In his speech to the assembled world leaders at the UN before the signing ceremony, Trump said the agreement gives the US “permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory”. “No US adversary will ever be permitted to establish a military presence in Greenland any more, or make sensitive investments there without our express written approval,” Trump said. Trump signed the ⁠agreement along with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen in a trilateral ceremony after Trump gave his UN speech. Frederiksen described the agreement as a deal that can “last forever” and ‌said it underlines the importance of the Nato alliance and respects Greenland’s right to self-determination. Nielsen emphasised the importance of Nato in the Arctic region. “We believe that it is vital to keep Nato strong, also in the Arctic, where the alliance has a key role to play,” he said. At a press conference ‌after the signing, Nielsen said Greenlanders must now go through a process of restoring trust with the US. Trump’s threats to take the island by force had strained ⁠relations with both Greenland and Denmark. “I believe the ⁠crisis is over now, but I don’t think the conflict is over in the sense that this agreement could very well be used – if the Americans wish – as a platform to force through further concessions,” said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political-science professor ‌at the University of Copenhagen. Greenland, a former colony and now a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, sits between the Arctic and North America and holds vast energy resources. The US already operates Pituffik Space Base in remote northwestern Greenland. The deal opens two ‌new military ‌sites: Narsarsuaq, a former Cold War airbase whose population has dwindled to just a few dozen, and Mestersvig, currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit. “We will immediately begin ‌the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate location. We will be building two very major military bases,” Trump said in his UN speech. Trump’s refusal to rule out military or economic force ⁠to acquire Greenland triggered a diplomatic crisis in January within Nato and forced Denmark and the island’s government into months of intensive negotiations. The text of the agreement says it amends a 1951 defence treaty that ⁠had been the legal basis for the US presence. It adds that Washington may seek further bases in the future, with details decided by mutual agreement. The deal has no end date, grants US aircraft and vessels broad access across Greenland and its territorial waters, and bars non-Nato states from establishing military installations on the island. It also restricts foreign investment, ‌effectively blocking states and investors from countries outside Nato, Nato ‌partners and the European Union from holding control or significant influence in sectors deemed particularly sensitive, including critical infrastructure and resource extraction. The deal, which needs approval by the parliaments of Denmark and Greenland, marks a shift from Trump’s earlier ambitions for an outright acquisition of Greenland, an island three times the size of Texas with a population of only 57,000 scattered along its rugged coastline. But it represents the first major increase in US military infrastructure in Greenland since the Cold War, when the US maintained 17 installations and more than 10,000 personnel there.

title: Hong Kong on way to securing green fuel supply to safeguard aviation hub status
description: Policy chief notes city to consider sustainable aviation fuel mandate, saying clear targets are needed to draw investment and build supply.
content: Hong Kong risks losing its status as an international aviation hub if it fails to secure a reliable, credibly certified supply of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the head of the government’s think tank has warned. Stephen Wong Yuen-shan, head of the Chief Executive’s Policy Unit, made the remarks at the Sustainable Aviation Futures China Congress on Tuesday, days after the government set out its fuel strategy in the city’s first five-year plan and policy address amid mounting global competition. “It is a question of whether Hong Kong can remain an international aviation hub as the economics and rules of global aviation change,” he said. He added that future demand for SAF was increasingly being driven by policy rather than voluntary action, with the European Union and the United Kingdom introducing mandates and Singapore and Japan setting their own targets. SAF is a renewable fuel made from materials such as used cooking oil and agricultural waste. It can cut life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel. As a drop-in substitute, it can be safely blended with conventional jet fuel and used in aircraft engines without modification. Wong said the shift formed part of a broader push by the International Civil Aviation Organization, which aims to cut global aviation emissions by 5 per cent by 2030 on the path to net zero by 2050. Against that backdrop, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has set a target for SAF to account for 1 to 3 per cent of fuel used on flights departing Hong Kong by 2030 under the city’s first five-year plan. “That is not just an aspiration; it is a planning signal you can build a model against,” Wong said. The latest policy address also commits to studying a SAF mandate by 2028. “A voluntary target attracts interest. A mandate attracts capital,” Wong said. “That is the difference between a pipeline of pilots and a pipeline of projects.” He noted that in Lee’s blueprints, SAF had its own heading covering a production base, a consumption ratio, a mandate study with a deadline and a certification pathway. Wong stressed that building a new industry required a longer time frame than an annual policy cycle, as investors, producers and airlines needed to know where Hong Kong aimed to be five years from now. “When long-term planning and annual execution move together, a policy signal can become an investment decision; individual projects can become a value chain; and an emerging fuel can become a strategic industry,” he said. Wong also stressed that a valuable opportunity existed in building the industry at scale in the Greater Bay Area. He pointed to EcoCeres’ new SAF production facility in mainland China’s Dongguan, which is targeted to begin operations in 2030 and is expected to produce about 450,000 tonnes of SAF and renewable diesel a year at full capacity, as a sign that the supply side “is becoming real”. EcoCeres is a Hong Kong-based biofuel company backed by the family office of tycoon Peter Lee Ka-kit, who is also chairman of Henderson Land Development and the Hong Kong and China Gas Company (Towngas). He said the planned facility had also helped establish the bay area’s first end-to-end SAF value chain, with waste-based feedstock collected across the region, refining and production carried out in Dongguan, and research, development and headquarters functions based in Hong Kong. Wong cited the Hong Kong International Airport’s Dongguan Logistics Park as an example of how the city could extend its economic infrastructure into the rest of the bay area while strengthening its global connections. He said the green-fuel industry could follow a similar model. “Not by duplicating every function in every [bay area] city, but by combining the strengths of the region into one globally competitive system,” he said, describing the approach as “regional specialisation by design”. He added that Hong Kong’s role should be to finance SAF, verify its environmental integrity and connect it with global buyers, rather than host every stage of production. Hong Kong brings distinctive strengths to that role, including its common law legal framework, deep financial markets, international connectivity and credible systems for certification, carbon data and settlement, Wong said.

title: Indonesia breathing issues spike to over 170,000 cases amid wildfire haze
description: As blazes blanket some areas and neighbouring nations in toxic smog, oxygen canisters have been given out. Over 40,000 toddlers are affected.
content: More than 170,000 respiratory cases were recorded in regions affected by haze in Indonesia, a health ministry official said on Tuesday, as the country continues its battle to control fires that caused the toxic smog. Blazes in Borneo, Sumatra and Papua have blanketed parts of the vast archipelago of more than 280 million people with haze, as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore, sending air quality indices plummeting. The toxic smog contains pollutants including PM 2.5, a fine particulate matter smaller than a human hair that could carry health risks such as respiratory infections, health ministry official Then Suyanti told a press conference. “There were 174,694 cases of acute respiratory infections between August and September 21 in areas affected by forest and land fires,” she said. More than 40,000 of the recorded respiratory cases affected toddlers, she said. The overall figure, reported in seven haze-affected provinces across Indonesia, was up from over 113,000 cases reported as of September 9. The health ministry had mobilised aid including oxygen concentrators, face masks and oxygen canisters to the affected regions, Then said. We advise (the public) to reduce outdoor activities when air quality worsens, use masks and maintain hydration Then Suyanti, health ministry official The health ministry had mobilised aid including oxygen concentrators, face masks and oxygen canisters to the affected regions, Then said. “We advise (the public) to reduce outdoor activities when air quality worsens, use masks and maintain hydration,” she said. Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, which typically runs from July to October. But the blazes are more intense this year, coinciding with what is expected to be the strongest El Nino climate phenomenon since comparable records began four decades ago. Experts also blame climate change, decades of forest degradation and slash-and-burn land-clearing practises that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape.

title: Japan fears hosting ‘worst Asian Games ever’, blames French firm for organisational woes
description: Organisers address reports of poor dining and housing; local media attribute chaos to lack of Japanese input, involvement of French operator.
content: Plagued by controversy ranging from athlete accommodation and dining complaints to severe operational blunders including misrecorded scores and incorrect national anthems, Asian Games host Japan has faced criticism for deflecting blame onto delegations and foreign contractors rather than addressing its own shortcomings. And now some in the country are worried they could be landed with the label of hosting the “worst Asian Games ever”. On Tuesday, the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games Organising Committee (AINAGOC) issued a statement addressing reports of poor athlete dining and housing conditions, while local media analysis attributed the operational chaos to the absence of major Japanese agencies and the heavy involvement of a French operator. In its statement, the committee acknowledged it was “aware” of the confusion reported on social media by some delegations boarding the cruise ship on September 16. To reduce costs, local organisers have accommodated athletes ⁠and officials in a mix of hotels, temporary wooden containers and a cruise ship rather than build a traditional Games village. Responding to reports that “AINAGOC’s failure to submit accommodation information to the accommodation system led to delays in boarding,” officials stated that “this was not the cause.” “We understand that the primary reason for the boarding delays and confusion was the time required to resolve issues with incomplete documentation submitted by some delegations,” the statement read. Regarding cruise ship operations, AINAGOC stated it was coordinating closely with Costa Cruises and JTB Corporation, adding that “AINAGOC will continue to work closely with relevant service providers to ensure the smooth reception of the athlete delegations.” Addressing criticism on social media regarding meal quality at the teqball competition venue, the committee similarly noted it was “aware”, but added that “however, these items were not provided by the AINAGOC”. According to official website information from last October, Australian firm Global Hospitality Group K.K. Japan was appointed as an official supplier for the 20th Asian Games and 5th Asian Para Games. “The appointment reflects Global Hospitality Group’s strong reputation of continuous feeding for world-class elite athletes and operational excellence,” the Australian company stated at the time. Meanwhile, Japanese media outlet Tokyo Sports on the same day attributed the Games’ operational troubles to the absence of major domestic advertising agencies and the deep involvement of veteran French event firm GL Events. Its report noted that domestic advertising giants failed to secure contracts because of corruption scandals tied to the 2021 Tokyo Olympics and Paralympics. “Although Aichi prefecture and Nagoya city formed the core of the organising committee, they lacked the expertise to handle unexpected situations,” the report stated. Before the Games, the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) pushed for the host city contract limit of athletes and officials to exceed 15,000. The media said although Aichi Prefecture expressed difficulties, the OCA insisted, leading to numerous obstacles before the opening ceremony. A sporting association official expressed frustration, noting that without the long-accumulated experience of major agencies, managing a tournament of this scale was very difficult. Another key factor cited was the “intervention” of French firm GL Events. Headquartered in Lyon, the company oversees venue design, infrastructure set-up, access control, accreditation and victory ceremonies. An event insider expressed frustration, stating: “Even when we see points of concern, that company refuses our input, saying ‘this is our domain’.” Moves to bypass traditional agencies appear to have backfired. South Korea’s chef de mission ⁠Lee Sang-hyun criticised the organisers on Tuesday for logistical failures that had inconvenienced athletes and said concrete measures had to be taken to ensure the problems were not repeated. Lee said his delegation had requested a meeting with senior Games officials and wanted a formal apology “at a higher level” after South Korean athletes were affected by transport and accommodation issues at the event in ‌Japan. “I hope the organising committee and the OCA (Olympic Council of Asia) will give these issues greater attention,” he said at Korea House, the team’s hospitality hub in Nagoya. “More than simply apologising, I believe it is important for them to come up with concrete measures to prevent these problems from happening again and put those measures into practice. “However, they have not yet provided us with any concrete plans for how they intend to improve things going forward.” South Korea moved their men’s basketball ‌team out of their container units at Garden Pier and into hotels because they said the beds were too short and after one of the units flooded during heavy rain. Lee said the containers were “extremely cramped” for the basketball players and ‌that administrative confusion on the cruise ship over bookings and room assignments had inconvenienced athletes. The men’s team had to cancel a training session hours before their final against Japan because their shuttle bus did not show up. Transport issues have affected other South Korean athletes, including the men’s football team, the defending Asian Games champions. The OCA, which governs the quadrennial Asian Games, did not provide immediate comment. Amid recurring issues, operational staff lamented that the chaos was “so terrible it is hard to believe this tournament is being held in Japan”. Repeated transport dispatch failures have also drawn criticism, with a major event management insider noting: “While there were disappointing international events in Japan before, this far exceeds expectations.” Even volunteers raised concerns, saying: “The management is truly full of problems, which makes us very sorry. Why is a French firm involved in the first place?” Tokyo Sports warned that if conditions continued to deteriorate, the event risked going down in history as the “worst Asian Games ever”.

title: Taiwan coastguard’s rare missile firing reveals deepening links with navy
description: Further integrating the agency with the military would multiply threats to the PLA Navy in a conflict, analysts say.
content: Taiwan’s coastguard fired a supersonic anti-ship missile during a military exercise last week, an unusual move by a civilian law enforcement agency that analysts say could be aimed at complicating potential war plans. The drill matters not only because it highlights the growing integration between the agency and Taiwan’s navy, experts argue, but also because missile-armed coastguard vessels would add another threat the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) would have to account for in a conflict. On Friday, the Anping-class coastguard patrol vessel Qijin launched a home-grown Hsiung Feng III, or HF-3, which hit a decommissioned navy frigate more than 100km (62 miles) away, according to local media. The coastguard also fired an HF-2, an older subsonic anti-ship weapon, during the drills, which involved Taiwan’s army, navy and air force. This means at least three named vessels of the coastguard’s 12-ship Anping class have now fired Hsiung Feng missiles, underscoring a broader effort to turn them into an additional pool of naval strike platforms. Based on the navy’s Tuo Chiang-class corvette, the vessels are designed to be armed with up to 16 HF-2 and HF-3 anti-ship missiles upon wartime mobilisation. John Bradford, executive director of the Yokosuka Council on Asia-Pacific Studies and a former US Navy officer, said the developments made long-standing arrangements between the coastguard and navy more visible while also showing that their cooperation was taking new forms. “The two forces are definitely getting closer, learning to cooperate and identifying ways to complement each other,” he said. “What was going on before is becoming more visible while they are simultaneously doing things never done before.” The practice of arming coastguard vessels with anti-ship missiles is unusual internationally, as coastguards are generally associated with law enforcement, safety and patrol duties rather than military and long-range strike missions. There is some precedent, however. During the late Cold War, the United States Coast Guard fitted some Hamilton-class vessels with Harpoon anti-ship missiles. The Mellon patrol vessel fired one in January 1990 before the capability was removed. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration remains a civilian agency in peacetime, but its wartime role is built into the island’s defence framework. The island’s National Defence Act allows the government to bring the coastguard into the military order of battle during a conflict. A 2021 special defence procurement law went further by funding wartime weapons and related support systems for coastguard vessels under a peacetime-to-wartime conversion programme. Beijing has taken a different route towards integrating its coastguard with the military. In July 2018, the China Coast Guard was transferred from civilian administration to the People’s Armed Police, placing it within a structure under the Central Military Commission. Beijing’s Coast Guard Law, which took effect in 2021, also allows the agency to carry out defence operations under the commission’s orders. Its director, Zhang Jianming, is a former navy officer. The PLA Navy has also transferred ships to the coastguard, including 22 Type 056 corvettes from 2021, with their missile and torpedo launchers removed. Beijing has also deployed coastguard formations during major exercises around Taiwan, including Joint Sword in 2024 and Strait Thunder-2025A, using them for patrols, inspections and other law-enforcement operations – moves seen as possible rehearsals for a blockade. That said, Simona Grano, head of Research Area China-Taiwan Relations at the University of Zurich, cautioned against viewing Taipei’s approach as an attempt to replicate Beijing’s model. While the mainland had integrated its coastguard into a military command structure, Taiwan retained a civilian coastguard in peacetime and was preparing it for wartime operations, she said. “The institutional models and the political purposes are quite different,” she said. Taipei’s preparations date back at least to 2005, when the Wei Hsing patrol vessel fired an HF-2 during the annual Han Kuang military exercises. Within the Anping class, the Anping fired an HF-2 in 2022 and the Bali fired an HF-3 in 2024, while an unidentified vessel of the class fired two HF-2s in 2025, according to a navy report to lawmakers. The approach became more visible during this year’s Han Kuang iteration in August, when the Bali was fitted with Hsiung Feng missiles and operated alongside navy Kuang Hua VI missile boats in a coastal-strike drill involving the navy’s newly established Littoral Operations Command. There is no indication the exercise changed the coastguard’s wartime command arrangements, but it showed a coastguard patrol vessel operating alongside navy missile boats in a strike role. Those operational preparations have been accompanied by moves to strengthen links between the navy and coastguard leadership. Hours after Friday’s drill, Ocean Affairs Council Minister Kuan Bi-ling said a navy flag officer would fill the coastguard’s restored third deputy director general post, describing the move as part of closer cooperation between the two services. The position was restored under legislation passed in June, with the government citing peacetime-to-wartime conversion and the coastguard’s expanding military-related duties among the reasons for adding another deputy. A Taiwan coastguard expert, speaking anonymously because he was not authorised to comment publicly, said that arming coastguard vessels with anti-ship missiles could help close the gap between law enforcement and military responses if a confrontation involving mainland Chinese warships escalated into armed conflict. However, the expert said the approach also risked blurring the line between law enforcement and military action, complicating crisis responses. For the PLA, this would mean treating some Taiwanese coastguard “white hulls” – not just naval “grey hulls” – as potential anti-ship missile threats, the expert added. Despite that added complexity, Bradford said the missile-armed coastguard vessels would not fundamentally change the military balance. “Given the size of the PLA Navy and [PLA] Air Force, these are not going to be a game-changer,” he said. “Yet in naval warfare, every opposing vessel adds risk to your plan and forces you to make increasingly difficult choices.” Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but most are opposed to changing the status quo by force.

title: Review | Heart of the Beast review: Brad Pitt and his loyal combat dog brave the Alaskan wilderness
description: Brad Pitt is good but his canine companion is better in this story about an ex-soldier and his former combat dog’s battle to survive.
content: 4/5 stars American writer-director David Ayer has built a career on tough-guy films featuring unlikely team-ups – from mismatched policemen Denzel Washington and Ethan Hawke in Training Day (2001) to Will Smith and an orc in Bright (2017) to Jason Statham and some bees in The Beekeeper (2024). However, Heart of the Beast, a soulful survival drama scripted by Cameron Alexander, represents Ayer’s best combination yet. A grizzled Brad Pitt stars as retired special forces officer James Belmont, who flies into the Alaskan wilderness in his seaplane to hunt and fish, taking his best pal, Odin – played by an equally rugged German shepherd called Uber and several stunt pups – for company. A former combat dog, Odin has a metal leg and titanium teeth from missions that went wrong. Belmont’s scars take a little longer to spot. It is easy to see what draws them to the wilds. The scenery is absolutely stunning – from the bright, spreading glaciers to muddy, Mordor-like swamps, all handsomely shot by Mauro Fiore – and there is nobody around for miles. Well, almost nobody. “There’s nothing like the quiet of nature; a whole world all to yourself,” notes a weathered old-timer played by JK Simmons, who briefly interrupts their idyll. When the pair fly back to civilisation, however, Belmont suffers a heart attack at the controls. A terrifyingly realistic crash – mostly shot from inside the plane – sees Odin flung free, while Belmont is trapped in the wreckage at the bottom of a lake. Touchingly, as the plane goes down, Odin tries to protect his master, though much worse is to come for both of them. What follows is a tale as old as Jack London’s The Call of the Wild – though Belmont prefers Cormac McCarthy’s The Road. Our injured heroes are forced to trek cross-country, facing inhospitable terrain, angry predators and PTSD flashbacks as they try to reach safety. Crucially, Ayer has the confidence to build the sense of danger slowly, giving the audience plenty of time to witness the depths of their bond – and the beauty of the landscape – as the noose tightens inexorably around them. While not as dramatic as The Grey or as ambitious as The Revenant, the film still features tense moments, such as a hair-raising canyon crossing and a fearsome nighttime encounter. Along the way, Belmont requires various forms of assistance from his fiercely loyal four-legged friend – there is even a scene in which Odin helps him reset a bone. However, there are also some surprisingly lame CGI interlopers and a coda so syrupy sweet it might deter more cynical viewers. A film as stark and simple as this stands or falls on the chemistry of its leads, and both deliver. Pitt is good, but Uber is the real star of the show. To remain unmoved by their obvious love would take a heart of stone. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Fatal dog attacks trigger safety fears in Hong Kong. Here’s how to protect yourself
description: Canine experts explain what to do, what to avoid and how to protect yourself during an attack.
content: The death of a cyclist in a suspected canine attack in Hong Kong’s Yuen Long on Saturday night has sparked fierce discussion on social media, with users sharing similar encounters and debating how to stay safe. The woman was discovered along Pok Wai South Road in the early hours of Sunday. She had suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal. Nearly a month earlier, a 33-year-old dog handler was found dead near her pet training centre in Ta Kwu Ling after being mauled by a canine. To help residents stay safe, the South China Morning Post has spoken with canine behavioural experts and dog rescuers to share essential safety tips. 1. What should you never do? Jacqueline Cheung, founder of the non-profit Love Adopt Animal Society, said it was important to never run from a dog. Running away could trigger an animal’s hunting mode and cause it to give chase, she noted. “And a dog will in most cases run faster than a human,” she said. Cheung said that anyone who encountered an aggressive dog should stand tall and avoid bending low. They should also avoid direct eye contact, as it could be seen as a sign of hostility, and instead focus on the surrounding environment in case more dogs emerged, she said. Jet Chow Wing-yin, a canine training instructor at My Dog Fits, said that dogs preparing to attack would be in a high state of alert, noting their tails would typically be very stiff and straight while wagging extremely fast. 2. How should I respond if a pack starts barking? Cheung said it was important to take a deep breath first and try to remain calm before finding an object, such as a backpack, to shield yourself in case a dog rushes in to bite you. Chow said that people should slow down if they spot a pack of dogs from far away. If a person was riding a bicycle, they should dismount while placing it between them and the animals as a physical barrier, he added. “As you slow down, do not stare directly at the dogs, and do not face them head-on. If possible, take a wide arc around the outer perimeter and leave slowly,” he said. Chow said it was best to walk sideways, keep the dogs in sight and retreat slowly without exposing your back, as it could make you appear vulnerable. 3. What about if dogs get close? Chow advised that if a pack suddenly charges and barking erupts right next to you, do not quickly dismount from the bicycle, as it would be easier to lose balance and fall. “Once you fall to the ground, you will easily become an attack target. Dismounting at close range means you might be attacked either way,” he said. “In that split second when they are too close, going full speed on the bike might give you a chance to escape. “Usually once you reach a certain distance and are out of their territory, they won’t keep chasing you.” Since a human cannot outrun canines on foot, the next best course of action would be to yell loudly at the dogs to try to scare them away, Chow said. In that situation, immediately grab any item you have, such as a backpack, to create a barrier and give the dog something to bite, which could help satisfy its initial urge to attack, he said. “If a dog actually pounces to bite, you can use [the bag] as a shield and thrust the backpack into its mouth,” he said. “Once they bite down on an object, their initial urge to bite is satisfied, and they might just tug on the backpack. This buys you time to get away safely without taking personal injury.” 4. What to do if a dog attacks? Chow said that if a person came under attack, they should defend, block or shout loudly to discourage the dog from seeing them as vulnerable prey. “If you continuously dodge or run, they will view you as prey and keep attacking,” he said. “Do not fall to the ground – your body language tells the dogs that you are down, making you look extremely vulnerable, and they will attack even more aggressively. “If you unfortunately fall and cannot fight back, your posture is vital to protect your life: curl your body up like a shrimp, cover your head with both hands, and tuck your elbows in tightly to shield your neck and throat.” He added that instinct prompts dogs to bite humans on the limbs and neck, making it important to protect vital organs. “So if you fall, cover your head and throat with your hands, clamp your elbows around your neck, and curl your body up,” he said. “Never uncover your hands from your neck.” 5. What about gadgets and other gear? Chow said dog deterrent devices such as ultrasonic gadgets were ineffective against dogs with heightened alertness, as the animals’ emotions were already worked up and the devices might just provoke them further. “Their internal adrenaline and emotional state completely override the disturbance of the ultrasonic wave,” he said. Chow also warned that weapons such as metal pipes and baseball bats might make the situation even more dangerous. “Adding extra body movements like swinging a racquet or pipe makes it look like you are threatening or trying to hit them, which provokes the dogs into feeling threatened and triggers an attack,” he said.

title: Some family offices eyeing Chinese investments as US-China tensions ease: report
description: European, Middle Eastern and African family offices are increasing their exposure to China as they diversify their portfolios, report finds.
content: Ultra-wealthy families in Europe, the Middle East and Africa view China as their most favoured market for future investments, as concerns over tensions between Beijing and Washington ease, according to a survey by Citigroup. The latest edition of the Global Family Office Report, published on Tuesday, analysed the investment plans of 351 family offices – private companies set up to manage the assets of ultra-wealthy families – from more than 40 countries around the world. In the survey, 29 per cent of respondents from Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) said they planned to increase their exposure to the Chinese market, the highest figure for any geographic region. The next most popular investment destinations among that group were the rest of the Asia-Pacific market, with 26 per cent, and North America on 25 per cent. The findings coincided with a significant easing of concerns over US-China tensions. Only 22 per cent of family offices surveyed viewed US-China tensions as a top concern this year, compared with 43 per cent in 2025. The results suggested that EMEA family offices were seeking to diversify their portfolios, and China was a popular choice as it had less political uncertainty compared with other regions, said Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank. “China can be a hedge to US dollar-denominated assets with opportunities in the tech sectors,” said Ng, while cautioning that valuation and exit strategies remained an issue in China due to frequent regulatory changes and limited liquidity. While stocks traded in Hong Kong and mainland China have underperformed those in other markets this year, China’s trade with the European Union and Africa has continued to grow strongly, rising 12.4 per cent and 23.3 per cent year on year, respectively, in the first eight months of 2026, Chinese customs data showed. China was also a popular investment destination with family offices in Asia-Pacific, the survey found, with 27 per cent of respondents from the region saying they planned to increase their exposure to the Chinese market. Globally, China was the fourth most favoured market among family offices, with 19 per cent of respondents intending to deploy new capital in the region. North America, the rest of Asia-Pacific and Europe were the top three choices, selected by 39 per cent, 29 per cent and 20 per cent of respondents, respectively. But China was the third pick among family offices with more than US$500 million of assets under management, according to the report, behind only North America and Asia-Pacific excluding China. This year, inflation and interest rates have replaced trade disputes and US-China tensions as the top concerns among family offices, with 63 per cent of respondents saying they were worried about inflation. Meanwhile, 38 per cent said they were concerned about the stability of the global financial system. Asia’s ultra-wealthy families are particularly interested in artificial intelligence, with more than 80 per cent of Asia-Pacific respondents saying they intended to invest in the sector – far higher than the global average of 51 per cent. Healthcare was also popular with Asia-Pacific family offices, on 43 per cent, while traditional sectors including automotive, finance and real estate were at the bottom of the list in the region. Asia-Pacific investors were the most ambitious in terms of their target gains this year, with 22 per cent of respondents in the region eyeing annualised returns of 15 per cent or above – compared with a global average of 11 per cent. Citi attributed the higher returns target partly to the large number of relatively young wealth creators in the region who aspired to be serial entrepreneurs. “Family offices globally are balancing conviction with resilience, opportunity with discipline, and growth with stewardship,” said Dawn Nordberg, head of integrated client solutions and the global family office group at Citi Wealth, in a statement.

title: Philippines races to turn Pax Silica into reality before political changes derail dreams
description: Philippines’ Marcos is due to leave office in 2028 while Trump faces US midterm elections next year that could change control of Congress.
content: The Philippines has less than two years to turn its ambitious Pax Silica project from a US-backed plan into a functioning industrial hub before a change of government in Manila – and potentially Washington – puts its future to the test. Pax Silica is an initiative by US President Donald Trump’s administration to diversify US supplies of critical minerals and semiconductors. The Philippines is seeking to position itself as a manufacturing base for companies looking to reduce their dependence on China. With Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr due to leave office in 2028 and Trump facing the midterm election in November that could change control of Congress, the project needs to move quickly to establish agreements and infrastructure that can survive political change, according to Jonathan Ravelas, a former chief market strategist at the Philippines’ largest bank, BDO. “The faster the government can institutionalise agreements and deliver infrastructure, the lower the political risk,” Ravelas, now managing director of eManagement for Business and Marketing Services, told This Week in Asia. The question is whether Manila can deliver the reliable power, infrastructure and regulatory certainty investors need to commit billions of dollars before the political clock runs out. For now, much of it remains on the drawing board. On April 16, Washington accepted an offer from Manila to convert a 1,600-hectare (4,000-acre) plot of land – rent-free for two years – into the “Pax Silica coordination office”. The site sits inside the 9,450-hectare New Clark City – part of the much larger Clark Freeport and Special Economic Zone, a master-planned development envisioned to host government offices, sports facilities and other major infrastructure. As China dominates the supply and processing of several critical minerals used in advanced manufacturing, supply-chain diversification is a strategic priority for Washington. In February, the Philippines signed a memorandum of understanding on critical minerals with the US. Joshua Bingcang, president and chief executive of the state-owned Bases Conversion Development Authority (BCDA), which manages the area, admitted to This Week in Asia on Monday that nearly everything in the Pax Silica hub – since renamed the Clark Advanced Manufacturing Park – was still in the planning stage. That is, except for one foreign company “tenant” whom he would not name. Bingcang told the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines on Monday that the company “signed an agreement [to lease] last week”. It will start hiring local engineers by October to be trained in Taiwan. These engineers would be “the ones to set up the machines, the factory lines” as part of technology transfer, he said. ‘Transcends political colour’ Bingcang believes Pax Silica can withstand political change because the BCDA has a history of pursuing major projects across administrations. “Our projects started two or three administrations ago, and they’ve seen the impact, so it’s really a no-brainer on the value we bring.” Pax Silica “transcends any political colour or any terms” because it was long-term, according to Bingcang. “The Philippines has a good track record of implementing multi-administration projects.” Alvin Camba, a trained political economist and sociologist who is chief scientist at Lyvi, a US defence technology company, said the issue, though “extremely sensitive” in the Philippines, would be able to weather political winds in Washington. “Pax Silica is not politically sensitive in the US. I don’t expect it to be something that Democrats would reverse if they happen to take both houses in November 2026 or win the presidency in 2028,” he said. “There is already near bipartisan consensus on taking a tougher stance on China. At the same time, there is a huge push from the big tech companies to expand their AI models and infrastructure in different parts of the world. So Pax Silica is really supported by both sides of this equation: the Department of [Defence] and the big tech firms.” He said the biggest concerns for foreign investors in the Philippines were “local political and regulatory conditions that could affect their operations, as well as energy and transportation costs”. “Regulations matter because companies do not want to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in a country that could stop or reverse their operations once the money has already been sunk and operations have begun.” Energy obstacle For investors, political continuity is only one part of the equation. “Pax Silica reminds me of the old button soup story. The idea is exciting, but a great soup needs more than a button – it needs ingredients,” Ravelas said. These ingredients include reliable power, world-class infrastructure, skilled talent, regulatory certainty and policy continuity. “The opportunity is real because global companies are looking to diversify supply chains, and the Philippines is well positioned to benefit. But interest is not the same as investment. The reported land lease commitment is encouraging, yet most of the names being mentioned remain prospective investors rather than signed commitments.” From an investor’s perspective, Ravelas said, “the biggest concern is not politics or regulation per se – it is execution”. Investors wanted assurance that infrastructure would be completed on time, power would be available at competitive prices, environmental and ancestral domain issues would be addressed transparently, and policies would remain stable beyond election cycles in both countries, he said. Those concerns are particularly significant in the Philippines, where energy costs and reliability have long posed challenges for manufacturers. “The main issue, more than anything else, is energy. This has been a failure of successive Philippine administrations since the 1980s. The lack of abundant, reliable and cheap energy makes it difficult for companies to operate,” Camba said. “This is actually one of the biggest reasons why companies have gone to Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Vietnam rather than the Philippines. In the end, they can simply operate more cheaply and with fewer problems in those countries.”

title: Opinion | Xi and Trump face their greatest challenge yet: building US-China trust
description: AI is the test case. A foundational agreement will prove trust is possible – otherwise, mistrust will harden and the detente will dissolve.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House is not just another ceremonial exchange. It is a test of whether the world’s two largest powers can build trust in an age where mistrust has become the default. Artificial intelligence (AI) is on the agenda. Both sides see danger but have yet to come up with meaningful regulatory cooperation. If this summit fails to deliver workable agreements, the tactical detente could collapse into a new cold war. If the leaders succeed in their personal desire for friendship and systemic, competitive cooperation, they may forge a new kind of major power partnership that, with effort, can last beyond the Trump presidency. Chinese officials are not monolithic. Simply put, in the southern coastal provinces, officials can be more pragmatic, focused on economic growth, trade and the daily mechanics of development. In the north, nationalism might run deeper in mindset – competition with the US is seen as destiny itself. This duality matters. China’s bureaucracy is not simply marching in lockstep behind a single ideology; instead, China is and must be seen as a historic nation wrestling with its own contradictions. Outsiders who fail to grasp this complexity are liable to misread it. The United States, meanwhile, is obsessed with the idea of being overtaken by China. Many in Washington believe China’s rise is proof of American decline, or that China’s assertiveness reflects a deepening belief in US decline. Chinese decision-makers may also interpret US anxiety as weakness. The result is a mirror of insecurities. Each side sees the other through the lens of its fear. This is why the Washington summit matters. If an AI agreement can be reached, it will not be because of technical pragmatism alone – runaway super AI can harm everyone. It must also be because both strong leaders chose trust over suspicion. And although Europe and the US seem to agree on little these days, some in Beijing continue to see disjointed Western efforts as potentially a conspiratorial network to restrict China’s rise. This perception is not paranoia alone. It is rooted in China’s long history of foreign encirclement. Western democracies dismiss this as authoritarian defensiveness, but for Chinese officials it is lived memory. The US far-right dreams of total decoupling from China. It imagines that cutting ties will limit Beijing’s ambitions. In reality, it would only sharpen them. China would double down on rare earths, chips and other bottleneck industries. It would accelerate self-reliance. Decoupling is not a strategy; it is stupidity presenting itself as provocation. American and other Western liberals must also consider abandoning their ancient playbook on China. Today’s China is different. It is integrated into global commerce, technologically ambitious and internally anxious. The only path forward is to deal with China as it is. Otherwise, both sides will eventually sleepwalk towards a confrontation. Wise leaders must look beyond the current situation. China is not simply another rising power like Germany or Japan in the last century. It is a civilisational state with unique internal challenges, and it has repeatedly said it does not wish to export its political model. Philosophy helps us see this clearly. Immanuel Kant argued that perpetual peace was not a dream but a wager: humanity could choose peace through insight or be forced into it through catastrophe. Hegel saw reconciliation as the synthesis of contradictions. Confucius taught restraint, not expansion. China’s nationalism is often inward-facing. It is an internal dialogue, not a blueprint for global conquest. Western observers who misread this restraint as aggression risk turning dialogue into confrontation. I recall Xi’s last state visit to Washington. In response to a reporter’s question, he promised not to militarise the South China Sea. That was not part of the agreed script. It was a gesture meant to dial down nationalism, to show China’s rhetoric is not always directed outward. Such moments matter. They reveal that beneath the slogans, there is room for moderation. But moderation requires trust. Without trust, every gesture is dismissed as deception. And Chinese leaders must also respond to internal sentiments reacting to perceived Western pressure on China. Three lessons emerge from the current geometry of recognition. First, recognition is not binary. It is shaped by silence, signal and timing. Second, smaller states can matter. From Japan’s signalling to Singapore’s balancing, agency is not reserved for great powers. Third, misalignment is dangerous. When gestures are misread as provocation or interference, dialogue collapses into confrontation. China often perceives external pressure as coordinated encirclement. Western democracies often misinterpret Chinese restraint as overreach. Both sides are wrong to some extent, and both sides are trapped by their misreadings. AI is the test case. If the US and China can reach a foundational agreement, they will prove that trust is possible even in the most sensitive domain. If they cannot, mistrust will harden, and the tactical detente will dissolve. The stakes are not abstract. They are immediate. A failure to build trust will accelerate the slide into a cold war neither side can afford. An agreement, however fragile, could anchor cooperation for the next decade. China is a historic nation. Its ambitions are limited, but its anxieties are expansive. The US is a republic haunted by itself. Together they face a choice. They can continue to mirror each other’s fears or they can choose trust. The summit is about whether two civilisations can step back from the edge and imagine a partnership. The wager is Kant’s: peace through insight or peace through catastrophe. The choice is theirs.

title: Mother seeks justice 7 months after Thai-Swedish son’s fatal crash in Pattaya
description: The grieving family of 15-year-old Tommy Boulanger accuses police of failing to execute an arrest warrant seven months after the fatal crash.
content: The mother of a 15-year-old Thai-Swedish teenager who died after his motorbike crashed into a truck illegally reversing into oncoming traffic has made an emotional appeal for justice, accusing police of failing to execute an arrest warrant for the alleged driver, a Chinese national, seven months after the fatal crash. Tommy Boulanger, an aspiring footballer, was left in a coma following the February 20 crash in the Nongpure district of Chonburi, near the resort city of Pattaya. He never regained consciousness and died six days later. Widely circulated CCTV footage of the crash shows a pickup truck reversing onto the main road without indicating – in an apparent attempt to make a U-turn outside a karaoke bar – leaving Tommy unable to brake in time before slamming into the back of the vehicle. Tommy’s death has gripped the Thai public, reviving complaints over the country’s often sclerotic justice system and fuelling a mounting sense that wealthy foreign nationals are able to gain preferential treatment. The Pattaya Provincial Court issued an arrest warrant on March 2 for the suspect – whose name has not formally been released to the media, though he is believed to be well known locally – on charges of reckless driving causing death. Seven months later, however, the arrest warrant has not been executed, leaving Tommy’s despairing family to push senior detectives for action while dealing with a crippling hospital bill from his care. Speaking to This Week in Asia, Tommy’s mother, Saitharn Singstrand, said justice had been denied to her, leaving “nothing but emptiness” following the death of her son, a talented youth footballer and Liverpool FC fan who dreamed of one day representing the Thai national team. “The man who did this to my child is still living comfortably. It’s just not fair. It feels like the death of a child didn’t matter to them [the police], but we are under their authority – we can’t fight them,” the 38-year-old said. “I want the person responsible to go to prison … so he can feel the pain that my family and I have had to endure.” In a video that went viral on Monday, a visibly distressed Saitharn could be seen confronting officers during a delayed raid on a property linked to the Chinese suspect – only to find he had already fled. Saitharn told officers at the scene that she had reported seeing the suspect weeks earlier and had alerted police, but officers did not respond at the time. Tommy’s case gained national attention two weeks ago after featuring on Hone Krasae, a popular Thai television current affairs programme, where Saitharn accused police of dragging their feet. Phoning in to the broadcast, Chonburi Provincial Police Commander Major General Pongphan Wongmaneethet said officers had “not abandoned the case.” He added that police were preparing a case file for Interpol to request a Red Notice for the suspect. “If the suspect makes a move or tries to leave the country, he will be arrested immediately,” Pongphan said. The handling of the case has drawn further scrutiny to the Chonburi police force, which faced public criticism in August over its slow investigation into a missing Thai family. The family members were later found murdered during a search for two missing Russian siblings, who had been killed by a Thai serial offender recently released from prison. At the time, criminologists urged Thai police to prioritise investigations based on urgency rather than media attention or pressure from foreign embassies.

title: Hong Kong to bar firms with integrity offences from building renovation lists
description: Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn says applications to pre-qualify will open next Wednesday and lists rolled out by year-end.
content: Hong Kong building maintenance consultants and contractors prosecuted or convicted of integrity-related offences in the past three years will be excluded from pre-qualified lists set up for owners undertaking renovation projects, the development minister has said. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Tuesday that applications to join the lists – covering inspection consultants, supervision consultants and building works contractors – would open next Wednesday and close on October 23. The lists would be set up by the end of the year, she added. Linn told the Legislative Council’s development panel that the lists would be reviewed every two years, as authorities tightened oversight of integrity standards. “If they are convicted of integrity-related offences, they will be removed from the pre-qualified lists immediately,” Linn said. The pre-qualified lists are part of the measures proposed in last Wednesday’s policy address to step up support for private owners conducting building maintenance work. The initiative follows a fire during renovation work at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, which killed 168 people and displaced about 5,000. Subsequent media reports revealed that the current lists failed to screen out companies with criminal records. The new lists will replace the current ones. Only consultants and contractors on the pre-qualified lists will be eligible to bid for building renovation projects under the support service. Eligibility criteria cover four areas: technical competence, integrity, financial capacity and past performance. Companies and their directors, partners and specified employees who are currently under prosecution for integrity-related offences or convicted in the past three years are barred from joining the lists. Such offences include bribery, corruption, anti-competitive behaviour and crimes related to false instruments and forgery. Those who fail to pass background checks by police and the city’s corruption watchdog, the Independent Commission Against Corruption, will not be included. Linn said the background checks served as a “safety net”, addressing concerns raised by lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu that firms under a cloud could join the lists given the lengthy process of integrity-related prosecution and conviction. “Some cases may have yet to reach the prosecution stage … The background checks serve as an effective safety net, allowing them to take action behind the scenes when they cannot speak publicly,” she said. To qualify, professionals and companies must have completed at least three inspection or repair projects under the mandatory building inspection scheme over the past five years or equivalent work. Over the past year, they must not have had their professional registration revoked or been convicted of a certain number of offences related to site safety, employment, buildings or fire safety. The lists also feature a mechanism for suspending the pre-qualification status of the professionals and companies if they are prosecuted for an integrity offence or are involved in a major site safety incident. Conviction of an integrity offence will lead to removal from the lists. Furthermore, firms will be delisted if they submit false statements during enrolment or project bidding, or if their professional or contractor registration is revoked. Linn expressed confidence that a sufficient number of companies and professionals would qualify under the “stringent and pragmatic” arrangement. She expected tenders utilising the pre-qualified lists to be introduced as early as the first quarter of next year.

title: Nicaragua govt responsible for at least 8 deaths in custody since 2018: UN
description: Experts also documented the disappearance of at least 161 people since 2018, when a crackdown on dissent began after mass protests.
content: The Nicaraguan government is responsible for at least eight deaths in custody since it began its crackdown on dissent and assault of democratic institutions in 2018, UN experts said Tuesday. The report from the UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua was the latest condemnation of the government of married co-Presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo, which has crushed dissent since 2018 mass protests and recently cancelled elections. “A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance,” said Jan-Michael Simon, the group’s chair. The report detailed inconsistencies in the government’s account of the in-custody death of Indigenous Miskito leader Brooklyn Rivera, who was imprisoned for 32 months with almost no contact with his family before he died in May. A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance Jan-Michael Simon, UN Group of Human Rights Experts The official statement after his death linked it to complications following a previous Covid-19 infection, which previous statements in the days before never mentioned. An independent assessment from Physicians for Human Rights said the explanation was “not medically coherent”. Its assessment also found that the “timing of the illness and the pattern of organisms identified both point to the infections having been acquired in custody or in hospital, rather than in the community”. The statements around his death could not be independently verified because no independent investigation or autopsy was ordered, the report said. Its authors called on the government to release Rivera’s body to his family for a burial under Miskito traditions. Murillo said Rivera received medical care and family support throughout his illness. The government did not respond to a request for additional comment. The report also detailed the failures of care in the deaths of Ortega’s estranged brother Humberto Ortega, former Sandinista guerrilla fighter Hugo Torres and lawyer Carlos Cárdenas Zepeda. The experts documented the disappearance of at least 161 people since 2018. It called on the government to release information on 29 people whose whereabouts remain unknown and to release anyone detained on political grounds.

title: China’s Huawei trims mobile chip gap with Apple as Tau Scaling Law pays off: Bernstein
description: Kirin 9050 Pro chip, the first based on Tau framework with 7nm technology, outperforms Apple’s 3nm A17 Pro in tests, research firm says.
content: Huawei Technologies’ latest smartphone processor, the Kirin 9050 Pro, unveiled earlier this month, has narrowed its gap with Apple’s chips to about three years, from roughly four years in the previous generation, according to equity research firm Bernstein. The chip, which Bernstein estimated was produced using technology equivalent to a 7-nanometre process node, outperformed Apple’s 3nm A17 Pro in Geekbench 6 multicore tests, a widely used benchmark that measures how effectively processors handle tasks across multiple central processing unit cores. Apple’s A17 Pro, released in 2023, was the world’s first mass-produced 3nm smartphone processor. The Chinese tech giant’s latest chip nevertheless remained around 30 per cent behind Apple’s newest 2nm A20 Pro in performance, while its single-core performance was closer to processors using Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s (TSMC) older 4nm-class technology, Bernstein said in a report on Monday. The research firm estimated that the Kirin 9050 Pro was manufactured using Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp’s “N+2” or “N+3” process technology, equivalent to a 7nm-class node achieved through deep-ultraviolet lithography, rather than the more advanced extreme-ultraviolet tools unavailable in China due to US sanctions. Bernstein described the advance as an “underestimated breakthrough”, adding that the chip’s architecture improvements had driven Huawei’s catch-up. At the centre of the progress is LogicFolding, a technique developed under Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law framework that stacks logic vertically and uses dense interconnections between layers. The approach reduces the distance signals travel within a chip instead of relying primarily on shrinking transistors. According to Bernstein, the technique increased transistor density to 238 million transistors per square millimetre from about 155 million – a gain of more than 50 per cent. Compared with the previous Kirin 9030 Pro, the new chip delivered about 20 per cent higher multicore performance in Geekbench tests, a 39 per cent improvement in graphics performance and around 150 per cent higher neural processing unit throughput. Huawei’s own tests also showed significant reductions in power consumption at comparable performance levels. Huawei introduced the Tau Scaling Law earlier this year as an alternative path for improving computing performance as further transistor miniaturisation becomes increasingly difficult. LogicFolding is one component of the framework, alongside software-chip co-design and system-level technologies such as UnifiedBus. The company last week said the same framework would guide future Ascend artificial intelligence processors, including the Ascend 970 and 980 planned for 2028 and 2029. Since US restrictions cut Huawei off from TSMC’s most advanced manufacturing processes, the company has increasingly sought to extract more performance from less advanced chipmaking processes through design, packaging and system-level engineering. That strategy has helped underpin Huawei’s return to advanced smartphones powered by domestically made processors and is now being extended to AI computing. The Tau Scaling Law serves as an umbrella for these efforts, combining technologies such as LogicFolding with faster chip interconnects and large-scale “supernode” systems. The Kirin 9050 Pro, which debuted in the firm’s Mate XT 2 trifold smartphone this month, is the first commercial chip to showcase LogicFolding and offers an early test of whether the approach can help offset China’s manufacturing disadvantages.

title: Taiwan’s opposition casts doubt on ‘rock solid’ US ties ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: KMT seizes on reported limits on Washington visits as a ‘wake-up call’ for Taipei, warning that US policy is driven by self-interest.
content: Reports that Taiwanese officials have been asked to scale back visits to Washington have sparked debate over whether the island’s ties with the United States remain as “rock solid” as Taipei has maintained. The New York Times reported on Monday that some Taiwanese officials travelling to the US had been told by Trump administration officials to “curtail their visits to research groups in Washington”. The report came as US President Donald Trump prepared to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a summit in Washington on Thursday. Taiwan is expected to feature in their discussions, and Beijing has been pressing Washington to halt or further delay arms sales to the island. Citing Brookings Institution senior fellow Ryan Hass, the report said the move reflected Trump’s preference to ensure Taiwan did not become an “obstacle” to his ambitions in dealing with Beijing. A proposed US$14 billion arms package to Taiwan has been awaiting Trump’s approval for months. After meeting Xi in Beijing in May, Trump described the package as a “very good negotiating chip”. Taiwan’s opposition seized on the developments to question the strength of ties with Washington. Chen I-hsin, communications director for the Kuomintang, the island’s main opposition party, said on Tuesday that the report was a “wake-up call” for Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te’s administration to recognise that US policy towards Taiwan was driven primarily by American interests. As evidence of frictions in ties, he cited Lai’s inability to transit through the continental United States, as well as delays in US arms sales and reported restrictions on Taiwanese officials’ visits. Yet the Lai administration continued to proclaim that US-Taiwan relations were “the best in history”, Chen said. He also criticised Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung’s recent assertions that “Taiwan’s interests are America’s interests” and that Taipei and Washington should “manage” Beijing, describing them as “naive and wishful thinking”. “US interests have never been identical to Taiwan’s interests,” Chen said, calling on the government to reassess its approach to Washington. Huang Kuo-chang, chairman of the smaller opposition Taiwan People’s Party, said Trump’s approach had raised questions about whether ties were really as strong as the government claimed. “At this point, we cannot afford to offend the United States,” Huang said. “But many of the things Trump and his administration have done regarding Taiwan make us reconsider one question: is the so-called rock-solid US-Taiwan relationship really that solid?” In response, foreign ministry spokesman Hsiao Kuang-wei said he did not know the source of the report about restrictions on Taiwanese officials, noting that government officials continued to travel regularly to Washington. Hsiao said exchanges continued at various levels, while Taiwanese ministries remained in regular contact with their US counterparts. “This is certainly not self-deception,” he said. “So when you say Taiwan-US relations are facing severe challenges, I don’t know from what perspective [Chen] is making that assessment.” As for Lai’s overseas trips, Hsiao said any transit through the US would have to fit the leader’s itinerary and would be arranged “when the timing is right”. He also said Washington had repeatedly stressed that arms sales to Taiwan were continuing. Ahead of the summit, issues such as large-scale US arms sales to Taiwan, Lai’s transit through the United States and visits to Taiwan by senior US officials have all been subject to considerable constraints Chang Wu-ueh, cross-strait studies expert Fan Yun, legislative caucus secretary general of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party, said questions about whether the US could be trusted tended to resurface whenever a Xi-Trump summit approached. But she said the US State Department and White House “have repeatedly reiterated that Washington’s policy towards Taiwan remained unchanged and that it opposed coercion or attempts to forcibly change the status quo”. Analysts said the Xi-Trump summit was unlikely to produce a major deal over Taiwan, but highlighted the risks of Taipei relying too heavily on Washington. Lee Shying-jow, former director general of the island’s National Security Bureau, warned that Taiwan could not base its security strategy on the assumption that the United States would definitely come to its aid. He added that international commitments were conditional and countries ultimately acted according to their own interests. “Our survival cannot possibly be the highest priority in another country’s calculations,” he said. Chang Wu-ueh, a cross-strait studies expert at Tamkang University in New Taipei City, said Washington and Beijing were “unlikely to make significant new declarations or strike a major deal over Taiwan”. Instead, he expected the summit to focus on “managing differences and establishing boundaries” to prevent the Taiwan issue from triggering a confrontation between Washington and Beijing or further cross-strait escalation. “Ahead of the summit, issues such as large-scale US arms sales to Taiwan, Lai’s transit through the United States and visits to Taiwan by senior US officials have all been subject to considerable constraints,” Chang said. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Asian Games: Pan Zhanle says ‘fire inside’ fuels his successful 100m freestyle title defence
description: The 22-year-old admits rival Kim Young-beom saying, ‘He [Pan Zhanle] is intimidating, but I don’t think he is unbeatable’ spurs him to victory.
content: Pan Zhanle admitted he had a “fire burning inside” during his successful title defence of the men’s 100m freestyle at the Asian Games. Motivated by a rival’s claim that he was not unbeatable, the 22-year-old “controlled his anger” to overturn two South Korean swimmers in the final 10 metres to snatch gold. A day later on Monday, swimming the third leg in a team with Xu Haibo, Fei Liwei and Zhang Zhanshuo, he led China to its first men’s 4x200m freestyle relay Asian Games gold in 16 years, breaking the team’s own Asian record. Those performances caused social media users to speculate whether Pan only performs at his best when fuelled by anger. After the 100m freestyle race, when asked by a reporter from state media how he managed the comeback, Pan replied: “Before the race, I saw their comments saying ‘Pan Zhanle is not unbeatable.’ “I actually had a fire burning inside me and wanted to prove myself,” he said. A month before the Asian Games, 20-year-old South Korean rival Kim Young-beom, holder of the Korean national 100m freestyle record, expressed his confidence to local media about beating Pan, stating: “He [Pan Zhanle] is intimidating, but I don’t think he is unbeatable. I am working as hard as he is, so I think gold is possible.” Pan won the race with a time of 47.61 seconds, and Kim ultimately took silver in 47.65 seconds, followed by countryman Hwang Sun-woo in third (47.79 seconds), while Zhang finished fourth with a personal best of 48.23 seconds. The time was Pan’s best since the 2024 Paris Olympics. Pan trailed early as the field turned together at 50 metres, with Kim turning first and Pan in third. Executing a late surge in the final sprint, Pan touched the wall 0.04 seconds ahead of Kim. “When I reached the 99-metre mark, I thought I might lose,” Pan admitted after the race, insisting he is not naturally gifted. “Maybe I was just lucky today.” Beyond luck, Pan credited his major tournament experience for the victory. “This is a good start, and I believe I will swim better in the future,” he said. Kim was not the first rival to get under the skin of the Chinese swimmer. Pan made headlines after complaining during a post-race interview about Australian swimmer Kyle Chalmers ignoring his greeting in the pool at the Paris Olympics. While others might have let it pass, Pan raised the subject immediately after breaking the world record with a time of 46.40 seconds to win Olympic gold: “I greeted Chalmers earlier, but he completely ignored me. It felt like he looked down on us.” The remark ignited a firestorm on social media. Reflecting on his recent struggles, Pan noted that mindset rather than capability was the issue: “When I was younger, I was on an upwards trajectory. If I kept that old mindset, I might swim slower and slower. I am working to rediscover myself.” Turning to the relay, Pan joked that Zhang was placed as the anchor leg due to his individual title and long reach: “With all conditions aligned, he always produces miracles on the final leg. He is the ‘Son of Miracles.’” He self-deprecatingly added that the first two legs were assigned by skill level: “I am the weakest, so I was placed on the third leg.” Having previously considered himself a junior athlete, Pan joked that he felt “old” seeing competitors born in 2006 and 2007. “I wouldn’t say I’m being challenged by younger swimmers,” he said. “Over the past two years, I’ve just been breaking through my own limits and surpassing who I was back then.”

title: Meet Paige Price, who is divorcing Malcolm in the Middle star Frankie Muniz
description: The actor, who took up stock car racing in recent years, announced his divorce from Price in July after 10 years together; the pair share a five-year-old son.
content: Actor Frankie Muniz, best known for playing the titular character in the hit sitcom Malcolm in the Middle, seems to be going through a rough patch. The 40-year-old, who is also a professional stock car racing driver, recently shared on Instagram that the last few weeks of his life have been “a nightmare [he’s] praying to wake up from”. Describing the situation as “hitting rock bottom”, the New Jersey native remains hopeful, writing, “In five years I believe I’ll look back at this exact low point and feel grateful for it, because the high I’ll be standing on then only exists because I went through this.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Frankie Muniz (@frankiemuniz4) The candid post comes around two months after Muniz announced his divorce from his wife, Paige Price, in July. The actor said at the time that they were separating after “10 beautiful years together”, but they remain determined to co-parent their five-year-old son, Mauz Mosley Muniz, as friends. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Frankie Muniz (@frankiemuniz4) Just a day after admitting his life was “falling apart”, the actor posted a family photo on Instagram, showing him spending time with his wife and son in Scottsdale, Arizona. So, who is Paige Price? Here is what we know. What is Paige Price’s background? According to her IMDb bio, Paige Price hails from Washington County, Pennsylvania, where she grew up in a borough called Marianna. Not much is known about her family and background, except that her nickname is Pog and she once aspired to become a forensic pathologist. What does Paige Price do? Paige Price began modelling at the age of 18 and joined a golf network as a presenter at 21, per IMDb. She hosted several segments, attended events and interviewed players. People magazine reported that it was in February 2016, while she was covering the 28th annual Frank Sinatra Celebrity Invitational in Indio, California, that she met Muniz. In 2018, Muniz and Price co-starred in the film The Black String and started running an olive oil shop they bought in Scottsdale, Arizona. “It’s a lot of work, but it’s really rewarding when people come in and rave about the product,” Muniz told The Republic. View this post on Instagram A post shared by pog and mauz (@pogandmauz) Price has also launched a business called Pog and Mauz, named after her nickname and her son. It is described as “A limited collection of thoughtfully curated items” on its Instagram page. When did Frankie Muniz marry Paige Price? Price went Instagram-official with the Big Fat Liar actor in August 2016, posting a photo on her profile captioned “my main squeeze”. Muniz proposed at a lantern festival in Arizona in November 2018, before the couple eloped in October 2019, per People magazine. They held an official wedding on February 21, 2020, marking the fourth anniversary of the day they met, and welcomed their son on March 22, 2021.

title: Who from China’s side will be in the room at this week’s Xi-Trump summit?
description: A look at past Sino-US summits offers insight, with trusted presidential aides and policy expertise expected to take centre stage.
content: When Xi Jinping sits down with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Thursday, the Chinese leader’s side of the table will be filled with senior aides bringing extensive policy expertise. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed on Monday that Xi would pay a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday. The trip – Xi’s first state visit to Washington since 2015 – will also mark his second face-to-face meeting this year with Trump, as the world’s top two economies seek to stabilise a relationship tested by trade, technology and national security disputes. A look at Sino-American summits over the past decade offers insight as to who from the Chinese side will be in the room. The president’s aides The innermost circle is likely to include Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, who oversees the Chinese leader’s administrative and security coordination. Cai is a Politburo Standing Committee member, first secretary of the ruling Communist Party’s secretariat, and director of the Central General Office. He has served right next to Xi on almost all the Chinese leader’s trips within China and abroad. While Cai is not a diplomat himself, he has always been seated at Xi’s right at high-profile summits. He has also received some important US figures in recent years, including Blackstone CEO Stephen Schwarzman in Beijing in 2024. Tang Fangyu, the newly appointed director of the Central Policy Research Office – the party’s top policy research body – is also likely to be there, as his predecessors have been. Lu Luhua, a top personal secretary to Xi handling foreign affairs, is almost certain to appear alongside Xi during the Washington visit, consistent with past protocol. The diplomatic apparatus Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi will certainly be in the Chinese delegation, leading Beijing’s diplomatic apparatus with several of his top lieutenants. The senior envoys expected to join the summit table are likely to include Ma Zhaoxu, executive vice-minister of foreign affairs, who visited Washington in July to pave the way for Xi’s visit. Others include Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the US, serving as the main liaison between Washington and Beijing; Hong Lei, the Chinese foreign ministry’s protocol chief; and Cai Wei, an assistant minister of foreign affairs. The economic and trade command The country’s top economic officials will join the Chinese delegation, as they help Beijing navigate complex trade negotiations, technology controls, as well as fiscal and financial alignments. Beijing’s economic team in Washington will be anchored by Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, China’s economic and financial hand, who arrived a few days before Xi did for talks with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Expect Zheng Shanjie, chairman of the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), to be among the top economic and financial bigwigs to join China’s side of the negotiating table. The NDRC is China’s top economic planning agency, guiding macroeconomic strategy and industrial policy discussions. Others include Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, who oversees bilateral trade, market access and commercial frictions, and Finance Minister Lan Foan, who oversees financial working groups and macro-fiscal policy alignment. The military angle Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun could join the Chinese team as Beijing’s liaison official for bilateral military talks, as both sides seek to strengthen military-to-military ties. Dong sat on the Chinese side of the table during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May as the counterpart of US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

title: 4 dead in Ukraine after Russian missile and drone attacks on industrial cities
description: As Russia says metals, chemicals, energy and arms areas were hit, Ukraine warns of mass starvation in frontline town of Oleshky.
