content: Russia fired ballistic missiles at the southern Ukrainian industrial cities of Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih and Pavlohrad overnight, killing at least four people and wounding six, the governor of the Dnipropetrovsk region, Oleksandr Hanzha, said on Telegram on Tuesday. The casualties occurred in Dnipro, he said, where people are still believed to be trapped under the rubble of a hit industrial facility. The Russian Defence Ministry confirmed attacks on Ukraine’s metals, chemicals, energy and arms industries, in a Telegram post. It said cruise missiles and combat drones were used in addition to missiles. In the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, air raid alerts sounded several times overnight. Three people were injured in drone attacks, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A logistics facility caught fire and a five-storey residential building was damaged. Ukrainian armed forces attacked the refinery in the Russian city of Samara on the Volga River with drones, Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels reported. A fire broke out at the facility, according to the reports. A drone attack on industrial facilities killed one person and damaged civilian objects but had otherwise been repelled, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev wrote on Telegram. Russia has been trying since early 2022 to subjugate Ukraine with a large-scale invasion. Diplomatic efforts to end the war have so far produced no result. They were to be continued on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was set to speak with US President Donald Trump. Ukraine will also be urging the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the hunger-stricken southern town of Oleshky, Kyiv’s foreign ‌minister said. Some 6,000 residents of the Russian-occupied town and nearby area in Ukraine’s Kherson region – including 200 children – were “dying from hunger and cold” under a “full blockade” by Russian forces, Andrii Sybiha said in a Facebook video on Monday. “The occupiers are not allowing humanitarian aid through. We have been negotiating evacuation for a long time … and Russia is giving no reply,” ⁠said Sybiha, who is in New York for the annual UN gathering. “We will talk about ‌Oleshky here, at the highest level, and we will apply pressure so that the world hears this and makes Russia provide humanitarian access.” The Kremlin said ‌on Monday that the town was facing critical problems with food and medicine supplies, but ⁠that Russia’s military was working ⁠to resolve them. The plight of civilians in the frontline town on the Dnipro River, ‌which separates Russian and Ukrainian forces, has drawn growing concern from international monitors. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: China tightens control on more fentanyl precursors ahead of Xi-Trump meeting
description: Two more chemicals added to export control list days after US president calls for ‘more aggressive action’.
content: China tightened its controls on the export of fentanyl precursors to the United States, Canada and Mexico, adding two new chemicals to its list requiring export licences on Tuesday, one day ahead of President Xi Jinping’s announced visit to the US. China’s Ministry of Commerce, together with four other government agencies, added two N-phenethyl piperidine esters to part one of China’s Catalogue for the Administration of Exports of Precursor Chemicals to Specific Countries (Regions), according to a statement from the ministry. The list now includes 18 chemicals, all of which could be used in fentanyl production. The licensing requirement for these substances applies only to North America, with a separate section covering 41 chemicals bound for Myanmar, Laos and Afghanistan. The news came on the day before Xi is set to depart for the US on his highly anticipated state visit. Fentanyl has been a core issue in US-China trade negotiations since the Trump administration returned to power last year. US President Donald Trump raised the issue again in a letter of determination to the US Congress published on Wednesday, urging Beijing to take “more aggressive action” to reduce the flow of fentanyl precursors. Washington has been publishing an annual list of major drug transit and illicit drug producing countries – known as the Majors List – for decades. The latest version, issued last week, named 23 countries including China. Trump’s letter recognised China’s efforts, making reference to the export licensing regime that was introduced last year. Washington reduced its fentanyl-related tariffs from 20 per cent to 10 per cent in November. But Trump noted that China continued to be “the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used to illicitly produce fentanyl, methamphetamine and other deadly synthetic drugs”, adding that he had raised the issue directly with Xi. During Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, both leaders discussed the need to do more to curb the flow of fentanyl precursors to the US, according to a statement published by Washington following the visit. China’s readout from the meeting, however, did not mention any such discussions. At a congressional hearing in June, witnesses described Chinese money laundering networks as the financial fuel behind Mexican cartels and pressed Trump to raise the issue directly with his Chinese counterpart. The testimony pointed to money laundering as a distinct strand of the fentanyl trade, alongside the supply of precursor chemicals. Efforts to tackle the drug issue have been mounting in the build-up to Xi’s US visit. China’s Ministry of Public Security announced on September 10 that it had worked with the US Federal Bureau of Investigation on a transnational case involving the manufacture and trafficking of synthetic cannabinoid precursors. The ministry called it proof that the bilateral counternarcotics law enforcement mechanism was operating efficiently and a visible result of closer cooperation between the two countries’ agencies. FBI Director Kash Patel also travelled to Beijing in July to meet with China’s public security minister, Wang Xiaohong, for talks that focused on cracking down on fentanyl precursors.

title: Asian Games: Ryan Choi ‘very upset’ after falling just short in battle for foil gold
description: Ryan Choi loses breathtaking final to Japan’s Kazuki Iimura at Aichi Sky Expo after battling back from 10-6 down.
content: Hong Kong’s Ryan Choi Chun-yin came with a whisker of winning Asian Games gold on Tuesday, and said after suffering a losing run in mahjong he felt his luck had been about to change. The 28-year-old former world champion had dominated for much of the day, and even when behind, launched a stunning fightback in the final of the men’s individual foil competition. Battling local hero Kazuki Iimura, Choi found himself in a hole early on at the Aichi Sky Expo, and slipped 4-2 behind quite quickly. Iimura turned that into an 8-4 and then 10-6 lead, before Choi found his feet and battled back to 12-12. But roared on by a vocal partisan crowd, Iimura pulled ahead for good to win 15-13. “I’m very upset now because I just lost the match, but I think overall I’ll be happy in 10 minutes because it’s still a silver medal,” Choi said. “Today I feel pretty lucky. I liked all my match-ups. I think this luck just came to me. Sometimes it happens and you don’t know why. I can’t explain it but I felt it would be a lucky day.” While compatriot Cheung Ka-long had a day to forget, crashing out in the last 32 having struggled through the pool stage despite being defending champion, Choi emerged unbeaten from his pool, earned a bye into the last 16, and then ran the table on the way to the final. A close semi-final with South Korea’s Youn Jeong-hyun aside, Choi had appeared largely untroubled, until he came up against Kazuki. “I’ve played a lot of mahjong games with my friends recently and I lost them all,” Choi said. “I feel like God was planning to give me all the luck today. “Finally today, after suffering from losing in mahjong games, I get paid off.” Unsurprisingly, Iimura was “genuinely happy” to have been able to win in front of the home fans who had given him “so much power”. The 22-year-old said he had been able to hear them chanting for him when he was briefly struggling during the bout. “To be honest, I was panicking when I didn’t manage to score, and my head went blank,” he said. “But the support of everyone and their chants made me feel calm. “All my family members are here in the stands. I want to dedicate this medal to my family and the people who have supported me.” Choi will eventually consider this to have been a good day, especially when Hong Kong’s athletes combined to add gold, another silver and a bronze to the city’s medal tally, which crept up to 12 overall. Siobhan Haughey’s heroics in the pool came after cyclist Chloe Leung Wing-yee came third in the women’s road race, and wushu exponent Lau Chi-long second in the men’s nanquan and nangun event. Lau picked up third-place finishes in the morning and afternoon sessions, giving him 19.456 points, just behind China’s Li Jianming, who took gold with 19.563 points. Chinese Taipei’s Liu Chang-min claimed bronze with a score of 19.430. The Hongkonger said the key to his medal had been about harnessing the pressure that came with competing at such a high level. “This sport is so stressful,” Lau said. “You need concentration. You need full body preparation and commitment. Physically and mentally you have to do it over 100 per cent. “The stress is so much. Stress can be very useful though, and you need to learn how to control it in your performance.” Away from the medals, and Hong Kong’s men and women struggled to make an impact in the team table tennis. The women were knocked out 3-2 by Singapore in the first knockout round, the men made it to the quarter-finals before being swept aside 3-0 by South Korea.

title: Hong Kong bans caterer from importing workers for year over local hiring breach
description: Labour Department action follows findings that Kwai Chung-based firm Happy Up Corporation did not maintain local-to-imported worker ratio.
content: Hong Kong’s Labour Department has terminated Kwai Chung-based catering firm Happy Up Corporation’s application to import workers after it failed to meet the required local hiring ratio. The company has also been barred from applying to import workers for a year. A department spokesman said on Tuesday that the administrative sanctions had taken immediate effect under the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme (ESLS) following an application previously submitted by the company. He added that following an investigation, the department found the company had breached the scheme’s requirements by failing to maintain the required ratio of two local employees for every imported worker. “Employers applying for the importation of workers under the ESLS should strictly comply with the scheme requirements, including giving priority to employing suitable local workers,” he said. “If an employer violates labour or immigration laws … the [department] will impose an administrative sanction on the employer.” The department added that possible sanctions included ending the processing of an employer’s application, revoking approval for imported workers already granted and refusing to process any subsequent applications by the employer. In August last year, the department barred Top One Dance Club & Chinese Cuisine in Tsim Sha Tsui from importing workers for two years after it dismissed local employees. That same month, the department announced that Alama, a local pest control company, had been barred from importing workers for one year after it was found to have failed to give priority to hiring local staff before applying to import labour. The scheme was introduced in September 2023 to address a shortage of semi-skilled workers. It allows employers to apply to import workers for jobs, including waiters, junior cooks, transport drivers and telephone operators, provided they can show they have faced difficulties recruiting suitable local staff. Hong Kong had 56,482 imported workers in the city by July this year. The department had imposed administrative sanctions on 54 employers as of August 2026.

title: Can China’s grain reserves protect food security against El Nino?
description: As climate shocks and supply chain disruptions push global food prices higher, Beijing believes it has the tools to fend off rising risks.
content: Amid mounting global concern over food security risks posed by the El Nino weather pattern, Chinese officials have moved to reassure the public that national grain reserves remain well above international safety thresholds. “China has a solid foundation and sufficient capacity to withstand risks and challenges such as El Nino,” said Li Chao, an official from the National Development and Reform Commission, at a press conference on Tuesday. The remarks followed comments on Monday by Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, who said the domestic grain market had held steady despite volatility in global food markets. Liu noted that China operated a multi-tiered reserve system covering central and local government stockpiles alongside private sector inventories. He stressed that the nation’s stock-to-consumption ratio – the share of stored grain relative to demand – remained “significantly above” the 17 to 18 per cent benchmark recommended by international agencies. These reserves, he said, could be used to balance supply and demand and bring stability during periods of unexpected market volatility. On the production side, Liu said grain output had also remained stable. Annual grain output reached 715 million tonnes in 2025, he noted, while per capita grain availability exceeded 500kg (1,102.3 pounds), surpassing the global average. “China’s vast territory allows different regions to offset fluctuations in production, strengthening the overall resilience of the country’s grain supply,” Liu said. China’s summer grain harvest exceeded 150 million tonnes for the first time this year, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. These official assurances come amid a challenging global backdrop. Earlier this month, the World Meteorological Organisation reported that El Nino was “firmly established” and projected it would “intensify into a very strong event in the coming months”, warning of severe weather disruptions. Compounding these climate pressures, global supply chain disruptions to commodity and fertiliser shipments – linked to the US-Israel war on Iran – pushed the UN Food and Agriculture Organization global food price index higher in August after it reached a more than three-year peak in July. At Monday’s press conference, Liu said China’s food processing industry had enough capacity to produce finished staple goods such as flour, rice and cooking oil to meet domestic consumption needs. “Ensuring national food security is an ongoing task. We must remain confident and steadfast while staying prepared for potential risks, closely monitoring changes in the situation and responding proactively,” Liu said. Beijing has long prioritised agricultural self-sufficiency, with top officials repeatedly invoking the maxim that China must “keep its rice bowl firmly in its own hands”. Under its planning targets, the country aims to further expand comprehensive grain production capacity to about 725 million tonnes by 2030.

title: Turkey teen arrested after 11 pupils injured in shotgun shooting
description: In the third such incident in six months, the youngster opened fire near his school, leaving three in intensive care.
content: A teenager opened fire outside a secondary school in western Turkey on Tuesday, wounding 11 pupils, before being detained in the country’s third such shooting in six months, officials said. Three of the victims were in serious condition following the attack outside a school in Turgutlu near the western city of Izmir. “The treatment of 10 minors is ongoing, including three of whom are in intensive care,” Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci told a press conference in the nearby town of Manisa, saying one victim had been discharged. Gunshots rang out. He was swearing as he walked towards the side street. He was shouting Unnamed local resident One resident told the IHA news agency that they saw the gunman moments after the attack, saying he appeared to be angry. “Gunshots rang out. I immediately went out onto the balcony. He was swearing as he walked towards the side street. He was shouting,” the local said. “He fired at people here with the gun he was carrying. We could not intervene because he had a rifle,” another eyewitness told IHA, which did not name either interviewee. Although shootings are rare in Turkey, the latest incident comes five months after two back-to-back attacks by teenagers on consecutive days in April that shocked the nation and sparked public concerns about security in Turkish schools. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek confirmed that all of Tuesday’s victims were minors. He said the suspect’s parents and his grandfather had been detained for questioning over the attack, which saw police and rescuers rushing to the school with panicked parents. HaberTurk news channel said the assailant was a student at the school. The report added that he arrived at the scene armed with a shotgun and fired randomly near the school before trying to flee on foot. The motive of the attack was not known, according to Gurlek, who said two chief prosecutors were appointed to investigate the shooting, including claims that the student was bullied at school. Anxious parents rushed to the school and confrontations broke out between them and the police who blocked entrance to the building, Cumhuriyet newspaper reported. The attack came months after Turkey was shocked by two other school shootings. The government increased security at educational facilities at the start of the academic year last week. In April, 16 people, mostly students, were injured when a former student opened fire at a high school in Sanliurfa province in Turkey’s southeast. The assailant later took his own life. The next day, a 14-year-old student opened fire on two classrooms at his school in nearby Kahramanmaras province, killing eight students and a teacher and injuring 13 others. The attacker was killed by police. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: How Mid-Autumn Festival lanterns are traditionally made and an artisan defending the craft
description: Hong Kong lantern artisan Wan Wong explains why she keeps the traditional craft alive, barriers she faced as a woman and the key techniques.
content: While mass-produced Mid-Autumn Festival lanterns of every size, shape and style can be bought with a single click these days, a dedicated few in Hong Kong are defying the fast consumerism trend by keeping the objects’ traditional craftsmanship alive. Among them is Hong Kong fashion designer and lantern artisan Wan Wong, 52, who spends hours every year crafting traditional bamboo, wire and cellophane lanterns by hand. Lanterns remain a cherished centrepiece of the Mid-Autumn Festival, a Southeast and East Asian celebration falling on the 15th day of the eighth month in the Chinese lunar calendar (between September 7 and October 8). While modern celebrations focus less on agricultural harvests and more on family unity, traditional customs like moon gazing, lantern appreciation and sharing mooncakes remain favourites. For Wong, taking the extra time to craft her own lanterns adds a sense of festivity that evokes fond childhood memories. “I grew up in quite humble conditions in the 1970s and 80s, living in a public housing estate,” she says. “Every year during the Mid-Autumn Festival, stationery and paper-craft shops were hung with hundreds of colourful paper lanterns. I’d walk past them after school and desperately look up at the rabbit lanterns in the storefronts. But my mum would only let me pick between a cellophane goldfish or a butterfly, which were cheaper.” In those days, lanterns were crafted using rice paper, bamboo and cellophane, illuminated from within by real wax candles. Wong had her share of accidental fires and fragile materials snapping. “Yet they remind me of the good old days of sitting outdoors at our public housing estate, watching people boil wax and playing with lanterns,” she says. “Life was tough back then, but we didn’t know what poverty was – we were just happy. It was also one of the rare times my dad had time off work to celebrate with us.” After building a career in fashion design, Wong happened upon a television programme featuring a local lantern artisan. “I’ve always loved handicrafts, but nothing captured my interest quite like traditional paper crafting,” she says. She tracked down the master online and called him, hoping to learn the craft. “As soon as he heard I was a woman, he instantly refused to teach me.” Perspectives have shifted since then. In 2018, Wong met another artisan skilled in making lanterns and lion heads (for lion dances) who was willing to mentor her. “Traditionally, masters only passed skills down to male family members,” Wong says. “But the younger generation, myself included, cannot pursue this as a full-time career because you cannot make a proper living from it. Once the lantern masters realised the art couldn’t survive without adapting, they had no choice but to open their doors.” Crafting a traditional lantern involves five key steps. The process begins with preparing bamboo strips (zuk mit), which requires splitting raw bamboo stalks and shaving the strips until pliable. These strips are used in zaat (constructing the frame), followed by pok (applying paper or cellophane), se (painting the surface) and zong (decorating with fabrics or embellishments). Rabbit lantern frames are typically made from bamboo strips due to rabbits’ rounded bodies, whereas metal wire is preferred for intricate animal shapes like goldfish because it bends more easily. Festive tradition demands vibrant, auspicious colours such as red, yellow or orange. Traditional lanterns rarely feature pure white or blue, which are associated with mourning and funerals. Wong says that a single lantern can take seven or eight hours to construct. “Not many people have the patience for it, and your fingers get chapped and calloused from the glue and shaving bamboo,” she says. Yet she considers the effort deeply rewarding. Beyond their visual charm, traditional lanterns carry auspicious meanings: the rabbit pays homage to the Jade Rabbit, the celestial companion of Chang’e in Chinese folklore symbolising longevity and selflessness; goldfish represent joy and prosperity; and the Chinese words for star fruit – yeung tou (Cantonese) or yang tao (Mandarin) – sound similar to auspicious phrases denoting a smooth and fortunate path in life. Wong also experiments with playful contemporary designs. In her studio, traditional paper-crafting techniques yield lanterns shaped like hot-air balloons and Labubu art toys. “Young people shouldn’t view paper-crafting as old-fashioned,” she says. “Even my teacher praised my modern designs, feeling I had opened a new path.” Wong is eager to share the craft with a broader audience. She has hosted lantern-making workshops for four years, including a recent collaboration with the Hong Kong Design Centre, and she dreams of creating large-scale lantern installations for global exhibition platforms. “Ai Weiwei’s massive paper installation Er Xi at Le Bon Marché Rive Gauche department store in Paris was breathtaking. I’d love to transform traditional paper-crafting into contemporary fine art installations,” she says. “I don’t want this beautiful craft to vanish. Today’s world moves too fast. Sitting down for hours to make a lantern brings me a deep sense of inner calm and appreciation for the creative process.”

title: Constructive. Strategic. Stability. Chinese state media spell out Xi-Trump summit aim
description: Front-page article in Communist Party’s top newspaper also lays out Beijing’s red lines for the relationship.
content: The Communist Party’s flagship newspaper has set the tone for the summit on Thursday between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, calling for the two sides to build on the “constructive strategic stability” agreed upon during Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing. The Chinese government and state media have also spelled out Beijing’s “red lines” days ahead of the high-stakes event in Washington. The leaders will provide “strategic guidance” on how the two powers can develop a stable relationship during this week’s summit, according to a front-page article published by People’s Daily on Tuesday. The newspaper cast a rosy light on the state of China-US ties since the pair last met in Beijing during Trump’s trip four months ago, saying that “positive factors in bilateral interactions continue to increase”. Xi’s visit this week was aimed at “keeping the positive momentum going”, an article posted on Chaoyang Shaoxia, a social-media channel widely believed to be affiliated with the Chinese foreign ministry, said on Tuesday. The ministry, Chinese embassies and ambassadors posted videos in both Chinese and English to social media on the same day, highlighting that “from Beijing to Washington DC, the China-US relationship must stay on course towards constructive strategic stability”. At their meeting in Beijing, Xi and Trump agreed to maintain “constructive strategic stability”, although the White House statement on the talks also included demands for “fairness and reciprocity”. Beijing has emphasised that the concept should guide China-US relations “over the next three years and beyond” – at least for the remainder of Trump’s presidency – which state media echoed on Tuesday. “Managing ‘Taiwan independence’ is a key part of building constructive strategic stability between China and the US,” the front-page People’s Daily piece noted, framing pro-independence forces as a “common enemy” of Beijing and Washington. “The US side must handle the Taiwan question with the utmost caution and take concrete action to safeguard the stable development of China-US relations and peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait,” it warned. It also reiterated that “Taiwan, democracy and human rights, the path and system and development rights are four red lines” for Beijing. “These are the guardrails and safety net for China-US relations,” said the article, which was published under the byline Guo Jiping, a pen name used for editorials which express the Communist Party’s position on major international matters. Beijing considers Taiwan to be part of China and has not renounced the use of force to bring the self-governed island under its control. Most countries – including the US – do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that the Trump administration was considering delaying the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. The Guo Jiping commentary also argued that having the “correct strategic understanding” was “the first button that must be fastened properly” in building China-US constructive strategic stability. It warned that the “root” of all problems in the bilateral relationship laid in the “cold war mentality” that was held by some in the US, who viewed China as a strategic rival and hyped a narrative of strategic competition. “China and the US should be partners and friends. This is what history teaches us, and what reality requires,” it added. The Chaoyang Shaoxia article said China’s overall national strength had “comprehensively” increased since Xi’s last state visit to the US in 2015 and its international influence had also “steadily” risen. After more than a decade, Washington should understand that “cooperation between China and the US is greater than their differences, there is no benefit in testing each other’s limits, and decoupling from China is even less realistic”. Instead, the US was urged to “focus on expanding cooperation” to “serve the common interests” of both nations. Chinese policymakers have repeatedly said in recent months that the concept of “constructive strategic stability” does not deny the existence of competition between China and the US but calls for avoiding full-scale confrontation and maintaining dialogue to manage the countries’ differences. “Economic and trade cooperation should continue to serve as the ballast and propeller” of the relationship, the Guo Jiping article said. As part of preparations for the summit, the two governments held a round of trade talks in New York over the weekend. They also agreed to establish dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI), while China stepped up purchases of US soybeans in recent days. Beijing on Tuesday added two drug precursor chemicals to its export control list for North America. Chaoyang Shaoxia said that as the technology continued to develop, competition between China and the US in AI was inevitable. “But what we seek is a race in which each side strives to catch up and both advance together, rather than a life-or-death, zero-sum struggle that exhausts both sides,” it said. “By steadily breaking the ice and building trust in lower and moderately sensitive areas, even if each step forward is only a small one, we can help ensure that global technology advances in a positive direction and benefits the world.” The People’s Daily article called on the two countries to make AI a “new frontier” of cooperation. It also said China-US constructive strategic stability would serve as a “precious public good” for the whole world. The article described the concept as a solution to the “Thucydides Trap”, a theory in which a rising power and an established hegemon are destined for war. The article described the theory as being rooted in a zero-sum narrative of confrontation drawn from the West’s history. “Major powers bear special responsibilities,” it said. “China and the US should … properly handle regional flashpoints with a strong sense of responsibility by doing more practical and beneficial work to promote peace talks and reconciliation,” it added, referring to conflicts in the Middle East, the war in Ukraine and tensions on the Korean peninsula. It argued that the back-to-back multilateral gatherings of the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 summit in Miami in December would create a “historic linkage” to help coordination between the two countries. “The year 2026 is bound to be a historic and landmark year in China-US relations that carries forward the past and ushers in the future,” it said.

title: South Korean graduates protected from deepfake abuse by new photo tech
description: The alumni-built technology embeds photos with signals that confuse AI generators to prevent images from being manipulated.
content: A South Korean university has embedded graduation photos with anti-deepfake technology to prevent a repeat of a scandal two years ago, when portraits of female graduates were used to create sexually explicit manipulated images. Seoul National University’s (SNU) use of StealCut Protect, created by a start-up founded by SNU alumni, marked the first time it was used for a university graduation album in the country, The Korea Herald reported. StealCut provided the technology to SNU free of charge. Deepfake models generally work by analysing facial structure characteristics to generate manipulated content. StealCut Protect inserts minute, pixel-level signals – largely invisible to the human eye – into images to disrupt this process. If a deepfake generator tries to manipulate a protected photo, the result is a distorted or unidentifiable face. The technology differed from existing tools that detected or flagged deepfakes after they were created, StealCut said, as it secured the image at the source – reducing the need for content moderation. SNU, ranked among the top three universities in South Korea, was at the centre of a scandal in 2024, when illegal deepfake pornography created from women’s graduation and social media photos was shared in chat rooms on Telegram, an encrypted messaging service. Two men, both SNU graduates, were arrested in May that year, according to The Korea Times. Police identified at least 61 victims, including 12 SNU alumni and students. During their trial in October 2024, prosecutors said that one of the men, surnamed Park, had created over 400 manipulated images and videos and distributed more than 1,700. Park was sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges including producing and distributing sexually exploitative and falsified media. His co-defendant, surnamed Kang, was sentenced to four years. Sexual misconduct at South Korean universities had hit its highest level in five years, news outlet Chosun Biz reported on Monday, citing figures received by opposition People Power Party lawmaker Jeong Seong-guk. From 2022 to this year, 160 crimes, acts of misconduct and school rule violations involving enrolled students were reported across nine universities, according to Jeong, a member of the National Assembly’s Education Committee. Sex-related cases accounted for 71 of these incidents, or 44.4 per cent. Such cases have risen for three straight years, after falling from 12 in 2022 to 10 in 2023. This year 21 cases have been recorded so far, compared with 12 in 2024 and 16 last year. The types of sex offences have also diversified beyond sexual harassment and sexual violence. Digital sex crimes, such as illegal filming, distribution of filmed material and production and distribution of deepfake sexual exploitation content, are on the rise. Kyungpook National University recorded the highest number of sex-related cases over the past five years with 25, followed by Jeju National, Gyeongsang National, SNU, Chungbuk National, Kangwon National, Chonnam National and Jeonbuk National universities. Kyungpook National said it had provided psychological and legal support to victims and taken strict disciplinary action against offenders. But Jeong said action “should not end with simple post-incident discipline”. “Preventive education should be actively supported to raise students’ gender awareness, and relevant laws and systems should be improved to respond to new types of sex crimes such as deepfakes,” he said.

title: Stand News editor had no intention of harming national security, court hears
description: Appeal judges say Patrick Lam failed to fact-check article containing false information, but still ran story after police countered claims.
content: A former acting chief editor of the now-defunct Stand News was fulfilling his duty to publish articles and had no intent to undermine national security in Hong Kong, his lawyer has said while appealing his conviction for sedition. A panel of High Court justices pointed out on Tuesday that the presiding trial judge had ruled Patrick Lam Shiu-tung’s decision to run material containing false information from interviewees had the seditious effect of inciting hatred against authorities. They noted the point was among the grounds for the appellant’s earlier conviction. In August 2024, Lam was found guilty of a joint conspiracy charge of publishing and reproducing seditious material along with former editor-in-chief Chung Pui-kuen and Best Pencil (Hong Kong), Stand News’ holding company. Lam, who was Chung’s successor before the outlet closed in December 2021, later lodged an appeal against his conviction. But David Ma Wai-kwan, Lam’s defence counsel, argued before the Court of Appeal on Tuesday that the trial judge had erred in law by failing to consider whether Lam had “seditious intent” when he published an article reflecting interviewees’ feelings about the 2019 anti-government protests. The article in question was a feature that focused on two alumni of the Chinese University of Hong Kong, who told the author that they were deeply upset by the stand-off between protesters and police at the university in November 2019 and blamed law enforcement for the ruined state of the campus. The piece was among 11 articles found to have been published by the defendants between July 2020 and December 2021 that demonstrating a “criminal mind” to put such seditious material online. Ma argued on Tuesday that Lam was simply an employee of Stand News. “It was part of his job to fulfil the publishing duties,” the lawyer said. Mr Justice William Tam Yiu-ho, meanwhile, said the interviewees had given information that was not entirely true and carried a seditious effect. The judge said that Lam, as a media professional, was obliged to conduct fact-checking, but had still published the interviewees’ statements in their original form. “The interviewees had said things that were seditious, and the editor obviously knew about that. Wasn’t he in the wrong when he allowed [the article] to be published?” Tam said. Chief Judge of the High Court Jeremy Poon Shiu-chor noted that under the colonial-era law applied in the original case, sedition was considered an “inchoate offence”, a category intended to stop harmful acts before they cause damage to society. He also questioned why Lam had not discontinued the article’s dissemination after police issued a statement to counter the allegations. Derek Lau Tak-wai, senior assistant director of public prosecutions, said that while the public enjoyed freedom of the press, such a right was not “absolute” and remained bound by law. “[Stand News] crossed the line when they published material that was known to be seditious,” he said. In 2021, Lam and Chung became the first media professionals to be charged under the colonial-era sedition law since Hong Kong’s return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997. The pair were convicted in August 2024. While Chung was sentenced to 21 months in prison, the court factored in the time he spent incarcerated before he and Lam secured bail in the middle of the trial, leaving him with nine months to serve. Lam avoided serving the remainder of his term, 21 days, as the judge took into consideration his need for treatment of a rare disease. For Lam’s appeal, the justices are expected to hand down their judgment within six months.

title: Were the Serbian military’s new robot dogs built using Chinese technology?
description: Analysts say the nations are deepening their collaboration, with China seeing Serbia as a gateway to the European market.
content: Cutting-edge Chinese technology could gradually be becoming part of Serbia’s weapons systems with the appearance of robot dogs in a Serbian military drill on the weekend soon after the opening of a Chinese robotics factory in the Balkan country, according to observers. Robodogs equipped with machine guns, grenade launchers and rocket launchers were among the major weapons systems unveiled at Serbia’s Pobednik 2026 large-scale tactical live-fire exercise on Sunday. The event involved its army, air force, air defence, special forces and military police and, according to Serbian media reports, the robodogs were designed to enter dangerous areas and secure entry routes for special forces, operations that were part of the military drill. The robodogs’ debut comes only a few weeks after Europe’s first factory for mass-producing humanoid robots and robotic dogs began production in the western Serbian city of Sabac. During factory’s opening ceremony on August 29, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that the country would unveil domestically produced combat robots in action “in 15 days”. The robot factory was jointly established by Taiwan-headquartered automotive supplier Minth Group and mainland Chinese robotics company AgiBot. AgiBot, which provides technological support for the Sabac factory, said that the company “neither manufactured nor sold” the quadrupedal robots involved in the military drills, and that the products it developed and sold were intended exclusively for civilian purposes. However, Minth Group, which actually operates the factory, did not respond to the South China Morning Post’s request for comment. While the US is thought to be a leader in robodog technology, military exports are strictly controlled. This leaves China as the most likely source of Serbia’s robotic dogs, given the two countries’ existing defence collaboration and China’s 80 per cent share of global robodog production. “[One can] only assume the dog robots were manufactured in Sabac,” said Vuk Vuksanovic, lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy education at King’s College London. “The issue remains: how advanced is the Serbian defence system, and does it allow integration of Chinese robotics, given that Serbian defence procurement is not always based on long-term strategic planning. “For China, the main reason for these transactions is to win new defence markets, and Serbia can be used as a potential short cut to European defence markets.” China is one of the world’s largest suppliers of parts for uncrewed platforms, often with the potential for both civilian and military uses, and is rapidly integrating robotics technologies into its own military. During a military parade in Beijing in September last year, the People’s Liberation Army showcased robodogs equipped with combat rifles and reconnaissance gear. China also unveiled similar robotic dogs during February’s World Defence Show 2026 in Saudi Arabia, potentially in an attempt to drum up overseas sales. On display was the PF-070 system, which carries four anti-tank guided missiles. Martin Sebena, a lecturer at the University of Hong Kong who specialises in China-Europe relations, said there was “both industrial and geopolitical logic” to the countries’ “intense collaboration” on drone production, with the Serbian Ministry of Defence explicitly describing China as a partner in air defence and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV). “Together with robotics, this gives rise to a dual-use industrial cluster,” Sebena said. “On the geopolitical side, production in Serbia can be seen as hedging, as it allows AgiBot to localise production in Europe in case import restrictions are imposed on it in the future. “Robotics production has the cover of a Sino-Serbian strategic partnership and goes in line with Serbia’s recent military purchases from China, which has become Serbia’s largest arms supplier.” Sebena said that given the UAV precedent, the integration of Chinese robotics technology into the Serbian military “could go quite far”. “The Chinese have first sold drones to Serbia, then helped it develop its own UAV systems until the Serbians were able to produce UAVs themselves,” Sebena said. “The same could repeat here, with the Chinese providing the know-how, platform and software, and the Serbian side adapting the technology and integrating it into their military.” Serbia is a major customer for China’s arms industry, buying 6.8 per cent of Beijing’s arms exports between 2021 and 2025 – the second-biggest buyer after Pakistan, which accounted for 61 per cent, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Belgrade’s recent military drill also featured other Chinese-made weapons systems, showing intelligence collection using CH-95 long-range reconnaissance and strike UAVs and tackling swarms of low-flying drones and combat aircraft with the HQ-17AE short-range surface-to-air missile system. Chinese weapons systems play a particularly significant role in Serbia’s air defence network, which reportedly operates Chinese-made HQ-9 long-range and FK-3 surface-to-air missile systems. Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said Serbia would likely integrate Chinese robotics, sensors, AI, autonomy software and networking technologies into its drone-enabled formations. Meanwhile, China saw Serbia as a “strategic European manufacturing and technology partner” that was politically receptive to Chinese investments and technology transfers, she said. “I expect cooperation to be deepened gradually over the next three to five years, especially in drones,” Odgaard said. “The opening of the robotics factory and recent military cooperation suggest growing institutional links.” Odgaard added that Serbia was likely to balance these ties against its relations with the EU and other partners, which could mean that “incremental integration” and co-production were more likely than wholesale dependence on Chinese military robotics. Stefan Vladisavljev, programme director at the Serbia-based Foundation BFPE for a Responsible Society, said Belgrade traditionally maintained a policy of military neutrality, which did not limit its cooperation with different actors. “As Serbia and China have developed their relations over the span of the past two decades, an increased amount of military-type equipment has been purchased from China,” Vladisavljev said. “With the development of military technology, now we are entering a phase in which Serbia – in order to build its own capacity – is purchasing new types of equipment.”

title: Indonesia presses ahead with Russian oil imports despite ‘real risk’ of US penalties
description: Analysts say Jakarta made the ‘right decision’ for the country’s energy security but urge dialogue with Washington to maintain transparency.
content: Indonesia plans to press ahead with discounted Russian crude oil imports to secure domestic energy supplies and manage fiscal pressures, despite the risk of higher US tariffs as Washington moves to tighten economic pressure on Moscow. On Friday, US President Donald Trump signed into law an act that would give him authority to impose sanctions on Russia and slap tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five buyers of Russian crude oil, gas and military equipment, or countries that help Moscow evade sanctions. The legislation, named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, also targets Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers. The term refers to a network of ageing or obscurely owned vessels that Russia uses to transport oil while seeking to evade Western sanctions and the Group of Seven’s price cap on Russian crude. The ships often operate under complex ownership structures and flags of convenience, making them harder to trace and regulate. In April, the European Commission sanctioned Indonesia’s Karimun port for its “connections with the shadow fleet and circumvention of the oil price cap”. A day after the US Congress passed the Graham Act, Indonesia’s Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Bahlil Lahadalia said the second phase of Russian crude oil imports was still on track. “Our crude oil supply is, God willing, secure, including those supplied by Russia. I will explain the technical aspects of [the second phase of crude oil import] from Russia at the appropriate time,” Bahlil told reporters on September 17. Indonesia received around 770,000 barrels of Russian crude oil valued at about US$75 million under the first phase in June, according to Bloomberg, citing customs data. The oil was delivered by the Sierra tanker under a Cameroon flag. The tanker is sanctioned by several countries including Britain, the European Union, Canada and Australia. In April, Hashim Djojohadikusumo, President Prabowo Subianto’s brother and his special energy envoy, said Jakarta had secured a commitment from Moscow for 150 million barrels of crude oil “at a special price”, of which 100 million barrels would be sent immediately and the rest would be bought out of necessity. The government’s fuel import decisions would always be based on “economic principles”, Bahlil said. “We look for the best. We look for the cheaper one, that’s what we will buy.” Indonesia is a net importer of oil, as domestic production of about 600,000 barrels a day cannot fulfil its demand of more than 1.6 million barrels per day. In the first six months of this year, Nigeria became the largest crude oil supplier to Indonesia, followed by Angola and Saudi Arabia, statistics agency BPS said last month. Tariff threat Analysts warn that Jakarta’s decision to continue buying Russian oil risks attracting higher tariffs on its own exports to the US. A 10 per cent levy is currently applied to Indonesian goods, following the signing of the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade in February. “There is a real risk, although Indonesia’s exposure is different from that of India or China because Indonesia is not among the world’s largest buyers of Russian crude,” Ronny Sasmita, a senior analyst at the Indonesia Strategic and Economics Action Institution, told This Week in Asia. “Indonesia should not assume that its relatively small Russian-oil purchases make it immune. Washington could look not only at the volume of purchases but also at whether Indonesia is considered to be materially supporting Russia’s energy revenues.” Additional US tariffs would have “very large consequences”, as Indonesia’s exports to the US were much more valuable to the economy than its purchases of Russian crude oil, he said. Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at maritime intelligence firm Kpler, said Washington’s actual enforcement of such heavy tariffs would largely depend on global crude price levels. “I don’t think [Washington] will impose any tariffs until oil prices come down. At US$70 [per barrel], there is a risk of tariffs, but at US$100 oil, they are not trying to take more oil off the market. They are actually trying to get Ukraine to stop hitting Russian infrastructure to keep oil on the market. So, I find the odds pretty low until prices come down,” Brouhard said. Yayan Satyakti, a lecturer in energy economics at Padjadjaran University, nevertheless suggested that Indonesia “hedge” its Russian crude purchase by importing it on a smaller scale to avoid becoming one of the top five buyers. “Indonesia is a neutral country. We buy oil from Russia, but we are also committed to buying oil from the United States,” Yayan said. “I believe Indonesia’s policy will not harm trade relations between Indonesia and the US.” Yayan added that buying Russian crude oil for a strategic reserve was “a lawful exercise of sovereignty” and Indonesia was not obliged to follow the “unilateral sanctions” the US and EU imposed on Moscow. “In this difficult situation, I believe that taking oil from Russia, even in the shadow of potential sanctions, is the right decision to protect Indonesia’s energy security right now,” he said. “If we don’t have that, it will be quite difficult for Indonesia to maintain energy accessibility and affordability, alongside managing a fiscal burden where we are experiencing very crucial challenges.” Yayan estimated that fuel reserves in Java were enough for 28 days of consumption but stock in the eastern part of the country could last only 14 days. To avoid higher US tariffs, Sasmita urged Jakarta to maintain dialogue with Washington, ensure full transparency that the Russian crude is for domestic energy needs, comply with applicable sanctions, and diversify its crude oil suppliers. “The broader lesson is that Indonesia should avoid turning an energy-security decision into a geopolitical dependency,” Sasmita said. “Russia can be part of Indonesia’s energy portfolio, but it should not become the foundation of it. In the current geopolitical environment, diversification itself is an economic asset.”

title: Chinese son’s video of mum’s final 14 days before sudden leukaemia death moves hearts online
description: Son reflects that if a life is measured by its depth rather than its length, his mother’s life was rich and complete.
content: A man in northern China created a poignant record of his mother’s final 14 days, documenting her rapid decline from a vibrant woman to her last moments. Gao, hailing from the Inner Mongolia autonomous region, shared that his mother travelled to his city for medical treatment after developing a fever and a persistent cough. On August 29, he captured her arrival at the railway station. Dressed in her favourite red coat, she appeared energetic and in good spirits, walking with confidence and a spring in her step. A hospital examination revealed inflammation in her lungs, but at that time, she remained independent, still managing daily tasks such as cleaning and doing laundry. However, her condition soon worsened – she lost her appetite, became increasingly frail, and struggled to get out of bed. Realising he might not have much time left with his mother, Gao began recording videos of her each day. On September 6, she developed breathing difficulties and severe pain throughout her body. As relatives gathered at the hospital, she began sharing her final wishes with Gao and her daughters. Her health declined further, leading to her transfer to a Beijing hospital where she was admitted to the intensive care unit. Once moved out of the emergency room, Gao’s mother expressed that she had no regrets about her life. She requested to be cremated after her death and took the time to call Gao’s mother-in-law to thank her family for their unwavering support. Honouring her wishes, the family decided to withdraw further treatment and took her home. Surrounded by her children and husband, she sat upright on her bed, carefully selecting the clothes she wanted to wear after passing. Gao’s mother died on September 11 at the age of 63 due to multiple organ failure caused by acute leukaemia. The videos he recorded became a cherished visual record of her final days. Gao reflected on how rapidly her illness progressed, leaving the family with little time to prepare. He realised they had underestimated the severity of her condition and sought medical help too late, though he expressed gratitude for the hospital’s efforts. His mother had been in good health until she delayed seeking medical attention for a cough that began in February. Leukaemia was only suspected after she entered intensive care and was confirmed posthumously. What touched Gao the most was his mother’s calm acceptance of her fate. “If life is not measured solely by its length, then my mother’s life was rich and complete. I recorded these videos so that, after she is gone, I would still have a way to remember the traces she left behind,” he stated. Gao also cautioned others not to dismiss minor health issues, as delaying treatment could lead to dire consequences. The video resonated with viewers on mainland social media, garnering over one million likes. One online observer commented: “Human life is genuinely fragile. Gao’s mother was a strong and brave woman, and her children displayed immense love and devotion.”

title: Meet Sienna Miller’s daughter, Marlowe Sturridge, who attended the premiere of War
description: Sporting a Chloé Paddington bag on the London red carpet, the 14-year-old has earned the nickname “a young Anna Wintour” from her mother.
content: Sienna Miller’s 14-year-old daughter, Marlowe Sturridge, recently made a rare public appearance, joining her mother on the red carpet for the world premiere of Miller’s forthcoming television series War – a co-production of HBO and Sky – in London on September 16. Stepping out in contrasting styles, Miller wore a black feathered Dilara Findikoglu gown, while Marlowe took a relaxed approach in a graphic yellow baby tee and a black silk midi skirt. She finished the ensemble with Mary Jane flats and Chloé’s iconic Paddington bag in black. So, what do we know about Sienna Miller’s teenage daughter? Read on to find out. She is Sienna Miller’s oldest child Marlowe Sturridge was born to Sienna Miller and her then-partner Tom Sturridge in July 2012. Miller began dating the British actor in 2011, and they got engaged in January 2012. The couple eventually split in 2015 but have remained friends and continued to co-parent Marlowe. Miller is engaged to actor Oli Green, whom she has dated since February 2022. The couple reportedly welcomed a baby girl together in early 2024, before welcoming a son in May this year. She has a strong sense of style If her red carpet look at the premiere of War is anything to go by, Marlowe is en route to becoming Hollywood’s future “It” girl. Miller has previously praised her teenage daughter, calling her a “young Anna Wintour”. “She’s so stylish. And very critical. She’s like a young Anna Wintour in her total disdain for some of the things I wear,” the Alfie actress told The Guardian in 2024. Marlowe apparently also likes to browse through fashionista Alexa Chung’s wardrobe – Chung is currently engaged to Sturridge. “She’s got it all going on. She’s very cool,” Miller told British Vogue in a recent interview. “She says she likes bottom halves from me and top halves from Alexa – and she doesn’t hold back with the criticism.” Her red carpet appearances Marlowe has made several high-profile appearances alongside her mother. In April last year, the teenager joined the actress and Green for an event at the Four Seasons Hotel London at Tower Bridge. In 2024, Marlowe joined Miller and Green at the screening of Horizon: An American Saga at the Cannes Film Festival.

title: Amazon and Shorea Capital deals underscore foreign interest in commercial property
description: Shorea plans to turn The Pemberton in Sheung Wan into high-quality accommodation; Amazon Data Services snaps up two data centres in Fanling.
content: Foreign investors continue to pile into Hong Kong’s commercial real estate, with a unit of online retail giant Amazon and Singapore-headquartered Shorea Capital among the latest to snap up assets, according to agents. Shorea won the tender for The Pemberton, a mixed office and retail property in Sheung Wan, for an undisclosed amount, Colliers said, underscoring Southeast Asian investors’ continuing robust demand for real estate assets in Hong Kong. Colliers was the lead agent and broker for the transaction. The property, with a gross floor area of 5,388 square metres (58,000 square feet), was last acquired by AEW Via HK 1 Limited for about HK$344.34 million (US$43.9 million) in a deal registered in 2010, according to the Land Registry. Colliers said Shorea plans to submit applications for the conversion of the 24-storey commercial building into high-quality living accommodation. The building comprises five levels of commercial space in the basement and on the upper ground floor and first to third floors, with office space from the fourth floor upwards. The office floors feature a glass curtain wall facade and offer flexible floor plates of about 214 to 409 square metres. “Hong Kong is a market that we have followed closely, and this acquisition provides a strong entry point for Shorea Capital,” Shorea CEO Eugene Teo said. “The Pemberton combines a well-connected location and long leasehold tenure with a clear potential for value creation through active repositioning. “With the potential of transforming the property into living accommodation, we can unlock its highest and best use while directly addressing the structural shortage of such accommodation in Hong Kong.” The deal “demonstrates continued investor appetite for well-located assets with strong repositioning potential in core urban districts”, said Andrew Ng, head of restructuring services and executive director for capital markets and investment services at Colliers. International technology companies remain optimistic about Hong Kong’s digital infrastructure market Samuel Lai, CBRE Hong Kong Meanwhile, Grand Ming Group said in a stock exchange filing on Friday that it had agreed to sell two data centres in Fanling to Amazon Data Services, a unit of the US-based e-commerce firm, for a maximum price of about HK$2.44 billion. Amazon Data Services currently occupied one of the properties, the filing said, while the second one was under construction. The sellers, Regal Development Limited and Golden Ford Limited, are both indirect wholly owned subsidiaries of Grand Ming. “International technology companies remain optimistic about Hong Kong’s digital infrastructure market,” said Samuel Lai, executive director and head of industrial and logistics at CBRE Hong Kong. “Although Hong Kong is a mature data centre market, with new supply constrained by limited land and power resources, demand remains resilient. “This underscores strong long-term confidence in Hong Kong’s role as a regional digital hub and international financial centre.” The deals highlight foreign investors’ robust demand for Hong Kong commercial properties. Southeast Asian investors, led by Singapore-based capital, have emerged as the largest non-local buyers of Hong Kong commercial property, Savills said. The property consultancy said that in deals worth more than HK$50 million, local and non-local investors – including those from mainland China – had spent an estimated HK$30.36 billion on Hong Kong commercial property so far this year. Southeast Asian investors contributed HK$3.37 billion – or more than 11 per cent – of the total value, Savills said. Mainland Chinese buyers contributed HK$1.75 billion, or 5.8 per cent, while Hong Kong-based capital accounted for HK$25.25 billion, or 83.2 per cent.

title: Free sports drinks with suspicious pinhole marks leave 14 Hong Kong students ill
description: Police investigating after drinks were handed out during lunch near school athletics meet at sports ground in Wong Tai Sin.
content: At least 14 students have been sent to hospital after drinking free beverages that were found with suspicious pinhole marks near a sports ground in Hong Kong, prompting a police investigation. Students from Maryknoll Secondary School in Kwun Tong reportedly posted messages on social media claiming that free bottles of a sports drink had been handed out during lunch on Wing Ting Road, a short distance from the Hammer Hill Road Sports Ground, where the school was holding an athletics meet on Tuesday. A police spokesman said a parent called the force at about 2pm. As of 10pm, 14 students had been sent to United Christian Hospital, with half of them later discharged while the rest were listed as in a stable condition. The four boys and 10 girls were aged between 11 and 17. Officers visited the site to investigate. Plain-clothes officers were seen searching rubbish bins outside the sports ground and removing plastic bottles carrying the brand name “Scream” for examination. Detectives also entered the venue to conduct inquiries. The South China Morning Post has contacted the distributor of the sports drink for comment. The case has been handed to the Kowloon East district crime squad. A message posted on the social media platform Threads carried photos of the event. It read: “We found pinholes in some of the drinks and suspect that an unknown liquid may have been injected into them. Teachers have since collected all the drinks.” The school said the incident involved food safety concerns after free bottled drinks were distributed outside the venue during its athletics meet by individuals not associated with the school. After some bottles were found to have suspected damage, the school advised students not to consume the beverages and collected the affected drinks, it said. The school added it was fully cooperating with authorities and urged parents to closely monitor their children’s health.

title: No need for Hong Kong to match Singapore’s HK$400,000 birth perk, top official says
description: Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk says 11-measure policy drive is ‘comprehensive’ approach tailored to local needs.
content: Hong Kong does not need to emulate Singapore’s generous childbirth incentives, a senior official has said, defending the city’s latest 11-measure policy drive to encourage births as a “comprehensive” approach. Addressing concerns that Hong Kong’s approach was too incremental compared with Singapore’s multi-tier sustained funding, Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said on Tuesday that each jurisdiction has its own unique set of circumstances. “Some people ask, ‘Why don’t you learn from Singapore by pledging a HK$400,000 [US$50,984] package?’” he told a radio show. “We approach the matter in different ways and I think it is appropriate for us to launch the current 11 measures.” Cheuk also rejected suggestions that Hong Kong’s package was “pretending to be generous at the expense of others.” “What we put forward is a fairly comprehensive package. So if people feel they have short-term cash flow issues, there are measures for that,” he said. “If it is about housing or making things easier at any stage of raising a baby, this is also where we can help.” In 2025, Hong Kong’s fertility rate stood at 0.733 – or 733 live births per 1,000 women – making it one of the lowest in the world. By comparison, Singapore’s rate was 0.87. In his latest annual policy address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced a raft of measures to encourage childbirth. Among them, a one-off HK$20,000 baby bonus was extended for another three years, while the incentive for a second or subsequent child was raised to HK$30,000. The annual tax allowance tied to a second or subsequent child was raised from HK$140,000 to HK$160,000. On the housing front, “white form” applicants – non-public housing residents buying subsidised sale flats – with newborns will only need to pay 5 per cent of the total property price as the down payment. Lee also pledged to enhance nursery capacity to relieve parental pressure. Under Singapore’s new package, which shifts from one-off birth incentives to sustained funding, each newborn will receive almost S$70,000 (US$54,874) – equal to more than HK$430,000 – in direct financial support from birth until the age of 17, starting from April 1, 2027. This includes a S$10,000 baby gift and S$2,000 in “child credits” from ages one to 16. The government also heavily subsidises their early education, healthcare and post-secondary education expenses. Cheuk also defended the focus on second and subsequent children, citing last year’s figures showing 43 per cent of Hong Kong births were second children. He noted that many households wanted multiple children, arguing that existing parents who had already addressed basic needs such as housing were better positioned to expand their families. Cheuk admitted that workplace family-friendly measures, such as longer maternity leave and a flexible family leave system that would be launched for civil servants, could offer more incentives than financial drivers alone. “But if you’re talking about citywide measures, that involves a lot of other stakeholders such as employers and it is a very complex issue,” he said. “We first launched what we can do now, and will do more where we can.” The Hong Kong government moved away from a non-interventionist stance in 2023, introducing a HK$20,000 baby bonus to encourage childbirth. Although the number of newborns rose to 35,723 in 2024, it fell to just over 31,000 the following year. Only 19,255 infants were born in the first eight months of this year, nearly 10 per cent lower than in the same period in 2025. The government would review the effectiveness of the package two years after its implementation.

title: Hong Kong regulators to flesh out new yuan strategy after Beijing meetings
description: HKMA, SFC officials expected to outline new measures to deepen yuan usage and cross-border market links following meetings in Beijing.
content: Beijing and Hong Kong are laying the groundwork for a new phase of offshore yuan development and other goals after the city unveiled its first five-year plan, with banking and securities regulators set to provide more details on Wednesday. The city’s market regulator, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), would outline further details of the blueprint, chairman Kelvin Wong Tin-yau said on Monday. Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man is also expected to elaborate on yuan internationalisation in a keynote speech at the Treasury Markets Summit 2026 on Wednesday. The summit is one of the city’s most important annual banking conferences, attracting hundreds of senior bankers. Yue, together with SFC CEO Julia Leung Fung-yee, joined Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po in Beijing on Monday to meet senior officials, including People’s Bank of China (PBOC) governor Pan Gongsheng and National Financial Regulatory Administration Minister Ding Xiangqun. Hong Kong officials and regulators briefed mainland Chinese officials on the city’s first five-year financial development plan unveiled last week, according to a Hong Kong government statement on Monday. The exchanges between policymakers and regulators were expected to pave the way for additional measures aimed at strengthening Hong Kong’s role as an offshore yuan trading centre, according to analysts. The Hong Kong five-year plan explicitly stated that internationalisation of the yuan and establishing significantly closer links with China’s financial products and markets were key priorities, said Tommy Ong, managing director of financial advisory firm T.O. & Associates Consultancy. Ong said Hong Kong was expected to build more infrastructure to support international investors trading yuan-denominated products, including a proposed fixed-income and currency trading platform jointly developed by the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) and bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX). The SFC’s Leung said in July that the platform had applied for a licence from the commission. The new platform would connect with the Bond Connect schemes, allowing global funds to trade onshore sovereign bonds through streamlined offshore access channels, Ong said. “At a later stage, the platform could be expanded to serve short-term treasury and cash management desks, enhancing bond repo transactions involving non-cash collateral denominated in yuan and Hong Kong dollars,” he said. “This would improve price discovery and execution for both northbound and southbound instruments.” Northbound trading allows global funds to invest in mainland Chinese markets, while southbound trading permits mainland investors to buy assets listed in Hong Kong. ⁠Beijing increased the Bond Connect quota to 800 billion yuan (US$119 billion) from 500 billion yuan in July. It also allowed HKEX in August to launch the first offshore government bond futures contracts. “These measures would improve international demand for onshore yuan bonds while enhancing Hong Kong’s role as the leading offshore pricing centre for yuan products,” Ong said. Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary president of the Institute of Securities Dealers, said Hong Kong regulators had spent months advancing a multi-year effort to expand the offshore yuan ecosystem. The Hong Kong government also pledged in its five-year plan to explore wider use of the yuan in official payments. “All of these measures will strengthen Hong Kong as a leading yuan trading centre,” Chan said.

title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over 2019 Easter bombings, 9 acquitted
description: Suicide bombers targeted three hotels and three churches, killing 279 people and wounding about 500. The trial has gone on for five years.
content: Sri Lanka’s High Court has found 15 of the 24 men accused of being directly involved in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings guilty. The attacks killed 279 people and wounded around 500. The three-judge bench found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act. A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted. The presiding judge on the three-judge bench told a packed court that sentencing would be done later on Tuesday. Suicide bombers struck three luxury hotels and three churches on April 21, 2019, in the deadliest attack against civilians in the island’s history. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead. Investigators blamed the massacre on a home-grown Islamist extremist group. One of the 25 men initially indicted – all of them from Sri Lanka’s Muslim minority – died in custody, leaving 24 defendants to stand trial. Police said extraordinary security measures were in place around the court complex on Tuesday. “Considering the interest in this case, we are making special security arrangements,” police said in a statement. The trial made legal history in Sri Lanka, with prosecutors filing 23,270 charges, the highest number ever brought in a single case. Prosecutors identified Mohamed Naufar as the alleged ringleader who provided support to the eight-member suicide squad that carried out the coordinated bombings. All defendants denied involvement. Local media had said earlier that if convicted, some could face the death penalty, even though Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976 and capital punishment is typically commuted to life imprisonment. The prospect of capital punishment gained prominence in July when two security officials were sentenced to death in a separate case for failing to prevent the attacks despite intelligence warnings. Three of the defendants were also charged by US authorities with terrorism-related offences linked to the bombings in December 2020. Five Americans were among the dead, including a US Commerce Department employee who was in Colombo on official business. Other foreigners killed included citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, India, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey and Britain. The trial unfolded against the backdrop of a separate and highly sensitive investigation into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state may have had links to those responsible for the attacks. Former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is in custody facing accusations that he orchestrated the bombings, allegations he denies. Public Security Minister Ananda Wijepala told parliament in June that investigators believed Sallay was the “mastermind” behind the attacks and had worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out. Investigators allege the network was cultivated to manufacture a security threat that would in turn bolster political support for the Rajapaksa family, which returned to power several months after the attack with Gotabaya Rajapaksa’s election as president. According to court filings, investigators believe the objective was to create chaos and present Rajapaksa, a former defence chief credited by supporters with crushing Tamil separatist rebels in 2009, as the leader best placed to restore security. The Rajapaksa camp, supporting the once powerful family that dominated Sri Lankan politics for nearly two decades, has rejected allegations of state involvement. Successive Rajapaksa administrations have acknowledged using Islamist militants as intelligence assets during a decades-long civil war that ended in 2009. But supporters maintain the militants had double-crossed their handlers and carried out the 2019 attack independently. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Dominant Siobhan Haughey ‘pretty satisfied’ after storming to second Asian Games gold
description: Hong Kong swimmer takes women’s 100m freestyle title with ease in Tokyo, says parents being able to watch makes her happy.
content: Siobhan Haughey was already the best swimmer Hong Kong has ever produced, much more like this and she will easily be the best athlete in the city’s history. The Hongkonger stormed to her second gold inside 24 hours at the Asian Games on Tuesday, sweeping all before her in the women’s 100m freestyle. Haughey touched the wall at Tokyo Aquatics Centre in 52.45 seconds, with China pair Yu Yiting and Cheng Yujie grabbing silver and bronze in 53.21 and 53.47 respectively. “I’m pretty satisfied,” Haughey said. “I think I still need to go back and review my split times, but overall, it was pretty good.” Unlike her previous time in Tokyo five years ago, when Japan hosted the Olympics in the middle of Covid, Haughey’s parents were able to be poolside to watch her race. “Now that they can watch it on site, actually I don’t know how many more opportunities I’ll have to compete in front of them,” Haughey added. “So, having my family here tonight, along with so many Hong Kong people supporting me here, I feel really happy.” Haughey had earlier qualified fastest for the evening final. At 53.60 seconds, she was the only swimmer to go under the 54-second mark in the heats. Compatriot Li Sum-yiu, who finished in 55.58, also qualified for the final in eighth place. Ultimately, her day ended in a tie for seventh alongside Japan’s Shiho Matsumoto, with the pair touching the wall in an identical 55.45. In the women’s 200m backstroke, Cindy Cheung Sum-yuet earned a final spot – in fifth overall – after touching the wall in 2:12.54, and was fifth in the final too. Her time of 2:12.06 was some way back of China’s Peng Xuwei, who gold in 2:05.77, with compatriot Sun Mingxia claiming silver in 2:08.65, while Japan’s Rio Shirai was third in 2:08.70. Meanwhile, Gilaine Ma came seventh in the women’s 400m freestyle final, in a time of 4:15.03. China’s Li Bingjie took gold in 4:02.71, Singapore’s Gan Ching Hwee was second in 4:06.81, with bronze going to Japan’s Ichika Kajimoto, after she came home in 4:07.45.

title: BlackRock gains QDII status in China’s US$149b market as Beijing leans into opening up
description: The qualification allows firms to raise funds in China and deploy them in overseas asset portfolios.
content: US asset manager BlackRock has obtained Qualified Domestic Institutional Investor (QDII) status in China, making it the first wholly foreign-owned public fund manager to obtain the qualification, with more such developments likely as Beijing signals broader financial opening. This qualification allows firms to raise funds in China and deploy part or all of the proceeds for overseas securities investment management through asset portfolios. New York-based Neuberger Berman, another foreign-owned public fund manager, submitted a QDII application in July. The fund-management businesses of JPMorgan, Manulife and Morgan Stanley obtained QDII status during their joint‑venture era and kept the qualification after converting to wholly foreign‑owned public fund firms. For instance, the fund business of JPMorgan became wholly foreign-owned in April 2023. BlackRock would complete relevant preparatory work within six months of the approval and would be able to launch its overseas securities investment management business only after passing an on-site inspection, the China Securities Regulatory Commission said in a statement last week. “The company’s cross-border product roll-out is expected to accelerate further,” said Guosen Securities analysts in a report on Sunday. The country’s QDII market topped 1 trillion yuan (US$149.3 billion) in January, with cross-border investment volume continuing to expand, according to the Asset Management Association of China. BlackRock’s approval comes at a time when Beijing is seeking further financial liberalisation. The People’s Bank of China (PBOC), China’s central bank, held a meeting with foreign-funded financial institutions on Monday to discuss ways to further improve the business environment and carry forward high-level financial sector opening.
