Representatives from foreign financial institutions including Bank of America, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, HSBC and Standard Chartered attended the meeting. “We will continue to advance high-level financial opening-up, refine policy support, steadily expand two-way opening of financial markets, optimise cross-border payment services, and facilitate the international use of the renminbi,” Pan Gongsheng, governor of the PBOC, said during the meeting. According to the PBOC, foreign financial institutions said during the meeting that the bank’s measures this year on financial opening, business climate and yuan internationalisation had made progress. They hoped policies would be further refined and that market communication would continue to improve, the PBOC added. Meanwhile, US-China trade talks in New York on Sunday showed an optimistic tone. The two sides had in-depth and constructive discussions on key shared economic and trade priorities, including advancing bilateral trade and investment ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington later this week, according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.

title: Once key economic weapon, US-China soybean trade may now offer rare common ground
description: As the two nations address disputes ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, some American soybean farmers say they are in a better position than in 2025.
content: As American farmers begin harvesting soybeans across the Midwest this month, some are feeling a sense of relief absent a year ago, when China – which typically buys around half of all US soybean exports – halted imports amid an escalating trade war. This season is unfolding differently. Ahead of President Xi Jinping’s coming meeting with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, China has rapidly scaled up purchases of American soybeans once again. “US farmers genuinely appreciate the business relationship we have developed with Chinese buyers,” said Stan Born, who runs a soybean and corn farm in Illinois and is a former chair of the US Soybean Export Council. Geopolitical tensions had overshadowed a decades-long relationship between US farmers and Chinese buyers, Born said, but he was “glad” the meeting between the two presidents was taking place. While agricultural trade was once a key weapon in US-China economic hostilities, it may now offer a rare point of stability as Washington and Beijing confront far thornier disputes over areas such as artificial intelligence. By early September, China had purchased roughly 15.7 million tonnes of soybeans this year, averaging purchases of at least 1 million tonnes per week recently, according to Hugh Grant-Chapman, a fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). That was a stark contrast to last year, when China recorded no soybean imports from the US after August – the first such halt since the 2018 trade war under the first Trump administration. The pace also puts Beijing well on track to meet its annual commitment of 25 million tonnes of American soybean purchases through 2028. Both sides were “very keen to have a flagship achievement to point to” at the upcoming Trump-Xi summit, Grant-Chapman said. “Agriculture ... is, at least from Washington’s perspective, an economic relationship that does not have the baggage of other hot-button issues like technology”, he said, adding that consensus would be far harder to reach on those disputes, such as Chinese open-weight AI model distribution and US restrictions on Chinese drones and network hardware imports. The United States also exported around US$4.6 billion in non-soybean agricultural products to China in the first seven months of the year, according to CSIS calculations. Although unlikely to reach the US$17 billion annual target set during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May – despite assertions otherwise by US officials – these export figures are set to surpass 2025’s full-year total of US$6.4 billion, which could let officials claim some progress is being made, Grant-Chapman said. Kang Mengjie, a policy analyst at advisory firm Hutong Research, similarly noted that agriculture was one of the clearest avenues for a commercial deliverable. She expected Xi’s visit to reaffirm and implement the commitments made in May, with the possibility of additional purchase announcements. “Soybean, beef, poultry and other purchases support farm income and give Trump a concrete result to present to agricultural states ahead of the midterm elections,” Kang said. Farmers and ranchers formed a core Republican voting base, especially in states critical to the party’s prospects in the November midterms, she noted. Beef has become a particularly sensitive topic after Trump expanded imports at lower tariff rates late last month in response to high domestic prices, angering American farmers. Increasing Chinese purchases would create fresh export demand to help ease those concerns, Kang said. “For Beijing, agricultural purchases remain a relatively low-cost way to stabilise relations with Washington,” she said, noting that targeted buying would be useful diplomatically as Beijing understands the domestic political importance of farmers to Trump. “China needs imported soybeans and selected meat products,” Kang added. Soybean imports accounted for around 85 per cent of China’s total supply in 2023, according to a report last year by S&P Global. Most of these imports are used as an affordable protein source for animal feed. Brazil is China’s primary supplier, with its crop holding a price advantage over American soybeans. “There is a market logic headwind to sticking with US imports,” Grant-Chapman said, predicting that Chinese buyers would taper off American purchases after meeting commitments in favour of cheaper sources elsewhere. However, Kang noted that select US agricultural goods, including soybeans, could regain commercial appeal among private Chinese buyers if Beijing granted exemptions from the 10 per cent tariff currently still in place for all American imports. Following the top-level diplomatic meeting in May, Washington and Beijing established a Board of Trade to negotiate reciprocal tariff reductions covering US$30 billion worth of non-sensitive goods on each side. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told media after US-China trade talks on Sunday that the two sides were launching the operation, which could include Chinese exports of consumer and low-tech goods and American exports of energy, agricultural products and medical devices. “There’s a lot of hope riding on [the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting] because farmers have felt a big squeeze from other parts of the economy,” Grant-Chapman said. Fertiliser and diesel prices have surged following shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, while land and labour costs are also rising in the US. He described the prevailing mood as one of “cautious optimism” – an outlook shared by Illinois farmer Born. While Born welcomed news of the summit, he remained doubtful that increased Chinese purchases of soybeans would persist. “The track record of purchase decisions is being driven by political positioning and not by science, economics, and efficiency,” said Born. “But I believe soy is not as high on the hit list as it once was,” he added. Perhaps commercial reasons, such as some Chinese buyers’ preference for the quality of American soy, “will have more weight in purchase decisions if we are in the ‘shadow’ of other issues like AI,” Born said.

title: John Lee appoints Kelvin Kong head of police’s National Security Department
description: Force veteran Kong takes over from Andrew Kan as city leader praises his ‘steadfast and courageous’ leadership.
content: Senior Hong Kong police officer Kelvin Kong Hok-lai has taken over the force’s National Security Department, succeeding Andrew Kan Kai-yan, who began pre-retirement leave on Tuesday. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu appointed Kong as deputy police commissioner (national security) under Article 16 (2) of the national security law. The appointment took effect immediately after Kong took the oath of office. Lee said Kong, formerly the director of national security, had served with the Hong Kong Police Force for three decades and worked in the department since the promulgation and implementation of the national security law. “He has shown outstanding performance, an exemplary commitment to serve, and exceptional leadership with a high awareness of national security. He is steadfast and courageous, and remains resolute in safeguarding national security,” Lee said. “I recognise his work and have confidence that he will take on more responsibilities in his new position and make greater contributions to safeguarding national security.” The national security law requires police to establish a department for safeguarding national security with law enforcement capacity. The head of the department is appointed by the chief executive, who must seek the written opinion of the Office for Safeguarding National Security before making the appointment. No successor has yet been announced for Kong’s former post as director of national security. Currently, two assistant commissioners – Dick Wong Chung-chun and Kenneth Kwok Ka-chuen – report to the director of national security. It was understood that both Wong and Kwok would hold acting roles until the end of this year, when a decision on the appointment would be made. Kong joined the force as an inspector in 1996. He spent most of his career in the Security Wing, a department responsible for a range of security-related matters, including VIP protection, counterterrorism and security coordination. He also held various posts at police headquarters and in frontline operational command. He was involved in security operations providing protection for visiting state leaders, including then vice-premier Wu Bangguo in 2000 and Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2017, a police source said. He was seconded to the Security Bureau between 2013 and 2016, serving first as assistant secretary of the Emergency Support Unit and later as exercise director of the interdepartmental Counterterrorism Exercise Planning Team. He was promoted to senior superintendent in October 2015. After his tenure at the Security Bureau, Kong commanded various formations in the Security Wing, where he was involved in security operations, VIP protection, intelligence operations and liaison work relating to security issues. He was promoted to chief superintendent and appointed district commander of Tseung Kwan O in May 2018. He returned to the Security Wing the following year as its second officer-in-charge. He was appointed assistant commissioner of police, National Security (2), in July 2020, following the enactment of the national security law. He was promoted to senior assistant commissioner of police and appointed director of national security in April 2023. Kong has received training at various institutions, including Tsinghua University, the China Executive Leadership Academy in Pudong, the Canadian Police College, the Australian Institute of Police Management and the US Asia-Pacific Centre for Security Studies. He holds a bachelor’s degree in management sciences and a master’s degree in public administration.

title: After flood disaster, young Nepalis battle climate dread and demand justice
description: The massive glacial collapse at Nepal-Tibet border killed more than 1,400 people, and young people want environmental action, not empty sympathy.
content:
Alina B.K. should be preparing for her end-of-year university exams, but news of devastating floods along the Nepal–Tibet border has kept pulling her back to a troubling question – what kind of future awaits her?
The 21-year-old forestry student, who coordinates the Pokhara network of Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, said she struggled to concentrate as reports of death and destruction deepened her fears about a changing climate.
“With the floods and deaths happening around us, it is really hard not to feel anxious and emotionally overwhelmed,” she said.
The August 26 disaster, triggered by a glacier collapse, has left more than 1,400 people confirmed dead across Nepal and Tibet, with thousands still missing.
Scientists have not yet established whether the collapse was directly caused by climate change and several factors could have been involved.
But experts say the disaster fits a broader pattern across the Himalayas, where rising temperatures accelerate glacier melt, weaken frozen slopes and increase the risk of cascading hazards such as ice-rock avalanches, landslides and flash floods.
Nepal faces these mounting risks despite contributing little to the emissions driving them: a 2022 World Bank report put its share of global greenhouse gas emissions at about 0.1 per cent. And the number of people in Nepal affected each year by climate-linked river flooding could more than double to 350,000 by 2030, up from 157,000 in 2010.
For young Nepali activists like Alina , that means building a future in a country acutely exposed to a crisis it did little to create.
The latest catastrophe has deepened anxieties that already shape their studies, family lives and future plans, adding urgency to their demands for climate justice.
A 2024 Unicef report, citing a U-Report poll of 2,506 young respondents in Nepal, found that 46 per cent were very or extremely worried about climate change, with another 32 per cent a little worried.
Those concerns sit alongside the trauma experienced by survivors. Activists and development specialists say the emotional toll deserves greater attention, even as communities scramble for basic shelter and survival.
Bimal Regmi, a senior consultant for climate change and disaster risk management at Oxford Policy Management Nepal, said losses were not just economic. Bereavement, psychological distress and the destruction of places of worship and community spaces were often overlooked.
“People’s [lives] can’t be judged in economic value,” he said. “People’s culture, loss of biodiversity, mental and other stresses can’t be counted in US [dollars].”
For Alina, concerns about the future begin right outside her window in the Annapurna Rural Municipality of Kaski district, where Machhapuchhre – the twin-pointed Himalayan peak also known as Fishtail – dominates the skyline.
She long associated the mountain with snow and light. Recently, however, its appearance has changed dramatically. “I used to see the white, shining mountains, but Machhapuchhre is becoming like a black rock,” Alina said.
She described hotter summers in a region where fans and air conditioning once seemed unnecessary, as well as erratic rainfall that had disrupted planting and reduced harvests for her family, who relies mainly on agriculture.
Alina said her forestry studies had heightened her awareness of ecosystem threats, making it harder to switch off. She said she often imagined what Nepal might look like in 50 years and where displaced mountain communities would go.
“Nepal is a small country,” she said. “What will happen if the snow melts? If the glacier outbursts, what will happen to the people from the mountains? Will the land of Terai [Nepal’s southern lowland belt] be enough for them, for all the shifted people?”
Aakriti Dotel, national network coordinator at Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, saw the fear in flood-ravaged regions first-hand while researching disaster-related trauma in Melamchi in 2024.
She found children haunted by a mix of fear for the future and grief for the past. Many told her they were frightened by the sound of the river. Others had lost contact with friends who had moved away, while damaged infrastructure blocked their routes to school and destroyed their play areas.
Khusbu Paudel, a programme coordinator at Ipas Nepal focused on climate change and gender health, said the urgency of saving lives and recovering belongings often sidelined mental healthcare.
“In affected regions, people are thinking more about how to save [their] lives, how to get [their] belongings and everything,” she said. “And the people affected in the disasters … I think the psychosocial thing [is not] a priority for people.”
Although government agencies and other organisations were increasingly adding counselling services into disaster-relief health camps, Paudel said support remained inadequate and social stigma could discourage people from seeking help.
Efforts to bridge this gap followed the August disaster. Unicef said on Thursday that it was deploying psychiatrists, clinical psychologists and psychosocial counsellors alongside government teams to help affected communities.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts
description: Hong Kong does not mention ‘climate change’ in its five-year plan, yet it already has many ingredients of climate leadership.
content: Hong Kong deserves credit for its first five-year plan, accompanied by a detailed policy address. The plan establishes a useful framework beyond the annual policy cycle. Precisely because this is an important first effort, it is worth asking what could make the framework even stronger. One striking omission is that the five-year plan never explicitly mentions climate change. This does not mean Hong Kong is failing to act. On the contrary, the plan and policy address contain many measures dealing with decarbonisation, adaptation, resilience and nature. But because climate change is not highlighted as a unifying focus, these measures appear fragmented. Consider the binding indicators. They include the long-standing reduction in carbon emissions per unit of gross domestic product and increasing the proportion of zero-carbon energy in electricity generation. The plan also addresses cleaner power, electric vehicles, green maritime fuels, sustainable aviation fuel, energy efficiency, hydrogen, waste reduction and carbon trading. The policy address adds detail. It commits Hong Kong to increasing zero-carbon electricity, developing hydrogen, expanding electric vehicle infrastructure, and building sustainable aviation and maritime fuel value chains. It proposes the interesting idea of carbon emissions accounting for green maritime fuels, cross-boundary carbon trading and green hydrogen certification. Climate adaptation is also taken seriously. The policy address refers to global warming and extreme weather, improved infrastructure design standards, studies of risks from extreme rainfall, storm surges, waves and sea-level rise, and continuing drainage and coastal protection projects. It connects adaptation with better weather forecasting, climate insurance, and transition and adaptation finance. Nature is part of the picture too. The five-year plan includes ecological protection, wetlands, marine and terrestrial protected areas, ecological corridors, biodiversity and blue carbon restoration. The policy address reiterated the commitment to the Hong Kong Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2035. Hong Kong has many ingredients of climate leadership. What it surprisingly lacks is a clear narrative that these activities form part of one strategic transformation. This becomes apparent in the chapters on innovation and talent. The plan promotes new energy, energy storage, advanced materials, and artificial intelligence (AI). It proposes an industry-academia-research collaborative system and an international hub for science, technology and talent. Yet it does not identify climate change as a major challenge towards which these formidable capabilities should be directed. The omission is especially noticeable in the Northern Metropolis sections. University towns are at the heart of the development. This is an opportunity to create a living laboratory for green buildings, clean mobility, smart energy, urban cooling, nature-based designs and climate-resilient infrastructure. Yet climate change adaptation is not articulated as a key driver. Similar fragmentation appears in finance. “Finance + Green Development” is included, but the missing narrative is the need to transition from the brown to the green economy globally. Carbon markets require far more than a trading platform. They need credible data, methodologies, verification, legal rules, risk management and investible projects – these are not explained adequately. Building retrofits likewise require aggregation, performance standards, predictable cash flows and financing structures. A climate lens would connect environmental objectives with the financial and market infrastructure needed to deliver them. Public health provides another example. The healthcare chapter covers primary care, chronic disease, ageing, surveillance and system resilience, but not the effects of extreme heat, air pollution or climate-sensitive diseases. Yet extreme heat affects elderly people, outdoor workers, poorly ventilated homes, electricity affordability, urban planning and emergency healthcare. It is a cross-departmental challenge. This brings us to governance. The plan calls for a holistic approach to development and security, prevention-based governance, risk warning, interdepartmental collaboration, infrastructure resilience and clearer accountability. Climate change is an ideal test of this approach. It crosses the boundaries between environment, development, transport, housing, health, labour, welfare, finance, education and security. The contrast with the national 15th five-year plan is instructive. That explicitly calls for climate mitigation and adaptation, control of carbon and other climate warming emissions, assessment of risks to vulnerable sectors and regions, stronger responses to extreme weather and active participation in global climate governance. Climate action is connected with carbon peaking, energy transformation, technological innovation, industrial development and international cooperation. Hong Kong need not rewrite the plan – the next administration can use climate change as a unifying focus for its policy address next year. It could apply a climate-and-nature lens across implementation, budgeting and annual reporting. This could identify shared missions, assign cross-bureau responsibility, connect research with public needs, develop investible project pipelines and measure combined economic, social and environmental outcomes. Such a lens could also strengthen Hong Kong’s international role. The city can connect mainland green technologies with international capital, science, insurance, professional services, standards and markets. Its work on hydrogen certification, sustainable fuels, carbon trading and green Belt and Road Initiative cooperation already points in this direction. Hong Kong does not lack climate action. It lacks a sufficiently visible climate narrative to pull its many efforts together. Bringing the existing pieces together would help the administration deliver the integrated governance promised by its first five-year plan and show Hong Kong intends not merely to respond to climate change, but to help lead the solutions.

title: King of Thailand’s estranged son seeks return for urgent brain surgery
description: Chakriwat Vivacharawongse says he faces paralysis or death from brain tumours as he appeals to receive medical care in Bangkok.
content: The third son of Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn has said he wants to return home for urgent brain surgery. Chakriwat “Than Aong” Vivacharawongse posted a video on social media on Monday saying he had two large brain tumours requiring surgery. The 43-year-old doctor said he wanted to receive treatment in Thailand. “I want to return to Thailand for treatment because Thai doctors are highly capable,” he said in the video. Chakriwat said he did not have enough money to pay for the surgery in Malaysia or the United States, where he had been living, adding that he could be bedridden or even die if he did not receive proper treatment in time. Chakriwat is the third of four sons born to the king and Sujarinee Vivacharawongse. The former actress had five children with the then crown prince while he was married to his first cousin, Princess Soamsawali. Sujarinee married the crown prince in 1994, but following their divorce two years later, she was exiled to the US with her sons. All four of Sujarinee’s sons have long been estranged from the palace and do not use any royal titles. In August 2023, Chakriwat and his older brother, Vacharaesorn, returned to Thailand for the first time in 27 years. “This was a fast week. There were many things we wanted to do and see in Thailand but there wasn’t a lot of time,” Vacharaesorn said at the time before leaving from Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport, according to Reuters. “We received love and warmth from everyone we met.” Their short visit passed without incident, but when their brothers, Juthavachara and Vatchrawee, later tried a similar trip, they were denied entry at the border. Chakriwat has been living with neurofibromatosis type 2 since he was 13. The genetic condition, also known as NF2-related schwannomatosis, can cause tumours to grow along nerves and inside the brain and spinal cord. While most of these tumours are generally benign, their size and location can still cause serious problems by putting pressure on the brain, spinal cord or nerves. By 2015, Chakriwat had already undergone 10 open operations alongside several Gamma Knife and CyberKnife radiation procedures, according to news outlet Thai Enquirer. His worsening health became public earlier this month when he shared that he was unwell. “I’m determined to get better. I’m trying every day,” he wrote. On Friday night, he posted photos and videos of himself in hospital, saying: “My health is truly in terrible condition, and I am at risk of becoming bedridden or facing death. This is the honest opinion of three to four neurologists I know. I am in urgent need of brain surgery.” His brothers later released a message expressing alarm over his condition. They said they did not know where he was or what treatment he was receiving, and offered to help him if he responded. This year has been a difficult one for the king. In June, Princess Bajrakitiyabha, his eldest child and only daughter with Princess Soamsawali, died at age 47 after spending more than three years in a coma. Her death raised questions about succession in the House of Mahidol. The 74-year-old king has seven children. With Chakriwat and his three brothers outside the line of succession, the eligible choices are Chakriwat’s sister, Princess Sirivannavari, and 21-year-old Prince Dipangkorn Rasmijoti, the king’s son with his third former wife, Srirasmi Suwadee.

title: China seeks German help to stave off EU trade sanctions days before Xi-Trump summit
description: Phone call between Wang Yi and Johann Wadephul underlines Beijing’s push to protect European partnerships alongside US relations.
content: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has urged Germany to help steer the European Union away from protectionist measures against China, saying that Beijing and Brussels should not engage in trade wars just days before President Xi Jinping’s high-stakes US visit. “China and the EU are comprehensive strategic partners, and a trade war should not be fought between them,” Wang told his German counterpart Johann Wadephul in a phone call on Monday. According to a statement from China’s foreign ministry, Wang said open dialogue was the viable way to address each other’s concerns and encouraged Brussels to “stay on the right track of open cooperation, dialogue and consultation”. He also called on Berlin to “maintain a rational and pragmatic approach” and play a positive role within the EU in “promoting the upholding of free trade and rejecting protectionism”. EU leaders are scheduled to meet in mid-October to assess the bloc’s trade deficit with China and consider new policy tools to counter what Brussels views as unfair Chinese trade practices. Strain has been building as China’s trade surplus with Europe surged to a record high in the first half of this year, stoking fears within the bloc that the region’s industrial capacity is being weakened. In June, EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic met Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao to launch ministerial-level discussions on trade disparities and export restrictions. The second round of China-EU trade talks will take place in early October. Commenting on China-German ties, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Beijing and Berlin should jointly enhance strategic communication and mutual trust, and deepen practical cooperation as the world faces growing unilateralism and anti-globalisation. The appeal comes as China-Germany ties also face mounting economic pressures and amid Berlin’s concerns about the trade imbalance with China. Germany’s trade deficit with China widened to around €55 billion (US$63 billion) in the first half of 2026, while exports to China fell more than 12 per cent year on year to just under €37 billion, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest. Yet China reclaimed its spot as Germany’s top trading partner in 2025 from the US, with the Trump administration’s protectionist tariffs damaging German exports to America. Beijing is seeking to manage trade disputes on multiple fronts. With Xi heading to Washington this week for his first US state visit in more than a decade, the engagement with Germany indicates Beijing’s approach of sustaining European partnerships. The phone call also touched on the Taiwan issue, with Wang Yi expressing hope that Germany would “take concrete action to maintain peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, creating necessary conditions for high-level exchanges”. The comment appeared to reference a recent visit by Taiwanese officials to Europe, including its top diplomat Lin Chia-lung’s rare visit to Germany in June, which drew protests from Beijing. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Germany, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. In a brief statement, Germany’s foreign office said Wang and Wadephul agreed that “a stable global economy is in China’s, Germany’s and Europe’s interest” and that “trade relations have to be based on fair rules and a real level playing field”. The two foreign ministers also discussed regional crises, including Iran and Ukraine. According to the Chinese statement, Wang reiterated that “China is always committed to achieving peace and promoting talks”, expressing willingness to “continue to strengthen communication and coordination with Europe”. The German statement said Wadephul asked China to use its “considerable influence on Russia to encourage peace negotiations on Ukraine” and urged Beijing to “constructively use its influence on Iran”.

title: Indonesia’s UN Security Council bid tests non-aligned diplomacy
description: Jakarta wants a fifth term on the council, but faces accusations of hypocrisy and being a ‘fence-sitter’, analysts say.
content: Indonesia’s bid for another term on the United Nations’ premier security body stands a good chance of success given Jakarta’s growing global engagement, analysts say, but its balancing act between competing powers could complicate efforts to speak for the Global South. Jakarta’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that it would launch its campaign this week for a fifth term as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for 2029–2030. The ministry said it was seeking the seat to represent the priorities of developing countries at the UN’s most powerful body and that its campaign would focus on peacekeeping, preventive diplomacy, conflict prevention and civilian protection. “Indonesia aims to act as a bridge builder, establishing common ground, maintaining dialogue within the council and seeking practical solutions. We will also bring the voice and priorities of the Global South,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Yvonne Mewengkang told reporters on Thursday. “Indonesia [also] wants a Security Council that delivers results. It might sound overly ambitious, but why not? That is precisely what Indonesia aims to bring: an effective and responsive Security Council,” she added. The council has 15 members: five permanent members with veto powers – China, France, Russia, Britain and the United States – and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. Indonesia has previously served four terms on the council: 1973–1974, 1995–1996, 2007–2008 and 2019–2021. Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in Padang, West Sumatra, said the country’s bid stood a good chance considering its active global engagement under President Prabowo Subianto. “Popularity does matter,” he said, adding that securing the seat could help strengthen Prabowo’s goal of making Indonesia an active contributor to the international community. Since taking office in October 2024, Prabowo has visited nearly 30 countries and attended a number of high-profile summits to position Jakarta as an active mediator and independent middle power. Apart from joining Brics as its first Southeast Asian member, Prabowo has actively advocated for the Global South at international forums such as the G20, emphasising fairness and strategic autonomy for developing countries. Radityo Dharmaputra, a foreign-policy analyst and lecturer at Surabaya’s Airlangga University, said the odds of a fifth term on the council “are in Indonesia’s favour”, adding that Jakarta was one of the most consistent contributors to UN peacekeeping troops. He said Indonesia was expected to push hard for Palestinian statehood, humanitarian access and for any stabilisation mission to remain anchored in a UN mandate rather than in a US-led framework. “On Ukraine, I would expect Indonesia to present itself as a bridge builder calling for a ceasefire and dialogue,” Radityo added. However, Indonesia will still need to mount a strong diplomatic campaign, taking lessons from the Philippines’ defeat by Kyrgyzstan last June. Manila lost to Bishkek for a non-permanent seat by a wide margin of 142 to 49 votes – a loss partly resulting from Manila’s treaty alliance with the US, which worked against it among non-aligned nations. Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate international relations professor at Jenderal Achmad Yani University, said that while Indonesia stood a good chance of getting a seat, the UN might look to consider other countries. He pointed out that former Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi was appointed UN special envoy on water in November 2024. The Security Council bid also reflected the “personal ambition” of Prabowo, who had often sought high-profile arenas to “showcase his leadership”, Yohanes added. A voice for the Global South? Rifki said a seat on the council might not automatically make Indonesia the voice of the Global South due to Jakarta’s mixed positions on several international issues. “Jakarta’s external approaches under Prabowo have been confusing for many Indonesians. Many have criticised his unclear direction in exercising foreign policies,” he said. “How can Indonesia support the freedom of Palestine while sitting side-by-side with Israel on the ‘Board of Peace’, a problematic organisation led by [US President Donald] Trump?” Indonesia strongly supports Palestinian independence and a two-state solution, maintaining that it will only formally recognise Israel as a sovereign state once Palestinian statehood is established. In January, Indonesia joined Trump’s “Board of Peace” to oversee post-war governance, reconstruction and demilitarisation of the Gaza Strip, but Prabowo later suspended his country’s participation. Rifki said that Indonesia’s ability to exert influence on behalf of the Global South would also be constrained by the “privileges of veto power” held by the five permanent members of the council. “To make the council more effective, reform is a must,” Rifki said. Critics have long called for reform of the council as its permanent members, in place since 1945, each wield a veto power that often paralyses its ability to resolve international conflicts and crises. Apart from sharp disagreements among nations on how to expand the council, amending the UN Charter governing its make-up would require a two-thirds majority in the UN General Assembly as well as ratification by two-thirds of member states – including all five permanent members of the council. Radityo said that other countries might see Indonesia as a “fence-sitter” or a “hypocrite” for championing Palestine’s statehood while remaining neutral on Ukraine. Indonesia had consistently framed the Ukraine war “as a tragedy to be ended through dialogue rather than as an act of aggression”, he said. Abstaining from votes would be harder to hide on a 15-member council than in the General Assembly, Radityo said. “So ambiguity becomes much harder to maintain,” he said, adding that Indonesia could contribute credibly as a non-Western, non-aligned voice in humanitarian areas – such as helping with prisoner exchanges, returning deported Ukrainian children and ensuring nuclear safety in war zones like Zaporizhzhia. “By 2029, the council may be dealing with monitoring a ceasefire rather than the war itself,” Radityo said, adding that Indonesia’s peacekeeping experience would serve it well should this outcome come to pass. For Prabowo, winning the council seat would indicate “to the world and to the domestic audience that Indonesia is respected”, he added.

title: China eyes chip-industry foothold with a tiny Han Xin code to challenge US standard
description: After failing to unseat the QR code years ago, Beijing is betting that a “micro” version of its home-grown barcode can gain a foothold in the global semiconductor supply chain.
content: China is attempting to breathe new life into its nearly 20-year-old Han Xin code by promoting a miniaturised version to use on semiconductors, marking the latest chapter in Beijing’s long-running attempt to secure a foothold for its home-grown standards in global industrial supply chains. The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) said on Monday that the “Micro Han Xin” code – a scaled-down iteration of the 2007-era symbology – had entered the formal international standardisation process. The effort aims to mark components that are too small for conventional labelling, specifically computer components. These ultra-compact codes give unique identities to sensors, microprocessors, controllers, memory units and other components, allowing them to be tracked across complex fabrication, packaging and testing workflows. The move reflects a strategic recalibration as China looks to challenge the established foreign technologies being used in high-specification industrial applications. The SAMR acknowledged how the domestic semiconductor sector currently relies heavily on foreign systems such as Data Matrix, which was created in the United States nearly 40 years ago and is already the global standard for marking and tracking semiconductors, silicon wafers and electronic components. The original Han Xin code was intended to supplant the widely used QR code but failed to achieve widespread adoption as the Japanese-developed format became the de facto standard for everything from mobile payments to logistics. Today, the SAMR claims that the Micro Han Xin code matches or exceeds Data Matrix in information density and damage resistance, packing anywhere from dozens to more than 100 numbers or characters into a space barely visible to the naked eye. The regulator said China planned to integrate the technology into a future revision of ISO/IEC 20830, which defines the requirements for the broader Han Xin framework. The formal revision process started in late May and was expected to take about two years. This came after representatives from the Article Numbering Centre of China in April presented the Micro Han Xin code at a meeting about international automatic-identification standards, prompting a working-group resolution to initiate standardisation work, the state-backed Science and Technology Daily reported in June. The centre is the official national body responsible for managing commodity barcodes, article numbering and automatic-identification systems in the country. By pushing this refined technical architecture into global supply chains, China is attempting to bypass its past inability to displace entrenched leading foreign standards in consumer markets. However, widespread adoption could present a separate challenge from winning international-standard status, given the installed base of existing identification systems across the semiconductor supply chain. While the original Han Xin code garnered some recognition for its compact design, a 2021 assessment by global standards body GS1 noted that adoption outside China and global scanner support remained limited. However, it also pointed out that Han Xin’s encoding efficiency could result in smaller symbols than the QR code and Data Matrix. Although the QR code’s dominance in everyday life once allowed it to eclipse the Han Xin version, this time around Beijing is betting on the much narrower battlefield – chip manufacturing – in hopes that technical merit, rather than mass adoption, will decide the winner.

title: Hong Kong school urged to rethink language policy after Cantonese ban uproar
description: Good Hope School faces scrutiny after a viral claim that it banned Cantonese in graduation videos, sparking an outcry and official intervention.
content:
Hong Kong’s education authorities have called on a local secondary school to reassess its event arrangements after a post alleging that the school prohibited Cantonese from being used in graduation videos sparked an online outcry.
In a response to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, the government said the school had activated its crisis management team to follow up on the issue and sent an email to all teachers and students to clarify the matter.
“The Education Bureau has urged the school to review the relevant event arrangements and maintain effective communication with stakeholders,” a government spokeswoman said.
“The bureau will remain in contact with the school to provide appropriate guidance and support.”
The issue came under scrutiny after a recent viral post on social media platform Threads that shared internal presentation records from Good Hope School, a semi-private girls’ school in Ngau Chi Wan.
Referring to “a Band 1A girls school on Clear Water Bay Road”, the user posted images resembling presentation slides titled “Language Standards”, which stated that classes would have to mute the audio and redo sound effects if Cantonese was detected in the voice tracks, with only English and Mandarin permitted.
Amid the escalating controversy, Good Hope School principal Gary Harfitt clarified that Cantonese was not forbidden at the institution.
In an internal email to students and parents that circulated online on Saturday, Harfitt addressed the social media posts and comments on guidelines given to Form Six students regarding their graduation ceremony next year.
“Today a PowerPoint slide that had not been revised was regrettably issued to Secondary Six students. It contained inappropriate language and I deeply regret this,” Harfitt wrote, referring to the incident on Friday.
He said the institution recognised the importance of Cantonese and Mandarin alongside English.
He added that he took full responsibility for the oversight and stressed that the slide’s message did not reflect school policy.
“A high school farewell ceremony only happens once in a lifetime, and we do not want it to end with regrets,” the Threads user wrote, adding that the city had no future if its students lacked the freedom to speak Cantonese.

title: Japan begins clean-up after Typhoon Dujuan kills 4, batters east
description: Landslide warnings remained in force on Tuesday after the 25th typhoon of the season left thousands without power and ruined holiday plans.
content: Residents of a wide swathe of eastern Japan were picking up the pieces on Tuesday after Typhoon Dujuan tore through the area the previous day, causing extensive flooding, landslides, power outages, flight cancellations and at least four deaths. Nearly 2 million people were instructed to evacuate their homes in low-lying coastal areas, or be prepared to move at short notice, after the Japan Meteorological Agency had warned that the typhoon posed an “imminent threat to life”. While the evacuation order has since been lifted, authorities are still warning residents to beware of landslides in areas where heavy rain has destabilised hillsides. The storm hit at the start of a three-day “silver week” national holiday, affecting travel plans, festivals, outdoor musical performances and sporting events, including the 20th Asian Games being held in central Japan. Mitsue Nagasaku, an office worker from Yokohama, had planned to go camping with friends, but cancelled late last week when it became clear how strong the winds would be. “There have been a lot of typhoons already this year but this one was very strong,” she said. “It rattled the windows for hours and the road outside our house was like a river … It was so noisy that I had to shout to be heard on the phone when I called my mother to see if she was OK.” Chiba prefecture, primarily comprising a peninsula jutting out into the Pacific east of Tokyo, was once again among the hardest-hit regions, recording widespread flooding and two deaths. A man in his fifties was killed after being knocked down by a landslide while operating a digger in the town of Sodegaura, the Chiba Nippo newspaper reported. The unnamed man had been attempting to clear an earlier landslide when he was struck by the subsequent slip. Local authorities issued a level five emergency warning, the highest alert, for the tens of thousands of residents living along low-lying areas of the Yoro River as raging floodwaters threatened to burst the banks. Nearly 38cm (15 inches) of rain fell on Kimitsu city in the 24 hours to 6.50pm on Monday, the Japan Meteorological Agency reported – a record high. Some towns received more rain in the space of a single day than was typical for the entire month of September, the agency added. Other deaths occurred in Kanagawa prefecture, south of Tokyo, where a woman’s house collapsed in a landslide and where rescuers were still searching on Tuesday for an elderly couple whose home had similarly collapsed. An estimated 60,000 households in Tokyo and Chiba prefecture were left without power in the storm’s immediate aftermath. All Nippon Airways cancelled 140 scheduled flights, including all services to the outlying Hachijojima island that lay directly in the typhoon’s path, while Japan Airlines grounded 135 flights. Railway operator JR East partially suspended operations on lines connecting the capital to Chiba prefecture. Meanwhile, the extra day that had been planned for this year’s Tokyo Game Show, held at a convention centre in Chiba, was scrapped as a precaution. Organisers of the major video game expo said in a statement they were prioritising the safety of all attendees, exhibitors and staff, “as well as ensuring everyone can return home safely”. The final day of the Rock in Japan music festival in Chiba was also cancelled on Monday, alongside a number of baseball matches. Less badly affected were the Asian Games in Nagoya and Aichi prefecture, although some equestrian events had to be rescheduled due to the weather, with organisers also blaming such concerns for empty seats seen at the opening ceremony. Typhoon Dujuan was the 25th named storm of the Pacific season, with sustained winds of 130km/h (80 mph) and gusts up to 194km/h (121 mph). As of Tuesday afternoon, the storm had veered northeast over the Pacific Ocean. An analysis published in June by Tokyo-based forecaster Weathernews predicted 28 typhoons forming in the northwestern Pacific this year, with around half expected to affect Japan. Japan’s typhoon season typically ends in mid-October, though disruptions could emerge with this year’s “super El Nino” weather phenomenon, which threatens to extend the season into November.

title: Indefinite time in psychiatric ward for Hong Kong man who fatally stabbed 2 in mall
description: Judge accepts Szeto Sing-kwong’s diminished responsibility after he attacked two women at shopping centre during schizophrenic episode in 2023.
content: A Hong Kong man suffering from a severe mental illness has been sentenced to an indefinite period in a psychiatric hospital for stabbing two women to death in a frenzied knife attack at a shopping centre three years ago. The High Court on Tuesday ordered former warehouse worker Szeto Sing-kwong to receive mandatory psychiatric treatment and supervision at the Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre in Tuen Mun, noting that he continued to display limited insight into his mental condition after killing two people for no apparent reason. The presiding judge also praised a chef at the shopping centre who stopped the assailant and prevented him from leaving the scene until police arrived. Szeto, 43, pleaded guilty to two counts of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility after prosecutors accepted that he should not be held liable for murder as he had experienced an acute relapse of paranoid schizophrenia at the time of the offence. The unprovoked attack at Plaza Hollywood, which was captured in CCTV footage that later went viral, stoked safety fears among residents at a time when the city was still dealing with the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic. The court heard Szeto had gone to the shopping centre in Diamond Hill on June 2, 2023, to buy a sushi knife to replace an old one at his public rental flat. He told police he had removed the 30cm (12-inch) knife from its packaging right after the purchase because he felt a “strong discomfort” and wanted to “find someone to vent” his pent-up emotions on. The defendant wandered around the shopping centre wielding the unsheathed knife and crossed paths with Fong Hiu-tung, 26, and Lau Kai-hei, 22, outside a Sasa cosmetics shop at around 5.10pm. Szeto claimed that the two women had scoffed at him and made him feel “unhappy and uncomfortable”, so he assaulted the pair to “teach them a lesson”. He added that he felt “relieved” after the crime. Video footage showed the defendant approaching Fong from behind and repeatedly stabbing her in the chest and abdomen for nearly a minute until she stopped moving. Lau attempted to intervene several times, only to be stabbed herself moments later. Szeto only stopped when a 64-year-old chef, identified only by his nickname Fai, hit the assailant with a stool he had grabbed from a Chinese restaurant where he was having his meal break. The chef continued to engage Szeto until police arrived a few minutes later. Medical findings showed that Fong sustained 27 knife wounds, while Lau sustained eight. They both died of blood loss and respiratory failure. Szeto, who was declared bankrupt in 2019, had relied on cash allowances under the Comprehensive Social Security Assistance scheme since becoming unemployed in 2012. He was first diagnosed with psychosis in May 2020 after being remanded in the Siu Lam Psychiatric Centre on suspicion of punching and threatening his elder brother with a chopper. After serving a two-month sentence in Siu Lam for charges arising from the 2020 incident, Szeto continued to receive inpatient and outpatient psychiatric treatment and was assessed to be mentally stable just days before the killings. Defence counsel David Boyton acknowledged on Tuesday that there was no other suitable sentence for his client and that the crime had a devastating impact on the two victims’ mothers. “It is clear that this defendant is a danger to society … It is quite clear what the sentence is likely to be,” the lawyer said. Madam Justice Esther Toh Lye-ping noted that the mothers of both victims had declined psychological counselling. Fong’s mother explained she feared treatment would strip away her grief, which she viewed as the last remaining connection to her daughter. The judge urged the two mothers to reconsider seeking support and said they should remember the happy memories with their daughters instead of the horrific attack. “It is unfortunate and tragic that both the deceased who were out on an innocent shopping expedition at a shopping mall, should meet such a painful end to their young lives,” she said. “Of course, the court has many available ways to punish the defendant. However, in view of the psychiatric reports, I am also of the same opinion that a hospital order for an unspecified period is the only fit sentence to pronounce.”

title: Who needs a degree? South Korea’s chip boom rewires university-obsessed culture
description: ‘When I think about the pay I’ll be getting at Samsung, I’m not worried at all,’ a student at a semiconductor school says.
content: Inside a brightly lit cleanroom at Chungbuk Semiconductor High School in South Korea, a group of teenagers in head-to-toe protective suits carefully handled silicon wafers, learning the same production processes used in commercial chip plants. About half of the school’s graduates head straight to large companies such as Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix without ever setting foot in a university classroom. The scene illustrates how South Korea’s semiconductor boom is beginning to challenge the country’s deeply entrenched belief that a university degree is the only route to a successful career. Even graduates of prestigious universities struggle to land jobs at large companies that are looking for experienced workers rather than new graduates. The school, which became the country’s first meister high school specialising in semiconductors in 2010, trains about 300 students across three departments covering semiconductor manufacturing, equipment and chemicals. As a government-backed vocational school designed to equip students with the skills and knowledge needed to enter the industry immediately, the three-year institution provides hands-on training in six on-site cleanrooms equipped for the full chipmaking process, from wafer fabrication to packaging. Some of the equipment was donated by SK Hynix. The school in Eumseong, North Chungcheong province, about 130km (80 miles) southeast of Seoul, has maintained a job placement rate of 96.4 per cent to 99.1 per cent in recent years, compared with nationwide averages of 38.2 per cent for vocational programmes at general high schools and 55.2 per cent for vocational high schools overall. Among the 105 students who graduated earlier this year, 23 were hired by Samsung Electronics, Samsung Electro-Mechanics or Samsung Display while three joined SK Hynix, according to school data. Some 14 per cent of South Korean workers find jobs at large companies, according to the Korea Development Institute. Jobs at large companies such as Samsung are highly sought after because employees of such firms earn roughly twice as much as those at smaller companies. Song Jun-hee, an 18-year-old bound for Samsung Display through the company’s scholarship programme, said he chose the school over a conventional academic track after developing a passion for machinery in middle school. His decision initially drew strong objections from his parents, who could not understand why he wanted to forgo university despite his decent grades. “I believed I would be more competitive if I entered the workforce early rather than spending years at university,” Song said, adding with a smile that his family’s scepticism quickly disappeared after he secured a job at Samsung. “They were thrilled,” he said. Yang Seung-hyun said he wants to contribute to what he called “the crown jewel of Korean industry”, much as his father contributed to society as a firefighter, while Park Seung-yun, a Seoul native, said the financial prospects eliminated any doubts he had about skipping university. “When I think about the pay I’ll be getting at Samsung, I’m not worried at all,” said Park, who will join Samsung Electronics after graduation, noting that employees can still earn university degrees through the company’s in-house programme. As generous performance bonuses at Samsung and SK Hynix make headlines amid the current semiconductor boom, interest in the school has also reached unprecedented levels, according to principal Seo Un-seok, who has spent more than two decades in vocational education. Registrations for the school’s coming admissions briefing surged past 400, compared with 80 to 90 in previous years, prompting the school to relocate the event to a larger venue, Seo said. He added that inquiries about enrolment have increased three to fourfold and now include those from overseas, including China and Vietnam. Competition for places rose from roughly 1.5 applicants per opening two years ago to 2.3 last year, and Seo expects it to intensify further this year. Jung Jae-won, a teacher who has overseen student employment at the school for five years, said demand among industry partners seeking recruits now far exceeds the roughly 100 graduates the school produces each year. “We simply don’t have enough students to send,” Jung said. Seo noted that the school has signed recruitment agreements with more than 100 companies, meaning graduates can pick and choose among prospective employers. The school’s graduates also enjoy a striking head start in their careers, with some reaching managerial positions as early as age 27, when university graduates are typically just starting their first jobs. “Our students are already section chiefs while their university-educated friends are walking in as fresh hires,” Jung said. With the school’s model gaining popularity nationwide, the Ministry of Education in June designated six new meister high schools, including two specialising in semiconductors, that are set to open in 2028. Each will receive 5 billion won (US$3.35 million) in government funding over two years. Seo, who assumed the principalship last year, said the school has always been guided by the conviction that South Korea needs to move beyond its long-held belief that a university degree is a must to become “successful”. “Our vision from the start was to shift from a society that values academic backgrounds to one that values competency,” Seo said. “We’ve walked this path for over 15 years. The change didn’t begin with the current boom, but has been building from the ground up.” On their days off, graduates regularly return to the Eumseong campus to buy meals for the students, share advice about working life on the semiconductor production lines and cheer on students heading to job interviews. Seo regards these small rituals as evidence that the school offers its students something beyond a fast track to a well-paid job.

title: Hisense unit gains in Hong Kong debut amid rush of mainland Chinese corporate spin-offs
description: Ligent’s steady market debut comes as Hong Kong moves to streamline spin-off requirements.
content: Television maker Hisense Group Holdings’ optical communications unit made a steady debut in Hong Kong after raising HK$5.6 billion (US$714 million), adding momentum to a fresh wave of mainland Chinese conglomerates spinning off business units to tap overseas capital and support technology expansion. Shares of fibre-optic communications equipment maker Ligent Technologies jumped as much as 19.2 per cent on Tuesday morning, valuing the company at more than HK$35 billion. The stock pared early gains to close 4.6 per cent higher at HK$34.48. Following the initial public offering (IPO), Hisense retains a 40.1 per cent stake in Ligent, which like its parent is based in Qingdao, eastern China’s Shandong province. Ligent’s fellow subsidiaries include Shanghai-listed Hisense Visual Technology and dual-listed Hisense Home Appliances Group. The debut comes as the Hong Kong stock exchange seeks to further relax spin-off rules. It proposed to shorten the post-listing waiting period for spin-offs to one year from three years, according to a consultation paper released on Monday. At least seven mainland Chinese conglomerates have announced plans to spin off businesses and seek listings in Hong Kong. Fosun International, backed by billionaire Guo Guangchang, has filed for a Hong Kong IPO for holiday resort operator Club Med. Xinyi Glass has also applied to list its nearly 40-year-old auto glass business on the main board. China Travel International Investment Hong Kong, GenScript Biotech and Sunny Optical Technology have announced spin-off plans this year. “This benefits new and hi-tech enterprises, which have large funding needs and can list mature businesses in a short time,” said Andrew Lam, managing director of accounting and advisory firm BDO. “They can also use the proceeds raised in Hong Kong for overseas acquisitions.” Spin-offs have emerged as a primary growth driver for Hong Kong IPOs. Zijin Mining Group’s spin-off of Zijin Gold International raised HK$25 billion in September 2025, making it the city’s second-largest IPO that year. At the listing ceremony, Hisense Group CEO and Ligent chairman Yu Zhitao pointed to the rapid growth of the global artificial intelligence economy. “The Hong Kong listing provides a launch pad to expand Ligent’s global [research and development], manufacturing and delivery capabilities to integrate into global AI computing networks,” Yu said. Ligent manufactures optical transceivers, optical chips and network terminals used across data centres, cloud computing and telecommunications networks.

title: Cambodia hosts anti-scam summit as scepticism lingers
description: Phnom Penh is gathering global law enforcement to showcase compound closures, but critics point to the missing billions and elite ties.
content: Cambodia is set to present the outcome of its crackdown on scams to global governments and security agencies gathering in Phnom Penh this week. Yet questions remain over where the missing billions have gone – as well as the role of the country’s elite, who for many years denied the problem existed at all on Cambodian soil. Scam compounds took over declining mega-casinos during the pandemic. As borders closed, gamblers were replaced with scam workers: many tricked, trafficked and forced to commit cyber fraud for Chinese criminal networks. Under intense pressure from Beijing and Washington, Cambodia last year took belated action. Compounds have since been closed across the country and tens of thousands of scam workers have been detained and deported. Some crime bosses have been arrested, while many have fled to Myanmar and beyond. On Wednesday, Cambodia hosts the International Conference on Combating Online Scams, supported by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and Interpol. It is a chance for Prime Minister Hun Manet to tout his government’s enforcement actions against cyber scammers, an effort he has called “cleaning our own house” of an issue that has badly damaged his country’s reputation. Hun Manet will open the conference, where organisers hope to secure an agreement on a framework for greater intelligence sharing and victim protection. The aim is to build transnational capacity to combat scam networks that change bases and business models faster than authorities can act. Ahead of the conference, government-guided tours of emptied compounds in Phnom Penh and nearby Prey Vang province offered the media a glimpse into the scale and sophistication of the now-defunct operations, with banks of mobile phones, SIM cards, stacks of passports and official uniforms used in elaborate cons. Cambodia had deported 21,102 foreign nationals of 38 nationalities as of June 30, according to official figures. Reputational rehab? Critics of Cambodia’s response to the scam crisis say this week’s conference is an effort by Phnom Penh to mark its own homework as it seeks to move on from the damaging scandal. Bringing global parties together was an attempt to secure endorsement for Cambodia’s self-declared “mission accomplished”, said Jacob Sims, a transnational crime expert and visiting fellow at Harvard University Asia Centre. “Everything they [the Cambodian government] have done reflects a country that recognises it has incurred severe reputational damage to the formal government apparatus,” he said, suggesting the Cambodian elite were now happy to “cut their losses” after raking in untold wealth and closing down the industry. A July report by the UNODC estimated losses from scams across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand were between US$88.3 billion and US$114.1 billion for 2025 alone. The World Bank put Cambodia’s gross domestic product at just over US$51 billion last year. “No one is denying the scam compounds are mostly shut down,” Sims said, urging greater accountability over where the money had gone and independent monitoring to make sure cyber-enabled crime did not return in any form. Elite ties and international pressure The main driver behind the crackdown was the alleged involvement of Cambodian elites, whose exposure only grew as international law enforcement closed in. In April, the US Treasury sanctioned Kok An, a Cambodian senator and prominent tycoon accused of controlling scam compounds throughout the country. Known for his close ties to Hun Sen, the current prime minister’s father and a strongman ruler who led the country for over three decades, Kok An was already the subject of an arrest warrant issued by Thailand. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent warned earlier this year that fraudsters and scam centres “that steal billions of dollars from hardworking Americans” were in his government’s crosshairs “no matter where they operate or how well connected they are”. Several other Cambodian tycoons, provincial officials and government figures have also faced scrutiny, alongside prominent Thai politicians and businessmen. Many were named in a letter sent last week by US lawmakers urging Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio to investigate their eligibility for sanctions. Profits from scam centres had equalled as much as 60 per cent of Cambodia’s formal GDP, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said in the letter. Sims said the amount of money involved suggested “state capture”, adding that any cash laundered through Cambodian banks raised urgent questions over the safety of those institutions. Critics of Cambodia’s government have urged representatives meeting in Phnom Penh this week to demand greater accountability from their hosts, alleging that the same authorities now poised to hail a scam crackdown had allowed the industry to thrive in the first place. “Hosting an international conference in Phnom Penh while the system protecting these scam compounds remains entirely intact is an exercise in political theatre,” said Mu Sochua, president of the Khmer Movement for Democracy, a former leading opposition lawmaker to Hun Manet’s party and a Nobel Peace Prize nominee. “Every raid we see today targets the lowest tier of this machinery: the victims forced into cyber-slavery and the low-level operators on the floor. Meanwhile, the high-level bosses, the politically connected tycoons and the complicit government officials who lease the land, grant the security and pocket the proceeds remain entirely untouchable.”

title: ‘Do teachers not have families?’: kindergartens’ Mid-Autumn events draw backlash
description: Events underscore demographic pressure as subsidies tied to number of enrolments fuel recruitment push.
content: At least four Hong Kong kindergartens will hold Mid-Autumn Festival open days and parties on a night traditionally set aside for family reunions, sparking criticism that teachers are being forced to work overtime to bring in pupils amid falling enrolment. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, the Education Bureau said on Monday that preschools should maintain good communication with stakeholders, including teachers and staff, to make appropriate arrangements when planning various activities. For the festival, which falls on Friday this year, many employers in Hong Kong traditionally allow staff to leave work a few hours early so they can attend or prepare for family dinners. But according to promotional posters seen by the SCMP, at least four preschools have planned activities and open days themed around celebrating the festival for parents and children in the community for Friday evening. Two kindergartens operated by the same school sponsoring body in Tsuen Wan will hold a “campus open day” for the community from 6pm to 8pm on Friday, featuring photo booths and complimentary lanterns. “We welcome kids who are under six years old and their parents to join for free,” its promotional leaflet said. A kindergarten in Sham Shui Po is planning a Mid-Autumn Festival party in an open area of a shopping centre nearby from 6pm to 9pm on Friday. The event will offer lantern-making, booth games and face and body painting. Another preschool in Tuen Mun said its night party would include parent-child fitness play, Beyblade battles, game booths and a talent show in an open space near its campus. The nighttime promotional events drew online comments expressing sympathy for teachers and staff at the preschools. A viral post by an internet user named “snowmanseekingtruth” sharing the event fliers, which attracted thousands of comments and hundreds of shares, urged the bureau and Social Welfare Department to intervene and issue clear guidelines. “Do teachers not have families? … This toxic trend of schools holding events on the actual day of a festival must not be allowed to spread any further,” the internet user wrote. A parent, named “dreamland.craft” on Threads, also voiced disapproval of these events. “Forcing teachers to work overtime so late on a holiday is genuinely heartless. The true meaning of Mid-Autumn Festival is to spend time with family. I really do not see the point of attending these events,” the parent said. A former teacher also left a comment saying that on top of being on duty that night, educators had to do a lot of preparatory work, such as decorations. “While you teach children in class that Mid-Autumn Festival is about family reunions, these teachers do not even get to see their own families,” the person said. “Principals and school management, please reflect on this.” The controversy also highlights the sector's struggles with changing population demographics. Under the government’s Kindergarten Education Scheme, participating schools receive operating subsidies based on the number of students they enrol, prompting some preschools to adopt aggressive strategies to attract pupils. Children entering the first year of kindergarten the next academic year were generally born in 2023, when Hong Kong recorded its third-lowest birth rate, with only 33,100 babies born that year. Official figures showed that first-year kindergarten enrolment at subsidised institutions had experienced a steep decline between 2020 and 2025, falling from 40,730 pupils to a low of 24,177 – a drop of about 41 per cent. Many parents are now signing up for kindergartens a year in advance of their child’s first year, while kindergartens are holding a raft of open days and activities during the application peak season.

title: Man shot by ICE in Texas says bullet still inside him
description: Lawyer says Venezuelan DoorDash driver is experiencing left-side paralysis following Austin encounter.
content: A Venezuelan national shot and wounded by a US immigration agent in Texas was jailed with the bullet still inside his body, his lawyer said Monday. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, told reporters he was delivering an order for DoorDash on Sunday when his vehicle was rammed by an ICE agent and he was shot. “I’m in a lot of pain because the shot fractured my clavicle and at the hospital where they took me they couldn’t remove the bullet because it’s close to the spinal cord … I’m not doing very well, I still have the bullet inside,” he told reporters by phone. Hours later, his lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garces Perez was “moved to another hospital as he is now experiencing left side paralysis,” in a post on X. The shooting in Austin, Texas, on Sunday marked the latest instance of violence by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents tasked with enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. Homeland Security Investigations, which is a part of ICE, is leading the investigation into the shooting with the assistance of the FBI, the Department of Homeland Security said. Garces Perez had “illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal,” DHS said on X. But his lawyer maintains he was in the US “legally with a work permit”. Lincoln-Goldfinch told a press conference that he had earlier been transferred from a hospital to a detention centre in Pearsall, some 215km (135 miles) southwest of Austin. “He was shot here in his back, and they didn’t take the bullet out, and they didn’t give him pain medication, and they transferred him to ICE, to a processing centre where he spent the night without a bed,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. About a hundred demonstrators gathered outside the Texas Capitol on Monday night to protest ICE’s actions. “We are less safe when they’re around,” Rosalie Kendall, 40, said. “They’re kidnapping our neighbours. They’re disappearing people who are part of our community.” Garces Perez confirmed that account Monday. “I was on my way with an order from the DoorDash app and then a truck pulls up next to me. It doesn’t turn on its lights or anything, it just tries to hit me,” he said. Then a black pickup cut him off and an agent got out and demanded his documents, Garces Perez said. Garces Perez asked to be allowed to pull over from the middle of the road, but agents refused. “I made a U-turn and that’s when he started chasing me, thinking I was going to run away, but I was looking for a place to leave my car safely,” Garces Perez said. “That’s when he hit me twice and shot me.” He doesn’t know how many shots were fired at him. “There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said. “This is why we’re calling for a stop to ICE traffic stops. ICE officers are over armed, overpaid, undertrained, and violent.” Garces Perez said after he was shot, an ambulance arrived and he couldn’t move. At the hospital, he said he was told tests were being run to prepare for surgery, but the operation to remove the bullet was halted. “A doctor comes in and tells me no, because they were in a hurry to discharge me and have me taken” to the detention centre. “I told the doctor, ‘How are you going to leave the bullet in there if it still hurts?’” Garces Perez said. He maintains he did not receive adequate medical care at the hospital. In the early morning, a nurse gave him a painkiller, he said. Then he was taken to a room with no bed at the detention centre, he said. A makeshift shrine with flowers, candles and a sign reading “Justice 4 Wilber” was placed near the site of the shooting. On Monday, a work crew painted over expletive-laced graffiti nearby, which expressed local outrage about ICE and the ongoing immigration crackdown. Nearly 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the United States in August, according to DHS figures. Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was shot by ICE in March 2025, in what the Texas Tribune said was the first known killing by immigration agents of an American in Trump’s second term. More recently, a Mexican man, Lorenzo Salgado, died in July after he was shot by an ICE officer in Houston, Texas. Two Americans – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were shot and killed by federal immigration agents in separate incidents in Minnesota during a crackdown on undocumented migrants in the northern state earlier this year.

title: Alibaba teases 10-trillion-parameter model, debuts ‘China’s most powerful’ AI chip
description: The tech giant also aims to scale its Alibaba Cloud global data-centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032.
content: Alibaba Group Holding has introduced what it called China’s most powerful artificial intelligence chip and teased plans to train an AI model with up to 10 trillion parameters, as top executives reaffirmed the tech giant’s ambition to pursue artificial superintelligence (ASI). Speaking at the company’s annual Apsara Conference in Hangzhou on Tuesday, group chairman Joe Tsai highlighted Alibaba’s commitment to building end-to-end capabilities. “Alibaba is firmly investing in building full-stack AI ... to let AI move from a technological breakthrough to value creation,” Tsai said during his opening remarks at the flagship event, which runs through Thursday. CEO Eddie Wu Yongming outlined the company’s road map during a keynote address, identifying “AI models, AI chips and the AI cloud” as the three cornerstones of the machine intelligence era. The company aims to scale its Alibaba Cloud global data-centre capacity to more than 20 gigawatts by 2032. “As AI unlocks greater capabilities and penetrates into every domain, a profound shift is under way: machines are becoming the primary force behind thinking, turning intelligence into a commodity supplied at scale,” Wu said. To advance towards ASI – AI that matches or beats human intelligence – Alibaba’s Qwen development team planned to train its Qwen 5 AI model with 5 trillion to 10 trillion parameters, designed to execute complex tasks over extended periods. Alibaba’s current flagship model, Qwen 3.8-Max – the second-highest-scoring Chinese system on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index – features 2.4 trillion parameters, while Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, China’s largest open-weight model, boasts 2.8 trillion parameters. Liu Dayiheng, head of the Qwen large language model (LLM) project at Alibaba Token Hub, presented the road map outlining plans for the Qwen 4, Qwen 4.5, and Qwen 5 series. The presentation marked Liu’s most prominent public appearance since taking charge of the project. He joined Alibaba in 2021 and has served as a core researcher for the Qwen line. Liu highlighted progress in recursive self-improvement using empirical feedback, as well as upgrades across Qwen’s speech, vision and multimodal model families. Alongside its frontier model push, Alibaba launched Qwen Intelligence, a full-stack agent platform designed to give smartphone makers access to Qwen-powered tools for developing AI phones capable of executing tasks across apps. The company confirmed earlier it had been collaborating with Apple on AI features for iPhones sold in China. On the hardware front, Alibaba debuted the Zhenwu V900 processor, billing it as “the most powerful AI chip in China today”. The new chip delivered three times the performance of its predecessor, the Zhenwu M890, according to the company. A computing cluster built around the V900 can link up to 500,000 chips to handle both training and inference for frontier models, according to the company. Wu said Alibaba expected a “significant” increase in annual AI chip shipments, though he did not provide a specific target. Alibaba’s semiconductor subsidiary T-Head laid out a road map extending to 2028. Gao Hui, vice-president of T-Head, said the Zhenwu V900 would feature 216 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory and inter-chip bandwidth of 1.2 terabytes per second. Mass production and commercial availability were scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.
