T-Head also previewed the next-generation Zhenwu J900, scheduled for release in the third quarter of 2028, alongside plans for next-generation proprietary central processing units (CPUs) tailored for agentic AI tasks – the Yitian 720 and Yitian 730, both due in 2027. The Yitian 730 would be T-Head’s first CPU built on an in-house microarchitecture. Alibaba faces stiff competition from local rivals, including Huawei Technologies, which last week unveiled its new Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster powered by its Ascend 960 chips. Huawei expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year, according to rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun. Despite US export controls designed to restrict China’s access to advanced chips, China’s most advanced AI models were still being trained on Nvidia processors, the South China Morning Post reported last month, citing sources at major Chinese AI developers. The firm said on Tuesday it was also accelerating the expansion of its power-intensive infrastructure to support rising computing demands. “Alibaba will join forces with all our partners to commit fully to AI infrastructure development, forging an AI cloud designed for the machine-intelligence era,” Wu said. Alibaba’s Hong Kong-listed shares rose 3 per cent to HK$166 as of midday. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: China breaks ground on the world’s first supercritical CO2 and molten salt energy plant
description: Ruitan demonstration project in Shandong aims to reduce energy waste and stabilise grid electricity supply.
content: China has broken ground on the world’s first utility-scale combined supercritical carbon dioxide power generation and molten salt energy storage project, which could help reduce energy waste and improve grid stability. Construction began on the Ruitan demonstration project at China Huaneng’s Bajiao power station in Yantai last week. The project in Shandong province, eastern China, is expected to go into operation next year. During periods when energy demand is low, surplus electricity generated by the plant’s existing coal power units will be used to heat up molten salt, according to a report by state news agency Xinhua on September 16. During hours of peak energy demand, the stored heat will power a supercritical unit that uses carbon dioxide rather than steam to produce electricity. The first phase of the project will feature a 50-megawatt supercritical unit and a 100MW, or 400 megawatt-hour, molten salt energy storage system. Traditional power plants burn fuel such as coal to heat water into steam, which then drives a turbine to produce electricity. In a supercritical system, carbon dioxide is held at a critical temperature and pressure, at which point it behaves like both a gas and a liquid. This dense fluid directly powers a turbine and can recirculate in a closed-loop system. These plants are smaller than traditional units, do not require water, have higher power generation efficiency and produce fewer carbon emissions. Their turbines can also be rapidly adjusted between zero and maximum load, with an adjustment rate four times greater than traditional coal-fired power units, according to Xinhua. Heat used to power supercritical systems can come from different sources, such as solar energy, geothermal energy, and even waste heat produced by industrial plants. The world’s first commercial supercritical carbon dioxide power generation – Chaotan One in China’s southwestern Guizhou province – began commercial operation at the end of last year and uses waste heat from a steel production plant. Unlike battery energy storage, which stores electricity as chemical energy, molten salt energy storage stores excess energy as heat or thermal energy within liquid salts in large tanks. This can allow it to be converted back into electricity using power generation units or used directly for other purposes. While battery storage is more versatile and better suited to mobile applications, molten salt storage can offer cost advantages and is more suited to large-scale projects, according to the Spain-based engineering company RPow. The China National Nuclear Corporation, which developed the Chaotan One unit, has initiated a project that aims to integrate molten salt energy storage and supercritical carbon dioxide power generation by 2028, according to state media reports. Elsewhere in the world, projects have also been initiated to develop combined units, including the European Union’s SOLARSCO2OL project, which aims to develop a supercritical power unit driven by molten salt within a concentrated solar plant. Supercritical plants are of interest for future nuclear technology, including mobile nuclear units for spacecraft, for their ability to provide a closed-loop and steam-free alternative to traditional turbine units. A molten salt storage system has been implemented at the 50MW Dangxiong concentrated solar power plant under construction in the Tibet autonomous region, which is also expected to be completed next year. The storage system will allow the highest-altitude concentrated solar plant to convert excess energy during the daytime into heat for use during peak electricity demand.

title: Singaporean fined US$3,920 for dumping urine, faeces outside neighbour’s flat
description: Martin Chua, who pleaded guilty to two counts of insulting behaviour, suspected that the victim had punctured his tyres.
content: Believing that a lorry driver in the same neighbourhood had punctured his tyres, a private-hire driver twice left urine and faeces outside his neighbour’s flat in Singapore. Martin Chua Kim Soon, a 67-year-old Singaporean, was fined S$5,000 (US$3,920) by a court on Tuesday. He paid the fine in full after pleading guilty to two counts of insulting behaviour under the Protection from Harassment Act. The court heard that Chua was a private-hire driver with Tada at the time of the offences and lived in Bukit Batok Central. He suspected that the victim, a 73-year-old lorry driver, had punctured his tyres. The victim lived in the block across from Chua. At around 2am on April 28, Chua went to the victim’s flat and threw a mixture of urine and faeces outside. He returned to the flat again at around 3.15am on May 4 and repeated his actions. The victim was alarmed when he discovered the substances and called 999 both times, saying someone had poured “smelly stuff” outside his flat. Chua, who was arrested on May 4, has no prior convictions. He did not say anything in his oral mitigation. For insulting behaviour under the Protection from Harassment Act, he could have been jailed for up to six months, fined up to S$5,000, or both. This story was first published by CNA

title: Search for stray dogs expanded as new CCTV cameras installed in Yuen Long
description: Hong Kong authorities ramp up public safety efforts and monitor area beyond road where cyclist was suspected to have been mauled to death.
content: Hong Kong authorities have expanded their search radius to capture stray dogs and installed new surveillance cameras in the area where a suspected fatal canine attack took place, in a bid to “completely remove” safety risks in the neighbourhood. The heightened measures came three days after a 27-year-old woman was found dead on a cycling path in Yuen Long after being chased by three dogs. She suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with some of the wounds believed to have been fatal. The attack occurred in a rural area along Pok Wai South Road, which has a river on one side and warehouses and fish ponds on the other. Dr Jackie Yip Yin, assistant director for inspection and quarantine at the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD), told a radio show on Tuesday that there had been difficulties in tracking down unattended dogs in a “relatively large area”. She said officers from the department and police were expanding the search radius to capture stray dogs in the wake of the suspected canine attack on Saturday evening. “Our current review focus is to look beyond just the main road itself and check the surrounding vicinity as well. Since the dogs might roam around those areas, we want to ensure that the risks in the neighbourhood are completely removed,” she said. “Our goal is to locate as many unattended dogs in the area as possible, and this operation will remain ongoing for some time.” A source said it was still too early to determine whether the captured dogs were involved in the attack, adding that the animals did not appear to be unusually aggressive, making it difficult to draw any conclusions at this stage. The AFCD earlier said it had conducted seven search-and-capture operations from June to August following four canine nuisance complaints in that area, but had not found any stray dogs. Police also said the force had installed four sets of temporary security cameras in the area to track stray dogs and “improve the efficiency of capture operations”. The move came a day after Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said authorities should consider more factors before installing additional security cameras in the low-crime area. “If stray dogs or other animals posing potential danger to the public are spotted, we will immediately notify the AFCD to arrange timely control operations to safeguard public safety,” police said on Tuesday. The force previously said they suspected the woman had been mauled to death, but further investigation was needed to confirm whether the dogs had indeed attacked her, as wild boars were also present in the vicinity. A joint search by the AFCD and police led to the capture of five stray adult mongrels in the area, including two on Tuesday. Authorities said earlier that they would conduct DNA tests and bite mark analyses to determine whether the animals caught were involved in the attack. Yip said the department received more than 1,000 stray dog-related complaints annually in recent years, including concerns about their gathering in packs and scavenging through rubbish for food. But the number of complaints had decreased by 90 per cent over the past 20 years, she noted. “No matter the circumstances, even a single tragedy is one too many,” Yip said. “In the short term, when dealing with stray dog black spots, such as the current area, we will conduct risk-based capture operations.” Captured canines would be sent to the AFCD’s animal management centre for inspection, she said. Those with good temperaments would be sent to partner organisations for public adoption, while those deemed to pose public safety threats could be euthanised. “Looking beyond that, we must also consider whether enforcement efforts in certain places need to be stepped up – specifically regarding legal action against irresponsible dog keepers, requiring proper control and enhancing public education,” she said. Under Hong Kong law, injuring animals, causing them unnecessary suffering or neglecting their care are all considered animal cruelty, which is punishable by a HK$200,000 (US$25,492) fine and up to three years’ imprisonment upon conviction. Separately, animal abandonment is an offence under the Rabies Ordinance and carries a maximum penalty of a HK$10,000 fine and six months’ imprisonment. Police said they had received 50 reports of animal cruelty in the first seven months of this year and arrested 37 people. For the whole of 2025, the force recorded 76 such cases and made 47 arrests. Appearing on the same radio show, agriculture and fisheries sector lawmaker Chan Pok-chi noted that it was still common among dog owners in rural Hong Kong to allow their pets to roam freely, with some choosing not to microchip the animals to avoid responsibility if any mishaps occurred. “The root of the problem must lie in dog owners,” he said, noting that it was a statutory requirement for owners not to abandon their dogs and to keep them from roaming unattended. “Some exploit [enforcement] loopholes by saying the dogs came [to them] on their own, or that they regularly feed the dogs while refusing to take up the responsibility of being dog owners. This is extremely undesirable.” Chan said that authorities would need to take more pre-emptive steps to manage a potential rise in dogs being abandoned in the area during land resumption efforts for the Northern Metropolis megaproject. Without going into specifics, the lawmaker said a “multipronged” solution was needed to engage different stakeholders, including dog owners and community organisations. The latest attack followed another fatal incident in late August, when a 33-year-old dog handler died after being mauled by a dog at her training facility in Ta Kwu Ling. Days before that attack, a large unattended dog killed two smaller canines in Yuen Long town centre, leading to the arrest of its owner. Additional reporting by Danny Mok

title: China signals greater market access, offshore yuan growth in meeting with banking giants
description: PBOC governor Pan Gongsheng vows to promote ‘high-level financial opening-up’ in meeting with foreign banks and investment firms.
content: China’s central bank has pledged to further open its financial sector during a meeting to solicit feedback from foreign financial institutions, amid broader efforts to shore up foreign corporate confidence and accelerate yuan internationalisation. Speaking to representatives from 15 foreign banks and investment firms on Monday, People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng vowed to promote “high-level financial opening-up”. “[We will] steadily expand two-way financial market access, optimise cross-border payment services, and further facilitate the international use of the renminbi,” Pan said, according to a readout by the central bank. The foreign financial institutions expressed hopes that Chinese regulators would continue to optimise relevant policies and strengthen communication with the markets, the PBOC said. Representatives from the Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, HSBC, Standard Chartered, Deutsche Bank, DBS Bank, First Abu Dhabi Bank, Bank Mandiri, BNP Paribas, Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, UBS Securities, Manulife, Brookfield Asset Management, and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board were present. They also acknowledged China’s progress in deepening financial reform, improving the business environment and broadening global use of the yuan, according to the PBOC statement. Pan also vowed to “implement a moderately loose monetary policy and create a favourable monetary and financial environment for stable economic growth”. The meeting follows Beijing’s recent push to improve its central banking system and expand international use of the yuan. The PBOC recently unveiled a rare five-year plan for the period covering 2026-2030, outlining its ambitions to build what Beijing called a “financial powerhouse”. The term first emerged in 2023 during the twice-a-decade central financial work conference, and is defined by President Xi Jinping through six core pillars, including a strong central bank and a strong currency widely used internationally. Earlier this month, the PBOC pledged in a press conference to expand bilateral currency swap agreements and local-currency settlement while improving the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System – a Chinese alternative to Western-dominated settlement networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, or Swift. The central bank said it would also expand cross-border use cases for the digital yuan and QR-code payments, and planned to optimise market access schemes – including Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Swap Connect – to further open up China’s onshore financial markets. Authorities also pledged to reinforce Hong Kong’s role as the premier offshore yuan hub as well as Shanghai’s development as a global hub for yuan asset allocation and risk management. In a separate meeting on Monday, Pan met with top Hong Kong finance officials, including Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po and Eddie Yue Wai-man, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority. The two sides discussed enhancing Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre, expanding cross-border market connectivity, and strengthening the city’s offshore yuan market, according to a PBOC statement.

title: A shift by China towards service-based economy could help trade imbalance: EU group
description: The nation has seen little progress towards addressing ‘involution’, with output still growing beyond absorption rate, says an EU trade group.
content: As Beijing and Brussels prepare for October talks on trade imbalances, an EU trade association has called for more concrete action, such as China shifting towards a more service-based economy, to address the country’s domestic supply-demand imbalances that have contributed to trade tensions. The European Union Chamber of Commerce in China (EUCCC), which has more than 1,600 member companies, said persistent supply-demand imbalances had fuelled neijuan or “involution” – a form of excessive competition marked by sluggish demand, excess supply and eroding margins. While China’s latest five-year plan has called for greater efforts to address these structural problems, the chamber said it hoped those commitments would translate into meaningful action. “The Chamber hopes [China’s latest five-year plan] ... can alleviate third market concerns over China’s increasing exports and the subsequent trade imbalances that have developed,” it said in its annual position paper released on Tuesday. A shift towards a more service-based economy would be beneficial both in terms of curbing the flow of excessive support into manufacturing and responding to the growing needs of China’s ageing population, the paper argued. While still at a very low level relative to other economies, the service sector now accounted for more than half of China’s gross domestic product, with its contribution steadily growing, the paper said. Developing the sector was also in line with the country’s five-year plan through 2030. The chamber also recommended restructuring talent-development policies to steer more students into service-related fields, while encouraging greater private sector participation and removing barriers to foreign participation to support the sector’s growth. “We don’t really see any progress in terms of resolving the fundamental issue of involution,” EUCCC president Jens Eskelund told the media ahead of the paper’s release, pointing to August data showing China’s industrial output growing at a pace far beyond what the domestic market could absorb. “The imbalances are growing considerably,” he said, adding that he didn’t see any signs of China’s exports slowing down. China’s swelling exports and widening trade surplus have fuelled mounting unease across Western economies, prompting the EU and others to impose trade curbs and demand that Beijing redress the imbalance. The EU now has the largest trade deficit with China of any economy, with China’s trade surplus with the bloc growing by about €1 billion (US$1.15 billion) a day, according to the chamber. The bloc has set an October deadline for Beijing to deliver “tangible” progress in rebalancing trade or risk facing further trade restrictions. “We are looking into a reality where trade is becoming much more unstable unless we are able to identify value creation for both sides,” Eskelund said. He expected China to “push hard to maintain unfettered access” to overseas markets, while warning of the risk of new tariffs if the two sides failed to find a solution to address EU economic concerns. The trade tensions come as European companies continue to face a challenging business environment in China, with overall business confidence remaining low despite a modest uptick in sentiment this year. The chamber’s annual Business Confidence Survey, released in May, showed the share of respondents optimistic about profitability over the next two years rose to 17 per cent, while the share expecting growth increased to 35 per cent. At the same time, European companies are increasingly integrating into China’s cost-effective and comprehensive supply chains to remain competitive. Fifty-six per cent of respondents said they were increasing onshoring in China, while just 7 per cent said they were only increasing offshoring, the survey showed. “If you are to be able to compete on price and quality, very often the only way you can do so is by becoming a part of the Chinese supply chain yourself,” Eskelund said. The position paper called on both sides to establish a framework defining areas essential for economic security while providing greater openness, reliability and predictability for businesses. For China in the longer term, the paper said this could include clearer export-control licensing processes, more explicit rules governing data flows and easier cross-border payments and trade.

title: Chinese doctor quits 20-year medical career to open steamed bun shop for mental health relief
description: Her story mirrors a growing trend of doctors trading prestigious, high-stress medical careers for simpler lines of work.
content: A woman in China, who dedicated over two decades to her career as a doctor, made a surprising choice three years ago to leave her profession and open a steamed stuffed bun store. As time passed, her store not only survived but flourished in the competitive food industry, prompting her to launch a second outlet in July. “When I was a doctor, the thought of quitting often crossed my mind. Now, running a bun shop keeps me busy and tired, but I am so happy that I can’t stop,” said Dong Min, 48, in an interview with the Changjiang Daily. In 2023, Dong garnered significant attention after starting her steamed stuffed bun shop in Wuhan, Hubei province, after a 20-year medical career. She graduated from Wuhan University School of Medicine in 1999 and began her career as a gynaecologist in Shenzhen. Years later, she returned to Wuhan to assist her mother in managing a private clinic. Upon her mother’s retirement, they closed the clinic and returned to their hometown of Tianmen, also in Hubei, where Dong took a position as a doctor and the legal representative of a small community hospital. “As a doctor, I faced considerable mental stress. In addition to treating patients, I had to devote significant energy to managing non-medical affairs, such as dealing with frequent inspections from various government agencies,” Dong explained. “It is well-known that the relationship between hospitals and patients is often tense in China. In cases of medical disputes, I bore the full responsibility since I was the legal representative of the hospital,” she added. In stark contrast to her prior role, Dong expressed that she currently experiences no psychological pressure, despite working more than 10 hours daily. Her interest in the steamed stuffed bun business sparked in 2023, inspired by a friend whose family owned a similar store. Initially, Dong invested in a bun shop, but when the chef abruptly resigned, she took it upon herself to learn the art of bun-making. She quickly mastered the skills, finding joy in the process. Ultimately, Dong chose to leave her medical career to fully dedicate herself to the operation of the bun store. Initially, her family opposed her decision, as being a doctor is traditionally regarded as a “decent and respected” profession. In response, Dong stated: “I am nearly 50 years old and have gone through many experiences. I don’t care what others think of me. I just want to live a life I love and live for myself.” Gradually, her mother and brother began to support her, occasionally lending a hand at the store. “There is no definitive answer in life. It is never too late to make a change,” Dong remarked. “I hope to run my bun store until I can no longer move.” Dong represents a growing trend of medical professionals leaving their careers to pursue what some may consider less prestigious occupations. In 2024, a doctor with 13 years of experience in a clinical laboratory at a major hospital in Yiwu, Zhejiang province, also quit to start a street snack stall. He noted that his income from the stall significantly exceeded his previous earnings of less than 10,000 yuan (US$1,500) per month. “Doctors are not merely burdened by physical exhaustion; they also suffer from mental burnout. This is a structural issue affecting the entire industry, not just individuals,” commented the Xing Lin Yuan Community, a social media account catering to doctors in China. “They encounter endless non-medical tasks and the risks associated with patient complaints, yet their income does not reflect the extensive education and effort they invest,” the editorial concluded.

title: 7 of the best attractions at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, from Star Wars to Banksy
description: Seeing everything at George Lucas and Mellody Hobson’s huge new Los Angeles museum in one day is a tough ask, so here are some highlights.
content: George Lucas and Mellody Hobson want their massive spaceship of a museum to be an experience. Across 300,000 sq ft (27,000 sq metres) and 11 acres (4.5 hectares) of park space, there is a lot to take in. Staring up at the 90-foot (27.4 metre) oculus four storeys above the entrance plaza makes one feel like a speck in the galaxy. Instead of trying to conquer everything at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art on the first visit – there are more than 1,300 works – maybe focus on some of the highlights below. You are guaranteed a good time if you aim to simply walk around the striking building, designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong and his firm MAD, and view a mishmash of masterpieces, children’s illustrations, Star Wars-heavy movie memorabilia and comic strips. Whoosh up in the glass-tube lifts to the massive fourth floor to begin. It is best to explore the bulk of the galleries when your tank is full. Then head up a floor to see the murals. Take a break at the rooftop Skywalker Grill before heading to the library and grounds. Skip the first floor’s “History of Narrative Art”. The exhibition is mostly screens, projections and reproductions, with a handful of great works from the 16th and 17th centuries, and feels superficial at times. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens today (September 22). Prepare to get your steps in and feel a little turned around. Admission is US$25 for adults, free for children. Here are the highlights. 1. Get your Star Wars on Tracey Bates, the museum’s chief executive, says Star Wars comprises only 7 per cent of the museum’s inaugural exhibitions, but there is still plenty for fans – even casual ones – to sink their teeth into. In the Slavko Vorkapich Theatre on the first floor you can watch parts of an unreleased animated comedy series called Star Wars Detours, which was created by Lucas as a parody of the franchise in the early 2010s but never aired. In the “Star Wars in Motion” exhibition on the fourth floor, you can stand before Luke’s landspeeder from the 1977 original film. The unassuming lozenge-shaped vehicle stands ready to conjure reverence in anyone who holds childhood memories of that film dear. For sheer spectacle, behold the first physical build of General Grievous’ Wheel Bike, an invention previously only realised in CGI but built specifically for the museum at Lucas’ request. 2. Gaze at a remarkable self-portrait of Frida Kahlo After the Lucas Museum acquired a 1940 work by Frida Kahlo titled Self Portrait Dedicated to Dr. Eloesser, then-museum director Sandra Jackson-Dumont called it the “Mona Lisa of Mexico”. It is easy to see why Jackson-Dumont was excited. Kahlo painted dozens of self-portraits, many relating to the excruciating physical pain she continued to suffer as a result of a childhood accident. This one is different. Besides a necklace of thorns, which draws small drops of blood, Kahlo appears to be more focused on the relief of healing. The painting is dedicated to the Bay Area doctor that Kahlo was seeing to treat her ongoing pain, with a small banner at the base of the picture painted with the words (in Spanish, but translated here): “To Dr Leo Eloesser, my doctor and my best friend. With all my love. Frida Kahlo.” The silver hand-shaped earrings Kahlo wears in the portrait were a gift from Pablo Picasso. 3. See rare and exciting comics Lucas is an unabashed comic fan, and his love shows in his extensive collection, highlighted in the large comics and graphic stories galleries. The crowning glory of the collection is arguably the first Flash Gordon comic strip. There is also an original splash page from Black Panther as well as original Peanuts strips from the 1950s and 60s. But fans of vintage comics of all kinds will be happily satiated with panels from Alley-Oop, Garfield, Tarzan and Prince Valiant. Here, as in all the other galleries, looking closely is key to finding hidden treasures. There is a stacked manga gallery for fans of that genre too. 4. Banksy was here After getting married, Lucas gifted Hobson a Banksy, concrete wall and all, to sit across from a prehistoric turtle he got her while they were dating. They had to reinforce the floor of their Chicago flat to support the pair’s weight. Lucas also invited Banksy to the museum to remake some well-known works, including Girl with a Balloon, Bates says. Banksy’s stencil works are with the murals on the fifth floor. Black paint spots stain the wood floor below one piece known as Crayon House. “George and Banksy had a real meeting of the minds,” Bates says. 5. Reserve now for November at Skywalker Grill View this post on Instagram Getting a coveted table at the luxe restaurant – which is small relative to the size of the museum – requires a reservation. As of writing, the next reservation for two is not available until late November. Still, it is worth putting this treat on your calendar if you are planning a trip to the Lucas. The room is lovely, with mid-century modern touches including curved cherry wood walls, illuminated white onyx Corian surfaces and low lighting. It also has a full bar and an outdoor patio with sail blinds and stunning views of the Los Angeles skyline. There is no marquee chef attached, but it is operated by the team that runs a variety of posh venues inside London’s Royal Albert Hall. The food is described as classic American cuisine made with California-sourced ingredients, and it is open for lunch, dinner and weekend brunch with hours that extend past the museum’s closing time – showing that it hopes to become a dining destination in its own right. 6. Browse the stacks The museum’s library is open to visitors without a ticket and is all dressed up in dark wood, with cosy lighting and plenty of comfortable chairs and tables. A wall of windows looks out onto the lush main lawn, providing both a quiet place to read and a perfect perch for people-watching. It is not a lending library, but you can enjoy the more than 3,000 art books on site. As an added treat, the third and top floor of shelving contains a variety of art books donated by actor and avid art collector Steve Martin (the public can only access the first floor). On your way out, be sure to leave books on the bright orange carts featuring signs of Yoda imploring guests to follow the golden rule: “Reshelve, do not. Leave books here, you must!” 7. Stroll the grounds Take a good book or your selfie stick on a stroll of the museum’s stunning garden campus designed by Mia Lehrer and her LA firm Studio-MLA. Featuring various zones of native vegetation alongside bougainvillea and jacarandas, the park is dotted with generous public seating and has an amphitheatre for outdoor events or general lounging. A tranquil hanging garden and rolling green hills are mirrored with dreamlike precision on the museum’s curved roof. There is also a smattering of sculptures, including a joyful mother and child by Fernando Botero, and a series of full-scale creations featuring some of Star Wars’ most beloved characters. You will find Yoda standing with Baby Yoda just behind him towards the back of the park, while a giant bronze in the ample grass lawn below the museum shows Princess Leia choking Jabba the Hutt with her chains – an iconic scene from Return of the Jedi. For a quiet moment of reflection, head to the north edge of the museum, where you will find a large waterfall dubbed “The Rain,” which doubles as a cooling mechanism for the building and attracts plenty of seagulls.

title: South Korean killer’s escape foiled, Singapore minister’s Mandarin speech: 7 Asia highlights
description: From Singaporean minister’s Mandarin diplomacy to Indonesia’s Whoosh debt burden, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. South Korean killer’s drone escape from Philippine prison foiled by test footage A South Korean crime lord convicted of murder in the Philippines reportedly planned to escape prison by strapping himself to a drone – until his own accomplice’s rehearsal footage gave the game away. 2. Why the ICC is cracking down on ‘fake news’ as Duterte trial looms As Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes-against-humanity trial looms, an international tribunal faces the challenge of managing a sprawling prosecution case around the health of an 81-year-old former president of the Philippines, on top of shielding the proceedings from a highly charged media environment. 3. Singapore minister Chan Chun Sing’s Mandarin diplomacy strikes China chord Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state. 4. Malaysia’s Loke resigns as minister following Najib’s house arrest approval A senior ally of Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim announced his resignation from cabinet on Saturday – a day after confidence in the prime minister’s administration took a severe hit when disgraced former leader Najib Razak was allowed to serve out his jail term under house arrest. 5. Who will shoulder the debts behind Indonesia’s China-backed Whoosh railway? Indonesia’s finance ministry is preparing to absorb debt payments for Whoosh, the China-funded high-speed railway connecting Jakarta and Bandung, in a move officials say will ease financial pressure on the state-owned enterprises that built and operate the line. 6. ‘Gone too far’: Thai PM Anutin slams foreign lawbreakers as backlash builds Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has issued a withering rebuke to foreigners behaving badly in Thailand following a wave of scandals involving illegal businesses and landholdings including a cemetery, saying the cases have “gone too far” by breaching Thai law and hospitality. 7. Crouching dragons: the suicide divers Japan never sent to war Japan’s wartime kamikaze pilots remain among the most recognisable symbols of the Pacific war: young men flying aircraft into Allied ships on missions from which they were not expected to return.

title: Hong Kong stocks eye fresh inflows from mainland China’s insurers sitting on US$6 trillion
description: Volume spike in exchange-traded funds seen as evidence insurers are taking advantage of recent regulator approval to diversify their assets.
content: Hong Kong’s stock market is getting a dose of optimism from mainland China’s 41 trillion yuan (US$6.1 trillion) insurance industry, as some insurers are widely speculated to have bought exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in the city one month after regulators approved such purchases. Market observers highlighted a spike in trading volume for several Hong Kong-listed ETFs on Monday as evidence of buying by the mainland insurance companies. The National Financial Regulatory Administration, the watchdog of China’s banking and insurance industries, allowed insurers to access Hong Kong-listed ETFs through the cross-border Stock Connect programme last month. Some Chinese insurers recently received specific rules on investing in the ETFs and may have already started buying, with more industry peers to follow, the China Securities Journal reported on Monday, citing an unspecified source. The approval of ETF investments is the latest in a series of measures by Beijing to reinforce Hong Kong’s position as a global financial hub. Earlier, it allowed mainland insurers to buy bonds trading in the city and gave permission to commence trading of offshore Chinese government bond futures in Hong Kong. More onshore institutional inflows should support Hong Kong stocks, which have been lagging global peers because of a lack of listings directly tied to the artificial intelligence boom. The new investments by Chinese insurers will add a new source of mainland buying to the southbound trade of the decade-old Stock Connect scheme, which allows onshore traders to access a large part of Hong Kong’s stock market. Chinese onshore buying now holds sway over Hong Kong equities, accounting for about one-third of daily turnover. “Overseas investments are effective in boosting overall investment returns among financial institutions,” said Luo Zuanhui, an analyst at Shenwan Hongyuan Group, which estimated that mainland insurers invested a combined 1.61 trillion yuan in Hong Kong stocks through the connect programme by the end of 2025. Hong Kong-listed ETFs have been eligible for trading through the Stock Connect since 2022. In the first seven months of this year, the daily trading value of the securities jumped by 61 per cent from a year earlier to HK$5.8 billion (US$739.3 million), according to bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing. Chinese traders bought a combined HK$391.8 billion of Hong Kong stocks in the first eight months, with buying concentrated on technology shares, according to exchange data. Such buying largely countered an exodus of overseas investors who shifted to AI bets in the US or South Korea, leaving the Hang Seng Index little changed this year. Hong Kong stocks are facing tighter liquidity after the Federal Reserve raised the interest rate in the US for the first time in three years last week and the Bank of Japan followed suit, boosting borrowing costs to a 31-year high. Sovereign bond yields in the two nations also hit multi-year highs on jitters over inflation and a glut of debt supply. Chinese insurers are diversifying investments beyond domestic assets to sustain growth after reporting strong profit increases in the first half. China Life Insurance reported a more than 200 per cent surge in profit and Ping An Insurance Group posted a 36 per cent increase, driven by increased investment gains from the stock market. China Life, Ping An and four other peers received the regulatory approval in June to buy fixed-income products in Hong Kong through the Bond Connect scheme.

title: Home at last? Why house arrest for Malaysia’s Najib is no done deal
description: The former PM has been granted house arrest, but an unpaid US$12 million fine and a second prison term stand in his way.
content: Malaysia’s former prime minister Najib Razak appears to have entered the home stretch of his years-long bid to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest. The 73-year-old has spent nearly two years fighting to serve his sentence at home, after claiming a royal order issued alongside his 2024 sentence commutation granted him that privilege. The 2024 decision had already halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine – to 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) – for misappropriating funds from SRC International, a former unit of state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). Najib must first settle that fine before he can be released from prison, but even if he manages to raise the funds, his future is far from certain. Malaysia has no law governing house arrest and the rules for Najib’s detention are still being worked out. Here’s what we know so far about how it will work, what Najib needs to do to go home – and why he could yet find himself back behind bars. Crowdfunding freedom Najib was granted his request for house arrest on Friday, when the Federal Territories Pardons Board, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim, agreed to let him serve the remainder of his six-year SRC sentence – until August 23, 2028 – at home. He must first pay the fine, however, and comply with the pardon’s other conditions. Any breach would void the arrangement and see him returned to prison, according to the official statement announcing the decision. His supporters in Umno – the Malay nationalist party he led for nine years until his government was ousted in the 2018 election – have already started passing the hat around. A solidarity fund launched by the party raked in 1 million ringgit within a single day, with many supporters reportedly chipping in 10 ringgit or 50 ringgit apiece. Attorney General Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said on Monday that Najib’s family had yet to pay the fine, which must be settled with the Kuala Lumpur High Court registrar before any transfer from prison can go ahead. Yet even once the money was paid, the process “may take some time”, Dusuki said. Najib’s lawyers have said raising the money is complicated because a “significant part” of his assets, bank accounts and properties remain frozen or subject to government enforcement proceedings. Decree deja vu The pardon Najib was granted in 2024 by then king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah not only cut his jail sentence and slashed his initial 210 million ringgit fine, it was also accompanied by a separate decree Najib’s lawyers insisted allowed him to serve the balance of his prison term at home. The document did exist, but the High Court ruled in December that it was unenforceable since house arrest had not been deliberated at the Pardons Board meeting and Malaysian law contained no provision for carrying it out. Najib then withdrew his appeal in April. Article 42 of Malaysia’s Federal Constitution gives the king broad powers to grant pardons, reprieves and respites. But the text does not spell out precisely how far that clemency can go, according to Malaysian constitutional lawyer Andrew Khoo. “The actual ambit of the Pardons Board, in terms of the scope of the clemency that may be granted, is not specified in the constitution or in regulations connected therewith,” Khoo said. “Given that this provision relies on the historical royal prerogative that has been received by convention, it could be argued that there are no limits to the scope of the clemency.” Home as a prison Malaysia still has no law specifically governing house arrest, leaving authorities to look to existing prison rules for a way to make Najib’s new arrangement work while the government develops separate legislation on home detention. Police and prison officials have assessed Najib’s residence in the upmarket Langgak Duta neighbourhood of Kuala Lumpur, local media reported on Monday, with a mobile police station deployed nearby. Authorities said the bungalow had not yet been formally confirmed as his detention site. “One possible technical way the prison authorities can enforce a house arrest is to designate Najib’s house as a prison,” Malaysia-based constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said. Such an arrangement could also subject Najib to prison-style restrictions, Lim said, including limits on electronic devices, food and who he can meet. “There are restrictions … I’m not sure whether that is in line with the idea of a house arrest,” he said. Back behind bars? Even a successful move home would only cover Najib’s SRC sentence, relating to some 42 million ringgit that was transferred into his personal accounts. In December, the High Court convicted him in a separate 1MDB case involving 2.3 billion ringgit (US$564 million) and sentenced him to a further 15 years in prison. Justice Collin Lawrence Sequerah rejected Najib’s claim that the case was a politically motivated witch hunt, pointing instead to “cold, hard and incontrovertible evidence” against him and ordering the new prison term to begin only after his SRC sentence ends. Najib is currently appealing that conviction, but as things stand, he would be legally bound to return to prison in 2028. “If he remains convicted in the 1MDB matter and his house arrest period has finished, he has to go back to the normal prison,” Lim said. “Unless, of course, there is a further clemency bid by him which is successful.” Pardon the politics Friday’s pardon decision followed a strong year at the ballot box for the United Malays National Organisation. Its Barisan Nasional coalition swept 48 of 56 seats in Johor in July, then took 18 of 36 in Negeri Sembilan the following month – more than any other bloc. Umno continues to press for its former president’s release, ensuring the issue remains one of the most sensitive in the party’s uneasy governing partnership with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition. That has never sat well with the Democratic Action Party (DAP), a key coalition partner for Anwar and one of Najib’s fiercest critics over 1MDB. Tensions flared again following the house-arrest decision, with DAP secretary general Anthony Loke offering his resignation as transport minister in protest. Political scientist Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid called Najib’s house arrest “a double-edged sword” for Umno. “Malay voters are now divided,” he said. “Some who have supported Umno all along will continue to do so, but floating voters [such as] those without any party loyalty will likely distance themselves from Umno [even] further.” While house arrest for Najib could “marginally improve Umno’s prospects” in some of its traditional strongholds, it also risked alienating middle-class Malay and anti-corruption voters, Ahmad Fauzi said.

title: Beyond Phoebe Gates’ Phia: 5 female-owned fashion-tech apps to have on your radar
description: From Indyx and By Rotation to SSQRD, these apps help you organise your wardrobe, rent clothes and discover indie brands at the tap of a button.
content: Female tech entrepreneurship is a rapidly growing field, but not all female founders, it seems, are shown equal treatment. That’s why Phoebe Gates, the 24-year-old daughter of now-divorced Bill and Melinda Gates, made headlines this summer as controversy surfaced over her AI-powered shopping app Phia, which she launched with her former Stanford University classmate Sophia Kianni just last year. Phia was, for all intents and purposes, a huge success story upon launch – the start-up counted Khloé Kardashian, Karlie Kloss, Eileen Gu, Sydney Sweeney, Paris Hilton, Hailey Bieber and even LVMH scion Alexandre Arnault as investors and boasted nearly 10,000 retail partners. The app and browser extension tool works by scanning the internet as you shop online to find alternative links at Phia’s affiliate partners to purchase whatever item you’re looking at, be it the same item at a discount or a similar version of the item being sold second-hand. Phia uses these affiliate commissions to make money, taking a cut of all purchases made using its extension. This July, however, Bloomberg reported that Phia had been claiming affiliate commissions on sales it did not actually drive, a fraudulent practice commonly referred to as “cookie stuffing” because it involves tracking the usage of unauthorised cookies, or small data files, stored in an individual’s web browser. The Phia extension claimed commissions from various retailers even in cases where the sale wasn’t necessarily completed by the shopper and overrode legitimate referrals from other external sites. In the weeks since the story first broke, Phia has continued to deny any intentional malpractice, first attributing the “cookie stuffing” to a bug, which it later claimed to have resolved, adding that it would reverse any misattributed transactions for affected brand partners. Bloomberg further reported on leaked messages that showed Phia’s founders may have been aware of, and actively pushing, “cookie stuffing” practices for months, a narrative a Phia representative later denied. And leaked internal documents reviewed by Bloomberg showed that average daily revenue at Phia has dropped significantly since those practices were exposed and disabled. Neither Gates nor Kianni has been charged with any crimes, though in the United States “cookie stuffing” could constitute wire fraud with a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison plus fines. Following the publication of this article, a Phia spokesperson provided the following statement to Style: “One of Phia’s many features involved finding and displaying free coupons for shoppers and, in connection with that feature, placing an affiliate cookie.” The statement further reads, “Following feedback from brand partners, Phia updated the coupon feature so that affiliate cookie placement now requires a shopper to click on the coupon pop-up. We’ve also been doing voluntary transaction reversals as a gesture of goodwill to our partners. In the three months since, we’ve rebuilt our codebase, hired a new head of compliance, and brought on senior leaders in partnerships and engineering. With stronger systems in place, we’re continuing to work closely with thousands of brands.” Controversy aside, the Phia scandal has also shone the spotlight on other female founders who are hustling to make their mark in the same space, perhaps without the Gates legacy and “cookie stuffing” allegations to their names. Some, like Kristine Locker of the shopping app Locker, have even alleged they were building products similar to Phia around the same time, only to be denied capital by several of the same investors, according to Forbes. Here are five fashion tech apps – and the women who built them – you should have on your radar right now. 1. Indyx by Yidi Campbell View this post on Instagram A post shared by Indyx | Your Digital Wardrobe (@myindyx) Former investment banker and retail industry veteran Yidi Campbell, who previously held strategy and operations positions at Gap Inc. and Athleta, launched the digital closet app Indyx in 2022, with the help of her co-founder and now head of growth, Devon Rule. Today Indyx is more than just a digital wardrobe; through the app, users can also book on-demand professional styling services. 2. SSQRD by Nabihah Ahmad Nabihah Ahmad started building her start-up, SSQRD (pronounced S-Squared), while still an undergraduate at Columbia University. SSQRD, a global shopping search engine, seeks to build the world’s largest e-commerce repository. But perhaps more importantly, Ahmad aims to use the SSQRD directory to highlight independent brands from around the world that would otherwise struggle to stand out above the noise: users can filter for Black-owned brands, sustainable ones and much more. 3. By Rotation by Eshita Kabra-Davies Investment manager Eshita Kabra-Davies first launched her clothing rental service By Rotation as a side hustle in 2019, and says she was inspired to do so after seeing the plethora of textile waste on a honeymoon visit to her home country of India. By Rotation proclaims to be the UK’s first social fashion rental app, operating on a peer-to-peer business model. Despite competition from American rental pioneer Rent the Runway and the Urban Outfitters-owned upstart platform Nuuly, By Rotation expanded into the US in 2023. 4. Selleb by Chloe and Claire Lee Ever wondered what the world’s coolest people are actually buying? Sisters Chloe and Claire Lee came up with the idea for their receipt-sharing app, Selleb, after spending their teenage years blogging about their own favourite finds and purchases, fine-tuning their personal taste, so to speak – and later developing a devoted following on fashion resale marketplace Poshmark. Selleb, which is still invite-only, allows users to see what other members of the app’s curated community are actually spending their money on rather than blindly following recommendations online. You can read users’ unfiltered reviews of purchases, too, from luxury clothing items to a meal at one of New York’s most hyped restaurants. 5. Daydream by Julie Bornstein View this post on Instagram A post shared by Daydream (@daydream) Like Phia, Daydream is also an AI-powered shopping app which profits off commissions, but its user experience is more akin to ChatGPT than anything. Powered by multiple AI models, including OpenAI, Google Gemini and various open-source tools, Daydream is a conversational shopping engine and assistant. It’s also not founder Julie Bornstein’s first excursion into the tech space – the former chief operating officer and board member of Stitch Fix, an online personal styling service, is an e-commerce veteran who helped launch American department store Nordstrom’s website all the way back in 1999. She also founded a venture-backed fashion recommendation app called The Yes, which was later acquired by Pinterest.

title: How are China’s Type 052D destroyers shifting the balance in the western Pacific?
description: The warship was used to launch a hypersonic anti-ship missile in July and could be strategically important in a Taiwan contingency.
content: When state television aired footage in July of a Type 052D destroyer launching a YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile it signalled a significant expansion of the Chinese navy’s long-range strike power. The missile had previously been associated with China’s larger Type 055 destroyers. Showing it fired from a Type 052D – a class the People’s Liberation Army has built in far greater numbers – suggests Beijing may be able to spread the weapon well beyond its much smaller force of Type 055s. That would boost the number of PLA Navy warships able to threaten US and allied naval forces approaching Taiwan from the western Pacific if a conflict broke out. The launch highlighted the continuing evolution of one of China’s most important warship classes. Building on the air-defence capabilities of the preceding Type 052C, the Type 052D – known to the US military as the Luyang III-class – introduced a more flexible missile-launch system. Its vertical-launch capacity increased from 48 to 64 cells, divided equally fore and aft, allowing it to fire a wider range of surface-to-air, anti-ship and anti-submarine missiles. The July footage showed that the system could cold-launch a YJ-20 – ejecting the missile before engine ignition – from the ship’s forward cells. Open-source estimates put the YJ-20 at just under 9 metres (29 feet) long and less than 850mm (33 inches) wide, meaning it could fit the deepest version of China’s universal missile-launch cells. It is, however, not publicly known which Type 052D production batches have cells of that depth. Since the lead ship, the Kunming, entered service in 2014, China has continued building the design while introducing changes to its sensors, aviation facilities, weapons and networking systems. One of the most visible changes came with a lengthened version of the Type 052D, commonly referred to by analysts as the Type 052DL. Its flight deck is about 4 metres longer than on earlier ships, a change viewed as a move to better accommodate larger helicopters such as the naval Z-20, alongside smaller types such as the Z-9. Images circulated in August appeared to show a Z-20F operating from a Type 052DL, potentially the first known example of the helicopter operating from that class of ship. A further upgraded variant, commonly designated the Type 052DM, has improved sensors, weapons and networking systems. In January, official PLA outlet China Military Online said upgrades aboard the Loudi destroyer had improved its air defence, missile defence, anti-ship and anti-submarine capabilities. Imagery of newer ships also shows a new mast-mounted radar replacing the mechanically scanned radar used on earlier vessels. Chinese military expert Fu Qianshao told state-run Global Times in January that the new radar was likely to be a dual-face rotating active electronically scanned array, offering significant improvements over the mast-mounted radar on earlier Type 052Ds. The installation also appears visually similar to the radar fitted to China’s Type 054B frigates. Beyond these technical upgrades, the Type 052D’s strategic importance lies in the scale at which China has built the class. Open-source counts put the force at about 35 ships, against 10 of the newer Type 055s. While each Type 052D carries fewer vertical-launch cells than the larger Type 055, the class has become a regular escort for China’s growing carrier fleet, providing area air defence against aerial threats, including aircraft and missiles, with long-range surface-to-air weapons such as the HHQ-9 family, backed by shorter-range defensive systems. Type 052Ds have repeatedly deployed as part of the Liaoning and Shandong aircraft carrier groups, including through the first island chain and into the Philippine Sea. In May 2025 one of the newer ships was tracked by Japan sailing between Okinawa and Miyako into the Philippine Sea. The following year, the Type 052D Kaifeng joined the Liaoning on a roughly 40-day deployment through the South China Sea and into the Philippine Sea alongside the Type 055 Wuxi, the Type 054B frigate Luohe and the replenishment ship Hulunhu. Those operational patterns would be especially relevant in a Taiwan contingency, as shown in multiple Taiwan-focused drills by the PLA. During Joint Sword-2024B, the Type 052D Urumqi operated east of the island alongside the Liaoning and the Type 055 Anshan. In Strait Thunder-2025A, the Type 052D Zhanjiang deployed with the Shandong carrier group during drills around Taiwan. PLA descriptions of later exercises show the kinds of missions these ships could support in a conflict. During Justice Mission 2025, for instance, the Eastern Theatre Command said its forces practised blockading key ports and areas, gaining control of the battlespace and deterring forces outside the first island chain. In such a scenario, the size of the Type 052D force could allow the PLA to protect carrier and amphibious groups, escort replenishment ships, support anti-submarine operations and also maintain surface forces on Taiwan’s eastern approaches. That said, long-range strikes against moving warships would still depend on a wider network of land-, air-, sea- and space-based sensors. The Pentagon’s 2025 China military report said the PLA’s growing space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network had dramatically increased its ability to monitor, track and target US and allied forces. It also said land-based sensors, including Skywave over-the-horizon radars, could probably detect ships and aircraft between the first and second island chains. The report – which primarily assessed developments through 2024 – said the PLA still faced challenges with time-sensitive battle-damage assessment and coordinating complex multiservice strikes. Beyond those operational hurdles, technical uncertainties remain. Weapons compatibility may differ between production batches, the precise anti-submarine sensor fit is unclear in open sources, and China’s missile-defence claims for newer ships remain unverified. But the broader trajectory is clear. Since the first Type 052D entered service in 2014, China has kept producing and upgrading the class as the PLA Navy has pushed farther into the western Pacific. In a conflict over Taiwan, the Type 052D’s importance may therefore lie less in any single weapon than in the combination of capability, adaptability and numbers – potentially giving Beijing enough modern destroyers to support several naval operations at once.

title: Ant Group consolidates Alipay operations in big bet on AI ‘agentic commerce’
description: Agentic commerce is entering a phase of ‘explosive, large-scale growth’, Ant CEO Cyril Han Xinyi said in an internal letter on Monday.
content: Chinese fintech giant Ant Group has revamped its online payments operations by creating a new business group for Alipay, as it sharpens its artificial intelligence focus on “agentic commerce” to drive new growth. Ant, an Alibaba Group Holding affiliate, merged its Digital Payment Business Group, Alipay Business Group and Zhima Credit Business Group into a new business unit dedicated to Alipay, according to an internal letter from CEO Cyril Han Xinyi on Monday, as reported by Chinese media outlet The Beijing News. The company also appointed Wu Minzhi, a veteran executive at Ant and previously at Alibaba, to lead the new Alipay Business Group while serving as Ant’s chief people officer. The restructuring aimed to “further consolidate technology, product and ecosystem capabilities and strengthen the merchant service system”, Han said in the letter. “As AI technology advances and industry adoption accelerates, agentic commerce is entering a phase of explosive, large-scale growth,” Han said, according to excerpts of the letter seen by the South China Morning Post. Alipay has built a solid foundation for the era of agentic commerce by expanding its footprint across AI payments and AI wallets, while also developing an ecosystem that connected multiple hardware devices, according to the excerpts. Ant did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. Alibaba owns the SCMP. The latest reshuffle comes nearly two years after Ant split its Alipay business group into two units, the Digital Payment Business Group and Alipay Business Group, in late 2024. The previous Digital Payment Business Group focused on the development of innovative payment products, while the Alipay Business Group focused on user base growth and monetisation of the digital wallet. In the current age of agentic AI, Ant would equip users with personal AI wallets and life assistants, enable merchants to grow their businesses on Alipay’s AI platform, and build a trusted AI agent ecosystem, Han noted in the letter. Ant has been accelerating its agentic AI efforts to prepare itself for the next generation of commerce. The company introduced an interactive assistant named Ah Bao in June, the biggest overhaul of Alipay in two decades, aimed at transforming its ubiquitous mobile-payment app into a native AI platform with autonomous agents. In late May, the Hangzhou-based company launched a new suite of AI payment tools, including an AI Wallet integrated within the Alipay app and designed to let users manage and authorise tasks carried out by AI agents. It also debuted Token Pay, a specialised business-to-business product engineered for AI-model providers.

title: Letters | Hong Kong can provide its snowboarders with a route to success
description: Readers discuss how the city can support its snowboarders, former chief executive Tung Chee-hwa’s contributions, and the AI poses.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong sent four athletes to the Winter Olympics in February, its largest team ever, and 74 to the Asian Winter Games in Harbin the year before, also a record. Neither delegation contained a snowboarder, however – and the old explanation no longer holds. Guangzhou now has a 75,000 square metre (807,293 square feet) indoor snow park with a covered alpine track of about 400 metres. For parallel snowboard racing, which involves gates on short courses, the Guangzhou track is a usable training venue within a day’s trip from the city, which no earlier generation of our racers had. The frameworks exist too. In March last year, the Sports Federation and Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China, signed a memorandum of understanding with the Heilongjiang Sports Federation and Harbin Sport University on joint training and talent development. Last November, Hong Kong joined a four-party agreement with the General Administration of Sport of China, Guangdong and Macau covering youth and athlete exchange. As far as I know, no snow sport programme has been announced under either. We know what a route is worth. The sport of short-track speedskating has rinks, a place in the Sports Institute’s top tier and a route a junior can see – and Joey Lam Ching-yan’s seventh place at Milano Cortina is this city’s best Winter Games result. The reverse also holds. The International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) records that Vic Wild, later a double Olympic champion, was forced to step back when the US Ski and Snowboard Association shut down its alpine snowboarding programme after the 2010 Winter Olympics; the discipline survives there mostly through non-profit organisations and clubs. As a snowboarder holding an FIS licence for Hong Kong, I accept the obvious objection: our snow athletes are few, and the Sports Institute’s tiers are rightly earned by results, as triathletes’ fight to keep triathlon’s top-tier status shows. However, a route is different from a tier, and no pool forms without one. In July, the International Olympic Committee added a second alpine snowboard event to the 2030 Winter Olympics programme. The promised review of support for Hong Kong’s athletes after this month’s Asian Games is the moment to respond. A snow sport pathway under the agreements already signed, with the Ski Association of Hong Kong, China, as partner, and a snowboard entry at the 2028 National Winter Games in Liaoning, would need no new instrument and no new venue. Hanson Meng, Pok Fu Lam Tung steered Hong Kong through a difficult period I agree with the letter saying that we owe Tung Chee-hwa much more that we gave him during his time as Hong Kong’s first chief executive (“Tung Chee-hwa deserved better from Hong Kong”, September 17). The position Tung occupied was always going to be extremely demanding, involving the necessity to accomplish several impossible things at once. Even under the most favourable circumstances it was going to be a very delicate task. But Tung was faced almost immediately with the Asian financial crisis, followed by the exigencies of severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars). This double blow meant that his well meaning and, in hindsight, farsighted policies could not readily be carried out. Added to this, of course, was the opposition in the Legislative Council, which seemed almost determined to be unhelpful, to put it mildly. I admire the man for the way in which he stood fast in the face of all these insurmountable difficulties and managed to steer Hong Kong through a very difficult period. May he rest in peace. David Gwilt, Sai Kung A pause on AI development is warranted Anyone who watched the CNBC interview with Mustafa Soleyman, Microsoft’s artificial intelligence (AI) CEO, woud have come away with deep concern about how the world is progressing with this technology. Unfortunately, the developers of AI who have created the problems appear to be unable to fix the issues with the technology. There seems to be only one solution and that is a total ban on AI development for a period of time. But obviously that is not going to happen. Duncan Hancock, Lamma Island

title: Asian Games, day 3: Choi into foil gold medal bout, after silver for Lau, Leung’s bronze
description: Cheung Ka-long’s early exit leaves Ryan Choi to chase foil title alone, after wushu medal for Lau Chi-lung, cycling success for Chloe Leung.
content: Ryan Choi Chun-yin will fight for individual foil gold at the Asian Games on Tuesday, after Cheung Ka-long’s early exit left him carrying the city’s hopes all on his own. Choi breezed through the knockout rounds of the tournament, displaying some sparkling form on the piste, and winning all five of his bouts in the pool stage. Alongside South Korean’s Lee Kwang-hyun and Youn Jeong-hyun, he was one of only three foilists to receive a bye straight to the round of 16. There, he quickly dispatched Kazakhstan’s Tiomfey Semyonov 15-4 to ease into the quarter-finals, and followed that by beating Singapore’s Samuel Elijah Robson 15-12 to set up a semi-final against Youn. The pair were evenly matched in the battle for the final, but Choi prevailed to face Japan’s Kazuki Imura for gold. In contrast, double Olympic champion Cheung struggled through Pool 3, losing three of his five bouts to rank fourth out of six fencers at the Aichi Sky Expo. There had been hopes for a double success, but Cheung lost 15–13 to Daniil Kravtsov in the round of 32, having previously been beaten by his Uzbekistan rival 5–4 in the pool stages. In the women’s épée, Kaylin Hsieh Sin-yan won all five of her Pool 3 bouts to reach the knockout stage and received a bye to the round of 16, where she lost 13-10 to China’s Yang Jinwen. Chan Wai-ling made it through to the round of 32 with four wins out of her six bouts in Pool 1. The Hongkonger then brushed aside Zainab Alhosani of the United Arab Emirates 15-5, before an equally comfortable 15-7 win over Tang Junyao took her into the last eight. And there was plenty to cheer for the city’s supporters elsewhere, with cyclist Chloe Leung Wing-yee taking bronze in the women’s road race, and wushu exponent Lau Chi-lung winning silver in the men’s nanquan and nangun event. Lau’s medal was the latest to be added to Hong Kong’s growing tally, and his 19.456 points over the disciplines put him second behind China’s Li Jianming, who took gold with 19.563 points. Chinese Taipei’s Liu Chang-min claimed bronze with a score of 19.430. There had been hopes for a double success at Aichi Sky Expo, but Chueng lost 15–13 to Daniil Kravtsov in the round of 32, having previously been beaten by his Uzbekistan rival 5–4 in the pool stages. Cyclist Leung, meanwhile, overcame the disappointment of finishing fourth in the time trial and a host of pre-Games injuries to take a well-deserved bronze. The Hongkonger battled away with China’s Li Guo, who took gold, and Afghanistan’s Fariba Hashimi, but ultimately couldn’t close the gap in the race for the line. “I was upset after the time trial because I came in fourth again,” Leung said. “At the last Asian Games, I’d been fourth too [in the time trial] and I was quite disappointed. “I also felt that my legs weren’t great today. I tried, in the first lap, to speed up a little bit, but I knew I would suffer from the beginning [doing that]. In the last lap, I just thought, ‘screw it, I’ll just go. If I try, no matter the result, at least I tried’.” Meanwhile, the city’s table tennis teams have suffered mixed fortunes, with the men moving on and the women crashing out. The men thrashed Qatar 3-0 in the round of 16 to set up a quarter-final clash with South Korea later on Tuesday, with veteran Wong Chun-ting, youngster Baldwin Chan Ho-wah, and Lam Siu-hang each winning a point for the team at Sky Hall Toyota. The city’s women, however, suffered a heartbreaking 3-2 loss at the hands of Singapore and crashed out in the first knockout round. Su Tsz-tung and Pedrey Ng Wing-lam twice gave Hong Kong a lead at 1-0 and 2-1, but Su missed the chance to seal the victory in the fourth match, while veteran Doo Hoi-kem lost both of her matches, in the second and fifth match of the tie.

title: What Saudi Arabia’s exit means for China-led mBridge amid global de-dollarisation
description: The departure sends political signal rather than materially threatens project, analysts say.
content: Saudi Arabia’s withdrawal from a China-led digital currency platform would carry greater symbolic than operational significance, analysts say, highlighting pressures facing countries caught between US influence and alternatives to dollar-based payments infrastructure. In a response to inquiries from the South China Morning Post, the Saudi Central Bank said it had participated in mBridge – a multilateral central bank digital currency platform seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system – only on a limited proof-of-concept basis, which it successfully completed on May 13 last year, after which it was “no longer a participating member of mBridge”. The move appeared “more significant symbolically than operationally” and did not “necessarily undermine the project’s viability”, said Matteo Giovannini, senior finance manager at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China. “It does … underline the geopolitical sensitivity of building alternative cross-border payment infrastructure at a time when the dollar-based financial system remains deeply intertwined with global trade and security relationships,” said Giovannini, who is also an AsiaGlobal Fellow at the University of Hong Kong. “The more important question is whether these participants can move mBridge from a successful technical experiment towards meaningful real-world adoption and a broader network of users.” Saudi can still watch the platform privately, so mBridge’s future looks narrower and more regional, not dead Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis Project mBridge, together with China’s Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, is widely viewed as part of Beijing’s broader push to establish alternatives to traditional US dollar-centric payment networks. That effort has gained momentum in recent years amid heightened tensions between the world’s two largest economies and growing concerns over the weaponisation of the US dollar. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis, also characterised the move as “a political signal more than a technical one”. “[It] dents the ‘anti-dollar coalition’ story without stopping mBridge among [mainland] China, [Hong Kong], Thailand, UAE [United Arab Emirates] and Macau,” she said. “Saudi can still watch the platform privately, so mBridge’s future looks narrower and more regional, not dead.” Aside from Saudi Arabia, which joined the project in 2024, mBridge includes the central banks of mainland China, Hong Kong, Thailand and the UAE, as well as Macau, which joined in June. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), which helped launch mBridge in 2021, withdrew from the project in October 2024. A BIS official told the media at the time that its withdrawal was because the project had reached a stage where its central bank partners could take it forward independently, rather than for political considerations. De-dollarisation efforts have nevertheless faced pressure from Washington, with US President Donald Trump previously threatening 100 per cent tariffs on Brics countries if they move to create a new currency or replace the US dollar. Brics began as an association of five major emerging national economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa – but has expanded significantly. “Third countries are increasingly being squeezed by the great power competition, with the US usually on the offensive side,” said Xu Tianchen, an economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. “It has intervened in projects in Brazil and Nicaragua, and Saudi Arabia may be under US [influence] as well.”

title: Rare earths friction threatens to stall trade truce extension ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: US trade representative blames China for creating ‘uncertainty’ but observers point to benefits for both sides in delaying agreement.
content: With the clock counting down to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington for a state visit, the US and China continue to wrangle over extending the 2025 Busan trade agreement – even as they report progress on implementing a narrow tariff-reduced trade mechanism. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Monday blamed China for creating “uncertainty” over the pact’s extension, saying Beijing was still holding out on supplying enough strategic mineral exports to the United States. “They have limited rare earth exports. They’ve controlled them,” Greer said in an interview with Bloomberg News. “President Xi and President Trump have a good relationship, but we need these extensions or other things to go incrementally to make sure that there’s compliance.” China’s shipments of rare earth magnets to the US fell 13 per cent year on year to 512 tonnes in August. This was despite Beijing resuming some export approvals following trade negotiations, and shipments recovering from their lows in 2025. Greer’s expressed frustration underscores a key dynamic of a bilateral relationship marked by complimentary language at the leader level papering over a significant number of irritants. His remarks – a day after the US and China agreed to launch a dialogue on artificial intelligence and kicked off a bilateral body to manage tariff-reduced trade – followed eight hours of negotiations in New York. Greer – who was part of the discussion, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, at JPMorgan’s headquarters – asserted on Monday that he did not expect an extension of the Busan deal to be announced this week, given the rare earth concerns. But he added that “both sides want” to extend it. “This isn’t until November that it expires, and I think we have time between now and then to talk about the terms of it,” he said. However, a source familiar with the discussions termed it “shadow boxing” between the two sides to maximise their leverage. The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The October truce in Busan, South Korea, helped to avert a full-blown crisis in the wake of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April last year. Beijing responded to the tariffs with sweeping restrictions on seven rare earths, triggering supply disruptions and temporary factory shutdowns around the world, including in the US. The export controls gave Beijing a powerful bargaining tool in trade negotiations, forcing Washington to back down from some of its demands as the disruptions exposed US dependence on China for rare earths. China controls much of the world’s processing capacity for these critical metals, particularly for the heavy rare earths that are used in high-performance magnets for defence systems, robotics and electric vehicles. It also has a dominant position in the processing and production of other critical minerals, including graphite, gallium and germanium. The South China Morning Post previously reported that the trade truce agreed by Xi and Trump in Busan was likely to be extended, though Washington was not expected to push for a breakthrough at the coming meeting. The agreement expires on November 10. The package deal lowered US tariffs on some Chinese goods, suspended additional restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, paused certain Chinese rare earth export controls for a year, and secured Chinese commitments on US soybeans and fentanyl precursors. According to sources, Beijing would prefer an extension that runs through to the end of Trump’s presidency while Washington is seeking a shorter-term deal. Greer on Monday indicated that the Trump administration would prefer an extension of three to six months, which was “probably the right kind of range”, he said. Sourabh Gupta, resident senior fellow at the Institute for China-America Studies, said the Busan consensus “was a very major outcome”, adding that it would be “understandable” if the two sides “choose to kick the tyres on renewal a few more times”.
