Gupta said Trump’s expected attendance at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November could give both sides another opportunity to meet in the run-up and finalise a deal before the deadline. “So the Americans might choose to leave the Chinese on tenterhooks until then,” he noted. Gupta also observed that it would be “too tempting for both sides” to leave the extension out of the “deliverables” coming out of the September 24 meeting. Most analysts expect this week’s summit to produce few major new deals, with both Washington and Beijing likely to focus on consolidating existing agreements and managing outstanding trade disputes. Negotiations over the Busan extension continue, even with Sunday’s launch of the US-China Board of Trade, while talks on the Board of Investment remain in a preliminary stage. Both mechanisms were announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. Under the trade mechanism, both Beijing and Washington are selecting non-sensitive sectors and products to be eligible for a tariff-reduced trade capped at US$30 billion for each side. Greer on Sunday said that teams from both sides were still working to finalise a list of goods that could be traded separately from future trade measures. “The teams right now upstairs are continuing to work through this to see if they can find some critical mass of goods,” he said, describing them as “non-sensitive” items that could be traded “in a balanced way” to create “a kind of ballast for the relationship”. “We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side, on the US side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices and other things like that.”

title: Malaysian resort under investigation after intruder molests tourist
description: A minister told tourism operators to prioritise visitor safety as police arrested a teen suspect linked to the incident in Sabah.
content: Malaysia’s Sabah state has ordered a full investigation into the Semporna resort where a female tourist from China was allegedly molested and assaulted inside her room by an intruder early last Saturday. State Tourism, Culture and Environment Minister Jafry Ariffin said he instructed tourism authorities and enforcement agencies to investigate the security lapses that led to the incident and the resort’s licensing status. “I have instructed the relevant tourism authorities to immediately look into the accommodation concerned, including its licensing status, safety and security measures,” Jafry said in a statement on Monday. “They will coordinate with the relevant enforcement agencies where necessary,” he said. Jafry warned that tourism operators, including accommodation providers, must ensure that their premises provide a safe and secure environment for guests and address weaknesses that arise. “As we move towards Visit Sabah 2027, we will not compromise on visitor safety. Sabah must continue to be a destination where visitors feel safe, respected and welcomed,” he said. He also welcomed the police’s swift arrest of the 18-year-old suspect linked to the incident. “I view the reported incident involving a Chinese tourist at a resort in Semporna with utmost seriousness. The safety and security of every visitor to Sabah must remain our highest priority,” Jafry added. On Sunday, Semporna Superintendent Tan Hiap Wah said a teenage suspect was arrested in connection with the alleged molestation and assault of a 25-year-old tourist from China in a room at a resort on Jalan Kamiri at 3am on Saturday. He said initial investigations found that the woman was sleeping alone when she realised an unknown man was inside her room. She managed to flee the suspect during the assault and hid in nearby bushes until a resort worker found her the next morning. She suffered injuries during the incident. The case is being investigated under Sections 448 and 354 of the Penal Code for house trespass and assault or use of criminal force with intent to outrage a person’s modesty. This story was first published by The Star

title: Brazilian serial killer suspect nicknamed ‘Mosquito’ dressed as a woman
description: Investigator reveals new details on suspect caught in a dress and wig carrying an unrelated baby after evading police for years.
content: A man accused of killing 16 people in a remote part of Brazil avoided capture by hiding in the woods, the police investigator responsible for his arrest said on Monday. Douglas Garcia, the investigator who led the two-day pursuit for 33-year-old Jorlan Lopes da Silva that ended on September 13, told Associated Press that the suspect used to hide in the thick bush in his own makeshift camps. The killings linked to da Silva occurred within the last three months in the isolated region of Mulungu in Brazil’s northeastern state of Paraiba. Garcia added that da Silva was nicknamed “Mosquito” by locals because of his frail build. “That allowed him to evade capture for years,” Garcia said. “Jorlan lived mostly in the woods, that’s why it was so hard to find him and link him to crimes that didn’t seem to be connected at first.” Garcia said police finally saw the link between da Silva and other crimes after he shot an 18-year-old dead in a public square. The investigator said the serial killer claims he has only attacked criminals, but evidence collected thus far shows that was not the case. Garcia also said da Silva is providing evidence he committed more crimes than those he is being prosecuted for but added he cannot discuss further details as some investigations continue and others are being reopened. The investigator said the identity of the victims and details about their deaths are being kept confidential so the prosecution can do its work. Da Silva was captured wearing a black dress with white stripes, a wig and painted nails. He was carrying a baby that authorities confirmed was not related to him, but they did not provide any other details. “This is a very different person, he said he killed for the first time at age 13,” Garcia said. “We caught him because he wasn’t able to reach his tent in the woods, so he, out of desperation, got that disguise, took that baby that is not his and was ultimately arrested,” Garcia said. Police said at the time that da Silva was a member of a criminal gang that has killed dozens of people in the region. He denies any affiliation with local gangs and told investigators upon his arrest that he was “in a personal war”. The region of Mulungu, where the recent killings took place, lies 2,500km (1,553 miles) north of Rio de Janeiro.

title: After chaotic start, are five-time Hong Kong champions a club in crisis or transition?
description: Eastern in funk following three defeats, manager’s exit, vice-captain’s resignation and player quitting after one match.
content: Having long ago agreed to coaching duties with Hong Kong this week, the interim Eastern head coach Cristiano Cordeiro has landed himself with a calendar clash. “It’s chaos,” he said, a light-hearted comment that would aptly describe Eastern’s embryonic campaign. Beaten in their opening match by newly promoted Supreme Sha Tin, who have since lost four straight games, Eastern then received two red cards in a 4–1 defeat by Tai Po. One of them went to Leung Kwun-chung, who duly resigned as vice-captain. Respite arrived the following week in the shape of a 4-0 victory over Kowloon City, a match lit up by the deft forward play of Lolo Pla, who crowned his debut with a fine individual strike. The result was not enough to save Manu Torres, the head coach, who multiple sources have told the South China Morning Post was unpopular among Eastern’s players and staff. He left on September 8, along with three of his backroom team. Appointed in January, Torres was given carte blanche to recruit 12 players this summer, including three from his native Spain, and another two with dual Spanish nationality. The 50-year-old also sanctioned the releases at the end of last season of key figures and big personalities in Calum Hall, Dani Almazan, Wong Tsz-ho, Manuel Bleda and Gil Martins. Days before Cordeiro managed the team in a banana-skin fixture away at bottom-team BC Rangers on Sunday, striker Pla, the father of a very young child, quit the club for “personal reasons”, leaving a beleaguered fanbase with wistful memories of his lone appearance. Eastern had the better of the game against Rangers in every metric other than where it mattered, failing to take a handful of chances before sloppily conceding the only goal to Flavio Tico with eight minutes remaining. After four straight defeats to begin their season, Rangers are off the mark. “Our start has been typical of the Hong Kong league this season, because there’s been a bit of turmoil everywhere,” Cordeiro said. “Everything is happening so fast, there are so many opinions, and you have less time to actually work.” Immediately after the Rangers loss, combustible midfielder Lam Hin-ting, 26, and Leung Chun-pong, the veteran captain, were seen engaging in a furious row. Subsequently, Cordeiro, Frankie Yau Wing-keung, the vice-chairman, and experienced keeper Yapp Hung-fai, back in a matchday squad for the first time since he tore an anterior cruciate ligament while earning his 112th Hong Kong cap in Bangladesh last year, staged an extensive post-match debrief on the Tsing Yi Sports Ground sidelines. They had a lot to pick over, given that Eastern have appeared a club treading water at best since a macabre AFC Champions League 2 campaign late last year. Across their closing four matches, they conceded 26 goals and scored one. After a 7-0 home defeat by Ratchaburi of Thailand last November, head coach Roberto Losada told the SCMP: “I’m devastated, we built up something very beautiful over the past three years, and it’s gone. Just like that … it’s gone.” The following month, so was he, Losada appointed Hong Kong boss after 4½ years with Eastern in which he delivered two FA Cups and one Senior Shield, and was three times named the city’s manager of the year. Cordeiro, 53, who had two years in charge of five-time Hong Kong champions Eastern from 2013, said that after the ACL 2 humblings, “we suffered a lot and morale went down a bit”. “But we have 12 new players, and we’re trying to get on track,” Cordeiro said. “Football happens in cycles, we’d been doing well for four years, and eventually you have one or two seasons where you have to readapt and find solutions,” he added, pointing to the example of Kitchee suffering a trophyless campaign in 2024-25, before winning the league title last season. “You learn and change until things get better.” Damian Dai, the formerly influential development director, has taken a step back this term, leaving Yau with the majority of decision-making responsibility. Cordeiro was non-committal over whether he wanted a job once held by England’s World Cup-winning captain Bobby Moore, saying only that “We’re in a transitional period, and as long as the club needs me to help, I’ve no problem with that”. He added that Eastern power brokers were “taking their time” before appointing, “because they want to make sure the guy they bring here is going to be fit for the job, and for the idea they have for the club”. Other than a League Cup game against Kitchee on Saturday, which they can afford to lose and still stay in the peculiar iteration of this season’s competition, Eastern have 18 days until their next match. Nonetheless, a home date with powerful North District on October 9 looks like a hospital pass for any prospective new manager. Cordeiro is set to oversee the Kitchee fixture, then rejoin Hong Kong to assist Losada for the city team’s opening Asean Cup game against Laos the following day. A former Hong Kong defender who was the city’s footballer of the year in 2001 and 2005, the Brazil-born Cordeiro said there had been a change in mood since Torres’s exit. “There always is after a manager leaves, no matter whether they were winning or losing,” he added. “The players are more open, and they’re embracing the ideas we’re giving them. “Their effort in training has been amazing, and if we’d converted one of the chances against Rangers in the opening 15 minutes it would have been a different game.” Ultimately, they ran out of legs against a team that, at 25.2, boasted an average age three years younger than Eastern’s 28.2. The district team fielded two 39-year-olds in Leung and Marcos Gondra, who is worryingly indispensable, and only three players under 25. One of them, the versatile 17-year-old Fred Yang Wong, delivered a tenacious performance at left-back that offered hope of brighter days ahead. He was replaced towards the end by Uriel Contiero, one of three 16-year-olds on the bench. “Fred has so much to develop, but he’s a kid you can count on to give 100 per cent of what he has,” Cordeiro said. “In Hong Kong, that’s more than enough. He has qualities, and he’ll keep developing. We’re trying to find solutions, and I think he’ll be part of the club in future.”

title: Style Edit: Fashion Asia Hong Kong 2026 asks what’s next for design and who will shape it
description: This year’s programme debuted the 10 Asian Designers to Watch runway, featuring labels from Hong Kong, mainland China, South Korea, Thailand, and the Philippines.
content: Fashion rarely stands still, and the forces shaping it – from changing consumer tastes and regional growth to the need for more convincing brand narratives – are moving particularly fast. At Fashion Asia Hong Kong 2026, the Fashion Challenges Forum turned its attention to those pressures, bringing industry figures together at Kimpton Tsim Sha Tsui Hong Kong on September 4. Rather than treating fashion as a purely aesthetic pursuit, the forum approached it as a business in connection with culture, commerce and new audiences. The Luxury Dialogue examined business strategies for leading luxury brands, while a session on the rise of Southeast Asian luxury considered Thai commercial milestones and emerging-market opportunities. Elsewhere, speakers discussed the global growth of menswear, the cultural role of fashion exhibitions and the value of authentic storytelling for brands seeking consumer connection. The line-up reflected that wide-angle view and included globally renowned fashion sourcer Gab Waller; Kayla Wong, founder of Los Angeles-based concept store Lang; Longchamp Asia-Pacific general manager Samy Redjeb; Sara Sozzani Maino, creative director of Fondazione Sozzani, among others. Running in parallel was the 10th edition of 10 Asian Designers To Watch, which made its runway debut on September 3 alongside the Hong Kong Fashion Fest Gala. Ten designers from Hong Kong, mainland China, South Korea, Thailand and the Philippines presented collections, placing contemporary Asian design and its range of approaches centre stage. The cohort included Hong Kong’s Kinyan Lam and Tigerstrolling; Chén Sifān, Nullus, Sean Suen and WMWM from mainland China; Leje from South Korea; Disaya from Thailand; and Maligaya Clothing Co. and Novel from the Philippines. Meovv member Gawon attended in exclusive looks by Disaya and Leje. To give the public a closer look beyond the runway, an accompanying exhibition was held at Peak Galleria until September 13. Fashion Asia is a flagship programme of Hong Kong Fashion Fest, sponsored by the Cultural and Creative Industries Development Agency under the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau, and organised by Hong Kong Design Centre.

title: Opinion | How Hong Kong can keep the talking going when US-China officials don’t
description: Hong Kong can’t set the terms of the contest, but with Track 1.5 diplomacy, it can decide if it is the room in which competition is managed.
content: When Tung Chee-hwa died, the obituaries predictably described a Hong Kong shipping mogul who became the city’s first postcolonial chief executive. How his government navigated the Asian financial crisis and severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) epidemic and its retreat from Article 23 were highlighted. There was less attention paid to the political hybrid he embodied. Tung sat as vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, until 2023 – state-leader rank, no diplomatic portfolio. His working instrument was the China-United States Exchange Foundation, which he established in Hong Kong in 2008, the year marking the 30th anniversary of Sino-US relations, to keep senior Americans and Chinese talking when their governments would not. Standing without a mandate, exercised through a private vehicle: that is Track 1.5, and Tung was very good at it. At the recent China-US Track 1.5 Dialogue in Beijing, Liu Haixing, head of the Communist Party’s International Department, said both countries should expand the “pie” of shared interests and reject zero-sum games to reach “normal stability with controllable disagreements”. This is not the stuff of summit headlines but of realistic ambition: neither a friendship nor a divorce, but a managed rivalry where shared interests can grow and the rest is fenced off. Track 1.5 is a hybrid of official governmental negotiation and purely unofficial civil society dialogue. Its participants – former officials, scholars, trusted business figures – engage in unofficial discourse. They move faster than foreign ministries, without bureaucratic protocol or legislative oversight, and can explore common ground as a foundation for future diplomacy. The format survives when everything formal has frozen. Hong Kong should care about this more than any other Asian city, and stop treating it as something that happens elsewhere, about Hong Kong, rather than here, because of Hong Kong. The city is already downstream of every one of these conversations. Hong Kong-registered entities sit in the path of each new round of American trade enforcement, and semi-official dialogue is where boundaries get signalled before anyone reaches for a designation – and where the specifics of how export controls land on a hub like ours get parsed. Because Hong Kong runs on a distinct legal framework, its forums are also where global business makes the case to both capitals that decoupling would hurt everyone. When official contact stalls, these networks keep the lines open. Three lanes suggest themselves. The first is research and development. Five Hong Kong universities sit in the Quacquarelli Symonds global top 100 ranking and, for the first time, two in the top 20. Research is the least securitised corner of the US-China relationship – climate, public health, ageing, learning science. Where a mainland university and an American one now hesitate to sign directly, a Hong Kong institution can host the laboratory, hold the data and lead the steering committee. That is Track 1.5 in a lab coat. The second is institution-based exchange. Hong Kong already houses bodies, such as the Yidan Prize Foundation, whose mandate is cross-border and non-political by design. These are the natural scaffolding for semi-official contact – institutions with standing in both capitals, able to seat a former assistant secretary beside a retired vice-minister without a flag on the door. The third is student-to-student exchange. The generation that managed the opening up of China and the US to each other in the 1970s had lived in each other’s countries. Today, fewer than 2,000 Americans study in mainland China, down from around 11,000 in 2019. Hong Kong – English-speaking, common law, half an hour from Shenzhen – is the most credible place to rebuild student ties. Plans to allow non-locals in public universities to rise to half of the local cohort are an invitation the city has not yet fully sent. Track 1.5 is not one conference; it is the critical mass of events that makes a city the default choice. Hong Kong holds most of the pieces: a three-runway airport, the Skycity and AsiaWorld-Expo expansion beside it, the “Study in Hong Kong” brand, and the convening power this year’s HSBC Global Investment Summit showed. Student accommodation is the binding constraint; converting commercial buildings into hostels is a start, not a solution. Visas should be processed in days. The peripheral programme – open days, industry visits, the reasons a delegation’s junior researchers want to return – matters as much as the plenary. And the talent pipeline must close the loop, so an exchange student can stay to work. “Normal stability” is rehearsed, by the same people meeting in the same rooms over years, until disagreements become controllable because people know each other. Hong Kong cannot set the terms of this competition, but it can decide whether it is the room in which the competition is managed. Tung spent two decades building one such room. The question is who builds the next, and whether it’s ready when needed.

title: Shadow of Xi summit hangs over Trump’s high-stakes talks with Japan’s Takaichi
description: Tokyo is determined to ensure its vital interests are not traded away when US and Chinese leaders meet later this week, analysts say.
content: When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi meets US President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, the leader casting the longest shadow over the meeting will not even be in the building. Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on Thursday – two days after Takaichi meets the US leader on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly. It will be Xi’s first state visit to the US in over 10 years. Faced with an unpredictable American president eager for tangible results ahead of what could be a tough November midterm election, Japan is working to ensure its vital interests are not traded away at the Xi-Trump summit. The Takaichi-Trump talks will unfold amid frosty ties between Tokyo and Beijing. Takaichi’s remarks last November that an attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan infuriated Beijing and sparked months of diplomatic freeze. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Experts said the timing of Takaichi’s meeting revealed Tokyo’s determination to prevent Washington from making concessions at the expense of Japan’s regional security and economic interests. They added that Beijing’s rare earth export controls and Taiwan would be featured in the Trump-Takaichi talks, with the Japanese prime minister using the opportunity to reiterate Tokyo’s perspective to the US leader. Beijing confirmed on Monday that Xi would make a three-day state visit to Washington from Wednesday to Friday - his third face-to-face meeting with Trump since the US president returned to office last year. Ahead of a meeting with Xi in South Korea last October, Trump visited Tokyo for hours of direct discussions with Takaichi. She reciprocated the visit in March for bilateral talks at the White House. This pattern reflects a deliberate strategy by Tokyo: maintaining personal rapport with Trump and securing assurances before Washington enters critical talks with Beijing, even as unpredictable US rhetoric continues to test allies’ coordination. “Tokyo’s priority is to prevent a US-China stabilisation deal from coming at the expense of Japan’s economic security or regional deterrence,” said Kenichi Doi, senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Japan. Japan would welcome more reliable flows of rare earths and other critical inputs, he added. “Tokyo will also want Washington to treat China’s dual-use restrictions on Japan as an alliance-wide supply-chain issue, given their potential spillovers through Japanese production into US industries,” he said. Doi said Takaichi was likely to seek confirmation of Washington’s commitment to peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait, along with closer alignment on critical minerals, export controls and wider economic security. Following Takaichi’s Taiwan comments, Beijing enforced strict dual-use export controls covering items destined for Japan, including critical minerals, rare earths and advanced tech. The rare earth restrictions loom large in Tuesday’s discussions. China controls 90 per cent of the world’s processed rare earths and at least 60 per cent of rare earth extraction, giving it considerable leverage. Asked on Monday whether rare earth exports to Japan would be addressed at the Xi-Trump summit, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said that restrictions on dual-use items were a necessary step to curb Japan’s remilitarisation and nuclear ambitions. Beijing has defended its restrictions as a direct countermeasure against Tokyo’s defence build-up. “In her own words, Takaichi sees Taiwan’s security as inextricably linked to Japan’s own,” said Sean King, senior vice-president at New York-based business advisory firm Park Strategies, adding that the Japanese leader was “unnerved by” Trump’s continued delay of an arms sales package to Taiwan. “She will surely be keeping a close eye on Trump’s summit with Xi Jinping to see if Trump again appears swayed,” he said, adding that Takaichi might worry the Diaoyu Islands, known in Japan as the Senkakus, could be next on the US president’s “reeducation list” if Trump were to start siding with Beijing on Taiwan. The Diaoyus are a group of uninhabited islands in the East China Sea claimed by Tokyo, Beijing and Taipei. The South China Morning Post reported earlier that Washington was considering postponing the announcement of arms sales to Taiwan until the end of the year, pointing to a planned bilateral meeting between Trump and Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and Xi’s expected visit to Florida for the Group of 20 summit in December. According to Doi, Tokyo’s worst-case outcome for the Xi-Trump summit would be if the US leader secures economic concessions from Beijing in exchange for shifting Washington’s position on the Taiwan Strait or technology controls “without sufficient coordination with its allies”. The timing of the meetings raises the question of whether Trump intends to use the impending Xi summit to squeeze Tokyo for concessions on burden-sharing, base hosting costs or currency valuations. However, analysts believe obvious discord between the US and its foremost Asian ally would undermine Trump’s own diplomatic leverage. “Trump is transactional with Japan, but he has little incentive to manufacture a visible dispute with Tokyo two days before negotiating with Xi,” Doi said. “Extracting marginal concessions now at the cost of displaying alliance friction would weaken, rather than strengthen, Washington’s hand with Beijing.” Doi said Tuesday’s meeting between Trump and Takaichi would be more about showing policy alignment before Xi’s visit. King agreed that Washington’s commercial posture towards Tokyo was relatively stable, noting that Japan remained the top foreign direct investor in the United States. “The purpose of Tuesday’s talk is to remind everyone that Japan is America’s premier Asian ally and that mainland China is a geostrategic rival, and Japan is the US’ anchor in Asia, as it were,” he said.

title: Hong Kong animal groups call for tighter pet laws after suspected fatal mauling
description: Former guard dogs may turn aggressive due to territorial instincts or past trauma, welfare advocates warn as government pledges review of policies.
content: Animal welfare groups in Hong Kong have called for a legal loophole in pet ownership laws to be closed to better protect public safety, after authorities pledged to review stray dog policies following Sunday’s suspected fatal mauling of a woman. The groups said that, based on their experience, the 27-year-old victim was more likely to have been attacked by former warehouse guard dogs than strays. But existing legal provisions made it difficult to prosecute owners who failed to microchip or properly secure their animals, they said. Police suspect a pack of dogs attacked the woman, who was found unconscious beside a bicycle in Yuen Long on Sunday and later died, less than a month after a similar canine-related case. The victim suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs. Police said that, in addition to stray dogs, wild boars had also been spotted in the area. The incident prompted police and the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) to round up strays in the area. At least three mongrels had been captured by Monday evening. A source said that bite-mark analysis and DNA tests were being carried out to determine whether any of the captured dogs were involved in the attack. Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan pledged on Monday to review policies on stray dogs and further reduce the risks they pose. But Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, argued that dogs born as strays rarely attacked humans, while former warehouse dogs were highly protective of their territory. “Stray dogs in Hong Kong rarely attack people as they are very scared of humans,” Luk said. “Many strays constantly cower and shrink back as many have been bullied and are afraid other dogs will attack them.” Luk said he had been barked at and chased by warehouse dogs while travelling through rural areas to carry out rescues, although he noted that the animals were merely trying to drive him away from their territory. “Dogs bark out of fear,” he said. Luk said warehouses had previously operated near the site of the attack, but it was unclear whether guard dogs had been rehomed after the facilities were demolished or had become abandoned, free-roaming dogs in the area. Mark Mak Chi-ho, executive chairman of the non-profit Veterinary Services Society, also said that, while authorities had yet to identify the animals involved, warehouse dogs had strong territorial instincts that could trigger defensive or retaliatory aggression against trespassers. Mak said the primary distinction was between dogs socialised as pets and those that were not. Domesticated pets were cherished by their owners, did not have to fight for basic survival or food, and rarely attacked or bit people without provocation, he said. Dogs that had not been socialised tended to live in packs led by a dominant animal and could be aggressive at times, he added. “They are forced to live this kind of life in society with these capabilities just to survive,” Mak said. Mak said a legal loophole made it difficult to prosecute the owners of free-roaming dogs, because they had little incentive to microchip the animals. “As long as one does not microchip the dog, one can deny abandoning it,” Mak said. He urged the government to incorporate a strict “duty of care” into the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Ordinance – requiring owners to ensure their dog’s safety, walk them responsibly and fulfil basic care obligations – to hold negligent owners accountable. “If you have possession of a dog without microchipping, and without fulfilling your duty as a keeper, that should directly constitute an offence,” Mak said. He noted that free-roaming warehouse dogs were unique to Hong Kong. “These are not stray dogs, but unrecorded, unregistered free-roaming working dogs; they come and go without a trace,” he said. Luk said he had experienced warehouse dogs chasing his car, possibly because they had been traumatised after being hit by vehicles. He also cited cases in which cyclists startled by barking had thrown stones at dogs, potentially conditioning the animals to associate bicycles with threats. He said the AFCD had told him that one of the three dogs caught on Sunday carried a microchip registered in his name, and that he had been asked to give a statement on Wednesday. He explained that it was common practice among dog rescuers to microchip animals under their own names after treating their injuries or spaying them because unchipped dogs would otherwise have no registered keeper and could face euthanasia if they bit someone and were captured. Some owners were reluctant to have their dogs microchipped, and even claimed that the animals were not theirs and that they merely fed them, so as to avoid legal responsibility, Luk added. According to the AFCD, the number of strays captured fell from 463 in 2023 to 398 in 2025. Complaints involving stray dogs rose from 1,230 in 2023 to 1,554 in 2024, before declining slightly to 1,232 in 2025. There were 482 complaints in the first three months of 2026. Under Section 22 of the Rabies Ordinance, an animal keeper who abandons an animal without reasonable excuse commits an offence punishable by a maximum fine of HK$10,000 (US$1,274) and six months’ imprisonment, an AFCD spokesman said. But no prosecutions have been brought under that provision. “While the evidential threshold for prosecution against abandonment is high and may be difficult to achieve, the AFCD will generally proceed to prosecute keepers failing to keep their animals under control and causing that animal to wander into a public place, where prosecution shall be pursued in accordance with Section 23 of the Rabies Ordinance or Section 9 of the Dangerous Dogs Regulation,” the spokesman said. Prosecution figures in the past three years in accordance with Section 23 or Section 9 stood at 258, 215 and 206. The spokesman added that anyone who caused unnecessary suffering to an animal, whether through an act or omission, could be prosecuted for animal cruelty and face a maximum fine of HK$200,000 and three years’ imprisonment.

title: Despite higher costs, Hong Kong’s student residences attract mainland Chinese renters
description: Dedicated housing offers greater convenience, security and value despite higher rents, students say.
content: Purpose-built student accommodation is drawing mainland Chinese university students away from Hong Kong’s traditional rental market, as professionally managed residences gain favour despite charging higher rents than many private flats. Some students said dedicated student housing offered greater convenience, stronger security, more predictable costs and a better living environment, helping offset higher rents and, in some cases, longer commutes. Qi Zhonghao, a mainland Chinese student pursuing a master’s degree in robotics at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), said he spent a year living in a subdivided unit – converted from a village house near the university – because of the limited availability of on-campus housing, before moving to an off-campus student residence. “Rents for this type of subdivided unit are relatively low,” he said. “A single room with a private bathroom costs around HK$7,000 [US$890] to HK$8,000 a month, and it’s quite close to university.” However, the units lacked communal kitchens and generally prohibited cooking, forcing residents to rely on takeaway food or eat at restaurants, which could significantly increase living costs over time, Qi said. He added that such accommodation typically offered limited security and property management services, leading to slower responses when repairs were needed. “I currently live at Brim Youth, a private student accommodation,” Qi said. “The facilities here are comprehensive, including a gym, a communal kitchen and activity spaces. What’s especially convenient is the weekly cleaning service, which gives me a lot of time to rest.” According to its website, Brim Youth is the first flagship long-term youth rental project in Hong Kong developed by China Resources Longdation. The property, formerly Hotel Cozi Oasis (Tsuen Wan), is about a 10-minute walk from Kwai Hing MTR station. Monthly rents for single rooms start at HK$9,600. The accommodation comes fully furnished, so there’s no need to buy any furniture Fan, Hong Kong Polytechnic University student “The rent is still within my budget,” Qi said. “Since it includes utilities like water, electricity and internet charges, monthly housing expenses are relatively clear and fixed.” The appeal of purpose-built student housing comes as demand for accommodation rises. CBRE estimated earlier this month that the number of higher-education students in Hong Kong would increase by 150,000 by 2035, creating demand for at least 70,000 additional student beds. Driven by immense market demand, a number of Chinese giants – including China Resources Longdation, China Merchants Group, JD.com and CICC Capital – have made high-profile moves over the past two years, acquiring hotels and commercial-residential buildings for student housing projects. China Merchants Commercial Real Estate Investment Trust (CMC Reit) announced late last month it had completed a HK$528.5 million acquisition of The Quad – a student accommodation building in Hung Hom – from Easyknit International. The property has since been incorporated into the company’s CM+U student housing brand, providing 205 beds. In response to inquiries from the South China Morning Post, CMC Reit said occupancy at CM+U in Hung Hom stood at 100 per cent. Average monthly rent was about HK$8,000 for a bed space and between HK$12,500 and HK$17,000 for a single room. Market sources said the project’s net yield was projected at 4.8 per cent after operating costs, based on its 184 rooms and 205 beds. Brandy, originally from Beijing and currently a master’s student in Chinese history and culture at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, lives at CM+U in Tsim Sha Tsui. She said student accommodation offered better value than many private housing options. She said surrounding private residential estates often felt crowded because of high building density, while some developments had ageing facilities and long waits for lifts during the morning rush. Brandy also praised the strict management standards in student residences. “You have to submit your university offer letter upon check-in to prove your student status,” she said. “This ensures a consistent resident profile for the entire building, making it feel safer.” Fan, a first-year master’s student in language science and technology at Hong Kong Polytechnic University, lives at the same accommodation as Brandy. While rents were not low compared with private housing, she said the accommodation offered excellent value for money. “The accommodation comes fully furnished, so there’s no need to buy any furniture,” she said. “When I moved in, they even provided daily essentials, which saved me the hassle of moving and settling into a new environment.” Private residential estates along railway lines have traditionally been popular among mainland Chinese students, but they are now facing competition from student accommodation. Now Wong, district associate director at Midland Realty, cited City One Shatin as an example. “There has been a noticeable drop in the number of tenants at City One Shatin this summer,” he added. “In previous years, the estate would face a severe shortage of available rental units by early August. This year, a significant number of units remained available for viewing even as late as the end of August.”

title: China’s MLCC market splits in 2 as AI server demand outpaces consumer electronics
description: Shenzhen distributors say speculative buying in consumer MLCCs is fading, but demand for AI server parts continues to strain supply.
content: In China’s hardware hub in Shenzhen, the speculative frenzy around consumer multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) has cooled into a sharp price correction, but prices for artificial intelligence server components remain elevated. Spot prices for consumer-grade MLCCs, often dubbed the “the rice of the electronics industry”, have fallen by two-thirds from their peak two months ago, according to Wang Jun, an MLCC distributor in Huaqiangbei, a commercial zone in the city known for electronic parts. However, prices remained higher than before the rally, which was “more speculative rather than driven by downstream demand”, said Wang, manager at Tongxin Chuanghui Technology, which trades imported MLCCs from global leaders including Murata Manufacturing and Samsung Electro-Mechanics (Semco). The segment recently saw a modest rebound after reports emerged that Murata would discontinue production of some consumer MLCC models, Wang said, adding that prices for mainstream products were likely to stabilise. “From what I see, the market for consumer MLCCs is reaching saturation, and domestic companies have ramped up aggressively to meet that demand,” Wang told the South China Morning Post on Monday. In contrast, demand for server-grade MLCCs remains robust in Huaqiangbei. Another distributor said prices of high-capacitance MLCCs used in AI servers had risen by up to five-fold over the past year. “Supply for server MLCCs is definitely the most critically tight,” said the vendor, who trades MLCCs from major Japanese makers including Murata, TDK and Taiyo Yuden. A report by Chinese national broadcaster CCTV on Sunday cited Huaqiangbei vendors saying some high-demand models had surged to as much as 10 times their original prices after the rally began in June, while gains in consumer-grade MLCCs proved short-lived amid weak demand for consumer electronics. As leading suppliers scale back lower-margin mature parts numbers, Chinese manufacturers appear well positioned to expand sales in those areas Kazunori Ito, Morningstar MLCCs are among the smallest but most essential components in modern electronic devices, from smartphones to electric vehicles. The rapid buildout of AI data centres has fuelled demand for AI server-grade MLCCs, which require more advanced specifications, including smaller sizes, ultra-high capacitance, and long-term reliability. While spot prices for consumer MLCCs in Huaqiangbei have fallen from their peak, contract prices from major manufacturers have continued to rise. Semco was expected to raise prices for consumer-grade products by an average of 25 to 30 per cent, as it sought to curb orders and free capacity for higher-end production lines, according to a TrendForce report in August. Global leaders are increasingly shifting their capacity away from mature parts to meet AI-related demand. Murata, the world’s largest MLCC maker, was expected to halt production of selected models across nine product series for general-purpose and automotive applications, according to a report by Taiwanese outlet Commercial Times earlier this month. “As leading suppliers scale back lower-margin mature parts numbers, Chinese manufacturers appear well positioned to expand sales in those areas,” Morningstar director Kazunori Ito told the SCMP on Monday. While Chinese MLCC makers still lagged behind major Japanese and Korean suppliers in the highest-end categories, they had been improving their competitiveness in standard products and parts of the mid-to-upper range by leveraging local material sourcing, proximity to Chinese electronics manufacturers, and cost advantages, Ito said. “As Japanese and Korean suppliers continue shifting capacity towards the highest-end products, opportunities for Chinese manufacturers to win customer qualifications in the mid-tier segment are likely to expand,” Ito said. Local vendors also expect Chinese firms to catch up in AI server MLCCs. “Domestic MLCCs for AI applications are still in the trial phase, but I believe they will achieve major breakthroughs in the near future,” said a manager surnamed Wei at Lanbaike Electronics, a distributor of electronics components.

title: Moscow’s asset seizures unnerve Japanese companies in Russia
description: The takeover of Swiss and French brands raises the spectre of retaliation against some 230 Japanese businesses still in Russia.
content: More than 200 Japanese companies still operating in Russia face growing uncertainty following Moscow’s seizure of three Western firms’ assets, amid deteriorating diplomatic relations. The Kremlin announced on Friday that the assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, French retailer Auchan and home improvement chain Lemana Pro had been transferred to Russian entity LEV Management under a decree signed a day earlier by President Vladimir Putin. “These are unfriendly nations,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said while announcing the decision to introduce “external management”. He added that the countries involved were either “actively involved in military actions against our country” or had “engaged in strikes by the Kyiv regime on our civilian and economic infrastructure”. About 230 Japanese-affiliated companies continue to operate in Russia, according to the Japan External Trade Organisation, though many have frozen operations or halted new investments. More than three-quarters of these companies expected to maintain a business presence in Russia for at least the next two years, a survey conducted in June by the organisation found. “Japanese companies are going to be watching very closely what happens next, and they are going to be concerned,” said Yakov Zinberg, a professor of international relations at Tokyo’s Kokushikan University. Japan-Russia ties have been in the doldrums since the Ukraine war began in 2022, with Tokyo joining other G7 nations in imposing broad economic and diplomatic sanctions. While surveys indicated almost half of British, 33 per cent of Canadian and 27 per cent of US companies completely withdrew from Russia following the invasion, few Japanese firms followed suit – likely hoping for a swift end to the war, according to observers. But tensions between Moscow and Tokyo have been ratcheting up in recent months. Eisuke Mori, the speaker of Japan’s House of Representatives, visited Kyiv this month to meet President Volodymyr Zelensky, who invited Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to visit the Ukrainian capital. He condemned Russia’s invasion as “a barbaric act that shakes the international order and the values that the international community has built over decades”, in comments to Ukraine’s parliament. It followed a high-profile visit last month by Putin to a chain of disputed islands north of Hokkaido that Tokyo protested against and Moscow summarily dismissed. Russia later unveiled a statue depicting a Soviet soldier crushing a border marker bearing the symbol of Japan’s emperor. Moscow would be closely watching the UN General Assembly in New York this week for a potential Zelensky-Takaichi meeting, said James Brown, an international-relations professor specialising in Russian affairs at Temple University’s Tokyo campus. “Up until now, the Japanese side has been able to avoid a face-to-face meeting for any number of reasons, but it is going to be much more difficult for Takaichi to do that when they are both in New York and this is at the request of the Ukrainians,” he said. “Not meeting Zelensky would not be a good image and would indicate that Takaichi is trying to distance herself from Ukraine.” But agreeing to the meeting could prompt Russia to target Japanese companies, Brown said, adding that Tokyo would be “very wary about losing its stake” in Russian liquefied natural gas projects. Japan held a 10 per cent stake in Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project in northern Siberia and a 30 per cent stake in Sakhalin 1, north of Hokkaido, he said. Concerns over energy security explained why Takaichi had been so “timid” in her dealings with Moscow, Brown said. Yet closing down Japanese companies’ operations would also be “self-defeating” for Russia, he said. “These businesses pay taxes and seizing them would cut off a significant amount of tax for the Russian government,” Brown said, adding that consumer backlash over the loss of popular brands would also pose a challenge. Zinberg said he expected both sides to proceed with caution, even as they “keep complaining about the other”. “Russia’s policy towards Japan is still rooted in old Soviet attitudes and their leaders are aware that they still need Japan,” he said. “The old approach was to try to drive a wedge between Japan and the US, and they are still following that approach.” This Week in Asia contacted seven major Japanese companies operating in Russia for comment, including Panasonic, Olympus, Japan Tobacco and cosmetics firms Kao Corp and Shiseido, but had received no response at the time of publication.

title: Bukhara Biennial spearheads cultural blossoming of the city as well as the wider Uzbekistan
description: With site-specific artwork displayed in restored or adapted historical structures, the inaugural Bukhara Biennial heralded the development of a cultural district designed for residents and visitors alike.
content: It might sound and look like an odd juxtaposition: chef-nun Jeong Kwan, of Netflix documentary series Chef’s Table fame, unearthing kimchi she has been fermenting for 10 weeks next to a new installation by British sculptor Antony Gormley. Yet, set in Bukhara’s 16th century Khoja Kalon Mosque, the two made perfect sense as collaborative highlights of the closing ceremony of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, which ran from September 5 to November 23 last year. A contemporary art festival, the Bukhara Biennial was conceived by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF) and forms part of a broader plan to revitalise Uzbekistan’s living heritage as well as establish a permanent cultural district in the historic city. Its first theme, “Recipes for Broken Hearts”, was inspired by Uzbekistan’s national dish, plov. A hearty meal of rice layered with meat, spices and vegetables, the ideas of healing and restoration imbued in plov were the conceptual crux of the gastronomy, art, craft, architecture, music and performance on display. Gormley’s Close (2025) – created from mud bricks with Uzbek artist Temur Jumaev – channelled the theme by exploring vulnerability, communal recovery and a reconnection to ancestral roots. Jeong Kwan’s kimchi was woven into a collaborative culinary performance with Indian artist Subodh Gupta. Blending Korean temple food with Bihari fare, the hybrid meal was served inside Gupta’s pavilion-like installation, Salt Carried With the Wind (2024-25), situated outside the Ayozjon Caravanserai, one of four in an interconnected complex, on a site once occupied by Bukhara’s spice market. All through the event, the locations were significant, as the Bukhara Biennial was designed to house site-specific installations, soundscapes and performances not in purpose-built, white-cube galleries, but in restored or adapted caravanserais (merchant inns), madrasas (educational institutions), trading domes and mosques. While fellow Silk Road stopover Samarkand and the national capital, Tashkent, are undergoing their own cultural transformations, this preservation-first approach is what sets Bukhara apart. Since its establishment in the 6th century BC as one of the main centres of the Persian Empire, Bukhara’s status grew as a spiritual nexus for Sufism and as an intellectual hub and home to scholars, poets and artisans. That Bukhara has lived many lives is evident from both its monumental buildings, spanning the 5th to 20th centuries, and the most intricately embroidered gold zardosi motifs and ikat prints on silks and various textiles found in the shops of the Old Town. In the city’s Registan square, the curved, mounded walls of the Ark of Bukhara, a sizeable citadel, stand tall. Built in the 5th century, the compound housed rulers and their courts until 1920, when it was attacked by the Soviet Red Army, which deposed the emir of Bukhara and established Bolshevik rule. Next to the fortress stands the most prominent reminder of that later era: the steely, industrial Shukhov Tower, a water supply, forming a visual paradox that differentiates Bukhara from the more uniform Tashkent, where the Soviet influence is starkly evident in the brutalist buildings that dominate that city. Across the street from the Ark of Bukhara, the early-18th century Bolo Hauz Mosque dazzles with its intricate, three-dimensional muqarnas decoration and vibrant mosaic tilework. Its linear lines present a striking contrast to the more rounded, ancient structures elsewhere in the Old Town, both charting the evolution of Islamic architecture. Just a short walk away stands the 10th century Ismail Samani Mausoleum, the soft, circular geometry and woven pattern capturing an aesthetic from when the region’s prominent Zoroastrian community was in the early stages of converting to Islam. Revitalising these venerated sites, and others, was a crucial aspect of the agenda, as “the plan to reanimate restored and previously closed landmarks and open them up as living sites of making and dialogue was […] appreciated not only by the inhabitants of Bukhara, but also the tourists”, claims Gayane Umerova, chairwoman of the ACDF and the commissioner behind the inaugural Bukhara Biennial. She enlisted Dubai- and Tokyo-based Lebanese architect Wael Al Awar and his studio, Waiwai, to execute this vision, to revive and make accessible to its inhabitants as much of Bukhara’s history as possible. In addition to repairing mosques, caravanserais and other structures, the most dramatic intervention the architect made was to pedestrianise large parts of the Old Town. “We created outdoor spaces, seating and platforms where the local community could gather recreationally, and use beyond the biennial,” says Al Awar. Aligned with Umerova’s desire to present Uzbek artists and artisans on a global stage, the curatorial theme of the first Bukhara Biennial was born from curator Diana Campbell’s interest in rice cultures. “Most cultures use rice in some way, and there’s some version of plov in every culture,” says Campbell, citing the likes of biryani, paella, Korean bap with kimchi and West African jollof rice, all of which were served to the public at the Rice Cultures Feast, another part of the closing programme. A key aim of the event was to stimulate local communities, the ACDF having spent seven years researching and mapping out the forms of craft across the country. “Supporting artisans is part of a strategy to develop the creative industry in Uzbekistan,” says Umerova. “We are looking at ways to nurture what we have already, by protecting our heritage and developing a framework that is sustainable and inclusive for artisans.” All 70 artworks – each a collaboration between a recognised artist and a local craftsperson or -people – were made on site, in Bukhara. “By placing artisans and craft masters at the heart of the programme and pairing them with international artists, we invited visitors to experience craft not as a souvenir product, but as a living, sophisticated cultural practice,” Umerova says. “It frames craftsmanship as something to observe, learn from and respect.” Some of the most transformational and noteworthy works were housed in the 16th century Gavkushon Madrasa, and highlighted the specific artisanal crafts Bukhara is celebrated for. Local ceramicist Abdulvahid Bukhoriy’s Blue Room (2024-25), made with coppersmith Jurabek Siddikov, was lined entirely with blue-glazed tiles produced by hand, the immersive installation featuring a central metal sculpture and delicate ceramic panels, the elements depicting aquatic motifs often found in Uzbek textiles – a nod to age-old beliefs that fish possess the power to absorb human illness. Miniature master Davlat Toshev transformed two adjoining rooms with his signature hand-painted “wallpaper”. Featuring traditional visual themes such as pomegranate trees, Toshev employed ebru, a marbled-paper painting technique widely believed to have originated in Bukhara. Toshev has a large studio in Bukhara’s Old Town, where he conducts workshops for deaf and mute children, using art as a method of expression and communication, as well as a way to keep traditional mediums alive. Less than 200 metres (656 feet) from the Gavkushon Madrasa, Brazilian artist Marina Perez Simão and Bukharan mosaic master Bakhtiyar Babamuradov mirrored the heavens. Across the courtyard floor of the Fathullajon Caravanserai – a 19th century Silk Road resting stop – they laid out Untitled (2024-25), a fantastical celestial map. Quickly becoming one of the event’s most photographed works, the vibrant installation paid homage to Uzbekistan’s legacy in astronomy and the creation of early space-mapping instruments. Kwan’s involvement in the Bukhara Biennial was more significant than it might have seemed at first glance, with members of the Koryo-saram, the Korean diaspora in Bukhara, assisting in the preparation of the kimchi and the resulting meal. In 1937, Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, concerned about the military threat from Japan, exiled 172,000 Koreans from the Russian Far East to Central Asia. Now, Uzbekistan is home to the world’s fifth-largest overseas Korean population. Increased global attention on Uzbekistan as a result of the Bukhara Biennial has established a gateway into a historically under-visited destination, and the massive funding poured into the exhibition marks an effort by the Shavkat Mirziyoyev administration to build cultural infrastructure, revitalise the nation’s creative landscape and attract foreign investment after nearly three decades of post-Soviet stagnation. “We want to inspire younger generations to take the creative path and to equip those already in the creative industries, including artisans, with the same opportunities and infrastructure they’d experience internationally,” says Umerova, noting that 40 per cent of the country’s population is under 35 years of age. Projects in the works for the city’s new cultural district include the Jadids’ Legacy Museum, scheduled to open in 2027. Set in the restored 19th century home of Usmon Khodjaev, a leader of the Jadid reform movement and the first president of the short-lived Bukhara People’s Soviet Republic (1920-24), the destination will be dedicated to the initiative that modernised education across Central Asia. Farther afield, in Tashkent, the Centre for Contemporary Arts (CCA Tashkent), housed in a former tram depot, opened earlier this month, and the National Museum of Uzbekistan is scheduled to launch in March 2028. “Since we launched the 2025 Bukhara Biennial, Uzbekistan has become globally recognised for its role in fostering arts and culture across Central Asia,” says Umerova, who notes that the opening of the CCA Tashkent marks “an exciting next step – and a historic moment, not just for the people of Tashkent, but for the citizens of Uzbekistan more widely. As the country’s first contemporary art centre, I believe it will inspire the next generation of artists, curators, poets and thinkers”. Bukhara’s inaugural biennial surpassed all expectations, clocking up a total of 1.8 million visitors. Umerova credits it with encouraging “a more thoughtful kind of tourism. People came not just to see monuments, but to understand the stories embedded in them”. Dates for the next edition of the Bukhara Biennial have been set for September 3 to November 21, 2027. Thai architect Kulapat Yantrasast will direct it, leaning on themes of urban space, ecology and sustainable development. In line with the ACDF’s mission to foster community involvement, admission to venues and public spaces will remain free. “When you bring art tourists, who actually look, care and value the work and sites, that’s a genius strategy,” says Campbell, who specialises in curating large-scale exhibitions centred on community engagement in regions with sparse cultural infrastructure, most notably as the artistic director of the Dhaka Art Summit, in Bangladesh. In an era defined by content overkill, the ability to evoke genuine awe and wonder sometimes feels like a lost art. In Bukhara, it is simply an ancient art form being powerfully revived.

title: Style according to … Dior Maison and Baby Dior’s artistic director Cordelia de Castellane
description: The Paris-based designer behind Sofitel’s Le Vestiaire uniform collection shares her favourite books, beauty essentials and travel finds.
content: Designer Cordelia de Castellane, artistic director of Dior Maison and Baby Dior, has recently partnered with Sofitel – one of the world’s top hotel brands – on Le Vestiaire, a collection of uniforms for Sofitel’s 25,000 employees. We asked the Paris-based designer to tell us about the range, which blends functionality and elegance to cater to the needs of the company’s staff, from front of house to housekeeping. She also shares her favourite finds from Paris and around the world. Beauty ritual A beautiful fragrance is essential to me – it creates a memory immediately. I also love nourishing skincare, especially products that give the skin comfort and glow rather than a “made-up” effect. I am faithful to elegant, timeless brands such as Dior, Guerlain, Sisley and La Mer. Insta inspo I love accounts that feel personal and visually generous. I enjoy following antique dealers, artists, decorators and artisans because they share a real eye for detail. Two of my favourite accounts are @themontydon and @willowcrossleycreates. Parisian soul I love places that feel intimate and full of soul: Musée de la Vie Romantique – it has such a poetic, hidden charm; Jardin du Palais-Royal – elegant, peaceful; Deyrolle – a magical cabinet of curiosities; Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen – wonderful for antiques and inspiration; [upscale brasseries] La Pagode de Cos and Le Voltaire – for that timeless Parisian atmosphere. Designing Le Vestiaire I didn’t want to impose one fixed look, but to create a flexible wardrobe that allows personal expression while still preserving Sofitel’s elegant French identity. We had to design for 25,000 employees across [more than] 120 hotels with very different climates, cultures and environments – from vibrant city hotels to peaceful resorts. Storied stays I have always admired hotels such as Claridge’s in London, The Carlyle in New York, and La Mamounia in Marrakech – each has a soul, a history and a very distinct elegance. I am also passionate about Scotland and its dramatic landscapes. Style icon I am inspired by women who have a natural sense of elegance rather than a constructed one. [American socialite] Lee Radziwill, for example, had that rare balance of sophistication, simplicity and personality. I also admire women who create their own world – not just through clothes, but through interiors, gestures, taste and attitude. Personal adornment My favourite pieces are always the ones with a story. I love jewellery that feels inherited even when it is new – something delicate, meaningful, and not too ostentatious. A jewel should accompany you, not overpower you – like my Jar ring. Cultural immersion I am very drawn to films, books or plays that create a world you want to stay in. I love classics as much as contemporary culture: a beautiful period film, a well-written novel, or a theatre production where every detail matters, from the costumes to the lighting. For books, I love Proust and Anna Karenina, while three of my favourite films are Lost in Africa (1994), Pretty Woman (1990) and The Leopard (1963). Objects of affection I love gifting something that feels personal and useful: beautiful linen napkins, a candle, a small antique object, or something for the table. France has such a strong culture of hospitality, so I like gifts that bring a little of that art de vivre into someone’s home.

title: Asian Games: Haughey back in action, fencers enter mix, 5 things to know on day 3
description: Siobhan Haughey, Cheung Ka-long and the women’s road race cycling team all have gold medals to defend in Japan.
content: The Asian Games is well under way, and for Hong Kong the belief that day three will bring more medals is largely guided by the fact that athletes who have been there and done that are back in action. Fencing starts at the Aichi Sky Expo on Tuesday, the swimming continues in Tokyo, and the women’s road cycling has the potential to serve up a surprise. Here there are five things to know as the region’s best get ready to do battle once again in Japan. Chasing gold Siobhan Haughey cruised to victory in the women’s 200m freestyle on Monday; she’s back little more than 12 hours later to start the defence of her 100m title. The Hongkonger has been in imperious form over the past two days, and anyone doubting her ability to still compete at this level, or at a higher one, should take a long hard look at themselves. From wondering whether she would retire after last year’s National Games, or if the drive was still there to be elite every day, now the question should be, what’s stopping her from going to Los Angeles and adding another Olympic medal to her collection in 2028? Haughey has the fastest qualifying time ahead of the morning heats, and also owns the Asian record and Games record over the distance. Cheung or Choi? The double Olympic champion or former world champion, Cheung Ka-long and Ryan Choi Chun-yin will probably meet at some point in the fight for individual foil gold. Kept apart in the pool stage, with Choi in Pool 2 and his teammate in Pool 3, the pair should cruise through the early stages before the serious business of the elimination rounds begins by lunchtime. There will of course be plenty of competition. Three years ago in Hangzhou, South Korea’s fencers dominated proceedings, winning half of the 12 golds up for grabs. With China also strong, they are likely to be the biggest hurdles that Kaylin Hsieh Sin-yan and her teammates face, with the women’s individual épée also taking place on Tuesday in Nagoya. A surprise ride It is easy to forget among all the talk of Ceci Lee Sze-wing’s goals and golds that the women’s road race title is also one Hong Kong is defending in Japan. In Hangzhou, Yang Qianyu was propelled to the front by the team’s collective efforts, taking a gold that was as much a surprise as any won three years ago. A short-lived retirement followed, but the task of trying to hold on to the gold medal this year falls to Chloe Leung Wing-yee, Kwan Tsz-kwan and Guardiola Cheung Li-tong. There will be the usual challenge from China, with Zhang Hao coming into the competition having won the road race at the Asian Cycling Confederation Road Championships in Al Qassim, Saudi Arabia, in February. Just be polite The Asian Games organisers probably deserve a bit of a break, so not having to navigate the perils and political pitfalls of an India v Pakistan clash in the final of the women’s cricket should feel like a win. India and Sri Lanka will battle it out for gold, while Pakistan and Bangladesh do the honours in the bronze medal match. All four teams will be at Korogi Athletic Park for their matches, so you might assume they will all meet at some point. Apparently, a handshake is too much for the Indian players to muster when the cameras are on; you’d hope for a certain level of civility, dare one say grown-up behaviour, away from the spotlight. Naughty, naughty Thai badminton player Pitchamon ⁠Opatniputh has been handed a provisional doping ⁠ban after returning a positive test for a banned substance. Opatniputh, ranked 18th in the world, was expected to play in Thailand’s team event against China on Tuesday, but tested positive for furosemide, a substance that ⁠can be used to lose water for rapid weight ‌loss. The 19-year-old Thai athlete was pinged for a sample given when training in Nagoya last Thursday, two days before the formal opening ceremony of the Asian Games. “The athlete has been informed of the case and has been provisionally suspended with immediate effect until the resolution ‌of the matter in line with the World Anti-Doping Code and ‌the ‌OCA Anti-Doping Rules,” the International Testing Agency said.

title: Brigitte Bardot’s personal items sell out at Paris auction
description: Nine-hour sale of late French star’s belongings nets €953,531 for her animal foundation and son.
content: Personal belongings of the late French film icon Brigitte Bardot fetched nearly €1 million at auction in Paris on Monday. More than 280 items from Bardot’s estate sold for a total of €953,531 (nearly US$1.1 million) including fees, auction house Millon said. Every item found a buyer. The auction at the Hotel Drouot lasted almost nine hours. Around 15,000 people had visited the auction house in the six days beforehand to view the personal possessions of the actress, who died in 2025. The items included personal mementoes from Bardot’s properties in Saint-Tropez – La Madrague and La Garrigue – as well as from her Paris flat. Among those sold were an Olivetti typewriter on which Bardot wrote the second volume of her memoirs, Repetto ballet shoes, portraits, soft toys and numerous small everyday objects. Estimated prices had ranged from €20 to €10,000, with most items valued at less than €100. The proceeds will go to the Fondation Brigitte Bardot and her only son, Nicolas-Jacques Charrier. Bardot, who rose to international fame with films such as And God Created Woman, died on December 28, 2025, at the age of 91. She retired from acting in the mid-1970s and devoted herself to animal welfare, founding the Fondation Brigitte Bardot in 1986.

title: UK confirms Manchester to host G20 summit in 2027
description: City served by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as mayor for nearly a decade will host global leaders.
content: The leaders of the world’s biggest economies will descend on Manchester next year after the UK government confirmed the English city will host the Group of 20 (G20) summit. Prime Minister Andy Burnham will use his first trip to the United Nations General Assembly in New York to announce the city he led as mayor for almost a decade as the venue for the leaders summit, according to a statement on Monday from his office. The decision to choose Manchester in the northwest of England as the centre of the UK’s G20 presidency was made before Burnham came to power. But with the city now the site of his new No 10 North office launched to rival the government’s base in London, the location only serves to complement the new premier’s regional growth and devolution-focused agenda. The UK will take over the presidency of the G20 from the US in December, and with one eye on the volatile global picture putting pressure on Britain’s economy, Downing Street was keen to highlight the potential benefits for Britain that the global leadership role creates. Burnham’s spokesman, Tom Wells, told journalists on Monday that it offered the chance for Britain to argue for a global economic approach that creates the conditions for stable growth and fair trade to improve the lives of voters across the UK; a move away from the current turmoil threatening to worsen cost-of-living challenges at home. The prime minister is travelling on Tuesday to New York, where he will hold his first in-person meeting with US President Donald Trump and address the UN. He will use the trip to push like-minded countries for greater cooperation on global security and defence, according to his office. Alongside the Manchester Summit, scheduled for November 27-28, 2027, regions across the whole of the UK will host a series of events throughout the year, Downing Street said. The UK last hosted the G20 in April 2009, in London. Gatherings of the group of major economies are usually held in big cities, as opposed to the smaller G7 and G8 summits, which tend to be hosted in smaller, more rural locations. This year’s G20 summit will be held in Miami, Florida at the Trump National Doral Miami on December 14 and 15.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong must address the systemic lapses behind hospital lift failures
description: Authorities must determine how multiple layers of checks failed to stop substandard construction work before it spiralled into a public scandal.
content: Faulty lifts are not uncommon in a high-rise city like Hong Kong, but it’s not every day such problems escalate to its top leader for attention. The 24 malfunctioning lifts at a newly commissioned clinical building at Queen Mary Hospital require not only prompt mechanical repairs but also a thorough investigation and punishment for those responsible. The saga first came to light in mid-August when the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block was delayed by the defective lifts. Only four of the 28 lifts in the 34-storey building were working, resulting in delays in moving clinical services into the building, which was originally scheduled to start from the end of last year. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu set the right tone by tasking the Development Bureau to investigate the bungle and submit a report within a month. Commenting on the incident for the first time last week, Lee promised to identify and rectify all systemic inadequacies. He vowed to hold those responsible accountable – including contractors, subcontractors, engineering professionals and government officers – but stopped short of responding to why the government had not invoked its “heads of department accountability system” introduced to improve governance and accountability. Hong Kong must ask how, despite the layers of checks, substandard construction work could have snowballed into a scandal that warrants top-level intervention by the government. In a joint statement last month, the Architectural Services Department, the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department (EMSD) and the Hospital Authority first attributed the work delay to “defect rectification” of the building’s lift works and negative-pressure systems, adding that the repairs were expected to finish within the fourth quarter this year. More details surfaced a month later. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said the authorities had found that some lift components were improperly installed. There were also “dimensional deviations in the lift shafts” that resulted in insufficient clearance for the smooth operation of the lifts. She said the relevant departments had not publicly disclosed all the problems at this stage to avoid legal disputes with the contractors that could affect the government’s position and rights in pursuing future claims, and gave assurance that remedial work could finish by the end of the year as promised. The public can be excused for having the impression that the government sought to downplay the severity of the problem. Between July 2025 and June this year, seven lift equipment failures in the hospital new block were reported to the EMSD, accounting for 28 per cent of all lift issues reported across the city. Six involved passengers trapped due to electrical or component faults, while one involved a passenger tripping because of a levelling inaccuracy. The authorities said that the main contractor, a Paul Y Engineering Group joint venture, and lift subcontractor Anlev Elex Elevator, would be required to bear all remedial work costs. While officials are right to pursue compensation over the faulty installations, the scale of the lift breakdown is too serious to be treated as an isolated case of mechanical failure or contractor dispute. The onus is now on the government to establish openly and independently how the defects passed through layers of monitoring and approval. Beyond the usual costs of project delays, this scandal calls into question the quality of civil engineering, the professionalism of the industry and the effectiveness of government monitoring. The South China Morning Post reported that a senior civil servant who oversaw the lift installation was asked to resign and left her post last month over the incident. But the government denied it was a case of “forced resignation”, saying she quit for “personal reasons”. The public expects nothing short of a credible investigation, transparent disclosure and proportionate punishment, without which confidence cannot be restored. The authorities must confront the internal and external inadequacies identified during the probe and ensure the problems do not spill over to other public works projects.

title: How a Hong Kong-style milk tea shop in Tokyo has customers queuing out the door
description: Despite none being from Hong Kong, the three founders of Urushi to Hibi have created a unique – and popular – cultural fusion experience.
content: With its dark-wood-furnished interior that is part-boutique, part-workshop and part-cafe, there is a lot to notice about Urushi to Hibi in Tokyo. The daily line of customers outside the door, however, is mostly here for one thing: its Hong Kong-style milk tea. Behind the counter, the three co-founders – Lei Shengyu, Zhang Qingyue and Ji Qiuzi – work tirelessly, alternating between taking and prepping orders. On this day, Ji is making the milk tea, face full of concentration as he strains it again and again through a cloth tea bag. For those acquainted with the drink, the signs are clear: this Hong Kong-style milk tea is not only the real deal but is made with exceptional dedication and craft. Craft is the keyword that binds the three Chinese co-founders together. Lei, Zhang and Ji met at Tokyo University of the Arts while pursuing their individual artistic interests. Lei, 32, grew up in Hunan and Zhang, 35, in Shanxi, two Chinese provinces that boast strong lacquerware cultures, which sparked their interest in the Japanese equivalent. Ji, 36, from the Ningxia Hui autonomous region, went to Japan to study design, but was captivated by woodworking after discovering it at the university. These creative backgrounds are evident throughout the venue. The shelves are lined with lacquerware cups, chopsticks and jewellery, and the trio often hold craft workshops in the space. In this unusual setting, Hong Kong’s afternoon tea culture has become the centrepiece. A dark wooden counter is laden with freshly baked egg tarts and scones, setting the stage for the tea theatre taking place behind it. How they fell in love with Hong Kong-style milk tea Hong Kong-style milk tea was not originally part of the plan. Immersed in their studies, the three friends were determined to continue their involvement with Japanese crafts upon graduation. In 2022, they founded Kogeishincho, a company under which they hold exhibitions and workshops and produce handcrafted works for daily use, leading to their own line of lacquer chopsticks and accessories. “Over the course of about three years of activity, our desire to ‘bring crafts closer to daily life’ grew stronger,” Lei says of their idea to open the shop. “We wanted to create a space where production, exhibition and hands-on experiences could coexist naturally alongside human interaction.” As three non-Japanese nationals, finding a location was no easy task – more than 100 places rejected them before they found a willing landlord, they say. Eventually, in July 2025, they struck lucky with a small spot near the Sumida River estuary in Tokyo. Then began half a year of preparation – and the birth of their passion for Hong Kong-style milk tea. “It was while considering the concept of the space that we encountered Hong Kong-style milk tea,” Lei explains. “The more we learned about it, the more we saw parallels with the world of crafts – not only in the underlying culture and techniques but also in the craftsmanship itself, which involves carefully layering each step and precisely managing time and temperature to achieve the final result.” It was Ji – an ardent fan of Hong Kong culture, including cinema and music – who first introduced the idea. The three soon dove deep into Hong Kong milk tea culture.
