They began following the work of Cui Hanpeng, a Shenzhen-based Hong Kong-style milk tea practitioner and champion of the 2024 National & Greater Bay Area KamCha Competition (HK Milk Tea), who works to spread the craft to younger generations. After studying theory and extraction methods online in Japan, they travelled to Shenzhen to take part in one of Cui’s workshops. They practised daily and even participated in the KamCha competition’s Shenzhen regionals in November 2025. They continued practising after returning to Japan. In January 2026, they felt ready to launch Urushi to Hibi as a fully fledged cafe. Their tea-making process and tea blend “The most important thing in Hong Kong milk tea is the quality of the tea itself,” Lei says. “When choosing a tea, you have to consider the ratio and the preparation method to strike the right balance – balancing the tea’s aroma and strength with the smooth texture that emerges after adding milk. While those three factors are important, we believe the quality of the brewed tea itself is the most crucial element.” The trio primarily use Sri Lankan Ceylon tea, blending four or more types or grades, including coarse Broken Orange Pekoe leaves, known as BOP; finer Broken Orange Pekoe Fannings, or BOPF; and very fine dust-grade tea. Because each contributes different qualities – such as aroma, body, colour and astringency – they adjust the balance according to the condition of the tea leaves and the results of each brew. They also add a commercial-grade Lipton leaf tea to further enrich the aroma and lingering finish of the black tea. They follow a traditional tea-making process. First is blending, known as kau cha. Then the mix is simmered in a kettle, a stage known as bou cha. Next comes zong cha, literally “crashing tea”, where the brewed tea is repeatedly poured through a traditional cloth filter at height to extract its aroma, body and depth. “By repeatedly pouring the tea through a cloth filter, we draw out the full aroma and richness of the leaves, creating the signature Hong Kong-style milk tea qualities of heung [aroma], nong [richness] and waat [smoothness],” Lei explains. The tea is then left to rest and infuse during the guk cha (steeping) stage. Finally, there is zong naai, “crashing milk”, where the strong brewed tea is combined with evaporated milk – they use the ubiquitous Black & White brand to emulate the taste familiar to Hong Kong’s cha chaan tengs. More than just a drink The trio say their tea is authentic Hong Kong-style milk tea, but take care to point out that everyone has different tastes. When it comes to Hong Kong customers, some say it is just right or very delicious, while others prefer a stronger flavour. The trio tried many milk teas across Hong Kong and found each varied from cafe to cafe. As such, they simply aim to make the tea to their own tastes as diligently as they can. “At our store, we perform all these processes by hand rather than by machine, and it takes about 28 minutes to complete one pot of milk tea,” Lei says. “While this sometimes means a wait, many of our customers understand the process and enjoy the time spent waiting for their drink to be prepared. “Just as craftsmanship takes time, the flavour of Hong Kong-style milk tea can only be achieved by carefully executing each step of the process. We view the time spent waiting as part of the experience – an opportunity to appreciate the value of this handcrafted work.” The resulting cup of tea is extraordinary: the aroma and flavour are rich, with no astringency, resulting in a cup that expands from the aroma into a deep, lingering flavour. The dedication to every step is evident – customers who order their drink cold will receive their glass with an ice cube of frozen tea to ensure the flavour does not dilute too much. As non-Hongkongers, the three admit to intense debate over whether they were pursuing the right path. The more they thought and learned about Hong Kong-style milk tea, however, the more they felt it was a traditional craft similar to the ones they had pursued: both techniques of making Hong Kong-style milk tea and Japanese lacquerware are registered as intangible cultural heritages by their respective governments. “For us, Hong Kong-style milk tea is more than just a drink – it is a gateway connecting people and cultures,” Lei says. “We believe that both traditional crafts and Hong Kong-style milk tea are endeavours that preserve culture through handcrafting and foster connections between people.” Urushi to Hibi continues to evolve with this sentiment. The trio plans to host more lacquer and woodwork workshops at the space, as well as an art exhibition focused on Hong Kong-style milk tea for the store’s first anniversary. They also plan to entwine their crafts more deeply. “In the future, we would like to serve our drinks and food in vessels made of lacquerware,” Lei says. “Our milk tea is also crafted entirely by hand. For us, every single cup is a work of art.” Urushi to Hibi, 1/F, Glanffice, 1-28-33 Shinkawa, Chuo City, Tokyo

title: AI poses new national security threat, outgoing Hong Kong deputy police chief warns
description: Andrew Kan discusses using AI to fight AI, ongoing threat of soft resistance and what lies ahead after retirement.
content: Retiring deputy police commissioner Andrew Kan Kai-yan has said artificial intelligence (AI) poses a new threat to national security in Hong Kong, with the force turning to the emerging technology to help combat the issue. Kan raised the alarm after state security minister Chen Yixin warned last week of rising national security risks posed by AI. The senior mainland Chinese official also called for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the technology. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined plans in his annual policy address last week to adopt an AI risk‑governance strategy, focusing on combating the use of such technologies in criminal activities and formulating safety‑management guidelines for AI agents. Kan, 57, who headed the National Security Department, began his pre-retirement leave on Tuesday after 35 years on the force. Discussing the new threat, the outgoing police official said he had seen overseas examples of AI agents launching attacks on critical infrastructure and other companies’ computer systems, as well as generating misinformation. Anti-government forces could also use AI to commit crimes related to national security, he said. “I totally agree … that AI poses a new security threat to national security,” he said. “We have been working to improve our capability in AI in this aspect. I can also tell you one of the tactics to combat AI crime is using AI.” Kan pointed to AI tools used to help screen social media posts to identify potential “soft resistance” against the government as an example. “As computers and AI become more powerful, the chances of successfully hiding your criminal intent or criminal acts are actually getting slimmer. So, it’s better not to test the law,” he warned. The police official also said that anyone who used AI to commit crimes should be held responsible. Kan said the current legislation was adequate for now to tackle such threats, but he did not rule out the need for new legislation in the future. “Maybe in the future we need new laws,” he said. “Of course, technology grows very fast. We do not know next year or five years later, what the world will be.” Discussing the relevant legislation, he cited Section 50 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, which governs acts of endangering national security in relation to computers or electronic systems, saying that authorities had anticipated AI-related threats while drafting the law. He also pointed to the Protection of Critical Infrastructures (Computer Systems) Ordinance, which safeguards critical infrastructure and banking systems from attacks. In his announcement of Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint last week, Lee touched on plans to enhance the legal system and enforcement mechanisms to safeguard national security. Kan said the four main national security threats that would require vigilance over the next five years were soft resistance, home-grown terrorism, foreign influence and espionage. Earlier this year, national security police raided three independent bookstores over allegations that they had displayed or sold titles with seditious intent. The deputy police chief said his officers had actually read the books and sought legal advice from the Department of Justice before taking enforcement action. “There is no such thing as blind enforcement or making arbitrary arrests,” he said. Kan also rejected the idea of publishing a banned books list with book titles or ISBNs, arguing booksellers were responsible for ensuring the books they were selling complied with local national security legislation and comparing the situation to how restaurant owners needed to ensure food safety. “If we issue a banned books list today, and tomorrow you publish another book that turns out to be illegal after our investigation, you’ll say, ‘hey, why are you arresting us if it wasn’t on the list?’ This simply cannot resolve the problem,” he said. He suggested that sellers read the books before offering them and seek legal advice if in doubt. “If you say it is not easy to get legal advice … then don’t sell it,” he said. “If you say, ‘you will not publish the book list, and I don’t know where the red line is’ – I feel this is a bit of … soft resistance,” he said, adding that there was a clear definition of sedition under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance. Kan said more people were engaging in soft resistance, which had become even more discreet and underground after the enactment of national security laws. He added that people used different platforms, including cultural, arts and online media, to spread misinformation, incite hatred and instigate public resentment towards the local and central governments. On the distinction between soft resistance and freedom of speech, he said that the key determining factors were whether the expression was intended to incite others and whether the criticism was based on concrete facts. On September 11, three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil were sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail for inciting subversion. Kan said that whether it was legal to commemorate the anniversary of the Tiananmen Square crackdown on June 4 in the future should be judged on a case-by-case basis. He said that when evaluating applications for protests, police assessed threats to national security, public order and safety, as well as the potential impacts on the freedoms of others. “Of course, if the rally or protest you join is explicitly taking up the mantle of the alliance’s ideology, or ideas aimed at opposing China and destabilising Hong Kong, then you really need to think twice about whether you’ll end up breaking the law,” he said. Commenting on the effectiveness of putting bounties on wanted persons who had breached national security laws, Kan said: “Justice may be delayed, but it will not be denied. “Just because they haven’t returned now does not mean they never will … world politics can change drastically. “Will those sheltering you today betray you tomorrow? I wouldn’t rule it out. It’s certainly not impossible. When you beg others for protection and shelter, what happens to you once your usefulness runs out? We shall wait and see.” Kan also noted that national security police had arrested people suspected of handling funds or donations on behalf of absconders, largely cutting off their means of survival. Asked whether he would join the Committee for Safeguarding National Security after retiring, he said he wanted to take a good rest and spend time with his family first, adding that he did not have any current plans for the future.

title: Swire Coca-Cola gets robots for heavy lifting in satisfying Chinese consumers’ thirst
description: New automated facility to help meet increasingly diverse demand across emerging sales channels, company says.
content: Chinese consumers are demanding more variety from the drinks sections in their local stores, and Swire Coca-Cola is employing robots to help quench this increasingly diversified thirst. The company began using a robotic system for order picking this month in a factory in Zhengzhou, capital of central China’s Henan province, where it has invested 900 million yuan (US$134.3 million). “China is a growth market, and consumer habits are changing,” said Peter Mills, chief supply chain officer of Swire Coca-Cola, in Zhengzhou on Friday. “We need to have a more flexible and responsive supply chain to meet the shifting needs, covering emerging sales channels including convenience stores, vending coolers and snack stores.” The facility automated shrink-wrapped order picking, which was a heavy challenge in markets where manual labour was still used, according to Mills. “They use the traditional human lifting way, which is inflexible with high costs,” he said. “We plan to launch this solution in other factories in China next year and scale it in overseas markets in the future.” Swire Coca-Cola, a subsidiary of Hong Kong-based Swire Pacific, operates in its home market, Taiwan, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos and Thailand in addition to mainland China. The latter is its largest market even though it shares franchise territory with state-owned Cofco. The Zhengzhou facility has three sets of robots developed by Seth Robotics, a start-up in Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province. Orchestrated by an artificial intelligence-based brain, the robots could identify products from live orders, compute efficient warehouse routes and handle the heavy-duty picking for a range of products, according to the company. With each robot capable of carrying up to 40kg (88.2 pounds) of goods and processing 600 cases per hour, the system had the highest payload and fastest picking speed among comparable solutions globally, Seth Robotics said. China was one of the markets driving Coca-Cola’s global volume growth, alongside India, the US and Brazil, according to its second-quarter earnings report. Swire Coca-Cola’s mainland sales volume rose 12 per cent in the first half of the year, while profit climbed 24 per cent to HK$727 million (US$93 million) as demand rebounded after a challenging 2025, the company said in its interim results. The competitive landscape continued to be reshaped by strong growth in emerging channels such as e-commerce and snack shops, as well as an expansion in immediate, occasion-based consumption, it added. “Increased Chinese consumer spending on health will bolster growth in the beverage and supplement sectors,” said Maggie Xie, associate director at S&P Global Ratings. “While consumers remain cautious about spending, demand will likely grow for experiences and products they see as emotionally satisfying.” Swire Coca-Cola said its priorities in China were emerging sales channels, digital platforms and tourist destinations, as well as continued investment in sparkling drinks, especially the low- and no-sugar segment. The company is pressing ahead with a 12 billion yuan investment plan for the mainland market, unveiled in 2023, that covers new facilities and equipment over a 10-year period. In late May, two new plants began operations, one in Kunshan, in the eastern province of Jiangsu, and another in Guangzhou. A new facility in Haikou, in the southern province of Hainan, is under construction and scheduled to open in December 2027.

title: US, China need nuclear-style AI safeguards, congressman says before Xi-Trump summit
description: Top Democrat on the House China committee calls for international inspections of leading AI laboratories and a ban on self-improving systems.
content: The US and China should agree on international regulatory standards for artificial intelligence (AI), akin to atomic-era guardrails, said Ro Khanna, the ranking member of the US House Select Committee on China, in New York on Monday ahead of the two countries’ high-stakes summit. The remarks come two days before Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive in Washington to meet with US President Donald Trump for a closely watched summit where AI is expected to be on the agenda after the two countries agreed to establish a dialogue on the technology a day earlier. “I hope there will be an agreement between Trump and Xi Jinping to have some safety standards,” Khanna told the South China Morning Post. “To have a ban on recursive self-improving AI and also a certification standard and inspection standard to make sure we don’t have AI models that lose control or that are misused.” Khanna, a Democrat, said the two leaders planned to discuss AI but needed a concrete framework to reach an agreement. Speaking with Kevin Rudd, president of the Asia Society, at an event earlier on Monday, Khanna proposed an international inspection regime to monitor frontier labs in both countries, citing Chinese firms Alibaba, Moonshot and DeepSeek alongside US labs. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. “I don’t expect our president or the Chinese president to know all the details,” Khanna told Rudd, a former Australian prime minister and a prominent China scholar. “They just need to say, ‘Yes, we need regulation. Yes, we’re committed to doing it in an international framework,’ and set a goal of three months to come to some basic understanding.” Khanna’s comments came after eight-hour long talks in New York on Sunday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng. US proposes new AI safety notification mechanism with China Bessent said the US had proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism with China, saying Washington wanted a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. “Winning an AI war is like winning a nuclear war; it is catastrophic to civilisation. America’s AI labs may be winning today, but nobody wins if humans lose control over AI, or if bad actors unleash chemical or biological attacks,” Khanna said. “There are two AI superpowers in the world today. One’s called the United States of America, the second is called the People’s Republic of China, and then there’s a gap a million miles long before you get to anybody else,” Rudd added. The pair discussed topics ranging from AI governance to US economic competitiveness and strategic diplomacy in Monday’s talks. Khanna again urged both the US and China to ban self-recursive AI while it remains in development. “Especially because these labs will tell you they haven’t gotten there yet,” he said, adding that it wouldn’t ban something that already exists but rather impose a pre-emptive pause. The comments come during a particularly busy week for China watchers, as Washington prepares to host President Xi for his first state visit to the United States since 2015, when Barack Obama was in office. “At the invitation of [the] President of the United States of America Donald J. Trump, President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from September 23 to 25,” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in an official statement on Monday. The visit will take place the same week as the United Nations General Assembly in New York and comes hot on the heels of Trump’s visit to Beijing for a bilateral summit in May. Xi will be in Washington from Wednesday to Friday with his wife, Peng Liyuan, where he will be hosted by the US president alongside first lady Melania Trump, an event described as a diplomatic “double date”. Researchers say AI could pose existential threat to humanity The meeting between the two presidents comes as concerns about AI continue to mount after researchers said the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity in the next decade. They also follow weeks of reports that AI agents have been acting beyond their assigned tasks. Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic over concerns about how AI was being developed, was among those who sounded the alarm, warning that AI could threaten humanity while urging the US and China to cooperate to slow down their development and address safety concerns. “I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual slowing,” he said.

title: In Focus | The US-China tech war has evolved since the last Xi-Trump summit. Who has the edge now?
description: The two sides have found new sources of leverage across AI, chips, rare earths and wider technology supply chains since the US leader’s May visit to Beijing.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the fourth part of this series, Sylvia Ma looks at the economic and technological levers available to both in their protracted rivalry. For years, Huawei Technologies has served as a central battleground in the contest between the world’s two largest economies. As Washington tightens restrictions, the Chinese tech giant continues to find new ways forward – to the point that “becoming Nvidia” is now an internal goal. Days before President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States for a high-stakes meeting with his American counterpart Donald Trump, Huawei announced a major technological breakthrough: a system that it said was capable of enabling up to 1 million processors to operate as a single, unified computer. The announcement followed earlier semiconductor advances, namely the Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture, which aim to deliver high-performance chips without relying on the most advanced lithography tools, whose sale to China remains restricted. Ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, Huawei rotating chair Xu Zhijun last week voiced a widely shared hope among entrepreneurs that the world’s two superpowers could “coexist and get along in a peaceful way” and that government actions would avoid interfering with normal, innovation-driven market competition. “With increasing geopolitical tension, those days [of globalisation and full competition] are leaving us,” Xu said, asserting that enterprises were now trapped in a reality where “you cannot buy what you want to, you cannot sell what you want”. As geoeconomic competition continues to reshape US-China relations, the sources of leverage available to Washington and Beijing are also coming under scrutiny. Four months after Trump visited the Chinese capital in May, when both sides agreed to work towards “constructive strategic stability”, traditional economic levers, such as pledges to order Boeing aircraft, have almost flatlined. At the same time, the technological contest has accelerated, spanning China’s push to catch up in artificial intelligence and semiconductors and Washington’s drive for self-reliance in rare earths – one of Beijing’s main trump cards. “The more interesting change is that both sides appear increasingly conscious that their leverage is reciprocal,” said Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Centre for China and Globalisation. “Neither side has a decisive advantage without imposing significant costs on itself.” While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis Chasing the AI frontier Since May, Chinese AI developers have increasingly sought to combine powerful open-weight models, whose parameters are made available for developers to download, modify and run, with a broader domestic hardware base to reduce reliance on Nvidia chips. When Moonshot AI launched its 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 in July, it made the weights available to developers. The model was soon adapted to run on Alibaba Group Holding’s Zhenwu M890 and Huawei Technologies’ Ascend 910C chips, while new models from Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and Alibaba – owner of the South China Morning Post – have followed. Paul Triolo, a partner and technology policy lead at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, said the release of such “capable models” had “arguably” narrowed the gap at the frontier. Although the US still leads in proprietary frontier models, Washington has increasingly shifted its focus to how Chinese developers gain access to those capabilities. A report released by three US government agencies earlier this month accused six Chinese AI firms of using “distillation” – a technique in which a smaller system is trained on responses generated by a more powerful one – to extract capabilities from American-developed models. China’s Ministry of Commerce rejected the allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation as groundless, warning that Beijing would retaliate if Washington weaponised the claim to stifle the country’s tech sector. Elly Rostoum, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at the Centre for European Policy Analysis (CEPA), disagreed that China’s progress could be explained solely by distillation, calling such claims “short-sighted”. “Even if they distil it, they are smart enough to take the technology, distil it and build on it within six weeks – in such a short time – as we’ve seen with Moonshot AI,” she told a media briefing last week. Meanwhile, Joe Khawam, managing director of legal and AI policy at the Law Reform Institute in Washington, said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials had weighed sanctions over distillation, some policymakers could favour a diplomatic solution given the risk of Chinese retaliation. “One of the big questions is how truly important distillation is for specific Chinese AI companies to maintain their position as fast followers in frontier AI models,” he said. Yao Xu, secretary general of the Centre for Global AI Innovative Governance at Fudan University, said the two countries held leverage in different parts of the AI technology ecosystem. “The United States has the chips, but lacks effective planning and public persuasion,” he said. “China can do better at planning and securing public trust in policy, but we lack the chips.” The battle over advanced semiconductors Although the US retains a major advantage in cutting-edge chips, Chinese players have spent the past four months bolstering the domestic hardware ecosystem underpinning the country’s AI models. “The US has a lot of leverage around ... [the] ecosystem for advanced chips,” Kevin Allison, a senior fellow with the tech policy programme at CEPA, told the same media briefing. “China has yet to catch up, although it’s been making progress kind of under pressure from US export controls.” Unable to access the machines capable of extreme ultraviolet lithography – the cutting-edge chipmaking technology dominated by Dutch giant ASML – Chinese companies such as Huawei and Alibaba’s T-Head division are pursuing alternative ways to improve performance. Huawei, for instance, anticipates a major domestic shift towards its AI infrastructure for model training next year, as its Ascend processors gain ground on Nvidia in China despite supply bottlenecks. Washington continues to bar Chinese firms from accessing the most advanced Nvidia chips, even after approving sales of the H200 model, and has yet to close loopholes that allow remote access to processing power hosted in overseas data centres. In early August, Bloomberg reported that US regulators were reviewing how Chinese AI companies accessed Nvidia chips through computing power rented overseas. “While the US still holds the leading-edge chip advantage, it is now treating it as a bargainable asset rather than a hard wall,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis. Alex Capri, a senior lecturer at the National University of Singapore’s business school, said he expected the coming Xi-Trump talks to renew interest in Beijing’s push to secure relief from export controls on high-end chips and lithography equipment. That could include Washington extending its suspension of the “50 per cent affiliates rule”, which would otherwise expand tech export restrictions to overseas subsidiaries that are at least 50 per cent Chinese-owned. The suspension is set to expire in November. As foreign memory-chip giants increasingly devote production capacity to high-bandwidth memory, which supports AI computing, Chinese manufacturers such as Yangtze Memory Technologies (YMTC) and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) have continued expanding their presence in conventional memory, strengthening China’s domestic memory supply chain. Data released by Counterpoint Research last month showed that YMTC had entered the world’s top three NAND suppliers by shipment volume for the first time, accounting for 14 per cent of global bit shipments. Leverage beyond rare earths Beyond AI models and chips, both the US and China have increased their use of restrictions and export controls across technology and other supply chains, creating additional sources of potential leverage. On the American side, the regulatory dragnet is expanding rapidly into downstream hardware. The Federal Communications Commission expanded its Covered List in July to include foreign-made advanced robotic devices and connected power inverters. It is also reportedly drafting a ban on new Chinese-made optical transceivers used in data centres, with officials aiming to publish and implement the measure later this year. Analysts at Bernstein described the recent US ban on new foreign-made mobile robots as “the formal beginning of US-China decoupling in robotics,” in a note published last month. Although China’s robotics industry remained reliant on US AI chips and simulation platforms, it had moved faster in scaling training datasets and acquiring high-value data, the analysts said. Data would consequently be Beijing’s “base case” response, with rare earth magnets potentially serving as an escalation lever, they added. China accounts for about 60 per cent of global rare earth mining and nearly 90 per cent of processing, according to the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies. As the world’s leading producer of rare earth elements, it has long used critical minerals as a strategic lever in its protracted trade conflict with the US. Washington has accelerated efforts to reduce its rare earth dependence, with Elon Musk earlier this month touting the Cybercab’s rare-earth-free motor, although analysts regarded the development as only a slight step towards meaningfully weakening China’s leverage across industries. At the federal level, USA Rare Earth secured access to up to US$1.6 billion in US government funding in June to build out a domestic mine-to-magnet supply chain – though Rostoum of CEPA said China had “a 20-year head start in going around the world” on a “shopping spree” to secure critical minerals. “The Chinese definitely have the upper hand when it comes to rare earths,” she told the media briefing last week. Beyond rare earths, analysts also pointed to China’s ability to leverage its position in global manufacturing and supply chains. “As the US seeks to de-risk from China, Beijing retains considerable leverage through the depth and scale of its industrial ecosystem, something that is much harder to replicate quickly than individual supply chains,” said Giovannini, also a fellow at the University of Hong Kong’s Asia Global Institute. “The key question ahead of the meeting is therefore less about which side has more leverage and more about which side is willing to bear greater economic costs in exercising it.” Additional reporting by Coco Feng, Iris Deng, Howard Liu, Vincent Chow and Wency Chen

title: Canadian province sues OpenAI in US over school shooting
description: Lawsuit alleges tech giant failed to report shooter’s ChatGPT activity before attack that killed eight.
content: British Columbia filed a lawsuit on Monday against OpenAI in California over the company’s failure to report violent activity on its ChatGPT service by the person who committed a mass school shooting in the western Canadian province. British Columbia Attorney General Niki Sharma said in July that the province planned legal action against the US tech giant for its connection to the deadly February gun violence in the tiny mining town of Tumbler Ridge. Sharma told reporters that the suit filed earlier on Monday is seeking “accountability and change” from OpenAI, which previously apologised for not flagging the account linked to Jesse Van Rootselaar, an 18-year-old transgender woman who killed eight people at her home and a school. Tumbler Ridge families impacted by the shooting have filed separate lawsuits against the US tech giant in California. OpenAI has already moved to dismiss those family lawsuits, arguing that any legal actions related to the shootings should be heard in British Columbia. The financial damages that could be awarded by a Canadian court would likely be substantially smaller than a prospective award from a US court. Reporters asked Sharma why British Columbia believed California was the appropriate venue for its action. “The decision not to report happened in California,” she said. “What we’re alleging in our claim is that AI knew that there were serious things happening in that chat and they failed to report.” Sharma declined to specify how the province might use any settlement funds but said resources would be devoted to building a new school in Tumbler Ridge. In April, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologised to residents of Tumbler Ridge, saying in a public letter that he was “deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement to the account that was banned in June”. OpenAI has said that it did not report Van Rootselaar’s account at the time of the suspension because it saw no evidence of an imminent attack. But it has also said that under updated security guidelines imposed after June 2025, the account would have been reported to police. Lawyers for the families suing the company have alleged that OpenAI chose to stay silent about Van Rootselaar’s account because “reporting one case would mean reporting thousands”. Their lawsuit also claims that when an account is shut down for dangerous behaviour, OpenAI instructs the individual on how to resume use of the service, including tips on how to circumvent the 30-day suspension period. Van Rootselaar killed her mother and brother at the family’s home before heading to the local secondary school, where she shot dead five children and a teacher. She died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound after police entered the building.

title: Top US Senate Democrat Jeanne Shaheen warns Trump not to waver on Taiwan ahead of Xi meet
description: Jeanne Shaheen also said new law allowing tariffs on buyers of Russian oil ‘sends Beijing a message’ before this week’s summit in Washington.
content: The top Democrat on the US Senate’s foreign policy panel urged Donald Trump on Monday not to signal any retreat from Taiwan when he hosts Chinese President Xi Jinping this week. Speaking at the Concordia Summit in New York, Senator Jeanne Shaheen said she hoped the president “will not say anything that indicates a lack of support for Taiwan” during his talks with the Chinese leader. Shaheen is the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which reviews US arms sales abroad, including those to Taiwan. “In Congress, there is very strong bipartisan support for our historic position with respect to Taiwan,” she said. The island, she added, “is a huge producer of semiconductors that are very critical to the United States”. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with the mainland, by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington opposes any attempt to change the status quo by force and is committed to supplying the island with defensive weapons. The Chinese Embassy in Washington said China’s position about Taiwan “has been consistent and clear”. Shaheen co-led Senate delegation to Taipei in March In March, Shaheen co-led a bipartisan Senate delegation to Taipei with Republican Senator John Curtis, meeting Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te and pressing the island’s legislature to approve a special defence budget. Beijing’s foreign ministry denounced the trip and urged Washington to stop “sending any wrong signals” to separatist forces. Days before that visit, she told the press she was concerned about Trump’s commitment to “reinforcing the United States’ support for Taiwan and not undermining their sovereignty”. Her committee has since advanced bills to codify Washington’s “Six Assurances” to Taipei and to prepare sanctions in case of a Chinese attack. Meanwhile, a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan is still awaiting final approval. The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that Washington was considering holding back announcements of major arms sales to the island until after the Apec summit in Shenzhen in November. Chinese officials had asked the US not to announce new sales before Xi’s trip, a source told the SCMP. Beijing confirmed on Monday that Xi will pay a state visit to the US from Wednesday to Friday, his first to Washington since 2015. He and Trump are due to hold talks at the White House on Thursday, four months after the US president travelled to Beijing. Shaheen hoped the leaders would also discuss “how to proceed on AI and the threat from AI that Americans are very much feeling”. She pointed to a sanctions law Trump signed on Friday, describing it as “a very strong message to Russia and to China and the users of Russian oil and gas”. The law, she said, was “an important message for the president to be able to go in to any meeting with President Xi, to let him know that Congress is paying attention to the support that China is giving to Russia and their help in funding the war in Ukraine”. Named after Lindsey Graham, the Republican senator who championed it until his death in July, the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act was co-written with Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal. The Senate passed it 86-11 in August and the House approved it 262-159 last week. New law will see tariffs on buyers of Russian oil The law directs tariffs of up to 500 per cent on Russian imports. It also lets the president impose duties of up to 100 per cent on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, a list led by China and India. Putin, senior Russian officials and banks are targeted too, along with the “shadow fleet” of tankers that carry Russian oil around Western restrictions. The law extends existing sanctions on Iran for five years and allows Trump to waive the measures if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said last week that Beijing opposed “long-arm jurisdiction” without a basis in international law or UN Security Council authorisation. China’s trade with other countries was based on equality and mutual benefit, he added. Moscow called the measure “unfriendly” and warned it could affect talks to end the war in Ukraine. India said it would keep securing energy for its 1.4 billion people through diversified sourcing. Shaheen also accused the administration of “playing footsie with China and Russia” during the US war with Iran, arguing that both countries were helping Tehran target American bases, troops and allies in the Middle East. She called it “totally unacceptable and unconscionable”. Several media outlets reported in March that Russia was sharing intelligence on US military positions with Iran. Citing leaked Iranian military documents, the Financial Times also later reported that Tehran had covertly acquired a Chinese-built satellite to watch US bases. Beijing denied the accusations. Additional reporting by Han Li

title: Opinion | Why Trump-Xi summit must put Korean peninsula back on the agenda
description: US and Chinese indifference risks reinforcing North Korea’s calculation that the world will settle for merely managing its nuclear threat.
content: The September 24 summit between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump is no ordinary engagement. Their May summit took place in Beijing and largely centred on economic issues. This one will be on Trump’s home turf and is expected to put strategic questions on the table. Will the Korean peninsula and North Korea’s nuclear programme again be pushed to the margins? In Beijing, both sides focused on their immediate national interests, such as trade, semiconductors, rare earths and Taiwan. The issue of the peninsula’s security threat never appeared on the agenda. Trade, technology and artificial intelligence are again expected to dominate the agenda in Washington. Yet the North’s arsenal is no side issue – it is the most explosive variable capable of destabilising northeast Asia. North Korea has tested intercontinental ballistic missiles that are capable of reaching the continental US, according to Congressional testimony, and Trump has specifically said that North Korea possesses 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. When a US president counts another state’s warheads in public, Pyongyang hears something close to acknowledgement. North Korea is no longer a target for persuasion; it treats its nuclear status as a fait accompli. It has redefined inter-Korean ties as “two hostile states”, seeking to write the South out of the discussion. Diplomatic silence has not produced stability; it has bought Pyongyang time. Dropping the peninsula from the agenda would send the wrong message. Indifference from the world’s great powers risks reinforcing Pyongyang’s calculation that the world will settle for managing, not resolving, its arsenal. A problem unaddressed does not vanish but returns more dangerous. The timing of the latest Trump-Xi summit compounds concerns. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un hosted Xi in June, the latter’s first visit to Pyongyang in seven years. Denuclearisation was not mentioned. Trump has indicated he wants to meet Kim around November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, and Beijing appears ready to help broker it. Meanwhile, Trump ordered the Ulchi Freedom Shield joint exercise between US and South Korean forces cut from 11 days to five, with Seoul receiving no advance notice. This summit sits at the centre of that sequence, and how the North’s status is framed will shape what follows. There is a clear case for making the peninsula and the nuclear question a formal agenda item. North Korea’s weapons transcend bilateral concerns as a clash or nuclear crisis there would be catastrophic for everyone. If the two powers mean to honour the “constructive strategic stability” they agreed in Beijing, managing this risk is the minimum common ground on which that stability rests. The longer both sides stay silent, the more Pyongyang will misread it as an opening to recognition as a nuclear power, undercutting the very stability Beijing championed. What each side should do is clear. The US must restore strategic clarity. Washington must reaffirm denuclearisation and show that the North’s weapons are no bargaining chip in its dealings with Beijing. If the US finds the word “denuclearisation” burdensome, Pyongyang will read that as its own victory. China must move from bystander to responsible stakeholder. Its readiness to help arrange a Trump-Kim meeting is a start, but convening one is not owning its substance. Beijing is not being asked to manage North Korean caprice but to meet the minimum obligation of a permanent Security Council member: not leaving cracks in the non-proliferation regime unattended. Sanctions enforcement, trade controls, drawing Pyongyang to the table – none of this works without China. Treating the issue as a shared regional risk befits China’s stature as a global power. South Korea’s role matters, too. It is the most exposed stakeholder, yet the discussion proceeds without it. Settling an issue this vital to its security in its absence is dangerous, as August’s abrupt exercise cut showed. To prevent a repeat, Seoul must be involved in any coordination with Washington and Beijing before and after the summit. President Lee Jae Myung has called a nuclear freeze “a feasible, realistic alternative”. This would be a first step towards negotiated denuclearisation, not a substitute for it. Seoul should act not as a bystander but as the author of its own road map and peace vision. If the peninsula is again pushed to the margins of great power politics, the peninsula and the entire region will pay the price. That is why the issue must make the agenda in Washington. North Korea’s nuclear programme does not shrink on its own accord; the longer the problem is ignored, the more intractable it becomes. This summit will be judged less by what the two powers trade away than by what they responsibly confront. What is needed is recognition in both capitals that the peninsula and the North’s nuclear threat cannot be left off the table.

title: Burnham to meet Trump, make UN debut after offering UK support for Saudis
description: British prime minister targets Middle East stability and AI governance on New York trip.
content: Andy Burnham once said he would refuse to meet Donald Trump. Now Britain’s prime minister is about to hold his first meeting with the US president, with Ukraine, the risks and opportunities of artificial intelligence and the soaring cost of conflict in the Middle East dominating his agenda. In a sign of the stark decisions facing the neophyte prime minister who took office just two months ago, Burnham announced Monday that he would send a Royal Air Force plane to help Saudi Arabia repel attacks from Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. The UK says the plane will refuel Saudi planes during “defensive” missions. Burnham told reporters en route to New York, where he will meet Tuesday with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, that he is “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region”. He said Britain wants to see an end to the conflict in the region “as quickly as possible and we stand ready to play our part”. The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has reignited, with Houthis aiming missile and drone strikes on Saudi Arabia, including one that targeted Riyadh on Saturday before being intercepted. The Houthis also declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, attacking Saudi-linked vessels and oil facilities inside the kingdom, the world’s top oil exporter. Burnham is set to address the annual gathering of world leaders on Tuesday, setting out his vision of Britain’s place in an increasingly fractured and perilous world. In his speech, he said he would set out his vision of the UK as an “honest broker” when it comes to balancing the risks and opportunities of AI, which he plans to make the focus of Britain’s presidency of the G20 group of nations in 2027. “We have obviously the closest of relationships with the US. We have that deepening relationship with Europe. But also I’ve spoken to President Xi and we’ve maintained a strong dialogue with China,” he said. “So we are, I think, uniquely positioned to play a leadership role on AI and it’s very clear to me that the G20 presidency gives us that opportunity.” Burnham’s only other foreign trip since taking office in July was to Kyiv, and he has said he will urge Trump to send interceptor missiles to bolster Ukraine’s air defences ahead of another winter of war. The British government also wants to discuss ways to restore free movement of ships through the Strait of Hormuz, largely blocked since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February. The closure of the key route has sent oil prices spiking, complicating Burnham’s efforts to jump-start Britain’s sluggish economy and ease the cost of living. Like many Labour Party politicians, Burnham was strongly critical of Trump in the past. In 2017, Burnham, as the mayor of Greater Manchester, said the president wouldn’t be welcome in the city. Two years later he said he would refuse to meet Trump if he visited. On Monday he said he would seek “common ground” with Trump, adding that the two men had “found a connection” during two phone calls since Burnham replaced Keir Starmer at the helm of the centre-left governing party. Trump has called Burnham “a nice guy”, but has also recently needled UK officials by expressing support for Irish unification and musing about the future of the Falkland Islands that are claimed by both Britain and Argentina. Starmer went out of his way to flatter Trump, presenting him in the Oval Office in February 2025 with an invitation from King Charles for an unprecedented second state visit to the UK. British officials felt Starmer’s approach was vindicated when the UK struck a trade deal with the Trump administration. But Trump soured on Starmer over his refusal to join the Iran war. The president also has repeatedly criticised the UK’s immigration and green-energy policies, urging the country to open more of the North Sea up to oil drilling. Burnham is expected to announce a decision soon about whether to approve new oil and gas fields off Scotland. UK officials also are braced for criticism of Britain’s ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and efforts to regulate big American technology firms. Trump’s threats to seize Greenland alarmed the UK and other European allies earlier this year, and Burnham was among leaders expressing relief at the announcement of a deal between Greenland, Denmark and the US to bolster the American military presence there but keep the Arctic island under Danish control. Trump has other, more high-profile, international meetings this week, including one at the White House with Xi. Burnham’s trip comes as middle-sized powers, led most vocally by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, try to forge closer alliances in the face of Trump’s “America first” foreign policy. Burnham’s government wants Britain to be bolder on the world stage, and to restore some of the ties with Europe severed when the UK left the European Union in 2020. At the UN, Burnham will host a meeting on reviving hopes of a two-state solution for Israel and the Palestinians, alongside Carney, French President Emmanuel Macron, Saudi Arabia’s Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres.

title: Zelensky and CIA chief meet during refuelling stop in Ireland
description: Sources say the pair met at Shannon Airport as the Ukrainian leader travelled to the UN meetings in New York.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ⁠met US CIA chief John Ratcliffe at Shannon Airport in Ireland, two people familiar with the matter said. The meeting took place on Monday, one of ‌the sources said. The other source said the pair spoke informally while their planes were being refuelled without specifying a date. Both sources, who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, declined to disclose details of their conversation. The ⁠meeting happened as Zelensky was travelling to New York to take ‌part in the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations. Ratcliffe was on ‌his way back from meeting Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi, ⁠one ⁠source said. Ratcliffe’s meeting with Zelensky comes less than a month after the CIA ‌chief travelled to Moscow to meet Russia’s top intelligence officials. Neither Ratcliffe nor ‌the CIA ‌have publicly disclosed what was discussed in Moscow. One ‌of the sources, who confirmed the Zelensky meeting to Reuters, ⁠said Ratcliffe had been in Moscow to discuss Ukraine but they ⁠declined to elaborate. The New York Times reported last month that Ratcliffe used his trip to share his ‌bleak assessment of ‌the state of the Russian war against Ukraine and to urge the Russians to cut a deal before their position weakens.

title: US, Japan and South Korea launch economic-security talks before Xi summit
description: Three allies target economic coercion and industrial overcapacity while reinforcing calls for stability across the Taiwan Strait.
content: The United States, Japan and South Korea announced a new economic-security consultation and reinforced their support for stability across the Taiwan Strait on Monday, sending a coordinated message on two of Beijing’s most sensitive issues just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s summit with US President Donald Trump. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu and South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun unveiled the initiative after meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The three governments pledged to stand against economic coercion and “non-market policies and practices” that produce harmful industrial overcapacity and distort markets, as well as arbitrary export restrictions that disrupt global supply chains. They also agreed to strengthen an existing trilateral supply-chain early warning system, according to a joint statement released by the US State Department. Trump is scheduled to meet Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday, two days before his talks with Xi at the White House, giving Tokyo an opportunity to convey its priorities directly to the US president ahead of the summit. Takaichi also met Trump at the White House in March, less than two months before the US president travelled to Beijing for talks with Xi. Trump spoke with her again by phone after the May summit, providing what Takaichi described as a detailed account of his discussions with the Chinese leader. Xi is expected to arrive in the United States on Wednesday for a three-day state visit, with trade, artificial intelligence and other economic and security issues expected to feature prominently in his meeting with Trump. China not identified as target of new economic-security consultation The trilateral statement did not identify China as the target of the new economic-security consultation. But its references to economic coercion, industrial overcapacity and export restrictions closely tracked long-standing complaints by Washington and its Asian allies about Beijing’s economic practices. China’s dominance of critical-mineral processing and its restrictions on exports of some strategically important materials have become major concerns for the US and other advanced economies seeking to reduce their dependence on Chinese supply chains. The statement also called for closer cooperation among the three countries on semiconductors and for stronger protections around critical and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, quantum technology, digital infrastructure and biotechnology. The three governments said they would “cooperatively reinforce advanced-technology stacks and supply chain resilience” and expressed interest in expanding cooperation among their national laboratories. The announcement comes as Washington and Beijing hold their own economic talks ahead of the Xi-Trump summit. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in New York over the weekend to discuss possible summit deliverables, including trade and artificial intelligence. Taiwan Strait concerns raised at meeting Alongside the economic-security measures, Rubio, Motegi and Cho emphasised the importance of maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and encouraged the peaceful resolution of cross-strait disputes. They opposed unilateral attempts to change the status quo and expressed support for Taiwan’s “meaningful participation” in appropriate international organisations. The language is likely to draw scrutiny from Beijing, which regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The three officials also supported freedom of navigation and overflight, unimpeded lawful commerce and other lawful uses of the sea in the Indo-Pacific, in accordance with international law as reflected in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. On energy security, Washington, Tokyo and Seoul agreed to work towards stronger regional supply resilience by increasing oil stockpiles and encouraging cooperation between energy-producing and consuming countries. They also committed to implementing a July memorandum to accelerate the deployment of small modular nuclear reactors in third countries under nuclear safety, security and non-proliferation standards. The meeting also covered North Korea, with the three officials reaffirming their commitment to the complete denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula and calling on Pyongyang to return to dialogue. They pledged to continue efforts against revenue-generating activities that support North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, including illicit cyber operations and the overseas deployment of North Korean information-technology workers. Rubio reiterated US defence commitments to Japan and South Korea, including Washington’s extended nuclear deterrence, while the three countries promised to continue security cooperation and consultations at all levels.

title: Trump approval hits career low as living costs bite, new poll shows
description: Just 17 per cent of Americans endorse the president’s handling of inflation ahead of midterm elections.
content: US President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to 32 per cent – the lowest of his political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found. The poll, completed on Sunday, was conducted over a four-day period that saw Trump throw three major news organisations out of the White House and muse that Washington’s iconic Kennedy Centre for the Performing ‌Arts – named after slain President John F. Kennedy – could be torn down if Trump’s own name could not be added to it. It found voters leaning away from supporting Trump’s fellow Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. Trump’s overall approval was down from a reading of 35 per cent in last week’s Reuters/Ipsos poll, with support among his own Republicans down to 73 per cent from 82 per cent a week earlier. Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was sworn in, he enjoyed a 47 per cent approval rating. Just 17 per cent of respondents in the new poll ⁠approved of his handling of the cost of living – the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November. Dissatisfaction among Republicans on inflation has been growing since Trump ‌launched the war on Iran in February that has pushed petrol and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump’s handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up – 51 per cent to 44 per cent. Trump’s approval rating is lower than any recorded ‌for his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, whose presidency was also marked by surging inflation and who ultimately ended his re-election bid after a poor debate performance heightened concerns ⁠about his age. Biden’s low was 35 per cent, ⁠reached in late October 2024. Only 34 per cent of the most recent poll respondents approve of the strikes on Iran. The conflict has cut the world off from a significant slice of the oil and gas produced in the Middle East, and threatens ‌to stoke higher inflation in the US and elsewhere as businesses pass on higher fuel costs to consumers. Trump initially said the conflict would last a few weeks and that Iran needed to be bombed to stop it from developing nuclear weapons. Earlier ‌this month, ‌the Republican leader pledged the war would end “immediately after” the election. But Iran has shown no sign of giving up and in recent weeks Tehran and its allies have threatened further disruptions ‌to oil markets. Some 82 per cent of poll respondents – including nine in 10 Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans – said the conflict would likely go on for an “extended period of time”. The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered ⁠voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans – 43 per cent to 35 per cent – when asked how they would vote in the midterms. The 8-point gap was the biggest lead for Democrats in Reuters/Ipsos polling ⁠this year. For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his term. The poll results on congressional voting plans provide an overall view of which party Americans nationwide want to see in charge in Congress, though the results do not capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that ‌determine control of the Senate and House of Representatives. Trump ‌remains popular among Republicans on the issue of immigration – with 79 per cent of his party backing him – but only 36 per cent of Americans overall support his approach to the matter and 55 per cent disapprove. Some Republican allies in Congress have warned that his aggressive campaign to deport people in the country illegally risks alienating voters with family who recently immigrated to America, like some Hispanics. Some 35 per cent of poll respondents approve of Trump’s approach to fighting crime, compared to 50 per cent who disapprove. The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

title: Trump inaugurates White House helipad as major networks skip ceremony
description: Broadcast boycott leaves the US president without pool cameras for his maiden flight from the new helipad.
content: US President Donald Trump showed off his new White House helicopter landing pad on Monday, attempting to brush aside a First Amendment firestorm even as major television networks kept their cameras away in protest of CNN being banned from the grounds. A light drizzle fell on the South Lawn as Trump used oversized gold scissors to cut a red, white and blue ribbon. He then exchanged handshakes with officials and some members of a construction crew wearing green smocks and hard hats – seeking to portray business as usual. If he had words to mark the occasion, however, it was impossible to hear them over the noise of his waiting helicopter. Normally, TV network crews work to capture clearer audio. Trump did not answer reporters’ shouted questions before climbing aboard Marine One on his way to New York. Instead, he wrote on his social media site: “We are just leaving the White House Lawn on the maiden voyage from the newly built, and very beautiful, Heliport!” MS Now, Politico and CNN have sued after Trump announced Friday that he was banning them from covering the White House in a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts – in the courts and through administrative action – to restrict news coverage he finds objectionable. CNN normally participates in a five-network rotation that provides pooled footage of daily events at the White House. When the network was barred from taking its assigned turn on Monday, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News agreed collectively to the extraordinary step of skipping Trump’s helipad ceremony. Trump has long crowed about how the new helipad – featuring extensive granite that he boasts will have a “million-year life”, as well as a large insignia reading the “Seal of the President of the United States” – would impress Chinese President Xi Jinping, who arrives Wednesday for a state visit. He has been focused on wowing Xi even as he decried Democrats as communists in an attempt to help Republicans retain control of Congress in coming midterm elections. But his effort to curb access for media outlets to the White House has overshadowed Trump’s pet building projects and Xi’s visit. Igniting constitutional questions over media access also eclipsed the reason Trump was lifting off from the helipad – the annual trip to attend the United Nations General Assembly beginning on Tuesday. Speaking later to reporters in New York after meeting with the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, Trump tried again to shrug off the lack of network TV coverage of his movements. “It’s interesting because they said they were gonna boycott me. But they never boycott me,” the president said, before adding: “I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair”. The US president has spent large swathes of his second term focused on building projects even as his administration struggles to find a way out of the ongoing war in Iran. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk with only about six weeks before Election Day, where voters are increasingly worried about inflation and a potentially weakening economy. His successor in the Oval Office could move to undo much of his renovation work at the White House. And, in line with Trump’s assertions that the new helipad granite could last a million years, the president has made other grand pronouncements about his prowess with renovation projects that quickly fell flat. He said the refurbishing of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool would last a century, only for the paint to fade and its liner to peel away in chunks just days after it was laid. The helipad work began in June. Trump also ripped out the original Tennessee flagstone along the West Wing’s colonnade and replaced it with black granite. He similarly refurbished the traditional walkway from the White House’s diplomatic entrance with white granite, along with a portion of the asphalt driveway around the South Lawn. Trump rushed to finish the project before Xi arrives and has argued that visiting dignitaries will be dazzled by the project – despite Marine One being the only aircraft that lands so close to the White House. The president says the improvement was required since Vietnam war-era choppers that long had been used as Marine One are being replaced by modern ones that are too powerful to land on the White House lawn without damaging the lawn’s grass. Trump has spent months repeatedly talking about grass as a way to promote his various building plans, even though many of the construction projects required ripping up turf. Trump said in July that the helipad project would be privately funded and estimated its cost at up to US$6 million. Additional changes, including extensive efforts to level the ground around the helipad, have made calculating the exact expenditure difficult. The once storied South Lawn has become a major construction site this year. In June, Trump erected a fighting cage and temporary arena for a UFC fight marking his 80th birthday. Then, crews got down to work on the helipad. Trump says Sikorsky Aircraft – a subsidiary of defence contracting giant Lockheed Martin – would be paying for the helipad, since the company made the newer, larger helicopters. In his online post, Trump thanked Lockheed Martin’s CEO. Some of Trump’s projects have relied on public money, even when the president initially suggested otherwise. When crews originally demolished the White House’s East Wing to make room for Trump’s US$400 million ballroom, the president said it would be paid for by private donors. But his administration later sought US$1 billion from Congress to make security improvements to the structure.

title: UK brings first charges over the 1994 Rwanda genocide
description: Vincent Brown, 65, is accused of inciting and aiding murders of Tutsis after seven-year British investigation.
content: Prosecutors said on Monday they had brought the first-ever charges in the UK against a man for his alleged role in the 1994 Rwanda genocide, after a complex seven-year investigation. Vincent Brown, 65, was arrested and charged on Monday with one count of being an ancillary to genocide and six offences of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, prosecutors and the London police said. “He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others” against the Tutsi, said Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, in the first ever such charges in the UK. Some 800,000 people, mostly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were beaten, shot, or hacked to death with machetes in 100 days of slaughter. “This is the first time charges relating to the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda have been brought in the United Kingdom,” the Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement. A number of other countries have previously prosecuted suspects in the Rwandan genocide. Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is in custody and will appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday. Brown was formerly from Kigali in Rwanda but has been living in the Islington area of London. UK media said on Monday he was a Rwandan national but Agence France-Presse reported in 2006 that he had become a British citizen. Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said the case had “involved a huge amount of work and determination from officers in the War Crimes Team” which launched their investigation in September 2019. “This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” she added. Brown was first arrested in 2006. But his extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was finally refused by a British court in 2017. The Rwandan government then asked the UK government to investigate directly those allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994. Flanagan said “a number of other investigations remain ongoing” in the UK into similar offences committed during the Rwanda genocide. The genocide followed years of tension between ethnic Hutu and Tutsi populations and was triggered by the death of president Juvenal Habyarimana, whose private plane was hit by two missiles.

title: Thousands of US flights snarled before FAA resolves communications problem
description: Eight-hour outage cleared after construction crew cuts backup line on arrival day for world leaders in New York.
content: Thousands of flights across the US were snarled on Monday, with incoming flights halted for hours at major East Coast airports, before the Federal Aviation Administration resolved a telecommunications problem late in the afternoon. The issue started around 9.45am when workers accidentally cut a telecom line in New Jersey used by the FAA. This forced a halt to incoming flights at major airports on the day that 130 world leaders and dozens of ministers were arriving in New ‌York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. The FAA stopped arrivals at all three major New York-area airports as well as Philadelphia and Boston and two smaller airports in the New York area. The problems were not fully resolved for eight hours. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X late in the afternoon that telecom lines had been repaired and normal operations throughout the Northeast were resuming. He said it would take time to resolve existing delays and urged passengers to check the status of flights they were waiting for. FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said about 7,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, including 1,400 flights at the three major New York-area airports. More than half of all flights were canceled ⁠at Newark, a major United Airlines hub. United said it issued a travel waiver to help impacted passengers. The issue also forced the diversion of more than 100 flights to other airports. The incident demonstrated the ‌fragility of the aging US air traffic control system, which Congress awarded US$12.5 billion for upgrades last year. New Jersey Transit said a crew had been digging at one of its work sites 3 metres (10 feet) away from the utility markings and it was still trying to determine if Verizon or the contractor made ‌the markings. Duffy initially blamed an Amtrak construction crew, which he said accidentally cut into a fiber line in New Jersey near New Brunswick, causing a telecom outage ⁠and forcing FAA to pause flights in the ⁠Northeast. Amtrak said it was not responsible. Around 5.30pm, New Jersey Transit said most of the fiber cables had been repaired and should be coming back online shortly. Newark Airport reopened for arriving flights after eight hours and LaGuardia also reopened ‌after being shuttered for flights for much of the afternoon. Verizon said it was working to repair the damaged cable near the Amtrak rail line and to restore connectivity as quickly as possible. Flights at Philadelphia had again resumed late in the afternoon after a second ‌ground ‌stop was lifted. Reagan Washington National Airport also halted flights for more than an hour because of volume issues. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said a replacement circuit had failed at Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach ‌Control, which was the primary communications for the center. A ground stop at Boston, which stopped accepting flights because of spillover volume, was also lifted. “The timing is absolutely horrible and I’m very sorry ⁠for the delays and cancellations,” Bedford told reporters. He stressed that safety was the top priority. “We’re going to do what is necessary to make sure the airspace is safe.” The loss of communications was ⁠tied to a failed circuit at a Philadelphia air traffic control facility that handles air traffic for the airports, Bedford said. Then authorities discovered that the construction crew had accidentally cut a backup fiber line. “When it went to flip into the backup, we discovered that the backup fiber had a break, and that fiber break is probably 13 hours ‌to repair. It’s massive, I’m told. Meanwhile, we’ve ‌got the new circuit ready to install now,” Bedford said. Philadelphia is an American Airlines hub. In May 2025, the Philadelphia facility that guides air traffic in and out of Newark airport suffered a series of significant communications outages. The FAA said last year a telecommunications outage impacted communications and radar displays at Philadelphia TRACON. Technical issues can quickly have extensive knock-on effects for flights. In the UK on Monday, a brief glitch knocked out operations at a crucial center in Scotland, leading to delays. The issue followed two weeks after a massive countrywide disruption in UK airspace. Last year, Congress approved US$12.5 billion to start upgrading the aging air traffic control system, and boost controller hiring following decades of complaints over airport congestion and flight delays and a series of technology issues in recent years. Duffy said Congress needed to approve another US$17.5 billion to finish the job. “This is unacceptable in America,” Duffy said. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Sisters of Pakistan’s Imran Khan arrested in Lahore, jailed ex-PM’s party says
description: The purported arrests, ahead of ‌a protest planned for September 27, involved Khan’s sisters Aleema Khan, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Khan.
content: Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan’s party said on Monday that his three sisters had been arrested ahead of ‌a protest ⁠march planned for September 27. “Punjab police have raided Aleema Khan’s home and have abducted Imran Khan’s other two sisters, his nephews and their children,” Zulfi Bukhari, a spokesman for Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, said on social media. “Khan’s sisters and their children were taken into custody but the children were released,” PTI’s information secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram told Agence France-Presse. “All three sisters have been sent to Kot Lakhpat Jail, Lahore,” he added. The purported arrests involved Khan’s sisters Aleema Khan, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Khan. The deputy commissioner of Lahore passed two separate orders on Sunday, the copies of which were seen by Agence France-Presse, for the three sisters’ 30-day detention under the Maintenance of Public Order law of Punjab province. Punjab police did not respond to a request for comment. Khan’s party has announced a protest call for 27 September. Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Sunday the protest call was illegal. “We will not allow them to block roads and disrupt people’s lives,” Tarar said. Khan has been in prison since 2023 and was sentenced late last year, along with his wife, to 17 years in jail on corruption charges they both deny. The 73-year-old Khan, who was also a former Pakistan cricket captain, was prime minister from 2018 to 2022 before being removed in a no-confidence vote during a political crisis over tensions between his government and Pakistan’s powerful military establishment. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: President Xi Jinping calls on China, US youth to advance bilateral cooperation
description: In a reply to letter from students from US universities, Xi tells them to ‘shoulder the mission of the times’ ahead of state visit to Washington.
content: President Xi Jinping has expressed hope that the younger generation will advance Sino-US cooperation, foster mutual understanding and ensure steady, long-term development of bilateral ties, according to Chinese state media. Xinhua reported on Monday that Xi’s remarks came in his reply to a letter from students at 10 US universities who shared their thoughts and experiences after attending a youth exchange programme in China earlier this month. “Young people from China and the United States share the same planet Earth and jointly shoulder the mission of the times,” the report cited Xi as saying. “He expressed hope that the students would join the vast number of young people in both countries in striving to carry forward, uphold, and advance China-US friendly cooperation, and work together to foster mutual understanding and affinity between the two peoples and to ensure the steady and long-term development of bilateral relations, so as to contribute to the vitality of youth to building a better world.” Xi’s comments came ahead of his state visit to Washington to meet US counterpart Donald Trump between Wednesday and Friday. According to Xinhua, Xi cited the students’ letter in which they shared their appreciation for Chinese civilisation, their hope for friendly cooperation between China and the US, and their willingness to act as envoys of friendship across the Pacific region. He also expressed delight that the students had enjoyed their journey in China. The students told Xi that they hoped to serve as “ambassadors of friendship across the Pacific”, as they wrapped up a Sino-US youth tour in early September, according to one of the organisers, the Hong Kong-based Ng Teng Fong Charitable Foundation. Jointly organised by the foundation and the Beijing NGO Network for International Exchanges, the programme – Future Makers 2026 China-US Youth Tour for a Shared Asia-Pacific Future – was held between September 1 and 7.
