The programme hosted 170 young attendees from China and the US, of whom about 100 were from US institutions such as Harvard University, Columbia University, the University of Chicago and the University of Washington. Participants visited Jinan and Qufu in Shandong province as well as Beijing, touring landmarks such as the Temple of Confucius, the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the Great Wall. The foundation said the programme showcased traditional Chinese culture and values, and introduced China’s advanced technology through visits to an autonomous driving demonstration area in Beijing and the Xiaomi Auto Factory. It added that the Chinese and American youth also planted white-bark pines at Yanqi Lake in Beijing to symbolise enduring friendship between the younger generations of the two countries. Foundation director Daryl Ng Win-kong, also the chairman of Sino Group, said Xi’s reply was a “tremendous source of encouragement”. “His letter reflects the importance he places on youth development, as well as his long-standing support for youth exchanges and people-to-people ties between China and the United States,” he said. “President Xi has consistently shown great care for young people and a strong belief in the role they play in shaping the future. His message is both encouraging and inspiring, conveying his hope for deeper mutual understanding, lasting friendship and continued positive engagement between our two peoples.” He added that the foundation would continue to support international youth exchanges and dialogue, as well as foster greater understanding and connections across borders. Ng also said the foundation would leverage Hong Kong’s unique role as a “superconnector” to strengthen exchanges between China and the rest of the world. In May, Xi also replied to a letter from students attending a separate China-US youth friendship programme, including Liu Runjie from a local institution, the Chinese University of Hong Kong. In that reply, Xi expressed similar sentiments about his appreciation for the deep friendships forged between young people from the two countries through the programme. He also encouraged them to continue contributing to cultural exchange and mutual understanding between China and the United States. The letter was disclosed after Trump concluded a landmark visit to China earlier that month. Xinhua also reported that Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang met members of a youth delegation from Hong Kong and Macau at the Great Hall of the People on Monday morning, conveying Xi’s greetings to them. The delegation comprises nearly 1,200 students from primary and secondary schools and institutions of higher education in Hong Kong and Macau, who were on a trip in Beijing to pay tribute to the national flag. Ding said Xi has always cared for and supported the development of youth in Hong Kong and Macau, emphasising that when young people thrive, so do the two cities and the country. Noting that Hong Kong and Macau have ushered in the best development period in history, Ding called on the students to carry forward the cause of “one country, two systems”. Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, also attended the meeting, according to Xinhua.

title: Gaza children return to in-person schools for first time in 3 years
description: The move is a fragile milestone; the conflict with Israel has killed around 22,000 youngsters and over 770 education workers.
content: Hundreds of thousands of children in Gaza have returned to in-person teaching for the first time in nearly three years, albeit in damaged or makeshift school buildings and tents, and with uniforms, notebooks and pens unaffordable for many families. The United Nations Children’s Fund (Unicef) says 98 per cent of schools in Gaza were either destroyed or damaged during the war, and Gaza education ‌officials say about 660,000 students have been deprived of in-person learning and regular participation in education. The reopening on Saturday was a fragile milestone for Gaza after a conflict that has killed around 22,000 students and more than 770 education workers, including 532 teachers, according to Ibrahim Ramadan, director of education for East Khan Younis. “The last time I have been to school was three years ago. Now, we are starting the school year, it is year of joy, happiness and success,” said Moayed Abu Mustafa in Khan Younis. Mustafa said he was determined to learn even though he will sit on the floor in a tent ⁠lacking ventilation, he has no decent shoes, nor a notebook and pen, and lost friends during the war. “Despite all of this we will learn, we will learn ‌even in a tent.” Fifteen-year-old displaced student Samar Abu Salmi, who lives with her family in a tent, is also returning to class. “We studied on phones and we haven’t seen our teachers … now, we are back pursuing our dream … from one tent to another,” she ‌said, speaking in the yard of her new makeshift school. She also lacks much of the essential equipment, which has become unaffordable for her ⁠family. “Before the war, everything was available ⁠for us – notebooks, pens, goods, clothes, outings, things that we could get cheaply,” Salmi said. We used to wake up happy to go to ‌school... now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything Yamen Abu Samra, 14 Despite the devastation in the enclave, the Ministry of Education, backed by international and local organisations, has moved ‌ahead with the 2026-27 academic year, establishing dozens of temporary schools made of tents, tarpaulins, sheet metal and wood to accommodate pupils. Some are built on sandy ground, others have classrooms with only some mattresses and a blackboard, ‌into ‌which students cram. Others are still housing dozens of displaced families. Attending another school was 14-year-old Yamen Abu Samra. “We used to wake up happy to go to ‌school … now, when we come to school, we’re afraid of stray bullets, rockets, strikes, everything,” he said. “Now, I’m sitting in a tent that has absolutely nothing, just the sun ⁠and the heat,” he added. At least 540,000 students are expected to attend in-person classes this year in makeshift private schools, temporary learning centres and educational points, with ⁠Unicef support, according to education officials. Online learning will continue for those who cannot attend classes or who left Gaza during the war. Israeli forces remain in control of more than 60 per cent of Gaza despite last year’s ceasefire, which halted major fighting but failed to end the conflict. Palestinian authorities say more ‌than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s ‌assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023. Stationery trader Khaled Aliyan, 30, said Israeli import restrictions have reduced supplies and hiked prices. “This notebook, which used to cost 3 shekels (US$1), now costs 15 [shekels]. All stationery items are expensive,” he said. Israel’s COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on restrictions on supplies and strikes on schools. Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of using schools for military purposes, which Hamas denies.

title: First ladies step forward as Trump lays on rare honours for Xi
description: Three-day itinerary from September 23 to 25 will feature extensive ceremonial honours along with dedicated cultural exchanges and events.
content: US first lady Melania Trump is set to lead key cultural diplomacy events during the coming official state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, marking their first visit to the White House since 2015. According to an official itinerary released by the first lady’s office, the three-day visit, scheduled from September 23 to 25, will feature extensive ceremonial honours alongside dedicated cultural exchanges highlighting Sino-American relations. Melania will join US President Donald Trump to officially welcome Peng and President Xi to the White House on Thursday following their scheduled arrival at Joint Base Andrews the previous evening. The SCMP reported on September 17 that Trump would greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, not only at the White House, a rare presidential airport welcome. The official reception will take place across the South Lawn, State Floor and Rose Garden of the White House. It will begin with military pageantry along the White House grounds, where an Armed Forces honour guard will line the South Drive alongside displayed US and Chinese flags. The arrival proceedings will feature a full honour guard display by 479 military personnel across all branches of the US Armed Forces, a presidential salute, and military demonstrations by the United States Marine Corps Silent Drill Platoon and the Old Guard Fife and Drum Corps. A joint military flyover featuring a B-2 Spirit stealth bomber and four F-22 Raptors will conclude the morning’s lawn ceremonies. A major focus of the first lady’s agenda will take place on Thursday afternoon following the official State Arrival Ceremony on the South Lawn. Melania and Peng will visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art – the Smithsonian’s first art museum, housing over 45,000 works spanning thousands of years of Asian heritage. On Thursday evening, Melania will co-host a formal state dinner in the East Room of the White House for the visiting couple. Both presidents will speak at the start of the event. Officials said the American guests would include Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser and Tim Cook. “It’ll be a very popular and hot-ticketed event here in Washington,” a senior official said last week. The diplomatic schedule will continue into Friday morning, September 25, when Trump and the first lady will greet President Xi and Peng at the South Portico for morning tea in the White House Red Room. It would be the first time since 2017 that Melania and Peng have held separate engagements during a Trump-Xi summit. Melania did not accompany Trump to Beijing in May, but joined him on his 2017 trip to China, when she and Peng took part in several joint activities. In Beijing, she visited the Banchang Primary School alongside Peng, attended the Peking opera and took part in a variety of classes, including astronomy, calligraphy, cooking and Chinese architecture. Her interactions with Peng also drew comparisons between the two first ladies – from their pre-marriage lives to their fashion choices and public demeanour. During the trip, Melania remained in Beijing after Trump left for Vietnam, visiting the Beijing Zoo’s panda exhibit and touring the Great Wall. At the zoo, Melania fed a giant panda named Gu Gu and interacted with schoolchildren. “Thank you to the Beijing Zoo! Wonderful to meet Gu Gu! Melania Trump,” she later wrote on a panda print. After visiting the Great Wall, Melania posted a one-minute video on social media with a caption, “Thank you #China!”

title: Siobhan Haughey leads by example, inspiring the next generation of Hong Kong swim stars
description: The 28-year-old was in the 200m freestyle final with Gilaine Ma, while Adam Mak and Nicholas Cheung were in men’s 100m breaststroke.
content: China’s Yu Zidi was less than a year old when Siobhan Haughey first made the world sit up and take notice of her talent in the pool, 13 years later they are both Asian Games gold medallists and young talent is the order of the day. On Monday, Haughey defended her women’s 200m freestyle title with a crushing victory, and Yu laid down an Asian record in winning the women’s 200m individual medley. Three years ago in Hangzhou, it was Haughey setting regional and Games records, and while not “as fast as I would like”, the 28-year-old Olympian was also quick to highlight the way the sport was developing the next generation. “The general consensus is we have more and more great young swimmers swimming well,” Haughey said. “When Summer [McIntosh] first started she was also very young and swimming fast, so I think that’s kind of the ‌trend these days. “Hopefully, swimming well that young, you can also translate to as you get older and well into your 20s ‌and ‌beyond, so it’s exciting for the swimming world.” It’s not just the global talent that has Haughey excited, there was also the fact she was not the only Hongkonger in her race or others. Debutant Gilaine Ma, 18, also made the final, while there were appearances too for Adam Mak Sai-ting, 20, and Nicholas Cheung Chi-kit, 21, in the men’s 100m breaststroke. “The fact that it’s not just me swimming in the final this time is amazing and rare,” Haughey said. “It tells you that the development of our swimming team over the past few years has been really good; this is very encouraging.” Monday’s victory marked the fourth multi-sport games medal Haughey had won in this venue, after taking home two silver medals at the Tokyo Olympic Games five years ago, but she said the experience was almost incomparable. “The settings are different; and here we have the full crowd as well, whereas there was no one on the stands back then,” said Haughey, who pushed her Asian Games gold medal count to three. “It’s almost difficult to imagine it’s the same venue, but the memories come back when I walk past the warm-up pool or some other areas.” Still, it was not just the effort of the veteran swimmer that should be celebrated. Just one day after the decorated Haughey heaped praise on the city’s young generation of swimmers, Ma, who was part of the squad that took the women’s 4x100m freestyle relay silver on the opening night, put herself in the same bracket as some of the region’s top swimmers. Ma’s qualifying time of 2:00.57 in the heat was only 0.08 seconds off her personal best, eventually finishing fifth out of the 10 finalists, and she did it in style, slicing 0.74 seconds off her previous best time, which was achieved only in April at a local time trial event. “I think I did really well; in some previous major tournaments I felt nervous, but I was very calm so far,” Ma said. “Of course, there can still be a lot of improvement for me, but in terms of my competitive form this time, it’s 100 marks for me. “For everything I had prepared [in my training], I left it all in the pool. Obviously, I am very happy, and I also feel there is so much hope [regarding my future]. I am just beginning my university years, and with this result, I think there’s just so much hope in my training for the next four years.” From looking up to her idol Haughey, to swimming the opening relay leg before handing over to her, Ma has now even competed in the same final as Haughey, just a couple of lanes from the four-time Olympic medallist. “She’s still my idol no matter what, and after I had experienced so much with her, I learned more about her,” she said. “Aside from her outstanding athletic performance, she has a great personality – she really cares about her teammates and, since we’re younger, often gives us pointers and guidance. “Siobhan is both hardworking and humble; she inspires me to strive for improvement in swimming while also becoming a better person outside of the pool.” With the 200m freestyle her major event, Ma was following in the footsteps of Haughey not only in the water, but also outside of the pool. The Diocesan Girls’ School graduate was embracing her first year at the University of Michigan, where Haughey, who majored in psychology, graduated in 2019. Ma said, “I want to be a doctor in the future,” but revealed she still has a year before she decides on her major subject. With Haughey potentially swimming towards the end of her career with each appearance, she was delighted to see her young teammates stepping onto the bigger stage together. “It’s truly meaningful to see someone who had idolised me for years swimming next to me in an Asian Games final,” she said. “I’ve always said, yes, I am doing my own thing in the water, but if I can inspire someone else, it’s very good. “Gilaine, she may have been watching me compete and train just a few years ago, and now, seeing she’s right beside me doing the same thing, it’s like what I did was endowed with more meaning. “I just said, ‘Add oil, good luck, you’ve got this’ to her before the final. Yes, they may be young, but all of them have their own ways to deal with these major tournaments, so just some encouraging words will do, telling them that they’re not alone in this race, and that they have another teammate with them.”

title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico sue Trump over White House press ban
description: Lawsuit alleges First Amendment violations as major TV networks suspend presidential pool coverage in protest.
content: CNN, MS ⁠NOW and Politico sued US President Donald Trump and other members of his administration on Monday for banning them from White House grounds, saying the action violated their rights to free speech and a free press under the US Constitution’s First Amendment. The news outlets are seeking a temporary restraining order to block Trump’s action in federal court in Washington DC, with a hearing scheduled for Wednesday. “This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit stated. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference,” the outlets wrote in a joint statement. “The government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” Trump announced the ban on Friday on social media, saying those news outlets “shouldn’t ‌be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” and defended it in another post on Monday. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump wrote on Monday, without providing evidence of a national security threat. Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets. The White House launched a “Trump TV” stream on Monday evening, days after Trump banned the media outlets from the White House. The White House said the stream will run videos and highlights of what it calls the Trump administration’s achievements but a press freedom advocate said it amounted to “a steady diet of government propaganda”. A 60-second trailer displayed the Republican leader’s 2024 presidential win and the first video streamed after the ⁠platform went live was Trump’s remarks on July 3 at Mount Rushmore. The stream had only about 8,000 live views 15 minutes after it was launched on YouTube. “This just makes it even clearer that the real goal here is to ensure that the American public is fed a steady diet of government propaganda,” Jameel ‌Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said. CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country. CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Monday, but was not able to ‌provide a pool feed. In response, the other major TV networks suspended presidential pool coverage. This effectively eliminated the most widespread video source for White House events just as Trump is set to meet with numerous world leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly and ⁠host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington later in the week. “This is to ⁠advise that, effective today (Monday), the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the President,” Bryan Boughton, who runs the Fox News Washington bureau and is the current TV pool chair, said in an email Monday. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.” Otherwise, it was business as usual in the White House press room on Monday as reporters planned for the ‌day’s events, including an afternoon ribbon-cutting ceremony for the Republican president’s new Marine One helipad on the South Lawn. The audio on the White House’s own live stream of the ceremony, which it promoted as an alternative to the pool feed, was inaudible. Trump’s party is seeking to retain its narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections. Polls show the public souring on Republicans and Trump’s own approval ratings ‌stand near ‌historic lows. A person familiar with the matter, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Natalie Harp, a close presidential aide, showed Trump clips and graphics of recent news coverage, which contributed to his decision to ban the three outlets. Trump has been “very unhappy” with coverage of the midterm elections, the person added, and his frustration ‌intensified after last week’s Supreme Court ruling that blocked his attempt to limit mail-in voting. “The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office,” the White House said in response to Reuters questions about the lawsuit, Harp’s role and Trump’s views on election coverage. “They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside.” The ⁠affected news organisations moved quickly to present a united front. Within 10 minutes of Trump’s announcement on Friday, CNN reached out to MS NOW and Politico to discuss joint legal action, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter, speaking on condition of anonymity. “Banning news organisations from the White House prevents them ⁠from confronting government officials face-to-face and perhaps eliciting off-the-cuff unguarded comments that might shed new light onto political matters, which is especially important during an election year,” said Victor Pickard, a professor of media policy and political economy at the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg School for Communication. Last year, Trump banned the Associated Press from the pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt his preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico. The AP has sued over the ban. His administration also has limited the access of many journalists to the Pentagon. In ‌his first term, Trump’s White House sought to take away the credentials of then-CNN ‌correspondent Jim Acosta and Playboy correspondent Brian Karem. Federal judges ordered their White House press passes be restored. The lawsuit was assigned to US District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017. It was Kelly who ruled against Trump in 2018 in the Acosta case. Trump has stepped up his actions targeting the media since winning a second term, suing multiple outlets and repeatedly urging broadcasters to drop programmes he deems unfair. He has called on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavoured broadcast stations of their licenses. David Ellison, son of Trump ally and Oracle Executive Chairman Larry Ellison, took control of Paramount and its CBS news unit, leading to a shake-up at 60 Minutes, the most popular US TV news magazine. Ellison is now seeking to acquire CNN parent Warner Bros, in a move approved by Trump’s administration.

title: China gets closer to Jupiter mission by bringing Nasa’s StarNAV concept to life
description: The tech uses subtle shifts in starlight to track speed and position, allowing spacecraft to navigate deep space alone.
content: Chinese researchers have tested a new way for spacecraft to navigate in deep space, putting a concept funded by Nasa into practice and paving the way for the country’s planned mission to Jupiter in 2030. Known as stellar aberration navigation, the approach uses tiny shifts in the relative position of stars to work out how fast a probe is moving and in what direction, allowing autonomous real-time navigation without constantly relying on tracking and commands from Earth. In a low-Earth-orbit experiment in January, the Tianhui-7 satellite used this method to determine its position to within about 5km (3.1 miles), a performance comparable to Nasa’s antenna-based Deep Space Network. Jupiter can be up to 900 million km from Earth, with radio signals taking more than 50 minutes to travel one way. That made it impossible for ground controllers to intervene in real time, wrote researchers from the China Academy of Space Technology – the country’s main spacecraft manufacturer – in a paper that will be published in the Journal of Deep Space Exploration. While China can track spacecraft as far away as Jupiter, it cannot track objects in deep space as precisely as Nasa or the European Space Agency, the researchers said. Tianwen-4 will be China’s first mission to explore the Jupiter system, studying the giant planet and its moons, including their evolution, environment and internal structures. Tianhui-7 was launched aboard a Long March 4B rocket from northwestern China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre on December 30, 2025. At the time, state news agency Xinhua said only that it would be used for geographic mapping, land surveys and scientific research. According to the new paper, the satellite carried three highly precise star cameras and an infrared sensor to test the navigation technology for 20 hours in orbit about 500km above Earth, with the planet standing in for Jupiter. The cameras photographed different patches of the sky, while the infrared sensor observed Earth. Together, these measurements allowed the satellite to work out its own position and speed, which researchers then compared with GPS data to gauge the method’s accuracy. Stellar aberration is not a new concept. It was discovered about 300 years ago by English astronomer James Bradley, who noticed that stars appeared to shift slightly in the sky as Earth travelled around the sun. The stars themselves are not moving back and forth. They appear a tiny bit ahead of where they really are because Earth is moving forward to meet the incoming starlight. The effect can be compared to watching rain through the windscreen of a moving car. Even if the rain is falling straight down, it seems to slant towards you because the car is moving towards the raindrops. The same happens with starlight as Earth or a spacecraft moves through space. The effect is tiny, but predictable. For centuries, stellar aberration was something that had to be corrected when measuring the positions of stars. However, scientists later realised they could use the effect as a navigation tool. By measuring how far the stars appear to shift, they can work backwards and calculate how fast a spacecraft is moving and in what direction. In 2020, Nasa funded the StarNAV experimental project that aims to perform the extraordinarily precise measurements of star positions needed to navigate by starlight. Angles must be measured in milliarcseconds, equivalent to the apparent width of a grain of rice seen from 500km away. The star cameras aboard Tianhui-7 were accurate to about 50 milliarcseconds. To make such measurements useful, the Chinese team added an optical reference system that kept track of tiny shifts in the cameras themselves, caused by launch vibrations and temperature changes. Over the 20-hour test, the navigation settled at a margin of error of around 5km for position and 5 metres (16.4 feet) per second for velocity, compared with GPS data, the researchers reported. Correcting systematic errors later improved those figures to better than 4km and 4 metres per second. But the team cautioned that conditions around Jupiter would be very different, and whether the technique could perform as well in orbit around the gas giant remained to be tested. China is also developing a new generation of even more precise milliarcsecond-level star cameras. A prototype has been built and put through ground tests, according to a 2025 article published on the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation website.

title: Survey finds US public opinion shifting in favour of engagement with China
description: Beijing seen as less of a threat in Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey, although a partisan divide exists.
content: On the eve of this week’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Americans feel better about China, according to a poll released on Monday. They see Beijing as less of a threat, are less supportive of Taiwan and are more likely to favour engagement over containment than last year or in 2024, when views hit an all-time low. As with almost everything in the US these days, the Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey revealed a partisan divide. And while the views expressed were less hawkish than in recent years, 40 per cent of Americans still supported limiting China’s power. “There’s not a bipartisan consensus among the public in favour of a competitive containment approach,” said Craig Kafura, the Council’s public opinion and foreign policy director. “If Americans were really hawkish on China, I think that would bode poorly for stability.” The survey found that 57 per cent of Americans favoured engaging with China, an increase from the all-time low in 2024 and the highest result in Council polling since 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. But it is still below the high mark of 68 per cent in 2019. Using a “feeling thermometer” that measures cold to hot views on a 0 to 100 scale, Americans rated China at 39 this year, still relatively cool but warmer than the 26 in 2024. The highest heat rating for China was 53 in 1986. This year’s figure is also below the 44 level posted in 2015 during the last summit between a US and Chinese president on US soil. “After a year of escalating economic tension between Washington and Beijing, Trump’s May 2026 trip to China ended with agreements to stabilise the relationship,” the report said. “This marks only the second US state visit for Xi, the first held in 2015 under US President Barack Obama.” “American public opinion of China has also shifted over the past decade, with views turning sharply negative in the late 2010s and early 2020s – and now shifting again.” Trump’s approval rating in recent US polls, as low as 32 per cent, appeared to be lower than China’s, one senior Chinese diplomat recently noted. US views of China steadily declined from 2020 to 2024 in part because of the steady parade of negative news, Kafura said, including the pandemic, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan, the strained summit in Anchorage, Alaska, and the “spy balloon” overflight. In another survey result most likely to please Beijing, just 38 per cent of Americans favoured using US troops if the mainland attacked Taiwan, down from 52 per cent in 2022. This comes as Trump, a transactional president, has made several statements about the self-governing island that are closer to China’s view than those of past US presidents. After meeting with Xi last October, Trump openly questioned why the US should fight a war involving Taiwan 9,500 miles (15,000km) away and suggested that US defence guarantees involving the island were conditional. “The president sees Taiwan security as something that’s negotiable,” said Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow with the Foundation for the Defence of Democracies. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. The survey also highlighted the partisan divide endemic in US politics. Democrats were far more supportive of engagement with China, with 72 per cent of liberal Democrats and 64 per cent of moderate or conservative Democrats saying as much. This reflects in part a negative response to Trump’s unpopular trade tariff policy and a desire for less confrontation, Kafura said. Meanwhile, as with other issues such as military interventions and the lack of disclosures related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, Trump increasingly diverges from his base. Sixty-three per cent of Make America Great Again (Maga) Republicans advocated limiting the expansion of Chinese power, compared with 40 per cent for Americans overall. And just 36 per cent were in favour of engagement. “This shift towards cooperation and engagement matches the general direction that Trump has taken since his May 2026 meeting with Xi in Beijing,” the survey said. “But it is not one embraced by his base: most Maga Republicans continue to favour limiting the growth of China’s power rather than cooperation.” Analysts said this harder line among Republicans dovetails with Beijing’s long-standing contention that Washington is keen to prevent China’s development. The survey also found many Americans believe China’s position in the world is improving while their own country is not doing very well. One-third of Americans said China was more respected than a decade ago, more than double the percentage who said so in 2021. And 62 per cent felt the US was losing global respect relative to a decade ago, roughly consistent with the view in 2021. Looking at the partisan breakdown, some eight in 10 Democrats and two-thirds of independent voters said the US was less respected in the world relative to 10 years ago, compared with four in 10 Republicans. One ongoing question as Trump becomes increasingly unpopular at home and abroad is how much of China’s improved – or less negative – popularity is attributed to China’s actions and how much is related to its standing relative to Trump and US policies, an issue this survey did not address directly. “Yes, countries have a more favourable view of China today than they did three years ago,” said Ryan Hass, China director at the Brookings Institution. “How much of that is because China is doing well? How much of it is because people are angry at Donald Trump?” The Council survey was carried out between July 10 and July 21 by polling firm Ipsos involving 2,156 Americans from all 50 states and the District of Columbia, with a margin of error of 2.3 percentage points.

title: Air China makes special pre-summit New York flight over objections of US aviation group
description: Major American carriers protested to US Transport Department, saying Chinese rivals gain an unfair edge from access to Russian airspace.
content: A special Air China flight from Beijing reached New York over the objections of a trade association representing the biggest US airlines, according to a flight data tracker, and a second additional flight by the same Chinese carrier is being considered for Friday. The flight took off from the Chinese capital around 4pm on Saturday and landed after 6pm local time the same day, according to global flight tracking and data platform FlightAware. Flight 621 was the first US flight China’s flagship airline had proposed in tandem with President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, independent aviation analyst Li Hanming said. He said the flight carried diplomats, business leaders and reporters from China. Aviation regulators probably made no public announcements because the flight was for “diplomatic” purposes, Li said. The US Department of Transportation had not disclosed the September 19 flight on its website as of Tuesday Hong Kong time – days after the trade group Airlines for America filed an objection to the department. Airlines for America, which counts Delta Air Lines and United Airlines among its 11 members, said it was unfair that US-based carriers could not fly over Russian airspace while Chinese peers could. In a document filed with the department on September 17, the association said “as the department is well aware, Chinese airlines operate with [the] benefit of access to Russian airspace, which provides for shorter, less costly and more economical routing on flights to and from China and the United States.” It added that US airlines were “effectively banned from serving the very same important non-stop markets on the East Coast in the US for which Air China seeks authority”. Russia has banned a host of European and North American airlines from its airspace over their home countries’ sanctions against Moscow relating to the war in Ukraine, which has given Chinese carriers the advantage of shorter flight times on China-Europe routes. The granting of extra flights would let Chinese carriers operate above current limits set by both countries and “could create a precedent for incremental additions outside that framework”, the association said. Aviation analysts said it was unclear whether Air China’s proposed September 25 flight – noted in the Department of Transportation document – would get US approval. It would be a return flight and had not yet been given a flight number, Li said. Neither Air China nor the US consulate in Hong Kong replied to requests for comment.

title: World leaders meet at UN as planet grapples with climate change, wars, runaway AI
description: As we face ‘three existential threats,’ says the UN chief, ‘international cooperation is more necessary than ever’.
content: Under a global cloud of wars and bitter divisions, world leaders meet at the United Nations in New York this week facing new fears that runaway artificial intelligence could threaten humanity even as climate shocks and escalating prices are already making life much tougher for hundreds of millions of people. The annual high-level gathering at the UN General Assembly will also be consumed with major wars in Iran, Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, Congo and Myanmar and a persisting question: can the leaders do anything to end them? And what can they do about the relentless rise of global warming threatening the future of the planet, the growing inequalities within and among nations, and shocks to the global economy as blocked shipping routes and supply chains increase the cost of living and slow growth? The future of the UN will also definitely be on the agenda. At 81, its powers are still the victorious nations from World War II, not the 21st century’s major global players. The UN’s 193 member nations have agreed to a wide-ranging reform package that includes updating key institutions such as the powerful UN Security Council, where the US, Russia, China, Britain and France hold inordinate sway because of their veto power. Reform, however, is easier said than implemented. Behind the scenes, there will be speculation about who will lead the United Nations next. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ second five-year term ends on December 31, and no clear successor has emerged. Meeting remains pivotal There is still no question that the UN remains THE gathering place for its 193 member nations and their leaders. Some 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak at the General Assembly starting on Tuesday along with dozens of ministers. Among the headliners will be US President Donald Trump and French President Emanuel Macron. Both will speak on Tuesday after Guterres’ opening “state of the world” address. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian speak on Wednesday. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – whom New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani wanted arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza until he learned he has no such authority – will address the assembly on Thursday. For a second year, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will not be coming to the UN because the US has refused to give him a visa. He will nonetheless address the assembly by video the same day. The United States, under its agreement with the UN to host the organisation, is required to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend meetings. Equally telling is who else is not coming. China’s President Xi Jinping is meeting Trump in Washington on Wednesday, yet he is skipping – some diplomats say snubbing – the UN gathering and sending a vice-president instead. Russian President Vladimir Putin is not coming either, and Indian President Narendra Modi has backed out. France’s UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, said it is “extremely critical” for world leaders this week to support the UN as the place where the world’s nations meet, especially at a time of such polarisation. “We believe in multilateralism,” he said, “and we believe that the high-level week is the occasion for countries in the world to reaffirm that they prefer cooperation and dialogue to confrontation.” There is no doubt it has been a tough year for the world body. It has been pushed to the sidelines when it comes to its key responsibility of ensuring international peace and security and trying to end major conflicts in the Mideast and Ukraine. The US failure to pay billions of dollars in outstanding arrears has left the organisation’s finances in a rocky shape. But veteran UN watcher Richard Gowan, the International Crisis Group’s global issues and institutions programme director, says 2025 was even worse. A year ago, he said, people were contemplating that Trump would use his UN speech to announce that the United States would leave the world organisation. Trump did not announce a pull-out last September and the UN muddled through the past 12 months with financial troubles that forced cutbacks to its peacekeeping operations and humanitarian aid. In recent days, the US paid US$725 million of its dues to the UN’s regular operating budget for this year, enough to keep the Trump administration from losing its vote in the General Assembly. The payment was a strong indication that Trump will keep the US in the United Nations. The UN is no longer “in free fall”, Gowan said, but it “is stuck in an open-ended or permanent crisis”. Put more graphically, he said, “the UN may not be in emergency care like it was last year, but it does seem to be trapped in a trauma centre for the foreseeable future”. Former UN deputy secretary general Mark Malloch-Brown, a United Nations Foundation board member, said that “while the world still trusts the UN, the global public is eager for change”. The rise of AI The future of artificial intelligence has pushed to the forefront of global concerns, with its speeding advances and the dawning recognition that there are no industry controls, let alone any global guardrails for a technology that has many advantages but also many disadvantages and unknowns. Days before the global gathering, leaders of three major AI companies warned about the technology getting out of human control and called for a pause, but Trump dismissed their concerns as “a hoax” and urged continued advances to keep the US ahead of China. The UN Security Council added a high-level meeting on AI to its agenda on Wednesday afternoon, a sign of the growing apprehension and need to address the issue. It was already slated to hold a high-level meeting on Ukraine with Zelensky on Wednesday morning. For the UN chief, this will be his last assembly meeting with global leaders. He previewed his speech last week, telling UN reporters that power is shifting in “an era of deep uncertainty”. “At a time when the world faces three existential threats,” he said, “international cooperation is more necessary than ever.” Others will be vying for the spotlight on issues from rising sea levels and funding education to the fight for gender equality. Hundreds of private meetings will also convene in UN cubicles, hotels, diplomatic missions and restaurants. Esther Brimmer, a senior fellow in global governance at the Council on Foreign Relations and former US assistant secretary of state for international organisation affairs in the Obama administration, said in-person meetings can help countries hash out ideas that get implemented months later. She called the situation in 2026 “much more serious and complex than in decades past”. “With that said, I’m also not without hope as well,” Brimmer said. “Over the past decades we’ve learned a lot about international cooperation.”

title: Hong Kong school withdraws graduation video guideline on Cantonese after backlash
description: Good Hope School has expressed regret and withdrawn guidance after a viral post alleged Cantonese was banned from graduation videos.
content: A leading Hong Kong secondary school has expressed regret and withdrawn guidelines accused of banning Cantonese from graduation videos after the policy sparked controversy. Good Hope School issued a public statement on Monday evening, saying it had heard concerns from the wider community and had “fully and formally withdrawn” the guidance paper for next year’s Form Six graduation class video. “Good Hope School wishes to state unequivocally that it has never been our ethos to constrain the mother tongue of any child entrusted to our care, and nor shall it ever be. Drawing on our deeply ingrained and cherished culture of biliteracy and trilingualism, we remain dedicated to nurturing young minds,” it said. “We acknowledge, with profound contrition, that our previous document caused distress, misgiving, and sorrow among our students, parents, alumnae and the wider community. For this lapse, the school bears full responsibility.” The school came under scrutiny after a recent post on social media platform Threads went viral, sharing what appeared to be internal presentation materials from Good Hope School, a semi-private girls’ school in Ngau Chi Wan. Referring to “a Band 1A girls’ school on Clear Water Bay Road”, the user posted images resembling presentation slides titled “Language Standards”. The slides stated that classes would have to mute the audio and redo sound effects if Cantonese was detected in voice tracks, with only English and Mandarin permitted. The public statement came a day after the Education Bureau urged the school to review arrangements for the event and maintain effective communication with stakeholders. In Monday’s statement, the school said its leadership team had taken several measures to “address the crucial issue of trust”. It said it had immediately revoked the guideline and begun consulting student leaders, the graduating class and parent representatives to draft a new document jointly on the graduation videos. It added that it would ensure every student was “free to recount her school days in voices and accents that ring clearest to her heart”. On Saturday, principal Gary Harfitt clarified that Cantonese was not forbidden at the institution, according to an internal email to students and parents that was circulated online. He said a PowerPoint slide that had not been revised was regrettably issued to Secondary Six students and contained inappropriate language. He added that he took full responsibility for the oversight and stressed that the slide’s message did not reflect school policy.

title: Hong Kong athletes enjoy day to remember with 6-medal haul at Asian Games
description: Success across wushu, triathlon, karate and swimming took the city’s overall tally to eight, with fencers entering the mix tomorrow.
content: Hong Kong’s athletes had a Monday to remember at the Asian Games, picking up six medals, and if Siobhan Haughey’s gold was more expected than hoped for, the reverse was true elsewhere. Success across wushu, triathlon, karate and swimming took the city’s overall tally to eight, with the belief more should follow when the city’s fencers enter the mix for the first time on Tuesday. Lydia Sham Hui-yu got things started with victory in the women’s wushu changquan, and there were sighs of relief all round when the city’s triathletes claimed bronze in the mixed team relay. Swimmer Ian Ho Yentou took silver in a seriously fast men’s 50m freestyle race, while Howard Hung Ho-wai and Wong Cheuk-lee added bronze in karate. One of the city’s flag bearers at the opening ceremony, Sham could not believe her time had finally come, or how quickly it passed, at her third Asian Games. “It’s been eight years for 1.5 minutes of competition, and then it ends,” she said. “I don’t know what happened, but I just tried my best. “I just tried to tell myself that it’s just a moment to enjoy, even though it’s a very very, very nervous moment.” The city’s triathlon quartet – Oscar Coggins, Robin Elg, Cade Wright and Bailee Brown – could well have been forgiven for having nerves, given their future was largely hanging on them getting to the podium, and sitting fourth heading into the final leg of the mixed team relay was not part of the plan. Still, Elg kept his head, was fortunate that rival Park Sang-min briefly lost his on the bike, and was eventually able to add another bronze to the city’s collection, which was “a very special thing”, as the medal secured their sport’s elite status in Hong Kong. It is, of course, nothing in comparison to the runaway train that is the China team, who count 23 golds in 38 medals collected so far, and sit happily at the top of the medal table. Swimming sensation Yu Zidi provided one of the gold medals, setting an Asian record in her domination of the women’s 200m individual medley. The 13-year-old said she felt “even happier about this gold medal” than the first one she picked up in the women’s 200m butterfly on Sunday. Tokyo Aquatics Centre is proving a happy hunting ground for the mainland delegation, and included in the other triumphs was Xu Jiayu adding the men’s 50m backstroke title to the 100m one he claimed the day before. It is a place of happy memories for Haughey too. It was the scene of her 200m freestyle silver at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, when she came home in an Asian record time of one minute, 53.92 seconds. Not nearly as quick this time, she raced to victory in 1:54.96, comfortably clear of China’s Li Jiaping, who was second in 1:56.58 and Lu Yaxin, who took bronze in 1:57.53. “I’m really happy to win a gold medal,” Haughey said. “I gave it my all, and even though the time wasn’t quite what I imagined, I’m still satisfied with it.” As Haughey pointed out to reporters afterwards, “it’s a long week”, and Tuesday brings the defence of another gold she won in Hangzhou three years ago, the women’s 100m freestyle.

title: Former top PLA generals expelled from Communist Party for factionalism and disloyalty
description: Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli are both accused of severe violations of party discipline and suspected of serious duty-related crimes.
content: The Communist Party accused former military leaders Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli of factionalism and disloyalty, expelling them from the party and the armed forces following a Politburo meeting on Monday, state media reported. Zhang was once a vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) and the highest-ranking uniformed member of the Chinese military, second only to Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The CMC is China’s top military decision-making body. Zhang was also a member of the party’s 24-member Politburo. Liu was a CMC member as well and formerly served as chief of its Joint Staff Department. They are among the most prominent figures brought down in the anti-corruption campaign within the People’s Liberation Army. In a sternly worded read-out released on Monday, the two generals, who were placed under investigation on January 24, were accused of severe violations of party discipline and suspected of serious duty-related crimes. “Investigation found that Zhang and Liu … transgressed red lines and bottom lines,” according to the statement. “They severely violated political discipline and rules by forming cliques and factions, demonstrating disloyalty and dishonesty to the party.” Their offences included “taking advantage of their positions to seek promotional benefits for others in exchange for huge amounts of money”, “accepting gifts and money in violation of regulations”, “failing to fulfil political responsibilities for full and rigorous self-governance of the party” and “failing to properly educate and restrain their relatives and close staff”, it added. “Their political and economic infractions were intertwined, combining corruption and enrichment with dereliction of duty, involving exceptionally large sums of money, extremely severe circumstances and highly damaging impacts.” Besides being expelled from the party and the PLA, Zhang and Liu had their qualifications as delegates to the 20th party congress terminated, the statement continued, with their cases transferred to military procuratorial bodies for legal review and prosecution. The cases showed the Central Committee and the CMC’s determination to continue the fight against corruption, it said, “reaffirming the resolute stance that anti-corruption efforts in the military know no forbidden zones, allow no exceptions and tolerate zero corruption”. “There can be no place for corrupt elements to hide within the armed forces,” the statement added. In recent years, the massive anti-corruption campaign has seen the downfall of dozens of the PLA’s top brass. Before Zhang and Liu, CMC members He Weidong, Li Shangfu and Miao Hua were also removed, leaving only Xi and Zhang Shengmin of the seven-member commission elected in 2022.

title: Foreign chambers back Hong Kong 5-year plan, urge progress on Northern Metropolis
description: Focus on city’s role in helping mainland Chinese businesses go global is attractive to foreign investors, chamber heads say.
content: Representatives of foreign business chambers who met Hong Kong’s leader have said the five-year plan provided clear policy priorities for companies’ strategic planning, but called for more concrete timelines and visible progress on the Northern Metropolis project to attract investment. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu held a briefing on Monday for consuls general and heads of foreign chambers of commerce, during which he stressed that Hong Kong’s five-year plan was not a planned economy. The session included representatives from the United States, United Kingdom, Australia and the European Union. “[The five-year blueprint] is a planning process which combines government policy with market forces, allowing everybody to find the best way to achieve the target with the best results and allowing flexibility in the process, making adjustments when circumstances are beyond your control,” he said. After the briefing on Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the policy address unveiled last Wednesday, some chamber leaders said the road map provided policy certainty. They added that the blueprint allowed firms to align their own long-term strategic planning, which was often measured in three- to five-year intervals. “It tells us exactly where and when the resources will be deployed, and that gives business the confidence to move forward and to be able to invest here,” Mary Simpson, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said after the briefing. She said the plan channelled the city’s established pillars – which her chamber viewed as finance, law and logistics – into new growth areas, including artificial intelligence, green technology and critical minerals. Johannes Hack, chairman of the European Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, described the plan as a practical road map for communicating the city’s developmental direction to overseas investors. Hack and Simpson, who both returned from their chambers’ “door-knock” missions to their home region in recent weeks, said the focus on Hong Kong’s role in helping mainland Chinese businesses go global was attractive to investors in Europe and Australia. Hack said his chamber’s visit to Brussels and Strasbourg was intended to bridge the gap between his organisation’s on-the-ground experience in the city and what he called a “stuck” perception of Hong Kong that predated its post-pandemic economic recovery. He said he saw a role for European businesses to advise small and medium-sized Chinese firms in overseas investments on the continent via Hong Kong. “I think this was a journey more towards re-establishing the overall importance of Hong Kong, and the easiest way we found of doing that was to talk about finance, where it’s very clear that there is a very strong franchise and there is very strong trust,” he said. Under the five-year plan mapping out the city’s development direction between 2026 and 2030 with both binding and anticipatory targets, fast-tracking the Northern Metropolis has been designated a top priority. The 30,000-hectare megaproject is designed to house technology parks, university campuses and up to 186,000 homes. Other goals included enhancing the city’s status as an international hub for a variety of industries from finance to innovation, and deepening Greater Bay Area connections. However, foreign business leaders stressed that attracting overseas capital would require clear execution markers, including “visible” assurance of development timelines. Simpson of the Australian chamber said her country’s medical technology, infrastructure and logistics firms were keen to raise capital in Hong Kong. She added that firms in her country could lend expertise in public-private partnerships, urban planning, education and healthcare development. “I think for overseas enterprises to commit to capital, they need to have visibility on the ground,” she said. “They want to know that their infrastructure follows certain timelines, that where the precincts are focused, how there is cross-boundary collaboration, where that will all actually work in practice.” Hack highlighted the need for a compelling narrative for business chambers to sell the megaproject to firms back home, noting that few European companies had heard of the project so far. “The KPIs aren’t really something you can sell to an investor easily, you need storytelling around that,” Hack said. The chairman said examples of the megaproject’s achievements, such as a novel drug developed there with participation from the Greater Bay Area, would help convince European investors. Paul McComb, executive director of the British Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong, said the city government’s “whatever it takes” mindset to remove hurdles around the Northern Metropolis project was an encouraging sight, and that the project’s benefits would begin to show as businesses moved into the proposed tech parks. “I think they’ve got the right frame of mind to make the Northern Metropolis a huge success,” McComb said.

title: Subsidised physiotherapy places slashed by third amid graduate job crunch
description: Cuts come as physiotherapy graduates face a tight job market amid ongoing healthcare budget constraints and a surge in new practitioners.
content: Hong Kong education authorities have cut the number of subsidised places for physiotherapy and occupational therapy programmes at three self-financing institutions by about a third for the 2027-28 academic year, amid a jobs crunch for graduates. A physiotherapy association backed the reduction to avoid worsening unemployment in the sector, saying any future increase in places would depend on government funding. The Education Bureau on Monday announced that its Study Subsidy Scheme for Designated Professions or Sectors (SSSDP) would fund 4,711 places across 59 undergraduate programmes at eight self-financing institutions in the coming academic year. The overall number of subsidised places fell by 70 from the current year, a drop of about 1 per cent. “The programmes and numbers of subsidised places under the scheme are determined by the Education Bureau in consultation with relevant policy bureaus and departments,” the bureau said. In a separate reply to the South China Morning Post, the Education Bureau said it previously consulted the Health Bureau on the number of subsidised places in healthcare-related programmes. “Based on the findings of the 2023 Healthcare Manpower Projection, the supply-demand gaps for certain healthcare professions have gradually narrowed. To promote sustained development and meet the manpower needs of relevant healthcare professions, and having taken into account the latest service needs, the government has reduced the number of subsidised places for relevant programmes under the SSSDP,” an Education Bureau spokeswoman said. She added that the Health Bureau was conducting another projection to cover 13 healthcare professions, with the results expected to be announced in the first half of 2027. The study subsidy scheme covers 10 disciplines identified as having strong manpower demand: architecture and engineering, computer science, creative industries, financial technology, healthcare, insurance, logistics, sports and recreation, testing and certification, and tourism and hospitality. Three physiotherapy programmes saw a sharp reduction in places, with total intake falling from 175 in 2026-27 to 120 in 2027-28, a 31 per cent cut. Tung Wah College and Saint Francis University each had their Year One intake cut from 60 to 40 places, a one-third reduction. Hong Kong Metropolitan University’s (HKMU) intake fell from 55 to 40 places, a 27 per cent reduction. The SCMP has approached the three institutions for comment. The cuts come as physiotherapy graduates face a tight job market, amid continuing healthcare budget constraints and an increase in the number of new practitioners. Tung Wah College’s occupational therapy programme was similarly affected, with its intake set to fall by one-third, from 60 to 40 places next year, because of comparable job shortages in the sector. Alexander Woo Chuen-hau, president of the Hong Kong Physiotherapy Association, said he supported the cuts given the weak hiring outlook. He said the Hospital Authority and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) no longer had the budget to employ as many graduates as before. “To avoid a mismatch of graduates and jobs, I agree with cutting places in the coming school year. I expect Polytechnic University, the public one, will also suffer a cut in intake places in the future too,” he said Woo added that some NGOs were now hiring physiotherapy graduates as programme workers on monthly salaries of less than HK$20,000 (US$2,549). The Hospital Authority hired about 90 physiotherapy graduates this year, compared with around 130 annually before the government began its three-year budget cuts last year, Woo said. The government reduced recurrent public expenditure by 1 per cent for 2025-26 and by 2 per cent in each of the following two years. Aside from allied health, subsidised places were also cut by 29 per cent for landscape architecture and by 25 per cent for translation technology programmes. At the same time, more resources were directed towards emerging digital industries. HKMU’s applied degree in robotics and automation engineering was allocated 40 places, with 30 for Year One and the remaining 10 for Year Two. Hong Kong Shue Yan University’s digital solutions for entertainment and game applications programme received 25 places – 15 for Year One and 10 for senior-year entry. The scheme was first introduced in the 2015-16 academic year. Final tuition subsidies under the scheme vary according to programme costs. Annual government subsidies for laboratory-based and non-laboratory-based courses are HK$81,450 and HK$46,780 respectively. For applied degree programmes, the annual subsidies are HK$89,620 for laboratory-based courses and HK$51,880 for non-laboratory-based ones.

title: As AI safety fears mount, can a US-China hotline prevent a global crisis?
description: Washington and Beijing are seeking new ways to manage risks as competition intensifies, though analysts warn establishing effective safeguards may prove difficult.
content: The United States and China’s agreement to establish an official AI dialogue, including a proposed threat-notification system, marks a pragmatic step towards crisis prevention in their tech war, even as deep-seated divisions over chip access, model distillation and market dominance threaten to limit its impact, analysts said. Announced following high-level talks in New York on Sunday between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Vice-Premier He Lifeng, American officials said the new operational channel built on earlier discussions held in Beijing. While Bessent described the talks on AI and trade as “successful”, analysts cautioned that establishing a communication framework alone would do little to bridge the structural policy and commercial divides separating the two AI superpowers. Su Lian Jye, chief analyst at consultancy Omdia, called the launch of a formal dialogue a “good start” but said it was not enough to resolve fundamental conflicts of interest. “I don’t think the dialogue will remove all concerns and differences on distillation, pricing competition and [AI] pacing,” Su said. The planned AI dialogue comes as the technology emerges as one of the highest-stakes battlegrounds between Beijing and Washington, with tensions escalating sharply in recent months. Despite Washington maintaining strict controls on Chinese access to advanced AI semiconductors, US officials have accused the country’s developers of using “distillation” – a widely used technique where a smaller AI model learns from the output of a more advanced one – to replicate the capabilities of leading American systems. Beijing has dismissed the allegations as groundless, saying distillation was a standard industry practice. At the same time, Chinese AI firms have shaken the global tech sector with a rapid succession of model launches since earlier this year. By offering strong performance with aggressive pricing, they are making inroads into global markets and challenging established American giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic. The acceleration on both sides has fuelled debate over whether AI capabilities are outstripping the safeguards designed to contain risks. Leading US companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have advocated for “AI pacing” – intentionally slowing or regulating the deployment of advanced models – warning that rapid, unfettered progress could pose existential risks to humanity. Qiu Zhenhai, founder of the independent think tank Centre for Globalisation Hong Kong, compared Sunday’s AI safety discussions with Cold War-era arms control negotiations, arguing that intensifying competition had made risk-management channels increasingly important. AI now occupies a central place in the US-China tech rivalry, creating an urgent need for communication despite limited mutual trust, Qiu wrote on his WeChat public account. “Having dialogue is always better than having none,” Qiu added, noting that the initial communication channel could pave the way for wider negotiations. The centrepiece of the new agreement is a proposed “notification mechanism” through which one side can alert the other to serious AI security incidents. Bessent said the two countries aimed to build a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. “Having a notification mechanism will promote more transparency,” said Su of Omdia. But turning the proposal into an effective tool would require both countries to agree on risk classifications, notification triggers, response protocols and regular review procedures, he said. Still, the initiative marks a clear shift from previous exchanges, including formal government talks on AI risks in Geneva in 2024 and an academic dialogue active since 2019. Unlike those discussions, the latest initiative takes an operational approach and lays the groundwork as President Xi Jinping prepares to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington this week. If the two powers managed to establish workable ground rules, analysts said the impact could ripple beyond bilateral ties. “[The dialogue] could lead to the potential establishment of a global AI governance framework,” Su said.

title: South Korea gets a new internet star as Busan shark sighting goes viral
description: Nearly 20,000 visitors flocked to the North Port Waterfront Park over the weekend to see the shark, which has also spawned a flood of memes.
content: A 3.5-metre-long shark that wandered into a Busan waterfront channel has become an unlikely internet celebrity in South Korea, drawing nearly 20,000 spectators over the weekend as authorities opted to leave the animal alone rather than risk provoking it. The shark was first spotted on Friday in the waterway at North Port Waterfront Park, where it has remained for at least four consecutive days despite repeated efforts by the public to catch a glimpse of it. South Korea’s National Institute of Fisheries Science (NIFS) has provisionally identified the animal as a copper shark, also known as a bronze whaler, but experts caution that its exact species has not yet been confirmed. The Korea Coast Guard initially spent about six hours on Friday trying to guide the shark towards the open sea, deploying specialist personnel and patrol vessels, but stopped the operation after fisheries officials warned that forcing the animal through the narrow channel could provoke aggressive behaviour or injure it. Authorities have since been monitoring the shark and urging people to keep their distance. “Since the shark could turn aggressive, we ask that residents refrain from approaching the water’s edge at the waterfront park in case of any danger,” the coastguard said in a statement on Friday, according to Seoul Economic Daily. The warnings, however, have done little to dampen public interest. The Busan Metropolitan City Government estimated that nearly 20,000 people flocked to the waterfront park on Saturday and Sunday – roughly four to five times the site’s normal weekend traffic – with about 10,000 people visiting on Sunday alone. The shark has also spawned a flood of memes, including AI-generated images imagining it as a guest on the popular tvN variety programme You Quiz on the Block and others depicting a planned North Port baseball stadium redesigned in the shape of a shark. Social media users have suggested turning the animal into a Busan mascot, while the nickname “Bukangi” has begun circulating online, combining “Bukhang”, the Korean name for North Port, with the familiar “-i” suffix often added to Korean nicknames and names to make them sound more informal or endearing. Busan-born actor Han Sang-jin separately suggested calling the shark “Buk”, a play on “Bukhang” and Boogi, the city’s official seagull mascot, whose name is itself a Korean-language play on “Busan” and the word for seagull. 가을인데 부산 북항에 상어가? 어디서, 왜 들어왔을까.. 9월 18일 부산 북항 친수공원 수로에서 대형 상어가 발견됐다. 국립수산과학원은 이 상어를 무태상어로 추정했다. 아직 종이 확정됐다고 표현하기보다는 ‘추정’이라는 말을 붙이는 게 정확하다. 무태상어는 백상아리와는 다른 흉상어과… — Gallery X (@realgalleryx) September 20, 2026 The animal’s unexpected visit may have an ecological explanation. Ji Hwan-seong, a researcher at NIFS, told YTN that the shark appeared to have followed warm-water prey fish into the inner part of the waterway while searching for food. NIFS has also linked the shark’s presence to warmer waters and an increase in warm-water fish, which have helped bring species such as copper sharks closer to Korean coastal areas. The shark’s continued presence has generated a second, more speculative subplot. A fish measuring about 1 metre was reportedly spotted deeper inside the waterway on Sunday, prompting online speculation that the larger shark had given birth and was remaining in the channel to protect its young. Authorities have not established whether the smaller animal was a shark or if it was related to the larger one. Experts have also cautioned against drawing conclusions from the sighting, noting that while copper sharks are live-bearing, there is insufficient evidence to establish that the North Port waterway is a birthing site or that the two animals are connected.

title: In a China first, low-altitude sector hits turbulence as subsidies face reality check
description: Hangzhou tech hub looks to end financial incentives for development of light aerial vehicles, including eVTOLs, signalling more optimised regulations after June crash.
content: A major Chinese tech hub is moving to pull the plug on dedicated funding for its low-altitude economy, making it the first city in the country to propose repealing a full financial support package for the sector. The proposal in Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province, comes after the deadly crash of a small aircraft into Beijing’s tallest skyscraper in June. Still, some analysts contend that the reversal does not signal broader policy tightening for the low-altitude economy, but rather a shift towards more optimised and targeted industry regulations. Hangzhou’s initial policy took effect two years ago and was originally set to remain in force through the end of next year. It spans key segments of the sector – from enterprise establishment and technological innovation to new low-altitude flight routes and infrastructure buildout – offering differing amounts of fiscal rewards. Without spelling out the reasoning behind the move, the Hangzhou Municipal Bureau of Finance noted on its official website that “following internal review and consultations with relevant government departments”, it was determined that “the document has grounds for repeal”. The month-long public consultation period ends on October 7. Tan Chaochen, chairman of the Shenzhen Bao’an Low-Altitude Economy Industry Association, said Hangzhou’s proposed repeal should not be seen merely as a routine regulatory clean-up, but as part of Beijing’s broader push to regulate local industrial policies and build a unified national market. For instance, the top fiscal reward offered by the Hangzhou government hits 200 million yuan (US$29.87 million) for anchor enterprises, while the maximum payout for newly registered firms tops 10 million yuan. “The proposed repeal may be linked to China’s strengthened fair-competition review regime,” Tan said. “Local governments have competed for low-altitude economy companies through relocation incentives, but such selective subsidies may distort competition. “Hangzhou’s cash rewards for newly established companies may no longer fully align with national efforts to regulate local investment incentives.” A Shanghai government official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the matter’s sensitive nature, shared Tan’s view. The official said Hangzhou’s incentive programme was seen by other cities as creating an unfair competitive advantage, and the matter had been brought to regulators’ attention. “The proposed repeal of the support measures does not mean Hangzhou is scaling back its backing for the sector,” Tan Chaochen added. “The focus is moving from attracting companies to helping them fly and build viable businesses.” Hangzhou’s ambitious goals remain, as the city aims to nurture more than 600 firms across the low-altitude industrial chain, with total sector output topping 60 billion yuan by 2027. As of the end of 2025, both targets were said to be more than 70 per cent fulfilled. The once-hyped vision of intracity air-taxi services has effectively run its course in China Ma Liqi, Aircontainer founder While Hangzhou still trails Shenzhen and Guangzhou in aircraft manufacturing, key components and industrial depth, it has strengths in digital technology, e-commerce logistics, and tourism, according to Tan. “The decisive factor will no longer be which city offers the largest subsidies, but which can first establish safe and profitable business models,” Tan said. Meanwhile, the low-altitude sector has been forced to pivot in the wake of June’s crash involving the electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) light aircraft. Ma Liqi, founder of Aircontainer, a Shanghai-based eVTOL start-up, said the incident laid bare safety vulnerabilities within urban low-altitude airspace for regulators, industry participants and the general public. “The once-hyped vision of intracity air-taxi services has effectively run its course in China,” Ma said. “Going forward, intercity routes and flight corridors linking major economic regions are set to become the application scenarios for eVTOLs.” China’s low-altitude sector has maintained robust growth momentum since the first quarter of 2024, according to a UBS report in April. The bank’s analysts, led by Chen Xin, noted that financing for the domestic low-altitude economy reached 3.9 billion yuan in the first three months of 2025, marking a 60 per cent jump, year on year. Financing growth peaked in the third quarter of last year, with estimated quarterly financing topping 10 billion yuan, up by 77 per cent, year on year.

title: Opinion | Success of Xi-Trump summit lies in what happens afterwards
description: The real value of the Washington meeting between the presidents of the US and China is whether its understandings survive the next bilateral dispute.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, after the May talks in Beijing and before the November Apec summit in Shenzhen. This sequence of diplomacy will test if the commitment to building a “constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability” translates into practical arrangements. The Washington meeting faces clear limits. Differences over trade, technology, industrial policy, Taiwan and regional security are deeply embedded in the relationship. Washington will want results Trump can present at home: tariff reductions, greater Chinese purchases of agricultural and energy products, reliable access to critical minerals and new commercial contracts. Beijing will seek greater consistency in US policy, particularly on Taiwan, technology restrictions and trade measures. There is room for a phased agreement, provided it rests on reciprocity and addresses major concerns for both sides. Trade offers the most immediate opportunity. The two economic teams are discussing a tariff reduction framework covering around US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. The meeting could produce agreement on product lists, implementation schedules or additional market access. It would help businesses in both countries and reduce some of the pressure that tariff uncertainty has placed on Asia-Pacific supply chains. The lasting value of any package will depend on implementation. After rounds of tariff increases, suspensions and policy reversals, new purchase commitments or tariff adjustments could quickly lose value if overtaken by disputes over technology, subsidies or national security. A credible outcome requires clear timetables, working-level channels and procedures to manage disagreements. Taiwan remains the most sensitive issue. For China, it is the “core of core interests”. Some US allies in Asia have expressed concern about possible changes in Washington’s language on Taiwan, reflecting wider unease over the possibility of a policy trade-off. A summit statement that creates uncertainty about either side’s intentions could encourage competing interpretations across the region. Greater clarity, backed by restraint in policy and military signalling, would do more to reduce risk than carefully worded ambiguity. The South China Sea disputes require similar caution. The United States is a treaty ally of the Philippines, one of several Southeast Asian claimant states.
