More frequent maritime encounters, growing military activity and US alliance commitments have increased the risk that an incident involving a Southeast Asian state could draw Washington and Beijing into a direct confrontation. Washington and Beijing need to maintain rules for encounters at sea and in the air, keep crisis communication channels open and avoid treating every tactical incident as a test of strategic resolve. The region has avoided sustained armed confrontation, but the frequency and proximity of maritime encounters leave little room for complacency. Artificial intelligence should also feature in the talks. China and the US will continue to compete over advanced chips, export controls, technical standards and industrial capacity. But the application of AI to cyber operations, military decision-making, intelligence analysis and nuclear warning systems introduces risks neither side can manage alone. AI safety and strategic risk are an area of possible dialogue. A comprehensive China-US AI agreement remains out of reach. But their governments could establish regular contact, explore notification procedures for serious AI-related incidents and begin discussions on the most dangerous military applications. Dialogue on the role of AI in nuclear command and early-warning systems would be particularly valuable. Even limited progress could complement the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum’s work on digital and AI cooperation. What happens at the Washington meeting will ripple out. China has set this year’s Apec theme as “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, with openness, innovation and cooperation as its main priorities. If Washington produces workable economic arrangements and more reliable communication, the Shenzhen meeting will have a stronger foundation for progress on trade, AI, energy, climate and sustainable development. If the results depend mainly on the Xi-Trump personal relationship, renewed bilateral friction could again overshadow the regional agenda. Asia-Pacific economies accept that China-US competition will continue – their concern is the cost. Policy shifts disrupt investment and supply chains, maritime incidents heighten security pressures, and bloc politics constrains countries seeking productive ties with both Beijing and Washington. A more stable bilateral relationship means not having to choose sides or accept a China-US condominium over regional affairs. It would mean greater space to pursue their own development and security interests. For European governments, the wish is for greater stability in global trade and technology policy, even as they remain wary of any deal that sidelines multilateral rules or shifts economic pressure onto European industries. A more predictable China-US relationship could ease tensions between Europe’s economic ties with China and its security coordination with the US. Another cycle of temporary bargains and renewed restrictions would reinforce efforts to diversify supply chains and tighten economic security controls. Across the Global South, many countries share concerns about the economic costs of major-power rivalry. Their priorities include market access, affordable energy, food security, development finance and access to new technologies. Smaller and less diversified economies are especially vulnerable to tariffs, policy uncertainty and disruptions to global value chains. Greater China-US stability could create more room for cooperation on climate finance, debt, public health, infrastructure and AI capacity building, while also improving prospects for cooperation in multilateral forums. The real value of the Washington meeting is whether its understandings survive the next bilateral dispute. The key tests will be whether tariff arrangements are implemented, working-level negotiations continue, crisis communication channels remain open and dialogue on AI risks begins. The Shenzhen Apec meeting will provide an early test of whether the momentum generated can be sustained.

title: Hong Kong developer New World gets nod to spin off K11 Shanghai assets
description: Shanghai listing of Reit worth US$570 million will ‘recycle capital for more value-accretive projects’, analyst says.
content: New World Development (NWD) received the green light from the Shanghai Stock Exchange to spin off and list a Reit (real estate investment trust) on the bourse, according to the distressed developer controlled by one of Hong Kong’s wealthiest families. The expected offering size for the NWD C-Reit was about 3.82 billion yuan (US$570 million), from which the group’s estimated net proceeds would be 3.24 billion yuan, Hong Kong-based NWD said in a statement on Monday. The underlying assets of the Reit comprise the Shanghai K11 Art Mall and the Shanghai K11 Atelier New World Tower. The assets, located on Huaihai Road Central in Shanghai’s Huangpu district, have a gross floor area of 130,384 square metres (1.4 million square feet). NWD was the indirect whole owner of the properties, the company added. Following the spin-off, the group would continue to operate the asset, which would continue to be marketed under the group’s K11 brand. “The NWD C-Reit will be the first among Hong Kong enterprises,” said Echo Huang, the developer’s executive director and CEO. The establishment of NWD C-Reit showed the “strong brand equity” of NWD and K11 in the mainland market and was an “important milestone in advancing the group’s asset management and capital deployment capabilities”, she added. The spin-off would “open up opportunities for the group to access new forms of capital from institutional and retail investors in the region”, and allow NWD to “unlock asset value and redirect resources to support future growth through other projects”, Huang said. The spin-off was consistent with NWD’s intent to divest select assets in mainland China, according to Jeff Zhang, equity analyst at Morningstar. “We view the spin-off as optimal to recycle capital for more value-accretive projects,” he said. “Overall, we expect the spin-off to have no major impact on NWD’s equity valuation, as it only accounts for less than 5 per cent of the firm’s asset value and earnings.” In the first half of its financial year, NWD posted a net loss of HK$3.73 billion (US$475 million) as asset writedowns continued to weigh on earnings. The loss narrowed 44 per cent year on year for the six months ended December 31, as impairments on investment properties eased and financing and tax expenses related to mainland projects fell. Total debt declined by HK$1.7 billion to HK$144.3 billion. However, net debt rose by HK$2.6 billion to HK$122.7 billion, with the gearing ratio increasing to 59.7 per cent from 58.1 per cent a year earlier. The developer is scheduled to announce its annual results on September 30. Chief financial officer Edward Lau attributed the rise in net debt to the accounting treatment of Hong Kong joint ventures, as well as repayments of construction loans tied to those projects. NWD would subscribe for at least a 20 per cent interest in the NWD C-Reit, while the rest would be subscribed by strategic investors, institutional investors and retail investors, the company said. NWD owns and operates a number of mainland assets. The Hangzhou K11 Art Mall and the K11 Elysea project in Shanghai were expected to be completed in the near future, it said. The developer’s controlling shareholder is Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, the business of Henry Cheng Kar-shun and family. With an estimated net worth of US$26.1 billion, the family ranked third on a Forbes list of Hong Kong’s richest individuals and families, released in February.

title: Nearly half of Taiwanese lack confidence in US defence commitments, survey finds
description: ‘Deeply worrying’ result comes as US$14 billion arms package to island stays stalled ahead of this week’s Xi-Trump summit in Washington.
content: Nearly half of Taiwanese lack confidence that Washington will continue military aid and arms sales to the island, a new survey shows. The results of the poll were released on Monday, ahead of this week’s summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The poll by Taiwan-based United Daily News found 47 per cent were not confident the United States would continue providing military assistance and selling weapons to Taiwan, slightly exceeding the 44 per cent who remained confident. Nine per cent had no opinion. Conducted by the newspaper since 2010, the annual survey also found fluctuating expectations about direct American military support. Two years ago, 49 per cent believed the US would send troops to help defend Taiwan, compared with 42 per cent who thought it would not. Last year, 49 per cent said Washington would not intervene. This year, the balance was reversed again, with 47 per cent expecting US military troops to come and 43 per cent saying Washington would not send them. “Faced with the threat of military action from mainland China, Taiwan can only rely on US security commitments, yet fewer than half of respondents have confidence in those commitments,” the newspaper said in a commentary. “This is a deeply worrying figure,” it said. The findings come as a proposed US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan remains stalled and Beijing presses Washington over weapons sales ahead of the Xi-Trump meeting in Washington on Thursday. The South China Morning Post reported on Saturday that Washington was considering postponing the announcement of major Taiwan arms sales until after the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in November. Multiple sources said there was a strong possibility Trump could extend the delay until the end of the year, given another planned meeting with Xi at Apec and the Chinese leader’s expected attendance at the Group of 20 summit in Florida in December. According to William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the Brussels-based International Crisis Group, Xi was likely to press Trump over arms sales, including the delayed US$14 billion package. “Beijing hopes that further delays will deepen doubts in Taiwan and among US allies about Washington’s commitment to the Indo-Pacific,” Yang said. Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at Washington-based Defence Priorities, said Chinese interlocutors she had spoken to suggested one of Beijing’s objectives was to have the package cancelled altogether rather than merely postponed or suspended. But she rejected suggestions that Trump was preparing to trade Taiwan for concessions from Beijing, saying neither side was likely to view the issue in those terms. Instead, Trump’s focus on economic ties with Beijing and reluctance to disrupt that relationship meant the package could stay stalled for some time, Kavanagh told a panel organised last week by ReThink Media, a US non-profit strategic communications group. “I think this topic will definitely come up on the arms sale,” she said. “I think it’s most likely just going to get kicked down the road.” If Trump and Xi meet two more times this year as expected, the package might remain stalled until 2027, Kavanagh added. Uncertainty over new sales comes as Taiwan grapples with delays involving weapons it has already bought from the US. The first two of 66 new F-16 Block 70 fighters ordered by Taipei are still in Hawaii, a month after leaving the continental US. The aircraft, numbered 6727 and 6728, arrived at Joint Base Pearl Harbour-Hickam on August 21 but have yet to continue to Taiwan. An attempted departure earlier this month was aborted, with no official explanation given for the delay. The timing has fuelled speculation in Taiwan that political considerations surrounding the Xi-Trump summit could be involved, although technical problems, tanker availability and weather have also been cited as possible explanations. No evidence has publicly established a political reason for the delay. Lin Pei-hsiang, a legislator from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang, said such delays helped explain the survey results. Lin questioned how the public could have confidence when weapons bought from the US were not arriving on schedule. “If weapons could not be delivered on schedule or did not meet Taiwan’s actual requirements after they were purchased, public confidence would inevitably suffer,” he said. Su Chi, honorary chairman of the Taipei Forum Foundation and a former senior Taiwan security official, was more pessimistic, saying the chances of new US arms sales had become “very, very low”. Beijing had made its opposition to Taiwan arms sales clear during Trump’s May meeting with Xi and would react strongly to further approvals, he argued. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. The survey also found that 56 per cent of respondents regarded cross-strait military relations as tense, little changed from last year but below a peak of 64 per cent in 2022. Another 27 per cent described relations as moderate and 10 per cent considered them friendly. Despite those tensions, respondents generally considered the likelihood of war relatively low. On a scale of one to 10, with 10 representing the highest likelihood of conflict, the average score was 4.4 – broadly unchanged over the past five years but 1.2 points higher than a decade ago. Asked without being given a list of options what was contributing most to cross-strait tensions, respondents most frequently identified Taiwan independence as the biggest variable.

title: Hong Kong stock exchange moves to ease spin-offs and shareholder approval rules
description: Proposals aim to streamline corporate actions and align Hong Kong more closely with rival markets, HKEX says.
content: The Hong Kong stock exchange has proposed easing requirements for listed companies to disclose corporate transactions and seek shareholder approval, while also making it easier for issuers to spin off businesses, according to a consultation paper released on Monday. The 10-week consultation, which runs until November 30, proposes removing the profit test currently used to determine whether a transaction requires disclosure or shareholder approval. Companies would instead use market capitalisation or net asset value, whichever is higher. The proposal would also reduce the number of transactions requiring shareholder approval. Deals equivalent to between 25 per cent and 50 per cent of a company’s size would require disclosure only, rather than shareholder approval under current rules. According to the consultation paper, regulators in the UK and Singapore had already relaxed similar requirements, increasing pressure on Hong Kong to remain competitive. The exchange has also proposed expanding the definition of connected subsidiary by raising the voting-rights threshold to 30 per cent from 10 per cent. Separately, the exchange wants to relax spin-off rules by allowing eligible companies to assess proposed spin-offs without seeking prior approval from the exchange. The exemption would apply to companies with a market capitalisation of more than HK$10 billion (US$1.3 billion) and annual revenue exceeding HK$1 billion, or those that would retain businesses accounting for more than 50 per cent of revenue and assets after a spin-off. The proposal would replace the current requirement that all spin-offs obtain the exchange’s prior approval. The exchange also wants to shorten the post-listing waiting period for spin-offs to one year from three years. “This reform seeks to give issuers greater flexibility and certainty in their corporate transactions, increasing efficiency in terms of costs and time while upholding investor protection through timely, meaningful disclosure and strong board accountability,” said Katherine Ng, head of listing at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), the holding company of the stock exchange. “At HKEX, we are committed to enhancing our listing framework so that it meets the evolving needs of Hong Kong’s increasingly diverse ecosystem of issuers and investors.” Ng said the proposals represented the second phase of the exchange’s listing reforms, following changes introduced in July that eased listing requirements for companies with weighted voting rights.

title: Southeast Asia supports multilateralism, wary of US or China leadership: survey
description: A recent Rockefeller Foundation survey shows strong regional belief in global cooperation and a reluctance to accept superpower dominance.
content: Southeast Asia remains comparatively confident in international cooperation even as scepticism grows over whether the United States or China should take a leading global role, a new survey has found. Analysts said the findings reflected a long-standing regional preference for keeping strategic options open, particularly among smaller and middle powers wary of an international order dominated by either Washington or Beijing. “Seeking Security and Opportunity in a Stormy World”, released this month by The Rockefeller Foundation, surveyed more than 35,000 people across 34 countries on their assessment of global affairs. Its Southeast Asian grouping covered Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore. Southeast Asia was among the regions most positive about whether global cooperation was working effectively, scoring 63 per cent compared with 37 per cent for the US and Canada, 32 per cent for Oceania and 31 per cent for western Europe. At the same time, the survey suggested limited global appetite for either Washington or Beijing assuming a leading role, with 39 per cent comfortable with the US doing so and 37 per cent saying the same of China. Another 61 per cent supported countries working together to address global problems without either superpower taking the lead. The combination pointed to “a more fragmented global order”, said Alejandro Reyes, a senior fellow at the Centre on Contemporary China and the World at the University of Hong Kong. “There is widespread recognition of both American and Chinese power, but much less willingness to accept either as the natural or dominant leader of the international system,” Reyes said. Joanne Lin, a senior fellow and coordinator of the Asean Studies Centre at ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said comparable regional polling showed that both countries remained highly consequential even as concern about their influence persisted. “In Southeast Asia, China and the US are still seen as the two most consequential powers, but being influential does not mean being welcomed,” Lin said. She added that the economic and military weight of both powers meant their actions could sometimes be perceived as “narrowing the choices available to smaller states”. “For countries that do not have comparable power, there is naturally some unease with an international order in which ‘might makes right’ or where the strongest powers can set the rules for everyone else,” Lin said, adding that Southeast Asian nations “increasingly want alternatives, more choice and institutions or coalitions that are not dominated by either”. Charmaine Misalucha-Willoughby, an international relations professor at De La Salle University in Manila, said this preference aligned with the structural position of smaller states. “As small and middle powers, Southeast Asia is predisposed towards cooperation, multilateralism and norms like territorial integrity,” she said. The US-China divide Country-level results showed that this desire for strategic space did not translate into a uniform regional view of either major power. Among the Southeast Asian countries surveyed, 73 per cent of respondents in Indonesia perceived Washington as a major threat, compared with 31 per cent who said the same of China. The pattern was nearly reversed in the Philippines, where 70 per cent called China a threat compared with 33 per cent for the US. In Singapore, the figures stood at 25 per cent for China and 41 per cent for Washington. “The common theme is that Southeast Asia cannot easily be divided into pro-US and pro-China camps,” Reyes said, adding that several countries were resisting pressure to choose and instead balancing between the two powers on different issues. Lin said these differences partly reflected national concerns, including Jakarta’s anxieties over US foreign and economic policy, and Manila’s long-standing disputes over the South China Sea and territorial sovereignty. Singapore, meanwhile, maintained close defence and security cooperation with Washington without being a formal treaty ally, while keeping up extensive economic ties with China, she said. Collins Chong Yew Keat, a foreign affairs, security and strategy analyst at Universiti Malaya, said the survey suggested a “temporary perceptual advantage for Beijing rather than evidence of an irreversible geopolitical realignment”. He said Southeast Asian economies still relied heavily on Chinese capital, infrastructure, technology, industrial investment and access to its vast market. At the same time, concerns over US tariffs, political unpredictability, potential disengagement and developments in the Middle East had weighed on Washington’s image. But that did not mean regional concerns over Beijing’s strategic ambitions had disappeared, Chong added. “Economic attraction should not be confused with the disappearance of strategic apprehension,” Chong said. Demand for middle power agency The results also suggest that while middle powers in Southeast Asia remain tied to larger powers, there was a growing demand for them to exercise greater agency, analysts said. “While middle powers are bound to the superpowers in more ways than one, they also recognise that a bit more agency will benefit them. Doing so is a way to protect against the future,” Willoughby said. “Preparing for a world without the US or China is an insurance policy for middle powers,” she added. Lin said there was likely a desire for a wider distribution of global leadership, even if it did not mean the emergence of a formal middle power bloc. “Respondents are probably open to the idea that international cooperation does not always have to be organised around the two superpowers. That creates more space for countries and groupings such as Japan, the EU, Australia, India, South Korea, Canada and others to lead in particular areas, whether trade, climate, technology, development or security,” she added. Asean could play a larger role provided it maintained sufficient cohesion and capacity, Lin said, adding that the objective was to “build a denser network of partnerships so that Asean countries have more options and are less dependent on any single power to promote greater strategic autonomy”. Reyes shared this assessment, pointing out that an important opportunity existed for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to open doors to new partners. “Asean does not necessarily have to see the international order as a choice between Washington and Beijing. Its traditional approach has been to widen its partnerships, preserve strategic space and keep Asean-based institutions relevant. The Rockefeller finding suggests considerable public support for exactly that kind of international cooperation,” he said. However, Chong warned that while middle-power cooperation provided a strategic buffer, it could not replace the role and impact of major powers such as the US, including its military capabilities, alliance system and deterrent capacity. “Southeast Asia may presently be more critical of the United States, but that does not mean it necessarily wants less [of] Washington’s role here. That remains the essence of Southeast Asia’s hedging strategy – and also a long-time dilemma,” he said.

title: Moonshot’s Kimi K3 lands on Amazon in key test for Chinese open-source AI revenue
description: Open-weight models allow users around the world to use, copy, modify and distribute the software without paying the model developer.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up Moonshot AI has begun supplying its flagship Kimi K3 model to Amazon Web Services (AWS), one of the world’s largest cloud services providers, in a major test case for how open-weight AI models can generate higher revenue from third-party platforms. The model is now available on Amazon Bedrock, AWS’s tool for building generative AI applications, offering “a powerful new option for coding and knowledge work”, Amazon said in an announcement on Friday. While neither company has publicly disclosed financial terms, the arrangement appears to have triggered Moonshot’s updated commercial licensing terms. Revised in July upon K3’s release, the open-source licence mandates a paid arrangement if any firm or its affiliates host the model as a service and generate more than US$20 million in aggregate annual revenue. AWS reported in July that its AI business had surpassed US$25 billion in annual revenue run rate. Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. An Amazon representative referred the South China Morning Post to its Kimi K3-Bedrock announcement last week, which did not address revenue-sharing arrangements. Open-weight models like Kimi K3 allow users around the world to use, copy, modify and distribute the software without paying the model developer. However, companies like Moonshot, Alibaba Group Holding and MiniMax have moved to adjust their commercial terms with selective entities. Last month, when Alibaba released Qwen 3.8-Max, it required a separate deal for those running a “model as a service” or “AI work assistant” business whose aggregate revenue exceeded US$50 million over any consecutive 12-month period. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Similarly, MiniMax in an April policy change asked for separate commercial agreements for businesses exceeding US$20 million in annual revenue. It also prohibited its models’ outputs from being used to train competing models. Besides Moonshot, the Amazon Bedrock tool has added dozens of open-weight models from other Chinese providers, including DeepSeek, MiniMax and Alibaba, according to the announcement last week. DeepSeek does not impose commercial restrictions, while the models available on the AWS tool from Alibaba and MiniMax are older ones dating to before the companies adopted the new commercial licenses. The tie-up between Moonshot and Amazon comes as Chinese AI labs lag behind their US rivals in terms of monetisation. Seven major Chinese AI developers combined generate only about 10 per cent of the revenue reported for OpenAI and Anthropic, according to a report from US-based research firm Rhodium Group. The Chinese players have increasingly expanded overseas. Kimi K3 is also available on Microsoft’s Foundry platform through third-party inference provider Fireworks AI. Moonshot was also in talks with Microsoft and Google over revenue-sharing agreements to host Kimi K3 on their cloud platforms, seeking as much as 30 per cent of revenue, Reuters reported last month. AWS said customer data sent to Kimi K3 would remain within its cloud security boundary and would not be shared with Moonshot or used to train the model. The service also offers zero data retention for inference requests, an arrangement aimed at making open-weight models easier for companies with security and compliance requirements to adopt. MiniMax made its models available not only through Amazon, but also Microsoft and Google’s cloud platforms earlier this year. The company said its business-to-business revenue surged more than 700 per cent in the first half of 2026, with overseas markets accounting for about 60 per cent.

title: Uzbekistan has a brand new arts centre but can it rival Dubai as the next global art hub?
description: The Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent’s inaugural exhibition sees 10 global artists examine the East through their own perspectives.
content: Uzbekistan, with its rich history of ancient Silk Road craftsmanship and later influences from Imperial Russia to the Soviets, is a country shaped by layers of conquest, trade and intellectual exchange. At the Uzbek capital’s new Centre for Contemporary Arts Tashkent (CCA), the inaugural exhibition – titled “Hikmah” and featuring sculptures and installations by 10 artists from around the world, including Palestine and the United States – sets out to explore the complexity of that cultural cross-pollination. “The theme of ‘Hikmah’ comes from the Naqshbandi Sufi [religious] order,” says Sara Raza, the CCA’s chief curator. The word, adopted from Arabic, translates as “wisdom” in Persian and Uzbek. Raza refers to beliefs within Sunni Islam in which the Naqshbandi order has 11 principles that shape believers’ daily lives and conduct, such as keeping an awareness of time, awareness of number and awareness of the heart. Building on themes from her 2022 book, Punk Orientalism: The Art of Rebellion – which examines the former Soviet Union’s relations with Central Asia, the Caucasus and the Middle East – Raza grounds her curatorial intention in an East-East dialogue. “When we think about Orientalism, it was always this very vertical way of thinking about how the West sees the East,” she says. “But I split horizontally to think about how the East sees the East … how it examines itself, what are the relationships, both solidarity and friction.” What’s on display at ‘Hikmah’? The pieces exhibited at the CCA are a mix of newly commissioned and pre-existing works. Uzbek artist Shokhrukh Rakhimov’s new work, The Colour of Silence, In Search of Truth (2026), is a sculptural installation of large-scale ceramic orbs that welcome visitors from the courtyard. Born in 2002, he is the youngest of the 10 artists featured in “Hikmah”. As a seventh-generation Uzbek ceramicist, Rakhimov mixed ancestral methods with local minerals and raw pigments to glaze the pieces, highlighting the interplay of the four primary elements – water, air, earth and fire. Perhaps one of the more recognisable pieces exhibited is Nadia Kaabi-Linke’s Flying Carpets (2011). This installation of hanging stainless steel squares, previously displayed at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, is a meditation on Venice’s street vendors, primarily of African, Arab or South Asian descent. To create the piece, the Tunisian-Ukrainian artist, 48, directly transposed the dimensions of display rugs that migrant street vendors use to scoop up their goods when evading police. Speaking during a tour of the CCA, she explains that the work bridges romanticised orientalist tropes of the flying carpet with the harsh realities faced by undocumented immigrants. The CCA also commissioned new pieces from existing works, such as Tarik Kiswanson’s Nest (2025). The Paris-based artist, from a Palestinian family exiled and settled in Sweden, often focuses on rootlessness and metamorphosis in his work. Kiswanson, 40, shaped this cocoon-like sculptural fibreglass resin by lying on his studio floor and drawing a charcoal line around his body, the artist explains on the tour. Latched to an interior wall, it levitates metres off the ground. Walk through the centre too quickly, and one might even mistake the piece for part of the architecture. “You can say that the building and architecture itself are the 11th artist, and all these artists are going to cross-circulate around it,” Raza says. CCA is a major project led by the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF). Though the centre was originally scheduled to open in September 2025, construction delays pushed the launch to March 2026, which was postponed again due to the conflict in Iran. Finally, in early September, the ACDF officially opened the space as a permanent platform for contemporary art, research and international exchange. Looking beyond exhibitions The CCA is, aside from the physical centre, also directing its attention to arts education. A library on the top floor holds specialist research collections devoted to art and critical theory, and there are plans to host book clubs. Since October 2024, the CCA has also been hosting artist residency programmes in Tashkent. One former resident is Mohamed Benchellal, a couturier born in 1984 who merges fashion with architecture, and was previously invited by the Hong Kong Fashion Designers Association to show his work in Hong Kong in 2025. A sister programme in the Uzbek city of Samarkand is set to launch by the end of 2026. Furthermore, through CCA commissioning, 78-year-old Kyrgyz-Uzbek artist Vyacheslav Akhunov is presenting a collateral exhibition “Instruments of the Mind” at the 2026 Venice Biennale. Akhunov’s work was critical of the government and, having lived under Soviet rule, he hid many of his artworks for decades to avoid persecution. Even as recently as 15 years ago, there was no support in the country to exhibit conceptual works such as Akhunov’s, Raza says, explaining the tremendous changes in the Uzbek art scene. With so much support now funnelled into the art scene, is Uzbekistan positioned to become the next top international art hub – effectively “the next Dubai” at a time when the Gulf city’s reputation as a haven is threatened? “Uzbekistan has existed for a millennium,” Raza says. “These are open-air museums, archaeological sites, ancient madrasas, ancient techniques of architecture. I don’t think that is comparable with the next Dubai … if the West or whoever is just catching up to that, they need to read a book.” That is why she firmly stands behind the theme of Hikmah as a way to consolidate Uzbekistan’s history; a theme both grounded in the past yet forward-facing.

title: China allows foreign visitors to skip police stations, register stay online
description: Tourists staying outside hotels can fill in paperwork online, in the latest move to make visiting the country easier.
content: Foreign visitors to China who choose to stay somewhere other than a hotel can now register their accommodation with the authorities online, which analysts say will make travelling to the country more convenient. China’s Exit and Entry Administration Law mandates that foreigners register their accommodation with the police within 24 hours of arrival. Those who fail to do so could be issued a warning or fined up to 2,000 yuan (US$298). This applies both to foreign visitors arriving in the country and those moving from one part of China to another. Hotels are usually able to complete this process on guests’ behalf, but those staying elsewhere previously had to visit a local police station in person to register. Under the updated rules, they could now fill in the paperwork on the website of the National Immigration Administration, its official app, or services within the WeChat or Alipay platforms, the administration said in a statement on Monday. Either the visitors or their hosts can complete the registration. Foreigners who have their own homes in China or have residency documents do not need to re-register each time they return to the country, according to the statement. On March 20, a pilot programme for online registration was launched in seven provinces and regions – including Hebei, Zhejiang and Sichuan. This had made the process “more convenient and better organised”, the immigration administration said at a press conference in July. “We will gradually extend online accommodation registration for foreigners to the entire country so as to deliver more efficient and convenient government services to foreigners who work, study and live in China,” a spokesman said at the time. In the past, the inconvenience of paperwork and the relatively lax enforcement of the rules meant that many foreigners simply did not bother to register when travelling, expats said. A Beijing-based American who wished to stay anonymous said that when he went to a village in Hunan province, the local police did not know how to register him. Yannick Benichou, a French manager at a biotech firm who has lived in China for nearly two decades, said foreigners knew in theory that they needed to register, but in practice, many people skipped it because it was too much trouble. “Now that they provide online registration and it’s definitely more convenient, that is a good thing,” he said. Einar Tangen, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, sees this as a worthwhile modernisation. “It makes it easier for foreigners to comply with an existing requirement while also giving the authorities a more efficient and standardised way to maintain information about where foreign residents and visitors are staying,” he said. Some foreigners might have seen registering as intrusive if their own governments did not carry out the same procedures, he said. But in China, the concept was less unusual – as part of a broader administrative culture that included the hukou household registration system applied to all Chinese citizens. “China is constantly adjusting its administrative systems to changes in its national and local environment. The characteristic feature is that these changes are generally implemented through planning, pilots and controlled expansion rather than through sudden policy changes,” Tangen said. China has introduced a series of policies in recent years to attract foreign tourists, including expanding visa-free entry for travellers from dozens of countries and simplifying access to digital payment platforms.

title: How Hong Kong is positioning for a bigger role in Asia’s family wealth transition
description: City courts next-generation wealth as family businesses reinvent themselves and deploy capital into new sectors and markets.
content: Hong Kong is strengthening its position as Asia’s hub for family business succession and cross-border capital allocation as wealthy families navigate economic uncertainty and a generational transfer of wealth, financial regulators and industrial executives said on Monday. Speaking at the South China Morning Post’s Redefining Hong Kong: Next Generation Wealth Conference, Undersecretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Joseph Chan Ho-lim highlighted what he described as the city’s unique structural advantages for ultra-high-net-worth families. “Under our unique ‘one country, two systems’ principle, Hong Kong is the only city in the world that converges both the China advantage and the global advantage,” Chan said. The framework guaranteed the free flow of capital, a common law legal system, a simple low-tax regime and a compatible regulatory environment, providing “certainty, security, transparency and predictability” for wealthy families, he added. Chan’s remarks come as a growing number of Asian family enterprises prepare for leadership transitions. Speakers at the conference said younger generations increasingly viewed succession as an opportunity to reinvent businesses rather than simply inherit them. Asia’s next generation of business leaders were moving beyond passive asset stewardship, seeking to forge distinct track records across new geographies, business models and emerging sectors, such as artificial intelligence and green technology, according to Sun Life Private Wealth CEO Sujoy Ghosh. “These [next-generation leaders] are change-makers,” Ghosh said during a panel discussion. “They want to put their names behind what they are inheriting.” Christina Gaw, managing principal at Gaw Capital Partners, said younger family members were showing “a lot of interest” in emerging markets as they sought to diversify risk. At the same time, they were deploying capital into traditional, high-cash-flow sectors like shipping, as well as energy transition, which requires active modernisation amid persistent global supply disruptions. To achieve greater scale, family businesses increasingly needed institutional capital – including from insurers, banks, family offices and pension funds – to support growth, Gaw said. Carlo Pesenti, chairman and CEO of Italy-based investment company Italmobiliare, echoed that view, saying a broader base of institutional investors could boost family enterprises’ financial firepower and enable larger deals. Hong Kong had positioned itself as a base for these evolving strategies, offering the market depth and liquidity needed to “meet diverse investment objectives and execute complex global portfolio strategies”, Chan said. To sharpen its competitiveness, the city is rolling out legislative proposals to expand tax concessions for family offices and funds. The measures would broaden eligibility to alternative assets, including private credit, digital assets and carbon derivatives. In its five-year plan released last week, the government underscored its ambition to bolster Hong Kong’s standing as a premier global hub for cross-boundary wealth management. Hong Kong currently hosted more than 3,380 single-family offices – a 25 per cent increase over the past two years – with the sector injecting more than US$10 billion annually into the local economy, according to official data.

title: China economists urge Beijing to act fast on local-level debt before low prices vanish
description: Prominent advisers note importance of central authorities expanding borrowing to fund infrastructure before the current window of subdued inflation closes.
content: Beijing should expand central government borrowing and accelerate local debt restructuring, as China’s relatively low price levels offer a rare window for stronger fiscal support to bolster demand, according to some prominent Chinese economists. “With oil shocks pushing up prices, and inflationary pressures spreading globally, China currently has the lowest price levels, while prices elsewhere are significantly higher,” said Yu Yongding, a former member of the People’s Bank of China’s Monetary Policy Committee who is now an academician with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. “This window of opportunity cannot be missed,” Yu warned, speaking on Saturday at the Tsinghua PBCSF Chief Economists Forum in Beijing. “Once it is gone, it will not come back. By the time [China’s] inflation picks up and prices rise, it will become much more difficult to pursue expansionary fiscal and monetary policies.” Additional borrowing could support infrastructure investment, which historically serves as an effective driver of economic growth and creates a positive cycle that eventually boosts consumption, he added. Li Xunlei, chief economist at Zhongtai Financial International, agreed that China had room to expand government borrowing, noting that previous increases in government debt had not triggered significant inflationary pressures. He argued that further expansion should come from the central government rather than local authorities, given their already heavy debt burdens. “As Chinese households have only just begun to deleverage and local governments are already carrying high levels of debt, the central government is the only sector with room to increase leverage to help maintain economic balance,” Li said at the forum. “Past experience has shown that local government borrowing has not been sufficiently efficient in generating economic returns,” Li added. Local government debt remains a long-standing concern for China’s economy. By the end of 2023, Beijing had identified 14.3 trillion yuan (US$2.14 trillion) in hidden local government debt and set a target to address the liabilities by 2028. Through a series of debt-swap programmes backed by special bonds, the outstanding amount was cut to 6.5 trillion yuan by the end of 2025. Li said the immediate priority should be reducing local governments’ financing costs and debt pressures through debt swaps. He argued that existing fiscal tools such as special bonds had become less effective because strict project requirements made it difficult for local-level officials to find suitable investment projects, which he said was reflected in this year’s weaker-than-expected investment growth. Overall fixed-asset investment – covering major areas such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction – fell 7.2 per cent in the first eight months of 2026, year on year, widening from a 6.7 per cent decline in the first seven months, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics. Also at the Tsinghua event, Lin Yifu, an economics professor at Peking University and former World Bank chief economist, said local government debt swaps should be accompanied by a clearer distinction over responsibility, as not all local government debt was created for the same purpose. “Debt from projects pursued mainly for local governments’ own interests, such as image-building projects, should be their responsibility, while debt incurred to support central government policies should be taken on by the central government,” Lin said. “This would allow local governments to reduce their burden and move forward with less pressure.”

title: Asian Games: Typhoon Dujuan could force cruise ship housing athletes to set sail
description: Rowing and equestrian have been postponed due to the expected heavy rain, while table tennis player Zhu Yuling shares a strong wind advisory.
content: A coming tropical storm could force the cruise ship housing athletes at the Asian Games to set sail from Nagoya to seek refuge out at sea, while some events have been postponed due to the expected heavy rain. Japan’s meteorological authorities forecast Typhoon Dujuan to hit the Izu Peninsula and Tokyo before reaching the coast of Nagoya on Monday. Heavy rain warnings have been issued across several regions, with maximum sustained winds of 90km/h and gusts reaching 126km/h, casting a shadow over the Games. Under contingency plans released by the organising committee and the Nagoya Coast Guard, an advance evacuation order will be issued if the Port of Nagoya area is severely affected, requiring the Costa Serena to set sail with whoever is on board at the time. Athletes who fail to return to the vessel in time will be relocated to alternative facilities to ensure their safety. On Sunday night, Macau table tennis player Zhu Yuling shared a strong wind advisory on her social media, sent by the management of the cruise ship. “Just got a message from the hotel saying strong winds are expected in Nagoya over the coming days,” Zhu wrote. “I have a match early tomorrow morning – wish us luck.” The management notice advised athletes to take precautions and secure their belongings. “Strong winds are expected in Nagoya Bay over the coming days. We kindly ask all athletes who have clothes or other items on their balconies to bring them inside and keep them in their cabins to prevent them from being blown away,” the notice read. The storm forced the postponement of equestrian events held at the JRA Baji Koen Equestrian Park in Tokyo from Monday to Tuesday, with Hong Kong eventing riders Patrick Lam Lap-shun, Annie Ho Yuen-yan, Su Yuxuan and Nicole Michele Pearson competing. At the Nagara River International Rowing Course in neighbouring Gifu prefecture, heavy rainfall forced organisers to delay and condense the six-day rowing regatta into just two days. Originally scheduled for September 20–25, the rowing events are now September 23 and September 24, with semi-finals and repechage rounds across multiple events cancelled to mitigate typhoon risks. The approaching storm was not just affecting the Asian Games, marathons, football matches and other public sporting events were cancelled in Tokyo, as well as in neighbouring Kanagawa and Chiba prefectures. The organising committee stated that if certain competitions cannot proceed as planned, it will consult the Olympic Council of Asia and relevant international federations to adjust schedules.

title: Flights axed, over 1 million urged to evacuate as Typhoon Dujuan hits Japan
description: Four people died in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures, while over 46,000 households near Tokyo were without power.
content: More than 1 million people were under evacuation advisories in Japan early on Tuesday and hundreds of flights have been cancelled as Typhoon Dujuan brushed past Tokyo, bringing torrential rain, flooding and landslides to the region. Four people have been confirmed dead as heavy rainfall triggered landslides in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures near Tokyo, local governments reported according to Japanese media including the Kyodo News agency. Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, and other storms have already disrupted some events at the Asian Games being hosted in the country. Dujuan was bringing winds of some 144km/h (89mph) on Monday as it moved to around 130km/h south of Katsuura City near Tokyo. By early Tuesday, the storm had shifted away from the coast and was heading northeast out to sea, with slightly diminished winds, the Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. Japan Airlines cancelled 135 flights and All Nippon Airways scrapped 140, while more than 46,000 households near Tokyo were without power. More than 1.6 million residents in and around the capital were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations are not mandatory. Landslide warnings were issued for Tokyo as well as for Chiba, Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures. Railway operators in Tokyo and neighbouring regions suspended services on some lines. In areas where warnings have been issued, “there’s a risk the rain will continue as the typhoon moves north”, the JMA’s Takuya Hosomi told reporters. The JMA warned on Sunday that rain and winds were expected to intensify even before the typhoon’s arrival. “The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain,” the agency said. Dujuan forced the early closure of the Tokyo Game Show, one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs, on Monday, its final day. A major outdoor music festival and a baseball match both scheduled to be held in Chiba were also cancelled. Social media posts showed images of roads in front of Kamakura station, a popular sightseeing spot, that were flooded. “There is flooding in various parts of the city, so travelling by car is dangerous,” Kamakura City Mayor Takashi Matsuo said on social media. Flooding also inundated parts of Ichikawa city east of Tokyo.

title: Former Shenzhen mayor Qin Weizhong under corruption probe by China’s discipline watchdog
description: Announcement from China’s Central Commission for Discipline Inspection comes in the lead-up to Apec meetings in tech hub.
content: Qin Weizhong, former mayor of the southern technology hub of Shenzhen, is under investigation for corruption, the country’s top watchdog has confirmed. According to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection on Monday, Qin is “suspected of grave disciplinary and law violations and is currently undergoing review”, which usually means a corruption probe. Qin was appointed deputy party secretary and mayor of Shenzhen in May 2021. On August 24 this year, those positions were filled by banking veteran Li Yun, while Qin was announced to have resigned because of a “change in work post”, with no further details given. Shenzhen will host Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meetings, including a leaders’ summit, in November. Qin has not been expelled as an alternate member of the party’s 20th Central Committee, which is expected to sit until next year when the 21st party congress will be held. Qin’s last public appearance was on August 28, when he attended a meeting of the Guangdong Provincial People’s Congress Standing Committee on economic performance oversight to support building a modern industrial system. Before taking up the positions in Shenzhen, Qin was responsible for housing, the environment and big data management in Guangdong province. Qin, who holds a PhD in chemical engineering from Tsinghua University in Beijing, was a deputy general manager at the China National Petroleum Corporation before being appointed vice-governor of Guangdong in 2019. While in Shenzhen, Qin worked under Communist Party chief Wang Weizhong, another alumnus of Tsinghua, which is also the alma mater of President Xi Jinping. During his career, Qin crossed paths with Ma Xingrui, a member of China’s Politburo and the former party chief of Xinjiang. Ma was placed under investigation in April before being stripped of party membership and dismissed from public office in July. Ma served as the party chief of Shenzhen from 2015 to 2016, before being promoted to governor of Guangdong, a position he held until 2021. Qin was vice-governor of Guangdong from 2019 to 2021.

title: Hong Kong woman, 80, loses HK$6 million to fake online investment expert
description: The case was among over 50 investment scams reported in Hong Kong last week, with total losses approaching HK$30 million.
content: An 80‑year‑old woman has lost HK$6 million (US$764,772) to a fake investment expert she met online, Hong Kong police have disclosed. The case was among more than 50 investment scams reported over the past week, with total losses approaching HK$30 million, according to a post on the force’s CyberDefender social media page. The victim, a retiree, first met the fraudster posing as an investment expert on Facebook before moving their conversations to WhatsApp, where the suspect built a relationship with her over six months. After learning she was retired and held fixed deposits, the scammer pitched a high-return stock investment plan supposedly tailored for seniors. Trusting the scheme, she transferred more than HK$6 million by depositing cheques into an unknown personal bank account and delivering cash to a relative of the fraudster. When she later attempted to withdraw her funds, the suspect vanished, and she realised she had been duped. Police warned that scammers were increasingly targeting retirees through social media and messaging apps, luring them with promises of safe, customised investment schemes.

title: South Korea beats foreign student target, but struggles to keep them
description: New university rankings show while South Korea has enjoyed an international student boom, gaps in support and post-graduation outcomes remain.
content: South Korea has surpassed its 2027 target of attracting 300,000 international students a year ahead of schedule, and universities must now find ways to retain and develop them, a new rankings assessment has shown. First launched last year and described as the country’s most internationalisation-focused assessment to date, The Korea Times University Rankings assess institutions on seven indicators, including the ratio of exchange and international students to total enrolment, diversity of the cohorts’ nationalities, proportion of international students meeting language proficiency requirements, and foreign student retention rate. This year’s evaluation aims to look beyond the number of international students to assess how well South Korean universities are building the broader ecosystem needed for globalisation. Results show that while the universities have been good at attracting and managing international students, many still lag in areas such as international faculty, financial support and post-graduation outcomes. All performed well in education but scores are lower in student support and lowest in graduate outcomes – underscoring the challenge of building an environment that looks after international students throughout their studies and beyond graduation. Seoul’s three most prestigious universities – collectively known as SKY from the first letters of their names – topped the list. Korea University took first place with 149.52 points out of 200, followed by Seoul National University with 142.22 and Yonsei University with 140.74. Sungkyunkwan University, Hanyang University and Sogang University rounded out the top six. All retained their positions from last year. Sejong University was the best performer, breaking into the top 10 by climbing six spots from 13th last year to seventh. Its education score rose sharply from 32.8 points to 47.93. It also was among the top performers in research for the second consecutive year with 39.6 points. It took the place filled last year by the University of Seoul, which slipped to 11th as its education score fell from 47.02 points last year to 41.41. Completing the top 10 list were Ewha Womans University, Kyung Hee University and Dongguk University, who all retained their positions from last year. There was little change in the universities making up the top 30 from last year, with Yeungnam University and Kookmin University being the only newcomers. Yeungnam’s rise was driven largely by its strong performance in international research. The private university in Gyeongsan, North Gyeongsang province, ranked ninth in the research category with 30.95 points. The biggest contributor to Kookmin’s climb was its score in international student retention, which increased by 2.55 points from the previous year. The results also showed a heavy concentration of globalised universities in the capital region. Of the top 30 universities, 23 were in Seoul, Gyeonggi province or Incheon, while only seven were based elsewhere. As in its inaugural edition, the assessment places far greater weight on international attractiveness than conventional university rankings. This year’s evaluation also introduced several changes to sharpen that focus. The number of universities assessed expanded to 60 from 54. The scoring framework was broadened to 19 indicators worth a total of 200 points, up from 18 indicators and 190 points. A new 10-point indicator measuring the proportion of international full-time faculty was added, while student retention was limited to degree-seeking students. “This year’s rankings showed progress in several areas, particularly with the addition of indicators measuring the ratio of international full-time faculty and international student retention rate,” said Shin Jang-sup, a professor of economics at the National University of Singapore, as quoted by The Korea Times. “The move to strengthen the evaluation framework for international students is also a positive step.” This year’s rankings also align with changes in South Korea’s immigration policy, according to Shim Hwa-yong, CEO of international student services platform Hirediversity. “Immigration policy is increasingly shifting towards regional areas, long-term settlement and quality management,” he told The Korea Times. “This year’s rankings reflect those priorities and represent a clear improvement in both validity and reliability from the inaugural assessment.” The most consequential change to this year’s rankings was limiting the pool to only degree-seeking international students for the retention indicator. Universities that previously had high dropout rates among non-degree students benefited from the new calculation, while those with high attrition among degree-seekers were more likely to lose ground. Private and public universities showed the widest gap in the newly introduced indicator measuring the proportion of international full-time faculty. The 14 public universities assessed averaged just 0.95 points out of 10, compared with 4.05 points for the 46 private institutions. The rankings were more spread out at the top but became increasingly tight towards the 30th-place cut-off. From 24th to 30th, several universities were separated by only fractions of a point, meaning even small changes in a single indicator could significantly shift their positions. Strengths also varied by category among the top 30. Handong Global University, for example, ranked second in student support but 44th in research, while Hankuk University of Foreign Studies placed 12th in education but 58th in student support. This showed that a high overall ranking did not necessarily translate into strength across all areas. So prospective international students should look beyond the overall ranking to the areas that matter most to them.

title: Chinese woman, 65, plays dual roles of beautiful doctor and mum to con man out of US$25,000
description: Reviewing Yu’s videos, police spotted a tiny ‘AI-generated content’ disclaimer that the victim had missed.
content: A 65-year-old Chinese woman used artificial intelligence (AI) to impersonate both a young doctor and her mother, successfully scamming 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) from a man. Liu Hui, a resident of Shanghai, connected with a woman named Yu Xiuzhen on a social media platform in 2021. Yu asserted that she was a 29-year-old doctor at a prestigious Grade 3A hospital in Shanghai, claiming influence over her hospital’s property engineering projects. Over the past five years, Yu frequently shared details of her daily life on her profile, amassing nearly 7,000 video posts and attracting 10,000 followers. Liu, a property contractor, believed that Yu could assist him in securing projects, prompting him to pursue a romantic relationship with her. Despite living in the same city, Yu claimed she could not meet Liu due to her mother’s disapproval. She stated that they could only meet if he provided a dowry of 300,000 yuan (US$45,000) and bought property in Shanghai. Over the course of five months, Liu transferred a total of 170,000 yuan to Yu, even though they never met in person. At times, Liu’s requests for video calls were also declined, as Yu claimed her mother was present. Furthermore, Yu never advanced the engineering project as she had promised. Sensing something off, Liu contacted the police. The authorities swiftly located the scammer Yu, who was actually born in 1961. She possessed no medical qualifications and worked merely as a cleaner at a hospital. The account used to receive the funds was registered under another man’s name. Upon reviewing Yu’s videos, the police discovered small characters in some that indicated, “This work contains AI-generated content.” It was revealed that Yu used AI to enhance her appearance and fabricate her attractive doctor persona through compositing scenes. On occasion, she also portrayed her mother to convince Liu that her mother was obstructing their relationship. Liu remarked that he had never noticed the small characters and had no understanding of AI. The police disclosed that Yu had spent the money she scammed on cosmetic surgery, skincare, and clothing. Additionally, she had a prior conviction for fraud and was sentenced to four years in prison in 2009. Recently, police publicised the case to alert people to a new type of AI-driven online dating scam. According to data from the Ministry of Public Security, over 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) was involved in telecommunications and online fraud nationwide in the first half of last year. In just the first quarter of last year, instances of AI face-swapping and voice-mimicking fraud cases surged by 45 per cent. An online observer quipped: “This 65-year-old woman is better at AI than me, a 35-year-old.” Another remarked: “The man fell for the scam also due to his greed for business opportunities.”

title: Expect ‘high tide’ of Chinese biotech deals as threat of US curbs fades: analysts
description: Stocks jump on reports Washington will allow most licensing deals under ‘substantially softer stance’ than had been feared, analysts say.
content: US-China biotech deals are expected to thrive because Washington is reportedly leaning away from sweeping restrictions, according to analysts, giving Chinese healthcare firms a major boost following Beijing’s ambitious five-year plan for the sector. Out-licensing deals between China and the US would “ride on a high tide” in the favourable environment, said Nomura’s head of China healthcare research Jialin Zhang, in a research note on Sunday. The US Treasury Department was drafting investment rules for American pharmaceutical firms that would preserve their ability to license most Chinese drugs, barring links to pathogens or weaponisable biotechnology, Reuters reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources. That stance would represent a “substantially softer stance” than had been feared based on restrictions outlined in two US bills earlier this year, said Tony Ren, head of Asia Healthcare Research at Macquarie, in a note on Monday. The Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (Coins) Act, signed into law in December and slated to take effect by March 2027, restricted outbound investment in sensitive foreign technologies including semiconductors and quantum computing, authorising the Treasury Department to add to the scope. As biotechnology was not identified as a restricted sector under the legislation, two lawmakers – John Moolenaar, chairman of a House Select Committee on competition with China, and Debbie Dingell – introduced the Biotech Investment National Security Act (Binsa) bill in June to add it. US pharmaceutical licensing deals, joint ventures, and equity investments in Chinese biotech firms would be subject to Treasury review under Binsa, as such cooperation would “hand Chinese companies another chokehold over our economy”, the two lawmakers said. The bill has not yet passed. The industry strongly resisted such restrictions. A broad ban on Chinese biotech deals would conflict with both “the desire for longer, healthier lives” and large pharmaceutical companies’ business models, Macquarie analysts said on Monday, adding that global pharmaceutical corporations they had consulted “universally” opposed such a ban. The reported US plan to allow most cross-border biotech deals showed that the industry’s extensive lobbying efforts had paid off, according to Macquarie. China is playing an increasingly prominent role in the global healthcare industry as multinational pharmaceutical giants snap up cost-efficient innovative assets coming out of the country. The value of out-licensing deals involving China-made innovative drugs this year jumped 36 per cent from a year earlier to US$120 billion, state-run news agency Xinhua said last week, citing data from China’s National Medical Products Administration. Based on the strong momentum of domestic biotech firms, Beijing has laid out its ambition to become a global biomedicine powerhouse. A new five-year plan for the sector calls for Chinese first-in-class innovative drugs to account for at least 25 per cent of the global total by 2030, when the country’s large pharmaceutical enterprises should generate combined revenue of no less than 3.5 trillion yuan (US$522 billion). These developments would support a re-rating of China’s biotech sector, despite the prospect of further geopolitical volatility ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Macquarie said. Shares of Chinese biotech and pharmaceutical firms listed in Hong Kong rallied on Monday. Among those seeing the biggest gains, GenFleet Therapeutics jumped 13.7 per cent, Shanghai Junshi Biosciences rose 12.7 per cent and Akeso added 9.7 per cent.

title: Meet Maria Sten, the Reacher star leading spin-off series Neagley
description: The former Miss Denmark Universe almost missed out on her role in the Alan Ritchson-led series, but now she stars in a spin-off alongside Greyston Holt.
content: The Alan Ritchson-led crime television series Reacher has topped Amazon Prime Video’s viewership charts this week, but its own spin-off Neagley may be coming for the crown. Reacher’s Season 4 finale aired on September 16, the same day Neagley premiered. The spin-off is centred on Maria Sten’s Reacher character, former US Army Master Sergeant Frances Neagley, who takes on Chicago as a private investigator. Per Men’s Journal, the show, which also stars Greyston Holt, jumped to third place on Prime Video’s most-watched list on the day of its release. Speaking to Entertainment Weekly, Reacher showrunner Nick Santora, who co-created Neagley with Nicholas Wootton, gushed over Sten being “great all through Reacher”, before adding, “Now giving her the torch to carry as the lead of the show, she’s also been great.” Lee Child, author of the Jack Reacher novels, also called Sten the “surprise star” of the show. Seeing the show’s success, the 36-year-old actress told Entertainment Weekly that she was “so excited about the world getting to know Neagley a little bit better”. So, what do we know about Maria Sten? Read on to find out. What is Maria Sten’s background? Maria Sten was born on October 29, 1989, in Copenhagen, Denmark, and has Danish, Swedish and Congolese roots, per IMDb. Her mother is Danish painter Nina Sten-Knudsen, who has Swedish heritage, and her father is a Congolese artist, the actress revealed on the Danish Originals podcast. Sten grew up with her mother and older sister, Julie, who is a writer and poet. She has seven other siblings, according to her interview with fashion editor Linda Tatiene. What are Maria Sten’s credits? Ever since she could walk, Sten posed for her mother’s paintings and photographs, the actress told Tatiene. She got into modelling at a young age and also took up music, gymnastics and rhythmic gymnastics. She began acting in primary school and learned various dance forms, including ballet, flamenco and hip-hop. Determined to make a living through the performing arts, she graduated from secondary school at 17 and saved up to move to New York at 18, where she studied dance before moving to Los Angeles to attend an acting school. In 2008, she was crowned Miss Denmark Universe. Sten has since appeared in shows like Persuasion and Channel Zero and was a writer on Big Sky. She has also written and produced the shorts When It Burns (2016) and Wild Things Run Free (2017). How did Maria Sten land her role in Reacher? When Sten first auditioned for the role of Neagley, she was rejected, per Backstage. However, when the character’s direction changed, the team brought her on board. Now, with her own spin-off, the actress hopes to graciously represent leading women of colour on television, she told Entertainment Weekly.

title: China’s Djibouti base upgrade may give PLA eyes on foreign military in Middle East
description: Commercial imagery reveals two new communication sites built near foreign military bases in East Africa, US think tank says.
content: China has upgraded its military base in Djibouti with communications equipment a US think tank says is “likely enhancing” the country’s ability to collect signals intelligence – potentially giving the PLA a window on foreign military operations in Djibouti and the wider Middle East. The Chinese facility sits within 16km (10 miles) of US, French, Italian and Japanese military bases, according to the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), in an unusually concentrated environment in which several foreign militaries operate in close proximity. Beijing opened the Djibouti facility in 2017, describing it as a support base for naval escort, peacekeeping and humanitarian missions. It has since become a hub for Chinese naval operations in the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea. The upgrade could be particularly significant as US Air Force budget documents describe nearby Chabelley Airfield as the only location in East Africa from which armed intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets are authorised to operate. Meanwhile in August, Japan began flying P-1 maritime patrol aircraft from its Djibouti facility for counter-piracy and Middle East information-gathering missions. Analysis of commercial satellite imagery published by CSIS on Thursday shows two communications compounds have been built at the Chinese base since mid-2024, with most of the work completed by mid-2025. The larger compound includes three roughly 30-metre (98-foot) high-frequency (HF) antennas, two VHF/UHF antennas, three steerable satellite dishes, four probable 5G arrays and a radome structure enclosing an unidentified asset. The smaller compound has two further HF antennas and a second radome. Timothy Heath, head of defence research firm Perceptum, said the communications infrastructure was likely “first and foremost” to serve PLA forces, improving communication with Chinese ships, aircraft and personnel in the region and reducing the risk of mishaps. But it could also strengthen situational awareness and help collect intelligence on US, Japanese and other forces, he said. CSIS said the radio equipment could potentially pick up nearby signals and help determine where they were coming from, while the satellite dishes could potentially intercept satellite downlinks. Actual collection has not been confirmed. Not all the equipment appears intended for intelligence gathering. CSIS said one radome may house a weather radar and it considered collection through the probable 5G arrays unlikely. The think tank stressed that open-source information could not confirm whether the PLA was actively intercepting communications using the new equipment. But it said the systems could allow China to “draw valuable insights into US and other militaries’ operations by observing the direction, origin, frequency, and pace of their signals”. Heath said the new capabilities could allow the PLA to monitor US and Japanese ships and aircraft operating nearby, including counter-piracy patrols and US operations related to the conflict with Iran. “Although the content may be encrypted, the PLA could observe the patterns in emissions to include which platforms are emitting signals as well as when, where and how often,” he said. “This could give a clearer picture of the tempo of US and Japanese operations and insight into how they operate.” Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said such information could also have electronic warfare value. “Even gathering data on things like the types of radio communications, the frequencies foreign militaries employ and how often they ‘frequency hop’ is useful,” he said, adding that such data could support operations such as jamming. Heath said data on the technical parameters of military communications could also help the PLA add to its “database on US military communications signals”. He said observing real-world operations could reveal how US and Japanese forces behave in practice – including procedures, patterns or shortcomings – that might not be apparent from military doctrine or exercises. That information could be shared “with forces in the Pacific theatre that need to train and prepare for possible operations against the US and Japanese militaries”, he said, adding that electronic warfare would probably play a major role in any such operations. The Chinese upgrade comes as Djibouti takes on greater significance for Washington. Bosack said the country had become “much more important given the continued targeting of US bases in the Middle East and the scope of the damage sustained thus far in the region”. “The US needs viable basing options for its regional assets,” he said, meaning Djibouti “could see a post-war uptick in American presence”. That growing importance is also reflected in US plans for Chabelley. The Air Force is seeking US$27 million for power upgrades at the base to support round-the-clock intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance or ISR operations. The budget request underscores Chabelley’s role as a US surveillance hub in the region – and the kind of sustained military activity that could make communications and emission patterns valuable to monitor. Meanwhile, Japan’s facility, established in 2011 near Camp Lemonnier, is the Self-Defence Forces’ only overseas base. Then defence minister Gen Nakatani said last year that its role included counter-piracy, Middle East information gathering and potential evacuation operations. The concentration of foreign military facilities has also generated Chinese concerns about surveillance in the other direction. In 2019, Aboubaker Omar Hadi, chairman of the Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority, said Chinese officials had complained several times to Djibouti’s foreign ministry that US helicopters and drones were flying over the Chinese base. He said Beijing claimed the flights were being used for intelligence gathering. Washington has acknowledged counter-intelligence concerns. In 2018, US Africa Command said it was “carefully monitoring” China’s military presence in Djibouti, while the command’s then-chief General Thomas Waldhauser said the US was taking “significant steps on the counter-intelligence side”. The communications buildout may not be finished. CSIS said reinforced cable trenches laid at one of the communications sites last year suggested more antennas could be added. “The PLA base in Djibouti is maturing with more capable communications equipment,” Heath said. “This could signal PLA interest in upgrading the tempo and variety of operations it conducts from the base.”

title: Meet Laysla De Oliveira, who plays Cruz in Taylor Sheridan’s Lioness
description: The Brazilian-Canadian actress was discovered by a model scout as a teenager before securing her breakout role as the villain Dodge in Netflix’s Locke & Key.
content: Taylor Sheridan’s spy thriller show Lioness has wrapped up its third season with a shocking finale twist. Inspired by a real-life unit of undercover female agents fighting terrorist organisations, the show boasts an A-list cast led by Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman and Morgan Freeman. The final minutes of Season 3’s last episode spotlight Cruz Manuelos, a young Marine and CIA operative played by Laysla De Oliveira. In a dramatic turn, it is revealed that the multiple attempts to abduct Lioness team leader Joe McNamara (Saldaña) were orchestrated by Aaliyah Amrohi – a woman Cruz befriended in Season 1 in an attempt to kill her terrorist father. While fans are eager for confirmation on whether the show will be renewed for another season, here’s everything to know about De Oliveira. How did she get her start? Laysla De Oliveira was born in January 1992 in Toronto, Canada. Of Brazilian descent, she was raised in a Catholic household but has said she is no longer a practising Catholic. De Oliveira was just 14 years old when she began her modelling career after being discovered on the street by an agency scout. What roles has Laysla De Oliveira played? De Oliveira attended Rosedale Heights School of the Arts in Toronto. She decided to become an actress after her very first drama class at the school. At university, De Oliveira acquired an agent and got busy attending auditions. She landed her first on-screen role in a 2012 episode of the spy thriller Covert Affairs. Her first starring role came soon after, in the 2013 television film Gothica, also starring Tom Ellis and Melissa George. But it wasn’t until 2020 when she landed a recurring role as Dodge, one of the main antagonists in Netflix’s Locke & Key, that De Oliveira’s career really started to take off. The actress is clearly in demand, with three upcoming projects listed on her IMDb profile. Is Laysla De Oliveira single? De Oliveira wed her long-time partner, Jonathan Keltz, in May last year. The couple, who had been dating for 13 years, eloped and tied the knot at the Santa Barbara courthouse. A fellow actor, Keltz is known for playing Jake Steinberg on the HBO series Entourage.

title: Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan royal crisis escalates as chief minister defies ruler
description: The disagreement centres on competing interpretations of Negeri Sembilan’s state constitution.
