content: Malaysia’s royal crisis in Negeri Sembilan spilled into a new constitutional fight on Monday after the state’s chief minister refused to accept the ruler’s dismissal of the entire executive council – a dispute that has already brought down one government and triggered a snap election. The latest showdown comes less than a week after the executive council backed a disputed bid to remove the ruler, putting the palace and state government in conflict over both the throne and executive control. Chief Minister Ismail Lasim said the councillors remained legally in office and would continue working as usual, directly contradicting an order issued late on Sunday by state ruler Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir. “I was never consulted and never at any time advised on the termination of any Negeri Sembilan executive councillor,” Ismail said in a statement on Monday. “There is therefore no need to submit a new list of executive councillors because the existing exco remains valid and will carry out its duties as usual.” The disagreement centres on competing interpretations of Negeri Sembilan’s 1959 state constitution. Citing Article 38(5), the palace argued that executive councillors – excluding the chief minister – hold office at the pleasure of the ruler. In its statement, the palace said Muhriz had revoked the appointments “with immediate effect” after finding that the councillors had violated the oath of office they took before him on August 7. “They have breached that oath by their actions and statements on September 15,” the palace said. Each councillor was informed individually, while Ismail was ordered to submit a new line-up for royal approval. The state executive council is effectively Negeri Sembilan’s cabinet, made up of elected lawmakers who help the chief minister in governing and managing portfolios ranging from infrastructure and investment to education and welfare. Ismail, however, argued that Article 38(5) could not be read on its own. He said it had to be considered alongside Articles 38(4) and 40(1), which required the ruler to act on the advice of the chief minister and executive council in matters of state administration. Any attempt to dismiss a councillor without his advice, Ismail said, was “a legal error, unconstitutional, and has no legal effect whatsoever”. Royal rupture The palace intervention came days after the same executive council backed a disputed April 19 proclamation seeking to remove Muhriz and install Tuanku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar in his place. Ismail confirmed last week that the council had unanimously considered the proclamation at its September 15 meeting and instructed the state secretary to proceed with its gazettement. Malaysia’s Attorney-General’s Chambers rejected that move, finding that the April proclamation failed to meet mandatory constitutional requirements and that neither the chief minister nor the executive council held unilateral authority to remove a ruler. The chambers added that there was no evidence that any grounds for disqualification under Article 10 applied to Muhriz, noting that the matter was before the High Court in Seremban under an interlocutory injunction. The state secretary’s office subsequently refused to gazette or enforce the proclamation, citing the Attorney-General’s Chambers’ position that doing so would be unconstitutional. Negeri Sembilan, south of Kuala Lumpur, is Malaysia’s only elective state monarchy. Its ruler, titled the Yang di-Pertuan Besar, is chosen by four territorial chiefs known as the Undang, rather than succeeding automatically through primogeniture. The system has its roots in Adat Perpatih, a matrilineal customary system introduced by Minangkabau settlers from Sumatra that remains central to the state’s governing structure. Earlier this month, a special sitting of the Dewan Keadilan dan Undang – the state’s highest customary council – ruled the April 19 attempt to remove Muhriz invalid, finding that constitutional requirements for removal had not been fulfilled. The royal dispute has simmered since April, causing the collapse of the previous administration ahead of a snap state election in August. Ismail, a veteran of the United Malays National Organisation (Umno), was sworn in as chief minister before Muhriz on August 2. His 10 executive councillors took their oaths before the same ruler five days later. Salim Bashir, a former president of the Malaysian Bar, said that removing executive councillors would not by itself bring down the state government. “The state government does not collapse if excos are sacked, provided the MB [Menteri Besar] stays in office,” he said, adding that new appointments would have to be made quickly to avoid government disruption. Salim said that while a ruler could revoke a councillor’s appointment on the chief minister’s advice or following a breach of oath, anyone seeking to challenge the dismissals could turn to the courts. Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said Ismail now faced a difficult choice as submitting replacement names required the approval of the ruler whom his administration had declared removed only days earlier. “Ismail has a dilemma right now. He cannot function without the exco,” Azmi said. “I think that this matter needs to be resolved by the court,” he added, describing the judiciary as a neutral forum to settle state constitutional law with customary traditions.

title: Chinese regulator drafts rules to protect teenagers from ‘intimate’ AI companions
description: The latest proposals come two months after China introduced its first dedicated rules governing humanlike AI interaction.
content: China’s top internet watchdog has drafted new rules to regulate how social platforms and game developers should protect minors, including a ban on offering “virtual intimacy services” to those under 18 as artificial intelligence-powered companions gain traction. The rules, titled “Ensuring minors’ safe and healthy use of the internet”, would ban online platforms from providing “virtual relatives or companions”, and prohibit them from offering services that “induce minors to become addicted or otherwise harm or may seriously affect their physical and mental health”. The regulations would also ban online social networking services among strangers, except for those aged above 16 who rely on their own wages, according to the document published last Friday by the Cyberspace Administration of China. The document requires platforms to activate minors’ mode when operating online games, social sites and offering AI services that “could affect the cognition of” users under 16. Operators were also required to more accurately identify underage users and ban them from using algorithms that “induce emotional dependence, addiction or excessive spending”. Violations could carry fines of up to 10 times the income earned by the platform if it exceeded 1 million yuan (US$149,000), and punishment would include having all the income confiscated. The proposals, now soliciting public comment through October 17, represent the latest restriction on screen time by teenagers. Those aged between six and 19 accounted for 18 per cent of all Chinese internet users, or 112.5 million people, as of the end of 2025, according to data from the state-run China Internet Network Information Centre. “The key question in defining a ‘virtual intimate relationship’ is whether a service is designed to simulate or substitute for real family or partner relationships and build sustained emotional bonds through character settings and emotional guidance,” said He Qianggao, a lawyer and director at Geason Law Offices. He added that ordinary AI chats or functional role-playing would generally fall outside the scope, but services that effectively encouraged emotional dependence or replaced real-world relationships could still come under scrutiny even without being labelled as an AI companion. He said the bigger compliance challenge for AI companies would go beyond verifying how old users were to determining what services they could access once identified as minors. Platforms may consequently see rising costs across product design, technical infrastructure and compliance reviews. The latest proposals come two months after China introduced its first dedicated rules governing humanlike AI interaction, which took effect in July and targeted AI systems that excessively cater to users or encourage emotional dependence in ways that damage real-world relationships. To comply, ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen disabled customised agent functions that had allowed users to create characters with fixed names, personalities and speaking styles. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Fan Ho’s poetic photos of mid-20th century Hong Kong show in an unlikely place
description: An Italian palace in Turin is hosting a new exhibition of Fan’s works that capture everyday human activity in 1950s and 60s Hong Kong.
content: “Photography is a universal language that transcends the barriers of culture and time.” These wise words from Fan Ho perfectly encapsulate the premise of a new exhibition celebrating his poetic camerawork at the Palazzo Falletti di Barolo in Turin, Italy. A Baroque noble residence might not be the first place that comes to mind when looking to discover Ho’s mid-20th century Hong Kong compositions, but the show invites viewers to look beyond the obvious and make connections to those scenes from a faraway land. The exhibition, titled “Fan Ho. Il Maestro della Fotografia di Hong Kong” (Fan Ho. The Master of Photography of Hong Kong), premiered on September 11 in the aristocratic residence in the city centre. This marks the first time Ho’s photographs have received such extensive attention in Europe, with around 100 works curated by Elisa Maupas on display. Maupas worked closely with Sarah Van Ingelgom – also known as Sarah Greene – from Hong Kong’s Blue Lotus Gallery, the exclusive representative of Ho’s photographic works. Maupas has curated several high-profile photography exhibitions in Turin in recent years, including a particularly memorable one on Vivian Maier in 2022. “Turin has a special relationship with photography,” she says. “It is where the first photographs ever taken in Italy were shot, and the home of the first active camera clubs.” Turin’s long-standing affiliation with the artistic discipline has inspired her to seek out talent across the globe, not just the expected names. “I don’t know why Fan Ho hasn’t been showcased much outside Hong Kong and the United States, so it’s actually an honour for us to be able to realise the project here,” she says. Van Ingelgom notes that the show’s scale surpasses nearly all the Fan Ho exhibitions she organised in Hong Kong. She also points out that the show marks Ho’s second meaningful encounter with Italy; the photographer had previously met the legendary film director Federico Fellini in Rome’s Cinecitta, where they reflected on how much an artist’s status could influence public opinion of their craft. While that trip fulfilled Ho’s personal quest to come face-to-face with someone he had long idolised, one could imagine that this posthumous event decades later allows him to engage with the Italian public on his own terms, using Hong Kong as a canvas to experiment with different forms of stylistic representation of human activity and interaction. Before visitors even see the first photos, their senses are immediately heightened as they enter the venue. Palazzo Barolo was built in the 17th century and boasts all the glamour one expects from an Italian palace: a monumental marble staircase, crystal chandeliers, frescoed ceilings and more. The opulent surroundings are a stark yet intriguing contrast to the pieces featured. While the flamboyant interior details scream, Ho’s mainly black-and-white works whisper with his play of light and shadow. The purposeful geometric structure and stillness in the photos become more pronounced. Maupas is confident that viewers will not be distracted by the surroundings. “We hung the photos on gallery panels [to put them in focus], but at the same time, they are in a dialogue with the existing tapestry of the space,” she says. “I think it actually adds to the experience.” Local visitors are likely to recognise common ground between 1960s Hong Kong and Italy during the post-World War II era, a time of rapid industrialisation and social transformation. The ways societies and peoples forged ahead with limited means in Italy were immortalised through the street photography of Gianni Berengo Gardin, Paolo di Paolo and fellow realists. As Maupas points out, the often-captured moments of people engaging in everyday activities – having lunch or sitting idly in a stairwell – are the same kind of subjects that Ho favoured. What is immensely fascinating is the distinct visual language Ho chose to tell those shared stories. While the Italian maestros homed in on the vivacity and emotions of the characters inhabiting the public space, his camera – aided by intervention in the darkroom – strikes a contemplative tone. Photos like Coolies and Hawkers (1958) and Different Directions (1958) are prime examples of Ho seeking to distil harmony out of Hong Kong’s crowded urban landscape. Van Ingelgom also singles out the photograph Private (1960) – an image featuring a couple framed in a window above a “private” street sign – that epitomises his keen sense of observation by calling attention to the way spatial boundaries mediate perceived and actual intimacy. “His ability to connect to the human experience is what makes his photography so strong and powerful,” Maupas adds. Beyond Turin’s Museum of Oriental Art, which is just a stone’s throw from Palazzo Barolo, the city has seen an increasing number of Asian art exhibitions in recent years, something that could well see locals develop a stronger affinity for Ho’s oeuvre. Though public interest remains geared towards ancient genres such as Ukiyo-e woodblock art and Jingdezhen porcelain, the Fan Ho show contributes to a continuing phenomenon in which Italian art lovers recontextualise Eastern creativity through a modern, auteur-driven lens. “Fan Ho. Il Maestro della Fotografia di Hong Kong” is showing from September 11, 2026, to January 10, 2027, at Palazzo Falletti di Barolo, Via delle Orfane, 7, 10122, Turin, Italy.

title: Will Anwar’s coalition in Malaysia implode amid Loke exit, Najib house arrest?
description: Observers say the numbers in cabinet remain in Anwar’s favour for now, but warn that a DAP walkout could embolden rival Umno.
content: Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has suffered a double whammy as his Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition scrambles to placate public outrage over disgraced ex-leader Najib Razak being granted house arrest and the shock resignation of his transport minister in protest against the royal clemency. But observers do not expect the administration, already reeling from PH defeats in two recent state elections as federal allies turned against the coalition, to implode just yet. Anwar and PH’s reformist credentials took a hit on Friday after the Pardons Board announced that Najib would be allowed to serve out the remainder of his prison term at home, provided the former prime minister settles his 50 million ringgit (US$12.2 million) fine. In response, Anthony Loke, secretary general of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), announced on Saturday that he would resign from cabinet in a move widely seen as decrying Najib’s house arrest. Loke is the most senior figure in the largest party within Anwar’s coalition government. He is widely seen as the highest representative of Malaysia’s ethnic Chinese population, which for more than two decades has overwhelmingly voted against Najib and his former ruling Umno party. This opposition was driven by allegations of endemic corruption that culminated in the multibillion-dollar 1Malaysia Development Berhad scandal. However, PH’s dalliances with the United Malays National Organisation – with which it formed an alliance to govern the country after a deeply split 2022 general election – led to accusations from supporters that Anwar and his allies had abandoned their commitment to reform to stay in power. “[Loke’s resignation] is more to placate DAP’s base … so if the question is if it is enough for DAP’s supporters, I don’t think so,” said Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, an associate professor of political science at the International Islamic University of Malaysia. It is not clear when Loke intends to formally resign from his post as transport minister. In a statement on Monday, his ministry said he would remain in post to represent Malaysia at the 12th Apec Transportation Ministers’ Meeting in Beijing before heading to Shanghai to join Anwar on an official visit later this week. Anwar said on Sunday that he had yet to accept Loke’s resignation, adding that he would like to discuss the matter first before making any decision. “He has informed me, but I haven’t had the chance to discuss anything with him yet,” he was quoted as saying by the Bernama news agency. “I need to hear his views, but I understand because he is a man of principle.” Friday’s decree by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, who chairs the Pardons Board and is constitutionally empowered to grant pardons to convicts serving out their sentences, followed PH’s defeat in two recent state elections by federal partner Umno. The defeats were partly attributed to a resurgent Umno capitalising on a campaign to unify the majority Malay-Muslim vote, as well as PH being rejected by former supporters unhappy with its failure to bring substantive reforms to a government system still seen as compromised by systemic corruption and abuse of power. In announcing his resignation, Loke said it sent a clear signal that the DAP remained firm in its stance against corruption. However, the DAP still has 11 other ministers and deputy ministers in government. Analysts say this undermines any grand declarations made by the party and potentially lends weight to long-standing allegations that it seeks to erode the political and cultural dominance of the country’s Malay majority. “By making a big deal of it by calling a special meeting, [Loke] actually added oil to the fire,” said James Chin, a professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania, referring to the DAP’s emergency meeting on Saturday. “This had nothing to do with the PH government or the DAP; this was the king’s prerogative. If he had said that, most people, especially the Malays, would accept it.” But Chin said PH would have been in a far worse position if the DAP had decided to resign en bloc from government, emboldening Umno, which demanded snap polls just two weeks ago as it sought to capitalise on the momentum of its political revival. The numbers remain in Anwar’s favour, for now. Even if the 30 MPs under the Umno-led Barisan Nasional coalition pull out, the prime minister would still have just enough seats in parliament to remain in power. But a DAP walkout from Anwar’s cabinet could tip the calculus in Umno’s favour, analysts warned, as it could easily be painted as a dismissal of the country’s royal institution by the Chinese-majority party – and by extension PH. “If Anwar keeps things [as they are], it should blow over soon. Because truthfully, there is not much that can be done now, except to demand an explanation,” Syaza said.

title: Asia investors demand AI revenue proof as focus shifts from exposure to earnings: BofA
description: Investments in artificial intelligence increasingly hinge on monetisation, Bank of America survey finds, as ‘fundamentals drive everything’.
content: Investors in Asia are demanding clearer evidence that artificial intelligence can translate into revenue and earnings, rather than simply seeking exposure to the technology, as the sector moves into a more mature phase, according to Chris Oberoi, head of Asia-Pacific research at Bank of America (BofA) Global Research. “The issue increasingly is: does it add to productivity, and is it being monetised,” Oberoi said. “And the answer is, ‘absolutely yes’.” Separately, President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump are preparing to meet in Washington on Thursday, with trade and technology expected to feature in talks between the world’s two largest economies. In an interview on Friday, ahead of BofA’s Asia-Pacific Conference that began on Monday in Hong Kong, Oberoi said discussions with clients around AI had become “more nuanced” than a year ago. Investors were moving beyond simply seeking AI exposure to examining models, semiconductors, memory and whether companies can turn investment into revenue, he added. That shift was reflected in BofA’s September Asia Fund Manager Survey. Four out of five respondents said proven, tangible AI monetisation would most increase their conviction to add to AI-related stocks. The survey polled 190 investors managing US$512 billion in assets, including 87 regional specialists managing US$211 billion. At the same time, 55 per cent of respondents said AI’s positive impact was already fairly or more than fully reflected in equity valuations, up from 37 per cent in August. “Fundamentals drive everything, and if you can monetise, then you can fund, and investors will be interested,” Oberoi said. BofA was still expecting the AI capital-expenditure (capex) cycle to continue, with Taiwan and Japan among its preferred Asia-Pacific markets, according to its report on the survey results. Taiwan and the United States were tied as the markets most expected by fund managers to benefit from the next AI cycle, with Taiwan exposed to advanced chips, packaging and servers. Meanwhile, South Korea was benefiting from memory demand, and Japan offered exposure to industrial automation and robotics. China has a broader role in the buildout, according to the bank, supplying the global AI chain while expanding its own infrastructure. “China is a critical component in the supply chain on the global buildout,” Oberoi said. “But they also have a big capex cycle going on internally to build this out.” He described a “smile curve”, with semiconductors and memory at one end and models such as those from Kimi, Anthropic, ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding at the other, while robotics and industrial applications faced more intense competition over monetisation. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. BofA expected some progress on trade during the coming presidential summit, including possible tariff reductions in areas such as agriculture or aerospace, and an extension of the existing trade truce. But Oberoi said the meeting was unlikely to fundamentally alter the broader technology rivalry between the two countries. Going forward, rising interest rates could still become a tail risk for Asian markets, Oberoi said. “Markets are based on fundamentals. Investors do take into account the direction of rates in their analysis,” he added. The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point last week – its first increase in more than three years. BofA maintains its base case, expecting two more quarter-percentage-point increases before the end of the year. The Bank of Japan on Friday raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent – the highest level in 31 years – as it continues to move away from its long period of ultra-loose monetary policy. BofA expects the Bank of Japan to eventually reach 2 per cent and forecasts the yen at 149 to the US dollar at the end of 2026, strengthening from 157 on Monday. “Markets tend to reflect information as best as they can,” Oberoi said. “Revenues and earnings tend to be key drivers for investors.”

title: Rising toll of US-China trade, tech curbs in focus ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: Impacts of reciprocal restrictions eroding profits, disrupting supply chains and intensifying market competition are back in the spotlight.
content: With President Xi Jinping expected to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, attention is again turning to the tit-for-tat trade and technology restrictions between the two nations – a friction that continues to escalate despite occasional reprieves. Over the past year, tech firms and industrial manufacturers on both sides have been casualties of the ever-intensifying rivalry, even as some benefit from growing state support to cushion the blow. From lost sales and squeezed margins to supply-chain disruptions and rising competition, this piece breaks down how the restrictions are affecting companies in the world’s two largest economies, drawing on earnings reports from 18 listed firms. 1. Direct financial hits Many of the firms reported direct financial impacts from US-China restrictions, including lost revenue, lower profits, cancelled orders and substantial inventory writedowns. US chipmaker Nvidia, for example, recorded a US$400 million charge in the first half of its financial year 2027, which ended in July, for excess inventory and purchase obligations related to the H200 graphics chip. The charge came despite Washington granting licences for limited H200 shipments to China, as Beijing also reportedly imposed restrictions on the chip’s sale and import. “We have been unable to sell all the products for which we have licences,” the company said in its August filing. In China, auto-parts maker Bohai Automotive Systems swung to a net loss of 3.09 million yuan (US$460,630) in the first half of this year, from a profit of 301.5 million yuan a year earlier. In its half-year report published last month, the company said one of its subsidiaries, which is subject to US tariffs on auto parts and raw materials including aluminium, reported lower orders and revenue because of “US-China trade tensions”. Smart-furniture makers MotoMotion and Haier Smart Home also reported double-digit declines in first-half profits, citing higher tariffs that added to pressure on operating costs and profitability. 2. Losing ground to rivals US semiconductor equipment makers Applied Materials and Lam Research both said in their August filings that export restrictions on China had limited the market for some of their products and services while increasing competitive pressure from rivals. “There can be no assurance that we will continue to compete successfully in the future,” read Lam Research’s report. While the US revoked Qualcomm’s licence to sell 4G and certain integrated circuit products to Huawei Technologies in 2024, the US chipmaker continued to say it did not expect any revenue from the Chinese firm in its latest quarterly report in July. It also warned that Huawei’s growing share of China’s smartphone market could further weigh on its operations and cash flow. Meanwhile, server maker Super Micro Computer highlighted the escalating operational challenges of navigating US trade curbs on advanced processors. “Compliance with ever-changing regulations is complex and time-consuming,” the company said in its annual filing for the financial year ended June 30. It cautioned that licensing delays and compliance burdens could make technical support “more cumbersome”, ultimately encouraging customers to seek alternatives from competitors. 3. Supply chain risks Chinese chipmaker Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), which has been on the US Entity List since 2020, said in its latest half-year report that the list’s trade restrictions had created challenges for supply chain security and business stability. Some of its affiliates were also added to the list in 2024. The company warned in the report published earlier this month that tighter restrictions could further limit its access to equipment, materials, software and services needed for production. Similarly, ACM Research Shanghai, a wafer fabrication equipment manufacturer, was placed on the list in 2024 along with some of its subsidiaries. In its latest half-year report published in August, it warned that its suppliers must obtain US export licences before selling certain US-controlled items to the company, meaning any licence denials could constrain its ability to procure them. For some US companies, the risk increasingly runs through China’s tightening control over certain critical materials such as rare earth elements. China accounts for about 60 per cent of global rare earth mining and nearly 90 per cent of processing, according to the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies. Applied Materials flagged supply-chain risks tied to Chinese government restrictions on the export of rare earth minerals last year. Lumentum, an American manufacturer of optical and photonic products, said that China’s export controls on rare earths and other critical minerals had constrained its access to these materials, threatening to inhibit its ability to sell products or purchase necessary equipment and supplies. 4. Greater regulatory uncertainty KLA, a US semiconductor-equipment supplier, said some products destined for China had recently been held by US Customs and Border Protection because of questions over customers or product capabilities, creating the risk of shipment delays or cancellations that could further affect its financial condition and operations, according to its annual report for the financial year ended June 30. US chipmaker Marvell also said it had faced delays or denials in obtaining licences to ship some products to China, with no guarantee that future requests would be approved. Chinese buyers accounted for 42 per cent of the company’s total net revenue in the quarter ended August 1. Qualcomm said if US-China relations remain strained, “our ability to consummate any transaction that would require approval … in China may be severely impacted”, while completed acquisitions could face government reviews, fines or forced divestitures. Several companies also warned that restrictions could trigger countermeasures from the other side. US chipmaker AMD said complying with US restrictions could expose the company and its affiliates to Chinese countermeasures, leading to restrictions on its operations and transactions in China, supply-chain disruptions and reputational harm, any of which could materially affect its business, operating results and financial condition. Nvidia has likewise warned that tighter US export controls could provoke responses from foreign governments, including China, that disrupt its supply chain or its ability to serve customers worldwide.

title: Top official to determine responsible department in complex 1823 cases
description: When assigning complaints that involve more than one government department, responsibility will be fairly distributed, Warner Cheuk says.
content: A top official will determine where responsibility lies when a public complaint spans multiple departments under a new handling mechanism for the 1823 hotline, set to be implemented early next year. Deputy Chief Secretary for Administration Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said on Monday that he would ensure a “very fair” distribution of responsibility when assigning complaints that involved more than one government department. The reform, which will take effect in the first quarter of next year, will see Cheuk make the final call on which bureau or department should handle complaints with ambiguous or overlapping responsibilities. “If every department has a similar share of the responsibility, we will operate a roster system like the chief executive mentioned. We will make sure everyone has a turn,” he said during a press briefing. “If one department acts as the leading department this time, the next time other departments will take the lead in coordinating, so this is a fair system.” If the designated lead department disagrees with the assignment, it must appeal to 1823 within a few days, and Cheuk will then make a final decision. Cheuk was responding to a question about how responsibilities would be assigned if residents of a building undergoing renovation suspected that repair materials did not meet fire safety requirements. Before the Wang Fuk Court fire, which claimed 168 lives, residents had repeatedly complained to the government about issues including the use of styrofoam to seal windows, openings in fire escape stairwells and workers smoking on site. Hearings by a judge-led independent committee found that departments told residents they were contacting the wrong offices and effectively turned a deaf ear to the fire risks. Cheuk said that under the new mechanism, the lead department, on behalf of all teams involved, would give the complainant a preliminary response within 10 calendar days and a substantive response within 30 calendar days. He clarified that his decision-making would depend on the nature of the complaint and which department could “most effectively” respond to residents’ needs. Of the 750,000 complaints received last year, about 30 per cent involved multiple departments, he said. Cheuk said his new role would reduce finger-pointing by departments claiming others had similar capacity to handle cases. “Under the new mechanism, situations where departments say they do not have the authority, knowledge or money to handle the complaint will no longer exist,” he said. He emphasised that such cases made up only a minority of all complaints, as the 1823 service was able to efficiently allocate cross-departmental complaints to the relevant authorities “99 per cent” of the time. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his annual policy address last week that a lead department would be designated to coordinate the handling of interdepartmental service requests and complaints to resolve them more efficiently. Departments will handle cases within their respective purview under the coordination of the lead department and report on case progress. Each department will assign a directorate officer to monitor its efficiency and effectiveness in handling service requests and complaints lodged by members of the public.

title: The View | Why a hawkish US Fed won’t derail Hong Kong’s property recovery
description: Higher interest rates may dampen momentum, but solid demand, improving sentiment and effective policy execution will prove more decisive.
content: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city’s de facto central bank, probably anticipated the rise in US interest rates last week. However, it is unlikely it foresaw the extent to which the Federal Reserve shifted in a hawkish direction. Even Fed watchers were surprised by the unanimous vote to increase borrowing costs and the unambiguous signal that the central bank plans to raise interest rates further in the coming months. While the HKMA, which moves in lockstep with the Fed to safeguard the local currency’s peg to the US dollar, followed its US counterpart by raising borrowing costs for the first time since 2023, the city’s commercial banks have yet to increase their prime lending rates. Given that the Fed’s move almost certainly marks the beginning of a tightening cycle, it is only a matter of time before mortgage rates in Hong Kong start to rise again. When Morgan Stanley called the bottom of Hong Kong’s housing market in June last year, it said the uncertain outlook for US monetary policy could “remain an overhang in the property market”. The question is whether the underpinnings of the recovery in the residential and commercial markets are strong enough to withstand higher interest rates. The Fed’s hawkish turn coincides with another policy headwind that contributed to a slowdown in housing prices and sales in the last few months: Beijing’s clampdown on outbound investment, which limits mainland buyers’ ability to fund property purchases in Hong Kong. Were investors and advisers too optimistic about the recovery? Not necessarily. First, the narrative around Hong Kong real estate was so bearish for so many years that any improvement in the performance and outlook for the market was bound to have an outsize impact on sentiment. Moreover, the speed and scale of the revival in the city’s capital markets since the beginning of last year have overshadowed the comparatively modest improvement in the fundamentals of the property market. While second-hand home values have risen 20 per cent since June 2025, they are still 15 per cent below the August 2021 peak. Furthermore, although commercial property transaction volumes this year have almost reached the level for last year as a whole, they are just 17 per cent of 2018 volumes, data from CBRE shows. Second, interest rates are just one of several determinants of the performance of real estate markets. More important factors include supply-demand dynamics, the liquidity and depth of investment markets, economic and geopolitical resilience, policy support and stability, the talent pool and the quality of infrastructure. Even though Hong Kong recorded one of the strongest increases in commercial property investment activity in the Asia-Pacific in the first half of this year, transaction volumes in Singapore were more than double those in Hong Kong. “Investor sentiment towards Hong Kong has materially improved,” said Tim Graham, global lead of international and strategic capital in JLL’s capital markets business. However, “the strength and depth of the Singapore market have been a bigger driver” of investment in the region. Even so, the reassertion of Hong Kong’s role as China’s global financial hub has been a crucial underpinning of the recovery in the property market. The influx of mainland Chinese capital and talent has proved a boon for the luxury residential, office and nascent student housing markets. In the second quarter of this year, Hong Kong was the second most actively traded market for sales of homes worth US$10 million or more among 12 leading residential markets around the world, data from Knight Frank shows. Furthermore, rents for Grade A offices in Central grew 12.7 per cent, the fastest rate among central business districts in leading cities in the Asia-Pacific. Third, the biggest challenge facing Hong Kong’s real estate industry in the coming years is policy delivery. The government’s first-ever five-year plan, released alongside its annual policy address on September 16, prioritises innovation as a new growth engine, putting the Northern Metropolis at the core of a growth strategy to create a new ecosystem spanning technology, education, talent, industrial policy and private capital. While the sweeping economic blueprint could spur demand for residential and commercial property, regulatory and infrastructure bottlenecks need to be overcome to attract residents, occupiers and investors to the region. Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services at CBRE in Hong Kong, said the acid test will be whether the plan can “attract real capital, whether the transport milestones hold, and whether the talent the university towns are designed to attract actually chooses to live and work in the Northern Metropolis”. The Fed’s hawkish pivot adds to the uncertainty over the strength of the recovery in Hong Kong’s property sector. Yet at least there is a recovery, and a strong one in parts of the market. A broader-based and durable upturn will require an improvement in fundamentals and effective policy support. The Fed is not the decisive factor.

title: Cargo ship slams into Chinese fishing boat in Singapore Strait
description: Dramatic footage shows the moment a Panama-flagged bulk carrier collided with a Chinese trawler in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes.
content: Footage of a cargo ship ploughing into a Chinese fishing boat in the Singapore Strait, sending seawater surging across the smaller vessel’s deck as its crew scrambled to hold on, has circulated widely online. The 229-metre-long (750-foot) bulk carrier First Margaux struck the Luqing Yuanyu 108, a 49-metre (160-foot) Chinese fishing vessel, at around 5pm on Thursday last week, according to ship-tracking data cited by The Maritime Executive. Both vessels had left anchorage near Singapore at roughly the same time that morning and entered the same westbound channel under the traffic separation scheme – a routing system designed to prevent collisions in one of the world’s busiest maritime choke points. Video that surfaced over the weekend, filmed from aboard the fishing boat, shows the cargo ship bearing down on the smaller vessel from behind before ploughing into its side. The impact spun the fishing boat around, with crew members seen clinging to railings as water poured onto the deck. No injuries were reported among the crew of either vessel and no pollution arose from the incident, said the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore on Tuesday. “The fishing vessel took on water during the incident but remained afloat and stable, with the crew taking measures to manage the situation on board,” the authority said. The vessel was towed to Raffles Reserved Anchorage for assessment, it added. Essential crew remained on board to support the tow and the Singapore Civil Defence Force helped transfer the other crew to shore. The port authority issued navigational safety broadcasts to keep other boats clear of the tow and escorted the vessel into port with a craft. It is investigating the incident. The Luqing Yuanyu 108 kept transmitting its automatic identification system signal after the collision and was still being tracked as of Sunday, indicating it survived the encounter and later reached a nearby berth, The Maritime Executive reported. First Margaux reportedly carried on westbound at a steady speed of 10 knots (18.5km/h) for roughly two hours before stopping, circling back and anchoring. The Japanese-owned, Chinese-managed bulk carrier was overtaking the fishing boat when its bow made contact, according to The Maritime Executive’s reconstruction, travelling up to three knots faster. Maritime analyst Sal Mercogliano suggested on social media that First Margaux might have been boxed in by a third vessel, another bulk carrier, leaving the fishing boat pincered between two larger ships. “One of the problems of ship collision videos is you only get one perspective,” he wrote, adding that the Singapore Strait “is one of the most complicated and busy traffic areas on the planet”. First Margaux is a three-year-old bulk carrier of about 80,000 deadweight tonnes, flagged in Panama and carrying a clean inspection record. The Panama Maritime Authority confirmed in a statement to local media that it had launched an investigation into the incident. The straits of Singapore and Malacca form one of the world’s busiest and most critical maritime trade corridors, carrying nearly 40 per cent of global trade and about a third of the world’s seaborne oil – making it the busiest corridor for crude oil and petroleum liquids by volume.

title: Cathay calls on Hong Kong to map out long-term sustainable fuel plan beyond 2030
description: Cathay Group CEO Ronald Lam says scalability remains challenge, notes SAF still accounts for ‘well under 1 per cent’ of global jet fuel use.
content: Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways has urged the government to develop a longer-term plan for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) beyond 2030, including mandatory targets and consistent policies to help scale up the industry and meet the city’s climate goals. The airline made the call after a mainland Chinese official on Monday proposed that authorities in the Greater Bay Area introduce more favourable policies, including subsidies, to boost sales of sustainable fuel. Cathay Group CEO Ronald Lam Siu-por said scalability remained the main challenge, noting that SAF accounted for “well under 1 per cent” of global jet fuel use. “No airline, producer, city or government could change that alone,” he said. “We need supply, demand, policy and finance to move together.” SAF is a renewable fuel made from materials such as used cooking oil and agricultural waste. It can reduce life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 80 per cent compared with conventional jet fuel. In the city’s first five-year plan, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu set a target for SAF to account for 1 to 3 per cent of fuel used on flights departing Hong Kong by 2030. Lam said Cathay Group was actively supporting the market through direct purchases – including Chinese-manufactured SAF – while investing in future supply chains and next-generation technologies. The company was also working with corporate and cargo customers to create demand through its corporate SAF programme and to help build a wider ecosystem through the Hong Kong Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition and partnerships with industry, universities and research institutions, he said. “The next step is to provide greater certainty,” Lam said. “Producers need confidence that demand will be there. Airlines need fuel that is available and affordable. Investors need clarity on the direction of policy. A well-designed policy can connect these needs.” Grace Cheung, Cathay Pacific’s general manager for sustainability, told the South China Morning Post on Monday that she hoped the government could have a clearer long-term strategy. “Policymakers need to give us what we call a longer-term road map, so that we as an airline can prepare accordingly,” she said. “For example, we could tell producers that the mandatory usage target is going to keep rising, so we might as well lock in multi-year procurement agreements in advance.” Cheung pointed to the European Union’s SAF road map to 2050 as a model that could help the industry plan over a longer time frame. She added that Hong Kong and mainland authorities should communicate to ensure policy consistency, and address whether SAF produced on the mainland would face customs and tax requirements. On ramping up the use of SAF, Cheung said Cathay would continue to support voluntary purchases through its corporate programme and the coalition but noted that mandatory usage requirements would be needed to drive scalability. She said Cathay’s SAF use stood at about 0.7 per cent in 2025 – a relatively high proportion given that the global average remained below 1 per cent – but added that further expansion would depend on market and policy developments. On the same day, Qu Yong, head of the energy division at the Guangzhou Development and Reform Commission, suggested that authorities in the Greater Bay Area – which encompasses Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in neighbouring Guangdong province – introduce financial subsidies and policy incentives to convert SAF production capacity into actual sales. Qu observed that while expanding production capacity was straightforward, converting that potential into active output, sales and practical application required greater effort. Qu added that the government should promote research and the recognition of standards to broaden the range of eligible feedstocks beyond used cooking oil.

title: Despite stock stress, CATL likely to retain EV battery dominance in China, analysts say
description: CATL’s tech edge and brand safeguard its EV battery lead, though carmakers are seeking alternative suppliers.
content: Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited’s (CATL) dominance in the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) market is unlikely to slump over the coming year given its brand recognition and edge in technology, analysts said, though its shares have already tumbled amid the battle with profit-squeezed EV makers. Chinese carmakers have been doubling down on efforts in recent weeks to reduce their reliance on CATL – in September, Xiaomi and Li Auto highlighted their partnership with tier-two battery manufacturers, including CALB Group, while Xpeng planned to make in-house battery packs this year. Amid concerns about a potential loss of market share, CATL’s Shenzhen-listed shares have lost 25.7 per cent since mid-August and 36.5 per cent from their all-time high seen in early May. On Monday, the equities of the Fujian-based firm fell by a further 1.6 per cent in Shenzhen and 0.59 per cent in Hong Kong. The diversification away from CATL, which commanded over 41 per cent of the Chinese EV battery market in August, comes as the battery giant’s net profit outstripped that of mainland carmakers, which have been caught in a domestic price war since last year. In August, CATL led the EV battery market in China, followed by BYD at 21 per cent, CALB at 6.51 per cent, EVE Energy at 5.95 per cent and Gotion High-Tech at 5.87 per cent, data from CABIA showed. The profitability gap, which is unusual in the industry, had motivated carmakers to cultivate smaller battery makers, said Yale Zhang, managing director at the consultancy Automotive Foresight in Shanghai. “But it will take some time – say, a year or two – before we can see whether this trend will actually unfold as planned by the carmakers,” said Zhang. CATL rivals needed to deliver on the technology and quality of their products and win over consumers, while maintaining a low pricing strategy, Zhang noted. Otherwise, CATL would largely maintain its market share, he added. Notably, CALB’s batteries received some market attention in July after one of its models, commonly used in ride-hailing vehicles, was found to have warped into the shape of a banana following about two years of use. Kenny Ng Lai-yin, a strategist at Everbright Securities International, said he believed CATL’s stock was oversold, as the diversification strategy had not caused any loss in the battery giant’s market share or earnings. Ng also expected CATL’s market share to remain steady for the foreseeable future, as the EV battery industry had high barriers regarding capital and technological investment and talent accumulation. “Supply-chain diversification by some Chinese carmakers is unlikely to threaten CATL’s global leadership, given its diversified customer base, technology edge, and strong position in the faster-growing overseas EV battery and [energy storage system] markets,” said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. Yang added that it is unlikely for carmakers targeting the premium segment to exclude CATL, given its strong consumer brand recognition built through sustained marketing efforts.

title: China boosts crude oil, LNG imports from Canada as Ottawa-Washington relations sour
description: China’s imports of Russian energy products also rise sharply as Beijing diversifies its energy supplies.
content: China sharply increased its imports of crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Canada in August amid an escalating trade dispute between Ottawa and Washington. The country’s imports of Russian energy products also rose sharply last month, as geopolitical risks including war in Iran accelerated Beijing’s efforts to diversify its energy supplies. Customs data released on Sunday showed that the volume of China’s crude oil imports from Canada rose nearly 35 per cent year on year in August, while their value increased 64 per cent to US$782.3 million. That contrasted with a nearly 23 per cent year-on-year decline in China’s overall crude oil imports during the month. With the months-long war around the Persian Gulf disrupting regional oil shipments, China’s crude imports from six Middle Eastern countries, including Saudi Arabia, fell 45.5 per cent last month from a year earlier. Meanwhile, China’s imports of Canadian LNG surged 227 per cent by volume year on year, while the value of sulphur imports jumped 398 per cent, despite the volume rising by less than a fifth. Although overall China-Canada trade grew only modestly in August, China’s imports from Canada were increasingly driven by energy commodities, particularly those whose global supplies have been disrupted by the Persian Gulf conflict. The data came after US-Canada trade talks collapsed in late August, prompting US President Donald Trump to impose 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods. Ottawa retaliated with tariffs of between 15 and 50 per cent on more than 700 US products, leaving the two neighbours locked in an escalating trade war. By contrast, China-Canada relations have stabilised since the start of the year following years of diplomatic and trade tensions. The two sides agreed in January to lower tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and Canadian canola and other agricultural products while expanding cooperation in energy and trade. Canada is the emerging partner Xu Tianchen, Economist Intelligence Unit “China is an opportunistic player in the global oil market, buying when prices fall and drawing on its stockpiles when they rise,” said Xu Tianchen, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. Beijing’s systematic expansion of its oil reserves in recent years had also strengthened its ability to withstand elevated prices, he added. Xu said China used a brief period of US-Iran detente in late June and early July to purchase more oil, with those shipments arriving in August and lifting imports from the previous month. But the window quickly closed as tensions in the Middle East escalated again, probably causing Chinese purchases to fall afterwards, Xu said. Russia remains one of China’s largest energy suppliers, although Beijing’s diversification strategy limits how much it can increase its reliance on Russian imports. “Canada is the emerging partner,” Xu said. “Improvement in diplomatic ties under [Canadian Prime Minister Mark] Carney is creating trade opportunities between the two countries, including in oil.” Xu added that the outlook for China-Canada trade from 2026 to 2028 was “quite rosy”, as Ottawa would seek alternatives following its falling out with Washington while Beijing would diversify its commodity supplies. However, he cautioned that bilateral trade remained closely tied to political cycles in China and Canada, as well as developments in the US. The earlier deals between Beijing and Ottawa have also prompted China to step up purchases of products including canola oil, with import volume from Canada rising nearly 42 per cent year on year in August. The value of China’s crude oil imports from Canada also increased 40.2 per cent in the first eight months of the year. Elsewhere, war-related disruptions to energy supplies are accelerating economic and trade flows between Beijing and Moscow. China’s imports from and exports to Russia both grew by around 40 per cent last month. Energy products were the main driver of import growth. China’s crude oil imports from its northern neighbour rose 41 per cent year on year by volume in August, while its purchase volume of Russian LNG increased 43 per cent. China also continued to increase its overall coal purchases during the month, extending an earlier trend towards greater energy diversification amid elevated crude oil prices.

title: Some of China’s 11,000 mega bridges could be at risk from small drones: study
description: Chinese researchers simulate attacks on a typical suspension bridge and find a precisely targeted small strike could trigger collapse.
content: Scientists in China have simulated a drone attack on one of the country’s major suspension bridges to determine the vulnerability of key transport hubs to modern warfare tactics. The researchers found that a drone carrying just 30kg (66lbs) of TNT could trigger a bridge collapse if it detonated within inches of the main suspension cable at the point where it meets a support tower. The targeted bridge strikes that have featured in Russia’s war on Ukraine show that warfare has shifted from mass firepower to precision strikes, turning once hard-to-reach structures into prime targets, they said. “These events starkly reveal the extreme vulnerability of modern bridges to unconventional explosive attacks,” the team wrote in a paper published in the September issue of the Chinese-language Journal of Railway Science and Engineering. “Conducting a systematic study on the damage mechanisms and blast resistance of suspension bridges subjected to precision unmanned aerial vehicle-delivered explosive attacks holds urgent engineering significance and strategic value for national defence.” Earth-anchored suspension bridges feature a roadway that is hung from massive cables supported by pylon towers and secured by anchorages at either end. The researchers, from Southwest Jiaotong University and the China Railway Major Bridge Reconnaissance & Design Institute Company, simulated attacks on a suspension structure with a main span of 538 metres (1,765 feet). The dimensions matched the Dimuhe River Bridge in southwestern China’s Guizhou province, which is frequently used in Chinese engineering papers as a simulation benchmark. China has more bridges than any other country, including most of the world’s largest, longest and highest overpasses. Among them are more than 11,000 “super-large” or mega structures, according to transport ministry data. Record-breaking bridges include the highest on Earth, which crosses Huajiang Canyon, also in Guizhou, as well as the Zhangjinggao Yangtze River Bridge in eastern Jiangsu province, which will be the longest suspension structure in the world when completed. The study was prompted by the continuing Russian war on Ukraine, which in 2022 saw the Ukrainian military strike Antonovsky Bridge – the main crossing over the Dnieper River in the Kherson region – that Russia was using to transport supplies and troops. Ukraine’s military has also launched several attacks on the Crimean Bridge, which has served as a vital part of Russian military logistics since the start of Moscow’s invasion in late February 2022. The team noted that while early research established safety thresholds for individual bridge components, studies on complete suspension bridge systems remained limited and lagged behind modern warfare threats like drone strikes. To find out how much damage drone blasts could have on a suspension bridge, the team created a model that included the deck, main cables, hangers and pylon towers, according to the paper. The study focused on the potential blast impact on the bridge’s high-altitude components, specifically the main cables and support towers rather than the bridge deck, it said. The researchers modelled a 50kg TNT blast – equivalent to the warhead payload carried by a typical medium-sized drone – at a distance of 20cm (8 inches) from key structural areas. A blast at such close range targeting a cable near a support tower triggered a domino effect of snapping cables, flipping the deck and causing the bridge to collapse, according to the paper. This showed that a near-field explosion of this magnitude “poses a catastrophic threat to the suspension bridge”, it said. The team also modelled smaller explosive charges and found that even low-yield blasts could trigger a collapse if they detonated at close range, including 30-40kg of TNT if it exploded 20cm away from the main cable anchorage. A drone armed with just 5kg TNT would also be capable of severing a main cable if it exploded on contact with the tower junction, according to the study. The researchers noted that “precision contact capability warrants greater defensive attention than merely increasing the explosive yield”. Because an explosion at the point where the suspension cables are anchored to the tower could trigger a chain reaction, the team identified this area as the critical vulnerability against realistic drone threats. “Defence strategies against realistic drone threats should prioritise protecting the main cable anchorage zones and mitigate risks associated with close-range or contact threats,” the researchers wrote. According to the paper, an increase in cable dimensions could help to mitigate blast damage, though this measure was more suited to the design of new bridges. For existing bridges, retrofitting main cables with a high-density polythene protective sheath offered a more practical solution to reduce damage, it said. The team also simulated extreme blasts, ranging from 300kg to 500kg of TNT – far beyond the payload capacity of a single drone – to serve as an upper-bound scenario for compound attacks. Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: Hong Kong Ballet to move to city’s first dedicated dance venue in 2027
description: Group says move to Dancehouse at WestK Performing Arts Centre allows for more than 40 per cent increase in performance weeks annually.
content: Hong Kong Ballet will relocate to the city’s first dedicated dance art venue for at least five years, starting in April 2027, according to the institution and the West Kowloon Cultural District (WKCD). The move to the “Dancehouse” at the soon-to-be-finished WestK Performing Arts Centre will follow the ballet company’s departure from its base of 16 years at the government-run Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui. An announcement last December that the city’s flagship ballet company would be departing the Cultural Centre prompted concerns that the group would be left without an appropriate venue. In an interview with the South China Morning Post ahead of the announcement, Hong Kong Ballet artistic director Septime Webre expressed relief at being able to finally reveal the news of the move. In his annual policy address last week, city leader John Lee Ka-chiu described the Dancehouse as “the first dedicated venue for dance art in Hong Kong” and said it was “built to the highest international standards”. Webre said the new venue would allow the group to increase its number of performance weeks annually by more than 40 per cent, from seven to 10. He added that the rise could amplify the company’s impact. “That’s the main thing we exist to do – to perform at an excellent international level,” he said, adding that the ballet company and the WKCD shared a synergy that could take Hong Kong dance to a higher international level. Webre likened the cultural district’s importance to dance at an international level to the way its contemporary art museum M+ had put Hong Kong on the map in the visual arts world, becoming “an important part of the international discourse” at events such as Art Basel and the Venice Biennale. “Because of their international reach, by extension, it puts an international spotlight on us,” he said, adding the move could enhance Hong Kong Ballet’s existing international tour programme. He noted the dance company had already undertaken nine trips in the past 18 months, including two visits to New York. Webre said the “single biggest and most important change” was the enhanced access to the 1,450-seat grand theatre, the biggest of the three at the performing arts centre, as the company’s primary performance venue, which would enable the group to host more shows. For rehearsals, the company will be based at the centre’s Dancehouse. The centre will have 1,000 square metres of space dedicated to the company in total, including a dedicated physiotherapy room for dancers and more spacious changing and shower rooms. Webre noted that performers had no privacy for physiotherapy in the past, with treatment previously conducted in a corner during rehearsals. He added that the company would have access to three studios 24 hours a day and could also book the other five. He described the extra amenities as an “upgrade to our life”, as the company was required to leave the Cultural Centre after 6pm on weekdays and had no access to its facilities on weekends. Paul Tam Siu-man, executive director of the cultural district’s performing arts division, also highlighted that all the studios had floor-to-ceiling windows, similar to those at the Oslo Opera House, noting they were previously unavailable to the company. Tam stressed that not only did the glass panels allow natural light into the studios, which was very important for dancers’ circadian rhythms and well-being, but they also enabled visitors to see performers’ creative process as they walked into the district from the direction of Kowloon MTR station. He pointed out that the collaboration was not just a tenancy, with the ballet company being “structurally hard-wired into our modus operandi” as part of a strategic, creative and learning community partnership with the centre. “We will co-invest in select future productions, including [a Bruce Lee-inspired show], and co-curate learning and participation programmes with the ballet company,” Tam said. The late Hong Kong kung fu legend will serve as the inspiration for the company’s opening gala production at the centre. Tam elaborated on “the limitless potential” of the collaboration, which ranged from co-curating merchandise designs to seeking sponsorships together and promoting international collaboration. The WKCD and Hong Kong Ballet were currently planning programmes for the next three to five years, with their sights set on a long-term partnership, he said. The arts hub would work with other dance companies and artists on a project-by-project basis. Tam said the arts hub had struck deals with different groups in mainland China, France and the UK, including Sadler’s Wells and Studio Wayne McGregor, “and I would love to talk to Hong Kong Ballet to see how we can utilise these kinds of international relations”. “The [memorandums of understanding] we signed are not just for ourselves. They’re for any partners that we have … Hopefully this is going to be a new [collaboration] model. I think Heidi is a model inventor,” Tam said, referring to Heidi Lee Yik-shuen, executive director of Hong Kong Ballet. Lee said the collaboration was not just about access to new hardware, as it was no easy feat for any company to attract audiences in the thousands to pack a theatre for 10 weeks every year. “A new venue also needs high-quality content to brand it, to make a strong identity, just like the David H Koch Theatre of the Lincoln Centre is the New York City Ballet company’s base,” she added.

title: Chinese President Xi Jinping will pay state visit to US this week, Beijing confirms
description: Rare airport welcome by Donald Trump will precede talks on trade, tech and other areas of friction during second in-person summit of 2026.
content: Chinese leader Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, Beijing’s foreign ministry has confirmed. “At the invitation of President of the United States of America Donald J. Trump, President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from September 23 to 25,” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in an official statement on Monday. The trip – Xi’s first state visit to Washington since 2015 – will also mark his second face-to-face meeting this year with Trump, as the world’s top two economies seek to stabilise a relationship tested by trade, technology and national security disputes. According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun, Xi will “have an in-depth exchange of views with Trump on major issues concerning bilateral ties and world peace and developments”. “The exchange of visits by the two presidents within the span of half a year will mark a milestone of historic significance,” Guo said at a regular press briefing on Monday, stressing the importance of head-of-state diplomacy in China-US relations. He also highlighted Beijing’s pledge to boost dialogue with Washington under a framework of “constructive strategic stability” to manage differences and bolster global peace and prosperity. Xi and Trump last met in Beijing in May, a summit that ended with a pledge to pursue a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”. In the United States this week, the two leaders are expected to discuss trade, technology and other areas of friction, with artificial intelligence (AI) likely to be among the top issues on the agenda. In a rare presidential gesture, Trump will personally greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday ahead of a two-day summit in Washington, the US has confirmed. The state visit begins on Thursday with a State Floor arrival ceremony at the White House and a Rose Garden military review, followed by sit-down talks. The East Room state dinner later will be attended by top US executives including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Apple chief Tim Cook and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk, Huang and Cook were among more than a dozen top American executives who accompanied Trump on his May 13-15 state visit to China. On Friday, Trump will host Xi for a private White House tea followed by a tour of the National Archives before the Chinese leader departs. The South China Morning Post reported earlier this month that Beijing was considering sending a group of top executives from the technology, electric vehicle and aerospace sectors to accompany Xi on his visit to Washington. The selection was being modelled on the US business delegation that accompanied Trump to Beijing in May, sources told the SCMP. One source familiar with the planning said both sides were treating every aspect of the visit as a matter of reciprocity – including the composition of the business delegation. On Sunday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng met in New York for a final round of discussions, agreeing to establish a dialogue on artificial intelligence and to put into operation a bilateral trade body. Both sides agreed in May to launch an intergovernmental dialogue focused on AI safety and governance, though no formal talks on this track have been publicly confirmed. Washington accuses Chinese companies of obtaining advanced AI capabilities through the unauthorised extraction of US models and has been closely watching how Chinese firms gain access to advanced chips. Beijing has rejected the allegations as groundless, warning that any attempt to use such claims to curb China’s technological development or constrain its AI sector could trigger retaliation. The AI friction comes as both sides try to preserve a fragile trade truce struck after Trump and Xi met in Busan, South Korea, last year. A fresh wave of economic disputes is also testing relations. In recent months, Washington has expanded its blacklist targeting alleged forced labour in China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, banned Chinese robotics and power inverters, and sanctioned Chinese firms doing business with Iran – prompting swift retaliatory sanctions from Beijing. Last month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Washington to help “remove interference and overcome obstacles” to high-level exchanges during a meeting with US ambassador David Perdue in Beijing. And in a phone call with US counterpart Marco Rubio last week, Wang said that the two sides should “send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive relationship of strategic stability and jointly promoting world peace and development” – echoing the core outcome of the May presidential summit. Ahead of his meeting with Trump, Xi has sought to reinforce China’s diplomatic position through a series of international engagements, most recently at the Brics summit in New Delhi. Addressing the summit on September 12, Xi called for deeper cooperation on AI and indirectly criticised US policies as he promoted China’s vision of a more inclusive approach to global governance. Trump and Xi could meet in person two more times this year – at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit in south China’s Shenzhen in November and the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December.

title: Neither the US nor China can win the AI race alone, BofA analyst says
description: American power grid limits and China’s reliance on overseas chips mean both nations must lean on international cooperation.
content: Neither Beijing nor Washington can win the race for artificial intelligence dominance without relying on other countries, a Bank of America analyst said ahead of this week’s high-stakes bilateral summit, citing deeply entangled global tech supply chains. While China’s advantages had emerged in areas like power grids and manufacturing equipment, the country remained reliant on overseas suppliers for advanced chips, memory and some high-end materials, said Matty Zhao, co-head of China equity at Bank of America in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Monday. The US faced different constraints, including an ageing power grid averaging 30 to 40 years old, compared with 15 to 20 years old in China, Zhao said. Across the US, data centres have fuelled widespread political and community pushback over fears of surging power costs. While power could constrain US growth, China still needed “breakthroughs” in high-end chips, Zhao said. “Various countries have various limitations,” she added. “This race cannot be done by one country,” Zhao told SCMP on the sidelines of the BofA 2026 Asia-Pacific Conference in Hong Kong. The US and China would still need to cooperate with other countries, she said, pointing to South Korea’s strength in memory chips and Japan’s dominance in high-end materials like copper foil – a major material used in the production of printed circuit boards – and manufacturing equipment. “There will be competition and cooperation for sure,” Zhao added. Zhao’s comments come ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s meeting with US President Donald Trump in Washington on Thursday, where AI was expected to feature alongside trade and other geopolitical issues. Setting the stage for the summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng on Sunday agreed to set up a dialogue on AI and launch a bilateral trade body after eight hours of talks in New York. “We had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI,” Bessent said. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who also attended, said the initiatives were aimed at “helping President Trump and President Xi continue their relationship” and laying the groundwork for a successful summit on Thursday. The Chinese delegation did not speak to the media. The diplomatic push comes amid deepening technological distrust between the world’s two leading AI powers. Washington has repeatedly accused Chinese developers of distilling capabilities from leading US models, while Beijing has criticised recent US calls to pace frontier AI development as potentially entrenching American dominance. Amid talk of greater cooperation, the two countries have also sought to reduce reliance on each other for critical technologies. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has urged the US government to strengthen chip export controls on China, while China has pushed domestic tech firms to adopt home-grown semiconductors. Yet the infrastructure required to develop and deploy powerful AI systems remained deeply globalised, complicating efforts by either country to become technologically self-sufficient, BofA’s Zhao said. China has become a major global supplier of AI infrastructure, particularly power equipment and energy storage systems. Its exports of electrical transformers – equipment used to regulate voltage across power grids – rose about 30 per cent last year and had grown at a similar pace so far this year, Zhao said. The country shipped a record 64.6 billion yuan (US$9.6 billion) worth of transformers in 2025, according to data published earlier this year. But China remains dependent on foreign suppliers for parts of the AI supply chain, including specialised Japanese machinery and materials, as well as advanced chips and some optical technologies from the US and elsewhere.

title: Once the world’s most-visited city, Hong Kong now converts hotels into student dorms
description: As the city positions itself as a global education hub, hotels are being converted into premises for student occupation.
content: Late last month, an open tender for Hotel Cozi Harbour View in Kwun Tong was announced, with interested parties given until October 15 to submit bids. The 598-room hotel, located in Hong Kong’s eastern Kowloon Peninsula, a former industrial area, was taken over by Nanyang Commercial Bank for HK$1.87 billion (US$238.4 million) in 2025, with the bank now looking to dispose of the asset to the highest bidder. Just a week after the announcement of the tender, Nina Hospitality, one of the largest hotel operators in Hong Kong, unveiled the completion of the HK$120 million (US$15.3 million) renovation at Nina Hotel Island South. The refurbishment transformed the hotel’s lobby and guestrooms and launched both balcony suites and family rooms. It is the second major refurbishment project of the hospitality arm of private developer Chinachem Group, following the renovation of guest rooms at its flagship Nina Hotel Tsuen Wan West, completed in 2024. The renovation of Tsuen Wan’s lobbies are still under way, with the group earmarking HK$225 million for the project, part of Nina Hospitality’s rebranding announced in 2021. The two investment strategies illustrate contrasting outlooks for Hong Kong’s hotel industry. The city consistently held the crown as the world’s most-visited city before 2019, according to consultancy Euromonitor International. With 29.26 million overnight visitor arrivals in 2018, Hong Kong’s hotels saw their average occupancy rate increase by 2 percentage points to 91 per cent that year, according to the Tourism Commission. In 2025, Hong Kong saw 23.19 million overnight visitor arrivals, according to official data, still 20 per cent below their 2018 peak. The average hotel room occupancy rate, meanwhile, was at 87 per cent. It is no surprise that with higher financing costs, brought about by an increase in interest rates, many asset owners found the hotel business challenging. Those who were unable to service debts had to dispose of their assets, either by selling them at huge discounts or facing asset liquidation by their creditors, recent cases have shown. Many of these hotels sold were acquired by new owners for conversion into student accommodation. So far this year, Hong Kong has recorded HK$8.2 billion worth of hotel property deals involving about 2,550 rooms, according to Colliers. Most of these transactions were for student accommodation conversions, and some were a hybrid of co-living – targeted towards students or young professionals – and hotel offerings, the property consultancy added. With the government’s bid to turn Hong Kong into a global education hub, JLL estimated that the city faced a shortfall of more than 140,000 student beds by the 2029-2030 school year. “For investors, the sector presents a compelling opportunity underpinned by resilient demand and income visibility that is largely insulated from broader real estate market cycles,” said Cathie Chung, senior director of research at JLL Hong Kong. For Nina Hospitality, refurbishing its hotels was a way to prepare for higher accommodation demand from tourists, managing director Simon Manning said. “While recovery is slower than pre-pandemic levels, we are encouraged by the government’s initiatives such as mega-events, sports-related programmes and efforts to attract new markets, which are driving positive momentum,” Manning said. “By upgrading our hotels and services, we ensure Nina Hospitality is optimally positioned to capture demand and exceed guest expectations as tourism continues to strengthen.” Since the 50,000-seat Kai Tak Stadium in Kowloon opened in March last year, the mammoth venue had “quickly emerged as one of Asia’s leading event venues and top three internationally in terms of ticket sales in its first year,” according to Colliers.
