In the first half of the year, about 1.75 million visitors were drawn to more than 130 events in Hong Kong, generating around HK$5.8 billion in spending and contributing HK$3.3 billion to the economy, according to Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po. As the city also books global performers amid a growing demand for student accommodation, the hotel property industry was likely to see more hotel conversions and also investment in existing and new hotels, analysts said. In particular, hotels in the higher market segment could see more capital deployment to refresh and improve their amenities, while well-priced midscale assets could be primed for student accommodation conversions, said Shaman Chellaram, senior director for hotel advisory and valuation and advisory services at Colliers. “Each segment caters to different demand drivers and end users with very distinct operating and business models,” Chellaram said. Location might determine whether a hotel was suitable for a student dormitory asset or a tourist accommodation, said Cleavon Tan, senior vice-president of hotels and hospitality group at JLL Hong Kong. “Hotels in established tourism and business districts, with strong demand drivers, can offer a compelling case for continued hotel use and further investment,” Tan said. “For properties outside these core locations, particularly where hotel performance is weaker but access to universities and public transport is good, student accommodation may offer a more attractive use. A location that is less competitive for tourists can still work well for students.”

title: Why China is weighing into the debate on how to respond to shrinking coastlines
description: Rising sea levels are not an existential threat to China, but their impact on international law could have a knock-on effect in other areas.
content: For low-lying Pacific island states such as Tuvalu and Kiribati, rising sea levels are not just an existential crisis but also one that calls into question the very foundations of statehood. At the heart of this lies a contentious question: should maritime boundaries shift with changing coastlines, or should they be frozen in place? The answer carries profound implications not only for the survival of vulnerable islands but also for the rest of the world. Some analysts have argued that China should position itself as both a legal advocate and technical partner for Pacific nations to offer tangible support – such as surveying expertise, coastal protection technology and advocacy for fixed maritime boundaries. They said such support could not only help vulnerable states survive but could also advance Beijing’s strategic interests and align with its South China Sea claims. Projections from Nasa in 2024 showed that sea levels in the Pacific would rise by an average of 15cm (6 inches) over the next three decades. Beyond the immediate physical threat, shrinking coastlines also pose a fundamental challenge to the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). Maritime zones are measured from coastal baselines tied to the physical low-water line. These include territorial seas, which extend 12 nautical miles (22km) from the coast, and exclusive economic zones, which can cover 200 nautical miles. Such zones grant coastal states exclusive sovereign rights to explore, exploit and manage natural resources ranging from fish stocks to minerals and offshore energy. However, under Unclos, a land feature must be able to “sustain human habitation or economic life of its own” to have an exclusive economic zone. If rising seas severely undermine an island’s freshwater supplies, habitability or capacity to sustain an economic life of its own, this could raise questions about how the feature should be classified under Article 121 of Unclos, according to Chen Yitong, an associate professor of international law at the Ocean University of China. “This could affect the maritime entitlements generated by the feature and may also have implications for baselines or for pending maritime delimitation where the feature is relevant,” Chen said. “It should not, however, be taken to mean that maritime boundaries already established by treaty or other applicable international legal means can be reopened.” The legal dimension “The major legal obstacle [to keeping existing boundaries] is an adjustment of the long-standing legal rule that baselines are ambulatory, which means they can move and be adjusted over time,” said Donald Rothwell, a professor of international law at the Australian National University. “That rule is reflected in state practice and not in the precise rules of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.” The fallout from discussions about how rising sea levels should be reflected in maritime law reaches far beyond the South Pacific. “If a coastal country claims its features are full-fledged islands that generate full maritime rights, talks on rising sea levels protect and maintain those features’ surrounding zones and maritime rights will make a significant difference on their claims,” said Chen Chen-Ju, a professor specialising in the law of the sea at National Chengchi University in Taiwan. Beijing claims sovereignty over almost all islands and reefs in the South China Sea, as well as rights to the adjacent waters. Its claims overlap with those of Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam. In a formal 2016 statement that claimed sovereignty over the Pratas, Paracel, Spratly and Zhongsha islands, Beijing said this also covered territorial seas, exclusive economic zones and the continental shelf, as well as historic rights across the waterway. Chen from the National Chengchi University warned that rising sea levels could see countries losing territory, which raised fundamental questions over statehood as well as maritime boundaries. She added that a report from the International Law Commission last year said these aspects and the question of climate refugees were all “inextricably linked”. As a result, “the legal response tends towards either offering contemporary interpretations of existing international instruments and rules, or formulating dedicated legal frameworks and mechanisms tailored to climate-related sea-level rise”, she said. An emerging consensus Faced with an existential risk, Pacific island states have already demanded that their statehood, established baselines and maritime zones should remain perpetual regardless of physical changes. “There are a variety of processes [for freezing baselines]. One is to modify the convention, but this will be diplomatically and politically challenging,” Rothwell said. “The other is through the development and evolution of state practice and its wide-ranging acceptance by states throughout the international community. There is evidence that this is occurring.” The international consensus has begun leaning in their favour, with the International Law Commission recommending that states should not be obliged to update the baselines deposited with the UN even if there are physical changes. The UN is also planning a high-level meeting on rising sea levels on Thursday. China’s role Chen at Ocean University said Pacific nations must continue surveying and officially depositing and publishing their baselines and maritime boundaries under Unclos requirements, while broader and more consistent state practice would also help to consolidate the emerging legal approach. She argued that China could support these efforts through practical, demand-driven cooperation. “Beyond financial assistance, China can help island nations conduct maritime surveying, verify coordinates for UN deposit and support domestic ocean legislation and law capacity-building, while integrating coastal protection and climate monitoring with protection for affected populations,” Chen said. She added that China needed to ensure developing countries had a full say in rule-making, while “systematically documenting and articulating its own practices” in sea-level monitoring, coastal protection and maritime surveying – so that they can be properly understood and taken into account in the international legal process. “Active engagement in international lawmaking, supported by scientific evidence, clearly articulated state practice and concrete legal proposals, is necessary if China’s interests and perspectives are to be properly reflected in emerging rules.” Beijing has already laid the groundwork for this role. Last year, it pledged to combat rising sea levels through infrastructure upgrades and disaster early-warning systems, as well as expanding cooperation in coastal restoration and sustainable fisheries. Chen said supporting Pacific island states over the issue of maritime boundaries aligned with a wider interest shared by coastal states, including China: preventing climate-related physical change from automatically producing an additional loss in law. “Maritime boundaries established by treaties or other international mechanisms must remain stable and final,” she said. “The underlying principle is that physical harm caused by climate change should not automatically be converted into a loss of existing lawful maritime entitlements.” Historic rights Diplomatic hurdles nevertheless persist. China’s UN representatives have suggested that legal debates on rising sea levels should incorporate the concept of “historic rights” alongside baseline stability. “Rules in customary international law concerning historic waters, historic title, and historic rights are equally important foundations for asserting a nation’s maritime entitlements,” Wang Chen, a Chinese representative at the UN, told a meeting to discuss the issue last October. “The concept also provides legal support for impacted nations seeking to preserve maritime areas and rights. “China notes that useful discussions on the issue of historic waters were held but not reflected in the final report [by the International Law Commission], over which China expresses its concern.” Chen from National Chengchi University said: “When China raises the issue of historic rights when discussing sea-level rise, other nations quickly associate it with its historic claims in the South China Sea, which make them wary due to recent maritime frictions.” Common interests Nations threatened by climate change know that waiting for legal recognition alone may not be enough to preserve their existence. Some are already seeking immediate guarantees of their statehood. In the first agreement of its kind, in 2024 Tuvalu and Australia signed the Falepili Union Treaty, which guarantees Tuvalu’s statehood and maritime rights even if submerged, and opened the door to permanent migration to Australia. Meanwhile, Rothwell said major powers had shown rare convergence on interpreting maritime law to accommodate rising sea levels. Chen from Ocean University said Beijing need not rule out issue-specific cooperation with other-interested countries, as they shared mutual interests in technical standards for baseline coordinates, navigational safety, hydrographic surveying and legal capacity-building. “The key is adhering to transparent cooperation led by island states’ needs and priorities, without attaching political conditions. In this way, China is not pitching a competing framework against other powers but offering a public good that island states can put into use and that can be woven into global rules.” “Pacific island states should be treated as co-designers of the relevant rules, not merely as aid recipients or as states expected to choose between major powers,” Chen added. Meanwhile, climate-threatened nations know that legal recognition alone cannot preserve their heritage. In 2022, Tuvalu launched the world’s first digital nation project, using 3D lidar (light detection and range) scanning to build a virtual replica of the country.

title: Easy access to family guns fuels Philippine school shootings
description: Three fatal attacks since June have been traced back to state-linked weapons, exposing fatal flaws in official gun control.
content: The Philippines has suffered three deadly school shootings since June. In each case, at least one weapon belonged to a relative working in government or law enforcement, whether as an official service issue or a privately licensed firearm. On Friday, a student at Banga National High School in South Cotabato province shot dead two classmates, wounded several others and then killed himself. He reportedly used the licensed firearm of his father, who works in the Education Department’s risk reduction unit. Last month, a student at the privately run Ateneo de Zamboanga University’s junior high school live-streamed the attack, killing a fellow student before turning the gun on himself. The service-issued firearm recovered from the scene belonged to the student’s father, a customs official. And in June, two teenagers aged 14 and 15 killed three students at San Jose National High School in Tacloban, Leyte province, injuring many others. One of the firearms used in the attack belonged to a suspect’s aunt, who works in the police. The problem of children gaining access to these guns pointed to a “very serious failure of responsibility inside the home” and within the institutions issuing the weapons, said Raihan A. Yusoph, a conflict resolution researcher and assistant professor of history at Mindanao State University. Yusoph said the string of recent incidents reflected an “apparent lack of institutional learning”, arguing that the Tacloban shooting should have triggered an immediate cross-agency review of service firearms kept at home. Friday’s attack “showed that the risk also extends to privately licensed firearms in the homes of public officials”, he said, adding that authorities had been treating “each tragedy as an isolated incident instead of recognising a recurring access problem”. He called for stricter compliance measures to be undertaken such as regular firearm inventories, documented authorisation for take-home possession and independent, public reviews carried out whenever a service weapon was lost. “Otherwise, attention will fade, individual personnel may be blamed, and the institutional weaknesses that allowed the firearm to escape official custody will remain unchanged,” Yusoph said. Violent backdrop Permissive gun laws and a long history of internal armed conflicts against groups spanning communist rebels to Muslim separatists provided the backdrop to the recent violence, said Georgi Engelbrecht, a senior analyst for the International Crisis Group. He cited his own work in the southern Philippine region of Bangsamoro, which found that firearm availability had fuelled clan-related violence that sometimes spilled over into wider society. Philippine society had become further desensitised to violent imagery under former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose war on drugs, anti-communist campaigns and siege of Marawi in 2017 meant “blood and violence were often on television screens and sometimes not considered as an exception any more”, Engelbrecht said. He added that post-conflict trauma was widespread in many parts of the southern Philippines, where schools and rural communities often struggled to provide mental health support. “Teachers and school workers may not always be well equipped to address these needs,” Engelbrecht said. “Sometimes also there are not simply enough people.” Yusoph, who has studied firearm proliferation in the southern Philippines, said gun culture there had grown out of a long history of armed resistance, clan conflict and inconsistent state protection – not any inherent local disposition towards violence. “Firearms do not create every conflict. They change what a conflict can become,” Yusoph said. “A grievance, psychological crisis, experience of bullying or violent fantasy becomes far more dangerous when a weapon is within reach.” Officials have also examined the shooters’ online activity for evidence of radicalisation. Authorities launched investigations into platforms including Roblox after the Tacloban attack, while the suspect in Friday’s shooting reportedly engaged with “true crime” subcultures and was a heavy user of the so-called dark web, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said on Saturday. There was a degree of “mimetic violence” in such attacks, said security analyst Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow at Verve Research who has researched online extremism in Southeast Asia. She cited premeditation and a desire for infamy as factors linking the shootings, as well as the suspects borrowing and co-opting elements from online subcultures. Yusoph agreed, noting that some attackers would “adopt political or religious language to give a larger meaning to personal grievances”, while the motivation of others could be “invisible to investigators” until after the fact. “Separate attacks can still emerge from a common environment that normalises violence, rewards notoriety, circulates extremist narratives and makes weapons accessible,” he said, adding that the real crisis was the authorities’ “repeated failure to identify escalating threats, control access to weapons, intervene before grievances become violent and build public confidence in institutions”. Audits and intervention Much more needs to be done, according to Yusoph, who is calling for an immediate audit of service firearms kept in private residences by police and other armed government personnel. He also wants to see centralised national databases tracking school violence and tracing firearm sales, alongside school-based threat assessment teams combining educators, mental health professionals, social workers and law enforcement. “There is no single profile of a school shooter,” he said, urging confidential reporting channels and trained staff capable of evaluating warning signs such as abrupt changes in behaviour, bullying, suicidal ideation and a fixation on weapons or violent online communities. “At present, policy appears to be developing from one tragedy to the next,” Yusoph said. “A centralised firearm tracing and school violence monitoring system would allow authorities to identify recurring patterns.” We should not wait for more children to die before treating the pattern as a national warning Raihan A. Yusoph, conflict resolution researcher Engelbrecht agreed that managing access to guns was only part of the solution. Rural areas such as those in Bangsamoro needed more community-oriented law enforcement and forums where psychologists could engage more directly with parents and children, he said. This would help investigators “grasp the deeper answers” that were driving the violence, he added, “beyond only superficial culprits such as games and cults”. Yusoph said the spate of recent shootings was “already enough to show repeated system failure and a possible process of imitation or diffusion”. “The firearm did not create the anger, humiliation, isolation, bullying, psychological distress or exposure to violent online material that may have preceded these attacks,” he said. “But firearms gave those conditions immediate lethal capacity.” Gun availability in the Philippines and Thailand, where a 14-year-old killed seven people and himself in a school shooting last month, certainly increased “the feasibility of the attack”, Munira said. But she agreed with other analysts that “we need to understand first what’s driving these kids, what is the source of grievance and why it’s manifesting this way”. “This didn’t use to be a problem 10 to 15 years ago, and now it’s coming in clusters,” Munira said. “Why is it a problem now?” “We should not wait for more children to die before treating the pattern as a national warning,” Yusoph added.

title: Xi and Trump will meet this week. Here’s the exclusive info you need to know
description: From potential talking points to the Chinese entourage, here’s what you need to know before Xi and Trump meet in Washington.
content: We have put together stories from our exclusive coverage of Xi and Trump’s upcoming meeting in the US. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Chinese CEOs fly to US on own, await invites to Trump’s state dinner for Xi Jinping A small group of Chinese CEOs holding US visas has arrived in Washington after travelling separately from President Xi Jinping’s official entourage, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. 2. Fissures over US investments stall plans for Chinese business leaders to join Xi visit Differences between Washington and Beijing over potential investment announcements have created roadblocks for a Chinese business delegation expected to accompany President Xi Jinping on his state visit to the US, according to sources. 3. China, US may unveil measures to boost military ties when Xi visits Washington China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post. 4. AI fight shadows final preparations for Xi Jinping’s White House visit Rising tensions over artificial intelligence are shaping the final preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States. 5. Tech, EV and aerospace execs likely to join Xi’s US trip to mirror Trump team Beijing is weighing plans to send a group of top tech, electric vehicle and aerospace executives to accompany Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington later this month, as the two sides race to finalise details for the closely watched visit. 6. US weighs delaying Taiwan arms sales until after Apec and G20 summits The United States is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, multiple sources told the South China Morning Post. 7. Once sidelined, China stands ready to broker fourth Trump-Kim handshake China is willing to help broker a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, sources have said. 8. As Xi’s US visit approaches, basic details of planned AI talks remain uncertain Washington and Beijing are still struggling to arrange a hoped-for dialogue on artificial intelligence, with the venue, participants and scope of the talks yet to be settled. 9. Claims Hegseth close to exit raise questions over future US-China defence ties Speculation is growing that Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth is at increasing risk of losing his job, raising questions about the possible implications for US-China relations, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. 10. BYD, Xiaomi, Innolight likely on guest list for Xi Jinping’s US trip: sources Figures from some of China’s most prominent firms – including electric vehicle maker BYD and smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi – are likely to accompany President Xi Jinping on his trip to the US, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. 11. Chinese officials rattled by White House chaos weeks ahead of Xi-Trump summit Just months ago, disorganised planning from Washington in the lead-up to US President Donald Trump’s landmark China visit frustrated Chinese officials. Now, Beijing is watching the same story play out on the other side of the world. 12. US-China ‘Board of Investment’ stalls before expected Trump-Xi meeting The US-China Board of Investment, one of the key outcomes of the May summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, is unlikely to be among the deliverables for their meeting in Washington, according to the head of a leading bilateral business group. 13. Trump envoy Daines to return to Beijing as US and China lock in Xi summit agenda US Senator Steve Daines is expected to return to China for another round of talks ahead of President Xi Jinping’s planned September visit to Washington, according to people familiar with the preparations.

title: Communist Party sets October plenum date as Xi prepares for Trump summit
description: The Politburo meets early to decide date, allowing Chinese President Xi Jinping to consolidate party affairs before arriving in Washington.
content: The Communist Party has set a date for its most important political gathering this autumn, the news coming shortly before Beijing confirmed Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US. The fifth plenary session of the party’s 20th Central Committee will be held from October 26 to October 29, according to official news agency Xinhua on Monday. The meeting of political elites is likely to be the most important gathering ahead of next autumn’s national party congress, a five-yearly event marked by massive top-level reshuffles. The decision was made during Monday’s meeting of the 21-member Politburo, which is chaired by Xi. In a departure from its typical schedule, the Politburo convened the meeting a week early – just two days before Xi’s high-stakes trip to the United States. The expedited timing allows Xi to consolidate party affairs before arriving in Washington for a reciprocal summit with President Donald Trump, who visited Beijing in May. Soon after the release of the Politburo meeting details, Beijing’s foreign ministry confirmed Xi would make a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday. The visit is expected to include a tarmac reception by Trump at Joint Base Andrews and a White House state dinner. Xi will be accompanied by a delegation of top Chinese executives from the tech, electric vehicle and aerospace industries to address agenda items such as artificial intelligence (AI) safety, rare earths and trade ties. At the centre of Monday’s Politburo meeting was the review and approval of a draft policy decision by the Central Committee regarding “strengthening full and rigorous party self-governance with perseverance”, Xinhua said. Regional officials, central party organs and non-party organisations have already been consulted about the document, which will be submitted to the Central Committee for final deliberation and approval during next month’s plenum, according to the news agency. The Politburo urged the party to focus on enhancing its “long-term governance capacity, maintaining its advanced nature and purity, and preserving its close bond with the people”. It also called on the party to maintain a strict stance on self-governance, Xinhua reported. “We must fully promote the enthusiasm, initiative and creativity of the entire party, and continuously realise the party’s self-purification, self-perfection, self-renewal and self-progression,” it said. It said stronger self-governance would ensure the party always remained a “vigorous Marxist governing party that stands at the forefront of the times, wins the wholehearted support of the people, withstands the tests of all kinds of storms and waves and serves as the strong core of leadership” of China’s development. When Xi became the party’s top leader in late 2012, he inherited an organisation severely weakened by systemic corruption, disciplinary lapses, official inertia and ideological drift – vulnerabilities that were seen as an existential threat to the party’s rule. Xi’s response was an unprecedented anti-corruption campaign that has snared millions of cadres, from low-level “flies” to “tigers”, or top senior officials and military generals. As the campaign matured, Beijing has had to shift from emergency clean-ups towards setting up a more permanent disciplinary system. “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building” – a new branch of the Chinese leader’s political thought – has emerged directly out of this transition. According to party documents, at the centre of this doctrine is the concept of the party’s “self-revolution” – the idea that it can continuously cleanse, reform and update itself from within, eliminating the need for Western-style multiparty competition or independent judicial checks. The new doctrine is regarded by party leaders as vital to its rule. This is because Beijing views internal cohesion as its primary weapon against domestic and international risks as China navigates industrial rebalancing, trade and technological containment by the West, and geopolitical friction. A more disciplined corps of cadres can help Beijing mitigate risk when implementing national strategies to avoid local protectionism, bureaucratic paralysis and rent-seeking.

title: Hong Kong triathlon star tempers Asian Games medal joy as he wrestles with individual blow
description: Oscar Coggins acknowledges ‘mixed feelings’ as city quartet claim third straight Asiad bronze, athletes hail spirit after injury battles.
content: Oscar Coggins said he had “mixed feelings” after Hong Kong claimed Asian Games triathlon mixed-relay bronze on Monday, as the Tokyo Olympian wrestled with self-recriminations over his flat individual performance 24 hours earlier. Fancied by head coach Andrew Wright to challenge for gold, Coggins came home in a “very disappointing” seventh place on Sunday. Described by teammate Bailee Brown as “the most dedicated person” in the city squad, the 26-year-old buried his angst long enough to summon a characteristically full-throttle second leg at the Gamagori City Triathlon Venue, helping Hong Kong take relay bronze for the third straight Games. Pursuing the podium spot that would preserve triathlon’s Tier A Hong Kong Sports Institute status for at least four more years, Wright sent out the 2025 National Games silver medal quartet of Cade Wright, Coggins, Brown and Robin Elg. Unused squad member Wong Tsz-to took aim at his exclusion on social media, intimating that he believed the selection process lacked transparency. “From the three selection rounds for the Asian Games, all the way to the final squad announcement, it remained unknown whether I’d get to compete,” Wong wrote. “Every time, the answer was ‘I don’t know’. And I don’t know the criteria “This isn’t the first time this has happened; there are others who don’t even have to meet the requirements.” China won gold in one hour, 25 minutes and 54 seconds, while silver went to hosts Japan in 1:26:45. Hong Kong stopped the clock on 1:27:25. An individual National Games bronze medallist last year, Coggins said: “I have very mixed feelings because yesterday was very disappointing, and I’m struggling. It was just a job that I had to do today. I haven’t had a chance to really process [the individual race] yet. “I really wanted to take some pressure off the team today, for yesterday. I was able to make up for that in some sense, and just get us back into a medal position. I don’t want to be a downer, because we did [secure a] medal.” Ahead of competing in the under-23 World Triathlon Championship Finals in Spain on Friday, Cade Wright came into the relay comparatively fresh, after she sat out the individual women’s race, where twin sister Tallulah competed instead and finished 10th. After a year in which a number of the Hong Kong contingent have been managing injuries, Cade Wright, who is no relation to her coach, said the “main goal today was to have four healthy athletes and to be as fit as possible”. “We felt the pressure this year to push in every training, and to see how much our bodies could handle. “A lot of us got hit with overtraining, and we had to work on our nutrition.” Coggins advanced Hong Kong from fifth to third during his turn over the 0.3km swim, 6.6km bike and 2km run course. Eighth in the individual women’s race, third-leg athlete Brown handed over to Elg well adrift of the Chinese and Japanese athletes, but neck-and-neck with South Korea. Also part of Hong Kong’s bronze medal teams in 2018 and 2023, Brown, who only recently recovered from a stress fracture of a shin, said: “It’s been a really tough year … we’re always trying to push it to our limits, and it showed. I think we all want to lift, but it’s about finding that balance.” Elg’s has been a remarkable tale of grit since the National Games 10 months ago. While his teammates staged overseas camps to prepare for Gamagori, Elg was condemned to staying alone in Hong Kong to use an AlterG Anti-Gravity treadmill because of a persistent stress problem in his fibula that would not allow him to run on hard surfaces. He emerged from his competitive hibernation to finish sixth in the individual competition, then on Monday shook off South Korea to ensure his sport did not return home empty handed. “I think I handled the pressure pretty well,” Elg said. “Oscar and I wanted to take pressure off from yesterday, [when] we both had pretty average days. Being able to bounce back and contribute to the medal count is a very special thing.” Other than Cade Wright’s pursuit of global honours later this week, Andrew Wright’s squad will next compete in their home Triathlon World Cup on November 7 and 8. Their primary remaining 2026 target is the Asia Triathlon Sprint Championships in Jordan, in late November, where a worthwhile helping of Olympic qualifying points will be up for grabs. “I know how hard all these guys work,” Brown said. “Oscar is the most dedicated on the team, and Robin is so dedicated, even when he had so much adversity this year. “The bronze [means] more than just third place. When we hurt, or when someone on the team hurts, we all hurt. When somebody has a victory, we all celebrate, and I’m just really glad that we got to do that today. “I know how talented they all are. All I have to do is put my faith in them, and our coach, who has trained us for so long.”

title: Singapore retrenchment rates hit highest level since pandemic
description: The number of job vacancies declined in the second quarter, especially in the financial services and information and communications sectors.
content: Singapore’s retrenchment rate in the second quarter of 2026 hit its highest level since the height of the Covid-19 pandemic in late 2020, driven by business reorganisation and restructuring, the manpower ministry said on Monday. There were 4,620 retrenchments in the second quarter of this year, up from the 3,830 retrenchments posted in the first quarter of the year, the ministry said in its labour market report for the period. It is the highest since the 5,640 retrenchments recorded in the fourth quarter of 2020 during the Covid pandemic. Retrenchments fell after 2020, when Singapore’s population declined as travel curbs and job losses encouraged foreign workers to leave the business hub, creating a tighter labour market. The manpower ministry said that the quarter-on-quarter increase was “concentrated in outward-oriented sectors, including manufacturing, information and communications and financial services”. It ‌also noted that the proportion of retrenched residents who returned to employment within six months ‌declined ‌to 54.9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 from 60.7 per cent in the first. The 12-month ‌re-entry rate remained broadly stable, at 69.8 per cent. Singapore’s overall unemployment rate remained stable at 1.9 per cent, with resident and citizen unemployment rates holding at 2.9 per cent and 3 per cent respectively. The ministry said the number of job vacancies declined in the second quarter, with fewer opportunities for professionals, managers, executives and technicians in financial services and information and communications. However, vacancies continued to outnumber the number of unemployed persons, with the ratio at 1.48 to 1 in June 2026, the ministry said.

title: Who is Rande Gerber, the late Presley Gerber’s father and Cindy Crawford’s husband?
description: The son of the supermodel and businessman, and brother of Kaia Gerber, has died aged 27 following a struggle with mental health and addiction.
content: Cindy Crawford’s son Presley Gerber has sadly passed away. The 27-year-old reportedly died on Sunday, September 20, at a rehab facility, as per TMZ. Presley’s parents, Crawford and Rande Gerber, as well as his younger sister Kaia Gerber, have asked for “privacy during this very difficult and painful time”, TMZ reported. Presley’s official cause of death has yet to be announced. The late model was known to have struggled with his mental health and an opiate addiction. Just last month, Kaia opened up to Vogue about her brother’s decade-long drug addiction and how it had impacted her family. “When something like that happens in a family, it kind of levels everyone,” Kaia told Vogue in an interview published on August 11. “I think that’s also why I started to self- identify as the easy one and never wanted to ask for help. Because it felt like too much to have two children who were needing.” Last December, Presley had also spoken at length about his mental health struggles and dependency on multiple medications he had been prescribed by 15 different psychiatrists. “The doctors say a lot of different things, so it’s kind of scary, but hopefully between my research and their research … and God, we can figure this out,” he said in a video he had shared on Instagram on December 1, 2025, which is no longer available as of Monday afternoon. “The things that scare me are the things you need to take … if you don’t take them, something not good happens. And there’s a spectrum there on how intense the withdrawal from certain medications is.” “I’d like doctors to be like, ‘Take this three times a day’ … but every psychiatrist I’ve had – I’ve had 15 – are like, ‘Here’s 20 medications and take this if you feel like this … and I’m like, ‘No, don’t get me that much leeway.’ I need some direction,” he said. He added he hoped his video “reaches people in many ways”. “So you feel like you’re not alone, because that is how I feel most of the time and I have a feeling that if I say all of this, a lot of people will at least know that there’s someone else going through it. And the second thing is, hopefully I find some people out here [who] are willing to help or know someone that can help,” he said. In 2024, Presley revealed that he had fallen into a coma for several days after a near-fatal fentanyl overdose, according to media reports. Supermodel Crawford and businessman Gerber welcomed Presley in July 1999. In 2021, Rande celebrated his son’s birthday with a touching Instagram post featuring a snap of the father embracing a young Presley. “Happy Bday Prez! The love and bond we have means everything. I’m so proud of the man you have become and the work you have done this past year personally and professionally. Ready to launch! I love you,” Gerber captioned the post. Here’s everything you need to know about Presley Gerber’s grieving father, Rande Gerber. What is Rande Gerber known for? Aside from his famous wife, 64-year-old Gerber is known for being a businessman in the entertainment industry. Per his bio on the University of Arizona’s alumni section, he founded nightlife companies Midnight Oil and the Gerber Group with his brothers and launched Casamigos Tequila with George Clooney and Michael Meldman in 2013. As reported by CNBC, Casamigos Tequila was sold to Diageo for as much as US$1 billion in 2017. He is also a former model who was scouted by Ford Models when he was just 16, according to The New York Times. What is Rande Gerber’s net worth? In a 2018 Business Insider report, Gerber was listed as having an impressive net worth of US$100 million. That figure has since been upped to an estimated US$400 million, according to Celebrity Net Worth. How does Rande Gerber know George Clooney? Gerber and Clooney have reportedly been friends for years. As Gerber revealed in a 2015 interview with The Times, they met over 20 years ago at a bar he owned in New York City. “We had a couple of drinks,” he told the publication. “We started hanging out. We just enjoyed each other’s company.” Where did Cindy Crawford meet Rande Gerber? As per People, Crawford and Gerber met in the early 1990s as friends – but they were both in relationships with other people at the time. In a 2015 interview with Harper’s Bazaar, Crawford opened up about her romance. “We met at my agent’s wedding,” she said. “When I met him I was still with Richard [Gere] and he didn’t want to go to the wedding with me … Rande also had a girlfriend at the time so he wasn’t looking to meet anyone either and that’s the best time to meet someone because that’s when you’re truly yourselves. We became friends and after Richard and I broke up then we started dating.” When did Crawford and Gerber get married? The Sports Illustrated Swimsuit model and her beau tied the knot in the Bahamas on May 29, 1998, when Crawford was 32 and Gerber was 36, per People. Crawford told Harper’s Bazaar how they wanted to keep the nuptials hush-hush. “I wore John Galliano off the rack because the wedding was supposed to be secret,” she shared. “We married in the Bahamas in front of our friends and family and it was so special – it was different for my second wedding. We walked each other down the aisle.” Renowned photographer Arthur Elgort photographed the lavish event, adds People. The stylish couple share two children, who both entered the fashion industry. Presley had worked for Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger and Dolce & Gabbana, and did a Super Bowl ad with his mother in 2018. Kaia is a rising supermodel, having worked with brands from Saint Laurent and Fendi to Miu Miu and Prada. She is also a budding actress and dated Elvis star Austin Butler between 2021 and 2024.

title: 4 mainland Chinese firms jump into cooling Hong Kong IPO market
description: Led by RoboTechnik and Kinwong Electronic, quartet aims to raise up to US$1.8 billion in total, but most debuts this month have declined.
content: Four Chinese companies launched initial public offerings (IPOs) in Hong Kong on Monday, aiming to raise as much as HK$14 billion (US$1.8 billion) in total, with strong backing from cornerstone investors countering apparent weakness in the market so far this month. Automated equipment manufacturer RoboTechnik has the biggest target, planning to raise as much as HK$5.18 billion. The new entrants are braving a market that shows signs of slowing. After a blistering year so far – Hong Kong listings raised about US$43 billion in the first eight months, according to bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing – only one out of six new listings this month gained ground. RoboTechnik said on Monday that it was selling shares at up to HK$436, representing a 40 per cent discount on the closing price of its Shenzhen-listed shares on Friday. Based in Suzhou in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, the company attracted 16 cornerstone investors, including Singapore investment company Temasek and Chinese asset-management company E Fund Management. Together the cornerstone investors committed to 35 per cent of the offer. The company’s products include manufacturing equipment as well as complete production lines and smart manufacturing systems for the photovoltaic and silicon photonics industries. Shenzhen Kinwong Electronic aims to raise HK$5.10 billion in its IPO, offering more than 72.9 million shares globally at a maximum of HK$69.88 apiece, representing a 42 per cent discount from Friday’s closing price for the company’s Shanghai-listed stock. The maker of printed circuit boards attracted 14 cornerstone investors, including optical transceiver manufacturer Zhongji Innolight and Kingboard Holdings subsidiary KHL, which together committed US$310 million, or 47 per cent of the total fundraising. For the first half of this year, Kinwong’s revenue rose 21.4 per cent to 8.6 billion yuan (US$1.3 billion), though net profit fell 6.5 per cent to 612 million yuan. The other two companies that launched IPOs on Monday are Shanghai-listed materials manufacturer Red Avenue New Materials, which plans to raise up to HK$3 billion, and electric motor supplier Direct Drive Tech, which targets HK$1.08 billion. First-day margin orders for the retail tranches got off to a slow start. According to data from several brokerages, as of 4pm on Monday only Direct Drive Tech – the smallest of the four offerings – was fully subscribed, while the remaining three issuers fell short of full coverage. Shares of all four companies are expected to begin trading on September 29. Among September’s six IPOs so far, only Excelland Robotics rose in its debut, gaining 153 per cent on September 9. Transwarp Technology, which debuted on Monday, lost 9.18 per cent, closing at HK$44.50. The other four listees – Shein, Longsys Electronics, Medcaptain Medical Technology and Mech-Mind Robotics – have lost between 18 and 45 per cent since their debuts.

title: Be inspired by globally recognised scientists in face-to-face dialogue this November
description: Designed for shortlisted secondary students, the exclusive in-person dialogue ‘The Shape of Success: A Conversation with The Shaw Laureates 2026’ brings scientific visionaries together to share the insights and stories behind their achievements.
content: This highly anticipated event will do more than satisfy the curiosity of science-loving students: it will spark inspiration and answer the many questions they bring. It aims to set shortlisted students on their own paths to scientific discovery because dialogue is where curiosity meets experience and where the abstract equations and clinical trials they read about in class become human, lively and thrilling. On stage will sit celebrated scientists – figures whose names are already etched into the story of modern science – whose presence signals a passion for passing wisdom to the next generation. Expect the five 2026 Shaw Laureates in Life Science & Medicine and Mathematical Sciences to candidly share practical road maps for their breakthroughs: how to frame a question, how to design an experiment, how to recover when data disappoints and how to translate theory into tools that change lives. Beyond technical details, the laureates will reveal the mindset that fuels discovery. For students, hearing these candid reflections is transformative: the path from classroom to lab bench or research institute becomes visible and attainable. The laureates’ stories turn abstract ambition into concrete next steps – what to study, whom to seek out and how to build the resilience that research demands. Presented by the Shaw Prize Foundation and organised by SCMP Learn, “The Shape of Success: A Conversation with The Shaw Laureates 2026” is a living masterclass in innovation and practice – a rare chance for Hong Kong’s brightest, science-minded students to engage directly with world-class mentors. In this setting, wisdom is exchanged in close, in-person interaction: students ask, laureates answer and together they sketch the future of science – one question, one experiment and one bold idea at a time. Shaw Laureates 2026 Professor Anne Dejean, Professor Hugues de Thé and Professor Zhu Chen – co-recipients of The Shaw Prize in Life Science & Medicine 2026 Anne Dejean is Professor Emerita at the Institut Pasteur, France; Hugues de Thé is Professor and Chair of Cellular and Molecular Oncology at the Collège de France, and Hospital Saint Louis in Paris, France; and Zhu Chen is Professor at Ruijin Hospital, School of Medicine, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China. They have been honoured for uncovering the molecular and cellular bases of acute promyelocytic leukaemia and for pioneering a synergistic targeted therapy that has transformed the disease from one of the deadliest to one of the most curable cancers. Professor Emmanuel Candès and Professor Camillo De Lellis – co-recipients of The Shaw Prize in Mathematical Sciences 2026 The journey “The Shape of Success: A Conversation with The Shaw Laureates 2026” is the starting point for shortlisted students to unlock their potential. Join this voyage of discovery. Application: The journey begins with a short challenge: each applicant is invited to submit an essay of 100-250 words reflecting on their passion for Life Science, Mathematical Sciences or other scientific fields, and explaining how direct engagement with the laureates could inspire them to strive for excellence. Shortlisting: The SCMP editorial team will evaluate submissions and shortlist up to 60 students who stand out for their passion and potential to contribute positively to the programme. Pre-event preparation: On October 31, 2026, shortlisted students will be invited to an online workshop, including a sharing session led by the Shaw Prize student representatives to introduce the 2026 laureates, highlight their award-winning research, and provide context to help students prepare for the discussions. Next, students will take part in a complimentary English journalistic writing workshop curated by SCMP, focusing on interview techniques and storytelling. The day of inspiration: Shortlisted students should mark November 13, 2026, in their diaries. They will be split into two groups – Life Science & Medicine and Mathematical Sciences – to gain a deeper understanding of the Shaw Prize, engage with laureates in dialogues moderated by SCMP, and sharpen their English interviewing skills in a panel-discussion format. Share reflections: To deepen their experience, students will submit a 250-word post-event reflection accompanied by a photo taken during the event. The top three essays will be published in the Young Post, sharing those insightful reflections with a global audience. “The Shape of Success: A Conversation with The Shaw Laureates 2026” serves as a launch pad for future leaders in science. Seize this opportunity and let an inspired journey of discovery begin. Key dates at a glance Application period: Now until October 16, 2026 Online English journalistic writing workshop & pre-event briefing session: Saturday, October 31, 2026 Event day and venue: Friday, November 13, 2026, at Shaw Studios in Tseung Kwan O Apply here: https://bit.ly/4dvEsXs

title: Japanese surgeon removes healthy brain tissue, leaving woman on ventilator
description: The veteran doctor ignored negative biopsy results during the 10-hour surgery at Kyoto University Hospital, leaving the tumour intact.
content: A Japanese woman was left unable to breathe on her own after a veteran surgeon mistakenly removed healthy tissue instead of a benign tumour from her brain. Kyoto University Hospital apologised for the medical error and vowed to take measures to prevent similar incidents, local news outlet TV Asahi reported. The woman, in her fifties, was diagnosed with a benign brain tumour after consulting doctors for dizziness and unsteadiness. Although she was able to carry out her daily activities, she agreed to undergo surgery to remove the growth, which had formed inside the cerebellopontine angle deep within the brain. The 10-hour operation was considered complex as there were nerves surrounding the area. A team of three surgeons – led by a doctor with more than 20 years of neurosurgery experience – performed the procedure in late July. According to the hospital, the surgeon performed tests twice during the operation to determine whether the removed tissue was tumorous. Despite the initial biopsy result indicating that the tissue was “not a tumour”, the surgeon continued with the excision, believing “only the edge of the tumour tissue had been taken”, the hospital said, according to the Sankei newspaper. When a second pathological test showed the same result, the doctor concluded the tumour had been completely removed. But the patient did not regain consciousness after the operation and was unable to breathe unassisted. An MRI scan later revealed that a healthy section of her brain, including the brainstem – which controls breathing and movement – had been damaged. The tumour remained intact. While she has since been able to respond to questions by blinking, she remains dependent on artificial ventilation. When asked whether the lead surgeon – who had performed more than 100 such surgeries – had made the wrong decision by continuing despite the negative test results, the hospital’s chief of neurosurgery, Yoshiteru Ara told the broadcaster: “I perform surgeries myself, and that kind of thing happens sometimes. Even if we report it twice, we are told it’s not a tumour. It’s something we experience often.” Asked if the error was due to overconfidence stemming from experience, Ara replied: “I think so.” He said that the surgeon had since reviewed the video of the operation and post-operative magnetic resonance imaging scan, and was “apologetic for the misdiagnosis”. Kyoto University Hospital performs an average of 156 brain tumour surgeries annually. “We offer our deepest apologies,” hospital director Akifumi Takaori said. “We will do our best to provide the best possible treatment, and we will investigate the cause and formulate effective measures to prevent recurrence.” The hospital has since implemented a system where more than one person has to verify test results during a brain tumour removal surgery. Japan introduced a medical accident investigation system under the Medical Care Act in October 2015, mandating internal reviews for unexpected deaths. However, a study published in the JMA Journal in 2023 found that under-reporting persisted because of fears of legal liability and a lack of strict penalties for non-compliance.

title: Over 11,000 sign up for Hong Kong taxi, ride-hailing test, beating expectations
description: Transport minister says response has exceeded expectations, adds that authorities to arrange for applicants to take test within two months.
content: More than 11,000 Hong Kong residents have applied to take a new joint examination required to qualify for a taxi driving licence or ride-hailing permit, exceeding government expectations, the city’s transport minister has said. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also shared details on Monday about a separate scheme enabling mainland Chinese yachts to enter city waters, noting that candidates taking the required certification exam achieved a strong pass rate. Hong Kong recently passed legislation to regulate local ride-hailing services, capping the total number of vehicle permits at 10,000. Under the new rules, residents must pass a joint assessment to apply for either a taxi driving licence or a ride-hailing permit. However, existing valid taxi driving licence holders can apply directly for the permit without retaking the test. “The response was really beyond our expectations,” Chan told a radio programme. “Since the opening of applications for the examination, we have received many sign-ups per day, and the number has [only] recently stabilised.” Under the regulatory framework to be launched next year, drivers operating approved ride-hailing vehicles must be the registered owners. Ride-hailing platform operators will also be required to obtain dedicated licences. Chan said that more than 20 organisations had attended the government’s briefing session on platform licensing, and obtained the application forms and relevant documents. The minister said that more than 11,000 residents had signed up for the test since registration opened on August 3, adding that the Transport Department would arrange for them to take the exam within two months. Four sessions had been arranged so far, she said. Turning to maritime travel, Chan revealed more details about a scheme allowing mainland-registered yachts to enter Hong Kong waters, expected to launch next month. A parallel initiative permitting Hong Kong yachts to sail northbound was introduced in June. Currently, mainland yachts have to secure bookings for berths at private clubs before they are permitted to enter Hong Kong waters. Under the new arrangement, they will be permitted to anchor without prior reservations across five designated areas: Tai O, Three Fathoms Cove in Tai Po, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay and Stanley Bay. “The surrounding bays of the five anchorage areas designated by the Marine Department are remarkably beautiful, with excellent natural resources. These are also places that many yacht owners have frequently expressed a desire to visit in the past,” Chan said. She added that the department had activated a dynamic monitoring system to check the availability of anchorage spaces in each location, and would liaise closely with mainland yachts using the system. “If we spot any vacancies, we will update mainland yacht operators, and they can anchor at designated locations – as long as there is still room – without any prior application to yacht clubs,” she said. To support the initiative, authorities established training and examination centres across six mainland locations to certify captains operating vessels bound for Hong Kong. To date, more than 60 candidates have passed, reflecting what Chan described as a solid pass rate. Chan also expects the initiative to deliver a boost to the local economy. “Based on our previous understanding of the industry, yachts can drive a whole chain of supply services. For instance, vessel maintenance and repairs, or the provision of water and food supplies for passengers, and all these related service industries can be stimulated,” she said.

title: Black robin rules roost in New Zealand’s Bird of the Year vote
description: The critically endangered bird received more than 26,000 votes, beating the kakapo and karearea falcon to the title.
content: A record number of New Zealanders turned out at the polls this month, not for national elections but to vote for their Bird of the Year – the critically endangered black robin. The diminutive native lives on the remote Chatham Islands, 800km (500 miles) off the South Island’s east coast. In 1980, only five of the birds remained, including a single breeding female. Now there are about 350. The black robin topped the pecking order ahead of the famed flightless parrot, the kakapo, and the native karearea falcon, which came in second and third. The annual Bird of the Year competition is run by independent conservation organisation Forest and Bird, and has been the subject of significant controversy in the past decade. In 2019, there were accusations of Russian interference after hundreds of votes were registered from IP addresses in the country. Forest and Bird deemed most of the votes were legitimate, and said it did not affect the victory of the hoiho, or yellow-eyed penguin. In 2023, the puteketeke won the title after receiving the celebrity backing of Last Week Tonight comedian John Oliver, who urged his viewers to vote for the lake dweller. Forest and Bird’s Rebecca Hatch said voter numbers had soared this year, but not due to foreign interference. “This year has seen record numbers of votes with 105,000 people choosing their favourite,” Hatch said. “New Zealanders have really shown up for nature. Roughly one in every 50 Kiwis voted,” she said, referring to the country’s people and not the native, flightless birds. The black robin received more than 26,000 votes. The Chatham Islands Landscape Restoration Trust ran the campaign for the black robin and is seeking to create a third habitat for the birds to expand their biodiversity.

title: Geopolitical risks see institutional investors rush to stockpile cash, survey finds
description: Report says net cash allocation intentions rose 35.5 percentage points to a positive 22 per cent in poll conducted in June and July.
content: Global institutional investors and wealth managers are stockpiling cash at the fastest pace on record while quietly retreating from US and UK equities as persistent inflation and mounting geopolitical risks dominate portfolio decisions, according to a report by Marsh Investments. The institutional investment consultancy polled 430 asset owners managing a combined US$5.76 trillion and found that 37.8 per cent planned to increase cash allocations over the next 12 months, up from just 9 per cent in a similar survey last year. Net cash allocation intentions rose 35.5 percentage points to a positive 22 per cent – the sharpest year-on-year swing of any asset class in the survey. United States and United Kingdom equities were the only two asset classes where more investors planned to cut exposure than add, with net allocation intentions falling to negative 10.3 per cent and negative 16.5 per cent, respectively. “These shifts suggest asset owners are adopting a deliberate barbell position – strengthening downside protection and diversification while retaining flexibility to respond to market opportunities,” Niall O’Sullivan, Marsh’s global chief investment officer, wrote in a report published on Monday. The survey, conducted in June and July, found that geopolitical risks and inflation were the two most-cited concerns shaping near-term decisions – being considered significant by more than 70 per cent of respondents. At a media briefing in Hong Kong earlier this month, before the US Federal Reserve’s decision last week to lift its benchmark rate by a quarter of a percentage point, Mike Sebastian, Marsh’s global head of multi-asset investing, said the professional services firm held a “positive near-term view on equities”, supported by strong corporate earnings, though the medium-term picture was less certain. Private markets have become easier to access but harder to manage well Garvan McCarthy, Marsh Investments “In the medium term … you can see there being some volatility there,” Sebastian said, attributing the pressure to geopolitically driven yield moves, rising energy costs and tight credit spreads. He also urged investors to diversify and reassess their exposures. The survey found that asset owners were positioning themselves for that kind of pressure, with over half the respondents planning to raise infrastructure holdings and nearly half targeting increased exposure to emerging market equities. This shift away from single-market concentration extended across the Asia-Pacific region, where 53 per cent of investors had adjusted their geographic exposure over the past year, compared with nearly half of respondents globally. Private markets continued to draw broad engagement, though investors were showing greater restraint. About 44 per cent of respondents reported maintaining their existing commitments while applying stricter selection criteria. “Private markets have become easier to access but harder to manage well,” said Garvan McCarthy, the firm’s global chief investment officer of alternatives, in the Marsh report. He added the next phase of investing would favour asset owners who could “pace commitments, maintain underwriting discipline”, and properly assess the impact of individual exposures on overall liquidity and risk.

title: Tapestry depicting English history’s ‘most important event’ back in UK after 1,000 years
description: The Bayeux Tapestry is expected to draw 1 million visitors to the British Museum before its exhibition ends in July 2027.
content: After a wait of almost 1,000 years and a journey of hundreds of miles, the Bayeux Tapestry’s big moment is here. The embroidered panorama depicting the last successful invasion of England has gone on public display at the British Museum in London this month, back on British soil for the first time since the 11th century. Tickets have sold out months in advance, and the museum expects 1 million visitors to see the tapestry before the exhibition ends in July 2027. Schoolchildren across the UK will get special history lessons on it. King Charles and French President Emmanuel Macron have already had a private viewing. It is an extraordinary level of excitement for what UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham jokingly called a 70-metre (230ft) long “reminder of one of Britain’s biggest defeats”. Like a medieval comic strip, the tapestry tells a vivid tale of betrayal, bloodshed, suffering and conquest, depicting a pivotal moment in European history: the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. It illustrates the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings, where William, Duke of Normandy, defeated King Harold’s Anglo-Saxon army. The invasion crowned William the first Norman king of England, introduced the French language and settlers, and forever intertwined the two countries’ fates. At an exhibition preview, curator Michael Lewis called 1066 “the most important event in English history” and noted a “propaganda element” stitched into the tapestry. He said it was designed to tell English people that “Harold was king, you probably weren’t crazy to follow him, but the status quo has completely changed now. William is king, and you need to kind of accept the new reality.” The tapestry’s 58 scenes begin with English nobleman Harold Godwinson travelling to France, where he swears an oath to William, perhaps agreeing to back the duke’s succession to the English throne. But when English ruler Edward the Confessor dies, Harold is crowned king, leading William to assemble a fleet and set sail for England. The final sections depict the climactic battle: archers with bows, charging cavalry, sword-wielding knights, hand-to-hand combat and mutilated bodies. Brutal violence sits alongside domestic detail. Soldiers steal livestock, cook dinner, eat using their shields as plates and burn down an English house as a woman and child flee. People steal from the bodies of the dead. Margins at the top and bottom of the fabric brim with people, fish, dogs and winged beasts, sometimes acting as ironic commentary on the main action. It remains remarkably vivid, and would have been even more powerful for its 11th century viewers, Lewis said, adding, “Maybe they would even have tried to pick out themselves in the story of these events.” Centuries of secrets For historians, the tapestry is an invaluable source of insight into 11th century life: shipbuilding, fashion, cuisine, architecture, armour, even astronomy. At one point, Halley’s comet streaks across the sky, as it really did in 1066. Scholars still debate its mysteries. Was the arrow that hits Harold in the eye, killing him, a later addition? A final scene, possibly depicting William’s coronation, is missing. Historians even argue about the exact number of equine and human penises on display – either 93 or 94. Leonie Hicks, professor of medieval studies at Canterbury Christ Church University, said one reason the tapestry remains so famous is that its vivid, childlike illustrations are “very meme-able”. “It can be used to comment on current politics or mark memorable events,” Hicks wrote in a blog post, noting a recent magazine cover showing Burnham on horseback advancing on his predecessor Keir Starmer, who was depicted as Harold with an arrow in his eye. “The [cover’s] margins contained Big Ben and Larry the cat.” The tapestry was probably commissioned by William’s half-brother Bishop Odo of Bayeux and has spent almost 1,000 years in the French town. But historians believe it was probably stitched by women in southeast England, not far from the site of the battle. King Charles noted at a reception with Macron in early September that it might just as accurately be called the Canterbury Embroidery. A diplomatic triumph Governments on both sides of the English Channel have hailed the tapestry’s loan as a symbol of Franco-British friendship. But getting it to London took years of diplomacy. After decades of failed British requests to borrow the tapestry, an agreement was announced in 2018, delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic and Brexit tensions, and finally confirmed by Macron during a state visit to the UK in 2025. Some French cultural figures, and the late British artist David Hockney, opposed the move because of the risk of damage to the fragile artefact. Insured for €960 million (US$1.1 billion), the tapestry was nestled inside climate-controlled shockproof packaging before being transported by road and rail to the museum under police escort, arriving in the dead of night. It is being displayed flat in what curators say is a robust state-of-the-art case, rather than hanging as it was in Bayeux. Lewis said the “phenomenal expertise” of teams in France and Britain allowed it to arrive unscathed. “But we’ve learned so much in that process,” he added. “I’m confident that we’ve learned a lot that helps us be sure that going back is going to be as good.”

title: Who is Frank Adams, WNBA star Sophie Cunningham’s rumoured new beau?
description: The Indiana Fever guard, who faced backlash over her comments on trans athletes, has been spotted cosying up to a Grand Canyon University sports trainer.
content: WNBA player Sophie Cunningham repeatedly made headlines earlier this year when she publicly protested the inclusion of trans athletes in professional sports. “I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans,” the Indiana Fever guard told ESPN about the backlash she received from fans and the internet. “And I’m like, ‘I never once said that.’ I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.” More recently, however, Cunningham has been stirring the internet’s interest for an entirely different reason – it seems that the 30-year-old baller has a new man in her life. On September 12, Fever Updates, an X page that gives Fever fans the latest news on the WNBA team, uploaded two pictures of Cunningham cosying up to Frank Adams with the caption “Sophie Cunningham revealed her new boyfriend”. While Cunningham has yet to confirm her relationship status, here’s everything you need to know about her rumoured new man, Frank Adams. What is Frank Adams’ background? According to Adams’ LinkedIn profile, he attended Young Harris College in Georgia, where he studied biology from 2010 to 2013. During his time there, he was part of the school’s men’s basketball team. He went on to earn his bachelor’s degree in athletic training in 2015 from Florida Southern College and graduated from Hardin-Simmons University with a master’s degree in kinesiology, sports and recreation in 2017. Since then, Adams has gone on to work as an athletic trainer at various universities, including a six-year stint as the assistant athletic trainer for the Phoenix Suns from 2019 to 2025. Currently, he is employed as the head athletic trainer for Grand Canyon University in Arizona. How did Sophie Cunningham and Frank Adams meet? While neither Cunningham nor Adams has spoken publicly on their speculated relationship, they reportedly crossed paths during Adams’ time with the Phoenix Suns, as Cunningham was with the Phoenix Mercury at the time. Cunningham has shared little about her private and romantic life in the past, but she was confirmed to be dating Jakob Neidig, a University of Missouri athlete, from 2019 to 2020.

title: China’s collection of stock stamp duty jumps more than 80% as AI frenzy boosts trading
description: Average daily trading values on mainland China’s stock markets rose 72 per cent in first eight months of the year.
content: China’s revenue from stamp duty on stock sales jumped more than 80 per cent in the first eight months this year as improved sentiment bolstered trading activities. China collected 216 billion yuan (US$32.3 billion) from the tax between January and August, up 82 per cent year on year, data released by the Ministry of Finance showed. Average daily trading values on mainland China’s stock markets rose 72 per cent in the first eight months of the year as the artificial intelligence boom bolstered demand for equities. While the benchmark CSI 300 Index has remained flat this year, much of the trading has focused on technology stocks, driving the chip-heavy Star Market 50 Index up by 23 per cent in the first eight months of the year. Stocks worth a daily average of 2.67 trillion yuan changed hands on the mainland’s exchanges this year, according to industry data. The stamp duty is seen as a barometer of China’s stock market, as Beijing often adjusts the tax rate to influence investor sentiment. It was halved in 2023 to stem a decline in stock values and now stands at 0.05 per cent – payable by investors selling stocks. Beijing began cutting the stamp duty in 2007 to encourage stock trading. It slashed the rate from a high of 0.3 per cent that year and scrapped its application to those buying stocks in 2008. Growth in stamp-duty revenue moderated in August, recording an 18 per cent year-on-year increase for the slowest growth this year, as the unravelling of the global AI trade hurt sentiment and discouraged trading. The Star Market 50 Index rebounded by 3 per cent last month after a record 26 per cent plunge in July. The outlook for technology stocks has been clouded by monetary tightening by central banks around the world and elevated sovereign bond yields. The US Federal Reserve raised America’s benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years on Thursday, and the Bank of Japan followed suit a day later. Long-end yields in the two nations have touched multi-year highs this month on unease over inflationary pressure and a glut of debt issuance. “There will be a divergence of the AI trade going forward,” said Li Lifeng, an analyst at Huaxi Securities. “The next leg of the trade will feature selective buying of quality bets, deviating from the previous rally characterised by general gains in AI stocks and speculative trading in small-capitalisation stocks.” In a move seen by some industry players as an effort to boost market sentiment, the China Securities Regulatory Commission said last week that it would reward whistle-blowers in 17 cases of disciplinary breaches ranging from non-compliant corporate disclosures by listed companies to insider trading and fraudulent accounting.

title: China tests first practical submarine solar power plant at 10-metre depth in the open sea
description: Scientists successfully charge batteries and power a LED using lead halide perovskite solar cells in world-first test.
content: In a breakthrough that could power the future of underwater operations, Chinese scientists have built and tested the world’s first submarine solar farm, successfully operating a perovskite-based photovoltaic system at a depth of 10 metres (33 feet) in the open sea. The submerged array charged batteries and powered an LED panel, proving that solar energy can be harvested even in the dim, blue-green twilight of the ocean. The achievement by a team from Yunnan University was published on September 11 in the journal Joule. The feat overcomes a long-standing barrier: sunlight fades rapidly underwater, and conventional silicon solar cells are ill-suited to the narrow spectrum that remains. At 10 metres below the surface, only about 10 per cent of sunlight penetrates. And red light, where silicon cells perform best, is almost entirely absorbed. The researchers chose lead halide perovskite solar cells with a wide band gap of about 1.96 electron-volt, which matches the blue-green light underwater. Perovskites can be tuned and work better in dim light. But in seawater, they can become unstable because of corrosion, pressure, packaging problems and possible lead leakage. To address this, the team added polyhexamethylene guanidine hydrochloride or PHMG – as a crystallisation additive to make the cells more stable in seawater. “Previous underwater solar cells focused on very shallow water depths of only 2 metres or less, far from useful for practical applications,” Zhang Wen-hua of Yunnan University said in a Cell Press report. “This work presents the first functional validation of submerged solar cells practically operating at a water depth of up to about 10 metres.” In laboratory tests that simulated sunlight at a depth of 10 metres, a small cell measuring 0.0895 sq cm (about 0.014 sq inch) reached a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 34.71 per cent. A larger module measuring 28.79 square centimetres reached 29.4 per cent, showing that even weak light could be used efficiently. Durability was a highlight of the work. The team provided the perovskite solar cells with multilayer encapsulation – acting as waterproof, pressure-resistant, and corrosion-resistant armour – using butyl rubber and cover glass, topped with a transparent epoxy resin outer protective layer. In simulated seawater, the encapsulated device retained 99.58 per cent of its initial PCE after 1,000 hours of continuous immersion under illumination at a depth of 10 metres. Further calculations suggest that at 25 degrees Celsius (77 degrees Fahrenheit) under a simulated 10 metre underwater light, the cell had a T80 lifetime of 48,094 hours, meaning it could still keep 80 per cent of its output after about 5½ years. The team also carried out underwater tests near Weizhou Island in the South China Sea. They integrated perovskite solar cells with an underwater robot, which carried the perovskite solar modules to charge lithium-ion batteries at depths of 2, 6, and 10 metres. Under two hours of light, the system charged 1,416 milliwatt-hours at 2 metres, 752 mWh at 6 metres, and 324 mWh at 10 metres. It successfully lit an LED panel. “Moreover, we have achieved scaling from small-area laboratory cells to large-size modules,” said Zhang, dean of the materials and energy school at Yunnan University and corresponding author of the Joule paper. “The combination of the laboratory investigations and the in-field experiments provides strong evidence for the operation of underwater photovoltaics.” The work opens new frontiers both for perovskites, which are traditionally considered unsuitable for humid environments, and for the increasingly human-occupied underwater world. The technology could be used in underwater sensors, detectors, cameras, communication systems, underwater robots and submersibles, where it could serve as a long-term power node. According to the paper: “This work paves the way for the practical deployment of perovskite photovoltaics in underwater environments, offering a promising route toward self-sustained marine energy systems and autonomous underwater devices.”

title: Suspected DMZ landmine blast injures 3 South Korean soldiers
description: Three people were hospitalised. Hundreds of thousands of mines, if not more, are thought to be buried in the area.
content: Three South Korean military officers were injured in an explosion during an operation near the heavily mined border with North Korea, Seoul’s military said Monday. The incident occurred south of the military demarcation line inside the demilitarised zone (DMZ), one of the world’s most heavily fortified and mined frontiers. Two of the injured officers were evacuated by helicopter, while a third was due to be transported by road before being airlifted, the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said. It was not immediately clear whether the explosion was caused by a North Korean mine, a South Korean mine, or another explosive device. The three officers “were injured by an explosion of unknown cause while conducting an operation at a location south of the MDL”, the JCS said in a statement. The military did not immediately provide details on the severity of their injuries. The DMZ is a 248 km (154-mile) long and roughly 4 km (2½-mile) wide buffer zone that has divided the Korean peninsula since the 1953 armistice – with no peace treaty – that halted the Korean war. While the zone itself is officially demilitarised, its northern and southern boundaries are among the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers and remain littered with landmines. Around 800,000 mines are estimated to be buried around the area, according to military data cited by the Yonhap news agency, many dating to the Korean war – although mine laying has continued in recent years.
