Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un designated South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy”, Pyongyang’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the border as part of efforts to permanently seal off the frontier. South Korea’s military has previously said several North Korean soldiers were killed or wounded in accidental mine explosions during those works. Landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas. In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded when a landmine exploded on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs. Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the military demarcation line to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied. The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts along the border. The latest incident comes as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has repeatedly called for unconditional dialogue with the North, overtures that have so far gone unanswered by Pyongyang. North Korea has dialled up animosity with a run of military displays this month, including short-range ballistic missile launches, live-fire missile and artillery exercises, and the commissioning of a new warship as leader Kim Jong-un flaunts his growing nuclear programme despite US calls to revive diplomacy. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Singapore nets US$862,000 from first auction in money laundering case
description: The frenzied bidding is in sharp contrast to the lacklustre reception for luxury real estate tied to the same illicit network.
content: A fierce 30-minute bidding war for a rare Louis Vuitton x Yayoi Kusama pumpkin bag – seized in Singapore’s S$3 billion (US$2.35 billion) money laundering case – sent its final price soaring on Sunday night. The limited-edition yellow monogram leather piece, which was a collaboration between the luxury fashion house and the Japanese artist who recently died at 97, eventually went under the hammer for an eye-watering S$87,000. A flurry of 42 last-minute bids pushed the closing price to more than five times the auction house’s initial estimate of S$12,000 to S$16,000. The auction, that closed on Sunday, is part of a series of 15 online auctions for items from the money laundering case, scheduled to run from this month until May next year. Conducted by auctioneer Hotlotz, the sale of the first tranche of 337 handbags and accessories from the high-profile case concluded on Sunday night. All items were sold with the total coming in at over S$1.1 million (US$862,000). Like the pumpkin bag, several other lots saw strong interest from bidders. Necklaces, bracelets and a ring from Chrome Hearts mostly scored 30 bids or more, with the final sale prices coming in at several times higher than the estimates. A diamond double cross pendant necklace sold for S$11,000, about 10 times the estimated S$1,000 to S$1,500. Another Hotlotz auction for 286 pieces of fine jewellery seized in the case will stay open until September 27. Together, the two auctions were estimated to bring in between S$2.9 million and S$3.9 million in total. The frenzied bidding stood in sharp contrast to the lacklustre reception for luxury real estate tied to the same illicit network, where not a single seized property found a buyer when put up for auction on September 17. Bestselling bags Chanel bags, which made up the largest portion of luxury bags up for sale, and the Chrome Hearts jewellery were among the most popular items. A diamante-studded beige goatskin Chanel mini flap bag sold for S$15,000 – about a third of the 28 bids were made on Sunday. Loveholic founder Elaine Fung, whose firm sources for luxury items, said she expected iconic styles like the Chanel classic flap bags and Lady Dior bags to attract strong interest. These styles were widely recognisable even among those who did not usually follow luxury fashion, she added. “We also expected prices to be slightly above normal resale levels because of the publicity surrounding the auction. However, some bids have gone much higher than anticipated,” Fung said. For example, a Chanel classic flap in caviar leather that was on auction sold for S$13,000. Comparable pre-owned pieces generally sell for below S$10,000, according to Fung. “The strong interest did not surprise us. The bid amounts did. The publicity and competitive atmosphere may be encouraging people to bid more aggressively,” Fung said, adding that some bidders may also be unfamiliar with the current retail and resale prices. Hotlotz charges a “buyer’s premium” of 20 per cent on top of the closing bid, which includes Singapore’s goods and services tax that can be waived for foreign buyers. Towards the end of each auction, if a bid is placed in the final five minutes before a lot closes, the bidding period for that lot is extended by a further five minutes. This continues until a full five minutes have elapsed without another bid having been placed, Hotlotz explained on its website. This is why all of the lots in an auction usually close only a few hours after the scheduled closing time. The assets from the money laundering case were handed over by police to audit firm Deloitte for liquidation in August last year. Proceeds would be paid into the government’s consolidated fund, which is similar to a bank account held by the government. According to the parliament website, Singapore’s revenue is paid into this fund and it is also used to provide for government spending. This article was first published by CNA

title: Letters | What Hong Kong educators can learn from Yidan Prize winners
description: Readers discuss the foundations that help a child arrive ready to learn, a key moment in a Hong Kong school’s history, and the value of Hongkong Post.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. In Hong Kong, a child’s education can be planned before the child can talk. The 2026 Yidan Prize laureates give that instinct an evidence base: factors shaping how well children learn are in motion long before their first day of class. Professor Paul W. Glewwe, the laureate for education research, has shown how socioeconomic circumstances, health and nutrition shape learning outcomes. He was instrumental in introducing children’s and parents’ literacy, numeracy and abstract-reasoning indicators into World Bank household surveys, and pioneered the use of randomised controlled trials to evaluate education programmes and policies. The education development laureates – Professor Susan P. Walker, Professor Sally Grantham-McGregor and Dr Susan M. Chang-Lopez – followed the evidence into the home. Their Reach Up approach helps caregivers talk, play and respond to children aged zero to four, using low-cost, culturally adaptable activities rooted in daily routines. It has been implemented in more than 21 countries through health, social protection, education and humanitarian systems. Its curriculum and materials are free, continuously evaluated and adapted. The common thread is a wider view of where learning happens. Glewwe makes the conditions surrounding learning visible; the Reach Up team turns research into practical support. Together, their work asks us to identify a child’s barrier, test a response and adapt support to local conditions. For Hong Kong, the lesson is additive. The Education Bureau’s digital education blueprint calls on schools to integrate artificial intelligence into learning. The laureates’ work points to what belongs alongside it: nutrition, health and responsive caregiving in a child’s earliest years. Kindergartens and primary schools could work with clinics and social service groups on voluntary family sessions demonstrating talk, play and responsive interaction. Simple multilingual activity cards could extend learning at home, with outreach beginning among families least able to buy private enrichment. Policymakers could pilot such support in representative communities, agree outcomes in advance and publish null results alongside positive ones. They should measure attendance, language development and social-emotional growth, not examination scores alone. Effective approaches could travel through health, parent education and community channels, supporting teachers rather than adding to their load. Hong Kong has the ambition and technology. The laureates supply a discipline: identify what holds a child back, then test whether the support offered moves them forward. AI may extend what teaching can do; it cannot replace the foundations that help a child arrive ready to learn. Marina Watt, doctoral student in education, University of Bristol A letter of significance in Kellett School’s history Fifty years ago, a parent in Hong Kong wrote to these pages asking a question that changed countless lives. That letter, penned by Joanne Elliott in 1976, sparked a conversation among families who shared a common belief that children deserved an ambitious, nurturing, British education in Hong Kong. From that conversation came a school that is now firmly part of Hong Kong educational history. Half a century later, that school of 44 children has grown into a thriving community of more than 1,600 students, yet the principles remain unchanged. Kellett is still parent-founded, parent-governed and not-for-profit, with an unwavering commitment to an education that fosters a love of learning and confidence for life. As Kellett celebrates its 50th anniversary, this milestone is not simply an opportunity to look back. It is a chance to thank Hong Kong for being our home and to reaffirm our commitment to the future. The letter that started our story was written because one parent believed more was possible for her child. Fifty years on, that same spirit drives us forward. In a rapidly changing world, our aim at Kellett is not just to keep pace with change, but to help define what a world-class education should look like for generations to come. Paul Tough, principal and CEO, Kellett School Hongkong Post cannot be compared with newcomers I refer to “Wider options for Hongkong Post” (September 5) , which points to the stiff competition posed by courier giants such as SF Express. Hongkong Post provides a well-priced service locally. Also, overseas delivery by Hongkong Post, with its first-class postal connections, beats the ever-changing commercial options. Last winter, the letter I sent by registered post to our law firm’s client in Hanover, Germany, coincided with a local train workers strike. I wondered whether the letter would reach, but the tracking system showed that the German postal service had made the delivery. The cost of private courier services for such tasks can be too high. Private companies can be very sensitive to market and economic upheaval, causing them to shake up, cut staff or even cease business. We should not treat companies established not long ago the same as a veteran government department, with over a century of history. Edmond Pang, Fanling

title: Japan asks for US$43 million to weed out cherry tree-devouring longhorn beetle
description: Further growth in the ‘invasive’ beetle population could make it difficult to enjoy cherry blossom viewing in the spring.
content: Japan’s Environment Ministry is stepping up measures against longhorn beetles that are devouring cherry trees, with a request for 6.7 billion yen (US$43 million) to counter invasive species in the next financial year’s initial budget. According to the ministry, the requested amount, which is an increase of 11 times the initial budget of 600 million yen for the 2026 financial year, will be used to eradicate the red-necked longhorn beetle and strengthen measures to protect trees, including plum and peach trees, from infestation. The ministry has said that further growth in the beetle population could cause agricultural damage, make it difficult to enjoy cherry blossom viewing in the spring, increase the risk of falling trees and affect ecosystems. In response to the nationwide damage, the environment and farm ministries set up a task force in July and adopted a strategy earlier this month, which pledged to provide local governments with technical and financial support. According to the ministry, the longhorn beetle is native to China, the Korean peninsula, Taiwan and Vietnam, among other places. The beetle measures about 2.5cm (one inch) to 4cm in length. It was first confirmed in Japan in 2012 and has since been spotted in various parts of the country. The adult beetles are most prevalent from May through August. The larvae hatch from eggs laid in cracks in trees and burrow into the wood, where they feed on the tree for two to three years before pupating. In 2018, the beetle was designated an “invasive alien species”. It is prohibited to breed, keep, import, sell or release it into the wild. To prevent the beetle from spreading further, some local governments have begun offering bounties to those who capture and kill it. The town of Kawajima in Saitama prefecture has paid 100 yen for each beetle, while the city of Oyama in Tochigi prefecture pays 500 yen for 10 beetle carcasses. The ministry said that for the 2026 financial year, an additional 600 million yen was allocated from the international tourist tax revenue to protect cherry trees as an “important tourism resource”. The ministry added that the sum for the next financial year has yet to be determined.

title: Bite-mark, DNA tests used to identify dogs after woman dies in suspected attack
description: Hong Kong environment chief says policies on handling strays will be reviewed after cyclist’s death from suspected attack in Yuen Long.
content: Hong Kong’s environment chief has vowed to review government policies on handling stray dogs after a cyclist was killed in a suspected canine attack in Yuen Long, while an insider has said that bite-mark analyses and DNA tests are being conducted on three dogs captured by authorities to confirm whether any were involved in the deadly incident. Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan made the promise on Monday morning, months after shelters warned of pets being abandoned in the New Territories amid land resumption operations. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD), which operates under Tse’s bureau, said early on Monday that it had worked with police to capture three stray mongrels near Pok Wai South Road on Sunday evening. The operation followed the death of a 27-year-old woman along the same road on Saturday after she was chased by dogs. The victim suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal. Aside from stray dogs, officers also spotted wild boars in the area. A source close to the investigation said on Monday that forensic pathologists were conducting bite-mark analyses and DNA tests on tissue that may have been left by the canines, to determine whether any of the three dogs had attacked the victim, noting the tests would take time to complete. An AFCD spokesman said all the captured dogs were mongrels and two were microchipped. The department would contact registered owners based on licence records and if sufficient evidence showed they had failed to meet their legal responsibilities, then they would be prosecuted. The spokesman added that the department would continue to coordinate with police and carry out further operations in the area to capture stray dogs and ensure public safety. Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, told the SCMP on Monday that one of the three dogs caught had a microchip under his name and that he was asked to give a statement on Wednesday. Luk said it was a common practice for dog rescuers to register rescued dogs under their name after treating their injuries or spaying them. If they were not properly microchipped and registered, such dogs risked being euthanised by authorities if captured after a biting incident. He said some owners were reluctant to have their pets microchipped so they could deny ownership and avoid responsibility when dog attacks occur. Tse expressed deep sadness over the cyclist’s death and offered condolences to her family. “This incident also serves as a reminder for us to look further into the situation to see how we could do better regarding stray dog operations, thereby further reducing the risks posed by stray dogs,” he said during a media briefing. Tse emphasised that the bureau aimed for a “proper and balanced” approach to managing stray dogs in the Northern Metropolis and would try its best to “avoid methods that require the euthanasia of dogs.” Without citing public complaint figures, Tse noted that the number of strays rounded up by the AFCD annually had dropped from more than 11,000 in 2002 to 400 in recent years, illustrating improved management. He said the AFCD would first assess a dog’s physical condition, personality and temperament after capturing or receiving the animal. In the vast majority of cases, the general approach was to spay and release the dogs, the minister said. However, aggressive or severely ill canines may be euthanised, which he described as the “best arrangement for the dog’s welfare and public safety.” He added that the AFCD adhered to guidelines from the World Organisation for Animal Health when handling stray dogs. In July, dog shelters told the South China Morning Post that more animals, including dogs, had been displaced in the New Territories during land resumption works for the Northern Metropolis megaproject. The Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, which is based in Yuen Long, reported receiving an average of 1.9 rescue calls per day in the first half of this year, up from 1.3 in 2025. However, Tse said that while investigations into Saturday’s incident were still ongoing, the likelihood that dogs displaced by clearance works were involved in the attack was “relatively low”. But he pledged to work with the Development Bureau to review strategies for managing dogs displaced by the Northern Metropolis development. Dr Jackie Yip Yin, the AFCD assistant director overseeing inspection and quarantine, said it was not immediately clear whether the three captured dogs were the ones that had chased the cyclist. “We will continue with our operation to capture unattended dogs near the area to safeguard public safety,” she said. Saturday’s incident marked the second suspected fatal dog attack in less than a month. In August, a 33-year-old woman who operated a canine training centre in Ta Kwu Ling was attacked by a dog at the facility and later found dead nearby. Days earlier, a mongrel with genetic traits of a mastiff also mauled two smaller dogs to death in Yuen Long’s town centre. Discussing ongoing operations, Wilson Wong Ka-keung, deputy district police commander for Yuen Long, said the force had mobilised drones to help locate stray dogs. The force has identified several hotspots for future patrols, with officers instructed to immediately report any further sightings to the AFCD. Tse on Monday also addressed the potential use of genetic tests rather than physical assessments to identify “fighting dogs”. The AFCD earlier said it was considering genetic testing as a supplementary tool for identifying breeds after enforcement action against suspected fighting dogs sparked public outrage. But Tse said that genetic testing “may not be a particularly good method” as dogs have interbred freely over time and many now carry fighting-dog genes. “The crucial point is whether possessing these genes could lead the dog to develop the stature, build and temperament of a fighting dog,” he said, asserting that physical examinations remained more effective for classification. He acknowledged there were borderline cases where dogs would be more difficult to assess, and invited veterinarians to contact the AFCD experts for professional help. In the event of a dispute, a statutory committee could make a final determination on whether a pet was a fighting dog, he added. Speaking on a radio show on Monday, Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung said authorities should consider more factors before deciding whether to install additional security cameras in the area, given the spot had a relatively low occurrence of crime. “Thieves may stop committing crimes out of fear, knowing that there is a security camera. But dogs will not stop biting [regardless of] surveillance,” he said. Nonetheless, he acknowledged that the latest dog attack could trigger fresh safety concerns extending beyond crime prevention.

title: Philippines tribe vows to stand ground against US-led Pax Silica: ‘listen to us’
description: The Aetas have been offered just 50 US cents per square metre of land to make way for the sprawling tech hub. All have refused.
content: Tribal leader Petronila Munoz walked across the sweeping Philippine grasslands she has called home for generations, uncertain about its future, as a sprawling tech hub for a US-led initiative takes shape. With little information and no prior consultation, the indigenous chieftain said her Aeta Hungey tribe was uncertain how much of their land could be affected or what would become of the livelihood it provided. “There’s still no clarity,” Munoz said inside the tribe’s traditional meeting hall. “What will happen to us? That’s our biggest question.” In April, the United States announced that the Philippines had joined Pax Silica, a US-led effort to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors and rare earth elements and reduce participating countries’ dependence on China. The Philippines has designated a 1,620-hectare (4,000-acre) site in New Clark City in Tarlac province, north of Manila, for a manufacturing hub aimed at producing high-end components for use in artificial intelligence data centres. The government estimates the initiative could attract up to US$70 billion in investment and create about 190,000 jobs, a major boost to a country with more than three million unemployed people. The project has a long timeline. No tenants have been confirmed. Plans to domestically process the country’s mineral resources could be even further away. For about 1,000 Aetas, however, the prospect of displacement is already here. In July, they received a letter from the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) warning that the project “could affect your occupied lands”. Munoz said visiting BCDA employees told them to leave by December and relocate to an area about 16 km (10 miles) from their current home, without providing a master plan showing which parts of their ancestral domains would be affected. She said the BCDA offered them just 30 pesos (50 US cents) per square metre (10 square feet) for their lands, an offer they all declined. “Our lives, our livelihood and our culture are tied to this ancestral land,” Munoz said. “Land is more important. Money runs out.” The BCDA declined to address specific questions about the Aetas’ situation and rejected a freedom of information request for the site’s official boundary map and geospatial data. It said the information was being “withheld temporarily until the official action is finalised or published”. At a Senate hearing last month, BCDA president Joshua Bingcang said the Aetas were living on government land. Like many indigenous groups in the Philippines, they hold no land title. Environmental impact Civic groups have also raised concerns about the project’s environmental impact, particularly the demand for water and electricity in a country plagued by droughts and rotational power outages. The US Statement Department said “environmental, water, energy, and community-impact studies” would inform the project’s design. “Before any major development happens, we expect rigorous stakeholder impact assessments will take place,” a representative said. Bingcang told the Senate that investors would be required to build their own power and water systems. Alvin Camba, research director at an AI firm focused on supply chains and risk assessment, said Manila’s close relationship with the United States could motivate investors to set up shop despite the power concerns. Last month, reports said Washington planned to warn countries they could be excluded from Pax Silica if they joined a rival framework backed by Beijing. “This is where the advantage of the Philippines comes in. The Philippines is the least affected by Chinese capital in Southeast Asia,” Camba said, adding that the country would offer foreign companies the ability to “disentangle” from China. Political economist Calixto Chikiamco said Pax Silica represented a “historic opportunity” for the Philippines to move beyond its traditional wheelhouse of microchip testing and packaging. “We have to open up to foreign investment so that technology transfer [to the Philippines] will happen,” he said. The BCDA had been conducting public consultations in Tarlac and nearby provinces, but the agency had yet to hold talks with her tribe, Munoz said. The Aetas remain uncertain if the government will help them build new homes or provide land to cultivate for income if they are moved. “I wish they would listen to us. They’re just talking among themselves,” she said, adding that she worried her tribe would not be qualified for the sort of new jobs Pax Silica promised. While a proponent of the initiative, Chikiamco said the government was doing “a terrible job” explaining the benefits and trade-offs it represented. Why do we have to be the ones to sacrifice for the kind of development they want? Petronila Munoz, Aeta Hungey tribal leader Camba agreed. “I would actually advise the Philippine government to be very transparent about what’s happening. A big problem is transparency.” Still, the benefits outweigh the risks, he said. “Every country that has … jump-started development has had to make sacrifices.” But 63-year-old Munoz, who hopes to be buried in her tribe’s traditional burial ground, said she would not leave, even if a backhoe flattened her home. “Why do we have to be the ones to sacrifice for the kind of development they want?” she asked.

title: Chinese woman in her 70s wakes up in coffin before dying for good 2 days later
description: Woman likely experienced ‘apparent death,’ a comatose state where vital signs drop to a nearly undetectable level, says doctor.
content: A woman in her 70s in northern China briefly exhibited signs of life after being placed in a coffin, but ultimately died two days later. The woman, from Hebei province, had been suffering from cerebral thrombosis for decades and was also battling cancer, according to reports from mainland sources. After doctors concluded that her cancer was no longer treatable, her family brought her home for end-of-life care. On September 8, relatives found no apparent signs of life and placed her in a refrigerated coffin to preserve her body while awaiting the return of family members from out of town for a final farewell. However, the following evening, her daughter-in-law heard faint “humming” sounds coming from inside the coffin. The family promptly removed the elderly woman from it. When relatives arrived on September 11, the woman had regained consciousness and could open her eyes, although she remained in critical condition and was unable to eat or drink. Sadly, she died later that night and was laid to rest on September 13, with family members attending the funeral. The incident was shared online by a family member, leading to questions regarding its authenticity. The poster defended the account, stating: “No one would fabricate a story about the life and death of their own family member.” Some local residents also claimed to have heard about the incident in the village. According to a village official, the family used the refrigeration function of the coffin, rather than the deep-freezing mode, to keep the body cool while awaiting the return of relatives. This arrangement is believed to have enabled the woman, who was reportedly in a state of extremely low physiological activity, to exhibit signs of life. Doctors indicated that the case may have involved “apparent death,” a condition in which vital signs become exceedingly difficult to detect. Individuals in such a state may display barely detectable breathing and heartbeat, experience a slowed metabolism, and fall into a deep coma, as reported by Health Times. Medical professionals adhere to strict criteria when determining death and continue resuscitation efforts even when a patient appears to show no signs of life. This unusual case has generated significant discussion on mainland social media. One online observer commented: “This kind of ‘return to life’ must have been a painful experience for the woman. I hope she has found peace in the afterlife.” “The family should have obtained a formal death certificate from a hospital first,” remarked another. A third user reflected on traditional mourning customs, noting: “In the past, families often kept the deceased at home for three days. Today, everything moves so quickly that some individuals are cremated soon after being declared dead.”

title: As Chinese consumption of gold jewellery slumps 34%, sellers look to markets abroad: WGC
description: Domestic gold jewellers are seeking to leverage advanced crafting techniques as market sees turbulence, says World Gold Council executive.
content: Chinese gold jewellers are seeking opportunities in the Middle East and India, leveraging their advanced crafting technologies as the industry struggles amid the precious metal’s price volatility, according to an international association for the sector. At the most recent Jewellery & Gem World Hong Kong fair, buyers from the two regions accounted for most visitors, said Wang Lixin, China CEO of the World Gold Council, in a recent interview with the South China Morning Post. The interest was driven by the increasing demand for new jewellery products as the metal’s price fluctuates rapidly and the progress of Chinese producers in so-called hard pure gold, a new product category using a crafting technique that made the jewellery thinner and harder without contributing extra weight, Wang added. As consumers in the Middle East and India favoured inlaid jewellery, Wang expected Chinese jewellers could capitalise on their expertise to find local buyers. “In the past, overseas buyers from these markets have traditionally sought out Chinese manufacturers primarily to find cheaper suppliers for existing designs. But now, [Chinese firms] need to add value to the products with designs and technologies,” Wang said. China’s consumption of gold jewellery slumped 34 per cent year on year to 132 tonnes in the first half of the year, while the sales of gold coins and bars for investment increased further by 28 per cent year on year to 339 tonnes, data from the China Gold Association showed. In the second quarter, India surpassed China to become the world’s largest gold jewellery market, accounting for 27 per cent of global demand in the April-June quarter, according to a WGC report. “The domestic market is currently undergoing a period of adjustment and transition characterised by the interplay of macroeconomic factors and high gold prices,” Wang said. “Challenges certainly exist, and they are not likely to subside any time soon.” To connect overseas buyers with Chinese producers, the WGC organised major Middle Eastern wholesalers to visit Shenzhen to inspect factories and showrooms and also facilitated visits by the largest retailers in India to global exhibitions to explore collaborations. Yuehao Jewellery, a Shenzhen-based producer whose origins trace back to 1926, also noted an increase in clients from the Middle East and India, adding that they saw strong interest from Japan and South Korea, said Sharon Weng, vice president of branding and products. To cater to the Japanese market, Yuehao launched two series featuring “black gold” last year, in which electroplating or oxidation were used to give gold a black appearance, Weng added. Gold prices remained resilient despite the higher probability of further interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, as bullion was expected to be backed by the continuous buying from global central banks amid sticky geopolitical tensions. Wang of WGC said jewellery producers should double down on improving crafting techniques and design capabilities, areas in which Chinese companies were working hard, rather than focusing on the high cost of materials. “The manufacturing and processing capabilities of our domestic manufacturers are completely different from what they were five years ago,” Wang emphasised. “It is truly changing with each passing day.”

title: In Focus | As the US weighs restrictions on cloud computing, how will China’s AI sector adapt?
description: If Washington expands its tech blockade to include cloud networks, China’s AI sector will face its most severe choke point since the chip bans.
content: When Chinese artificial intelligence developers want to train their next-generation frontier models, they all face the same daunting wall: they cannot legally buy the world’s most powerful AI chips. However, the country’s tech giants and start-ups have still managed to quietly keep pace with global rivals. Their secret is an elusive workaround: moving heavy training workloads across borders through the cloud. By setting up proxy entities in foreign jurisdictions, domestic firms have for years leased server space in data centres across Southeast Asia, Japan and the Middle East, according to a broker in Shenzhen who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the matter. Under contracts signed by non-Chinese entities, models have been trained on cutting-edge Nvidia processors housed thousands of miles, away outside the reach of US authorities, he said. That critical lifeline could be on the verge of collapsing. Washington is reportedly moving to expand its tech blockade from physical hardware to cloud networks. As the US Congress weighs legislation to restrict foreign remote access and executive agencies review cloud-leasing loopholes, China’s AI sector faces its most severe choke point since the chip bans began. The impending US crackdown threatens to reshape the global AI ecosystem, challenging Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, squeezing Nvidia’s international revenues and forcing Beijing into an acceleration of its domestic chip push. The cloud escape hatch Developing AI infrastructure across borders has long been common practice among Chinese developers looking to bypass hardware bans while avoiding US regulatory hurdles, according to observers. “For a long time, Chinese AI companies have circumvented chip export bans by leasing overseas data centres,” said Arisa Liu, chief director and research fellow at Taiwan Industry Economics Services, a unit of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research. “[This] has indeed contributed a significant amount of overseas market demand to Nvidia.” To make good use of these remote servers, some Chinese teams have taken extraordinary measures to overcome technical bottlenecks. Chinese engineers personally carried hard drives storing 80 terabytes of data from Beijing to Malaysia to train an AI model at a local data centre, saving months of digital transfer time, The Wall Street Journal reported last year. Driven by the global AI boom, demand for high-performance computing power has sent global cloud rental rates soaring. Leading AI infrastructure provider Nebius Group raised rental prices on certain Nvidia chips by roughly 30 per cent in June, with a further 21 per cent increase to come into effect on October 1. Hyperscaler rates for Nvidia’s A100 processors rose to US$3.75 per hour in late August, up from US$3.71 a month earlier, according to tracking firm Silicon Data. To maintain secrecy and navigate cross-border payments, some Chinese teams have even executed cloud-leasing transactions via blockchain-based smart contracts and paid in cryptocurrency to keep both parties hidden behind anonymous digital wallets, the Journal reported in 2024. However, the regulatory net in Washington is rapidly closing. The administration of US President Donald Trump was reviewing remote access arrangements and was working on policies to curb it, according to reports by Bloomberg and The Information. In January, the US House passed the Remote Access Security Act, which, if signed into law, would expand American export controls to remote cloud computing access. “If the US passes and implements relevant legislation that extends restrictions from physical chips to cloud leasing, Nvidia’s overall sales growth momentum will inevitably be curtailed to some extent,” Liu said. Legal experts noted that current compliance remained a grey area. Currently, there are “no regulations or similar provisions in place to restrict or prohibit” such remote access, said Hong Jiayang, managing partner of US law firm Joint-Win Partners. The only measure that came close to banning the practice was the “AI Diffusion Rule”, said Hong, who focuses on trade compliance. The regulation, which requires US cloud service providers to exercise caution when providing cloud services for Chinese AI models, was introduced by the Biden administration in January 2025 but rescinded by the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) after Trump came to power. The Remote Access Security Act “was introduced for a similar purpose”, Hong said. However, once it goes into effect, “the businesses of cloud service giants such as Oracle and Amazon.com will be significantly impacted, which is bound to provoke a strong backlash”. Even if the US did not enact legislation to regulate cloud services, the BIS could “theoretically impose penalties on data centres and even model developers that use illegally smuggled chips” on the grounds of “General Prohibition 10”, which penalises transactions conducted with knowledge that a violation has occurred, Hong explained. “Hi-tech companies should avoid becoming entangled in such legal liabilities at all times,” he added. Southeast Asia’s data centre boom If Washington closes the cloud computing loophole, the immediate shock waves will hit Southeast Asia, one of the world’s fastest-growing data centre hubs. Local data centre capacity in the region was projected to expand at 35 per cent each year from 2023 through 2028, outpacing the global average of 15 per cent, according to market intelligence platform Speeda. Chinese tech giants, including Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – Tencent Holdings and TikTok owner ByteDance, have spent years building out regional infrastructure to serve the Chinese market. Asian hyperscalers preferred the region for several reasons, including “competitive development costs across construction, equipment and human capital; and lower operating costs”, according to Vivian Wong, lead analyst for APAC at DC Byte, a market consultancy in the data centre industry. If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market Alex Cordovil, Dell’Oro Group “If you want to win customers in a market, you need availability zones in that market … Southeast Asia is the natural first step for that expansion, given proximity, existing business ties, land and power availability,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group, a market research firm in the telecommunications, security and data centre industries. Beyond local demands, the region has attracted international workloads, “including from Chinese internet and cloud companies”, Cordovil said. “Export controls are part of that picture: certain accelerator architectures are only available outside mainland China, so workloads that depend on them naturally gravitate to locations where that supply is accessible.” The region also offers competitive energy economics. In Southeast Asia, electricity prices average US$118 per megawatt hour (MWh), with the lowest in Indonesia at US$60 per MWh, according to Wood Mackenzie, a consultancy focusing on the energy, chemicals, renewables, metals and mining. While higher than China’s average industrial rates - between 600 yuan (US$89) and 700 yuan per MWh, and half that in energy-rich regions like Inner Mongolia and Guizhou – Southeast Asia remains cheaper than US hubs like northern Virginia and Silicon Valley, where prices range between US$70 and US$120 per MWh. In comparison, European centres like Germany and Ireland see prices ranging between €150 (US$174) and €250 per MWh, according to state-backed media China Energy News. Should remote access become a constraint for certain customers in Southeast Asia, it would “likely create a transient imbalance between supply and demand in the region”, he said, adding that the imbalance was expected to be “short lived” as demand was deep. Wong held a similar view, saying that “any released capacity is likely to be taken up relatively quickly by other customers”. The domestic bottleneck For Chinese AI firms, losing overseas cloud access will lay bare a troubling reality: despite heavy state investment, domestic hardware is not yet fully equipped to handle frontier model training at scale. Despite China’s push for self-sufficiency in chips, the country’s most advanced AI models are still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP previously reported. The AI development life cycle involves training and inference – the use of a trained model to generate new content. Systems such as DeepSeek-V4 and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 have been successfully adapted to Chinese hardware for inference work only. For now, the most advanced Nvidia chips remain unavailable in China, including the B200, B300, H100 and H800. Chinese firms either use Nvidia chips they have in inventory or gain access through cloud computing. The H200, the latest of Nvidia’s Hopper-series chips but a generation behind the Blackwell family, was approved for import by both Washington and Beijing but is only available in small quantities. ByteDance and Tencent Holdings each received about 10,000 H200s and a few other Chinese customers obtained shipments of a similar size, the Financial Times reported in August. “There is a massive gap between this quantity and the actual demand of such top-tier tech giants, which often consume tens of thousands or even over 100,000 advanced [graphics processing units],” said Liu of the Taiwan institution. Nvidia in late August reported that shipments of H200s to China accounted for less than 1 per cent of its US$89 billion data-centre revenue in the quarter that ended July 26. However, it said it did not expect any data-centre computing revenue from China in the following quarter. Liu added that even though Nvidia’s income might be temporarily curtailed if the US imposed the ban on remote access, “this shortfall may be partially offset by massive orders from other international tech giants” given strong AI demand globally. Accelerating self-reliance If the US bans Chinese companies from renting Nvidia-powered data centres overseas, it may lead to higher domestic rental rates, the Shenzhen-based data centre broker noted. For now, rates for B300 chips outside China are two to three times higher than local prices, not including differences in electricity costs. Even if there were no restriction on renting overseas data centres, replacing Nvidia with domestic chips was “the main trend”, said a semiconductor designer at one of China’s biggest chipmakers, who requested anonymity. “Who knows if Nvidia processors have back doors,” the person said. Nvidia has repeatedly said that there are no back doors, kill switches or spyware in its products. Some Chinese teams have started using local chips for AI training. In June, Meituan released LongCat-2.0, a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that it said was fully trained and run on a 50,000-card domestic computing power cluster, without naming the supplier. Huawei Technologies’ rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun expected a major domestic shift towards its AI computing infrastructure for model training next year. The semiconductor design engineer said the best domestic AI chip currently was the Ascend 950 from Huawei Technologies, not only for its performance but for the whole ecosystem from architecture to networks. Huawei announced last week that the next-generation Ascend 960DT, designed for model training, will be ready in the first quarter of 2027, nine months ahead of schedule. However, transferring training workloads from Nvidia to domestic chips is a steep engineering bottleneck. The hurdles included the software ecosystem, as Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) platform has long been the industry standard for AI development, the SCMP reported in August. Migrating existing workflows to Huawei’s Ascend chips could add at least 50 per cent to training time and cost, according to researcher James Wang. Still, China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade. The supply of advanced-node wafers made using 7-nanometre processes and below was projected to grow at 46 per cent annually between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a recent report. That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035 from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank. As Washington moves to extend its tech blockade from hardware shipments to virtual server networks, Chinese AI developers may soon lose their refuge in the cloud. What remains to be seen is whether the squeeze will stall China’s frontier AI ambitions or simply accelerate its push towards technological self-sufficiency.

title: Mariko Mori’s ‘All That Shines’ at Mori Art Museum: inside her landmark Tokyo exhibition
description: From 1970s anime to ancient Jōmon culture and Buddhist thought, the Japanese artist’s retrospective explores cosmic connections.
content: Growing up in the outskirts of Tokyo in the 70s, Japanese artist Mariko Mori has fond memories of the popular science-fiction series Astro Boy. “I was part of the generation of Osamu Tezuka’s animation and this was his projection of the future,” she recalls. “I remember playing with my friends, thinking about what the future may look like … we imagined different worlds.” Decades later, not much has changed for her. Mori is still imagining alternate realities and inviting viewers into these worlds of her making. Now 59, she has become known for works ranging from provocative performances in the heart of major metropolises to ethereal installations embedded in nature. From delving into the depths of human consciousness through technology to paying homage to prehistoric sites across cultures, her work invites us to reflect on what binds us together. From October 31 to March 28, 2027, a landmark retrospective, “All That Shines”, traces more than three decades of her artistic journey at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum. Her first major exhibition in her home country since 2002, the show is a collaboration with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, and curated by Alexandra Munroe and Mami Kataoka. Traversing themes of archaeology, science, spirituality and technology, the exhibition brings several works to Japan for the first time while offering a glimpse into Mori’s process through her sketches, notebooks and ancient objects from her personal collection. The daughter of an art historian mother and inventor father, Mori began her career studying fashion design and briefly worked as a model in the 80s. She then returned to school to study art, first in London and then in New York. In her early works, she instinctively began using her own body as a medium. The show begins with works from the 90s, when she assumed multiple striking guises, ranging from a sultry cyborg riding the subway to a futuristic goddess floating above a lotus flower. Drawing from Japanese animé culture, her performances explored timely issues of gender stereotypes, consumerism and post-humanism. Gradually, however, her focus shifted from the concerns of the physical world towards metaphysical questions and Buddhist ideas. A turning point came when her father passed away in her early 20s. “It was such a big loss. I started to search and question: ‘Where did he go?’” she says. Mori began investigating quantum physics and the ideas of parallel universes but hit a dead end. She then turned to Zen Buddhism and Esoteric Buddhism to explore reincarnation: “I had a couple of spiritual experiences that led me to understand the idea of oneness and the existence of an invisible world.” Soon, she began unpacking these through artwork and installations. At first, Mori continued to use her body in works such as the video installation Link, 2000. In it, she appears in a bodysuit lying horizontally inside her “body capsule”, a translucent, coffin-sized Plexiglas pod. In the work, her body appears to have transcended time and space as she lies motionless in the heart of frenetic city streets, including Hong Kong, as well as at ancient sites such as the Giza pyramids. Over time, Mori disappeared from her works altogether, as she embraced more intangible themes and invited viewers into immersive experiences. A highlight of the exhibition is Wave UFO, 1999–2002, one of Mori’s most ambitious installations, which she created with the help of scientists and engineers. The work has travelled to 11 cities across the globe, including Venice, where it was presented as part of the 51st Venice Biennale in 2005, but this is the first time it has been exhibited in Japan. It is a futuristic teardrop-shaped structure designed for three people. Once inside, the three participants wear special headsets that project images of their brainwaves overhead using biofeedback technology. If all three enter an alpha-wave state, a circle of light appears. A video animation exploring a journey into deeper consciousness is then projected onto the ceiling of the structure. “The idea was that you entered the artwork as individuals but through experiencing this work, I’m hoping people release the idea of division, and can experience a connected world,” she says. At the time, the work was groundbreaking as few artists were harnessing technology to explore human consciousness in this way. “It was like a new vocabulary for art,” she says. “I thought that the possibility of using a new medium by collaborating with engineers and scientists could lead to new kinds of ideas – a new world and new vision.” Beyond exploring the ideas of unity among humankind, Mori began to create work with the aim of deepening viewers’ connection with the natural world. In the 90s, she started travelling to remote natural sites including the Dead Sea in Israel and the Silk Road outpost Turpan in China. “I was confronted with the vastness of nature, especially when I arrived in Arizona’s Painted Desert,” she says. “Humans think we are the centre of the world but we are so small compared to nature. I realised that we are so vulnerable.” Eventually, she turned her attention to prehistoric sites, from Idojiri and Oyu in Japan to Orkney in Scotland, where she became fascinated by both Jōmon and Celtic ideas, and their relationship to nature and the cosmos. Some of the most profound works to emerge from these explorations – such as Primal Rhythm: Sun Pillar, 2011, a crystal-like column rising from a rock in Seven Light Bay on Japan’s Miyako Island – are embedded in remote natural landscapes. The translucent tower casts a shadow across the bay when aligned with the sun at the winter solstice. As part of the Rio Olympics’ cultural programme in 2016, she created Ring: One with Nature, 2016, a luminous acrylic ring. Suspended above the Véu da Noiva waterfall in Brazil, it changes colour throughout the day and becomes golden when it aligns with the sun at the southern hemisphere’s winter solstice. A new immersive video installation captures footage of both of these sites. “I wanted to illustrate the feeling of being in front of these works and share some essence of it,” the artist explains. Mori sees art as a means to rekindle our primal relationship with the natural world. “In prehistoric times, our remote ancestors took the position of being caretakers who honoured nature,” she says. “It’s something that the modern human lost, but it’s still within us because we are an extension of nature.” The Japanese exhibition title, “Sansan”, which means “shining”, echoes these ideas. “It’s not just referring to the visible shine of the sun, planets or moon. It’s a reminder that we ourselves are shining,” explains Mori. “Every living being shines.” “Mariko Mori: All That Shines” shows at Mori Art Museum, Tokyo from October 31 to March 28, 2027

title: Style Edit: Chow Tai Fook’s Song collection gives the Chinese drum a golden update
description: Double-drum forms, gourd motifs and diamond-set details express blessings, family ties and traditions passed down through the generations.
content: Few objects carry the cultural weight of the Chinese drum. Its sound has long marked moments of ceremony and celebration, from ancient rituals to family gatherings, where its rhythm has come to signify harmony, prosperity and shared joy. For Chow Tai Fook, the drum now finds a new expression in gold and diamonds with Song, a collection that translates one of China’s most enduring symbols into contemporary jewellery. The collection takes its name from the Chinese character “頌”, associated with praise, and draws on the visual language of the drum rather than attempting a literal interpretation. At its centre is a distinctive double-drum silhouette, formed by two contrasting circular elements. The smaller form sits above the larger one, creating a visual dialogue between Heaven and Earth – an idea deeply embedded in Chinese philosophy. Together, the two shapes suggest blessings descending from above and prosperity rising from the earth. There is another layer to the design. Seen as a whole, the paired forms recall the rippling movement of sound waves spreading from a drumbeat, while their outline also echoes the auspicious shape of a gourd, traditionally associated with good fortune, well-being and abundance. The result is a piece of jewellery whose symbolism is quietly woven into its proportions and geometry. Angular contours reinterpret the form of the Chinese character “頌”, while square elements evoke the shape of a home. Roof-like lines suggest shelter and family, bringing an architectural quality to the designs. An interlocking triangular detail recalls an hourglass, a reference to the passage of time and the idea of blessings being carried forward from one generation to the next. The craftsmanship reflects the same theme throughout the collection – diamond-set halos follow the rounded profile of the drum, while carefully worked textures recreate its characteristic riveted surface. The effect is tactile rather than merely decorative, giving the gold a sense of depth and movement. Layered three-dimensional engraving and nano-layered polishing further refine the surfaces. Traditional goldsmithing techniques meet contemporary technology to reproduce the precise, orderly texture of the drum in miniature. A concealed clasp, inspired by the form of a drumstick, is integrated into each piece. The paired elements can be worn together as a complete composition or separated to reveal individual forms, giving necklaces, bracelets, rings and earrings a versatility that moves easily between everyday dressing and more formal occasions. For Chow Tai Fook, the collection also continues a broader dialogue between Chinese heritage and contemporary luxury. Founded in 1929, the house has built its identity around combining traditional craftsmanship with modern design, while its signature collections – including Rouge and Joie – have explored different facets of Chinese culture. Song extends that conversation through an object whose significance is both historical and deeply familiar. The Chinese drum has always been about more than music. Its rhythm gathers people, marks occasions and carries wishes into the future. Song turns the idea of rhythm into jewellery through gold, diamonds and texture. Each piece is designed to reflect the joy and blessings associated with music and celebration. The collection also looks at how jewellery carries meaning over time, becoming part of family traditions and something that can be passed from one generation to the next.

title: Style Edit: Zegna’s new Hong Kong store at Harbour City embodies an Alpine-inspired retail vision
description: Natural materials and curved interiors frame the Italian maison’s expanded menswear offering, from tailoring and leisurewear to footwear and fragrances.
content: For a house built on top-notch textiles, Zegna has long understood that luxury is as much about atmosphere as it is about a beautifully cut jacket. The brand’s new Hong Kong boutique – or negozio, Italian for “store” – brings that approach to Tsim Sha Tsui’s Harbour City shopping complex, where a 250-square-metre space places warm materials, soft architecture, subtle Alpine inspiration and a full menswear wardrobe at the centre of the customer experience. Located on the ground floor of Gateway Arcade, the new store is Zegna’s first Hong Kong location to adopt the maison’s latest retail design. The facade makes for an elegantly understated entrance: a signature wooden pattern set above two walls of travertine marble. Beyond it, the boutique is arranged as a sequence of distinct but connected areas, beginning with a bright space dedicated to leisurewear and showcasing tailoring, shoes and fragrance. Inside, contoured dropped ceilings and curved travertine platforms direct the eye, giving the grand scale of the space a more intimate feel and unhurried rhythm. Embodying the contemporary vision of Zegna’s artistic director, Alessandro Sartori, the design takes cues from Oasi Zegna, the spectacular 100-square-kilometre nature reserve in the Biellese Alps that surrounds the company’s historic wool mill and remains a central reference point for the family-led Italian label. Natural materials and a palette of wood and stone lend the Harbour City interior a sense of calm – it’s an urban setting, but one that nods to the bucolic landscape from which the brand’s textile heritage has emerged. That heritage began in 1910, when Ermenegildo Zegna founded the business in northern Italy. More than a century on, Zegna remains part of the Ermenegildo Zegna Group and is still led by the Zegna family. Its original expertise in fabric has evolved into a broader vision of men’s dressing, spanning tailoring, leisurewear, footwear, accessories and fragrance. The shift is also apparent in the company’s contemporary attitude: once closely associated with formal suiting, Zegna now presents a more expansive wardrobe, including its bestselling Triple Stitch sneaker collection. At Harbour City, the entrance opens onto the leisurewear selection, where visitors will find key pieces such as Il Conte chore jackets, Triple Stitch shoes, the brand’s signature Mocassin loafers and the new Memorie fragrances. The line-up is a concise expression of how the house now approaches modern menswear: tempering formal craftsmanship with the ease and utility required by a less rigid way of living. The store arrives alongside Zegna’s fall/winter 2026 Su Misura campaign. In a world flooded with fast fashion, Su Misura takes the opposite approach. Italian for “custom-made”, its premise is that garments should not only be worn, but also kept, remembered and passed on. That sentiment also informs the label’s emphasis on supply chain transparency: since 2024, its Oasi Cashmere and Oasi Lino fibres have been certified as 100 per cent traceable. The new address also makes a statement about Zegna’s wider position in Hong Kong’s fashion retail landscape: a place where the boundaries between tailored dressing and leisurewear are increasingly fluid. Here, the house’s familiar hallmarks – superior textiles, understated construction and relaxed Italian style – are presented as elements of a complete wardrobe rather than separate categories. The result is a space that invites careful browsing, whether for a precisely tailored piece, a pair of finely crafted shoes or a new fragrance. It’s a forward-looking retail setting, but one shaped by the preference for longevity over novelty. In a city accustomed to high-gloss luxury retail, the new Zegna negozio makes a more restrained suggestion: focus less on spectacle and more on texture, comfort and the finest materials.

title: Style Edit: 45R marks 20 years in Ginza with new 4-storey flagship store
description: The Japanese brand’s latest Tokyo address brings indigo-dyed denim and seasonal collections into a striking new space, with matcha and art on the top floor.
content: After 20 years in Ginza, Japanese fashion label 45R this month opened a new four-storey flagship in the Tokyo district, ahead of the brand’s 50th anniversary next year. The Seiko Ginza 5-chome Building now houses the label’s denim and natural indigo collections among old brick, stone and warm wood. At street level, reclaimed details shape the entrance. A teak facade and Takine stone frame an automatic door fashioned from chestnut. Just inside, a small garden separates the street from the shop, with salvaged stepping stones underfoot. 45R worked with traditional carpentry atelier Sankakuya, using solid wood and vintage materials rather than composite boards and glue. The approach draws on a Japanese building tradition in which structures and materials can be dismantled, relocated and reassembled. Across its four floors, chestnut, teak, hinoki (Japanese cypress), keyaki (Japanese zelkova) and ash have been selected for their grain and scent. The same interest in materials that change over time runs through 45R’s denim and indigo-dyed pieces, designed to soften, fade, and become personal through use. On the first floor, the focus is on the label’s core wardrobe: selvedge denim (a premium denim that develops a distinctive fade with wear), denim shirts, T-shirts and bandanas alongside the gender-neutral 908 line. Chestnut display tables and a textured, naguri-finished rear wall sit alongside a teak fitting-room floor in the same tactile treatment. The result is characterful without being theatrical. The second floor turns to seasonal womenswear and Yasuminate, a presentation styled by 45R’s chief designer and executive director, Yasumi Inoue. The space also carries forward elements of the brand’s former Ginza shop, including the familiar curved R-wall and a Bubinga-wood display table reused and reworked for its new setting. Reclaimed keyaki columns and chestnut latticework extend the sense of continuity. Indigo takes centre stage on the third floor at Ai Shokunin (indigo artisan), the brand’s second space dedicated to its blue-hued craft after the one at the iconic Hankyu Umeda department store in Osaka. Here, 45R traces its entire process, from cultivating indigo plants through to dyeing and garment making, while a sewing room keeps the focus on the labour behind the finished pieces. Indigo-toned cypress flooring and pearlescent blue plaster provide the backdrop for “Ai-hiko” and “Ai-hime”, boy and girl figurines by sculptor Satoshi Yabuuchi that depict stages of the dyeing process. The fourth floor, Chabatei, shifts the emphasis from wardrobe to hospitality. Here, matcha is served alongside a programme of exhibitions by Japanese artists, with 24 planned each year. Wood-fired hexagonal floor tiles, a cypress-bark roof and a counter made from kihada (Amur cork tree) lend the space the calm of a small pavilion. In a district defined by newness, 45R makes a case for materials that improve with time.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong’s 5-year plan plays it too safe
description: The series of anticipatory goals – only five out of 22 are binding – gives the impression of a cautious, not confident, government.
content: For the first time, Hong Kong’s chief executive rolled out his policy address together with a five-year plan for the city. The much anticipated release of these two supremely important documents – the final policy address of John Lee Ka-chiu’s current term as well as the first five-year blueprint in the city’s history – cements a road map for Hong Kong for the next five years. There were few surprises, although there shouldn’t have been. By combining the consultations for the five-year plan and the policy address, the administration made clear from the get-go the importance of Hong Kong aligning with the country’s plans – deepening economic integration, pushing ahead with the Northern Metropolis, leveraging Hong Kong’s traditional strengths, upgrading more of what we do well and supercharging our capacity to connect the country with the world. There has been very little disagreement on the desired destination and none over the need for Hong Kong to deliver on expectations set in the nation’s five-year plan. To that end, the chief executive has set goals in a range of areas. There are 22 indicators in Hong Kong’s five-year plan. Of these, only five have binding targets while 17 have anticipatory goals. Interestingly, it looks like the government has the most confidence in meeting environmental protection goals. Four of the indicators on the government’s to-do list are under environmental protection and all of them are binding. For a city that couldn’t even get its residents to pay for their own trash, with the Municipal Solid Waste Charging Scheme crashing and burning before it could hit the ground, that is intriguing. One wonders where the new-found confidence in environmental protection is coming from or if the government has set itself up for success with easier goals. The only other binding goal on the list is “‘Spade-ready sites’ available in the Northern Metropolis in five years”, one of the 14 items under “Economy, innovation and infrastructure development”: 900 hectares are to be available by 2030-31. The government should have been more ambitious for the other goals. Some of these should be easy-peasy. Take, for instance, being an “international cross-boundary wealth management centre”. We are already ranked first globally. Why would strengthening that position be an “anticipatory” goal? What these anticipatory goals suggest, especially when it comes to items like “median monthly employment earnings of employed persons” and “real gross domestic product growth”, is that the government has taken an overly cautious stance. Of course, we know we are at the whim of geopolitical and prevailing economic conditions, but should the goal of achieving GDP growth “within a reasonable range” be anticipatory? One would hope median monthly employment earnings are going to be “in line with economic growth” without this having to be set as a goal, let alone an anticipatory one. Unfortunately, these goals fall way short of the confidence Lee has expressed. What happened to being “firmly convinced that the [five-year] plan, and its vision for economic and social development will … safeguard and improve people’s livelihoods”? What about Lee’s direct answer to a Hongkonger’s question about what these economic issues have to do with ordinary residents? Lee said that he wants “every one” of us “to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment”. Maybe the authors of the five-year plan didn’t get the memo but with these anticipatory goals, which essentially translate as “if all goes well, we’ll strive to make them happen, but there are no guarantees”, the blueprint doesn’t exactly inspire confidence. Rather it seems to come with the sort of fine print one sees in bad deals. When we are nearly doubling our investment in innovation as a percentage of GDP and boosting new industries, the government can’t just say it anticipates modest results if all goes well. Funding for the new projects takes money away from others – we are shutting schools, for example. Speaking of which, the government has chosen to expand the baby bonus scheme even though the education secretary has said the declining pupil population is an irreversible trend. We are also supersizing our three new university towns, but the government is effectively saying: don’t come to us for money. Our education chief has said institutions that don’t require a loan will be favoured. Cognitive dissonance is beginning to set in. Is our government confident this is the way we should be headed? Yes, but fingers crossed? Or yes, but none of us can be held accountable if things don’t quite work out?

title: Asian Games, day 2: Yu Zidi takes gold, Haughey defends 200m title, Ho wins silver
description: China teen Yu Zidi adds second gold in women’s 200m IM, Siobhan Haughey, Ian Ho add to Hong Kong medal haul on Monday.
content: China’s Yu Zidi added another Asian Games gold to an already glittering resume on Monday, after Siobhan Haughey had defended her 200m freestyle title and Ian Ho Yentou grabbed silver in a fast 50m race. Yu moved through the gears in the women’s 200m individual medley at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, and her time of two minutes, 06.10 seconds, was an Asian record. That mark had been set by compatriot Yu Yiting when she won the race in Hangzhou three years ago, but the record holder was no match for her 13-year-old teammate and had to settle for silver in 2:07.99. Japan’s Mio Narita took bronze in 2:10.40. Minutes earlier, Haughey had completed a victory that was just as emphatic, and Ho had done well to hold on in a men’s 50m freestyle that also happened at record pace. Haughey got clear of the field early and stayed there, winning comfortably in a time of one minute, 54.96 seconds. China’s Li Jiaping was second in 1:56.58, while compatriot Liu Yaxin took bronze in 1:57.53. Hong Kong debutant Gilaine Ma, who won silver alongside Haughey in the women’s 4x100m relay on Sunday, finished fifth in 1:59.75. Moments before, Ho had held on in a fast final won by South Korea’s Kim Young-beon in a Games record time of 21.66. Ho came in just behind in 21.76, with Kim’s fellow South Korean Ji Yu-chan third in 21.94. Expectations for Haughey are always high and never more than from herself. While she finished well ahead of Li, her time was some way off the 1:54.12, a Games record she posted to win the same event in 2023. “I’m really happy to win a gold medal,” Haughey said. “Maybe the time wasn’t as fast as I expected, but my goal today was just to achieve my best for today. I gave it my all, and even though the time wasn’t quite what I imagined, I’m still satisfied with it.” Ho, meanwhile, said he had not held any expectations going into the race after what he said had been “a pretty tough” season, despite winning National Games gold in November. “Training this year has been more challenging, as recovery starts to get a bit harder,” the 29-year-old said. “The time is great. Every time I go under 22 [seconds], I’m happy. I think it’s a good result and I congratulate the Koreans. They’ve been great.” Haughey’s gold was not Hong Kong’s first of the games however, that honour was claimed earlier in the day by Lydia Sham Hui-yu, who won the women’s wushu changquan at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall. One of the city’s two flag bearers at the opening ceremony in Nagoya, Sham scored 9.713 points to see off the challenge of Macau’s Sou Cho-man, who took silver with 9.710, and Eugenia Diva Widodo of Indonesia, whose 9.706 was good enough for bronze. “I really can’t believe it, because this is my third time competing at the Asian Games, so it’s been eight years for 1.5 minutes of competition, and then it ends. I don’t know what happened, but I just tried my best,” Sham said. “And as I’m the flag bearer for Hong Kong as well the pressure just adds on with that. But I’m proud of myself, because I was able to bear the pressure and go up without any mistakes, and I’m more than satisfied.” Sham’s performance set the tone for a relatively successful morning for the city’s delegation, and shortly after at the Gamagori City Triathlon Venue, triathletes Bailee Brown, Cade Wright, Oscar Coggins and Robin Elg grabbed the bronze medal they need to secure their sport’s elite status in Hong Kong. Elg battled back from fourth at the start of his leg to overhaul South Korea and get Hong Kong across the line in 1:27:25. China won gold in a time of one hour, 25 minutes and 54 seconds, while Japan took silver in 1:26:45. “Both me and Oscar wanted to take off pressure from yesterday from the individual [race],” Elg said. “I think we both had pretty average days yesterday. Being able to bounce back today and contribute to the medal count of Hong Kong is is a very special thing.” And a day after Grace Lau Mo-sheung took home silver in the women’s kata, there was bronze in the men’s individual event for Howard Hung Ho-wai at Toyohashi Gymnasium. In what could be the 34-year-old’s last Games, Hung beat Malaysia’s Mohamad Haznil 5-0 to win the first Asian Games medal of his career. “Who knows what will happen in the future?” Hung said. “Maybe this will not be my last Asian Games medal. Maybe there will be many more, or maybe this is where it stops. But right now, I’m enjoying it.” Wong Cheuk-lee added a second karate bronze later in the day in the women’s -68kg category. As part of the Jockey Club’s athlete award incentive scheme, Sham and Haughey will both earn themselves HK$1 million for their gold medals. A sliding means individual silver is worth HK$500,000 and bronze HK$250,000. The city’s triathletes, meanwhile, will share HK$500,000 for their collective efforts, while any team winning gold will split HK$2 million, with silver bringing HK$1 million.

title: Mainland China’s stock exchanges mount charm offensive amid Hong Kong IPO boom
description: Domestic bourses are lobbying mainland firms to reconsider Hong Kong listing plans, sources say.
content: Mainland China’s stock exchanges have stepped up lobbying of companies and regulators to prioritise their boards for listings after Hong Kong stole their thunder in fundraising activities in recent years, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Figures from the exchanges recently met representatives of some mainland companies planning Hong Kong listings, especially first-time issuers and firms in sectors supported by national policies, a source said. “Exchanges emphasised the benefits of listing on the mainland, including valuations that are generally higher than in Hong Kong, a clearer and more controllable timetable, and more policy resources for sectors that fit Beijing’s priorities,” the person said. Another source, an intermediary who helps companies with Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs), said such lobbying efforts, while routine, had intensified as exchanges operated as businesses “competing for market rankings”. “Competition between exchanges for quality technology firms will be much more intense going forward,” the person added. Following the outreach and persuasion from mainland exchanges, some clients are now rethinking plans to offer Hong Kong shares, also known as H shares, and choosing A-share offerings in Beijing, Shanghai or Shenzhen instead, a source said. The heated competition comes as Hong Kong’s IPO fundraising – a majority involving mainland companies – topped HK$340 billion (US$43 billion) in the first eight months of this year. The figure has already surpassed last year’s total, with hundreds of firms still waiting in the queue. “The market previously relied heavily on a single offshore platform,” said Edward Au Chun-hing, a managing partner at Deloitte China. “The policy encouraging quality domestic firms to leverage Hong Kong’s platform has never changed. National policy has always stressed that the mainland A-share and Hong Kong markets are ‘dual platforms, dual tracks’.” China’s market regulator introduced a package of measures to encourage Hong Kong listings in April 2024, including simplified filing steps, clear support for qualified industry leaders and shorter review times. Battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and optical module supplier Zhongji Innolight successfully listed in Hong Kong over the past two years, helping the city’s bourse operator, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, reclaim the global IPO crown last year. The mainland A-share market recorded 102 IPOs, raising 177 billion yuan (US$26 billion) in the first eight months of 2026, also beating last year’s total, though growing at a significantly slower pace than Hong Kong. The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges recorded 26 and 23 new listings during the period, respectively, raising 100.56 billion yuan and 58.61 billion yuan, according to Deloitte figures. The Beijing Stock Exchange, which focuses on supporting “specialised, refined, distinctive and innovative” firms and “little giant” enterprises, was the best performer among the three mainland exchanges in terms of growth in the number of deals. It recorded 53 new listings, raising 18 billion yuan. Mainland bourses have received some backing from officials. Li Chao, vice-chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission, said last week that the regulator would implement more inclusive policies for IPOs and mergers, making the A-share market “the top priority listing destination”. Speaking at a news briefing, Li said the average review cycle for A-share IPOs in Shanghai and Shenzhen had been shortened to about six months, with refinancing approvals for top-tier companies taking less than a month.

title: How Beyblade helps Hong Kong children learn science and make connections
description: The battling spinning tops toy teaches kids about physics and resilience.
content:
On a Friday afternoon inside a school hall, Daniel Keung Tsz-chung proudly opened his toy box. He revealed his prized collection of Beyblades.
Then, the 10-year-old tugged a cord and launched a custom spinning top. The Primary Four pupil had locked into a fierce battle with two classmates.
Daniel is a student at Lions Clubs International Ho Tak Sum Primary School in Tin Shui Wai. There, Beyblade tournaments have become a regular breaktime sight.
The spinning top is a nostalgic childhood toy for many older Hongkongers. It was first released in 1999 by Japanese toy company Takara.
Today, the old-school craze has made a comeback – with a new spin.
Across Hong Kong, the game is attracting players of all ages. It ranges from primary school pupils to full-grown adults.
Daniel has been an avid fan for three years. He has invested in his passion. His collection of Beyblades is worth nearly HK$4,000.
But the real value of the game for him is the human connection.
“Spinning tops can keep people from getting addicted to their phones and help build really great friendships,” Daniel said.
Daniel’s school principal, Wong Wai-lap, agreed. He explained why he encouraged Beyblades on campus.
“Being able to play outside and connect through a shared interest – something everyone plays together – naturally sparks communication,” the principal said.
Wong said playing with Beyblades was an excellent way to teach science. The spinning toy helps students understand abstract physics concepts.
The school has even added Beyblades into its new Primary One and Primary Four science curricula.
The Primary Four curriculum focuses on fair testing and friction.
