So Wing-sum is the school’s science panel head. She said that spinning tops matched these scientific concepts.
“[For example], there is contact friction between the top and the arena, which is why it ultimately comes to a halt,” So explained.
The educators also believe the toy can build emotional resilience . The nature of the game teaches children the ability to handle failure.
“You see yourself lose instantly,” So said. “Some children do cry, but I believe this is a valuable experience for them to have at a young age, learning that even if they lose and cry, they can pick themselves up and try again.”

title: South Korea steps up to plug Europe’s jet fuel deficit
description: South Korea is the latest large source of jet fuel shipments to Europe, exporting 129,000 barrels per day, the highest since October 2022.
content: Europe faces a fourth-quarter jet fuel deficit, even as it turns to far-flung suppliers including South Korea, which is set to boost its jet exports to Europe to a four-year high in September, according to analysts and shipping data. The continent has been importing more jet fuel from nations including Nigeria, the United States and Canada since the outbreak of the Iran war over half a year ago, which hit Middle Eastern supplies and cut off around half of Europe’s jet imports. Europe remains highly exposed to the risk of further supply disruption as Middle Eastern tensions rise. Consultancy Energy Aspects forecasts that Europe will see a fourth-quarter jet fuel deficit of 510,000 barrels per day, against surpluses of 18,000 in the United States and 419,000 in Asia-Pacific. The third-quarter trend is largely the same. South Korea in September has become the latest large source of jet fuel shipments to Europe, according to flows data. European imports of the fuel from the Asian nation so far in September stand at 129,000 barrels per day according to commodities intelligence firm Kpler, the highest since October 2022. LSEG data shows similar ⁠volumes. With the continent expected to remain short of jet fuel, Europe’s imports were set to continue, said James Noel-Beswick, head of commodities at market intelligence firm Sparta Commodities. Jet fuel is one of the so-called middle distillates, which include diesel and gas oil. European diesel hit a record high this week, firmer than Asia’s diesel ‌markets. The widening spread between the Asian and European benchmarks was making it more profitable to export barrels into Europe, Noel – Beswick added. Imports from South Korea also coincide with low inventories, with stocks held independently in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp oil refining and storage hub hitting their lowest in seven years in the week to September 10. Asia is a swing supplier of jet fuel to Europe and traders typically turn there when they judge the arbitrage – the relative prices between the two regions – profitable. Average monthly exports last year were 1.5 million barrels, Kpler data showed. South Korea’s jet fuel output for July hit a seven-year high of almost 13.89 million barrels, while exports reached a 3½-year high, government data showed. An increase in refinery crude processing rates has contributed to this rise in output, and traders expect crude runs for August to be firmer than July. Provisional government data showed July refining runs at 2.7 million barrels per day, up by 16 per cent from June.

title: The importance of safe drinking water in East Timor
description: Clean water is essential to avoid disease and danger, but it is not easy to access in this Southeast Asian country.
content:
For many people in East Timor, clean water does not come from a household tap. In this Southeast Asian country, many have to walk very far.
In July, a group of secondary school and university students from Hong Kong and Macau visited the island nation. They hoped to understand its barriers to healthcare – for example, limited access to clean water.
Their trip was part of the Youth Ambassador Programme by GX Foundation, an NGO that sends medical aid to developing countries .
East Timor is home to 1.4 million people. After centuries of Portuguese colonisation and a violent Indonesian occupation, the country became independent in 2002.
For Candice Cheung On-yu, the trip was a chance to leave her bubble of worrying just about grades.
“It’s crucial for our generation … to realise how hard life is for others,” the 17-year-old pupil at St Paul’s Convent School said. “[We should] learn to treasure what we have.”
The youth ambassador trip was built around a potable water project. GX Foundation donated 100 water purification machines to hospitals, churches, schools and more in East Timor. But the machines are only one small step towards clean water for all.
“Taking water from nearby pipelines or river sources is more convenient,” Candice said. She explained that residents might understand that clean water would be better for their health, but they grew up drinking river water.
Changing people’s thinking was key to the NGO’s mission, she said.
During the trip, the ambassadors visited households and surveyed families. They taught residents about the dangers of dengue fever and unclean water.
One local, Americo, recalled how his nephew once got sick from drinking unfiltered water.
Now, he understands the need for clean water.
“Sometimes, I take about 20 to 40 litres of water from the machine at the church,” he said through a translator.
He added that he would also boil the water before using it.
“[Now,] there is less diarrhoea and gastrointestinal disease,” he said.
He also knows now that you cannot wait when treating dengue fever: “When it’s already two days, we have to go to the community health centre.”
Medical students from the Universidade Catolica Timorense (UCT) in East Timor also joined the visiting group.
Sartelizia Constantino de Fatima is a final-year student in UCT’s first medical class. But the university lacks essential lab equipment, so Sartelizia spent two months practising at an Indonesian hospital last year.
Studying has added an immense financial burden on the 24-year-old, but she hopes her medical knowledge will help others.
She will return to Indonesia for a two-year clinical residency . Students like Sartelizia form the foundation for the future of health in East Timor.

title: Chinese AI chipmaker Hygon plots expansion from data centres to robotics
description: New chip targets range of physical AI applications, where machines interact directly with their environments.
content: Chinese chipmaker Hygon Information Technology is set to release a new chip targeting complex real-world applications including robotics, an expansion from its current focus on data centres. The product launch, slated for Tuesday, marks Hygon’s move into a new chip category powering machines that interact directly with their environments, as physical artificial intelligence becomes increasingly important. The new chip, an iteration of the company’s CPU1000 series, is designed to meet “low-power, embedded and edge computing requirements”, targeting a range of physical AI applications in sectors including robotics, machine vision and intelligent manufacturing, according to reports by state-owned business news outlets Jiemian News and China Securities Journal on Sunday. The company’s slogan for the launch event, set to be held in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen, was “Let computing power reach the physical world”, according to a post on the company’s official WeChat account on Sunday. The post did not disclose more information. Hygon’s expansion comes amid a broader industry trend where computing demand is increasingly migrating out of centralised data centres and towards the so-called edges of networks at active physical industry sites. Unlike data centre chips which prioritise raw computational output, chips deployed in robotics and edge applications must meet stringent demands for real-time processing, power limits and robust security in unpredictable settings. Hygon, which designs central processing units (CPUs) and deep computing units – a type of accelerator card designed specifically for AI – is playing an increasingly critical role in Beijing’s broader drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency, a campaign that has taken on greater urgency as US trade restrictions limit the country’s access to advanced chips. Its current CPU product lines include the 7000 series for high-performance data centres, the 5000 series for “middle-level” industry clients in cloud computing and edge computing and the 3000 series, which boasts cost efficiency. The Shanghai-listed chipmaker is one of the country’s premier developers of x86-compatible CPUs. Iterations of the x86 architecture, originally developed by US semiconductor giant Intel, are still the basis for most server, desktop and laptop computers. The company’s first-half revenue rose 66.5 per cent from a year earlier to 9.1 billion yuan (US$1.4 billion) amid strong demand for high-end domestic chips.

title: Feature of the Week: Ophelia Chan’s short story titled ‘Cindy’s Magical School Journey’
description: The 10-year-old from Man Kiu Association Primary School shares a tale about a young girl who attends a magical school.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
Cindy wanted to be a diligent student, so during the summer she decided to attend a magic school after the holidays. She was very excited and spent her last day of holiday packing.
After the summer holiday, Cindy started her first day at Rainbow Primary School. She brought her broomstick, bag and a long magic wand with her. She flew all the way to school and arrived with a sense of anticipation.
Upon arrival, she met her class teacher, Miss Lui. In the classroom, she spotted a desk, chairs, pots and sticks, and realised it was time for a music lesson.
Cindy tried to create music using her long wand but unfortunately it didn’t work as she had hoped.
The next lesson was art, where she used her spells to create beautiful artwork.
After working hard over the next few years, Cindy passed her exams. She proved to be a diligent student and earned several awards.

title: Letters from readers: Cut food waste, an Indian girl’s Hong Kong life, love for penguins
description: This week, students write about minimising dining waste, their favourite hobbies and why they love reading.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
Ng Sze-wing (aged 10), Lok Sin Tong Leung Kau Kui Primary School
If you are planning to open a restaurant, here’s a helpful tip to reduce food waste.
Consider putting up a sign in front of your establishment that says, “If you finish all your food with no leftovers, you can deduct HK$10 from your bill!”
Additionally, you could create another sign stating, “If you don’t finish your food, you will be charged an extra HK$5.”
This approach can benefit both you and your guests, encouraging everyone to avoid food waste.
Divina Mulani (aged 11), Kowloon Junior School
I am of Indian origin and was born in Hong Kong. Some of my favourite hobbies include art, dancing and talking with my friends and family.
My favourite activity is creating art pieces. My favourite colours are pink, blue, white and light yellow. Some of my friends are Saanvi, Mishka and Nairra, but my best friend is Prisha.
The extracurricular classes I take include maths, swimming, Chinese and dance. My favourite foods are pizza, hotpot and lentils, and my favourite drinks are boba and other cold, refreshing beverages. A few things I am skilled at are finger knitting and dancing.
Bella Cai Shiyao (aged 9), CPC Yao Dao Primary School
My favourite subject is Chinese because it is both easy and interesting.
Reading is my biggest hobby. It lets me travel to different worlds and learn new things.
My favourite birds are penguins. They look super cute as they waddle on the ice. I often watch documentary videos about penguins.
My best friend is Ellie, and she lives in Shanwei. We live very far apart, so I can only see her when I go back to the countryside. We always have fun together.

title: Nearly 50% rise in drug seizures by Hong Kong customs in first half of year
description: About 60 per cent of 5,704kg of narcotics seized in six-month period was cannabis and ketamine, with notable increases in smuggling via air and sea.
content: Hong Kong customs recorded a nearly 50 per cent year-on-year rise in drug seizures during the first half of 2026, driven by notable increases in smuggling activities via air and sea routes. The Customs and Excise Department confiscated 5,704kg (12,575lbs) of illegal narcotics in the first half, a 49 per cent increase year on year, according to figures seen by the South China Morning Post. Nearly two-thirds of the seized narcotics, or 3,408kg, were found at the airport, a 46.6 per cent year-on-year increase at that port of entry. Those on sea routes accounted for one-third, or 1,954kg, representing a 55.6 per cent rise. The remaining 342kg were confiscated at land checkpoints and other parts of the city. Cannabis and ketamine accounted for about 60 per cent of the drugs seized in the first six months, marking a rise of 40 per cent and 78.8 per cent of those substances, respectively. The number of drug cases detected by customs and the number of arrestees also recorded a slight increase. A senior customs officer said while there was an obvious trend of syndicates recruiting air passengers to smuggle drugs, the rise in maritime confiscations was primarily due to large quantities found in a few particular cases. “Sea routes have always been used by smugglers to diversify risk. When they ship drugs by sea, the volume per shipment is usually larger. So whenever a confiscation happens, a single case can end up involving a larger quantity [of drugs],” he said. Last week, customs made the city’s largest-ever sea shipment drug seizure, uncovering HK$125 million (US$15.93 million) worth of marijuana in a 40-foot container and arresting three people. According to the officer, syndicates mainly concealed drugs in different goods, such as by mixing them among buckets of sugar cubes or hiding them in hollowed-out timber and pool tables. In some cases, they recruited crew members of ocean liners to carry drugs for them. But air travel remained the largest contributor to the overall rise in drug seizures, with 95 cases committed by air passengers in the first half of this year representing a 35.7 per cent year-on-year increase. Earlier this month, customs smashed an international drug trafficking syndicate that recruited students during the summer holiday. The department seized about 6.1 tonnes of suspected drugs worth more than HK$1.4 billion. He said trafficking by air also led to the amount of drugs seized at land ports increasing almost fivefold because some courier companies moved their distribution centres to Shenzhen and Guangzhou, with some air cargo logged as ground interceptions when they moved through Hong Kong’s land checkpoints. The officer said customs expected that drug smugglers would change their methods of moving contraband in the second half of the year in response to authorities’ enforcement efforts. Many air passengers recruited to carry drugs who were caught at the start of the year, for instance, had flown directly from Thailand. Afterwards, they changed their routes slightly by flying via a transit airport to prevent being targeted by customs. “We found that if they discovered we had stepped up enforcement in certain channels, they would change their modes of smuggling … We will monitor closely [to see] if the trends change,” he said. The officer said the surge in cannabis seizures was mainly due to the legalisation of the drug in certain countries and an increase in the number of users globally. Most of the cannabis seized this year came from Thailand and North America. On ketamine, the officer said the synthetic drug was relatively easy to detect during the production stage in Hong Kong, and most of it seized by customs came from Europe, where there was more space to manufacture it. Incoming ketamine could be supplied locally or transited elsewhere. The officer said customs would step up intelligence exchanges with overseas law enforcement agencies and enhance communication with local logistics companies. He added that customs would help the logistics industry identify suspicious clients, such as those who placed urgent orders, made last-minute changes to delivery instructions or failed to provide direct contact information. A customs spokesman said the department had adopted an intelligence-led strategy while working closely with local, mainland and overseas law enforcement agencies to execute joint operations, identify drugs at their source and block illicit narcotics from entering Hong Kong. He said strict control measures were enforced across all sea, land and air control points, with risk assessment frameworks and advanced technology, such as specialised X-ray systems and ion mobility spectrometers, used to enhance detection capabilities.

title: Hong Kong’s newest sporting star and heir to Cheung Ka-long throne set for Asian Games bow
description: Given ‘11 out of 10’ billing by Greg Koenig, Harris Ho announced talent to global audience with flawless world championships final effort.
content: Their adrenaline pumping in the immediate aftermath of competition, sportspeople can tend towards hyperbole. Mike Tyson took the biscuit, poleaxing Lou Savarese, then calling out future opponent Lennox Lewis with the immortal line “I want your heart, I want to eat your children.” Not remotely as graphic, but after unfancied Bangladesh had ended New Zealand’s 17-match home unbeaten streak in a gripping 2022 Test, their excited seamer Taskin Ahmed praised his side for “giving 110 per cent”, a familiar cry in victory or defeat. Even Greg Koenig recently allowed himself to go a little overboard: the erudite foil coach, who has done so much to revolutionise fencing in the city, awarded Harris Ho Hing-shim “11 out of 10” for his flawless display in Hong Kong’s gut-wrenching Kerry Fencing World Championships team final defeat by Italy. In this instance, Koenig could be forgiven for his excitement after his 17-year-old charge had beaten the Italian trio of Guillaume Bianchi, Filippo Macchi and Tommaso Marini, the world Nos 3, 4 and 13, respectively. “He showed up very well, which we didn’t expect,” Macchi told the South China Morning Post. Zheng Kangzhao, Hong Kong fencing head coach for the past 15 years, called Ho the “biggest surprise” of the world championships, albeit he had labelled him “one to watch” earlier this year. Ahead of Ho’s Asian Games debut this week, Koenig continued the narrative on the teenager’s lightning emergence. “Before the world championships, nobody knew him,” the Frenchman said. “Now the whole world knows him. In every competition, when people see they have to compete with Harris Ho, they’ll think, ‘I really have to take care because this kid is not a joke’.” With elder siblings who fenced, Ho “followed in their footsteps and tried to learn from very young”. Aged four when he first picked up a sword, it was around a decade later it dawned on Ho that he had the capacity to mix in elite circles. “My results made me happy and gave me the motivation to continue improving,” he said. Ho’s contrasting approaches to watching Cheung Ka-long claim his two Olympic golds were illustrative of a sharpening focus. Only 12 when Cheung won in Tokyo to ignite a fencing craze in his home city, Ho watched quietly with his parents, then retired to bed. “Then he thought, ‘I want to perform like this guy, I can do it because I’m from Hong Kong, too, and there’s no reason we won’t succeed’,” Koenig said. “When you have this mindset, wow, of course you work harder.” Sitting in front of his television with friends when Cheung retained his title in Paris two years ago, Ho treated the day “more like a learning session”. “It wasn’t just cheering for him, we were discussing how Ka-long and his opponents were fencing,” Ho said. As fencing grew more serious, Ho increasingly struggled to combine sport with lessons at Diocesan Boys’ School. “I’m not a clever guy when it comes to studying, so it took me a lot of time and it was hard to balance both,” Ho said, although he was equally self-critical of his English, which is very good. “Now I have given up most of my academics and I just focus on fencing,” Ho added. He received senior Hong Kong recognition at 16, comfortably meeting his “expectation to get into the team before I was 20”. “It was like a dream to train with a two-time Olympic gold medallist, and a world champion [Ryan Choi Chun-yin],” Ho said. “If I told the 12-year-old me this would happen, he wouldn’t believe me.” Confirmation that Ho was setting himself apart from his contemporaries came with the cadet gold he won from April’s Junior & Cadet Fencing World Championships in Rio de Janeiro. The previous month, he had reached the Lima Foil Grand Prix quarter-finals in Peru, beating 2023 world champion Marini in the process to become the youngest member of the world’s top 50. He has since climbed to No 26. Also part of Hong Kong’s silver medal team at the Asian Championships in June, Ho nonetheless acknowledged that he “didn’t think I would do as well as I did in the world championships”. “It was unbelievable for me, but I don’t feel extra pressure because of it,” said Ho, who also won all six of his individual qualifying bouts at the global competition, before a narrow first-round defeat by Great Britain’s Jaimie Cook. “I haven’t thought about [rivals knowing me better], because it’s a future thing. If they just know 20 per cent of me [currently], it’s not enough for me to change my fencing.” Told about 2024 Olympic silver medallist Macchi’s admiration for his world final efforts, Ho could not suppress a faint smile. Still, there was a distinct undertone of Macchi throwing down the gauntlet when he was informed that Ho had stated his ambition to win gold in Los Angeles in 2028. “Anybody can say anything [regarding their targets], and I think he’s very strong [but] we have to see what he’s going to do,” Macchi said. “He has two examples to learn from in Ka-long and Ryan, and I hope for him that he achieves his goals.” Choi in particular has taken Ho under his wing. At the beginning of this year, he told the SCMP that his fellow left-hander was among a new Hong Kong generation who “haven’t unlocked their potential yet, but you can see they have the ability to be strong; maybe stronger than us [Choi and Cheung]”. In the fortnight’s holiday that Koenig allowed his foilists after their world championships exploits, Ho accompanied Choi to coach at the six-day Fencer’s Paradise elite training clinic in Hawaii. “I’m getting to visit countries I never would have if it wasn’t for fencing, and I like travelling, so I feel very lucky,” Ho said. Next destination Japan. Ho tempered expectations for Tuesday’s individual foil competition, but said a Hong Kong team that also features Cheung, Choi and the 21-year-old Leung Chin-yu “can get gold” on Friday, “Japan and Korea are our biggest opponents, they’re strong but we’re also strong, so they’re afraid of us,” Ho said. “I just hope I can fence how I always do, and that it will be OK for me.” Koenig added: “Although people now know they have to fight hard against him, he’s so strong and so smart that it will be complicated for every opponent he faces. I’m quite confident about the next 10 or 15 years for Hong Kong fencing.”

title: Upgraded but underperforming: Philippines’ growth lags behind
description: High living costs and delayed public works drag growth projections down far behind regional front runners.
content: The Philippines’ rise to upper-middle-income status was supposed to mark a new phase for one of Southeast Asia’s most closely watched emerging economies. Instead, analysts say the milestone has done little to shield the country from short-term pressures weighing on growth: sluggish public spending, delayed infrastructure, high living costs and the fallout from investigations into alleged irregularities in flood control projects. Those strains have left the Philippines looking like a regional laggard. Bank of America is forecasting gross domestic product growth of 2.5 per cent for 2026 – tying with Thailand for the slowest pace in the region – even as it raised its overall Asean growth forecast to 5 per cent, up from 4.7 per cent at the end of the second quarter. “The Philippines is expected to see a sharp slowdown relative to 2025,” the bank said in its September report, comparing that to Singapore’s projected 5.1 per cent growth, Malaysia’s 5.2 per cent, Indonesia’s 5.3 per cent and Vietnam’s 8.2 per cent. As other members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations surge ahead, the growing growth disparity raises serious questions about whether Manila can convert its long-term strengths – a young population, a robust consumer base and an expanding services sector – into the growth momentum seen elsewhere in the region. Modest consumption gains and a bottoming-out of investment spending could support limited growth in the second half of the year, Bank of America said, while targeted subsidies for vulnerable consumers and the transport sector could cushion the impact of energy shocks. “Compared with its Asean peers, the Philippines is currently facing a relative slowdown,” said Jonathan Ravelas, a Filipino economist and market strategist. “Countries such as Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia are benefiting more from manufacturing expansion, supply-chain relocation and stronger foreign direct investment inflows.” The Philippine economy had been “heavily dependent on consumption and that engine has been tempered by higher borrowing costs, elevated living costs and slower public spending”, he said. Michael Ricafort, chief economist at Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation, said increased government “catch-up spending” on infrastructure was the “missing element or link that could once again accelerate Philippine economic and GDP growth”, offsetting the underspending seen since late 2025 amid ongoing flood-control corruption investigations. “This would lead to better fiscal performance, in terms of increased government tax and revenue collections, narrower budget deficits and a lower, better national government debt-to-GDP ratio,” Ricafort said, adding that such spending “would be the major catalyst to pump-prime the economy”, counteracting geopolitical factors that had driven up prices, inflation and interest rates. Ravelas said the slowdown in infrastructure spending was concerning because public construction “has a strong multiplier effect on the economy”. Most investors were less troubled by the corruption investigations than by the delays they had caused, he said. “Transparency and accountability are positive for investor confidence but projects must continue moving forward. The challenge for policymakers is to clean up the system without slowing down execution,” Ravelas added. The Philippines’ challenge is sustaining and accommodating growth Jonathan Ravelas, economist Ricafort agreed that governance reforms would be vital to restoring investor confidence in the Philippine economy. Piled on top of the infrastructure slowdown and governance issues is another worry: forecasters have warned of El Nino-driven drought conditions stretching into early 2027, threatening food prices and agricultural incomes just as households are already feeling the strain of rising living costs. Ricafort wants to see the gap filled with targeted, non-monetary relief such as ayuda (aid) payments and job programmes aimed at the poorest Filipinos, to ease price pressures “largely caused” by the Iran war. Some of these measures are already being rolled out: subsidies have been directed at transport, agriculture and fisheries, among other hard-hit sectors, in an attempt to stop higher costs being passed on to the public, along with financial support for low-income households. But Ricafort said more needed to be done. “Technology, on top of education, is one of the biggest equalisers that would lift more people from poverty, especially in the countryside,” he said, pointing to raised productivity across agriculture and manufacturing that would also increase the country’s global competitiveness and strengthen food security. Philippines vs Thailand Despite the sluggish growth outlook, analysts say the Philippines still has room to catch up. “I would not read the Bank of America forecast as the Philippines losing its long-term growth story,” Ravelas said. “The country’s elevation to upper middle-income status reflects the progress it has achieved, while the BofA outlook is more about the near-term challenges it faces.” That upgrade, announced by the World Bank on July 1, was based on the strength of the Philippines’ 2025 gross national income per capita, placing it in the upper middle-income bracket. This year’s slowdown has since tempered expectations, but Ravelas says the investment case for the country remains intact. He said investors liked the Philippines’ young population, sizeable domestic market, resilient consumer base and growing services industry, but were “looking for stronger execution, particularly in infrastructure, foreign investment attraction and policy implementation”. Before the Covid-19 pandemic, the Philippines actually had one of the region’s fastest-growing economies and had kept growing steadily since, Ricafort said. Analysts say the comparison with Thailand is instructive because the two Southeast Asian economies have arrived at the same 2.5 per growth figure from different directions. “Thailand is a net exporting country with relatively lower inflation and interest rates, while the Philippines is a net importing country, with inflation and interest rates among the highest in the region,” Ricafort said. Ravelas pointed to other differences. “Thailand has strong infrastructure, manufacturing and tourism, yet it is constrained by an ageing population, weak domestic demand and slower labour force growth,” he said. “The Philippines, on the other hand, benefits from a young population, strong consumer spending, remittances and long-term demographic momentum, but continues to struggle with productivity, infrastructure gaps and inflation volatility.” Put another way, Thailand struggled to find new sources of growth, “while the Philippines’ challenge is sustaining and accommodating growth”, Ravelas said, pointing to energy, water and transport networks that need to “keep pace with urbanisation and economic expansion.” “Ultimately, the Philippines still has the fundamentals to outperform over the long term,” he said. “But turning potential into growth will depend on the quality and speed of policy execution.”

title: Wing Shya: photographer to Wong Kar-wai on working with the great and good of Hong Kong cinema
description: Wing Shya’s candid Hong Kong photography journey – from street snaps to Wong Kar-wai collaborations, Leslie Cheung portraits and iconic film stills – reveals art born of instinct, accident and unwavering passion.
content: I WAS BORN in Hong Kong in 1964. My parents came from Shandong province, in mainland China, arriving illegally, later legalised – a common story for that generation. I went to the all-boys Salesian School, in Chai Wan, and was not a good student. I spent all my time messing around with friends. Then, at 17 or 18, I watched a film called Boat People (1982) and there was a character holding a camera who looked cool. Something happened in me. “I want to be that,” I thought. Not the actor – the photographer. I saved every dollar I made from part-time jobs until I could buy a camera, then I started to photograph everything: friends, family, the street, skateboarders. I didn’t really have a plan. I just liked looking through that little window. MY ENGLISH WAS so bad and I didn’t do well in my exams, so university in Hong Kong wasn’t possible. Art school was the only door open to me and, I’ll admit, a good excuse not to get a real job yet. I went to a technical college, the Lee Wai Lee Technical Institute (in Kowloon Tong), before I found the Emily Carr College of Art and Design, in Vancouver, Canada – the only overseas school I could afford, where tuition for international students was the same as for local students. I WORKED THREE or four jobs at a time, sometimes illegally, as I was on a student visa. I delivered food for a Chinese restaurant, waited tables and even cleaned houses that were a two-hour drive from the city. On weekends, I would sell my drawings in Stanley Park. I DID A double major: graphic design and fine art. In the summer, I’d drive to San Francisco, or fly to New York on the cheapest ticket I could find. I could earn a few dollars drawing people in Washington Square Park, in Greenwich Village. I had so much energy then. AFTER GRADUATING IN 1991, six classmates and I opened a graphic-design company in Vancouver. Eight months in, we were doing well. One afternoon at a restaurant in Chinatown, I picked up a Hong Kong gossip magazine and looked at the layout. I said to my friends, “I have to go back – this design is terrible. I want to do something in the city.” They tried to talk me out of it. But within a week, I’d sold my car and bought a ticket home, without telling my mother. I flew back and rang the doorbell. She opened it and said, “Why are you here? You’re not welcome. We have no space.” I slept on the sofa. WORK WAS HARD to find, but in 1992, I won a biennial photography prize and gave the money to my mother – it’s the right order of things. In 1993, I got a job at J. Walter Thompson (JWT), the advertising agency, but only lasted about a year; I had too much ego and was always fighting clients. I ran into an old school friend, Jan Lamb Hoi-fung – a singer who DJ’d at Commercial Radio Hong Kong – on the street by chance and he got me hired as the creative director there. It was a tiny department, just two of us, responsible for everything – stage design, ads, CD covers, concerts. I worked hard and I loved it. I got to know the biggest Cantopop stars: Jacky Cheung Hok-yau, Andy Lau Tak-wah and Faye Wong – she was there all the time. THROUGH A FRIEND, Eric Kot Man-fai, my portfolio landed in front of Wong Kar-wai, in 1996. He said I could shoot some promotional pictures. On a Japanese commercial he directed, I hid behind a sofa so the crew wouldn’t throw me out of the tiny set – and when the official photographer could not get enough pictures, my photos were the only ones that worked. Because of that, Wong Kar-wai sent me to Argentina a year later, for Happy Together, starring Tony Leung Chiu-wai and Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing. I HAD NEVER done film stills professionally. I didn’t even own a sound blimp – the soundproof box for your camera so you can’t hear the shutter going off. Because of this, I mostly shot between takes. I captured the actors sitting, waiting, hanging out: Tony and Leslie just breathing, not performing. One afternoon, on a rooftop, the street noise was so loud that my shutter was no longer an issue and I could finally shoot freely. Most of my images that you know from that film came from that one afternoon. THEN, THE COLOUR. I was shooting slide film. Wong Kar-wai demanded to see the images immediately, but there were no labs where we were in Argentina that could process slide film. We found a shop that only did negative film. Because slide film is positive film, they ran mine through the wrong chemicals, and that turned everything green. Argentina’s grey walls became luminous. In the end, Wong Kar-wai loved it. It became the visual language of the whole film. I can call it a mistake, or I can call it, “I had no choice. It ended up like this.” After that, I left the radio station and started my company, Shya-la-la Workshop. ONE DAY, WE were shooting in a train station – it was too noisy for sound recording – so I could shoot freely. Leslie was annoyed at me for distracting him. My shutter was too loud, but I kept going. I explained to him, “I’m only scared of Wong Kar-wai, not you. Because he hired me, only he can fire me.” He looked at me for a long moment, then said, “I like your attitude. When we get back to Hong Kong, you’ll work for me.” HE MEANT IT. From that day until he died, I shot almost every photograph of Leslie for his work, his concerts, behind the scenes, albums and tours. He was the most considerate person I’ve known in this industry. He remembered everyone’s habits, every name, if you took milk in your coffee. He looked after the whole crew, from driver to delivery boy. We travelled together for concerts, shot in countries I’d never been to. I still think about him. FOR In the Mood for Love (2000), Wong Kar-wai gave me one instruction: the film is about red. He gave me some music to listen to, and that was it, initially. So, in 1999, I went to Tokyo, bought 40 or 50 different rolls of film, shot test after test and laid every print in front of him. He picked one: an old, obscure film – barely still in production, its colour deeply reddish. I called the manufacturer; they were closing the following month because nobody was buying their film any more. “How many rolls remained,” I asked. “Two hundred,” they said. I bought every single one. THAT PHOTO FILM was made in the 1960s or 70s, and its dyes were slowly failing – that’s why my shots for In the Mood for Love look the way they do. After we finished the film, there was none left anywhere in the world. THERE ARE PEOPLE who I learned almost everything from. One, of course, is Wong Kar-wai, who gave me access to everyone, all these famous faces. I learned how to crop a photograph by watching him on the monitor. But another one of my real teachers is William Chang Suk-ping – the famous production designer and art director. Even now, we work together regularly. Just the other day, I was on a shoot, with William beside me. I learned what makes a picture by watching what Wong Kar-wai and William chose to keep and what they threw away. I don’t think of my work as mine alone. It is a long conversation with two people I deeply respect. IN 2010, FOX came to Hong Kong to make a Chinese film – my feature-film directorial debut, Hot Summer Days. Stars such as Jacky Cheung, Maggie Cheung Man-yuk, Nicholas Tse Ting-fung and Daniel Wu Yin-cho all appeared in it, for very little money, as a favour to me because we had 20 years of trust. DIRECTING FELT LIKE another universe. You have to think about logistics, 80-people crews, egos, dangerous rigs, scenes and even the crew lunches! I’ve made more films since. I still shoot fashion campaigns, recently for Chanel and Bottega Veneta, and – fingers crossed – I am now writing a television drama. MY FIRST BOOKS came about because cultural curator Shelly Verthime told me at a dinner many years ago that she wanted to make a book. One day, in 2015, she called from Hong Kong International Airport, so I put a hard drive with every photo I owned into a taxi and sent it to her, at the terminal. She spent a year and a half editing alone. An investor funded the printing and an exhibition in Shanghai, in 2017. My shows in Japan (in Tokyo and Kyoto), the books (Chaos [2020], Solace [2024], Is [2026] and more) – they happened all because someone pushed. I never start these things myself. MY WORK HAS been in the Mori Art Museum, in Tokyo, and in the V&A, in London. I don’t think about it much. I’ve done it already, and the future is more exciting to me than the past. What I still love is being on set – the mess, the crew eating together, the gossip, the waiting. I think the universe already has a script written. My job is only to follow my heart and see what page it turns to next. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

title: Chinese province urges firms to seize the day as Xi-Trump meeting provides trade stability
description: Eastern manufacturing centre Zhejiang asks traders to find opportunities for US exports in rare period of detente in run-up to leaders’ summit.
content: As final preparations are being made for President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington this month, one export-oriented Chinese province has urged businesses to “grasp the window” of relative stability in China-US ties to boost shipments. The hope among regional officials for more trade lays bare the dependence some key Chinese localities still have on America despite diversification and decoupling. Major manufacturers in Zhejiang – which helped the coastal province grow its annual export value to the second largest among all localities in China – have been asked by local authorities in recent weeks to increase production and expedite delivery of US-bound goods, the South China Morning Post has learned. The move comes after Zhejiang officials deemed that bilateral economic and trade ties would remain “settled” and in turn create a “favourable climate” for expanding exports to the US, the province’s largest overseas market. It also represents how China’s powerhouse provinces aim to capitalise on and contribute to the opportunities presented by this year’s flurry of meetings between the two countries’ top leadership. One of the enterprises to receive official encouragement was Wanxiang Group, according to a source with knowledge of related communications. Wanxiang is an auto-parts maker that has, over the years, built sprawling operations across America through investments and acquisitions. In May, its group chairman and CEO, Lu Weiding, was among a group of top-flight executives who sat down with their American peers for a state banquet hosted by Xi for US President Donald Trump inside the Great Hall of the People. The encouragement from Zhejiang authorities also followed a June visit by Katherine Clark, Democratic Whip in the US House of Representatives, to Wanxiang’s US headquarters. Enterprises in the cities of Ningbo and Wenzhou have also been exhorted to dispatch sales teams to scout out fresh orders in the US, amid recent exchanges between Zhejiang cadres and American politicians. US businessman-turned-Senator and Trump ally Steve Daines visited Zhejiang at the end of August. There, together with US ambassador to China David Perdue, Daines was assured by Zhejiang Governor Liu Jie that the province would “substantively” strengthen cooperation with America in economy and trade, the Zhejiang Daily reported. Liu added there was a golden window of opportunity thanks to the presidential meetings, and Zhejiang may have a role in bringing the world’s two largest economies closer. On September 3, Liu also received a delegation from the US-China Business Council, led by council president Sean Stein. Liu told Stein that Xi and Trump had established a constructive, strategically stable China-US relationship and that Zhejiang will “earnestly implement” the consensus reached by the two leaders in industry, trade and people-to-people exchanges and tap new markets in the US. Such optimism stems from the uptick in top-level interactions. Xi is tipped to head for Washington this month - his first trip to America in more than a decade - following a state visit by Trump to China in May. The two may meet for a third time this year in November, when Xi receives a number of state leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in Shenzhen. With the stage set at Apec for a potential fourth meeting between the two, Xi could again be on US soil in December for the Group of 20 meeting in Miami, Florida. A common belief among officials appears to be that these encounters could insulate trade from shocks, in stark contrast to the stunned reaction to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and China’s retaliation that pushed duties through the roof in April and May 2025. And despite the country’s efforts to diversify its trade partners, the comments and encouragement suggest a continued reliance on US buyers to sustain the province’s economic growth. Zhejiang’s exports grew 10 per cent year on year to 2.66 trillion yuan (US$396.5 billion) in the first seven months, with America and Europe remaining the largest destination with a combined share of 30 per cent, according to China Customs data. The province is lagging China’s overall diversification, as Southeast Asian nations are now the country’s top export market by bloc. China’s shipments to the US, meanwhile, were down 1.3 per cent year on year to 1.78 trillion yuan in the first seven months. Qin Shili, a senior researcher at Zhejiang Development and Planning Institute, an official think tank, said the recent stabilisation was great news for the province. “It’s a timely opportunity for Zhejiang businesses to once again deepen participation in [US-led] global supply chains and economic and trade exchanges,” he said. Qin also argued, despite heated rivalry in hi-tech and other sectors, some of America’s constraints have “eased” in areas like light industries, consumer goods, small commodities and mid-range manufacturing. “These areas align closely with Zhejiang’s industrial and export focus.” Since May, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has stated that the US-China Board of Trade, one deliverable from Trump’s China trip, would focus on “non-strategic, non-critical goods”. Bessent explained that the US would identify Chinese imports in categories his country does not want to reshore – citing fireworks and “very low-end” consumer goods – and remove tariffs on them. “These goods are going to keep coming from China no matter what,” Bessent said.

title: Nigerian game show helps diaspora reconnect with their language roots
description: Participants embrace their roots as entertainment, social media and technology bridge cultural connections worldwide.
content:
A television game show in Nigeria has a strict rule: if you speak English, you lose.
For Tomi Adeshokan – who lives in the United States and is learning her parents’ native language, Yoruba – being in the audience of this show is a great way to practise. Yoruba is one of Nigeria’s most widely spoken languages.
Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees the show as part of a wider shift.
“We are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots,” he said.
This show is part of a new wave of interest in African languages that were pushed to the side by many years of colonial rule.
Experts say people of African descent living in other places are finding new ways to connect with their roots through social media and entertainment.

title: 18 suspects in 2021 Haiti president’s killing sent to US for trial
description: Suspects flown to Florida as US prosecutors expand case over mercenary plot against Jovenel Moise.
content: Eighteen suspects in the 2021 assassination of Haitian president Jovenel Moise have been transported to Florida to stand trial, US officials said Sunday. Moise, 53, was gunned down on July 7, 2021, at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him. “Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on X. In the same post, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the Southern District of Florida”. “Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing. Among those extradited is a main suspect in the probe - Joseph Felix Badio, a former anti-corruption official at Haiti’s Ministry of Justice, Haitian government and police sources said. The others are Colombian mercenaries, according to the same sources. Colombia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs released a statement Sunday saying it is closely monitoring “the transfer of 17 Colombian citizens from the Republic of Haiti to the United States”. It said Bogota “did not intervene in the decision or in the process that led to the transfer of its citizens to the United States, a matter that falls under the jurisdiction of the competent authorities of the countries involved”. In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moise, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad. The men face possible sentences of life in prison. All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moise’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors. Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil. Haiti has spiralled into deeper chaos since Moise’s killing, and currently has no president. It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on December 13 - if security conditions allow. Gangs control around 80 per cent of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation. A United Nations-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesman said earlier this month.

title: Scientists hope to keep glaciers cool with wool, slowing melting in Swiss Alps
description: Researchers are testing if biodegradable wool can be an eco-friendly alternative to plastic tarpaulins.
content:
Switzerland is struggling to stop glaciers in the Alps mountain range from melting. Thus, researchers are trying to see if sheep’s wool can protect ice from melting during the summer.
For years, reflective tarpaulins have been laid over ice and snow to reduce heat absorption in the summer. But these tarpaulins are typically made from plastic and can shed polluting microfibres.
Instead, the “Keep It Wool” project is using wool to slow the melting of the Tsanfleuron Glacier. The team wanted to explore a biodegradable alternative using Swiss wool that would otherwise have been discarded.
In June, two prototype wool blankets were laid on the Tsanfleuron Glacier. Early results showed the wool covers limited melting as well as the synthetic ones would.
Still, scientists stress that lowering greenhouse gas emissions is the only meaningful long-term way to slow the loss of glaciers.

title: Olympian Siobhan Haughey nurtures meaningful discussion at book club
description: Local writers Lam Sam-wai and Eva Wong joined the star swimmer for a discussion about Xi Xi’s ‘Mourning a Breast’ at the event tailored for young women.
content:
Hong Kong Olympic swimmer Siobhan Haughey’s latest community book club gathering focused on empowering women while nurturing critical thinking, self-confidence and meaningful literary dialogue.
The project, titled Empower Through Reading, was launched three years ago in partnership with Chanel and aims to foster consistent reading habits and self-expression in young Hongkongers.
Although Haughey has spearheaded the initiative since its inception , this summer gathering marked the first time she stepped up as the sole host and lead moderator for three sessions.
“Balancing my own thoughts while keeping time, reading the room and steering the flow was a completely new challenge, but it pushed me out of my comfort zone in the best way possible,” she said.
The latest student sessions were specifically tailored to provide young women with a safe space to share their distinct life perspectives through literature.
“We actively encouraged open discussion to help nurture confidence and compassion,” Haughey said. “We built an environment where respectful disagreement was welcomed because true community grows when people feel safe to voice diverse opinions and explore meaningful discourse.”
Around 100 participants attended the sessions, where Haughey guided discussions on two featured texts: Mourning a Breast by the late Hong Kong author Xi Xi and Lessons in Chemistry by American novelist Bonnie Garmus.
Student representatives Inaaya Saeed, 17, a pupil at Pok Oi Hospital Tang Pui King Memorial College, and Hayden Ma, 17, a student at the Academy of Innovation (Confucius Hall), sat alongside Haughey to share how they were inspired by Mourning a Breast – writer Xi Xi’s memoir about battling breast cancer.
Local authors Lam Sam-wai and Eva Wong also joined Haughey for a panel discussion on the book.
“I hope students learn about the experiences of women in the 1990s, including their mothers and grandmothers, to build intergenerational empathy and understanding,” Lam said. “I also want them to realise that life offers choices and that they have the right to express or choose not to express themselves.”
Wong highlighted the subtle depth of Xi Xi’s writing style in the memoir: “Xi Xi’s work can be understood without using a dictionary, but as you read slowly, you discover very deep meaning expressed through a child’s perspective of caring for the world,” she said.
“I want students to feel a sense of hope. The title sounds sad, but it is actually a book that offers hope rather than just pain. There is growth within hardship.”
Wong added that observing young participants engage with classic Hong Kong literature demonstrated how meaningful books remain across generations.
“Seeing that students could connect with the text ... made me very happy,” she said. “Good books can transcend time and region, remaining relevant for discussion over many years.”
Held at Commaa, a coffee shop in Sheung Wan, the book club session gave secondary school participants a chance to address topics such as illness and body image.
“Back in the ’90s, people were most likely more reserved and wouldn’t share their illnesses with others, but then Xi Xi did something unusual,” said Cherish Chiu, 16, a student at Leung Shek Chee College, after attending the event.
“She wrote it out as a book, as a biography, with some funny slang and descriptions, and it makes reading her book quite enjoyable.”
The discussions also prompted participants to reflect on the physical impact of academic pressure while preparing for public exams.
“How often do we feast on knowledge, yet starve our own bodies?” asked Cherine Yip Cheuk-kiu, 18, a student at the True Light School of Hong Kong.
“During Xi Xi’s brave battle with breast cancer, she struck upon a startling truth: while we eagerly enrich our intellects with academics and soothe our souls with music and literature, we routinely neglect our physical selves.”
Yip noted that her preparation for the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) examinations mirrored this dynamic. “Now, transitioning into university offers a perfect opportunity to break this unhealthy cycle,” she said.
“We hear so much about work-life balance, but maybe it’s time we start championing body-mind balance, too.”
For student writers, Xi Xi’s playful approach to narrative structure provided a model for creative expression.
“Xi Xi’s willingness to lay bare her cancer journey was revolutionary for her time,” said Emily Lam Hin-kwan, 18, a student at Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College.
“When illness was heavily stigmatised and viewed through a lens of judgment – as though getting sick was somehow a personal failure – Xi Xi became a pioneer. She broke the silence not with bitterness but with a lighthearted, gentle courage.”
The student writer added that analysing the text broadened her understanding of creative writing techniques.
“I found Xi Xi’s narrative style to be a complete revelation,” she said. “She refused to let storytelling remain rigid, seamlessly stepping out of the plot to break the fourth wall ... Seeing how effortlessly she blurred the boundary between reality and prose taught me to be less tense in my own creative work.”
To Haughey, the discussions and the lessons students learned illustrate the importance of literature.
“Whether you read every day or haven’t picked up a book in years, I invite you to open one today, even for just a few pages, to rediscover the quiet power, clarity and sanctuary that reading brings to your life,” she said.

title: What makes glacial instability on the Tibetan Plateau even more dangerous?
description: Scientists say glaciers falling from high altitudes can trigger destructive mudslides.
content:
Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau might become more unstable and could cause more disasters.
“Over the past 60 years, the glacier area on the Tibetan Plateau has shrunk by around 24 per cent, with around 7,000 small glaciers disappearing,” Gao Rong, deputy director of China’s National Climate Centre, said earlier this month. He said glacial disasters would likely become more frequent.
This warning came after last month’s deadly landslide on the China-Nepal border. It was caused by a falling glacier.
A study was published by the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, along with other institutions. It found that downstream erosion played a big role in the damage.
When ice and rocks collapsed, they slid down the valley, scraped the riverbed, pulled debris from the banks and mixed with the water. This turned a collapse into a mudslide. Scientists stress the need to improve risk assessment and monitoring systems.

title: ICE agent shoots and wounds man in Texas
description: Man in custody pending removal as Austin mayor demands local police be involved in shooting investigation.
content: An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas, on Sunday, city officials said, adding that the man was in serious but stable condition. The man was shot in the torso and taken to a local hospital, officials told reporters at a press conference. The ICE agent shot him during a brief pursuit on foot shortly before 1pm, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said. Immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch identified the victim to multiple news outlets as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, and posted on social media that she is representing his family. Lincoln-Goldfinch said he was released from the hospital on Sunday into the apparent custody of ICE. Perez is an undocumented immigrant from Venezuela, a law enforcement source told CNN. Lincoln-Goldfinch told the Texas Tribune that her client entered the United States legally. The Department of Homeland Security said in a post on X that its Homeland Security Investigations unit is leading the investigation of a case of an officer-involved shooting in Austin ⁠on Sunday with the assistance of the FBI. The post said the person shot was a Venezuelan who entered the United States “illegally” during the Biden administration and was subject to ‌a final removal order, adding the person is stable and in federal custody pending removal. ICE is an agency within the Department of Homeland Security. City officials did not identify the man who was shot, and said they did not know the identity of the ICE ‌agent involved. Austin Police Chief Davis said she had not been briefed yet by federal officials and had few details about the incident. The shooting ⁠is the latest in a series ⁠of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and whose actions have drawn scrutiny and calls for accountability from rights advocates. Austin Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said ‌he wants city police involved in the investigation, with the additional participation of the Texas Rangers. “From my perspective, the credibility of ICE doing some form of an investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate,” Watson ‌said, ‌adding that he is angry about the shooting but not surprised by it. ICE recently started detaining more people in Austin, Watson and US Congressman Greg Casar, a Texas ‌Democrat, said. “Just a few weeks ago, as we saw the ICE surge come to Austin, especially to North Central Austin, I and others said that ICE needed to leave ⁠before someone was shot,” said Casar, whose district includes parts of Austin. Local TV news coverage on Sunday afternoon showed protesters gathered across the street from a blue Toyota ⁠Corolla that had sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby. Rights advocates say the federal immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump violates free speech and due process rights. Trump defends his actions by saying he aims to improve domestic security. Federal immigration officials have been involved in ‌multiple shootings this year, including the killing of ‌two US citizens in Minnesota, which sparked a widespread backlash. More than 50 people have died in ICE detention since Trump returned to office last year. The killing of US citizen Renee Good in Minnesota earlier this year showed that ICE cannot be trusted to provide accurate information about its shootings, Casar said. “It is important for us to have transparency and the true facts in this case,” he said. “Unfortunately, ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities.”

title: Editorial | Tung Chee-hwa’s legacy helps lay foundations for better tomorrows
description: Hong Kong’s first chief executive will be remembered for his commitment to the ‘one country, two systems’ principle and for ideas that have proved to be visionary.
content: Tung Chee-hwa’s passing unleashed a torrent of tributes from the community at large. Public condolences further affirm Beijing’s praise of Tung’s invaluable contribution to the “one country, two systems” principle. That says something about the legacy of Hong Kong’s first post-handover chief executive. The public outpouring of grief and gratitude from all walks of life set the stage for a moving state funeral and public memorial service on Sunday, and framed the eulogy delivered by Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and top vice-chairperson of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. Condolences included those from President Xi Jinping and other top state leaders. Earlier, Xi instructed the central government’s liaison office in Hong Kong to ensure Tung received the best possible medical treatment during his illness. State news agency Xinhua described Tung as a staunch patriot and close friend of the Communist Party. Shi’s address represented Beijing’s official praise and final assessment of Tung’s role in implementing and upholding the one country, two systems principle. In that regard, he highlighted Tung’s role in bravely speaking up for the government’s efforts to quell the 2019 social unrest and in safeguarding national security. Tung had firmly supported the government in curbing violence and chaos in accordance with the law, and strongly condemned foreign interference, at a time when one country, two systems was seriously challenged. In 2020, Tung spearheaded the establishment of the Hong Kong Coalition, uniting forces across all sectors of society to forge consensus and propel Hong Kong towards a fresh start. Shi also praised Tung for pushing Hong Kong-mainland collaboration, a direction he set early in his term as chief executive. In addition, he city’s former leader will be remembered for enhancing China-United States ties, having been one of the earliest to establish an unofficial channel known as “track 2” diplomacy, by funding and promoting people-to-people exchanges. It is telling that not only heavyweights from almost all sectors paid tribute to Tung but also many ordinary people, all with a similar message: Tung’s policies were visionary. It is good to see his foresight is now better understood and appreciated by the public. As chief executive, Tung consistently placed the fundamental interests of the nation and Hong Kong above all else. After stepping down as chief executive, he often stepped forward to defend the bottom line of the one country, two systems principle, safeguarding sovereignty, security and development interests. Tung backed the establishment of a sound legal system and enforcement mechanisms for safeguarding national security in Hong Kong as well as the enactment of the Hong Kong national security law. He publicly supported the National People’s Congress Standing Committee decision to revamp Hong Kong’s electoral system to allow only patriots to rule Hong Kong, emphasising that improving the electoral system would return the operation of the Legislative Council and the governance of Hong Kong to the right track. Shi said Tung was a pioneer in practising one country, two systems in Hong Kong. Tung once stated that the principle was an unprecedented undertaking that could not be allowed to fail, because its success or failure concerned the fundamental well-being of the people of Hong Kong and the historic cause of national unification and rejuvenation. Major policy challenges under Tung’s administration included his handling of the Asian financial crisis and defence against foreign financial predators who targeted the Hong Kong dollar in 1998 as well as his leadership during the severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) pandemic in 2003. Tung had introduced numerous long-term plans for the economy, livelihoods and education, including mother-tongue teaching reform, the Mandatory Provident Fund system, shortening wait times for public housing and increasing Comprehensive Social Security Assistance for the elderly. He drove structural reforms within the government, introducing the Principal Officials Accountability System to improve efficiency. Tung’s legacy will last. It helps lay the foundations for better tomorrows, with Beijing’s backing and by grasping national development opportunities. Ultimately, that is the best way to commemorate Tung.

title: Why dementia is preventable – and the new tools that can reduce your risk
description: On World Alzheimer’s Day, a look at advances in dementia diagnosis and treatment, and why much of the risk may be within our own control.
content: This is the 98th instalment in a series on dementia, including the research into its causes and treatment, advice for carers and stories of hope. Dementia news is almost relentlessly grim – a steady drumbeat of rising cases and elusive cures. More bad news came in 2025, when semaglutide, the blockbuster GLP-1 drug celebrated for treating diabetes, obesity and various other conditions, failed to slow Alzheimer’s progression. The setback prompted semaglutide’s developer, Novo Nordisk, to pull the plug on its high-profile dementia trial. Beyond the headlines, however, a quieter, more encouraging shift is under way. Significant strides in brain health research are helping us tailor treatment, refine diagnosis and manage risk far more effectively. Most importantly, science is revealing that much of this risk is within our own control. It marks a profound shift in thinking: we have gone from assuming dementia was an inevitable part of ageing to knowing increasingly that it is not. Blood tests move into everyday practice Advances in blood-based diagnostics mean they are now moving into real-world clinical use. A large real-world study in Sweden found that an Alzheimer’s blood test helped family doctors diagnose the disease with nearly the same accuracy as specialists. Covering 1,300 patients and 165 doctors, the study showed diagnostic accuracy jumped from 65 per cent to 93 per cent when doctors had access to the test results. The findings are significant because early diagnosis can slow the condition’s progression, helping patients remain independent for longer and giving families more time to plan. Another study pushed the blood test even earlier, to before any symptoms appeared. Researchers at Harvard Medical School followed nearly 2,700 cognitively healthy older adults for up to a decade, measuring the same class of protein biomarker (p-tau217). Those with very high levels had an estimated 78 per cent chance of developing cognitive impairment within 10 years, and roughly a two in five chance within five years. But would you actually want to have a test like this, and what would the results mean for you? Deborah Kan, who launched the Being Patient platform after her mother’s Alzheimer’s diagnosis to bridge the gap between patients and science, says a question she gets asked often is: should you get tested for Alzheimer’s if you have no symptoms? The general consensus, Kan says, is no. You can have a biomarker result that indicates high risk and remain clinically free of symptoms – but the result can create enormous, often needless, worry. A more useful approach, for now, is to monitor blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar. Managing those supports whole-body health, and brain health along with it. There is still no cure for Alzheimer’s – but the race to find one continues, and a broadening view of what causes the disease might help win that race. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Deborah Kan (@dkbraintalk) The drug pipeline is diversifying The GLP-1 trials may have been abandoned, but about 158 drugs are being tested across 192 active clinical trials – up from 138 drugs in 182 trials in 2025, and 127 drugs in 164 trials in 2024. This is an increasingly active space. Scientists are looking far beyond just one cause for Alzheimer’s. For years, research focused mainly on amyloid, a sticky protein that clumps together in the brain to form plaques, blocking communication between brain cells and driving memory loss. While amyloid remains an important factor, researchers now view Alzheimer’s as a “perfect storm” caused by several overlapping issues. The focus of Alzheimer’s drug trials has shifted over the past decade. Amyloid treatments, which once made up a third of all research, have dropped to about 20 per cent. Meanwhile, treatments targeting tau – a protein that forms tangles inside damaged brain cells – and treatments for immune dysfunction and brain swelling have grown, with each now accounting for a further fifth of trials. Amyloid is not seen as the sole culprit, but as part of a bigger gang. The more culprits scientists identify, the more targets they have to develop new ways to fight back. Lifestyle interventions still deliver real benefits Findings from the LatAm-Fingers study, which looked at ways to prevent cognitive impairment in Latin America, suggest lifestyle changes can bring benefits. It built on the original Finger trial – the landmark Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability. The study was built on lifestyle interventions you can count on your fingers: diet, physical activity, cognitive training, social engagement and stress management, and cardiovascular health. LatAm-Fingers adapted this model for more than 1,000 older adults across sites in 11 countries, tailoring it to local cultures. For example, researchers incorporated salsa and tango dancing into the physical activity component, and used locally available foods such as avocado and quinoa in the diet component. Over two years, participants showed a 55 per cent greater improvement in overall memory, thinking and reasoning than those following a self-guided programme that was not necessarily Finger adherent. It is a strong reminder of how much power we have to improve our own brain health – and how easily interventions can be adapted. Retinal AI tool assesses dementia risk At the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), professors Carol Cheung and Vincent Mok developed the world’s first retinal AI tool for assessing Alzheimer’s risk: i-Cog Brain Health (ICBH). Using special photographs of the back of the eye, ICBH tracks changes linked to brain health. As Mok explains, the retina is a neurosensory tissue that, anatomically and physiologically, is essentially an extension of the brain, which mirrors changes in it. With an accuracy of more than 81 per cent, ICBH helps identify people at risk of future dementia and motivates them to adopt brain-healthy habits. It is not a diagnostic tool but is effective at flagging risks that people can act on. Preliminary results suggest that tailored brain health management – lifestyle changes, for instance – in people who test positive with ICBH can slow cognitive ageing by two to three years, potentially reducing dementia cases by 20 to 30 per cent. It has found practical applications. CUHK worked with Hong Kong-based Charles K. Kao Foundation for Alzheimer’s Disease to launch a free community-based Alzheimer’s disease screening using ICBH for at-risk Hong Kong residents. Hong Kong healthcare provider Humansa has also incorporated ICBH into an early dementia detection programme for its clients. ICBH is also in use at Hong Kong’s Asia Pacific Institute of Healthy Ageing and the CUHK Medical Centre. Beyond flagging individual risk, ICBH’s real value may be as an educational tool. Mok suggests it may motivate at-risk people to adopt brain-healthy behaviours and help the public understand that dementia is, to a certain degree, preventable. Sometimes, simple is best Being Patient’s Kan attended the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference – the world’s largest annual meeting dedicated to advancing dementia science – in London in July 2026. For her, the most significant takeaway came not from the cutting-edge science presented, but from simple advice from a doctor friend. When she asked him how best to monitor brain health, he recommended buying a simple, inexpensive blood pressure cuff. His advice was straightforward: check your blood pressure – or that of a loved one – three times a week, aiming for a reading of around 120/80. If either number is consistently higher, consult a doctor. After all, your brain health depends directly on your heart and blood vessels. “[I was] surrounded by the most advanced Alzheimer’s science in the world, and the best advice I left with was a click away,” Kan says. Kan ordered a cuff online, and it was waiting for her at home by the time she got back. The science around dementia is big and important – but sometimes, it really is the simple things that matter most. After all, as the saying goes: healthy heart, healthy brain. Like what you read?
