title: 66-year-old Kau Kee’s Hong Kong fish balls are bouncing back in Mong Kok shop
description: Before the retail store opened last year, the factory’s fish balls were supplied only to food stalls and eateries.
content:
Anita Lee Yan-kwan grew up in a family business that sold fish balls to street food stalls and restaurants in Hong Kong.
For many years, the fish balls from Kau Kee Food Factory were known only to industry operators.
But last December, Lee, the second generation in her family to run the business, opened the company’s first retail store for everyday customers. It is located in Mong Kok.
Kau Kee has been a quiet leader in the food industry for 66 years, providing fish balls to almost 1,000 eateries and stalls around Hong Kong.
“Before opening the retail shop, if you were to ask people about Kau Kee on the street, they would probably not know about it,” Lee said. “Yet it’s likely almost every Hongkonger has eaten our fish balls.”
The 30-year-old used to work in the government. She changed careers during the Covid-19 pandemic and took over the family business. At the time, street food vendors were struggling to attract customers, so shops were ordering fewer fish balls. In 2023, Lee launched the company’s first online store to sell directly to consumers.
For Lee, the venture is about ensuring that the pulse of the 66-year-old business continues to beat for many years to come.

title: Barristers dismiss calls for solicitors to gain senior counsel status in Hong Kong
description: Bar Association labels push to expand elite title ‘premature’, while Law Society argues appointments should be merit-based.
content: The professional body for Hong Kong barristers has dismissed as “premature and largely academic” calls by solicitors for legal changes so fellow lawyers can gain recognition as senior counsel and rights to represent clients in higher-level courts. The Law Society, the governing body for the city’s solicitors, is calling for the higher status for its members as lawmakers scrutinise the latest round of omnibus legislative updates in Hong Kong. But the Bar Association, the body for barristers, questioned the need for such changes, noting that the city had about 100 solicitor advocates with such representation rights, but most of them had not exercised the privilege in the past two years. “A review of judgments handed down from the beginning of 2024 to the end of 2025 shows that the number of judgments where a solicitor advocate has exercised higher rights of audience in open court as lead or sole advocate is fewer than 15 cases,” the association said. “This demonstrates that the current arrangements between solicitors and the Bar work for the benefit of the litigants and [are] ... consistent with the wishes of solicitors who choose to instruct counsel.” The association added that the limited, sporadic exercise of higher rights by solicitor advocates was a result of the size of the local legal services market, its fragmentation into mostly small and medium-sized firms and a natural reluctance for firms to instruct a solicitor advocate from a competing firm. “Conversely, as barristers only take on instructions by referral, they are never competitors in the same sense,” it said. “Based on the present situation, the debate regarding the eligibility of solicitor advocates for appointment as senior counsel remains premature and largely academic.” Hong Kong’s legal system follows the English common law model, where solicitors and barristers have different responsibilities and are governed by separate rules. Each branch regulates itself. Broadly speaking, solicitors have limited rights of audience. They cannot cross-examine in the High Court or give oral submissions in the Court of Final Appeal. They handle litigation, documents, property, wills and advice, and often instruct barristers for higher courts. Barristers have unlimited rights of audience in all courts and specialise in litigation and oral submissions. Similar to solicitors, barristers can also draft legal documents or give legal advice to their clients. But lawyers practising as barristers are not allowed to serve as solicitors at the same time and vice versa. Another distinguishing feature of barristers is that they, unlike solicitors, can be appointed as senior counsel – known as queen’s counsel before the 1997 handover – by the chief justice. This elevated status is given to a small minority in recognition of their ability, standing in the profession, experience and legal knowledge. In Britain, solicitors with higher rights of audience have been eligible to apply for queen’s or king’s counsel status since 1995. Following legal changes in Hong Kong in 2012, solicitors have been allowed to gain higher rights of audience as senior advocates who can represent clients in higher courts. In 2021, the government also amended the Legal Practitioners Ordinance to allow government solicitors to qualify for promotion to senior counsel. Hong Kong currently has more than 1,700 practising barristers and 109 senior counsel. There are over 12,000 practising solicitors, including 119 solicitor advocates, according to the Law Society. The society has been lobbying for amendments to the Legal Practitioners Ordinance so that solicitor advocates who have the required experience and standing in advocacy work can apply for senior counsel status. Under Section 31A of the ordinance, only barristers are eligible to be appointed as senior counsel. The society recently renewed its calls in a submission to the Legislative Council committee studying the Statute Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill. The professional body said the proposed reform was not intended to alter that role or to diminish the standing of senior counsel. “Rather, it seeks to ensure that eligibility for appointment is determined by merit, excellence and professional standing, irrespective of the branch of the profession through which those qualities have been demonstrated,” it said. “It is consistent with Hong Kong’s long-standing commitment to meritocracy, fairness and excellence within the legal profession.” In its statement, the association argued that big law firms might be subject to intense commercial, media, government or administrative pressure that might compel them to decline representation or drop litigants. Barristers are generally required to accept any instruction within their field if a reasonable fee is offered, under what is known as the cab-rank rule aimed at ensuring unpopular clients or controversial causes still receive legal representation. The association said that rule and barristers’ self-employed status ensured all litigants were guaranteed access to justice.

title: For China’s hi-tech IPOs, it’s Hong Kong vs the mainland – but how much does it matter?
description: Firms weigh benefits of international reach against higher domestic valuations, but the dual-track dynamic is just the start, and it all aligns with Beijing’s goals.
content: Competition between mainland China and Hong Kong for hi-tech initial public offerings presents emerging technology firms with a dual-track strategic choice rather than a zero-sum battle, according to an executive at a national cross-border innovation platform. “There is naturally a degree of competition,” Lu Peng, general manager of Beijing-based Zhongguancun International, said in an interview on Thursday, referring to how tech firms select their primary listing venue. “However, the two markets ultimately target different types of enterprises and investor bases.” Firms focused on international expansion tend to view Hong Kong as the preferred venue, Lu said, while those chasing a higher valuation multiple often stay onshore, where domestic investors typically reward growth stocks with richer price-to-earnings ratios. The competition has intensified as Beijing has moved to facilitate, rather than restrict, a wave of Hong Kong listings by mainland firms, streamlining cross-border approval procedures since 2024, even as domestic exchanges remain a deeper pool for capital. In total, Beijing-based firms had accounted for 484 A-share listings, or 8.72 per cent of all A-share companies nationwide, as of August 31, according to a report by the Listed Companies Association of Beijing. Their combined market value had reached 23.74 trillion yuan (US$3.54 trillion), representing 20.39 per cent of the entire A-share market – the largest share of any region in China. Even so, Lu argued that the distinction between the two markets faded over time. Once a technology company lists, its long-term ambition is almost always to become “a great global company”, meaning many will eventually pursue listings in both venues, regardless of where they start. He said this dual-track dynamic aligned with China’s broader economic goals while supporting Beijing’s “dual circulation” strategy, which anchors growth in the domestic market while staying integrated with foreign trade and international capital. Lu spoke ahead of his plan to lead a Beijing delegation of five artificial intelligence companies to Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK – the city’s flagship financial and technology festival – in November. The delegation is likely to include Yuequan Bionics, a humanoid-robotics developer that Lu described as the group’s likely front-runner for a Hong Kong IPO, with its immediate priority being to raise capital. The other attendees are expected to be Zhongguancun Kejin, a large-language-model firm; PanaPay, a cross-border payments platform targeting emerging markets; and two other fintech-focused companies. Hong Kong’s appeal to these companies, Lu said, comes down to three roles: “a gateway, a connector, and a hub”. The city provides direct access to international capital and distribution channels, and it has a compliant environment to validate products before entering Western markets, he explained. King Leung, the global head of financial services, fintech and sustainability at InvestHK – the Hong Kong government’s investment-promotion arm, as well as one of the upcoming festival’s organisers – said the city’s fintech evolution was “directly benefiting real economy operations”. China has dubbed robotics, AI and innovative drugs its “next new three” – successors to electric vehicles, batteries and solar panels that drove the last export wave. Exports of industrial robots alone rose 18.6 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to official data. November’s festival is expanding beyond traditional finance to support the government’s “AI+” and “Finance+” push, Leung said, noting that the pivot was tailored to growing overseas demand for real-world industrial applications, where mainland firms hold a strong advantage. Industrial AI, new energy, and advanced materials for energy storage are among the new areas of focus. InvestHK said it helped 413 overseas and mainland companies set up or expand in Hong Kong during the first half of 2026, and mainland firms comprised nearly 60 per cent of the total. The investments were expected to bring in more than HK$53 billion (US$6.76 billion), with innovation and technology forming the single largest sector.

The city invested HK$251.2 billion into its health budget last year. Public funds accounted for 51.8 per cent of that spending.

But the city aims to slash the subsidy rate to 90 per cent by 2030, following an overhaul of payment systems earlier this year. The cost of visiting a general outpatient clinic also tripled from HK$50 to HK$150.

title: How to make your own Beyblade at home
description: Create your own battle top and learn more about friction as you test it at home.
content:
Beyblades are all the rage. Before your next battle spins out of control, see what you can learn about friction through this toy. Friction is the force that stops an object from moving freely on a surface.
To maximise your chances of winning, let’s take a closer look at the friction in different home environments. You can also make your own version of the popular top!
large rubber eraser (at least 4-5cm in diameter and no more than 1cm in height)
craft knife or scissors (with help from an adult)
drawing pin or push pin (at least 1.5-2cm long)
Start by creating the base of the top. It must be a perfect circle. Using the compass, draw a circle on the eraser that measures at least 4-5cm from end to end. Then, trace over the circle with a marker.
Ask an adult to help you cut the eraser along the line with a knife or scissors. Ensure that the surface is even and round. This is your top’s base.
Find the spot where you had placed the point of the compass. This is the centre of your circle. Force the pushpin through the spot. Make sure the needle goes through to the other side, but be careful not to poke yourself.
Test your home-made Beyblade using the pushpin’s head as a handle. If it wobbles, double-check that your pushpin is in the centre.
Add decorations to give your Beyblade unique powers. For attacks, cut out spiked edges and glue them onto the top’s surface. If you want it to have better defence, cut out a protective ring and attach it to the top of your Beyblade for more stability.
Now that you have your own home-made Beyblade, let’s find out which surface is the best for a competition: the floor, a carpet or a glass dish.
Take out your stopwatch and get ready to click “start”.
On a hardwood floor (or any smooth, flat surface in your house), spin the Beyblade and click “start” on your stopwatch.
Click “end” on your stopwatch when the Beyblade stops spinning. Record the time in the table below.
Repeat the test two more times, and then find the average of the three trials. Do this by adding up the total spin time from the three tests. Then, divide the sum by three.
Test your top on the other surface types and record the results.
Ask yourself: which surface has the longest average spinning time? Do you know why one surface might be better than another? Which surface causes more friction?

Medication is often cheaper across the border
Some Hong Kong public schemes have expanded to cover services in the Greater Bay Area
With healthcare costs continuing to rise in Hong Kong, many residents are now going to the Greater Bay Area to save money on medication and medical procedures.
According to Clement Chan Wai-kit, the chairman of the Cancer Patient Alliance, a local NGO, Hong Kong patient groups are organising regular weekly trips to reputable medical institutions in the bay area to help residents familiarise themselves with the mainland system and access treatment.
Chan said prices on the mainland were better for cancer patients needing expensive and innovative treatments – such as targeted therapy – thanks to a tough enlistment regime and bulk purchasing power. He estimated that prices could be a third or a quarter of medical fees back home.
Raymond Li, a 65-year-old lung cancer survivor, said he received his targeted therapy drug in Hong Kong for HK$36,000 a month.
The cost of treatments had since been reduced to HK$9,000 per month due to the drug maker’s assistance programme, but the price of the same drug at the University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen Hospital was even lower, at HK$5,000, Li noted.
“For someone like me who has lost the ability to work due to cancer, the prices mean the difference between unaffordable and affordable,” he said.

Li said many Hong Kong patients get a diagnosis from a trusted practitioner in the city first before heading to the bay area for cheaper prescriptions.
The process sometimes required an extra examination and diagnosis by mainland doctors but would still be less expensive overall than getting the medication in Hong Kong, he said.
The expansion of the Elderly Health Care Voucher scheme has also affected where Hongkongers receive medical services.
Chan noted that since the scheme’s expansion last year to cover 21 service points across nine bay area cities, such as Guangzhou and Shenzhen, many residents had travelled north for services such as dental care.

title: Slimy Japanese natto gains popularity worldwide
description: Known for its strong smell, this fermented soybean dish is packed with nutrients.
content:
Natto is a healthy Japanese food made from fermented soybeans. It is becoming popular worldwide. Between 2017 and 2025, Japan sold three times more natto to other countries than before. Most of it was sent to China and the United States.
The dish is a traditional Japanese breakfast food. It is packed with nutrients (see graphic). It also contains beneficial bacteria.
Many believe eating this snack can help you build a stronger immune system and digest food better. They also think it can build stronger bones.
But it has a strong smell. It also has a sticky texture and a unique taste. Not everyone likes it, even in Japan.
In China, people are becoming more health conscious. They are also showing interest in Japanese foods.
Natto is also famous in Japan for being affordable. A pack of 40 to 50 grams of natto sells for around 100 Japanese yen (HK$5) at supermarkets. It usually comes with little packets of mustard and soy sauce.
“I hope an era will come when people will collectively see high-quality, high-end natto as worth shelling out their money on,” Yoshihiro Noro said. He is the former head of the Japan Natto Cooperative Society Federation.
The 72-year-old is also the owner of his family-run business, Kamakurayama Natto. His company makes high-quality natto. It is “extremely stringy” but minus “stinkiness and bitterness”.
Kamakurayama Natto is about three times more expensive than average.
Still, in recent years, it has secured orders from many different places. These include Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore and even Norway.
“I’ve heard that in some countries, people have been told natto is good for their health, so they force themselves to eat it even though they strongly dislike the taste,” Noro said.
“But keep eating it, and you will definitely get hooked.”

title: Listen Up: Struggling Indian families turn to firewood amid oil crisis
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.

This week’s podcast is voiced by Graeme Acres, a production editor on SCMP’s Hong Kong desk, and Cathy Hilborn Feng, SCMP’s health and wellness editor.
Voice 1: Tovi Murru doesn’t remember exactly when his family started using firewood to cook. It was sometime in April, he said. Housework for him has doubled since. Murru, who lives in the Indian town of Kohima, gathers bits of wood from dead trees in the forest, brings them home and chops them. He also does most of the cooking now.
Voice 2: The family used to cook with cylinders of LPG, short for liquefied petroleum gas. His wife, Atoshi Ayemi, ran the kitchen back then, but cooking over a fire is too much work for his wife to manage. Murru pointed out that the rise in fuel prices has made it hard to find LPG cylinders, and everyday people are suffering. Power has been out most evenings. The couple use their mobile phones to find their way around.
Voice 1: When the United States and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. Roughly a fifth of the world’s traded oil passes through the strait, and its closure has had a significant impact on energy prices. In India, which imports nearly 90 per cent of the crude oil it uses, the war has hampered vehicles that need petrol and millions of homes and restaurants that use LPG.
Voice 2: Murru is a driver, and he lives with his wife, daughter and two dogs in a house provided by his employer. He muses that if he had to pay rent, then it would be hard to survive in the present times. Every month, he earns US$125, which is about HK$979. An LPG cylinder, if he is lucky enough to find one, costs almost a quarter of his salary on the black market, more than double what it used to cost before the start of the Iran war.
Voice 1: Murru is dexterous. It took him less than a day to build the hearth. The skilled cook can start a fire and boil eggs and broth to be eaten with rice. His three-year-old daughter loves eggs.
Voice 2: More than 4,000km from Tehran, this tiny town of Kohima also bears the brunt of the Iran war. Like many people, Murru doesn’t understand why a war that isn’t theirs is affecting everyday life. Murru is a Naga, part of an Indigenous group living in northeastern India and areas of Myanmar.
Voice 1: The family’s eyes tear up from the smoke. Wiping his brow, Murru said the smoke was bad, but he would be more affected by the heat from the fire. Ironically, the family serves their meal by an empty gas cylinder.

title: US prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court: sources
description: Trump administration readies entity-wide measures that could severely disrupt tribunal’s war crimes probes.
content: US President Donald Trump’s administration has prepared sanctions against the entire International Criminal Court (ICC) and plans to announce them soon, two sources familiar with the matter said, ‌a move that would step up its attack on the global tribunal that prosecutes war crimes and genocide worldwide. The Trump administration has made no secret of its disdain for the court and has worked to undermine it. US officials want the court to drop its arrest warrants against Israeli leaders as well as a past investigation into American troops in Afghanistan. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in July announced a campaign to isolate the court, calling on other countries ⁠to withdraw from the tribunal. Washington has imposed sanctions on a number of ICC judges and prosecutors but has so far held ‌off from imposing sanctions on the court itself, although the move has long been considered one of the options. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sanctions against the ‌court have been prepared, the sources said, even though the exact timing of an announcement remained unclear. The Wall ⁠Street Journal cited officials ⁠who said the decision could be finalised as soon as this week during the United Nations General Assembly meeting. Targeting the entire organisation directly, as well as entities that ‌cooperate with it, could severely undermine the court’s work. Any entity-wide sanctions imposed by the US Treasury would prohibit US citizens and companies from providing funds, goods or services ‌to the ‌court without a licence from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). Banks often over-comply with such US sanctions because ‌they depend on access to the American financial system. Among the court’s operations that could be affected by sanctions against the entire organisation ⁠are the procurement of IT services and insurance, the hiring of investigators and the conducting of everyday financial transactions, such as paying dozens of ⁠American employees, the ICC’s registrar and president have warned. Trump’s opposition to the court goes back to his first term. It surfaced again with a plan to penalise ICC officials, an idea developed in November 2024 when Trump was ‌reelected and the ICC issued an ‌arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza conflict. The ICC was established in 2002 by the international community to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. It asserts jurisdiction only if a member state is unable or unwilling to prosecute atrocities itself. The United States has never been a member.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): Australia’s new social media algorithm regulations
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] Social media algorithms are a powerful feature of online life, serving up content to users based on their browsing habits or personal data. Australia could soon give citizens the choice to opt out of algorithms under new legislation that also threatens big tech companies with fines if they fail to protect young users from harmful content.
[2] Open TikTok, Instagram or other platforms and you’ll see a scrolling feed or recommendations bar showing content targeted to your interests. These posts are selected for users based on programming rules called algorithms that predict what you will engage with – whether it’s something you like or that riles you.
[3] Broadly speaking, the recommendations are based on what the machine knows about you: what you’ve interacted with or posted about online, or information such as your age, job and location. Social media giants usually keep the coding behind these algorithms – the so-called “secret sauce” that drives traffic to their platforms – closely guarded.
[4] It’s a familiar pattern for many – open your phone on a break and before you know it, an hour has passed, and you’re still scrolling. That’s by design, researchers and activists say. “These platforms have engineered addictive features that keep children and adults online longer than they intend, often at the expense of sleep, well-being and real-world connection,” Mark Williams, an honorary professor of cognitive neuroscience at Australia’s Macquarie University, said.
[5] In a landmark trial in Los Angeles this year, tech giants were accused of creating “addiction machines”. Experts point to strategies companies use to encourage scrolling, like never-ending feeds, intermittent rewards and time-sensitive notifications. “This unpredictability triggers the dopamine system, creating a compulsive cycle of seeking and anticipation,” wrote Quynh Hoang, a lecturer at the University of Leicester in Britain.
[6] This can create dependence similar to substance addiction, research published in the online medical journal Cureus last year found. By pushing people to content they respond to emotionally, many say social media can drive us into “rabbit holes” that are difficult to escape. The recommendations “are designed to hold our attention, and too often that means privileging provocative and extreme content because outrage drives engagement and engagement drives profit”, said Steven Roberts, from Monash University in Australia.
[7] Under Australia’s new rules, social media giants must allow users to “opt out” of the algorithm. It also holds the firms responsible for protecting under-18s from pornography, online bullying and content that glorifies crime or encourages eating disorders. The initiative aims to bring social media back to the basics – a feed focused on updates from friends, family and pages you follow.
[8] “The government has handed Australians a switch. Whether anyone flips it is another matter,” said Lisa Harrison, a lecturer in communication and media at Australia’s Flinders University. She noted a 2025 survey of over 6,000 people in six countries, in which only one in five said they would switch off personalised recommendations if they could.
Source: Agence France-Presse, September 9

Tiangong Ultra – a white, headless humanoid – finished the sprint in 9.39 seconds, according to state broadcaster CCTV. This surpassed Bolt’s best of 9.58 seconds, set in 2009.
[3] The robot was developed by a local government-backed research centre in Beijing. It also shattered the 400-metre world record by nearly five seconds. It finished in 38.16 seconds – later revised to 38.15.
[4] In one 400-metre heat, a white-shelled robot thrashed its arms side to side as it propelled itself around the track. As it leaned dangerously forward, fans wondered aloud if it would fall. The robot wobbled as it stormed towards the finish but managed to remain upright.
[5] Fans were just as pleased to watch the robo-athletes flop, as multiple robotic runners failed to start. Others made their way around the track at the pace of a brisk walk or crumbled immediately after the gun start. Children and their parents giggled as a toddler-sized robot kicked a football off the pitch over knee-high barricades. Each clunky, barely defended goal earned the waddling humanoids roars of applause from the stands.
[6] Spectators erupted into laughter as a humanoid in a boxing ring stumbled off to the side and folded over the ropes, where it stayed motionless until humans lifted it away.
[7] The weekend’s robot records left 72-year-old spectator Hou Yali wanting to watch the machines go against humans. “We’ll be able to see more clearly whether machines can surpass humans,” said Hou, who is retired. “Right now, this is just running … a competition of speed. It’s not a test of intelligence or hiring someone to do household tasks,” she said.
[8] Hou pays people to clean her home and make meals for her weekly. She said she would like to see robots do those tasks. “People have more money in their pockets, and they may decide to use robots,” she said.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): Hidden politics of time and how clocks, calendars came to be
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] It flies. It heals all wounds. It can be of the essence, and it can be money. We’re warned not to waste it, since we cannot turn it back – even as we try to make up for it when it’s lost. The methods different peoples and communities have used to track their lives have been shaped by culture, religion, economics, technology and the governing principles both within nations and among them.
[2] “Every measurement of time is arbitrary,” said Elizabeth Cohen, a political science professor at Boston University in the United States who has written about how we chronicle time and how it impacts the way people relate to each other. Take calendars. We use them to give structure to our lives, but the spectrum of what that has looked like has been vast throughout human existence.
[3] Some followed the sun, others the moon and others still a combination of both. Even today, when the main calendar in use globally is the Gregorian calendar, with its 12 months and leap years, other calendars are still consulted for religious or cultural purposes in places ranging from Israel to Thailand.
[4] It’s not just about the how. When we think about how culture evolved around time, there’s also the why. For most of human history, there were ties to the rhythms of the natural world: the phases of the moon, the rising and setting of the sun, the ebb and flow of the tides. And in agricultural societies, the importance of when to plant and when to harvest.
[5] Industrialisation – in the form of the Industrial Revolution that started in 18th century England and spread – pushed people to shift notions of time. No longer was it about the sun’s cycle or the turn of the seasons. Industrial production meant schedules – people paying attention to the clock because they were due for specific shifts. “It was one of the goals of industrialisation to instil in people this regular, unvarying sense of time,” said Michael O’Malley, professor of history at George Mason University in the US.
[6] Time zones themselves “are about politics,” said Kevin Birth, a professor of anthropology at Queens College, also in the US. He pointed out that they are not divided in a standard format. Countries decide their own, and in the US, individual states can decide whether to observe Daylight Saving Time.
[7] A prime example is China, which stretches more than 5,000 kilometres across Asia. It has one official time zone for the country, instituted when the Communist Party took power in 1949, as a form of national unity. The entire country runs officially on Beijing time. However, the reality on the ground is that when the sun rises in eastern China hours before it does in western China, people adjust to their local times for daily life, Birth said.
[8] Time can also be a tool used in a society to manage dissent and protest, Cohen added. She pointed to examples like governments instituting curfews or protesters engaging in slowdowns or strikes. “Time has a lot of power, and people are battling over it to try and impose themselves on others or remove the yoke that has been imposed on them,” she said.

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): Amsterdam museum unveils Yayoi Kusama show after artist’s death
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] More than 300 works by Japanese contemporary artist Yayoi Kusama went on display in Amsterdam earlier this month. The exhibit has become a tribute to the “polka dot queen,” who died in August. The exhibition at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum features dozens of ceramics, etchings, and drawings from Kusama, one of the world’s best-known artists, as well as her trademark polka dot pumpkins.
[2] Around 50 of the pieces have never been displayed before, said curator Leontine Coelewij. She pulled together works from several museums in Japan, including in Tokyo and Kusama’s birthplace, Matsumoto. “I think the show will be a highlight for people who do not know the work of Kusama, but also [for] people who’ve seen her work on several occasions,” Coelewij told Agence France-Presse. “I think there will be many surprises,” the 62-year-old curator added.
[3] The centrepiece of the exhibition is a huge “infinity room” with black walls covered with yellow polka dots, featuring mirrors that give visitors the disorienting impression that the dots are never-ending. Kusama died aged 97, after a career spanning 70 years, during which her work was exhibited around the world.
[4] She channelled hallucinations and well-documented battles with mental illness into vibrant art that inevitably featured polka dots – how she saw the world. “What I think is very characteristic of Kusama is that for her, making art and drawing what went on in her mind was a way to deal with the difficult issues she had,” Coelewij said. “Art can be like a healing power.”
[5] After studying art in Japan, Kusama moved to the United States in the late 1950s, becoming a leading figure in New York’s avant-garde scene. On her return to Japan in the 1970s, she checked herself into a Tokyo psychiatric hospital, where she lived and worked right up to her death.
[6] News of her death came as the Amsterdam exhibition was being installed. “We were very sad when we heard the news ... On the other hand, we could say that this exhibition is a great celebration of her work, a tribute to a wonderful life and a wonderful body of work,” Coelewij said. Curators decided not to make any changes to the exhibition, as they had worked with Kusama on the composition. “This is how she wanted the show to be,” Coelewij explained.
[7] But Coelewij said she felt a weighty responsibility to put on an exhibit that has come to mark what she called a “full stop” on Kusama’s career. “So we can take a step back and look at her work and see this as a marvellous tribute to what she has done through the years, more than 70 years of making art,” she said.
Source: Agence France-Presse, September 9

title: Open Questions | Former WTO head Pascal Lamy on the EU’s China choice: get a rebalance, or go protectionist
description: He says Chinese authorities’ lack of interest in addressing structural macroeconomic imbalance a ‘huge problem’ for European Union.
content: Pascal Lamy served two consecutive terms as director general of the World Trade Organization from 2005 to 2013. Before that, he spent decades in various French government roles, contributing to the building of the European Union. He was chief of staff to European Commission president Jacques Delors from 1985 to 1994, and European trade commissioner from 1999 to 2004. Here, he discusses Europe’s trade tensions with China, the continent’s growth potential problem and the WTO’s need for stronger enforcement mechanisms. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. In France, many have expressed doubts about the future of free trade. Former finance minister Eric Lombard said last year that free trade is dead, killed by the US and China. Do you agree? No, free trade is not dead. And by the way, I never ever use the expression “free trade”. I’ve been in this business for decades now, and I’ve never used this expression, which is for one simple reason: it is misleading. Trade is never free. It is either more or less open. Free trade is not dead, it was never born. The question is whether the previous decades we’ve seen, which have consistently moved in the direction of more open trade – this being evidenced by the growth of the volume of international trade – whether this volume is still growing or not. If you look at the numbers, which we have to do, especially if we discuss trade, trade is still growing in volume. This means that trade is more open than it used to be. But there is a catch: the growth of international trade, at least benchmarked against the growth of the economy, has slowed. The slowdown can be attributed to many reasons. Starting with the main factor, which is the fragmentation of production systems that has led to the global supply chains that now span the world. The expansion of the supply chain, the fragmentation of production, has limits. It is efficient and productive at some stage, for some products in some conditions. But we’ve probably reached a stage where the efficiency gains stemming from the multi-localisation of production systems are slowing, with decreasing yields, like any productivity curve. At some stage you reach a level where economies of scale are less important than at the beginning of the process. Reason No 2 is that trade openness trends are now counterbalanced by trade-restricting attitudes among a number of international trade players, given the United States’ position and the huge growth of China’s exports and surplus. There are also growing reactions in some places to the expansion of international trade for social or environmental reasons. Its growth is slowing because of various reasons, but overall, international trade is still expanding. So what, in your view, are the main problems facing the global trade system? As Europeans, we have three problems in global trade today. A small one, a medium-sized one and a big one. The small one is the US. The US has embarked on a protectionist crusade, which stems from the deep belief by US President Donald Trump that tariffs are the Swiss army knife of the 21st century economy, which is not so. The ones who pay the price for that at the end of the day are US consumers. But even if he makes a lot of noise about his attempt to de-globalise the planet, this will not happen. Then we have the medium-sized problem, which is that the World Trade Organization, the international institutional engine for opening trade, is not working in the way it used to work. This is mainly a problem of organisation. The fact that the US de facto left the WTO. The fact that although a new dispute-settlement system has replaced the previous one, it does not work with the US. The fact that all decisions, including on minor issues, are still taken by consensus, and that the secretariat is not allowed to exercise its potential authority based on its first-class expertise. And that third one, in my view, is the main reason. The WTO has not been able to develop new trade-opening agreements in areas where international trade has moved a lot – digital trade for instance, which matters a lot for services – and we should always remember that international trade is goods plus services, plus the invisible part of international exchange trade today, which is about trillions of pieces of data. Then we have a big problem, which is China, which is a problem for every country. It’s a huge problem for us Europeans because we have a mega trade deficit, growing in an unsustainable way. And for the European Union, addressing this problem is a very tough task. The main reason behind it is the macroeconomic imbalance of China, which is structural, which Chinese authorities have not addressed, do not want to address, although they’ve been saying for many years that Chinese growth should be rebalanced – with more domestic consumption. China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later? It is not happening, and we are in a situation where industry in China produces twice as much as it consumes in industrial goods, hence the debate about overcapacity. China now has comparative advantages in most of the supply chains in manufacturing. Not yet in agriculture, and not yet in services. But I believe China wants to get there, following a policy developed by the Chinese government, mostly since 2010. China already has plans to make itself self-sufficient in food – why not in services too later? Because of the strategic concept that China has to become more self-reliant. In energy, in manufacturing, in technology, China has, so far, been formidably efficient in constructing self-sufficiency; other sectors will come. This is a major systemic problem, because trade opening has always been based on the theory of comparative advantage. I do something better than you do. You do something better than I do. We have a rational interest to trade, which is, by the way, the philosophical basement of the WTO. The WTO is built with the mission of promoting open trade because opening trade is a good way to create growth and welfare, because it is based on the efficiencies stemming from the exchange of comparative advantage, the international division of labour. This game seems to be over with China today. China has gained comparative advantages all along the industrial production chain for various reasons. Some of which are legitimate. They have a huge market. They have a formidable education capacity, and this is something where they have built their own comparative advantage, and they have a political regime that allows a level of strategisation, coordination, multilayered intervention, which is incredibly efficient. This has a lot to do with the political regime, and this is something, of course, that we Europeans would hesitate to emulate for a variety of reasons. China also uses its state-owned sector, its state-owned banks, its budget to heavily subsidise sectors – which is not in the spirit of a fair international division of labour – benefiting from the fact that WTO disciplines on subsidies, state support and state ownership, have remained very weak. This is the situation we Europeans now have to face. It’s not just a bit different from what it was before, where maybe we could adjust the recipes here and there with a bit more or a bit less of anti-dumping or countervailing duties. The size of the deficit is now out of reach of the normal instruments which the WTO provides to regulate trade and absorb import shocks. With China trade dynamics, we are entering a new world, a new paradigm, which opens a lot of questions about WTO disciplines. The French government’s high commission for strategy and planning has called for 30 per cent tariffs on all Chinese imports, and Paris and Berlin have expressed a desire for fast measures rather than long WTO-style investigations. Is China right that the EU is turning protectionist, and would Brussels be better off saying so openly, telling Beijing it has no choice if it wants to keep its industry? You are absolutely right, we Europeans are reaching a moment of truth with trade and China. Either we can convince China to rebalance the system and decrease its exports or we will have to go protectionist. Let’s test the willingness of China to seriously address the problem. This is the first option and in my view, the good option, provided China shows signals that it is ready to address the problem. This is Plan A. We need a Plan A, but we also need a Plan B. Some in the US argue it was a mistake to let China into the WTO. You were the one who closed the EU’s bilateral accession deal in Beijing in May 2000. With hindsight, was the mistake letting China in, or was it what the West failed to write into the terms? Would you sign the same text today? Yes and no. I think letting China into the WTO was the right thing to do precisely because it brought about an exchange of comparative advantage, and China wanted to join the WTO to benefit from an insurance policy against export restrictions. China paid a high price for subscribing to this insurance in opening its economy. China opened its economy as a developing country, roughly three times more than its developing country equivalents at the time and more than Russia 10 years later. The maximum tariff China accepted on goods was 10 per cent. China made a big effort, which led to a big divide within the Chinese leadership: between those who said [former paramount leader] Deng Xiaoping was right, we have to open to better combine Chinese characteristics and Western characteristics, and this is the way to go to grow China more rapidly, represented by [former premier] Zhu Rongji. And then there was another camp, more conservative within the leadership, that thought that opening trade with Western countries might make China more vulnerable. The first camp won and China opened its economy, which became very profitable for the rest of the world during the next 10 years. There was an end to that, which roughly coincided with the aftermath of the 2008 crisis, where the Chinese government switched back to a more ideological approach. Self-sufficiency became the new strategic priority to reach total strategic autonomy in the future. The Chinese economy was, from then on, run on a geopolitical basis, not on a geoeconomic basis. China then pushed, very successfully, to go from low-wage value addition, which was a comparative advantage 25 years ago, to where China is now, competing with the US on the frontiers of technology. To answer your question, we were right to let China in, and we were wrong not to reinforce the WTO’s rules on subsidisation and state support before China entered. The reason we did not do that – “we” being the big shots at the time: the US, EU and Japan – was we thought that we might end up restricting our ability to support our champions such as Airbus or Boeing, or Japan’s programmes to foster innovation. We were subsidising a small part of our economy, and we mistakenly remained defensive. We did not forecast how large a part of the Chinese economy would remain de facto under state control and support. Or the importance of the state-owned sector, which had actually shrunk in the first 10 years after China joined the WTO and then grew again from 2010 on. We did one thing right, which was letting China in, which benefited everybody for quite a bit of time, but we did not properly identify the risk that China’s state-owned system would drive the economy in such an efficient way, including in subsidising a strategic industry heavily at the beginning, then creating a lot of competition. The best example is what we see in electric vehicles, which were heavily subsidised at the start, and now there’s cutthroat competition within China until the system stabilises with maybe a handful of surviving producers. How do you see the current EU-China negotiations, with Brussels demanding “tangible progress” by October? Can both sides still avoid a trade war? Some argue China and the EU are already in one. Do you agree? First of all, I don’t think we should use the word “war” about trade. I’m talking to you from Ukraine, I was a naval officer in my youth. I know the meaning of the word “war”, and we shouldn’t use it lightly. We have trade frictions, we have trade disputes, we have trade tensions. There are trade tensions between China and the US. There are trade tensions between the US and Canada that were triggered by Trump because he thinks Canada should become a new US state. We have trade tensions between the EU and China, which stem from the fact that we have such a huge and growing deficit with China. The European Union today still has a trade surplus as a whole. What does this mean? This means that, overall, the EU, in what is traded today, can compete with the rest of the world. We have a trade surplus vis-a-vis the US. We have a trade surplus with many of our trade partners, except with China. If you remove €350 billion (US$407 billion) of trade deficit between the EU and China, we have a big trade surplus, which means that we are competitive with anybody on this planet except China. Now there are reasons for that, which I can totally understand. It stems from what I describe as Chinese organisation: they’ve been extremely good at gaining a comparative advantage all along the supply chain, including, for instance, in critical materials, which is extremely important for electrification and the economy. Of course, China did not do it for the pleasure of doing it. China built a comparative advantage in critical materials because China wanted to electrify, and the reason China wanted to electrify was that it wanted to be less dependent on oil or coal or gas imports. We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively It’s not because China suddenly became a believer in the necessity to reduce emissions – although I’m happy that China is doing this. China built the comparative advantage in rare earths to become less dependent on fossil fuel imports. They built this control, which now gives them a monopoly that they can weaponise. We Europeans have to try to convince China that it is in their interest, as it is in our interest, to reduce our trade deficit massively, not just by €10 billion or €20 billion. We have a €350 billion trade deficit, and this cannot be addressed by a little bit of this or a little bit of that. The problem is the magnitude of the problem. Either we can convince China to address this problem, which will need a lot of unilateral market power exercised by the Chinese side to export less, or we will have to look for other options. I hope we do not have to do this. I interpret the Sefcovic mission [aimed at rebalancing trade] and the time between now and the October deadline as a test of whether China is serious about addressing this or not. As usual, the EU gave priority to negotiation, consultation, discussion. We are not the US, and nobody wants to play Trump on the EU side, we are not brutal. We try to understand problems. We try to address this peacefully, respectfully and through negotiation. But if that does not work, we have to look at other options. Europe says it wants to be neither dependent on the US nor overwhelmed by China. Is a third position actually available, or does reducing exposure to one side mean aligning with the other? Solving this issue will not, by itself, solve Europe’s No 1 problem, which is growth. The EU’s growth potential is half of that of the US, one-third that of China and one-quarter that of India. This is a worrying situation, and one we will have to work hard on to improve our competitiveness. But becoming more competitive will not solve our China trade problem, given its magnitude and the threat it represents to the survival of some of our production systems. How did we get here, to this level of trade imbalance? Is that a story about Chinese competitiveness or industrial policy? It is overall competitiveness, all along the supply chain, which leads to this. If you have a competitive advantage all along the supply chain, there is no more fair trade. You are absolutely right, this is the result of Chinese competitiveness. Chinese competitiveness has various sources, which I mentioned: the size of the market, the organisation of the state and its capacity to subsidise efficiently. It’s not just subsidising, because you can subsidise inefficiently too. The Chinese system has learned to use subsidising efficiently, giving the industrial policy a coherent logic: what strategic priorities, what the state does, in which sector, what the regions do and what the municipalities do. There is a lot of competition within. It’s a formidable mix of non-competition, which is the state, and competition, which is a part of the economy. What would China have to do to prove that it is a defender of multilateralism and free trade? Beef up domestic consumption. Stop pushing, pushing and pushing for increasing manufacturing, which is way beyond the consumption capacity of Chinese consumers. Chinese households have a saving rate that is way too high, coming from the fact that they want to hedge against old age, children’s education spending, pensions and so on, so China also needs to create somewhat of a welfare state. Secondly, import more, export and subsidise less. Or in the case of subsidies, renegotiating the WTO rules on subsidies – what we in the EU call “state aids” – to level the playing field, which is now heavily unbalanced in the subsidisation capacity between China and Europe. And convince China to invest more in Europe in areas where tech transfers and ownership arrangements are doable, which was China’s position 30 years ago. Boosting Chinese investment in Europe is, in my view, part of the solution.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): Hong Kong cafes and coffee shops to try this month
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
Read the following text and answer the quiz below.
[1] This month, the city’s cafe scene welcomes the return of a decade-old favourite to its original neighbourhood, as well as new establishments in Sai Ying Pun. Here are four new coffee shop openings to visit in Hong Kong in September.
[2] How Dept started as a furniture showroom-slash-cafe hidden in an industrial building in Kwun Tong. It has branches in Hysan Place, K11 Art Mall and other malls. Now, it returns with a new location on the same street it occupied a decade ago.
[3] The ground-floor space at The Angle looks out over the bustling streets. Its upgraded menu includes snacks such as Sichuan spicy beef nachos and mains such as cheese egg rolls with dried sakura shrimp and salmon roe. There is also an extensive coffee selection. Shop G01, G/F, The Angle, 98 How Ming Street, Kwun Tong
[4] Coffee Boats was founded in late 2025 as a social initiative. It was supported by Caritas Hong Kong to empower young people and women from marginalised communities through work opportunities and training. Its coffee beans are sourced directly from farmers. The beans are roasted by professionally trained women from Caritas Hong Kong’s Healthy Neighbourhood Kitchen Project.
[5] Coffee Boats has held various small pop-ups and events across Hong Kong. Now, it’s taking on its most ambitious project. It is collaborating with the charity One Bite Social to take over the historic Chun On Pawn Shop in Wan Chai. The takeover runs until December 19. Twenty per cent of the revenue will be donated to Caritas Hong Kong. G/F, 91 Wan Chai Road, Wan Chai
[6] Brown Heart is a humble operation with a small menu. It is the latest in a string of coffee shops to occupy its corner spot near Sai Ying Pun MTR. The food is simple but bursting with flavour. Signature sandwiches include burrata, Parma ham and green grapes with truffle balsamic glaze, and crabmeat and mentaiko with mascarpone cheese, basil and cheddar. 176 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun
[7] Urban Coffee Roasters is a home-grown roastery. It has opened a second outlet in Central following its Hollywood Road location. The IFC store features four branch-exclusive coffees, including a fruity single-origin Ethiopian bean with notes of passion fruit, blood orange and grape, and a Geisha blend with notes of flowers, honey and tangerine. The Geisha coffee is also made into a gelato for the perfect pairing. Shop 1032, 1/F, IFC Mall, 8 Finance Street, Central

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): History of 5-kernel mooncakes, a classic Mid-Autumn treat
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
Read the following text and answer the quiz below.
[1] When you think of mooncakes, the ones that come to mind tend to be the classic sweet lotus paste versions with salted egg yolk, or maybe a more modern interpretation like one with a salty-sweet baked custard filling.
[2] Historically, the first mooncakes were made with a mix of nuts and seeds. The five-kernel ( wuren ) mooncake – filled with ingredients including walnuts, almonds and sesame seeds – was considered the height of sophistication from the 1950s to the 1970s.
[3] Five-kernel mooncakes originated from the Hu cakes introduced during the Han dynasty (206BC-AD220), when Chinese diplomat and explorer Zhang Qian brought back nuts, such as walnuts and sesame seeds, from the western regions, laying the foundation for their use in mooncakes.
[4] Later, during the Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties, these small cakes filled with nuts became popular among the common people, gradually becoming associated with the Mid-Autumn Festival. Similar multi-nut-filled cakes appeared in Qing dynasty (1644-1912) publications such as the Chinese classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber and the gastronomical guide Recipes from the Garden of Contentment .
[5] The five kernels symbolise completeness and harmony, making it a classic representative of Cantonese mooncakes. The typical kernels would include walnuts, almonds, olive kernels, melon seeds and sesame seeds, which symbolised the virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and trustworthiness – in that order.
[6] Long before white lotus seed paste or modern snow-skin flavours took over the market, wuren was the undisputed king of mooncakes across mainland China and Hong Kong. In times of material scarcity, the calorie-dense components of rich nuts, Jinhua ham and cured pork fat were highly precious, luxury food items.
[7] In the early 1950s, imported nuts were rare in Hong Kong, so the traditional five-kernel filling was often replaced with the more common peanuts, melon seeds, sesame seeds and candied winter melon. This new version was usually called a five-nut fruit mooncake, said Tse Jing-yuen, the operator of Tai Tung Bakery, one of Hong Kong’s oldest bakeries.
[8] According to Tse, there have been many variations of the five-kernel filling. The most common sweet version included candied winter melon, while the savoury version included preserved mustard greens. By the 1960s, people wanted more novelty when it came to flavours. Gradually, fillings such as five-kernel rose sweet mooncake, straw mushroom braised chicken mooncake, and roast duck mooncake appeared.
[9] Modern five-kernel mooncakes have also evolved. For example, Lung King Heen, a two-Michelin-starred Chinese restaurant in Hong Kong, has added pistachios for a more satisfying bite, saying it wished to “enhance the overall flavour and texture” of the treat.
Source: South China Morning Post, September 1

title: Opinion | Pacific island states are trapped in Cold War 2.0
description: Geopolitically, it’s like a feudal hierarchy: small island nations as vassals, Australia and New Zealand as local lords and the US as king.
content: In early July, China fired a test missile from a nuclear submarine into the South Pacific for the first time, a weapon capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Washington and Canberra were livid. The Pacific has long been the exclusive testing ground for such long-range missiles from the United States. How dare China! The reaction from Pacific island states was more measured. While leaders from Tuvalu, Palau and the Solomon Islands strongly criticised the test, the 18-member Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) failed to draft a united statement. Last month, foreign ministers again failed to agree on criticising Beijing, with Kiribati and Nauru reportedly refusing. Finally, this month, a PIF statement that “registered concern on the recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test” was issued. China was not named, and Nauru disassociated itself. Kiribati previously said singling out China was unfair when the US regularly tested such missiles near the Marshall Islands. In March, the US launched a Minuteman III ICBM from California, landing near the Marshall Islands 6,700km away; it followed a similar test in November last year. The US has test-fired at least 15 ballistic missiles into the Pacific since 2021. The historical precedent weighs heavily. Between 1946 and 1996, the US, Britain and France conducted over 300 nuclear tests in the Pacific, particularly in French Polynesia and the Marshall Islands, resulting in radioactive contamination, mass displacement, high cancer rates and generational trauma. The double standard is glaring. Geopolitically, the region resembles a feudal hierarchy: small island nations as vassal states, Australia and New Zealand as local lords, and the US as king. Since its Aukus alliance with Britain and the US, Australia has increasingly resembled just another vassal. According to a recent Guardian report, US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil – what some analysts describe as a “colonisation”. Data by California’s Nautilus Institute shows the US military controls 17 facilities on mainland Australia and has access to 75 more, with defence corporations accessing an additional 18. Meanwhile, under the Compacts of Free Association, the Marshall Islands, Micronesia and Palau operate as US defence outposts, with Washington exercising defence veto power over their foreign conduct. Australia’s diplomatic recalibration towards China reveals a troubling disconnect. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese initially pursued stabilisation after Beijing lifted punitive sanctions. China ended embargoes on Australian wine, barley and lobster by December 2024 as bilateral trade soared. Yet stability proved ephemeral. Albanese now speaks openly of China seeking “hegemony” – clearly an exaggeration, paranoia or both. He defended the US missile tests, saying there was no comparison with the Chinese test. He is right – who can compare with America when it comes to weapons tests? This tougher posture coincides with alarming developments. As US President Donald Trump’s erratic Asia policy erodes Washington’s credibility, Canberra doubles down, gambling its strategic future on a declining Pax Americana. Australia’s flurry of Pacific defence pacts with Fiji, Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu signals renewed great-power competition even as Aukus submarine deliveries remain uncertain. Beijing has warned of “measures” over any challenge to the Chinese lease for Darwin port even as it distances itself from what it calls “selfish political gains”. Australian public opinion diverges from elite consensus: 61 per cent view China as an economic partner rather than a security threat. Yet Australia’s security establishment reflexively adopts Washington’s hawkish assumptions precisely as their foundation crumbles. As Laura Tingle, ABC’s global affairs editor, wrote recently: “The world is a particularly confusing place just now. But no one seems more confused about their place in it than Australia.” Meanwhile, former New Zealand prime minister Helen Clark has issued a pointed warning: Wellington’s rush into Pacific security pacts threatens to erode its cherished tradition of independent foreign policy. Clark – who also led the UN’s development arm for eight years – argued that such moves undermine the Pacific’s future as “a zone of peace”. For decades, New Zealand balanced independence from superpower blocs with maintaining a nuclear-free Pacific. Both pillars now face strain. “The Australians being in the market for nuclear submarines isn’t helpful,” Clark said, predicting Canberra will host an American base for such vessels. Her critique targets the premise that Washington can indefinitely guarantee Pacific security while managing global commitments. Invoking Australian strategist Hugh White’s argument that China’s rise makes US primacy unsustainable, Clark cited America’s Iran preoccupation as evidence of overreach. “Apply that to the Asia-Pacific context. It’s not real, is it? So this is all a game of bluff.” Australian public opinion diverges from elite consensus: 61 per cent view China as an economic partner rather than a security threat. Clark warned that “New Zealand must never be seen as a proxy”. Her 2003 refusal to send combat troops to Iraq defined her premiership’s principled independence. She accused the current coalition government of having made “unfortunate moves”. On China, Clark counselled pragmatism: “We need to continually work on how we maintain good engagement and dialogue”. Small nations preserve agency through principle, not alignment. Wellington should remember that. As usual, however, the interests of small island nations are being trampled on amid their larger neighbours’ strategic muddle. The Pacific islands deserve better than to become pawns in a new cold war. Their residents suffered generations of trauma from nuclear testing conducted by powers that now demand their loyalty in condemning others for far less. They face existential threats from climate change while watching wealthy Western nations prioritise military competition over climate action. Australia and New Zealand style themselves as Pacific champions, but their actions reveal different priorities. Canberra’s strategic panic drives deeper military integration with Washington, while Wellington’s traditional independence frays. Neither has offered Pacific islanders a vision beyond choosing sides in someone else’s conflict. Washington, Canberra and Wellington cannot credibly claim to champion Pacific interests while maintaining double standards on missile testing. The US is militarising Australian territory while reducing island states to defence outposts. Australia cannot reconcile economic interdependence with China and security anxieties through military posturing. New Zealand is surrendering the independent foreign policy that gives it moral standing. The small island states’ months-long hesitation before issuing a mildly worded statement without naming China shows they no longer automatically align with the Anglo-American sphere. They need to assert greater agency if they are to have a fighting chance against climate change and outside dominance.

title: Trump and Mamdani set to meet in New York
description: Meeting marks first sit-down on the mayor’s turf following series of cordial exchanges between political opposites.
content: US President Donald Trump will meet New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when Trump travels to the city for the UN General Assembly. The meeting is scheduled for Monday at Gracie Mansion, the official mayoral residence, according to Anna Bahr, Mamdani’s communications director. Bahr said the two will discuss issues affecting the city and New Yorkers. The White House confirmed the meeting will take place but did not offer more details. Mamdani, a democratic socialist who upset former Governor Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic primary before winning the general election in November, has been a frequent and favourite political foil for Republicans. But Trump has often been warm to Mamdani and seemed charmed by the young mayor. Their first meeting after Mamdani’s election was quite cordial, with Trump saying at the White House that the then mayor-elect would “surprise some conservative people”. The Republican president had called Mamdani a “100% Communist Lunatic” in a social media post during the 2025 campaign. During a February meeting, Mamdani gave Trump a mock New York Daily News front page that said “Trump to City: Let’s Build”. That was a riff on the famous front-page headline from 1975, “FORD TO CITY: DROP DEAD”, referring to former president Gerald Ford’s promise to veto financial help to the city. Mamdani’s aides said at the time that it was meant to show Trump the reaction and support that new federal investments in housing could have in the city.

title: Ukraine’s Zelensky to meet Trump in New York
description: Planned meeting comes as Washington pushes for fresh, face-to-face peace talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has announced plans to meet US President Donald Trump in New York in the coming days as efforts intensify to revive negotiations aimed at ending the war in Ukraine. Zelensky said he had spoken to Trump by phone and discussed a range of issues ahead of the meeting, which is expected to take place while both leaders attend the United Nations General Assembly. A meeting in New York “could achieve a lot,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Sunday, pointing to the possibility of renewed negotiations to end the war. “The diplomatic momentum is there,” he said. Zelensky did not give a date for the meeting. Zelensky met US chief negotiator Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner earlier this month when they travelled to Kyiv. It was the pair’s first visit to Ukraine in their role as mediators in the conflict. They had previously made several trips to Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four and a half years ago. Plans are under way to revive direct negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow under US mediation, with Russia saying talks could resume in October. Negotiations reached an impasse last winter and were subsequently suspended during the Iran war. Witkoff and Kushner, who were also involved in mediation efforts in the Middle East, are now making a fresh push to help resolve the conflict in Ukraine. There are ideas for de-escalation steps and fundamental security issues – energy, food, protecting people’s lives. We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram. He did not provide further details. Zelensky has called on the United States to provide additional air defence missiles to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks. Russia and Ukraine have frequently accused each other of lacking genuine interest in ending the fighting. Ukraine, backed by Western military aid, is also seeking to regain territory occupied by Russian forces.

title: Putin’s party retains power in Russian vote marked by massive drone attack
description: Electoral chief says results show United Russia – dominating for 25 years – won 355 of the Duma’s 450 seats, the party’s highest ever.
content: Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party won a record supermajority in the Duma, authorities announced on Monday, after a tightly controlled three-day election without parties critical of the Kremlin or the war in Ukraine. Electoral chief Ella Pamfilova said preliminary results showed United Russia – which has dominated Russian politics for 25 years – won 355 of the Duma’s 450 seats. The result handed Putin’s party an increased supermajority and beat its previous record of 343 seats. The supermajority means it can change the constitution, if it needs to. The result is expected to further tighten Putin’s grip on power. The Kremlin said the result of the first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in early 2022 showed Russians were united around their leader, who has been in power since New Year’s Eve 1999. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a press briefing. Elections under Putin are tightly controlled and few in Russia doubted United Russia would win. The Communist party came second, winning 40 seats. The nationalist LDPR party took 25 seats and the New People party won 20. Putin had encouraged Russians to vote in support of troops in Ukraine and Moscow also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. The president cast the vote as a show of support for Moscow’s troops and an “answer to those who want to weaken Russia”. Moscow has banned criticism of its military campaign and the only party that called for an end to the war was removed from the election. Pamfilova said turnout was over 59 per cent, thanking Russians for voting despite what she called “psychological pressure” on the country. Kyiv hit Moscow with its biggest drone attack of the war on Sunday, the last day of voting, killing two people and setting an oil refinery ablaze. A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, officials said. There was a wave of cyberattacks too. “Despite the extreme situation, we were successful in ensuring the maximum security of these elections,” Pamfilova told a press conference, thanking security services for ensuring the vote went ahead. The conflict with Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and hit ordinary lives in Russia more than ever this year. Ukraine has targeted Russian infrastructure with drones, in retaliation for Russian bombardment of its own towns and cities. Russia’s defence ministry accused Ukraine of attempting to “disrupt the democratic will of Russian citizens”. “In response to the Kyiv regime’s attacks on civilian targets within Russia, the Russian army will continue and intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kyiv,” the ministry said. The Ukrainian attack during the election involved around 1,600 drones, 450 of which were aimed directly at the capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky praised the strikes, saying “our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night”. While diplomatic efforts to end the war have not prevented mutual strikes from escalating in recent months, Zelensky spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump, who in recent days has urged Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries. The men are expected to meet in New York this week. The Kremlin’s chief political opponents have been driven into exile, while Putin’s main rival, Alexei Navalny, died in an Arctic prison in 2024. In Berlin and London, dozens of opposition supporters gathered outside Russian embassy buildings in protest at the vote in Russia. Electoral chief Pamfilova said there had been a wave of cyberattacks targeting election infrastructure. She did not say who was responsible. The attacks appeared to have been carried out by “highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools”, she said. “Over the past period, more than 1,000 waves of DDoS attacks have been recorded against infrastructure in Russia that is specifically involved in the electoral process,” Pamfilova was quoted as saying by Russian news agencies. DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attacks involve overwhelming a system with internet traffic so that it is unable to function normally. She warned on Saturday that saboteurs had also severed communication lines in Russia’s far east, in an apparent attempt to frustrate the voting. The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas said “the veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia”.

title: Thousands march in France against ‘licence to kill’ draft law
description: Protesters target legislation granting officers presumption of legality when using firearms.
content: Thousands of people marched in Paris and other French cities on Sunday against a proposed law on the legitimate use of force that critics say would be a “licence to kill” for police and gendarmes. In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the bill which says that any police official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally when using their weapon. It now faces a vote in the Senate. Politicians, rights groups and other activists joined the Paris demonstration, among them Mathilde Panot of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party. “The police kill already,” Panot told the crowd, calling for the bill to be voted down in the Senate. “In the Republic there can be no organised police impunity,” she added. “In the Republic, there cannot be a category of citizens who have the right of life or death over other citizens.” Amal Bentousi, the sister of Amine, a robber who was shot in the back by police in an incident in 2012 at Seine-Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, was among the marchers. What she described as a “licence to execute” was intended to “reverse the burden of proof” in such incidents, she said. Amnesty International, France’s magistrates’ union and the country’s League of Human Rights also took part in the protest. Scores of other marches against the bill were organised in cities around France this weekend. Police said 4,500 people had rallied in Lyon and 3,700 in Toulouse. A petition against the bill on the National Assembly website gathered 730,000 signatures but a parliamentary law committee dismissed it in July. Defenders of the bill say it would avoid police officers automatically coming under suspicion or being detained when using armed force. But in the Marseille protest, Cedric Picard, of Amnesty International, said “we are afraid police violence would only grow with this law”. “In a country where police abuse is among the worst, this law risks worsening the situation,” said one protester, a high school pupil who gave his first name as Hugo. On Saturday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called on police to be “particularly vigilant” during the protests, fearing incidents. In the city of Rennes, officials said eight people were arrested and three police officers were injured after protesters threw projectiles at them.

title: ‘Disaster’: Germany’s embattled chancellor suffers bruising election defeats
description: Friedrich Merz is under pressure as the far-right AfD party wins another vote and his conservatives crash out of a state parliament.
content: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz faced a struggle to stabilise his position and keep his agenda on track on Monday after voters inflicted two more defeats on his party, ejecting it from a state legislature for the first time in its eight-decade history. The unpopular Merz vowed to stay on and push through reforms to Germany, Europe’s biggest economy, minutes after polls closed on Sunday in regional elections in Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural eastern region on the Baltic Sea coast. Still, final results underlined the extent of what Merz conceded was a “disaster” in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The votes have compounded widespread discontent with his leadership, as the chancellor has struggled to push through unpopular economic, health and welfare reforms seen as crucial to reviving the sluggish economy. His centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) fell just below the five per cent of the vote needed to keep seats in the regional parliament, the first time that has happened in 77 years of modern Germany’s federal republic, after losing over half its support. The CDU also dropped to second place in Berlin behind the hard-left Left Party, which is in pole position to lead the next city government – although Merz’s party could, depending on how coalition talks go, still retain city hall. Neither state is one of Germany’s political heavyweights. The CDU’s 2023 win in Berlin was its only one in the past 25 years in the capital, which has tended to lean left, and the party was already weak in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
