But the manner of its defeat in the latter in particular adds to the headwinds Merz faces after a stinging defeat by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) two weeks ago in Saxony-Anhalt – another region in the formerly communist east – damaged his authority and set off speculation that he might be replaced. AfD emerged as the strongest party in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but the centre-left Social Democrats – the junior party in Merz’s national governing coalition – were fairly close behind after a campaign focused squarely on the state governor, Manuela Schwesig, as a bulwark against the far-right party. That polarisation helped squeeze other mainstream parties, including the CDU. A left-leaning three-party coalition under Schwesig would have a majority in the new regional legislature. Schwesig and others in the governing parties have cast doubt on aspects of the federal government’s reform agenda, which is meant to bolster a chronically sluggish economy. The reform plans include a potentially painful overhaul of the creaking pension system, a reduction of Germany’s stifling bureaucracy and cuts to income tax for low- and middle income families. The head of the Social Democrats’ group in the national parliament, Matthias Miersch, said it was clear that “we need reforms”. But he told ARD television that “we must also take people’s concerns seriously”. On Monday there were mixed responses to the election results, even from within the chancellor’s own conservative ranks. CDU deputy chairman Karl-Josef Laumann, arriving at party headquarters in Berlin for post-election consultations, stressed that “the party leadership stands behind the chancellor”. But Family Minister Karin Prien said the results showed that her party “lacks empathy” to understand people’s problems. Much depends on the CDU’s influential regional leaders; the party’s eight state governors last week backed the chancellor, although questions remained about how wholehearted their support was. There are no more electoral tests this year. However, five state elections are scheduled next year, three of them in April. They include one in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, currently led by a prominent CDU figure often cited as a possible successor to Merz, Hendrik Wust. None of the five elections is in the east, where the AfD is strongest. Additional reporting by dpa

title: UK’s Burnham congratulates Trump and Danish PM on Greenland deal
description: British prime minister praises deal to bolster Arctic defence after Trump threatened to take island by force.
content: Andy Burnham has congratulated Denmark and the United States on a deal to “strengthen security in the Arctic” after the two countries reached an agreement over Greenland. The prime minister and his Danish counterpart Mette Frederiksen “welcomed the US’ commitment to the region” in a call on Sunday morning, Downing Street said. In a readout, a No 10 spokesperson said: “The two leaders began by discussing their upcoming visits to New York for the UN General Assembly (UNGA). The Prime Minister said he would use the trip to drive forward work on issues that matter to people at home, including reducing the cost of living through greater global stability and delivering security for people through closer international partnerships”. “Turning to defence and security, the two leaders discussed the forthcoming signing of a new deal to strengthen security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area between the US, Greenland and Denmark this week,” the spokesperson added. “They welcomed the US’ commitment to the region and underlined the strategic and shared importance of the High North for Euro-Atlantic security.” “The Prime Minister congratulated Prime Minister Frederiksen and the Kingdom of Denmark on negotiating a deal benefiting the US, Greenland and Denmark, and said he would pass on his congratulations to President Trump. “The leaders also discussed the situation in Ukraine, and the Prime Minister said he hoped to make further progress with partners on stepping up support for Ukraine during UNGA and in the coming weeks.” “The leaders agreed to stay in close touch,” the spokesperson added. On Saturday, the US president said he had a deal with Denmark to bolster America’s military presence in Greenland after months of threatening to take the island by force from the Nato ally.

title: Meloni pushes for burka ban in Italy’s schools, cap on foreign students
description: Italian prime minister tells party rally that foreigners must ‘respect our rules’ under proposed integration package.
content: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Sunday she will soon introduce a measure to her government that would cap the number of foreign pupils in classrooms and ban the wearing of burkas and niqabs in schools. Meloni told the youth wing of her nationalist conservative Brothers of Italy party that the measure would also make Italian language lessons compulsory for parents of foreign pupils having “serious difficulties integrating into the school system”. “For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules,” she said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. “It is the only serious way to welcome them.” Meloni specifically referred to a ban on the burka, an all-covering dress worn by some Muslim women, and the niqab, the veil worn by the most conservative Muslim women, in which, at most, only the eyes show. But Meloni did not mention the hijab, the headscarf worn by some Muslim women. Once approved by the government, the measure would need parliamentary approval within 60 days to pass into law. Meloni, who has political roots in the far-right, has consistently been hawkish on migration. But she has evolved politically over her tenure as prime minister, shifting from a nationalist outlier to an establishment figure among European Union politicians. However, she is also keen to boost her popularity before a general election next year and is introducing a string of policies that achieve that aim, including an exemption from a hated property tax on small- and medium-sized cars and scooters. Earlier this month, Meloni’s conservative administration became Italy’s longest-serving uninterrupted government since World War II.

title: US announces AI dialogue with China, launches Board of Trade
description: Key outcomes released after eight-hour marathon meeting in New York.
content: The United States and China agreed to establish a dialogue on artificial intelligence (AI) and put into operation a bilateral trade body following eight hours of negotiations in New York, just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced the outcomes after meeting Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng at JPMorgan’s headquarters. “We had a very successful engagement with the Chinese on trade and AI,” Bessent said. Greer added that the negotiations had turned earlier ideas of a Board of Trade and AI talks into concrete initiatives. “We started in Beijing with notions on a Board of Trade and AI dialogue. Today, those notions have become reality.” He added that the effort was aimed at “helping President Trump and President Xi continue their relationship”. “What matters today is that we are preparing the groundwork so that when President Xi comes to Washington on Thursday, President Trump and President Xi will be able to have a successful summit,” Greer said. The Chinese delegation did not speak to the media. The South China Morning Post reported last month that the Board of Trade was likely to be operationalised during Xi’s visit, even as discussions on the investment forum remained stalled. On AI dialogue, the Treasury secretary said they had proposed a “notification mechanism” between the two countries, and sought a “shared vision of common goals and common threats”. Chinese ambassador to the United States Xie Feng said the two sides had “candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges during consultations on economic and trade issues in NYC”. “The two sides engaged in exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, as well as the implementation of consensus reached in previous talks. They also held dialogues on AI-related issues,” he wrote on social media. The AI channel has struggled to make progress because the two sides differ over the meeting’s agenda and scope. The US side wanted to focus narrowly on AI safety and the technology’s risks, while China sought a broader conversation on global AI governance. In the run-up to the Bessent-He meeting, Washington repeatedly criticised Beijing for allowing Chinese AI companies to distil technology from US models, raising concerns over the use of American AI systems to accelerate their own development. “One of the ways we can push back against China, because the Chinese models distil from the US models, which is a polite scientific word for steal,” Bessent said on Tuesday. “As a person who manages the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal.” Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones. The Chinese embassy in Washington earlier rejected the US allegations, terming distillation “a common technical practice used by AI developers worldwide, including US companies”. As Chinese companies have closed the gap with US firms in frontier AI models, US firms and Trump administration officials have increasingly accused Beijing of using American technology to accelerate the development of its own AI systems. On the operationalisation of the US-China Board of Trade, Greer said teams from both sides were still working to finalise a list of goods that could be traded separately from future trade measures. “The teams right now upstairs are continuing to work through this to see if they can find some critical mass of goods,” he said, describing them as “non-sensitive” goods that could be traded “in a balanced way” to create “a kind of ballast for the relationship”. “We expect that the types of goods you’ll see in those lists are consumer goods, low-tech items coming in from the Chinese side, on the US side, energy products, agricultural goods, potentially medical devices, and other things like that.” They did not announce any update on the extension of the Busan trade deal, but Greer said that “US export controls were not on the agenda”. The SCMP previously reported that the bilateral trade truce agreed by Xi and Trump in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025 was likely to be extended, though Washington was not expected to push for a breakthrough at the coming meeting. At the time, the two sides agreed on a package deal that included lower US tariffs on some Chinese goods, a suspension of additional US restrictions on Chinese-affiliated companies, a one-year pause on certain Chinese rare earth export controls, and Chinese commitments on US soybeans and fentanyl precursors. On Friday, the White House raised concerns over the flow of rare earths from China and said it would be a part of Sunday’s discussion. “China’s performance in that respect has not been up to par of what we would expect,” a senior White House official said. The creation of the Board of Trade was also announced in May following Trump’s visit to Beijing, alongside a new Board of Investment, as mechanisms for managing business ties between the world’s two largest economies. Under the trade mechanism, both sides are selecting non-sensitive sectors and products eligible for a tariff-reduced trade capped at US$30 billion for each side. On Thursday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi also held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “Wang Yi stressed that the two sides should act in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit” and “make good preparations for high-level engagement in the next stage”, Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said on social media. Wang also called on the two sides to “send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive relationship of strategic stability and jointly promoting world peace and development”.

title: ‘His love for Hong Kong was profound’: Tung Chee-hwa honoured at state funeral
description: In sombre ceremony, political and business elite pay final tribute to city’s first postcolonial leader, as President Xi sends condolences.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping and other top leaders sent condolences from Beijing as Hong Kong bade farewell to the city’s first postcolonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, at a sombre yet poignant state funeral on Sunday. A report by the official Xinhua News Agency praised Tung, who died on September 8 at the age of 89, as “an outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’, a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of” the Communist Party of China. “While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition,” it said. “Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the [liaison office in Hong Kong] to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.” Xinhua also reported that following Tung’s death, Xi, Premier Li Qiang and other members of the leadership “expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to [Tung’s] family”. They included Zhao Leji, chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress; Wang Huning, the chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC); Politburo Standing Committee members Cai Qi and Li Xi; Vice-President Han Zheng; and former president Hu Jintao. Tung was a shipping tycoon elected to run Hong Kong after the 1997 handover from British to Chinese sovereignty. He resigned midway through his second term in 2005, citing health reasons, and served as a vice-chairman of the CPPCC, the country’s top political advisory body, until 2023. As residents stood watching and row upon row of white floral wreaths of tribute spilled onto the pavements around the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point, figures drawn from the highest circles of power in politics and business in mainland China and Hong Kong arrived for the state funeral, only the third in the city since the handover. Among those paying their final respects were Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and first vice-chairman of the CPPCC; Wang Dongfeng, CPPCC vice-chairman and secretary general; Leung Chun-ying, a CPPCC vice-chairman and former city leader; and Xia Baolong, director of the State Council’s Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office. Also attending the funeral were incumbent city leader John Lee Ka-chiu, who together with CY Leung was among the pallbearers. Predecessors Donald Tsang Yam-kuen and Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor were also present. The ceremony began at around 9am with attendees standing in silent tribute. A portrait of Tung hung in the funeral hall, surrounded by white orchids symbolising love and respect. A banner on top read “Deepest condolences to Mr Tung Chee-hwa”. Delivering a eulogy, Shi praised Tung for his role in helping to build US-China relations, as well as in quelling the 2019 social unrest in Hong Kong and in safeguarding national security. “He always placed national interests first and throughout his life upheld the belief that patriotism is a natural conviction,” said Shi, who visited the city as chairman of Tung’s funeral committee. “His patriotism was in all sincerity and his love for Hong Kong was profound. He had a broad vision and a staunch stance. He was a practitioner and contributor to the great cause of ‘one country, two systems’.” The principle, adopted upon the handover, governs relations between Hong Kong and mainland China. Shi also highlighted Tung’s handling of major challenges during his tenure, including the 1997 financial crisis and his defence against foreign financial predators who attempted to “snipe” the Hong Kong currency in 1998 and the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome in 2003. He recognised Tung’s efforts to promote the nation’s foreign ties and cooperation, particularly the stable development of Sino-US relations, including by founding the China-United States Exchange Foundation in 2008. He called on the public to remember Tung’s legacy, carry forward his patriotism and spirit of perseverance and dedication, and resolutely implement the “one country, two systems” principle to ensure Hong Kong’s long-term prosperity. “[Tung’s] passing is a major loss to Hong Kong and also a major loss to the country,” Shi said. The funeral ended at around 10am, and Tung’s coffin, draped in the national flag, was accompanied by sombre pallbearers, white roses tucked into the front-breast pocket of their black suits. Wearing white gloves, Leung and Lee led the coffin out of the hall with eight others, including liaison office head Zhou Ji, Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king, Chief Justice Andrew Cheung Kui-nung and tycoon Victor Fung Kwok-king. The coffin was placed in a hearse, which was escorted by police vehicles with lights flashing and residents watching silently as it wound through the streets east to the Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan for the cremation. Tung’s widow, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, was supported by family members as she left the funeral home. Members of Tung’s governance team, including his chief secretary Anson Chan Fang On-sang, his financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung and his justice secretary Elsie Leung Oi-sie were also seen attending either the funeral or the vigil held on Saturday. At several condolence points set up by the government, Hongkongers lined up to write messages in memorial books. At the North Point Government Offices, Chan Kam-wai, 78, recalled that Tung visited her family at Wah Fu Estate decades ago and praised him as a “kind man who improved the city’s housing policy”. “I think he just headed off to another world to keep working,” said Chan, referring to Tung’s famous “7-11” dedication to putting long hours into the job. A resident surnamed Cheng recalled Tung as a good leader, despite pushback against some of his policies. “Sometimes differing views are inevitable,” Cheng said. “Given that era and circumstances he faced, it can only be said that the situation was not in his favour.” State-run China Central Television reported Tung’s funeral in its main evening newscast, running footage of the proceedings and the hall packed with guests dressed in black. The 3½-minute report, carried as the third item, showed the rows of wreaths from Xi, Premier Li, the State Council, the CPPCC, the National People’s Congress and various central government units lining the funeral hall. Other senders included Foreign Minister Wang Yi, former president Hu and former premier Wen Jiabao. The Jockey Club also cancelled Sunday’s race meeting as a mark of respect, and all off-course betting branches were closed. Tung shares the rare distinction of a state funeral with industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006, both of whom were also CPPCC vice-chairmen. A resident signing the public condolence book in North Point recalled Tung as a patriot and kind leader, who displayed courage and calm despite criticism over his policies. “I never saw him speak with anger,” the 64-year-old woman surnamed Tang said. “He was so gentle, so kind, warm and welcoming to everyone he met. “Even facing heavy criticisms, he stayed calm and good‑natured. He could always respond with a smile. This made me admire him deeply. In my heart, he was absolutely the best.”

title: Rare earth exposure can triple low birthweight risk: Chinese study
description: Research tracking pregnant women in Wuhan over a two-year period shows link between critical mineral exposure and low baby birthweights.
content: A new study finds that prenatal exposure to rare earth elements can raise the risk of low birthweight, with some substances increasing the danger by more than three times. Researchers tracked 4,891 pregnant women who gave birth at Wuhan Maternal and Child Health Hospital between 2012 and 2014. They measured the concentration of 13 rare earth elements including cerium, ytterbium, and lanthanum in urine samples collected from the mothers. After adjusting for confounding factors such as maternal age and body mass index, each 1 microgram per gram increase in a single rare earth element was linked to a 25.6 to 51.4 per cent higher chance of delivering a low birthweight baby. When the scientists assessed the combined impact of all 13 elements using a weighted quantile sum regression model, the overall risk more than doubled, yielding an odds ratio of 2.004. Odds ratio indicate how a one‑unit change in an exposure shifts the odds of a health outcome. Cerium stood out as the dominant contributor, accounting for nearly half of the mixture’s harmful weight. In several analyses, exposure to certain individual rare earth elements or their mixtures produced odds ratios that soared past 3 or even 4, signalling a three-fold or greater surge in low birthweight risk. In the study group, the incidence of low birthweight was 0.8 per cent, while 7.9 per cent of newborns were classified as small for their gestational age. No significant association was found between rare earth exposure and babies being small for their gestational age, the researchers noted. Rare earths are vital for smartphones, green energy and advanced weaponry, but their extraction and processing have long polluted China’s environment and threatened public health. For decades, China exported these strategic minerals at rock-bottom prices, fuelling global hi-tech industries and Western militaries while absorbing the environmental and health costs at home. Recently, Beijing imposed export quotas and restrictions, triggering outcry from affected nations that viewed the move as retaliation in the ongoing trade war with the United States. Inside China, however, many argue that the price of rare earths must rise to compensate for the damage done to rivers, soil and the bodies of Chinese citizens. The new study provides a “chilling example” of that damage, showing that even unborn children are paying a price, according to a Beijing-based rare earth expert. “Why should Chinese newborns suffer so that American fighter jets and missiles can be built cheaply and used in conflicts that kill children in places like Palestine and Iran,” he said, requesting anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media. The study’s authors, led by Wang Youjie with Huazhong University of Science and Technology, caution that their findings are based on a single urine sample and need confirmation through more extensive prospective research. The paper was published in the September 2026 issue of the Journal of Environmental Health, a peer-reviewed publication run by the Chinese Preventive Medicine Association.

title: Trump says his big arch would be a ‘military complex’ with drones and snipers
description: US president claims massive monument will store ammunition as critics call national security framing a legal pretext.
content: US President Donald Trump said Sunday that the massive arch he wants to build between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery would become a “top grade military complex” able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition. It is one more example of how Trump is insisting that his initiatives to beautify the White House and the city are also serving a defensive purpose. Trump has been calling the new White House ballroom a “military complex” and arguing it is necessary for national security purposes. The Pentagon said it had no information beyond the US president’s statement. Trump’s announcement also comes as the arch, like his other projects, faces legal challenges. Though the arch has received early approval from the US Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued, saying the project needs to be approved by Congress. “The President’s belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality,” Nicolas Sansone, one of the lawyers representing the litigants, said on Sunday. “Congress has not authorised the arch and unless and until Congress does so, the project should not be permitted to move forward.” The Republican president said in a social media post that he had agreed, at the “strong request” of the military, to convert the planned 76-metre-tall (250-foot) memorial arch “into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage”. The arch is proposed for a circle adjacent to the Memorial Bridge, which is a heavy traffic area as one of a handful of connecting bridges between the nation’s capital and northern Virginia. Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat who represents the area, noted another potential problem, given the proximity to the Washington airport. “Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” Beyer wrote on X. “Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic.” The project is one of several that the Republican president is pursuing to leave his lasting imprint on Washington. Among the others are the White House ballroom, renaming and renovating the Kennedy Centre, refurbishing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuilding a golf course in East Potomac Park, which could significantly reduce the public’s access to running and biking paths. The groundbreaking for the arch was to have happened sometime this month. The project has not yet received final approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, which greenlit the site and preliminary plans at its July meeting. The commission was expected to take up the matter again this autumn.

title: Asian Games 200m butterfly gold just the start for Chinese swimming sensation Yu Zidi, 13
description: After bursting onto international scene last year, Hebei native clinches first regional title on debut appearance, with promise of more ahead.
content: The sky is the limit for Chinese swimming starlet Yu Zidi after the teenage girl stormed to her maiden Asian Games gold medal on her regional multi-sport games debut on Sunday. Yu powered to the women’s 200 metres butterfly crown, leading from start to finish at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre before touching the wall first in a Games-record time of two minutes and 5.08 seconds, taking over the honour from compatriot Zhang Yufei, who set the time in Hangzhou three years ago. Yu, 13, was already three seconds faster than the next swimmer, Chiho Mizuguchi of Japan, in the morning heats; even compatriot Chang Mohan, who claimed a silver medal in the evening, was more than three seconds behind in 2:08.44 in the race for gold. It was the first of three individual events Yu is scheduled to compete in. “It was only so-so,” a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal. “I hope I can swim even faster. I improved my time by 0.9 seconds here, and I believe I will perform better next time.” Saying that her “technique is still slightly lacking”, Yu added that “I need to lower my head earlier, reach farther forward and improve the movement of my legs”. It has been a swift rise for Yu, who was born in Baoding on October 16, 2012. What was meant to be a fun father-and-daughter trip to the water park one day in 2018, to escape the summer heat, turned out to be the opening of a new door. “It was really hot that summer, so I went to the water park with my dad,” recalled Yu, who was only six years old when she visited the park. “The summer vacation was very long, and I often went to the swimming pools, and that was when a coach noticed me.” It was Yu’s “exceptional feel” for water that caught the eye of a swimming coach, and it was suggested that she join a swimming team. While other children her age were still afraid of water, Yu could already float on the surface of the water on her own, and her movements were also particularly smooth. Under the guidance of enlightenment coach Li Chao, Yu showed remarkable improvement after receiving formal training. She was among the national top 10 in the women’s 400m individual medley (IM) when she was 10 years and five months old. She also reached the level of a national first-class athlete – after only four years of systematic training – when she was 12, and was then selected for the second-tier training squad of the Hebei provincial swimming team. On the team, Yu is often guided by teammate and Olympic medallist Li Bingjie, who also clinched gold with ease on Sunday, defending her 1,500m freestyle title in a time of 15:53.52. The Hebei pair are close, with Yu idolising the 24-year-old and often calling her “sister”. “Olympic champions like Ye Shiwen and Zhang Yufei are role models for all young swimmers,” Yu was quoted as telling state media Xinhua News. “But for me, my idol Li was much closer to me; I trained with her every day, after all. “I had heard about her for long, [and] since joining the same elite camp, I always trained with 200 per cent effort. I feel especially honoured to be able to train with her; it’s also a rare learning opportunity. “Sometimes when I didn’t quite understand the training content, she would patiently explain it to me and share her own experience with me. This helped me a lot and encouraged me greatly.” A host of national results, at both junior and senior levels, in 2024 showed a glimpse of her talent, but those successes did not come without hitting a hump or two along the road. Yu recalled almost giving up swimming before April’s national championship in 2024. “The dual pressure of training and studying left me exhausted,” she said. “Fortunately, with the support of my coach, teammates, friends, and parents, I realised that swimming had become an indispensable part of my life, and I simply couldn’t live without it. “I often encourage myself, telling myself that as long as I train hard, I’ll get good results.” She was right, and the next 12 months were a transformative year. At the national championships in May last year, Yu, then 12, set the fastest time in the age group – by male or female – in the 200m IM. In the subsequent World Championships in Singapore, she helped China reach the 4x200m women’s freestyle relay final. Despite not swimming in the final, in which China finished third, Yu still won a historic bronze and became the youngest-ever medallist at the Worlds. After also finishing just outside the podium in three other events – 200m butterfly, and the 200m and 400m IM – in Singapore, Yu added three National Games gold medals in November on her debut, including clocking a time of 2:07.41 to smash a 13-year-old Asian record in women’s 200m IM along the way. The previous record belonged to Chinese swimmer Ye Shiwen, who achieved it on July 31 at the 2012 London Olympic Games – Yu was not born until 78 days later. Yu’s regional record, however, has since been chalked off by compatriot Yu Yiting in June, the Zhejiang native further chopping 0.59 seconds off the time. The current women’s 200m butterfly Asian record of 2:01.81 belongs to retired Chinese swimmer Liu Zige, who achieved that feat in Jinan back in 2009. While Yu had chopped 0.63 seconds off her personal best record in the event, the few seconds difference with the regional-best time might prove a gap too far at this moment. Turning 14 only next month, Yu now holds the baton in the race to catch up with Liu, and if she is able to take down the 2:01.81 Asian mark from 17 years ago, the world record – set by Canadian swimmer Summer McIntosh in July, which is only 0.16 seconds faster – could be next. Do not forget: when swimming events kick off at the SoFi Stadium in California on July 16, 2028, Yu will still be three months away from her 16th birthday.

title: Chinese AI firm Z.ai faces reputation hit after users spot unauthorised uploads
description: ‘It’s basically like stealing something from users, and the malicious intent is what concerns me,’ Shanghai-based AI developer says.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai is facing a trust crisis after developers discovered that its coding assistant tool, ZCode, was silently uploading local workspace data to external servers without explicit user consent. Even though the company, also known as Zhipu AI, apologised and patched the vulnerability, developers said the incident was likely to weaken its reputation, especially at a time when cybersecurity is becoming a central issue in the AI industry. The issue came to light on Friday when an independent Chinese technical blogger known as Ferstar inspected a local directory in ZCode and found that a compressed file of 313 megabytes was pending upload to Alibaba Group Holding’s cloud storage service after failing 564 times, while a smaller 15-kilobyte file had been successfully sent. Both files were encrypted, he said. The larger file, according to visible filenames, contained a snapshot of a commercial project he was working on, including the project’s Git history. He said the archive could not be opened by him or the ZCode client and could be decrypted only with a private key held on Z.ai’s back end. The upload mechanism was enabled by default, and there was no button to turn it off, he said. Other users spotted similar issues. Tech blogger Feng Ruohang said in a post on Friday that he had seen at least three files uploaded. In a statement posted in its official Feishu community on Friday, Z.ai said it had fixed the issue and apologised to affected users. It added that it planned to open-source ZCode’s codebase and invite third-party assessors to review it while publishing updates on the review. It would also give all ZCode users an additional weekly quota reset as compensation, it said. Z.ai sought to assure users that the data had been immediately destroyed once uploaded. But Ferstar, the blogger who first discovered the vulnerability, questioned how to verify the “immediate destruction” claim in a Saturday update. To address ongoing privacy concerns, Z.ai said late Sunday that its model-as-a-service (MaaS) platform would introduce a data non-retention policy to prevent the persistent storage of user inputs and outputs, although certain data may still be retained for some application programming interface services, or to satisfy legal requirements. Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday. A Shanghai-based AI developer, who goes by Tuxi, said the ZCode incident was likely to have a bigger impact on community trust than on Z.ai’s underlying models. “It’s basically like stealing something from users, and the malicious intent is what concerns me,” Tuxi said. The developer said the episode could damage Z.ai’s reputation, particularly among overseas users of its GLM models, although the impact on the models themselves could be limited because developers can use GLM with other coding tools such as OpenAI’s Codex. A software engineer at a leading Chinese robotics company, who asked not to be named because they were not authorised to speak publicly, said the company had internally banned the use of Z.ai’s tools over security concerns. The incident follows similar incidents involving Anthropic’s Claude Code and Grok Build from Elon Musk’s xAI, now part of SpaceX, earlier this year. The global AI community is increasingly attaching importance to user privacy and cybersecurity. The topic may be a key point of dialogue during an expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump next week.

title: Macron, Carney pledge closer ties in Atlantic island meeting amid strains with Trump
description: Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the European Union amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the United States.
content: The leaders of France and Canada on Sunday pledged closer ties to grapple with rising geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values, after they met in the French territory of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon off Canada’s Atlantic coast. The two leaders’ visit to the territory, the first by a French president since 2014 and the ‌first by a Canadian prime minister, followed just weeks after US President Donald Trump posted an image showing the islands, as well as all of Canada and other countries in North America, covered by the US flag. Ottawa has been seeking closer ties with the European Union amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war with the United States. “Our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals, caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and new threats to our sovereignty,” Carney said in a statement alongside Macron. “The time ⁠has come to strengthen our ties.” Macron added that the two allies agreed to forge closer ties in sectors ranging from space and climate to ‌energy. “We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for international law, respect for free and fair trade, science as the basis for our decisions and the strategic autonomy that we defend,” he said. Diplomats said the visit by Macron, who was en route to the annual United Nations General Assembly of world ⁠leaders, had a symbolic weight ⁠following Trump’s social media post. The image Trump shared showed the US flag draped over a map of the United States, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, ‌and was labelled “United States of America”. It included Saint-Pierre and Miquelon and French Caribbean territories. Responding to questions on Trump’s post, Macron dismissed any notion that the territories could not be French and ‌said ‌he did not need to reaffirm that point every day just because “people have strange ideas or say strange things”. For France, Saint-Pierre and ‌Miquelon is strategically important due to its location on the doorstep of the US and the Arctic. The territory also occupies a key place in ⁠France’s cooperation with Canada, including over energy. Macron, whose government is facing increased pressure at home over rising fuel prices, said the talks had opened ⁠the door for bilateral discussions aimed at sealing concrete deals. Paris hopes Canada will broaden its exports of liquefied natural gas to Europe rather than primarily to Asia. “Canadian liquefied natural gas projects can help. They are important for Europe,” Macron said. The two ‌leaders also discussed Canada’s relationship with the ‌EU after the bloc opened the door to Ottawa becoming its first associate member, something Macron said France supported. Any move towards deeper integration, however, is likely to face hurdles. More than a decade after the EU and Canada agreed to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, and nine years after its provisional application began, several EU member states have yet to ratify the accord, including France.

title: China elevates Li Chenggang to top international trade role ahead of Xi’s US trip
description: Appointment comes as Vice-Premier He Lifeng leads a delegation to the US ahead of expected Xi-Trump meeting.
content: China has elevated veteran trade diplomat Li Chenggang to the country’s top-level international trade representative post, giving him a prominent role ahead of an expected meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. Li has been officially appointed by the State Council as China’s international trade representative, carrying a minister’s rank, Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday. He was previously the international trade negotiator of the Ministry of Commerce, and the revised official title vests him with a national-level mandate, strengthening the country’s economic relations with its key trading partners. China’s Vice-Premier He Lifeng is leading a Chinese delegation to the US for consultations on economic and trade issues of mutual concern from Saturday to Wednesday. A seasoned expert in multilateral trade rules and bilateral economic consultations, 59-year-old Li holds a bachelor’s degree in law from Peking University and a master’s degree in law and economics from the University of Hamburg. He was appointed as the commerce ministry’s international trade negotiator and vice-minister in April last year. Following the appointment, Li played an important role in US-China trade talks amid heightened tariff disputes in 2025. Li has decades of experience in World Trade Organization (WTO) dispute settlement and high-level negotiations with major global economies. In his previous tenure as China’s WTO ambassador, he was involved in handling intricate cross-border trade disputes and bridging divergences between major trading powers. In addition to Li’s promotion, the State Council rolled out a series of appointments across key economic, industrial and public service sectors. Multiple senior officials have taken up new posts, including new deputy leaders for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, the National Financial Regulatory Administration and the Cyberspace Administration of China. Meanwhile Ling Ji, vice minister of commerce, was appointed as deputy international trade representative of China.

title: Opinion | New North Korea-Russia bridge delivers a powerful message to China
description: The Yalu bridge remains unused years after completion – a reminder that despite economic reliance on Beijing, Pyongyang still decides where to invest its political attention.
content: The recent opening of a new road bridge between North Korea and Russia may look like a modest infrastructure project. In reality, the 1km stretch across the Tumen River carries implications far beyond the movement of vehicles between two border towns. For China, it is a reminder that its influence over North Korea is no longer as secure as it once appeared and that Russia may be increasingly capable of challenging Beijing’s interests on its northeastern periphery. The bridge, inaugurated on September 7, is the first dedicated road crossing between Russia and North Korea. It links the North Korean city of Rason with Russia’s Khasan, with Russian authorities saying the bridge will reduce transport costs and facilitate trade, economic cooperation and year-round traffic. But the bridge’s importance is not simply economic. Its location gives it an important strategic dimension for China. Beijing has long had an interest in gaining greater access to the Sea of Japan – also known as the East Sea – through the Tumen River. China’s northeastern provinces, particularly landlocked Jilin and Heilongjiang, are close to the sea but lack a direct maritime outlet. The Tumen River reaches the sea only a short distance from China’s border, but the river’s final stretch runs between Russian and North Korean territory. Gaining access thus requires cooperation from both Pyongyang and Moscow. The bridge doesn’t legally block China’s Tumen navigation rights, but it reinforces the physical and political barriers around Beijing’s access to the East Sea. By deepening Russia’s presence on the river, it gives Moscow and Pyongyang more say over the corridor – and shows Russia can shape access to something Beijing wants without asking. For Pyongyang, the project offers another opportunity to exploit differences between Russia and China. North Korea has become remarkably adept at maintaining relationships with both powers while avoiding overdependence on either one politically. The speed with which the Russian bridge was completed makes that point particularly stark: it took less than two years from start to finish. In contrast, China’s New Yalu River Bridge has been sitting there since 2014, still unused, and North Korea didn’t bother connecting a highway to it until 2020. The contrast sends a powerful message to Beijing: Pyongyang may depend heavily on China economically, but it still decides where to invest its political attention. That is particularly uncomfortable for Beijing because the Russian bridge comes as China has been actively trying to repair its relationship with Pyongyang. Since last year, Beijing has made increasingly visible efforts to rekindle ties that had cooled amid North Korea’s growing relationship with Moscow. While the political and maritime dimensions of the bridge deserve attention, it’s the military implications that would arguably be of most concern to China. The bridge creates a land route that could facilitate continued transfers of weapons, military personnel and other strategically important materials from North Korea to Russia. North Korea says the bridge will support “personnel exchanges, tourism and trade”. But one Ukrainian investigative organisation has argued that its primary purpose could be to establish a covert military logistics corridor supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine. The bridge’s capacity, while small, is still significant: Russian media said the crossing can eventually accommodate up to 300 vehicles and 2,323 people per day. Regular movements could also make certain military transfers more difficult to monitor. The bridge adds further weight to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s warning in July that Russia was preparing to receive another 30,000 North Korean troops. Whether that deployment materialises remains uncertain, but another major North Korean contribution to Russia’s war effort would further complicate Chinese-North Korean ties and could undo much of Beijing’s progress. In the long term, the bridge could also facilitate a two-way flow of military cooperation, potentially including Russian assistance to North Korea in a conflict involving the latter. And unlike ammunition shipments, a permanent road connection cannot simply be switched off when the Ukraine war ends. Even after the war, it could support trade, tourism, labour flows and more frequent government exchanges in fields ranging from agriculture and science to medicine and education. Beijing, however, still has a few strategic assets unavailable to Moscow. One is its clear status as a critical economic lifeline, both for Russia and North Korea. The other is its diplomatic capital. The latter could be especially crucial in the near term given the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China in November. With US President Donald Trump repeatedly expressing interest in resuming talks with Pyongyang, the summit could give Chinese President Xi Jinping an opportunity to reinforce China’s role as an indispensable diplomatic actor on the Korean peninsula. Although a Trump-Kim summit may be difficult to arrange given the limited time and Pyongyang’s unwillingness to engage with Washington, a lower-level meeting between American and North Korean officials could be feasible. China has played a mediating role before, particularly through the four-party and six-party talks, and could do so again. If Beijing can help facilitate even a modest diplomatic breakthrough in November, it would show something that infrastructure alone cannot: that China still possesses unique political leverage in Pyongyang and can prevent Kim Jong-un from further sidelining Xi in favour of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russia may be building physical bridges to strengthen its leverage over Beijing, but China can build bridges of its own through diplomacy, thereby strengthening its hand not just with Pyongyang and Moscow but also Washington.

title: Hong Kong secures expanded equal treatment and investment guarantees across Asean
description: Hong Kong authorities say signing of the protocol will bring legal certainty, enhance the investment environment and boost investment flows.
content: Hong Kong firms will benefit from expanded non-discriminatory treatment and investment guarantees in 10 Asean states after a protocol amending an investment agreement with the bloc was signed on Sunday. The protocol was signed in Manila – where Asean economic ministers are meeting – ahead of dedicated trade consultations between Hong Kong and the bloc. Undersecretary for Commerce and Economic Development Bernard Chan Pak-li signed the protocol for Hong Kong, alongside Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque and Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Commerce Suphajee Suthumpun. The protocol enables local enterprises to enjoy treatment no less favourable than that accorded to domestic or foreign enterprises in the 10 Asean states. It mainly incorporates the schedules of reservations into the investment agreement to give effect to articles, which state that a party shall accord other parties’ enterprises and their investments non-discriminatory treatment, except for reserved measures. Hong Kong authorities said the protocol would bring legal certainty, enhance the investment environment and boost investment flows. Asean has been the city’s third-largest destination for outward direct investment for four consecutive years, with investments worth HK$671.2 billion (US$86 billion). “Our flourishing investment relations have been boosted by the investment agreement which has strengthened Hong Kong’s position as an international investment hub,” a spokesman for the Commerce and Economic Development Bureau said. “We are confident that the signing of the protocol and its subsequent implementation will drive steady growth in Hong Kong’s economic, trade and investment relations with the Asean region. We will work side by side with our Asean partners to strive for further economic development and investment growth in the region.” The existing free trade agreement already guarantees equal treatment for Hong Kong service providers operating in specified sectors, including those with a commercial presence in these states. Complementing this, the amended agreement will accord enterprises and their investments in non-services sectors equal and most-favoured-nation treatment once the new rules take effect. Beyond equal treatment, the agreement guarantees that Hong Kong investments will be physically protected and treated fairly, with full freedom to transfer capital and profits. It also promises standard compensation if assets are seized or lost due to war or conflict. The 10 states from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) covered by the agreement are the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar. Extension of the agreement to East Timor – Asean’s 11th member – remains subject to the bloc’s internal procedures.

title: Does Trump’s new AI Force signal tech race escalation ahead of Xi Jinping summit?
description: Move may either aid AI risk talks or become containment tool targeting China, one analyst says, as others expect more intense tech rivalry.
content: US President Donald Trump has unveiled a new “AI Force” just days ahead of a state visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, in a potential escalation of the high-stakes technology race between the rival powers. Experts said the proposed AI Force – whose exact structure remains unclear – could give Beijing a clear counterpart for AI safety talks, but warned it risked becoming an instrument of further technological containment and export controls targeting China. In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said that “the decimation, or destruction” of artificial intelligence (AI) was among the many hoaxes generated by the “Radical Left Democrats”. “I, as President of the United States, will not stand by and let this happen,” he said. “For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force,” Trump said, adding that he would be announcing “the AI ‘czar’” in the near future. It remains unclear whether Trump intends the AI Force to be a branch of the military like the Space Force, floated by him in March 2018 during his first term in office. The Space Force was officially established in December 2019. Trump also rejected recent calls to slow down AI development, saying the US must protect its lead. “AI is the next industrial revolution … We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!” The announcement comes at a time of heated US debate over AI safety and guardrails, following calls from leading tech executives to slow the development of increasingly powerful machine learning systems over fears they could spiral out of human control. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows,” Trump said in his Saturday post, adding that the US criminal and civil justice system could handle the “BAD” of the industry. AI is also expected to feature in the broader US-China economic dialogue when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Vice-Premier He Lifeng meet in New York on Sunday. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the new force could have two contrasting effects on the intensifying US-China AI rivalry. “If the AI Force becomes a relatively centralised mechanism for coordinating risk governance within the US, future China-US AI safety talks could actually benefit from having a clearly defined policy counterpart on the US side, including on issues such as cyberattacks, loss of control over AI models and communication mechanisms for major AI incidents,” Sun said. “But if the institution primarily operates around maintaining US technological leadership, strengthening export controls and pursuing national security competition, China would be more likely to worry that ‘AI safety’ is being used as an instrument of technological containment.” Other experts contend that the new force would only lead to more intense AI competition between the rival nations. “The US military application of AI is no secret. As the US now seeks to build such a force, China – being among the leading nations in AI – will certainly perceive the competitive dynamics at play,” said Zhou Bo, a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army. “In terms of strategic balance, when one side takes action, the other is bound to respond,” said Zhou, who is also a senior fellow at the same Tsinghua University security and strategy centre. Zhou said while he “wouldn’t be surprised” if AI talks featured at this week’s expected leadership summit in Washington, “reaching an agreement on actionable, joint measures remains a very distant goal”. Sun also said the latest US move could prompt China to further strengthen cross-departmental coordination at the national level, even though the announcement carried “more political symbolism than institutional significance”. As for China mirroring the move, Sun said it was more likely to build upon its existing governance system rather than copy an American “AI Force” model with such a strong political branding component. Shi Yinhong, an international affairs professor at Renmin University of China, said the AI Force was mainly designed to compete with China and that any bilateral regulation was unlikely. “Trump has just declared that competing against China is his first priority on AI rather than any of the [other] dangers to humanity … [His] first priority is [to compete] against China. Establishing an AI Force is not a way to deal with domestic worries at all,” Shi said. Sun noted that there was no indication whether it would be a new military branch like the Space Force, but emphasised the symbolic weight of the framing. “By using the term ‘AI Force’ and deliberately drawing a comparison with the Space Force, Trump appears to be signalling that he wants to elevate AI into a long-term strategic capability comparable to space,” he said. “I am therefore more inclined to think that, at least initially, it could take the form of a White House-led inter-agency coordination mechanism rather than a military ‘force’,” Sun said, citing the absence of any executive order, budget or organisational blueprint for the AI Force so far. A new US military branch would require congressional approval through legislation, rather than a presidential order alone. Xi and Trump agreed in Beijing in May to set up an intergovernmental AI dialogue mechanism, distinct from the economic talks led by Bessent and He. However, the AI channel appears to have struggled to gain traction, with basic details of the planned talks still unresolved as Xi’s visit approaches.

title: Boeing’s 200-jet China deal could hinge on Trump-Xi talks: industry insiders
description: Beijing agreed to buy 200 Boeing jets during Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and could depend on summit outcome.
content: When President Xi Jinping travels to Washington later this month, he is likely to hop over the Pacific on a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. He will also hold the fate of the American planemaker’s much-touted China deal in his hands. Beijing agreed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft during US President Donald Trump’s visit to China in May. But the deal has yet to materialise – and the negotiations could depend on the outcome of Xi’s coming meeting with Trump in the Oval Office, according to industry insiders. With key details still needing to be agreed – especially the time frame for any purchases – the final deal was likely to be shaped by the broader economic and political bargaining between the two presidents, they said. “It’s all about the three Ws: whether, when and what,” said a retired aviation executive, who previously oversaw fleet management and engineering at one of China’s largest state-owned airlines. “With Trump’s Beijing trip in May and the 200-jet deal announcement, the ‘whether’ part is now agreed upon … But a call on when to place actual orders needs to be determined by Chinese trade officials, a vice-premier or even needs a nod from the top leader.” In May, China agreed to purchase at least 200 Boeing planes as a key deliverable from Trump’s state visit – the country’s first deal with the US aviation giant for nearly a decade. At the time, China’s Ministry of Commerce said aviation was an area where both nations could deepen “mutually beneficial, win-win” cooperation, adding that the two presidents had reached an “important consensus”, without elaborating. The White House, meanwhile, called the 200-jet deal an “initial purchase”, with Trump claiming that China could commit to buy up to 750 aircraft if certain conditions were met. The deal has appeared to stall in the months since. No details have been released regarding the number or models of Boeing aircraft involved, nor which Chinese airlines will be placing orders. No Chinese government agencies have provided updates on the deal’s status. There have not been any related announcements from Chinese airlines, either. But the silence does not mean the deal is off. Xin Qiang, a professor with Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said Beijing had been facing growing domestic calls to buy from Boeing in recent months – and that Xi’s US trip could present an opportunity to advance the deal. “Many US-focused analysts and government departments have since this year made stronger recommendations to the top leadership [to place orders with Boeing],” Xin said. “With Xi’s coming visit to Washington – which in itself is a sign of continued easing of tensions – the decision to advance the purchase makes perfect sense,” he added. “The reality is that there are very few high-end industrial products – Boeing aircraft being a prime example – that China has the need to buy and the US is able to sell.” In May, Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg cautioned that “official orders” from China “will come later in the year”, as the company was still working to iron out specifics with Chinese clients. “My primary objective was to reopen that [Chinese] market … and we accomplished that,” said Ortberg, who was part of the US business delegation that accompanied Trump on his trip to Beijing. “I think people focused a bit too much on the initial quantity,” he continued. “The order is a good start.” In July, Ortberg told CNBC that Boeing was in the process of finalising the contracts. “China will allocate the total quantity to individual airlines, then we negotiate the contracts with individual airlines,” he said. “We are in the process right now. We will have contracts here shortly.” A source with flag carrier Air China confirmed the airline was involved in discussions over a potential Boeing order. “We are involved in this, but it is not something on which individual airlines can make a final decision – it requires coordination and advancement by the National Development and Reform Commission,” the source said, referring to China’s top economic planning body. Beijing was currently maintaining a “silent period” regarding the deal status, the person added. “Our approach is to proceed and be ready, without making public comments.” The last time China bought from Boeing was in 2017, when a US$37 billion, 300-plane contract was announced during Trump’s first state visit to Beijing. But the US firm was later frozen out of the world’s second-largest economy, as US-China tensions rose and Boeing experienced a string of safety issues. In the meantime, China has directed huge orders to the company’s European rival, Airbus. Airbus has landed a series of fresh contracts in China in recent months, with Chinese airlines including China Eastern, China Southern, Air China, Xiamen Air and Spring Airlines signing formal agreements for hundreds of European-made aircraft. Switching wholesale to Airbus, however, would not be easy for China. Several Chinese airlines – including China Eastern-owned carrier Shanghai Airlines and Air China subsidiary Shandong Airlines – have all-Boeing fleets. These carriers have needed new aircraft for years to renew their ageing stock, according to independent aviation analyst Li Hanming. “China does need Boeing,” said the retired airline executive, who declined to be named as he was not authorised to speak with the media. “The art of the deal [for Beijing] is to balance commercial need with geopolitical bargaining.” For some market observers, one of the concessions Beijing will want to extract before proceeding with any Boeing deal will be securing supplies for China’s domestically made C919 passenger jet. While the C919 is assembled in China, many of the plane’s parts are sourced from overseas – including the Leap-1C engine, which is produced by CFM International, a consortium between America’s GE Aerospace and France’s Safran. In May, China’s commerce ministry said the US would “provide China with adequate supplies of engines and spare parts” for its aviation firms. The Boeing deal could be tied to firming up that guarantee. For the executive, the coming Xi-Trump meeting could provide an opportunity for “breakthroughs” in such negotiations. “What’s better than the two presidents meeting face-to-face again?” Additional reporting by Zhu Wenqian

title: Hong Kong customs seizes 13kg of suspected ketamine at airport, man arrested
description: Officers found suspected ketamine in checked luggage of a 22-year-old man who arrived in city from Frankfurt.
content: Hong Kong customs has seized about 13kg of suspected ketamine, worth an estimated HK$4.7 million (US$599,067), at the city’s airport and arrested a passenger arriving from Germany for alleged drug trafficking. According to the Customs and Excise Department, officers found the suspected ketamine in the checked luggage of a 22-year-old Japanese man who arrived in Hong Kong from Frankfurt on Sunday. “During customs clearance, customs officers found about 13kg of suspected ketamine inside his check-in suitcase. The man was subsequently arrested,” the department said, estimating the drugs’ street value at about HK$4.7 million. An investigation was ongoing, it said. “Customs will continue to apply a risk assessment approach and focus on selecting passengers from high-risk regions for clearance to combat transnational drug trafficking activities,” it said. It also reminded the public to remain alert and refrain from involvement in drug trafficking for monetary gain. Under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, those convicted of trafficking dangerous drugs face a maximum penalty of a HK$5 million fine and life imprisonment.

title: North Korea fires 2 missiles in 3 hours amid tensions over US drills
description: North Korea’s ‌Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of Kim Jong-un, blamed US-led military drills for worsening tensions on the Korean peninsula.
content: North Korea fired two missiles off its eastern coast on Sunday, its second set of tests in roughly a week and days after Pyongyang accused the US of driving tensions on the Korean peninsula through a series of military drills. Nearly three ‌hours after launching a short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) towards the East Sea, or Sea of Japan, on Sunday afternoon, North Korea ‌fired a similar missile, according to South Korea’s defence ministry. If the subsequent launch is confirmed to be a ballistic missile, it will mark two consecutive ballistic missile tests by North Korea within a three-hour window. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the first test firing from the Wonsan area at around 3pm, identifying the weapon as a ballistic missile. Japan’s defence ministry also said it appeared to be a ballistic missile. Japanese public ⁠broadcaster NHK said the projectile had come down outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone. The ‌first projectile flew around 450km (280 miles) and is presumed to belong to the Hwasong-11 series, according to South Korea’s military. The second short-range missile, which was also fired from Wonsan ‌at about 5.50pm local time, flew more than 600km (373 miles). “South Korean and US intelligence authorities have been tracking and sharing ⁠related developments from ⁠the initial stage of the launch, and have also shared information regarding the ‘North Korean ballistic missile’ with Japan,” the Joint Chiefs of Staff ‌said. South Korea’s National Security Council condemned the short-range missile launch, which follows a test on September 12. The council urged Pyongyang to immediately cease ‌missile activity, warning ‌the test directly violated UN Security Council resolutions. “We are ‌aware ‌of the recent missile launches and are consulting closely with our allies and partners. Based on current assessments, these events do not ‌pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies,” the US Pacific Command wrote in a social media post. Japan also lodged a protest through embassy channels in Beijing, according to a Nikkei report. “This series of North Korean actions threatens the peace and security of Japan, the ⁠region, and the international community,” Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi was quoted as saying by Nikkei. On Saturday, North Korea ⁠dismissed a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against Pyongyang’s nuclear programme. Pyongyang last week also condemned a US-led naval drill which included South Korea and Japan and which ran from August 29 to ‌September 10 near Guam. North Korea’s ‌Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong-un, on Friday blamed US-led military drills for “ever-worsening” tensions on the Korean peninsula and vowed no change in the country’s course to strengthen its nuclear arsenal.

title: China needs US-style immigration policy to win tech rivalry with Washington: expert
description: Li Mingbo, of Guangzhou Institute of the Greater Bay Area, says China should create English-friendly environment to attract foreign talent.
content: China can learn from US immigration strategies to attract foreign talent and stay competitive in the intensifying global tech race, a Chinese public policy analyst has said. Li Mingbo, deputy dean of the Guangzhou Institute of the Greater Bay Area (GIG), said China must be more efficient in promoting its new K visas for young science and technology specialists from overseas, noting that the country lacked an immigration system tailored for hi-tech talent. “Although the US has tightened its visa policies, I think it still offers valuable lessons for China, particularly in attracting international hi-tech talent, an area where China remains relatively weak and overly conservative,” Li said earlier this month. He said conflict-affected countries such as Ukraine, Russia and Iran were home to incredible tech talent, including top engineers and mathematicians looking for safer, better places to live. “China actually has an urgent need for certain technical professionals, and those countries have plenty of them,” Li said. “It would be great if we could bring them in through a technical immigration pathway, yet we currently lack relevant policies.” Beijing aims to become a tech superpower by 2035, and views young talent as a cornerstone of that vision. In its latest five-year plan – covering 2026 to 2030 – China has pledged to “establish an immigration system for hi-tech talent” and “attract and cultivate outstanding talent from around the world”. The pledge follows last year’s introduction of a new K-visa category, a scheme designed to draw young science, technology, engineering and mathematics, or STEM, professionals from overseas by offering streamlined entry, residence and employment options without requiring a local employer or inviting entity. The United States, China’s main geopolitical rival, has long been a magnet for global talent. Its H-1B visas are widely used by tech companies to hire professionals and serve as a major gateway to permanent residency. Data from the 2020 census showed that only 845,000 foreign nationals were living in mainland China, representing just 0.06 per cent of its overall population. By comparison, the US was home to 52 million immigrants as of June last year, accounting for about 15 per cent of residents. But Washington has tightened visa policies for highly skilled foreign workers, including a recent proposal to scrap the 60-day grace period for H-1B holders after job loss. Li and a fellow GIG researcher submitted a proposal in December in line with Beijing’s push to attract foreign visitors and residents. The proposal advocates for a unified identity authentication system that shares data across departments and platforms, creating a single identity framework for the visitors’ entire stay in China and eliminating day-to-day operational hurdles. They also suggested linking personal information to a unique permanent ID, rather than a passport number that changes upon renewal, for seamless access to services such as banking, accommodation, transit and work. However, Li said he did not know how the proposal was progressing. Beyond simplifying work permits, residence visas and identity authentication systems, Li emphasised the need for an English-friendly environment to attract more foreign visitors and residents. He suggested standardising English translations on public signage and introducing English-language interfaces for ride-hailing and navigation apps. But Li warned that top-level efforts to attract foreign talent could face resistance from domestic public opinion, urging people to be more open-minded on increased immigration. The debut of K visas in August last year triggered an online backlash in China, with many arguing the plan overlooked the country’s high youth unemployment and competitive job market. Additional reporting by Fan Chen

title: A guide to Hong Kong’s bitter herbal teas and how Gen Z is reviving the health tradition
description: These century-old ‘leung cha’ cooling teas for ailments such as excess internal heat are finding new fans among health-conscious Gen Z.
content: In the first instalment of a four-part Health Matters series on traditional Chinese medicine, Lisa Cam and Ashlyn Chak explore how a new generation of health-conscious youth is discovering century-old leung cha and helping neighbourhood tea shop owners safeguard a dying trade. Long before modern chain pharmacies and over-the-counter painkillers were readily available in Hong Kong, there were leung cha: intensely bitter herbal “cooling teas” brewed in massive brass cauldrons in traditional open-front shops. To the uninitiated, these dark, earthy, grassy decoctions served in ceramic bowls are an acquired taste at best. For generations of local workers, though, these century-old remedies have been consumed to ease sore throats, flush out seasonal “dampness” and reset bodies run down by urban stress. The stores function as everyday street clinics. Not unlike espresso bars in Italy, customers approach the counter, buy their tea, have it while standing – and leave. Unlike coffee, however, leung cha is drunk purely for functional wellness rather than taste or aroma. The practice of drinking cooling teas originated in Guangdong, a southern province of China, says Hong Kong author and food writer Lui Ka-chun. “So the tonics are usually for very southern ailments such as dampness and excessive heat, which you won’t find so much in northern China. These are home remedies from farming communities.” From mountain foragers to street corner clinics The concept of cooling tea shops started as an offshoot of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) clinics. People who worked for practitioners gained some knowledge, then prepared and sold their own ready-to-drink remedies. Soon, enterprising hawkers began selling bowls of cooling tea on food carts. “Seeing a practitioner is expensive and sometimes drinking cooling teas can nip some conditions in the bud,” Lui explains. “It is not unlike taking over-the-counter medicine before you get really sick and have to go to the clinic to see a doctor.” He adds: “I’ve interviewed Hakka communities in the northern districts of the New Territories [in Hong Kong], and they still go up the mountains to forage herbs.” Leung cha shops proliferated in Hong Kong during the city’s industrialisation in the 1920s. “As factories started springing up in Hong Kong and people entered the workforce, they had less time to make home remedies, so it was only natural that more of these cooling tea shops opened,” Lui explains. The shops were more than just providers of these tonics – they also served as community centres. They opened where busy people congregated, near cinemas and industrial areas with a lot of factories, such as in Sham Shui Po in Kowloon. When not every household could afford a television or a radio, a tea shop was the place to go. People dropped in to listen to the news or a programme while taking a break in their busy day. It was also a common place to meet up for dates before cafes or cha chaan tengs – bustling tea restaurants serving a blend of Cantonese fast food with Western-influenced comfort dishes – were common. The cultural importance of the trade was formally recognised in 2006, when herbal tea was inscribed on China’s first national list of Intangible Cultural Heritage. According to records from Hong Kong’s Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, there were 385 Chinese herbal tea shop permits in force in the city as of late 2025 – a network that operates alongside hundreds of commercial chain outlets and Chinese medicine dispensaries. Keung Wai-kwan, 60, is the second-generation owner of the Pak Po Tong cooling tea shop, which opened on Temple Street, between Jordan and Yau Ma Tei, in 1982. Her shop, like others in the city, sells several varieties of cooling tea, all based on TCM remedies, including the popular 24 herbs and five flower teas. Because everyone’s body is different, each brew uses a distinct combination of herbs to target specific health needs and achieve different results, Keung explains. In a place like Hong Kong, where the weather is relatively humid, people generally drink these teas to remove dampness. How over-clearing ‘internal heat’ can backfire Like over-the-counter medications, cooling teas should be used as needed rather than consumed indiscriminately, Hong Kong TCM practitioner Samuel To Ching-shan says. These herbal brews are intended as short-term treatments for acute “internal heat”, rather than everyday hydration. They are best reserved for sudden flare-ups marked by systemic signs like dark yellow urine or constipation, alongside upper-body symptoms such as a bitter taste in the mouth, dry throat, swollen gums, mouth ulcers or a feverish, flushed face. Misusing cooling teas can easily strip the body of its essential yang – or internal warmth – and exacerbate underlying digestive issues. “It is entirely unsuitable to drink them if your body already lacks warmth,” To cautions. “If you frequently feel cold, have icy hands and feet, or are prone to bloating, stomach pain and loose stools, your spleen and stomach are already weak. These herbs will only deepen that chill.” The popularity of tea shops has waned over the years as factories closed, people found other places to go, and the teas started being sold in cans, bottles or as ready-mixed powders in supermarkets and convenience stores. “They have lost their spot in the community,” Lui says. “There is an abundance of places for people to hang out, and there are over-the-counter medicines for everything. The knowledge of which teas to drink for different conditions has also been lost in the younger generations. If someone drinks the wrong kind of tea for their symptoms, they will simply chalk it up as ineffective.” Several cooling tea shops in the city have recently closed – the businesses operate on thin profit margins and high turnover, making it hard to sustain as commercial rents increase. Keung, however, says this decline is not happening at Pak Po Tong. “Many long-time patrons who supported us back in the day still come back,” she says. Students who used to drop by after class at nearby schools still visit decades later. “Now, they’ve become mothers and bring their husbands and kids along.” Gen Z’s focus on wellness, too, has triggered a resurgence in the popularity of leung cha, she adds. “Surprisingly, more young people are coming now. Over the past few months, I’ve noticed that young people are super health-conscious. Maybe through the internet and various sources, they know [leung cha] is good for them. [These new customers] are in their twenties, and they’ve already built a solid health foundation. Some people come regularly as a form of health maintenance.” Just as an established restaurant owner is not threatened by instant meals or fast-food chains, Keung does not see commercially sold home-brew packets or large chains selling cooling tea as her competition. “First off, your recipe is different,” she says. “Secondly, ours is freshly brewed. Freshly brewed versus machine-manufactured are two completely different things, totally distinct. “We start at around 6am, brew it until about 10am or 11am, then it gets delivered here to us. So ours is 100 per cent made in Hong Kong, with absolutely no additives at all.” Keung concedes that many traditional tea shops face a problem: if they are family-run, they often find the next generation unwilling to take over. Other traditional shops in Hong Kong, such as goldsmiths, are disappearing one by one because the children are not interested in continuing the businesses.
