Keung is proud that her 26-year-old son, Li Ming-hin, continues to work at Pak Po Tong. “I told him I don’t believe this trade is a sunset industry or that it will fade away,” she says. “Because wherever there are people, or wherever there’s this humidity, there’s a need for cooling teas. The demand will naturally be there.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by 阿雷 Alex (@xalexmartini) Popular leung cha offerings – ingredients and benefits 24 herbs tea (ya sei mei): A potent, intensely bitter blend of up to two dozen medicinal plants designed to clear severe internal “heat” (yit hay) and toxins. Five flower tea (ng fa cha): A milder, naturally sweeter floral infusion – traditionally including kapok, frangipani and honeysuckle – used to clear summer heat, detoxify the liver and soothe throat irritation. Hemp seed drink (fo ma yan): Made from roasted hemp seeds blended with sesame and almonds into a sweet, nutty drink known in TCM for aiding digestion and relieving constipation. Self-heal spike tea (ha fu chou): A cooling, slightly bitter herbal tea made from Prunella vulgaris, targeted at clearing “liver fire”, relieving eye strain or headaches, and soothing swollen glands. Turtle jelly (gwai ling gou): A firm, dark, herbal jelly traditionally made with powdered turtle shell and cooling herbs, eaten to nourish yin and clear toxins. Many modern shops now offer a plant-based version. Turtle tea (gwai ling cha): A liquid decoction featuring similar cooling, detoxifying herbs as turtle jelly, brewed into a drink for relieving internal heat. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Hong Kong school told to review arrangements after alleged Cantonese video ban
description: Education Bureau steps in after viral post, as Good Hope School principal Gary Harfitt clarifies that Cantonese is not forbidden at institution.
content: Hong Kong’s education authorities have urged a local secondary school to review its arrangements for events after a post alleging the school banned Cantonese in graduation videos sparked outrage online. In a response to the South China Morning Post on Sunday, the government said the school had activated its crisis management team to follow up on the issue and sent an email to all teachers and students to clarify the matter. “The Education Bureau has urged the school to review the relevant event arrangements and maintain effective communication with stakeholders,” a government spokeswoman said. “The bureau will remain in contact with the school to provide appropriate guidance and support.” The issue came under scrutiny after a recent viral post on social media platform Threads that shared internal presentation records from Good Hope School, a semi-private girls’ school in Ngau Chi Wan. Referring to “a Band 1A girls school on Clear Water Bay Road”, the user posted images resembling presentation slides titled “Language Standards”, which stated that classes would have to mute the audio and redo sound effects if Cantonese was detected in the voice tracks, with only English and Mandarin permitted. Amid the escalating controversy, Good Hope School principal Gary Harfitt clarified that Cantonese was not forbidden at the institution. In an internal email to students and parents that circulated online on Saturday, Harfitt addressed the social media posts and comments on guidelines given to Form Six students regarding their graduation ceremony next year. “Today a PowerPoint slide that had not been revised was regrettably issued to Secondary Six students. It contained inappropriate language and I deeply regret this,” Harfitt wrote, referring to the incident on Friday. He said the institution recognised the importance of Cantonese and Mandarin alongside English. He added that he took full responsibility for the oversight and stressed that the slide’s message did not reflect school policy. “A high school farewell ceremony only happens once in a lifetime, and we do not want it to end with regrets,” the Threads user wrote, adding that the city had no future if its students lacked the freedom to speak Cantonese.

title: China’s CXMT touts new chip manufacturing platform as close to ‘world’s most advanced’
description: Fifth-generation process narrows gap with global leaders Samsung and SK Hynix as the DRAM maker shows two 24-gigabit chips.
content: Chinese memory chip giant Changxin Memory Technologies (CXMT) said on Sunday that it adopted its new-generation technology platform for mass production, narrowing the advantage of global leaders including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in manufacturing nodes. CXMT’s fifth-generation technology platform, dubbed G5, achieved a “quantum leap” in storage density, with the number of dies produced per wafer increasing by at least 50 per cent from the previous generation while maintaining better energy efficiency and cost control, the company said in a statement on Sunday. As dominant players – including South Korea’s Samsung and SK Hynix – are using 10-nanometre (nm) process technology, CXMT said it had reached the 11.95nm threshold using “quadruple exposure” technology, bringing it close to the level of “the world’s most advanced mass production memory platforms”. CXMT also displayed two mass-produced LPDDR5X products based on the G5 platform. The high-speed, low-power dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chips for mobile devices each featured a capacity of 24 gigabits, a 50 per cent increase over the previous generation of similar products. The company said the products fit the needs of “mid-to-high-end smartphones and portable consumer electronics”, and it vowed to “continue to advance technological iterations to meet global market demands” in the future. The announcement – at the World Manufacturing Convention in CXMT’s hometown of Hefei, capital of central China’s Anhui province – comes as the firm is gaining ground with domestic smartphone vendors. Some of its high-end chips have found their way into flagship Chinese handsets as vendors push into the premium market. ZTE-backed Nubia’s NaviX Ultra, which went on sale on Wednesday integrating ByteDance’s Doubao artificial intelligence assistant, uses LPDDR5X DRAM chips from CXMT. Xiaomi and Transsion, the latter known for its budget phones in emerging markets, are also among the customers using CXMT’s LPDDR5X line. Shanghai-listed CXMT, which became China’s most valuable listed tech firm after a blockbuster initial public offering in July, began producing its LPDDR5X chips based on its previous platform in May 2025. Its share of global DRAM revenue rose to 9.5 per cent in the second quarter from 7.6 per cent in the first quarter, according to data from TrendForce in early September. Samsung led the global market with a share of 39.4 per cent, followed by SK Hynix at 24.9 per cent and US company Micron Technology at 23.3 per cent.

title: Chinese Good Samaritan arrested for manslaughter after kindness leads to fatal accident
description: The tragedy sparks heated online debate, with many mourning a misfortune where good intentions ironically ‘paved the road to hell’.
content: Online community in China is heart-wrenched over a driver’s goodwill in pulling a rope across a road as a warning sign, which ultimately took the life of a passer-by. The case emerged after the driver, surnamed Xie, was arrested for manslaughter in central China’s Henan province on September 11. While driving along a dirt road in a village, the concrete mixer truck driver noticed potholes that caused a bumpy ride. With some leftover concrete mix in his truck, Xie volunteered to fix the road himself. He then tied a dark-coloured cable between two trees across the road to warn drivers and passers-by of the wet concrete in that section of the passage. However, that kind gesture ended in tragedy. A 45-year-old villager was strangled by the suspending rope while riding an electric bicycle on the road early on August 10. She fell to the ground and was suffocating when discovered by her secondary school son, who had ridden about 10 minutes behind her, according to the woman’s relative. She was taken to the hospital for emergency treatment but could not be saved. The woman, Wu Xia, supported three children with her monthly earnings of 4,000 yuan (US$600) from odd jobs and farming. She had gone to town for the market earlier that morning and was just over a kilometre away from home when she was killed by the cable. A relative stated that it was a finger-thick cable, strung at the end of a downhill slope, suspended about one metre above the ground. The woman’s family tracked down Xie, who had paid tens of thousands in funeral expenses. A government worker from the village told the Chinese media outlet Hongxing News that they have been following up on the case. They confirmed that Xie was arrested for manslaughter. In China, the crime of manslaughter, known as causing death through negligence, carries a standard sentence of three to seven years of imprisonment. The tragedy sparked heated discussions online, with many expressing pity for the misfortune caused by good intentions. “Good intentions paved the road to hell,” commented an online observer. “A cable like that could warn no one. Not to mention it would be invisible at night; even during the day, it can be easily overlooked by fast riders,” remarked another. “The driver should have placed an eye-catching warning sign there, or at least tied some bright-coloured fabrics to the cable,” suggested a third. “Ignorance is more dangerous than malice,” commented another. This was not the only case of harm caused by suspending ropes and kite strings. In April, a 13-year-old boy, also in Henan, suffered severe neck injuries after a rope strung across a rural road caught his throat while he was riding an electric bicycle. The boy’s trachea was severely ruptured, and his lungs also suffered internal bleeding. He was transferred to a hospital in Beijing and treated in the intensive care unit. His life was saved, but he still faced a long and challenging recovery ahead.

title: Meet Catrine Spencer, the 4th wife of Princess Diana’s brother Charles Spencer
description: The earl, whose memoir Swan Song: Diana, My Sister publishes next week, married the archaeologist earlier in May.
content: Charles Spencer, the brother of the late Princess Diana, has made headlines recently with the claim that King Charles III said she, his ex-wife, would soon be forgotten after her death in a 1997 car accident in Paris. In his book Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, due to be published next week, Spencer claims then-Prince Charles told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” He also accuses Charles of having “contempt” for his ex-wife and of sounding “elated” after her death. While Buckingham Palace has refuted the claims, saying grief can “colour memory in ways others do not recognise” in an unusually robust statement, the death and troubled married life of Princess Diana have once again been thrust back into the spotlight. Attention has turned to the earl himself, with his complicated family life now news fodder. Spencer’s turbulent relationships have themselves made headlines over the years, most recently when he wed his fourth wife – 18 years his junior – earlier this year. Spencer’s new bride, Catrine “Cat” Spencer (née Jarman), 44, whom he wed this May, had lodged a claim against his then-wife Karen Spencer over the “misuse of private information” in October 2024. The lawsuit was settled in late 2025, per People. Here’s what we know about Earl Spencer’s new wife. What is Catrine Spencer’s background? Dr Cat Spencer holds a PhD in archaeology and specialises in the Vikings. According to her Academia profile, she advises on the development of the Museum of the Viking Age in Oslo, set to open in November 2027, “providing research and written texts as background for creating the museum’s new exhibits and online content”. She is also a freelance author and historical consultant for television and media. How did she meet Charles Spencer? The couple reportedly met while she was searching for the remains of an ancient Roman villa on Althorp’s grounds for a Channel 4 documentary, according to The Telegraph. Spencer confirmed they were dating when he told The Times in October 2024 that they “are close”. They officially tied the knot in a private ceremony in Arizona in May this year. The 62-year-old earl took to Instagram to announce the news and shared a carousel of wedding photos. “15 May 2026 – the happiest day ever”, he wrote. “A very close friend said to me, months ago: ‘The thing about Cat is, she’d want to be with you if you lived in a hut. Little did I know she’d also be happy to marry me in a desert,”’ he continued. Charles Spencer has been married four times. Besides Catrine and Karen, he also wed Victoria Aitken and Caroline Freud (formerly Caroline Hutton before she married Matthew Freud). He reportedly has seven children in total, including glamorous socialite daughters Lady Kitty Spencer and twins Lady Amelia and Lady Eliza Spencer. They host a history podcast together Spencer and Catrine co-host the podcast The Rabbit Hole Detectives with Reverend Richard Coles, where they “chase the provenance of historical objects both real and metaphorical”, per Apple Podcasts. However, it’s unclear whether they still run this, as the most recent episode was posted over a year ago in April 2025. Catrine and Karen’s legal dispute In October 2024, Catrine sued Karen for “alleged misuse of private information” regarding her multiple sclerosis diagnosis. Karen fired back two months later, accusing her ex-husband and Catrine of having an affair since 2022 and launching a “bullying campaign” against her. In December 2025, a spokesperson for Karen shared a statement with People announcing that she and Catrine had settled their legal battle. “Countess Spencer confirms that the legal proceedings brought against her by Cat Jarman have been resolved in an agreed settlement,” the statement read. “There was no admission of liability or wrongdoing, and Earl Spencer has been ordered to pay the legal costs, which are expected to be in excess of £2m [US$2.6 million] together with £4,500 [US$6,000] in damages to be paid to his girlfriend Cat Jarman.” With additional reporting by AP

title: Low pay, job insecurity for China’s trainee doctors a turn-off for young talent
description: A sharp drop in the number of candidates for clinical medicine has highlighted the challenges of pursuing a medical career.
content: Huang Qiaoyuan has just a year to go before she completes her undergraduate medical training in southern China, but she is thinking of quitting the field and going into consulting. Huang, a fifth-year clinical medical student in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, said she was initially drawn to the idea of being a doctor during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the contributions of health workers came to the fore. She also thought it would be a financially secure choice in a country where the career has carried high prestige. “I truly believed that medicine was a skill-based career that would protect me from unemployment,” she said. But the reality of the work has made her reconsider her choice. Huang said that during the 12-month unpaid internship of the final year, the interns rarely performed procedures, instead spending most of their time on mundane administrative tasks. The risk of injury in medical disputes was also a factor, she said, but the main factor was everyday workplace pressures. “The main driver is the squeeze on young and mid-career doctors caused by ‘cost-cutting and efficiency-enhancing’ measures, namely the lack of job opportunities, low pay and heavy workloads,” she said. While medicine still attracts some of the nation’s best and brightest, the shine is coming off the career as general work conditions and competition from other industries encourage students to look elsewhere. That trend is reflected in the admissions for medical schools, which draw applicants from all over the country. Among the top 10,000 participants in this year’s college entrance exam in Zhejiang province, medicine was still the top choice overall but the threshold for getting into many medical schools was lower, according to Chinese media reports. For example, the lowest-scoring Zhejiang candidate admitted to study medicine at Sun Yat-sen University, a top school in Guangdong province, was 1,300 places lower in the exam rankings than the lowest performer last year. It was a similar situation at Southern Medical University, also in Guangdong, where the lowest scorer allowed in was 2,000 places further down on the list than in 2025. The decline was even sharper among candidates from within Guangdong. The minimum entry threshold for a Guangdong resident to get into Southern Medical University fell by more than 10,000 places compared with 2025. I truly believed that medicine was a skill-based career that would protect me from unemployment Huang Qiaoyuan, medical student The decline was concentrated among the five-year undergraduate clinical medicine programmes, like the one Huang has almost finished. Graduates with these degrees must go on to complete three years of residency at a hospital, but the competition for places to do this training is fierce, so much so that a master’s degree or higher is now the baseline requirement. Going down this path would take at least 11 years. Meanwhile, long-term tracks offering a faster route to advanced degrees – such as “5+3” integrated bachelor’s and master’s programmes – remain sought after, and admission rankings for other medical disciplines, including dentistry, stayed relatively stable. Even if a graduate makes it into a residency programme, the pressure is not over. Trainees must complete clinical rotations across key departments, gaining well-rounded hands-on experience that mirrors the clinical workload of a full-time hospital staff member – all for little pay. “I’m almost 30, but I’ve yet to achieve a stable professional status. I still have to rely on my parents for financial support,” one commenter said. China is not the only country that requires a long-term commitment to complete a medical education, but overseas trainee doctors often benefit from a more established residency system with stronger financial safeguards. In the United States, for instance, many resident physicians are salaried hospital staff who are entitled to benefits such as health insurance, paid time off and relocation help. Their pay typically starts around US$60,000 to US$70,000 in their first year with annual increases, providing a basic financial safety net during training that is on a par with the national average salary. In contrast, the income for Chinese medical students during their residencies remains precarious. On top of base pay and hospital performance subsidies, they should receive a central government allowance. But while central authorities allocate 30,000 yuan (US$4,500) annually per trainee, a 2020 survey by medical platform DXY revealed that nearly 28 per cent of residents were paid less than 1,000 yuan each month, with 8 per cent receiving no income at all. Only 32 per cent of those surveyed earned more than 3,000 yuan a month, a level many described as barely enough to get by. Emerging degree subjects such as artificial intelligence are also growing in appeal, contributing to the shift away from the traditional discipline, observers say. However, among commenters online, the tough conditions for would-be doctors were the main cause. “Even if we get hired by a hospital, we still face heavy workloads and endless night shifts, all while having to do academic research and take constant exams,” one commenter wrote. “And amid the economic downturn, many hospitals have slashed salaries, upending the long-held balance between effort and compensation.” According to Chen Zhiwen, an academic committee member at the Chinese Society of Educational Development Strategy, universities nationwide have generally seen an increased intake for other, more popular majors. Chen told China Comment, a social science journal supervised by the Communist Party, that this meant the lower entry rankings were affecting other majors and were not unique to medicine. Speaking to the same publication, Jin Hui, head of the clinical nutrition department at Southeast University’s Zhongda Hospital, also said she considered the trend to be normal. “In any major, some people will drop out halfway while others remain genuinely passionate,” she said, adding that improving the support system for young doctors could rebuild the industry’s appeal.

title: UK media is ‘cancerous’ to Harry and Meghan, Diana’s brother says
description: Diana died in a car crash as photographers pursued her, sparking a reckoning over whether the media bore responsibility for her death.
content: The media’s treatment of Prince Harry and his wife Meghan ⁠is on a par ⁠with that faced by his mother ⁠Diana, the late princess’s brother said in an interview published on Sunday, warning that lessons needed to be learned from that period. Diana died aged 36 in a 1997 Paris car crash as photographers pursued her on motorbikes, sparking an outpouring of ‌grief and a reckoning over whether the media bore some responsibility for her death after splashing details of her life across front pages for years. “If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant,” Diana’s brother, Earl Charles Spencer, said. “And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example.” “I’m not ‌here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their ‌life.” Harry, Diana’s youngest son, and Meghan cited the impact of what they called ⁠a toxic media on ⁠their lives before they quit royal duties and moved to the United States in 2020. They also sued much of ‌the British tabloid press – with varying degrees of success – before they moved back to Britain in August. Spencer has made headlines around the ‌world ‌in the last week after his book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister”, was serialised in the Daily ‌Mail, accusing her former husband, the now King Charles, of sounding “giddily elated” in the hours after ⁠her death. The palace responded by saying the king “is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud ⁠reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” The publication of the book and the return of Harry ‌and Meghan to Britain are ‌another challenge for the king, who is still undergoing treatment for cancer. Diana’s family accused the royals of showing a lack of support or care towards the late princess before her death, a charge that was repeated by Harry, who is now largely estranged from the rest of the royal family.

title: China’s trade limits continue to bite into Japan’s imports of rare earths, other minerals
description: Rare earth magnet imports fall 17 per cent, following a 52 per cent plunge in July, amid deteriorating ties between Beijing and Tokyo.
content: China’s exports of key materials to Japan remained on a downward trend in August, with shipment volume of rare earth magnets falling 17.1 per cent from a year earlier, according to the latest customs data. China exported about 212 tonnes of rare earth permanent magnets to Japan last month, down from nearly 256 tonnes a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data released on Sunday. That followed a 52.2 per cent year-on-year plunge in July. Other rare earth products and critical materials also recorded declines last month. Exports of rare earth metals to Japan fell 11.2 per cent year on year, while exports of rare earth compounds dropped 48 per cent. Exports of natural flake graphite and other natural graphite fell 36.5 per cent and 77.1 per cent, respectively, while exports of unwrought tungsten plunged 94.7 per cent. The extended decline comes amid deteriorating ties between Beijing and Tokyo since late last year, after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made controversial remarks on Taiwan. Beijing has since taken a series of steps to curb economic ties with Japan, from warning Chinese citizens against travelling to the neighbouring country to tightening export curbs on “dual-use” items, referring to goods that have both civilian and military applications. China banned exports of dual-use items to Japan in January and subsequently added 40 Japanese entities to its export control list. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, a think tank under China’s Ministry of Commerce, described August’s decline as “a normal reaction under the current system of rare-earth export controls on Japan”. “The controls have raised concerns among market participants, and they are adjusting their expectations accordingly,” he said, adding that the shift in expectations “presents a very tangible shock for Japanese firms”. China’s exports of rare earths and related products to Japan were unlikely to see meaningful improvement if Takaichi’s stance towards China continued, he added. Rare earth magnets are critical components in electric-vehicle motors, wind turbines, certain consumer-electronics products and advanced defence applications. China is the world’s largest supplier of the magnets, as well as rare earth materials more broadly. As trade tensions with the West have escalated, Beijing has increasingly used its dominance in rare earths and other critical minerals as a source of leverage in economic and trade relations. Japan ranked seventh among destinations for Chinese rare earth magnet exports in August by volume, with Germany, South Korea and the US being the top three. China’s shipments of rare earth magnets to the US declined 13.2 per cent year on year to 512 tonnes in August, despite Beijing resuming approvals for some rare earth shipments and easing some restrictions on critical-material exports following trade negotiations in November. Shipments to Germany fell 22.4 per cent by volume, while total shipments to EU member states declined about 21 per cent, based on calculations by the South China Morning Post based on customs data. Overall, China’s rare earth exports by volume fell by 18.25 per cent year on year in August.

title: Asian Games: Hong Kong women claim historic swim silver, Yu leads China domination
description: City’s 4x100m freestyle relay team finish second in record-setting pace, while teen star Yu Zidi enjoys golden debut in Tokyo.
content: Hong Kong’s women made Asian Games history on Sunday, winning silver in the 4x100m freestyle relay, while China’s contingent dominated the day in the pool from start to finish. Olympian Siobhan Haughey pushed her team, who were in fourth after Gilaine Ma’s opening leg, into second, and Li Sum-yiu and Natalie Kan Cheuk-tung held their position to finish in three minutes, 36.59 seconds, a new Hong Kong record. The previous best of 3:39.10 was set in Hangzhou, where they claimed bronze, as they had done on four previous occasions. It was just the second silver the team have ever managed, after one in 1994. Haughey, who was part of the team that won bronze in Hangzhou, was proud of the collective efforts of the swimmers. “I felt really happy for sure; we have two Asian Games debutants on the team, and we scored a medal on the first day,” Haughey said. “It shows that we actually have quite a lot of young swimmers who have great potential. I believe our swimmers will perform great in the following days.” Ma, who was making her Asian Games debut, enjoyed soaking up the atmosphere of the event. “It’s my first Asian Games, the atmosphere was really good, and I can feel it instantly the moment I stepped into the competition hall. I am happy to be swimming here, and I wasn’t thinking about the outcome; I was just trying to do the best I could. I am happy to be swimming with this team.” Haughey added: “Swimming relays is more fun and anxious compared to competing in individual events, as you need the four of us to work together. You can’t control the outcome just by yourself, so it’s the collective effort of all four of us in winning this medal.” China, meanwhile, took gold in a Games record time of 3:33.10, while Japan claimed bronze in 3:39.09. Earlier, teenage swim sensation Yu Zidi had put an exclamation point on her Games debut with a record-setting victory in the women’s 200 metres butterfly in Japan. Pan Zhanle followed shortly after and proved he was still the best 100m freestyle swimmer after storming back from behind to defend the title he won in Hangzhou. The 13-year-old Yu led from start to finish at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre, as China’s dominant swimmers added more gold to a day that had quickly become full of it. Yu’s time of two minutes and 5.08 seconds sliced almost half a second off the previous record, set by compatriot Zhang Yufei at the Hangzhou Games three years ago. It was also 0.63 seconds faster than her personal best, achieved in March in Shenzhen at the China Open Swimming Championships. Compatriot Chang Mohan took silver more than three seconds behind in 2:08.44, with Japan’s Misa Okuzono claiming bronze in 2:09.67. In the 100m freestyle, Pan was third at the midway point but the Paris Olympic champion exploded in the second half to take out halfway leader Kim Young-beom of South Korea to win the gold medal. The 22-year-old finished in 47.61 seconds, while Kim, who clocked a time of 47.65 seconds, and compatriot Hwang Sun-woo (47.79 seconds) rounded out the podium. And just some six hours after smashing her own Asian Games record in the women’s 50m breaststroke, China’s Tang Qianting did it again in the final, chalking off another 0.05 seconds to finish in 29.45 seconds to win a second regional multi-sports games gold. Japan’s Satomi Suzuki, who finished in 29.91 seconds, was sandwiched between a pair of Chinese swimmers as Yang Chang claimed bronze in 30.24 seconds. In the men’s 100m backstroke final, China’s Xu Jiayu dominated all the way to clinch gold in an Asian Games record time of 51.98 seconds. Second and third place were only 0.01 seconds apart, with Hidekazu Takehara of Japan claiming silver in 53.93 seconds, just ahead of South Korea’s Lee Ju-ho. Li Bingjie comfortably defended her 1,500m freestyle title.

title: Opinion | Middle powers don’t have to wait for a Trump-Xi-Putin summit
description: Rather than waiting for great powers to reshape the world, middle powers can find agency by deepening connections between hubs of cooperation.
content: The prospect of United States, Chinese and Russian leaders meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen this November has revived the Yalta analogy. Talk of a Trump-Xi-Putin summit – echoing the 1945 meeting that reshaped the world – surfaced during the first Trump term, and speculation returned last year with the 80th anniversary of the second world war. No such meeting occurred. However, Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted the two presidents back-to-back in Beijing this May, and Moscow now says a three-way meeting in Shenzhen is possible. The symbolism would be potent: the three leaders around one table as the international order fragments. It would also evoke an enduring instinct – the belief that disorder is ultimately managed by a handful of great powers. A literal 21st century Yalta remains improbable. Yet its underlying logic is increasingly visible as trade, technology, finance, infrastructure and development are organised through great-power bargains and rivalries. Middle powers have a limited ability to stop great powers from competing or concerting. They have far greater scope, however, in preventing that competition or concertation from becoming the organising principle of international cooperation. Their opportunity lies in a largely overlooked feature of world politics: the geography of multilateralism. Global governance operates through specialised hubs. New York concentrates universal political legitimacy. Geneva brings together trade, health, labour, humanitarian, human rights and technical institutions. Vienna anchors nuclear governance and arms control; Nairobi environmental governance; Brussels regulatory power; Basel central banking; Bangkok regional development; Singapore finance and shipping. And new centres are emerging. Shanghai hosts the Shanghai Gold Exchange, the New Development Bank and, since July, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). These are ecosystems where governments, international organisations, regulators, firms, experts and civil society interact repeatedly. The next task is to connect these hubs more deliberately. A system of polycentric functional multilateralism would link specialised centres through recurring institutional relationships, allowing cooperation across geopolitical divides and outside the rhythm of great-power summits. Its basic unit could be a functional multilateral corridor. A Geneva-Shanghai corridor on AI governance, for example, could connect Geneva’s technical, intellectual property, labour and development institutions with Shanghai’s emerging AI architecture. A Geneva-Nairobi corridor could address the energy, water and environmental costs of AI infrastructure. Basel, Singapore and Hong Kong could deepen cooperation on digital finance and financial stability. Geneva and Doha could connect mediation with humanitarian diplomacy. Such corridors require more than conferences. They need regular working groups, staff secondments, joint fellowships, shared data sets, reciprocal observer arrangements, compatible reporting systems, pooled funding and predictable annual work cycles. The test is simple: cooperation should survive the minister who launched it. This creates a distinctive role for host states. Switzerland, Kenya, Thailand, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates can supply the physical, legal and diplomatic infrastructure. Hosting multilateralism is itself a form of statecraft. The strategic objective should be to make each hub valuable through its connections. Middle powers without major international headquarters can be connectors. South Korea, Indonesia, Brazil or Turkey can finance cross-hub initiatives, bridge regulatory approaches, bring regional organisations into global processes and co-chair functional coalitions. Their leverage would come from shaping the edges between institutions. Repeated connections can generate institutional momentum. Regular meetings become routines; staff exchanges create professional networks and institutional memory; joint projects create constituencies among bureaucracies, companies, universities and NGOs. Shared infrastructure and funding create sunk costs. Standards create interoperability. Each layer raises the cost of rupture and lowers the cost of cooperation. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub offers a partial model. Its teams operate across Switzerland, Hong Kong, Singapore, London, Stockholm, Toronto and a Frankfurt-Paris centre, while BIS maintains a strategic partnership with the US Federal Reserve. Financial authorities can collaborate on problems without first resolving geopolitical disagreements. The United Nations is moving in a similar direction internally. The UN80 reform process envisages regional commissions as physical hubs and is developing joint knowledge hubs. Extending that logic beyond the UN system could connect established institutions with regional and emerging centres. This is especially consequential as China builds new governance infrastructure such as Waico. Established hubs and middle powers have an entry point: technical cooperation, institutional links and participation can encourage openness, compatibility with wider standards and broader representation. The danger is that polycentricity simply reproduces blocs: Washington-Brussels-Geneva vs Beijing-Shanghai-Moscow. Cross-bloc connectivity must therefore be the measure of success. A resilient system needs multiple pathways between political camps, with redundancy to survive broken relationships and functional autonomy for technical cooperation to continue during diplomatic crises. Twenty-first-century functionalism should carry modest political expectations. Technical cooperation will not dissolve strategic rivalry. Its strategic value lies in containing rivalry’s spillovers: keeping finance, health, climate, AI safety, humanitarian affairs and trade from collapsing whenever relations among major powers deteriorate. The coming order will still have great powers. It can also have many centres of governance and many states capable of connecting them. Middle powers may struggle to determine what happens around a table of great powers. They can do much more to ensure the rest of the world does not have to wait for that table to function.

title: Forget colour analysis – how colour pyramids can help you dress your best
description: Don’t conform to a rigid palette with colour analysis, style experts say – instead focus on proportion, texture and your own preferences.
content: Colour analysis has won fans from across diverse cultures looking to optimise their complexion. The system, which typically involves draping fabric of different hues across your chest, determines which shades of clothing, make-up, jewellery and hair colour best complement a person’s natural skin, hair and eye tones, matching people to a core season: spring, summer, autumn or winter. Colour analysis has gained popularity – especially in South Korea in recent years – because it simplifies shopping by immediately eliminating unflattering shades, making building cohesive capsule wardrobes seemingly effortless. “Many people are overwhelmed by shopping options and want to find boundaries or guidelines for what they buy,” says Sera Murphy, a Singapore-based personal fashion stylist and founder of The Reoutfitter, a wardrobe consulting platform, in an email. “With so much choice out there, it was only a matter of time before consumers wanted to shop for things that work for them on a personal level.” The limitations of colour analysis But although the goal of colour analysis is not to restrict what you wear, that is what often happens. “I don’t practise it because I don’t believe in it,” says Samuel Gilzean, a Hong Kong-based personal stylist for men. “People can wear almost any colour they want, within reason and situation. Limiting people to certain colours – I think it’s very restrictive.” Gilzean acknowledges that the trend’s popularity is not without reason. With endless shopping options and algorithmic recommendations, seasonal colour analysis offers clear, digestible boundaries. “A lot of people don’t understand colour and how colours work together, so they’re looking for advice,” Gilzean says. “It sounds very scientific as well – an ‘analysis’ by an ‘analyst’ – so they must know what they’re talking about.” Murphy, who also avoids rigid colour systems, notes that clients who had previously undergone colour analysis found it had either not worked at all, or they had adhered to it so rigidly that their wardrobes became stale. “By wearing the same colour tones for years, their wardrobes can feel stale and lack options of ‘newness’,” Murphy says. “They end up feeling like they can’t shop or can never find anything that ‘flatters’ them, when in reality they just need to change what colours and cuts they are restricting themselves to.” She also pointed out the practical disconnect: fashion brands do not design collections around your season. “Fashion designers aren’t thinking about whether the colour of a garment is flattering to a certain skin tone,” she says. “They are designing based on the story they want to tell.” For Gilzean, a wardrobe stocked entirely with bright colours is just as impractical as one filled with nothing but dark shades. “It’s unreasonable,” he says, because neither extreme offers the flexibility required for everyday dressing. A wardrobe of only bold hues makes it difficult to build cohesive outfits without clashing, while one of only dark tones leaves no room for personality or visual interest. The solution, Gilzean says, lies in balance: grounding bright pieces with neutrals and injecting occasional accents into darker palettes, so that every item has a role to play. The colour pyramid So what replaces the seasons? Gilzean advocates a different approach: the colour pyramid. The colour pyramid is a proportional system with three tiers that work with anyone at any time. At the base – comprising roughly 40 to 50 per cent of a wardrobe – are core colours: black, navy, olive green, khaki, brown, off-white and white. These are earthy, versatile shades that mix effortlessly. “If you want a professional vibe, go for dark navy,” Gilzean says. “If you want to be relaxed and summery, go for beige or off-white.” The middle tier – about 35 per cent – is for tonal and seasonal colours: light blues, pastel pinks, heather greys and mustard yellows. These add flavour while still pairing well with the core base. At the top – around 15 to 20 per cent – are pop colours, prints and patterns: tropical prints, stripes, bold reds and oranges. These are the statement pieces. “They’re harder to mix and match,” Gilzean says. “If you have too many in one outfit, it can look messy.” For him, the question is never “does this colour suit my skin?” but rather “what vibe do I want to give off?” He points to Pierce Brosnan and Hyun Bin: different complexions, similar colour choices. “They’re not choosing based on being white or Asian,” he says. “They’re choosing based on the vibe – white and blue for summer, brown for warm and approachable, black for impact.” Murphy similarly encourages clients to treat colour as one tool among many. “If a person’s outfit fits them well – the cut, the drape, the construction – and is comfortable and represents who they are, all of those can ‘flatter’ someone in ways that are deeper than the surface,” she says. She also challenges the notion that “allowed colours” build confidence: “Changing clients’ mindsets out of their ‘allowed colours’ can free up so many more options.” One of Gilzean’s key principles is that bold accents are not reserved for “winters”, referencing a client he styled in a burnt orange suit – a colour that would never appear on a muted seasonal palette. “I knew he could pull it off,” he says. “He had the personality and confidence.” What about someone who lacks that confidence? The pyramid offers a gradual on-ramp. “You build the outfit through core colours,” Gilzean says. “Then you do the swap trick: swap a white shirt for a patterned one, or navy trousers for pastel pink. It teaches people how colours work together, rather than just saying, ‘Here are your colours’.” Getting started For anyone ready to abandon the seasons system, Gilzean’s first step is counterintuitive: don’t buy anything. “You can’t fix style issues just by buying more clothes,” he says. “That complicates the problem.” Instead, lay out your entire wardrobe. Identify the pieces in core colours. If you lack them, plug the gaps. And crucially, let go of items you do not actually like. “If a client doesn’t like black, I say: fine. There are plenty of other core colours,” Gilzean says. For Hong Kong’s humid climate, he recommends prioritising core colours that stay cool – khaki, beige, white and warm browns – and avoiding dark “heatsinks” like heavy navy and black in the summer. Fabrics matter too: linen over cotton for moisture-wicking. The rise of colour analysis reflects a genuine desire for guidance. But both Gilzean and Murphy argue that the answer is not a rigid palette. It is understanding proportion, texture and – above all – your own preferences. “I tell my customers: if you like a colour, you like a colour,” Gilzean says. “We’ll incorporate it. If they don’t like a colour, even if it’s a core colour, we won’t wear it.” Murphy adds: “Dressing one’s body goes way beyond what the colour of the garments is. It’s much deeper – dressing in a way that answers the question: ‘Is this me? Do I like the garment and how it represents me in the world?’” Gilzean thinks people worry too much about what colours work best for them. “All this colour analysing, colour wheels and skin tone stuff is needlessly complicated,” he says. “It’s more about what colours you like, and the vibes you want to give off.”

title: Woman chased by 3 dogs before suspected fatal attack in Hong Kong
description: Security footage shows woman leaving Yuen Long MTR on shared bike, then being chased by dogs minutes before she was found unconscious.
content: Hong Kong police suspect a pack of dogs attacked a 27-year-old woman who was found unconscious beside a bicycle in Yuen Long and later died, less than a month after a similar canine-related case. The woman was discovered on Pok Wai South Road at 12.42am on Sunday, according to the force. The victim, who worked as a background music operator, was taken to Pok Oi Hospital in Yuen Long and pronounced dead at 2.09am. Security camera footage showed her leaving Yuen Long MTR station at 11.40pm on Saturday and riding a shared bicycle home, acting assistant Yuen Long district commander Cheung Chun-tong said. By 11.55pm, three dogs were seen chasing her along Pok Wai South Road, about 30 metres (98 feet) from where she was later found near a Drainage Services Department sewage pumping station. Passers-by reported seeing three to four stray dogs nearby when they discovered her, Cheung said. Officers also saw wild boars and stray dogs in the area. The victim suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal. Investigators are still trying to locate the dogs, described as medium-sized. They could not confirm whether fighting-dog breeds were involved because the footage was unclear in the dim light. The case is being handled by the Yuen Long district crime squad. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department said it was deeply concerned about the suspected dog attack. It said it was fully cooperating with police in their investigation, and joined officers in conducting dog-catching operations in the area on Sunday night to safeguard public safety. The incident followed recent dog attacks that have heightened public concern in the city. In August, a large unleashed mastiff-type dog mauled two smaller pets to death in Yuen Long, drawing public anger. A few days later, a woman, 33, who operated a canine training centre in Ta Kwu Ling, North district, was attacked by a dog at the facility and later found dead nearby. The animal involved was a fighting-dog crossbreed, prompting calls for tighter control of aggressive breeds and better enforcement of stray management. Pok Wai South Road is a well-used route for local residents who regularly cycle or jog to and from home. Overlooking the Nam Sang Wai wetlands and ponds, it is a renowned scenic spot, particularly at sunset. A resident in his sixties from nearby Wing Kei Tsuen, who cycles past the location daily, said he was shocked by the incident and had never heard of anything similar in his 20 years of living in the neighbourhood. He said there were very few stray dogs in the area and that they were generally not aggressive. Nor were there any active construction sites nearby where security‑conscious guard dogs were usually kept. Asked whether he would take extra precautions, the resident said he rarely cycled out at night when he suspected stray dogs were more likely to roam.

title: Murder trial of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi’s former relatives to begin
description: Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong, 35, face a joint count of murder.
content: Hong Kong prosecutors are set to open the murder trial of three former relatives of slain socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung later this week, three years after her killing shocked the city and drew international attention. The High Court will hold the first trial hearing on Monday for parties to sort out preliminary issues. Jury selection is expected to take place later in the week before the prosecution delivers its opening statement. The 28-year-old influencer’s death came to light in February 2023, when parts of her dismembered body were discovered in a flat inside a three-storey village house in Tai Po’s Lung Mei Tsuen. Choi’s former husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, his father Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, will stand trial on a joint count of murder. The trio have also been charged with preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. The case had undergone a lengthy legal process since the defendants first appeared in Kowloon City Court on February 27, 2023, with multiple adjournments over the years before it was transferred to the Court of First Instance for trial. The Department of Justice has engaged Charlotte Draycott SC to lead the prosecution in the trial, which has been set down for 45 days and could run until December. Known as the first European woman to become a senior counsel in Hong Kong, Draycott specialises in commercial crimes and cases involving children. She appeared for a co-defendant in the trial of Henry Chau Hoi-leung, a convicted murderer who killed his parents and dismembered their bodies in 2013. Alex Kwong, Kwong Kau and Anthony Kwong are represented, respectively, by veteran barristers Andrew Raffell, Oliver Davies and Trevor Beel. The trial will be presided over by Deputy Judge Brian Keith, who served in the Court of Appeal between 1999 and 2001. Since his retirement from the High Court in England in 2014, the 82-year-old Keith has overseen a number of high-profile criminal cases in the city’s Court of First Instance on an ad hoc basis. They included the manslaughter trial arising from the 2012 Lamma ferry disaster and, more recently, the retrial of a former university professor who used a gas-filled yoga ball to kill his wife and daughter in 2015. The judiciary will arrange a live broadcast of the trial to accommodate the large number of attendees expected.

title: Housing prices surge near new Huanggang Port as buyers eye ‘dual-city’ lifestyle
description: The new port is expected to dramatically speed up crossings between Shenzhen and Hong Kong, making cross-border living more convenient.
content: Prices for properties near the new Huanggang Port are already soaring months ahead of the border crossing being put into operation, with many buyers attracted by the idea of a “dual-city lifestyle”, according to property agents. The new border facility, which is set to open before the end of the year, is expected to make crossing between Shenzhen and Hong Kong far quicker and more convenient, with plans for 24-hour operations, a “co-location arrangement” and a “joint inspection” clearance model that could reduce crossing times from 30 minutes to just five. Located in Shenzhen’s Futian district, just across from the Lok Ma Chau control point in Hong Kong, the border crossing will create a “half-hour living circle” encompassing the two cities, leading to a surge in cross-border commuting, according to Henry Chung, senior managing director at Midland Realty. Demand for housing near the border was rising among a range of different groups, including students and professionals looking to live in Shenzhen but travel into Hong Kong during the week, Chung said. The area was also expected to attract a growing number of retirees and scientific research personnel from Hong Kong, he added. “Year-to-date, residential transaction volume in the Huanggang area has risen by 50 per cent compared with the same period last year, with a noticeable increase in property viewing inquiries,” Chung said. The Shenzhen Beike Research Institute has also recorded a strong uptick in sales of second-hand residential properties in the Huanggang area during the first half of the year. The average transaction price for those properties had risen by 5.6 per cent over the period, faster than the 3.7 per cent increase recorded for the Shenzhen market as a whole, data showed. Rents in the area have also been creeping up in recent months, especially since the opening of the Hong Kong-side port area in late July, according to Chung. “Taking Huangyuyuan as an example, rents in the estate rose by nearly 20 per cent in the first half of the year,” he said, referring to a housing complex near the border crossing. “August and September mark the peak season for rentals, which drove rents up by nearly another 10 per cent.” The average monthly rent for a two-bedroom flat in the complex had increased from about 5,000 yuan (US$745) last year to reach 6,500 yuan, he added. Hong Kong buyers currently drive about 28 per cent of the residential property market in Futian district and about 20 per cent of the market in the Huanggang Port area, according to data from Midland Realty. Hong Kong residents also account for as much as 30 per cent of residential tenants in the area, the data indicates, with much of the rental demand coming from cross-border commuters, students and families accompanying students. A Hongkonger surnamed Ngai recently bought a 60-square-metre (645-square-foot) two-bedroom flat at Huangyuyuan for 3.5 million yuan. “Compared to apartments of the same layout two or three months ago, the price has risen by over 200,000 yuan – an increase of 8 per cent,” he said. “I believe the opening of the new port will drive foot traffic in the area and boost housing demand.” Another Hong Kong resident surnamed Chan bought a 42-square-metre flat at Huangyuyuan last month. “I bought the property for personal use, believing that the opening of the new Huanggang Port will facilitate commuting between Shenzhen and Hong Kong,” Chan said. Joyce Lai, executive director at Shun On Home Realty Company, said two young women from Hong Kong had rented a two-bedroom flat at Langqiao International – a residential complex next to Huanggang Port – for 8,500 yuan per month in late June. “Some Hong Kong residents choose to relocate to Huanggang to enjoy a dual-city lifestyle – working in Hong Kong while living in Shenzhen,” Lai said. “The daily commuting cost via cross-border bus and metro through the Huanggang Port is about HK$70 (US$9). If switching to the high-speed rail, the daily round-trip fare is equivalent to about HK$150. Both options fall within an acceptable range for dual-city commuting in the Greater Bay Area.” The commercial property market in the Huanggang area was also heating up, agents said, with shop rents and valuations increasing as the market anticipates that massive cross-border flows of people will drive a surge in business for merchants. “During the reconstruction of Huanggang Port, the occupancy rate for street-front shops in the surrounding area was less than 30 per cent,” said King Lau, regional investment director for the Greater Bay Area at Yui Yin Property. “However, the occupancy rate for street-front shops in core malls near the port – such as Langqiao International and Huangyuyuan – surged to near-full occupancy between August and September this year.” According to market sources, a Hong Kong investor last year bought four street-front shops and the entire second floor in the Jinling Holiday Apartment complex’s shopping arcade for tens of millions of yuan. Lau, however, pointed out that whether they were investors who had already entered the market or tenants rushing to secure space, they were essentially acting based on expectations because the area had yet to truly benefit from the passenger flow generated by the border crossing. Chung also noted that if the flow of people fell short of expectations after the border fully reopened, merchants would face significant operational pressure and retail rents might undergo a downward correction.

title: Hong Kong start-up’s app alerts users if their pet’s poo has problems
description: The founders of Petalife want to help pet owners identify health problems as soon as they show up in the animal’s urine, stool or vomit.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Have you ever been worried that your pets were acting strange but you could not tell why? That feeling inspired Eugene Siu Cheuk-wing and her brother Oscar Siu Chak-lam to start Petalife in 2023.
The Hong Kong start-up helps people track the health of their cats and dogs. Using the app, pet owners can create a digital log of their animals’ well-being by uploading photos of their stool, urine or vomit.
In 2015, the siblings were shocked to find out that their dog, Oreo, had cancer. They only found out about the illness when it had already become deadly.
But Eugene said symptoms in cancer’s early stages could be as small as suddenly not eating much or being less active.
“For these very small things ... if the owner is not really around for 24 hours or is not very experienced, they will not notice,” said Eugene, 30, Petalife’s chief executive officer.
Inspired by the sudden loss they faced, the siblings considered how other people might want a tool to alert them about their pets’ health issues.
Petalife’s app has about 10,000 users. When Petalife notices something unusual in users’ uploads, it alerts them and suggests seeing a vet if there are risks.
The company said its app had an overall accuracy rate of about 93 per cent. But it stressed that Petalife is meant to support, not replace, professional vet care.
To analyse stool, the app uses artificial intelligence (AI) to create a health assessment based on the Bristol Stool Scale. This is a medical guide that groups faeces by shape and texture.
Based on the records uploaded by users, an AI chatbot gives suggestions.
“The AI chatbot may ask some questions – for example, about what [the pet] has eaten in the past 24 hours – to make the owner recall if there was anything special,” Eugene said.
She shared how a user panicked over what looked like blood in his dog’s stool. But the app noted that the colour was orange, not red. The chatbot then asked the owner what he had fed his pet and traced the colour to a carrot mixed with the dog’s steak.
A post shared by Petalife | AI Cat Health App (@petalife.global)
The siblings began developing their idea in 2022 through start-up competitions, where they met vets and got advice from experts.
They worked with vets and other partners in Hong Kong, Britain and the Greater Bay Area to collect about 100,000 sets of raw data to train Petalife’s AI model. They used datasets that covered cats and dogs of different breeds, ages and sizes.
Vets made sure the AI model’s ability to analyse photos matched standards at an animal clinic. Experts continue to independently check the AI’s accuracy.
Eugene is in charge of the business side of the company, while Oscar, 27, works on the app’s technology. He is Petalife’s chief technology officer.
In university, he found his passion through a start-up competition. He designed a machine that mixed water with pet food to create a paste. He won funding to build a prototype and learn about how things are manufactured .
At Petalife, Oscar built the app’s AI model himself, and he continues learning new skills to improve it.
Both siblings agree that real-world experience is key to finding your passion.
“Studying and actually working are two different things,” Oscar said. “The newest technology cannot be learned in university ... [You should] look at more things outside school.”

title: University calls for government funds for shared sites in Northern Metropolis
description: Saint Francis University head says authorities should contribute more towards facilities that will be jointly used by institutions in megadevelopment.
content: Hong Kong authorities should shoulder a larger share of the cost of facilities jointly used by institutions at the Northern Metropolis university towns, a varsity president has said, while calling for dedicated research funding to encourage collaboration among campuses. Professor Stephen Cheung Yan-leung, president of the private Saint Francis University, said that while individual institutions could finance the construction of their own campuses, the government should contribute more towards shared infrastructure such as research and student entrepreneurship centres. “For facilities that everyone will use, the government could contribute more,” he told a radio programme on Sunday. Cheung said universities had the money to develop campuses, adding that many had expressed an interest in doing so. His remarks followed the government’s announcement that institutions seeking sites in the three planned university towns in the new development along the border would receive favourable consideration if they did not require public loans to build their campuses. Education minister Christine Choi Yuk-lin earlier said institutions could apply for government loans, but priority would be given to those that did not require one or could offer financially competitive repayment proposals. Under indicative terms set by authorities, institutions proposing a 20-year repayment period could receive an interest-free loan for the first six years. The rate would then rise to about 2 per cent between the seventh and 10th years and around 5 per cent for the remaining decade. The government previously earmarked HK$10 billion (US$1.28 billion) for a loan scheme supporting the Hung Shui Kiu University Town. Successful institutions will also pay a nominal land premium of HK$1,000. Cheung also called on the government to establish research funds that universities could jointly apply for, encouraging institutions, students and technology companies to collaborate rather than operate separately. Universities had room to improve cooperation both with one another and with industry, he said, adding that placing researchers, students and technology firms in proximity could generate new ideas and help turn academic research into marketable products. “If these people are put together and allowed to exchange ideas, it will certainly create synergies,” he said. Cheung urged authorities to review the experience of Cyberport and the Hong Kong Science Park to identify what had not worked before developing the university towns. He also called for regulations and approval procedures to be streamlined, warning that excessive red tape and year-long waits for approvals could hinder collaboration and development. Saint Francis University itself would find it difficult to finance another campus in the Northern Metropolis, Cheung said, as the self-funding institution was already preparing to begin construction of a second campus in Tai Wai early next year. But the university would be willing to use and help manage shared facilities in the new towns, including entrepreneurship and research centres where its students could work with technology companies, he added. The three university towns in Hung Shui Kiu, San Tin and Ta Kwu Ling will cover 26, 100 and 180 hectares (64, 247 and 444 acres), respectively, forming a major part of the government’s strategy to turn the Northern Metropolis into an education and innovation hub. Applications for the first three sites in Hung Shui Kiu will close at the end of this year, with results expected in early 2027. Authorities have not set a limit on the number of institutions that can be granted land. No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki has said the Hung Shui Kiu town and adjoining technology and industrial areas would be developed into a centre for applied post-secondary education, smart manufacturing and global talent cultivation. Institutions seeking sites there will be required to collaborate with industries on curriculum design, internships and applied research, form partnerships with leading mainland Chinese and overseas universities, and develop shared facilities. Cheung said the university towns offered an opportunity to better connect Hong Kong’s higher education sector with industry, describing tertiary education as one of the city’s better-performing sectors amid pressure on retail, catering and commercial property. “The higher education sector can create synergies, drive other industries and generate economic benefits,” he said. “It could become an important direction for Hong Kong’s future economic development.”

title: ‘Staunch patriot, close friend’: Beijing official hails Tung Chee-hwa’s legacy
description: ‘He always placed national interests first and throughout his life upheld the belief that patriotism is a natural conviction,’ Shi Taifeng says in eulogy.
content: Hong Kong’s first post-colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, has been lauded as a pioneer of “one country, two systems”, a staunch patriot and a close friend of the Communist Party who also contributed to Sino-US relations, according to a eulogy delivered by a senior Beijing official. In his remarks at Tung’s state funeral on Sunday, seen by the South China Morning Post, Shi Taifeng – a Politburo member and first vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) – also hailed Tung’s role in supporting the government in quelling the 2019 social unrest and in safeguarding national security. “He always placed national interests first and throughout his life upheld the belief that patriotism is a natural conviction,” said Shi, who visited the city as chairman of Tung’s funeral committee. “His patriotism was sincere and his love for Hong Kong was profound; he had a broad vision and a staunch stance. He was a practitioner and contributor to the great cause of ‘one country, two systems’.” The principle, adopted upon the handover from British to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, governs relations between Hong Kong and mainland China. Beginning with Tung’s life story, Shi said the city’s first chief executive was born in a turbulent era and developed a deep sense of patriotism under the influence of his father, shipping magnate Tung Chao-yung. He described the younger Tung as a “staunch patriot” and a “close friend” of the Communist Party. Shi said Tung, who chaired his family shipping business in his earlier days, firmly supported the country’s reform and opening-up and its modernisation drive, including establishing shipping lines connecting the mainland to North America and Europe, backing the country’s external trade and helping the city develop into a global shipping hub. As the city’s first chief executive, Tung made exceptional contributions to the smooth transition and handover in 1997, including his role in drafting the Basic Law – the city’s mini-constitution – and forming the local government, Shi said. “During his tenure as chief executive of Hong Kong, he always prioritised the fundamental interests of the country and Hong Kong, dedicating himself wholeheartedly and pouring all his energy into the role,” he said. “As the first chief executive, he resolutely implemented the initiative of ‘one country, two systems’, ‘Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong’, and a high degree of autonomy as well as the Basic Law. He carried out a great deal of pioneering work.” Shi highlighted several major policies under Tung’s administration, including his handling of the Asian financial crisis and his defence against foreign financial predators who attempted to “snipe” the Hong Kong dollar in 1998, as well as his leadership during the Sars pandemic in 2003. The late leader was also praised for advancing cooperation between the mainland and Hong Kong, including the signing of the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement – a free-trade deal with the central government after Sars. Tung also took an active part in key national policies as vice-chairman of the CPPCC, China’s top political advisory body, after he stepped down in 2005 and supported the administration in restoring social order during the 2019 social unrest, Shi said. He noted that Tung had “condemned external forces that sought to disrupt the city”, founded the Hong Kong Coalition in 2020 to help the city weather the storm and endorsed the ensuing enactment of the national security law and the electoral revamp. “After stepping down as chief executive, whenever events in Hong Kong touched the bottom line of the ‘one country, two systems’ principle, he always stepped forward promptly to speak out unequivocally,” Shi said. “[He] unswervingly safeguarded the sovereignty, security and development interests of the country.” Shi also recognised Tung’s efforts to promote the nation’s foreign ties and cooperation, particularly the stable development of Sino-US relations, including founding the China-United States Exchange Foundation in 2008. He said the organisation fostered exchanges among politicians, business leaders and academics on both sides, and initiated more than 1,000 people-to-people dialogues, which deepened mutual understanding. “[Tung] made many friends at home and abroad. He used his special status and influence to promote the mainland’s achievements in opening-up and modernisation, and to introduce the success of ‘one country, two systems’, ‘Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong’, and a high degree of autonomy,” Shi said. “He made contributions to the nation’s friendly exchanges and the fostering of mutual trust with other countries.” Concluding his eulogy, Shi cited Tung’s famous quote: “If Hong Kong is good, China will be good. If China is good, Hong Kong will be even better”, adding that the late statesman had lived up to his words. He called on the public to remember Tung’s legacy, carry forward his patriotism and spirit of perseverance and dedication, and resolutely implement “one country, two systems” to ensure Hong Kong’s long-term prosperity. “[Tung’s] passing is a major loss to Hong Kong and also a major loss to the country,” Shi said. “His patriotic sentiment, sense of responsibility and sincere character will forever deserve the world’s respect and remembrance.”

title: Ukraine pummels Moscow with drones on last day of Russian election
description: Two people were killed in the Moscow region and the Russian capital’s oil refinery was also struck.
content: Ukraine launched ⁠what Moscow’s mayor called the biggest ever drone attack on the Russian capital on Sunday, in what he said was an unsuccessful attempt to disrupt the final day of a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for Russia’s war in Ukraine. The drone strikes killed two people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, according to Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and election ‌authorities. A facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged. “The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled. Since yesterday, more than 1,600 drones have been shot down across all fronts. Of these, 450 were approaching Moscow,” Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said in a statement on Telegram. One of the drones had struck a residential building, but none of its residents had lost their lives, he said. “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” Sobyanin said. The election authorities say the three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite cyberattacks reported on ⁠Saturday. Turnout was at over 50 per cent by early afternoon Moscow time, Interfax news agency reported, citing the Central Election Commission. In the village of Sofyino, south of Moscow, a body covered in a stained blanket lay in front of a damaged apartment ‌block, the upper windows of which were blown out. “Glass went flying, people started screaming ⁠and shouting. I turned around, ⁠and the entrance doors had already been blown out, debris everywhere,” said resident Vitaliy, who gave only his first name. The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, is expected to see the ruling United Russia party easily retain its dominance in a political system critics ⁠say do not tolerate dissent. The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II, now in ‌its fifth year with no sign of ending soon. Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail ‌terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict deemed illegal by authorities. Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences. In a ⁠small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”. The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts ‌the conflict as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West and says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia. Russian electoral officials said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow ‌had ‌come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election”. Putin on Friday also accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he ‌said was a Ukrainian strike on the home of an election official in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that killed Elena Astanina, the official. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack ⁠and there was no comment from Kyiv. Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated “a foreign agent”, ⁠said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain. “The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the country and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on the ballot,” it said in a note. It said the Communist party ‌and the New People party could attract votes the ‌authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in line with United Russia on major issues. Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine. “Your choice, and your will, will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared values, historical memory and love for our homeland, and that no one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” Putin said. Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 1800 GMT on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

title: US Congress investigates diversion of sensitive F-35 parts to Hong Kong: report
description: Jet’s canopy among components missing, sparking fears of potential reverse engineering, as city’s authorities decline to comment.
content: The United States Congress has reportedly launched a probe after a shipment of sensitive F-35 fighter jet parts was said to have been unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong and went missing, with the city’s authorities declining to comment on the case. A spokesman for the Hong Kong government said over the weekend that it would not comment on individual cases, a day after US media outlet Politico reported the story. Citing three anonymous sources, Politico said the F-35 parts were shipped from Australia to the United States for repairs and were diverted to Hong Kong as they transited the Pacific Ocean this summer. The Pentagon’s F-35 Joint Programme Office confirmed it was “aware of a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 Lightning II components”, saying it was working with US authorities and industry partners “to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence”. The US State Department declined to comment when reached by Politico, while the Chinese embassy reportedly said it was not aware of the incident. According to the report, US State Department and Pentagon officials first briefed congressional staff on key national security committees about the incident in June, with multiple additional briefings expected in the coming weeks. Two sources told Politico that the shipment included one of the jet’s canopies, which covered the cockpit and contained stealth technology that only the US and its allies had access to, sparking fears of potential reverse engineering. F-35 manufacturer Lockheed Martin managed the programme’s overall supply chain and used commercial shipping providers to transport parts. The company said in a statement it would not discuss the status of shipments for security reasons but stressed it followed all US regulations for shipping aircraft components. “Our teams handle every shipment with the utmost diligence and safeguards to ensure the integrity of the F-35 programme and the security of our allied partners,” it said. In recent years, the US Defence Department has stepped up oversight of the F-35 supply chain. However, Lockheed Martin, rather than the department, accounted for spare parts in the pool. A 2023 Government Accountability Office report found that more than 1 million F-35 spare parts had gone missing in the past five years. The watchdog agency concluded the department had not been able to review spare part losses worth tens of millions of US dollars because Lockheed Martin controlled the information.

title: IOC president impressed by ‘beautiful’ Asian Games shipping container-style huts
description: Kirsty Coventry admits the cabins are ‘a little tighter’ than similar accommodation at the Milano-Cortina Winter Olympics earlier this year.
content: IOC president Kirsty Coventry called the shipping container-style huts for Asian Games athletes “beautiful” on Sunday – but conceded they were “a little tighter” than similar accommodation at the Milano-Cortina Winter Olympics. Asia’s biggest sporting spectacle, which opened on Saturday in the Japanese city of Nagoya, has split with past Games by having no traditional athletes’ village. To save costs, the more than 17,000 Asian Games participants will stay in temporary huts, hotels and a cruise ship. Some countries have criticised the wooden cabins as too small, with beds that are too short. But after touring the lodgings, International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Coventry said she could not understand the negativity. “We had similar cabins in Milano-Cortina [Winter Games this year] and the athletes were very happy. And the cabins here are really nice,” the Zimbabwean former Olympic champion swimmer said. “They’re a little tighter. So, you know, if you want something negative, it’s a little smaller. “But I don’t think it’s a negative thing. I love the village.” About 2,000 participants are staying in the lodgings by the water in Nagoya. Coventry said: “The cabins are quiet, they’re very cool. The air conditioning is working well. “The flooring and the walls are beautiful.
