It’s better than some of the villages I’ve stayed in. “So I think to be very fair to Japan and to the organising committee, I was really impressed. “I had only been reading everything that had been said. And I was expecting something completely different to when I walked in.” Asked if she would happily see the temporary cabins and also a cruise ship serve as accommodation at the Olympics, she said she had not been to the vessel. But she pointed to the accommodation at Milano-Cortina, and said those “very closely” resembled the ones in Nagoya. “It’s not a new concept,” she added. “And it is a concept that I think, for me, when we talk about an athlete experience, being an athlete ... as soon as I go in, I’m not necessarily concerned about the look.”

title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan to give firms more long-term certainty: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief says blueprint’s targets and timelines will help businesses align investment decisions with government goals.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will give businesses greater certainty to make long-term investment decisions amid a volatile external environment, the city’s finance chief has said. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the plan’s targets and timelines would allow companies to see the city’s direction over the next five years and better align their plans with the government’s. “The significance of planning lies not only in the document itself, but also in looking at today from the perspective of the future and turning a vision into indicators and action plans that can be reviewed year by year,” Chan wrote in his weekly blog on Sunday. “The more volatile the external environment becomes, the more the market needs certainty that extends beyond a single year.” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled Hong Kong’s first five-year plan last Wednesday, mapping out the city’s directions between 2026 and 2030, alongside the annual policy address. Among its targets are the production of 900 hectares (2,224 acres) of formed land in the Northern Metropolis, raising the contribution of manufacturing and new industrialisation to 5.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) and increasing expenditure on local research and development to 3 per cent of the economy. Chan said that each annual policy address would translate these goals into tangible targets for that year’s work, with specific departments overseeing progress evaluations. He said at least 200 hectares of formed land would be produced in the Northern Metropolis over the current and next financial years. All nine new development areas within the megaproject had been launched, with work under way in four of them covering about 800 hectares, he added. Chan also outlined how different sites would support the innovation and technology (I&T) sector. He said the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park in the Lok Ma Chau Loop would focus largely on research and development (R&D), while the San Tin Technopole would provide space for pilot testing and mass production. The Sandy Ridge Data Park would provide computing power, completing a chain extending from R&D to production and the market, he said. More than 100 technology companies and institutions have moved into the park, while its two wet laboratory buildings are fully leased. The San Tin Technopole will provide 210 hectares of innovation and technology (I&T) land, while the operator of the Hung Shui Kiu Industrial Park is in substantive talks with companies involved in sectors including advanced construction and testing and certification. The government has expanded the planned area of three university towns in the Northern Metropolis to more than 1,000 hectares. Research postgraduate places will rise gradually from 7,200 to 9,600, while the number of Hong Kong PhD Fellowship Scheme awards will increase from 400 to 550. On financial initiatives, Chan said about 20 fund management companies had been shortlisted for the I&T Industry-Oriented Fund, which was expected to be launched this year. The government also plans to submit an amendment bill by the end of the year offering concessionary tax rates – either 5 per cent or half the prevailing rate – to selected companies in finance, advanced manufacturing, I&T research, headquarters operations, logistics and supply-chain management.

title: Chinese firms keen on investing in Oman’s International Financial Centre: official
description: Neutrality amid US-Israel war on Iran cited as an advantage, as well as location of ports away from Strait of Hormuz.
content: Chinese firms have shown “very strong interest” in investing in Oman – across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran – as they aim to tap the lucrative Middle East market while minimising risks, an Omani official said. Banks, asset managers and law firms from China were getting in touch every day to ask about setting up in the International Financial Centre Oman, a free-standing legal zone in the country, the centre’s associate director for business development, Al Hussain al-Qalhati, said. The International Financial Centre Oman will open in Muscat, the Omani capital, by early next year. Chinese professional service companies that served Chinese vendors and manufacturers in the Middle East were looking to Oman for safe proximity to their clients, Qalhati said. Oman continued to remain neutral towards Iran, Israel and the US, he added, naming the principal actors in an economically destabilising war that was launched by the United States and Israel in late February. “Most of the Chinese companies come because they want to diversify,” Qalhati said on the sidelines of the Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this month. “Oman has a big advantage with stability and neutrality.” The International Financial Centre Oman had received “very strong interest” from Chinese investors, whose inquiries had outnumbered those from many other countries, he said. A survey by professional services firm PwC last year found that 86 per cent of Chinese enterprises were planning to expand operations in the Middle East. Chinese direct investment in Oman rose from 887.3 million Omani rials (US$2.3 billion) at the end of last year to 901.5 million rials at the end of the first quarter this year, according to investor advisory firm Oman Verified. It is far safer to transport goods to and from Omani ports than to attempt to travel through the strait at present Azad Zangana, Oxford Economics Chinese professional services firms formerly focused on expanding in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, said Annelle Sheline, a programme research fellow with the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a think tank based in Washington. Iran has fired on both Saudi Arabia and the UAE during this year’s war. “It makes sense for more firms to establish a presence in Oman,” she said, adding that Oman was “likely to retain a working relationship with Tehran”. Chinese investors would require support from legal and accounting firms, especially those with a local presence and familiarity with Middle Eastern laws and regulations, said Sheline, formerly of the US State Department. Chinese companies with those needs had often invested in Middle Eastern energy, hi-tech and infrastructure projects, she said. Analysts said Oman’s 20-year-old free-trade agreement with the US and international financial centre tax exemptions lasting up to 50 years would give Chinese investors further incentives. They also said Oman’s economic zones were to the east of the Strait of Hormuz, meaning they could provide access to global markets by sea without the threat of strikes by Iran. “It is far safer to transport goods to and from Omani ports than to attempt to travel through the strait at present,” said Azad Zangana, head of macroeconomic analysis for Gulf countries at Oxford Economics. But some experts cautioned that Oman lacked the development level of countries such as the UAE. “The degree of development is not as great as the UAE [and] Oman is smaller,” said Warren Bailey, a Cornell University professor of finance. “It’s a bit more distant from the Gulf than, say, Dubai, plus there is political distance.”

title: Hong Kong founders of AI app Petalife on using poop to get the scoop on pet health
description: Inspired by their dog’s death, siblings hope their start-up can alert owners about possible issues using their animals’ stool, urine or vomit.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Have you ever panicked when you noticed that your pets were a bit off but you couldn’t tell why? That feeling inspired Eugene Siu Cheuk-wing and her brother Oscar Siu Chak-lam to start Petalife, an app for owners to track the health of their cats and dogs.
Launched in 2023, the Hong Kong tech start-up enables owners to build a digital log of their pets’ well-being by uploading photos of their stool, urine or vomit.
In 2015, the siblings were shocked to find out that their beloved dog, Oreo, had cancer – they only discovered the illness when it was already critical.
But Eugene said she learned later that minor symptoms in cancer’s early stages could be observed: they could be as small as “suddenly not eating much [or] suddenly being less active”.
“But for these very small things, actually, if the owner is not really around for 24 hours or is not very experienced, they will not notice,” said Eugene, 30, the chief executive officer of Petalife.
Inspired by the sudden loss they faced, the duo considered how other people might need a clear, accessible way to notice pets’ subtle health issues.
Petalife’s app, which has about 10,000 users, is designed to help pet owners and vets monitor an animal’s health and spot risk signals.
When Petalife detects something unusual, it alerts users and suggests seeing a vet if there are risks. The company said its app had an overall accuracy rate of about 93 per cent, but it stressed that Petalife is not a medical diagnostic tool and is meant to support, not replace, professional vet care.
For stool analysis, it uses artificial intelligence (AI) to generate a health assessment based on the Bristol Stool Scale – a medical guide that classifies faeces based on shape and consistency.
Based on the records input by owners, an AI chatbot gives advice.
“The AI chatbot may ask some questions – for example, about what [the pet] has eaten in the past 24 hours – to make the owner recall if there was anything special,” Eugene said.
She shared how a user panicked over what looked like blood in his dog’s stool, but the app identified the colour as orange, not red. The chatbot then prompted the owner to recall what he had fed his pet, tracing it to a carrot mixed with steak.
The founders think Petalife is also useful for vets as it stores stool records they can reference for diagnosis.
“We specifically found veterinarians to help us tailor … [the records] to be most convenient or most suitable for them to look at,” Eugene said.
The siblings began developing their idea in 2022 through local start-up competitions, where they built networks with vets and got feedback from industry experts.
They collaborated with veterinary teams and other partners across Hong Kong, Britain and the Greater Bay Area to collect about 100,000 sets of raw data to train their AI model.
They used diverse datasets covering cats and dogs of different breeds, ages and body sizes. From the start, vets labelled the data and ensured the models aligned with clinical standards. Today, veterinary experts continue to conduct independent validations and verify the AI’s precision.
The idea of analysing stool came from Eugene’s early career in skincare marketing, where AI was used to assess human skin health. But since skin scans are less practical for furry animals, the duo changed their focus to researching how stool consistency can indicate pet health.
Eugene manages the business operations, while Oscar drives the app’s technical development.
Oscar, 27, Petalife’s chief technology officer, studied surveying at Polytechnic University of Hong Kong but found his true passion through a school start-up competition during his first year.
Rooted in his love for pets, he designed a smart feeder that mixed water with pet food to create a smooth paste.
He won funding to build a prototype and learn about product manufacturing. After graduating, Oscar built Petalife’s AI model himself, and he continues learning new technical skills to improve the application.
Both siblings agree that real-world experience is essential for figuring out your passion.
“Studying and actually working are two different things,” Oscar said. “The newest technology cannot be learned in university … Actually, I think [you should] look at more things outside school.”
A post shared by Petalife | AI Cat Health App (@petalife.global)
To make pet health tracking effortless, Petalife is trying to merge its technology into public spaces and homes.
Following the July launch of Hong Kong’s scheme allowing dogs in licensed food premises, Eugene saw growing interest from commercial spaces looking to build pet-friendly environments. For example, they have partnered with local malls to offer prizes for people who use Petalife’s app.
The team also plans to automate pet health monitoring with a camera designed to sit in a cat’s litter box, sending information to the app to analyse the animal’s habits.
“We know [Petalife] cannot replace any veterinarian to do any diagnosis,” Eugene said. “Instead, before a disease is diagnosed, we hope to know earlier whether those pets are suffering … so that owners can help them.”

title: Pending US$12.3 million house arrest fine keeps Malaysia’s Najib in prison
description: The former prime minister mulls how to pay the penalty as significant part of his assets and bank accounts remain frozen.
content: Former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak said on Sunday that he would remain in Kajang Prison as he and his legal team study the conditions attached to his “conditional pardon”, including the payment of a 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine before he can be transferred to house arrest. In a statement issued on his behalf by Messrs Shafee & Co, Najib said his transfer to house arrest depended on the conditions of the pardon being fulfilled. “Until the fine is paid to the court, our client remains in Kajang Prison. Our client and our legal team are presently studying those terms and their practical implications,” the statement said on Sunday. The statement said a significant part of Najib’s assets, bank accounts and properties remained subject to freezing orders and enforcement proceedings by the government. “As their disposal is not presently within his sole control, his ability to satisfy the condition therefore turns in part on matters that do not lie in his own hands,” it said. Najib was taking legal advice and considering his options on how best to meet the condition, it added. Malaysia’s ⁠Prisons Department said ⁠in a statement on Sunday that it and the home affairs ministry were waiting for official written confirmation ‌of the pardon before taking any action. By law, the home affairs minister has the power to gazette ‌any premises ‌as a prison, which could be used to designate Najib’s home as ‌a place to serve his sentence. Najib expressed gratitude to Deputy Prime Minister, Umno president and Barisan Nasional chairman, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, as well as the Umno supreme council and party members and supporters for standing by him. He also thanked Malaysians who had offered help towards meeting the condition. However, Najib said he did not want Umno members, supporters, or members of the public to feel burdened or obliged to assist him. Umno had ‌raised almost 1 million ringgit by Saturday noon, local media reported. He also thanked his family, friends and those who had kept him in their prayers and asked that his family’s privacy be respected. The statement said his legal team would not comment further at this time. Najib has been serving a prison sentence at Kajang Prison in Selangor state since August 23, 2022, for misappropriating 42 million ringgit from a former unit of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. On Friday, Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar granted a “conditional pardon” to Najib at the 64th meeting of the Pardons Board for the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur, Labuan and Putrajaya, allowing Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence, due to end on August 23, 2028, under house arrest. This story was first published by The Star Additional reporting by Reuters

title: What to expect from MasterChef Asia 2026? Judges open up on series’ comeback
description: We talk to chefs Edward Lee, Pichaya ‘Pam’ Soontornyanakij and Kelvin Cheung on the new series returning to screens after a decade off air.
content: For much of the world, Asian cuisine is often seen as just a menu category rather than a rich tapestry of histories from a vast continent. A few familiar dishes have come to represent thousands of regional techniques, ingredients, migrations and memories. The reboot of MasterChef Asia, after a decade off the air, seeks to change that by placing the region’s home cooks, flavours and ambition on screen. Having Asian cuisine represented and judged by chefs with deep, personal connections to the region is important. Chefs Edward Lee, Pichaya “Pam” Soontornyanakij and Kelvin Cheung will not simply decide whose dish is best. They will help define what it means to represent Asia now, an evolving conversation among cultures. “This is MasterChef Asia, not MasterChef Thailand, the Philippines or India,” says Cheung, who runs modern Chinese restaurants Jun’s and Jooksing in Dubai. “A champion must be able to move beyond a single comfort zone and represent modern global cuisine and modern techniques.” A continent under the spotlight The new judges are adamant that the region’s food deserves a broader yet more nuanced perspective. Lee, a breakout star from the first season of Netflix’s Culinary Class Wars, says curiosity about Asian food is at “an all-time high”. That curiosity, he hopes, can move past the familiar shorthand of noodles, fried rice and a few celebrated classics. “Asian food is so diverse,” he says. “There’s so many layers, so many histories. Every region has its own specific story.” Pichaya, chef of Michelin-starred Restaurant Potong in Bangkok, points to the diversity within countries themselves. India, she notes, cannot be reduced to one familiar dish when its northern and southern traditions hold so much more to discover. The new season, she says, is an opportunity to shine a light on “lesser-known flavours and food from Asia.” At the same time, contemporary cooking does not mean leaving history behind. “In Thailand, chefs are experimenting with fermentation again, which we did a lot because [our ancestors] didn’t have fridges,” she says. “It’s very interesting to see that, moving forward, we’re moving back in a way.” Cheung’s perspective is similarly personal. Lauded as the pioneer of “third-culture cuisine”, the chef was often referred to as “the Canadian” in his father’s Chinese kitchen and later as “the weird Asian kid” in Western fine-dining kitchens. The experiences made him acutely aware of the limitations imposed on Asian chefs. A chef of Chinese heritage, for example, should not automatically be expected to cook only Chinese food, he says – the point of MasterChef Asia is to embrace the diversity and complexity of the whole region. Representing Asian food today The original run of MasterChef Asia in 2015 established a regional stage for talented home cooks, but ran for only one season to give way to more country-specific editions such as MasterChef Singapore in 2018. This reboot is deliberately not built around nostalgia. Lee says the team is trying to define the season “as a stand-alone and something exceptional”, representing Asian food as it is today and bringing a fresh, innovative face of Asia to the screen. The returning franchise invites 10 alumni contestants from previous MasterChef seasons, including the popular Vietnamese-Australian chef Khanh Ong – a fan favourite and finalist from MasterChef Australia – and Malaysian pastry chef Marcus Low, who appeared in the original MasterChef Asia. The reboot is especially relevant in the social-media era. Lee says the gap between professional chefs and home cooks has narrowed because recipes, images and techniques are now readily available online. “There’s no excuse any more,” he says. “You have access to everything.” Pichaya agrees, adding that social media has opened up possibilities, but cautions that access does not guarantee originality. The real challenge, she says, is creating something that is genuinely one’s own rather than a copy of what is already online. Cheung puts the issue more bluntly: “Social media flavour is not always going to be real flavour.” There are no bonus points for a plate with 800 garnishes if a three-ingredient fried rice is executed better Kelvin Cheung, MasterChef Asia 2026 judge The new season will not be a competition in which visual spectacle alone triumphs. The judges will be looking for dishes that are personal, but also delicious; innovative but rooted in a coherent idea; visually striking but technically sound. Asked what separates a good dish from a winning one, Pichaya says flavour comes first. “It has to be something that makes me want to eat it again and again,” she says. Cheung emphasises execution, from texture and planning to every component on the plate. Lee concludes that the best dishes transport the judges into a contestant’s story and thought process, while still getting the details right. The qualities to survive The judging will not treat traditional food as untouchable or innovation as an automatic virtue. Lee says there are objective parameters across cuisines such as balance, texture, seasoning and proper technique. Pichaya offers a more emotional test: a radically reworked dish can still be right if, when tasted, it feels familiar and “like home”. Cheung’s formulation is characteristically practical. “There are no bonus points for a plate with 800 garnishes if a three-ingredient fried rice is executed better,” he says. The contestants, meanwhile, will be assessed as individuals as well as cooks. Lee wants them to infuse food with story, heritage and personality rather than merely replicate a recipe. Cheung adds that grit, confidence, passion, and the capacity to adapt when something goes wrong are the high-pressure qualities required to survive. The judges see their role as more than critics; they want to mentor contestants towards the chefs they may become. And what of the trio’s on-screen chemistry? There is always the funny judge, the mean judge and the nice judge. The chefs’ playful response offers a glimpse: Pichaya is the nice one, Cheung is the funny one, and Lee – while clearly happy to be called many things – prefers to be known as “the honest one” or “the professor” rather than the mean one. MasterChef Asia streams on HBO Max and TLC from September 22, and Discovery Channel from September 23.

title: The cooling trap: how Asia’s air conditioners are making heatwaves worse
description: As heatwaves intensify across Asia, soaring air-conditioner use is threatening power grids and warming urban nights.
content: As heatwaves become more frequent and intense across Asia, the region faces a dangerous power paradox. Soaring demand for air conditioning threatens to push electricity grids closer to failure just as extreme heat puts the infrastructure under greater strain, raising the risk of cooling disappearing when people need it most. That risk has been visible across the region this summer. In South Korea, President Lee Jae Myung called a record heatwave a “national disaster” in August after the death toll rose to 19, ordering officials to inspect power systems as air-conditioning demand surged. In Japan, 39 people died of heatstroke across Tokyo’s 23 central wards in August. Of those deaths, 37 occurred indoors, with 31 involving people who were not using air conditioning. In India, an extended spell of hot weather pushed peak electricity demand close to a record in May. Cooling needs kept demand at about 267 gigawatts over several days, leaving nearly a third of coal-fired power plants operating with critically low fuel stocks. Heatwaves drove spikes in electricity demand as more people turned to air conditioning, especially during peak hours from late afternoon to early evening, said Eduard Muljadi, a power systems expert and electrical engineering professor at Auburn University in the US. “At the same time, the grid’s infrastructure, especially transmission lines and transformers, is stressed by the heat itself,” Muljadi said on the university’s website. “These components can overheat, lose efficiency and become more prone to failure.” He added that the efficiency of both thermal plants and renewable energy sources could drop during peak heat. Karachi offers one of the starkest examples of what happens when extreme heat and power failure collide. Eleven years ago, as Pakistan endured a record-breaking heatwave, chronic outages left residents with few ways to escape scorching temperatures, contributing to more than 1,200 deaths. The city’s grid repeatedly failed for 12 hours or longer, turning fans and air conditioners into useless ornaments. As air-conditioning ownership expands across Asia, the number of people and power systems exposed to those risks is likely to grow. Total demand for cooling technologies rose by 50 per cent from 2015 to 2025, according to data from the International Energy Agency. In 2025, global demand reached roughly 2,900 terawatt-hours – more than the European Union’s total electricity consumption that year. By 2035, the IEA estimates total global demand for space cooling will reach 4,500 TWh. In Asia, the combination of intense heatwaves and rising middle-class incomes is set to fuel a rise in air-conditioning ownership over the coming decades, particularly in developing nations. In Indonesia, the IEA expects the share of the population owning an air conditioner to rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 85 per cent by 2050. That growth is not being driven by heat alone. Yuyu Zhou, a geography professor at the University of Hong Kong, said extreme heatwaves and rising incomes across Asia’s developing economies both contributed to the cooling demand spike. Rising household incomes made air-conditioning purchases feasible for more families over time, while extreme heat served as the immediate catalyst for those purchases, he said. “We find that countries like India and Indonesia are right at the steepest part of the curve, where one extreme heat season, combined with rising incomes, can unlock a huge amount of new demand almost overnight,” Zhou said. But as more units are installed, they change the urban environments they are meant to make more bearable. Air conditioning directly adds to the urban heat it is meant to relieve, according to Yuan Chao, an urban climate researcher and architecture professor at the National University of Singapore. Each unit releases hot air back into the atmosphere, contributing to “anthropogenic heat” or heat generated by human activity. Zhou added that air-conditioning use could drive up nighttime temperatures in particular, pointing to Chongqing’s 37-day extreme heatwave in 2022 that pushed temperatures to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit), making it the Chinese city’s hottest August since records began in 1961. Urban waste heat – including heat expelled by air conditioners – accounted for almost half of the total nighttime warming during that heatwave, Zhou said. Simply using less air conditioning was not a viable answer because cooling could also protect health, particularly among elderly and vulnerable people, Chao said. “If it’s very hot outside, they stay at home 24 hours,” Chao said. “But they don’t want to use AC [air conditioning] for 24 hours, otherwise it will be very expensive. They just tolerate, tolerate, tolerate.” Singapore offers an example of how governments can address these competing pressures. Under its Climate Friendly Households Programme, eligible households can claim S$400 (US$312) in vouchers towards energy-efficient air conditioners. Meanwhile, the city state’s national heatwave response plan opens air-conditioned cooling centres in public community facilities when extreme temperatures are forecast, prioritising vulnerable residents and older people. Zhou said making air conditioning more efficient and affordable was an important part of the solution. Models currently on the market vary widely in efficiency, with older, less efficient units typically costing less up front. To encourage people to buy more efficient models, Zhou suggested vouchers, rebates or trade-in programmes. Governments could also enforce minimum energy performance standards to prevent inefficient systems from entering the market entirely, he said. But reducing the need for mechanical cooling is also important. When implementing urban cooling measures in existing cities, Chao said planners should first identify key air passages that allow wind to ventilate dense neighbourhoods. Those areas could be designated as “no-build zones”, he said, with planners advised against putting up additional structures that could block the flow of cooler air. Other strategies include strategically planted shade trees, cool roofs painted in light reflective shades and sky gardens. For cities with tighter budgets, Chao said improving wind ventilation was the most cost-effective first line of defence. “Wind is free,” he said. Cities could also ease grid pressures by encouraging people to use fans instead of or alongside air conditioners and shifting their non-essential energy use away from peak demand hours, Zhou said. “This integrated approach protects public health while limiting waste heat, emissions and blackout risks during extreme heatwaves,” he added.

title: Opinion | Reporter’s note: two Delhis, one weekend – when the world came to dinner
description: The Indian capital was prepared for the 18th Brics summit like a house before company, if at times the cost of its finery fell unevenly.
content: I grew up in Delhi. Not Lutyens’ Delhi, that quieter, greener stretch of tree-lined avenues and high-walled colonial bungalows where the VIPs live. But close enough to know that two cities share one name. One Delhi is generally messy. Rubbish piled into small mountains by the roadside. No footpaths to walk on. Narrow streets marked as one way, with every kind of traffic coming at you from every direction, and then simply stuck. And the dust. Not a film on the windowsill, but something you breathe. It hangs in the heat, gets into your throat, burns your eyes and sets off the sneezing before breakfast. The other is the Delhi that gets dressed when the world comes to dinner. Last week, that second Delhi was out in full. The 18th Brics summit was historic: 20 years of the grouping, 11 members, and the Bharat Mandapam convention centre rising on the old Pragati Maidan exhibition grounds I remember from school holiday fairs. The capital had been prepared like a house before company. Banners on the flyovers. Flags. Faces. The theme in many languages, including simplified Chinese: building for resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. Buildings were lit up. The venue itself, glass and steel now, stood on the same earth where we once queued for the annual trade fair. For a few days, the city looked as if it had been dry-cleaned for the occasion. It had. That dressing had a cost, which fell unevenly. Ordinary people waited for hours while VVIP motorcades used the wide roads of the clean city. Janpath, Shanti Path, Mathura Road: names from childhood, now corridors of barricades. Delhi Police said the city was not shut, only regulated. From a wet pavement, regulation still means standing still. Lutyens stayed Lutyens. The rest of us learned, again, which Delhi the cameras were meant to see. Inside Bharat Mandapam, the day belonged to the summit. The international media centre was buzzing with action. But the Wi-fi did not work at all. In a room built to file to the world, phones became hotspots. The copy still went out. What did work, without pause, was the food: free-flowing, plentiful and entirely vegetarian. Most Indians are not vegetarian. Some 60 to 80 per cent eat meat. Still, the old instinct held: a guest must not go hungry. Indian coverage was buoyant, and not without reason. After a year of fractures inside the bloc, leaders adopted a unanimous New Delhi Declaration. It named the April 2025 Pahalgam attack in India-administered Kashmir, in which 26 people were killed. It also pushed for United Nations reform and gave the Global South a voice in one long careful document. Leaders stood on the lawns in a light September rain, planting banyan saplings. Chinese President Xi Jinping was in India for the first time in seven years. His meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi was read as a thaw: partners, not rivals; differences that should not become disputes; peace on the disputed Himalayan border as the ground on which everything else might stand. What stayed with me was the floor of the media centre. Chinese and Indian crews were not only working side by side. Presenters and commentators from China’s state broadcaster also appeared on India’s national broadcaster DD News and wire service ANI, where they were interviewed repeatedly, saying warm things about the visit and the venue. My Chinese friends were surprised. I was too. For a few hours, the hall felt like a ceasefire you could hear, not in the communique, but in the chatter. Then the day ended. Media had been promised shuttles from a fixed point to the venue. In the mornings, it worked. We were collected there and taken in. At night, the return buses did not come. Colleagues waited for hours at Bharat Mandapam then walked, then met roadblocks. About 40 of us, with kits, cameras and live units, were packed into a Delhi Police van that was never built for that many people. Most of us stood – packed like chickens in a cage. It took more than 40 minutes in the sticky heat and dust-filled air before they dropped us at the same point from which we had been collected that morning. From there I found a cab. Roads were blocked again. Another hour and a half to the hotel. My driver made a point of getting me there safely. Still, I was content. India had done a good job of hosting world leaders and clinching a big diplomatic win on the global stage. And for a few hours, it had felt like a good day for China and India’s ties too. It did not last the week. By Wednesday, Islamabad and Beijing were holding the first meeting of a Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission, a body that touches on territory India says Pakistan illegally occupied and then ceded to China in 1963. New Delhi rejected it at once: no legal basis and no Pakistan-China boundary over land that India still claims. On Indian channels, the warmth of Saturday had cooled. That, too, is this neighbourhood. A handshake in Bharat Mandapam and a map in Islamabad can occupy the same week. I keep both pictures. Similarly, both Delhis are real. The Delhi of barricades and motorcades. The Delhi of dust, traffic and dead Wi-fi. The Delhi that can frustrate you before breakfast and feed hundreds of foreign guests without a second thought. The Delhi that can spend weeks arguing with itself and then, when the world arrives, somehow make room. This is the city that raised me. For one historic weekend, it stood up straighter, opened its doors and reminded me why leaving never quite means leaving.

title: Letters | On English usage, the Trump effect needn’t be the last word
description: Readers discuss the ‘dumbing down’ of spoken English attributed to the US president, and how teachers can engage with today’s digitally savvy students.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Traditionally, the rationales for using “good” English with precision have been well explained. First, as George Orwell argued in his essay “Politics and the English Language”, the decline of standards in politics and that in the use of English can reinforce each other: our language becomes ugly and inaccurate because our thoughts are foolish, but the slovenliness of our language makes it easier for us to have foolish thoughts. Second is the need to appear respectable, which Bergen and Cornelia Evans assumed in the 1950s everybody in America had. As late as 1985, both of these rationales were cited at the beginning of a well-respected guidebook for English usage. More recently, however, these considerations appear to have been, at least to a certain extent, brushed aside, resulting in the “dumbing down” of the English language in US President Donald Trump’s America as described in “Reflections of a reformed grammar Nazi” (August 25). Francis Fukuyama recently explained the Trump phenomenon on BBC’s Newsnight by referring to several trends, two of which are relevant to the discussion on language use. The first one is the tremendous resentment of the less educated in the United States against the educated elite now running many of the country’s big institutions. The second is the rise of the internet and social media on which, Fukuyama said, “anyone can say anything”, by implication including “in any way they like”. It remains the responsibility of those intent on preserving the quality of English in general use – as opposed to fossilising it – to express themselves through different channels in such ways as to prevent the coming into operation of the equivalent of Gresham’s law in the realm of English usage. The pull of the need to appear respectable through proper use of English may have significantly attenuated for those who are so frustrated economically and socially that respectability has simply become a minor or non-existent consideration. On the other hand, as Orwell said, “the process is reversible”. The possibility of a future charismatic American political leader who is much more linguistically sophisticated than Trump exercising a different kind of influence on the public cannot be ruled out. Bowen C. Chow, Heng Fa Chuen Teachers can engage with pupils in the digital world As the old saying goes, “If you can’t beat them, join them.” In education, this need not mean giving in to students’ attachment to screens. It can mean meeting them in a digital environment they already understand, then using it to lead them towards deeper learning. When digital education is discussed today, attention often turns to devices, coding, artificial intelligence and online platforms. School libraries can seem to sit at the edge of that conversation, still associated with bookshelves, borrowing and quiet revision. Yet they remain highly relevant. They are among the places where students learn not only to access information but also to find it, organise it, question it and use it responsibly. This thinking informed the creation of Library Smash, a 3D educational game I developed as a school librarian. Set in a fictional Hong Kong secondary school library, it places students behind the counter during a busy period. Players process loans and returns, locate and shelve books, handle reservations, use equipment and respond to everyday disruptions. The game draws on ordinary library work. A book placed on the wrong shelf may become unavailable to another reader, and an incomplete return process can create further problems. By taking on the role of library staff, students are invited to consider why procedures, call numbers and rules matter. They are not merely administrative requirements but part of how people share resources and space fairly. The tasks also introduce classification, cataloguing and information searching. These skills connect with wider learning: organising materials for project work, managing digital files and searching online with greater purpose. Digital literacy is woven into the game’s scenarios. Students consider the reliability of information, whether AI-generated material needs checking, how copyright applies to online content and why personal data should be handled with care. The intention is to create opportunities for discussion about judgment, consequences and responsibility. Schools rightly encourage students to spend time away from their phones and return to books. But digital media and reading need not be opposing forces. A game may provide an entry point into the library, and teachers and librarians can then guide students towards inquiry, reading and the use of real resources. Developing this game has also reminded me that teaching ideas often emerge from close observation. Looking more closely at these familiar moments may help educators find fresh ways to engage students, while showing them that teachers, too, continue to explore, learn and adapt. Tseng Tsz-ching, Sha Tin

title: Some Western politicians stoking Nato-Russia clash as Ukraine war strategy falters: Fico
description: The Slovak leader said Europe was closer than ever to a large-scale war ‌erupting from the Ukraine conflict.
content: Some Western politicians are seeking conflict between Nato and Russia after ⁠a “failed” strategy to defeat ⁠Moscow in its war with Ukraine, ⁠Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Saturday. Long-time Slovak leader Fico, who has kept up warm relations with Russia and refuses military aid for Ukraine, said this week that Europe was closer than ever to a large-scale war ‌erupting from the Ukraine war. At the same time, some European leaders, such as those in France and Poland, have warned of Russian hybrid attacks. In his video message, Fico said, “we face a mortal danger” while watching the West “pour fuel on the fire” with its support for Ukraine, which he said had been to no avail. “The failure of the ⁠strategy to destroy Russia through the war in Ukraine has led some Western politicians to believe ‌that if the goal cannot be achieved through the Ukrainian army and full support for it, then every effort must be made to trigger a conflict ‌between Nato and Russia,” Fico said in the video posted on social media. He ⁠said the war ⁠in Ukraine was not Slovakia’s nor Nato’s war but said, “certain war hawks within Nato are trying, at any cost, to ‌turn this war into a conflict between Russia and Nato”. Earlier this week, Fico warned a drone incursion could spark the ‌activation of ‌Nato’s collective defence clause and he wanted to prevent Slovakia, which neighbours Ukraine and ‌is a member of the Nato military alliance, from becoming part of an armed conflict. He said on ⁠Saturday that creating a pretext to start a war was easy and reiterated Slovakia would ⁠not send soldiers to fight under a fabricated pretext. French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that Russia was intensifying its campaign of hybrid attacks against Europe and he cited ‌an attempted drone attack ‌at Leipzig airport in August, which the German government concluded Moscow was behind, as evidence of the changing nature of Russian aggression. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday, citing unnamed intelligence agencies, that Russia planned to launch hybrid drone and missile attacks against countries supporting Ukraine.

title: Will fresh incentives give China’s housing market more than a short-lived rebound?
description: Sales of new units in cities like Shanghai and Shenzhen have risen following central government moves designed to revive buyer confidence.
content: Property brokers in China’s major cities are expecting busier days as would-be homebuyers take a cue from a recent policy shift by Beijing aimed at reviving the slumbering real estate market. Some say they are being swamped by inquiries and are trying to seal as many deals as possible amid a recovery in confidence, while others are keeping their fingers crossed for more government stimulus to sustain the growing momentum. “Government support always holds the key to the performance of the home market,” said Yang Keju, a broker at a Lianjia property agency branch in Pudong, Shanghai. “We are worried that the current high transaction volume could become short-lived.” The central government published a package of incentives late last month in an effort to bolster the housing market. It included extended mortgage terms and encouraging sales of completed homes. A longer mortgage repayment cycle – from 30 years to 40 years – can save a homebuyer thousands of yuan in monthly payments, and buying completed flats helps them dodge risks from developer defaults. China Real Estate Business, a newspaper run by the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development, said sales of new residential units in major cities like Shanghai, Shenzhen and Nanjing jumped in the first week of this month. But while brokers said the policy shifts had sparked a short-term buying spree, they were not enough to trigger a broad market turnaround. Analysts say China’s real estate sector and related industries, such as home appliances and construction materials, still account for about a quarter of economic output. The grim reality is that policy support can only effectively release pent-up demand You Liangzhou, Baonuo property agency Early this year, Qiushi, a Communist Party journal, said in a commentary that the property sector was an important part of Chinese households’ wealth, which was taken by the market as an indication that the central and local governments would map out more stimulus measures to stabilise home prices and encourage home buying. “The grim reality is that policy support can only effectively release pent-up demand, while few of our clients hoping to upgrade their living conditions have been willing to take action because they expect a further price drop,” said You Liangzhou, the owner of the Baonuo property agency in Shanghai. “In Shanghai, homebuying restrictions are still preventing some buyers from owning more units and further market deregulation is needed to fully restore consumer confidence.” Fitch Ratings said in a report published this month that the new policies would not boost housing demand materially or alter the weak sales and investment outlook for the real estate sector. “Housing demand is likely to remain weak as the mortgage easing is unlikely to offset high inventory levels and low buyer confidence,” it said. “New-home sales are likely to continue declining, while near-term home prices remain broadly stable at the national level.” Brokers in Shanghai said most owners trying to sell lived-in homes still had to offer discounts ranging from 5 to 10 per cent to secure a sale. Shanghai’s property market was once overheated and the municipal government began tightening limits on home purchases in 2011 to cool it down. The measures included a ban on local households owning a third flat that was designed to rein in speculation. But the municipal government has been gradually easing ownership rules since October 2024 in an effort to spur the local housing market, and now allows people who are not registered residents to buy homes in the city. Since mid-2025, Beijing has been cutting insurance or income tax payment requirements for non-local families wanting to buy homes within the Fifth Ring Road that circles the city centre. Non-Beijing residents are now eligible to buy homes within the Fifth Ring Road after completing at least one year of local income tax or social security payments, down from a three-year rule previously.

title: Face Off: Should driverless cars be allowed on public roads?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
Imagine cars smoothly lining up and gliding along the road without drivers. This is no longer just a dream; driverless cars have already been tested at locations like Hong Kong’s airport and the West Kowloon Cultural District.
While some people are sceptical about the presence of autonomous vehicles on public roads, it is clear that they offer more benefits than drawbacks to society.
Allowing driverless cars on the road introduces a new commuting option that provides significant advantages in terms of safety, accessibility and efficiency.
Driverless cars have the potential to significantly reduce traffic accidents by eliminating human error. According to an analysis published in 2024 in the journal Nature Communications, human drivers generally are more prone to accidents than cars with advanced driving systems.
By reducing these traffic risks, autonomous vehicles can create safer road conditions for both passengers and pedestrians.
One of the key benefits of driverless cars is their potential for accessibility. They offer increased mobility for the elderly, disabled individuals and others who are unable to drive themselves. This technology enhances the confidence and autonomy of these groups, contributing to a more inclusive community.
Some people are concerned about job losses for drivers. However, driverless cars do not eliminate the need for human expertise.
The knowledge of drivers can be redirected to maintaining, repairing and enhancing autonomous systems, complementing the work of engineers and IT developers. This shift creates new opportunities.
Some people point out that autonomous vehicles may increase power consumption for navigation. While this may be true at present, allowing these vehicles on public roads will motivate scientists to develop more environmentally friendly models.
History has shown that widespread adoption often accelerates breakthroughs in energy efficiency, as seen with smartphones and electric vehicles. Driverless cars can follow a similar path.
Driverless cars should be permitted on public roads. By taking this important step, we can embrace technological advancements and work towards a more sustainable future.
While driverless vehicles are often praised and celebrated, they also have significant flaws and dangers. Therefore, they should not be allowed to operate on public roads at this stage.
Autonomous driving technology presents unresolved safety concerns for all road users. Driverless vehicles rely on sensors to monitor real-time road conditions.
However, the camera sensors integrated within these self-driving systems are essentially algorithms and do not possess the capabilities to make decisions in response to real-world incidents.
The readings of automatic sensors can be affected by natural weather conditions and challenging visibility situations like dim street lighting at night, overwhelming glare from sunsets and scattered debris.
When a driverless vehicle’s programmes fail to assess the current environment or respond accurately, this can lead to dangerous misjudgments. Such errors can put pedestrians, bicyclists and citizens’ private property at risk during traffic collisions.
Unlike human drivers, who can make critical life-or-death decisions during sudden roadside emergencies, automated driving systems are limited to operating within the scope of their training.
This significant difference suggests that driverless cars should be banned on public roads.
Additionally, there is currently no fair legal framework to determine liability when a driverless car causes an accident, leaving victims caught in prolonged and unfair disputes. In accidents involving traditional human-driven vehicles, liability is clearly assigned to the driver’s negligence.
However, with autonomous vehicles on public roads, accountability becomes blurred. Who should be held responsible after a serious collision? Is it the vehicle manufacturers, whose defective sensor hardware may be the cause of the system’s misjudgment?
Currently, the absence of a legal standard for addressing fatal collisions involving autonomous vehicles leads to significant regulatory uncertainty.
Overall, driverless vehicles still face safety issues related to their technology, and the global legal system has yet to establish clear guidelines for resolving liability disputes in the event of accidents. Therefore, driverless vehicles should remain banned from public roads.

title: Chinese man sues AI firm after chatbot’s ‘auspicious’ date suggestion leads to disaster
description: Many noted the ultimate irony of the man using the same AI chatbot to draft a lawsuit against its developer for allegedly giving him faulty advice.
content: A man in eastern China filed a lawsuit against an AI company after he followed a chatbot’s recommendation for his mother’s burial date, which he later claimed was linked to a family misfortune. According to Jimu News, Shi, from Jiashan county in Zhejiang province, lost his mother to a sudden illness in April. As the youngest of five siblings, Shi sought an auspicious date for her burial. Such dates, derived from traditional Chinese almanacs reflecting ancient beliefs about celestial movements, are considered by many Chinese to be guidance for significant life decisions. After consulting a feng shui master, Shi and his family initially selected April 20 as a suitable burial date. However, Shi became concerned that it fell on the fourth day after his mother’s death, as local customs regard even-numbered days as unlucky. He subsequently turned to an AI chatbot for further guidance. The chatbot recommended April 19 and advised burning paper horses and paper money before the funeral procession, a traditional practice believed to provide the deceased with essentials for their journey to the afterlife. Shi followed this advice but later received conflicting information regarding the burial time: while the chatbot suggested 7am to 9am, it simultaneously stated that April 19 was not an auspicious date. By this time, he had already informed relatives of the arrangements and could not change the date. Shortly after the funeral, one of his relatives suffered serious injuries in a traffic accident, though the specific timing of the incident was not disclosed. Some family members attributed the incident to the burial date, believing it had disrupted the family’s feng shui and attracted bad luck. Shi, a frequent user of the AI chatbot who relied on it for tasks such as organising work contracts, felt the AI provided misleading advice that contributed to strained family relations. He later filed a lawsuit against the AI company, seeking an apology and compensation. Notably, the chatbot also assisted him in drafting legal documents and outlining litigation procedures, though the amount of compensation sought has not been disclosed. The software provider in question is Beijing Chuntian Zhiyun Technology. Its terms of use state that AI-generated content is provided for reference only and does not constitute professional advice, while users accept the relevant service agreement by using the software. The case has recently been heard at the local court and remains ongoing. The company argued that no online infringement had occurred, while Shi countered that the user agreement unfairly shifted responsibilities onto users, offered insufficient warnings, and lacked adequate review of the information sources utilised by the AI. Online observers had varying opinions; one commented: “AI is only a tool. It is unfortunate for those who cannot evaluate its answers independently.” Another noted: “The irony is that this man is using AI to sue the AI company. If this trend continues, people may eventually turn to AI lawyers for legal disputes as well.”

title: Chinese lawyers offer coaching for when corruption busters come knocking
description: Suspects should learn what to do before being detained, lawyers say, as they might spend months cut off from legal counsel.
content: Zhang Dongdong has been fielding ever more requests for legal advice from jittery entrepreneurs, nervous government officials or their desperate relatives. They usually do not tell him the whole story, and sometimes say it happened “to a friend”, but most want to know the same thing: what to do when they are targeted by China’s corruption busters. “Some had received a tip-off that they were being investigated, some got a call from disciplinary inspectors asking them to cooperate, but in most of the cases, the suspects had already been held by disciplinary authorities, and their families came to us,” said Zhang, a partner at Beijing Han Heng Law Firm. “We even ran into some extreme cases. Once, someone who had given bribes agreed to cooperate after being promised that they wouldn’t be investigated, but the authorities went back on their word after the bribe-taker was sentenced. In the most serious case, the client died after being taken into custody and the family came to us.” It’s a black box. Everybody knows that it’s terrifying, but they do not know how exactly. A Beijing-based criminal lawyer Last month, Zhang began advertising consulting services for “bribery and corruption crisis response”. In a social media post, he said that as the authorities intensified their efforts to root out corruption across society, individuals faced “unprecedented criminal, financial and professional risks”. His move comes as law enforcement authorities further toughen their approach to corruption. In April, the Supreme People’s Court and Supreme People’s Procuratorate made it easier for corruption suspects to be charged with criminal offences. As President Xi Jinping’s anti-corruption campaign moves further into its second decade, the scope of suspicion has increased. A South China Morning Post analysis found that last year, watchdogs handed down punishments to 983,000 people and the number of senior officials taken down last year was three times the total for 2013. As fears of being targeted grow, more state employees are reaching out to seasoned criminal lawyers like those in Zhang’s team to find out how to best protect themselves. According to Zhang, few people were prepared to deal with a corruption investigation. A common reaction is to run. Once, a senior manager from a state-owned company fled to another province and claimed he was on a business trip to headquarters, while others escaped overseas, he said. Another common reaction is denial. In one case he dealt with, the briber and recipient coordinated their stories and decided to deny the charges altogether, Zhang said, adding that the consequences of denial could be serious if bribery were proven. His team could provide clients with strategies on how to present evidence, avoid detention by the supervisory authorities, reduce their sentences and safeguard their assets, he wrote. Suspects needed to be able to draw a distinction between conduct that constituted a crime and conduct that did not, and must understand how leniency worked in the judicial system. Another reason he launched corruption consultation services was that suspects were usually cut off from their lawyers after being detained by the disciplinary authorities, Zhang said. Custody is generally three or six months and can be as long as 14 months under special circumstances. “When they are in custody, and the authorities tell their families to return any bribes, families do not know what to do. Do they pay or not? In some cases, authorities take a couple and leave only the elderly and young children at home,” he said. The opacity of the system was partly why such investigations were so hard to deal with, said a Beijing-based criminal lawyer who wished to remain anonymous. “It’s a black box. Everybody knows that it’s terrifying, but they do not know how exactly,” she said. The most valuable time to get advice would be before disciplinary detention, said legal expert Zhang Qingfang. After that, a defence lawyer’s room for manoeuvre was narrow and it did not matter much whether families sought legal help, he said. “But under some circumstances, if the requests raised by law enforcement authorities to families are illegal, if lawyers give legal and correct suggestions, it will avoid suspects being framed or their sentences becoming heavier,” he said. Clients often missed the critical defence opportunities that appeared at every stage of the proceedings in these cases, Zhang Dongdong said. Lawyers can spot the key issues that can potentially affect sentencing, including whether to define the alleged bribe as a legitimate social courtesy, how to determine the amount of money involved and whether an individual or their employer should be liable. Family members should also record the extent of searches and which items were confiscated by the authorities and refuse to cooperate with illegal requests such as making false confessions, according to Zhang Zhiyong, a lawyer from the Chongqing Zhihao Law Firm. In an article he published on social media, he wrote that he had been in the business for more than 20 years and had multiple senior officials’ sentences reduced. In one case, he defended a vice-governor who was accused of abuse of power and taking a large amount of bribes. He successfully argued that his client deserved leniency because they had turned themselves in, returned their illicit gains and admitted their guilt. In another case, Zhang Zhiyong found new evidence in the case of a director of a public hospital who had been charged with embezzlement. He used the evidence to persuade the authorities to downgrade the charge to the lighter “unlawful possession of property”. Lawyers, however, were not always able to turn things around, the Beijing-based lawyer said, especially if the authorities used illegal measures such as torture to extract confessions. There was usually more space for legal defence for bribe givers than bribe takers, even though these cases were usually investigated together, she said. If bribe givers cooperated with the disciplinary authorities, they might get off the hook as the authorities focused mostly on officials receiving bribes, she said. But the restrictions on lawyers did not mean they could not develop effective strategies based on the evidence, said Zhang Dongdong, the lawyer from Han Heng Law Firm. His clients “need professionals familiar with the law, the disciplinary authorities’ policies and their proceedings”, he said.

title: Anwar was on song in India. Will Malaysia reap the rewards?
description: The Malaysian PM’s rendition of a Bollywood ballad went viral, but his India trip was about more than just the music.
content: Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim caused a bit of a stir in India recently with his spirited rendition of a Bollywood classic – a lighthearted moment that also neatly captured his broader push to deepen ties with the South Asian giant. A video of Anwar singing, from memory, Kishore Kumar’s 1965 hit ballad “Khwab Ho Tum Ya Koi Haqeeqat” (“Are you a dream or are you reality?”) was first posted to his social media accounts last Sunday before quickly being picked up by Indian news outlets. The performance came as Anwar joined leaders from across the Global South in New Delhi from September 12-13 for the annual Brics summit, where Malaysia took part as a partner country. Guru mintak izin nyanyi kejap ok! pic.twitter.com/NzazFHV509 — Anwar Ibrahim (@anwaribrahim) September 12, 2026 Viral recitals aside, the visit’s underlying importance lay in Malaysia’s attempts to widen its economic and strategic options at a time of intensifying rivalry between the US and China. After meeting his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi, Anwar toured the country, pressing the case for more capital and opportunity to flow between the two nations with political leaders and captains of industry alike. The outreach was an exercise in Malaysia’s “friend to all, enemy to none” foreign policy, analysts said, as it sought to broaden its pool of partners and insulate itself from the prolonged trade and technology rivalry between the US and China – its two largest trade and investment partners. “Closer cooperation with India gives Malaysia another important economic and security partner without requiring Putrajaya to move decisively into any one camp,” said Kamles Kumar, associate director for Malaysia at strategic consultancy Asia Group Advisors. Untapped promise Malaysia’s economy is heavily dependent on the US and China: two-way trade with the superpowers was valued at more than 900 billion ringgit (US$220 billion) in 2025 alone. The US is also Malaysia’s largest source of foreign investment, while China supplies the raw materials and equipment that keep the Southeast Asian nation’s industries running. Both are vital buyers and suppliers for Malaysia’s all-important semiconductor sector, which meets an estimated 13 per cent of global chip assembly, testing and packaging demand and accounts for about 7 per cent of the country’s annual revenue. Malaysia’s economic relationship with India is underdeveloped Yeah Kim Leng, economics professor But with Washington and Beijing increasingly pressuring partners to pick a side in their years-long economic rivalry, Malaysia has been forced to actively strengthen other partnerships to help steady its footing as it straddles the interests of the world’s two largest economies. Malaysia’s ultimate goal is preserving its “strategic autonomy” as a relatively small trading nation by tightening ties with other major powers, such as India, to balance out the influence of the US and China on its economy, according to Eric Low, a partner at Kuala Lumpur-based strategic advisory firm Densui. “Strengthening Malaysia-India ties in this regard is not so much about shifting away from China or the United States, but rather, expanding Malaysia’s economic and strategic options and position, especially for the long term,” Low said. Getting there will take some serious work, however. Malaysia has yet to tap the enormous potential of India’s market of more than 1.4 billion people despite signing a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2024. Bilateral trade between the two nations was valued at 79.3 billion ringgit in 2025 – a fraction of what Malaysia trades with the US and China. While India’s bureaucracy is notoriously difficult for foreign investors to navigate, experts say it is up to Malaysia’s government and businesses to negotiate better access to the world’s largest population. “Malaysia’s economic relationship with India is underdeveloped. With weakening growth and rising structural problems facing both [the US and China], looking for alternative markets becomes an urgent imperative,” said Yeah Kim Leng, an economics professor at Sunway University. “Apart from boosting trade and investment with Asean member countries, India is the closest neighbour with the greatest potential for boosting Malaysia’s exports,” he added, referring to Southeast Asia’s 11-member diplomatic bloc. Chips, oil and missiles Analysts point to semiconductors as a natural entry point for both nations to supercharge trade and cooperation, with Malaysia’s strengths in advanced packaging and testing complementing India’s expertise in integrated circuit design and front-end chip fabrication experience. Yeah said Malaysia could also look to sell more of its palm oil to India – the world’s largest consumer of vegetable oils – and buy more Indian rice to shore up its own food security. Beyond trade, India has the potential to become a valuable addition to Malaysia’s list of defence partners. Following his meeting with Modi, Anwar announced an interest in procuring the BrahMos air-to-surface missile system developed jointly by India and Russia, a move that could reduce Malaysia’s reliance on US or US-aligned nations to meet its defence needs. Diversifying defence partnerships in this way was also about preserving strategic autonomy, Asia Group Advisors’ Kamles said, though it could raise a few eyebrows in Beijing. “Given the missile’s range and versatility, it could also affect perceptions of Malaysia’s deterrence posture in the South China Sea,” Kamles said of the waterway over which China and Malaysia have overlapping claims. “Putrajaya would therefore need to communicate clearly that any acquisition is intended to strengthen national defence, rather than target a particular country.” Malaysia can expect more pressure from the US and China to pick a side should it grow closer to India, observers say, especially with the three nuclear powers increasingly jostling for dominance. But that only made it all the more important to maintain a principles-based and non-aligned approach to foreign policy, said Hafidzi Razali, chief executive at policy advisory firm Strategic Counsel. “Malaysia has always hedged its position through diversification and maintaining a neutral position. It deepens its relationship with other states often in parallel to each other,” Hafidzi said.

title: Opinion | What Hong Kong cinema can take away from a popular Chinese war film
description: If productions need not be set in China to be seen as Chinese, why must Hong Kong films rely on language or place as proof of identity?
content: In late August, I took my parents to see Once Upon a Time in the Middle East in their small-town cinema on the mainland. Built around an unnamed conflict widely understood to be the US-led Iraq war, the film has become the kind of phenomenon no marketing budget could buy, projected to reach 2.5 billion yuan (US$372.5 million) largely through word of mouth. Its Hong Kong and overseas release will revive geopolitical arguments over a Chinese commercial film entering a narrative world long associated with American power and war. My parents offered another kind of review, which was neither about geopolitics nor historical responsibility. Their take was simply that any war brings immense suffering to ordinary people. For 50 years, the Middle East had reached my parents largely as television news. The film gave those distant wars ordinary faces. They said little else on the drive home. I kept returning to a question from my research: why do some films travel across borders while others remain trapped by the expectations attached to where they were made? I have heard the standard diagnosis of the decline of Hong Kong cinema: co-productions corroded the craft; filmmakers chased mainland money; the cure is to become more authentically Hong Kong, more local, more unmistakably ours. It all has the comfort of a familiar hymn. Those complaints might explain what went wrong with some films. They don’t explain what happened to the market. There is nothing wrong with wanting Hong Kong cinema to look and sound like Hong Kong, but local identity is not an industrial policy. Treating it as one mistakes an industry problem for an identity problem. The old Southeast Asian Chinese-language market was not merely an export destination for Hong Kong cinema. In the 1950s and 1960s, Singapore-based studios such as Shaw Brothers helped finance films made in Hong Kong, then distributed and exhibited them through cinema networks across the region. Migration and language networks held this system together. From the late 1950s onwards, Cold War-era nation-building drew new cultural borders across the region: Indonesia closed Chinese-language schools and newspapers; Malaysia withdrew funding from Chinese-medium secondary schools; Singapore pushed dialects aside in favour of Mandarin. When the Teochew-dialect film Dear You reached Singapore this summer, some pressed for more screenings in Teochew, despite the fact that in 2025, 58.1 per cent of Singapore residents aged five and over spoke English most often at home. Chinese-language audiences remain, but the regional film market that once linked them has fractured. Making films more recognisably Hong Kong cannot put that market back together. Hong Kong films can no longer assume that language or location will carry them across the region; their stories must work beyond both. Mainland cinema offers a counterpoint. It serves a larger domestic market, faces stronger pressure to affirm national identity and operates under tighter content controls. Even so, some recent commercial hits have set their stories beyond China without losing mass audiences at home. Viewers followed the story without needing to recognise the place. Some of this flexibility began under pressure. Crime, corruption and other sensitive subjects are easier to depict when shifted from recognisable Chinese locations to invented foreign settings, but the workaround has matured into a commercial language. The formula did more than evade censorship: it loosened the assumption that a Chinese film must look geographically Chinese. Hong Kong cinema ... helped write the textbook. Bruce Lee needed no subtitles. Jackie Chan carried his comedy into Hollywood. Chow Yun-fat’s gunmen travelled far beyond Hong Kong streets Sheep Without a Shepherd was one such hit, grossing about US$191 million in China. It was adapted from Drishyam, a Malayalam thriller remade in several Indian languages. Malaysian-born director Sam Quah shot it in Thailand with mainland Chinese backing for China’s domestic market. The production map is remarkable, but Chinese audiences did not need to read it; on screen, a father is trying to save his family. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East is the latest proof. Much of its setting was built on sound stages and backlots in Qingdao. My parents did not care where the desert really was; they cared what happened to the people in it. Hong Kong cinema should recognise the pattern: it helped write the textbook. Bruce Lee needed no subtitles. Jackie Chan carried his comedy into Hollywood. Chow Yun-fat’s gunmen travelled far beyond Hong Kong streets. A Better Tomorrow is unmistakably a Hong Kong film, but the city was the setting, never the entrance fee. Hong Kong was the workshop. Its filmmakers turned migration, crowded cities, ambition and desire into action, comedy and melodrama that audiences everywhere recognised. As Once Upon a Time in the Middle East opens in Hong Kong, its mainland success raises a question. If a mainland Chinese film need not take place in China to be recognised as Chinese, why must a Hong Kong film turn local landmarks and language into proof of its identity? Hongkongness can shape a film without becoming a test viewers must pass before the story begins. People sometimes forget that cinema is an art of illusion. Shaw Brothers built some of the cinematic worlds now regarded as quintessentially Hong Kong on backlots and sound stages. They were artifice, and no less Hong Kong for it. The least authentic thing Hong Kong cinema can do now is demand authenticity. That identity was never simply about soil. It was shaped by filmmakers drawing on Cantonese and English, tapping Shanghainese capital and talent as well as Southeast Asian audiences. The mixture produced films strangers wanted to watch. That is the habit worth recovering. Enough borders stand in the way of Hong Kong cinema. A self-made barrier is the last thing the industry needs.

title: Ed Sheeran calls Gaza situation ‘unjustifiable’ after Macklemore exit furore
description: The pop star decried the ‘devastation and loss of children’s lives’ in the Palestinian enclave during a concert in Philadelphia.
content: Ed Sheeran opened a concert on Saturday with comments about Gaza after controversy swirled around his tour and supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage. Sheeran began the concert alone on stage with no opener, but was joined by other musicians later in the show. Sheeran said he wanted his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. But he said the attacks in Israel of October 7, 2023, were horrific and what was happening in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable”. “I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” Sheeran said during his performance at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia. “My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians’ lives, of children’s lives.” Sheeran then addressed the controversy that unfolded since his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore. Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original US opener, had been replaced by the Danish band Lukas Graham and the Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out. Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week. Before Saturday’s show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators congregated outside the stadium. Hillary Steinberg, 34, of Philadelphia, said she got tickets a year ago but wound up getting a refund and attending the demonstration instead, disappointed that Sheeran did not take a stand. “I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice – even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit – is a political choice.” The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a September 5 show in New Jersey. Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran’s statement on Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew. Diane Savitz, a 53-year-old concertgoer from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, got her tickets to the show months ago and is a big Sheeran fan. She said she does not think that he did anything wrong or that a concert is the place for politics. “A concert should be for people enjoying the music. Music should bring people together,” Savitz said. “Everyone has their right to freedom of speech, but not every platform is the place for it.” Macklemore said on Wednesday he was donating US$1 million to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift; a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate US$2 million but have not specified where the money will be directed. Sheeran’s representatives have not responded to multiple requests for comment. Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over US$7 million per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the No 3 top-earning concert act since 2021. Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore. The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he would not be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans do not come to his shows to hear about these issues. He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.
