While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran’s magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows. Sheeran told the crowd in Philadelphia that everyone was welcome at his concerts and they can have opposing points of view while still singing his songs, which are about “love, hope and unity”. He also told fans that he was worried about venues pre-approving performances. “This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” Sheeran said.

title: Xi sends condolences as Hong Kong holds state funeral for Tung Chee-hwa – as it happened
description: President Xi Jinping and other top Chinese officials, including Premier Li Qiang, pay tribute after funeral attended by 200 members of city’s establishment and family.
content: Hong Kong bid farewell to its first post-colonial chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, at a state funeral on Sunday – only the third time a Hongkonger has received such an honour since the 1997 handover. Tung, who died at the age of 89 on September 8, led Hong Kong through a series of ups and downs, including the 1997 Asian financial crisis, the 2003 Sars outbreak and the V-shaped economic recovery that followed. Sunday’s funeral follows a vigil held the previous day at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point, which drew dozens of political and business heavyweights paying their respects to the late leader. The state funeral was arranged by an 87-member committee chaired by Shi Taifeng, top vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and a member of the Communist Party Politburo. Members of the public can pay their respects by signing condolence books at three community halls until noon on Sunday. title: Why AI giants are choosing Singapore to turn models into real-world tools
description: The city state is emerging as a regional hub for turning frontier AI models into practical applications.
content: When Jordan Seow joined OpenAI in June 2025, he became the company’s first locally hired forward-deployed engineer in Asia-Pacific, joining a Singapore office that then had fewer than 20 employees. The 29-year-old is now part of a fast-growing workforce built in Singapore by the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies. Experts say the city state is emerging as a regional hub – not for training the latest AI models, but for the increasingly crucial task of deploying and adapting them for practical use. Seow told This Week in Asia that the growing presence of global AI firms was opening new doors for local talent. “It also makes roles that combine technical depth, customer engagement and practical implementation more visible,” Seow said. “You don’t necessarily have to follow a purely research or software engineering path to contribute meaningfully to AI.” On Wednesday, Anthropic became the latest AI firm to announce plans for a Singapore office, joining the likes of OpenAI, Meta Platforms’ Superintelligence Labs and Alphabet’s Google DeepMind. Anthropic is currently advertising nine roles in applied AI, finance, marketing, public benefit and sales. OpenAI has committed to creating more than 200 Singapore-based technical roles as it builds its first Applied AI Lab outside the United States. The influx reflects Singapore’s appeal as a stable, well-connected base with direct access to Southeast Asian markets and global talent. But for the city state, a key question remains: how effectively will this foreign investment translate into high-value jobs and skills for Singaporeans? Seow, a 2021 National University of Singapore business analytics graduate, worked at an AI start-up before OpenAI. As a forward-deployed engineer, he works with clients to build and integrate technical solutions into their existing infrastructure. Singapore’s AI expansion comes against the backdrop of a tech rivalry between the US and China, with global companies navigating a complex geopolitical environment. US AI firms are reportedly increasingly turning to Singapore to recruit international engineers without facing the tightening visa restrictions, high processing fees and longer wait times common in the US. At the same time, Singapore is pursuing its ambition to become what its Economic Development Board calls the world’s “most AI-powered economy”. The city state currently offers a Tech.Pass for top tech talent, which will be replaced in January by a dedicated One Pass for AI and tech specialists. Under its updated national AI strategy, Singapore aims to help 10,000 enterprises make meaningful use of the technology over the next three years. Starting in 2027, businesses will also receive enhanced tax deductions on spending towards adopting AI. Deployment advantage Stefan Winkler, head of AI & Data Science at the Singapore Institute of Technology’s Infocomm Technology Cluster, said Singapore’s appeal lay in its access to Southeast Asia’s digital economy, regulatory stability, strong intellectual property protections and highly skilled talent pool. For companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, Singapore offered a base for “regional market development, enterprise deployment, partnerships, customer support, policy engagement, and talent recruitment”, the professor said. In return, Singapore gained high-value jobs, talent development, foreign investment and closer integration between leading technology providers and local universities, start-ups and state bodies, he added. Laurence Liew, director of AI innovation at AI Singapore, put the distinction more bluntly: “Frontier pre-training is not here.” While some localised adaptation research was taking place, Liew said the “thickest layer” of Singapore’s industry was deployment engineering. OpenAI committed more than S$300 million (US$235 million) in May under a joint agreement with the Singapore government. Google Cloud opened an engineering centre in the city state on Tuesday – partnering with regional giants Grab and DBS – while Microsoft is investing US$5.5 billion in local cloud and AI infrastructure through 2029. “What is being built here is the layer that turns a model into something a bank, a hospital or a ministry can run in production,” Liew said. “That layer is the one Singapore has spent nine years getting good at.” Do companies hire locally? Linda Teo, country manager at ManpowerGroup Singapore, said tech multinationals typically hired locally for roles requiring an understanding of regional regulations, market dynamics and business culture. But other employees were often relocated from global headquarters to support set-up and early launch phases. Liew agreed, saying local hiring tended to expand as operations matured. To bridge this gap, AI Singapore runs an apprenticeship programme that has trained over 500 apprentices, adding more than 100 every year. About 99 per cent of graduates were placed in roles within six months, with several companies working with AI Singapore to recruit forward-deployed engineers directly from the programme. Some government grants also came with local hiring requirements, he said. That means the gains for Singaporeans may come less from taking the most senior roles immediately than from a gradual widening of technical, customer-facing positions as companies deepen their operations. The city state also faces the challenge of managing the risks that come with wider AI deployment, particularly as the technology moves into sectors such as finance, healthcare and public services. “In many ways, Singapore’s approach has been pragmatic,” Winkler said. “Remain open to innovation, but ensure that organisations deploying AI are accountable for how these systems are used.”

title: Hong Kong’s Asian Games relay silver the big surprise on day when results went as expected
description: Siobhan Haughey leads city to just second 4x100m freestyle silver as Grace Lau wins medal, China win six pool golds, hosts win opening gold.
content: There was something almost inevitable about the way the first day of competition at the Asian Games in Japan unfolded on Sunday, and the only real surprise would have been finding someone surprised by it all. That is until Hong Kong’s women came second in the 4x100m freestyle relay in the final event at Tokyo Aquatics Centre. Just the second silver the team has ever managed in the discipline, it was as unexpected as the city-record time that accompanied it. Much earlier in the day’s proceedings, organisers got the quick start they needed to briefly silence the dissenting voices: China raced to the top of the medal table, and will no doubt stay there, and swimmer Yu Zidi was equally quick in dispelling any notion that she will not be a global star. The 13-year-old won the women’s 200m butterfly by a gap of more than three seconds, capping a golden debut for an athlete who surely has eyes on a greater prize, given she rated her performance as “so-so” and was already evaluating areas for improvement so she could “perform better next time”. Yu’s gold, which came in a Games-record time of two minutes, 5.08 seconds, was one of six China won in the pool, with others coming in modern pentathlon, shooting, triathlon and wushu, taking the total to 11 overall. At least the honour of securing the first of the week went to the host nation, with triathlete Takumi Hojo coming home ahead of the rest in the men’s race at the Gamagori City Triathlon Venue.. “As it’s our first gold medal, it’s given the Japanese team a real boost, and we’ve managed to pass the baton on to the women and our teammates for the relay,” Hojo said. While revelling in his achievement at finishing second, China’s Zhang Xiuri said he was “disappointed to be behind Japan”. It didn’t take long for roles to be reversed, with Lin Xinyu beating teammate Huang Anqi across the line in the women’s race and finishing almost a full second faster than Japan’s bronze medallist, Hayashi Manami, who came home in 58 minutes and 36 seconds. Hong Kong’s quartet will be hoping they can again prove to be greater than the sum of their parts in Monday’s team relay. Robin Elg and Oscar Coggins finished sixth and seventh respectively in the men’s outing, while Bailee Brown and Tallulah Wright were eighth and 20th in the women’s event. Not that the city’s delegation was limited to just one silver. After back-to-back bronzes in Jakarta in 2018 and Hangzhou three years ago, Grace Lau Mo-sheung finally upgraded her karate medal, although she was denied gold by a familiar foe, Japan’s Maho Ono. Not that Lau was entirely happy, saying this had been the year she was “really ready to get the gold medal”. “In 2018 and 2023, I was very close in the semi-finals, but I always missed it,” she added. Still, it was a costly day for the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s athlete incentive award scheme, which will pay out HK$500,000 to Lau for her result, while the swimmers will get to share HK$1 million. Siobhan Haughey, meanwhile, was delighted at a performance involving two debutants, Gilaine Ma and Li Sum-yiu, that “scored a medal on the first day”. Ma led out the city quartet, Haughey and Li did their jobs in the middle, and Natalie Kan Cheuk-tung held on to bring them home in 3:36.59, in a race China won in a Games record time of 3:33.10. Bronze went to Japan. “It shows that we actually have quite a lot of young swimmers who have great potential,” Haughey added. “I believe our swimmers will perform great in the following days.” The expectation will be that she is among them. Haughey opted out of the women’s 50m breaststroke on Sunday to focus on defending her women’s 200m freestyle title on Monday and her 100m freestyle 24 hours later. It was probably a sensible decision given China’s Tang Qianting won in a Games record 29.45 seconds. Other golds were won by Pan Zhanle in the men’s 100m freestyle, Li Bingjie in the women’s 1,500m freestyle, and Xu Jiayu in the men’s 100m backstroke. There will be more gold to be won in Tokyo tomorrow, and Haughey is aware of the pressure that rests on her shoulders. Not only as one of the most experienced swimmers in the squad, but as a double Asian Games gold medallist in Hangzhou and with four Olympic medals to her name. “I am one of the older swimmers here, but that comes with a lot of experience as well and I think that is a big advantage,” she said. “I’ve been to many big meets so I kind of know what to expect and how to deal with the nerves when it happens. “Pressure is a privilege, but I’m here to do my job and to swim well, and I can’t wait to see what I can do this week.”

title: Hong Kong coach spells out big change needed after Fiji overpower city team
description: City team beaten in their second WXV Challenger fixture, poised to complete campaign against Samoa next Saturday.
content: Tumua Ioane said Hong Kong would make tangible progress only when they had their sevens players available for major 15s tournaments, after his spirited team lost 54-26 to Fiji at Kai Tak Youth Sports Ground on Saturday. Last-ditch victors over Brazil last Sunday, the hosts will expect to end their WXV Challenger campaign with victory over hapless Samoa next week. But in a four-try blitz shortly before half-time, the bustling and buccaneering Fijians brutally exposed the gulf that exists between Hong Kong and the leading second-tier nations. Missing a number of players who are preparing for next month’s Asian Games 7s competition in Japan, the city team led 14-12 following a cleverly worked 26th-minute try for Sabay Lynam. In the space of 10 sobering minutes, however, Varanisese Qoro, Atelaite Bune, twice, and Merewairita Neivosa all crossed for converted tries to kill off the game as a contest. Ioane, the lead coach, praised his team’s “relentlessness and hard work”, but acknowledged that to bridge the gap to “dynamic” Fiji “we need more games, and access to our sevens players at these big tournaments”. Also the head coach of Women’s Premiership team Gai Wu, Ioane said: “[Player absences were] something we knew was going to be a factor, but the way this group has come together and are performing, the door is open for us to keep growing once we have all our players available. “In the short term, the Premiership is doing some good things in terms of the quality, which has risen in the two years I’ve been here.” Introduced this year to provide emerging unions with more competitive international fixtures, the WXV Challenger has allowed Hong Kong’s players a rare concerted period of training and matches. Currently 16th in the global standings, the city team have targeted qualification for the 16-team 2029 World Cup. “We’ve come so far, we’re not a full-time programme, and to perform like that in the first half [before Fiji’s try spree] was outstanding,” Grace Hood, the Hong Kong No 8, said. A full-time 7s player who, as a non-passport holder, is ineligible for the Asian Games, Hood said the 15s team need to “keep driving and pushing”. “We have a lot of evening training, camps and some competitions abroad, but if we can perform like today, who knows what will happen for us in the future,” she added. The position of Hong Kong head coach has been something of a hot potato of late. This year, Bella Milo led the team in the Asia Rugby Women’s Championship, where the city team lost heavily to Japan and drew with hosts Kazakhstan. Milo is now bossing Samoa, who went down 61-21 to Spain on Saturday. New Zealander Ioane was at the helm for victories over Belgium and hosts Germany in November last year, on an uncapped tour that he said “gave players experience of how different international rugby is from the club game”. Royce Chan Leong-sze, Andrew Douglas and Lewis Wilson have all had spells in charge over the past 2½ years. Ioane recently signed up for three more years in Hong Kong. “We’ll talk about what that looks like moving forward after this tournament,” he said. “I love these girls and this programme, and I’ll be open to filling whatever role is in front of me.” On the back foot against Fiji after early scores for Salote Nailolo and Qoro, Hong Kong responded with a try from Tanya Dhar, adding to the pair she managed against Brazil six days earlier. So reliant on the rolling maul to hurt the Brazilians, Hong Kong summoned a measure of flair when Roshini Turner and captain Lara Schats combined to send the impressive Lynam over in the corner. Lauren Knowler, a former England under-20 inside centre, brilliantly converted. “When we scored the first try, a belief switch flicked in our heads,” Hood, sporting a fresh and vivid shiner, said. “We thought, ‘we can do this’. “We knew this was a game where we needed to get the ball wide and it worked for the second try.” Their tails tweaked, Fiji summoned a passage of irresistible, unforgiving rugby to put Hong Kong to bed. “It’s disappointing,” Ioane said. “We put ourselves in a good position, but letting them score 28 points in 10 minutes changed the game. We were always chasing it from there.” Zipporah Sorocacika and Vasemaca Duva added second-half tries for Fiji, while Knowler, who finished with 14 points, and Lucia Bolton, at the death, replied for Hong Kong. “We speak about being relentless and working hard for each other,” Ioane said. “The girls have worked on their condition for two months, and we’re seeing the fruits of that late in these games.” Ioane reminded his shell-shocked players at half-time that they were not on the field to merely participate, while Schats issued an impassioned rallying cry. “When you’re in dark places, the only thing that can pick you up outside of your own mentality is everyone around you,” Ioane said. “They know what it’s taken to build that trust between them. Credit to them, they’re like a family.” After Georgia Cutt became Hong Kong’s latest debutant off the bench, Ioane, a former Dunedin player who switched to refereeing at 26, said the city’s talent pool was “getting deeper to a point”. “The last year’s been brilliant in terms of giving opportunities to more people,” he added. “There’s a bit of work we have to do, but I can’t fault the players’ effort.”

title: Named as an enemy: Indonesia’s uneasy Aukus moment
description: Aukus inquiry testimony in Australia cast Indonesia as a foe in a hypothetical war, reviving old suspicions.
content: A former Australian official’s use of a hypothetical “aggressive Indonesia” to make the case for Aukus at a public inquiry has been called “clumsy diplomacy” by analysts, who say the comments risk reviving old suspicions as Jakarta and Canberra try to strengthen security ties. Michael Pezzullo, a former deputy secretary of strategy in Australia’s defence department, made the remarks in testimony on September 2 to the Aukus Public Inquiry, an independent, crowdfunded review of the trilateral defence pact. Making the case that Aukus’ nuclear-powered submarines offered Australia its best route to undersea military dominance, Pezzullo used Indonesia as an illustrative adversary arguing that in a hypothetical conflict, Australian forces would seek to “rapidly destroy as much of the enemy’s fighting power as possible” without having to call on the United States or other allied forces. His remarks were first published by media outlet News24 on September 5, then edited and republished two days later by The Strategist, a journal run by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, under the headline “Aukus has put Australia’s submarine effort back on track”. The institute, which was established by the Australian government in 2001, receives partial funding from the Department of Defence. Abdul Rahman Yaacob, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates, said Indonesian defence officials were “unhappy” and had raised the matter informally with their Australian counterparts in Jakarta on the same day the article was published. “It is always good not to mention one’s potential adversary publicly when relations are good,” Rahman said. “That is clumsy diplomacy.” It comes seven months after Australia and Indonesia, under a landmark agreement signed in February, committed to regular high-level consultations on regional and national security challenges and to expand defence cooperation, including through joint military training. If mismanaged, the fallout from Pezzullo’s remarks could damage ties, Rahman said, noting that Canberra had periodically viewed Indonesia as a threat. As recently as the early 2000s, Australian opinion polls had Indonesia “far outranking” other regional states as a perceived security threat, he said – likely a legacy of East Timor’s bitter struggle for independence from Indonesia that prompted an Australian-led military intervention. Suspicion exists on both sides. Rahman pointed to revelations, leaked by former US National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden in 2013, that Australian intelligence had monitored the mobile phone of then president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono. In response, Jakarta recalled its ambassador to Canberra and suspended bilateral cooperation for a time. Building trust Indonesia’s defence establishment was unlikely to see the country as Aukus’ intended target, regardless of a former Australian official’s remarks, said Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. Indonesian forces have clashed with Australian and British troops in the past, including during the “Konfrontasi”: president Sukarno’s 1963-66 armed campaign against the formation of Malaysia. Relations hit another low point in 1999, when Australia led an international peacekeeping force into East Timor as the territory voted for independence – a move Jakarta viewed as an affront to its sovereignty. But Gatra said ties had moved well beyond that era, with Australia increasingly regarding a strong, stable Indonesia as important to its own security. Joint exercises, military training and personnel exchanges in recent years pointed towards “a relationship built around cooperation rather than contingency planning against one another”, he said. “There are already serious efforts to build trust and confidence through regular training, personnel exchanges and combined exercises,” Gatra added. Jakarta’s chief concern centred on the practical risks of nuclear-powered submarines themselves, he said, including the potential impact on fisheries and the marine environment in the event of an accident. Troubled waters Aukus, established by Australia, Britain and the US in 2021, aims to equip Australia with two types of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines: US-made Virginia-class boats and a newly developed Anglo-Australian class known as SSN Aukus. Febry Triantama, an international relations lecturer at Paramadina University in Indonesia, said Aukus carried strategic implications for Jakarta given its non-aligned, “free and active” approach to foreign policy. That balancing act could be unsettling Australia, which might be using Aukus to discourage Indonesia “from siding with China” in any possible future conflict, he suggested. A hypothetical conflict between China and Aukus would pose serious risks for Indonesia given the strategic value of its archipelagic sea lanes, which any combatant could exploit to move troops and weapons, Febry said. “If this happens, Indonesia is at high risk of being dragged into the conflict or becoming a target of foreign military reconnaissance activities,” he said. Foreign underwater drones have been discovered in Indonesian waters – most recently in April, when a fisherman found a 12-foot (3.7-metre) cylindrical drone in the Lombok Strait between Lombok and Bali bearing the logo of China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation. “Indonesia’s seabed warfare capabilities must be maximised immediately,” Febry added. To reinforce February’s security pact with Australia, Febry suggested strengthening confidence-building measures through “Track 1.5 diplomacy” – informal dialogue bringing together officials and independent researchers – to discuss sensitive issues including Aukus, maritime security and threat perceptions, and thereby “erode remaining suspicions and bridge the strategic understanding of both parties”. Rahman recalled that when Aukus was first announced in 2021, Indonesia’s defence establishment “then perceived Australia’s defence engagement as superficial and insincere”, a perception Canberra had since worked to change. Anxiety was likewise stirred in Australia last year when reports emerged of Russia seeking access to an Indonesian airbase, prompting Jakarta’s defence minister to publicly state that Russian military aircraft would not be permitted to operate from Indonesian territory. Even so, Indonesia continues to hold joint drills with both Russia and China, alongside equipment-manufacturing plans and technology sharing. “Canberra must understand that as part of Jakarta’s strategic culture,” Rahman said, adding: “Indonesia is always part of Canberra’s security calculus.”

title: Editorial | China must enforce high standards of integrity for scientists
description: Beijing’s ambitions for scientific leadership require not just investment but trust from the international community and the Chinese public.
content: China today is a pre-eminent technological powerhouse. Over multiple generations, Beijing has marshalled enormous resources to build one of the world’s largest pools of research talent. Under President Xi Jinping, Beijing has doubled down, with the 15th five-year plan projecting research and development spending to grow by at least 7 per cent annually. Yet quantity alone cannot secure scientific leadership. The nation’s future depends equally on quality. That demands an unwavering commitment to scientific integrity. The latest misconduct revelations underscore this imperative. The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) published details late last month about 31 new misconduct cases at universities and hospitals across China, involving more than 40 researchers - its largest such public disclosure to date. Among them were four prominent professors publicly named in April by a whistle-blowing blogger. All four had been recognised by the National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars, an honour that typically serves as a stepping stone to scientific elite membership in China. Three had served as deans or associate deans. The foundation revoked their funding and titles, ordered them to return more than 10 million yuan (US$1.49 million) in grants, and barred them from reapplying for three to seven years – effectively ending their academic careers. Collectively, the misconduct cases point to systemic failures. According to a recent study, slightly more than half (52.8 per cent) of 579 Chinese universities maintained academic integrity web pages, and only 16.8 per cent released annual research integrity reports, as required by the Ministry of Education. This institutional neglect has created a permissive environment where misconduct is frequently left unchecked. “Student Geng”, a former biomedical PhD student at Beihang University, has emerged as China’s most prominent online whistle-blower on academic misconduct. His full-time vlogging has uncovered duplicated images and questionable data in papers authored by credentialed researchers. With 3 million followers, he enjoys a visibility beyond most other whistle-blowers. His exposés have galvanised often sluggish institutions into investigating prominent scientists. That it takes an outsider wielding statistical tools and public pressure to enforce standards shows the inadequacy of oversight mechanisms. The structural drivers of misconduct are well understood. China’s research evaluation system emphasises publication counts, journal rankings and grant acquisition when determining promotion. This creates intense pressure to produce results or use short cuts. The rapid expansion of research funding compounds the problem. In 2023, the NSFC received 318,000 proposals from 2,404 host institutions and approved 52,500 awards with funding of 31.9 billion yuan. As volume grows, so must vigilance. Xi has rightly demanded stricter standards to tackle misconduct and foster a clean research ecosystem. But that needs to translate into action. The foundation’s August disclosure shows progress, yet many of Student Geng’s allegations have yet to draw responses from universities or the foundation. Incomplete accountability breeds cynicism. What is needed is zero tolerance. Universities must maintain functioning integrity offices and publish annual reports, as regulations already mandate. Penalties must carry real consequences – not just funding suspensions. Evaluation criteria should shift from publication quantity towards research originality and reproducibility. And whistle-blowers deserve more legal protection and institutional channels. The stakes could not be higher. China’s ambitions for scientific leadership require not just investment but trust from the international community, collaborators and the Chinese public. A nation’s research prowess is only as good as the integrity of its researchers. China’s house of science must rigorously enforce high standards. Anything less risks squandering decades of valuable national investment and the aspirations of millions of honest researchers who deserve better.

title: The inspiring story of Hong Kong dancer and filmmaker who began at 48 after leaving Apple
description: Patsy Lo talks about making her latest dance film in Patagonia, being struck down by illness, and why she left Apple to pivot to dancing.
content: Patsy Lo has just flown into Hong Kong from Tokyo, where she is now based, and the humidity is doing what humidity does. It is a far cry from Patagonia, where just months ago, Lo and a small arts team from Asia spent days hiking in punishing conditions to shoot Anamnesis II. The 10-minute experimental dance film blends contemporary movement with the raw, unforgiving beauty of the Patagonian Steppe shared by Argentina and Chile. Shot in the shadow of Mount Fitz Roy, the film is the second instalment in Lo’s Anamnesis series – a Greek-derived word meaning “recollection” or “remembrance” – and explores how memory is written into the body through exhaustion, intimacy and sustained movement. But to understand the film, one must first understand the journey that brought Lo there. Before committing to an artist’s life, hers was anything but. Now 57, Lo had the textbook zero-to-hero story: growing up in a 500 sq ft (46 square metre) flat in Hong Kong’s Mong Kok district shared with five family members, she pushed through school and climbed the corporate ladder until she landed her dream job at Apple. But that dream came at a cost. In her early forties, while working for the company in Beijing, she developed shingles. What followed was a spiral: she saw countless doctors and was prescribed a flurry of sedatives and antidepressants alongside medication for her physical symptoms, all of which she refused to take for fear of becoming dependent on them. Eventually, she grew so unwell that she could not wear clothes, leave her bed or eat without throwing up. From illness to health – and dance One night, desperate and exhausted, she prayed. “I said, ‘OK, God. All my life, I’ve worked really hard and chased what success meant to me. I will take these pills. If it means that I am turning into someone dependent on drugs to find balance, I accept this life.’ Because I’d done my best, and it didn’t seem to work.” Lo recovered two months later, aided by acupuncture and natural therapy. She stayed at Apple for another three years, working in Singapore and California, before finally walking away in 2018. What followed was an unexpected pivot: she moved to Paris and enrolled in the Paris Marais Dance School, training 20 hours a week at 48. “It was because I saw Cirque du Soleil in Macau,” she recalls. “It wasn’t the acrobats or performers doing crazy things that moved me. It was this boy rocking back and forth to the side of the stage. Anyone could do that, but he did it in a way that was so present. You could tell there was no noise in his head. And I thought, ‘I want that. Give me that.’ “In Europe, people say you don’t have to have technical skills to dance if you have something to say with your body. You can lie there and still call it dance.” Lo’s dance journey began with no prior experience, and the early years were gruelling. She was not flexible, struggled with turns and constantly compared herself to classmates who had trained since childhood. She had to learn how to stop judging every step. “Two years ago, I finally felt I could dance,” she says. Not long after, she founded her own performance arts company, SML Dance. Filming Anamnesis II Her first trip to Patagonia came four years ago, and everything changed for Lo again. She was struck by the honesty of the landscape – the unrelenting wind, the ancient mountains, the impossibility of control. “There was a moment when I was pinned against the wall of a cliff and couldn’t move,” Lo says. “There was nothing I could do except wait. But those moments were so peaceful. My brain wasn’t spinning. I wasn’t worrying about the future or regretting the past. I was just there.” That peace became the foundation for her art. “Nature is honest,” she says. “It doesn’t lie. And I wanted to capture that.” Anamnesis II was financed by Lo and shot with a team of six: director Takuya Setomitsu, co-choreographer Yuh Egami of Hong Kong Ballet, dance artist Hiroki Ichinose, visual artist Shi Shimu, casting and logistics lead Miki Sato, and Lo. Professional Patagonian mountain guide Facundo Jios shepherded the expedition, drawing on his experience of climbing to the summit of Fitz Roy and other peaks in the region. The result is a film that Lo describes as a “quiet opening” – an invitation to experience the vulnerability and awe she found in Patagonia. It premiered across the Upper House hotel group’s properties in Hong Kong, Shanghai and Chengdu this month, with behind-the-scenes footage and intimate conversations with the creative team. It follows her first Anamnesis film, shot on Japan’s Sado Island in 2025, which blended traditional Japanese Noh theatre with contemporary dance. More instalments are planned, including one in Kyushu and another focused on femininity. “Art is very personal,” Lo says. “I did it for me.” Anamnesis II will be released on YouTube and Instagram later in 2026, alongside a small number of curated in-person screenings in Hong Kong and beyond.

title: Meet Gary Oldman’s wife, Gisele Schmidt, who hit the Emmys red carpet with the Slow Horses star
description: Schmidt served as Oldman’s assistant on Darkest Hour, where the Oscar-winning actor proposed in a full Winston Churchill costume.
content: The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards ceremony was held on September 14, and the internet is still buzzing over television’s biggest night. Gary Oldman brought extra sparkle to the red carpet, stepping out for the glamorous evening alongside his wife, Gisele Schmidt. The Slow Horses actor, 68, was nominated for Outstanding Lead Actor in a Drama Series but lost to Noah Wyle for The Pitt. This was one of four losses for Slow Horses, which was nominated for five Primetime Emmys. Saul Metzstein won Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series for Season 5’s episode, Scars. The show also received four nominations for the Primetime Creative Arts Emmy, which honours technical crafts including editing and sound mixing, but did not win. Nevertheless, Oldman looked triumphant when he attended the Apple TV Emmy Awards Celebration at NYA Studios with Schmidt. Two days later, Season 6 of Slow Horses premiered on Apple TV. So, what do we know about Gisele Schmidt? Read on to find out. She is Gary Oldman’s 5th wife Oldman and Schmidt met at a gallery where she worked while the actor was hunting for a Richard Miller photograph of Elizabeth Taylor and James Dean, according to an article the couple wrote for Hollywood Authentic. They married in August 2017 at the Beverly Hills home of Oldman’s manager, Douglas Urbanski, in front of close friends, per AP. Oldman was married four times before his wedding to Schmidt. He wed Lesley Manville in 1987, welcoming their son, Alfie, the following year before the couple split in 1990. That same year, he married Uma Thurman, divorcing in 1992. He later married Donya Fiorentino in 1997, with whom he has sons Gulliver and Charlie, before they parted ways in 2001. Oldman then married Alexandra Edenborough in 2008, divorcing in 2015. Schmidt has a son named William from a previous relationship, per the LA Times. In a recent interview with the outlet, Oldman shared that he felt “happier than [he’s] ever been”, thanks to his wife. “I’m with someone who gets me and understands what I do,” he said, while Schmidt added, “I might be the fifth one, but I am the one.” What does Gisele Schmidt do for work? The LA Times described Schmidt as an art curator, writer and photographer. Hollywood Authentic said Oldman encouraged her to take up photography. She also executive-produced Lauren Vance’s documentary short The Carnival of Dreams (2016) starring her husband. She was on the set of Darkest Hour Schmidt served as Oldman’s assistant on Darkest Hour (2017), with Oscar-winning special make-up effects artist Kazuhiro Tsuji describing her as a “key person” on the actor’s team. It was on the set of the film – while Oldman was in full Winston Churchill costume – that he proposed. Years later, Schmidt suggested showing the scarred foot of Oldman’s character, Jackson Lamb, in the Season 5 finale of Slow Horses, entertainment news site TheWrap reported.

title: In Focus | Analysts tip a stronger hand for China ahead of Xi-Trump summit in Washington
description: Chinese confidence could be boosted by US push to make progress on its war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, experts say.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the second part of a series, Fan Chen looks at Beijing’s stronger position going into the high-stakes visit. Beijing is poised to begin this week’s summit with Washington from a position of strength, bolstered by a flurry of recent diplomatic outreach. Chinese confidence could be further reinforced by the United States’ latest push to make headway on conflicts in Ukraine and Iran – wars that observers say Washington may need Beijing’s cooperation to help resolve – even if a near-term truce remains unlikely. Just weeks before his Washington trip, Chinese President Xi Jinping embarked on one of his most intense overseas itineraries, paying a state visit to Egypt after wrapping up the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. Xi also attended the Brics summit in New Delhi last weekend, marking his first trip to India in seven years. In his address, the Chinese president took a veiled swipe at US policies and urged the bloc’s members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence. Through a joint declaration, the two-day summit also forged a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” policies – all without naming Washington. Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University in Shanghai, noted that Beijing’s diplomatic blitz strengthened its hand ahead of the second US-China summit of the year. “Xi’s visit to Egypt – a major Middle Eastern power – underscores China’s rising influence in the region,” he said. “As Washington is currently entangled in conflict with Iran, this serves as a reminder to the US that it cannot overlook China’s regional clout when managing its bilateral ties with Beijing.” Amid escalating conflicts in the Middle East, Xi used his first Cairo visit in a decade to urge the countries of the region to build a self-led security model and “take charge of their own future”. Observers noted that the approach nudged the countries in the region away from Washington, without committing Beijing to a role as a replacement security guarantor. US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that Xi would visit on September 24 and that they would have “a lot of good things to discuss”. Beijing has yet to confirm the trip, in line with its practice of leaving official travel announcements to the last minute. Wu added that Beijing’s diplomatic whirlwind highlighted its focus on Asia and the Global South, showing its expanding reach as a global power and standing in sharp contrast to a US administration that has alienated traditional allies. His view was echoed by Ali Wyne, International Crisis Group’s senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations. As Trump undermined US alliances, Xi was building “China’s portfolio of transactional alignments”, Wyne said, although he added that Beijing was “unlikely to establish a coherent counterbalancing coalition”. “Still, the Trump administration’s foreign policy enables Beijing to present itself as a more stabilising force than Washington.” According to Wyne, while Xi would avoid upstaging or upbraiding his counterpart, he might enter the Washington summit far more confident than in May, buoyed by Trump prioritising their relationship over allegations of Chinese election interference and support for Iran. Patricia Kim, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Brookings Institution, said Xi’s multiple tours showed that China had other important relationships and diplomatic options. They aimed to portray Beijing as “increasingly central to a more multipolar international order”, she said. “The message Xi wants to project is that Beijing can engage Washington without making the US the centrepiece of its foreign policy.” In Bishkek, Xi praised the SCO approach of peaceful coexistence “without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”, taking a veiled swipe at the US military alliance system. Bloc leaders – representing Central Asian states, Iran, Russia, Pakistan, India and Belarus – condemned military strikes on Iran as international law violations and backed Tehran’s right to a peaceful nuclear programme, directly countering US demands for total nuclear abandonment. Meanwhile, pressed by November’s midterm elections and the approaching summit with Beijing, Washington has also stepped up efforts to resolve the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran. Following a phone call on Tuesday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said, though not for the first time, that he thought his Russian counterpart wanted to make a deal to end the war in Ukraine. The call came after US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks with Putin on Saturday. Both sides have signalled optimism and that plans for next steps could be expected soon. Witkoff and Kushner travelled to Kyiv on Sunday for talks aimed at resuming Russia-Ukraine negotiations – their first visit to the Ukrainian capital after numerous trips to Moscow since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. While no breakthrough was announced, Witkoff said he was “confident there would be a good resolution”. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukrainian, European and US officials would meet to continue talks, while reiterating his call for a trilateral meeting involving Russia and the US. Zelensky also said he expected the war with Russia to continue into the winter. On Wednesday, Trump addressed the Middle Eastern front where the US has been deeply embroiled since February. The war with Iran would end immediately after the midterms, he said, and hinted that negotiations “could possibly happen”. Surging oil prices and broader inflation from the US-Israel war in Iran have plunged Trump’s approval ratings to new lows, stoking Republican fears of what the midterms may bring. Though neither conflict has a clear end in sight, analysts say that Washington might need China’s cooperation to resolve them, giving Beijing a stronger hand ahead of the Xi-Trump talks. According to Zhu Junwei, director of Chinese think tank Horizon Insights, Trump – unable to resolve the conflict in Iran – is pursuing alternative wins in North Korea and Ukraine to project a “can’t stop winning” narrative in a bid to distract voters and boost his political prospects. “None of these crises can be resolved quickly. If Trump wants quick, tangible wins to boost his midterm prospects, he is likely to need China’s help,” she said. “Even if he approaches this by applying pressure, it fundamentally comes down to needing Beijing’s cooperation.” Trump has repeatedly signalled a desire to revive personal diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, saying he expected to meet him later this year after scaling back last month’s US-South Korea military drill, widely seen as a conciliatory gesture. On Thursday, the South China Morning Post reported exclusively that China was willing to broker a leaders’ meeting between Pyongyang and Washington and would support all credible efforts leading to resumed dialogue. Zhu also noted that calming the Ukraine and Middle East conflicts – even if impossible overnight – “ultimately benefits Beijing, regardless of its impact on US-China rivalry, as it significantly improves China’s external environment and creates new opportunities”. Sun Yun, director of the China programme at US think tank the Stimson Centre, echoed this view, saying that China could help the US resolve both conflicts and describing Beijing’s role as a potential bargaining chip in broader US-China talks. However, both Sun and Wyne of the International Crisis Group noted that Beijing was not the main driver behind Trump’s pre-summit rush to resolve both conflicts. “While the Trump administration would indeed have more diplomatic bandwidth were it to freeze the Russia-Ukraine war and reach a fresh ceasefire with Iran, it has not prioritised China policy nearly as much as many observers had anticipated when Trump retook office,” Wyne said. Even though Putin might view Trump as a more favourable interlocutor than his predecessor Joe Biden, Moscow “is unlikely to weaken its relationship” with China for a fragile US truce under Trump, knowing American leadership was likely to revert to a hostile stance towards Moscow, he added. Even without major deliverables, the summit could still prove useful if it maintained a cordial rapport between the leaders and sustained a “tactical thaw”, Wyne stressed. According to Kim from Brookings, the leaders’ meeting was “unlikely to produce a significantly expanded bilateral agenda or result in a fundamental reset” of ties. Instead, the focus remained on extending the trade detente and sustaining leader-level diplomacy as the main buffer against further deterioration, she said. Zhu noted that while Trump aimed to stabilise ties with China, an overall hawkish US bipartisan consensus meant there was “still a long way to go” towards achieving “constructive strategic stability” – the framework introduced at the Beijing summit in May. “A single summit cannot resolve every issue; if this meeting yields partial economic and trade agreements and temporarily manages differences, it should be viewed as a success.”

title: Opinion | What China really means when it says it’s being ‘strategic’
description: Rather than geopolitical manoeuvring or calculation, this diplomatic label aims to convey seriousness, patience and a willingness to work for mutual long-term benefit.
content: On September 12, Chinese President Xi Jinping met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Brics summit in New Delhi. In their talks, Xi said China approached the relationship “from a strategic and long-term perspective”. He called for an objective and rational “strategic” perception. That means the two sides should treat each other as partners rather than rivals, and as opportunities rather than threats. In Chinese official and diplomatic language, the term “strategic” is routinely used to denote matters of high importance, long-term significance and central weight in the nation’s interests and development. When China defines a bilateral relationship as “strategic”, it signals that the relationship is viewed from a high level, beyond immediate disputes or short-term calculations. It implies a willingness to invest sustained political attention and effort, and a belief that the engagement can generate mutual benefits and positive externalities for the wider region or the world. China’s partnership diplomacy is organised in a clear ladder. At the basic level are ordinary “strategic partnerships”. Higher up are “comprehensive strategic partnerships”, which China has established with a wide range of countries including Brazil, France, Indonesia, Egypt and Saudi Arabia. Still higher tiers include “comprehensive strategic cooperative partnerships” with some countries and the special formulation of “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership” with Pakistan. A “comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era” is uniquely set with Russia. Contrary to the common perception that the term “strategic” in these partnership labels primarily signals military or security-related importance, this usage is typically intended to convey goodwill and a commitment to long-term cooperation, rather than a tactical, opportunistic or merely convenient partnership. The same logic applies in domestic and diplomatic discourse. Labelling something as “strategic” elevates it above routine or tactical matters, underscoring that it has been carefully considered at the highest level and is intended to shape the country’s direction over an extended horizon. Clearly, the phrase is never about clever tactics or indirect manoeuvring. But here is where problems might arise. In English, the word “strategic” frequently implies calculated action – manoeuvring to achieve goals that cannot be reached by straightforward means. When people say someone is “being strategic”, the phrase often carries an undertone of foxiness or calculated deception, suggesting clever positioning, hidden motives or the manipulation of appearances to gain an advantage. In discussions of “war strategies”, the term commonly evokes cunning, misdirection and the art of outmanoeuvring an opponent rather than confronting them openly. Indeed, Sun Tzu’s The Art of War is frequently read as a treatise devoted almost entirely to strategies of deception and psychological manipulation, even though the text also addresses broader questions of preparation, timing and the avoidance of unnecessary conflict. In political science, “strategic voting” refers to deliberately supporting a second-preference candidate to prevent a worse outcome. In bilateral relations, “strategic ambiguity” means intentionally keeping one’s position unclear to preserve flexibility or deter others. In these contexts, the word suggests shrewd calculation, positioning and the smart use of means rather than open-ended commitment or goodwill. Therefore, when Chinese leaders describe a relationship or decision as “strategic”, English-speaking audiences may subconsciously hear this second shade of meaning. What is intended in Chinese diplomatic language as an expression of seriousness, patience and mutual long-term benefit can be received as evidence of geopolitical manoeuvring. Chinese authorities are aware of the potential misunderstanding that the terms “strategic” or “strategy” can generate. Several years ago, the government officially required state media, think tanks and academics not to translate or refer to the belt and road plan as a “strategy”. It chose the term “initiative” instead, presumably to project a softer, more inclusive image and to avoid the impression of “outsmarting” counterparts that the word “strategy” might convey. Yet despite this caution in specific cases, Chinese official and diplomatic discourse continues to place heavy weight on the word “strategic” or “strategy” as a way of conveying importance, centrality, goodwill and long-term commitment and devotion. The cultural and linguistic gap remains serious. How, then, might China address this gap? A simple approach is to pair the term with clearer, more transparent phrasing that helps reduce ambiguity. Formulations such as “a long-term and constructive approach”, “a serious and sustained commitment to mutual benefit”, or “viewing the relationship through the lens of long-term shared interests” will help reduce misunderstanding among English-language audiences. When the term “strategic” is still used, it should be briefly defined in the same context. A short clarification – that it denotes a willingness to invest sustained effort, manage differences with patience, and pursue outcomes that benefit both sides over the long term – can help anchor the audience’s understanding. Emphasis in public messaging can also usefully shift towards sincerity, mutuality and concrete shared benefits, rather than relying on the term “strategic” to convey these meanings. Using clearer language is likely to communicate the intended goodwill and long-term commitment more effectively.

title: Houthis claim attacks on Saudi capital, after flames seen near Riyadh airport
description: The militants say they targeted ‘sensitive’ sites, along with an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu.
content: Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh on Saturday with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city’s main airport. Saudi Arabia had sent alerts overnight warning of potential danger around Riyadh, amid an escalation in attacks by the Houthis in the kingdom. Reuters video and photographs ‌showed a huge pillar of black smoke rising in the area, with the airport highway, main terminal building and other facilities in the foreground. At one point in the video, flames were visible rising from behind what appeared to be fuel tanks. While the Iranian-backed Houthis have launched repeated attacks against Saudi Arabia since July, Saturday’s claim appeared to be their first reported strike on Riyadh since the current escalation began. The Houthis did not specify what they had targeted in Riyadh, but said they had also attacked an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil export hub. The Houthis said the operation came as a response to an attack in the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group towards Riyadh early on Saturday. In a statement, the coalition also said it had foiled attacks targeting civilians in the Saudi cities of Bish and Farasan in the southwest and Taif ⁠in the west, as well as Yanbu on the Red Sea coast. It did not say whether there was any damage. Saudi civil defence sent the alerts by phone overnight for potential ‌danger of aerial attacks in Riyadh and the city of Al-Kharj east of the capital, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning. A Reuters journalist in Riyadh’s Olaya area heard booms before the all-clear was sent. Although some alerts had been issued in Riyadh this ‌year after the start of the US-Iran war, these were the first since the escalation with the Houthis began in July. A US State Department security alert issued on Saturday for Americans in the Middle East cited Houthi attacks. The State Department urged US citizens in the ‌region to “exercise heightened vigilance” and that Americans outside the Middle East “should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region”. The Houthis, who ⁠control the most populous parts of ⁠Yemen and much of the north, have been launching attacks against Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, with strikes targeting Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. The attacks have targeted Saudi ‌cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, creating new threats to global oil supplies and putting at risk the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains blockaded. On Friday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya ‌Saree said ‌the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” in the Yemeni capital Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The Iran-aligned group, which seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast in ‌a lightning advance this month, says the Saudi Air Force has conducted hundreds of air strikes against it in recent days. The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as ⁠a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme ⁠National Security Council, told Al Jazeera in an interview aired on Saturday that Tehran wanted the war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to end, adding that he believed Yemenis also wanted a settlement with Saudi Arabia. Rezaei also said Iran had conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in stalled negotiations ‌with the US, including “ending the war on ‌all fronts”. Consultations were continuing with Qatari and Pakistani mediators and Tehran was awaiting a response from US President Donald Trump, Rezaei said. The UN Security Council in a statement on Friday “condemned in the strongest terms continued Houthi attacks against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including attacks impacting civilian and energy infrastructure, which have resulted in the injury of civilians, including women and children”. In the statement, the Security Council also condemned “Houthi military escalation in Yemen”.

title: Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’, name AI tsar
description: ‘We will not in any way hinder or stifle’ the growth of the industry, the US president insisted.
content: US President Donald Trump ⁠said in a social media post ⁠on Saturday that he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as an “AI tsar”, and create an “AI force”, though he did not provide details about either initiative or how they would be implemented. Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed ‌by AI technology on humans and property. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary. “We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said on social media. “Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it ‌grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.” If Trump follows through ‌on the pledge, it would be his second AI tsar. Venture capitalist David Sacks ⁠previously served in the role ⁠before stepping down in the spring and moving into an external advisory position. Sacks has echoed Trump’s scepticism of new AI regulation. Speaking ‌at a Politico event on Wednesday, he said AI developers should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products and could be ‌held ‌liable if problems arise, adding that new federal rules are unnecessary. The White House did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment on Trump’s post. Trump’s post comes ahead of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President ⁠Xi Jinping on Thursday. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in artificial intelligence, which both governments view ⁠as vital to their economic and military strength. Trump and technology executives have argued that excessive regulation would slow US AI development and undermine American companies’ ability to compete with Chinese ‌rivals, a claim that safety advocates ‌often refute. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York to discuss AI security, trade and other economic issues, a person familiar with the planning said on Saturday.

title: White House bars CNN, MS Now and Politico reporters after Trump ban
description: All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were ‌confiscated on Saturday morning.
content: The White House on Saturday denied access to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump’s announcement that he would ban them from the building’s grounds. All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were ‌confiscated on Saturday morning when their journalists went to the White House. They have signalled that they may contest the ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press. A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban “an illegal assault” on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS Now and Politico said they ⁠would “defend our First Amendment rights”. MS Now said it intends to “take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment ‌rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy”. CNN and MS Now said they would continue reporting on the Trump administration, and Politico said it stands by ‌its reporters covering the White House. A social media post by Trump on Friday accused the outlets of “reporting ⁠FAKE NEWS” and said ⁠that they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”. He added: “Other Fake ‌News Media Outlets to follow.” Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Trump answered a question about what he meant by other outlets ‌by describing The New York Times and The Washington Post as examples of “fake news”, although he did not specifically say he would ‌ban them from the White House. The New York Times in a statement called Trump’s latest ban “yet another ⁠retaliatory and unconstitutional threat” and said the newspaper “stands in support of the news organisations being unfairly targeted by the president”. The Washington Post ⁠in a statement on Saturday said its access to the White House was a “non-negotiable constitutional right” and called the president’s actions “a ⁠clear form of intimidation meant to silence coverage”. Trump ⁠previously has tried to keep certain news outlets or specific journalists out of press gatherings. Last year he banned Associated Press from the pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news ‌agency did not adopt Trump’s preferred ‌name for the Gulf of Mexico after the president instructed the executive branch to call it the Gulf of America. AP has challenged the ban. In his first term, Trump’s White House sought to revoke or suspend the credentials of Playboy correspondent Brian Karem and CNN’s Jim Acosta, but federal judges ordered their White House press passes restored.

title: Hong Kong’s political, business elite pay final respects to Tung Chee-hwa
description: Beijing leaders send wreaths ahead of former chief executive’s state funeral as residents stream into community centres to sign condolence books.
content: Hong Kong’s political and business elite bade a solemn farewell to Tung Chee-hwa, the city’s first chief executive, at a vigil on Saturday, as Beijing leaders sent wreaths ahead of his state funeral and members of the public streamed into community centres to sign condolence books. Hundreds of wreaths lined the pavement at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point, spilling into a nearby playground, while inside the hall the mood was hushed as top officials, former politicians and business chiefs filed in to pay their respects at the invitation-only vigil. The hall was decorated with white orchids and pine trees, with wreaths from Tung’s widow, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, and their three children placed in front of the altar. She did not attend the vigil, the South China Morning Post learned. One attendee said the ceremony followed the format of a typical local vigil. A master of ceremonies invited visitors to pay their respects and bow to Tung at the altar before they turned to his family to offer their condolences and receive their thanks. “The mood is solemn and very quiet. Many visitors stay for about half an hour before leaving,” the attendee said, adding that some of Tung’s close friends were allowed into a room to view his body. Tung, who died on September 8 at the age of 89, led Hong Kong during a pivotal era following the city’s return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, with his tenure defined by the Asian financial crisis in 1998, the Sars epidemic in 2003, early efforts to enact domestic national security legislation, a post-Sars V-shape rebound in the economy, and more. At the entrance of the hall was a banner reading “Tung family funeral” framed by white chrysanthemums. Inside, a portrait of Tung was displayed, showing him smiling. Former and current Beijing officials sent wreaths, including tributes from vice-premiers He Lifeng and Liu Guozhong, Central Committee Publicity Department head Li Shulei, Politburo member Chen Miner and Communist Party secretary of Guangdong, Huang Kunming. Politburo member Shi Taifeng, the top vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), who heads Tung’s funeral committee, also sent wreaths, as did former premier Wen Jiabao, former National People’s Congress Standing Committee chairman Li Zhanshu and Jia Qinglin, the former chairman of the National Committee of the CPPCC. Among the first officials to arrive was Zhou Ji, director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong, at around 2.30pm. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu came after 3pm – the official start time – and spoke briefly to Tung’s son, Andrew Tung Lieh-cheung. Three former chief executives – Leung Chun-ying, Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor and Donald Tsang Yam-kuen – paid tribute with family members and left together. Key figures from Tung’s cabinet – former chief secretary Anson Chan Fang On-sang, former financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung and former justice secretary Elsie Leung Oi-sie – also visited. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po and deputy finance chief Michael Wong Wai-lun also attended. Other political heavyweights paying their respects included Rita Fan Hsu Lai-tai, the first Legislative Council president after the handover, Tam Yiu-chung, formerly the city’s sole delegate to the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, and Macau’s first chief executive, Edmund Ho Hau-wah. “He was truly dedicated and gave his all to Hong Kong. It was particularly difficult during the handover period, combined with the Asian financial crisis in 1998,” Tam said. “He faced many challenges during his tenure, but he was able to lead us in overcoming every difficulty. He was a good-natured person with deep patriotic feelings who made immense contributions to both our country and Hong Kong.” Property tycoons turned out in force. Raymond Kwok Ping-luen of Sun Hung Kai Properties and his brother Thomas Kwok Ping-kwong arrived together at the funeral parlour. Henry Cheng Kar-shun, chairman of property developer New World Development, attended with his daughter, Sonia Cheng Chi-man, CEO of Rosewood Hotel Group. Gordon Wu Ying-sheung, chairman of property developer Hopewell Holdings, and Adriel Chan, chairman of Hang Lung Group and Hang Lung Properties, also paid their respects. Among the early arrivals were the Li family of the Bank of East Asia dynasty – Arthur Li Kwok-cheung, David Li Kwok-po and David Li’s son, Brian David Li Man-bun. Also paying tribute were CLP Holdings chairman Michael Kadoorie and Solina Chau Hoi-shuen, a director of the Li Ka Shing Foundation. Top Hong Kong Jockey Club officials also paid their respects. Chief executive Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges, chairman Martin Liao Cheung-kong, and deputy chairman Lester Huang attended together. Local residents paid tributes at several community centres. At the Moreton Terrace Activities Centre in Causeway Bay, retiree Anbie Tsang, 70, said Tung’s death was a great loss for Hong Kong. “I feel so sad. He is like a father to me,” said Tsang, who paid his respects with his wife. “He had a great vision for Hong Kong, and he has done so much for the city.” Retired Catholic leader Cardinal Joseph Zen Ze-kiun also visited the centre. Members of the public can also visit the Kai Tak Community Hall or Sai Lau Kok Garden in Tsuen Wan to sign the condolence book until noon on Sunday. A memorial service for Tung will be held from 9am to 11am on Sunday, followed by a funeral procession. He will be cremated at Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan, the South China Morning Post learned.

title: Denmark cautiously optimistic over Trump’s Greenland deal
description: The Arctic island’s leaders have echoed that, saying the security agreement, which maintains Danish control, was long in coming.
content: Denmark’s government was cautiously optimistic on Saturday following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal on Greenland to bolster US military presence there but keep the island under Danish control after months of threats by the US president to seize the semi-autonomous territory of a Nato ally. The Arctic island’s top leaders echoed that stance and said the deal, which has not yet been made public, was long in coming. US, Greenlandic and Danish officials had quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the territory of roughly 56,000 residents. With the announcement of the pact, Trump is able to tout a foreign policy achievement ahead of the midterm elections in the United States. Trump said on Friday that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns”. Denmark and the US already have a long-standing security agreement that allows the US to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal would be different from that. “I think it’s obvious that we can expect more bases in Greenland. But it’s important to say that if we look in the past, especially during the Cold War, the US had immense military presence in Greenland,” said Marc Jacobsen, an associate professor at the Royal Danish Defence College and the head of research at the Centre for Arctic Security Studies. He said it was a win for Trump. “It’s important for him to show that he’s a good businessman, that he kind of forced the pressure on Denmark and Greenland into something new.” A period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic – and thus also our shared security within Nato and Europe Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen After Trump’s announcement, the office of Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal will be signed next week at the United Nations General Assembly. Parliamentary action was still needed by the Danish and Greenlandic governments before it can be enforced, she added. “Next week could be a good week … for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States alike,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen wrote on Instagram on Saturday. “A period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic – and thus also our shared security within Nato and Europe,” he added. Greenland’s government leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal would benefit “not only our collective security, but also the continued development here in the country”. The island’s foreign minister, Múte B. Egede, was “pleased that we finally have an end product within reach”, he told Denmark’s TV2 broadcaster. “It’s about time.” Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the Nato Military Committee, said later on Saturday in Copenhagen, the Danish capital, that the agreement was “very, very welcome”. Speaking after a meeting of Nato countries’ chiefs of defence, he said that from a military perspective the alliance is “taking great care” of the area and that “attention toward the north is one of our top priorities because we want to keep that area under control”. Trump said that with the agreement, the US would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory. The US held several bases and installations on Greenland through the Cold War, before dialling back its presence. It still operates the remote Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, built after the US and Denmark signed the Defence of Greenland Treaty in 1951. The base supports missile warning, missile defence and space surveillance operations for the US and Nato. A US State Department official said the agreement bans any non-Nato base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland, and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base on the island. The official was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. Denmark and Greenland did not explicitly confirm any of the specifics in Trump’s statements, nor did they provide more details. After his return to the White House, Trump had called on Denmark to sell the island to the US, while insisting Greenland is crucial for US security. He pointedly would not rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a Nato ally of the US. Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. The US push for Greenland was also fiercely opposed by Russia and much of Europe. Greenland grassroots pro-sovereignty activist Orla Joelsen wrote on X that “our fight against Trump’s ambition to take over Greenland has been won”. He (Trump) obviously didn’t get in this agreement what he originally set out to have, that is sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher and Arctic security expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies “The new agreement explicitly recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination,” the activist added. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher and Arctic security expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said that Trump has tried to sell the situation as a win. “He obviously didn’t get in this agreement what he originally set out to have, that is sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States.” In Denmark, many expressed relief that a deal with the US seemed close. Michael Burgaard from Gentofte, north of Copenhagen, was hopeful the crisis was over “because just a fortnight ago, Donald Trump posted this map showing Greenland … as part of the US”. “We were kind of worried that he would take all of Greenland by force,” added the 56-year-old telecommunications worker. “So the fact that we can settle this in a diplomatic way … I think it’s good.” Michael Frees, a 51-year-old teacher in Copenhagen, said he thinks the agreement is “the most realistic solution for us right now”. “We are a small nation and of course we have to cooperate with bigger countries and also the European Union,” he said. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Is China’s fabled Empress Dowager Huayang buried near an airport? A study says yes
description: Researchers say a looted tomb near Xian’s main runway belongs to the adoptive grandmother of the country’s first emperor.
content: An airport is an unlikely place to search for national origins but researchers say they have uncovered the tomb of the woman behind the man who unified China – next to a major city runway. The researchers said the tomb was believed to belong to Empress Dowager Huayang, the adoptive grandmother of Qin Shi Huang, who unified the warring states more than 2,200 years ago. “I believe the most likely identity of the tomb owner is Empress Dowager Huayang,” Zhao Hanqing, from the Shaanxi Provincial Institute of Archaeology, said in a paper published in the Chinese journal Archaeology and Cultural Relics in July. Huayang was central to Qin Shi Huang’s rise. She was the wife of a Qin prince but, with no sons, she adopted his father, Ying Yiren, an impoverished hostage prince from a rival state. Her husband became King Xiaowen but died after a brief reign, enabling Ying Yiren to become king. He was then succeeded by his son, Qin Shi Huang. The tomb was found in an area that had been set aside for the expansion of Xian Xianyang International Airport and although heavily looted, yielded a range of artefacts, including hundreds of pottery, bronze, iron, jade, agate and glass items. Announcing the results to the public on Friday, Zhao said that because of the severe looting, the tomb did not yield objects that could confirm the tomb owner’s identity or identifiable human remains. However, based on historical records and the burial system of the Qin state during the Warring States Period, archaeologists narrowed down the most likely owner of the tomb to an empress from that time. The theory was supported by radiocarbon dating of bones from the tomb, which yielded a range of 389-208 BC, or about 2,250 years ago. Archaeologists began surveying the site in 2018 and confirmed that it contained a large tomb with an independent cemetery. In 2022, they excavated the northern part of the cemetery and conducted additional surveys, clarifying its overall layout. The tomb was initially thought to belong to an emperor from the Northern Zhou era (557-581AD) but the researchers concluded that it was a royal tomb from the Qin state. Until Huayang’s era, Qin tradition dictated that a king be buried with his queen but King Xiaowen had two wives and discontinued this practice. He is buried 2.3km (1.4 miles) away from the airport tomb site in an area on the Xianyang Plain called Shouling. When Empress Dowager Huayang died in 230BC, she was described as having been buried alongside King Xiaowen in Shouling. But on Friday, Zhao said the historical references to a “combined burial” could suggest that the king and the queen were buried in two separate but nearby independent cemeteries. The burial system from this time was a turning point in the development of the Qin royal burial system. Its main features, including separate mausoleums for kings and queens, paved the way for the design of Qin Shi Huang’s tomb, now a World Cultural Heritage site.

title: Methanol-tainted Nigeria drink kills 48, 182 made ill: government
description: Fifteen people have been arrested in connection with the production and sale of a locally brewed beverage, say officials.
content: Nigeria’s food and drug regulator on Saturday said alcoholic concoctions tainted with methanol killed 48 people and sickened 182 in recent weeks. The deaths occurred in three districts of Nigeria’s southwestern Ondo state after victims consumed the locally brewed mixture, which local media said is known as “Monkey Tail”. Methanol is highly toxic and causes death by organ failure as well as blindness. The country’s National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) said five people had been made totally blind and two had partially lost their sight. The first cases of poisoning were reported earlier this month and the toll has gradually been rising.
