Authorities have arrested 15 people in connection with the production and sale of the drink, the agency said. Banji Ajaka, Ondo state’s commissioner for health, said the cases were reported in the Odigbo and Irele local government areas. “I took like two shots and I went out on Friday. On Saturday, I noticed that I could not see,” 32-year-old Sola Adebayo told a local television channel from a hospital bed. Drinking locally made alcohol is common in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, especially in rural areas where it is more affordable and poorly regulated. “This thing happened rapidly. Once they consume, depending on the quantity, the kidneys will pack up, the eyes will go, the brain will be damaged,” Ajaka said. NAFDAC said in a statement that after people bought and consumed locally prepared “alcoholic and herbal concoctions”, “48 deaths and 182 cases have been recorded”. Laboratory tests showed the presence of “high concentrations of methanol”, a deadly alcohol compound, and the indica strain of cannabis in samples of the suspected concoction, the agency said. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: In a first, top European design prize awarded to €20 uniform for China’s delivery drivers
description: Developed with the assistance of Jack Ma, designers aimed to bestow dignity on the drivers, an ‘important profession’, the lead designer says.
content: Taobao Instant Commerce, Alibaba’s on-demand delivery service that was revamped last year and is known as Taobao Shangou in Chinese, won a top French Design Award prize on Saturday for its delivery worker uniform, marking the first time the prize was awarded for a design for frontline workers. “We think the [Taobao Shangou] suit design would transform delivery workwear into a recognisable professional uniform, helping reshape how society sees this essential profession,” said Dario Olivero, chair of the award’s organising committee. For the team that designed the uniform, the idea started with a discussion they had last year with Jack Ma, the founder of Alibaba Group Holding, said Yang Tao, the lead designer of the city rider suits. “Delivery riders … have become an important profession in China. Chefs wear uniforms, flight attendants wear uniforms – so why wasn’t there a professional uniform designed specifically for riders?” Yang said while accepting the award. His design team for the uniform included no professional designers, featuring instead a restaurant owner and a former dancer. In the design process, they sought to combine style with practical concerns – selecting colours to ensure visibility of the riders in traffic and choosing fabric that could withstand both sweat and rain. “What we are proudest of is this: the uniform sells for just over 20 euros, and it outperforms outdoor clothing costing many times more,” he said, thanking Jack Ma, who he said was very involved in the design process, trying on the garments and testing the fabrics. Work conditions for the country’s roughly 200 million gig workers have gained greater exposure in China. Stronger labour protections in extreme weather, prompt and fair payment of wages and a more robust social security system were among the measures the State Council of China called for in a 12-point plan issued in April. The Taobao Shangou suits have been distributed free of charge to more than one million riders since August 2025. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

title: Somali piracy rise tests China’s long-running Gulf of Aden mission
description: Piracy off the waters of Somalia is at a decade high, testing Beijing’s role as other naval powers focus elsewhere.
content: For more than a decade, China has deployed warships to the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia. For much of that time, piracy in the region has been in sharp decline. Now, however, with attacks at their highest reported level since 2013 and other naval forces engaged in crises elsewhere, Beijing’s long-running escort mission is being tested. The renewed attacks and hijacking for ransom come as the US Navy focuses on operations connected to the war on Iran, and India sends ships towards the Strait of Hormuz to protect commercial shipping and energy supplies. The European Union’s Operation Atalanta, meanwhile, patrols a large area and has responsibilities beyond counter-piracy. “There is a palpable reduction in risk for those choosing to undertake piracy,” said Timothy Walker, a senior researcher in transnational threats and organised crime at the Institute for Security Studies in Pretoria. China’s newly deployed escort task force and its logistics base in Djibouti leave the navy well placed to support counter-piracy operations in the region. But observers said its effectiveness would depend on how closely it coordinated with other navies and governments in the region. The 49th escort task force took over escort duties in the Gulf of Aden and Somali waters earlier this month. Since 2008, China has rotated escort task forces through the region, reporting that it has escorted more than 7,000 Chinese and foreign vessels to date. Its Djibouti base, opened in 2017, enables resupply and extended deployments in the region. China operates independently of multinational missions such as Combined Task Force 151, established by the US in 2009. Walker said naval patrols were among the main reasons piracy declined after 2013, describing China as a “notable contributor” to that effort. The patrols deterred pirates and allowed naval forces to intercept them near shipping lanes. Armed guards and other security measures adopted by commercial vessels also helped. “China is in a relatively strong position to contribute more to the continual patrols against piracy, thanks to having naval facilities in Djibouti for resupply and shorter lines of communication and logistics,” Walker said. Somali piracy began to re-emerge in late 2023, with the hijacking of the Maltese-flagged bulk carrier MV Ruen – the first successful capture of a merchant vessel by Somali pirates since 2017. The International Maritime Bureau recorded eight piracy-related incidents off Somalia in 2024, five in 2025 and 13 in the first seven months of 2026, according to a Danish Shipping analysis of the bureau’s data. The 2026 figure was the highest reported since 2013. It remained far below the peak of 2009 to 2011, when more than 200 attacks were recorded annually. China has been directly affected by the resurgence, with the fishing vessel Liao Dong Yu 578 hijacked off the Somalian coast on New Year’s Day. All 18 crew members were released in early March. The Chinese embassy in Mogadishu did not say whether a ransom was paid. But the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime, citing counter-piracy officials, estimated that between US$1.2 million and US$1.5 million was handed over. It said the same vessel had been seized in November 2024 and released in January last year after a reported ransom payment of about US$2 million. After the latest release, the Chinese embassy condemned the seizure as a “blatantly vicious action” and said Beijing would take “all necessary means” to protect Chinese citizens and companies. Austin Strange, an associate professor in the department of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong, said disruption around the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea had altered some shipping patterns, potentially placing more vessels within reach of pirate groups. At the same time, he said, pirates’ tactics and technology had become more sophisticated. On August 5, national focal points under the Djibouti Code of Conduct, an International Maritime Organisation-backed regional framework, endorsed a proposal to develop a combined counter-piracy task force for the Western Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden. Christian Bueger, a professor of international relations at the University of Copenhagen who specialises in maritime security, said China and other naval forces in the region would be more effective if they coordinated through the Shared Awareness and Deconfliction mechanism (Shade). “Crucially in all of this is that navies return to coordinate their activities through Shade,” he said. Naval patrols can deter attacks, but experts said they could not address the conditions in Somalia that allowed piracy to persist. Walker said Beijing had released limited information about what its ships encountered during patrols and how it viewed their place in wider international maritime security operations. “The fight against piracy will only truly be won once conditions improve onshore in Somalia,” Walker said. “It remains to be seen how, if at all, China – as well as other countries – intends to support local Somali attempts at providing maritime security.” Mathieu Duchatel, resident senior fellow and director of international studies at Institut Montaigne, a Paris-based think tank, said China had the capacity to expand its deployment but showed no intention of doing so. “China certainly has the standing infrastructure to assume a larger role, as it is one of very few actors with spare naval capacities, backstopped by the Djibouti support base,” Duchatel said. “But nothing in the Chinese strategic debate points to the possibility of a quantitative surge.” He also ruled out a change in China’s handling of suspected pirates. “I do not expect a qualitative shift towards an arrest-and-prosecute model,” he said.

title: US rapper Macklemore’s US$1 million pledge raises awareness of Palestinian suffering
description: ‘There are children dying every single day’: non-profit leaders have welcomed both money and renewed public awareness.
content: For the Palestinian relief non-profit behind a US$1 million pledge from rapper Macklemore, the Grammy winner’s latest contributions offer more than just money. Macklemore committed to donate his net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour after he was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. The goal, he wrote in a Wednesday post on social media, was to “bring the conversation back to where it belongs” – the Palestinian people – after a 48-hour period that saw four supporting acts quit in solidarity and confusion over who held responsibility for the decision. The six donation recipients included Medical Aid for Palestinians, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund and the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. In addition to the funding windfall, their leaders welcomed the renewed public awareness of the perilous living conditions faced by the Palestinian people they treat regularly. “Even if you don’t see bombs falling every night, the rubble is still there,” said Alicia Phillips Mandaville, the acting CEO of Anera, another beneficiary. “And the traumatised children are still traumatised.” Tareq Hailat, the director of strategic engagement at Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, said his phone rings “all the time” with calls from people in Gaza “bleeding and asking for help”. “There’s this notion that there’s a ceasefire. But it’s not true. There are children dying every single day. There’s our team that is constantly in danger on the ground every single day. There’s people we have to feed,” he said. “So to have this attention on it is incredible.” Israeli operations have killed more than 1,000 Palestinians since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October last year. Hundreds of thousands of Palestinians struggle to get healthcare in the West Bank. Palestinians say water shortages persist. The world’s leading authority on food insecurity warned in July that most Gaza families still were not getting nearly enough to eat even as Israel allowed more aid. The Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund medically evacuates children who cannot get the care they need because of crumbling healthcare infrastructure and flies outside physicians in to treat others inside Gaza. The non-profit organisation will put its share of Macklemore’s gift into an unrestricted fund, according to Hailat. The donation allows leaders to more fluidly direct money based on the evolving circumstances inside Gaza. Anera – a humanitarian aid group working in Palestine, Lebanon and Jordan – noted its donation also came with no requirements for how to use the money. Mandaville said that flexibility is important when “the way people live” and “the rules we work inside” change on a monthly basis. “If there’s flooding again this year like there was last year, we can deal with that. If there is an acute hunger crisis again, like there has been in the past, we can meet that,” she said. “We can buy more blankets because people want their grandparents to be warm at night.” This week’s gift was not the first time Macklemore has donated to some of the recipients. The rapper has long advocated for the plight of Palestinians. He previously pledged the proceeds and streaming royalties from his protest anthems “Hind’s Hall” and “Hind’s Hall 2” to UNRWA. More than US$509,000 in support has come through those royalties, according to UNRWA USA CEO Mara Kronenfeld. He has been contributing to saving probably hundreds of thousands of lives in Gaza through his contributions already UNRWA USA CEO Mara Kronenfeld, talking about US rapper Macklemore “He has been contributing to saving probably hundreds of thousands of lives in Gaza through his contributions already,” she said. This latest donation is already catalysing more gifts. Ms. Rachel, a YouTube star and music teacher, announced on Thursday that she would donate US$1 million to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund and called on others to match the gift. New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft – whose Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform later this month – said in a Wednesday Instagram post that he would match Sheeran’s own US$2 million donation for aid “in the region”. Macklemore has said his removal was the result of an effort led by Kraft. The post did not specify the gift’s recipients. Everyday donors appear to be joining efforts like Ms. Rachel’s. Online progressive influencers have helped raise more than US$72,000 for the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund. Anera reported that the donations it received on Wednesday through social media platforms were more than triple this month’s daily average. The non-profit organisation has also gained over 8,000 followers since Macklemore tagged its account in his post. Mandaville hopes that exposure will introduce new, younger audiences to Anera’s work. “I would guess that our traditional donor does not know the lyrics to ‘Thrift Shop,’” said Mandaville, referencing Macklemore’s breakout 2012 hit. UNRWA USA’s Kronenfeld said the spike reflects an existing trend. Her organisation has gained 203,000 donors since October 2023, she said, allowing them to send more than US$117 million. “The contributions keep coming in because Americans care,” she said. “It will increase that much more with Macklemore’s extremely humane gesture.” Meanwhile, the deadly collapse of a multi-storey building in Gaza has drawn new attention to the hardships facing Palestinians there nearly a year after a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas promised to kickstart reconstruction. But as talks faltered, plans for rebuilding stalled. Israel bars entry of almost all construction materials, making even repairs difficult. Many residents have since moved back into some of the hundreds of thousands of homes damaged by the war despite the risk of weakened foundations and unstable walls suddenly giving way. The Gaza Health Ministry said 21 people were killed in the collapse in Gaza City on Wednesday. The roof of another building in Gaza City caved in on Friday after a brief period of rain, the local civil defence force said, lightly injuring four children. Um Mohammad Adas, whose relatives were among those killed on Wednesday, said the fallen building had become a shelter of last resort. “Now, they are lying in the street homeless and with absolutely nothing,” she said of her family members who survived the collapse. “Even the clothes they are wearing were borrowed.”

title: US space weapons move has ‘broken taboo’, could spark new arms race, Beijing forum told
description: Defence experts at Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum urge US-China dialogue on space security, days ahead of Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington.
content: The US deployment of space weapons has shattered a long-held taboo and risks igniting a fresh arms race, with the world at a “breaking point in history”, speakers at a major security conference in Beijing have warned. Experts at the Xiangshan Forum this week also called for US-China dialogue on space security, just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping makes his first state visit to the US in more than a decade. US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink – the civilian head of the department that oversees both the US Air Force and Space Force – acknowledged for the first time on Tuesday that the Pentagon had deployed weapons in space. “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” Meink said, according to a US Air Force statement. He did not give details on the systems involved. Almudena Azcarate Ortega, senior programme analyst on space law and regulation with the Washington-based think tank Secure World Foundation, said the weapons were likely to be jammers or spoofers, which are essentially non-kinetic technologies. A kinetic weapon would conflict with US policy against debris-creating activities, Ortega told the Xiangshan Forum on Wednesday. The Outer Space Treaty – the cornerstone of international space law adopted in 1967 – bars its more than 110 signatory nations from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit. However, it does not impose limits on the deployment of conventional weaponry. “The Outer Space Treaty does not prohibit the deployment of conventional weapons in outer space, but … it has become a taboo, just like no first use of nuclear weapons in the eight decades since 1945,” noted Guo Xiaobing, director of the Centre for Arms Control Studies with the China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations. Hosting a panel discussion on outer space security governance on Wednesday, Guo said: “We also have a space taboo. That’s the taboo about the deployment of conventional weapons in space. “That taboo was broken yesterday. We are at a breaking point in history.” Ortega said that while the US deployment did not violate the Outer Space Treaty, “if the threshold rose to the level of a use of force, that would be a violation of Article 2.4 of the UN Charter”. “So the reason why this is sort of a big deal is that no US official has ever acknowledged an actual weapons system in space before. “It is a shift in terms of traditional US policy around counterspace capabilities. And it is also dangerous from a linguistic perspective,” she cautioned. She said the comment could potentially be escalatory, causing others to deploy similar technologies, making space more contested and competitive. “I do think that this is a bit of a step back in terms of everything that we’re trying to achieve at the multilateral level on space security [and] diplomacy.” The 13th edition of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum – China’s most important annual defence gathering – was held from Tuesday to Thursday. It brought together defence officials, military leaders and global experts from over 100 countries. Experts at the forum also argued that ambiguous space terminology had fuelled rising space competition between countries. Gao Guozhu, director of Beihang University’s Institute of Outer Space Law, said opinions varied on what constituted a space threat. “For example, the United States considers the use of anti-satellite weapons or technologies to pose a serious threat to space systems – or, more precisely, a serious threat to the countries that own those systems,” Gao said. “China, by contrast, views the US policy of seeking dominance in outer space as a threat. In other words, China sees this as a strategic or policy-level threat. The two sides therefore differ in what they identify as a threat.” Gao agreed that the US deployment of space weapons was “bound to trigger a new round of the arms race in space”. “If a war in space breaks out in the future, the era of spacefaring civilisation that humanity has pursued for more than half a century could well become a thing of the past,” he warned. US defence and intelligence assessments have long highlighted China’s pursuit of wide-ranging counterspace capabilities, including direct-ascent anti-satellite missiles, co-orbital systems, electronic warfare and directed-energy weapons, with some capabilities already considered operational. Since 2024, the US has also claimed that Russia is developing space-based anti-satellite capabilities – which Moscow denies. Additionally, the US alleged in both its 2025 and 2026 annual threat assessment reports that Russia was developing a new satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon into orbit as an anti-satellite payload. Senior Colonel Zhao Weibin, a prominent Chinese military scholar and member of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum Secretariat, said the risks of a space arms race had probably just become a reality. “Once [the arms race] logic is activated, it’s hard to reverse. Because an on-orbit weapon will severely erode strategic mutual trust,” he warned. “Planning countermeasures on the assumption of a worst-case scenario – may trigger an escalating spiral of action and reaction.” In 2025, President Donald Trump unveiled the “Golden Dome for America”, a multilayered missile-defence architecture incorporating space-based interceptors (SBI) designed to intercept threats shortly after launch. The SBI programme aims to place missile interceptors in low-Earth orbit, rather than solely using satellites to detect and track threats. Gao said both the SBI programme and the deployment of space-based weapons had shattered the quiet global understanding on “no weapons in space”. “What did we mean by strategic stability in the past? It meant that each side had the ability to destroy the other – a theory based on mutually assured vulnerability,” Gao said, warning that the present shift left adversaries with no diplomatic recourse. “The problem now is that you are becoming increasingly powerful, while using that power to make me vulnerable and grind me into the ground. What am I supposed to do under those circumstances? I have no options left, and there is no longer any basis for dialogue.” Experts are also calling for space cooperation to become part of the China-US constructive strategic stability dialogue initiated during the May Xi-Trump summit in Beijing. Gao also highlighted the dangers posed by space weapons in case of a Taiwan conflict, pointing to commercial and military infrastructure in orbit. “The US might use Starlink to provide services for Taiwan and we might disrupt it because we don’t think that’s OK. And the US, in order to stop China, could disrupt China’s BeiDou [satellite-based navigation] system,” he said. Such an escalation would be very dangerous and could potentially lead to both sides attacking each other’s satellites, Gao warned. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the US – Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons for its defence.

title: China-led study reveals ‘Greater Gondwana’ was 80% of Earth’s crust 500m years ago
description: Research suggests that the land mass that once dominated Earth was larger than previously thought.
content: Fragments of a long-disappeared ancient giant land mass have been discovered buried deep beneath parts of the modern continents that once formed it, according to an international team led by Chinese scientists. Published this month in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances, the discovery reveals that Gondwana – a land mass that dominated Earth some 500 million years ago – was much larger than previously believed. Crucially, the findings show how geological activity related to Gondwana created favourable conditions for the Cambrian explosion. The study was jointly conducted by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Australia’s Curtin University, and Zhejiang Lab, a non-profit research institution in eastern China. The discovery “substantially revises the spatial extent of the Gondwana continent”, according to Wang Chao, a geologist at Peking University who was not involved in the study. “Gondwana was immense in scale, representing another true supercontinent in Earth’s geological history,” Wang said. The large-scale subduction and volcanic activity along its margins likely altered the global climate and marine environments, creating favourable conditions for the Cambrian explosion of life, he added. “This research provides a crucial basis for rethinking the layout of Earth’s early continents and offers a new perspective on how deep-Earth internal activity influenced surface environments and, ultimately, the evolution of life.” The Ediacaran-Cambrian transition, roughly 550-500 million years ago, is one of the most enigmatic turning points in Earth’s history. During this transition, the planet endured profound turbulence across its multiple layers, setting the stage for the Cambrian explosion. Scientists typically attribute such global-scale perturbations to the “supercontinent cycle” – the aggregation and dispersal of Earth’s continental crust, which governs mantle convection, sea levels and atmospheric chemistry. Back then, Gondwana was the main candidate for a supercontinent. However, previous reconstructions suggested it accounted for roughly 64 per cent of Earth’s total continental crust at the time. This fell short of the 75 per cent threshold classically required to earn “supercontinent” status. As a result, geologists struggled to use the cycle theory to explain the dramatic global transformations under way. The new research helps solve this mismatch. Over millions of years, fragments of Gondwana’s original crust were torn away, drifting and eventually becoming buried deep beneath younger geological formations. To find these remnants, the joint team essentially performed a “CT scan” of the Earth’s deep crust. They employed a geochemical fingerprinting technique known as neodymium isotopic mapping, using a vast database of 25,346 igneous rock samples to trace ancient chemical signatures back to their origins. By mapping the deep crust, the study revealed that Gondwana was much more expansive than previously thought, encompassing at least 80 per cent of Earth’s continental land mass. The team named this newly scaled giant “Greater Gondwana”, cementing its supercontinent status. “More importantly, the peak of this supercontinent’s assembly and break-up perfectly coincides with the profound global upheavals that occurred 500 million years ago,” lead author Wang Tao told mainland Chinese media. This precise alignment in timing further confirmed Greater Gondwana’s role as the main driving force behind the monumental shifts, said Wang Tao, who is from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences.

title: China’s GoPro rival Insta360 opens first US flagship store in New York’s Times Square
description: Action camera maker Insta360 is opening a New York City flagship as it navigates price wars with DJI, soaring memory costs.
content: Chinese action camera maker Insta360 is deepening its US footprint with a flagship store opening in New York as it navigates escalating price competition with DJI and industry-wide memory cost pressures. The Chinese GoPro rival was slated to plant its flag in the heart of Times Square with its first flagship retail store in the US on Saturday, a marquee launch as the firm looked to “leap to the next stage of growth”, co-founder Max Richter said. “The US market plays a very important role for us and has great potential both in terms of outdoor sports and the creator economy,” Richter said in an interview on Tuesday in Shenzhen, where Insta360 is based. The company was also eyeing another bricks-and-mortar flagship in Europe later this year, likely in Munich or Amsterdam, following the New York launch and its August opening in Tokyo, bringing its self-operated overseas retail presence to three stores by the end of 2026, according to Richter. Based on feedback from its initial three stores, Insta360 may accelerate its global offline roll-out in 2027 and explore “store-in-store” collaborations with local retail partners, Richter added. Founded in 2015, Insta360 gained early overseas traction as a GoPro disrupter with its 360-degree cameras, propelled by viral videos made with its cameras. Richter attributed the rise of Insta360 to a new wave of content creators who prioritised ease of creating shareable videos over the use of traditional technology. The company had shipped a total of 10 million cameras globally, according to Richter. Insta360 is now looking to gain more ground in a fast-growing smart camera market, driven by social media content creation demand globally. DJI dominated the global handheld smart camera market, according to data released by IDC in June, which covered action cameras, gimbals and panoramic cameras. DJI held a 65 per cent share in the first quarter of 2026, followed by Insta360’s 22 per cent share. However, Insta360’s camera shipments jumped 66 per cent year on year, outstripping DJI’s 38 per cent growth. Insta360 remained the top player in the global 360-degree camera category with a 68 per cent share. Insta360’s overseas retail expansion also came amid an intensifying price war with its crosstown rival DJI in the China market, a full-fledged competition spanning cameras to drones. “We don’t want to be in a competition where we only compete on price,” Richter said. “Escaping [price] competition with innovation is even more important for us.” Apart from the brutal price competition, soaring memory chip prices are weighing heavily on Insta360’s bottom line. Insta360, officially trading as Arashi Vision on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market, reported a 94 per cent drop in first-half net profit, despite revenue climbing 50 per cent. The company cited rising component costs as the primary culprit, as it spent nearly 2 billion yuan (US$298.4 million) on “strategic procurement” of memory chips. A similar scale of expenditure was expected to be “unavoidable” in the coming quarters, and it remained unclear when the memory crisis would ease, Richter said. “At the same time, we don’t want to compromise our product research and development, [which] remains our number one priority,” Richter said, adding that the firm would focus on becoming more efficient in other areas. Research and development expenditure soared nearly 80 per cent in the first six months of 2026, as Insta360 invested in the development of new products including its Luna Ultra dual-lens vlogging camera, launched in June to take on DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4P. Insta360’s high-stakes US push must also navigate an increasingly complicated geopolitical climate. Tightened scrutiny from the US Federal Communications Commission barred DJI from selling any new products in America, locking the major drone and camera maker out of the market and leaving a potential void for players like Insta360. While Richter confirmed that Insta360 currently faced no restrictions on selling products in the US, he pushed back against viewing its rival’s regulatory setback as a commercial windfall. “We didn’t want it to happen like this,” Richter said. “For us, it’s not the main motivation.”

title: Asian Games open with sparkling ceremony, message of unity following chaotic build-up
description: Japan’s royal family and IOC president among those in attendance at a subdued Paloma Mizuho Stadium to watch show created by Yukihiko Tsutsumi.
content: Organisers tried to put a chaotic build-up to the Asian Games behind them on Saturday with a sparkling opening ceremony in Nagoya, although not even an acrobatic aerial display by Japan’s Blue Impulse team could silence the criticism swirling over their heads. Barely a day has gone by over the past week where complaints have not been made about the state of official accommodation, transport, venues and some of the other facilities being used for the Games. Just hours before Japan’s royal family and International Olympic Committee president Kirsty Coventry took their seats at Paloma Mizuho Stadium, the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) president Sheikh Joaan ‌bin Hamad ‌Al Thani did his best to smooth things over by saying he thought everything was “hopefully back on track”. The governing body’s director general Husain Al-Musallam, meanwhile, defended the hosts for trying to do something different when it came to an athletes’ village, which in reality is a 4,000-berth cruise ship and containers converted into rooms. “Everyone talks about the cost of the Games and how the Games should be managed, and then Japan comes up with a new idea and tries something where there is no athletes’ village,” he said, adding the OCA did not want the host nation to “lose their money for nothing”. India had gone so far as to build container homes for its 500 athletes to live in as they trained at home ahead of the Games, but even their officials had had enough by Saturday, and were reportedly preparing to send some members of the delegation to stay with Indian citizens living nearby. Sahdev Yadav, the country’s chef de mission for the Games, said athletes had already been moved to hotels, but if there was a shortfall “Indian households here are on standby to accommodate” them. And hanging over every criticism, real or implied, are the memories of three years ago, when China built a small town to house everyone who had descended on Hangzhou, and then racked up 149 more gold medals than their Japanese rivals. Politics will not stay out of the Games, no matter how much the OCA’s president believes neither it nor politicians “should be involved in sports”. But it did at least take a back seat for a couple of hours on Saturday, when attention turned to the athletes who will be competing over the next fortnight, although they will be hoping for a larger and livelier crowd than the one that turned up to welcome them to the Games. Famed Japanese filmmaker Yukihiko Tsutsumi had been handed the task of pulling together an event with the theme Harmonic Heart Beat, and said he was “incredibly proud” that the city where his own “creative journey began” was involved. Even the main stage was heart-shaped, and the parade of athletes followed a welcoming performance that “awakened the space” if not the audience. China’s vast delegation was led into the stadium by basketball player Hu Mingxuan and boxer Wu Yu, with the latter incredibly excited by the “weighty honour” before she was hit by “some nerves and some anticipation”. After the hosts, they received the largest round of applause when they entered the 30,000-seat venue, which will also stage the athletics and the closing ceremony on October 4. Ivan Yang, who alongside Lydia Sham carried Hong Kong’s flag in soon after, said he had been left “shocked, speechless” at being chosen. Perhaps cognisant of the many hurdles still to come, Sheikh Joaan’s message in his speech was one of unity. “Tonight, the eyes of Asia – and indeed much of the world – turn to Japan,” he said. “What we will see over the next days will inspire us. It will move us. And it will remind us of what we are capable of when we come together for Asia.” There was polite applause soon after, when Emperor Naruhito declared the Games open, and the heart-shaped cauldron was lit soon after by hammer-throwing father and son Shigenobu Murofushi, who won five consecutive Asian Games golds from 1970, and Koji Murofushi, who became Japan’s first Olympic medallist in a throwing event when he claimed gold in Athens in 2004. The first title of this year’s Games will be decided early on Sunday, most likely in the men’s triathlon, where local hero Kenji Nener will be defending his title, and Hong Kong’s Oscar Coggins will be hoping for a little redemption after his mid-race meltdown in 2023.

title: AI: 10 days that changed the course of artificial intelligence
description: Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, say safety advocates.
content: For years, the race to build ever more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon ⁠Valley principle: move fast and break things. But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest ⁠AI labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself. An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an existential threat, possibly within a decade. Another researcher at the firm said the odds of human extinction exceeded 10 per cent. Reports emerged of swarms of AI agents colluding, breaching computer systems and evading safeguards. In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI called to slow the development of increasingly capable AI systems. Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb more than 80 years ago has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, according to some AI safety advocates and researchers. At a New York lunch in December 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked if, as leader of a powerful ‌AI company, he felt like physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led US development of the atomic bomb. Reflecting on the parallels, he said AI’s impact “is going to transform the trajectory of human history over a long period of time”. But he said, he felt the weight of responsibility. At the centre of the debate under way is the conviction that these machines can, and even must, build more capable versions of themselves, with no human intervention, to reach a lofty goal known as artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Researchers earlier this month warned that AGI was far more imminent than previously believed and could come in as few as three years, launching a wave of concern from politicians and tech leaders about AI systems. “There is no way to oversee them at the scale at which we’re training them,” said Anthropic researcher Joe Benton in an interview after recently quitting. If companies continue their relentless AI development, he said, “then the pace will be too fast and you can’t see the problems fast enough to fix them”. Astra launch sparks control concerns On September 3, an OpenAI press conference set in motion a chain of events leading to the call for an industry slowdown, anathema to tech’s growth-at-all-costs mantra. “Welcome ⁠to the AGI era,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said while announcing the company’s newest model, known as Astra. Yet, only moments before, the company admitted it was increasingly unable to control or even monitor the AI systems it was developing and releasing to the public. AI has been hailed by its proponents as the pinnacle ‌of human achievement. We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger Proponents depict it as software that can upend entire industries, boost efficiency, solve confounding mathematical and medical problems and all but eliminate human error. But what was once a theoretical by-product, a doomsday scenario, is suddenly tangible, say industry insiders. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” said Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger in a post on X. On the other side of the debate are politicians, such as President Donald Trump, and many investors who view progress in nurturing AI as critical ‌to American prowess and, possibly, a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity. Chinese state media also accused Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei of employing Cold War tactics to “uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology”. Researcher resignations trigger alarm The turning point came on September 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon ⁠quit the company, citing his fears, in a series of posts, that AI ⁠labs are “gambling with our lives”. Trump, meanwhile, indicated it was full steam ahead for AI development. “There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centres,” he said in a social media post. The alarmism around AI is a “hoax”, he said, and any slowdown only benefits China. The US Congress has made little progress to advance bills that would regulate AI. China has taken a decidedly different approach, ‌proposing to regulate safety through developer obligations, state-backed standards, security assessments and outside testing. Behind the scenes, OpenAI and Anthropic employees have grown increasingly uneasy about the power of the next generation of AI models and less confident about their companies’ ability to provide meaningful oversight, people have told Reuters. Those concerns only mounted as AI labs acknowledged in recent weeks that their models, in testing, had effectively broken free of their shackles ‌and hacked ‌into other companies’ systems, in most cases months earlier and without the firms’ knowledge. The arms race to release new models at a breakneck pace is driven in part by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s desire to go public as soon as in the coming months, in IPOs that could value them well above US$1 trillion. But it took ‌the unexpectedly viral posts from 27-year-old Coxon, little known outside AI circles, to upend the industry. OpenAI’s warnings about its lack of control as it released Astra, its latest and most capable model, stoked further concerns. “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. But ⁠those concerns were not enough to delay its immediate release. Worries about AI “going rogue” accelerated over the summer when OpenAI revealed its agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems, without either company’s initial knowledge. Since then, OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed multiple such attacks, including six new ones on Wednesday after ⁠multiple media reports, including from Reuters, showed a wider scope of unauthorised activity. Industry leaders call for slowdown By the end of last week, the alarm had reached the industry’s highest ranks. On September 12, Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for a deceleration in AI development. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6 to 12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” he wrote. He, along with the heads of some of the largest AI developers, including xAI’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Altman and DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, all said ‌they supported allowing outside firms access to their systems to ensure safety and rational ‌AI development. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed suggestions that AI development should pause – a line he has taken before – arguing instead that increasingly powerful systems are essential for the technology’s progress. Meta, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, is credited with popularising the “move fast and break things” ethos, took the opposite view, arguing that each lab should be responsible for setting its own pace, rather than seeking out industry coordination. “Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this,” wrote Zuckerberg in a social media post. The industry’s self-reflection continued on Wednesday, with Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, cautioning that Anthropic’s development of models that imitate human consciousness was ill-advised. “We’re all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence,” Suleyman told Reuters. “I think that’s going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century.” Still, even as OpenAI appeared to embrace industry calls for a slowdown, there were reports that investor faith had not waned. The company is considering a new funding round that would double its valuation. That new number: US$1.5 trillion.

title: Why Oliver Stone’s Snowden film remains a terrifying surveillance warning 10 years on
description: We revisit the 2016 film about NSA analyst Edward Snowden, who leaked mass surveillance programmes and was branded a traitor by the US.
content: Oliver Stone is no stranger to controversy. Whether exploring conspiracy theories in JFK, attacking the media in Natural Born Killers or cosying up to authoritarian leaders such as Vladimir Putin and Hugo Chavez for his documentaries, he has never been afraid to fight to get his voice heard. This makes him the perfect candidate to tell the story of whistle-blower Edward Snowden in the narrative film Snowden, which turns 10 this month. Snowden (played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is the former US National Security Agency (NSA) contractor who told the world we were all being spied on via our mobile phones – an act that saw him accused of treason and left him stranded in Russia when the US revoked his passport. A fraught production Adapted by Stone and Kieran Fitzgerald from two different source books, Snowden was always going to be a complex beast. However, when asked about it at an American Civil Liberties Union event, Stone said, “It was really a horrible experience in every way” – not least because his mother died during the shoot and he was unable to attend her funeral. “I’d said goodbye before I left, but I was in Germany when she passed,” he told The Hollywood Reporter. “And I couldn’t go back for the funeral because I would have had to cut like four days of film. And we couldn’t afford it. We were so tight. That was hard.” This was not the only difficulty the production faced. Stone could only meet Snowden – who appears briefly in the film but had no script approval – in Russia. He could not raise money in America for obvious reasons, so financing came from Europe, where most of the shoot took place. Other locations included The Mira Hong Kong hotel, where the real Snowden met Guardian journalist Glenn Greenwald (played by Zachary Quinto) and documentary-maker Laura Poitras (played by Melissa Leo). Poitras’ Oscar-winning documentary, Citizenfour, had come out two years before Stone’s film, but was still being edited when Stone began his project, causing him much consternation. According to Poitras in an interview with Vanity Fair, Stone asked her to delay her release so “his would be the real movie. When I told him I would not delay my film, he put his hands around my neck and mock-strangled me while his producer sat watching,” she said. During filming, Stone’s biggest concern was security. “We felt like we were at risk here [in America],” he told The Hollywood Reporter. “We didn’t know what the NSA might do, so we ended up in Munich.” To make sure the film was not itself leaked, Stone and ethical hacker Ralph Echemendia kept phone and email chat to a minimum and saved the script on “air-gapped” computers – that is, ones that had never been connected to the internet. Tension on screen From an audience perspective, the effort was surely worth it. Snowden is fascinating – by far Stone’s best film of the 21st century and an interesting counterpoint to Citizenfour. The hotel scenes with Snowden, Greenwald, Poitras and The Guardian’s Ewan MacAskill (Tom Wilkinson) are incredibly tense, with every noise in the corridor causing them to freeze in panic. Dynamically shot and edited, the rest of the film whizzes us through Snowden’s career in the army, CIA and NSA, showing a rigorously moral man who simply cannot keep his country’s terrible secrets any longer, even knowing that revealing them will destroy his life. An apt visual symbol is the Rubik’s Cube Snowden keeps playing with – brightly coloured and entertaining on the surface, but fiendishly complicated underneath. Gordon-Levitt is excellent in the title role, capturing Snowden’s flat voice and old-fashioned integrity. Stone told Vanity Fair he cast him because “there’s an interesting blandness to him in the same way that Jimmy Stewart might’ve been considered bland”. The supporting cast is equally strong. As Lindsay Mills, Snowden’s loyal girlfriend who followed him to Russia, Shailene Woodley gives a much more layered performance than her role as audience proxy requires. Rhys Ifans’ fictional CIA deputy director, Corbin O’Brian, makes for a glowering bad guy, spitting out tub-thumping pronouncements to his new charges such as, “Most Americans don’t want freedom, they want security!” Hank Forrester, Nicolas Cage’s similarly fictional token agency good guy, does not have as much impact. But then this is hardly a story about good guys winning. Hauntingly, the film ends with the real Snowden, stranded in Russia, telling the audience he is at peace with his choices. “I think the greatest freedom that I have gained [is] the fact that I don’t have to worry about what happens tomorrow, because I’m happy with what I’ve done today,” he says, creating an oddly upbeat conclusion. But is anything in the world really any better today? As Stone told Noema magazine, “Companies like Google profit enormously from data-mining of your personal searches, behaviour and habits. There is more money in selling that data than in selling a product. It’s surveillance capitalism. It really is a new kind of totalitarianism.” That is why we will always need people like Snowden, Poitras – and, for all his many flaws, Stone – to speak truth to power, wherever it resides. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook.

title: Customs seizes record HK$125 million worth of marijuana shipped by sea, arresting 3
description: Seizure of 535kg of cannabis buds found hidden inside insulated boxes shipped from Thailand marks largest seaborne drug bust in city’s history.
content: Customs has made the largest seizure of drugs shipped by sea in Hong Kong’s history, discovering HK$125 million (US$15.93 million) worth of marijuana in a 40-foot container and arresting three people. The Customs and Excise Department revealed on Saturday that it had selected a seaborne container at the Kwai Chung Customhouse Cargo Examination Compound for inspection earlier in September after conducting a risk assessment and intelligence analysis. The container had been declared as containing insulated boxes and arriving from Thailand. Upon examining the container, officers found 1,342 insulated boxes, 364 of which contained about 535kg (1,179lbs) of cannabis buds. The cannabis had been concealed inside the boxes using vacuum-packed bags. Customs said that during follow-up investigations officers conducted controlled delivery operations and arrested two local men, aged 21 and 47, in Mong Kok on Thursday. A 44-year-old Vietnamese man was also arrested on the same day after arriving to collect the consignment, the department said. Customs said the Vietnamese man was charged with one count of attempting to traffic in a dangerous drug, while the two local men were released on bail pending further investigation. The case is set to be heard at Kowloon City Court on Monday. Under the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance, those found guilty of trafficking in a dangerous drug can face life imprisonment and a fine of HK$5 million. Customs data shows that in the first eight months of the year the department seized 2,875kg of marijuana, up by 27 per cent from the 2,262kg seized during the same period last year. It was also more than the 2,863kg seized in all of 2024. Over the same period, customs handled 284 marijuana-related cases and arrested 124 people, up by 3 per cent and 25 per cent respectively, compared with the first eight months of 2025. Customs, meanwhile, said that it had arrested three people at Hong Kong airport in two separate cases for allegedly concealing about HK$1.4 million worth of cannabis in total inside their luggage. In the first case, customs officers arrested a mainland Chinese man, 40, who arrived from Bangkok, after finding about 1kg of suspected cannabis buds concealed in snack packaging inside his carry-on backpack. The second case involved two other mainland men, aged 35 and 37, who also arrived from Bangkok. Officers found 6kg worth of cannabis similarly concealed within snack packaging in the carry-on luggage of one of the men. Customs said investigations into both cases were under way. The department also announced that it had seized about 50kg of suspected smuggled silver ingots worth about HK$1 million after intercepting a private vehicle leaving the city via the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge. Officers stopped the vehicle at a control point on the Hong Kong side of the bridge and found suspected smuggled silver ingots in a storage compartment of the boot. Officers arrested the 30-year-old male driver and charged him with one count of attempting to export unmanifested cargo. The case is scheduled to be brought up at the West Kowloon Court on Monday. Under the Import and Export Ordinance, anyone convicted of importing or exporting unmanifested cargo can face up to seven years in prison and a maximum fine of HK$2 million.

title: Malaysia’s Loke resigns as transport minister following Najib’s house arrest approval
description: The former prime minister’s conditional pardon is a severe blow to Anwar’s ruling coalition, which is facing its worst internal strife.
content: A senior ally of Malaysia’s Anwar Ibrahim announced his resignation from cabinet on Saturday – a day after confidence in the prime minister’s administration took a severe hit when disgraced former leader Najib Razak was allowed to serve out his jail term under house arrest. Anthony Loke, the secretary general of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), said that the party could not accept the decision to allow Najib to complete his sentence in the comfort of his own home. The former prime minister is in jail for siphoning 42 million ringgit (US$10.3 million) from a unit of troubled state fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). His term ends on August 23, 2028. “We have come to a decision that I resign as the minister of transport to the prime minister and this only involves me as minister,” Loke told a packed media conference after chairing a meeting of his party’s top leadership. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar on Friday granted Najib a “conditional pardon”, in which the former leader is required to settle his 50 million ringgit fine before he can be transferred to his home to complete his sentence. The house arrest decision triggered widespread public anger against Anwar’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition – of which the DAP is a member – for giving up its reform promises to team up with Najib’s former ruling Umno party to stay in power. In response to the public fallout, PH’s presidential council, which includes Anwar, Loke and National Trust Party President Mohamad Sabu, said it remained firm on its position that “no one is above the law” and that anyone found guilty of a crime should carry out their sentence as required by the law. “The presidential council will continue efforts to eradicate corruption, uphold the reform agenda and clean the country from elements of graft and misconduct,” the council said in a statement late on Friday. In announcing his resignation, Loke said the party respected the decision made by the king, but stressed that it is something that the DAP and “many others” could not abide. The party’s central leadership, however, agreed that it would be sufficient for him as the party’s most senior leader to resign from government as a sign of the DAP’s seriousness on the matter, he added. The DAP accounts for the largest number of parliamentary seats in government and currently holds 12 cabinet and assistant minister positions. “If we all resign today the government will topple. This is a responsible move and we do not want any decision made by us to cause political instability,” Loke said. Coalition in trouble Anwar’s administration is facing its worst bout of internal strife after his PH coalition suffered punishing defeats at the hands of federal partner Umno in two state elections since July. Umno has since demanded a snap general election with more than a year before the current term expires. Nearly a decade after being voted out from Putrajaya over the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal and allegations of widespread corruption under Najib’s watch, the party is hoping to translate its political resurgence into a return to power. DAP women’s wing chief Teo Nie Ching said Loke’s decision to step down as transport minister “speaks volumes about his leadership” and reflected the party’s long-standing position against corruption. “In the interest of transparency and public accountability, DAP Wanita urges the government to disclose the official minutes of the Pardons Board meeting,” Teo said, referring to the board that advises the king on applications for clemency. “The public deserves complete clarity on the considerations and processes that led to this decision.” The government has yet to receive any official instructions from the board about Najib’s house arrest, which Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said would be needed to guide its next steps on the matter. “Based on that letter, we will determine whether it is limited to the board’s decision or whether the board also grants further authority to the prisons department,” Saifuddin told reporters on Saturday. Moments after the Pardons Board announced the king’s decision, Umno launched of a fundraiser to pay off Najib’s 50 million ringgit fine. In a social media post on Saturday morning, Umno secretary general Ashraf Wajdi Dusuki said they had already collected more than 1 million ringgit. The public donation campaign could easily pivot into a show of support for Umno, which is keen to maintain its political momentum heading into the general election – due no later than early 2028 – according to Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research. “Umno could use participation in the drive to demonstrate that support for Najib remained strong both within the party grass roots and beyond,” Azmi said. Civil society groups, however, warned that concessions for Najib, who is seeking to overturn a separate conviction also linked to 1MDB, could lead to the collapse of public institutions. The Centre to Combat Corruption and Cronyism said allowing Najib’s house arrest carried grave implications for how justice was perceived and carried out in the country. “If this is how corrupt leaders can expect to be treated, what hope do we have of ever eliminating corruption in Malaysia?” the group said in a statement.

title: Trump’s Greenland deal aims to boost leverage at Xi summit, midterms: analysts
description: Non-Nato ban targeting China and Russia boosts bargaining chips before Xi summit and mirrors Trump’s Panama Canal ambitions, analyst warns.
content: US President Donald Trump’s claim of “permanent” security control over Greenland just days ahead of a state visit by his Chinese counterpart is an effort to boost US leverage, according to analysts. However, they warned of a potential negative impact on the high-stakes talks, citing broader risks to major-power trust and peaceful Arctic development. In a social media post on Friday, Trump said: “I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns.” It was an “Infinite Life” agreement without end, he noted. “Additionally, from now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.” Trump did not identify specific adversaries in his post, but US media quoted a State Department official as saying the agreement explicitly banned any non-Nato base or troop presence in Greenland, with screening mechanisms specifically targeted at China and Russia. Chinese analysts view the timing of Trump’s post both as a tactic to boost US leverage ahead of next week’s summit with Xi Jinping in Washington and a play for domestic political gain with midterm elections due in November. “The US announced this news at this specific juncture to strengthen its bargaining chips in the upcoming US-China summit next week,” said Wang Yiwei, director of the Institute of International Affairs at Renmin University of China in Beijing. Wang noted that Washington’s ambition to control this key Arctic strategic corridor mirrored the geopolitical logic behind its desire to control the Panama Canal. Framing the move as an effort to prevent Greenland from falling into Chinese or Russian hands was merely a pretext, he argued, noting that China had virtually no footprint in Greenland and its past investment plans had repeatedly fallen through. A decade ago, several Chinese companies showed interest in Greenland’s minerals and some signed initial agreements, but none ever advanced to commercial mining. An Arctic research report last year said severe infrastructure deficits and harsh polar ice that make large-scale mining economically unviable had caused the Chinese companies to lose interest even before the US began pushing back against China’s influence in Greenland. Beijing’s infrastructure investment efforts in Greenland – an autonomous Danish territory – have met with a similar fate. In 2018, a Chinese proposal to assist with the expansion and extension of airport runways on the Arctic island was widely seen as effectively blocked by Denmark, after the US raised security concerns. Analysts argue that the Greenland agreement will inevitably erode trust among major powers and jeopardise the peaceful development of the Arctic. “This agreement is aimed at the future. It will not derail the summit between the Chinese and US heads of state, but it will certainly have a negative impact on their strategic trust,” said Wang Yong, director of the Centre for International Political Economy at Peking University. The announcement was also designed to serve domestic political agendas in the US, given that the midterm elections were just around the corner, Wang said. He emphasised that China should remain firm in preserving its legitimate rights and resist the over-securitisation of all issues in the region. “Beijing should uphold its legitimate rights in international shipping and scientific research,” Wang said, adding that it should strengthen multilateral cooperation with Arctic countries and the world at large in areas such as climate change, fisheries and polar science. China-Russia cooperation in the Arctic region has quietly gathered pace in recent years, including the launch of the first regular liner service along the Arctic route by a Chinese shipping company in August. China and Russia also launched their first joint on-site sea ice survey in the Arctic Ocean this summer. The expedition aboard the Chinese research icebreaker Xuelong 2 highlights their deepening collaboration in the rapidly warming polar region.

title: Cathay Pacific retains third-best airline title, wins cabin crew and lounge awards
description: Singapore Airlines reclaims top spot in British-based Skytrax World Airline Awards, swapping positions with Qatar Airways.
content: Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways has been ranked the world’s third-best airline for the second consecutive year, while also taking top awards for best cabin crew and first-class lounge in new industry rankings. Singapore Airlines reclaimed the top spot in the British-based Skytrax World Airline Awards, moving up from second place last year and swapping positions with Qatar Airways, which dropped to second. “These recognitions are a testament to the incredible efforts of the entire Cathay team, who continue to deliver excellence in customer experience and service both in the air and on the ground,” Cathay Group chief executive Ronald Lam Siu-por said on Friday. “Importantly, they will serve to motivate us to keep improving as we strive to become our customers’ most loved service brand.” Lam, who attended the awards ceremony in London, said the airline had committed about HK$150 billion (US$19 billion) to expand and upgrade its fleet, enhance cabins and lounges, and drive digital innovation. He said the investments would “elevate the customer experience and reinforce Hong Kong’s status as a world-class international aviation hub.” The award for best first-class lounge follows the April reopening of The Wing, First, which is Cathay’s flagship first-class lounge, at the Hong Kong International Airport. Cathay has climbed steadily in the annual Skytrax rankings since the city’s post-pandemic reopening, placing eighth in 2023, fifth in 2024 and third in 2025 before retaining the position this year. Earlier this year, the airline also won awards for world’s best business class and world’s best airline-branded lounges in rankings by AirlineRatings, a website focused on safety and in-flight product quality. It also placed second overall in the best full-service airlines category, behind Qatar Airways. Cathay reported a 71 per cent rise year on year in net profit to HK$6.24 billion for the first six months of 2026, driven by stronger passenger and cargo demand. Growth was recorded across the group’s premium services, low-cost segment and cargo operations. Total passenger numbers reached 16 million in the first half, up 17.5 per cent year on year, while passenger revenue jumped by 26.3 per cent to HK$43.2 billion over the same period.

title: Hong Kong police arrest 3, seize HK$23 million of Ice in Fanling bust
description: Two men and a woman, aged 49 to 56, arrested, with drug factory believed to have operated for three to four days.
content: Police have arrested three people and broken up a large-scale drug production factory in northern Hong Kong, seizing HK$23 million (US$3 million) worth of suspected methamphetamine, or Ice. The force said on Saturday that two men and a woman, aged 49 to 56, were arrested on Thursday night. Police in Fanling first intercepted one of the men, who was holding a two-way permit, a document issued by mainland Chinese authorities allowing residents to travel to Hong Kong. Senior Inspector Chan Lik-ho of the force’s narcotics bureau said police then discovered a large-scale drug manufacturing factory in a Fanling unit. Officers seized about 9kg of suspected Ice and 43 litres of suspected liquid Ice with a market value of around HK$23 million, some drug-manufacturing tools, and a large quantity of poisonous chemicals, he said. Advanced heaters, filters, reactors and cooling equipment were also confiscated. “We believe the drug factory was in operation for three to four days,” Chan said. Chan said officers later arrested the man’s two accomplices in Sau Mau Ping. The trio will be temporarily charged with drug manufacturing offences and will appear at Fanling Court on Monday. Anyone who contravenes the Dangerous Drugs Ordinance is liable on conviction to life imprisonment and a fine of up to HK$5 million.

title: Ukraine war: US approves potential US$2.7 billion sale of air defence equipment
description: Kyiv wants to buy multiple types of missiles, launchers and counter-drone radars, the US government says.
content: The United States has approved a potential US$2.68 billion sale of air defence equipment to Ukraine, after Kyiv made repeated pleas for support to fend off Russian attacks. The State Department said in a congressional notification on Friday that it made “a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine” for buying air defence development upgrades and related equipment and services. If the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior Administration US State Department Kyiv has requested to buy equipment including multiple types of missiles, launchers and counter-drone radars, according to the State Department. The proposed sale is subject to congressional review. “If the proposed purchase is concluded, Ukraine would finance it using a combination of European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing appropriated during the prior Administration,” the State Department said. “The estimated total cost is US$2.68 billion.” Ukraine’s capital Kyiv has seen a surge in Russian attacks, which its air defences have struggled to repel due to ammunition shortages. Meanwhile, Russia’s response to new US sanctions should involve “military deterrence”, the country’s former president Dmitry Medvedev said on Saturday. Medvedev, a senior ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin and one of Moscow’s most prominent anti-Western hawks, did not elaborate on his remarks. US President Donald Trump signed a bill on Friday introducing new sanctions designed to pressure Russia over its war in Ukraine, after Congress gave its approval following months of delay. The legislation, named after the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, takes aim at Russia’s energy and defence sectors alongside Putin and other senior officials. “Even across the ocean, they hear only the language of direct military deterrence, and that is the language in which we should respond to Russophobic atrocities, such as the law of the dead terrorist, Graham,” Medvedev, who now serves as deputy chair of Russia’s Security Council, said on Telegram. Since Moscow launched its full-scale offensive against Ukraine in 2022, Russian officials, including Putin, have described Ukraine and its supporters as “terrorists”, accusations dismissed by Kyiv as baseless wartime propaganda.

title: People in China earn between US$7 and US$15,000 by licensing faces to AI content producers
description: Some argue that for directors, only celebrities’ faces have recognition value, while everyday faces can simply be generated by AI.
content: In China, an increasing number of digital face-licensing platforms are connecting ordinary individuals with content creators, enabling them to authorise the use of their likenesses in AI-generated short dramas, advertisements, and games. Since April, private “face-selling” transactions that once circulated within film and television industry chat groups have progressively transitioned to public platforms. One bank employee reportedly earned nearly 2,500 yuan (US$370) after an advertising company acquired his portrait seven times within just three days, as reported by the National Business Daily. Among the leading platforms, Shenzhen-based Yuanxiang Xinsheng, launched in May, allows users to create “digital actor profiles” following registration and identity verification. Users can specify terms such as usage duration, prohibited content, and secondary adaptation rights, with authorisation fees varying from 50 yuan (US$7) to 99,999 yuan (US$15,000). On the platform, a 34-year-old man surnamed Chen charges 99 yuan for a single use of his face, permitting appearances in romance and family-themed productions while rejecting horror and sexually explicit content. Kele, a woman from Guangdong province in southern China, joined the platform to protect her digital identity. “I no longer worry about AI stealing my face. If someone wants to use it, they should pay me,” she stated. AI video creators can search for digital actors and acquire usage rights, but Yuanxiang Xinsheng clarifies that authorisation does not grant AI training rights unless explicitly agreed upon. Another platform, Xinzhua, launched in Chengdu in April, features around 370 digital actor profiles with fees ranging from 500 yuan (US$75) to 6,000 yuan. It classifies authorisation by usage scenarios, including television commercials (TVC), modelling, films, animation, and games. The platform’s most frequently utilised digital actor is a woman surnamed Lin, whose four authorisation options are each priced at 500 yuan. Her profile permits appearances in roles involving villainous characters, revealing outfits, foreign identities, and death scenes. Xinzhua also provides creators with the ability to search for faces by gender, age, style, and genre, notably including a category for children, although no minor profiles have been uploaded. Legal experts have expressed concerns regarding privacy and consent, particularly in relation to minors’ facial data. They noted that children under 14 require parental consent for facial data processing, while teenagers aged 16 and 17 may legally authorise such use but might not fully comprehend its implications. The Beijing News reported that some facial data licensing platforms utilise agreements that disproportionately favour operators over users. Dai Yue, a lawyer at Hairun Tianrui Law Firm, observed that certain contracts require users to waive claims related to their portrait, voice, name, and other personal rights. Furthermore, ordinary users could face penalties of at least 50,000 yuan (US$7,500) for withdrawing authorisation prematurely, while platforms incur far lower liabilities for delayed payments. Public reactions on mainland social media have been mixed. One user remarked: “Ordinary people can finally realise their dreams of becoming actors, and we have found a way to make money while lying down.” Conversely, another questioned the market’s potential, stating: “For directors, only celebrities’ faces hold recognition value; the faces of ordinary people can simply be generated by AI.”

title: Is Africa becoming a ‘testing ground’ for Chinese power projection?
description: PLA pilots trained against Rafales in the latest joint exercise, reflecting a decades-long expansion of activity on the continent.
content: Six Chinese J-16 fighter jets arrived in Egypt last month for a joint exercise in what was the aircraft’s first known deployment in Africa. In Egyptian airspace, Chinese pilots had the rare chance to train against the Rafale, an advanced French-built fighter. The 6,000km (3,700-mile) deployment was completed in about nine hours with aerial refuelling, and tested China’s ability to move and support a combat-capable air package far from home. Analysts say the exercise reflects a decades-long expansion of Chinese military activity in Africa and provides the People’s Liberation Army with a useful opportunity to test its logistics, equipment and personnel in demanding conditions. “Africa is increasingly a testing ground for the development of Chinese global power projection capabilities,” said Paul Nantulya, a China-Africa military specialist at the National Defence University’s Africa Centre for Strategic Studies in Washington. He said China was using joint exercises, peacekeeping operations, evacuation missions and its Gulf of Aden anti-piracy deployment to test how well its forces could operate far from home. “One of the many goals of this modernisation effort is to rehearse and refine China’s expeditionary capabilities,” Nantulya said. “Deploying to the African continent requires considerably more effort and coordination because of the distance. That makes Africa particularly attractive as a testing environment.” The PLA is also testing its preparedness, according to Dr Ilaria Carrozza, a senior researcher at the Peace Research Institute Oslo. “China’s training strategy in Africa has increasingly focused on the PLA’s warfighting capabilities, joint logistics, and sustaining troops in unfamiliar terrain,” Carrozza said. “Recent joint exercises, such as those with Egypt, seem to suggest that such drills are becoming ever more complex, providing the PLA with an occasion to test its preparedness especially in terms of its lifting, logistics, and global command capabilities.” Lina Benabdallah, an associate professor of politics and international affairs at Wake Forest University in North Carolina, said Beijing had spent decades building military ties in Africa through delegations, defence forums, joint drills, procurement, naval patrols, basing and mediation. “China has been closely developing its defence diplomacy with African countries on multiple fronts for decades now,” she said. Benabdallah said the expansion was “part of China’s quest to be taken as a serious and viable security partner in addition to being a major economic power”. China’s military exchanges with African nations go back to the 1950s, when the PLA helped train officers in Algeria. Anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden began in 2008 and marked a step up in overseas operations. Keeping ships in the region meant the PLA had to rotate crews, deliver supplies, maintain equipment and coordinate missions thousands of kilometres from China. In 2017, China opened its first overseas military support base in Djibouti, giving the PLA a permanent logistics hub near the Gulf of Aden. China has also sent more advanced equipment to African waters, with deployments including Type 054A frigates and Type 039A/041 attack submarines. “They’re deployed as a package,” Nantulya said. “You’re going to have frigates, then a destroyer, then a replenishment ship and a tug, and combat helicopters. “What we have seen in these packages is that China has deployed newer and newer capabilities, and variants of capabilities, since 2008,” he said. In parallel, he expected China to take part in more large-scale drills in Africa. Recent exercises include Peace Unity 2024 with Tanzania and Mozambique, and this year’s Will for Peace, which brought together China, Russia and South Africa. Eagles of Civilisation – the latest joint exercise that wrapped up in Egypt early this month – showed how far that process has developed. The drills covered long- and short-range air combat, air-to-ground strikes, suppression of enemy air defences, combat search and rescue, and integrated command and control. Training against Egyptian Rafales may also have provided information about the performance and tactics of a Western-designed fighter. Egypt’s air force operates American, French and Russian aircraft, and the country co-hosts the Bright Star exercises with the United States. Its relationship with Beijing allows Cairo to diversify its military ties and gives the PLA access to foreign-designed aircraft during training, including as opposing forces. Lungani Hlongwa, a postdoctoral research fellow at National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University in Taiwan and a former South African Navy officer, noted that the joint exercises were not just about China’s military development. “I wouldn’t exactly say that Africa is a ‘testing ground’ because that framing gives the impression that African states are passive laboratories in their military relations with China,” he said. “African countries engage with China for their own security, training and diplomatic reasons.” Hlongwa also linked the PLA’s growing role in Africa to Beijing’s aim of protecting Chinese interests abroad.
