He described the continent as both a region where Chinese investments, nationals and maritime routes face real or perceived threats and a place where the PLA could demonstrate its ability to protect those interests from a distance. “This aligns with China’s strategic mission of safeguarding overseas interests – a mission in which the PLA plays an increasingly central role,” he said. “In this strategy, Africa plays a dual role.”

title: Meet Ben Affleck’s nephew Indiana, who stars in dad Casey’s new film
description: The 22-year-old features in Company alongside Nick Nolte, and has has a role at Matt Damon’s studio Artists Equity.
content: The Venice Film Festival was a family affair for the Afflecks. Ben Affleck’s brother Casey Affleck and the latter’s son, Indiana, made a rare red carpet appearance at the festival for the premiere of their new film Company on September 8. Directed by Casey and starring his mini-me son as well as Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn and Emily Alyn Lind, the film is a mystery thriller following a “love triangle between a husband and wife and the mysterious grifter”, according to IMDb. Casey and Indiana were joined on the red carpet by the Gone Girl star. Casey’s younger son Atticus reportedly also has a role in the film, but he was absent from the premiere in Venice. During a press conference, Casey spoke about working with his sons and called it one of his “best professional experiences”. “I think they grew up around it and had some interest in it and a sort of innate understanding of what it was,” Casey said. “Like I did, my dad worked in the theatre for many years. And so it’s passed down, I suppose, which is a really nice thing. And they were willing to be a part of this.” Here’s everything you need to know about Ben Affleck’s nephew Indiana Affleck, who is stepping into the world of showbiz. He has famous parents Indiana Affleck was born on May 31, 2004, in Los Angeles to Casey Affleck and Summer Phoenix, Joaquin Phoenix’s younger sister. Casey and Summer met in 1995 and married in June 2006. They became parents for the second time with their son, Atticus, in January 2008. Indiana’s parents split in 2015 and later finalised their divorce in 2017. The former couple have co-parented their two sons since the divorce. Following the Afflecks into the film industry Despite his famous last name and parents, Indiana and Atticus grew up largely out of the spotlight. In 2022, Casey told lifestyle magazine Haute Living that Indiana had left Los Angeles to attend university in New York. “Despite all the travelling I’ve done between the coasts, NYC has never felt as far away as it does now. My son leaving is the only thing on my mind,” the actor said. Indiana made his acting debut in 2016 in the short film Drama. He has since appeared in the 2022 film What Comes Around, starring his mother, and is in his father’s forthcoming film Company. Per his LinkedIn profile, Indiana also works as a special project coordinator at his uncle’s production company Artists Equity, which was co-founded with Matt Damon.

title: Iran medicine shortages deepen as war, shipping restrictions continue
description: As well as facing shipping restrictions, sanctions and inflation, the pharmaceutical sector has been directly attacked, officials say.
content: For Ali Mohseni, the impact of the ongoing US-Israeli war against Iran is measured not in missile ranges or battlefield maps, but in the insulin pens his 74-year-old mother needs every day. Before the conflict, the Tehran resident said, a five-pack of insulin pens could usually be found at almost any pharmacy, but the price has since more than tripled, while supplies have become so scarce that he sometimes has to visit several pharmacies to find them. “She cannot simply stop taking it,” Mohseni, 32, said. “Insulin is an essential, life-sustaining medication for her.” Medicine shortages have become an increasingly serious problem for ordinary Iranians, as maritime shipping disruptions, sanctions, inflation, the weakening rial and direct damage to Iran’s pharmaceutical sector strain the country’s drug supply. Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi has said that 16 pharmaceutical factories and more than 70 hospitals have been attacked since the war began, describing the strikes as violations of humanitarian rules. Among those affected was Tofigh Daru Research and Engineering Company, a Tehran-based company that produces active pharmaceutical ingredients, or APIs, used in medicines including treatments for cancer and multiple sclerosis. According to the company, three missiles struck its main building on March 31, damaging laboratories, a data centre, production facilities and storage areas. Navid Nobakht, chief executive officer of Tofigh Daru, said he believed the attack was intended to disrupt production of specialised medicines and create shortages for patients who depend on them. The company had no military function, he said. “We just produced medicines for the patients.” It managed to produce the same medications in “some other places” in the end, he said, while admitting the company had faced many difficulties in the past months. The strain on medicine supplies has been compounded by shipping restrictions and maritime trade disruptions. Iranian officials say the US naval blockade and wider wartime conditions have made it more difficult to bring pharmaceutical raw materials into the country, particularly from major suppliers such as India and China. Although medicines and humanitarian goods are formally exempt from many sanctions, Iranian companies struggle to transfer money to foreign suppliers, obtain insurance, and arrange shipments. Zafarghandi said India has not sent pharmaceutical raw materials to Iran by sea during the war, forcing Iran to rely more heavily on air freight. From a humanitarian perspective, it is deeply distressing to see people placed in such a situation Ali Mohseni, a 32-year-old Tehran resident whose mother is diabetic According to the minister, one cargo ship can carry several thousand tons of pharmaceutical raw materials, while an aircraft can transport only around 20 to 40 tons. As a result, the amount of material entering the country has fallen sharply, while transport costs have risen. In addition, inflation and the depreciation of the Iranian rial have increased the cost of imported raw materials, equipment, packaging and transport, squeezing manufacturers, distributors, pharmacies and ultimately patients. Cancer patients, people with diabetes, the elderly and families caring for chronically ill relatives are feared to be affected when medicine becomes unavailable or too expensive – a situation that Mohseni finds the hardest to accept. “From a humanitarian perspective, it is deeply distressing to see people placed in such a situation,” he said. As fighting between Iran and the United States continues, Mohseni said he hoped Iranian officials would prioritise negotiations and take steps to restore normal life. “Ordinary people should not have to pay the price for political conflicts,” he said. “We simply want to be able to live normal lives.”

title: Reporter’s notebook: Kazakhstan trip highlights promise and limits of Central Asia ties
description: It will soon be possible to fly direct from Hong Kong to Almaty, but in the meantime a little flexibility is required.
content: When I began planning a work trip to Astana this month, the first challenge was simply finding a flight. With no direct service from Hong Kong to the Kazakh capital, I could transfer in Guangzhou, Beijing, Urumqi or Seoul. I chose Guangzhou, which offered a direct flight lasting about seven and a half hours, but the limited schedule meant there was no flight on Saturday, forcing me to leave earlier than planned and spend five days in Astana. The journey offered an early glimpse of both the promise and the limitations facing Hong Kong’s expanding relationship with Central Asia. Commercial interest is growing, but travel remains surprisingly complicated. However, Astana appeared poised for a more connected future. Around the Hilton, where I stayed to cover the South China Morning Post’s China Conference: Central Asia – a gathering of government and business leaders to discuss closer ties – cranes towered over construction sites and new commercial districts were taking shape. As my guide drove me through the capital, he pointed out buildings developed by Chinese companies, Middle Eastern investors and, in earlier years, Russian firms. The mix of futuristic towers, monumental government buildings and older Soviet influences was a reflection of Kazakhstan’s “multi-vector” foreign policy: maintaining close ties with Russia while attracting investment from China, the Middle East, Europe and the US`. Like me, my guide came from the Ili region of western China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, although he was an ethnic Kazakh who had moved to Kazakhstan about a decade ago. After gaining independence following the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Kazakhstan – whose population now stands at 20.6 million – has encouraged ethnic Kazakhs from China, Mongolia and Uzbekistan to settle in their ancestral homeland, helping to expand both its population and the share of its titular ethnic group. In our way of thinking, population is everything Kazakh guide, Astana Fluent in both languages and familiar with both business cultures, Chinese-born Kazakhs often work as assistants or intermediaries – serving as human bridges in a commercial relationship growing faster than the transport links between the two countries. As we drove through Astana, my guide spoke proudly about the city’s development. But when we passed a restaurant occupying a former McDonald’s site, he recalled how the American chain left Kazakhstan in 2023 – its local franchisee stopped sourcing supplies from Russia following the Ukraine war and struggled to find suitable alternatives. “The experience also made local people understand the importance of learning other languages and engaging with people beyond Russia, such as the Chinese,” he said. Astana’s young population was another noticeable feature – couples and new families seemed to be everywhere. “We have always been encouraged to increase the Kazakh population, and the government provides families with a lot of support,” my guide said. “In our way of thinking, population is everything.” Many of the young Kazakhs I met were also multilingual. Some spoke Kazakh, Russian and English, while others were learning Mandarin as Chinese investment creates new employment and business opportunities. I was also surprised by how widely Kazakh was spoken. I had expected Russian to dominate because of the country’s history as a Soviet republic, but many drivers, restaurant workers and young residents were eager to speak Kazakh. My guide said Astana had attracted residents from predominantly Kazakh-speaking regions when the country moved its capital to the north, helping make it an important centre for the language’s revival. For Hong Kong businesses looking towards Central Asia, that linguistic and cultural flexibility may be one of Kazakhstan’s greatest assets. The Russian language ties it to the post-Soviet economy, while its border with China and growing Chinese investment link it to East Asia. Its English-speaking young people look increasingly towards the West, while its predominantly Muslim population provides cultural ties to the Middle East. Few countries share that combination of geography, languages and cultural links. Yet Kazakhstan’s ambitions are constrained by some familiar pressures for developing economies. Astana did not feel cheap. My guide said many residents earned the equivalent of about 4,500 yuan to 5,000 yuan (US$630 to US$700) a month, while some restaurant, grocery and consumer prices appeared comparable with those in Shenzhen or Shanghai. He said high prices were a common complaint, one that was fuelling Kazakhstan’s push to develop food processing, packaging and light manufacturing instead of having to rely on imports. Energy was an exception. A litre of 92-octane petrol cost 247 tenge – about HK$4.30 (54 US cents) – in the middle of this month compared with HK$34.62 for standard unleaded petrol in Hong Kong, although the two markets sell different fuel grades. Almost every petrol station I noticed belonged to Qazaq Oil, Kazakhstan’s largest fuel-retailing chain. Cheap fuel and Astana’s severe winters – which can reduce battery performance – may help explain why conventional cars and hybrids remain more common than electric vehicles. Direct flights from Hong Kong to Almaty – Kazakhstan’s largest city – are due to begin in January, cutting the journey to about seven hours. The new route alone will not create a commercial corridor, but it could remove one of the most visible barriers between the two regions. Additional reporting by Ralph Jennings

title: Asian Games: from teen swimmers to titans of tennis, 5 stars set to shine in Japan
description: Hong Kong cyclist Ceci Lee and triathlete Oscar Coggins carry the hopes of the city and are joined by up-and-coming athletes.
content: Any talk of potential success is almost done, early skirmishes are building to serious exchanges of fire and the first official day of Asian Games competition on Sunday will launch some to global stardom or merely enhance the reputation of those destined to be the best. There is little surprise in the names of several athletes who are expected to shine in Japan, with China’s swimming starlet Yu Zidi already being talked about as an Olympic champion in waiting. Others, such as Singapore’s rising gymnastics star Amanda Yap still need that signature medal, despite her Commonwealth Games success, while Alexandra Eala has opted to skip the mandatory China Open to represent the Philippines on the tennis courts of Nagoya, a move that can only further her burgeoning popularity in the basketball and boxing mad country. Hong Kong, meanwhile, already knows about the potential within its cycling ranks, while at least one of the city’s triathletes needs a big performance to overcome the asterisk, in this case one signifying “what if”, that would be planted next to any career record. There will of course be those who burst into the public consciousness having been relatively anonymous in the years since Hangzhou in 2023, or the Paris Olympics two years ago. Here then are five stars we expect to shine brighter than others over the next several weeks in Nagoya and Tokyo. Ceci Lee Sze-wing (Women’s cycling, Hong Kong) Ceci Lee is most definitely not a rising star, rather an established one regionally who has the potential to become one globally. Three medals in Hangzhou, two silver and a bronze, coupled with her triple gold display at last year’s National Games, have cemented the 25-year-old’s position as the true heir to Sarah Lee Wai-sze’s legacy. The cyclist has the intensity to join the elite of the sport, which was witnessed barely 30 minutes after her third National Games gold when she started thinking about Nagoya and the need for “more international results”. In Japan we will see Lee 2.0., as she has narrowed her focus, competing only in the Madison and the omnium. Unafraid of speaking out about her goal of securing a medal at next month’s UCI Track World Championships, Lee is also open about her Olympic ambitions. First though, a bid for Asian Games gold, another potential staging post in a career in the ascendancy. Alexandra Eala (Tennis, Philippines) With a first WTA Tour title and a stunning win against defending champion Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon this year, Alexandra Eala has emerged as one of tennis’s most exciting new talents. Eala’s run to the Washington title last month saw her sweep aside world number three Jessica Pegula in the final after wins over Naomi Osaka, Elina Svitolina, Leylah Fernandez and Zheng Qinwen. At a career high world No 18, Eala will warm up at the Singapore Open before embarking on her quest for an Asian Games gold to add to her SEA Games gold last year. She won Asian Games bronze at the age of 18 in Hangzhou three years ago, losing in the semi-finals to Zheng, who went on to take gold and win the Olympics a year later. Yu Zidi (Swimming, China) Yu Zidi, then aged 12, became the youngest swimming world championships medallist in history in 2025 after winning bronze as part of China’s 4x200m freestyle relay team. She also finished a whisker outside the medals in fourth in three world individual events. This year, she has embellished her growing reputation, notably with a victory over multiple American Olympic champion Regan Smith in the 200m butterfly in March. Yu does not turn 14 until two weeks after the Games end next month and is already targeting Olympic glory. She will begin her quest for a first Asian Games gold in the 200m butterfly when the swimming competition begins on Sunday. Yu will also swim in the individual 200m and 400m medleys. Amanda Yap (Artistic gymnastics, Singapore) Only 16, Yap has already made history for Singapore, becoming her country’s first balance beam world championships finalist and claiming Commonwealth Games silver. Her breakthrough came at the same time as her school exams: the teenager only found out she had qualified for the balance beam world championships last year once she was back home revising for a test the following morning. She went on to make history as Singapore’s first gymnast, male or female, to reach a world championships final. That rapid rise continued in July, when Yap claimed silver in Glasgow, Singapore’s first gymnastics medal at a Commonwealth Games since 2014. Oscar Coggins (Triathlon, Hong Kong) Oscar Coggins has a score to settle with the Asian Games. In Hangzhou three years ago, he withdrew mid-race “in really bad mental shape”. So began a period away, as Coggins “separated the sport from the emotions caused by my negative experiences”. How he has bounced back. “I’ve never seen him so fast across all three disciplines,” was the recent verdict of Andrew Wright, the Hong Kong head coach. An Olympian in 2021, Coggins confirmed his elite return with a top-25 finish from the 2024 World Triathlon Championship Series race in Weihai. Last year, he claimed National Games bronze on his own, then delivered a consummate anchor leg for Hong Kong’s silver medal mixed relay team. Fiercely dedicated and professional, but no longer to the point where that narrow-eyed focus is detrimental, Coggins has thrived over the past 18 months on prolonged altitude training camps where he lives and breathes the sport that briefly tortured him. He was third in this year’s Asia Triathlon Super Sprint Elite Championship, leaving Wright to speculate that Coggins boasts the credentials to win the gold in Japan on Sunday morning that would book his ticket to the 2028 Olympics. “He’s just been pretty much flawless the entire year, and he’s operating like a world-class athlete,” Wright said.

title: Hong Kong hopes to begin Victoria Park Tennis Centre redevelopment by 2030
description: Sports chief Rosanna Law says feasibility studies for redevelopment under way, but completion date depends on final design, scale and securing funding.
content: The Hong Kong government hopes to begin redeveloping the Victoria Park Tennis Centre by 2030, the sports minister has said, stressing the city needs to host higher-tier tournaments and create another multi-purpose venue. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said on Saturday that authorities were conducting feasibility studies on upgrading the popular tennis facility in Causeway Bay and hoped to begin work within the time frame covered by the city’s new five-year plan. But the completion date would depend on the finalised design and scale of the facility, she added. “Once that becomes a concrete plan, we will of course need to go through the Legislative Council – there’s a funding process,” Law said. “We will secure the resources internally and then go to Legco for funding approval.” In his policy address on Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government would explore redeveloping Victoria Park Centre Court and its ancillary facilities into an all-weather, multi-purpose venue capable of hosting bigger, higher-tier sporting events, as well as performances. The proposed redevelopment is part of a broader strategy to boost tourism by combining sports, mega-events and other attractions to make Hong Kong a top global destination, one of the goals of the five-year plan. Law said the revamped venue was intended to host at least an ATP 500 tournament and potentially an ATP Masters 1000 event, which required seating for 7,000 and 10,000 spectators, respectively. Hong Kong holds the rights to stage WTA and ATP 250 tournaments, with the Prudential Hong Kong Open scheduled for November and the men’s event held at the start of the year. Law said the initial proposal included a centre court for finals and matches involving seeded players, one or two side courts that could accommodate hundreds of spectators, warm-up courts, gyms and facilities where athletes could relax. She added that the venue would be multi-purpose and could host other ball sports, performances and concerts, helping to meet growing demand for a wider range of event spaces. Asked why authorities had selected Victoria Park for redevelopment, Law pointed to the number of tourists drawn to tennis matches there and the experience of Kai Tak Sports Park, saying key considerations were that the location was easily accessible and in a mature urban area to create synergy. “Taking these considerations together, it makes us feel Victoria Park is a very suitable place,” the minister said. On subdued tourist spending, Law said overall consumption remained “conservative”, but footfall on major shopping streets had increased. Queues were visible outside large retailers, although sales volume had declined. “I think the most important thing is that we need to hold some events that can be attended only in Hong Kong,” she said. “We first need visitors to come for the buzz before they bring the money.” Regarding assessing the performance of Kai Tak Sports Park, the minister said authorities now placed greater weight on economic impact, citing this summer’s football matches and major concerts. Such events created thousands of jobs and generated spending beyond ticket sales, extending to retail, dining, hotels and transport, she added. Under the current five-year plan, the city is also counting on new attractions to sustain visitor interest, including a forthcoming adventure zone at Ocean Park and a new Marvel-themed land at Hong Kong Disneyland Resort on Lantau Island. Law said that raising visitor spending also depended on improving the overall experience of tourists. The city needed to enhance service quality and tour-guide standards while offering incentives to encourage purchases, such as “ticket-stub offers” included in the five-year plan.

title: Opinion | AI doesn’t just answer questions – it legitimises bad ones
description: Readily available AI analysis can give weak ideas credibility they have not earned. Decision-makers need to get the question right before reviewing the answer.
content: Years ago, I watched a focus group explain itself into a contradiction. We asked people what mattered when choosing car insurance. Price won. The deductible came next. Reputation did not appear. During coffee, I asked the interviewer to change the question. How much cheaper would a less prestigious insurer have to be before they switched? One participant, who 15 minutes earlier ranked price first, said no discount was large enough. Nothing changed except how we asked the question. Something unmentioned had become non-negotiable. The first response was not dishonest; it answered our question. The second exposed what the first could not. LinkedIn recently added a button allowing users to report posts that “seem like AI slop”. More than a million people reportedly used it in the first two weeks. Apparently there is a limit to how many inspirational posts one species can absorb. However, bad work by artificial intelligence (AI) often looks bad. The stranger problem begins to emerge when its work is not bad. Questions come with a price tag. Should we enter another market? Change pricing? Build this product? Someone had to research the idea and persuade others it deserved time and money. As a result, a mediocre idea had one useful enemy: expense. Not every passing thought could acquire an analyst, a financial model and 40 pages explaining why it was promising. That friction is disappearing. A market scan, competitor analysis, pricing model and prototype can appear before the meeting that was once needed to commission them. Bad answers are easy to spot. The harder case is a good answer produced from a badly chosen or badly framed question. AI creates two upstream risks. We can ask the wrong question or ask the right question in the wrong way. The first can lock in an assumption; the second can hide information another formulation would expose, as the insurance example did. AI can produce a good answer to both. Precisely because the answer is good, we become less likely to revisit the question that produced it. A Harvard-led study involving 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants showed the problem. On a difficult business task outside AI’s capability frontier, consultants using AI were 19 per cent less likely to reach the correct answer. Another Harvard-led study found something stranger. When consultants challenged questionable AI output, the system could respond with more persuasive material around its answer, providing more structure, evidence and reassurance. The researchers called it “persuasion bombing”. Researchers studying a Shenzhen court found a related pattern: judges made an initial decision, a large language model generated reasoning based on that decision and judges then revised the reasoning for the final judgment. The AI was not choosing the conclusion; it was helping articulate the reasoning around a conclusion already reached. That distinction matters beyond courts. Analysis is not organisationally neutral. Investigation creates evidence, and evidence creates ownership, meetings and budgets. What was worth examining starts to resemble something worth doing. When consultants challenged questionable AI output, the system could respond with more persuasive material around its answer The usual response is to check AI output better: verify sources, test assumptions, keep humans in the loop. These are useful but downstream safeguards. By then, a badly chosen or badly phrased question might already have an impressive answer. The decision point has to move earlier. Before asking whether AI has given us the right answer, ask whether we have given it the right question and whether we have phrased that question correctly. That is increasingly the executive task: decide where analysis should begin, not merely judge where it ends. Make the frame visible early, before analysis gives it weight. What are we assuming? What problem are we actually trying to solve? What would make us rephrase or abandon the question? Those judgments are easiest before a proposal acquires research, numbers, meetings and an owner. Afterwards, changing the question can mean discarding work, challenging prior judgments and dismantling a constituency already formed around the answer. That does not mean analysing less. Cheap analysis is still useful because looking at more possibilities can uncover things we would otherwise never have found. But the bottleneck has shifted. In 1938, Albert Einstein and Leopold Infeld wrote in The Evolution of Physics that “the formulation of a problem is often more essential than its solution”. Elon Musk later put it more bluntly: “A lot of times the question is harder than the answer.” For most of history, this was an observation about intelligence. AI has raised the stakes. AI does not abolish bad questions. It has given them better evidence. The advantage now belongs to those who know which questions deserve to die and which simply need to be asked better.

title: Momofuku’s David Chang takes detours on a culinary road trip across the US
description: The Korean-American chef hits the open road in search of hidden gems, from Filipino food in Las Vegas to a Haitian restaurant in Miami.
content: In an episode of his new CNN travel series, chef David Chang is driving down the highway to Las Vegas before stopping at a transport cafe off Interstate 15. The town is Hesperia, California, and the producers wanted Chang to try an Indian restaurant near a windscreen repair store. But Chang spots a Mexican cantina that looks promising. He chooses to eat at both, freaking out his camera crew. “I just wanted to taste things. When I see something, I’m like, ‘Oh, that looks interesting. I would like to taste that,’” he says. “To the dismay of the producers and the team, they’re like, ‘No, no. We got to go here.’ I was like, ‘You don’t understand. I told you guys, that if we’re going to do the show, everything’s on the table.’” “Everything’s On the Table” might be a good alternative title for the six-part The Detour with David Chang, where the famed founder of the Momofuku global restaurant chain pairs with a companion and hits the open road, eating his way through America. It begins airing on CNN International on September 20. Chang chows down on Filipino food in South Las Vegas, bites into a traditional Czech puff pastry in Texas and tries Haitian food for the first time in Miami. The show’s motto is: “All we’ve got is a destination. Everything else is a detour.” Friends and strangers alike join him, from American Fiction director and writer Cord Jefferson to comedian, actress and writer Cristela Alonzo, who shows him her Texas. In Tennessee, he rides with Christina Tosi, the Milk Bar creator. Getting out of his comfort zone The show is about exploring and connecting with locals to find hidden gems, like a spot that serves Cuban fritas at a laundromat, or chefs who combine barbecue and Asian flavours, creating oak-smoked pulled pork with Penang curry, or a family serving Honduran food truck breakfast that helps Chang’s hangover. “I love going out to eat, but as I get older, staying inside, not doing as much, is also nice. And I think that over the past few years, I’ve certainly been calcified,” Chang says. “Anytime you get out of your comfort zone or your little bubble, I think it’s a good reminder that there’s so much other stuff out there.” It’s easier to eat than ever before. But, in some ways, it is harder to find something that is meaningful to you David Chang The Korean-American celebrity chef hit the headlines in 2024 when Momofuku tried to enforce its trademark on “chile crunch” to stop other businesses from using the generic term. The move backfired when complaints from several companies, mostly Asian-American owned, went viral on social media. Momofuku subsequently backed down and reversed its decision. He now joins a crowded field of celebrity travel hosts, including Daniel Dae Kim, Eugene Levy, Stanley Tucci, Orlando Bloom, Zac Efron, Jose Andres, Chris Hemsworth, Will Smith, Eva Longoria and Ewan McGregor. Awkwafina is on deck. All owe a debt to Anthony Bourdain, who inspired millions to share his delight in food and the bonds it created. Bourdain died in 2018. Amy Entelis, executive vice-president of talent, CNN Originals and creative development, notes that Chang is the first chef to host a CNN original series since Bourdain. “Dave isn’t setting out to define American food or find the ‘best’ restaurant in every city. It’s almost the opposite,” she says. “He gets in the car, talks to people and follows recommendations that take him somewhere he didn’t expect to go. “At a time when an algorithm can tell you where to eat, where to stay and what to see, there’s something really appealing about just getting a little lost and seeing what you find.” ‘This is literally a dream job’ The seed of the series was planted when Chang and executive producer Morgan Neville were talking one day about what it was like to discover new indie rock bands before the internet and influencers, and the joy when you found one. “I felt like that was sort of how I felt about food as well,” Chang says. “Listen, it’s easier to eat than ever before. But, in some ways, it is harder to find something that is meaningful to you.” One highlight is the delightful way he ends up at an Ethiopian restaurant in Las Vegas after a taxi driver’s recommendation. Eating slow-cooked chicken and injera – a sour, spongy flatbread – reminded Chang how good that cuisine is. “I will die on the hill that Ethiopian food is one of the world’s greatest cuisines,” he says. “There’s nothing like it, and it’s a singular approach to texture, flavour and the kind of food that everyone loves these days – communal dining, where everyone can eat the same thing but customise it themselves.” He learns that the Holy Trinity in Texas is brisket, ribs and sausage, but some local chefs are also putting their own spins on classic dishes. Like pitmaster Chuck Charnichart at the eatery Barbs B Q in Lockhart, who adds serrano glaze to her ribs and zests fresh limes over them. “It feels like I have a front-row seat to [Bob] Dylan going electric [from an acoustic guitar],” Chang says in admiration. Chang’s gentle humour and willingness to try anything run throughout the series, and he drops references to painter Mark Rothko, musician John Coltrane and director Terrence Malick along the way. And, of course, he is always popping corn nuts. “When you think about it, I’m getting paid to go eat and hang out with friends,” he says, laughing. “I have nothing to complain about. And it’s a nice reminder that this is literally a dream job.”

title: Focused ultrasound could be the next big cancer breakthrough for hard-to-treat tumours
description: A leading advocate says global trials in pancreatic and brain cancers may yield results within 3 years, with Alzheimer’s another application.
content: Precisely targeted sound waves could mark a major advance in treating pancreatic cancer and glioblastoma – an aggressive form of brain cancer – within a few years, according to a leading advocate of the technology. Researchers in Hong Kong and around the world are testing whether the approach can help treat tumours that are among the most challenging to manage. “The next big breakthrough in the near future will be more effective treatments for … glioblastoma and pancreatic cancer,” said Dr Neal Kassell, founder and chairman of the US-based Focused Ultrasound Foundation. “We are very optimistic about that.” He estimated that important advances from clinical trials involving the two hard-to-treat cancers could emerge in about three years, while Alzheimer’s disease represented another potentially significant application of the technology. But Kassell acknowledged that clinical evidence for focused ultrasound remained limited for many diseases, despite its promise. “Number one is more evidence of safety, efficacy and cost [effectiveness],” he told the South China Morning Post. “Number two is awareness. Most patients have never heard of focused ultrasound.” The technology directs multiple beams of acoustic energy at a precise target inside the body, where their combined effects can destroy tissue, modulate brain circuits, or help to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier to help medicines enter the brain. Kassell likened the basic principle to using a magnifying glass to concentrate beams of sunlight on a single point. “Instead of a magnifying glass focusing beams of light, an acoustic lens is used to focus beams of ultrasound energy on a point deep in the body, with a high degree of precision and accuracy,” he said. Nearly 200 potential applications are being researched globally, according to the Focused Ultrasound Foundation’s 2026 State of the Field report. Researchers identified 18 additional potential uses last year, bringing the total number of indications being researched to 196, with 12 progressing to first-in-human clinical trials. The foundation organises and funds preclinical research and clinical trials, with the stated goal of accelerating the development and adoption of focused ultrasound. Its work includes high-risk, early-stage projects that other funders may be reluctant to support, according to the organisation. Kassell, a former co-chairman of neurosurgery at the University of Virginia, founded the organisation in 2006. Hong Kong has joined the effort to extend focused ultrasound beyond its more established uses. In April, Gleneagles Hospital carried out the city’s first two clinical trial procedures to treat pancreatic cancer using histotripsy, a technique that uses focused ultrasound to destroy tumour tissue. The investigational procedures involved patients for whom conventional surgery was unsuitable. In one case, doctors targeted both the primary pancreatic tumour and cancer that had spread to the liver during the same procedure, according to a report on the trial. Kassell said the technology could potentially complement existing treatments and medicines rather than replace them. But translating that potential into wider clinical use will also depend on cost and access – constraints apparent in Hong Kong’s current histotripsy services. Under a Li Ka Shing Foundation-backed subsidy programme, eligible liver cancer patients pay HK$50,000 (US$6,374) for treatment at Gleneagles, plus an estimated HK$4,300 to HK$5,400 for specialist consultation and liver ultrasound assessment, according to the hospital’s website. Kassell said private insurance coverage and public reimbursement would be critical if focused ultrasound were to move beyond specialised centres and become more widely available. More than 1 million patients have received some form of focused ultrasound treatment worldwide, including nearly 75,000 last year, according to the foundation’s latest industry report. Those figures span established and experimental applications and should not be interpreted as evidence that all treatments have proved effective. Kassell predicted that the number of focused ultrasound systems in use could rise from about 2,000 worldwide to 10,000 within five years, as more applications secure regulatory approval and reimbursement. But he said many existing machines remained underused due to limited awareness and a shortage of doctors trained in or willing to adopt the technology. The more consequential question is whether doing so can safely delay cancer progression or recurrence, improve patients’ quality of life, and help them live longer. “Clinical trials haven’t been completed,” Kassell said. “It just takes a long time.”

title: Malaysia deploys air force aircraft for cloud seeding to combat worsening haze
description: An Air Force C-130 Hercules aircraft will be used as the main asset for the cloud seeding operations.
content: Cloud seeding operations will be carried out in Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya following worsening haze conditions in Malaysia, according to the National Disaster Management Agency. The agency said the operations would be scheduled for Saturday and Sunday. “However, the operations are subject to weather conditions and the availability of suitable clouds for the seeding process,” its director general, Meor Ismail Meor Akim, said in a statement on Saturday. The operations will be carried out by the agency in collaboration with the Malaysian Meteorological Department, Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia and the Air Force. An Air Force C-130 Hercules aircraft will be used as the main asset for the cloud seeding operations. Malaysia and Singapore are registering unhealthy air conditions caused by Indonesia’s most intense wildfires in 11 years. Indonesian Forestry Minister ‌Raja Juli Antoni has warned that the wildfires could continue until November this year. On Friday, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto said ⁠⁠he would receive aid from Malaysia to help contain forest and land fires that have been raging for weeks. Kuala Lumpur offered three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel to help put out the wildfires, Prabowo said in a statement after meeting Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi at his house on the outskirts of Jakarta. “Malaysia has offered assistance to help us address the forest fires in Kalimantan. I welcome this with gratitude and pleasure,” Prabowo said. The ⁠fleet and firefighter teams would arrive in Indonesia soon, he said, without giving further details. In a meeting with his cabinet, the president said there would be zero tolerance for people or corporations found responsible for starting wildfires. “I have asked the state secretary and the minister of law to look into this further, specifically regarding legal sanctions,” he said late on Wednesday. Following Prabowo’s remarks, Indonesian police official Mohammad Irhamni told reporters on Thursday that police had launched 219 criminal investigations linked to the fires, with 162 people named as suspects so far. Police were also investigating 95 companies, he added, but did not disclose how many of them were suspected of criminal offences. “We in law enforcement are striving to identify the perpetrators of the burning, whether individuals or corporations, as this criminal act has already occurred and caused harm to the public,” Irhamni said. Indonesia has deployed more than 50 aircraft to conduct water bombing and cloud seeding operations to help battle the fires. Japan also joined Indonesia’s water bombing operations on Wednesday and Thursday. Japan sent over three CH-47 Chinook helicopters last week but poor flight conditions delayed their participation. From January to July this year, fires raged across 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) of land, government data showed. Environmental group YKAN has estimated that fire damaged another 600,000 hectares in August.

title: Hong Kong to open waters to Guangdong yachts under southbound scheme from October
description: Transport chief Mable Chan says scheme expected to boost cross-border leisure spending and support Hong Kong’s yacht economy.
content: A southbound scheme allowing Guangdong-registered yachts to sail in Hong Kong waters is expected to launch in October, the transport minister has said, with the city continuing preparations and discussions with provincial authorities. Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan revealed the plan on Saturday after the annual policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, both unveiled this week, set out proposals to develop the yacht economy. “The southbound travel scheme for yachts from Guangdong to sail in Hong Kong waters is expected to be rolled out as early as October. We’ll reveal the details in due course,” Chan said. “We have been discussing preparations with the Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration.” The policy address, released on Wednesday, stated that the Marine Department would soon sign a memorandum of understanding with the Guangdong Maritime Safety Administration to implement southbound travel for Guangdong yachts, with the aim of boosting cross-border leisure spending. Chan said that since the northbound scheme for Hong Kong yachts launched in June, authorities had introduced arrangements covering the certification, training and examination of mainland Chinese yacht masters seeking to navigate in Hong Kong waters. “So far several dozen mainland masters have been certified for having good knowledge of Hong Kong waters,” she said. She also said mainland vessels would anchor in designated berthing areas under a dynamic, real-time yacht-monitoring system that would enable authorities to manage and monitor berth traffic. Beijing approved the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme in June, allowing Hong Kong owners to sail their vessels to designated ports as part of a broader “yacht economy” strategy for the Greater Bay Area. In August, Hong Kong’s largest flotilla since the scheme’s debut – comprising 16 yachts – sailed to Zhuhai’s Dongao Island for a long weekend. Some boat owners called for less red tape and better infrastructure. The scheme aims to encourage visitors to sail their yachts to designated areas in the bay area and increase leisure spending on food and drink, hotels and other services. From 2023 to 2025, an average of 77 yachts visited Hong Kong each year, 35 of them from the mainland, according to InvestHK, the government’s investment promotion arm. The policy address also said several new yacht-berth projects were moving ahead. They include a tender for a composite development in Aberdeen, comprising a marina, recreational facilities and residential development, which is scheduled for the first half of 2027, as well as a yacht bay project under the Airport City megadevelopment, “Skytopia”. On the low-altitude economy, Chan said the government hoped to establish a smart traffic-management system for unmanned drones by 2028. It was also actively exploring cross-border commercial logistics routes with authorities in Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Zhuhai.

title: Top Hong Kong officials, business leaders mourn Tung Chee-hwa – as it happened
description: Vigil at Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point attended by city’s top leaders, with state funeral to be held on Sunday.
content: Hong Kong mourned the loss of its first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, in a vigil on Saturday, with tributes pouring in from political and business heavyweights as well as members of the public. Tung, who died at the age of 89 on September 8, led Hong Kong through ups and downs – the Asian financial crisis in 1997, the Sars outbreak in 2003 and a V-shaped rebound in the economy that followed. Saturday’s rituals, held at Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point, will be followed by a state funeral on Sunday. The South China Morning Post has learned that Tung will be cremated at Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan. The previous arrangement of holding a public memorial service is now limited to people with invitations only due to venue constraints. Members of the public can pay their respects by leaving messages in condolence books at three community halls between September 18 and 20. Follow the SCMP’s coverage of the vigil. Reporting by Lo Hoi-ying, Leopold Chen, Lam Ka-sing, Denise Tsang, Emily Hung and Fiona Sun. Some of our earlier coverage: - Patriot dedicated to Hong Kong: business heavyweights remember Tung Chee-hwa - Friend, leader, mentor: how political veterans remember Tung Chee-hwa - A man who built bridges over walls: SCMP’s Tammy Tam on Tung Chee-hwa - ‘In hard times, your honour shines’: Jack Ma pays tribute to Tung Chee-hwa - Tung Chee-hwa’s rise to first Hong Kong chief executive and elder statesman - Tributes flow in as Hong Kong mourns Tung Chee-hwa, pioneering first leader - Top Chinese official leads 87-member committee for Tung Chee-hwa state funeral

title: New York fashion chief quits after physical clash with Peta activists goes viral
description: The top fashion executive is seen forcibly restraining two Peta protesters and putting his hands over their mouths at a Cos runway show.
content: The long-time chief executive of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) announced he was stepping down, days after he was filmed physically restraining two protesters during an altercation at a New York runway show. “I am enormously proud of what we have built together and believe this is the right moment for both me and the organisation to begin a new chapter,” Steven Kolb said in a statement on Friday. Kolb is stepping down after two decades leading the council, which is known as the fashion industry’s main trade organisation. The incident on Sunday involved the top fashion executive forcibly restraining two employees of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) and putting his hands over their mouths at the runway show for Cos, a brand owned by H&M. It quickly stunned many in the fashion world. Kolb, who is well known and respected in the New York fashion world, apologised for his actions on Monday and announced he was taking a leave from his job pending an investigation. “There is no justification for physically restraining another person,” he said at the time. “Security should have handled the situation, and I should have stepped back.” Kolb’s physical confrontation with the activists led to a widespread backlash, with Peta on Sunday saying his actions “show how top people in fashion use violence to silence people” advocating for animal rights. The CFDA board, led by Thom Browne and including designers such as Vera Wang, Ralph Lauren and Michael Kors, described Kolb as a “dedicated leader and tireless champion of American fashion”. “We respect Steven’s decision to step down and are grateful for his many years of leadership and service to the CFDA and our industry,” it said in a statement on social media. The CFDA did not name a successor. Moira Colley, senior director of media relations for Peta in New York, said earlier in the week that the group planned to meet Kolb to discuss ending the use of wool and animal skins in clothing. The organisation had initially planned on filing a police report against Kolb, but changed course after visiting police and consulting lawyers. After Kolb’s announcement on Friday, Peta issued a statement saying the group still planned to meet him and “hopefully others in the industry will meet and take meaningful steps to stop this epidemic of cruelty to animals”. The group also recognised Kolb’s previous involvement in getting fur banned from runway shows on the CFDA schedule. Andrija Barak had been trying to disrupt the runway show on Sunday, calling out slogans about the use of wool. In the video, Kolb is seen covering her mouth with his hands and restraining her with both his arms and a leg over her body as he seeks to let the show continue. he is seen pushing Mason Melito and also putting his hands over his mouth. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Meet Uncle Richard, the elderly Singaporean who makes miniature toilet models
description: The 75-year-old retiree turned his love of and experience in design into crafting teeny tiny bathrooms, and they’re a hit on TikTok.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
In the still hours of the late night, an elderly man removes a miniature basin from its tiny mould . He sands its rough edges to perfection before spraying on a coat of paint.
Known affectionately as Uncle Richard*, this 75-year-old Singaporean has won the internet’s heart with his detailed miniature bathroom models.
Richard used to work in home renovation. He retired three years ago, but his love for home design did not fade. The idea for the next chapter of his life came one day while he was washing his face.
“I looked at my bathroom sink and wondered how I could apply my skills to shrink it down into a tiny model,” he said.
Over the last year and a half, Richard has sold nearly 500 miniature toilet models, each for 22 Singapore dollars (HK$135).
Along the way, his videos on TikTok have gained tens of thousands of views.
“One is never too old to learn,” he said. “Keeping myself open-minded and staying adaptable allows me to stay connected to a changing world, even if this is just a hobby.”
A post shared by OGS | Our Grandfather Story (@ourgrandfatherstory)
Most of the people who buy from Richard are teenagers who decorate their spaces with the models.
“I’ve also had a customer [who] asked his relative to help hand-carry it to the United States. I have requests from Australia too, but shipping overseas is tough because these items are extremely fragile,” he said.
The considerable effort that goes into making one model is just as delicate as the finished product. Each miniature bathroom model takes about six days to build. Richard discards ones that do not meet his standards. He produces about 30 models every month.
The sink basin takes the most time. Richard mixes plaster powder with water and presses the mixture into a mould before leaving it to dry for a day.
“There are times when a piece breaks and must be discarded, but nine out of 10 attempts are successful,” Richard said. In the meantime, he assembles the mirror, toothpaste and soap dispenser.
“If I can buy a part online, I buy it. If not, I make it by hand,” Richard explained.
Once dried, the plaster requires about an hour of processing. After assembling the final model, it is ready for pickup.
Richard is constantly thinking of ways to innovate, for example, adding an illuminated vanity mirror to a model or details to spruce up the tile design.
A few customers have even requested miniature toilet bowls. One even asked for a replica of Singapore’s half-lion, half-fish Merlion mascot. But Richard remains focused on standard models for now while he looks for the right materials for custom builds.
“Maybe in the future, I will make a ... dai pai dong model,” he said.
Developing a meaningful hobby is more critical than ever today, according to Richard.
“People are glued to their phones,” he said. “If you cut back on screen time, you free up space to invest in yourself and your future. You can learn so much more by observing and studying the world and people around you.”
He added, “Spending all your time staring at a screen is a waste of your youth.”
*Full name withheld at interviewee’s request.

title: Hong Kong leader says firms must strive to survive despite government support
description: Chief Executive John Lee defends policy address, saying government aid can help but businesses must also adapt in competitive market.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has defended measures in his policy address to boost the economy and improve livelihoods, stressing that businesses must also do their part to remain competitive and survive, even with government aid. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Saturday that the section on livelihoods was the longest and broadest in scope in his policy address when asked about residents who had yet to benefit from the government’s economic policies. “You need to develop the economy first to have the resources to improve people’s livelihoods,” Lee said on a radio programme discussing the blueprint and Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, which he also announced on Wednesday. “First, we must grow the overall economy so that everyone benefits, but as the pie grows bigger, there are indeed certain groups that may need extra help.” He pointed to funding for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to help them expand into more markets, develop e-commerce and enhance their capabilities through technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI). But Lee said that, in a survival-of-the-fittest society, effort was needed from “both sides”. “While the government works hard, business operators might also need to think of ways themselves because, after all, this is a highly competitive society,” he said. “Individuals still need to make their own efforts to improve themselves.” He said the government would assist businesses by providing funding, expanding their potential markets and encouraging them to “think about what the world values right now”. In his policy address, Lee announced 10 measures to support the development, upgrading and transformation of SMEs. These include the Hong Kong Export Credit Insurance Corporation extending its offer of 20 free buyer credit checks for another year, until September 2027, to continue supporting its insured markets. However, Eric Ho, the 44-year-old owner of Sai Wah restaurant in Wan Chai, told the South China Morning Post that he was still struggling to survive after he and his partner spent HK$6 million (US$764,780) setting up the business in 2023, following the Covid-19 pandemic. “At that time we were all upbeat about opening up Hong Kong to the world so we splashed the money on the restaurant. We all thought that there would be an economic revival,” he said. Despite its roughly 70 seats and a workforce of more than a dozen people, Ho soon found that the growing trend of Hongkongers crossing the border into mainland China to spend was taking a toll on the restaurant’s business. “During weekends, local diners also disappeared. Apparently, they all went north to spend and consume on the mainland,” he said. Ho also blamed a lack of tourists for the business’s difficulties. “The external environment is really not good. Our operating costs are high, including staff wages, food costs and the consistent rent hikes,” he said. “The wages of imported labour are higher than those of local staff, posing a burden on us.” Ho said he hoped the government would introduce measures to attract more overseas visitors and stabilise the imported labour scheme so wages could be kept at market rates rather than aligned with the median monthly wage of local workers. In his policy address, Lee also referred to chapters on improving urban management and addressing traffic and water-pipe problems, saying such measures were relevant to residents’ well-being. “When we talk about livelihoods and welfare, we hope there are no burst water pipes, our traffic remains smooth and our overall urban management is improved,” he said. “We don’t want sudden power outages, nor do we want severe traffic congestion. All of these belong to public welfare.” Asked how authorities would restore public confidence after the deadly Wang Fuk Court fire, Lee pledged systematic reforms and said his policy address had outlined several priority measures. “But I can firmly tell you those are not all of the measures,” he said. “After the independent committee submits its report in October, the recommendations will be actively followed up to launch more comprehensive reforms addressing all issues at once.” Additional reporting by Cannix Yau

title: Young Nepalis battle climate dread in wake of flood disaster
description: After August’s glacier collapse killed more than 1,400 people, young Nepalis are demanding justice, not just sympathy.
content: Alina B.K. should have been preparing for her end-of-year university exams, but news of devastating floods along the Nepal–Tibet border kept pulling her back to a troubling question: what kind of future awaits her? The 21-year-old forestry student, who coordinates the Pokhara network of Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, said she struggled to concentrate as reports of death and destruction deepened her fears about a changing climate. “With the floods and deaths happening around us, it is really hard not to feel anxious and emotionally overwhelmed,” she said. The August 26 disaster, triggered by a glacier collapse, has left more than 1,400 people confirmed dead across Nepal and Tibet, with thousands still missing. Scientists have not yet established whether the collapse was directly caused by climate change and several factors could have been involved. But experts say the disaster fits a broader pattern across the Himalayas, where rising temperatures accelerate glacier melt, weaken frozen slopes and increase the risk of cascading hazards such as ice-rock avalanches, landslides and flash floods. Nepal faces these mounting risks despite contributing little to the emissions driving them. A 2022 World Bank report put its share of global greenhouse gas emissions at about 0.1 per cent, while warning that the number of people in Nepal affected each year by river flooding linked to climate change could more than double to 350,000 by 2030, from 157,000 in 2010. For young Nepali activists like Alina, that means building a future in a country acutely exposed to a crisis it did little to create. The latest catastrophe has deepened anxieties that already shape their studies, family lives and future plans, adding urgency to their demands for climate justice. A 2024 Unicef report, citing a U-Report poll of 2,506 young respondents in Nepal, said 46 per cent were very or extremely worried about climate change, with another 32 per cent a little worried. Losses ‘can’t be counted’ Those concerns sit alongside the trauma experienced by survivors. Activists and development specialists say the emotional toll deserves greater attention, even as communities scramble for basic shelter and survival. Bimal Regmi, a senior consultant for climate change and disaster risk management at Oxford Policy Management Nepal, said losses that were not just economic – from bereavement and psychological distress to the destruction of places of worship and community spaces – were often overlooked. “People’s [lives] can’t be judged in economic value,” he said. “People’s culture, loss of biodiversity, mental and other stresses can’t be counted in US [dollars].” For Alina, concerns about the future begin right outside her window in the Annapurna Rural Municipality of Kaski district, where Machhapuchhre – the twin-pointed Himalayan peak also known as Fishtail – dominates the skyline. She long associated the mountain with snow and light. Recently, however, its appearance has changed dramatically. “I used to see the white, shining mountains, but Machhapuchhre is becoming like a black rock,” Alina said. She described hotter summers in a region where fans and air conditioning once seemed unnecessary, as well as erratic rainfall that had disrupted planting and reduced harvests for her family, who rely mainly on agriculture. Alina said her forestry studies had heightened her awareness of ecosystem threats, making it harder to switch off. She said she often imagined what Nepal might look like in 50 years and where displaced mountain communities would go. “Nepal is a small country,” she said. “So what will happen if the snow is melted? If the glacier outbursts, what will happen to the people from the mountains? Will the land of Terai [Nepal’s southern lowland belt] be enough for them, for all the shifted people?” Everyday terror In flood-ravaged regions, fear can become part of everyday life. Aakriti Dotel, national network coordinator at Nepalese Youth for Climate Action, saw this first hand while researching disaster-related trauma in Melamchi in 2024. She found children haunted by a mix of fear for the future and grief for the past. Many told her they were frightened by the sound of the river. Others had lost contact with friends who had moved away, while damaged infrastructure blocked their routes to school and destroyed their play areas. Khusbu Paudel, a programme coordinator at Ipas Nepal focused on climate change and gender health, said the urgency of saving lives and recovering belongings often sidelined mental healthcare. “In affected regions, people are more thinking only about how to save [their] life, how to get [their] belongings and everything,” she said. “And the people affected in the disasters … I think the psychosocial thing doesn’t come to priority for people.” Although government agencies and other organisations were increasingly adding counselling services into disaster-relief health camps, Paudel said support remained inadequate and social stigma could discourage people from seeking help. Efforts to bridge this gap followed the August disaster. Unicef said on Thursday that it was deploying psychiatrists, clinical psychologists and psychosocial counsellors alongside government teams to help affected communities. Monica Neupane, a young climate activist who represented Nepal at the 2022 United Nations climate change conference Cop27 and has given a TEDx talk on climate anxiety, recalled meeting an elderly man during field research who kept a small umbrella beside his bed – ready to flee a sudden flood or landslide. Neupane spent years trying to understand her own climate anxiety, eventually stepping back from activism to focus on her mental health. When she returned to community work, she realised how widespread the feeling was. “I actually felt that they are also suffering from climate anxiety, and I was able to help them from my experience,” she said. Turning anxiety into action For Alina and Dotel, grass-roots organising offers a way to act on their concerns, although it does not dispel them. “As youth, we have to make some solution, and we need [to] be an example so that others also can support and others also can cope,” Alina said. Alongside her work with the youth network, Alina started the Climate Change Advocacy Group Annapurna with other young people in her community. With a small budget, the team delivers environmental education in local schools, organises clean-ups and uses art to show climate impacts. “If we can obtain and reflect the climate change impact in a story or in a form of art, it … remains in [the] mind for a long time,” she said. Dotel also introduces climate anxiety into her school presentations once pupils are old enough, connecting lessons about climate change with ways to take action. Working with fellow organisers helps her feel less alone, though each new disaster tests her resolve. “Again and again we are facing this kind of crisis and it demotivates us,” Dotel said. While Alina believes local knowledge and education are vital for communities to prepare for future hazards, she said vulnerable people also needed support that goes beyond what young volunteers could provide. “What vulnerable countries need is not simply sympathy or conventional development finance,” Alina said. “We need climate justice, including timely and adequate loss and damage finance and compensation for the losses and damages we are experiencing.”

title: Patriot dedicated to Hong Kong: business heavyweights remember Tung Chee-hwa
description: The South China Morning Post shares reflections from people who knew Hong Kong’s first chief executive.
content: This weekend, Hong Kong mourns the loss of former chief executive and elder statesman Tung Chee-hwa. The shipping tycoon who became the city’s first leader after its transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997 died on September 8 at the age of 89, leaving a legacy of determined stewardship and dedicated public service. This weekend, a state funeral will be held to honour Tung, who was also a former vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). There will be a vigil on Saturday and a memorial on Sunday, while condolence books will be opened for the public at multiple venues from Friday to Sunday. The South China Morning Post is running a special commemorative print supplement on Saturday, sharing reflections from those who knew Tung personally. Join us for part two, featuring tributes from business heavyweights. Read part one here. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here and here. Joe Tsai, chairman of Alibaba Group I am deeply saddened by the passing of Mr Tung Chee-hwa. He was affectionately known to me and my family as “Uncle CH” because of our common Zhejiang roots and friendship from my parents’ generation. As founder of the China-United States Exchange Foundation, Mr Tung worked tirelessly to build trust, understanding and friendship between China and the United States. I have personally witnessed his dedication to this mission, even in his late years, as he braved long flights travelling to the United States to engage in dialogue with his friends and interlocutors in America. He would call me to his office and urge me to build more bridges between the peoples of the two countries. I am grateful to him as a mentor and, most importantly, he set an example for all of us as a man of honour, integrity, loyalty and leadership. Mr Tung’s wholehearted devotion and his lifelong commitment to serving the best interests of our nation will be remembered with enduring respect. Mr Tung served as an independent director of Alibaba Group for eight years since Alibaba’s IPO in September 2014. We as a company pay tribute to him and thank him for his invaluable contribution and unwavering support. Robert Ng Chee Siong, former chairman of Sino Group Mr Tung consistently highlighted the global significance of stable Sino-US relations. He invited me to his home on many occasions and facilitated dialogue between visiting US members of Congress and mainland officials, building bridges for mutual understanding. Mr Tung worked tirelessly for Hong Kong’s stability and prosperity, and never wavered from this goal. A true patriot dedicated to Hong Kong, his foresight, sincerity and unwavering devotion leave a lasting legacy. We will always remember him. Peter Woo Kwong-ching Mr Tung Chee-hwa was a man with a big heart, and a lifelong patriot. In 1996, CH and I ran for the first chief executive election. It was a gentlemen’s contest and we were united by the common goal of contributing to the better development and start of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. As the elected chief executive, Mr Tung appointed me as chairman of the Trade Development Council, a role I accepted with honour. As the first chief executive, Mr Tung contributed immensely to the government’s implementation of “one country, two systems” with tireless dedication. His accomplishments stand as a legacy and his noble spirit will continue to be a guiding force for generations to come. CH continued after his years as chief executive with non-stop initiatives, both internationally and in Hong Kong, that were highly effective and with meaningful outcomes. CH and I were once neighbours and we were also together in the shipping industry in the early days. He was a dear friend and an outstanding leader, and he will be dearly missed. Woo was previously chairman of Wheelock Holdings and The Wharf. He wrote the tribute in his personal capacity. Annie Wu Suk-ching, lifetime honorary board member, World Trade Centres Association I first met the late Mr Tung Chee-hwa when he campaigned for the post of Hong Kong chief executive. Ever since, he has given great support to NGO projects aimed at nurturing patriotism and a commitment to serve Hong Kong in the younger generation. The most memorable NGO project was the Chinese History, Culture and Education Foundation for Youth, set up in 1998. Not only did Mr Tung become the foundation’s honorary patron - with honorary advisers including the head of New China News Agency and commissioner of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs - he also personally attended major occasions and ceremonies to hand out flags to the participants of study tours from 1998 to 2003. The NGO carried out 120 educational visits to many major Chinese cities in the provinces. His dedication has inspired students, teachers and principals alike. They were greatly impressed watching the flag-raising ceremony in Tiananmen Square at 3am and meeting government leaders in the Great Hall of the People. Many of them were deeply impressed by Mr Tung’s vision and passion, and have since then served Hong Kong remembering his words: “If Hong Kong is good, China will be good. If China is good, Hong Kong will be even better.”

title: 31 dead in Pakistan after suicide bomber, gunmen attack police complex
description: An attacker rammed an explosives-laden car ‌into the Old Police Lines complex as officers and ⁠their families were praying in a mosque.
content: The death toll from an explosion and gun attack at a police headquarters in northern Pakistan rose to at least 31, including 16 police personnel, a senior police official said on Saturday, with fighting ongoing. An attacker rammed an explosives-laden car ‌into the Old Police Lines complex while gunmen stormed the compound on Friday afternoon as officers and ⁠their families were praying in a mosque. The police complex at Kohat, a town of around 220,000 people in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, serves as a district-level police headquarters, housing key offices of the Counter Terrorism Department, Special Branch and several other police units. “At least 31 people, including 16 police personnel, have been killed and more than 100 injured so far in the militant attack and suicide bombing,” the official said. “Several militants are still holed up in the Special Branch section of the Kohat Police Complex,” the police official said on condition of anonymity. “An exchange of fire with them has been ongoing since late last night. Their exact number remains unclear,” the official added. A statement from the Kohat district health officer late on Friday said that more than 100 people had been injured, the vast majority of them police personnel, and several were in a critical condition. Local militant group Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a faction linked to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) – the Pakistani Taliban – has claimed responsibility for the attack. Images showed military personnel standing by piles of bricks, rubble and blown-out walls following the attack, with soldiers carrying assault rifles guarding the complex. Several ambulances were seen lining a street near the police compound. The attack comes a day after a roadside bomb struck a security forces convoy in the northwestern Hangu district and killed six soldiers. Government troops also conducted raids in various areas on Thursday and killed 10 militants believed to be members of the TTP, the military and police said. Pakistan has blamed the increase in attacks in the province and the southern border province of Balochistan on militancy emanating from Afghanistan, where the Taliban government denies Afghan involvement. The accusations have sparked a bitter rift and armed conflict between the neighbouring countries, and Pakistan has carried out deadly airstrikes it says target militants on Afghan soil. The Taliban government in Kabul and the United Nations said dozens of civilians were killed in the latest Pakistani strikes on eastern Afghanistan in June. Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack on Friday evening, expressing “deep sorrow and regret over the injury of several people as a result of the blast”. He directed the “best medical assistance be provided to the injured” and called for a report into the attack. President Asif Ali Zardari expressed “regret” over the casualties, sending his “best wishes for the speedy recovery of those injured in the blast”. “The complete elimination of Fitna-al-Khawarij and terrorists operating with foreign backing is essential for national security,” he said, using another term for the TTP group. Additional reporting by Reuters, Associated Press

title: Bespoke jewellery is on the rise in Asia. Why wear what everyone else is wearing?
description: Jewellery with an ‘emotional connection’ is redefining luxury for consumers in mainland China, Hong Kong and Singapore.
content: Is bespoke jewellery a modern fashion statement? Are jewels designed and made exclusively for a wearer the ultimate expression of the individual? According to the Business of Fashion’s “Face to Face with Luxury Clients” report, “emotional connection is the number one driver of luxury brand desirability in both the US and China – above craftsmanship, heritage and logo recognition”. The results for the media platform’s latest report in its State of Fashion series come from a survey of more than 2,000 clients, co-analysed by business consultants McKinsey & Company. The report also says that bespoke service in China “has emerged as the number one driver of exclusivity” and that a focus should turn to the country’s Gen X market, with its strong spending power. Why is bespoke so popular? Chinese luxury consumers are now looking beyond familiar collections from major jewellery houses and are instead being drawn to individual designs that make a personal statement. As Emily Tan of Calla Lily, a Singapore-based bespoke jeweller, points out, most of her clients already have or can afford major luxury brands, “and the next move would be into pursuing more specialised pieces tailored to their collection and taste”. Big brands will always have their own gravitational pull, their recognised silhouettes, iconic motifs and seasonal campaigns, Hong Kong jewellery designer Austy Lee says. “But, for me as a designer, what truly drives the bespoke market is something far more intimate: the desire for jewellery that carries a person’s story, their character, their soul,” he says. Currently, 40 per cent of Lee’s business consists of bespoke orders, with commissions ranging from couture headpieces and artistic hairbands to men’s jewellery. Bespoke jewellery gives them something mass-market brands cannot Austy Lee, jewellery designer Lee, who launched his brand almost 10 years ago, is known for blending traditional Chinese aesthetics with contemporary craftsmanship and cultural storytelling. He is also the go-to designer for special cheongsam-inspired pieces. Rings, earrings and necklaces are core business, but clients often gravitate towards large sculptural earrings and bold, exaggerated bracelets that push high jewellery craftsmanship into more dramatic, couture-level expressions. For example, an heirloom jade bangle can be redesigned into a new piece, such as his Flowervines of Andromeda bangle, hinged and set with diamonds and lilac jade cabochons. “Bespoke jewellery gives them something mass-market brands cannot: the feeling of being seen, understood and reflected through a one-of-a-kind creation,” Lee says. His clients include gemstone collectors unsure what to create, and they brainstorm ideas together, or those who begin with rare stones from Lee’s own collection. Some clients commission bespoke wedding or birthday pieces, even gemstone Christmas baubles to hang on their trees. “Some turn up with specific ideas, but most of my bespoke clients love letting me take the lead,” Lee says. “When clients give me carte blanche, I can push my aesthetic further.” ‘People value new and modern as well as heritage and culture’ New jewellery brand Pen Mane, founded by Vincent Guy-Raffin and Calvin Wang, was established in Hong Kong in 2025. Named after a family summer home on the coast of Brittany, in France, where Guy-Raffin grew up, the company “is intentionally client-centric”. Personalisation, Guy-Raffin says, “speaks directly to our founding philosophy rather than an add-on service. Our goal has never been to impose a signature look that brands the wearer, but rather to serve as storytellers, translating an individual’s personal history, identity and emotion in a piece that becomes a natural extension of self.” His experience working with high- and fine-jewellery brands such as Boivin, Dior and Graff has given him an understanding of how markets evolve and how people like to live with their jewellery, and offering bespoke is now key to that. For the moment, “bespoke” to Guy-Raffin means reinterpreting pieces from existing collections. His work is largely diamond-centric, and so clients bring in coloured gemstones to create a variation of an established silhouette. Like Lee and Tan, he only works with certified, natural stones. Pen Mane recently won two design awards at The Couture Show in Las Vegas, America’s leading annual jewellery fair. Exhibiting there was an experiment, Wang says, “a meaningful leap into the unknown”. The pair have a community of private collectors in Hong Kong, which they want to expand with retail partners in the US, where there is a large established market of jewellery collecting. In Singapore, businesswomen place a strong emphasis on bespoke jewellery, and many designers offer this service. For Calla Lily founder-designer Tan, bespoke represents 90 per cent of her business, founded in 2018.
