Starting in bespoke design, transforming vintage pieces and loose stones into modern creations, provided momentum for her as a young designer. “It was very helpful in gaining insights into the various tastes in Singapore, where it is a melting pot of East meets West,” she says. “People value new and modern as well as heritage and culture.” Her designs currently fall into three categories: modern art deco, nature-inspired and modular travel jewellery, which allow for daily customisation. Some of her clients, she says, “have a vision of what they are after, but just can’t seem to find the right combination for that perfect piece”. The designers place firm boundaries on the commissions they accept, and none of them would accept a request to replicate another designer’s work. Their dream commissions, however, are another thing entirely: Lee wants to design a series of haute couture watches, while Guy-Raffin fantasises about resetting the 45.52-carat Hope Diamond, which is on permanent display at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of Natural History in Washington, in the United States. As for Tan, “A crown of the finest Paraibas [tourmalines] with water opals and antique-cut diamonds for the late Queen Elizabeth,” she says. “I always admired pictures of her elegance in her youth with her elaborate crowns, and I can just imagine how beautiful it could possibly be.”

title: Google says Gemini AI model breached real systems in security test
description: Asked to access a fictional firm with the same name as a real company, Gemini guessed a password and hacked into the real company’s website.
content: Google’s consumer AI model Gemini hacked multiple systems through guessing login credentials, the company said, the latest case of rogue AI cybersecurity transgressions, which have generated safety concerns. The hacks, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, took place in May and were discovered by Google in July. “In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, Google’s vice-president of security engineering, said in a statement on Friday. The hacks happened during the same tests run by the AI security vendor Irregular that led to breaches previously disclosed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms. Irregular confirmed on Friday that the breaches were all part of the same issue and that the firm had disclosed them to the relevant AI developers in late July. One of the Google breaches occurred when Gemini was asked to retrieve information from a fictional company that happened to have the same name as a real company. The model guessed a password to access the real company’s service. The other Gemini hacks occurred when the model performed web searches with the name of the company. Adkins said that led the model to public online repositories containing credentials belonging to other companies that it used to access more systems. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped,” she added, without specifying which organisations were breached. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes.” In July, two OpenAI models escaped the closed environment they were meant to stay in, got onto the internet on their own and broke into the internal systems of the AI platform Hugging Face. The incident fed worries that AI giants cannot keep their own models under control, as similar episodes have been reported at Anthropic and China’s Moonshot AI. “These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins emphasised. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei has called for an industry-wide slowdown in the development of the technology – a proposal endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and others. US President Donald Trump, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg are among those who have pushed back against the idea of new regulation, however, arguing among other things that companies should be capable of regulating themselves. Some AI upstarts have also warned that more regulations threaten to make it harder for smaller companies to compete against larger rivals. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: Friend, leader, mentor: how political veterans remember Tung Chee-hwa
description: Figures from Hong Kong and beyond reflect on Tung as a friend, city leader and elder statesman.
content: This weekend, Hong Kong mourns the loss of former chief executive and elder statesman Tung Chee-hwa. The shipping tycoon who became the city’s first leader after its transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997 died on September 8 at the age of 89, leaving a legacy of determined stewardship and dedicated public service. He is remembered for steering Hong Kong through uncharted waters following the end of colonial rule, as well as his tireless efforts as a state leader and business heavyweight to help repair, maintain and improve Sino-US relations. Tributes have been pouring in locally and from overseas to reflect the high regard in which he was held, many remembering him as a wise, kind and exceptionally hard-working leader with a deep love for Hong Kong and the country. He was a pioneering steward of the unprecedented “one country, two systems” experiment, the governing formula for Hong Kong that he oversaw in its initial application and supported in its continuing success. Tung’s tenure from 1997 to 2005 as chief executive was tested by a series of major challenges, from the Asian financial crisis and the deadly Sars epidemic to mass protests over national security legislation. He stumbled at times, drawing criticism, but was unwavering in his commitment to Hong Kong’s stability and prosperity, and initiated policies that laid the groundwork for the city’s current success. As a Shanghai-born patriot born into a shipping family, Tung had a strong network of influential global contacts. He put them to use in service of the nation in his lifelong efforts to advance dialogue between China and the US. He is one of the few Hong Kong politicians to have officially met two US presidents, Bill Clinton and George W Bush. This weekend, a state funeral will be held to honour Tung, who was also a former vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC). There will be a vigil on Saturday and a memorial on Sunday, while condolence books will be opened for the public at multiple venues from Friday to Sunday. Tung is the third Hongkonger to be accorded a state funeral, following industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Shi Taifeng, a Politburo member and top vice-chairman of the CPPCC, is overseeing the arrangements. The South China Morning Post is running a special commemorative print supplement on Saturday, sharing reflections from those who knew Tung personally. Join us for part one, which features tributes from past and present officials and other political figures. Read part two here. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here and here. Goh Chok Tong, emeritus senior minister and former prime minister of Singapore My friendship with Tung Chee-hwa goes back to the early 1970s, when we were both in the shipping industry. Together with three other shipping lines, we formed a container consortium in the Far East-Europe route. Our friendship developed and endured as we went on to lead Singapore and Hong Kong, respectively. CH first visited Singapore as chief executive in 1997, and I made my return visit as prime minister in 2000. In our numerous meetings, we discussed the challenges that Singapore and Hong Kong faced and explored opportunities to strengthen bilateral relations. Later, he was preoccupied with getting the United States and China to understand each other better. He was well-placed as he had influential friends in both countries. I have always enjoyed meeting CH. He was a helpful, sincere and trustworthy friend who exuded humility and warmth. I will miss him dearly. Leung Chun-ying, vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference A solemn tribute to Mr Tung Chee-hwa, the first chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, vice-chairman of the 10th to 13th National Committees of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), and vice-chairman of the Preparatory Committee for the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the National People’s Congress. Mr Tung spearheaded the establishment of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region and its government. Earning the highest trust of the nation, he implemented the principles of “one country, two systems”, “Hong Kong people administering Hong Kong”, and a high degree of autonomy, while charting the course for Hong Kong’s long-term development and addressing the city’s deep-rooted livelihood issues. Kind-hearted, wise, and principled, Mr Tung was a true exemplar of leadership and service. May Mr Tung rest in peace. (from Leung’s Facebook post) Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor, former chief executive of Hong Kong I deeply mourn the passing of Mr Tung Chee-hwa and extend my profound condolences to Mrs Tung and their family. As the first chief executive of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, Mr Tung guided Hong Kong into a new era under “one country, two systems” with profound patriotism, extensive international experience, and a humble approach to governance – a monumental legacy that serves our present and benefits generations to come. With insight into Hong Kong’s deep-seated social challenges, he mapped out long-term strategic plans for housing, education and elderly care. Having served as director of social welfare during his tenure, I profoundly felt his care for the elderly. As a younger fellow native of Zhoushan in Zhejiang, I will always remember Mr Tung as a truly benevolent elder. How fondly I cherish the memories of having lighthearted conversations with him at his home. I pay my highest respects and deepest tribute to Mr Tung Chee-hwa. Donald Tsang Yam-kuen, former chief executive of Hong Kong I first met CH in the 1990s, when we served together on the then Executive Council. From the outset, I was struck by his gentle grace and breadth of vision. He guided Hong Kong masterfully through the historic transition in 1997, setting out, with extraordinary foresight, his priorities for the administration of Hong Kong by the people of Hong Kong. Working under his leadership, I witnessed first-hand his selfless and tireless devotion. He worked long hours every day, through weekends and throughout the year; holidays scarcely featured during his term of office. Through his unwavering dedication, he transformed tertiary education, raising enrolment from 14 to 50 per cent. Drawing on his extensive experience and commercial networks, he opened vital diplomatic doors with the United States, creating valuable new opportunities for Hong Kong’s trade and strengthening bilateral relations. CH also successfully championed the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement, securing a vital economic foundation for Hong Kong’s development and closer integration with mainland China. When Hong Kong was battered by the Asian financial crisis, he gave me his unreserved support as we fought off unscrupulous speculators. And when the Sars epidemic struck, his quiet resolve helped steer us through the storm. I shall forever cherish CH’s gentle smile, gracious disposition, unyielding spirit and profound patriotism. He devoted his life to Hong Kong, and his legacy will endure. Andrew Li Kwok-nang, chief justice of Hong Kong from 1997 to 2010 I have known Mr Tung well for over 35 years. As chief executive, he respected the rule of law with an independent judiciary. He is one of the finest men I have the privilege of knowing. He was patriotic and served the motherland and Hong Kong with selfless dedication. He was a visionary leader who influenced the course of history. He had utmost integrity, courage, perseverance and wisdom. He always set a good example and had a great generosity of spirit. He was a gentleman in the Confucian tradition. I have never heard him bad-mouth any person. He always addressed the matter and not the individual person. Over the years, I learned a great deal from him. In particular, I learned the importance of humility and that, as a leader, one must have broad shoulders and put people in the right places. Henry Tang Ying-yen, former financial secretary of Hong Kong Mr Tung was a visionary leader with a warm heart. He was always kind, patient and thoughtful towards those around him. I was honoured to work with him, to benefit from his wisdom, and to be inspired by his persistence, impartiality and benevolence. Amid political pressure and economic challenges, he remained committed to protecting and preserving Hong Kong’s interests under “one country, two systems”. To me, Mr Tung demonstrated not only the qualities of great leadership, but also the values that truly elevate Hong Kong. He inspired and encouraged me to shoulder greater responsibilities as financial secretary during critical times, and I will never forget that. His devotion to Hong Kong and the motherland set an excellent example for all of us to follow. Mr Tung may be gone from this world, but he will never be gone from my heart. I believe the same is true for the people of Hong Kong. Bernard Charnwut Chan, former convenor of the Executive Council of Hong Kong Though my late parents were long-time friends of Mr Tung Chee-hwa and his wife Betty, my personal journey with him began when I joined the Legislative Council in 1998. Appointing me to the Executive Council in 2004 and later inviting me to Our Hong Kong Foundation in 2017, he gave me the privilege of observing his tireless dedication first-hand. Behind the scenes, Mr Tung worked round-the-clock with extraordinary magnanimity. He never harboured anger towards critics, striving instead to bring diverse stakeholders together to address deep-seated challenges in our economy, housing, and youth development. It was his evident authenticity and profound, genuine love for both our country and city that inspired so many of us to rally behind him and contribute. Even when he could have chosen a quiet retirement with his family, he continued to serve selflessly. Above all, Mr Tung was a kind man with a generous heart. I will forever cherish his warmth, wisdom and steadfast friendship. Regina Ip Lau Suk-yee, convenor of the Executive Council of Hong Kong I worked for Mr Tung for seven years as director of immigration and then as secretary for security. He was a visionary leader – the first to promote Hong Kong as a global tech hub. He had extensive global connections and Hong Kong benefited immensely from his international connectivity. He was highly respected by many global leaders. As a person, he was a caring and considerate boss. When I was studying at Stanford University, he visited me in my apartment and invited me to dinner in San Francisco from time to time. Frederick Ma Si-hang, chairman of the Hong Kong Trade Development Council Meeting Mr Tung Chee-hwa changed my life. His invitation to enter public service gave me a new purpose and a lasting sense of responsibility to Hong Kong. I deeply respect his dedication to Hong Kong and his vision for realising “one country, two systems”. His efforts to develop technology and innovation, his foresight in opening up the mainland market for Hong Kong, and his work to improve people’s lives are a powerful reminder of what public service means. What I cherish most is the man behind the public role. His integrity and sincerity have left an indelible impression on me, and his trust inspired me to persevere through difficulties and serve with dedication. To me, Mr Tung will always be more than the leader who brought me into government. He is someone whose example continues to guide and inspire me every day.

title: How will Beijing receive the most senior Taiwan official at Apec events this year?
description: Hung Sun-han will be the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te to travel to mainland China.
content: In a rare development, Taiwanese Labour Minister Hung Sun-han is expected to travel to Nanjing on Sunday, becoming the first cabinet-level official under William Lai Ching-te’s administration to visit mainland China. Hung will attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) ministerial meeting on Monday to discuss employment, vocational training, social security and the impact of artificial intelligence on jobs. Hung will be the most senior Taiwanese official to visit the mainland for Apec events this year. The island’s vice-minister of economic affairs, Lai Chien-hsin, took part in the energy ministerial meeting in Beijing last week and then chief trade negotiator Yang Jen-ni participated in a trade ministers’ meeting in Suzhou in May. While Hung’s visit is being closely watched for signs of a possible thaw in a prolonged cross-strait stand-off, analysts have cautioned against interpreting it as an icebreaking trip or a resumption of official exchanges between Taipei and Beijing. The trip will also take place just days before US President Donald Trump is expected to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, putting Taiwan under renewed scrutiny as the two powers seek to manage their differences. Ahead of his departure, Hung stressed that Taiwan was a full Apec member under the name “Chinese Taipei”. He said he would take part under the grouping’s established arrangements and the principles of “equal participation and reciprocal dignity”. Nevertheless, with official cross-strait dialogue suspended, Hung’s visit carries symbolic weight because no cabinet minister – particularly a political appointee – has travelled to the mainland since Lai took office in May 2024. “A small step by Hung Sun-han would be a big step for cross-strait relations,” said Lee Yen-hsiu, a lawmaker from the main opposition Kuomintang, a Beijing-friendly party. Lee questioned whether the trip signalled a change in the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) approach towards Beijing after more than two years of promoting its “resist China, oppose China” agenda. She said Hung’s visit could be seen as “a possible test by Lai of whether cross-strait relations could begin to thaw”. DPP lawmaker Wu Szu-yao urged Hung to remain alert to “potential personal safety concerns and the possibility of unequal treatment or politically motivated difficulties” while on the mainland. But DPP legislative caucus whip Chuang Jui-hsiung dismissed such concerns. “Are you kidding? If holding Apec in China meant there was a threat to someone’s personal safety, it wouldn’t just shock Taiwan – the whole world would be shocked by China,” Chuang said. Analysts said Taipei might hope the trip created an impression of easing tensions, particularly ahead of the Washington summit. “It is especially important before the sensitive Trump-Xi meeting to create an impression that Taiwan is not a troublemaker and hopes cross-strait relations can ease,” said Wang Kung-yi, head of the Taiwan International Strategic Study Society, a Taipei-based think tank. But Wang said the trip could not be regarded as a genuine advance because Hung was attending a multilateral meeting and not direct talks with Beijing. “If there were really a breakthrough, there would inevitably be substantive interactions, such as Hung meeting mainland officials,” he said. Li Da-jung, a professor of international relations at Tamkang University in New Taipei City, similarly argued that the arrangement was standard. “Taiwan is a full member of Apec, and to maintain its position in the international organisation, it has to send officials to attend the meeting,” Li said, adding that participation also helped maintain the island’s international visibility. More important for Taipei, he said, would be the consequences of the coming Trump-Xi summit. “Its impact on Taiwan remained uncertain, but Taipei would be watching closely to see whether Washington’s approach to the island – including pending arms sales – is affected by Trump’s talks with Xi,” Li said. Analysts also doubted Beijing would create difficulties for Hung over his entry arrangements. “Long-established arrangements have already governed participation in Apec meetings, and this is mainland China’s third time hosting the leaders’ meeting after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014,” Wang said. Hung should therefore be able to enter using his Apec invitation letter under existing arrangements instead of using a mainland-issued Taiwan compatriot permit, he added. Beijing has skirted questions over whether Hung must hold the permit. “Since 1991, Taiwan’s participation in Apec meetings and activities has been handled in accordance with the ‘one-China principle’ as well as the provisions and established practices of relevant Apec memorandums of understanding,” Chen Binhua, a spokesman for the State Council’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said last week. Zhu Fenglian, a spokeswoman for the Taiwan Affairs Office, reiterated on Wednesday that under the one-China principle, the “Taiwan region” took part in Apec under the name “Chinese Taipei” and as a regional economy. Taipei rejects that interpretation, saying its 1991 Apec accession memorandum contains no reference to the “one-China principle” and provides for participation on an equal basis with other members. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Wang said the DPP could benefit politically if Beijing created difficulties for Hung – and thus Beijing was unlikely to take action that could inadvertently help the party electorally. Huang Kwei-bo, a diplomacy professor at National Chengchi University in Taipei, said the DPP government was likely to stress that Hung was attending an international meeting rather than engaging in bilateral cross-strait exchanges. He also cautioned against using the trip as a barometer of cross-strait relations because Beijing, as this year’s Apec host, was expected to invite representatives from all member economies, and Hung was only visiting because the Apec meeting happened to be held on the mainland. Huang said Taipei’s choice of representative to the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen in November would be a more significant test.

title: Opinion | Why the Global South keeps its doors wide open to Russia
description: Far from being isolated, Moscow’s relationships across the non-Western world are a geopolitical constant the West cannot break.
content: Over the past two weeks, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin staged a major diplomatic blitz. Across three events in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Vladivostok in Russia’s Far East and New Delhi, India, as well as a state visit by Vietnam’s leader, he met some 18 heads of state. Among them were the leaders of heavyweights of the Global South such as China, India, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia and Turkey, just to name a few. The Ukraine war certainly featured in these conversations. Russia has recently ramped up its attacks, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up losing the war. Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit. Here’s why Russia is deepening ties with many partners in the Global South – and what these meetings tell us about the impacts of Western efforts to isolate Putin. Fuel and energy Fuel and energy security is becoming a mutual concern for both Moscow and its partners in the Global South. Ukraine’s deliberate offensive campaign targeting Russia’s oil refining capacity has resulted in noticeable fuel shortages in the country. It has forced the Russian government to import refined fuel from countries it has traditionally exported to, such as Belarus, Turkey and India. At the same time, the Kremlin continues to push for the expansion of its energy exports. This includes finalising the contract to build the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which intends to deliver 50 billion cubic metres (1.77 trillion cubic feet) of natural gas annually from Russia to China via Mongolia. Last week, Russia also signed a deal to establish a new strategic oil reserves hub in Vietnam. Moscow is also expanding cooperation on nuclear power, which was part of the discussion agenda with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Vietnam’s President To Lam (during his state visit to Russia), and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Deeper ties The ongoing sanctions war between Russia and the West has made its economic and trade relations with the Global South pivotal for the country’s survival and future development. Two friendly interstate bodies, in which Russia plays core roles, are becoming especially important. The first is Brics, a group of 11 economies comprising Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. The Brics economies now account for about 40 per cent of global gross domestic product. Last year, mutual trade turnover between Brics member states exceeded US$1 trillion for the first time. The second is the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. This is a political and security bloc spanning countries in Europe, Asia and the Indo-Pacific. According to Putin, Russia’s trade turnover with the SCO exceeded US$400 billion in 2025. Overall, Asia accounted for 73.4 per cent of Russia’s trade turnover last year. It’s no surprise that Moscow’s trade links with Asia featured in almost every conversation in Bishkek, Vladivostok and Delhi. Bypassing disruption Despite its friendly ties with Iran, Russia and its clients aren’t immune from the ongoing disruption to transport and trade routes through the Middle East. To mitigate these risks, Russia is actively lobbying two relatively new transcontinental transit networks. The first is the 7,200km (4,470-mile) combined rail-road-maritime International North-South Transport Corridor. This route connects Russia’s Baltic Sea ports with Mumbai in India, via the Caspian Sea and Iran. Russia reportedly discussed this route with the Indian and Iranian delegations this month. The second is the 5,600km (3,480-mile) maritime Northern Sea Route, which connects Asia’s ice-free ports with Russian and European ports as part of a maritime passage across the Arctic Ocean. In August, Beijing launched commercial operations along this route for the first time. Political signalling Russia walked away from this month’s diplomatic blitz with some clear wins. In addition to securing US$7.7 billion worth of investments in Vladivostok, along with some lucrative deals with Vietnam, Putin could also claim some political success. First, although challenging at times, Putin’s interactions with his counterparts showcased how Moscow’s relationship with major non-Western international players remains a geopolitical constant, even in the fifth year of the Ukraine war. For leaders of emerging centres of global influence, whether India’s Modi, Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto or Vietnam’s Lam, interacting with Russia forms part of their countries’ foreign policy approach based on the notion of “strategic autonomy”. This sends a powerful signal to the United States and its allies, amid the latest round of high-level consultations involving the CIA and US Treasury chiefs and their Russian counterparts. Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump sent his own personal envoys to Moscow and made a follow-up phone call to Putin. Second, Russia and its core partners in Asia jointly signalled they would continue to maintain strategic partnership links. This includes the question of importing Russia’s fossil fuels, nuclear power and other goods, and exporting processed fuel back to Russia. Fuel security is particularly relevant to the Russian authorities’ attempts to stabilise the domestic situation. The Kremlin is under pressure to mitigate the aftershocks of the escalating war with Ukraine amid coming parliamentary elections from Friday to Sunday. Concerns persist Still, many in the Global South remain concerned about the growing impact of what seems to be becoming a forever war in and over Ukraine. The latest round of tit-for-tat attacks against merchant shipping in the Black Sea triggered fears of grain and wheat shortages. In mid-November, China will host the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. This is tipped to be a possible venue for the first trilateral meeting between Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump. Here, Moscow might feel increasing pressure to settle the war by political means from its partners. These countries don’t want to feel the effects of the sanctions war between the West and Russia, let alone be dragged into it. Alexey D Muraviev is senior research fellow at the School of Arts and Humanities at Edith Cowan University. This article was first published by The Conversation.

title: Pickle-flavoured tart, anyone? Japanese convenience stores turn to AI for novelty sweets
description: Lawson is launching three new food items created using AI around the theme: ‘What on earth is this? But it’s delicious’.
content: Fears that advanced artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity have dominated global headlines, but in Japan the technology is being used for a sweeter purpose – developing never-before-seen convenience store desserts. For customers tired of the usual egg sandwiches and rice balls, major chains are turning to AI to develop products, including some unexpected flavours. Lawson, one of the country’s biggest convenience store operators, said on Tuesday it would roll out three new food items, including a pickle-flavoured lemon tart and a bread roll filled with red bean paste, margarine and yogurt cream. These products, to be launched this month in Tokyo and neighbouring regions, were created using AI around the theme: “What on earth is this? But it’s delicious.” “To generate ideas unconstrained by existing ways of thinking or market trends, we used AI during brainstorming, without relying on past sales figures or market data,” a company press release said. Meanwhile, rival FamilyMart said they fed sales data into AI to help develop a new dessert – a French-style canele pastry made with dough containing sweet potato puree and topped with caramel sauce. The dessert would hit shelves nationwide next week, a spokeswoman said, adding that the company had wanted to create something new but likely to sell. Like Lawson’s products, AI was used primarily for brainstorming, while human specialists were still involved in product development, according to the company. It will not be FamilyMart’s first dessert product suggested by AI. In July, the chain test-launched its first AI experiment – a biscuit sandwich filled with thick milk cream. It proved a success, so the company decided to properly pursue AI in product development and planned to launch more of the items in the coming months, the spokeswoman said. The rapidly advancing capabilities of AI have sparked a global panic in recent days, as researchers warn of the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems that could evade human control. Leading US AI labs have called for a coordinated slowdown of their cutting-edge work, while debate rages over how governments should regulate the technology.

title: Letters | Why a Chinese farmer’s reunion with a US teacher moved me to tears
description: Readers discuss an American’s return to a part of China he helped transform, and how the country is taking climate change seriously.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Last month, American educator Ronald Sakolsky travelled back to China’s Mu Us Desert for an emotional reunion with national “model worker” Yin Yuzhen, 26 years after he raised US$5,000 to help her plant trees. Watching the two embrace amid the towering canopy they built together, I found myself moved to tears. Their story involved an act of selfless generosity, an unyielding vow and a cross-border friendship that endured decades of silence. In the late 1990s, Sakolsky, then teaching in central China’s Henan province, watched a television programme about Yin and her husband’s punishing, solitary battle against the encroaching Mu Us Desert. When Sakolsky visited the desert in 2000, holding fragile green shoots amid howling winds, he shook his head in quiet disbelief, viewing it as an impossible dream. Yet his contribution planted the seeds of a miracle. Yin made a silent promise to prove that a humble Chinese farmer could keep her word. For decades, lacking machinery, she and her husband relied on manual labour – and steel bars, shovels and water buckets – to battle sandstorms and freezing winters. Crucially, Yin never diverted a single yuan of the donation to her family’s comfort; all the money went towards the trees, transforming the barren wasteland into a flourishing green space. For over a quarter of a century, Yin never forgot her distant benefactor. When Sakolsky accepted her invitation to visit this year, her household spent months preparing. Knowing that Sakolsky had undergone cervical spine surgery, she arranged to have the rugged dirt road near her home flattened to ensure a smoother ride. She prepared the hand-pulled noodles he loved decades ago, picked fresh fruit from her orchard and stitched traditional embroidered shoe insoles. When they finally embraced at the airport, tears fell freely. Yin represents all the Chinese farmers who have reclaimed green spaces from the desert. Yet, the true power of her and Sakolsky’s story lies in its universality. Behind grand geopolitical headlines, individual human hearts remain capable of profound empathy and steadfast honour. A simple act of kindness from a foreigner met an unwavering spirit of perseverance, proving that even in the driest desert, humanity can bloom. Jianlu Bi, senior fellow, Institute for Policy Studies, Washington Like China, countries must get tough on climate change Hong Kong recorded a maximum temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) on August 9, the hottest since records began in 1884. Some people have been taking refuge from the heat in shopping centres while others insist on not turning on the air conditioning. This is the hottest weather many of us have ever experienced. The heat gripping the planet is a global emergency and demands a global response. Global warming is a known crisis, but this year it has found a powerful partner. The World Meteorological Organization says a strong El Nino is expected to intensify in the coming months, with above-normal temperatures forecast across most land areas. Europe and North America have also experienced severe heat. This is precisely what the world has to confront, urgently and collectively. China has responded to the challenges of climate change with good governance. In 2018, the National People’s Congress amended the constitution to formally enshrine “ecological civilisation” as a national principle. That constitutional commitment has produced tangible results. In 2025, China added more than 430 gigawatts of new wind and solar capacity, a record high, pushing renewables past 60 per cent of the country’s total installed power capacity and generating nearly 4 trillion kilowatt-hours of electricity. Most significantly, China’s landmark Ecological and Environmental Code took effect on August 15. Spanning 1,242 articles, it consolidates more than 30 existing laws, 100 regulations and 1,000 local rules into a single unified legal framework covering pollution control, ecological protection and low-carbon development. It is a pioneering codification effort, turning years of policy pledges into an enforceable statute. None of this cools heated cities overnight and neither does it mean the work is finished as enforcement gaps and overlapping penalties remain real challenges. Instead, China’s shift from constitutional principle to detailed legal code shows what sustained follow-through looks like. As heat records keep falling worldwide, the world would do well to treat environmental protection with the same seriousness. Caleb Hon Chi-wang, youth ambassador for the Hong Kong Association for External Friendship

title: South Korea justice minister nominee withdraws over Covid-19 drug trial scandal
description: Kim Seung-won, who has denied the allegations, says he does not want to add any burden to President Lee’s administration.
content: South Korea’s Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won withdrew his nomination on Saturday following allegations concerning his involvement in a Covid-19 treatment and approval of its clinical trials. “After much deliberation, I decided to step down as the nominee for minister of the justice ministry. I apologise for failing to live up to your expectations,” Kim said during a press conference at the National Assembly. Kim, who said he did not want to add any burden to Lee Jae Myung’s administration, criticised a conservative lawmaker who had accused him of lobbying regulators over a drug trial and of financial irregularities. Kim ⁠has denied the allegations. “I gravely accept that I did not ‌meet the public’s expectations, and I will deeply reflect on my shortcomings,” ‌Kim said. The two-term lawmaker of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) served as a judge at the Jeonju District Court and the Suwon District Court before joining the presidential office under the liberal Moon Jae-in administration, where he worked in the office of political affairs. He was elected to the 21st National Assembly in 2020 and later served as DPK’s legal affairs committee chief. On Friday, Lee admitted to failures in the cabinet candidate vetting process. “We did our best, but unexpected issues continued to surface … Failing to prepare for those aspects was our fault,” Lee said during a press conference at Cheong Wa Dae, adding that “we are currently working to re-examine our personnel system”. Lee faces declining approval ratings amid resistance to his proposed policies and contentious reform efforts, as well as concerns over his cabinet nominees. A Gallup Korea poll released on Friday put Lee’s public approval at 37 per cent, the lowest since he took office in June 2025, a decline pollsters have partly linked to criticism over his personnel appointments. Addressing Kim’s nominee issue, Lee said: “While we believed we had made the best possible selection, various controversies have emerged during the public confirmation process.” The scandal surrounding Kim unfolded against the backdrop of an unusually high attrition rate among Lee’s cabinet nominees. The most recent casualty was Yong Hye-in, who stepped down as gender equality minister nominee on Sunday amid public criticism over her decision to retain her parliamentary seat alongside the cabinet post, prompting opposition parties to renew their attacks on Lee’s vetting process. Kim’s and Yong’s exits bring to five the number of ministerial nominees who have failed to be appointed since Lee took office last year, following education minister nominee Lee Jin-sook and gender equality minister nominee Kang Sun-woo in June 2025, and planning and budget minister nominee Lee Hye-hoon in December 2025. The rate compares unfavourably with past administrations over equivalent periods: Moon had three failed nominations over a similar time frame, while Yoon Suk-yeol, Park Geun-hye and Lee Myung-bak each had two – a record critics attribute to a shallow talent pool within the ruling camp. This article is a combination of articles published by The Korea Times. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: ‘In hard times, your honour shines’: Jack Ma pays tribute to Tung Chee-hwa
description: Alibaba Group co-founder looks back on his ties to Hong Kong’s first chief executive, spanning business and philanthropy.
content: Alibaba Group co-founder Jack Ma reflects on his ties to Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa. Those connections spanned both business and philanthropy, encompassing Tung’s eight years on Alibaba’s board of directors and his inspirational role in Ma’s youth entrepreneurship foundation for local youths. Ma’s reflections are part of the South China Morning Post’s special commemorative print supplement published on Saturday. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here, here and here. I knew Mr Tung for many years. When he served as the chief executive of Hong Kong, Alibaba was expanding its businesses in the city. As we pursued our mission to “make it easy to do business anywhere”, Mr Tung offered us invaluable guidance and care. After he stepped down as chief executive, I invited him to serve as one of the inaugural independent directors on Alibaba’s board in 2014, a role he graciously accepted. We were privileged to work alongside him for eight years. During his tenure as an independent director, Mr Tung was exceptionally conscientious and dedicated. With profound wisdom and vision, he staunchly supported Alibaba’s innovations across various fields. He appreciated the core values of integrity and kindness that define Alibaba and he looked forward to seeing the company expand globally and earn the world’s respect as a Chinese enterprise. Although Mr Tung has passed away, Alibaba’s continued development serves to realise his aspirations. I believe this is the finest tribute we can pay to his memory. The qualities Mr Tung demonstrated during our years together had a profound impact on both me and Alibaba. He possessed a deep devotion to the country, matched with a forward-looking, global perspective. He was a tireless innovator who remained pragmatic and humble. He viewed the encouragement and mentorship of young people as his lifelong, unwavering duty. Over a decade ago, inspired by his vision and call to action, we launched the Alibaba Hong Kong Young Entrepreneurs Foundation to help young people realise their dreams of innovation and entrepreneurship. This foundation stands as part of Mr Tung’s enduring legacy. Gone is the man, enduring is his legacy. Standing steady for the nation and city; in hard times, your honour shines. Sharing great responsibilities shoulder to shoulder, as a mentor and friend, your unwavering devotion will be remembered.

title: Chinese miners partner to tap Tibet’s critical minerals amid Beijing’s resource push
description: Xizang Zhihui Mining and Zhaojin Nonferrous Mining will pursue joint investment in mining projects in the autonomous region.
content: Two established Chinese mining companies plan to jointly acquire and develop gold, copper and other critical mineral projects in Tibet, marking the latest corporate push to tap the region’s resources as Beijing seeks to strengthen domestic supplies of strategic raw materials. Privately controlled Xizang Zhihui Mining and state-owned Zhaojin Nonferrous Mining signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement on Thursday to pursue joint investment in mining projects in the autonomous region. In a statement, Zhihui Mining said the partners would target reserves of strategic minerals including copper, molybdenum, chromium, antimony, gold, tungsten and zinc. “Importantly for the market, the joint venture will not be restricted to Tibet,” the company said. “The model, once proven, could be replicated for high-quality non-ferrous mining projects elsewhere in mainland China, further expanding the scope of investment.” The agreement is the latest example of state-owned and private-sector miners taking part in Beijing’s most recent nationwide drive to expand mineral exploration, which began in 2021. The campaign has gained urgency as competition intensifies over rare and critical minerals used in military equipment, advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies, particularly amid growing geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about global supply-chain security. “Tibet is not only an important national ecological-security barrier, but also a strategic reserve base for the country’s natural resources,” Zhihui Mining said. At least nine strategic minerals found in Tibet rank among China’s top three by known resource volumes, according to regional authorities. The region ranks first nationwide for identified resources of copper, chromium, antimony, salt-lake lithium and boron. These minerals are used extensively in power grids, electric vehicle batteries, renewable energy equipment, aerospace, semiconductors, defence systems and high-performance alloys. “Tibet has a significant and diverse mineral resource base,” said Liu Wenjing, a member of the AIFC Executive Council for the Mining Sector and founder and principal adviser of Elistra Advisory Limited. “Copper, chromium, lithium, lead, zinc and gold are among its notable mineral resources, and there remains considerable exploration potential. “What the market is increasingly looking at is not simply one or two metals, but a broader group of minerals that are becoming increasingly important to the energy transition, advanced manufacturing and supply-chain security,” she said. “Tibet has significant exposure to several of these strategic and critical minerals.” The China Geological Survey said last year that more than 20 million tonnes of copper resources had been newly identified across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau since the start of the country’s 14th five-year plan in 2021. The public institution under China’s Ministry of Natural Resources estimated the plateau’s total copper potential at 150 million tonnes and said the area could become a world-class copper resource base. “Having substantial resources underground does not necessarily mean they are straightforward to develop,” Liu said. “High-altitude operating conditions, infrastructure and logistics constraints in some areas, environmental and permitting requirements, and development costs all need to be taken into account. “The next thing to watch is whether this framework can translate into specific, investable mineral projects,” she added. “Then the key questions will be the scale and grade of the resources, the stage of exploration, permitting status and ultimately the development economics.” Listed in Hong Kong in 2025, Tibet-focused Zhihui Mining operates the Mengya’a zinc-lead-copper mine in Nagqu. Its open-pit operation began production in 2007, while its underground section entered commercial production in 2025, giving the mine a combined ore-supply capacity of about 400,000 tonnes a year. Zhaojin Nonferrous, meanwhile, develops gold and base-metal resources, operating mines across several of China’s mineral-rich provinces, including Yunnan, Guizhou and Shandong. Tibet is already home to some of China’s largest state-owned mining operations. Among them is the Yulong mine, which contains copper, molybdenum, iron and gold and produced about 152,000 tonnes of copper in 2025.

title: Your Voice: Can-do robots, SBTI and labels, balanced diets and the effects of AI use (letters)
description: This week, students reflect on life lessons and a personality test, and consider artificial intelligence and how what we eat and drink affects our brains and bo
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Bonny Liu, SKH Leung Kwai Yee Secondary School
Using two robots, Hong Kong artist Orson Li tells us a story about life. The first of the robots is Canbot, a miniature sculpture, only 3.5cm tall, made by folding discarded aluminium soda cans.
The second is Nick the Lost Robot, a character illustrated by Li that has gone from picture books to the city’s public education programmes. It is also one of Hong Kong’s distinctive home-grown licensed IPs.
Li graduated from the University of California, Los Angeles with a degree in economics and worked as an auditor before turning to art and design.
His journey reflects a broader shift in Hong Kong’s creative economy, from making parts for other companies to creating original art toys and character-based intellectual property.
Canbot represents a “can-do” spirit, and Nick the Lost Robot is its personified extension. Li explained that just as a discarded soda can could be upcycled into valuable artwork, human life could also be changed.
That idea is seen in the five core elements of Nick’s story: dreams, beliefs, time, imagination and a positive mindset.
Nick’s story does not avoid wounds. Instead, Li places one on the most visible part of the character: the lightning-shaped crack on his chest, which symbolises turning imperfection into strength.
Li noted that everyone gets hurt while growing up, but standing up again makes us stronger. He added that the robots do not compare themselves with others but focus on completing their own tasks.
He summed up the lessons humans could learn from the robots: do not compare, do not judge and do not complain. From auditor to creator, what Li really offers is not just a toy but a way to show how adversity can push us onwards.
Sylvia Xu, Hangzhou Yungu School (Zhejiang)
Recently, a new personality test – the Silly Big Personality Test (SBTI) – has gone viral on Chinese social media.
WeChat and RedNote are filled with posts of netizens sharing their test results. However, some of the test results use labels like FAKE and JOKE-R, which have sparked debate.
While some people find them funny and entertaining, others worry that these labels may influence how young people see themselves and others. Some experts have warned that online labels may become a trap. I strongly agree.
The SBTI is a play on the popular Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) personality test. According to Ding Daoshi, a veteran analyst in the internet sector, test results have become social currency.
He said the memes-based quiz “rewrites the logic of youth socialising: the meme is the message and participation is more important than the result itself. Taking the test becomes a lawful ticket to belonging.” Teenagers may feel pressured to take a test in order to take part in their peers’ conversations.
I am also concerned about the illogical nature of the test result, as it seems to pull from an online encyclopaedia of memes, giving users different personality types on each try. It captures only a moment or aspect of the test taker, rendering the label meaningless.
But while the SBTI labels may not be scientifically accurate, they do encourage self-reflection and social interaction. SBTI labels do not have rigid definitions, and this creates a low-stress space where people can explore various sides of themselves.
During the peak of SBTI’s popularity, I took the test out of curiosity. My result surprised me. I felt it deepened my self-awareness and gave me a humorous and lighthearted perspective. The test neither confirmed my identity nor defined who I was, but it helped me become aware of traits and characteristics I had not considered before.
Additionally, another merit of these labels lies in their ability to establish connections.
In today’s fast-paced online culture, bold yet funny personality labels provide an easy topic for conversation and help people express themselves more comfortably.
I shared my test results with my classmates and friends, which led to unexpected connections with old and new friends. We compared the “labels” and used them to better understand each other.
Labels like the SBTI types are neither entirely harmful nor entirely beneficial. They reflect young people’s desire to understand themselves and one another. What is most important is remaining self-aware. Labels can promote self-expression and connection but they should never become the final definition of who we are.
Sunny Chan San-yeung, St Mary’s Canossian College
At 9am, do you feel like your brain is running on only 2 per cent battery? Many of us rely on fast food, snacks and heavy caffeine to survive the day. But a poor diet will affect your school performance, sleep and mental health.
On one hand, junk food often saves time. Just grab a snack and you’re done! But this can significantly hurt your health. Fast food and sugary drinks only give us energy for a short amount of time. Then, we crash: drained, irritated and unfocused.
Over time, poor nutrition leads to stress, insomnia and even depression.
Major advantages of fuelling up on balanced, nutritious food are that it sharpens your memory, improves your concentration and maintains your mental stability. Eating nutritious food before a huge exam is like a secret cheat code for hitting peak mental alertness and memory.
Upgrading your diet does not have to be complicated and costly. Start by always eating a quick and healthy breakfast, for instance, a boiled egg or an apple. Drop your daily sugar intake by cutting out Coke, Fanta and other unhealthy drinks – even Coke Zero! For snacks, try fruits and nuts instead of chips.
Eating healthily is about creating habits that help you feel and perform better.
Elidi Yang Ya-ching, French International School
A recent study by MIT Media Lab, a research laboratory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, reported that excessive reliance on artificial intelligence (AI) may contribute to “cognitive atrophy”. This means our critical thinking skills are weakening as well as our ability to comprehend and assess.
The study was reported on in The Harvard Gazette, which asked ChatGPT whether AI makes us dumber or smarter. I asked two AI assistants the same.
First, the Chinese start-up DeepSeek replied “both”, saying that AI’s effect on us comes down to what we use it for. For example, if AI always corrects our grammar, our brain will begin to shut down the section we use to spot and fix errors.
DeepSeek also suggested AI can help us become smarter if we use it as a personal tutor.
Google Gemini had a similar response: “It depends on whether it is used as a tool or a crutch”.
Are we using AI for help or are we depending on it to fix our problems for us? At the end of the day, AI use seems inevitable as we keep up with technological advancements. But it is our choice whether it affects us negatively or positively.

title: Protesters surround Kennedy Centre over Trump demolition fears
description: The Kennedy Centre board voted to close the centre indefinitely after a court blocked its plans to return Trump’s name to the building.
content: Thousands of people joined outside the John F. Kennedy Centre for the Performing Arts on Friday evening to protest President Donald Trump’s plans for the facility, lending their voices to a chorus of organisations and individuals who have been horrified that he might make good on his threat to close and tear down the storied institution. The crowd streamed in from the nearest subway stop, crowding streets in the Foggy Bottom area of Washington and locking down traffic as they walked, many carrying signs, as they joined in “Hands Around the Kennedy Centre”. Many carried signs, wore costumes and booed when the president was mentioned during the programme. Chris Raleigh, co-founder of Hands Off the Arts, which set up the gathering, said in an interview that he hoped the event would show that people were willing to fight to keep Trump’s plans for the building at bay. One of the most iconic buildings on the Potomac River waterfront, the Kennedy Centre has been a focus of Trump’s remake of Washington since 2025, when he began installing favourites onto its governing board. Late last year, he had his name placed on the centre. A judge ruled that Trump’s name was illegally added and ordered it removed. The Kennedy Centre board, which is aligned with the president, voted on Tuesday to close the centre indefinitely for repairs hours after US District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked its plans to return Trump’s name to the building. On Thursday, the judge ordered the Kennedy Centre to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major physical changes to the building, including demolishing it. Raleigh said he, like others, was concerned that Trump could take the step without notifying the court. “Look at the East Wing,” he said. “We got up one morning and there was a giant hole there.” Raleigh said the Kennedy Centre was more in the public eye than the East Wing was. He added he did not believe the president fully understood why people were so upset “but that’s our job, right? This may be the line that no one expected but this is where the line is going to be”. Importance of arts Protesters talked about the importance of the centre as the pinnacle of the nation’s performing arts world. Bud Wilkinson, a local member of the arts community, set up a chalkboard with Trump’s name written on it hundreds of times. Protesters flocked to him to erase the names and replace them with hearts. “The Kennedy Centre is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” Wilkinson said. “This is not just about putting the president’s name on the Kennedy Centre. It’s about censoring the performances and the programming. That’s what started all this. So that’s what the nitty-gritty really is about. So I want to replace all of this with love. That’s why there’s a heart.” Alina Baciu talked about the opportunities and relationships that students at the Duke Ellington School of the Arts had with the centre and how those relationships might be impacted by what was going on. Her daughter had numerous opportunities to take advantage of all the centre had to offer as a student at Duke Ellington, she said. “They borrowed the beautiful costumes and the beautiful dresses from the Washington National Opera for their performances at Duke Ellington,” she said. They also performed on the centre’s Millennium Stage. “All of those things have gone away because of this craziness. And it just hurts my heart.” Laura Steinberg, a volunteer for the last 10 years, said the loss of performances has already been heart-wrenching. “This reminds me of that picture from Tiananmen Square, where that young man stood in front of the tank,” she said of the throngs present. “This was my visceral response to this. I’ll stand in front of the wrecking ball if it’s going to come to that. My guess is many of these people would come down because we saw what he did to the East Wing. Nobody thought he would actually do it. So I think the shock has mobilised people.” Friday’s event followed a tumultuous week in federal courts in Washington where filings and counter-filings flooded the courts as the administration continued to push for the president’s vanity projects. The administration has made substantive steps to begin work on a number of projects, despite the fact they are still being litigated. Such projects include Trump’s triumphal arch, and the administration’s takeover of East Potomac Golf Links and the US Institute of Peace. Speaking from the Oval Office, Trump said he was willing to save the centre, which he said was losing money. He did not address a question about demolishing it. “We have a lot of people working very hard on it to save it,” he said. “I can save it easily, but why should we be doing that and then raise money for the rest of our lives to keep it afloat? Because that’s what you have to do, if we get no recognition. I think the Trump administration should be recognised as having saved the Kennedy Centre.”

title: Postcard from Nagoya: Asian Games opening hour nears, but teething problems remain
description: The opening ceremony takes place on Saturday, but some athletes have already competed and bowed out, and then there are transport issues.
content: The Asian Games opening ceremony at Paloma Mizuho Stadium on Saturday will fire the starting gun on the first official days of competition in Nagoya and Tokyo, even if some athletes have already finished their events. Various team sports such as basketball, football and volleyball are working their way through the group stages, while some poor unfortunates, such as Hong Kong’s Shum Chun-hei and Liu Hei-yu, have already competed and bowed out. The pair were taking part in the modern pentathlon, which is making its Games debut, and did not qualify for the medal round on Sunday. Would you stay for the opening, or in their case, closing, ceremony? As usual, the media has descended in their thousands to cover the regional sporting bonanza, although with some events based in Tokyo, the need to go to pick up accreditation in Nagoya caused a certain amount of irritation. Previously, at the Olympics in Paris and before that Tokyo, and at the Games three years ago in mainland China, most credentials were sent to a journalist’s point of origin long before their departure on their overseas mission. With Japan’s capital hosting diving, swimming and equestrian events, the bibs photographers have to wear were also supposed to be available at Tokyo Aquatics Centre, only for journalists to discover on arrival banks of deserted help desks and service tents. “No one was working, and it wasn’t even 7pm yet,” one journalist said. “There were some other staff, but they knew nothing about those bibs, and they had no idea when the service tents would resume. “All of them keep speaking in Japanese and don’t care whether you understand or not.” Just like other years, free shuttle buses connect official hotels, venues and the main press centre, but are certainly not up to the host nation’s famously fastidious approach to punctuality. On the bright side, everyone is being treated equally. Standing alongside the media’s massed ranks waiting for a connecting bus to the Aichi International Arena was the Japan women’s basketball team. Saving the best for last, of course. And then there is the technology. This time around a different login is required at each of the venues for the Wi-fi essential for the media to tell the stories of the day in a timely fashion. Quite what happened to the universal passwords that solved that particular problem at the previous edition in 2023, and then in France two years ago, is anyone’s guess.

title: Foreign carer scheme may drive up wages, leave poor without help, employers warn
description: Hong Kong will admit foreign carers with more advanced training and experience in elderly care under pilot scheme unveiled in policy address.
content: A new pilot scheme to bring in foreign domestic carers for the elderly to deal with an ageing population could disrupt Hong Kong’s existing helper market, driving up wages and putting care beyond the reach of low-income older residents, some employers and agencies have warned. They said the measure, announced by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in his policy address on Wednesday, was likely to prompt existing helpers to demand higher pay or quit to take up the new employment opportunity, adding to families’ financial burden. Authorities revealed on Friday that the minimum wage for carers under the pilot scheme would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that for existing helpers. The current minimum allowable wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month. Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Domestic Helpers Association, said 30 per cent of the city’s more than 378,000 foreign domestic helpers were already caring for elderly people, questioning the need for a separate category of workers. “There are many low-income people in Hong Kong who are retired but need a domestic worker to take care of them,” she said. “But with expected rising wages for workers, how can the government help these families? The new measure could lead to only the well-off being able to afford it.” Yung added that some employers feared helpers would move to the new scheme to earn more, leaving families struggling to recruit workers to care for children and other family members in need. She also questioned whether authorities could monitor whether carers had completed the required training and met the qualification requirements before arriving in Hong Kong under the scheme. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that the newly created jobs were unlikely to have an impact on the helpers’ market. He said existing helpers hoping to switch to the new role would have to return to their home country to receive relevant training and meet other requirements before they could return to Hong Kong to take up the carer job. Lee announced that the government would admit carers with more advanced training and experience in elderly care on a pilot basis, under a scheme modelled on the city’s existing foreign domestic helper regime, to help meet the home-care needs of older residents. A government source said those employed under the new scheme, to be launched next year, must have experience in caring for the elderly and undergo relevant training in their home countries. Thomas Chan Tung-fung, chairman of the Hong Kong Union of Employment Agencies, said it was expected that carers admitted under the new scheme would be paid more. “If you require a worker, in addition to doing housework, to also have special skills such as medical care skills, the worker will require a higher salary,” he said. Chan said helpers equipped with such skills currently earned about HK$1,500 to HK$2,500 a month above the minimum allowable wage. “Currently, 30 per cent of helpers are caring for elderly residents or patients, most of them earning a monthly salary of HK$5,100. If the new carer scheme is implemented in the future, it might lead workers doing the same type of job to question why there is unequal pay for equal work,” he said. This could prompt some helpers to demand a pay rise or quit to join the new scheme, he said. “It could inadvertently drive up costs for employers,” he said. While acknowledging the demand for elderly care in ageing Hong Kong, Chan urged authorities to provide allowances for families under financial pressure to hire carers under the scheme. Phobsuk Gasing, chairwoman of the Federation of Asian Domestic Workers Unions, also questioned the necessity of the new scheme, calling instead for recognition of current helpers’ work through better wages. “Domestic workers have already been doing this job. Our skills should be recognised with better pay,” she said. The pilot scheme was among a series of measures Lee announced in the policy address to build an age-friendly society. In Hong Kong, the number of people aged 65 and above is projected to nearly double from 1.45 million in 2021 to 2.74 million by 2046, when more than one in three residents will be elderly. Despite concerns from employers and helpers, experts and NGOs said the new scheme to bring in skilled domestic carers could help meet some families’ elderly care needs but called for more to be done. Chou Kee-lee, chair professor of social policy at the Education University of Hong Kong, said the scheme would make it easier for households to find workers specifically trained to care for older family members. “The scheme will enable a systematic approach with clearer standards for assessing whether carers are qualified to perform more complex care procedures,” he said. Chou suggested that authorities model the qualifications for foreign carers on the requirements for workers caring for elderly residents in the city’s care homes, which he said would increase public confidence in them. But he added that the measure would mainly benefit better-off households, as low-income families might not be able to afford carers under the scheme, calling for more support for these families. The Society for Community Organisation described the pilot scheme as an innovative approach to meeting the home-care needs of older residents but suggested that the government subsidise people to hire carers. It also urged the government to ensure the workers possessed basic local language communication skills and training in medical or caregiving work to meet older residents’ needs.

title: Chinese scientists find first evidence of ancient nose-chopping punishment for cattle thieves
description: Under the rule of the King of Qin (247 BC–221 BC), severed noses accumulated like mountain peaks, and carts overflowed with amputated feet.
content: Stealing someone’s cattle is a serious crime, and in many places, the thief would end up in jail. However, ancient Chinese justice could result in a truly horrific form of mutilation: the amputation of the nose. This harsh consequence has been well-documented by historians as one of the infamous “five punishments” from the penal system of the Xia dynasty (2070 BC–1600 BC). Until now, no physical evidence of this punishment had been discovered. A team of researchers from China and the US recently announced the finding of a female skeleton dated between 1298 and 1404 (from either the Yuan or Ming dynasties) that showed clear evidence of nose removal as part of a criminal sentence. “It wasn’t a surgery for disease or trauma,” stated Qian Wang, a professor at the College of Dentistry at Texas A&M University in the US and one of the authors of the study. Wang explained to the SCMP that one major takeaway from the skeleton is the strong evidence of post-injury care. The team believes that procedures were implemented to stop the bleeding, prevent infection, and alleviate the woman’s pain. The thief survived for years after the punishment – a remarkable achievement given the substandard medical practices of the time. She died at the age of 40 to 45. The research team hypothesised that the woman might have worn a prosthetic to conceal her mutilation. This theory is supported by the healing of the bones around the wound, suggesting adaptation to a foreign object. After her death, the body was buried face down, and hers was the only skeleton interred in that position. This unique treatment likely served as a form of social ostracisation, a way to separate her from the rest of society in death. “She had a normal diet for her time as a commoner and might have worn a nasal prosthetic to cover the scar, indicating that she attempted to return to normal life,” said Wang. “However, given that she was buried face down in an isolated area, she may have experienced discrimination from the community at large, if not from her immediate family.” Upon investigating the skull more closely, the team discovered that the pear-shaped opening where the nose would have been was much wider than normal. The nasal bones had been severed, and bone spurs indicated trauma in the region. Yet, there was no evidence of blunt force trauma, such as indications of a severely broken nose. Additionally, there were no signs of diseases like leprosy that would have caused such disfigurement. Theoretically, the nose was sliced off from the bottom up. Textual records support the widespread use of this punishment. In the notorious 81 BC debate known as the “Theory of Salt and Iron,” there is an account that describes the gruesome scale of such penalties: “During the reign of the King of Qin, severed noses were piled up like mountains, and severed feet filled carts.” Wang stated that other skeletons would likely show evidence of nasal amputations, but such findings may have been overlooked. “Many skulls found are often broken or fragmentary, which could lead to nasal amputations being missed,” explained Wang. This particular skeleton was unearthed as part of a project called the Global History of Health Project Asia Module, initiated by Wang. The project aims to analyse skeletons spanning tens of thousands of years to understand how health is influenced by the environment, economics, climate change, and interpersonal conflicts. Her remains were initially flagged during routine screening but received special attention due to their unique and revealing characteristics, ultimately shedding new light on the realities of ancient justice and survival.

title: A man who built bridges over walls: SCMP’s Tammy Tam on Tung Chee-hwa
description: SCMP publisher recalls Tung as ‘humble and unpretentious personality’ who helped foster ties between China and the United States.
content: South China Morning Post publisher Tammy Tam reflects on her encounters with Hong Kong’s first chief executive, the late Tung Chee-hwa, looking back on memories from her days as a frontline reporter, his regular exchanges with media representatives and Tung’s rare appearance at an SCMP conference in 2020 to advocate US-China dialogue. Her recollections are part of a special SCMP commemorative supplement that features heavyweights from various sectors paying tribute to Tung. You can also find other tributes from the supplement here, here and here. “Are you Ms Tam? Mr Tung wants to speak to you.” The call from former chief executive Tung Chee-hwa’s office came shortly after I joined the South China Morning Post more than a decade ago. It was at a time when Hong Kong’s newspaper of record was busy preparing its annual flagship China Conference event. Tung was always among those at the top of the guest list for the event since its inaugural edition in 2015. Now that he is gone, the memories come flooding back. As a journalist, I started to encounter Tung from 1996, when the Sino-British talks over Hong Kong’s future entered their final stage, and the then shipping tycoon emerged as the most likely candidate to lead Hong Kong after the transfer of sovereignty in 1997. We reporters door-stepped, hounded and grilled him regularly, both before he became chief executive and throughout his seven years in the post. We would not let him go even after he stepped down to become a state leader as a vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body. Tung was well known for his humble and unpretentious personality, although he was understandably a bit camera-shy in the beginning and did not necessarily like answering the questions we yelled out at him. He would run the media gauntlet by simply waving with a “hello, good morning” as he walked past us, but always with a smile on his face. Of course, he would meet senior members of the media regularly during and after his tenure as chief executive to exchange views on many pressing issues pertaining to the city and the wider world. I remember how he would always pick the same classic Shanghai restaurant, which led to some of us developing a real taste for Shanghainese cuisine. That morning more than 10 years ago, when his office put me on the line with him, Tung’s voice was as warm and familiar as in my frontline reporting days. “Tammy, I’m very glad that you are now with the SCMP, so I’m calling just to share with you some more background information on why the China-US relationship matters,” he said. “I do hope the SCMP can explain the latest about China to your global audience, and break down the most important bilateral relationship in language that people can understand – I don’t mean just writing something in English, but using words that matter and make sense for everyone to grasp your meaning.” I have never forgotten that piece of advice and encouragement from Tung. The South China Morning Post positions itself as a highly credible go-to source for comprehensive and meaningful Greater China news, starting with what happens in our home city by sticking to fair and fact-based journalism. We unbox the complexities and bring out the nuances in our China and Hong Kong coverage, reading between the lines to glean the information that matters, and present it using the kind of language needed for better understanding. Not just in English, as Tung said. The last time I saw him was in December 2020, when he graciously accepted our invitation to speak again at the China Conference. We were in the middle of the Covid crisis and it was risky for elderly people in particular to be out and about socialising, but Tung put on a mask to attend our event, along with his beloved wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping. While this was a virtual conference attended online by hundreds from around the world, Tung made a physical appearance in our studio to read out his keynote speech on camera, which was then broadcast live. He went off script and kept emphasising how “we can solve all the problems” if only Beijing and Washington would work together. Looking back, I realised Tung was well aware that his health problems might soon keep him away from public activities and he felt the need to seize every opportunity to speak up while he still could. I learned later that he was already under his doctor’s advice to reduce public engagements as much as possible. But it was typical of him to keep his word and set aside inconveniences if he felt what he was doing was meaningful for everyone else. There was another phone call from his office that is still etched in my memory – this time on a summer’s day in July 2008. “Ms Tam, this is from Mr Tung’s office. He wants to invite you to the August 8 Beijing Olympics opening!” It had been quite a while since I had last talked to him, and I was gobsmacked by what seemed to be an invitation from out of the blue. Then I remembered what it was all about. Back in 2001, when I was a television journalist, my crew and I followed Tung all the way to and across the United States for his meeting with then president Bill Clinton. It was a roadshow for Hong Kong’s “one country, two systems” governing formula, but Tung was also pushing for China’s accession to the World Trade Organization, and was on a “secret” mission to convince Washington not to openly oppose China’s bid for the Olympics. Come July 13, 2001, Tung was anxiously waiting for the announcement on television in his US hotel suite, where we had gathered for a live interview. “The Games of the 29th Olympiad in 2008 are awarded to the city of Beijing,” International Olympic Committee president Juan Antonio Samaranch announced, delighting all of us glued to the screen. An excited and jubilant Tung made an announcement of his own right there and then: “I’ll invite all of you in this room to Beijing in 2008!” And there I was, seven years later, realising that Tung had really meant what he said and remembered to save a ticket for me. I told his office that I had already secured my media credentials to cover the Games and suggested the precious ticket should go to someone more in need. My phone rang again 10 minutes later and I was told: “Mr Tung agrees with your suggestion, but he insists on inviting you to a celebration dinner hosted by him when he arrives in Beijing ahead of the opening.” I accepted without hesitation. Over the years, my colleagues and I at the SCMP have received groups of visiting American students and academics touring Hong Kong and the mainland, sponsored by the China-US Exchange Foundation set up by Tung using his own money. These visits present opportunities for candid and engaging conversations on many sensitive and thorny issues – just the kind of thing we need to enhance mutual understanding on both sides of the geopolitical divide. Tung was 89 years old when he left us, but it still feels too soon, considering how much more there is to do in the mission he dedicated the last decades of his life to. I have never found the right moment to say this to him until now: thank you, Mr Tung, for your leadership, generosity, kindness, sincerity and genuine love for our city and nation; we will never forget you, and we will always remember the shining example you have set in building bridges over walls for everyone’s benefit.
