title: Australia’s backpacker visa cuts threaten working holiday dream
description: Interior minister Tony Burke has announced plans to cut the number of visas issued – and detain tourists who overstay.
content: Briton Johnny Gibbs has been in Australia for six months, surfing and working part-time – like countless other young people drawn to the country’s pristine beaches and laid-back way of life. He is one of thousands that venture Down Under on so-called “working holiday visas” – a chance to work, and play, in Australia for as long as three years. But the future for some backpackers is now in doubt, following the government’s announcement of plans to cut the number of visas issued – and detain tourists who overstay. “A lot of places you can’t surf and work at the same time, so it’s kind of perfect,” said Gibbs, 22, from near Croydon in London. “They’re not really losing much by getting people to work in their country,” he said, his surfboard still wet from an afternoon dip at Sydney’s famed Bondi Beach. “I’ve done a lot of different types of work on the working holiday visa, and that helps out the Australians as well. I’m not a harmful person. I’m only doing good.” As a Briton, Johnny is lucky; he is not affected by the changes thanks to an agreement between London and Canberra. But many of his compatriots will be left waiting. Interior minister Tony Burke said this week that a backlog of applications from the UK for working holiday visas would continue to be processed slowly after a record 80,000 applications last year. For other nationalities, Burke said visas for a second-year stay will be cut to 45,000 places from 57,000 last year – and applicants will be required to carry out 88 days of regional work. Those that want to stay a third year will need to enter a ballot to stay – with only 5,000 places available. Australia’s ruling Labor party denies it is tightening visa rules in response to the rise of the far-right One Nation, now one of the country’s most popular parties with pledges to drastically slash migration. Graham Carson, 55, an Australian lawyer who was sunbathing with his family, said the crackdown was “ironic”. “We send criminals back to England – which you know in a way is quite funny, given that they were sending their convicts here,” he said. For some on Bondi – long known as a backpacker’s paradise for its chill vibes and carefree lifestyle – the crackdown is a surprise. “Maybe this was the wrong impression I had of Australia, but I thought they were very open,” said Stina Svensson, 27, from Gothenburg in Sweden. She and her friend Alva Johanssen are both in Australia on working holiday visas – not working yet, but hoping to soon. “People speak so highly of the working holiday visa programme. And I feel like it’s also good for Australia,” she said. “Like we – OK, not yet because we’re unemployed – but we would do the work that Australians don’t want to do,” she explained. “We wanted to have, like, just a regular fun job at the beginning, but then do the remote work or, like, farm work, but, like, now we don’t want to do that. Because we don’t know if we’re even going to get a second year.” Her friend, Alva, said the new rules would likely mean she would cut her stay short. “We wanted to stay before this came up. But now I think I’ll go home.” “I think we would rather just go to Southern Europe then, because that’s just easier,” Stina said.

title: Crouching dragons: the suicide divers Japan never sent to war
description: Sealed in diving suits with mines attached to poles, Japan’s ‘fukuryu’ frogmen waited beneath the waves for an invasion that never came.
content: Japan’s wartime kamikaze pilots remain among the most recognisable symbols of the Pacific war: young men flying aircraft into Allied ships on missions from which they were not expected to return. Far less well-remembered are the fukuryu – suicide frogmen trained in the closing months of World War II to walk into the sea with mines on bamboo poles, then wait beneath the waves for an Allied invasion fleet. Kanade Hamamoto was one of many Japanese people who had never heard of them, despite spending years on the same stretch of coast where they once trained. The 25-year-old photographer knew Inamuragasaki, on the Shonan coast south of Tokyo, only as a scenic seaside spot until a friend mentioned that the remains of a military base could still be seen near the cape, in tunnels cut into the cliff face. “My friend’s comments kept nagging away at me after I got home, so I did an online search and came across the term ‘Fukuryu Special Attack Unit’ for the first time,” Hamamoto told This Week in Asia. She has since turned that discovery into “ー・・”, a bilingual photo book published in 2025 that won the 50th Kimura Ihei Photography Award, one of Japan’s most prestigious honours for emerging photographers. The title, rendered in English as “Arrived at the seabed”, refers to the Morse code-style signal – one long tug and two short ones – that the divers would use to tell colleagues on shore they had reached the bottom. Once underwater, the fukuryu could communicate only through such coded tugs on a rope. Their bodies were sealed inside heavy diving suits, with weighted shoes and helmets fastened shut with four screws. As those screws were tightened, surviving members of Japan’s wartime fukuryu units later described a piercing, high-pitched sound right next to their ears. In his memoirs, former fukuryu Takaichiro Monna wrote that it felt “as if I were being placed in a coffin while I was still alive”. Other survivors of the little-known unit, which was tasked with the last-ditch defence of the Japanese homeland in the closing stages of the second world war, reported that even years afterwards, they could still hear the whistling sound. Few of the estimated 1,200 men who completed fukuryu training before Japan’s surrender on August 15, 1945, are likely to still be alive, but Hamamoto has helped return their story to public memory. A different kind of kamikaze The first organised kamikaze attack came during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, off the Philippines, in October 1944, when Lieutenant Yukio Seki crashed his Zero fighter into the US Navy escort carrier St. Lo, causing an explosion that sank the vessel in minutes. Kamikaze air attacks on Allied shipping grew more frequent over the following months, alongside one-way missions by kaiten crewed torpedoes and shinyo motorboats laden with explosives. The tide of the war could not be turned, however, and the fukuryu – meaning “crouching dragon” – were conceived as virtually the last line of defence against an Allied invasion of Japan. The plan was simple: when an invasion fleet was sighted offshore, the fukuryu would wade out from the beaches, wait for a warship or landing craft to pass overhead, then strike it with a mine fixed to a five-metre-long (16.4 foot) bamboo pole. The 15kg (33lb) explosive would be devastating to the enemy vessel – and to the frogman holding it. In some places, underwater structures were installed a short way off the beach to store extra mines and offer the divers some shelter. The 71st Arashi unit, based at Yokosuka, was tasked with defending the beaches of Sagami Bay with about 1,000 men. Additional units were stationed at Kure in central Japan and Sasebo in Kyushu. Although the divers were never called upon to face an invasion fleet, since Japan surrendered first, their training was far from safe and at least some of the men died in accidents. It is not clear how many were killed during training, however, because many records were destroyed after the surrender. Surviving accounts describe isolated incidents, including one evening when bioluminescence at sea was mistaken for an approaching invasion fleet and the men were ordered into the water. “When I read reports that said many of the bodies could not be recovered and many people were still missing, I began to wonder if they might still be there, somewhere beneath the sea where I had spent time since I was a teenager,” Hamamoto said. “I felt their presence not as something that belonged to the past, but as something that exists in the present. I felt it not as something that concerned someone else, but as something that concerned me personally.” While researching her book, Hamamoto concluded that the fukuryu were relatively unknown today for a number of reasons: firstly because the war ended before they saw combat, secondly because the unit’s records were destroyed and thirdly because the area where they trained was long off limits to civilians. Garren Mulloy, a professor of international relations at Daito Bunka University and a specialist in military affairs, pointed to yet other reasons that the fukuryu frogmen’s stories had been largely overlooked for so long. “When the first kamikaze aircraft started hitting warships in the Pacific in 1944, it was caught on film and shocked everyone who saw it,” he said. “There was also attention on how the kamikaze were first thought up, then the technology was developed and deployed, but with the fukuryu, it was just diving suits and a pole with a mine on the end.” Sending young men to their certain deaths armed only with a mine illustrated the desperation of Japan’s military in the waning days of the conflict, Mulloy said. Other last-gasp defences were planned too, including soldiers being ordered to crouch in beach foxholes and wait for enemy tanks to pass overhead before detonating a mine beneath them. “I imagine that even in those extreme circumstances – with reckless training regimens and makeshift diving suits, as well as the grim necessity of carrying out a suicide mission – the waves and winds off Yokosuka must have been just as calm as they are today,” Hamamoto said. “In that beautiful sea, human beings were attempting to kill their fellow human beings and, in the process, were losing their own lives.” Preserving the memory of the fukuryu was essential to ensure that history did not repeat itself, she said. “I simply cannot bring myself to view this as a distant event that has nothing to do with me.”

title: Opinion | Now Hong Kong must turn its international edge into national impact
description: The city can bridge China and the world, adding value to every connection, but to deliver on this promise, it needs everyone on board.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan marks a new chapter for the city and will prompt discussion about individual priorities and initiatives. But there is another question worth asking: what can Hong Kong bring to the national journey over the next five years? As China begins its 15th five-year plan, Hong Kong has an opportunity to think more deliberately about its distinctive contribution to national development. Much has been said about Hong Kong’s role as a “superconnector”. The description remains apt, but that role is evolving. Hong Kong’s value does not come simply from sitting between China and the world. It comes from its ability to help businesses, capital, talent and ideas move between different markets and systems. That capability has been built over generations. Hong Kong combines deep connections with the mainland with an international financial system, common law tradition, professional expertise and extensive global business networks. These attributes are particularly valuable as geopolitical tensions, technological change and shifting supply chains make cross-border business more complex. For much of Hong Kong’s modern economic history, its intermediary role was associated with bringing the world into China. International companies used the city to understand, invest in and do business with the mainland. That function remains important, but an increasingly significant flow is in the other direction as mainland companies look overseas for new markets and opportunities. Recent figures illustrate this two-way role. Last year, InvestHK helped a record 560 non-local companies set up or expand in Hong Kong, a city home to a record 11,070 companies with non-local parents. Of the 560 non-local companies, 298 were from the mainland and most of these, according to the government, either planned to use Hong Kong to go global or were already doing so. This points to an important opportunity for Hong Kong over the next five years. The city can continue to provide a platform for international companies seeking opportunities in China while becoming an even more effective springboard for mainland enterprises expanding overseas. Doing this successfully requires more than connecting companies with markets. A mainland enterprise expanding internationally may need to raise capital, understand unfamiliar laws and regulations, manage risks, protect intellectual property, build its brand and identify reliable partners. International companies entering China similarly need local knowledge, professional advice and trusted networks. Hong Kong has accumulated decades of experience in many of these areas. The Task Force on Supporting Mainland Enterprises in Going Global (GoGlobal Task Force) is one example of how those capabilities are being brought together, drawing on expertise across finance, law, accounting, marketing, logistics, technology and other professional services. This is also where Hong Kong can fulfil its role as a “super value-adder”. Its contribution should not be limited to providing a point of connection. It should use its international experience and professional capabilities to make cross-border connections work better and create greater value from them. There should therefore be no contradiction between Hong Kong becoming more closely integrated with national development and maintaining its international character. The more internationally connected Hong Kong remains, the more it can contribute to a China increasingly engaged with the world. Also, deeper participation in national development can strengthen Hong Kong’s ability to connect international businesses, investors and talent with opportunities across the country. Being backed by China and connected to the world are complementary strengths. Making the most of them, however, cannot be a government undertaking alone. This is also consistent with the approach set out for the next five years. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has made clear that while the government will lead, coordinate resources and set policies, achieving the best results will require everyone to play their part. That wider participation matters because much of what makes Hong Kong internationally relevant resides across society: companies with experience in global markets, professionals accustomed to working across jurisdictions, universities with international networks, entrepreneurs seeking opportunities beyond familiar markets, and people able to operate across languages and cultures. Businesses and institutions should therefore consider how their strengths can contribute to Hong Kong’s role over the next five years. Companies can invest and build partnerships across the mainland and overseas. Professional services can help businesses navigate an increasingly complex international environment. Universities can deepen cooperation with institutions on the mainland and around the world, strengthening the movement of knowledge, research and talent. Hong Kong must also continue to be outward-looking. The city has prospered because people, capital, businesses and ideas from different parts of the world have been able to meet here. Maintaining that openness while participating more deeply in national development strengthens rather than diminishes Hong Kong’s distinctive contribution. Ultimately, the benefits must extend beyond businesses and economic indicators. A competitive, prosperous and internationally relevant Hong Kong should create better opportunities for the next generation and give young people confidence that they can build their futures here. The choices made over these five years will help shape the city they inherit. China’s 15th five-year plan provides a broader national framework, while Hong Kong’s first five-year plan gives the city direction within it. Turning that direction into progress will require the government, business and society to work together. Hong Kong is an international city backed by China and connected to the world. Over the next five years, it should use that position to bring more of the world to China, take more of China to the world and add value to the connections between them. That is a contribution Hong Kong is uniquely placed to make, and a shared mission worth pursuing.

title: How much has Iran war cost US? Pentagon estimates US$43.6 billion so far
description: Polls show Americans increasingly oppose the war, partly over its impact on the economy, as the November midterm elections approach.
content: The Iran war has cost US$43.6 billion as of this month, the highest official estimate to date, the Pentagon told Congress’ defence oversight panels this week. The cost estimate comes as polls show Americans increasingly oppose the war, partly over its impact on the economy, and the issue is looming large as the November midterm elections approach. The Pentagon’s latest figure comprises US$11.2 billion already obliged for operating expenses – for fuel, combat pay, aircraft, medical care, parts and the like – plus US$32.4 billion in unfunded replacement costs for munitions, damaged aircraft and other assets, according to a Pentagon document submitted to Congress. The estimate does not include the cost of addressing potentially billions of dollars in damages to US military facilities in eight Middle East countries. The figure also does not account for future potential costs, which the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimates may be US$2 billion to US$3 billion a month. Moreover, the Defence Department estimate does not take into account the effect of inflation, which has risen because of war-related restrictions in shipping routes in the region. The Pentagon’s new partial estimate is close to figures publicised earlier this week in separate reports from the department’s inspector general and the CBO, both of which cited US military cost figures as the source of their estimates. The new Pentagon estimate of US$43.6 billion was current as of September 3, the document said – the most recent reckoning. By comparison, the CBO said the war cost US$38.1 billion through July. It noted that its estimate did not cover costs associated with diplomatic operations or foreign aid, nor expenses related to military personnel killed or injured, future veterans’ healthcare and disability compensation, or spending or future maintenance costs for military assets used in the conflict. The inspector general, meanwhile, put the figure at US$33.4 billion. Its estimate ran through June. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth testified in July that the war would cost US$37.5 billion through the end of September. The Pentagon has asked Congress for US$67.1 billion in supplemental spending, partly to recoup war costs. The department’s latest cost estimate arrived on Capitol Hill about the same time that nearly every Senate Democrat and independent senators Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine were signing on to a letter to Hegseth calling for a complete accounting of the war’s costs.

title: Trump, Melania to host China’s Xi and Peng Liyuan for White House ‘double date’
description: Officials outline a two-couple White House state visit, confirming AI, rare earths and US car market access are on the agenda.
content: US President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump will host Chinese leader Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan across two days in Washington next week. The itinerary: a White House welcome, a state dinner at which both presidents speak, a private tea and a tour of the United States’ founding documents. At a briefing late on Friday, senior US officials described a state visit built around the two couples as a diplomatic “double date” – with the hard bargaining underneath. The pageantry will sit beside talks on artificial intelligence (AI), a trade truce that expires in November, rare earths, fentanyl and detained foreigners. Officials also hinted that Chinese investment in the US car market could be discussed, but only if existing US national security rules were met. “I think the president’s comments speak for themselves,” a senior official said of the US car market. Trump is “not interested in compromising on our national security”, the official added, “so some of the rules and regulations that present hurdles would still have to be met for some of these types of investments to occur”. The briefing confirmed much of what the South China Morning Post has already reported: AI will be folded into the pre-summit economic talks, the Busan trade truce and tariff talks are central, and that the visit will be built as a full state occasion rather than a single day of meetings. The two couples On Thursday, September 24, the Trumps will welcome Xi and Peng to the White House for an arrival ceremony on the State Floor, followed by a military review in the Rose Garden. The two presidents will then hold talks, while Peng will leave that track for a separate programme with the US first lady. That evening, the Trumps will host a state dinner for the Chinese delegation in the East Room. Both presidents will speak at the start of the event. Officials said the American guests would include Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser and Tim Cook. “It’ll be a very popular and hot-ticketed event here in Washington,” a senior official said. Friday, September 25, is the quieter half. Officials said the Trumps would host Xi and Peng for a private tea at the White House, then the two couples would tour the National Archives – where the US keeps its founding charters – as the country marks 250 years of independence. Xi will then depart from Washington. The SCMP reported on September 17 that Trump would greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, not only at the White House, a rare presidential airport welcome. Bargaining points The policy list matches the ground that the SCMP has been reporting for weeks. Senior officials said AI and the US-China trade arrangement, the “Busan truce”, struck in South Korea last October and due to lapse in November, were both on the agenda. “Those are both on the agenda, both AI and the current ‘Busan truce’, and we’ll know more once the two leaders meet,” a senior official said. The SCMP reported on September 12 that Washington and Beijing were discussing folding a long-delayed AI dialogue into the broader economic meeting before the summit, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent handling both files in one sitting. Bessent is in New York this weekend for high-level talks with Chinese counterpart He Lifeng to prepare the leaders’ meeting. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will join Bessent. “Secretary [Bessent] has mentioned that we’ll be up in New York this weekend, talking about this with the Chinese at a very high level at his level,” a senior official said. “I don’t want to get ahead of any conclusions or agreements or non-agreements that may occur over the next couple of days.” China’s Ministry of Commerce announced on Saturday that He, vice-premier of the State Council, would lead a delegation to the US from September 19 to 23 to hold economic and trade consultations with the US side. “Both sides will be guided by the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and conduct consultations on economic and trade issues of mutual concern,” the ministry said. On the rest of the economic front, officials set out several markers. Washington will not trade additional export control relief for rare earth supplies that officials say were already negotiated. “China’s performance in that respect has not been up to par of what we would expect, and that I’m sure will be a topic of discussion.” The two sides have discussed cutting tariffs on a “narrow band” of goods that are neither strategic nor sensitive. On any opening of the US car market to Chinese firms, Trump was “not interested in compromising on our national security”. Fentanyl, prisoners and Iran Officials said Washington wanted Beijing to treat fentanyl chemicals as a systemic problem. China, they said, remained “the overwhelming, predominant supplier of precursor chemicals to the cartels in Mexico”. “We do need them to do more on the fentanyl front,” a senior official said. A few recent arrests were not enough. “We’d like to see much more systemic change.” Trump is expected again to raise people the US regards as wrongfully held in China, including Americans and – as officials said – some non-US nationals. “Every time … when he meets with Xi Jinping … he raises Americans that have been wrongfully detained,” a senior official said. “If I had to guess, he will be consistent again this time.” Sanctions on mainland Chinese and Hong Kong firms accused of helping Iran earn revenue, including from oil, “will continue”, officials said.

title: Exclusive | US weighs delaying Taiwan arms sales until after Apec and G20 summits
description: Sources say the decision is expected to be a compromise between Donald Trump, Washington’s China hawks and Taipei’s lobbyists.
content: The United States is considering postponing the announcement of major arms sales to Taiwan until after November’s Apec summit in Shenzhen, multiple sources told the South China Morning Post. The potential delay comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares to travel to Washington next week for a state visit. The sources said there was a strong possibility US President Donald Trump could extend the delay through to the end of the year, pointing to a planned bilateral meeting between the two leaders at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and Xi’s expected visit to Florida for the Group of 20 (G20) summit in December. One source said Trump was considering various options to postpone the signing of Taiwan arms sales, but the final outcome would be a “compromise between him, the China hawks and Taiwan’s lobbyists”. “President Trump has considered delaying the [Taiwan] arms sales decision till end 2028 or January 2029, that is, towards the end of his current term. However, he faced very loud opposition from hawks after floating the idea,” he said. “Delaying it after Apec and G20 seems to be the decision for now. There is also a high chance that he will continue to sit on it next year, as Beijing has signalled very strongly against the military sales to Taiwan,” he said. Noting the existing delivery backlog for Taiwan, the source said a postponed approval “might have limited impact on the actual delivery timeline”. Taiwan’s orders remain stuck in a long manufacturing queue as American defence contractors prioritise urgent US military inventory replenishment and active combat theatres, especially in the Middle East. Chronic constraints within the US defence industry – amplified by supply chain bottlenecks and skilled labour shortages – have contributed to the backlog. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. According to a source familiar with Chinese planning, officials have privately pressed the US to hold off on any new arms sales to Taipei before Xi’s trip to Washington, echoing the message they sent ahead of Trump’s Beijing visit in May. While Beijing would want sales pushed back as long as possible, officials recognised that Washington could not stall forever, he said. Meanwhile, Taiwanese officials had voiced concerns about the possibility of Trump delaying arms sales until the end of his presidency, he added. Two other people familiar with the discussions said the Trump administration could announce a smaller arms package in the window between next week’s Washington summit and the Apec meeting in November, but emphasised that a multibillion-dollar deal like those seen in past years was less likely to materialise. They said Trump had been advised by some China hawks to take a “piecemeal approach”, approving a small sale first to pacify Taipei. The Trump administration may give Beijing advance notice of any smaller sales to ensure it is not caught off guard and does not view the move as a breach of their understanding, according to sources. While the Chinese side will certainly oppose a small arms package and publicly express its displeasure, Beijing may reluctantly come to accept it without major retaliation, according to a person familiar with the matter. Another source described the delay as unsurprising, noting there had been similar delays in the past. Days before Trump’s May visit to China, his administration put on hold a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan that had been approved by the US Congress. The package included advanced air and missile defence systems, including PAC-3 Patriot interceptors and the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, or Nasams. Six months earlier, Washington had announced a separate US$11 billion arms sale to Taiwan, drawing a strong reaction from Beijing. The current US arms sales delay is not without precedent. Former US president Barack Obama froze arms sales to Taiwan from 2011 to 2015, and George W. Bush did the same from 2007 to 2008. A source pointed out that Sino-American military ties and the resumption of security dialogue hinged on Washington’s assurances regarding Taiwan. The SCMP reported on Thursday that the two sides were discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington. Sources said both Beijing and Washington were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship. Another potential deliverable under discussion is the resumption of arms-control talks suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan. The dialogue could potentially include military personnel.

title: Perfect Diary owner Yatsen doubles down on skincare, R&D after business overhaul
description: The Chinese beauty firm has snapped up a string of overseas skincare brands, but it now plans to focus on expanding its existing portfolio.
content: Yatsen Group, the Chinese beauty company behind Perfect Diary cosmetics, plans to deepen its push into skincare and new product research to sustain its growth, after a years-long overhaul of its business that has seen the firm acquire a string of overseas brands. The Guangzhou-based company will slow its acquisition spree for now and instead focus on expanding its existing portfolio of skincare offerings, while maintaining – and potentially raising – its research and development spending, which currently hovers at 3 to 4 per cent of annual revenue, according to founder and CEO David Huang. “We still think there will be pretty big potential for our existing brands,” Huang said during a media event at the company’s manufacturing and R&D facility in Guangzhou earlier this week. “At this stage, we will remain focused on growing our existing framework.” But Huang did not rule out further acquisitions of businesses with strong brand equity and products. The strategy marks the next phase of a major transformation for Yatsen, which rose to prominence through its mass-market colour cosmetics brand Perfect Diary before listing in New York in 2020. Colour cosmetics accounted for more than 80 per cent of the company’s sales that year, with skincare contributing just over 12 per cent, according to the company’s 2020 annual report. The group, however, has since built a skincare portfolio including French brands Galenic and Eve Lom, as well as the mainland China business for Taiwanese dermocosmetics brand Dr Wu, while investing more than 700 million yuan (US$104 million) in R&D since 2020, according to company figures. The strategy has turned Yatsen’s revenue mix on its head. Skincare sales jumped over 40 per cent year on year in the second quarter of 2026 to reach 816 million yuan (US$122 million), accounting for more than 70 per cent of the group’s total revenue. Colour cosmetics revenue, meanwhile, fell by more than 35 per cent. Despite the strong growth in skincare, Yatsen’s net loss widened from 19.5 million yuan a year earlier to 90.8 million yuan in the second quarter as the firm’s sales and marketing costs jumped 11.8 per cent to 807.6 million yuan, according to the company. Yatsen ranked seventh among listed Chinese beauty companies by revenue in the first half of 2026, according to Qingyan, a research and intelligence provider specialising in the beauty industry. It was the only company among the top 10 to post a net loss. One idea the company is pursuing to rejuvenate its business is “skinification” – applying its skincare research to its colour cosmetics business to develop new make-up products that incorporate skincare functions. Huang said technology developed across the two categories could create synergies in R&D, distribution and consumer insights, with Yatsen seeking to build a multi-brand beauty group rather than simply replace cosmetics with skincare.

title: Hong Kong civil servants to get hourly leave but businesses unlikely to follow
description: Civil servants expect to receive an annual entitlement of 10 to 12 hours of family care leave, with the arrangement taking effect in early 2027.
content: Hong Kong civil servants could receive flexible hourly family care leave next year as part of the government’s wider drive to boost birth rates, the South China Morning Post has learned, though business leaders warn the private sector has little incentive to follow suit, citing manpower and financial constraints, especially for smaller firms. Under the “promote fertility” section of Wednesday’s policy address, the government said it would introduce family care leave for its employees to enhance family-friendly measures. A government source said that civil servants could apply for leave by the hour for personal matters, such as accompanying family members to hospital or attending parent-teacher meetings. The Civil Service Bureau was formulating details and would conduct further consultation with government employees, the insider added. Tsoi Koon-lung, president of the Hong Kong Chinese Civil Servants’ Association, welcomed the proposal, saying it would give colleagues greater flexibility. He said he expected each civil servant to receive an annual entitlement of 10 to 12 hours, with the arrangement taking effect in early 2027. Currently, even staff who needed only one or two hours for family matters had to take at least half a day off, Tsoi said. “Some civil servants feel this wastes their annual leave, while the government ends up short-staffed for half a day,” he said. The hourly system would allow civil servants to respond to family matters more flexibly without wasting their annual leave, he added. But Tsoi also cautioned that the entitlement might be insufficient for those with multiple children and called for ongoing reviews. “After the implementation, the government should constantly monitor the use of such leave to see if many colleagues report that the entitlement is insufficient.” Ngan Man-him, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Federation of Civil Service Unions, echoed Tsoi’s view, adding that the application procedures should also be simple and flexible so that civil servants could better respond to different emergencies. “For emergencies, we might just tell our boss the reason via WhatsApp and then complete the procedure with supporting documents afterwards. We hope to keep it simple,” he said. Labour sector lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, also an honorary adviser to the Hong Kong Civil Servants General Union, said the measure could encourage young government workers to start a family. “Some youngsters can enjoy a relatively stable working environment after joining the civil service, and they would be more inclined to have children with such family-friendly measures,” he said. Lam added that the government could act as a role model for the private sector, although adoption could be difficult, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). “For SMEs, their resources and manpower are short, and they may find it difficult to make such arrangements,” he said. Lam added that such arrangements would also put greater financial pressure on private-sector employers, making them reluctant to follow the government’s lead. “The government can do the maths, and if the budget permits, it could consider paying the wages on such days off on behalf of the private sector so that all workers in Hong Kong can benefit from family leave.” Danny Lau Tat-pong, ­honorary life chairman of the Hong Kong Small and Medium Enterprises Association, said even if the government were to subsidise family leave wages, it would still be difficult for SMEs to make such arrangements. “Even if the government pays the salaries, we are still short-staffed,” he said. “When employees are only away for a few hours, it is impossible for us to hire a part-timer to fill in.” Lau added that while private firms might avoid formal family leave policies, employers typically granted short, discretionary leave for emergencies. Lawmaker Jonathan Lamport, who also represents the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, said larger corporations with more resources would be more likely to adopt the practice. “In a micro-enterprise with only a few staff, ad hoc leave can significantly disrupt daily operations because there is simply no buffer,” he said. “We hope the government can act as a partner by providing practical incentives – such as tax concessions to help SMEs overcome these operational hurdles and build a family-friendly workplace.” The government is the largest employer in Hong Kong, with more than 170,000 civil servants. In 2024, it introduced childcare leave for staff, entitling each civil servant to three days of leave annually for each child under three years old.

title: How a game show in Nigeria helps people connect with their mother tongue
description: The show tests people on their knowledge of Yoruba, one of the most widely spoken languages in the country.
content:
A television game show in Nigeria has a strict rule: if you speak English, you lose.
Tomi Adeshokan lives in the United States and is learning her parents’ native language, Yoruba. For her, being in the audience of this show is a great way to practise Yoruba. It is one of Nigeria’s most widely spoken languages.
Olalekan Fabilola, the show’s host, started it in 2024. He sees the show as part of a wider change.
“We are in the age ... [when] people want to go back to their roots,” he said.
This show is part of a new wave of interest in African languages. For many years, colonial rule pushed these languages to the side.
Experts say people of African descent living in other places are finding new ways to connect with their roots through social media and shows.

title: India’s Modi caught between Russian oil needs and US trade threats
description: Cutting Russian oil imports could avoid price rises ahead of key polls but keeping such purchases could cripple access to its largest market.
content: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is caught in an energy policy bind with no easy exit. Cutting Russian oil imports to avoid potential new US tariffs could increase fuel prices ahead of key regional elections, or stress government finances. Maintaining such purchases could cripple Indian exports to its largest market. India, the world’s third-largest oil importer and among the biggest buyers of Russian crude, reacted unusually strongly on Thursday to a US congressional bill that would allow Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on countries, including India and China, for major purchases of Russian oil. The sharp response showed how an energy trade that has delivered India billions of dollars in savings since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is now colliding with its broader strategic and commercial interests. New Delhi said it had warned the United States that the measure could damage bilateral relations and disrupt global energy markets, vowing to keep “ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” by buying from diversified sources. But holding firm could further strain ties with Washington after a turbulent year marked by repeated disputes over trade and tariffs under President Donald Trump. A planned trade deal between the two countries has already faced multiple delays. Two Indian sources said the latest tensions did not mean Delhi would abandon hopes of striking a trade deal with Washington, though they said India might increasingly need to lean on deals elsewhere if additional US tariffs hit exports. Since last year, India has signed a trade deal with Britain, finalised one with the EU and is looking to conclude talks on another one with Canada by the end of the year. Delhi is hoping for a breakthrough when Modi travels to the US for the G20 summit in December, where he could meet Trump on the sidelines, according to one of the sources. The White House and the Indian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ‘Biggest blow yet’ “The US-India relationship has suffered over the last year for a range of reasons, including US tariffs,” said Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council in Washington. “But this new legislation, which enjoyed strong bipartisan support and takes the most maximalist position possible on punishing India for its Russian oil buys, may be the biggest blow yet.” If Washington delayed implementing tariffs or applied them only lightly, the damage could be manageable, he said, adding the legislation nevertheless could widen the trust gap in Delhi for a trade deal and make it harder for Indian negotiators to agree to last-minute concessions needed to secure a deal. “From the perspective of the trade talks, this new legislation couldn’t have come at a worse time,” he said. “The two sides are not far from the finish line, but getting there will require careful diplomacy.” The bill has already become a political issue in India, with the opposition urging Modi to adopt a tougher stance. Any hike in pump prices would be risky for Modi, whose party faces elections in India’s most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Modi’s home state of Gujarat starting early next year. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party runs both Uttar Pradesh and Gujarat. Before Trump, India was courted by the United States for decades as a strategic counterweight to China, but the world’s fifth-largest economy has repeatedly been left reeling over the past year by decisions taken in Washington. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, India sharply increased purchases of discounted Russian crude, which now account for more than 40 per cent of India’s overall oil supplies. The stepped-up purchases were partly the reason Trump imposed tariffs of as much as 50 per cent on Indian goods in August 2025, among the steepest levied on any country. In February, Trump rolled back those duties in exchange for what he said was India’s commitment to halt Russian oil purchases and lower trade barriers. But Delhi only briefly reduced purchases from Russia early this year. They have since jumped, especially since the supply shock that followed the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. Delhi has repeatedly resisted pressure to scale back purchases, arguing that its large population and growing economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies. Indian refiners have already secured crude supplies for September and October that include Russian oil, according to sources familiar with the matter. Indian analysts said the country’s purchases of Russian oil were not financing the Ukraine war, but only helping stabilise global supplies and keeping domestic prices in check. “Tariffs of up to 100 per cent would punish Indian exporters and American consumers, disrupt trade and give the US president excessive power over major partners,” said Ajay Srivastava, founder of Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative and a former trade ministry official.

title: Reflections | A Polish priest’s perilous mission to save a doomed Chinese dynasty with Catholic links
description: In 1651, the embattled Ming court, which included several Christian converts, sent Michal Boym to seek the Pope’s aid. It never came.
content: I spent a week in Warsaw and ate more pierogi than I could shake a stick at. These beloved traditional Polish dumplings come filled with potatoes, cheese, meat, mushrooms and even fruit. Boiled or fried, they may look familiar to anyone acquainted with jiaozi, the Chinese dumpling, although their flavours are distinctly Polish. This is not to suggest that dumplings travelled directly from China to Poland. One theory posits that dumpling-like foods – from Nepalese momo and Central Asian and Turkish manti to Georgian khinkali – spread westwards from their origin in East Asia through Central and South Asia, the Middle East and, eventually, Europe. Another posits that filled dumplings emerged in multiple places independently rather than from a single source. Whoever invented the dumpling, the resemblance of a Polish pierogi to a Chinese jiaozi is not the only connection between Poland and China. At a time when China was being convulsed by the fall of one dynasty and the rise of another, a Polish Jesuit priest found himself carrying a desperate appeal from a doomed imperial court across half the world. His name was Michal Boym (1612-59), also known by his Chinese name Bu Mige. Born in the Polish city of Lwow (present-day Lviv in Ukraine), Boym travelled to China as a missionary in the 1640s, arriving in Macau at a moment of extraordinary upheaval. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was collapsing. In the north, Manchu invaders had seized Beijing and established the Qing dynasty (1644-1912). Ming loyalists in the south and southwest continued to rally around a scion of the Ming ruling house, Zhu Youlang (1623-62), known in history as the Yongli Emperor. Yongli’s court possessed an unusual connection with the Roman Catholic world. Members of his household, including his stepmother (the Empress Dowager Wang), his birth mother, his wife and his son and heir, had converted to Christianity. For this reason, Jesuit missionaries had direct access to the inner circle of the Zhu family, whose members had ruled China for the previous 270 years. Boym became involved when he was entrusted with a mission of immense urgency and desperation: to carry Yongli’s appeal for help against the Manchu invasion to the Pope and the Catholic powers of Europe. In 1651, accompanied by a Chinese companion, Boym left China and embarked on a journey as arduous as it was perilous. He travelled overland across the Indian subcontinent, Persia and the Ottoman Empire before eventually reaching Europe. When Boym finally arrived in Rome, his mission attracted attention but not the assistance he had hoped for. Pope Alexander VII received him in 1655 but only offered words of encouragement and sympathy. There would be no European army sailing east to rescue the Yongli Emperor and the Ming loyalists. Boym turned around and headed back towards China. By the time he arrived in East Asia, the cause he had represented was nearing its end. Qing armies had continued their advance south, driving the Yongli regime deeper into southwest China towards Yunnan province. Boym eventually reached Guangxi in 1659, but he died there in June. Yongli himself would be executed three years later by the Qing forces. Yet Boym’s legacy was not confined to a failed diplomatic mission. Alongside his work as a missionary, teacher and envoy, he was an energetic observer, recorder and illustrator of Chinese plants, animals, medicine and geography. His writings helped introduce European readers to a China that was still only dimly understood in the West at the time. His best-known work, Flora Sinensis, published in Vienna in 1656, was an important early European account of Chinese plants and animals. As a bridge between two worlds, Boym left behind something far more enduring than the cause of the ill-fated Chinese dynasty he had tried to save. In his writings, however, there was no mention of dumplings.

title: China makes progress in 3-nm chips without advanced lithography tools
description: The breakthrough by the Chinese Academy of Sciences is far from mass production but shows China is tracking the road map of global leaders.
content: Chinese researchers have made early strides in pushing semiconductor processing nodes below 3-nm using older lithography technology, as more advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) tools from ASML remain blocked under US sanctions. The breakthrough marks the latest progress in China’s drive to chart an alternative path to advanced chipmaking amid US export restrictions. Under current export control rules, Dutch equipment giant ASML is barred from selling its state-of-the-art EUV machines – essential for producing chips below the 7-nm node – to Chinese clients. In the latest development, state-backed Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) has established a preliminary gate-all-around (GAA) device development path using the less advanced deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography, Taiwanese media Digitimes reported on Thursday, citing a speech by Ye Tianchun, a veteran from the academy’s Institute of Microelectronics (IMECAS). Ye said the institute had finished early integration for stacked nanosheet-channel GAA CMOS transistors using DUV tools. He described the result as a “new early-stage MOS transistor process path for China’s sub-3-nm advanced manufacturing”, according to the Digitimes article. The breakthrough also reflects how China is closely tracking the architectural road map of global semiconductor leaders despite its lack of cutting-edge tools. GAA transistor architecture is seen as the next critical evolution in semiconductor production beyond the widely used FinFET, or Fin Field-Effect Transistor, designs. Samsung Electronics is already mass-producing 3-nm chips using GAA, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company transitioned to GAA for its 2-nm node in late 2025. Still, the breakthrough by CAS seems far from ready for mass production. Ye noted that the development remained at an early stage. Whether the institute’s latest GAA technology can transition into mass production will depend on future wafer validation performance on actual manufacturing lines. Ye, a veteran semiconductor technologist who previously headed IMECAS, also served as chief technologist for China’s high-profile “02” project, a major state initiative to advance domestic chipmaking equipment and fabrication capabilities. CAS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday. Recent US proposals have threatened to extend export bans on ASML’s DUV business in China. Chinese semiconductor companies, therefore, have been exploring novel architectures to extract advanced performance out of mature tools. The latest breakthrough builds on years of research by CAS to seek innovations that can potentially bypass the need for advanced lithography tools in chipmaking. In 2025, the institute developed an all-solid-state DUV laser capable of emitting 193-nm coherent light – the crucial wavelength used in current semiconductor lithography. Beyond the state-backed institute, the biggest leap in China’s chip self-sufficiency drive so far this year is from Huawei Technologies, which unveiled the Tau Scaling Law in May that redesigns chip architecture based on “time scaling”. The company expects its self-developed high-end chips, based on the new scaling law, to feature transistor densities equivalent to 1.4-nm processes by 2031.

title: South Korea wants free ‘AI for All’. Is society ready?
description: Seoul’s roll-out of free, unlimited AI is set to shake up classrooms, careers and crime – for better or worse.
content: In Silicon Valley and beyond, the architects of artificial intelligence are increasingly warning about the risks it poses to humanity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wants the industry to slow down. A former engineer at his company, who also worked at its rival OpenAI, told reporters after quitting earlier this month that he was “genuinely frightened” unchecked AI development might mean “we could all die in the immediate future”. Even Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, has warned of the existential threat posed by the technology should it escape human control. Concerns about AI run the gamut from autonomous weapons, mass unemployment and machine-driven cyberattacks to deepfake-fuelled misinformation, algorithmic bias and a dangerous overreliance on automation. South Korea has seen all this – and decided now is the time to hit the accelerator. Under President Lee Jae Myung’s “AI for All” initiative, the government is preparing to hand every citizen free access to artificial intelligence, integrating it into hospitals, schools, government offices and daily lives in a way few countries have attempted. “The idea is to substantially lower barriers to access so that the benefits of the technology are distributed evenly rather than enjoyed by only some people,” Seoul’s Ministry of Science and ICT said in a statement to This Week in Asia. The government, which has a 10 trillion won (US$7.3 billion) AI budget for the current financial year, has allocated an additional 250 billion won for the roll-out through 2027. A beta version is set to launch later this month, introducing free, unlimited-access general-purpose chatbots and AI agents developed by three consortiums – led by telecoms giants SK Telecom, KT and Kakao – using hundreds of state-of-the-art Nvidia B200 graphics processing units lent to them by the government. From next year, officials envisage the temporary trial will become a permanent, taxpayer-funded public utility, eventually connecting to government systems to allow citizens to book doctor’s appointments, go house hunting, get tax advice and the like, all through AI intermediaries. To manage the risks involved, Seoul is relying on its landmark AI Basic Act, which came into force in January, to ensure human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory impact assessments and clear watermarking of synthetic content. Meanwhile, a state-funded AI Safety Institute has been tasked with serving as a technical watchdog to evaluate the pitfalls and ensure that public AI utilities remain trustworthy, secure and answerable to the citizens who use them. “Going forward, the government plans to establish an autonomous reliability-assurance system”, the ICT ministry said in its statement, adding this would be based on the seven “AI Ethics Principles” it laid out last month: accountability, human-centredness, privacy protection and fairness among them. South Korea hopes its “AI for All” push will help it become one of the world’s three leading AI powers, alongside the United States and China, with the government seeing the technology as an antidote to a shrinking workforce and as a way to strengthen its export-driven economy. But the same society racing to put AI in every pocket is also confronting the consequences of what that means, as workers worry about automation eliminating jobs, police struggle to combat a surge in deepfake crimes and educators watch a generation’s reading scores slide. Sovereignty is another concern. Of the roughly two-thirds of South Korea’s 51.6 million people who have tried or regularly use AI, 23.45 million are active users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, 8.45 million of Google’s Gemini and 2.41 million of Anthropic’s Claude, according to government figures. Yet access to these platforms cannot be guaranteed, as the ministry noted in its statement. “As we saw recently, foreign AI services can have their availability limited at any time depending on decisions made by foreign governments or companies,” it said, in a possible nod to Washington’s recent attempts to block access to the newest models. In July, Science and ICT Minister Bae Kyung-hoon unveiled plans for South Korea to develop its own cybersecurity-focused AI model by the end of this year, following the US clampdown. Brewing with bots At Unicup Coffee, an independent cafe vying for business against 11 low-cost chain rivals in Busan International Finance Centre, owner Bae Kyung-han, 31, credits AI with helping him beat the competition. What began a year ago as a cost-saving experiment, with Bae teaching himself how to use generative AI to create promotional posters and menu images, has since taken over nearly every part of the business. “It’s now running my research, proposal developments, communications and advertisements,” he said, adding that the AI system – his only office-based “colleague” – had also orchestrated a shift in focus towards bulk orders instead of walk-in customers. Five employees handle customer orders, serving some 13,000 people a month and generating card sales that are, according to Bae, roughly double those of his competitors. He has also built a second business around the technology, registering as a vendor under one of the government’s chosen AI consortiums to teach novices how to ask better questions of their chatbots. “The biggest advantage of AI in the workplace is that it reduces the psychological burden of managing people,” Bae said, describing the relief of no longer having to coordinate schedules, repeat instructions or manage employees’ feelings. “With AI, I can ask questions whenever I need to and revise plans whenever I want to. It’s just more efficient.” Yet he is still sceptical of the government’s AI strategy, questioning whether domestically developed models – even ones that are provided for free – would actually be able to wean people off premium foreign made tools. “People who are used to using AI would likely pay for a more expensive US-based model like ChatGPT rather than use a free domestic service,” Bae said. That is, unless the models were specialised and purpose-built for specific problems, as opposed to another general-purpose chatbot. “That changes the conversation,” Bae said. “That could do wonders for businesses like mine.” Elsewhere, at a jobs fair in Seoul’s Yonsei University, technology companies crowded the floor, competing for the attention of soon-to-be graduates before they had even finished their degrees. Kwon Il-geun, an electronic engineering student hoping to work at semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix, said AI proficiency had never been more important. “My skills in using AI tools have nearly doubled in the past year,” he said, comparing the shift to the first industrial revolution or the arrival of the personal computer. “This is just part of the changing times.” No juniors needed? Not everyone is sharing in the spoils, however. The number of young South Koreans aged 15 to 29 who were in work dropped by 285,000 between June 2022 and June this year, according to the central bank, which estimated that 94 per cent of that decline was in sectors highly exposed to automation, including publishing, IT services and computer programming. And the Korea Development Institute, a government-run think tank, projected in July that AI could wipe out roughly 256,000 jobs a year within the next decade. This has had a knock-on effect on students’ ambitions, with enrolment reportedly falling at academies teaching graphic design and coding, even as institutions preparing young people for stable public-sector careers enjoy booming interest. At the SKY Entrance Exam Academy in Seoul, enrolment in its military and policy preparation track is up 70 per cent year on year. Yun Ji-sang, a recent school leaver, is among those preparing to commit himself to five years of officer training and a military career of 15 years minimum. “Some people think this is a long time to be trapped inside the military, but I just view it as a long time of having a stable job,” he said, noting that it was also one that came with a pension. The number of young South Koreans in employment fell by 143,000 in August compared to the year before, the Chosun Daily newspaper reported on September 9, marking the 46th straight month of decline for those aged 15 to 29. Meanwhile, the number of civil servants being recruited nationwide increased this year for the first time in five years, according to the Ministry of Personnel Management. “I used to want to live as an entrepreneur who would travel abroad frequently and live freely,” Yun said. “But what use is that when we are constantly worrying about making a living?” Conventional wisdom surrounding which jobs were most at risk from automation had been flipped on its head by the rise of generative AI, said Ko Hak-soo, a law professor at Seoul National University. “When ChatGPT first emerged three or four years ago, there was widespread concern that jobs involving workers with relatively low levels of education … would be at highest risk,” he said. “But now, there is a much stronger view that jobs requiring a great deal of human labour may actually be relatively safe while professional occupations, especially entry-level and junior workers in these fields, might gradually disappear.” New roles were likely to emerge as AI became more integrated into workplaces, Ko said – while warning there was “little understanding of the reality of the shifting labour market”. Kim Myuhng-joo, executive director of South Korea’s AI Safety Institute, said the disruption was already under way. “Until just a few years ago, programmers were extremely highly valued, and their salaries were rising rapidly,” he told This Week in Asia. “But AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding … without needing as many junior-level developers.” Kim further voiced concerns that a new cohort of workers coming of age in the “AI for All” era might never develop the skills needed to operate without the technology. “In less than 10 years, we could see a new generation entering the workforce that is overly dependent on AI,” he said. “Companies may expect these new employees to have the capabilities of previous generations, but they … could end up becoming people who are incapable of doing anything without AI.” AI-fuelled abuse South Korea’s most visceral fears surrounding AI stem not from the threat of rogue tech, however, but from the recent reality of criminal misuse. The Nth Room case of 2020 – in which encrypted social media channels were used to produce, sell and distribute sexually exploitative material and blackmail victims – and subsequent scandals led to the country strengthening its deepfake laws in 2024. Producing such material can now result in seven years behind bars or a 50 million won (US$37,000) fine, while possessing or knowingly viewing it can mean three years in prison or a 30 million won penalty. Yet police still recorded 1,553 deepfake-related offences last year, accounting for over 35 per cent of all reported cybersex crimes, according to statistics presented at a recent forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea. In the first half of this year alone, police apprehended 419 suspects for deepfake offences, 17 of whom were physically detained while awaiting trial. The National Office of Investigation said in a statement that officials were “developing police response technologies at a pace that exceeds the speed at which technology itself is evolving”, including by expanding forensic video expertise and the use of AI-assisted detection tools. Won Eun-ji is less convinced that technology alone will solve the problem. As director of Team Flame, which investigates digital sex crimes, she has spent much of this year infiltrating roughly 50 Telegram chat rooms alongside investigative outlet Newstapa, documenting how AI tools have swelled the ranks of anonymous perpetrators and lowered the age of victims. “Even today, many initial leads in these investigations often come from victims themselves,” she said. “The police need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities.” Kim, of the AI Safety Institute, said the government needed to prepare for the unintended consequences of increasing access to AI. “Once AI becomes embedded in society, it is difficult to remove it,” he said, describing it as “an irreversible change”. “We need to conduct thorough impact assessments from the beginning, considering what effects the technology might have and whether it could be misused, abused or overused.” To combat crime, Kim said he would support police undercover investigations “depending on the circumstance” alongside greater use of invisible watermarking to trace AI-generated content back to its creator or means of distribution. “Online platforms should take more active steps to identify online crimes” and prevent abuse material from being circulated, he said, adding the children “need to receive education on these issues as part of broader civic education and AI literacy”, starting in primary school. Generation chatbot Yet in the classroom, an upside-down hierarchy of knowledge has begun to emerge, according to Moon Sung-ho, the 16-year-old editor-in-chief of Tokipul, an independent student-run newspaper. “In many cases, students actually know more about AI than teachers, resulting in students using AI to complete all of their assignments while teachers don’t really know how to stop them,” he said. Song Keun-sang was among the educators who protested last year against the government’s short-lived 1.2 trillion-won plan to roll-out AI-powered textbooks. “Once we actually tried using AI in the classroom, we realised that it wasn’t as useful as we had expected,” said the fifth-grade teacher at a school in South Chungcheong province. While good teaching pushes students to learn more about the world, AI short-circuits this process, according to Song. “It simply gives you the answers,” he said. “It doesn’t have much educational value.” Song had once thought that AI might be useful to help isolated students or those struggling to make friends, but that changed after a child in neighbouring North Chungcheong province died by suicide following conversations with a chatbot. “I wonder whether it is really beneficial for students to be exposed to chatbots that constantly cater to them and reassure them,” he said. “They are essentially designed to tell you what you want to hear, so you will never be challenged or face disagreements.” The effects of this may already be starting to be felt. South Korean 15-year-olds topped global reading charts in 2006, as measured by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment. Yet in 2025 they posted their lowest average reading score since the country first began taking part in the assessments in 2000, the OECD reported earlier this month. “Other countries are starting to ban social media and other online devices for adolescents, but South Korea is moving in the exact opposite direction,” Song said. “We can already expect serious declines in academic achievement and literacy skills.” The more pressing concern for him, however, is social rather than academic. “Cooperation and communication between students ultimately develops the skills they will need to succeed in society later on,” he said, predicting that interacting with AI chatbots might make it “much more difficult to form relationships with other people.” Moon has seen this happen among his own classmates and friend group, who once went to internet cafes and played football together, while also asking for help with homework assignments. “Students these days increasingly ask AI chatbots about these questions,” he said. “It feels like it’s become more difficult to talk with people.” This Week in Asia contacted South Korea’s Ministry of Education for comment on this article. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Hong Kong cycling star Chloe Leung ready for race of truth in bid for Asian Games gold
description: City rider expects to shrug off finger injury and go for glory in Japan, while Vincent Lau prepares for potentially his last Games road race.
content: After all the meticulous preparation, the talking and the injury frights, Chloe Leung Wing-yee is ready for the clock to start ticking on her race of truth in the remote hills of Shinshiro City on Sunday. The little finger on her right hand that Leung broke following a racing crash in Italy in July has been a nuisance, but she has reconciled with the fact that it is just one more challenge, besides the slopes and corners that characterise a deeply technical course, to overcome in her pursuit of Asian Games individual time trial (ITT) gold. Still taped to its neighbouring digit, the offending finger is likely to be more of a pain, both literally and metaphorically, when Leung competes on the track in the Madison, where riders use their hand to sling their teammate back into the race. “I haven’t done much track training because of this,” Leung said. Instead, she has buried herself in getting ready for the road; twice paying exploratory visits to the tight Japanese roads that will stage this weekend’s time trial, and spending time practising on the narrow, winding streets of Girona in Spain. “In Girona, we were working on my skills,” she said. “The biggest thing about going to Japan was to prepare for the weather. We expect it to rain on race day, so I’m ready for the worst, rather than expecting great weather, then suddenly it’s raining.” Still, wet skies and slick surfaces on Sunday would suit Leung down to the ground. She marries fearlessness with judiciousness to navigate weaving descents at breakneck speed, and even left male counterpart Vincent Lau Wan-yau trailing on the race course last week. “I like [rainy conditions] because I’m more confident than ever before: going into corners, doing the downhills and the turns, everything,” Leung said. “Vincent was a bit hesitant in the rain. I went faster in it.” An elevation gain of 326m over the rolling 24.4km route will also play into Leung’s hands. “She’s one of the best climbers in Asia,” Herve Dagorne, the Hong Kong head coach, said. “We are thinking about gold.” Experience has taught Leung to wear that expectation lightly. It still rankles that she finished one place outside the medals in Hangzhou three years ago. “I think at that time I was really feeling pressure, but now I just want to enjoy this,” Leung said, perhaps leaning into memories of the ITT 2018 Games bronze she won as a 21-year-old. “I didn’t expect anything then and the medal was 100 per cent a surprise,” she added. “I think there will be a little bit of pressure [on Sunday] but confidence, too. I’m hoping that on the start line I feel only happiness, and don’t think about anything else.” Unlike Hong Kong’s gun cyclist, Ceci Lee Sze-wing, who is skipping the road in Japan, Leung is about to enter one month of intense competition. She will compete in the Games road race on Tuesday, alongside Kwan Tsz-kwan and Guardiola Cheung Li-tong, before teaming up with Lee in the Madison. The pair are set to race in the same event at next month’s UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai. “I trust the coaches and we’ll do everything we can to maintain our fitness, then try to improve on our last world championships,” Leung said. Fifteenth in 2024, Leung and Lee have come on leaps and bounds – technically, physically and psychologically – in the intervening period. Rather than bemoan her workload, Leung wishes she could add to it by competing in the 2026 UCI Road World Championships, which clash with the Asian Games. Leung went so far as to investigate the possibility of flying to Montreal for the women’s road race on September 26, before returning for the Games track programme from September 29. “I really want to go, but the time difference is too difficult,” Leung said. “I want to know where I am now compared to last year [when she was 22nd and 39th in the time trial and road race, respectively].” Mention to Dagorne that Games organisers this year are staging road races before their track counterparts, a reversal from 2023, and watch the steam rise from the Frenchman’s ears. Leung is more relaxed over the switch, “I prefer having the road first, because it helps me prepare for the track,” she said. The 29-year-old has two bigger-picture targets: to qualify for her first Olympics in 2028, and to secure a contract with a team on the UCI Women’s World Tour. She attracted interest following her 2025 World Championships exploits. “It’s always my dream, and I’ll keep going for it,” she said. Leung acknowledged it would be complicated for her and Lee to replicate their golden Madison effort from last year’s National Games. She has noted with interest, however, that the Japanese favourites “mention the China team every time they do an interview”. “I watch it and read it,” Leung said. “If they only focus on them and leave us alone, we can do what we want. That’s the best scenario.” In Japan, Leung will have to do without elder sister Boey Leung Bo-yee, who retired soon after joining Chloe in the team pursuit quartet that established a city record to claim bronze from March’s Asian Track Championships. Stripped of Boey Leung, Dagorne has chosen not to enter Hong Kong in the women’s team pursuit in Shizuoka, because “we’d have no chance of a medal”. “I haven’t thought about Boey not being there, I’m just focusing on myself,” Leung said. “We message a lot, and she’s always sending videos and pictures of her cats. “We can’t change that we’re not in the team pursuit, we have to concentrate on what we do have.” Lau, the ITT Games bronze medallist from 2023, acknowledged there would be “an element of danger” in Sunday’s race against the clock, but said “you have to manage the risk”. “You need to be brave, but also know your limits,” he said. “My medal last time shows I have the level to be competitive, and I’ve gained more experience and grown physically in the past three years.” Dagorne reckons Lau is among around six riders in a stacked field capable of claiming a podium finish. The competition has been heightened after talented 23-year-old Athit Poulard last year changed his allegiance from France to his mother’s native country of Thailand. “I know my limits and how to pace a time trial course better than I did in 2023,” Lau said. “Your opponents grow, too, but you have to see where you’re at. It’s not really my type of course, but I’ve prepared for it and I’m very eager to get the race going.” Lau, who will turn 30 on the day of the men’s road race next Wednesday, when he will compete alongside teammates Wu Chun-yin, 20, and 19-year-old Daniel Yip Hon-man, raised the possibility of stepping aside after next year to leave the coast clear for the coming generation. “I haven’t lost the passion but I’ll see if I still have the energy,” he said. “I’ll ride next year, for sure, then think about it at the end.”

title: Kirsten Dunst in Manolo Blahnik heels features in new Marie Antoinette book
description: Photographer Andrew Durham documents life on and off the lavish set of Sofia Coppola’s Oscar-winning cult classic, shot on location at the Palace of Versailles.
content: This year marks the 20th anniversary of Marie Antoinette, director Sofia Coppola’s third film. Starring Kirsten Dunst as the Queen of France and Jason Schwartzman as King Louis XVI, the film is still remembered for its performances, cool soundtrack and Oscar-winning costume design, not to mention the countless trays of Ladurée macarons and Manolo Blahnik heels that also played pivotal roles. The film’s enduring legacy lies in its ability to present historical narrative in a modern, vibrant way. This approach helped cement its status as a piece of cinema that continues to resonate with audiences today. Coppola’s long-time collaborator Andrew Durham was there to capture the key moments on a still camera. His book Making Marie Antoinette documents the production of the cult movie, from its conception and filming within the hallowed grounds of the Palace of Versailles, to the Cannes premiere. The release of the book coincides with an exhibition at Versailles, on view from September 22 until January 24, 2027. The exhibition will give visitors a look behind the scenes of Coppola’s cinematic work, featuring original costumes by Milena Canonero, as well as the director’s early storyboards, filming accessories, annotated scripts, set photographs and set design sketches that brought her vision of Marie Antoinette and eighteenth-century France to life. Screenings held in the very rooms where scenes were shot will allow visitors to revisit key sequences from the film. Beyond cinematic artefacts, the exhibition also explores the film’s cultural resonance, delving into how Coppola’s vision, and the “Marie Antoinette style”, continue to have a lasting impact on art, fashion, design and photography. Additional contributions by Alexa Vernice Pacis

title: Escape Manila’s heat for northern Luzon’s pine-scented hills, hanging coffins and other hidden wonders
description: They may not make for a typical Philippine holiday, but the highlands of northern Luzon are a world apart from Manila and the tropical lowlands, finds Thomas Bird
content: Travellers rolling north through Metro Manila along the Skyway are treated to an elevated perspective of the Philippine capital. The land is pancake flat but the buildings – from bric-a-brac slums to gilded high-rises – reach for the heavens. My partner and I, too, are headed higher. Our aim is simple – to escape the city heat and exchange the pervasive congestion for nights that aren’t polluted by light, and days by smog. The most obvious solution would be to take a ferry to some exotic isle – after all, the Philippines has 7,000 of them – but we’ve resolved to head in the opposite direction to the Boracay-bound sun-seekers, to the pine-scented hills of Luzon. The first quarter of the day is spent on a Victory Liner coach, staring at an undulating sea of rice, with only the volcanic profile of Mount Arayat suggesting there may be mountains ahead. Once we pass the city of Tarlac, lowland farms begin to submit to hill country, as the coach lurches from a cane-straight highway to a winding road that traces the contours of the land. The temperature cools with the altitude and the natural world evolves in tandem. Brilliant wildflowers line the passage north and menacing raptors circle overhead. Eventually, we encounter the strangest of things in the tropics – forests of conifers, which dominate the slopes on the outskirts of what’s been aptly dubbed the City of Pines. Baguio, where we plan to spend the night, is a little over 200km (124 miles) from Manila. But it’s the altitude, not distance, that distinguishes it most from the capital.
