At 1,400 metres (4,600 feet) above sea level, the Americans found a cool spot on a former Spanish ranchería to build a summer capital in the vogue of Shimla, in British India, and duly designed one of the country’s most pleasant cities. Lungfuls of pine-scented air explain why administrators from Boston and Chicago chose to escape here from the muggy oppressiveness of Manila during the worst months of the year. As we circumvent Burnham Park – a public lake garden designed by architect Daniel Hudson Burnham that remains the city centrepiece – the laid-back atmosphere of Baguio eases our work-frenzied minds. Although many of the finest old houses have been lost to war and the catastrophic earthquake of 1990, a few period buildings – log and stone constructions designed to blend with the mountainous pine forest – still dot the neighbourhood. Drawn northwest of the park by the imposing City Hall, we stumble upon Café by the Ruins, an American house bombed during World War II only to be reconstructed by local artists using indigenous materials such as bamboo and nipa, the sense of place enhanced by photographs of mountain tribes on the wall and a menu that mixes classic Filipino fare with international dishes. Tortang talong (grilled aubergine omelette with carabao cheese and tomatoes) washed down with tapuey – the local rocket fuel, made with rice, roots and ginger – kindles a satisfied glee at the end of a hard day’s travel. About 1.5km (one mile) to the north, the Baguio Village Inn is a prim wooden lodge overlooking the city suburbs, which carpet a series of steep hills, resulting in topsy-turvy, chaotic little districts catering to a quickly expanding population. The following day, morning light is creeping over the hills when we hop a Jeepney to the City Market in search of breakfast. We get more than we bargained for; mountain-grown strawberries are piled outside shop fronts throughout the labyrinthine bazaar, where peanut brittle, sweet wine and honey are offered for sale along with textiles from the ethnically diverse mountains stretching ahead of us for more than 320km (200 miles) and over six provinces. A brass band appears, and marches through the throng, the trumpets and drums cultivating the feel of a fiesta, recalling the Spanish influence in the Philippine cultural mosaic. However, Iberian colonists didn’t make it far into the cordilleras and mountain peoples were largely spared the corrupting influences of the outside world until the completion of the American-made Halsema Highway, in 1930. It is along this 96-year-old road that we embark on the next leg of the journey. You can’t pre-book, we just have to wait for a minivan ride at the Sto. Niño Bus Terminal. Although, not for long; we’re soon travelling through villages in eyeshot of the terraced hills that turn whole mountainsides into a laddered patchwork of rice fields. It’s a stunning vista, but our driver – a 20-something heavy smoker with a novelty skull dangling from the rear-view mirror – handles the minivan as though he’s driving in the Macau Grand Prix. It’s a roller-coaster trip that ends only after six hours of bouncing and clinging on for dear life, when we’re unceremoniously deposited roadside in Sagada. This remote mountain settlement found its way onto the hippie trail with the arrival of electricity, in the early 1970s, after which intellectuals flocked here to write, paint and make merry on tapuey. Western beatniks followed, “and the artistic influence has left its mark in the form of little boho cafes and inns and a distinctly laid-back atmosphere”, according to my guidebook. Grandma’s Yellow House is not quite “boho”, but homely and convivial nonetheless. Members of the owning family are cooking and offer us food when we arrive. We have a second-floor room with thick blankets on the beds – it gets cold at night – and our own bathroom, with running hot water some of the time. It’s not the Ritz, but not bad given the remoteness of Sagada. The town, it turns out, is no longer the getaway for scribes and bohemians it once was. What Sagada can claim to be, though, is blissful, the alpine cool and whispering pines a balm for travellers with stiff limbs and sore buttocks. The town is dotted with weaving houses - selling everything from traditional scarves to guitar straps - and cafes serving local specialities, notably lemon pie. As the sun sets, the plummeting temperature impels us to return to Grandma’s Yellow House for an early night. The following day, having risen with the cock crow – literally – we rendezvous with Wihlis Talanay on the terrace of the building that houses Saga Tours a little after sunrise. Inside, our guide for the day offers us a variety of hikes, cave tours and terraced mountain viewings. We opt for a tour to Echo Valley and its famous hanging coffins. After compulsory registration with the tourist office, he walks us to the church that overlooks Sagada, a not uncommon sight in a Catholic country, except that this one, the Church of Saint Mary the Virgin, “is Anglican, the Spanish never got here”, explains Talanay. “It’s the Americans who introduced Christianity, this church was built in 1904.” A Protestant church might be out of the ordinary but the traditional burial sites set on the cliffs of Echo Valley are truly extraordinary. “The hanging coffins were hung up high as it was believed the higher the dead were placed, the greater chance of their spirits reaching a higher nature in the afterlife,” Talanay explains of a tradition that is fast disappearing. The coffins are those of distinguished members of the Kankanaey (an ethnic grouping of the Igorot people) and are in various states of repair. They are jammed into crevices, roped to outcroppings and balanced on brackets on sheer cliff faces as if floating. Some have been broken into by foraging animals, the skulls and bones visible as if the dead were preparing to rise. Our walk across the rooftop of the Philippines proceeds along a mountain track deep in the forest, which is home to cloud rats, forest mice, warty pigs and deer, according to Talanay. Hunting and timber were the economic mainstays in Sagada but recent decades have seen the introduction of cash crops, most notably coffee. “Welcome to Sagada’s Starbucks,” says Talanay, pointing to the thatch-roofed Baw-eng Coffee Shop, which has a backdrop of vegetation, stands on a coffee farm and serves mountain-grown brews to thirsty hikers. We pair ours with lemon-cream cookies. Fortified with caffeine, we trek on into the forest. The path climbs then descends to follow a stream, leading through dark caves and patches of upland meadow until it opens onto a clearing drenched in midday sunlight. Butterflies flit everywhere, birdsong chorusing from the tree canopy. We could walk indefinitely in temperatures this conducive and surroundings this seductive, the pull of nature impelling us towards wherever it is Talanay is leading us, for we have no destination in mind. The act of walking is enough. Like so many Filipinos, Talanay once travelled overseas to find work, in his case to Britain. No doubt it was hard to make a living in Sagada but, as the last leg of the hike takes us out of the forest to cultivated land marked by a wooden fence, the mud path becoming a narrow stone road, I begin to understand why he returned to this pristine corner of Earth. We conclude our hike, as all good hikes should end, in a pool beneath a waterfall – feeling a lot farther from Manila than the 400km a crow would fly.

title: Sikh trucker stabbed in Wyoming, stirring fresh fears in US community
description: The attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh drivers led to debate about licensing requirements and rising anti-immigrant sentiment.
content: The stabbing of a truck driver at a remote Wyoming rest stop had US Sikhs on edge on Friday amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular. The Sikh victim was attacked from behind early Sunday while in a restroom at the Bitter Creek rest stop on Interstate 80 midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents. He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived. While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver’s licensing requirements – sparking hatred towards Sikhs as a group, community leaders said. Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California. “I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years,” Singh said. “I never felt this kind of hate before.” Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said. “We have zero motive,” Sheaman said. The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and did not see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case. Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming. A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak’s truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit. Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak. Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit. Bzdak remained jailed on US$1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday. A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, was not immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell. Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the US. Many live in California. Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the US. In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver’s U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed. Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said. Both drivers were in the US illegally, according to the US Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts. One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs – well over 100,000 in the US and millions worldwide – have the last name Singh. No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism towards Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim. “We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.” The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said. But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive. “We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I’m not surprised that it has happened.”

title: Editorial | Global monetary tightening tests China’s 2-speed economy
description: While the domestic hi-tech sector builds momentum, traditional exporters struggling with shifting trade patterns will need targeted support.
content: The US Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates by 25 basis points marks a pivotal moment not just for American monetary policy, but for China’s increasingly fractured economy. As borrowing costs rise globally in response to persistent inflation – exacerbated by Middle East conflicts pushing oil prices skyward – China faces an uncomfortable reality: its economic fortunes depend on which sector you examine. As for Hong Kong, major local banks kept their prime rates unchanged, but funding costs such as the benchmark one-month Hibor (Hong Kong interbank offered rate) are already edging higher. Higher borrowing costs could squeeze corporate profit margins, raise funding costs for artificial intelligence infrastructure investments and suppress the stretched valuations of technology stocks. The Fed’s unanimous vote to lift rates to between 3.75 and 4 per cent reflects a determination to restore credibility amid a bond market rout. A pre-emptive approach to curbing inflation is sound. Markets have responded with cautious approval; global central banks concur. The European Central Bank delivered a hawkish outlook last week, the Bank of Japan raised its rate to a 31-year high, and markets anticipate four Bank of England increases over the next year. For China, these synchronised rate hikes will inflict damage – but unevenly. The artificial intelligence investment boom shows little sign of abating despite higher borrowing costs. America’s AI hyperscalers such as Amazon and Microsoft, locked in fierce competition with Chinese counterparts, are unlikely to curtail data-centre plans over modest increases in debt costs. With these companies reporting surging AI revenues and forecasting even larger returns, a 5 per cent US 10-year Treasury yield would just be a speed bump. This resilience benefits Chinese tech exporters. Chip shipments have more than doubled in dollar terms so far this year, while computer and server exports have surged 50 per cent. These sectors ride a wave largely immune to interest-rate headwinds; greater threats come from calls to slow AI development and opposition to data-centre expansion in the US. The picture darkens for traditional Chinese exporters. Higher US mortgage rates will further depress America’s weak housing market, dampening demand for Chinese furniture and related goods. These categories have grown less than 10 per cent this year. Already battered by China’s domestic real-estate crash and tariff-driven production shifts overseas, these manufacturers now face deteriorating conditions in their largest export market. American consumers, squeezed by rising petrol prices, were showing weakening confidence even before the rate rise. The University of Michigan sentiment index fell more than expected in September, signalling reduced appetite for discretionary purchases – mainly sourced from China. In Hong Kong, the monetary ripples arrived swiftly. The Monetary Authority raised its base rate in lockstep with the Fed, maintaining the currency peg. Yet all three note-issuing banks – HSBC, Bank of China (Hong Kong) and Standard Chartered – held prime rates steady. Beyond interest rates, darker clouds gather. The widening US-China yield gap – American yields spiking amid persistent inflation and fiscal concerns while Chinese bond yields decline amid weak demand and disinflation – risks accelerating pressure on capital outflows. China’s direct US Treasury holdings have already fallen to an 18-year low of US$618 billion. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s recent State of the Union address at the European Parliament raised trade-war spectres, while the US Congress passed legislation authorising tariffs as high as 100 per cent on China for purchasing Russian oil. Domestically, Chinese oil prices briefly hit records this month. For China, a monetary tightening cycle illuminates a challenging structural reality: the economy’s future increasingly belongs to hi-tech sectors riding global megatrends, while traditional manufacturing faces compounding headwinds from higher rates, geopolitical tensions and shifting trade patterns. Beijing has its work cut out as policymakers tackle this two-speed economy and respond accordingly, supporting industries that can weather global headwinds while mitigating the social costs of others struggling to adapt.

title: How much sex should a couple have? Focus on quality over quantity, experts say
description: Satisfying sex boosts relationship happiness more than frequency, and intimacy thrives on connection, not a number, according to experts.
content: Recently, an acquaintance told me about her brother’s marriage break-up. “They had sex once in eight years,” she said – as if that were the sole reason. It would not have been: the couple’s collapsing relationship was the reason. The absence of sex – except for that single occasion in eight years – was a symptom that likely made it worse. It raises the question, though: is there a sweet spot for sex in a relationship? How many times a week or a month should we be “doing it” to keep a relationship alive and well? A decade ago, researcher Amy Muise, a professor in the department of psychology at York University in Toronto, Canada, and a past president-elect of the Canadian Sex Research Forum, published a study that asked whether having sex more often makes a person happier. The answer was yes, up to about once a week, and then it plateaus. The pattern held only for people in relationships. For single people, sexual frequency was not significantly linked to well-being at all. Notably, once a week was roughly the average frequency among established couples in the data. There was a lot of press response to the study, with headlines like “More sex makes us happy, but once a week may be enough”, “Couples who have sex weekly are happiest” and “For a happier life, have sex once a week”. In August 2023, the Family Planning Knowledge, Attitude and Practice in Hong Kong Survey – conducted every five years – found that the Hong Kong couples polled were having sex 3.1 times a month, down from 3.7 times in 2017 and 4.3 times in 2012. Is more sex better? Jill Carter, a sex-therapy specialist and co-founder of Momentum Counselling in Hong Kong, says that before we get worked up over how much sex we ought to be having, the question we need to ask ourselves should be: “Is more sex really better?” “One of the problems with asking how often happy couples have sex is that the question itself can reinforce the idea that there is a ‘normal’ amount of sex couples should be having,” Carter says. “There really isn’t a magic number.” She refers to the work of American sex educator and researcher Emily Nagoski, author of books including the bestseller Come as You Are. Carter says Nagoski “encourages us to move away from measuring sexual well-being by frequency and towards looking at the quality and experience of the sexual connection”. Everybody is different in their sexual wants and whens. “The problem often begins when couples start comparing themselves with what they think everyone else is doing,” Carter says. “Keeping score doesn’t necessarily lead to better intimacy. In fact, sometimes keeping score is precisely what gets in the way of it.” That will come as a relief to those with stressful lives, especially in Hong Kong, where many couples deal with long working hours, demanding careers, small living spaces, children and little privacy. Stress is key to sexual desire, Carter says. “People respond to stress differently. For one person, sex may be a wonderful way to decompress and reconnect. For their partner, stress and exhaustion may make accessing desire extremely difficult. Neither response is wrong.” Confined living spaces can add another layer – they feel less private, especially when there are children in them. “Imagine two new parents living in a small flat,” Carter says. “They’re exhausted, one or both are working, the baby wakes at night, privacy has disappeared and their conversations revolve around logistics: feeding, sleep, childcare, appointments and who’s doing what. Sex may decline dramatically, but the problem isn’t necessarily sex.” Rather than suggest that they need to have sex once a week, “they need help to rebuild the conditions in which intimacy can emerge again”, she says. It’s not all about sex Intimacy does not necessarily mean intercourse either, Carter stresses. It can include kissing, massage or simply being physically close. And it does not end with touch. Emotional intimacy matters too: talking, laughing, going out for dinner without phones. “When couples are struggling sexually, one of the things I sometimes encourage is a once-a-week ‘intimacy date’, where the goal isn’t intercourse,” Carter says. That reminds them both of something important: the other person is not just someone they run a household and raise children with, but their partner and lover. “That can be incredibly bonding.” Returning to the couple who only had sex once in eight years – what might Carter say to them? “When a couple tells me that sex has virtually disappeared from the relationship, I’m interested in what else has disappeared,” she says. While little intimacy – and no intercourse – in a relationship can be the consequence of life and exhaustion getting in the way, there can be bigger things at play beyond the superficial stress. “There may also be unresolved resentment or conflict, or they may no longer have fun together.” In a case like this, Carter says she would want to understand what happened to the connection between these two people. The Gottman Method for couples counselling highlights how healthy relationships are built through small positive interactions, not grand gestures. “It doesn’t always have to be a romantic dinner,” Carter says. “It’s smiling at your partner, touching them as you walk past, laughing together, saying thank you, showing appreciation, kissing goodbye or demonstrating that you’re interested in their day.” Enjoyable sex beats frequency for couples’ happiness Nearly a decade after her original study, Muise’s latest research finds evidence of a shift: a satisfying sex life leads to a happier relationship rather than the reverse. Simply having more sex may not lead to greater satisfaction, but rather, greater sexual enjoyment leads to more frequent sex, and an enjoyable sex life can be more important than the mere frequency of sex for a happier relationship. As Muise, now director of the Sexual Health and Relationships (Share) Lab at York University, puts it: “When sex is more satisfying, you are more likely to have more of it in the future.” In short, frequency is not the key to a happy relationship – it is the payoff. Satisfaction is what actually drives both a stronger relationship and a more active sex life. Aiming for a specific number misses the point entirely: sex-life frequency is a sign of a thriving relationship, not the tool used to build one. Carter says we should not use a certain number of times a week or a month as a prescription. Rather, we should use the research as a reminder that intimacy matters. Jill Carter’s tips for nurturing intimacy Schedule the opportunity for connection, not the obligation to have intercourse. Agree to protect that time – put away your phones, step out of your roles as parents or professionals. Broaden the “menu” of what intimacy means – being close, being playful, laughing. Do not ask yourself: “Did we have sex this week?” Ask yourself: “Did we create space for pleasure, affection and connection with each other this week?” Do not judge your sex life by other people’s – especially from reading headlines in the media. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Top 10: Your funniest memory from summer
description: Readers share amusing stories of time spent with friends and family during the recent holidays.
content:
Our next question: If every time you opened your school bag, it could magically spawn one item that never ran out, what would you want inside? To take part, drop us a line via this form by 12pm on Tuesday, September 22 .
Chan Tsz-yin, 13, Stewards MKMCF Ma Ko Pan Memorial College: I went to a butterfly farm, and lots of butterflies landed on me. I was having a lot of fun while others looked very envious of me. It was so funny!
Hannah Ip, 10, Hong Kong Baptist University Affiliated School Wong Kam Fai Secondary and Primary School: My friend came to sleep over at my house. We played games on our phones and on the Nintendo console. We also talked about funny things while drinking bubble tea, and I almost choked when she told me hers. I started giggling. Do you know what she told me? She said, “Let’s stay up at night, creep out for snacks and play hide and seek.” She added that we should bring back really heavy things and keep them by the dinner table and see how my parents react.
Chong Hok-yu, 14, Ho Yu College and Primary School (Sponsored by Sik Sik Yuen): During summer, my friends and I were playing table tennis when something unexpected happened. One of my friends wears glasses. We were playing normally until, from the side, my best friend’s strong forehand shot smashed the ball into my friend’s glasses, and they broke. It was the funniest thing I have ever seen.
Zofie Wong, 13, Renaissance College: I, a girl, went with my friend, who is a boy, to eat sushi and just hang out. But my female friends from school ended up going to the same restaurant. I had to deal with them teasing me and my male friend for the whole hang-out session. So embarrassing!
Haylie Lam Hiu-yu, 14, Pui Tak Canossian College: During a visit to Jiangmen, in southern China, a group of my friends and I were getting off a bus that had the lights off. Two of my friends started playing around, and, as one of them was distracted, he bumped his head on the compartment above while standing up. Ouch!
Lauren Lee, 10, French International School: I asked my mother, “A bat and a ball cost $1.10 altogether and the bat costs a dollar more. So how much does the ball cost?” She answered incorrectly, and she was so insistent she was correct that she resorted to searching the internet to prove herself. It was so amusing.
Zhuang Kai-wing, 16, Fung Kai Liu Man Shek Tong Secondary School: I tried making home-made dumplings with my family. My filling was too salty, but we still ate them all. The messy‑but‑warm meal became my funniest summer memory, full of joy and laughter.
Ryan Cheung Yin-yuk, 15, CCC Kung Lee College: Watching Spider-Man: Brand New Day at the cinema with my friends. It was a blast! Spider-Man dive-kicked through a car window to stop reckless driving, and Frank wore Spider-Man’s mask as a double agent. You should definitely watch it.
Leung Yan-yu, 14, Ho Yu College and Primary School (Sponsored by Sik Sik Yuen): I went shrimp fishing with my dad and little brother. My brother was very excited. He shouted so loudly when a shrimp came up to us that it almost swam away. We laughed a lot. At the end of the day, we caught three small shrimp.
Cathy Tsoi Tsz-ching, 17, Fung Kai Liu Man Shek Tong Secondary School: Without a doubt, the best moment of my summer was the Animation-Comic-Game (ACG) expo. Cosplayers, fan art and game demos thrilled me. But the real joy was talking with fellow fans in queues – exchanging favourites and tips. That instant connection and collective passion turned a fun day into an unforgettable summer memory.

title: Trump signs bill targeting China’s Russia energy imports days before Xi’s US visit
description: US president gives backing to ‘Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026’ before next week’s Xi-Trump summit in Washington.
content: US President Donald Trump on Friday signed a new sanctions bill into law that targets Russia’s leading energy buyers – China and India – just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for a state visit. The White House issued a brief statement, saying that the President had “signed into law” the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026,” which “authorises and expands statutory sanctions, tariffs, and prohibitions on Russia and extends existing sanctions on Iran.” The US House of Representatives passed the bill by a comfortable 262-159 vote on Wednesday. The Senate cleared the bill last month by an overwhelming 86-11 vote. The legislation, originally backed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, gives Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five biggest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, adding another layer to his tariff-driven approach to foreign policy. The bill would also tighten restrictions on Russia’s energy and defence industries, target its tanker fleet used to evade existing sanctions, and introduce further measures against Iran. The bill does not explicitly name the countries that could face tariffs, but its provisions are expected to affect major importers such as China and India. Countries including Japan, France, Hungary and Belgium could potentially be exempt as they source smaller volumes from Russia and are taking steps to reduce their dependence. China on Thursday criticised the move, saying that Beijing “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit”. “China opposes long-arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said. The developments come just days before US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng are due to hold their final preparatory talks ahead of the Chinese leader’s visit next week. The two sides are expected to settle the summit’s potential economic deliverables, including lower tariffs on agricultural goods, while seeking to extend the fragile trade truce agreed in October last year, the South China Morning Post reported earlier. The bill targeting Russian oil exports to Beijing and other major buyers adds another point of potential friction as Washington presses China to sever commercial ties with Iran under its “Operation Economic Outcast” sanctions campaign. “With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart, [Vice-Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing on Tuesday when asked whether Washington planned to target Chinese banks over their alleged links to Iranian entities. However, Washington is unlikely to target Beijing given the fragile trade understanding between the two countries and its previous decision to penalise only India over Russian oil purchases while leaving China’s imports untouched. Last year, Washington hit New Delhi with a 50 per cent tariff over its purchases of Russian oil, which it lifted in February. India also warned on Thursday that the new law carries “potential implications” for the US-India relationship. “India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people.” India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement. “It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” the statement added. During his second term, Trump has pushed the limits of his executive authority and wielded tariffs aggressively to pursue political and economic goals, from pressuring trading partners to change their policies to advancing US economic interests. Most recently, he imposed new tariffs on goods from Canada and Brazil, further expanding the list of trading partners facing higher US duties. Many House Democrats voted against the Russia sanctions bill, arguing that it would give Trump “sweeping new tariff authorities that he can abuse to raise costs on the American people”. “With this language, he would be able to place tariffs on nearly any country he wants, using sanctions evasion as a pretext,” said Gregory Meeks, a Democratic representative from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. “Does anyone seriously believe President Trump will not use this broad language to target whichever government he is personally angry at?” Washington’s expanding use of tariffs and sanctions is also pushing targeted countries to explore alternatives and reduce their reliance on the US-led global financial system. Last week, Brics leaders agreed to deepen trade and expand the use of local currencies for cross-border payments, advancing the bloc’s efforts to reduce reliance on the US dollar. Brics comprises 11 countries, including China, India, Russia and Iran.

title: Trump says son told him he’ll repay Russian oligarch for wedding parties
description: Democratic lawmakers have launched an investigation into reports that Umar Kremlev contributed thousands to Don Jnr’s festivities.
content: US President Donald Trump ⁠said on Friday that his son Donald Trump Jnr has told him he would pay back a Russian oligarch who bankrolled wedding celebrations for him in the Bahamas in May. Democrats in ‌the US Congress launched an investigation this week into reports that Umar Kremlev, a wealthy Russian businessman and president of the International Boxing Association, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the wedding festivities. ProPublica, which first reported Kremlev’s involvement, said he has close ties to the Russian ⁠government. Trump told reporters on Friday that when he asked his son about the ‌report, he responded: “‘No, I’m paying it back, Dad.’ And that was a while ago. So I heard he’s paying.” A ‌person familiar with the situation confirmed that Don Jnr planned to ⁠reimburse Kremlev. Kremlev ⁠and the IBA did not immediately respond to requests for comment late on Friday. The president, ‌who did not attend his son’s wedding, said in a statement earlier in the week that ‌he does ‌not know Kremlev and that the wedding controversy is “not a big ‌deal!” Trump said on Friday he has given wedding parties to “numerous people” ⁠at “beautiful places” like his Mar-a-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida. “They get married, I ⁠give them a party,” Trump said. “With all of that being said, I understand that Don’s paid him back.” Don Jnr’s wife, Bettina ‌Trump, in an social media ‌post on Monday called Kremlev a friend who extended an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift”, stressing that Kremlev paid for two after-parties, not the wedding itself.

title: Trump says Xi state dinner is ‘a very tough ticket’ as business guest list takes shape
description: US president says White House seats about 125 guests, while Chinese executives facing scrutiny in the US are considered for Xi’s delegation.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he had turned away friends hoping to attend next week’s state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, as reports emerged that executives from some of China’s biggest companies could join the visit. “This is a very tough ticket for me,” Trump told reporters. “I’ve told a lot of very good friends of mine, you just can’t come.” The president said the White House had room for “about 125 or so people”, although thousands would like to attend. He lamented that its planned ballroom was not yet open, saying it could have accommodated 2,000 guests. First lady Melania Trump shared a video on Thursday showing details of the preparations, including the menu and flowers. Trump’s remarks came as Washington and Beijing were finalising a Chinese business delegation for Xi’s visit, according to Reuters. Executives from electric vehicle maker BYD, battery producers Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Gotion, smartphone maker Xiaomi, electronics manufacturer Hisense, auto parts supplier Wanxiang Group, Bank of China and state-owned agriculture group COFCO were among those under consideration, the news agency reported, citing people familiar with the plans. The list has not been finalised, and inclusion does not mean an executive has received a dinner invitation. Chinese executives selected for the visit are expected to attend the White House dinner, Reuters reported. On the US side, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and Apple board chairman Tim Cook are planning to attend, according to ABC News. The White House has not publicly confirmed the guest list. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is meeting with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday to discuss the likely economic outcomes of the Trump-Xi summit and begin preparatory dialogue on artificial intelligence safety and governance. The possible presence of Chinese executives would put some companies facing US restrictions or political scrutiny in the room for the leaders’ meeting. CATL and BYD have been placed on a Pentagon list of companies alleged to have links to China’s military, while US rules and tariffs present substantial barriers to Chinese electric vehicles entering the American market, Reuters reported. The business component would also echo Trump’s May visit to Beijing, when his delegation included executives from US companies that have faced regulatory or market access difficulties in China. Beijing had proposed a round table for US and Chinese chief executives during Xi’s visit, but the White House rejected the idea, according to reports. Trump said he expected “a very good meeting” with Xi. Asked whether the two leaders would discuss an artificial intelligence safety deal, he said they intended to make “a lot of different deals”, without giving details. “We’re going to have some pretty important meetings,” he said.

title: Who is Karen Spencer? Meet Charles Spencer’s ex-wife as he releases new Princess Diana memoir
description: Buckingham Palace has denied claims surrounding King Charles in Spencer’s new book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – but who is the earl’s ex-wife?
content: Buckingham Palace has forcefully denied a claim by the brother of the late Princess Diana that King Charles III said his ex-wife would soon be forgotten after her death. In a new book, Charles Spencer recounts the traumatic days after Diana was killed in a car crash in Paris in 1997 at the age of 36. He alleges that he argued with his sister’s former husband over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to walk behind her coffin during the funeral procession. Spencer says he told the then-Prince Charles that Diana would not have wanted her boys to undergo the ordeal. He claims the prince told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough.” Spencer also accuses Charles of having “contempt” for his ex-wife and of sounding “elated” after her death. The Daily Mail tabloid newspaper is publishing extracts from Spencer’s book, titled Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, which is due to be published next week. Buckingham Palace responded late Wednesday with an extremely strong statement by the measured standards of the royal household. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” it said. While Spencer’s book has once again thrust Princess Diana’s death and troubled married life in the palace back into the spotlight, the earl who tied the knot with his fourth wife earlier this year has had a complicated marital life of his own. In 2025, Spencer was accused of ending his 13-year marriage to Karen Spencer by text and then resorting to “bullying” her with the help of his then-mistress, Dr Cat Jarman, now fourth wife, according to People magazine. It all started with the alleged affair – Karen suspects their trysts began in 2021. In the course of investigating her husband’s relationship with Jarman, Karen found out about the other woman’s multiple sclerosis diagnosis – information she shared with her inner circle. Jarman, who had been keeping her condition under wraps to avoid prejudice, sued Karen for disclosing private information without consent. The countess hit back in her filing, claiming her actions were “entirely justified and legitimate”, given she had just found out about Spencer’s infidelity. Spencer and Karen – who share a 14-year-old daughter, Charlotte Diana – announced their divorce in June 2024, with the earl hiring King Charles’ former divorce lawyer, Fiona Shackleton, to represent him. He made his romance with Jarman public in October 2024, but denied their affair in an interview with the Daily Mail. So just who is Karen Spencer, the ex-wife of Charles Spencer? Here’s what to know. What is Karen Spencer’s background? Karen Spencer was born in June 1972 in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. Growing up, she moved house 22 times and attended 10 different schools because her father worked as a national parks administrator, per Forbes. She grew up with two younger siblings and went to college in Toronto, but dropped out to launch a modelling career. She’s been married before Karen Spencer was previously married to renowned Hollywood producer Mark Gordon, who helped produce Saving Private Ryan (1998) and the popular television series Grey’s Anatomy. The pair met while she worked as a receptionist at the Four Seasons Hotel in Toronto. The couple had two daughters and divorced in 2003. She’s a philanthropist A year after separating from Gordon, reported Forbes, Spencer put part of her divorce settlement money into founding Whole Child International, an NGO dedicated to supporting the emotional needs of vulnerable children in developing countries. “I didn’t finish college, I’d never been to a third-world orphanage, and I didn’t speak Spanish. Everybody thought I’d lost my marbles,” she said. Today, she’s the board chair of her charity after serving for 20 years as its CEO. The countess’ philanthropy earned her an Ashoka Fellowship, a University of Northampton Honorary Fellowship and a Pikler/Lóczy USA Founders Award. She also made People’s list of 25 Women Changing the World in 2017 and co-founded Catalyst 2030 – a movement of social entrepreneurs collaborating to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals set out by the United Nations. She is also a board member of the Centre for Global Development. With additional reporting by AP

title: Exclusive | Word to the wise on organising a Chinese leader’s US visit
description: Ex-senior US intelligence official Dennis Wilder reflects on his experience of Hu Jintao’s 2006 White House visit ahead of Xi-Trump meeting.
content: Let me begin by wishing those planning Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to the US on September 24 the best of luck, something I didn’t have in 2006, when president George W. Bush invited president Hu Jintao to the White House. After you read this, you may wonder how I was able to keep my job. All I can say is, Bush was a very forgiving boss. This story begins in January 2006. I had just been elevated from China director to acting special assistant to the president and senior director for Asian affairs on the National Security Council. My predecessor Michael Green had returned to his position as a professor at Georgetown University. To say I was wet behind the ears is an understatement. As 2006 began, Beijing was pressing for a state visit by Hu to Washington. Bush had made a highly successful visit to China just two months earlier as part of a four-nation Asian tour. China was playing a key role as host of the six-party talks on North Korea and not standing in the way of the war on terrorism. On that trip, the US president had made his strongly held views on religious tolerance clear not by haranguing Beijing but by attending a Protestant church service. He also participated in an extraordinary mountain bike ride with young Chinese Olympic aspirants that was heralded in the Chinese press and supplanted the boring men-in-suits images so typical of US-China summits. Bush was willing to consider a visit by Hu but not a state visit with an elaborate black-tie dinner. Bush had made the decision that only those with boots on the ground in Iraq would be afforded such an honour. Of course, the Chinese had refused to join the coalition. Thus, the counterproposal to the Chinese ambassador was a “social lunch”. The Chinese were dismayed and only agreed with the stipulation that Bush accord Hu the honour of the traditional White House lawn welcoming ceremony. As the April visit approached, I knew I was in trouble. Ever since 1999, the Chinese government had persecuted Falun Gong, and they were intent on disrupting Hu’s visit to the United States. Indeed, on the night before the event, they used megaphones to keep Hu, who apparently suffered from insomnia, from a good night’s rest. The Chinese ambassador repeatedly called me in the night, demanding I do something. I explained that they were within their constitutional rights, but he seemed unimpressed. The weather on April 20 was perfect for a midmorning lawn ceremony. But to begin the ceremony, the announcer intoned, “Ladies and gentlemen, the national anthem of the Republic of China”. Of course, that was a mistaken reference to Taiwan. Fortunately, the Marine Band had been provided with the correct sheet music. My real moment of horror came when Hu stepped to the podium to deliver his remarks. A woman stood up in the press bleachers and began shouting in English and Chinese for Bush to stop Hu from persecuting Falun Gong. At this point, I was writing my resignation letter in my head. I began praying at this point that the Secret Service would step in. I was wrong. I later found out that it is the responsibility of the uniformed White House police to deal with peaceful protesters. However, on the advice of intelligence officials, we had put the uniformed officers along the perimeter because we had information that Falun Gong members would try to jump the fences. Thus, as I remember it, I waited for what seemed like forever for the officers to run across the expansive White House lawn and detain her. But my nightmare was not over. Bush urged Hu to finish his remarks, and after that, it was time to leave the podium and review the US military honour guard. However, Hu tried to leave the stage by the wrong stairs and Bush had to reach out and grab him by his suit. At this point, I was writing my resignation letter in my head. In the ensuing Oval Office meeting, Bush simply said to Hu that “my mother taught me to treat guests better than this”. The Chinese leader graciously accepted this, although the Chinese foreign ministry never let me forget it. For my sins, the president sent me to the White House press briefing room to “explain” what had happened to the world. One senior New York Times reporter later told me that he had never seen such a pathetic briefing. Bush did not fire me, but it took him a long time before he decided to make me permanent senior director for Asia. title: Trump claims US Greenland security deal, China reportedly among adversaries being kept out
description: US president says Washington will expand its military presence on the island; sources report the restrictions include China.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that the United States had reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives Washington permanent authority over security on the Arctic island and requires American approval for military activity or sensitive investment by US adversaries. In a Truth Social post, Trump described the arrangement as giving the US “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland. He said no US adversary could establish a base, maintain a military presence, or make sensitive investments there without Washington’s express written approval. The US would immediately begin developing a large military presence on the island, Trump said, adding that Washington would work with Greenlanders on its development and construction. He said the agreement had no end date and would come at no cost to US taxpayers. Greenland and Denmark offered a more cautious account in a joint press release on Friday, saying they expected to sign a security agreement with the United States next week, during the UN General Assembly in New York. They said the agreement would then need to pass through the necessary parliamentary procedures before taking effect. The release did not say the United States would gain permanent control over Greenland’s security. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the prospective agreement would recognise the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination. Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it would recognise Greenland’s interests. Fox News Digital reported that the restrictions cover China and Russia, citing a senior US official. The official said the deal grants the US permanent access, basing and overflight rights, and allows it to establish additional military installations. Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed an agreement to Fox News, calling it a guarantee of US security interests in the Arctic. Trump’s announcement follows earlier reports that Washington and Copenhagen were nearing a deal to expand the American military presence in Greenland. One person familiar with those talks said the parties had discussed limiting Chinese presence and influence on the island, while both sources said any agreement would fall short of Trump’s ambition to acquire it outright. The announcement comes less than a week before Trump is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24. Trump did not name China in his post or specify which investments would require US approval.

title: Being Chinese | The unspoken reason my Chinese friends choose America
description: When friends say they can just ‘exist’ in the US, they mean they can stop performing to the Confucian expectations that define Chinese life.
content: A friend who is three years into her doctoral programme in the San Francisco Bay Area texted me the other day to say she had finally figured out what was different about living in the US. “I don’t need to perform any more. I am allowed to just … exist.” Naturally, I asked for elaboration. She said that back home in China, every decision she made came with an interview she did not sign up for. Every Chinese New Year, some relative would probe into her personal life with forensic precision. In America, on the other hand, nobody’s uncle asks anything. I laughed, because I had heard versions of this from different people since I came to Berkeley. And every time, my instinct would be to blame Confucius, a man who has been dead for 2,500 years and whose core professional achievement has been making an entire civilisation feel obligated and stressed. Even now, he is still shaping the Chinese group psyche. The funny thing is, as I am typing this, the idea of criticising Confucius actually makes me pause with guilt. Writing an article questioning his role in shaping our civilisational psyche feels like heresy, and my internal brakes engaged automatically. How dare I do something so outrageous! But here’s the thing. If judged by the standards of his own time, the Chinese philosopher wasn’t up to the mark. He spent years touring different states and pitching his vision of benevolent governance to different dukes – much like a start-up founder, but with little success. Historical accounts describe how, at one particularly low point, he was spotted standing alone at a city gate and looking like a dejected “dog from a family in mourning”, a description he himself famously agreed with. It took a few centuries before he could be effectively rebranded as an “exemplary teacher for tens of thousands of generations”. It was not Confucius who built the cult of Confucius. Instead, it was a Han dynasty official named Dong Zhongshu, who made Confucianism the state ideology and advocated a hierarchical society. In this system, roles such as ruler or subject, father or son, teacher or student are meticulously prescribed, so everyone just needs to perform according to the script handed to them and make sure the person above them is OK with their performance. It is a genuinely elegant piece of social engineering. And here’s the part nobody says out loud: everyone is perpetually, quietly trying to be the director, and they secretly hope there is no one above them. Every Chinese person wants to be the one writing the script, as opposed to just reading from it. This is most evident at home, where parents lecture their children incessantly, usually along a one-way street. Then there is lecturing as a competitive sport, with uncles correcting nephews, seniors admonishing juniors and strangers correcting one another. The grand arena of mutual lecturing, of course, is the online forum. Once you enter, you will find quite a few people who think they know how to perform your role better than you. The moment you step out of line, all these self-appointed directors will rush in to magnify your misstep and readily have something negative to say. Here’s the part nobody says out loud: everyone is perpetually, quietly trying to be the director ... Every Chinese person wants to be the one writing the script, as opposed to just reading from it Sadly, although nearly every Chinese person wants to be their own director, almost nobody actually gets to be one. The genius of the system is how every performer is convinced that if they perform well enough, want it enough and make enough sacrifices, people around them will leave them alone and they will eventually get to wield the pen and write the script for others. Most of them never do. Therefore, when my friends tell me they can just “exist” or “be” themselves in the United States, what they are really saying is: they now have the option to stop performing. Almost nobody I know moved here for the dirty streets, wilful public transport system and expensive Asian food. They are here to live the unwatched life. Here, there is no audience running a silent audit of how you behave, no perpetual appraisal of your earning power, your waistline, your marital status or your choice of partners, and no disapproval of you daring to sit down on public transport without earning it first. It’s a small freedom, but dignifying. It just happens to be the kind of thing a very orderly society hasn’t got around to offering in thousands of years. Confucius would probably disapprove of the case I am making, while Dong Zhongshu might be disappointed. Both might find it hard to understand why people would want to stop performing by choosing America. Quite likely, they would expect me to shut up and fall in line, wherever the line has been drawn for me.

title: Trump ‘banning’ CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House
description: The US president’s targeting of three major news outlets is his latest move to crack down on the free press.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he is banning three major news outlets – CNN, MS ‌Now and Politico – from the White House in his latest move to crack down on the independent press. Trump said that, “effective immediately, I am banning” the outlets for allegedly “reporting FAKE NEWS” in a move that is likely to be challenged as conflicting with the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United ⁠States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump said on social media. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” CNN, ‌MS Now, Politico and the National Press Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN’s team remains at the White House working as if it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN ‌reporter Brian Stelter said on air. Trump has a long history of bickering with members of the press ⁠corps and has stepped ⁠up his complaints during his second term in office. And he has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programmes he dislikes or which ‌have joked about or criticised him or his administration, calling on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavoured broadcast stations of their licences. In 2019, the White House credential ‌of Brian ‌Karem, a Playboy magazine correspondent, was suspended after he traded insults with Sebastian Gorka, then an aide to the president, ‌in the White House Rose Garden. A judge later ordered the White House to reinstate Karem’s credential. Since returning to the presidency ⁠in January 2025, Trump has openly badgered reporters, particularly from US television networks. Last year, he also banned Associated Press from ⁠the usual pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Trump’s preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump has instructed executive branch employees to refer to as the Gulf ‌of America. US congressman Frank Pallone, ‌the lead Democrat on the House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee, called Trump’s action censorship. “If Trump thinks banning media outlets from the White House will make his presidency seem less like a failure, he’s delusional,” Pallone said.

title: Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ goes on show amid clash between brother and King Charles
description: The outfit became a symbol of the royal couple’s troubled relationship and the public breakdown of their marriage.
content: Princess Diana’s “revenge dress” went on display in London on Friday, days after new claims about King Charles’s reaction to her death, as the shadow cast over the royal family by the so-called “people’s princess” lingers nearly 30 years on. The dress became a symbol of the rancour between Charles and Diana during the public breakdown of their marriage in the early 1990s, when she made a public appearance in the off-the-shoulder black silk number soon after Charles admitted his infidelity. This week scrutiny of their troubled relationship has resurfaced thanks ‌to extracts published in a forthcoming book by Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, who accuses the king of being “giddily elated” in the immediate aftermath of her death. Buckingham Palace has hit back at the claims, suggesting that the author’s memory had been affected by his loss. The dress was unveiled in Sotheby’s, its first stop on a world tour that will take it to Hong Kong, Geneva and New York, underlining Diana’s enduring and global allure. It will be auctioned at its last stop in December, with a guide price of between US$150,000 and US$300,000. Her appearance in it in 1994 was widely seen as a show of strength as the public feasted on details of the royal couple’s separation – an interest that has come back strongly this week. Humiliated by her husband’s affair with Camilla, ⁠whom he went on to marry in 2005, Diana opted for an outfit which she had had in her wardrobe for years but had previously seen as too daring. “We can imagine it’s a night where she had ‌to decide – whether I go and what do I wear?” said Morgane Halimi, Global Head of Handbags and Fashion at Sotheby’s. “So she decided to wear something that would make her look the most beautiful, the most powerful,” Halimi added. “It’s about being self-assured, being empowered, and not only the negative part of the revenge, but ‌really, ‘This is my life and I stand up for myself.’” As crowds came in to see it on Friday, Spencer’s claims dominated newspaper front pages, airwaves ⁠and pub talk in Britain, showing the challenge ⁠faced by the 77-year-old king who will never quite shrug off his role in a toxic marriage blamed for damaging the hugely popular Diana. “Everybody liked her, so her story will never die,” Merete Lund Jensen, a 54-year-old paediatric nurse said. As well as her sense ‌of style, Diana was known for the easy affection she showed when meeting homeless people, children in hospital or Aids patients, a natural warmth which contrasted with the more formal approach of King Charles. Diana was 36 when she was killed in 1997 in a car crash ‌in Paris, leaving ‌Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, without a mother. She and Charles had finalised their divorce a year earlier. At the time, Diana’s death plunged the monarchy into crisis. The stiff upper lip ‌shown by the royal family was so at odds with the outpouring of grief across the country, that it caused widespread public anger, forcing the institution to change tack and begin to show emotion expected by the ⁠public. But the allegations from Spencer that the king was “giddily elated” over her death have been rejected in unusually strong terms from Buckingham Palace. Spencer’s claims come at a tricky time for the king, who continues treatment for ⁠cancer, while trying to repair the relationship with his semi-estranged son Harry, and navigate the fallout from the arrest of his younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. The book, which is being serialised in the Daily Mail and will be published on Tuesday, claims Charles said about Diana “we’ll forget her soon enough”. Her brother said in the book: “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences ‌and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated – like a ‌lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.” A Buckingham Palace spokesman said on Wednesday: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” Royal commentator Afua Hagan said that Buckingham Palace’s reaction showed that 29 years after Diana’s death the royal family continued to be out of touch with how well-loved she continues to be. “I do think it was quite cold, quite aloof, and that kind of harks back to what people said about the royal family in those days after Princess Diana died. It’s definitely not a good look,” she said.

title: China hawks join forces in US Congress  to pressure Trump ahead of Xi’s visit
description: Trump administration criticised for focusing on achieving economic gains from Beijing while neglecting political and human rights issues.
content: US lawmakers critical of China had a busy week on Capitol Hill, stepping up their activity ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to President Donald Trump in Washington next week. China-focused members of Congress and commissions held multiple hearings on issues ranging from human rights to trade and supply chains – an apparent effort to put a range of issues on Trump’s agenda for his talks with Xi. A former senior US official said congressional Republicans had given Trump “a huge leash” to negotiate with Beijing during his first 20 months in office, but that there had now been “a shortening of the leash” as lawmakers pressed ahead with China-related initiatives. The House Select Committee on China, the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) and the House Foreign Affairs Committee have all held China-related hearings this week. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi also took part in a “shadow hearing” on Tuesday organised by Democratic members on human rights in China, criticising the Trump administration for focusing on economic benefits while neglecting political and human rights issues. “If we do not speak up for human rights in China because of commercial interests, we lose all moral authority to speak up for human rights any place in the world,” Pelosi said at the event. “Apparently, we seem to be abdicating that right.” Pelosi, 86, a San Francisco Democrat and long-time hawkish voice to Beijing, is retiring from Congress. Jonathan Stivers, a commissioner on the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission and the US Director of the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation, also testified at the hearing. A CECC hearing focused on Jimmy Lai Chee-ying and urged Trump to raise his case with Xi, while a newly introduced bill sought sanctions. Lai, the former Hong Kong media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years under the national security law. The congressional activity drew condemnation from Hong Kong officials. Liu Chang, a spokesperson at the Chinese Embassy in Washington, said Beijing opposed using human rights and Hong Kong-related issues to interfere in its internal affairs and “politicising” trade and technology issues. He called for dialogue to safeguard stable and smooth global industrial and supply chains. The congressional activity has extended beyond Hong Kong. On Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs hearing, titled “Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America”, examined covert foreign influence, with China repeatedly cited as a US adversary and a source of risks to American society. On Wednesday, the committee’s East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee held another hearing titled “Lives, Not Leverage: The Long Arm of China and North Korea’s Repression”. One of the witnesses was Sylvia Zin, the wife of US citizen and Myanmar-focused scholar Min Zin, who was detained in China in June on suspicion of espionage and endangering national security. Beijing has rejected the “wrongful detention” designation, saying Min Zin was subject to criminal coercive measures as part of an investigation and that his legitimate rights had been fully protected. Also on Wednesday, the House Select Committee on China held a meeting focusing on import controls and supply-chain risks posed by China. The CECC is scheduled to hold a hearing next Tuesday on political prisoners in China. Congress also passed a Russia sanctions bill this week that could affect China, adding another source of tension ahead of Xi’s visit. The legislation authorises Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian energy, potentially including China. Beijing criticised the measure, saying its economic cooperation with other countries should not be disrupted or subject to US coercion. Steve Yates, a senior research fellow and China expert at the Heritage Foundation, stressed the importance of raising political and human rights issues with Beijing while acknowledging that Trump has a broad range of issues on his agenda, including Russia, Iran and fentanyl. “There’s a broad menu. And I would make no bones about it,” Yates said. “There’s a full menu, and China has made the menu more full.” It remains unclear how much of this congressional activity will make its way onto Trump’s agenda. The two leaders are expected to meet in Washington on September 24, with a White House state dinner also planned. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio have held discussions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng are expected to meet this weekend as the two sides continue working on potential deliverables. Xi’s coming trip would be his first state visit to the United States since 2015, when he met then-President Barack Obama in Washington. His most recent US visit was in 2023, when he travelled to San Francisco for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Additional reporting by Teresa Frontado

title: Over 2,000 UK flight cancellations traced to millisecond software defect
description: The September 8 chaos stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers for hours on UK airport runways and in terminals.
content: A preliminary report on Friday blamed a millisecond-software defect for the cancellation of over 2,000 flights in and out of the United Kingdom last week. NATS, formerly known as National Air Traffic Services, said on Friday that the glitch on September 8 was behind the mayhem at British airports and beyond, rather than any human failings – as many had speculated at the time. It said a software defect in the National Airspace System, which allocates codes so air traffic controllers can identify flights on radar, was behind the decision to axe the flights. The move affected hundreds of thousands of travellers. “This happened in the space of a millisecond,” the report said. The chaos, which stranded passengers for hours on airport runways and in terminals and took days to clear up, was the latest embarrassment to afflict NATS, which operates the UK air traffic control system. It prompted mounting calls for its CEO Martin Rolfe to stand down. “This was a software issue in a specific part of our flight data system that we have traced to a small subsection of coding,” he said, adding that mitigation measures are in place while a permanent fix is tested and deployed. Apologising once again for the chaos, Rolfe said it was not a result of “any incorrect actions by either military or civil operators”. Rolfe also said the latest incident was not connected to a previous outage in 2023 or a radar issue in July last year. UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander met Rolfe in the aftermath of the flight chaos and ordered his organisation to complete a full investigation into the incident to make sure lessons are learned. “I have now received NATS’ report and, while I am pleased to see that the safety of passengers was protected, it’s clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos,” she said. Alexander said she has tasked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review to check NATS’ findings and investigate their investment plans to enhance resilience in the future, along with regulatory accountability. The UK government owns 49 per cent of NATS, making it the largest shareholder and giving it a veto over key decisions. Airlines, airports, investors and employees own the remaining shares in the public-private partnership.

title: Chaos, tepid public interest at Asian Games so far, but things will heat up when it counts
description: Hong Kong team among those hit by issues such as housing, but the enlarged multi-sport event will see its share of world-class competition.
content: The Asian Games open in Japan on Saturday, against a backdrop of complaints over athlete accommodation, venues that have leaked under record rainfall, and a host city still at odds with the Olympic Council of Asia over the ballooning number of those taking part. Chaos has been the theme in the week before the opening ceremony, with transport data errors at Nagoya airport leaving teams stranded for hours without food, while basketball players who did manage to get to their rooms found themselves forced to bed down in converted containers that barely held their two-metre (seven-feet) frames. Hong Kong’s delegation has not been spared either, with the table tennis teams sent to different accommodation when they arrived on Thursday. The players and coach Liu Guodong of the men’s team were sent to the newly arrived Costa Serena cruise ship, which will house some 4,000 competitors over the next two weeks, as was women’s coach Zhang Rui. The rest of the players and coaching staff, plus a host of support staff, were sent to locations across Nagoya. “It’s quite difficult for us, to be honest, all the staff in one place while the athletes are in another place – it’s complete separation,” Liu said. “Our players can only receive massages at the arena for now, or we have to try getting day passes for our medical staff; we’ll figure it out. “We are not going to complain too much. It’s important to keep a positive state of mind because these situations cannot affect our players.” Three years after China built a small city to house athletes, officials and media at the Hangzhou Games, the less impressive Japanese version has caused angst for a variety of reasons. Three of the four players representing Hong Kong in men’s 3x3 basketball have complained of seasickness associated with the rolling of the cruise ship. “We were all very hungry after finally getting out of the airport following lots of procedures,” Ivan Yang Bo-wen said. “There were a lot of people waiting in the lobby when we arrived at the cruise ship, and everyone was facing the same problem; I was expecting better arrangements.” Multi-sport events such as these, however, have a habit of coming good when it counts, and five years after Covid deprived the nation’s capital of the Olympic party it had hoped for, Japan will stage its third regional Games, although not with the enthusiasm it might have hoped for from its residents. Public interest has been low, with officials struggling to sell tickets and Nagoya’s desire for a “simple, streamlined and functional event” slamming headfirst into the OCA’s far grander vision. An initial local budget that banked on around 15,000 athletes, coaches, medical staff and the usual assorted hangers-on has risen to some 17,000, partly because of the addition of new sports such as padel and mixed martial arts (MMA). While the Paris Olympics had 329 medal events in 32 sports, Nagoya will feature 469 medal events in 43 sports, up from 40 sports in 2023. While cramming in more, the hosts have also dropped a number of non-traditional competitions that were held in Hangzhou. Chess, Go, xiangqi and bridge have all been ditched, as have dragon boat racing, roller skating and open water swimming. Instead, spectators will get MMA, ⁠padel and surfing, as well as virtual taekwondo and teqball, a ball sport that combines elements of table tennis and football. Esports will again be a medal event, while ‌breaking has been retained, despite its less than impressive display in France in 2024. Competition will be fierce in Asia’s traditional strengths of table tennis, badminton and weightlifting, while athletes will be competing for ⁠Olympic quota spots for the 2028 Los Angeles Games in archery, hockey, sailing, squash, surfing, tennis and triathlon. The Tokyo Aquatics Centre will be laden with global quality ⁠when the swimming launches on Sunday, when Siobhan Haughey could yet compete in the women’s 50m breaststroke, as she looks to defend the two gold medals she won three years ago. The Olympic men’s 100m freestyle champion and world record holder Pan Zhanle leads a strong Chinese squad, though it might be his 13-year-old teammate Yu Zidi who steals the show. Filipino tennis player Alex Eala, whose every move on the WTA Tour has drawn ‌excited crowds of compatriots, will bid for ‌gold three years after claiming bronze in the singles and mixed-doubles events at Hangzhou. Enthusiasm levels for the Games are likely to improve among home fans with a few gold medals. Japan finished third with 20 golds at the Paris Olympics, upstaging Great Britain, Australia and hosts France. Javelin thrower Haruka Kitaguchi, the first Japanese woman to win Olympic gold in a field event, will lead the hosts’ athletics hopes, while triple Olympic gymnastics champion Shinnosuke Oka will also be bidding for gold.

title: In Focus | Why China is playing it cool amid Trump’s disruption and churn
description: Despite months of US ambivalence, Beijing’s patience and composure at key Washington summit can show they are ‘the new adults in the room’.
content: When the presidents of the United States and China meet in Washington, the world will be watching to see whether their two countries can make good on their agreement to work towards “constructive strategic stability”. In the first part of a series, Mark Magnier looks at expectations in the US for the summit. Chinese planners have been frustrated for months at the slow speed of decision-making and limited engagement by a distracted US administration as the days tick down to next week’s high-stakes summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. This may advantage Beijing by precluding trade and security concessions that require extensive groundwork, according to former US officials, analysts and people involved in coordinating the visit. “How are we going to get anything done if we can’t even agree on the basic logistics,” said a person involved in planning. “The Chinese are … not thrilled with it. But as a result, we have ever-shrinking expectations for the visit, and the Chinese are OK with that too.” Any expectation of a massive soy deal or a large number of Boeing aircraft was a long shot, he added. “The Chinese are all signalling that their expectations are very low, that there should have been more preparation,” said Bonnie Glaser, managing director with the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “It’s hard to identify anything that is a sure thing,” she added. “I haven’t heard the term ‘deliverable’ even used.” But reduced expectations also speak to a US president who disparages planning in favour of in-person deals with his “gut” – and to increasingly frequent presidential summits. “This is not a relationship where you can expect big numbers or major gift packages being announced any more,” said Yun Sun, China director at the Stimson Centre. “We seem to have unrealistic expectations that these two leaders should come together, sit down, announce the ending of all wars and world peace. That’s just unrealistic.” While planning has picked up ahead of the first full US-China state visit in Washington since 2015, arrangements have been creaky as the White House juggles the Iran war, rising inflation and Trump’s declining popularity. “There probably won’t be breakthroughs because Trump’s team is not capable of that,” said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group. “But there also won’t be a breakdown.” Drawn-out issues include a US$30 billion for US$30 billion, or “30-for-30”, reciprocal tariff reduction deal likely to be a summit cornerstone; extending a trade truce that expires next month; when, where, and on what issues meetings will be held; and who will meet an expected Chinese business delegation. One impediment has been the small circle of White House decision-makers. “It’s a bandwidth issue,” the person involved in planning said, citing a reluctance to involve the US president too early. “You’ve got folks who don’t want to bring Trump into the discussion yet because they think he might land someplace different than they land,” he said. “The longer they put it off, the better people are going to be able to shape a contained visit.” What each side hopes to achieve For Trump, the summit is an opportunity to celebrate his power, host a strong leader he admires and bask in the pomp and ceremony he relishes. “Trump wants a diversion, something showing he is a ‘big guy’ peer and managing China to good effect,” said Kevin Nealer, a partner with The Scowcroft Group consultancy. “My worry is they lack any affirmative agenda. There’s nothing we’re doing together and plenty that divides.” Xi, meanwhile, can showcase China’s growing clout, solidify gains made on Taiwan and show that Beijing faced down the US on trade and prevailed. “They want the world to see they can manage Trump and they want the world to say, ‘look, we’re being treated as the equal,” said Ryan Hass, China director at the Brookings Institution and former National Security Council (NSC) official. “Part of their broader narrative is, we’re the new adults in the room; it’s the US that is the disrupter.
