They’ve got a lot of reasons that they want this to go right.” Summit format to mirror Trump’s May trip to Beijing The summit format will be a meticulous mirroring of Trump’s May trip to Beijing, lasting no more than 48 hours, with no additional stops, speeches or side trips out of the capital. This suits China’s equal footing messaging, analysts say. It also blunts criticism that Chinese business leaders accompanying Xi are outsourcing American jobs, since they are only replicating Trump’s entourage. A key focus is likely to be the 30-for-30 tariff reduction framework. Washington wants to include US farm exports to appease Trump’s rural farm base hit by higher costs tied to the Iran war and his aggressive tariff policies. It also wants China to export so-called 4A products to the US, such as apparel, footwear and televisions, to ease voter affordability concerns and address China’s failure to fully satisfy the 2020 phase one agreement. China, however, would rather export higher-value goods and has expressed interest in a package larger than US$30 billion that Washington reportedly balked at. On the political front, China at one point offered over a dozen non-economic issues for discussion, according to one source, only to see these largely rebuffed, with the administration laser-focused on three: a possible November Xi-Trump meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen; a possible December meet-up at the G20 in Florida; and China’s help in pressuring Iran, something Beijing rejects given its ties with Tehran. “It’s basically been the Chinese in a holding pattern, waiting for the US to stand up some sort of interlocutor,” the source, who declined to be named, said. “Two of those are logistics, and one of those is a non-starter … So, we have nothing to discuss on the political-diplomatic track.” What was likely, analysts said, were some largely symbolic announcements on law enforcement, space, military communication and something on artificial intelligence, arranged this weekend by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng. “We should have exceedingly low expectations for the AI dialogue. In all likelihood, it will be a one or two-hour conversation in consecutive translation between two men in their 60s and 70s,” said Jon Czin, a Brookings fellow and former CIA analyst. “Moreover, the administration does not have a coherent view on what – if anything – should be done about regulating AI at home, never mind in tandem with our principal competitor.” Expect US-China trade truce to be extended Another likely announcement is an extension of the trade truce Xi and Trump reached in South Korea last year. But even this had seen wrangling, analysts said. China pushed for a 24 or 27-month extension, while Washington sought six to 12 months, reportedly believing this boosted its leverage amid the lingering distrust over phase one outcomes. Looming over the talks – and a source of Beijing’s growing confidence – is China’s tight control over global rare earth production essential for hi-tech products. While Beijing wants to cement its constructive strategic stability framework, those close to negotiations said Washington saw it more as a holding action until it eased China’s grip and potentially resumed its trade war. “If it’s two years, it’s not strategic stability,” said the person involved in planning. “China has got one definition and Washington has got a very different definition.” Taiwan not on the agenda Taiwan was not expected to be contentious, sources said, given Beijing’s satisfaction with Trump’s suggestion in May that the US would not fight a war over Taiwan. “If I were the Chinese, I would say “you got basically everything out of Trump that you are likely to get’,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow with the conservative American Enterprise Institute. “Anything else that he does carries at least a 50 per cent chance that he says something that you’re not going to like. So why poke this issue?” Beijing will, however, likely convey its displeasure with any Taiwan arms sale soon after the summit – as seen with December’s record US$11 billion package – any interaction with Taiwanese officials or any record weapon sales. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is traditionally opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed by law to supplying it with weapons. Within the administration, meanwhile, mud wrestling and competing objectives abound. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been sidelined from most China discussions, partly given his prominent role in threatening 50 per cent tariffs against China leading up to “Liberation Day”. That backfired when China imposed rare earth restrictions. “That revealed the American underbelly to the Chinese,” a Washington insider said. Bessent remains the lead on the China file but has numerous other responsibilities, while US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer oversees the 30-for-30 framework, keen on helping achieve balanced trade and blunting Chinese exports that could further deindustrialise the US. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a long-time China hawk, meanwhile, had been noticeably quiet, potentially burnishing his anti-Communist credentials for any 2028 presidential run, analysts said. This weekend’s expected Bessent-He meeting and Thursday’s call between Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi just days before the summit, also point to ineffective planning or outcomes. “Maybe the Chinese are happy to have that,” said Cooper, a former NSC and Defence Department official. “But if anyone wanted a deliverable out of the summit, the last thing you’d do is wait until three days before arrival to try and hammer out the details.” At least the two were talking, however, analysts said. “Just to think how deeply hostile we were,” Sun said. “I’m not sure if it’s going to end well, but it’s already a miracle. “The evaluation of whether this visit is a success should not just be contingent upon the big-ticket items. “It’s also the overall stabilisation of the bilateral relationship, which people should remember could generate the largest nuclear war in human history. So on low expectations I would argue that no bad news is good news.”

title: Review | Netflix K-drama The Scandal review: Son Ye-jin, Nana anchor Dangerous Liaisons adaptation
description: Netflix’s The Scandal reimagines Dangerous Liaisons in Joseon-era Korea, exploring seduction, power and societal constraints.
content: 4/5 stars Lead cast: Son Ye-jin, Ji Chang-wook, Nana Les Liaisons Dangereuses (Dangerous Liaisons), an 18th century novel by Pierre Choderlos de Laclos, is an erotically charged tale of aristocrats indulging in illicit games of seduction that may not seem like an ideal fit for a Joseon-era Korean adaptation at first. The period’s patriarchal nature, however, makes it the perfect backdrop for The Scandal, Netflix’s glossy adaptation of the novel starring Son Ye-jin (No Other Choice), Ji Chang-wook (The Worst of Evil) and Nana (Mask Girl). It is not the first time a Korean filmmaker has tackled this celebrated text in a historical setting. In one of her most iconic roles, Jeon Do-yeon starred in E J-yong’s Untold Scandal (2003), another Joseon-set take on the material that directly inspires this new drama. Hur Jin-ho also adapted the story, moving it to 1930s Shanghai for the 2012 Chinese production Dangerous Liaisons, which paired Zhang Ziyi and Jang Dong-gun. The Scandal is helmed by veteran director Jung Ji-woo, who is no stranger to carnal dramas following films such as Happy End and Eungyo. Jung previously partnered with Netflix on the dark serial killer thriller Somebody. Son stars as Lady Cho, a brilliant noblewoman who presents herself with perfect poise and decorum but secretly bristles at the stifling conventions of the time. In a society that denies women a voice, she has tried to circumvent the patriarchal order through her close friendship with her cousin, Cho Won (Ji). When they were younger, Lady Cho gave Cho Won her writing to use in his exams, which earned him great respect among the nobility. As an adult, Cho Won leans towards a decadent, libertine path, but the unusual connection between them remains as charged as ever. When Lady Cho must welcome concubine Lee So-ok (Shin Youn-ha, Oasis) into her household to help her husband father a male heir, she asks Cho Won to seduce the woman as part of a wicked plan. The plan takes on a new dimension when Ahn Hui-yeon (Nana), a young widow celebrated for her devotion, arrives. Hui-yeon intrigues the bored Cho Won, who sees her as a worthy challenge compared to the easy prey he is used to. Cho Won suggests switching his target of sexual conquest to Hui-yeon. Should he succeed and bring back written proof of the deed, Lady Cho will grant him his most cherished wish: allowing him to share her bed. So begins a complex game of duplicitous courtship that will push its conniving instigators to confront unexpected feelings. While The Scandal hews quite close to Untold Scandal, using the same names and departing from the original text in many similar ways, this is a much longer adaptation of the book. Consequently, the social tapestry is richer but also more Byzantine. The social complexities Lady Cho must navigate are presented in greater detail, but while the added layers of decorum and hierarchy deepen the proceedings, they also become more disorienting. Unable to show her desires in public in a society with few private spaces, Lady Cho has only ever been herself around Cho Won, whom she recognised as a kindred spirit. Yet Cho Won, as a man, is free to pursue a dilettante’s life, partly insulated by the reputation of his intellect – a status Lady Cho’s words granted him. Inevitably, when Cho Won ultimately falls for Hui-yeon, he acts on his desires despite his feelings for Lady Cho and the danger that romance could present to Hui-yeon, stripping her of her status as a “virtuous woman” and ruining her. Lady Cho has only ever dropped her guard when alone with Cho Won, but after years of bitterness hardening her, it is no longer clear whether she still does so. In one of her most challenging roles, Son excels as a graceful, calculating noblewoman who always seems to be putting on an act. With his sharp command of tone, Jung orchestrates a tale that rewards viewers – though occasionally demanding their patience – through powerful performances, lyrical dialogue and keen social observations. Meanwhile, Nana delivers a transformative turn and has never been better. Challenging and complex, The Scandal is another worthy adaptation of Les Liaisons Dangereuses, adding new dimensions to the novel’s timeless exploration of social double standards. The Scandal is streaming on Netflix.

title: Patient who needed soft food dies after choking on regular meal at public hospital
description: Prince of Wales Hospital says man, 54, lacked identification and was given temporary identity, which contributed to wrong food order.
content: A Hong Kong patient died after suffering a heart attack when he was fed a regular meal instead of the required soft food and choked at Prince of Wales Hospital. The public hospital in Sha Tin issued a public apology on Friday and said it had appointed an eight-person panel to look into the blunder. A report, along with recommendations for improvement measures, is expected in eight weeks. The 54-year-old male patient was admitted to hospital on Wednesday morning “due to deteriorated mental status”, the Hospital Authority said in a statement reporting the sentinel event. The man had no identification document upon admission, so the hospital generated a “pseudo identifier” for registration. Given his clinical condition, the attending doctor subsequently gave a “diet as tolerated”, or DAT, order for nursing staff. DAT generally refers to a medical instruction indicating that a patient should consume food and fluids according to his or her individual tolerance and comfort level. But the hospital’s catering management system defaults to arranging a regular meal for patients registered under a pseudo identifier. “A nursing staff member did not complete checking the patient’s previous diet records to adjust the diet order, [and] a regular meal was served to the patient that night,” the hospital said. He started feeling unwell while fed by a patient care assistant. Doctors were called to help remove the obstruction in the patient’s airway, but during the emergency treatment, he went into cardiac arrest. His condition continued to deteriorate, and he died late that night. “Upon reviewing the patient’s history after the incident, the hospital found that the patient had been frequently hospitalised before due to underlying diseases,” the authority said. The patient was said to have suffered from dementia and had a history of stroke. “Following speech therapy assessment, a purée diet was recommended for the patient due to dysphagia,” it said, referring to difficulty swallowing. The hospital said it was deeply saddened by the death and had met with the patient’s family to explain the incident, extending its sincere apologies and condolences. “The hospital has devised immediate measures, including reminding healthcare staff to thoroughly assess patients’ clinical conditions and diet orders before making meal arrangements and reviewing the default meal setting of the [dietary and catering management] system,” it said. “The nursing staff member and [patient care assistant] concerned have been temporarily arranged for non-clinical duties.” A similar blunder was reported at Caritas Medical Centre in March last year when a 75-year-old patient choked to death after a nurse misunderstood the doctor’s instructions due to a communication error and gave him the wrong food. The man, who was supposed to be on a puréed diet, was fed solid food instead.

title: Alibaba open-sources medical AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
description: Tested on nearly 40,000 real-world exams, the model outperformed most radiologists, according to a new study published in Science.
content: Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts. The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday. The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy. The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”. In a comparative study involving 26 human radiologists from multiple hospitals, the model’s average accuracy exceeded that of 23 participants, according to the study. With the model’s help, the radiologists also managed to improve their ability to prevent missed diagnoses by 10 per cent while reducing the time required by more than 30 per cent, Damo said. The research was published on Thursday in the journal Science. Several institutions took part in the study alongside Alibaba, including a hospital affiliated with Zhejiang University. The model’s release builds on a string of recent medical AI advances by Alibaba as Chinese technology giants increasingly explore the use of cutting-edge technology in healthcare settings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. In recent years, Damo Academy has focused on developing AI screening tools to help doctors identify conditions including pancreatic, stomach and colorectal cancers, as well as aortic dissections. In April, the division released the Coca AI model, which it said was more sensitive than radiologists in spotting early-stage colorectal cancer from CT scans. The model was co-developed with Chinese institutions including the Guangdong General Hospital.

title: Foreign carers for elderly to get 10 to 20% more pay than current helpers
description: Carers must also have received elderly care training recognised by Hong Kong and possess at least three years of experience looking after older people.
content: Foreign domestic carers brought to Hong Kong to look after elderly residents under a proposed government pilot scheme would receive 10 to 20 per cent more pay than existing helpers, the labour minister has said. Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han on Friday revealed additional details about the arrangement for foreign domestic carers, as the government also released a comprehensive report outlining strategies for an ageing society. The report listed 73 measures spanning 11 areas, many of which were revealed in the policy address earlier this week. “The rapid development of the ageing population has an immense impact on the economy and different areas of society, and both challenges and opportunities exist,” Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said. “The government must actively formulate strategies as early as possible based on population changes and make forward-looking plans.” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced in last year’s policy address the formation of a working group on ageing society strategies, chaired by Cheuk and tasked with submitting a report on the blueprint this year. The pilot scheme to introduce foreign domestic carers, announced in the policy address on Wednesday, is among measures to tackle manpower shortages exacerbated by the greying population. Sun said the minimum wage for carers would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that of current domestic helpers. The carers must also receive elderly care training recognised by Hong Kong and possess at least three years of experience looking after older people. The current minimum wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month. “People can choose,” Sun said. “If you only need a foreign helper, you can continue to recruit from the foreign helpers’ market. “But if you need someone with greater ability and they are accredited to take care of elderly people, you can pay a bit more to hire a foreign domestic carer.” The minister added that the initiative would provide reassurance to local families seeking workers with proven experience in caring for elderly people. Hong Kong is struggling with a rapidly ageing population. The number of people aged 65 and older is projected to increase from about 1.8 million in 2025 to 2.74 million by 2046, at which point more than one in three residents will be elderly. Sun expressed confidence that the scheme would not disrupt the market for foreign helpers. “If existing helpers want to change their job and become foreign domestic carers, they would need to return to their home country, receive relevant training and meet other requirements before they can come to Hong Kong,” he said. “We do not want the newly created job causing concern to current [employers] of foreign domestic helpers.” A government source on Wednesday said that the scheme would be launched next year. Alice Lau Yim, permanent secretary for labour and welfare, said the carers would be required to work in a domestic setting and live with their employers, similar to the current arrangement for helpers. “The main target is to raise the quality of foreign domestic helpers who are now taking care of elderly people and offer one more option in the market to families in need,” she said. Currently, about 380,000 foreign domestic helpers work in Hong Kong. More than half are from the Philippines, followed by Indonesia and other countries. Johannie Tong Hiu-yan, a community relations officer with the Mission for Migrant Workers, said a 2018 survey by the NGO found 40 per cent of helpers were already looking after elderly with different degrees of disability. Many were therefore puzzled when authorities announced the plan for dedicated carer positions, he said, adding none had yet indicated an interest in flying back home for the training. Tong said unionists had been campaigning for a 10 to 20 per cent basic salary increase for helpers, taking into account the unique position they held in the Hong Kong market. “If we were paying specialised carers this amount, it is not enough at all,” he said. Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Overseas Domestic Helpers Association, warned that the scheme could disrupt the market for domestic helpers. She said the government had consulted employers’ groups beforehand but decided to press ahead despite opposition. Yung noted many helpers had already undergone training before coming to Hong Kong and had been caring for elderly people for several years, making specialised carers unnecessary. “Some dissatisfied helpers may just leave their jobs for better pay and higher status … and their flight back home [for the training] is covered by the employers,” she said. She also highlighted the financial burden on employers, claiming that they already spent about HK$7,000 a month to cover the wages and living-in costs of helpers.

title: Are the doors to German universities closing for China’s STEM researchers?
description: As Berlin pursues de-risking, hundreds of visa applicants in China are rejected each year, an investigation finds.
content: Chinese AI researcher “Joy” waited more than seven months to hear that his visa application for Germany had been rejected. The 30-year-old had been offered a postdoctoral position at a German technical university but the rejection letter said there was an Ausweisungsinteresse, or public interest in denying him entry. Citing Section 53 of Germany’s Residence Act, the letter said that for applications involving “study, research and similar employment”, particular attention had to be paid to the possibility that knowledge acquired in Germany could be misused in ways that harmed protected legal interests or other significant German interests. The letter did not specify which aspect of his research, personal background or application materials amounted to a security risk. And Joy said he was not contacted by German authorities about his research, education or work history during the months of waiting. “I did not know where exactly the application was stuck, or whether any additional security screening was taking place,” he said. Joy’s experience corresponds with reports of long wait times and refusals for Chinese researchers applying for visas to take up positions at German universities as Berlin puts higher scrutiny on security risks in research. According to a joint investigation by the German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung and public broadcasters NDR and WDR, the number of visa applications from Chinese science researchers that are rejected by Germany’s foreign office each year is in the triple digits. The report said that around 400 Chinese applicants were turned down last year, of whom around 200 had doctorates. China has made high technology in strategic sectors one of its top priorities in its drive to move up the industrial value chain and secure a firmer footing in its rivalry with Washington. These sectors – such as aerospace, semiconductors and automation – are precisely the areas where Germany most frequently denies visa applications, according to the investigation. The investigation said Germany’s foreign office declined to comment on rejection rates for specific countries, citing the need to “protect international relations”. On Chinese social media, young researchers have discussed ways to overcome these application hurdles. Some suggest “desensitising the research direction” while others advise avoiding overly specific research descriptions in visa materials, especially for fields such as AI and computer vision. There is no official guidance but experience of the US’ screening policies informs the crowdsourced advice. “Sailor”, a 31-year-old computer science PhD graduate from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne, thought he did not have any red flags. Sailor was offered a postdoctoral position in computer vision in Germany but his visa application was rejected after 132 days, also in relation to Section 53 of the Residence Act. He said he had “no academic or professional background connected to the ‘Seven Sons of National Defence’ in China or the military”, a group of Chinese universities that have been subject to US government restrictions because of their links to China’s defence sector. Washington launched such curbs in 2020 during US president Donald Trump’s first term, restricting entry for Chinese graduate students and researchers tied to Beijing’s military-civil fusion strategy. Cui Hongjian, a research fellow at Beijing Foreign Studies University’s Country and Area Studies Academy, said Germany’s visa rejections were part of Europe’s broader embrace of “research security”. “Just as Europe limits its companies from engaging with China in hi-tech or strategic industries, the same basic attitude and direction are now being applied to research,” said Cui, a former diplomat. He said the trend had been developing for several years but was becoming more visible as European countries incorporated national-security considerations into their China policies. This is the case in Germany, where Berlin is pushing forward with its “de-risking” strategy towards Beijing. Under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Germany is trying to preserve vital commercial ties with China while shielding sensitive technologies. Cui said the outlook for China’s ties with Europe was still relatively optimistic compared with that for relations with the US, with debate on the continent about the harm that Europe could inflict on itself by extending security concerns to science and education. “However, the future remains uncertain,” Cui added. “If mutual trust between China and Europe – and between China and Germany – continues to erode, they [Europe] may adopt even harsher measures against educational and scientific exchanges to divert domestic political pressure outward.” Rebecca Arcesati, co-head of the science, technology and innovation programme at the Mercator Institute for China Studies, said several European countries were undergoing a “transition and recalibration in the way they approach research collaboration with China, especially in critical technology fields”. Germany had previously started from a position where there was “hardly any rigorous scrutiny of potential national security risks”, she said. She said it was very important for governments to step in now – with resources, advice and regulatory action where appropriate – “to provide the scientific community with strategic clarity”. Cui described the tightening restrictions as a “lose-lose approach”. He said Beijing would hope these visa rejections remained isolated incidents. “I believe relevant Chinese authorities in charge of science and education will raise these issues with their counterparts in Germany,” he said. Reversing the trend would require joint effort, Cui added, stressing that both sides needed to stem the tide of tightening controls while identifying fresh avenues for collaboration. “It has to be a two-way street: China also needs to consider how we can maintain mutual trust and mutual benefit in our scientific and educational engagement with Europe.”

title: Saudi oil pipeline closure puts Asia’s economic resilience to the test
description: Experts say the loss will hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region.
content: Asian economies heavily dependent on imported energy are facing an even sharper squeeze after the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline removed a key escape route from the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, deepening an energy shock that has already pushed crude oil above US$100 a barrel. Analysts said the loss of that bypass would hit Asian refiners first before feeding through to inflation, currencies and economic growth across the region. Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, confirmed that the pipeline was shut as a precaution following an attack last week but did not disclose the extent of the damage, the number of affected pumping stations or a timetable for restarting operations, according to a Rystad Energy report on Monday. The closure leaves Saudi Arabia with fewer ways to keep crude moving to Asian buyers, raising the risk of delayed or reduced deliveries if the outage drags on. Benchmark Brent crude oil, which surged to US$108 a barrel following the attack, was trading at US$104.6 during Asian evening hours on Friday, up more than 70 per cent year to date. Before the attack, Saudi crude reaching Yanbu on the Red Sea coast could bypass the contested Strait of Hormuz, with tankers then able to head south through Bab el-Mandeb towards India and the rest of Asia or move north towards Egypt. Rystad said Saudi Arabia had increasingly favoured the northern route because of the growing threat of attacks by Houthi militants. Flows through Bab el-Mandeb should decline because fewer Saudi cargoes would be available to sail south, although the reduction would be partly obscured by already loaded vessels and non-Saudi traffic, Rystad added. Asian oil refiners have the greatest direct exposure. Most Chinese and Indian customers had been instructed to lift September barrels from Yanbu, while Japanese and South Korean customers had increasingly been offered supplies through Sidi Kerir, an alternative route, the report said. The market should therefore first see delayed or reduced deliveries into China and India, it said. Janiv Shah, vice-president at Rystad, told This Week in Asia that Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam were among the most exposed to the oil supply disruption because of their dependence on imported energy and the resulting impact on transport, manufacturing and electricity costs. “Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh are more vulnerable through inflation, foreign exchange rates and balances, while India faces a substantial increase in its overall import bill,” he said, adding that while Japan and South Korea were also highly import-dependent, they had stronger financial and strategic stock buffers. Shah warned the development was likely to weigh on Asian countries’ economic growth. “A short-lived price above US$100 per barrel should slow growth, but prices remaining elevated for multiple months would raise inflation, weaken consumption and increase fiscal pressures. The likely outcome is slower, more inflationary regional growth rather than an immediate recession,” he said. The recent disruption would challenge global supply and demand “as we flip from a relatively balanced market currently to one that is heavily undersupplied in the next few months”, said the Rystad report. An Oxford Economics report published on September 10 noted that neither an oil price shock nor higher trade tariffs imposed by the US had derailed Asia’s economic growth this year, driven by demand for AI-related hardware. However, it predicted the region’s growth would drop by around 0.4 percentage points to 4.2 per cent next year, noting that Asian governments had absorbed much of the initial energy shock to protect consumers. “Asian economies would feel the shock unevenly but the direction is clear. Southeast Asia would be particularly exposed because it sources close to 60 per cent of its crude from the Middle East,” said Ausaf Sayeed, India’s former ambassador to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. He noted that regional officials had estimated the pipeline would remain largely out of service for three to five weeks. The pressure would spread through several channels, including larger import bills and current account deficits, higher prices for food, fuels and fertiliser, as well as weaker currencies and heavier subsidy outgo for their governments, he added. US tariff threat India, Asia’s second-largest crude oil importer, is facing a double whammy. The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed legislation that could enable President Donald Trump to impose sanctions on Russia and up to 100 per cent tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. It will need Trump’s approval to be made into law. India and China have been among the largest buyers of Russian oil. Analysts believe China will keep buying Russian oil because overland pipelines protect its supply compared with maritime supplies, and the benefit of cheaper oil is likely to outweigh the US tariff threats. Sayeed said the proposed legislation gave Trump the authority to grant waivers on the grounds of national interest. “The bill does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on every country that buys Russian energy.” Nevertheless, India will have to grapple with the dilemma of buying more expensive crude oil from elsewhere or potentially exposing its exports to substantial US tariffs. “The immediate effect is therefore heightened policy and commercial uncertainty, not an already operative 100 per cent tariff,” he said. India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement on Thursday expressing concern about the proposed US legislation. “India remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people. It will continue to do so through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics,” the statement said. “This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.” Russian oil supplies were not just another commercial option for India but an important diversification source when flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb were under stress, said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at Indic Researchers Forum. The loss of Saudi supplies also made other South Asian countries – Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh – vulnerable as energy imports affected their limited fiscal space, Sayeed said. “Countries with weaker currencies, limited foreign-exchange buffers and large fuel subsidy burdens will feel a prolonged period above US$100 per barrel oil price more acutely than richer East Asian economies,” said Uday Chandra, a professor at India’s Ashoka University.

title: China’s crude imports are rising again. What will that mean for oil prices?
description: China’s plunging oil imports prevented a bigger price spike after the Iran war broke out, but its crude purchases are now ticking up again.
content: China is showing early signs of stepping up imports of crude oil after months of subdued buying amid the US-Israel war on Iran, threatening to erode a buffer that has helped prevent a larger surge in global oil prices. But analysts do not expect China to quickly return to its pre-war import levels, as elevated crude prices could squeeze margins for Chinese refineries and the country’s stockpiles are still large enough to last for several months. Signs of a rebound in Chinese demand emerged in August, when China’s crude imports rose 6.2 per cent compared with the previous month to hit 37.9 million tonnes, according to Chinese customs data. The figure was the highest import level seen for four months, though still more than 23 per cent lower than a year earlier. The recovery has continued this month, with China’s crude imports running at 7.84 million barrels per day (bpd) in September, up from 7.25 million bpd the previous month, according to trade intelligence firm Kpler. A year ago, the figure was 9.76 million bpd. The uptick in Chinese purchases has come amid renewed turbulence in the oil market, as the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East cause further disruptions to global supplies. According to Kpler, China’s imports from Iraq shot up from 177,000 bpd in August to over 1 million bpd this month, but its purchases from Iran and Saudi Arabia are set to decline. “A recent partial rebound in Chinese import demand coincided with increased uncertainty regarding crude oil supply availability from the Middle East – following attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline – and Russia due to Ukrainian attacks on the Novorossiysk export terminal,” said Ivan Ryabov, head of oil trading analytics at Kpler. “As two major exporters with remaining spare crude production capacity, these disruptions created upwards pressure on prices and raised supply security concerns for importing countries.” Chinese firms “have held back on buying for several months, but have come back to the market to reduce their drawdown rate and support increased crude runs to replenish domestic product inventory”, said June Goh, a senior oil market analyst at Sparta. The return of Chinese buyers comes after months of weaker imports, which helped partly offset a global supply shortfall and limit upwards pressure on prices after the outbreak of the Iran war. China’s crude imports from April to August were about 3.2 million bpd lower than a year earlier, largely because refiners drew on inventories and consumers increasingly switched to new-energy vehicles, according to a report by Huatai Securities published on Tuesday. But that China buffer is now weakening as inventories fall. China’s vast crude oil stockpiles have been declining since April, with inventories falling from about 1.25 billion barrels to 1.14 billion barrels in September, data from Kpler showed. “China’s oil inventories have fallen significantly from the levels built up before the Strait of Hormuz closure, making it harder to sustain the ‘China buffer’ that had helped keep oil prices in check,” the Huatai Securities report said. Goh agreed that China’s muted crude buying in recent months had helped contain upwards pressure on oil prices, while its return had partly contributed to the recent gains in global oil benchmarks. “Now, the crude market cannot rely heavily on China to rebalance again,” said Sun Jianan, a senior oil analyst at Energy Aspects. Even so, analysts do not expect Chinese buyers to return to the market aggressively. “We see no imminent risk to China’s crude supply,” Sun said, adding that China still had ample crude stocks that could meet more than 80 days of demand and cushion potential supply losses. Goh estimated that China still had around four to six months of inventory at current consumption rates, when factoring in both commercial and strategic reserves. Global oil benchmarks such as WTI and Brent rose more than 20 per cent from late August to nearly US$110 a barrel on Tuesday, before falling back to about US$100 a barrel on Friday. Higher prices are one reason Chinese refiners are unlikely to rush to rebuild inventories. “Higher crude prices are now eroding Chinese refining margins, as domestic product prices are regulated above US$80 per barrel,” Sun said, adding that he did not expect China to “significantly increase crude purchases with flat prices above US$100 per barrel”. Similarly, Terine Ooi, associate director of energy markets at Dow Jones Energy, said she did not expect China to quickly return to pre-war import levels. “Chinese buyers remain highly price-sensitive, particularly when domestic demand is weak,” Ooi said. “At current elevated crude prices, aggressive restocking becomes less attractive and could move the market against China’s own interests.” A prolonged disruption to Saudi exports could push up crude prices and further pressure refiners’ margins, while Beijing could also tighten refined-product exports to prioritise domestic supply, she added.

title: Singapore Airlines takes world’s best carrier crown from Qatar Airways
description: Asian carriers dominated the Skytrax rankings and only one European airline – Air France-KLM – made the top 10.
content: Singapore Airlines was awarded the title of world’s best airline in the annual rankings by Skytrax, taking the top spot from Qatar Airways in a year that saw Middle Eastern carriers come under significant pressure from the ongoing war in Iran. The award, which is based on a survey of almost 25 million travellers, was announced in London on Friday, with a list dominated by Asian carriers. Only one European airline – Air France-KLM – made the top 10, and not a single US company, despite their efforts to upgrade their passenger experience and premium cabins. The Skytrax recognition gives airlines bragging rights with the flying public at a time when premium travel is rising in popularity around the world. Besides the overall ranking, Air France was also awarded the top prize for its La Premiere first class, which the French airline is expanding amid booming demand. The conflict in the Middle East has proved a major challenge for airlines worldwide, with soaring oil prices and dampened consumer demand. Ultimately, the Gulf carriers were the worst hit in the immediate aftermath, forcing Qatar Airways and Emirates to temporarily suspend their service after the conflict erupted. Last year, Qatar Airways won the best airline title, a position for which it has duelled with Singapore Airlines over the past decade.

title: Beijing, Taipei need peace deal before reunification, Taiwanese scholar says
description: An agreement ending hostilities could allow the two sides to discuss the future on an equal footing, Chang Ya-chung.
content: A formal peace deal between Beijing and Taipei should be signed to build trust before discussions on post-reunification political arrangements, a prominent Taiwanese political scientist has argued at a security conference in Beijing. Chang Ya-chung, who heads the Taiwan-based Sun Yat-sen School advocacy group, said the “one country, two systems” formula, which has been applied to Hong Kong and Macau, had so far failed to resonate in Taiwanese society. “If reunification means that one side, with greater power, puts forward a proposal and the relatively weaker side simply decides whether to accept it, it is only natural for people in Taiwan to have concerns,” Chang said on the sidelines of the Xiangshan Forum, Beijing’s leading security platform. “One country, two systems is an arrangement after peaceful reunification. But people in Taiwan may care more about how the two sides can move from their current hostility towards peace before reunification. That is the more important issue,” Chang separately told a panel discussion during the forum on Wednesday. The remarks were made amid renewed discussion on potential political arrangements after any future reunification among scholars on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. Last week, Beijing’s Taiwan Affairs Office welcomed a proposal by a Taiwanese scholar on detailed arrangements for Taiwan after reunification, saying it was pleased to see more people on the island discussing the scenario and offering suggestions. Chang told the South China Morning Post that this reaction showed Beijing was “thinking about how to make post-reunification arrangements more concrete and comprehensive”, but such proposals had not generated a comparable level of public interest in Taiwan. The framework has been deeply unpopular on the island, with polls conducted in August by Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council indicating that more than 80 per cent of Taiwanese reject one country, two systems. “What most people in Taiwan want to know first is why reunification is necessary and how it would come about, and whether Taiwan can participate on an equal footing, maintain its security and retain its dignity and autonomy throughout the process,” Chang said. Chang, a pro-reunification activist who ran to be Kuomintang chairman in 2021 and 2025, was the sole Taiwanese voice at Beijing’s flagship security forum, which this year brought together defence officials, diplomats and academics from nearly 100 countries. In 2019, Chinese President Xi Jinping called for more exploration of how one country, two systems could apply to Taiwan, a process he said should involve various political parties and groups from both sides of the strait. Beijing has offered scant detail on how it thinks such a framework could be structured, but mainland scholars have been studying possible arrangements. Last week, more than 20 mainland scholars reached a 12-point consensus on a plan for Taiwan during a seminar in Beijing. These included maintaining a People’s Liberation Army presence in Taiwan and implementing patriotic education. Chang said he was “pessimistic” about cross-strait relations, citing a shift towards a solely Taiwanese identity, with fewer people identifying as Chinese, and the KMT’s traditional support base dwindling when compared to that of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party. Cross-strait tensions intensified after William Lai Ching-te took office as the island’s leader in May 2024. Efforts to secure peace should be prioritised, Chang said, adding that this should include signing a peace agreement, formally ending hostilities, restoring full exchanges, promoting social integration and building trust. Then, the two sides could move into discussions on an equal footing regarding post-governance arrangements, Chang suggested. These arrangements, he said, should not be unilateral concessions but the result of joint negotiations, commitments and agreements. A conflict could erupt “with just a single thought”, Chang warned during the panel, urging the two sides to seek dialogue. “Even under the most difficult circumstances, we must keep talking, try every possible way to maintain dialogue and find areas of common ground,” he told the panel. Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but are opposed to a change of status quo by force.

title: China table tennis stars describe Asian Games cruise ship living as a ‘unique’ experience
description: Sun Yingsha, Wang Chuqin and Wang Manyu have adapted to living aboard the Costa Serena, but arrangements have descended into chaos for others.
content: Just one day before the official opening of the Asian Games, chaotic accommodation arrangements have surfaced on the cruise ship hosting athletes in Nagoya, with Chinese table tennis stars including Sun Yingsha and Wang Chuqin describing living on board as a “unique” experience. On Thursday, the Chinese table tennis team held their first practice session in Nagoya following a rocky arrival that significantly compressed their training and rest schedule. The team also had to quickly adapt to living aboard the Costa Serena cruise ship, which serves as the offshore athletes’ village. “This is genuinely the first time in my life living on a ship,” Wang told CCTV after his first training session in Japan. “It’s docked at the pier and the ship is large, so it feels fine with little swaying; it’s quite unique. Because the rooms are close together and there are many people, it feels different from staying in a hotel.” As a lead figure on the men’s squad, Wang added that his goals remained firm, and he aimed to fight for every point while preparing for a marathon-like competition. “We will certainly face many difficulties, but the Chinese table tennis team is never afraid of hardship,” he said. Sun expressed a similar calm and optimistic mindset towards her first stay on a cruise ship. “We just arrived yesterday. Overall, there isn’t much swaying. It’s my first time staying on a cruise ship, and I find it unique,” she said. The Costa Serena is docked at Kinjo Pier in the Port of Nagoya, roughly 30 kilometres from the table tennis venue, Sky Hall Toyota. The one-way commute takes more than an hour, amounting to an almost three-hour round trip. In contrast, the host Japanese team are reportedly staying near the venue, with a 30-minute one-way commute. Wang Manyu admitted feeling slightly disoriented navigating the vessel’s layout at first. “It’s a bit winding and disorienting, but I think it will get better after walking around more,” Wang said, noting that she spent time rearranging her room to maximise the space and familiarising herself with routes and schedules. Facing both team and individual events, she emphasised maintaining physical condition and executing techniques honed during training. Sun noted that managing time would be crucial, taking into account transit times and movement on the ship. “For me personally, the most important thing is not to take the wrong shuttle bus or be late,” she said, adding that her injury recovery was progressing and she aimed to enjoy every match without setting rigid goals. The Asian Games table tennis competition begins on September 20. All three Chinese athletes are Olympic champions embarking on their third Asian Games appearance. However, Japanese media outlet Yahoo Japan reported that accommodation arrangements on the cruise ship have descended into chaos, with reports of male and female athletes initially assigned to the same rooms. Some Japanese athletes were paired with coaches of the opposite sex or placed in mixed-gender rooms, prompting the Japanese delegation to urgently reassign rooms and secure emergency hotel accommodation. Hisashi Mizutori, deputy head of the Japanese delegation, cited an example at a press conference where a squad of five male and five female athletes was assigned five double rooms based strictly on head count. “On paper, the numbers matched,” Mizutori said. “In practice, it caused many problems, men and women were placed together, coaches shared rooms with athletes, and physiotherapists needing space for heavy medical equipment were forced to share rooms.” The Japanese Olympic Committee had pre-booked backup hotels in Nagoya because of prior concerns. Mizutori confirmed that for difficult cases, “we are considering using the backup accommodation prepared in advance by the Japanese delegation”. Upon arriving in Nagoya earlier, the Chinese national table tennis team were stranded at the airport transit centre for almost six hours because of glitches in both the organising committee’s registration and transport dispatch systems, and were unable to board shuttle buses to their cruise ship accommodation. However, China were not the only delegation to face logistical nightmares. According to Thai media outlet Main Stand, the Thai sepak takraw team spent almost 24 hours trying to check in after organisers failed to enter their accommodation details into the system, forcing exhausted athletes to sleep on the floor. 【恥ずかしすぎる名古屋でのアジア大会】 名古屋で開催の第20回アジア競技大会(2026)はタイ人からの日本評価を爆下げすることになるかもしれない。… pic.twitter.com/yOuyegdn5z — タイニュースPK(พี่เค) 🇯🇵🇹🇭 (@Thainews_PK) September 18, 2026 The squad departed Thailand late on September 15 for the Costa Serena, but began entering their rooms only around 10.30pm the day after. Chalirat Chantarubeksa, deputy head of the Thai delegation, said the contractor hired by the Japanese host made an error by failing to input the team’s paperwork, resulting in lost records. As an interim measure, Thai athletes were temporarily placed in unassigned rooms of delegations that had not yet arrived, with organisers pledging to reassign them to permanent accommodation the following day. Meanwhile, the Thai teqball team shared a video online showing sparse Asian Games meal portions, consisting of a single mouthful of vermicelli, a small cup of rice and a few pieces of broccoli. Addressing fan outrage over athlete nutrition, the Thai teqball team stated they had already arranged additional meals for their athletes outside the venue.

title: Ant International embeds AI agents  across all platforms in biggest-ever product upgrade
description: The new suite features accounts tailored for AI agents, allowing users to delegate specific tasks without relinquishing account control.
content: Ant International, the overseas affiliate of China’s Ant Group, is executing an artificial intelligence overhaul across its entire suite of global financial services, introducing AI agents designed to help manage payments, foreign exchange and treasury operations. Described by the company as its largest-ever product upgrade, the initiative embeds AI-native solutions across all platforms: cross-border payment network Alipay+, merchant services provider Antom, account and treasury platform WorldFirst, and digital credit platform Bettr. The global roll-out has begun and would extend through winter, the company said. Peng Yang, CEO of Ant International, said the shift would prepare global commerce for a “fully agentised future”, adding that fintech providers needed “a future-ready trust infrastructure” paired with financial AI models and connected AI-native solutions. The move follows a roughly US$1.2 billion series A funding round in July, backed by Ant Group, Alibaba Group Holding and other institutional investors. Carved out as an independent operating entity in 2024, Ant International said it connects over 150 million merchants to more than 2 billion consumer accounts, processing over 25 million daily transactions across 210 markets. The upgrade spans nearly 100 products, including AI assistants for payments and account management, tools for cash-flow forecasting, currency hedging and global payouts, and services supporting billing, tax filing, marketing and access to credit. Ant said it also introduced a business account designed for AI agents. “We’re a problem solver for merchants,” Gary Liu, CEO of Antom, said in an interview with the South China Morning Post, noting that 89.5 per cent of Antom’s merchants already used AI agents, with 81.4 per cent of payment tasks receiving AI assistance. Liu said agent authorisation should depend on the task and its spending limits, rather than the job titles used to determine employees’ authority. “It matters what the task is,” he said. According to Ant International, the overhaul relies on two proprietary systems: a payment foundation model - called Antom 3-in-1 Transformer - that processes structured records, sequences of behaviour and relationships between users, merchants and devices to assess transactions, and FalconTST, a forecasting model for cash flows and currency exposures. Ant International said FalconTST had achieved over 93 per cent forecasting accuracy and reduced corporate currency hedging and capital allocation costs by 30 to 60 per cent in real-world applications. On top of the Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, the company built a second security layer, with a “know-your-agent” (KYA) framework linked to its Agentic Mobile Protocol, which connects mobile wallet networks to agentic transactions. The security layer includes AgentSafePay, which offers a fund-back guarantee against losses from agent-specific risks. To combat security risks tied to autonomous transactions, the firm relies on its Antom Shield framework to guard against AI-driven fraud, as well as AgentSafePay, an indemnity scheme covering merchant losses from agent errors. Ant International is also partnering with Visa and Mastercard to establish global agent verification standards through its Agentic Mobile Protocol. Alibaba is the owner of SCMP.

title: Tesla auditing Chinese suppliers ahead of Optimus roll-out: sources
description: The supplier audits come as Elon Musk’s firm aims to quickly ramp up production of its Optimus humanoid robot after its release later this year.
content: Tesla officials and engineers have begun auditing part of the firm’s Chinese supply chain, as Elon Musk’s company aims to quickly ramp up production of its Optimus humanoid robot after it hits the global market later this year, according to sources with knowledge of the matter. Chinese companies set to undergo supplier audits included heat-control component manufacturer Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, auto parts supplier Ningbo Joyson Electronic, and chassis producer Tuopu Group, two corporate executives with business ties to the manufacturers told the South China Morning Post. Most of the firms being examined by Tesla as potential Optimus suppliers already provide automotive components used in the company’s electric cars, and they are all based in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. A supplier audit is a process in which a vendor’s production and compliance standards are evaluated to ensure product quality. According to the sources, this round of audits comes as Tesla plans to place additional orders for components, as mass production of the firm’s Optimus robots will soon begin at its plant in Fremont, California. Tesla China declined to comment on the issue. Tesla is locked in a race with several competitors in the United States and China to mass produce humanoid robots – artificial intelligence-powered robots that can be deployed in scenarios ranging from factory production lines to elderly care centres. In January, Tesla signalled it was pivoting towards becoming a physical AI firm, with CEO Elon Musk announcing the company would halt production of its Model S and Model X cars in Fremont so the plant could focus on building robots. The Chinese vendors had signed non-disclosure agreements with Tesla, which would subject them to penalties worth millions of dollars if they failed to comply, the sources said. “The audits show that those Chinese suppliers are an important part of Optimus’ supply chain,” said Chen Jinzhu, CEO of the Shanghai Mingliang Auto Service consultancy. “They enjoy cost and technological advantages over their domestic and overseas rivals.” Chinese carmakers such as Xpeng were viewed as strong rivals to Tesla in robotics due to their manufacturing heft and complete, cost-effective supply chains, analysts said. In December, Musk endorsed Xpeng’s Iron humanoid robot on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla. In April, Tesla’s China president, Allan Wang Hao, said the company’s Shanghai Gigafactory had the potential to produce humanoid robots, as it benefited from China’s complete supply chain and advanced manufacturing techniques.

title: Xi-Trump summit preview: what to watch for as investors brace for best and worst scenarios
description: Tariff cuts or a new 7.5 per cent duty on China? Possible outcomes on the cards as leaders navigate a trade truce and a widening tech schism.
content: President Xi Jinping is scheduled to sit down with US President Donald Trump in Washington next week, and their planned summit looks to be closely watched as an indicator of the current state of ties between the world’s two largest economies. Economic issues appear poised to drive the agenda again, as they did when Trump travelled to Beijing in May with more than a dozen top American CEOs, including the heads of Tesla, Apple, Nvidia and Boeing. At stake are an extension of their current truce and further cuts on high tariffs, as well as deals that could see China buy more American goods. Here is a breakdown of the outlook from the perspectives of global financial institutions and policy analysts. What is the market consensus for the Xi-Trump summit results? The bar for next week’s meeting, slated for Thursday, is relatively low, according to some research houses and research organisations. The results of a recent Goldman Sachs investor survey showed that most respondents expected the meeting to be symbolic, though onshore Chinese investors were relatively constructive: 38 per cent expected incremental progress, compared with 26 per cent among offshore respondents. Financial institutions Barclays and BNP Paribas defined the baseline outcome as a managed stabilisation of China-US economic ties and an ongoing commitment to stability. Dividends might include extending the 2025 tariff truce and finalising earlier trade commitments – upbeat but short of a grand bargain. Chinese leaders are treating strategic US-China competition as an enduring one and seeking to buy time while calculating the lowest cost to sustain an uneasy calm, the Brookings public policy think tank said in a September 9 analysis. What’s a realistic best-case scenario? China might buy key US goods, and both sides could formally lower tariffs that soared past 100 per cent on both sides last year. Progress could include reciprocal tariff cuts on roughly US$30 billion in trade on each side, which the two sides agreed to after Trump’s trip in May. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday that the economic and trade teams of both sides were maintaining close communication on relevant issues, and that further updates would be released in due course. The US side has also hinted at carrying forward earlier Chinese agreements to buy US agricultural products, energy and aircraft. Chinese soybean purchases have been a particular sticking point this year. Steadying the supply chain for critical minerals – where China has reserves that the US needs – has a shot at seeing progress next week as well. What constitutes the worst-case summit scenario? Trump could move towards a 7.5 per cent overcapacity tariff on China, echoing earlier threats. Trump also has warned that an “economic D-Day” package would harm countries and entities that support Iran – a descriptor taken by some to mean actors in China. Tech ties could fray further. BNP Paribas warned that a China-US technology schism was broadening into AI, and that the world was moving towards two distinct tech ecosystems as the US tried to limit China’s access to advanced AI chips and models. Beijing’s latest rare earth export restrictions continue to deepen supply-chain tensions, and institutions previewing the summit were not forecasting any positive outcome on this topic. What are the likely market impacts? According to Goldman Sachs, 46 per cent of offshore respondents and 38 per cent of Chinese respondents expected moderate gains in Chinese equities one month after the visit, if things go well. Respondents anticipated limited upside for the yuan in foreign-exchange markets. Goldman Sachs said most investors expected the pace of yuan appreciation against the US dollar to remain unchanged or to slow into late October. If the summit ends poorly, BNP Paribas and Barclays indicated that investors would veer towards safe capital flows, even at the risk of lower returns. They also pointed to possible losses of scale for companies operating in the tech ecosystems of both China and the US. About two-thirds of investors surveyed by Goldman Sachs expected US-China tensions to be broadly unchanged after the US midterm congressional elections in November, while roughly 15 per cent expected moderate improvement and another 15 per cent expected moderate deterioration.

title: Opinion | Ending the nuclear arms race starts with cities doing their part
description: As cities are the main targets of nuclear weapons, they have a responsibility to speak out and encourage efforts to eliminate them.
content: The catastrophic danger posed to cities by nuclear weapons is nothing new. Putting major urban areas at risk across generations is, in fact, the point of these weapons of terror. The practice of doing so is benignly called nuclear deterrence, but it requires holding the cities of adversaries – real and imagined – under constant threat. The use of even the smallest nuclear weapons in today’s arsenals would cause a humanitarian emergency in cities. That is why city leadership should have a voice in nuclear policymaking. Attacking cities or other densely populated areas has always been part of warfare. Whether it’s medieval sieges to unseat ruling powers or drone attacks on Kyiv, cities are not safe from war. Efforts to restrict or limit civilian suffering in cities and populated areas have included the endorsement by 91 countries of a political declaration on explosive weapons in populated areas. Through this, nations are looking for ways to reduce and prevent the known reverberating effects of explosive ordnance contamination in urban areas, effects which are compounded and made long-lasting by the destruction of cultural, educational, commercial, infrastructure and healthcare facilities. Nuclear weapons are highly explosive weapons which also leave a lasting radioactive legacy. No country is prepared to respond to the use of nuclear weapons. A 2014 report from the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research showed that there are unique problems associated with nuclear weapon use, including radiation and radioactive fallout, large numbers of injured people with multiple trauma, serious burn injuries and radiation-related illness. They also found “there are inadequate specific procedures and systems appropriate to nuclear weapon detonation events as these differ from civil nuclear accidents in significant ways”. A recent study from the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force Characteristic Medical Centre, which was published in the Chinese Journal of Radiological Health, was a stark reminder that while low, the probability of a nuclear attack on cities is not zero. Any such attack would overwhelm emergency services. The International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN) published a study looking at the response capacity in key global cities, including Beijing. In that study, we found even if just one average-sized, 100-kiloton nuclear weapon was detonated over Beijing today, the immediate health impact would be catastrophic. There are not enough medical personnel or hospital facilities to treat what could amount to 1.2 million casualties. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) put it succinctly, saying: “There is no adequate humanitarian response capacity in case of use of nuclear weapons.” The ICRC, UN humanitarian agencies and more than 100 governments recognise the only way to ensure protection from nuclear weapons is by preventing their accidental or intentional use. The legal framework to do so exists. The framework of nuclear weapons-related agreements, from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), offers a way to move towards verifiable and irreversible nuclear disarmament. As cities are the main targets of nuclear weapons, municipalities have a special responsibility to their populations to speak out against any role for nuclear weapons in national security doctrines and encourage efforts to eliminate the risk of nuclear weapons. Mayors and other municipal leaders are rising to the challenge. More than 1,000 cities in 24 countries have called on their national governments to join the TPNW as a way to halt the nuclear arms race. Cities such as New York, Canberra, Berlin, Paris, Rome and Washington have all encouraged their governments to join the TPNW and eliminate their nuclear arsenals. Through the ICAN Cities Appeal, these cities are empowered to act locally on global issues such as nuclear disarmament, stand up for the protection of those living in their cities and demand action. The gruesome images of the two cities destroyed by nuclear weapons, Hiroshima and Nagasaki, are a reminder of everything at risk from nuclear dangers. In efforts to protect civilians, leadership might not always come from the highest levels of government. Instead, it might rise from the cities, the communities and the people who see nuclear weapons as a threat. The growing support for the ICAN Cities Appeal and the TPNW, especially in countries where national governments are clinging to outdated policies that allow for the use of nuclear weapons, shows that leadership.

title: Australian man pleads not guilty to murder of Thai teen girl found in suitcase
description: A court also denied Simon Peter Carman’s bail application after prosecutors opposed his release.
content: An Australian accused of murdering a teenage girl in Thailand and abandoning her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty in court on Friday, citing self-defence. Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested at a Bangkok airport in June as he prepared to take a flight back to Australia after the 17-year-old victim’s friend had reported her missing. The young woman’s body was found in a suitcase near a railway track in Pattaya, a seaside resort city south of the capital, Bangkok. Police said she died of suffocation. Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya Provincial Court, where he denied all charges, citing “self-defence and a mistaken belief about the victim’s age”, a court statement said. It did not elaborate further. The Australian is charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor aged between 15 and 18 for indecent purposes. The court denied Carman’s bail application after prosecutors opposed his release, saying he posed a flight risk. The next court date was set for October 12. Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase. The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism.

title: CUHK instructor triggers backlash over WeChat attendance registration policy
description: Department later clarifies rule after students raise privacy concerns over using mainland app and location tracking to register class attendance.
content: An instructor at Hong Kong’s second-oldest university has faced a backlash over asking students to use mainland Chinese messaging app WeChat to register their attendance and keep its location services enabled, before later saying the arrangement was optional. The policy was revealed after a screenshot of an email from a teaching staff member in the information engineering department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) was posted to the social media platform Threads on Friday. “Starting from the next class, attendance will be recorded by scanning a QR code through WeChat. Please install the WeChat app and enable location services before coming to class,” the email said. “Your attendance will be considered valid only if your location is detected within the classroom, such as CUHK faculty of law, CUHK Library Road, CUHK Lee Shau Kee Building.” It added that a test QR code had been provided to students to ensure the app was working properly. The post attracted hundreds of replies and was forwarded thousands of times. Some students questioned online why the department had not adopted the university’s own app for checking student attendance. A spokeswoman for CUHK said a part-time instructor for one class had asked students to record their attendance using a non-official system on his own initiative. “After becoming aware of the incident, the relevant academic department immediately reminded the instructor to use the university’s official systems instead,” she said. Other users also criticised the department and staff for using an app other than CUHK’s to track attendance and raised concerns about potential data leaks. “Am I studying in mainland China now or what?” the author of the post, nemui._.desuyo, wrote. The user wrote that he had already sent an email to the department to follow up on the matter and ask why it had not adopted the CUHK-developed app instead. “How can they force us to install a third-party app just for taking attendance? Who’s going to be responsible if there’s a security breach?” another commenter said. A user named iireneliui wrote: “CUHK has its own attendance system, plus card readers to tap student IDs. Or worst-case scenario, just use a plain old sign-in sheet. Why on earth do we have to use WeChat?” The department later sent an email to students clarifying that they could use either WeChat or sign a paper attendance sheet in class. “You only need to use one of these two methods. If you do not normally use WeChat, there is no need to install it just to record your attendance,” the email stated. However, the email said students would still need to enable location services if they chose to use WeChat. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said it had not received any inquiries or complaints about the matter, adding that it would not comment on individual cases. The privacy watchdog also said personal data should only be collected for lawful purposes directly related to a function or activity by the relevant organisation, provided the information was “necessary, adequate but not excessive”.

title: Could China’s sixth-generation fighter carry a laser to defend against incoming missiles?
description: Beijing expo display offers strongest public hint yet that China is developing airborne laser systems for advanced fighter aircraft.
content: China may be aiming to equip its sixth-generation fighter jets with laser weapons that experts say could help defend them against incoming missiles. At the 14th China International Defence Electronics Exhibition, held in Beijing from September 15 to 17, the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) Beijing Precision Engineering Institute for Aircraft Industry presented details of a “fighter aircraft laser-weapon tracking and aiming system”. According to social media posts, the booth display said the system weighed less than 380kg (838lbs), although key performance figures were partly obscured. Transmission power was listed as “*00kW” – implying at least 100kW if the asterisk concealed a single digit – while the system’s dynamic tracking accuracy, a measure of how precisely it could maintain its aim over time, was redacted as “* μrad (RMS)”. Precision tracking is critical for airborne laser weapons, which must keep a beam fixed continuously long enough to damage or dazzle a target despite aircraft speed, vibration and manoeuvring. The promotional poster paired the tracking system with an image of a large tailless aircraft which Andreas Rupprecht, an author and researcher on Chinese military aviation, has identified as the J-36. J-36 is the unofficial name for the three-engined jet first seen flying over Chengdu in December 2024 and believed to be a sixth-generation fighter under development by Chengdu Aircraft Corporation, part of state-owned AVIC. Rupprecht said the AVIC display gave the strongest public indication yet of the existence of such a laser system. Mark Cazalet, editor-in-chief of international defence news organisation Warsight, agreed that the illustration appeared to depict a J-36 and said the aircraft “likely has sufficient space, weight and power” to accommodate a high-energy laser. “Lasers are in many ways easier to implement on larger aircraft than smaller aircraft,” he said, with larger platforms more likely to have the space, weight and power available for the systems. That could also make the systems potentially relevant to larger high-value aircraft, including bombers, transport aircraft and airborne early-warning platforms. However, the expo display leaves important technical questions unanswered, starting with what the advertised weight covers. Cazalet said the 380kg figure likely included the beam director, laser source and cooling system, but the poster did not make clear whether the weight applied only to the tracking-and-aiming unit or to a broader laser system, nor did it give details of its electrical power requirements. There is also no public evidence that such an airborne laser system has been fitted to or flight-tested aboard a Chinese fighter aircraft. Because their limited range restricted lasers in air-to-air combat, their main use on aircraft would be to destroy incoming missiles or damage and dazzle their seekers, Cazalet said. Lasers could burn holes in physical targets only at short ranges – typically several kilometres – while they could damage or dazzle optical sensors at greater distances, Cazalet said. He said that with the United States developing or fielding long-range air-to-air missiles such as the AIM-174B, AIM-260 and AIM-424, the emergence of Chinese systems that could potentially counter them was “not altogether surprising”, though many questions remained about how lasers would perform in reality. China’s existing high-energy laser systems have largely been ground-based. Developing one for an aircraft as a form of active protection “represents a different challenge”, Cazalet said. China has signalled interest in airborne lasers before. In 2020, PLA procurement notices sought suppliers for an “airborne laser attack pod” and control software for a “laser attack platform”, while a military programme affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV said China had developed a prototype airborne laser, citing academic research on energy storage and power supply. The following year, a Chinese study used flight data from a transport aircraft to simulate how an airborne laser could remain accurate despite aircraft movement and vibration. The US experience also illustrates the difficulty of turning the technology into an operational airborne weapon. The US Air Force’s Self-protect High Energy Laser Demonstrator, or SHiELD, sought to show that a pod-mounted laser could defend fighters against incoming air-to-air and surface-to-air missiles. In 2021, programme manager Jeff Heggemeier cited wind speeds, turbulence and rapid aircraft manoeuvres as among the “hard problems” encountered. The project concluded in 2024 without a laser pod being mounted on a fighter test bed. AVIC has previously disclosed field tests of other directed-energy tracking systems. A report in China Aviation News, an AVIC publication, in July said researchers at the institute had built and field-tested one system within a year. The report described a trial in March 2024 in which the system kept a lock on a drone despite clouds, birds and increasing distance, and said later versions had been tested on multiple platforms. However, it did not identify those platforms or link the work to the fighter-specific system.

title: China emerges as key growth market for ICC in bid to expand cricket worldwide
description: Women’s team have climbed 10 places in world rankings over the past two years, but were knocked out of Asian Games without a ball being bowled.
content: China is emerging as a key target for growth as the International Cricket Council seeks new fans worldwide, its chief executive says. While South Asia accounts for about 90 per cent of cricket’s billion-plus fans, the ICC is seeking to expand the sport’s fan base by 500 million and sees China’s 1.4 billion people as a potentially huge audience – helped by the steady progress of its women’s team. “The continued success of their women’s team has provided a major boost to cricket in the country,” ICC chief executive Sanjog Gupta said. China became a focus market after hosting cricket at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and through the progress of its women’s national team, which have climbed 10 places in the world rankings over the past two years. There is still far to go, however. In the ICC T20 rankings the women are ranked a modest 36th, while the men languish in 92nd place. The women were also knocked out of the Asian Games on Thursday without a ball being bowled, two days before the opening ceremony. A sodden outfield caused by days of rain in Nagoya, Japan, prevented any play from taking place in China’s morning quarter-final against Bangladesh, who went through to the semi-finals by virtue of being the higher-ranked team.
