Still, China is one of several markets the ICC sees as crucial to broadening cricket’s appeal beyond its traditional strongholds of South Asia, England and Australia. The ICC has spent US$1.5 million in China to boost the sport over the past five years. The country now has three top-level cricket venues, including a new 1,500-seat stadium in Taicang expected to host domestic and international matches and provide a training base for the national teams. The ICC has begun testing the appetite for the sport in China. Some women’s T20 World Cup matches were broadcast in Mandarin, and the final week of the 2026 men’s T20 World Cup generated 4.4 million video views in China. The country’s potential emergence is particularly significant for the ICC because, unlike several newer cricket nations, its men’s and women’s teams are made up largely of home-grown players rather than players from South Asian communities. Indonesia, a country of around 280 million people, has also been identified as a market with growth potential. Its men’s team T20 ranking is No 63 and the women’s team are No 23. “If even segments of the population in China and Indonesia start engaging with the sport, then they could power the next leap in the scale of cricket’s fandom,” Gupta said. “It can play a significant role in the sport’s ambition to add 500 million fans to its global fan base, which is the ICC chair’s stated ambition.” The ICC believes cricket’s return to the Olympics at the 2028 Los Angeles Games could provide another boost, with men’s and women’s T20 tournaments set to award medals for the first time since the sport’s lone previous appearance in 1900. The ICC’s push into new markets has paid off elsewhere. Italy offered a glimpse of the potential of another non-traditional market when it made its men’s T20 World Cup debut earlier this year, beating Nepal and pushing England close. The ICC push has the backing of the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC), custodian of the game’s laws. “MCC is very pleased to be sending a women’s team for an overseas tour of China in 2027,” MCC director of cricket and operations Rob Lynch said. “We see this tour as a huge opportunity to be able to grow the game in China,” he added.

title: Howard replaces his father, Warren Buffett, as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
description: The US$1 trillion conglomerate said the 96-year-old will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately.
content: Warren Buffett is stepping down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway after serving in the role at the conglomerate for more than 50 years. Buffett, 96, will become chairman emeritus and will take on his new role immediately, the company said on Friday. His son, Howard, will become Berkshire Hathaway’s new chairman, part of a long-planned succession. Howard Buffett has been on the Berkshire Hathaway board since 1993. Warren Buffett will remain a director. He has served as Berkshire Hathaway’s chairman since 1970. Greg Abel took over for Buffett as the CEO of the US$1 trillion conglomerate to start the year, but Buffett remains one of the most influential investors in the world. “I have served Berkshire since 1965,” Buffett said in a letter to shareholders. “Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world. That is not something many people my age can say, and I have never felt better about what comes next.” Buffett said that he was confident in Abel and his son Howard leading Berkshire Hathaway. “Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet,” he said. “Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.” Buffett’s fortune has been amassed through Berkshire Hathaway stock. It was worth more than US$140 billion in July 2026. He has already given away roughly US$66 billion worth of stock since 2006. Buffett has built a devoted following and when Berkshire Hathaway reveals the stocks that the company has acquired or sold in public disclosures, it can shake markets. During his time as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, the company nearly doubled the returns of the S&P 500, with a 19.9 per cent compounded annual growth rate compared with the index’s 10.4 per cent gain. “Warren’s impact on Berkshire and its owners is without parallel in the history of American business,” Abel said in a prepared statement. “The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian.”

title: Hong Kong to recruit AI chief by mid-2027, with confidence in local talent pool
description: Post will pay up to HK$278,200 per month, authorities reveal, adding they also understand public concerns over bolstering cybercrime laws.
content: Hong Kong will begin recruitment for an artificial intelligence (AI) commissioner in the second quarter of next year to assist in drafting policies for the technology and risk governance, with authorities confident the city does not lack suitable talent. Tech authorities on Friday revealed details of the new post under the Digital Policy Office, which will pay between HK$262,125 and HK$278,200 (US$33,414 to US$35,436) a month. Permanent Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Kevin Choi Kit-ming said that recruitment for the post would begin in the second quarter of 2027. “Their job scope will include providing their expertise and advice on various AI-related activities,” Choi said at a press briefing. In his policy address on Wednesday, city leader John Lee Ka-chiu said that the commissioner was expected to take up the role next year and would oversee seven key areas of AI risk governance. These include combating AI-related crimes, such as deepfake porn and online scams, and empowering authorities to remove online content linked to financial fraud. Choi said the commissioner was also expected to be familiar with developments in the AI industry, including risk governance, global trends, its impact on public administration and its application in local industries. Choi, who is responsible for the recruitment, said the commissioner would be hired in a recruitment exercise open to both the private and public sectors. “I deeply believe that the development of AI in Hong Kong is not bad, so we are not worried about a lack of suitable candidates,” he said. Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan and latest policy address placed a heavy focus on AI as a main driver of the city’s industrial transformation. “Artificial intelligence” appeared more than 190 times in the policy address alone. Four pages were dedicated to the use of AI across eight industries to boost Hong Kong’s role as an international innovation and technology centre, including taking forward the ‘AI-plus’ initiative, a concept championed by China to integrate the technology into every sector of the economy and society. Authorities will consult the public on strengthening the legal framework surrounding the technology and improving the detection of AI-generated fraudulent content. The government will also review whether existing laws adequately address liability for accidents or damage caused by AI products, promote market assessment of ethical risks, step up protection for minors using the technology and ensure they use it with the proper values. Regarding the timeline for regulating deepfake AI crimes, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok noted that the cybercrime subcommittee under the Law Reform Commission was reviewing the laws, but he was unable to give a “concrete timeline” for the reform. “Because the [commission] is an independent body comprising members from different industries, it is difficult to state definitively when a final report will be completed,” he said. However, Lam said he understood public concerns about deepfakes, especially those involving the generation of sexual images or used in fraud. He said he would urge the commission to complete its study as soon as possible. The new laws would incorporate maximum flexibility to prevent legislation from becoming obsolete as AI technology evolved, he added. “Many existing laws use technology-neutral language. For example, fraud offences focus on the intent to deceive using tools, regardless of whether those tools are primitive or advanced,” he said. Flexible “soft laws,” such as industry codes of conduct and public education, could be employed alongside legal measures, Lam added.

title: Singapore minister Chan Chun Sing’s Mandarin diplomacy strikes China chord
description: Chan quoted ancient philosopher Mencius in his speech at Xiangshan Forum, winning praise on social media for his knowledge of Chinese thought.
content: Singapore Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing’s use of Mandarin and Chinese philosophy in his speech at a major security forum in Beijing has won him praise on Chinese social media, while shedding light on how cultural familiarity and language can be diplomatic tools for the city state. Videos of Chan at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum quoting ancient philosopher Mencius, or Mengzi in Mandarin, have gone viral on platforms such as Weixin and Baidu, with users hailing his command of the language and knowledge of Chinese thought. Observers say that through resonating with the hosts, Chan managed to convey Singapore’s sterner message of a call for major powers to build trust instead of coercion, though there is a risk that linguistic bonds may raise the expectation for Singapore to sympathise with Beijing’s interests. At the summit on Wednesday, attended by delegates from nearly 100 countries and helmed by Chinese defence chief Dong Jun, Chan spoke mostly in English but switched to Mandarin occasionally and cited Mencius, saying: “Power may compel others to comply. But in the end, it is trust that truly wins others over.” Social media users also drew comparisons between Chan and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth, praising the former for displaying wisdom which exceeded that of a counterpart helming the military of a much larger country. On Chan’s use of Mandarin, a Weixin user commented: “This minister is not an ordinary person; he knows Chinese culture like the back of his hand.” Many also said Chan’s Mandarin was proof that the language and Chinese culture were gaining traction on the global stage. The Singapore minister also urged superpowers to shoulder higher expectations from smaller states, stressing that countries should strengthen their own security but not at the expense of others. “The more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be,” he said in Mandarin. Singapore welcomed China’s aspiration to be a “responsible major country”, Chan said, adding that Beijing’s “reform and opening up” policy had contributed greatly to regional and global prosperity. “As the People’s Liberation Army approaches its centenary, there is much potential for it to make a positive contribution to global stability and security,” he said. Diplomatic move? Observers hail Chan’s use of Mandarin and historical references as a clever diplomatic move, showcasing an appreciation and understanding of China and its culture. Stefanie Kam, an assistant professor at S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS), described Chan’s switch to Mandarin as deliberate and a “clear effort to show cultural awareness and diplomatic tact”. “For a defence minister to quote an old Chinese classic like this is quite strategic; it makes it hard for the Chinese audience to disagree because they would be disagreeing with their own classic,” she said. Adam Liu, a political scientist and assistant professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, pointed out that Chinese leader Xi Jinping often quoted ancient Chinese teachings. “Speaking in Mandarin and drawing on Mencius is a way of saying: I am addressing you in your own idiom, on your own terms. That tends to land well,” he said. While Chan’s Mandarin switch-up was largely well received, some netizens were unimpressed, arguing that it should be expected that Chan – who hails from a country where 74 per cent of citizens were of Chinese ethnicity – would be fluent in Mandarin. As English strengthens its hold as the main language for Singaporeans, the government has reinforced the importance of maintaining a bilingual edge, implementing measures such as public speaking contests and cultural workshops. According to a 2020 census, the use of Mandarin as the language most frequently spoken at home fell from 35.6 per cent in 2010 to 29.9 per cent in 2020. Dylan Loh, associate professor of foreign policy at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University, said the speech showed Singapore’s bilingualism and an ability to code-switch. “Beyond citing Mencius specifically, the broader context in which it was used is also important,” he said. “The message was respectful and paid compliment to Chinese history and philosophical heritage.” But Loh said the code-switch was not necessarily a strategic move in itself, noting that leaders had in the past done the same at various forums. Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, warned that the Chinese public could view affirmations of culture and ethnic similarities as synonymous with political alignment. While using a Chinese philosophical expression “may be tactically helpful to smooth ties”, Chong said it could also “create disappointment when a person or the entity they represent take positions that diverge from prior expectations associated with race, culture and politics”. On Chinese social media, some users interpreted Chan’s speech as veiled criticism of the United States, though observers note the script was vague and aligned with Singapore’s foreign policy. In his speech, Chan said: “We must work even harder to strengthen our domestic fundamentals, rather than try to externalise our domestic issues.” He also illustrated Singapore’s journey to the global stage since its independence in 1965, through which “leaders avoided exploiting foreign policy for political gain”. While Chan did not explicitly name a country, some online users who appraised Chan’s speech likely interpreted the reference to winning by force as implying American actions, Kam said. Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and coordinator at the China Programme at RSIS, said Chan’s speech was broad and in line with the city state’s “pro-Singapore” policy. “It’s not surprising the Chinese read this as a reference to the US, but the case that China’s domestic issues are not absent in its foreign policy can also be made,” he said. “If you look past the idioms, which are obviously for the Chinese audience, it’s general and mostly speaking on principle.” Liu said Mencius’ quote was consistent with Singapore’s non-alignment. “The hope is for an international order built on trust, rules and moral principles, which is a position one can hold without pointing at anybody.”

title: Thailand makes weight-loss pens prescription-only to counter glut of illegal medicines
description: The country’s consumer watchdog aims to help patients receive ‘higher quality, safer, and more appropriate for their treatment’.
content: Thailand has moved to make weight-loss pens prescription-only, as a glut of the GLP-1 medicines – which mimic the hormones released once someone is full – floods the black market and influencers swarm TikTok to extol the quick wins of the simple injections. The Southeast Asian nation, which is never far behind wellness or aesthetic trends and has a notorious black market in counterfeit drugs, has seen the uptake of GLP-1 medicines skyrocket, doctors say, including the market-leading Ozempic brand. But doctors have warned that the US$240 to US$360 monthly cost of having the drugs prescribed by doctors has caused a black market to mushroom, including a tsunami of fake and potentially dangerous smuggled medicines. As of Tuesday, Thailand’s consumer watchdog, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), designated weight-loss pens as a “specially controlled drug”, meaning buyers need a doctor’s prescription to access them at pharmacies. “Following the discovery of inappropriate use of the medication, as well as problems with counterfeit drugs and unregistered drugs in the market, the Thai FDA is also advancing a Track & Trace system to monitor the drug’s journey throughout the entire supply chain,” the FDA said in a statement. The aim was not to stop patients who “genuinely need the medication”, the statement added, “but rather to help them receive drugs that are of higher quality, safer, and more appropriate for their treatment”. GLP-1s (glucagon-like peptide-1) are the blockbuster class of drugs that many patients hail for shedding large amounts of weight quickly, as well as managing blood sugar for Type 2 diabetes. In beauty-obsessed Thailand, where wellness clinics line every main road, the drugs have found a ready market. An army of young content creators are amplifying their virtues over social media, alarming doctors over the reach of the new generation drugs and their potential dangers. Across Thai TikTok, how-to-use guides showing mainly young women self-administering pak pakaa (“stab the pen” in Thai, as the jabs are known) are popular among a Gen Z desperate to get thin, but often without the time to exercise or money to pay for prescriptions. In its place, a shadow market made the drugs affordable, one unlicensed GLP-1 seller told This Week in Asia. “The pens I sell are three times cheaper than the ones sold by clinics,” the trader said, requesting anonymity, of the US$80 to US$90 black-market jabs. “Of course mine are not FDA approved. But people keep buying them – even if they don’t admit it to avoid judgment and also in case it affects their health insurance records later at some point.” One pharmacist with a string of outlets told this Week in Asia that beauty clinics had sprung up offering the short cut to looking thin, irrespective of staff training or quality control over the pens’ contents. The pharmacist, who asked not to be named to avoid backlash, said it was also easy to find black-market GLP-1 pens from unscrupulous clinics, online sellers and pharmacies. “I’ve seen young people injecting themselves on social media without the knowledge of how to safely use the needle,” the pharmacist said. “It is one of the most ludicrous industries in the entire country, with almost no oversight. The Thai beauty standard is thin equals beautiful, no matter what the FDA does, it will not make the problem of abusing weight-loss drugs like this go away.” As GLP-1 drugs are being explored for their wider potential to help human conditions including asthma, doctors have warned of potentially serious effects from self-administering unknown, unregulated drugs at unsafe doses. “Weight-loss pens should only be considered after you have exhausted other methods of losing weight, because there are many factors to take into account, including your pre-existing medical conditions. Do not buy them and use them on your own,” said Pitsri Khumanuwong, or “Dr Mom”, a doctor who gives social media advice to her 600,000 followers on TikTok.

title: 3 Jellycat, Labubu plushie thieves jailed for up to 2 years and 2 months
description: Three men, aged 33 to 36, stole 83 plush toys from two claw machine shops on the instructions of other suspects who remain at large.
content: Three repeat offenders have been sentenced to up to two years and two months behind bars for stealing 83 Jellycat and Labubu plushies worth a total of HK$115,200 (US$14,770) from a Hong Kong shopping centre last year. The District Court heard on Friday that the three men had stolen the popular merchandise from two claw machine shops at Kwai Chung Plaza on the instructions of other suspects who remain at large. A waiter, Tang Lik-ming, 35, and a wood painter, Wong Wai-chun, 36, pleaded guilty to two counts of burglary for taking part in the crimes in the early hours of June 9 and June 12 last year. Part-time warehouse worker Ho Ka-keung, 33, admitted one count of burglary for driving an accomplice to the scene during the second incident. All three defendants had previous brushes with the law, with Ho and Wong committing the current offences shortly after they were released from prison in 2024 and 2025, respectively. A prosecution summary of the case said Tang and Wong first met outside the shopping centre at about 3am on June 9. Carrying four tote bags that Wong gave him, Tang used what appeared to be a stolen key to open a claw machine inside a shop on the second floor and took 23 Jellycat soft toys, each valued at HK$1,000. The two men left the scene separately 10 minutes later. At about 5am three days later, the pair returned to the shopping centre alongside a wanted suspect to steal 60 Jellycat and Labubu from another shop on the ground floor. The plushies were worth a total of HK$92,200. Surveillance camera footage revealed that Ho was behind the wheel of a car that took Wong to the shopping centre that morning. Police subsequently seized from the vehicle three tote bags and other items Tang used to commit the offence on June 9. Under caution, Tang and Wong said they had agreed to take part in the scheme for a reward of up to HK$9,000. Wong said he recruited Tang to commit the crimes at Ho’s instructions, adding that another wanted suspect had provided the keys to the claw machines to Ho in advance. Judge Ada Yim Shun-yee said the offences were highly premeditated and all three defendants were aware of their respective roles in the scheme. She jailed Tang for two years and Ho and Wong for two years and two months each. Claw machine shops typically operate 24 hours a day, with staff making only occasional visits while relying on CCTV cameras to detect theft. Burglary is punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment in Hong Kong. The Court of Appeal has set 2½ years’ imprisonment as the customary starting point for sentencing burglary offences outside domestic premises, and three years for offences committed in a domestic setting.

title: Hong Kong’s metal storage hits 30,000 tonnes in push to become global commodity hub
description: Financial services minister Christopher Hui also says city will pay for Dongjiang water using yuan as part of internationalising renminbi.
content: Hong Kong’s push to develop into a premier gold and commodity trading hub has gained momentum, with local metal storage surpassing 30,000 tonnes, a minister has said, as the administration positions the city as the “must-choose destination” for global capital. Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu also said on Friday the government would expand renminbi settlement of payments for mainland Chinese services, such as buying water from the Dongjiang, in a bid to boost the globalisation of the yuan. “The significance of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan is a shift in mindset. We must plan Hong Kong’s financial development with a longer-term perspective and a broader vision, and respond with flexibility and diversity,” Hui said. “Every measure I introduce revolves around one goal: to elevate Hong Kong from a ‘must-pass route’ for capital to a ‘must-choose destination’ for capital.” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out an array of measures in his annual policy blueprint on Wednesday to accelerate the growth of the city’s international gold trading market, including a Joint Working Group on Commodity Trading chaired by Hui. The government will halve the profits tax rate for qualifying physical commodity traders from the standard 16.5 per cent to 8.25 per cent by next year, and the city’s Exchange Fund, used to defend the local currency, will increase its gold portfolio. The policies followed the launch of the trial operation of Hong Kong’s gold clearing and settlement system in July, which aims to establish the city as a major trading centre and price-setter for the precious metal. The system is expected to begin operation officially in the first quarter of next year. Speaking at a press conference, Hui noted total metal storage within Hong Kong’s London Metal Exchange warehouse network had crossed 30,000 tonnes, underscoring the drive to advance commodity trading. Hong Kong has recorded robust demand for gold imports as banks and logistics companies bet on Hong Kong’s expansion of its vaults for the precious metal. Data from the Census and Statistics Department showed about 107 tonnes of gold entered Hong Kong in July, up from 72.16 tonnes in February. Hui noted that the trial operation of the gold clearing system had proceeded smoothly, attracting substantial deposits. Beyond the 11 banks taking part in the trial, authorities received inquiries from other institutions interested in joining the gold trading ecosystem, which Hui described as a “good sign”. On government payments, the policy address proposed expanding yuan payments for services rendered by mainland authorities. Hui said the arrangements were already in place on a limited scale and described the increase as a natural next step. He added that officials were considering paying in yuan for Dongjiang water supplies – which account for up to 80 per cent of the city’s fresh water from the Taiyuan Pumping Station in Dongguan city – as well as for training programmes run by mainland institutions. At the same press conference, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah revealed that authorities were liaising with more than 40 companies interested in establishing a presence in the Northern Metropolis. “Many of them are in innovation and technology, including hydrogen energy [and] new energy development, and the other one is in quantum science, and we got another one building a logistics park,” Yau said. To attract enterprises to the 30,000-hectare (74,130-acre) megaproject, which will feature several innovation hubs and university clusters, the government is offering tailored incentive packages featuring land-use facilitation, co-investment options and tax breaks based on operation scale.

title: US hands over 64 smuggled artefacts to China in diplomatic push before summit
description: Beijing praises repatriation of looted treasures as concrete proof of constructive US-China cooperation before high-level talks.
content: The United States has returned dozens of cultural relics to China ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s coming visit to Washington, a goodwill gesture to help pave the way for a positive summit. At the handover ceremony at the Chinese embassy in Washington on Wednesday, China officials received 58 cultural relics and palaeontological fossils from the cultural property, art and antiquities programme of US Homeland Security Investigations. A further six items were returned a day later by the Manhattan District Attorney’s Office in New York. “The repatriation marks the latest step to implement the common understandings reached by the two presidents in their meetings in Beijing, and also demonstrates the broad prospects of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Friday. “China and the US should go in the same direction in the spirit of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit so as to accomplish more great and concrete things for the good of our two countries and peoples.” According to the Chinese embassy in Washington, the returned items included a Bodhisattva statue from the Tianlong Mountain Grottoes in the northern province of Shanxi, which was looted and taken overseas more than a century ago. Xie Feng, China’s ambassador to the US, said the repatriation reflected both sides’ responsibility for history and showed that China-US cooperation based on mutual respect and benefit could deliver many “major, practical and meaningful achievements”. The handover took place with less than a week to go until Xi’s scheduled visit to Washington. It is a reciprocal trip following US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, where the two leaders agreed on a new positioning for China-US relations – to build a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability. “This repatriation stands as a tangible outcome of both sides implementing this new positioning,” Xie said. He said the returned cultural relics – ranging from pottery figurines and stone sculptures to dinosaur and fish fossils, all of which were illicitly trafficked into the US before being seized by US law enforcement – carried “high historical, cultural and scientific value”. He added that cultural heritage preservation had become a fruitful area of Sino-American cooperation. China and the US signed their first intergovernmental memorandum of understanding to prevent the illegal entry of Chinese cultural artefacts into the US in 2009. It has since been renewed in 2014, 2019 and 2024. Guo said the memorandum had so far enabled the return of more than 700 artefacts from the US. The largest single repatriation of Chinese cultural relics from the US occurred in 2019, with 361 items handed over. According to the China Cultural Relics Academy, more than 10 million Chinese cultural artefacts have been lost overseas since the opium wars in the mid-19th century, mostly because of wartime looting and illegal trafficking. In response, Beijing has been stepping up efforts to become a petitioner and setter of standards in global heritage restitution. In April, China published the Collection of Chinese Bronzes in Overseas Collections after 14 years of investigation, serving as a toolkit for its intensifying campaign to reclaim lost cultural heritage.

title: Mainland Chinese tax drive flags Hong Kong MPF accounts as offshore trusts
description: As Beijing tightens tax collection, some mainland residents who previously worked in Hong Kong are being asked to explain their MPF accounts.
content: For Michelle Zhao, a Shanghai resident, offshore trusts had long appeared to be the preserve of people far wealthier than herself. That assumption was upended two weeks ago when she received a “baffling” text message from the Hongkou district branch of the Shanghai Municipal Tax Service. “The message said I might have taxable gains stemming from offshore trusts that I was required to declare. Yet I have never held any form of trust. I assumed the message was sent to me by mistake, so I ignored it at first,” she recalled. A few days later, the tax administration followed up with a phone call, shedding light on the SMS: the alert was linked to Zhao’s Hong Kong Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) account. She explained to the tax officer that the account had been set up by her former employer in 2022 when she worked in Hong Kong, and she had no trust holdings. “The officer said he would record my statement, and nothing further,” Zhao said. Her experience is far from unique, with multiple posts describing confusion over similar tax notices surfacing on the Chinese social media platform RedNote. A Beijing-based user of the platform, posting under the handle @Will, said he, too, had been contacted by local tax officials by text message and phone about potential offshore trust gains. Like Zhao, he had previously worked in Hong Kong. In his case, the inquiry also led back to an MPF account. Beijing tax officials emailed @Will a form requiring him to explain the account, sign the form and affix his fingerprint. So why are MPF accounts, a type of pension fund, being flagged by mainland tax authorities as offshore trusts? According to the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority (MPFA), master trust schemes are the most common type of MPF plan. They pool contributions from multiple employers and scheme members for consolidated administration and investment, harnessing economies of scale. That structure may be at the root of the confusion: the word “trust” appears in the official name of the retirement schemes. It is difficult for local officials to determine whether MPF accounts constitute offshore trusts or simply retirement savings, so taxpayers are expected to clarify on their own Ge Yuyu, Shanghai National Accounting Institute “Under the Common Reporting Standard, information on MPF accounts is [shared with] mainland tax authorities, where the accounts are categorised as trust-related holdings,” said Ge Yuyu, an associate professor at the Shanghai National Accounting Institute. “It is difficult for local officials to determine whether they constitute offshore trusts or simply MPF retirement savings, so taxpayers are expected to clarify on their own,” he added. Beijing has tightened scrutiny of overseas assets over the past two years, extending its tax net to offshore trusts, returns on cross-border insurance policies and overseas share investments as domestic tax and land-related revenues soften. In July, the Ministry of Finance and the State Taxation Administration for the first time set out detailed provisions addressing individual income tax on offshore trusts. The rules apply a uniform 20 per cent rate to relevant taxable income at each stage of a trust’s life cycle: the transfer of assets into the trust, income earned during its operation, and its eventual wind-up. Ye Yongqing, a tax lawyer at Beijing-based Anli Partners, said trusts and MPF schemes had similar legal structures, which could explain why MPF accounts were being categorised as trusts under the tax system. Ge said tax authorities could readily verify whether an MPF pension account was involved by requiring supporting documents from the scheme provider. According to Hong Kong’s Inland Revenue Department, since 2020, MPF schemes have fallen within the definition of a reporting financial institution and no longer qualify for exemption. Both Ye, the lawyer, and Ge, the professor, said MPF accounts enjoyed tax-exempt status and were not subject to the tax framework for offshore trusts. The MPFA also notes on its website that “upon withdrawal of MPF by scheme members, the sum derived from mandatory contributions is not taxable”.

title: Fok fudges but Hong Kong football chiefs appear ready to make Gianni Infantino their man
description: Fifa president set to visit city for Asean Cup final next month, as chairman hails local association’s close ties with global governing body.
content: The local football association has planted its flag in the camp of Gianni Infantino, the embattled Fifa president who is expected in Hong Kong for the final of the second-tier Asean Cup on October 3. At a media event to announce details for the coming competition on Friday, Eric Fok Kai-shan fudged the direct question over whether Infantino retained his organisation’s backing. But the chairman of the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) said that “whoever supports Hong Kong football development, we will support, and we are working closely with Fifa on delivering this landmark event”. Busy trying to curry favour with member associations ahead of March’s election, Infantino’s grip on power weakened after his cloak-and-dagger plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was exposed in July. Exactly two months before the deadline for candidates to put their hands up to challenge Infantino, the Swiss lawyer appeared on video at the Fifa Asean Cup press briefing, congratulating the HKFA for their involvement in “this spectacular event”. “You will see the best of football in Southeast Asia: emotions, passion and goals,” Infantino said. “You will see the best of Fifa at your doorstep, and broadcast to the entire universe.” Setting aside for a moment the absurdity of Infantino’s grandstanding over a tournament in which world No 156 Hong Kong are the highest ranked of the six entrants, his remote appearance further underlined the strengthening ties he has forged with local officials. Last week, the HKFA posted an image on its Instagram account that captured Infantino sandwiched by Pui Kwan-kay and Charles Cheung Yim-yau, the HKFA president and general secretary, respectively. “[HKFA] is a member of the Fifa family, and we strive to bring in more tournaments,” Fok said. “Working with Fifa and having this tournament being developed in Hong Kong shows [Fifa’s] trust in Hong Kong’s professionalism and [ability to] bring more international football.” Pressed on whether the HKFA’s self-stated tight relationship with the global governing body could be interpreted as support for its figurehead, Fok said that was “a decision for the board”, and that this was “not the time to talk about it, because it’s not on the agenda, right now”. “The [election] will be next year, and we’ll be closely looking at the whole process,” Fok added. “But we see big support from Fifa for the development of Hong Kong football and we’re working closely [together]. They’ve delivered this tournament and we’re excited to have all the matches.” While India reneged on their initial interest in joining the inaugural Asean Cup’s “Premier Division” in Indonesia, in favour of hosting friendlies against Brazil, Uruguay and Panama, and traditional rivals Singapore recently secured home friendly dates with Paraguay and Brazil, Hong Kong are poised for games against Laos and Brunei, Nos 185 and 194 in the world, respectively. Assuming they do not come unstuck, the city team will probably face either world No 158 Myanmar or 175th-ranked Cambodia in the final. Those sides are grouped with Timor-Leste, who are 201st in the global standings. The South China Morning Post has been told that Uruguay, now managed by former Kitchee striker Diego Forlan, expressed interest in coming to play Hong Kong in the forthcoming Fifa window. They will instead have matches in Japan and South Korea before going to India. Fok said the HKFA had received “many enquiries” but that “for us it’s about bringing quality tournaments during the Fifa windows”. “It’s important to progress our ranking, and to play at Kai Tak Stadium where we can have more supporters,” Fok said. “I believe this is a prestigious tournament with prestigious teams. We should be positive and look forward to it.” After the HKFA announced on June 5 that it planned to stage the Asean Cup “Challenge Division” there was a 97-day information vacuum before they confirmed arrangements on September 10. Theodore Giannikos, who flew in for the soft launch three months ago in his role as Fifa’s director of strategic projects partnerships and media, quietly left the organisation in July. He was appointed CEO of English Premier League club Nottingham Forest this month. Fok said that HKFA had been dictated to by “Fifa’s protocols and timetable” but that conversations over staging the Asean Cup began late last year. “We appreciate the trust [invested in us] because it shows Hong Kong has the environment, infrastructure and professionalism to host such a tournament,” Fok said. For Roberto Losada, the Hong Kong head coach, the competition will provide an opportunity to kick-start his tenure. Appointed in June, he began with a flat 2-0 victory over Mongolia, before feeling the full fury of supporters following a tame 2-0 surrender in Cambodia. “That’s the life of a coach,” Fok said. “The HKFA is giving the best support to the fans, to the players and to the coaches. That’s our role, and we believe we’ve done our part.” Fok had no news over who the city team would face in Fifa’s November window, but did not reject the prospect of the two-leg Guangdong-Hong Kong Cup being played then instead of in its traditional December and January slot. “We’re reviewing everything, but our priority is the Asean Cup,” he said. “We have different enquiries for different periods, so we’re looking for the best combination and we hope to set a clear calendar going forward.” Tickets to watch Laos play Brunei, and Myanmar tackle Timor-Leste, at Mong Kok Stadium on September 24 will cost HK$150. Hong Kong’s Kai Tak game against Laos on September 27 will be followed by Cambodia against Myanmar. The city team meet Brunei at the same venue on September 30, directly after Timor-Leste clash with Cambodia. Tickets for both dates, as well as for the final, are priced between HK$80 and HK$200. A three-day Kai Tak package is available for HK$520. “It’s kicking off very soon, I will be there and enjoying it,” Infantino said. “Congratulations to president Pui from the Hong Kong FA.”

title: ‘Sadfishing’: China teacher probed over sacrifice claims – 23 years away, US$300,000 spent
description: Facing a hyper-competitive academic market, young educators must publish, secure grants, teach under tight deadlines to avoid dismissal.
content: A Chinese professor has ignited controversy after asserting at a university conference that her extreme commitment to research involved sleeping less than two hours a day for a decade, investing two million yuan (US$300,000) of her own money, and completely sacrificing her personal and family life for over 20 years. The public health professor, Lu Chan, from the Xiangya School of Medicine at Central South University in Hunan province, sparked widespread debate after presenting these extraordinary claims to her research group on September 10. Lu, who became a professor immediately after earning her PhD in 2018, reportedly shared her remarkable undertakings during the China National Teachers’ Day Commendation Conference held at her university. According to a presentation displayed on a large screen, which served as evidence of her dedication to research, Lu claimed to have slept “0 to 2 hours every day” without taking a day off since graduate school until December last year. She also revealed that she had “not met up with her parents for 23 years.” At the age of 44, she remains single and views her students as her children. Lu stated that she invested around two million yuan from her own finances, including 800,000 yuan from her parents’ pension, into her research group. Last week, she even allocated 200,000 yuan, originally earmarked for her mortgage, to support her students’ research. Lu was one of 10 teachers honoured during the China National Teachers’ Day on September 10. The university released a photo showcasing the content of her presentation, which a netizen subsequently shared on social media, inciting a wave of backlash. Critics have questioned the credibility of the presentation’s claims, expressing concerns about the university’s values in promoting what they perceive as “sadfishing.” “If she truly sleeps for less than two hours a day for over a decade, she should evaluate her own well-being,” commented one individual. “What she shared is not inspiring; it’s alarming,” remarked another. “If I were a student searching for a research group, I would avoid hers. Her work ethic seems excessively demanding,” a third observer noted. “Genuine scientific research and education should be rooted in rational inquiry and a commitment to humanistic care, rather than a competition of who can be harsher on themselves and their families,” one person commented. Some critics believe Lu’s presentation employed vague language to embellish the facts. One individual suggested it would make more sense if she had not met her parents for “two to three” years instead of “23,” and if she mentioned “naps 0 to 2 hours” rather than “sleeping 0 to 2 hours” a day. A staff member from the School of Medicine informed The Beijing News that Lu’s statements reflected her personal experiences and did not violate any rules or contain seriously inappropriate remarks. He mentioned that the school would investigate whether her claims regarding her sleeping patterns and familial interactions are exaggerated. The SCMP reached out to Lu for comment but had not received a response at the time of writing. On a knowledge-sharing platform, a self-proclaimed university teacher noted that it is common to “embellish” details when competing for performance awards. However, he stressed that such embellishments should remain grounded in “basic human nature.” Several observers also commented on the intense pressure faced by many young university teachers in China. Due to the escalating competitiveness in the academic job market, many young educators are forced to sign “up or out” contracts, which require them to fulfil a series of demanding tasks – such as publishing in top journals, teaching, and securing grants – within a limited time frame to avoid termination.

title: Collision near Sabina Shoal sparks fresh escalation between China and the Philippines
description: Two sides blame each other for deliberate ramming near the contested atoll in the South China Sea, fuelling tensions over strategic waterway.
content: China and the Philippines exchanged blame over a clash on Friday in disputed waters in the South China Sea, further fuelling tensions over the strategic waterway that has become a dangerous regional flashpoint. In a brief statement released on Friday afternoon, China’s coastguard accused a Philippine vessel of deliberately ramming a Chinese patrol vessel near the contested Sabina Shoal. “Philippine vessel No 3015 intentionally adjusted its course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow of the Chinese coastguard vessel, resulting in a collision,” said Jiang Lue, a Chinese coastguard spokesman. Manila’s actions “severely violated international law and basic norms governing international relations, endangering the safety of Chinese vessels and personnel”, Jiang added. Demanding that Manila immediately cease all “infringements and provocations”, Jiang warned that the Philippines would bear full responsibility for any escalation and that Chinese law-enforcement forces would continue their operation to safeguard national sovereignty and maritime rights. Video footage released by the Beijing-based think tank South China Sea Strategic Situation Probing Initiative – and purportedly captured by the Chinese coastguard – showed the Philippine vessel altering its course before sideswiping the Chinese ship. The clash was the latest in a series of increasingly sharp confrontations at sea and comes amid growing concern that the maritime stand-off could draw in the US, a treaty ally of the Philippines. The Chinese statement came shortly after Jay Tarriela, a spokesman for the Philippine coastguard, accused Beijing of “deliberately” ramming a civilian government vessel and endangering the lives of its Filipino crew. According to Tarriela, the incident occurred about 54 nautical miles off the Philippine island of Palawan on Friday morning, when the Chinese coastguard vessel cut across the stern of the Philippine boat at a distance of about 10 metres (about 33 feet). The Chinese coastguard vessel repeated the manoeuvre and struck the Philippine boat, inflicting damage that extended to the starboard side and resulting in debris scattering across the deck, Tarriela wrote on social media. He added that the Chinese vessel subsequently made another manoeuvre, passing about five metres behind the damaged Philippine boat, and that surface and air assets were deployed to the location to help and ensure the safety of its crew. “Let us be clear about what this vessel was doing,” Tarriela wrote. “It was bringing fuel to Filipino fishermen so they can keep fishing in our own waters and keep food on Filipino tables.” “The China Coast Guard deliberately rammed a civilian government vessel on a humanitarian and livelihood mission, endangering the lives of its Filipino crew.” In a short video that Tarriela posted, crew members aboard the Philippine ship could be heard shouting “collision”. Another video captured the Chinese ship pulling away after a Philippine crew member reported over the radio that the vessel was just “five metres” away. It is not clear whether any crew members from either side sustained injuries. Friday’s encounter marks one of the most serious escalations between the rival claimants in recent months. Beijing claims sovereignty over most islands and rock features in the South China Sea. Some of its territorial claims in the resource-rich waterway overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and others. Beijing has in recent months ramped up its patrols to maintain a presence in the disputed waters in the Spratly Islands and Scarborough Shoal, now at the centre of its territorial disputes with the Philippines. Sabina Shoal is an atoll in the Spratly Islands in the South China Sea and claimed by China, the Philippines and others. It serves as an important staging ground to monitor or block Philippine resupply missions to nearby Second Thomas Shoal while also functioning as a strategic buffer zone controlling access to Reed Bank’s massive untapped natural gas and oil reserves.

title: Where to celebrate Negroni Week 2026 in Hong Kong, September 21–27
description: Enjoy classic and eclectic variations of the Italian cocktail with guest bartenders, free-flow packages and more at these venues.
content: Negroni Week returns for its 14th edition, running from September 21 to 27. Launched in 2013 by the US-based Imbibe Magazine, the annual celebration has grown into a worldwide drink-for-a-cause movement. More than US$5 million (HK$39.2 million) has been raised to date, with proceeds supporting the work of the Slow Food global movement. This year marks the programme’s most extensive Asia-Pacific presence yet, with visiting bartenders appearing across 18 venues in mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, Thailand, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. Here are a few events happening in Hong Kong. 1. Zuma Zuma in Central kicks off the week with a double guest shift on September 21, hosting two of Bangkok’s most recognised bar talents for one night only. The opening party at the Landmark venue will feature Matteo Cadeddu, bar manager of Opium Bangkok – which placed No 25 on this year’s Asia’s 50 Best Bars list – alongside Michele Montauti, director of beverage and bars at Aman Nai Lert Bangkok. Between them, they will serve six drinks made with Campari – including a truffle negroni and cafe latte negroni – while Zuma’s own bar team will feature two cocktails available only during the week: a roasted negroni with hojicha gin and a banana negroni fizz with coffee Campari. Zuma, Level 5&6 Landmark Atrium, 15 Queen’s Road Central 2. Qura To celebrate Negroni Week, Qura has created a three-cocktail menu called L’Avanguardia Italiana that riffs on Italian ingredients and traditions, with each cocktail priced at HK$160. L’Oliveto takes a savoury route, combining Los Siete Misterios Doba Yej Mezcal, Mancino Rosso Amaranto and Campari with olive and cacao. The result is smoky, briny and bittersweet. Il Frutteto shifts towards fruit, blending Cascahuin Blanco Tequila, Campari, Vecchia Romagna 18 Brandy, toasted almond, peach and soda water. Think a stone-fruit highball with a bitter Italian spine. Last but not least, La Drogheria completes the trio with No 3 London Dry Gin, Cocchi Vermouth di Torino Rosso and Campari, plus coconut and Abracadabra licorice liqueur. Qura Bar, Lobby Floor, Regent Hong Kong, 18 Salisbury Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui 3. Cassio Social Club Negroni Night Fever takes over Cassio in Central on September 24, from 7pm to 10pm. The three-hour free-flow line-up covers the negroni, the rosita and the Campari spritz, with live music from the bar’s resident DJ throughout the night. Tickets are HK$198 plus service charge, making it one of the more accessible ways to dive into the week’s bitter-and-bubbly programme. For anyone who wants a social, high-energy Negroni Week experience rather than a seated tasting, this is likely to be the stand-out party. It is also a rare chance to try a rosita alongside the classics without committing to a full cocktail menu. Cassio Social Club, 2/F, 33 Wyndham Street, Hong Kong 4. Dio Cosy coffee bar Dio will host a negroni cocktail workshop on September 26, an intimate hands-on session limited to a small group. Led by Campari’s Oscar Choi and Dio’s bar manager Wing Chan, the workshop covers the history of the Campari brand before guests craft three cocktails of their own: a classic negroni, a Canton negroni and a Garibaldi. Dio Cafe Bar, New Central Mansion, 8 Aberdeen Street, Central

title: Why Singapore’s big-box gyms are losing to niche fitness studios
description: Traditional gyms are struggling to compete with 24-hour budget chains on price and specialised boutique studios on community experience.
content: Property agent Raymond Heng had suspected True Fitness was struggling, but he did not expect the gym he had visited for more than a decade to disappear overnight. The closure was not entirely surprising given the region’s fiercely competitive fitness industry, but its abruptness left Heng, 47, in disbelief after paying S$8,800 (US$6,900) for a lifetime membership in 2013. “I guessed that they might not have been doing that well since branches have been closing over the years, but I did not expect the whole chain to disappear just like that,” he said. Heng is among the many fitness fans left searching for a new gym after True Fitness abruptly ceased all operations in Singapore last week. Parent company Kontafarma China Holdings cited cost pressures and intense market competition for winding up the business. Industry experts said the closure did not necessarily point to a saturated market in Singapore, but instead reflected shifting consumer preferences. Gym-goers are increasingly splitting into two camps: those seeking value and convenience, and those looking for specialised experiences beyond traditional big-box facilities. Low-cost, 24-hour chains and niche boutique studios offering structured, guided classes are squeezing traditional full-service fitness centres from both ends of the market. While the large-format gym model was attractive two decades ago, the market had fragmented, said Jack Tong, an assistant professor of business at Nanyang Technological University. Operators now had to compete on all fronts, including experience and the sense of community they provided, he added. “This leaves traditional full-service gyms potentially squeezed in the middle. They may find it difficult to compete with low-cost gyms on price while also struggling to compete with specialised operators on experience,” Tong said. Natthavut Srinara, a lecturer and consultant at EHL Hospitality Business School in Switzerland, said that the old business models were falling out of favour. “Demand is now spread across many formats and price points, which makes the middle of the market increasingly difficult.” Following True Fitness’ closure, budget and boutique gyms moved quickly to court displaced members, with franchises like Body Fit Training and Anytime Fitness waiving sign-up fees and offering complimentary sessions. Price vs experience A short walk from a closed True Fitness branch, Stella Loh laces up her boxing gloves. Three times a week, the 60-year-old rotates between strength and Muay Thai classes at Hybe Fit, a hybrid training gym where curated programmes and attentive instructors make workouts less intimidating. “Technique and safety are more important than simply lifting heavy weights,” Loh said. Boutique studios like Hybe Fit have been popping up across Singapore in recent years, offering specialised workouts and personalised coaching that mass-market gyms rarely provide. Hybe Fit co-founder Nuovo Tan said the studio had welcomed an increasing number of members seeking structured training since opening in the city state’s Orchard Road shopping district last month. “We have [had] some conversions from open gyms, such as those who have been going to the gym for a while but don’t see progress due to a lack of a proper programme or guidance,” Tan said. The popularity of functional fitness events like Hyrox has also provided a boost, with studios launching targeted programmes to prepare participants. Ground Zero, which launched as a spin studio in 2017 during the global rise of indoor cycling gyms, has expanded its offerings to include functional fitness and strength training while remaining open as a gym between classes. Ground Zero founder Jeong Fok said their community-driven nature was a key selling point for boutique gyms. “People who train at such studios want somewhere they can call their own, meet like-minded people, and actually feel like they belong … It almost becomes a modern-day version of a club or community space,” Fok said. “I think that’s also connected to the rise of events like Hyrox – people just aren’t participating individually any more.” But these specialised experiences come at a premium. An unlimited monthly pass at Hybe Fit costs S$360 – dropping to S$300 on an annual plan – while weekly access at Ground Zero ranges from S$70 to S$80. Consumers’ willingness to spend substantial sums on fitness was no surprise, Srinara said. “Consumers are becoming much more specific about what they want,” he said. “Premium customers are willing to pay more for better service, wellness experiences and networking opportunities.” At the other end of the spectrum, price and accessibility top the priority list for Justina Tay, 26. The consultant pays S$95 a month for an Anytime Fitness membership, giving her 24-hour access to roughly 160 locations across Singapore. “Convenience is the most important to building a consistent routine and Anytime Fitness has the most number of outlets,” Tay said. The chain operates on a franchise model, with fitness group Inspire Brands Asia the master franchisee for Southeast Asia since 2020. Inspire Brands Asia did not immediately respond to requests for comment from This Week in Asia. Calls for stronger protections The sudden closure of True Fitness – which reportedly left customers suffering losses exceeding S$600,000 – has renewed calls for stricter consumer protection standards around long-term prepayments. Holly Yang, a professor of accounting at Singapore Management University, said that while financial distress was evident in public filings from Kontafarma and True Fitness, ordinary consumers could not be expected to scrutinise financial statements before buying a gym membership. In Singapore, financial records for companies such as True Fitness and True Yoga are available via the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority for a fee. However, tracking cross-border corporate structures is challenging. Singapore operates a voluntary accreditation scheme called CaseTrust, under which participating firms that collect qualifying advance payments must implement prepayment protection measures. A government-run Consumer Protection Review Panel is currently evaluating whether existing safeguards for high-value packages are adequate. Yang urged regulatory authorities to consider making insurance requirements mandatory for large advance membership fees. “[The] information existed, but people had no reason to think they needed it, and no costless way to obtain it,” she added. Kontafarma China Holdings, which is listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange, has been contacted for comment.

title: Could mystery Shanghai vessel be a mothership for China’s underwater drones?
description: Satellite images show an unusual craft under construction that analysts say may be designed to deploy very large uncrewed submarines.
content: An unusual vessel taking shape at a Shanghai shipyard has been assessed as a possible mothership for China’s large uncrewed submarines – a capability that, if confirmed, could enable Beijing to operate the drones far from its own coast for sustained periods. Open-source naval analyst H.I. Sutton said satellite imagery of the roughly 200-metre (656-foot) hull at Hudong-Zhonghua showed a large internal hangar and an opening at the stern that appeared designed to launch and recover extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles (XXLUUVs). Sutton said the vessel was most likely a dedicated submarine-drone mothership. An experienced military imagery analyst who reviewed the same September 10 imagery for the South China Morning Post said he could independently identify the apparent stern launch-and-recovery system. The analyst, who was not authorised to speak publicly on the matter, said a lifting frame, or cradle, positioned behind the vessel in the dry dock appeared narrow enough to pass through the stern opening. The area inside the opening might lack a floor, he added, potentially allowing the cradle and any underwater craft it carried to be lowered into the sea or hoisted back aboard using the surrounding support structures, as Sutton described. The analyst said the configuration was inconsistent with a cable-laying ship. Such vessels normally carry large horizontal drums for storing cable, either exposed on deck or housed within the hull. The drums or their fittings would be visible during construction, he added. The observations support parts of Sutton’s reading of the imagery but do not establish what the ship will be used for. Sutton’s interpretation builds on earlier imagery showing unusually large, submarine-shaped craft being handled from floating docks. In early 2025, open-source researcher M.T. Anderson spotted a craft about 40 to 45 metres (131 to 148 feet) long, with no visible sail, inside a floating dock at Guangzhou Shipyard. Sutton later assessed the craft as an XXLUUV, linked the dock to a vessel named Special Floating Dock 001, and reported that it subsequently operated around Hainan. An SCMP examination of China Classification Society records found that a vessel of that name – Special Floating Dock 001, a 70.2-metre (230-foot) semi-submersible floating dock completed in October 2024 – is owned and managed by the Kunming branch of the 705 Research Institute. The institute, also known as the Xian Precision Machinery Research Institute, is a Chinese underwater-weapons research body. A Shanghai Stock Exchange filing describes it as responsible for the overall research and design of underwater weapons and their launch systems. Its specialist journal, launched in 1993 as Torpedo Technology, was renamed the Journal of Unmanned Undersea Systems in 2017. The SCMP has not independently established that the dock seen with the 40- to 45-metre craft was the 705-owned vessel, nor is it confirmed that the craft is uncrewed, or that either is connected to the Hudong hull. If floating docks can already transport such large underwater craft, the question is what a dedicated mothership could add. Peter Jones, a retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral and adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra, said such a vessel could function much like a submarine tender, providing maintenance, forward support and transport. “For UUVs with their slow transit speeds, there is utility in having a forward-deployed support ship” to shorten transit time to the patrol area, he said. Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said the vessel could be understood as a “hybrid mothership and mobile support dock”. Such a ship could carry fuel, batteries, armaments and other supplies, he said, allowing China to “operate underwater drones on a sustained basis at distant locations”. It could support intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance UUVs searching for submarines, or deploy attack UUVs or mines closer to an adversary’s shores. Lyle Goldstein, director of the Asia programme at Defence Priorities and head of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School, said Sutton’s interpretation was “quite plausible” given China’s long-standing work on very large UUV prototypes. Floating docks were useful for “testing and experimentation”, Goldstein said, but sustaining XLUUV operations at sea over extended periods could justify a dedicated mothership. An XLUUV could carry torpedoes, mines or even missiles but would probably have “quite limited magazine depth”, he said, meaning it would need to be rearmed after firing only a limited number of weapons – a problem that also confronts the US Navy’s submarine force. One plausible wartime role, he said, would be supporting patrols east of Taiwan or between the first and second island chains, where mainland Chinese surface ships or aircraft could provide some protection. Goldstein was sceptical though of Sutton’s suggestion that the drones could be deployed off the US west coast, given their vulnerability to interception. Such a ship would also be a large, vulnerable target. Heath said it would be better suited to operating relatively close to China in less hostile conditions, leaving crewed submarines to operate in the most contested waters. Goldstein likewise cautioned that survivability would be limited in a conflict with a peer military power. Experts also do not rule out the vessel having a civilian or scientific role.

title: Will AI adoption shrink office space? Asia-Pacific firms are on the fence in survey
description: AI currently has a more significant impact on office operations than on real estate requirements, CBRE says.
content: Nearly one-fifth of surveyed companies in the Asia-Pacific region believe wider adoption of artificial intelligence will reduce their real estate needs, a new study by CBRE has found. More than half – 56 per cent – held a neutral view, believing either that AI had no impact on office space demand or that it was too early to determine its effect, according to the property consultancy’s poll of corporate real estate executives in the region. The remaining 25 per cent said AI adoption would require them to expand their office footprint. The survey was conducted between May 26 and July 10 across nine markets, including Hong Kong, mainland China, Singapore, Japan, Australia and India. It received 651 responses, with those from the mainland and India weighted more heavily to “reflect those markets’ share of Asia-Pacific grade A office stock”. The results pointed to AI currently having a more significant impact on office operations than on real estate requirements, CBRE said. “Although there is speculation that AI could reduce office demand, our findings suggest most organisations remain in the early stages of assessing its impact, with minimal short-term effect on real estate requirements,” said Ada Choi, head of research for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “At the same time, many occupiers remain confident in business growth and continue to plan for expansion. As companies rebalance their office portfolio, future growth will be concentrated in higher-quality workplaces, while lower-value space is rationalised.” What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market Tom Gaffney, CBRE AI has been blamed for lay-offs across various sectors, with lower headcounts often linked to reduced office space needs. Last year, a study by the Switzerland-based World Economic Forum found that 41 per cent of employers across 22 industries in 55 economies planned to reduce their workforce as AI automated certain tasks. Among CBRE respondents, 46 per cent identified themselves as AI adopters or active movers in applying AI to corporate real estate operations, up from 9 per cent in 2024. Meanwhile, nearly nine in 10 respondents reported that employees worked in the office at least three days per week, the highest level since the Covid-19 pandemic. Another 85 per cent said office attendance had reached a steady state. “With attendance and utilisation largely stabilised at higher levels, companies are no longer focused only on bringing employees back to the office,” said Tom Gaffney, head of leasing for Asia-Pacific at CBRE. “They can now concentrate on transforming the workplace to improve experience and efficiency. What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market, with companies selectively growing their portfolio and prioritising premium workplaces.”

title: Hyrox Beijing athlete apologises to China, competitors after soiling herself
description: Joanna Wietrzyk says she should have stepped off the track at Hyrox Beijing, announces her retroactive withdrawal from race, loss of points.
content: Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has issued a public apology after soiling herself during Hyrox Beijing, admitting she should have stepped off the track while announcing her retroactive withdrawal from the race and forfeiture of her points. The 24-year-old elite athlete completed Saturday’s race covered in faeces after organisers failed to intervene, leaving more than 1,000 subsequent participants to compete on the contaminated track and shared equipment. Wietrzyk previously posted “a win is a win” on social media, a statement she later deleted before turning off comments and direct messages as she faced five days of intense online backlash alongside criticism of organisers for negligence. On Thursday, after the event and following official apologies and rule updates from organisers, Wietrzyk published a statement on social media expressing regret over the impact on fellow competitors, spectators and staff. “I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the Hyrox organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” she wrote in the statement. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Joanna Wietrzyk (@joannawietrzyk) Wietrzyk stated she felt physically fine at the start of the race and did not anticipate any discomfort, but acknowledged upon reflection that she should have left the track, taking responsibility for her decision to continue. “I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice,” she said. “I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.” Adding that she would learn from the experience, including remembering that “there is more to life than racing” and recognising “when it is right to step away”, Wietrzyk announced she had retroactively withdrawn from the race and relinquished her earned points. She also thanked supporters who showed kindness, noting she would temporarily step back from public attention. “I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise,” she wrote. Many social media users remained sceptical of the delayed apology, viewing it as a public relations effort to protect commercial sponsorships. “The main issue is that this athlete is sponsored by Puma,” one user noted. “Hyrox is inherently a highly commercialised event, and a lot of people are paid by sports brands to promote it.” Another asked: “Will people look down on me if I wear the Puma and Hyrox co-branded gear I bought?” Wietrzyk had recently noted that Puma maintained a long-term partnership with Hyrox and that she would receive multi-year support from the brand. She also recently featured in campaigns for Puma’s PWRMODE collection and promoted its footwear line ahead of the Beijing race. Following the incident, dedicated “Joanna Wietrzyk x PUMA” landing pages and certain promotional materials on official Puma websites in mainland China and Hong Kong became inaccessible, with related search results redirecting to error pages. However, identical pages on Puma’s Polish and Czech websites remain active and list multiple items, indicating localised adjustments to regional access rather than a total global removal of the partnership. As of Friday, Puma has not issued any public statement or comment regarding the controversy. Promotional videos featuring Wietrzyk remain live on the Puma Training account, while her personal social media profile continues to list her sponsorship with the brand. “If she truly wanted to apologise, she wouldn’t have said ‘a win is a win’ at the start,” one user commented. “Apologising now is just because she got scared of the backlash.” Another Chinese user wrote: “It seems Hyrox still wants to do business in China, and we should also have our own race brands.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by PUMA Training (@pumatraining) However, others urged leniency, arguing that taking responsibility was still a step forward. “The apology doesn’t fix what happened, and yes, she handled it wrong. She acknowledged that,” one user wrote in defence of Wietrzyk. “You can say the apology didn’t come fast enough or that it feels fake, and sure, that can be true. But what can ALSO be true is that she took time to actually sit with what happened … We all have moments we don’t handle correctly. Growth is something we should WANT from people.” Wietrzyk’s statement follows an earlier apology from Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste, who confirmed coming rule book revisions after initial official explanations failed to appease the public. The governing body has since officially updated its global rule book to introduce a mandatory Did Not Finish (DNF) protocol across all race divisions, allowing race directors to pull athletes off the track if blood, vomit, urine or faeces pose health or contamination risks. On Wednesday, Hyrox China also emailed affected afternoon heat participants from the September 12 Beijing event, offering full ticket refunds. Originating in Germany, the event is an indoor fitness competition featuring eight 1km runs interspersed with eight functional strength exercises and is often described as the “marathon of fitness”.

title: Why the ICC is cracking down on ‘fake news’ as Duterte trial looms
description: Presiding Judge Joanna Korner warns parties to ‘avoid speculation’ and urges prosecutors to trim their witness list and evidence.
content: As Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes-against-humanity trial looms, an international tribunal faces the challenge of managing a sprawling prosecution case around the health of an 81-year-old former president of the Philippines, on top of shielding the proceedings from a highly charged media environment. Those pressures came into focus at an International Criminal Court (ICC) status conference on Wednesday, when Presiding Judge Joanna Korner urged prosecutors to trim their witness list and evidence ahead of the November 30 trial opening while delivering a blunt warning against lawyers using the media in ways that could fuel “fake news”. Legal experts say such warnings are not unusual in international criminal cases, but the breadth of Korner’s remarks reflects the particular difficulty facing the court as its proceedings are scrutinised, interpreted and sometimes distorted across the Philippines’ political and social media landscape. Duterte was arrested in the Philippines and surrendered to the ICC in The Hague in March 2025. In April this year, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber confirmed all three counts of crimes against humanity against him – involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed as part of his war on drugs between November 2011 and March 2019 – and committed him to trial. He appeared in person at the pretrial conference for the first time, looking thinner but walking unassisted and without a cane. News agencies said he waved to the audience and smiled slightly but did not speak. Blunt reminder During the case conference, Korner bluntly told defence and prosecution lawyers: “We see no reason why counsel should feel it necessary to make any comment to the media. The appropriate forum for counsel to raise matters is in the courtroom. Trials are not conducted by the court of public opinion, but by this court during the course of the proceedings.” She criticised in particular Duterte’s former counsel Nicholas Kaufman, who she said had made “wholly inappropriate” personal comments in at least three media interviews about decisions by the Pre-Trial Chamber and Appeals Chamber despite “a reminder to him to remember that he had a professional duty to be respectful and courteous to the chamber”. Korner noted that “this case has attracted, not surprisingly, a substantial amount of media interest in the Philippines in particular” – in mainstream and social media – “as to have provoked suppliers of what is undoubtedly fake news and obviously fake news”. “The first thing we wish to emphasise is the need for the media to report to the public accurately and fairly what is said in court and above all to avoid speculation,” Korner said. Two legal experts on the ICC told This Week in Asia that Korner’s reminder was not unique to Duterte’s case, although the former president’s rise to power and continuing political influence have been closely intertwined with social media. For British legal expert Tom Smith, who has been closely following Duterte’s case and other ICC proceedings, the judge’s warning “is not unprecedented”. “What is striking here is the breadth and bluntness of Judge Korner’s warning, and her explicit recognition of the Philippine disinformation environment,” said Smith, an associate professor in international relations at the University of Portsmouth and academic director of the Royal Air Force College. “This was not simply concern about an indiscreet lawyer. Kaufman’s interviews were feeding an enormous political and social media ecosystem in which incomplete or inaccurate claims about the ICC could be turned into supposed facts within hours.” Smith stressed that the court had not imposed a formal gag order on the media, but warned of “a danger for the ICC”. “If the lawyers stop speaking and the court does not communicate the proceedings clearly and quickly, the resulting information vacuum will be filled by the Duterte political network,” Smith said. “The ICC cannot defeat disinformation simply by asking everyone to remain silent. It must explain its own decisions far more effectively to Filipinos.” . The ICC had issued warnings in previous cases, said Ruben Carranza, a senior expert at the International Centre for Transitional Justice, which advises victims in cases before war crimes tribunals such as the ICC, including on reparations. Carranza recalled that in the case of former Kenyan president Uhuru Kenyatta, his indicted co-accused were warned by ICC judges “to not issue statements to the media or to the public that would tend to incite more political violence in Kenya”. ‘Enormous’ amount of evidence Korner also told prosecutors to “think long and hard” about trimming some 15,000 exhibits – including documents and videos – and their witness list covering 57 separate incidents. Lead prosecutor Julian Nicholls said prosecutors had already begun cutting both, after initially estimating they would need between 175 and 200 hours just to present witnesses. Duterte’s lead counsel Peter Haynes called the volume of evidence “enormous” and raised concerns about duplicate and incomplete records. Legal experts said such large volumes of material were not unusual in crimes against humanity cases, where prosecutors must prove not only individual killings but also a broader attack on civilians and the accused’s connection to it. Carranza indicated that Haynes was familiar with handling an enormous amount of evidence, as Haynes had handled the case of the convicted Congolese politician Jean-Pierre Bemba Gombo on appeal where he had to review “over 5,700 pages of evidence and [testimonies of] more than 70 witnesses”. Bemba was acquitted in 2018. “This case is also unusually documentary because Duterte was president and the Philippine police and government generated extensive records,” Smith said. “Even the prosecution acknowledged that there is more material than in other cases its lawyers have handled.” The defence, however, had “legitimate concerns [about] … duplicate records, individual pages being treated as separate exhibits and incomplete documents”, Smith added. “The raw number tells us very little about the strength of the case.
