Sixty-two thousand disclosed items are not the same as 62,000 pieces of compelling evidence.” Smith said the prosecution’s estimated courtroom hours also excluded cross-examination and procedural arguments, meaning the trial could run substantially longer once proceedings began. His “cautious” estimate was: “Two to four years from the opening of the trial is more realistic, particularly if health disputes and appeals continue.”

title: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case
description: Woman, 55, with no recent travel history reported as city’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case this year.
content: Doctors in Hong Kong have been urged to arrange blood tests for patients with symptoms of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history, after the city recorded its first local case of the mosquito-borne disease this year. The Centre for Health Protection issued a reminder to doctors on Thursday after a 55-year-old woman with no recent travel history was reported as Hong Kong’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case in 2026. “To facilitate early diagnosis and timely public health intervention, please consider arranging diagnostic testing for any patient presenting with symptoms suggestive of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history,” the centre wrote in a letter to doctors. Testing for the mosquito-borne disease is free of charge at the public health laboratory service under the centre. The latest infected woman, who lives on Li Tak Street in Tai Kok Tsui, started to develop symptoms such as fever, headaches and joint pain in her fingers and wrist last Monday, followed by a rash on her face and body. She sought medical care at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan on Wednesday and was admitted on the same day for treatment. She was in a stable condition. The woman did not travel during the incubation period, but recalled receiving mosquito bites at her residence and in areas around Cherry Street Park and Lok Kwan Street Park. The centre is still conducting an epidemiological investigation into the case. It urged people who had visited Li Tak Street or the two parks and exhibited symptoms such as fever, rash or joint pain to seek medical advice or contact the centre. The woman is Hong Kong’s third confirmed chikungunya fever case this year. The first two were imported cases reported in January. Last year, 82 chikungunya cases were recorded in Hong Kong, including 11 local cases. Mosquito activity, as measured by the government’s Gravidtrap Index, started to pick up in some areas in Hong Kong this month. In Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun, the initial index for September was 32.1 per cent, falling within the level three readings that indicated the distribution of Aedes albopictus mosquito was “extensive”. Aedes albopictus is a type of mosquito that can spread diseases such as dengue fever, chikungunya and the Zika virus. Aberdeen and Ap Lei Chau recorded an index of 26.9 per cent, also reaching the third-highest level in the distribution of mosquitoes under the four-tier system.

title: Top Chinese AI models make 10% of OpenAI, Anthropic revenue despite high valuations: report
description: ByteDance led the Chinese group in ARR at US$4 billion as of July, followed by Alibaba at US$2.4 billion in August, Rhodium Group found.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence models from seven major developers combined generate only about 10 per cent of the revenue reported for OpenAI and Anthropic, even as investor enthusiasm remains intense, according to US-based research firm Rhodium Group. The Chinese AI models earned an estimated US$10.7 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) from March to August, a fraction of the more than US$100 billion combined for OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Rhodium report published on Thursday. The report covers DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, MiniMax, Alibaba Group Holding, ByteDance and Kuaishou Technology, which runs the Kling AI video generator. ARR, a widely used measure for fast-growing companies, projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period. ByteDance led the Chinese group in ARR at US$4 billion as of July, followed by Alibaba at US$2.4 billion in August. By comparison, OpenAI reached US$40 billion in August and Anthropic was at US$65 billion in July. DeepSeek and Kling had the lowest ARR among the major Chinese AI companies tracked by Rhodium, at US$500 million each as of June and March, respectively. They were followed by MiniMax at US$800 million and Moonshot at US$1 billion, both as of August. Executives at Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, told investors on Wednesday that the company’s ARR had reached US$1.8 billion. The report stated that Z.ai’s ARR from its API business was US$1.6 billion in August. Despite the gap, investors have continued to pile into Chinese AI companies. Rhodium said their valuations remained “substantially lower” than those of OpenAI and Anthropic, and some looked far more expensive relative to revenue. Moonshot has been undergoing a funding round that could value it at roughly US$50 billion and has filed confidentially for a Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), while DeepSeek was also nearing the completion of a pre-IPO funding round valuing it at about 500 billion yuan (US$74 billion), the South China Morning Post reported previously. Meanwhile, Anthropic was expected to go public later this year with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, according to media reports. OpenAI had discussed a new funding round that would value it at about US$1.2 trillion, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday. “Valuations relative to revenue appear exorbitant for Moonshot and DeepSeek at present,” the Rhodium report said. Their estimated valuation-to-ARR multiples stood at 50 times and 163 times, respectively, compared with 34 times for OpenAI and 21 times for Anthropic. The numbers underscore a central challenge for China’s AI industry: how to turn AI models into sustainable businesses while spending heavily to keep pace at the technological frontier. Revenues for these Chinese AI companies have grown rapidly. Z.ai recorded a 400 per cent increase year on year in first-half revenue to 953.9 million yuan, while MiniMax’s revenue surged 283 per cent to US$116.6 million during the same period. Still, Z.ai and MiniMax, both listed in Hong Kong, could remain loss-making through 2030 due to spending required for computing power, Macquarie Group’s head of Asia internet and software research Ellie Jiang told the SCMP last week. Investors have so far been willing to tolerate those losses while AI adoption remains at an early stage, she said. The findings come as Chinese developers have rapidly narrowed the performance gap with their US counterparts while competing aggressively on price and embracing open-source and open-weight models. However, the open-weight strategy has made Chinese models harder to monetise, Rhodium said. Third-party cloud providers can deploy open-weight models and sell access without paying the original developer. “This could be changing, as Moonshot and Alibaba are pushing for revenue-sharing agreements with major users of their open-weight models,” Rhodium said. For example, Moonshot was in discussions with Microsoft, Amazon and Google, with its potential share of revenue reaching as much as 30 per cent, Reuters reported last month. Alibaba owns the SCMP.

title: North Korea’s nuclear tests awaken fault lines pointing to huge volcano at China border
description: Researchers find evidence of persistent earthquake activity that has also steadily intensified along two distinct paths.
content: North Korea’s underground nuclear tests have triggered a chain of seismic events, activating ancient fault lines that stretch towards one of the most dangerous volcanoes on Earth, about 100km (62 miles) away, according to a paper published by the journal Science. The joint Chinese and South Korean study, which appeared on Thursday, found that the five nuclear explosions conducted between 2013 and 2017 at the Punggye-ri test site beneath Mount Mantap fundamentally altered the region’s geological stability. Instead of fading quickly, the earthquake activity had not only persisted for nearly a decade, it had also steadily intensified, the researchers found. It is now propagating along two distinct parallel fault zones heading directly towards the China-North Korea border. At the end of those fault lines is Changbai Mountain, known on the Korean peninsula as Mount Paektu, a dormant but restless volcano that had its last major eruption in AD946 – one of the largest on the planet in the past 2,000 years. “Our paper concerns the delayed reactivation of pre-existing faults and the prolonged seismicity within several tens of kilometres of Mount Mantap,” corresponding author Kwang-hee Kim, from Pusan National University in South Korea, told the South China Morning Post. On whether the tests could disturb the massive volcano, Kim said that “the short answer is that an influence on the volcanic system of Mount Paektu is physically conceivable, but it has not been demonstrated by observations”. “Based on the published studies that I am aware of, there is currently no direct observational evidence that the … underground nuclear tests – or the subsequent earthquakes around Mount Mantap – changed volcanic activity at Mount Paektu or increased the likelihood of an eruption,” he said. Cold War-era research – by the United States at the Nevada National Security Site and the Soviet Union at its Semipalatinsk Test Site in Kazakhstan – indicates that explosion-induced seismic activity generally lasts from a few days to a few weeks, is mostly confined to the vicinity of the epicentre and decays rapidly. But North Korea’s nuclear test site is different. In 2017, the last and largest nuclear test explosion at the Mount Mantap site was estimated to have a yield of 100-250 kilotonnes of TNT – about seven to 17 times the power of the atomic bomb the US used to destroy Hiroshima in 1945. Before this nuclear test, the global seismic catalogue showed no earthquake records within a 50km radius of the area. Afterwards, seismic activity increased significantly. In May the following year, North Korea announced it was dismantling the Punggye-ri site. However, until May 2025, when the experimental data collection ended, both the earthquake occurrence rate and the seismic moment release rate – the total energy released by earthquakes over time – in the region continued to rise. The Chinese and South Korean researchers conducted high-precision relocation of the 955 recorded seismic sources and found that seismic events after 2017 delineated two nearly parallel structural zones extending north-northwest from the test site. Along these structural belts, seismic events form a coherent fault-scale structure rather than a diffuse earthquake swarm, suggesting that they were caused by the large-scale nuclear tests rather than occurring randomly, according to the paper. “Our observations indicate that repeated underground explosions modified the local stress field and progressively damaged the shallow crust, easing the delayed reactivation of pre-existing structural weaknesses rather than producing only short-lived, localised responses,” it said. “A 2016 study by Yonsei University in South Korea estimated the dynamic stresses that hypothetical large underground nuclear explosions could produce at the surface and within the magmatic system of Mount Paektu,” Kim said. “Their study demonstrated a possible physical mechanism but it did not observe an actual volcanic response to a nuclear test.” Asked about his research, Tae-Kyung Hong, author of the 2016 paper, said “the exact situation at Mount Paektu is still unclear”. “This is because there are many limitations in the investigation of the Mount Paektu area. The exact state of the volcanic magma chamber is still unclear,” he said in an email. According to ancient Japanese and Korean historical records, volcanic ash from the AD946 eruption of Changbai Mountain drifted as far as Nara, falling like heavy snow in November. Several centimetres of ash accumulated in northern Japan, while in the Korean capital Goryeo and its Japanese counterpart Kyoto, a continuous drum-like roar could be heard throughout the winter and even into the following spring. The eruption also produced a pyroclastic flow – a fast-moving, superheated avalanche of hot gas, ash, and rock fragments – of up to 100 metres (328 feet) thick that formed around the volcanic crater, eventually filling with rainwater to create what is now known as Heaven Lake at the mountain’s summit. Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: As I see it | Why mainland Chinese despise the British – but Hongkongers don’t
description: Whereas Hong Kong people experienced a milder form of colonialism, mainland Chinese were subjected to the extremes of Western imperialism.
content: What explains the vastly different attitudes of Hong Kong people and their mainland Chinese counterparts towards the United Kingdom? The first and easiest answer is, of course, Western freedom and democracy as allegedly practised – or at least taught – in colonial Hong Kong, as opposed to Chinese communist propaganda on the mainland. That is the most oft-cited claim, at least in Western media and public discourse, so I will not repeat it here. You can easily look up such arguments. Perhaps you have made them yourself. Rather, I would argue that the vastly different, even opposing, attitudes of these two socially and historically distinct but ethnically similar populations – in Hong Kong and mainland China – ultimately stem from different facets of Western or British colonialism and imperialism. Put simply, these facets were experienced differently over the past two centuries on either side of the border. I will also distinguish between the two isms below. Historians and political scientists have identified different types of modern colonialism, practised not only by different dominant societies and groups but by the same society in different times and places. There is extractive colonialism, which focuses on essentially stealing local natural resources, often through forced labour or slavery; plantation colonialism, closely associated with the transatlantic slave trade; settler colonialism, which has often been genocidal; surrogate or proxy colonialism; internal colonialism, which Western critics often associate, rightly or wrongly, with the Chinese takeover of Tibet and Xinjiang; and commercial colonialism, which arguably most closely resembles that practised by the British in Hong Kong. I will cite one more type: contemporary neocolonialism. It replaced traditional colonialism following global decolonisation by Western powers after the second world war. It is the ongoing economic, cultural and political dominance exercised by developed nations over sovereign developing countries, often through financial systems and trade policies rather than direct military rule – though military intervention has remained common for the American imperium to this day. Extractive colonialism has been among the most brutal, even genocidal, such as that practised in the Congo Free State under Belgium’s King Leopold II to extract ivory and rubber. It is what people call the resource curse. Commercial colonialism may be the least brutal and is more open-minded than most types of colonialism. Throughout history, free ports have tended to enjoy greater freedom of movement and employment, cultural exchange, and racial and religious tolerance, whether they were independent or governed by an external authority. The Romans may have invented the world’s first duty-free port on the Greek island of Delos in the second century BC. In the early modern era, ports under the Hanseatic League enjoyed tax privileges and varying degrees of political and legal autonomy. During the early 18th century, Trieste under Habsburg emperor Charles VI became a cosmopolitan melting pot of multi-ethnic merchants. And there was Gibraltar, declared a free port by the British a decade earlier. “One country, two systems” or “one empire, several systems” was often implicit in free-port arrangements. In the 19th century, Singapore and Hong Kong became British colonial trading outposts. Becoming a tax-free free-trade haven naturally entailed a very different experience for Hong Kong’s local population – entirely predictable from the experience of other free ports in prior centuries – than for their counterparts on the mainland. For mainland Chinese, Hong Kong and the British concessions in Tianjin, Hankou, Jiujiang, Zhenjiang, Guangzhou and Shanghai, along with “extraterritoriality” – whereby foreigners in designated Chinese territories were subject to the laws of their own countries rather than Chinese law – were the outcomes of outright Western imperialism. Whereas Hong Kong people experienced a milder form of Western colonialism, mainland Chinese were subjected – until the communist unification in 1949 – to the most extreme Western imperialism. Hong Kong’s freedoms ultimately depend on its status as a free port and financial centre It has sometimes been argued that after the 1997 handover of sovereignty, many Hongkongers, especially younger ones, took up identity politics that ultimately led to the anti-government riots – or democratic protests, depending on your political sympathies – of 2019. Many identified as Hongkongers rather than Chinese and believed they were fighting for universal franchise and resisting Chinese communist tyranny. Superficially, that sounds plausible, especially when it suits the Western narrative that enabled and justified foreign interference in Hong Kong. For explanations, though, I prefer studying history to appealing to political ideology. Historically, freedom is not a constant. It is not binary but a matter of degree. It ebbs and flows over time under any political regime, whether democratic or authoritarian. Just look at the United States under Donald Trump today. Hong Kong’s freedoms ultimately depend on its status as a free port and financial centre, not on democratic franchise or lack thereof.

title: Chinese paint cuts wall temperature by 25 degrees Celsius in summer test: report
description: The super-coating, which can help cool buildings, goes into mass production, making the leap from lab to industry.
content: China has begun mass production of a super-coating that can cut wall temperatures by 25 degrees Celsius in summer, according to the state-run Science and Technology Daily. The material, which has undergone six months of real-world testing at a petrochemical plant in the southern island province of Hainan, uses the principles of radiative cooling. It requires neither electricity nor cooling agents and its overall performance is reportedly the highest among known global competitors, according to the report published on September 7. The coating may also have potential for broader use in public infrastructure and homes. The need to reduce the effects of heat on buildings was apparent in Europe this summer when record heatwaves left many residents sweltering in homes without air conditioning. The coating has already transitioned from a laboratory innovation into mass production. Following dozens of trial batches, the research team has established manufacturing standards – spanning raw material grinding and formulation, right through to final product testing. The annual production capacity was 600,000 tonnes, the report noted. At a petrochemical refinery in Hainan, the scorching sun routinely bakes a row of 3,000 cubic metres (106,000 cubic feet) spherical liquefied gas tanks. Without immediate cooling, internal pressures would surge, posing severe safety risks. Previously, the facility relied on highly water-intensive sprinkler systems to cool the tanks. Now, clad in this super-coating, the tanks achieve a remarkable self-cooling effect with zero energy consumption. Composed of tailored inorganic fillers and polymer resins, the coating boasts the dual properties of high solar reflectance and strong thermal emittance. It reflects most solar radiation while emitting the tank’s accumulated heat outwards as infrared energy – without the need for power or refrigerants. The pioneering material was jointly developed by the state-owned China Construction Eco-Development Company, headquartered in Suzhou, and the Harbin Institute of Technology (HIT) in Heilongjiang province. According to an R&D director from the Suzhou-based venture, on a clear 30-degree (86 Fahrenheit) day, a treated tank’s surface temperature can drop by roughly 25 degrees, reducing internal temperatures by about 7 degrees. Achieving an equivalent cooling effect via traditional sprinklers would consume an estimated 35 tonnes of water daily per tank, by some estimates. “Even during extreme heatwaves, the cooling coating can maintain the tank’s interior at a safe temperature,” the report quoted Li Xiang, head of the R&D centre at China Construction Eco-Development, as saying. This is made possible by a specific infrared emission window. Scientists have long known that within the atmospheric infrared band of 8 to 13 micrometres, heat can penetrate the Earth’s atmosphere and dissipate directly into the freezing vacuum of space. However, thick applications are required for traditional radiative cooling materials to be both highly reflective and highly emissive. This bulkiness leads to a host of drawbacks, including higher costs and impaired heat dissipation efficiency. The research team overcame this hurdle by taking biomimetic inspiration from the microscopic structure of human skin wrinkles. By assigning various functional fillers to work collaboratively, they achieved both high reflection and emission within a much thinner layer. This design reportedly reduces the coating’s thickness from 500 micrometres to 100 micrometres – thinner than a standard sheet of A4 paper – while driving both solar reflectance and infrared emissivity up to 97 per cent. The coating is also exceptionally durable. During its 180-day on-site trial in Hainan, it endured 40,000 scrub tests without the paint film blistering or peeling. Based on this ageing rate, developers estimate its effective lifespan at up to 15 years. The project is an example of scientific research bridging the gap to industrial application. Wang Fuqiang of HIT developed the foundational coating during his academic research. However, after publishing his findings, the project was largely shelved – until Wang crossed paths with the state construction corporation, which had been hunting for exactly this type of advanced cooling solution. The two parties then joined forces to drive the technology towards commercialisation. Starting with laboratory samples, they spent several years on testing, optimisation and validation. Ultimately, they forged a manufacturing process capable of stable, large-scale production without compromising the material’s optical performance.

title: South Korea’s president rejects US request for Iran war support
description: President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a firm line against sending troops or assets to the Middle East, defying pressure from Washington.
content: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has drawn a clear line against any US request for Seoul to join the war against Iran, explicitly ruling out the dispatch of troops or military assets that could involve his country in the conflict. The stance comes amid mounting public opposition to any military deployment and growing pressure from Washington for Seoul to contribute to efforts to secure freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Lee’s government faces the difficult task of balancing its security alliance with the United States against the risks of becoming entangled in a distant conflict that could expose South Korean forces, citizens and commercial interests to Iranian retaliation. “There will be no dispatch of troops or military assets that would lead to involvement in a conflict. There will be no engagement or involvement in war. I can say that clearly,” Lee said during a televised press conference on Friday. “We’ve been sticking to this principle, and this principle won’t change.” His remarks represent the clearest signal yet of Seoul’s position regarding US President Donald Trump’s demands. Washington argues that countries benefiting from American operations in the Strait of Hormuz should contribute to the military effort. South Korea initially appeared to be weighing a role in the strategic waterway, sending a fact-finding team to the Middle East while balancing US pressure against Iranian threats of retaliation. A security briefing on the team’s findings – originally scheduled for Thursday – did not take place ahead of Lee’s press conference. Lee ruled out sending combat troops or placing them under foreign command, an issue of particular sensitivity as his administration seeks to regain wartime operational control over South Korean forces from the US military leadership by 2030. He acknowledged that distinguishing between defensive protection and military involvement could be challenging, but he said Seoul would not cross that line. “Let me make it clear once again: there will be no deployment for war,” Lee said. However, Lee said South Korea would maintain “the minimum level of activities” to protect its merchant ships, crude oil transport routes and citizens abroad, pointing to the deployment of the Cheonghae Unit – a naval anti-piracy task force operating in Middle Eastern waters. He said the government was considering ways to strengthen the unit’s defensive capabilities without escalating into direct military intervention. Trump’s pressure South Korea’s president noted that several other countries had deployed military assets near the Strait of Hormuz, with some committing to post-conflict recovery while others focused strictly on protecting commercial shipping and their citizens. Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Lee “firmly stated his stance against dispatching military assets or troops to the raging war”. But he noted that Seoul had promised to support post-war efforts to restore freedom of navigation through the strait, a route that accounted for roughly 70 per cent of South Korea’s crude oil imports before the war and a significant share of its natural gas and petrochemical feedstocks. “His statement on this issue will help put domestic controversies and concerns to rest, although Washington is unlikely to be happy with it,” Yang said. Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said Lee had made it clear that a deployment would only be for “post-conflict multinational stabilisation efforts”, such as mine clearing. The Trump administration has repeatedly singled out South Korea over its reluctance to help the US in its war against Iran. Speaking to reporters at the White House last month, Trump recounted a conversation in which Lee rejected his request for support. “I called him, I said, ‘Would you like to give us a little hand? We don’t need help with Iran. But if you would like, give us a hand with Iran.’ He said, ‘No thanks’,” Trump recalled. “And I said, ‘Wait a minute. We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbour. And you’re not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran?’ That’s strange.” South Korea hosts about 28,500 US troops. A delicate balancing act Aside from Hormuz, the two allies are currently navigating several other major economic, trade and security issues. These include the implementation of South Korea’s commitment to a US$350 billion investment package in the United States – which includes US$150 billion for shipbuilding – regulatory scrutiny over US-listed technology platforms such as Coupang and stalled progress on Seoul’s acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines. Against this backdrop, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun left for Washington on Thursday for talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Domestically, Lee is also under pressure. Jhee Byong-kuen, a political-science professor at Chosun University, said that the president was “putting his foot down” on the deployment issue to avoid further damaging his sliding approval ratings, which took a hit from recent real estate reforms. Hundreds of South Korean civic, religious and labour organisations have held rallies demanding that the government reject US demands. Opposition to military action has also surfaced within the ruling coalition. “Even US public opinion polls show that 66 per cent of Americans do not support this war. We could be driving our young people into a situation where their lives and safety are jeopardised,” said Woo Won-shik of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, a former National Assembly speaker. South Korea sent about 320,000 troops to the Vietnam war – the second-largest foreign force after the US – and sent 3,600 personnel from the non-combat Zaytun Division to northern Iraq in 2004 under liberal president Roh Moo-hyun. The Iraqi deployment sparked deep domestic political divisions and severely eroded Roh’s support base. Roh later reflected in his memoir, Destiny: “I authorised the deployment not because I believed it was right, but because it was an unavoidable choice … The Iraq troop deployment will go down in history as a wrong decision.” Professor Jhee said: “President Lee must have learned a lesson from former president Roh’s bitter experience”.

title: How Astrid Jorgensen’s Pub Choir shows anyone can sing. No auditions, no judgment
description: From a Brisbane pub to America’s Got Talent – Australian vocalist Astrid Jorgensen shares her story ahead of her Hong Kong show.
content: As someone who started playing the piano at age two and later trained in violin and singing, Astrid Jorgensen has always had a close relationship with music. Still, something felt off. “I’ve always been a really musical person looking for that outlet of music and creativity, but I didn’t really find it,” says the 36-year-old vocalist and conductor. Born in Hamilton, New Zealand, to a Singaporean-Chinese mother and a father of European descent, Jorgensen emigrated to Australia as a child, settling in Brisbane. Later, while studying for her arts degree at the University of Queensland, she specialised in aural musicianship and choral conducting in an attempt to make sense of why making music still “didn’t feel good”. In 2017, after spending a few years working as a high school music and vocal teacher and conducting community choirs, the then 27-year-old set up Pub Choir in a Brisbane pub. The project, for which entry to early sessions cost A$5, was born of a desire to flip the script on traditional live music events by inviting audience members – no matter how untrained, off-pitch or unmusical they may be – to perform. Jorgensen had finally found what she had been missing: the opportunity to make music in a way that felt good. Pub Choir steadily gained traction throughout the late 2010s and early 2020s in Australia, where Jorgensen says she now teaches “around 3,000 to 4,000 people” at every rehearsal. But make no mistake, Pub Choir is not about formal music education – which has long been synonymous with harsh discipline and perfectionism – in fact, it is in many ways the antithesis of it. No sheet music, no judgment Pub Choir is about reclaiming music as a joyful form of expression accessible to all. Accordingly, there is no sheet music and no judgment, and participants need no prior musical training. “I teach everything from zero for everyone,” Jorgensen says. “Every single person in the room, no matter your experience, has to learn something new. “You will have to sing and learn something, but it is the easiest music lesson in the world. At the end of it, we all get to enjoy what we made together.” Jorgensen also recommends Pub Choir to those with a musical background. “If you’re a good singer, you get to feel really clever at the show and help people around you,” she says with a laugh. “You become a leader. It’s good if you want to feel smug.” Taking Pub Choir global In June 2025, Jorgensen accepted an invitation to appear on the reality TV show America’s Got Talent. Rather than performing herself, she helped the thousands of audience members in the auditorium find sonic harmony with each other, splitting the crowd into three sections to sing Toto’s “Africa”. “It’s me saying ‘America’s got talent,’” Jorgensen says. Although Jorgensen did not win the contest – not that she intended to – the audition clip blew up online and brought Pub Choir global recognition and opportunities to tour internationally. In the year or so since that television appearance, Jorgensen has toured Australia and the United States extensively. In Asia, she has taken the act to Singapore and Tokyo, and will debut her show in Hong Kong, the birthplace of her maternal grandmother, on September 21. “I’m really curious because I’ve never been to Hong Kong,” Jorgensen says. “I don’t know how people feel there. The entire show is improvised; I don’t have a script at all and can’t ever predict what is going to happen. But I have great aspirations to explore more of my own roots, to meet more friends and to see if singing feels the same everywhere.” Jorgensen already knows that the audience’s willingness to participate in Pub Choir varies depending on gender and culture. “I can say with confidence that it’s always more women,” she says. “Women feel really comfortable going out with their girlfriends and being kind of vulnerable. But I did notice that at the Singapore and Tokyo shows last year, there was a bigger proportion of men than I would expect in, say, Australia. “I really love that maybe it’s not shameful to sing in Asian cultures. In Australia, the men would stand with their arms folded, and I have to really break down that stigma.” Living in the moment To add an element of surprise, Jorgensen does not announce beforehand which songs will feature in each of Pub Choir’s two-hour shows. There is also a strict no-phone policy. For those eager to document their experience, there is a team, including a professional videographer, who record the sessions from the stage with a smartphone, to be shared with audience members at the end. “It’s a better perspective,” Jorgensen says. “You don’t have to worry about taking a s*** phone video. We will do that for you so you can feel it. My favourite thing is probably that you have to look up and participate. “The instructions are on the screen; you have to think, and there’s no time for being on your phone and taking a video.” “For me, singing is magic – you can’t see anything, it’s just a feeling,” she says. “Only you know how to cast your spell. I can explain singing to somebody, but you have to figure out how it feels for yourself. You carry it with you all the time. It’s free. “I think it’s time we take away the other stuff that makes us feel so judged. Who cares? It’s not illegal to sing out of tune. “Music is a beautiful way to connect with other people. It’s not like I don’t want people to be excellent, but it doesn’t have to be everybody’s goal.” “Pub Choir: Just Think About It World Tour”, September 21, 8pm, at Portal, 1/F, The Burrow, 212 Choi Hung Road, San Po Kong, Hong Kong. For more information, visit ticketflap.com/pubchoir.

title: How China plans to ‘firmly rank at the global forefront’ with 25% of first-in-class drugs
description: New five-year plan aims to turn the sector into a pillar industry by 2030, driven by breakthroughs in technologies across critical fields.
content: China has set its sights on becoming a global biomedicine powerhouse by 2030, targeting key technological breakthroughs and at least a quarter of the world’s first-in-class drugs market under a new five-year plan for the sector. By the end of the decade, China would “firmly rank at the global forefront” in biopharmaceutical research and development and applications, with its “core competitiveness” and international influence making a significant leap, authorities said on Friday. The biomedical industry will emerge as a “pillar industry” for the nation, according to the pharmaceutical industry development plan published jointly by eight government agencies, including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA). The plan sets 10 measurable targets, including requiring large pharmaceutical enterprises to generate combined revenue of no less than 3.5 trillion yuan (US$522 billion), and for the country to produce at least 50 drug makers with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan each. Sinopharm, China’s largest drug distributor, generated 575 billion yuan last year. China’s innovative drugs market is expected to grow at an annual rate of more than 20 per cent by 2030, with at least five products achieving global annual sales of above US$1 billion, according to the plan. Chinese first-in-class innovative drugs would account for at least 25 per cent of the global total, authorities said. First-in-class drugs broadly refer to therapies using a completely new and unique mechanism to treat a condition, even though this is not a formal regulatory category. The targets are significantly more ambitious than the sector’s 14th five-year plan, released in December 2021, which did not have quantifiable indicators for innovative drugs and focused on increasing R&D investment. The push comes as China rapidly emerges as a biotech innovation force, highlighted by growing demand among Western pharmaceutical giants for Chinese-developed innovative therapies. The total value of out-licensing deals involving Chinese innovative drugs has reached US$120 billion so far this year, up 36 per cent from a year earlier, news agency Xinhua said earlier this week, citing NMPA data. The latest plan also calls for “systematic breakthroughs” in core technologies across “critical fields”. In a report published earlier this month, Xinhua Think Tank Research, a journal under the state-run news agency, identified cell and gene therapy, green manufacturing of chemical drugs, biomedical big data and synthetic biotechnology as among key areas. China should also expand the use of artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and supercomputing in pharmaceutical R&D, while deepening the application of frontier technologies like gene editing and brain-computer interfaces, according to the government agencies. The plan outlines several critical areas requiring breakthroughs, including artificial life system synthesis, organoids and organ-on-a-chip, as well as universal cell therapies.

title: Pride or practicality? Indonesia receives first aircraft carrier amid fears of upkeep cost
description: Jakarta has approved US$450 million for the aircraft carrier programme but some lawmakers warn the final bill could be higher.
content: Indonesia welcomed its first aircraft carrier on Friday, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelago nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities. The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short take-off and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, was welcomed with a military ceremony upon its arrival at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok seaport. Rome in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the Southeast Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship. “We intend to use the ship primarily for military operations other than war, although it can also be deployed for combat missions if necessary,” Indonesian Navy chief Admiral Muhammad Ali told reporters after the ceremony. He said the carrier could serve the navy for another 15 to 20 years and could accommodate 14 helicopters or more, depending on their size. Indonesia will become the second country in Southeast Asia with an aircraft carrier. Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump jets. Ali said the carrier would be commissioned into the navy next week as the KRI Sriwijaya, honouring the Srivijaya empire, a maritime kingdom based in Sumatra that became one of Southeast Asia’s dominant naval and trading powers between the seventh and 13th centuries. Previously, the navy said it would name the carrier KRI Gajah Mada. Defence development was one of the top priorities for President Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, and missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries. But the Garibaldi acquisition has raised questions about whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship. Indonesia’s Finance Ministry approved US$450 million in financing for the aircraft carrier programme in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of Parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16 trillion rupiah (US$900 million). Disaster response Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, uncrewed aircraft and maritime operations across its thousands of islands. Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of Southeast Asia with hazardous haze. “We will refurbish it and convert it into a carrier for helicopters and drones,” Prabowo said in a video briefing. “This will greatly help our disaster response.” He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters. Monsoon flooding, earthquakes and volcanic activity are common across Indonesia. Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster relief needs. The acquisition comes as Southeast Asia’s largest economy faces growing financial pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding an ambitious free nutritious meals programme and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenue and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects. “The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. He said policymakers should weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure. Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints. “The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.” Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers were not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters. “Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said. But he added that if Indonesia was seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions”.

title: 3 students killed in Philippine school shooting, including gunman
description: The attack at Banga National ‌High School ‌in South ‌Cotabato also left eight others injured.
content: A 16-year-old student shot dead at least two fellow students and then killed himself at a school in the southern Philippines on Friday, provincial officials said. Eight others were injured, with four in critical condition. All the victims – Grade 9 students at Banga National High School – were aged 14 to 17, said Albert Palencia, mayor of Banga town in South Cotabato, where the shooting took place. The incident follows two fatal gun incidents since June at schools in the Philippines, where school shootings were previously rare. “The ⁠suspect supposedly sat beside his friends and told them to go home ‘because after lunch, I will ‌be executing my plan’. His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker,” Palencia said. “After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit ‌10 students before killing himself,” Palencia added. He said in a radio interview that the suspect, the son of Department of Education officials, had taken the gun from a home safe. South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Tamayo said the suspect’s best friend told local officials that he was a member of a “true crime community”. “Our police force is investigating this and what this internet organisation entails,” Tamayo said. He said the alleged shooter had used a “very well-maintained” 9mm handgun and acted alone. Tamayo urged parents to ensure guns were kept out of reach of minors. “We need to be responsible in storing firearms. Gun ‌owners, in particular, must make ‌sure that minors do not have access to them,” he said. “We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address.” In a video posted to social media, a man can be seen carrying what appears to be a wounded child from the school, rushing him into the sidecar of a waiting motorbike. The Department of Education expressed deep concern about the incident and offered to provide psychological first aid and mental health support to those affected. “Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel,” it said in a statement, calling on the public to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information. Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow at Verve Research, said the latest shooting appeared to have similarities with the attacks that occurred in August and June. “They all seem to be a part of some online community in one way or another. They have friends, but they’re online and nobody knows who they’re talking to or who’s goading them,” Munira said. Based on screenshots from the Cotabato suspect’s purported social media accounts, she said he displayed indications of premeditated behaviour, including “peacocking” or showing off references to violence before the attacks. A student in Zamboanga also expressed these tendencies. She added that personal grievances matter more than ideology in assessing school attackers’ risk profiles. Last month, a student live-streamed himself shooting and killing ⁠another student in ⁠a classroom in Zamboanga in the country’s south before taking his own life. In June, at least three students ‌were killed and about 20 others injured in an attack at a public high school in Tacloban, where two classmates opened ‌fire on ‌campus. The Philippines has relatively strict gun ownership regulations, including background checks and psychological evaluation requirements, although ‌illegal firearms remain in circulation. Friday’s shooting also follows a high-profile incident in Thailand in August, ⁠where a student went on a shooting rampage at a school on the outskirts of the ⁠capital, Bangkok. Additional reporting by Sam Beltran, Agence France-Presse

title: From US Fed rates to China’s global export share: 4 figures shaping markets
description: The US central bank raised rates for first time since 2023, Hong Kong followed and Goldman Sachs projects a sharp rise in Chinese firms’ global export share.
content: The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point this week, followed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Bank of Japan, while the 10-year US Treasury yield fell back below 5 per cent. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. Fed raises interest rates for first time since 2023 The US Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously on Thursday to raise rates by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75 to 4.00 per cent. This marked the central bank’s first rate increase in three years, as Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh pledged to tackle inflation that had been “too high” for “too long”. 10-year US Treasury yield drops below 5 per cent Following the Fed’s announcement, the US 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 4.94 per cent on Friday, retreating below the crucial psychological threshold of 5 per cent reached earlier in the week for the first time since 2023. Hong Kong ranks as No. 3 global financial centre The Hong Kong Monetary Authority raised the city’s base rate to 4.25 per cent in response to the Fed’s move, even as the city’s three note-issuing banks – HSBC, Bank of China (Hong Kong) and Standard Chartered – kept their prime lending rates unchanged. The city also retained its status as Asia’s top financial hub for a fourth consecutive edition of the Global Financial Centres Index, which evaluates five main categories: business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial sector development and market reputation. Hong Kong scored 756 this year, just one point behind London on 757, while New York topped the index with 761. Singapore ranked one spot below Hong Kong with 755. China’s global export share projected to reach 31 per cent by 2035 The average market share held by Chinese companies in export markets is projected to surge from 18 per cent this year to 31 per cent by 2035, with their revenue growing 3.6-fold by then, according to a new Goldman Sachs report. The biggest growth potential lies with what the investment bank called “latecomers” – including companies in sectors such as robotaxis, e-commerce and surgical robots – while “early achievers” such as carmakers would face more contested paths.

title: Chip foundries better insulated in an AI slowdown than Asia-Pacific tech peers, S&P says
description: Contract chipmakers like TSMC are well protected against spending contractions by hyperscalers, based on stress tests by the ratings agency.
content: As market fears mount over waning Big Tech spending and calls to slow down frontier artificial intelligence development, Asia-Pacific semiconductor foundries are better positioned to withstand a potential downturn in AI investment than other tech hardware firms in the region, according to S&P Global Ratings. In a report published on Thursday, the rating agency said it had stress tested four key Asia-Pacific sectors – foundries, memory manufacturers, cooling component suppliers and original design manufacturers that assemble servers – against two downside scenarios for the AI boom. The first possibility involved a drop in capital expenditure from major hyperscalers like Amazon and Microsoft. The second stemmed from bottlenecks that could delay AI projects, such as power grid constraints and land scarcity. Under both scenarios, contract chipmakers, which manufacture chips for semiconductor designers such as Nvidia, were expected to prove the most resilient. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest foundry, was highlighted as particularly well insulated due to its dominant lead in advanced manufacturing. The findings underscore how top regional foundries were uniquely positioned to shrug off temporary spending lulls. Behind TSMC and second-ranked Samsung Electronics, mainland Chinese players hold significant market share. Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC) and Hua Hong Group ranked third and sixth globally by revenue in the second quarter this year, according to research firm TrendForce. By contrast, memory chipmakers such as Samsung and SK Hynix could face more pronounced earnings declines if investment appetite peaked early, the report noted. “Rated Asia-Pacific tech-hardware issuers maintain sufficient buffers against delays in AI spending plans,” said S&P analyst Clifford Kurz, though he cautioned that a fundamental shift in long-term AI demand could still pose credit risks. The report comes amid heightened nervousness on Wall Street and other markets, where an AI-driven stock rally is facing fresh scrutiny. Prominent US industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have recently urged the sector to temper its breakneck pace of advancement to establish safety guardrails. While some analysts believe clearer rules would be beneficial for the industry in the long run, the proposed pause has unnerved some investors accustomed to aggressive buildouts. Capital expenditure by China’s major tech companies was set to more than double to around US$140 billion this year – up from US$65 billion in 2025 – and reach US$165 billion by 2027, according to a Moody’s report earlier this month. Meanwhile, five major US hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Oracle – alongside AI cloud provider CoreWeave, were projected to spend more than US$785 billion this year alone, approaching US$1 trillion by 2027. S&P maintained its base-case forecast that demand across the AI value chain would remain strong over the next two years. In a separate report released on Thursday, S&P noted that mainland China’s AI buildout would disproportionately enrich a handful of top-tier cities. Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou were set to reap the biggest gains due to their dense pools of research talent, established engineering bases and deep capital reserves, according to the report. “Benefits will reach the places best equipped to host firms building out related infrastructure and services. The rest of the country will have to hope and wait for second-order effects,” the agency wrote. Shanghai’s dominant position is already evident. Official data showed that the city’s three frontier industries – integrated circuits, biopharmaceuticals and AI – had surpassed 2 trillion yuan (US$298.5 billion), with its chip sector alone accounting for roughly a third of China’s national total.

title: Chinese star Zheng Qinwen gets massive show of sponsor support as she surges up rankings
description: Despite a loss of form, the Olympic champion’s total earnings had risen this year to US$22.6m, placing her seventh among tennis players.
content: Zheng Qinwen’s sponsors have proved even more excited than her long-awaiting fans, kicking off a new round of commercial campaigns to capitalise on her 69-spot surge to world No 52 after her comeback run at the US Open. Following her amazing comeback victories at the year’s final grand slam event in New York, where she lost only to eventual champion Elena Rybakina in the quarter-finals, her sponsors posted celebratory campaigns, competing to highlight their early faith in her resilience. Among them, Turkish Airlines’ official Chinese account congratulated her, writing: “It is easier to fly against the wind. Next stop, fly higher, Queen Wen!” Nike’s Chinese campaign read: “You believed in yourself back when you had no world ranking. How could current ups and downs shake you now?” SAIC Audi wrote: “Is a 12 per cent win probability enough? For the brave, it is enough.” Meanwhile, tea chain Chagee featured the slogan: “Point by point, finding back your familiar self.” In Forbes’ 2025 list of the world’s highest-paid female athletes, Zheng ranked fifth with about US$21 million, trailing Eileen Gu, who placed fourth with around US$23 million in off-court earnings, bringing both Chinese athletes to a similar commercial tier. A separate ranking of the highest-paid tennis players released by the publication in late August showed Zheng’s total earnings over the preceding 12 months had risen to US$22.6 million, ranking seventh globally. The magazine estimated her 2026 prize money at around US$600,000, while endorsements and off-court income had reached US$22 million, accounting for more than 97 per cent of her total income. This meant that for every US$100 earned, more than US$97 came from brand sponsorships and less than US$3 came from tournament play. Fuelled by a broad portfolio of global and domestic brands, her commercial partnerships continued to expand despite injuries affecting her world ranking. In October 2025, Chagee upgraded her from global health ambassador to its first global brand ambassador. In January, Alibaba’s AI platform Qwen named her a global brand ambassador, with Turkish Airlines doing the same in February. In May, Lancôme promoted her from skincare ambassador to global skincare spokesperson. Currently holding one of the most diversified endorsement portfolios in women’s tennis, Zheng represents more than 10 brands across cosmetics, sportswear, luxury accessories, consumer electronics, automotive, FMCG, technology and finance. Besides Audi, Chagee, Nike, Qwen and Turkish Airlines, her sponsorship roster also includes Alipay, Beats by Dre, Dior, Gatorade, L’Oréal, Rolex, Wilson and Yili Group, positioning her as a key figure in the WTA’s expansion into Asian markets. “Zheng Qinwen has signed away virtually everything from head to toe,” a user on Chinese social media observed, highlighting a level of commercial scale that explains why her off-court earnings have remained consistently high. Rather than focusing solely on her reaching the last eight, her sponsor brands aligned around her recovery from injury, ranking drop and gritty comeback trajectory. According to a report by National Business Daily, an industry insider noted that an athlete’s persona often outlasts match outcomes. “I remember Nadal rushing over to comfort a ball girl who got hit by a ball, but I no longer remember what match that was or what the score was,” the insider said. “In fact, the persona an athlete leaves behind during a match is remembered far more easily than victory or defeat.” Zheng’s commercial footprint erupted in 2024. In January that year, she finished as runner-up in the Australian Open women’s singles, marking her best grand slam result and the finest performance by a Chinese player since Li Na. Seven months later, she captured the women’s singles gold medal at the Paris Olympics, becoming China’s first Olympic singles champion in tennis and transforming her from a promising athlete into a national icon. Zheng is represented by sports agency IMG, which also manages Chinese stars including Eileen Gu, Su Yiming and Li Na, under parent company Endeavor, the world’s largest talent agency.

title: Senior HSBC bankers face double blow as school-fee subsidy cut adds to job risks: sources
description: HSBC axes education benefits worth up to HK$300,000 as integration with Hang Seng Bank threatens jobs – but investors stay upbeat.
content: Senior bankers at HSBC are facing a double blow of losing a key employment benefit while also confronting potential job losses as the lender carries out a range of measures to cut costs and achieve fair treatment for all staff, according to sources. HSBC, the biggest lender in Hong Kong, will scrap an education subsidy programme for all newly hired or newly promoted senior executives from Friday, according to an internal memo seen by the South China Morning Post. Employees who were already in the bank’s top three grades as of Thursday, including managing directors and department heads, will continue to enjoy the benefit, which provides subsidies of up to HK$300,000 (US$38,240) for secondary school fees and HK$220,000 for primary school fees per year. “It is a double blow to management like me as we are seeing more benefit cuts while also being among those most likely to lose our jobs in the current restructuring and integration of back-office teams between HSBC and Hang Seng Bank,” a source said. HSBC, which completed a US$14 ­billion buyout of shares it had not yet owned from subsidiary Hang Seng Bank in January, has recently begun integrating seven back-office functions across the two lenders. The functions are corporate communications, company secretaries, compliance, information technology, internal audit, finance and operations. “After the integration, six of the seven combined units are headed by Hang Seng Bank executives and only one by HSBC,” the source said. “It is really scary because I do not know if I will still have a job tomorrow.” Another HSBC source said the moves were aimed at reducing costs while ensuring fair treatment for global staff. “It should be noted that neither Hang Seng Bank nor HSBC’s operations in other markets offer education benefits, with Hong Kong being the exception. The bank has discussed cutting these benefits for several years,” the source said. “The arrangement allowing Hang Seng Bank executives to lead most of the combined back-office functions also shows a fair approach that gives opportunities to both HSBC and Hang Seng Bank.” While some bankers may be concerned about the changes, shareholders appear to have taken a different view. HSBC’s strong share-price performance suggests investors have broadly supported CEO Georges Elhedery’s strategy since early last year of streamlining global operations to reduce costs by US$1.5 billion. That target was achieved in the middle of 2026, six months ahead of schedule. “It is definitely a good move for HSBC to integrate with Hang Seng Bank to reduce excess staffing, unnecessary spending and costly benefits because that could help profitability. There is no point maintaining two separate large teams to do the same job,” said Charles Cheng Kai-min, who has been an HSBC shareholder for more than 20 years. “I am very happy with HSBC’s share-price performance because the value of my holdings has risen more than 50 per cent over the past year – thanks to the bank’s cost-cutting measures.” HSBC shares rose 1.1 per cent to close at HK$161.60 on Friday. The stock has risen around 52 per cent over the past year, outperforming the Hang Seng Index, which dropped 8 per cent during the same period. HSBC co-CEOs for Asia and the Middle East, David Liao Yi-chien and Surendra Rosha said in Thursday’s internal memo that the lender would continue to invest in talent. “We’re investing in our people, providing competitive, fair and inclusive benefits that reward high performance while supporting our long-term growth ambitions,” the co-CEOs said. “We want to be intentional about how we allocate resources and will invest in benefits and support that are accessible to a wide range of colleagues.” An HSBC spokesman said on Friday that the bank remained focused on “rewarding our employees fairly and competitively”. He added: “HSBC employees in Hong Kong have access to a broad and market-competitive total rewards package.”

title: Hong Kong youth discuss 2026 policy address: job scheme, university town
description: Youth support new 30,000-spot career programme and innovative Northern Metropolis campuses, but some unsure if they can access these benefits.
content:
Background: Alongside the last policy address of his term, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan, which is meant to align the city more closely with the national development blueprint.
Big number: 30,000 full-time jobs, internships and training positions will be available for the youth over the next two years
Think about it: What are the benefits and potential consequences of the government’s job scheme for youth? What areas of study will benefit most from the university towns in the Northern Metropolis? To what extent do you think this is positive for Hong Kong’s development?
Hong Kong secondary students have mostly welcomed new government initiatives targeted at easing their transition into the job market, highlighting a flagship 30,000-place internship scheme and university town development discussed in the city’s latest policy address.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the measures on Wednesday alongside the city’s first five-year strategic blueprint aimed at boosting global competitiveness.
Thirteen-year-old Megan Lam Hoi-ching said she was “impressed” by the blueprint and how it could alleviate some of the stress the city’s youth face.
“I worry a lot about AI taking over the job market after I graduate, so this sounds like a great plan to solve it. There’s a lot of money being put into helping young people and building new stuff,” said the Form Two student at Heep Yunn School.
“But some of it sounds like it will take forever to happen – like the [Northern Metropolis] university towns won’t be done until I’m basically a grown-up with a job. So I’m impressed by the big ideas, but I’ll believe the cool parts when I actually see them.”
For the government’s two-year “30,000 Youth Employment and Internship Programme”, which will begin in 2027, 16-year-old Cherish Chiu Cheuk-wing said it would help youth overcome early career barriers.
“Young people with limited or no work experience face [a] well-documented ‘catch-22’ – employers demanding experience, but no one will give them the first opportunity,” noted the Form Five student from Leung Shek Chee College.
“A government-backed scheme with business-sector partnership can break that cycle.”
The programme offers 10,000 full-time roles starting in 2027, with public subsidies covering up to HK$6,000 or one-third of monthly salaries for six months. This comes alongside expanded spots under the STEM Internship Scheme, the Home and Youth Affairs Bureau Youth Start-up Internship Programme and a Construction Industry Council training scheme.
In total, these programmes will provide at least 30,000 placements to help youth build their careers.
While Megan appreciated how this could help young people get their first jobs, she worried whether this short-term placement would translate into permanent roles.
“What if some companies just use young people for six months and then throw them away?” she asked.
“I think the government could enforce a new policy to ask the companies to at least keep a few of their top young employees employed by this programme.”
Year 13 student Huang Ziyan, from Harrow International School, also cautioned about the high demand for spots.
“One thing I might be aware of, though, is how this could end up being very, very popular and competitive,” the 17-year-old said.
Beyond youth employment subsidies, the government also plans to expand tertiary education infrastructure through three dedicated university towns in the Northern Metropolis: Hung Shui Kiu, San Tin and Ta Kwu Ling.
Lee said the Hung Shui Kiu site would be prioritised, with invitations to construct campuses opening this year and land allocations expected by the 2027-28 academic year.
The university towns will operate under a “one town, five elements” framework, integrating education, technology, industry, talent and urban living across 1,000 hectares, including 300 hectares earmarked specifically for campuses.
Cherish pointed out that physically linking higher education with commercial sectors represented a crucial shift in the city.
“Traditional university campuses [in Hong Kong] are often isolated from industry and from the communities around them,” Cherish said.
“The framework acknowledges that universities do not exist in a vacuum – they are anchors for regional economies ... Concentrating universities, technology areas, industry areas and living communities in one place can generate the kind of innovation ecosystem seen in Cambridge, Boston or Shenzhen.”
While Megan noted that the university towns would take years to build, she appreciated that it could help students get internships and jobs near their schools.
“It sounds like a good idea to put universities, tech companies and housing all in one place instead of having them scattered everywhere. That way, students don’t have to travel super far, and they can maybe get jobs nearby,” she said.
In addition to other requirements, institutions in the university towns will have to partner with renowned mainland Chinese and overseas institutions.
Ziyan noted that this could widen options for students seeking global exposure without moving overseas.
“If the plan to bring in many different universities and international institutions can truly be achieved, it would be amazing for students who want a global education and international exposure but cannot afford [it] or for other reasons cannot go abroad,” she said.
To further support higher education development, the government will allocate an additional HK$20 million per academic year for knowledge transfer starting in 2027-28 while increasing the annual quota for the Belt and Road Scholarship from 150 to 200 places.
These targeted youth initiatives form part of a macro-level strategy laid out by the chief executive.
By publishing a five-year plan alongside his annual policy address, Lee aligned Hong Kong’s economic trajectory directly with mainland China’s 15th five-year plan. Framing the city’s future around 22 major key performance indicators, Hong Kong’s plan signals an attempt to transition Hong Kong from short-term management to medium-term integration into the Greater Bay Area.

title: Could Chinese explorers have settled New Zealand before the Maori?
description: Mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, but researchers say acknowledging lesser-known history could alter national identity.
content: For generations, the narrative of New Zealand’s human settlement has held that Polynesian voyagers – the ancestors of the Maori – arrived and settled the islands in the 13th century, followed by European explorers in the 17th century. This timeline underpins New Zealand’s history and its political model. The Treaty of Waitangi, signed in 1840 between the British Crown and about 540 Maori chiefs, served as New Zealand’s founding document, paving the way for Britain to claim sovereignty and incorporate the country into the British Empire. Outside the halls of universities and government institutions, two independent researchers are on a quest to discover pre-Maori Chinese presence in New Zealand. Citing underwater shipwrecks, carbon-dated structures and anomalous artefacts as evidence, scholar and author Sheng-Wei Wang has proposed a theory that a Chinese “treasure ship” fleet met its end there around 1435-1436 owing to the impact of a meteorite. Wang also contends that Chinese mining and trading activities date back to 190BC, challenging the accepted 13th-century Maori settlement timeline and suggesting that these pre-European contacts have been overlooked or suppressed. While mainstream academics and Maori groups voice scepticism, Wang and others argue that acknowledging this lesser-known history could reshape New Zealand’s national identity and improve its relations with China. Speaking this month at the Commonwealth of World Chinatowns conference in Penang, Malaysia, Wang raised the question of whether fleet leader Zheng He died in New Zealand during his final voyage. Zheng was a Chinese admiral who led seven massive naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean during the early Ming dynasty. While Zheng is widely believed to have died in 1433 in Calicut, or today’s Kozhikode, a coastal city in southern India, after setting sail in 1431, his exact fate was still unverified, Wang said. “We know that Zheng disappeared during the seventh voyage. There were different kinds of proposals about what happened to him. “Could he [have died] while he visited the Americas? Or in India near Calicut – he was ill, and because the weather was so hot that his body couldn’t be brought back to China? Or just like in this case that he died because of the unexpected tragic event?” Wang said a meteorite was believed to have crashed in the Tasman Sea, southwest of New Zealand. “My estimate of the date is around 1435 or 1436, when a squadron of the Ming Treasure Fleet reached New Zealand after they explored the Americas during their seventh voyage to the Indian Ocean and beyond,” she said, adding that the impact carbonised all the ships in the harbour. “One of the possibilities is that the whole fleet disappeared there, which may have included Zheng because there is no satisfactory evidence to show where or when he died,” she said. “There was no convincing record, so I am proposing that.” Wang’s research draws on field surveys by the late independent British surveyor T.C. Bell, who used magnetic anomaly surveys to detect underwater and buried structures throughout New Zealand. The method measures local variations in the Earth’s magnetic field to locate metal objects. “When Bell went to New Zealand for surveys in 2003, 2006 and 2017 … he was able to detect 78 shipwrecks of various dimensions,” she said. “Twenty-four of them are of the super-junk or treasure-ship size. They are around over 100 metres (328 feet) in length, about 40-something [metres] in width, and all these large ships are characterised by their unique double-fluke anchors.” The specialised Chinese anchor consisted of a central wooden bar connected to two huge rocks, Wang said, and was designed to cut into the sea floor to secure the ship in place. She proposed a route for Zheng’s last voyage that “went to America for several months and came back by rounding the southern part of South America, Cape Horn. They followed the Humboldt Current, then the [South] Equatorial Current and they could have gone to Asia”. “Naturally they would have been brought westward to New Zealand.” Wang described the seventh fleet as on its way back to China. Carbon dating results indicated a Chinese presence in New Zealand predated the seventh Ming voyage, extending from as early as 190BC through 1600, Wang said. She pointed to a “scrub-covered, small-moated Chinese fort platform” at Governors Bay, South Island, which was carbon-dated to 190BC, and the years 800 and 1600. “In my opinion, in Bell’s opinion, [New Zealand] became the headquarters of Chinese business trading ships.” “There were already many Chinese who had lived there for thousands of years,” Wang said, explaining they were attracted by “coal mining and other metallic ores in New Zealand”, including “very rich ores” of gold and silver. She also noted the presence of canals, smelter sites and barrack blocks that she believed bore Chinese characteristics. “It is clear that a Chinese presence in New Zealand started at least from 190BC and lasted until the tragic [meteorite] event took place,” she said. “The next wave of Chinese immigration started in the 19th century.” Wang also cited stone carvings as possible evidence, with a massive gateway rock on the North Island bearing an elephant petroglyph and linear script. “New Zealand does not have native elephants, and the Maori had no history of carving elephants either,” she said. “Even the Europeans did not do much elephant carving. This is very interesting. But the Chinese knew elephants.” However, according to Li Yuelin, president of the Seven Seas Institute of Chinese Calligraphy in Illinois, the workmanship on the elephant rock carving “seems quite primitive and its origin remains uncertain”. Li, who is also a physicist at the Argonne National Laboratory near Chicago, said that by the period Wang identified, from 200BC to 1000AD, the Chinese writing system had already evolved well beyond the petroglyph stage into a mature script, and the carved symbol did not match early oracle bone forms for “elephant”. “Regarding the carving itself, the tool marks and overall technique seem relatively rudimentary and do not exhibit features typically associated with Chinese stone inscriptions from the period in question,” he said. As for a piece of rock bearing a symbol resembling the Chinese character for mountain, found by Bell’s son Dave in the Moeraki cliffs in the South Island, Li said the motif could not “be confidently associated with the Chinese character”. A 3D scan showed a raised form where the surrounding material was removed so that the motif stood above the surface, he added, rather than a traditional intaglio method typically preferred in Chinese stone inscriptions in which the strokes were cut below the surrounding rock for efficiency. “Even if we consider the form as a raised, positive-relief character, the background around such carvings is usually cut back to a fairly even depth to make the strokes stand out clearly,” Li said. “That kind of consistency is not present here; the surrounding relief is irregular and lacks the controlled excavation one would expect from a deliberate raised-relief inscription.” Nevertheless, Wang maintained that “the hidden history of New Zealand has to be uncovered so that the government will have to implement more balanced policies for a lasting peace and future”, especially regarding the country’s relations with and protection of the rights of the indigenous Maori people. In that vein, Robert Jones, director of the forthcoming New Zealand Museum of Anomalous Antiquities, said a growing collection of enigmatic artefacts discovered across New Zealand could indicate pre-European Chinese contact largely overlooked by mainstream academia. “While we can explain away some evidence and anomalies in isolation, when you count the sheer quantity of anomalies, it begs the question: when does it become a pattern?” Jones asked at the conference in Penang. He and his team presented replicas of several artefacts, including the Korotangi, a dark green serpentine stone bird discovered in 1878. The bird of sorrow is a sacred artefact believed to have been brought to New Zealand on the Maori Tainui canoe. “The carving displays extremely fine feathering detail and shaping, which is consistent with the kinds of things that could only be produced by metal tools, not the traditional stone tools that were used by the Polynesians,” Jones said, adding that the stone likely originated from Indonesia or China. Jones also singled out the Tamil Bell, a bronze ship’s bell discovered in about 1841 by a missionary in a Maori village where it was used as a pot for cooking potatoes. The bell has an inscription in Tamil, a language mainly spoken in southern India, Sri Lanka and Singapore.
