Jones raised a theory that the artefact could be linked to the treasure fleets of the Ming dynasty under Zheng. “If the 15th-century dating is true, the bell would tie neatly into what researcher Gavin Menzies proposed in his book 1421: The Year China Discovered the World, in which he theorised that a Tamil ship could have appeared with one of Zheng He’s treasure fleets for protection from pirates or pursuing trade opportunities,” he said. “Subsequently, it was marooned, with its cargo later dispersed and all looted by local Maori.” Jones further cited the discovery of porcelain crates in Northland, a region in the North Island, that he said matched the style of blue-and-white porcelain produced during the Ming dynasty Yongle Emperor period (1402–1424), while Zheng’s voyages were known to carry Chinese porcelain for trade. “[The discoverer’s] description of translucent plates through which the sunlight could visibly pass matches the type of eggshell porcelain that was first introduced during the Yongle period,” he said. Jones acknowledged that such theories faced opposition, including from indigenous Maori who have secured settlements from the New Zealand government based on their status as the country’s first inhabitants. “We can be charitable and remove the possibility of any cover-up of these Chinese connections,” he said. “But we can also infer that public officials in New Zealand would be scared to pursue lines of inquiry that could potentially undermine the Eurocentric accounts of our history.” “The significance of recognising these connections is not simply historical but existential, especially as we enter into a new multifaceted cold war with China, which I might add, is currently New Zealand’s largest trading partner.” “We are still almost completely alone in searching for the true provenance of these artefacts,” he added. “The Chinese connections, however, are certainly not so easily dismissible as others have since tried to claim.” For Jones, uncovering this hidden past is both culturally and geopolitically vital. He argued that New Zealand’s traditional Eurocentric perspective had historically entangled the country in “foreign imperialist wars that had nothing to do with us”. “The reality is New Zealand is a nation in the South Pacific, and China is a major power in the Pacific, and as our main trading partner and having genuine historical ties, we are much closer to China than we are to [Britain],” he said. “If New Zealanders could appreciate that China is a part of our history, and that the Chinese are not some ‘other’ out there who are foreign or alien … I think Kiwis would actually appreciate our museum initiative and uncover greater clarity in their sense of self.” While stating that he and his team were not credentialled academics, Jones said they were committed to rigorous inquiry. “It is usually outsiders who have unique perspectives who contribute very interesting things. We do not have any qualifications. We are just curious, but we try to follow the scientific process and proper procedures of archaeological excavations as closely as possible.” Mainstream historians remain sceptical of pre-Maori theories, but Jones described his museum as seeking to fill a void for discussion and research into New Zealand’s early history. “We do think there is a genuine interest among young people,” he said. “There is this hesitancy because people know that this is a very sensitive thing.” “Hopefully, once the institution is up and running, there will be that legitimacy and that authority that people will be able to defer to and have confidence that they can research this without being completely destroyed economically, socially or politically.”

title: Ancient recipe for Cola-like drink discovered in Tuscany’s monastery
description: A 19th century tonic featuring coca leaves and kola nuts predates modern cola beverages.
content:
A 19th century recipe recently found in the pharmacy of Saint Mark’s Monastery in Florence describes a drink that may be a precursor to modern cola beverages, according to monks in the Italian city.
Dominican friar Manuel Russo explained that the recipe is written on a faded advertisement for a “fortifying wine elixir” made from coca leaves and kola nuts.
The drink is described as a tonic to relieve exhaustion, headaches and weakness.
It was one of the pharmacy’s bestselling products at the time, Russo said.
According to the records, missionaries brought coca leaves and kola nuts from South America to Tuscany.
In 1886, US pharmacist John Stith Pemberton created Pemberton’s French Wine Coca. It was a tonic containing coca leaves and kola nuts.
When alcohol was banned for some time, Pemberton replaced the alcohol with water and sugar syrup. This eventually became Coca-Cola.
The exact recipe for Coca-Cola is a secret. According to Coca-Cola, Pemberton never wrote down the original formula.
It was first committed to paper in 1919 and is now stored in a secure vault.
The newly discovered Tuscan recipe is several decades older than Pemberton’s invention. But Russo stressed there is no evidence of any direct connection between the monastery’s drink and the later drink.
Saint Mark’s Monastery is famous for its early Renaissance frescoes by Fra Angelico.
Its pharmacy, founded in 1436, is one of the oldest in Florence. For centuries, Dominican monks supplied people with medicinal herbs, essences and scented waters. The pharmacy no longer operates as it did originally.
A 330ml can of cola contains 35.3 grams of added sugar, or about eight teaspoons. This is more than the World Health Organization’s recommended limit of six teaspoons per day. Drinking too much Coca-Cola and other sugary sodas can harm your health (see graphic).
If you want to drink less soda, try these simple tips:
When you fill your cup with ice, there is less room for soda. This means you drink less sugar as long as you save the rest of the can or bottle for another day.
Check the nutrition label on the bottle or can to find drinks without added sugar.
If you like the bubbly feeling of soda, sparkling water is a great replacement. You can also add fresh fruit or real fruit juice to your sparkling water. If you buy flavoured sparkling water, check the label to make sure it has no added sugar.

title: John Lee keeps Hong Kong talent target unchanged despite 300,000 arrivals
description: City leader also says professionals arriving under Top Talent Pass Scheme could add about 1.2 per cent to local GDP each year.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has said he does not plan to change the government’s annual target for attracting talent despite the city admitting more than 300,000 people since expanding its drive four years ago. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Friday that about 20 per cent of overall arrivals came from places outside mainland China. “We have met our targets better than we set,” Lee told a phone-in radio programme, days after delivering his policy address and unveiling the city’s first five-year plan. Lee noted he had originally set a target of attracting about 30,000 people annually when the government launched its talent drive four years ago. Official government documents put the goal at a minimum of 35,000 arrivals annually between 2023 and 2025 under various admission schemes. “If [talent] doesn’t join my side, they join the competitor’s side,” Lee said. “So when you have this competition game, I have to ensure that Hong Kong has the best people.” Lee also said the individuals brought in via the Top Talent Pass Scheme could add about 1.2 per cent to the city’s gross domestic product (GDP) each year. “These [professionals] will create an extra GDP of probably 1.2 per cent every year because they are very well qualified,” he said. “They can do jobs that will receive higher pay and that will reflect the contribution they can make to the economy.” Lee added that more than 50 per cent of the talent admitted to Hong Kong through the scheme were willing to extend their stay in the city. A supplement to the latest policy address showed that more than 61,000 extension applications under various admission schemes were received between January and August this year, with about 58,000 approved. The government had earlier set a target of approving at least 50,000 extension applications annually between 2025 and 2027. Lee linked the talent drive to Hong Kong’s manpower needs, noting that the city recorded a natural population decline of about 20,000 people annually. The city’s population stood at around 7.5 million after rising by about 19,000, despite deaths outnumbering births by around 20,000 annually, he said. Hong Kong’s population is expected to remain flat over the coming years, with only minor increases supported by talent schemes, imported workers and one-way permit holders from the mainland. Lee said that even when the population increased, it would be just a “very moderate” upward trend. He added that the labour and welfare authorities would release an updated manpower projection soon to determine how many more people the city needed to attract. A projection conducted in 2023 indicated Hong Kong would face a shortage of about 130,000 workers by 2028, Lee said. He warned that the shortfall could reach around 300,000 without new talent arrivals. The government will consider adding more artificial intelligence-related professions to the Talent List, which currently covers 60 occupations facing local manpower shortages, according to the policy address supplement. Authorities will also relax extension requirements under the Top Talent Pass Scheme for some technology start-up operators in the first half of next year.

title: Torrential rain in Vietnam leaves 3 dead, 16,000 homes flooded
description: More heavy rain is expected through the weekend, with some areas forecast to receive a deluge of over 100mm.
content: Heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides across northern Vietnam, killing three people and damaging thousands of homes as well as more than 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of crops. The northern region has experienced downpours since Monday, with some areas receiving as much as 653mm (26 inches) of rain, according to a statement on the government’s website. More than 16,000 houses have been inundated while rice and other crops have been damaged. National and provincial roads have been affected by 11 landslides and flooding in 30 locations, causing traffic tie-ups. The Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City railway was flooded to a depth of about one metre. Several train services on the north-south railway were suspended on Thursday and Friday. More heavy rain is expected from Thanh Hoa province to the city of Hue through the weekend, with some areas forecast to receive a deluge of over 100mm. In Thanh Hoa, more than 29,000 officials and soldiers were mobilised for emergency aid. Some Hanoi schools switched to online classes or gave students the day off on Thursday as streets inundated with as much as one metre of floodwaters caused gridlock in the centre of the capital city, state media reported. “The flood happens every year,” Ninh Binh resident Tran Ngoc Tai told national broadcaster VTV, adding that people were prepared with fresh water and food. Vietnam’s long coastline makes it vulnerable to storms roaring in from the South China Sea, while climate change and deforestation have increased the country’s potential for severe damage. As many as five more storms are expected off the coast the rest of the year, with one or two possibly sweeping over Vietnam’s mainland. Natural disasters have killed or left 63 people missing in Vietnam so far this year, causing total losses of around 2.2 trillion dong (US$84.6 million). Financial losses are down 84.9 per cent from the same period last year when the country was hit by severe typhoons and flooding, according to a separate government statement. Last year, Tropical Storm Wipha brought heavy rain and flooding in July, followed by more flooding and landslides in August when Tropical Storm Kajiki struck. Typhoon Bualoi killed at least 26 last September while a month later, the historic cities of Hue and Hoi An in central Vietnam flooded, along with much of the north. Meanwhile, El Nino is expected to reduce rainfall in central and southern Vietnam by 10 per cent to 50 per cent later this year, potentially affecting around 350,000 hectares of rice in the Mekong Delta. Severe water shortages are also forecast in the central highlands, the country’s largest coffee growing region. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Russians begin voting in parliamentary election in shadow of war
description: Kremlin’s United Russia party set to maintain a tight grip on the Duma alongside a handful of Putin-aligned groups.
content: Polling stations opened Friday in Russia’s Far East, kicking off a three-day election that President Vladimir Putin’s party is all but guaranteed to win in the fifth year of war with Ukraine. It will be Russia’s first parliamentary election since Moscow sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022. The conflict has since killed hundreds of thousands. Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s dragging military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine. While few in Russia doubt Putin’s United Russia party would sail to victory again, the vote is an opportunity for the Kremlin to gauge public support for the Ukraine war, the effects of which have hit home more than ever this year. In a grim reminder of the fighting, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Kyiv launched 350 drones at the Moscow region overnight, adding most were destroyed. The vote to renew the 450 seats in the Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament, would run until Sunday. Russia’s Kamchatka peninsula and Chukotka – on the Pacific – were the first of Russia’s 11 time zones to begin voting. Putin has ruled Russia since New Year’s Eve 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated Russian politics since the early 2000s. Moscow has banned criticism of its Ukraine campaign and the Russian elections, tightly controlled by the Kremlin, are bringing few surprises. United Russia is only facing parties who back most of Putin’s policies and the war in Ukraine: the Communist Party, the nationalist LDPR, A Just Russia and New People. Yabloko, which called for an end to fighting, was barred from running shortly before the vote. One of its main figures, Lev Shlosberg, was imprisoned for criticising the war. Ahead of the vote, the 73-year-old Putin called on Russians to vote to show troops that “behind our fighters stand millions of people” and to demonstrate a “common answer to those who want to weaken Russia”. The war has broken Moscow’s ties with the West, which has hit Russia with massive economic sanctions. In the absence of a public debate and with protests banned, the vote will serve as a barometer for the Kremlin of public frustration with the conflict, which has no end in sight. This year, the war hit ordinary Russians more than ever, with Ukrainian strikes reaching as far as the Urals and Siberia, and causing billions of roubles in damage – as well as civilian deaths deep inside Russia. Putin’s political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny – who once brought thousands to the streets during elections – died in an Arctic prison in 2024. Russia’s exiled opposition called on anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but to vote “against Putin’s party”, publishing recommendations of who to back in which region. Some fear the post-election period in Russia will bring a new military mobilisation, similar to the one in 2022, when Putin called up 300,000 reservists. That hugely unpopular move led to an exodus of draft-age men out of Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused the Kremlin of planning a fresh mobilisation campaign “this autumn”, a suggestion Putin has denied.

title: Thailand’s Muslim separatists vow to fight for independence ‘until the end of time’
description: Since 2004, over 7,000 militants, security forces and civilians have been killed in the region, once part of a Malay-Muslim sultanate.
content: Two decades into an insurgency that has killed thousands in southern Thailand, a leader of the main Malay–Muslim separatist group has vowed to keep fighting until it achieves its goals. “This struggle will continue until the end of time,” Nikmatullah Seri, the spokesman for the Barisan Revolusi Nasional (BRN) peace negotiation delegation, said in a rare interview. “As long as our objectives remain unachieved, we will continue to fight.” Militants from BRN have fought for an independent Islamic nation in Thailand’s Muslim-majority south since the 1960s, although the current unrest began in 2004. Thailand has been negotiating with the BRN under Malaysian mediation since 2013, the most recent high-level talks taking place in December. But the process has repeatedly stalled, and Bangkok suspended dialogue in July following an attack that killed five soldiers. “The objective remains the same, which is the demand for independence,” Nikmatullah said in a hotel in the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur. The southern region was once part of the former Malay-Muslim Patani sultanate, but was annexed by Buddhist-majority Thailand, then Siam, in the early 1900s. Since 2004, more than 7,000 people – militants, Thai security forces and civilians – have been killed, according to monitor Deep South Watch. Nikmatullah neither confirmed nor denied the BRN’s responsibility for a recent flare in violence, but said it was the “driving force behind a struggle”. He said the group had proposed a power-sharing arrangement with Bangkok, and implied the BRN would take office without elections. “We want political power. That is, the BRN should be able to govern” over the region, spread across four Thai provinces near the Malaysia border. It would be administered by sharia police and courts following Islamic law – although only for Muslims, he said. There would be a “transitional period of five or 10 years during which we govern”, he said. “After that, we will hand it over to the people to choose democratically.” Nikmatullah said ethnic Malay Muslims faced “obvious discrimination” against their language and culture, and “have never felt safe” – something Thailand has rejected. Bangkok’s lead negotiator, Thanut Suvarnananda, told local media in August there was “no talk of secession at the negotiating table”. Instead, Thanut – appointed in April – said ceasefire zones and reducing checkpoints and other security measures that disrupted daily life were under consideration. Tight security Since 2005, the region has been administered under special security laws allowing Thai authorities to detain suspects without charge and impose curfews, drawing criticism from rights groups. Nikmatullah said the BRN’s military wing recorded 1,000 fighter deaths over the past two decades, but said “warfare was a last resort”. “We do not target vulnerable groups – our target is the government,” said the negotiator, who was born in southern Thailand and joined the BRN at 18. Last month, scores of coordinated nighttime attacks injured several people and damaged government property and private businesses. In July, five Thai soldiers died in a shooting and bomb attack at a checkpoint that also injured six civilians, according to Thai authorities. Nikmatullah would not say if the BRN was involved: “We are not intelligence agents for the colonisers.” But the soldiers’ deaths caused Thailand to put dialogue “on hold”, the foreign ministry said, while stressing it remained committed to the process. In a statement, it said it was focused on a three-pronged approach to the south, “namely socio-economic development, maintenance of security and peace dialogue”. Wearing a black leather jacket and songkok, a traditional black cap worn by Muslim men, he was vague about where he lived. But he claimed the BRN had the support of local people and was funded by members' donations. Weapons were taken from its “enemies”, he said. “We take them for free, because they’ve come here and are wreaking havoc on our land.” Nikmatullah said the peace talks had been hampered by the absence of a Malaysian mediator, but said the BRN could potentially go to “backchannel negotiations” with Thailand in October. Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin said in a statement the appointment of a new mediator was “under consideration”. He said Kuala Lumpur’s priority was a peaceful resolution. “Malaysia respects Thailand’s sovereignty and recognises that matters concerning its citizens are within Thailand’s domestic jurisdiction,” Mohamed Khaled said. He declined to apportion blame for the unrest, but said Malaysia would not allow itself “to be used as a refuge or hideout by any party that resorts to violence or rejects the peace process”. Nikmatullah said the BRN was playing the long game. “This is not a short-lived struggle. It will take a long time.”

title: Hong Kong IT analyst charged with murdering wife at their flat
description: Wong Chi-Kwong, 51, remanded in custody after police found his wife dead in their flat in Heng Fa Chuen estate on Wednesday and arrested him.
content: A Hong Kong IT analyst has been remanded in custody after being charged with killing his wife in a flat at a private residential estate two days ago. Wong Chi-kwong, 51, was brought to Eastern Court for the first time on Friday to face a count of murder. Police arrested him on Wednesday after his wife, 53-year-old Wong Yuk-ting, was found dead in a flat in block 2 of Heng Fa Chuen estate in Chai Wan. The defendant appeared composed in the dock when the murder charge against him was read out. He told the court he understood that he was accused of killing his wife and that he now faced criminal proceedings. Prosecutors asked for a 12-week adjournment for further investigation. Their request was granted by Principal Magistrate David Cheung Chi-wai, who set the next hearing for December 11. Police said on Wednesday the woman was confirmed dead at the scene. Heng Fa Chuen is a private waterfront residential estate built directly above the MTR depot in Hong Kong’s Eastern district. Developed in the 1980s, the self-contained community has 48 residential towers and a shopping centre.

title: Saudis scramble to solve ‘humiliating dilemma’ after US rejects Red Sea intervention
description: Riyadh is now working frantically to build a coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea and defend the kingdom against Houthi attacks.
content: Saudi Arabia faces a “humiliating dilemma” after the United States refused to militarily intervene to prevent the Iran-aligned Houthi militia from tightening its blockade of the kingdom’s key backup maritime trade route with Asia, according to analysts. US President Donald Trump on September 12 dismissed the Houthi seizure of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast as a problem that “only affects one country”. Iran has already blockaded the Straits of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia’s main oil and petrochemicals export lane from the Gulf. This stance has “deeply disturbed” the Saudi leadership, according to Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia. It was “deeply frustrating, to say the least” for Riyadh, Ratney said at a webinar hosted by the Washington-based Arab Gulf States Institute on Wednesday. Trump’s belief that all would be “fine and dandy” contrasted starkly with the suspension of Saudi oil exports from the Red Sea the same day, after drone strikes by Iran-allied Iraqi militias badly damaged the east-west pipeline that had enabled the kingdom to bypass Hormuz since the Iran war erupted on February 28. Having invested about a century and hundreds of billions of dollars in building a strong military and strategic partnership with the US, Saudi Arabia had expected it “to be there in the breach” now that it was under attack by its “mortal enemies”, Ratney said. Instead, Riyadh found that “for the most part, the US has not taken their concerns and vulnerabilities into consideration” in its war against Iran. Those vulnerabilities were exposed when the Yemeni government forces that the Saudi leaders “were banking on” to seize territory from the Houthis instead surrendered control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to the Iran-aligned movement without much resistance last week, said Bernard Haykel, professor of Near Eastern studies at Princeton University. Riyadh now had to “rethink really everything”, he said at the webinar. Haykel said Iran and the Houthis were using “the same playbook” against Saudi Arabia and the other Gulf Arab states. “Essentially, they can disrupt flows of oil and other goods, so they’re basically in the extortion business.” Coalition call With US military support not forthcoming, analysts are not optimistic about Saudi Arabia’s chances of wriggling out of the straitjacket being forced on it. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s administration is now working frantically to build a multinational coalition of regional and Western states to protect shipping in the Red Sea and defend the kingdom against Houthi drones and ballistic missiles. Analysts say the underlying Saudi strategy is to ramp up military pressure on the Houthis while engaging diplomatically with Iran in the hopes that Tehran will rein in its Yemeni ally. A temporary framework agreement between Iran and Oman, scheduled to be signed on Monday, was scuttled by Saudi objections to the text, which granted Tehran permanent privileges over the strategic waterway. It also provided no guarantees that commercial shipping activity could resume. Tehran had made opening Hormuz contingent upon the lifting of the US naval blockade and other conditions agreed by the two sides under the Islamabad Declaration in June. Alongside Mecca Defence Pact partners Pakistan and Turkey, Saudi Arabia hopes to receive defensive support from Britain, France and Egypt. But none of these countries want to directly engage the Houthis in kinetic warfare, analysts say. “The coalition is much more likely to become an enabling coalition than a war-fighting coalition,” said Andreas Krieg, associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London. Pakistan and Turkey could provide air defence, counter-drone capabilities, intelligence, surveillance, training, munitions and personnel to protect Saudi territory. That would give the Mecca agreement, signed in August, “some practical meaning without forcing either country to invade Yemen”, Krieg said. Egypt has a “huge interest” in protecting Bab al-Mandab because the security of the Suez Canal – its major foreign revenue generator – begins there, according to Krieg. But Cairo has “no stomach whatsoever for an expeditionary operation in Yemen”, which remains a “historical trauma for the Egyptian military” following its intervention in a previous civil war there in the 1960s. Its cooperation would likely be limited to naval surveillance, intelligence and maritime coordination with Saudi Arabia, Krieg said. Western powers, meanwhile, could contribute naval escorts, surveillance, mine countermeasures and protection of international shipping. “The Americans are still crucial even if they do not want to bomb Yemen themselves,” Krieg said. Intelligence, targeting data, early warning, air defence and the broader command-and-control architecture “remain areas where Washington is extremely difficult to replace”. So Saudi Arabia might discover that it could build a substantial coalition “around the conflict while still being largely alone” in any offensive inside Yemen, he said. Financial compensation Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics risk consultancy, was less sanguine. “Saudi Arabia faces a humiliating dilemma in which Riyadh has no good options,” he said. “I have a difficult time imagining Saudi Arabia not making concessions to the Houthis as part of a grander deal.” Haykel agreed, saying the Saudis “sooner or later, will have to pay off both the Iranians and the Houthis to back off from attacking them”. Some form of Saudi financial compensation while distinguishing “very clearly between paying the Houthis and paying Iran” looked likely, Krieg said. Riyadh was being forced to “demonstrate whether it can actually organise regional power rather than simply possess it”. Keeping open a diplomatic channel with the Houthis while coordinating with its partners would demonstrate a “much more mature form of leadership”, Krieg said. However, if it chooses to launch another open-ended war on its southern border with Yemen, “the limits of Saudi power become much more visible”. “This is the real test,” Krieg said. “It means Saudi Arabia is able to construct an architecture in which different partners contribute different capabilities, while Riyadh remains the political centre of gravity.”

title: China to see major shift to Huawei for AI model training in 2027: deputy chair
description: The firm’s Ascend chips are ahead of Nvidia in domestic market, Huawei’s Eric Xu Zhijun says.
content: Huawei Technologies expects a major domestic shift towards its artificial intelligence computing infrastructure for model training next year, as its Ascend processors gain ground on Nvidia in China despite supply constraints, according to rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun. “I believe that starting from next year, a lot of the AI model training will be based on the SuperPoD or SuperCluster based on Ascend 950DT,” Xu told reporters during the Huawei Connect 2026 conference in Shanghai on Thursday. Xu said Huawei’s proprietary Ascend chips had overtaken Nvidia in domestic market share, although he did not provide specific figures. Nvidia confirmed last month that it had begun shipments of its H200 processors to China under a new US licensing arrangement after a months-long lockout, although those sales represented less than 1 per cent of its second-quarter data-centre revenue. Huawei has been pushing its own alternative computing infrastructure amid US export controls that were designed to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors, such as those from Nvidia. China’s most advanced AI models were still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP reported last month, citing sources at major Chinese AI developers. “Even though there might be some gaps between Ascend and some of its competitors, it offers the strongest support for mainland Chinese customers,” Xu said, adding that many clients chose Ascend due to geopolitical risks and a preference for multi-vendor strategies. “Pushing full chip self-sufficiency is the certain path forward for China,” Xu said. “I believe it will become a reality sooner or later.” However, international availability for Huawei’s latest hardware remains constrained. While the Shenzhen-based tech giant unveiled its new Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster on Thursday – powered by Ascend 960 chips and boasting double the training and inference performance of its predecessor – production limits would keep the systems mostly within China, Xu said. “Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don’t have the plan to expand [SuperPoD systems] to the international market in a fully fledged way,” Xu said, though he noted the firm has been shipping small quantities overseas for testing in high-demand regions. Huawei’s previous-generation Atlas 950 SuperPoD, powered by the Ascend 950DT chip, had increasingly been deployed for AI model training with encouraging initial testing results, according to Xu. Huawei had deployed over 1,000 Atlas SuperPoD units across more than 370 enterprise customers, the company said. On Thursday, Huawei also introduced its Peerium Computing Architecture, a technology designed to interconnect 1 million processors to function as a single computer. Already deployed on Atlas 950 systems, Peerium was undergoing testing on the new Atlas 960 hardware, the company said. Despite its technological leaps, Xu cautioned that computing supply still lagged behind China’s surging AI demand. He projected that global AI computing supply and demand would reach equilibrium around 2029, with China reaching a balance slightly later in 2030.

title: China launches Pinglu Canal; Hong Kong unveils first 5-year plan: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From Chinese defence chief’s forum speech to a Beijing Hyrox athlete’s faecal row, here are top stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. China launches Pinglu Canal, slashing transit time to Southeast Asia China officially opened its landmark Pinglu Canal to navigation on Wednesday, creating a new maritime gateway for the country’s southwestern hinterland and providing a shorter route to Southeast Asia as Beijing seeks to deepen trade with the region. 2. Chinese defence chief skirts flashpoints at Xiangshan Forum ahead of Xi-Trump summit With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday. 3. Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy. 4. Has a Chinese DF missile been used for the first time in the Middle East? Debris from a Chinese-made short-range ballistic missile has been found in Yemen for the first time, suggesting Chinese weapons systems may have been used during the heated conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. 5. Hyrox Beijing athletes get full refund, new rule on hygiene risks comes into force Hyrox China has given full refunds to competitors affected by last weekend’s incontinence incident in Beijing, while the global governing body has updated its rule book to allow race directors to remove athletes if they pose a risk to the hygiene of the event. 6. South Korean killer’s drone escape from Philippine prison foiled by test footage A South Korean crime lord convicted of murder in the Philippines reportedly planned to escape prison by strapping himself to a drone – until his own accomplice’s rehearsal footage gave the game away. 7. Knife attack in China’s Guangzhou leaves multiple people injured Police in Guangzhou said on Monday they had apprehended a man in the southern Chinese city’s university town district after receiving reports that he was wielding a knife and injuring pedestrians.

title: Malaysia’s Najib Razak allowed to serve rest of jail term under house arrest
description: Given a ‘conditional pardon’, Najib has to settle his US$12.3 million fine before he can be transferred home to complete his sentence.
content: Malaysia’s Pardons Board on Friday agreed to allow disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak to serve out the remainder of his jail term under house arrest. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar granted Najib a “conditional pardon”, where the former leader is required to settle his 50 million ringgit (US$12.3 million) fine before he can be transferred to his home to complete his sentence, due to end on August 23, 2028. “He must abide by these conditions, and should he fail to fulfil any of these conditions, his conditional pardon will be nullified and must immediately serve the remainder of his sentence in jail,” the Pardons Board said in a statement. The decision came a week after the board deferred discussions on Najib’s pardon application, stoking intense speculation and public anger over the possibility that he could walk free from his conviction in a case involving 42 million ringgit siphoned from a former unit of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. Royal pardons are the prerogative of the king, who is constitutionally empowered to grant clemency to convicted felons serving their sentences on the advice of the Pardons Board, which typically includes the federal territories minister, attorney general and several other appointed members. In an immediate response, Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi expressed the party’s gratitude for the king’s decision to allow his predecessor to serve out his term in the comfort of his own home. Zahid, who is also a deputy prime minister, announced that Umno would launch a fundraiser to cover the cost of Najib’s fine. “Umno calls on its leadership, members and party supporters and all who wish to lend their support to make voluntary contributions to this initiative that will be carried out transparently, in order and in line with all regulations and laws,” he said in a statement. Earlier on Thursday, rumours that Najib had been granted house arrest went viral, with images of a document purportedly signed by the king and Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh making their rounds on social media. Yeoh said the images of the said document were fake and that her press secretary had since lodged a formal report with the authorities on the matter. “I have never signed a house arrest order as has been going viral on social media. The Pardons Board has yet to meet,” she said in a social media post ahead of Friday’s meeting. This is the second pardon for Najib, who holds the dubious distinction of being Malaysia’s first former prime minister to be jailed for corruption in 2022. In 2024, then king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah halved his 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fine from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit. Najib later attempted to secure a court order to compel the government to enforce an alleged “addendum” to the decree allowing him to serve out the remainder of his sentence under house arrest. But he dropped his bid in April after more than a year of pushing his case. No reason was given for his decision. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the Pardons Board’s ruling does not change his government’s stance on corruption, stressing that he had fulfilled his role in advising the king. “As prime minister, my role is to provide advice on the legal implications, national stability, the principles of law and to follow the advice and guidance provided at length by the attorney general,” Anwar was quoted as saying by state news agency Bernama. “But in the end, the constitution provides absolute power to the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, and I hope we accept [the decision],” he added, using the official title of the king. It was not immediately clear whether Najib’s transfer would happen today or how it would be handled. Friday’s decision also drew immediate public backlash, with hundreds of angry social media posts decrying what was described as the collapse of the nation’s institutions. “We cannot even pretend to be shocked any more and that’s the most depressing part. Each time we express outrage, adjust, and move on. This is how faith in institutions dies,” read a post by Khoo Ying Hooi, an expert in international relations and human rights at the University of Malaya. Najib’s transfer to house arrest also raised complaints of alleged preferential treatment for the country’s elites, with many blaming it on a failure of Anwar and his ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition to push through its promised reforms. “The last straw for Pakatan Harapan believers. PKR, DAP, Amanah. You guys are over,” said a post, referring to the three component parties of PH, the People’s Justice Party, Democratic Action Party and National Trust Party. Syaza Shukri, a political scientist at the International Islamic University Malaysia, told Reuters the pardon was bad news for Anwar and a boon for Najib’s Umno ahead of the next election. “The impact on Anwar and his government is really bad unless they can explain to the people the constitutionality and limitations they face,” she said. “This is a big win for Umno and they would feel more confident and emboldened going forward to get things going their way, looking like they will be the next government in waiting.”

title: From Cheng Pei-pei to Michelle Yeoh, Hong Kong cinema’s history of action heroines
description: Hong Kong studios embraced female action stars long before Hollywood. Here’s how some of the biggest triumphed in wuxia and kung fu films.
content: For decades, Hong Kong’s film industry has cultivated an extraordinary roster of female screen warriors, defying the city’s historically conservative gender roles. From 1960s icon Cheng Pei-pei – known as the “Queen of Swords” – to the globally recognised Michelle Yeoh, the city’s male-dominated studios have consistently given women the chance to fight just as hard as the men in their fabled martial arts films. This offers an interesting comparison to Hollywood. The United States has produced its fair share of 21st century films featuring heroines such as Wonder Woman, but female performers have generally continued to work outside the action genre. Before that, action was largely regarded as men’s work, save for B-movies and exploitation films. So why did female fighters thrive in Hong Kong? The answer lies in a mix of cultural history, an industry that allowed producers to take chances, and the gumption of the women themselves. Actresses had to hold their own in scenes dominated by men, becoming stars in their own right through their skills – whether that meant Angela Mao Ying’s superior kung fu or Brigitte Lin Ching-hsia’s fearsome screen presence. Female fighters were part of martial arts films from the start, drawing on a long tradition of female knights-errant (nuxia) in Chinese literature and folklore. As Stephen Teo noted in his book Chinese Martial Arts Cinema: The Wuxia Tradition, the first ever wuxia (sword-fighting) film, 1925’s Lady Knight Li Feifei, featured a female knight-errant. Such heroines regularly anchored early martial arts films, which tended to be more phantasmagoric than realistic. The rise of the cinematic swordswoman Martial arts heroines became extremely popular in Hong Kong in the 1950s, when film producers were focused on attracting a female audience. “The female knight-errant was a standard part in the repertoire of roles for female stars in both the Cantonese and Mandarin cinemas of the 1950s,” Teo wrote. Cantonese stars such as Yu So-chow (known as “Black Peony”) and Wu Lizhu were the first female performers to define themselves as action heroines in Hong Kong cinema. They were careful to present a feminine side even while they fought, and the men were generally portrayed as relatively weak both morally and physically. That approach continued into the early 1960s, when the young duo of Josephine Siao Fong-fong and Connie Chan Po-chu became a very popular sword-fighting team, with Chan sometimes playing a boy. “Siao and Chan were loyal to their school, sexually neutral, and more like children than women,” noted film historians Law Kar and Frank Bren. The situation for women in martial arts films changed radically in the mid-1960s when legendary director Chang Cheh became the predominant creative force at Hong Kong’s powerful Shaw Brothers studio. Chang railed against sword-fighting heroines and mild-mannered male heroes, bringing macho male stars such as Jimmy Wang Yu to the fore. Films like One-Armed Swordsman (1967) were a massive success, and women suddenly found themselves excluded from the action. The situation was mitigated by Chang’s contemporary, King Hu, whose elegant, stylised approach to martial arts filmmaking was almost antithetical to Chang’s penchant for blood and guts. Steeped in Chinese literature, Hu’s stories about female knights-errant simply reflected the heroines he had read about rather than making a point about gender roles. Hu brought various women into the genre who went on to forge durable careers as fully fledged action stars, notably Cheng Pei-pei, the lead of Hu’s Come Drink with Me (1966), and Taiwanese actress Hsu Feng, the star of his masterpiece A Touch of Zen (1971). Come Drink with Me turned Cheng into the first of Hong Kong’s modern female action superstars. She had trained in martial arts at the Shaw Brothers film school, but Hu picked her for her background in jazz dance, believing her knowledge of rhythm would translate to elegant on-camera movement. Cheng always said that while other actresses had better combat skills, her dancing brought sophistication to her martial arts moves. Although Cheng was a big success, masculine action still ruled at the box office, and she did not start a wave of leading ladies. Shaw Brothers saw a successor in Shih Szu, a tough and boisterous fighter – the two were paired in the superior The Lady Hermit (1971) – but disagreements with the studio and, possibly, an injury hampered her career. The shift to kung fu The next female action superstar did not arrive until kung fu took over from wuxia in the 1970s. Established performers did not want to offend Shaw Brothers by working with the fledgling Golden Harvest studio, so for their first signing, Harvest hired a young Peking opera performer from Taiwan, Angela Mao Ying, specifically to cultivate as an action star. While women did not generally learn kung fu at martial arts schools, female Peking opera performers learned stylised combat techniques and tended to be especially good with weapons, which provided producers with a ready pool of screen warriors. Mao played fighting roles (wudan) in Peking opera, was good with weapons, and could defend herself from 12 spears thrown in succession with just her foot. She originally appeared in the wuxia film The Angry River (1971), but after the death of Bruce Lee, Golden Harvest switched Mao – who had studied the Korean style of hapkido – to kung fu and promoted her as his successor. Films such as Lady Whirlwind (1972) were incredibly popular abroad, and Mao continued to make great films throughout the 1970s. But the focus on Bruce Lee clones meant no one was groomed to follow in her footsteps. It was not until the mid-1980s that Hong Kong’s next two female action stars, Michelle Yeoh and American import Cynthia Rothrock, rose to fame. By then, modern-day action was in fashion, so the duo made their debut as police officers in the hard-hitting 1985 hit Yes, Madam!. Both Yeoh and Rothrock have said fight choreographers Sammo Hung Kam-bo and Corey Yuen Kwai gave them no special treatment because they were women. They got bruised and injured while shooting but dismissed such events as part and parcel of Hong Kong’s rough-and-tumble filmmaking. Rothrock went on to forge a durable career in Hong Kong before moving back to the US to appear in Western films, while Yeoh ultimately morphed into a global icon. This time, a few others did follow in their footsteps, notably Cynthia Khan (real name Yeung Lai-ching), but none hit the same heights. Modern-day action Brigitte Lin Ching-hsia, Hong Kong’s last bona fide female action superstar, is an interesting case. Lin knew no martial arts and did not feel the need to learn any; she simply struck dramatic poses. This worked incredibly well. Already a highly successful dramatic actress, Lin became a cultural phenomenon after being cast as the transgender sorcerer Invincible East in the Tsui Hark-produced 1992 wuxia fantasy Swordsman II. She quickly took a slew of similar roles before withdrawing from acting. “I seem to embody some kind of fantasy about a beautiful woman performing violent acts,” she told this writer in a 1993 interview. Hong Kong’s interest in action heroines declined along with the industry as a whole in the late 1990s. Action films such as Gen-X Cops (1999) morphed into ensemble showcases for glamorous young stars, and no female performers arose with the requisite skills to take on the mantle of their forebears. It does, after all, take a lot of gumption and a love of danger to be a female action star. “Making action films is very tough,” Yeoh said of the making of Tai-Chi Master in 1993. “But I really enjoy it. You can spend a sleepless night because you know there’s a stunt ahead of you, but at the same time it gives you a rush. You know if you do that stunt, it will look incredible.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Hongkongers pay tribute to late leader Tung Chee-hwa at community halls
description: Residents lay flowers and leave messages in condolence books ahead of vigil on Saturday and state funeral on Sunday.
content: Residents visited three community halls across Hong Kong to pay tribute to the city’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, bringing flowers and writing heartfelt messages in public condolence books on Friday. The arrangements came ahead of a vigil on Saturday and a state funeral on Sunday honouring Tung, who died aged 89 on September 8. “Tung’s contribution to Hong Kong is conspicuous and his death made everyone sad,” said Peggy Lam Pei Yu-dja, a former member of the nation’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), who paid tribute at the Moreton Terrace Activities Centre in Causeway Bay in the morning. “He was not only our first chief executive, but also a leader in the business sector, the political sector and for all Hong Kong people.” Tung was appointed a vice-chairman of the CPPCC after stepping down as city leader in 2005, midway through his second term. Lam, a former chairwoman of Wan Chai district council, recalled her experience working with Tung at the CPPCC, as well as the unwavering support of Tung’s wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, when Lam founded the Hong Kong Federation of Women. She said she would attend the vigil on Saturday. Wan Chai Police District Commander Liauw Ka-kei also signed the condolence book at Moreton Terrace Activities Centre. A resident surnamed So came to the Causeway Bay community hall to pay tribute, saying Tung had left a lasting legacy for Hong Kong people. “Chief Executive Tung, you devoted yourself selflessly so that Hong Kong could make a smooth transition. Hong Kong people will remember you forever,” he wrote. So said Tung had devoted his life to the city, but noted that some of his policies were not rolled out at the right time, which affected his political career. A retiree surnamed Tang, who lives in Sha Tin, also went to Causeway Bay with flowers and recounted the time she met Tung at her younger daughter’s wedding. She had invited him to the wedding through friends and remembered him as a “kind and amiable gentleman”. Tang wrote “thank you” in the book and hoped Tung would become “an immortal”. She added: “I think of how much he loved his country and how much he loved our Hong Kong.” A 70-year-old Eastern district resident, surnamed Chan, said he appreciated Tung’s pledge in 1997 to build 85,000 flats every year, which would have made it easier for lower-income families to buy homes. However, the ambitious target was quietly dropped following the onset of the Asian financial crisis. “Tung did many things for Hong Kong residents,” Chan, who lives in public housing, said. “He was the first chief executive after the handover, and many things were still in the exploration stage, but he managed to do it.” Chan also thanked Tung in the book, saying he felt deeply sad about the former leader’s death. Another retiree, surnamed Cou, said Tung’s policies were very forward-looking, but the financial crisis prevented him from implementing some of them. “Tung, as a businessman running a large enterprise, wouldn’t necessarily need to engage with politics. But he had the central government’s trust at the time, and he also had an international outlook,” she said, referring to the former leader’s time at the helm of his father’s Orient Overseas Container Line. “Combined with his leadership experience in the business world – knowing how to expand a business – these were all factors, I believe, that contributed to him being chosen as the first chief executive.” Hong Kong authorities have also set up condolence points at the Kai Tak Community Hall and the Sai Lau Kok Garden Multipurpose Room for members of the public to sign condolence books between Friday and Sunday. Tung will be accorded a state funeral for his service as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework. A vigil will be held from 3pm to 10pm on Saturday at the funeral home in North Point and a memorial service will start at 9am on Sunday. The memorial service, originally planned as a public event, will instead be by invitation-only due to venue constraints, the Office of Former Chief Executives announced on Thursday.

title: US to allow Iranian leaders to attend UN meeting in New York amid wartime stand-off
description: US again imposes strict conditions on the Iranian delegation for the UN General Assembly in New York.
content: The Trump administration has approved visas for top Iranian officials, including the president and foreign minister, to attend next week’s UN General Assembly high-level meeting in New York even as the two countries are locked in a stalemated war. The State Department said Thursday that it had approved visas for Iran’s “core delegation”, along with essential staffers to participate in the UN meetings. The core delegation includes President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, according to US officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to visa privacy laws. The move is unusual due to the more than six-month-long conflict between Iran and the United States and no sign that agreements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to talks on Iran’s nuclear programme are close. US President Donald Trump has said he has a “big decision” to make over his stalled war with Iran - mainly whether he should “annihilate” the Islamic Republic or not. “I have a big decision coming up,” he told the Axios news portal for a story published on Thursday. “Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me.” Trump did not specifically mention Iran, but he has repeatedly threatened to destroy the country. The UN gathering comes as Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up attacks on Saudi infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, another major maritime route in the region where impediments have helped drive a surge in global oil prices. In addition, Iran remains the world’s leading state sponsor of terrorism, according to the United States, which has imposed significant sanctions against the country and launched a new campaign in recent weeks aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines”. As the host country for the United Nations headquarters, the US is generally limited in what it can do to prevent foreign leaders from coming to the General Assembly. However, it has in the past denied visas to - or discouraged applications from - leaders involved in active conflicts with the United States. For last year’s UN meetings of world leaders - which took place before the Iran war began on February 28 but after the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025 – the State Department also approved a limited number of visas for Iranian diplomats but also imposed rigid restrictions on the delegation’s movements. Those included severe limitations on how far Iranian officials could travel in New York City from their UN mission and barred them from shopping at wholesale membership stores, such as Costco and Sam’s Club. “Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level week,” the State Department said. “The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year.” “While ordinary Iranians endure brutal repression, water and electricity shortages, and soaring inflation, the regime’s officials want to go on shopping sprees in New York,” US State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott wrote on X. “Not on our watch. We will not let the Iranian regime’s elites exploit [UN General Assembly] for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people’s suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran’s wealth to support its terrorist proxies.” The decision on the Iranian visas was announced just a day after the State Department denied visas to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and his delegation to come to the General Assembly. The department accused the Palestinian Authority - which administers parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank – of trying to “internationalise” the Israel-Gaza war by bringing cases to the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court as well as continuing to pay stipends to prisoners jailed in Israel for attacks on Israelis. The Palestinian Authority condemned the move and called Israel’s actions “the real threat to the two-state solution and prospects for peace”. It also said it remained committed to long-stalled negotiations but defended its efforts to gain Palestinian recognition through international bodies and courts. “Punitive measures and restrictions imposed on Palestinian officials do not contribute to advancing peace or combating violence,” the authority’s foreign ministry said in a statement. “Rather, they weaken the Palestinian partner committed to a political solution and encourage forces working to undermine the two-state solution and impose the reality of occupation, settlement and annexation by force.” The US does not recognise the Palestinian Authority as the government of a full UN member state. The UN General Assembly, however, along with various UN agencies and organisations, does. Additional reporting by dpa

title: City tennis chief ‘quietly confident’ Alexandra Eala will play at Hong Kong Open
description: Filipino superstar is ‘super excited’ to return and Michael Cheng is hopeful Leylah Fernandez and Naomi Osaka will also come back.
content: The city’s tennis chief is “quietly confident” that Filipino superstar Alexandra Eala, and fellow main attractions Paula Badosa and Diana Shanider, will show up for the 2026 Prudential Hong Kong Tennis Open in November. In the past two years, Michael Cheng Ming-git has seen Naomi Osaka and Emma Raducanu both withdraw with injuries on the eve of the WTA 250 tournament. But the president of the Hong Kong, China Tennis Association said the “issue about no-shows has got nothing to do with the conviction of the players”. “It has everything to do with it being the end of term, everyone is tired and sometimes they get injured,” Cheng added. Aiming to lure more marquee names to the city, Cheng said he hoped that 2023 champion Leylah Fernandez would return for this year’s event, whose main draw begins on November 2. Whether he would try to make it third time lucky with Raducanu, the 2021 US Open champion, was a “separate conversation”, although Cheng added that “if Naomi Osaka can play, she’ll play”. Beaten in the second round last year by eventual champion Victoria Mboko, Eala, 21, said: “I loved playing in Hong Kong last year, and I’m super excited to come back. The crowds were amazing, and I love the city.” Despite being injured, Osaka visited the 2024 edition. The four-time grand slam champion played in 2017 as a 20-year-old, beating Venus Williams in round two but falling to eventual champion Anastasia Pavlyuchenkova in the last eight. Cheng said the Japanese world No 17 had cited her fondness for the food and the humidity as reasons for wanting to come back, along with remembering that “before she became famous, we really looked after her”. “I can’t control their physical conditions, but I don’t want to invest in players who just come for [their own ends],” Cheng said. “I want them to enjoy being and competing in Hong Kong. That’s the requirement, and it’s how we have an authentic line-up. “We’re not like some other countries that invest big time in player appearances. That’s not the philosophy or business model of HKCTA.” Having climbed to world No 18 this year, the wildly popular Eala is sticking to her guns over playing in the Asian Games, despite having to miss the China Open, which is a WTA 1000 event and therefore mandatory for players. Eala has asked for a release, but if it is not granted she can expect ranking and financial penalties. On the men’s side, Carlos Alcaraz, the world No 2, recently said he planned to start ignoring appearance demands to preserve his body. Cheng acknowledged that “we want to get a piece of the top players everywhere they go”, but added that the WTA Tour “wants protection, and comfort that the players are fit and playing the events they want them to play”. It has been a landmark week for Hong Kong tennis, after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced in his annual Policy Address on Wednesday that Victoria Park Tennis Stadium would be redeveloped. Opened 44 years ago, the site is fit to host only the lowest-tier tournaments on the men’s and women’s tours. Revealing that work on the upgrade would begin “as soon as is practicable”, Cheng said that “Hong Kong should be targeting 500-level events, minimum, for men and women”. Should the women’s Hong Kong Open be bumped up from 250 status, it could conceivably move from its end-of-year graveyard slot. Cheng said the HKCTA would “see what works for the tour”, but observed that the women’s players decamp en masse to Asia from late September until November. “You’re looking at those slots to see what makes sense for Hong Kong and for the tour,” he added. Despite the positive news, Hong Kong tennis is also facing one of its most important months in recent years. Having failed to meet the requirements for Tier A status at the city’s Sports Institute, it needs an Asian Games medal to be spared the axe. Cheng pointed to the sport’s “consistent performance” and pair of National Games medals last year, but said, with his lawyer’s hat on, that “we have to follow the rules”. Not winning a medal, the responsibility for which is likely to fall to Coleman Wong Chak-lam in the men’s singles, would mean not having “the same infrastructure or funding support, and we’d have to figure it out ourselves”. Nonetheless, Cheng pleaded tennis’s case on account of its “four main pillars being on the way up”. “My heart says, Everything is moving on the right trajectory, do we really want to put a brake on it?” The task of obtaining the medal that would earn a reprieve will fall squarely at the feet of the world No 112 Wong, who is ranked higher than any player in the city’s history and was briefly inside the top 100. “It’s such a brutal sport,” Cheng said. “This is where I challenge the [HKSI] rules, because you’re looking at one result over consistency, which isn’t fair. In tennis, you need consistency to break into the world’s top 100.” Hong Kong will discover its fate before Badosa, the former world No 2, who decided she wanted to play during a training visit to the city last year, 2024 champion Shnaider and crowd darling Eala arrive in November.

title: Bail out or downsize? Malaysia’s stark choice as AirAsia losses mount
description: Rival carriers lack commercial incentive to take over unprofitable routes, which could force the government into a subsidy dilemma, analysts say.
content: Malaysia could struggle to preserve some domestic air links if low-cost carrier AirAsia is forced to scale back operations, analysts have warned, as rival airlines would have little commercial incentive to take over unprofitable routes. That reality could leave the government facing a stark choice: allow domestic flight services to shrink or step in with subsidies for essential routes, rather than assuming competitors will automatically fill any void left by the country’s largest budget airline. The concern has taken on added urgency as AirAsia seeks fresh financing following a sharp rise in jet fuel costs, which contributed to heavy losses across its wider airline group. The government had already sounded out full-service flag carrier Malaysia Airlines and hybrid operator Batik Air on whether they could expand into AirAsia’s domestic routes should its financial position worsen, Reuters reported on Wednesday. Both carriers indicated a willingness to take on more routes, but doing so at scale could require them to assume AirAsia’s existing aircraft leases, according to two sources familiar with the discussions. Batik Air chief executive Chandran Rama Muthy separately told national news agency Bernama that the carrier was able to “bring aircraft in quickly” to help meet domestic demand if required. According to data from the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia, AirAsia handled a third of all passengers passing through Malaysian airports in the first quarter of the year, compared with 17.1 per cent for Malaysia Airlines and 10.3 per cent for Batik Air. Malaysia has no other large-scale budget operator; Firefly, the next largest domestic carrier, accounted for just 4 per cent of traffic. Domestic difficulty Analysts said rival airlines were most likely to prioritise adding capacity to commercially attractive routes, leaving thinner, secondary domestic services vulnerable. Wang Kun, an assistant professor at Hong Kong Polytechnic University’s department of industrial and systems engineering, said international routes within Southeast Asia were generally more attractive to carriers because of established demand and existing low-cost competition. “If the expected commercial return is insufficient, other airlines may choose not to enter the route or may provide less capacity unless an appropriate support mechanism is available,” Wang said. He added that even profitable routes could not be replaced overnight, as expansion would depend on aircraft availability, staffing, airport slots and other operational bottlenecks. Fu Xiaowen, a transport economist and head of the same university department, agreed that while competitors would probably move into AirAsia’s profitable routes over the medium to long term, they could not stretch existing fleets and crews indefinitely. “There’s a safety limit on the number of hours a pilot can fly,” Fu said, adding that the government could protect essential links by allowing fewer flights rather than trying to match AirAsia’s previous schedules. Wang said routes deemed essential but not commercially viable could be sustained through targeted passenger or seat subsidies, government purchases of capacity or competitive tenders in which airlines bid to operate them. Malaysia already uses such a model: the federal government pays 209 million ringgit (US$50 million) annually to subsidise rural air services in Sabah and Sarawak. Those routes are now operated by state-owned AirBorneo, which took over the operations from Malaysia Airlines’ regional arm, MASwings, in January. Extending such frameworks could protect vital domestic links without requiring a broader state bailout of an airline. Fu said government intervention would come with significant costs, including to taxpayers and through the precedent it set for future rescues. “But if you do not intervene, it’s going to create a disruption to the whole economy,” he added, pointing to the effects on passengers, creditors, suppliers and local government. Fuel squeeze The contingency planning comes as AirAsia’s parent group faces mounting financial pressure caused by this year’s surge in global fuel prices. While Malaysia Airlines and Batik Air were similarly exposed to the rising costs, AirAsia faced the spike largely unhedged after shelving its hedging plans in January. By April, chief executive Bo Lingam acknowledged the carrier could not afford to hedge at prevailing prices. Jet fuel prices surged to average US$183 a barrel in the second quarter amid market disruptions due to the Iran war. AirAsia Group subsequently reported a headline net loss of 830.5 million ringgit, which included 331 million ringgit in foreign-exchange losses. The group said its core short-haul operations in Malaysia remained profitable, with losses concentrated in its long-haul business and regional subsidiaries in Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia. Wang said budget airlines were particularly vulnerable to fuel price volatility because fuel made up a large share of their variable operating costs compared with full-service carriers, which generated additional revenue from services including meals and checked baggage. AirAsia’s second-quarter accounts show current liabilities of 18.4 billion ringgit against 954 million ringgit in cash reserves at the end of June. The carrier is seeking up to US$1 billion in international debt and 700 million ringgit in local credit lines, though sources cited by Reuters say it needs at least US$3 billion. In a September 2 statement, AirAsia Group said its fundraising was primarily aimed at debt restructuring, refinancing and consolidating its balance sheet. Fu said the exact size of the funding shortfall would heavily influence policymakers’ response. “If they are close to a deal, the government only needs to provide some support,” Fu said, while a much larger shortfall could be a signal for the government to proceed more cautiously. In a press release issued on Friday, AirAsia Group said it was managing industry-wide pressure from fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and higher costs through fare adjustments, capacity cuts and fleet optimisation. The company said it would not be “distracted by unsubstantiated speculation from anonymous sources”. Lingam said in the same release that AirAsia had recovered about 70 per cent of second-quarter fuel-price increases through dynamic fares and lower non-fuel operating costs and that the group had returned 25 older, less fuel-efficient aircraft to lessors on what it described as favourable commercial terms, reducing its fixed lease burden. He explained that the airline had cut third-quarter capacity by 20 per cent to 25 per cent during a traditionally weaker travel period but was preparing to raise capacity again towards pre-war levels in the fourth quarter as year-end demand strengthened. Wider economic costs Mohd Harridon Mohamed Suffian, an associate professor at the University of Kuala Lumpur, said AirAsia’s low-fare model supported a wider network of small businesses, hospitality vendors and technical subcontractors dependent on passenger volumes. “AirAsia employs thousands of workers, and there are numerous subcontractors,” he said. Allowing AirAsia to collapse would be “financially calamitous” for Malaysia’s economy, Harridon said, though he stressed that the carrier should first try to raise funds privately. Should state-backed guarantees or loans eventually be needed, Harridon added, the government “should have a say in AirAsia’s financial operations”. AirAsia had previously said it did not comment on market speculation. However, deputy group chief executive Farouk Kamal told Reuters the airline remained focused on business continuity and continued to see strong demand. Any job losses would also reverberate through an already saturated aviation labour market. A representative for the National Union of Flight Attendants Malaysia said on September 10 the country was “overflooded with aviation professionals, especially technical engineers and pilots”, adding that qualified Malaysian staff were also being recruited by overseas operators, particularly airlines in the Middle East.

title: Letters | Northern Metropolis can offer a clean slate for educational innovation
description: Readers discuss the planned education hub near the city’s northern border, and smart traffic management systems.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. With education designated as a growth engine in Hong Kong’s new development blueprint, the planned Northern Metropolis university town faces a pivotal moment. Artificial intelligence (AI) is dismantling the foundations of traditional learning. Simply expanding science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) programmes or enrolment capacity will not set us apart. If Hong Kong is to become a premier global education hub in the AI era, it must pioneer a fundamental pedagogical transformation. Higher education must pivot away from theory-heavy knowledge recalls and towards essential human skills development: systems thinking, emotional intelligence, critical thinking and ethical reasoning. These must be cultivated through active, interdisciplinary learning and real-time problem-solving. Beyond standard exchange programmes, universities must forge strategic partnerships with companies and civic leaders around the world, enabling students to tackle live business and social challenges. Cross-border virtual internships are gaining traction, directly mirroring a modern economy where remote collaboration across time zones is the baseline for 21st century commerce. We also need a fundamental overhaul of assessment, moving from summative knowledge exams to formative evaluation of transferable skills, a shift now enabled by AI. This also requires unbundling the traditional four-year degree into stackable microcredentials, allowing students to cycle fluidly between full-time employment, remote modules and campus-based sprints over a lifetime. While legacy institutions can struggle with innovation amid administrative inertia, the Northern Metropolis offers a clean slate to deploy modern pedagogical and operational models. The San Francisco-based Minerva Project offers a reference point. Free of traditional physical campuses and powered by digital technology, Minerva engages students through active learning, continuous rubric assessments and immersive real-world projects across global cities. Founded in 2011, Minerva recently launched a global university system to scale the cultivation of “critical wisdom” in the AI age. Governments, philanthropists and educational institutions are invited to support and join its network of member institutions. We do not need bigger and shinier versions of 20th century universities in the Northern Metropolis. To become a true international education hub in the AI era, we must pioneer the future of human intelligence. Hong Kong institutions can pursue two complementary paths: fast-tracking innovation by joining Minerva’s global university system or engineering a home-grown 21st century model tailored to the Asian economy. This is the moment for policymakers, university leaders and philanthropists to unite behind a bold vision and act together. Rachel Chan, North Point Give pedestrian countdown timers the green light The Hong Kong government’s recent announcement of 30 new artificial intelligence-powered projects to enhance public services sounds promising on paper. However, the Transport Department plans to deploy AI-controlled traffic lights at the busy junction of Great George Street and Gloucester Road in Causeway Bay, which officials claim will reduce pedestrian waiting times by up to 20 seconds, raises questions. What exactly is the algorithm driving these smart lights, and how can pedestrians verify that their waiting times have actually decreased? A simple, effective solution would be to install pedestrian countdown timers, a tool the Transport Department has resisted for decades. After a brief trial in 2006, the department removed the timers, arguing they did not improve safety. Subsequent small-scale trials in 2018 and 2023 yielded little progress. Today, Hong Kong pedestrians are still forced to play a guessing game at crossings, rushing before the green light starts flashing – a signal that legally bars them from stepping onto the road. Meanwhile, the use of a red light projected on the ground to remind pedestrians not to cross the road seems to be expanding, but it’s unclear how helpful this is. Cities like Taipei, Bangkok and New York have long embraced countdown timers. Some show the remaining crossing time, while others display the remaining wait time. It is paradoxical that a world-class city with Hong Kong’s immense traffic density still lacks this basic infrastructure. Transparency and accountability are the cornerstones of effective governance. If the government wants the public to embrace its “smart city” vision, it must prove its policies work. I strongly urge the Transport Department to reconsider its pedantic stance, share the rationale behind the algorithm that controls the traffic light and install pedestrian countdown timers to make our streets truly smart and user-friendly. Karl Shieu, Mong Kok

title: On This Day | Ngong Ping 360 cable car opens in Hong Kong after typhoon delay - SCMP archive
description: Attraction officially launches after 3-month delay following Typhoon Prapiroon damage.
content: This article was first published on September 18, 2006. Breezy launch is on the cards By Dennis Eng The Ngong Ping 360 cable car will open today in one of the windiest months of the year, according to the Hong Kong Observatory. Windy conditions with gusts reaching 90km/h occur on 5.5 days for a total of 52 hours in September on average, according to measurements taken at Ngong Ping between 2002 and last year. June, July and August are typically the windiest months. The Observatory’s forecast for today is for moderate north to northeasterly winds. The cable car is scheduled to open at 1pm after three months of delays due to glitches and further testing. Electrical and Mechanical Services Department staff will be on site to monitor the inauguration. The department will also conduct both prearranged and surprise inspections during the initial period. The system suffered some damage in Typhoon Prapiroon seven weeks ago. Early this month, the Observatory submitted its study on wind patterns in the area to the cable car operator, Skyrail-ITM. Secretary for Economic Development and Labour Stephen Ip Shu-kwan has said the system is designed to handle local weather conditions. Its operator also manages the Skyrail Rainforest Cableway in Cairns, Australia, which it said experienced similar weather conditions to those of Hong Kong. But “wind conditions in Australia and Hong Kong can be quite different”, said Lo Kok-keung, a Polytechnic University engineering expert. “Even though the system is designed to cope with wind speeds in excess of 100km/h, it’s no longer safe to carry passengers.” Mr Lo attended a trial run of the cable car on June 14, a few hours before Chief Executive Donald Tsang Yam-kuen enjoyed his first ride. Three days later, in another trial run, a cabin approaching the Ngong Ping terminal collided with another cabin, triggering an automatic safety mechanism that halted the system and stranded 500 people in their cabins for two hours. The problem was blamed on a failure in the cabin spacing system.

title: ByteDance spin-off Anew Labs raises US$290m as AI drug developers enjoy fundraising boom
description: As AI’s role in drug design advances rapidly, Chinese start-ups are ramping up fundraising efforts.
