content: China is seeing a fresh fundraising boom for artificial intelligence-powered drug developers, with start-ups including a ByteDance spin-off raising hundreds of millions of dollars this week as investors rush to back domestic challengers to Anthropic and Isomorphic Labs. Anew Labs, a Shanghai-based AI drug discovery firm and former unit of Chinese tech giant ByteDance, has raised US$290 million at a valuation of US$1.5 billion, according to an informed source. Investors included prominent venture capital firms such as HSG – formerly Sequoia China – IDG Capital and 5Y Capital, the source said, with ByteDance maintaining a 56 per cent stake. Anew Labs, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, operates a range of AI models for biomolecular structure prediction and design. They include AnewFold, its in-house foundation model, and Protenix, an open-source reproduction of AlphaFold 3, the most advanced biomolecular prediction AI model from Google DeepMind and its Isomorphic Labs spin-off. The Chinese company said on its website that it has four drugs in its development pipeline, including an oral small-molecule drug for immunological diseases. On Thursday it launched its AnewDDE agentic platform, which it said was designed to address “fragmented” AI workflows in drug discovery. AI’s role in drug design is advancing rapidly. Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo, formerly Novo Nordisk, announced a partnership with Anthropic on Wednesday, saying it would use the US AI firm’s models and its Claude Science platform to accelerate the discovery and development of new medicines. Anthropic said in June that its Mythos 5 model, only available to selected partners, made aspects of the drug design process around 10 times faster. The company said last month that its Claude Mythos Preview and Opus 4.8 models had designed protein binders from scratch that succeeded against 14 of 15 targets. Start-ups in China have ramped up their fundraising efforts. Nutshell Therapeutics, a Shanghai-based biotech firm focused on developing small molecule drugs with AI, said on Tuesday that it had raised tens of millions of US dollars in a C+ round, with backers including Citic Capital, Decheng Capital and state-backed Fortune Venture Capital. With nearly 20 planned drugs in its pipeline, the company’s lead programme targeting tumours was advancing through phase one and two clinical trials in the United States and China, it said on its website. Beijing-based AI drug discovery firm AIPher, started in July and incubated by Tsinghua University’s Institute for AI Industry Research, said this week that it had completed an angel round of financing worth about 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million). The start-up’s fastest-progressing pipeline, targeting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, is in the pre-preclinical candidate stage, according to an article published on its official WeChat account on Monday.

title: Can the new Pinglu Canal become China’s Yangtze of the southwest?
description: The 134.2km waterway promises shorter routes to the sea and lower transport costs, potentially reshaping the fortunes of landlocked regions.
content: The opening of China’s first new river-to-sea canal since 1949 – which will boost trade links with Southeast Asia – could transform the economy of the country’s landlocked southwestern interior in ways comparable to the Yangtze’s role in Shanghai’s rise, according to its operator. The 134.2km (83.4 mile) Pinglu Canal, which opened on Wednesday, links a major tributary of the Pearl River in the southern Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region with the Gulf of Tonkin, known as the Beibu Gulf in China, serving as a short cut for cargo moving between western China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). The project was prioritised to ease severe congestion at traditional logistics hubs and additional projects were already under way to maximise the waterway’s economic potential, the operator said. “China was forced to build a new canal by the aggravating ‘chokepoints’ along the Yangtze and Pearl rivers,” executives from Guangxi Pinglu Canal Group said during an event at the annual China-Asean Expo on Thursday in Nanning, Guangxi’s capital. “Goods from Sichuan, Chongqing, Yunnan and other western regions bound for Southeast Asia are usually stuck in major hubs like Shanghai and Guangzhou as well as the Three Gorges Dam, where ships may have to wait for days to pass.” Construction on the canal, which involved levelling mountains and carving out artificial waterways through Guangxi’s rugged terrain, took 48 months following regulatory approval. To widen and deepen river beds, engineers deployed heavy-duty dredgers designed for island-building operations in the South China Sea, local media reported, citing the canal’s chief engineer, Wei Dejian. The vessels blasted through rock and sucked up sand at a rate of up to 6,000 cubic metres (211,888 cubic feet) per hour, excavating as deep as 35 metres (114.8 feet) below the riverbed. More than 315 million cubic metres (11.12 billion cubic feet) of soil and granules were removed to make way for the canal. The operator noted that Pinglu was one of only three waterways in China, alongside the Yangtze and Pearl rivers, capable of accommodating 5,000-tonne capacity vessels travelling in both directions. “Its significance cannot be overstated … If the Yangtze’s shipping capacity was behind the rise of Shanghai and other cities like Nanjing and Wuhan, Pinglu may also bring the same change to southwestern China, which is still an economic backwater,” Wei told local media. But to accommodate that much shipping, engineers had their work cut out. The operational demands required the canal to be at least 80 metres (262.5 feet) wide and 6.7 metres (22 feet) deep, with a minimum turning radius of 360 metres (1,181 feet) at bends. Numerous bridges were demolished or raised to ensure sufficient navigational clearance. Overcoming a 65-metre (213.3 feet) height difference between the canal and its coastal outlet in Qinzhou, where the canal empties into the Gulf of Tonkin, posed a significant obstacle. Engineers addressed it by building three massive two-way ship locks, some as deep as 40 metres (131.2 feet). Despite the authorities’ promise of economic benefits, the project faced scrutiny and even resistance from some Guangxi residents. There were widespread concerns over inadequate water during the region’s dry season, which runs from October to March and can bring long spells of low rainfall, according to a Pinglu Canal Group expert who declined to be named. Residents in Qinzhou and other areas also raised objections over potential saltwater intrusion during low-discharge months, which could threaten local freshwater supplies. To mitigate these risks, engineers incorporated water-saving designs, including storage pools stacked on top of each other at major ship locks. The coming dry season could provide the first real-world test in a region known for its fragile ecosystem. On Wednesday, the governments of Guangxi and Yunnan launched a partnership framework to streamline shipping along the Pinglu Canal. The new route is expected to shorten journeys by 560km (348 miles), reducing transport costs and travel time. Previously, export goods from Yunnan had to follow a tortuous route to Guangzhou before being shipped overseas. Guangxi is also promoting supporting projects intended to unlock more of the canal’s economic potential, including another proposed waterway linking the central province of Hunan with Guangxi and connecting to the Pinglu Canal.

title: Brussels announces dates for second round of China-EU trade talks in Beijing next month
description: October 8-9 schedule revealed after video call between European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
content: The next round of China-EU trade talks is set to take place in Beijing from October 8 to 9, Brussels announced on Thursday following a video call between European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, adding that Europe wanted to see a “credible” outcome. The European Commission said that during a call lasting more than an hour, the two sides reviewed “extensive work” carried out at senior-official level covering issues including the management of Chinese exports to Europe, European firms’ access to the Chinese market and China’s export controls on rare earths. Brussels said it was important that the first concrete outcomes be delivered at the second round of talks under the EU-China Trade and Investment Consultations framework next month, which would signal that both sides were “moving from rhetoric to results”. “That outcome needs to be credible,” the European Commission said in a statement, adding that a European team would travel to Beijing for preparatory work later this month. The Commerce Ministry in Beijing released a one-line statement that said Wang held a video meeting with Sefcovic at the latter’s request. The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Brussels was seeking a commitment from Beijing to restrict sales of made-in-China hybrid vehicles to about 15 per cent of the EU market. The bloc also wanted China to apply similar policies in several other sectors, such as chemicals, and buy more EU exports, it said. The European Commission did not reply to a request for confirmation of the report. China urges the EU to abide by WTO rules, keep its market open [and] amend the discriminatory provisions He Yadong, Ministry of Commerce A Chinese source said Beijing was frustrated by Brussels’ unwillingness to make any compromises over the summer – before an EU team travelled to China at the end of last month. Ministry of Commerce officials were annoyed by the EU’s approach, the source said, viewing it as no way to run a negotiation. During European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s state-of-the-union speech on Wednesday, she warned that a “second China shock” was already affecting Europe and vowed that Brussels would use all available tools to rebalance its trade relationship with the country. At a news conference on Thursday, Ministry of Commerce spokesman He Yadong said China would not engage in “megaphone diplomacy”, nor would it participate in a “war of words” with the EU. He said the EU had rolled out legislation this year – including an amendment to the Cybersecurity Act, the Industrial Accelerator Act and the Public Procurement Act – that would introduce “discriminatory provisions, and continuously tightening market-access conditions”. “China urges the EU to abide by WTO rules, keep its market open, amend the discriminatory provisions … and create a fair, transparent, and non-discriminatory business environment for enterprises investing and operating in Europe,” He said. “China will closely monitor the EU’s legislative process and evaluate the relevant impact in a timely manner.”

title: China’s ‘future Elon Musk’ solves daily problems with AI; vocabulary method draws 20 million views
description: Looking ahead, Yang is driven to become a programmer or AI researcher, determined to leave his own mark on the world.
content: A 13-year-old boy from eastern China has garnered significant attention online for his ability to leverage artificial intelligence and programming to solve everyday challenges. Yang Xizhe, a junior secondary school student from Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, stands at an impressive 1.9 metres tall and has amassed a following of over 500,000 on mainland social media platforms. Growing up in a city celebrated for its vibrant technology ecosystem, he identifies as an “AI native.” Yang believes that for his generation, AI is becoming as vital as air and water. In February last year, he gained recognition when a video demonstrating his use of AI to memorise English vocabulary attracted 20 million views. He uploaded a photo of the vocabulary list to Doubao and created prompts to guide the chatbot in generating engaging stories and personalised exercises based on the words. Yang’s AI-driven learning strategy resonated with parents and educators. Some viewers noted that the video had inspired greater interest in learning among their children, while a teacher expressed the desire to incorporate his approach into their first lesson of the new school term. This year, he transitioned from online learning to hands-on innovation by taking part in several hackathons – time-limited programming competitions where teams collaborate to create software projects. His first project was an AI-powered vision system designed to assist visually impaired individuals in applying make-up. This product secured first place at the Moonshot 48 Hackathon. Later, he took part in HackMIT China 2026, where his team was awarded the Best Pitch Award and secured second place in their category. Their project, a smart lunchbox equipped with AI vision and sensors, provides personalised dietary suggestions based on users’ profiles and meals while enabling parents to monitor their children’s eating habits at school. In April, Yang formed a team with an average age of 13 to compete in RedNote’s hackathon championship. His team developed an AI-powered diagnostic and optimisation tool for original content creators, which earned a special award and attracted a purchase offer of 100,000 yuan (US$15,000) from a company. In a speech, Yang reflected on how his passion for programming began in Primary Two. After playing The Legend of Zelda, he became captivated by the idea of creating his own game. Following his father’s advice, he began to teach himself the visual programming platform Scratch, subsequently advancing to C++ and vibe coding. According to Dushi Express, neither of Yang’s parents have a formal technology background, but they have actively educated themselves about AI to keep pace with their son’s interests. As Yang’s profile has risen, some Chinese technology influencers have referred to him as a “young genius” and “a future Elon Musk.” Nevertheless, Yang and his parents have reportedly approached such labels and accolades with modesty. Yang has also established personal guidelines to balance schoolwork and AI exploration, with the aim of maintaining above-average grades while dedicating three hours each day to programming. Looking to the future, he aspires to pursue a career as a programmer or AI researcher. “If possible, I hope to make even a small difference in the world,” he shared with the media. One online observer remarked: “In the future, Yang could become the kind of employee every company desires, with a decade of programming experience by the age of 23.” “I hope that someone like Yang, with his curiosity and determination to learn, will evolve into an entrepreneur who makes a significant impact on the world,” another added.

title: Authorities aim to launch revamped Huanggang Port on October 12
description: Start date will meet government’s fourth-quarter target, with travellers able to clear Hong Kong and mainland immigration under joint system.
content: Hong Kong’s redeveloped Huanggang Port could begin operations as early as October 12, allowing cross-border travellers to complete dual immigration procedures in a single inspection under a new joint clearance system. The South China Morning Post learned on Friday that authorities were aiming to open the facility on that date, although the decision would depend on its operational readiness. An October 12 launch date would meet the government’s target of starting operations in the fourth quarter this year. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his policy address this week that the facility would adopt a co-location arrangement and introduce a new “collaborative inspection and joint clearance” model to improve efficiency and passenger clearance experience. Under the system, travellers will be able to complete Hong Kong and mainland Chinese immigration procedures in one go by having their documents read or their faces scanned at automated channels. Cross-border drivers will similarly be able to complete procedures for both jurisdictions through a “five-party inspection” arrangement at joint one-stop vehicle lanes. The complex, located in Shenzhen’s Futian district, will replace the existing Lok Ma Chau-Huanggang crossing arrangements, under which passengers must clear Hong Kong immigration, take a shuttle bus across the Shenzhen River and undergo mainland clearance separately. Authorities said the new system could reduce the typical clearance time from about 30 minutes to five. Huanggang will be the first boundary control point to use the joint inspection model, under which travellers queue only once despite being processed by officers from both jurisdictions. The opening follows about six years of redevelopment and months of operational tests. Security chief Chris Tang Ping-keung said in August that authorities would conduct more than 100 exercises, including large-scale drills involving at least 10,000 participants, to test passenger flows, transport arrangements and emergency responses. Authorities have said the redeveloped port will initially be able to handle 200,000 passenger trips a day, with capacity potentially rising to 300,000 in future. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, released alongside the policy address, also identified a Northern Link spur line connecting to the new Huanggang Port as one of the major railway projects supporting the Northern Metropolis megaproject. The redeveloped Huanggang crossing will increase the capacity of Hong Kong’s boundary control points and facilitate the movement of cross-border passengers, according to the five-year blueprint. The additional capacity comes as cross-border travel continues to grow. Hong Kong received 36.67 million visitors in the first eight months of this year, an 11 per cent increase from the same period in 2025, with mainland travellers accounting for about 78 per cent of the total.

title: US firm Waymo to launch robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028
description: Trained specialists will drive Jaguar I-Pace vehicles and help Waymo adapt its technology to Singapore’s road layouts and other conditions.
content: Waymo plans to launch its robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028, giving the US company its first foothold in Southeast Asia. Fully electric Jaguar I-Pace vehicles were due to arrive in the city state in the coming months, ahead of preparations for a commercial launch, the company said on Friday. From 2027, trained autonomous specialists will manually drive the vehicles to help Waymo adapt its technology to Singapore’s road layouts, monsoon conditions and other local features. The service is expected to open to the public through the Waymo app in 2028. Waymo, a subsidiary of Google parent Alphabet Inc., operates ride-hailing services using driverless, or autonomous, vehicles. It announced its Singapore plans at a press conference with the Ministry of Transport and Land Transport Authority. “Singapore has built one of the safest, most efficient, and most forward-thinking transportation ecosystems in the world. Their focus on reliability, sustainability, and human-centric progress directly mirrors how we have built Waymo’s technology and service,” said Tekedra Mawakana, co-CEO of Waymo. “As we begin our journey here, we are committed to listening to the community, creating high-skilled local operational jobs, and working hand in hand with national leaders to complement Singapore’s world-class public transit network.” Earlier this year, Singapore’s major ride-hailing companies Grab and ComfortDelGro were given the green light to collaborate with leading Chinese AV manufacturers WeRide and Pony.ai, respectively, to test and deploy shuttle taxi services on public roads in Punggol. “Waymo brings world-class technology and operational expertise to Singapore, and will move us towards our vision of creating new transport options for Singaporeans,” said Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow. “The partnership will also strengthen our ecosystem and create new capabilities and jobs here.” Waymo said it planned to complement Singapore’s public transit network by bridging first- and last-mile transit gaps while offering zero direct emissions. At the launch on Friday, Siow said the feedback on autonomous vehicles (AV) in the Punggol trial had been overwhelmingly positive with 99 per cent of passengers saying that they would recommend the experience to someone else. The AVs, which currently shuttle passengers to fixed points along loops, will soon be tested for point-to-point service within Punggol. This will be done progressively by adding more pickup and drop-off points. Testing and preparation for Waymo will begin for deployment in the western part of Singapore, starting with the Labrador and Harbourfront area. “This will include new use cases such as travelling to work, weekend travel, and serving industrial areas which have fewer transport options,” Siow said. Singapore expects to increase its total fleet to several hundred vehicles in the next two years, according to Siow. Earlier this month, ride-hailing app Grab announced that it was expanding its fleet from 10 to 50. As the industry grows, new jobs will be created and people will be needed to manage the vehicle fleets, operate the vehicles remotely, maintain sophisticated systems, test new applications, analyse data, and ensure that the services run safely and reliably. Some of these jobs will be open to taxi and private hire car drivers, Siow said. “The government will subsidise up to 90 per cent of salaries during training, because we are committed to supporting any driver who wishes to take on new opportunities,” he added. According to Mawakana, peer-reviewed data shows that Waymo dramatically reduced serious injury crashes and pedestrian injury crashes compared to humans, had a 94 per cent reduction in injury-causing crashes, and 84 per cent fewer cyclist crashes with injuries compared to human drivers in the United States. “By offering 24/7 safe transportation, we hope to support Singapore’s green vision while serving everyday needs, from helping students get home safely to supporting an ageing demographic,” she said. “We look forward to working side-by-side with the Singaporean government, community partners, and local residents to ensure our service directly reflects the needs of Singapore’s residents and visitors alike.” The company on Tuesday announced it aimed to launch Japan’s first fully autonomous commercial taxi service in Tokyo in 2027. It also has plans to launch in London and Munich.

title: Filipino fishers count the cost of South China Sea dispute
description: Blocked from accessing Scarborough Shoal and hit by local dredging, Zambales fishermen say their weekly incomes have collapsed.
content: For fishermen like Joey Marabe in the Philippine province of Zambales, the geopolitical contest playing out in the South China Sea can be measured in dwindling catches and shrinking incomes, as the presence of Chinese vessels around a contested shoal increasingly limits where they can work. “It’s a huge drop. Before, a lot of us who could go out to Scarborough Shoal used to bring home around 15,000 pesos (US$238) a week, a comfortable amount for our families,” said Marabe, a resident of Masinloc town and provincial coordinator for the national fisherfolk federation Pamalakaya. “But now, since we’ve been restricted from going out that far, and we’re limited to our own nearer waters … we’re down to 600 to 700 [pesos], struggling hard just for one day.” The decline in earnings has coincided with rising fuel and operational costs, piling further pressure on fishermen who say they are being pushed into overcrowded waters closer to shore. At the centre of their struggle is Scarborough Shoal, or Huangyan Island – a coral atoll and rich fishing ground known in the Philippines as Bajo de Masinloc. Claimed by both countries, the shoal lies about 124 nautical miles (230km) west of Zambales and has been under Beijing’s de facto control since a tense, months-long stand-off in 2012. In 2016, a Hague-based arbitral tribunal ruled that Scarborough Shoal was a traditional fishing ground for several nations and declared that China had unlawfully prevented Filipinos from fishing there. The tribunal did not rule on sovereignty over the feature. Beijing rejects the ruling as “illegal, null and void”, maintaining that the shoal is Chinese territory and that its coastguard patrols are legitimate exercises of sovereignty. That maritime presence has intensified recently. The Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative recorded 933 Chinese coastguard ship-days – a unit of measurement equal to one vessel operating in an area for one full day – around Scarborough Shoal in the first half of 2026 alone, almost matching the 1,099 ship-days logged across the whole of 2025. For Filipino crews, the patrols make reaching or remaining at the shoal risky. Fishermen report being chased, ordered away, targeted by water cannons or having their anchor lines cut. Beijing says its coastguard acts lawfully within Chinese jurisdiction, defending the use of warnings and blockades against Philippine vessels it accuses of intruding into its waters. Reduced access to the shoal is only one part of a wider economic crisis hitting Zambales fishing communities. Declining nearshore fish stocks, rising fuel prices, temporary no-sail zones for military exercises and coastal dredging are all taking a heavy toll. “No fisherman can come near the shoal,” said Leonardo Cuaresma, head of the New Masinloc Fishermen’s Association, adding that Chinese ships patrolled the area “24/7”, forcing many Filipinos into crowded municipal waters where catches were smaller. “Some go hook-and-line fishing here in municipal waters, but only catch two or three kilos, sometimes as much as five kilos, because almost all our municipal waters really have weak fish stocks now,” he said. Rising fuel costs have made longer journeys harder to sustain. Marabe recalled how crews used to travel 80 to 100 nautical miles offshore in convoys, whereas most now opted for short, quick trips to save fuel. Rough seas add another layer of difficulty. The southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat, has long forced fishermen to scale back trips, but Marabe said falling earnings were pushing some to take greater risks. “We usually comply with guidelines on when we can and cannot fish … but we have to force ourselves and try for our families’ needs,” he said. Local waters were also temporarily disrupted by Balikatan, the annual joint military exercises between the Philippines and the US, which included live-fire drills and temporary no-sail zones off Zambales. Cuaresma said the fallout outlasted the exercises, which scared away fish and damaged sensitive coral ecosystems. Dredging concerns Fishermen are also worried by extensive river and estuarine dredging across Zambales. Government officials have defended sediment removal as part of flood control measures, saying the extracted sand generates provincial revenue and supplies infrastructure and land reclamation projects, including Manila Bay and the international airport in Bulacan, north of Manila. But environmentalists and fishing communities warn that large-scale extraction could alter river and coastal ecosystems, particularly during extreme weather. These concerns intensified after heavy rainfall and lahar – volcanic mudflows – caused severe flooding in parts of the province. In August, the Zambales Ecological Network called for an investigation after torrential floods collapsed a bridge in San Marcelino town, cutting off the village of Santa Fe. The group questioned whether changes to the Santo Tomas sediment system caused by dredging had affected natural drainage patterns during extreme rainfall. Marabe said dredging made the water murky. “Silt and everything ends up in the sea,” he said. “And that kills a lot of fish and marine life.” Fernando Siringan, a professor of marine and coastal geology at the University of the Philippines Marine Science Institute, said industrial noise and suspended sediment could disturb marine habitats and spawning grounds. “If you have a boat that’s loud, and material gets suspended in the water, it’s the noise and the suspended material that directly impact the presence of fish,” Siringan said. Dredging has also become politically contentious after reports surfaced last year alleging the involvement of Chinese companies. Representative Leila de Lima sought a congressional inquiry into foreign contractors involved in the operations, including China Harbour Engineering Company, a subsidiary of the state-owned China Communications Construction Company. Government officials have disputed allegations of Chinese involvement and rejected claims that Zambales sand was being used to build artificial islands in the South China Sea. For Marabe, however, the more immediate concern is making fishing viable again. He said longer-term support should include resources for small-scale fishermen, such as shared cold storage to preserve their catch, alongside greater protection for those trying to make a living at sea. “We’re grateful for the five kilos of rice [from the government]. But that’s not what we’re truly after,” Marabe said. “We need protection as fishermen, to be allowed to go out to sea and not be left behind. That’s the freedom we want.”

title: Ancient recipe reveals monastic drink preceding modern Coca-Cola
description: Discovery at Florence’s Saint Mark’s Monastery sheds light on the early origins of cola.
content:
A 19th century recipe recently found in the pharmacy of Saint Mark’s Monastery in Florence describes a drink that may be a precursor to modern cola beverages, according to monks in the Italian city.
The discovery was made while cleaning out the archives. The yellowed recipe outlines the ingredients, which include 30 grams of kola nuts, 10 grams of Bolivian coca leaves and one litre of an alcoholic mixture.
Dominican friar Manuel Russo explained that the recipe is written on a faded advertisement for a “fortifying wine elixir” made from coca leaves and kola nuts.
The advertisement promotes a “fortifying wine elixir” designed to alleviate physical and mental exhaustion, headaches and the weakness that can accompany ageing or extreme exertion.
According to him, this drink was one of the pharmacy’s bestselling products at the time. Missionaries are known to have brought both coca leaves and kola nuts from South America to Tuscany.
If you’re interested in making the drink at home, your ability to obtain the ingredients will depend on your location. While you might be able to find coca leaves, they are not readily available everywhere.
Additionally, in many countries outside South America, laws do not differentiate between coca leaves and other substances containing cocaine, making the possession of coca leaves illegal.
Today’s Coca-Cola is generally recognised as having been invented in 1886 by US pharmacist John Stith Pemberton. He initially created a tonic called Pemberton’s French Wine Coca, which contained coca leaves and kola nuts.
However, when alcohol prohibition made the original formula impractical, Pemberton replaced the alcohol with water and sugar syrup, ultimately creating what we now know as Coca-Cola.
The recently discovered Tuscan recipe predates Pemberton’s invention by several decades. But Russo emphasised that there is no evidence of a direct connection between the monastery drink and Coca-Cola.
Meanwhile, the exact recipe for Coca-Cola has long been and continues to be one of the world’s most famous trade secrets.
The company states that only a limited number of employees are aware of the complete formula, and strict confidentiality agreements bind these individuals. Their identities are kept confidential as well.
There is even a popular myth that only two people know the recipe and that they are never permitted to travel on the same aircraft. The company claims this story is false.
According to Coca-Cola, Pemberton did not personally write down the original formula. The formula was first documented in 1919 and is now kept in a secure vault.
Saint Mark’s Monastery, also known as Convento di San Marco, is one of Florence’s most famous landmarks, renowned for its early Renaissance frescoes by Fra Angelico.
The monastery houses the Antica Farmacia di San Marco, founded in 1436 and one of Florence’s oldest pharmacies. For centuries, Dominican monks provided local residents with medicinal herbs, essences, elixirs, and scented waters.
Today, the pharmacy operates differently.
A single 330ml can of cola contains 35.3 grams or about eight teaspoons of added sugar. This exceeds the World Health Organization’s recommended limit of six teaspoons per day. Drinking too much Coca-Cola and other sugary sodas can harm your health (see graphic).
If you want to drink less soda and stay healthy, try these simple tips.
When you fill your cup with lots of ice, there is less room for soda. This means you drink less sugar in one cup. Just remember to save the rest of your can or bottle for another day instead of finishing it.
Check the nutrition label on the bottle to find drinks without added sugar. You can also try unflavoured bottled water with added electrolytes. These usually have zero sugar.
If you like the fizzy, bubbly feeling of soda, sparkling water is a great replacement. If you buy flavoured sparkling water, check the label to make sure it has no added sugar. A better alternative is to buy plain sparkling water and add fresh fruit or real fruit juice.

title: Style Edit: YDC 2026 spotlights Hong Kong’s fashion trailblazers
description: Up-and-coming designers brought personal stories, experimental craft and fresh perspectives to the runway at the Centrestage annual showcase.
content: The Hong Kong Young Fashion Designers’ Contest (YDC) has always been a barometer of the city’s creativity: a place to test ideas under runway lights. This year’s finale was held on September 5 during the closing of Centrestage – Asia’s premier annual fashion event hosted by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC) – and saw 10 emerging local designers respond to the theme “You” with collections rooted in memory and experience. The top prize went to Tsui Ao-lung for The Tide, a collection inspired by the Cantopop classic “Kuang Chao” (Surging Tide). Depicting the four stages of a woman’s life, Tsui’s pieces stood out for their intricate craftsmanship and unconventional materials. He received HK$60,000 and an overseas internship. Kenneth Cheang King-tung took the Excellence Award and won best art direction for Nostalgia, a poetic exploration inspired by Andrei Tarkovsky’s 1983 film of the same name. Cheang translated his memories of Hong Kong into garments through hand-dyeing, sewing and experimental materials, winning cash prizes totalling HK$50,000 and overseas study trips including a five-day course at the Vogue College of Fashion in London. Jenny Lam Chun-ni’s The Old Si-Fut and New Chai, which explores tensions between workplace veterans and young recruits, was voted My Favourite Collection by the public. Through shifts in proportion, structure and detail, Lam examined the pressure to conform alongside the impulse to push back. The contest was judged by a panel led by HKTDC Garment Advisory Committee chair Katherine Fang. Finalists were mentored by Alex Po and Derek Cheng of gender-fluid fashion label Ponder.er, while Mini Hong Kong marked a decade as YDC’s lead sponsor with a limited edition car-wrap collaboration. Elsewhere at Centrestage, Fashionally.com – the HKTDC’s online platform for promoting local fashion talent – presented its Collection 26, featuring new work by Marcch, Murfi Lau and Ous. Phenotypsetter, Oplus2 and Szmannie, meanwhile, unveiled collections through Fashionally Presentation. Next year, YDC will reach its 50th anniversary – a significant milestone for a contest that continues to offer Hong Kong’s up-and-coming designers a public platform.

title: Style Edit: Loro Piana’s baby cashmere and summer-to-autumn layers
description: Rare raw materials and exacting craftsmanship inform the maison’s approach to exceptional fibres and its fall/winter 2026-27 Back to School collection.
content: There are impulse wardrobes, and then there are considered wardrobes – the kind not shaped by seasonal novelty but rather by materials and craftsmanship with a longer story to tell. For Loro Piana, that story begins in nature: with the changing of the seasons, the knowledge of local herders, and the scarcest, most precious materials. At the heart of this philosophy is baby cashmere, a very rare fibre gathered from the first fleece of a certain breed of domestic goats (Capra hircus) when they are less than a year old. The kids grow an exceptionally fine, downy underfleece to ward off the extreme cold of their home range on Inner Mongolia’s Alashan Plateau. As temperatures rise in the spring, the kids naturally shed this ultra-soft layer, which is gently combed off by herders at exactly the right moment. With each kid’s underfleece yielding only about 30 grams of usable fibre, there is no way to scale up such production. The delicate threads have an average diameter of 13.5 microns, compared with some 15.5 microns for adult cashmere – a difference that is felt as much as measured, with baby cashmere possessing an extraordinary lightness to the touch. The idea for baby cashmere came from Pier Luigi Loro Piana, grandson of the maison’s founder, while he was visiting goat herders in China in the mid-1990s. Just getting the concept off the ground would take immeasurable patience, however. For a decade, the maison worked with select herders to separate the first fleece of the kids from the adult cashmere with which it had traditionally been blended. Then, in Italy, Loro Piana developed the technical expertise to spin and weave the delicate raw material without compromising its character. The first baby cashmere creations finally arrived in 2008. That same respect for provenance, process and performance carries into Loro Piana’s fall/winter 2026-27 Back to School collection, which approaches early-autumn dressing through light layers, relaxed silhouettes and materials chosen for the changeable weeks between high summer and the cooler months. The Spagna jacket, an icon introduced in 1998, appears in Pecora Nera (dark undyed merino wool), while the suede Maremma bomber offers a contemporary interpretation of the Tuscan country jacket. Elsewhere, heritage wools take centre stage with varieties such as Sopra Visso and Merino d’Arles used in tweed outerwear, featuring felted finishes rendered in the rich, earthy shades of a woodland walk: moss green, burnt orange, rust, brown and beige. The season’s most quietly persuasive innovation may be CashDenim, which combines Japanese denim with fine cashmere. Woven slowly on rare vintage looms in Japan, the material brings denim’s familiar utility into dialogue with cashmere’s warmth, appearing in straight-leg jeans and sporty jackets in indigo and mid-blue. It is a material proposition for the in-between season: familiar in appearance, yet notably softer and warmer to wear.

title: Style Edit: Rolex’s timeless commitment to tennis shines at the US Open
description: As the official timekeeper of all four grand slam events, the Swiss watchmaker counts elite players including Carlos Alcaraz and Coco Gauff among its testimonees.
content: When the greatest sporting achievements are forged, Rolex is there. The most iconic of Swiss luxury watchmakers marks the defining moments in the most resonant of athletic spectacles, supporting the leading competitions and events as both timekeeper and sponsor, in sports ranging from equestrianism to motorsport to golf. But nowhere is its involvement quite so profound as in the uber-glamorous world of tennis. Rolex is the official timekeeper of all four grand slam tournaments, beginning its association with The Championships, Wimbledon, as long ago as 1978, and subsequently adding the Australian Open, Roland-Garros and the US Open. The last of these recently concluded its 2026 edition at Flushing Meadows. There, the 23,800-capacity centrepiece is Arthur Ashe Stadium, the largest arena in world tennis, which saw a continuation of the tournament’s and the brand’s long history of remarkable achievements, on and off the court. Many of the US Open’s most memorable moments have been created by players drawn from the ranks of Rolex Testimonees, the select group of elite performers with which the brand partners. They include contemporary stars such as Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz, Coco Gauff, Iga Swiatek, Zheng Qinwen, Stefanos Tsitsipas and Taylor Fritz – as well as numerous legends of the game from the past: the likes of Roger Federer, Li Na, Björn Borg and Chris Evert. These are the players who have been involved in some of the US Open’s most unforgettable encounters. Evert, for example, overcame one of the tournament’s greatest-ever challenges when it moved to Flushing Meadows, and from clay to hard courts, in 1978 – the same year that Rolex first became the official timekeeper of a grand slam event. It meant that she was forced to defend her singles title on an unfamiliar surface, one to which her game was less well suited. It was a challenge she overcame in spectacular style, not dropping a single set during the entire tournament to take home the silverware for an incredible fourth consecutive year. It’s an example of the indefatigable spirit shown over and over again by the sport’s leading stars, one that was dramatically in evidence at this year’s tournament – as ever, with Rolex’s unstinting support.

title: Australia’s Sydney Airport staff shortages prompt plan to close tower overnight
description: To compound the problem, hundreds of Qantas ground workers are set to strike over pay and working conditions next ‌week.
content: Australia’s major airlines have backed a proposal to close Sydney Airport’s control tower overnight to free up air traffic controllers, the latest step to address a persistent labour shortage that is disrupting flights and raising safety concerns. “It sounds like an opportunity we should absolutely explore,” said Stephen Beckett, chief executive officer of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, the group that represents Qantas Airways, its low-cost carrier Jetstar, and Virgin Australia Holdings. “There seems to be some merit to this proposal,” he said in an interview. At least six safety incidents, close calls and mistakes on the tarmac at Sydney since late July have put a spotlight on the lack of controllers and the impact on air travel. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson last month called for the issue to be fixed after 60,000 passengers were affected by flight delays in July alone. The proposal to close the tower was raised at the meeting of a task force specially formed last month to address the disruption in Sydney. Sydney Airport’s existing 11pm – 6am curfew means commercial air traffic would be largely unaffected by any tower closures. But a plan to have no operational tower at Australia’s biggest aviation hub, even temporarily, reflects the urgency of the labour shortfall. Flights exempt from the curfew, such as those dealing with emergencies or carrying medical patients, would have to fend for themselves when landing or taking off. Airservices Australia manages the country’s airspace and employs air traffic controllers at airports. Beckett said the roster of controllers at Sydney had been too fragile for too long. “That’s had a significant impact on passengers,” he said. The unexpected absence of just one controller at the airport on September 11 was enough to cause significant flight delays the same morning. Closing the tower at night would free up two controllers who could, in theory, be deployed during the day. In an email, Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority said, “Airservices Australia is exploring an option to temporarily vary the operating hours of Sydney Air Traffic Control Tower services overnight.” But the agency said it had not received an application seeking approval for such a proposal. Airservices Australia was “considering all options to ensure the efficient use of our qualified workforce,” it said in an email. “Any changes to air traffic services at Sydney Airport would be subject to “thorough safety assessment processes”, including approval by the regulator. Workers strike The labour shortage is expected to become even more acute if hundreds of ⁠Qantas ground workers who handle freight and its QantasLink regional flights go ahead with a strike over pay and working conditions next week. Workers would strike for a 24-hour period on Wednesday in Victoria state and Thursday in the rest of the country, the Transport Workers Union said in a statement on Friday. “Workers do not take this action lightly. Any disruption to freight, including Australia Post shipments, sits solely at the feet of Qantas management ⁠and its brutal disregard for customers and the workforce,” said Michael Kaine, the union’s national secretary. Qantas ‌did not ‌immediately respond to a request for comment. The airline outsourced the jobs of more than 1,800 ground workers in Australia who handled its broader network during the Covid-19 pandemic, in action later deemed illegal. A court last year ordered the airline to pay a record fine of A$90 million (US$64 million) over the matter.

title: China publicly names officials in ‘unprecedented’ hidden-debt crackdown. Can it work?
description: The escalating campaign comes as officially identified hidden debt shrinks, even as broader estimates of local financing vehicle liabilities remain far larger.
content: A recently issued official circular has put China’s long-running problem with hidden local government debt back in the spotlight. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) and the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) jointly outlined six typical cases spanning six provinces where local authorities had fallen short of targets to resolve unrecorded liabilities. “For hidden-debt penalty announcements, it is unprecedented to have the CCDI alongside the MoF,” said Qiao Yide, vice-chairman of the Shanghai Development Research Foundation think tank. “Previously, the MoF alone would issue these case notifications. Bringing in the party’s highest internal disciplinary body sends a sobering reminder to fiscal officials,” Qiao added. The first case concerned Bijie in southwestern China’s Guizhou province. The circular departed from past practice by naming Wu Shenghua, the city’s former Communist Party secretary, in full. Earlier documents typically disclosed only officials’ surnames. According to the circular, Wu had “failed to take effective actions on debt-resolution efforts” between 2022 and 2025. It also said he had made contentious remarks at multiple public gatherings, including the comment: “These debts were run up by previous administrations. Why should I have to pay them back?” Excluding government subsidies, more than 2,100 LGFVs we tracked all posted losses and their earnings capacity is eroding Luo Zhiheng, Yuekai Securities The other five cases in the circular concerned local officials who were faulted for sluggish progress in repaying debt or for irregularly taking on new off-book borrowings. “The revelation of specific cases of breach with official names suggests the government is very determined to resolve the hidden debt issue. This comes at a time when we see a risk that the government may need to deal with new hidden debt,” said Ding Shuang, chief economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered. Ding said declining land-sale revenues had left local governments with spending obligations that could not be fully covered by fiscal revenue. In his assessment, this meant officials were still “incentivised” to borrow outside official budgets, although he expected the amount to be relatively small because of tighter monitoring and disciplinary action. Official data showed that hidden debt identified by Beijing had reached 14.3 trillion yuan (US$2.13 trillion) at the end of 2023, when the central government pledged to eliminate such liabilities by 2028. Following successive rounds of debt swaps funded through special bonds, this had fallen to 6.5 trillion yuan by the end of 2025. But the decline in officially identified hidden debt did not mean broader financial risks had disappeared, according to analysts. Davis Sun, senior director of international public finance at Fitch Ratings, cautioned in a report published on Sunday that China’s 2028 target was “mainly a political and accounting milestone” rather than evidence that most local government financing vehicles (LGFVs) had become financially independent. LGFVs are companies established by local governments to raise funds and finance projects such as infrastructure, and their borrowing has long been an important source of local government financing. Under China’s official definition, meanwhile, hidden debt refers specifically to certain liabilities that rely on government budget allocations for repayment or carry a formal government guarantee. However, some LGFV debt that Beijing does not classify as hidden government debt is included in broader measures used by some global institutions, including the International Monetary Fund. Luo Zhiheng, chief economist at Guangdong-based Yuekai Securities, estimated that total LGFV liabilities nationwide stood at more than 71 trillion yuan – almost 11 times the stock of officially identified hidden debt at the end of last year. Ding at Standard Chartered gave a similar estimate of 73 trillion yuan. In a research note released in early September, Luo said short-term debt accounted for 27.6 per cent of total LGFV liabilities at the end of 2025, one percentage point higher than a year earlier. He added that their underlying ability to generate cash had “continued to weaken” amid a sluggish property market. “Excluding government subsidies, more than 2,100 LGFVs we tracked all posted losses and their earnings capacity is eroding,” Luo said. “Their median return on equity stood at 0.8 per cent last year, meaning every 100 yuan (US$14.90) of equity generated less than one yuan in net profit.” Against this backdrop, Sun of Fitch Ratings suggested that China’s 2028 “no hidden debt” target was unlikely to mark the end of government support for LGFVs. “China’s current debt-substitution programme has eased near-term refinancing pressure, but does not resolve the sector’s underlying debt-service weakness,” he said in the Sunday report.

title: Opinion | Like Shenzhen, the Northern Metropolis is animated by the spirit of experimentation
description: As the flagship project of Hong Kong’s five-year plan, the cross-border hub is built to function as a sandbox – a special zone for bold policy and economic innovation.
content: At the heart of Hong Kong’s first five-year plan lies the Northern Metropolis – a massive tract of land spanning roughly a third of our entire city. Much ink has been spilled over what this project represents and why it matters, but if I had to summarise it in a single sentence, I would call it the “Shenzhen of Hong Kong”. To me, Shenzhen stands as the most miraculous growth story on Earth. Forty-eight years ago, it was a sleepy fishing village with a single muddy main road and just tens of thousands of residents. Today, it is the undisputed tech capital of China and one of the world’s premier innovation hubs. While the exact circumstances, history and status of Hong Kong and Shenzhen differ, both the Northern Metropolis and Shenzhen stem from the very same strain of Chinese political thinking – one that is frequently overlooked and misunderstood by the outside world. Back in 1979, China was an isolated, impoverished nation freshly emerging from the trauma of the Cultural Revolution. The new leadership under Deng Xiaoping desperately wanted to open the economy, yet they faced entrenched domestic resistance, a lack of funds and technical know-how and no proven blueprint to follow. Opening up too quickly on a national scale risked severe political instability, and the cost of failure was simply too high. Xi Zhongxun, the father of future president Xi Jinping, was in charge of Guangdong province at the time. In April 1979, he proposed that Beijing allow Guangdong to establish experimental economic zones in Shenzhen, Zhuhai and Shantou. Deng immediately endorsed the idea, designating them China’s first “special economic zones”. These zones were granted the latitude to learn from the best business and economic practices of the capitalist West – particularly from Hong Kong, sitting right across the border. They functioned both as a contained buffer for experimentation and as a beacon to inspire the rest of the country. Rather than wasting years debating theory or building ideological consensus, the tangible success of these zones blazed a trail for the nation, gradually winning over even the most staunch initial sceptics. This model allowed the Communist Party to maintain socialist governance on the mainland while digesting, adapting and localising capitalist best practices. Eventually, these trial policies were rolled out nationwide, sparking one of the greatest economic booms in human history. Today, Hong Kong faces a strangely familiar crossroads. Our traditional model as a city of compradors is no longer sustainable. Our future depends on seizing the opportunities created by China’s economic rise and actively integrating into the national blueprint. Hong Kong needs fresh land, capital, talent and big ideas to jump-start its engine and resolve deep-seated social issues. Yet, as the city recovers from the aftermath of the 2019 unrest, many people remain hesitant – worried that closer integration might jeopardise the city’s capitalist system and the “one country, two systems” foundation. Enter the Northern Metropolis. It is designed to function as a special zone within our Special Administrative Region – a sandbox where bold new ideas can take root and flourish, rather than an attempt to fix legacy problems within the confines of the existing framework. It allows for new regulatory approaches, a seamless technology ecosystem and the freer movement of cross-border capital, data and people. All these, if they were to be introduced citywide, would entail much more debate and a longer period of adjustment. Instead, they now can be tested in designated zones free from the straitjacket of traditions and ideological rigidity. Positive results here will foster further reforms and create a virtuous feedback loop. Fortunately for us, unlike Deng and Xi, who had to launch the Shenzhen experiment blind, we actually have a proven playbook to reference. This approach highlights the pragmatic core of Chinese statecraft: prioritising tangible results over ideological dogmatism. It requires staying flexible and adaptive while remaining vigilant not to undermine the fundamental principles holding society together. Progress relies on balancing speed with stability, using initial wins to generate momentum, and focusing on maintaining dynamic growth rather than getting bogged down in minor details and debates. Nobody in 1979 could have scripted every detail of Shenzhen’s meteoric rise. Deng could never have predicted that a quiet border town would become a global nexus for electric vehicles, telecommunications, drones, smartphones and advanced microchips – most of these hadn’t even been invented yet. At the same time, Shenzhen’s miracle was no accident; it was the fruit of methodical planning across successive generations of leaders. Long before others caught on, Shenzhen drew up visionary policies – launching comprehensive schemes to attract top-tier global talent over two decades ago, and building a citywide EV charging network as early as 2009, well before “EV” became a household term. Shenzhen is a masterclass in striking the balance between top-down planning and bottom-up innovation. It is a cliché to say that innovation cannot be commanded by decree, but often it also needs a guided push to break inertia or create the right environment. In his book Complexity, science writer M. Mitchell Waldrop described this as “the edge of chaos”: a delicate balance point between order, purposefulness and enough room for flexibility. That, he says, is the key for any creativity.

title: Singaporean climber dies on Nepal’s Mount Manaslu, first foreign casualty of season
description: The 50-year-old felt unwell as he was descending from around 6,000 metres after an acclimatisation rotation.
content: A Singaporean climber died on Nepal’s Mount Manaslu, the world’s eighth highest peak, expedition organisers said. Lau Wee Seng, 50, felt unwell as he was descending from Camp II at around 6,000 metres after an acclimatisation rotation, according to The Himalayan Times newspaper. “He passed away this morning; arrangements have been made to airlift his body,” Pemba Sherpa of 8K Expeditions said on Thursday. The mountaineer had arrived in Samagaun on September 7 as part of a team aiming to scale the peak during the autumn climbing season, Nepal News online portal reported. He was the first foreign fatality of the season. Lau’s family had been notified, Sherpa said. “A helicopter was mobilised to retrieve his body, but it could not land due to bad weather conditions,” Raj Kumar Shrestha, spokesman for the District Police Office in Gorkha, told Xinhua news agency. This season, 480 climbers are attempting to reach the summit of the 8,163-metre (26,800-foot) high mountain in Nepal. This month, 20-year-old Nepali porter Tashi Sherpa was found dead in his tent at the mountain’s base camp. He had reportedly gone to sleep inside a tent housing a generator without telling others. Autumn expeditions on the Himalayas are less popular because of the shorter, colder days, snowy terrain and a narrow summit window compared to the busy spring. Nepal has issued 536 permits, taking US$1.44 million in royalties, for nine peaks – a little over half of the total permits issued in spring. Organisers have been conducting acclimatisation rotations while transporting essential equipment to higher camps. By September 4, over 200 climbers and support staff had reached the base-camp area through Samagaun, the Himalayan Times reported. Nepal is home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks and foreign climbers who flock to its mountains are a major source of revenue for the country. Fears for the industry rose after a devastating flood hit Nepal in late August, but expedition organisers say most climbers have not cancelled their expeditions. Additional reporting by SCMP’s Asia desk

title: Scientists trace half the DNA in Xinjiang’s oldest tombs to Yellow River farmers
description: Study of Bronze Age remains uncovers a population with roots in both Yellow River farmers and Eurasian steppe groups.
content: Nestled between the Tianshan Mountains and the Gobi Desert, the Hami oasis in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region is a land of little rain, battered by wind and sand year-round. It is also home to the region’s oldest known burial site, the Tianshanbeilu cemetery, located around 500km (310 miles) east of Urumqi, the regional capital. More than 700 Bronze Age tombs have been unearthed here, long assumed to belong to Eurasian nomads who migrated eastward from the steppes. But a study published on Friday in the journal Science upends that view, revealing a previously unknown, genetically mixed population that lived in the eastern Tianshan region 3,600 years ago, during China’s Shang dynasty (1600-1050BC). About half of this population’s ancestry can be traced to the millet-farming groups of the Middle and Late Neolithic period (around 4000-2000BC) along the Yellow River. The other half originated with Chemurchek-related populations in the Altai and Dzungaria regions. “These interactions began nearly 1,800 years before the historic Silk Road, revealing deep prehistoric foundations for trans-Eurasian mobility and exchange,” wrote corresponding author Fu Qiaomei, a researcher at the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The Tianshanbeilu cemetery has vast expanses of evenly spaced circular pits or rectangular burial grounds that contain one or more human skeletons, dating back between 3,000 and 4,000 years. The circular tomb chambers also contain burial objects such as bronze and pottery. The researchers obtained whole-genome data from 135 ancient individuals across 11 sites at the cemetery. The oldest of these people lived around 3,580 years ago. The scientists combined this data set with 735 published ancient genomes and 2,850 modern samples from previous databases. By analysing the genetic data, they found that most Bronze Age individuals from the eastern Tianshan region belonged to a distinct, newly discovered genetic group whose members shared remarkably similar ancestry. Compared with other ancient Xinjiang populations, this group was genetically closer to modern East Asians. At the same time, they had a mix of both Eastern and Western Eurasian heritage – a finding consistent with local archaeological evidence. As an oasis, Hami was visited by travellers moving between east and west and was home to both grassland nomadic culture and East Asian crop cultivation. The researchers’ genetic modelling showed the population was a mix of East Asian roots and ancestry from the Chemurchek – a Bronze Age culture distributed along the southern foothills of the Altai Mountains in Xinjiang. Human samples from tombs at the Tianshanbeilu cemetery have a nearly identical genetic composition, suggesting that this core Bronze Age population with mixed ancestral origins was widely distributed across the eastern Tianshan region. Further genetic analysis revealed that more DNA from outside groups entered the local gene pool starting around 1000BC, though the local Bronze Age population remained the genetic foundation. This shows that Iron Age populations in Xinjiang grew out of repeated waves of genetic mixing, combining the local Bronze Age population with groups arriving from East Asia, the Eurasian steppe and Central Asia. The findings reveal that long before the Silk Road emerged, human migration, crop dispersal and cultural transmission between East and West had already become deeply intertwined in what is now China’s Xinjiang region.

title: How will Japan’s rate increase affect capital flow in global financial markets?
description: Tokyo’s bond yields are seeing multi-decade highs as Bank of Japan boosts borrowing cost to three-decade high.
content: Japan is adding a fresh layer of uncertainty to global financial markets by potentially triggering a new bout of turmoil in bond markets and dampening the appetite for risk assets, as Tokyo’s pursuit of bigger government spending stokes concerns about fiscal discipline and sends sovereign bond yields to multi-year highs. The nation’s 10-year bond yield hit 3.03 per cent this week, a level not seen in three decades, while 30-year bond yields traded at 4.1 per cent, also nearing a 30-year high. The sell-offs, in which bond prices move inversely with yields, came amid speculation that Japan would seek to boost its defence budget to 3.5 per cent of its gross domestic product from around 2 per cent. The Bank of Japan’s decision on Friday to raise the interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent may further fuel the yield gains. With investors repricing a broader central-bank risk, turmoil in Japanese bonds would probably unleash fresh sell-offs in long-end debt in the US and Europe which are already grappling with elevated yields, according to market observers. An increase in risk-free interest rates typically dents investors’ appetite for assets such as stocks by demanding a higher risk premium, draining funds that spawned the frenetic artificial intelligence trade that has buttressed the bull market over the past few years. Rising bond yields “change the investment calculus,” said Gary Dugan, CEO of The Global CIO Office, which advises family offices and ultra-high-net-worth investors. “Bonds are real capital competitors instead of being portfolio insurance, and equity arithmetic follows suit.” “There’s a price to pay for owning equities,” he added. China’s financial markets remain vulnerable to an external shock, with the yield on the 10-year government bond trading close to a one-year low of 1.7 per cent and the outlook for tech stocks dependent on global sentiment. Japan’s elevated yields underscored rising fiscal spending as their persistent driver. Its government ministries requested a total budget of 143.1 trillion yen (US$918.5 billion) for the 2027 financial year, an increase of 16 per cent from the previous year, according to its Ministry of Finance. There was an upside risk for the final figures because of the large number of unspecified requests, particularly for military spending, Bank of America said in a report this month. While Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to limit bond issuance to around 40 trillion yen in the coming financial year, it hardly dispelled concerns among bond investors about Tokyo’s unbridled spending. Japan’s aggregate government debt is equivalent to 230 per cent of its gross domestic product, the highest among the developed nations, after Tokyo resorted to heavy borrowing as a way to lift the nation out of decades of deflation. Global risk assets from stocks to commodities are under pressure after the US Federal Reserve raised the benchmark interest rate for the first time in three years on Thursday, with chair Kevin Warsh signalling more increases ahead. The yield on 10-year US Treasuries surpassed 5 per cent for the first time since 2023 this week, and the 30-year Treasury yield rose to a nearly two-decade high of 5.4 per cent as investors priced in a prolonged oil shock and Washington competed for capital with AI hyperscalers for debt issuance. With the Bank of Japan following the Fed with monetary tightening, the move – alongside expectations for further tightening – would entrench the elevated sovereign yields, according to Sumitomo Mitsui Banking. Japanese government bonds trading at generational yield highs are not merely a market curiosity Stephen Innes, SPI Asset Management US money manager T. Rowe Price projected Japan would deliver between three and four rate increases in the coming 12 months to cool inflation and prop up the yen, while Swiss private bank Julius Baer foresaw three increases in December, March and July. “The resulting increase in expectations of further rate increases in Japan is another factor pushing Japanese longer-term yields higher,” said Hirofumi Suzuki, a strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking. “For the time being, upwards pressure on longer-term yields is likely to remain strong, particularly in the US. As a result, Japanese longer-term yields are also likely to remain under upwards pressure for some time.” The yen weakened 0.8 per cent against the US dollar on Friday, with Tokyo’s rate increase widely anticipated to reduce immediate fears of an unwinding of the carry trade financed by the Japanese currency. A surprise hike by the Bank of Japan in 2024 led to a melt-down across global financial assets, as investors scrambled to exit their carry trade positions, spurring brutal sell-offs in high-yield assets bought with the cheaper yen. For investors to regain their appetite for risk assets, the yield rise in developed markets such as Japan needed to pause, according to Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “Japanese government bonds trading at generational yield highs are not merely a market curiosity,” he said. “They represent a higher global discount rate, intensified competition for capital and a reminder that resilient growth and perfection pricing can coexist only until they cannot.”

title: Scientists are seeing if sheep’s wool can slow melting of glaciers in the Alps
description: The team hopes that this natural material can be just as effective as synthetic tarpaulins.
content:
Switzerland is struggling to stop glaciers in the Alps mountain range from melting. Thus, researchers are trying to see if sheep’s wool can protect ice from melting during the summer.
For years, reflective tarpaulins have been laid over ice and snow to reduce the heat that is absorbed in the summer. But these tarpaulins are usually made from plastic and can shed polluting microfibres.
Instead, the “Keep It Wool” project is using wool to slow the melting of the Tsanfleuron Glacier. The team wanted to explore a natural material – Swiss wool that would otherwise have been thrown away.
In June, two wool blankets were laid on the Tsanfleuron Glacier. Early results showed the wool covers limited melting as well as the tarpaulins would.
Still, scientists stress that lowering greenhouse gas emissions is the only long-term way to slow the loss of glaciers.

title: Exclusive | Blanket of security planned for state funeral of Tung Chee-hwa in Hong Kong
description: Beijing officials Shi Taifeng, Wang Dongfeng and Xia Baolong to arrive on Saturday, but memorial service will be invitation-only, sources say.
content: Hong Kong police will impose a high level of security for this weekend’s state funeral of the city’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, including providing protection for the three top Beijing officials attending the event, the South China Morning Post has learned. However, the memorial service, originally planned as a public event, will instead be by invitation only due to venue constraints, the Office of Former Chief Executives announced on Thursday. A command centre would be set up at the police headquarters in Wan Chai, and officers would be stationed at “every road junction and on every flyover” on the route taking the hearse carrying Tung’s body from the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point to the Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan, sources said. A vigil will be held from 3pm to 10pm on Saturday at the funeral home and a memorial service will start at 9am on Sunday. Tung died on September 8 at the age of 89 and was accorded a state funeral for his service as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework. He became a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), the nation’s top political advisory body, after stepping down as city leader during his second term in 2005. The three top Beijing officials attending the event are: Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and first CPPCC vice-chairman; Wang Dongfeng, a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and CPPCC vice-chairman and secretary general; and Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO). Shi chairs the 87-member committee of political and business heavyweights overseeing the funeral arrangements, while Wang and Xia serve as deputy directors. The two other deputy directors are Leung Chun-ying, a CPPCC vice-chairman and former Hong Kong chief executive, and current city leader John Lee Ka-chiu. The force’s VIP Protection Unit will help guard the three visiting Beijing officials, who are expected to fly into the city on Saturday to attend the vigil, sources said. The Airport Security Unit will be on duty to ensure safety. A command centre will be set up at the force’s Wan Chai headquarters, led by the regional commander of Hong Kong Island, while police tactical units will be deployed to surrounding areas, according to two sources. “The security will be of the highest level,” one insider said. “It will be unprecedented as there has not been a funeral for a [former] chief executive before.” Checks for suspicious items and bombs at the funeral home will be conducted by the force’s Key Points and Search Division, according to one source. The Force Escort Group will be deployed to escort the hearse, another insider said. Special traffic arrangements and road closures are expected during the journey. “There will be officers at every road junction and on every flyover,” the first source said. Officers will also be stationed at the three public condolence points in Causeway Bay, Kai Tak and Tsuen Wan from Friday, he said. The event this weekend is the third state funeral held since Hong Kong’s handover from British to Chinese rule in 1997. Industrialist Ann Tse-kai and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung were granted state funerals in 2000 and 2006 respectively. Like Tung, both served as vice-chairs of the CPPCC. The state funerals of Ann and Fok were coordinated by the central government, with the committees handling the arrangements each chaired by a CPPCC vice-chairman. The committee for Ann’s funeral had 65 people while Fok’s consisted of 74. Both funerals were attended by senior mainland Chinese officials, including the HKMAO director, with the coffins draped in the national flag and state leaders laying wreaths in tribute. Tung and Fok were among the pallbearers for Ann’s 2000 funeral. The industrialist was buried in Dapengwan Cemetery in Shenzhen. Fok’s state funeral was also held at the Hong Kong Funeral Home, with the businessman buried at the Hong Kong Buddhist Cemetery in Chai Wan. Governor Edward Youde was given a British state funeral after he died in December 1986. Additional reporting by Fiona Chow

title: Poland eyes deeper Philippines defence ties following Black Hawk deal
description: Warsaw is targeting drones, air defence and artillery exports to Manila as European rearmament fuels global arms ambitions.
content: Poland’s delivery of Black Hawk helicopters to the Philippines has given Warsaw a foothold in Manila’s defence market as it seeks to expand exports from its growing defence industry, with analysts saying drones, air defence and potentially co-production could pave the way for a broader partnership. Polish deputy foreign minister Wladyslaw Bartoszewski said on Tuesday that Warsaw was keen to pursue further defence partnerships with the Philippines, as Poland has poured US$50 billion into strengthening its defence industry and expanding exports. His comments came after the Philippines received its final seven S-70i Black Hawk helicopters in August. Manila acquired 32 of the helicopters in a US$509.6 million deal signed in 2022 with PZL Mielec, a Polish subsidiary of Sikorsky, which is owned by US defence contractor Lockheed Martin. Bartoszewski said Poland wanted to sell reconnaissance and combat drones, radar equipment, anti-aircraft missiles and armoured personnel carriers to Manila, Reuters reported, adding that a Philippine military delegation had recently visited Poland to explore other potential acquisitions. Analysts said the push reflected Poland’s ambition to become a more significant defence manufacturer and exporter at a time when the war in Ukraine and uncertainty over transatlantic security had accelerated European rearmament. “We can see this in Warsaw’s push to indigenise its defence capabilities, driven in part by the changing security environment in Europe, including the ‘Trump effect’ on Nato and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” said Joshua Espena, an international relations lecturer at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines. Espena added that Warsaw’s outreach suggested a deliberate effort to move away from an import-heavy defence ecosystem and build greater domestic production capacity. Poland’s Black Hawk helicopters show it has developed its manufacturing capabilities enough to compete with traditional military suppliers while providing cost-effectiveness and interoperability, according to Chester Cabalza, president and founder of the Manila-based International Development and Security Cooperation think tank. “Poland’s S70i Black Hawk was co-developed with the US,” he said. “The helicopters it sold to the Philippines are signs that it can fare better in terms of interoperability and cost-effectiveness compared to other hard power.” Vincent Kyle Parada, a foreign-policy analyst at policy advisory firm FACTS Asia, said that though most Polish arms exports currently went to Ukraine, Warsaw offered lower prices than leading Western manufacturers while remaining fully compliant with Nato standards. Parada said Polish equipment presented advantages as it was “tried and tested on the battlefield against Russia”, adding that Poland’s own history of hostilities with Moscow had helped develop its outsize military capacity and institutional interoperability with Nato allies. This offered clear advantages to Manila, he said, as Polish capabilities closely aligned with the Philippines’ current defence requirements. “Throughout past iterations of Balikatan [annual joint drills], we’ve seen a greater emphasis on coastal defence and anti-landing exercises. Heavy artillery systems like Poland’s AHS Krab are key to this. They can suppress and destroy enemy forces from a distance as they attempt to establish a beachhead,” Parada said. The Philippines faced a severe deficit in air defence capabilities, he added, with its military mostly restricted to three batteries of the Israeli Spyder system. To bridge this gap, Parada said Manila could look towards Poland’s domestically produced Piorun portable air-defence system, which had become a highly sought-after export among Nordic and Eastern European countries bordering Russia. “For the Philippines, acquiring such systems fills a critical capability gap when it comes to short-range air defence, allowing troops to threaten low-flying aircraft and drones in support of ground operations,” he said, leaving more sophisticated systems to deal with higher-altitude threats. Analysts say Warsaw is also ramping up drone development to adapt to evolving battlefield tactics, producing variants that can serve as interceptors against incoming missiles. “Exports range from reconnaissance drones to one-way attack drones similar to what we’ve seen in Iran and Ukraine,” Parada said, adding that while Philippine military officials had shown interest in unmanned systems, tangible progress towards the acquisition of lethal drones had yet to happen. Co-production opportunities Observers said there was an opportunity for Manila to deepen its defence ties with Warsaw through joint drone production, particularly as Poland positioned itself as a competitive player within the European Union’s Defence Technological and Industrial Base. “If this trajectory continues … it could also provide Warsaw with a platform for expanding defence-industrial linkages with Indo-Pacific partners such as the Philippines,” Espena said. Poland and the Philippines both faced “the same strategic ambiguity in terms of their national security”, Cabalza said, adding that the “historic delivery” of Polish Black Hawks not only made the Philippines the largest operator globally of that variant of the helicopter, but also “shows a common strategic collaboration”. Poland could also help the Philippines develop autonomous drones to strengthen its asymmetric warfare capabilities, he said. Espena agreed, adding that Poland’s defence-industrial cooperation with South Korea was also “worth watching, including in air defence and armoured systems”. “The Philippines could potentially leverage existing Manila–Warsaw–Seoul linkages to develop a more diversified and resilient defence supply chain,” he said.
