However, logistics and supply chain constraints could complicate broader collaboration, Parada said. “Apart from Ukraine, the rest of Poland’s exports mainly cater to Europe,” he said. “It’s reflective of Poland’s emerging status as a regional rearmament hub rather than a global arms exporter.”

title: Choosing a school in Hong Kong: local, DSS, private and international options
description: From curriculum and language to fees and admissions, understand Hong Kong’s school choices and identify the best fit for your family.
content: For new families and those arriving in Hong Kong for the first time, the school search can feel both exciting and overwhelming. The city offers a wide range of choices in four broad streams: government and aided local schools, Direct Subsidy Scheme schools, private independent schools and a large international sector. Local schools are the backbone of Hong Kong’s education system. Government and aided schools are publicly funded, generally follow the Hong Kong curriculum and lead to the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE). Many local schools teach largely in Chinese, though some are English-medium schools. They are low cost compared with private and international options and educate most of Hong Kong’s children. Direct Subsidy Scheme schools (DSS) sit between the public and private sectors. Introduced in 1991 to inject greater variety into the system and enhance parental choice, they receive government subsidies but have more flexibility in curriculum design, resources and admissions. They may charge fees, but are required to offer fee remission and scholarship schemes. In the 2026/27 school year, there are 78 DSS schools, including 57 secondary schools and 21 primary schools, with nine operating as secondary-cum-primary schools. Private Independent Schools (PRI) also belong to the private school sector and are often considered alongside international schools, offering immersive Chinese-English bilingual curricula. Most offer non-local curricula and are intended to provide more diversity and choice. Unlike international schools, however, they primarily serve local families seeking an alternative to public sector schools and are required to maintain at least 70 per cent of their student population as Hong Kong permanent residents. International schools are private, self-financing and market-driven. They serve non-local families, particular cultural or linguistic communities, and students who do not wish to sit local examinations. Curricula include American, Australian, British, Canadian, French, German, Japanese, Korean and Singaporean programmes, as well as the International Baccalaureate. There are currently 53 international schools operating in Hong Kong, though some have more than one campus. For many expat families, international schools offer continuity: a familiar curriculum, English-language instruction and smoother transitions to schools or universities overseas. However, continuity should not be confused with lower academic expectations. Educational consultant and mother of two Katie Shull says one common misconception is that “local schools hold a monopoly on academic rigour”. While local and DSS schools are known for demanding workloads, she says top international schools can also deliver strong academic outcomes, often across broader and more inclusive cohorts. The difference is in education structure: a creative, collaborative student may find a rigid exam-driven environment stressful, while a child who thrives on structure and clear metrics may feel unsettled in a more open, self-directed setting. Curriculum and language Curriculum choice is closely linked to a family’s timeline. If a family expects to be in Hong Kong for only two or three years, a school aligned with a home-country curriculum may reduce disruption. For families staying longer, DSS, private and some English-medium local schools can offer stronger exposure to Hong Kong society, Chinese language and local friendships, while still providing international elements. Julie Ma, principal of St Stephen’s College, a DSS school, calls language “perhaps the single most consequential decision”. English may dominate in international schools, while Chinese is often taught as a second or foreign language. In local Chinese-medium schools, most instruction is in Cantonese with written Chinese. DSS and English Medium of Instruction (EMI) schools may offer a mixed model, with English as the medium for many subjects and Mandarin taught seriously. “If you plan to stay in Hong Kong for the long term, or if you want your child to be genuinely trilingual and biliterate, do not underestimate how difficult it is to acquire strong written Chinese later,” Ma adds. “A child who begins Chinese seriously at age five is in a very different position from one who begins at age 11.” Admissions, wait-lists and timing Rosie McColl, head of Harrow International School Hong Kong, says demand remains strong at many leading international schools, particularly from relocating families, but cautions parents not to be discouraged by talk of long wait-lists. For DSS and local schools, admissions may be tied more closely to local allocation systems, school-specific entrance procedures or year-level vacancies. Newly arrived families should also be aware that the Education Bureau provides placement assistance and support services for children new to Hong Kong, as well as education services for non-Chinese-speaking students. Fees and selecting your optimal school Fees vary dramatically. Local government and aided schools are free from Primary 1 to Secondary 6, only charging for miscellaneous and activity fees. DSS schools are government subsidised and charge tuition, but must provide fee remission and scholarship schemes. Private independent and international schools generally have higher fees and may also require debentures, capital levies, application fees, trips, uniforms, buses and so on – all of which are outlined within this guide. McColl says families comparing financial options should look beyond tuition alone, weighing educational philosophy, curriculum, language of instruction and future pathways. Ma is equally blunt: “The assumption that paying more guarantees a better education” is one of the persistent misconceptions in Hong Kong, and that it only “buys a particular kind of educational environment, which may or may not suit your child”. One parent of an eight-year-old at an international school says families should not assume money alone will open doors. “You can’t get in with just money – each school will be looking for the right families to fit them.” Both school heads return to the same advice: visit schools, ask questions and observe the community closely. Parents should also consider the daily realities: commute, pastoral care, counselling, parent communication, co-curricular life, class size, language support and transition points. A child travelling 90 minutes each way may struggle no matter how strong the school’s reputation, Ma advises. Above all, begin with the child. Don’t get too caught up in the weight of other people’s anxiety and league tables; the “best” school is not necessarily the most expensive, most famous or hardest to get into. It is the one whose curriculum, language environment, community and expectations best fit your child – and your family’s time in Hong Kong.

title: Hong Kong’s Cheung Ka-long ready to rise to challenge overcome by Djokovic, Guardiola
description: Hong Kong’s first fencing superstar set for fourth Asian Games but motivation not coming so easily having won it all.
content: A big believer that elite sporting performance is entirely dictated by an athlete’s brain, Greg Koenig is busy convincing Cheung Ka-long that the Asian Games remain an important date in his calendar. Hong Kong’s first fencing superstar, Cheung has been there and done it over the past five years. He brilliantly won a pair of Olympic golds, first as an unfancied underdog, then as the foil king his rivals all wanted to dethrone, either side of becoming Asian Games champion in 2023. Of Cheung’s teammates in Japan this month, Harris Ho Shing-him and Leung Chin-yu, 17 and 21 respectively, will be making their debuts. Ryan Choi Chun-yin has a world title but is still desperately coveting his first Olympic medal. “The psychological planning for Ka-long is different from the others, because he’s won everything,” Koenig said. Finding direction and motivation after career-defining achievements is an age-old challenge for high-achieving competitors and coaches. Josh Kerr, the 2023 1,500m world champion, broke the 27-year-old world mile record earlier this year. Before he banked US$150,000 for winning the 1,500m at last weekend’s World Ultimate Championship, Kerr told the South China Morning Post that he had “already left behind my achievements from this year”. “For me now, I’m doing this for the joy of it, and I love what I do,” Kerr said. “The routine I find myself in, day in, day out, is very fulfilling, and it allows me to maximise my life.” Already the owner of a record 24 men’s grand slam titles, Novak Djokovic said last year that his desire had not dimmed because he “still feels a connection with the inner child, the four-year-old boy who took a racquet and said, ‘I love this sport, I want to play it all day’”. Originally keen to replicate the route of his basketball-playing parents, Cheung transferred his sporting affections, aged 10, after he joined a Hong Kong Fencing Association summer course. He has been going at it full-time since 2014, the year he swapped Lam Tai Fai College for Hong Kong Sports Institute, and, at 17, claimed team foil bronze from the Asian Games. He would pair team silver with individual bronze four years later, while his solo gold three years ago was coupled with another team bronze. Koenig said that since his first Olympic gold in 2021, Cheung had undertaken “five years of almost non-stop hard training”. “When you do this, your body tries to tell you, ‘Come on, you should calm down a bit’,” Koenig said. “But I tell all my athletes that everything comes from the brain. Even when you’re tired, if the brain is ready, it will give good information and you’ll be able to push harder.” Last year, Cheung told the SCMP that he had been “quite tired for the past four years”, a period stretching back to the months before he scythed through a sequence of supposedly superior opponents to claim a shock Olympic gold. Defending his title in Paris in 2024, when expectations were through the roof, was perhaps the more impressive achievement after Koenig had warned: “When you’re the Olympic champion, you have the maximum pressure, and we have to see how he will handle it.” On the Olympic front, Cheung is adopting a similar stance to that adopted by Pep Guardiola after he masterminded Manchester City’s treble in 2023. “No one has won four [Premier League titles] in a row, why don’t we try?” Guardiola asked, immediately bleeding renewed purpose into his squad. After they duly sealed that fourth straight crown, Guardiola said: “Now I don’t know what exactly the motivation is because it’s difficult to find it when everything is done”. We are not there with the 29-year-old Cheung just yet. He is enthused by the prospect of becoming the first man to win three Olympic foil golds, but has hinted that regardless of the outcome, the 2028 Games could spell the end of the road. In the context of what is on the line in Los Angeles in two years, the Asian Games could easily feel like small fry. “I try to convince him that it’s important, and I think he understands that for Hong Kong, for all of us, it is,” Koenig said. “Deep down, the motivation can’t be the same when you’ve already won. Nor the excitement, you don’t have the eyes of a kid discovering something different. But he’s also calmer. “We have some fun between us, I tell him that having two Asian Games golds, to go with the two Olympics would be a good thing.” Koenig said that in Hangzhou in 2023 he had detected on competition day that Cheung was “not in a good mood”. The coach’s solution was to show his charge the picture of a car he wanted, telling him he would be able to buy it if he won gold. “He said, ‘Oh, right, let’s go,’” Koenig said. “We’re trying to be serious, but it was a joke between us. A tiny game. “Sometimes, you need to remind athletes that we have a nice life. When we chit-chat now I remind him how he felt after winning the last Asian Games. I say that this is the feeling he’ll have if he fights hard and finds the motivation for this competition.” Cheung has usually permitted himself time to rest and enjoy his achievements, falling somewhere between the manner in which fellow fencer Enzo Lefort and Roy Keane celebrated their major triumphs. Keane, the former Manchester United midfielder, has said that a “fear of letting people down” pursued him throughout his career. After winning silverware, therefore, “the enjoyment was very, very brief, I’m afraid”. Frenchman Lefort claimed the first of his three Olympic medals, team foil silver, in Rio in 2016. He stayed in the Brazilian city for nine days afterwards and “partied for eight of them”. “The day we got the medal, I went to the French house and partied until 6am,” Lefort told the SCMP. Following his second Olympic gold, the more sober Cheung “took a long break and rested mentally and physically”. He has acknowledged that he needs to “take care of my body, I have a lot of injuries from overuse”. “I can’t push him as much as I used to,” Koenig said. “When he was 24 [at the time of his first Olympic triumph], it was easy for me to tell him that, ‘If you work hard, you can achieve this, this and this’.” “Now he’s achieved this, this and this, so sometimes I have to remind him that he can still do more.” A quarter-finalist in June’s Asian Championships, Cheung was comfortably beaten by Kirill Borodachev in the last 16 of the following month’s Kerry Fencing World Championships in Hong Kong. He was a team silver medallist in both events. Koenig told his athletes to go away and forget about fencing for a fortnight after the global event. “It can be hard to wake up and come to train every day, but he’s training hard to be prepared,” Koenig said. “I’m pretty sure he will find the motivation and his brain will give a good signal when the competition starts.”

title: Ode to the horse: 5,000 years of human-equine connection on display in new Kazakh museum
description: In rural Kazakhstan, a father and son have built a temple to our equine companions – the animal that once carried monks, traders and armies across the steppes. PostMag visits their museum, where myth and reality graze side by side.
content: On the scenic drive east from Almaty, in Kazakhstan, along the old corridor of the A351 highway, towards the Charyn Canyon National Park, and the Xinjiang border beyond that, sits an unassuming museum run by an unlikely duo. Nurbol Baimukhanov, 50, is an independent, published researcher of shezhire – traditional Kazakh genealogies, historically memorised and passed down through generations – and an award-winning documentary producer who speaks in equal parts archaeology and mysticism. His son Ilyas, 23, with a MacBook tucked under his arm and an eye for systems, is pursuing a master’s in management at Satbayev University, the nation’s oldest technical institute. On a quiet stretch of the A351, father and son have built a showcase dedicated to the ancient Botai, the multi-hyphenate people of the Eurasian steppes – hunter-gatherer-herder-settlers – who some archaeologists believe were among the first to domesticate the horse more than 5,000 years ago. Located around 70km from Almaty, the Ush Qiyan Open-Air Museum sits near the village of Akshiy, in the Enbekshikazakh district – the kind of place most travellers pass without noticing. Opened this summer, it rises from the flat landscape as three circular log dwellings with sloping roofs – constructed from more than 1,000 logs, the exhibition brochure proudly proclaims – and is designed to evoke what some researchers believe are among the oldest known permanent settlements of the steppes. Ush Qiyan receives no government funds, has launched no grand marketing campaign – it is just a father, his son and their semi-domesticated horse named Ayan grazing outside. “Kazakh culture is, first and foremost, the culture of the horse,” says Nurbol. “In gratitude to these beautiful animals, we built this museum as a temple of knowledge to enlighten people.” Before there were empires and criss-crossing trade routes, before valiant steeds carried armies across continents and monks towards enlightenment, there was a culture that first looked at a wild horse and saw something more than prey. It is believed that the Botai people lived in what is now northern Kazakhstan, in the 4th and 3rd millennia BC. Mighty they were not. As far as archaeologists could detect, the Botai built no cities, wrote no epics and erected no monuments that would survive the centuries and catch the eye. Instead, what they left behind were traces of dwellings, scattered pottery and the bones of horses – thousands upon thousands of them, now housed at the North Kazakhstan Regional Museum of History and Local Lore, in Petropavl. Archaeologists around the world now widely believe that the Botai were the first to domesticate the horse, though the claim is debated each time new evidence comes to light. Experts argue that the proof is in the bones, which show signs of bit wear on the teeth, from the bridle gear used to control them, and in the residue of mare’s milk found in their pottery, leading them to theorise that the Botai were not just hunting horses, but riding them, milking them and living alongside them. If true, it would be one of the most consequential partnerships in human history. Migration, trade, warfare, the spread of ideas and empires – all of it would eventually travel on horseback. And yet, there is a twist. Genetic research suggests that the animal the Botai domesticated is actually the ancestor of the Przewalski’s horse – the stocky, pot-bellied wild horse that still roams parts of Central Asia. In other words, the first horse believed to be part of human culture eventually returned to the wild, rather than develop into the modern steeds we see today. Ush Qiyan attempts to capture this paradox – the last wild-horse species being descended from domesticated ancestors, raising questions around whether the breed is truly wild or simply feral – telling a complicated story about a partnership that was formed, dissolved and formed again, as the modern horse, tamed later in the Early Bronze Age, became the engine of human history. It all started with Ayan, a stallion who seems to straddle both worlds. In the spring of 2021, Nurbol went looking for a light-hued horse in the Altai mountain range, in eastern Kazakhstan. He had no particular reason for doing so; he says he simply, suddenly, felt like having one. A friend had told him about a remote village with no internet and a horse bearing a rare isabelline colour. Having negotiated a price, it took Nurbol three nights by truck to take Ayan back to Almaty. “He was born wild, near Lake Zaysan,” says Nurbol. Ayan is, according to Nurbol, a Zhabe – one of Kazakhstan’s oldest horse breeds, distinguished by its stout frame, thick neck, muscular croup and substantial body weight. But with a pale, almost metallic coat that glows golden in sunlight, Ayan is no ordinary Zhabe. Whether the isabelline colouring is genetically possible for this breed is another matter, but Nurbol is not a man to let science get in the way of a good story. “It was a sign from above,” he says, referencing the heavens. “Our horse bears all the hallmarks of an ancient celestial horse. It has a powerful mind and transmits information telepathically.” Separating fact from fiction is a secondary concern for Nurbol. He is a researcher whose published works focus on history, archaeology and ancestry. At the same time, he is a believer who sees little boundary between myth and reality. In his telling, Ayan the horse is both a living animal and the latest chapter in a legend that began with the Botai people and culture five millennia ago. “In the Chinese epic Journey to the West, the White Dragon Horse came from the West,” says Nurbol, noting that, in the text, “the tale of the monk [Tang Sanzang] who met a White Dragon Horse happened somewhere in our area. [Kazakhstan] is a land of legends where myth and reality intertwine”. Ayan eventually inspired the construction of Ush Qiyan, which began in the summer of 2024. It took about two years to finish, building only in the warmer months, with a small crew, and involved no architects or contractors in the conventional sense – just workers stripping bark from logs under a punishing sun. “Construction was not easy,” Nurbol recalls. “It was very hot. People were breaking down like matchsticks.” All the logs had to be processed and cut by hand, following what Nurbol dubs “experimental archaeology” – a scientific approach to understanding how ancient nomads built their dwellings, and the physical labour involved. It was, in his words, an attempt to recreate not just the look of the Botai world, but the toll it took. Money for the project came entirely from the Baimukhanovs, and though that choice was deliberate, it had consequences. Nurbol remembers days when, due to a lack of funds, “we were idle and wondering how to raise money to continue construction. [But] this was our conscious choice, and we are pleased with the result”. Ilyas was born in Almaty and grew up tagging along on his father’s scientific expeditions across Kazakhstan. Ush Qiyan, in some ways, is the culmination of a childhood spent among artefacts and open landscapes. Now in his early adulthood, Ilyas speaks with the composure of someone a decade older. “My father and I are like-minded people,” he says. “I represent the younger generation, a new perspective.” While Nurbol supplies the vision, the younger Baimukhanov thinks about sustainability, management systems and visitor services. His own “eureka!” moment came years earlier, in the Botai region of northern Kazakhstan, where he met the influential archaeologist Viktor Fedorovich Zaibert, who discovered, excavated and opened the Botai settlement site in 1980, in the Aiyrtau district. In doing so, Zaibert gave the world some of the earliest evidence for horse husbandry and domestication. “He [was] an amazing person,” Ilyas recalls. “He told fascinating stories about history.” What struck him were the traces of ancient circles still visible in the earth – the outlines of dwellings long gone – and the bones and pottery scattered across the ground, some more than 5,000 years old. “I am happy to have interacted with such a great archaeologist and seen the artefacts in person. It’s unforgettable,” says Ilyas. Zaibert died in 2022, but his influence, legacy and memory live on in the log walls of the museum. A visitor to Ush Qiyan moves through the three log structures, each roof shaped like an inverted basket, echoing the ancient yurts of the early nomads. Inside, scientific replicas of nomadic dress from various periods, made from materials such as hide, bone and leather, created for the 2018 documentary Equus: Story of the Horse, which Nurbol co-produced, hang alongside other props. Installations showing reconstructions of historical dwellings and horse sculptures fill the spaces between, and films are screened for guests who want to linger. In another room, Daniyar Sarbassov, a 36-year-old artist from the Bayanaul district, showcases his work: castings of horses, mostly. “Daniyar is our friend,” says Nurbol. “He’s a talented sculptor with great potential.” But the connection to the museum runs deeper than friendship. Sarbassov’s horses are not decorative – they carry, as Nurbol puts it, “the code of the Great Steppe”. One of his pieces, an aluminium-and-bronze statue titled Zhuyrik (2022), was sculpted earlier, in his studio, when Sarbassov had no knowledge of Ayan, or the world Nurbol was building. But when he spotted the ivory-coloured horse, something shifted. “After seeing Ayan, I decided that this work would be better placed at the entrance of the museum,” he says. In Sarbassov’s description, Zhuyrik is not simply a horse running. It is “a creature that merges with the wind and moves together with the air”. Its smooth surface catches the natural light from the structure’s oculus as it shifts throughout the day, seemingly dissolving the boundary between the horse’s body and the surrounding space. “A truly swift horse is difficult to perceive in its entirety,” he says. “Its speed is often experienced through the impression, trace and sensation of movement left in our memory.” As its metallic shine echoes Ayan’s coat, Sarbassov calls it “a spiritual symbol of the museum”. He hopes it will remain there permanently, and that visitors will find their own meaning in the work: “One viewer may see freedom in the image of a horse, another may be reminded of their ancestors, while a third may discover an entirely different meaning. My hope is that they will pause for a moment to reflect on their own history, their homeland and their place as human beings within this vast expanse of time.” Outside, Ayan grazes, unaware of the symbolism attached to him. Nurbol considers him the living echo of the story Ush Qiyan exists to tell: the wild horse that came to humans, changed their world and still carries that independence in its blood. Whether that story belongs to history or to myth is, by now, beside the point. Between them, a father and son have built a temple to the horse, raised by hand, off the beaten track. “We live in a complex era of digital technology; it’s difficult to be surprised by anything,” says Nurbol. “But at the same time, we look to the future without forgetting the past. Our museum is like a time machine.” But a time machine moves forwards, too. More visitors will be drawn by the same road that connected cultures. Ush Qiyan sits beside it, ready to welcome those who pause on their way to somewhere else. “The Great Steppe has always been a place of meeting,” says Nurbol. “We are open to dialogue with the world.”

title: Help! How can I stay focused when I feel overwhelmed by schoolwork?
description: Each week, we respond to a question from our readers and give advice and resources they can turn to.
content:
Do you have a personal question you’ve been too afraid to ask? Whether it is about school, family or your social life, you can share it with us through this form . Don’t worry, you’ll remain anonymous.
I am having a hard time getting started on my assignments. Even though I know what I need to do, I feel stuck and can’t seem to begin. My teachers and parents think I am lazy, but I am actually trying. I feel like I can only work when I am in the mood. What should I do?
When we feel overwhelmed , it’s often because we have too much on our plate. Think of it like a phone with too many apps running at once. The device starts to lag, may even crash, and, as a result, the battery drains faster.
Before you begin, take a moment to set a specific goal. For example, you might aim to complete three pages of maths homework. Being as specific as possible will provide you with a clear sense of direction.
Once you’ve established your goal, break it down into smaller, more manageable tasks. For instance, you could read one chapter, complete a single page of a worksheet, or write just one paragraph.
When we have a lot to accomplish, it’s easy to lose track of our progress, which can affect our motivation . To help you stay organised, it can be beneficial to create a daily plan for yourself. Be sure to include a few breaks as well.
During breaks, make sure to step away from your current activity to give yourself a chance to recharge. It’s important not to wear yourself out. Aim to take a few minutes to step away from your study table, do some stretches, or get a glass of water. This will help you feel refreshed.
If you find it difficult to refocus and return to work after taking breaks, consider setting a timer or alarm. On days when you feel motivated, you might want to give yourself more time for your tasks.
However, on days when you’re not as motivated, having a plan can help you stay on track. Place this plan in a visible location, such as on your fridge or on the wall in your bedroom. This way, it can help you regain your focus whenever you feel lost.
I understand that it can be discouraging and make you feel misunderstood when your teachers and parents label you as “lazy”. However, let’s concentrate on taking small steps to help ourselves move forward.
In the end, even minor achievements will demonstrate to them that you are putting in effort. The most important thing is how you feel and how to stay focused when everything seems overwhelming.
This question was answered by Dr Carmen Ip, a clinical psychologist at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: King Charles was ‘giddily elated’ after Diana’s death, her brother says
description: Then-Prince Charles sounded ‘like a lottery winner’ because he felt freed to marry again, Earl Spencer writes in new book.
content: Britain’s King Charles sounded “like a lottery winner” after the death of ⁠his late first wife Diana, ⁠her brother writes in his forthcoming ⁠book, new extracts of which were published on Thursday. Diana’s brother Charles Spencer said the then-Prince Charles was “giddily elated” in the immediate aftermath of Diana’s death in 1997, possibly because he felt it meant he was freer to marry again, according to passages in the Daily ‌Mail. Spencer also claimed that in another conversation days after her death, the future king told him: “Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”. Charles on Wednesday took the unusual step of responding to criticism after the first extracts of Spencer’s book were published in the Daily Mail, saying via a spokesman that grief could impact reason, judgment and memory. There was no new comment from the king on the latest excerpts, which also stated that Diana went to a site of many suicides on Britain’s south coast, but ⁠that her love for her sons, William and Harry, “stopped her from going further”. “It is a sad fact that, ‌in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all,” Spencer said. Diana was ‌killed at the age of 36 when the car carrying her and her lover Dodi Fayed crashed in Paris ⁠as it sped away from chasing paparazzi photographers on motorbikes. Spencer said in the book that he spoke to Charles shortly after Diana’s ‌death was confirmed, writing: “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily ‌elated – like a ‌lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time”. Spencer added: “Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first ‌reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman ⁠he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not”. Charles and Diana separated in 1992 ⁠and divorced in 1996. That was a year after Diana told the BBC that “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, in reference to Charles’ relationship ‌with Camilla Parker Bowles, ‌whom he married in 2005. A Buckingham Palace spokesman said on Wednesday: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss”. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong, mainland China won’t genuflect to Silicon Valley’s moral panic over AI
description: Mainland China’s AI strategy focuses on economic transformation while addressing concrete risks, an approach which aligns with Hong Kong’s five-year plan.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan makes artificial intelligence development and governance a policy priority amid apocalyptic warnings from Silicon Valley’s leading AI bosses. While American executives speak of slowing development, the city and mainland China are systematically embedding AI across industries – a measured strategy focused on tangible economic transformation. China tightly regulates AI and so largely avoids the existential worries the technology provokes in the US. Recently, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that “we must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models”; rival OpenAI’s Sam Altman agreed. By effectively dividing AI development into “responsible” systems regulated by trusted guardians versus “dangerous” open-source models requiring constraints, they establish a binary that advantages their business models. Calls to slow AI’s development squarely target China’s progress, especially since Amodei is well known as an AI hawk. Beijing agrees to the need for global AI governance through a multilateral organisation like the United Nations. It objects to any nation or tech insider unilaterally dictating rules and imposing them on others. The safety discourse serves domestic American purposes. If catastrophic AI risk becomes the dominant narrative, who regulates it? Not government bureaucrats lacking technical knowledge, but the very companies issuing warnings, the same actors who create the alleged threats in the first place. This allows frontier labs to position themselves as indispensable gatekeepers while gaining autonomy from oversight. Legitimate safety concerns exist, and China takes them very seriously. The distinction lies in approach. China’s regulators require pre-deployment safety assessments for generative AI and last year removed over 3,500 non-compliant AI products from the market. China’s 15th five-year plan elevates AI to the organising logic of industrial transformation, with targets including growing digital industries to 12.5 per cent of gross domestic product and achieving “decisive breakthroughs” in foundational technologies. This prioritises rapid economy-wide diffusion, moving AI from consumer novelty to industrial backbone. Hong Kong’s own five-year plan is in alignment. The Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster covering 110,000 square metres is expected to deliver computing power of 180,000 petaflops by 2032, 36 times the current capacity, supporting the city’s intelligent computing industry. Cyberport’s AI Supercomputing Centre is expected to deliver 3,000 petaflops. The practical focus is evident in deployment priorities, which cover finance, healthcare, law, construction, transport, social welfare, tourism and media. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s generative AI sandbox has been expanded beyond banking to securities, insurance and retirement funds. Rather than hypothetical threats, local policymakers address concrete challenges: training thousands of employees, establishing AI literacy and supporting businesses. AI is expected to feature prominently when US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet soon at the White House. The fundamental question is whether AI development should be governed by market leaders claiming special insight into existential risk or by transparent frameworks addressing demonstrable harms. Hong Kong’s answer is clear: AI governance must serve economic development and social welfare, not the strategic interests of particular companies. By focusing on computing infrastructure, talent development, sector-specific deployment and practical safety measures, this approach delivers tangible benefits while managing real risks. The apocalyptic narrative serves those who directly profit from it. Hong Kong and China recognise AI as a transformative technology requiring serious governance but refuse to cede that governance to self-appointed guardians whose warnings conveniently advance their position. As Hong Kong implements its first five-year plan, embedding AI across industries with proper safeguards, it shows that responsible development need not genuflect to Silicon Valley’s moral panic. The practical path, grounded in economic reality and genuine oversight, offers a more credible model.

title: No time for the gym? How micro-workouts could help busy professionals improve their health
description: Studies suggest bursts of activity bring benefits, but can ‘exercise snacks’ replace longer gym sessions for the time-poor? Experts weigh in.
content: For many professionals, finding an hour for the gym is about as feasible as finding an extra day in the week. There are deadlines, family obligations, late-night calls and the small matter of getting enough sleep. That is why “exercise snacks” – or micro-workouts – have become so appealing. Rather than reserving exercise for a long session, the approach breaks activity into short bouts: a brisk climb up stairs, a few squats between meetings or an interval session squeezed into a lunch break. The evidence suggests that these doses are not meaningless. But they are not a reason to abandon longer exercise either. A recent meta-analysis of 27 trials found that short, intensive bouts of exercise improved cardiorespiratory fitness and decreased fasting blood glucose and cholesterol levels, body fat percentage, waist circumference and blood pressure, compared with doing no exercise. The studies varied in their protocols, however, and the wider evidence base remains relatively young. “I haven’t done a traditional gym workout in 10 years, and I’m stronger than ever” Beatrice Chan, founder of EMS Fitness Another growing body of research concerns vigorous intermittent lifestyle physical activity, or Vilpa – strenuous movement performed incidentally in daily life, such as fast stair climbing or hurried uphill walking. In an accelerometer-based study of more than 25,000 non-exercisers in the UK, even three or four minutes a day of Vilpa was associated with a substantially lower risk of mortality compared with doing no exercise at all. As an observational study, it cannot prove that the short bursts themselves lead to improved outcomes, but it strengthens the case that exercise does not need to be done in a single, gym-based block. The science of microbouts For Professor Parco Siu Ming-fai, head of the Division of Kinesiology at the University of Hong Kong’s School of Public Health, the key is to avoid confusing any kind of movement with proper exercise practices, such as interval training. The latter, he explains, “involves alternating periods of vigorous exercise with lower-intensity active recovery exercise or simply rest. The exercising heart rate during vigorous exercise always exceeds 85 per cent of the estimated maximum heart rate”. In a recent study, Siu tracked adults with extra weight around their middle who did 75 minutes of brisk interval walking a week for four months. Whether they knocked it out in a single weekend session or split it over three days, the results were the same: participants lost belly fat, reduced their body fat percentage and boosted their cardio fitness compared with those who did not exercise. The relevance to Hong Kong is obvious, Siu says: “Time constraints are a major barrier to exercising multiple days per week for many adults with central obesity who struggle to balance work, study, family and other commitments.” Quality over duration James Campion, founder, CEO and trainer at HIT Personal Training in Central, Hong Kong, says his clients are likewise people with demanding careers, family responsibilities and limited time. And while many overestimate how long they need to spend in a gym, they also underestimate the importance of structuring it properly. Campion suggests that, in many cases, 90 to 120 minutes of purposeful weekly training can be enough to produce significant changes. “It’s more of the quality of the time that you spend,” he says. For short sessions, Campion favours combining movements that do not excessively fatigue the same muscles. Pairing push-ups with lunges in “supersets”, for example, means one muscle group can recover while another works. The format can keep the cardiovascular system engaged while also training strength and muscular endurance. Frequency is also important. “You will get more results if you hit a muscle very hard for a short period of time, more frequently throughout the week,” he says. Campion is circumspect about micro-workouts. “To do one of those, you have to be pretty knowledgeable about how to get a really effective 10 minutes done … to make it challenging, safe and effective,” he says. Consistency is key Heather O’Brien, founder of Hong Kong-based HKM Fitness, says the most effective programme is one a person can sustain. “For a workout to be generally effective, it has to be something that you can remain consistent with,” she says. “That is the underlying foundation of everything.” For someone who can only train three times a week for 20 minutes, O’Brien would prescribe full-body strength sessions using supersets. This approach makes better use of limited time, while allowing each worked muscle group a brief recovery period. She says 10-minute workouts – short cardio, mobility or flexibility sessions, for example – can be worthwhile, but building substantial muscle usually requires more effort. “You do need to be looking at the 20-minute mark,” she says, pointing out that progression and good form take priority. “People can build a significant amount of muscle with 20-minute workouts at least two to four times a week.” Steps build a strong foundation There is also value in the most basic form of movement: walking. Campion says clients can break up prolonged sitting by taking calls while walking or going out for a coffee rather than ordering in. The point is not that every movement must leave someone breathless but that regular low-intensity activity is a useful foundation on which more structured exercise can be built. The World Health Organization recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, alongside muscle-strengthening activity involving major muscle groups on two or more days. Micro-workouts can help people hit those targets, especially if they are otherwise inactive, but they should be understood as a tool – not a loophole. A brisk stair climb, a properly planned 20-minute strength session and a walk to the supermarket can all be part of the same solution: doing more of what can realistically be repeated. EMS fitness: can 20 minutes replace a gym session? Electrical muscle stimulation (EMS) is being marketed as a more efficient method of resistance training for Hong Kong professionals who struggle to find time for conventional exercise. Research supports its utility, with caveats. A study published in October 2025 in the Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness found that while 25-minute EMS sessions and 90-minute traditional workouts both improved strength and body composition over 20 weeks, traditional weightlifting still yielded significantly greater strength gains and fat loss. Researchers concluded that EMS is a viable, time-efficient option for those unable to lift heavy weights but it does not fully match standard gym training. Yet for clients at EMS Fitness, which has studios in Hong Kong’s Central and Discovery Bay neighbourhoods, the convenience is what counts. They wear a fitted suit that delivers electrical impulses to muscles during weekly supervised 20-minute sessions. Founder Beatrice Chan says her clients are mostly professionals aged between 30 and 70, who are balancing tight schedules with injuries, joint pain or an aversion to crowded gyms. “Hong Kong moves incredibly fast,” Chan says. “Everything is about speed, and the saying ‘time is money’ is deeply true in this city. Time is the ultimate luxury here.” Chan notes a common misconception is that clients simply lie still while the suit does the work. Rather, trainers guide them through active movements under stimulation. “Even though it’s highly efficient, it still requires consistency like any workout,” she says. But there are limits. Chan acknowledges EMS cannot replace heavy powerlifting or cardiovascular training but sees it as an ideal bridge for time-poor professionals. “I haven’t done a traditional gym workout in 10 years,” she says, “and I’m stronger than ever.” While clients often report visible toning after 10 sessions, experts say individuals with medical conditions, implanted electronic devices or pregnancy-related concerns should seek medical advice before starting EMS. title: White House pulls Trump nominee to head ICE
description: No reason was given, but ex-Marine Lance Schroyer’s confirmation had been stalled in the Senate.
content: The White House on Thursday withdrew its nominee to head US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency tasked with carrying out President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown. Lance Schroyer, a former US Marine and Oklahoma state trooper, was named by Trump earlier this year to be the next ICE director, a post subject to Senate confirmation. In a brief statement on its website, the White House said Schroyer’s nomination had been withdrawn. No reason was given but the nomination had been stalled in the US Senate. ICE is currently being run by an acting director after the previous interim chief stepped down in May. Individuals nominated to head federal agencies are supposed to be confirmed by the Senate, but that has not happened with ICE since 2017. Its leaders since then have been interim directors. Schroyer has been serving as an adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin pending his Senate confirmation. Trump campaigned for the White House on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken a number of actions since taking office aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings. Nearly 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the US in August, according to Department of Homeland Security figures, surpassing the previous record high of 50,200 in July.

title: Hong Kong malls bet on Asian Games to boost footfall, tenant sales amid spending shifts
description: Mall operators are expanding sports-themed campaigns and experiences as retailers fight for consumer attention.
content: Hong Kong shopping mall operators are extending a strategy used during this year’s Fifa World Cup into the Asian Games, leveraging major sporting events to draw visitors and support tenant sales as retailers face competition from Shenzhen, overseas shopping and online spending. Sino Group is among the landlords expanding the strategy beyond tournament broadcasts. It has projected foot traffic across its four malls to increase during its Asian Games campaign, with selected merchants forecast to record double-digit year-on-year sales growth. The strategy builds on the group’s experience during the World Cup, when foot traffic across three flagship malls rose by about 10 to 15 per cent year on year and overall sales recorded double-digit growth. Bella Chhoa, chief commercial officer at Sino Group, said the Asian Games and World Cup generated different consumption patterns. The World Cup attracted a “concentrated football fan base” while the Asian Games encompassed multiple sports and were expected to attract a broader mix of visitors, she said. “The competitive schedule, viewing patterns and customer journeys are therefore fundamentally different,” Chhoa added. Sino is using athlete-themed displays, promotions and interactive activities alongside live broadcasts to encourage visitors to spend more time at its malls and engage with retailers. The strategy reflects a wider shift in how mall operators view their role in the retail market. Over the long term, malls will need to look beyond sports to other experiential uses as new trends emerge Roy Ng, Newmark Sino described sports programming as an “important pillar of experiential retail”, as landlords sought ways to increase dwell time and give consumers reasons to visit physical stores beyond shopping itself. “Consumer spending has already shifted structurally towards experience-led consumption,” said Roy Ng, head of research at the property consultancy Newmark. “Over the long term, malls will need to look beyond sports to other experiential uses as new trends emerge.” The Asian Games officially open on Saturday in Nagoya, Japan, though preliminary events have already begun. The event runs until October 4. For mall operators, the immediate challenge is converting higher visitor numbers into spending. Ng said the sector’s biggest hurdle was turning footfall into sales, with neighbourhood malls facing greater pressure as consumers channel spending online, overseas and across the border with Shenzhen. Major sporting events could help neighbourhood malls foster a stronger sense of community and generate spending through event-related promotions, Ng said, adding that Hong Kong’s shortage of sports venues gave malls an opportunity to use large atriums and other spaces for temporary sporting activities. Henderson Land Development is also extending its World Cup strategy into the Asian Games. Its MCP Central and MCP Discovery malls in Tseung Kwan O will roll out six sports-related programmes, including Asian Games broadcasts, basketball tournaments, an indoor dragon boat event and a pickleball competition. “The strong public response reinforced our confidence in using sports events as a marketing tool,” said Terence Chan, general manager of portfolio leasing at Henderson Development. MCP said it expected visitor numbers to rise by double digits in the second half, extending growth recorded during the World Cup period, and named sportswear, lifestyle retail and food and beverage tenants as beneficiaries from the additional traffic.

title: School open day checklist: the key questions parents should ask
description: Open days offer more than a look at facilities – asking the right questions can reveal how a school teaches, supports students and builds community.
content: The school website and other marketing materials provide comprehensive information, but it is during the school tour when parents get a true understanding and experience of the institution and whether it is a good fit for their child. Below is a checklist of questions and key points to keep in mind when attending a school open day. 1. The learning environment In addition to knowing what type of curriculum the school follows and fully understanding it, you can use the opportunity to find out more about how students are assessed and whether it is the most suitable form of assessment for your child. For example, you might ask: beyond traditional pen‑and‑paper tests and exams, do teachers assess learning through projects, oral presentations, practical tasks or group work? Do you use formative assessments such as class observations, quizzes or portfolios to track progress, and how is this feedback shared with parents? These questions will help you gauge whether the school’s assessment approach is aligned with your child’s learning style. If it is an international school that uses English as the primary language for teaching, parents wanting their children to learn Chinese as well can ask if Mandarin will be taught as an additional language and whether simplified or traditional Chinese characters will be used. You can also probe how seriously the school treats Chinese within an English‑medium environment by hearing how many hours of Chinese is scheduled each week, and whether this is the same across all year groups. You might want to ask if Chinese is taught as a stand-alone subject, or is there any dual‑language or bilingual immersion where subjects such as maths, science or social studies are taught partly in Chinese? Or if the school has a one‑teacher‑per‑language model. 2. Student support Some students might require different learning needs from the rest of the class, and a school’s open day is a prime opportunity for you to have a face-to-face conversation about this with the teaching staff. It can also be worth discussing how the school balances academic requirements with the social and emotional well-being of its students. Whether in primary or secondary school, some children might require counselling support at times and an open day is the best time to ask about a school’s counselling resources and how they can work with families when such scenarios arise. 3. School management Getting to visit a school and talk to the principal, vice-principal and teachers, as well as other parents, can provide valuable insights into how the school is managed at the senior level. In addition, you can get an idea of the teacher-to-student ratio, as well as the general retention levels of staff and students at the school. For a secondary school, it can also be useful to see if there is an active alumni network for graduates, which helps promote an ongoing sense of community around the school and provides networking and social opportunities. 4. Extracurriculars and more To ensure that your child gets a well-rounded experience in school, you can ask for details of the sports, arts and STEM programmes on offer, and if outdoor education and other experiential learning programmes complement the main curriculum. With university environments in mind as well as ways to prepare children for the working world, you can also explore opportunities for student leadership within the school, and involvement in any student teams or organised competitions, either locally or internationally. 5. Parent–school relationship Once a child is enrolled in the school, it is also the start of a years-long relationship between the school and the parents. During the initial visit, you can find out how the school and the teachers will communicate with parents and how you can be more involved in your child’s school life and the school community in general. Ask for details of the PTA (Parent-Teacher Association) and how it works alongside in-house school structures.

title: In Focus | China has gained pace in the space race by recovering rockets – but can it relaunch one?
description: SpaceX might have a head start in reusable rockets, but Chinese commercial space companies are exploring ways to catch up in the cost-saving tech.
content: As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead. US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components. Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain. Last month, Chinese private aerospace company LandSpace landed the booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket on deployable landing legs at a site in the northwestern province of Gansu, marking the country’s first successful ground-based controlled recovery using landing legs, an approach that closely resembles that of SpaceX’s Falcon 9. The significance of landing a launched rocket goes beyond the spectacle of bringing a booster back intact, according to industry experts. Rocket reuse was “essential for achieving low-cost, frequent and sustainable [launches] … and providing new opportunities for large-scale commercial space exploration”, a team from three major Chinese aerospace research institutions said in a paper published in March. LandSpace said the first stage represented “about 70 per cent” of a rocket’s cost, with reuse able to spread that expense over multiple missions, underscoring the cost advantages of reusing first-stage boosters. Some Chinese launch services can cost around US$20,000 per kilogram (about US$9,070 a pound) of payload, compared with roughly US$2,700 to US$3,000 for SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9, according to a report published by the Mercator Institute for China Studies in February. The large gap helps explain why rocket makers are racing to develop vehicles that can be recovered and reused. The Chinese paper from March said there were several different approaches to bringing a rocket back, including recovery using parachutes or wings to slow the vehicle for a safer arrival. Other approaches include landing leg recovery, with the booster using its engines to control its descent before touching down vertically on deployable landing legs. While China still lags behind the US in landing leg recovery, it is also betting on a different approach to booster recovery: an offshore net-capture system that uses a recovery vessel to catch the descending booster. In July, it successfully retrieved part of a Long March-10B reusable rocket following its maiden launch by using a unique sea-based net-capture system for the first time. Compared with the landing leg recovery approach, net-capture had relatively less demanding requirements for the booster’s final landing-point accuracy, avoided the need to install heavy landing-support structures on the rocket and allowed the offshore recovery platform to be deployed flexibly, Wang Long, the founder of space technology consultancy Nihao Taikong, was quoted as saying in a report by Shenzhen-based Securities Times in July. Hao Jinjie, an engineer at China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, told state broadcaster CGTN the net-capture method was “like dropping a pen from the 100th floor into a pencil holder, while keeping its speed and orientation under control”. China’s pursuit of reusable rockets draws on both its state aerospace groups and its ability to mobilise the private sector behind national priorities through the deployment of industrial policy. Galactic Energy’s kerosene-fuelled Pallas-1 reached orbit earlier this month, with a recovery attempt deliberately deferred to later missions. The rocket is designed to carry up to 7 tonnes to a low-Earth orbit, intended for use on the first stage of at least 25 flights. ISpace flew the same low-altitude methane demonstrator twice in 2023, though its orbital SQX-3 has yet to launch. Space Pioneer, Orienspace, Deep Blue Aerospace and Space Epoch also have reusable rockets at various stages of testing or development. To make reusability economically viable, a booster needs to be able to re-enter space and survive repeated launches. Dai Zheng, chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, said those were areas in which China had little experience. China had no established technical framework covering rocket reuse standards, inspection procedures or rules governing component replacement, Dai told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview last month. “China has just solved the question of whether a rocket can come back,” he said, adding that there was “no system yet for determining whether a recovered rocket can fly again”. In a research report published last month, analysts at Jinyuan Securities emphasised that a reusable rocket required a complete post-recovery processing cycle, including safely draining and disposing of residual propellant, isolating potential hazards and conducting non-destructive inspections of the vehicle’s structure, welds and propellant tanks. Other necessary steps involved assessing the remaining life of engines after repeated thermal and pressure cycles, replacing worn components such as seals and valves, and carrying out system-wide functional tests before another flight. LandSpace has said it plans to reuse the Zhuque-3 booster recovered last month in a space mission in the next six months, while the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology has said it aims to conduct a reuse flight of the first-stage Long March-10B by the end of this year. Success in those endeavours would mark a crucial shift for China from demonstrating that it can recover a booster to proving that it can fly one again – essential to realising its commercial space ambitions. A decade ago, a central government white paper called for research into low-cost launch vehicles and reusable transport systems capable of travelling between Earth and space. Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency Xu Ying, GalaxySpace What began as a research objective has moved through engineering trials and become a national industrial push. China’s latest five-year plan made building the country into a “space power” a priority, and specifically mentioned the development of reusable launch technology, including a reusable heavy-lift launcher for deep-space programmes. Every serious ambition China has in space – from constellations of broadband satellites to orbiting computing networks and missions to the moon – will depend on reusable launch systems. “Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency,” said Xu Ying, general manager of public affairs at satellite manufacturer GalaxySpace. Only then, she added, could “space infrastructure” be deployed at scale and become commercially viable. China’s two flagship broadband projects show the size of the task. China Satellite Net plans for its Guowang constellation to have 12,992 satellites, with roughly 1,300 scheduled to be in orbit by 2029 and the full network deployed by 2035. Shanghai-based SpaceSail’s Qianfan network is aiming for more than 15,000 by 2030, but the two Chinese companies combined have less than 500 satellites in orbit at present – around 4 per cent of Starlink’s orbiting fleet of more than 11,000. LandSpace launched 10 Qianfan satellites into orbit on Tuesday, marking the first deployment for a large-scale satellite internet constellation by a private Chinese rocket company. Another eight were launched on Wednesday. SpaceSail aims to expand the Qianfan constellation to 324 satellites by the end of the year – up from 256 at present – leaving a narrow window of just over three months to launch 68 more. A space industry researcher based in Xian, capital of northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, said some experts were optimistic that China would be able to make steady progress in the reusable rocket race. He said that while SpaceX – founded in 2002 – had a head start in many aspects of the commercial space sector, Chinese companies were making progress. However, he added, China’s industry might encounter difficulties due to a comparative lack of experience in advanced rocket engines, as “no one from outside China would teach you how to design them”. Engines accounted for more than 50 per cent of the total cost of a rocket, Wang Zijing, an analyst at Soochow Securities, wrote in a research note issued this month. Jinyuan Securities said engine life and repeated ignition were among the biggest technical challenges in the reuse of boosters. A reusable booster must restart its engines during ascent, re-entry and landing and operate reliably across a wide range of thrust levels, meaning that key components including its turbopumps, combustion chamber, nozzle and valves must be able to withstand repeated thermal and pressure cycles as well as vibration loads. No Chinese rocket engine has yet made a second orbital flight. Meanwhile, a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster was sent into space for the 37th time last month. “Reusable technology remains a new field that requires continued learning,” Lou Luliang, the chief designer of the Long March-10B, told Beijing-based China Aerospace News in a report published in July. “The thermal and mechanical conditions during an actual return, component damage and the patterns of reuse cannot all be fully understood through ground testing alone”.

title: Meet Cillian Murphy’s mini-me son Aran, set to appear in HBO Max series Youth
description: The Oppenheimer star’s youngest child made his screen debut in 2022’s Lola and has three releases lined up, including one with Amy Adams and Jenna Ortega.
content: Cillian Murphy’s son Aran is his father’s mini-me. The 19-year-old, who will appear in the upcoming HBO Max series Youth, walked the red carpet at the show’s premiere in London on September 11 and the internet can’t get over how much he resembles his father. “[At] first sight, I thought it was Cillian Murphy! He’s super cute!” one user commented under an Instagram post that showed Aran speaking to the media at the premiere. “Looks so much like his dad!” another fan wrote. So who is the Irish actor’s lookalike son Aran? Read on to find out. He was raised in London Aran Murphy was born in 2007 to Cillian Murphy and Yvonne McGuinness. He also has an older brother, Malachy, who was born in 2005. Malachy and Aran were raised in London for much of their childhood, but the family moved to Ireland, where both Murphy and McGuinness hail from, in 2015. During a 2022 appearance on the Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard podcast, Murphy revealed that he and McGuinness moved the family to Dublin because they “wanted their children to be Irish”. “They were sort of at that age where they were preteens and had very posh English accents, and I wasn’t appreciating that too much. So we decided to come back,” the Oppenheimer star said. When did Aran Murphy start acting? While his older brother has chosen to stay out of the spotlight, Aran has been acting since he was young. Aran was only 11 years old when he landed the titular role of Hamnet in Irish theatre company Dead Centre’s play about William Shakespeare’s only son. The play toured in the US, Europe, Australia and Hong Kong. He made his on-screen debut with the 2022 sci-fi film Lola and will soon appear in Youth, a show starring Sharon Horgan as a 50-year-old divorcee who juggles her single life while looking after her parents and son. He is also set to appear in HBO’s television series War, as well as Taika Waititi’s upcoming film Klara and the Sun starring Amy Adams and Jenna Ortega. Cillian Murphy is a proud father The Peaky Blinders actor has previously spoken of his two sons, commending them on their confidence and sense of self. “They seem better adjusted than I was. More sure of themselves,” Murphy told The Guardian in 2016. “I’m happy about that. For me, it was something that took a long time to figure out: that it’s all right to be you, that it’s all right to be an individual.” He also said on the Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard podcast that his sons were “good boys”. “This is such a cliché, but I just want them to be happy and confident kids, that’s all. And to know themselves, I think that’s the most important thing. And they’re heading that way; they’re good boys. But I try not to project stuff onto them; it’s impossible not to do it entirely, but let them find their own way.”

title: Why one family’s perfect school may not be quite right for another child
description: Beyond the rankings, results and reputation, parents must find the school environment where their child can truly thrive.
content: When choosing a school in Hong Kong, families have a wealth of information at their disposal outlining everything from curriculum content and pathways to language options, clubs, community activities and educational philosophy. However, amid all these considerations, it generally comes down to one key question: not is this the best school by reputation or results, but is it the right place for this child? As both parents and teachers are well aware, finding a good fit takes time and thought. It means assessing how various factors will help each individual to thrive and understanding what it takes to inspire different talents and temperaments. “Families who are thinking carefully about fit tend to ask thoughtful questions about the school’s culture, values, learning environment and community,” says Câline Fonteneau, director of admissions at Hong Kong International School (HKIS). “Rather than focusing solely on academic outcomes, they are looking for a place where their child will feel known, challenged and supported socially and emotionally, and where the general philosophy aligns with their family’s goals and expectations.” During information sessions for secondary-age pupils, the discussions naturally touch on the HKIS AP (Advanced Placement) programme of college-level courses, university destinations and basic steps in the admissions process. Typically, though, there is just as much interest in daily schedules, transition support, after-school activities, opportunities to volunteer and how these contribute to the overall experience. “Our admissions process is designed to develop a holistic understanding of each applicant and their readiness to thrive at HKIS,” Fonteneau says. “We are interested in a child’s authentic developmental profile, learning needs and the way they approach new experiences.” The first few weeks of the school year are intentionally organised to help students build connections, establish routines and feel a sense of belonging. This provides a strong foundation for academic and personal success, and each secondary grade also has a pastoral care group leader to assist students and parents with aspects of well-being and navigating school life. “Finding the right balance is a priority for us,” Fonteneau says. “Research consistently shows that students thrive when they are engaged physically, creatively and emotionally. We realise too that a positive school culture benefits every member of the community and has a lasting impact far beyond the classroom.” At Korean International School (KIS), Anson Lam can view the matter of best fit for pupils from three distinct perspectives. She is a mother of two, a professional counsellor and the designated safeguarding lead at KIS, meaning she encounters relevant issues while at home, as an adviser and on campus. What interests her most is a school’s heart and soul, which includes its general atmosphere, signs of a safe and nurturing environment, whether teachers are kind and approachable, and how results are achieved without affecting the children’s happiness. “I expect parents to ask about the structure of our support systems and how the safeguarding and academic teams work together,” Lam says. “That tells me they are thinking long term and want to know their child will build good friendships and enjoy a positive school life where well-being and learning are equal priorities.” When advising families, she always encourages them to get a feel for the school’s culture as soon as possible. This can be by connecting with current parents or following KIS on social media channels to see daily life in action – extracurricular activities (ECAs), special events, pastoral care and smiles on faces. “The ‘best’ school isn’t the one with the highest cut-off score,” Lam says. “It is the one where your child wakes up genuinely wanting to go to class.” The common misconceptions she still has to address include the idea that a high-pressure, academically selective environment guarantees future success and the notion that a long list of ECAs inherently provides balance. “True balance is about depth, emotional well-being and quality of experience, not sheer quantity,” Lam says. “We must also be realistic about children’s niche passions, whether that is excelling in ballet or mastering the piano. The school provides essential exposure and encouragement, but going further requires specialist training from external experts. The primary focus at KIS is to give students a caring environment where they can develop unshakeable confidence, resilience and a love of learning.” For the International Montessori School of Hong Kong (IMS), known for its mixed-age, bilingual English-Mandarin classrooms and non-traditional approach, creating a good fit depends on respect for a core concept. That is, the belief that Montessori learning does not just happen at school, but is a way of life, with school and family coming together as a partnership to support the child’s all-round development. The shared values underpinning this include the view that every child is an individual who progresses at their own pace, and that long-term growth, curiosity, independent thinking and a willingness to embrace challenges outweigh test scores. “Parents want to see how we prepare pupils for transitions to primary, secondary and beyond, but also how our bilingual environment works for everyday learning,” says Sandy Tsang, head of admissions and marketing at IMS. “They ask about our routines, emotional support, and how we help children build self-discipline, focus and confidence in a mixed-age classroom.” The objective of workshops and campus tours is to show how structure and freedom for self-directed learning coexist, and that academic rigour is not about memorising worksheets, but ensuring pupils know how to learn and can reflect on and record their own progress. “Adjustment takes time, so we offer a multi-tiered support system with individualised scaffolding, manageable steps, peer mentoring and experienced learning support teams,” Tsang says. “Our teachers notice subtle behavioural shifts very early and look for continuous patterns over time rather than isolated incidents of anxiety, withdrawal or outbursts of frustration. When children feel safe and respected, their natural curiosity is unlocked and learning flourishes.”

title: Exclusive | US families ramp up efforts for loved ones’ release from China ahead of Xi’s visit
description: Cases of US citizens detained in China gain greater attention as their families increase pressure on Trump administration to help them.
content: Chen Youlin, a Chinese-American scientist, travelled back to China in October 2024 for a month-long holiday, including to celebrate his mother’s 80th birthday. As he prepared to leave, authorities arrested him at the airport in Beijing. For more than 670 days, his wife, Rong Yufang, and other family members have not been able to see or speak with him. “Sometimes I realise I can no longer clearly remember the sound of his voice, and that breaks my heart,” Rong told the South China Morning Post. “Our home feels empty without him and the uncertainty surrounding his future has become a prison for our family as well.” Ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to Washington next week, cases of several US citizens detained in China are gaining greater attention as their families step up pressure on the Trump administration to press Beijing for their release. As well as Chen’s family, the relatives of Americans Min Zin, Dawn Michelle Hunt and Nelson Wells Jnr are pressing Washington to intervene with Beijing – but their cases vary. Chen and Zin are being held on national security-related allegations, while Hunt and Wells Jnr have spent over a decade in Chinese prisons over drug convictions. Families like Chen’s face a dilemma: pursue quiet diplomacy or go public to pressure Washington and Beijing. Many initially favour a low-profile approach, but turn to public advocacy when private efforts fail. The cases highlight the risks American citizens can face in China’s legal system, even as US President Donald Trump and Xi seek to stabilise ties and Beijing courts foreign investors, academics and tourists. US government lists individuals as being ‘wrongfully detained’ Chinese authorities have accused Chen of espionage, likely linked to his previous work analysing seismic data, including North Korean nuclear tests. Another recent well-publicised case involves American scholar Zin, who was detained in China in June. Chinese authorities accused him of espionage and endangering China’s national security. Both Chen and Zin have been formally designated as “wrongfully detained” by the US government, a status that means officials will prioritise efforts to secure their release. A lawyer has been hired to represent Chen and US consular officials have been allowed to visit him. Rong, Chen’s wife, raised concerns about his health and weight loss during his detention. She told the SCMP that senior US officials had assured her that Trump would raise Chen’s case. “President Trump and his senior team have been 100 per cent on my side,” Rong said. The State Department’s Office of the Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs has also publicly addressed the issue, saying: “Hostage diplomacy has no place in the US-China relationship.” Chen’s family initially worked behind the scenes, according to its representative, Eric Lebson of Global Reach. It went public after Trump raised Chen’s case with Xi in May but secured no breakthrough. Trump also raised the cases of Pastor Ezra Jin, who was later freed, and jailed Hong Kong media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying. Lai’s family and supporters want Trump to raise his case again next week. For Zin’s case, the circumstances are less clear. The Wall Street Journal reported that US officials believe his background as a former student activist in Myanmar and his US-funded academic work may have drawn the attention of Chinese security services. Edgard Kagan, a China expert at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said the detention of Chen and Zin is likely linked to their academic work, and he expects Trump to press for their release. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey is leading a bipartisan resolution condemning China’s wrongful detention of American academics. The James W. Foley Legacy Foundation says 12 Americans are currently wrongfully detained in China, including some subject to exit bans. It has assessed 42 cases since 1998, though the total number of Americans caught up in China’s legal system may be higher. In 2024, US diplomacy secured the release of three Americans held for years; Beijing said the US returned four people to China. The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment. Beijing has firmly rejected the “wrongful detention” designations. Asked about Chen’s case, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said there is no “wrongful detention” in China and that judicial agencies handle cases in accordance with the law. The embassy spokesperson offered more detail on Zin specifically, telling the Wall Street Journal that he is subject to “criminal coercive measures,” meaning he is under investigation, and that his “legitimate rights have been fully guaranteed.” Two other high-profile cases involving Americans Two other high-profile cases involve Americans Hunt and Wells Jnr, both of whom have been imprisoned in China for more than 12 years after being convicted on separate drug charges. Unlike the scholars’ cases, which have been designated as “wrongfully detained”, the families are pursuing the humanitarian release route and say that they are speaking on behalf of ordinary “rank-and-file” Americans. The families have joined forces, saying both detainees unknowingly carried drugs out of China. Dawn Michelle’s brother, Tim Hunt, said scammers lured her there with a purported competition prize, then gave her purses with drugs sewn into the lining.
