Wells Jnr was arrested after agreeing to carry someone else’s suitcase containing hidden narcotics, his family said. Both have worsening health problems, their families say. Wells Jnr’s father said his son has seizures, high blood pressure and diabetes, and was recently diagnosed with hepatitis C. Peter Humphrey, a former SCMP China correspondent and fraud investigator who was imprisoned in China with his wife from 2013 to 2015, is working with the families. Since his release, he has advised foreign detainees and their families on how to navigate China’s system. “We have been constantly hearing from our lobbying contacts in Beijing that the Chinese side is very ready to consider a humanitarian release, so long as there is a request from the American president,” Humphrey said. Joi Chaney, a legal expert working with the families, called the lack of a US-China prisoner transfer treaty a “blockade” the US has placed on itself. Chinese law allows transfers through bilateral negotiations in special cases, but Washington has historically maintained that US law does not, said Humphrey. He said the US State Department asked China in May 2025 to release Wells Jnr and Hunt on humanitarian grounds. In response to an SCMP inquiry, a US State Department spokesperson said it has repeatedly raised serious concerns about Wells Jnr and Hunt’s health with Chinese officials. “We have called upon the Chinese to release them unconditionally on humanitarian grounds, at every opportunity, and we will continue to do so,” it said, while adding that decisions on humanitarian release are at the discretion of the host government. Additionally, in 2025, bipartisan lawmakers introduced the “Nelson Wells Jnr and Dawn Michelle Hunt Unjustly Detained in Communist China Act”, seeking to strengthen the government’s response to Americans detained in China and support their families. The bill has stalled since its introduction. “We’re not famous people, we’re not sports stars,” Chaney said, arguing that ordinary Americans should be able to count on their government to bring them home. Both families have histories of military and public service. “If you say you respect the people who serve, show us,” Tim Hunt said in a plea to Trump. “Ask for their release.” When asked about Hunt and Wells, the White House offered a general response rather than addressing the individual cases. Families put faith in Trump as Xi summit approaches “President Trump is always concerned about Americans detained abroad. That is why he has brought over 100 individuals – a record number – home from around the world,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said. Both families said they were disappointed when their loved ones were not released after the last Xi-Trump summit. Wells Snr described feeling out of it in the weeks after, not wanting to talk. Tim Hunt found it hard to speak to his sister, who felt she had false hope in the lead-up to the meeting. Addressing the US president directly ahead of next week’s summit, Wells Snr said: “I would tell President Trump that he’s a father. If he had a child that was in the same situation as our child or Tim’s sister, he would do everything in his power to try to bring them home.”

title: Opinion | What the China-Nepal floods teach us about crisis communication
description: In an unfolding disaster, families need quick, practical updates and journalists need access the moment safety allows.
content: The Himalayan disaster that tore through the China-Nepal border last month was a human calamity before it became a media story. A torrent of ice, rock, mud and debris swept through valleys, destroying key infrastructure, severing roads and communications, and leaving families desperate for news. In Gyirong county in the Tibet autonomous region, the disaster hit a major border crossing and created a rescue environment as physically difficult as any imaginable. The human toll extends beyond the confirmed dead. With people unaccounted for and recovery work continuing, families on both sides of the border are still waiting for answers. In terrain like this, uncertainty is unavoidable. Rescue operations were hampered by unstable slopes, damaged roads and difficult conditions in a narrow gorge, delaying the arrival of heavy machinery. Those constraints also restricted the flow of information from the area in the first few days. The initial picture was fragmented and the lack of detail gave speculation room to spread. Much of the early international reporting relied on images and accounts from Nepal, while the earliest material from the location itself largely came from CCTV and other Chinese state outlets. That left foreign audiences with a narrow evidentiary base. Tibet’s distance from major news centres and its restrictions on foreign media access made independent reporting even harder. On social media, limited early information fuelled speculation about the disaster’s scale and cause, including false claims about casualties and allegations that Chinese dam construction was responsible. Initial reports indicated that part of a glacier collapsed on the Nepali side of the border. The precise trigger remains under investigation, but the impact was immediate: communities in both countries were caught in the same disaster. For families waiting for news, the line between a rescue operation and a communication failure is not always clear. A blocked road or a damaged signal tower could leave relatives with the same unanswered questions as official silence. That is why the first hours of any disaster are so difficult: uncertainty creates its own story, especially when video, rumour and grief move faster than verified information. In Gyirong, the mudslide cut off roads, power and communications, while damage to the main access route kept heavy machinery from the core disaster area for days. Rescuers also had to contend with an upstream barrier lake, which briefly forced operations to stop amid fears of another flood. Chinese media gave viewers an early picture of the destruction on the Chinese side. After emergency repairs reopened the route, the authorities invited journalists from eight overseas outlets, including CNN and NBC, to visit the hardest-hit areas and attend a government news conference. The reports that followed added another layer to the story. CNN and NBC showed their audiences the scale of the damage at Gyirong and the obstacles facing rescue and recovery crews. That does not settle every question about the early flow of information. It does, however, underline what is needed in a crisis: quick, practical updates for families, followed by access for reporters when conditions allow. For families waiting for news, more reporting was valuable because it shifted attention back to what mattered: finding out what had happened, where the damage was worst and who had been affected. Other overseas coverage focused on China’s handling of information. BBC reporting questioned access to Gyirong and said widely circulated flood footage had become difficult to find on Chinese social media. It later amended its headline to acknowledge that some footage was being shown, though it maintained that coverage was heavily censored. Chinese commentators and state media countered that official updates, video and rescue coverage were already available, and accused foreign outlets of presenting an incomplete picture. In the process, the people who had lost homes, relatives and livelihoods risked being pushed to the margins. That matters because the danger isn’t going away. The Himalayas are becoming an increasingly exposed frontier of climate and geological risk. Glacial instability, extreme weather, the steep terrain and infrastructure development make cross-border early warnings, data sharing and rapid coordination more important, not less. China and Nepal share a practical interest in ensuring the next warning travels faster than the next wall of water. People in valleys below need to know when a lake is forming, a slope is moving or a river is rising. That means the two countries must share information quickly and make sure it reaches the villages, road crews and border posts most exposed to danger. In the Himalayas, warmer conditions, less reliable snowfall and thawing permafrost are changing a mountain environment already prone to sudden, cascading hazards. The next landslide or glacial surge is not a remote possibility, and this disaster teaches that cooperation matters most before the emergency begins.

title: US trade chief pressed Brazil to review Anglo American nickel sale to China
description: Jamieson Greer asked Brasilia to curb ‘non-market’ buyers of critical minerals in exchange for relief from Trump’s tariffs.
content: US Trade Representative (USTR) Jamieson Greer asked Brazil to review the sale of Anglo American’s nickel mines to a Chinese state-controlled miner in exchange for tariff relief, two people familiar with the negotiations told the South China Morning Post. Washington made the request during talks to lift the 50 per cent tariffs US President Donald Trump imposed on Brazilian goods last year. First reported by Brazilian newspaper O Estado de S. Paulo and CNN Brazil on Thursday, the proposal would have given Washington advance notice of mining asset sales before those deals closed, subjected transactions involving rare earths to US review, and opened a window for American companies to buy the assets before any sale won approval. Greer also asked Brasilia to limit investment by “non-market actors” and foreign entities of concern in mining, refining and other critical industrial sectors. Brazilian officials read the phrase as a reference to China, the country’s largest trading partner and a growing source of investment in its mining sector. Officials at the foreign ministry rejected the terms and said Brazil applied the same rules to foreign investors regardless of where their capital came from. They also rejected a second and shorter proposal in January that repeated several of the demands. The US embassy in Brasilia and the USTR could not be immediately reached for comment. The American Iron and Steel Institute had asked Greer to intervene months earlier. Lobby group letter warns of China’s ‘direct influence’ if sale goes ahead In a letter sent in August last year, the lobby group warned that if the sale succeeded “China would gain direct influence over a substantial portion of Brazil’s nickel reserves, in addition to its dominant position in Indonesian production”, and urged its office to press Brasilia to explore alternatives that “would preserve market-oriented ownership of these strategic nickel assets”. Kevin Dempsey, the institute’s Chief Executive, filed the letter in the public docket of the Section 301 investigation into Brazil. That investigation covered digital payments, tariffs, intellectual property, ethanol access and deforestation, but nickel was not on the list. Anglo American agreed in February last year to sell the business to a Singapore subsidiary of MMG for up to US$500 million, with US$350 million payable on completion and the rest tied to nickel prices and a final investment decision on new projects. The sale was part of a restructuring the London-listed miner launched after it fended off a takeover approach from BHP. The assets include the Barro Alto and Codemin ferronickel operations in Goias state, which together produced 39,700 tonnes of nickel contained in ferronickel last year, and undeveloped projects at Jacare in Para and Morro Sem Bone in Mato Grosso. MMG and its parent China Minmetals are controlled by the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission. China does not produce ferronickel and instead relies on nickel pig iron, a cheaper, lower-grade substitute smelted mostly in Indonesia from ore that Chinese companies control. Brazilian ferronickel has a higher nickel content and, because the mines run on a lower carbon footprint, European mills have struggled to source it elsewhere. Brazil’s antitrust authority, known as Cade, opened an inquiry in August last year after a complaint from CoreX Holding, a Netherlands-registered group controlled by Turkish billionaire Robert Yuksel Yildirim, which said it had offered US$900 million for the same assets and took the same objection to regulators in Brussels. Regulators in Brasilia examined whether the transaction should have been notified in advance, which carried a fine of up to 60 million reais (US$11.5 million) for Anglo American, and Cade’s investigative arm shelved the case. Anglo American said MMG submitted the strongest offer after weighing guarantees, operating record, and long-term management capacity alongside price. European Commission’s in-depth investigation into deal The European Commission opened an in-depth investigation last November and sent MMG a statement of objections on Wednesday, warning that the miner could redirect low-carbon ferronickel towards affiliated Chinese steelmakers and away from European producers. The Commission said such a diversion “could adversely affect the price of low-carbon ferronickel” and the resilience of European stainless steel producers. MMG rejected the assessment, offered guarantees to European customers and said it would supply at least the volumes Anglo American currently delivers. The Commission has until November 30 to decide. Brazil and the United States resumed talks on August 31 after months without formal negotiations, and Brazil’s minister of development, industry and trade, Marcio Elias Rosa, is due to meet Greer in the US on the sidelines of a G20 meeting later this month. Until then, two rounds of US tariffs remain in force, reaching 37.5 per cent when combined and covering about 23 per cent of Brazilian exports to the American market, though rare earths are already exempt.

title: US approves sale of 48 F-35 jets to Saudi Arabia despite Israeli concerns
description: US says the sale would improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter ‘current and future threats’.
content: The United States has approved a US$24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 stealth warplanes to Saudi Arabia, the State Department said Thursday, the kingdom’s latest major arms purchase since the start of the Iran war. Saudi Arabia has long sought to buy F-35s, but officials from Israel – currently the only country in the Middle East to operate the jets – have voiced concern about their sale to Riyadh despite a push for the kingdom to normalise relations. “The proposed sale will improve Saudi Arabia’s capability to deter current and future threats by strengthening its homeland defence, and improving interoperability with US forces,” the State Department said in a statement. It “will also augment Saudi Arabia’s operational aircraft and enhance its air-to-air, and air-to-ground self-defence capability,” the statement said. The Saudi embassy in Washington praised the transaction, saying it “reflects the strength and enduring nature” of the relationship with the United States. It added that the security cooperation between the two countries “has contributed to regional stability, strengthened our collective defence capabilities, and advanced our shared security interests”. Saudi Arabia has been repeatedly targeted with drone and missile strikes by Tehran’s forces since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February, and has also been hit by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Yemen’s civil war had been dormant for years, but fighting between Houthis and the internationally recognised, Riyadh-backed government reignited in July, with the rebels declaring a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Washington has not directly entered the conflict, but a US official said earlier this week that an American military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces. The State Department has notified Congress about the proposed sale, which would require the approval of US lawmakers. It did not provide a time frame for the delivery of the jets. The F-35 sale “will not alter the military balance in the region,” the State Department said, in keeping with long-standing US policy that Israel must have a military edge over potential regional adversaries. “We should always be a few rungs above. And if they give them the F-35, we’ll get the B-2, for argument’s sake,” Eli Cohen, a member of Israel’s security cabinet, told Channel 14 in November, referring to the stealth bomber used by the US to attack Iranian nuclear sites in June. The “Israeli edge must be preserved and insisted on,” he said. The Saudi Air Force flies a mix of fighter aircraft ‌including Boeing F-15s, European Tornados and Typhoons. The United States has so far only allowed the sales of F-35s to its closest allies, including a number of European Nato allies and Israel. Washington kicked Nato member Turkey out of the F-35 programme in 2019 because Ankara’s purchase of a Russian air defence system sparked fears that Moscow could acquire the plane’s technology. Washington also has concerns about potential Chinese espionage related to the jets. The New York Times reported this week that US intelligence analysts have raised the possibility that Beijing could acquire F-35 technology through its partnerships with Riyadh. US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi, a Democratic member of the House Intelligence Committee, expressed opposition to the sale on those grounds. It should not go ahead “when our own intelligence community is warning that it could put the crown jewels of American military technology within reach of the Chinese Communist Party,” Krishnamoorthi said in a statement. The F-35 sale is the latest in a series of major arms buys by Saudi Arabia this year. The State Department announced the approval of a US$5 billion sale of more than 10,000 bombs – including highly destructive 2,000-pound weapons – to Riyadh earlier in September. Washington also signed off on the sale of 60 tank engines and related equipment to Saudi Arabia at a cost of US$750 million this month, and a US$1.96 billion deal in July for the kingdom to buy guidance sections that can convert rockets into precision weapons. Additional reporting by Reuters and Bloomberg

title: Trump says ‘major progress’ made towards US base in Poland
description: Announcement comes despite a wider US review of troop levels in Europe and tensions over Nato defence spending.
content: US President Donald Trump said Thursday there had been “major progress” towards establishing an American military base in Poland, after Warsaw said it was holding talks with Washington on the issue. “Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a US Army base in Poland,” Trump said on social media. “If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.” Trump’s announcement comes despite his administration launching a formal review of its military presence in Europe, raising fears among allies that it could cut back its forces in European nations. But Poland, which borders both Ukraine and Russia on Nato’s eastern flank and spends around 5 per cent of its GDP on defence, is working to strengthen the US presence on its soil. “We are ready to continue our efforts to strengthen our defense cooperation: seriously, responsibly, and always together,” Nawrocki said on X. “I can assure you that the Polish government will do its utmost to provide the best possible location for the US Army base.” Nawrocki is a conservative ally of Trump, and he visited the White House last year. During that visit Trump offered to send more US troops to Poland. Polish deputy defence minister Pawel Zalewski said in August that his country was discussing with the United States whether to set up a permanent US base on its territory. “We have already completed the initial stage (of the process), not to mention the political will, which was expressed long ago,” Zalewski told public broadcaster TVP. Almost 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in Poland - which is also an EU member state - but almost exclusively on a rotational basis. Washington has levied heavy criticism against a number of European countries that refused to allow US forces to use Nato bases on their territory in their war with Iran. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had also threatened to reduce his country’s contribution to the alliance’s budget if certain states refused to honor the commitments made last year at the Nato summit in The Hague. At that summit, Nato allies pledged to devote by 2035 at least 4 per cent of their GDP to security spending, including 3.5 per cent devoted strictly to military expenditures.

title: AFC Champions League 2: Hong Kong champions Kitchee survive red card to make point
description: Hosts impress and lay down marker in Mong Kok Stadium stalemate with Gangwon FC, Tai Po lose down under.
content: Kitchee survived playing the final 25 minutes with 10 men, after a debatable red card for captain Ruslan Mingazov, to draw 0-0 with Gangwon FC on Thursday night in their opening AFC Champions League 2 match. Although a point against the strongest team in the group represented a sound return, it could have been even better for the Hong Kong club on their return to Asian competition after three years away. Mingazov and Victor Camarasa, the former Cardiff City midfielder, were both inches wide with first-half attempts at Mong Kok Stadium. In front of a healthy 2,899 crowd, Marcao headed over a Camarasa cross shortly after half-time, then Koldo Obieta aimed wastefully wide following good work from Adrian Revilla. Pong Cheuk-hei, the Kitchee goalkeeper, produced a pair of athletic stops to deny the Koreans’ 18-year-old midfielder, Lee Yong-jae, either side of the break. Already in the book following a loose challenge, Mingazov received a second yellow card after using his hand to meet an Everton Camargo delivery at the back post. The winger and his teammates were incensed, circling referee Ahmad Yacoub Ibrahim to vehemently plead that Mingazov had been impeded as he stretched to reach the ball. Hong Kong’s other entrants, FA Cup holders Tai Po, were beaten 3-0 by Adelaide United in Australia.

title: US sanctions boost China’s science-driven innovation by over 70%, study finds
description: US tech restrictions have driven Chinese firms to expand and deepen their scientific research sourcing through citations and research.
content: US-sanctioned Chinese companies are increasingly turning to open-source research to innovate and reverse-engineer restricted foreign technology, with a 72 per cent surge in scientific literature citations in their patent applications, according to a new study. While the United States said it expanded its Entity List to safeguard national security and preserve its technological edge, an analysis of Chinese patent filings over the 12 years until 2022 showed that US restrictions on access to technology had driven Chinese firms to widely source publicly available scientific knowledge and conduct more of their own research. “Our analysis reveals that US trade sanctions, such as the Entity List, have generated consequences that US policymakers may not have fully anticipated,” the researchers wrote in a policy article published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on Friday. “Though hindering the targeted firms’ short-term operations, sanctions may also catalyse these firms’ development of internal capabilities and drive strategic shifts, potentially leading to the emergence of separate technological systems that compete with, rather than integrate into, the current global innovation ecosystem,” they wrote. “This strategic adaptation by Chinese firms under external constraints unfolds against the background of rising corporate science in China, where firms have been deepening their integration with science, as evidenced by the rising number of science-linked patents and scientific publications.” “Although the list limits access to US-origin proprietary technologies, sanctioned Chinese firms do not stop sourcing US-produced science,” the authors said. Following sanctioning, targeted companies added nearly 0.99 patents citing domestic science, 0.27 citing non-US foreign science and 0.2 citing US science. To examine how trade controls alter corporate strategy, researchers from Shenzhen University, Tsinghua University and the University of Hong Kong analysed a firm-level data set of Chinese patents filed domestically and internationally between 2010 and 2022. They found that Chinese companies were more engaged with science, both as consumers who increasingly cited scientific publications in their patents and as producers who generated a growing volume of academic publications. Study author Wang Yanbo, associate director of the Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at HKU Business School, said US trade restrictions were inadvertently accelerating technological self-reliance in China. “Once they get blocked from this US-dominated global innovation system, they have to reinvent the wheel,” Wang said. In addition to reverse engineering, “underneath every technology there are certain scientific principles. What is the best way to look into the scientific principle? You read academic papers. “This is why these Chinese firms are extremely motivated to search the scientific literature, incorporate the knowledge into innovation and even to produce scientific knowledge by themselves,” he said. “As long as you make a sufficient amount of effort and have some luck, you are going to invent something similar, something that you can use to substitute the US technology. “Essentially what the US has been doing is forcing China to become independent and develop a separate technological system.” The findings showed that among targeted firms, placement on the US Entity List induced an average 72 per cent surge in science-linked patents that cited academic literature. While Chinese firms’ science-linked patents grew 13.4-fold compared to a 1.3-fold increase for US peers, Chinese companies still lag behind American counterparts in both scientific breadth and depth, according to analysis of patents granted by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. In 2022, 37 per cent of US firms’ patents cited scientific literature, compared to 22 per cent for Chinese firms. Furthermore, among science-linked patents, US companies cited an average of 17.5 scientific publications per patent, compared to five for Chinese firms. In international scientific publishing, US publicly listed companies maintained substantially higher output, rising from an annual average of 12 papers in 2010 to 20 in 2021. By contrast, Chinese listed firms produced an average of four international papers in 2021, despite a 6.5-fold growth in international publications. On the other hand, China used its dominance over rare earth mining and processing as a powerful chokepoint to counter US trade restrictions, Wang said. “The US government and some US firms have been trying really hard over the past several years to identify alternative supply chains and potential substitute technologies, and whether they can develop some kind of magnets without rare earth materials,” he said. “We are all sitting in the same boat. Now these two big guys are quarrelling with each other and we feel the boat is getting rocked. We would not feel comfortable.” If this decoupling continued to its extremes, Wang warned, two separate technological ecosystems would emerge – one dominated by the US and one by China. “I am not sure whether this is what the US policymakers really want to see.” “A certain level of competition is healthy for knowledge production and commercialisation,” he said. “But at the same time, do we really want to see a fragmented global scientific or innovation community? Probably not, because that means knowledge flow will become very inefficient. “However, from where we are to that extreme, the distance is huge,” Wang added. “China has become one of the leading scientific knowledge producers on this planet. That also means working with China’s scientific community can bring a lot of benefits to the US.”

title: New cat species identified in Bolivia, first in over a century
description: The Tilcayo is part of a group of South American tiger cats and was found in the lush Yungas cloud forest.
content: A ⁠diminutive wild cat that inhabits Bolivia’s cloud forest has been identified as ⁠a previously unknown species, marking the first time a new living cat species has been formally named and described in more than a century. The cat, called Tilcayo by local communities, is part of a group called tiger cats found across much of South America. It was found in Bolivia’s lush Yungas forest, a mountainous region where forests are often covered by clouds and surrounded by high humidity, according to researchers. It measures about 18 inches (46cm) long and ‌weighs around three pounds (1.4 kg), making it smaller than the average domestic cat. Researchers used genetic data to confirm that the cat is a new species and gave it the scientific name Leopardus tilcayo, retaining its local name. “Its fur is light brown … with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body,” said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, a National Geographic Explorer and one of the authors of the study describing the newly identified species published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology. Little is yet known about the cat’s biology and lifestyle. Remains of small rodents in scat samples suggest they may form part of its diet, while camera-trap evidence indicates it could be more active at night, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Tiger cats are so-called cryptic species, ⁠meaning they cannot easily be distinguished merely by appearance, said evolutionary biologist and study co-lead author Jonas Lescroart of the University of Antwerp in Belgium. Tiger cats previously had been considered a single ‌species, but genetic studies decades ago suggested the existence of multiple species. Referring to the new species, Lescroart said: “Our information at this moment is limited to the two live individuals that we examined, and a small number of camera-trap records.” One of the live cats is a 10-year-old male that now lives ‌in Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary after being kept by a local family in their home. Observing the Bolivian cat drew interest because “its characteristics did not match ⁠the descriptions, most of them based on Brazilian ⁠cats”, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. “This made us wonder: what tiger cat do we actually have in Bolivia?” The team analysed DNA from 38 cats sampled across several South American countries, including eight museum specimens. The study found that tiger cats are in ‌fact five genetically distinct species. “We never expected this Bolivian tiger cat to be a separate species, and no one had ever proposed it as a different animal, subspecies or otherwise,” Lescroart said. Genetic analysis suggested that the Tilcayo lineage separated from other tiger ‌cats about ‌1.4 million years ago. “The more differences in their DNA, the longer the time that we estimate those lineages to have been physically separated,” Lescroart said, adding that such a gap ‌is generally considered a species-level divide in cats. The research team also described a new tiger cat subspecies in Peru’s Yungas, naming it Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo after Antisuyu, the region of the old Inca ⁠Empire that included the area it inhabits. The International Union for Conservation of Nature, or IUCN, Red List tracking the status of species currently treats tiger cats as two “vulnerable” species with declining ⁠populations. The researchers have shared their findings with the IUCN, whose upcoming review will assess the five lineages separately. That could give a more accurate picture of risk, Lescroart said, and species such as the Tilcayo could potentially be considered endangered when assessed on their own. The need for a clearer assessment is particularly acute in the Yungas, one ‌of the region’s most threatened ecosystems. The mountain ‌forests face growing pressure from deforestation, agricultural expansion, human-caused fires and mining, Nogales-Ascarrunz said. Restoring forest patches damaged by fires, protecting remaining native forest and maintaining connections between habitats are urgent priorities, Nogales-Ascarrunz added. “Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats … there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message,” said Eduardo Eizirik, an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil and senior author of the study. “There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them.”

title: Hong Kong hits out at US panel over Jimmy Lai hearing and sanctions bill
description: Government says US Congressional-Executive Commission on China is trying to ‘intimidate’ officials with sanctions.
content: Hong Kong authorities have hit out at a US congressional commission for colluding with “anti-China politicians” to hold a hearing on jailed former media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying and introducing a bill to “intimidate” local national security officials with sanctions. The government issued the condemnation on Thursday night after the US Congressional-Executive Commission on China (CECC) held a hearing the previous day on Lai, founder of the now-defunct Apple Daily newspaper. During the hearing, Lai’s son appealed for his father’s release. Lai’s national security case and prison conditions, as well as his 20-year sentence, press freedom and rule-of-law issues in Hong Kong were also discussed. The heads of the CECC also introduced the Jimmy Lai Hong Kong Political Prisoner Accountability Act of 2026. The bipartisan bill seeks to establish a framework requiring the US State Department to investigate within 30 days any death of a “Hong Kong political prisoner” in custody linked to abuse, medical neglect or inhumane conditions. It would then mandate sanctions within 60 days against responsible or complicit mainland Chinese and Hong Kong officials. The bill also requires regular reporting to the US Congress on the health of and access to Lai, 78, and other “political prisoners”. A Hong Kong government spokesman strongly condemned the move. “The anti-China politicians have once again clamoured at the so-called ‘hearing’ to intimidate the relevant officials safeguarding national security with so-called ‘sanctions’,” the spokesman said. “All relevant government officials are not intimidated at all and will continue to resolutely discharge their duty of safeguarding national security.” The spokesman also rejected claims that the case involved press freedom, saying Lai and others had used journalism as a cover to create social conflicts, incite hatred and collude with foreign forces seeking sanctions against the central and Hong Kong governments. “Anyone who vilifies the rule of law and the human rights situation in [Hong Kong] by exploiting the Lai Chee-ying case is distorting the facts and reversing right and wrong,” the spokesman said. Lai was jailed for 20 years in February after he was convicted of two counts of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces and a third count of conspiracy to print and distribute seditious articles. He did not appeal against the conviction or sentence. The spokesman also dismissed claims about Lai’s health and prison conditions as fabrications, saying the Correctional Services Department had provided adequate medical care.

title: Will Trump demolish the Kennedy Centre? Air Force One photo offers clue
description: US president seen through aircraft window holding a placard showing the apparent demolition of famed venue.
content: A photo of US President Donald Trump examining a depiction of Washington’s Kennedy Centre apparently being demolished sparked widespread attention on Thursday after he threatened to tear down the revered arts venue because he has been blocked from renaming it after himself. In the image captured by Agence France-Presse photographer Brendan Smialowski late on Wednesday at Joint Base Andrews, the Republican leader was seen through the windows of Air Force One holding a placard with visible text in red declaring: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS …” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame but Trump has mused repeatedly about razing the Washington arts venue. Below the words is a large picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building. Smialowski, who was photographing Trump’s return to Washington from a rally in North Carolina, said he was watching carefully as the president appeared to be sitting in a different seat than usual. “It’s an interesting photo,” said Smialowski, who has covered the White House for 20 years. “The Kennedy Centre’s in the news right now, and their future is in the news.” The images were viewed millions of times on social media and made headlines in many US news outlets. They were also included as evidence in a court filing Thursday by Joyce Beatty, a Democratic Ohio congresswoman and Kennedy Centre board member who is challenging Trump’s overhaul of the institution. With his approval ratings in the low 30 per cent range amid discontent over the war against Iran and the rising cost of living, Trump has fixated on getting the Kennedy Centre renamed in his honour. He threatened to tear down the venue after a judge ruled this week that his name cannot be added to the building’s exterior. Trump said his administration planned to carry out needed multimillion dollar renovations, then would have to “subsidise it for years to come”. “I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition because, frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down,” he said Wednesday. Trump and his hand-picked Kennedy Centre board members have argued that its main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair. The facility was closed on Wednesday for seven days “to assess existing safety risks”, according to a Trump administration court filing on Thursday. It came after a staff member of the law firm representing Beatty tried to visit the Kennedy Centre on Wednesday morning and was stopped by staff who told her it was closed. In her own court filing, the employee described how the centre had been blocked off by gates and witnessed how a forklift had “run into and hit the pillars on the building several times”. Trump installed himself as chairman of the centre, which is named in honour of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963. The venue’s board voted in December to call it the “Trump-Kennedy” Centre and installed signage with his name on it. A judge ordered Trump’s name removed from the exterior and overturned the board’s decision to rename the institution. Workers removed Trump’s name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since. The Kennedy Centre takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump’s brand on the US capital, including lavish gold trim in the Oval Office, a triumphal arch near the National Mall and a half-billion-dollar ballroom at the White House.

title: Rare honour: Trump will greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews, not just White House
description: US president will personally greet Chinese counterpart on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews in Washington when Xi lands next Wednesday.
content: US President Donald Trump will personally greet Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews when Xi lands in Washington next Wednesday, a rare airport reception, a US official confirmed on background. Trump will attend Xi’s arrival ceremony at Andrews, where the Chinese president’s aircraft is expected around 4pm local time on September 23. The president almost never meets visiting heads of state at the airfield. He typically waits at the White House. The gesture is not a perfect mirror of what Trump received in Beijing a few months ago. When Air Force One landed at Beijing Capital International Airport on May 13, Xi did not come to the tarmac. Vice-President Han Zheng led the reception, joined by ambassadors and senior foreign ministry officials, along with an honour guard, a band, and flag-waving youth. Xi’s formal welcome came the next day outside the Great Hall of the People, with a military review Trump later called “incredible”. Airport greetings by a sitting Chinese president are themselves uncommon. Xi has not made a habit of meeting foreign leaders on the runway. Washington is pairing the airport honour with a full state arrival ceremony. White House pool guidance circulated this week lists a “State Arrival Ceremony and Welcome” by Trump for Xi on Wednesday, September 23. An honour guard has been rehearsing at the White House since Tuesday. Troops in ceremonial dress have been drilling on the driveway and lawn in a formation meant to echo the pageantry Trump received in Beijing. A newly completed granite helicopter pad on the South Lawn was rushed to be ready for the visit. Trump has said he wanted the pad finished in time for Xi. His unfinished US$400 million ballroom will not be. The trip is the return half of the May state visit. At a Beijing banquet on May 14, Trump invited Xi and Peng Liyuan to the White House on September 24. After arrival on the 23rd, the core of the summit will take place on the 24th and Xi’s departure on the 25th. Xi is not expected to participate in the UN General Assembly in New York, happening at the same time. September 24 is expected to include bilateral meetings and a formal state dinner. On Thursday, First Lady Melania Trump posted a short video of the table settings being prepared, with the caption “THE WHITE HOUSE STATE DINNER” and the line that every detail had been considered “for our distinguished guests”. The clip showed crystal glassware, floral arrangements, a place card for “The President”, and a printed welcome from the President and Mrs Trump “on the occasion of the visit of His Excellency Xi Jinping”, with Peng also named. Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are among US executives reported as likely dinner guests. Beijing is assembling its own business entourage. The grouping is expected to parallel the coterie of chief executives Trump took to Beijing in May and could signal room for investment deals at the summit. The South China Morning Post earlier reported that executives from electric vehicle maker BYD and smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi are likely to accompany Xi. Sources familiar with the planning say some limited sightseeing may be added around the official programme, though Beijing and the White House have not published a public hour-by-hour itinerary. China typically confirms travel details only days in advance. The protocol burst comes as both sides try to lock down the agenda. China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke by phone on Thursday. According to a Chinese readout, they focused on high-level exchanges, preparing the next phase of leader-to-leader contact, and the principle of equality, respect, and mutual benefit. They also discussed the Middle East. The call follows earlier Wang and Rubio contacts in late June and a lengthy meeting in Manila in July that Rubio said was largely about laying groundwork for a “very positive visit”. Separately, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to meet Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng this weekend. US media reported that the meeting will take place in New York. Bessent told Congress that the talks would continue private discussions on trade, rare earths, Iran-related financial sanctions, and artificial intelligence, and would carry into Xi’s state visit.

title: Hong Kong to legislate against persistent child sexual abuse and ‘cyberflashing’
description: Security Bureau says government will include targeted offences in sex offence amendment bill after public and legal groups express broad support.
content: Hong Kong authorities have said they will legislate against persistent sexual abuse of children and the act of sending images of genitals to others online without consent after consulting the public. In a consultation report published on Thursday, the Security Bureau stated that with the city’s two professional legal associations expressing broad support for a dedicated law targeting persistent child sexual abuse, the government would include the crime in an amendment bill overhauling sex offence laws. “In advancing this proposal, the government will study relevant laws in other jurisdictions so as to formulate targeted laws to address perpetrators’ persistent sexual abuse against children, while upholding the principles of presumption of innocence and fair trial,” the bureau wrote. The public had “widely recognised and supported” the series of proposed measures to strengthen protection for minors and mentally incapacitated people from sexual exploitation and abuse, it added. The government earlier said the review was necessary to modernise sexual offence laws two decades after the Law Reform Commission set up a subcommittee in 2006 to examine them. While the original set of proposals did not include a separate offence targeting persistent, long-term sexual abuse of children, advocates have urged authorities to plug the legal loophole. Victims often have difficulty recalling details of abuse that span years. This created a hurdle for prosecutors who must prove under a precedent set by the Court of Final Appeal in 1999 individual acts with sufficient detail for each charge. The Bar Association also reversed its opposition to creating the new offence during the public consultation. However, the 2001 proposal was eventually shelved after the Bar Association and the Law Society opposed the suggestion, saying it would not be possible to specify a representative number of charges, while defendants might not have a clear idea of the allegations against them. Bar Association vice-chairman Martin Hui Siu-ting said last month that the barristers' group now “broadly supported” creating the offence, but cautioned that it would require some “safeguards” to ensure fairness for defendants and victims, as well as the integrity of court rulings. “The [association] in principle supports the introduction of this new offence which no doubt [will] be subject to sufficient safeguards being in place to ensure a fair trial,” a spokeswoman said late on Thursday. Separately in the consultation report, the bureau agreed to adopt suggestions to criminalise “cyberflashing” – the act of sending images of genitals to other people online without their consent. Responding to public concerns over the scope of application for a legal defence of a defendant’s “genuine but mistaken” belief of consent, the bureau said it would follow the Law Reform Commission’s recommendation that the court should determine whether such a belief was reasonable. The use of the term “rape” would also remain in the amendment bill despite an expansion of the offence to sexual penetration without consent in areas other than the vagina. The bureau explained this was to express the gravity and severity of the offence with a broadly understood term. A spokesman for the Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women said he welcomed the government’s addition of the two offences. However, he said the government’s approach to the “genuine but mistaken belief” defence was flawed, as frontline experience showed that a court’s judgment of a reasonable belief would not be able to eliminate prejudice against victims. On the retention of the term “rape”, the spokesman raised concerns over public confusion in understanding the new, expanded offence when the name of the old one would remain in use.

title: 100 start-ups joining Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub to get top mentors
description: Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park submits proposed list of sector-specific firms to access cross-border data flows in pilot.
content: Around 100 start-ups selected to join Hong Kong’s flagship border tech hub will undergo mentorship programmes ranging from five to eight years, backed by industry heavyweights, the operator has revealed. Vincent Ma, CEO of Loop Hong Kong Park Company, said in an interview on Thursday that the start-ups were chosen to join the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (HSITP) following a months-long screening process. “We have chosen 100 start-ups to enter our park soon following a few months of selection … and the park will offer a mentorship programme for them,” he said, adding that some of the firms were drawn from local universities. The mentorship will be delivered by established firms operating in the park, such as pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca and battery manufacturer Xiamen Hithium Energy Storage Technology. A longer eight-year path was better suited to life-science start-ups, Ma noted. He cited the example of new medicine development, which required a much lengthier research and development timeline than artificial intelligence (AI) firms, which operated on much shorter cycles that aligned well with a five-year track. Meanwhile, the operator has submitted a list of sector-specific firms, including new energy companies, to authorities for a pilot scheme enabling cross-border data flows later this year. Ma emphasised that seamless data flows, along with the movement of capital, materials and personnel, were key to the park’s development. Around 10 AI and biotech firms will be the first to access cross-border data transfers under the pilot initiative this year, according to a government source on Wednesday. “We have proposed a list of sector-specific firms, such as new energy companies, for the data flow pilot scheme which is expected to roll out this year,” he said. The Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park is located in the Hetao cooperation zone at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, a project proposed by Beijing in 2017 comprising two parks on either side of the border. The Hong Kong park covers 87 hectares (215 acres) while Shenzhen’s encompasses 302 hectares. The development forms a core component of the Northern Metropolis megaproject aimed at diversifying the city’s economy, a key priority in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan. Ma highlighted the park’s role as a springboard for mainland and international companies expanding globally. As an example, he cited Topxgun, a leading agricultural drone manufacturer based at the HSITP, which recently secured a new client in Kazahkstan’s capital Astana, following a visit to the country as part of the park’s delegation. Commenting on the park’s recent land tender for four parcels, which drew a better-than-expected six bids, Ma revealed that one firm had submitted a single bid covering all four sites. The six submissions were almost split evenly between Hong Kong and mainland CHinese firms focusing on frontier technologies. Ma dismissed direct comparisons to a July land tender in Hung Shui Kiu – also part of the Northern Metropolis – which drew just two bids. The Hung Shui Kiu site is the first large-scale land sale to combine property development with the creation of an innovation and technology (I&T) hub. He explained that the two developments serve different purposes, noting that the park offered no residential plots for sale, with the four sites earmarked for laboratories and talent accommodation spanning more than 76,000 square metres (818,000 square feet). Separately, the Development Bureau revealed on Thursday that the projected supply of spade-ready land in the Northern Metropolis over the next 10 years would total around 2,500 hectares. Annual supply is expected to peak at 380 hectares in 2031-32 before tapering to 120 hectares in 2036-37. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on the same day that the overall land supply remained sufficient, noting that land delivery naturally fluctuated across cycles. Most of the supply will stem from new development areas in the Northern Metropolis, with the remainder coming from Tseung Kwan O, Lung Kwu Tan and Tuen Mun West.

title: Self-funded campuses favoured in Hong Kong’s new university towns
description: Education chief Christine Choi says institutions may seek government loans to build campuses, but those that do not will be given priority.
content: Tertiary institutions seeking to establish campuses in one of three university towns planned for the Northern Metropolis megaproject will be given “favourable consideration” if they do not require a government loan to build their facilities, Hong Kong’s education minister has said. The government has expanded all three university towns – formally named in Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s annual policy address on Wednesday – and opened applications for interested institutions to submit their proposals for the first, in Hung Shui Kiu, by the end of this year, with the results to be announced in early 2027. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin said on Thursday that institutions could opt to take out a government loan to build their campuses, but those that did not do so would be given priority. “Institutions may reference the indicative terms set by the government to submit competitive loan proposals; favourable consideration will be given to the institutions that do not require a loan or that are able to offer a financially competitive proposal,” she said. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Hong Kong’s No 2 official, added that whether an institution applied for a loan was only one factor in vetting proposals, not the sole condition. Under indicative terms set out by the government, institutions are encouraged to propose repayment terms, including the period and interest rate. SCMP · Self-funded campuses favoured in Hong Kong’s new university towns The indicative terms state that if the repayment period is 20 years, universities can enjoy an interest-free period for the first six years, pay an interest rate of around 2 per cent from the seventh year to the 10th year, and around 5 per cent from the 11th to the 20th year. Institutions that apply for a loan may seek to extend the repayment period to no more than 25 years at an interest rate of around 5 per cent. Lee, who also unveiled Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan on Wednesday, said the 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) Northern Metropolis project, located near the border with Shenzhen, would serve as a key platform for the city’s participation in the Greater Bay Area and for national development. Chan reiterated the point on Thursday. “The Northern Metropolis University Town is not only an educational infrastructure project, but also a crucial platform for Hong Kong to deeply participate in the development of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area, actively integrate into and serve the overall national development, and enhance Hong Kong’s international connectivity,” he said. Chan also updated the sizes of the three university towns: the Hung Shui Kiu University Town will cover 26 hectares; San Tin University Town, 100 hectares; and Ta Kwu Ling University Town, 180 hectares. He added that the sizes of the San Tin and Ta Kwu Ling sites might be adjusted before the applications opened for those locations. All proposals will be examined by a designated vetting group led by Chan, who said the government had not set a limit on the number of institutions to be granted land. The Hung Shui Kiu town and its adjoining technology and industry areas will be developed as a “centre for applied post-secondary education in smart manufacturing and global talent cultivation”. Chan said institutions in the town would be required to focus on cutting-edge scientific research, collaborate with local industries on curriculum development, teaching and learning, internships and applied research to cultivate talent. They would also have to partner with renowned mainland Chinese and overseas institutions, strengthen linkages and collaboration with leading enterprises and develop shared facilities. Under the government plan, institutions can build permanent premises to expand their capacity, re-provision existing campuses and provide or enhance teaching and other ancillary facilities such as libraries, laboratories, student guidance centres, research facilities and student hostels. The government previously earmarked a HK$10 billion loan scheme for Hung Shui Kiu University Town. All three plots in the town are subject to the same building density rule – a maximum plot ratio of five. The largest site measures 16.5 hectares, which can yield 826,000 square metres of total floor space, with the plot to be handed over in stages from 2026 to 2029. The second covers 5.3 hectares, with 264,000 square metres of floor space. The handover is scheduled between 2027 and 2029. The smallest measures 4.4 hectares, allowing 218,500 square metres of floor space under a 110-metre height limit, with the site handover scheduled for 2027. Asked if the government was subsidising the construction of campuses, Chan said it had already offered a land premium concession, as successful institutions would only need to pay a nominal land premium of HK$1,000. He added that no institutions had told him they would not be financially viable if they were allowed to operate in the towns, adding that they could generate income by charging non-local students, whose fees were generally higher than those for local students.

title: China’s Wang Yi holds phone call with Rubio days before Xi visits US
description: Top diplomats’ call likely to have locked down final details for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s first US state visit in more than a decade.
content: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday, just a week ahead of President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the United States. “Wang Yi stressed that the two sides should act in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit” and “make good preparations for high-level engagement in the next stage,” said Mao Ning, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on social media. He also called on the two sides to “send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive relationship of strategic stability and jointly promoting world peace and development”. The call is expected to have locked down final details of Xi’s closely watched visit and expected summit with US President Donald Trump. The two top diplomats held a similar call roughly two weeks ahead of Trump’s state visit to China earlier this year. Rubio last met Wang Yi in July on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ gathering in Manila. Both leaders held a 90-minute engagement and discussed possible outcomes for the September summit. The phone call on Thursday comes just days ahead of the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s weekend meeting with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng to finalise the agenda for the Xi-Trump summit. “With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart, [Vice-Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing on Tuesday. Bessent was responding to a question about the alleged role of Chinese banks in facilitating commercial transactions with Iran and Washington’s plans to take action against them. Bessent and He are expected to finalise the likely economic outcomes of the summit and begin preparatory dialogue on artificial intelligence safety and governance. Sources said Bessent is expected to discuss AI and economic issues with He in a single meeting, rather than hold separate high-level talks. Bessent leads the US side in both dialogues, while the tight schedule before the summit has made it increasingly difficult to arrange a second meeting. With Xi’s trip just a week away, Beijing and Washington are racing to lock in possible deliverables. The South China Morning Post previously reported that one key deliverable could be an extension of the trade deal struck in South Korea last year, when Xi and Trump met on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit, though Washington was not expected to push for a breakthrough. The SCMP also reported on Thursday that both sides are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties. Another issue under discussion, and a possible summit deliverable, is resuming arms-control talks suspended in 2024 over US arms sales to Taiwan, potentially with military personnel taking part in the dialogue. Sources said both sides were exploring ways to expand military communication channels and strengthen existing ones, providing a rare area of cooperation in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship. As Washington and Beijing prepare for the leaders’ meeting, the US Congress on Wednesday passed a bill to strengthen sanctions against Russia by targeting Russia’s leading energy buyers – China and India. The legislation, championed by late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, authorises Trump to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian oil and natural gas, expanding his favourite tactic of slapping tariffs to maximise leverage and retribution. China on Thursday pushed back against the sanctions bill, saying that Beijing “carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit”. “China opposes long-arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said. Xi is expected to hold talks with Trump in Washington on September 24, marking his first state visit to America since 2015.

title: Hong Kong 999 callers can send real-time audio, video data from 2028: Chris Tang
description: Security minister reveals timeline for upgrades to emergency call services, a day after new features announced in Hong Kong policy address.
content: Callers to Hong Kong’s 999 hotline will be able to send real-time audio and visual information to emergency call centres using instant messaging apps in 2028, Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung has said. The security minister revealed the timeline for the upgrade on Thursday, a day after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced in his latest policy address that three new functions were set to be introduced to enhance 999 call services. Alongside providing “real-time audio, image and video data” to help centres appraise situations, the new features will ensure crucial data can be instantly sent to the Fire Services Department to help fast-track rescue efforts. Authorities are also expected to employ new technology to triage incoming calls, ensuring the most critical cases are prioritised during major incidents or busy periods. Tang said the three functions would be introduced in 2028. “In extreme situations with a high volume of calls, our system categorises what people are reporting,” he said. “Say it’s a fire. That is obviously more urgent, so we take that call first. But if it is a dispute over a parking spot, that is relatively minor.” Tang also provided an update on the revamped Huanggang Port. The border crossing is expected to begin operations in the fourth quarter of this year, according to the policy address. The security minister said a concrete opening date would be announced after adjustments to the facility’s computer systems were completed, which included the fine-tuning of facial-recognition cameras. The facility had already passed a large-scale operational drill, with follow-up improvements made to the site’s Wi-fi system and anti-skid works completed on road surfaces, he said. Tang said the redeveloped Huanggang Port could serve 200,000 people daily, up from the previous capacity of 40,000. He expected this figure to reach 300,000 once the Northern Link rail line fully opened in 2034. The minister also discussed sections on national security in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, which was unveiled alongside the annual policy address on Wednesday. While the plan stated the city would “strengthen the top-level structure to robustly safeguard national security under an authoritative chain of command”, Tang said this did not mean a new command tier would be introduced. He added that the future work of both the central government’s Office for Safeguarding National Security and the Committee for Safeguarding National Security – including its chairman, consultants and secretariat – would be further strengthened. Tang was also asked whether Hong Kong planned to introduce anti-sanction laws, given Macau had included improving its “anti-sanction mechanism” in its own five-year plan. The security minister replied that staying “on guard against activities endangering national security by hostile forces” was part of Hong Kong’s five-year blueprint, and “anti-sanctions” was already covered in the plan.

title: Exclusive | China, US may unveil measures to boost military ties when Xi visits Washington
description: Two sides have been discussing ways to improve communication channels, according to sources familiar with the talks.
content: China and the United States are discussing possible announcements to strengthen military-to-military ties during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington next week, multiple sources familiar with the discussions told the South China Morning Post. Another item that is being discussed, and a possible deliverable, is restarting the arms-control talks that were suspended in 2024 over US weapons sales to Taiwan, with the dialogue potentially including military personnel. In a phone call on Thursday to make final arrangements before the summit, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that both sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchange in the spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit. “[We should] strengthen communication, advance cooperation and manage differences, respect each other’s core interests, and send a positive message that China and the United States are committed to advancing a constructive and strategically stable relationship and to jointly promoting world peace and development.,” Wang said, according to Xinhua. The two also discussed the situation in the Middle East, Xinhua reported. Sources said both sides were discussing ways to activate more military communication channels and bolster the existing ones – marking a rare bright spot in an otherwise fiercely competitive relationship. They said officials in the two militaries were interacting at various levels, with the frequency and level of engagement increasing substantially in the past few months. Despite a still-contentious economic relationship marked by tit-for-tat tariffs, export controls and sanctions, military ties between Washington and Beijing have moved in a more positive direction, with regular dialogue and public commitments to maintaining peace and increasing mutual understanding. Sources said both sides were rebuilding military channels to speak frequently and prevent any misunderstanding and miscalculation about each other’s intentions. Ending a two-year hiatus, China and the US held command-level talks late last month in Canada, with a meeting between Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the Pacific Command. The US Pacific Command said Yang and Paparo discussed the importance of maintaining open lines of communication between senior American and Chinese military leaders to reduce the risk of miscalculation and to promote safe and professional conduct between forces. One source said China and the US were seeking military dialogue at three levels. Those talks would be between the two presidents, who are also commanders-in-chief of their countries’ armed forces; also at the ministerial level, including the US Department of Defence and China’s Central Military Commission; and between frontline commanders, in particular the US Pacific Command chief and the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command chief. “The presidential-level and frontline commander-level talks are progressing,” the source said, referring to recent meetings between Xi and US President Donald Trump and the talks between Paparo and Yang. “But actual ministerial-level talks might take a while. One problem has been China’s anti-corruption campaign that [almost] wiped out the CMC, leaving Zhang Shengmin [as the only uniformed official in the body],” he said. “But we believe they will take place in the near future.” Another person familiar with the matter said both sides had made clear they wanted new communication channels. One of the channels could be to revive dedicated arms-control talks between the US State Department and China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which gained momentum in 2023 before being suspended in July 2024 over Washington’s continued arms sales to Taiwan. A source described the talks as a give from the Chinese side that could eventually be broadened to include military personnel – a long-standing US request – “if things go well”. Washington had planned to send a more senior Pentagon China official to Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum this week, after last year dispatching only the defence attache. But the official withdrew before the forum, with the US delegation instead led by Brigadier General Stacy Kihara of the embassy in Beijing, leaving the official level unchanged from 2025. A third source said military-to-military contact under Trump’s second term had become more stable but remained “shallow”. The source said deliverables for the Xi-Trump summit were discussed and locked in when Yang and Paparo met face to face in Canada – their first in-person meeting. The person called that progress “unique” under a Republican president, describing Trump as “a different sort of Republican president”. A fourth source said the two militaries were working to follow the “strategic stability” guidance agreed by Trump and Xi during their May meeting in Beijing. After the summit, the two sides referenced the concept of “strategic stability” in their statements, while differing over its phrasing and interpretation. In July, a senior Pentagon official – for the first time in more than five years – attended and spoke at a reception at the Chinese embassy in Washington marking the 99th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Liberation Army. “Under the leadership of Secretary [Pete] Hegseth, we are actively repairing a once broken military-to-military channel and making clear, steady progress,” said Alvaro Smith, deputy assistant defence secretary for China, Taiwan and Mongolia. He added that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years” and said Washington was not seeking a “conflict with China”. “This is how two powerful militaries should engage, and over the last year and a half, we made this a reality.” US undersecretary of defence for policy Elbridge Colby also hosted Chinese Foreign Vice-Minister Ma Zhaoxu at the Pentagon, later saying on social media that the US interacted with its “Chinese counterparts in a spirit of respect, candour, and realism”. In another sign of closer military engagement, China is cooperating with the US military to recover the remains of American soldiers who went missing in China during World War II. As part of those efforts, US defence recovery teams travelled to China in early July to resume searches for missing service members. The renewed engagement marks a significant shift from the Joe Biden administration, when a series of incidents escalated tensions and left military-to-military communication largely stalled. Beijing suspended several key military dialogue mechanisms with Washington in 2022 after then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi travelled to Taiwan on a high-profile visit. Taiwan has been the most sensitive issue between Beijing and Washington. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent nation, but Washington opposes any attempt to seize the self-governing island by force and has pledged to supply it with weapons.

title: China trusted more than US, EU on AI regulation in Pew survey of middle-income countries
description: US think tank study finds middle-income countries have ‘more positive views of China’ when it comes to regulating AI effectively.
content: Amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence (AI) competition and global concerns about the technology, China appears to have an edge over the US and European Union (EU) in trust to regulate AI among mostly middle-income countries. A new Pew Research Centre report released on Thursday found that, on a median basis across 11 countries and two territories, more people trust China than the US or the EU to regulate AI effectively. China was not among the countries surveyed in the broader report. “Middle-income countries tend to have more positive views of China than high-income countries,” Pew’s associate director of research Laura Silver told the South China Morning Post. “We see that trust in a country to regulate AI and views of that country tend to be closely related.” The 11 countries are Bangladesh, Chile, Colombia, Ghana, Malaysia, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka and Thailand. The two territories are the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Most, but not all, of the nations are middle-income countries. Pew said the group skews middle-income because it consisted largely of countries newly added to this year’s survey. A median of 43 per cent across these countries said they trusted China to regulate AI effectively, compared with 35 per cent for the US and 34 per cent for the EU. China was the country people trusted most to regulate AI in five of the places surveyed: Bangladesh, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the West Bank and East Jerusalem. The gap was widest in Pakistan, where 87 per cent said they trusted China to regulate AI, compared with 28 per cent for the US and 33 per cent for the EU. The Philippines was the only country where the US was more trusted than both China and the EU. The findings contrast with Pew’s 2025 survey of a different group of 25 countries. That survey found a median of 53 per cent trusted the EU to regulate AI effectively, compared with 37 per cent for the US and 27 per cent for China. Trust in China was relatively strong in four middle-income countries surveyed in 2025 – Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Indonesia. Silver said views of China “have risen in many places since last year”, which likely contributed to some of the high levels of trust in China on AI regulation this year. The report comes as Washington and Beijing spar over AI and work to structure a long-planned AI dialogue ahead of a planned visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to meet US President Donald Trump in the US next week. The two sides have clashed over a wide range of AI-related issues, including chip export controls, model distillation and intellectual property as each country figures out how to handle AI’s disruptive effects on jobs and industry. The Chinese embassy in Washington said China advocates a people-centred, open and inclusive approach to AI and supports dialogue and cooperation. “China stands ready to work with all parties to bridge the digital divide, strengthen international cooperation and global AI governance,” the embassy’s spokesperson Liu Chang said. The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Chris Miller, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, downplayed China’s stronger showing in some middle-income countries. “In terms of trust in China versus the US, AI companies are unlikely to focus heavily on the views of small economies,” he said, because the primary markets will be the US, Europe and the major Asian economies. In the long run, Miller said, he expects each country to impose its own AI regulations, much as countries have developed somewhat different rules governing social media. The report also found sharp anxiety in wealthy countries over AI’s effect on jobs. The concern was most pronounced in Australia and South Korea, where 76 per cent said AI would lead to job losses, and in the US, where 71 per cent said the same – up seven percentage points from when Pew last asked the question in 2024. Trump has meanwhile dismissed growing domestic concern over AI, calling warnings about the technology’s risks a “hoax” and rejecting calls for stronger guardrails. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” he wrote on social media.

title: Pets and personal touches: how China’s luxury hotel market is changing
description: Today’s Chinese guests expect hotels to offer cultural experiences, personalised touches and a pet-friendly environment, Hang Lung director says.
content: Chinese customers’ growing desire for personal expression and cultural experiences has raised the game in the country’s hospitality sector, creating opportunities for leading lifestyle hotel brands, according to a director at Hong Kong developer Hang Lung Properties. “An ideal hotel is the one that can redefine hospitality with personal touches,” said Herman Chui, the company’s senior director of office, hotel and residence, during a media briefing on Wednesday. “Guests can select a teapot to their liking. The hotel also offers tailor-made key cards and other items. More importantly, a client is allowed to bring their pet along.” Chui’s remarks were made ahead of the inauguration of Hilton’s new Xi Zhe Wuxi hotel in Hang Lung’s Center 66 commercial complex in Wuxi, eastern China’s Jiangsu province. The developer’s push into lifestyle hotel brands echoes recent forecasts by industry officials and analysts that the hospitality sector needs to focus on creating products and services that provide “emotional value” for Chinese travellers. Last year, Shangri-La Group launched its super-luxury hotel brand in China, Shangri-La Signatures, which features a convergence of cultural heritage and nature aimed at attracting wealthy ­tourists with unique offerings. In July, Hilton introduced a new brand Tempo to China, as Alan Watts, the group’s Asia-Pacific president, described the move as an effort to help hotel owners capture growing demand for lifestyle-oriented hospitality via a scalable model. Mainland China’s tourism industry raked in revenues of 3.21 trillion yuan (US$478.7 billion) in the first half of 2026, up 2 per cent from a year ago, according to data from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. The pace of growth lagged the 4.7 per cent overall rise in China’s gross domestic product during the same period. Despite the lacklustre overall market, Chui said that pet-friendly hotels that also offered curated experiences such as yoga training could be well received by young travellers on the mainland, who increasingly preferred to spend on immersive story-led hospitality rather than displays of luxury.
