The new hotel in Wuxi – part of the Curio Collection by Hilton portfolio – would bring local culture to life through distinctive hospitality experiences, said Weber Lo Wai-pak, CEO of Hang Lung, in a statement. The developer and Hilton would create lifestyle synergies and further enhance the overall appeal of the Center 66 project, he added. Hang Lung has developed 11 premium mixed-use complexes under its signature “66” brand on the mainland, which are located in cities including Shanghai, Wuxi, Hangzhou and Tianjin.

title: Sweden’s PM Kristersson resigns after left-wing wins slim majority in election
description: Magdalena Andersson’s left-wing bloc, splintered over ideological differences, faces laborious negotiations to form the new government.
content: Sweden’s conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson announced his resignation on Thursday after the left-wing opposition won a slim majority in parliament in the country’s general election. “It is now the speaker of parliament who will lead the next steps on the path towards forming a new government. In order for this work to begin immediately, I hereby request to be relieved of my duties as prime minister,” Kristersson said in a letter to the speaker which he posted to social media. The four parties in the left-wing bloc, led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats, hold a three-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Kristersson’s right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. But only around 50,000 votes separated the two sides in the country of 10.6 million people. “The Swedish people have voted for a new direction for our country. Voted for unity and against division,” Andersson said in a speech posted to social media shortly after Kristersson announced his resignation. She added that the people “have voted to move Sweden forward, and I want to realise the new direction that you have voted for”. With the opposition deeply splintered over ideological differences, Andersson’s negotiating skills will be put to the test to unite the bloc, made up of the Social Democrats, the Left Party, the Greens Party and the Centre Party. The 59-year-old, Sweden’s first woman prime minister in 2021–22 and finance minister for seven years before that, is known as a hard-nosed technocrat with a direct and no-nonsense style. The negotiations could drag on for weeks, and if Andersson were to fail, Kristersson would be waiting to try to build his own majority. After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government, much shorter than the 134 days it took to do so in 2018. Andersson will in particular need to find a path to reconcile differences between the socialist Left Party and the liberal Centre Party. The Centre Party has said it will oppose a government that includes cabinet posts for the Left Party, which has insisted on having a minister. Andersson has previously ruled out a government that includes the Left Party, but wants their support in parliament. On Sunday’s election night, Andersson already declared that if the result held “Sweden will have a new government”. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, heading one of the few left-wing governments in Europe, hailed the win. “Social democracy has won the elections in Sweden. After four years of a right-wing government with the far-right, the Swedes are once again backing the welfare state, social justice and the green agenda,” Sanchez said in a social media post. Parliament can vote on a new prime minister on September 29 at the earliest. Kristersson said on election night that he would respect Andersson’s attempts to form a government, but wished her “good luck” given the divisions among her left-wing bloc. He said he was ready to explore options to find a majority among “non-socialist” parties. He is seen as wanting to woo the Centre Party, which used to belong to the right-wing bloc, though it is staunchly opposed to a government that includes the Sweden Democrats. Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist on election night stressed the party had “been clear that we are going into the election on the basis that the extremes should not dominate a government”. The Social Democrats, which ruled the Scandinavian country for most of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest party, also looked to be heading for their worst score in over a century with 28.0 per cent of the vote. In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which entered parliament in 2010, lost support for the first time, garnering 17.5 per cent of the vote, down three percentage points from the last election in 2022.

title: Asian Games: China athletes stuck at Nagoya airport with no food, way out for 7 hours
description: A data entry glitch at Chubu Centrair International Airport transport centre meant athletes were unable to get buses to their accommodation.
content: Athletes from multiple countries arriving in Japan for the 20th Asian Games were stranded at Nagoya airport because of a technical glitch, leaving some Chinese team members stuck for seven hours without food. According to state media, the plane carrying the country’s delegation from Beijing landed on schedule at around 12.15pm, with buses already waiting at Chubu Centrair International Airport to take them to their accommodation. However, athletes and officials soon found themselves trapped at the transport centre after a data entry error meant many of them were not listed in the departure system. With only water available, officials, coaches and athletes from numerous countries and places had to find a space to sit down. 体操中国代表、张博恒選手（かなり有名）に起こった出来事を語ってくれています 有り得なすぎて…怒りを通り越して悲しいです 皆さん、想像できますか？ 僕達は日本で宿泊する場所に着くまでに、なんと丸一日かかりました そして、一番ありえない、一番ありえないことは、↓ https://t.co/44ZEldKuXu — yuzuco🐼 (@Yuzuco48) September 17, 2026 An Indian rowing coach said his team had landed at around 10am but were stuck at the transit hub for more than four hours. “Staff members could not find our athletes’ information in their system, so they couldn’t arrange vehicles,” the coach said. “There are teams that arrived even earlier, two or three hours before us, who still haven’t boarded buses.” China’s gymnasts told a similar story. Of the 21-strong squad, only the information for two athletes was available, preventing the whole team from being able to leave. During the wait, several Chinese athletes unrolled yoga mats and pulled out foam rollers and resistance bands to stay limber. Among them was table tennis star Sun Yingsha, who was seen stretching in a video. “Nobody could tell us when the buses would arrive; everything was just waiting,” one delegation member said, adding that staff appeared equally bewildered when asked. “Everyone was just asking each other.” China’s badminton team took matters into their own hands, and tried to take public transport. But with insufficient tickets available, only a few of the team were able to get away. Staff from the Chinese Consulate-General in Nagoya relied on the services of Chinese citizens living nearby to drive the rest to where they were staying soon after. Members of the table tennis, wushu and rowing teams finally got buses around 5pm, while the gymnastics team did not leave for another hour, nearly six hours after landing at Nagoya airport. The last members of the delegation did not leave the airport until around 7pm. “We barely ate anything all day. It’s been over five hours since we got off the plane and we’re exhausted, sleepy and hungry, with training scheduled for tomorrow,” one athlete said. Another athlete, who was only partly joking, said the ordeal had been “harder than the actual competition”. Discussing the incident on his social media, Chinese gymnast Zhang Boheng called his arrival at the Games an “awkward trip,” and said it was “outrageous” that he had not eaten for 12 hours. In his video, he outlined his day, which involved waking at 3.30am, having breakfast just after 7am, boarding his flight at 8am and landing in Nagoya at noon, only to then be trapped at the airport until 6pm. “By the end, I really couldn’t hold on any more,” he said. Zhang and his teammates had been assigned accommodation on the Costa Serena cruise ship, which is being used to house around 4,000 of the 17,000 athletes and officials in Japan for the Games. However, the heavy rain that has battered Nagoya for the past week left Zhang and his team stuck in the athletes’ village, where containers are being used as rooms for competitors. They ultimately decided to check into a local hotel to rest, which left Zhang “extremely, extremely tired”, and ruing a “wasted day”.

title: Hong Kong eyeing gold expansion and Northern Metropolis vaults to cement hub status
description: Finance chief says HKMA playing greater role in gold market will enrich city’s financial ecosystem and that Hong Kong not considering interest rate rise.
content: Hong Kong’s plan to raise its gold holdings will further cement the city’s status as an international financial centre, with the possibility of building vaults in the Northern Metropolis megadevelopment, according to authorities. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also said on Thursday the city was under “no pressure” to raise interest rates following a US rate hike, but stressed authorities would “keep a close watch” on the situation. Speaking at a conference the day after the policy address and the first local five-year plan were unveiled, Chan elaborated on a proposal to increase the Exchange Fund’s gold portfolio, which currently represents a tiny fraction of the war chest used to defend the local dollar and is managed by the city’s de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). SCMP · Hong Kong eyeing gold expansion and Northern Metropolis vaults to cement hub status Noting that other central banks had shown an interest in moving some of their gold to Hong Kong due to geopolitical concerns, Chan said the stewardship would offer the HKMA a further opportunity to accelerate the city’s transition into a global trading hub for the precious metal and other commodities. “The move by HKMA is very positive to Hong Kong in terms of not just holding the gold physically, but at the same time giving assurance to the other central banks as to the status of Hong Kong in this aspect,” the minister said. “On this basis, with real gold here, we can develop a lot of derivative services, and also on gold, we can also develop certain connect arrangements with Shanghai, for example. That will further enrich the financial ecosystem of Hong Kong. “This is good for Hong Kong, good for our financial centre status.” While HKMA chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man also said on Thursday the authority was considering increasing its exposure to gold, Chan explained he could not disclose further investment plan details. The policy address delivered by city leader John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday also called for establishing metal vaults approved by the London Metal Exchange in the Northern Metropolis, which would promote clustering of physical delivery, as well as financing and risk management services. The Northern Metropolis aims to turn 30,000 hectares (74,131 acres) near the city’s border with mainland China into an economic powerhouse and a housing hub. Speaking at the same event, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the government had been discussing gold vaulting with stakeholders and the Development Bureau had an office dedicated to exploring building the secure storage areas in the Northern Metropolis. But any facilities in the megaproject would not compete with the 1,000-tonne-class warehouse project at the Hong Kong International Airport on Lantau Island, he said. “They do not really compete with each other because, in our estimation, the demand for such facilities far outstrips the capacity that can be provided at the airport,” Wong said. “So we do need more. The government said in July that it had earmarked industry land across new development areas in the Northern Metropolis, which can meet commodity warehousing demand. Since the London Metal Exchange included Hong Kong in its global warehousing network last year, the city’s storage area has exceeded 60,000 square metres (14.8 acres), with an inventory of more than 20,000 tonnes of metal so far. Financial chief Chan also elaborated on the government’s plan to take the lead in driving the settlement of more government expenditure in yuan in suitable scenarios. The initiative was laid down in the city’s first five-year plan, also unveiled on Wednesday, to strengthen Hong Kong’s role as the world’s largest offshore renminbi trading hub. Chan said the government would try to settle its bills in yuan at mainland entities taking part in cross-border social welfare schemes. He added that the government would also issue more renminbi-denominated bonds, while considering costs, as well as interest rates and hedging currency risks. Separately, Chan also addressed the US interest rate hike and said Hong Kong did not need to follow suit at the moment. He cited assessments from the Hong Kong Association of Banks, which said the United States was facing the risk of higher inflation due to the Middle East war. While the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar, Chan noted that the city had special advantages, such as “very ample” liquidity in its banking system. Despite forecasts of another US rate rise before the end of this year, Chan said it would depend on the economy, employment and inflation in the US. “There is really at the moment no pressure for us to raise the interest rate, but we will keep a close watch,” he said.

title: Von der Leyen’s ‘China shock’ speech aimed to send Beijing a message: analysts
description: The EU leader’s speech was light on specifics, but aimed to signal firm stance ahead of looming trade talks with Beijing, analysts say.
content: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s state-of-the-union speech offered few details on new trade measures targeting China, but its sharp tone was designed to send a message to Beijing, analysts said. During her speech on Wednesday, von der Leyen warned that a “second China shock” was already affecting Europe and vowed that Brussels would use all available tools to rebalance its trade relationship with the country. Her remarks came as the European Union’s October deadline for securing tangible results in rebalancing trade with China approaches. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic held a video conference with his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao as planned on Thursday. Though the speech was light on specifics, the fact that China was the third topic addressed and explicitly mentioned as a threat to Europe was significant, according to Peter Chase, senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund and a former US diplomat in Brussels. “Where it was placed and how explicitly she spoke were the more important messages than the actual words that she used,” he said. For Chase, von der Leyen’s statement that Europe would always defend the rules-based order, but could no longer rely on it to protect European interests, was clearly a message to Washington and Beijing. “[The message is] when there are countries that are not adhering to the rule of law, we can no longer use the rule of law to address the problems we have,” he said. Others nevertheless saw the speech as a sign that von der Leyen still wanted Europe to deal with China within the framework of the World Trade Organization. “For me, the important signal is that there was no reference to new instruments,” said Ignacio Garcia Bercero, a senior fellow at Bruegel and former director at the European Commission’s trade department. Von der Leyen’s vow to use all the tools at Brussels’ disposal was a signal that any potential autonomous actions coming from the EU would be framed within the context of legitimate actions under the rules of the WTO, according to Garcia Bercero. The fact that she refrained from mentioning any specific measures also indicated that the priority was still for both sides to see what could be achieved during a coming round of trade talks in October, he said. Analysts agreed that the ongoing trade talks could be a reason von der Leyen did not announce any new measures. “It would be inappropriate to say, ‘we already committed to this deadline for these negotiations, but we’re going to go ahead and start doing all this stuff anyway’, that would be very unusual by European diplomatic standards,” said Jacob Gunter, head of programme for economy and industry at the Mercator Institute for China Studies. It would also be politically risky for von der Leyen to go too far in her speech, given the delicate power balance between Brussels and member states, which could hurt the EU’s ability to build a political consensus next month and take concrete actions, according to Gunter. Von der Leyen’s announcement that the bloc would work with Canada to make it an associate member of the EU also reflected her will to work together with like-minded countries, he added. “It is a very clear signal that there are serious major powers in the world who, because of course some of what China has done, but really what Donald Trump has done, are trying to find alternative coalitions,” Gunter said.

title: Malaysian woman scuba diving in Bali dies after being swept away by currents
description: Siti Nuraini was on a diving trip with several others when the incident occurred at Crystal Bay.
content: A Malaysian woman has died while scuba diving after she was caught in strong currents in Bali, Indonesia. According to local media portal Bali News, the victim, Siti Nuraini Rusidi, 40, was on a diving trip with a divemaster, boat captain and several other divers when the incident occurred at 11.10am local time on Wednesday. The trip’s divemaster, Eugenius Franciso Ray, 33, had reportedly raised concerns over her health when he noticed her coughing when the group was at the first dive site at Manta Bay. He asked Siti Nuraini about her condition but she said she was able to continue with the dive. The group then completed their dive and proceeded to Crystal Bay. However, the group encountered extremely strong sea currents at the second dive site. Three divers were swept away by currents and Siti Nuraini was later found dead. The incident has reignited concerns about safety at Indonesian tourist sites. Over the years, maritime and other transport accidents have cast a spotlight on poor safety standards, faulty equipment, decrepit infrastructure and a lack of accountability in the country. In May, two Austrian tourists died on the island of Flores after a wooden suspension bridge they were crossing near the famous Cunca Wulang Waterfall collapsed, throwing them onto the rocks below. A Saudi national was killed in a jet ski accident in West Java in January while riding in rough seas. And in December last year, four Spanish tourists died when the wooden tourist boat they had chartered sank near Padar Island close to Labuan Bajo in Flores. This story was first published by The Star Additional reporting by SCMP’s Asia desk

title: ‘Gone too far’: Thai PM Anutin slams foreign lawbreakers as backlash builds
description: Anutin says foreigners ‘should not come here and take advantage of us’, as Thailand acts to close legal loopholes and deter transgressions.
content: Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has issued a withering rebuke to foreigners behaving badly in Thailand following a wave of scandals involving illegal businesses and landholdings including a cemetery, saying the cases have “gone too far” by breaching Thai law and hospitality. Facing mounting public backlash against illegal foreign ownership of swathes of the country enabled by endemic corruption, Anutin’s government has halved the visa-free entry period to 30 days for most countries and fast-tracked deportation proceedings against criminals. Authorities have also launched a crackdown on “nominee” businesses that use Thai citizens as paper owners of companies, while vowing to tighten rules that have allowed foreign nationals to buy citizenship and therefore own land restricted only to Thais. Chinese, French, Indian and Russian nationals have been among the targets of the snowballing crackdown, which has been closely watched by nationalist hardliners who have started street protests against transgressions by foreigners – and the official corruption that has allowed portions of the country to slip beyond the control of Thais. Most recently Israelis, who have poured into the country since their war on Gaza, have stirred public ire for the alleged operation of nominee businesses that span entire southern islands – as well as a Jewish cemetery in eastern Chachoengsao province. “I think this has gone too far – it’s beyond the limits of what we can accept,” Anutin told officials on Thursday. “We’ve already been generous by allowing them to come here. If they come, they should make an honest living. But when they die, they should go back and be buried in their own country. They should not come here and take advantage of us.” This week, four bodies were exhumed from the cemetery, which appears to have been legitimately bought by Thailand’s Jewish community but allegedly continued operating under a permit that lapsed a few years ago. “If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that – whether it’s a church, a temple, a crematorium or an existing cemetery. We have no objection whatsoever,” Anutin said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here. That is not acceptable.” As the latest scandal erupted on Wednesday involving a Chinese fugitive who attempted to launder tens of millions of dollars through a tyre shop registered to his Chinese child – who held a Thai national identity card illegally bought for 500 baht (US$15) – the Ministry of Interior said it would swiftly amend the country’s 50-year-old nationality law. The aim is to “close legal loopholes that have allowed grey-market capital and foreign nominee networks to Thai citizenship as a gateway for illicit businesses”, the government said in a statement. The behaviour of foreigners has come under the microscope since Thailand launched a 60-day visa waiver in 2024 to kick-start post-pandemic tourism in a nation where a fifth of the economy is tethered to visitor spending. But that policy has backfired. Thousands of cyber scammers and other criminals have abused the visa-free stay to set up illicit businesses and launder money made in the scam rooms of neighbouring Cambodia and Myanmar into Thai property, companies and resorts. Endless viral moments of culture clashes, rudeness, bill-skipping and fighting by drunken foreigners have also fuelled anger among Thais that their hospitality has been abused. With the country facing the tension point between welcoming the tens of millions of tourists each year it needs to keep hotels occupied and resort economies spinning – and the increasing number of scandals – Anutin said people “must come in a way that benefits both sides.

title: Opinion | A new Trump-Kim summit would be a nightmare for everyone but Pyongyang
description: A bilateral deal that is acceptable to both Washington and Pyongyang would come at a steep cost to US allies and the region as a whole.
content: It is clear that US President Donald Trump is pushing hard for a fresh summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in the coming months. To achieve that, he appears prepared to downgrade and jeopardise the US-South Korea alliance, as seen in his recent move to scale back joint military exercises. For Trump, this will be a purely bilateral exercise, with both Seoul and Beijing totally sidelined, let alone Moscow and Tokyo. Equally, there is now a general acceptance that the issue of denuclearisation will not be on the table at any future summit. Trump is looking for an outcome that protects US security interests, while Kim’s interests are in de facto recognition as a nuclear weapons state, sanctions relief and investment. Kim has a functioning nuclear arsenal but lacks any reliable intercontinental delivery system. South Korea and Japan are easy targets for his short and intermediate range missiles, but Pyongyang currently has only tested engines for an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) that can hit the mainland United States. It lacks re-entry technology, payload capacity for multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles and pinpoint guidance capacity. In these circumstances, constructing a bilateral deal where both sides can credibly claim a win – at least to their own domestic audiences – is a challenge but nevertheless possible with some misdirection. However, this will come at considerable cost to their friends and neighbours who will suffer serious collateral damage. Washington and Pyongyang can be expected to collude to save face. An undated promise for future denuclearisation talks that take place well after Trump’s term ends will mitigate embarrassment in Washington. Kim will glibly announce that North Korea has completed all necessary nuclear and ICBM testing and is henceforth shifting efforts from development to production. However, an end to ICBM testing and the prospect of early testing of a second hydrogen bomb and warhead miniaturisation leave Kim a serious and dangerous threat to Seoul and Tokyo, even as Washington gets a pass. Kim would be rewarded with the North being recognised as a nuclear power, a partial lifting of UN sanctions, some degree of normalisation of relations with the US and the prospect of massive industrial investments in its rare earth deposits. He would also see either the creation of a triad of new see-saw relations between Moscow, Washington and Beijing or North Korea being welcomed out of its current pariah status when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine ends. Meanwhile, Trump would be able to claim he has made the US safer, secure access to the North’s rare earths for American corporations and possibly break off a piece of the Beijing-Moscow-Pyongyang axis. A deal that protects the US at the price of leaving its Japanese and South Korean allies exposed is dangerous for northeast Asia and the world as a whole. It would change the regional calculus with its threat to roll back the American nuclear umbrella over northeast Asia, regardless of Washington’s official rhetoric. Seoul and Tokyo would be totally exposed to future asymmetric negotiations over cost-sharing with the US. Worse still, trust that takes decades to build would be destroyed in days. South Korea’s response would almost certainly be to go nuclear. A Gallup Korea poll from last month showed almost two-thirds support for the country acquiring its own nuclear weapons, and such a deal would see any remaining opposition fall away. Pyongyang would welcome such a move as a retrospective justification of its own programme and a guarantee that there would never be any future suggestion of their denuclearisation. Tokyo would certainly follow Seoul’s path. Japan has already prepared legislation to allow a referendum to revise Article 9 of the country’s constitution, and nationalist Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is keen to put it to use. The fear factor whipped up will carry the legislation to a majority. Taipei might even follow. Europe and China might threaten sanctions over such a move, but Trump would not join in given his repeated demands that Seoul play a bigger role in its own defence. This would signal the end of nuclear non-proliferation as the current club of nine nuclear powers would grow to 11 or 12. Around the world, the unthinkable would become likely. Countries that saw possessing nuclear weapons as impossible would start to see them as an option. The current crisis on the Korean peninsula might in fact be nothing compared to what might follow its resolution. As things stand, the most significant danger to international arms control is a deal between Trump and Kim. This article is based on a speech given at this week’s Xiangshan Forum in Beijing.

title: 3 firms fined over HK$900,000 each for role in apprentice electrician’s death
description: Main contractor, two subcontractors found to have played role in fatal electrocution of worker handling wiring for solar panels amid rain.
content: A main contractor and two subcontractors have been fined more than HK$900,000 each for their role in the death of a 38-year-old worker who was electrocuted while handling wiring for solar panels during wet weather at the Hong Kong Science Park three years ago. Magistrate Jeffrey Sze Cho-yiu said China Power International Development, the main contractor for solar panel installation works at the park, had not conducted any on-site supervision “in the slightest”. The project involved three subcontractors: A Kourage, Skynet Engineering Company and Towngas-China Power (HK) Integrated Energy Company – a joint venture between China Power and the Hong Kong and China Gas Company. The magistrate said each tier had committed “serious negligence” by failing to ensure safety measures were in place. He pointed out that Towngas-China Power, which was supposed to handle operational works, had not even inspected the sites or ensured workers had completed the relevant safety training. The West Kowloon Court previously heard that the victim, an apprentice electrician, was asked to connect the wiring for the solar panels without wearing insulated gloves, a necessary safety item that was not provided by the employer. The worker also did not have the qualifications to carry out such work. While China Power, Towngas-China Power and A Kourage denied any role in the worker’s death, the court found them guilty of a total of more than 20 summary charges, including failing to take measures to prevent electrical hazards. A Kourage was fined HK$904,250 while the other two companies were fined HK$908,000 each. The charges against the companies all fall under the Factories and Industrial Undertakings Ordinance and the Occupational Safety and Health Ordinance. Sze noted the two ordinances were amended in 2023 to increase the relevant penalties. Under the legislation, offenders can face a fine of up to HK$10 million and a maximum prison sentence of two years. The magistrate said that when determining the appropriate sentence, cases involving casualties carried a certain weight. Looking at the evidence, Sze said China Power was only concerned about transferring the project to Towngas-China Power. “There was never any intention to fulfil the duties of a main contractor right from the bidding stage,” he said. Sze said China Power and the joint venture firm had committed serious negligence and had failed to report the incident to authorities within seven days of its occurrence. He added that A Kourage had equally contributed to the serious negligence as it had not taken up any supervisory duties after commissioning Skynet Engineering and another company to hire electricians. A Kourage also failed to ensure the two latter companies had exchanged communications about workplace safety, he added. Sze also stressed that Skynet Engineering nonetheless bore the primary liability as it must have known that the deceased was not a registered electrical worker and should not have performed high-risk work. Skynet Engineering pleaded guilty to ordering an unauthorised person to enter a designated area without supervision and several other charges before trial. It was fined HK$417,000 after the court applied a discount to reflect the plea. Esther Tse Yan-yin, an organiser for the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims, welcomed the verdict and said the ruling reflected the gravity of fatal industrial accidents. She noted that the penalty was “fairly heavy” compared with other fatal accidents that led to prosecutions and expressed hope that it would send a clear message that breaching occupational safety rules would lead to serious consequences.

title: UN investigators cite US over Iran strikes that constituted war crimes
description: UN-backed experts also accuse the Iranian government of carrying out crimes against humanity during a domestic crackdown.
content: A UN fact-finding mission on Iran said on Thursday it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States was behind two military strikes on a school and sports facility in Iran in February, and that these constituted war crimes. It also found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their deadly crackdown on anti-government protests. The findings in a new report by the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran, to be submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, examined US conduct during the Iran war ‌that began in February and the Iranian government’s response to nationwide unrest that began in late December. The Pentagon declined to comment on a report conducted by an outside organisation. “Our investigation remains ongoing, and we have nothing to announce at the moment,” it said in a statement. White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in response to the report that the UN Human Rights Council had “accomplished nothing for human rights”, adding that Iran was the only party in the current conflict that had committed war crimes. The Iranian permanent mission in Geneva did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. US officials have previously said military operations are conducted in accordance with the law of armed conflict, while Iran has consistently rejected allegations of systematic rights violations. UN Fact-Finding missions are investigative, ⁠not judicial bodies, and therefore do not initiate any criminal cases. Their findings, however, can be used in criminal investigations by national courts or international tribunals such as the International Criminal Court. States will discuss the ‌findings of the report when it is presented to the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday. The UN experts said they found reasonable grounds to believe US forces were responsible for an attack on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School in the city of Minab, where more than 150 people were killed, including ‌around 120 schoolchildren, according to Iranian officials. The attack constituted an indiscriminate attack causing civilian deaths and damage to civilian infrastructure, amounting to a war crime under international law, the ⁠mission concluded. According to the report, the US ⁠failure to update information in relation to the school, which was adjacent to an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval complex, in its targeting databases and to confirm the building was a military objective amounted to more than mere negligence. “Rather, the US directed the strikes ‌at the building of the school while being aware of a substantial risk of striking a civilian object and acting recklessly as regards the possibility that this would happen.” In June, US President Donald Trump said that “nobody” purposefully attacked a girls’ school in Iran in February, citing ‌an investigation ‌into the incident. Reuters first reported that an initial internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for the fatal strike in Minab in southern Iran. The Pentagon has since elevated the ‌probe but it has not published any preliminary findings. UN experts said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian object and found no evidence that it was being used for military purposes. The experts reached a similar conclusion ⁠over a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd. The report said the attack damaged nearby residential buildings and a school and killed and injured 22 civilians. It concluded that the strike was indiscriminate and ⁠therefore constituted a war crime. US Central Command said in a statement in March that US forces did not launch any strikes into the city of Lamerd on that day. The UN mission probe found that the Iranian authorities carried out a widespread and systematic attack against civilians during protests that erupted in late December last year, involving unlawful killings, torture, ‌arbitrary detention, enforced disappearances and severe restrictions on freedom of expression. Rights ‌groups say bystanders were among those killed during the biggest crackdown since Shiite Muslim clerics took power in the 1979 revolution. Tehran blamed “terrorists and rioters” backed by exiled opponents and foreign foes the US and Israel. The probe said it could not independently verify the death toll, but that it believed the number of dead and injured was likely far higher than official figures which say 3,038 people were killed, and 25,000 people injured. The government’s response to the protests – including violence and killings, cutting off the internet and use of the death penalty – marked a significant escalation from previous patterns of suppressing dissent, the report said.

title: Warning against Japan’s military build-up surfaces at Beijing Xiangshan conference
description: Chinese scholars say Tokyo’s security expansion and US ties could trigger regional instability.
content: Chinese panellists and experts at the Xiangshan Forum have warned against Japan’s remilitarisation amid reports that Tokyo is considering raising its midterm defence spending to 3.5 per cent of GDP. Japan might raise its midterm budget to 3-3.5 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product in line with Nato and other US allies, Bloomberg reported earlier this week, as the US pushes its allies in Asia and Europe to boost their own defences. At the three-day defence gathering in Beijing on Thursday, Zhou Rong, senior fellow with Renmin University of China’s Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies, said the US was not the only influence on Japan’s decision to expand military spending. “Their increase in military expenditure by 3.5 per cent of GDP does indeed have an American factor. It also has to do with the frantic clamour of their own domestic conservative forces, who hold a hostile attitude towards China or perceive China as a security threat,” Zhou said in an interview on the sidelines of the event, which ended on Thursday. Japan has been accelerating its defence spending and will revise its landmark three security documents before the end of the year as part of its military build-up under Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, whose comments on Taiwan set off a decline in Sino-Japanese ties. Japan says it has already reached its goal of spending about 2 per cent of GDP on defence ahead of schedule. Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, said Japan risked becoming the “Israel of East Asia”, a development that would be harmful for the region. “In the Middle East, for example, Israel has ‘hijacked’ the United States … There is a similar trend in East Asia. If Japan wants to become the ‘Israel of East Asia’ and ‘hijack’ the United States, it would be a disaster for our region,” Zheng said. Japan has shifted away from its post-World War II pacifist policies and embarked on a military build-up. It is acquiring long-range missiles, embracing drones and expanding defence partnerships stretching from Canberra to London. But on Tuesday, Japan’s defence ministry denied that defence officials had indicated to US officials that Tokyo was prepared to significantly increase its defence spending to meet the 3.5 per cent of GDP target adopted by other allies. Speaking at a breakout session at Xiangshan Forum on Wednesday, PLA Senior Colonel Xiao Tiefeng said Japan’s refusal to reflect on its history of aggression and push for “remilitarisation” in recent years was among the factors constraining security cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. “We must oppose bloc confrontation, but we must also oppose the resurgence of militarism,” said Xiao, who is a research fellow at the Institute of War Studies of the PLA Academy of Military Sciences. Last November, Takaichi said an attack on Taiwan could trigger military intervention, angering Beijing, which called on the prime minister to retract the remarks. Zhou said it was unlikely that Japan would change its unfriendly China policy in the short term, and that the rising defence budget was a part of that. He said the scale of Japan’s arms sales and whether Japan would send its Self-Defence Forces overseas as combat troops rather than just as peacekeepers remained to be seen. Zhou said the process of increasing the defence budget was gradual and “the direct result of the investment remains to be seen”. Juerg Lauber, vice-president, International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), also warned against rising defence budgets in northeast Asia at the Xiangshan Forum this week. “Asia-Pacific military spending reflects a global upwards trend and is already at record heights against this backdrop. The ICRC encourages the states to de-escalate and to reject the notion of inevitable and unending war,” Lauber said.

title: How Huawei plans to bypass US chip curbs with its new UnifiedBus technology
description: The Chinese tech giant is leveraging its UnifiedBus technology to link hundreds or thousands of chips into single computing unit.
content: Huawei Technologies on Thursday unveiled a new computing architecture that it says could make as many as 1 million processors work as a single computer, putting its UnifiedBus interconnect technology at the centre of an ambitious effort to rethink how large data centres are built. The Peerium Computing Architecture combines nested parallelism, unified memory addressing and peer-to-peer interconnect, with UnifiedBus serving as the high-speed fabric connecting processors, memory, storage and networking equipment. Huawei said an Atlas 950 SuperCluster containing 256,000 computing cards was already being deployed, while its next-generation Atlas 960 system using near-packaged optics, or NPO, was under testing. Known in Chinese as Lingqu, UnifiedBus has become central to Huawei’s efforts to extract more computing power at the system level, a strategy that has taken on greater importance as US restrictions constrain the company’s access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing technologies. Here is what you need to know about UnifiedBus, how it works and why it matters for China’s artificial intelligence ambitions. What is UnifiedBus? UnifiedBus is Huawei’s high-speed interconnect protocol designed for what the company terms as “SuperPoDs” – systems that tightly link hundreds or thousands of processors into a single logical computing unit. Huawei now positions the technology as the key interconnect underpinning Peerium, its newly named computing architecture. UnifiedBus uses a single open protocol to link CPUs, NPUs, memory, solid-state drives, network interface cards and switches, with the longer-term goal of extending the concept of a single computer to systems containing as many as 1 million processors. In a traditional AI cluster, servers communicate with one another over conventional network connections like Ethernet. While easy to expand by adding more machines, larger clusters also face bandwidth bottlenecks and latency spikes when moving data between processors, leaving expensive AI chips waiting idle for data. Scale-up interconnects like UnifiedBus aim to address this structural limit directly. By providing higher bandwidth and lower latency between processors, memory and storage modules, UnifiedBus allows different hardware components to share data through unified memory addressing and communicate on a more peer-to-peer basis, according to Huawei. The protocol’s first commercial implementation, UnifiedBus 1.0, was deployed in Huawei’s Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoD, linking up to 384 Ascend AI processors. It began shipping in March 2025. Huawei subsequently expanded the scale to 8,192 processors with its Atlas 950 SuperPoD. The 256,000-card system disclosed on Thursday goes further still, although it is a SuperCluster made up of multiple SuperPoDs rather than a single 256,000-card SuperPoD. Why did Huawei develop it? US restrictions have made system-level innovation more important to Huawei, but rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun rejected the idea that UnifiedBus was merely a workaround for China’s limited access to advanced chipmaking technology. Asked whether the technology represented a China-specific path or one the wider industry would eventually follow, Xu called UnifiedBus “a path for the future” in the AI era. “In the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit,” he told the South China Morning Post on Thursday, adding that Huawei made the UnifiedBus protocol open to all because it believed “the whole industry will move toward the same direction”. Xu acknowledged that Huawei remained constrained by advanced manufacturing. “There is no problem from [a] design perspective for Huawei,” he said, but the company was limited by “the availability of sophisticated process nodes in China”. By making multiple processors work as one computer, Huawei believed it could compete at the system level, an area where Xu said the company had global leadership. He also stressed that the work predated US sanctions. “Those activities started not after the US sanction, but before,” Xu said. Huawei unveiled its first AI chip and AI strategy in 2018 and began investing more heavily in new computing architectures and interconnect technologies after launching SuperPoD and SuperCluster products in 2019. Xu said Huawei had invested more than 1.8 trillion yuan (US$268.2 billion) in research and development since 2007, with about 10 per cent going towards basic research. How about Nvidia’s NVLink and other Western alternatives? Western tech giants are also pouring resources into high-speed interconnects, which have become a key battleground for next generation AI infrastructure. Nvidia’s dominance in AI hardware relies heavily on its proprietary NVLink and NVSwitch technologies, which bind multiple graphics processing units (GPUs) inside systems, such as its rack-scale platforms, into a unified domain. Meanwhile, an industry coalition – including Advanced Micro Devices, Intel, Google, Microsoft, Meta Platforms, Amazon Web Services and Alibaba Group Holding – is backing Ultra Accelerator Link, or UALink, as an open standard to counter Nvidia’s ecosystem lock-in. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. By publishing the technical specifications for UnifiedBus 2.0 late last year, Huawei is seeking to build a domestic ecosystem that encourages Chinese chipmakers, server vendors and software developers to standardise on its architecture.

title: China hits back as US Congress approves tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy
description: Passed just ahead of Xi Jinping’s expected US visit, the bill gives Washington power to penalise Beijing over its Russian fuel imports.
content: Beijing has pushed back after the US Congress passed a bill on Wednesday that would allow US President Donald Trump to sanction Russia and its largest energy importers, including China. The bill, named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, authorises tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the top five importers of Russian oil and natural gas. In response to a question about the bill, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing had always opposed “long-arm jurisdiction” lacking a basis in international law and authorisation from the United Nations Security Council. “China has consistently carried out normal economic and trade cooperation with countries around the world on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” Guo said on Thursday. “Such cooperation neither targets any third party nor is subject to interference or coercion from any third party.” The bill’s passage comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s anticipated visit to Washington next week, which would be his first trip to the US since the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in November 2023. Ahead of Xi’s visit, Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent are set to conduct final preparatory talks over the weekend. Since returning to office for his second term early last year, Trump has aggressively deployed tariffs and sanctions as tools of geopolitical leverage. This has included targeting Russia’s defence and energy sectors in an attempt to disrupt Moscow’s ability to fund its war on Ukraine. Last month, Washington also launched a sanctions campaign targeting Iran to isolate it from global trade and financial systems. The move was widely seen as an attempt to exert pressure on Beijing to sever its commercial ties with Tehran. While the new bill does not explicitly name China, it states that tariffs will be increased on goods imported from countries that are “among the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas” if they continue buying these products after the law is enacted. The bill, which also expands sanctions on Iran, allows the US president to waive the requirements if national interests are at stake. It also introduces other prohibitions related to Russia, including sanctions on people involved in Russia’s defence base, financial institutions and fleets that transport Russian energy. China is the top buyer of Russian fossil fuels – ahead of India and Turkey – and has bought half of Russia’s crude oil exports since late 2022, according to data compiled by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Helsinki-based think tank. The European Union continues to be a major purchaser of Russian gas. Amid escalating US pressure on Russia and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, China has maintained its energy relationship with Moscow and pushed back against Washington’s tariff threats. China and Russia now settle most of their trade and payments in local currency. At the Brics summit in India last week, members of the bloc of emerging nations – which also include South Africa, Brazil and Iran – agreed to expand the use of national currencies in cross-border trade. The China-Russia energy relationship still has its sore spots. The Power of Siberia 2 gas pipeline project has remained stalled for years despite being high on Moscow’s agenda. Former US vice-president Mike Pence said on social media that the new bill targeted the “lifelines sustaining [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s war machine”.

title: India and Vietnam aim to turn ‘China plus one’ rivalry into trade gains
description: New Delhi and Hanoi are looking to join market scale with manufacturing capacity to build new trade links, analysts say.
content: India and Vietnam could turn their competition for “China plus one” investments into a complementary partnership, analysts say, combining New Delhi’s scale and technology capabilities with Hanoi’s manufacturing agility and links to East Asian supply chains. Such a shift could deepen both nations’ roles in global production networks across high-value industries – from electronics and pharmaceuticals to renewable energy – while giving companies reliable alternatives as they diversify supply chains beyond China. The idea has gained momentum after Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung called for closer economic integration with India, including new economic corridors and supply chains and a potential bilateral free-trade agreement. During a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Delhi on Saturday on the sidelines of the Brics summit, Le urged both countries to accelerate a review of the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement – a pact launched in 2010 to lower tariff barriers between India and members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. According to an Indian government statement, the two leaders also reviewed progress made since ties were elevated in May to an “enhanced comprehensive strategic partnership” during a visit by Vietnamese President To Lam. The nations have set a target of boosting bilateral trade to US$25 billion by 2030, up from US$18.28 billion in 2025–26. From competition to complementarity Experts said a deeper partnership could reinvigorate a range of industries while strengthening global supply-chain resilience. “The real significance of the proposal is larger than tariff reduction,” said Swaran Singh, a former professor of diplomacy and disarmament at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s School of International Studies in Delhi. He added that both nations should look beyond a preferential trade pact to co-creating integrated supply chains. Both India and Vietnam have actively sought to take advantage of the “China plus one” strategy, which accelerated following pandemic-era supply disruptions as global firms sought to diversify. Vietnam has emerged as one of the premier and most successful beneficiaries of this supply chain diversification, with small and lean facilities across electronics assembly, garments, footwear and technology components. “The shift that needs to be effected is one from ‘China plus one’ competition to ‘China plus one’ complementarity,” Singh said. Vietnam excelled in export-focused manufacturing and integration with East Asian supply chains, while India brought vast domestic market scale, design capabilities and digital services expertise, he said. “Instead of competing for the same factory, the two can collectively calibrate their respective niches in the value chains,” Singh added. “The strategic prize will be the creation of a South and Southeast Asian production corridor connecting Indian scale with Vietnamese manufacturing agility.” While a free-trade agreement could unlock business opportunities in pharmaceuticals, agriculture, electronics, machinery and services, Singh said the true test would be reducing non-tariff barriers, streamlining administrative procedures and improving cross-border logistics and investments. Deepening ties Indian officials say Vietnam is a core pillar of Delhi’s “Act East” policy – an initiative aimed at deepening economic and security ties across Southeast and East Asia – as well as its broader Indo-Pacific maritime doctrine. Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, said that the existing Asean-India free-trade agreement already provided zero-duty access to more than 80 per cent of bilateral trade by value. During the financial year ending March 2026, Indian exports to Vietnam, including meat and aluminium products – reached US$6.7 billion, while imports from Vietnam totalled US$11.6 billion, dominated by electronic products. “Before negotiating a separate FTA, both governments should assess why existing Asean–India FTA preferences remain underused and identify areas where deeper commitments could generate new and more balanced trade,” Srivastava said. He highlighted electronics, semiconductors, precision manufacturing, pharmaceuticals and food processing as key sectors for mutual integration. Combining maritime capabilities – ranging from port connectivity and shipbuilding to joint naval exercises – could help support a rules-based order in regional sea lanes. Vietnam has long voiced concern about China’s growing maritime assertiveness in the South China Sea, making security cooperation with India an attractive counterweight. “A partnership with India gives Vietnam fresh sources of military technology, maritime cooperation and potentially, defence co-production,” said Uday Chandra, an assistant professor at India’s Ashoka University. “Both India and Vietnam would also favour free navigation and open seas, whether around Malacca or in the South China Sea.” “In other words, this is about China, but also beyond China,” Chandra added. Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at the ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, said that Vietnam’s interest in Indian investment naturally aligned with Delhi’s dominance in generic pharmaceuticals and back-office technology. “These are natural areas where Vietnam would particularly welcome foreign investment,” Lim said, adding that Hanoi was following a playbook used by newly industrialised economies that relied heavily on foreign investment to build up industrial capacity. Lim added that diversifying foreign investment away from a heavy reliance on Beijing remained a priority for Hanoi. “I suspect that the diversification of its main investment partner – especially from China – is also at the back of the mind of Vietnamese officials, who understand that its symbiotic relationship with southern Chinese firms and investors often comes with the risk of becoming a client state of China,” Lim said. However, balancing these relationships would require careful diplomacy. “Vietnamese officials will have to tread carefully, since they certainly do not wish to alienate the otherwise healthy economic ties between their country and China, even as it seems to strengthen its relationship with India,” he said.

title: Hong Kong give Yang, Sham honour of carrying city’s flag at Asian Games opening ceremony
description: Basketball and wushu athletes Ivan Yang and Lydia Sham to lead city’s delegation into event, as official urges team to ‘achieve new heights’.
content: The 20th Asian Games officially get under way in Japan on Saturday, and the honour of leading the Hong Kong delegation into the opening ceremony has been handed to Ivan Yang and Lydia Sham. At a welcome event on Thursday, Wong Po-kee, the chef de mission for Hong Kong’s more than 800-strong delegation, said the pair would be the city’s flag bearers for the event at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Officials and some of the city’s athletes attended a flag-raising at Nagoya Port Garden Pier, where they were joined by the delegations from China and Macau. Wong, who is also honorary deputy secretary general of the Sports Federation & Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China, said he and his colleagues would do everything they could to support the 580 athletes who will represent the city across 38 sports. “I hope they [the athletes] will enjoy competing and engaging with Asia’s top athletes, give their best performance and achieve new heights,” he added. “At the same time, I call on everyone to support and stand behind every athlete.” Yang captained Hong Kong’s under-22 men’s basketball team at the National Games last year, and will represent the city in the 3x3 event in Japan. Sham, meanwhile, has hopes of coming back with a medal from her third Asian Games, having had an outstanding 2025, during which she won gold in the women’s Changquan – Jianshu – Qiangshu Combined event at The World Games in Chengdu, as well as gold in the women’s Changquan event at the World Wushu Championships. With the first day of competition on Sunday involving Hong Kong’s cyclists, triathletes and swimmers, who are in Tokyo for their events, several teams are likely to miss the opening festivities. Hopefully that will not be the case for 16-year-old Shum Chun-hei and Liu Hei-yu, who have already made history this week. Hong Kong has entered the modern pentathlon for the first time, with Shum in the men’s event and his teammate in the women’s. The city’s wrestlers and padel players are also making their debuts at the regional Games. The Asian Games take place from September 19 to October 4.

title: After the US Fed’s rate increase, will China still move ahead with monetary easing?
description: Analysts weigh whether Beijing is set to push ahead with a rate cut to bolster China’s economy despite the US Fed raising interest rates.
content: Following the rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, some analysts argue Beijing may still push ahead with rate cuts this year to shore up flagging domestic growth, though a rate increase by the US typically limits room for monetary easing by China’s central bank. The Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 on Wednesday, bringing the benchmark target range up 0.25 percentage points to between 3.75 and 4 per cent. The Federal Reserve’s move has not “significantly” narrowed China’s room for easing, said Shao Yu, chief economist with the Sci-tech Innovation Centre at Fudan University’s School of Management, though Chinese policymakers may enter a brief period of cautious observation. “China is currently one of the few economies globally whose economic cycle is moving in the opposite direction to that of the US dollar, which allows us to be more proactive in our monetary policy,” said Shao, who expected Beijing to cut the reserve requirement ratio and interest rates this year to support the economy. The Fed’s rate increase comes amid persistent inflation in the United States, with another increase possible later this year. By comparison, China continues to grapple with weak domestic demand. China’s economy has been slowing since the second quarter, when it grew just 4.3 per cent. With sluggish consumption and a deepening investment slump, markets are largely expecting additional policy support to help hit Beijing’s full-year growth target of around 4.5 to 5 per cent. Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, similarly noted that there was still a “solid case” for the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) to cut rates in the coming months. “Given the strength of the yuan this year, the Fed rate increase is unlikely to be a major factor in the PBOC’s rate decision,” Song said, adding that he expects the yuan to continue appreciating, though at a slower pace compared with so far this year. “The wider yield spread has not stopped yuan appreciation so far, but it may be a factor that is increasingly worth monitoring moving forward,” Song said. The PBOC set the yuan’s midpoint rate – also known as the daily fixing rate – at 6.7580 against the dollar on Thursday, the strongest level since February 2023. While a Fed rate increase typically triggered capital outflows from emerging markets towards higher-yielding US assets, Shao expected any downward pressure on the yuan to remain limited, supported by China’s strong export performance. Additionally, growing concern over Washington’s ability to service its ballooning US$40 trillion debt amid higher interest rates could prompt a reallocation into non-dollar assets, including the yuan, further insulating the currency against depreciation, Shao said. Foreign holdings of US Treasury debt fell for a second consecutive month in July, with Japan and China – two of the three largest creditors – trimming their positions, according to the latest data released on Wednesday. However, not all observers agree that rate cuts from China’s central bank are on the horizon. Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at French investment bank Natixis, did not expect any monetary easing from Beijing this year, citing the wide interest rate differential with the US. Instead, she expected authorities to focus on local-level fiscal support, such as expanding local government special bond issuance for infrastructure projects in sectors including data centres and grid upgrading to arrest the decline in fixed-asset investment. China’s top economic planner, the National Development and Reform Commission, has held a series of meetings in the past month calling for the acceleration of major construction projects and disbursement of fiscal funds to boost investment. Nevertheless, Garcia-Herrero expected the yuan to remain stable, noting that significant dollar reserves parked in Hong Kong would remove some of the pressure from Chinese banks continuing to move funds into short-term US money market paper for higher yields.

title: Carney seizes Canada-EU associate membership plan despite Trump’s ire
description: Welcoming the idea that Trump called ‘laughable’, the Canadian PM told the European Parliament, ‘we do not seek power to dominate others’.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday welcomed a proposal for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member, but said he did not mean for a closer alliance to create a new bloc that would rival the world’s great powers. The remarks came after US President Donald Trump suggested the proposed arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened heavy tariffs on Europe if he judged its intentions to be unfriendly. Trump also called the idea “laughable”. “We welcome this ambition,” Carney told the European Parliament of European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal, unveiled on Wednesday. Carney said plainly what he was proposing: deeper Canada-Europe integration across trade, defence, critical minerals, artificial intelligence, energy, space, research and financial services to make both sides less vulnerable to economic and geopolitical pressure. “I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” he said. “We do not seek power to dominate others.” Carney said the goal instead is to build Canada’s resilience so that no country can control its markets, undermine its sovereignty or dictate its choices. The prime minister received an ebullient welcome when he walked into the chamber, with many lawmakers approaching him to shake his hand and ask for selfies – and a standing ovation after he spoke. One parliamentarian had donned a Canadian hockey jersey. For generations, Canada built its economy around integration with the United States. Trump’s tariffs, demands for economic concessions and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state are now driving Ottawa to reduce that dependence and seek a deeper economic, security and political relationship across the Atlantic. Von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU’s first associate member – a status that does not currently exist in the bloc’s treaties and would have to be created. She said Europe wants to take its relationship with Canada to “the highest level possible”. Carney, sitting in the front row of the European Parliament chamber, nodded and rose to embrace von der Leyen as lawmakers gave the proposal a standing ovation. This time, Europe is offering Canada another path. Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU should move beyond their existing free-trade agreement and create an “alliance for the future” encompassing a “common prosperity and economic security space”. Carney will host EU leaders for a Canada-EU summit in Montreal on October 29-30, where the two sides are expected to discuss the proposed new relationship in more detail. Canada sends roughly 70 per cent of its exports to the US, making it highly exposed to Trump’s tariffs. Ottawa has retaliated and rejected demands Carney says threaten Canadian sovereignty. Europe took a different path, shelving retaliation and accepting tariffs of up to 15 per cent on most EU exports to the US. Carney has repeatedly urged middle powers to resist that kind of economic coercion. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he warned that when countries negotiate alone with a dominant power, “we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered”. Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday that Canada is not seeking full EU membership because that would require surrendering some sovereignty. Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to Europe while increasing Canada’s independence. Exactly what associate membership would mean remains to be negotiated. Canada has already taken a major step towards European integration. This year it became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150 billion (US$173 billion) Safe defence procurement programme, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe increases defence spending. The two sides have also discussed closer cooperation on energy, critical minerals, AI and digital trade. “The policies and rhetoric of the Trump administration are clearly pushing both Canada and the EU to imagine a world without strong US leadership and to act accordingly,” said Daniel Beland, a political-science professor at McGill University in Montreal. Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s handling of Trump has heightened European interest in the Canadian leader. “Carney’s shrewdness in dealing with Trump has captured Europe’s attention,” Wiseman said. Wiseman said Europeans have long regarded Canada as a country that understands the US particularly well because of their deep economic and political ties. Carney’s willingness to resist Trump rather than quickly accept Washington’s demands has reinforced that perception, he said. Beland said Carney may avoid naming Trump on Thursday while leaving little doubt about the target of his broader argument. “He knows that, beyond Europe, the world will be watching, including the White House,” Beland said.

title: President Xi’s industrial power play sees China bet big on AI, chips and smarter factories
description: Beijing is accelerating its push for resilient supply chains amid geopolitical tensions and domestic weaknesses.
content: President Xi Jinping has reiterated calls for China to make its supply chains more resilient and self-sufficient while accelerating the creation of a modern industrial system underpinned by advanced manufacturing. Xi’s latest directives, issued at a national conference on advanced manufacturing in Beijing on Wednesday and Thursday, were said to be aimed at strengthening the Chinese economy, the state-run Xinhua reported. Xi’s push this week echoed Beijing’s previous statements and came as the world’s second-largest economy has been growing at a slower pace amid employment worries, soft consumption and a persistent property market downturn. Upgrades to the industrial sector, the president said, were essential to securing China’s global competitiveness, Xinhua reported. In recent years, the so-called world’s factory has increasingly upgraded its industrial base, moving from traditional sectors towards a hi-tech, AI-heavy industrial base led by domestic inputs. The shift also reflects Beijing’s focus on self-reliance and its efforts to reduce dependence on foreign chips and hardware designs. With China and the United States racing to develop advanced technologies, including artificial intelligence models and semiconductors, geopolitical tensions have become a major obstacle to cooperation between the countries. Premier Li Qiang reinforced Xi’s message at the conference, calling the roll-out of advanced manufacturing a long-term strategic priority in China’s drive to become an industrial superpower. Li added that next-generation smart manufacturing would be the sector’s primary direction. Smart manufacturing refers to the use of data, connected equipment and automation to improve factory production. The premier called for a broader push into digitisation, technological self-reliance, low-carbon production and cross-sector integration to ensure that Chinese manufacturing becomes “smarter, greener and more interconnected”, Xinhua reported. “China is so large that we must dedicate ourselves to the real economy,” Xi previously said, according to an earlier Xinhua report on Tuesday. The real economy refers to production and trade in actual goods and services, rather than financial transactions or monetary instruments. Xinhua added that Xi also called for the country to “lead overall industrial revitalisation through scientific and technological innovation” as Beijing continues to enact its strategy for “new quality productive forces” – a term the president has used since 2023 to describe a shift away from traditional means of production towards a more tech-driven model. “To boost manufacturing, innovation-driven development is at the core,” Xinhua quoted Xi as saying, citing the goal of turning China into a greater manufacturing powerhouse.

title: Ancient Chinese scholars drank ink for poetic inspiration or poor handwriting penalties
description: Unlike today’s inks made from industrial pigments, ancient Chinese ink was produced using soot from burning natural plants or animal oils.
content: While the Chinese idiom, “Having ink in their stomach”, serves as a metaphor to commend the knowledgeable, the act of ingesting ink was a common practice among ancient literati. The earliest documentation of ink drinking dates back to the Northern and Southern dynasties (420–589), where it was used as a sanctioned punishment for scholars with illegible handwriting. According to the Book of Sui, the official history of the Sui dynasty (581–618), during an exam administered by a palace attendant to assess local officials, scholars who presented poor handwriting faced the penalty of consuming one sheng of ink. This traditional Chinese unit of volume varied by dynasty, with one sheng equating to 600 millilitres during the Sui period. This rule was abolished after Li Shimin ascended the throne in the Tang dynasty (618–907). Nevertheless, some scholars willingly consumed ink to enhance their literary skills. For instance, the Tang dynasty poet Wang Bo (650–676) was noted for having drunk “several shengs of ink” when he felt creatively blocked, which effectively enabled him to complete an essay in one continuous effort, without making any revisions. Wang’s action of consuming ink is likened to “creating mental drafts.” In another example, the Song dynasty (960–1279) wordsmith Su Shi (1037–1101) famously stated: “If I were to don the hemp robe once more, the exam ink would indeed be worthy of my drink.” In the Brush Records of Qiuchi, believed to be authored by Su, three literary figures from the Song dynasty were also recorded grinding ink for both writing and drinking during their gatherings as a scholarly pastime. The text describes how “True pine soot yields a lingering aroma, naturally imbued with the fragrance of ambergris and musk.” Unlike today’s inks, which are made from industrial pigments and chemical additives harmful to health, ancient Chinese ink was produced using soot from burning natural plants or animal oils, making it safe for consumption. Moreover, some inks were infused with traditional Chinese medicinal herbs. One such ink from the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), known as Eight Treasures Five Bile Medical Ink, featured a unique formula incorporating a dozen precious Chinese herbal medicines, believed to possess beneficial properties for disease prevention and beauty care. Though the practice of drinking ink is no longer carried out today, the idiom, “Ink in the stomach”, continues to describe well-informed individuals. For instance, during discussions about casting for an upcoming TV drama portraying the renowned female Song dynasty poet Li Qingzhao (1084–1155), actress Chen Duling, who holds a bachelor’s degree in aircraft manufacturing engineering, was recommended because she “has ink in her stomach.” Additionally, some cultural organisations have introduced drinkable ink products to connect with this historical practice. For example, last year, the Nanjing Imperial Examination Museum of China unveiled a drinkable ink product made from black mulberry, blueberry, and plum juice, allowing visitors to “experience traditional culture in a fun way.”

title: Malaysia confronts complexities of schizophrenia after school killing ruling
description: One woman details her experience of living with schizophrenia, saying ‘I had no idea what was real’ during severe psychotic episodes.
content: When Cindi suffered her first severe psychotic episode a decade ago, she could no longer tell where reality ended and her imagination began. “My reality and fantasy [were] all distorted. I had no idea what was real, what was not,” the 38-year-old, who asked to be identified only by her first name, told This Week in Asia. “It was so severe to the point that I couldn’t even recognise my own family members. My mother was there, my brother was there, but they didn’t feel like my mother or my brother.” Her experience has taken on new resonance in Malaysia after a court acquitted a 15-year-old boy of murdering his schoolmate Yap Shing Xuen, 16, on the grounds that severe schizophrenia had left him legally insane when he killed her at their school in Bandar Utama, outside Kuala Lumpur, last October. Yap was found dead in a school toilet after suffering at least 180 stab wounds, according to a forensic report, in a killing that shocked Malaysia and intensified concerns over safety in the country’s schools. On Monday, the Shah Alam High Court accepted testimony from forensic psychiatrist Ian Lloyd Anthony that the teenager had severe schizophrenia and was incapable of understanding the nature of his actions or that they were wrong. His lawyer Kitson Foong earlier told This Week in Asia that the boy’s condition had gone untreated for several years before the attack. “The court held that, because of his illness, the child offender did not know the nature of what he was doing and did not know that it was wrong or against the law,” Foong said. After his acquittal, the boy was sent to Hospital Bahagia Ulu Kinta, a psychiatric hospital in Perak state, for treatment, counselling and medication. Foong said the boy would remain there until he was assessed to no longer pose a threat to society, with any eventual release dependent on medical and psychiatric reports presented to the Sultan of Selangor. But much of the anger since the ruling has centred on the word “acquitted”, with some Malaysians questioning why the boy should escape a murder conviction and others arguing that an insanity verdict had been mistaken for freedom. In one online forum, the verdict quickly split opinion. Some users called for the death penalty and invoked “a life for a life”, while others stressed that the boy had not simply walked free and remained in psychiatric custody. Yap’s mother, Wong Lee Ping, has also urged the public to back a petition calling on Malaysia’s Attorney-General’s Chambers to appeal against the acquittal, saying her family had few avenues of its own to challenge the decision. “We are neither judges nor prosecutors. We are simply a family who has lost our daughter,” Wong said on social media, adding that the family wanted the proper legal process, including any available right of appeal, to be considered. Cindi said she understood why the case frightened people because her own first psychotic episode in 2016 took her to a place she still struggles to explain. At one point, frightened and feeling alone, she took out knives. After her mother locked her in an outside kitchen, Cindi repeatedly stabbed the door trying to get out. “I felt very out of control, basically,” she said. “It’s like I’m witnessing everything from a different point of view, but I don’t know why or how to explain why I do this. I feel like I’m just looking at what I’m doing, but I cannot stop it … by then it was too late because I’ve already done the action.” Police eventually took her to a psychiatric ward, where she was observed for about two weeks before being diagnosed with schizophrenia. She then went seven years without another psychotic episode and today works, raises a five-year-old son and attends therapy, although severe stress can still trigger symptoms. During a recent episode, Cindi called a crisis hotline and told her family she needed their help. As someone on the line talked her through what she was experiencing, she said the negative voices gradually stopped and she began to feel normal again. “With the right intervention, with the right medication, with the right support, we are just as normal as anyone else,” she said. Diagnosis in the dock About 27 million people worldwide, or roughly one in every 300, live with schizophrenia, according to the World Health Organization, which lists persistent delusions and hallucinations among symptoms that can profoundly alter how a person perceives reality.
