Mariani Md Nor, a psychologist and vice-chancellor of SEGi University, said severe psychosis could seriously impair judgment and a person’s understanding of their actions, but that was not the experience of everyone diagnosed with schizophrenia. “We should not assume that schizophrenia means violence. Most people with schizophrenia are not violent,” she told This Week in Asia. “The risk may increase when someone is experiencing severe untreated psychosis, particularly when other factors such as alcohol or drug misuse are involved. In fact, people with serious mental illness can also be victims of violence, discrimination and stigma.” We need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia Chua Sook Ning, clinical psychologist A review published last year examining 47 longitudinal studies involving more than 203,000 people with psychosis found that a previous criminal history had the strongest association with later violence, followed by substance misuse, with many treatment-related factors linked to a lower risk. Clinical psychologist Chua Sook Ning, founder of mental health organisation Relate Malaysia, said the danger after a case such as the Bandar Utama killing was that the diagnosis itself could become the explanation for what happened. “A diagnosis can become a very easy one to reach for. That can make schizophrenia sound as though it explains the violence by itself,” she said. “Most people with mental illness aren’t violent, and acts of violence can occur in the absence of mental illness, so we need to be careful about taking one case and allowing it to shape how we see everyone living with schizophrenia.” Cindi has felt those assumptions in her own life. She kept her diagnosis private for almost a decade and said the father of her son refused to marry her because his family was afraid of her schizophrenia. “Schizophrenia is a treatable disease. It’s lifelong, but it’s treatable,” she said, adding that she now had an accepting workplace, supportive friends and continued access to therapy. Much of her attention now is on raising her son, whom she hopes will never have to experience the same illness and upheaval that have marked the past decade of her life. “I just hope that my son doesn’t get it. That’s all,” Cindi said. “I don’t want my son to go through the same suffering that I have … so let the struggle end with me.”

title: Prime Video K-drama A Love Other Than Yours: Seo Kang-joon, Ahn Eun-jin face 10-year itch
description: Seo Kang-joon and Ahn Eun-jin play a long-term couple yet to tie the knot whose relationship is challenged when newcomers enter their lives.
content: Lead cast: Seo Kang-joon, Ahn Eun-jin, Jo Aram, Lee Joo-ahn Latest Nielsen rating: 2.8 per cent Romantic comedies have long been the bread and butter of the Korean drama industry, full of meet-cutes, misunderstandings and the promise of falling in love with a forever partner. While these remain the gold standard, recent years have witnessed a steady rise in romantic dramas that follow long-term couples navigating their evolving relationships. Some series, such as the smash hit Queen of Tears, still exist in a highly heightened K-drama environment, while others in the vein of LTNS offer a more grounded view of what relationships can look like several years down the line. The latest series to explore mid-romance malaise is the KBS drama A Love Other Than Yours. It revolves around Namgoong Ho (Seo Kang-joon, Undercover High School) and Lee Mi-do (Ahn Eun-jin, My Dearest), a couple who have been dating for 10 years but are no closer to tying the knot despite family members pressuring them to do so. Ho is an ordinary office employee working as an assistant manager at Hunmin Confectionery. His relatively stable work life stands in stark contrast to that of Mi-do, a film director grappling with a troublesome star and a brewing media scandal threatening to scupper her career before it truly begins. Amid these contrasting work environments, which present varying stresses and encompass very different work hours, Ho and Mi-do are also confronting changes within their relationship. Although they have known each other since they were seven and remained close through school, it was only in their 20s that they became a couple. They do not officially cohabit, but they live in one-bedroom flats across the hall from each other and freely move between them, whether to visit or borrow toothpaste. This serves as a clean visual metaphor for their relationship: close and comfortable, but not yet truly united. A decade into their romance, they are as comfortable as ever around one another, but something has changed: the spark has faded. Their status quo is then challenged when new people enter their respective work lives. In Ho’s case, Park Su-ah (Jo Aram, formerly of the K-pop group Gugudan) joins his workplace and a comfortable rapport quickly builds between them. While dealing with the fallout of her clash with an actress, Mi-do meets Han Tae-seung (Lee Joo-ahn, Bon Appétit, Your Majesty), a legal adviser for the company bankrolling her project, who is tasked with negotiating her settlement. Initially, their dealings are highly contentious, but the fire between them suggests that something else could build over time. The appearance of these newcomers forces Ho and Mi-do to take a hard look at their relationship and feelings for one another, forcing Mi-do to make a rash judgment call. Mi-do has been delaying their engagement, wanting to debut as a feature filmmaker and achieve stability first. Ho is endlessly supportive of her desires, doing his best to help her navigate these challenges, but Mi-do no longer wants to lean on him and cannot face the thought of failing as a filmmaker while being protected by Ho and his steady job. These thoughts come spilling out one night when Mi-do suggests they break up. Unfortunately, this is the very evening Ho had intended to propose. This is not the end of the road for Ho and Mi-do, but it does send their relationship into murky waters. To navigate them, they must also overcome the obstacles presented by potential love interests Su-ah and Tae-seung. The question going forward is not whether they will get back together, but rather whether they should. They care for one another, but – particularly for Mi-do – is this the right kind of support? For couples balancing personal and professional lives, relationships should not just be about building safe spaces. Partners also need to challenge and push one another to strive for their goals. That appears to be the kind of support Mi-do is craving. With a total of 14 episodes, there is plenty of runway ahead for A Love Other Than Yours to explore the complex balance that two working professionals continually strive for in a relationship. A Love Other Than Yours is streaming on Prime Video.

title: Hong Kong will lack 130,000 workers by 2028, fewer than projected due to talent policies
description: Shortage mitigated by AI development and talent import policies, labour chief says, as top talent visa renewal to be relaxed for tech founders.
content: Hong Kong will be short of 130,000 workers by 2028, about a third less than originally projected, a reduction the city’s labour chief attributed to the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and government policies to import labour and top talent. A day after the release of the city’s first five-year plan and annual policy address, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Thursday that authorities would exempt start-up founders approved under the Top Talent Pass Scheme from needing to provide proof of company income when renewing their visas to better support these entrepreneurs. “Our previous manpower projection found that we will be short of 180,000 workers by 2028, but in the latest study, to be announced in detail next week, the shortfall will be reduced to 130,000,” he said. “That reflected a change in our economic structure, the impact of the rapid development of AI on labour demand, and the result of our labour and talent policies, which helped fill some of the vacancies. Without these policies, the predicted shortage would be 300,000.” The Labour and Welfare Bureau last conducted a manpower projection in 2023. It predicted that the labour supply would reach 3.56 million in 2028, while demand would be 3.75 million, resulting in a shortage of 180,000 workers, based on the assumption that the economy would grow by 3.2 per cent each year. The manpower shortage in 2023 was 50,000. To support talent development, Sun said the government would relax the visa extension requirements under the Top Talent Pass Scheme for technology start-up professionals. He said proprietors of technology start-ups that had secured support from the Hong Kong Science Park, Cyberport or the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park would be exempted from providing proof of company income when applying for an extension of stay under the Top Talent Pass Scheme. “Start-ups often experience financial losses in the first few years, but they have very bright prospects in the longer run. If we want to foster a thriving start-up environment, we should make some small adjustments according to their unique ecosystem to support them,” Sun said. “We hope that it can offer more convenience to people aspiring to start a business.” He added that authorities noted the impact of AI on youth employment and would support young people under the 30,000 Youth Employment and Internship Programme, a new two-year joint initiative between the government and businesses announced on Wednesday. He said the government would work with six major business chambers to provide at least 10,000 additional jobs in two years. For each young person admitted under the scheme, the government would cover up to one-third of their monthly salary or HK$6,000 (US$765) for six months, with the rest to be paid by the companies. Sun said only Hong Kong permanent residents under the age of 29 would be eligible to apply, regardless of their academic qualifications. The remaining 20,000 opportunities will come from the STEM internship scheme, the Home and Youth Affairs Bureau’s start-up internship programme and an on-the-job training subsidy scheme for graduates in the construction industry. Meanwhile, the government would continue to update the Talent List, the official registry of high-demand professions with local labour shortages, to include workers in the AI sector. The update was expected to be completed by next year, he said. Under the Talent List, companies can hire foreign professionals and workers without providing proof that no suitable candidates are available locally. The scheme allows applicants to receive a work visa in as little as four weeks.

title: Exclusive | ‘Provocation’ could accelerate Taiwan reunification, retired PLA major general says
description: Island’s leader William Lai has ‘challenged our red lines’, Luo Yuan says on sidelines of Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum.
content: Progress towards reunifying with Taiwan hinges on factors like the island’s level of provocation, retired PLA major general Luo Yuan told the South China Morning Post, warning that Taiwan’s leader had challenged Beijing’s red lines. Speaking on the sidelines of the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing on Wednesday, Luo said the timeline for reunification with mainland China was shaped by “the development of our national strength, our defence needs, the global security environment, as well as the degree of provocation from Taiwan”. If Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te “continues to provoke, the Taiwan Strait will be plunged into a dangerous situation fraught with the risk of conflict”, added Luo, who is widely regarded as a hardline figure. Luo’s remarks came amid heightened cross-strait tensions since Lai, of the independent-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), took office in 2024. Luo also referred to Lai’s description last year of mainland China as a “foreign hostile force”, saying it had “challenged our red lines”. Beijing has repeatedly denounced Lai as a separatist and accused him of fuelling tensions since his inauguration. “Peaceful reunification remains our sincere aspiration,” the retired PLA major general said. “But whether it is achieved through peaceful means, force or other non-peaceful means, these are merely means. The ultimate goal is to achieve reunification,” he added, calling reunification “irreversible”. Luo is a senior adviser to the Xiangshan Forum, China’s flagship security conference. The gathering is often seen as a counterpart to the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore. Defence officials and academics from nearly 100 countries are attending this year. In a departure from last year’s conference, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun did not mention Taiwan in his keynote speech to the forum on Wednesday. Still, the issue remained prominent in panel discussions, drawing particular attention ahead of an expected summit in Washington next week between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump. Beijing has described Taiwan as “the first red line that cannot be crossed” in Sino-US relations. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Luo said an important aspect of the Taiwan issue was US arms sales to the island, likening them to “playing with fire”. With a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan reportedly awaiting Trump’s approval for months, weapons sales are an especially sensitive issue ahead of Xi’s expected state visit. Chang Ya-chung, a Taiwanese political scientist who attended this year’s Xiangshan Forum, warned of a difficult situation in the Taiwan Strait, pointing to what he described as Japan’s increasingly prominent security role around Taiwan. Speaking at a panel session on Wednesday, Chang, who now heads the Taipei-based Sun Yat-sen School, said a “tacit security alliance” was emerging between Taiwan and Tokyo, citing their cooperation in the drone industry as an example. Relations between Beijing and Tokyo deteriorated following remarks in November last year by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi regarding Taiwan. Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a PLA attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially allowing Japanese forces to intervene. During Wednesday’s panel, Chang called for the swift resumption of institutionalised communication between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait. The arrangement was suspended after Tsai Ing-wen of the DPP became Taiwan’s leader in 2016. Chang also called for a crisis-management channel to help maintain peace across the strait, arguing that “the foundation of peace across the Taiwan Strait remains political dialogue between the two sides”. Chang is an advocate for reunification. He ran unsuccessfully for the chairmanship of the Kuomintang (KMT), Taiwan’s main opposition party, in 2021 and 2025. “The two sides should resume institutionalised communication as soon as possible, establish mechanisms for military crisis management and mutual trust, and begin political dialogue on ending hostilities and signing a memorandum of peace,” Chang said.

title: Hong Kong property market gets reprieve on rates, but position remains precarious
description: Major banks hold rates steady despite Fed action, but some sellers and buyers are already anticipating increases later, agents say.
content: Hong Kong’s property market dodged an immediate hit from the Federal Reserve’s rate hike on Thursday as major local banks kept their prime rates unchanged, but another increase could puncture the market’s relatively fragile recovery, according to industry insiders. The Fed raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point at its latest meeting on Wednesday in the US, but HSBC and other major Hong Kong banks left their prime rates unchanged. The decision should have no immediate impact on the local property market, said Joseph Tsang, chairman of JLL Hong Kong. “However, the market outlook depends on whether US rate hikes will continue.” If rates rose further, higher mortgage costs would weigh on homebuyers and raise developers’ financing costs, potentially prompting them to accelerate sales to reduce financial pressure and dampening their appetite for land, Tsang said. Developers have been testing higher prices. On Thursday, Chow Tai Fook-owned State Residence priced its first batch of flats more than 10 per cent higher than the prices at neighbouring State Pavilia’s 2025 launch. Meanwhile in the second-hand market, some sellers are already narrowing discounts. In North Point, negotiating margins narrowed to 1 to 2 per cent from 3 to 4 per cent immediately after HSBC announced it would not raise its rate, while viewing appointments rose 20 per cent, said Chris Wong, executive director at Century 21 Sunrise. A homeowner surnamed Tsang, who is selling her 807-square-foot flat in the district, raised her minimum price to HK$10.8 million from HK$10.67 million, citing stable rates and promotional mortgages. The firmer tone was also evident at City One Shatin, where owners were generally unwilling to cut asking prices despite remaining open to negotiations, said Now Wong, district associate director at Midland Realty. At the same time, a property investor surnamed Lam contacted an agent looking for “bargains to be snapped up”, saying he was ready to buy if further rate hikes triggered distressed sales. Funding costs are already edging higher despite unchanged prime rates. The one-month Hibor (Hong Kong interbank offered rate), the basis for most mortgages, had recently approached 2.8 per cent to 2.9 per cent and could move above 3 per cent in the near term, said Raymond Chong, CEO of mortgage brokerage StarPro Agency. If the Fed increased rates again by the end of the year, Hong Kong banks could raise prime rates by up to a quarter point, Chong said. Rising funding costs would also prompt banks to withdraw popular fixed-rate mortgage plans by the end of the year, he added. At the top end of the market, sellers remain cautious. Most owners with properties for sale in The Peak and Southern district were taking a wait-and-see approach and inviting offers rather than setting asking prices, said Joseph Yan, senior principal district sales director at Centaline Property. For now, much of the rate pressure had already been absorbed, said Elliott Hau, head of financing valuation at Colliers. Residential transactions fell to 4,019 in August from 7,650 in June, suggesting buyers had priced in expectations of higher rates. Colliers said it would maintain its forecast for residential prices to rise between 8 and 10 per cent this year. However, if borrowing costs remained elevated for a prolonged period, “some capital could be diverted to alternative investment products offering competitive returns”, Hau said. The commercial property market could face greater pressure if rate increases continued, said Tsang at JLL. “Buyers will ask for higher rental yields, and property owners may need to lower asking prices in order to sell,” he said. Additional reporting by Cheryl Arcibal

title: Who is Kevin Costner’s rumoured new girlfriend? Meet lifestyle coach Jennifer Milburn
description: Once linked to Jennifer Lopez after divorcing Christine Baumgartner, the Yellowstone actor is now reportedly dating an ex-Delta flight attendant 31 years his junior.
content: It seems Yellowstone star Kevin Costner is no longer dating actress and producer Kelly Noonan Gores, who is 24 years younger than him. The 71-year-old actor was reportedly dating 47-year-old Gores, the ex-wife of billionaire Alec Gores, earlier this year. A source told Page Six that Costner was “not looking for a serious relationship or marriage any time soon” at the time, and that the pair were spending time together at his Santa Barbara estate in California. However, more recently, Costner was spotted in Santa Barbara with a “mystery blonde”, whom the Daily Mail identified as 40-year-old Jennifer Milburn. The rumoured new couple were seen grocery shopping together and Costner was reportedly being “extremely affectionate” with Milburn, per the Daily Mail. What do we know about Kevin Costner’s new date, who is more than 30 years his junior? Read on to find out. What is Jennifer Milburn’s background? Milburn is from Aspen, Colorado, where Costner’s 65-hectare Dunbar Ranch is located. Milburn, who is identified as a “lifestyle coach” by various media outlets, worked as a Delta Air Lines flight attendant and is also a model. She also worked for Western gear retailer Kemo Sabe, frequented by Costner, for several years, per the Daily Mail. The British news outlet also reported that she currently works as director of partnerships for author and inspirational speaker Simon Sinek’s The Optimism Company. “We are here to inspire people to do the things that inspire them so that, together, each of us can change our world for the better,” the company bio reads. Who else has Kevin Costner dated? While it is unclear when and how Costner and Milburn’s speculated romance first started, his romantic relationships have been a hot topic since his high-profile split from Christine Baumgartner in 2023 after 18 years of marriage. Since then, Costner has sparked dating rumours with Jennifer Lopez after the pair were seen together at Kemo Sabe in 2024. He was last known to be dating Gores. There is little information available on Milburn’s personal life.

title: Record influx of university graduates pushes China’s youth unemployment rate to 18.9%
description: Anxieties over AI’s growing threat to entry-level roles add to existing concerns about economic doldrums caused by weak domestic demand.
content: China’s urban youth unemployment rose last month, as a record influx of university graduates struggles to find work in a job market weighed down by weak domestic demand and the growing adoption of artificial intelligence. The jobless rate for those aged 16 to 24, excluding students, rose to 18.9 per cent in August from 17.9 per cent in July, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Thursday. This figure, as well as the identical number from August last year, represents the highest reading since Beijing revised its calculation methodology to exclude students in 2023, following a peak of 21.3 per cent under the old rubric reported in June of that year. A record 12.7 million university students were estimated to have graduated this summer, entering a labour market already weakened by slowing economic momentum. While the rise in youth unemployment is partly seasonal, anxiety is growing over the threat that the emerging adoption of AI poses to entry-level roles. Zhang Lin, a recent software engineering graduate from a university in Tianjin, said she had spent over a month searching for work in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen to no avail. She attributed her difficulty partly to AI, which she suspected had reduced entry-level coding roles and heightened competition. “For certain tasks, AI doesn’t just write code faster than you, but it writes it better, too,” Zhang said. She said she had sent out over a hundred applications and messages to recruiters, but the vast majority had gone unanswered. Even when she did secure a response, intense competition often cut the process short. In one instance, she began a work trial with an e-commerce company only to be told on her second day that a candidate who had tested earlier in the week had just been hired for the position. “The job market is really not great,” Zhang said. “There are too many people competing for a single role.” Around 7.5 per cent of the jobs held by workers aged 15 to 29 in East Asia are in occupations highly exposed to AI, according to a report published by the International Labour Organization last month. If just 10 per cent of those positions disappeared, the region would see 1.5 million young people face unemployment, shift into another job, or leave the workforce entirely, the UN agency said. Chinese authorities have expanded vocational education and technical training to address workforce mismatches, but some jobseekers – like Zhang – remain sceptical that additional qualifications will improve their prospects. “I just have to keep applying,” Zhang said. “The priority is to land a job, earn a living and regain my momentum.” Meanwhile, the unemployment rate for those aged 25 to 29, also excluding students, stood at 7.5 per cent in August, up from 7.2 per cent in July. China’s overall urban jobless rate edged up to 5.3 per cent in August, from 5.2 per cent in July.

title: ‘War without battle’: Europe struggles to tackle mounting Russian hybrid attacks
description: From sabotage and arson to cyberattacks and airspace violations, officials say Moscow’s hybrid actions have moved deeper into Europe.
content: Over the course of the summer, Russian attacks have been pushing ever deeper into European territory. On August 11, military divers destroyed two drones floating off the coast of Romania near a €4 billion (US$4.7 billion) energy project. Nine days later, Bucharest scrambled two F-16s to take out a maritime drone near the same Black Sea gas platform with hundreds of workers on board. Earlier that month, German police detected an armed UAV at Leipzig airport, while this week Nato jets downed another unmanned aircraft that entered Lithuanian airspace from neighbouring Belarus, an ally of Moscow. In all these cases, the authorities pointed the finger squarely at the Kremlin. As Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine grinds on with little movement on the battlefield and thousands of casualties each week, so-called hybrid attacks on Europe are increasing not just in number, but in their recklessness. Companies on the front line find themselves caught in a grey zone between war and peace and European officials, who asked not to be named discussing sensitive issues, fear that it is only a matter of time until there are civilian casualties. “It’s clear that the European defence industry is working in a different security environment than a few years ago,” said Kuldar Vaarsi, CEO of Estonian defence firm Milrem Robotics, which was targeted by a suspected arson attack in August. “As a company whose systems are used by several Nato member states and other ally and partner nations, including Ukraine, we need to take the resultant risks into account.” Just this week, the US Justice Department accused the Russian intelligence service of “conspiring to finance terrorism and commit murder for hire” in Europe at the behest of the Kremlin. Defence plants, public utilities, transport systems and communications networks have all been attacked, presenting Europe’s leaders with their greatest security threat in decades. So far, it is unclear if they are up to the challenge. “We struggle to counter so-called hybrid attacks with open societies that make it easy for the attacker,” said James Everard, former Nato deputy supreme allied commander Europe. “This is war without battle and behind their nuclear shield Russia believes it can act with impunity, acting directly or through proxies.” Germany is the “daily target of hybrid warfare” by Russia, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on September 1. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said those accusations were “completely unfounded”. The past two months have seen a shift in Russia’s focus towards defence-industrial and logistics targets directly connected to support for Ukraine, according to one Nato country official, who added that this more aggressive campaign presents higher risks. With Moscow continuing to structure operations so that it can deny direct responsibility, the campaign is more significant strategically than for the physical damage caused so far, the official said. That assessment could change as Russia ups the ante with incidents such as last weekend’s drone assault at a railway station near the Ukraine-Polish border as European and US dignitaries were passing through. Such attacks had been largely taboo until now, offering further evidence of a growing brazenness and willingness to risk foreign victims. Where once Russia stood accused of election interference and weaponising migration, it is now suspected of sabotage, arson, tampering with critical infrastructure, cyberattacks and airspace violations, including an incident last week that resulted in two civilian deaths at a border post between Ukraine and fellow European Union aspirant Moldova. The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said Europe was experiencing “a wave of increasingly kinetic hybrid attacks”. The difficulty in responding to hybrid attacks has at times led to a reluctance to blame Russia openly, both to avert escalation and avoid revealing intelligence methods, officials say. Many incidents, especially cyberattacks and hacks targeting critical infrastructure, are barely reported if at all, meaning the scale of the problem is far wider than is made public. Many arms makers in Germany are targeted by regular cyberattacks, according to a person familiar with the matter. In 2024, arsonists set fire to the home of Armin Papperger, the CEO of defence giant Rheinmetall, and Western intelligence agencies warned that Russia was plotting to kill him. He now travels with a heavy security detail and Rheinmetall has increased its overall security measures. German radar and sensor maker Hensoldt is increasing drone and perimeter surveillance at its plants and wants to build the infrastructure required to down drones itself, CEO Oliver Dorre said in an interview. It needs approval from the federal police to do this and Dorre said guidelines are needed sooner rather than later, before the situation becomes worse. Poland, as a major conduit for aid to Ukraine, has suffered a spate of suspicious incidents, with multiple cyberattacks on public utilities like water, energy infrastructure and hospitals, and damage to the rail line between Warsaw and the Ukrainian border attributed to Russian intelligence. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described a fire at a plant for one of Europe’s largest drone makers, WB Electronics, in August as an “act of sabotage”, though no public link was made to Russia. Poland announced this month it was expanding protection of its airspace and strengthening rapid-response defences, citing the threat from “Russian provocations”. Europe’s largest weapons makers are mostly undeterred by the increasing level of Russian activity aimed at their facilities and personnel, according to a person at one such company. Security has been tightened and lingering “muscle memory” from the Cold War is feeding a vigilance that borders on paranoia, the person said. Other key businesses are less well able to defend themselves. Achieving 100 per cent protection of electricity networks is impossible, “especially when you may not even know what you are facing”, said Juha Rasanen, CEO of Savon Voima, an energy company in eastern Finland. “Physical security, physical monitoring, cameras and different types of detection methods are being increased all the time,” he said. “But the most important thing is that people learn to tolerate power outages.” That kind of resilience points to another reality: Russia’s campaign has so far failed to substantially reduce European support for Ukraine. The rise in high-profile incidents has instead reinforced arguments for more European defence spending, tighter counter-intelligence coordination and new sanctions. As one official put it, the Kremlin’s campaign may be disruptive but is proving counterproductive for Moscow. Germany, for example, made it known after Leipzig that a delivery of additional Iris-T air defence missiles to Ukraine is planned for September, and that Berlin will also soon provide Kyiv with several thousand strike drones. As hybrid actions move deeper into Europe, the lid is occasionally peeled back to reveal what authorities are confronting. In early September, a British man was arrested and charged under the National Security Act with giving details about drone manufacturing sites in England to a Russian intelligence unit and preparing to commit sabotage. His lawyers said his allegiance lies with the UK. That comes on the back of suspected arson attacks on former British prime minister Keir Starmer’s home, Russian submarine activity around critical infrastructure in the British Isles and drones launched from shadow fleet vessels in UK and Irish waters, including during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s visit to Ireland this year. Governments from London to Warsaw are scrambling to ratchet up their individual and collective responses before more serious damage spirals into open conflict with Russia. Nato is strengthening deterrence in the nations affected, officials say, but a coordinated strategy continues to elude member states. The understanding among security officials is that Putin is testing how far he can push Nato members to expose indecision among the allies while staying below the threshold that would trigger retaliation under the Article 5 collective-defence clause. Yet that probing raises the chances of miscalculation and accidents. “Russia is consistent in identifying weaknesses in Nato’s infrastructure and is willing to attempt multiple tactics and targets in a flexible and increasingly risk-taking manner,” said Emily Ferris, associate fellow at the London-based Royal United Services Institute. Ferris published a report in March on sabotage attacks attributed to Russia in Nato countries and found the alliance “unprepared”. Six months later, her verdict has not changed. “In the absence of clear red lines from Nato about the consequences of attacks like this, Russia is expanding to fill the space of the uncertainty,” she said. The only time that Article 5 was invoked was by the US after the September 11 attacks of 2001. Western intelligence agencies are now applying counterterrorism methodology developed since then and the fight against al-Qaeda and Islamic State to Russian hybrid warfare, according to two officials. Russia and terror groups both use proxies, often recruited online. Hence for Western agencies, there are similarities in identifying threat actors. The difference is that those recruited to Moscow’s service are not ideological, but paid. Western security officials say that Moscow is acting out of desperation after Ukraine’s drone attacks targeting energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses damaged the Russian economy. The view from Moscow is that the more painfully Ukraine hits Russia, the stronger will be the voices who want to make Europe pay. A person close to the Kremlin put it more bluntly, saying that Russia will make life hell for Europe through asymmetrical hybrid operations over its support for Kyiv. To those on the front line like the Baltic states, Russia has long since crossed any notional boundaries. “This is not hybrid, this is about explosives that can cause damage. There can be casualties. People may die,” said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys. “If we won’t stop this, it will escalate.”

title: Indonesia faces reckoning over maritime safety after deadly ferry disaster
description: Experts say poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continue to leave passengers vulnerable, amid a rise in maritime incidents.
content: Indonesia’s latest ferry disaster has exposed persistent weaknesses in maritime safety oversight, experts have said, with poor enforcement and inadequate supervision continuing to leave passengers vulnerable across the sprawling archipelago. The capsizing of the Virgo Transport 8 in the Java Sea on Sunday has intensified scrutiny of a system that analysts say too often comes under pressure only after deadly accidents, rather than preventing them. Six people have been confirmed dead and 129 remain missing after the passenger and cargo ferry capsized amid high winds and rough seas while travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan. According to Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency, 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – were aboard the vessel when the captain reported bad weather at about 2am local time on September 13. A total of 108 people were rescued after personnel from agencies including the Indonesian Army and the Search and Rescue Agency were deployed, in the latest of a string of maritime incidents that have renewed questions over how Indonesia regulates and enforces safety at sea. The latest disaster follows a string of other maritime incidents in recent months. In August, five people died after a ferry caught fire off the island of Madura, while a blaze aboard another ferry travelling from Bali to Lombok killed one person. In July, a ferry sank in the Bali Strait leaving 19 people dead and 16 missing, and another ferry went down in waters close to South Sulawesi, killing three people with 14 still missing. In May, a tourist boat capsized close to Bengkulu City in Sumatra, resulting in eight deaths. Following the latest sinking, lawmakers and experts have called for a comprehensive investigation into the incident and a tightening of maritime safety regulations. In a statement provided to This Week in Asia, Usman Hamid, the head of Amnesty Indonesia, described the Virgo Transport 8 incident as “a humanitarian tragedy” that exposed the state’s failure to protect the safety rights of sea transport users. Hamid called for an “immediate, independent, impartial and thorough investigation” to determine whether negligence by regulators, the vessel’s owners or other parties had contributed to the disaster, adding that anyone found responsible should be held legally accountable. He also pointed to survivor testimony that no emergency alarm sounded when the ship capsized in the middle of the night while many passengers slept in cabins below deck. “The availability of life jackets has also come under scrutiny,” Hamid said, citing survivor accounts that some passengers could not find them and that many people on life rafts were not wearing them. Data from Indonesia’s Search and Rescue Agency showed 601 maritime incidents between January and August this year that required search and rescue deployment, including passengers falling overboard, engine failures and fires aboard vessels. In 2025, there were a total of 450 incidents from January to December. Rise in incidents Soerjanto Tjahjono, head of the National Transportation Safety Committee, told This Week in Asia he could not comment on the Virgo Transport 8 incident as it was still under investigation but that data compiled by the independent government agency also showed maritime incidents in Indonesia were on the rise. “However, we do not yet have a definitive conclusion for why that is,” he said. “What we do know is that extreme weather should never be blamed. We have to learn how to deal with the weather at sea and avoid it. It is not a reason for accidents, but it can be a contributing factor. There are also technical issues such as human factors.” Tjahjono said the committee was currently conducting a wider investigation into boat safety, and aimed to publish a list of recommendations in the coming months. One family member still anxiously awaiting news of a loved one aboard the Virgo Transport 8 is Fredy Manuhua, whose younger brother Stefiansa Manuhua, 44, played keyboard in the boat’s band to keep passengers entertained during the voyage. Manuhua, 48, said he last contacted Stefiansa on Friday and later heard about the ferry incident around 7am on Sunday. “I went straight to the port in Surabaya and the ferry company confirmed it,” he said. “I have been waiting there ever since and will not leave until there is news.” Lack of oversight Aji Suraji, director of postgraduate programmes at the University of Widya Gama in Malang, who specialises in transport safety and engineering, told This Week in Asia that maritime safety was a shared responsibility. “It is the responsibility of boat operators to ensure that all the standard operating procedures on their vessels are being followed,” Suraji said. “However, it is also the responsibility of external stakeholders such as the Department of Transportation to make sure that vessels are adhering to these procedures.” While the Department of Transportation had tightened some regulations in recent years, particularly regarding the compilation of accurate boat manifests, Suraji said there was still room for improvement. “Adhering to standard operating procedures and external oversight of these are weak points in Indonesia when it comes to transport safety,” Suraji said, adding that “there needs to be more control and supervision, with clear and enforced sanctions in place”. Suraji lamented that too often, transport safety in Indonesia gained attention only when incidents such as the Virgo Transport 8 happened and went viral. “But after that, people forget and are too forgiving. We need to be better at identifying potential issues before they happen and anticipating them.” The incident has left Manuhua grappling with questions such as why no alarm apparently sounded, and why the captain of the Virgo Transport 8 and 11 crew members left the vessel and were rescued while other passengers were still aboard. “I hope there will be a full investigation, and I will push for anyone to face the full extent of the law if they were at fault,” he said. “I am devastated by what has happened. I am so close to my brother and I pray every night to our parents, and tell them that he is still lost and to please send him back to us. “There are still so many things that we want to do together. I am not ready to lose him.”

title: Hyrox Beijing athletes get full refund, new hygiene rule will allow competitors to be axed
description: Athletes finished after women’s elite winner Joanna Wietrzyk on Saturday to get cash back. Australian would have been removed under new rules.
content: Hyrox China has given full refunds to competitors affected by last weekend’s incident in Beijing, while the global governing body has updated its rule book to allow race directors to remove athletes if they pose a risk to the hygiene of the event. The commercial fitness competition has faced intense public backlash since elite Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk suffered incontinence during the solo women’s event but was allowed to carry on and win. Her mid-race left track surfaces and shared equipment contaminated for more than 1,000 subsequent participants. In an email sent to participants on Wednesday, organisers offered to refund entry costs to those who started before 2.40pm on Saturday but had not finished by that time, as well as all athletes who departed in heat batches between 2.40pm and 8.40pm. Wietrzyk’s solo women’s race began at 2.40pm and she needed little more than an hour to triumph across the 8km and eight-obstacle course. “First, when the unexpected incident occurred during the afternoon session on September 12, we failed to timely arrange for the involved athlete to leave the track,” Hyrox China said. “Due to this operational oversight, you did not receive the good event experience you deserved, and for this we are deeply sorry.” Officials added that on-site staff immediately disinfected the venue and completed a full track carpet replacement later that evening. Hyrox China noted that after a complete internal evaluation, the decision was made to issue full refunds, instructing runners to contact them if funds are not processed within 10 working days. The financial remediation followed Hyrox officially updating its global rule book for the 2026-27 season, introducing emergency protocols for biological contamination. Under the updated penalty section for all divisions, the rule book now explicitly addresses medical and hygiene risks on track in 12.3 Did Not Finish (DNF). “If a racer’s blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers, a Race Director may withdraw the racer from the race on medical grounds, in line with Hyrox’s medical and hygiene SOPs. Any such withdrawal is recorded on the leaderboard as DNF.” The refunds and policy overhaul follow days of escalating criticism, which was initially fuelled by the initial response from officials in China. In a statement released 48 hours after the incident, in which Wietrzyk soiled herself midway through her race, Hyrox World acknowledged organisational lapses but defended the 24-year-old, praising her “courage, resilience and refusal to give in …[as] precisely what makes elite athletes so extraordinary”. The statement failed to appease competitors and the public, with Chinese social media users condemning local organisers as “arrogant” for prioritising competitive perseverance over public health and equal rule enforcement. Before the change in the law book, athletes could be handed a two-minute penalty for spilling water or spitting on the course, but not an incident where faecal matter was left on the course. Co-founder Moritz Furste ultimately had to step in with explicit apologies. He admitted the organisation made a mistake by “not reacting immediately during the race,” while Hyrox China conceded the global rule book lacked mechanisms to penalise competitors in such situations, pledging that the structural changes that have now been made.

title: Taipei donates coastguard vessel to Manila as South China Sea tensions mount
description: As it faces off against Beijing in the region, Manila has been expanding its unofficial security cooperation with Taipei.
content: Taiwan has quietly acknowledged donating a coastguard vessel to the Philippines, potentially adding to Manila’s maritime patrol capacity amid its long-running stand-off with Beijing in the South China Sea. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration said on Wednesday that “this case” was being handled in line with previous transfers of vessels to the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu. Unlike those three Pacific states, which all maintain formal diplomatic ties with Taipei, Manila recognises Beijing under its one-China policy. In its remarks, the Taiwanese agency did not identify the vessel, its specific Philippine recipient or intended mission. Taiwanese media have linked the transfer to the Philippine-flagged BLING NO.1, which is classified by commercial ship-tracking services as a law enforcement vessel. Sources familiar with the transfer told the Post that the vessel was the retired Kinmen patrol ship and that BLING NO.1 was a temporary name being used for its delivery voyage to the Philippines. The identification is consistent with a report by Taiwan’s Liberty Times newspaper, which cited naval enthusiasts’ comparisons of the bows of the Kinmen and its sister ship, the Lienchiang. The Lienchiang and Kinmen were built in 2008, are about 61 metres (200 feet) long and displace 688 tonnes (758 tons). Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said this represented “a notable shift” from Taiwan’s previous vessel donations. “Whereas those transfers centred on capacity development, delivery of this vessel to the Philippines provides an asset that could have a direct impact on contestation with China,” he said. Operationally, Bosack said, a vessel of its size and capability would “better position the Philippine Coast Guard to hold firm” against the Chinese coastguard, while cautioning that it remained unclear whether Manila would use it for other missions or “in managing Chinese presence operations”. The transfer has drawn criticism from Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang. KMT legislator Ma Wen-chun questioned why Taipei was donating a law enforcement vessel to the Philippines given continuing disputes over fishing rights and overlapping maritime claims. Pointing to the fatal shooting of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine coastguard personnel in 2013, Ma asked whether Taipei could guarantee that the donated vessel would not eventually be deployed against Taiwanese fishing boats. She also called on the government to disclose the refurbishment costs, funding source and any restrictions or conditions attached to the transfer. Simona Grano, head of Research Area China-Taiwan Relations at the University of Zurich, said a vessel of this size could provide the Philippines with “additional flexibility for maritime law enforcement, search and rescue, fisheries protection and sustained presence operations”. “The vessel should not be viewed as a substitute for the larger and more capable ships that the Philippines needs to monitor its extensive maritime domain,” she said. “However, it could help expand the number of platforms available for routine patrols and allow the Philippine Coast Guard to distribute its existing resources more effectively.” Manila has been expanding its unofficial security engagement with Taipei amid increasingly tense encounters with Chinese mainland forces both at sea and in the air over parts of the South China Sea. Citing a senior Philippine government official, the Japan Times reported last year that exchanges with Taiwanese security officials had increased, including contact between senior military personnel. The official described a more deliberate effort to informally draw Taiwan into the defence architecture of the Philippines and the wider region. Grano said maritime security and coastguard cooperation offered “relatively discreet channels” through which Taiwan and the Philippines could deepen engagement “without necessarily crossing Manila’s diplomatic red lines concerning its relations with Beijing”. But she cautioned that “we should be careful not to interpret this single transfer as evidence of a formal security partnership”, adding that Manila’s growing exposure to Chinese maritime pressure created “clear incentives for closer practical cooperation with Taiwan”. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr said last year there was “no way that the Philippines can stay out” of a US-China conflict over Taiwan. He has also highlighted the need to evacuate Filipinos living and working in Taiwan if a conflict erupted. Bosack said Taiwan’s low-key approach pointed to practical cooperation rather than “a ceremonial dig” at Beijing. Manila’s relationship with Beijing remains fraught. On Wednesday, in response to Taipei confirming its plans for a new representative office in Cebu, the foreign ministry in Beijing urged Manila to abide by the one-China principle. The donation adds Taiwan to a growing list of partners helping to expand the Philippines’ maritime capacity. Much of that support has come from Washington, Manila’s treaty ally, and its partners. Grano said it would be “premature to conclude that Taiwan has established a systematic regional maritime assistance programme comparable to Japan’s”. The comparison was nevertheless useful, she said, because both Japan and Taiwan could strengthen their partners’ resilience “while operating below the threshold of direct military cooperation”. Japan has supplied the Philippine coastguard with 10 44-metre and two 97-metre response vessels and is financing five more 97-metre ships. The United States handed over two former US Coast Guard 27-metre patrol boats in August, while France is financing the acquisition of 40 new 35-metre patrol vessels from French shipbuilder OCEA. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force.

title: Once reliant on Samsung and SK Hynix, Chinese smartphone makers are turning to CXMT
description: Fuelled by a global memory shortage, China’s CXMT is winning spots in flagship handsets from ByteDance-powered AI devices to Xiaomi’s top models.
content: China’s leading memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) is gaining ground among local smartphone vendors, with some of its high-end chips finding their way into flagship Chinese handsets as vendors push into the premium market. ZTE-backed Nubia’s NaviX Ultra that went on sale on Wednesday used LPDDR5X DRAM chips from CXMT, the companies announced earlier this month. The handset was dubbed the Nubia Doubao phone due to its integration of TikTok parent ByteDance’s Doubao artificial intelligence assistant. CXMT said the tie-up with Nubia marked the first large-scale use at that level of domestically made LPDDR5X chips, which have a data transfer speed of up to 10,667 megabits per second (Mbps). The flagship handset, priced from 5,999 yuan (US$885), according to ZTE’s website, was also the first mass-market smartphone equipped with an AI agent, the company claimed. The consumer version of ByteDance’s Doubao smartphone assistant provides the phone with capabilities to respond to spoken instructions and carry out tasks on a user’s behalf. CXMT’s LPDDR5X chips support speeds of 8,533 Mbps, 9,600 Mbps and 10,677 Mbps, with the two slower versions already in mass production since last year. The adoption of LPDDR5X by the Nubia Doubao underscores how CXMT is breaking into the premium mobile memory chip segment at a time when on-device AI is boosting demand for faster and more capable memory. Chinese smartphone-to-vehicle giant Xiaomi and Transsion, known for its budget phones in emerging markets, were also among customers using the LPDDR5X line, CXMT said in its 2026 interim report published last month. CXMT said last month that its newer and faster LPDDR6 chips had entered mass production, with Xiaomi’s 18 Fold becoming the first flagship smartphone to commercially deploy the memory product. The memory chip offers a capacity of 16 gigabytes and supports a maximum data rate of 12,800 Mbps, which was “sufficient data bandwidth to meet the high-performance computing needs of flagship smartphones and edge devices”, CXMT said. Huawei Technologies’ Kirin 9030 Pro, the processor in its Mate 80 Pro Max released in February, uses a mix of memory components from Samsung Electronics and CXMT, according to a teardown report published in June by SemiAnalysis. The Chinese memory chip giant has been rapidly gaining traction in the global DRAM market. CXMT’s share of global DRAM revenue rose to 9.5 per cent in the second quarter from 7.6 per cent in the first quarter, according to market consultancy TrendForce in early September. However, it still trails the three global memory giants by a wide margin. Samsung accounted for 39.4 per cent of global DRAM revenue in the second quarter, followed by SK Hynix at 24.9 per cent and Micron Technology’s 23.3 per cent, according to TrendForce. CXMT’s growing capabilities have also appeared to attract the attention of Apple. The US tech giant has reportedly been testing the Chinese firm’s memory chips for potential use in products including iPhones and MacBooks, particularly those for sale in China, according to a Wall Street Journal report last month, citing sources. Neither Apple or CXMT have publicly announced any tie-up so far. Apple’s exploration of Chinese chips comes as the global industry is grappling with a memory chip supply crunch, with surging demand from AI data centre buildouts squeezing supplies of conventional memory chips for smartphones and other consumer electronics, pushing up prices.

title: Macroscope | Who’s in control of Japanese monetary policy? Tokyo or Washington?
description: Bessent’s intervention could have adverse implications for Japan’s economy, the BOJ’s credibility and tech-heavy stock markets in Asia.
content: Before the unexpected intervention in Japan’s foreign exchange market by the US Treasury Department on July 31 – the first time both countries joined forces to support the yen via outright purchases since 1998 – the probability of the Bank of Japan raising interest rates at its policy meeting on September 17-18 was less than 30 per cent. Fast forward to today, and the chances of an increase have shot up to almost 100 per cent. In fact, expectations have shifted so dramatically that bond markets are pricing in a one percentage point rise in borrowing costs to 2 per cent by the third quarter of 2027. JPMorgan is even more hawkish and expects Japanese interest rates to rise to 2.25 per cent by the end of next year. While several factors are at play, the most important one is the unprecedented pressure exerted by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Japanese policymakers to take more forceful action to strengthen the yen. The coordinated intervention to support Japan’s currency, which had fallen to its weakest level against the dollar since 1986, has fuelled speculation about the terms of the cooperation, particularly given Bessent’s active interest in Japan’s economic affairs, which dates back to his years as a hedge fund manager. In a report on August 13, Citigroup said that “it makes sense to interpret concerted intervention as suggesting US authorities have received a convincing pledge regarding an adjustment in the direction of the Takaichi government’s economic policy. One aspect of this is likely promotion of BOJ monetary policy normalisation.” Even if such assurances were made, it would be politically unwise for Bessent to play up the fact that he was able to extract them. Although investors’ perception that the BOJ is under pressure to raise interest rates more aggressively to prop up the yen has caused the currency to strengthen 4.6 per cent versus the dollar since July 28, Bessent has overplayed his hand. Last week, he warned traders not to bet against the yen, claiming he has “asymmetric information” that gives him “pretty good insight into … what Japanese policymakers are going to do”. He even boasted: “I am the house now. You can bet against me if you want.” Never mind that Bessent’s credibility in the bond markets has already suffered – his intervention to bring down long-term US bond yields failed to prevent the 10-year yield from breaching 5 per cent earlier this week – and that the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East makes the policy dilemmas facing the world’s central banks more acute. The overt pressure exerted by the US Treasury Secretary on Japan, especially his blunt tone, is bound to backfire. While Japanese policymakers have, for the most part, refrained from commenting publicly on Bessent’s intervention, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said his reference to himself as “the house” was “a bit scary”. If the Trump administration tried to meddle in Chinese policymaking in such a brazen manner, there would be hell to pay. Although Japan is a close ally of the United States, the flagrant foreign interference in the domestic economic affairs of a leading economy – one whose policies have a major bearing on global financial stability – beggars belief. Bessent’s intervention could have adverse implications for Japan’s economy, the BOJ’s credibility and technology-driven stock markets in Asia. First, while borrowing costs need to rise – real interest rates are still negative, Japan’s corporate sector has proved extremely resilient and wage growth is picking up – household consumption was flat in the second quarter. Although Bessent believes Japan has overcome decades of deflation, Japanese policymakers are not so sure. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was already worried about the risk of excessive tightening before Bessent’s intervention. Her fears are certain to have intensified since the escalation of the US Treasury’s pressure campaign. Second, the perception that the BOJ is stepping up the pace of interest rate increases as a quid pro quo for US support in propping up the yen could severely undermine the Japanese central bank’s credibility. It is bad enough that the politicisation of US monetary policy contributed to the Federal Reserve’s decision on September 16 to raise interest rates in order to maintain credibility. By jeopardising the independence of the BOJ, Bessent is playing with fire. Third, if higher interest rates in Japan cause the yen carry trade – a widely-used strategy in markets whereby investors borrow cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets overseas – to unwind, technology-heavy stock markets such as South Korea and Taiwan could suffer. Moreover, higher Japanese bond yields could draw capital away from the US Treasury market, which is already under pressure because of the Fed’s hawkish pivot. “Japan’s rate reset matters beyond its borders: shifting capital flows could add to upward pressure on global yields”, said BlackRock. What is clear is that while the US is putting pressure on Japanese monetary policy, Japan could end up putting global markets under more strain.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, September 18-20
description: A rooftop market, a free mini music festival and an all-you-can-eat pizza block party are among our picks this weekend in Hong Kong.
content: With fine weather forecast in Hong Kong for the coming few days, it’s a sign to spend the day outside this weekend. Whether that’s shopping, eating, drinking or exercising, you’re sure to find something on this list. Read on for all the details. 1. Rooftop Moonlit Market Start the Mid-Autumn Festival celebrations early with the Rooftop Moonlit Market in Lai Chi Kok on Saturday, September 19. Along with local bites, handmade crafts, live music and a full afternoon of family-friendly activities, the market will also host workshops across the day. The line-up includes charm bracelet workshops, lip stain and gloss classes, and even sound baths with journaling therapy. View this post on Instagram A post shared by the Hive Hong Kong (@thehivehongkong) Carnival game booths will offer a chance to enter a lucky draw for prizes including a portable photo printer, a mini popcorn machine, a suitcase and more. The event is open to both children and pets, and entry is free for those who reserve a ticket in advance. For more information, click here. 13/F, The Hive Lai Chi Kok, Tai Cheong (Liberal) Factory Building, 3 Wing Ming Street, Cheung Sha Wan 2. Chilled Steps at Tai Kwun The mini music festival held in Central is back, this time with a spotlight on American jazz. Titled Boundless Soundscapes, the event is curated in collaboration with First Half Arts in Concept, bringing together local and international musicians for an alfresco concert. The three-day music festival celebrates the fusing of American jazz with global traditions as well as Cantonese folk music, featuring musicians such as jazz icon Patrick Lui, vocalists Mandy Chan and Rachel Sung, guitarist Huang Zhihong, and violinist Bob Pang. For those planning to attend, it is advised to arrive early at the Laundry Steps in Tai Kwun to secure a good spot. No registration is required for this free event. For more information, click here. Tai Kwun, 10 Hollywood Road, Central 3. Motorino Pizza Block Party Motorino Wan Chai is once again throwing a neighbourhood block party on Saturday with unlimited pizza, free-flow drinks and a little friendly competition. Starting at 3pm, the event invites guests to drop by any time during the two-hour window for a HK$298 (US$38) ticket that covers two hours of unlimited pizza by the slice alongside bottomless wine and beer. A beer pong tournament adds a competitive edge to the afternoon, with winners walking away with exclusive Motorino socks and a complimentary pizza for their next visit. Tables are available on a first-come, first-served basis, and guests are encouraged to spill out onto the streets. For more information, click here. Motorino, 15 Ship Street, Wan Chai 4. AIA Annual Healthy Living AIA’s free two-day wellness festival is back in Wan Chai, running over the weekend on September 19 and 20. While admission is free, places are allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. Visitors can use the AIA+ app to secure slots. This year, visitors can put their strength, endurance and determination to the test at a series of fitness stations, with challenges including the SkiErg, rowing machine, sandbag lunges and wall balls. Professional coaches will be on hand to offer guidance. The designated area also offers family-friendly interactive games for all ages and fitness levels. There will be a range of talks and panels from local celebrities and experts such as Carol “Dodo” Cheng Yu-ling, who will be sharing insights on mental well-being, family and future planning across eight sessions over two days. Advance registration is required and each user may register for one session only. Other wellness activities include Pilates, body composition assessments and sound experiences, with prizes and rewards available for selected activities. For more information, click here. 19/F, Crystal Court, Hopewell Hotel, Wan Chai 5. Look Back Unveiled last week at the Venice International Film Festival – just three months after he took the somewhat disappointing Sheep in the Box to Cannes – Hirokazu Koreeda’s Look Back, in which a childhood friendship shapes an artistic dream, is an elegant work that once again underlines the Japanese director’s preternatural skills at working with young actors. Adapted from Tatsuki Fujimoto’s work – which was turned into an equally charming animated feature of the same name in 2024 – Koreeda’s film is full of surprises and beautifully rendered, much like the manga at the heart of the story. Handled with the director’s usual warmth and accompanied by a soaring score, the film finds one of its greatest pleasures in watching the girls at their desks, drawing, shading and sketching. Paying great attention to their surroundings and their clothing, Koreeda delivers a film awash with childhood memories, both sad and special. Read the full review. Look Back is in cinemas now.

title: ‘Depraved’ Singaporean paedophile, who abused daughter, granddaughters, jailed
description: The 71-year-old man has blood cancer, but the judge said it was clear neither age nor condition had stopped his ‘appalling’ crimes.
content: A diagnosed paedophile who sexually abused 11 girls over 33 years, with the acts ranging from molestation to rape, was sentenced by a Singapore court on Thursday to 21 years’ jail. The victims were as young as five, and included his daughter, granddaughters, nieces and students at an enrichment centre he ran with his wife. The judge noted that the jail term should not be crushing or amount to a life sentence for the 71-year-old man, who suffers from a rare blood cancer called myelofibrosis. At the same time, she rejected the defence’s call for the exercise of judicial mercy in this case, saying it was not appropriate. Justice Mavis Chionh said this was a tragic case of persistent sexual offending by a diagnosed paedophile against his own family members and students, who trusted him. This was despite the man being punished and prosecuted twice, and despite his diagnosis in 2021. The elderly Singaporean cut a shrunken figure in the dock, with a folded wheelchair nearby. He had pleaded guilty to 10 charges including rape, sexual assault and unnatural sex, with another 23 taken into consideration. Across all offences, he began abusing victims in 1990 and this continued until 2023. He started sexually abusing his daughter in 1997 when she was between six and seven. He later raped her when she was 15, telling her not to tell anyone because it would split up the family. The man was incarcerated twice, in 1999 and 2020, for similar sexual offences against minors. However, the full extent of his predatory conduct came to light only after he started preying on his granddaughters following his second release from prison. He molested his five-year-old granddaughter in 2023, and showed her sister pornography and sexually abused her. When the granddaughters told their mother about the abuse, the man’s daughter then revealed the offences against her. ‘Particularly heinous’ Deputy Public Prosecutors Jiang Ke-Yue and Ronnie Ang had sought 32 to 36 years’ jail for the man, while defence lawyers Nakoorsha Abdul Kadir and Dwi Heryanni Mohamad asked for 15 years’ jail. Justice Chionh said neither position correctly applied what is known as the totality principle, a legal concept where a court reviews the combined sentence to see if it is just, fair and not too harsh. The prosecution’s position breached the first limb of the totality principle, which considers whether the total sentence is substantially higher than the normal sentence for the most serious of offences faced. The most serious offence in this case was punishable by between eight and 20 years’ jail. The second limb of the totality principle requires a court to consider if the total sentence is crushing, and not in keeping with the man’s past record and future prospects. While the prosecution had argued that it was appropriate to breach the first limb because of the man’s overall criminality, the judge rejected this. She said she had no doubt that the case was egregious and the offender’s conduct was reprehensible, but the sentence sought by the prosecution was “disproportionate” to the man’s overall criminality, especially when compared with similar cases. Justice Chionh said she had to consider whether the sentence amounted to life imprisonment, and any terminal illness the man had must be considered. The offender’s life expectancy is reduced because of his blood cancer, with the latest medical report estimating a 13 per cent chance that he will live beyond 2031. On the other hand, the judge did not agree with the defence’s position for 15 years’ jail. She adjusted the sentence to sufficiently reflect the man’s overall criminality, arriving at 21 years’ jail, and declined to add any additional jail term in lieu of caning because of his age and illness. Still, Justice Chionh said the offences the man committed were “particularly heinous”, with some of them involving his daughter, granddaughters and niece. “The full extent of his offending is appalling,” she said, pointing to his repeated and brazen sexual abuse and repeated offending even after previous stints in jail. She said it was clear that neither his age nor condition had put a stop to his “depraved” criminal conduct. He stopped his serial sexual offending only because he was caught, and a report from the Institute of Mental Health states that he is a paedophile with a sexual attraction to prepubescent girls. The report also noted he poses a danger to children. This article was first published by CNA

title: Donald Trump presses China on fentanyl precursors ahead of US summit
description: White House designates China as the top source of core synthetic drug chemicals despite joint enforcement progress.
content: US President Donald Trump has urged Beijing to take “more aggressive action” to curb the export of drug precursor chemicals, noting to the US Congress that he had raised the issue “directly” with his Chinese counterpart. Trump’s call comes just days ahead of a planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and just a week after security agencies from the two countries praised progress in cooperation on counternarcotics law enforcement. The call was noted in an annual list sent to the US Congress of designated major source or transit countries for illicit drugs affecting the United States. Releasing the list on Wednesday, the White House again labelled China “the world’s largest producer of many of the precursor chemicals used to illicitly produce fentanyl, methamphetamine and other deadly synthetic drugs”. In an annual presidential “determination” sent with the list, Trump noted that the Chinese government last year implemented new requirements for companies to obtain licences before exporting designated precursor chemicals to North America, adding that the move was made at his request. Still, he accused “criminals” in China of continuing to find ways around those controls by using unregulated precursor chemicals. “The [People’s Republic of China] needs to take more aggressive action to effectively reduce the flow of these substances by scheduling additional chemical precursors and substances requested by the United States,” Trump wrote in the presidential determination. “This enhanced cooperation will enable timely prosecution of the criminals responsible for supplying drug traffickers with deadly precursor chemicals.” Also known as the Majors List, the Presidential Determination on Major Drug Transit or Major Illicit Drug Producing Countries has been issued annually for nearly four decades. The latest version, published this week for the US government’s 2027 financial year beginning on October 1, named 23 countries, including China, India, Mexico and Panama, a composition that is unchanged from last year. Since 2003, US law has required the president to notify Congress of the designated countries by mid-September each year. Notably, this year’s release comes just before Trump and Xi are expected to meet in Washington on September 24 for their second face‑to‑face talks of 2026. Fentanyl and cross‑border drug trafficking have consistently been high on Washington’s agenda in negotiations with Beijing, which are expected to feature at the summit. During his visit to Beijing in May, Trump “highlighted the need to build on progress in ending the flow of fentanyl precursors into the United States” during his conversation with Xi. But as the two powers work to keep bilateral ties stable despite intense strategic competition, counternarcotics has emerged as a prominent area in which they could work together. In a sign of efforts to build an upbeat tone ahead of Xi’s visit to the US, China’s Ministry of Public Security announced last Thursday it had jointly investigated a transnational case involving the manufacture and trafficking of synthetic cannabinoid precursors with the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Beijing described the case as “a demonstration of the China-US counternarcotics law enforcement cooperation mechanism’s efficient operation” and “another visible outcome of deepened practical cooperation between Chinese and American counternarcotics agencies”. According to a statement from the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Texas on September 9, the FBI-Ministry of Public Security counternarcotics working group, established in January, allowed collaborative efforts to dismantle the transnational criminal network. “These results represent a major milestone in US-China counternarcotics cooperation and underscore the effectiveness of sustained, structured coordination between both countries in addressing the international illicit chemical supply chain,” the office said. In July, FBI director Kash Patel visited Beijing to meet Chinese Public Security Minister Wang Xiaohong for discussions that focused on tackling fentanyl precursors. Ahead of Trump’s visit to China in May, Beijing also announced that the two countries had jointly dismantled a transnational drug-trafficking network. China was first placed on the Majors List in 1992, then removed for a period from 2005, and was relisted in 2023 under former US president Joe Biden after an expanded definition of precursor chemicals. It has remained on the list since. US documents state that a country’s presence on the list “is not necessarily a reflection of its government’s current counterdrug efforts, or coordination” with the US, but is “due to a combination of geographic, commercial and economic factors that allow drugs or precursor chemicals to transit or be produced, even if a government has engaged in robust and diligent narcotics control and law enforcement measures”.

title: Malaysia seizes 3 Israeli-bound containers as Anwar pledges to stop shipments for Gaza war
description: The seizures follow an initial detainment of a container for Israeli defence technology firm Elbit Systems, suspected of containing weapons.
content: Authorities in Malaysia have seized several more Israel-bound shipments at one of the country’s biggest ports, according to people familiar with the matter, an apparently new level of scrutiny in a nation where anti-Israeli sentiment runs high. Three containers bound for Ashdod Port south of Tel Aviv were detained at Malaysia’s Tanjung Pelepas port in mid-August and to date had not been released as authorities investigate their contents, the people familiar with the matter said, asking not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly. The seizures follow an initial detainment of another container on August 7 that originally came from the Philippines and that was suspected by the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency of containing weapons because it was headed to Elbit Systems, an Israeli defence technology firm, according to a statement from the agency at the time. Tracking data from Hapag-Lloyd, the container line carrying the cargo, show the shipment still at Tanjung Pelepas. The other three seizures happened on August 19, the people said. Those containers housed electric bike parts that were being shipped from a Chinese manufacturer, Chongqing Mobimax Technology, according to manifests. Tracking data from the liner carrying those cargoes, A.P. Moller-Maersk, also show them still at the busy transshipment port almost a month later. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, commenting on the August 7 seizure, said the Southeast Asian nation would not be a conduit to trade flows that can support or contribute to “the cruelty of the Israeli regime”. Malaysia does not have diplomatic or trade relations with Israel, reflecting its long-standing position on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Malaysia’s customs legislation prohibits trade with Israel, but excludes transit goods. The Strategic Trade Act 2010, however, bars transshipment of military, strategic dual-use goods. “Any suspicious shipment will be subject to inspection and investigation in accordance with Malaysian law. Where a violation is established, decisive action will be taken,” Anwar said on social media on Tuesday, in an apparent reference to the latest seizure. “We will not allow our country to be used as a conduit for any shipment that supports or contributes to Israel’s military capabilities and its atrocities against Palestinians and other innocent lives.” We will not allow our country to be used as a conduit for any shipment that supports ... Israel’s military capabilities Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim A representative from the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency said the matter was currently under investigation and the agency was unable to comment further. The Royal Malaysian Customs Department, whose legislation the agency uses to conduct enforcement at ports, declined to comment. The Johor Port Authority, which oversees ports in the Malaysian state, also said the matter was under review. Malaysia’s Ministry of Transport did not respond to a request for comment. Representatives for Elbit Systems declined to comment while Mobimax Technology did not respond to a request for comment. Representatives for Hapag-Lloyd and Maersk declined to comment. Pro-Palestinian sentiment has long been strong in Muslim-majority Malaysia and intensified after the Gaza war began in October 2023, driving widespread public protests and consumer boycotts. Anwar, who has been a vocal Israel critic, in December of that year banned Israeli shipping company ZIM Integrated Shipping Services from using Malaysian ports.
