More recently, authorities in July this year closed crypto investor Balaji Serinivasan’s start-up academy, the Johor-based Network School, following an investigation triggered by claims that Israeli students were studying at the tech commune in breach of Malaysian immigration rules. Malaysia also has no diplomatic ties with Israel and passport holders are banned from entering without permission. The Port of Tanjung Pelepas is located near the Strait of Malacca, one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. It is Malaysia’s second biggest port but its largest in terms of transshipment volumes, which account for around 90 per cent of the cargo it handles.

title: Tribute exhibit for Leslie Cheung; Hong Kong’s Gen Z coffee boss: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From famous Chinese women in folklore to Year of the Horse eighth month predictions, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Leslie Cheung would have been 70 this year. An exhibition celebrates the star For those too young to have attended a live concert by Hong Kong Cantopop icon Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing, who died on April 1, 2003, appreciation often relies on recordings of his performances and exhibitions dedicated to his career and legacy. 2. The Hong Kong Gen Z coffee boss filling market gap with her can-do attitude Few would guess that Hong Kong’s first plant-based canned coffee brand, Busy Brew, is run by a 23-year-old. One might be tempted to see it as a Gen Z entrepreneur fairy tale: a student spots a gap in the market, builds a cult following for her canned oat milk lattes, lands incubation funding and watches the product fly off shelves in some of the city’s largest retail chains. 3. Is the Year of the Horse’s eighth month lucky for you? Forecasts for all signs The elements play a powerful role in the eighth month of the Year of the Fire Horse, with a surge of metal energy bringing clarity to some zodiac signs and obstacles to others. 4. Why are Chun-Li’s thighs so big? All about the Street Fighter character In the 1990s, Chun-Li was not only the first female playable character introduced in the Street Fighter video game franchise – she was also the first female playable character to gain mainstream recognition in the arcade and fighting game industry. 5. Hong Kong as Asia’s next fashion hub? Fashion Fest could help make it happen Can Hong Kong realise its ambition as a premier fashion hub in Asia? The answer may have lain in this year’s Hong Kong Fashion Fest. 6. Famous Chinese women in folklore, from Mulan to a dynasty-toppling consort Women are vastly under-represented in ancient Chinese literature. The few who appear, often in myth or semi-fiction, serve primarily to reflect that era’s moral expectations for women. 7. Why sleeping less than apes helped humans become Earth’s dominant species For most people, bedtime is a routine matter of turning off the lights and hoping for eight hours of rest. For David R Samson, an associate professor of evolutionary anthropology, it often means venturing deep into the wild or far back in evolutionary time.

title: Teodoro for president? Philippine defence chief draws 2028 election buzz after China clash
description: His viral moment in Seoul has raised his profile among supporters, but analysts say weak polling and past losses remain hurdles.
content: Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has won a burst of online support among Filipinos who see him as one of Manila’s most outspoken senior officials against China, with some already asking whether it could give him enough political momentum to carry him into the 2028 elections. His latest boost came after a viral moment at the Seoul Defence Dialogue on September 8, where he read out a handwritten note reiterating Beijing’s rejection of the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling while on stage. Forum organisers said the note came from a military attaché at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who had passed it to a staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap. Teodoro read parts of the note aloud, including Beijing’s position that the 2016 award was “illegal, null and void”, before saying the move was disrespectful to the forum’s South Korean hosts and showed disregard for international law. “So, perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do … This is actual coercion, bullying and aggression,” he said. Beijing hit back, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning accusing Philippine officials of “grandstanding and lying” and urging “certain people in the Philippines” to stop undermining China-Philippines relations and stability in the South China Sea. China does not accept the 2016 ruling by an arbitral tribunal in The Hague, which found Beijing’s claims to historic rights within the nine-dash line had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos). Beijing argues the tribunal had no jurisdiction because the case involved territorial sovereignty and maritime delimitation and says the Philippines abused the Unclos dispute settlement mechanism by bringing the case unilaterally. The Seoul episode followed Beijing’s June sanctions on Teodoro, his wife and child over what China said were erroneous remarks that undermined its interests and damaged bilateral relations. The move barred them from mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau and restricted Chinese organisations and individuals from dealing with them, but Teodoro remained defiant, saying the sanctions would not stop him from doing his job. Even before his latest viral moment, some social media users in the Philippines had begun urging Teodoro to run for president, vice-president or the Senate in 2028. On Facebook, a page entitled “Filipinos for Gibo Teodoro 2028” had sprung up by June and had 35,000 followers as of the time of writing. One user commented “if Sec Gibo decides to run for President, we should all support him”, while another said: “He’s my President in 2028.” His Seoul response also drew support from public figures, including Senator Erwin Tulfo, who said Teodoro had done “the right thing”, and Senator Panfilo Lacson, who said the episode showed what Teodoro’s “brilliant mind” could bring to the world stage. But political observers said Teodoro’s path to higher office would depend on whether he could translate a burst of online attention into sustained support – a challenge made clearer by his previous unsuccessful runs for national office. Teodoro was criticised over disaster rescue operations after Typhoon Ketsana in 2009, when he was defence secretary, before running the following year as president Gloria Macapagal Arroyo’s official candidate and finishing in fourth place. After that defeat, he largely shunned politics until 2022, when he offered to be the vice-presidential running mate of Davao City mayor Sara Duterte-Carpio. When Duterte-Carpio decided to seek the vice-presidency herself, Teodoro instead ran for one of 12 Senate seats up for election that year under the poorly funded People’s Reform Party, but finished 15th and missed out. Dr Ranjit Rye, founding president of poll firm Octa Research, told This Week in Asia that Teodoro was “not yet” ripe for the vice-presidential race but said a Senate run could be more realistic. In Octa’s July poll of the public’s senatorial preferences, Teodoro placed No 29, with 11.2 per cent of respondents saying they would vote for him, while WR Numero Research’s June survey put him at No 35, with 6 per cent support. Barry Gutierrez, who was spokesman to former vice-president Leni Robredo and is himself an ex-congressman, said survey numbers were “the most immediate measure” of viability, though not the only one. “Unfortunately, Secretary Teodoro’s numbers are fairly low across the board at this point,” Gutierrez told This Week in Asia, adding that Teodoro “is not even considered in publicly released presidential surveys”. “To me this indicates that, as of now, he is not top of mind when it comes to choices for the top posts in 2028,” he said. Ronnie Holmes, Pulse Asia president and a professor of political science and development studies at De La Salle University, said the pollster “will include his name for a long list on presidential preference in our third-quarter survey”. “I can’t comment on viability until we see the survey results,” Holmes said. Gutierrez said Teodoro’s numbers could improve if his recent prominence became “the start of a more sustained visibility as a national leader”, but added that this would require “a sustained and consistent effort over time, and not simply one viral moment two years before the elections”. “Gilberto Teodoro is qualified to run for higher office in 2028. He has the credentials and experience,” said Manuel Mogato, a defence and security analyst. “But experience, expertise, and his high qualifications are not enough. Winnability is also important,” Mogato said, adding that current opinion polls suggested Teodoro still had significant ground to make up before 2028. University of the Philippines political-science professor Dr Jean Franco said Teodoro was “definitely viable given his background, experience, and competence”, but that his association with Macapagal Arroyo, elite family background and lack of mass appeal could count against him. “I believe, however, that if he is paired with a strong presidential candidate and if he has good campaign strategists, he can be a strong contender. He can carry the China issue, which I believe is something that resonates across classes,” she said. Asked by radio station DZBB on September 11 whether he was eyeing an elective post, Teodoro said he was keeping his options open because “you know it’s hard to plan now. It’s hard to plan because I am focused on my work here”.

title: How Hong Kong’s new 5-year plan courts global capital with an eye on market dominance
description: Expanded investment products and stronger mainland-market links aim to deepen Hong Kong’s wealth-management edge and lure more international investors.
content: Hong Kong is broadening its equity markets, deepening its offshore yuan business and expanding further into gold trading under its first five-year plan for economic and social development, as the city seeks to defend its standing as Asia’s top financial centre and close the gap with London. Unveiled on Wednesday by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu alongside his 2026 policy address, the blueprint outlines a package of financial plans to “consolidate and enhance Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre”. The plan arrives with Hong Kong having retained its position as the world’s third-ranked financial centre and Asia’s top hub in the latest Global Financial Centres Index. With a score of 756, the city sat five points behind top-ranked New York, one point behind second-placed London and one point ahead of regional rival Singapore, highlighting the razor-thin margins in the battle for market dominance. At the core of Hong Kong’s strategy is a revitalised equities market. The local exchange is set to study looser listing rules – including adjusted market-capitalisation thresholds – for technology companies of “strategic importance” while broadening secondary listing channels by adding the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange to its recognised-bourse list. SCMP · How Hong Kong’s new 5-year plan courts global capital with an eye on market dominance To deepen capital links with mainland China, Hong Kong’s stock exchange will also strengthen ties with the Qianhai Equity Exchange in Shenzhen to connect more mainland firms with global capital – part of what Lee called Hong Kong’s role as a “two-way” platform for listings flowing in and out of the mainland. Hong Kong’s exchange ranked second worldwide for combined initial public offering and secondary-listing proceeds in the first half of 2026 – a total that jumped 84.3 per cent, year on year, to US$26.4 billion. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing CEO Bonnie Chan said in a statement on Wednesday that these priorities would “attract global long-term capital” and create a “vibrant marketplace that reinforces Hong Kong’s position as the pre-eminent global financial centre”. Currency mechanisms form another major pillar of Hong Kong’s financial-development strategy, with plans to introduce a tendering facility for seven-day offshore yuan liquidity and to build out a local yuan yield curve through short-term debt instruments. While Hong Kong remains the world’s largest offshore yuan centre – with average daily turnover surging 64.8 per cent from 2022 to US$315.1 billion in 2025, according to the Bank for International Settlements – competitors are moving fast. London’s cumulative yuan-clearing volume reached 48.15 trillion yuan (US$7.18 trillion) last year, with daily average clearing volume jumping 55.33 per cent to 191.09 billion yuan, buoyed by its position as the world’s primary foreign-exchange hub. Yuan internationalisation is also central to Hong Kong’s newest push: gold trading. Lee said the city was considering tapping its Exchange Fund to buy more of the metal and would let the Hong Kong Monetary Authority trade directly in local spot and futures markets. The fund is the city’s main financial war chest and is used to defend the local currency. While much of global gold trading still clears through London – whose bullion market has long set the global benchmark price – Hong Kong is building a regional alternative. The city rolled out trial operations earlier this year for a new clearing and settlement infrastructure tailored to settle gold trades in yuan. The blueprint also targets asset and wealth management – a move that analysts said was designed to maintain Hong Kong’s edge over Singapore, as both hubs roll out competing tax exemptions to attract family offices and fund managers. Stephen Yan, chairman of Singapore-headquartered wealth manager WRISE Prestige, said the five-year blueprint would help attract top professional talent, noting that “a growing number of clients who previously opened accounts in Singapore are shifting business back to Hong Kong”. He added that Hong Kong’s broader array of investment products and deep integration with mainland Chinese markets – alongside planned enhancements to the Bond Connect scheme and local exchange-traded funds – gave the city a distinct competitive edge that would “significantly bolster its wealth-management sector”.

title: Hong Kong police officer left paralysed in 2005 knife attack dies
description: Jacky Chu was honoured with bravery medal for continuing to pursue knife-wielding attacker despite bleeding heavily from neck injury.
content: A former Hong Kong police constable who was left paralysed and bedridden for 21 years following a knife attack during a stop-and-search has died, the force has confirmed. Jacky Chu Chun-kwok, who was in his fifties, died on Wednesday, a source said. The force confirmed Chu’s death on Thursday, saying it would extend condolences to his family and provide necessary support. Frankie Leung Chun-kit, chairman of the Junior Police Officers’ Association, said on Thursday that the force’s management supported burying Chu in Gallant Garden, a dedicated site at Wo Hop Shek Public Cemetery for public servants who died in the line of duty. Leung also said he had suggested holding a funeral with either full police honours or police honours to pay tribute to Chu. On the morning of July 19, 2005, Chu was critically injured during a solo patrol when a man stabbed him in the neck with a six-inch knife. The attacker, Liu Chi-yung, was carrying the knife with the intention of robbing pedestrians when Chu, a member of the Police Tactical Unit, stopped him for an identity check outside the Po On Road Municipal Services Building in Cheung Sha Wan. When the 30-year-old constable grew suspicious and confronted him, Liu pulled out the knife, stabbed Chu in the neck and fled. Despite his severe injuries, Chu took off in pursuit but eventually collapsed from excessive blood loss. His fellow police officers arrived at the scene and stabilised him, but his injuries resulted in brain oxygen deprivation and left him completely paralysed and in a vegetative state. Later that afternoon, Liu surrendered to another police officer at Prince Edward MTR station. Liu, 23 at the time of the offence, admitted at the High Court in April 2006 to possessing an offensive weapon and assaulting an officer. He told the court he planned to commit robbery with a knife before Chu intercepted him. He was initially given six years in prison, with the sentence later increased to 10 years on appeal. Liu was released on parole in 2011 after serving more than five years. Chu was awarded the Medal for Bravery (Gold) in 2006. In its commendation, the government noted the police officer had showed extraordinary courage despite his injuries in the attack, making every effort to arrest the armed assailant until he collapsed.

title: 22 months’ jail for Hong Kong driver who fatally struck student at traffic junction
description: Court slams Ernest Au Yeung’s reckless behaviour after NGO worker accelerated car to almost 100km/h to beat amber light on his way to work in 2024.
content: A Hong Kong man has been sentenced to 22 months behind bars for driving dangerously and causing a 19-year-old student’s death at a pedestrian crossing two years ago. The District Court on Thursday also disqualified Ernest Au Yeung Shiu-hong from driving for five years and criticised his “extremely dangerous and irresponsible” attitude that led to Lisa Pun’s death on November 7, 2024. Au Yeung, an NGO event organiser, drove his Tesla Model Y past a box junction on On Lok Road in Yuen Long at almost 100km/h (62mph) at around 8am, as he tried to beat an amber light on his way to work in Tsim Sha Tsui. Pun, who crossed the road while the pedestrian light was red, was sent flying through the air upon collision and suffered serious injuries all over her body. She was certified dead in hospital six hours later. The defendant told police he had not expected anyone to be on the road when he drove past the junction. He admitted in court that he did not pay proper attention to the surroundings and accelerated his car unnecessarily to almost double the 50km/h speed limit as he approached the intersection. The court was told that Au Yeung had seven previous traffic violations since obtaining his driving licence in January 2015, including a conviction for careless driving in November 2024, for which he was fined HK$1,200 (US$153). Defence counsel Danny Chan Kin-keung said his client was deeply remorseful and had suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and major depressive disorder since the accident. Chan added that Au Yeung had made significant donations to charitable causes after the tragedy, giving HK$50,000 each to a primary school and a fund set up to help those affected by the devastating fire in Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court last year. In sentencing, Deputy Judge Bernard Chung Wai-keung said the defendant committed the crime recklessly because he was unwilling to wait for a short time before the red light. “[The defendant] told the probation officer that he rushed through the traffic light because he feared he might be late for work in Tsim Sha Tsui. His driving attitude was extremely dangerous and irresponsible,” Chung said. “No matter how the court sentences the defendant, it cannot save the life of this 19-year-old young woman or redress the permanent suffering and grief endured by her family following the loss of their loved one.” Chung set a starting sentence of three years but knocked off 14 months in recognition of Au Yeung’s guilty plea and mental condition after the offence. The deputy judge declined to grant an additional reduction for the defendant’s donations, noting that he had only made those contributions out of guilt. Dangerous driving causing death is punishable by up to 10 years’ imprisonment but is capped at seven years at the District Court level. The Court of Appeal’s sentencing guidelines stipulate that an offender should be sentenced to no more than three years behind bars if the case only involves a momentary dangerous error of judgment or the driver’s irresponsible or habitually unacceptable conduct.

title: Russia employs North Koreans to build drones for Ukraine war: report
description: The move shows how military ties have expanded beyond weapons and troops into labour and industrial production, the report says.
content: Russia is increasingly mobilising North Korean workers to build military drones for use against Ukraine in defiance of international sanctions, giving Pyongyang a key source of revenue to fund its unlawful weapons programmes, according to a report by the US and its allies. Up to 25,000 North Koreans were believed to be working in Russia’s drone industry, including at facilities in Alabuga, Tatarstan, where unmanned aerial vehicles were assembled, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team said in a report released on Wednesday. The report said North Koreans abroad – largely IT workers – were estimated to have earned up to US$800 million for the Kim Jong-un regime last year, providing funds for its unlawful nuclear and ballistic missile programmes in violation of UN Security Council resolutions. The development underscores how the deepening military ties between Russia and North Korea are expanding beyond weapons and troops into labour and industrial production. Russia gets a new pool of workers for industries supporting its war in Ukraine, while Kim’s regime gains access to foreign currency that helps finance its nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, further eroding a sanctions framework Moscow itself once helped enforce. North Korean workers in Russia were disguised as students under a visa scheme to evade sanctions, the report said. A North Korean worker there earns an average of US$7,500 in wages a year, most of which is confiscated by the Kim regime. In some cases, the forfeited amount exceeded their actual earnings, the report said. Monthly wages earned by North Koreans working in Russia may be up to five times higher than what they can earn in China, making Russia an increasingly lucrative destination for Pyongyang. At the end of 2025, an estimated 20,000 to 70,000 North Korean labourers were working in China, while another 15,000 to 30,000 were in Russia, the report said. “DPRK authorities exercise extreme control over labourers’ movement and interactions with outsiders in order to prevent defections, while labourers who do defect risk reprisals against family members remaining in North Korea,” it said, using the initials for North Korea’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. The US and its allies, including South Korea and Japan, are part of an 11-nation team that monitors the enforcement of sanctions on North Korea. The group was launched after a Russian veto in 2024 ended the mandate of a United Nations panel that had reported on North Korea’s sanctions evasion and development of its nuclear arsenal for 15 years. Additional reporting by Kyodo

title: Huawei quickens AI chip pace, promises next entrant 3 quarters early
description: Company says ‘performance-doubling’ Ascend 960DT training chip to debut in first quarter, followed by 960PR inference chip in third quarter.
content: Huawei Technologies said on Thursday that it would launch its next-generation artificial intelligence chip in the first quarter of 2027, moving the target launch forward by nine months as the firm aggressively expands its ecosystem amid China’s self-sufficiency push. David Wang Tao, rotating and acting chairman for Huawei, said on Thursday that the Ascend 960DT chip, an AI chip designed for model training, “with performance doubling”, would be “ready in the first quarter of 2027”, three quarters ahead of schedule. The Ascend 960PR, designed for AI model inference, would launch in the third quarter of 2027, a quarter earlier than expected. Speaking at the Huawei Connect 2026 conference in Shanghai, Wang said that the Ascend series would “continue to follow an annual upgrade cycle”, with the Ascend 970 and 980 launching in 2028 and 2029, respectively. The announcements came ahead of expected high-level trade talks between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump next week, where AI and semiconductor exports are set to top the technology agenda. The Ascend 950, Huawei’s most powerful current processor, has been used for AI workloads as an alternative to the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) from Nvidia, which remain unavailable in the domestic market due to US export controls. The US-sanctioned firm has been playing a central role in advancing China’s AI ambitions without relying on American technologies. In May, days after Trump concluded his trip to China, the Shenzhen-based company unveiled its Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture – semiconductor breakthroughs that aim to deliver performance equivalent to chips built using a 1.4-nanometre manufacturing process by 2031 without depending on advanced lithography tools that are inaccessible in China. “Guided by innovation based on the Tau Law, we aim to continue doubling computing performance while also significantly increasing bandwidth, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth,” Wang said on Thursday. At the Thursday event, Huawei also announced the Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster, which is slated for late 2027. The company said the system, powered by Ascend 960 chips, would improve performance in training and inference for 10-trillion-parameter models by 2.3 and 2.5 times, respectively, compared with its predecessor the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, which is slated to be deployed by the fourth quarter of this year. AI training is the computationally demanding process where a model takes in massive data sets to learn basic patterns. Inference is the use of a finished model to answer user queries and generate output.

title: Hong Kong targets 240 air destinations by 2030, eyeing new Uzbekistan routes
description: Cathay also reveals passenger numbers, including those handled by HK Express, reached monthly record of more than 3.6 million in August.
content: Hong Kong aims to expand the number of global destinations connected to its airport from 220 to 240 by 2030, with authorities exploring the launch of routes to Uzbekistan. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the goal in the city’s first five-year plan, stating authorities would explore aviation partnerships with 10 or more countries each year between 2026 and 2030, with at least 40 per cent involving nations belonging to the Belt and Road Initiative. Beijing launched the initiative in 2013 to bolster trade links, with it now covering more than 150 countries. According to the blueprint, priority will be given to regions with “further development potential and new growth areas”, such as South America, Central Asia, Africa and the Middle East. Hong Kong will also integrate into the country’s “one circle, six corridors and five channels” framework – the international network model in China’s civil aviation development plan. A government source cited city flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways’ launch of a direct service to Kazakhstan next January as an example, adding that the government had also established traffic rights with Uzbekistan and was in talks with airlines about launching a new route to the country. The insider also noted that the administration was targeting new traffic rights in traditional markets such as Europe, North America, and Australia, given the high demand in those regions, while also pursuing emerging markets. According to Lee’s policy address, delivered along with the five-year plan on Wednesday, Hong Kong has updated air service agreements or entered into new ones with 20 aviation partners. Between June 2024 and August this year, 40 airlines launched 94 new routes linking Hong Kong with destinations in Asia, Europe, Africa and North America, while frequencies on 15 existing routes were increased. Hong Kong International Airport has also been expanded, with its three-runway system having started operations nearly two years ago. Meanwhile, the airport reported on Thursday that passenger numbers rose by 10.1 per cent year on year to 44.3 million between January and August, while flight movements increased by 3.5 per cent to 269,900. Passenger traffic in August reached 5.86 million, up 3.5 per cent from a year earlier, while flight movements rose by 0.5 per cent to 34,995, according to the airport. “Growth was mainly led by traffic with the Chinese mainland and South Korea, while the decline in the Middle East moderated further,” it said. On the cargo side, an 18.2 per cent rise in transshipment and 3.6 per cent growth in imports in August partly offset an 8.8 per cent fall in exports. Total cargo volume nevertheless declined by 1.2 per cent, year on year. Total cargo throughput for the eight months rose by 2.6 per cent from the same period last year to 3.34 million tonnes. Andrew Yuen Chi-lok, executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Aviation Policy and Research Centre, said the cargo traffic in July and August reflected an adjustment following the European Union’s removal of the de minimis exemption and the introduction of a temporary per-item duty on low-value consignments from July 1, rather than a dip in Hong Kong’s hub status. “The data is consistent with a policy-induced contraction on one origin-destination lane being offset by increased connecting traffic through Hong Kong,” Yuen said. “That pattern is characteristic of a mature cargo hub absorbing an external regulatory shock.” Cathay Pacific also revealed on Thursday that its overall passenger numbers, which combine figures for the carrier’s premium services and those of budget arm HK Express, set a new monthly record of more than 3.6 million passengers in August – an increase of 4 per cent year on year. Cathay Cargo carried 8.6 per cent more cargo in August than a year earlier, while total tonnage for the first eight months increased by 8.2 per cent compared with the same period in 2025.

title: Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ to cost initial HK$200m, but ‘won’t catch thieves’
description: John Lee and Eric Chan stress new system will consolidate data to improve city management and won’t be used for crime detection or surveillance.
content: Hong Kong’s proposed “AI city brain” will cost HK$200 million (US$25.5 million) for the first phase and will connect to the police’s citywide security camera network, authorities have revealed, while stressing that the new system would not be used for crime detection or the surveillance of residents. Speaking at a Legislative Council question and answer session on Thursday following his annual policy address a day earlier, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also emphasised the system would not tap into personal data or pose privacy concerns. In his address, Lee proposed establishing an “AI city brain”, deploying the technology for data analysis within a data-sharing environment that would provide early warnings and trend forecasts, improve interdepartmental collaboration in response to extreme weather or major incidents, and manage public order and control crowds. SCMP · Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ to cost initial HK$200m, but ‘won’t catch thieves’ No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki stressed the initiative driven by artificial intelligence was designed for better city management. “The function of the ‘AI city brain’ is not for personal surveillance or monitoring criminals. It is not for catching thieves. It is not our target,” he said at a press conference. Chan explained that data scattered across different departments, for example the ones for transport, drainage and water services, would be incorporated into the system by the first quarter of 2028, and the government’s 1823 complaint platform would be connected by the third quarter of the same year. He said the police’s CCTV network, SmartView, would also be connected to the new data system because it was useful in monitoring traffic. He did not rule out integrating data from private companies in the future. HK$200 million would be needed initially to connect different systems, Chan said, adding that he did not have an estimate of the total project cost. The AI-driven “brain” would carry out risk assessment and suggest preventive measures, for example, carrying out repairs for potential pipe bursts, he explained. “In case of an incident, emergency responses, decision-making and resource allocation across departments can become much more efficient and precise,” he said. He said that given the experience of mainland Chinese cities, for example Shanghai and Hangzhou, it would take six to nine years for the system to come into full force. In response to lawmakers’ questions, Lee explained that the new platform would only consolidate data held by different departments and would not involve personal information. “For example, for traffic data, [we gather] figures on daily MTR passenger flows … they do not involve personal privacy. We handle the information in full compliance with privacy requirements,” he said. The city leader added that he hoped the initiative would encourage departments to adopt a more proactive mindset in sharing data. An AI interdepartmental task force chaired by Chief Secretary Chan will oversee the plan. The first phase of the platform, expected to launch by the second quarter of next year, will integrate the Security Bureau’s Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre to improve the city’s response to extreme weather before the next typhoon season. The platform will pull data from departments including the Observatory, the Drainage Services Department and the Fire Services Department, as well as information from the government’s emergency and public inquiry hotlines, enabling a faster, more proactive response, according to the government. “For example, the golden week [National Day] holiday is coming soon. If we already have [the ‘AI city brain’], we can monitor how many people are at each tourist hotspot,” Lee said. “We can immediately issue messages saying that in half an hour the queuing time may increase from one hour to two hours, and we may be able to divert them elsewhere.” Golden week refers to mainland China’s week-long National Day and Lunar New Year holidays, as well as the five-day Labour Day break. After Lee delivered the final policy address of his current five-year term and the city’s first five-year plan on Wednesday, legislators lauded his performance over the past four years and the vision he set out in the two blueprints. Reflecting on his role, Lee compared a leader to the captain of a ship, saying the most important task was to build a strong team and enable it to perform its best. “The captain does not necessarily need to know how to send telegrams, cook meals, or be as skilled as the navigation officer with the maritime charts,” he told lawmakers on Thursday. “What matters most is that the captain builds the team, knows how to manage it, has a clear plan and direction, and ensures that once everyone agrees with it, they work together towards it. “I have 15 bureaus. I do not want any of my ministers to be less capable than me. Each of them must be the strongest in their own field.”

title: After far-right AfD win, Germany’s embattled chancellor faces more election tests
description: Chancellor Friedrich Merz braces for a potential double election blow this weekend as pressure mounts on his leadership.
content: Two German state elections Sunday could deal a double blow to embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz, two weeks after his party suffered a stunning defeat at the hands of the far-right AfD. Tight races for power – each with their own unique electoral dynamics – are expected in the city state of Berlin and the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The Alternative for Germany is expected to make strong gains in both, a fortnight after it trounced Merz’s centre-right CDU by a margin of almost 44 to 17 per cent in the ex-communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD triumph badly rattled Merz and fuelled speculation that the 70-year-old leader, who took power in May last year, may not sit out the end of his four-year term as leader of Europe’s top economy. Amid speculation about a potential change at the top, eight CDU state premiers closed ranks Wednesday and declared jointly that Germany needs “stability now more than ever” rather than “discussions about personnel”. Merz has vowed to reboot Germany’s flagging economy, rearm the country to deter a hostile Russia and contain irregular immigration to soothe voters’ fears and lure them away from the AfD. Instead, the AfD now leads nationwide polls, Merz’s personal approval ratings hover around 10 per cent, and his coalition with the centre-left SPD is increasingly torn by infighting. “In Merz’s case, we are now observing the possibility of a tipping point – an implosion rather than a slow erosion of authority,” said Oliver Lembcke, a political scientist at Ruhr University Bochum. “When election defeats, poor personal ratings and internal party doubts reinforce one another, political authority can collapse very quickly.” In one election Sunday, in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Merz’s party is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD of popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD. While the AfD was polling at 37 per cent against the SPD’s 35 in the latest INSA survey, Merz’s CDU, at just 7 per cent, may drop dangerously close to the 5 per cent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament. A CDU crash below that line would be a historic first and heap enormous pressure on Merz. If the CDU “were indeed to fail to clear the 5 per cent threshold, I consider it quite likely that Mr Merz would be pressured by his party to step down,” said Ursula Muench of the Academy for Political Education in Tutzing. “Barring such a drastic turning point, I do not foresee this happening for the time being.” In Berlin, the ruling CDU is running a neck-and-neck race against the far-left Die Linke, which is popular with many young people and promises drastic steps to solve a dire housing crisis. A CDU defeat in the capital would be another black eye for Merz. The AfD is meanwhile expected also to do well in Berlin, although it is set to remain shut out of power in both states because all other main parties have agreed on a “firewall” of non-cooperation with it. Whoever wins either poll, the AfD is sure to again channel voter discontent with the mainstream parties. “I do hope they vote for the AfD here, I can tell you, because the CDU have been in power for years and they haven’t got their act together,” said Berlin retiree Manuela Schmidt, 63. She pointed to poverty-stricken pensioners collecting bottles off the streets to collect the deposits. “They’ve worked for 45 years, get a pension of 500-something (euros per month), and go out at night to collect bottles, only to be driven away by foreigners in the end … and that simply can’t go on,” Schmidt said. Merz – bracing for a tough Sunday evening – has scheduled a CDU executive committee meeting then to quickly discuss the election results and the way forward. He also cleared his calendar for the coming week by scrapping plans to travel to the UN General Assembly, sending his foreign minister to New York instead. “Dissatisfaction is evidently running high” in the CDU camp, said Muench, adding, however, that cooler heads might eventually prevail to avoid boosting the AfD under co-leader Alice Weidel. “It must surely be clear to level-headed CDU politicians that replacing the CDU chairman and chancellor would not serve their own interests,” she said. “It would just fuel the AfD’s pipe dreams of a ‘Chancellor Alice Weidel’.”

title: Exchange Fund weighs bigger gold holdings to support Hong Kong’s trading hub plan
description: A larger allocation to precious metals could improve diversification and align with the city’s gold hub strategy, says HKMA’s Eddie Yue.
content: Hong Kong’s Exchange Fund, the war chest used to defend the local currency, is considering increasing its exposure to gold and other precious metals as part of the government’s push to develop the city into a gold trading hub. Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said on Thursday that the Exchange Fund would continue to invest mainly in US dollar assets to support the Hong Kong dollar’s peg with the US currency. Yue said the Exchange Fund could increase its allocation to gold, which currently accounted for only a small portion of its portfolio, but he did not disclose the scale or timing of any potential purchases. The Exchange Fund, which had total assets of HK$4.463 trillion (US$569 billion) at the end of June, backs the issuance of banknotes and helps defend the Hong Kong dollar against speculative attacks. The HKMA, the city’s de facto central bank, manages the Exchange Fund’s investments across Hong Kong and overseas equities, global bonds, overseas property, long-term projects and a small allocation to commodities. “By increasing its buying of gold and other precious metals, the Exchange Fund would diversify risk within its investment portfolio,” Yue said at a media briefing on Thursday after announcing Hong Kong’s first base rate rise in three years. He added that investing more in gold would align with the Hong Kong government’s five-year plan to develop the city into a major commodities trading centre and gold trading hub. The plan for the Exchange Fund to increase its gold holding was unveiled by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu in his annual policy address on Wednesday, alongside the city’s first five-year development plan. Lee said the HKMA would consider investing more in local gold spot and futures gold markets, while also studying the transfer of the Exchange Fund’s physical gold holdings to designated vaults overseen by the Hong Kong Precious Metals Central Clearing Company as part of efforts to build a gold-trading ecosystem. The Exchange Fund reported investment earnings of HK$134.7 billion in the first six months of this year.

title: Exclusive | BYD, Xiaomi and Innolight executives likely to join Xi Jinping on US visit: sources
description: Sizeable business delegation – mirroring US President Donald Trump’s entourage in Beijing – suggests potential for investment deals at the summit.
content: Figures from some of China’s most prominent firms – including electric vehicle maker BYD and smart manufacturing giant Xiaomi – are likely to accompany President Xi Jinping on his trip to the US next week, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. The entourage would draw a parallel to the coterie of CEOs that US President Donald Trump brought to Beijing in May, and could signal greater potential for investment deals as part of the high-profile summit. According to one of the sources, who asked not to be named due to the sensitivity of the issue, representatives of Zhongji Innolight – a leading producer of optical transceivers used in artificial intelligence data centres – could also join, despite recent reports the firm would be on the receiving end of US export restrictions. Bank of China, the country’s most internationalised lender with an established presence in the US, might also be invited, the person added. Another source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) could be another company on the guest list. “It will be significant if CATL [also] joins the trip,” the person said, referring to BlueOval Battery Park Michigan – a collaboration between American auto giant Ford and the Chinese battery maker – announced in 2023 and scheduled to start operations this year. The 1.8-million-square-foot battery manufacturing plant, one of the most prominent China-US joint ventures on American soil, drew strong opposition from local residents and lawmakers amid broader tensions between the two countries. The actual number of companies in the delegation is unknown, as the list is being regularly modified. None of the firms mentioned by the sources immediately responded to requests for comment by the South China Morning Post. In May, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Tesla’s Elon Musk, Apple’s Tim Cook, BlackRock’s Larry Fink and Boeing’s Kelly Ortberg were among the business leaders joining Trump on his state visit to China. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed that he will meet Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng this weekend for final preparatory talks, less than a week before Xi is scheduled to travel to the US. “The industry breadth of a delegation could signal that Beijing … puts commercial engagement alongside strategic diplomacy and gives businesses a stake in stabilising ties,” said Han Shen Lin, China managing director for The Asia Group. Lin added the summit could lay the groundwork for future talks at multilateral forums such as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting and the Group of 20. “Both sides want to buy time, but it’s a good sign if this summit confirms further engagement.” James Downes, director of the Europe-Asia programme at the US-based Centre for Explanatory Research and Scientific Prediction, said that Xi’s business delegation would be less about securing a breakthrough deal than about containing the economic fallout from the countries’ broader strategic rivalry. “A major trade deal, broad technology detente or sizeable Chinese investment commitments are extremely unlikely,” he added. Among the agreements reached at the May summit was the establishment of bilateral trade and investment councils, but action on the latter body has stalled amid wariness from US legislators and other figures within the Trump administration over welcoming Chinese investment. According to a White House fact sheet released after the summit, the US-China Board of Investment would provide a “government-to-government forum for discussing investment-related issues” while the corresponding Board of Trade would focus on bilateral trade in non-sensitive sectors. “The most realistic outcome is a structured channel for commercial engagement,” Downes said. “Clearer procedures for trade and investment screening, and cooperation in less sensitive policy areas such as agriculture, consumer goods, selected green supply chains and industrial inputs.” In July, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposed rules to tighten authorisation requirements for devices containing certain hardware components made by entities on the Covered List – a US blacklist of foreign technology equipment and service providers deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to national security. Earlier this month, the US regulator issued its final decision on the rules, excluding optical transceivers and easing market anxieties over a potential ban. Zhongji Innolight’s share prices went up by 4 per cent the day of the FCC’s announcement. Additional reporting by Ann Cao

title: Pop-up ad accused of delaying life-saving call during Chinese woman’s heart attack sparks debate
description: Pop-up ads frustrate everyone; their exit buttons are hard for sighted users to find and nearly impossible for the visually impaired to locate.
content: Intense public discussions surrounding the downsides of technology have been sparked by a Chinese man accusing a phone company’s lock screen feature of obstructing his father from calling an ambulance, which he claims contributed to his mother’s death. On September 10, a 19-year-old man named Zhang shared on social media that his mother suffered a heart attack around 4am on August 30. His father attempted to dial the 120 emergency medical number, but accidentally swiped to the phone’s magazine page instead of unlocking the device, rendering him unable to exit that page. Zhang said that his father, who suffers from long-term effects of a stroke, had to go door-to-door seeking help from neighbours. Consequently, this delay hindered his mother’s rescue efforts, and she ultimately died. According to her death certificate, Zhang’s mother was pronounced dead at home at 5.51am. The smartphone in question was manufactured by Honor, a Chinese consumer electronics company, and features their proprietary “Magic Pictorial.” A test video posted by another user demonstrated that swiping left or right on the screen activates this function. If someone attempts to unlock the phone by swiping up – a gesture common across many brands – they would instead find themselves scrolling through the magazine’s page rather than exiting it. The user, under the handle @yuanlaiwoshixiaocaitui, also highlighted that the magazine pages sometimes included app advertisements that allowed users to download apps without unlocking the phone. Initially, Zhang sought compensation from the brand’s customer service for his loss, an apology, or the removal of the feature. However, all his requests were denied. Later, Zhang deleted his post and issued an apology, stating that the phone did not prevent his father from calling for help. According to Southern Metropolis Daily, a third-party analysis of Zhang’s father’s phone confirmed that he successfully made 10 calls between 4.40am and 5.40am. The system log indicated that the father accessed the “Magic Pictorial” page after making those calls, but exited the page after eight seconds. Honor expressed empathy for Zhang’s distress following his mother’s passing and decided not to hold him legally responsible for any damage to the brand’s reputation. Subsequently, Zhang deleted his apology post and turned off direct messages. Despite this turn of events, public outcry regarding intrusive advertising features persisted. Not only did Honor’s “Magic Pictorial” face backlash, but other familiar irritants, such as pop-up ads and shake-to-trigger advertisements, also drew criticism. Various news reports document cases of elderly users trapped by splash screen ads when they attempt to make a call or take a photo. In another incident, a woman in Shenzhen trying to report a fire was redirected to a pop-up ad after clicking a link sent by the dispatcher, with the ad slowing the uploading process of an on-site video for firefighters to analyse the situation. Such ads also create challenges for individuals with visual impairments, who may struggle to locate the exit button on their screens. Even for sighted individuals, many ads feature indiscernible exit buttons, complicating the process of closing them. Calls for stricter regulations to combat these types of ads, likened to “viruses,” have gained traction. A study led by Sun Yi at Hangzhou City University found that over 95 per cent of respondents wanted a switch to permanently disable pop-up ads. Current Chinese regulations only require that pop-up and splash screen ads “clearly display an exit button to ensure one-click closure.” Additionally, China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has issued warnings against the use of shake-to-trigger ads. Some commenters have likened these ads to viruses and ransomware. “Certain apps’ Chinese versions feature these repugnant ads, while their international counterparts do not. We must question why Chinese users are the only ones affected by such nuisances,” commented another observer.

title: IT worker, 51, allegedly killed wife with knife after financial disputes: police
description: Hong Kong police say 53-year-old woman found in bedroom with knife wounds after suspect turned himself in on Wednesday and confessed to killing her.
content: A man believed to be more than HK$1 million (US$ 127,470) in debt is suspected of murdering his wife in their flat after previous financial disputes, according to preliminary investigations by Hong Kong police. Superintendent Kwan Chun-ting, assistant district commander of Eastern district crime squad, said on Thursday that a 51-year-old man had turned himself in at Kowloon City Police Station at 7.30pm the previous day and confessed to killing his wife. “We believe the incident happened between the early hours and daytime [on Wednesday] when they were inside the same room,” he said. Police arrested the suspect on Wednesday evening after officers found his 53-year-old wife dead on the bed in the master bedroom of their flat at Heng Fa Chuen private housing estate, with knife wounds on her neck, torso and hands. “The deceased and the arrestee had a dispute inside their home, with the arrestee attacking her with a kitchen knife,” Kwan said. The couple’s two sons, aged 22 and 15, also lived in the same flat, but the superintendent did not mention their presence when recounting the incident. While Kwan said police would still have to investigate the suspect’s motive, preliminary findings showed he had a record of risky investments and debts of more than HK$1 million. “This caused disputes with the deceased. Their relationship, we believe, was quite poor,” Kwan said. The suspect was an IT professional with a stable income, while his wife was a homemaker, he added. The family had no previous record of disputes or domestic violence. The case remained under investigation and the man was still in custody as of Thursday morning.

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo mulls labelling wildfires as ‘ecological terrorism’
description: Indonesia is battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, with the hazardous haze also affecting neighbours Singapore and Malaysia.
content: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for stricter regulations and sanctions against those who use slash and burn methods to clear land, as the country struggles to contain wildfires that have been raging for weeks. Indonesia is battling its most intense wildfires in 11 years, with “super El Nino” weather parching ‌the country’s forests and fields. The islands of Borneo and Sumatra have been the worst hit, with the hazardous haze causing a spike in respiratory illnesses. Transboundary pollution has also caused unhealthy air conditions in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia. Prabowo, in a meeting with his cabinet, said there will be zero tolerance for people or corporations found responsible for starting wildfires. “I have asked the state secretary and the minister of law to look into this further, specifically regarding legal sanctions,” he said. “And perhaps we should ask the House of Representatives to stiffen the laws, classifying this as ‘ecological terrorism’. This is a very serious matter,” he added, according to a palace statement issued late on Wednesday. He also instructed regional governments to immediately abolish exemptions that allow smallholders to clear small plots of land using fire. Prabowo also called for the police to ‌launch criminal investigations against corporations found to be violating fire safeguards. Cases of wildfire-related respiratory illness in seven affected provinces more than doubled to 113,336 from September to September 9, with residents of West Kalimantan among the people suffering the worst from hazardous fire emissions. Indonesia has deployed more than 50 aircraft to conduct water bombing and cloud seeding operations to help battle the fires. Japan also joined Indonesia’s water bombing operations on Wednesday. Japan sent over three CH-47 Chinook helicopters last week but poor flight conditions delayed their participation. From January to July this year, fires raged across 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres) of land, government ‌data showed. Environmental group YKAN has estimated that fire damaged another 600,000 hectares in August. Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni warned that the wildfires could last until early November with the rainy season expected to arrive later than previously estimated.

title: On the Menu | Is New York’s Bar Leone a copycat of Hong Kong’s ‘World’s Best’ original?
description: Hong Kong’s Bar Leone says it has no connection with its namesake in Lower Manhattan, which officially opened on September 10.
content: I was at a dinner the other night when a guest excitedly asked: “Did you know Bar Leone just opened in New York City?” The original Bar Leone is a famed Hong Kong cocktail bar on Bridges Street in Sheung Wan. Opened in 2023 by Italian bartender Lorenzo Antinori, the popular watering hole has already been named Asia’s Best Bar twice (2024-5) by 50 Best and is its current World’s Best Bar. Last year, it opened its second location in Shanghai’s Huangpu district. In March, the team served cocktails at the invite-only Governors Ball – the official after-party for the Oscars. Given the similarity between the Hong Kong and New York bars’ names, and the fact that both employ a similar burgundy colour scheme and use motifs featuring a 2D lion holding a tray of cocktails, you would probably think that this was yet another chapter in the Hong Kong bar’s international expansion. The thing is, the two are not connected at all. In May, Antinori and his team were made aware of an Instagram account that had opened bearing the Bar Leone name. They quickly distanced themselves from it with announcements on their website and social accounts. They have since updated an official statement that reiterates they “are not affiliated, associated, or in any way connected with the New York venue now trading under the Bar Leone name”, and that they have “not authorised, licensed, endorsed or sponsored it in any way”. As the case is still an “active matter”, the Bar Leone Hong Kong team was unable to comment any further when approached by the South China Morning Post. The SCMP has also reached out to Bar Leone New York for comment. So who is behind the NYC opening? That would be Andres Diaz, described in the venue’s press release as “a New York City hospitality veteran with more than 15 years of experience in the restaurant industry”. He is also the founder of La Rubia and Her Name Was Carmen; Bar Leone took over the space previously occupied by the latter. In an interview with Women’s Wear Daily, Diaz said the idea for Bar Leone’s lion theme came from someone on his branding team who had gone to see The Lion King on Broadway, and that the colour scheme of the theatre production happened to match the bar’s interior design. It’s not the first time an internationally recognised hospitality name has had its name pilfered. In 2023, a Malaysian company attempted to launch The Chairman restaurant in a Kuala Lumpur shopping centre. The name and logo were nearly identical to those of The Chairman in Hong Kong, this year’s No 1 on the Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list and a former winner in 2021. In 2014, Jia Group’s popular Thai restaurant Chachawan was also duplicated without authorisation in Shanghai. That restaurant was forced to change its name following a social media uproar. More recently, a new restaurant by the name of Amber has opened in Quarry Bay, though it serves modern Chinese cuisine – and has no affiliation with the three-Michelin-star French restaurant of the same name by chef Richard Ekkebus in Central’s Mandarin Oriental The Landmark hotel. It is not just restaurants and bars. Eagle-eyed cafe hunters recently spotted the soft opening of a stylish cafe named Lowkey in Central’s Old Bailey Street, matching the minimalist aesthetic of a popular mini chain of coffee shops in Seoul. The South Korean cafe has since confirmed that the Hong Kong shop is not one of its own and that it does not have any international outlets yet. Whatever the motive, naming your business after something significantly more famous is a bit of an own goal. It strips you of the opportunity to craft your own narrative, creates a very specific set of expectations and, honestly, makes it look as though you have been living under a rock all this time.

title: Hong Kong’s John Lee vows to review IVF support for women over 40
description: City leader says he will examine current policies but acknowledges no single measure can reverse Hong Kong’s declining birth rate.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has vowed to examine whether the government can better support women aged over 40 seeking assisted reproductive treatment, while acknowledging that financial incentives alone will not reverse the city’s falling birth rate. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu made the pledge during a radio phone-in programme on Thursday, when residents described obstacles to having children, including job insecurity, a day after the leader unveiled a raft of measures aimed at boosting the birth rate. Among the callers was a woman surnamed Lee, who said a medical condition and a lengthy recovery had caused her to miss what is considered the optimal childbearing age. “I will go back and look into this, as it involves professional medical considerations,” the city leader said. “We will examine the age issue and how the government may be able to help.” The woman, who said she and her husband both worked in education, told Lee that they wanted children and could afford to raise them but had been unable to obtain public assistance because she was over 40. She said the couple had felt “disheartened and helpless” and had been forced to seek costly treatment in the private sector. Under current Hospital Authority policy, women must begin publicly funded in vitro fertilisation treatment before the age of 40. Private patients can undergo treatment cycles until they are 45. The chief executive said the government aimed to foster a broadly family-friendly environment by addressing financial pressures, housing constraints, workplace demands and childcare needs, rather than relying on individual incentives. He acknowledged that one-off measures could provide only a temporary stimulus and said no specific payment could guarantee an increase in births. “Who can guarantee that if we provide a certain amount [of money], it will result in a certain number of new babies? Nobody can answer that,” he said. “That is why, since it is difficult to calculate scientifically, we need to create a comprehensive and friendly environment.” Lee said the government had based its approach on its own surveys and research by think tanks, universities and overseas institutions, which had identified broadly similar factors influencing decisions about whether to have children. He said economic pressures were among the main considerations, citing the government’s newborn bonus, tax allowances and housing support. He added that authorities had sought to ease the burden on working parents by expanding childcare and after-school care services. But Lee said reversing the long-term decline in births would be difficult because of structural and highly personal factors that could not be addressed through a single measure. “Structural factors include many women having higher education levels, placing importance on their careers and, nowadays, also talking about freedom,” he said. “These are very personal matters that cannot be dealt with through a single measure.” Concerns about job security also featured heavily in the programme. A resident told Lee that repeated lay-offs at large companies and public bodies had left younger workers afraid to make long-term commitments. “Many young people do not dare to do it. Forget about having children – they do not even dare to get married,” he said. Lee said Hong Kong’s economy was performing better than last year and that the government had upgraded its full-year growth forecast to between 3.5 and 4.5 per cent. He added that the city’s first five-year plan was intended to give residents and international investors greater confidence in Hong Kong’s future, with economic diversification expected to create a broader range of jobs. Asked whether Hong Kong could extend statutory paternity leave to match places such as Singapore, Lee stopped short of making a commitment. He said any change would have to take account of the operating pressures faced by the city’s many small and medium-sized enterprises. The latest policy address increased the newborn bonus from HK$20,000 (US$2,549) to HK$30,000 for a family’s second or subsequent child, alongside higher tax allowances and housing-related support. The government also announced expanded childcare and after-school services, as well as increased capacity for assisted reproductive treatment at public hospitals. Another planned measure to help boost the birth rate was raising the mortgage loan-to-value ratio to 95 per cent for families with newborns who are applying to the Home Ownership Scheme with “white form” status, which refers to non-public housing residents. At a Legislative Council question and answer session with city leader Lee, lawmaker Scott Leung Man-kwong called for the measure to be extended to young couples and other families with older children. He also urged the government to consider additional financial support to boost the city’s birth rate. “I have seen many sandwich-class families applying under the ‘white form’. Their children have already passed the newborn stage, but they still need a stable living environment as they grow up,” Leung said. “And for many young people who are still single, or those preparing to get married, having a stable place to live is a basic precondition when they consider whether to marry and start a family.” The sandwich class refers to those who earn too much to qualify for public housing but cannot afford to buy a home in the private sector. In response, Lee stressed there was a need to allocate public resources prudently. “If we expand the scope of the measure, we have to consider whether our financial commitment and responsibility can be sustained. The sustainability of a policy must be taken into account when allocating public resources,” the chief executive said. “For example, during the most difficult period of the Covid-19 pandemic, we provided large-scale support, but that approach was not sustainable, and it was why we began to face fiscal challenges.”

title: Hong Kong to support rocket, satellite IPOs as SpaceX-led sector takes off
description: Exchange will examine listing-rule changes to attract space IPOs in alignment with Beijing’s prioritisation of space technology.
content: Hong Kong aims to adjust listing rules to grab a share of initial public offerings by mainland China’s space companies, in line with Beijing’s priorities and heightened activity in the sector following the blockbuster June listing by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. That could lead to more head-to-head competition between the Hong Kong stock exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which is now drawing a majority of applications, including commercial space launch providers and reusable rocket makers CAS Space and Landspace Technology. The objective was revealed on Wednesday in the annual policy address by Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu, who said that bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) would, in the first half of next year, launch a consultation on revising Chapter 18C of the city’s listing rules to court space-related IPOs. The move aimed “to attract enterprises in emerging industries such as aerospace to raise capital in Hong Kong, consolidating our position as a financing hub for new economy enterprises”, Lee said. The consultation would include a review of the market capitalisation threshold, Lee added. Introduced in 2023, Chapter 18C defines special listing rules for companies in five technology sectors, placing commercial aerospace under advanced hardware and software. Eligible space activities under Chapter 18C include spacecraft development, space exploration and space-based communication and services. The bourse operator introduced a three-year temporary reduction in Chapter 18C’s minimum market valuation requirements in August 2024. Effective through August 31, 2027, the modification lowers the valuation threshold for pre-revenue companies to HK$8 billion (US$1.02 billion) from HK$10 billion and reduces the requirement for firms with at least HK$250 million in annual revenue to HK$4 billion from HK$6 billion. The consultation should ease requirements for research and development milestones, commercialisation and disclosure standards, given the long investment cycle and heavy capital needs of aerospace technology, said Edward Au Chun-hing, a managing partner at Deloitte China. “Authorities could lower the shareholding or investment ratio threshold for ‘Sophisticated Independent Investors’ and broaden the categories of recognised senior investors to help the market conduct reasonable valuation and validation,” he added. Lee also said the Securities and Futures Commission would begin consultation on streamlining prospectus disclosure requirements in 2027. This would facilitate Hong Kong listings by quality overseas enterprises by further reducing compliance and financing costs for technology companies, he said. Earlier on Wednesday, Hong Kong released its first five-year plan to align with Beijing’s 15th five-year plan. The national framework set a clear goal of making China a strong aerospace nation. Excitement in advance of the US$75 billion Nasdaq listing of SpaceX sparked a space-technology boom in capital markets. The Shanghai Stock Exchange allowed pre-revenue rocket makers onto its Nasdaq-style Star Market last year, drawing many companies into the queue. Hong Kong has attracted some peripheral firms. Aerospace-related tool manufacturer Shanghai Top Numerical Control Technology was listed in May, and Adaspace Technology – which is focused on building AI computing facilities in space – also chose the city for its listing destination. As of the end of August, funds raised through IPOs in Hong Kong topped HK$340 billion, surpassing last year’s total. However, the SpaceX listing put Nasdaq above the city’s exchange in the global ranking of IPO venues. In a statement on Wednesday, HKEX chairman Carlson Tong said the bourse operator was looking forward to working closely with the Hong Kong government and other stakeholders to deliver on the government’s strategic priorities and “bolster the city’s position as a premier gateway for capital, opportunities and ideas between China and the world”.

title: This Hong Kong home was designed to be family-friendly without feeling immaculate
description: Architect Darius Woo transformed a 1,500 sq ft Happy Valley flat into a real home with thoughtfully designed focal points.
content: Just when they thought life could not possibly become more chaotic – full-time jobs in finance, the whirlwind of a toddler and the imminent arrival of a second child – William Li and Sara Browne decided to add one more variable to the equation: buying a 1,500 sq ft (139 square metre) flat in Happy Valley, Hong Kong. Wanting to craft a permanent home for their growing family, they were drawn to the property’s generous bones, its coveted location and its proximity to Li’s mother. On paper, the four-bedroom, two-bathroom flat was perfectly habitable. In reality, its 1980s soul was crying out for a modern makeover. The couple initially considered tackling only the most critical rooms but friend and architect Darius Woo Ching-fung, of Kasawoo, advised them that a full renovation, executed while they were comfortably ensconced elsewhere, was the only way to achieve the home they wanted. We were deliberately restrained with colours and materials Architect Darius Woo Working around structural constraints, which became part of the design challenge, Woo minimised unnecessary demolition, both to cut waste and to keep construction costs under control. “The guiding principle was clarity,” says Woo, who is based in London, Britain, and worked on the project remotely, with an on-site project manager. “We were deliberately restrained with colours and materials so that every room has a clear focal point – whether it’s a kitchen island or a run of cabinetry. Everything else plays a supporting role. “We try to avoid filling a space with too many competing materials … We believe richness comes from carefully considered composition rather than an abundance of finishes.” Browne and Li wanted a home that was visually arresting yet profoundly calming – a space that could handle the entertaining pandemonium of early parenthood but possessed the architectural maturity to evolve alongside their children. Woo’s response was a masterclass in subtle spatial engineering. Although the Hong Kong instinct is to remove walls to make spaces feel larger, he did the opposite. He reconfigured the layout of the main suite, adding a slatted timber walk-in wardrobe to trim the overly large bathroom and give the bedroom a greater sense of intimacy. He also borrowed square footage from the disproportionately large living area, adding partition walls to carve out substantial bedrooms for the couple’s son and their soon-to-arrive daughter. “The whole idea was to create a family-friendly environment that didn’t feel immaculate,” Browne says. “The children play in the living room now but they will crave privacy as they get older, so we wanted to make their bedrooms a generous size.” Having traded the grey skies of Britain for the energy of Hong Kong eight years ago, she was keen to weave a thread of English domesticity into the urban modernity of her adopted city – a place Li has always called home. Rather than recreating a traditional English interior, however, Woo drew out, through conversations with his clients, the qualities they associated with it: Shaker-style cabinetry (minimal ornamentation, simple pulls or knobs), a confident use of colour and warm natural materials and textures. “We reinterpreted those qualities through contemporary architectural language, using modern detailing and restrained compositions so that the apartment feels cohesive rather than a collage of different styles,” he says. “The goal was never to mimic English interiors but to distil their essence into something that feels fresh and appropriate for Hong Kong.” Colours that Browne and Li naturally gravitated towards became the defining feature of the flat. Deep blue panelling stretches from the far end of the living room through to the kitchen (see Tried + tested), cleverly disguising the front door and storage. In a fourth bedroom, which doubles as a study off the living room, a sage green unit takes centre stage, creating a calming, work-conducive atmosphere. Here, Woo’s ingenuity shines in the details: he engineered the end section of the built-in desk to be entirely removable, allowing the sofa to be pulled out into a guest bed without awkward furniture rearrangement. “We aren’t afraid of colour but Darius helped us choose the ideal blues and greens to go with the slatted panelling and flooring and give the whole flat an earthy, organic feel,” says Browne. “Good design isn’t necessarily about expensive materials or extravagant gestures,” says Woo. “For us, luxury comes from generosity of thought rather than generosity of expenditure.” Living room Sofa and footstool from Bo Concept. Coffee table from Rove Concepts. Rug from Miss Amara. Rizzatto 301 ceiling light from Nuura. Eros table lamp from Honoré. Nabila wall light from Tooy Lighting. Bespoke television cabinet by BiGi Wood HK. Kitchen Kitchen, designed by Kasawoo and made by Kitench. Study Cabinetry designed by Kasawoo and made by Skywill Far East Engineering (tel: 9456 6633). Chair from Cozymatic and jute rug from Bali, Indonesia. Main bedroom Random Cloud ceiling light from Lodes. Bed from Decor8. Bedside tables by BiGi Wood HK. Lamps from Ikea. Artwork by Xingfa Ke from Guangdong Contemporary Art Centre. Ecowood slatted panels in oak finish from Nexon Building Materials. title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan, John Lee’s 2026 policy address: everything you need to know
description: From Hong Kong’s first five-year blueprint to new initiatives to boost birth rates, here are highlights from John Lee’s final policy address.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage of John Lee’s 2026 policy address. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. 14 key takeaways from John Lee’s policy address, Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has placed deepening integration with mainland China and developing new economic engines centre stage as he unveiled the city’s first-ever five-year plan alongside the last policy address of his term. 2. Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries The city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, sets targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy. 3. Hong Kong’s HK$30,000 bonus for second child among 11 new measures to boost births Hong Kong authorities have rolled out 11 new initiatives to encourage residents to have children, including an expanded cash bonus scheme and a reduced down payment for subsidised housing for parents with newborns. 4. Hong Kong’s new training visa could be available in first quarter of 2027 A new visa intended to attract international talent to participate in short-term training programmes in Hong Kong could become available as early as the first quarter of next year. 5. Hong Kong to woo finance and tech firms with new tax breaks Hong Kong will introduce various tax incentives for new finance and technology industries to attract businesses and reinforce the city’s role as a leading financial hub. 6. First building in Hong Kong’s university town project to be ready in months The first building in the 1,000-hectare (2,472-acre) university town project in the Northern Metropolis will be completed by the end of this year, Hong Kong’s leader has said, revealing that the flagship tower is called Loop Academy One. 7. Hong Kong leader pledges building maintenance reforms after fatal Tai Po fire John Lee has pledged to overhaul the city’s building maintenance regime and improve emergency response as part of the government’s response to last year’s fatal Tai Po fire, while authorities study criminalising bid-rigging and plan to submit a proposal later this year. 8. Hong Kong launching pilot scheme to bring in foreign carers for the elderly Hong Kong will introduce a pilot scheme next year to bring in foreign domestic carers to look after older residents as part of a broader package of measures announced in the policy address to deal with an ageing population. 9. Hong Kong targets gold trading, FPS-UnionPay link to boost yuan use 10. Hong Kong targets film tourism boom and higher-level tennis tournaments Hong Kong will introduce themed tourism routes showcasing the city’s most recognisable filming locations and explore upgrading Victoria Park’s Centre Court to host higher-level tennis tournaments, as authorities seek to significantly increase the sector’s economic contribution under the city’s first five-year development plan.

title: Casino, not bakery: Philippine e-payment firms urged to improve merchant vetting
description: The central bank found thousands of payments of as little as 80 US cents being made to generally unremarkable merchants past midnight.
content: Electronic payment providers need to be more diligent in vetting companies that use their platforms to protect people from fraud, the Philippine central bank said.
