The requirement came after Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas found thousands of illegal businesses on the payment platforms, including many online casinos masquerading as more ordinary companies like beauty salons and bakeries. “We want to protect consumers from online fraud, illegal activities and also from money launderers,” Deputy Governor Mamerto Tangonan said in an interview. “You cannot expand digitalisation if people’s money is being stolen” or they are being scammed. His comments came after Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas released a draft document that put the onus on payment service providers to improve screening of the merchants they partner with. Alarm bells started ringing for the central bank after surveillance discovered many merchants, which on paper were unremarkable, were accepting thousands of payments of as little as 50 pesos (80 US cents) past midnight and into the early hours of the morning, according to Tangonan. Authorities discovered the payments were bets on online casinos, he said. Mom and pop stores were also among the enterprises used by over 8,000 merchants whose accounts have now been closed for allegedly illegal activities. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation Chairman Alejandro Tengco said the state regulator was aware that many innocuous-sounding businesses were in reality unregistered online casinos and was working with the central bank. “Unfortunately, we don’t have control over that,” Tengco said. The discovery also highlights the problems that arise when e-payments companies use intermediaries, called merchant aggregators, to help them aggressively expand their business. Financial inclusion is a big push in the archipelago of over 7,000 islands, and merchant aggregators are incentivised to link many small – mostly legitimate – businesses in far-flung areas to formal payment channels. The Philippines central bank will now require payment platforms to collect more information on merchants being linked up, including owner details and licenses. It also wants them to set up databases of legitimate merchants. Repeated violations could lead to revocation of payment licenses, the central bank official said. “If there are illegal activities and you’re not able to stop it, then you are accountable,” Tangonan said. Use of online payments in the Philippines has exploded in recent years amid the popularity of mobile wallets like GCash, whose parent Mynt is set to hold a record initial public offering next month. Maya, a large e-wallet and digital bank operator backed by KKR & Co and PLDT, is also considering going public. Maya said the company supported measures that “strengthen the integrity, safety and trustworthiness of the digital payments ecosystem”, adding that it had merchant onboarding, due diligence and monitoring processes in place. The EMoney Association of the Philippines said the group fully supported the central bank’s goals of safeguarding and improving the country’s payment system. “It is important that there is accountability from the industry to ensure that we have a safe digital ecosystem for the market,” a representative said in a text message. The association is currently reviewing and evaluating the central bank’s proposed circular. GCash did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Digital payments accounted for around two-thirds of total retail transactions in the Philippines in 2025, up from 57 per cent in 2024 and a share of just 10 per cent in 2018, when the central bank started reporting data. While more stringent due diligence may temporarily slow the expansion of digital payment activities, Tangonan said it should set the sector up for more sustainable growth. “You shouldn’t sacrifice safety for growth,” he said. “There’s no trade-off there.”

title: Chinese runner becomes first athlete to complete 330km Tor des Géants in under 66 hours
description: Guizhou-born Zhao Jiaju uses ‘fragmented sleep’ strategy to win gruelling Italy race, makes history as first Asian to win the event.
content: Chinese runner Zhao Jiaju became the first athlete to complete the 330km Tor des Géants in under 66 hours on Wednesday, breaking the course record to claim victory in Italy using a “fragmented sleep” strategy. Wearing bib No 1, he crossed the finish line in Courmayeur at 9.55am with a winning time of 65 hours, 55 minutes and 22 seconds, making history as the first Asian competitor to win the event. Widely regarded as one of the world’s most gruelling ultra-trail races, the flagship event offers no prize money and serves as a supreme test of human endurance. Competitors face a 150-hour cut-off with no mandatory rest stops, leaving sleep management entirely up to the athletes. Held in Italy’s Aosta Valley and starting and ending in Courmayeur, the 330km loop features more than 24,000 metres of total elevation gain, equivalent to climbing Mount Everest twice, and crosses 25 high-altitude passes, some exceeding 3,000 metres at the foot of Mont Blanc, the Matterhorn and Monte Rosa. Runners also endure extreme weather shifts, ranging from summer valley heat to sub-zero mountain snow. Born in Guizhou in February 1995, Zhao showed extraordinary endurance and tactical discipline, running the first 150km in just 24 hours. According to reports, Zhao made his first checkpoint stop only after running for 35 hours and 42 minutes, halting after being strongly urged by his support team. He spent a total of 50 minutes at the station changing clothes, eating and resting, with his actual sleep accounting for only about 20 minutes. In contrast to second-place finisher Jonathan Schindler of Switzerland, who took intermittent sleep during the first half, Zhao subsequently adopted a fragmented sleep strategy, taking several quick 10-minute power naps at checkpoints. View this post on Instagram A post shared by RUN'IX (@run_ix) After the 203km mark, Zhao leveraged his strengths in night and downhill running to regain the lead and steadily pull ahead of record pace until the finish. Zhao prepared by arriving in Europe a month early to adapt, using the 60km OCC race at UTMB (Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc) as training. In 2025, after placing 10th in the 174km UTMB, Zhao made his Tor des Géants debut but withdrew after the 200km mark because of exhaustion, pledging at the time that he would “definitely return” to break the record. In his autobiography, Wang Qian Pao (which means “running forward”) with the English title Run, Zhao recalled working as a food delivery worker in Hangzhou around 2014, delivering orders on foot rather than by bicycle as “paid long-distance training” to build mileage, laying the foundation for him to turn professional in 2017. The previous course record of 66 hours, eight minutes and 22 seconds was set by Frenchman Richard Victor in 2025. The previous best finish by a Chinese runner was sixth place, achieved by Zhang Weiqiang in 2025. Germany’s Katharina Hartmuth, a PhD in climatology, finished as the top female competitor and third overall after battling Schindler over more than 100km by taking seated micro-naps at checkpoints. As of 1am on Wednesday, only these three runners had completed the race, with Chinese runner Zhang currently running in fourth place.

title: Hong Kong watchdog probes buy one, get one free deals at supermarkets
description: Consumer Council finds some offers deliver smaller-than-expected discounts or no savings at all, urges shoppers to compare unit prices.
content:
Hong Kong shoppers may be saving less than expected – or nothing at all – with supermarkets’ buy one, get one free and bulk-buy promotions, a consumer watchdog has warned.
On Monday, the Consumer Council released the findings of a survey covering 222 products sold by Aeon, ParknShop and Wellcome between September 2025 and July this year. It found that the actual discounts offered in some promotional campaigns were less attractive than consumers might expect.
It urged residents to compare unit prices rather than rely on promotional labels.
During the period, 48 products at two supermarkets were offered under bulk-buy promotional campaigns such as buy one, get one free, choose any two and get one free, and get one more for HK$1.
But for some of these products, the single item cost more during the promotional period than during non-promotional periods, meaning the actual discount fell well short of the about 50 per cent consumers might expect, the council said.
The findings add to long-standing concerns over whether supermarket multi-buy promotions always offer the savings suggested by their labels.
Alaina Shum Jiu-fai, the watchdog’s chief executive, suggested grocery stores and supermarkets list their unit price somewhere to make it easier for consumers to choose products.
“Hong Kong is a free market, and the merchants have the flexibility to adjust the prices any time,” she explained. “But it’s not a prudent move to adjust the price immediately before the promotion – it will affect the consumers’ confidence.”
In one example, a 150-millilitre bottle of sesame oil was sold under a buy one, get one free campaign at one supermarket for HK$20 or HK$22 per item – much higher than its pre-promotion price of HK$10 to HK$14.
“Consumers’ expectations [are] that a buy one, get one free offer is equivalent to nearly a 50 per cent discount,” the council said.
The same product was offered at a discount of up to 21 per cent under a choose any two and get one free promotion at another supermarket, the council said.
“Under both promotions, the average price per item during certain periods was even about 10 per cent higher than the corresponding non-promotional prices,” it said.
Similar patterns were observed for other items, including a 410ml bottle of soy sauce for steamed fish, for which the effective discount was about 16 per cent.
In another case, discounts on a 280-gram pack of rice vermicelli only ranged from zero to 29 per cent. This was despite both being sold under bulk-buy schemes.
The council also found that larger pack sizes did not necessarily offer better value. Of the 15 product groups compared by unit price, the larger pack cost of seven was found to be between 2 and 35 per cent more per unit than the smaller version during certain periods.
The watchdog received 359 complaints about supermarkets in the first eight months of this year, up by 16.9 per cent from the same period last year. About 20 per cent concerned service quality at physical stores, followed by disputes over product quality and pricing.
The council pressed consumers to compare products using their “unit price” and historical selling prices, rather than making purchasing decisions solely based on promotional formats or pack sizes.
It also directed shoppers to its Online Price Watch platform, which provides shopping budget calculations and target price alerts for about 2,800 products across nine retailers.

title: US House holds billionaire Leon Black in contempt over Epstein probe
description: Lawmakers refer billionaire investor to Justice Department as his lawyers call contempt move ‘outrageous’.
content: The US House of Representatives held billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress on Wednesday for defying subpoenas issued in its investigation into notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The resolution was adopted by unanimous consent, without a recorded vote, a day after the House Oversight Committee unanimously recommended the action. The matter will now be referred to the Justice Department, which will decide whether to pursue criminal charges. “No one is above the law. Leon Black defied two subpoenas, and the US House of Representatives acted swiftly to find him in contempt of Congress,” panel chairman James Comer said in a statement. “We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors in our investigation of the federal government’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell criminal cases.” Black, the billionaire co-founder of Apollo Global Management, failed to appear for a September 3 deposition and did not fully comply with a separate subpoena seeking nondisclosure agreements. His lawyers called the House action “outrageous”, accused lawmakers of rushing the process and said they would continue a court challenge to the subpoenas, US media reported. Black had appeared voluntarily before the committee in June, acknowledging that he paid Epstein US$158 million for tax and estate planning advice. But that session ended early after he declined to answer questions about some nondisclosure agreements, prompting lawmakers to demand further testimony and documents. Black has repeatedly denied wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities. Black is the latest among several prominent figures, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, who have been asked to appear as part of the Oversight Committee’s long-running probe of Epstein. Survivors of Epstein’s alleged sexual abuse have told personal stories of being young women in a trafficking enterprise organised by Epstein and his colleague Maxwell. Epstein died in federal custody in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges involving minors, in what authorities ruled a suicide. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Indian transgender patients left in limbo following legal amendments
description: The amendment introduced penalties for forcing someone to assume a transgender identity through surgical, chemical or hormonal procedures.
content: When transgender woman Kali Sidharth Medepalli began hormone replacement therapy in India, she expected to complete her medical transition and undergo surgery within a year. But just months after she began treatment earlier this year, India’s parliament amended the country’s transgender law, and the clinic where she was receiving care stopped her medicines. “Everything shut down,” the 23-year-old communications specialist and LGBTQ rights activist said in the southern city of Hyderabad. Kali said she went 10 days without a testosterone blocker, experiencing hot flushes and body aches. The amendment introduced penalties for forcing someone to assume a transgender identity through surgical, chemical or hormonal procedures. Authorities say the changes are meant to better protect vulnerable groups by strengthening penalties for exploitation, forced identity and trafficking. The government said it does not criminalise consensual, medically supervised care, but activists and doctors say the amendment created uncertainty for thousands of people. “The healthcare system is very fearful right now,” said transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, a member of a Supreme Court advisory committee on transgender welfare. The lack of clarity, she said, could “scare away even the ones who have the best interests for the trans people”. Kali later managed to obtain her medicine using her existing prescription but was forced to self-medicate. “Ideally, you should have a doctor doing this for you,” she said. Care dilemma The case illustrates the dilemma facing transgender people seeking safe medical care, according to Sanjay Sharma, head of the Association for Transgender Health in India. Doctors face a choice. Continuing treatment could expose them to legal risk, but refusing care could conflict with their medical responsibilities. “How can I refuse care? I took an oath that above all do no harm,” said Sharma, a doctor and retired air force commodore. Some private clinics have continued treatment but are taking extra precautions, including additional paperwork, consent forms and charging patients more. “Private clinics will now give care, but they lawyer up,” Sharma said. It is particularly difficult for people without supportive families, established doctors or money for private care. Mumbai-based Meghna Kulkarni, who supports her child’s transition, said the amendment “immediately rang danger bells”, but unlike others, they had a support network. “We already knew the doctors, the surgeon, the psychiatrist.” There are no official figures for how many transgender people receive gender-affirming healthcare in India, making the scale of the disruption difficult to assess. India does not have a current estimate of its transgender population. While India’s official 2011 Census recorded roughly 488,000 transgender individuals, human rights groups and experts estimate that the actual population is between five and six million people. The uncertainty over the amendment also affects transgender identity certification. Bhukya Ahalya, 21, who transitioned in 2025, wants regular employment but has struggled to update her identity documents, which still identify her as a man. She now survives by begging at traffic signals. “Everyone wants me to move on from this life,” she said. “But when I want to move on, when I want to earn a respectful life, I don’t get a TG [transgender] card.” The government website for applying for a transgender identity card – the first step towards changing other key documents – has not functioned since the amendment came into force in March. The amendment has added an extra layer of scrutiny to the process. Now a designated medical board must recommend certification, after which a magistrate can issue the identity certificate. The amendment is being challenged in the Supreme Court. Petitioners cite constitutional protections including dignity, autonomy and privacy, as well as the right to self-identification. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment has not responded to requests for clarification on the amendment, its rules and the identity-card portal. For Kali, her carefully planned medical transition has become uncertain. “I don’t know the future,” she said. “I can’t plan it any more”.

title: Letters | What Brics wants: a non-Western, not an anti-Western, world
description: Readers discuss the recent Brics summit, and former Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa’s time in office.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Brics has a strange habit of confounding both its supporters and its critics. The group is often portrayed as an emerging anti-Western bloc led by China and Russia. Others dismiss it as an unwieldy talking shop whose members share little beyond dissatisfaction with Western dominance. The recent New Delhi summit suggests both interpretations miss something important. For an organisation supposedly united by opposition to the West, Brics spends much time demanding reform rather than revolution. Its latest declaration calls for “a reinvigorated and reformed multilateral system”, not the dismantling of the existing one. That distinction goes to the heart of what Brics has become. Its members are not abandoning the United Nations, International Monetary Fund and World Bank, nor are they constructing a coherent alternative order. Instead, they are building institutions and mechanisms alongside existing ones. The New Development Bank, expanding trade in national currencies and efforts to improve cross-border payment systems are intended not as replacements but as additional options. This helps explain why Brics often appears simultaneously divided and influential. China and India remain strategic rivals. Russia’s confrontation with the West is not shared by much of the membership. Expansion has added further complexity, bringing in states with their own priorities and regional disputes. Even the Delhi summit reflected differing levels of political commitment, with some members choosing not to send their heads of government to the event. But disagreement over methods should not be confused with disagreement over direction. Across Brics there is a broadly shared view that the international system should become more multipolar and that emerging powers should have greater room to manoeuvre within it. The debate over de-dollarisation illustrates this point. Some have limited interest in strengthening the financial influence of any of the group members’ currencies or provoking confrontation with Washington. Yet trade in national currencies continues to expand and work on alternative payment mechanisms continues. Brics should therefore be judged less by its internal disagreements than by its ability to widen the choices available to other states. What binds its members together is not a common ideology or a shared opposition to the West, but a common desire for a world in which Western institutions remain important without remaining the only points of reference – a non-Western world, rather than an anti-Western one. Dr Zeno Leoni and Dr Rishika Chauhan, King’s College London, and Dr Maria Papageorgiou, Newcastle University Tung Chee-hwa deserved better from Hong Kong The recent passing of Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, deserves more than the usual post-event political analysis. He was a humble and diligent leader, yet for most of his tenure he was met with mockery, blame and disrespect. Three of the most controversial episodes of his time in office illustrate how that disrespect was manufactured. First, the 1999 right-of-abode case. The Court of Final Appeal delivered a ruling that significantly expanded eligibility for permanent residency. Tung’s government was right to seek an interpretation from the National People’s Congress Standing Committee under Article 158 of the Basic Law to restore the true legislative intent of the Basic Law. This was not an attack on the rule of law but rather an effort to uphold the Basic Law as written. Second, the handling of the 2003 severe acute respiratory syndrome outbreak. Public criticism at the time was intense, yet a Legislative Council select committee noted that the chief executive was very concerned about the outbreak and was prepared to consider drastic measures to control the spread of the disease. It specifically found that he was the first official to raise the question of whether it was necessary to quarantine family members of infected people. Third, the attempt to legislate under Article 23 of the Basic Law. Tung’s government simply sought to fulfil this clear constitutional responsibility. The effort was turned into a political nuclear bomb by its opponents to split the ruling coalition and undermine Tung’s authority. These three episodes were systematically hijacked by Tung’s detractors. They were spun into a false narrative of personal incompetence and weak leadership. Beneath his amiable face, Tung had a strong sense of duty. The overwhelming and relentless attacks from the media and other quarters could sting. Hong Kong owes him an apology, a simple acknowledgement that a decent and hardworking man was treated with disproportionate harshness while he tried, under extraordinary constraints, to keep the city stable and prosperous. Hongjie Chen, Ma On Shan

title: China cuts US Treasury holdings to 18-year low amid global bond sell-off
description: Persistent concerns over sustainability of Washington’s finances see overall foreign holdings shrink for second consecutive month.
content: China cut its holdings of US Treasuries to an 18-year low in July, as overall holdings by foreign countries fell for a second consecutive month amid deepening worries over the sustainability of American government debt. China’s holdings fell to US$618 billion in July from US$633.4 billion in June, data released by the US Treasury Department showed on Wednesday. The July figure was the lowest level since August 2008, when its holdings tumbled to US$573.7 billion, according to Chinese financial data provider Wind. Meanwhile, overall foreign holdings of US Treasuries dropped to US$9.25 trillion in July, down from US$9.3 trillion in June, the US Treasury Department said. In July, persistent concerns over the sustainability of Washington’s finances – with investors demanding greater compensation for holding US government debt over longer horizons – continued to weigh on long-term US Treasuries, pushing 30-year Treasury yields to their highest level since 2007. In late July, Washington and Tokyo intervened to stem the Japanese yen’s slide, marking their first joint yen-buying intervention since 1998, with observers widely speculating that US involvement might also help limit selling pressure on US Treasuries. Among other major Treasury holders, Japan, the largest foreign holder of US debt, cut its holdings to US$1.1 trillion in July from US$1.12 trillion in June, while the United Kingdom’s holdings rose to US$998.3 billion from US$939.9 billion, official data showed. Long-term bond yields continued to rise even after the US Treasury Department said last week that it would buy back up to US$6 billion of long-dated debt – a move widely seen as an effort to support the market and ease pressure on longer-term yields. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed above the 5 per cent mark on Monday, for the first time since 2023, and has hovered around that level since. Meanwhile, the impact of the US Federal Reserve’s decision on Wednesday to increase interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point due to inflation concerns – the first rate increase in over three years – remained a key focus for investors. China slipped to third place among foreign holders of US Treasuries in March last year – behind Japan and the UK – continuing a gradual but uneven retreat that began during US President Donald Trump’s first term amid rising tensions and concerns over the weaponisation of the US dollar. In contrast to its broader sell-off of US debt, China has steadily added to its gold reserves, widely viewed as a hedge against geopolitical and financial risks. Official data showed the People’s Bank of China increased its bullion holdings for the 22nd consecutive month in August, bringing the total to 76.73 million troy ounces.

title: China airports climb global-connectivity ranking as international routes rise: OAG report
description: Third terminal helps Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport jump 17 places in global standings, while airports in Beijing, Shanghai and Hong Kong also improve.
content: Among the world’s most connected airports, Guangzhou’s hub has posted the fastest rise through the latest rankings, according to an annual list compiled by aviation data firm OAG. And overall, Chinese hubs stood out as carriers expanded their international networks with added flights. Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport in southern China jumped to 19th place, from 36th last year, in OAG’s Megahubs 2026 report, released on Wednesday. An OAG spokeswoman called its jump the biggest of any airport globally. The addition of the airport’s third terminal in October has since facilitated air connections throughout the region, including neighbouring Hong Kong and Macau. Passenger and flight volumes increased “sharply” at the airport in early 2026, reflecting a rebound in air-travel demand, according to the Guangzhou Foreign Affairs Office. The airport now handles 146 international routes, served by 80 airlines. Elsewhere in China, Shanghai Pudong International Airport climbed to 14th from 19th, while Beijing Capital International Airport advanced 10 spots to 44th. Hong Kong International Airport improved two places to 20th. The ranking evaluates airports based on the ratio of possible scheduled international connections to the number of destinations served. OAG’s 2026 rankings placed Turkey’s Istanbul Airport in the top spot, up from second in 2025. Istanbul traded places with last year’s No 1 hub, London Heathrow Airport. Amsterdam Airport Schiphol retained its third-place position. Chinese airports have enhanced connectivity by adding international flights since the Covid-19 pandemic, and after a “cautious” phase focused on domestic networks, noted OAG chief analyst John Grant. “In the last two years, we have seen some changes … with more new routes being launched to Europe from China and a return of Chinese airlines to Australia in large volumes as bilateral relations improved,” Grant said. “The addition of each new international route has a multiplier effect on [a hub’s] ranking position, so that has been a key factor,” he added. Airlines in China have been riding a wave of interest in outbound tourism, with online travel agencies finding that Chinese travellers were seeking experience-based trips to far-flung destinations such as Egypt and Norway. At the same time, Grant said, “megahub” airports in other countries had seen cuts to the number of flights handled. In the Middle East, he explained, all major airports were “significantly down” as local airlines had not recovered capacity amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, and with overseas carriers in that part of the world reducing services. “It’s a bit of growth in the local Chinese airport networks alongside those cutbacks in other airports that traditionally score highly in the megahubs ranking,” Grant said. This year, airports in the Asia-Pacific region account for eight of the world’s top 20 hubs, more than in any other region.

title: Is Japan’s Okinawa finally moving past anti-base politics?
description: Frustrated by economic hardship, Okinawans have rallied behind a new governor, leaving long-standing anti-base resistance in disarray.
content: Okinawa has handed a landslide victory to a conservative who accepts Tokyo’s plans for relocating a controversial US airbase – delivering a blow to 12 years of anti-base politics in Japan’s southernmost prefecture. Genta Koja’s victory on Sunday over two-term governor Denny Tamaki raised a question cutting to the heart of Okinawa’s post-war politics: is it finally starting to move on from the US military base issue? Koja, a 42-year-old conservative backed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, campaigned on economic revival and accepting Tokyo’s plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station from densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko district in Nago, both on Okinawa Island. Tamaki, by contrast, had opposed the base project for his entire tenure as governor, a stance he inherited from his late predecessor after winning 2018’s election on an anti-base platform. Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News on Sunday found that nearly half of voters ranked economic revitalisation as their top concern, while barely one-fifth of respondents cited issues related to US bases. That was reflected in the election results. Koja, a former deputy mayor of Okinawa’s capital Naha, defeated Tamaki with 59 per cent of the vote, officials said on Monday. He will become the prefecture’s first governor born after its return to Japanese sovereignty by the United States in 1972 and the first in over a decade not to have built his career on opposition to US military bases. Generational rift Okinawa has been seen as a bastion of pacifist, left-leaning opposition forces for years. Despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of Japan’s total land area, it hosts roughly 70 per cent of the land dedicated exclusively to US military facilities in the country – a burden that has made it central to arguments over the US-Japan alliance. Tamaki and his All Okinawa movement, a broad political and civic alliance that opposes the relocation and construction of US military bases on Okinawa Island, had long framed the dispute as a test of local autonomy against central authority. Sunday’s result illustrated a generational divide, according to Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science. While voters over 60 largely backed Tamaki and All Okinawa, “younger voters were more concerned about the economy”, he said. The outcome reflected “pragmatism as well as frustration” with Tamaki for failing to stop new base construction, Maslow said – though that did not mean voters were unconcerned about national security implications. Japan’s “Nansei shift” – the build-up of defence capabilities across its southern islands – was expected to continue under the new governor and “this will place an even higher burden on Okinawa”, he said. Masato Kamikubo, a political scientist and professor at Ritsumeikan University, said successive LDP governments dating back to Shinzo Abe’s administration had cut subsidies to Okinawa in an attempt to “bully” the prefecture for its confrontational approach to central authority. A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics Masato Kamikubo, political scientist “Faced with rising prices and other economic difficulties, Okinawan voters appear to have wanted a way out of the present situation and therefore prioritised the economy over the military base issue,” he said. The election result reflected a move away from the decades-old contest between conservative and liberal blocs, Kamikubo said, arguing that All Okinawa’s “crushing defeat” revealed a movement built on ideological resistance struggling to hold a new generation’s attention. “A younger generation is now beginning to create a new form of politics from the grass roots, moving beyond the traditional divide between left and right,” he said. “This election may have symbolised that emerging transformation.” Meanwhile, Takaichi’s firm stance on national security, particularly the tough line she had taken on China, also resonated with Okinawan voters, Kamikubo said. “Okinawa is on the front line in confronting the perceived threat from China,” he said, noting that liberal politicians such as Tamaki and the All Okinawa movement had done little more than appealed for peace. “Some voters are anxious about whether these groups would actually be able to protect them in the event of a crisis.” Tokyo’s cash carrot On Monday, following Koja’s victory, Takaichi pledged to raise Okinawa’s budget to more than 300 billion yen (US$1.94 billion) from around 260 billion yen in recent years. Kamikubo said he expected her “to present Okinawa as a model demonstrating that economic growth can be achieved and rising living costs overcome when the central and prefectural governments work together”. “For a prime minister struggling with declining approval ratings, the victory in Okinawa will be seen as a significant glimmer of hope,” he added. A recent poll by national broadcaster NHK found public approval of Takaichi’s cabinet at 53 per cent, down from 66 per cent in November last year, amid concerns about inflation and the rising cost of living. Koja’s economic focus and his image as a fresh face – in contrast to Tamaki, who staked his political legacy on opposing the US military presence – had all helped at the polls, said Rintaro Nishimura, a Tokyo-based senior associate at strategic advisory firm The Asia Group. But Sunday’s result did not mean that Okinawans no longer cared about the base issue, he said, nor that they would accept every central government policy. “He [Koja] has been clear in how he views his role: a coordinator who will seek out the most practical and best option for the people of Okinawa,” Nishimura said. Still, the LDP backing a winning candidate for governor in a historically anti-LDP prefecture was “a good narrative for Takaichi to build on”, he said – particularly heading into next year’s local elections, as it helped counter concerns that the party was unpopular at the local level. Masaaki Gabe, a professor emeritus at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa, said many Okinawans had voted out of dissatisfaction with rising prices and economic hardship rather than security concerns. “The sense of immediacy regarding a potential conflict stemming from the Taiwan Strait crisis remains relatively limited,” he said, adding that further militarisation of Okinawa was likely to be “tolerated” by a significant segment of voters. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but are opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force. The two central challenges facing Okinawa today were poverty and the burden of hosting US bases, Gabe said. “Regardless of who serves as governor, these two challenges continue to exist with unwavering force and successive prefectural administrations have been compelled to confront them,” he said, adding that “the central government holds the upper hand on the base issue and its control over policy is unlikely to be shaken”. Okinawa consistently ranks as the least economically developed of Japan’s prefectures, with average incomes and employment roughly 20 to 30 per cent behind mainland standards.

title: Huawei unveils latest tech to boost AI power in push to break China’s Nvidia reliance
description: Its SuperPoD will face off against offerings by US rivals in the global computing power arena, including Nvidia’s NVL system.
content: Huawei Technologies on Thursday unveiled its latest Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster and an upgraded version of its UnifiedBus interconnect technology, key components of the Chinese tech giant’s strategy to build advanced artificial intelligence systems despite US semiconductor-related restrictions. At the Huawei Connect 2026 conference in Shanghai, the Shenzhen-based firm introduced near-packaged optics (NPOs) – a placement structure enabling higher speeds and lower energy use – to the company’s SuperPoD architecture for the first time. Huawei said the combination of its UnifiedBus interconnect technology and Hi-ONE optical system would allow a SuperPoD to connect as many as 4,000 processors, extending high-speed optical connections deeper into the computing system. The Atlas 960 SuperPoD, powered by Ascend 960 chips, promises a 2.3-fold and 2.5-fold improvement in training and inference for 10-trillion-parameter models, compared to its predecessor Atlas 950 SuperPoD. Huawei rolled out the Atlas 950 SuperPoD commercially last year, bringing total deployment of its Atlas SuperPoD line to over 1,000 units. While the Atlas 950 SuperPoD is powered by 8,192 Ascend neural processing units (NPUs), the Atlas 960 SuperPoD expands its scale to run on up to 15,488 Ascend cards across 220 cabinets covering 2,200 square metres. “Supernodes are an inevitable choice for building ultra-large-scale data centres,” said David Wang Tao, rotating and acting chairman for Huawei, on Thursday at the Huawei conference in Shanghai. “Huawei is set to begin mass production of the world’s first NPO product with an integrated light source,” he added. Huawei’s new development underscored the firm’s ongoing efforts to build a self-reliant computing power infrastructure to break the US stranglehold on advanced chips from the likes of Nvidia, aimed at curbing China’s AI advancements. Its SuperPoD will face off against offerings by US rivals in the global computing power arena, including Nvidia’s NVL system. Its UnifiedBus protocol is looking to challenge Nvidia’s NVLink, the US giant’s proprietary interconnect technology that supports communications between graphic processing units within cabinets. The announcements also came ahead of high-level trade talks between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump later this month, where AI and semiconductor exports are expected to top the technology agenda. Speaking on Thursday, Wang said development of the Ascend 960 DT, an AI chip designed for model training, was ahead of schedule. “Our Ascend 960 chip is progressing faster than expected, with performance doubling. We have brought the target launch for Ascend 960 DT forward by three quarters, and it will be ready in the first quarter of 2027.” The Ascend 960 PR chip, designed for AI model inference, is set to launch in the third quarter of 2027, also moving ahead of schedule by a quarter. “Our Ascend chips will continue on an annual upgrade cycle. In 2028 and 2029, we will successively launch the Ascend 970 and 980,” Wang added. “Guided by innovation based on the Tau Law, we aim to keep doubling computing performance, while also significantly increasing bandwidth, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth.” A Huawei paper posted to arXiv on the same day said the company was already deploying a 256K-node-class single AI computing system, extending the same architecture far beyond an individual SuperPoD. The paper, authored by Huawei researcher Liao Heng, described the system as “one machine”, rather than a network of more than 200,000 separate machines, with UnifiedBus and Huawei’s Nested BSP computing model spanning the system end-to-end. The development builds on Huawei’s UnifiedBus 2.0, the technology it first made public in September 2025. Huawei also unveiled a portfolio of 11 chips powered by UnifiedBus across computing, storage, management and interconnect for SuperPoDs and Superclusters. Known as Lingqu in Chinese, UnifiedBus is designed to connect large numbers of processors, memory modules and computing resources, allowing separate chips to function as a single computer. US-sanctioned Huawei has been playing a central role in advancing China’s AI ambitions without relying on American technologies. In May, the company unveiled its Tau Scaling Law and LogicFolding architecture, key semiconductor breakthroughs aiming to deliver transistor performance equivalent to a 1.4-nanometre process node by 2031 without depending on advanced lithography tools that are inaccessible in China. The company planned to deploy LogicFolding on its flagship Ascend 990 AI chip around 2030.

title: Risk of unrest in Asia as Iran war, El Nino threaten food supplies
description: Over half of countries at high risk on Verisk Maplecroft’s Food Security Index also sit at the top of its predictive Civil Unrest Index.
content: Severe weather disruptions will amplify food security risks in Asia, potentially triggering civil unrest and political instability in vulnerable countries such as India, Indonesia and the Philippines, according to consultancy Verisk Maplecroft. The warning comes as the war in Iran has already disrupted fuel and fertiliser supplies, both of which are key agricultural inputs. Now, weather extremes linked to a powerful El Nino are further threatening crops across the region. Indonesia, the world’s biggest palm oil producer, is suffering from a rash of hard-to-control wildfires that have disrupted harvests. The monsoon rains that top rice exporter India relies on are running 15 per cent below normal, and Thailand’s sugar harvest is set to sink. The twin threats of war and weather are driving up food inflation – an established trigger for unrest, the risk consultancy said in a report released on Thursday. Over half of countries that are at high or very high risk on Verisk Maplecroft’s Food Security Index also sit within the two highest categories of its predictive Civil Unrest Index. Those include India, as well as Bangladesh, the Philippines and Indonesia, where protests have already broken out in recent weeks. “The data suggest if food price and availability pressures intensify, and governments are seen to respond ineffectively, unrest and political instability could emerge in these higher risk markets,” the report said. For conflict-stricken nations like Afghanistan and Myanmar, a food shock would raise the risk of a humanitarian catastrophe, it added. Thailand, highly reliant on imported energy and fertilisers, is also under growing pressure from debt-laden farmers ahead of the next planting season. “The impacts are increasingly visible,” said Verisk Maplecroft. “In many key agriculture regions, planting and fertilisation decisions were made during the peak of the disruption, meaning negative impacts may now be locked in even if the geopolitical situation improves in the coming months.”

title: Hong Kong stocks decline after Fed raises interest rates and signals more to come
description: Investors look to Japan’s next rate decision after the Fed points to further tightening this year.
content: Stocks in Hong Kong and mainland China fell on Thursday, after the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in three years and signalled that further tightening remained on the table. The benchmark Hang Seng Index dropped 0.4 per cent to 24,604.29 at the close. The Hang Seng Tech Index lost 0.3 per cent. Rate-sensitive stocks such as property developers and gold producers led the decline. On the mainland, the CSI 300 Index slipped 0.5 per cent, while the chip-heavy Star Market 50 index retreated 0.6 per cent. The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to a target range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent at its September policy meeting. The so-called dot plot, which the US central bank uses to signal its outlook for the path of monetary policy, pointed to one more increase this year. Resilient growth and higher rates could benefit sectors such as financials, consumer discretionary and industrials Tai Hui, JPMorgan Asset Management in Hong Kong Fed chair Kevin Warsh described the increase as the removal of a “dose of accommodation,” language that traders interpreted as signalling that policy remained accommodative rather than restrictive. “There are no immediate signs that inflation will ease. This means the Fed may continue tightening in order to achieve its target,” said Tai Hui, a strategist at JPMorgan Asset Management in Hong Kong. “Resilient growth and higher rates could benefit sectors such as financials, consumer discretionary and industrials. We still see [Asian] technology benefiting from ongoing demand expansion despite caution around model development.” With the rate rise potentially heralding a new tightening cycle, investors are shifting their attention to how many additional increases lie ahead. Higher borrowing costs could squeeze corporate profit margins, raise funding costs for artificial intelligence infrastructure investments and suppress the stretched valuations of technology stocks. The outlook adds to challenges facing Chinese equities, which are already contending with uneven economic growth characterised by fragile domestic demand and strong exports. The rate rise also adds to a difficult macro-environment for global stocks. Over the past few weeks, equities have faced pressure from bond sell-offs that drove up the 10-year US Treasury yield to nearly 5 per cent, coupled with a sustained energy shock triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran. Those headwinds have been partly offset by resilient corporate earnings and the AI boom. “The message points to a Federal Reserve that is increasingly confident in the US economy and labour market, while remaining concerned about second-round inflation effects from supply-side shocks,” said Michael Langham, an economist at Aberdeen Investments. “We therefore continue to expect another [0.25 percentage-point rise] in December before the Fed pauses through most of 2027.” The Fed decision came in line with Warsh’s commitment to bring inflation back to 2 per cent and restore the credibility of the world’s biggest central bank, which is under pressure from US President Donald Trump to lower borrowing costs. Sun Hung Kai Properties sank 1.3 per cent to HK$108.20 and Hang Lung Properties fell 2 per cent to HK$6.60 after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority followed the Fed by raising the city’s base rate by 0.25 percentage points. Higher rates tend to dampen housing demand by increasing mortgage costs. Laopu Gold shed 3 per cent to HK$363 and Zijin Mining Group slid 1.6 per cent to HK$33.86 as higher interest rates traditionally diminished the appeal of non-yielding assets such as gold. Gold prices, however, rebounded on Thursday morning as analysts remained bullish on the metal’s long-term outlook. Investors will now keep a close watch on Japan’s looming rate decision on Friday, when the nation’s central bank is expected to raise borrowing costs by 0.25 percentage points to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent. The move is expected to have a substantial impact on risk assets globally that were bought by the Japanese yen-financed carry trade.

title: North Korea at Japan’s Asian Games: sports diplomacy or propaganda stunt?
description: Pyongyang is sending its largest-ever delegation to Japan, signalling a calculated bid to test Tokyo and pave the way for US re-engagement.
content: North Korea’s decision to send a record delegation to the 2026 Asian Games in Japan could serve as a calculated opening for limited diplomacy with Washington and Tokyo, even as major obstacles to formal talks remain. State media reported on Wednesday that a delegation led by Kim Il-guk, North Korea’s sports minister, had left for Japan to attend the Games. The 20th Asian Games are being held in Nagoya and surrounding Aichi prefecture and run from Saturday to October 4. North Korea’s 180-strong delegation is made up of 107 athletes competing across 14 sports – including football, weightlifting, table tennis and wrestling – alongside support staff. It is the country’s largest sporting delegation ever to visit Japan, according to Kyodo News. Tokyo generally bars North Korean nationals from entry under sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes, making this a rare exception. Observers say North Korea is using the international stage to project stability and shed its image as a pariah state. Oh Gyeong-seob, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said the move reflected Pyongyang’s desire to shed its “rogue state” label. “The North’s presence at the Games could provide an opening for cautious contacts for potential dialogue, but chances are slim,” Oh said. He noted that Kim Yo-jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, said in March that a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi would not happen as long as Tokyo maintained what she called its “anachronistic” approach. This was apparently a reference to Japan’s demands for denuclearisation and the return of Japanese nationals abducted by Pyongyang in the 1970s and 1980s. Her remarks came after Takaichi told reporters in March that she had expressed “a very strong desire” to meet Kim Jong-un during a Washington summit with US President Donald Trump. Lee Won-deog, a professor of international relations at Kookmin University in Seoul, said South Korea and Japan had hoped to take advantage of Pyongyang’s presence at the Games to pursue diplomatic outreach. “But their efforts have hit a stone wall,” Lee said, as Pyongyang had shown no interest in dialogue with anyone other than Trump. Victor Cha, Korea chair at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, said last month that Kim might see an opportunity in re-engaging the US leader. “Aside from the US president’s expressed desires to meet, North Korea surmises that Trump’s commitment to denuclearisation as the premise of any negotiation is malleable at best, as the president alternates between supporting such a goal and admitting that North Korea is a ‘nuclear power’,” Cha said. Observing the US war against Iran might have convinced North Korea that maintaining contact was the best way to manage Trump’s unpredictability, Cha added. “Kim may target a meeting with Trump, potentially after a US midterm election loss for the party in power,” Cha said, suggesting a possible return to a framework on improved ties and denuclearisation reached in Singapore in 2018. He added that Pyongyang’s diplomatic strategy might also extend to Tokyo. “The best chance for engagement is with someone of Takaichi’s ilk – a hawkish, not dovish, leader,” Cha said, noting Kim could seek to revive a declaration Japan and North Korea reached in 2002 to unlock billions in economic aid and normalisation settlements. The 2002 agreement, signed by then Japanese prime minister Junichiro Koizumi and late North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, pledged mutual efforts towards diplomatic normalisation alongside progress on the abduction issue, economic aid and nuclear compliance. “Pyongyang’s goal is to achieve a position where the North Korean leader has summits with both the US and Japan – a feat not accomplished by any previous leader – as a nuclear weapons state, while dividing US-Japan-South Korea trilateral cooperation,” Cha said. However, interests may not align. “Takaichi may justifiably see too much risk in such diplomacy,” he said. “But she may also see opportunity in trying to reduce the threat of North Korean short-range missiles aimed at Japan, whereas Trump cares only about long-range ballistic missiles targeted at the US.” Direct engagement with South Korea was off the table, Cha said, pointing to Pyongyang’s definition of ties as those between “two hostile states”. But he said Beijing could play a role in promoting Trump-Kim diplomacy to ingratiate itself with Trump while counterbalancing Russia’s growing influence over North Korea. Pak Seong-bin, a Japanese affairs expert at Ajou University in South Korea, said there were too many obstacles standing in the way of North Korea resuming dialogue with Japan. “Dialogue between North Korea and Japan could take place only after a breakthrough is made through US-North Korea talks, including on the nuclear issue,” he said. Beyond geopolitics, the Games serve a vital domestic function for Pyongyang. Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said sending a record delegation signalled confidence in the stability of its political system and offered a low-risk platform for state propaganda. “By taking part in international sports exchanges, which are relatively insulated from international sanctions, North Korea can project the image of a normal state,” Yang said, adding that victories against rivals like South Korea or Japan would be heavily featured at home to showcase the “superiority” of the North Korean system. The North is also expected to mobilise pro-Pyongyang Koreans living in Japan to project solidarity, while strictly enforcing isolation between its delegation and South Korean athletes and officials. “Particular attention should be paid to possible tensions during direct South Korea-North Korea matchups, including the women’s football match scheduled for September 21,” Yang said. “Such encounters could involve considerable psychological and verbal sparring between the two sides.” North Korea performed well at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games, finishing 10th overall with 11 gold, 18 silver and 10 bronze medals – winning a six-gold sweep in weightlifting.

title: Opinion | CityU’s response to disco night ‘misconduct’ an overreaction
description: Two adults, both at least partially dressed, took part in some harmless fun. Where is the crime in that?
content: In response to the August 27 case of a young man lifting up and carrying a young woman at a party, City University authorities have established a student discipline panel. The man was reportedly half-naked while the woman was clad in only shorts and a bra. Am I the only person to think that a mountain is being made out of a molehill here? We run the risk of using a sledgehammer to crack the proverbial small nut. One aspect of this case does merit further examination: the issue of consent. Who among those attending what was essentially a private gathering consented to be filmed? Who among the students present at the event thought it was acceptable to film proceedings at a closed function and release the footage to social media? If anyone is to be disciplined in this case, it should be that person, for intruding on the privacy of fellow students, betraying their classmates’ trust and perhaps tarnishing the reputation of the institution. It is the practice of local universities to organise orientation events to help young adults cope with the transition from a heavily scripted secondary school setting to the more freewheeling atmosphere of life in a tertiary institution. However, some of our universities have run into controversy with these well-intended programmes. There have been allegations of various types of misconduct: a groping incident at the University of Hong Kong, reports of voyeurism at Education University and a kissing game at Lingnan University. To help prevent similar incidents at City University, the authorities there require all organisations putting on such programmes to undergo anti-sexual harassment training. This is entirely appropriate. The fact that activities are taking place in an informal setting is not an excuse for misbehaviour by a small number of individuals. Criminal activity should always be called out and handled by the police. It is not a matter for student discipline. The Management Sciences Society of the university’s student union organised a three-day programme with the reported aim of helping new students understand university life and prepare for their academic studies and growth. At the end of the first day’s formal proceedings, there was a disco party so students could mingle and get to know each other in a more informal setting. There are several important points to note: the incident took place in the students’ own time after the main work had finished; the event itself was not open to the public; and the ethos of the event was informal, with the objective of breaking down barriers. There is no hint in the media reports that what took place was not consensual. So we have two adults, both at least partially dressed, neither under duress nor pressure of any kind, taking part in some harmless fun of their own free will. Where is the crime in that? Finally, there is the matter of clothing, and here I detect a clear case of double standards. Let’s be honest: nobody cares that the man was shirtless. All the attention has been focused on the report that the woman was wearing only a bra above the waist. What is deemed appropriate clothing in any setting depends on the circumstances. As we go about our daily lives, we often see people exercising in public. Men are sometimes in shorts and a singlet, while women wear similar relaxed clothing. Form-fitting clothing is worn openly on the street and in shopping malls as people head to and from exercise classes. It is a similar case at our beaches and swimming pools. Every day, men and women enjoy themselves in swimming shorts and bikinis. We think nothing of it; we just shrug and move on. That is what the university authorities should have done in this case. The main point is that this course was not designed to equip kindergarten children to cope with life in primary school; it was intended to help young adults transition from a school setting to life in college. These students were not in class and the serious part of proceedings for the day had already ended. They were attending a disco party in their own time and deserved their privacy. The local media would also benefit from some maturity. In my days as a reporter half a century ago, we asked three questions of any news report coming in: anyone dead, anyone injured, anyone naked? If all three were negative, there was not really much of a story.

title: Concert proposal in China stirs controversy when woman’s reaction blocks, angers spectators
description: As clip went viral, discussions about incident garnered over 110 million views, challenging the romanticised perception of public engagements.
content: A romantic marriage proposal at a concert in northern China attracted significant backlash after the couple blocked the view of other spectators, leading to numerous complaints. On September 12, Chinese folk singer Zhao Lei performed at Beijing’s National Stadium, known as the Bird’s Nest. As tens of thousands of fans sang along, a man in the front section of the audience stood up to propose to his partner. Videos circulating online featured the woman in a white wedding dress, complete with a veil. Overcome with emotion, she stood up, raised her arms, and waved towards the stage. However, this romantic moment sparked vocal complaints from fans seated behind the couple, who expressed frustration at having their view obstructed. A viral clip clearly captured many attendees shouting: “Sit down!” Before the proposal, the couple had also distributed wedding candies by tossing them towards nearby audience members, prompting security staff to intervene. Some attendees were heard saying: “That’s enough, stop throwing them!” The individual who recorded the video, identifying only as Xie, noted that the couple remained standing for more than five minutes, leaving those behind them “completely unable to see the stage.” After the clip went viral, discussions about the incident garnered over 110 million views on mainland social media platforms. Many users criticised the couple’s actions, arguing that concertgoers had paid to see their favourite singer perform, not to witness a stranger’s personal celebration. “The audience was already being polite by merely shouting ‘sit down.’ If it were me, I would have shouted ‘get divorced,’” one commenter remarked. Another user commented: “A proposal at a concert feels awkward because no one is truly concerned about your happiness.” Conversely, some urged for greater understanding from the audience. A widely shared comment read: “A proposal deserves congratulations as long as it does not inconvenience others. The couple could have quietly exchanged rings or waited until the concert ended.” Following the incident, the couple requested the removal of the viral clip and indicated that they had contacted the police, according to Jin Evening News. Concert proposals have long been popular in China and were once regarded as highly romantic gestures. However, the incident at Zhao’s concert challenged this perception, with some fans asserting that romance should not infringe on others’ rights. In September, singer Li Ronghao’s concert in Chengdu, southwest China, saw multiple couples proposing. Li expressed that he was honoured to witness these happy moments and playfully stated that he had become a “wedding host.” This trend has also sparked a niche resale market for concert seats that hold symbolic meanings. Seats with numbers linked to phrases such as “I love you” or “forever” are often considered ideal spots for proposals. Reports indicated that at Jay Chou’s Hong Kong concert, a pair of adjacent seats numbered 13 and 14 was resold by ticket scalpers for 12,013 yuan (US$1,800), while a single ticket originally cost HK$1,380 (US$180). The numbers 13 and 14, when combined, sound similar to “one life, one lifetime” in Mandarin, signifying “a whole lifetime.” One ticket scalper even shared tips on how to attract attention from stage cameras and performers, noting that the more dramatic the action, the greater the likelihood of being featured on screen. In China, however, ticket scalping is illegal, with serious cases potentially leading to criminal penalties.

title: India, Pakistan summon each other’s diplomats after naval ships collide in Arabian Sea
description: This is the first overt military tension between the nuclear-armed neighbours since they engaged in a four-day conflict last year.
content: New Delhi and Islamabad summoned each other’s top diplomats to lodge strong protests after an Indian and a Pakistani naval vessel collided in international waters. India’s foreign ministry said that it had called in Pakistan’s senior envoy to formally register a strong objection over what it said was “unacceptable and unprofessional conduct” of Pakistani naval units that led to a collision with an Indian warship. Pakistan’s foreign ministry also said it had officially called upon the charge d'affaires of the Indian High Commission in Islamabad to convey disapproval over what it called “highly provocative and unacceptable action” by an Indian navy vessel. This was the first overt military tension between the nuclear-armed neighbours since they engaged in a fierce four-day military conflict last year that raised fears of a wider war before a ceasefire was reached. Both sides blamed the other for the incident late on Tuesday. Indian sources said the collision occurred when a Pakistani naval ship moved closer to a frontline Indian warship on a routine surveillance mission in the north Arabian Sea at high speed. The impact did not cause any major damage, but Pakistan’s conduct was “in direct contravention” of a 1991 agreement between the two countries governing military exercises, manoeuvres, and troop movements, the Indian ⁠foreign ministry said. The agreement mandates that naval ships and submarines of the countries should keep a distance of at least three nautical miles from each other to avoid any accident in international waters. “The charge d’affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides ‌in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents,” the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. The top Indian diplomat in Islamabad was also instructed to lodge a similar protest with Pakistan’s foreign ministry, it said. The Pakistani foreign ministry, however, said later on Wednesday that the Indian vessel had carried out “aggressive manoeuvres in dangerously close proximity” to a Pakistani naval ship that was taking part in biennial exercises, and the charge d’affaires had been asked to convey to the Indian government that the country rejected the Indian action. “The charge d’affaires of the Pakistan High Commission in New Delhi will lodge the same demarche with India’s Ministry of External Affairs”, the foreign ministry statement said. India and Pakistan do not have ambassadors in each other’s capitals as they downgraded their diplomatic relations over their Kashmir dispute in 2019, with their missions headed by a charge d’affaires since. The arch-rivals have fought three major wars, two of them over Kashmir – which is divided between them but claimed in full by both – and numerous armed skirmishes since independence from British colonial India in 1947. In May 2025, the two countries fought a deadly four-day conflict after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in Kashmir. Delhi blamed Islamabad for the attack, a charge Pakistan denied. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Gold rebounds after Fed rate rise as banks back long-term demand outlook
description: Investment banks say central bank purchases and demand from China and India should support bullion prices.
content: Gold prices bounced back after the US Federal Reserve’s interest rate increase, as analysts and investment banks maintained a positive long-term outlook for the metal, citing structural challenges facing the world’s largest economy. Spot gold traded at US$4,326 an ounce at 4pm on Thursday in Hong Kong, up 1.52 per cent since the market opened at noon. The bullion once dived as much as 2.7 per cent to US$4,234 at 3am in Hong Kong, right after the Fed meeting. The US central bank announced a widely expected 0.25 percentage-point rate rise early on Thursday, its first in three years, with the new Fed chair Kevin Warsh saying inflation had remained “too high for too long”. The move followed weeks of market expectations for a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s September meeting, amid persistent inflationary pressures and renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Investors were now shifting their focus to whether the Fed would raise rates again, a move that could trigger short-term volatility in gold prices, said Kenny Ng Lai-yin, a strategist at Everbright Securities International. He projected one more Fed rate increase by year-end. Nearly 50 per cent of traders were betting on another 0.25 percentage-point rise in October, up from 43.5 per cent before the Fed meeting, according to CME FedWatch data based on Fed funds futures contracts on Thursday. “But in the long run, the Fed rates will head downwards again because the United States is facing structural economic challenges, huge government debt and declining global central bank holdings of US Treasury,” Ng said. Those factors could help push gold prices back to US$5,000 per ounce again next year, Ng added. Meanwhile, UBS urged investors to look beyond a single Fed rate decision, arguing that purchases from central banks and recovering demand from China and India should support gold prices in the final quarter of the year, according to a note on Monday. “Gold may still be vulnerable to hawkish surprises, but it appears increasingly more sensitive to positive catalysts,” said Joni Teves, precious metals strategist on the global economics and strategy research team at the Swiss bank. Julius Baer shared a similar view that rate rises themselves, historically, had little market impact when fully anticipated. The bank cited market performance across 20 rate-rise days under former Fed chairs Janet Yellen and Jerome Powell. After hitting an all-time high of above US$5,400 per ounce in January, gold prices surrendered as much as one-third of their gains this year amid concerns over the US-Israel war on Iran and soaring debt linked to major US artificial intelligence firms. The metal regained investor interest in late July amid global diversification from the sell-off of artificial intelligence and semiconductor stocks. UBS also said central banks continued to add to their gold reserves at “historically meaningful rates”. China increased its gold holdings for a 22nd consecutive month in August by some 650,000 ounces to reach 76.73 million ounces, while the Dutch central bank decided to move around 85 tonnes of gold from the US and Canada to London. “Strong reported purchases would reassure investors that official demand can continue to support the market amid headwinds from expected Fed tightening,” Teves of UBS said. ANZ analysts Soni Kumari and Daniel Hynes said in a report last week that US rate rises were unlikely to obstruct gold’s recovery. “Gold’s sensitivity to US yields is shifting. Fiscal stress is becoming more relevant for gold, with investors increasingly focused on debt sustainability and currency debasement following the latest US Treasury intervention,” they wrote. Institutional banks from JP Morgan to Goldman Sachs projected gold prices to range between US$4,500 and US$4,900 an ounce by the end of the year, according to their previous forecasts.

title: Japan’s Natuna port proposal highlights Indonesia’s balancing act on China
description: Tokyo offers port upgrades to boost maritime security, but analysts say Jakarta is being pragmatic, not taking sides against Beijing.
content: Japan’s proposed port upgrades in Indonesia’s Natuna Islands reflect Tokyo’s push to bolster South China Sea security without building an overt military footprint. However, analysts stress that the move does not mean Jakarta is siding with Japan in its efforts to contain Beijing. Japan, which earlier this year eased its restrictions on lethal weapons exports, is ramping up security cooperation with Indonesia – a crucial bellwether for Southeast Asia. The expanding partnership includes joint defence industry development, intelligence cooperation and expanded military exercises in strategic waterways. Citing Japanese government sources, Kyodo News reported earlier this month that Tokyo was planning to use its official development assistance to help upgrade Indonesia’s fishing ports to allow patrol vessels to operate in more areas. According to the report, one potential location will be the Natuna Islands, which lie along the southern edge of China’s nine-dash line – a boundary outlining Beijing’s expansive claims in the South China Sea. In a commentary, state-owned Global Times framed Japan’s offer as a geopolitical tactic to expand Tokyo’s intelligence gathering and strengthen its presence in the South China Sea. “Japan seeks to push countries like Indonesia to the front lines of South China Sea rivalry, while hiding behind the scenes to orchestrate its ‘proxy gambit’,” it said. “This allows Japan to avoid risks of direct confrontation yet reap intelligence and strategic dividends. Indonesia and other Asean nations must be particularly vigilant against this ‘wolf in sheep’s clothing’ ploy,” it continued. The Natuna Islands lie to the northeast of Sumatra and west of Borneo in the South China Sea. The archipelago and its adjacent waters – officially named the North Natuna Sea by Indonesia in 2017 – sit astride a key shipping route. The area is also a hotspot for commercial fishing. Chinese, Vietnamese and Indonesian fishing vessels, often escorted by coastguard ships, have occasionally clashed over marine resources in recent years. Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, noted that Jakarta’s push to upgrade the remote resource-rich islands served both economic and sovereign ends. He said that policymakers in Jakarta had long been wary of foreign military presence in the region, especially the Chinese. “Indonesia has sought to develop Natuna Islands, particularly its fishing resources, and has looked to expand its military presence in the region so as to consolidate its control in the region,” he said. Chaula Rininta Anindya, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Indonesia, noted that the project was expected to address the “grey-zone” tactics Jakarta faced in the North Natuna Sea by bolstering frontline maritime deterrence. However, she said the plan was broader than a simple response to South China Sea issues. Rather, she said, it reflected Indonesia’s attempt to enhance its “Large Islands Defence” strategy through the dual use of ports – hosting civilian vessels as well as military and coastguard fleets when needed. Under its “Free and Open Indo-Pacific” strategy, Tokyo has prioritised helping Southeast Asian partners build capacity and increase awareness of maritime threats so they can safeguard critical sea lanes. Heng Yee Kuang, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said efforts to upgrade fishing ports were a result of the Japan-Indonesia summit in March. At that meeting, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi emphasised cooperation in the fisheries industry, especially as Indonesia faced challenges related to illegal fishing and smuggling in the South China Sea, according to Heng. He added that the initiative illustrated the continuity of cooperation between the two countries, as Japan had provided patrol boats for the Indonesian coastguard since the early 2000s. The stakes for Japan are significant. Roughly 80 per cent of its energy imports and much of its maritime trade flow through the South China Sea, making stable sea lanes a core national interest. “Indonesia’s importance to Japan has grown because of its geostrategic archipelagic location astride maritime chokepoints and key shipping lanes within Japan’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific Vision. Helping Indonesia address its maritime challenges is also in Japan’s enlightened self-interest,” Heng said. However, Beijing has become increasingly alarmed by Tokyo’s growing security footprint in the region amid a downturn in Sino-Japanese ties. Chen said that by offering security aid to Southeast Asia, Tokyo might be trying to distract Beijing from territorial disputes in the East China Sea. “In a sense, Japan is … hoping to use the Southeast Asia region to relieve pressure or draw attention away from the East China Sea,” he said. “More importantly, I think Japan is now engaged in a full-spectrum competition against China, not just in northeast Asia but in Southeast Asia as well, in terms of the economy, the military and diplomatic influence,” Chen said. In the past two years, Japan and the Philippines have signed two deals to strengthen the logistics and sustainment capabilities of their armed forces, including the Reciprocal Access Agreement, which came into force last September. At a defence ministers’ meeting in Jakarta in May, Japan and Indonesia signed a defence cooperation agreement covering military personnel development, defence industry collaboration and a mechanism for integrated defence dialogues. It institutionalises exchanges between senior officials and operational-level engagements between Japan’s Self-Defence Forces and Indonesia’s armed forces. More crucially, the two sides also agreed to explore cooperation on defence equipment and technology aimed at boosting maritime deterrence, opening the door to future Japanese arms transfers. Anindya said Indonesia’s role as the largest country in Southeast Asia – by size and by population – and its critical role as a co-founder of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) had made it an agenda setter in the region. “It seems that Japan is expecting Indonesia to share a common understanding on the issue in the region, then the message could be conveyed as well at the regional level,” she said. She added that military cooperation between Indonesia and Japan should not be seen as an alliance to counter China but a pragmatic strategy by Jakarta to work with its partners around the world. “Indonesia is simply being pragmatic, and I believe it does not want to risk escalating tension with China. Indonesia will be careful in establishing cooperation with various countries and will remain committed to its ‘free and active’ foreign policy,” she said. Heng noted that Japan and Indonesia did not yet have an intelligence-sharing framework for sensitive information. He said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto had also been careful to balance relations with China, “so Beijing can be reassured on this point”.

title: You can now buy Kau Kee’s fish balls, used in almost 1,000 Hong Kong shops
description: The company’s second-generation owner explains why the factory has opened its first retail shop in Mong Kok.
content:
Anita Lee Yan-kwan grew up in a family business that sold fish balls to street food stalls and restaurants in Hong Kong.
For many years, the fish balls from Kau Kee Food Factory were known only to people in the industry.
But last December, Lee, the second generation in her family to run the business, opened the company’s first retail store for everyday customers. It is located in Mong Kok.
For 66 years, Kau Kee has provided fish balls to almost 1,000 eateries and stalls around Hong Kong.
“Before opening the retail shop, if you were to ask people about Kau Kee on the street, they would probably not know about it,” Lee said. “Yet it’s likely almost every Hongkonger has eaten our fish balls.”
The 30-year-old used to work in the government. She changed careers during the Covid-19 pandemic and took over the family business. At the time, street food vendors were struggling to attract customers, so shops were ordering fewer fish balls. In 2023, Lee launched the company’s first online store to sell directly to consumers.
Lee wants to make sure that her family’s business can continue for many years to come.

title: Only ‘idiots’ expect North Korea to give up nuclear weapons: Kim Yo-jong
description: The powerful sister of leader Kim Jong-un says ‘familiar silly talk’ about denuclearisation will not change the country’s status.
content: The powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un said on Thursday that the country’s nuclear-armed status was “absolute”, calling those hoping for its denuclearisation “idiots”. North Korea has legally enshrined its status as a nuclear weapons state, with its leadership declaring the country’s nuclear arsenal permanent and irreversible.
