US President Donald Trump recently said Pyongyang possessed 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons, with Seoul putting the figure at between 80 and 120. “The DPRK’s position as a nuclear weapons state is absolute, which cannot be reversed by anything,” Kim Yo-jong said, using initials for the North’s official name, the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal “makes a significant contribution to deterring the outrageous acts of international rogues”, she said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency. Kim’s statement came during the ongoing General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency in Vienna, where she said the “familiar silly talk” of efforts to denuclearise the North was expected. “If they believe that it is really possible, they will only hear the word of idiots,” she said. “No matter how rhetorically the hostile forces may deny, the reality in which the nuclear position of the DPRK has been permanently settled physically and legally cannot change even a bit.” The North’s nuclear arsenal has expanded since a second summit between Kim and Trump collapsed in 2019 over what Pyongyang would receive in return for taking steps towards denuclearisation. On Saturday, a day after the US, South Korea and Japan ended a trilateral military drill that Pyongyang views as a provocation, North Korea launched multiple short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea. North Korea’s ballistic missile launches, the first in about three weeks, came as the country was continuing its weapons display after rebuffing Trump’s decision to scale back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea in a goodwill gesture. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected the launches of several missiles from North Korea’s eastern coastal Wonsan area. It said the missiles flew about 250km (155 miles) each in a direction towards North Korea’s eastern waters. The Joint Chiefs of Staff said it had boosted its surveillance posture and was closely exchanging information on the launches with the US and Japan. The US Pacific Command said the North’s launch event did not pose an immediate threat to US territory or to its allies. It said the US remained committed to the defence of the US homeland and its allies in the region. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Hong Kong’s 5-year plan, policy continuity offer investors more stability, experts say
description: Explicit directions set by John Lee seen as ensuring persistence in policies even if there are changes in government leadership.
content: Longer-term vision and policies with continuity mapped out in Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan, along with the latest policy blueprint, offer investment opportunities and greater stability for investors, according to experts and commentators. Hong Kong marked a historic milestone on Wednesday when Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out the city’s first five-year development plan with his fifth policy address to align with China’s long-term national strategy. The explicit directions Lee set for Hong Kong in terms of economic and social development are seen as ensuring policy continuity even if there are changes in government leadership. This is Lee’s final policy address of his current five-year term as chief executive. “It is an important start,” Our Hong Kong Foundation vice-president Kenny Shui Chi-wai said. “For the first time, the message is clear on the purposes of the two documents. The five-year plan provides mid- to long-term vision with indicators, and the policy address stipulates how to attain the goals.” The 22 indicators in the five-year plan include five binding and 17 anticipatory goals, which will be covered in Lee’s annual work report to Chinese President Xi Jinping. In the 60,000-word five-year plan running to 2030, Lee spelled out the city’s core positioning under the “four centres, one hub” concept, which refers to Hong Kong as a financial, maritime, aviation and trade centre, as well as a high-calibre talent hub. The policy address, at over 40,000 words, offers five major development opportunities spanning talent, industry, business investment, institutional safeguards and international cooperation. This is in addition to 25 key livelihood initiatives ranging from youth development, housing and healthcare to artificial intelligence and education. SCMP · Hong Kong’s 5-year plan, policy continuity offer investors more stability, experts say “Many of the developments mean investment opportunities, for example, the Northern Metropolis project,” Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce CEO Patrick Yeung Wai-tim said. “This time, it gives investors more confidence because previously, the policies on the Northern Metropolis were less organised.” The centrepiece of development will be the 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis, a business, education and housing megaproject near the border with Shenzhen. It will serve the important strategic goals of promoting high-standard tertiary education via a university town, innovation and technology, industrial development and talent aggregation, aligning with the national five-year plan. The megaproject is subject to a binding target of raising “spade-ready sites” from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030. Other anticipatory goals include increasing the number of completed homes in the Northern Metropolis to 70,000 from the current 11,000, hitting an average annual increase of 4 to 5 per cent in the number of companies in Hong Kong with parent firms located outside the city, and boosting the value-add of the tourism industry to HK$126 billion (US$16.1 billion) from HK$86.2 billion during the five-year period. Hannah Jeong, head of valuation and advisory services with CBRE Hong Kong, said the five-year plan offered the Northern Metropolis “its clearest and most actionable” timeline yet. “The next chapter will be defined not by planning ambition but by execution discipline: whether the commercial frameworks attract real capital, whether the transport milestones hold, and whether the talent the university towns are designed to attract actually chooses to live and work in the Northern Metropolis,” she said. Lee’s call to expedite the building of an international gold trading market and the city’s offshore renminbi businesses, developing an international asset and wealth management centre and risk management centre, enhancing the securities market and expanding fixed-income and commodity trading, also presents greater opportunities to local and foreign investors. Billy Mak Sui-choi, an associate professor at Baptist University’s accountancy, economics and finance department, pointed to the five-year plan’s emphasis on yuan globalisation, saying it would create synergies with the annual policy and drive the gold trade while consolidating the city’s status as a foreign exchange hub. “The current problem with offshore renminbi is that its functions are too limited, and the policy address makes it clear that Hong Kong will expand the sales, valuation and clearance of renminbi-denominated assets in the city,” he said. “When this is promoted, it will help Hong Kong with its foreign exchange business.” Hong Kong is China’s largest offshore yuan business hub, with 1.1 trillion yuan in offshore deposits as of June and handling more than 70 per cent of all global offshore yuan payments, according to official statistics. According to Mak, the yuan push went hand in hand with Hong Kong’s vision to build a commodities ecosystem, especially with measures to expand gold trading in the city, as backing renminbi-denominated assets with gold bullion stored in Hong Kong would offer more assurance to investors. “If Hong Kong, as an offshore renminbi centre, is to further develop the offshore renminbi market, it needs gold to serve as a backup,” he said. “Putting the two together is just the right fit.” Andrew Gaw, managing director of trader Solid Gold Investments, said the precious metal was a hot asset and gold trading was crucial to the city’s strength as a global financial centre. “Many investors are sceptical about the US dollar and want to diversify into gold to hedge investment risks,” he said. “China is a huge market, which means huge opportunities for Hong Kong, so what the government should do is to bring the two markets even closer.” However, Hong Kong is facing strong competition from markets such as London and Singapore in the gold business. Gold prices jumped about 17 per cent over the past year to HK$34,099 per ounce on Wednesday. Yeung of the chamber said gold trading also served to strengthen the financial security of the city and even the country amid intensifying Sino-US rivalry. “Hong Kong has built a solid foundation in its standing as an international financial centre, which has become an alternative market for gold investors and risk management,” he said. In February, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowed to scrutinise more closely Beijing’s use of Hong Kong for sandbox experiments in gold-backed digital assets that could rival the US dollar. Shui of the think tank said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s plan to introduce a tendering mechanism for seven-day offshore renminbi liquidity and explore issuing short-term debt instruments was among the investor-friendly measures to boost the currency’s liquidity. He pointed out that government safeguards and initiatives such as building a global capital of mediation and combating the use of artificial intelligence in criminal activities would offer protection to investors. “In light of the controversies surrounding AI developers like Anthropic and DeepSeek, the AI initiative will at least offer some legal protection, like what the EU and South Korea are offering,” Shui said. The European Union and South Korea heavily penalise perpetrators of scams using AI. Yeung of the chamber said the series of investment opportunities, particularly in the Northern Metropolis, would drive the city’s economic growth in coming years, benefitting livelihoods. “What we will see is a major transformation in Hong Kong,” he said. “The city has to grasp this critical window of opportunity, even though the Northern Metropolis development is very much like crossing the river by feeling the stones.” Additional reporting by Leopold Chen

title: US rate increase should only have short-term impact on Hong Kong stocks: CICC
description: Rise in US interest rates could put pressure on Hong Kong stocks, but the impact is likely to be short-lived, investment bank says.
content: Hong Kong stocks could face greater volatility from renewed US monetary tightening, but the impact should be short-lived unless the Federal Reserve embarks on a sustained rate-increase cycle, according to China International Capital Corporation (CICC). The Fed rate increase would not necessarily spell losses for Hong Kong stocks, as monetary conditions were only one of several factors driving the market, said Liu Gang, chief offshore China and overseas strategist and managing director at CICC Research. “When fundamentals can outweigh [the impact of higher rates], it is not a major factor,” Liu said at a media briefing on Wednesday afternoon. But Hong Kong stocks currently appeared vulnerable to changes in US Treasury yields and global liquidity, as China’s domestic fundamentals remained relatively weak, Liu said. “When overall fundamentals are not that strong – and that happens to be the situation now – it will amplify the market’s reaction to US Treasury yields,” Liu said. “That is also why we have seen relatively more market reaction and concern in recent days.” The US central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage points on Thursday for the first time since 2023 to curb persistent inflation. The duration of any Fed tightening would be critical, according to Liu. A prolonged cycle similar to 2022 would put broad pressure on global assets, while a brief or relatively dovish increase might only have a temporary effect, particularly if tighter policy had already been priced in by investors, he said. Hong Kong stocks have already underperformed relative to the global market this year despite a stronger yuan, dashing market expectations at the end of last year that a rising yuan would attract foreign capital inflows and lift the market. The city’s benchmark Hang Seng Index was down 3.6 per cent for the year as of Wednesday’s close, while the tech-focused Hang Seng Tech Index was down by more than 20 per cent. Liu attributed the underperformance partly to the composition of the Hong Kong market, which has greater exposure to weaker parts of China’s economy, including consumer goods, e-commerce and electric vehicles. Meanwhile, much of this year’s technology rally has been driven by mainland-listed hardware and tech companies. Liquidity conditions have also tightened in Hong Kong, as capital inflows from the mainland have slowed from last year, a heavy pipeline of initial public offerings has absorbed market liquidity, and higher US Treasury yields have added an external headwind, according to CICC. CICC maintained its view that Hong Kong’s benchmark indexes would remain rangebound, as the factors needed for a substantial improvement – such as a fiscal stimulus or recovery in private-sector credit flows on the mainland – did not appear to be emerging, according to Liu. A sustained rebound would only be triggered by something like another “924 moment” – a reference to the stimulus package launched by Beijing in September 2024 – or a “DeepSeek moment”, where the artificial intelligence start-up’s success sparked a wave of investment into Chinese tech stocks last year, Liu said.

title: Hong Kong Premier League on up but Kitchee face AFC Champions League test against Koreans
description: Local champions poised to begin continental campaign against Gangwon FC at Mong Kok Stadium on Thursday.
content: Although he cheesed off some of his England players when he accused them of being “sloppy” and committing “lots of technical mistakes” following their World Cup quarter-final victory over Norway this summer, Thomas Tuchel’s angst perhaps stemmed from the knowledge that a much tougher test was around the corner. So it would prove, the head coach’s team punch-drunk by the end of their semi-final capitulation against Argentina. For Tuchel two months ago, and indeed Alex Ferguson after the 1983 Scottish Cup final when he labelled his victorious Aberdeen side a “disgrace”, read Inigo Calderon, the Kitchee head coach, last weekend. It has been a bright start to the local Premier League season, with four-figure crowds increasingly the norm for a regular diet of competitive and unpredictable matches. Nonetheless, the acid test for whether we are seeing genuine improvement will be supplied when the AFC Champions League 2 begins this week. With Tai Po a shadow of their former selves and probably in for a rough ride away against Adelaide City on Thursday, it is Kitchee that will shoulder the responsibility of positioning Hong Kong football back on the continental map. They start against powerful Gangwon FC at Mong Kok Stadium, also on Thursday, but with the unheralded pair of Phnom Penh Crown and Kuching City completing their group, the local champions should have designs on becoming the first Hong Kong club to legitimately advance to a continental knockout round since they themselves did it in 2016. Although Kitchee progressed in 2022, they needed only a pair of wins against Chiangrai United to escape their group in a truncated, joyless Covid-19-affected AFC Champions League. Kitchee won 3-1 at Southern on Saturday, but any players expecting a pat on the back from their boss afterwards were in for a rude awakening. Calderon gathered his squad together on the boggy Aberdeen Sports Ground surface and issued a furious dressing down. When he had had his say, the Spaniard angrily marched alone back to the changing room. His poise recovered about 45 minutes later, Calderon said that at 2-0 up and seemingly cruising, he suspected some players’ minds had begun drifting towards the more glamorous Gangwon fixture. “When you’re winning, it’s easy to start thinking, ‘Let’s try to not get injured, I want to play on Thursday’,” Calderon said. He accepted that self-preservation in the circumstances was natural, and Calderon had himself nodded towards the bigger test as he substituted a series of key figures. The young right-back Jay Haddow’s reward for keeping going at full pelt was to sustain what he suspected was a hamstring tear in the closing minutes. Hobbling off to hospital afterwards, he was devastated. With Victor Camarasa, the former Cardiff City midfielder, sent off shortly after Haddow’s enforced withdrawal, Kitchee found themselves down to nine men and under siege. “Everything you don’t want when you talk about controlling a game,” Calderon said, alighting on the primary cause of his irritation. Repeat their indiscipline against streetwise South Koreans Gangwon and Kitchee will be punished. “We suddenly started missing easy passes,” Calderon said. “I don’t know if it’s because we were tired, or whether it was a lack of concentration. We were too open, which is the last thing you want when you’re winning. “I hope they learn, and it’s always better to learn when you win. [Against Gangwon], we need to have more personality and to keep the ball better.” Only midfielder Tan Chun-lok remains from the Kitchee team that last played an Asian match, the meaningless 2-0 win against Lion City Sailors in December 2023 that concluded an otherwise miserable group-stage effort. Classy young defender Jason Kam Chi-kin, an unused substitute for three of those six matches, could potentially make his continental bow this week. The 22-year-old grew in stature over 19 league appearances during a breakthrough campaign last season, emerging as one of Hong Kong’s most elegant and effective defenders, and winning the first of three senior international caps in March. Kam has wanted for action this term following the summer arrivals of central defensive duo Dudu and Marcao, but he came on against Southern and was surely one of the players exempt from Calderon’s criticism. “He told us we need to have the guts to play the ball and not just kick it away, even when we’re players down and the opponents all press,” Kam said. “It’s more of a challenge for me this season, but mentally, I have to force it. “Lots of young players have one big season, then disappear in the next one. I don’t want to be one of them.” Preparing to manage in Asian competition for the first time, Calderon has leaned on the collective experience of Fernando Recio, Jordi Tarres and Ken Ng Kin, his assistant, technical director and boss, respectively. Recio and Tarres both played Asian football for Kitchee. “I’m the new one here,” Calderon said, acknowledging that, for the first time since he took over last summer, Kitchee would enter a match “knowing that we are worse than our opponents”. “We’ll have less of the ball, which is something we don’t really like,” Calderon said. Calderon has occasionally deployed a back three and should he choose to go that way against Gangwon, it could open the door for Kam. Regardless of his set-up, the Basque manager vowed to not compromise on his attacking ideals. “When I was managing Bristol Rovers, we went to Ipswich in the FA Cup [in January 2025]; they were in the Premier League, but we didn’t change,” he said. “I don’t know another way, I can’t sit back and counter-attack.” Music to the ears of Kam: christened Bec-Kam-bauer by supporters in recognition of his ability to surge from defence with the ball at his feet. “The biggest challenge will be the tempo of the game; we don’t have enough quick matches in Hong Kong,” Kam said. “I want to figure out the distance between us and the top Asian clubs, so it’ll be a valuable experience for me.” Only last December, Kam questioned whether he was ready for Hong Kong recognition. Now he is prepared to acknowledge that he was disappointed to be told club duties would prevent him from competing in this month’s Asian Games. Currently following a dedicated gym programme, and enthusiastically embracing the instruction to eat more as he fills out his long, slender frame, the 1.9-metre (6ft 3in) Kam, who added 7kg in the 2025 off-season, said: “You only get one chance to go to an Asian Games, but I accepted it. It’s just the way it is. “I am believing in myself now. If I don’t, who will?” With Kitchee since the age of eight, Kam said he had noticed “football in Hong Kong getting more attention”. “But if we do well in ACL2, then there will be more attention from around the world,” he said. “Maybe more players will get opportunities in other countries.” Still, Calderon neatly summed up the scale of Kitchee’s task against a Gangwon side currently fifth in their strong domestic league. “If we play the perfect game, not like against Southern, and avoid them having a good game, we’ll have a chance,” he said. Elsewhere, Premier League newcomers Supreme Sha Tin have parted company with head coach Kenneth Kwok Kar-lok. Appointed this summer after previous boss Lo Kwan-yee was arrested on match-fixing charges, Kwok was at the helm for only four matches. He won his opening game against Eastern, but their 3-2 defeat by struggling Wofoo Kowloon City on Sunday was Supreme’s third straight loss and spelled the end for Kwok.

title: Will Takaichi visit Kyiv? Zelensky’s invite puts Japan PM in diplomatic bind
description: Analysts say a Ukraine trip will be an ‘excellent opportunity’ for Takaichi to show her mettle, despite concerns about chilly Russia ties.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s invitation for Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi to visit Kyiv has created a diplomatic dilemma for the Japanese leader, who is under pressure to show firmer support for Ukraine without further antagonising Russia. Zelensky extended the invitation through Eisuke Mori, speaker of Japan’s House of Representatives, during his visit to the Ukrainian capital earlier this week. Mori, who helped establish the cross-party Japan-Ukraine parliamentary friendship group in 1995, is widely regarded as one of Japan’s more experienced parliamentary voices on Ukraine and did not hold back during his visit. In a speech to the Supreme Council in Kyiv on Tuesday, Mori condemned the Russian invasion as “a barbaric act that shakes the international order and the values that the international community has built over decades”. He added that “unilateral changes to the status quo by force will never be tolerated”. In their meeting, Zelensky expressed his gratitude for the “solidarity” Mori showed, adding: “We will always be glad to welcome the prime minister of Japan, Sanae Takaichi, to Ukraine.” Zelensky has been working hard to convince more senior Western political figures to call on him in Kyiv – Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Britain’s former leader Boris Johnson have been recent visitors – and analysts say the invitation may have been a calculated effort to encourage Takaichi to state her support for Ukraine more explicitly. Still, it leaves the Japanese leader with a choice, analysts say. She can travel to Kyiv and win approval from Ukraine’s partners and some critics at home, but risk further antagonising Russian President Vladimir Putin at a time when Tokyo-Moscow relations are already at their lowest point in decades. Or she can delay and hope to preserve limited diplomatic space with Russia regarding Japan’s claims to northern islands seized by Soviet forces in 1945. That dispute over what Japan calls the Northern Territories and Russia terms the Southern Kurils has prevented both sides from signing a formal post-war peace treaty. Tokyo also relies on energy supplies from the Russian Far East, including liquefied natural gas from the Sakhalin-2 project. “Yes, Takaichi is in a difficult position, but she has brought it on herself because she did not respond more forcefully when Putin visited the disputed islands in August,” said James Brown, a professor of international relations specialising in Russian affairs at Temple University’s Tokyo campus. Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party is a “big tent party” with numerous factions, Brown pointed out, adding, “My sense is that there are many people in the party who were dissatisfied with her weak-kneed response to Putin’s visit and they are taking it on themselves to do what she would not.” Mori’s visit to Kyiv was the most high-profile demonstration of that, he said, with the house speaker clearly willing to take a more confrontational line towards Moscow. Go Ito, a professor of international relations at Tokyo’s Meiji University, says the invitation is an “excellent opportunity” for Takaichi to show her mettle. “I actually think that she would like to go in response to Putin going to the Northern Territories,” he told This Week in Asia. “It could very easily be seen as a mirror action, which would make it harder for Moscow to complain too loudly.” Perhaps a larger consideration would be Washington’s response, Ito said, with US President Donald Trump’s position on Ukraine fluctuating and difficult to predict. “I’m sure other Western leaders would like her to go and show her support – and it is conspicuous that she has not met Zelensky one-on-one so far – but Takaichi is very eager not to attract Trump’s attention,” he said. The Japanese government is working hard to keep the Trump administration onside as it navigates national security concerns and economic threats, notably tariffs on Japanese imports. Brown believes Takaichi could “diplomatically fudge” the issue by pleading domestic political challenges and sending Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi to Kyiv in her stead, or arranging a meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York next week. “Personally, my feeling is that she should go to Kyiv,” Brown said. “Why shouldn’t she? She’s a national leader, she has modelled herself as the ‘iron lady’ of Japanese politics and if other leaders have run the gauntlet of Russian missiles, then she should as well.” Any such visit to Russia’s battlefield enemy could worsen relations with Moscow, however. “Things can certainly get chillier,” Brown said. “Russia is always ready to apply more pressure, as we have seen with Putin’s visit to the disputed islands and the unveiling of a statue marking Russia’s victory over Japan in the war.” He also pointed to Russia’s use of proxies to set fire to the home of Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer last year, and an attempt to destroy a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig airport in August. In recent days, Moscow had visibly ratcheted up the pressure with a great deal of naval activity around Japan, Brown said. Russian warships have sailed through Japanese waters between mainland Japan and islands to the south of Tokyo that are administratively part of the city, apparently on course to circumnavigate the Japanese archipelago. A Russian intelligence-gathering vessel, meanwhile, has been operating in the Tsushima Strait between southern Japan and the southern tip of the Korean peninsula. “It would be very easy for Russian intelligence officers to use the tokoryu criminal groups to carry out mischief on their behalf here,” Brown said. “Japan has not directly sent weapons to Ukraine so far, but I can easily see a reaction from Russia if Takaichi did take that step.”

title: Tooro Kingdom mourns the untimely death of young King Oyo Nyimba
description: A bitter succession dispute follows as Uganda’s beloved monarch is laid to rest at 34 amid claims of an heir.
content:
King Oyo Nyimba of Uganda was once the youngest monarch in the world. He was buried on September 12 amid a bitter succession dispute that has troubled the royal family and captivated the nation.
The traditional monarch, who became the king of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995, died last month from cancer at the age of 34.
Elders from the ruling clan of the kingdom stated that Oyo, who was unmarried, never declared an heir to them. This contradicts the accounts of others in the kingdom, who claim that he left behind a son born out of wedlock.
The son has not been publicly identified, leading to sensational claims on social media about at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo’s children.
On September 9, a committee of Tooro elders announced their decision to select a prince who works as a journalist to succeed Oyo. The move was praised by traditionalists who desire an adult on the throne.
Oyo’s closest relatives expressed their disapproval. His sister, Ruth Komuntale, said the announcement sought to “bring division and turmoil”.
Queen mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death: “I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said. “Let us grieve and bury my son.”
In the East African country, many cherish traditional monarchs despite their lack of formal governing power.
Oyo was crowned king in 1995 at the tender age of three, following his father’s death. He was a curious child, dressed in colourful robes and became an object of adoration. During his coronation, he took part in a series of tribal rituals, including a significant coming-of-age ceremony.
The issue surrounding Oyo’s successor may still be brought before the courts, as his family claims that the Tooro elders have disregarded the will he left behind.
Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king and was a captivating figure, even for global leaders who met him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela.
Until he turned 18, Oyo was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom.
“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” said Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, in a eulogy posted on social media.
The late Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi developed a close friendship with the Tooro royal family, treating them as if they were part of his own family. He made several trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for many years before his death in October 2011.
After Uganda gained independence from British colonial rule, a republican president banned Uganda’s traditional kingdoms to unify the country.
These kingdoms were restored in 1993. Although they have no political power and are legally prohibited from taking part in partisan politics, the monarchs play an important role as guardians of tribal culture.

title: 4 plush shearling accessories for autumn, from Saint Laurent to Prada
description: From sandals to mittens, here are four shearling accessories worth investing in to keep you cosy through the cooler months.
content: Shearling accessories are always a favourite choice for the cosiest months of the year – they add warmth and texture to clean, sharp and minimalist looks. Here are four plush pieces to invest in this season. Burberry sandals Burberry’s Check Shearling Urchin sandals (HK$7,350) feature an embossed outer and adjustable jacquard-woven straps with the maison’s signature check motif in sand beige. It is fitted with logo canvas straps inspired by the ribbons used to tie gifts. They are crafted from sheepskin, offering natural insulation and protection against the cold.

title: Our cheat sheet for the best things to do in Hong Kong, September 17-26
description: Meet Ocean Park’s scaly new residents, a supersized patchwork cat at Hong Kong Design Centre, then enjoy the Wagyu masters’ offerings at Gyu+Bar by Miyoshi and wash it all down with a neon-inspired cocktail at The Pontiac.
content: DO THIS Reptile Territory at Ocean Park Hong Kong Not a fan of soft, furry critters? What about cold-blooded, scaly ones? Ocean Park Hong Kong cut the ribbon on its new reptile sanctuary late last month, so it’s high time to meet this cohort of four-legged tenants, from the plant-loving rhinoceros iguana and the endangered Chinese crocodile lizard to the stunning panther chameleon with its colour-changing abilities, the semi-aquatic sailfin lizard with its fan-like dorsal crest, the giant horned lizard that resembles an armoured dinosaur and more. Resident animal caretakers lead daily talks to introduce guests to these quirky species, offering an engaging learning experience. The Summit, Ocean Park Hong Kong, 180 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Aberdeen SEE THIS Meow‑cation – With Cats, We Connect As part of an initiative to bring communities together and encourage participation in the arts, the Hong Kong Design Centre invited more than 130 individuals to collaborate on stitching a supersized installation. “Meow‑cation – With Cats, We Connect”, running until November 2, reveals the result: a patchwork mass in the shape of a feline in mid-stretch. Harking back to Sham Shui Po’s enduring legacy of textile manufacturing and craftsmanship, the artwork – a visual cacophony of fabric, thread, buttons and zips, all sourced from the neighbourhood – is a tangible embodiment of the relationships between humans and cats. The Square, G/F, DX Design Hub, 280 Tung Chau Street, Sham Shui Po EAT THIS Gyu+Bar by Miyoshi Self-taught marvel Tsutomu Ito’s Hong Kong outpost opened quietly earlier this year, but with his recent visit to officially inaugurate the space comes a Wagyu-focused menu that distils the essence of his one-Michelin-star restaurant, Niku no Takumi Miyoshi, in Kyoto, into 10 refined courses. Starting with the slow-simmered truffle beef “wine” – a consommé to be swirled before enjoyed – through to such dishes as the delicate Wagyu sashimi, Wagyu sushi prepared in signature Miyoshi style (seared and chopped) and topped with a crown of sea urchin and caviar, and wood-fired Wagyu tenderloin, served with a trio of house-made condiments but also utterly scrumptious without, the meal journeys through technique, heat, texture, richness and aroma, exhibiting the versatility of the hero ingredient. Shop 401 & 404, 4/F, Lee Garden One, 33 Hysan Avenue, Causeway Bay DRINK THIS The Pontiac It’s time to rock ’n’ roll again at Hong Kong’s liveliest dive bar, with a side of neon-lit dazzle. Honouring the irresistible aesthetics and cultural importance of neon signs through mixology, partner and general manager Jen Queen and her team shake up fresh cocktails and revive old favourites to match the theme, taking cues from the unapologetic personalities and histories of the Pontiac crew. Midnight Sun, a libation of blended Scotch whisky, blackberry and shiitake cordial, and Angostura bitters, recalls the famous San Francisco LGBTQ club of the same name, while the rum-based Teaches of Peaches is a nod to feminist activist Peaches. G/F, 13 Old Bailey Street, Central

title: Trump threatens EU over ‘hostile’ proposal to make Canada associate member
description: US president warns of severe trade action as Ursula von der Leyen pitches historic partnership to Mark Carney.
content: US President Donald Trump threatened on Wednesday to cut trade with the European Union after the bloc proposed to make Canada its first-ever associate member. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen raised the prospect a day before Canadian leader Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament. Her pitch comes as both Canada and the EU seek to pivot away from an aggressive US under Trump’s leadership. “I think it’s laughable,” Trump told reporters when asked about the plan. “If they do that, if I think it’s at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe, on many things.” He added: “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe, which is a possibility.” Von der Leyen pitched closer cooperation on tech, defence and energy to Carney, who became the first non-European head of government to attend the annual “State of the European Union” speech. The German told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that, as democracies face a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. “I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told the Canadian leader, drawing a standing ovation in the chamber. Carney has been pursuing closer ties with the EU as Canada gets drawn ever deeper into a trade war with the US. He addressed the parliament on Thursday, with his visit meant to act as a catalyst ahead of an EU-Canada summit in Montreal next month. “Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak, no one is going to dictate our culture, or with whom we can strike agreements internationally,” Carney said. Von der Leyen said it was time to move from cooperation based on trade to a broader “alliance for the future” and “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible”. “We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project,” she said. She listed energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, cyber and economic security as other fields of cooperation. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. But both the EU and Canada have been buffeted by tariffs and territorial threats from the US and competition from China. “In a more dangerous and divided world, Canada is forging stronger relationships with trusted partners,” Carney’s office said in a statement. While EU treaties do not envision the possibility of becoming an “associate member”, the idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz this year for Ukraine. Under that plan, which met a cold reception from a country pushing for full membership, Ukraine would have been allowed to attend the bloc’s summits and have a representative in the European Commission. It would have also benefited from parts of the EU budget, but without full voting rights. “We don’t really know yet what it means,” said Tobias Cremer, a centre-left European lawmaker from Germany and the main sponsor of a resolution urging stronger EU-Canada cooperation, after von der Leyen’s “associate membership” pitch. Under EU rules, member states have to approve any form of partnership with a third country and it was unclear how much support von der Leyen’s proposal would receive from capitals. Brussels and Ottawa already enjoy a considerable level of cooperation. The CETA free-trade agreement that abolished almost all tariffs has been credited with boosting trade in goods and services by more than 80 per cent since 2016. And this year, Canada became the first non-EU country to join a flagship defence loan programme. Seeking to further diversify its defence ties away from the United States, Canada has also formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military coalition, Carney’s office said on Wednesday. The force, a rapid response military partnership of 10 Nato member states, comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, and the United Kingdom. The announcement followed a bilateral meeting in northern England between Carney and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The two leaders discussed opportunities for defence industrial cooperation through the Global Combat Air Programme, an advanced fighter jet project that Canada joined as an observer in July. The bilateral talks were held ahead of an Everton football match in Liverpool, which both leaders attended together before Carney returned to Strasbourg for his Thursday address to the European Parliament. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Health crisis grips Indonesians enduring haze: ‘my eyes sting, my head hurts’
description: ‘While working, my chest feels tight, my head dizzy, my eyes burning. Even with this unhealthy air, we still must work,’ a resident says.
content: Struggling to breathe through the acrid haze emanating from wildfires on Indonesia’s Borneo Island, residents said on Wednesday they feared for their health but had little to do but wait out the foul-smelling hazard. Indonesia, which shares Borneo with Malaysia and Brunei, is grappling with forest fires that have ravaged swathes of the island, partly caused by the El Nino climate phenomenon that has also affected other countries in Southeast Asia and beyond. In Pontianak, the capital of West Kalimantan province, the thick, yellow smoke was so intense that it had paralysed the international airport over the weekend. “My eyes sting, my head hurts. Over the past week it’s been getting worse,” resident Anggita Putri said. “While working, my chest feels tight, my head dizzy, my eyes burning. Even with this unhealthy air, we still must work,” she said. The air quality index for Pontianak briefly exceeded 1,100 over the weekend, Anggita said – nearly four times the hazardous limit. “I leave my child at home, so of course I have worries that go beyond just my own health. I’m also concerned about my child’s condition,” said the 28-year-old, who has a three-year-old son. Another Pontianak resident, 35-year-old university lecturer Djunita Permata Indah, also said she was concerned for her two children, aged two and four. “The situation is quite bad. I’m worried about the children’s health. Even as an adult, I feel my head aching and dizzy because of the smoky air,” she said. “But parents still must work, so the children are forced to keep going to day care, where they remain exposed to the smoke that has already started to enter the house.” The health ministry said last week that more than 113,000 cases of upper respiratory tract infections had been recorded across seven provinces since the fires began raging early this year. Brief rainfall on Tuesday, which some residents had hoped could alleviate the risk, did little to help and only intensified the thick smoke, Djunita said. Local authorities said they were intensifying efforts to bring the haze under control, including by waterbombing and cloud seeding. Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, which typically runs from July to October, but the blazes this year have been particularly bad in part because of the powerful El Nino – expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago. Experts also blame climate change, decades of forest degradation and slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape. From Borneo, the haze has also spread to neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia. The Indonesian government has said that between January and July, more than 202,000 hectares (499,152 acres) of land burned across the country. The Nusantara Atlas project put that figure close to 300,000 for the same period, and last week estimated the total area affected, including August, was nearly 896,000 hectares. For many residents on Borneo, the haze has not only affected their health but also disrupted their livelihoods. “My house is surrounded by smoke … For more than a month, I haven’t opened the windows,” said snack seller Desia, who like many Indonesians only has one name. She said she had stopped working two weeks ago because she could no longer spend much time outside. “It’s like we’re breathing toxin every day,” she said. Desia’s two children, aged 10 and 11, have not gone to school in over a month, spending most of their time in the only room in the house that has an air purifier. “Right now, I just hope for rain,” she said. “I’ve stopped hoping for anything from the government.”

title: Editorial | Dual policy plans will help Hong Kong grab new opportunities
description: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the chief executive’s latest policy address set the right macro directions for the city’s development.
content: A new chapter is unfolding with Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiling two much-anticipated documents crucial to the next critical phase of Hong Kong’s development. The joint release of the city’s first five-year plan and Lee’s fifth policy address, the final one of his current term, is no routine policy cycle. It is a pivotal moment that shapes the city’s trajectory up to 2030 and beyond, aligning a visionary blueprint with state development strategies, setting concrete targets and outlining measures to ensure that national priorities and local livelihoods advance in tandem for the mutual benefit of the city and the country. The 28-chapter plan comprises clear goals and indicators for enhancing core and new industries as well as public governance and people’s livelihoods while the 103-page policy address lists 25 key livelihood initiatives, such as the pro-fertility bonus and tax incentives as well as AI adoption and risk governance. There is also a wide range of economic measures, including enhancing global offshore renminbi business, green finance and gold trading. Lee said the five-year plan was a pivotal milestone for Hong Kong’s new journey “from stability to prosperity”. “Not only is it an action agenda for Hong Kong to better integrate into and serve the overall national development, but also the strategic plan gearing up Hong Kong to capitalise on the aggregate advantages arising from the national and international opportunities, as well as a sustained pathway to enhancing social well-being,” he said. The five-year plan should not be seen as replacing free markets with a planned economy, nor is it a top-down and centralised control over what individual sectors must do. Rather, it enables strategic planning so Hong Kong can better grasp opportunities arising from national development while adapting to fast-changing geopolitical uncertainties. Lee has said that the existing governing model of “one country, two systems”, the rule of law and the capitalist system will be upheld. The release of the two documents is unique in Hong Kong’s history. This is the city’s first five-year plan to align with the country’s blueprint up to 2030. The Hong Kong plan sets out how the city will move along with national policies in areas such as innovation and technology, international finance, trade and logistics, and regional integration, along with measures to speed up the Northern Metropolis mega-project and initiatives to improve education and housing. Efforts to strengthen mainstream media’s overseas reach have also been incorporated into the five-year blueprint, which means the government will continue to facilitate the development of a healthy media ecosystem. This year’s policy address is more than a review of Lee’s achievements and outstanding targets. Crucially, it translates the five-year plan’s broad vision into actionable measures for the coming year and beyond, transcending the tenure of the chief executive and the administration. The link between the two documents is both symbolic and pragmatic. Symbolically, it signals continuity in development. Pragmatically, it ensures that long-term strategic goals are not divorced from deliverable targets. The plan is essentially a macro, directional blueprint with anticipatory goals, complemented by the policy address laying out pragmatic measures for implementation and the annual government budget. The new framework – “Five-Year Plan leads, Policy Address implements, Budget supports, annual report gives accounts” – ensures progress, continuity and accountability. Understandably, national security continues to feature significantly. In an era of intensifying geopolitical rivalry between China and the United States, Hong Kong’s role as an global financial hub and gateway to the mainland carries both opportunity and risk. There is a need to enhance national security on all fronts so that Hong Kong can continue to thrive as a trusted superconnector and super value-adder while safeguarding national interests and its own safety. The city’s future hinges on whether it can make the most of opportunities. Now that the two documents have set out clear directions and specific measures for implementation, it is incumbent upon the authorities and all sectors to forge ahead so that the city can make better use of its unique edges to act as a bridge between the country and the world and to enable the public to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment.

title: The tragic Qing dynasty politician whose legacy lives on in descendant’s new novel
description: The life of Duanfang inspires E.L. Shen’s novel Foreigners, about identity, queer awakening and the immigrant experience in modern America.
content: Few figures in Qing dynasty (1644-1912) history embody the tragedy of shifting tides quite like Duanfang, a Manchu statesman born in 1861. Duanfang rose through the imperial ranks, earned distinction for his service during the Boxer Rebellion (1899-1901) and went on to hold major regional posts, such as governor of China’s Hubei province and viceroy of the Liangjiang region. His career took a bizarre turn when he was stripped of his viceroyalty in 1909 for supposedly showing disrespect by photographing Empress Dowager Cixi’s funeral procession. Just two years later, while leading troops to quell an uprising in Sichuan, he met a brutal end when his own soldiers executed him in 1911. But beyond his dramatic downfall lay a deeper complexity. Duanfang lived, spoke and governed as a Manchu official, using only his given name in adherence to Manchu traditions. Yet beneath this assimilated identity, his lineage revealed a curious truth – he was ethnically Han, caught between the dominant culture and the ruling elite he faithfully served. More than a century later, a descendant of Duanfang is releasing a novel inspired by his life. E.L. Shen, a Chinese-American writer living in the US state of Connecticut, was drawn to her great-great-great-grandfather’s life and how the two could share different yet eerily similar experiences of feeling like a cultural “impostor”. Set to be released on September 22, her new novel Foreigners (2026) is a sweeping intergenerational story that follows three family members in different times who experience marginalisation in China and modern America. A story told across three periods In the modern day, Dawn is a student at a New England boarding school grappling with her burgeoning queer identity. Running parallel to Dawn’s story is that of her grandmother, Zhengyi, a new US immigrant in the 1960s. Then there is Duanfang, an ancestor of both women, as he navigates his identity among the warring communities of the Han and Manchu in late 19th century imperial China. “I wanted to know, ‘What does it mean to be an impostor?’” Shen, 30, says, explaining the inspiration behind her book. “You could be an impostor in a physical sense – pretend to be someone else. You could also have impostor syndrome. And you could also be doing this sort of subtle thing where you’re really trying to fit in with a country and an identity that is foreign to you.” Shen straddled the line between staying true to historical facts while also adding fictional flair when attempting to “get into the head” of Duanfang. His chapters are written in a “folktale-esque” voice, whose secrets affect the generations that come after him. This may not be the right book for those looking for hard historical facts, Shen warns, as she has heavily dramatised Duanfang’s life story. The book takes creative liberties with unknown information lost to time, such as the name of Duanfang’s wife. Her connection with Duanfang When Shen was in high school and first discovered her connection to Duanfang, she thought it was a joke. “But then, some of my family members went to China and started doing a family history project, and it was quite legitimate,” she explains. Struck by this lore, she sought out a professor at the University of Rochester in New York who had written her dissertation on Duanfang. She helped Shen trace her family lineage. Shen experienced this history not only through textbooks and dissertations but through family heirlooms too. “My grandma just whips out this insane 10-carat ring and asks, ‘Oh, do any of you want this?’ She was like, ‘Oh yeah, like, it’s from Duanfang but I don’t know what to do with it.’” Shen’s mother eventually remade the ring into a necklace. Today, it remains with the family. “I’m really excited that it’s part of our family and we can pass it down to future generations,” Shen says. A historical collection While working as a government official, Duanfang also collected Chinese antiquities – spanning bronzes, jades, steles, calligraphy and paintings. He fostered connections with Chinese art and history scholars and with foreign figures like American collector John Calvin Ferguson and Japanese art critic Taki Seiichi, introducing them to traditional Chinese bronze connoisseurship. When speaking with experts about her family lineage, Shen also discovered that Duanfang travelled to the United States, various European countries and even Egypt as an imperial commissioner to study constitutional government. In 1906, he bought 51 antiques in Cairo, including a limestone stela of Queen Cleopatra of Egypt, thus creating the first Egyptian collection in China and one of the earliest in East Asia. Today, some of Duanfang’s other collections can be spotted at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The Met houses his ritual altar set – which includes three wine containers, three wine warmers, five drinking cups, a wine mixer and a rectangular table – that likely dates back to the Zhou conquest of the Shang in around 1046BC. Their varying designs suggest that they were made at different times and passed through generations in a family. According to the Met, these bronze vessels were found in the early 1900s and went into Duanfang’s collection. The story goes that Shen’s family was left destitute after Duanfang’s death, so they sold his collection to a French collector. The ritual set eventually ended up in the hands of Ferguson and was later sold to the Met in 1924. When Shen’s grandmother immigrated to New York in the 1960s – which directly inspired the character of Zhengyi in Foreigners – she was able to get her first job in the city thanks to the Met curator’s daughter. “[My grandmother] always looked at her with such fondness. I think the daughter even went to her wedding,” Shen says. It was a strange yet fascinating experience to see Duanfang’s collection at the Met, Shen recalls. “It almost felt like impostor syndrome because I feel so separate from this reality – I’m a third-generation Chinese-American,” she says. “I feel like it did bring me closer to my culture and my heritage, but it also made me feel like, ‘Oh, do I even belong in this place when I have such an important family history?’” ‘Every grandparent has something really interesting to tell’ Duanfang, a Qing dynasty official who navigated the treacherous politics of the early 20th century, probably could not have imagined that his life would one day inspire a novel about identity, queer awakening and the immigrant experience in 21st century America. But beyond being a statesman and antiques collector, Duanfang fought to abolish foot binding in China and established China’s first formal public kindergarten while serving as the governor of Hubei in 1903. At a time when female literacy was not prioritised, Duanfang sent more than 20 girls to study pedagogy in Japan. “I hope that [this book] encourages people to talk to any living grandparents [or] relatives about their own family histories, because I really do think that every grandparent has something really interesting to tell,” Shen says. She also hopes that Foreigners will prompt people to confront the same questions she had while writing the book: in what ways do you live as a foreigner or an impostor in your own land, and do you treat others as foreigners too?

title: After US rate hikes, HKMA says Hong Kong dollar could come under pressure
description: HSBC and other major banks keep prime rates unchanged after HKMA raises base rate by a quarter-point in lockstep with Fed.
content: The Hong Kong dollar may come under pressure against the US dollar after the first interest rate rise in three years, but the city does not face a heightened bad-debt risk despite higher borrowing costs, according to the head of the city’s de facto central bank. Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said the US Federal Reserve’s rate rise on Thursday would widen the gap between the market interest rates of the US dollar and the Hong Kong dollar, encouraging more carry trades as investors switch to US dollar assets to earn higher yields. “The increase in carry trades may result in a weaker Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar,” Yue said at a media briefing on Thursday. “The US interest rate outlook remains full of uncertainties, which will also have an impact on Hong Kong’s market and economy. The public should be aware of interest rate risks when buying property or making other investment decisions.” Yue, however, played down worries that higher interest rates would lead to more bad debt, noting that the sector’s overall bad-loan ratio had fallen since late last year as the property market stabilised. His comments came after the HKMA increased its base rate by a quarter of a percentage point on Thursday, hours after the US Federal Reserve raised its target range for the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points to tackle inflation amid conflict in the Middle East. The HKMA lifted the city’s base rate to 4.25 per cent after the Fed raised the target range to between 3.75 per cent and 4 per cent following the sixth meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) this year. The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long Kevin Warsh, US Federal Reserve The city’s three note-issuing banks did not follow suit. HSBC and Bank of China (Hong Kong) kept their prime lending rate at 5 per cent, while Standard Chartered maintained its prime rate at 5.25 per cent, according to separate statements from the lenders. All three institutions set their Hong Kong dollar savings rate at 0.001 per cent for customers with deposits above HK$5,000 (US$637), while balances below this threshold would continue to earn no interest. HSBC, however, said it would increase its savings rate for US dollar deposits to 0.125 per cent from 0.001 per cent per annum, effective Friday. The Hong Kong dollar traded at 7.845 per US dollar as of late Thursday afternoon, its weakest level in a month. The moves marked the first rate rises by the Fed and the HKMA since July 2023, when they also increased rates by a quarter of a percentage point. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” said Kevin Warsh at a news briefing after presiding over his third FOMC meeting as Fed chairman. “Price stability is foundational to economic growth, and I think we took an important step today to deliver it.” The Fed’s decision was widely expected, with 93.5 per cent of traders forecasting a rise and the rest expecting no change, according to CME FedWatch data based on Fed funds futures contracts on Wednesday. Following the rate rise, about 48.7 per cent of traders expected another quarter-point increase at the October FOMC meeting, while the remainder expected no change. “Warsh was arguably more hawkish than the projections, saying financial conditions are not particularly restrictive and suggesting further tightening may be needed,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo Group. Barclays Research said it expected the FOMC to deliver another quarter-point increase in December. The Fed and the HKMA both reduced their key policy rates by a total of three-quarters of a percentage point last year, following a full percentage point cut in 2024. At the beginning of this year, analysts forecast two to three rate cuts in 2026, but the tide turned after the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in late February. The United States’ inflation rate in August was 3.4 per cent, unchanged from July and down from 3.5 per cent in June and 4.2 per cent in May. But, driven mainly by rising energy costs, it remains above February’s 2.4 per cent and far from the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System introduced in 1983, the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar, which means the HKMA always adjusts its base rate when the FOMC decides to do so. However, the city’s commercial banks can decide when and how to adjust their prime and savings rates.

title: Asian Games: when it starts, how to watch, what’s new, where Hong Kong could win gold
description: Event officially starts on Saturday, with karate star Grace Lau a potential early medallist before Siobhan Haughey gets into action Monday.
content: The Asian Games get officially under way on Saturday with the opening ceremony in Nagoya, although early rounds in several sports have already taken place. Hong Kong’s men began their football campaign on Wednesday, losing 2-0 to hosts Japan, while their female counterparts started two days earlier with a 5-1 defeat at the hands of China. It will not be until Sunday that the first gold is handed out, with triathlon and road cycling the most likely candidates to get their athletes on the podium before everyone else. The city’s best hope of a medal on day one lies with karate star Grace Lau Mo-sheung, who won bronze in the women’s individual kata in Hangzhou three years ago. That was one of 53 medals Hong Kong’s athletes brought home last time around, made up of eight gold, 16 silver and 29 bronze. Here then is a look at how they might do this time, where gold could be found in Japan and how those at home can cheer on the city’s 580-strong delegation without being there. How to watch In Hong Kong, the Asian Games is being broadcast live on three free-to-air channels under Cable TV – Hoy 76, Hoy 77, Hoy 78 – as well as being streamed on the company’s mobile app, website and official Facebook account. Coverage of Saturday’s opening ceremony is expected to start at 4pm Hong Kong time, with the event itself due to start an hour later. Siobhan Haughey defends her 200m freestyle gold on Monday and her 100m title the day after. The medal races are in the evening session in Tokyo, starting at 4pm (HKT). The Games run until October 4, and fans will be able to see all the top athletes in action for the duration of the multi-sport event. Where else to watch As with previous major events involving the city’s best athletes, several shopping centres and sports venues will be broadcasting some of the action on big screens. Kai Tak Sports Park will stage a host of events, including having a pop-up store showcasing the uniforms the city’s athletes will wear in Japan. Starting on Saturday, a giant screen at the Atrium of Kai Tak Mall 2 will broadcast some events live, while MOSTown in Ma On Shan and Metro City Plaza in Tseung Kwan O will also have screens showing the action. In addition, the Leisure and Cultural Services Department will set up “Asian Games Focal Sites” at designated sports centres across the city’s 18 districts. These will be open from 5pm to 8pm on Saturday, and daily thereafter from 8am to 9pm. Who to watch Well, Siobhan Haughey, obviously, but also fencing kings Cheung Ka-long and Ryan Choi Chun-yin, who begin their latest quests for foil glory on Tuesday, September 22. And after her triple gold medal display in the National Games, how could you ignore cyclist Ceci Lee Sze-wing? Much will be riding on the 25-year-old’s shoulders, with the team now firmly hers. The women’s road race, in which Hong Kong took gold last time out, will take place while Cheung and Choi are chasing titles of their own. A busy start to the week awaits Hong Kong’s fans. Of course, success is not just of the yellow variety but of the silver and bronze ones too. In Hangzhou, Hong Kong’s athletes also took to the top step of the podium in rowing, rugby, golf and bridge, and grabbed numerous others in everything from equestrian to esports. The expectation is they will do so again. The city’s men will look to make it a three-peat in the men’s sevens, which is almost certain to involve needing to beat Japan at some point, while Taichi Kho’s golf gold is one of the last on the line, with the final round scheduled for Saturday, October 3. There will undoubtedly be the odd surprise along the way, although there should be little when Chinese swimming star Yu Zidi and javelin phenom Yan Ziyi shine as they are expected to.

title: China pushes back against US sanctions bill targeting Russia’s top energy buyers
description: Beijing braces as US House clears ‘Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026’ before next week’s Xi-Trump summit in Washington.
content: China on Thursday pushed back against a new US sanctions bill targeting Russia that could also have a major impact on Beijing, a major Russian energy importer. The US Congress on Wednesday passed the bill to strengthen sanctions on Moscow by targeting Russia’s leading energy buyers – China and India – just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in Washington for a summit with President Donald Trump. “China carries out economic and trade cooperation with countries on the basis of equality and mutual benefit,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said. The cooperation did not target any third party and should not be disrupted or be under the coercion of any third party, Guo added. “China opposes long-arm jurisdiction that has no basis in international law or the authorisation of the UN Security Council.” The US House of Representatives cleared the “Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026” by a 262-159 vote, making its way to the White House for Trump’s signature. The Senate passed the bill last month by an overwhelming 86-11 vote. The legislation, championed by late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, authorises Trump to impose up to 100 per cent tariffs on the five largest importers of Russian oil and natural gas, expanding his favourite tactic of slapping tariffs to maximise leverage and retribution. While buyers of Russian energy are not explicitly named in the bill, it is set to target major buyers such as China and India, while potentially exempting countries including Japan, France, Hungary and Belgium, which source smaller shares from Russia and are taking steps to reduce their reliance. The bill would also impose additional measures on Russia’s energy and defence sectors and its fleet of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions, while slapping more sanctions on Iran. Congress’s move comes as US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng are set to hold their final preparatory talks this weekend ahead of the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington next week. Both sides are expected to finalise the summit’s likely economic outcomes, including tariff reductions on agricultural trade, while extending the fragile trade truce reached in October last year, the South China Morning Post earlier reported. The bill targeting Russian oil exports to Beijing and other major buyers adds another layer of economic pressure as Washington presses China to sever commercial ties with Iran under its “Operation Economic Outcast” sanctions campaign. “With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart, [Vice-Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing on Tuesday. Bessent was responding to a question about the alleged role of Chinese banks in facilitating commercial transactions with Iran and whether Washington planned to take action against them. During his second term, Trump has tested the limits of his executive authority and used tariffs extensively to pursue both political and economic objectives, including pressuring trading partners to change policies and advancing economic interests. He has recently imposed new tariffs on Canadian goods and Brazilian imports, adding to his broader use of tariffs as a negotiating tool. Many Democrats in the House opposed the Russia sanctions bill, saying it handed Trump “sweeping new tariff authorities that he can abuse to raise costs on the American people”. “With this language, he would be able to place tariffs on nearly any country he wants, using sanctions evasion as a pretext,” said Gregory Meeks, a Democratic representative from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. “Does anyone seriously believe President Trump will not use this broad language to target whichever government he is personally angry at?” Since the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump’s expansive tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act were unconstitutional, the administration has sought to replace them with a range of other measures under the 1974 Trade Act and other lesser-known laws and regulations. In July, it imposed tariffs ranging from 10 to 12.5 per cent on 60 economies, including China, Japan, South Korea, India and European Union member states, under Section 301 of the Trade Act over allegations of forced labour. The administration is also expected to slap additional duties on 16 economies, including China, India, Japan and South Korea, following another Section 301 investigation into industrial capacity. Trump also invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to impose 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods last month after trade talks with Ottawa collapsed at the last minute. The obscure 1930 trade enforcement provision, passed at the height of Depression-era protectionism, had never been used before and, in theory, gives Trump broader, faster and less-restricted authority to levy tariffs than almost any other trade statute on the books. Washington’s growing reliance on tariffs and sanctions is also prompting targeted countries to seek workarounds and reduce their dependence on the US-led global financial architecture. Last week, leaders of Brics countries agreed to expand trade and payments in local currencies, making another step towards de-dollarisation as the bloc seeks to counter an assertive United States. Brics is an 11-nation grouping that includes China, India, Russia and Iran, spans four continents and represents nearly half of the world’s population. The pledge was part of the “New Delhi Declaration 2026”, adopted unanimously at the Brics summit. The 45-page declaration said the group’s Payment Task Force had studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and held talks on using local currencies for “trade settlements and investments”.

title: King Charles responds to criticism from Princess Diana’s brother in rare move
description: Charles Spencer says the royal told him ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’ after his sister died in a Paris car crash.
content: Britain’s King Charles took the unusual step ⁠on Wednesday of ⁠responding to criticism by ⁠the brother of his late first wife Diana, saying via a spokesman that grief could impact reason, judgment and memory. The assertions, made in a soon-to-be published book, relate to the now-monarch’s ‌conduct in the days after Diana’s death in 1997. Diana was killed at the age of 36 when the car carrying her and her lover Dodi Fayed crashed in Paris as it sped away from chasing paparazzi photographers on motorbikes. Her brother, Charles Spencer, alleges in a soon-to-be-published ⁠memoir that the then Prince Charles told him “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, ‌according to a report in the Daily Mail, which begins serialising the book on Thursday. The reported comments were made in ‌an argument over whether Diana and Charles’ children, princes William and ⁠Harry, should walk ⁠behind her coffin during her funeral – something Spencer objected to, the report said. Diana became the ‌most photographed woman in the world after marrying Charles in a glittering ceremony in 1981. However, ‌the marriage turned ‌sour and the couple eventually divorced in 1996. Asked about the ‌report, a Buckingham Palace spokesman said: “While we do not comment on books ⁠as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of ⁠fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.” Before the book’s release, ‌Spencer said: “The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective … I want to speak on Diana’s behalf and do so in an openly positive way.”

title: Huawei accused of stealing robot tech to get hands on T-Mobile’s trade secrets
description: US prosecutors claim Chinese tech giant officials were intent on finding out about technical specifications of the robot, dubbed Tappy.
content: The criminal trial of Huawei Technologies on racketeering charges shifted this week into a slower, more laborious pace in what is expected to be a weeks-long trial as the US Government sought to establish on Wednesday that Huawei was intent on learning about a proprietary robot developed by US telecommunications carrier T-Mobile. Matthew Skurnik, assistant US attorney for the Eastern District of New York, spent hours running FBI Special Agent James Diclemis through a series of emails that appeared to show keen interest by US and China-based Huawei officials in the technical specifications of the robot, dubbed Tappy. Developed in 2006 at the company’s State of Washington engineering lab, Tappy was used to automate quality-assurance testing on smartphones before they were approved for sale. The main advantage of the then-innovative technology was that its mechanical robotic arm and rubberised tip allowed it to replicate a human’s tapping, swiping and typing on smartphone touchscreens. This allowed T-Mobile to simulate weeks or months of customer use in a few hours, saving time and money and, presumably, reducing boredom while discovering software bugs, latency issues, touch-latency delays and mechanical screen defects before a phone went to market. The Shenzhen-based company has pleaded not guilty to all 14 federal counts in Brooklyn, New York, including bank fraud, wire fraud, trade secret theft and racketeering tied to alleged criminal activity dating back to 1999. Huawei has termed the allegations “demonstrably false” and argued that innovation, not intellectual property theft, has driven its global success. Emails presented to the jury on Wednesday appeared to show Huawei colleagues instructing Prachi Kathale, a Huawei engineer, in October 2012 to elicit technical specifications from T-Mobile during an upcoming demo the US company was giving her. These included robot stroke/range, position accuracy and repeatability accuracy, according to an attachment included with the email. Kathale reportedly responded that the questions were extremely detailed, leaving her unsure whether T-Mobile would disclose the specs, but that she would try her best. In another email exchange presented in court, Richard Yao, then a Huawei technical representative, reported back to headquarters after meeting with T-Mobile engineer Joseph Mantz in September 2012. “Joe told me that TMO won’t like to share the details of the robot tech/doc,” he reportedly wrote, using TMO as shorthand for T-Mobile. Skurnik spent hours establishing the identities of some dozen Huawei employees on the various email chains, including Cui Jiangao, then chief executive of Huawei Device USA, a subsidiary of Huawei Technologies USA. Drawing on immigration, Huawei payroll and internal company documents, Skurnik linked the various Huawei officials before asking Diclemis to attach each of their photos to a divided whiteboard marked with Chinese and American flags, depending on which side of the Pacific they worked. “Since he’s in Texas, we’ll put him on the US side,” Skurnik said of one such employee, engineer Dong Yongjian. The jury and jury alternates were roughly equally balanced between men and women of varied races, including two who appeared to be of Asian descent. T-Mobile sued Huawei in a civil suit in 2014, alleging that Huawei employees – who had received lab access to test their own handsets – secretly took photos and measured components. It also alleged that Huawei employees physically removed a robotic arm piece from Tappy to build their own testing system. T-Mobile won a US$4.8 million breach-of-contract judgment in 2017. A key piece of government evidence is a video allegedly showing the Huawei employee spiriting away part of the Tappy technology. While cutting edge at the time, Tappy’s skills have been far outdistanced by software and AI-driven commercial robots that can now routinely do multi-finger gestures, pinch-to-zoom, dynamic pressure sensing and continuous swiping. Tools tapping into a phone’s operating system directly now work millions of times faster than a physical arm, allowing companies to run stress tests across thousands of virtual or physical devices at the same time. Racketeering requires the government to prove a pattern rather than a series of incidents, which legal experts say suggests why the government has widened the trial’s scope to two decades. Huawei is also charged with violating US sanctions on Iran and deceiving major banks about its Iran ties, all of which the company denies. If convicted, Huawei faces fines and forfeiture of proceeds gained during the alleged criminal activity, potentially one of the biggest US corporate fines ever. China has accused the US of “economic bullying” and framed the Huawei case as a false pretext for “oppressing Chinese companies”.

title: In Focus | China’s rocket boom has made Hainan a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
description: Factories, supercomputing centres and satellite businesses are springing up in the province as officials push to build a fully fledged aerospace ecosystem.
content: As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism. On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms. No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility. Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan a catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services. Today, the island province is working to build a more diversified and sustainable growth model and, together with its ambition to host a premier free-trade port, is embracing a hi-tech future increasingly centred on the space economy.
