From coconuts to rockets: Hainan’s economic reboot “Commercial space flight could give Hainan a clearer manufacturing focus while complementing its traditional strengths in tourism and consumer services,” said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government. Home to more than 10 million people and comparable in size to Belgium, Hainan now boasts a growing industrial cluster known as Wenchang International Aerospace City. At its centre are two state-owned rocket launch facilities: one serving national programmes and another handling commercial missions. The Wenchang Space Launch Site staged its first launch in 2016 and focuses mainly on lunar exploration and human space flight. Just a few miles away sits the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, China’s first dedicated commercial launch platform. Since its inaugural mission in November 2024, the commercial site has completed 21 launches and has sent 221 satellites into orbit, according to Xu Xikai, deputy head of the development department at Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch, the site’s operator. Two more general-purpose liquid-fuel launch pads were also under construction and could host their maiden missions by the end of this year, Xu noted. Longer-term plans envision as many as eight large coastal launch pads, together with tracking facilities and systems for recovering rockets at sea. We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains Xu Xikai, Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch Wenchang’s coastal geography gives it a major advantage. Massive rockets can be delivered directly by sea, bypassing the road, tunnel and bridge constraints faced by inland facilities. And at about 19 degrees north latitude, rockets gain an extra momentum boost from the Earth’s rotation, reducing fuel requirements or allowing heavier payloads, Xu explained. “For large-diameter, heavy-lift rockets in the future, coastal launch sites will increasingly have an advantage,” he said. Geography, however, is also one of Hainan’s economic weaknesses. The island has historically lacked a heavy industrial base, meaning much of the specialised hardware and construction materials required for space manufacturing must be shipped in. Inside Wenchang’s manufacturing ambitions The challenge for Hainan is transforming launch sites into the nucleus of a wider industrial ecosystem – and early signs are encouraging. Wenchang International Aerospace City recorded a surge in revenue amid an “unprecedented” pace of rocket launches, according to a June report by Nanhai Net, a state-run news portal operated by the Hainan Daily Press Group. The aerospace park’s revenue jumped 85 per cent in 2025 to 23.53 billion yuan (US$3.5 billion), while manufacturing output from its rocket supply chain more than doubled to over 8 billion yuan, the report stated. Under a provincial action plan from 2025 to 2027, Hainan also aims to raise annual operating revenue at Wenchang’s aerospace cluster to 10 billion yuan by 2027, while building an integrated supply chain spanning rockets, satellites and data services. The expansion comes as Beijing presses ahead with reforms to open the island further and develop new sources of growth – though competition is intensifying. Two other commercial launch sites have already begun operating in Gansu and Shandong provinces, while at least four more are under development nationwide. To stay ahead, Hainan’s strategy is to push further up the industrial chain. Its action plan prioritises a “super factory” next to the launch pads, designed to produce up to 1,000 satellites annually. The location would allow freshly assembled satellites to move straight from production line to launch pad with very little transit time, the Star Market Daily, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet focused on technology and capital markets, reported in December. Described by local authorities as Asia’s largest satellite-manufacturing facility, the industrial complex is also expected to support China’s Qianfan low-Earth-orbit constellation. A planned special bonded zone for satellite data would further leverage Hainan’s free-trade policies to attract data from overseas, according to the report. “We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains,” said Xu of Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch. The infrastructure buildout is already reshaping launch activity. After more than two years of development, the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has moved from experimental testing to routine operations. It handled more than 30 per cent of China’s commercial satellite launches in 2025 and successfully carried out the country’s first offshore rocket booster recovery. Business beyond the launch pad Putting a rocket into orbit, however, is only one part of the emerging space economy. Ye Shiyang, a Wenchang native who chairs the company behind the Aerospace Supercomputing Centre in Wenchang International Aerospace City, argued Hainan must capture a larger share of the value generated after a rocket launches. “Over the past few years, we have connected the entire chain – from collecting and receiving satellite data to storing, processing, applying and trading it,” Ye said. Completed in 2023, the supercomputing centre occupies about 40,000 square metres (about 431,000 square feet), with about 22,400 square metres of floor space. A guide at the centre said it offered peak computing power of 100 petaflops – a measure of processing capacity – and was designed to accommodate about 2,000 server racks. Meanwhile, three of the centre’s remote-sensing satellites operate as part of Jilin-1, which is described by its developer as the world’s largest commercial sub-metre Earth-observation constellation. The centre has also built 13 ground stations, according to a guide there. The practical applications could be numerous. Satellite images processed in Wenchang can distinguish food crops from cash crops, identify fallow land and monitor crop growth, assess pest outbreaks and track the effects of typhoons. Such imaging tools can also help to detect water pollution, illegal logging and unauthorised land use. These services, Ye argued, could generate steady demand from agricultural, environmental and land-management authorities, giving Hainan a revenue stream that is less dependent on the schedule of rocket launches. The aerospace city is also developing a space tourism business. The Jixing Meteorite Museum, for instance, displays more than 400 specimens gathered from around the world, while exhibitions introduce visitors to satellite data and supercomputing. “We are developing space tourism in response to market demand,” Ye said. “Visitors should not only watch a launch or see a rocket or satellite. They should also understand the industry and technology behind them.” In 2025, tourism, modern services, hi-tech industries and tropical agriculture – Hainan’s four pillar sectors – accounted for 65.9 per cent of the province’s gross domestic product, according to the provincial government. “The Wenchang launch site has already become a tourist attraction, and this could give Hainan an economic model built around tourism, consumer services and aerospace manufacturing – and give its manufacturing sector a much clearer direction,” said Peng of the Guangdong Society of Reform. For a Wenchang native surnamed Xie, the transformation has been drastic. Growing up in a village in Longlou town, he once walked barefoot along unpaved red-earth tracks. Today, working as a taxi driver, he has watched the sprawling aerospace complex reshape the place he calls home. As the launch site and surrounding projects expanded, local families were relocated and farmland acquired. While some households received hundreds of thousands of yuan in compensation, Xie noted how traditional livelihoods were quickly fading, leaving coconut processing as one of the few legacy industries remaining. “Farmers around here barely farm any more,” he said. In Longlou, the coconut palms still remain – quiet reminders of a past that existed before the rockets arrived, even as a new economy takes shape around them.

title: Meet Anthony Ippolito, who stars as Sylvester Stallone in upcoming biopic I Play Rocky
description: From playing a young Adam Sandler in Pixels to Al Pacino in The Offer, Ippolito continues his streak of portraying Hollywood’s biggest names.
content: Anthony Ippolito may be a rising star in his own right, but the 27-year-old seems to have found his niche playing famous Hollywood actors. He first gained recognition playing Al Pacino in The Offer, the Paramount+ miniseries chronicling the behind-the-scenes story of cinema classic The Godfather. Now, Ippolito is set to play Sylvester Stallone in the upcoming biopic I Play Rocky, which reveals the true story behind Stallone’s fraught journey to landing the lead in the 1976 classic he penned. Speaking in a recent interview with Fandango, Ippolito discussed getting into character by studying Stallone’s archival interviews and connecting with the star over Zoom. “He couldn’t have been more gracious and generous in sharing what that experience was for him,” Ippolito said of their brief yet “inspirational” call. So, who is Anthony Ippolito, the breakout talent playing a young Stallone in Amazon MGM Studios’ I Play Rocky, set for release this November? How did Anthony Ippolito land the Stallone role? Ippolito reportedly won the role of young Stallone with a bold approach, bypassing the traditional casting process by self-recording an unsolicited audition tape and sending it directly to the producers, per The Hollywood Reporter. In August 2025, the actor shared his emotions about getting the role with Entertainment Weekly: “It’s an honour and a privilege to portray Sylvester Stallone in this inspiring story. It is an absolute dream come true.” What other roles has Anthony Ippolito played? Ippolito’s breakout role arrived during the Covid-19 pandemic, when he played secondary school student George Wright in the Netflix drama series Grand Army. His earlier credits include bit roles in the short film Fool’s Day (2013) and the sci-fi feature Pixels (2015), where he played a younger version of Adam Sandler’s lead character. Ippolito also lent his voice to an episode of the renowned children’s animated series Go, Diego, Go!, voicing Billy the Beaver and various river animals. He later gained wider recognition for his performance in Netflix’s 2022 romantic drama Purple Hearts. How did Anthony Ippolito break into acting? While the rising star is making strides in showbiz, acting wasn’t Ippolito’s original career plan. “It was something I started when I was really young, originally just wanting to get commercials or something to pay for college, but then I ended up developing a passion for acting itself when I was around 16,” the actor told Vulkan magazine. When asked, during the same interview, what he’d likely be doing today if not acting, Ippolito said he “would probably be away at college majoring in psych, philosophy or cultural anthropology”.

title: US must prepare to fight around moon, top Trump military adviser says
description: General Dan Caine urges preparation to fight from the ‘seabed to cislunar space’ after US reveals deployment of space weapons.
content: American troops need to prepare for combat not only in Earth’s orbit but around the moon, President Donald Trump’s top military adviser said on Wednesday, looking ahead to a new frontier in warfare after the US revealed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space. General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, told service members and industry figures at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference outside Washington that the US military should adapt now so it “is prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”. Space Force, the newest military service, which was created by Trump in 2019, is preparing to fight in space and around the moon because “humanity is advancing deeper into space – the Space Force’s job is to help be prepared to defend US interests,” Lieutenant General Gregory Gagnon, head of the force’s Combat Forces Command, told reporters separately. The announcement that the US military is ready to fight in the area between high Earth orbit and the moon itself comes days after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed at the same conference that the US has fielded “on-orbit space control weapons”. The spate of announcements about space weaponry from military officials over recent days flies in the face of long-standing conventions and international understandings that have held outer space as only to be used for peaceful purposes and remain non-militarised. While multiple nations, including the US, have shown the ability to shoot down satellites in Earth orbit, those demonstrations have taken place from the ground against their own satellites. However, according to Gagnon, “the intelligence community has been clear that potential adversaries have been seeking to extend warfare into space” and that the US military needs to react. “Our potential adversaries such as the PRC are actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space,” Gagnon said, referring to the People’s Republic of China, the country’s official name. China established its own military space troops in 2024, charging them with boosting capability to manage space crises. When asked about the US announcement on deploying weapons in space, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters on Tuesday that “China always upholds the peaceful use of outer space, maintains outer space security and opposes the weaponisation, militarisation and an arms race in outer space”. Guo also urged the US to “stop expanding its military preparations in outer space”. It is not clear whether deploying weapons in space or possible plans to use them around the moon will run afoul of international treaties that prevent the militarisation of space. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, which the US and China have signed, says celestial objects such as the moon are to be used “exclusively for peaceful purposes”, nuclear weapons cannot be placed in space and countries are “liable for damage caused by their space objects”. There was a renewed push two years ago to further bolster anti-militarisation measures in the United Nations following US reports that Russia was developing a space-based weapon. Russia vetoed a joint US-Japanese resolution that would have called on all countries not to develop or deploy nuclear arms or other weapons of mass destruction in space, as banned under the treaty. A rival Russian resolution to ban all weapons in space “for all time” also ultimately failed. When asked about the 1967 treaty and other similar obligations, Gagnon said the US Space Force “will continue to execute safe and responsible space operations in all the reaches of space”. However, he would not say what Space Force or overall US military policy was on the use of weapons like bullets or projectiles in space. He directed questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. Gagnon also said the US aims to double the size of the Space Force over the next five years – to roughly 25,000 service members – and that about two-thirds of that growth would be focused on Combat Forces Command. “We have capabilities in the military because we are preparing to defend the nation,” Gagnon said. “The reason we have the capabilities is to help create deterrence.”

title: Opinion | Why women in China are still at risk of abduction and forced marriage
description: The latest incident has exposed many failings in local authorities’ work in a country where a mindset of favouring sons over daughters still exists.
content: One stormy night last month, a driver surnamed He saw two tall men get out of a car in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen and pull a young woman off the street and into the vehicle. During the struggle, her umbrella fell to the ground. She did not appear willing. Suspicious, He followed the vehicle and later reported the incident to local police, supplying them with footage he had recorded. Thanks to him and the police, the abducted 18-year-old was rescued from a forced marriage. According to media reports, the teenager, originally from Lanzhou, Gansu province, had been promised to a man by her parents without her knowledge or consent. After receiving the agreed price from the prospective groom’s family, her parents forced her to drop out of school. The teenager sought help via online posts and eventually a non-profit organisation found her a job in a Shenzhen coffee shop. But her parents, intent on marrying her off, tracked her down and sent a team to stake out her workplace and ambush her, driving her over 20 hours back towards home before they were stopped by the police. This young woman was lucky that the motorist saw what happened and alerted the police, who then worked quickly to rescue her. But what if she hadn’t been so fortunate? The incident has exposed many failings in the work of local authorities to ensure the welfare of women. For one, the young woman’s parents reportedly found her Shenzhen address through their local police station. How was that legal and not an invasion of privacy? Furthermore, it’s not clear what the local chapter of the All-China Women’s Federation, the official organisation representing women’s interests, had done for her or whether it was even alerted. The civil code is clear: forced marriages are not allowed. This is not just about overly controlling parents and it is certainly not a “family matter” to be settled behind closed doors. The young woman’s parents clearly saw her as an “asset” over which to exercise control. Planning an abduction and taking a woman against her will bears all the hallmarks of trafficking. When a woman has to count her lucky stars that her abduction is foiled by chance, and when not every abduction attempt is even reported to the police, there is a desperate need for community organisations to step up. It might be a shock to some that women can still be treated so badly in this day and age in China. After all, it is decades since Mao Zedong declared that “women hold up half the sky” and authorities began to advance women’s rights. But the fact is that, despite the laws, campaigning and propaganda, the mindset of favouring sons over daughters still exists. This gender bias is reflected in the birth ratio of boys to girls. According to national statistics, in 2021, more than 108 boys were born for every 100 girls, rising in 2024 to nearly 112 boys per 100 girls – above what is globally considered to be a stable ratio of 103-107 boys per 100 girls. Also in 2021, China’s seventh national census found that there were 35 million more men than women, with the ratio of third children born at nearly 133 boys per 100 girls. Though society has moved on from many traditionally accepted gender biases, as long as a preference for sons exists, daughters will continue to be cast aside as subordinate, good for little more than marrying a man and bearing his children. In rural areas, this bias manifests itself in the common practice of passing land down to sons rather than daughters. And in the workplace, women are still more likely than men to be asked how marriage and family planning figure in their careers. As a direct result of the skewed gender ratio, men are competing for far fewer women. Prospective grooms find themselves offering ever higher prices for a bride. And yet, so much of the blame is still being directed at women, who are accused of being greedy and materialistic. So yes, forced marriages can still happen. And the shifting of mindsets can take time. But at the same time, there could be more targeted measures, including additional media reports of gender inequality, more efforts to improve women’s educational levels and more monitoring of the mindset where sons are favoured over daughters across the country, including through national sample surveys.

title: Saudis turn to Western, regional allies as missile defences run low
description: Regional officials say kingdom appeals to France, UK, Pakistan, and Egypt for help against Houthis amid US interceptor shortages.
content: Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for help as its stand-off with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on, two regional officials said on Wednesday. The officials said the Saudis have asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air-defence support to the region to help defend against missiles and drones fired by Houthis and other Iran-backed groups. The outreach was initiated because Saudi Arabia’s main ally and arms supplier, the United States, has seen its own stock of interceptors dwindle over the course of a six-month war with Iran, one official said. Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media. Saudi officials did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment. The fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is the latest front to erupt as a result of the Iran war. On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city with a drone; the region responded with condemnation but no sign of military support. The kingdom declared Mecca, the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, a “red line” and said it had intercepted the drone. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca, about 1,100km (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. With the world’s biggest oil exporter under fire from rebels backed by the Saudis’ regional adversary, the kingdom needs a safe outlet for its crude as well as military aid. There is no clear path to either. A crucial Saudi pipeline has been shut down, reportedly for weeks, after an attack by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. The Houthis have been targeting infrastructure in the kingdom and its shipping on the Red Sea, where they have seized several islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And Iran is still targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices remain above US$100 a barrel. One of the regional officials said Saudi Arabia is in a “very difficult position”, since it has to protect not only its military bases and vital government installations but also oil facilities across the kingdom. The second official said Saudi Arabia was also seeking to rally its international allies to launch a collective response against the Houthis. “But the decision now is to give diplomacy a chance,” the official said, adding that Oman and Egypt were leading efforts for de-escalation in Yemen. Last weekend, Oman hosted a meeting between US and Houthi representatives to discuss the regional tensions, said two people familiar with the matter, including a Houthi official. They gave no further details and spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media. On Tuesday, the British prime minister’s spokesman, Tom Wells, confirmed the UK has a “close defence partnership” with Saudi Arabia. But he declined to say whether Saudi Arabia has asked for military aid or say whether British troops are in the country. US and Nato officials have previously acknowledged a critical shortage of missile interceptors in Europe, raising questions about Europe’s ability to assist. A Turkish government official said Turkey was engaged in talks with Iran and the United Arab Emirates to try and lower tensions. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to speak on the issue publicly, did not provide further details. The attacks are the first test of a new defence pact among Saudi Arabia, Nato member Turkey and nuclear power Pakistan. But officials from Turkey and Pakistan said they have not received a Saudi request for support in response to the Houthis’ escalation. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak publicly on the issue. Amid the condemnation of the attempted attack on Mecca, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said his country and the Saudis stand “unwaveringly, shoulder to shoulder”. Turkey’s foreign minister expressed solidarity and said no country can “remain indifferent”, state-run Anadolu Agency reported. The United States has sold billions of dollars in weapons to Saudi Arabia and has committed to other support, but top US officials have indicated a lack of desire to get involved in the conflict. US Vice-President J.D. Vance on Monday said Washington had been in “constant contact” with the Saudis and had “engaged in direct conversations with the Houthis”. When asked whether Saudi Arabia had requested intervention, a US official said the US military’s Central Command has a task force in place for “enhancing intelligence sharing and planning support with Saudi forces”. The US military hosted senior military leaders from eight countries last week at a conference in Germany to discuss “opportunities for enhancing security cooperation in the Middle East”, the official also said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly. The official did not confirm which countries attended. The Houthis claimed on Wednesday that they shot down an F-15 fighter jet operated by the Saudi-backed coalition over Yemen’s central province of Marib, releasing a video of wreckage. In a video posted on social media, the burning wreckage of an aircraft could be seen in the desert and fighters posed with a part of the plane that appeared to show a Saudi flag. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: T. rex was warm-blooded and had body temperature close to ours, study finds
description: Scientists used chemicals in fossilised teeth to help pin down how warm the iconic dinosaur was.
content: Using fossilised teeth, scientists have finally taken the T. rex’s temperature – and it wasn’t too different from our own. Researchers once thought that dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded creatures. Later findings challenged that, suggesting that older dinosaurs were warm-blooded and could control their body temperature. Most scientists agree that Tyrannosaurus rex was warm-blooded, but pinning down the exact core temperature of an extinct creature is difficult. “We can’t just use a thermometer to do that,” said Jasmina Wiemann, a palaeobiologist at Johns Hopkins University who had no role in the latest work. Scientists tried other methods like studying how T. rex grew or searching for clues in its bones, but a firm number eluded them. In a new study, researchers hunted for chemical clues in the fearsome predator’s teeth. It turns out that atoms within the enamel clump together in different patterns based on an animal’s body temperature. “We figured out how warm the most famous animal of all, a T. rex, was,” said co-author Aradhna Tripati, a geochemist at the University of California, Los Angeles. Readings from three teeth revealed an average body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit (36 degrees Celsius). That is similar to modern elephants and not too far from the average body temperature of humans, which ranges from 97 to 99 degrees Fahrenheit (36 to 37 degrees Celsius). The findings were published on Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. “I almost would have expected a higher body temperature,” Wiemann said. Based on her prior work, she thought the predator could have run a few degrees hotter – similar to modern birds, dinosaurs’ warm-blooded descendants. Knowing how hot or cold the T. rex was can help scientists piece together how the dinosaur might have lived. At 97 degrees (36 degrees Celsius), T. rex could have lived across most of prehistoric North America, Tripati said, maintaining a stable internal thermometer across both cooler and hotter regions. The findings could also shed light on the kinds of prey the dinosaur had to hunt to keep its energy up. Scientists say it will be important to test these methods on other dinosaurs to see how warm or cold they ran. It is possible T. rex’s temperature could have been one of the keys to its dominance as one of the dinosaur age’s top predators. “There’s lots of interesting, charismatic species that could be explored using this,” said study co-author Robert Eagle, a geobiologist at UCLA.

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for first time in 3 years, irking Trump
description: US president demands immediate rate cuts as Chair Kevin Warsh warns inflation remains ‘too high’.
content: The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, defying President Donald Trump’s demand for cuts, as central bank chief Kevin Warsh stressed the need to combat inflation that has been “too high” for “too long”. The Fed’s Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates by 25 basis points to between 3.75 and 4.00 per cent. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” Warsh told a press conference, adding that the decision was a “serious” but necessary one. And Wednesday’s rate hike may not be the last – the vast majority of Fed policymakers indicated that at least one more rate hike was likely necessary before the end of the year, according to their Summary of Economic Projections (SEP). US households and businesses have been battered by years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of Trump’s war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom. The US president reacted angrily to the decision Wednesday, calling it a “raise against Trump” and accusing the Fed’s rate-setting committee – which he called “hostile” – of making decisions for political reasons. The president has launched an unprecedented assault on the Fed’s independence since taking office, attempting to fire a Fed Governor and launching a criminal probe against Warsh’s predecessor in his quest for lower rates to spur economic activity. Wednesday’s statements refrained from directly insulting or criticising Warsh, as Trump did with former Fed chair Jerome Powell. Trump’s Republican Party faces a stern test in coming midterm elections, with rival Democrats seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress and economic issues front-and-centre for voters. The Fed had held rates steady since January, choosing to wait to gauge the effects of the Iran war’s energy price shocks and to let the impact of tariffs on prices ripple through the economy. Since July, however, a growing faction of policymakers had indicated a rate hike may be required to tame inflation, as the war grinds on and prices remained elevated, particularly for energy. On Friday, August’s consumer price index came in at 3.4 per cent – unchanged from the month before, but still well above the Fed’s long-term 2 per cent target. Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said inflation had “forced the Fed’s hand”. “Price pressures remain too elevated and too persistent for policymakers to look through, while the economy and labour market have held up well enough to absorb tighter policy,” she said. In its SEP, the Fed raised its forecast for its preferred gauge of inflation – the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index – by 0.1 percentage points to 3.7 per cent by year-end. The Fed also raised its projection for GDP growth by year end to 2.3 per cent, up 0.1 percentage points. Warsh reiterated his belief in the “resilience” of the US economy, citing its strength as being a marker of its ability to absorb tighter financial conditions. US stock markets largely priced in Wednesday’s rate hike, but they were still down on the news – expected with any rate hike as investors adjust their portfolios. Yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds – which have surged in recent days as uncertainty on long-term inflation has spiked – were also up past the 5 per cent threshold, a sign that uncertainty remains a factor. Warsh was named to his position after a contentious Senate confirmation process, during which Democratic lawmakers accused him of being a “sock puppet” for Trump, which he denied. The Fed has a dual mandate to deliver maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term 2 per cent target. It mainly achieves these goals by setting the key US interest rate – lower rates tend to spur economic activity but fuel inflation, and hiking them cools both activity and prices. The Fed’s SEP showed that at least 12 of 18 policymakers who participated in the projection expected one more rate hike would be required before the end of the year. Four policymakers expect two more rate hikes to be required. Warsh has criticised the Fed’s policy of offering such projections in the past and did not participate in the previous iteration in June. This projection also included only 18 policymakers, suggesting he had once again withheld his contribution.

title: As EU cosies up to Canada, Burnham’s Brexit Britain feels sidelined
description: The bloc prioritises deepening ties with Ottawa over warming up to the UK leader’s overtures to reset post-Brexit relations.
content: Andy Burnham was for years a staunch opponent of Brexit and a vocal supporter of rejoining the European Union. When he became Britain’s new prime minister in July, this seemed to augur well for UK-EU relations – but instead, Brussels is looking past its neighbour and cosying up to Canada. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the EU, creating a tailor-made title in a bid for the trading bloc to expand its borders and reinvent itself following Britain’s infamous exit. It remains to be seen what associate membership means in practice, and this may take years to determine. Still, it signals that Canada is well ahead of Britain in establishing better relations with the bloc on both trade and security. British officials shrugged off the announcement. One said they could not judge what it meant without any details. Another downplayed it as a political move rather than one that would necessarily have any major trade or economic impacts any time soon. Nonetheless, figures across the Labour government, both under former prime minister Keir Starmer and his successor, are disappointed that the EU has not shown much desire to use the ousting of the Conservatives in the 2024 general election to reset post-Brexit relations. Burnham’s ambitions for closer ties have been largely shelved as new UK negotiators immediately got bogged down in the same difficult negotiations on food standards and a youth mobility programme that were taking place under Starmer. A UK-EU summit has been delayed amid the lack of progress. The United Kingdom’s government is still bound to its red lines on remaining outside the single market and customs union – a commitment made at the last election. British officials involved in negotiations believe there is no prospect of a significant improvement in trading terms unless Labour breaks its electoral promise. Still, some in London were surprised to read EU officials suggesting the bloc is more interested in closer relations with Canada than Britain. One official described it as needlessly divisive when Western allies should be pulling together against Russian aggression. They referred to a view in the UK, shared in some European capitals, that von der Leyen had erred by asking for exorbitant fees from Starmer to join the bloc’s Safe defence procurement programme. Canada has been granted access. Another official said that, in any case, the UK, France and Germany had forged a more effective geopolitical bloc than the EU in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is the so-called E3, made up of those three countries, which has led on the most important problems facing Europe in recent years, they said. That is in part because the EU as a wider bloc is slower and less united, so on issues such as Ukraine it made sense for western Europe’s major players to work together. Nonetheless, some in Britain are calling for Burnham to throw off the shackles of Labour’s red lines on Europe at the next election. The Liberal Democrat party wants the UK to rejoin the single market and customs union and says rejoining the EU as a whole is a long-term objective. The next election will bring a focus on whether the prime minister is bold enough to put his past views on the EU in front of voters. Until then, Britain may have to face up to a relationship with Brussels that is largely on ice.

title: Hong Kong targets gold trading, FPS-UnionPay link to boost yuan use
description: ‘We will consolidate and enhance Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre,’ John Lee says.
content: Hong Kong will expand the use of the yuan in areas including gold trading and cross-border payments, as policy blueprints call for the city’s biggest push yet to internationalise the Chinese currency. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday devoted part of the city’s first five-year plan and his annual policy address to developing a gold trading ecosystem and creating a regional intellectual property trading centre in the city. “We will consolidate and enhance Hong Kong’s status as an international financial centre, and stay committed to our global positioning,” the city leader said. “Hong Kong will deepen the development of its global offshore renminbi business and capital market, develop an international asset and wealth management centre and international risk management centre, enhance the securities market and expand fixed-income and commodity trading.” Lee added that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the city’s de facto central bank, would introduce a tendering mechanism for seven-day offshore yuan liquidity and explore issuing short-term debt instruments to encourage wider use of the currency. A government source said the mechanism could let banks manage liquidity more easily as demand for the yuan expanded. The insider also said authorities aimed to announce the system within this year, allowing market players with yuan shortages or surpluses to trade short-term debt instruments to manage their holdings. The HKMA would also promote linking the Faster Payment System with mainland China’s bank card and payment system UnionPay by the end of the year. The move would allow users to make payments in Hong Kong dollars and renminbi while in Hong Kong, on the mainland or elsewhere, the insider said. In addition, the HKMA is also expected to encourage more foreign banks in Hong Kong to directly join the Cross‑border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to expand the clearing network. The source said the CIPS offered banks and other institutions an alternative channel for clearing and settling transactions in yuan to the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication system, better known as Swift. Under the five-year plan, authorities have pledged to “actively promote the use of renminbi to settle government expenditure”. At present, the Hong Kong government mainly uses renminbi for bond repayments and spends about 20 million yuan (US$2.98 million) monthly on welfare and medical programmes in Guangdong and civil servant training, the source said. The source said the government could use the currency more extensively in future to pay mainland suppliers. As part of its efforts to develop a gold trading ecosystem, Hong Kong will launch its central clearing and settlement system for the precious metal in the first quarter of 2027, building on its current trial operation. The insider said board members of the clearing company included Chinese and foreign institutions such as HSBC and Standard Chartered. All direct participants would need to be vetted by the board based on criteria such as experience, once it officially launched, while admission rules would also be set by the board, the source said. David Liao, HSBC co-chief executive for Asia and the Middle East, said a mature gold trading hub supported not only storage, trading, clearing, and settlement, but an ecosystem of financial products, including gold loans, inventory finance and risk management tools. “As the world’s largest offshore yuan centre, Hong Kong has a unique advantage in developing more renminbi-denominated gold products,” he said. “We’re excited about the prospect of growing a scalable gold market in Hong Kong, underpinned by internationally recognised standards for risk management and controls.” The city’s stock exchange is expected to reveal details of new renminbi-denominated, physically settled gold futures contracts this year, which would boost the yuan’s global influence in terms of pricing precious metals. The source added that the trading of other commodities in yuan would be considered in the future. The insider said that gold had different warehousing requirements compared with other commodities because the precious metal was more valuable relative to its size and served as a benchmark product. Authorities also set their sights on developing a regional intellectual property trading centre. The new measures include expanding the Intellectual Property Department’s in-house examination capacity for original grant patent applications in major technology fields. The government source said the department had obtained resources for a headcount of 40 people and would continue to expand. The department was still studying pilot facilitation measures to roll them out for relevant original grant patent applications next year, the insider said. Other key initiatives include releasing the second-stage consultation on increasing the competitiveness of the listing mechanism by the end of this month, with the source saying authorities would see if the system could be further relaxed.

title: Hong Kong aims to raise innovation spending to 3% of GDP by about 2030
description: Chief Executive John Lee unveils ambitious goal, together with measures to boost frontier technologies, including aerospace research.
content: Hong Kong will strive to raise its expenditure on innovation activities to a level equivalent to 3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) by around 2030, nearly double the current rate, according to the city’s first five-year plan. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the ambitious goal, together with measures to boost frontier technologies, including aerospace research, on Wednesday. Among the 22 indicators laid out in the plan, the government aims to raise the ratio of total domestic expenditure on innovation activities to GDP from 1.63 per cent in 2024 to 3 per cent around 2030. The government expects the increase in average annual expenditure on innovation activities to be around 10 per cent. “This is indeed aggressive. The government is putting pressure on itself,” a government source said. “We hope our economy can be more diverse.” The insider said the government hoped to attract leading enterprises in areas such as life technology, AI and robotics to Hong Kong as their activities could help boost GDP. The total domestic expenditure on innovation activities will cover R&D, and spending on enterprises’ application development and other activities such as product design and pilot testing. To elevate the city’s role as a regional innovation hub, Lee said the government would press full steam ahead with three major tech parks – the Science Park, Cyberport and the San Tin Technopole and the Loop Hong Kong Park at the Lok Ma Chau Loop – and five institutes. They are the Hong Kong Productivity Council, the Hong Kong Applied Science and Technology Research Institute, the Hong Kong Microelectronics Research and Development Institute, the Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute, and the Life and Health Technology Research Institute. The authorities will also capitalise on 15 state key laboratories and three existing InnoHK research clusters to speed up innovation development. The move aligns with neighbouring Guangdong’s latest five-year plan, announced in April, which highlights the need to connect with the city’s InnoHK clusters and develop state key labs. The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau will also set up a task group on frontier technologies to formulate a development strategy for areas covering artificial intelligence, new energy, new materials, aerospace technology and quantum technology. The task group, to be formed next year, will comprise experts from engineering and biotechnology fields, according to a source. It will make recommendations to a committee chaired by innovation and technology minister Sun Dong for policy formulation and industry planning. Aerospace, an emerging pillar technology identified by Beijing, will also get a boost. The Innovation and Technology Commission will inject HK$300 million (US$38 million) into a subsidy programme targeting research related to national space missions. The programme would not cap the number of subsidised projects or set a ceiling for the subsidy amount, the source added. In a move to translate local research outcomes, the bureau will also support the Science Park in establishing the Hong Kong Innovation and Technology Application Scenario Promotion Centre, which will help line up innovative solutions with organisations from the public and private sectors that could benefit from those inventions. On the medical innovation front, the International Clinical Trial Academy will be set up to train talent conducting clinical trials that are up to international standards. The Hospital Authority will also match innovative medical technologies with potential uses in public healthcare settings through a new unit called the HA Technology Convergence Hub. The hub could serve as a dedicated office to help link drugs, medical devices or prototypes with the authority to run trials, another source said. The Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation said it welcomed the five-year plan, and would fully support the implementation of the measures listed in it and the policy address.

title: Police arrest man after wife found dead with knife wounds in Heng Fa Chuen
description: Woman, 53, found in flat in block 2 of private residential estate in Hong Kong’s Eastern district.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a man on suspicion of murder after his wife was found dead in a flat at a private residential estate. The force said the woman, 53, was discovered with knife wounds to her neck in a flat in block 2 of Heng Fa Chuen estate in Chai Wan at about 7.50pm on Wednesday, a police spokesman said. She was confirmed dead at the scene. Officers arrested the man, 52, and announced that an investigation was under way. Heng Fa Chuen is a major private waterfront residential estate built directly above the MTR depot in Hong Kong’s Eastern district. Developed in the 1980s, the self-contained community has 48 residential towers and a shopping centre.

title: Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries
description: Blueprint sets goals for economic development, livelihoods and environmental protection, policy address targets 5 key areas of development.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy. In a historically significant new approach, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu prefaced his annual policy address on Wednesday with a comprehensive set of binding and anticipatory or aspirational longer-term targets for Hong Kong up to the year 2030. The two documents would go hand in hand, Lee said, promising to take the city’s economic development to the next level by creating a new innovation engine in the Northern Metropolis megaproject, while building on Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, aviation, maritime services, trade and technology. He also focused on improving living standards and social well-being, announcing initiatives ranging from higher baby bonuses to encourage childbirth and increased healthcare spending to more subsidised housing and shorter waiting times for public flats. “[China’s] 15th five-year plan, which outlines a blueprint for future national development and also places a heightened demand for Hong Kong’s better integration into and service of the overall national development, presents major opportunities and opens up new ground for the growth of our city,” Lee said in his speech to the Legislative Council. “Hong Kong’s economic structure still leaves room for enhancement, the mission of transitioning to new growth drivers remains formidable, and deep-seated social problems still require speedy resolution.” The five-year blueprint, a seven-part document described by Lee as “an action agenda” for Hong Kong’s medium- and long-term development, lists 105 indicators, including 22 major targets covering economic and innovation development, livelihoods, and environmental protection. The major indicators are divided into 17 anticipatory goals and five binding targets, some of which would be affected by geopolitical uncertainties and other external factors. “If the binding targets are not met at the end of the day, there is a need to be held accountable,” Lee said. “But we need to appreciate that some things may be out of our control, such as economic development. Some countries might suddenly change their policies.” The anticipatory goals include 10 per cent annual increases in two key technology indicators: nearly doubling spending on innovation activities to 3 per cent from 1.63 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) over five years; and raising the economic share of value-added manufacturing to 5.5 per cent from 3.8 per cent. Another anticipatory target is to increase by 4 to 5 per cent annually the number of companies whose parent firms are based outside Hong Kong. Four of the five binding targets concern environmental protection. They include cutting carbon emissions per unit of GDP by 32.5 per cent and raising the share of zero-carbon energy in Hong Kong’s electricity fuel mix to 30 per cent from 25 per cent over the five-year period. Goals for the Northern Metropolis, the massive undertaking near the Shenzhen border to build a 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) business, education and housing zone, include a binding target to raise the “spade-ready sites” available from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030, and an anticipatory target to increase the number of homes completed in the zone to 70,000 from the current 11,000. On livelihoods, Lee pledged to raise the doctor-to-population ratio to 2.43 from 2.25 per 1,000 residents, and lower the risk of early deaths caused by chronic conditions to 6.9 per cent from 7.3 per cent. Lee’s long-term blueprint dedicates a chapter to national security as a priority for the city’s success and prosperity, stressing that “a holistic approach” will be adopted to strengthen economic resilience by improving the city’s legal system and enforcement mechanisms. The wide-ranging, traditional policy address that followed the announcement of the five-year plan was titled “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era, Driving Reform and Boosting Development, Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihood”. The address, which was the last of Lee’s current term, set out priorities targeting five major areas of development opportunities, alongside 25 key livelihood initiatives. Measures offering immediate benefits to residents include one-off cash incentives and subsidies. While extending the HK$20,000 (US$2,549) newborn bonus for three years, Lee said the government would increase the amount for second and subsequent children to HK$30,000 and offer subsidies to employers providing an extra 10,000 full-time jobs to young people entering the workforce. Expediting the development of the Northern Metropolis is a key highlight of the policy address, which matches the “dual-core planning” vision set out in the five-year plan that clusters innovation and technology (I&T) sectors near the northern border and places finance sectors south along Victoria Harbour. Describing the northern development zone as “an important strategic vehicle” for integrating I&T and industry, Lee said selected strategic industries establishing a presence there would receive targeted tax breaks. While developing three university towns that will span 1,000 hectares in the northern zone, the government will invite universities to build campuses in Hung Shui Kiu from this year. Authorities are also studying the feasibility of a southern extension of the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Western Rail Link to enhance connectivity. The Northern Metropolis will seek to improve living conditions in space-starved Hong Kong, with its housing projects increasing the proportion of more spacious flats with an area of about 45 square metres (484 square feet) to 25 per cent from the original 20 per cent. Both policy documents devoted significant space to consolidating Hong Kong’s role as an international financial centre under the broader “Four Centres, One Hub” strategy. The strategy seeks to strengthen the city’s position as an international financial, maritime and trade centre, develop it into an international innovation and technology centre, and establish the city as a hub for “high-calibre talent”. The chief executive said the city would introduce an auction system allowing banks to bid for short-term yuan liquidity to meet their short-term financing needs. Lee said his administration would actively promote the use of the Chinese currency to settle government expenditure, for example purchasing fresh water from Guangdong, and expand the dim sum bond market, while the operator of the city’s stock and futures markets would launch an offshore renminbi bond index and introduce new products. Following the official launch of Hong Kong’s central clearing and settlement system for gold earlier this year, the government is considering tapping into the Exchange Fund to buy more gold and participate in the spot and futures markets. The policy address also outlined growth strategies for emerging sectors, including dispute resolution, international property and marine services. A new task force on frontier technology will spearhead deeper research on aerospace, marine and quantum technologies. Addressing housing issues that Beijing has often instructed Hong Kong to resolve, Lee said the aim was to reduce the waiting time for subsidised rental flats to 4.5 years from 4.8 years by 2027, and to bring it below four years after 2030. The long-term plan envisages public rental housing accounting for 40 per cent of total supply, with subsidised sale flats and private homes each making up 30 per cent over the next 10 years. Lee put a heavy emphasis on leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) in various policy domains, which will include establishing an “AI City Brain” system to strengthen responses to extreme weather events, major incidents and public order management. A new AI commissioner’s post will be created to tackle emerging challenges. Lee told the media later that while AI boosted efficiency, it also created “operational and societal risks”, prompting his administration to introduce seven risk governance guidelines, with a particular focus on protecting students. Lee expressed confidence that the targets would improve livelihoods, strengthen economic development and deepen Hong Kong’s integration into the national development agenda. “I hope and I’m confident that in five years, for everyone, whether it’s their income or development, there will be an improvement,” he said. “Our industries will be more diversified, education enhanced, [the city] more international, and we will be a highly technologically empowered Hong Kong.”

title: China uses 100,000 home-grown AI chips to build leading weather forecast system
description: The Sugon 8,000 system can predict weather 10 days in advance, bringing the country closer to its ambitious forecasting goals.
content: China said it can now predict weather 10 days in advance at a cutting-edge resolution of 5km (3.1 miles), finer than most major systems in routine use around the world. The advance was achieved by a Chinese-developed weather forecasting model running on Sugon 8,000, a massive home-grown computing system built entirely with domestically made AI chips. Most major global forecasting systems have resolutions of roughly 5km to 10km, according to the China Meteorological Administration and Beijing-based computing company Sugon, which jointly announced the results on Tuesday. For instance, the Global Forecast System – the main global weather model run by the US National Weather Service – has a maximum resolution of about 13km. The team has already tested the system at an even finer global resolution of 3km, according to Sugon, bringing it closer to a goal set out in China’s latest five-year meteorological plan: 1km forecasts nationwide and resolution down to 100m (328 feet) in key areas by 2030. Numerical weather models work by dividing the atmosphere into a three-dimensional grid, then calculating how wind, temperature, air pressure and moisture change across it. Smaller grid cells allow forecasters to see weather systems in greater detail, but at a steep computational cost. For instance, halving the distance between grid points can demand an eightfold increase in computing power. The Chinese model is known as the Mesoscale Convective Vortex. To handle the huge workload, it was adapted to run on Sugon 8,000, a computing cluster unveiled in July that links 100,000 powerful computing units that can work on calculations simultaneously. What sets Sugon 8,000 apart is its ability to handle different kinds of computing on the same system, according to the company. Traditional supercomputers are built for the highly precise calculations used in scientific simulations, while AI systems typically trade some precision for the ability to process huge amounts of data quickly. Sugon 8,000 was designed to do both, using domestically developed chips, storage and networking technology. In the latest test, it produced a 10-day global forecast in about an hour. That calculation time is not unusually fast by itself. During tests, the US Global Forecast System has completed a 10-day forecast in about 45 minutes. But Sugon said its one-hour turnaround met the requirements for routine weather forecasting. Getting results within that window could give forecasters more time to assess approaching typhoons, heavy rain and other severe weather, it said. Sugon 8,000 has also been used for large-scale simulations in areas including protein research, molecular dynamics and turbulence. According to the company, the system has been adapted for nearly 200 applications and more than 500 mainstream AI models across over 30 research and industrial fields.

title: Hong Kong leader vows support for media’s global reach, to review TV practice code
description: Hong Kong to review television practice code to help local broadcasters adapt to modern industry trends and digital competition, John Lee says.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has expressed renewed support for the local media industry, including strengthening its global reach and reviewing the code of practice for television to ensure it keeps abreast with the times. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu made the pledges in both the city’s first five-year plan and the policy address he unveiled on Wednesday. In the section on “Develop an East-meets-West Centre for International Cultural Exchange” under the five-year plan, Lee said: “We will strengthen the global reach of the mainstream media”. And in the part discussing measures to strengthen the city’s status as an international trade centre in the policy address, Lee said: “The government will continue to assist the local media to expand their network beyond Hong Kong, telling the good stories of Hong Kong.” The South China Morning Post earlier reported that the initiative would assist local media, which report in Chinese and English, in reaching readers beyond the city for the second consecutive year. The industry could offer media services particularly in countries under the umbrella of China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Lee also said on Wednesday that the administration would review the Generic Codes of Practice for Television. “We aim to ensure that regulation keeps pace with the times, and that diversified and quality programmes are broadcast, expanding the reach of the ‘Hong Kong Brand’ to the Asia-Pacific region,” he said. The codes govern the programme, advertising and technical standards of television broadcasting in Hong Kong. This includes regulating the use of language, violent and sexual content and indirect marketing in television programmes. The Newspaper Society of Hong Kong and the Hong Kong News Executives’ Association welcomed the government’s inclusion of support for the media in the two blueprints. “The society believes that such strategic direction and policy support will foster media development and competitiveness, promoting a healthier evolution of the industry amid the immense technological disruptions and challenging operating environment it currently faces,” it said. The association said that with the government’s support over the past year, media organisations had been expanding their networks outside Hong Kong and exploring new directions to improve their competitiveness. “The association firmly believes that the healthy development of the media industry is inextricably linked to Hong Kong’s overall prosperity,” it said. “The industry remains committed to upholding professional standards to ensure its continued healthy growth.” The Hong Kong Federation of Journalists also welcomed the measure, saying it would foster the “healthy development” of the media industry and strengthen its global competitiveness and communication capacity. Lawmaker Christine Fong Kwok-shan said traditional broadcasters operated under strict advertising and content restrictions while streaming platforms and social media such as Netflix and YouTube operated with minimal regulation, draining away advertising revenue. She said she hoped the updated codes would allow broadcasters to diversify their revenue streams through more flexible sponsorship arrangements. Fong also said generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools continued to scrape news and multimedia content without licensing, eroding the value of original intellectual property. She said the government should take the lead in establishing guidelines or a legal framework to help protect copyright content created by media from AI data mining. But lawmaker Elizabeth Quat said the emergence of AI had made copyright issues more complicated and harder to resolve. Quat said that if AI absorbed different content and generated something on its own rather than copying it directly, it would be hard to define the copyright, as it was the AI’s own creation. Regarding the code, Quat said it had been in place for many years with only minor amendments, yet it must contend with today’s industry competition and the development of the multimedia ecosystem. She said television broadcasters in many places were facing serious difficulties. “So on one hand, they need to proactively transform themselves, but on the other hand we also need to look at whether the current codes of practice and regulations can keep pace with the times,” she said.

title: Hong Kong to offer ‘attractive’ merger deals for schools beyond those struggling
description: Source says demand exist even among schools with healthy enrolment, provided authorities offer more resources and support.
content: Hong Kong education authorities will offer a “very attractive” proposal and policy support to encourage schools without survival issues to merge amid the shrinking student population, according to official sources. The government said it might allow aided schools and semi-private Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS) schools to merge and operate across two campuses, though all arrangements remained subject to the forthcoming announcement of further details. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced that the government would launch the “Confluence and Elevation – School Excellence Project” for publicly funded schools in the 2026-27 school year. “This will encourage and support mergers of suitable publicly funded primary and secondary schools, consolidating resources and raising the quality of education,” he said. His proposal comes as schools struggle to survive amid falling enrolment, with the number of babies born between 2021 and 2025, who will enter Primary One in the coming years, continuing to decline and hitting a record low last year. The bureau expects the number of six-year-olds to fall to just 31,500 by 2029, a 16 per cent drop from the 37,600 Primary One pupils allocated school places in aided and government schools this academic year. In the first eight months of 2026, the number of registered births stood at 19,255, a 10 per cent drop compared with the same period in 2025. If this trend continues, the total annual birth count this year is likely to fall below 30,000. A government source noted that schools without survival issues also showed demand for mergers, provided authorities offered more resources and supportive measures. The source urged schools with complementary strengths to merge so they could enhance their combined capabilities and become stronger institutions. “The plan is not meant for schools struggling with student recruitment. It is designed for quality schools, and we will set clear criteria for institutions joining the scheme to become stronger,” the source said, adding that the requirements might include the number of classes the schools were now operating. The source promised that the coming scheme details would be “very attractive”, offering not only monetary resources but also policy facilitation and transitional support, such as teacher manpower and ensuring that class numbers would not be reduced as a result of a merger. The government may also permit institutions with different funding models, such as aided and semi-private DSS schools, to merge and operate across two campuses. However, the source said that government schools would not be eligible to merge with aided or DSS schools because their personnel were civil servants. But government schools may still consider merging among themselves. The source added that school governing boards should consider whether parents would overwhelmingly object to the merger. The current rules only require public primary schools failing to secure at least 16 pupils to enter their Primary One in the coming school year to submit survival plans including merger. Schools choosing this option would be given a one-off allowance of HK$1 million (US$127,500) each to cover additional expenses. Secondary schools being unable to admit 29 students to operate two Form One classes in the coming school year could choose to merge to survive and they would be offered a one-off allowance of HK$500,000 for each merging level to cover the additional expenses. In March, the Education Bureau announced that a record 15 primary schools would not be allowed to operate subsidised Primary One classes for this academic year because they had failed to secure at least 16 pupils. Eight of them eventually chose to merge. Choy Sai-hung, a primary school principal whose institution is popular among parents, said while the proposed plan might not attract top-tier ones to merge, it might interest those with strengths in particular areas and who were hoping to create an institution with distinct features. “For instance, two schools with strengths in teaching non-Chinese students could merge to become a strong institution for ethnic minorities,” he said. He added that schools in different districts might also consider merging. He noted that a past merger involving two underperforming institutions still resulted in insufficient student enrolment, which might be why the government introduced this new scheme. Meanwhile, the policy address will launch a new pilot scheme to help around 200 primary and secondary schools provide support for students with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Schools with a certain number of such pupils will be included in the scheme. Under the initiative, non-governmental organisations will enter schools to offer small-group training for these students to improve their behaviour, learning adaptation and social skills. Teachers will also receive training to better support these students.

title: Who is Abdul Malik al-Houthi, the elusive Yemeni commander behind Red Sea-Saudi blitz?
description: He has transformed the Houthi group from tribal insurgency to a fighting force, threatening Riyadh and controlling the vital waterway.
content: Abdul Malik al-Houthi, an elusive figure who commands ⁠a battle-hardened force, scored his biggest military victory in years when his Iran-aligned Houthi militant group swept through Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and tightened their grip on a vital shipping waterway, rattling oil superpower Saudi Arabia. The offensive, which has been accompanied by attacks on Saudi Arabia, has put the Houthis in a strong position to call the shots in the Bab el-Mandeb strait by potentially halting global trade in one of the world’s most important conduits for goods and commodities, including oil. Al-Houthi has transformed his men, fierce mountain fighters often in sandals and hooked on the green leaf stimulant khat, into ‌a force of tens of thousands who withstood years of air strikes by a Saudi-led coalition in Yemen’s civil war and built an arsenal including drones and ballistic missiles. A 2022 UN-brokered truce halted heavy fighting in the war but failed to lead to a lasting settlement in the impoverished country. The following year, al-Houthi’s militants surfaced to disrupt Red Sea shipping in support of Palestinians in the Gaza war. Now, they have grabbed the spotlight by opening another front in the Middle East conflict, giving strategic leverage to Iran after it had already effectively closed off the Strait of Hormuz. As head of the group, al-Houthi has emerged as Iran’s most prominent and resilient Arab ally after Israel killed the leaders of Lebanon’s Hezbollah and Palestinian group Hamas. Enigmatic with a reputation as a fierce commander, al-Houthi remained defiant despite US military retaliation for his group’s attacks on shipping during the Gaza fighting. ⁠He threatened military action if the US and Israel sought to displace Palestinians from Gaza and called US President Donald Trump a criminal. “We reaffirm our steadfast position against American and Israeli-Zionist tyranny, which targets our entire nation under the banner of ‘changing the ‌Middle East’,” he said in August in a speech to mark the Prophet Mohammed’s birthday. In another speech during the Gaza war, al-Houthi, appearing with a traditional Yemeni dagger in his belt, described Israel’s blockade of Gaza as a crime against humanity and accused Arab and other Muslim states of inaction. Al-Houthi has survived in a ‌country with a history of complex, shifting alliances. After veteran former president Ali Abdullah Saleh switched sides in the civil war, abandoning his Houthi allies in favour of a Saudi-led coalition, Houthi fighters stopped ⁠his armoured vehicle with a rocket-propelled grenade in an ambush ⁠then shot him dead, sources said at the time. Since the start of the civil war – widely seen as a proxy conflict between Riyadh and Tehran – foreign officials who dealt with al-Houthi are not known to have met him in person, a source familiar with the matter said. Many seeking meetings were ‌asked to travel to the Houthi stronghold Sanaa, where a security convoy would take them to safe houses and conduct security checks before leading them to an upstairs room, where al-Houthi, fearing assassination, would appear only on a screen. The Houthi movement was formed to fight ‌for ‌the interests of the Zaydi Shiites, a minority sect that ruled a 1,000-year-old kingdom in Yemen until 1962 but felt marginalised during the 1990–2012 rule of Saleh, unified Yemen’s first president. The Houthis deny being puppets of Tehran and say they ‌are fighting a corrupt system in Yemen and regional aggression. Saudi Arabia and its allies accuse Tehran of arming and training them, which Tehran denies. The civil war killed tens of thousands, devastated Yemen’s economy and left millions hungry. During its most intense phase, ⁠the Houthis launched attacks on Saudi Arabia. In January 2022, they also launched a missile attack on a commercial hub in the United Arab Emirates. In a speech in 2022, al-Houthi said his goal was to be able to strike ⁠any target in Saudi Arabia or the UAE, both US allies and major oil producers which view Iran and its proxies as major security threats. Al-Houthi, who traces his lineage to the Prophet Mohammed, has asserted that his movement is under siege because of its religion. “We must focus on preserving the authenticity of our Islamic affiliation and identity,” he once said. With al-Houthi largely out of public view, ‌his military spokesman, Yahya Saree, has become the public face ‌of the movement. Standing rigidly in his uniform, Saree reads statements in a theatrical cadence, stretching certain words and sharply raising his voice for emphasis. The distinctive delivery has made Saree instantly recognisable to audiences across the region. In 2024, Saree earned a master’s degree in diplomacy and international relations from the Yemeni Academy for Graduate Studies, according to Houthi websites and his personal social media account. His thesis had a subject close to his day job: “the threat of the Israeli presence in the Red Sea to the national security of the Republic of Yemen, 2010–2022”. In a statement on Sunday, he declared: “We affirm to the criminal Saudi enemy that the continuation of its aggression against our people will be met with more severe and larger operations deep inside its territory and the consequences will be dire, God willing.”

title: Hong Kong’s new training visa could be available in first quarter of 2027
description: New visa category among spate of new talent-trawling measures unveiled in city leader John Lee’s policy address.
content: A new visa intended to attract international talent to participate in short-term training programmes in Hong Kong could become available as early as the first quarter of next year, the South China Morning Post has learned. The final policy address of Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s current term also put the spotlight on five existing or soon-to-launch academies that would seek to train overseas professionals and organise international events. They and the new visa category were among a spate of talent-trawling measures unveiled on Wednesday, with the latter allowing non-locals to take part in government-recognised training programmes lasting less than 12 months. “It will advance Hong Kong’s development into a regional training hub,” an insider said. The government source said various public and private bodies had set up other training academies in recent years, including the MTR Corporation, the Airport Authority and Cathay Pacific Airways. The insider noted the city lacked a suitable visa category for those who wished to attend short-term training in Hong Kong, limiting their chances of receiving training in the city. Further details about the new visas are expected to be announced by the end of this year. The source said applications could open as soon as the first quarter of 2027. She added that anyone holding the new visas would be prohibited from working part time during their stay, except for internships provided by the programmes, and could not remain in the city after completing their training. “If they engage in part-time jobs, they will become illegal workers,” she said, adding that the government would conduct checks to prevent employers exploiting such visas to employ “cheap labour” through long-term bogus internships. SCMP · Hong Kong’s new training visa could be available in first quarter of 2027 Another measure is the expansion of the Immigration Facilitation Scheme for Invited Persons to cover Central Asia and the Middle East, and allow all government bureaus and departments to issue invitations for guests to take part in activities in Hong Kong. The scheme currently covers Asean member states, with just five government bureaus and departments allowed to send invites. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations comprises the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor. The government source said the visa application process would be simplified and the invited visitors would be allowed to use e-channels to enter Hong Kong under the scheme. The latest policy blueprint also includes plans to add more talent categories related to artificial intelligence (AI) to enrich the list of desired professionals, in addition to relaxing the extension of stay requirements under the Top Talent Pass Scheme for employees at technology start-ups. Under the revised requirements, start-up talent will be exempt from submitting proof of company income when applying for a visa extension if their enterprise was supported by designated public sector organisations, as their business performance would be considered unstable during such early stages. Lee also highlighted five established or planned academies for training international talent, namely the International Clinical Trial Academy, the Maritime Academy, the Hong Kong International Legal Talents Training Academy, the Hong Kong Intellectual Property Academy and the Hong Kong International Academy of Policing. The Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute is set to establish the International Clinical Trial Academy next year, with plans to help train practitioners to meet global standards and potentially pave the way for smoother drug registrations in the future. The government said it would promote the creation of the Maritime Academy in Hong Kong and support prominent industry institutions looking to establish a presence in the city to help train talent. The policy address touched on the Hong Kong International Legal Talents Training Academy, which was established in 2024. The institution organises a wide variety of programmes, conducts research on cross-jurisdictional topics covering common law and other legal systems, and regularly holds international seminars. The Hong Kong Intellectual Property Academy will launch in the fourth quarter of this year to provide more on-the-job training programmes that offer a higher level of recognition. The academy will seek to raise the intellectual property literacy of practitioners in sectors such as technological innovation, cultural and creative, commerce and industry, and professional services. The Hong Kong International Academy of Policing will be established in November, with plans for it to organise 20 global training programmes and forums by the end of next year. It will aim to train about 1,000 law enforcement officers every year, including around 200 from overseas.
