The academy is expected to organise a police leadership forum called “ConvergeHK”, which will be held annually starting from 2027. Organisers will invite police officials from Asean and Middle Eastern countries, as well as nations under the Belt and Road Initiative, to join the event, according to the policy address. The blueprint called for a revamp of the website for the Education Bureau’s “Study in Hong Kong” campaign to help attract more high-calibre professionals to study in the city. On top of the revamped website, the bureau is expected to launch the “Hong Kong: Your World-class Campus” promotion campaign and organise exhibitions in belt and road countries and other target locations. The policy address also calls for a two-year extension of a pilot scheme allowing graduates from bay area campuses of Hong Kong universities to apply for visas under the Immigration Arrangements for Non-local Graduates policy. The scheme allows such graduates to apply to work in Hong Kong. Other measures include raising the annual quota for the Belt and Road Initiative Scholarship to 200 places, up from 150, from the next academic year. Public universities plan to organise more than 160 recruitment activities in mainland China and overseas in the current school year as part of efforts to attract outstanding students from around the world.

title: Malaysia to invite Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing for Rohingya repatriation talks
description: Anwar Ibrahim says it is necessary to formally recognise Minh Aung Hlaing’s government if Malaysia wants to resolve the Rohingya crisis.
content: Malaysia will formally invite Myanmar leader Minh Aung Hlaing to visit Kuala Lumpur to discuss efforts to repatriate nearly 200,000 refugees from the war-torn nation that Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says have placed a heavy social and economic burden on his country. Refugees from Myanmar, particularly ethnic Rohingya, have faced worsening hostility in recent months in Malaysia, where they are accused of causing social problems and taking over small local businesses in areas where they have set up temporary settlements. Muslim-majority Malaysia is a key destination for Rohingya refugees fleeing religious persecution by successive Myanmar administrations and sectarian violence in Rakhine state over the past decade. On Wednesday, Anwar said formally recognising Min Aung Hlaing’s government was necessary if Malaysia were to find a lasting solution to the plight of the Rohingyas. “If we do not recognise the government of Myanmar, who do we negotiate with?” Anwar said in a podcast that aired on Wednesday. “I want to let [Minh Aung Hlaing] know that we can be friends, we can trade, we can accept Myanmar. But Myanmar must accept [taking back the refugees]”. Buddhist-majority Myanmar refuses to recognise ethnic Rohingyas – who are predominantly Muslim – as citizens. About 1.2 million Rohingya, mostly pushed out of Myanmar’s western Rakhine state, are based in Bangladesh, mainly in refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar. But conflict and dwindling aid have forced them on deadly journeys across the Andaman Sea. Most who survive the squalid conditions on cramped boats managed by human traffickers end up as undocumented migrants in Malaysia. Anwar’s plan to recognise Min Aung Hlaing’s administration puts him at odds with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which has barred Myanmar’s top officials from attending the bloc’s meetings after a 2021 military coup that triggered a civil war. Minh Aung Hliang transitioned from junta leader to president in April after the military won a national election, which the UN and international rights groups widely panned as a sham meant to legitimise the junta’s claim to power. More than 1,600 civilians were killed in over 5,400 armed clashes and 1,416 air raids in Myanmar during the first six months of 2026, according to figures compiled by Altsean-Burma from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project. The conflict has displaced nearly 3.8 million people and left more than 16 million others in need of humanitarian help in Myanmar, according to the UN, as continued fighting, movement restrictions and blocked aid access have deepened the crisis. “Everyone is saying we cannot accept the Myanmar government, they are harsh and [rule with an] iron fist,” Anwar said. “We have ties with dozens of other countries that are ruled with an iron fist, we have ties with many nations that are cruel. Why not with Myanmar?” Anwar’s announcement comes just weeks after he revealed that he had negotiated a deal with Myanmar to repatriate 5,000 Rohingya refugees. The first batch of 1,500 refugees was expected to be sent back to Myanmar “in a week or two”, Anwar said, adding that Malaysia would cover the cost of food and clothing for the journey. The prime minister insisted, however, that Malaysia would only proceed with the mass repatriation plan if Myanmar guaranteed that the refugees – especially the Rohingya – would be safe. “If they bring them back and kill them like before, we cannot accept that either,” Anwar said. “The negotiations are not only to send them back. We also ask to guarantee their safety, where they can have a safe zone in Rakhine for Muslims so they are not disturbed.”

title: China affirms support for Iran, but warns against Yemen spillover
description: In talks with his Iranian counterpart in Beijing, Foreign Minister Wang Yi calls on Tehran and Washington to stay rational.
content: In talks with his Iranian counterpart in Beijing on Wednesday, China’s foreign minister reaffirmed Beijing’s support for Tehran, called for a political settlement to the country’s conflict with the US and warned that regional tensions must not further spill over into Yemen. Wang Yi also urged the earliest possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Abbas Araghchi’s trip to China, his second since the US launched large-scale strikes on Iran in late February, came as Washington expanded sanctions and warned of further measures against those who allegedly support Tehran, including Chinese firms. Alongside trade and technology, the conflict is likely to be a key topic during Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected summit with President Donald Trump in the United States next week. Araghchi last visited Beijing in May, shortly before Trump’s own trip to China. According to the official Chinese readout, Wang told Araghchi that Beijing was ready to play a constructive role in resolving international disputes as the turbulent situation in the Middle East was seriously affecting international peace and development. He said Beijing was ready to strengthen its cooperation with Tehran to safeguard Iran’s legitimate rights and interests. He urged both Iran and the US to “remain rational”, return as soon as possible to their Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, re-establish negotiations and engage in substantive consultations on issues of mutual concern. “The continued protracted conflict between the US and Iran is not in the common interests of the parties involved or the international community,” he said. On regional diplomacy, Wang expressed support for Iran’s engagement in dialogue with Persian Gulf countries on the basis of mutual respect for territorial sovereignty and national security. He urged all parties to take effective measures to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “at the earliest opportunity”. The conflict is also threatening to expand further into Yemen. Fighting has flared between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in the country, with Riyadh accusing the militant group of targeting Mecca, a claim the Houthis have denied. The Houthis’ seizure of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – including the stretch near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping lane – has added pressure on global energy markets and pushed the price of Brent crude oil above US$100 a barrel. “We do not wish to see regional tensions further spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea,” Wang said. He also highlighted the four‑point proposal for a new Middle East security architecture that Xi unveiled earlier this month. “The current situation once again demonstrated that the existing security architecture in the Middle East was imperfect and needed to be reformed and strengthened,” Wang told Araghchi. According to the Chinese statement, Araghchi briefed Wang on the latest Middle East and Gulf developments. “Iran does not wish for the conflict to continue and hopes to return to diplomatic channels for resolution, while firmly safeguarding its own rights and interests,” he was quoted as saying. He said Tehran believed the Islamabad memorandum signed in June was still valid and urged Washington to honour its commitments. Araghchi added that Iran was willing to engage in dialogue with states in the region to build good neighbourly relations. Last week, Xi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian joined other leaders at the Brics summit in New Delhi in a joint statement urging maximum restraint in the Middle East conflict. Without naming any country, the New Delhi declaration also expressed concern over the escalation of the fighting and condemned deliberate attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities. Following a meeting between Abu Dhabi’s Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan and Pezeshkian on the Brics sidelines, Iran and Oman are preparing to unveil a temporary shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has stressed that the arrangement will not amount to a full reopening, and a planned regional foreign ministers’ meeting has been postponed amid renewed fighting involving Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis. The diplomatic push comes as the cost of the conflict is mounting. Araghchi on Tuesday mocked US claims that Iran had been left defenceless, citing a Pentagon report to Congress that detailed extensive damage to US bases across the region, calling the losses “the tip of the iceberg”. A separate congressional estimate put US war costs at US$38 billion in five months, with monthly outlays of at least US$2 billion and projected inflationary effects. On Tuesday, the US House of Representatives voted for a third time to curb Trump’s war powers. China is Iran’s most important economic partner and the main customer for its oil, often buying Iranian crude at discounted prices and providing Tehran with a vital source of revenue amid sanctions, according to media reports. Beijing has denied these reports, saying its cooperation with Iran is in line with international law. Relations between Beijing and Tehran were elevated to a comprehensive strategic partnership in 2016 and reinforced by a 25-year cooperation agreement signed in 2021. But China has not committed to defending Iran militarily and Beijing’s investment in the country has been constrained by the risks of US secondary sanctions, banking restrictions, infrastructure bottlenecks and commercial caution. In 2023, Beijing helped broker the restoration of diplomatic relations between Iran and Saudi Arabia, presenting the agreement as an example of its preference for regional dialogue over US-led security arrangements. Iran is also instrumental to Beijing’s regional strategy due to its location at the intersection of routes linking China with Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Persian Gulf and Europe. Beijing has promoted transport and logistics links through Iran under the its Belt and Road Initiative, while Tehran has sought Chinese investment in railways, ports, energy and industry.

title: Hong Kong targets film tourism boom and higher-level tennis tournaments
description: Policy blueprint sets HK$126 billion tourism target by 2030, with film tourism and major sporting events among its priorities.
content: Hong Kong will introduce themed tourism routes showcasing the city’s most recognisable filming locations and explore upgrading Victoria Park’s Centre Court to host higher-level tennis tournaments, as authorities seek to significantly increase the sector’s economic contribution under the city’s first five-year development plan. The 2026-30 blueprint aims to raise the tourism industry’s value added from HK$86.2 billion (US$10.9 billion) in 2024 to HK$126 billion by 2030 – an increase of about 40 to 50 per cent. It also targets increasing the proportion of non-mainland Chinese visitors among overnight travellers to 40 per cent by the end of the decade. Among the more immediate measures unveiled alongside the plan in Wednesday’s policy address were a series of “+ Tourism” initiatives aimed at combining travel with mega-events, finance, industrial brands, ecological conservation and heritage. The government will also promote film tourism, yacht tourism, urban renewal and homestay accommodation on outlying islands. “The Hong Kong Tourism Board will offer visitors an immersive experience of Hong Kong’s unique urban landscape and lifestyle, weaving together classic Hong Kong films, district characteristics and local culture,” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Wednesday. A government source said the initiative would be a campaign that the board aimed to launch on its website within the year, promoting famous filming locations across the city. “The programme will also look at businesses around these landmarks and recommend what visitors can shop for and eat nearby,” she said. The second phase of a film exhibition at the Old Yau Ma Tei Police Station will also open in early 2027. The attraction welcomed about 77,000 visitors in its first eight months, with more than 90 per cent of those who registered attending, the source said. Authorities will also establish a one-stop Support Unit for Non-local Film Productions in the first quarter of 2027 to help mainland and overseas crews hoping to use Hong Kong as a filming location. Another source said it would help with logistical matters such as visas, venue finding and coordination with government departments. “For example, if you want to close down a street in Tsim Sha Tsui to film a car-chase scene, it involves a lot of departments, including police, and we can help with that,” the source said. On sports, the government will begin a study next year into redeveloping Victoria Park’s Centre Court into an all-weather multipurpose venue capable of hosting larger higher-level sporting competitions and performances. “Hong Kong’s overall tennis sector has high potential to develop as an industry, whether in terms of public interest or the performance of local athletes,” a government source said. The existing venue can host tournaments at around the ATP 250 level, while authorities want an upgraded stadium capable of staging at least ATP 500 events. This would require capacity for about 7,000 spectators among other improvements. The government source added that construction could begin in about four to five years. The initiatives form part of a broader five-year tourism strategy calling for deeper thematic travel experiences, more city-walk routes, horse racing and culinary tourism, island-hopping activities, and world-class mega-events combining sport and culture. Hong Kong will also seek to become a “core demonstration zone” for multi-destination tourism and a southern gateway for overseas visitors entering mainland China. Authorities hope to encourage travellers to extend their Hong Kong trips to the Greater Bay Area and other mainland destinations. A third source said the concept was intended to showcase multi-destination travel, with Hong Kong serving as an entry or exit point for overseas visitors because of its connectivity and ease of travel. Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said successful measures needed to be “deepened, broadened and sustained”, while long-running policies should be adjusted or expanded where necessary. “Good hardware and appropriate policies are not enough. We still need to tell Hong Kong’s story well,” she posted on social media shortly after the documents’ release. The policy address also eased the way for homestay accommodation on outlying islands by allowing the Home Affairs Department to disregard deed restrictions on guest house use when processing licence applications for buildings of three storeys or fewer. Operators will still need to obtain a guest house licence and comply with requirements, including fire-safety rules.

title: First building in Hong Kong’s university town project to be ready in months
description: Tower called Loop Academy One, city leader says, while also revealing official names for the three university towns in Northern Metropolis.
content: The first building in the 1,000-hectare (2,472-acre) university town project in the Northern Metropolis will be completed by the end of this year, Hong Kong’s leader has said, revealing that the flagship tower is called Loop Academy One. Announcing Hong Kong’s first five-year plan on Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also revealed the official names of the three Northern Metropolis developments: San Tin University Town, Hung Shui Kiu University Town and Ta Kwu Ling University Town. The three towns, proposed in 2024, are intended to drive synergy among industries, academia and research to achieve the integrated development of education, technology and talent. According to the five-year plan, authorities will step up efforts to attract world-famous institutions or first-class scientific research institutes to establish a presence in the towns. A source said No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki would announce the updated sizes of the three towns, whose core campus alone is 300 hectares. San Tin was originally allocated 52 hectares, while Hung Shui Kiu and Ta Kwu Ling were given 22 and 40 hectares respectively. For the San Tin town, located at Hetao or the Lok Ma Chau Loop, a new large plot of land near the rail station would be added, a government source added. “The educational facilities within the 300-hectare campus area of the university towns will be connected to the adjacent strategic industry area, distinctive conservation area, recreational, sports and cultural facilities, as well as the surrounding living community. The total area of the three towns has been expanded to over 1,000 hectares,” the plan read. The site spanning Hung Shui Kiu is expected to be ready this year and universities can begin bidding this month, while those in Ngau Tam Mei and the New Territories North are set to be ready in 2028 and 2030, respectively, according to the government insider. The first building of the university town, located in San Tin University Town, will be completed at the end of this year and positioned as the flagship project, according to the policy address, which Lee also unveiled on Wednesday. “It will bring together the frontier research capabilities of leading local and non-local universities and institutions, including InnoHK and other new initiatives. It will promote interaction and connection between universities, research and development and industries,” Lee said. He added that the building was named Loop Academy One, which reflects the three-part mission anchored in academia, with research and development a core part and underpinned by technology. The second building of the university town would be funded by the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, which has also allocated HK$3 billion to support the construction of another integrated teaching and scientific research building. It will focus on educational and scientific exchange as well as the cultivation of scientific research talent and will make its facilities available for other institutions to use. Public universities will have a presence and laboratories in the two buildings. The policy address and the five-year plan also listed the positions of each town. The San Tin University Town will focus on the development of medicine, life and health technology, artificial intelligence, robotics, microelectronics and emerging industries. The one in Hung Shiu Kiu will be positioned as a cultivation centre for smart manufacturing and applied post‑secondary education. The Ta Kwu Ling University Town will incorporate arts and development elements combining natural water features and green spaces, while reserving strategic development space for future needs. But according to the five-year plan, authorities would only offer land and loans for the university town, with the government source saying the project would be self-financing. “In terms of financial arrangements, the government will provide full support through a multipronged approach such as land premium exemption and loans,” the plan stated, adding institutions could mobilise their reserves or issue bonds. The government said the institutions should make good use of the business capital to fund their building projects in the towns, such as offering research collaborations, as overseas university towns did.

title: Iranian and Saudi panellists spar at Xiangshan Forum over Middle East attacks
description: Verbal battle erupts at security conference over Tehran’s targeting of US bases in Saudi Arabia.
content: A plenary session at a Beijing security conference turned into a heated exchange on Wednesday, when a senior Iranian defence official and a Saudi think tank chief clashed over the conflict in the Middle East. In the city where just a few years ago Iran and Saudi Arabia signed a peace deal, Prince Turki al-Faisal, chairman of the Saudi think tank the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies, accused Iran of not respecting “the sovereignty of the Arab states”. In a clear reference to Tehran’s attacks on the US’ Arab allies, Prince Turki told the Xiangshan Forum that this had culminated in “aggressive and unlawful attacks on [the allies’] territories and assets in the recent war”. Brigadier General Mohammad Taghi Osanlou, deputy for operations of the General Headquarters of the Armed Forces of Iran, swiftly rejected the suggestion of any wrongdoing by Tehran, saying the attacks were aimed at US assets. “We have not attacked any Arab countries or their territories. We only attacked US military bases in Arab countries,” Osanlou said. “We not only targeted Saudi Arabia. We launched strikes against US military bases in Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar, not just those in Saudi Arabia. Our target is the United States, not other Arab countries.” In his address to the forum, the Iranian military official laid blame for the conflict, now in its seventh month, squarely at the feet of the United States. Hundreds of defence officials and researchers in the audience fell silent as Osanlou raised his voice and slammed the US for challenging Iran’s bottom line. “We strongly condemn the crimes committed by the United States against Iran and in the Middle East. It has deepened divisions in the region … its pursuit of hegemony is aimed at establishing its own unilateral hegemonic order across the world,” he said, speaking through the event’s interpreter. Osanlou said the United States should withdraw its military presence from the Middle East. “As long as the US remains in the region, there can be no peace or stability in the Middle East,” he said. The Iranian official also said Tehran would not allow the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane that has been largely blocked following US and Israeli strikes in February. “How can we open the Strait of Hormuz? Iran has made hundreds of years of efforts in building up its military capabilities, which is greatly attacked in this war. So we would never allow the reopening of the strait,” Osanlou said. Researchers and officials from dozens of countries are taking part in the forum, which Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun described in his keynote address as an opportunity to “open doors to dialogue and listen to diverse voices”. Throughout the Wednesday plenary session, Prince Turki accused Iran multiple times of violating the two nations’ agreement to restore diplomatic relations, signed in Beijing in 2023 after a seven-year rupture. Prince Turki said that given that China had served as the guarantor of the agreement, Iran had disregarded China’s position by attacking Saudi Arabia. He expressed hope that China would ensure both parties honoured the agreement and determine whether Iran or Saudi Arabia had failed to comply. Prince Turki also criticised Western nations, particularly the US and Germany, saying their backing of Israel had fuelled regional conflicts. He added that the 2003 US invasion of Iraq led to the collapse of alliances among several neighbouring countries, thereby enabling the rise of powerful proxy forces allied with Iran. Both Prince Turki and Osanlou cited and endorsed Beijing’s proposals to address Middle East issues.

title: Hong Kong to woo finance and tech firms with new tax breaks
description: Chief Executive John Lee says Hong Kong aims to attract more commodity traders to set up or expand their businesses in city.
content: Hong Kong will introduce various tax incentives for new finance and technology industries to attract businesses and reinforce the city’s role as a leading financial hub, the city leader has announced in his policy address. Tax concessions to draw intellectual property (IP) businesses and selected industries to the city were among the new measures Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced on Wednesday, while the halving of the profits tax rate for gold traders would be sped up. To speed up the growth of Hong Kong’s international gold trading market, the city will push to slash the profits tax rate for qualifying physical commodity traders from the standard 16.5 per cent to 8.25 per cent by next year. The aim was to attract more commodity traders to set up or expand their businesses in Hong Kong, Lee said. With the official launch of Hong Kong’s central clearing and settlement system for gold in the first quarter of 2027, financial authorities also aim to explore providing tax concessions for qualifying activities within the gold and commodity trading ecosystem for consultation with the Legislative Council next year. Since the London Metal Exchange (LME) included Hong Kong in its global warehousing network last year, the city’s storage area has exceeded 60,000 square metres, with an inventory of more than 20,000 tonnes of the metal to date. The city in July launched a trial gold clearing and settlement system involving 11 Chinese and international banks, including introducing a two-way physical gold transfer mechanism, dubbed Delivery Connect, linking the local market with Shanghai. This is in line with the national policy to establish a commodity trading ecosystem. Separately, to attract businesses to set up corporate treasury centres and sourcing centres, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau plans to introduce an amendment bill to provide preferential tax rates to certain industries to Legco by the end of this year. “A tax concession of 5 per cent or half rate may be offered under the preferential policy packages on attracting enterprises and investments, depending on the investment plan of individual enterprises and their actual contribution to Hong Kong’s economy,” Lee said. These include enterprises in key sectors such as finance, advanced manufacturing, research and development in I&T, headquarters activities and logistics and supply-chain management. A government source said this applied to sizeable companies that authorities would like to invite to set up shop in, or “steal”, to Hong Kong, if they asked for a lower tax rate as a condition for relocating. Criteria include the investment size, the number of staff to be recruited in the city and economic contribution. Although the Inland Revenue Department is responsible for this initiative, the company will also need to seek support from the relevant bureau for its industry. For example, an aviation company needed support from the Transport and Logistics Bureau, while large finance firms should be supported by the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau, the source added. For the IP industry, the government will introduce a bill this year to implement tax deduction arrangements for capital expenditure incurred in purchasing IP rights, or for the licence to use IP rights, to support developing Hong Kong into a regional IP trading centre. According to the source, when the measures are implemented, the costs will be deducted from the buyer’s revenue when calculating profit, which acts as a tax allowance. This applies even if the buyer is an associate company of the seller, if they can prove they were not evading tax or the amount involved is not unreasonably high. The aim is to encourage more buying and management of IP. For example, a company can group all its IP under one subsidiary, which can be costly now, according to the source. Hong Kong protects eight major forms of IP – patents, trademarks, designs, copyright, trade secrets, plant varieties, performances and integrated circuit layout designs. Currently, the IP industry accounts for about 30 per cent of Hong Kong’s gross domestic product and jobs.

title: 10 AI, biotech firms in Northern Metropolis to get early cross-border data access
description: ‘White list’ to ease cross-border movement for more than 1,000 workers willl be ready next year, city leader reveals.
content: About 10 artificial intelligence (AI) and biotech companies will be the first to access cross-border data flows under a new pilot scheme, securing an early edge over roughly 100 other firms set up in Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub at the border. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu revealed on Wednesday during the final policy address of his current term that more than 100 innovation and technology firms had moved into the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, while a “white list” to facilitate cross-border movement for more than 1,000 workers would be ready next year. “Among the four cross-border flows of data, capital, materials and personnel, a pilot scheme for data flow involving around 10 firms is expected to be rolled out this year, while the talent white list will be ready by mid-next year alongside the completion of the connection bridge on the Western side,” an insider told the South China Morning Post. The government source added that while the white list would eventually cover more than 1,000 workers, the final number remained subject to how many companies established their presence in the park. The bridge is one of two cross-boundary corridors over the Shenzhen River that will link the Shenzhen park and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Park, also known as the Hong Kong park. The government earlier said it would set up dedicated boundary control facilities at a Western bridge linking the two parks to serve people on a white list. Only personnel directly involved in the development and operation of the Hong Kong park would be included, and they would still be required to undergo immigration and customs clearance, it said. The Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park is located in the Hetao cooperation zone at the Lok Ma Chau Loop proposed by Beijing in 2017, comprising two parks on either side of the border. The Hong Kong park covers 87 hectares (215 acres) while Shenzhen’s encompasses 302 hectares. The project is part of the Northern Metropolis mega development, which aims to diversify the city’s economy and is one of the highlights in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan. The 100 entities include industry heavyweights such as the pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca and battery manufacturer Xiamen Hithium Energy Storage Technology alongside roughly 100 mainland Chinese and overseas start-ups selected from a few hundred applicants to join the park soon, according to the insider. The source added that tenant numbers were expected to grow steadily. Beyond the flow of personnel and data, attention has also turned to the remaining cross-border flows of capital and materials such as biological samples. The insider noted that strong capital flows were already reflected in the high turnout for the park’s recent land tender. He cited the tender for four land parcels in the park, which drew a better-than-expected six bids earlier, and revealed that submissions were almost split evenly between Hong Kong and mainland firms focusing on frontier technologies, mostly bidding individually. The strong interest underscored capital inflow from the mainland into Hong Kong, the source added. The sites are earmarked for laboratories and talent accommodation with a combined gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres. Vincent Ma, CEO of Loop Hong Kong Park Company, said the park had “achieved remarkable outcomes in investment promotion”. Ma added that more than 100 innovation and technology entities had signed agreements to set up operations since the park’s official launch last December. He also said that the first two wet laboratory buildings were fully leased, while five remaining buildings were scheduled for completion by year-end.

title: China’s Z.ai raises revenue target 25% after US$5 billion cash injection
description: The AI firm said its computing power bottleneck was no longer a ‘primary constraint’ thanks to its fresh US$5 billion war chest.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence developer Z.ai has raised its year-end annual recurring revenue (ARR) outlook by 25 per cent to US$3 billion, as the firm indicated its fresh US$5 billion war chest had helped clear its computing capacity bottlenecks for the time being. The updated ARR projection, up from a previous estimate of about US$2.4 billion, was disclosed during an investor call on Wednesday, according to a transcript seen by the South China Morning Post. The revised guidance comes days after Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, announced it had raised US$5 billion through a share placement and convertible bond sale. The firm will use the funds to expand its computing power to support the training of new models and meet a surge in demand for its AI services. Z.ai’s ARR – a key metric projecting a firm’s monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – had reached US$1.8 billion so far this year, executives said during the call. “In the short term, computing power supply is no longer the primary constraint on the company’s rapid revenue growth,” they added. The company’s shares rose 5.9 per cent to close at HK$720 in Hong Kong on Wednesday, helping to offset a combined loss of 14.3 per cent over Monday and Tuesday amid a global slump in AI-related stocks. Despite recent stock volatility, the firm is still trading at more than six times its January listing price. The easing of the firm’s computing constraints marks a turnaround from earlier this year, when Z.ai was forced to temporarily suspend sales of its Coding Plan after the release of its GLM-5 model in February, due to a shortage of computing reserves. Momentum appears to have picked up since then. Z.ai’s coding user base expanded by more than 1 million in the two weeks following the release of its first-half results in late August, the company said. Management also said a planned 30 billion yuan (US$4.5 billion) infrastructure push could add up to 100,000 petaflops of computing power, with 40 per cent reserved for model training and research and the remaining 60 per cent for inference. That inference capacity could generate as much as 40 billion yuan in annual revenue, executives said, while cautioning that actual returns would depend on factors including utilisation, customer discounts and computing costs. On AI applications, Z.ai said its co-working tools were gaining traction beyond coding products. Industry orders had exceeded 1 billion yuan since the launch of GLM-5.3 in August, with about 100 cybersecurity companies integrating GLM models into their products and workflows, it said. The Beijing-based company is also expanding commercialisation beyond direct application programming interface (API) sales. It has signed revenue-sharing agreements with several major domestic and overseas cloud service providers, with related revenue expected to be recognised from October, according to company executives. In August, Z.ai reported a 400 per cent increase in first-half revenue to 953.89 million yuan, driven by explosive growth in its open platform and API business. The extra revenue helped the firm narrow its total loss for the period by 12.1 per cent to 2.07 billion yuan, despite higher research and development spending.

title: China mulls bid for Apec free-trade area to taunt US, tantalise Asia
description: Anticipated push for the FTAAP, covering all 21 Apec members, will burnish China’s reputation by casting the US as an obstacle, analysts say.
content: China is increasingly expected to push for a trade agreement binding a wide swathe of the Pacific Rim, including the US, when it hosts a forum of major Asia-Pacific economies in November, but a real deal may be hard to secure as Washington is likely to resist, according to analysts. The anticipated push for the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific (FTAAP), covering all 21 members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, would – even if unsuccessful – earn Beijing goodwill from other Pacific Rim countries because it would be proposing action to cut export costs, they said. “It should be high on the agenda especially given [US President Donald] Trump’s anti-international trade position and his constant tariff threats,” said Chen Zhiwu, chair professor of finance at the University of Hong Kong. The FTAAP accord, which would bind China, the US, Russia and numerous Asian manufacturing powerhouses, was introduced to the Apec agenda 20 years ago but has lain largely dormant due to geopolitical rivalries and protectionist policies. China was willing to use the idea’s 20th anniversary “as an opportunity to promote the coordinated development of regional economic and trade rules”, Chinese Vice Minister of Commerce Li Chenggang was quoted as saying in May. Officials from China were trying for an “agreement to implement” a deal at this year’s Apec forum, member country Indonesia’s official Antara news agency reported in August. Apec members normally make decisions by consensus rather than majority votes. “Trump basically in his first term already couldn’t accept any free trade agreements, so I don’t see any possibility to have one with Apec countries,” said Liang Yan, a professor of economics at Willamette University in the US. “Trump really wants to use tariffs as an economic tool and for geopolitical reasons.” Trump opposes multilateral trade deals and last year slapped tariffs of more than 100 per cent on imports from China. The US president would oppose an Apec deal partly on concern that China could “use” the other countries in the pact as “stepping stones to export goods to the US”, Chen said. The Ministry of Commerce in Beijing said that Apec ministers in January had “in-depth discussions” about the trade area. Months later, it adopted a “Beijing road map” to help achieve it, according to a ministry statement. China, the trade area’s key proponent for years, could use its Apec host role in 2026 to spearhead the issue, said Jayant Menon, a visiting senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. The area was proposed to align two-way and multi-country free trade agreements that had expanded after a collapsed round of World Trade Organization talks in 2006. Tariff cuts and market liberalisation are common hallmarks of the deals – including two that already bind China to the giant Southeast Asian trading bloc. Chinese President Xi Jinping said at an Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting last year that the group should help the pan-Asian Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership trade pact and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership deal “align with each other and progress together so as to inject impetus into the development of the FTAAP”. China would welcome the trade area to “counterbalance the pressure and the rhetoric” from the US and Europe against Chinese export practices, Chen said, adding that any agreements of this scale would allow Chinese exporters, a backbone for the world’s second largest economy, to ship at lower costs. Beijing’s advocacy of the Apec trade area would cast the US as an obstacle to regional trade, assuming Washington protested it while other Pacific Rim countries favoured it, Chen said. “Pushing on the [trade area idea] may or may not lead to substantive deliverables, but simply keeping it in the headlines can allow China to portray itself as a champion of open trade and demonstrate that other countries want more trade with China,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at Gavekal Dragonomics in Hong Kong.

title: Former director of leading Chinese museum jailed 3 years after art-selling scandal
description: Xu Huping found to have abused his position at Nanjing Museum and taken bribes, including money and property, state media says.
content: A former director of a state-owned museum at the centre of a rare high-profile art scandal was sentenced to three years in prison, Chinese state media said on Wednesday. Xu Huping was found to have abused his position at the Nanjing Museum in eastern Jiangsu province and taken bribes, including money and property, for helping others secure projects and business collaborations. He was sentenced to prison for three years and fined 200,000 yuan (US$29,800), according to state news agency Xinhua. Before this, he had been expelled from the Communist Party and stripped of benefits after an investigation into allegations that arose in December last year that the museum had secretly sold donated paintings. Xu, who was found to have mishandled artworks, was central to the investigation. The controversy centred on five paintings from a large collection donated by the family of collector Pang Laichen. The paintings were found missing during a court-ordered inventory review last year. The review came after one of the works – a painting titled Spring in Jiangnan by Qiu Ying from the Ming dynasty – surfaced at an auction house. A months-long investigation initiated by Jiangsu provincial authorities and the National Cultural Heritage Administration found that some of the five works were illegally sold, transferred or lost. They found that in the 1990s, then vice-director Xu had violated procedures when he approved the transfer of paintings to a state-owned relics store. Following the investigation, Xu was placed under formal disciplinary review in February. Xu served as the museum’s director from 2001 to 2005 and retired in 2008. A relics store employee surnamed Zhang was also placed under investigation for allegedly altering the price tag of Spring in Jiangnan to orchestrate its resale to a private collector. Authorities found more than two dozen people responsible for the mismanagement and illegal sales of artefacts, with 24 still alive to face punishment. The timing of the revelations struck a nerve among the Chinese public, which has become increasingly interested in traditional Chinese art and culture in recent years. The scale of systemic mismanagement at the Nanjing Museum, one of China’s largest and most prominent museums, raised public concerns over the potential for management issues in other museum collections. In April, the National Cultural Heritage Administration launched a year-long nationwide campaign to inventory all state-owned collections. Zhang and others, including provincial officials, were also held responsible for violations, such as failing to properly perform their duties or the unauthorised transfer or sale of artworks. Wednesday’s report did not specify Zhang’s punishment but said that those implicated would face disciplinary action such as dismissal and demotion. The provincial culture and tourism department and relics bureau, along with the Nanjing Museum, have said they will strengthen the safety management of state-owned museum collections.

title: Philippines seek WTA exemption as Alexandra Eala skips China Open for Asian Games
description: Games and Open have overlapping schedules and Philippines tennis body wants world No 18 to compete at Aichi-Nagoya without penalties.
content: The Philippines Tennis Association (Philta) has filed a ⁠request with the ⁠WTA on behalf of ⁠Alexandra Eala, requesting an exemption from the mandatory China Open so that the world No 18 can represent her country at the Asian Games. Eala, who has become a fan favourite ‌with wins over some of the biggest names on the circuit including Iga Swiatek and Coco Gauff, is the highest-ranked player in the women’s singles draw at the Asian Games, which begin on Saturday and conclude on October 4. However, the Aichi-Nagoya ⁠Games schedule overlaps with the China Open, a mandatory WTA 1000 tournament, which ‌starts in Beijing on September 30. Skipping a mandatory WTA 1000 competition without an official exemption results in a ranking penalty and may attract fines. “We have formally requested an ⁠exemption and we ⁠respect the WTA’s process. At the same time, Alex has made her decision to ‌represent the Philippines at the Asian Games, and we fully support her,” Philta secretary general ‌John ‌Rey Tiangco said in a statement to media on Tuesday. The WTA has been reached for a comment. Earlier this week, Indonesian ⁠Janice Tjen withdrew from the Asian Games as she was unable to ⁠secure an exemption from taking part in the China Open. Eala, however, will compete at the Asian Games regardless of the WTA’s ‌decision, Philippine Olympic Committee ‌president Abraham Tolentino said in a statement. “The WTA has its rules and breaking the rules has penalties. But Alex will be in Nagoya, for flag and country,” he added.

title: Australia to ban student dependants as Labor fends off far-right pressure
description: Canberra plans to cap net migration at 225,000 and stop visa hopping as a housing crisis and the far-right One Nation party turn up the heat.
content: Australia is set to introduce sweeping changes to its immigration policy by barring international students from bringing dependants, in a bid to ease housing pressures and fend off a growing political challenge from the far-right. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke will announce the measures at the National Press Club in Canberra on Thursday, outlining plans to trim net overseas migration from 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028. The issuance of temporary residence permits would also be reduced to curb “visa hopping” and ensure migrants leave Australia once their visas expire, according to national broadcaster ABC. Between July last year and June this year, Australia granted 337,427 student visas, 45,991 of which were for dependants or family members. International education is one of Australia’s largest export sectors, contributing A$36.4 billion (US$25.96 billion) to the economy in the 2022–23 financial year. Speaking to lawmakers on Wednesday, Burke said the government would enact the revamp through legislation, but remained open to other “levers” if the ruling Labor Party’s plan failed to pass parliament. “Since the Hawke and Howard years, a whole lot of our immigration system has been demand-driven, and processing speeds are one of the only things, with planning levels, we currently have available,” he said, referring to former prime ministers Bob Hawke and John Howard. “The best form of outcome ... if we are able to sort our way through, [is] for a legislative option,” Burke added. “In the absence of that, there are still more levers the government will be able to use.” The crackdown targets people on bridging visas – which allow holders to remain and work in Australia – following accusations of applicants “gaming the system”. This group includes temporary migrants whose claims for protection have already been rejected by the Department of Home Affairs. The department handles about 1,580 protection claims a month, mostly from Chinese, Indian and Malaysian nationals on student or visitor visas. Although about 90 per cent of these claims are dismissed, applicants can appeal – a process that can take up to eight years. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s government faces mounting pressure from Pauline Hanson, leader of the far-right One Nation party, who has blamed the nation’s housing crisis on migration. Hanson, whose populist party has been performing well in opinion polls, has proposed reducing the number of temporary migrants by roughly 750,000 over three years. “A larger economy on paper means nothing if Australians are poorer per person and cannot afford a home, find a hospital bed or get ahead,” Hanson said in a statement on Monday, reported by Bloomberg. Support for One Nation stood at 31 per cent in a June Newspoll survey, ahead of Labor on 30 per cent. Migration has long been a vital engine of Australia’s economic growth, helping the country avoid a recession since the early 1990s, outside a brief contraction during the Covid-19 pandemic.

title: Hong Kong leader pledges building maintenance reforms after fatal Tai Po fire
description: Government will conduct a legal study on criminalising bid-rigging in major building maintenance works and submit a proposal to the Legislative Council this year.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to overhaul the city’s building maintenance regime and improve emergency response as part of the government’s response to last year’s fatal Tai Po fire, while authorities study criminalising bid-rigging and plan to submit a proposal later this year. The measures were outlined in Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address on Wednesday, amid pressure on the government to strengthen oversight of renovation works after the city’s deadliest fire in decades at Wang Fuk Court, where all eight blocks were covered in scaffolding. He said the government would conduct a legal study on criminalising bid-rigging in major building maintenance works and submit a proposal to the Legislative Council this year. The government would also introduce “pre-qualified lists” of consultants and contractors to help owners select professionals for renovation works. Authorities would vet applicants through background checks conducted by law-enforcement agencies. As the government planned to begin accepting applications later this month and roll out the list by the end of this year, an insider said the applicants would be assessed on several criteria. “We will look at their technical ability, integrity, financial background and their work records,” the source said. The insider added that the government would conduct background checks on the directors and authorised persons of renovation and consultancy companies to prevent nominal appointments and ensure they were capable of supervising works. An authorised person is a professional registered under the Buildings Ordinance to coordinate and supervise private building works. Lee’s address also proposed further amendments to the ordinance to strengthen oversight and increase penalties for large renovation projects. According to a government source, authorities were considering requiring major renovation works at multi-block estates to be carried out in phases unless contractors introduced specified safety measures. The insider said the government was also considering tighter oversight of certain minor works at large-scale maintenance projects that did not currently require the Buildings Department’s approval. The final proposals, however, would be tabled only after the government considered the report of the independent committee investigating the causes of the Tai Po fire, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 residents. The committee is expected to submit its report and recommendations next month. Its lead counsel, Victor Dawes SC, has attributed the disaster to six “human factors” and pointed to systemic regulatory failures and suspected fraudulent acts by contractors. The factors listed included the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, widespread installation of combustible polyfoam boards over windows and deactivation of the fire-alarm system. The policy address also highlighted efforts to enhance fire safety and emergency responses. Another insider said firefighters from neighbouring Macau and Guangdong province were ready to assist local officers during future “ultra-large-scale fires”. The source said equipment of the firefighting teams in Macau and mainland China was aligned with Hong Kong standards. Their duties at the scene would depend on the circumstances, the source added. The policy address also said the Fire Services Department would optimise its mobilisation protocol, command systems and casualty handling procedures, as well as leverage artificial intelligence and technology to improve efficiency. According to the source, the department has been using lightweight robots to tackle fires in narrow spaces. It will soon introduce smart systems to track firefighters’ status, record their entry times and monitor air levels in their breathing apparatus, the insider added. The measures follow the death of firefighter Ho Wai-ho at the Tai Po fire. He lost contact with colleagues at the scene, and a post-fire visual inspection indicated that he might have been in prolonged contact with hot or burning objects. The policy blueprint also said the department would further apply its Internet of Things (IoT) fire alarms to cover old buildings of seven storeys or more by the end of the year. The IoT system can provide real-time detection and rapidly transmit fire-alarm signals, which helps improve safety in buildings.

title: Opinion | Why Russia’s AI-powered economic future lies in its Far East
description: With a 10-year plan, the Far East gives Moscow what mature economies lack: room to redesign systems at regional scale.
content: I attended this year’s Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok and took part in a dialogue on technological development. There, I had a deep discussion with Maxim Oreshkin, Russia’s deputy chief of the presidential executive office, who co-chairs the country’s national AI headquarters. I left Vladivostok with a broader impression: Russia increasingly sees its Far East as a place to build a new version of its economy. For decades, Russia’s Far East has been understood through geography. It is vast, resource-rich and sparsely populated. At the forum, those characteristics were recast as strategic assets. President Vladimir Putin presented an updated development strategy running to 2036 and called for the Far East and Arctic to serve as testing grounds for advanced technologies. A special legal regime due to begin next year is intended to speed up experimentation. The government is planning new data centres, stronger power infrastructure and next-generation transport systems. The Far East offers Russia something increasingly scarce in mature economies: room to redesign systems at a regional scale. A logistics network can be built around autonomous operations from the outset. New industrial projects can assume that artificial intelligence (AI) will be part of daily work. Public services can be designed around digital tools as they expand. The region has the potential to become a greenfield laboratory for an AI-era economy. Geopolitics gives this experiment urgency. Russia’s confrontation with the West has reduced its access to Western technology, capital and markets. Its economic gravity has consequently moved eastwards. Vladivostok sits at the front edge of a Russia increasingly connected to China and the wider Asia-Pacific. A shift born from geopolitical pressure can still create a development opportunity: old dependencies weaken and new systems have to be built. The strongest consensus I heard at the forum and dialogue was that AI is becoming societal infrastructure. Its long-term importance will come from widespread use, much as electricity transformed economies by becoming ordinary, dependable and cheap enough to be embedded everywhere. I have argued previously in the SCMP that accessibility may become one of the defining sources of advantage in the AI era. A capable model creates value when millions of people and businesses can afford to use it repeatedly. Russia enters this transition with a powerful upstream asset: energy. According to the US Energy Information Administration, Russia remains one of the world’s largest producers of natural gas and oil, while its electricity system also draws heavily on nuclear power and hydropower. In an AI economy, energy can be converted into computation and computation can be converted into intelligence. A country that can supply this chain reliably has a path towards lower-cost AI. The opportunity is real although it depends on execution. Parts of the Far East currently face power capacity constraints and industrial electricity prices have been under pressure. Data centres only become strategic assets when the grid can support them. Russia’s energy advantage is best understood as an upstream advantage that still needs to be converted into reliable electrical capacity and modern computing infrastructure. The human side may be even more important. The economic return from AI depends heavily on whether people learn to work with it. Russia’s challenge is to cultivate a population comfortable with using AI as an ordinary tool. In this context, logistics is an obvious starting point. Large distances and labour constraints make route optimisation, autonomous delivery and coordinated warehousing unusually valuable. Logistics is not only an economically valuable use case but also a setting in which broad-based AI literacy can develop through daily work. This is also why regulation should support learning at scale. The Far East’s proposed experimental legal regime could become important if it creates a controlled environment where organisations can deploy useful systems, measure their effects and improve the rules through experience. The AI infrastructure challenge has three layers: energy, compute and models. Its energy base gives it a strong starting point. Turning that energy into intelligence requires accelerators, servers and data-centre systems at scale. The final layer is a supply of capable models that can be adapted to Russian language, industry and public services. This is where cooperation with Asian partners becomes commercially significant. China has developed increasingly competitive open-weight language models and a growing domestic compute ecosystem. Chinese firms could find demand in Russia for model deployment, inference hardware and the systems needed to connect AI with industrial processes. Such projects would need careful structuring around export controls, sanctions exposure, payments and Russian localisation requirements but the underlying business need is clear. The more interesting opportunity is larger than selling chips or models. If Russia can assemble the full infrastructure, the Far East could become a place where AI is integrated into the design of a region while that region is still being built. That creates a rare chance to study what an AI-powered society looks like when AI enters ordinary economic and public life as part of the underlying operating system. Russia’s eastwards turn was forced by geopolitical rupture. Forced innovation, however, can produce institutional changes that gradual reform rarely attempts. The Far East gives Russia the space to build new infrastructure and a reason to experiment with new rules. It also places the country next to Asian partners that can supply technologies and markets. The Eastern Economic Forum left me with a question that reaches beyond Russia: what happens when a country begins to treat AI the way earlier generations treated electricity? If the experiment works, the Far East may be where Russia’s technological future is built.

title: Hong Kong to set up ‘AI city brain’ to boost disaster response and public safety
description: Government also creating new role of AI commissioner, who is expected to begin next year overseeing key areas of risk governance, John Lee says.
content: Hong Kong will create an “AI city brain” system to strengthen its response to extreme weather events, major incidents and public order management, while creating the role of artificial intelligence commissioner to tackle emerging challenges. While the city’s first five-year plan set out a vision to advance technology development, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu outlined seven key areas of AI risk governance in Wednesday’s policy address, including efforts to combat the use of AI in crime and introducing management guidelines for AI agents. “We will push for AI development comprehensively … as it enhances efficiency in all aspects including governance,” Lee said. “[But] global AI development is advancing so rapidly that I believe the world is thinking about how to promote its growth while properly managing the risks; [therefore we] introduce regulatory measures.” The policy address detailed plans to apply AI to improve governance, including setting up the “AI city brain” system. To be spearheaded by an interdepartmental task force chaired by No 2 official Eric Chan Kwok-ki, the platform will use AI analysis, big data analytics and a data-sharing environment to provide early warnings and trend forecasts, improving interdepartmental collaboration in response to extreme weather, major incidents and public order management, such as crowd control. In the first phase, expected to launch by the second quarter of next year, the system will integrate with the Security Bureau’s Emergency Monitoring and Support Centre to improve the city’s response to extreme weather before the next typhoon season. A government source said the system would draw data from departments including the Observatory, the Drainage Services Department and the Fire Services Department, as well as information from the 999 emergency hotline and the 1823 public inquiry and complaint hotline, enabling a faster, more proactive response. He added that in the case of a heavy rainstorm, AI could help anticipate which areas were at high risk of flooding and help in the rapid deployment of officers and resources. A new “interdepartmental major incident platform” would also merge existing systems to support real-time data exchange among emergency response units, the insider said. Another component of the “brain” will be a traffic management platform that will use big data and access real-time traffic information, such as traffic and passenger flows and road conditions, with a trial to be launched in Aberdeen next year. The platform is also expected to help the government and public transport operators formulate contingency plans in extreme weather. The administration will study overseas examples and assess the computing power demands of the entire system, before later putting it out to tender, a government source said. He also stressed that the system would use only the government’s internal computing resources and a private cloud to ensure security. Other applications of AI in governance include site supervision for public works, property management at public housing estates, the facilitation of service arrangements at hospitals and the identification of high-risk patients. AI will also be applied in the 1823 hotline to identify recurring complaints, allowing authorities to formulate targeted solutions, moving away from a post-complaint management approach. Lee also announced the creation of the new post of commissioner for AI, who will come under the Digital Policy Office. The externally recruited commissioner is expected to take up the role next year and will oversee seven key areas of AI risk governance. These include combating AI-related crimes, such as deepfake porn and online scams, and empowering authorities to remove online content linked to financial fraud. The government will consult the public on enhancing the legal framework and improving the detection of AI-generated fraudulent content. As the government has already piloted AI agents capable of autonomously integrating and executing multiple tasks, it will work with the Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute to release society-wide guidelines on AI agent management next year. The government will also review whether existing laws adequately address liability for accidents or damage caused by AI products, promote market assessment of AI ethical risks, step up protection for minors using AI and ensure they use the technology with the proper values and attitude. Another government source said an additional HK$1 billion would be allocated to the Artificial Intelligence Subsidy Scheme, launched in 2024 to help local research and development centres, start-ups and educational institutions access computing power at Cyberport. The policy address also revealed that the Sandy Ridge Data Facility Cluster is expected to deliver computing power of 180,000 petaflops by 2032, 36 times the current capacity, providing support for the city’s intelligent computing industry. The two pilot lines on the research and development and trial production of third‑generation semiconductors will also commence by the end of the year. Lawmaker Duncan Chiu. who represents the technology and innovation sector, welcomed the government’s measures, saying the “AI city brain” would help departments communicate better and resolve long-standing bottlenecks in the use of the technology within the government. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, cautioned that establishing the traffic management platform would be challenging because it would involve technical hurdles such as inconsistent data standards, requiring trials and adjustments across varying commuting modes in different districts.

title: China’s AI chip stocks face crucial test as MetaX lock-up period expires
description: The Chinese AI chip firm enjoyed a blockbuster market debut in December, but its stock is now under pressure ahead of a major share release.
content: China is bracing for a potential massive sell-off of a high-profile artificial intelligence chip stock on Thursday, when a lock-up period affecting 14 million shares in MetaX Integrated Circuits is set to expire. Analysts expect MetaX to face “significant selling pressure” when the restricted shares are released for trading, after the expiry of a similar lock-up period for shares in fellow AI chip firm Moore Threads last week sparked an avalanche of sales that wiped nearly 49 billion yuan (US$7.3 billion) off the company’s value in a single day. The looming release of the MetaX shares is seen as a crucial test for China’s AI chip stocks, which have attracted huge investor interest as China strives to develop domestic challengers to US graphics processing unit behemoth Nvidia. Moore Threads and MetaX both enjoyed blockbuster market debuts on Shanghai’s Star Market in December, with their share prices skyrocketing by several hundred per cent amid a wave of investor hype. The companies are known as part of the “four little dragons” in China’s AI chip sector alongside Biren Technology and Enflame. But their shares are now coming under pressure as some early backers look to cash in on their gains. When a lock-up period affecting 26 million shares in Moore Threads expired last week, the company’s share price quickly plunged by 20 per cent – triggering the Star Market’s daily downward limit. Moore Thread’s stock has continued falling since then, shedding more than 30 per cent and wiping out tens of billions of yuan in market value. The rout has led to expectations of a similar sell-off when MetaX releases its own restricted shares, which are worth an estimated 6.7 billion yuan (US$998 million) based on the company’s share price on Wednesday. “When the restricted shares are released, the stock price is likely to face significant selling pressure,” said Kenny Ng, a strategist at Everbright Securities International, adding that the scale of the sell-off would depend on the actual cost basis of the original investors who bought in. “The initial investment cost for these restricted shares was quite low. Although AI stocks have recently undergone a price correction, compared to the entry cost of the original investors the current profit margins are still high.” MetaX, which went public 12 days later than Moore Threads, already saw its shares tumble more than 22 per cent last week as investors pre-emptively unloaded positions to avoid being caught in the expected correction. Both companies are currently seeking listings in Hong Kong. The anticipated sell-off, however, would be more a structural market function than a reflection of MetaX’s operational health, Ng stressed. And despite the recent price drop, early institutional investors in the company are still sitting on massive paper gains. MetaX listed in December 2025 at an IPO price of 104.66 yuan per share. With the stock closing at nearly 478 yuan on Wednesday, early backers still boast a profit margin of over 350 per cent. Analysts, meanwhile, maintain a positive outlook on the company’s product road map amid fierce domestic competition. MetaX started mass production of its next-generation C600 processor in May, and the firm is expected to proceed with a “gradual ramp-up” of production over the second half of 2026 and 2027, according to a Goldman Sachs research note published last week. The company was also the first among the “four little dragons” to achieve first-half profitability. It posted a net profit of 612 million yuan for the first six months of 2026, reversing a loss of 186 million yuan a year earlier. Moore Threads saw its net loss narrow from 271 million yuan a year ago to 11.6 million yuan during the same period.

title: Hong Kong’s HK$30,000 bonus for second child among 11 new measures to boost births
description: ‘The current-term government has shifted from a non-interventionist approach to actively promoting fertility,’ city leader John Lee says.
content: Hong Kong authorities have rolled out 11 new initiatives to encourage residents to have children, including an expanded cash bonus scheme and a reduced down payment for subsidised housing for parents with newborns. In the latest policy address delivered on Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced that the HK$20,000 (US$2,550) newborn bonus scheme, expiring on October 24, would be extended for another three years. He added that the cash bonus for second and subsequent children would increase to HK$30,000, while the tax allowance for such children would also rise from HK$140,000 to HK$160,000. “The current-term government has shifted from a non-interventionist approach to actively promoting fertility, working to create a conducive environment for childbearing,” he said. SCMP · Hong Kong’s HK$30,000 bonus for second child among 11 new measures to boost births A government source estimated that the incentives would reduce tax income by HK$15 million in the first year of implementation, while the amount would climb to HK$200 million in 26 years’ time, describing the impact as “manageable”. Other measures include waiving stamp duties for families who buy properties from one year before to two years after childbirth, capped at HK$20,000, and raising the mortgage loan-to-value ratio for White Form family applicants – non-public housing residents – with newborns applying for subsidised flats under the Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) to 95 per cent to ease their down payment burden. Hong Kong launched the HK$20,000 baby bonus in 2023 as a measure to drive fertility. Although the number of newborns rose to 35,723 in 2024, it fell to just more than 31,000 the following year. Only 19,255 infants were born in the first eight months of this year, nearly 10 per cent lower than in the same period in 2025. Professor Michael Wong, chairman of the Hong Kong Future Economy Institute and an economics professor at the University of Hong Kong, said the lack of affordable housing was a critical problem for young families. “Youth home ownership has declined dramatically over the last thirty years,” Wong said. “The government’s decision to help young households with children obtain a mortgage at a lower rate is a step in the right direction.” But not all young families could benefit, as another source said only those with children no older than three years on the day of application were eligible for the 95 per cent mortgage rate. A mother of two who asked to remain anonymous said her younger daughter would turn three years old next month, meaning the family would not be eligible if the next round of HOS flat sales happens after their girl’s birthday. Renting a 200 sq ft home in Sham Shui Po, the woman and her husband were hesitant to buy a subsidised home despite hoping to provide a larger living space for their daughter and 11-year-old son. The mother, who is in her thirties, added that the family had not benefited from the current HK$20,000 baby bonus because her daughter was born before the measure was introduced in the 2023 policy address. The four-person household, which earns just over HK$20,000 a month, could not benefit from the tax perks either. The couple was hesitant to have one more child despite the expanded bonus scheme. “The HK$30,000 baby bonus is of little help. The parents have to bear the costs on their own in the long run,” the woman said. She said relaunching the HK$2,500 non-means-tested student grant would be more helpful, as they paid HK$3,000 already on her son’s textbooks in the first term this year. The mother, a part-time clerk, also hoped the government could provide childcare help so she could work full time to share her husband’s burden. To improve upward housing mobility, Lee also said the government would relax the restriction period for the reselling of HOS flats sold between 2022 and 2025 from 15 to 10 years. The city’s first five-year plan vowed to boost property ownership, as the government set out a housing supply planning basis for the coming decade, with 40 per cent of public rental homes, 30 per cent of subsidised sale flats and the remainder for private homes. The housing minister told the media in 2024 that the ratio was 5:2:3. Lee also announced in the policy address to improve the career prospects of young people. Starting from the first quarter of 2027, the government would collaborate with the business sector to roll out 10,000 full-time positions for young people newly entering the workforce over two years, with the government subsidising up to HK$6,000 of their monthly salaries. There will also be 10,000 government-subsidised internships in the science, technology, engineering and maths sectors, also known as STEM, and another 10,000 on-the-job training places for construction industry professional graduates. Fresh university graduate Derek Liao Ka-chung described the new initiatives as “incremental”. “Even if I am allocated a HOS flat and my parents could make the down payment, I still have to repay the mortgage. But when consumer prices are so high in Hong Kong, I don’t know if I can even survive,” said the 23-year-old religious studies graduate from the Chinese University of Hong Kong. For Liao, who was still hunting for a job, employment was a more urgent issue than property ownership, adding that the 10,000 job positions would be less beneficial to arts faculty graduates like him.

title: Hong Kong launching pilot scheme to bring in foreign carers for the elderly
description: Chief Executive John Lee says in policy address that the government will admit carers under a scheme modelled on domestic helper regime.
content: Hong Kong will introduce a pilot scheme next year to bring in foreign domestic carers to look after older residents as part of a broader package of measures announced in the policy address to deal with an ageing population. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said in his address on Wednesday that the government would admit carers under a scheme modelled on the city’s existing foreign domestic helper regime. “With reference to the existing regime for admitting foreign domestic helpers, the government will admit foreign domestic carers with more advanced training and experience in elderly care on a pilot basis,” he said. “This will help meet the care needs of elderly persons living at home.” A government source said the pilot scheme aimed to expand the pool of recruits and attract people with relevant skills in response to Hong Kong’s ageing population. Those employed under the new scheme must have experience in caring for the elderly and undergo relevant training in their home countries, he said. The source added that authorities had not ruled out setting a higher minimum monthly wage for recruits under the new scheme than the amount paid to helpers. The current minimum allowable wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month. The source also said basic requirements for the existing regime for helpers, including the live-in rule, would apply to the new scheme. The scheme would be open to people from countries currently covered by the domestic helper regime, he said. No quota would be imposed on the number of carers admitted under the pilot scheme, he added. The government was in talks with relevant consulates to work out details, including the content and duration of the training required for recruits, the source said, adding that the scheme would be launched next year. Hong Kong had more than 378,000 foreign domestic helpers last year, mostly from the Philippines and Indonesia. The pilot scheme was among a series of measures Lee announced on Wednesday to build an age-friendly society, including the setting up of three new residential care homes for the elderly, providing about 400 places. The government will increase the number of community care service vouchers for the elderly by 2,000 to 18,000 in the 2027-28 financial year, while the number of residential care service vouchers for the elderly will rise by 1,000 to 8,000. Five new subsidised day-care facilities for the elderly will be established, providing about 200 service places. In rapidly ageing Hong Kong, the number of people aged 65 and above is projected to nearly double from 1.45 million in 2021 to 2.74 million by 2046, when more than one in three residents will be elderly.

title: Hong Kong aims to raise zero-carbon energy share of fuel mix to 30% by 2030
description: Target is one of four binding environmental protection targets revealed in city’s first five-year plan.
content: Hong Kong has pledged to boost the share of zero-carbon energy in its electricity generation fuel mix to 30 per cent by 2030, up from the current 28 per cent – one of four binding environmental protection targets set out in the city’s first five-year plan on Wednesday. The binding goal aligns with existing climate protection strategies that target a zero-carbon energy share of between 60 and 70 per cent by 2035, as part of the city’s broader push towards carbon neutrality by 2050. “With these efforts, we strive to strengthen energy security, lower energy generation costs and stabilise electricity tariffs to minimise the impacts of the war in the Middle East, which has driven up liquefied natural gas prices,” a government source said. Natural gas currently accounts for most of Hong Kong’s electricity generation, making up more than 50 per cent of the fuel mix as of June this year, followed by coal at under 20 per cent, and nuclear and renewable energy at around 28 per cent. “As we advance green transition goals in alignment with the national plan, it goes hand in hand with carbon reduction,” the source said.
