Between now and 2030, Hong Kong would aim to import more nuclear, wind and water energy from mainland China via the Clean Energy Transmission System, the source said. The system, under which CLP Power connects to the Daya Bay Nuclear Power Station and the China Southern Power Grid, underwent enhancements in March to strengthen overhead cables for energy supply. The source added the city had sufficient electricity reserves to meet an anticipated rise in demand from the coming data facility at Sandy Ridge in the Northern Metropolis. The facility, which aims to boost Hong Kong’s overall computing power, is scheduled to begin operations in 2029. “Regarding the power usage effectiveness [for data facilities], our stance is to strike a balance,” the source said. The government has long regulated the electricity market through Scheme of Control Agreements signed with the city’s two energy providers, HK Electric and CLP Power. The parties signed a 15-year agreement in 2017 to run until 2033, with the next interim review set for 2028. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, which contains 22 major indicators, aims to align the city’s priorities with the nation’s 2026-30 development blueprint. Similar to the national five-year plan and Guangdong province’s own blueprint, all environmental targets are binding goals that must be achieved by 2030. Addressing the media on Wednesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said environmental targets were made binding because they involved “critical” factors affecting livelihoods. “Environmental factors [are] important because … everyone needs to breathe, right? So we have to ensure that these factors that will affect health [heavily] are something we must do well to achieve … and devote all resources and actions to,” he said. Another binding goal in the five-year plan is to ensure more than 90 per cent of Hong Kong’s 30 main rivers and streams meet water quality standards – up from 88 per cent – with key parameters including acidity and oxygen levels. The plan also touches on expanding producer responsibility schemes to raise recycling rates for plastic bottles, although the blueprint does not include a timeline. Greenpeace called for the scheme to be implemented in 2027 and for companies to be required to disclose plastic bottle usage volumes and reduction progress annually. The non-profit organisation stressed that tackling waste reduction at the source was “the first step in addressing the city’s waste problems”. In 2021, Hong Kong announced its own climate action plan, which included a target of achieving carbon neutrality before 2050 – 10 years ahead of the rest of the nation. Authorities are also set to implement the second phase of a push to ensure energy efficiency standards for building services installations later this month. The policy is expected to cut the annual electricity consumption of about 150,000 three-person households by 2035. To support the city’s more than 180,000 electric vehicles, the government also aims to boost the number of fast chargers to 4,000 by 2030, before reaching 10,000 by 2035 to support about 500,000 electric vehicles.

title: Trump taking notes from India? US$5,000 cash pitch draws ‘freebie’ comparisons
description: Indian politicians and commentators accuse the US president of mimicking South Asia’s election playbook to woo voters ahead of the midterms.
content: Donald Trump’s proposal to give adult Americans US$5,000 if Republicans win November’s midterm elections has drawn an unusual accusation from India: that the US president is borrowing from the country’s welfare-heavy political playbook. Speaking days after Trump floated the US$5,000 proposal on September 9, Karnataka Deputy Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar told an event held by India’s main opposition Congress party: “Trump is copying us.” Shivakumar argued that the pledge reflected the wider influence of Karnataka’s welfare model. Political analysts and party leaders credit Karnataka’s targeted welfare promises – aimed at easing inflation, empowering women and supporting youth – as a defining factor behind Congress winning a decisive victory in the state in 2023. To Indian observers, Trump’s conditional payout promise sounded familiar. Social media users compared it to pre-poll pledges often made by domestic politicians, posting memes and saying “freebies” had reached America’s shores. Trump’s proposal comes as the US economy battles persistent inflation and rising interest rates, partly because of a long and costly war with Iran. But the US president has claimed the payouts would be possible because of the economy’s strength. It is unclear how – or if – Trump’s proposal could be implemented. Some commentators see the move as a bid to win back voters who have drifted from the Republican Party because of the effects of the prolonged war with Iran. “Trump has to find an alternative way to appeal to voters, especially those in his Maga base,” said Priyajit Debsarkar, a London-based independent political commentator writing on South Asia. He said such handouts had produced mixed results in India, where discerning voters knew what was in their larger interest. Indian commentators described the staggering US$1 trillion-plus proposal as a classic populist manoeuvre to revive flagging popularity ahead of the midterms. Harsh Ramaswamy, a political commentator, said welfare programmes in India and other developing nations, such as Brazil, were originally designed to address historic inequities in poorer communities. “By making such a proposal, he is also accepting that it means America is becoming poorer,” Ramaswamy said. He added that if democracy was to remain healthy, welfare initiatives should be offered by elected governments for targeted, needy families rather than dangled by political leaders in the run-up to polls. Ramaswamy also said support should ideally come in the form of essential supplies, such as food staples, rather than cash. “When you offer money like this, people will be spoiled,” he said, warning that cash payouts risked being misspent on alcohol or illegal drugs. Economists and other political observers have also voiced concerns about the potential effects on inflation and the national balance sheet, saying the proposal resembled a desperate political gambit. Ramaswamy said that as a 250-year-old democracy, the US should set an example for younger democracies like India, which is 76 years old. “American democracy was exemplified because of its performance and functioning. It is a sad thing that the spirit of American democracy is being murdered,” he said. Trump had previously pledged to distribute payments of US$2,000 or more using savings from the Department of Government Efficiency and tariff revenues, though none of that materialised. An opinion piece in The Times of India, one of the country’s leading daily newspapers, made a similar comparison: “From voter ID to $5,000 cheques: Trump goes desi, mimics India’s election toolkit.” “US President Donald Trump may never admit it, but it’s self-evident,” the article read. “The self-proclaimed oldest democracy is beginning to borrow from [the] political toolkit of the world’s largest democracy.” “It first reflected in Trump’s photo identification for voting. Now comes the promise of money.” Voter identification Trump has repeatedly pushed for mandatory photo identification and proof of citizenship in federal elections. Proponents argue these rules strengthened public confidence and election security, while critics say they were cumbersome and risked disenfranchising legitimate voters. In an August 17 post on social media, Trump cited India’s voter identification system to advocate for the SAVE America Act: “India’s last Election had 646,000,000 Voters! Less than 1% voted by mail, and every single Voter had to have a VALID Photo Identity Document.” The post followed what Trump described as a question from Indian Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on why US elections did not require photo identification. Ramaswamy said citing India’s voter ID cards to push for a similar system in the US was not the right comparison. Given India’s large population, mandatory identification was needed to prevent confusion about voters’ identity, particularly among voters with similar names. “We needed identification to map these people. You don’t need that in America,” he said. Debsarkar said the proposals indicated a shift in the US political undercurrent since the last election cycle.

title: Chinese defence chief skirts flashpoints at Xiangshan Forum ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: Dong Jun makes rare public offer of foreign military aid at major security conference and skips mentions of Taiwan and South China Sea.
content: With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday. Speaking at the annual Xiangshan Forum in Beijing, Dong took veiled swipes at Washington and its allies but – unlike last year – appeared to pull his punches, skipping mentions of contentious issues such as Taiwan and the South China Sea. He also said Beijing would share its experience in “military building” and “provide assistance within our capabilities” to foreign armed forces, a rare public offer by the country’s top defence officials. Beijing seems increasingly confident of its military prowess heading into the People’s Liberation Army’s centenary next year, with a belief that it is closing the military gap with Washington. At the same time, there are signs of improving defence ties between the two powers. A senior Pentagon official said earlier that US-China military communication was “stronger than it has been in years”. At the forum, Dong described the global landscape as complex and international security as “fragile”, saying there was an “urgent need” to improve global security governance. “We must promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive, forging a new path to security based on dialogue rather than confrontation, partnership rather than alliance and win-win outcomes rather than zero-sum games,” he said. While he did not name any country, Dong alluded to the US and its actions in the Middle East on several occasions, including urging “major powers” to shoulder the responsibility of maintaining global stability and upholding multilateralism, and calling on countries to “resist reckless moves that use security as a bargaining chip”. “We must not tolerate provocations that attempt to hijack the overall interests of countries and regions for private gain or the interests of small cliques. We must work together to rein them in,” he added. “The persistence of global conflict serves as a sobering reminder that … force cannot resolve the root of the problem. Coercion and pressure only widen rifts and create more difficulties.” His comments took tacit aim at the United States as the Donald Trump administration resumed strikes against Iran in a bid to end a conflict now in its seventh month. Dong instead positioned Beijing as a “responsible major country” that has maintained an impartial stance, capable of acting as a “positive and stabilising force” in resolving conflicts. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi hosted his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Beijing on Wednesday. Even as Dong took veiled jabs at the US, his tone was markedly more measured than at the same forum last year. A year ago, he still did not name any country but described military alliances as groups driven by “selfish interests”. Urging countries to stand up against “disguised hegemonic logic and bullying acts”, he also said the time that the world was overshadowed by a “cold war mentality, hegemonism and protectionism” – phrases Beijing routinely uses to describe Washington’s actions. Unlike last year, when Dong asserted that the return of Taiwan to Beijing was “an integral part of the post-war order” and that Beijing was “ready to thwart any external military interference”, he left out Taiwan from this year’s speech. Zhou Bo, senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, described Dong’s tone on Wednesday as “relatively mild” but stressed that the omission of Taiwan did not mean the issue was any less important. “Not mentioning Taiwan does not mean that China is less concerned with the issue,” said Zhou, a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army. “It doesn’t mean that China is not paying attention to it.” Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Beijing has repeatedly said that Taiwan is its core interest and a “red line” that must not be crossed in Sino-US relations. The issue is expected to be raised again by Xi when he sits down with Trump next week. Nor did Dong make any mention of the South China Sea. Last year, he criticised “extra-regional powers” for using freedom of navigation to stir up tensions in the disputed waterway. According to Zhou, Dong’s offer to help with military development in other countries reflects Beijing’s growing confidence in its military. That offer came a day after Dong hosted senior officials attending the forum, including the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar, according to China’s defence ministry. The PLA has also held a series of joint training exercises with other militaries, including those of Belarus, Egypt, Singapore and Thailand in the past month. Meanwhile, according to Zheng Yongnian, dean of the school of public policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, it was good for the world that the US and China had agreed to establish stable relations since Trump’s visit to China in May. Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University’s school of international studies, said the forum was aimed at promoting security cooperation between Beijing and the world, so Dong’s speech could not solely focus on “these contentious issues”, referring to the omission of Taiwan and the South China Sea. Beijing’s offer to help build other militaries stemmed from the turmoil roiling global affairs, Zhu added, saying that while China could deepen cooperation through multilateral platforms, it also needed to work together with smaller states if they faced internal problems. “This also demonstrates China’s responsibility as a major country in the face of various current tensions,” he said. With China-Japan relations still strained following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks on Taiwan in November last year, Dong said the world “must bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against … hegemonism, militarism and historical revisionism”. Among other things, the Chinese defence chief also called for countries to deepen cooperation in areas including joint exercises and training as well as engage in dialogue on artificial intelligence, outer space and the deep sea. The three-day Xiangshan Forum is expected to gather defence delegations from close to 100 countries, regions and international organisations. The forum, seen as Beijing’s answer to Singapore’s annual Shangri-La Dialogue, marks its 20th anniversary this year.

title: Hong Kong Jockey Club to plough HK$3b into new research facility in Northern Metropolis
description: HKJC says its Charities Trust donation has been “approved in principle” for construction of Life and Health Academic Research Building.
content: The Hong Kong Jockey Club has said it will funnel HK$3 billion to support the construction of a Life and Health Academic Research Building at the city’s new Northern Metropolis University Town. During his policy address on Wednesday, Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu announced the creation of an integrated teaching and scientific research building in the Northern Metropolis. In a statement issued soon after the chief executive’s speech, the club said its Charities Trust had made a donation that had been “approved in principle”, and was in support of the National 15th five-year plan, and in alignment with Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, details of which Lee revealed alongside his annual address. “As a patriotic world-class horse sports organisation, as well as a charity institution deeply committed to our country and Hong Kong, the club is honoured to work alongside the HKSAR Government to support the long-term development, prosperity and progress of Hong Kong as it advances from stability to greater prosperity and success,” Martin Liao, the HKJC chairman, said. According to the HKJC, the new facility will provide more than 30,000 sq m of gross floor space in support of life and health science research. It added that the new building reflected its “long-standing commitment to nurturing cutting-edge talent and research”. The club pointed to its JC Stem Lab initiative and the associated early career research fellowship that provides “funding, capacity-building and industry exposure to turn innovative ideas into impactful real-world applications”. Alongside its work at City University of Hong Kong, the club said that this underscored its dedication to academia and research institutions. “The club’s support for the Life and Health Academic Research Building, like all of its charity and community initiatives, is made possible by its unique value creation model through which racing and wagering generate tax contributions, charity support and employment opportunities for the community,” the statement said. Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, a non-official member of the Executive Council and Legislative Councillor who chairs both the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company and the Vocational Training Council, told the South China Morning Post the new building represented a critical step for the area. “As part of the Northern Metropolis University Town, this life and health technology building can forge a vibrant ecosystem,” Lam said. “It will focus on educational and scientific research exchanges, as well as cultivating research talent.” He noted that the facility’s equipment and resources could also be made accessible to other institutions to maximise regional collaboration. “I believe this dedicated ecosystem can become a catalyst for driving the commercialisation of health and medical research outcomes, transforming them into viable healthcare solutions,” Lam said. “This will foster a favourable business environment, enhance talent cultivation and ultimately benefit society.” Duncan Chiu, the lawmaker representing the technology and innovation functional constituency, also welcomed the Jockey Club’s contribution, noting the club’s history of backing public infrastructure. “HKJC did sponsor schools and hospitals in HK with their reserve fund, so it’s not out of the ordinary for them to support this project,” Chiu told the SCMP, adding that “it is of course significant for HKJC to support this.” Chiu emphasised the need to accelerate development within the hub to capture growing international interest. “We need to speed up the building at the hub to attract universities, research labs, companies and talent to HK,” Chiu said. “We should leverage all resources private and public to support the zone.” Pointing to a recent surge in university admission scores as evidence of rising demand from international applicants, Chiu called for rapid expansion to accommodate incoming talent.

title: Chinese travel platform sparks debate with US$760,000 space flight package
description: The Chinese travel platform now allows users to book space flight packages with US-based provider Virgin Galactic for nearly US$760,000.
content: Chinese online travel platform Trip.com has launched a space-flight package priced from 5.1 million yuan (US$759,900), compared with Virgin Galactic’s publicly announced ticket price of US$750,000. The six-day trip includes several days of preflight training followed by a 90-minute suborbital flight operated by US-based provider Virgin Galactic, which departs from Spaceport America, near Truth or Consequences, New Mexico. The first four days are devoted to preparation and training, with the air-launched space flight taking place on the fifth day, according to Ctrip, Trip.com’s mainland China platform. The 5.1 million yuan price tag covers the space-flight programme, related accommodation and membership of Virgin Galactic’s Future Astronaut community, while return air fares to the United States, visas, insurance and other expenses are charged separately. According to Ctrip’s AI chatbot, two customers have booked the package through the Chinese platform since the 2027 programme was launched on Tuesday. Virgin Galactic said its astronaut community now comprised more than 700 people worldwide. The launch of the package – the most expensive publicly available space-tourism product in the Chinese market – has generated widespread discussion on Chinese social media. Ctrip labelled the experience a “sport for the elite” on its homepage, describing it as more than simply a “rich person’s game”. Commercial space flight has become an emerging investment hotspot in recent years, with a slew of private operators in China and the US launching their own ventures. Before the flight, passengers will undergo G-awareness training, cabin and seat familiarisation, and classroom-based preparation, according to Virgin Galactic. The programme is designed to ensure customers understand each stage of the flight and minimise distractions during the experience. During the flight, passengers will experience several minutes of weightlessness and can view Earth through the spacecraft’s 17 windows. After landing, they will receive a “commercial astronaut” certificate from the Association of Space Explorers, according to the itinerary. Founded by British entrepreneur Richard Branson in 2004, California-based Virgin Galactic operates suborbital flights for private passengers and researchers from Spaceport America in New Mexico. Its VSS Unity spaceplane completed 12 space flights, including seven commercial missions between June 2023 and June 2024, before being retired. The company is developing its higher-capacity Delta-class spacecraft as part of its effort to make commercial space travel more widely accessible. During its second-quarter earnings call in August, Virgin Galactic said it had completed the sale of a batch of tickets offered from March at US$750,000 each. The company expects to operate at least 10 flights a month by the end of the second quarter of 2027 and achieve positive quarterly cash flow sometime that year. China, meanwhile, has yet to conduct a commercial space-tourism flight, but domestic companies including CAS Space, Deep Blue Aerospace and Interstellor are developing suborbital tourism vehicles. Deep Blue Aerospace began selling its first batch of suborbital space-tourism tickets in October 2024, priced at 1.5 million yuan each, with the goal of conducting a crewed flight in 2027. CAS Space has said it aims to begin crewed space-tourism flights around 2028.

title: Hong Kong theatre legend Fredric Mao launches foundation to boost city’s performing arts
description: Fredric Mao has launched a new foundation to strengthen Hong Kong theatre as mainland China’s arts scene grows at ‘incredible speed’.
content: “When you’re my age, you start to think about legacy,” says 79-year-old Fredric Mao Chun-fai, a Hong Kong theatre veteran behind many of the city’s original stage productions and a pioneer in connecting the local theatre industry to the world. This month, he launched the Mao Chun-fai Performing Arts Charity Foundation to further talent development, research and creation across Hong Kong’s theatre landscape. The foundation aims to: nurture the next generation of theatre talent and develop international productions rooted in local culture; help mid-career theatre artists further their careers through new productions and research projects; and cultivate theatre appreciation within the community. For five decades, Mao has been instrumental in shaping Hong Kong theatre. He studied acting in New York under Sanford Meisner, performing on Broadway in the 1970s before returning to Hong Kong in 1985 as the first head of acting at the then newly established Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts’ School of Drama. In 2001, he became the first artistic director of the Hong Kong Repertory Theatre (HKRep) after its incorporation, producing original Cantonese plays and musicals including The New Love in a Fallen City (2002) and Sweet and Sour Hong Kong (2003). These works were some of the earliest Hong Kong productions to tour regionally. “We had good actors, we had good productions, and we performed in our own dialect of Cantonese,” Mao recalls of those early days. However, that formula was not enough to bring the global recognition he felt HKRep deserved. “From its founding in 1977 up until 2001, hardly anyone abroad even knew we existed,” Mao says. “That was a shame. That’s why I was determined to take us overseas. The process was tough but necessary.” Today, HKRep is the city’s longest-standing and largest professional theatre company. Since the 2000s, the company has established a footprint across North America, Greater China and the broader Asia region. Mao stepped down as HKRep’s artistic director in 2008, going on to promote Chinese opera in Hong Kong as the founding dean of the HKAPA’s School of Chinese Opera while remaining active in the city’s theatre scene. A mission to accelerate growth Many would be satisfied with retirement after such an accomplished career. Mao, though, is far from done. “We are in a different era now,” he says. “It’s time for this generation of theatre practitioners to develop a fresh perspective and artistic touch. The continuation of our industry doesn’t mean blindly re-enacting what has been done in the past but discovering new meanings and cultural identities.” Mao believes Hong Kong’s mindset has transformed, from focusing on black-and-white morality to foundational questions. “Who am I? How do I choose? How do I become a complete human being? How do I become a hero? That is modern thinking,” he says. “Plays built on this mindset are the ones that connect with contemporary audiences.” Despite the rise of new arts festivals in the Greater Bay Area and state-of-the-art infrastructure in mainland China – where the Shanghai Grand Opera House is slated to open in October 2026, followed by the completion of the Shenzhen Opera House in 2028 – Mao remains confident Hong Kong will not be outcompeted. “Mainland China has undergone an immense transformation over the past 20 to 30 years, moving at an incredible speed,” he says. “Whether in Shenzhen or Shanghai, you can watch any kind of show – foreign, local or experimental. They have the space, resources and technology to test new ideas. Yet, because they move so fast, they sometimes lose their way and miss the essence of the craft, settling for superficial form.” Immersive theatre is a prime example. “True immersive theatre allows the audience to genuinely feel and experience the narrative within a living space,” he says. “It isn’t just about constructing a fancy set to create an illusion of engagement.” That said, Mao admits that the development of Hong Kong’s theatre scene is “far too slow”. “The government certainly supported us early on, but that support still feels confined to a very small scale. I don’t mean the physical size of productions. I hope we can be a bit more ambitious in strengthening and expanding the whole theatre ecosystem.” With his new foundation, Mao hopes to accelerate growth by offering a platform where artists can focus on researching contemporary productions and artistic experiments without constantly worrying about their financial prospects. The foundation’s debut production will be a yet-to-be-decided Chekhov play in 2027. Mao has no interest in repeating his past Chekhov productions, even though they were critically acclaimed. “The goal is to inspire the cast to discover where the true value of Chekhov lies today,” he says. “Chekhov understood human nature better than anyone, laying it bare with utmost honesty. Isn’t that something we still need to learn today?”

title: Hong Kong tennis bosses hail Victoria Park revamp plans, eye WTA, ATP 500 tournaments
description: The decades-old facilities in Causeway Bay are to be redeveloped into an all-weather, multi-purpose venue in the years to come.
content: Hong Kong’s decades-old tennis facilities at Victoria Park will be redeveloped, the city’s leader said on Wednesday, a move that could open the way to holding bigger tournaments in the future. Speaking during his annual Policy Address, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the plan was “to strengthen the promotion of ‘sports and mega-events’.” At the moment, Hong Kong holds the rights to stage a WTA and an ATP tournament, both at the 250 level. The first of those is the Prudential Hong Kong Open in November, with the men’s event at the start of the year. “We will explore the redevelopment of Victoria Park Centre Court and other ancillary facilities into an iconic all-weather, multi-purpose venue for holding larger-scale and higher-level sports events, as well as performance activities as required,” Lee said. Opened in 1982, the 3,600-seat facility is only eligible to host the lowest tier of men’s and women’s professional tennis. But the redevelopment plan is expected to more than double capacity, with local tennis bosses pushing for between eight thousand and nine thousand seats. A government source said tennis was considered to have “high potential to develop as a sports industry, whether it’s public interest or local athlete performance”. “The goal is to upgrade the court to be able to host at least an ATP 500 – which is a 7,000-seat venue, among other requirements,” the source added. Hong Kong tennis chief Michael Cheng Ming-git called Victoria Park a “one of a kind” location, and said it represented “a very unique brand of Hong Kong as Asia’s World City”. “Victoria Park is one of a kind on a global scale, given its heritage and its prime location in the heart of the city. It represents a very unique brand of Hong Kong as Asia’s World City,” the 56-year-old said. “This decision today demonstrates Hong Kong has the conviction and vision to bid for credible world-class sporting events in Hong Kong,” the 56-year-old said. Reconstruction was not expected to involve any reclamation of the city’s harbour, while nearby facilities such as the indoor swimming pool, basketball courts and football pitches, would not be affected, those with knowledge of the plans told the South China Morning Post. The redevelopment would also turn existing facilities into a multi-purpose venue capable of hosting other sports events, and the owner of a Hong Kong basketball team backed the move. Tony Chin To, owner of Hong Kong Bulls, hailed the forward-looking planning in Lee’s speech, and said he hoped to eventually make the new space “our team’s home court for future Chinese Basketball Association competitions”. A government source said the goal was to begin the reconstruction of Victoria Park Centre Court in “four to five years”. Cheng said there would be an implementation and transition plan for the WTA and ATP Tour events already in place for when the work began. “HKCTA has a plan to use the Hong Kong Stadium as an interim measure, with a view to ensuring professional tennis tour events will continue without disruption,” he said. “We are discussing with relevant parties of the government and with the professional tour. “We are all actively exploring to make sure there is an implementation and transition plan in place in an orderly manner, and make sure we have a plan in place while the new tennis stadium is under construction.” Hong Kong Sports Institute, the city’s training agent of elite athletes, also supported the government’s initiative. “Upgrading Victoria Park Tennis Court into an international-standard centre venue will support the hosting of larger-scale and higher-level sports events in Hong Kong, giving elite athletes more opportunities to train and compete in major events on home ground where they can fully showcase their talents,” Tang King-shing, the HKSI chairman, said. Separately, the city’s leader in his five-year plan also aims to raise the tourism industry’s value added from HK$86.2 billion in 2024 to HK$126 billion by 2030, an increase of about 40 to 50 per cent. It also targets increasing the proportion of non-mainland visitors among overnight travellers to 40 per cent by the end of the decade. Among the more immediate tourism measures unveiled alongside the plan in the Policy Address on Wednesday were a series of “+ Tourism” initiatives aimed at combining travel with mega-events, finance, industrial brands, ecological conservation and heritage, while also promoting film tourism, yacht tourism, city renewal and homestay accommodation on outlying islands. “The Hong Kong Tourism Board will offer visitors an immersive experience of Hong Kong’s unique urban landscape and lifestyle, weaving together classic Hong Kong films, district characteristics and local culture,” Lee said. A government source explained it would be a campaign, which the board aimed to launch within the year on its website, that would promote iconic filming locations around the city. “The programme will also look at businesses around these landmarks and recommend what visitors can shop and eat nearby,” the source said.

title: As US slashes funding, UN peacekeeping head says global body can rely on China
description: Jean-Pierre Lacroix tells Beijing’s Xiangshan Forum that UN is struggling with fewer resources and a shrinking field presence.
content: The United Nations can count on China’s support, the UN’s peacekeeping chief said in Beijing as he flagged the body’s financial strains – due in large part to Washington’s funding squeeze. Speaking at the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing on Wednesday, UN undersecretary general for peace operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix said the international system was under severe strain and the UN urgently needed to adapt its tools to modern realities. Lacroix warned that the global body’s financial situation “is concerning member states” and it cannot be expected to deliver the same results with “steadily fewer resources, reduced mobility and a shrinking field presence”. He said the UN had a responsibility to be “efficient, disciplined, transparent and accountable” when using the pooled resources of member states. “We are committed to nurturing a culture of efficiency and responsible stewardship of resources,” he said. “A tighter focus on realistic, adaptable goals and constructive cooperation with host nations is necessary to maximise the return on invested resources. “We know that we can count on China’s support for these efforts. “China’s global initiatives [have] called for strengthening the central role of the United Nations and for making international institutions more effective in addressing today’s peace and security challenges.” Lacroix’s appeal in Beijing comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump looks to disengage from international institutions and pare back its financial contributions to the UN. Trump has publicly called out the UN for not living up to its potential and demanded sweeping reforms in exchange for the support of its one-time largest donor. The Trump administration did not pay anything to the United Nations in 2025, leaving nearly US$5 billion in dues unpaid – US$2 billion owed towards the regular budget and US$3 billion for peacekeeping operations. Under Trump, the US has also withdrawn from UN organisations such as the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco, and pulled funding from dozens of others. In August, the State Department laid out plans to pay US$725 million towards the regular UN budget and US$125 million for UN peacekeeping operations in Haiti and the Democratic Republic of Congo. In February, the Trump administration made a single payment of US$160 million shortly after UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres warned that the institution was facing imminent collapse unless its financial rules were overhauled or all 193 member nations paid their dues. Lacroix’s message on Wednesday was clearly directed at the US, which has been billed for about 22 per cent of the UN’s regular budget. China, which is now paying US$686 million, or about 20 per cent of the UN’s regular budget, paid its remaining dues early this month. During his address, Lacroix painted a sobering picture of the global security landscape, noting that the number of armed conflicts was at a level unseen since 1945. He warned that conflicts were becoming more internationalised and protracted, with civilians bearing the heaviest costs amid deep geopolitical polarisation. The peacekeeping chief also highlighted the rapidly changing nature of warfare, pointing to the convergence of transnational organised crime, climate change and the misuse of new technologies. “We currently see a drastic increase in [the] use of uncrewed systems, drones,” Lacroix said, citing conflicts such as the civil war in Sudan. He warned that some of these systems “can now operate without any help or control from the human”, transforming battlefields at a fraction of the cost of traditional weapons while threatening civilians and peacekeepers alike.

title: EU’s von der Leyen vows tough China-trade stance: ‘words are good, but deeds are better’
description: Brussels is looking to reduce reliance on Chinese raw materials, and Beijing again urges the EU to avoid protectionist policies.
content: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has reaffirmed the bloc’s resolve to use all available tools to rebalance trade with China. After opening remarks about energy and innovation during her annual State of the Union speech at the European Parliament on Wednesday, she quickly pivoted to the EU’s trade deficit with China and contended that the “second China shock” had already arrived. She argued that European firms must compete on a level playing field, noting that while Brussels was engaged in dialogue with Beijing, such talks must lead to results. “Let me be clear: we will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship. Words are good, but deeds are better,” von der Leyen said. She added that China’s weakened domestic demand made it dependent on Europe’s market, creating a shared interest in working together and finding solutions. She also vowed to continue reducing the EU’s “dangerous dependencies” on Chinese critical raw materials, stressing the importance of establishing a European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials to help with the bloc’s procurement efforts. Von der Leyen also promised to work with Canada to make the country the first associate member of the EU. The comments on China follow previous remarks from the EU’s trade chief, Maros Sefcovic, demanding tangible results by October, when the second round of trade talks is set to take place in Beijing. The stance was also echoed by certain groups listening to the speech in the European Parliament, especially the centrist Renew Europe group led by French President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party. Valerie Hayer, president of the Renew Europe group, called for tough EU trade actions, advocating for a retaliatory tariff strategy matching the US and China with European levies. She also asserted that Washington, Beijing and Moscow only understand the language of power. Sefcovic was scheduled for a videoconference with China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, on Thursday as both sides prepare for the next round of trade talks and the October deadline looms. On Wednesday, Beijing again urged Brussels to avoid protectionist policies, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun commenting on an open letter from Connect Europe, a trade group representing European telecoms operators. “Protectionism cannot buy competitiveness,” Guo said, arguing that “it will only mean missing out on the opportunities for digital transformation, damaging Europe’s economic and social development – and its image as an open market – and undermining the confidence of companies from around the world in investing in Europe”. The open letter, published on Tuesday, was signed by 17 senior executives, including the CEOs of Orange in France, Deutsche Telekom in Germany, Telefonica in Spain and Elisa in Finland. They warned that a proposed ban on high-risk suppliers under the Cybersecurity Act Revision (CSA2) – a measure widely viewed as targeting China without naming it – would cost the industry up to €40 billion (US$46.16 billion) in replacement costs, and that this would “risk draining the sector of the very capital needed for fibre, 5G and 6G”.

title: Kimi creator Moonshot draws global funds seeking ‘top-tier’ Chinese AI developers: sources
description: Start-up draws intense international interest through offshore vehicles chasing alternatives to US systems, insiders say.
content: China’s Moonshot AI has attracted global investor interest spanning Europe, Asia and the Middle East, people familiar with the matter say, as international capital scrambles for access to Chinese frontier artificial intelligence labs, betting on their high-stakes race against US rivals. The Beijing-based developer of the Kimi family of AI models has seen mounting interest from overseas players ranging from European investment firms to Middle East family offices, with some seeking indirect exposure through special-purpose vehicles (SPVs), according to people familiar with the matter, as well as public disclosures. Moonshot was among the top three Chinese tech targets driving a surge in global inquiries alongside TikTok parent ByteDance, which remained privately owned, and humanoid maker Unitree Robotics, before it listed in Shanghai, according to a Hong Kong-based venture partner backed by Asia-Pacific family offices. The person, who asked not to be identified as the discussions were private, said a dozen US-based funds had recently made inquiries about securing investment opportunities. Chinese tech companies including Moonshot had “withstood enormous pressure” from various headwinds, earning respect among foreign investors who viewed them as bets worth backing, the person added. The deal was a chance to gain exposure to a potential global top-tier AI developer ... and alternative to proprietary US frontier models Investment firm Pyratz Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. The company counts South China Morning Post owner Alibaba Group Holding as a backer. Investors backing Moonshot include Singapore-based K3 Ventures, Paris-based Cathay Capital, Singapore’s Granite Asia, and investment firms Japanese Orix Group and South Korean Mirae Asset Financial Group, according to people familiar with the matter. The companies did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. The surging appetite comes as Chinese AI labs face soaring training and inference costs to keep pace with Silicon Valley peers. Moonshot has raised around US$5 billion since its founding in 2023, according to Paris- and Barcelona-based investment firm Pyratz, which announced earlier this month an investment in Moonshot. The figure still lags the tens of billions being poured into leading US counterparts. To broaden its financial runway, Moonshot has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, the SCMP reported earlier in September. Offshore investment vehicles have become a key pathway for international funds looking to bypass direct investment hurdles. Pyratz said it invested in Moonshot through Techmind Moonshot AI, an SPV established with Paris venture firm Techmind.vc, in a round that valued the Chinese developer at US$30 billion pre-investment. In an interview with the SCMP on Wednesday, Pyratz CEO Bilal El Alamy said Moonshot had “very good” product positioning in offering capable open-weight models that could be post-trained or self-hosted to cater to different needs. Pyratz described the deal as a chance to gain exposure to “a potential global top-tier AI developer, a leading Chinese technology company, and an open-weight alternative to proprietary US frontier models”. Other international backers have built positions through similar structures. London-listed Shaires Holdings said it committed US$5 million last month for an indirect economic interest in Moonshot. Malaysia’s Falnas Capital and Dubai-based Stella Capital have also disclosed exposure to the Chinese start-up. The rush for equity reflects a broader capital drive across China’s generative AI sector. Hong Kong-listed Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, recently launched a roughly US$5 billion equity placement and convertible bond offering in Hong Kong to meet rising computing demand for its next-generation GLM foundation models. That fundraising came just two months after Z.ai raised HK$31.4 billion (US$4 billion) in a July share placement, underscoring the relentless pace at which China’s AI champions are tapping global markets to build out their capabilities. Additional reporting by Chong Ming Lee

title: Hong Kong to invest in primary care to cut premature death risk to 6.9%
description: Chief Executive John Lee also unveils Hong Kong’s first integrated ambulatory care hospital at King’s Park, featuring AI-assisted radiology and expanded cancer services.
content: Hong Kong aims to reduce the risk of premature deaths from some major chronic diseases to 6.9 per cent by 2030 by investing heavily in primary healthcare and prevention, authorities have said. Delivering his annual policy address and the city’s first five-year plan, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday also unveiled plans to develop the city’s first integrated ambulatory care hospital at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital site in King’s Park after its relocation to Kai Tak. The facility will offer high-volume cataract surgery, radiology and radiotherapy services to shorten patient waiting times. “We will strive to make the healthcare system more sustainable to better cope with an ageing society, the increasing prevalence of chronic diseases and the development of innovative drugs and medical devices, thereby strengthening the role of the public healthcare system as a safety net for all,” he said. Under the five-year plan, the government aims to reduce the risk of premature mortality, defined as the unconditional chance of dying between ages 30 and 70 from cardiovascular diseases, cancers, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases, from a baseline of 7.3 per cent in 2024 to 6.9 per cent in 2030. A key focus is enhancing primary healthcare services, including increasing cumulative membership at district health centres from 600,000 as of the end of June to 1 million over the next five years. Of these, 700,000 will receive services under the co-care network, such as cancer screening and chronic disease management. Authorities will also steadily increase resource allocation to primary healthcare programmes, with an estimated 30 per cent rise from current levels by 2030-31, to promote systematic preventive care through a life-course approach. The life-course preventive care plan, built on a family medicine model, will provide residents across different life stages with screening for chronic diseases and cancers, as well as age-specific health advice, to enable early prevention, identification and management. The policy address outlined further measures to strengthen the primary healthcare system, including providing about 220,000 additional family medicine outpatient service spots annually from next year, including 10,000 reserved for evening slots. The cataract surgery centre is also set to begin operations in the fourth quarter of next year, providing 5,500 procedures annually. The waiting time for the 90th percentile of patients is expected to fall to 18 months by 2032, down from 32 months. For computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), service capacity will increase by about 40 per cent compared with general facilities, with AI-assisted annotation and triage at the radiology centre. Increased capacity at the radiotherapy centre will also accelerate treatment procedures for cancer patients. A government source said radiology and radiotherapy services would begin to be offered in the first half of next year, with the radiotherapy centre treating 11,300 patients annually, and those in the Kowloon West hospital cluster expected to benefit first. On cancer management, the insider said the city would set up three cancer centres in Kai Tak, Kowloon East and King’s Park. Since January, 16 new innovative drugs, including seven cancer treatments, had been added to the Drug Formulary used by public hospitals. Meanwhile, 27 drugs had their indications broadened to benefit more patients, including 14 for cancer, the source said. The Hospital Authority has also set a target to halve waiting times for first consultations for stable new cases across seven specialist services over five years, with a 10 per cent reduction targeted in 2027-28 in the first phase. The seven specialities covered include psychiatry, surgery, ophthalmology and gynaecology. To achieve this, the authority would avoid unnecessary referrals and divert stable cases to primary healthcare facilities for follow-up consultations, alongside enhancing service capacity, Lee said.

title: How wildfires are threatening Indonesia’s economy and carbon market
description: Total economic and health costs from January to August as a result of the haze could reach US$6.9 billion, analysts warn.
content: Forest and peatland fires raging across Indonesia are threatening to become more than an environmental emergency, with analysts warning that the thickening haze could weigh on economic activity, strain public health and test confidence in the nation’s fledgling carbon market. Indonesia is no stranger to forest and peat fires, but this year’s super El Nino has helped make it the country’s most intense wildfire season in 11 years. Toxic haze and smoke have also drifted to neighbouring countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines, forcing some employers to impose work-from-home policies while numerous schools have resorted to remote learning. A health crisis is also in the offing. Data from the Indonesian health ministry last month showed that acute respiratory infection cases topped 15.6 million from January 1 to August 20 this year. The ministry recorded 400,000 new respiratory infection cases per week at the height of the dry season between the end of July and the beginning of August. According to a report released by Jakarta-based think tank the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios) earlier this month, the total economic and health costs from January to August could reach up to 123.1 trillion rupiah (US$6.9 billion), though the estimate does not yet account for a scenario in which fires continue to expand through the end of 2026. Celios estimated the total economic costs arising from the loss of physical assets and economic activity could reach nearly 30 trillion rupiah, or 0.23 per cent of Indonesia’s gross domestic product last year. The fires could also result in 269.89 billion rupiah in lost potential tax revenues, the group warned. Total healthcare costs for people diagnosed with fire-related health conditions could hit 93.56 trillion rupiah, or “equivalent to 67.6 per cent of Indonesia’s total national health-sector budget in the 2026 state budget”, Celios added. Its economic director Nailul Huda said these figures reflected a contraction across several commercial sectors. “Our estimation isn’t merely about the value of burned timber or other forest products, but rather a broader disruption in economic activities of the community and trade,” Nailul told This Week in Asia. “Regarding healthcare costs, these will be borne by either the state or individuals. If the patients don’t have universal healthcare, they will inevitably have to cover them privately. These are the [spending] losses that must be taken into account too.” During the catastrophic 2015 forest fires, the worst in recent history, the World Bank estimated total economic damage to Indonesia alone reached US$16.1 billion, equivalent to 1.9 per cent of its GDP. In Singapore, the haze, which lasted for two months, cost the country an estimated S$1.83 billion in lost tourism, reduced productivity, healthcare expenses, and cost of mitigation actions by the city state’s government, research published in the Journal of Asian Economics in 2021 showed. Celios did not estimate the cross-border fallout from the haze this time. The first major haze episode in 1997-1998 from fires in Indonesia caused US$9.3 billion in economic losses across Southeast Asia, according to the Asian Development Bank. Carbon market integrity The widespread wildfires could also threaten the appeal of Indonesia’s fledgling carbon market, which launched its national carbon registry system, known as SRUK, in July. Carbon markets allow projects that reduce or remove emissions to generate tradeable credits, which companies or governments can buy to offset their own emissions or meet climate targets. During the initial roll-out, Indonesia approved four carbon projects covering roughly 225,000 hectares of peatlands and rainforest, including three restoration projects and one social forestry project, Rohmat Marzuki, deputy minister of forestry, said in July. According to Rohmat, the projects are expected to issue more than 31 million carbon credits, with an estimated value of 5 trillion rupiah, of which 500 billion rupiah would go to state coffers as non-tax revenue. Burning peatlands increased Indonesia’s carbon emissions from September 1 to 7 to 19.7 million metric tons, making up more than a third of the global total, according to Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate ‌monitoring service, last week. “I would not expect a blanket discount on Indonesian carbon credits as a direct result of the ongoing wildfires. However, the scale of these fires is likely to increase buyer scrutiny and due diligence, particularly for forest and peatland projects,” said Bjorn Fonden, international policy manager and Asia-Pacific lead at the International Emissions Trading Association. “Prospective buyers or investors will want to understand whether a project has been directly affected, its historical fire exposure, the assumptions underpinning its baseline, the risk of future reversals, and the measures in place to prevent and manage fire-related carbon losses.” Going forward, the revenue from Indonesia’s carbon projects should strengthen measures against peat and forest fires, Fonden said. These would include rewetting drained peatlands through canal blocking and water-table management, maintaining firebreaks and access corridors, and establishing community-based fire prevention and response systems. He warned, however, that carbon finance would not close the financing and institutional gap. “Indonesia also needs coordinated action by national and provincial governments, local communities, civil society, donors and the private sector to map fire risks, address illegal logging and land conversion, improve hydrological monitoring, establish early-warning systems and rapid firefighting response mechanisms,” Fonden said. For environmentalists such as Belgis Habiba, the ongoing land degradation strengthens their scepticism about Indonesia’s credibility in the international carbon market. “Indonesia’s carbon achievements should have been considered a failure from the very start, because it couldn’t protect peatlands as one of the largest carbon sinks,” said Belgis, a forest campaigner with Greenpeace Indonesia. “So if you ask about its carbon market integrity, it has already failed. It failed the moment the fires occurred.”

title: Former Kosovo president Thaci gets 25 years in prison for war crimes
description: A tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of 96 political opponents during the 1990s conflict with Serbia.
content: Former Kosovo president Hashim Thaci was found guilty of ‌war crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention by the Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday. Thaci, 58, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes committed as top commander of the ethnic Albanian Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the territory’s violent break from Serbia in the 1990s. The tribunal said ⁠he was guilty of the murder of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with ‌Serbian security forces by Kosovo Liberation Army forces during the conflict. He was also convicted for the arbitrary illegal detention of 385 people, ‌torture of 303 people and cruel treatment of around 50. The court said ⁠Thaci had “actively ⁠participated in and encouraged crimes”. Thaci, who stood in silence as the judge read out the conviction and ‌the sentence, had denied all charges. The ruling was closely watched in Kosovo and Serbia, where the legacy ‌of the ‌1998-99 conflict and Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence remain a source of ‌tension between ethnic Kosovo Albanians and Serbs. Thaci remains a revered figure for many ⁠Kosovo Albanians, while the tribunal itself is deeply unpopular in Kosovo. In Pristina, thousands of ⁠people watching the verdict on a big screen booed the verdict and chanted “Thaci, Thaci” as some burst into tears. Outside the Kosovo Specialist Chambers ‌in The Hague, dozens of ‌Thaci supporters had gathered ahead of the verdict waving KLA flags and chanting “UCK”, the Albanian acronym for the army.

title: US military prepares ceremonial welcome for Xi Jinping at the White House
description: Video clip shows honour guard drill mirroring the welcome extended to Donald Trump during his China trip.
content: A US military honour guard held a rehearsal at the White House as Washington fine-tuned diplomatic protocols and preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the United States next week. A video clip posted on social media by Fox News correspondent Lucas Tomlinson on Tuesday afternoon Washington time showed service members from various military branches dressed in ceremonial uniform and standing in formation. The drill mirrored the welcome extended to US President Donald Trump on May 14 during his visit to Beijing, where China hosted an elaborate ceremony featuring a People’s Liberation Army honour guard in the square outside the east gate of the Great Hall of the People. In an interview with Fox News, Trump praised the Chinese military’s marching as “incredible”. “We certainly got a very nice greeting and today was beautiful,” Trump said at the time. U.S. military Honor Guard rehearses at the White House ahead of visit by General Secretary Xi Jinping next week. pic.twitter.com/HvwvBvdg09 — Lucas Tomlinson (@LucasFoxNews) September 15, 2026 His satisfaction with China’s reception was also evident on social media, with both the official White House account and Trump’s personal account posting multiple photographs highlighting the honour guard. Renovations at the White House are being wrapped up in anticipation of Xi’s arrival. The Washington Post reported earlier this month that workers had removed the drapes shrouding the North Portico, and the surrounding scaffolding is expected to be dismantled soon. The North Portico project is part of a broader series of White House construction and renovation projects initiated by Trump, who aimed to complete several upgrades before hosting Xi for a planned state dinner. Officials from both nations are working to prepare for the summit while adopting a distinctly milder tone ahead of the high-stakes meeting. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed on Tuesday that he would meet Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng this weekend for final preparatory talks, less than a week before Xi’s scheduled arrival. Meanwhile, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun delivered a 20-minute address at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on Wednesday, advocating China’s vision for global security governance. Dong called for maintaining global stability through multilateralism amid world turbulence. Striking a moderate tone, his speech refrained from naming any specific country and omitted mention of the Taiwan issue, marking a shift in rhetoric compared with last year’s speech.

title: Developer family’s deals highlight capital shift across Hong Kong property sectors
description: A Mid-Levels transaction comes on the heels of the family’s commercial divestment, tracking a wider reallocation across the city.
content: A third-generation member of a long-established Hong Kong developer family has bought a HK$98.8 million (US$12.6 million) luxury flat in Mid-Levels, weeks after the family sold a long-held North Point property, highlighting a broader market trend of capital shifting across real estate sectors. John Lai Sung-ziang agreed to buy a high-floor unit at Estoril Court on August 31, Land Registry records showed. The price for the four-bedroom flat, which has a saleable area of 2,888 square feet, translates to HK$34,211 per square foot. According to Chinese media reports, Lai is part of the family behind Majestic Textiles and St Louis Land Investment, a property developer and owner. The family had held North Point Terraces as a rental property for more than four decades before selling it to Chinachem for about HK$1.9 billion earlier this year. Majestic Textiles and St Louis Land Investment could not be reached for comment. Selling an older rental building and buying residential is not a negative view on property. It is an asset-allocation decision Nicholas To, Savills Hong Kong The transaction also offers a contrast to some families moving more decisively out of property. In a recent case, the next generation of a wealthy family sold their investment properties, redirected capital into financial assets for greater liquidity and returns, and chose to just rent instead. While cautioning against reading too much into two transactions, Nicholas To, senior associate director of investment at Savills Hong Kong, said the Lai family move reflected a broader trend of investors shifting between property sectors. “Selling an older rental building and buying residential is not a negative view on property,” To said. “It is an asset-allocation decision.” Non-residential transactions worth more than HK$50 million totalled HK$30.36 billion so far this year, up 25 per cent from a year earlier, according to property consultancy Savills. Local capital accounted for more than 80 per cent of investment volume. Some of that capital is moving into alternative uses. More buyers are acquiring hotels and offices for conversion into student accommodation or co-living, reflecting demand for income-producing assets tied to living uses. Hotels accounted for HK$7.3 billion of non-residential transactions above HK$50 million this year, 69 per cent more than the full-year total in 2025, according to Savills. For families that continue to own property, To said the next generation could increasingly assess each asset on its investment merits rather than its place in the family portfolio. “Property now competes with other asset classes inside the same portfolio, and each asset is expected to justify itself on its own returns rather than on family history,” he said. Family wealth could also become divided among branches over generations, making individual residential units more practical to own than entire buildings, To said. Hong Kong’s residential market has performed differently from other property sectors. Home prices rallied earlier this year, rising over 7 per cent in the first half, while office, retail and industrial capital values remained below year-earlier levels, according to government data.

title: New ‘wall-hanging’ trend sees jobless Chinese youth working 1 day, ‘lying flat’ for 3
description: Guo hopes the struggles of ‘wall-hanging youth’ will no longer go unnoticed, and that they will face less prejudice.
content: In the early hours of the morning, 29-year-old Guo Zihao awoke in a 24-hour billiards hall in Shenzhen, southern China. For months, such places had served as his makeshift shelter. At his lowest point, he found himself with merely 20 yuan (US$3) left in his pocket. “That period was more than a financial struggle,” Guo told the SCMP. “Every minute, every second, felt like torture.” Just a few years earlier, Guo was far removed from the image of a young man living on society’s fringes. Raised in a relatively affluent family in Hunan province, central China, he graduated with a degree in economics and management and once envisioned a predictable path towards success. However, a bereavement and a failed investment profoundly upended his life. With his income vanished, Guo drifted between temporary jobs in food delivery, manual labour, sales, and internet cafés. As his confidence eroded, he withdrew from friends, fearing they would perceive him merely as someone seeking financial aid. Eventually, Guo discovered a term circulating online in China that resonated with his situation: guabi, or wall-hanging. This lifestyle offered him a means to escape problems he felt helpless to address. Originally denoting objects hanging on a wall and left unused, the term has evolved into a descriptor for young people who navigate lives sustained by minimal incomes. This phenomenon parallels Shenzhen’s “Sanhe Gods,” a term popularised online in 2018 to describe young migrant workers who congregated around the Sanhe job markets, surviving on short-term daily employment. Their motto was “work for one day, lie flat for three.” The term guabi is believed to have emerged from the slang prevalent among this group. Yet, the face of China’s “wall-hanging youth” is evolving. They are no longer confined to young workers struggling in factories. An increasing number now includes university graduates who have lost the support systems that once anchored their lives. While “lying flat” is often interpreted as a deliberate withdrawal from social competition, “wall-hanging” encapsulates a broader and more precarious existence. In March, an internet cafe in Guizhou province, southwest China, gained viral attention after becoming a hotspot for “wall-hanging youth.” The cafe charged a mere 0.6 yuan per hour. Among its regulars was a 28-year-old man known as Little Beard. After his wife lost 200,000 yuan (US$30,000) to gambling, the couple divorced. He recovered part of the bride price through legal action, only to be told by his mother to leave home for being “a failure.” He cancelled his phone number and withdrew from social life. Mainland media reports have also highlighted diverse paths into “wall-hanging” life. Some young people spend their days wandering the streets, sleeping in public spaces, or earning meagre incomes through live-streaming, while others grapple with mental health challenges or addiction. For Guo, becoming “wall-hanging” was not a conscious choice but a state he gradually fell into. During his darkest times, he battled depression, shed 20kg, and faced frequent breathing difficulties. Overwhelmed by guilt towards his family, he repeatedly contemplated ending his life. What kept him persevering was his one-year-old son. For young people in similar predicaments, there is no singular route back into society. Sociologists emphasise that meaningful support necessitates not only employment opportunities but also a healthier online environment. In Guo’s case, the turning point arrived when he encountered individuals willing to extend a hand. Two former classmates offered him financial and emotional support, while a relative provided him with a job opportunity in August. Guo hopes the struggles of “wall-hanging youth” will no longer remain hidden, and that they will encounter less prejudice. Above all, he is learning to coexist with the painful memories of his past. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, dial +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page

title: Meet Mariska Hargitay’s 3 children, who joined her at the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards
description: The Law & Order: SVU star’s children are no strangers to the spotlight, having joined their mother at the Cannes Film Festival and other high-profile events.
content: Mariska Hargitay just turned the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards into a family affair. Before the Law & Order: Special Victims Unit star hosted the big night on Monday, the 62-year-old turned heads on the red carpet – posing with her husband Peter Hermann and their children, August Miklos Friedrich, Amaya Josephine and Andrew Nicolas. The mother and daughter matched in stunning red dresses, while the father and sons looked dapper in black suits. By the end of the night, Hargitay had not only achieved the immense feat of becoming the first woman in 15 years to host the Emmys since Jane Lynch in 2011, but she also took home two awards – Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special and Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program – for her 2025 documentary, My Mom Jayne: A Film by Mariska Hargitay. The actress previously won an Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for Law & Order: SVU two decades ago. Here’s everything to know about her children. Mariska Hargitay became a mother at 42 Hargitay and Hermann first became parents on June 28, 2006, when the actress gave birth to August at 42. The family expanded when the couple adopted Amaya and Andrew in April and October 2011 respectively. “I basically pulled Amaya out,” the Emmy winner recalled of the little girl’s birth in an interview with Good Housekeeping, calling the subsequent moment of embracing the birth mother “one of the most meaningful moments” of her life. As for Andrew, Hargitay called his addition to the family “divinely right”. Speaking to People magazine, Hargitay described her family as a “whole, happy, joyful, chaotic, crazy unit”, and the kids inspired their father to write the 2008 children’s book If the S in Moose Comes Loose. Her children are not camera-shy From August visiting the Law & Order: SVU set as a young child to Amaya attending the Los Angeles premiere of Taylor Swift’s The Eras Tour concert film with her mother in 2023, Hargitay’s children have never shied away from the spotlight. The siblings celebrated their mother at her Hollywood Walk of Fame ceremony in 2013, were spotted at the opening night of New York City’s Big Apple Circus in 2019 and even enjoyed some family time at Walt Disney World in 2022. In 2025, the family of five appeared together at the Cannes Film Festival. What are their interests? Hargitay told Entertainment Tonight that her children are “super funny”, but they haven’t caught the acting bug yet. August, 20, is a philosophy major, per Variety, and enjoys swimming, per Parents.com. Amaya, 15, loves music and dancing, and Andrew, 14, is an anime fan, per People. He particularly enjoyed watching Tales from Earthsea (2006), where his mother voices Tenar in English.

title: Geologists find unexpectedly large water sources in Xinjiang beneath China’s largest desert
description: Discovery offers an answer to sand control and agricultural demands along the arid region’s edge.
content: Geologists have discovered two large water sources beneath China’s largest desert, potentially offering the northwestern region a vital new tap for sand-control projects and agriculture. The desert region has drawn attention for extensive afforestation and anti-desertification efforts taking place around its edges under the Great Green Wall initiative, alongside a rainfall trend that is transforming arid western China. The groundwater discoveries were made as part of a water-finding project in the Taklamakan Desert conducted in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region by the region’s geological bureau, according to a report by CCTV Finance on Monday. The findings challenge the perception that “there is only stagnant water and salt water underground in the desert”, according to the report. Stagnant groundwater is a source that has slowed or stopped moving, allowing bacteria and chemicals to build up and making it unsuitable for drinking and food production. One of the new sources was found at the southern edge of the Taklamakan Desert – which is also the world’s second-largest shifting sand desert – in Andir township in Minfeng county. The second was discovered south of the Mazartag Mountains, within the desert’s interior. As part of the water-finding project, researchers also built a test station to use brackish water – which has more salt than fresh water but less than seawater – for irrigation and desertification control along the desert’s edge. Fresh water makes up only a few per cent of the Earth’s total water supply. Brackish water is seen as an underutilised resource that could help meet growing water demands, such as crop irrigation and cooling artificial intelligence data centres. According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation, non-conventional water resources, including brackish water, could be used to meet irrigation needs but are used in limited amounts and require an understanding of the local climate, soil and crops. Researchers around the world, including in China, have been testing the use of brackish water for growing salt-tolerant crops, though desalination may still be required for certain applications. Located in Xinjiang’s Tarim Basin, the Taklamakan Desert covers an extensive area of 337,600 sq km (130,350 square miles), about the size of Germany. The desert has been dubbed the “sea of death” due to its shifting dunes and harsh climate. In 2015, researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography discovered that an underground ocean with a volume greater than all five Great Lakes in North America combined could lie below the basin. The Taklamakan Desert has historically had little annual precipitation and extreme evaporation. However, global warming has caused a rise in intense recent rainfall and unprecedented flooding that threaten local infrastructure. China’s largest desert has been a major site for the country’s afforestation and anti-desertification efforts under the broader Great Green Wall initiative. In 2024, a 3,050km (1,900-mile) green belt of trees, shrubs and sand-blocking solar panels surrounding the desert was completed in a bid to prevent sandstorms and safeguard regional infrastructure. Alongside these barrier projects, China is also cultivating crops along the desert’s periphery to boost food security. These efforts include a desert wheat farm built in the county-level city of Kunyu at the southern edge of the desert. Although water-saving measures such as pivot or drip irrigation methods have been employed in China’s arid regions to support sand control and agriculture, water supply continues to be a concern for the desert crop initiatives.

title: Meet Brooks Nader’s parents Holland and Breaux – as the Baywatch star defends going topless around them in Italy
description: The Sports Illustrated model has hit back at criticism over her Sardinia family holiday, saying her financier father was ‘half-blind’ and didn’t care.
content: Last month, Baywatch actress Brooks Nader made headlines while she was enjoying a family holiday in Sardinia, Italy. Images obtained by Page Six showed the 29-year-old standing topless on a luxurious yacht in front of her family, including her father. While Brooks’ parents Holland and Breaux Nader seemed unfazed, the internet was quick to question the actress. “This is weird,” one user commented under Page Six’s Instagram post sharing snaps of a topless Brooks on holiday. “That's very weird to do in front of your dad unless you’re under the age of 5 or something,” another comment read. Last week, Brooks responded to the criticism she received while attending the Tommy Hilfiger spring/summer 2027 show on September 10 in New York City. “I had the time of my freaking life,” Brooks told Entertainment Tonight. “I don’t care if I’m not from Europe. I’m from Louisiana. I grew up in an all-girl household. We’re always naked together as sisters.” She added that her father was “half blind” and didn’t notice that she was topless, nor did he care. “He has selective hearing and selective seeing,” the Love Thy Nader star told the outlet. “I was just having the time of my life and really not thinking that anyone was documenting some of it, but we love it. It’s great.” Here’s everything you need to know about Brooks Nader’s parents, Holland and Breaux Nader. What does Breaux Nader do? Breaux graduated from Louisiana Tech University and currently works as a senior financial adviser at Longbridge Wealth Management. Before that, he spent more than 14 years at Wells Fargo Advisors. According to his bio on the Longbridge Wealth Management website, Breaux and his partner were named in the 2023 Forbes Best-In-State Wealth Management Teams list. “Away from the office, my wife Holland and I enjoy visiting our four daughters in New York. I also enjoy supporting the LSU Tigers, playing golf and tennis as well as reading, travel and spending time with family and friends,” Breaux’s LinkedIn profile reads. When did Holland and Breaux Nader marry? Breaux and Holland tied the knot in August 1995. Little information is available about Holland’s life before she wed the financier. They had their first child, Brooks Claire, in February 1997 before welcoming three more daughters – Mary Holland in October 1998, Grace Ann in April 2000 and Sarah Jane in February 2002, according to People magazine. They were raised in Maringouin, Louisiana. “[Maringouin] means mosquito in Cajun French,” Brooks told the New York Post in a 2023 interview. “It really did have a lot of mosquitoes because it was between two bayous. It’s really gross now that I think about it.” The model went on to recall growing up with “humble beginnings” and living on her grandparents’ property in a two-bedroom house. They are a tight-knit family Breaux and Holland have a close relationship with their children. Brooks’ younger siblings have all followed in her footsteps and signed with various modelling agencies. The four sisters also have their own reality television show, Love Thy Nader, which debuted in August 2025 and was renewed for Season 2, set for release this winter. The couple are often spotted attending events with their children, while Holland regularly celebrates her daughters’ milestones on Instagram.

title: 14 key takeaways from John Lee’s policy address, Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan
description: Chief executive lays out how the five-year plan will align the city more closely with the national development blueprint.
content: Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has placed deepening integration with mainland China and developing new economic engines centre stage as he unveiled the city’s first-ever five-year plan alongside the last policy address of his term.
