During his landmark speech on Wednesday, which ran just one minute shy of three hours, Lee laid out how the city’s first five-year plan would align the city more closely with the national development blueprint, while the policy address would serve as the “action agenda”. The South China Morning Post looks at some takeaways from the policy blueprint, including how authorities will build the Northern Metropolis megaproject while also tackling some of the city’s most pressing issues, including a low birth rate and artificial intelligence (AI). SCMP · 14 key takeaways from John Lee’s policy address, Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan 1. Twenty-two major indicators The five-year plan has set 22 major indicators, with 17 being anticipatory goals and five being binding targets. Four of the five binding targets focus on environmental protection, such as reducing carbon emissions per unit of GDP, as well as raising the number of “spade-ready sites” in the Northern Metropolis by 2030. Anticipatory goals include increasing the number of completed domestic units in the Northern Metropolis from the current 11,000 to 70,000, an average annual increase of 4 to 5 per cent in the total number of companies in Hong Kong with parent firms located outside the city, as well as boosting the value added of the tourism industry from HK$86.2 billion (US$11 billion) to HK$126 billion. 2. ‘Four centres, one hub’ to hone Hong Kong’s global edge The five-year plan states that to ensure Hong Kong’s long-term prosperity and stability, the city will have to leverage its existing advantages while expediting the development of “new quality productive forces” – a term first coined by President Xi Jinping in 2023. The plan calls for the enhancement of Hong Kong’s status as international financial, maritime and trade centres, as well as developing the city into an international innovation and technology centre and a hub for “high-calibre talent”. Doing so would further strengthen Hong Kong’s edge amid global competition, Lee said. 3. Northern Metropolis ‘key platform’ for integration into national development Lee said the 30,000-hectare (74,131-acre) Northern Metropolis development project would serve as a key platform for Hong Kong’s participation in the Greater Bay Area and for national development. Under the city’s first five-year plan, the government has set a target of increasing the number of “spade-ready sites” available in the Northern Metropolis from 120 to 900 hectares by 2030. Lee said authorities would also guide the future layout of the city under the South-North Dual Engine – a strategy that leverages the city’s traditional strength in finance in the south with an innovation hub in the Northern Metropolis. 4. Three university towns in Northern Metropolis Three university towns are planned within the Northern Metropolis – San Tin University Town, Ta Kwu Ling University Town and Hung Shui Kiu University Town. Lee said the government would prioritise the development of Hung Shui Kiu University Town, with universities expected to occupy sites in 2027-28. The government will invite universities to build campuses starting this year. The government would use various measures to support tertiary institutions taking part in the university towns, such as offering land premium exemptions, he added. 5. Greater Bay Area as ‘strategic fulcrum’ of national development The five-year plan describes the Greater Bay Area – comprising Hong Kong, Macau and nine Guangdong cities – as the “strategic fulcrum of the country’s new development paradigm”. During his speech, Lee introduced a variety of measures to deepen integration with the bay area, including enhancing connectivity through a rail network, promoting mutual recognition of professional qualifications and aligning rules and mechanisms. The government will also enhance cross-border collaboration in emerging areas such as innovation and technology, hydrogen and satellite development. 6. New strategy for housing supply The five-year plan set out new strategies for future housing development. Housing supply plans spanning the future decade will earmark 40 per cent for building public rental homes, 30 per cent for building subsidised sale flats and 30 per cent for private homes. The composite waiting time for public rental flats, including temporary homes offered under the light public housing scheme, would be cut to four years or below in 2030-31, down from 4.8 years now, Lee said. He also said overall public housing supply in the coming five years would reach 196,000 flats, with more than 35,000 to be completed annually starting from 2027. 7. ‘Holistic national security approach’ According to the five-year plan, a “holistic national security approach” will serve as a guiding principle to “fiercely” crack down on infiltration, sabotage and subversion, separatism by “overseas hostile forces” and other “local anti-China destabilising” forces. The inclusion confirmed an earlier SCMP report that national security would remain an integral part of the five-year plan despite calls from parts of the business community to shift the city’s focus towards economic growth. National security also featured prominently in Lee’s policy address, which stated that “the fundamental premise of the ‘one country, two systems’ principle was to safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests”. 8. Tapping Exchange Fund to buy gold and promote trading To boost the gold trading market in Hong Kong, Lee announced a series of initiatives such as considering tapping into the Exchange Fund to buy more gold and allowing the city’s de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, to participate in the local spot and futures markets. Tax incentives will be offered to boost gold and commodities trading with plans to add more storage facilities. 9. AI risk management and tackling ‘deepfakes’ Lee said Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, the city’s No 2 official, would coordinate the government’s efforts on AI risk management, while the Digital Policy Office would also create the post of commissioner for AI to facilitate relevant work. He listed seven key areas of work in which the Law Reform Commission was studying to tackle deepfake porn and online scams. He added the government aimed to empower authorities to take down content that could be used for potential financial fraud, and that authorities would consult the public on enhancing the legal framework and strengthening the sector’s ability to detect AI-generated content. 10. Target for 30,000 internship places Lee announced a new two-year scheme, the “30,000 Youth Employment and Internship Programme”, targeting young people with limited or no work experience. To reach the target, the government will collaborate with the business sector, expand the STEM Internship Scheme and the HYAB Youth Start-up Internship Programme, and allocate funding through the Construction Industry Council for on-the-job training subsidy schemes. A dedicated one-stop platform will be established to provide information and streamline the application process for the various schemes. 11. Baby incentives given a boost To further incentivise childbirth, Lee said the HK$20,000 baby bonus he rolled out in 2023, which is set to expire soon, would be extended for another three years. For families having a second or subsequent child from Wednesday, the baby bonus will be increased to HK$30,000. The tax allowance for a second child born on or after Wednesday will be increased from HK$140,000 to HK$160,000, while permanent residents who have a newborn on or after Wednesday will be eligible for a stamp duty reduction of up to HK$20,000. 12. Victoria Park tennis courts to be upgraded The government will upgrade the Victoria Park tennis courts in Causeway Bay as the city aims to host higher-level tournaments in the future. It currently hosts one ATP 250 and one WTA 250 event in men’s and women’s professional tennis. The court facilities were opened in 1982 and are expected to be expanded to accommodate a few thousand more seats. The expansion will allow the city to host ATP 500 and WTA 500 events and potentially even top-tier events in women’s tennis, as WTA 1000 venues do not have a strict universal minimum seating capacity requirement. 13. Building renewal arrangements after Tai Po fire In response to the deadly Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po, Lee said the government would make a series of improvements to the city’s building management issues, including legislative proposals to tighten requirements on fire service installation and maintenance, stricter disciplinary mechanisms for professionals and owners’ voting requirements. The government was also studying criminalising bid rigging, he added. Authorities will also launch professional consultation services for homeowners undertaking major building overhauls, while a stricter pre-approved list of contractors, with background checks by law enforcement, will be open for application this September. 14. Measures to boost yuan use and globalisation Lee announced a raft of new measures to promote the usage and globalisation of the renminbi. Apart from settling government payments in yuan for mainland services, the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing will also announce details of commodities trading, including gold, in the currency. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority will also link the Faster Payment System with UnionPay, allowing people to make purchases in yuan. The government will also expand financial services using the yuan, including for short-term financing needs, while supporting the building of an offshore renminbi yield curve.

title: People’s Daily rejects US claims of malicious AI distillation, warns of countermeasures
description: Beijing vows to take action if Washington tries to contain China’s firms, as tensions over advanced AI systems heat up before expected Xi-Trump meeting.
content: China’s ruling Communist Party mouthpiece has rejected US allegations that Chinese artificial intelligence companies conducted “industrial-scale” distillation of American frontier models, warning that Beijing would respond if Washington continued to suppress China’s AI industry. In a commentary published on Wednesday, People’s Daily said the US claims were “without factual or legal basis” and accused Washington of “politicising” a normal technical and commercial practice. The strong stance came just a week before an expected meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump on September 24, where AI may emerge as a key point of dialogue. The newspaper called for the two sides to “work towards a common goal, and manage risks through dialogue and communication”, and it warned that Beijing would take “countermeasures” if Washington used the allegations as a pretext to contain Chinese companies. Distillation is a machine-learning method in which a smaller “student” model learns from the outputs of a larger “teacher” model. The technique is neutral and widely used, with the commentary pointing out that certain American companies had distilled Chinese AI models for their own systems, without naming any specific firm. One example is Thinking Machines Lab, co-founded by OpenAI’s former chief technology officer, Mira Murati. Its first model, Inkling, which was launched in July, used other models - including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K2.5 - to generate some early training data. AI “should not be the exclusive domain of big nations”, the People’s Daily article said, adding that the US was expanding its restrictive measures from chip controls and computing power blockades to AI model access – a move said to be “rooted in deep-seated anxiety over the potential erosion of its technological dominance”. The commentary pushed back against allegations made last week by three US government agencies that six Chinese companies – DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba Group Holding, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.ai – conducted “aggressive, malicious and targeted” distillation campaigns of advanced American models, allegedly with Beijing’s awareness. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week that China could “never get ahead” of the US in AI because of distillation. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also linked the issue to the strategic competition between the two countries. In an essay published on Saturday, he called for a crackdown on unauthorised distillation by companies in authoritarian countries, and said that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world”. Anthropic has identified several Chinese firms, including DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai and Alibaba, as companies it said had distilled its models. In its latest report last week, Anthropic said that the Chinese firms were engaged in a form of “illicit” distillation because of the “industrial” scale of their efforts to access the outputs of Anthropic’s models – which the company does not permit to be used in China – through fake accounts and stolen credit cards. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Monday rejected the suggestion that China’s progress in AI posed a risk to US national security. “The development of AI concerns the shared well-being of all humanity,” Guo said at a regular press briefing, urging countries to promote AI that was open, inclusive, broadly beneficial and oriented towards the common good. Spreading threat narratives and pursuing confrontation or malicious competition, he said, would only disrupt global AI governance and serve no one’s interests.

title: X Games League to hold first winter draft, with Eileen Gu expected to be top pick
description: Draft follows debut of X Games Summer League, with both events aiming to cement ties with Olympic Games, build on strong audience growth.
content: The MoonPay X Games League will hold its inaugural winter draft this week, ⁠betting that a team-based format and ⁠closer ties with the Olympic movement can build on ⁠strong audience growth for action sports, CEO Jeremy Bloom said. Eileen Gu, the most decorated freestyle skier in Olympic history with three golds and three silvers, is expected to be selected first overall. The draft follows the debut of the X Games Summer League, which featured teams representing Los Angeles, New York, Sao Paulo and Tokyo competing ‌across events in California; Chiba in Japan; and New Orleans. The title race went down to the final event in New Orleans, where New York secured the championship and a US$500,000 prize for its athletes after injured BMX rider Daniel Sandoval delivered a fourth-place finish that proved decisive. “It was a walk-off win for New York,” said Bloom, describing the dramatic finale as evidence that athletes had embraced and helped shape the league concept. View this post on Instagram A post shared by X Games (@xgames) The summer series drew 18.3 million television viewers in the US, up 78 per cent from ⁠a year earlier on linear television, Bloom said, while generating more than 200 million video views globally. The winter format presents different challenges, including ‌staging events at ski resorts rather than in more controlled urban venues. But Bloom said the X Games’ established brand, which has run for three decades, gave it confidence that fans would respond. This ‌year’s Aspen X Games attracted 15.3 million US television viewers, up 43 per cent year-on-year. The event sold out in ⁠three weeks and drew almost ⁠50,000 spectators over the weekend, while also featuring music performances from artists including Gunna, Disco Lines and Kaskade. The Winter League will begin with a draft on Wednesday, with athletes ‌to be allocated to teams rather than competing primarily under national flags. Bloom said the approach would distinguish the X Games from the Olympics, where national representation remains central, while allowing the ‌two properties ‌to complement each other. Action ‌sports once sat outside the sporting mainstream when the X Games launched in 1995. Now, its core disciplines are Olympic events, with ⁠skateboarding and BMX set to appear in their third Olympic cycle at the Los Angeles 2028 Games. The Olympics can turn athletes into global ⁠stars during a concentrated period of competition, while the X Games can sustain their profiles, stories and commercial appeal during the four years between Games. “The more that we can help build global icons, the better their ratings will be and ‌vice versa,” Bloom said. In addition to ‌Gu, who was born in San Francisco but represents China, Bloom highlighted snowboarders including Mark McMorris as well as skier Alex Hall. The Winter League is scheduled to include stops in Aspen, Calgary and Ruka in Finland, combining competition with live music and festival programming. Bloom said that mix would remain core to the X Games identity. “The X Games has done more to shape youth culture than it has done in even snowboarding and BMX,” he said.

title: Chinese research ship completes month-long mission near Scarborough Shoal
description: The vessel surveyed the geology and environment of a South China Sea feature claimed by Beijing and Manila.
content: China confirmed on Wednesday that a research vessel conducted a month-long, wide-ranging geological survey in the waters near Scarborough Shoal, a South China Sea flashpoint between Beijing and Manila. The Haiyang Dizhi Shihao, or Marine Geology No 10, carried out the survey from August 11 to September 8, with the aim of “gaining a comprehensive understanding of the basic geological features and ecological environment” of waters under its jurisdiction, the Ministry of Natural Resources said on Wednesday. The data and samples collected would support research into the area’s seabed, geology and marine environment while “providing a scientific basis for comprehensive management” of the waters around Scarborough Shoal, the ministry said. The 75-metre (246-foot) Haiyang Dizhi Shihao is a multidisciplinary geological survey vessel equipped for marine geological, geophysical, hydrological and environmental research. The ministry’s statement came a day after the Armed Forces of the Philippines said the vessel had stayed 28 days near the shoal, which China calls Huangyan Island and the Philippines calls Panatag Shoal. According to the armed forces, it was the first time the ship had been seen near the shoal. It was previously monitored in 2024 in waters north of the Philippines and in the vicinity of the Philippine Rise, or Benham Rise, a vast undersea plateau in the Philippine Sea off the eastern coast of Luzon. The armed forces said there were no signs that the Chinese research vessel conducted seabed drilling operations. “The presence and the track would indicate that they were conducting surveillance or research activities,” the official Philippine News Agency quoted the military as saying. “As to any report of drilling activities, there was none that was confirmed nor were there any reports given by our monitoring capabilities.” Beijing claims sovereignty over most islands and rock features in the South China Sea, claims that overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei. Scarborough Shoal has been controlled by China since 2012 and has been a persistent source of tension between Beijing and Manila. To underline its claim, China released baselines for the territorial sea around the shoal in 2024. The Philippines – which challenges the Chinese claim with occasional ship and aircraft activities in the area – filed its own territorial sea baselines for the shoal with the United Nations in July. The same month, China approved the construction of a marine environmental observation station to monitor an area that includes the shoal. The planned station is expected to “fill a key gap” in marine monitoring in what China refers to as the Zhongsha Islands and complete China’s ecological observation network across the entire South China Sea, according to the South China Sea Institute of Oceanology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, which proposed the project. The Zhongsha Islands, part of which is also known as Macclesfield Bank, are a group of reefs and atolls in the central South China Sea. Beijing approved the Scarborough Shoal National Nature Reserve in September last year. Last month, Beijing issued an administrative regulation on biodiversity and ecological protection near the shoal.

title: Sweden’s long election night ends without answers – but caution on China seems certain
description: Despite close result, main parties agree on reducing economic dependence on China and pushing Europe towards a tougher line on Beijing.
content: Sweden found itself in political uncertainty this week, as its parliamentary election on Sunday turned out to be extremely tight. With 95 per cent of the votes counted, the opposition left-wing bloc holds a three-seat lead over the governing right-wing bloc, with final results expected on Thursday. I’ve been to multiple election night parties across Europe as a journalist. The one on Sunday night with the Social Democrats, the main centre-left party seeking to regain power, was definitely on the calmer end: no free champagne was served, so you had to pay for your own drinks. The race was so close throughout the night that when the initial exit poll projected a left-wing victory, a reporter friend could not find anyone willing to give a reaction – as the potential interviewees were unsure whether the results would hold. Some journalists wondered if the Social Democrats’ leader, Magdalena Andersson, was ever going to speak. She eventually took the stage close to midnight; by that time the hall had thinned out, as many supporters had already gone home. Swedes are now waiting to see who will form their new government. But what I sensed during my days in Stockholm was a bigger feeling of uncertainty in the business community about the future of global trade and the country’s economy. “We are seeing globalisation turning into regionalisation,” a senior Swedish executive told me, adding that protectionism was on the rise across major markets including the US, China and India. Even within the EU, with far-right nationalist political parties on the rise, companies lack long-term predictability about how the bloc might develop and evolve. When Chinese companies invest in factories in Sweden, nothing good comes of it Senior Chinese executive According to the executive, who asked not to be named due to the topic’s sensitivity, the prosperity of Swedish businesses would lie partially in whether they could adapt quickly to local protectionist policies. China did not feature much during the campaign cycle, probably because the major parties do not have large disagreements on the subject. In August, before the vote, Swedish media platform Kvartal asked the main parties whether Sweden should actively reduce its economic dependence on China and push Europe towards a tougher, more defensive line on Beijing. Every party that responded said “yes”. The Left Party abstained. Swedish companies, on the other hand, still have many reasons to stay in China despite the tough realities of the market, increasingly for its advantages in innovation, research and development. “We still see a net inflow of companies into the [Chinese] market, and I do believe that for most companies – even if the market is very challenging – they’re still there for the long term,” said Per Porten, Sweden’s trade commissioner to China. Apart from weak domestic demand, key concerns of Swedish companies in China include export controls as well as “buy local” restrictions in public procurement and tenders. In practice, many local governments still exclude Swedish companies with local supply chains or Chinese subsidiaries owned by Swedish companies in public procurement, despite them meeting the requirements set out by the central government. Beijing’s export control regime is also hurting Swedish companies that use China as a hub to supply their global supply chain, according to Porten. Meanwhile in Sweden, Chinese firms face their own challenges, as the business environment and mindset are very different from those at home. “When Chinese companies invest in factories in Sweden, nothing good comes of it,” said a senior Chinese executive with decades of experience in Sweden. Investing in production in Sweden is risky, the executive said, because many Chinese firms struggle to cope with the country’s regulations and environmental policies and political turnover adds to the uncertainty. Chinese firms also tend to arrive with performance benchmarks that are too ambitious for the Swedish market or the way Swedes do business – for instance, one company vowed to become No 1 in Sweden within three years, the executive said – and end up fighting among themselves or engaging in other aggressive market behaviour. Nevertheless, one thing is sure. For many analysts and those in the business community in Sweden who I have spoken with: whoever the next prime minister might be, that person should travel to China soon. With no state visits since Stefan Lofven attended the World Economic Forum’s 2017 “Summer Davos” summit – held in northeast China’s Dalian – it has been nearly a decade since a Swedish prime minister set foot on Chinese soil.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong must prepare for the impact of heat-related work stoppages
description: We need to start discussing when work may need to stop, who should be compensated when it does and how the cost of adaptation can be shared.
content: At the beginning of August, when temperatures in Hong Kong hit highs not seen for at least 140 years, the Labour Department’s Heat Stress at Work Warning system remained at the amber level, the lowest of three tiers. The controversy that followed raised a broader question: are our heat warnings adequately protecting people who work outdoors? The Labour Department has since announced changes that will lead to earlier heat-stress warnings. These improvements to worker protection are welcome. But they also force us to confront a harder question: what happens when dangerous heat becomes common enough that protecting workers’ health begins to conflict with construction schedules, noise controls, workers’ incomes and the normal functioning of the city? Let us for a moment consider the wider impact of the updated rules. After this summer, it is not hard to believe that heatwaves will become increasingly long and common. Together with the newly lowered warning thresholds, this is likely to lead to more rest time or time when work has to be halted completely during the hours in which much construction activity is normally scheduled. Cramping activity into shorter available periods on hot days will result in a set of new trade-offs for the affected parties. For outdoor workers, the time stress caused by more frequent heat-related warnings may aggravate the already high work accident rate. It may also lead to a loss of income for workers under precarious contracts, with many preferring to continue to work to receive a steady pay cheque. After all, a warning is only effective if those warned can afford to obey it. For employers and contractors, stricter heat regulation will affect productivity, deadlines and costs. For society and affected neighbourhoods, it is a question of environmental nuisance like construction noise, the length of disruptions and the date of infrastructure delivery. The cost of extreme heat does not disappear when work stops; it simply moves from one party to another. These trade-offs can be summarised in a single question: If midday work becomes unsafe more frequently, who will absorb the cost? Extreme heat stress is just one example of the changes coming our way. We will have to continuously rethink and renegotiate societal trade-offs, such as the balance between heat protection, environmental nuisances, social security and business costs. In this process, we have one major advantage: the future is not entirely unknown. Climate projections can tell us the direction in which Hong Kong’s heat is moving, and other societies already live in conditions Hong Kong may increasingly experience. We also don’t have to wait for existing arrangements to repeatedly fail before redesigning them. Adaptation is not just a matter of better climate modelling. It is also a matter of institutional learning. As extreme heat becomes more common, our society must be able to continuously rethink the approach to outdoor labour protection. Solutions may be found in the regulatory space – or outside it. In India, where some regions frequently suffer extreme heat, a novel heat insurance scheme for workers shows a shift towards innovative and market-driven solutions by providing workers with income protection when extreme heat prevents them from working. Adjusting heavy workloads away from midday heat is already common in countries like Spain, showing how regional regulations can prioritise human physiological limits over rigid work schedules. Lastly, adaptation measures such as fan-cooled jackets can play an important role and may be faster and cheaper to realise than regulatory change. With a mature insurance industry, could Hong Kong consider similar protections, whether through insurance or mandatory compensation for certain heat-related work stoppages – alongside a more nuanced approach to environmental nuisances when schedules shift? Hong Kong’s extreme heat challenges will not be solved by a better warning system alone. All options, including choosing not to do anything, will incur costs. Rather than stopping at the technical details of the warning system, we need to start discussing when work may need to stop, who should be compensated when it does and how the costs of adaptation can be shared. Extreme heat is becoming a question not only of meteorology, but also of labour, economics and social policy. The Office of the Commissioner for Climate Change is well positioned to coordinate these developments. Now is a good time to think about not only when work should stop but also whether we will allow working hours to shift, how rules on environmental nuisance can be adjusted, who will pay for heat-related downtime, who bears construction delays and what protections should be mandatory rather than advisory.

title: HBO Max K-drama The Ordinary Jackpot: Lee Joon-hyuk hides a lottery win in workplace drama
description: Lee Joon-hyuk plays a timid office worker who decides to stop bottling up his emotions after a significant lottery win changes his life.
content: Lead cast: Lee Joon-hyuk, Seo Hyun-woo, Oh Dae-hwan Latest Nielsen rating: 3.9 per cent In a refreshing departure from the recent slew of workplace romantic comedies, The Ordinary Jackpot brings the focus back to the office dynamics of Seoul’s salary workers, but with a twist: what if you had enough money to never fear getting fired again? Lee Joon-hyuk, who appeared in last year’s office romcom Love Scout, leads the series as Gong Eun-tae, the hard-working head of sales team five at Hongseong International. Over his years at the company, he has kept his head down and quietly risen through the ranks, earning a reputation for turning around seemingly hopeless accounts. Unfortunately, he is also seen as a pushover who never raises his voice and meekly accepts when the brands he has saved are transferred to another team to help a different team leader earn a promotion. Eun-tae has an ally at work in Jeong Seon-hyuk (Oh Dae-hwan, Filing for Love), the leader of team four, but this support doesn’t extend much past commiseration during rooftop breaks. Meanwhile, he has a difficult relationship with a direct subordinate, the moody assistant manager Yang Joon-ho (Seo Hyun-woo, Behind Every Star), who is older than him and openly defiant. Eun-tae’s life revolves entirely around work, with each day unfolding much like the last. That changes one evening when he drops by a convenience store for his daily wind-down beers. With the card machine broken and a lack of change in the till, he is convinced to buy a lottery ticket as well. He thinks nothing of it until he sees the lottery results and remembers the ticket. He is stunned to discover he has won close to 2 billion won (US$1.5 million) – or, at least, about 1.3 billion won after tax. It is a life-changing sum for someone who earns 70 million won a year, but given it is about the same as the average cost of a Seoul flat these days, it is not enough to retire in the lap of luxury. Eun-tae daydreams about showing off his money, sticking it to his colleagues and quitting in style, before accepting that this is not in his nature. After careful consideration, he decides to stick with his job and keep his windfall a secret, with one crucial difference: he will no longer bottle up his emotions. He got the idea while collecting his winnings, inspired by a conversation with an elderly fellow winner. When asked what she will do with the prize, she replies, “I’m going to get angry. I’ve never really got angry in my life. I’ve put up with too much all this time. Maybe it’s time I started letting myself get angry.” And so he does. When Joon-ho defies him again, Eun-tae refuses to take it, reprimanding him on the office floor. This initially makes both men uncomfortable, but once they talk privately and lay their cards on the table, the dynamic begins to shift, allowing them to move forward. While The Ordinary Jackpot is not an office romcom, romance is still in the air. Eun-tae occasionally shares after-work meals with Jin Hae-joo (Ok Ja-yeon, Mine), another hard-working Hongseong manager working on the floor above him. He seems a little too consumed by his anxieties to think of her as more than a late-night dining partner, but Hae-joo appears to be biding her time, waiting for him to open up. As Eun-tae gains confidence from his windfall and becomes more assertive in the workplace, there is hope he will soon be able to apply that energy to his personal life. Much like last year’s hit series The Dream Life of Mr Kim, The Ordinary Jackpot takes pains to present a grounded story of an ordinary worker – albeit a ridiculously handsome one – while depicting recognisable scenarios of workplace microaggressions and miscommunication. Most viewers will not be lucky enough to receive the same windfall as Eun-tae. However, this series suggests that while the money gives him the freedom to come out of his shell and embrace life once more, the cash itself is incidental. The ability to change his life was inside him all along, as it is for us all – it just needed to be teased out. The Ordinary Jackpot is streaming on HBO Max.

title: Germany’s Merz cancels trip to UN in New York as pressure mounts at home
description: Friedrich Merz opts to remain in Berlin following far-right AfD gains and ahead of crucial regional votes.
content: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has cancelled a trip to the UN General Assembly next week as he faces mounting pressure at home during a string of difficult state elections. A government official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they couldn’t publicly discuss a trip that hadn’t been announced officially, said Wednesday that Merz won’t travel to New York as originally planned because “his presence is required in Berlin”. Merz had been expected to speak at the General Assembly next Wednesday. There was no word on why his presence in Germany was required. But speculation has mounted that Merz’s job is in danger following a stinging defeat for his centre-right party by the far-right Alternative for Germany party in an election on September 6 in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt. That damaged the already unpopular chancellor’s authority as he tries to push through reforms to Germany’s sluggish economy. Two more regional elections follow on Sunday: one in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, another largely rural eastern state, and the other in Berlin, the capital. The AfD is expected to make significant gains in both, though it has no realistic path to power in Berlin and faces a much stronger challenge from the current centre-left governor in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania than it did from Merz’s party in Saxony-Anhalt. The prospects for Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union are bleaker, 16 months after the 70-year-old became Germany’s leader. It could lose the mayor’s office in Berlin that it has held since 2023 and, if things go very badly, fail for the first time to win seats in a state legislature anywhere by falling below 5 per cent of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a region where it was already weak. The general debate of the UN General Assembly takes place every year in September. Merz also chose not to attend last year. Instead, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul spoke on behalf of Germany. Additional reporting by dpa

title: US crypto bill stumble sparks call for Hong Kong to seize ‘critical strategic window’
description: City urged to act fast as window could vanish once Washington regains regulatory momentum.
content: The US Senate’s rejection of the Clarity Act – a landmark bill meant to regulate cryptocurrency market structure – has opened a window for Hong Kong to accelerate its digital asset ambitions, industry insiders say, even as the sector remains mired in a slump after a brief rally last month. Beijing’s ban on crypto remains in force in mainland China, but Hong Kong has received approval to develop itself as a digital asset hub, with the stalled push in Washington presenting the city with what analysts called a “critical strategic window” to secure a regulatory lead. US Senators on Wednesday blocked the bill, which was expected to accelerate the integration of digital assets into mainstream finance. Senate Democrat Elissa Slotkin slammed the bill’s ethics provisions as “thin” in a post on X on Wednesday, and accused US President Donald Trump of “making billions of dollars” from crypto by “bilking everyday Americans out of their hard-earned money”. It remains uncertain whether the city can turn this temporary lead into a lasting one Allen Ding, Bitfire Research The delay had given Hong Kong a “critical strategic window”, said Allen Ding, director of Bitfire Research, a unit of Hong Kong-listed crypto asset management firm Bitfire Group. But he added Hong Kong’s digital asset regulatory advantage over the US “may be temporary” due to its small domestic market and the global influence of US regulatory standards. “It remains uncertain whether the city can turn this temporary lead into a lasting one,” Ding said. A predictable regulatory environment has been Hong Kong’s pitch to global businesses. At an industry conference in April, lawmaker Duncan Chiu Tat-kun swiped at US political uncertainties while touting the city’s “steady progressive build-up” of digital asset regulations. “The failure of the Clarity Act does not change the long-term direction of the digital asset market, but it does extend a period of regulatory uncertainty in the US,” said Shawn Yan, founder and CEO of Hong Kong-based enterprise digital asset wallet provider Cregis Technology. “For Hong Kong, this makes the development of its own regulatory framework increasingly relevant.” The city should now focus on “building infrastructure that can operate across regulatory boundaries, rather than waiting for any single jurisdiction to define the market for everyone”, Yan added. Republican Senators including Cynthia Lummis and Jon Husted said on social media that rejecting the crypto bill meant ceding digital asset leadership to China. Hong Kong’s bid to become a hub has faced headwinds as companies struggle with high compliance costs and a prolonged market downturn. CoinEx, which is based in Hong Kong but is not among the city’s 13 licensed exchanges, said earlier this week it would cease operations amid uncertainties “exceeding reasonable boundaries”. Bitcoin briefly broke above US$80,000 for the first time in three months in August amid a broader rally in alternative assets, but has since retreated and remained nearly 40 per cent below its record high of US$126,000 in October. On Wednesday, the world’s largest cryptocurrency token dropped nearly 5 per cent to below US$75,000 after the US Senate vote.

title: Hong Kong court winds up Wang Fuk Court renovation consultant over debt
description: Will Power Architects, involved in HK$336 million renovation project at estate, is ordered wound up after failing to oppose creditor’s application.
content: A Hong Kong court has ordered the winding-up of an engineering consultant behind a HK$336 million (US$42.8 million) renovation project at the fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court over an unspecified debt. The High Court on Wednesday granted Tong Yiu-kwok’s application to wind up Will Power Architects after the company neither filed a statement in opposition nor sent a representative to explain its position at the hearing. The court did not disclose Tong’s relationship with the firm or the amount of debt involved. It also ordered Will Power to bear the costs of the civil proceedings. Will Power director Wong Hap-yin has been remanded in custody since being charged with 16 offences in connection with the deadly blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last year. The 40-year-old previously told West Kowloon Court that he had difficulty arranging legal representation for the company because he was in custody. The fire, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000, was the deadliest in the city’s recent history. The tragedy exposed loopholes in fire-risk management for large-scale renovation projects and shed light on widespread collusion among engineering firms to manipulate the lucrative building maintenance market. The housing estate’s high-rise towers were wrapped in scaffolding when a piece of safety netting caught fire at one of its eight blocks. A preliminary investigation found that substandard scaffolding mesh and polyfoam boards used to protect windows during the works contributed to the blaze spreading rapidly to six other blocks in the estate. Concerns over possible bid-rigging also emerged after the estate’s renovation budget more than doubled from a preliminary estimate of HK$152 million in September 2023 to HK$336 million in 2024, when the most expensive option was adopted. In June, police and the Independent Commission Against Corruption laid a total of 25 charges of manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering, attempting to pervert the course of justice and tax evasion against seven individuals and two companies, including Wong and Will Power. In separate criminal proceedings initiated earlier this month, the Buildings Department and the Labour Department laid a total of 284 charges against Wong, Will Power and other defendants in connection with the fire. The charges included allegedly permitting the use of defective building materials and failing to ensure workers’ safety.

title: Singapore court rejects 90-year-old’s spousal support claim against ex-wife, 89
description: The ex-wife claims that after she retired in 1992, she supported the household and gave her husband half of her monthly pension.
content: A Singapore family court rejected a 90-year-old man’s claim for spousal maintenance from his 89-year-old wife, noting that both of them are in the twilight of their lives. The court also noted that the man would receive more than S$2 million (US$1.6 million) from the matrimonial pool, comprising the couple’s assets to be divided in the divorce, and his wife was a retiree living on a pension. The former couple were married for more than 64 years and have three children, all aged above 60, a judgment published on Wednesday said. They were not named in the judgment, as is usual for a family court ruling. Most of the value in the matrimonial pool came from their joint asset, a S$5.8 million house. The couple married in January 1960 and were granted an interim judgment for divorce in September 2024. There were no issues of custody or child maintenance since their children are adults. Dealing with the division of matrimonial assets, Justice Dedar Singh Gill added about S$14,500 in the man’s name to the pool. Most of this is from his Central Provident Fund (CPF), Singapore’s mandatory social security savings scheme. He added about S$80,000 from the woman’s assets to the pool, including almost S$20,000 in CPF. Disputed contributions The woman argued that she had contributed 100 per cent to the matrimonial home and financed it alone. She said she had bought their previous property under the Teacher’s Estate housing scheme, which provided homes for educators. The sale proceeds from this property were used fully to buy the matrimonial home, to which her husband contributed “nothing”. The man sought a 50:50 division of all matrimonial assets, claiming to have contributed to both the Teacher’s Estate property and the matrimonial home. However, the judge noted that neither side’s account was supported by documentary evidence. The woman sought a ratio of 80:20 in indirect contributions in her favour, arguing that she bore virtually all the financial and non-financial burdens of the family throughout the marriage. She said she was the main provider during the first half of the marriage when both of them worked, paying for the children’s tuition and courses, family holidays and a domestic worker to care for the children when she was at work. She also said that she gave her son S$50,000 to start a business that failed, and footed the bills for her children’s weddings. After she retired in 1992, she claimed that her husband had no income and contributed “nothing” while she supported the household from her pension of about S$2,400 a month. She gave her husband half of this amount each month, she added. She also said that she was the primary carer for her children, cooking for the family and supervising the various domestic helpers and overseeing the repairs and maintenance of the household. The husband sought an equal or near-equal division of indirect contributions, claiming that until retirement, both parties had pooled their incomes in joint accounts. From these, all the household expenses were paid. After retirement, he said the expenses were paid from their pooled savings in joint accounts, and thereafter from his wife’s joint accounts with their son and oldest daughter. He said he did his “fair share of being involved in the care and upbringing of the children”. Justice Gill said the indirect financial contributions for the first half of the marriage were difficult to determine, given the couple’s differing versions of events without objective evidence. However, the position is clearer for the second half of the marriage after their retirement. It was undisputed that the man had no income beyond his monthly annuity of S$485.75 from insurer NTUC Income, and that the only income stream was the woman’s monthly pension of about S$2,400, of which she gave her husband half. The woman also produced payment records showing that she paid the property tax bills up to 2024, as well as receipts for household bills she continued to cover on her own. Family carer The judge also found that the wife contributed the greater share in indirect non-financial contributions, with detailed evidence of her caregiving and home-making. She was the primary carer of her children from birth and even when she worked, helping them with their homework and managing their schooling and activities. She also ran the household, cooked for the family, organised family gatherings, and trained and supervised the various domestic workers they hired. “The husband, on the other hand, does no more than assert in general terms that he did his fair share,” Justice Gill said. “He descends to no particulars of caring for the children, their schooling, their health or their emotional needs. I also consider it significant that the husband neither disputed most of what the wife says she did for the family nor offered any competing account of his own.” He assessed indirect contributions at 70:30 in favour of the woman. The woman sought a 2 per cent increase of her share of the matrimonial pool, saying that her ex-husband had illegally excluded her from the home from March 2025 and placed a padlock on the gate. The man, however, claimed that his ex-wife and their oldest daughter moved out of their own accord. Justice Gill noted that this complaint of illegal exclusion surfaced for the first time only in written submissions, and both parties would obtain substantial sums from the pool in any event. He declined to raise the woman’s share of the assets on this basis. In total, the ratio across direct and indirect contributions was computed to be 60:40, in favour of the woman. Accordingly, she was to get S$3.5 million, while her ex-husband obtained S$2.4 million. The man sought maintenance as an incapacitated former husband under the Women’s Charter, pointing to his medical and mobility issues, his inability to earn a livelihood, his minimal income and his wife’s departure from the matrimonial home. This has left him to cover the home’s expenses alone. If he did not get maintenance, the man asked for a lump sum equivalent to 5 to 10 per cent of his share of the matrimonial assets. The judge rejected the man’s claim for spousal maintenance and his request for the lump sum payment. He said that both parties are in the twilight of their lives, with neither having any earning capacity nor any expectations of improving their financial positions through work. Both of them rely on monthly pensions or payouts as their financial source, and they will each have very substantial sums from the matrimonial pool, Justice Gill added. The sum of more than S$2 million that the man will obtain is “more than sufficient to meet the needs of a 90-year-old retiree for the remainder of his life”. “Once the division takes effect, he will be amply provided for. In these circumstances, I do not think an order for maintenance against the wife, herself an elderly retiree living on a pension, would be just or necessary.” The man sought reimbursement from his ex-wife’s share for the property tax he paid on the house for the years of assessment 2025 and 2026, saying that she had paid nothing since moving out in March 2025. The judge acknowledged that the man should not necessarily bear the entire property tax simply because he lived there, but found his argument for his ex-wife to pay the full bill untenable. He said that the property tax for the two years must be borne equally by both parties. The home is to be sold on the open market within six months, with them having joint conduct of the sale. Each side will bear its own costs. This story was first published by CNA

title: Tesla revives China discounts; Iran war drives shift to electric cars: 7 EV reads
description: From China’s powerhouse plan for its car industry to Tesla’s rare-earth-free motor, here are seven EV stories you may have missed.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on electric and new energy vehicles from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Market squeeze: Tesla revives China price cuts to stem slumping deliveries Tesla China has launched discounts on its Shanghai-made cars for the first time since the end of 2024, responding to falling deliveries in the world’s largest market for electric vehicles (EVs). 2. ‘Key pillar’: the 5-year powerhouse plan for China’s car industry China is set to secure its place among the global automotive powerhouses by 2030 through further efforts to boost domestic sales and foster technological innovation, while a capacity alert mechanism will be introduced to guard against disorderly competition. 3. Over 65% of cars sold in China are now EVs as Iran war drives electric shift China’s EV adoption rate has hit an all-time high, as the Iran war drives motorists to shift away from petrol cars despite a sluggish automotive market. 4. Will Tesla’s rare-earth-free motor put China’s trade trump card at risk? As Tesla CEO Elon Musk touted the motor of his company’s Cybercab – which, he claims, contains no rare earth elements – debate has emerged over whether the technology could mark a meaningful shift in EV supply chains, or undercut one of China’s trump cards in its protracted trade conflict with the US. 5. BYD, Leapmotor buck EV market slowdown as pressure piles up on small rivals Top performers BYD and Leapmotor clawed their way up higher in terms of sales last month, even as China’s EV market was shrinking amid weaker consumer demand. However, smaller players were expected to face falling sales and mounting losses for the rest of the year as competition got fiercer, according to analysts. 6. China’s EV makers see synergy in their race to beat Tesla in humanoid robotics When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots. 7. Tesla to exhibit Cybercab robotaxi in China: can it spark buzz amid slow sales? Tesla is facing weaker sales in China this year, but the American EV manufacturer is looking to generate a buzz in its second-largest market by exhibiting its new self-driving vehicle, the Cybercab.

title: Israel prepared to ‘finish job’ in Gaza and remove Palestinians, minister says
description: Israel Katz says the IDF is prepared to resume fighting, eliminate Hamas and implement ‘the migration plan’.
content: Israel’s defence minister said Wednesday it was only a matter of time before the country resumes full-scale war in Gaza and moves to force out its 2 million Palestinians. Israel Katz, who is known for outspoken remarks, was responding to criticism from another right-wing contender ahead of October 27 elections. Katz said 70 per cent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population in the Israeli offensive launched after the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas. He said that an October 2025 ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump had “supreme value for all Israelis” by leading to the return of remaining hostages and ensuring “a commitment by the United States” to disarming Hamas. “We all understand that this is not going to happen - and the IDF is prepared, once given the directive to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan,” Katz said in a statement, referring to the Israeli military. He said earlier this month that Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the 2 million people would go. US ambassador Mike Huckabee has denied any plan to “displace people out of Gaza against their will”. Katz had described the migration plan as voluntary, saying most Palestinians wanted to leave. Nearly all of Gaza’s population has been internally displaced and most of the territory lies in rubble after the war. The Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 killed 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on Israeli official figures, the deadliest attack ever against Israel. Militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza. Israel’s retaliatory military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 73,700 people, according to the territory’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and does not distinguish between combatants and civilians, and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. While the 11-month-old ceasefire has reduced the level of violence, Israel has still regularly carried out strikes in Gaza. A total of 1,375 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire came into effect, according to the Gaza health ministry. Hamas said in late July that it was ready to disarm, in what Trump hailed as a breakthrough. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the latest stage of the plan and said there would be no Israeli withdrawal from Gaza until Hamas verifiably decommissions all weapons.

title: First update made to ISO 9001 in a decade, with China shaping AI, cybersecurity standards
description: Global organisation says China will play a greater role in writing tech rules which pave the way to a more ‘inclusive, sustainable future’.
content: China’s contributions and leadership were of considerable value to the revision of new International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards for artificial intelligence, intelligent transport systems and cybersecurity, according to the global body. The ISO made the comments as it released ISO 9001:2026 on Wednesday, which is the first major revision to ISO 9001 – an international benchmark for quality management – in a decade, it added. ISO Secretary-General Sergio Mujica told the South China Morning Post that China had shown great leadership and vision, heading around 100 ISO technical committees. International standards are crucial in facilitating the country’s participation in regional and international markets. “Beijing has been responsible for the development and revision of around 600 ISO standards. I expect the city to play an even greater role in international standardisation in the coming years,” Mujica said. “Beijing is an international centre for science and technology innovation, therefore it’s no surprise that it is home to more than half of all the ISO technical committee secretariats held by the Standardization Administration of China (SAC),” he added. The 2026 edition responds to an increasingly complex operating environment, where organisations must balance resilience with innovation and adapt quickly to changing markets and technologies, ISO said. The organisation launched its series of standards centred on ISO 9001 in the 1980s. China’s first ISO 9001 certificate was granted in Shenzhen in 1991. Now, certificates held by Chinese companies account for over one-third of the global volume, the world’s largest share for consecutive years, according to the National Certification and Accreditation Administration in China. As one of the global leaders in technological and industrial innovation, Chinese experts participate in nearly 800 ISO committees. Input from these experts and cross-sector stakeholders ensure ISO standards address market needs, reflect diverse user experiences and build trust. “By continuing to invest in national quality infrastructure and encouraging broader participation in standards development, China can bring its national priorities to the international table – helping to write the rules that shape economies and offer a pathway to a more inclusive, sustainable future,” Mujica said. As an ISO member body, the SAC plays a vital role in developing standards that address environmental and sustainability challenges such as renewable energy, greenhouse gas emissions and the circular economy. Beyond advancing emerging technologies, China, through the SAC, also leads ISO’s new technical committee on cultural heritage conservation, he added. This work supported the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, which calls for strengthened efforts to protect the world’s cultural and natural heritage to make cities and human settlements resilient and sustainable. “We are extremely grateful for the commitment and effort shown by the SAC and encourage it to go even further in engaging with the international standards community,” Mujica added.

title: Should Beijing use its maritime militia as a backup force in the South China Sea?
description: On the sidelines of the Xiangshan Forum, a leading Chinese researcher says there could be a role for the vessels at critical moments.
content: China should strengthen its maritime militia to be an extra force to collect information and maintain a regular presence in the South China Sea, where it is coming into frequent conflict with the Philippines. That was the suggestion Wu Shicun, the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, made on Tuesday on the sidelines of the Beijing Xiangshan Forum, an annual defence gathering in the capital attended by security officials and researchers from nearly 100 countries this year. “We need to strengthen our maritime capabilities, including our coastguard forces and even our maritime militia. Their main role is fishing, but at critical moments, there is nothing objectionable about using them to safeguard our maritime rights and interests,” Wu said. Most of China’s maritime militia members are civilian fishermen, and they have become more visible as confrontations have grown between Beijing and Manila in the South China Sea in recent years. The Philippines has repeatedly accused Chinese maritime militia vessels of operating around Scarborough Shoal, a particular flashpoint that China calls Huangyan Island and the Philippines calls Panatag Shoal. Three Chinese maritime militia vessels were involved in a confrontation in the area in July, according to the Philippine Coast Guard. Wu said the build-up of the maritime militia was driven by growing tensions over the shoal, tensions that he said could escalate as “actions by the Philippines and countries behind it that infringe on China’s interests around Huangyan Island intensify”. Wu’s assessment is unusual, given Chinese authorities have repeatedly denied the involvement of the “maritime militia” in South China Sea stand-offs. Even so, China’s 2013 defence white paper categorised the country’s militia as one of the three components of China’s armed forces, elevating its importance both on land and at sea. The maritime militia force is a supplementary option that could be used when necessary for maritime rights protection in addition to the China Coast Guard and the Chinese military, Wu said. “Their main occupation is still fishing, and they make their living from it. Their role in protecting maritime rights is only supplementary, when necessary, when China uses civilian means to safeguard its rights and claims,” Wu said. He said that depending on the situation, the militia could use their stronger steel-hulled vessels to protect other timber vessels during confrontations, help guard facilities such as drilling platforms, and monitor and collect information. “Keeping naval or coastguard vessels at sea for extended periods is too costly. Maritime militia vessels can range from several hundred tonnes to, at most, about 1,000 tonnes, so they are relatively inexpensive to operate. They can maintain a regular presence to observe, track and identify and provide information,” Wu said. A Philippine Navy assessment in January said Chinese maritime operations became more coordinated last year, with the People’s Liberation Army Navy increasingly operating alongside the China Coast Guard and what Manila identified as Chinese maritime militia. The Chinese defence ministry described the Philippine report as “smearing of China’s actions to safeguard its rights” and “an attempt to mislead public opinion”. It did not directly comment on the description of the maritime militia. China’s maritime militia was deployed in “record-high numbers” across the disputed South China Sea in 2025, the Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, a research programme affiliated with the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said in a report this year. It said an average of 241 maritime vessel deployments took place each day last year, “the highest level measured in any year”. In 2024, the daily average was 232 vessels.

title: Tips from top universities on acing admissions essays and interviews
description: Representatives from leading schools in the United Kingdom and United States advise students on writing applications that stand out from the rest.
content:
Applying to university can be overwhelming, but it’s important to choose a programme that fits your interests and needs.
We got advice from representatives of top overseas universities about how to figure out your passion and stand out in personal statements and interviews.
Speakers from the University of Oxford, University of Cambridge, King’s College London and New York University shared their tips at the Global Education Summit, organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier.
Sarah Hales, senior regional manager of admissions and access at the University of Cambridge, urged prospective students to dig into the content of a school’s courses.
“Go beyond the course headline. Go beyond the university ranking and actually look specifically at what you will be learning in that course,” Hales said. “It’s not just about getting into the university; it’s about getting on. Will you thrive? Will you be happy there?”
“One of the things that’s really different about some of the courses you can have at … [top] universities is the interdisciplinary nature of the courses and the ability to tailor your own learning to suit you,” Hales noted.
“We’re really looking for those students that have that passion, that commitment, that critical thinking [and] that desire to go beyond the curriculum to explore.”
Mandy Zhang, head of East Asia for the global student recruitment and admissions directorate at King’s College London, stressed the importance of student growth and resilience over time.
She said: “You may not be the very best at this course in the beginning. But gradually you’ll find your place [and] your passion through either coursework, projects or engagements with your tutor or your classmates. That’s really something we want to see – the drive [and] the curiosity.”
Admissions officers emphasised the need for authenticity and reflection over perfection.
Samina Khan, director of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Oxford, said: “This is a personal journey, so we are looking for you to tell us about you. What is it that’s unique about you? What are you bringing to the table from your experience of having lived in Hong Kong?”
She added: “If you’re studying history, what is it you’re reflecting upon in terms of Hong Kong’s history? … We’re looking for those personal reflections – your thoughts [and] your ideas, where you have gone into the depth of your academic subject that you want to study.”
William Sichel, assistant vice-president of undergraduate admissions at New York University in the United States, warned applicants against over-editing their personal statements and relying solely on artificial intelligence (AI) tools.
“You may end up with a perfect essay, but that has no humanity. That doesn’t tell us anything about you,” Sichel noted.
“We’re looking for authenticity. We’re looking to understand who you are. We’re looking to understand more about your story [and] more about what makes you, you.”
Admissions experts pointed out that interview styles could vary across different countries.
Bob Fan, managing partner at admissions consultancy True North Education, said British admissions interviews would usually be more academic while US ones were more conversational.
“[For schools in the United Kingdom], students are being asked about their thought process – how they approach certain questions. And so that’s how admissions officers really evaluate their intellectual abilities for UK universities,” Fan said.
“For US-style interviews, the admissions officers and companies that do interviews are trained to tease out specific details from students so that they can’t just avoid [answering] … about a certain passion.”
On the other hand, Khan, from Oxford, reassured reserved candidates that being shy would not be a barrier to admission.
“We are looking for somebody who is passionate about their subject, and they can have whatever personality that they come with. We cope with all different personalities,” she said.
“We will draw people out who are naturally reserved and quiet and be able to get the best out of them … So if you are naturally reserved, then one of the things that you may start to think about is building up your oracy skills in terms of being able to answer academic questions.”

title: Hong Kong court terminates trial after suspect in deadly 1991 hold-up dies of cancer
description: Wen Wenye, 62, who allegedly took part in murder and attempted robbery at second-hand goods shop, succumbs to lung cancer.
content: A Hong Kong court has terminated a trial arising from a deadly shooting during a botched robbery three decades ago after the defendant died in custody earlier this week. The High Court on Wednesday discharged a seven-member jury presiding over the trial of Wen Wenye, who allegedly took part in the murder and attempted robbery at Shun Fat Company, a second-hand goods shop in Sham Shui Po, on June 9, 1991. A government statement on Monday said Wen, 62, died in hospital that afternoon after he was found unconscious in the court’s holding cell during the trial’s adjournment. The presiding judge was giving instructions to jurors at the time, ahead of their closed-door deliberation. The jury had earlier found that Wen, a Shenzhen resident, could not be held criminally liable for the offences due to his cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer. The panel was nonetheless asked to decide if the defendant had committed the acts as charged in the indictment. Wen had been remanded in custody since his arrest at the Shenzhen Bay control point on November 11, 2023. He was allegedly one of three robbers behind the attempted hold-up, during which shop employee Cheng Kai-lam was fatally shot. During his incarceration, Wen was diagnosed with stage four lung cancer, with mutated cells spreading to his brain. He underwent surgery to remove damaged brain tissue on July 24, 2024, but had been wheelchair-bound since. In court, the defendant appeared drowsy and inattentive. He almost slid off his wheelchair on multiple occasions, prompting prison officers to help him up and reattach his hearing aid. The government statement said an inquest would be held to investigate Wen’s death.

title: Kowloon Bay’s new Amoy Footbridge set to draw neighbourhood closer together
description: The new elevated walkway builds on a long history in the area, starting with Amoy Gardens, the residential estate at the centre of the 2003 Sars outbreak.
content: Hong Kong is famous for its elevated walkways, which dot the city from Tsuen Wan to Mong Kok to Central, forming a sprawling pedestrian network built out over many decades. The newest addition to this network is the Amoy Footbridge in Kowloon Bay, which provides a roofed connection between the HK$4.1 billion East Kowloon Cultural Centre, Amoy Plaza mall, residential developments The Aperture and Amoy Gardens, and Kowloon Bay MTR station. Built by Hang Lung Properties as a community investment project, the footbridge opens at a time of meaningful anniversaries for the company and hence carries far more significance than its modest structure might suggest – from memories of the neighbourhood’s ordeal during the 2003 Sars outbreak to an illustration of how thoughtful urban planning can knit communities together. In 1977, Hang Lung acquired a 222,560 sq ft plot in Kowloon Bay, including the Amoy soy sauce factory, from the Amoy Canning Corporation. In 1981, the group opened the first phase of Amoy Gardens residential estate and Amoy Plaza shopping centre on the site. The opening of the new bridge therefore caps almost half a century of Hang Lung’s footprint in the district, aligning with the 66th anniversary of the group’s founding on September 13, 1960. At the opening ceremony, Leung Chun-ying, vice-chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, said residents could now move around “in a more comfortable, convenient and safe environment – whether it is raining heavily, as it was earlier today, or during the heat of summer”. He traced the project back to an accessibility drive from his tenure as Hong Kong’s chief executive, when the local government “promoted the idea of creating barrier-free, convenient access for all”. Hang Lung Properties “responded positively”, he said, in this collaboration between government, business and the community that produced “a genuine win-win-win outcome”. The project was enabled by public-private collaboration. In 2016, the government piloted a scheme allowing private developers seeking to build a footbridge or tunnel connecting their property to a public network to have the expensive land premium required to modify their land lease waived. The scheme was trialled in the Kowloon Bay and Kwun Tong business districts as part of the Energising Kowloon East programme. The new footbridge, delivered with the Energising Kowloon East Office and the Transport Department, is one of its results. Forged in adversity The origins of this public-private framework run deep, forged during one of the city’s greatest health crises. “My connection with the Amoy Gardens community began 23 years ago, during the Sars outbreak,” Leung recalled. Amoy Gardens was the site of Hong Kong’s largest single Sars cluster during the 2003 crisis: 329 residents were infected and 42 died, with almost half of all cases from Block E alone. Investigations by the government and the World Health Organization concluded that dried-out U-traps in bathroom floor drains – the water seal that keeps sewer gases out of a flat – had opened a route for the virus to travel between units, compounded by a “chimney effect” in the building’s light wells that drew contaminated air upwards between flats. In response, Leung, then Executive Council convenor and chairman of the Hong Kong Coalition of Professional Services, led a 2004 initiative to redesign Block E’s drainage with external water-seal pipes to act as insurance against the virus returning. The Coalition announced it would raise and spend HK$800,000 to retrofit Block E’s drainage system. “The new design is like a heart bypass operation, basically by providing water shields, in addition to what’s already inside [the flats], to make sure that this possible means for the spread of Sars and other diseases is totally and effectively dealt with,” Leung said at the time. Additional pipes fixed to external walls supplied a constant trickle of water to stop the traps drying out, requiring about a day’s work per flat with no need to replace drains inside homes. Crucially, the coalition gave the design away for free. “What we are going to do is to make this design totally public,” Leung announced in 2004, offering it to other buildings after a Buildings Department survey found that sewage systems in some 6,000 private buildings were defective or substandard. Persuading residents to agree to the retrofit fell largely on the shoulders of former district councillor Yip Hing-kwok, who was present at Monday’s ceremony. As chairman of the Amoy Gardens Owners’ Joint Committee during the crisis, Yip worked to secure household consent across the estate. The mutual trust forged between government, developers and residents during those crisis years laid the foundation for future civic partnerships – and Leung’s later policy focus as chief executive – ultimately paving the way for public-private initiatives like the Amoy Footbridge. Small links, big impact A hundred metres of covered walkway is the sort of thing that often goes unnoticed in a city as frenetic as Hong Kong. But these unremarkable pathways are among Hong Kong’s basic building blocks: the Highways Department was maintaining 1,171 footbridges and 564 subways as of June 2026, a network built piece by piece over many decades. Academics who study that layered system say that small pieces of infrastructure often punch above their weight. Sunny Choi, assistant professor at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University’s School of Design, said Kowloon Bay is exactly the kind of neighbourhood where an elevated link earns its keep, with a ground plane “overwhelmingly dominated by vehicular infrastructure, including heavy traffic arterial roads, bus bays, loading docks and continuous motor flows”. That makes elevated links essential “primary catalysts for neighbourhood walkability”. A well-placed link, “completely restructures how residents navigate between commercial, residential and cultural anchors,” she said. Others in academia agree. “In a dense urban fabric like Kowloon Bay, localised interventions like the new footbridge demonstrate how micro-connections can effectively knit together previously fragmented commercial, residential and civic nodes,” said Yung Yau, professor of Lingnan University’s Department of Sociology and Social Policy. Huang Jianxiang, honorary associate professor at the University of Hong Kong’s Department of Urban Planning and Design, said footbridges, tunnels and interconnected concourses “not only support commercial vitality but also encourage walking and help reduce pedestrian/vehicle conflicts and traffic accidents”. Choi highlights Hong Kong’s most famous elevated networks as proof of concept. The Central-Mid-Levels Escalator “began as a transit solution” but “transformed an entire hillside into a vibrant, human-scaled ecosystem,” Choi said. Its success, on her reading, lies in what it does not do: pedestrians moving between the CBD and residential blocks pass by scenes of ordinary street life instead of being sealed inside their estate’s podium. Hong Kong did not invent such systems, Huang said, “but it has become an outstanding example of how an extensive, interconnected pedestrian network can function within a dense urban environment”. However, experts caution that lifting pedestrians off the pavement does come with trade-offs. Yau warned that siphoning foot traffic upwards can drain street-level businesses and leave mobility-impaired residents overly reliant on lifts during severe weather. To counteract this, Huang suggests footbridges double as inclusive public spaces hosting informal gatherings, while Choi advocates for ground-level shade canopies and open-air stairs to keep both tiers active. Ultimately, as the Amoy Footbridge opens to daily commuters, its success will depend on how naturally it integrates into the community’s routine. As Huang noted, “Once the physical infrastructure is in place, the success of a footbridge depends as much on its management as on its design.”

title: ‘Baby boss’ in China wins hearts after clip shows him playfully courting customers outside eatery
description: Expat diner praises boy’s ‘five-star service’ for setting the table, gifting drinks, and encouraging slow eating.
content: A Chinese boy with a remarkable talent for engaging customers at his family’s restaurant in central China has gone viral, drawing entertaining reactions from both domestic and international netizens. The four-and-a-half-year-old child gained overnight fame after a Serbian expat in China posted a video of him being approached in front of a diner in Huangshan, Anhui province, on his account @saitie, on September 12. In the video, the young boy skilfully attracted customers in front of his family’s Anhui cuisine restaurant. He exhibited no stage fright while interacting with a foreigner, politely asking: “Would you like to dine in our restaurant?” Initially, Saitie declined, as it was 3pm and he had already eaten. The boy took the rejection in stride, quickly turning to engage another passer-by. Without hesitation, he responded “yes” when Saitie asked if he was the restaurant’s “little boss.” When queried about his recommended dish, he enthusiastically replied: “Anything you want.” The kind-hearted vlogger eventually stepped into the restaurant and ordered fried rice, wanting to avoid disappointing the little boy.
