He remarked that the boy provided him with “five-star service,” preparing the tableware, offering a complimentary soft drink, and gently reminding him to eat slowly with the small bowl, saying: “If you eat this rice too fast, isn’t there nothing left to eat?” Saitie expressed his admiration for this “baby boss,” praising him as kind and adorable. The video attracted 260,000 likes on a Chinese short video platform and was also shared on an international platform under the account @sj_china_vlog, where it received 50,000 reposts. Viewers responded with heartwarming and humorous comments. “Bro got rejected and instantly locked in on another target,” one commented, to which Saitie humorously replied: “He mastered the art of rejection.” “He is the one who drops his parents off at work and then goes to school. He doesn’t cry when getting a shot; he holds the doctor’s hand to comfort them,” joked another. A netizen in China praised Saitie as well, stating: “Saitie is a lovely person who dined at the restaurant even when he wasn’t hungry, just to avoid disappointing the boy. He also tolerates the boy playing at his table.” The boy’s mother later responded on the restaurant’s social media account, clarifying that they had never taught him how to engage customers; he learned it from observing adults. She explained that his motivation came from wanting to be “a little adult” and help his family. He would offer complimentary drinks and buns to customers and assist in setting their tables. The mother also commented on the boy’s adeptness at handling rejection, noting that he sometimes invited those who turned him down to “come back tomorrow.” She expressed her gratitude for Saitie’s kindness towards her son.

title: ByteDance’s AI-enhanced short-drama app eclipses China’s Netflix rivals combined
description: Acknowledging format’s popularity, award-winning director Jia Zhangke defends short dramas as valid art that can move audiences.
content: TikTok parent ByteDance has scored another hit in China with Hongguo, an artificial intelligence-powered short-drama platform. Launched in 2023, Hongguo quickly became a household name by riding China’s short-drama boom. A surge in AI-generated content propelled it past some of the country’s biggest professional streaming platforms, while iterations of AI-animated dramas – using AI video models including ByteDance’s Seedance – gave it further lift. Hongguo has overtaken the country’s four largest long-form video streaming apps including iQiyi – often dubbed China’s Netflix – in daily viewers as its free shows and expanding supply of AI-generated content transform competition in the online entertainment sector. Hongguo’s daily active users (DAU) reached 168 million in July, more than double from a year earlier, according to mobile analytics service QuestMobile’s data cited in a research note by Japanese securities firm Nomura in August. That exceeded the aggregated DAUs of Tencent Video, iQiyi, Alibaba Group Holding’s Youku and Mango TV apps – four of the largest long-form streaming platforms in China – according to Nomura. Whether a story runs for two hours or two minutes is a question of form, not pedigree Jia Zhangke, film director Hongguo’s rapid growth underscores ByteDance’s tightening grip on Chinese consumers’ attention, while traditional streaming platforms struggle with declining viewership. Total monthly time spent on Hongguo jumped 157 per cent year on year in July at the expense of its four long-form rivals that recorded various declines on the mobile front. Monthly time spent on iQiyi fell 27 per cent, while Youku posted the steepest drop at 47 per cent. Tencent Video and Mango TV recorded declines of 31 per cent and 24 per cent, respectively. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Hongguo lets users watch complete short drama series for free, generating revenue from advertising and sharing part of the proceeds with creators. Its rise comes despite long-standing criticism of short dramas for formulaic plots, uneven production quality and an emphasis on instant gratification. But as the format draws larger audiences, it is also seemingly gaining recognition from established filmmakers as an alternative form of storytelling. Chinese director Jia Zhangke, whose films have won prizes at international festivals, said in a recent social media post that whether a story ran for two hours or two minutes was “a question of form, not pedigree”. Jia added: “If two minutes move people, then they have done their job. If two hours fail to, they cannot apply for extra time.” Eight of the 10 titles on Hongguo’s popularity chart on Monday were AI-generated dramas or animated series, according to a check done by the SCMP. A separate Hongguo app focused on AI-animated series reached 16 million DAUs in July, up 37 per cent from June, Nomura said. Five ByteDance services ranked among China’s 20 most-used apps by monthly time spent in July: Douyin, Douyin Lite, Hongguo, news aggregator Toutiao and online reading platform Fanqie Free Novels. Together, they accounted for 35 per cent of the time users spent on the top 20 apps in July, according to Nomura, highlighting ByteDance’s commanding position in China’s mobile sector. Douyin also surpassed Weixin in monthly time spent for the first time, according to the report.

title: Hong Kong rated Asia’s top financial hub for fourth straight year: report
description: City also ranked third overall in the Global Financial Centres Index as Asian hubs strengthened their positions in the top 10.
content: Hong Kong has retained its status as Asia’s top financial hub for a fourth consecutive edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI), even as many of the world’s leading centres saw their scores slip slightly amid rising geopolitical headwinds. The city also ranked third globally in the 40th edition of the twice-yearly report, released on Wednesday amid a remarkably tight race at the top of global finance. Hong Kong scored 756, just one point behind London and a point ahead of Singapore. New York topped the index at 761. All four centres recorded lower scores than in the March edition as the conflict in the Middle East overshadowed much of the latest survey period. The index is compiled by Z/Yen Group and the China Development Institute (CDI). Across the index’s five main categories – business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial sector development and reputation – Hong Kong placed ahead of London, ranking first globally for financial sector development. Hong Kong also topped the report’s separate fintech ranking, a position it has now held for several consecutive editions of the report, and led the breakdowns for investment management, insurance and the wider finance sector. “Behind those numbers lies deepening connectivity with the mainland through the Stock, Bond and Wealth Management Connect scheme,” said Yu Peng, a senior researcher at CDI. He said the city remained the world’s premier offshore renminbi centre – handling 70 to 80 per cent of global clearing – and the top cross-border wealth management hub, with total assets under management touching US$2.95 trillion at the end of 2025. The ranking stands as Hong Kong’s stock exchange rides a rebound in initial public offerings. Hong Kong led the world in IPO fundraising last year and trailed only the Nasdaq in the first half of 2026, driven by a wave of listings by mainland Chinese technology companies. The report arrived as Hong Kong rolled out its first-ever five-year blueprint for financial development. The strategy outlines “five major objectives”, including seeking new grounds for economic development and boosting Hong Kong’s international competitiveness. The road map aligns Hong Kong’s financial trajectory with Beijing’s 15th five-year plan, giving the city “an unusually specific mandate” to strengthen its status as an international financial centre while expanding its offshore yuan, asset management and commodity trading sectors, Yu said. Beijing supported this framework in July with a fresh package of financial measures, expanding the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s renminbi funding facility to 500 billion yuan (US$74.54 billion) while raising the annual investment quota for the Southbound Bond Connect scheme from 500 billion yuan to 800 billion yuan. Other Asian financial centres also posted strong results in the GFCI report. Shanghai overtook San Francisco to reach fifth place as its rating rose 11 points – the only gain among the world’s top five centres this round. Shenzhen also advanced, rising one place to eighth – a climb Yu linked to its deepening technology-finance ecosystem and the Qianhai cooperation platform with Hong Kong. Asia-Pacific hubs now account for six of the global top 10 in the index. Tokyo posted the sharpest rise, climbing four places to sixth, while Seoul moved up one place to seventh. The Asia-Pacific region also saw its average financial rating climb 1.48 per cent, the highest rise recorded for any region and well above the average global gain of 0.8 per cent, the report noted. Despite the broad-based strength, the margins at the top remain thin. “Leadership in this index is contestable and it has to be defended,” Yu said.

title: Malaysian councillor resigns after DAP remarks at Umno assembly
description: In his speech at the Umno assembly, Zaidi claimed DAP feared losing power if Malays and Muslims came together.
content: A Malaysian city councillor has resigned over remarks he made about the Democratic Action Party (DAP) at the recent Umno general assembly. Permatang Pauh Umno division chief Mohd Zaidi Mohd Said’s resignation as a Seberang Perai city councillor took effect on Monday, according to a letter made public by state local government committee chairman Jason H’ng Mooi Lye on Wednesday. In the letter, Zaidi apologised for his remarks during the assembly in Kuala Lumpur on Saturday, where he represented Penang Umno. He acknowledged that as a councillor, he needed to be more careful when expressing views about parties that jointly formed and administered the state government. Zaidi said his remarks could have created a wrong perception of DAP, particularly in the context of cooperation within the Penang government. He said he had considered the matter carefully and decided to take full responsibility for his mistake by resigning. Zaidi stressed that the decision was made voluntarily and without pressure from any party. In his speech at the Umno assembly, Zaidi claimed DAP was uneasy over efforts to bring Malays and Muslims together because the party feared losing political power. He claimed DAP and coalition partner People’s Justice Party (PKR) depended on each other for political power and described Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s cooperation with PKR as a political strategy that would eventually weaken DAP. His speech, however, included praise for Penang Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow. In his resignation letter, he said Chow was a leader who cared about the people’s welfare, valued tolerance and carried out his responsibility in administering the state. H’ng thanked Zaidi for apologising and taking responsibility by stepping down. He said Zaidi’s letter recognised that the state government led by Chow was committed to the people’s welfare, tolerance and responsible administration. H’ng said this showed that the DAP-led Penang government had remained committed to the people’s welfare and the state’s development regardless of race, religion or background. The resignation comes amid heightened tensions between Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) and federal partner Pakatan Harapan (PH) following a series of pointed remarks at the general assembly. Ahmad Zahid had called for the 16th general election to be held as soon as possible and later challenged those who wanted BN out of the unity government to formally remove it and face the consequences in parliament. He said there were two options if BN was removed from the government: seek a fresh mandate through a general election, or remove it formally and hold a no-confidence vote in the house. His remarks prompted delegates to chant “bubar” (dissolve). Ahmad Zahid had earlier criticised uncertainties in government policies, including the handling of the Budi95 subsidised fuel quota. He questioned the use of the term “Madani government”, saying the administration was formed as a unity government. The remarks drew concern from PH leaders. DAP secretary general Anthony Loke said on Monday that he would propose a PH presidential council meeting to discuss the political developments, saying some statements at the Umno assembly raised concerns over political stability and could affect public and investor confidence. This story was first published by The Star

title: Where a champion Hong Kong barista goes for local comfort food and Italian dishes
description: Hasting Ng shares his favourite restaurants for cart noodles, soup pasta, fine Chinese dining and the flavours of Italy.
content: Barista Hasting Ng owns Blossom, a cafe in Kowloon City, and was crowned global champion at the DaVinci Gourmet Coffee Barista Championship 2025-26. He also curates speciality coffee experiences for Nordic restaurant Finds in Tsim Sha Tsui. He spoke to Andrew Sun. I grew up in Hong Kong and spent several years in the US, so I have lived between two food cultures. That experience has shaped my palate. Still, when it comes to comfort food, nothing replaces the familiar flavours of a cha chaan teng – especially an iced lemon tea and a plate of Hong Kong-style curry, both of which remain constant favourites in my life. Among Asian dishes, cart noodles have long been one of my greatest comforts. Part of their charm lies in their endless possibilities: fish balls, beef brisket, white radish, tofu puffs – each bowl can be tailored to mood and appetite. But beyond variety, cart noodles carry a sense of ease and familiarity. They are the kind of meal that works at any hour, whether it is a casual lunch, a late dinner or a midnight craving. Fei Gor Cart Noodles (Shop 55, Fook Tin Building, 38 Wai Chi Street, Shek Kip Mei. Tel: 2777 3089) is my favourite for this comfort food. Their house-made chilli sauce is one of the best in Hong Kong. La Volta (9 Lan Fong Road, Causeway Bay. Tel: 6978 8800) has become a comfort place. It is chef Roland Schuller’s new Italian home. I have known him since 2019, when he was at Octavium, and I have long admired the way he brings Eastern and Western ingredients into dialogue with one another. That sensibility is expressed beautifully through La Volta’s home-made pasta, antipasti and warm, comforting cocktails. Octavium (8/F, One Chinachem Central, 22 Des Voeux Road, Central. Tel: 2111 9395) still holds a special place in my memory. It is one of my favourite formal dining destinations. Their seasonal menu, imaginative use of fusion ingredients, refined service and excellent wine selection create an experience that feels both polished and alive. When friends visit, I often bring them to Australia Dairy Company (47-49 Parkes Street, Jordan. Tel: 2730 1356) not just for the food but the full local experience. This iconic spot is famous as much for its brisk efficiency as its unapologetic service style. Yet beneath that reputation lies something endearing, even charming. A bowl of soup pasta is surprisingly memorable, especially for visitors encountering local comfort food for the first time. For Chinese cuisine, my first choice remains The Chairman (3/F, The Wellington, 198 Wellington Street, Central. Tel: 2555 2202). It is one of Asia’s most celebrated restaurants for good reason. I always return for dishes such as camphor wood smoked Magang goose and stewed pork belly with preserved vegetable claypot rice. For a vibrant taste of Nordic-infused dining, Finds (1/F, The Luxe Manor, 39 Kimberley Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2522 9318) stands out as an iconic destination. Working together to merge distinct coffee craft with their newly launched “Afternoon Delight” menu has been an inspiring creative journey, offering guests a fresh perspective on contemporary cafe culture in their hotel venue. Beyond Hong Kong, travelling to Italy remains one of my favourite culinary journeys. I am drawn not only to pasta and pizza, but also to the country’s deeper traditions of fermentation, from balsamic vinegar to anchovy essence. Last year, I had the chance to dine at Osteria Francescana (Via Stella 22, Modena. Tel: +39 059 223912), chef Massimo Bottura’s legendary restaurant. More than a fine-dining meal, each course felt like a narrative, composed with precision, imagination and emotion. It is the kind of experience that stays with you long after the last bite.

title: South Korean killer’s drone escape from Philippine prison foiled by test footage
description: Convicted killer Park Wang-yeol reportedly spent some US$74,000 on his planned drone-assisted prison break.
content: A South Korean crime lord convicted of murder in the Philippines reportedly planned to escape prison by strapping himself to a drone – until his own accomplice’s rehearsal footage gave the game away. Park Wang-yeol, 47, was sentenced in 2022 to 60 years behind bars for the killing of three South Koreans in a sugar cane field outside Bacolod City in 2016, a crime that earned him the nickname “sugar cane field killer”. The drone-assisted escape plot was planned for earlier this year, in the weeks before his temporary repatriation to South Korea in March to face charges of importing 4.8kg (10.5lbs) of methamphetamine, Korean broadcaster JTBC reported on Monday. This was not Park’s first escape attempt. He had already escaped custody twice, in 2017 and again in 2019 while being transported from a court hearing. He reportedly spent about 100 million won (US$74,000) on preparations for the latest attempt, including buying a drone capable of carrying up to 75kg (165lbs). His associates had been banking on New Bilibid Prison’s apparent lack of signal-jamming technology to avoid detection, repeatedly rehearsing the flight at a site nearby. But it was one of those practice flights, caught on camera by a passer-by, that ultimately let the cat out of the bag. Philippine media initially broadcast the footage as a light-hearted human interest story before authorities linked it to Park. According to JTBC, Park had planned a simpler escape at first involving a prison transport vehicle being ambushed – with weapons already obtained for this purpose – until he switched to the more audacious drone plot. “A prison escape by someone like me should be on this scale,” an inmate who spoke to the broadcaster quoted him as saying. While held at New Bilibid Prison, Park is believed to have lived in relative comfort, paying the equivalent of 6 million won a month for a private, air-conditioned cell with a television and a mobile phone, according to the Asia Business Daily. From prison, he has been accused of running a drug ring smuggling large quantities of narcotics into South Korea via Telegram, working with accomplices in the Philippines to distribute the goods, Reuters reported. Escapes from Philippine prisons have declined in recent years, down from a high of 81 in 2012, when the Philippine Star newspaper reported there were 60 to 70 escapees per year on average, citing Bureau of Corrections and National Bureau of Investigation figures. Last year, at least 10 prisoners escaped, including a group who overpowered a guard and seized his firearm to flee a prison in Batangas province on July 28, the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported.

title: News helicopter crashes in Los Angeles, killing 3
description: NBC4 news chopper comes down in Chatsworth neighbourhood while covering a fatal bus crash.
content: An NBC local news helicopter crashed in the Chatsworth area of Los Angeles on Tuesday evening, killing three people, NBC said during a live television broadcast. NBC Los Angeles anchors on air identified the aircraft as their NewsChopper 4 helicopter. “We’ve been telling ‌you that we’ve been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper 4 went down just before 7 o’clock tonight in Chatsworth,” NBC anchor Colleen Williams said. Five patients were assessed at the scene, with three pronounced dead and two others taken to hospital, the Los Angeles Fire Department said at a news conference shortly after 9.30pm ⁠local time. At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the car park next to ‌a commercial building, said the fire department. It was not immediately clear whether the other two who were killed were on the ground or inside the aircraft. The NBC anchors did not say how many ‌people had been on board the network’s helicopter. The helicopter crash occurred after a vehicle collision in the area ⁠involving a Los Angeles ⁠Metro bus and a passenger vehicle earlier on Tuesday that killed at least two people. According to media reports, several TV news helicopters were in the area ‌reporting on the bus collision, when the NBC helicopter crashed. Reports said the helicopter crashed and burst into flames near a storage building in the San Fernando Valley, as ‌news crews were ‌covering the bus crash. At least four cars and two storage containers caught fire after the helicopter crashed, the fire ‌department said. The fire was quickly put out as more than 70 firefighters responded to the crash, the department said in its ⁠briefing. The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will investigate the crash, the fire department said. NBC said the helicopter ⁠was operated by Angel City Air, which is affiliated with the station. Angel City Air did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was “devastated” by the loss of life in ‌the helicopter crash and the ‌bus collision in Chatsworth. California Governor Gavin Newsom also shared his condolences and said “our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family”. NBC, owned by Comcast, and the Los Angeles Fire Department did not immediately respond to emailed requests for further details. Los Angeles, America’s second biggest city, is a competitive and crowded media market, where TV stations compete aggressively for stories. Many of them routinely make use of aerial coverage, sending helicopters into the city’s already busy skies to cover everything from fires to dramatic car chases. There are usually two people on board a news media helicopter – the pilot and the reporter-camera operator who frequently reports live from the sky. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: G20 summit: US scraps coal and gas power plant limits that hoped to curb climate change
description: Environmental groups say it’s ‘a gift to the fossil fuel industry’ and a ‘dark day’ as the policies protected people from a destabilising planet.
content:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has tossed out the limits on carbon emissions from coal and gas-fired power plants, the latest in a wave of dismantling regulations aimed at curbing climate change.
The changes were announced during a meeting of Group of 20 (G20) energy ministers in Houston, Texas. They roll back measures introduced under former US president Joe Biden – and go further, proposing to stop future regulations over the power sector, which accounts for roughly a quarter of the US’ greenhouse gas emissions.
“For over 15 years, the Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy,” US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement.
“The Trump Administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” he added.
Environmental groups have vowed to sue, describing it as a dark day for policies that protect people from the ravages of climate change and a gift to the fossil fuel industry.
The news comes amid growing signs of Earth’s climate system destabilising, setting the planet up for more frequent and destructive extreme weather events.
August was the hottest month ever recorded around the world, and the United States just experienced its hottest recorded summer. The main driver of global heating is the burning of fossil fuels, and this year human-caused warming is stacking on top of a historically intense El Nino weather pattern.
“They’re propping up fossil fuel industry profits and completely sidelining people’s health and well-being,” Rachel Cleetus from the Union of Concerned Scientists, a non-profit science advocacy organisation based in the United States, told reporters.
“The EPA has deserted its mission entirely, and they’re doing it in a way that’s cruel. They’re gleefully taking credit for it.”
The administration has repealed the 2024 Biden-era standards set under the Clean Air Act, the United States’ primary federal air quality law, intended to control greenhouse gas emissions from existing coal plants and new gas plants.
The rules required a reduction of up to 90 per cent in carbon dioxide pollution over time and would have required chimney carbon capture technology to achieve that goal. But in its now-finalised rule, the EPA has asserted that these standards were impossible to meet and the deadlines were too tight.
The second part of the package is a proposed rule making a broader statutory argument – that the EPA does not have the authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector at all, and that even if it did have the authority, doing so would be futile because it would not meaningfully address global climate change.
It builds on the US government’s February decision to overturn the 2009 Endangerment Finding, the scientific determination that greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare.
The agency said that the latest repeal would save US$310 billion (HK$2.4 trillion) while the proposed rule would save a further US$370 million (HK$2.9 billion) – figures that critics have voiced scepticism towards and vowed to examine.
Meredith Hankins, a legal expert at the US-based international environmental advocacy group Natural Resources Defence Council, told Agence France-Presse that the actions had contradictory legal justifications.
They noted that the technical repeal, at least in the draft phase, stated that the EPA had the authority to regulate greenhouse emissions but found the Biden administration had gone about it the wrong way.
“We’ll have to look at the final text of the rule,” Hankins said. “But I think on its face you can see the contradictions. So I’m certainly looking forward to seeing them in court.”
Trump often calls the concept of human-induced climate change “a hoax” and his policy rollbacks have included withdrawing the United States once more from the Paris climate accord and eliminating greenhouse gas standards for vehicle tailpipe emissions.
“Our government is ignoring the reality all around us that people are feeling every day of the impacts of climate change, and just putting their heads in the sand and saying, ‘We don’t care, it’s not our problem, next generation, figure it out yourselves,’” said Hankins.

title: Investors prepare for ‘super-central-bank week’ as US rate increase appears done deal
description: Traders are bracing for central bank decisions in the US, the UK and Japan and are weighing whether a Fed rate increase marks one-off move or new cycle.
content: With a US interest rate increase almost a done deal, investors are now trying to figure out whether it would be a one-off move or the start of a fresh tightening cycle, while also bracing for a borrowing-cost increase in Japan, which is highly likely and may jolt capital flows. As the odds of a 25 basis-point rate increase at the US Federal Reserve’s policy meeting on Thursday have risen to 92 per cent, stock traders have shifted the focus to whether the world’s biggest central banks would deliver further increases. A one-off increase may be interpreted as dovish, or even positive for equities, with the move helping to restore the Fed’s credibility and showing chair Kevin Warsh’s commitment to reining in inflation. If the Fed signals more rate increases to come, stocks may face severe challenges, with a mix of stretched valuations amid a persistent oil crisis. “A one-and-done outcome would allow the Fed to show that it is responding to inflation, respecting the message from markets and acting independently despite political pressure,” said Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “It would also take some of the guesswork out of the remaining meetings this year.” “The surprise risk may no longer be the increase itself. It may be anything in the guidance suggesting that one move will not be enough,” he added. Hong Kong and mainland China stocks have barely budged this week, as investors refrain from making big bets in a week packed with rate decisions in the US, the UK and Japan. The benchmarks in the US have dropped slightly for the week to trade near their record highs, reflecting optimism that the world’s largest economy is not set for a fresh cycle of monetary tightening. The Fed’s September rate decision meeting has drawn significant attention from investors, who have been navigating through a combination of soaring US Treasury yields, oil rising above US$100 a barrel and pressure from the White House to lower borrowing costs. The rate decision is also a test of whether Warsh would preserve the Fed’s independence after signalling it would prioritise policy to tackle inflation at the Jackson Hole symposium last month. While some institutions, including Macro Risk Advisors, predicted that the S&P 500 would respond to the Fed rate increase with a 10 per cent decline, Citigroup said that the bull trend would remain intact because of the resilience of the US economy. Historical data showed that global stocks initially wobbled at the start of a Fed rate-increase cycle and rose in the following six to 12 months, with the US market outperforming and value stocks beating growth names, Citigroup said. “It is not the first Fed increase that ends equity bull markets, although it does inject near-term volatility,” said David Groman, a strategist at the US bank. Japan’s policy-rate decision on Friday also takes centre stage, with the Bank of Japan widely expected to raise the benchmark borrowing cost by a quarter of a percentage point to a three-decade high of 1.25 per cent. Swiss private bank Julius Baer said it expected Japan to deliver three more hikes in December, March and July. The normalisation of monetary policy in Japan risks upending the yen-funded carry trade, by which investors borrow the cheaper Japanese currency to invest in other high-yield assets, such as technology stocks in the US and South Korea. The set-up may inject more volatility into equities, with investors selling risk assets to close out carry-trade positions. About 80 per cent of the Asian fund managers surveyed by Bank of America expected a rate increase in Japan on Friday, which would reduce the possibility of an intervention to support the yen.

title: Japanese monks embrace material world to raise cash as donations shrink
description: Temple upkeep costs are soaring while Japan’s Buddhist population has dropped about 14 per cent in the last two decades.
content: Koukyo Yoneta, a fifth-generation Buddhist priest in a small town in Japan’s Hokkaido, was struggling to keep up with the maintenance needs of his century-old temple, so he chose a path that would have been unthinkable for his predecessors – rather than wait for his congregation to give money they do not have, he invested what they had already donated. The move paid off. Within two years, his portfolio of US treasuries, Japanese real estate investment trusts and stocks including BYD and Hyundai Motor returned more than 10 per cent annually, helping to cover part of the roughly 25 million yen (US$160,000) in needed repairs. The extra money even allowed him to expand the renovations beyond the original plan. Having previously worked in retail sales at Daiwa Securities Group, Yoneta is an unusually finance-savvy priest but is also part of a growing wave of temple owners turning to financial markets to make ends meet. Costs for the upkeep of the ornate wooden buildings are soaring while the country’s Buddhist population has dropped about 14 per cent in the last two decades as elderly adherents die and younger generations in larger cities lose their ties to religious practices. “I’m just so thankful that the investments performed well,” said the 46-year-old, who inherited the Kongo-ji temple from his father in 2018 after leaving his job in finance and training as a monk. “With the funeral business shrinking, more and more temples will find they can’t just rely on donations to meet their funding needs; they will have to build up reserves and invest those funds.” The shrinking number of followers is hitting temples’ finances. About half bring in less than 4 million yen per year, according to a 2021 survey of 7,000 temples by one of the largest Buddhist groups, Jodo Shinshu Hongwanji-ha. The situation is particularly severe in rural areas, where it is common for monks to oversee multiple temples while also working day jobs like schoolteachers or civil servants. Moral dilemma Traditionally, funerals and maintaining graves have helped sustain temples as bereaved families would pay for more elaborate ceremonies and prayers. During the Covid-19 pandemic, people began spending less on funeral rituals and the trend has continued, particularly as inflation has increased households’ daily costs. Some temples that are popular with tourists charge entrance fees, but most lack other means. The need to cover higher costs through price hikes or investments poses a moral dilemma for some monks, whose religious principles call for detachment from greed. Daian-ji temple in Nara prefecture still holds most of its assets in cash, with around 10 per cent now allocated to foreign-currency denominated insurance products, which earn higher interest returns. Their investment style is “purely defensive” to avoid any conflict with the religion’s teachings, according to the deputy priest Yusho Kono. “There is an inherent contradiction in our position,” Kono said. “In principle, monks should not engage in profit-making activities. But if we do not take any action now, the temple could cease to exist.” Production costs for some of Daian-ji’s traditional silken amulets, which visitors buy to guard against misfortune or to bring good luck, have surged in the last two years. Monks should not engage in profit-making activities. But if we do not take any action now, the temple could cease to exist Yusho Kono, Daian-ji temple deputy priest Shifting attitudes among priests underscore the strain that persistent inflation is placing on traditional institutions long accustomed to stable prices. Although Japan’s consumer price inflation has fallen below the central bank’s 2 per cent target, thanks to a series of subsidies, rising prices are continuing to disrupt social and financial practices shaped by decades of deflation. Rising costs Issues surrounding surging living costs are a major political issue for the Sanae Takaichi administration. Opinion polls show her approval rating hovering near its lowest level after 11 months in office, after she was seen by voters to be concentrating too much on less pressing issues than the cost-of-living crunch. Temples’ limited ability to charge adherents more for services strengthens a case for asset management, according to Tsuyoshi Kawata, a senior researcher at SMBC Nikko Securities’ corporate investment strategies department, who published a study on asset management by religious organisations in 2023. “When the overall market is shrinking, raising prices is not really an easy option,” Kawata said. “Leaving cash sitting idle is probably no longer an option either. They would want to use whatever means they can to increase income, even if only slightly.” For some temples, returning to financial markets also means overcoming painful lessons from the past. In 2013, the Koyasan Shingon-shu sect was embroiled in a financial ordeal after reporting unrealised losses from its exposure to structured bonds. The sect declined an interview request, saying they were considering revising their asset management strategy. Even so, rising bond yields following the end of negative interest rates offer comfortable investment opportunities for risk-averse monks. Soto-shu, a Buddhist sect overseeing around 15,000 temples nationwide, has been taking advantage of higher yields. Of the 13 billion yen it manages across eight accounts, around 10 per cent is now invested in Japanese government bonds that it plans to hold to maturity, while another 2 per cent is invested in debt issued by the Japan International Cooperation Agency to finance development in emerging economies. Religious groups, schools and other non-profit organisations are collectively becoming a buying force of fixed-income products. Non-profit organisations, including schools and religious institutions, held roughly 5 trillion yen of corporate bonds as of March, about double the amount in 2023, according to Bank of Japan figures. Holdings of Japanese government bonds also increased to 2.9 trillion yen from 2.5 trillion yen over the same period. At Kongo-ji temple in Hokkaido, Yoneta hopes his investments will help fund future repairs as revenue continues to decline. At the same time, he is trying to safeguard the future by regularly hosting investment seminars for adherents at the temple, building a support network that the temple might one day be able to rely on. “The days when temples and their priests enjoyed a privileged status are completely over,” Yoneta said. “How temples plan their finances and manage their assets is becoming an issue we simply cannot afford to ignore.”

title: Student Academy Awards 2026: Oscars body champions emerging film talent at TIFF
description: Hosted at the Toronto International Film Festival and supported by Rolex, the awards connect a new generation of filmmakers with the global industry.
content: The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences (AMPAS) is best known as the organisation behind the Oscars – the entertainment world’s most prestigious awards – but for over 50 years the entity has also been supporting young talent through the Student Academy Awards (SAA). Established in 1972, the competition invites college and university students from around the world to submit films in four categories: animation, documentary, live action narrative and alternative/experimental. The award ceremony normally takes place in Los Angeles, where the Academy is based, but in 2024 it was held in London – in partnership with the BFI London Film Festival – and last year in New York during the New York Film Festival. The 53rd edition took place at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), where students from countries such as France, the UK, India and China presented their work and got the opportunity to experience North America’s most important film festival. “This is all part of the academy’s drive to be a more global organisation,” said Bill Kramer, CEO of AMPAS, in an interview in Toronto, adding that holding the event at festivals such as TIFF gives students the chance to go to screenings, take part in panel talks, learn about the industry, and network with fellow students and filmmakers. For each category, the Academy selects three works to be awarded a bronze, silver and gold prize. This year alone, the Academy received 2972 submissions from around the world. Among the gold prize recipients was Lei He, who won in the alternative/experimental category. Titled Drifting, her black-and-white short combines fiction and non-fiction to explore the life of a miner in Shanxi Province, where she grew up. The winner of the narrative category was The Dragon Letter by Stanzin Jigmet from Ladakh, a city in India near Tibet, while the gold prize in the documentary section went to Lara Dihmis, a New York University graduate who in The Lost People of Petra explored the plight of the Bdoul tribe in Jordan. “As an up-and-coming filmmaker, being here has been the most incredible opportunity,” said Dihmis before the ceremony. “To see all the actors and amazing directors, producers and meeting my fellow award winners has been very inspiring and has given me a real boost to want to be on an even bigger stage and do bigger things.” Given that past recipients of the award include household names such as Spike Lee, Robert Zemeckis and Trey Parker, Dihmis has a point. As part of the programme, all the winning films are also eligible to compete for an actual Oscar in the animated short film, live-action short film or documentary short film category. At various panels and talks, the students got the chance to ask questions to industry professionals about topics such as the rise of AI, how to build a community – especially in niche categories such as documentary filmmaking – the importance of storytelling and even practical matters such as how to get funding for their projects. TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey was thrilled to have the awards in Toronto this year. The festival is known for championing independent filmmakers and for its global perspective. This year’s sleeper hit Obsession, for instance, premiered at TIFF in 2025, before becoming an unexpected global blockbuster. “If there is talent there, if there’s an original voice, and if it continues to be an original voice, if a filmmaker keeps making work that’s pushing the boundaries or his own boundaries as an artist, then I think institutions like ours, have the privilege of supporting those artists by presenting their work,” said Bailey in an interview on the day of the event. The night before the SAA awards ceremony, Bailey attended the TIFF Tribute Awards, which began in 2019. The awards, which like the SAA are supported by watchmaker Rolex, honour individuals who have made significant contributions to cinema. At this year’s ceremony, A-list stars such as Helen Mirren, Penélope Cruz, Seth Rogen and Isabelle Huppert took the stage alongside lesser-known creatives like Polish cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz and director Siân Heder. The SAA and the TIFF Tribute Awards couldn’t be more different from each other but two topics that constantly came up during thank-you speeches – whether they were given by Oscar winners like Coda director Heder or a student filmmaker exploring her lack of sex drive in a tongue-in-cheek short video – were the vital role of storytelling and a new-found yearning for sharing collective experiences amid the rise of streaming networks. During the festival, TIFF Lightbox, the cultural centre where many screenings take place, was packed with fans from all walks of life lining up to catch screenings, a clear sign that the moviegoing experience is here to stay. Over the summer, blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day and smaller productions made on a shoestring like the aforementioned Obsession and Backrooms, broke records at the box office. “We want people to go back to theatres. We want people to experience cinema in a theatrical setting,” said Kramer. “It is where filmmakers create their art form to be seen.” “Young people are driving that interest, whether it is films that are about Gen Z or films that are about queer characters or films that reflect a kind of an identity that audiences are craving,” added Bailey. “That’s the other thing that’s driving this, not simply big spectacle films, as great as they are. It’s also films that feel very intimate and personal to people who haven’t had the opportunity to experience them together.” Earlier this year, the Academy launched the Academy Marquee Theater List, which will recognise the most exceptional movie theatres around the world and their efforts to preserve and champion the movie-going experience. In spite of young people’s new-found love for going to the movies, however, filmmakers with a different point of view – both established ones and emerging ones – still struggle to find funding for their work. Luxury companies have started to play a key role in supporting them, from Saint Laurent funding award-winning movies such as Emilia Pérez through its Saint Laurent Productions platform to A24’s recently announced partnership with Dior and Chanel’s long-time support of female filmmakers. “Brands understand the value of storytelling to reach audiences and the power of filmmaking and cinematic storytelling to reach people in a very profound way so I don’t think it’s a bad thing,” says Kramer about luxury houses’ involvement in filmmaking. “It’s interesting and it’s not new. You’re seeing a lot more of it happening now because I think this is the world that we’re living in; it’s about visual storytelling in a way that we have never seen. So to me, it’s logical.” As part of its Perpetual Arts Initiative, Rolex has been supporting cinema and the arts for more than five decades and has partnered with AMPAS since 2017. Filmmakers such as James Cameron and Martin Scorsese and actors like Leonardo DiCaprio are Rolex testimonees. The watchmaker, however, doesn’t get directly involved in filmmakers’ work nor does it expect its products to be featured in their movies. Rolex’s focus is on transmission and mentorship, as Bailey explained while talking about his long-time relationship with the brand. “I’ve been fortunate enough to sit on a couple of juries, to identify protégés and mentors,” said Bailey. “You’ve got an established filmmaker like Spike Lee or Zhang Yimou, who, through Rolex’s resources, is able to actually find international filmmakers at the beginning of their career, and they spend two years together. This is a remarkable programme to elevate a younger filmmaker but also the mentor and [connect] them with a new generation. Brands don’t have to do that but when they do, it really makes a difference.”

title: ‘Red line’: Saudi coalition accuses Houthis of targeting Mecca with drone
description: Drone intercepted heading towards the Saudi holy city, but Houthi official rejects claim as a ‘worn-out lie’.
content: The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis accused the rebels on Wednesday of targeting Islam’s holy city Mecca, sparking outrage across the Muslim world and deepening the conflict roiling the region. Fresh fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government has dragged in Riyadh, with the Houthis declaring a maritime blockade on the kingdom and targeting its ships in the Red Sea. Last week’s lightning offensive saw the group seize control of the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for Saudi oil exports as the wider Middle East war chokes off the Strait of Hormuz strategic shipping route. The Houthis swiftly rejected as a “lie” Riyadh’s report that it shot down a drone from the rebels heading towards the Saudi city of Mecca, which attracts millions of pilgrims each year. “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone,” Hazem al-Assad from the Houthis’ politburo said on social media. “I saw a few people panicking, running to the window to see what happened,” a Mecca resident who asked for anonymity said. “I think the alarm system creates panic. Life is normal in Mecca and there have been previous incidents in Mecca so this isn’t the first one.” The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a “red line”. “The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the Terrorist Houthi Militia,” the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on social media. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation – a bloc of 57 Muslim countries – condemned the “heinous” attack. In a statement on Wednesday, Arab League secretary general Nabil Fahmy said “compromising the security of Mecca and the sanctity of Islamic holy sites is a matter of extreme gravity”. Later on Wednesday, the rebels claimed, without offering evidence, that they shot down an F-15 fighter jet operated by the Saudi-led coalition over the central province of Marib. Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree did not say when the incident occurred, and the claim could not be independently verified. Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and across swathes of the kingdom’s south, which borders Yemen. The alerts, including the first one issued in Mecca since the Middle East war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom’s south. Fighting flared in July when the Houthis, who have for years controlled swathes of northern Yemen, launched a large-scale offensive against Yemeni government forces. The conflict in the Arabian Peninsula’s poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the United Nations. Yemen’s permanent representative at the UN, Abdullah al-Saadi, said Yemenis were fighting to restore “national institutions across every inch of their land”, and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis. Yemen’s plea came as Saudi Arabia and Egypt called for free navigation in the Red Sea following the Houthis’ offensive in the vital waterway. De facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi called on Tuesday for “ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation” through the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden, the Egyptian presidency said. The revival of Yemen’s civil war, dormant since 2022, has left Riyadh rushing to respond. US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but was turned down. The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb except for Saudi vessels. Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers. Disruption in the strait could cause Egypt to feel the pinch too, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, upon which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue. Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza. On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab el-Mandeb was closed, saying it would be “catastrophic for the entire world”. The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world’s leading crude exporter, helping push global prices above the US$100-a-barrel threshold. The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks “firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom”, and would take “all necessary operational measures to deter this … hostile and extremist approach”. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Tuesday that Saudi Arabia launched 52 air strikes on Yemen over the past 24 hours, accusing it of targeting civilian sites, including schools and bridges. But Riyadh’s strikes have failed to reverse the group’s gains. A US military task force is working to enhance intelligence sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official said on Tuesday. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Chinese scientists build world’s smallest CT scanner, weighing just 6kg
description: Compact and portable device can be used to analyse fossils and archaeological relics in the field, developer says.
content: Chinese researchers have developed the world’s smallest CT scanner, a portable device designed to produce images of tiny fossils and archaeological relics. Built by the Shandong province-based Rayim, the Xtomo-Cube is about the size of a desktop speaker and weighs just 6kg (13.2lbs). “The device can be held in one hand and is the world’s smallest and lightest CT system, earning it the nickname ‘palm-sized CT scanner’,” Liu Baodong, a senior engineer at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and general manager of Rayim, told the Science and Technology Daily on Monday. The machine had a spatial resolution of 80 micrometres, roughly the width of a human hair, and could analyse objects from snail shells to medicine capsules, Liu said. It consumed only about 200 watts, which meant it could be powered by an ordinary portable power bank during fieldwork, he said. Liu added that all the machine’s key components – including its X-ray source, rotating platform and detector – were developed and manufactured in China. The previous record holder for smallest CT machine was a German-developed device that weighed 19kg, according to the Science and Technology Daily. CT, short for computed tomography, uses X-rays taken from multiple angles to produce images of an object or organism’s internal structure. A computer then combines the images into a detailed 3D model. In 1971, the first clinical CT scanner was used on a patient in London to reveal a brain tumour. Developed by British engineer Godfrey Hounsfield, the 3-metre-long (9.8 feet) machine could only scan a patient’s head and took about five minutes to generate a pair of two-dimensional images. Today, hospitals around the world use CT scanners routinely to spot tumours, internal bleeding and other injuries or conditions. They are also used to peer inside fossils, archaeological finds and industrial components without damaging them. Despite their expanding uses, CT scanners have remained big, heavy machines. A typical hospital scanner is roughly 2 metres tall and wide and weighs around two tonnes (2.2 tons), while some industrial systems are even larger and can weigh several tonnes. “There are probably more types of CT scanners than cars – sports cars, trucks, you name it,” Liu said. “This one is the compact car of the CT world. It’s not meant to scan everything; it’s designed to look inside small things.” He said the challenge was to squeeze the X-ray source, detector and rotating platform into a four-litre package while maintaining fine imaging detail. Its small size and relatively low-energy X-rays could also make it useful in university classrooms and research labs. Unlike many commercial CT systems, its settings and raw imaging data were open to users, allowing students and researchers to experiment with how CT images are collected, reconstructed and improved, according to Liu.

title: SOTY 25/26: Sportsperson finalist balances study and sport
description: Chinese International School alum Rosalyn Chan Hau-ching has been proudly representing Hong Kong since age 11.
content:
On a tennis court, Rosalyn Chan Hau-ching is alert and adaptive, never settling into one rhythm for too long.
That quality has defined the 18-year-old’s path from an energetic child in Hong Kong, who tried almost every sport, to a three-time consecutive National Junior champion – a local record. Now, the former Chinese International School pupil is a student-athlete at the University of Chicago in the United States.
After trying sports like football, track and table tennis, she got hooked on tennis: “I suppose the variety and difficulty one can experience in the game of tennis particularly drew me in as a kid,” she recalled.
By the age of six, she was training four or five times a week and competing in local events. At 11, she was invited to represent Hong Kong overseas. She held her own at a tournament in Japan, but the results were secondary.
“More memorable than the results were the memories I had and the connections I made with players from other countries. It really helped me recognise the opportunities I was given representing Hong Kong,” she said.
“It’s nerve-racking to compete for something bigger than just myself, but I take pride in competing for Hong Kong,” she added.
Balancing that responsibility with the demands of the International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma required discipline.
“The first year and a half of the IB, heavy with long-term projects, tested me. But I was prepared by my years of experience as a student-athlete,” she said.
“I reached out for extra support, completed work while travelling and treated every training session as high value rather than high volume,” Chan explained.
“I recognised the value of quality over quantity, cutting down moderate but long sessions into shorter yet more productive practices.”
Calendars, to-do lists and an unapologetic willingness to ask for help became her quiet weapons.
“When you aren’t afraid to ask for help, many – if not most – are willing to support you,” she said. “I paid close attention in lessons so that catch-up work was minimised, dialled training down during the most intense academic stretches, then ramped it back up.”
The result surprised her: strong final IB results alongside continued progress on the court.
In 2025, she won four international titles, including a doubles crown she earned with a friend from Thailand at a higher-level J60 ITF event. It marked a personal high.
“It gave me confidence in my ability to compete at an international level, even against full-time players from other countries,” she said.
“It showed me my potential to continue improving and going even further in the future. I could see how frequently competing at an international level against high-level athletes improved my physical skill set as well as my mental approach.”
Last year, Chan also levelled a 40-year local record by capturing the National Junior Championships three years running.
Her hunger to win fuelled grit but also led to extreme pressure and stress not to lose.
She shifted her strategy when she began simply trying to play her best, point after point.
“This approach took off a lot of pressure and benefited my performance overall ... Being more focused on playing each point well instead of the score was a major contributor,” she said.
“As cheesy as it sounds, it really is helpful to forget about what has passed and focus on what’s in front of you.”
Competitive sports, Chan said, helped her build resilience and adaptability. She learned to switch to her backup plan when the first tactic failed – an instinct she also applies to analysing a book or navigating a sudden change of plans.
“I now perceive challenges as an opportunity for growth and improvement and to bounce back from setbacks by looking ahead,” she said.
Off the tennis court, Chan has poured her energy into mentoring younger students and community work.
For the past two years, she has shared her student-athlete journey through “OneInchVertical”, a service project in collaboration with the NGO Christian Action, which supports underprivileged children of different ethnicities and backgrounds.
“Sport is always a way for individuals to find a sense of belonging,” Chan said.
One memory stands out for Chan from her volunteering experience. She recalled how at first, the older boys she volunteered with were reluctant to play football with the younger girls. But eventually, “Persistence broke down those barriers until all-inclusive games became the norm. We tried hard to make it work and ultimately broke down the prejudices related to women and girls in sport.”
Chan’s achievements make her a role model for others. She was honoured for her hard work and persistence when she was recognised as a finalist in the Sportsperson category of the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.
This year, Chan began studying economics and biological sciences at the University of Chicago while competing in NCAA Division III tennis.
“My plan is to keep playing competitively and to join community outreach programmes that use sport for education and social mobility,” she said. “I want to encourage younger athletes to pursue both sports and studies rather than sacrifice one [for the other]. Sharing my own story and journey can inspire young student-athletes to balance both.”

title: How will the Okinawa governor’s race result reshape China’s local messaging?
description: Analysts say the election is a reality check for Beijing, which has sought to leverage local opposition to US-Japan military ties.
content: The leadership change in Okinawa could deal a quiet blow to Beijing’s attempts to leverage local opposition to remilitarisation and the US-Japan military alliance, according to analysts. They added that the shift would compel Chinese academics and state media to recalibrate their messaging and approach towards the strategically vital Japanese prefecture. Genta Koja, the 42-year-old backed by Japan’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party to become Okinawa’s new governor, defeated incumbent Denny Tamaki on Sunday. This brought an end to eight years of Tamaki’s leadership, characterised by vocal pacifism and active regional diplomacy with Chinese cities that historically maintained ties with Okinawa. For Beijing, which has long cultivated relationships with Okinawan leaders who challenge Tokyo’s defence policies, Koja’s win represents the loss of a sympathetic subnational partner. Analysts said the election result served as a reality check for China’s external messaging, requiring it to adjust its approach towards Okinawan voters who were prioritising bread-and-butter issues over opposition to American military bases. Okinawa prefecture is made up of around 40 inhabited islands and has a population of 1.5 million. It hosts roughly 70 per cent of all US military facilities in Japan despite accounting for less than 1 per cent of the country’s land area. The United States seized Okinawa from Japan after World War II. Washington returned administrative control of the islands to Tokyo in 1972, but it has maintained a substantial military presence that serves as a crucial node in checking Beijing’s regional ambitions. Before Japan annexed it in 1879, Okinawa was known as the Ryukyu Kingdom, an independent maritime kingdom that paid tribute to China during the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1911) dynasties. In July 2023, Tamaki visited Beijing as part of a Japanese trade delegation and paid respects at the historic Ryukyu Kingdom cemetery in Beijing’s Tongzhou district. Concerns have grown in Japan that Beijing may play the “Ryukyu card” – invoking the islands’ history to question Japanese sovereignty over Okinawa and counter Tokyo’s position on Taiwan. Positioned within the “first island chain”, which stretches along the East Asian coastline from the Kuril Islands down to Borneo, Okinawa acts as a barrier limiting the People’s Liberation Army’s access to the Pacific Ocean. It is expected to play a vital strategic role in the event of a Taiwan conflict. In addition to the American presence, Japan’s Self-Defence Forces have been expanding their deployments in Okinawa as part of Tokyo’s “southwest shift” – a defence strategy that bolsters the region with new missile systems, radar installations and troop deployments. Tamaki firmly opposed the construction of new American military facilities on Okinawa Island and also opposed a plan to relocate the US Marine Corps’ Futenma air station in southern Okinawa to the Henoko coastal area in the north. Koja supports this controversial plan but has also called on Tokyo to provide a clearer timeline on when the Futenma station will close. For decades, local Okinawans have protested against the American military presence, with residents long complaining of noise pollution, security risks and recurring cases of sexual assault by US servicemen. Xu Weijun, an associate research professor at the Institute of Public Policy at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, said that with Tamaki’s exit, China would lose an important interlocutor who could speak on behalf of the prefectural government to “publicly emphasise dialogue and oppose the expansion of US military bases”. “Koja’s victory could weaken the leverage Beijing has long relied on to constrain Tokyo through Okinawa’s local politics,” he said. Xu noted that Koja would be far more mindful of Tokyo’s foreign policy stance and would be likely to scale back reciprocal visits to China that carried obvious political symbolism. He is also expected to draw stricter boundaries on local matters that concern Beijing, such as the Ryukyu narrative, Taiwan and Japan-US military base arrangements, according to Xu. In recent years, Chinese state media have played up the historical ties between China and the ancient Ryukyu Kingdom while emphasising tensions between Okinawa residents and the US military. Chinese academics and state media have even suggested challenging Tokyo’s control of Okinawa. While Beijing has not openly done so, state media have increasingly called for more research into historical and legal claims over the islands. Xu said that following Tamaki’s defeat, it would be difficult for Chinese media and intellectuals to continue using the narrative that Okinawans generally opposed US-Japan security arrangements. Koja’s victory at least showed that a candidate who did not oppose the air station’s relocation could still win, he added. “This shift can weaken the credibility and factual foundation of China’s previous narrative, which relied on invoking Okinawan public opinion to criticise Japan-US military activities.” Xu suggested that Beijing should shift from emphasising the divergence between the prefectural government and Tokyo to focusing on the social consequences of the military build-up. “China’s focus should be on how these arrangements increase the local burden, exacerbate regional tensions and pose threats to the lives and property of Okinawan residents,” he said. Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, cautioned against overstating the impact of the election on China’s approach. “China does not have a formal Okinawa policy in official diplomatic terms, and the change in Okinawa’s leadership may not constitute a shock to existing policy from Chinese cities that have civilian exchanges with Okinawa,” he said. “During Tamaki’s tenure, he maintained relatively friendly communication channels with China at both the central and local levels. How Okinawa now adjusts and develops its relationship with China will certainly be a test for the incoming governor.” Yet Koja’s victory signals a recalibration of Okinawan priorities that may still offer Beijing room for regional engagement. Exit polls conducted by Kyodo News showed that only 21 per cent of voters prioritised issues related to US military bases, while nearly 50 per cent chose economic revitalisation when deciding who to vote for. Over half of the respondents said they supported the Futenma relocation. During the campaign, Koja pledged to double Okinawa’s average income – which remains among the lowest of all prefectures – expand the local government budget for childcare and increase tourist spending on the island. According to Xu, Koja’s success stemmed from tapping into Okinawa residents’ economic anxieties. “This suggests that his administration will still need to preserve commercial ties with China and remain open to advancing tourism, business and cultural cooperation,” he said.

title: India and Russia push to expand defence ties with more joint production
description: Analysts say offers of Su-57 stealth jet tech and BrahMos upgrades signal an exit from simple buyer-seller deals.
content: India and Russia are seeking to push one of Asia’s oldest defence relationships beyond arms sales and into a more technology-driven industrial partnership, analysts have said, with missile exports and fighter-jet offers emerging as early tests. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shook hands and embraced on Friday ahead of last weekend’s Brics summit in New Delhi, prompting Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal to post on social media: “A bond that keeps growing stronger!” Analysts said the meeting pointed to a deeper recalibration of defence ties, as Delhi and Moscow explored more joint production, technology transfer and export-focused weapons development. Srikumar Menon, a former Indian diplomat, said discussions on modernising BrahMos missiles and Moscow’s offer of technology transfer for Su-57 stealth fighter jets to India showed “the growing maturity, depth and strategic sophistication” of India-Russia defence cooperation. The two countries have also set a target of US$100 billion in bilateral trade by 2030, up from a current base of around US$60 billion. India has traditionally relied on Russian arms and equipment for its military, from tanks to fighter jets, although in recent years it has stepped up purchases from France, the US and Israel to secure more sophisticated technology and hedge against uncertain Russian supplies amid the war in Ukraine. “Russia has been hampered by Western sanctions since 2022 in accessing advanced components and technology, which in turn affected defence supplies to India,” Menon said. This has pushed both sides from a buyer-seller model towards joint production, technology transfer and localisation under a “Make in India” programme launched in 2014. The export success of BrahMos spotlights this shift. Travelling at three times the speed of sound and launchable from land, sea, air or under the sea, BrahMos has carved out a niche in a region increasingly anxious about maritime security. The Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam have already reached agreements to acquire it, while Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told NDTV last Saturday that Kuala Lumpur was in exploratory talks of its own. No contract for an advanced BrahMos variant emerged from the Putin-Modi meeting, but it raised “the political priority of the next generation BrahMos work that was already under way”, said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum. “We are jointly producing the BrahMos missiles,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last week. “It is time to think about improving those missiles, adding some additional characteristics, making them more competitive in the market and more effective.” Balakrishnan said upgrade proposals included a lighter, smaller variant of BrahMos for India’s Tejas jets, a submarine-launched version and a hypersonic variant capable of travelling at five times the speed of sound. “The next step should be to move from jointly producing an existing weapon to jointly developing the next generation of weapons,” he said. “If Moscow is genuinely prepared to deepen technology sharing, BrahMos could become the foundation for a much more ambitious Indian-Russian defence industrial partnership.” Eye on the future Also on the table is a US$11 billion programme to upgrade India’s ageing Su-30MKI fleet, which still forms the backbone of its air force, alongside a Russian proposal to jointly develop the Su-57 stealth fighter. India is developing its own fifth-generation stealth fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), but is having problems securing the engine, after General Electric reportedly raised the price of the GE-414 engine almost threefold, according to Ravi Gopal Krishna Kapoor, a former Indian Air Force air marshal. Delayed deliveries of the GE-404 engine that powers India’s Tejas Mk-1A fighter had also raised “a serious question on achieving first flight [for the AMCA] within a 2028-29 time frame”, he said. India is in dire need of a fifth-generation fighter Ravi Gopal Krishna Kapoor, former Indian Air Force air marshal “With both China and Pakistan strengthening their air forces with fifth-generation fighters and strong air defence, India is in dire need of a fifth-generation fighter,” Kapoor said, noting that the Su-57 was the only aircraft of comparable calibre on offer, amid indications Delhi might not opt for US-made F-35s. “India has a current stealth gap which is not likely to be filled for the next decade. Su-57s can fill that gap before 2030–31 to some extent,” he said. Meanwhile, talks with France over 114 Rafale jets have stalled, reportedly over Paris’ refusal to hand over core software source codes, handing Moscow an opening. Kapoor was careful not to oversell the Su-57’s abilities. Only around 30 had been built and the jet had yet to make a “visible impact” in Russia’s war with Ukraine, he said. Still, he argued that a limited order made sense, provided Moscow agreed to one condition. “It would be worthwhile for India to go in for a limited number of Su-57, with a caveat of source code being shared,” Kapoor said.

title: How Jet Li’s trainer Wu Bin, 89, ages well and still nurtures martial arts talent
description: Martial arts legend Wu Bin talks about mentoring Jet Li and other wushu stars, and how building good habits is key to health in older life.
content: At 89, many rely on glasses or hearing aids. Wu Bin needs neither. Daily runs and regular football games keep the legendary martial arts coach of action icon Jet Li in fighting form. Wu is a convincing advertisement for the wellness benefits of lifelong discipline. He still travels widely and recently presided over the 18th Hong Kong International Wushu Competition, where Dragon He, the son of another of Wu’s former students, Jaden He Jingde, was competing. A founder of the Beijing Wushu Team, Wu helped develop the traditional martial art into an elite modern sport. His eye for potential led him to the eight-year-old Li in 1971 and helped launch his career. Li’s mastery of Chinese martial arts would elevate him to the podium at championships and launch him onto cinema screens around the world. Today, Wu’s impact extends to a third generation of disciples. Rather than retire, he travels to encourage them. Wu was born in Huzhou, in China’s Zhejiang province, in 1937. His family fled to Shanghai during the Second Sino-Japanese War, when Wu was around two years old. His father made bricks, including those used to build Shanghai’s historic Park Hotel, which for years was Asia’s tallest building. If you imagine Jet Li’s master as a mystic elder armed with wushu’s deepest secrets, think again. “It was only after primary school that I liked reading martial arts novels,” Wu says. “I was most captivated by the stories of various combat styles.” Books such as Water Margin and The Seven Heroes and Five Gallants, which featured themes of brotherhood, martial prowess and rebellion against injustice, stirred his imagination – but he had yet to throw a punch. From weightlifting to wushu Wu boarded at Shanghai High School, where he served as captain of the football team for about half a year. A teacher recommended he train as a PE teacher. Wu had been offered early admission to Shanghai Teachers College when a chance bicycle ride changed his plans: he saw an advert for the Beijing Institute of Physical Education – now called Beijing Sport University – and decided to sit its entrance examination. He was accepted into the institute in 1958 and started weightlifting. Two years later, a teacher encouraged him to diversify. “You’d better stop practising weightlifting,” Wu remembers being told. “You’ve done it for two years, and that’s enough. Learn martial arts instead.” The teacher reasoned that weightlifting equipment would not necessarily be available to a future PE teacher, but martial arts could travel anywhere. Wu followed the advice and retrained as a wushu coach in Beijing after graduation. Having watched older pupils pulled away from sport by academic pressures, he decided to recruit younger children. In 1970, he began visiting primary schools. Among a group of prospective recruits at Beijing’s Changqiao Primary School, one boy stood out: Li Lianjie, who would later become known as Jet Li. Wu remembers that Li was unusually quick for an eight-year-old. “His memory was excellent, and his ability to mimic movements was very strong,” Wu says. “Whatever you taught him, he learned very quickly.” Li was one of around 10 children Wu coached into adulthood. A cultural calling card Warming relations between the United States and China in the 1970s triggered a rise in martial arts. US President Richard Nixon’s landmark 1972 visit to China ended 25 years of diplomatic estrangement and paved the way for broader, official athletic exchanges between the two nations. In 1973, a high-profile US collegiate all-star basketball delegation became the first American team-sports group to compete in China. Beijing needed a sport that could make an equally distinctive return statement in the US. “Track and field couldn’t beat the US, tennis couldn’t beat the US, and golf couldn’t beat the US either,” Wu says. “After thinking it over for a long time: martial arts.” The choice serendipitously put Wu’s wushu team in the spotlight. Within a few years, martial arts became China’s cultural calling card for a sporting visit to the US, and a young Li became a crowd favourite. Nixon subsequently invited the delegation to perform at the White House. Jaden He Jingde, a former national wushu champion, stuntman and martial arts school founder, is another of Wu’s former students. He says his sifu (master) taught him that an exceptional martial artist needs patience, exposure to different styles and respect for tradition. More importantly, He says that Wu’s method changed the way he himself approached teaching children. “Rigid, forced training never works,” He says. “We must first assess every child’s personality, natural talent and physical flexibility.” He has applied this thinking to his son Dragon, choosing weapons and routines suited to the boy’s strengths. For Dragon, the inheritance is moral as well as physical. “My sifu does not just teach me martial arts moves – he also teaches me about respect and self-discipline,” he says. One teaching has stayed with him: medals and victories do not last, and what matters is becoming a better person with every contest. Although Wu’s own daughter and grandson have chosen lives outside martial arts, he remains surrounded by the students and families shaped by his teaching. The secret to longevity One of the ways Wu ensures he ages well is by continuing to practise martial arts, although he says these days it is “just light activity”, not the punishing training he did when he was younger. “Now is the time for them to teach,” Wu says of his mentees, “while I am in the stage of nourishing life.” In Chinese, that concept is called yangsheng, the everyday cultivation of health. This entails having a routine. Wu still runs and prefers football to gentle qigong or breathwork, which is “not enough” exercise for him. He plays with mixed middle-aged and senior teams, sometimes alongside people in their twenties. He values sleep, going to bed at about 10pm and waking up at 6am without any interruptions. The key, he says, is building habits. “Living well includes your daily personal habits, lifestyle habits and of course, what we eat,” he says.
