Wu favours light, bland foods and emphasises balance and variety. “Steamed, stir-fried, or with less oil, but you need a variety of flavours,” he says. “You can’t just eat one type of food. Hong Kong’s food culture is quite smart in this respect – it combines variety with moderation.” Wu’s reputation helps him stay active, and he receives roughly 30 invitations a year to events across China and overseas. In November, 2025, he visited Russia to receive the Order of Friendship for his contributions to developing the country’s wushu team, one of the strongest teams in Europe. On his latest trip, he travelled from Xian to Hong Kong before heading to Hainan. He says that travel is “no problem … My health is great – no chronic conditions or illnesses at all.” This year, following the traditional East Asian practice that counts a newborn as one year old, Wu celebrated his 90th birthday. The gathering brought together many of his former students, including Li and He. Wu’s longevity is based on balance: staying active, making time for rest, eating with restraint but also pleasure, and nurturing younger people. Dragon says: “I try my best to stay humble and keep working to live up to what my sifu has taught me. I want to make my sifu proud of me.” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Policy address 2026: John Lee says accountability needed if 5-year plan targets missed – as it happened
description: City leader has set 22 major indicators in the five-year plan, with five being binding targets.
content: This live article is freely available to our registered users. Please log in or create an account. Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan at the legislature, followed by his annual policy address. The highly anticipated plan, unveiled after a two-month public consultation, aimed to align the city’s priorities with the nation’s 2026-30 development blueprint. Lee set 22 major indicators in the plan, with five being binding targets mostly focusing on environmental protection, while 17 were anticipatory goals. Lee said the five-year plan would provide a long-term blueprint and strategic direction for Hong Kong’s development with “far-reaching significance”, while the policy address would continue to serve as an annual report, setting out how the government would implement the plan in a given year. This year’s policy address was also the last of Lee’s current term. Read on for the South China Morning Post’s live coverage of this year’s session. You can find the key takeaways here. title: Dong Jun takes softer line on US at Xiangshan Forum as Xi prepares for Trump summit
description: Retired PLA colonel says defence minister’s speech signals growing confidence and lower tension with US.
content: Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun’s address to a defence gathering in Beijing on Wednesday carried a message for Washington but it was delivered in a notably softer, less critical tone, according to a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army. Zhou Bo, now a senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, said Dong’s tone was “relatively mild”, even as the Chinese defence minister made veiled references to the US and its actions in the Middle East. The address comes just a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the US and as US officials laud improved military-to-military communication between the two powers. In his speech at the Xiangshan Forum, Dong urged countries to build a new security approach based on dialogue rather than confrontation, and partnership instead of alliance – a reference to Washington’s military alliances that Beijing has long criticised as bloc confrontation. He also called on major countries to shoulder their responsibility, and for the international community to oppose actions that involved forming exclusive blocs. As Washington presses on with strikes against Tehran, piling pressure on Iran to seek an end to a conflict now in its seventh month, Dong said that “the causes of disputes cannot be resolved by force”. Dong also said the Chinese armed forces were willing to share their experience of military governance as the PLA approached its centenary goal next year to become a strong force. He added that Beijing could – within its capacity – help others in need of developing their armed forces. According to Zhou, the move reflected Beijing’s growing confidence in its military, noting that China had sought to ramp up efforts on this front. At last year’s conference, Dong also refrained from naming particular countries, including the US, but he described military alliances as groups with “selfish interests” and urged nations to stand up against “disguised hegemonic logic and bullying acts”. Dong did not mention Taiwan in his speech. Last year, he said the return of Taiwan to China was “an integral part of the post-war order”. Zhou noted that US defence chief Pete Hegseth had also avoided mentioning Taiwan in his speech at the Shangri-La security dialogue in Singapore earlier this year. “Not mentioning Taiwan does not mean that China is less concerned with the issue,” he said. “It doesn’t mean that China is not paying attention to it.” Taiwan remains a core interest to Beijing and the issue is expected to be raised again by Xi when he sits down with Trump next week. Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited with force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Dong singled out AI, outer space and the deep seas as three fields requiring communication and cooperation between countries. China and the US have seen a growing rivalry in AI and space technology. Dong said conflicts should be resolved through dialogue and consultation, and that countries should bear in mind “the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against hegemonism”, and prevent minor disagreements from escalating to major frictions. Shi Yinhong, a professor of international affairs at Renmin University of China, said Dong used his address to underline some of China’s long-held positions, including its opposition to the US forming closed alliances with Western countries to target China and its partners. He said Beijing’s offer to help build up other militaries signalled its ambition to expand its military influence globally but added that few countries beyond some developing nations were likely to take it up.

title: China launches new canal, first of its kind since 1949, giving inland access to sea lanes
description: Newly opened Pinglu Canal will allow cargo from inland provinces to reach the Gulf of Tonkin, avoiding a 560km detour, deepening trade ties.
content: China officially opened its landmark Pinglu Canal to navigation on Wednesday, creating a new maritime gateway for the country’s southwestern hinterland and providing a shorter route to Southeast Asia as Beijing seeks to deepen trade with the region. The 134.2km (83.4 mile) waterway links Nanning, the capital of the southern region of Guangxi, to the Gulf of Tonkin, known as the Beibu Gulf in China, allowing cargo from inland provinces to reach the sea without taking a roughly 560km detour via Guangzhou, cutting both transit times and logistics costs. With the canal’s opening, two new freight routes have begun operation – an international route linking Nanning with Can Tho in Vietnam, and a domestic route connecting Nanning with Yangpu in southern Hainan province, according to state broadcaster CCTV. About 30 cargo vessels carrying goods such as building materials, coal, minerals, steel and fertiliser are set to pass through the canal on its opening day, with Nanning Port and Qinzhou Port handling operations, the state media report said. The first of four passenger routes along the waterway has also begun operation, according to the live broadcast by official media. “Pinglu Canal is an important piece of innovative infrastructure,” said Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, a think tank under China’s Ministry of Commerce. “Beyond providing a more efficient route to the sea, connecting provinces and promoting economic cooperation, it also creates an opportunity to modernise China’s transport system,” he added. Zhou also said the canal provided a platform for exploring more efficient and more environmentally friendly forms of transport. “This could create important conditions for the Chinese economy and for greater coordination with neighbouring countries, while supporting the optimisation and upgrading of regional industrial and supply chains through greater use of smart technologies.” With a planned investment of 72.7 billion yuan (US$10.8 billion), the project, which began construction in August 2022, is designed to accommodate vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes and save more than 5 billion yuan in overall transportation costs each year. The canal is the first man-made waterway connecting a river to the sea to be built since the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, state-run Xinhua News Agency reported. It is equipped with a tiered navigation zone system to facilitate the movement of inland vessels, allowing qualified vessels to travel through the canal and into the sea without transferring cargo to another ship. The canal’s opening comes after a series of navigation tests. In mid-August, four merchant vessels ranging from 1,000 to 5,000 tonnes conducted phased trials along the canal’s main channel, testing the safety and reliability of the waterway, locks, anchorages and service areas, state media reported. Earlier that month, a maritime patrol vessel completed the first full-route transit test along the waterway, according to the canal’s operator. Late in August, the canal’s first command and management vessel was delivered to oversee navigation and handle emergency responses along the waterway. The canal aims to give China’s less-prosperous inland regions quicker and easier access to global sea lanes, boosting local industry and strengthening trade with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), China’s largest trading partner as a bloc. That ambition is already taking shape. Last Thursday, a multimodal freight train carrying more than 370 tonnes of construction machinery and other products arrived in Guangxi, after departing from Hunan province, with the cargo scheduled for export following the canal’s opening. The project is also part of a broader push to expand China’s inland waterways, with several other provinces, including Jiangxi, Hubei, Hunan and Henan, planning or advancing ambitious multibillion-dollar waterway expansions to boost local economic growth. By using the canal, provinces including Yunnan, Guizhou, Hunan and Sichuan, as well as the metropolis of Chongqing, could see their logistics costs reduced by around 18 per cent to 30 per cent, making it “the shortest, most economical and most convenient route to the sea in the western region”, according to an August 13 report by Yunnan authorities. The canal’s construction has also spurred a broader build-out of supporting infrastructure and transport links. At Nanning Port’s Liujing operations area, berths have been upgraded to handle vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes. The Beibu Gulf Port is also seeking to attract cargo from Chongqing, Sichuan and Yunnan, while cross-border railways such as the China-Laos Railway are expected to feed into the network, according to state media reports. The opening comes as China’s trade with Asean continues to grow. Beijing has increasingly sought to strengthen supply chains and economic ties with the region as tensions with the West persist over trade and technology. Total trade between China and Asean reached US$862.75 billion in the first eight months of this year, up 25.6 per cent from a year earlier, customs data showed. China’s exports to Asean stood at US$546 billion, up 25.8 per cent. In contrast, exports to the US rose 6.2 per cent in dollar terms over the same period. The opening came just ahead of this year’s China-Asean Expo in Nanning, an annual trade and investment fair showcasing products ranging from agricultural goods and food to machinery and hi-tech equipment.

title: South Korean court orders Pyongyang to pay US$32.5m for destroying border office
description: The lawsuit over the destruction of the Inter-Korean Liaison Office marks the first time Seoul has sought damages directly from the North.
content: A Seoul court ordered Pyongyang on Wednesday to pay roughly US$32.5 million for blowing up in 2020 an office in North Korea that was intended to foster relations between the two Koreas, Yonhap news agency reported. The lawsuit over the destruction of the Inter-Korean Liaison Office marks the first time the South Korean government has sought damages directly from the North, according to media reports. South Korea’s previous conservative government, led by former president ‌Yoon Suk-yeol, filed the suit in June 2023, before Yoon was ousted from office after his short-lived December 2024 martial law declaration. The office building was constructed in the dormant Kaesong Industrial Complex, where South Korean companies once employed North Korean workers. But Pyongyang blew up the building in June 2020 after days of rising tensions due to activists in the South sending balloons carrying anti-Pyongyang leaflets across the border, with the North denouncing the office as “useless”. “The North should pay the South Korean government 44.6 billion won in damages over the demolition of the liaison office,” the Seoul Central District Court said in its ruling, Yonhap reported. The office opened in September 2018, days before then South Korean president Moon Jae-in travelled to Pyongyang for his third summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. Around 20 officials from each side were stationed at the office in the following months until operations were suspended in January 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Fragility and cooperation: takeaways from Dong Jun’s Xiangshan Forum speech
description: The Chinese defence minister officially opens the security conference with a warning about ‘zero-sum’ mindsets.
content: Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun gave a keynote speech to the Xiangshan Forum in Beijing on Wednesday, with just over a week until a summit in the United States between the presidents of the two countries. In his 20-minute address, Dong outlined China’s goals for global governance, multilateralism, conflict prevention and the development of emerging technology. Global security at a ‘moment of fragility’ Dong started by warning that a “zero-sum mindset” could not resolve today’s problems. He said that while China upheld a cooperative security approach, global governance would either advance or regress. International security remained “fragile”, he said, calling for a new security approach to be forged based on dialogue rather than confrontation, partnership rather than alliance, and win-win outcomes rather than zero-sum games. Vigilance against ‘hegemonism, militarism’ Dong said multilateralism must be upheld in a turbulent world, describing it as “essential” to safeguarding overall global strategic stability. He called for major powers to shoulder their responsibilities, while ensuring equal participation of countries for security governance and development. He also said that countries should bear in mind the lessons of history and remain highly vigilant against hegemonism and militarism, and prevent minor disagreements from escalating into major frictions. The comment appeared to be a veiled reference to relations with Japan, which have declined since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested in November that an attack on Taiwan could constitute a Japanese military response. Beijing to share experience, expand military cooperation Dong said China was ready to share its experience of building and governing its military and help “within our capacity” countries in need with their military development. He outlined Beijing’s plan to expand practical cooperation in areas such as joint exercises and training, personnel training, and equipment and technology. Development and security Noting that “nothing in the world is difficult, as long as we are willing to climb”, Dong said the Chinese military was ready to work with all parties to maintain regional stability and safeguard peaceful development. He said the key to security governance was in narrowing the development gap, and that “development is the greatest guarantee of security” for countries of the Global South. AI and emerging technology Dong called on the international community to firmly oppose actions that involved forming exclusive blocs and exacerbating tensions. He also voiced support for cooperation on artificial intelligence, outer space and the deep sea, so that emerging technologies could better benefit all humanity. No word on Taiwan, South China Sea Dong did not make any direct mentions of Taiwan during the speech. It was a departure from his address last year when he said “Taiwan’s return is an integral part of the post-war order”. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Despite recently simmering tensions with the Philippines, Dong also did not comment on the South China Sea dispute. There was also no direct mention of Japan, although Dong called for the powers of justice to unite to prevent historical problems from reemerging.

title: GSK licenses Chinese firm’s cancer drug in US$750 million deal
description: The acquisition is the latest in a string of major licensing deals involving Chinese biotechnology firms.
content: British pharmaceutical giant GSK has agreed to acquire a cancer drug from Chinese firm Chimagen Biosciences in a deal worth up to US$750 million, underscoring China’s emergence as a global player in biotechnology. GSK announced plans on Tuesday to buy full global rights to a “potential best-in-class” T-cell engager (TCE) from Chengdu-based Chimagen, targeting treatment for multiple myeloma, a type of blood cancer. TCEs work by binding T cells, a kind of white blood cell, directly to cancer cells, triggering the immune system to attack the cancer. While current TCEs are effective at treating multiple myeloma, they often cause major side effects, and Chimagen’s new drug shows promise in both improved tolerability and more durable results, according to GSK. GSK will pay an undisclosed upfront fee to develop and commercialise Chimagen’s new TCE assets, followed by payments based on the drug’s successful development and commercialisation, the company said. The programme is expected to enter phase-one trials next year. The deal reflects China’s rapid progress in biotech innovation, which has drawn growing interest from global pharmaceutical giants and investors in recent years. The total value of out-licensing deals involving Chinese-made innovative drugs so far this year has reached US$120 billion, up 36 per cent compared with the same period last year, Xinhua reported on Tuesday, citing new data from China’s National Medical Products Administration. That has included several huge deals that dwarf GSK’s TCE acquisition. In January, Swedish-British drug maker AstraZeneca said it would license Chinese firm CSPC Pharmaceutical Group’s weight-management drugs, with payouts potentially reaching up to US$18.5 billion. In May, Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceutical – China’s largest drug maker by market capitalisation – secured an agreement with US pharmaceutical giant Bristol Myers Squibb covering 13 programmes spanning oncology, haematology and immunology, which could be worth up to US$15.2 billion.

title: Rodrigo Duterte appears in ICC courtroom for pretrial proceedings
description: The former Philippine president’s trial over his ‘war on drugs’ that killed thousands will start on November 30.
content: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte appeared in person at the International Criminal Court for the first time on Wednesday as he faces charges over his “war on drugs” that killed thousands. The 81-year-old had appeared by video link when he was first brought to the court in The Hague, but had since skipped hearings, with his defence team claiming he was too ill. Dressed in a dark suit and white shirt with no tie, Duterte sat with his chin resting on his hands as the proceedings opened. Judge Joanna Korner noted his appearance in court for the first time and said he could leave the court at any time without seeking permission from the bench. Duterte faces three counts of crimes against humanity, with prosecutors alleging his involvement in at least 76 murders between 2013 and 2018 during his offensive against drug users and sellers. He is the first Asian former head of state to face trial at the ICC, which prosecutes individuals for the world’s worst crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. Judge Korner has set November 30 as the start date of the trial, which could take months or even years. Wednesday’s hearing was a “status hearing” for the parties and the judge to fix logistical details. The only time Duterte had been seen since his arrest in March 2025 was an initial appearance via video, where he seemed confused and tired, his speech barely audible. His defence team has argued he is not mentally fit to follow proceedings and that his condition continues to deteriorate. Relatives of some of those killed in the anti-drugs campaign welcomed Duterte’s appearance in court. Randy Delos Santos, 48, an uncle of Kian Delos Santos, a teenager killed by police in August 2017, when Duterte was president, said: “Of course, we are very happy that he is now able to attend in person.” “Seeing that he is physically fit, we believe this could be the start of a process that will finally bring us, the victims, the justice we have been waiting for. We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings,” Santos said in Manila. In a submission published on Tuesday, Duterte’s lawyers said he suffered from “significant memory impairment that prevents him from retaining recent information and reliably accessing memories”. Judges are weighing whether he is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three experts. That assessment has not been made public but Duterte’s defence cited the results of examinations contained in the report. According to the defence, these examinations showed Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and could not recall the name of the current US president. During hearings in February, the prosecution alleged Duterte killed thousands of suspected drug dealers and users, first as mayor of Davao City, then as president. “Decades of murdering his own people, murdering the children of the Philippines, and he claims that he did it all for his country. He doesn’t deny it,” said Julian Nicholls, summing up for the prosecution after the hearings. “He ran a death squad in Davao that he created,” said Nicholls, referring to the city where he was mayor before he became president. “His promise was to kill thousands and he did.” The true number of killings during his campaign in the Philippines is thought to be in the thousands and lawyers for the victims have argued that a full trial could encourage more families to come forward. His then-defence lawyer Nicolas Kaufman told the court in February that his client “absolutely” maintained his innocence. Kaufman told ICC judges the evidence against Duterte was “wholly insufficient” and the charges “grievously misplaced and politically motivated”. He argued that while Duterte used “bluster and hyperbole” in his speeches, he also frequently ordered authorities only to shoot in self-defence. Duterte remains popular in the Philippines, where many favoured his tough approach to crime.

title: Opinion | Why more export controls won’t stop China’s industrial engine
description: Beyond cutting-edge tech, Beijing’s true manufacturing strength lies in its unmatched ability to scale the mature technologies that drive the modern economy.
content: The first “China shock” was fairly easy to understand. Beginning in the 1990s, cheap Chinese goods poured into global markets, displacing large parts of lower-end manufacturing across the world. Now, China shock 2.0 seems to be under way, with China taking the lead in electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, solar panels, semiconductors and other more technologically sophisticated industries. This is often perceived as a trade problem, with Chinese manufacturers producing too much, selling too cheaply and flooding global markets with subsidised goods. However, the more consequential question is not just why the United States and Europe run growing trade deficits with China. It is who is supplying the next round of industrial growth in Asia, Africa, Latin America and other emerging markets. That makes today’s industrial competition more of a production story than a trade story. Headlines on the technological race between China and the US are usually about the frontier: artificial intelligence (AI), advanced semiconductors, quantum computing, biotechnology and other fields in which scientific leadership could determine the future. China’s efforts to catch up with the technological and productivity frontier can make it look like the country’s industrial future lies entirely at the highest end of technology. However, much of China’s industrial expansion is happening in a different area: technologies that are less cutting edge but already proven and widely used throughout the world. Much of the modern economy does not run on frontier technology. Rather, it relies on mature technologies that are reliable, affordable and fit for the job. China is becoming one of the main suppliers of that kind of proven technology. Automobiles show why industrial competition is not just about the frontier. German industrial strength has never depended on producing every German car inside Germany. By 2010, German carmakers were already producing more vehicles abroad than at home. Much of the production shift has been visible in China and the so-called German-Central European supply chain. China presents a different challenge. It is not that German manufacturers are incapable of producing electric cars; Germany still remains a major EV producer. Rather, electrification has changed the source of much of the value, technology and strategic dependence. While the internal combustion vehicle rewarded decades of German expertise in engines, transmissions and mechanical engineering, EVs rely more heavily on batteries, semiconductors, software and digital architecture. Germany might still produce EVs, but a growing share of the components on which those cars depend now comes from China. The EV race is not just about having the latest technology. China’s battery dominance has been built in large part around lithium iron phosphate technology, a mature technology that is cost effective, reliable and suitable for mass-market vehicles. Automobiles also depend on mature chips. A Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago report estimates that an average internal combustion vehicle contains more than 1,000 semiconductors, around 95 per cent of which are mature or legacy chips. EVs use more sophisticated processors, but they still rely heavily on mature chips alongside other proven technologies such as batteries, software and digital architecture. These are precisely the areas in which China has built a dense domestic ecosystem. The semiconductor industry consists of much more than frontier processors. China’s share of global capacity for mature chips has expanded dramatically: it has grown three to four times during the past decade, rising from about 17 per cent in 2015 to 33 per cent in 2024 and a projected 45 per cent in 2027. Such chips will not power the most advanced AI models or graphics cards, but they do perform many of the less spectacular but key functions without which the modern economy cannot operate. China subsidising its industries is far from a new development, and the use of subsidies, tax incentives and below-market borrowing are hardly unique to China. What makes China different is partly where the money has gone. Financing technology-intensive industries does not necessarily mean financing only the most cutting-edge technologies. In fact, much of China’s capital is going into technologies that are already mature. Since 2021, China’s semiconductor industry has made more than US$75 billion in new investment, primarily in legacy technology nodes. China is competing in the race for advanced chips, but it is also pouring capital into the less glamorous technologies on which much of the industrial economy already depends. The central story is that the modern industrial economy does not simply replace mature technologies with frontier ones. Mature technologies are not obsolete technologies. They are becoming increasingly important to China’s position in the global industry as machinery, electrical equipment and transport equipment now account for more than half of the country’s exports. China is also exporting more of these products to emerging markets, especially within Southeast Asia. Now, the US and European responses to China still focus on controlling what enters their markets, but the deeper challenge is production capacity. Tariffs might keep some Chinese goods out of American or European markets, and export controls might slow China’s progress in some frontier technologies. However, neither does much to prevent Chinese machinery, components and capital goods from replacing Western products in emerging markets. The key question is not simply who invents the technologies of tomorrow; it is who produces, adapts and scales the mature technologies that the modern economy already runs on today. A country can remain at the scientific frontier while losing the ability to manufacture the technologies that support it. China’s manufacturing model makes one thing clear: industrial competition requires both innovation at the frontier and the ecosystems needed to produce proven technologies that support the industrial economy.

title: Viral ‘then and now’ photos of Chinese woman reunited with family spark trafficking debate
description: Sun, believed to have come from a relatively affluent Beijing family, was fluent in English and classically trained in ballet, ballroom dancing.
content: A woman from northern China has been reunited with her biological family after 26 years, with striking before-and-after images from her disappearance renewing public attention on the plight of human trafficking survivors. Sun Meihua, from Shandong province, was located after an online user known as Chuxin shared her story. During a visit to a village captured on video, Chuxin encountered Sun, who had greying hair, a frail demeanour and signs of cognitive difficulties. Chuxin soon learned that Sun was not from the area and had long harboured hopes of reconnecting with her family. Despite her intellectual challenges, Sun demonstrated remarkable abilities, including recalling foreign trade terminology and writing clearly. She was able to write her own name, as well as two names believed to belong to relatives, and identify several locations in Beijing. A now-deleted article published by a volunteer claimed that Sun was born in Beijing in 1968 into a relatively affluent family and was fluent in English, having trained in both ballet and ballroom dancing. However, these claims could not be independently verified. Sun reportedly disappeared in 2000, prompting her family to search for her unsuccessfully for many years. She eventually lost contact with them and settled in Shandong, where she lived with “Uncle Long,” a man about 20 years her senior. The nature of their relationship has not been disclosed. Chuxin managed to obtain Sun’s identification information by exchanging a mobile phone with Uncle Long. Later, volunteers assisted in arranging a DNA test, leading to the discovery of her biological elder brother in Beijing. Sun was subsequently reunited with her family, although her parents had already died. Reports also indicated that she had an elder sister living in the US. It remains unclear whether Sun’s case involved human trafficking or if anyone will face accountability. Local authorities have not revealed whether Uncle Long is suspected of any wrongdoing. Moreover, videos and reports concerning the case have been challenging to locate on mainland social media platforms. In China, individuals who abduct, kidnap, sell, purchase, or transfer women or children for trafficking purposes can face sentences of up to 10 years in prison. In more severe cases, penalties may escalate to life imprisonment or even the death penalty. On September 2, prominent missing-child advocate Du Xiaohua addressed Sun’s case in a video. Du’s six-year-old son disappeared in 2011, prompting him to spend over a decade searching across China. His experiences ultimately inspired the 2014 film Dearest. Du expressed relief over Sun’s reunion with her family, crediting local authorities and public support for this outcome. “I hope Sister Sun can live a safe and peaceful life in the future,” he added. The SCMP reached out to Du for more information about Sun but had not received a response by the time of publication. Sun’s story has ignited broader discussions online. One observer called for a thorough investigation, stating that “Sun’s life was destroyed” and that those responsible should be held accountable. Another commenter mused: “This brings to mind reports from the 1990s of women abducted to rural areas, forced into marriages, and deprived of their freedom. Despite social progress and enhanced legal protections, similar hidden cases still persist today.”

title: Tibetan Plateau’s unstable glaciers could cause more disasters in the future
description: This warning comes after the deadly landslide caused by a falling glacier on the China-Nepal border.
content:
Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau might become more unstable and could cause more disasters.
“Over the past 60 years, the glacier area on the Tibetan Plateau has shrunk by around 24 per cent, with around 7,000 small glaciers disappearing,” Gao Rong said earlier this month. He is the deputy director of China’s National Climate Centre. He said glacial disasters would likely happen more often.
This warning came after last month’s deadly landslide on the China-Nepal border. It was caused by a falling glacier.
A study was published by the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, along with other institutions. It found that erosion in the glacier’s path played a big role in the damage.
When ice and rocks fell, they slid down the valley. They scraped the riverbed, pulled debris from the banks and mixed with water. This turned a collapse into a mudslide. Scientists stress the need for governments to improve how they assess risk and monitor glaciers.

title: Japan’s Takaichi opts for stability in first reshuffle since taking over LDP
description: The reshuffle comes ahead of changes to Takaichi’s cabinet, in which she is likely to also retain key ministers.
content: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi retained many of her Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) executives on Wednesday, in her first reshuffle since taking the helm of the ruling party about a year ago. Takaichi kept the influential former prime minister Taro Aso as vice-president and his brother-in-law, Shunichi Suzuki, as secretary general, as she seeks to maintain continuity ahead of what is likely to be a packed legislative agenda into the end of the year. Policy chief Takayuki Kobayashi was also retained, while Hiroshi Kajiyama, a former industry minister seen as a safe pair of hands, replaced Haruko Arimura as head of the LDP’s decision-making General Council. Kajiyama’s former role as Diet affairs chief was filled by House of Representatives member Hideki Murai, previously a deputy chief Cabinet secretary under former prime minister Fumio Kishida. The appointment of a politician without cabinet experience as the LDP’s chief negotiator in parliament comes after he played a significant role in talks with opposition parties on key bills. Among other appointments, party election strategy chief Yasutoshi Nishimura and Executive Acting Secretary General Koichi Hagiuda, both of whom were implicated in a high-profile political slush funds scandal that emerged in late 2023 and dealt a heavy blow to the party, were kept on in their roles. Takaichi won the LDP’s presidential contest on October 4, 2025, and became the country’s first female prime minister later the same month. The reshuffle comes ahead of changes to Takaichi’s cabinet on Thursday, and as the ruling coalition of the LDP and the Japan Innovation Party prepares for an extraordinary Diet session, likely to start in early October. The session is likely to include deliberations towards passing a cut of the consumption tax on food products from 8 per cent to 1 per cent for two years from April, and on a controversial political reform bill reducing Diet seats that led to a boycott by the opposition in the previous session. In the cabinet revamp, she is tipped to retain a number of her top team, including Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. Minoru Kiuchi is likely to stay on as minister in charge of economic revitalisation, according to the Yomiuri newspaper. Markets been focusing on whether Kiuchi, known as ‌an advocate of expansionary fiscal and ⁠monetary ⁠policy, will retain his post for clues on ‌whether the recent bond sell-off could prod Takaichi ‌to water ‌down her big spending ‌plans. As minister overseeing the Cabinet Office, Kiuchi has the right to attend the Bank of Japan’s policy-setting meetings as one of the two government representatives. The Finance Ministry has the right to send the other government representative. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong policy address to unveil bold youth housing and mediation initiatives
description: City leader John Lee will seek to prioritise youth home ownership and position Hong Kong as global mediation capital in his address, SCMP learns.
content: Hong Kong’s leader will unveil two bold initiatives on housing and mediation in his policy address, the South China Morning Post has learned, with the government planning to boost home ownership rates among young couples and prioritise settling official commercial disputes through the city’s mediation body. The new measures, to be unveiled by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday, aimed to strengthen the city’s status as a global mediation capital while improving livelihoods, government sources said. “Hong Kong is actively building itself into a capital of mediation. Hence, authorities will prioritise including the International Organisation for Mediation (IOMed) as a dispute resolution option in government contracts involving international commercial matters, as well as in international agreements signed by the Hong Kong government,” an insider said. According to the source, authorities will also encourage the IOMed to handle disputes in emerging industries such as commodity trading and the space economy, and explore setting up a dedicated panel of mediators for commodity trading to lower cross-border transaction risks and attract overseas businesses to the city. The move is intended to deepen Hong Kong’s development as a global dispute resolution centre under Beijing’s national plan. Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah, secretary general of the IOMed, told the SCMP last month that the mediation body was ready to handle state-to-state disputes, with six countries having nominated more than 100 mediators from the legal, diplomatic and academic fields. She added that the organisation had already received a “not insignificant” number of inquiries and expressions of interest in its services. On the livelihood front, Lee is expected to boost subsidised home ownership among young couples by lowering the minimum down payment level for families with newborns. According to a second insider, one option under consideration is to lower the minimum down payment for a Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) flat for families with newborns under “white form” status, as part of broader efforts to boost the city’s birth rate. The minimum down payment could be cut to 5 per cent from the current 10 per cent of the property value, the second source said. The government currently sells subsidised housing under two major programmes: the HOS and the Green Form Subsidised Home Ownership Scheme (GSH). “Green form” applicants – families living in public rental housing – are eligible for both schemes and can buy a subsidised home with a minimum down payment of 5 per cent of the property price. White form applicants – families renting private homes – can only join the HOS provided that their initial down payment currently costs at least 10 per cent of the property price. HOS flats are priced based on affordability and sold at a discount on market values. The latest batch of flats, announced last December, was sold at 30 per cent off assessed market values. The batch of 7,000 HOS homes was 14 times oversubscribed, attracting 104,400 applications, 72,300 of which came from white form candidates. About 50 per cent of HOS buyers were below the age of 40, according to housing authorities, which estimated in July that more than 30,000 young families would benefit from the expanded supply of subsidised sales flats. The government is under mounting pressure to tackle demographic challenges, including declining birth numbers and a rapidly ageing society that threatens to shrink the city’s workforce. Hong Kong recorded a historic low of 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026, a drop that continued despite a HK$20,000 (US$2,550) baby bonus, tax relief and public housing perks for families with newborns. Experts have warned that increasing financial incentives alone are unlikely to reverse the slump in births, even as some point to Singapore’s recent push for more generous pro-family measures. Anthony Chiu Kwok-wai, executive director of the Federation of Public Housing Estates, said a reduced down payment would be of immense help to young parents. “This provides them with extra funds for home decoration or further studies, offering substantial financial relief,” he said, noting that families with children aged below three faced heavy financial pressures across all aspects of daily life, from food and clothing to housing and transport. Legal sector lawmaker Nick Chan Hiu-fung welcomed the new mediation initiatives. “Incorporating mediation into local procurement contracts previously was just a start. It’s natural to expand it to cover international contracts. Mediation is about achieving win-win solutions, which will benefit both parties in the contracts tremendously,” he said. He added that Hong Kong’s mediation talent and institutional neutrality were highly valued globally. With additional resources, along with the city’s safety and stability amid growing geopolitical tension, Hong Kong was well positioned to “take international mediation to the next level”, he said.

title: Xiangshan Forum: China’s defence chief on security in a fragile world – as it happened

title: Singapore ministers earn millions. What do other Asian leaders make?
description: Political pay structures elsewhere in Asia are shaped by factors including bureaucratic hierarchy, austerity and symbolic restraint.
content: Singapore’s ministers are among the world’s highest paid, a system its leaders have defended as necessary to attract capable people into public service and reduce the temptation of corruption. Its latest salary review has once again put the spotlight on that approach, while highlighting a wider regional divide over how Asian governments value political leadership and public service. Under the city state’s formula, the prime minister’s salary is pegged at twice the benchmark for an entry-level minister, which is based on the median annual income of the country’s top 1,000 Singaporean earners after applying a 40 per cent public-service discount. When Prime Minister Lawrence Wong’s annual pay benchmark rises to S$3.6 million (US$2.83 million) on October 15, it will be almost four times the basic annual salary of Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu. Wong has pledged to donate his S$1.4 million increase over five years, while serving ministers will only gradually move towards the S$1.8 million entry-level benchmark. For analysts, the issue extends far beyond the size of any one leader’s salary. Political pay structures reveal what governments value, what they expect citizens to accept and how much of a leader’s total compensation is visible to the public. While Singapore defends high salaries as a way to attract talent and guard against corruption, the balance looks very different across the rest of Asia – shaped instead by bureaucratic hierarchy, austerity, symbolic restraint or off-the-books perks that do not always appear in headline figures. Premium on talent Singapore’s high ministerial salaries stem from a broader choice about who should govern, according to Donald Low, a former civil servant in the city state and professor of practice in public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Rather than relying only on politicians who rise through party ranks, the long-ruling People’s Action Party (PAP) routinely recruits mid-career professionals and senior public servants. However, these new political entrants must still stand for election, engage voters and face public scrutiny, Low said. “It’s a very unusual model of how politics is done, and high ministerial salaries are almost inevitably a consequence of this model.” Low said Wong’s donation pledge and the gradual phase-in for serving ministers showed that public expectations remained a factor, even within a market-linked system. Hong Kong’s administrative benchmark Hong Kong’s chief executive also sits near the top of regional salary rankings, but that figure is set through a different system. Following a 1.3 per cent adjustment in July, Lee’s cash pay stands at about HK$475,600 (US$61,000) a month, or HK$5.71 million annually. Since 2007, the chief executive’s salary has been pegged at 112.5 per cent of the wages received by the chief secretary for administration. “Rather than asking what a political leader might earn in the private sector, Hong Kong has positioned the chief executive’s salary within an established public-service hierarchy,” Low said. The contrast also reflects different career arcs. Hong Kong’s principal officials often serve one or two terms before returning to another profession, making any private-sector pay cut temporary. “In Singapore, a ministerial appointment is more likely to become the final major phase of a person’s career,” Low said. Hong Kong’s former chief executives remain subject to a three-year post-office employment control period, which includes a total ban on outside jobs during their first year out of office. Institutionalised austerity in Japan Until December 2025, Japan’s prime minister and cabinet members who were also Diet members were entitled to additional executive pay and bonuses, in addition to their standard legislators’ salaries. However, Japanese leaders have long maintained a tradition of returning their executive pay and bonuses – a practice started by former prime minister Naoto Kan in the wake of the 2011 Fukushima disaster. What began as an emergency response survived as a long-standing norm of financial restraint under subsequent administrations. The practice was formalised when legislation was enacted last year stating that Diet members appointed as prime minister or ministers would receive no additional pay. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the change as “mi wo kiru kaikaku” – or self-sacrificing reforms. The revised law means Takaichi now receives standard Diet pay and year-end allowances, totalling about 21.9 million yen (US$141,000) annually, down from the 40 million yen figure often cited in older comparisons of Japanese prime ministers. Hidden figures and off-the-books perks In Malaysia, Anwar Ibrahim has refused a salary for both his roles as prime minister and finance chief since taking office in 2022. His cabinet also implemented a 20 per cent monthly pay cut that remains in place – gestures meant to show solidarity with citizens facing economic pressures. Bryan Cheah, a senior researcher with the anti-corruption non-government organisation Centre to Combat Corruption and Cronyism, said modest salaries and voluntary pay cuts could not answer wider questions about politicians’ wealth, investments and business interests. Malaysia has no statutory requirement for ministers and elected representatives to make comprehensive public asset declarations. “Such disclosures are entirely voluntary and lack a common protocol,” Cheah said. He pointed to instances where candidates published their bank statements during the last general election, calling them “wholly inadequate” as such documents “[do] not exclude the possibility that their wealth may be deposited with a family member”. Cheah cited enforcement cases involving the seizure of assets worth millions of ringgit as a reason official salary figures alone did not necessarily reassure the public. “Without the requisite institutional reforms that demonstrate the real earnings of ministers and elected officials, this gesture remains a gesture alone,” Cheah said. Indonesia presents a sharper divide between headline salary and the overall value of political office. A cabinet minister’s basic monthly salary is 5.04 million rupiah, with a 13.61 million rupiah position allowance bringing the published total to about 18.6 million rupiah (US$1,056). But ministers can also receive an official residence, vehicle and driver, health coverage, travel expenses and ministry-specific performance allowances. “No single public document tells a citizen what a minister actually takes home in total,” said Yanuar Nugroho, a visiting senior fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and senior lecturer at the Driyarkara School of Philosophy in Jakarta. “The 18.6 million rupiah figure is real, but it is a small and slightly misleading fraction of the real value of holding office.” President Prabowo Subianto has also floated salary cuts for ministers to improve budget efficiency. Nugroho said the gesture could matter politically, but not financially. He cited independent estimates that the move would save about 6.5 billion rupiah a year in basic pay, or 47.9 billion rupiah including allowances – roughly 0.0005 per cent of Indonesia’s 2026 state budget. Public anger over political privilege has already proved combustible. Protests erupted last August over a 50 million rupiah monthly housing allowance for legislators, before spreading nationwide after ride-hailing driver Affan Kurniawan was killed by a police vehicle. Indonesia could borrow Singapore’s clearer consolidation and disclosure of political pay, Nugroho said, without adopting its link to elite private-sector incomes. “Transparency travels,” he said. “The market-rate aspiration does not.”

title: For Phurba Tenjing Sherpa, climbing Everest now a way to help others ‘fulfil their dreams’
description: Part of a record-breaking mountaineering family, Phurba says reaching a peak ‘makes me happy’ and now enjoys sharing that joy with others.
content: Mount Everest, known to all, understood by few – including someone who has been up and down the treacherous peak almost 20 times. More than 7,500 individuals have reached the top of the highest mountain on Earth since it was first conquered by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on May 29, 1953, and there have been more than 15,780 successful ascents, with climbers and guides returning for repeated attempts. It has also claimed the lives of at least 346 people, which is the number since records began in the 1920s. Among those who have scaled the 8,849-metre (29,032-foot) giant multiple times is 18-time Everest summiteer Phurba Tenjing Sherpa, who was in Hong Kong this week for the premiere on Sunday of the Road To Everest documentary, which tells the story of Hong Kong climber Raj Gurung. Speaking to the South China Morning Post at the premiere, Phurba, who has climbed with Gurung and features prominently in the film, admitted that he used to see climbing Mount Everest as only “a job”, but now says it is “a bit of everything”. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Raj Gurung (@rajgrghk) “I was from the extremely remote Rolwaling village of Gaurishankar [mountain] in Dolakha, where we don’t have electricity, we don’t have internet and we don’t have good income sources,” the 37-year-old said. “We have no schools, and I have never been to one, but if I work in the mountains, it’s very easy to get money for me. “Now I have my own company. I am leading my group. It’s kind of like my passion, hobby and business. It’s a mix of everything.” The cost to climb Mount Everest ranges from the basic budget of US$30,000, or a little more than three times that to the more premium options. Ultra-luxury tours could start at US$150,000 and go up to 10 times the basic cost. Those numbers cover mandatory government permits and fees, including a climbing permit and garbage deposit, gear and logistics, flights, insurance, and of course Sherpa summit bonuses and tips. Born to Chhiring Nurbu Sherpa and Kimjung Sherpa, Phurba is one of 12 children in the family, and he said mountaineering was almost like a “family thing” for him, though only his siblings did it. “My father was a farmer; he took care of yaks and sheep and never climbed any mountains,” he said. “That’s why my father had many children: eight sons and four daughters.” The big group of brothers and sisters to date are holders of two Guinness World Records. Four of them have climbed Kanchenjunga, the third-highest mountain in the world at 8,586m, at the same time, in May 2019; eight siblings – six brothers and two sisters – have reached the top of the world’s highest mountain during their work as trekkers, guides and porters, as of May 2021. Three other siblings – Pasang Futi Sherpa, Lhapa Diki Sherpa and Sonam Temba Sherpa – have yet to climb, but Phurba’s elder brother, Nima Gyalzen Sherpa, who is a 14-peak conqueror and has summited Mount Everest 11 times, said any further records are unlikely as his siblings “do not climb; they are monks and Lamas and stay at home”. Widely considered to be a mountaineering legend of his generation, Phurba also held a record of his own among a list of other impressive achievements. “When I was 24 years old, I had already climbed Everest nine times; that was my record: the youngest person to climb many times,” he said. “I also had two ascents from the China side in 2007 when I was 17; that was my first time, and I did it two times within 10 days. “I had another two ascents in three days in 2008, and two ascents without supplementary oxygen in 2017. “I feel so strong at the Everest summit, and I told my mum after my third time: ‘Now I am strong enough, I can earn my money, I can allow myself to make a living [climbing]’.” While Phurba is a renowned mountaineer of Nepal today, he admitted to having had days when he wondered why people would even want to climb Mount Everest. “I was so shocked as to why people are coming here and losing their money, wasting their lives, you know? Why are they coming here?” said Phurba, who is now chief executive of Dreamers Destination Treks and Expedition. “Because there was nothing on the summit. If you are lucky, maybe you can see a little bit of the view. But why are the people coming? That was the question for myself. “But everybody comes for a dream; some people come for records, some come for other things. Now, I feel very happy when I am on the summit, because I am not going by myself but with my clients, and I help fulfil their dreams.” Phurba, who started his mountaineering career as a porter at 15, also said reaching the top of a mountain “makes me happy” and that he felt “bored” when staying in Kathmandu and not climbing a mountain. “I have to go to the mountains myself; actually I just got back from Europe. I did Mont Blanc and Matterhorn – one of the biggest, most difficult mountains in France and Switzerland,” he said. “I did two mountain summits within three days, and I just got back to Nepal yesterday, and the same night I flew here to Hong Kong.” Although he sees climbing as his way of living, the mountains have not always been friendly, at least not to his family, or those surrounding him. In 2006, he lost his brother Phurba Thundu in an avalanche on Mount Pumori. “I promised myself, my sister and my mum I would never go to the mountains. I never wanted to go to the mountains again,” Phurba said. “But I broke my promise after one year. “I went to my Rolwaling Valley, which is 4,200 metres high. Then after one year, I came back again to Kathmandu and again I went to Mount Everest.” In 2015, the Mount Everest avalanches, which were triggered by a massive 7.8-magnitude earthquake on April 25, struck Everest Base Camp and killed at least 24 people, among them Phurba’s brother-in-law. Last year, he lost three more close Sherpa team members in a devastating avalanche on Mount Yalung Ri. Phurba shared his thoughts on social media in November, saying: “I have been climbing all my life – this is the only thing I know. We mountaineers live constantly with life on one side and death on the other. “I know it is dangerous. I know we all have to die sooner or later. I know … I know! But how do I accept how fragile life is – that my brothers are not with me any more?” Still, there is unlikely to be anything that would stop Phurba from climbing mountains at all. “I like to travel! I earn money in Nepal and spend it travelling in Europe, the United States and Asia,” he said. “My wife [Rojita Buddhacharya] lives in America; she’s studying for her PhD at Howard University in Washington. “She’s doing astrophysics research and will be going to the moon in the future! She’s also an Everest summiteer and a science journalist too.” Phurba even has his 19th summit of Mount Everest planned and scheduled for next year, but he said there was never a number in his mind. Kami Rita Sherpa, from Nepal, currently holds the record for reaching the summit the most times – 32 – with his most recent one on May 17. “I don’t have exactly this kind of goal, how many times, this and that,” he said. “I keep climbing because there are many people interested in climbing with me, so I continue. “Next year I want to climb again to lead the group. People have different dreams – some want to climb Everest, some specifically want to climb with me.”

title: Southeast Asian buyers emerge as top non-local investors in Hong Kong commercial property
description: Southeast Asian capital, led by Singapore, now eclipses mainland Chinese as the city’s leading non-local commercial property investors.
content: Southeast Asian investors have emerged as the largest non-local buyers of Hong Kong commercial property, led by Singapore-based capital, according to Savills. As of Tuesday, local and non-local investors – including those from mainland China – were behind an estimated HK$30.36 billion (US$3.87 billion) in transactions involving commercial property deals above HK$50 million in Hong Kong so far this year, data compiled by the property consultancy showed. Southeast Asian investors contributed HK$3.37 billion – or more than 11 per cent – of the total value, Savills said. Mainland buyers contributed HK$1.75 billion, or 5.8 per cent, while Hong Kong-based capital accounted for HK$25.25 billion, or 83.2 per cent. “Southeast Asia’s share has risen against a much smaller non-local pool – it is roughly two-thirds of all non-local investment this year,” said Nicholas To, senior associate director for investment at Savills Hong Kong. Last year, mainland investors topped non-local buyers with HK$16.06 billion, or nearly 34 per cent, of the HK$47.32 billion total, followed by US and Canadian buyers with HK$7.58 billion, or 16 per cent. Southeast Asia ranked third with HK$1.74 billion, or 3.7 per cent, while those from Europe bought HK$940 million worth of commercial property assets or 2 per cent of the total. Western investors had been absent this year, Savills data showed. Some of the assets that Singaporean firms and investors bought so far this year included 152,000 square feet of space across several floors at The Center, which DBS Bank (Hong Kong) acquired for about HK$2.62 billion, and One Bedford Place, an office building with 184,041 square feet in Tai Kok Tsui, which Wee Hur Holdings purchased for HK$748.8 million. Although classified as an asset under residential property, luxury estate Jadebeach Villa in Chung Hom Kok, Southern district, was also acquired for nearly HK$1.17 billion by a Singapore-based group in a deal registered last week, according to Land Registry records. The Style Limited was named as the buyer of the 30-unit enclave. Its directors were Singapore passport holders Luk Kwok Wing and Wee Teng Yuan, according to the Companies Registry. Meanwhile, Centurion Holdings had provisionally agreed to purchase Yan Wo Building in North Point for HK$364 million, according to Land Registry records dated August 25. It is reportedly the local unit of Singapore-listed Centurion Corporation. To said that, based on the deals, Singapore investors fell into three categories: corporate occupiers such as DBS (Hong Kong), private family capital such as The Style Limited, and operator capital such as Wee Hur and Centurion, “which already run student accommodation platforms” in Singapore, Australia and the UK. “They are bringing an operating business into a market where policy created demand faster than supply could respond,” To said. He pointed to the “Hostels in the City” scheme, which allows commercial buildings to be converted into hostels without planning approval while preserving floor area. To said the quota for non-local students “has been raised from 20 to 40 and then 50 per cent”, further fuelling demand. Despite a potential interest rate increase, To added that Singapore-based investors were likely to keep buying Hong Kong assets. “Pricing has reset far enough for buyers without legacy Hong Kong exposure to underwrite assets that local owners are having to release,” he said. “I would expect all three [categories] to continue [buying], and the operator capital in particular to keep going into the living sector rather than into core commercial.”

title: Letters | How Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis should be judged
description: Readers discuss the mega-project being developed at the city’s northern border, and how Asian nations can ensure diversity thrives.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will preserve capitalism while creating jobs and opportunities for social mobility (“Hong Kong 5-year plan to stick with capitalism, uphold ‘one country, two systems’: John Lee”, September 14). The Northern Metropolis will be an important test, but not simply of whether government initiative can coexist with a capitalist economy. That proposition has become something of a cliché. Every successful market economy depends on public infrastructure, reliable institutions and long-term planning. The Northern Metropolis requires coordinated investment in land formation, transport, drainage, schools, healthcare, housing and environmental work that no individual company could reasonably undertake. The meaningful question is therefore not whether government should intervene, but whether its intervention enlarges the space for competition, investment and enterprise. The project should also be assessed against the correct time horizon. Large expenditure may produce immediate activity through construction contracts, employment and land transactions, but these are preliminary effects rather than the return Hong Kong should ultimately seek. The lasting return must come from higher productivity, new business formation, stronger connections with neighbouring markets and an urban environment capable of adapting as industries change. That return may take years to emerge. A long horizon, however, should not mean an absence of discipline: the government should publish milestones on costs, private investment, business occupancy and economic output so that the strategy can evolve with evidence. Most importantly, promises of jobs and upward mobility need a practical road map. Announcing employment targets is not enough. The government should identify the types of industries the Northern Metropolis is intended to support, the skills those industries will require and how residents can acquire them. Plans for vocational training, university partnerships, affordable housing and transport should be aligned with the arrival of employers. Small businesses and new entrants must also have genuine access to premises, procurement and financing, rather than opportunities being concentrated among established corporations. Preserving capitalism while pursuing government-led development should be the starting premise, not the final achievement. The real measure of the Northern Metropolis’ success will be whether public investment creates productive capacity that endures after the initial spending subsides – and whether that capacity gives ordinary people credible routes into better work, higher incomes and social advancement. Only then can the project become a source of sustained advantage for Hong Kong rather than merely another ambitious development programme. Martin Cheung Tat-ming, principal researcher, POD Research Institute Malaysia offers lessons in protecting diversity Malaysia Day offers more than a routine nod to history. It presents a timely case study for an Asia increasingly fractured by political polarisation, identity politics and economic anxiety: how can diverse, multi-ethnic societies build a common future without losing their distinct local identities? More than six decades after the Malaysian federation was formed, national cohesion across the region can no longer be taken for granted. In an era dominated by online echo chambers and divisive rhetoric, social harmony must be actively cultivated rather than passively assumed. Malaysia’s trajectory offers instructive lessons. Despite deep ethnic, religious and regional fault lines, the nation has maintained fundamental stability. Navigating the delicate relationship between peninsular Malaysia and the Bornean states of Sabah and Sarawak underscores that physical separation across the South China Sea need not dictate social or political division. While macro-level ties in trade, investment and infrastructure create the structural foundation for this federal unity, higher education provides the vital human connective tissue. Economic policies alone cannot overcome geographical isolation; meaningful interaction must bring together individuals who would otherwise inhabit parallel social worlds. As an academic, I observe daily how deliberate collaborative spaces allow young people to dismantle entrenched stereotypes. The practical value of this approach was recently demonstrated through Heriot-Watt University Malaysia’s EmPower programme. Student teams from peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak came together to tackle real-world community issues, partnering with 12 local charities and raising nearly 137,300 Malaysian ringgits (US$33,850) for initiatives tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The ultimate value lay beyond the money raised. Working side by side on tangible social challenges forced these young adults to navigate regional perspectives, confront implicit biases and build lasting mutual trust. It proved that a shared civic identity is built through action, not passive coexistence. Top-down government frameworks can establish political structures, but they cannot manufacture trust. As division increasingly commands global headlines, Malaysia Day serves as a reminder that national unity is not a static milestone but an ongoing project. Malaysia’s primary asset lies not merely in the richness of its diversity but in its sustained, everyday capacity to hold that diversity together. Dr Lee J. Peter, assistant professor, Heriot-Watt University Malaysia

title: The modular furniture trend loved by Justin Bieber, Kim Kardashian and Travis Scott
description: From Pierre Paulin’s Dune sofa to USM Modular Furniture’s iconic Haller system, modular pieces are becoming sleeker, smarter and more versatile than ever.
content: If Justin Bieber, Travis Scott or Kim Kardashian are anything to go by, then the latest must-have in interior design is a modular sofa, specifically the Dune by Pierre Paulin. Designed nearly 60 years ago in collaboration with Herman Miller, this space-age couch is enjoying a new lease of life thanks to its cool design, versatility and promise of exceptional comfort. Back in the real world, modular furniture is experiencing a renaissance beyond the living room. “Modular furniture first gained popularity in the 1970s with systems like those from Herman Miller, or Italian designs emphasising flexibility and mass production amid social and economic shifts,” explains Emma Maclean, founder of interior design studio Emma Maclean & Co. “It’s making a comeback for various reasons, including sustainability concerns and a desire for longevity in a fast-changing world. Clients want furniture that evolves with life stages, growing families, downsizing or reconfiguring for guests without constant replacements,” she says. By design, modular furniture – which is composed of interchangeable pieces – is well suited to the demands of modern life. With more people working from home and moving into urban areas, it allows for flexibility and space optimisation while promising a minimalist look. While many of today’s iterations pay homage to their predecessors – think utilitarian pieces in bold, colourful tones – there are differences, especially when it comes to aesthetics. Modern modular is sleeker thanks to engineering breakthroughs and technical advances like hidden mechanisms, resulting in more sculptural, less boxy shapes. Take, for example, the current designs of Swiss manufacturer USM Modular Furniture, which was established in the early 1960s and rose to fame with its steel-based storage and shelving systems. Its most iconic design, the USM Haller – part of the permanent collection of New York’s Museum of Modern Art – allows users to build, expand or reconfigure units thanks to a clever system of chrome-plated balls and tubes paired with powder-coated steel panels. New updates include sustainable manufacturing and smart features such as cable-free dimmable LED lighting and electromechanical locks that can be controlled via an app. “From its inception, the USM Haller system has been designed to last and continually adapt. It’s very simple, yet sophisticated,” says Laurent Crochet, CEO, France, and director, China and Japan, of USM Modular Furniture. “All new USM components and add-ons to the system are made backwards-compatible with vintage USM pieces that are half a century old.” The sheer variety of styles on the market has also expanded, with pieces such as modular sectionals and sofas built to move seamlessly between areas of the home while meeting multiple needs at once. “Styles like coffee tables with lift-tops or hidden compartments and modular media units address clutter in smaller homes while doubling as workstations. Ottomans and benches are also popular, and prove versatile as seating, footrests or coffee tables,” says Maclean. Crochet points to cabinets and low side tables, both of which fit naturally into a hybrid living space. A cabinet can double as a room divider, creating a defined home office corner, while a low table can transition from an occasional working desk by day to a coffee table by night. The idea is that everything is customisable according to the homeowner’s needs and personal taste. While there’s no doubting the practicality of modular furniture, many styles can run the risk of looking too utilitarian and segmented, which is why styling is key. Experts suggest pairing modular pieces with other luxe design elements such as sculptural lighting, natural wood accents and mixed textures to create a softer look. “Playing with contrast is becoming more popular. People love to enrich the clean, linear design of USM with organic or playful shapes, or the other way around, [to bring USM into] warm, wood-heavy interiors,” Crochet says. “In terms of colours, we’re seeing a comeback of earthy tones. Our new olive green is enjoying great popularity, and brown is experiencing a real revival,” he added. What customers value most about modular furniture, though, is the freedom to truly express themselves. “Modular furniture is more than just practical – it’s a thoughtful response to today’s key design priorities, including future-proofing and biophilic design. This approach allows your home to evolve alongside your story, rather than dictating it,” says Maclean. 5 tips for incorporating modular pieces into your home Design around your actual needs rather than a fixed layout. Prioritise versatility, and look for systems with multiple configurations. Think about details such as drawers, doors and shelving inserts to ensure a piece is used to its full potential. Go for construction that’s built to last: look for a sturdy frame, solid connections and tech-advanced hardware. Maintain visual cohesion – modular pieces can look segmented, so choose unifying elements, such as consistent materials or a cohesive colour scheme, for the rest of your space.

title: Digital Silk Road: Hong Kong acts as financial bridge between China and MENA
description: As the Middle East seeks economic diversification, Hong Kong acts as the financial gateway for investment.
content: The start and end points of the Silk Road at its historical peak are crucial to its significance. Land routes wound for thousands of miles from China over mountains and deserts, concluding in the Middle East, connecting the age’s two world leaders in scientific and economic power: the Tang dynasty and the Abbasid Caliphate. While systems of trade have radically changed in the centuries since, the modern iteration of this link, the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), has firmly established a new intercontinental network. What was cross-continental then is now intercontinental, with myriad trails connecting China to nations worldwide. Yet, while no longer the network terminus, the Middle East remains a key part of Hong Kong’s BRI investment road map. Since the start of this decade, Hong Kong’s government and industry leaders have eagerly ramped up engagement with the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Multiple delegations from Hong Kong’s education, technology, finance, and government sectors have been deployed. Chief Executive John Lee personally visited Saudi Arabia and the UAE in February 2023, followed by Qatar and Kuwait in 2025, while Financial Secretary Paul Chan journeyed to Saudi Arabia in October 2025. These excursions amassed 77 memorandums of understanding and agreements spanning trade, finance, technology, and sustainable development. These grand foundations are already yielding tangible commercial results. Alpha Lau, Director-General of Investment Promotion at InvestHK, notes, “The commercial base is already meaningful. In 2025, the Middle East was Hong Kong’s 10th largest trading partner, with bilateral trade in goods of HK$192.8 billion (US$24.7 billion), 1.8 per cent of Hong Kong’s global merchandise trade, and an average annual growth rate of 5.8 per cent over the past five years.” Diversifying the Gulf Beyond sheer trade volume, the nature of Hong Kong’s outbound investment in MENA is evolving. The early years of the BRI’s push into the region were defined by physical infrastructure like ports, industrial zones and railways. Today, investors are tapping into a much broader ecosystem. Financial professional Matteo Giovannini says, “The most significant story is not simply the number of traditional Belt and Road infrastructure projects in the Middle East. Rather, we are seeing an evolution of China-Middle East engagement towards a broader ecosystem of energy, infrastructure, industrial investment, technology, finance and logistics.” This shift perfectly aligns with the Gulf states’ race to diversify their economies away from an over-reliance on oil revenues. Achieving these long-term, innovative goals requires exactly what Hong Kong excels at providing. As Giovannini points out, these projects “require more than construction financing”. “They need international fundraising, cross-border banking, legal and professional services, risk management and access to Asian capital,” he notes. Backing this commercial pivot is a wealth of academic and professional expertise. Providing a strong institutional ballast to economic ties, more than 50 research collaborations had been forged between Hong Kong’s UGC-funded universities and MENA institutions as of November 2024. The “Digital Silk Road” ambiguity A major component of this new outbound investment wave is digital transformation. Under the banner of the “Digital Silk Road”, Chinese telecoms and tech giants like Huawei, Alibaba and Tencent have invested heavily in MENA data centres, cloud computing, and 5G networks. However, this blend of hi-tech start-ups and private joint ventures is blurring the traditional definition of the BRI, which was oriented around physical infrastructure. The initiative has increasingly become a catch-all buzzword stamped on projects with Chinese involvement for brand recognition, featuring a global mix of public and private stakeholders. Dr Zeynab Farhadi, Assistant Professor of International Relations at Hong Kong Chu Hai College, explains the resulting ambiguity: “How do we define projects that China has in Middle Eastern countries as either bilateral trade or foreign direct investment BRI projects? There are lots of questions about how we can describe a project as part of the Digital Silk Road, or what we might consider to be private-sector investments.” MENA capital accessing China While Hong Kong’s outbound efforts support MENA’s economic diversification, MENA’s reciprocal inbound investment into Hong Kong is far more laser-focused. Here, Hong Kong plays its mastered role as an advanced financial safe haven backed by robust legal protections, serving as MENA’s premier gateway to Mainland Chinese capital and assets.
