Recent milestones highlight this inbound strategy, including the October 2024 establishment of a US$1 billion joint investment fund between the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Furthermore, in February 2026, the UAE’s Central Bank was admitted to the HKMA’s Central Moneymarkets Unit, enabling direct UAE access to Mainland asset investments. Professor Michael (Jinghan) Zeng, Head of the Department of Public and International Affairs at City University of Hong Kong, says: “There has been Middle Eastern investment in Hong Kong, but so far it’s different from the way Hong Kong invests in the Middle East. The most visible Middle Eastern investment in Hong Kong is through the capital market, rather than the large-scale greenfield investment in the local economy.” Navigating risk and looking ahead Naturally, this cross-continental integration faces legitimate geopolitical headwinds. Regional tensions in the Middle East, stoked by conflicts involving the US, Israel and Iran, alongside fears that President Donald Trump’s ongoing trade war against China could open a new economic battlefront in MENA, pose undeniable risks to BRI investments. However, the overall outlook remains resilient. This optimism is anchored by the sheer volume of sovereign wealth capital seeking diversification and the deep, long-term strategic alignment between China and the Gulf states, which helps insulate these financial bridges from short-term geopolitical shocks. Lau summarises this strategic proposition: “Hong Kong’s proposition is to serve as the Asia-facing platform for Gulf capital, issuers and family offices, while helping Hong Kong and Mainland companies use the city to reach Middle Eastern growth opportunities. With its capital-market depth, professional services, international connectivity and Mainland access, Hong Kong is well placed to support a broader, more balanced and more practical partnership between Asia and the Middle East.”

title: Hong Kong’s hottest new openings, from Sugar Daddy’s Italian pastries to Japanese-Chiuchow fusion fare at Chiu San
description: Discover Hong Kong’s freshest F&B openings: Italian pastries at Sugar Daddy, Lingnan fine dining at The Canton Library, Japanese-Chiuchow fusion at Chiu San and whimsical heritage ice cream at Teemtonefai.
content: Sugar Daddy Fabio Bardi, patissier extraordinaire, wants to treat us right with … confectioneries, of course. At Sugar Daddy, the Italian colazione al bar tradition – a casual, speed- and convenience-driven breakfast at a cafe, typically consisting of coffee and a cornetto – comes to life. His signature maritozzo alla panna (a brioche bun filled with whipped cream) is the star of the show, but the chef-founder also levels up the options with a tiramisu variation. Other indulgences include a range of petite bites such as the tart yuzu cake and a handcrafted take on the Ferrero Rocher, gelatos such as pistachio and the sugar-free peanut and black sesame, and fresh cornetti. G/F, Fu Tung Building, 104 Queen’s Road East, Wan Chai The Canton Library Aqua Restaurant Group delves into the multidimensional world of Lingnan dining with The Canton Library, spreading its arms wide to honour cooking styles from across southern China, counting Guangxi, Hainanese, Chiuchow, Hakka and more within its purview. Executive chef Junno Li Zhenlong and executive dim sum chef Leung Kwok-wa commit to a coastal-contemporary approach for the menu, in which comforting creations such as succulent roast suckling pig with pickled-mustard pancakes, pan-fried buns reimagining Cantonese Da Ma Zhan claypot as dim sum, steamed pork belly with black bean and chilli, and wonton-hargow dumplings capture the diverse culinary influences inside the Lingnan region’s expansive reach. 29/F, One Peking, 1 Peking Road, Tsim Sha Tsui Chiu San Only in the cultural melting pot that is Hong Kong can a Japanese-Chiuchow fusion concept find fertile ground. Boldly venturing into uncharted territory, Chiu San experimentally marries two distinct gastronomic identities, combining the teishoku set-meal format with the umami-forward notes of both cuisines, balancing freshness and depth. Enticing dishes such as stone-grilled beef short rib doused in a Chiuchow satay sauce, soy-glazed chicken thigh marinated for 12 hours in fish sauce and finished with a black-garlic oil, deep-fried crab and shrimp balls, and plump, pomegranate-shaped chicken dumplings await. G/F, Kin Liong Mansion, 6 North Street, Kennedy Town Teemtonefai With the bricks-and-mortar opening of Teemtonefai, content creator Thomas Fung has fashioned himself something that looks a lot like the next step of growing his ice-cream empire. It was he, after all, who gave us corn-cob- and soap-bar-shaped frozen desserts, which, understandably, went viral on social media. Long awaited – 10 whole years, would you believe it – his brand, nurtured through pop-ups, collaborations and word-of-mouth hype, brings that same inimitable whimsy to a retro-nostalgic space on “Cat Street”, its 1980s look blending in seamlessly with the antique stalls. Behind the glass, crowd-pleasing classics such as Lotus Biscoff, mango sticky rice and ginger tofu pudding share space with Chinese-heritage-inspired flavours, built around spices, teas and local ingredients. G/F, 19 Upper Lascar Row, Sheung Wan

title: Carney sells Canada to global investors but says US ties still key
description: The PM shared an anecdote about how Trump gave him a key to the White House but jokingly warned that ‘maybe they’ll shoot you’.
content: Prime Minister Mark Carney pitched Canada as an investment haven on Tuesday at a gathering of global financial elite but conceded ties with the US remained crucial despite an escalating trade war. Carney convened the Canada Investment Summit as part of his push to diversify an economy he insists had grown too reliant on an increasingly protectionist US. The guest list for the event in Toronto included representatives of Gulf sovereign wealth funds, European banks, the China Investment Corporation, as well as Africa’s richest man, Nigerian tycoon Aliko Dangote, along with US investors. “Our goal is to catalyse C$1 trillion (US$720 billion) of investment in Canada over the next five years,” Carney told the event, promising tax deductions and less red tape to make the country more attractive to foreign capital. Carney said Canada had the reserves of critical minerals and clean energy that the world needs, calling these sectors the keys to “strategic autonomy”, also highlighting plans to build a new pipeline that will help bring “one million barrels of low-emission Alberta oil per day to Asian markets”. “We are unleashing our full potential as an energy superpower,” the prime minister said. He said Canada would open its four largest airports to private investment, a controversial move rejected by previous governments, which Carney said could generate billions of dollars in public revenue. The CEO of investment behemoth BlackRock, Larry Fink, told the summit that “if the Canadian government follows through with the plans that have been presented today … I do believe international capital will seek out these opportunities”. In his opening address, hours after Trump imposed new tariffs on certain Canadian goods, Carney offered an optimistic view of future US relations. “We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’ most important partner in many key areas,” he said. He recalled that the two countries had always maintained close ties, “even at times of disagreement”. When conditions allow, Canada will resume US partnership but from a “stronger” and more “independent” position, Carney said. He then shared an anecdote about a visit to the White House last year, when Trump gave him an honorary key. “He’s like, ‘Yeah, it’s a key to the White House. You just bring it, they’ll let you in,’” Carney told the audience. “And then [Trump] says, ‘Maybe they’ll shoot you.’” Trump’s public treatment of Carney has varied wildly, with the president occasionally praising the Canadian leader before mocking him as the “governor” of a US state. The prime minister said the key anecdote “sort of sums up the relationship that we have”, indicating it can be unpredictable. The summit closed with an address from former prime minister Stephen Harper, a Conservative who nevertheless has backed Liberal leader Carney’s posture towards Washington. To preserve Canadian “sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance upon the United States,” Harper said. “We cannot allow the Trump administration to hollow out our industrial capacities.” Carney later headed to Strasbourg, France, where he will become the first head of government to attend the State of the European Union address. Closer ties with the EU are at the core of Canada’s strategy to pivot away from the United States. Carney has said he is seeking a “unique alliance” with the bloc and was pressed on Tuesday for details on what that might include. He said Canada and the EU intend to hammer out their future relationship at a summit next month in Montreal. It is crucial for Canada to be “connected to partners on which we can rely”, Carney said.

title: US military fires on boats attempting to capture sailing drone off Iran
description: Central Command confirms engagement off Iranian coast as Tehran claims vessels were local fishing craft.
content: The US military said on Tuesday that it opened fire and destroyed two small Iranian boats this week that were trying to steal a drone ship in the waters off Iran, the latest back-and-forth fire in the stalemated war. Captain Tim Hawkins, US Central Command spokesman, said the Iranian boats “recently attempted to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel” but failed after the military “forcefully responded”. Iranian state media reported on Monday that a pair of fishing boats came under attack in Hormozgan province on Iran’s southern coast and that several fishermen were reported missing, citing a provincial official. It is the latest volley of fire in the more than six-month-old war as both sides seek control over the Strait of Hormuz, where the US has succeeded in recent weeks in loosening Iran’s grip over the critical energy shipping corridor. But the impact of the unpopular conflict has driven up the cost of oil and petrol prices, posing political problems for US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party before November’s congressional midterm elections. “Oil will drop like a rock as soon as the Military Conflict with Iran is over, and that will not be long,” Trump asserted in a social media post on Monday. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called the foreign minister of Oman to discuss the Gulf Arab country’s efforts to de-escalate tensions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the State Department said. Global oil markets have been further roiled by increased attacks from Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen against Saudi Arabia’s shipping and infrastructure. The new front in the Middle East conflict has cut off or hindered alternate routes for Saudi Arabia to get its oil to the world, including an attack days ago that damaged its biggest pipeline and advances that strengthened the Houthis’ ability to choke off Saudi oil exports out of the Red Sea. Besides the hit to the global economy, new reports out of Washington have detailed the US costs for the war against Iran, the reduction to stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors, and the damage that has been inflicted on American aircraft, bases and diplomatic outposts. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office said on Tuesday that the war has cost the Pentagon more than US$38 billion through August 1 and will cost up to US$3 billion a month or more depending on the intensity of the conflict. That figure largely aligns with what Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has told Congress that the fighting has cost so far. The CBO said the war is expected to contribute to inflation into the first quarter of next year. Iranian strikes also have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in the Middle East as well as dozens of American aircraft and drones, according to a report from the Pentagon inspector general released on Monday. Hawkins said Tuesday the sea drone involved in the latest clash is a “Saildrone” – a small, roughly eight-metre (25-foot) craft – which can operate by itself. US Central Command has been using them in the region for several years to surveil maritime traffic. Hawkins said all of the command’s surface drones “remain fully accounted for”. The military has long asserted that the technology on the Saildrones is commercially available and not sensitive in nature. Ahmad Nafisi, Hormozgan’s deputy governor, told the Islamic Republic News Agency that the two boats came under attack on Monday evening from what he described as an “enemy drone” in the Persian Gulf. The IRNA report did not mention an attempt by Iranian forces to seize a US drone. The latest incident, which was reported earlier by Axios, comes a week after Iranian state television reported that the country’s navy captured one of the US military’s underwater drones at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Hawkins said then that an Anduril Dive-LD drone had malfunctioned while it was surveying the waters in the region and the US military no longer had possession of it. He stressed that the drone was defective and noted that it was also an “older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”.

title: Editorial | To combat scams, Hong Kong needs stronger crackdowns, greater vigilance
description: The police’s latest efforts are encouraging, but with one Hongkonger duped by a fraudulent call every hour, there’s no room for complacency.
content: Hong Kong rightly prides itself on being one of the world’s safest cities with regard to violent crime. Yet the latest deception figures make clear that safety on the streets is no guarantee of safety over the phone and internet. Police are to be commended for their recent operations that smashed sophisticated fraud syndicates, including those employing hotel rooms as call centres and identity cards forged using artificial intelligence (AI) to launder money. But the underlying trend is hardly reassuring. Deception remains an entrenched, evolving problem that demands not only more forceful crackdowns but also greater public vigilance. The recent wave of unauthorised credit card transactions linked to pre-orders of Apple’s newest iPhones, involving more than 1,200 transactions worth HK$25 million (US$3.2 million), is another reminder of the city’s prevalent tech-scam problem. In the first half of 2026, the total number of deception cases edged down by 0.7 per cent compared with the same period last year while losses fell 0.8 per cent to HK$3.51 billion. Despite the nominal decreases, the trend appears to be persistent. Phishing scams surged 61 per cent to 1,113 cases, while phone scams jumped 45 per cent to 4,830 cases, with losses from phone scams alone reaching HK$900 million – up 56 per cent. Put simply, phone and online scams remain an issue of grave public concern. Police warnings must not be ignored. On average, one resident falls for a phishing scam every four hours and another is duped by a fraudulent call every hour. Each phone scam victim loses an average of HK$270,000. The largest single phone scam loss in the first half of this year involved nearly HK$4 million. The victim was tricked by scammers pretending to be customer service staff into making 13 bank transfers after clicking a WhatsApp link. The most rampant tactic now is impersonating customer service officers, accounting for nearly half of phone scams. Scammers send fake SMS alerts or place calls alleging delivery failures, account anomalies, urgent payments required or the need to cancel supposedly activated insurance policies. Victims are directed to counterfeit websites that mimic the real platforms, then instructed to enter account numbers, passwords and one-time codes – effectively handing over the keys to their personal finances. Deception cases accounted for nearly half of all reported crimes last year, with online investment fraud generating the highest losses: 5,135 cases involving losses of HK$3.58 billion, up 58.4 per cent. Even as total cases dipped slightly in 2025, the absolute level – 43,212 cases and HK$8.1 billion in losses – remains too high. This is not a marginal problem; it is a structural threat to personal and public wealth as well as confidence in digital commerce and crime prevention. Stronger law enforcement action is essential. The latest operation against a phone scam syndicate saw officers raid two hotels in Yuen Long and Tsuen Wan and arrest 269 suspects in connection with 203 cases involving HK$320 million. Commendable as that is, the crackdown will not necessarily undo the victims’ losses. Many more syndicates continue to prey on the weak and vulnerable every day. The first line of defence is heightened vigilance. Although it seems like common sense, the appeal to treat every unsolicited call or message about money, deliveries or accounts as deception until verified is, unfortunately, often ignored. Protecting one’s digital identity is equally important. Police have uncovered syndicates using AI-edited images to forge Hong Kong identity cards and open bank accounts for money laundering, and have warned the public never to share selfie photographs that can be misused to create convincing forgeries. Scammers are organised, cross-border operations and quick to adopt new tools, from AI-generated IDs to mass-generated fraudulent messages. Law enforcement, banks, tech platforms and companies must deepen intelligence sharing and take stronger action. Better safeguards for digital transactions are also needed. A more sceptical public makes each of us a harder target – and collectively raises the cost of doing fraud. In a city where one person is phished every four hours, vigilance is not optional but an essential part of online security and self-defence.

title: She’s telling Hong Kong’s culinary stories through an Instagram ‘staging’ series
description: Mel Ng’s series is a showcase of behind-the-scenes kitchen storytelling, from fish ball joints to Michelin-starred restaurants and beyond.
content: Mel Ng tosses a beef burger patty from one hand to the other. A vlogging camera sits atop a stainless steel container, filming her every move. The 36-year-old is working for the day at The Diplomat, a cocktail bar in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood famed for its globally ranked Wagyu burger. Next to her, the bar’s founder, John Nugent, explains the burger components to Ng ahead of service, while passing around slices of American orange cheddar to taste. The Diplomat was the 31st stop in Ng’s stagiaire series on Instagram; “stagiaire” is the French term for intern, commonly used in professional kitchens to describe a short-term, typically unpaid internship. Since posting her first stagiaire video in October 2025 on her account @melngtf, the culinary creative has staged in both traditional and modern kitchens in Hong Kong and abroad, from Ha Ming Kee, a famous fish ball noodle restaurant in Hong Kong, to Salira, a modern Indonesian restaurant in Jakarta. “The Hong Kong craft side to my staging series really resonates with a lot of diaspora people who are overseas, which is great because I feel like it’s like a way to connect people back to their roots,” Ng says. Stepping out from behind the camera Despite growing her account to nearly 55,000 followers on social media in less than a year, being a content creator is only a small part of Ng’s identity. Behind the camera, she has been running food and beverage (F&B) consultancy Off Mnu since 2019, helping clients with menu research, branding and operations. She is also the co-founder of Rumah, an Indonesian dessert brand she founded with content creator Kelly “Spoon” Chan in 2023. “I’ve never been a camera-facing person,” Ng says. “I’m quite introverted, so I actually don’t like being in front of the camera.” Chan pushed her into making content to enhance Ng’s identity as an F&B consultant. “She saw that I had a good network within the F&B community and thought that I could really do something with that,” Ng says. Ng initially began staging at restaurants where she already had connections, but as the series grew, businesses began inviting her into their kitchens instead. The Diplomat was one of them. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mel (@melngtf) “I don’t think I’ve ever had their food before [the stage],” Ng says (she usually gets burgers from Shake Shack instead). “Within a 30-minute time frame, 15 burgers went out. It was right when they opened at 6pm.” The staging series also brought her into the kitchens of local businesses, such as Chinese preserved sausage maker Yue Wo Hop Kee. “It’s very interesting because I would have never thought that these small heritage brands would be open to something like this,” Ng says, explaining that second-generation owners of family businesses tend to be more receptive to brand building and social media. ‘It’s tough work’ Before making content, Ng initially wanted to build a food festival, which she quickly realised would not be a profitable endeavour. “After that I was like, ‘Hmm, what else can I do?’” she says. “I started scrolling on Instagram and saw a lot of people doing behind-the-scenes chef content.” Given her industry network, as well as a lack of similar kitchen content in Hong Kong at the time, Ng saw an opportunity to showcase more insider knowledge, “rather than a normal foodie influencer perspective where you just go and show what you’re eating at the restaurant”. In her videos, Ng reveals the behind-the-scenes process of professional kitchens, from prepping ingredients to learning cooking techniques, such as for the hollow spring rolls at Duddell’s, a one-Michelin-starred Cantonese restaurant in Central. At the time of her first staging video in October 2025, the food services industry in Hong Kong was struggling with an unemployment rate of 5.7 per cent. That figure leapt to 6.4 per cent the following quarter. “First, I thought [the series] would be a great recruitment tool for chefs or people who are interested in entering the industry,” she explains. “The staging series was also a way for me to help diners understand what goes on behind restaurants and the operations – and it’s tough work.” From business to cooking Ng did not initially plan on working in food. After graduating from Chinese International School, she moved to Boston, in the US state of Massachusetts, to study business at Northeastern University. “I did not like it at all,” Ng recalls. “I did not feel like that was what I was meant to do or had any interest in those jobs.” During her undergraduate studies, Ng cooked often and hosted friends frequently, which partially inspired her to enrol in the International Culinary Centre in New York. “I’m gonna be honest. The reason I went to culinary school was that I wanted to move to New York,” she admits. “I knew that I wanted to be in the industry, but not specifically a chef. I thought culinary school was a good starting point.” After finishing culinary school, she brought what she had learned back home and into her first kitchen at Little Bao, chef May Chow’s modern Chinese bao restaurant, in 2013. “Little Bao was just opening on Staunton Street, so I helped with the opening – just as a part-timer because I wanted to ease my way into the industry,” she says. After a short stint at the restaurant, Ng spent a few months at the then newly opened Nur, a plant-focused fine-dining restaurant that later earned and lost a Michelin star, and ceased operations in 2016. At Nur, Ng realised she did not want to be a full-time cook. “I didn’t spend too much time in kitchen jobs in general because I found out very early on that doing it full time wasn’t really for me,” she says. Moving away from full-time cooking Nur introduced her to her mentor, who brought her onto her first menu consulting jobs. “He was a very, very good mentor to me. I learned a lot from him,” she says. Her next gig was at the co-working company Campfire, where she learned about the operational side of F&B projects and businesses, before moving on to the now-closed F&B incubator PMQ Taste Kitchen, where chefs could rent space for restaurant pop-ups. “There was one month where we couldn’t find a chef to do a pop-up. So I proposed, how about I try to do a concept myself?” Ng recalls. That was how Sando Ba was born, Ng’s pop-up concept that offered one sandwich: a Wagyu sando, with slices of toasted bread sandwiching a battered Wagyu steak, cut into four tidy pieces. “I did it for a month, and the concept took off,” she says. “It did really, really, really well to the point where there was this lady, a gallery owner from Beijing, who came to eat at my pop-up and she flew me to Beijing and was like, ‘Do you wanna open your concept in our gallery, in our museum?’” While Ng declined the offer, other doors kept opening. From branding requests to consultations, her pop-up helped start her consulting business Off Mnu. Today, her journey has temporarily led her back into kitchens. “There are always new ways or new roles to approach the industry,” she says. “My role is constantly changing. When the industry was at a low, that’s when I started doing content creation.” Despite now spending more time in professional kitchens, cooking for and hosting friends is now a thing of the past. “I’ve become even more introverted now,” she says. “I’m constantly evolving. I don’t really set anything in stone … I just go with the flow.” Ng’s five favourite stagiaire experiences Kamcentre Roast Goose “Siu mei [roast meats] is something we all grow up with in Hong Kong, and I think it’s definitely a dying trade. Everybody that you see in a siu mei shop is part of the older generation. There’s hardly any young blood entering this trade because of how tough it is. When I staged there, the sifu started work at 6am and he did everything by himself. His capacity for multitasking is crazy.” Yue Wo Hop Kee “This was my first experience learning about Hong Kong craft, so it was very memorable. I staged the day before it closed for Chinese New Year, so it was very special. Seeing this 50-year-old tradition of handmade Chinese sausage is a reminder of why these crafts are worth fighting for.” Ha Ming Kee “I’ve been eating fish balls since I was a child, and I can’t believe I didn’t know how fish balls were made. Everything is still made entirely by hand. No machines, just decades of pure muscle memory – from hand-kneading the fish paste to folding the perfect wonton.” Duddell’s “[This was] obviously more high-end Chinese cuisine, Cantonese cuisine, but what was memorable for me was that I have always wanted to learn how to make that spring roll puff. That’s where I learned the technique to make the puffed spring roll.” Wah Kee/Peter Seafood “When it comes to suppliers, it’s tied between these two: Wah Kee and Peter Seafood. It’s very interesting to see where restaurants get their produce. Peter Seafood is the bridge between the ocean and Hong Kong’s best menus. For Wah Kee, it’s intense, manual labour, but the quality of the vegetables and microgreens gives you a whole new respect for the supply chain.”

title: Top Chinese official leads 87-member committee for Tung Chee-hwa state funeral
description: Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and No 1 vice-chairman of CPPCC, is funeral committee head, with vigil on Saturday and public memorial service on Sunday.
content: The first vice-chairman of the nation’s top political advisory body is overseeing an 87-member committee of political and business heavyweights to arrange the state funeral for Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa. A vigil will be held from 3pm to 10pm on Saturday at the Hong Kong Funeral Home in North Point and a public memorial service will start at 9am on Sunday, according to an obituary placed by Tung’s family in the South China Morning Post on Tuesday. “In lieu of flowers, please make donations to charities of your choice,” the obituary read. The government announced on Wednesday night that members of the public could sign condolence books between Friday and Sunday at Moreton Terrace Activities Centre in Causeway Bay, Kai Tak Community Hall or Sai Lau Kok Garden Multipurpose Room in Tsuen Wan. Details of the state funeral were also announced in an advertisement published in the SCMP, with Shi Taifeng, Politburo member and top vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), heading the funeral committee. The committee has four deputy directors: Leung Chun-ying, a CPPCC vice-chairman and former Hong Kong chief executive; Wang Dongfeng, a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and CPPCC vice-chairman and secretary general; Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO); and current city leader John Lee Ka-chiu. The remaining 82 members include tycoons, political and business leaders from Hong Kong and mainland China. Among them are: Wang Yonghong, deputy secretary general of the State Council and a Central Committee member; Zhou Ji, liaison office director; Dong Jingwei, head of Beijing’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong; and local foreign ministry chief Cui Jianchun. Other members are billionaire businessmen Li Ka-shing, Peter Woo Kwong-ching, Henry Cheng Kar-shun and Peter Lee Ka-kit, former Macau chief executive Edmund Ho Hau-wah, former secretary for justice Elsie Leung Oi-sie, former Legislative Council presidents Jasper Tsang Yok-sing and Rita Fan Hsu Lai-tai and ex-chief executive of Bank of East Asia David Li Kwok-po. Also on the list are former city leaders Donald Tsang Yam-kuen and Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor, former chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority Joseph Yam Chi-kwong and president of the Legislative Council Starry Lee Wai-king, who is also Hong Kong’s sole delegate to China’s top legislative body, the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok, Chief Justice Andrew Cheung Kui-nung and various legislators are also committee members. The Hong Kong Jockey Club said on Wednesday that the race meeting scheduled on Sunday at Sha Tin Racecourse would be cancelled as a mark of respect for Tung’s funeral. All off-course betting branches will also be closed on Sunday. The SCMP previously reported that Tung would be honoured with a state funeral for his service as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework. The former city leader died peacefully in hospital with family members by his side last Tuesday at the age of 89. Following his death, Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to one country, two systems” and a “renowned patriot”. Since the 1997 handover, only two other local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Similar to Tung, both served as vice-chairs of the CPPCC. The state funerals of Ann and Fok were coordinated by the central government, with the committees handling the arrangements each chaired by a CPPCC vice-chairman. The committee for Ann’s funeral had 65 people, while Fok’s had 74. Both funerals were also attended by senior mainland Chinese officials, including the HKMAO director, with the coffins draped in the national flag and state leaders laying wreaths in tribute. Ann, a textile entrepreneur, was regarded as one of a handful of capitalists who had the ear of Chinese president Deng Xiaoping in the early 1980s and held key positions in major bodies that Beijing formed to prepare for the handover. Tung and Fok served as two of the eight pallbearers at Ann’s funeral at the Hong Kong Funeral Home after he died of heart complications at 88. Ann was buried in Dapengwan Cemetery in Shenzhen. The other pallbearers at the time included both mainland and local officials, including Leung, as well as the late entertainment tycoon Run Run Shaw and two of Ann’s long-time business partners. Fok, a tycoon with gambling, port and property interests, died on October 28, 2006, in Beijing at the age of 83 after a long battle with cancer. His coffin was flown to Hong Kong several days later in accordance with his wishes to be buried back home. His funeral was also held at the Hong Kong Funeral Home. He was buried at the Hong Kong Buddhist Cemetery in Chai Wan. Headed by Wang Zhongyu, a CPPCC vice-chairman at the time, the committee for Fok’s funeral had four deputy directors: then HKMAO director Liao Hui; Liu Yandong, head of the United Front Work Department at the time; Tung; and then chief executive Donald Tsang Yam-kuen. As Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung played a pivotal role in implementing the then-untested and novel one country, two systems model, under which the city has been administered since the end of British colonial rule in 1997. After resigning as city leader in March 2005 for health reasons, Tung went on to assume a prominent role at the national level and increasingly came to be regarded as an elder statesman.

title: Hong Kong commercial property downturn to worsen amid tightening credit: agents
description: Tighter bank lending is further weakening demand for commercial property in Hong Kong, and could tip the market into a ‘vicious cycle’, agency warns.
content: Commercial property prices in Hong Kong are likely to continue their downward spiral, as the market risks getting trapped in a “vicious cycle” of tighter bank lending and weakening demand, a property agency has warned. Banks in the city had adopted a more conservative approach towards approving mortgages for commercial properties over the past three years, introducing stricter approval standards and terms, said Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services, at a press conference on Tuesday. Only about 20 per cent of commercial property transactions in Hong Kong this year have involved mortgage loans – a sharp decline compared with levels seen during the market’s peak in the early 2010s, according to Tso. “In reality, only very powerful end users and investors are buying commercial properties these days,” Tso said. “Currently, only medium and small banks are more proactive in offering these mortgages in Hong Kong, while large banks tend to avoid the risks.” By contrast, when Hong Kong’s commercial property market was at its height in 2012 and 2013, about 30 to 40 per cent of transactions involved mortgages, Tso recalled. “Nowadays, banks – especially large banks – are reassessing loan customers,” Tso said. “These assessments include the mortgage applicant’s background and repayment ability, as well as their asset liquidity.” Banks will still lend money to those with strong financial backing, but it depends on the industry, according to Tso. They were also approving loans based on a property’s valuation, he added. “Banks tend to be more lenient when approving mortgages for commercial properties with larger scale, concentrated in grade A office buildings, and with more active trading,” Tso said. Some commercial property prices in Hong Kong have fallen by more than 40 per cent from their historical highs, according to Dave Ma Tai-yeung, CEO of Midland IC&I. Prices were still “in the process of bottoming out”, Ma said, with the average price per square foot for grade A and grade B commercial space hitting record lows. In August, grade A office prices were down 48.5 per cent from historical highs on average, while grade B office prices were down 49.2 per cent, according to Midland IC&I. Prices for industrial buildings were 37.2 per cent below their peak, while retail shop prices were down 47.1 per cent. Though the volume of commercial property transactions in the first eight months of 2026 rose 14.5 per cent year on year to 3,494, the combined value of those transactions was down 3.5 per cent year on year at HK$36.2 billion (US$4.6 billion), Midland IC&I data showed. The price downturn threatens to become self-reinforcing, given the importance of commercial real estate (CRE) as a form of collateral for corporate loan financing, according to Ma. “If CRE prices and rental values continue to decline, the borrowing capacity of owners and businesses may decrease, and some borrowers may face difficulties in supplementing collateral, accelerating repayments or refinancing,” he said. “If the market adjustment is too rapid, it could create a vicious cycle of valuation downgrades, credit tightening, forced sales and further price declines.” Rising caution from lenders risked harming swathes of the CRE market, Ma warned. “If banks generally become more cautious due to risk management considerations, not only will highly leveraged landlords or those with weak rental cash flow be affected, but the working capital turnover of retail, catering, logistics, trade, professional services and other SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises) may also be put under pressure,” he said. Ma believes that banks should focus on borrowers’ repayment ability, rental cash flow and business prospects, and provide appropriate refinancing or restructuring arrangements for CRE owners and SMEs with actual operating incomes, good repayment records and feasible restructuring options.

title: Meet Ethan Hawke’s youngest daughter Indiana, who made a rare red carpet appearance
description: Unlike her older half-sister Maya Hawke, who starred in Stranger Things, the Dead Poets Society actor’s youngest child with his second wife keeps a low profile.
content: Ethan Hawke recently made a rare appearance with his daughter Indiana Hawke at the Deauville American Film Festival in France on September 4. Indiana, 15, is the youngest of Hawke’s four children. He shares daughter Maya and son Levon with ex-wife Uma Thurman, and welcomed daughters Clementine and Indiana with second wife Ryan Shawhughes Hawke. Here’s everything you need to know about Ethan Hawke’s youngest daughter, Indiana. How did her parents meet? Hawke and Ryan married in 2008 after the Dead Poets Society actor met the Hollywood producer when she worked as a nanny for his children with Thurman. “I met Ryan through my literary agent, and she was indeed one of Maya and Levon’s nannies during a film shoot,” Hawke told The Guardian in 2009. “After a short period of working for me, Ryan went back to Columbia to get her degree. There were never any scandalous thoughts or actions back then. In the years that followed, my marriage disintegrated due to many pressures, none of which were remotely connected to Ryan.” The pair reconnected a year after Hawke and Thurman’s divorce in 2005. They welcomed Clementine Jane in 2008, and Indiana in July 2011. Will Indiana Hawke follow in her father’s footsteps? Hawke’s older children Maya and Levon have chosen to follow in their famous parents’ footsteps; Maya starred in Stranger Things, and Levon is set to appear in the upcoming queer film Girls Like Girls. Meanwhile, Clementine and Indiana have stayed largely out of the limelight except for rare red carpet appearances supporting their father. While she has yet to show off her acting chops, Indiana seems to enjoy music and even participated in a singalong with her three older siblings and father during the Covid-19 pandemic, as seen in an Instagram video shared by Maya in 2020.

title: Celebrated Everest guide Phurba Tenjing Sherpa fears way of life under threat
description: The veteran guide has scaled Earth’s highest peak 18 times, but worries global warming and societal change could put an end to climbing.
content: Phurba Tenjing Sherpa has climbed Mount Everest 18 times over the years but fears he may now be a dying breed, with climate change one day making it unscalable and societal change leaving fewer willing to risk its dangers. The 37-year-old, who runs his own business guiding people up and down Earth’s highest peak, said one of the biggest challenge his industry faced was the fact “the Sherpa community is no longer climbing”. While the veteran guide said he had never been to school, he believed the younger generation from Nepal had greater opportunities available when it came to education and making a living. “Young Sherpas are no longer going to the mountains because they are well educated,” Phurba said. “They have now moved to America, Canada, Australia and Europe because the mountains are quite dangerous and the earnings are low. In the future, a shortage of sherpas is going to be a big problem.” The Sherpa people are often associated with mountaineering, with many working as climbing guides, trekkers and porters in the Himalayan region. In the Road To Everest documentary film, which captured his ascent in May last year, Raj Gurung, an Everest summitter from Hong Kong, hailed the importance of the ethnic group. “We can never overemphasise their work. From logistics to guiding people safely, they do everything,” the 53-year-old said. “Without the Sherpas, I don’t think anyone could climb these mountains.” But a shortage of expert guides is not the only threat to mountaineering in the Himalayas. Global warming has resulted in melting glaciers and the loss of a vital source of drinking water for climbers. Rising temperatures are also thinning the Khumbu Glacier and melting the snow cover, exposing historic climbing paths, bodies and rubbish. “The effect of global warming is happening so fast. In the future, there will be no glaciers, no snow and no water,” Phurba said. “Even now, some mountains like Ama Dablam and Island Peak have no snow. “No snow means no glaciers and no water, so we can’t climb mountains because we melt snow to drink. We cannot carry enough water.” Thawing permafrost also destabilises rock faces, increasing the long-term risk of rockfalls and avalanches. However, this merely changes the level of difficulty rather than closing the mountain entirely. “Based on experience, there used to be much more snow on the mountains, which made climbing relatively safer,” Gurung added. “Now, due to melting glaciers, bare black rocks are exposed, significantly increasing the risk of rockfalls.”

title: Rob Reiner’s son Nick won’t face death penalty in trial for parents’ killing
description: The Hollywood icon and his wife Michele Singer were found stabbed to death at their home in an affluent Los Angeles neighbourhood.
content: The son of Hollywood icon Rob Reiner will not face the death penalty when he stands trial over the killings of his parents, Los Angeles County’s top prosecutor said on Tuesday. Nick Reiner, who turned 33 on Monday, was arrested in December 2025 after his parents’ bloodied bodies were discovered at their home in the affluent Brentwood neighbourhood of Los Angeles. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder, with the special circumstance allegations of multiple murders and murder by means of lying in wait. Rob Reiner, 78 – the director behind classics including When Harry Met Sally and A Few Good Men – and his wife Michele Singer, 70, were stabbed to death. Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said the decision not to pursue the death penalty followed “rigorous review” including discussions with the Reiner family. “They made their views very clear,” Hochman said at an early morning press briefing, referring to Nick Reiner’s siblings, Jake and Romy Reiner. “We took their views into consideration in ultimately deciding not to seek the death penalty.” The maximum sentence Nick Reiner will face is life in prison without possibility of parole. The prosecutor estimated a trial would not begin before 2027. Nick Reiner had a history of addiction and mental health issues. He lived in a guest house on his parents’ property and had attended a party at the home of comedian Conan O’Brien with his parents before their deaths, an event at which some attendees reportedly said he had behaved erratically. Rob Reiner, the son of legendary comedian Carl Reiner, started his showbiz career in acting. He won fame as the oafish son-in-law Michael “Meathead” Stivic on groundbreaking 1970s sitcom All in the Family before transitioning to directing. As a director, his output included classic films like 1984’s rock music mockumentary This is Spinal Tap, fantasy gem The Princess Bride from 1987 and seminal coming-of-age film Stand By Me.

title: Ed Sheeran tour in trouble as support acts quit over pro-Palestinian speech fallout
description: Musicians withdraw from British singer’s shows in solidarity with Macklemore after promoter drops rapper.
content: Ed Sheeran’s tour of North and South America was plunged into chaos Tuesday when four of his supporting acts abruptly quit in solidarity with the rapper Macklemore, who was dropped for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Hours after Sheeran posted on social media about Macklemore’s ousting and attributed the decision to the tour’s promoters, Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, the Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas posted on social media that they were leaving the tour. Rowe and Lukas Graham would have been replacements for Macklemore on Sheeran’s remaining US dates, while Beoga had been performing several songs – including some the Irish folk band co-wrote – with Sheeran around the middle of each set. Finneas, who is Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year. “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas said on social media. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.” The moves by his fellow artists put enormous pressure on Sheeran, who has tried to avoid politics and taking sides in the Gaza conflict, arguing that his fans do not come to his shows to hear politics. Rowe and Beoga each cited their country’s history in their statements explaining their decision. “We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be,” Beoga said. Rowe called Sheeran a friend and said the British singer-songwriter changed his life. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” he said, adding that he couldn’t “stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up”. Meanwhile, Lukas Graham, the band that had hits with “Mama Said” and “7 Years”, expressed gratitude to Sheeran and called it “a difficult decision”. “Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge,” the band posted, seemingly referring to billionaire Robert Kraft’s role in Macklemore’s removal from the tour. Emails seeking comment were sent to Sheeran and the tour’s promoter, the Messina Touring Group. Sheeran weighed in on Macklemore being dropped after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments onstage during their tour, saying the decision was made by the promoters alone. The British singer also said he refused to be drawn into a public discussion about the war in Gaza. “Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” Sheeran said on social media on Tuesday. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living.” Sheeran’s statement came a day after Macklemore said he was kicked off the Loop Tour after exclaiming “Free Palestine!” during the September 5 date at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium while introducing his protest song “Hind’s Hall”. “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you,” he said during the concert. Macklemore said on Monday on social media that several US venues told the promoter they would prohibit him from performing as Sheeran’s opening act, rallied by Kraft, owner of the NFL’s New England Patriots. His Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where the Patriots play. In a statement on Monday, Kraft said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”. Kraft’s representatives did not immediately respond to a Tuesday email seeking comment about the other musical artists’ actions. A growing chorus of organisations and experts say Israel’s wartime actions in Gaza amount to genocide – an accusation Israel vehemently rejects. Macklemore was scheduled to perform at eight of the 10 shows Sheeran has remaining on his stadium tour, which is scheduled to resume Saturday in Philadelphia. Ahead are stops at Gillette Stadium, Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium and Indianapolis’ Lucas Oil Stadium. In his social media post, Sheeran said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge”, but that “the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final”. He said that he tries to use his music to “bring people from all backgrounds and cultures together” and that while he has personal views about “this devastating conflict”, he chooses not to speak publicly because people who come to his shows “do not expect a political forum”. He added: “I am not complicit”. “I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes,” Sheeran added. “However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed.”

title: In Focus | Will China’s new local surtax provide relief for its regions’ fiscal headaches?
description: Analysts say the proposed surtax – a reworking of three local revenue sources into one semi-autonomous levy – should help streamline finances.
content: As even China’s wealthiest provinces continue to run deficits and rely on the central government to make ends meet, Beijing is loosening the reins on the country’s highly centralised fiscal system, with legislation for a new tax category – the local surtax – under way. Late last month, the Ministry of Finance unveiled a draft local surtax law for public consultation. The proposed tax would merge three existing levies – the urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge and local education surcharge – and would be charged on value-added tax (VAT) and consumption tax payments. Provincial governments would be allowed to set rates within an 11 to 13 per cent range. Analysts described the move as a modest but constructive step in China’s broader fiscal reform agenda. While far from a cure-all for local financial distress, the change would give local authorities much-needed flexibility to manage their spending, they said. “It appears that the top leadership has heard the calls [for fiscal reform] and is aware that many localities, including coastal regions, are becoming cash-strapped,” said a frontline official with a local finance department in Zhejiang. Although the eastern province is among China’s most financially self-sufficient, it still posted a fiscal deficit of 360.6 billion yuan (US$53.8 billion) in 2025. During China’s property boom, local authorities were able to rake in huge sums from selling land, enabling them to balance their books even as they handed over most tax revenue to the central government. But a prolonged slump in the housing market has effectively closed off that source of income, leaving local governments under mounting pressure as they fund an expanding range of public services for a rapidly ageing population – from public transport to healthcare – and work to meet heavy bond repayment obligations. The proposed local surtax marks the first move towards rebalancing the skewed fiscal relationship between China’s central and local governments – a long-term reform mandate laid out by the ruling Communist Party’s Central Committee at a plenum in July 2024. “There is only one core reason the central government is pushing ahead with this reform this year – it’s time for fiscal rebalancing,” said Li Xin, a partner at Shenzhen-based DeHeng Law Offices. “Local authorities are under such acute fiscal strain that adjustments have become unavoidable.” Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution Finance official, Zhejiang How does the new surtax work? Representing a “major component of China’s fiscal and taxation reform”, the proposed local surtax is poised to become “the largest single tax category” in China’s local tax system and a pillar source of income for provincial authorities, according to Tian Zhiwei, director of the Institute of Public Policy and Governance at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. But it was not designed to boost fiscal revenue, analysts from Moody’s Ratings said in a report this month, adding that the proposed local surtax rate was broadly aligned with the combined effective burden of the three existing charges it would replace, and that overall fiscal revenue was likely to remain broadly unchanged. Under the current system, the urban maintenance and construction tax is levied at 7 per cent, 5 per cent or 1 per cent of VAT and consumption tax payments, depending on the taxpayer’s location, while the education surcharge and local education surcharge are fixed at 3 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively. In 2025, the effective combined rate nationwide stood at 11.6 per cent, according to Xinhua, compared with the 11 to 13 per cent range proposed under the new legislation. The reform would change the institutional status of these revenue streams from three sources distributed across tax, non-tax and government fund accounts to a single tax that would be fully retained by local governments, the Moody’s analysts said, adding that this would improve revenue transparency and simplify fiscal administration. A key proposed change concerns the two education-related surcharges: by raising their status from fees to taxes, the reform would give provincial governments greater flexibility in spending the proceeds. Currently, the two surcharges are earmarked for education-related spending, including the purchase of teaching equipment and school building renovations. If enacted, the new law would allow local authorities to use the revenue at their discretion. In 2025, combined proceeds from the two education-related surcharges reached 396.4 billion yuan, according to Xinhua. If enacted, the reform would allow local governments to redirect the revenue towards repaying maturing debt and meeting civil service payrolls, with civil servants facing pay cuts and delayed salary payments even in some of China’s wealthiest regions. “Turning fees into tax and making it an income stream for local authorities marks a step towards a bigger solution,” the Zhejiang official said, on condition of anonymity. Meanwhile, experts said the reform would also streamline tax collection and cut compliance costs. “On collection, three separate sets of rules will be consolidated into one … Taxpayers will only need to submit one tax return, lowering manpower-related costs for both businesses and tax authorities,” said Li, the Shenzhen lawyer. With the two fees’ conversion into taxes, taxpayers who failed to pay or who underpaid their liabilities would face penalties, including overdue payment surcharges and fines, she added. “This gives local tax authorities much stronger incentives to bolster tax collection,” Li said. Relief for cash-strapped local governments? In total, the three revenue sources generated 913.4 billion yuan last year, according to Xinhua. Although the proposed local surtax would be the largest tax source fully retained by local governments, its revenue would remain relatively modest. Last year, domestic VAT revenue reached 6.9 trillion yuan (US$1.0 trillion), half of which is allocated to local governments under the current revenue-sharing arrangement. Corporate income tax revenue totalled 4.1 trillion yuan, and personal income tax revenue amounted to 1.6 trillion yuan. The central government kept 60 per cent, leaving 40 per cent for local governments. Consumption tax for the year brought in 1.7 trillion yuan. Imposed on certain categories of goods – such as alcohol, tobacco and fuel – the income generated goes entirely to the central government. “The issue is that even with our income dropping, a big portion still needs to be turned over to the central government as state tax, leaving us with limited fiscal resources … The main complaint is that the state is taking too much,” said the Zhejiang finance official. Daisy Xiao, director of Asia-Pacific international public finance ratings at Fitch Ratings, said the reform should modestly improve local revenue flexibility and spending discretion, but would be unlikely to materially ease structural pressure on local finances because debt growth had far outpaced the expansion of fiscal resources in recent years. “The extra tax income would be small against persistent structural deficits, which are largely financed through special-purpose bonds linked to capital spending,” Xiao said. “Even so, the measure is a constructive step in broadening more stable local revenue sources and giving local governments greater fiscal discretion,” she added. More broadly, the move was consistent with China’s fiscal reform agenda and longer-term objective of reshaping local fiscal incentives away from property-related revenue and towards economic growth, consumption and sustainable tax bases, according to the Moody’s analysts. “While incremental in nature, it represents a step in expanding provincial fiscal autonomy, supporting a more sustainable local revenue structure,” they added. Rare autonomy for rate-setting Under the proposal, provincial governments would be allowed to set the new rate within a range of 11 to 13 per cent, signalling greater flexibility. “This is notable because most major tax rates in China are set by the central government, leaving local authorities with few levers to adjust revenue,” Xiao said. Rate-setting discretion within an approved band would give provinces a limited additional countercyclical tool, allowing them to respond to changing revenue needs and local economic conditions, she added. That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best Tian Zhiwei, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics Tian, from Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, said final tax rates would be the product of provincial governments’ “trade-offs”. Authorities would need to strike a balance between retaining businesses and easing fiscal pressure: set the rate too high and they risk driving firms away; set it too low and they forgo revenue when public finances are already under strain, he said. “That is one reason why the central government gives provinces the discretion over setting tax rates – local authorities know their own circumstances best,” Tian added. Wealthier provinces may choose lower rates to strengthen their competitiveness, while fiscally weaker regions could opt for higher rates to bolster revenue, according to Moody’s. “As a result, fiscal management could become incrementally more province-specific, reflecting local economic conditions and policy priorities,” the analysts added. But the reform could also bring unintended consequences for some localities. Under the current urban maintenance and construction tax rules, a 7 per cent rate applies in urban areas, 5 per cent in counties and designated towns, and 1 per cent elsewhere, including rural areas and oil-producing fields. As the proposed legislation would replace that system with a single rate across an entire province, businesses in counties and rural areas could face a higher tax burden, according to Li, the lawyer. “From a provincial perspective, the overall tax burden may see little change, yet for individual companies, it translates into real-world cost increases.” Additional reporting by Frank Chen

title: Meet Jack Lowden, tipped as the next James Bond by his Slow Horses co-star Gary Oldman
description: The Scottish actor is married to Saoirse Ronan and has appeared in films including Dunkirk and Mary Queen of Scots – but will he succeed Daniel Craig?
content: Gary Oldman recently revealed in an interview with Canada’s Global that the next 007 has already been cast. While Oldman’s connection to the James Bond franchise is a mystery, the Oscar-winning actor went on to say that he had his fingers crossed for his Slow Horses co-star Jack Lowden to take over as the Omega-wearing spy from the most recent Bond, Daniel Craig. “It’s been rumored that he’s on the shortlist. We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack,” Oldman said. Here’s everything you need to know about the next James Bond – at least according to Gary Oldman – Jack Lowden. How did Jack Lowden get into acting? Lowden grew up in a village in the Scottish Borders. He has told interviewers that his family didn’t have a theatre background or even an interest in acting. Instead, he joined his little brother for ballet lessons. This little brother is Calum Lowden, now principal dancer at the Royal Swedish Ballet. The older Lowden quickly realised that his talent wasn’t in ballet and decided to “try words instead”, and that’s how his tryst with theatre began. He got his first job at 19 playing Cammy in Black Watch at the National Theatre of Scotland. He went on to graduate from the Royal Scottish Academy of Music and Drama (now called the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland). He’s not a method actor The 36-year-old actor is known for playing some incredibly dark and complex characters. However, his approach to such characters doesn’t follow “the method”. In an interview with Gentleman’s Journal, the Dunkirk (2017) actor revealed, “I don’t find that I carry the characters around with me … Because I’ve always gotten off on being one person one minute and another person the next.” When asked about getting into the mindset of his characters, especially that of Oswald in Richard Eyre’s 2014 adaptation of Ghosts, where the character has a fatal stroke on stage, Lowden quipped, “I’ve never been in that mindset! I’ve never had a stroke! It must be bloody knackering for an actor to inhabit the character that way!” He is married to Saoirse Ronan After acting with Saoirse Ronan for the first time in Mary Queen of Scots (2018), Lowden was full of praise for the American-born Irish actress. During an interview with the since-defunct talk show Build Series, he said: “The woman is a force of nature on and off screen, and utterly fearless and a brilliant leader … it’s just constantly amazing to me – not just her work, but how she is on a set is amazing.” Ronan – who at 32 is four years younger than her hubby – has also spoken fondly of him. She told People in 2022, “I completely trust his eye … I think that really helps, having someone that you really trust. And he’s a sort of typical Scot, where if there’s a problem, he’s the first one to try and solve it.” According to People, the Oscar-nominated actress tied the knot with her long-time partner in a private ceremony in 2024 – fittingly in Edinburgh, Scotland – in the presence of very close friends, all of whom were “sworn to secrecy”. Ronan gave birth to their first child last September, also per People. He ran a production company with Ronan On the professional front, Ronan and Lowden have been prolific collaborators. In 2019, Lowden co-founded the production company Arcade Pictures alongside producer Dominic Norris, with Ronan joining as a director in 2021. In 2024, together with Brock Media, they produced the film The Outrun, starring Ronan and based on Amy Liptrot’s memoir of the same name. While both actors have since stepped down from their roles in the company, Variety reported that they will “continue looking for more passion projects to develop together in the future”.

title: Will ‘transactional’ America assist India in a future border crisis with China?
description: India’s relations with US have frayed over trade and tariffs recently, but strong defence ties still remain between the two countries.
content: When Chinese President Xi Jinping met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi last week on the sidelines of the Brics summit, another country loomed large in the background, even in its absence: the United States. After the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to maintain peace at the disputed border and strengthen economic ties. Beijing’s readout, however, offered a pointed reminder of the US factor in India-China ties. The official Chinese statement claimed that Modi assured Xi that India adhered to an “independent foreign policy” and that its ties with China are “not influenced by any third party”, an apparent reference to Washington. While India did not endorse Beijing’s assessment, analysts said Washington’s shifting priorities in the Asia-Pacific region and strained US-India ties are reinforcing New Delhi’s instinct for strategic autonomy and influencing its approach to China. However, they added that despite uncertainty about Washington’s strategy, it would likely stand by India in a potential border crisis with China as it did during the 2020 Galwan clashes, but New Delhi should be ready to defend the territory on its own. “American assistance cannot be treated as automatic,” said Nirupama Rao, a former Indian foreign secretary. “If China attempted a significant unilateral alteration of the status quo. American support would likely be substantially stronger.” “India is going to its default position, which is strategic autonomy and multi-alignment,” said Aparna Pande, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, adding that the policy has been “reinforced over the last year and a half because of concerns over the global order under the second Trump administration”. During his second term, US President Donald Trump has frequently criticised allies and partners for taking advantage of the US, launched trade wars against them and questioned the security architectures in Europe and Asia as well as the costs of maintaining them. In August, Trump ordered the Pentagon to significantly reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, citing their cost and saying the drills sent an inappropriate message to North Korea. His approach has unsettled America’s friends, prompting a scramble among them to manage rivalries and forge new partnerships. India’s attempts to stabilise ties with China come as its relations with Washington have frayed over trade and tariffs, oil sanctions, visa restrictions and rising anti-India rhetoric and racism from Trump’s Maga base. While not a treaty ally of the US, India still maintains strong defence ties with Washington, focused on maintaining peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, a euphemism for checking China’s growing influence. Xi, Modi emphasise need for border stability During his bilateral talks with Xi, Modi emphasised that “peace and tranquillity in the border areas remain an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”, while Xi said both sides should commit to “parallel development and mutual promotion of bilateral relations and border issues”. Xi’s first visit to India in seven years followed the prolonged freeze in ties after the deadly Galwan clashes in June 2020, which killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops. Both sides deployed thousands of troops and heavy weaponry along the ill-defined border for more than four years. Border arrangements that began in 2024 eased tensions and revived high-level dialogue, regular flights and people-to-people exchanges. However, disagreements appeared to resurface last month over patrolling points in Arunachal Pradesh, a province in India’s northeast that Beijing claims as Zangnan or south of Tibet. The two sides contained the latest crisis and agreed to an eight-point consensus, including an “early and substantial harvest of boundary delimitation and border management”. Despite multiple border arrangements, thousands of troops remain deployed on either side, while the two countries continue to expand physical infrastructure across the difficult terrain. India’s Ministry of Defence said in its annual report last week that it witnessed a “significant reduction in the deployment of People’s Liberation Army [PLA] forces” along the LAC in the northern front, with around 40,000-50,000 PLA troops at the border and an equal number in designated training areas. The report did not disclose India’s troop numbers, describing its deployment as “robust, well poised and prepared to deal with any emerging contingency”. “All India is trying to do is manage, to the extent possible, the border issue so that it doesn’t flare up,” said Pande of the Hudson Institute. She added that New Delhi is attempting to balance a “very strong” China, a weaker Russia and a less dependable, transactional and “semi-isolationist America”. “India has to manage that,” Panda said. Rao, who has served as India’s ambassador to both China and the United States, said that “difficulties with Washington undoubtedly reinforce India’s instinct for strategic autonomy and increase the value of stabilising relations with China”. But she cautioned that there isn’t a “direct causal connection” between the two, noting that the India-China stabilisation process began well before the recent deterioration in India-US ties. Will US support India in a Galwan-like clash with China? During the 2020 India-China border crisis, the US largely stayed in the background but played an important supporting role, providing India with surveillance drones and logistical assistance. It reportedly provided India with MQ-9 drones for surveillance in record time, along with cold-weather clothing, tents, rifles and spare parts. In 2022, Washington shared real-time intelligence on Chinese positions along the LAC with New Delhi, according to reports, in what was the first known instance of the US providing such active assistance. Hundreds of Indian and Chinese troops wielding spiked clubs and tasers engaged in fistfights in December that year in the Tawang sector of Arunachal Pradesh. Neither side officially confirmed the extent of the US assistance, as details of the cooperation remain classified. On whether the US would extend its support to New Delhi again despite tensions in bilateral relations, Sameer Lalwani, a senior fellow in the South Asia Programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said he was optimistic and confident that it would. “I think our relationship is even better now than it was in 2020,” he said, adding that “there’s a lot more structural support” for defence cooperation. The India-US defence relationship has expanded in recent years from arms sales to technology cooperation and plans for greater defence co-production in India. Under the current administration, the two countries signed a new 10-year framework last October, focusing on operational coordination, information sharing and bolstering defence industrial capacity. The previous Joe Biden administration launched INDUS-X, the India-US Defence Acceleration Ecosystem, in 2023 to connect US and Indian defence companies, start-ups and investors. New initiatives help strengthen US-India relations The Trump administration has since strengthened the partnership through TRUST, a broader technology initiative, and INDUS Innovation, a network connecting defence start-ups, investors and research institutions in the two countries. The two militaries have also expanded joint exercises, including the tri-service Tiger Triumph and the Malabar naval exercise, alongside cooperation across air, land, sea, space and cyberspace. They also cooperate through the Quad, an informal grouping of the US, India, Japan and Australia that focuses on maritime security, including maritime domain awareness, coastguard cooperation and disaster response. Rao argued that the “precedent of 2020 is important” and any valuable assistance “would probably be discreet”. She added that Washington would probably “encourage de-escalation” and avoid “unnecessarily internationalising the incident” in the event of a small patrol confrontation, but American support would likely be “substantially stronger” if China attempted a significant unilateral alteration of the status quo at the border. “The essential qualification is that India is not a US treaty ally,” she cautioned. “US partnership should multiply Indian capability, not substitute for it.” According to Lalwani, India is seeking to build guardrails with China through the latest border arrangement to prevent “inadvertent crisis escalation”, but a meaningful thaw remains unlikely. “These two countries are clearly rivals, if not adversaries,” he said.

title: Opinion | Why I am grateful for Asean’s endless meetings
description: A modest lesson in a multipolar world is that sometimes the achievement is simply that disagreement does not end the conversation.
content: I remember 2011 well. Indonesia was chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and I was serving as deputy foreign minister for Asean cooperation. I learned a great deal, although if I had to summarise the experience in one word, I would say: meetings. Asean members meet. They talk. They disagree. They issue statements. Then, quite remarkably, they meet again. We meet in conference rooms, coffee shops and restaurants. We speak by telephone and online. And when matters become particularly serious, there is always durian. To outsiders, Asean consensus can appear tedious. Where is the breakthrough? Why does everything take so long? Yet the longer I work in diplomacy, the more I appreciate the willingness to meet again, especially after a disagreement. Agreement is important, but it is not the only measure of successful diplomacy. Sometimes, the achievement is simply that disagreement does not end the conversation. This is what I understand as the habit of dialogue. Working in Beijing, I see something familiar around Chinese dinner tables. A round table has no visible head, creating a sense of equality. Yet it does not remove order. Everyone has a place and everyone is expected to contribute. Those who have conducted business in China will understand that many important decisions are shaped around such tables. Trust is built gradually, through conversation, shared food and the willingness to spend time understanding one another. I wonder whether this habit offers a modest lesson for a world accelerating towards multipolarity. I use the word “accelerating” because the changing distribution of global power appears to demand immediate adjustment. Yet multipolarity does not tell us how power will be exercised or what kind of order will emerge. China’s vision of an equal and orderly multipolar world recognises this challenge. Its Global Governance Initiative similarly places sovereign equality at the centre. But how can sovereign equality become a working practice? How can countries create order without simply recreating hierarchy? Perhaps Asean can offer part of the answer. International order needs power to sustain it, but it also needs limits on how power is used. Institutions make those limits more durable. Countries accept restraint because predictability benefits everyone: they know broadly what others may do, what they are unlikely to do and how disagreements will be managed. The difficulty arises when power shifts. Established powers may fear that restraint gives rivals room to advance. Rising powers may question rules they had little opportunity to shape. When countries no longer believe restraint will be reciprocated, rules begin to give way to transactions. Every concession has a price. Every act of self-restraint starts to look like a favour that must be repaid. Cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon This is especially complicated because power today takes many forms. One country may possess greater military strength, another greater manufacturing capacity, another financial influence, advanced technology or essential mineral resources. Strength in one area often exists alongside dependence in another. Countries will not always share the same interests. But perhaps they can develop a shared understanding of how their different forms of power should be exercised. Indonesia has Asean’s largest population and economy. By accepting consensus, Indonesia accepts a restraint on its weight. This restraint is useful because, as Bilahari Kausikan, a good friend of mine, has explained, consensus reassures smaller members that Indonesia cannot impose decisions upon them. It also reassures Indonesia that smaller members cannot simply combine to outvote it. Each accepts limits in exchange for reassurance. No one gets everything but no one is expected to surrender everything either. This matters in a region of different political systems, cultures, levels of development and national interests. Such diversity complicates collective decisions. It also makes Southeast Asia difficult for any outside power to capture entirely behind a single agenda. Its members may not converge on every interest, but they can converge on certain procedures, protocols, principles or concepts, for example, the non-use of force, a zone of peace, freedom and neutrality, a nuclear-weapon-free zone, Asean centrality and Asean-plus. We have learned, imperfectly, how to disagree without immediately reaching for the divorce papers. There are, of course, limits to Asean’s experience. Consensus can take time. Dialogue can become repetitive. Meetings can produce more meetings, sometimes followed by preparatory meetings for the next meeting. I would therefore hesitate to present Asean as a complete model for the global order. Its lesson is more modest: cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything. It requires them to preserve the means of working through what they cannot agree upon. The habit of dialogue helps sustain this process. Equality gives every country a voice. Humility helps each country listen and recognise that it may not possess the whole answer. Repeated interaction gradually creates predictability. Admittedly, habitual dialogue cannot erase power differences. It cannot resolve every dispute. But it can do something essential. It can create time when decisions are moving too quickly. It can lower the temperature when tensions are rising. And it can help countries adjust to power shifts without allowing every disagreement to become a crisis. This is why I view the first Indonesia-China comprehensive strategic dialogue, held in Jakarta last month, with hope.
