Its importance lies not only in what was discussed but in the habit that made the discussion possible. And there is quite a momentum to protect. Since 2015, the bilateral trade volume has tripled and Chinese investment has risen over 12-fold. At this pace, US$300 billion of trade in the next four to five years is within reach. Through my years in China, I have walked its streets, met its people and spoken to many who will inherit whatever we build today. I do not know whether I have done enough. But I take some comfort in believing I have helped nurture the habit of dialogue. As long as we remain willing to meet again, we will always have something on which to build.

title: Trump threatens to keep Kennedy Centre closed for good after name ruling
description: US president conditions venue repairs on his name being added to the building.
content: US President Donald Trump threatened Tuesday to keep the Kennedy Centre closed for good after a judge ruled his name cannot be added onto the famed arts institution’s facade. Trump said his hand-picked board voted “almost unanimously” to shut the venue immediately for emergency renovations, just a few hours after the federal judge’s decision. But he warned the “very large and complex” repairs at the building in Washington cannot begin until a higher court rules on whether the centre can be renamed after himself. “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. The Kennedy Centre said in a statement that the board’s decision “reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritisation of safety above all else”. Shortly after beginning his second term, Republican Trump installed himself as chairman of the centre, which is named in honour of late president John F. Kennedy, a Democrat who championed civil rights before he was assassinated in 1963. The board voted in December to call it the “Trump-Kennedy” Centre and installed signage with his name on it. US federal judge Christopher Cooper previously ordered Trump’s name removed from the exterior and overturned the board’s decision to rename the institution. Cooper ruled on Tuesday that Trump’s name cannot be added back, rebuking the centre for trying to circumvent his earlier order. “Simply put,” wrote Cooper in his decision, the board “cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing”. Trump himself called into the board meeting and berated a Democratic congresswoman who serves on the board and filed the lawsuit that blocked its renaming, CNN reported. The Kennedy Centre takeover is one of several projects aimed at stamping Trump’s brand on the US capital, including a triumphal arch and a half-billion-dollar ballroom at the White House. Workers removed Trump’s name from the building in June, but scaffolding and tarps have remained ever since. Last month, the board moved forward with a plan to add a new signage on the building that would read “renovated and restored by President Donald J. Trump”. Cooper on Tuesday said that plan was in violation of his previous ruling. Trump and his chosen leaders of the Kennedy Centre have argued that its main building, which was constructed in the 1960s, is in a state of dangerous disrepair. As evidence of the safety problems, the president pointed to a recent incident in which a piece of the ceiling tumbled to the ground following a storm. “If the Building were open, innocent people would have been killed,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social before the judge’s ruling. Last month, as part of court proceedings, the Trump administration warned that the centre may need to be demolished, if its plans to renovate the building were blocked. A host of artists cancelled concerts at the venue in response to Trump’s takeover, while US media has reported that Kennedy Centre ticket sales have plummeted.

title: Unlikely allies Sanders and Bannon call for stronger AI oversight
description: Ideological adversaries warn of the dangers of artificial intelligence amid public concern over unregulated tech.
content: Progressive US Senator Bernie ⁠Sanders and Steve Bannon, a close ally of President Donald Trump, both called on Tuesday for stronger oversight of artificial intelligence, uniting two political adversaries around concerns that the technology will harm humans. The rare display of bipartisan concern at the same Washington gathering reflects deepening anxiety over unregulated AI, with lawmakers in both parties questioning Trump’s hands-off approach even as the technology raises fears about job losses, safety and the concentration of power among a handful of tech companies. “AI has the potential to eliminate tens of millions of jobs, wiping out entire professions and ‌making it harder for our young people to enter the workforce,” Sanders said. He added: “As many scientists believe could happen, this technology will escape human control with potentially catastrophic consequences”. Sanders drew applause from the room when he criticised tech executives for centralising control over AI technology, including SpaceX CEO and former Trump adviser Elon Musk. “Last month, we learned that AI has been used for the first time ever to create new viruses. In the wrong hands, this could lead to new bioweapons and a potential global pandemic that could lead to the deaths of tens of millions of people,” Sanders said. Sanders called on Trump to negotiate a treaty with Chinese President Xi Jinping at their summit next week to pause AI development. Bannon, a former White House strategist during Trump’s first presidential term, has criticised Trump’s approach to overseeing AI, ⁠placing the blame for the president’s unwillingness to regulate the technology squarely on tech companies. On his Monday podcast, Bannon said Congress should not pass laws that prohibit states from enforcing their own rules for the technology. “Here’s what ‌we have to do first: to slow down the pace so that we can understand exactly what’s going on,” Bannon said on Tuesday. He praised Sanders for the way he summarised the risks of AI and said the country has to rise above partisanship on the issue. “I don’t think you could find any too harder partisans ‌than Bernie Sanders on the left and Steve Bannon on the right,” he said. Bannon said Congress will take too long to pass legislation slowing the development of AI. “This is going to ⁠have to be executive action,” Bannon said. He said ⁠the US must cut off China from American-made computer chips. Trump on Monday played down concerns expressed by industry leaders over the weekend about the misuse of artificial intelligence harming people, saying the US already has guardrails in place for the powerful technology. Backing Trump’s position on Tuesday, ‌Republican US House Speaker Mike Johnson said there cannot be a moratorium on artificial intelligence development without losing the competitive edge to China and that AI companies can regulate themselves. “They can self-regulate. They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down. If they want to slow ‌it down, ‌they should,” Johnson told reporters. Speaking to reporters at the White House, Todd Blanche, the US Attorney General, accused Democrats of trying to influence November’s midterm congressional elections by politicising the issue of AI. The view that regulations will ‌harm US companies’ ability to compete with their Chinese counterparts is shared by tech executives, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Dario Amodei, the CEO of AI company Anthropic, speaking in San Francisco on Tuesday, called for better AI safety ⁠standards. “Let’s invest more in safety,” he said. Recent surveys have found majorities of Americans worry the technology could be used to eliminate jobs, raise costs for families or otherwise cause social harm. The US House ⁠of Representatives ended its long summer break on Monday, with members in the House and Senate holding private conversations about whether or not to legislate on AI, especially after Trump said there was no need for legislative action. Congress has been criticised in the past for lacking the collective expertise to rein in or regulate technology companies. Speaking to Reuters, Republican Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio said: “This process ‌of legislating takes so long. Imagine AI four years in. ‌We’re dealing with stuff that isn’t even relevant in four years”. Residents in several states have also challenged proposals for new data centres, a critical component of the AI boom. According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published in June, 77 per cent of Americans worry AI-driven data centres will raise electricity costs. Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon captured public attention last week when he said he resigned from the company, in part because the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. Also on Tuesday, Andrew Ferguson, the chairman of the US Federal Trade Commission, expressed suspicions over AI companies seeking antitrust exemptions while they also lobby for new regulations.

title: Dutch rail network crippled by suspected sabotage
description: Dutch authorities discovered items on railway tracks in around 30 separate locations.
content: Rail travel in large parts of the Netherlands ground to a standstill on Tuesday, after what authorities suspect were coordinated acts of sabotage with tubes attached to train tracks in multiple locations. Transport by train in most of the central and eastern parts of the country was virtually impossible after authorities discovered items on the tracks in around 30 separate places. “Materials were found at multiple locations on the track that were deliberately placed there,” said rail operator ProRail in a statement. “This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved,” added the operator. ProRail said its computer systems interpret an item on the track as meaning that section is occupied, even though there is no train. The system then turns all lights in that section red, meaning no trains can pass. One train did hit one of the tubes but there were no injuries, said ProRail spokeswoman Joke van der Cruysen. “Who is responsible for this and what the motive is is not yet known,” said ProRail, adding that a police investigation was under way. There was also a knock-on effect on road travel, as level crossings are also malfunctioning due to the sabotage. By around 3pm, the blockages had been removed from the tracks and traffic was able to resume. Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the alleged sabotage as “disruptive and life-threatening”. “We must now calmly await the police investigation. The police and the security services are doing everything they can to track down the perpetrators,” Jetten added. The action coincided with Prince’s Day, when the government lays out its budget plans. Tuesday also saw protests by farmers angry at the government plans, who set bales of hay alight alongside several country roads. No roads were closed as a result of the farmers’ protests, according to transport authorities, who also said there were no major delays in road traffic. The Farmers Defence Force had already announced they would take protest actions to coincide with Prince’s Day, but it is not clear if farmers were also behind the train sabotage. Climate group Extinction Rebellion was also active, throwing red paint at the route taken by King Willem-Alexander to parliament to make his Prince’s Day speech. The group denied having anything to do with the train sabotage, however. “Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today,” said ProRail. “ProRail finds the disruption experienced by travellers and shippers today very regrettable.”

title: Kim Kardashian awarded €1 over 2016 Paris armed robbery
description: French judge awards requested symbolic sum following armed robbery by ‘grandpa robbers’.
content: A Paris court on Tuesday awarded €1 (US$1.15) to Kim Kardashian for having been the victim of an armed robbery in the French capital in 2016, the amount of compensation she had asked for, according to a lawyer involved in the case. Kardashian has sought to move on since the court last year found eight people guilty for their roles in what the celebrity described as “the most terrifying experience of my life”. She and stylist Simone Harouche expressed gratitude to the French justice system in a joint statement. “The experience was deeply traumatic, and its impact has stayed with us. Today’s decision is not about the compensation, but about accountability and recognition,” the statement to Associated Press read. “We are thankful to the Court and everyone who supported us throughout this process, and we hope to now move forward and continue to heal.” The court awarded a former receptionist at the Hotel de Pourtales €109,516 (US$126,472), according to his lawyer. Kardashian had been staying at the hotel when the robbery gang targeted her. The receptionist said he had been traumatised by the October 2, 2016, jewel heist during Fashion Week. He had sought €550,000 (US$634,868) in damages and interest. His lawyer, Mohand Ouidja, welcomed the decision as a victory. The lawyer read the court’s written decisions pertaining to Kardashian and the others aloud to AP. The court awarded the hotel €50,000 (US$57,741). It awarded €1 – the amount she had requested – to Harouche, Kardashian’s stylist who was present during the robbery. Two of the robbers, dressed as police, forced their way into her suite, bound Kardashian with zip ties and tape and made off with more than US$6 million in jewellery, including a diamond ring she had worn that night to a Givenchy show. Because of their ages, the robbers became known in France as “les papys braqueurs”, or the grandpa robbers. Six of them were in their 60s and 70s when they were tried for armed robbery, kidnapping, gang association and other charges. With time already served in pretrial detention, none of those found guilty went back to prison. None of them appealed the verdict. Kardashian said in a statement issued after their conviction that she was “deeply grateful to the French authorities for pursuing justice in this case”. “The crime was the most terrifying experience of my life, leaving a lasting impact on me and my family,” the celebrity said. “While I’ll never forget what happened, I believe in the power of growth and accountability and pray for healing for all. I remain committed to advocating for justice and promoting a fair legal system.”

title: Scott Bessent confirms weekend meeting with He Lifeng days before Xi’s US visit
description: US Treasury Secretary to meet Chinese Vice Premier for final preparatory talks between two sides before key Trump-Xi summit in Washington.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday confirmed that he will meet Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend for the final preparatory talks between the two sides, less than a week before Chinese President Xi Jinping travels to Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump. “With China, we have had some very good private discussions, and I look forward to those continuing this weekend when I meet my Chinese counterpart Vice [Premier] He Lifeng,” Bessent said during a House Financial Services Committee hearing. Bessent was responding to a question about the alleged role of Chinese banks in facilitating commercial transactions with Iran and whether Washington planned to take action against them. Bessent is expected to discuss the likely economic outcomes of the Trump-Xi summit and begin preparatory dialogue on artificial intelligence safety and governance. Last week, the South China Morning Post reported that Washington and Beijing are set to fold the long-awaited AI dialogue into a broader economic meeting. The two leaders agreed in Beijing in May to establish an intergovernmental dialogue on AI, which ran separately from the economic talks led by Bessent and He for months. The AI channel has struggled to make progress, with basic details of the planned talks still unresolved as Xi’s visit approaches. Bessent set to address AI and economic issues in meeting with He Sources said Bessent is now expected to address both AI and economic issues in a single meeting with He, rather than hold separate high-level talks. Bessent leads the US side in both channels, while the tight schedule ahead of the summit has made arranging a second meeting increasingly difficult. The latest arrangements mirror those in May, when Bessent and He held talks in Seoul just days before Trump met Xi in Beijing. Another source familiar with the discussions said the upcoming AI talks are expected to be “fairly preliminary” and more about “agenda setting” than grappling with complex issues. On Tuesday, Bessent also weighed in on the AI safety debate, highlighting the tension between addressing concerns about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and maintaining US competitiveness with China in the race for AI leadership. “It does matter whether the good guys or the bad guys have this,” Bessent said in response to Massachusetts Democrat Stephen Lynch, who argued it probably wouldn’t matter whether the good or bad guys developed superintelligence if it couldn’t be controlled. “As a person who manages the relationship with China on AI, it matters a great deal,” Bessent added. Trump on Monday dismissed growing concerns about AI, claiming America already has guardrails to regulate the industry and warning that casting doubt on development only benefits China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ ‌that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on social media. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these ⁠companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data ‌Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.” Bessent echoed Trump’s stance on Tuesday, arguing that “AI is the most important technology of this century, and that we must maintain US leadership”. Bessent’s testimony came on the same day that Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump White House aide Steve Bannon joined forces at a Washington conference, dubbed the Pro-Human Assembly, to call for new policies to curb the rapidly accelerating development of AI. The AI safety issue gained prominence last week when a former Anthropic employee warned that the technology may lead to human extinction in the next decade. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-step framework to slow the pace of AI development and give policymakers and companies more time to address the risks posed by rapidly advancing technology. The proposal quickly won support from other prominent industry leaders, including xAI chief Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. However, the Trump administration is prioritising AI competition with China as a key driver of AI development and is unwilling to slow down. Concerns rise over Chinese AI models using ‘distillation’ from US rivals The Treasury Secretary once again raised concerns about Chinese AI models using “distillation” from US models, which he described as one area where the US could challenge Beijing. “One of the ways we can push back against China, because the Chinese models distil from the US models, which is a polite scientific word for steal,” he said. Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones. Last week, three US agencies – the National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI – accused leading Chinese AI companies of engaging in “aggressive, malicious and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale”. They alleged that the practice was carried out “likely with Chinese government awareness”. During an afternoon press conference at the White House on Tuesday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked whether the US Justice Department would “go after” China over the alleged distillation or whether Trump would bring it up when he meets with Xi next week. “When you say China, you’re talking about an entire country, and so those two presidents have a great relationship, and they get along, they make deals together,” said Blanche. “Are there separate issues with actors in China and companies in China and bad actors? That has existed long before this administration and will exist for the next several years.” Blanche said the US Justice Department and other executive branch agencies would continue to combat theft “in the right way”. “I don’t think it’s fair to just label China as a country,” he added. “There’s bad actors in China that are doing it, which we’re definitely going to go after.” The Chinese embassy in Washington rejected US allegations, terming distillation “a common technical practice used by AI developers worldwide, including US companies”. “The US allegations are unfounded and politicise a normal technological and commercial practice,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang told the SCMP. As Chinese companies have narrowed the capability gap in frontier AI models, US firms and Trump administration officials have increasingly accused Beijing of stealing and copying American technology to speed up the development of its own systems. Additional reporting by Mark Magnier

title: Paris court convicts school aide for sex abuse, orders ankle tag
description: The man, who admitted to having sexually assaulted the nine children aged five to 10, was also banned from working with children again.
content: A Paris court on Tuesday sentenced a man to one year under house arrest with an ankle tag for sexually assaulting primary schoolchildren in his care. The sentence is the heaviest imposed since multiple allegations of sexual or physical violence emerged in recent months against monitors the city employs to look after children at school outside the classroom. Michael M., 38, admitted during his trial to having sexually assaulted the nine children aged five to 10 between September 2022 and January 2024, and apologised for “what had happened”. The court handed him a five-year term, four of which were suspended and banned him from working with children again. It ordered him to serve the one-year term under house arrest with an ankle tag rather than inside prison. The investigation had shown that he had taken part in conversations on the sexual abuse of children in an online forum, the presiding judge said. A Paris court in July found a 25-year-old guilty of sexually assaulting a kindergarten-age girl in his care, handing him an 18-month jail sentence and banning him from working with children. He denied any wrongdoing. Since the start of the year, Paris has suspended 132 aides including 52 suspected of sexual abuse. Prosecutors are investigating whether the capital’s mayor Emmanuel Gregoire and his predecessor Anne Hidalgo, who served in her post for 12 years up to this year, should be held responsible after parents filed several complaints alleging mismanagement. Speaking to a fact-finding inquiry of the upper house Senate on the issue, Hidalgo described Tuesday the problems in the sector as a “collective failure” but stopped short of issuing any personal apology. “If we are here before you today, it is because our institutions – Paris City Hall, local authorities, the national education system, the police, and the justice system – have failed to protect our children,” she said, insisting she had personally been “deeply involved” in combating the problems. Gregoire – who says he was sexually abused during an after-school primary school swimming programme – has pledged to tackle such abuse since he took over in March, describing it as a “systemic problem”. He is due to speak to the fact-finding inquiry on Wednesday.

title: Japan jails man for forcing Thai girl, 12, into sex work
description: He had forced the girl to provide sexual services at his private-room massage parlour in Tokyo in 2025.
content: A Japanese court on Tuesday sentenced a 52-year-old man to five years in prison and fined him 1 million yen (US$6,500) for forcing a 12-year-old Thai girl to provide sexual services at his private-room massage parlour in Tokyo. The Tokyo District Court found Masayuki Hosono guilty of violating the child welfare law, saying the owner of the establishment had created a disorderly workplace environment and failed to verify the girl’s age. Prosecutors had sought a six-year prison term and a 2 million yen fine. Judge Hiroshi Ikegami said that while the girl’s 30-year-old mother deserved the strongest condemnation for pressuring her daughter to engage in sex work, Hosono had caused the child emotional distress “beyond imagination” by forcing her to serve customers in a foreign country and making her practise on him. Hosono had denied the charges by claiming the female store manager Punsiripanya Phakhaphon, 39, who is also on trial, was responsible for recruitment. But the judge dismissed the argument, citing messages showing that Hosono was involved in the process. According to the ruling, Hosono forced the girl to provide sexual services between June and August 2025. The girl’s mother was later arrested by Thai police and sentenced in June to seven years and six months in prison.

title: Hong Kong finance chief urges Cathay to keep fares attractive, add routes
description: Cathay Pacific targets 150 new aircraft and 150 global destinations over next decade, chairman Guy Bradley says.
content: Hong Kong’s finance chief has called on Cathay Pacific Airways to offer attractive fares and expand its route network, as China’s national development plan reinforces the city’s status as a global aviation hub. Speaking at Cathay’s 80th anniversary celebration on Tuesday, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po described the flag carrier as more than just a transport provider, calling it an ambassador for Hong Kong that reinforced the city’s status as a global aviation hub and “superconnector”. Chan emphasised that each new route drove trade, investment and economic opportunities, noting that bringing people together and unlocking new markets was especially vital in an uncertain global climate. He said that the three-runway system at Hong Kong International Airport – now nearly two years operational – provided more capacity for growth, adding that the government was pursuing new air services agreements and expanded traffic rights in such markets as the Middle East, Central Asia, Africa and South America. “As the government opens the way for wider air links, I encourage Cathay to seize these opportunities and add new destinations to your network,” Chan said. “I am sure passengers would be delighted to see one more thing: your excellent service accompanied by equally attractive fares. Guy and Ronald, I shall leave that in your capable hands,” he added, addressing Cathay Group chairman Guy Bradley and CEO Ronald Lam Siu-por. At the same event, Bradley highlighted that the group now operated scheduled passenger services to more than 100 destinations worldwide – including 24 in mainland China – via Cathay and its low-cost carrier, HK Express. He said the group planned to expand into more belt and road destinations, including Almaty, Kazakhstan, next January. He was referring to participating nations in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network. “In the next 10 years, we target to have 150 new aircraft join our fleet, and build a network serving 150 destinations worldwide, if market conditions are favourable,” Bradley said. Chan acknowledged that Cathay’s 80-year history included “difficult chapters”, recalling the Covid-19 pandemic period when the government led a HK$39 billion recapitalisation package for the airline in 2020. “During the pandemic, the government’s support reflected our determination to safeguard Hong Kong’s status as an international aviation hub and our confidence in Cathay’s role within it,” he said. “That was an investment in our shared future. And it was your people – their professionalism, perseverance and dedication – who helped turn confidence into recovery. “Your work matters far beyond air connections. For Hong Kong, every new route is another opening for trade, investment and opportunity. This is our ‘superconnector’ role in practice: bringing businesses to markets, and people to one another. “In an uncertain world, we must pursue these opportunities with prudence as well as confidence,” Chan said. “The case for bringing people together and opening up new markets is stronger, not weaker.” He said Cathay’s commitment of about HK$150 billion (US$19.12 billion) to investments in aircraft, cabins, lounges and digital innovation was a vote of confidence in Hong Kong’s future. “The national 15th five-year plan explicitly supports Hong Kong in consolidating and enhancing our status as an international aviation hub,” he said. “We are determined to translate that support into greater capacity, wider reach and lasting economic benefits.”

title: How Okinawa’s political shift could make Japan more prepared for a Taiwan contingency
description: Election of governor backed by nation’s ruling party could stabilise the US military presence and drive a defence build-up.
content: Okinawa’s election on Sunday of a governor backed by Japan’s ruling party ended 12 years of local leadership opposed to the relocation of a US airbase and elements of Tokyo’s defence build-up plans. While experts say that Genta Koja’s victory will not give Tokyo any new military authority in the region, it could lead to closer integration of civilian infrastructure into Japan’s defence network in case of a conflict – including one over Taiwan. Koja’s election would give Tokyo “room to expand its so-called Nansei shift, that is to concentrate its military build-up in the southwestern part of Japan to deter China’s military presence in the East and South China seas”, said Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo. Maslow said much of this shift would probably have happened regardless of the election result. But with a prefectural government backed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party, the process would be “less noisy and perhaps faster”. Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said Koja’s victory suggested Okinawan politics could become more receptive to a greater role for the prefecture in Japan’s defence planning. But Koja has drawn limits around his support for Tokyo’s defence build-up. During the campaign, he said he understood the need for the Nansei shift but believed there was no need “at present” to deploy long-range missiles in Okinawa. The clearest sign of Koja’s political break with his predecessors is his stance on the decades-old dispute over the US Marine Corps’ Futenma airbase in Ginowan, a densely populated city on Okinawa’s main island. Tokyo and Washington agreed in 1996 to relocate the station once a replacement facility was completed elsewhere in Okinawa. Successive Okinawan governors opposed relocating Futenma within the island but that facility is now being built beside the existing US Marine Corps’ Camp Schwab in Okinawa’s less-populated area of Henoko. Unlike his predecessors, Koja accepts the relocation of the airbase, although he has called for a clearer timetable for the closure of the Futenma base. “Koja’s win removes the political deadlock over the base issue,” Maslow said, adding that while anti-base protests would not stop, the election could help drive the relocation forward. For Beijing, the significance of the Henoko airbase lies less in the US military expanding in the region than in potentially making its presence in Okinawa more durable, reducing a long-standing source of political friction over the alliance’s forward posture near Taiwan. A more immediate effect of the leadership change could come from Tokyo’s “specified-utilisation” programme, intended to make selected civilian airports and ports more usable by the Self-Defence Forces (SDF) and Japan Coast Guard. Okinawa’s main airport at Naha is already in the programme and is managed by the central government. The city-managed Ishigaki and Hirara ports are also designated. By contrast, three prefecture-managed facilities – Ishigaki Airport, Miyako Airport and Nakagusuku Bay Port – remain outside the programme. The outgoing governor, Denny Tamaki, moved towards accepting their inclusion in February 2025, but eventually decided against it. Koja, however, indicated during the campaign that he was prepared to move towards accepting the designations after discussions over implementation. The government says the programme does not turn civilian airports and ports into military bases and that civilian use remains the priority. But it allows arrangements for smoother access and for upgrades that take security requirements into account. Maslow said Koja’s support for the programme sent “a clear signal” about strengthening Japan’s defence infrastructure and Okinawa’s role in deterring China’s regional military presence. “These efforts will bolster the islands’ role as defence hubs in the region, especially for evacuation operations in the case of a Taiwan contingency,” he said. Bosack said that expanding SDF operations into additional Okinawan airports and seaports would be a significant consideration for both Beijing and Tokyo in a Taiwan contingency. “One of the first considerations for military planners is logistics throughput and space,” he said. “There are only so many berthings and aircraft spaces available, so an increase in that capacity is important from both sides’ planning considerations.” He said US and Japanese planners had previously considered using additional civilian air and seaports for military purposes and non-combatant evacuation operations, but politics had limited how far such planning could go. The implications are particularly significant on Ishigaki and Miyako islands, where Japan has already stationed Ground Self-Defence Force units. Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said those facilities could add redundancy to Japan’s logistics network by providing alternative routes for moving personnel, fuel, equipment and supplies if major military bases were damaged or temporarily unavailable. But their military value would, at least for now, be constrained by limited parking, storage and loading capacity. Matsuoka also warned that increased military use could invite closer Chinese scrutiny and expose those sites to attack in a conflict.

title: How Canada’s Trump headache is fuelling a China trade boom
description: Exports to China hit their highest first-half level in decades as Ottawa looks to reduce dependence on its southern neighbour.
content: Canada’s exports to China jumped by 30.1 per cent in the first half of 2026, led by crude oil, copper and other energy and mineral products, as Ottawa stepped up efforts to diversify trade ties amid growing tensions with its largest trading partner, the United States. Exports to China reached C$21.74 billion (US$15.63 billion) over the period, marking the highest first-half value since 1997, according to a trade report released by the Canada China Business Council and the China Institute at the University of Alberta. The report, published on Monday, showed that energy and mineral products drove much of the growth. Energy products accounted for 35.8 per cent of the shipments, surging 81.8 per cent from a year earlier. Metal ores and non-metallic minerals made up 22.6 per cent, with exports rising 29 per cent. Crude petroleum exports more than doubled to C$5.96 billion, contributing C$3.2 billion to the overall increase. Exports of copper ore and concentrate rose by C$949 million to C$2.64 billion. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation – a think tank under the Ministry of Commerce – said the expansion reflected strong alignment between Canadian supply and Chinese demand for energy and critical minerals, backed by both governments’ willingness to strengthen ties. Diversifying trade partners had long been a Canadian objective, Zhou observed, noting that the strategy was accelerating as risks in Ottawa’s relationship with Washington grew. Zhao Minghao, deputy director of the Centre for American Studies at Fudan University, echoed that sentiment. “Mark Carney’s government is taking a pragmatic approach towards Beijing,” Zhao said. “Notably, he views improving relations with China as a way to achieve a degree of ‘de-risking’ from the United States.” Bilateral tensions between Washington and Ottawa have escalated since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025. Trump has publicly expressed his desire to annex Canada and quickly stepped up tariffs against the neighbouring country. After US-Canada trade negotiations broke down in late August, Washington imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting Ottawa to retaliate with measures that took effect earlier this month. According to Zhao, the latest friction had largely stemmed from US efforts to restrict Canada’s closer economic engagement with China, which he said Ottawa viewed as an infringement on its sovereignty. “As Carney said, the international order is undergoing a ‘rupture’, [so] he must improve ties with China,” Zhao stated, noting that Canada was actively repositioning itself as a “middle power” by deepening partnerships with the European Union, South Korea, Australia and other economies. “This highlights a longer-term shift towards foreign policy diversification – using its core strength in energy and critical minerals to hedge against US pressure,” Zhao said. Carney has set an ambitious goal of doubling Canadian exports to markets outside the US over the next decade, with China potentially playing an important role in that effort. During a visit to China earlier this month, Corey Hogan, parliamentary secretary to Canada’s minister of energy and natural resources, said there was “broad potential” for energy cooperation between the two countries. Ottawa, Hogan said, was willing to strengthen information sharing and policy exchanges with Beijing to create a favourable environment for trade and investment by energy companies from both countries, according to a statement from China’s National Energy Administration. The Trans Mountain Expansion Project (TMX), an oil pipeline system that provides Canadian crude with a direct route to the Asia-Pacific region independent of US pipelines, highlights the potential benefits of deeper energy ties with China. According to data released on Monday by Natural Resources Canada, China has become the leading buyer of seaborne exports shipped through TMX, accounting for about 60 per cent of shipments.

title: From barefoot hockey to Asian Games, India’s Lalremsiami Hmarzote chases golden dream
description: First Olympian and Asian Games medallist from Mizoram hopes to win gold medal in Japan for her country, build hockey facilities for her state.
content: When an 11-year-old Lalremsiami Hmarzote told her parents she wanted to leave home to take ⁠up a place at one of ⁠India’s top hockey academies, she first had to explain ⁠to them what the sport was. Less than a decade later, Lalremsiami would become the first female Olympian and the first Asian Games medallist from the northeastern state of Mizoram. Lalremsiami, who fell in love with the sport playing barefoot on dirt pitches in the Himalayan town of Kolasib, is now India’s offensive linchpin as they bid for a first Asian Games gold ‌since 1982. She said she had to overcome her parents’ resistance to the idea of her joining the Sports Authority of India’s academy in Thenzawl, about 170 kilometres from her hometown. “My family initially didn’t want me to join the academy, but eventually they agreed,” the 26-year-old said. “I told them I have to play it, I can only play hockey.” Hockey is one of India’s national sports but it remains a fringe pursuit in the tiny mountainous state of Mizoram, wedged between Bangladesh and Myanmar. Lalremsiami credited the geography of the mountainous ⁠region for helping her develop endurance and athleticism. “If you’re walking somewhere, you’re either going up or down the hill,” Lalremsiami said with a smile. “You ‌get used to the exhaustion, the heavy breathing … it helps you when you are training as an athlete.” Her fitness stood out when she debuted for India’s under-18 team and she was called up to the senior camp within ‌a year. In 2018, she won a Youth Olympics silver medal and scored four goals as the senior India team reached ⁠their first Asian Games final in ⁠20 years. She has earned 193 caps for her country and was the first Indian woman to score in three consecutive World Cup campaigns as they came fifth last month in ‌the Netherlands and Belgium, their best finish since 1974. The golden dream Lalremsiami said the India team, under Dutch coach Sjoerd Marijne, believe their World Cup performance has set them up for a shot ‌at gold ‌in this month’s Aichi-Nagoya Games after three bronzes and the 2018 silver over the past two decades. “We have the belief but we are not ‌overconfident … I know everyone’s expectations are high but we must stay calm and focused,” she said. Her ultimate dream, though, is to build training facilities ⁠in different parts of her state, so girls can pursue the sport without having to leave their homes, like she had to. “I did not have ⁠any equipment when I started. A former player was teaching us after school, she had some hockey sticks,” Lalremsiami said. “Sometimes football teams have issues with the grounds being used for hockey … there are only three hockey grounds in Mizoram – where will kids play? “During ‌the World Cup, my mother told ‌me an unknown person came up to her and said their daughter loved hockey but they did not know how and where to get into it,” Lalremsiami added. “I felt very bad that I could not help. How am I supposed to guide somebody? I can’t even say, go play in the academy, because it’s so far away. “It is my dream to build more hockey grounds in Mizoram … they will produce much better players than me, I can guarantee that.”

title: US-China ties haunted by lack of mutual trust, Beijing Xiangshan Forum told
description: No ‘illusion that things will be easy’ ahead, former Chinese ambassador to US says before President Xi Jinping is expected in Washington.
content: A lack of mutual trust and confidence haunts Sino-US relations, a major security conference in Beijing has heard, just a week before Xi Jinping travels to America for his first state visit there in over a decade. “[While] we have the agreement on this constructive strategic stability, we don’t have the illusion that things will be easy going ahead. There are always problems, sometimes very big problems,” said Cui Tiankai, a former Chinese ambassador to Washington, at a panel of the Xiangshan Forum on Tuesday. Cui praised the stability in bilateral ties since Xi hosted US President Donald Trump in May, including in terms of regular exchanges in diplomacy, economics, the military and law enforcement. “I expect things will remain the same in the next few months,” he said. However, Cui listed a number of issues in China-US relations that Beijing still believed needed to be taken seriously, saying “there are more attempts at more tariffs, more restrictions and sanctions against Chinese companies or even research and higher learning institutions”. The challenge that still needed to be overcome was the building of trust and confidence, he said. “I hope our American friends will have trust in our policy statements [and that] they will not see Chinese policy statements just as rhetoric,” Cui added. “For instance, when we say we want to be a partner and friend to the United States, we mean what we say … when we say the Taiwan question is the red line of the red lines, you better trust we mean what we say.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Cui’s comments came just over a week before Xi is expected to travel to Washington, the Chinese leader’s first state visit to the US since 2015. Despite weeks of preparations, Beijing has yet to officially confirm Xi’s schedule. On this point, Cui simply said it was necessary to wait for an “official announcement”. Trump announced the US invitation to Xi during his own state visit to Beijing in May, when the two sides agreed to seek strategic stability. According to David Finkelstein of the US-based Centre for Naval Analyses, the bilateral relationship was “in a better place after the summit” than it was beforehand. The consensus among analysts was that US-China relations had been more stable since Trump’s Beijing trip, Finkelstein said, but it was “still quite fragile”. The May summit had focused only on trade and investment issues, he added, with these areas representing just some of the points of dispute between the two sides. According to Finkelstein, strategic stability is critical in defence matters, particularly in crisis management. He said one sign of progress was the first meeting between Yang Zhibin, commander of the People’s Liberation Army’s Eastern Theatre Command, and US Navy Admiral Samuel Paparo on the sidelines of a conference for Indo-Pacific defence chiefs in Canada earlier this month. The meeting ended a two-year break in theatre-level military contact between China and the US. “I think all of us in the US agree that crisis management between the two sides is weak,” Finkelstein said. “We could do a lot better there.” A dialogue on nuclear issues, emerging technologies and strategic domains, such as cyber, hypersonic and space, would help build strategic confidence, he added. The three-day Xiangshan Forum, China’s most important annual defence gathering, is taking place in the Chinese capital from Tuesday to Thursday. It is widely seen as Beijing’s answer to the Shangri-La Dialogue held in Singapore. China this year is hosting defence officials and scholars from nearly 100 countries. No official delegations from Japan or the Philippines are attending, according to people familiar with the matter. The US had originally planned to send Cynthia “Xanthi” Carras, the Pentagon’s principal director for China, Taiwan and Mongolia, to lead its delegation. But she cancelled her attendance days before the forum, according to two sources familiar with the matter. One source said Carras pulled out because of an illness. Another source said Brigadier General Stacy Kihara, the senior defence official at the US embassy in Beijing, replaced Carras in leading the American delegation. Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun is expected to outline Beijing’s security position in a keynote speech at the forum’s opening ceremony on Wednesday morning. Dong on Tuesday held separate meetings in Beijing with senior officials attending the forum, including the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar, according to China’s defence ministry. Dong also met with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn and Brunei’s coordinating minister for national security, Halbi bin Haji Mohd Yussof. Meanwhile, Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University, said Trump might view stable US-China relations as an “asset” ahead of America’s midterm elections in November. According to Wu, who hosted Tuesday’s panel, Trump is unlikely to take action on Taiwan, including through arms sales to the island, that would upset Beijing in the period between the summit and the midterm elections. Cui said the elections had “no impact” on Sino-US relations. “For the past few years, people have told me that the only thing that is still bipartisan is to be tough on China,” he added. “Hopefully, there could be a new bipartisan agreement that we should together build constructive strategic stability.”

title: Review | Benjamin Grosvenor joins Hong Kong Sinfonietta for a memorable night
description: Norwegian Radio Orchestra conductor Holly Hyun Choe led proceedings on an evening starring Grosvenor playing Brahms’ ‘Piano Concerto No 1’.
content: What advantage does a left-handed conductor have? Before answering that, it is worth looking at another of Holly Hyun Choe’s strengths. In keeping with the Hong Kong Sinfonietta’s tradition, the guest conductor opened the concert with an introductory speech, immediately establishing herself as an excellent communicator. She recalled her excitement upon discovering that the orchestra had long been led by a female music director. Enthusiastic applause followed when Choe acknowledged music director emeritus Yip Wing-sie in the audience. Following this delightful icebreaker, Choe introduced the programme. The Sinfonietta has a strong record of promoting contemporary music, routinely featuring premieres or commissioned pieces. This concert’s Asian premiere was “Burn My Letters – Remembering Clara”, written by Swedish composer Albert Schnelzer in 2019 to mark the 200th anniversary of the birth of German pianist and conductor Clara Schumann. The piece highlights the enigmatic relationship between Schumann – who once asked her daughter to burn all her letters – and her contemporary Johannes Brahms. This was followed by Danish composer Carl Nielsen’s “First Symphony”, which Choe explained was almost like a work by Brahms – Nielsen had, in fact, actually shown the piece to Brahms. While it bears a clear resemblance to the older composer’s symphonic language, it also displays Nielsen’s own stylistic progressiveness. As principal conductor of the Norwegian Radio Orchestra, Choe is well placed to demonstrate the richness of the Scandinavian repertoire. It was no surprise, then, that two of the evening’s three pieces were from the region, all neatly tied together by a shared connection to Brahms. Returning to the question of a left-handed conductor’s advantage: although Choe is left-handed, she holds the baton in her right. Her hands operate with impeccable independence, but it is from her left hand that the finest musical details emerge. Whether lightly fluttering her fingers to cue the clarinets for a gentle offbeat accent or shaping broader dynamics, watching her agile left hand in action was a constant joy. Schnelzer’s “Burn My Letters” was pleasant, approachable and, at times, distinctly cinematic. Structured like an arch, it began and ended with a quiet “A” note that sandwiched passages of immense energy and delicate counterpoint. The musicians relished the performance, as did the audience, who responded with rapturous applause. Nielsen’s “First Symphony”, meanwhile, revealed the composer’s love of exploring orchestral colours. The woodwinds delivered a series of attractive passages, while the brass section produced a spine-tingling chorale, all beautifully executed by the Sinfonietta. These two works perfectly paved the way for the genuine Brahms item. British pianist Benjamin Grosvenor first mesmerised local music lovers during his Hong Kong debut with the Sinfonietta in 2014. This time, he tackled Brahms’ “Piano Concerto No 1” – a work originally conceived as a symphony and noted for its expressive depth – with profound artistic maturity. Grosvenor possesses an impressive dynamic range, which is crucial for delivering such a contrasting piece. The opening movement contains some of the stormiest passages in the piano concerto repertoire and gives way to a serene second movement designed as a remembrance of Brahms’ late mentor, Robert Schumann. Grosvenor captured these extremes of agitation and tranquillity remarkably well. His rendition of Brahms’ intense part-writing was particularly captivating, rendering the inner musical lines with a heavenly touch. The evening was not without a touch of offstage drama, as an audience member required medical attention during the final movement. Paramedics discreetly attended to the situation while Grosvenor offered a sublime encore of Alexander Siloti’s arrangement of Bach’s “Prelude in E minor”, bringing a soothing close to a memorable concert. “Great Piano Concertos: Benjamin Grosvenor Plays Brahms”, Hong Kong Sinfonietta, Hong Kong City Hall Concert Hall. Reviewed: September 12.

title: South Africa on alert after seventh woman’s body found near capital
description: The seventh body found in two months has sparked fears of a potential serial killer.
content: A woman’s body was found on Tuesday in the same area east of Johannesburg in South Africa where the discovery of several other victims in the past two months has sparked fear of a potential serial killer at large and led to a public warning by the police. According to South African authorities, the cases appear to be linked, though they did not confirm whether they are the work of the same killer. The South African Police Services (SAPS) has issued a public warning for women to be cautious when doing activities like jogging in the area. “While investigations are still under way and SAPS has not, at this stage, confirmed that the deaths are linked to a serial killer, the similarities are sufficiently concerning for the police to issue a public warning and intensify investigations,” police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said. President Cyril Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations. “I have directed that these cases be prioritised and that no stone be left unturned in bringing those responsible to justice. Our law enforcement agencies are undertaking this work in partnership with citizens, on whom we depend for any information that may help end these attacks on women,” he said in a statement. The police alert followed the discovery on Tuesday of a body in the Kwa-Thema area, about 34km (21 miles) from Kempton Park. Police said the victim was found fully naked and in an advanced stage of decomposition. On Monday, another body was found in Olifantsontein. On Saturday, the body of a 38-year-old woman was found after she went missing in Kempton Park last week while jogging. A frantic community and police search for Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo ended when her half-naked body was found. The public warning has highlighted long-standing concerns over violent crime in South Africa, particularly against women and children. The country recorded 5,427 murders between April and July – an average of 45 a day – according to the latest crime statistics. Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the UN’s agency for gender equality. A South African study in 2022 found that more than 35 per cent of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point. The Commission for Gender Equality has called for urgent preventive action, including a safety audit of the affected areas involving police, municipal officials, transport authorities and community safety structures. It said the audit should assess lighting, surveillance, pedestrian and public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency help. “Women should not have to be killed before an area receives heightened attention,” commission spokesperson Javu Baloyi said.

title: Tighter scrutiny of Hong Kong IPOs could slow deal flow, analysts say
description: CSRC and SFC wake-up calls to bankers and other intermediaries indicate emphasis on quality over quantity amid fervour for listings.
content: Securities regulators in Hong Kong and mainland China are doubling down on efforts to raise the quality of Hong Kong initial public offerings (IPOs), which could slow the flow of new listings but would not reduce underlying demand, according to analysts. In an unusual move, the China Securities Regulatory Commission recently asked nine mainland companies, which had already been pre-approved for listings, to provide supplementary materials detailing fund usage, shareholding structures and pending litigation. Hong Kong’s market watchdog, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), on Thursday directed the city’s bourse operator to suspend trading of US-based biotech firm Cloudbreak Pharma, explicitly expressing concerns that the company’s IPO could have been “rigged” to create an artificial impression of demand. “The launch of new projects has been affected,” said Hang Wang, chief representative of Baker McKenzie’s Beijing office and co-chair of its China capital markets practice, when asked about the regulator actions. “This has pushed mainstream investment banks to become more cautious when screening projects and potential clients.” This “tightening of quality oversight” would have a knock-on effect on intermediaries including law firms, auditors and industry advisers, which would lead to a reduction in the number of new projects being screened and launched, he added. In another recent case, the SFC instructed Futu Securities to freeze up to HK$125.2 million (US$16 million) in client assets linked to suspected artificial demand creation in July. Listing activity in the city’s stock market is running unusually hot, with hundreds of mainland AI, robotics and tech companies lining up to debut. At least 500 companies had submitted applications, excluding confidential filings, according to bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX). In the first eight months of 2026, companies raised HK$651 billion through IPOs and secondary placements in Hong Kong, with IPOs accounting for about HK$342 billion. “Every time the IPO market is hot, some substandard companies try to sneak through,” said Roy Lo Wa Kei, managing partner at accounting and consulting firm SW Hong Kong. “Since regulators stepped in, intermediaries have become much stricter in their gatekeeping.” The SFC said in a January circular that some listing documents had serious flaws, including a possible lack of thorough understanding of applicants and insufficient due diligence. It now limits signing sponsors to handling five deals at a time. Lo said the watchdog would strengthen sponsors’ due diligence duties, covering client knowledge, legal, intellectual property and financial checks. He also said he expected more guidance to be released soon on valuation reasonableness, so that high valuations for AI and new economy firms would no longer rely on companies “blowing their own trumpet”. Despite these hurdles, Baker McKenzie’s Wang said the city was not trying to raise listing thresholds or shut companies out. “HKEX remains committed to simplifying the listing process and lowering barriers, and continues to welcome strong companies to list in Hong Kong,” he said. The bourse operator implemented its most ambitious listing reform in eight years in July, significantly lowering the financial and market capitalisation thresholds for companies with weighted voting rights and allowing all new applicants to submit listing applications confidentially. “This may seem at odds with stricter quality oversight, but it isn’t,” Wang said. “HKEX is essentially trading quantity for quality. Regulators care more about bringing in high-quality companies with real investment value than about simply racking up the number of listed companies.” Underlying market demand had “never truly halted”, he added. “Taking our firm’s daily operations as an example, we continue to pitch to prospective clients and hold kick-off meetings each month. Overall, the Hong Kong IPO market is shifting towards a healthier, more manageable and sustainable trajectory.”

title: China make late change as they target 7 badminton gold medals at Asian Games
description: Men’s doubles player Chen Boyang withdraws from illness but 31-member squad for tough Aichi-Nagoya event remain stacked with experience.
content: The Chinese Badminton Association has announced, just four days before the start of the Asian Games, that men’s doubles player Chen Boyang had withdrawn because of illness, with He Jiting named as his replacement alongside Liu Yi. On Monday, the association revealed that Chen had suffered a sudden illness. Following consultations between national team doctors and specialists from several hospitals, medical experts confirmed his condition would prevent him from competing. “To protect the athlete’s health and fully prepare for the Games, the national team considered factors including competitive form, technical characteristics, partnership synergy and major tournament experience, deciding that substitute athlete He Jiting will replace Chen Boyang in the men’s team and men’s doubles events at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games,” the association said. The badminton tournament will run for 10 days starting on Sunday, the day after the opening ceremony, at the Ichinomiya City General Gymnasium and will bring together traditional powerhouses China, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and Malaysia. Although He and Liu will pair up for an international major for the first time, the duo said they frequently partnered in regular training and shared a strong “chemistry”. They added that they would maximise the remaining pre-tournament window for targeted preparation and would fight hard in every match to bring honour to the national team. Chen’s condition was reportedly under control and he was recovering, though he would require two to four weeks of rest. China have sent a 31-member squad anchored by veterans Shi Yuqi, Chen Yufei, Jia Yifan and Huang Dongping, alongside middle-generation players Li Shifeng, Wang Chang, Liang Weikeng, Jiang Zhenbang and Wei Yaxin, targeting all seven gold medals across the team and individual events. The team finals take place on September 24, followed by individual finals on September 29. At the Hangzhou Asian Games, China claimed four gold, three silver and two bronze medals, highlighted by a dramatic comeback in the men’s team final alongside titles in women’s doubles, men’s singles and mixed doubles. China faces stiff competition across all the disciplines in Nagoya. In men’s doubles, India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty pose a major threat with their balanced play, alongside strong pairs from Indonesia, Chinese Taipei, Japan and Malaysia. The women’s team event remains a duel between China and South Korea, led by world No 1 An Se-young following South Korea’s Uber Cup and World Championship triumphs. Hosts Japan also present a strong threat through steady endurance play in women’s singles and doubles. In men’s singles, Shi and Li face a stacked field including Jonatan Christie of Indonesia, Kunlavut Vitidsarn of Thailand and Kodai Naraoka of Japan, with both Chinese shuttlers working through recent injuries and form concerns. Women’s singles will see Chen and Wang Zhiyi challenge An, who went undefeated without dropping a set at the 2026 World Championships, alongside home favourite Akane Yamaguchi. While doubles remains China’s primary stronghold, world champions Liang and Wang Chang face stiff resistance from South Korea’s Kim Won-ho and Seo Seung-jae, and Indonesia’s Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohibul Fikri. In women’s doubles, Liu Shengshu and Tan Ning join Jia and Zhang Shuxian against South Korea’s Baek Ha-na and Lee So-hee, while top-ranked mixed doubles pairs Jiang/Wei and Feng Yanzhe/Huang Dongping look to bounce back from World Championship stumbles against Thailand’s Dechapol Puavaranukroh/Supissara Paewsampran and Japan’s Yuta Watanabe/Maya Taguchi.

title: DeepSeek AI engineer slams Anthropic, OpenAI over ‘pacing’ calls, invokes Nazi Germany
description: Heated rhetoric highlights tensions over how quickly artificial intelligence should advance and who should shape its future amid mounting safety concerns.
content: A DeepSeek engineer has issued a stark warning about the potential concentration of advanced artificial intelligence and resources in proprietary US developers Anthropic and OpenAI, intensifying a growing debate in China over calls by US industry leaders to “pace” AI development amid safety concerns. The comments preceded an expected meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump on September 24, where AI safety may emerge as a key point of dialogue as the two countries race for technological supremacy. Liu Shengyu, a DeepSeek engineer behind the company’s V4.1 models, said he did not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to make cutting-edge AI “open and affordable”, contrasting their closed-source approach with DeepSeek’s embrace of open-source models. “I especially don’t want Anthropic to master the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI,” he wrote in a social media post on Monday. AGI broadly refers to AI systems that match or surpass human-level intelligence. “Social mobility would become increasingly difficult,” Liu added. Liu compared the prospect of Anthropic controlling the most advanced AI to Adolf Hitler and Nazi Germany acquiring nuclear weapons before the Allies, noting that a belief in the fostering of inclusive and open-source AI was among the reasons Liu had chosen to remain at DeepSeek. Neither DeepSeek nor Anthropic immediately replied to emailed requests for comment on Tuesday. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on frontier AI companies to “pace” development, warning that capabilities were advancing faster than safeguards. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk have since backed his calls to slow the race. Other Chinese observers have similarly questioned the motives behind such calls to slow AI development. In a post on Tuesday, the Dongbuyaqiao Research Institute, an independent Chinese research platform, said Amodei’s comments could have been “an attempt to gain greater control over industry rules before they are fully established”. Amodei also singled out China, arguing that a Chinese lead in AI would pose a “grave danger” to the United States and the world. He called on Washington to maintain restrictions on exports of advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China. Despite the safety warnings, Anthropic was still expected to go public later this year, with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, according to multiple sources cited by Axios on Monday. The remarks drew a sharp response from Beijing. China’s foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiakun, said at a regular news briefing on Monday that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only hamper efforts towards sound global AI governance”. Also on Monday, Du Hengfeng, a commentator for National Business Daily, a major Chinese financial newspaper, wrote that “direct commercial returns are the deeper motivation” behind the US tech giants’ calls for safety and alignment. The heated rhetoric underscores an intensifying dispute over how the world’s most powerful AI systems should be developed and who gets to set the rules governing them. A commentary on Sunday in the state-run Global Times described Amodei’s proposals as a “quiet AI cold war”, arguing that they were aimed at preserving America’s technological lead while excluding China from global AI governance. Trump on Monday also dismissed calls for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that restraining American AI development could hand an advantage to Beijing. “AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX,” Trump said in one of a series of social media posts. “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” he added. The debate has spilled into financial markets, with US technology stocks declining on Monday as investors weighed the prospect of slower AI development. Shares of Nvidia fell 3.4 per cent, while Micron Technology lost more than 5 per cent. Broadcom and AMD each dropped more than 4 per cent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed 0.56 per cent lower, while the S&P 500 fell 0.48 per cent. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng AI Index – which tracks Hong Kong-listed companies across the AI value chain – slipped 1.65 per cent on Tuesday, extending Monday’s 3.3 per cent drop, reflecting broader weakness in Chinese AI-related stocks. Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and MiniMax both took a hit, closing down 5.69 per cent and 7.05 per cent on Tuesday, respectively.

title: Opinion | The world is not so much embracing China as recoiling from Trump’s US
description: The US is haemorrhaging goodwill around the world, but China will have to build up its own trustworthiness and credibility to win hearts and minds.
content: Global surveys show China is now more popular than the United States in most countries. The reality is China hasn’t become more popular, only that Uncle Sam has become odious. Two recent major summits demonstrate precisely why this erosion has occurred. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and the Group of 20 (G20) gathering in the US, the Trump administration faced withering criticism for policies that have destabilised global commerce, violated international law and alienated even Washington’s closest partners. The SCO summit, representing organisations that account for roughly 40 per cent of all the people in the world, issued a joint declaration that laid bare the depth of international opposition to American policy. The Bishkek Declaration condemned “military strikes on the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which have resulted in heavy civilian casualties and significant damage to the country’s economy”, stating that the US-Israeli attacks “violate the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter and create serious risks to international peace, security and stability”. The statement was signed by Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, among others. Without specifying US sanctions on Iran and Western sanctions on Russia, SCO members said in their declaration that they oppose any “unilateral coercive measures” that go against UN and World Trade Organization rules and that could have a “negative impact on the global economy”. This represents a direct challenge to Washington’s decades-long practice of wielding economic sanctions as a foreign policy tool. At the G20 meeting ostensibly organised to showcase US President Donald Trump’s economic policies, European allies used the platform instead to voice displeasure over American unilateralism. German Vice-Chancellor Lars Klingbeil told reporters that America’s tariff conflicts, including its escalating stand-off with Canada, were eroding trust in global trade and would “ultimately harm everyone involved”. European leaders complained that the war in Iran continued to hobble trade through key maritime routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz, upending global supply chains, the energy market and financial markets. They also raised concerns about Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s surprise decision to sell US holdings of euros to prop up Japan’s currency without telling European allies in advance. The head of Germany’s central bank, Joachim Nagel, noted that Europeans “were not really enthusiastic about the fact that there was no prior coordination”. A recent Pew Research Centre survey found a median of 75 per cent of respondents in 17 middle-income countries say the US interferes in other countries’ affairs, while just 45 per cent say the same about China. The United States has been haemorrhaging goodwill in the high-income democracies that were once its reservoir of admiration, while China gains in the Global South. In middle-income countries particularly, perceptions of China as a reliable partner have strengthened while America is seen increasingly as an interferer pursuing narrow interests. The contrast is stark. In many middle-income countries, more people see China as a reliable partner than the US and are more likely to say China contributes to peace and stability around the world. Washington’s unreliability under Trump – the unilateral withdrawal from agreements, the imposition of tariffs on allies, the military adventurism in Iran, the crude transactional diplomacy – has squandered decades of accumulated trust. The International Monetary Fund has noted that the administration’s war in Iran has slowed global economic growth, while German economists say Trump’s war and tariffs on Europe have dampened what would otherwise have been the strongest year of German growth since 2022. Soft power ultimately derives from credibility, and solid, credible foundations need to be laid to enhance China’s appeal on its own, not relative to Washington. This suggests the current moment represents not a permanent reordering and may yet reverse. In that case, Beijing has much work to do. After all, soft power is far more mercurial than hard power and public opinion can swing within a very short time. It’s not impossible for American institutions to revive lost credibility. A future administration could repair some of the damage by returning to predictability, respect for international law and genuine multilateral engagement. But who knows what will come next? It’s America’s unpredictability that scares everyone. Trust, once lost, is hard to recover. The world has not embraced China so much as it has recoiled from an unreliable and belligerent America that is contemptuous of international law and norms it once championed. While America has lost trust through its choices, Beijing must build up its own trustworthiness and credibility to win hearts and minds.

title: China mulls building nuclear-powered tank with 450km-range railgun in 2 decades
description: Further multi-physics simulations and vehicle-level testing needed before proposed systems could move towards practical deployment.
content: Chinese military researchers have outlined an ambitious plan to develop a nuclear-powered main battle tank armed with an electromagnetic railgun capable of hitting targets up to 450km (280 miles) away, possibly debuting after 2045. Detailed in a peer-reviewed paper published in June in the Chinese journal Acta Armamentarii, the concept envisions a 60-tonne armoured vehicle driven by a 10-megawatt-class small modular reactor (SMR) and a 50-megajoule (MJ) railgun. The paper was written by researchers from Inner Mongolia First Machinery Group – part of China’s defence industrial system and closely associated with the development and manufacture of tanks and armoured vehicles – and the Beijing Institute of Technology. The National Key Laboratory of Special Vehicle Design and Manufacturing Integration Technology funded the study through a special research project. The authors proposed a three-stage development path. Before 2035, the focus would be on integrating electromagnetic weapons into existing tank platforms using relatively mature power systems, with the paper envisaging a 60-tonne-class main battle tank equipped with a 150km range and 10MJ electromagnetic gun, 2MJ electromagnetic armour and a 1,500-horsepower diesel generator paired with hybrid-energy storage based on supercapacitors and flywheels. Between 2035 and 2045, the proposed system would move towards higher-energy weapons and denser on-board energy storage, with a 300km range and 20MJ electromagnetic gun and 10MJ active electromagnetic armour supported by a 2,000-horsepower diesel system, 5 tonnes of advanced energy storage, solid-state batteries, superconducting storage and an intelligent microgrid. After 2045, the researchers would aim to develop a fully nuclear-powered tank with a 50MJ railgun. The weapon could theoretically reach about 3.5km/s, giving a notional range of roughly 450km. For scale, 50MJ is roughly equivalent to the energy an electric car might consume over 90 to 100km, depending on efficiency. The proposed reactor would need to fit within 2 cubic metres (70.6 cubic feet), according to the paper, while its radiation shielding would have to weigh no more than 3 tonnes and its fuel replacement interval would need to reach at least five years. The difficulty, however, lies less in the total amount of energy than in delivering it in an extremely short pulse. The SMR remains the least mature part of the proposed system, with the paper describing a 10MW thermal lead-bismuth-cooled reactor and saying current work remained largely at the simulation stage. According to the paper, the reactor and its shielding would need to withstand about 30g (the impact of gravitational acceleration shock) of off-road shock while remaining small and light enough to fit inside a 60-tonne armoured vehicle. The authors wrote that further multi-physics simulations and vehicle-level testing would be needed before the proposed systems could move towards practical deployment. Yet, there are immediate questions over whether such a nuclear-powered vehicle would be practical. A veteran military equipment expert said a fission-powered tank would face problems extending far beyond the reactor itself. “Fission reactors are relatively mature and can be miniaturised, but applying one to a tank is still unrealistic,” said the expert, who asked not to be named, citing the sensitivity of the issue. The reactor would also require power-conversion equipment, radiation shielding and heat dissipation while competing for space and weight with armour, weapons and crew protection, he said. “Regardless of whether the technology and materials are sufficient, the overall volume and weight alone could make it lose its practical significance.” The military expert also questioned the military value of effectively unlimited on-board energy. “Even if a tank achieved ‘unlimited power’, the advantage would be limited because personnel still need rest and ammunition still needs replenishment,” he said. The problem of survivability could become more serious as anti-tank missiles and drones proliferate, he continued, because a reactor mounted on a crewed combat vehicle would add another liability if the vehicle were destroyed. The military expert instead suggested abandoning the traditional concept of a heavily protected, highly mobile crewed gun platform. “It should become uncrewed, use high-energy lasers or microwave weapons, and exploit the advantage of ‘unlimited electricity’ by carrying high-power radars and electronic-warfare equipment,” he added. Such a system could combine reconnaissance, strike, short-range air defence, communications and electronic warfare across a network of uncrewed vehicles. The South China Morning Post reached out to a senior researcher at Inner Mongolia First Machinery Group for comment.

title: China bets on chips and AI in new 5-year road map to challenge US tech dominance
description: Plan forecasts that operating revenue of enterprises and manufacturers in related sectors will exceed 30 trillion yuan by 2030.
content: An intensifying tech race with the United States, along with Beijing’s drive for technological self-reliance, has led China’s leaders to place greater significance and urgency on breakthroughs in sectors ranging from artificial intelligence to integrated circuits and chips in its latest five-year plan for electronics and information technology.
