The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the National Development and Reform Commission, China’s top economic planning agency, on Tuesday outlined priorities for the electronics and IT industry over the next half-decade. Key objectives include comprehensive progress across the entire integrated-circuit industry, including the development of open-standard RISC-V integrated circuits, to help reduce China’s dependence on Western technology. The plan also calls for a greater role for the indigenous BeiDou satellite navigation system as it competes with the US-led Global Positioning System. And China is prioritising next-generation battery and solar technologies, including perovskite tandem solar cells, which pair a perovskite layer with a conventional silicon cell to capture more sunlight and improve power-conversion efficiency. Advanced chips are foundational to these ambitions, according to the plan. As Beijing attempts to bring its home-grown products closer to the global technological frontier and narrow its gap with the US, developing high-end chips – including high-performance processors, high-density memory and highly reliable analogue and mixed-signal chips – is a central feature of the plan. The country also aims to boost its production capabilities in advanced process nodes. For AI, the plan contains dedicated measures to foster development, including substantially increasing compute-power supply capacity. AI is now at the front and centre of the China-US competition for global dominance, while a reliable and affordable electricity supply is one of the key determinants of the technology’s expansion. The plan also calls for a marked increase in the “penetration” and adoption of next-generation intelligent terminals, including AI-embodied humanoid robots and autonomous driving systems. The document also calls for greater compatibility between AI chips, large-scale models and databases. For Chinese consumers, the plan outlines a wider array of choices as China aims to drive the iteration and upgrading of AI products, from AI-enabled smartphones, PCs and smart glasses to audiovisual terminals and in-vehicle terminals. Beijing is seeking to broaden the technology’s use cases, widely seen as one of China’s most distinctive advantages over the US in the AI race. The plan forecasts that the operating revenue of enterprises and manufacturers in related sectors will exceed 30 trillion yuan (US$4.5 trillion) by 2030. By then, China aims to have developed a range of technologies and products – spanning chips, advanced computing, consumer electronics, basic electronic components and energy electronics – with an overwhelming competitive edge over foreign rivals. The drafting of the plan took more than a year, beginning in July 2025. Its release came as China and the US have shown no signs of easing their efforts to develop, test and deploy AI. On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump, in a phone call with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a live-broadcast panel discussion in Los Angeles, dismissed concerns about AI risks and underlined the need to win the geopolitical competition, especially against China. For its part, China has taken a stand against a pause in AI deployment. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun on Monday rejected calls to slow the technology’s advancement, stressing instead that global progress must remain open and inclusive. “Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve the interests of no one,” Guo said at a regular news briefing.

title: Denmark says Russian frigate fired flares at helicopter
description: The helicopter was on a ‘routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate’ in the waters off Denmark’s southernmost town.
content: Denmark and Russia were at a war of words on Tuesday after Danish authorities accused a Russian frigate of firing flares at a Danish military helicopter. The armed forces said in a statement late on Monday that “one of the air force’s Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser”, Denmark’s southernmost town. The frigate had fired “two flares towards the helicopter. One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter”, it added. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen on Tuesday slammed the incident as “reckless action from Russia”. “Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver,” Frederiksen said in a statement on social media. However, Vladimir Barbin, the Russian ambassador to Denmark, fired back, saying it was the helicopter that had been at fault. “The Danish side’s attempts to explain the helicopter’s provocative actions against the Russian frigate as ‘routine practice’ give rise to serious concern about the possible consequences of such recklessness,” Barbin said in a written statement to AFP. “The Russian side will thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident,” Barbin said while adding that “this is not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships when they were at sea and outside Denmark’s territorial waters”. Barbin said he had last year informed the Danish foreign ministry of “dangerous flyovers and low-altitude hovering” by a Danish Air Force helicopter over a large anti-submarine vessel. Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the actions were “completely unacceptable and could have put human lives at risk”. “I have therefore summoned the Russian ambassador for a discussion about the incident,” he said in a statement sent to AFP. “Russia is gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour,” he warned. “That is something we cannot accept,” he said. Danish media reported that Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus had summoned representatives of the parties in parliament for a briefing on the incident at the defence ministry. Tensions over the Baltic Sea have risen sharply since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Denmark, a member of Nato and staunch supporter of Ukraine, has accused Russia of conducting hybrid operations on its territory. In the autumn of 2025, unidentified drones flew over several Danish airports and the Skrydstrup airbase – where Ukrainian pilots are trained on F-16 fighter jets. The flights began just days after Denmark announced that it would acquire long-range precision weapons for the first time due to the threat posed by Russia. While investigators failed to identify those responsible for the drone flights, Frederiksen at the time pointed the finger at Russia. Danish intelligence agency PET in September warned that Russia was “actively preparing acts of sabotage targeting the defence industry in Denmark”. The agency said that Russia was recruiting “ordinary Danes” on social media to take photos that could be used in planning acts of sabotage. The Scandinavian country has also accused hacker groups linked to the Russian state of carrying out cyberattacks against Denmark.

title: Iran’s top diplomat heads to China for talks as Middle East diplomacy falters
description: The Strait of Hormuz remains closed and fighting has flared again in Yemen as Abbas Araghchi and Wang Yi prepare to meet.
content: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will meet with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi in China on Wednesday, amid stalled diplomatic efforts to de-escalate conflicts in the Middle East. The meeting comes during the countdown to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States for a summit next week with his US counterpart Donald Trump, when the war on Iran and disruption of energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are expected to be high on the agenda. Fighting has also erupted again between Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemeni government forces as well as Saudi Arabia, and a scheduled regional meeting that was expected to address the conflicts and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz has been postponed indefinitely. A meeting between the foreign ministers of Iran, Iraq, and the Gulf Cooperation Council nations – excluding Bahrain – was planned for Monday but was called off, according to Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi. According to reports, Iran later claimed the meeting was cancelled due to objections by Saudi Arabia. The talks on Wednesday could lay the groundwork for a visit by Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who was appointed as Iran’s special representative for China affairs in May. According to Iranian media, the speaker’s visit aims to deepen the partnership between the two countries, one that includes political coordination, investment, technology, infrastructure and regional security. There were reports that Beijing had set conditions for the visit, including reopening of the strait, but the office of Iran’s special representative for China affairs denied there were any prerequisites, the Iran International satellite TV service reported. Araghchi has had at least four phone calls with Wang since the US and Israel jointly bombed the country. They met in person in May when Araghchi visited Beijing to discuss bilateral cooperation, economic ties and the Gulf issues. Wang and Araghchi also met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation foreign ministers’ meeting in Kyrgyzstan in July, as well as on the sidelines of Brics gatherings in India earlier this month. During their meeting in July, Wang called for the resumption of negotiations and the implementation of the US-Iran agreement signed in June to establish a ceasefire, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and pave the way for a permanent peace deal, according to a Chinese statement. The temporary truce collapsed in early July, and negotiations stalled during the 60-day agreement window, which officially expired in mid-August.

title: Mainland Chinese joint venture launches new electric taxi in Hong Kong
description: SAIC-GM-Wuling unveils new six-seat Darion Taxi, but lawmaker warns lack of chargers in city remains challenge to hitting government’s 2027 target.
content: A mainland Chinese joint venture will introduce an electric taxi in Hong Kong next month, but a lawmaker has warned that a lack of quick-charging stations remains the biggest challenge to the government’s target of introducing 3,000 such cabs by next year. SAIC-GM-Wuling, a joint venture between SAIC Motor, General Motors China and Guangxi Automobile Group, on Tuesday unveiled its Darion Taxi, a new six-seater e-taxi to be launched in Hong Kong. DH Legend Motors, the joint venture’s sole Hong Kong distributor, expects to deliver the new model next month. Wong Kin-man, the distributor’s director and general manager, said the model had a 540km (336-mile) range and 30-minute quick-charging capacity, designed to meet demand in the city. “We promise to provide car owners and drivers across Hong Kong with the highest quality, most professional factory maintenance and repair services,” Wong said. “Our team will continuously strive for faster, better and more efficient after-sales support, significantly shorten repair waiting times to ensure smooth taxi operations across Hong Kong and give drivers peace of mind in making a living.” He said the new model would come with a 500,000km battery warranty and cost about HK$300,000 (US$38,248), adding that he expected the company to sell at least 300 cars. Wong added the company would also build Hong Kong’s largest battery repair centre next year, which would cut battery repair costs by about 60 per cent. Wong Po-keung, chairman of the Hong Kong Taxi Owners’ Association, said the new model’s quick-charging capacity was attractive to taxi owners. The vehicle’s real-world range could be closer to 400km once factors such as Hong Kong’s traffic congestion and air conditioning use were taken into account, he added. The Environment and Ecology Bureau said Hong Kong had 988 electric taxis in 2025, which accounted for a fraction of the city’s total of about 18,000 cabs. The government has set a target of introducing 3,000 electric taxis by 2027. Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said the biggest challenge to hitting the target remained the lack of quick-charging facilities for electric vehicles. He noted that the government was relying on the market to solve the problem, but called for authorities to introduce more quick charging stations specifically for taxis. “Many taxi [drivers] need to charge their cars within a short time – about an hour while having their meals – and they cover a lot of mileage every day. They can only provide service if they’re able to charge to a full battery [during these intervals],” he said. Chong suggested that the government set up more fast chargers at the airport, Disneyland and other tourist spots, adding that such facilities could also help divert traffic at gas stations for petrol and gas-powered taxis.

title: EU to propose curbing social media, online games for under 15s
description: The European Commission has come under pressure from some EU member states to take bloc-wide measures to protect children.
content: The European Union is set to propose curbing access to social media, video-sharing platforms, chatbots and online games to children under the age of 15, according to a draft legal document seen by AFP. A proposed new law – to be formally presented on Thursday – would mean banning minors under 15 from opening their own accounts, with a tiered system of access under parental supervision for younger children. As well as age limits, the new “EU KIDS Act” would force digital giants to make their platforms “safe by design” for children, meaning certain “addictive” features such as so-called infinite scrolling would have to be removed, the draft showed. The European Commission has come under pressure from several EU member states including France and Greece to take bloc-wide measures to protect children from social media harms, a push that intensified after Australia banned under 16s from such platforms. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen will provide a glimpse of what to expect from the new law on Wednesday during her annual address to the European parliament in Strasbourg, France. She will then join EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen the following day to present the proposal, which, according to the draft, would ban addictive features such as endless scrolling, artificial notifications and some reward features for children. The Commission, the EU’s digital watchdog, declined to comment on details of the draft. The new law “sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an autonomous account at the age of 15”, the draft says, with a tiered system applying to younger children. Minors aged 13 and 14 will have to ask their parents to set up “introductory” accounts on social media, AI or gaming platforms, with limited features and strict screen time use. Those accounts would also be under parents’ control. Those aged between three and 13 can access “fully parent-controlled accounts on ‘child-friendly’ services” with strict safety standards. Below the age of three, children in the 27-nation bloc would have no access at all to social media and other “risky services”, the draft says. The EU is simultaneously preparing to roll out an age-check app to ensure children are kept off such platforms. The rules on gradual access make the EU’s approach different from that chosen by Australia, where parents cannot consent to children below 16 having any access to social media. The law’s enforcement will be paid for by a supervisory fee on platforms. The EU already has powerful laws to protect children including the content rules known as the Digital Services Act (DSA), with which it has told Meta’s Facebook and Instagram and TikTok to change their addictive design. But in the document, the EU admits the “existing rules do not suffice”, since there is no “outright ban on common problematic features”. It said the new law would build on enforcement of the DSA, which allows in theory for fines of up to six per cent of a company’s annual global turnover. The EU’s approach “needs to limit the access of tech companies to our children and not the other way around”, the document says. Alongside a ban on addictive features, the draft says the EU would regulate so-called recommended systems – the algorithms that feed users more personalised content – to control the content promoted to children and avoid harm. The EU wants children’s accounts to remain private, with “risky settings” disabled by default and unknown users prevented from contacting minors. There will also be “tailored commitments” for online games and AI chatbots. The proposal will become law after negotiations between the EU parliament and member states.

title: Profile | ‘Real experiences’: Mondrian Hong Kong general manager on why community matters
description: Dirk Dalichau explains how a hotel’s message should be welcoming not just for guests but also for a city’s wider community.
content: Hong Kong’s five-star hotels can come across as intimidating, with more conservative properties wanting to shield their well-heeled visitors with ornate decor, black-uniformed staff and chintz seat cushions that ask: “Are you worthy?” For Dirk Dalichau, general manager of Mondrian Hong Kong in Tsim Sha Tsui, a hotel’s message should be welcoming – not only for guests but the wider community in the city. “I have been involved in so many projects that changed the hospitality landscape,” says the 58-year-old German hotelier who has also worked at The Mira Hong Kong, Ovolo Hotels and Eaton HK since landing in the city two decades ago. “But I want to emphasise that it’s never just me – I am always part of a team. And team members are endless sources of inspiration.” In March this year, to coincide with Hong Kong’s art week, Dalichau invited Bunny Cadag to share her story as a Filipino trans multimedia artist in “The Lullabies that Lived”. She performed at Mondrian’s Roofgarden and exhibited works at Mondrian’s annex space, The Corner Shop. “The Corner Shop is accessible to everyone,” Dalichau says of the street-level space located next to the hotel. “There are no barriers; people don’t even need to enter the hotel. “Corner shops around the world are where life happens. It is part of every community’s social fabric. Our Corner Shop gives Mondrian vibrancy. The neighbourhood understands that we are part of the local life, and some have told me that their businesses have improved since the hotel opened in late 2023.” How he fell in love with hospitality Dalichau first fell in love with the hospitality industry as a child, spending holidays hanging around hotel lobbies while his family was at the beach. He pretended he was a waiter and wrote elaborate menus, thrilled by the idea of providing beautiful moments through curated tables laden with scrumptious food. “I found hotels fascinating,” Dalichau says. “So much goes on in them. I had romantic ideas of the industry at the time. I still feel that now.” Born in Frankfurt, Dalichau grew up between London and Germany. His father, Dr Harald Dalichau, was a leading German heart surgeon and thoracic specialist, and the family relocated frequently for his research. Dalichau initially considered a career as a diplomat to fuel his travel bug and desire to work abroad. Eventually, his passion for hospitality led him to the Glion Institute of Higher Education, a Swiss hotel school, and management training at The Boca Raton resort and club in Florida. He got his start at Hilton in Germany, moving up the ladder to become its regional director of marketing for Central and Eastern Europe in 1997. “Wolfgang Neumann, then president of Europe for Hilton, was an amazing mentor,” Dalichau recalls. “He knew that I was a free spirit and couldn’t sit in an office. That’s how I got the chance to open The Trafalgar [rebranded The Trafalgar St. James London in 2017].” Making a move to Asia At The Trafalgar – where he was general manager from 2003 to 2005 – Dalichau met Martin Lee Ka-shing of Henderson Land Development. Lee was seeking a hotelier with no preconceived ideas about Asia to spearhead the transformation of Hong Kong’s 50-year-old Miramar Hotel into The Mira. “I had always wanted to go to Asia,” Dalichau says. “I love its many traditions woven into modern life. Henderson was so open-minded and willing to take a risk with me. The Hong Kong hotel industry at the time was very traditional. It was a steep learning curve.” Since then, with every hotel challenge that Dalichau tackles, he recalibrates and fine-tunes community building to suit. In 2017, he joined Eaton HK as managing director, a year ahead of the hotel’s major rebrand. He was told then that the concept for an inclusive space would never fly in its Nathan Road location. “It was the most visionary concept I had ever worked on,” he says. “Eaton was about diversity no matter what age, religion or social background. It embraced more than the LGBTQ community. “We wanted it to be as relevant as possible and ensure that people can use spaces without an obligation to spend money, such as attending a music event.” Music became a core feature, with a dedicated radio station built in the basement-level Food Hall, directly above the one-Michelin-starred Cantonese restaurant Yat Tung Heen. Over time, the Food Hall has become a popular neighbourhood hangout, while Eaton Workshop has hosted diverse events such as film screenings, yoga classes and Cantopop concerts in spaces dotted across the entire property. Why word of mouth matters Dalichau helped shape Mondrian Hong Kong, which opened in December 2023, from the ground up when he took over his current role in 2022. The hotel now has strong cultural pull and an identity that fosters dialogue between guests and locals. “There is a commercial aspect to our outreach. It replaces traditional marketing,” says Dalichau. “If locals embrace you, half the battle is won. Word of mouth is very powerful. If we create relationships, recommendations are genuine.” During the devastating Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po last November, Dalichau called Mondrian’s owner, Peterson Group, to suggest offering free emergency accommodation to victims affected by the tragedy. Today, the hotel’s art and culture events have helped bolster local talents ranging from choirs to graffiti artists by providing space and support. “As a business, we need to give back and celebrate a sense of place,” Dalichau says. “We can only do that if we involve the community. I’m convinced that if locals go there, tourists will follow for real experiences.”

title: Man arrested after HK$1 million in gems stolen from hotel guest asleep in lobby
description: Police say suspect allegedly took advantage of situation to search overseas businessman’s backpack and remove uncut gemstones.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a man and recovered uncut gemstones worth nearly HK$1 million (US$127,500) that were allegedly snatched from an overseas businessman as he slept in a hotel lobby. The force said on Monday that the suspected theft happened a day earlier while the businessman, a 29-year-old jeweller from Sri Lanka, was in the city for the “Jewellery & Gem World Hong Kong September” trade fair. The jewellery was allegedly taken from the victim as he slept in the lobby, while he was waiting to check in at a hotel near Hong Kong International Airport. Police said the suspect allegedly exploited the situation to search the businessman’s backpack, which he had placed on his luggage, and removed a batch of uncut gemstones valued at nearly HK$1 million before fleeing. Airport district officers launched an investigation and identified the suspect with the help of surveillance footage. About six hours after the alleged theft, officers arrested a 32-year-old Algerian man at a hotel in Tsing Yi, and recovered the precious stones intact. Police are investigating whether the suspect had any accomplices. The force reminded the public to safeguard personal belongings, adding that officers would step up patrols and monitoring for the duration of the jewellery exhibition. It also urged exhibitors to remain vigilant, watch their valuables and avoid disclosing storage locations for their items.

title: Wrise Prestige accelerates mainland China expansion with new offices, AI lab
description: The wealth management firm has invested HK$30 million in AI-related development as it focuses on scaling up its business on the mainland.
content: Wealth management provider Wrise Prestige is stepping up its investment in artificial intelligence technology as the firm looks to expand its footprint on the Chinese mainland and power its next phase of growth. The Singapore-headquartered firm planned to open an AI laboratory in Guangzhou next month to house its technology team, following a HK$30 million internal investment in AI-related development, senior executives said during a media briefing marking the company’s second anniversary in Hong Kong on Tuesday. The initiative will focus on building enterprise systems and streamlining operational efficiency across the group, with further capital expenditure planned for future tech initiatives, according to the company. Henry Shin, the company’s chief executive, said the plan aimed to merge technology with professional expertise rather than replace human advisers. “AI is meant to empower our business operations and elevate service efficiency, but the human wealth consultant remains the absolute core of our client relationships,” Shin said. The firm is moving from an “independent wealth consultant” to an “intelligent wealth consultant” model, according to Shin, which pairs human judgment with AI-driven research and analytics. “Independence remains a core pillar of the business,” Shin added, stressing that technology allowed advisers to objectively help clients select and design financial solutions. The initiative aligns with a broader push across Hong Kong’s financial sector to integrate AI into wealth management and capital markets. Trillions of yuan in wealth will undergo intergenerational transfer in the domestic market in the coming years Henry Shin, Wrise Prestige Regulators have been encouraging responsible adoption while urging financial institutions to prepare for a coming wave of autonomous systems. Earlier this month, a senior official at the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) noted at an industry event that the watchdog was considering further regulatory guidance for financial firms deploying autonomous “agentic” AI systems. The company said its Hong Kong business had expanded rapidly since launching in 2024, with assets under management rising 927 per cent, revenue increasing 301 per cent and client numbers growing 382 per cent compared with the end of 2024. Its network has grown to more than 400 wealth consultants. Beyond Hong Kong, the group was expanding its mainland presence with offices in Shenzhen, Chengdu, Changsha and Wuxi, focusing on investor outreach, research and family office education, the executives said. “Trillions of yuan in wealth will undergo intergenerational transfer in the domestic market in the coming years,” Shin said, pointing to rising demand for succession planning and advisory services. The expansion comes as Hong Kong reinforces its position as a global hub for private wealth. Total assets under management in the city’s private banking and wealth management sector rose 24 per cent year on year to HK$12.9 trillion at the end of 2025, according to SFC data.

title: Taiwan tests US-made MQ-9B drones to counter PLA ‘grey-zone’ operations
description: More advanced derivative of MQ-9A Reaper to be used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, island’s military says.
content: Taiwan has begun flight testing its newly acquired MQ-9B drones, giving the island a long-range reconnaissance platform capable of monitoring People’s Liberation Army (PLA) and grey-zone activities across vast stretches of surrounding waters. The first two of four MQ-9B SeaGuardians ordered from the United States took off from Hualien Air Base in eastern Taiwan on Monday, according to military sources. It was their first test flight since arriving in Taiwan by sea in June, following nearly three months of assembly, testing and preparations by the air force and US manufacturer General Atomics Aeronautical Systems. The drones were handed over to Taiwanese personnel in the US on March 17 before being shipped to the southern city of Kaohsiung and transported to Hualien county, where they were assembled in a US military-certified hangar. They will serve with the 12th Tactical Reconnaissance Squadron at Hualien Air Base. Military officials said the MQ-9Bs would be used mainly for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance rather than as strike aircraft, particularly to monitor PLA warships and mainland Chinese coastguard vessels involved in grey-zone operations around Taiwan. Taiwan has allocated NT$21.7 billion (US$684 million) between 2022 and 2029 for four MQ-9Bs, ground-control systems and related equipment. The remaining two aircraft are scheduled for delivery next year. With satellite communications, sophisticated maritime sensors and endurance measured in dozens of hours, the aircraft could conduct prolonged patrols over high-risk areas that would otherwise require repeated sorties by crewed reconnaissance aircraft. According to General Atomics, the MQ-9B is a larger and more advanced derivative of the MQ-9A Reaper, which the US military has used extensively for reconnaissance and strike operations. The MQ-9B has a wingspan of 24 metres (79 feet), has a maximum take-off weight of about 5.67 tonnes and can fly above 40,000 feet (about 12,200 metres). Depending on its configuration, it can remain airborne for more than 40 hours, although operational endurance with a full intelligence and surveillance payload is expected to be shorter. Kao Chih-jung, a researcher at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research, estimated that the MQ-9B could conduct missions lasting more than 24-30 hours. Kao said it had a maximum range exceeding 5,000 nautical miles (9,260km) and an operational radius of up to 1,200 nautical miles. At an altitude of 25,000 feet, its radar and electro-optical sensors could have a line-of-sight radius of about 194 nautical miles. “A single aircraft loitering in position could theoretically monitor the entire Taiwan Strait while covering parts of the Bashi Channel to the south and Miyako Strait to the northeast,” Kao said. Its maritime-search radar could scan through 360 degrees and detect, track and classify targets across “thousands of square nautical miles” every hour while updating information on hundreds of targets each minute, he added. Taiwan’s MQ-9Bs are equipped for maritime surveillance with systems including SeaVue radar and electro-optical and infrared sensors, as well as satellite communications that allow them to operate beyond the direct line of sight of ground-control stations. Taiwan’s air force has also tested the MS-110 reconnaissance pod in the US. Kao said the MQ-9Bs could help establish a broad “surveillance wall” along strategically important waterways in the first island chain, making it more difficult for the PLA to use the western Pacific for tactical manoeuvres or surprise operations. The first island chain runs along East Asia’s coastline, from the Kuril Islands through Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines down to Borneo. It forms an important part of the US-aligned security architecture in the region. According to Kao, the drones could use radar and electro-optical sensors to cross-cue targets before sending their coordinates through data links to other units, shortening the response time in the military’s “kill chain”. But he cautioned against relying heavily on a small number of large drones. “Although an MQ-9B could detect and classify large numbers of objects, operators would still have to visually identify some targets,” Kao said, noting that the number that could receive detailed, persistent surveillance at any one time would be limited. The aircraft should instead “perform wide-area searches and identify priority targets before passing intelligence to smaller drones, shore-based radar and other combat units”, he added. Su Tzu-yun, another senior analyst at the institute, described the MQ-9B as a “satellite within the atmosphere” because of its range and endurance. “Deployment of the drone could substantially reduce the burden on Taiwan’s crewed tactical reconnaissance aircraft, particularly during routine operations against PLA warships and [mainland] Chinese coastguard vessels,” Su said. The MQ-9Bs could also support coastguard maritime patrols and, because their communications systems were interoperable with those of the US and other friendly forces, potentially share information when required, he added. While the MQ-9B can carry weapons and Taiwan’s aircraft have the interfaces needed for future weapons integration, military officials have stressed that their immediate role is surveillance rather than attack. Su said four aircraft would provide only a basic operational capability and Taiwan “would eventually need a larger uncrewed reconnaissance fleet”. Rather than necessarily ordering more MQ-9Bs, Taipei could supplement them with locally developed drones such as the medium-altitude, long-endurance Teng Yun 2, allowing the military to expand coverage while controlling costs, he said. Taiwan’s air force is reportedly considering acquiring several Teng Yun 2 reconnaissance drones from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, Taiwan’s top weapons developer, potentially creating a “high-low mix” with the more capable MQ-9Bs. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: China is beating the US in consumer AI adoption, thanks to super apps: Morgan Stanley
description: While the US has a lead in frontier AI, China’s advantage stems from distributing services through platforms tailored to local habits.
content: China is surging ahead of the US in consumer AI adoption as technology giants like Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding embed artificial intelligence directly into popular everyday apps, even as American models lead in capability, according to Morgan Stanley. A survey conducted by the bank and published in a report on Monday showed that 80 per cent of Chinese respondents used AI for personal purposes at least weekly, compared with 54 per cent in the US. China’s generative AI user base grew from about 249 million in December 2024 to 602 million in December 2025, scaling significantly faster than mobile internet adoption did over a comparable period, the report said. While basic access to AI remained free in both nations, China’s advantage stemmed from distributing services through everyday platforms tailored to local consumer habits, rather than holding an edge in frontier model benchmark performance, Morgan Stanley noted. In China, generative AI functions – capable of producing text, images, video or code – are embedded directly into shopping, search, messaging and entertainment apps, allowing users to leverage AI without downloading stand-alone software. ByteDance’s Doubao, which received traffic from TikTok’s Chinese sibling Douyin, has emerged as the clear leader among native AI apps, reaching about 399 million monthly active users (MAU) in July, according to QuestMobile data cited in the report. It was followed by Alibaba’s Qwen – an AI agent designed to execute real-world tasks by plugging directly into Alibaba’s ecosystem of shopping, travel booking, navigation and payments platforms – with 161 million MAUs. However, “multi-homing” was becoming the norm, with 64 per cent of surveyed Chinese respondents using five or more AI tools, Morgan Stanley said. The low cost of switching between apps prevented a winner-take-all situation for stand-alone apps and favoured existing platforms that control user demand, proprietary data and transactions, according to the bank. As a result, incumbents with strong distribution networks were best positioned to benefit, according to Morgan Stanley. Tencent, in particular, was likely to see its WeChat ecosystem of social graphs, mini-programmes and payments enhanced rather than displaced by native AI tools. Alibaba remained a top stock pick for the bank for its full-stack capabilities, particularly in-app commerce features like Taobao’s Qwen shopping assistant, though analysts remained cautious about investments in the stand-alone Qwen app. Meituan and online travel agencies were also well-positioned because of their high conversion efficiency at low incremental acquisition costs. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

title: Who will shoulder the debts behind Indonesia’s China-backed Whoosh railway?
description: Jakarta plans to transfer the US$56.5 million annual debt into state accounts as critics warn taxpayers will subsidise the losses.
content: Indonesia’s finance ministry is preparing to absorb debt payments for Whoosh, the China-funded high-speed railway connecting Jakarta and Bandung, in a move officials say will ease financial pressure on the state-owned enterprises that built and operate the line. The government has argued that the burden is manageable after the debt was restructured over 80 years, requiring annual instalments of about 1 trillion rupiah (US$56.5 million). But the plan has also raised concerns that taxpayers are being left to subsidise a project that has strained state firms after its budget ballooned from an initial US$6.02 billion to about US$7.3 billion. The railway connects the Indonesian capital to West Java’s provincial capital in 45 minutes, far faster than driving, which can take up to three hours. Whoosh is operated by Kereta Cepat Indonesia-China (KCIC), a joint venture between a Chinese consortium and an Indonesian state-owned consortium led by national rail operator Kereta Api Indonesia (KAI). The project has weighed on the finances of its local backers. Last year, KAI head Bobby Rasyidin described the Whoosh debt as a “ticking time bomb”. The pressure is visible in the accounts of Pilar Sinergi BUMN Indonesia (PSBI), the Indonesian consortium that owns 60 per cent of KCIC, with the Chinese consortium holding the remaining 40 per cent. In the first six months of this year, PSBI recorded a net loss of 5.13 trillion rupiah (US$290 million), exceeding its full-year net loss of 4.99 trillion rupiah in 2025, according to KAI’s financial report released in June. The report also showed PSBI’s liabilities had edged past its assets as of June 30, while KAI carried the biggest share of the debt at roughly 3 trillion rupiah. Outgoing finance minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa said last week that his ministry would take over responsibility for the debt from Danantara, an Indonesian wealth fund that oversees hundreds of SOEs, including those in PSBI. “The total debt is huge, but [its tenure] is stretched to 80 years due to restructuring. The instalments are 1 trillion [rupiah] or slightly less per year,” Purbaya told reporters on September 8. “I’m relaxed. I will probably be dead [in 80 years], so it’s not as scary as we imagined.” Purbaya said the debt would be managed by a special mission vehicle under the Ministry of Finance – likely Sarana Multi Infrastruktur (SMI), an infrastructure financing institution, or the Indonesia Investment Authority sovereign wealth fund. Despite the mounting debt, Purbaya said that Jakarta was committed to working with Beijing to extend the railway line to Surabaya. “I’ve spoken to the Chinese minister of finance and the authorities there. They seem interested,” he said. Whoosh was originally budgeted at US$6.02 billion, with 75 per cent funded through a China Development Bank loan at a 2 per cent interest rate and KCIC financing the rest. A subsequent US$1.2 billion cost overrun was covered by an additional loan from the bank at an interest rate of 3.4 per cent. Danantara’s CEO Rosan Roeslani said on Monday that the debt takeover plan would continue under the new finance minister, Suahasil Nazara. After the ministerial handover ceremony on Tuesday, Purbaya told reporters that he “thanks God that I am saved” from managing the transfer. KCIC did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ‘People’s money’ Analysts warn that shifting the debt away from SOEs to state financial vehicles is an accounting change that still leaves the public on the hook. Muhammad Andri Perdana, research director at Jakarta think tank Bright Institute, said absorbing the liabilities into state accounts stripped away the commercial nature of the venture and placed a direct burden on public funds. “As the Whoosh debt is transferred to the Ministry of Finance, it could burden the Indonesian government,” Muhammad said. “Danantara should be the one to fix the problem, as it is tasked with improving the [financial] health of state-owned enterprises, such as those in the KCIC consortium.” The debt takeover could deplete state revenue and reduce SMI’s capacity to finance other national priority projects, Muhammad said. “Even though it appears we’re not using the state budget to pay off the debt, SMI’s or INA’s profits, which were originally supposed to be deposited into the state budget, will now be used to pay off the high-speed railway debt, which is tantamount to reducing the state budget.” Anthony Budiawan, managing director of the Political Economy and Policy Studies think tank, agreed that Whoosh’s debt would be paid off “using the people’s money". Budiawan said that choosing Chinese financing over Japan’s initial proposal doomed the project’s financial viability from the start. “If we had used the Japanese proposal at the time, the interest rate was extremely low at 0.1 per cent. China’s rates of 2 to 3.4 per cent mean KCIC has to pay around 2 trillion rupiah annually in interest alone,” Budiawan said. “KCIC’s operational earnings in 2024 were only around 345 billion rupiah. With Japan, annual interest would have been 90 billion rupiah, which earnings could easily cover. Instead, we have a massive gap that the company cannot pay.” Budiawan urged Jakarta to exercise caution to avoid repeating past missteps should the government go ahead with its plan to extend the high-speed railway to Surabaya. “If the financing structure for the Surabaya extension looks like what we have now, we will just be digging a deeper grave,” he said. “There must be a proper feasibility study this time. The project tenders must be done properly, and interest payment calculations must be factored into project costs from [the beginning], because interest costs dictate cash flow for decades.”

title: 85% of Wang Fuk Court owners sign sale deals as flat selection moves ahead
description: Housing Bureau holds computerised ballot to set flat-selection order, posts results online as rehousing scheme moves into next phase.
content: More than 85 per cent of owners at the blaze-hit Wang Fuk Court have signed agreements to sell their flats to the Hong Kong government as authorities move ahead with flat selection under a special rehousing scheme. Authorities said on Tuesday that 1,702 households – 85.8 per cent of flat owners across blocks A to H at the estate – had signed sale and purchase agreements as of Monday. On the same day, the Housing Bureau held a computerised ballot to determine the selection sequence for subsidised flats under the scheme. “The Housing Bureau conducted separate computerised random-ordering ballots for the two batches of applicants to determine the sequence of the last two digits of the application numbers held by the applicants,” a spokesman said. “Based on the ballot results, the Housing Bureau randomly generated the order of all applicants.” In the wake of the blaze last November, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000, the government announced a buy-back of all 1,984 flats at the subsidised housing estate in Tai Po. Under the scheme, flats are being acquired at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot depending on whether owners have paid the land premium. Participating owners can use the cash compensation to purchase a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to buy new subsidised housing under a flat-for-flat arrangement. Owners had until August 31 to submit acceptance letters. Those who indicated their intention to sell by June 30 are eligible for priority flat selection. The bureau said flat selection under the special sales exercise was expected to begin later this month. “The Housing Bureau will, in accordance with the order of priority, issue letters in batches to notify applicants of the priority order and invite eligible applicants to attend flat selection sessions,” a government spokesman said. Ballot results and the priority order based on the computerised draw had been uploaded to the designated website, the bureau added. The government has set aside more than 4,400 flats at 10 development projects for these owners, spread across Kowloon Bay, Kai Tak, Kam Tin, Tseung Kwan O, Ping Shan, Tung Chung, Tai Po, Fanling and Kwun Tong. Earlier, the South China Morning Post spoke to six residents who said they would not sell, arguing that no financial package could compensate for the loss of their homes and community ties.

title: Malaysia’s ex-PM Muhyiddin acquitted of 4 charges in US$49 million corruption case
description: Prosecutors decided not to proceed with three money-laundering charges and one of abuse of power against the former leader.
content: Malaysia’s former prime minister Muhyiddin Yassin won a significant court victory on Tuesday after he was acquitted of four charges linked to a government programme set up to help contractors during the Covid-19 pandemic. The Kuala Lumpur High Court cleared Muhyiddin of three money-laundering charges and one of abuse of power involving 200 million ringgit (US$49.1 million), after prosecutors said they no longer wanted to pursue those counts in his Jana Wibawa trial. The ruling removes four of the seven charges against Muhyiddin, although he still faces three abuse-of-power counts, keeping him among several of the country’s former prime ministers caught up in criminal proceedings. High Court judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin ordered Muhyiddin’s full acquittal after rejecting the prosecution’s request for a discharge not amounting to an acquittal, which would have allowed the charges to be revived later. “Accordingly, the court discharges and acquits the accused of the four charges,” she said, as quoted by local media reports. Deputy public prosecutor Ahmad Akram Gharib told the court that prosecutors had reviewed the case “as a whole” before deciding not to proceed with the four charges. No further reason was immediately given. Akram Gharib declined to comment on the decision to discontinue the charges when contacted by This Week in Asia. Muhyiddin, 79, who remains president of the opposition Bersatu party, was accused of using his positions as prime minister and party chief to obtain 200 million ringgit from Bukhary Equity Sdn Bhd for Bersatu and later laundering that same amount through the party’s bank accounts. Prosecutors acknowledged when the trial opened in March that the money did not enter Muhyiddin’s personal accounts, but argued he had an indirect interest because he was both prime minister and Bersatu president at the time. The allegations stem from Jana Wibawa, a programme introduced during Muhyiddin’s administration to help ethnic Malay and other indigenous contractors, known as Bumiputera, weather the economic fallout from the Covid-19 pandemic. Three abuse-of-power charges remain against him, involving 25.3 million ringgit allegedly received by Bersatu from Nepturis Sdn Bhd, Mamfor Sdn Bhd and parties linked to KCJ Engineering Sdn Bhd. Muhyiddin has pleaded not guilty and has repeatedly described the case against him as politically motivated. His acquittal comes two months after Malaysia’s Federal Court upheld the acquittal of former youth minister Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman on four charges involving criminal breach of trust, misappropriation and money laundering of funds belonging to his former Bersatu youth wing. Muhyiddin also faces a separate sedition prosecution over remarks made during a 2024 election campaign in which he questioned why Malaysia’s then king, Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah, did not appoint him prime minister following the inconclusive 2022 general election. Muhyiddin served as prime minister for 17 months from 2020 until 2021 after the collapse of the first Pakatan Harapan government. The latest ruling adds to a string of politically sensitive cases involving Malaysia’s former prime ministers. Najib Razak is serving prison terms for corruption linked to the multibillion-dollar scandal in which billions were siphoned from state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad, and is seeking another royal pardon. Ismail Sabri pleaded not guilty last month to failing to declare millions of dollars in cash, foreign currencies and gold to the country’s anti-corruption agency. Muhyiddin’s latest court victory came days after Malaysia’s Pardons Board deferred Najib’s latest clemency application. Najib, jailed since 2022, had his initial 12-year sentence halved in 2024 but later failed in a legal attempt to serve the remainder under house arrest. In December, Najib was handed another 15-year prison sentence after being convicted of four abuse-of-power charges and 21 money-laundering counts involving about 2.3 billion ringgit in 1MDB funds. He is appealing against that conviction.

title: ‘Lazy economy’: US$15 monthly rubbish services in China gain popularity, benefitting elderly
description: Trend highlights a growing market of convenient, time-saving services for people lacking the energy for daily chores.
content: A new business trend has emerged in China where young people get paid to throw out rubbish for others at a small fee – and it is proving to be a surprising success. While many people consider taking out the rubbish merely an incidental chore, it has evolved into a paid service in China. On social media platforms, some entrepreneurs promote their rubbish disposal services. Their fees range from three to five yuan (45 to 75 US cents) per pickup, with an option for a monthly package priced at around 100 yuan (US$15). The monthly service includes daily rubbish collection, requiring clients only to place their bag of rubbish outside their door for easy pickup. This represents a novel aspect of the lazy economy, characterised by time-saving, labour-saving, and convenient services, following in the footsteps of other viral offerings, such as picking up children from school and collecting parcels for clients. Some people find this business model puzzling. One person asked: “Isn’t this just a side task on your way out? Do people actually pay for such a service?” To their surprise, many people expressed a genuine need for this rubbish disposal service. One individual, coping with depression, shared: “I only dispose of rubbish late at night, worried about encountering others. This service is a necessity for me.” Another client from Shanghai, China’s first city to implement a mandatory household waste-sorting system, highlighted that certain residential compounds permit rubbish collection only for two hours in the morning and another two in the evening. “As an ordinary office worker, it’s easy for me to miss those four hours,” they explained. Additionally, homebodies who prefer staying indoors consistently find the service beneficial. Moreover, a service provider in Jiaxing, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, known by her surname Fei, mentioned that her team also assists elderly individuals with mobility issues who live on upper floors without lifts. Fei reported receiving three orders in her first month but remains optimistic about growth, planning to collaborate with communities while focusing on the needs of elderly clients. Another service provider from Hangzhou, Zhejiang, named Mihan, claimed to have secured over 20 orders just three days after launching her business. She occasionally picks up parcels for her clients as an additional service. Discussing the advantages of this job, Mihan noted: “I barely need to meet my clients in person.” She emphasised that the key to the success of this business model is affordability: “Today’s office workers are willing to spend a little money to save time.” Similarly, parcel collection costs three to five yuan per parcel and around 100 yuan for daily collection over a month. Picking up children is pricier, costing around 50 yuan per trip, but parents unable to leave work early still require this service.

title: ‘Doing a North Korea’? Why the Middle East could be entering a new nuclear age
description: A Saudi-US nuclear pact and further attacks on Iran could prompt Tehran to withdraw from the non-proliferation treaty, analysts warn.
content: The Middle East stands on the precipice of a new nuclear age, with Saudi Arabia set to acquire American uranium enrichment technology and Turkey eager to follow suit, as Iran weighs withdrawal from the treaty that bars it from making atomic bombs. Momentum is building: last week, the United States and Israel both threatened further air strikes against Iran’s nuclear facilities, accusing Tehran of attempting to resurrect its nuclear programme. The country’s three main complexes were buried deep underground after the US and Israel bombed them during their first, brief air war against the Islamic Republic in June 2025. The warnings from US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu followed the publication on September 9 of a study by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) claiming that a surge in construction activity at the so-called Pickaxe Mountain site “likely” meant it was being developed into an underground fortress for Iran’s nuclear programme. The CSIS report said the facility could either be a centrifuge assembly plant, an enrichment site or a safe haven for other “nuclear weapons-relevant” work such as uranium metal conversion. That same day, Trump said Western intelligence agencies had flagged the Pickaxe facility as a likely storage site for nuclear material. “We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard,” he threatened. In a video message on September 10, Netanyahu alleged that Iran, “after we destroyed its immediate capability to produce nuclear bombs … is trying again”. However, the CSIS findings were hotly disputed by eminent American nuclear weapons expert David Albright, founder of the Institute for Science and International Security. In a social media post on Monday, Albright argued that the construction activity at Pickaxe Mountain spotted by satellites in August had in fact been under way since last year’s air strikes and more likely showed Iran preparing the site for a potential US attack. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed the CSIS report on Tuesday as “much ado about nothing”. Still, its publication coincided with an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) decision to refer Iran’s file to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years. The resolution, brought by Britain, France and Germany, accused Iran of non-compliance with the nuclear non-proliferation treaty (NPT) on the grounds it had withheld information on its stockpiles of highly enriched uranium stored in the three facilities rendered inaccessible by American bunker-buster bombs and by denying IAEA inspectors access to the sites. The referral is not expected to yield further UN Security Council action against Iran, because of opposition from veto-wielding permanent members China and Russia. But the political fallout is already being felt in Tehran, where hardliners have seized on the move to renew calls for withdrawal from the NPT. Mohsen Rezaee, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned that the IAEA’s “politicised and disruptive actions will push countries towards withdrawing from the NPT”. Analysts who spoke to This Week in Asia said further US-Israeli strikes could prompt Tehran to take that very action. Barbara Slavin, distinguished Middle East fellow at the Stimson Centre, said such attacks would “increase political support within the regime for such a step”. Sina Azodi, author of Iran and the Bomb, called withdrawal “quite likely” given the war and Iran’s “strong dissatisfaction with the IAEA and the NPT itself”. Ali Alfoneh, author of Political Succession in the Islamic Republic of Iran, was more cautious, suggesting Tehran would only leave the NPT “if and when it has completed production of two nuclear weapons: one for testing and another to retain as a deterrent”. Slavin agreed that the likelihood of Iran “doing a North Korea” was increasing. Azodi also noted growing support within Iran for “weaponisation” since the previous strategy of enriching uranium to near weapons-grade without actually building a bomb had failed to deter the US and Israeli attacks. “Whether Tehran can actually sneak out and test a device is a separate issue,” Azodi said. Alfoneh similarly said he suspected that “technical obstacles, rather than an absence of political resolve, are the principal constraint on Iranian weaponisation”. A July 22 agreement between the US and Saudi Arabia to develop the kingdom’s nuclear power industry was expected to further strengthen Iran’s resolve to keep its uranium enrichment capabilities, analysts said. The deal, which Alfoneh calls “a sad joke”, has alarmed nuclear non-proliferation experts because it includes scope for future uranium enrichment activities using American reactors and Saudi uranium reserves. At the IAEA’s annual general conference in Vienna on Tuesday, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman announced the discovery of 110 million tonnes of uranium-bearing ore near the holy city of Medina. The agreement with the US makes proliferation safeguards a bilateral matter, sparing Saudi Arabia the intrusive nationwide inspection regime required by the IAEA. The Arms Control Association said in a statement published on September 1 that the Trump administration had “rejected key non-proliferation conditions for US nuclear cooperation that have long-standing bipartisan support and are internationally recognised best practices” in negotiating the agreement with Riyadh. While Saudi Arabia had insisted its interest in enrichment is purely for civilian purposes, the association observed that the same technology could create fissile material for a bomb – a risk it called “particularly troubling given that Saudi officials have openly threatened to pursue nuclear weapons to match any Iranian capability”. Analysts said Nato member Turkey was closely following all these developments. According to Gonul Tol, senior Turkey fellow at the Middle East Institute, Ankara sees the US-Saudi deal as “evidence that regional states are becoming more serious about preserving a nuclear option”. “Just as importantly, Turkish officials see Washington itself as becoming more flexible about non-proliferation,” Tol noted in a September 10 research paper. The Iran war, Turkey’s expulsion from the F-35 programme, Trump’s threats towards Nato and broader questions about US security guarantees had also “strengthened doubts in Ankara about whether Turkey can rely indefinitely on the American nuclear umbrella”, she said. Turkey would likely hedge by seeking “greater control over its nuclear supply chain and more indigenous nuclear capabilities”, Tol added.

title: Has a Chinese DF missile been used for the first time in the Middle East?
description: Video of a DF-15A rocket motor in Marib hints at secret arms deliveries as Saudi-Houthi fighting escalates.
content: Debris from a Chinese-made short-range ballistic missile has been found in Yemen for the first time, suggesting Chinese weapons systems may have been used during the heated conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Video clips circulating on social media in the past week showed debris from the booster stage of a short-range ballistic missile with “DF-15A” written on its side found in the Raghwan district of Marib governorate, about 170km (105 miles) by road from the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. The same images were carried uncensored by multiple Chinese online news outlets. The discovery marks the first time the DF-15A missile, and more broadly the Dongfeng missile series, has been found operating in the Middle East. There are no previous confirmed reports of its export to Middle Eastern entities, suggesting the Chinese-made missile may have been delivered covertly to the region. The DF-15A is the advanced variant of the Chinese DF-15 short-range ballistic missile, a series with a range of up to 900km. While the DF-15 series is classified as a single-stage solid-propellant missile system, the recovered hardware appears to correspond to the large solid-rocket motor casing used during the initial boost phase of flight. China is the only confirmed operator of the DF-15 family but there have been reports of its possible transfer to countries such as Egypt, Pakistan and Syria. The discovery comes amid intensified fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. Neither Saudi Arabia nor Houthi militants have publicly acknowledged operating the DF-15A, but analysis of the debris in Yemen suggests Riyadh may have imported and operated the Chinese-made missile, based on its previous covert introduction of the Dongfeng series. Saudi Arabia secretly acquired the DF-3A intermediate-range ballistic missile from China in the late 1980s, while the Houthis are known to mainly incorporate Iranian technology into their weaponry. More recent reports of satellite imagery and other open-source intelligence provide evidence of Saudi Arabia’s operation of Chinese-designed ballistic missile infrastructure linked to the DF-21 medium range ballistic missile family. Despite its operation of Chinese-made missiles, however, there are no known records of Saudi Arabia’s combat use of the ballistic missile systems, even in its conflict with the Houthis that began in 2015. It remains unclear how the debris of the DF-15A was found in the Marib region. The discovery of the booster stage suggests a stage separation from the initial boost phase of the flight, or that the missile broke apart during the flight, either by internal failure or external destruction. The Houthis are not known to have any weapons that could have intercepted it, while there have been several reports of Saudi air strikes nearby. On September 11, Houthi media said there had been 32 Saudi air strikes in the regions of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeidah. While Saudi Arabia imports most of its arms from the United States and European countries, it has recently strengthened its defence ties with Pakistan under the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed in September 2025. The treaty was speculated to play a role, with Pakistan providing a nuclear umbrella over Saudi Arabia amid escalating military tensions in the region. About 80 per cent of Pakistan’s arms imports are supplied by China and the DF-15A is assessed as nuclear-capable. Following Iran’s reported request to support its war against the US and Israel, the Houthi militants have engaged in offensives in their civil war against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, taking over strategically important Marib and Taiz and claiming control of the Yemeni coast along the Red Sea and blockading its entrance, the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb – a critical energy transport route – to Saudi oil traffic. The Houthis have also escalated missile and drone attacks against southern Saudi Arabia, targeting military and energy infrastructure and further constraining the global energy supply chain following Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

title: Meet Lee Pace, who stars as Ian Wright in Practical Magic 2 alongside Sandra Bullock
description: The actor, who is married to a Thom Browne executive, boasts an impressive list of fantasy credits, including The Hobbit trilogy and The Twilight Saga.
content: Lee Pace is no stranger to fantasy. The 47-year-old actor is known for playing Thranduil the Elvenking in The Hobbit trilogy, Ronan the Accuser in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Brother Day in Foundation and vampire Garrett in The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn – Part 2. Most recently, he joins Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in Practical Magic 2, and the internet has fallen under his spell. The newly released sequel to the 1998 film, which also stars Joey King and Maisie Williams, secured a US$30 million opening at the box office, taking over the top spot held by Spider-Man: Brand New Day for six weeks. Pace plays Ian Wright, a professor of magic history who gets involved with Bullock’s Sally Owens. Although Pace has found himself in hot water for suggesting during a recent Today show interview that a woman’s “magic power” was cooking, his heartthrob status remains unchanged. Here’s everything to know about Lee Pace. What is Lee Pace’s background? According to his IMDb, Lee Grinner Pace was born on March 25, 1979, in Chickasha, Oklahoma, to engineer James Roy Pace and teacher Charlotte Kloeckler. He grew up in a suburb near Houston, Texas, per Highsnobiety, but he also spent part of his childhood in Louisiana and Saudi Arabia because of his father’s work, per the Associated Press. Pace moved to New York at 17 and was accepted into the Juilliard School. “I definitely feel the Texan me,” he told Highsnobiety before adding, “I’m not really from anywhere.” He has a brother named Will and a younger sister, with whom the actor said he is “very close”, in his interview with lifestyle and culture magazine Mr Feelgood. How did Lee Pace get into acting? Pace caught the acting bug after he had to give up swimming due to painful earaches that required surgery, he told French magazine Crash. At his mother’s suggestion, he took a drama class around age 12 or 13 and became a “nerdy theatre kid,” Pace described his younger self in a recent interview with Flaunt magazine. He worked for Alley Theatre in Houston and later auditioned for Juilliard, where he eventually earned a bachelor’s degree in fine arts in performing arts. Pace has since been nominated for a Golden Globe for best supporting actor for his performance in Soldier’s Girl. He also received an Emmy nomination for outstanding lead actor in a comedy series for his role in Pushing Daisies. He debuted on Broadway in 2011 with The Normal Heart. Is Lee Pace single? Pace is married to Thom Browne executive Matthew Foley. According to Foley’s LinkedIn, his most recent position with the brand was global vice-president of marketing and communications. The couple was introduced by a mutual friend, per GQ Hype, and Pace described their marriage as “an endless sleepover with your weirdest friend”. They live in a 200-year-old upstate New York farmhouse, per Just Jared.

title: Meet Celine Dion’s 3 supportive sons, René-Charles and twins Nelson and Eddy
description: The ‘My Heart Will Go On’ singer’s emotional Paris comeback following her illness shines a spotlight on her children with late husband René Angélil.
content: For the first time in six years, Celine Dion returned to the stage and performed a full live show to kick-start her residency at the Plenitude Arena in Paris from September 12 to May 29, 2027. The 58-year-old was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome in late 2022, a rare autoimmune neurological disorder that causes muscle stiffness and painful spasms. The diagnosis led the songstress to step away from the limelight; she last performed a live full set in 2020 as part of her Courage tour. Dion’s comeback was an emotional one, both for her and her fans. Her shows were sold out within hours of the tickets going on sale, with more than 9 million fans trying to get their hands on tickets to see Dion, per The Guardian. The “My Heart Will Go On” singer shed tears on opening night, telling her fans: “I had promised myself not to cry. But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you. I’m going to sing, like you, without crying.” Dion is widely recognised as a musical icon, but in her personal life, she is a mother of three and has often said publicly that being a parent is what makes her proudest. In 2023, a source told People that Dion’s three sons were her “light” as she struggled with her health. Although they have remained relatively under the radar, Dion does occasionally share snippets of her kids on social media. So, what do we know about her three sons, René-Charles, Nelson and Eddy, who were recently spotted in Paris supporting their mother? Who is the father of Celine Dion’s children? René-Charles, 25, and twins Nelson and Eddy, 15, were born to the Canadian singer and her late husband René Angélil. According to People magazine, Angélil passed away in 2016 after battling throat cancer. “I feel extremely fortunate as a mother that – it’s probably the thing I’m the most proud of – I prepared my children for how to live … how to live with him without his presence,” Dion told Ellen DeGeneres in 2016. René-Charles Angélil Dion’s eldest child, René-Charles Angélil, was born in January 2001 and named after his father. Although he had a low-profile childhood, he has been in the spotlight more recently, after news emerged that he was pursuing a career in music like his mother. As previously reported, the budding musician, known to his peers as RC and also goes by the name Big Tip, has produced and rapped over remixes of songs by The Weeknd on his SoundCloud, which once shot to No 1 and 2 on the platform’s R&B & Soul New & Hot chart. In 2017, René-Charles also made a cameo in his mother’s live performance of Michael Jackson’s “Black or White” in Paris. Apart from making music, his hobbies reportedly include golf, hockey and poker. Nelson and Eddy Angélil Born in October 2010 in West Palm Beach, Florida, Nelson and Eddy Angélil were dubbed a “double blessing” by Dion and her husband. According to People, Dion went through six rounds of IVF and one miscarriage before announcing the news that she was pregnant with the fraternal twins. Eddy’s name was inspired by producer Eddy Marnay, who helped with Dion’s first five albums, according to People. Dion’s rep told the publication that “he was like a father to her. Eddy is a major influence in both Celine and René’s lives”. Nelson was named after the late former president of South Africa, Nelson Mandela, whom Dion once met on a tour, per the same source. “Celine and René want their children to be inspired by their names, because they were so inspired by these men,” Dion’s rep told the magazine at the time. When describing the twins, Dion told Hello! in 2010 that “one is more gutsy than the other”. The singer said Nelson “seems to have a little stronger personality”, adding he was “the tougher of the two”. Celine Dion is very close to her kids Dion has always been close with her three sons. They have helped each other get through the grief of losing Angélil. “So I got myself a huge, huge, huge bed and I sleep with my twins. They are comforting me a lot. I need them. I need them close,” Dion told The Sun in 2017. “And when it’s time for them to say they want their room, their room’s ready. But we watch a lot of TV together. I’m discovering Disney,” she added. In 2020, the “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now” superstar shared old photos of the twins on Instagram to mark their birthday. “Nelson and Eddy, you have been bringing so much joy, love and laughter into our lives every single day for the past 10 years,” Dion wrote. With additional reporting by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Forget AI KPIs: how China’s tech giants are rationing tokens for employees
description: Employees at Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent and ByteDance all report tightening token policies, with some staff asked to co-pay to use US AI models.
content: When generative artificial intelligence first swept through China’s technology sector, workers faced a clear directive from management: use AI and use it often. Consuming vast numbers of AI tokens – the basic unit of computing power needed to process text or write code – became a badge of honour, with companies often viewing a high token count as a sign that employees were productive and taking initiative. But those computing allowances are now being sharply rolled back as China’s leading internet companies introduce token quotas to rein in rising AI-related costs, according to staff who spoke with the South China Morning Post on condition of anonymity. At ByteDance, one employee said staff using closed-source models must co-pay out of pocket. The company reimburses roughly half of external tool costs, capping annual payouts at around US$1,000 for technical staff and interns, and US$300 for non-technical employees, according to the staff member. Alibaba Group Holding, meanwhile, allocates employees 3,000 to 6,000 monthly credits for its internal coding platform, QoderWork, with additional credits granted when needed, according to people familiar with the programme. Reimbursements for external AI tools are capped at US$200 a month and subject to security rules. At Baidu, developers start with a baseline allowance of 1,500 yuan (US$223) a month, with another 1,500 yuan top-up available upon request, according to employees. While routine development tasks typically only consumed about 500 yuan worth of tokens per month, staff using advanced models in “deep-thinking” modes could exhaust their monthly allowance much more quickly, they said. At Tencent Holdings, workers who previously had access to flat annual token allocations must now draw from departmental pools overseen by line managers, according to several employees. Those who ran out mid-month had to file requests with their supervisors for additional resources, the sources said. Tencent has reassured employees that it would not rank them by token consumption nor measure their performance solely by token usage. In response to queries, Tencent said on Saturday that it aimed to meet employee AI token needs as far as possible, adjusting allocations based on workload, demand and model capabilities. The company added that “tokenmaxxing” – excessive consumption merely to inflate usage numbers – should not be encouraged. Alibaba, Baidu and ByteDance did not respond to requests for comment. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The tightening rules reflect an operational headache brewing inside tech firms. As workers adopt increasingly complex agentic AI workflows – where software autonomously plans, executes code, searches for information and verifies its own work – a single prompt can rapidly burn through computational capacity. Data from Goldman Sachs highlights the scale of the demand. Enterprise and consumer token consumption was projected to jump 24-fold between 2026 and 2030, reaching 120 quadrillion tokens monthly, the bank said in a May report. While the cost to process each token was forecast to fall by 60 to 70 per cent annually, lower prices could encourage companies to run models more frequently, analysts said. Additional reporting by Ann Cao, Ben Jiang and Coco Feng

title: ‘New normal’: China to see slower loan growth amid sluggish consumption, investment
description: Loans reverse record contraction a month earlier but fall far short of expectations as property slump drags and deposits rise.
content: Slower but higher-quality loan growth may become a “new normal” for the Chinese economy as its financial structure undergoes a profound shift, China’s central bank governor Pan Gongsheng has said. “Maintaining past credit growth rates is difficult and unnecessary,” said Pan in an article published on Wednesday in the Communist Party’s theoretical journal, arguing that revitalising inefficient existing loans was essentially equivalent to new lending in supporting growth. This shift is part of the dynamic alignment between the financial sector and the ongoing industrial transformation – from real estate and infrastructure towards high-end manufacturing and green industries, he added. Pan’s comment came as the central bank’s latest credit data showed new lending by China’s banks returned to growth in August after a record contraction the previous month, but the scale remained subdued as sluggish consumption and investment continued to weigh on credit demand. The country’s real estate and local government financing vehicle loans still account for a large share of the more than 280 trillion yuan (US$41.7 billion) outstanding loan balance at present. However, both are shrinking – real estate loans fell by more than 2 trillion yuan between 2025 and the first half of 2026, he noted, adding that other sectors must first offset this decline before total credit can grow. The change was also unfolding amid a changing financial landscape in which the share of indirect financing, dominated by bank loans, continued to decline, while the share of direct financing, including bonds and equities, rose steadily. New bank loans totalled 60 billion yuan (US$8.94 billion) in August, reversing a record contraction of 340 billion yuan in July, according to data released by the People’s Bank of China on Monday. The figure, however, fell well short of the 380 billion yuan consensus forecast among economists surveyed by Wind. For the first eight months of the year, banks extended 10.44 trillion yuan in new loans, down 22 per cent from 13.46 trillion yuan in the same period last year. The credit figures were followed by economic data on Tuesday that pointed to deepening weakness in domestic demand. Retail sales grew just 0.4 per cent year on year in August, while fixed-asset investment fell 7.2 per cent in the first eight months, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. Corporate medium- and long-term loans increased by about 320 billion yuan last month, compared with an increase of 470 billion yuan a year earlier, calculations based on central bank data showed. Household credit demand remained restrained, with shrinking short-term borrowing pointing to weak appetite for consumer and business loans, while the property slump and early mortgage repayments continued to weigh on longer term lending, according to a report by Southwest Securities on Monday. “Loan growth is likely to remain weak, although the year-on-year decline may gradually narrow as faster fiscal disbursement and special treasury bond funding help banks increase longer-term lending for infrastructure and equipment upgrades,” the brokerage said. Weak home sales would continue to constrain mortgage demand, the report added. “Credit expansion in the fourth quarter may depend more heavily on policy funding, while a recovery in underlying financing demand will take time,” it said. The weakness in household borrowing contrasted with shifts in deposits. Household deposits rose by about 40 billion yuan in August after declining by roughly 630 billion yuan in July, while deposits at non-bank financial institutions, including brokerages, increased by about 560 billion yuan.
