BOC International (China) said in a report on Tuesday that financing demand from the real economy remained weak in August, extending the trend of previous months. “With domestic demand weak and uncertainty surrounding external demand still elevated, monetary policy should seek to meet the real economy’s financing needs by improving the structure of lending to businesses,” the brokerage said. It added that policymakers could work through financial institutions to strengthen monitoring of the financing needs and liquidity conditions of small- and medium-sized enterprises.

title: German industry wants tougher trade action on Beijing. So why are investments in China up?
description: Companies are caught between China’s growing competitive threat and its importance as a market, manufacturer and source of growth.
content: German companies have little choice but to keep investing in China if they want to remain globally competitive, according to a new study by the German Economic Institute (IW) published amid growing calls for Brussels to take a harder line on Chinese trade practices. German firms invested an additional €5.6 billion (US$6.46 billion) in China in the first half of 2026, up about one-third from the same period a year earlier, according to the IW study published on Monday, which cited German central bank data. The figure was broadly in line with the average for the first half of each year between 2020 and 2025, pointing to relatively steady investment over the longer term. It contrasts with a marked decline in German firms’ investment in the United States, which fell 65 per cent year on year to about €4.3 billion in the first half of this year, according to a separate IW analysis published last month. Juergen Matthes, the author of the study released on Monday, said that to keep pace with the “fierce global price competition” of Chinese firms, German companies needed to expand production in China and “take advantage of the competitive distortions there”. These included state subsidies for Chinese companies and an undervalued yuan, Matthes said, noting that they made production costs “artificially cheap”. The findings come as German businesses adopt a harder line towards Beijing. More than half of firms surveyed by the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK) earlier this month backed tougher trade measures, even if such policies risked harming their own operations. At the same time, the IW described China as both an important sales market and a “fitness ground” for some German firms. Businesses capable of surviving fierce competition in the world’s second-largest economy were more likely to succeed in global markets, according to the study. More than 85 per cent of German subsidiaries in China planned to at least maintain their presence, while more than half intended to increase investment, the IW noted, citing a survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China. That expansion was increasingly financed by earnings generated in China rather than capital from Germany, according to the study. Reinvested earnings – profits retained in China instead of being sent back to Germany – reached €7.8 billion in 2025, against an annual average of €5.4 billion between 2017 and 2024. A separate report released by the German Chamber of Commerce in China last week pointed to a similar dilemma. While the global expansion of Chinese companies was intensifying competitive pressure on German firms, it had also become a major business opportunity – with nearly half of surveyed firms supplying products or services to Chinese companies operating overseas. Even so, calls for tougher European Union action are mounting. Matthes warned production and jobs were moving to China and urged the EU to “put a stop to this unfair game” by imposing countervailing tariffs on Chinese imports. Berlin has long been reluctant to back aggressive trade measures against Beijing, but German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shifted course under mounting pressure from domestic industry. In late August, he tasked his cabinet with drawing up proposals to address the trade gap with China.

title: US judge blocks Trump’s ‘absurd’ visa caps for students, journalists
description: The last-minute freeze keeps old rules in place as legal challenge by university groups and labour unions makes its way through the courts.
content: A US federal judge on Monday temporarily blocked a new visa cap for international students, visiting scholars and foreign journalists, saying the Trump administration’s national security justification “borders on the absurd”. Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston said the rationale for the restriction was “exceptionally weak”, and the connection between the rule and the problems it purported to address was “exceptionally attenuated”. He wrote that the US Department of Homeland Security had built the case “almost entirely on a small handful of anecdotes, each of which involved incidents that the new rule would do nothing to prevent or even mitigate”. In July, the department published a final rule doing away with the long-standing “duration of status” system, under which holders of F, J and I visas may remain for the length of their programme or assignment. Under the new rule, which was scheduled to take effect on Tuesday, foreign journalists would be limited to 240 days in the US, with no way to appeal if the renewal was denied. For Chinese passport holders, excluding those from Hong Kong and Macau, the limit would be just 90 days. The US State Department issued 12,924 I visas to foreign media in 2024. Saylor, who was appointed by former president George W. Bush, said “the possibilities for abuse are rampant”, pointing to “the obvious likelihood” that the visas of foreign journalists critical of the government would not be renewed. The rule would limit international students’ stays to four years and restrict programme changes, transfers and second degrees at the same academic level. Additionally, it would cut the post-graduation grace period from 60 days to just 30 days. India and China together make up more than half of all foreign students in the US. India is now the biggest source, with 363,019 students in 2024-25, ahead of China’s 265,919, which was down by 4 per cent from a year earlier and well below its pre-pandemic peak of about 370,000. New arrivals are falling faster. US campuses reported a 17 per cent drop in first-time international enrolments in autumn last year. The Department of Homeland Security had argued that the “duration of status” policy let people linger and hop between programmes. Saylor said the agency failed to show how a blunt time limit would resolve those problems and criticised the department for treating a possible collapse in foreign enrolment as inconsequential. “The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be catastrophic,” Saylor wrote, adding that the cap “will have the unavoidable effect of making the United States a less attractive destination for the world’s top students”. Adam Rose, deputy director of advocacy at the New York-based Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the ruling “a victory for the United States”, saying the administration’s targeting of journalist visas was “fundamentally un-American and a betrayal of the First Amendment”. He warned that forcing journalists to renew visas every few months could enable content-based denials and “chill the ability to report freely”. The policy, he added, could also be weaponised by future administrations to target opposing viewpoints and critical coverage. A coalition of university groups and labour unions sued to challenge the rule last month. Until the lawsuit is decided, the old system stays: students, visiting researchers and foreign reporters may remain for the length of their programmes or assignments. The next hearing in the case will be held on October 2. US President Donald Trump’s administration is expected to appeal against the temporary freeze. The fight comes amid a wider squeeze on legal immigration. Last week, the Department of Homeland Security proposed ending the 60-day grace period that lets H-1B and other work visa holders stay and find a new sponsor following a lay-off. Last month, the agency floated a US$103,265 fee for most new H-1B petitions for skilled foreign workers. Additionally, after warnings last month from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, several institutions including Stanford University, Harvard University, the University of California, Berkeley and the University of Michigan paused or restricted off-campus internships for international students.

title: India scores Brics win with joint declaration despite divides
description: New Delhi ‘papered over’ differences to keep the bloc focused on trade and tech priorities, analysts say.
content: India scored a diplomatic win at the latest Brics summit, analysts have said, after steering an increasingly unwieldy bloc towards a joint declaration despite deep divisions over geopolitical conflicts and the global order. Observers said New Delhi achieved “pragmatic consolidation” by avoiding forcing members to assign blame for contentious geopolitical issues, keeping the focus on trade, technology and greater representation for the Global South. That compromise came at a cost, however, with analysts noting that differences over the Middle East and other regional conflicts were merely “papered over”. During the 18th Brics summit held in Delhi over the weekend, leaders from the expanded 11-member bloc addressed international conflicts, trade disputes and economic governance before adopting a unified joint declaration. In it, leaders called for maximum restraint in the Middle East, expressed firm opposition to the displacement of Palestinians and cautioned against the weaponisation of critical minerals and technology. Without directly naming the United States, the bloc also criticised protectionist trade policies and global tariff escalations. As host, India emphasised digital public infrastructure, fairer international financial systems and stronger representation for developing nations. Manoj Kewalramani, a geopolitical analyst and chairman of the Takshashila Institution’s geostrategy programme in India, said securing an agreed text was “no easy feat”. “The fact that New Delhi could balance competing interests while getting principled agreements is a success,” he said, adding that the declaration managed to focus on issues without getting into “the politics of apportioning blame”. Rityusha Tiwary, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Delhi’s Shaheed Bhagat Singh College, said India’s achievement as chair was one of “pragmatic consolidation rather than transformation”. She said Delhi kept the agenda focused on areas where cooperation was politically feasible and directly relevant to the developmental priorities of developing countries, pointing to trade, technology, agriculture and digital public infrastructure. “India has to manage a difficult balancing act. It wants Brics to strengthen the voice of the Global South while ensuring that the organisation does not simply become an instrument of Chinese strategic influence,” Tiwary said. Brics’ foreign ministers failed to issue a joint statement in May due to sharp disagreements between new members Iran and the United Arab Emirates over the Middle East conflict, said Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South programme at the Washington-based Quincy Institute. “India was able to find a solution to this impasse,” he said, referring to a paragraph of the declaration that expressed “deep concern” and called for “maximum restraint” over escalating tensions while omitting direct blame on specific countries. “The price of this consensus, however, was weaker language on the Middle East war,” Shidore said, noting that the final text only acknowledged various national positions. “So the divides in Brics were papered over,” he said, which allowed leaders to shift focus to developmental issues. India, for instance, contributed proposals on boosting small businesses and creating incubation and innovation ecosystems. Mihaela Papa, director of research and principal research scientist at the MIT Centre for International Studies in Massachusetts, said India advanced cooperation in global supply chains, industrial development, agriculture, trade, health, science and innovation. However, she added that little progress was made on the cross-border payments initiative or the Brics Grain Exchange, both endorsed in 2024, due to technical, regulatory and political roadblocks. ‘Anti-West vs non-West’ During the summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed key initiatives for “greater Brics” cooperation focusing on the Global South, artificial intelligence, trade, digital industry, smart manufacturing and talent development. Kewalramani said Xi’s summit speeches referencing a “Cold War mentality” and unilateralism were structured as a “pushback” against Western dominance. “The implied solution is an order in which Western structural advantage is reduced and in which China’s global initiatives provide an architecture,” he said. By contrast, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s focus was not on Western dominance but on the exclusion of developing nations. “The solution, therefore, is larger representation and a stake in rule-making. This is the anti-West vs non-West distinction between the two,” Kewalramani said. Tiwary said Brics should not be judged on whether it became a “coherent” geopolitical bloc, as its strength lay in being a flexible platform for issue-based cooperation among countries “that do not share a common strategic world view”. “The larger the grouping becomes, the greater its representational weight, but also the greater the diversity of interests it has to accommodate,” Tiwary said. Brics currently has 11 full members – including Brazil, Russia, India and China – and 10 partner countries, such as Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam. More than 30 additional nations, including Turkey, Pakistan and Bangladesh, have formally applied or expressed interest in joining. Tiwary said India’s chairmanship showed that strategic autonomy and Global South leadership can coexist with pragmatic economic cooperation. “The harder question is whether this can be sustained once the chairmanship passes to another member,” she added. As India prepares to hand over the presidency to China, Papa said the two Asian powers would need to work closely to ensure continuity. “China has been more engaged on artificial intelligence and the climate leadership agenda, so these areas may receive greater emphasis under its presidency,” Papa said. Beijing sees Brics as a way to balance Washington and reinforce its implicit claim to be leader of the Global South, according to Shidore. “India would like Brics to be more complementary to existing US-led institutions rather than directly rivalling them,” he said, adding that Delhi also competed with Beijing for leadership of the Global South. “But neither side has allowed their competitive elements to overpower their constructive engagement with Brics. In this sense, both have shown maturity as major powers in Asia.”

title: Opinion | As the American century ends, Asia’s renaissance begins
description: The businesses that adapt early to engage China, India and Asean will help draft Asia’s next chapter and profit from it.
content: The ending of the American century is coinciding with an Asian renaissance. America remains the world’s largest economy and will stay that way for another decade or two. But its economy no longer dominates the world. And its “America first” policy has partners and allies looking for alternatives for trade and investment – and for certainty. Simultaneously, everyone else is changing. The fastest-growing economies in the 21st century will be Asian. Business leaders must wrestle with the paradox that while America remains the world’s most powerful nation, it no longer dominates the world order it built because it is drifting away. US and European businesses that do not understand the geopolitical and cultural shifts under way, and which still operate under an obsolete rule book for trade and investment, will find that their operations and strategy no longer match what their bottom line requires. Already, we have seen significant shifts in the relative weightage of Asian economies, especially China and India. Three forces drive the return of Asia. First, a return to form: until about 1820, China and India were consistently the world’s two largest economies. Second, Asia owes the West a quiet thank-you: it absorbed to varying degrees the seven pillars of Western wisdom – free-market economics, science and technology, meritocracy, the rule of law, education, pragmatism and a culture of peace. Third, an explosion of Asian cultural confidence has followed. Wealth and confidence have risen together across Asia. Western companies need to fully grasp and then internalise what that combination means for how the region negotiates, does business and sees its place in the world. A crucial distinction sits at the heart of this shift, one many in the West struggle to see: modernising does not mean Westernising. A century ago, even Asia’s own thinkers believed otherwise. In 1885, reformer Fukuzawa Yukichi was credited with urging Japan to “leave the ranks of Asian nations and cast our lot with civilised nations of the West”. Sun Yat-sen, speaking after Japan’s 1905 victory over Russia, cast that triumph as proof that an Asian nation could master Western methods on its own terms. Now, few believe prosperity requires them to shed their Asian identities. For deal makers, the practical differences in approach matter. In the West, a signed contract secures a deal. In much of Asia, a trusted relationship matters at least as much. Brand America once opened doors across Asia almost automatically, built on decades of trade, education and cultural exchange. Amid today’s tariff disputes, immigration bans, student visa rejections and political volatility, while goodwill towards America has not vanished, it no longer travels as powerfully. We must understand the market in front of us and adapt to it. A region this diverse cannot be run off a single playbook designed in a Western headquarters – it requires as many strategies as there are markets. Business leaders must watch and understand the new “CIA”: China, India and Asean. All three act in their own self-interest while doing their best to adhere to the rules-based order, even while it is fracturing. Of the three, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is the hardest for outsiders to understand. The 11-member Asean governs by consensus across 240 million Muslims, 130 million Christians, 140 million Buddhists and seven million Hindus – a diversity so wide its progress compares to a crab walk: two steps forward, one back, one sideways. Judged year to year, Asean looks stuck. Judged decade to decade, Asean’s durability bests the others. It has been remarkably resilient compared with Saarc, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, Mercosur, the South American trade bloc, even the European Union, which could not keep Britain and struggles to respond collectively to China’s rise. China has been Asean’s largest trading partner every year since 2009. China-Asean trade exploded from US$40 billion in 2000 to over US$1 trillion last year, primarily because China was Asean’s first dialogue partner to conclude a free-trade agreement. India’s connections with Southeast Asia are as deep as China’s. From the turn of the Common Era, Indian traders and priests spread Hindu-Buddhist traditions that shaped how Southeast Asian kings ruled, how their subjects wrote, even what their cities were called – Singapore’s name comes from the Sanskrit for “Lion City”. Two thousand years on, that imprint runs through the region’s languages, systems of rule and maps. Western businesses in Southeast Asia today are not writing on a blank page. They are joining a story well under way, and it helps to know what came before. Business leaders must grasp three key new realities. First, that Asia is modernising on its terms. Second, that Asean’s pragmatism is a huge asset in a troubled world. Third, that the China-India-Asean triangle will provide major sources of global economic growth. The businesses that adapt first and engage the new CIA won’t just avoid being left behind – they’ll help to draft the next chapter of Asia’s story and be best positioned to profit from it. This is written from a fireside chat between Steven Okun and Kishore Mahbubani at the US-Asean Strategic Business Forum held in Singapore on September 4.

title: 16th Gwangju Biennale rises above controversies as one of art world’s best in recent years
description: Curators urged visitors not to be distracted by the bitter pre-opening dispute over the ‘Taiwan Pavilion’ naming. They needn’t have worried.
content: Despite a title that sounds like a barked order, “You Must Change Your Life” may be one of the most sensitive, nuanced and fulfilling biennale shows in recent memory. And no, this is not just the relief of a smaller, less foot-blistering marathon of a show than usual, though that too is very much part of the curatorial philosophy. The strong selection of artworks in the main exhibition of the 16th Gwangju Biennale is blessedly free of the moralising, clichéd tone that taints so many recent biennials and delivers on the curatorial promise of empowering change by shifting our perspectives. The title is taken from Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 poem Archaic Torso of Apollo. Artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen – a Singaporean visual artist, filmmaker and curator – was reading the poem on a train while feeling creatively depleted after a major solo exhibition in 2024. In those words, he found rejuvenation. Now, they have been transplanted to an exhibition in a historically charged city where the Gwangju massacre of 1980 paved the way to eventual democracy in South Korea. A deep, slow burn of an exhibition As an artist who often has to navigate an exhausting circuit of global art exhibitions, Ho rebelled against the expansionary model of modern mega-exhibitions by confining the main exhibition to a single venue – the Biennale Hall – and restricting the roster to just 43 artists and groups, compared with over 70 artists and nine venues in the 2024 edition. It is a deep, slow burn of an exhibition that encourages a rare intensity of attention rather than a sheer accumulative experience. As Ho explained in the opening press conference, he wanted to prevent biennial panic. You do not have to worry about missing anything with this exhibition, which frames change as a sustained, interconnected reconfiguration that starts with the self. We see this in the quiet, durational painting practice of Sasaki Ken, whose works recur across four different galleries like familiar travelling companions. Referencing Japanese yoga, or Western-style painting – a tradition reserved for heroic, masculine subjects – Sasaki tenderly uses oil painting techniques to document the mundane that forms part of himself: household objects, drawings by his brother who has a disability, boots belonging to a friend who founded an alternative art school. This memorialisation of the personal recurs throughout the halls. Goldin+Senneby’s Resin Pond (2025) is a show-stopper in an otherwise spectacle-free event. Two tonnes of luminous pine resin spread across the floor visually seduce while physically obstructing the space. Jakob Senneby – one half of the Stockholm-based artistic duo – has multiple sclerosis. The work brings home the reality of living with an immune system that has become toxic, while its broader social resonance ripples across the still pond. The body and perspectives Several other artists also address how the body and the mind change to accommodate a life with illness. Italian artist Rossella Biscotti explores the retraining of the body after illness in Alfabeto (2018). Indian photographer Sohrab Hura’s Life is Elsewhere (2015) is a collection of photos, videos and writings recording the years when his family isolated themselves while his mother suffered from acute paranoid schizophrenia. While Hura dreamed of life elsewhere, the intimate, grainy black-and-white photos of his mother are a record of pain, taboo and love. The exhibition continually shifts our macro and micro perspectives. Mumbai-based studio Camp’s Bombay Tilts Down (2022) was filmed via a single Mumbai CCTV surveillance camera to expose social hierarchies, challenging the genre of traditional landscapes. Australian dancer and choreographer Angela Goh’s Craft (2026) is a performance that functions like a multi-focal zoom, directing our gaze from minute bodily gestures to the wider city environment. Meanwhile, Swedish artist Nina Canell’s delicate assemblages show how micro-movements shape environments, sitting in contrast to the volcanic plugs from Jeju Island – listed as participating artists – that remind us of vastly different scales of transformation. Other artists tackle intimacy within a political context. Filipino artist Kiri Dalena’s Life Masks (2013-) portrays plaster-mask-wearing activists affected by state-sanctioned violence, memorialising the intimate trust built between artist and subject. Embracing political works Given the Gwangju Biennale’s emphasis on slowing down and quiet contemplation, it was a pleasant surprise to find that Ho and his team have not shied away from political works that help make the exhibition immediate and grounded in reality. At the opening press conference, the curators urged visitors not to be distracted by the bitter pre-opening dispute between Taiwan and mainland China over the “Taiwan Pavilion” naming in a separate section of the biennial. But quiet contemplation, it turns out, is not the same as political evasiveness: the exhibition examines the power dynamics of social change and the way small, individual acts can help carry collective change forward. A collective of women deeply affected by the 1980 Gwangju massacre, the May Mothers’ House, presents 322 paintings, turning decades of trauma into an active practice of solidarity and remembrance. A mini library in the exhibition contains the Gwangju Videos – anonymous compilations of videos recording what happened on May 18, widely circulated despite intense state scrutiny, and The Light in the Factory (1978), a recording of a secret musical drama about labour rights that was also widely copied and circulated at the time. Complementing this is Hong Kong-born, Los Angeles-based Sunik Kim’s new The Light in the Factory (2026), a 496-hour sound installation echoing degraded 1980s democratic labour songs. Installed in transitional spaces, it spans the biennial’s public opening hours to measure time through sonic degradation. Taiwanese-American artist James T. Hong’s Apologies – a video compilation started in 2012 – has grown longer as more politicians apologise in public. Projected on the facade of the exhibition hall every evening, the compilation’s meaning is ambiguous: is accountability just theatre, or are these significant instances of collective remorse? Palestinian artist Mona Benyamin uses bitter, gut-wrenching humour in videos starring her Palestinian parents to question whether laughter can survive occupation and terror. Contemporary Chinese artist Wang Tuo’s continuation of his Critical Theory of Absence (2026-) series navigates collective amnesia. Playing on overlapping screens, his works The Experimental Paradigm of Ownership and Autonomy and Ratchet Drill recreate scenes from the Gwangju uprising while examining the precarious reality of queer activism in China under blanket censorship. For ultimate transcendence, Chinese artist Lu Yang’s “Doku” film series (2022-) pushes individual world-making to the limit, merging Tibetan Buddhist concepts with video game aesthetics to navigate life’s illusions. The final gallery, a sanctuary with one work, is a masterstroke. American artist Jacqueline Kiyomi Gork’s Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose) (2026) is a giant inflatable labyrinth breathing in time to psychoacoustic techno music in an orange-lit room. It encapsulates an aspect of club culture that symbolises how we are all connected yet alone in this world. A focus on older works If there is a criticism of “You Must Change Your Life”, it is this: the well-travelled will recognise many of the older works on display across the biennial. It is an interesting contrast to the Busan Biennale, taking place concurrently, where 70 per cent of the exhibits are new commissions. However, knowing what you will get means curators can tightly control the experience and, in this case, rise above the pre-opening “Taiwan Pavilion” political drama. Titled “Instance Dungeons: Gray Zone”, the Taiwan show proved one of the strongest in the pavilion segment of the biennial – modelled on the Venice Biennale’s national pavilion system and organised separately from Ho’s exhibition. It became the centre of attention after the organiser, the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, protested the decision to call it the “NTMoFA Pavilion” instead of the “Taiwan Pavilion”. The Gwangju Biennale foundation backed down after criticism of censorship and allowing political interference. That prompted mainland China to protest, claiming the pavilion name amounted to acknowledging Taiwan as a nation, and withdrew from the biennial even though its own pavilion had already been installed. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Housed in the National Asia Culture Centre and curated by Chen Hsiang-wen and Lin Hsiao-yu, the Taiwan exhibition uses the video game concept of an “instance dungeon” – isolated copies of areas generated for single parties of players – an arena of endlessly recurring histories and conflicts – to tackle Taiwan’s precarious reality in the “new Cold War”. With stand-out works from artists such as Su Hui-yu, Li Yi-fan and Cheng Hsien-yu, the exhibition dissects cognitive warfare, disinformation and surveillance with gravity and humour. “You Must Change Your Life”, 16th Gwangju Biennale, led by artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen, together with curators Che Kyongfa, Park Gahee and Brian Kuan Wood. Gwangju Biennale Exhibition Hall, September 5 to November 15, 2026. A total of 27 pavilions are also holding exhibitions during the same period.

title: Chinese firms’ export share to reach 31% by 2035 as global expansion deepens: Goldman Sachs
description: The report says the biggest opportunities favour ‘latecomers’ in fields such as robotaxis, e-commerce, surgical robots and power equipment.
content: Chinese companies “going global” are moving from the peripheral to the core in the business world, with their average market share in export markets projected to rise to 31 per cent by 2035 from 18 per cent this year, according to a Goldman Sachs report on Monday. The global expansion of Chinese firms was not yet fully reflected in their share prices, but their revenue would grow 3.6-fold by 2035, according to the report, which covered 40 global companies in 11 sectors, including 21 Chinese players and 19 of their global peers. The report said the biggest growth opportunities favour the “latecomers”, including companies in sectors such as robotaxis, e-commerce, surgical robots, clear dental aligners and power equipment, which have the potential to expand their market positions. “Markets have yet to price in China’s global growth opportunity, with a number of sectors trading at less than 1x [earnings] in international markets excluding China,” said Trina Chen, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Goldman Sachs, in the report co-authored by 36 analysts globally. “We recognise there is far more complexity entrenched in the outlook for Chinese companies going global. We see a harder path and slower pace as the competitive ground shifts towards core segments, where the moat of the incumbents is widest.” Conversely, the outlook is less favourable for “early achievers”, including carmakers operating in Europe, who face more mature, contested and potentially price-destructive expansion paths. Consequently, implied revenue could come under greater pressure. For non-Chinese companies, Goldman Sachs estimated that their aggregate revenue would reach 1.6 times current levels by 2035, provided that its assumptions for Chinese company expansion played out. Meanwhile, the investment bank said sectors such as heating, ventilation and air conditioning, express delivery services, and industrial robots would be the hardest for Chinese competitors to penetrate overseas, given the incumbents’ competitive moats. Separately, the biggest share gains by Chinese players have been in emerging markets, followed by the European Union, despite US-China markets being perceived as the most contested. This year, Chinese companies’ market share is highest in emerging markets at 24 per cent, where their aggregate revenue growth has been nearly 15 times faster than organic market growth. In contrast, their market share is lowest in the US at 10 per cent, followed by the EU at 16 per cent, the report found. In nearly 70 per cent of cases, the Chinese companies entered the international market by pursuing a strategy of “disruptive innovation”, according to Goldman Sachs. This approach meant focusing initially on low-end market segments or emerging markets where demand was price sensitive but usually underserved by the non-Chinese incumbents. Although the consensus was that Chinese industrial products were more disruptive, Goldman Sachs said consumer products had the highest adoption rate in overseas markets.

title: China urges ‘constructive dialogue’ with EU in high-level call with France
description: Amid tensions over subsidies and deficits, Beijing’s top diplomat tells French counterpart the two sides should keep to their partnership.
content: In a phone call with his French counterpart on Monday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged the European Union to avoid escalating trade disputes and engage in “constructive dialogue”. The conversation, requested by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, comes as Brussels tightens investment screening, public procurement rules and anti-subsidy measures, particularly on electric vehicles over what the bloc has called unfair Chinese competition. Wang told Barrot that China and the EU should keep to their partnership, pursue mutually beneficial cooperation and openness, maintain mutual openness, properly resolve economic and trade frictions through constructive dialogue, and avoid escalating confrontation, according to a Chinese statement. “Protectionism will not enhance Europe’s competitiveness but will instead deprive consumers of high-quality and affordable products, drive up inflation and hamper the process of green transition,” Beijing’s top diplomat was quoted as saying. The call took place as France holds the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council this month and ahead of the 81st UN General Assembly, whose high-level general debate begins on September 22. While Paris has often positioned itself as more open to engagement with Beijing than some other EU capitals, it has also backed tougher EU scrutiny of Chinese investment and voiced concern about industrial overcapacity and subsidies, making France a pivotal player in internal EU debates on China policy. Beijing routinely denounces such moves as politicised trade barriers or disguised protectionism aimed at curbing Chinese companies. Describing China as one of the world’s largest markets, Wang said its development represented an “opportunity rather than a challenge” for the EU. He called on France, as a “major country with a strategic vision”, to take a “pragmatic and rational” approach and encourage Brussels to work with Beijing “in the same direction” and play a positive role in promoting the stability of China-EU relations, the Chinese statement said. Barrot, for his part, was quoted in the Chinese read-out as saying France was ready to promote constructive exchanges between the EU and China to find solutions, acknowledging “difficulties and challenges” in economic and trade relations. The French foreign ministry’s statement said Barrot voiced support for the ongoing EU–China trade talks but stressed that dialogue must deliver a substantial rebalancing of trade given what he called Europe’s unsustainable deficit. Europe’s large trade gap with China remains a persistent point of friction, with Paris and Brussels pushing for rebalancing. On Taiwan, which Beijing regards as part of its territory, Wang reiterated that the one-China principle was the “political foundation” of the comprehensive strategic partnership between China and France, according to the Chinese statement. Wang urged Paris to uphold it through concrete action, “refrain from any form of official engagement” with the self-ruled island and avoid sending “wrong signals” to “Taiwan independence” forces. The Chinese statement said Barrot reaffirmed France’s strict adherence to the one-China policy. The exchange followed recent visits by French lawmakers to Taiwan, which Beijing views as challenges to its sovereignty. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and France, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Wang and Barrot agreed that Sino-French relations had maintained a stable trajectory overall under the strategic guidance of their leaders, and highlighted their countries’ shared responsibility to address global risks as permanent members of the Security Council. They also exchanged views on Iran and the Ukraine crisis, with Wang briefing Barrot on China’s “principled position” and highlighting President Xi Jinping’s four-point proposal for a new Middle East security architecture as a “global public good”. The French statement said Barrot underscored Russia’s “irresponsibility” in its war against Ukraine, the difficulties Moscow faced and France’s continued support for Kyiv. Barrot also raised concerns about freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, calling the waterways crucial for stability and prosperity in Europe and Asia. He recalled a Franco-British initiative to guarantee navigation rights and urged continued exchanges with Beijing.

title: Cambodia, Thailand take US$300 billion seabed dispute to UN
description: A rarely invoked UN legal process is trying to untangle the two countries’ row over 27,000 sq km of oil- and gas-rich waters.
content: Months after deadly clashes that cost dozens of lives along their shared border, the foreign ministers of Cambodia and Thailand laid out opening arguments on Tuesday over a different kind of territory: 27,000 sq km (10,400 square miles) of seabed thought to hold a fortune in gas and oil. The venue was the Permanent Court of Arbitration’s Singapore office, where the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea’s conciliation commission is being asked to settle who controls a stretch of the Gulf of Thailand with hydrocarbon reserves worth an estimated US$300 billion. It is only the second time in Unclos’ history that the conciliation process has been used. The first, initiated by East Timor against Australia in 2016, took nearly two years to resolve. Cambodia said it had no choice but to turn to the UN after Thailand earlier this year tore up a 2001 memorandum of understanding that had kept alive the promise of jointly developing the disputed waters’ estimated 12 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and up to 700 million barrels of oil. Both countries are bound by Unclos to take part in the proceedings, though the commission’s eventual recommendations are non-binding and carry no legal weight. Cambodian foreign minister Prak Sokhonn spoke first, giving a 15-minute statement that ranged across a millennium of history – invoking the ninth-century Khmer Empire, French colonial rule, civil war and the Khmer Rouge genocide – portraying his country as a reluctant litigant rather than an aggressor. Cambodia had sought the Unclos conciliation commission’s intervention only after Thailand’s withdrawal from the MoU dashed any hope of a negotiated deal, he said. “Cambodia took this step to find a peaceful pathway forward in accordance with international law,” he said, describing the process as a “means to rebuild trust” and voicing hope that it might let both nations “turn a new page for their mutual benefit”. Thailand’s response, delivered by Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, was decidedly less conciliatory. He accused Cambodia of weaponising diplomacy, pointing to the phone call between Hun Sen and former Thai prime minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra that was leaked last June, setting off a political crisis that ultimately drove the latter from power. Cambodia “always claims that it respects international law and portrays Thailand as flouting it, but the claims are self-serving”, he said. “When Cambodia leaked a private telephone conversation between our leaders, when Cambodian rockets hit and killed innocent Thai civilians, and when our soldiers lost their legs to landmines planted by Cambodia, where was respect for international law?” Thailand walked away from the 2001 MoU only after a quarter-century of talks produced no progress, Sihasak said, accusing Cambodia of turning to international forums to cast itself as a victim through “false narratives and distortions of facts”. Yet for all the cutting accusations, Thailand’s top diplomat said Bangkok had entered the Unclos process “in good faith” and was “ready to engage … constructively” to find “a negotiated and equitable solution”. “Thailand stands firmly on the path of peace. Moving forward requires political will on both sides,” he said in his concluding remarks. “The choice is for Cambodia to make.” Thailand has made it clear it does not welcome outside interference in its land and sea disputes with Cambodia – a smaller, poorer and less heavily armed neighbour that appears to have suffered heavier losses in last year’s border conflict.

title: Hong Kong visitor arrivals hit post-pandemic monthly high in August
description: Arrivals rise by 6 per cent year on year to 5.46 million, while city welcomes 36.7 million visitors in first eight months, up by 11 per cent.
content: Hong Kong recorded its highest monthly number of visitors since the Covid-19 pandemic in August, provisional official figures show, with authorities preparing for an influx of mainland Chinese travellers during the coming “golden week” holiday. The Hong Kong Tourism Board said on Tuesday that the city received 5.46 million visitors last month, up by 6 per cent from a year earlier and the highest monthly total since the pandemic. Tourist numbers in the first eight months of 2026 also rose by 11 per cent year on year, fuelled by an influx of mainland and long-haul international arrivals. Also on Tuesday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government was preparing for the arrival of tourists during the National Day golden week from October 1 to 7, including stepping up publicity, improving crowd management and tackling “coerced shopping”. “Not only is this a crucial period for the tourism sector, but also an occasion for Hong Kong to promote itself as a friendly tourist destination,” he said. “We hope to deliver good experiences to tourists and that they will come again.” The Tourism Board attributed the increase in August to international conferences and mega-events held during the month, including the 16th Worldwide Chinese Life Insurance Congress & 2026 IDA Annual Conference, the Hong Kong Football Festival 2026 and the TMElive International Music Awards. “[These events] attracted a diverse range of visitors and helped drive visitor arrivals from the Chinese mainland, Singapore, the United Kingdom and other source markets,” it said. Provisional figures released by the board showed that nearly 4.6 million of the August arrivals came from the mainland, an 8 per cent increase from a year earlier. Long-haul arrivals also rose by 18 per cent year on year to 289,489, while visitors from new markets increased by 10 per cent to more than 65,000. Short-haul visitors from outside the mainland were the only segment to decline, falling by 16 per cent to about 405,000. For the first eight months of the year, Hong Kong welcomed 36.7 million visitors, 11 per cent more than in the same period last year. More than 28.7 million came from the mainland, representing growth of 13 per cent. The city also received about 4 million short-haul visitors during the period, down by 4 per cent year on year, while long-haul arrivals rose by 19 per cent to 2.6 million. Visitors from new markets reached 550,000, an increase of 15 per cent. The Tourism Board said the performance of the mainland and long-haul markets had remained stable. “Visitor growth in short-haul markets continued to face challenges owing to factors such as flight capacity, fuel surcharges and regional competition,” it said. It also highlighted coming flagship events, including the Sun Hung Kai Properties Hong Kong Cyclothon, the Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival and the New Year countdown celebrations, as further draws for tourists. Lawmaker Perry Yiu Pak-leung, a tourism industry veteran, said the results were “hard-earned” and the upward trend would help maintain momentum for the sector’s development. He remained “cautiously optimistic” about the prospects for the fourth quarter, citing major festivities in Hong Kong and the increase in visitors brought by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation finance ministers’ meeting. On the coming golden week, Yiu said it would be a good opportunity to stress-test the management measures for ecologically sensitive tourist attractions, notably the pilot scheme of the visitor reservation system for Po Pin Chau in Sai Kung. “We hope after the pilot scheme, the authorities can sit down with stakeholders to discuss how we can make good use of our natural resources to develop tourism, while maintaining sustainable development,” he said. Sai Kung district councillor Chris Cheung Mei-hung said the influx of tourists to the area would put the reservation system to a “real test”. “We will have to see whether the system is really feasible or if there is any room for improvement, such as introducing a penalty or charging scheme,” he said. Cheung also urged authorities to collect visitor data during the holiday to determine whether the reservation system or other restrictive measures should be extended to other tourist hotspots in the district, such as Sharp Island and the Ham Tin Wan campsite.

title: Indonesian finance minister found out about his firing in mid-meeting phone call
description: Purbaya ⁠Yudhi Sadewa said he was ‘upset’ over losing the top finance job, a move that also surprised markets.
content: Purbaya ⁠Yudhi Sadewa, who was sacked as Indonesia’s finance minister this week, said on Tuesday he was upset to be removed from his job, but was half expecting the decision. President Prabowo Subianto abruptly removed Purbaya as finance minister on Monday and named his deputy, Suahasil Nazara, to the top finance job, in a move that surprised markets but was ‌also seen as an attempt to restore trust in financial policies. After a terse handover ceremony at the finance ministry, Purbaya told reporters he found out about his termination in a phone call with the president’s spokesman Prasetyo Hadi on Monday. Purbaya was seen receiving a phone call and leaving in the middle of a parliamentary meeting just hours before Suahasil was sworn in. “Last night, going to sleep was difficult. I was upset, but now it’s not too bad,” Purbaya told reporters. “Tonight I can sleep soundly,” ⁠he said, adding he had half expected to be fired over a recent decision he took. He did not elaborate. While he said he ‌had no policy disagreement with the president, Purbaya said his sacking partly had to do with differences with other officials. Prabowo’s sacking of Purbaya came just days after the former economist marked one year as finance minister, ‌with Southeast Asia’s largest economy suffering a crisis of confidence among investors and analysts. Prabowo’s fiscal policies have been under ⁠scrutiny since he came to power ⁠in October 2024 because of costly campaign promises. Known for his candour, Purbaya’s tenure was marked by the fastest economic growth in three years, but also the widest budget deficit ‌in over 20 years outside the pandemic and credit rating outlook downgrades by ratings agencies Fitch and Moody’s. Capital outflows have also intensified this year, pushing the rupiah to an ‌all time ‌low, triggered by concerns about financial profligacy, central bank interference and transparency issues in capital markets, on top of global risk aversion ‌due to the war in the Middle East. Purbaya said his tenure was “decent”, citing rising economic growth. He said he would spend his retirement ⁠fishing in a pond at the back of his house. Speaking at the handover ceremony, Suahasil asked all stakeholders to ⁠open their doors for collaboration. He has pledged to safeguard Indonesia’s fiscal credibility and abide by the legislated fiscal deficit limit of 3 per cent of gross domestic product. A veteran technocrat, Suahasil, 55, is well known to investors and analysts, some of whom said ‌he would likely reassure investors. Shinta Kamdani, who ‌chairs business group Indonesia’s Employers Association, said Suahasil should provide policy continuity and institutional understanding. “We hope this continuity will help ensure that the leadership transition does not lead to a sudden shift in policy direction,” she said. Shinta said the business community understood the importance of a healthy budget and its limited financial space, but government support to bolster growth remained important to maintain purchasing power, boost investment and increase the nation’s productivity.

title: Thais stage rare Israel protest; Singapore ministers get pay rise: 7 Asia highlights
description: From Thai PM Anutin’s US$90,000 amulet to the Philippines’ big bet on railways, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. ‘Not for sale’: Thais take to streets in rare protest against Israel Hundreds of Thais, led by a veteran political activist, rallied outside the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok in a rare public protest against a group of foreign nationals. 2. Singapore ministers set for pay rise with entry-level pay up to US$1.4 million Singapore’s ministers will receive gradual pay increases following a 60 per cent jump in their baseline salary benchmarks, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has announced. 3. India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent. That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad. 4. Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air. 5. Thai PM Anutin’s US$90,000 amulet back in spotlight after disgraced monk’s arrest Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has come under intense social media scrutiny after photos resurfaced showing him wearing a high-value amulet created by a senior monk now at the centre of a fraud and sex scandal. 6. Philippines bets big on rail, but can it fix a broken transport network? A two-hour commute for a 14km (8.7-mile) journey. For Julius Dalay and millions of other Filipinos, this is just how public transport works in Manila: a mishmash of jeepneys, trains and buses that commuters are left to figure out for themselves. 7. Malaysian woman who stabbed boyfriend to death over sex demand gets 12 years A Malaysian court has nearly doubled jail time for a woman who stabbed her boyfriend to death for demanding sex after ruling that the sentencing court had been “over-sympathetic” towards the accused.

title: US judge blocks Trump limits on how long foreign students, journalists can stay
description: Rule would have capped duration of visas for international students at four years.
content:
A federal judge on Monday blocked US President Donald Trump’s administration from implementing a new rule that would limit how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the US without applying for extensions.
US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston ‌ruled in favour of a coalition of unions and higher education advocacy groups a day before the Department of Homeland Security’s rule was set to take effect.
Saylor said DHS adopted the policy based on “exceptionally weak” rationales. The agency had cited national security and the need to prevent fraud in the visa programme, but the judge found it had not adhered to its legal obligations to engage with concerns about a policy change or consider less burdensome alternatives.
DHS did not ⁠immediately respond to a request for comment.
The judge, an appointee of Republican President George W. Bush, wrote that the rule ‌upended a system through which the US for nearly five decades had issued visas to foreign students for their “duration of status.”
That system, he said, has permitted tens of millions of foreign students and ‌researchers to come to the US, leading to “groundbreaking research in science, medicine and technology, substantial economic growth and ⁠a host of other ⁠benefits, often on a vast scale.”
Saylor said the rule DHS adopted in July seeks to replace that system with one that would substantially restrict the overall number ‌of foreign students, professors and journalists in the country.
Under the rule, F visas for international students and J visas that allow visitors on cultural exchange programmes to ‌work in the ‌US would be capped at four years, while I visas for journalists, which currently can last years, would be ‌up to 240 days.
About 1.6 million people currently have F visas and another 500,000 have J visas. Major research universities like Massachusetts Institute ⁠of Technology and Harvard have large percentages of foreign students, particularly at the graduate level, the judge noted.
If the rule took ⁠effect, such universities would likely suffer hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and enrolment would decline, Saylor said.
“The damage to the higher education system and to the economy of the United States is likely to be ‌catastrophic,” Saylor wrote.
Miriam Feldblum, the head ‌of one of the plaintiffs, Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said the judge’s ruling recognised the harm the rule would cause to international students, universities and the economy if it was allowed to take effect.
“While the case continues, this relief preserves the long-standing system that enables our colleges and universities – and our country – to attract, educate and retain global talent,” Feldblum said.

title: Hong Kong’s employment outlook rebounds sharply to 14% in fourth quarter
description: Firms looking to hire after previous quarter’s slump as city’s economic environment improves, according to survey by ManpowerGroup.
content: Hong Kong employers’ hiring sentiment rebounded sharply in the fourth quarter, with far fewer companies expecting to cut jobs as confidence improved alongside stronger economic growth, according to a ManpowerGroup survey. The international human resources firm said the city’s seasonally adjusted net employment outlook rose to 14 per cent, up by 23 percentage points from minus 9 per cent in the third quarter of this year. The outlook is calculated by subtracting the percentage of employers expecting to reduce staffing from the share planning to increase headcount. Among 603 employers surveyed, 30 per cent expected to increase staffing, 16 per cent anticipated cuts and 54 per cent forecast no change. “If you look at the figures alone, you can see that the economic environment has continued to improve,” said Lancy Chui Yuk-shan, senior vice-president at ManpowerGroup Greater China. “Thirty per cent of employers plan to increase [their] headcount, compared with 23 per cent last quarter, while the proportion expecting to reduce staff has fallen from 32 per cent to 16 per cent.” The turnaround was driven not only by more companies planning to hire, but also by a sharp reduction in the number expecting to reduce staffing, she said. Chui attributed the improvement to a stronger economic backdrop, pointing to Hong Kong’s 5.1 per cent year-on-year real gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the first six months of 2026, an upgraded full-year government forecast of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent and stable unemployment at 3.7 per cent. The information technology sector recorded the strongest hiring outlook at 27 per cent, followed by finance and insurance at 21 per cent, professional, scientific and technical services at 15 per cent and trade and logistics at 10 per cent. Chui said demand in the technology sector was being driven by the wider adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and corporate digital transformation, with employers particularly seeking workers who could apply the technology in business settings alongside skills in data analytics, cloud architecture, cybersecurity and project management. Financial sector hiring was supported by stronger activity in initial public offerings, asset and wealth management and insurance, with demand expected for investment banking, compliance, fintech, risk management and customer service roles. Hospitality recorded a net outlook of 5 per cent, with the year-end festive season expected to support recruitment in hotels, catering, retail and customer service. Manufacturing remained relatively cautious at 7 per cent, with Chui saying much of the hiring involved staff replacement – particularly in technical roles – rather than significant workforce expansion. Health and social services was the only sector with a negative reading, at minus 3 per cent, although this was still five percentage points higher than in the previous quarter. Asked whether the rebound could be sustained, Chui said the longer-term trend would depend on the global economic outlook and Hong Kong’s labour market. She added that while Hong Kong showed a dramatic quarter-on-quarter recovery, its 14 per cent net outlook remained modest compared with many other global markets. The global fourth-quarter outlook showed the city lagging behind mainland China’s 34 per cent, Vietnam’s 36 per cent and India’s 54 per cent, although it was still ahead of Singapore’s 13 per cent.

title: Chinese woman’s search for kind former foreign tutor sparks flood of shared memories
description: To Wang, Evans was more than just an educator; he was a mentor and a guiding figure whose lifelong influence reshaped her perspective.
content: A Chinese woman’s quest to reconnect with a former foreign teacher who profoundly influenced her outlook on life has sparked a collective online effort to locate him. Wang Yu, a community worker in Shanghai, graduated from East China Normal University in 2005 with a degree in tourism management. Wang informed the SCMP that the teacher, known only as Evans, was an American who taught her an elective English course during her university years. For three years, he selflessly supported her academic pursuits by offering free tutoring outside of class hours. Beyond his teaching duties, Evans invested his own money to establish a small photo studio in the reception area, capturing cherished memories for his students. Wang estimates that Evans is now likely in his 70s. Two decades ago, he stood out with his curly grey hair, tailored suits, and fluent Mandarin. In his classroom, desks and chairs were arranged in a circle, with the centre reserved for students to sing, deliver speeches, and perform magic tricks. He even shared the joy of making dumplings with his students. His unique teaching style helped Wang build confidence in her English skills, influencing her professional approach later on. In 2019, while promoting child-friendly communities, she replicated Evans’ circular classroom layout, enabling children to draw and engage at the centre. Evans also expressed a deep appreciation for Chinese culture. His Chinese name, Wen Xiaofan, reflected his passion for sailing, along with his admiration for the free-spirited philosophy of the ancient Chinese thinker Zhuangzi, Wang noted. During one summer holiday, Wang explored Shanghai with Evans’ two daughters. The photographs they took together remain among her most treasured keepsakes. To Wang, Evans was more than just a teacher; he was a mentor and a guiding figure whose influence reshaped her perspective on life. He bestowed upon her the English name “Grace,” inspired by his grandmother’s middle name. However, after Wang graduated from university, the pair lost touch when she lost her phone. Each Teacher’s Day, Wang sends gifts to the educators who have impacted her life, but Evans is the only one she has been unable to reconnect with. In August, she posted an English letter on RedNote, hoping to find him. The post quickly went viral; former students shared memories and clues, including his full name, Curtis Roy Evans, and a possible birth year of 1953. Some recalled that Evans always carried a thick English dictionary, while others fondly remembered singing “Scarborough Fair” and “You Are My Sunshine” in his class. One former student noted their magic tricks performed under his guidance; another recalled his consistent reminders to wear helmets while cycling. A US-based online user suggested that Evans may have once lived in Hawaii but has since relocated. Wang has prepared gifts for China’s National Teachers’ Day, celebrated on September 10, including a notebook and pen holder. She expressed her willingness to welcome any form of contact, whether through emails, messages, or video calls. “I can accept that he may not want to be disturbed. I only hope to know that, somewhere in the world, he is safe and happy,” she added.

title: Newsom won’t run for US president in 2028 if Harris does
description: California governor says both he and former vice-president Kamala Harris campaigning would be a ‘gift’ to Republicans.
content: California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who is widely considered a contender for the 2028 presidential election, will not enter the race if former US vice-president Kamala Harris runs again, he told CNN in a clip shared on Monday. Newsom made the comment in an interview with CNN anchor Jake Tapper, during which the two men are standing knee-deep in a body of water while fishing. “I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said. He explained that both campaigning would split Democratic votes, which would be a gift to Republicans who might coalesce around a narrower set of potential nominees, including current Vice-President J.D. Vance. “Electorally it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it,” Newsom said. “Mutually assured destruction, it serves as no greater good.” Newsom said did not previously run against former president Joe Biden in 2024 because he “wasn’t ready” and thinks he would have lost anyway. “First of all, I wouldn’t do that,” Newsom said, referring to the 2024 race. “Second, if I did, I would have gotten crushed because I didn’t have a why.” His children will also be a factor if and when he ever decides to run. “I’ve got four kids. It’s the only thing that matters to me. They gotta be on board,” Newsom said. “Forget it, if they’re not on board, that’s a non-starter.” The comments from Newsom seemingly stunned Tapper in the two-minute clip, which teased a longer interview that is expected to air Tuesday morning. It might surprise other observers, too, who have watched Newsom’s political ascendance from the mayor of San Francisco to governor of the Golden State, both Democratic strongholds. He was elected governor in 2018, and re-elected to a second term four years later. As California governor over the past eight years, he survived a recall election, launched a podcast called “This is Gavin Newsom”, and oversaw emergency responses to natural disasters including wildfires and the Covid-19 pandemic. Earlier this month, he spent several days visiting right-leaning southern states where he stumped for Democratic causes. Newsom also celebrated a Supreme Court decision on Monday that allowed a lower court to block proposed changes to mail-in voting made by the Trump administration. “Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law, and the American people looking to exercise their Constitutional right to vote,” the governor said in a statement. “Trump’s attacks on democracy these last 20 months have been nothing short of un-American.” In June, Newsom accused the US Department of Justice (DOJ) of launching a politically motivated investigation against him and his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom. A DOJ source in Washington, who requested anonymity, told Agence France-Presse earlier this year that the investigation was not politically motivated and instead was focused on “tax activity” involving Newsom’s wife, a documentary filmmaker, and activities related to his former chief of staff and possibly current aides. “Donald Trump isn’t just coming after me because of my mean tweets,” Newsom said in June. “He’s coming after me because I am considering running for president. “One by one, anyone who has challenged Donald Trump has ended up on his hit list,” he continued.

title: China star Eileen Gu makes safety plea after fans flood New Zealand slopes seeking pictures
description: One year after training injury mishap in New Zealand, Olympic freestyle champion posts safety reminder on social media on return to venue.
content: Multiple Olympic freestyle skiing medallist Eileen Gu has urged fans to not ask for pictures while she is training, offering instead to meet supporters at the lodge after her sessions finish. Gu recently returned to Cardrona Alpine Resort in New Zealand for training, where fans took photos of the Chinese superstar and shared them online. On Monday, Gu posted a selfie on social media thanking supporters while issuing a safety reminder. “I’m excited to be back on snow and grateful for all the love!” she wrote. “I’d like to kindly remind everyone to not ask for photos while I’m in the middle of training.” She emphasised that freestyle skiing was a high-consequence sport and warned that “unexpected disruptions”, however well-intentioned, could be dangerous. “I am happy to meet everyone and share the joy of skiing, and will do my daily meet and greet in front of the lodge every day after training ends,” she added, thanking fans for their understanding and telling them to “be safe out there”. This is not the first time Gu has issued such a reminder. A year ago at the same resort, she updated social media after sustaining an injury during training caused by a “man-made accident”. The incident occurred just days into her first on-snow training in New Zealand following months of injury recovery. While her initial sessions had gone smoothly, Gu posted in August last year that “a very scary accident occurred due to human error” and that she had undergone medical imaging tests. Gu explained at the time that she needed full concentration during training, noting that being interrupted while preparing at the top of the terrain park was particularly dangerous and that she also needed to focus on visualising her tricks while on the chairlift. She had then also requested that fans refrain from filming or asking for photos during her sessions, and had written: “I am very happy to meet everyone inside or outside the ski resort restaurant after the park closes every day, around 3:30 to 4.00pm. Thank you for your understanding.”

title: China cracks down on big firms delaying payments to cash-strapped SMEs
description: New rules require large companies to pay suppliers within 60 days, with penalties for deliberate delays and incentives for clearing backlogs.
content: Beijing is planning a carrot-and-stick approach to stop large corporations from exploiting their market dominance to delay payments to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) as part of a broader campaign to curb cutthroat competition. “In recent years, we have observed that some large enterprises – in order to save on financial costs and gain a competitive advantage – have exploited their dominant market position to delay payments to suppliers,” said Cao Yuanyuan, director of financial markets at the People’s Bank of China (PBOC). “This not only harms the interests of SMEs, but also exacerbates ‘involutionary’ competition and imbalances between supply and demand on a macro level,” Cao added, referring to the self-defeating cycle of excessive competition that has taken hold of several sectors. Speaking at a press briefing in Beijing on Monday, Cao said public financial data showed that some large enterprises were capable of paying SMEs on time but refused to do so, forcing smaller cash-strapped suppliers to take out bank loans and effectively absorb the larger companies’ financing costs. By the end of June, outstanding loans to small and micro enterprises – a vulnerable subgroup within the SME category – totalled 38.5 trillion yuan (US$5.73 trillion), having grown at an average annual rate of 20 per cent since 2020, according to central bank data. Chinese SMEs, most of which are privately owned, form the backbone of the country’s economy, but many have struggled with cash flow because of delayed repayments. Beijing is now moving to curb the practice, with the State Council on Thursday publishing a document to address payment delays. The guidelines ordered large enterprises to pay SMEs within 60 days of delivering goods, projects or services, and specifically called on central and state-owned enterprises to take the lead in making timely repayments. To eliminate loopholes, industry regulators are required to strengthen payment settlement rules, such as clarifying when payment windows begin and which transaction methods are allowed. Authorities urged companies to pay in cash, such as through bank transfers, rather than through non-cash instruments such as commercial drafts. Additionally, listed companies with large accounts payable would face stricter reporting rules, requiring them to disclose average payment cycles, main settlement methods and any reliance on commercial drafts and digital vouchers. According to the guidelines, large enterprises that continued to abuse their market dominance by deliberately delaying payments or using non-cash instruments to extend payment terms would face penalties, with typical cases publicly named and shamed to deter repeat offences. Meanwhile, the central bank would encourage large corporations to clear arrears through debt-financing instruments such as bank loans and bond issuances. “Enterprises that demonstrate significant reductions in accounts payable and payment terms will be granted favourable treatment in bond issuance,” said Cao of the PBOC.

title: 2 brothers found dead in Hong Kong flat had withdrawn from social contact
description: Pair believed to have died several weeks apart, with their bodies discovered after elder sister made police report.
content: Two brothers in their fifties who were found dead in their Hong Kong flat had largely withdrawn from social contact and were financially supported by their parents, the South China Morning Post has learned. The exact cause of death has yet to be confirmed by postmortem examinations. No suspicious circumstances had been identified at this stage, the force said on Tuesday. An insider said the bodies were discovered after the men’s elder sister made a police report on Monday. The sister was alerted earlier that day by a security guard at Tung Yip House, Lei Tung Estate, who noticed an unusual odour coming from the flat. The guard knocked on the door but there was no response. Police, firefighters and paramedics arrived at the scene and forced open the metal gate and wooden door. They found the decomposing bodies of the two men in the toilet and on the top bunk of a bedroom, respectively. The men, aged 53 and 55, were pronounced dead at the scene at 2.45pm on Monday. Investigators estimated that one brother had died within the past week, while the other had died several weeks earlier. The pair lived together. No suspicious injuries were found on either man, and they were identified as Hong Kong residents through their identity cards. According to police’s preliminary investigation, the younger brother was believed to have died several weeks ago. The elder brother was unable to care for himself, and was suspected to have died in the past week as a result. The source said valuables, including HK$10,000 (US$1,275) in cash, in the flat were left untouched, and there were no signs of a struggle. The flat’s letterbox contained letters dated after July 2, while opened letters dated before July 1 were found on the dining table, the insider said, adding that no medical documents were discovered. There were no security cameras inside the flat, and a review of footage from the building also yielded no useful information, the source added. The insider said the younger brother had acted as his sibling’s sole carer since 2003. Neither was employed, relying instead on an automatic monthly bank transfer of HK$17,000 from their parents to cover their living expenses. The sister told police that neither brother had received a formal medical diagnosis. But she said the elder brother had a severe tendency to socially withdraw, rarely speaking to anyone, including family members, and went to great lengths to avoid social interaction. The source said the older man left school after Form Four and worked as a technician at a power station for about a year before becoming unemployed and reliant on his younger brother for financial support. The younger brother had also displayed mild introverted tendencies since childhood, the source said. He left school after Form Four and worked as a goldsmith for several years before leaving the job and becoming financially dependent on his parents. The insider said the sister last confirmed that the younger brother was in good health at a family gathering on February 18. The elder brother did not attend because of his aversion to social gatherings, and the family had not seen him for more than 10 years, the source added. Their parents, aged 93 and 83, were unable to visit because of mobility problems. The sister’s phone records showed that she had not received WhatsApp messages from either brother since May, and their last reply to her was sent on February 18. The sister did not live with the brothers and visited them every other month. If neither answered the door, she would usually push a handwritten letter containing cash through the letterbox and leave. Utility bills were paid by direct debit from their father’s bank account. Electricity consumption remained at normal levels between July and August 2026. Their parents bought the 400-square-foot flat fully paid in 2003 for the elder brother to live in. According to the source, neighbours only ever saw one of the brothers leave the premises even though they knew both lived there. No one had noticed any noises that were out of the ordinary before the siblings’ deaths or any unusual odours after. The neighbours also said the brother who left the flat did not usually greet or respond to others. Lawmaker Grace Chan Man-yee, who represents the social welfare sector, said there was a need for more proactive efforts to identify those struggling with social isolation, declining health, caregiving strain, financial difficulties and uncertainty over where to seek help, among other issues. “I believe there is no single cause, and this issue has never been one that a single [government] department can resolve on its own,” she said. The legislator said the current carer data platform was already linked to the Social Welfare Department, the Hospital Authority and the Housing Authority. She suggested that the platform should be gradually expanded to include more departments and public bodies, adding that high-risk households should be identified in accordance with privacy regulations. Chan stressed the importance of making effective use of the high-risk register to identify those in need, as well as ensuring that community support, such as care teams, had sufficient training, reporting channels and access to elderly care technology. “Case managers play a vital role in strengthening social services and providing greater support. They should be assigned to ensure ongoing follow-up for high-risk households,” she added. The lawmaker also noted that many residents did not always fully understand how to apply for financial assistance and urged authorities to simplify application procedures to ensure timely support.

title: Price of Epic Fury: Iran war’s toll on US bases, weapons and more
description: Pentagon inspector general offers an official accounting of the war’s costs in expended US munitions and damages.
content: A US government watchdog released its first report on Monday on the impact of the Iran war, acknowledging the military’s advanced weapons shortfalls and offering the first public look at the damage to American aircraft, bases and diplomatic outposts in the Middle East. Much of the information about Operation Epic Fury has been previously reported over the past six months, but the Pentagon inspector general’s report offered the fullest official accounting so far of the conflict’s costs in American lives, taxpayer dollars and physical damage. It included information from the watchdogs for the Defence and State departments as well as the US Agency for International Development. The report, whose publication was first reported by NBC News, noted that the US war with Iran “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply” in regard to advanced weapons. Experts have previously said it would take about three years for military contractors to replenish advanced missiles and defensive missile interceptors to pre-war levels. The Pentagon has repeatedly pushed back against reports of any munitions shortage, saying the US military has all the weapons it needs to fight any conflict.
