President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Monday that the US was “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History”. “They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East, and beyond,” he wrote. The watchdog report, which covers April 1 to June 30, also acknowledged that Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan. It noted that the US naval base in Bahrain, a US Navy logistics hub in the region, was targeted with Iranian drones and ballistic missiles. US Central Command (CENTCOM) had to shift supply lines to alternate hubs that were much farther away, including Diego Garcia, a US-UK base on an island in the Indian Ocean. It required “14- to 18-day logistics cycles” to support operations in the Middle East, the report said. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao acknowledged in an interview with The Epoch Times last week that “they blew the hell out of Bahrain” and said he has a task force looking into whether the US Navy would need to repair the base in Bahrain to sustain its forces in the region. Dozens of American aircraft and drones also were destroyed or damaged by Iran, including the destruction of as many as 30 MQ-9 Reaper drones that cost around US$30 million apiece, the report said. Seven KC-135 refuelling aircraft were damaged or destroyed, including five that were struck by Iranian munitions while on the ground in Saudi Arabia. Another KC-135 crashed in Iraq, killing six service members, following a collision with another KC-135. Those deaths, and the death of a pilot of a helicopter that crashed into the Arabian Sea, are listed as occurring during non-hostile events. Eleven other service members are listed as “killed in action” in Kuwait, Iraq, Jordan and Saudi Arabia. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told Congress in late July that the war had cost US$37.5 billion so far. The costs in physical damage to US diplomatic facilities, however, had not been previously publicly released. Such outposts in Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the UAE were damaged by Iranian strikes, with an estimated cost of US$184 million, according to the report. The State Department reported in early June that its other costs from the conflict came to US$113 million, with nearly US$80 million used to respond to contingency plans, including evacuation expenses for US personnel and their families as well as other American citizens and eligible third-country nationals. The State Department reported that in the weeks and months after the US and Israel first struck Iran on February 28, the Trump administration evacuated about 9,000 US citizens from countries in the Middle East and Europe. Through private and commercial flights as well as land and water travel, the cost of the department’s evacuation operation was more than US$11 million as of late June. “State determined that consular officers would not be able to fully document travel itineraries required to seek reimbursement from evacuees and therefore it would be impracticable to seek reimbursement from them,” the report states. The majority of the evacuations were made from Israel, with Iraq and Jordan following shortly behind. While the US only evacuated 1,200 Americans from the United Arab Emirates, those trips to Istanbul, Athens and Washington cost the most, at more than US$4 million. The State Department reported that more than US$44 billion in emergency and non-emergency military sales also were made in that span of time, with the majority of sales going to Saudi Arabia. Sales included military helicopters, munitions and munitions support as well as advanced precision weapons systems. Other regional countries, including Qatar, Kuwait, UAE and Israel, also received billions in sales, as Iran retaliated against nearly every country in the region that hosted a US military base.

title: US throws weight behind Thai submarine cable that skips South China Sea
description: The 18,507km long cable connecting Thailand with America would be built to US engineering standards.
content: The US Trade and Development Agency (USTDA) on Monday announced funding for a feasibility study on a new transpacific submarine cable linking the US with Thailand and as many as five other Southeast Asian nations, as Washington seeks to expand secure digital infrastructure in the region. The proposed cable that could extend up to 18,507km (11,500 miles) long would connect Thailand with the United States via Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam, “while avoiding the South China Sea and other routes that carry security risks”, the agency said in a statement. The project would be built to US engineering standards and is intended to replace Thailand’s ageing subsea connection to the US. The Thailand-US Submarine Cable System, or Thus, will “strengthen the resilience and diversity of our international networks, support the growth of Thailand’s data centre, cloud and AI sectors, and expand affordable connectivity”, said Colonel Sanpachai Huvanandana, president of the Thai state-owned National Telecom Public Company. The US, facing competition from China, has made a concerted effort in recent years to expand its role in building subsea cables, which carry nearly all international internet traffic. The Indo-Pacific is an increasingly important arena for such networks as countries build out digital infrastructure, while Beijing’s sweeping claims in strategic waterways, including the South China Sea, have complicated efforts to lay new cables. Nearly two dozen international cables are expected to be built across the Pacific between 2022 and 2030, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies. While the USTDA did not offer an expected price for the project, other estimates show the aggregate cost of new undersea cable construction is expected to reach over US$14 billion between 2025 and 2027. Last week, the USTDA announced plans to support the expansion of port facilities at the strategic Subic Bay in the Philippines and establish a nationwide public Wi-fi network. The agency will also develop liquefied natural gas and nuclear projects there to lower electricity costs and attract businesses into an investment belt that is seen to counter China’s supply-chain influence.

title: Unitree’s US$30 billion stock wipe-off spurs regulatory caution on humanoid robot IPOs
description: Beijing tipped to tighten approvals, heighten scrutiny of humanoid makers as leading robotics specialist reports a 44% stock slump.
content: A more than 40 per cent slump in Chinese humanoid robot maker Unitree Robotics since listing has sounded regulatory caution for the industry, with speculation swirling that Beijing may tighten approval of the peer listings. The regulators would heighten scrutiny over humanoid makers seeking initial public offerings (IPOs) on the mainland’s exchanges, according to media reports. The sustainability of revenue growth, earnings prospects and applicants’ key capabilities of tech innovation would be the focus of regulatory surveillance, they said. The shift is expected to affect companies including Deep Robotics and Leju Robot, which still remain unprofitable after filing for IPOs. The change of the regulatory stance on one of China’s strategic industries came after the tumultuous post-debut performance of Unitree, the industry champion that is also known as Yushu Technology. The stock has plunged 44 per cent, less than a month after it started trading on the tech-heavy Star Market on August 19, wiping out more than 200 billion yuan (US$29.8 billion) in market value. The rout stirred debates on whether the regulators are too lax with the listing bar for humanoid robot makers. While a retreat in speculative bets may partially explain the meltdown in Unitree’s stock, which surged 460 per cent on the first day of trading, the valuation has far run ahead of the fundamentals. Even after the decline, the Hangzhou-based company was capitalised at 190 billion yuan, translating into 347 times estimated earnings versus the average multiple of 118 for the Star Market. The stock was little changed at 469.80 yuan on Tuesday in Shanghai. “The company’s fundamentals are insufficient to justify its valuation premium,” said Kelvin Lau, an analyst at Daiwa Securities Group in Hong Kong. “Unitree needs to accelerate research and development spending in AI large models to stay competitive.” Unitree also needed to broaden its customer base for new revenue sources, with 70 per cent of its robot downstream applications concentrated on research and education, he said. Unitree’s fall from grace put under the spotlight the vulnerability of the humanoid robotic industry, where the ratio of industrial commercialisation is still low and most industry players are struggling to make profits. First-half profit for Unitree dropped 19 per cent from a year ago excluding extraordinary gains, while revenue growth slumped to 48 per cent from more than 300 per cent in 2025. Leju Robot, which has filed for an IPO on Shenzhen’s ChiNext board, reported a loss of 69.8 million yuan last year, the biggest over the past three years. Shenzhen Dobot expected its first-half loss to widen to as much as 120 million yuan because of increased costs. The Shenzhen exchange approved its stock sale in July. While Deep Robotics, whose listing application was accepted by the Shanghai exchange in May, posted a profit last year, the company said its profit margin might shrink in the first half because of falling product prices.

title: Top Singaporean chemist Lu Yixin to join Chinese university EIT next year
description: The distinguished scientist is the latest prominent academic to sign up with the privately funded research powerhouse.
content: Singapore’s most decorated chemist has confirmed he will leave his present position to join the fledgling Eastern Institute of Technology (EIT) in Ningbo, Zhejiang province, eastern China. Lu Yixin, a professor with the National University of Singapore (NUS), said he planned to move to the private research institute in early 2027, in a full-time role. Lu is a fellow of the Singapore National Academy of Science and president of the Singapore National Institute of Chemistry, in addition to his position as NUS Provost’s Chair Professor. “According to the plan, I will join EIT in Ningbo full time in January 2027,” he said, adding that he remained fully committed to his present duties at NUS for the coming months. Lu is the second high-profile academic to announce his departure from Singapore to EIT within the past month, with former Nanyang Technological University vice-president K. Jimmy Hsia joining in August. EIT was established in 2025 with a 30 billion yuan (US$4.4 billion) donation from Yu Renrong, a Ningbo-born semiconductor magnate. The institution is positioning itself as a research powerhouse, aggressively recruiting world-class talent. Lu said he was still working normally at NUS. “In the coming months, I will continue to diligently fulfil my responsibilities in teaching, research and management at the university,” he added. “Singapore, and NUS in particular, is where I have worked and lived for over 20 years. Here, I have many long-term collaborators, friends and students with whom I have grown together. “I have also established a very deep emotional and academic connection with NUS. Therefore, joining EIT full time does not mean that these connections will be interrupted.” Lu completed his undergraduate studies at Fudan University and obtained his master’s degree from Dalian University of Technology. He received his PhD from McGill University in Canada in 2000. He worked as a postdoctoral fellow at the Montreal Clinical Research Institute and later conducted research at Nagoya University under Ryoji Noyori, the Japanese Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry. Lu, who joined NUS in September 2003 and was promoted to full professor in 2014, has long focused on asymmetric catalysis and synthesis, with research spanning organic catalysis, metal catalysis, photocatalysis and sustainable chemistry. In simple terms, he uses various catalysts to precisely synthesise desired molecules for pharmaceuticals and catalysis. These methods can be shorter and more economical, paving the way for new drug synthesis. Lu has received multiple honours, including from the National Research Foundation in Singapore and the Asia Core Programme Lectureship. He also received the young scientist/outstanding scientist award from the science faculty at NUS, as well as the National Chemical Society of Singapore-GlaxoSmithKline organic chemistry prize. Lu was named a fellow of the Singapore National Academy of Science in 2022. He was elected president of the Singapore National Institute of Chemistry in 2025 and received the title of Provost’s Chair Professor. When asked why he joined EIT, Lu said that the institution was “at a critical stage of rapid development”. “For me, being able to participate in and witness the process of EIT gradually growing into a world-class institution is a meaningful challenge that I cannot refuse,” he said. “Another important factor is Ningbo. “Ningbo has a solid manufacturing foundation and a rich industrial base, while the Yangtze River Delta economic zone brings together a large number of universities, research institutions and hi-tech enterprises, providing a good ecosystem for scientific research innovation and the commercialisation of research outcomes.” Lu noted that chemistry “is not only an important component of basic sciences but is also closely related to application fields such as materials, medicine, energy, and advanced manufacturing”. “The industrial environment in Ningbo has established a broad bridge between basic research and industrial transformation, providing rich, real-world application scenarios for the development of the chemistry discipline,” he said. “This research and innovation environment, which combines academic potential with industrial support, is very attractive to me.” Lu said he would continue to focus on asymmetric catalysis and synthesis in his new role, with particular emphasis on biomedicine, green and sustainable chemistry. He will also promote the development of an interdisciplinary platform, he added. According to Lu, he had long conversations with Chen Shiyi, the EIT president, and other colleagues, while he was deciding whether to make the move. Their passion felt genuine and infectious, he said, and he was completely on board with what they were trying to build: a small, top-notch university led by research from day one. Lu said that in terms of China’s development there was a real need for a place that went after big scientific questions, tackled the country’s most important challenges and trained genuinely outstanding people. Lu said he hoped to take what he had learned over the years – in research, mentoring students and building academic programmes – to help EIT take off. Passionate about science? title: Who won at the Emmys? Widow’s Bay scores 14 awards, The Pitt takes best drama series
description: Widow’s Bay breaks the Emmys record for a comedy series, while The Pitt clinches best drama for a second year.
content: Widow’s Bay stormed the Emmy Awards on September 14, breaking a record for a comedy series with 14 awards, including best comedy series and three acting wins. The first season of the horror comedy created by Katie Dippold – about a New England island community reckoning with a centuries-old curse – spoiled the going-away party for Hacks, which had received the most comedy nominations of any show in its fifth and final season. It broke the comedy record set last year by The Studio, also on Apple TV, when it won 13. Widow’s Bay star Matthew Rhys won best actor, Stephen Root won best supporting actor and Kate O’Flynn won best supporting actress. Dippold won for writing and Hiro Murai for directing. The Pitt won the Emmy Award for best drama series for the second straight year, along with best actor for star Noah Wyle. HBO Max’s 24-hours-in-the-life-of-an-emergency-room series created by R. Scott Gemmill has now won best drama series for each of its first two seasons. The Pitt has sought to merge elements of network television from its 1990s peak with streaming-era prestige, and it has paid off with critical acclaim, cultural relevance and awards like the biggest prize on television’s biggest night. It won its first best drama Emmy as a rookie upstart, and it takes its second as a revered favourite, beating fellow nominees including Pluribus, Paradise and The Diplomat. The Apple TV horror comedy Widow’s Bay similarly rode into the night on a wave of buzz. It had already won eight Emmys at an earlier ceremony and added four more, including supporting actress for breakout star Kate O’Flynn and supporting actor for Stephen Root. Rhys also won best actor in a limited series for The Beast in Me, becoming the first man to win two leading actor categories in the same year. “The celebrations will be long, varied and I hope at times wild,” Rhys, 51, said backstage while holding both Emmys. Widow’s Bay creator Dippold is a first-time Emmy winner and first-time nominee, previously best known for an old viral tweet showing her dressed as “The Babadook” monster from a film of the same name. Jean Smart won her fifth best actress award in an unprecedented sweep for the fifth and final season of Hacks. No actor had won an Emmy every year for a series that lasted more than three seasons until she did it this year. “What a ride this has been,” an emotional Smart said after receiving a standing ovation. The 75-year-old has won eight Emmys overall in a career that was already more than respectable when she landed her defining role of Deborah Vance, a brash stand-up comic pushing back against age, obscurity and sexism in the HBO Max series. Wyle won the Emmy for the second season of The Pitt for playing Dr Michael “Robby” Robinavitch, a role that brought him a major career revival after starring in ER in the 1990s. “I grew up in LA; I’m a Hollywood kid. I was raised on television, and movie theatres were my place of worship,” Wyle, 55, said in his acceptance speech. “This is all I’ve ever wanted to do, and this is the only club I’ve ever wanted to join.” Rhea Seehorn won best actress in a drama for playing the lone central character on Apple TV’s Pluribus. The 54-year-old had been nominated twice without winning for her breakthrough role on Better Call Saul, created by Breaking Bad creator Vince Gilligan, who put Seehorn at the centre of Pluribus. Gilligan won his fifth career Emmy for his writing on the show. It was the first Emmy for both Widow’s Bay actors O’Flynn and Root. O’Flynn, a 40-year-old British actor whose previous acclaim came mostly for her work in theatre, plays Patricia Moyer, a city worker and social outcast dealing with a demonic darkness. “This is the role of a lifetime,” O’Flynn said from the stage. “This is for all the Patricias out there.” Root, one of the most ubiquitous character actors of the last few decades, beat out Harrison Ford, who many thought would get his first major competitive Hollywood award for his role on Shrinking. “Thank you, sir, for all your many years of great, great, great acting,” Root said to Ford during his acceptance. Root, 74, is the oldest person to win the category. Sally Field, 79, became the oldest woman to win best actress in a limited or anthology series or television movie for Remarkably Bright Creatures. The Pitt was the top overall nominee, but it lost in both supporting acting categories despite having four nominees in one and three in the other. Allison Janney won best supporting actress in a drama for her role in The Diplomat, over Katherine LaNasa from The Pitt, who won last year, and three of her castmates. Janney joined Smart as an eight-time Emmy winner. Tom Pelphrey won supporting actor in a drama for Task.

title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp announces half-price fares for ‘Thank You Day’ on October 24
description: Offer applies to Octopus, JoyYou and QR ticket users across heavy rail, eligible bus services and selected cross-border East Rail journeys.
content: Hong Kong’s rail operator will offer half-price fares across its network on October 24, as part of a “Thank You Day” promotion. The MTR Corporation said discounts would apply to Octopus and JoyYou card users on its railway, light rail and bus services in the northwestern New Territories, as well as to QR code ticket holders on the heavy rail network. Cross-border journeys to and from Lo Wu and Lok Ma Chau stations on the East Rail line will also be covered. Passengers can combine the half-price discount with interchange and fare saver discounts, a 25 per cent discount on connecting journeys under the monthly pass and the government’s HK$2 (25 US cents) concession scheme for elderly passengers and eligible people with disabilities. The discount will not apply to East Rail first class, the Airport Express, MTR feeder bus services, single-journey tickets, contactless card payments or the Hong Kong section of the high-speed rail. “The corporation will deploy additional staff at MTR stations to assist passengers and closely monitor train and station operations to suitably adjust train service and manpower arrangements when necessary,” it said. The promotional day falls under the MTR’s service performance rebate arrangement, part of the fare adjustment mechanism, which offers discounted fares on a designated Saturday or Sunday once the rebate fund reaches HK$25 million. Last year, Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan confirmed that the corporation had been fined HK$19.2 million over a five-hour disruption on the Tseung Kwan O line in May, with the penalty allocated to passenger rebates.

title: Malaysian mother honours slain daughter Yap Shing Xuen’s memory
description: Nearly a year after the school toilet stabbing, Yap Shing Xuen’s mother wrote of her grief and paid tribute to her brave daughter.
content: The mother of Malaysian schoolgirl Yap Shing Xuen has shared a moving tribute to her late daughter, who was stabbed to death nearly a year ago in a school toilet. On Monday, the Shah Alam High Court found Yap’s attacker, who was 14 at the time, not guilty of her murder on the grounds of insanity. Medical testimony accepted by the court established that the boy had severe undiagnosed schizophrenia since the age of nine. He was ordered into psychiatric confinement, where he will remain indefinitely. Earlier that same day, Wong Lee Ping wrote in a social media post that she had raised Yap and her younger sister largely alone after her marriage ended when Yap was two years old. The girls lived with their paternal grandparents during the week while Wong worked and were reunited with their mother only at weekends. “Because of this, we cherished every day we had together,” Wong wrote in Chinese. Those weekends were filled with running, hiking and swimming. Yap was “a very brave child”, trying parasailing, snorkelling and rock climbing with her sister, her mother wrote. “I knew I wasn’t a wealthy mother,” Wong wrote. “But I always told myself, as long as I was able, I would do my utmost to ensure my children were happy and had a childhood filled with love.” Yap emerged from that upbringing unusually self-reliant, according to her mother. She began helping with housework – mopping floors and washing dishes – aged five and rarely if ever asked her mother to buy her anything. She organised her own tuition classes as she grew older, telling her mother she hoped to study accounting, design or financial management. I will carry the love you gave me Wong Lee Ping, Yap Shing Xuen’s mother Sport was a big part of Yap’s life. She played badminton and volleyball, won gold at a school sports day and actively sought out opportunities to train and compete outside school. “As a mother, there wasn’t much I could do other than handle the driving,” Wong wrote. “Watching her put in the effort … for the things she loved made me incredibly happy and proud.” Yap never forgot her mother’s birthday or Mother’s Day, saving pocket money and cash from Chinese New Year red packets each year to buy presents, occasionally also baking a cake in secret. ‘Most unbearable day’ Wong described the day of Yap’s death, on October 14 last year, as the “darkest most unbearable day of my life”. “I am still living, still eating, sleeping and working,” she wrote. “But the most important place in my heart is now permanently empty.” She said people had tried to comfort her by saying time would heal her grief. “But only a mother knows, some pain does not disappear with the passage of time. We just learn, little by little, to go living while carrying that pain with us.” The tribute closed with a message addressed directly to her daughter: that she owed her mother no apology for the cost of her education or hobbies, and that being her mother had been the proudest and happiest experience of Wong’s life. “I miss you so very much,” she wrote, adding that she hoped Yap was now somewhere free of pain, with “sunshine, sea, badminton, volleyball and everything you loved”. “I will carry the love you gave me as I continue on my journey,” Wong added. “You will always be my daughter”.

title: Chinese carmakers GAC and FAW eye potential tie-up of their Toyota operations
description: The planned deal is seen as a precedent for cross-regional consolidation amid China’s efficiency push, analysts say.
content: Two Chinese state-owned carmakers, Guangzhou Automobile Group (GAC) and FAW Group, are weighing a restructuring that could integrate their joint venture operations with Japanese giant Toyota, industry insiders say, following Beijing’s call for consolidation amid weakening domestic demand. GAC planned to acquire part of FAW’s equity in a joint venture vehicle manufacturer through a share issuance and raise supporting funds, the Guangzhou-based carmaker said in an exchange filing on Monday night, following a full-day trading halt. The target asset involved a foreign-listed company, but GAC did not disclose its name or the deal value. The deal remained in the planning stage, subject to internal approvals and regulatory clearance, GAC said. Analysts and mainland media reports said the target company was FAW’s joint venture with Toyota. “From a strategic and synergy perspective, a Toyota-related target is more likely,” said Claire Yuan, director of corporate ratings for China autos at S&P Global Ratings, in a reply to the South China Morning Post. “This transaction could resolve the long-standing competition between GAC-Toyota and FAW-Toyota.” Yuan added it would mark a critical move for state-owned enterprises, which had largely lagged in the transition to electric vehicles (EVs). GAC has joint ventures with Toyota and Honda, while FAW – which is controlled directly by the central government – partners with Toyota, Volkswagen and Audi. The deal is expected to set an important precedent for cross-regional consolidation among central and local carmakers China International Capital Corporation The deal aimed to “promote the optimal integration of industrial resources among local and central state-owned enterprises, and enhance operational efficiency of listed companies,” GAC said in the filing. Investment bank China International Capital Corporation said in a research note on Tuesday that if the restructuring went through, it was “expected to set an important precedent for cross-regional consolidation among central and local carmakers, send a positive signal of ‘anti-involution’, and help improve market sentiment”. Involution, or neijuan, refers to excessive competition, where more resources are invested without increasing returns or reinvestment in research and development. GAC’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed 2.6 per cent higher on Tuesday. Trading in its Shanghai shares remained suspended. The announcement followed a pledge by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology – China’s industrial watchdog – and eight other agencies on Friday to intensify efforts to promote mergers, reorganisations and cross-regional integration among carmakers, while advancing reforms towards group-based management. Despite strong exports, China’s domestic vehicle sales have slowed sharply after years of rapid growth and subsidy withdrawal, squeezing profitability. Retail sales fell 20.8 per cent year on year to 11.7 million units in the first eight months of the year, while profit margins shrank by 1 percentage point to 3.6 per cent in the January-July period, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed. Joint ventures between local and foreign carmakers, which once dominated the mainland market, have struggled amid China’s rapid shift towards EVs. In August, joint venture retail sales of petrol-powered cars and EVs plunged 35 per cent year on year to some 310,000 units, accounting for just 4.3 per cent of China’s EV market, according to CPCA. Squeezed by domestic EV makers like BYD, GAC’s net loss in the first half of the year widened 76 per cent year on year to 4.5 billion yuan (US$670 million).

title: How a Vietnamese chef is turning family favourites into Michelin-starred feasts
description: Inspired by his roots, Hiep Truong is elevating traditional Vietnamese cuisine at his Upstairs Tasting Room in Ho Chi Minh City.
content: Even after winning a Michelin star for his restaurant, Upstairs Tasting Room in Ho Chi Minh City, the biggest source of chef Hiep Truong’s inspiration remains the same: his mother and the family table. The dish closest to his heart – the one that reminds him most of home – is the vit hon, a traditional Central Vietnamese dish where duck meat is braised with lemongrass, turmeric, coconut water and fermented shrimp paste. At his intimate tasting room in the Vietnamese city, the duck is dry-aged for 21 days, grilled over charcoal and served with peanuts, house-made duck sausage and wild fig. The rest of Truong’s menu holds the same familial warmth, drawing on childhood favourites and shaping them into 13 fine-dining courses. His current favourite is hen xuc banh da – stir-fried clams with laksa leaf, served on a rice cracker as a tartlet. Other crowd favourites include so nuong mo hanh (scallop and cockles) and ca nau me (fish with fermented rice), as well as a Wagyu beef salad with pickled young aubergines, egg yolk and spring herbs. “Upstairs is how I share the food I grew up with,” he says. Falling in love with cooking Truong came from a farming family and was raised near Chua Chan Mountain in Dong Nai province, roughly 100 kilometres (62 miles) east of Ho Chi Minh City. Corn, pepper, tobacco, cashews – the seasons constantly shifted what they grew throughout the year. With his parents busy with the crops, cooking at home often fell to Truong – a chore that would eventually become his life’s passion. He went straight into a two-year culinary programme after graduating high school. His routine consisted of class in the mornings, shifts at a nearby bistro from the afternoons until late at night, alongside ongoing internships. “When you do something you like, in your passion, it will never make you tired,” he says. After working at Villa Song Saigon and a few smaller restaurants, Truong landed at Quince Saigon, where he stayed for five and a half years, eventually becoming sous-chef under chef Julien Perraudin, his globally trained mentor. “I learned so many things,” he says. “I learned everything. With the wok, with fire, yes, and also flavours. [Chef Julien] was married to a Thai woman, so he cooked Vietnamese cuisine with Thai [techniques] mixed with French and Japanese.” After Quince, Truong moved to Little Bear, a gastro wine bar on the ground floor of a building that also housed an empty, unfinished unit above it. That bare space would eventually become Upstairs. The restaurant earned its first Michelin star within 18 months of opening in late 2024, a rapid rise for a chef who had never run his own kitchen before. An advocate for his home city Over the years, Truong has developed some firm opinions and observations about what defines his homeland’s food. Originally from Hue, his family settled among a community of central Vietnamese migrants after relocating. He is quick to note that both his accent and his cooking still carry the city he was born in – and he is especially proud of it. Contrasting the two regional Vietnamese cooking styles, he explains that he prefers the “salty, spicy and very herbal” Hue style over the “lighter and more sour” cooking in the north. The contrast is more than culinary: it speaks to how deeply his Hue roots have shaped his palate. It is regional, seasonal, personal. Take shrimp paste, for instance. He refuses to use the northern variety, which he bluntly says “smells funky”. Instead, he reaches for the darker, more mellow version from central Vietnam – the kind made in the Hue style, brown rather than purple and far less pungent. He may experiment with variations and adjust his flavour palates, but one thing never changes, no matter the region he is drawing from: fish sauce. “For me, Vietnamese cuisine without mam – fish sauce, fermented things – and fresh herbs, is not Vietnamese cuisine,” he says with a laugh. Reinventing traditional dishes Then there is the dish that divides his diners: kho quet, which centres on an intensely savoury, sweet and thick Vietnamese dipping sauce made by simmering fish sauce, sugar, crispy pork fat and dried shrimp in a clay pot. Boiled or fresh vegetables are used to dip into the sauce. Traditionally, it is a humble home-cooked dish. At Upstairs, Truong reinvents it, making the sauce creamier and richer, and serving it surrounded by vegetables. The result is polarising. “Vietnamese people don’t like it because they say it’s not kho quet,” he says. “But foreigners really love it.” He has noticed this pattern again and again: a dish that Vietnamese diners dismiss often becomes the one foreigners cannot get enough of. When asked why, he offers a simple theory: outsiders arrive with fewer expectations. He admits he has high expectations and harsh opinions, too. “When it’s a new cuisine, it’s easy,” he says. “But you, me, we already have a lot of these things every day for a very long time.” Upstairs, 36 Nguyen Ba Huan, An Khanh Ward (Thao Dien), Ho Chi Minh City

title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan to set goals, not alter economic system: John Lee
description: ‘I want to make it very clear: the five-year plan is not a planned economy,’ city leader stresses ahead of blueprint’s unveiling.
content: Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will include both binding and anticipatory targets, the city’s leader has said, stressing that the long-term blueprint will not signal a move towards a planned economy. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu also revealed on Tuesday that the plan, which will be unveiled alongside his annual policy address the following day, would feature a blue cover symbolising “blue skies”, openness, progress and steadiness. “There will be indicators which are binding and indicators which are anticipatory … There are things we must do and they are binding on the government particularly,” he told the media ahead of the weekly meeting of the Executive Council, the key decision-making body. “And there are things we want to do very much, but we need everybody to facilitate. The government will lead, and also the government will coordinate resources, make the right policies and everybody has to play their part in order to achieve the best result.” But he stopped short of saying whether specific indicators would be set for major initiatives such as the Northern Metropolis megaproject. Lee reiterated that the plan would not alter Hong Kong’s economic system. “I want to make it very clear: the five-year plan is not a planned economy. It is a plan which tells us where the strategic directions are, where we are heading and which are the priority areas,” he said. “It is a blueprint for us to implement in five years’ time. So when we each year roll out policies, we also have to ascertain priorities so that at the end of five years we will reach certain goals.” The city leader said the theme of the fifth and final policy address of his current term would be: “A Strategic Vision for a Bright New Era; Driving Reform and Boosting Development; Unleashing Opportunities and Enhancing Livelihoods”. He said the document would retain its green cover, symbolising policy continuity, vibrancy and hope, adding that it would carry special significance as the first policy address to follow the announcement of the five-year plan. “It means that we adopt a long-term perspective through the five-year plan to map out Hong Kong’s overall development, advance reforms, promote growth and create opportunities,” Lee said. “[We will] ensure that the benefits of economic development are shared with the public, and that we embrace the future.” He also thanked the public for their valuable feedback, which helped the government complete drafts of the two documents. Lee is scheduled to present both documents to the Legislative Council on Wednesday morning. He said they contained more than 100,000 words in total and that he would spend two to three hours outlining their key points. The government had prepared a summary to help the public understand the relationship between the two documents and their contents, he added. Lee said the two blueprints were rich in substance and that he would explain them to the public at a press conference and television forum on Wednesday, followed by a radio event the next day. He will also attend a 1½-hour question-and-answer session at the legislature on Thursday morning to answer lawmakers’ questions, his first such session this year. Authorities have said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan aims to align the city’s development more closely with the national blueprint for 2026-30, while providing strategic direction for the years ahead. The plan will outline the city’s vision for the Northern Metropolis, the advancement of innovation and technology, and the development of the finance, shipping and trading sectors. The policy address will serve as a progress report on the implementation of the plan, setting out policies and advancing its direction in response to the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments. The South China Morning Post earlier reported that the documents would introduce measures to remove hurdles to business development in the Northern Metropolis, as well as initiatives to strengthen innovation hubs, research efforts and technology applications. The government earlier concluded months-long public consultations on both documents. It held more than 100 consultation sessions and two town hall meetings, attended by more than 200 residents and district representatives, and received more than 17,000 submissions on the five-year plan and 11,000 on the policy address.

title: Citigroup hires veteran banker Sophia Wang to lead China institutional sales
description: Wang has more than 20 years of experience in the field, and her hire comes after Citi announced plans to expand its corporate headcount.
content: Citigroup has appointed veteran banker Sophia Wang as a managing director and head of China financial-institutional sales and senior relationship management (SRM), marking the latest move by the Wall Street lender to deepen its footprint in mainland capital markets despite ongoing geopolitical friction. Wang joined the bank on Tuesday, according to an internal staff memo. Based in Shanghai, she will oversee institutional sales coverage across rates, spread products, foreign exchange, commodities and equity derivatives. She will also manage high-level strategic relationships with key local financial institutions, as well as global SRM clients looking to access China’s markets for investment and financing. With more than two decades of international banking experience, Wang spent 15 years at Bank of America Merrill Lynch in London, where she led fixed-income, currencies and commodities sales targeting sovereign wealth funds and major Chinese financial institutions across the Europe, Middle East and Africa region. Earlier in her career, she held debt-capital-markets and treasury roles across London, Hong Kong and Shanghai at Standard Chartered Bank. In her new role, she will report locally to Jeff Wu, Citi’s head of markets sales for China, and regionally to Laiman Wong, head of SRM for Japan, North Asia, Australia and South Asia. Citi’s Shanghai-based institutional sales teams will report directly to Wang. The high-profile hire comes weeks after Citi’s announcement that it planned to expand its corporate banking headcount across North Asia and Japan by 25 per cent while establishing new China-desk hubs in Brazil and Europe to capture double-digit growth in cross-border client activity. The US bank is also awaiting Chinese regulatory approval for a wholly owned securities brokerage licence, which could come as soon as this month and would allow the firm to trade and underwrite shares onshore. That would put Citi alongside rivals JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, whose China securities units all posted sharply higher profits last year, according to reports by international media outlets. “Sophia is an accomplished markets leader bringing extensive sales expertise across FX, rates and local markets products,” Wu and Wong said in the memo.

title: Hyrox co-founder sorry for Beijing incident, pledges rule changes after backlash
description: Moritz Furste issues apology days after Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk’s accident during her race left faecal matter on course.
content: Hyrox co-founder Moritz Furste has apologised for the events in Beijing over the weekend, and said his organisation had begun revising event operations and updating its rule book. The commercial fitness competition has faced intense public backlash ever since elite Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk soiled herself during the solo women’s event, which she went on to win. The incident raised severe concerns over whether prompt sanitation was carried out and whether the hygiene rights of other competitors who used the same course and equipment were protected. Two days after the race, following an initial official statement acknowledging organisational lapses that failed to satisfy the public, Furste released a joint post on the official Hyrox World account addressing the fallout directly. “I need to address all of you directly concerning the recent events in China,” Furste said. “I apologise to all that were directly or indirectly affected, as well as to everyone who felt like we did not handle the situation like we should have.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Mo Fuerste (@mofuerste) He acknowledged that his organisation made a mistake by “not reacting immediately during the race,” adding that “in the end, it is my job to foresee these potential incidents, and I did not”. Furste said work had immediately begun to refine race operations and amend the rule book, with new rules and procedures already implemented to prevent similar occurrences. “We learn and try to get better every day,” he added. During the race in Beijing last Saturday, world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk suffered diarrhoea and incontinence but carried on to take first place in a time of one hour, one minute and 23 seconds. Footage of the incident quickly went viral across social media and fitness communities, triggering fierce debate over sportsmanship, venue sanitation and rule enforcement. Some questioned why Wietrzyk was not punished, while other athletes who spilled water outside designated areas were hit with two-minute penalties. For her part, the 24-year-old has said little outside a now-deleted Instagram story that said a “win is a win” and thanked everyone for their support.

title: Chinese plant extracts critical rare metals from lithium waste in world first
description: 500-tonne production line up and running for rubidium and caesium, critical to advanced technology including aerospace and quantum computing.
content: China has launched a 500-tonne production line to extract rubidium and caesium from lithium waste. A demonstration line in Jiangxi province – the world’s first with an annual capacity of 500 tonnes for continuous tower extraction and separation of low-grade rubidium and caesium – has achieved stable production, according to the Institute of Process Engineering under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). Rubidium and caesium are critical to aerospace, quantum computing, biomedicine, new energy and other frontier fields. But they do not exist in large amounts as independent minerals in the Earth’s crust. Instead, they occur as associated elements in lithium ores and salt-lake brines, at very low grades that make extraction extremely difficult. By recovering them from waste left after lithium extraction from ore, China has extended its new energy industry production chain and strengthened the secure supply of rubidium, a strategic rare and precious metal. China’s rubidium resources are not scarce. A 2024 paper estimated domestic reserves at about 1.16 million tonnes of rubidium oxide and 140,000 tonnes of caesium oxide. However, known rubidium resources are mainly associated with speciality lithium ores and salt-lake brines, with low grades and complex forms that make extraction and recycling very difficult. For example, lithium-bearing lepidolite in Jiangxi contains nearly 40 per cent of China’s rubidium reserves, but the traditional high-temperature sulphate roasting process can reach 800 to 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit), locking much of the rubidium and caesium in aluminosilicate waste that is eventually discarded with lithium slag. Pollucite is the main industrial source of caesium. China has no commercially viable pollucite mines, so it mainly imports from Canada, Australia and Zimbabwe. Like rubidium, China’s caesium is mostly found alongside lepidolite and salt-lake brines, which makes it hard to extract. The breakthrough relies on a high-efficiency tower extraction system for rubidium and caesium developed by the institute with independent intellectual property rights. It uses differential counter-current extraction and has advantages such as a small footprint, low extractant use and strong containment. According to the CAS website, a single extraction tower can be up to 15 times as efficient as a traditional extraction tank. It reduces extractant use by 40 per cent and equipment footprint by more than 50 per cent. The team designed an industrial unit with 17 extraction towers together with Jiangxi Ganfeng Lithium and other partners. It started up successfully on the first try and has run continuously and steadily since then, the institute said last Thursday. It recovers more than 98 per cent of the caesium and more than 95 per cent of the rubidium. Both products, caesium carbonate and rubidium carbonate, are more than 99.9 per cent pure and are already being sold in commercial batches. The system produces 500 tonnes a year of rubidium and caesium carbonates in all. The ratio of rubidium to caesium in the output is not yet clear. Still, the demonstration line proves that low-grade associated rubidium and caesium resources can be separated industrially in an efficient and green way, providing a technical model for larger-scale commercialisation. According to the CAS report, the technology is important for ensuring the development and use of China’s speciality lithium ores and the secure supply of rubidium and caesium resources. China already plays a dominant role in the global rubidium resource landscape. A March article in China Mining News said the country had the world’s richest rubidium resources and the most centralised production capacity. As of December 2025, China had built five core rubidium production lines – boasting world-leading technology and a total annual capacity of about 3,000 tonnes in rubidium salt equivalent. Meanwhile, China’s Sinomine Resource Group controls the world’s largest pollucite (caesium ore) mine – creating a closed loop of resources, technology and production capacity that cements the country’s dominant position in the industry. Looking ahead, breakthroughs in perovskite solar cells, solid-state batteries, quantum computing and other key technologies could broaden applications for rubidium salts, giving rubidium the potential to become the next rare earth.

title: Promoter behind Strikeforce, Bellator MMA, to launch new 32-fighter combat league
description: Veteran boss Scott Coker set to launch Ki MMA, with featherweight tournaments in Europe, Asia, and North America.
content: Veteran mixed martial arts promoter Scott Coker has ⁠unveiled Ki MMA, ⁠a new global promotion set ⁠to launch in the first quarter of 2027 with a 32-man featherweight tournament spanning four continents. The former head of Bellator MMA and Strikeforce announced the venture at a news conference in New York on Monday ‌alongside long-time MMA executive and matchmaker Rich Chou, who will lead athlete relations, and media executive Peter Levin, who will serve as the chairman. Ki MMA’s inaugural competition will feature eight featherweight fighters from each of North America, South America, Asia, and Europe. Regional events will determine one finalist from ⁠each continent, who will advance to an international semi-final stage. Who will fight has yet to be revealed. The promotion is targeting events in the US, Ireland, Hungary, Brazil, Japan, South Korea, and either Italy or France, Coker said. ‌The initial tournament will be contested at 145lb (66kg), a division ⁠that has produced ⁠some of the sport’s most prominent champions and fighters. Its fights will be held in a ring ‌rather than the fenced cage used by the UFC and many other leading MMA organisations, a format that ‌reflects Coker’s ‌long-standing interest in Japanese combat sports. Coker previously led Strikeforce, which emerged as ‌one of the UFC’s most significant rivals before it was acquired by UFC parent ⁠Zuffa in 2011. He later became chief executive of Bellator, which was purchased by ⁠the Professional Fighters League in 2023. Ki MMA enters a crowded market led by the UFC, with the PFL, ONE Championship and Japan’s Rizin ‌also competing for fighters, ‌media rights and international audiences. Coker’s record of building Strikeforce and Bellator, however, gives the new venture immediate credibility within the sport. The company did not disclose broadcast partners, financial backing or a timetable for announcing its first group of athletes.

title: Hong Kong leader vows accountability over faulty lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
description: John Lee orders report within a month over defective lift installation and says those responsible, including officials, will be held responsible.
content: Hong Kong authorities will hold construction firms and government personnel accountable for faulty lift installation work at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block, the city’s leader has said, as he tasked the Development Bureau with submitting a report within a month. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Tuesday that the problem should be rectified “very, very quickly”, adding that he had instructed the bureau, which had given him a preliminary briefing, to “thoroughly investigate the matter and report within a month”. “We will pursue accountability, including contractors, subcontractors, engineering personnel and professionals. And if there are government personnel involved, we will pursue their accountability as well,” he said ahead of his meeting with the key decision-making Executive Council. “We also need to identify where and whether the system has any inadequacies and rectify them. “To consider what further action we will do, we must fact-find very clearly about what happened, where are the inadequacies, and whether any person who should be held accountable, we should pursue their accountability. After we have found out the facts, then we will decide what further steps we shall take.” Lee’s comments came a month after defective work at the hospital – the largest on Hong Kong Island – came under scrutiny, with 24 of the 28 lifts in its new 34-storey clinical block deemed unfit for use. Sources previously told the South China Morning Post that Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the Architectural Services Department (ASD) who oversaw the development, had been asked to resign and left her post over the scandal. The department denied that there had been any “forced resignation”, saying Li had quit for “personal reasons” after giving three months’ notice. Lee did not directly address the SCMP’s questions about whether the resignation would affect the investigation and why the government had not invoked its “Heads of Department Accountability System”, proposed in his policy address last year to improve governance. He stressed that medical services were important to the public and that the new block should open as soon as possible. Widespread installation defects, revealed last month, have delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, raising serious concerns over project oversight and civil service accountability. The delay has prevented medical departments from moving into the block, although its blood bank and restaurants remain open. Construction began in 2018 and was largely completed last year. Health authorities had previously said that hospital staff had begun using the building, but that it had not yet been formally handed over by the ASD. Clinical services had originally been expected to begin relocating there from the end of last year. Last month, the ASD said the main contractor, a Paul Y Engineering Group joint venture, and lift subcontractor Anlev Elex Elevator would be required to bear all remedial work costs. But on September 4, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said her bureau had also instructed the ASD and the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department – both of which it oversees – to submit internal review reports assessing their handling and supervision of the project. Lawmakers and political observers have called for transparency and explanations from authorities over the scandal. Some also criticised the handling of civil service management lapses following Li’s departure, saying it had bypassed the established disciplinary mechanism.

title: Letters | Hong Kong must put child safety on the development agenda
description: Readers discuss the danger of child sexual exploitation shifting online, and the Hong Kong dollar peg.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. As Hong Kong’s chief executive prepares to unveil the city’s first five-year plan and his 2026 policy address on Wednesday, child safety should be recognised as a central part of the city’s long-term development agenda. With online grooming and artificial intelligence abuse continuing to escalate, telling children to “be careful online” is no longer enough. Protecting young people requires comprehensive sexuality education, strict digital safeguarding and clear systems for prevention, reporting and support. The landscape of child sexual exploitation is rapidly shifting online. Hong Kong’s police force recorded 100 cases of online child sexual grooming in 2025 with a further 40 reported in just the first four months of 2026, and at least one victim as young as 10. Crucially, 37 per cent of the 1,354 newly registered child protection cases in 2025 involved sexual abuse. These figures reveal an uncomfortable reality: harm is not limited to strangers or physical spaces. Schoolmates, friends and peers were among the most commonly identified perpetrators implicated in grooming, sexual exploitation and image-based abuse, meaning children can be harmed by people they know and trust. In fact, grooming rarely starts with obvious coercion but begins with attention, emotional validation and false friendship. Once trust is built, perpetrators may introduce secrecy or request intimate images. As a result, victims may feel too ashamed or confused to seek help. To address these risks, children need more than warnings about online dangers. Clear, age-appropriate and evidence-based education on consent, personal boundaries, healthy relationships, help-seeking and online safety must be prioritised. Plan International Hong Kong therefore calls for a comprehensive review of sexuality education to ensure every child receives consistent and practical learning, regardless of the school they attend. The rise of generative AI also creates further urgency. AI tools make it effortless to produce sexualised deepfakes used to humiliate, exploit or blackmail young people, with catastrophic psychological impacts when shared among peers or online communities. While government initiatives to strengthen AI literacy are welcome, education must extend beyond technical skills to include digital ethics, consent and online respect. Besides, Hong Kong should establish a formal AI safeguarding framework for schools, requiring clear operational protocols for handling disclosures, supporting affected students, limiting the spread of harmful content and reporting incidents appropriately. Children have a fundamental right to safety, dignity and privacy. As technology reshapes how children interact and experience harm, our education and safeguarding systems must evolve to keep children protected. Dr Kanie Siu Mei-kuen, CEO, Plan International Hong Kong A ‘golden’ Hong Kong dollar anyone? With the United States’ sovereign debt at US$40 trillion, the collapse of the US dollar seems like only a matter of time. When that day comes, the Hong Kong dollar, which is pegged to the US dollar, is likely to see a sharp fall in value. Panic selling of the Hong Kong dollar would be inevitable. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority would be forced to buy Hong Kong dollars on the foreign exchange market to defend the peg, and despite having around US$442.9 billion in the Exchange Fund, it could be badly outmatched by a much larger pool of sellers and speculators. A broken peg would be disastrous for Hong Kong, but there is a way to prevent this. Create a new “golden” Hong Kong dollar, fully backed by gold and freely exchangeable with the traditional Hong Kong dollar at 1:1. Both would remain legal tender in the city. At a gold price of US$5,000 per troy ounce, only around 500 tonnes of gold would be needed to back the roughly HK$640 billion (US$82 billion) currently in circulation. The central government has gold reserves far in excess of that. More importantly, if the US dollar collapses, Hong Kong dollar holders could convert their traditional holdings into golden Hong Kong dollars at par in an orderly manner. In a world short of gold-backed currencies, the golden Hong Kong dollar would be a uniquely secure safe harbour. Even if the US dollar never collapses, the golden Hong Kong dollar would still be a beacon that attracts global capital, strengthening Hong Kong’s role as an international financial centre. Guy Lam, Admiralty

title: Air quality across Singapore reaches unhealthy levels from Indonesian wildfires
description: The financial hub’s air currently ranks among the 10 most polluted cities in the world, according to IQAir data.
content: Singapore was shrouded in haze on Tuesday, with smoke from wildfires in neighbouring Indonesia raising island-wide pollution to levels that pose a health risk. All five regions of the city state recorded unhealthy air quality levels, the first time that has happened since September 2019, according to the National Environment Agency. Singapore’s air currently ranks among the 10 most polluted cities in the world, according to IQAir data, with the capitals of Malaysia and Indonesia also among the top spots. Indonesia often battles wildfires during its annual dry season, but hotspots this year have been higher than normal. There were more than 9,000 recorded in August, the most for the month in data going back to 2015, and more than 7,000 have been recorded so far in September, according to the forestry ministry’s fire-monitoring platform SiPongi. The situation is being exacerbated by the strengthening El Nino weather pattern, which causes drier weather in much of the region. Little immediate relief is expected from the weather, with dry conditions expected to persist across much of the south of Southeast Asia in the near term, according to the Asean Specialised Meteorological Centre. “The hotspot and haze situation in the region is expected to remain escalated with a continued risk of transboundary smoke haze,” the centre said in its latest forecast. Air quality in parts of Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions, where the fires are concentrated, was at dangerous or very unhealthy levels as of Tuesday, government data showed. Malaysia has also suffered, with choking haze in late August prompting the government to move its leader’s annual National Day speech to an indoor venue. A state of emergency was declared for part of Sarawak state earlier this month. A hotspot is defined as a location where satellites detect an elevated surface temperature, indicating a potential fire. The dryness has affected Indonesia’s vast natural resources sector, with water supplies dwindling at a major nickel complex and palm oil production expected to take a hit. Slash-and-burn methods used to clear farmland have previously been linked to the fires, and dry undergrowth can also ignite carbon-rich peatland, which can smoulder for long periods and be difficult to extinguish. Smoke plumes from fires in Kalimantan drifted towards Singapore because of a shift in winds, alongside smoke haze from Sumatra, the National Environment Agency said on Monday. The agency expects the haze to persist over the next 24 hours, with air quality ranging from high-moderate to mid-unhealthy conditions. Indonesia’s forestry ministry said in a statement that this year’s surge in forest fires was due to a combination of El Nino-driven dry weather and human-caused ignition, adding that each incident must be investigated individually. The country has expanded aerial firefighting operations, including with helicopters provided by Japan, it said. Malaysia has also offered help to tackle the blazes. There may be a slight uptick in rainfall in parts of Sumatra and Kalimantan next week, which could temporarily ease fire risks, according to Takahisa Nishikawa, senior decision support meteorologist at Atmospheric G2. “This may provide some relief, although it does not yet look like a widespread or sustained wetting pattern and forecast confidence is lower at that range,” he said. The fires in Indonesia add to a bad year for wildfires globally, with parts of Europe and North America also reeling from recent blazes. The current El Nino has a 75 per cent chance of becoming “a historic event”, surpassing all records dating back to 1950, the US Climate Prediction Centre said last week.

title: Meet Riverdale star Charles Melton’s wife, Camille Summers-Valli, who has directed Hermès and Burberry campaigns
description: The actor, who is reportedly in talks to star in Destin Daniel Cretton’s live-action Naruto film, confirmed his marriage to the director last month.
content: Riverdale star Charles Melton is enjoying a milestone year. Following his first Emmy nomination for Netflix’s limited series Beef in July, the actor is reportedly in final talks to star as Kakashi Hatake in Destin Daniel Cretton’s live-action Naruto adaptation. The actor’s personal life is equally busy. After welcoming his first child in March, Melton is embracing fatherhood and recently confirmed his marriage to Camille Summers-Valli. So, who is Camille Summers-Valli, Charles Melton’s wife and the mother of their daughter? Melton and Summers-Valli’s relationship timeline Melton and Summers-Valli have kept their relationship largely private. The actor first tagged Summers-Valli on his Instagram in a Coach campaign post, marking her as a director, in 2024. The couple offered more glimpses of their life together this January, when Summers-Valli posted a series of maternity photos – some of which featured Melton. In March, the Korean-American actor announced the arrival of their newborn daughter with a heartfelt Instagram carousel, captioning the pinned post “our family”. When Melton received the gold artistic achievement award at Gold Gala in May, he referred to Summers-Valli as “my partner, my fiancée, my wife, my girlfriend” in his acceptance speech, sparking the first wave of marriage speculation. The actor later confirmed their marital status by referring to her as his wife in an interview with People last month. In July, Summers-Valli shared a candid post about motherhood: “As girls we are told our power is in our beauty, in our sexuality, in our service to men. My daughter has taught me that in fact my power is within my ability to love on others in a world that needs more love. That my power is in my creativity.” What does Camille Summers-Valli do? Born in Bangkok and raised in Nepal, Summers-Valli is a multidisciplinary director who has led major art and fashion campaigns for brands including Hermès, Jean Paul Gaultier, Marc Jacobs, Stella McCartney, and Burberry, according to Onepointfour magazine. She has also collaborated with American rock band Haim, directing the music video for their 2025 single “Relationships”. Outside of fashion and music videos, Summers-Valli directed Big Mountain Diné Bikéyah (2015), a documentary about a remote Navajo community in Northern Arizona.

title: Man arrested for alleged HK$2.8 million Hong Kong school admission scam
description: Authorities say suspect accepted 23 payments from an education consultant in exchange for securing dozens of places at ‘Kiangsu-Chekiang College’.
content:
Police have arrested a man for allegedly defrauding an education consultant out of nearly HK$3 million (US$382,500) by claiming he could secure dozens of places at a Hong Kong school, the South China Morning Post has learned.
A police source said on Monday that the suspect, a 51-year-old Hongkonger who claimed to be a businessman, had signed a contract with a 45-year-old woman working as an education consultant on March 1, 2024, claiming he could provide dozens of places at a “Kiangsu-Chekiang College”.
Believing the claims, the consultant transferred about HK$2.84 million in 23 instalments between April and July 2024 to the man’s mainland Chinese bank account, covering application fees for 37 students, the source added.
He had allegedly promised access to 50 secondary school places at the college, assuring her that her students would also have guaranteed entry into universities in Hong Kong or Macau regardless of their Diploma of Secondary Education results.
But the source said none of the students received admission offers from the school or any other higher education institutions. He subsequently cut off contact, prompting the woman to file a police report in May this year.
Investigators intercepted him at Hong Kong International Airport on July 29 this year as he attempted to leave the city. He was arrested on suspicion of fraud.
There are three secondary schools and one primary school carrying the “Kiangsu‑Chekiang” name in Hong Kong. The three secondary schools are located in Sha Tin, Kwai Chung and North Point.
The one in North Point, Kiangsu-Chekiang College, is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents.
The primary school, the Kiangsu and Chekiang Primary School, is also in North Point.
Kiangsu-Chekiang College in North Point is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents.

title: ‘I just need an answer’: widow haunted by husband’s shooting seeks inquest
description: Two years after her mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li says she cannot forgive herself for calling for help.
content: Two years after her armed, mentally ill husband was fatally shot by a Hong Kong police officer, Mrs Li is still waiting to learn whether a death inquest will be held. On September 15, 2024, she called police when her 38-year-old husband, who had a history of mental illness, attacked his elderly mother and her at their North Point home. Officers wielding shields arrived and found the man holding a 30cm (11.8-inch) knife and a pair of scissors. Little did Mrs Li, who preferred to be identified by her spouse’s surname, expect that the day would end in tragedy. Police said an officer eventually shot the man at a distance of 1.5 metres (4.9 feet) after he allegedly ignored repeated warnings during a 30-second stand-off and attempted to attack them. Now, all she wants is for a death inquest to be held as soon as possible to bring closure to herself and her husband, to whom she had been married for 10 years. “I need no sympathy or pity. I just need an answer and hope to prevent this tragedy from happening again,” she said. “It’s been two years, yet there is still no news. I’m anxious that this matter will just be left unsettled, and my husband’s death went unexplained.” The then commissioner of police Raymond Siu Chak-yee defended the officer’s decision to shoot the man because he followed the guidelines on firearms use. Siu said police would submit a death investigation report to the Coroner’s Court and “recommend the court hold a death inquest as soon as possible”. But Li barely heard anything about it over the past two years. In February last year, she received a letter from a coroner confirming that the cause of death was a gunshot wound to the chest. In early April, she wrote to the court to inquire about a death inquest. In response, the court said police had been instructed to produce a death investigation report, and a decision on whether to hold an inquest would be made after receiving the complete report. Since then, she has called the Coroner’s Court general hotline every month to check on the progress, only to be told: “The investigation is still under way.” On the other hand, she stopped contacting police after the contact person who treated her kindly retired. Only an officer from the Complaints Against Police Office continued to check on her regularly, but declined to reveal details of their investigation. “Every step has been very hard for me … I’m always afraid that something bad will happen to me and no one will be left to follow up on my husband’s case,” she said. “I hope everything can go faster.” In the first few months after her husband’s death, she was unable to eat and sleep well, losing over 20 pounds (9kg) in just one month. Now, she suffers from a failing memory, slowed reaction times and wakes up repeatedly throughout the night. Whenever she has a moment to herself, the memory of her husband covered in blood and surrounded by police after being shot floods back into her mind. “I deeply regret calling police. I made a call, and then he died … I will not forgive myself for the rest of my life,” she said. “My intention was simply to have my husband taken to hospital, as we did before.” She questioned why officers discharged a fatal shot to the chest rather than retreating down the stairwell or deploying non-lethal options such as pepper spray and shields. In response to the South China Morning Post queries, police said they submitted the investigation report to the Coroner’s Court in June 2025. The court requested further information, which was provided this month, and police were waiting for further instructions from the court. As for the complaint filed with police, it is being handled in a “fair and impartial manner in accordance with established procedures”. The judiciary declined to comment on individual cases. It said the coroner would decide whether to hold an inquest after reviewing the report, and police might be directed to conduct further investigations if needed, with the deceased’s next of kin to be updated on the progress and decision on the inquest. Under Practice Direction 39 on coronial procedures, which took effect in June last year, if an investigation is not completed within nine months of the date of the interim report, or if no decision whether to hold an inquest has been made, the court will, where appropriate, update the family every three months on the reasons for the delay – which did not happen in Mrs Li’s case. The guidelines do not set a fixed deadline for supplying supplementary information once a report is submitted. Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a community organiser at the Society for Community Organisation who helped Mrs Li, said he believed that the case would rely on expert assessment of firearms use and police protocols to evaluate whether the officer’s actions were justified. “Without disclosing anything, families are left in this situation – with just one letter on hand and they have to reach out repeatedly in anxiety,” he said. “Even after the report is submitted, it takes time for the pre-inquest [reviews] to be scheduled before the formal hearing; more waiting is anticipated.” Delays of two to three years before a coroner’s inquest opens are not uncommon in Hong Kong, according to lawyer Jonathan Man Ho-ching. Man said police handled death investigations alongside routine work without a dedicated unit, according to his understanding. There are only three designated coroners in Hong Kong handling inquests while performing regular duties such as granting burial and autopsy orders, with their workload further compounded following major disasters such as the Wang Fuk Court fire that claimed 168 lives. The primary recourse for families is to query the Coroner’s Court directly regarding the progress of their case. “Just like any case, the longer a death inquest is delayed, the less ideal it is because witnesses might not be able to remember details, or might simply be unreachable any more, as seen during the Lamma ferry disaster inquests,” Man said. “A wait is often inevitable … which is very hard on families because an inquest allows them to understand what happened to their loved ones, providing closure and helping them move on.” Man said he believed Hong Kong could do better in strengthening communication with bereaved families during these prolonged periods. “In some jurisdictions, death inquiries are not treated purely as a legal procedure; caseworkers are assigned to families to help them navigate the process,” he said.

title: Singapore jails armed Malaysian gang for US$3.9 million ‘lightning heist’ at bungalow
description: The prosecution said the theft at the home, where a woman held high-stakes poker games, was one of the highest-value robberies in Singapore.
content: After learning that a woman regularly hosted high-stakes poker games at her home in Singapore’s affluent Bukit Timah area, two men plotted to rob the house, recruiting a group of people from Malaysia and conducting surveillance before carrying out the plan. Prosecutors said seven men entered the King Albert Park good class bungalow in the early hours of April 18, 2024, in a “lightning heist”, some of them armed with machetes and baseball bats. They tied up the people inside and stole about S$4.9 million (US$3.9 million) in cash, valuables and cryptocurrency. The men then fled Singapore with the loot in two cars, crossing the border into Malaysia through the Tuas and Woodlands checkpoints in what the judge called an “audacious and well-planned” operation disrupting peace and security. Most of the men in the group were subsequently arrested and taken back to Singapore to face prosecution. One man, 33-year-old Malaysian Muhammad Yusuf Kassim, remains at large and is believed to have left Malaysia for Thailand, court documents stated. On Monday, the six Malaysian men pleaded guilty to various charges, including armed gang robbery and removing criminal benefits from jurisdiction. They were sentenced to jail terms of between seven years and eight months and 12 years and 11 months, along with 24 strokes of the cane for those aged below 50. They are: Wong Chi Shan, 35; Goh Boon Tong, 30; Mohd Hamidon Ahmed, 49; Kartik Palaniappan, 34; Mohd Hashim Ismail, 51 and Muhammad Tauffiq Ahmad Fauzi, 34. The prosecution said this was one of the highest-value robberies in Singapore, if not the highest, in nominal terms. A gold bar case in the 1970s would be higher if inflation were accounted for. In November 2023, Wong and Goh learned that high-stakes poker games were being held at a house in the King Albert Park area, where many landed properties and good class bungalows are located. They knew someone who had taken part in the games, court documents stated. The games involved stakes of up to a few hundred thousand dollars, with payments settled using cryptocurrency, the court heard. Wong and Goh visited the house and observed that the gate was left open and the wooden door unlocked during the poker game. Several months later, in March or April 2024, Wong suggested robbing the house. But he and Goh knew they would need more people to carry out the plan. Goh approached Hamidon, whom he had met at an event where Hamidon had provided private security. Hamidon ran his own private security firm as well as debt-collection services. Wong and Goh met Hamidon to discuss the operation. Hamidon was to recruit men to intimidate and subdue the victims in exchange for 1.5 million ringgit (US$368,515), which would be split among his team. Hamidon obtained a deposit of 10,000 ringgit before recruiting the others. He did not initially tell them the details of the operation but they knew it involved illegal activity. Wong and Goh decided the robbers would wear black clothing, gloves and ski masks. On April 15, 2024, Wong drove into Singapore via Woodlands Checkpoint and checked into a hotel. However, despite a poker game ongoing at the house, Hamidon’s team was not ready and the robbery did not take place. Meanwhile, Hamidon’s team prepared themselves with black clothing, ski masks, gloves, duct tape and cable ties. The following day, Wong and Goh drove past the house but found that no poker game was taking place. They instructed Hamidon’s team to remain in Johor Bahru, Malaysia. The next night, however, a poker game was in progress. Goh and Wong instructed Hamidon to meet them at a car park in Geylang. Hamidon and his team entered Singapore through Woodlands Checkpoint in a vehicle at about 10.45pm on April 17. They met Wong and Goh at the car park, where they were shown photographs of the house and briefed on how to enter it. Machetes and baseball bats were placed in Hamidon’s vehicle. Before 2.05am on April 18, 2024, the seven men drove to the house and parked outside. Three of them were armed with machetes, while two carried baseball bats. The men entered through the unlocked gate and main door while the poker game was still taking place. Those in the house were: Li Xiaoyu, a Chinese national and the hostess of the game. Li Yang, her husband who was a tenant at the house. Hu Zhi Peng, a Chinese national who stayed at the house and helped Li with organising the poker game. Mo Ran, a South Korean woman hired as a card dealer. Yap Kian Yeap, a Malaysian hired to provide massages during the poker game.
