Seven poker players: Indonesian Andrew Halim, Chinese national Liu Yi and Singaporeans Macus Yap Jin Xin, Ceesvin Abraham Abdulla, Lim Yah Loon, Hoo Teng Yang and Ho Bao Qiang. The robbers first encountered Hu, who had just exited the toilet near the main door. They pointed a machete at him and taped his mouth, wrists and ankles before telling him to sit in the toilet. The robbers then moved into the living room and ordered the victims to put their hands in the air, lower their heads and place their phones on a table. The victims complied. They were tied up and had their mouths taped while the robbers searched the house for valuables. Goh and Wong checked the victims’ phones for cryptocurrency applications and discovered sizeable amounts of cryptocurrency in the hostess’ phone apps. The group carried out cryptocurrency transfers to a wallet they controlled, emptied cash from a safe in the living room and ransacked a bedroom. In total, this is what they took: From Li: S$210,000 in cash, about US$40,000 in cash, S$55,500 worth of Emirati dirhams, about S$3.6 million in cryptocurrency and a Patek Philippe watch worth more than S$500,000. From Abdulla: S$1,300 in cash and one Rolex watch worth S$55,000. From Hoo: S$3,000 in cash and one Rolex watch worth S$55,300. From Macus Yap: A Samsung Galaxy smartwatch worth S$452. From Yap Kian Yeap: A Huawei watch worth S$400 and S$1,000 in cash. From Ho: A Richard Mille watch worth S$320,000 and a Ferrari car key worth S$1,000. ‘Audacious’ armed gang robbery The seven men then left in their vehicle for another location where they split up from Goh and Wong. As part of their escape plan, Wong and Goh left in their car via Tuas Checkpoint at about 2.15am while the rest left via Woodlands Checkpoint in a second vehicle at about 2.40am. They arranged to regroup in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. They discarded the weapons and clothing used in the robbery along the way. Meanwhile, the victims managed to free themselves and called the police. They sustained minor injuries from being bound. Goh and Wong drove to Kuala Lumpur that same day, where Wong transferred about 1.1 million USDT to Goh as his share of the loot. USD Tether is a cryptocurrency pegged to the US dollar. Goh and Wong managed to find buyers for their coins while in Kuala Lumpur, receiving 1.49 million ringgit in cash for an unspecified amount of USDT. They handed the cash over to Hamidon and Yusuf in Kuala Lumpur as the remaining payment to Hamidon’s team in exchange for the stolen cash and valuables. Hamidon and Yusuf gave 100,000 ringgit to two friends in Malaysia who had helped to coordinate their activities. Hamidon kept 445,000 ringgit, while Tauffiq, Hashim and Kartik each received 100,000 ringgit. Yusuf kept 645,000 ringgit, of which his share was to be 245,000 ringgit. He claimed that he would safely keep the remainder for the team. The six Malaysian robbers were arrested in Malaysia by the Royal Malaysian Police between April 2024 and November 2024. Tauffiq was caught before he boarded a flight to Kota Kinabalu, while Goh was arrested at the airport before getting on to a plane for Japan. Of the S$4.9 million stolen, the Singapore Police Force managed to recover only about S$1.69 million. About S$3.21 million has been lost, lead prosecutor Dillon Kok said. Wong and Goh also pleaded guilty to other charges involving sex work by Japanese women. Kok sought various jail terms for the six men according to their relative culpability, with Wong and Goh pegged at the highest culpability. The jail terms sought by the prosecution range from the lower end of seven years and eight months to 13 years and one month, with 24 strokes of the cane. Wong was represented by Don Tan, while Goh was represented by Thangavelu, Tan Jun Yin and Sugenya Manogaran. James Gomez Jovan Messiah defended Kartik, while Ariffin Sha represented Hashim. Estelle Tai represented Tauffiq, while SS Dhillon acted for Hamidon. Gomez and Ariffin said their clients received only 100,000 ringgit each, while Tai said her client was largely kept in the dark about details of the robbery. Tan said no injuries were caused in the robbery. Dhillon said his client Hamidon was turning 50 in the coming months but did not cause any undue delay in the matter going to court to avoid caning. He said Hamidon had refused to prepare weapons for the robbery, instead preparing duct tape and cable ties. He was not armed at all during the robbery, the lawyer said. Sugenya said Goh helped authorities recover about 800,000 USDT out of the 1.1 million USDT he received, which she called a substantial recovery. In sentencing, Justice Aidan Xu said this was an “audacious and well-planned” armed gang robbery “which has disrupted the peace and security”. He said the sentence must deter any future such attempts and punish those involved. Justice Xu said Singapore is by and large a safe country, thanks to the efforts of law enforcement agencies and members of the public. “We expect our homes to be secure … those who disturb that peace and security … can only expect to be treated severely,” he said. Wong and Goh were each sentenced to 12 years and 11 months’ jail, 24 strokes of the cane and a fine of S$4,000. Hamidon was jailed for 10½ years and given 24 strokes of the cane, while Kartik and Tauffiq received seven years and eight months’ jail and 24 strokes of the cane. Hashim, who cannot be caned due to his age, was sentenced to eight years and eight months’ jail. For armed gang robbery, an offender can be jailed for between five and 20 years and is liable to 24 strokes of the cane. The Attorney General’s Chambers has been contacted about whether any action has been taken against the victims for illegal gambling. This story was first published by CNA

title: China’s economy under further pressure in August, as analysts expect rebound next quarter
description: The drop in overall fixed-asset investment widened last month, as retail sales grew 0.4 per cent year on year.
content: China’s economy came under further pressure in August, as sluggish investment and consumption highlighted persistently weak domestic demand, although analysts expect a rebound in the fourth quarter as state intervention begins to take effect. Retail sales, a major gauge of consumer spending, grew last month by 0.4 per cent year on year, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Tuesday. The reading was lower than a 0.73 per cent rise forecast by economists surveyed by Chinese financial data provider Wind, and was down from the 0.6 per cent increase in July. Overall fixed-asset investment – covering major areas such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction – fell by 7.2 per cent in the January-August period, year on year, largely in line with a Wind forecast of a 7.19 per cent decline. The drop widened from the 6.7 per cent decline recorded in the first seven months of 2026. Industrial output, meanwhile, grew by 5.2 per cent in August, up from the 4.5 per cent increase seen in the previous month. Ding Shuang, chief economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered, said economic conditions marginally improved from July to August. “If the current improvement continues, and proceeds from government bond issuance are fully deployed alongside sustained and faster fiscal spending, the economy is likely to perform better in the fourth quarter than in the third,” Ding said. “On this basis, we maintain our full-year growth forecast at 4.6 per cent.” The country’s economy has experienced a prolonged imbalance, with resilient exports supporting industrial activity while weak consumption and investment, coupled with a prolonged property downturn and labour market pressures, weigh on domestic demand. Economic growth slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, down from 5 per cent in the first, marking the slowest quarterly expansion since late 2022. Wang Guanhua, spokeswoman for the NBS, said that investment had been hindered by this year’s adverse weather, as well as companies adopting a more cautious approach as the economy transitioned towards new growth drivers. She noted that investment had shifted from a focus on scaled expansion to technological innovation, and that the roll-out of local government special-purpose bonds was accelerating. China’s top economic planner, the National Development and Reform Commission, has held a series of meetings in the past month calling to speed up major construction projects and accelerate the disbursement of fiscal funds to boost investment. Xu Tianchen, an economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the August data was perhaps a mark of an “intra-year bottom” for China’s economy, with growth likely to rebound in September as stronger government support for public investment began to take effect. “The impact on investment should start to emerge in September and become more visible in the fourth quarter,” Xu said, adding that a favourable base effect would also support growth. “I do not think additional stimulus is necessary, as the full-year growth target of 4.5 to 5 per cent remains within reach.” Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said China’s economy remained uneven, with resilient industrial production contrasting with rising unemployment and weak consumption and investment. “So far, there is no clear sign of stronger fiscal spending yet,” Zhang said. “The economy faces downside risks in the third quarter, as fiscal support takes time to be implemented and transmitted to the economy.” Property investment, a persistent drag on economic growth, fell 19.9 per cent in the first eight months of the year, compared with a 19.2 per cent decline between January and July. Sales of new homes by floor area contracted by 12.1 per cent between January and August, following an 11.8 per cent drop in the first seven months. China’s surveyed urban unemployment rate stood at 5.3 per cent in August, compared with 5.2 per cent in July. Zhang Yuhan, principal economist at the Conference Board’s China Centre, said the August data suggested China was becoming increasingly reliant on technological upgrades, productivity gains and overseas demand to absorb its expanding industrial capacity, as domestic consumption and investment remained weak. “China’s domestic slowdown and the globalisation of Chinese industrial capacity are increasingly two sides of the same story – with potentially important implications for outbound investment, trade relations and manufacturing competition globally,” Zhang said.

title: Philippine VP’s impeachment trial heats up as unexplained wealth takes centre stage
description: Prosecutors have so far tried to prove that Sara Duterte-Carpio’s office could not properly account for millions of pesos in confidential funds.
content: Philippine Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio’s impeachment trial entered a politically explosive new phase on Monday as prosecutors turned to allegations of unexplained wealth in proceedings that could end her term and bar her from a possible presidential run in 2028. The Senate hearing opened its 24th day with congressmen serving as House prosecutors beginning to tackle the third of four impeachment charges against Duterte-Carpio, whose legal troubles have intensified alongside her increasingly bitter feud with President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Once Marcos’ running mate in the 2022 election, Duterte-Carpio is now one of his fiercest critics, accusing him of corruption and political persecution as she fights both the impeachment case and a separate criminal charge. On Friday, Duterte-Carpio was due to be arraigned before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on charges of issuing grave threats against Marcos, his wife and his cousin – allegations that also form part of one of the impeachment charges against her. The court agreed to defer the arraignment after she filed a motion seeking a delay. The vice-president then called on Marcos to resign, accusing him of corruption and of using his power to politically persecute her and her family. “I cannot bring myself to just stay silent while I see you swimming through floods. Because I see you struggling so hard for your families. Because I witnessed the abuse of Marcos with my very own eyes,” Duterte-Carpio told supporters outside the court. “Remember to keep calling for the departure of our nation’s problem, whose name is Bongbong Marcos. Resign, get out of there. You are a liar, you are abusive, you are corrupt.” Asked about Duterte-Carpio’s remarks by reporters accompanying him to India for the Brics summit, Marcos brushed them aside. “You know, I hear about them, but I don’t really even have a response. If she feels very angry, I suppose, with what’s happening to her. And I am the target of that anger, or the main target of that anger. What can I do? You cannot force anyone to love you,” Marcos said, drawing laughter. On whether Marcos played a role in Duterte-Carpio’s recent legal and political troubles, observers told This Week in Asia that the question could not be separated from the evidence being presented against her. “Well, he may have something to do with it,” said Dr Jean Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines. “But it can still be true that there is enough evidence to charge her with grave threats and to impeach her and try her in the Senate. Both can be true. They are not mutually exclusive.” Barry Gutierrez, a professor of criminal law at the University of the Philippines College of Law, said public reaction would depend heavily on political loyalties, with pro-Duterte supporters likely to “scream persecution and constitutional violation”, while those backing conviction would welcome it. For those still undecided, “if there are truly any left”, Gutierrez said the response would probably depend on the final legal basis and explanation. “Of course, he is responsible and to blame,” said lawyer Vic Rodriguez, Marcos’ former chief presidential aide who is now a close ally of Duterte-Carpio. Even if others were doing the “thinking, planning and execution” for Marcos, Rodriguez said, “the buck stops with him”. The prosecution has spent much of the trial trying to show that Duterte-Carpio’s office and the Department of Education, which she headed from 2022 to 2024, could not properly account for hundreds of millions of pesos in confidential funds – money meant for sensitive security and intelligence-related spending. The alleged irregularities included military certifications that officers said were used to justify fund liquidations even though their units had not received any money, and cash payments allegedly channelled through Colonel Raymund Lachica, then commander of the Vice-Presidential Security and Protection Group. Philippine Statistics Authority assistant national statistician Marizza Grande testified on September 7 that of 2,669 “acknowledgment receipts” Lachica and his team had gathered from recipients of the confidential funds as proof of payment, 1,685 lacked birth, marriage or death records. At least 152 names showed up in the Civil Registration Service database, including 37 people who were already dead before they supposedly received payments, and 25 children. The youngest was Miko Alquizar, who was six months old when a receipt for 400,000 pesos was signed by someone bearing the same name. The defence maintained that the names used were aliases to protect whistle-blowers. Analysts say the next procedural battle will focus on the number of votes needed to convict Duterte-Carpio. Under the usual reading, Duterte-Carpio will be removed only if two thirds of the 24-member Senate, or 16 senator-judges, vote to convict her. But some senators have been absent or unable to participate because of criminal cases, an Ombudsman investigation, medical leave or, in the case of Senator Ronald Dela Rosa, an International Criminal Court arrest warrant. Gutierrez said the impeachment court had cause to review the threshold because “the circumstances of the current Senate are unprecedented, with four senators out and unable to participate, with possibly more to follow”. “That alone should be sufficient context to open the conversation,” he said. But Rodriguez warned that Duterte-Carpio’s camp would view any attempt to lower the required number of votes for conviction as “yet another legal anomaly”. With public anger already building over the flood-control scandal, other controversies and the worsening economy, “BBM is courting disaster,” Rodriguez said, referring to Marcos by his initials. Franco predicted that any such move “will divide the public. The important thing is that any decision on this will be perceived as impartial and legitimate”. While the case against Duterte-Carpio could have enough legal basis to convict her, Franco said “it can also be true that [the family’s] enemies are using these cases to politically disempower them”.

title: Style Edit: Tudor expands the Ranger collection and brings back the Northflag
description: Tracing its roots to 1929, the Ranger welcomes a compact 36mm option and a new ‘Dune white’ dial, while the Northflag returns in a 40mm iteration.
content: Few watchmakers have exploration so deeply woven into their history as Tudor. Its connection to adventure dates back to the 1950s, when Tudor watches accompanied the British North Greenland Expedition into one of the world’s most unforgiving environments. Decades later, that spirit of utility continues to inform Tudor’s approach to the modern tool watch, most recently through the expanded Ranger collection and the return of the Northflag. The Ranger traces its roots to a name registered by Hans Wilsdorf, founder of Rolex and Tudor, in 1929. Its defining visual language has remained remarkably consistent: a clean dial punctuated by oversized Arabic numerals at 3, 6, 9 and 12, designed for instant legibility. The contemporary collection refines that utilitarian formula without stripping away its character. Available in the existing 39mm and the new compact 36mm satin-brushed steel cases, the Ranger has an easy versatility that allows it to move between expedition-ready practicality and understated everyday wear. The “Dune white” dial brings a warmer interpretation to the collection, its softly domed surface adding a touch of character to the otherwise restrained design. The watch can be paired with a three-link steel bracelet fitted with Tudor’s T-fit clasp, which allows for on-the-wrist adjustment, or a Jacquard fabric strap produced by French artisans. Inside, the Manufacture Calibre MT5400 or MT5402 delivers COSC-certified performance and a 70-hour power reserve, underscoring the Ranger’s fundamental appeal: simplicity backed by serious mechanical credentials. The Northflag takes that philosophy in a more technical direction. Originally introduced in 2015 and now resurrected, the watch draws on the architecture of the 1973 Ranger II, translating its angular, functional aesthetic into a contemporary 40mm steel case with an integrated bracelet. A central GMT hand and 24-hour scale set into the angled rehaut give the Northflag a distinctly exploratory character, while also making it a practical companion for crossing time zones. Its most significant evolution, however, is mechanical. Beneath an open sapphire caseback sits Tudor’s Manufacture Calibre MT5652-U, certified as both a COSC chronometer and a METAS Master Chronometer. The movement is rated to an impressive 0/+5 seconds per day and offers resistance to magnetic fields of up to 15,000 gauss. A 65-hour power reserve and monobloc luminous ceramic hour markers complete the specification. Together, the Ranger and Northflag reveal two sides of Tudor’s expedition legacy. One distils the tool watch to its most considered essentials; the other pushes the same philosophy deeper into contemporary movement technology. Both demonstrate how a history born in the harshest environments can still shape what a modern adventure watch looks – and performs – like today.

title: Style Edit: Furla unveils Rome-inspired fall/winter 2026 collection and new Macau boutique
description: Blending Italian elegance with rich seasonal hues, designs like the Ginevra, Tonie and Iride take centre stage at Furla’s store inside The Venetian Macao.
content: There is a particular kind of Italian confidence that favours a beautifully engineered bag and the ability to keep everything else uncomplicated. Furla channels that panache in its fall/winter 2026 collection, drawing on Rome’s cinematic heritage while keeping its accessories grounded in the rhythm of contemporary life. The season is imagined as a long weekend in the Eternal City – perhaps a succession of coffee stops, leisurely lunches, gallery visits and evening invitations – each framed by a bag that becomes more of a characterful finishing touch instead of a status symbol. The palette borrows from wildflowers, then deepens for the cooler months into dark forest, winter bloom, chocolate and cherry, punctuated by red apple and rose-gold hardware. It is a rich but wearable range, aimed at women who value both colour and nuance. Among the stand-out silhouettes is the Ginevra, a generously proportioned, soft-leather shoulder bag with the relaxed, slightly slouchy attitude favoured by those who want their holdall to look as nonchalant as it is useful. Adjustable straps and arched buckles allow it to move from shoulder to crossbody, while its unfussy interior features a spacious compartment and an internal zip pocket. The Tonie takes a more tactile route. Available in soft textured leather, teddy fabric and velvet craquelé, it has detachable straps that shift its mood from practical crossbody to compact handheld piece. Meanwhile, the Iride brings a little evening drama: its diamond-cut Arch hardware catches the light, while new patent-leather and velvet finishes arrive in party-ready black, red apple, gold and winter bloom. Those looking to see the collection in situ can now do so at Furla’s new boutique at Shoppes at The Venetian Macao. Spanning more than 75 square metres, the space reflects the label’s increasingly polished retail direction, with lacquered surfaces, natural oak, glossy tiles and light gold accents set against white, ivory, burgundy and aqua green. The boutique features dedicated zones for handbags, charms, eyewear, textiles and small leather goods, alongside a magnetic display system to spotlight new arrivals. Warm lighting, tactile finishes and enough visual breathing room make browsing feel like part of the pleasure. It is a fittingly modern setting for a brand founded in Bologna in 1927, and one that makes accessories designed to go everywhere.

title: Opinion | Why Hong Kong’s economic future still hinges on national security
description: Whether under British rule or modern superpower competition, Hong Kong’s value as a strategic gateway makes it a vital security asset.
content: In any conversation about Hong Kong’s future, one question often emerges: when will the city pivot away from national security and back to economic development? To most, Hong Kong is fundamentally a commercial hub. After the turmoil of 2019, most reasonable people agreed that restoring public order was imperative. Today, the orchestrators of that unrest and the radicals are largely imprisoned or have fled. While occasional flare-ups and various forms of “soft resistance” persist, society at large appears to have reclaimed its traditional pragmatism. Few doubt that national security laws are here to stay, yet many wonder whether it’s time to turn the page and refocus on economic growth. As a journalist, I work in one of the most affected industries and this question is constantly on my mind. I have come to a conclusion that may sound counterintuitive, if not sacrilegious, coming from a media professional: national security will always remain a top policy priority for Hong Kong. It is not a handicap undermining our commercial interests; rather, our economic future depends entirely on our ability to manage these concerns to the nation’s satisfaction. Any sober examination of the facts, framed by current geopolitical realities, makes this conclusion inescapable. Hong Kong’s strategic position has always been dictated by national security considerations. When Great Britain took the territory by force from China in 1842, it was not seeking natural resources, but a protected gateway to a vast Chinese market and a naval stronghold for the Royal Navy. Admiral John Fisher, architect of Britain’s global maritime strategy, notably served at the naval headquarters here. The British colonised Hong Kong specifically to serve the security needs of the British Empire. Immediately after a modern China emerged from the chaos of World War II and a civil war in 1949, it entered a period of diplomatic isolation and internal upheaval. Yet a nation of that scale could not remain entirely severed from the world. Both China and the Western world needed a communication channel. Hong Kong served as the vital umbilical cord, facilitating flows of capital, intelligence, and people – legally or otherwise. To monitor and control these movements, London established the Special Branch in Hong Kong in 1933 – a formidable security apparatus operating with unchecked authority to gather political intelligence and neutralise threats to colonial rule. London disbanded the Special Branch just two years before the 1997 handover. Beijing, fully recognising the historical imperative of maintaining a safety valve, insisted on making Article 23 a constitutional obligation. Yet many of us embraced the idealised narrative of Hong Kong as merely a “free, business-first city”, treating security affairs as an unnecessary burden. This ignored the fundamental reality of the city’s origins. While colonial administrators preferred to withhold security deliberations from the colonised public, Beijing expected Hong Kong to exercise self-governance by proactively managing these risks. The failure to grasp this mandate proved costly to us. Today, we live in a world defined by intense China-US rivalry. During the transitional decades following the handover, Washington and Beijing maintained a complex but cooperative economic baseline. That dynamic has shifted dramatically. The United States now views China’s rise as a direct challenge to its global standing that must be contained. Washington is turning to its dominance over international financial and technological networks to achieve that goal. If the city is perceived as a point of vulnerability in this era of geopolitical competition, strategic opportunities will inevitably move elsewhere In response, while China leverages its strength in supply chains and critical materials, it is also focused on building resilient alternative systems to mitigate potential vulnerabilities. This structural shift presents Hong Kong with its greatest commercial opportunity. The city is uniquely positioned to help construct these alternative financial and technological ecosystems – serving as a premier offshore yuan hub, a wealth management centre for Chinese companies, the primary IPO market for Chinese tech firms, and an innovation nexus connecting mainland China with emerging global markets, particularly the belt and road economies. Capitalising on this opportunity requires a stable, highly secure environment. Hong Kong is simultaneously an economic bridge and a battleground for global financial and technological competition, drawing intense interest as it develops new financial technologies and cross-border settlement mechanisms. For instance, in February 2026, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that China might use Hong Kong’s large financial testing environment to launch gold-backed digital assets that could rival the US dollar. He vowed to closely monitor these sandbox experiments. Hong Kong offers distinct advantages in building these new infrastructures for China, but it is not without competition. Domestic financial centres like Shanghai and Shenzhen, as well as regional peers like Singapore, remain possible alternatives to Beijing. The more effectively Hong Kong addresses national security imperatives, the greater latitude it retains to experiment with novel financial frameworks and access mainland capital, technology and talent. If the city is perceived as a point of vulnerability in this era of geopolitical competition, strategic opportunities will inevitably move elsewhere. National security is not a distraction from Hong Kong’s business – it is the baseline upon which its business depends.

title: Chinese students ‘eating homework’ to relieve exam stress draws amused public reactions
description: For some children, consuming the very assignments that weigh them down offers a playful way to ease crushing academic pressure.
content: Children in China are embracing the trend of consuming “homework” made from rice paper as a way to alleviate their heavy study burdens, raising concerns regarding food safety. Recently, a snack called “homework” has gained viral popularity among primary and secondary school students. These snacks resemble miniature versions of Chinese textbooks and workbooks, but they are marketed as entirely edible. On China’s e-commerce platforms, these edible workbooks are priced at less than 0.50 yuan (7.5 US cents) each. Packaging often features promotional slogans such as “stress reducer.” Some online retailers even claim that these snacks can help “improve academic grades.” Inside each package is a thin piece of rice paper decorated with images of textbooks, dictionaries, certificates of merit, and occasionally, a bank card, which one shop explained is a representation of a scholarship card. The advertised benefits of these edible workbooks evoke memories of a well-known gadget from the anime series Doraemon, known as Memory Bread or Copying Toast. Doraemon is a robotic cat featured in a popular Japanese manga and anime. In the series, pressing this magical bread onto a textbook transfers the text onto it, allowing anyone who consumes it to instantly memorise the content. Historically, ancient China also held the belief that ingesting ink could enhance writing and calligraphy skills On online product listings, many parents leave comments noting that their children demanded these snacks after seeing them featured in social media videos. One person claimed that by eating the rice paper homework, their child would “become smart.” Another parent remarked that the snack’s main ingredient, starch, is “healthier than other snacks.” Some children also reported feeling their heavy academic pressure ease by consuming the homework that weighs them down. However, concerns have been raised by the state media outlet China National Radio regarding the food colouring used to print the textbooks, which may not conform to national food safety standards. These national standards prohibit the use of food colouring in starch products but allow it in candies. One manufacturer of these textbook snacks, however, asserted that they “produced them as candies.” Dr He Sijun, affiliated with the Mindong Hospital at Fujian Medical University, stated to the SCMP that rice paper and food-grade colouring are safe. However, if industrial colouring is used, it could potentially harm children’s liver and kidney functions. He advised parents to limit their children’s consumption of inexpensive snacks. As the autumn school term begins in China, market regulatory authorities in some regions have conducted special inspections of convenience stores, snack shops, and stationery outlets around schools, urging merchants not to sell these snacks.

title: Japanese delegations flock to China, but thaw hinges on Takaichi mending ties
description: Visits by Japanese lawmakers and business groups aim to ease ties ahead of Apec summit, but experts say Tokyo must send clearer signal.
content: With bilateral ties in a deep freeze since late last year, a flurry of planned China visits by Japanese lawmakers and business leaders has been interpreted as an attempt to break the ice ahead of November’s Apec summit in China. However, analysts warned that these efforts to carve out a diplomatic opening with Beijing might not achieve much unless Tokyo sends a clearer signal to mend ties from the very top. Relations reached their lowest point in a decade following Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks last November that a Taiwan contingency could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence. An eight-member cross-party delegation of junior lawmakers led by the Liberal Democratic Party’s Masahiro Takamura is visiting Beijing this week. Meanwhile, Keidanren – Japan’s largest business lobby – and the Osaka-based Kansai Economic Federation are also planning China trips in the coming months. Later this month, former Japanese foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya will lead a high-profile delegation from the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade, which is seeking to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping. These efforts are not going to lead to much unless there is a clear message from the very top – that is, the prime minister or her cabinet – to make proactive efforts to mend ties Rintaro Nishimura, senior associate at The Asia Group Rintaro Nishimura, a senior associate at The Asia Group strategic advisory firm, noted that Beijing probably viewed progress as requiring clearer signals from Japan’s top leadership. “These efforts are not going to lead to much unless there is a clear message from the very top – that is, the prime minister or her cabinet – to make proactive efforts to mend ties,” he said. “Diet members and business delegations seem to be trying to create that opening, but Beijing is also drawing a clear line between the Japanese government and other actors.” “These successive visits are largely intended to lay the groundwork and break the ice for a potential meeting between Takaichi and Xi in November,” said Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University. Takaichi is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen in mid-November, but whether she will secure a meeting with Xi remains uncertain. Wang said he was sceptical about the effectiveness of the business and lawmaker visits given the depth of deterioration in China-Japan relations and the gravity of what he called Takaichi’s “erroneous remarks” on Taiwan. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Wang added that it was unclear whether these delegations had received a mandate from Takaichi or her cabinet, or whether the prime minister even wanted them to visit China now. The fragile limits of parliamentary diplomacy were exposed in late August when a group of Japanese lawmakers met Lu Kang, vice-minister of the Communist Party’s International Department. According to a statement from the department, Lu told the delegation that history and Taiwan were at the centre of tensions between the two nations, and Tokyo needed to take “concrete actions” to improve ties. Lu added that he hoped Japanese politicians could urge their leadership to learn from history and handle the issue “honestly and faithfully in accordance with the one-China principle”. Toru Horiuchi, a China-Japan relations expert at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, noted that while these visits helped keep communication channels open, Japanese lawmakers “have not been able to meet with anybody in the Chinese leadership, and business delegations so far have been rather small”. He suggested watching who from the Chinese side would meet the delegation led by Iwaya – who is viewed as more China-friendly – as a potential sign of Beijing’s willingness to accept greater political contact with Japan. “China still demands that Takaichi retract her remark on Taiwan and continues to put pressure on Japan,” Horiuchi said. “So as long as Japan does not compromise in some way, a major breakthrough is unlikely.” During the 2014 Apec summit in Beijing, Shinzo Abe, Japanese prime minister at the time, had an ice-breaking meeting with Xi following a two-year freeze triggered by territorial disputes and Abe’s visit to the Yasukuni Shrine. Before that meeting, former prime minister Yasuo Fukuda went to China on a “secret mission” to ease a rapprochement and deliver Abe’s request for dialogue. But Wang said a similar breakthrough was out of reach today because the current rift was centred on Taiwan – a “red line” on which Beijing allows no compromise. “Both sides lack intermediaries with sufficient political capital and a foundation of mutual trust,” he added. According to observers, a deeper structural problem compounds the difficulties facing Beijing-Tokyo ties: a generation gap in Japan’s vital conduits to China. Older politicians such as Yohei Kono – who died in June – and Toshihiro Nikai previously wielded considerable influence within the Liberal Democratic Party and maintained long-standing trust with Chinese counterparts. The LDP’s former junior coalition partner Komeito, which positions itself as a party of peace and acted as a bridge between China and Japan, is no longer in government. “The major problem we’re facing now is that as this cohort of older-generation ‘China-knowledgeable’ politicians collectively exits the political stage, the younger generation has not done a good job in maintaining continuity in communication channels,” said Wang of Fudan University, describing it as an “alarming gap”. Nishimura noted that Japanese politicians today faced mounting domestic pressure that made China engagement politically perilous. “With sentiment towards China souring in Japan, it is becoming increasingly challenging for lawmakers to visit China or engage with Chinese stakeholders without being seen as ‘too cosy’ with Beijing or under Beijing’s influence.” He said this perception carried huge political costs, potentially damaging their standing within the LDP and alienating voters. “The recent acceptance of business and Diet member delegations suggests that Beijing is keen to gauge how Tokyo is thinking about China engagement and to encourage these delegations to communicate back to Tokyo that it needs to make efforts to re-engage Beijing, not the other way around,” he said.

title: Mitch McConnell returns to US Senate after lengthy health absence
description: Frail-looking 84-year-old Republican returns in a wheelchair following his June hospitalisation.
content: Republican Senator Mitch McConnell returned to the Capitol on ⁠Monday after a three-month absence spent recuperating from a fall ⁠in his Washington home that had raised questions about his fitness to serve in Congress. “I must admit. After two years of – decades, actually – dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today. But I’m glad ‌to see you. Time to get back to work, finish the job for this Congress,” the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican told reporters from a wheelchair outside the Senate chamber. Looking frail and speaking in a voice that sometimes faltered, McConnell said he was determined to work to pass new farm legislation, aid US relations with Nato and counter Russian aggression in ⁠Ukraine. He ignored a reporter who asked if he intended to serve out the remainder of ‌his Senate term, which ends in January. He then entered the chamber to vote for a Republican judicial nominee. A long-time Republican Party leader who ‌in 2025 announced his plan to retire from the Senate after the 2026 midterms, McConnell ⁠had been out ⁠of public view since mid-June, when he was taken from his home to a hospital in the Washington area for ‌reasons that went undisclosed for weeks. McConnell later said he suffered a fall that left him briefly unconscious. While hospitalised, he ‌developed ‌pneumonia and was treated with antibiotics, according to a separate statement that McConnell’s office attributed to ‌the attending physician. He was released from a rehabilitation centre in early August. The episode marked the ⁠latest in a series of health problems that have raised concerns about McConnell’s capacity to serve ⁠in the Senate, an institution long known for the advanced age of its members. The median age is just under 65 for the current Senate and just under 58 ‌for the House of ‌Representatives, according to Pew Research Centre. Speculation about his condition grew so intense at one point that Kentucky’s Democratic Governor Andy Beshear took the extraordinary step of issuing a public letter asking McConnell to update the public in a “transparent manner”. Earlier on Monday, McConnell issued a statement acknowledging that he was “not quite back to 100%” but adding that he had assured Senate Majority Leader John Thune that he would “do my best to be present for tough votes”. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong’s next policy address is just around the corner. Here’s what to expect
description: Sources say measures supporting Northern Metropolis and backing innovation are expected to be major highlights of John Lee’s policy address.
content: Hong Kong leader John Lee Ka-chiu’s coming policy address will introduce measures to remove hurdles for businesses setting up shop in the Northern Metropolis and include proactive initiatives to strengthen innovation hubs, research efforts and tech applications, the South China Morning Post has learned. Government sources said measures supporting the megaproject in the northern New Territories and backing innovation were expected to be major highlights of the chief executive’s policy address on Wednesday – the same day he will unveil the city’s first five-year plan. The SCMP also learned that Lee’s coming speech would last no more than three hours and be equally split between the five-year plan and the policy address. The five-year plan is expected to include aspirational and binding key performance indicators and goals. The latter will cover concrete targets for both the incumbent and future administrations. “The new policy address will feature a number of deregulation and streamlining measures,” one insider said. “The government will further streamline development procedures and facilitate business operations, including relaxing rules in various commercial and operational sectors to unlock market vitality.” The source said that, given the Northern Metropolis was considered a key testing ground, authorities were determined to remove red tape and scrap certain rules to help speed things up. But he added that the government would also work to safeguard urban planning, environmental protection and safety measures. A second source said streamlining the process for obtaining approvals from various departments during construction was one direction. “Cutting time means cutting costs for companies,” the insider said. The planned megaproject includes several innovation hubs and a university town, comprises 30,000 hectares (74,132 acres) and aims to diversify the economy through technology. It is also expected to create more demand for skilled jobs and learning opportunities for young people, while offering larger homes for a better quality of life. A third insider said that more details, including the fixed sizes of land plots for the three university town areas and the latest timeline for completing various infrastructure projects, such as new rail lines, would be covered in the policy address. The insider added that authorities were expected to increase the number of research postgraduate and doctoral places funded by the University Grants Committee, to help support local universities’ expansion into the Northern Metropolis. The first source also said Lee would announce more proactive policies to boost industrial development, reinforcing the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou innovation cluster’s status as a world-leading hub. Last week, the World Intellectual Property Organisation ranked the cluster first globally. The source also touched on how Hong Kong planned to develop synergy among three of its own innovation parks, as well as fostering collaboration among five other research and development (R&D) institutes to expand the city’s research capabilities. “The three major innovation and technology hubs will form a ‘North-Central-South’ spatial strategy, centred on the Hetao Hong Kong Park in the north, the Hong Kong Science Park system in the middle and Cyberport in the south,” the source said. “Building on existing research capabilities, the five major R&D institutes will further strategically expand into key domains such as microelectronics, artificial intelligence, and life and health sciences, forming an integrated ecosystem spanning education, technology, talent, industry and capital.” The five institutes are the Hong Kong Productivity Council, the Hong Kong Applied Science and Technology Research Institute, the Hong Kong Microelectronics Research and Development Institute, the Hong Kong Artificial Intelligence Research and Development Institute, and the Life and Health Technology Research Institute. The second source said one option for authorities was to invite smaller companies, local universities and organisations from mainland China and the rest of the world to take part in projects at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, the site of the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park. Such a move could nurture ideas and attract talent, help to sustain the integrated research ecosystem, the source said. The first source also said the government had plans to use artificial intelligence (AI) to develop Hong Kong society. “But authorities will attach great importance to the safety, ethics and responsibilities involved when using AI,” the insider said. The source added that the government would integrate the technology’s usage across various policy areas such as tourism, welfare, finance and legal services, while introducing the use of robots to communities. The third insider said authorities would also consider enacting legislation to combat cyber-dependent crimes. Observers are watching closely to gauge where the last policy address of Lee’s current term and the city’s first five-year plan will take Hong Kong, and whether such high-level strategic planning will be used by Lee to build momentum for securing a second five-year term next July. In an opinion piece published in the SCMP on Monday, Lee stressed that the five-year plan would not change Hong Kong’s capitalist system but instead fully exploit its advantages to map the city’s long-term development. This would ultimately “enable citizens to flourish” by creating jobs and upward mobility, the city leader wrote. “I want the people of Hong Kong – every one of you – to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment,” he added. Wingco Lo Kam-wing, president of the Chinese Manufacturers’ Association of Hong Kong, called for greater flexibility in investment models for the Northern Metropolis, including more flexible arrangements for land payments. He also proposed new approaches, such as allowing joint development between the private sector and the industrial park operators. Lo urged the government to publish a list of the industries it expected to develop in the megaproject, along with corresponding plans and a clear timetable, to give the business community greater certainty and enable better evaluation of economic gains. “People may still lack an understanding of the detailed planning of the Northern Metropolis. More promotion is needed in this area,” Lo said. “If [the business community] knows what stage of development will be reached by a certain year, that will allow us to make better plans.” Leonard Chan Tik-yuen, founding chairman of the Hong Kong Innovative Technology Development Association, said he expected the government to relax regulations on the testing of advanced driverless vehicles and drones in the Northern Metropolis, noting that some trials were difficult to conduct in urban areas. He also called for better cross-border flow of data, specimens and equipment, describing it as a unique advantage for the city. He added that the administration must clearly define the positioning of the three I&T clusters under the North-Central-South strategy and ensure proper coordination to avoid homogenisation and internal competition.

title: US Supreme Court blocks Trump mail ballot restrictions before midterms
description: Justices reject White House bid to restrict mail-in ballots, leaving state voting procedures intact.
content: The US Supreme Court dealt a major blow Monday to President Donald Trump’s attempts to restrict mail-in voting before the November midterm elections, denying his request to lift an order halting the divisive plan. Only two of the six conservative justices on the nine-member panel offered a dissent. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, in a concurring opinion with the majority, said Trump’s plan may ultimately be legal in the long run, but “state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections”. After the decision came down, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the president’s “plan to make it harder to vote was obviously unconstitutional. The Supreme Court had no choice but to make the right decision”. The case has major implications because nearly one-third of the country votes by mail. Several states, including North Carolina, have already begun sending mail-in ballots to voters. Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to restrict mail-in voting, saying without evidence that it is vulnerable to fraud. The order quickly prompted multiple legal challenges. Democratic-led states sued the administration on grounds that under the US Constitution, states - and not the federal government - retain broad control over the administration of elections. “Today is a good day for democracy, the rule of law and the American people looking to exercise their constitutional right to vote,” said California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose state led one of the lawsuits against the rule. “Trump’s attacks on democracy these last 20 months have been nothing short of un-American.” Trump’s executive order would require the compilation of lists of eligible voters and for the US Postal Service (USPS) to deliver ballots only to voters who are on the lists. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) hailed the Supreme Court’s decision as a “major win for voting rights, election integrity, and democracy”. “This administration keeps testing the limits of its power, as if the rules governing our elections are merely suggestions to ignore when they don’t suit the president’s agenda,” said Sophia Lin Lakin, director of the ACLU Voting Rights Project. “The president does not run our elections, the Postal Service does not get to decide whose ballot counts, and voters - not the White House - will decide November’s elections.” Officials from several states had warned that a lack of legal clarity around the plan was sowing chaos months before the November 3 vote. A USPS whistle-blower had also warned that millions of Americans may not receive ballots because the systems being used by the postal service have been put together in a “sloppy and rushed manner”. Trump has long been a critic of mail-in ballots but has frequently used them himself, including when he voted by mail in Florida’s Republican primary earlier this year. The president has for years claimed without evidence that mail-in voting is highly vulnerable to fraud, repeatedly linking it to his false assertion that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him by Democrat Joe Biden. Polls show that Trump’s Republican Party faces a serious threat of losing its narrow control of Congress in November, particularly the House of Representatives. If Democrats win, they have signalled they would block Trump’s agenda and could even move to impeach him for the third time. Additional reporting by Reuters and Associated Press

title: Fiery crashes and costly karts do little to deter Hongkonger Han from chasing F1 dream
description: Hongkonger John Han has won 2026 Junior FIA Karting Arrive and Drive Asia-Pacific Championship, a competition aimed at making sport accessible.
content: An innate talent, coupled with a novel concept designed to lower motorsport’s financial barriers, could one day deliver the answer to the question of, where is the next Zhou Guanyu? A reserve driver this season with newest Formula 1 team Cadillac, Zhou is the first, and so far only Chinese racer, to have had a full-time seat in the sport. And while we are not quite at the “remember the name” stage for those hoping to follow in his footsteps, 12-year-old Hongkonger John Han showed flashes of talent in pulling off a thrilling last lap overtake on Macau’s tricky Coloane Karting Track on Sunday to win the 2026 Junior FIA Karting Arrive and Drive Asia-Pacific Championship. The competition’s concept is as simple as it sounds. Introduced last year, as part of world governing body the FIA’s (Federation Internationale de l’Automobile) new global karting plan, it asks riders to compete in identical vehicles that they see for the first time when they turn up at the race venue. Engines are routinely swapped to avoid any competitors complaining that they have been stuck with a dud. Entrants paid €3,950 (US$4,550) to compete in Macau, in addition to their mechanics’ fees. Although expensive on the face of it, Akbar Ebrahim, president of the FIA Karting Commission, said it was reasonable in the context of usual all-in costs of up to €12,000. The junior category over the weekend was contested by drivers aged 12 to 14, while 14 to 18-year-olds vied for senior honours. “We’re providing a platform for people who are talented and do well in their home races, but who cannot compete at this level [because of expense],” Ebrahim said. “Talent scouts from all the big Formula 1 teams are watching these races, and we wanted to provide something with less engineering, which was more affordable and accessible.” All bases beyond the karts’ uniform chassis and engines have been covered to ensure a level playing field. On Friday’s practice day, in a marquee around 50 metres from the Macau circuit, staff from OTK Kart Group, the Italian manufacturers responsible for designing, building and transporting the karts, were studying various metrics being delivered to their computer screens from the vehicles. None of the data was shared with the riders or their mechanics, lest more experienced personnel gain a jump on their rivals. After first sitting in a baby kart at four, Han was drawn in by motor racing’s “speed and competitive challenges, and the need to solve problems”. With a driving simulator in his Beijing home, he is already doing what he can to separate himself from his rivals. Also leading the way in this year’s FIA Karting Academy Trophy, which counts Charles Leclerc, the 2026 British Grand Prix winner, among its former champions, Han said: “It’s hard to manage school and karting, because I need to be away a lot, but I have lots of online lessons.” Describing himself as “an aggressive driver … but I don’t do dirty moves”, Han said his parents had never tried to persuade him to focus on his second sport of tennis over the riskier pursuit in vehicles that in Macau were capable of top speeds of nearly 80 mph (128 km/h). In this month’s China GT Championship, British driver Ollie Millroy was dragged from his burning car by fellow competitor Loek Hartog following a three-vehicle collision. “Inherently, motorsport is dangerous, and it’s going to take someone aback when they see something like that,” Ebrahim, who in his earlier years competed in F2 and F3, said. “It felt safe when I raced more than 35 years ago, but the circuits, products and driver equipment have greatly improved. If you look at the number of accidents that happen over the kilometres run, I think the safety rate is pretty good. “If somebody is invested in the sport, they’re invested irrespective of what they see.” Han validated Ebrahim’s last point. “I know it’s a very dangerous sport, but I’m never scared on the track,” he said. “I focus on the speed rather than the danger.” A three-strong team of race stewards in Macau was responsible for enforcing safety rules. Drivers on the naughty step would enter blinking into a compact room overlooking the track where they had transgressed, apologising profusely and vowing to their inquisitors that they had learned their lessons. Some were handed “jokers”, their one-strike before being hit with race penalties. One unfortunate young fellow’s punishment for overtaking on a yellow flag was to have to report at 6.45am the following morning to accompany a steward on his safety inspection of the 1.2km circuit. The walk would be accompanied by a lecture on race etiquette. Ebrahim said it would be too simplistic to state whether he considered arrive-and-drive a success or a failure. Last year’s inaugural World Cup in Malaysia was oversubscribed, with 107 drivers eventually on the grid, but regional competitions have proved a tougher sell. Forty-three raced across the two age divisions in Macau. Punitive financial costs led to the abandonment of a plan to stage the Asia-Pacific championship over three separate race weekends, in favour of the one-off shoot-out in Macau. “We’re actually losing a bit [of money], but the FIA is there to invest to develop the sport and give opportunities to people who would otherwise not be able to compete at this level,” Ebrahim said, adding that around 65 per cent of his organisation’s arrive-and-drive outlay covered logistical and human expenses. Plans are afoot to change the model in 2028 to a global kart system that will feature more localised races under global rules. “We can’t sustain the freight prices,” Ebrahim said, revealing that FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem would like car manufacturing decentralised from its dominant Italian hub to strip back transport expenses. “Because of the geopolitical situation, the cost of getting the materials here from Italy, along with personnel, has increased by two or three times. “Whichever country adopts the global kart system must abide by our sporting and technical regulations. They’ll run it, and they’ll come with their own equipment.” Also a former professional cricketer for Tamil Nadu in his native India, Ebrahim said Asia lagged behind in producing elite F1 drivers because the continent boasts few “motoring countries”. “A lot of [Asian regions] have more connection to public transport than to automobiles,” Ebrahim said. “In the larger counties, travel is expensive and there are fewer circuits. If you don’t have the infrastructure, how will the sport grow? “Also, India and China are doing well economically, but it’s a very small percentage of the populations who have the wealth.” Seira Kojima, the 15-year-old Japanese driver who placed fifth in the seniors in Macau, said she was consistently racing in Europe to sharpen her competitive edge. “The level is very different,” she said. “In Asia, there’s about 30 drivers in each class, in Europe it’s more than 80 or 90, then only 36 in the finals. “The rules in Asia are stricter, too. If you hit someone, or look and block, you get a penalty. In Europe, those things are normal. If you don’t have any spoiling [tactics] you’ll find it hard.” Han will jet to Italy next month for the latest leg of his karting academy title pursuit. “I don’t think about the future,” he said. “The best thing for me now is to just do my best and try to win every race I can.” Ebrahim added: “This is a tough sport: mentally and physically, and also financially. “It’s not a walk in the park for someone who thinks they can come and have a punt at it. You get badly battered and bruised, both ego-wise and physically. “It’s only those who are very committed and who have an intense passion for racing who will sustain it.”

title: Iceland’s whaling ban plan threatens to leave Japan alone in defending industry
description: Reykjavik’s move to end hunts increases international pressure on Tokyo as low consumption of whale meat and high subsidies fuel debate.
content: Iceland’s move towards a whaling ban could leave Japan more exposed than ever as it defends an industry critics say relies on public money, political symbolism and a shrinking domestic appetite for whale meat. The Icelandic government has announced plans to submit a bill early next year to end whaling – a step that would leave Japan and Norway as the world’s only two nations still carrying out commercial hunts. For environmental campaigners, the move has renewed hopes that Japan will no longer be able to justify the annual killing of up to 412 whales. Public opinion in Japan has shifted away from support for whaling in recent years, according to surveys. Animal rights groups say negative publicity and a sense of isolation would intensify if Tokyo and Oslo were left standing alone. However, Japanese defenders of commercial whaling frame it as a matter of traditional culinary culture. Some argue that anti-whaling campaigns are rooted in Western bias, saying there is no moral difference between consuming whale meat and eating livestock or fish caught at sea. Anti-whaling campaigners say the key to ending the practice is convincing Tokyo to stop subsidising a loss-making business that produces food few people eat. International isolation “If Iceland does ban whaling, that will make Japan and Norway even more isolated than they already are,” said Wendy Higgins, a spokeswoman for Humane World for Animals, a global non-profit organisation based in Washington. “I do think a ban in Iceland, and the international applause that will inevitably create, could impact public awareness and opinion within Japan, which is already shifting away from support for whaling.” The most recent survey on public attitudes towards whaling was conducted by the Japan Wildlife Conservation Society and published in August 2024. It found that only 10 per cent of the 1,000 respondents felt that losing access to whale meat would affect their lives, while 49 per cent said it would have no effect at all. Just 7 per cent of those questioned had eaten whale in the previous 12 months. Yet, 16 per cent opposed a government ban – more than double the proportion of recent consumers, suggesting that resistance to a ban is driven by factors beyond culinary preference. When asked why whaling should continue, respondents most frequently cited the need to “maintain Japanese culture and tradition”. A sizeable number also pointed to the importance of taking a stand against outside pressure. Higgins said while traditionalists in Iceland had long fought to protect whaling, a policy shift there would resonate in Japan. “If a country like Iceland, with similar narratives around culture and national pride, chooses to end whaling and begin a new era of whale protection, that will be hard for the Japanese public to dismiss,” Higgins said. She added that Norway was in a similar situation, with only 1 per cent of its population eating whale meat. “If Iceland ends whaling, that will massively increase public pressure on the Norwegian government, particularly among younger voters,” Higgins said. “That would leave Japan completely isolated as the only nation to kill whales commercially.” Diplomatic pressure points Ren Yabuki, director of the animal rights organisation Life Investigation Agency, agreed that while total isolation would embarrass Tokyo on the world stage, an extra push would be needed to shut down the industry. External pressure, he said, could give the Japanese government a politically safe off-ramp to end the practice without losing face. “Even if Japan was isolated, I do not think that would be enough to halt whaling immediately,” Yabuki said. “When pressure is exerted during summit meetings with foreign leaders or at major international conferences – pressure that could affect trade and the economy – Japan would halt the subsidies it is currently channelling into whaling,” he said. “Whaling would only be completely halted once companies find they cannot continue to operate at a loss.” Yabuki pointed to another argument used by those in favour of whaling: as an island nation dependent on marine resources, Japan fears that giving ground on whaling could set a precedent as global fish stocks decline. “Whaling is used as a ‘breakwater’ in that debate,” Yabuki said. “If this breakwater were to be breached, international regulations could be imposed on other fish and shellfish. Japan is taking a firm stance to protect its right to harvest whales and other marine life.” Cultural sovereignty A segment of the Japanese public remains intent on defending what it sees as a key element of national identity and food heritage – and strongly resists outside interference. “Iceland halting whaling would have no impact on Japan,” said Ken Kato, a conservative Tokyo businessman. “Public opinion there has no meaning on the situation here. It would be unfortunate that a country that has long been an ally in the whaling industry goes back on that, but this is our culture, and nothing will change that.” Kato said foreign opposition to Japan’s whaling tradition stemmed from double standards. “The people who criticise us for whaling are not all vegetarian,” he said. “They eat meat and fish, so why is whaling different? Their opposition is based on misunderstanding, and trying to disrupt another country’s culture is racism. “If they want to ban whaling, what is next? Will our sushi culture also be banned?” he asked. “Other countries need to respect our culture.” This Week in Asia has contacted Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries and the government-run Institute of Cetacean Research for comment.

title: China targets offshore operations of brokerages in crackdown on pay loopholes, corruption
description: The move extends Beijing’s regulatory reach to financial institutions’ overseas activities, which have been a grey zone for corruption.
content: China’s securities regulator and its industry body are moving to close compensation loopholes for brokerage management and staff, extending anti-corruption oversight to overseas operations for the first time, as Beijing pushes the sector to build world-class investment banks. The Securities Association of China, a self-regulatory body under the supervision of the regulator, recently sent brokerages a revised draft of its rules on “clean practices”, seeking industry feedback by September 29, domestic media reported on Monday, citing industry sources. Under the proposed rules, offshore operations have been explicitly targeted for integrity oversight, marking a major expansion of Beijing’s regulatory reach into financial institutions’ overseas activities – a sector long viewed as a grey zone vulnerable to illicit transfers and kickbacks. Brokerages will be required to establish clawback mechanisms to recover bonuses and performance pay from employees who violate ethical standards or regulatory rules. Brokerages must also prepare an annual report on integrity management and have it reviewed by their board. Regulators are also introducing positive incentives to foster compliance. Employees who resist improper benefit transfers or flag major risks will be given priority for promotions and honours, according to the draft. The move follows a series of crackdowns earlier this year by the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), which penalised three brokerages for regulatory breaches and illicit cross-border activities, in an effort to “fully safeguard the order and stability of China’s capital markets”, the CSRC said. Beyond offshore expansion, the latest overhaul targets two other fast-growing risk areas: innovation and digital operations. Under the new provisions, firms must complete integrity risk assessments before launching innovative products, and are barred from using algorithm design or system access to generate improper gains through digital operations. The revisions also call for closer internal inspection of investment banking, bond trading, brokerage and marketing activities, while encouraging firms to protect whistle-blowers who report violations. The regulatory push comes as Beijing pressures brokerages to strengthen their international competitiveness. At a State Council briefing on September 10, CSRC vice-chairman Li Chao said the regulator would speed up efforts to build “first-class investment banks and institutions” with stronger governance and professional service capacity. The CSRC would also foster “a sound industry culture,” Li said, while supporting brokerages in tapping both domestic and overseas markets as part of broader opening-up efforts. The tighter regulatory scrutiny could directly impact Chinese brokerages in Hong Kong, which include major players such as China International Capital Corporation (CICC), Citic Securities International and Huatai International – which dominate the city’s equity and debt underwriting markets. CICC leads the pack in Hong Kong’s primary market, where companies raise funds through new share and bond offerings, capturing an 18.7 per cent share with HK$67.79 billion raised across all deals this year as of September 9, according to data from financial provider Wind.

title: How Sandrine Zhang Ferron built vintage furniture marketplace Vinterior – interview
description: While fashion resale has matured thanks to Vinted and Vestiaire Collective, Vinterior is scaling the untapped global market for antique and second-hand homeware.
content: Sandrine Zhang Ferron’s path to entrepreneurship was less a predictable trajectory and more a conscious pivot. She grew up between Suzhou in China, France and London, with her upbringing placing a premium on stable, conventional career paths rather than creative pursuits. “In my family, it was not an obvious thing to do,” notes the founder of Vinterior, the London-based vintage and antique furniture marketplace. “There was no tradition of design, entrepreneurship or art.” Zhang Ferron’s career ultimately became a story of personal reinvention. After establishing a secure foundation in the financial sector, she chose to step away from the industry to build something of her own, turning her focus towards the then-nascent world of digital design curation and online resale. The path to design was neither linear nor romantic. Armed with a master’s degree in finance, she arrived in London in 2007, entering the high-stakes world of financial markets. She eventually moved from a brokerage firm on the sell side to a boutique family office on the buy side. But the allure wore thin. “I just didn’t really see myself spending the rest of my life moving money, which is very immaterial, just to make rich people richer,” she says. The friction that birthed Vinterior was entirely practical. While moving homes in London, Zhang Ferron spent months navigating local shops and classified ads in a desperate bid to find high-quality, characterful furniture. The tipping point arrived courtesy of her cat, Misifu: wanting a yellow vintage armchair to match his striking yellow eyes, she launched a three-month hunt across London before finally unearthing a 1960s Poul Volther armchair in Dalston. “At some point, the hunt is not fun any more,” she adds, recalling an incident where attempting to sell a light fixture on eBay meant not only inviting a stranger into her home but having him muddy her floors and help himself to her bathroom. For a finance professional, the inefficiency (and awkwardness) was both maddening and enlightening. Zhang Ferron saw a chasm between the mainstream flat-pack retailers and the analogue world of antique dealers, which gave her the momentum she needed. She enrolled in a coding boot camp, learning how to build the platform’s architecture from scratch. If the venture failed, she reasoned she could slip back into finance. But it didn’t. Launched in January 2016, Vinterior began with a hyper-lean marketplace model – an asset-light approach directly inspired by her time in financial brokerage. Zhang Ferron applied her cold-calling sales skills to convince 12 sceptical London antique dealers to list a starting pool of 200 products. The platform’s very first order was a pair of black Belgian armchairs. Ten years on, the business has been profitable for a few quarters, with sales growth up around 22 per cent year-on-year. The scrappy solo operation has quietly scaled into a design force, capturing a digital audience of around half a million monthly visitors. While the broader resale narrative has long been dominated by fashion giants like Vinted and Vestiaire Collective, the furniture sector is less saturated. Zhang Ferron notes that a mere two per cent of all furniture is currently resold, and only nine per cent of UK consumers have bought second-hand furniture. “The challenge, obviously, is that it’s much harder to ship a three-seater sofa than a T-shirt.” Yet, macroeconomic headwinds, the rise of spending on interiors and growing awareness of overconsumption are shifting the temperature. Vinterior now connects buyers with over 3,000 professional dealers across 30 countries. Zhang Ferron is currently initiating Vinterior’s first major European expansion, launching localised operations in the Netherlands. Scaling a marketplace to 500,000 products, however, fundamentally alters the user experience. The early charm of digital rummaging quickly curdles into decision fatigue if not properly managed. To maintain Vinterior’s curation, the company is leaning into advanced matching algorithms and data-driven personalisation. This ecosystem is run by a lean team of just 20 employees – an agility that Zhang Ferron cites as a deliberate pivot back to her solo-founder roots. By integrating AI tools across the business, she has bypassed the bloated organisational structures that plague mid-stage tech start-ups. “We are training everyone in the company to become engineers so they can build directly and solve problems themselves,” she says. The shift has even allowed Zhang Ferron to return to the keyboard, actively pushing code to the live site. The founder’s personal interior style has similarly evolved from the mid-century aesthetic that first drew her in. Today, her London home is an eclectic, colourful study in texture. Her favourite piece? A mid-century Scandinavian Søren Nissen & Ebbe Gehl “Clipper” lounge chair. Bought as a bare, dilapidated frame for under £200 (US$270), it sat in her home for five years before she custom-reupholstered it in crisp green and cream stripes. “It feels unique and personal to me,” she says. Now 19 years into her London chapter, Zhang Ferron’s focus is on cementing Vinterior as the definitive global destination for antique furniture. It is a complex operational puzzle, but she remains grounded. Having raised US$15 million in venture capital over the decade, she advises the next generation of founders to look beyond pure data. “I’m a facts person due to my finance background,” she reflects. “But with hindsight, really nailing the storytelling and building something that people can feel an emotion about is what gets you the VC money.” Global locations for vintage furniture finds The Old Cinema, London 160 Chiswick High Road, Chiswick, London W4 1PR, United Kingdom A cinema-turned-showroom brimming with modernist sofas, 1800s desks and groovy Murano glass lamps – there’s something for every mood board. Paul Bert Serpette, Paris 110 Rue des Rosiers, 93400 Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine, France A legendary, sprawling market where high-end dealers showcase museum-quality space-age furniture and rare avant-garde lighting alongside archival Hermès and Chanel. Colt & Sonechika A, Tokyo 3-Chōme-11-5 Meguro, Meguro City, Tokyo 153-0063, Japan A stand-out gem nestled along Tokyo’s famous Meguro-dori interiors street, full of restored Scandinavian modern chairs, compact vintage desks and understated Japanese mid-century design.

title: Paul French lifts veil on final months of China’s last emperor in the Forbidden City
description: It is not the first biography of China’s Puyi, but Paul French’s latest book brings with it a feminine voice of modernity and fully exploits its place in the ‘doomed-monarchy’ sub-genre.
content: On a recent afternoon, Paul French – British author, broadcaster, blogger but definitely not, as he always stresses, an academic – is explaining his technique. “My trick, which I suppose is reasonably successful, is to try and write Chinese history linked to a genre that lots and lots of people read, [because] there’s that many people” – his finger and thumb indicate a space so narrow you’d hardly be able to pass a sliver of paper between them – “who read books on China. And there’s this many people” – his hands convey near-ceiling height – “who’ll read about true crime or gangsters or royalty.” Such an approach has, indeed, made him reasonably, and internationally, successful. In 2011, he published Midnight in Peking: How the Murder of a Young Englishwoman Haunted the Last Days of Old China, which made it onto the New York Times’ bestseller list, won both the 2013 Edgar Award for “Best Fact Crime” in the United States and Britain’s Crime Writers’ Association’s “ALCS Gold Dagger for Non-Fiction”, and was named “International Success of the Year” at the 2012 Australian Book Industry Awards. In 2018, his City of Devils: A Shanghai Noir was a Kirkus Reviews’ “Best Book of the Year”. In 2024, Her Lotus Year: China, The Roaring Twenties and the Making of Wallis Simpson received much coverage and quotably upbeat reviews (“Her Lotus Year stays in the mind as a bright, shining, lively snapshot,” says The Spectator. “Delightful to read.”). Now, it’s the turn of Puyi in The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City, which falls into a royalty subgenre that French calls “doomed monarchy”. Although he’s writing – primarily – for a Western audience, as a category, it has promising global reach. Earlier this year, French was told by his Chinese publisher that only one other foreigner has shifted (and signed) more books in China: British author and historian Simon Sebag Montefiore, whose 2016 work on those quintessential doomed monarchs, The Romanovs: 1613-1918, was a massive hit. Puyi, of course, didn’t meet his doom with an execution in a cellar. He was six years old in 1912, when the Manchu empire ended and the new Republican government decided to leave him behind the walls of the Forbidden City – an oddity, roaming around the “Great Within”, attended by eunuchs (“teapots without spouts” was the local term). With his peculiar upbringing and background, that child would grow into the adult who, during the second Sino-Japanese war (1937-1945), would become his country’s “Great Traitor”. French, who was a language student in 1980s Beijing and lived in Shanghai for many years before returning to Britain in 2014, had been marinating this story for a while. He sensed that – “a bit like Wallis Simpson”, the American socialite whose relationship with Britain’s King Edward VIII led to his abdication – people sort of knew about Puyi but not really. He’d been struck by the blank stares he met when he mentioned him to Chinese-language students at a couple of British universities.
