French realised that it’s been almost four decades since he, along with many others, had been “blown away” by the Bernardo Bertolucci epic, The Last Emperor (1987), which was – an amazing achievement – filmed inside the Forbidden City. While he was wondering how to tackle the topic, he wrote an article about Puyi’s wife, Wanrong, in 2024, for this magazine. “Wanrong is so beautiful and there are so many pictures of her and I thought it would be fun,” he says. “I did mention, in a couple of lines, that she’d had a tutor and this was one of the things the film had missed.” In fact, Joan Chen – who played Wanrong in the film – makes a single reference to her tutor as a “Miss Windsor”. Bertolucci, who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother-in-law, Mark Peploe, knew Wanrong was educated but not by whom, so they made up a name with British royal resonance. Wanrong’s tutor, however, was not British. Isabel Ingram was an American “mishkid” – a child of missionaries – born in Peking (Beijing) in 1902 and educated at Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, in the US. After the PostMag piece came out, French was contacted by a man called Kenneth Mayer, who told him he was Ingram’s grandson. “He said, ‘Thank you so much for noticing Isabel; no one else does,’” French recalls. “And then he said, ‘By the way, you really should read her diary and she has some letters from this Johnston guy …’” French was staggered. He hadn’t known about the diary, and the “Johnston guy” was Reginald Johnston, Puyi’s Scottish tutor, played in the film by Peter O’Toole. Johnston had written a memoir which, in its 486 pages, makes a single reference to “the Empress’s American friend who had been her teacher of English both before and after the Empress entered the Forbidden City as a bride”; and his letters and journals had been destroyed after his death in Edinburgh, in 1938. Diary! Letters! Such finds are history’s gold dust. Even better, Ingram, who died in Virginia in 1988, had typed up all of it. (French, who revels in his North London unacademic blokeishness, makes some cheerfully unrepeatable comments about the trials of handwritten research materials.) Once he’d read the Ingram documents, he knew he had his book. Ingram was 20 when she became Wanrong’s tutor, in October 1922. A few months later, on December 1, Wanrong, aged 16, married Puyi, also 16. French decided to focus The Last Emperor of China on the 23 months between that five-day wedding – “the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see”, he writes – and the couple’s expulsion into the “Great Without” on November 5, 1924, which brought an end to more than 500 years of (occasionally interrupted) dynastic occupation of the Forbidden City. Apart from sporadic chunks of necessary context, the book is like a wonderfully evocative play with four principal performers – a middle-aged Scottish man, a young American woman and two teenage Manchu royals – on a spectacular stage. French says he’s only too aware that he joins a long line of Puyi biographers, but what Ingram brings to his version is the voice of modernity. Formal lessons with Wanrong, who had a golden fountain-pen and silver inkwell, rarely took up more than an hour or two. Afterwards, there would be hair-braiding, hat-selecting, wardrobe-rummaging, dancing to gramophone records, chocolates and cigarettes. Ingram’s language – “I love her for life”; “cute little thing”; “the Empress is still darling”; “he nearly died on the spot” – could be that of a Californian blogger, and the film these scenes evoke isn’t the Bertolucci drama; it’s Clueless, in every sense. Her diary also testifies to Puyi and Wanrong’s genuine friendship as they go cycling and kite-flying and dog-walking around their vast, mouldering compound. Many happy photographs are taken. For French, Ingram is an important witness to the growing intimacy between the newlyweds. As he says, a great debate among biographers concerns Puyi’s sexuality and whether he was asexual or homosexual. Famously, on his wedding night, the last emperor had sloped off to the Hall of Mental Cultivation for a think. “He’s 16!” says French, and goes on to note that “the single most surprising thing [in the diary] is when Isabel writes about ‘the curtain being drawn’ and there are no lessons today … Obviously, like all young people, they work out what goes where”. But Puyi and Wanrong’s isn’t the only unexpected romance in the book. It becomes clear through his letters that Johnston, 28 years older than Ingram, is attracted to her. French believes he was “heartbroken” when she refused him, which is why her name was never mentioned in his memoir. Perhaps. (On the other hand, this reader thinks it was more about Johnston’s considerable, publicity-hogging ego.) At any rate, Johnston’s letters to Ingram veer in tone from housekeeper (“I am sorry to hear chewing gum has been introduced into the palace”) to stalker (“Who is the young man you kept looking at so earnestly all the time?”). Eventually, he becomes self-deludingly creepy. “Did you explain to the Lockharts how and why you refused to let me kiss you when we were on the Emperor’s swing together?” he writes. “And yet it would only have been a remote, innocuous fatherly salutation!” By then, the quartet had broken up. On November 5, 1924, several hours after the early-morning palace coup, Ingram was taken by rickshaw to the Forbidden City as usual, but was barred from entering. At the Gate of Divine Prowess, the commandant told her that Wanrong had gone into the “Great Without” “hatless, coatless, baggage-less”. Ingram, who would leave China in 1927, never saw her dressing-up companion again. In the Bertolucci film, when soldiers arrive to evict Puyi and Wanrong, they are playing tennis. In real life, he was peeling her an apple, that ancient symbol of expulsion, in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Soldiers took a – distinctly unhappy – photo, which is in the book, of his abandoned bedroom: an adolescent muddle of kung fu novels and toys. “Once they go outside the gilded cage, they’re lost,” says French. “You could write another book about Puyi in Manchuria and try and get into the psychology of what happened to that relationship when he’s manipulated, with no advisers, and she knows that they’ve made a horrendous mistake and slips into opium abuse.” In this immensely readable book, however, French steps only briefly beyond the palace gates and into that future when Puyi was crowned the emperor of Japan’s puppet state, Manchukuo, in 1934 – another doomed monarchy. Another sombre note is the contrast between Ingram’s spirited diary and the fate suffered by Wanrong in the final summary, which is heart-wrenching. Puyi survived and, in the 60s, made several return visits to the Forbidden City. Premier Zhou Enlai liked to keep an eye on him. Asked what he thinks of Puyi now, French replies, “I do take the Zhou Enlai line. He’s supposed to have invited Puyi to a lunch and told him, ‘You weren’t to blame for becoming emperor and what happened then. But you can be blamed for what happened after.’”

title: Editorial | Asia requires a flexible, conviction-led approach to philanthropy
description: A report released at a Jockey Club philanthropy forum in Hong Kong underscores both the sheer volume of giving in the region and the need for an efficient model.
content: Philanthropic giving in nine Asian jurisdictions is projected to hit US$1.5 trillion over the next decade, according to the Commission on Asian Philanthropy. That has immense potential to help make the world a better place, which is why ensuring charity is efficient in Asia is important. The commission was launched just two years ago at a Hong Kong Jockey Club forum – Philanthropy for Better Cities – to develop more effective solutions to Asia’s socio-economic and environmental challenges. Why such a potent force for good needs to be harnessed effectively was addressed by Jockey Club chairman Martin Liao Cheung-kong at this year’s philanthropy summit. “We are gathering at a critical time,” he said. “Philanthropy is growing in importance because governments are no longer alone in confronting the world’s most profound challenges. Today, communities, businesses and civic society are all grappling with ever more complex social needs, demographic shifts, technological disruption and the pressing realities of climate change.” The forum brought together about 2,000 delegates from across philanthropy, sport, government, business and academia. Liao said it had given the city a chance to showcase its credentials as a global hub while reinforcing its role as a bridge between East and West. The Commission on Asian Philanthropy comprises 13 charitable organisations from 10 jurisdictions across the region, including the Jockey Club Charities Trust. The jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, mainland China, Singapore, Japan and Saudi Arabia, account for 70 per cent of Asia’s population and 80 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP). Excluding the United Arab Emirates, whose data is not readily available, the commission’s interim report noted philanthropic giving across the other nine jurisdictions amounted to US$109 billion in 2024. The commission aims to develop strategies to “professionalise” philanthropic efforts at regional level. Citing an independent study by KPMG Advisory, the Jockey Club Charities Trust said in a report that it had contributed about HK$55.4 billion (US$7.07 billion) in economic value to Hong Kong during 2024-25. In a foreword to the report, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the Jockey Club’s “value creation model” was an important adjunct to Hong Kong’s growing role as a wealth management hub for family offices. The sheer volume of capital tells only half the story. Future development is not just about the amount of capital deployed, but also its agility, adaptability and willingness to embrace risk. Flexible philanthropy must become an important element of Asian development strategies. Historically, philanthropic capital across the region has often been constrained by rigid, transactional models, focused narrowly on traditional charity, short-term relief or risk-averse institutional projects. Yet, the complex nature of 21st century crises demands a fundamental reset. As research from the Centre for Asian Philanthropy and Society highlights, deployment of flexible philanthropic risk capital provides a vital bridge to viable, system-wide public solutions. An example of this evolving landscape is to be found in key financial and philanthropic hubs like Hong Kong. At the Jockey Club’s Philanthropy for Better Cities Forum 2026, sector leaders pointed out that corporate and institutional giving plays a crucial role in Hong Kong’s “giving” ecosystem. For instance, the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust alone generated economic value equivalent to roughly 1.8 per cent of the city’s GDP in the 2024-25 financial year. When major institutions and family offices leverage their resources flexibly, they do more than provide financial aid – they serve as catalysts for cross-border collaboration and structural innovation. Asia stands at a critical juncture. Wealth creation sweeping across the continent over the past few decades has created a pool of resources. But capital without flexibility risks remaining a passive buffer rather than an active engine for change. To build resilient, equitable and sustainable societies for the decades ahead, Asian philanthropists, corporate leaders and policymakers must embrace a flexible, conviction-led approach to giving, turning financial capital into catalytic, lasting impact.

title: Why are Chun-Li’s thighs so big? The Street Fighter character’s origin and cultural impact
description: We look at the Chinese martial artist’s backstory, sexualised design, the actors who played her – and a bizarre Jackie Chan cosplay moment.
content: In the 1990s, Chun-Li was not only the first female playable character introduced in the Street Fighter video game franchise – she was also the first female playable character to gain mainstream recognition in the arcade and fighting game industry. The fictional Chinese martial artist has become something of a pop culture icon over the years. She remains one of the world’s most cosplayed video game characters, while US rapper Nicki Minaj borrowed the heroine’s name for her 2018 single, “Chun-Li”. The character made headlines again recently when Canadian actress Callina Liang went viral for a fitness regimen that grew each of her thighs by 6.5cm (2.6 inches) to match the character’s physique for the upcoming Street Fighter film. Vancouver-born Liang’s 2026 reinterpretation wears a modernised version of the character’s iconic blue dress, retaining some cheongsam elements and adding black tights to cover her muscular legs. “I ate a lot, and I never skipped leg day,” Liang revealed in a Q&A session posted on the Street Fighter movie’s Instagram page. In another video, it was disclosed that her stunt double had to don butt pads to match Liang’s physique. But who is Chun-Li, and why are her thighs so thick? There are both practical and questionable reasons. The story behind a feminine icon Chun-Li, meaning “the beauty of spring” in Mandarin, first appeared in Japanese video game company Capcom’s 1991 smash hit Street Fighter II, becoming the series’ first female protagonist and first playable Chinese character. She is an Interpol operative and expert martial artist whose main objective is to avenge the death of her father, a Hong Kong village magistrate or police officer – depending on the adaptation – who was killed by the franchise’s principal antagonist, M. Bison (known in Japan as Vega), the leader of the powerful Shadaloo criminal syndicate. Driven by filial piety and a strong sense of justice, Chun-Li is a highly disciplined fighter trained in Chinese martial arts such as wushu, tai chi and qigong. As one of the few women among a cast of strong male fighters, she is known for her exceptional strength and agility. Although one of her super combo attacks is the Kikoken, or “Qigong Fist”, she is best known for her muscular legs, with her signature moves being the Lightning Kick and the gravity-defying Spinning Bird Kick, both of which involve throwing multiple kicks in one go. She can also bounce off walls and perform a Yosokyaku, or Head Stomp. The fetishisation of a warrior Capcom composer Yoko Shimomura revealed in a 2014 interview that the decision to give Chun-Li unusually thick thighs – contrasting with her petite and slim frame – was down to one of her makers, Japanese game designer Akira Yasuda. “It kind of got awkward when he started explaining his fetishes,” Shimomura recounted. “I mean, he has really strong feelings towards his creations.” Yasuda was not alone. According to Capcom producer Yoshinori Ono, Chun-Li’s other character designer, Daigo Ikeno, was also “kind of into thick girls. So as an artist he feels that the most beautiful thighs he can give Chun-Li would be of the wide variety.” Indeed, Chun-Li was created with the male gaze in mind, what with the frequent flashing of her underwear during her high kicks. She is also presented through a traditional lens of femininity: beauty and manipulation, but also a maternal instinct and a love for children. Yasuda was quoted as saying his initial idea “wasn’t very sexy” and “lacked visual impact and personality”, which led him to give her “bare legs and a bodycon dress”. He added: “That made her look like a female pro-wrestler, a sort of ‘fake’ kung fu fighter. It’s a little bit hard to describe in words, but it had a lot of impact, and I decided to go with it and release her to the world this way. She became far more popular than I had imagined; I was shocked. I guess part of it was that she was the only female character in the game.” In interviews by Capcom, Yasuda also said that the development team had wanted Street Fighter II to be “more entertaining than its predecessor”, and the addition of Chun-Li, as a female character, pushed things “towards the full-on entertainment side”. The human women (and one man) who played her The character’s first official live-action portrayal came from Macau-born American actor Ming-Na Wen in Street Fighter, a 1994 feature film based on the video game series. But perhaps the most pop-culturally iconic Chun-Li moment came a year before, when Hong Kong’s Jackie Chan cross-dressed as her in a bizarre fight sequence in City Hunter, a 1993 action comedy written and directed by Wong Jing. In both treatments, her hair is tied up in “space buns” – as popularised by Princess Leia in the Star Wars franchise – otherwise known as “ox-horn buns” or double buns. These buns on both sides of the head are a traditional Chinese hairstyle common among children and teens. In anime and manga, the hairstyle is known as odango and is worn by young women. Wen’s version wears a red, sleeveless cheongsam with fishnet tights, while Chan’s comedic spin-off is closer to the two-dimensional original, wearing a blue Chinese-inspired outfit with white trim and white ribbons in his hair. Both outfits have thigh-high slits. In 2009, Canadian actress Kristin Kreuk, who is of Dutch and Chinese-Indonesian descent, played the character in Street Fighter: The Legend of Chun-Li, a stand-alone origin story loosely based on the source material. The film stripped away much of her key lore, and it was poorly received at the box office and critically. Chun-Li is one of video gaming’s most loved characters and has even appeared in some of Capcom’s non-Street Fighter games. Her live-action revival coincides with the rise of the “muscle mommy” archetype, which has emerged in recent years as a pop culture and fitness trend. Whereas thin, frail and “delicate” bodies have long been idealised as the epitome of objectified femininity, mainstream media now also celebrates defined muscles for a broader representation of female athleticism that empowers women. While her youthful looks, large breasts and tiny waist all cater to the straight male fantasy, Chun-Li’s thick thighs may also serve to accentuate her strength and give her unprecedented agency in the male-oriented action world.

title: Ukraine says ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’ if Russia does same
description: Kyiv demands genuine commitment from Moscow as Trump claims deal to halt refinery and grid attacks.
content: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets. With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel. In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Monday that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure”. He added: “If this can become the first de-escalatory step – stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response – then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation”. Zelensky said “we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia’s war economy”. He noted that “so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the war”. “But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps.” Trump has insisted that Russia’s war in Ukraine, and not the conflict with Iran, was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November. A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the US-Israeli conflict against Iran, now in its seventh month. US envoys went to Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month without announcing a breakthrough. While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelensky has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defences as Russia intensifies its attacks. Russian strikes on Ukraine’s rail network are worsening each week, the CEO of the state Ukrainian Railways operator said on Monday, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend. “It’s growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one,” said Oleksandr Pertsovsky. Nato-member Poland said on Sunday that Russia hit a train near the Polish-Ukraine border, just days after Kyiv officials said road crossing checkpoints on the border with Moldova had been targeted. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that Warsaw had obtained information that Moscow might be planning attacks on border crossings. But European Union countries on Monday delayed a deadline for prolonging sanctions on Russia after France pushed for billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be removed from a blacklist, diplomats said. An EU list of almost 3,000 individuals and entities – which needs to be extended every six months – was set to expire by Wednesday. However, ambassadors from the 27 EU member states pushed back the deadline one week after the late efforts from Paris to remove 73-year-old Uzbek-Russian metals tycoon Usmanov drew opposition, the diplomats said. Usmanov, a former major shareholder in England’s Arsenal football club, was placed on the EU sanctions list in 2022 over what Brussels said were his close ties to the Kremlin. The French move surprised some EU states. “Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia’s war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefiting from it,” a spokesman for Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, said. The Financial Times reported, quoting people familiar with the issue, that France was making the push as part of a prisoner release deal involving French citizens held in Azerbaijan.

title: Huawei’s US trial puts jury to the test amid China, Iran links
description: More than 80 questions sought to uncover potential biases in the landmark criminal case against the Chinese tech giant.
content: The unique circumstances surrounding Huawei Technologies’ landmark trial in a US court made jury selection especially important to ensuring a fair trial for the Chinese tech giant, according to US litigation experts. Known as voir dire, the process allows the presiding judge and two legal teams to question prospective jurors before the trial begins to identify possible bias and conflicts that could impede their ability to adjudicate the case in a “fair and impartial” way. Richard Gabriel, president of litigation strategy firm Decision Analysis, said the high-profile nature of the case, eight years in the making, and its links to both China and Iran elevated the stakes of voir dire for both sides. “Given the nature of the case, its pre-trial publicity and potential international ramifications, they seemed to want to ask [prospective jurors] many questions to get a better sense of where they are coming from,” he said, referring to a questionnaire that was circulated among hundreds of prospective jurors before the trial. Consisting of more than 80 questions, the questionnaire was even longer than usual for such criminal cases, as both sides were likely eager to extract as much information about the jurors as possible, said Gabriel, co-author of Jury Selection: Strategy and Science. These included questions about whether jurors had “strong opinions” about the Communist Party or personal or professional ties to China. The US government has charged Huawei with 12 criminal counts, including violations of US sanctions on Iran and theft of trade secrets from US rivals such as T-Mobile and Cisco. Some of these fall under an umbrella charge of a racketeering conspiracy, which would deem Huawei a “criminal enterprise” if convicted under the US Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO), first applied to mafia organisations in the 1970s. Huawei denies all the charges. The jury selection process began long before the trial began on September 8, as the two legal teams spent months going back and forth over which questions to include. US District Judge Ann Donnelly, who is presiding over the case in the Eastern District of New York, finalised the questions and asked follow-ups on jury selection day. Following “peremptory challenges” by both legal teams, where they were able to dismiss a set number of jurors they deemed unfavourable to their side without having to provide any reasons, a final panel of 12 jurors and six alternates was selected. “Instead of selecting the jurors you want, you eliminate the jurors you don’t want. Each side does that, and you hopefully end up with a group that’s kind of in the middle,” said Gabriel. Huawei’s legal team would likely have focused on identifying prospective jurors with biases against China or Iran amid tense relations between the US and both countries, he noted. Given the “unusual” nature of a criminal case where no individuals are on trial, the defence will try to convince jurors that a large company like Huawei is bound to have some rogue employees who have had misconduct over the years, he said, adding that the company’s likely strategy will be to humanise the company in the eyes of the jurors. During opening statements last Wednesday, Huawei’s lawyer began his remarks by describing how company founder Ren Zhengfei built the world’s largest telecoms company from his flat nearly 40 years ago. “The delicate balance for the defence is to admit that, yes, some employees may have crossed the line, but this is not a companywide conspiracy,” said Gabriel. “This way, there’s an acknowledgement of some accountability while dismissing the overall charge.” Meanwhile, the prosecution will focus on convincing jurors that Huawei had masterminded a long-running criminal enterprise, said David Barnard, director of jury consulting at Magna Legal Services. In their opening statement last week, a US government lawyer accused Huawei of running a “far-reaching criminal scheme” over decades. Given the perception that New York residents are more liberal leaning, the federal prosecution may also have worried about jurors being biased against the US government under the current administration, said Gabriel. “Especially these days, there’s a lot of attitudes about the Department of Justice under the Trump administration, and whether there is political targeting of other countries and other companies,” he said. Perceptions of politicisation mean it's unlikely the prosecution would lean into using Huawei’s status as a Chinese company as the foundation of its case, said Barnard. “Typically, jurors will reject that because they want to do a good job. If jurors feel that [the prosecution] is relying on such tactics … that is something that is not likely to resonate with jurors and will actually create a backlash,” he said. “Based on my experience of watching hundreds of jurors deliberate and speaking to jurors after trials, what often comes through is that jurors really want to do the right thing, and that typically means applying the law as they understand it.” The trial is expected to run until December.

title: Iran says tanker exploded in Strait of Hormuz as US rejects account
description: IRGC says vessel hit sea mine in waterway as CENTCOM accuses Tehran of drone strike and intimidation.
content: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said late on Monday that an oil tanker had struck a sea mine and exploded in the Strait of Hormuz. The tanker El Gaia was travelling along the southern route through the strait, which was mined by Iran, state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the IRGC. The entire vessel went up in flames following the detonation of the mine, it said. The US military rejected that account. “The Panama-flagged oil tanker El Gaia was struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable. This weekend, Iran struck the tanker again with a drone while the ship sat in waters off the coast of Oman,” US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on social media. “The tanker is currently being towed by a regional partner. The IRGC’s false claim is yet another example of their lies and intimidation attempts while they try to impede commercial vessels in the strait.” The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization reported El Gaia was damaged on Saturday, but did not say how, and that two seafarers were missing. The IRGC’s naval command reportedly stated that “the Strait of Hormuz is closed and remains under our control”. It had previously warned against using the southern route. The navy has mined the southern passage, declared only a northern route along the Iranian coast to be safe and is charging fees for passage. The Strait of Hormuz has become a central point of contention between Tehran and Washington in the Iran war. Before the war, around a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through the strait. Liquefied natural gas and fertiliser from the Gulf states are also exported via this route. A meeting of foreign ministers from Gulf states scheduled for this Monday to discuss the Strait of Hormuz was cancelled at short notice. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: In Focus | New York City’s rich Chinese grapple with Beijing tax rules as enforcement deadline nears
description: With the 90-day grace period soon to run out, some ultra-wealthy living outside mainland China face complicated tax liability questions.
content: Months after Beijing unveiled a bevy of new tax rules for offshore trusts, the fallout has now reached New York City – home to one of the largest concentrations of mainland Chinese wealth outside Asia – after the changes swept across Hong Kong and Singapore. Under the rules, which took effect on July 24, mainland tax residents who transfer property or shares into an offshore trust – or receive distributions from one – face a 20 per cent tax on realised gains, plus an annual tax on income the trust generates. A 90-day grace period, running to October 22, allows taxpayers to declare and settle liabilities dating back to January 1, 2023, without incurring late-payment interest or administrative penalties. With just over one month before that window closes, advisers serving New York’s Chinese community said affluent families were racing to review their cross-border wealth holdings. “We’ve seen a clear uptick in families and their advisers reviewing existing offshore trusts,” said Larry Ikard, CEO of Yuvarra, an independent lender serving high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs). The greater worry, he said, was not the tax bill itself but whether a decades-old structure could “still deliver the original goals – protection, succession and practical liquidity – once ownership and family circumstances start changing”. Closing the capital loophole Offshore trusts have long been the bedrock of global wealth management for China’s elite, allowing for risk mitigation and serving as quiet vaults for succession planning and cross-border asset allocation. More than half of the country’s ultra-HNWIs – typically defined as those with a net worth or investible assets of at least US$30 million in value – managed their wealth using such vehicles, according to a report from KPMG, and frequently transferred shares or capital into entities registered in low-tax jurisdictions. Among the venues most favoured by Chinese investors are the Cayman Islands and the British Virgin Islands. The practice has expanded rapidly over the past two decades, as Chinese entrepreneurs sought access to international capital markets and global investments. Boston Consulting Group estimated that up to US$1.2 trillion in mainland wealth now sat in offshore, low-tax hubs, including Hong Kong and Singapore. Yet this staggering offshore capital pool created a persistent dilemma for Beijing: a massive, unchecked outflow of domestic wealth that left multibillion-dollar capital gains entirely outside the reach of tax authorities. While we cannot say there is a panic, we can definitely feel stress from our clients and other stakeholders Jean-Francois Harvey, Harvey Law Group To stem illicit capital flight and close these long-standing regulatory loopholes, Beijing is taking direct aim at the structure. Under the new policies, Chinese tax residents face a 20 per cent levy on assets transferred into offshore trusts, annual investment yields and ultimate liquidation payouts. In a joint statement announcing the measures, the authorities said the rules were designed to prevent individuals from using opaque, low-tax jurisdictions to “transfer assets, conceal wealth and evade tax”. Li Daokui, a Tsinghua University economist and former member of the People’s Bank of China’s monetary policy committee, further noted in a social media post in early August that this approach established explicit tax obligations across every stage of a trust’s life cycle – from set-up and operation to eventual termination. High-profile tycoons are already feeling the pinch. Soho China co-founders Pan Shiyi and Zhang Xin, who now live in New York, hold a major portion of their fortune via a Cayman Islands discretionary trust created before the developer’s 2007 Hong Kong listing. Domestic media reports indicated the structure could be exposed to billions of yuan in back-tax claims. A wider circle of entrepreneurs who once relied on offshore trusts to list companies abroad – including Pinduoduo’s Colin Huang, Xiaomi’s Lei Jun, Haidilao founder Zhang Yong and Longfor’s Wu Yajun – are also being closely watched for how they handle potential deferred liabilities. A calibrated approach to wealth For affluent Chinese families navigating cross-border holdings, the immediate concern is more than the 20 per cent tax bill – it is what the crackdown suggests about Beijing’s evolving posture towards private capital. “While we cannot say there is a panic, we can definitely feel stress from our clients and other stakeholders,” said Jean-Francois Harvey, founder and managing partner of Harvey Law Group. The deeper anxiety, he noted, was not merely the added financial cost, but “the Pandora’s box it may open” by pulling decades of offshore assets into sharp regulatory focus. Yet market analysts cautioned against viewing the offshore trust tax as a blunt war on private wealth creation. Instead, they said, the move reflected a broader, deliberate pivot to redirect capital into strategic domestic sectors crucial to China’s long-term industrial ambitions. The relative value of onshore and offshore assets shifts with economic cycles, a gap that periodically drives speculative “hot money” across borders, as investors seek higher short-term returns. That back-and-forth flow of capital, however, has done little to help the “real economy”, according to Xiao Geng, associate dean of the School of Public Policy at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen. Bringing offshore assets into a clear regulatory fold, he added, created a more predictable and stable environment that encouraged long-term investment at home. As decades of rapid expansion driven by real estate and speculative asset appreciation wind down, China is seeking more sustainable growth drivers. Strategic industries – including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing and renewable energy – have moved up on Beijing’s list of long-term economic priorities. China’s gross domestic product surpassed 140 trillion yuan (US$20.9 trillion) in 2025, expanding 5 per cent year on year. Within that total, added value generated by the “three new” economies – encompassing new industries, new business formats and new models – reached 25.79 trillion yuan, growing 6.2 per cent and outpacing overall economic growth. To foster growth in these sectors, enterprises that are officially recognised as hi-tech qualify for a preferential 15 per cent corporate income tax rate, compared with the standard 25 per cent, while technical staff who receive equity rewards for commercialised research could defer personal income tax payments for up to five years. The Private Economy Promotion Law, which took effect in May last year, backs private investment and entrepreneurship in strategic emerging and future industries, while offering stronger intellectual property protections. This shift is increasingly reflected in China’s wealth rankings, where tech innovators are displacing real estate tycoons. Forbes’ 2026 ranking put ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming at the top for the first time, while Xiaomi’s Lei Jun broke into the top 10 and Cambricon Technologies’ Chen Tianshi became the country’s wealthiest figure in the semiconductor industry. Levying taxes on offshore trusts, Xiao said, could help build “a clear, regulated framework” for cross-border capital flows and support China’s economic transition – measures he said would ultimately help stabilise both emerging tech drivers and traditional sectors. The residency question For New York City-based ultra-HNWIs, the immediate complication is determining whether they still fall under Beijing’s jurisdiction. Under the refined rules, an individual can be classified as a Chinese tax resident based on where their “primary economic interest” lies, not physical presence. A US green-card holder in Manhattan could still be a Chinese tax resident if their equity, corporate control or dividend income remains tied to the mainland. The picture is murkier still for mixed-residency families, who face a more tangled set of questions – including how the “primary economic interest” test interacts with existing tax treaties – that practitioners said remained unresolved. Waiting out the deadline is not a realistic option, either. Under the Common Reporting Standard (CRS), overseas institutions will send account details to Beijing by September 30, regardless of whether individual taxpayers have filed anything themselves. While some were exploring options to fast-track citizenship in third nations to relinquish Chinese nationality, Harvey said he doubted many would make it in time. “The odds of securing alternative citizenship in time … are exceptionally low, making this a mid-to-long-term fix,” he said, adding that many clients would still face hefty tax payments this autumn. Others are eyeing the US itself as a potential shelter, since Washington sits outside the CRS and does not automatically share domestic bank account data with foreign authorities. Advisers cautioned that the reasoning for this tactic was flawed. The US enforces compliance through its own Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act – requiring foreign institutions to report on US taxpayers’ offshore accounts – and stringent beneficial ownership information mandates. These frameworks imposed heavy tax and disclosure obligations on individuals, trusts and corporate structures, Ikard noted. He added that US tax law imposes a higher burden on non-resident aliens for estate or inheritance taxes. Unlike US citizens and green-card holders who enjoy a lifetime estate-tax exemption of roughly US$15 million, non-resident aliens receive an exemption of just US$60,000 upon death, with tax rates climbing to 40 per cent on any excess. “Simply parking assets in a non-CRS jurisdiction like the US does not automatically remove Chinese tax exposure for people still connected to the mainland,” Ikard said. “Moving the problem from one set of rules to another is rarely a clean solution.” The competitive edge will belong to places that can stay with families after the initial structures are in place … Not just attract the capital in the first place Larry Ikard, Yuvarra A shift to compliance Rather than rushing to liquidate assets, advisers reported that affluent families were taking a measured approach to bring their holdings into compliance before the deadline. They laid out a typical timeline: starting with rapid fact-finding on historical transfers and valuations, then preparing voluntary disclosures that cover 2023–2025 liabilities before the grace period lapses. They would then widen the review to whether trusts, insurance policies and financing arrangements still worked together as a coherent whole. A minority of clients were considering partial distributions, or limited restructuring, where doing so clearly reduced exposure or improved flexibility, but full unwinding remained uncommon, the advisers said. They added that most families preferred to adapt an existing platform rather than start over – and guidance was still evolving in places – but the deadline was firm enough that waiting was no longer the safer option for anyone with material exposure. “The vast majority of sophisticated families are focusing on understanding their exposure and preparing for compliance rather than making rushed structural changes,” said Neil Synnott, regional chief commercial officer for Asia-Pacific at IQ-EQ, a global investor services group. “The conversation has shifted from ‘How do we optimise taxes?’ to ‘How do we demonstrate transparency, control and compliance across jurisdictions?’” Wealth managers said they were not expecting Chinese families to abandon offshore trusts altogether. Instead, most anticipated a shift towards a structure built on stronger commercial, governance and succession rationales rather than pure tax minimisation. Across Asia, Synnott said, wealth owners increasingly wanted institutional-grade frameworks around their private capital, with greater emphasis on governance, reporting and operational infrastructure – a shift that was already under way before the new rules, but one they were likely to accelerate. “Greater regulatory clarity often encourages more disciplined planning and gives families a clearer framework within which to operate,” Synnott said. “In many markets, uncertainty is a bigger deterrent than taxation itself.” For Hong Kong and other established Asia wealth hubs, that dynamic could prove an advantage rather than a threat, Ikard said, pointing to predictable regulation, deep professional expertise and the ability to support families across generations. “The competitive edge will belong to places that can stay with families after the initial structures are in place,” he said. “Not just attract the capital in the first place.”

title: Beijing threatens ‘serious consequences’ after Panama lawmakers support Taiwan
description: Parliamentary exchange group set up despite pressure from China’s embassy and public disavowal by Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino.
content: China has warned Panama of “serious consequences” after most of the country’s lawmakers set up a parliamentary exchange group with Taiwan, defying pressure from Beijing’s embassy and a public disavowal by their own president. The warning came from foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun, who said on Monday that the group seriously violated the one-China principle upheld by Panama and urged what he called “those few politicians” to “see the real picture”. Beijing had noted the Panamanian government’s statement on the matter, he said, and hoped Panama would honour its commitment “with real actions to uphold the political foundation of China-Panama relations”. Guo devoted the closing part of his answer to Washington, urging the United States to abide by the one-China principle and the three joint communiques that underpin its recognition of Beijing, and to “stop disrupting and sabotaging China-Panama relations”. Panamanian deputies installed the body on September 8 at a closed-door ceremony in the National Assembly, nine years after Panama broke off relations with Taipei to recognise Beijing. Medin Jimenez, the Panamanian deputy heading the group, said 45 of the chamber’s 71 members signed the founding document and that others backed it but were unable to sign while it circulated in the plenary. New group breaks no rules, Panama lawmakers claim Panama recognised Taipei for decades before the 2017 switch, and commercial and academic ties survived the rupture, which lawmakers have used to argue that the group breaks no rules. Jimenez presented it as a commercial project, pointing to the free-trade agreement in force since January 2004, which outlived the diplomatic break, and to more than US$158 million in seafood and other Panamanian exports to Taiwan in the last financial year. Lawmakers involved were careful with the name, calling it a “multiparty exchange group” rather than a friendship group, a distinction that separates a gesture Panama can defend as legislative business from one Beijing treats as informal recognition. Joan Guevara, who chairs the assembly’s foreign relations committee and hosted the session, said the term was ruled out because “Panama has no diplomatic relations with Taiwan and the conduct of such relations belongs to the executive branch”. Taiwan’s foreign ministry described the body as a Taiwan-friendly parliamentary group and said assembly president Shirley Castanedas and two vice-presidents had joined, though the assembly has not confirmed the membership list. Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung recorded a congratulatory video for the ceremony, in which he said he looked forward to “deepening parliamentary diplomacy and expanding cooperation”. The launch followed nearly a year of parliamentary traffic to Taipei that Panama’s government had already disowned twice, with three delegations of deputies visiting the island since November. The lawmakers met Vice-President Hsiao Bi-khim, Lin and Legislative Yuan president Han Kuo-yu, and a mission in January discussed semiconductors and possible trade representation mechanisms. President Jose Raul Mulino distanced his government from the group within hours without taking any measures against it. “I reiterate: the approaches, trips and exchanges of assembly members with Taiwan do not mean that the executive endorses them,” he wrote on X. The Chinese embassy in Panama City expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm rejection” hours after the ceremony and demanded the deputies rectify their position, prompting several of them to accuse Beijing of interfering in the legislature. “The legislature has every faculty, power and responsibility to relate to the parliaments it wishes,” independent deputy Luis Duke said, adding that the group was not interfering in bilateral diplomacy because that was a matter for the executive. Panamanian diplomatic sources told the news site Infobae that Chinese officials had called, written and sought urgent meetings to stop the launch and had threatened some lawmakers. The embassy has not commented on those accounts. China keeps the pressure on Panama Beijing’s warning landed weeks after the two countries pulled back from a confrontation over the canal through which about five per cent of world seaborne trade passes. Panama’s Supreme Court ruled in January that the concession held since 1997 by Panama Ports Company, a CK Hutchison subsidiary, over the Balboa and Cristobal terminals at either end of the waterway was unconstitutional. The state took over both ports in February and handed them to units of Maersk and Mediterranean Shipping Company, prompting CK Hutchison to begin arbitration seeking more than US$2 billion and Beijing to warn that Panama would pay a heavy price. Detentions of Panamanian-flagged vessels in Chinese ports rose from March to about 470 in the first half of the year, against 256 in all of last year, according to figures compiled by Panama’s maritime chamber. The data comes from the Tokyo Memorandum, the Asia-Pacific regime under which port authorities inspect foreign ships, and Mulino said more than 200 vessels left the Panamanian registry, the largest in the world, describing the inspections as carrying a political message. Detentions returned to normal levels in June, and negotiators met in Beijing in July and agreed to renew a maritime transport agreement that expires this year. Neither government has said whether it has been signed.

title: Opinion | The classic Chinese parenting playbook won’t survive the AI age
description: Controlling and achievement-oriented parenting stifles creativity, autonomy and critical thinking – qualities that will be needed more than ever.
content: Like many Hong Kong parents, Ms Ng spends her weekend shuttling her eight-year-old son from one tutoring class to another across the city, hoping to strengthen his academic performance. Across Chinese communities worldwide, parents travel the same journey, investing time, money and energy. But as we enter the age of artificial intelligence, we must ask if such striving is still worthwhile. Industry leaders predict that AI will replace swathes of white-collar work in finance, law, accounting and computing, whereas blue-collar jobs such as plumbing, electrical or construction work remain largely irreplaceable. The reasons for this may not be what you think. Psychologist David Geary distinguished between two classes of cognitive ability. Biologically primary abilities such as speaking, counting and basic social understanding develop in all human children with minimal formal instruction. Biologically secondary abilities such as reading, writing and formal mathematics require sustained learning and only develop in specific cultural contexts. Richard Dawkins’ concept of the extended phenotype adds another layer. Dawkins argued that genes also express themselves beyond the organism, through its effects on the environment. For humans, our culture and technology are our extended phenotype. What we lack biologically, we make up for through accumulated knowledge, cultural products and technological advancement. In this framework, while AI represents the culmination of our extended phenotype and will replace us at our secondary abilities, it cannot replace our primary attributes. Physical presence, face-to-face communication and the tangible performance of a job that requires a body in a specific place at a specific time cannot be faked or replaced. The distinction between replaceable and irreplaceable work is not physical vs cognitive, but whether the work involves the physical person. Large-language models can generate a legal brief but cannot stand in a courtroom and argue with conviction. Music AI agents can write and sing but cannot perform on stage with the charisma of a live musician. A medical algorithm can diagnose diseases and its embodied AI can perform surgeries, but they cannot hold a patient’s hand while discussing the diagnosis or working out a treatment plan. A plumber fixing the sink or a kindergarten teacher comforting a crying child cannot be replaced by AI. This principle extends to athletic abilities, physical prowess, motor agility and any talent that involves the body, such as playing an instrument, dribbling a basketball or rolling a pencil across the fingers. Similarly with social interaction: in a post-AI world, the ability to connect with others in person, to look someone in the eye and communicate effectively, will define success more than any written products. These are all primary abilities, grounded in the physical self. Elon Musk predicts that AI and robotics will produce goods and services in such abundance that humans will no longer need to work. What will humans do then? John Calhoun’s “Universe 25” experiment placed mice in an environment of total abundance. One discovery about the mice, which the researcher called “the beautiful ones”, was their exclusive focus on grooming, maintenance and physical presentation. If Musk’s prediction holds, human behaviour may follow a similar path. A post-AI world will reward not the accumulation of knowledge but the presence of a real person who can speak, connect, create and decide Evolutionary fitness, in the ultimate sense, is about bringing out the best and maximum of a species’ primary attributes. It means being physically and mentally viable, resisting diseases and stresses, handling crises, making sound decisions under pressure and bouncing back from defeat. In a post-AI world of plenty, these primary attributes will be the new currency. It’s not just about looking good. It’s about being the survivor of the physically fittest in the truest Darwinian sense. Our focus should shift from the acquisition and accumulation of knowledge per se to critical thinking, creative problem-solving, inquisitive questioning, curious inquiring and sound decision-making. These are primary mental faculties that define human cognition. They are what our ancestors used to navigate uncertain environments and will be what we use to navigate the post-AI world where machines handle the tasks of secondary abilities. So how should parents raise children for the post-AI age? Chinese parenting is known for being authoritarian, controlling and achievement-oriented, specifically oriented to academic achievement. Authoritarian and controlling parenting stifles creativity, autonomy and critical thinking. When children are constantly told what to do and how to do it, they rarely learn to question, imagine or decide for themselves. Its academic focus is mostly on secondary abilities. Memorising facts, mastering formulas and even learning to write in a particular style are all things AI can do faster and better. Instead, focusing on physical training, social development and higher-order cognitive abilities redirects, rightfully, Chinese priorities away from the extended phenotype, what humans have created, towards the physical person, who we are. Western parenting, which tends to be more authoritative than authoritarian, is more suited to the post-AI world. Research shows that authoritative and supportive parenting encourages autonomy, supports individual expression, and fosters creativity and critical thinking. Yet Western parenting can be permissive, lacking the structure and supervision that help children develop resilience and perseverance and discriminate against misinformation. It may also undervalue the physical rigour and discipline that come from structured training, whether in sports, music or other embodied skills. Shuttling an eight-year-old across tutoring centres may not be the best investment of parenting effort for a post-AI world that will reward not the accumulation of knowledge but the presence of a real person who can speak, connect, create and decide. Parenting should aim to cultivate primary abilities, raising children who are physically fit, socially skilled, creatively minded and critically thoughtful, while letting AI perfect the tasks that depend on our secondary abilities.

title: US has weapons deployed in orbit, Space Force says
description: US acknowledges offensive and defensive capabilities against potential ‘hostile adversary action’.
content: The United States has weapons deployed in space, the US Space Force said on Monday, confirming the presence of such capabilities in orbit for the first time. “The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” a US Space Force spokesperson said in a statement that did not provide specifics on the weapons. “Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities,” the statement said, adding that “these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”. Both Russia and China – the two main geopolitical rivals of the United States – pose potential threats to US interests in space. China “develops and operates space and counter-space capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy”, while Russia “views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts”, according to the US Space Force. The militarisation of space is as old as the space race itself – as soon as Sputnik was launched into orbit in 1957, Washington and Moscow began exploring ways to both arm and destroy satellites. The biggest worry was once about nuclear weapons in space, but the superpowers and other countries signed the Outer Space Treaty in 1967, banning weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Since then, Russia, the United States, China and India have explored ways to fight in space outside that treaty, including by targeting rivals’ satellites, which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

title: Prince Harry’s children changing schools over security concerns
description: Decision comes weeks after the Sussexes’ return from the US and as the UK government reviews protection status.
content: The children of Britain’s Prince Harry and his wife ⁠Meghan are to swap ⁠schools after just two days because of ⁠concerns over the security of transporting them, the couple’s spokesperson said on Monday. Last month Harry, the younger son of King Charles, and his family relocated to Britain after six years of living in California, with Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, starting ‌school in September. The location of their new home and details of the children’s school have been kept private. But on Monday, a spokesperson for the couple, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, confirmed reports that Archie and Lilibet were changing schools after just two days. The distance between their home and the original school, with heavy traffic in the area, had caused concern for their security ⁠team. “The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security ‌team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” the spokesperson said. “The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they ‌have shown their family. This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection ⁠on the school or ⁠the exceptional care the children have received there.” The couple stepped down from royal duties and moved to the United States in 2020, ‌leading to estrangement and awkward relations with the royal family as they delivered a series of barbed comments about the institution. Their return came ‌as a ‌surprise, with even the monarch unaware of their plans until just days before it became public. Harry ‌and Meghan are not living in a royal residence and will remain non-working royals, as agreed with ⁠the late Queen Elizabeth before their move. Their status as private citizens was confirmed in a letter authorised by ⁠King Charles and sent to senior British officials last week, a step which their spokesperson said had come as a surprise to Harry and Meghan. The prince has also been critical of ‌the government’s decision to strip him ‌and his family of automatic police protection afforded to other senior royals, with a bespoke system put in place instead. Harry’s security is currently being reviewed by a government committee and the couple’s spokesperson confirmed that Meghan’s situation is also being looked at again for the first time since they moved away from Britain.

title: UN Security Council to meet on AI threat as rights chief warns of ‘unprecedented risks’
description: France calls high-level session during General Assembly amid urgent pleas to govern frontier models.
content: The UN Security Council will hold a meeting on artificial intelligence next week amid growing international concern over the threat from the fast moving technology, a French diplomatic source said on Monday. The meeting would be held during the United Nations General Assembly when a host of world leaders are at the UN headquarters in New York and France holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council. No details were given on the exact day. “In terms of global affairs, the issue of AI will be very high on the agenda through two different angles,” the diplomatic source told reporters, highlighting “the existential threat” that AI poses to global security as well as the risks for children. The United Nations rights chief, Volker Turk, called on Monday for countries and “frontier” artificial intelligence companies to act urgently to rein in a technology he warned posed “unprecedented risks”. In a letter sent to countries and AI developers and shared with the media, Turk cautioned that the world was “on the cusp of irreversible change, affecting not just us but generations of humanity to come”. “The current race towards ever more powerful AI is a step change towards greater existential risks to every aspect of our lives.” “I call on states and companies to mobilise urgently through multilateral fora to chart a path for action to govern advanced, frontier AI models, grounded in international human rights law.” The safety of AI has hit global headlines in recent weeks with even some AI technology company chiefs saying there has to be greater regulation to slow down development. But US President Donald Trump on Monday slammed suggestions that AI poses a threat to humanity, calling it a “hoax” and a “sick conspiracy”. The source said that events in Gaza, Lebanon and Ukraine would also feature strongly at the UN General Assembly and that France as monthly head of the Security Council and current G7 president would seek to defend multilateralism at a time when international institutions face mounting pressure.

title: Famed ‘Designer to the Stars’ Bob Mackie dead at 87
description: Oscars, Emmys, and Broadway creator dressed generations of icons from Marilyn Monroe and Cher to Zendaya.
content: Bob Mackie, the fashion designer whose visually provocative Hollywood style defined glamour for the 1970s – including putting Carol Burnett in some of her kookiest get-ups and Cher in her raciest ones – died on Monday. He was 87. “He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement on his social media accounts. Mackie died in Palm Springs, California, from pneumonia, his publicist said. Dubbed the “Designer to the Stars”, Mackie won nine Emmys, a Tony and was nominated for three Oscars, including one for Barbra Streisand’s 1975 film Funny Lady, in which she wore a sheer batwing gown. He was inducted into the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences’ Hall of Fame in 2002. Mackie designed gowns for Madonna, Streisand, Sharon Stone, Diana Ross, Whoopi Goldberg and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and concert costumes for Pink. When Marilyn Monroe delivered a breathy, seductive take on “Happy Birthday” at a fundraiser for President John F. Kennedy and the Democratic National Committee, she did it in a sheer, beaded gown that Mackie dreamed up in a sketch. His influence can be seen in the styles of Kendall Jenner and Bella Hadid. His archival pieces are worn today by the likes of Anya Taylor-Joy, Miley Cyrus and Zendaya, the latter who wore a Mackie gown to honour Cher at the 2024 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony. When Taylor Swift wanted to look like a showgirl on the cover of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl, she turned to some Mackie originals. Tributes came from fellow designers and those lucky enough to wear Mackie’s outfits. Actress Kristin Chenoweth called him a “legend” and designer Isaac Mizrahi wrote, simply, “heartbroken”. Actress Alyssa Milano called him “one of the best that ever was”. On Broadway, Mackie dressed the casts of On the Town in 1971 and Moon Over Buffalo in 1995. He also created costumes for Burnett in the revue Putting It Together, Debbie Reynolds in Debbie in 1976, Liza Minnelli in Minnelli on Minnelli in 1999 and, most recently, the cast of The Cher Show, winning his Tony Award. Mackie, from California, embraced the idea of Hollywood movie glamour as a young child, inspired by Technicolor musicals. He would dream elaborate costumes for his mother and sister and sketch them, and he was active in costume and set design of his high school plays. He went to Pasadena City College to study advertising and illustration, and then costume design at LA’s Chouinard Art Institute. He went to work for costume designer Edith Head, then got the job for The Carol Burnett Show. He and Burnett had a close friendship and collaborated on memorable characters such as Nora Desmond, Eunice and her take on Scarlett O’Hara in Gone With the Wind – called Starlet O’Hara – wearing her green curtain dress on its rods. Mackie’s television work continued on The Sonny and Cher Show, after Cher had guest-starred on Burnett’s show and took a liking to him. When Cher moved to films Mackie was invited to the Academy Awards. All those beaded, belly-baring outfits she wore on the red carpets came from Mackie. Mackie attended the 1974 Met Gala with Cher on his arm dressed in what is perhaps one of the most famous so-called naked dresses of all time: a sheer beaded gown with white feathered sleeves and a white feathered skirt. She and the dress ended up on the cover of Time magazine. Looks such as the 1986 beaded spiderweb – worn with complementary Mohawk – and the barely-there gown she wore for her best actress win in 1988 turned heads and set tongues wagging at the time. “The outfits are sometimes mistaken for fashion, but they’re costumes like for a character in a play,” Mackie said in 1999. “I want people to have fun. I want people to say ‘Wasn’t that interesting?’ or ‘Wasn’t that wild?’” Mackie had some retail success in the 1980s and 1990s, launching a ready-to-wear line in 1982 that would ultimately land on the catwalk at New York Fashion Week, and he was an early partner of QVC. Mackie also created dozens of different Barbie dolls for Mattel, with a wide variety of face sculpts, body types and storylines. He is credited as the first designer to create a complete doll. One was Lady Dracula Cher, with little baby fangs and her box resembling a coffin. The documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion debuted in 2024. A Mackie dress Cher wore in 1975 was auctioned off in 2024 for US$101,600, 25 times its original estimate. Mackie was married to showgirl Lulu Porter from 1960 until 1963; their son, make-up artist Robert Gordon Mackie Jnr, died from Aids at 35. Costume designer Ray Aghayan, Mackie’s long-time partner, died in 2011. He had said practicality was never a driving force in his design: “It’s all about looking good and living your fantasies.” In 2017, a 71-year-old Cher once again turned heads, dressed in two Bob Mackie specials at the Billboard Music Awards. It was a blast from a different era, unlike the boring fashion world he saw. “Nothing is very interesting any more,” he told Vogue in 2017. “You just keep seeing the same thing over and over again and there are no surprises. Unfortunately, you don’t see much fashion any more.”

title: Israeli army chief orders legal review of award-winning Gaza war film NAZA
description: Israeli-made Gaza documentary makes waves after winning the Venice special jury prize.
content: Israel’s top military officer on Monday ordered lawyers to examine steps against the filmmakers behind the Gaza war documentary NAZA that took the jury’s special prize at the Venice Film Festival. Chief of the General Staff Eyal Zamir instructed the military prosecutor to “examine and advance possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it”, the military posted on social media. The statement cited “the spread of false claims about soldiers of the Israeli army as well as possible implications for their personal safety and the security of the state”. NAZA by Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham examines the alleged mechanisms behind Israeli warfare in Gaza. In it, Abraham interviews 24 Israeli military and intelligence staff, with their voices and faces rendered unrecognisable. Those interviewed describe how targets in Gaza were selected and how many civilian casualties were factored into attacks. The film’s title derives from the Hebrew acronym for collateral damage. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu termed the film shocking. “We are fighting against antisemitic incitement worldwide, but when it comes from within our own ranks, it is intolerable,” he said in a video statement. The Israeli military has rejected the allegations made in the film. It particularly criticised the documentary for relying on anonymous sources whose identities and actual roles within the military cannot be independently verified. The army also denied claims regarding the use of artificial intelligence, stating that decisions on the selection and approval of strikes are made exclusively by human personnel. Zamir said this was not a critical film about the Israeli army but defamation and a “deliberate distortion of reality”. The army would “use all means at its disposal” to protect its soldiers and the military’s reputation, he said. In the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023, around 1,200 people were killed in Israel and more than 250 others were abducted to Gaza as hostages. The unprecedented attack triggered the Gaza war. Since then, according to the Hamas-controlled health authority, more than 73,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza.

title: Trump Jnr confirms Russian businessman paid for post-wedding parties
description: Couple defends gift from IBA head and ‘dear friend’ Umar Kremlev following investigative report.
content: A Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin paid for celebrations after the wedding of President Donald Trump’s eldest son and his new bride, the couple confirmed on Monday. Donald Trump Jnr and Bettina Trump said in a jointly signed post on Bettina’s Instagram account that their “dear friend” Umar Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights” of festivities in the Bahamas in May. The confirmation came after the ProPublica investigative website reported that Kremlev footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” said the post by Bettina and Don Jnr. President Trump did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to stay in Washington during talks on the Iran war. Kremlev is head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), with which the International Olympic Committee severed links after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns. Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the “Order of Friendship” award in April 2026, according to an IBA press release, which featured a photo of Putin and Kremlev shaking hands. “During the ceremony, the Russian President praised the IBA’s resilience in supporting athletes despite political pressures,” the IBA statement said. The IBA website also featured photos of Donald Trump Jnr on stage with Kremlev at an event in Istanbul in September 2025. Bettina Trump’s Instagram post was accompanied by 20 photos including one of the newlywed couple on a beach, and others of President Trump’s other children Eric Trump, Ivanka Trump and Tiffany Trump. “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” the post added. ProPublica posted a group photo from the wedding that it said showed the top of Kremlev’s head. According to Russian investigative media outlet Proekt, Kremlev is a Tajik native who worked as a mid-level boxing promoter and cultivated links with the Federal Protective Service (FSO), whose role is to protect high-level officials in Russia. Kremlev is also a member of the pro-Kremlin Night Wolves biker club, it reported. Members of the Night Wolves rode down en masse to Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula just after it was annexed by Russia in March 2014 and members have also fought side by side with pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine. Trump Jnr has previously been scrutinised over his Russian ties. During the 2016 campaign, his meeting with Russian lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya in Trump Tower was the subject of intense scrutiny by federal and congressional investigators probing whether the Trump campaign coordinated with Russia to meddle in the election. The meeting had been billed as an opportunity to discuss potentially incriminating information about the president’s then-Democrat opponent, Hillary Rodham Clinton, as part of the Russian government’s efforts to help Trump Jnr’s father win the White House. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: British man admits drugging, raping wife over more than 2 decades
description: Man pleads guilty to dozens of charges in Manchester court as 12 co-defendants face trial.
content: A British man on ⁠Monday admitted repeatedly drugging and raping his wife at their home over more than two decades, shortly before his trial was about to begin. The man – from northern England who ‌is in his 60s but cannot be named as it would identify his wife who is entitled to lifelong anonymity – pleaded guilty at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court to 45 charges, having previously admitted 15 offences. The man has now admitted charges including ⁠21 counts of rape, 15 counts of assault by penetration, 11 counts ‌of sexual assault and one count of sharing intimate images without consent in a period between 2004 and 2025. He ‌has also admitted an offence of administering a substance in ⁠order to ⁠stupefy his wife. Prosecutors say the woman was repeatedly raped and sexually assaulted in her own ‌home while she was unconscious, having been drugged by her husband. A dozen other men, aged ‌28 ‌to 74, are also charged with sexually abusing the victim from ‌2018 until 2025 and have all denied the offences which include ⁠rape. “Our focus remains on supporting the victim of this horrific campaign of abuse ⁠through what is a very complex investigation,” said Greater Manchester Police Assistant Chief Constable Rick Jackson. “Specialist support continues to be ‌provided to the ‌victim at the centre of this case.” The other men’s trial is due to take place at the same court and is expected to take several months. It is the latest in a string of UK criminal cases related to drug-facilitated sexual abuse (DFSA). Global awareness of the crime has grown following the high-profile conviction in France of Dominique Pelicot, who drugged and raped his then-wife Gisele for nearly a decade alongside strangers. In a separate case last week, a London man pleaded guilty to encouraging other men in an online group chat to sexually abuse their unconscious partners and exchange images of the abuse. And later this week, a man is due to be sentenced in central England after pleading guilty in July to 32 sexual offences against his girlfriend while she was allegedly drugged or asleep. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: German intelligence report warns of rising Chinese, Russian spy threat
description: A report by Germany’s counter-intelligence agency said some surveillance activities targeting military infrastructure can be linked to China.
content: Germany’s military counter-intelligence agency, known as MAD, has warned of a growing threat from hybrid attacks and the use of recruited contract agents, or low-level agents, saying Germany is a “prioritised target of Russian espionage activities”. According to the agency’s annual report released on Monday, it cited Germany’s geostrategic position in Europe and Nato the expansion of the Bundeswehr and the introduction of new weapons systems as reasons for the heightened targeting. “The hybrid threat situation in Germany has continued to deteriorate,” MAD says. These include cyberattacks, drone attacks, attempts at political influence, and disruptive attacks targeting transport, energy facilities and telecommunications. MAD said the potential threat of sabotage by low-level agents has also increased significantly. The report does not provide comparative figures, which could lead adversaries to draw conclusions from the data. It notes that embassies and semi-governmental organisations provide cover for Russian spying and also mentions press agencies. MAD expressed concern about German military staff travelling abroad, noting that some members of the armed forces had travelled to Russia and Belarus, often to visit family. During these trips, they had reportedly come to the attention of the respective intelligence services. “This creates a particular vulnerability to blackmail and threats from the security authorities there,” the report stated. Turning to China, the report noted that at least some surveillance activities targeting military infrastructure, including drone overflights and intrusions onto Bundeswehr property, can be attributed to Chinese intelligence services. These services also make use of the Chinese diaspora. The MAD has also recorded an increasing number of suspected cases of right-wing extremism within the Bundeswehr. In 2025, a total of 519 new “case investigations” relating to this area were opened, up from 413 in 2024, representing an increase of around 26 per cent. According to the report, the MAD identified 11 armed forces staff as right-wing extremists last year and 21 individuals for whom there was credible evidence giving rise to suspicion of disloyalty to the constitution. The report highlights incidents involving sexual misconduct, drugs and extremism among paratroopers, which repeatedly made the headlines. New youth groups are said to be gaining influence particularly through the use of social media, and the MAD notes a continuing “blurring of boundaries” in right-wing extremism, with far-right views increasingly being “normalised”. According to the report, these groups have repeatedly been involved in right-wing extremist disruptive actions against public events such as Pride celebrations or attacks on political opponents.

title: Trump condemns ‘sick conspiracy’ against AI, says he is only guardrail needed
description: US president criticises industry leaders’ calls for slowdown in development, as it only benefits China in battle for global tech dominance.
content: US President Donald Trump downplayed growing concerns about artificial intelligence on Monday, claiming America already has guardrails to regulate the industry and warning that casting doubt on development only benefits China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ ‌that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on social media. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these ⁠companies! There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data ‌Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.” In recent months, the US president has accused China of amplifying anti-AI and anti-data centre rhetoric, a sentiment he appeared to echo in Monday’s post. Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to visit Washington later this month for a summit with his American counterpart, where AI is expected to be on the agenda. “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!” Trump wrote. The president’s comments come as concerns about AI continue to mount after Anthropic researchers warned that the technology may lead to human extinction in the next decade. They also follow weeks of reports of AI agents acting beyond their assigned tasks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday proposed a three-step framework to help pace AI development and allow more time to mitigate the risks of rapidly progressing technology.
