Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman were among the high-profile industry executives who quickly endorsed the proposal. Trump claimed US tools have already stopped AI executives from doing bad “things”, while singling out Anthropic’s boss, Amodei. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like ‌Dario (Anthropic!), who is now ‌pretending to be a ‘perfect little angel’ – and we will continue to do so,” Trump wrote. As industry leaders at some of the world’s largest AI companies called for a slowdown in the pace of technological development, AI-related stocks fell sharply on Monday. US House Speaker Mike ‌Johnson said that AI providers were expected to meet at the White ⁠House either later this week or early next week. Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic over concerns about how the technology was being developed, warned about the future capabilities of AI models. “You’re building a human-level or superhuman-level mind, without understanding what it wants, or thinks, or the way it thinks,” Coxon said. He also urged the US and China, the two countries leading in AI, to cooperate to slow down their development and address safety concerns. “I do hope that the people in China who are looking at the same problems as we are, so they’re trying to build the same technology, will come to the same conclusion that it has to be done in a measured manner, and it should be easy to cooperate on some sort of mutual slowing,” he said. On Sunday, Trump again downplayed the need to check AI development, citing concerns about ceding the US’ lead over China in the race for global AI supremacy. “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that … shouldn’t be bringing it up, and they’re bringing up things that won’t happen,” he said while in Ireland over the weekend. “But whoever wins with AI wins.” Trump’s second term as president has seen him largely embrace AI, encouraging US companies to innovate in the field and imposing minimal constraints on its development. AI and data centres are set to be a key issue for both Republicans and Democrats in the lead-up to November’s midterm elections.

title: Brics leaders act to hedge – not revolt – against US dollar dominance
description: As New Delhi summit closes, the bloc pushes for a louder voice within global institutions while building parallel machinery, analysts say.
content: The family photograph did the political work the summit’s final declaration could not. Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi stood shoulder to shoulder as the Brics summit closed in New Delhi on Sunday – a single frame capturing an 11-nation bloc that now spans four continents and nearly half the world’s population. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres attended the gathering of emerging economies alongside World Trade Organization Director General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, New Development Bank president Dilma Rousseff and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank president Zou Jiayi. As Washington leans on tariffs and steps back from the institutions it once dominated, the United Nations, the WTO and the WHO sat at a table built by the Global South. What the leaders signed – the New Delhi Declaration – was neither a revolt against the dollar nor a blueprint for a new world order. It was a hedge. Experts say the document treats de-dollarisation as insurance. By promoting local-currency settlement, linked payment rails and a louder voice within the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, Brics members aim to ensure trade keeps moving even if the United States turns its dollar, or the institutions around it, into a political weapon. “As we move irreversibly to a multipolar world, all countries must work to strengthen and safeguard a multilateral system that delivers for all with the United Nations at its centre,” Guterres told the summit. Multipolarity, he said, required “reforming multilateral institutions, including the UN Security Council and the Bretton Woods system, to reflect the world of today”. “From Gaza, to the broader crisis in the Middle East, to Ukraine, Sudan and beyond, our world needs peace.” Brics finance ministers and central bank governors had already set the economic demand. Before the summit they called for quota changes at the IMF, a bigger voice for emerging economies at the World Bank, and leadership contests not locked to the West. “We reiterate the urgent need to reform the Bretton Woods Institutions to enhance their legitimacy,” their joint statement said. India closed the door on the idea of a common Brics currency – a door US President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to slam. “There is no proposal in the Brics for a Brics currency, as of now,” Sudhakar Dalela, India’s Brics sherpa, told reporters on Saturday. He added that local-currency settlement was “a practical mechanism to reduce transaction cost in bilateral trade” and had been “encouraged as complementary to the global payment and settlement system”. The declaration sent the Brics Payment Task Force back to work on interoperable payment and messaging channels and on settling trade in members’ own currencies, “acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach”. Chinese scholars who follow the grouping describe a double movement: press the old institutions to make space, and build parallel machinery in case they do not. Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, pointed out that “dissatisfaction with the US-led international order” was one of the key reasons Brics was established. Members were seeking both to reform the existing system and to build new mechanisms. Liu said moves towards a Brics payment system and greater use of national currencies were “especially driven by the constraints imposed by the US dollar-dominated financial system, particularly on countries such as Russia and Iran”. “These measures will gradually change the international financial system and enhance the strategic autonomy of Brics countries,” Liu said. Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies said these efforts were easy to misread. “I’d say it’s less about de-dollarisation, since much of their trade will continue to be denominated in dollars, and more to do with lessening the capacity for dollar weaponisation,” he said. Invoices can stay in dollars. Gupta said payment itself could move to infrastructure over which the US Treasury did not have jurisdiction, such as a network of correspondent banks, and be “routed amongst themselves but outside the plumbing of the dollar-based system.” The secondary aim is slower. Members want to “build out their own local currencies-based trading and settling directly with counterparts”, he said. “But this process will take a much longer time. That’s where central bank digital currencies come in too, at a later date.” According to Gupta, the nearer-term prize is more precise: “Transact in dollars, and instantaneously, while sitting outside the back office market infrastructure that is an essential basis of the dollar’s centrality, and via which Treasury can flex its jurisdictional powers.” That infrastructure is why the dollar is more than a unit of account. Cross-border dollar payments still run, in large part, through correspondent banks, the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (Swift) messaging network and US-centred clearing. After 2022, Russia learned what happens when those channels close. Iran has lived with that constraint for far longer. Other Brics members have watched tariffs and secondary sanctions and drawn the lesson without wanting to announce it. A more public experiment is Brics Pay, developed through the Brics Business Council rather than as a finished intergovernmental system, which aims to let people pay in national currencies across member countries. It is not yet operational. Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, was sceptical about the scale of any shift. Members had a shared interest in reducing reliance on the US dollar after facing sanctions from Washington, he said, adding that local-currency payments were moving “slowly but steadily”, though a Brics currency remained unrealistic. “Even if local currencies are used for settlement, it would not have a major impact on the dollar system,” Lin said, because Brics’ economic power remained fragmented and its members were not sufficiently united. The work still mattered, he added, because it was strengthening members’ “strategic autonomy” and their ability to respond to US pressure. Sarang Shidore, director of the Global South Programme at the Quincy Institute, put the retail project in that same modest frame. “The idea is that of a decentralised system based on blockchain technology in which Brics-wide settlement will be done of transactions by, say, a Brazilian tourist paying a restaurant bill in Mumbai or a Chinese student buying a T-shirt in a store in Cape Town,” he said. “They’ll be able to do these transactions on their phone via QR codes. It will cut out intermediary credit card companies that charge fat commissions and are typically American, and also avoid intermediate steps of dollar conversion.” Even success would leave the core of dollar power untouched. “The system has ways to go before being adopted, with barriers present, including the question of political will,” Shidore said. “Several Global South states don’t want to create the impression that they are trying to ‘de-dollarise’.” “Brics Pay, even if it were fully functional, would not touch the big wholesale trade transactions between countries that matter much more to dollar usage,” Shidore said.

title: Singapore’s Chan Chun Sing to visit China, speak at defence forum
description: The three-day visit comes at the invitation of Chinese defence chief Dong Jun and underscores both countries’ ‘warm and friendly’ ties.
content: Singapore’s Defence Minister Chan Chun Sing is set to visit China from Tuesday to Thursday at the invitation of his Chinese counterpart Dong Jun and will speak at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum for the second consecutive year. His visit comes as defence analysts tell This Week in Asia that ties with Beijing are important for the city state’s balancing strategy with Washington. Singapore and the United States are close strategic partners with deep defence cooperation. Singapore’s defence ministry said in a statement on Monday that Chan would meet Dong and other senior Chinese and People’s Liberation Army (PLA) leaders and speak at the forum. Chan also attended last year’s event as defence minister. The forum, co-hosted by the China Association for Military Sciences and the China Institute for International Strategic Studies, involves global high-level defence, military and foreign affairs leaders discussing regional and international security issues. The theme for this year’s forum is “Build Consensus on Stability, Advance Security Governance Together”. “Minister Chan’s visit underscores the long-standing, warm and friendly bilateral defence relationship between Singapore and China,” the defence ministry said. According to defence analyst Abdul Rahman Yaacob, while the US is a critical security partner for Singapore, the city state recognises that a defence partnership with China is also important as the latter is a significant global player and the two countries hold defence talks and conduct joint military exercises. “These engagements increase trust and provide platforms for the two parties to discuss sensitive defence issues,” said Rahman, a research fellow at the Rabdan Security and Defence Institute in the United Arab Emirates. Singapore and China conduct military drills code-named Exercise Maritime Cooperation, which include communications exercises, formation manoeuvres and aerial photography, at-sea replenishment, and joint search-and-rescue operations. “These exercises are less complex than those with the US, but the Americans have been Singapore’s exercise partner since the Cold War. Thus the exercise with China starts from a low base, but [is] growing,” Rahman said. He expected Chan to encourage his Chinese counterpart to attend the Shangri-La Dialogue, Asia’s premier defence forum, which is held annually in Singapore. China has in recent years opted not to send its defence minister for the dialogue. Faizal Abdul Rahman, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that China’s decision not to send a minister to the dialogue did not sour bilateral ties but was more likely a snub towards the Western powers and their Asian allies, whose interests typically dominated the agenda. Regarding Chan’s visit, Faizal said it was a continuation of Singapore’s defence ministers attending the annual Beijing Xiangshan Forum and underscored the regular high-level diplomatic engagements between Chinese and Singaporean leaders. He said Chan was also likely to discuss Singapore taking over as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) in 2027 since the country would need to work more closely with its 12 dialogue partners, including China, to advance the bloc’s interests. “Given the current tense geopolitical environment, Singapore also needs to ensure that the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting Plus remains a beneficial platform that maintains the participation of external partners, including China, some of whom increasingly regard each other as potential military adversaries,” Faizal said. During his speech at the forum last year, Chan stressed that all countries, big or small, had an agency and responsibility to reinforce the international rules-based order in an increasingly fragmented world and that Singapore would continue contributing to global stability by taking a principled approach.

title: Hong Kong district councillor remanded in custody after underage sex conviction
description: Sei Chun-hing, 39, set to become first elected officer to face imprisonment for a criminal offence since ‘patriots-only’ electoral overhaul in 2021.
content: A Hong Kong court has remanded a district councillor in custody pending sentence after convicting him of unlawful sex with a 13-year-old girl 15 years ago, rejecting his claim that the allegation was politically motivated. Yuen Long District Council member Sei Chun-hing, 39, is set to become the first elected officer to face imprisonment for a criminal offence since a Beijing-led electoral overhaul in 2021, which ensured only those endorsed by authorities as “patriotic” can assume public office. The District Court on Monday accepted the complainant’s testimony that Sei had committed sexual acts on her on March 14, 2011, telling her he expected the then secondary school pupil to reciprocate a month after he gave her a handcrafted Valentine’s Day gift. Sei, a personal assistant to former cultural and sports lawmaker Ma Fung-kwok, was convicted of unlawful sex with a girl under 16, an offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment. He was acquitted of a separate indecent assault charge relating to a 2008 incident on technical grounds. Judge Stanley Chan Kwong-chi also dismissed Sei’s contention that the woman’s evidence was tainted by her desire to punish him for his pro-establishment views or for ending their relationship. The government announced an internal inquiry following a petition by the Yuen Long District Council chairman and three other members to the secretary for home and youth affairs. “The government places great importance on the conduct and integrity of [district council] members, and will closely monitor the progress of the legal proceedings and follow up accordingly,” a spokesman said. The complainant, now 29 and identified only as X, said she was 11 years old and in Primary Six when Sei, then an assistant to the director of her school’s theatre production, molested her in November 2008. She said she avoided contact with the defendant after the incident until they met again in October 2010, reconciled and soon became a couple. The woman recalled Sei, who was 23 at the time, describing her as his wife and suggesting she could only demonstrate her love by having sex with him. On Valentine’s Day in 2011, Sei gave her a rose-shaped ornament engraved with their names and asked her to reciprocate a month later on White Day, usually celebrated as a second Valentine’s Day in East Asia. The complainant said she reluctantly had sex with the accused at his residence in Tin Shui Wai to maintain their relationship. In the witness box, Sei admitted developing romantic feelings for the girl but dismissed her allegations as pure fabrication. He insisted he met the girl for the first time a month after the alleged sexual assault in 2008, while contending he could not have had sex with the complainant at his home in 2011 because he was busy with work. Judge Chan rejected Sei’s account as untruthful, noting that metadata attached to images he submitted as evidence might have been altered to aid his defence. He stressed that the complainant’s motive for filing the police report was not pivotal to the court’s determination. “The alleged incidents of indecent assault and unlawful sex, if proven beyond reasonable doubt, are facts independent of whether X had filed a police report for political reasons or because her love had turned to hate,” he said. The judge said the complainant gave a credible and reasonable account of the event that took place on March 14, 2011, while rejecting the defendant’s claim that he was at a meeting with a theatre colleague that afternoon. Chan further held that he molested the woman when she was 11 in 2008 but said the prosecution failed to prove its case because the complainant was unable to show the incident took place at the time and place specified in the indictment. The court will hear oral mitigation arguments on October 27 before passing sentence. Under the District Councils Ordinance, a member is disqualified if sentenced to more than three months’ imprisonment for an offence. Additionally, performance monitoring guidelines mandated by the government stipulate that an officeholder can face sanctions for gross misconduct or a criminal offence attracting a jail term, even if the sentence is not severe enough to warrant disqualification.

title: Brics keeps de-dollarisation push alive despite no common currency plan: analysts
description: Analysts say lack of movement towards a common currency reflects a more pragmatic approach to reducing reliance on US dollar.
content: With the 11-nation Brics grouping pledging to boost cross-border payment links but making no move towards establishing a common currency, analysts said the vow marked a shift towards a more pragmatic de-dollarisation strategy rather than a retreat from the effort. A 45-page leaders’ declaration issued on Saturday at the Brics summit in New Delhi said the group’s Payment Task Force would continue working to facilitate “fast, low-cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe” cross-border payments among Brics countries. However, Sudhakar Dalela, secretary of India’s Ministry of External Affairs, told a news briefing on Saturday there was “no proposal in the Brics for a Brics currency, as of now”. Matteo Giovannini, a non-resident associate fellow at the Beijing-based Centre for China and Globalisation, said it was “less a retreat from de-dollarisation than a shift in its strategy, from trying to create a common Brics currency towards building the infrastructure that allows Brics members to reduce their reliance on the dollar in practical terms”. “This is a much more achievable objective,” he said, citing hurdles including differences in monetary policies, exchange-rate regimes, capital controls and economic structures across Brics members as reasons for the declaration’s more “pragmatic approach.” The declaration said the task force had also studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and had held talks on using local currencies for “trade settlements and investments”. The idea of a Brics currency has drawn widespread attention since Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva floated the prospect of a common trading currency in 2023. That later prompted US President Donald Trump to threaten 100 per cent tariffs on Brics countries if they moved to create a new currency or replace the US dollar. Each country has the incentive to bypass the dollar system Xu Tianchen, Economist Intelligence Unit Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the vision of a common Brics currency “lacks the business case”. He cited the absence of a single market among the 11 members of the group, the lack of a central body that could have a say in members’ policymaking – along the lines of the European Commission – and members’ differing ambitions to retain control. “These mean a collective political union, a single market and a unified currency will all be very difficult,” Xu said. The 11 Brics members are: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia. However, analysts said efforts to reduce reliance on the US dollar were likely to continue amid mounting geopolitical tensions and concerns over the dollar-dominated financial system, although they would follow a more practical and incremental path. “Each country has the incentive to bypass the dollar system,” Xu said. “So one possible way is for each country to build its local currency settlement networks and ensure interoperability within the various systems.” Giovannini, also an AsiaGlobal Fellow at The University of Hong Kong, forecast forecast a future with greater use of national currencies for intra-Brics trade, more interoperable payment and messaging systems, and potentially deeper cooperation around settlement and financial infrastructure. “I would expect Brics to make more progress on the plumbing of international finance than on creating a new currency,” he said. “The dollar is unlikely to be displaced in the foreseeable future, but the more important development may be the gradual creation of a parallel financial ecosystem in which the dollar is no longer the default intermediary for every transaction.”

title: Foundation collects tributes to Hong Kong’s Tung Chee-hwa for online memorial
description: China-United States Exchange Foundation has collected more than 100 reflections on Tung from political and business heavyweights.
content: The China-United States Exchange Foundation has launched a permanent tribute webpage to Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive, and collected more than 100 reflections from political and business heavyweights around the world. The foundation, established by Tung in 2008, said the webpage, which launched on Monday, included tributes from Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus and Max Baucus, former United States ambassador to China. “This permanent tribute not only placemarks his remarkable record of public service but honours his lifelong belief that dialogue can advance global peace, progress and prosperity,” foundation president James Chau said. “Above all, this tribute is intended to inspire a new generation to advance the cause to which Mr Tung was deeply devoted,” he said. “I saw first-hand Mr Tung’s exceptional sense of duty, generosity and conviction.” Among those who contributed to the memorial was Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Emeritus Senior Minister Goh Chok Tong of the city state. Goh said his friendship with Tung went back to the early 1970s when they were both in the shipping industry. “I will remember him as a helpful, sincere, trustworthy friend whom I had the privilege of knowing for more than half a century,” he said. Yunus said Tung’s life was one of quiet but determined service, highlighting how he guided Hong Kong through a historic and difficult transition as well as building understanding and trust between China and the US. “That kind of patient, long-term bridge-building is rare, and it leaves a lasting mark far beyond the institutions he led,” he said. Others who paid tribute to Tung included former US treasury secretary Hank Paulson; John Podesta, former White House chief of staff for Bill Clinton; and retired US admiral William Owens. “He was the epitome of a citizen diplomat. Despite strong differences between our systems and our governments, [Tung] had an unshakeable belief that the people of China and the people of the US had much in common and could share a prosperous and peaceful future through dialogue and understanding,” Podesta said. Mogens Lykketoft, a past president of the United Nations General Assembly, former World Health Organization director general Margaret Chan Fung Fu-chun and Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai also paid tribute to Tung on the website. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. A spokesman for the foundation said some tributes were conveyed privately to the family and therefore did not appear on the webpage. The tribute page also has a dedicated space where the public can share their own memories and reflections. Tung, who died on September 8 at the age of 89, is remembered for a tenure marked by difficult policy choices and successive crises, with former officials saying some of his past decisions had taken on a different significance with the passage of time. He largely withdrew from public view in his final years and was last seen publicly in July 2021, when he attended the premiere of a film marking the centenary of the founding of the Communist Party of China.

title: Chinese researchers chart 5-stage path toward ‘last AI built by humans’
description: Automating AI research has emerged as a battleground, though US firms have an early lead due to superior access to compute resources.
content: Researchers from China’s leading universities and tech giants are setting their sights on a crucial new front in the AI race with the US: developing systems capable of building better versions of themselves without human intervention. In a joint paper published on Thursday, researchers from ByteDance, Tsinghua University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, among others, outlined a five-stage road map for recursive self-improvement (RSI). The study, titled “The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement”, highlights a growing industry focus on automating the labour-intensive life cycle of training, evaluating, and fine-tuning AI models. The paper describes five progressive stages of autonomy. In the initial phase, an AI merely executes improvement procedures designed by human engineers. It then begins to choose how to upgrade itself, rather than simply carrying out preprogrammed instructions. In later stages, the system determines what new information or experiences it must acquire, adapting to changes post-deployment. The final stage would allow an AI to persistently refine the very methods used to improve AI itself. Unlike a chatbot correcting an individual response, RSI requires improvements to persist beyond a single task and be inherited by successor systems. The authors argue that the ability to automate parts of AI research could become a source of competitive advantage for model developers. If realised, this paradigm shift could shorten development cycles while slashing the labour and computational costs required to build foundation models, according to the authors. Automating AI research has emerged as a core battleground in US-China technological competition. While Chinese institutions continue to make rapid practical leaps, experts note that US firms maintain an early lead, largely due to superior access to compute resources. “American companies still appear several months ahead of China and have access to more compute for deployment,” said Erich Grunewald, senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. “Chinese researchers are very capable at squeezing performance from scarce hardware, but those compute constraints do still bite.” Despite the challenges, Chinese firms are doubling down on autonomous training infrastructure. Z.ai, known in China as Zhipu AI, said on Sunday it would allocate about 60 per cent of the net proceeds from its latest US$5 billion fundraising round to support the development of its next-generation GLM foundation models and its “fully self-training system”. Researchers behind MiniMax 2.7 said in an article titled “Early Echoes of Self-Evolution” earlier this year that the model could update its memory and build complex skills while executing reinforcement-learning experiments, with the resulting experience feeding back into its learning process. DeepSeek last month developed an agentic “harness” that gives models greater autonomy to navigate multi-step tasks, execute code and interact with external software. The authors noted in their paper that progression through the five stages would vary widely depending on the AI field. Software engineering presented a relatively clear path forward, whereas robotics and scientific discovery faced steeper hurdles. Safety remains another major concern. The researchers said that genuine RSI required strict safeguards, including verified testing environments to ensure updates were safe and beneficial before being deployed. The authors provided no timetable on when RSI could be achieved.

title: Man arrested over alleged HK$2.8 million Hong Kong school admission scam
description: Police say suspect, 51, accepted 23 payments from an education consultant in exchange for securing dozens of places at ‘Kiangsu-Chekiang College’.
content: A man has been arrested for allegedly defrauding an education consultant out of nearly HK$3 million (US$382,500) by claiming he could secure dozens of places at a Hong Kong school, the South China Morning Post has learned. A police source said on Monday that the suspect, a 51-year-old Hongkonger who claimed to be a businessman, had signed a contract with a 45-year-old woman working as an education consultant on March 1, 2024, claiming he could provide dozens of places at a “Kiangsu-Chekiang College”. Believing the claims, the consultant transferred about HK$2.84 million in 23 instalments between April and July 2024 to the man’s mainland Chinese bank account, covering application fees for 37 students, the source added. He had allegedly promised access to 50 secondary school places at the college, assuring her that her students would also have guaranteed entry into universities in Hong Kong or Macau regardless of their Diploma of Secondary Education results. But the source said none of the students received admission offers from the school or any higher education institutions. He subsequently cut off contact, prompting the woman to file a police report in May this year. Investigators intercepted him at Hong Kong International Airport on July 29 this year as he attempted to leave the city. He was arrested on suspicion of fraud. There are three secondary schools and one primary school carrying the “Kiangsu‑Chekiang” name in Hong Kong. The three secondary schools are located in Sha Tin, Kwai Chung and North Point. The one in North Point, Kiangsu-Chekiang College, is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents. The primary school, the Kiangsu and Chekiang Primary School, is also in North Point. Kiangsu-Chekiang College in North Point is a direct subsidy scheme school popular among mainland parents.

title: South Africa road accident kills at least 21 people
description: The collision was one of two major crashes that killed at least 29 people across South Africa over the weekend.
content: Two minibus taxis collided head-on, and an SUV crashed into them on one of South Africa’s main highways, killing at least 21 people and leaving four others seriously injured, authorities said on Monday. The crash on Sunday night in the Western Cape Province took place between the small towns of Prince Albert and Leeu-Gamka, around 380km (235 miles) east of Cape Town, according to the Road Traffic Management Corporation, or RTMC, the national traffic agency. The collision involved two Toyota minibus taxis and a Suzuki sport utility vehicle, police spokesperson Warrant Officer Christopher Spies said. Eighteen people were declared dead at the scene. Three others were declared dead after being taken to a hospital, bringing the toll to 21, Spies said. Four other people were seriously injured, according to the Western Cape Mobility Department. The death toll “may change as emergency services and authorities in the Western Cape continue their assessment of the scene”, RTMC said. The N1 highway was closed at the crash scene. Police opened a culpable homicide case, and the cause of the collision remained under investigation, Spies said. RTMC also sent investigators to the scene. The Western Cape collision was one of two major crashes that killed at least 29 people across South Africa over the weekend, the government said in a statement. Eight people were killed in a separate crash near Ermelo in Mpumalanga province early on Sunday. Minibus taxis are the main mode of public transport for millions of people in South Africa and are often involved in fatal collisions. Two separate crashes involving minibus taxis in January left at least 25 people dead, including 14 children.

title: Venice 2026: 10 of the festival’s best movies, from Woman Unknown to Possible Love and Musk
description: Indie dramas and documentaries, rather than big Hollywood productions, took the spotlight at this year’s festival. Here are 10 of the best.
content: The 83rd Venice International Film Festival was defined by surprises. While this year’s line-up lacked major Hollywood studio fare, the jury – led by American actress-director Maggie Gyllenhaal and including veteran Hong Kong filmmaker Johnnie To Kei-fung – still had plenty to chew over. Labour issues emerged as a prominent theme, while the festival looked controversially to the future with the selection of Be Brave, a documentary about Diesel founder Renzo Rosso that was partly completed using artificial intelligence. However, perhaps the biggest shock was the sight of a reunited Liam and Noel Gallagher walking arm-in-arm down the red carpet – who on earth would have predicted that a few years back? Featuring their reunion documentary Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger, here are 10 of the best films that screened at the festival. 1. Woman Unknown May el-Toukhy, the Danish-Egyptian filmmaker previously best known for her 2019 feature Queen of Hearts, will remember this festival for the rest of her life. Her formidable work Woman Unknown not only claimed the top prize – the Golden Lion – but also the Volpi Cup for best actress, for Mathilde Arcel. Set in Copenhagen in the summer of 1945, with residents still reeling from the Nazi occupation, the new film stars Arcel as Marie, a nanny who must hide her past at a time when women who fraternised with German soldiers are being weeded out and publicly shamed. It is painful to watch, sublimely executed and a deserved winner. 2. Musk It wasn’t the longest documentary playing in the festival – that honour went to Luca Guadagnino’s Joie de vivre, his seven-hour, 25-minute take on Italian filmmaker Bernardo Bertolucci – but Alex Gibney’s rigorous examination of the richest man in the world was still a marathon watch. Clocking in at four hours and featuring a 10-minute intermission, this study of Elon Musk took audiences through SpaceX and Tesla Motors to his Twitter takeover and time heading up Doge. Some elements flop, like using a computer-generated Musk to mouth real-life sound bites instead of an actual interview. But with ex-wife Justine among those spilling the beans, Musk makes for riveting viewing. 3. A Good Little Soldier French writer-director Stephane Brize picked up the best screenplay prize for this savage look at corporate culture. Alba Rohrwacher is stunning as an HR manager in an insurance company who succumbs to workplace pressures when she takes on a troublesome department manager. The moment she explodes at her own son over a video call because he is unable to complete his mathematics assignment is one of the festival’s stand-out scenes. Vincent Lindon, marking his sixth film with Brize, also shines as a ruthless boss who prioritises nothing but the bottom line. 4. Naza A late addition to the competition line-up, Naza is the latest documentary from Israeli journalist Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, who won an Academy Award for No Other Land. Shot on a rooftop in Tel Aviv, the film features interviews with Israeli military personnel – all speaking anonymously – who were involved in the systematic destruction of Gaza following the October 7 attack. Filled with shocking, heartbreaking and cold-blooded revelations, the film claimed the Special Jury Prize. One imagines that jury member Kaouther Ben Hania, who in 2025 brought The Voice of Hind Rajab to the festival, pushed hard for this. 5. Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger As one of the bigger surprises of the festival, Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern’s documentary about Oasis’ reunion tour hardly felt like Venice material, but it managed to strike plenty of poignant grace notes. The famously fractious Liam and Noel Gallagher, who had not spoken in years after the band broke up in 2009, were on reflective form across an impressionistic work that took audiences from rehearsals to gigs in Cardiff, Manchester and then abroad, including Tokyo and Buenos Aires. Crucially, the film includes the fans and explores what the band’s music means to them, serving as a testament to the healing power of music and the community it builds. 6. Possible Love For our money, this was the best film at the 83rd Venice Film Festival. The jury almost agreed, but ultimately, Possible Love took the Silver Lion Grand Jury Prize. Awards aside, Lee Chang-dong’s first film since 2018’s Burning is a mesmerising drama about the sparks that fly when two married couples – one wealthy, one not – cross paths. Featuring an all-star Korean cast – Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong – Lee’s film unfolds with an equal measure of mastery and mystery. Terrific performances, especially from Sul as a laid-off welder struggling to maintain his dignity, power this dense tapestry. 7. They’re Here Like Alex Gibney, Laura Poitras is one of the great truth-seekers of our age. The director of Citizenfour and the Venice-winning All the Beauty and the Bloodshed returned to the festival with a 25-minute short, which was among the festival’s most powerful offerings. Co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller, They’re Here follows anonymous Minnesotan residents as they resist the work of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers patrolling the streets on a Trump-ordained mission to detain undocumented immigrants. The sheer brutality of ICE tactics is laid bare. 8. Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? Following Cannes, this year’s Venice festival was also a strong showcase for Japanese cinema. Shinya Tsukamoto (the cult director behind Tetsuo: The Iron Man) delivered one of the highlights with his stirring English-language tale about real-life Vietnam war veteran Allen Nelson. A gripping, empathetic portrait of PTSD and how to face it head-on, the film benefits from Tsukamoto’s masterful casting of Broadway actor Rodney Hicks as Nelson, notably for his heartfelt scenes opposite Geoffrey Rush, who plays his therapist. It is a worthy tribute to the real Nelson. 9. Wild Horse Nine John Malkovich took the best actor prize for Martin McDonagh’s 1973-set black comedy, just as Colin Farrell did in Venice for the director’s last film, The Banshees of Inisherin. Here, Malkovich’s world-weary CIA agent feels like a character only he could play, from his sharp banter with his partner (played by Sam Rockwell) to his chilling pronouncements about the impending coup in Chile. Largely set on Rapa Nui – the Polynesian island also known as Easter Island and famous for its mysterious stone carvings – the film showcases McDonagh’s expert blend of the personal and the political, making for compelling viewing. 10. Look Back Tatsuki Fujimoto’s popular one-shot manga Look Back had already been turned into a 2024 animated film, but Hirokazu Koreeda takes it a step further with this live-action adaptation. Aju Makita, who marks her fifth collaboration with Koreeda, and Natsuki Deguchi star as teenagers who bond over their love of manga. While it can often be stultifying watching artists at work on screen, Koreeda delicately captures the rush of creativity and the fine penmanship it requires to bring such works to life. A film about dreams colliding with reality, Look Back is a marked improvement on Koreeda’s overly sentimental Cannes entry earlier this year, Sheep in the Box. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Can Trump’s White House ballroom top China’s vast Great Hall of the People?
description: US president says the under-construction ballroom will outdo its Beijing counterpart, despite being a fraction of the size.
content: President Donald Trump’s claim that the new White House ballroom will top China’s Great Hall of the People has thrust the Beijing landmark back into the spotlight just as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares for his US visit later this month. Speaking at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas last week, Trump described the Great Hall of the People – China’s most prestigious venue for legislative and ceremonial events – as “a serious hall”. “This is a very large hall, but we’re going to top it. You know, we’re going to top it,” Trump said. Trump stood inside the central Beijing landmark just months earlier. During his state visit to China in May, the US delegation attended a welcoming ceremony, bilateral meeting and state banquet in the Great Hall of the People. After wrapping up his visit, Trump posted to social media a photo of himself walking alongside Xi in front of the building, declaring: “China has a ballroom, and so should the USA!” He said the new White House ballroom, part of an ongoing revamp of the East Wing announced last year, would be “the finest facility of its kind anywhere in the USA” and was scheduled to open in September 2028. The Great Hall of the People, located on the western side of Tiananmen Square, was not built only to host grand banquets. It has served as a major venue for China’s legislative, state and diplomatic activities since its completion, and hosts the annual “two sessions”, the meetings of the National People’s Congress and the country’s top political advisory body. In 1972, then US president Richard Nixon visited the Great Hall during his historic visit to China, where he held talks with premier Zhou Enlai as Beijing and Washington moved towards normalising relations. Opened in 1959, it was one of 10 major construction projects in Beijing to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the People’s Republic of China. Construction began in October 1958 and was completed just over 10 months later. The main entrance opens onto Tiananmen Square, with the national emblem of the People’s Republic mounted above it. Twelve pale-grey marble columns, each 25 metres (82 feet) tall, frame the entrance, which is approached via broad granite steps. The building is monumental. It covers about 170,000 square metres (1.8 million square feet), with a 10,000-seat auditorium at its centre, a banquet hall capable of accommodating 5,000 people to the north and offices for the Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislative body, to the south. More than 300 meeting rooms, lounges and offices are spread across the complex, including rooms named after China’s provinces and regions, including Hong Kong and Macau, which are decorated to reflect their local culture. The grand auditorium has a domed ceiling centred on a ruby-red five-pointed star, with 70 radiating beams and 40 sunflower-shaped motifs. Hundreds of smaller lights are designed to evoke a starry sky against pale blue wall panels. The White House State Ballroom, by comparison, will have about 8,360 square metres of space and seating for 650 people, an increase from the 200-person seated capacity in the East Room of the White House. In 2025, Trump’s administration demolished the White House’s East Wing and began work on the ballroom without seeking congressional approval, prompting controversy over historic preservation and funding challenges. The administration has said the project is intended to address a long-standing shortage of space for large official functions. Trump has frequently complained about the White House’s limited capacity for formal dinners, which forces the US to use “unsightly tents” on the South Lawn. For visiting foreign leaders, China’s Great Hall of the People is also part of the choreography of diplomacy. Its grand reception halls serve as elaborate backdrops for welcoming ceremonies, talks and state banquets, putting the country’s architectural traditions and political symbolism on display at the same time. The East Hall, one of the building’s main reception spaces for foreign leaders and high-level meetings, spans more than 1,120 square metres. During the May state visit, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was filmed taking in the East Hall’s ornate ceiling, with the footage later circulating widely on Chinese social media. At one point, he pointed towards the ceiling and gave a thumbs-up, before drawing US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s attention to the details, the footage shows.

title: Southeast Asia weighs energy transition amid LNG supply crunch
description: At Gastech 2026, policymakers implore pragmatism over net-zero targets and closer cooperation to ensure affordable LNG supplies.
content: Energy ministers and executives met in Bangkok on Monday to discuss the prolonged price increase for liquefied natural gas (LNG) triggered by the Iran war, with Southeast Asia’s growth ambitions and climate goals on the line as the cost of powering economies shifting to artificial intelligence soars. On the first day of Gastech 2026, one of the world’s largest energy conferences, policymakers implored pragmatism over net-zero targets and closer cooperation to ensure affordable LNG supplies, particularly among Southeast Asian neighbours whose industrial plans remain hooked on gas generation. The region’s energy security has been brutally exposed since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, resulting in the virtual closure of the Strait of Hormuz and what Tengku Mohammad Taufik, CEO of Malaysian state energy giant Petronas, described as a “debacle” that has “curtailed, disrupted or disturbed” a fifth of the world’s gas supplies. Singapore’s economy is virtually fully powered by natural gas, most of it imported from Malaysia and Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s largest producing nations. Gastech host Thailand, meanwhile, has its own gas fields but their reserves are dwindling, increasing reliance on imports whose price has spiked. Main supplier Qatar was forced earlier this year to suspend LNG production due to drone strikes by Iran. The Southeast Asian kingdom aims to boost its capacity to handle LNG by 40 per cent from 19 million tonnes each year as its power needs surge, and it eyes greater imports and a future role as a trading hub. Natural gas would remain “an important foundation of Thailand’s power system”, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said, while renewables would also be gradually increased as a share of the energy mix. Fossil fuels would continue to underpin the economy “while we work to diversify supply, strengthen domestic energy security, improve efficiency and improve our exposure to global markets”. With LNG supplies from Qatar – the world’s largest producer – strangled by Iranian threats to ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, power plants across many Asian economies have faced delays or losses on pre-ordered gas deliveries, pushing them into expensive spot markets for the crucial energy source. An analysis of LNG purchases published by Bloomberg on Monday estimated that India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Thailand and Vietnam have collectively spent an additional US$7.4 billion on LNG since the Iran war, more than double the costs of the previous year. That has stirred debate and a rethink of where the future of energy lies. Some experts say that the price shock could nudge more countries towards speeding up their adoption of cheaper renewables like solar, wind and hydrogen. But delegates also raised the prospect of softening commitments to reduce fossil fuel consumption as the immediate needs of economies chasing technology-driven growth outweigh net-zero targets – and calls to tackle the climate crisis. “There’s a changing debate about energy in the world today,” Tony Blair, the former British prime minister, said during the conference. “I think arguments around climate change and fossil fuels are still there [but] people have understood that energy security is essential and energy supply is essential for growth,” said the head of the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, citing the increased demand for fuels from Indonesia, Vietnam and Thailand. The supply of energy, particularly natural gas, was “a vital part of development”, Blair noted. “It’s not that people have given up on clean energy – renewable energy investment is still more than the investment in fossil fuels – but I think people have come to an understanding that you can’t put the two against each other.” Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam and Malaysia have all set 2050 as an ambitious target to reach net-zero emissions. But they have also invested in strings of power-hungry data centres that will require a massive injection of fossil fuels if they are to come online speedily. In a sign of the tensions between the push for greater reliance on fossil fuels as a driver of growth and those stridently against them, Greenpeace Thailand hung a giant banner outside the Gastech venue. The banner depicted Anutin and the slogan “Your Gas Deal, Our Loss” – a reference to his government’s backing of new gas and oil terminals, power plants and other infrastructure, especially in the eastern coastal area. While gas will remain crucial to Singapore, Gan Siow Huang, minister of state in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Trade and Industry, said the ambition of establishing the Asean power grid – a vision to integrate a renewables-led electricity system across Southeast Asia, saving costs, losses of excess and slashing emissions – was a pathway towards sustainable and secure energy for the region. “Energy resilience is key and no single country can achieve [it] on its own. Multilaterally in the near term we are hoping to develop together with other Asean states the Asean power grid,” she said, referring to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “It’s very exciting … Asean is a growing economy; it needs power … there is renewable energy potential in the Asean states, but we need to unlock that.”

title: China’s oil demand could falter as Saudi pipeline shutdown raises costs
description: Supply relatively insulated in short term, but refiners could cut run rates amid rising crude prices, freight costs, analysts say.
content: As the shutdown of Saudi Arabia’s major oil pipeline tightens global crude supply, shipments to China remain relatively insulated in the near term, though rising prices and freight costs are set to dampen demand, according to analysts. Drone attacks launched from Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to shut its East-West pipeline, which connects its eastern oilfields to Yanbu port on the Red Sea and serves as a vital bypass around the Strait of Hormuz, where transit remains disrupted. The closure late last week has sent oil prices higher, with Brent crude rising around 3 per cent to US$107.72 a barrel at midday on Monday. While the disruption threatens global crude supply, flows to China are expected to remain relatively unaffected. “The impact on China is largely indirect, as Chinese refiners have stopped loading Saudi crude from the Red Sea since August,” said Emma Li, lead China oil market analyst at energy firm Vortexa. While other Asian buyers were sourcing Saudi crude that travels from Yanbu to the Mediterranean coast via ship and then a pipeline through Egypt, Chinese refiners were securing their barrels from Gulf ports to the east of the Strait of Hormuz, Li said. This is sometimes done through ship-to-ship transfers at sea. China’s cargo nominations for September had also largely concluded before the pipeline shut down, Li added. The East-West pipeline can carry around 7 million barrels per day at full capacity. Before the shutdown, it was diverting around 4 million barrels per day, and could reduce global oil supply by up to 4 per cent if not restored within days, Reuters reported. Authorities have not disclosed the extent of the damage or a timeline for reopening the pipeline. Saudi Arabia has faced increasing attacks and threats from Iranian-linked groups in recent days. Last week, the Iran-backed Houthis in neighbouring Yemen struck several oil facilities in the kingdom’s south and captured strategic locations in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. While a country-by-country breakdown of China’s imports for August is not yet available, the country’s total crude imports inched up around 6 per cent in August, compared with July, according to customs data. Rising crude prices and freight rates from the pipeline damage and increasing competition for Gulf barrels, however, were “not particularly attractive for new bookings” from China, Li said. Analysts from Huatai Futures similarly said that as Chinese refineries were already struggling with margins, the combination of high prices and shipping costs was likely to push refiners to cut run rates and suppress China’s crude demand. The pressure was particularly severe for independent “teapot” refiners, which have also lost access to heavily discounted sanctioned crude, the analysts said in a report on Monday. Nevertheless, most Chinese refiners have already secured enough feedstock to maintain operations for at least the next two months, according to Li. “The greater uncertainty is around November and December coverage,” she said. As the country heads into winter, Beijing may impose additional domestic fuel supply requirements. If that occurs, refiners could draw down existing crude inventories rather than significantly raise imports at inflated prices, Li said.

title: Opinion | China’s J-10CE has foreign buyers, but not yet a market
description: In service in Pakistan and Uzbekistan and on Bangladesh’s radar, the fighter jet is not yet a threat to Western market dominance.
content: Uzbekistan’s recent confirmation that China’s J-10CE fighters have entered into service in its air force ended months of speculation. It is the latest of three developments that include Pakistan’s use of J-10CEs in combat last year and Bangladesh’s draft procurement paper for the Chinese aircraft. Read separately, each looks like a win for the J-10CE. Taken together, however, they show something narrower: the Chinese aircraft is gaining export traction without yet winning a clean contest against a Western rival. Pakistan’s file is the one that changed the sales pitch. In May last year, Pakistan Air Force said its J-10CE fighter jets had fired at Indian aircraft during the conflict that followed India’s “Operation Sindoor” strikes. Pakistani officials claimed that five Indian aircraft were shot down, including three Rafales. By June, Eric Trappier, CEO of Rafale maker Dassault Aviation, was dismissing Pakistan’s claim, noting that India had not officially announced its losses. Reuters, citing US officials, reported that at least one Rafale had been lost. The count remains disputed. Pakistan is still the only J-10CE operator with a combat record. No air force really wants to be the first to test an unproven jet against a peer adversary; Pakistan absorbed that risk. A potential buyer can now point to someone else’s war instead of being the first to find out. Bangladesh has done so. Last month, Zahed Ur Rahman, the prime minister’s information and broadcasting adviser, said Bangladesh had “taken note” of the J-10CE’s performance in the war, asserting it was now “established” that the Chinese fighter jet could take down an Indian Rafale. This characterisation is being used to justify the government’s proposal to procure the J-10CE. In June, a local report cited an unnamed official as saying the government hoped to sign the purchase agreement by August; the proposal continues to await budget approval. The package is reportedly for 20 jets at over US$2.3 billion; while the flyaway price is US$62.7 million a jet, items such as training, technical support, freight and insurance push the effective per-jet cost to roughly US$115 million. Payments would run through the 2035-36 fiscal year, under a proposed government-to-government arrangement with China National Aero-Technology Import & Export Corporation (Catic): a decade of budget commitments to one supplier. This is not simply a question of sticker price. Bangladesh flies an estimated 35 Chinese F-7s and six Russian MiG-29s with an average fleet age of over 20 years. One of its F-7s crashed into a school in Dhaka in July last year, killing dozens, mostly students. The need for replacement is clear. The choice is not. Last December, Bangladesh Air Force also signed a letter of intent with Italy’s Leonardo to buy the Eurofighter Typhoon. Local reporting suggests it could seek up to 16 of the aircraft. Bangladesh is holding on to two options, but neither is yet a contract. As for Uzbekistan, its story runs through Moscow rather than Beijing. Its air force inherited MiG-29s, Su-27s and Su-25s at independence in 1991, and has leaned on Russian parts and overhaul capacity since, in a supply chain that has come under greater pressure since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The recent announcement confirms that its Chinese J-10CEs have arrived and are flying. What no one has confirmed – not Tashkent, not Beijing – are the details of the contract behind them: the reported figures of 24 jets for roughly US$1 billion are still just that – reported. It’s also not clear if Uzbekistan is retiring its Russian jets or simply adding to them. Bangladesh is weighing the J-10CE against a Western alternative. Uzbekistan is diversifying away from a Russian one. They may end up making the same choice, but they are starting from very different places. The tested buyers sit elsewhere. Indonesia bought 42 Rafales for US$8.1 billion in 2022 and has since moved towards more; while it has been named as a prospective J-10CE customer, no order has been confirmed. Egypt, which continues to expand its fleet of Rafales, has for years drawn unconfirmed reports that it is a buyer of J-10s. Both Indonesia and Egypt are still moving ahead with Western fighters. Neither has chosen the J-10CE. In comparison, Bangladesh is still deciding, with a Chinese draft agreement in one hand and an Italian letter of intent in the other. Neither has become a contract. Until a buyer signs for the Chinese fighter jet against a Western alternative or walks away from one, the J-10CE will keep collecting operators without answering the harder question: can it actually win over the market?

title: Knife attack in China’s Guangzhou leaves multiple people injured
description: Police apprehend suspect who appeared to target faces as online photos show bloodied victims sitting on ground.
content: Police in Guangzhou said on Monday they had apprehended a man in the southern Chinese city’s university town district after receiving reports that he was wielding a knife and injuring pedestrians. Emergency services started receiving calls around 5.20pm local time about multiple stabbings in front of a hotpot restaurant in the Xiaoguwei Island area of Panyu district, according to an alert sent out by the district branch of the Guangzhou Municipal Public Security Bureau. The bureau said in a social media post that police promptly arrived and the injured individuals were sent to hospital, with none in life-threatening condition after treatment. A 35-year-old male suspect surnamed Li was apprehended, and the bureau said the case was under further investigation. The island is home to a university park complex that includes several major universities. Earlier on Monday, online posts circulated about a knife attack at Gogo Xintiandi mall in Panyu’s Guangzhou University Town complex, with images circulating of multiple injured individuals along with an image of the presumed assailant wearing a face mask. Some online posts said that there was more than one attacker, but that information could not be immediately verified. Apparent CCTV footage posted on social media on Monday showed a man clad in black stabbing a woman in the face in a split second as he passed by her inside a shopping centre. Other videos showed the same woman later sitting on the ground being comforted by passers-by. Another series of graphic videos appeared to show the aftermath of another attack on an older woman, seen sitting outdoors covered in blood with a knife in her face, screaming for help. The knife-wielding suspect appeared to target the victim’s face and eyes. Footage was also posted of a police unit rushing into a shopping centre, as well as what appeared to be the officers apprehending a suspect inside the centre. Some videos posted of the event were removed from Chinese social media platforms, but others posted to Western platforms remain online. . The university town, which is officially known as Guangzhou Higher Education Mega Centre, is a major education hub and home to campuses of major institutions like Sun Yat-sen University and South China Normal University. Xiaoguwei Island also contains university dormitories, a science museum and cultural tourism sites. In recent years, China has seen high-profile knife attacks, including one in October 2024 at a supermarket in Shanghai’s Songjiang district that left three people dead and 15 injured. Other public incidents have also raised safety concerns, including a deliberate car-ramming incident in November 2024 outside the Zhuhai Sports Centre, also in Guangdong province, which resulted in 35 dead and dozens wounded.

title: Hong Kong urged to overhaul ecotourism planning and expand bookings for hotspots
description: Poll finds 71.8 per cent agree Hong Kong’s countryside resources could be developed into high-quality ecotourism products.
content: Hong Kong should overhaul its ecotourism planning and allow visitors to book ahead at more of its popular countryside attractions, a lawmaker has said, after a survey found most residents believed the city had strong potential for nature-focused experiences but lacked enough quality options. A poll of 651 residents commissioned by lawmaker Perry Yiu Pak-leung’s office and think tank New Youth Forum found 71.8 per cent agreed Hong Kong’s countryside resources could be developed into high-quality ecotourism products. But the same proportion said most visitors heading to the countryside were merely taking part in ordinary leisure activities rather than “genuine” ecotourism. “Hong Kong has very rich ecotourism resources, but unfortunately we have not made good use of them for a long time,” Yiu said. The survey, conducted by telephone between August 18 and 26, also found that 62.1 per cent of respondents felt the city lacked enough high-quality ecotourism products, while 59 per cent said they would be interested in taking part in more in-depth experiences. About 83.3 per cent agreed quality ecotourism should combine professional guiding, conservation education and sustainable development. Regarding visitor management, 75.8 per cent supported booking systems at popular ecological attractions, while 73.1 per cent said selected hotspots should be accessible only through accredited travel agencies and professional guides. Yiu, who represents the tourism sector in the Legislative Council, said the government should move away from what he described as a “passive, piecemeal and firefighting” approach to managing popular attractions and instead adopt a strategy based on policy coordination, capacity management and industry accreditation. He called for a high-level cross-departmental task force to oversee ecotourism development, saying the existing interdepartmental mechanism used to handle crowds during major holidays was insufficient for long-term planning. He highlighted that managing overtourism at the High Island Reservoir East Dam in Sai Kung alone required the involvement of the Transport Department, Tourism Commission, Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, Water Supplies Department, police and district authorities. Yiu suggested the government review the booking trial at the High Island East Dam and Po Pin Chau before considering extending similar arrangements to other popular sites. He cited Tai Mo Shan as one area that could come under pressure as authorities promote the “four peaks” green tourism initiative, which also covers The Peak, Lantau Peak and Sai Kung Hoi. Yiu noted the High Island reservation scheme had recorded a no-show rate of about 41 per cent over its first two weekends, but argued unused slots could be opened to walk-in visitors and that frontline staff should retain flexibility in managing entry times. Travel Industry Council chairman Tommy Tam Kwong-shun emphasised that crowd control is only the first step, arguing that ecologically sensitive or heavily visited sites should eventually be managed by accredited travel agencies and professionally trained guides. “If we genuinely want to achieve professional guiding, conservation education and sustainable development together, the government should consider allowing accredited professional travel agencies and guides to coordinate visits to designated ecologically sensitive and popular attractions,” Tam said. He also called for a dedicated accreditation system for eco-tour operators and guides, saying professionally trained operators could provide visitors with richer experiences. Additionally, Tam urged the Travel Industry Authority to strengthen online patrols of social media platforms, including RedNote, to target unlicensed cross-border tour operations at source. Derek Tse Yue-tak, general manager of Eco Travel, said transport restrictions and cumbersome permit procedures were making it harder for operators to develop quality countryside products. He also said unlicensed cross-border hiking tours organised by guides from mainland China had increasingly eaten into the business of licensed local operators.

title: Hong Kong to sweeten school merger deals, offer housing measures to lift births
description: Source says city leader John Lee will unveil additional incentives to boost births and encourage school mergers in policy address.
content: Hong Kong authorities are expected to provide more incentives to encourage under-enrolled public schools to merge to survive, while announcing housing measures and tax reductions to tackle the falling birth rate in this week’s policy address, the South China Morning Post has learned. A government source said the policy address by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Wednesday would offer additional incentives to encourage the merger of subsidised schools amid the shrinking student population. Currently, if a primary school merges with another institution to allow the affected pupils to continue their studies, a one-off allowance of HK$1 million (US$127,500) will be granted to cover additional expenses. In March, the Education Bureau announced that a record 15 primary schools would not be allowed to operate subsidised Primary One classes for this academic year because they had failed to secure at least 16 pupils. Among them, eight chose to merge with other schools – which is the most popular option – while four chose to close down after three years, and two opted to operate private Primary One classes. The remaining school is already in the process of merging with another institution. The survival challenge of schools is expected to become more serious, as the number of babies born from 2021 to 2025, who will be entering Primary One in the coming years, keeps declining and hit a record low last year. The bureau expects the number of six-year-olds will stand at only 31,500 in 2029, a 16 per cent drop from 37,600 Primary One pupils in public schools this school year. Jessie Cheung Chok-fong, a consultant at the Subsidised Primary Schools Council and a principal, said schools generally used the current allowance to cover pupils’ extra expenses incurred by the mergers. “If a school in one district merges with a school in another district, schools have to offer school buses for students to commute, and parents will also be given money to buy a new set of textbooks and school uniforms after joining the new school,” she said. “More resources are definitely good for schools planning to merge, but schools always look at how much they are given before spending.” At present, secondary schools that continue to operate Form One classes after a merger will be provided with a one-off allowance of HK$500,000 for each merging level to cover the additional expenses. Over the past few years, only four government secondary schools and two secondary schools operated by Caritas Hong Kong have chosen the merger option. The issue of a declining number of Form One students is not as imminent as it is for the primary section, as the local number of births started to fall in 2017. Secondary schools now have to secure 29 students to operate two Form One classes, or they will face survival risks. The source said the policy address would also try to boost the birth rate by offering tax incentives and rolling out housing measures, as authorities wanted to avoid depending solely on cash giveaways for families. Last month, Hong Kong recorded a record-low 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026, down 15.6 per cent from 35,200 for the same period a year earlier. The decline in births came despite the government’s introduction of a “baby bonus” scheme in 2023, offering a one-off HK$20,000 cash award to new parents to encourage families to have children. The scheme was planned for an initial three years. In June, city leader Lee said the government would conduct a consultation on its slew of pro-baby incentives amid persistently low birth rates, noting that delayed marriage and cultural shifts were limiting the effectiveness of such policies. He conceded that delayed marriage, driven by career pursuits and postgraduate education becoming more common, had disincentivised couples from having children. The median age for first marriage among Hongkongers rose from 31.2 years for men and 29.3 for women in 2015 to 32.6 and 31, respectively, in 2025. He also pointed to changing cultural values, including the decline of the traditional view that children serve as an old-age safeguard and the growing prioritisation of individual aspirations.

title: Taiwan defence logistics under fire over missing chargers for US drones
description: Island’s army reportedly discovered omission only after taking delivery and later asked American side to find alternative supplier.
content: Taiwan’s military has taken delivery of 291 one-way attack drones from US maker Anduril Industries, only to discover they came without chargers and require American assistance to recharge them. The revelation involving the Altius-600M loitering munitions has prompted Taiwan’s opposition lawmakers to question the military’s procurement and logistical planning, days before the drones join other weapons systems in a three-day live-fire exercise. The controversy comes at a sensitive time in Sino-American relations, with US President Donald Trump expected to host Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24 and Taiwan arms sales emerging as a potential irritant ahead of the summit. According to recent local media reports, chargers were not included in the US Letter of Offer and Acceptance for the drones because the original equipment contained mainland Chinese-made components and therefore failed to meet requirements for a so-called non-red, or non-Chinese, supply chain. The army reportedly discovered the omission only after taking delivery and subsequently asked the US side to find an alternative supplier. As recently as April, no replacement source had been found, meaning US technical representatives were needed in Taiwan to help recharge the systems, the reports said on Friday. Ma Wen-chun, a legislator from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang, asked why the military had failed to identify such a basic logistical requirement before placing the order. “The drones have been bought, but before they have even reached the battlefield, we already need US personnel to help when their batteries run out,” Ma said. “Can this kind of logistical support really be relied upon in wartime?” She also questioned reports that the army had ordered nearly eight times as many spare batteries as the 291 drones, saying the Altius-600M was an expendable system and its battery requirements should have been determined before procurement. “They failed to buy the chargers they needed but bought a huge number of spare batteries,” Ma said. “Who calculated these requirements? And who was responsible for reviewing them?” In response, the army rejected the battery claim, saying each Altius-600M had been bought “with one installed battery and one spare”. In a statement, it said Anduril had completed development of a charger that met “non-red” supply-chain requirements and that “the equipment would be delivered according to schedule”. The company did not say when. The drones had been delivered with their batteries fully charged, meaning the charger issue had not affected current combat-readiness requirements, the army said. Legislator Wang Ting-yu of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party defended the procurement, saying the Altius-600M provided important anti-armour and anti-landing firepower. Wang said Taiwan could not buy the original charging equipment because it contained components made in mainland China, but the Taiwanese and US sides had since “established non-red sources for batteries and chargers”. The drone batteries would eventually be manufactured in Taiwan, with an unidentified local company receiving technology transfers to produce them, he added. “The arrangement could help Taiwan develop a non-red drone supply chain and potentially turn local companies into suppliers for Anduril’s overseas customers with similar requirements.” According to Shu Hsiao-huang, an associate research fellow at the government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research, the episode showed that eliminating mainland Chinese components from drone supply chains remained a work in progress, including in the United States. “Altius-600M is not standard US military equipment,” Shu said. “Some of its components and peripheral equipment might not previously have been subject to stringent non-red supply-chain requirements.” He argued that the problem could “create opportunities for Taiwan’s companies to cooperate with US manufacturers in production, maintenance and research and development”, bolstering supply-chain resilience while helping upgrade Taiwan’s drone industry. The controversy comes as Taipei has substantially expanded its purchases from Anduril. In late August, Taiwan’s defence ministry awarded a NT$26.9 billion (US$850 million) contract for another 2,032 systems – involving 1,554 Altius-700M anti-armour attack drones and 478 Altius-600ISR surveillance and reconnaissance drones – with deliveries extending to 2033. Ma questioned whether problems identified with the first purchase had been rectified before the much larger follow-on order. Concerns have also been raised over the Altius-600M’s performance and suitability for Taiwan’s operating environment. The roughly 12kg (26lbs) fixed-wing loitering munition has a range of about 440km (273 miles) and an endurance of about four hours, but critics have questioned how effectively such a lightweight system would operate in Taiwan’s mountainous terrain, coastal winds, heavy rain and high humidity. They have also questioned its resilience against electronic warfare and whether its anti-armour warhead would be effective against fast-moving maritime targets in the event of a People’s Liberation Army amphibious operation. The drones nevertheless showed markedly improved results in recent Taiwanese testing. Three of five reportedly crashed during their first live-fire test last December, but the military said more than 10 systems launched during two exercises in June all hit their targets. The Altius-600M will undergo another test from Wednesday during a three-day joint precision-munition live-fire exercise at the Jiupeng military testing site in southern Pingtung county. Running until Friday, the exercise will also involve weapons, including US-made multiple-launch High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (Himars) and Patriot air defence systems, as well as locally developed Tien Kung air-defence missiles and Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles. The drills are intended to test the armed forces’ long-range precision-strike capabilities and newer weapons, including the Altius-600M, as Taiwan seeks to strengthen its ability to strike PLA forces approaching the island. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Asian Games: tiny beds, rooms that leak, is Japan accommodation ‘the worst ever’?
description: Some countries have been forced to move officials into Airbnb accommodation as others warn of ‘serious shortage’ in Nagoya.
content: Accommodation at the Asian Games in Japan is the “worst ever”, South Korean officials said on Monday, also warning of “a serious shortage” of rooms. Beds in shipping container-style huts are too short for players to stretch out, a South Korean basketball chief said, while officials from the Philippines resorted to Airbnb. There is no dedicated athletes’ village in Nagoya, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden cabins and hotels in a bid to cut costs. While the Games officially open on Saturday, football and basketball are already under way, with Hong Kong’s women opening their tournament with a 5-1 defeat to China on Monday. Their male counterparts, meanwhile, have an equally tough start, facing hosts Japan on Wednesday. Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP he was deeply unhappy with the cabins where the men’s basketball team are staying. “Based on my experience this is the worst it has ever been,” he said. “Athletes who are over two metres tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It’s unreasonable.” Byeon Jun-hyeong, from the basketball team, posted a video on social media showing a leaking sink and soaked floor in his hut. He posted the caption, “Please help us”.
