The huts are set to be home to 2,000 athletes and officials over the more than two weeks of the Games. Indian sports chiefs are so worried about the cabins that they built replicas to help get their athletes used to them. Jung accused organisers of failing to respond to South Korea’s concerns, and said he was “discussing extensively with the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee what to do about this”. Hundreds of athletes were briefly evacuated from their accommodation last week as record rainfall lashed Nagoya, with more rain forecast in the coming days. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected at the Games – a bigger number than the Olympics. Local organisers were initially expecting 15,000 and argued last month that they had “neither the manpower nor the budget” to deal with ballooning numbers. The Olympic Council of Asia later said that everyone would get a place to stay. A South Korean Olympic committee official told AFP that, with the Games just days away, there were problems. “At the moment there is a serious shortage of accommodation not only for the entire South Korean delegation to the Asian Games, but for delegations from around the world in the Aichi-Nagoya area,” the official said. “We are doing everything we can to resolve the issue and ensure there are no such problems.” Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino said all his country’s athletes had been given a room, but “some officials, like coaches, were moved to different hotels and Airbnb”. Asian Games organisers did not immediately respond to an AFP request for comment. The Italian cruise ship Costa Serena is expected to arrive in Nagoya on Tuesday, and between 4,000 and 5,000 athletes will stay on the vessel. The rest will be in hotels, including in Tokyo, where swimming, diving and equestrian events will take place.

title: US blocks Iran’s nuclear chief from Vienna meeting
description: US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Mohammad Eslami was blocked from entering Austria because he was a ‘sanctioned individual’.
content: Iran’s nuclear chief was blocked from attending an annual conference on Monday at the headquarters of the UN’s nuclear agency in Vienna after US pressure, both Washington and Tehran said. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright confirmed to reporters that Washington had applied pressure to stop Mohammad Eslami from entering Austria, saying “he’s a sanctioned individual and we don’t want sanctioned individuals evading their sanctions”. “He asked for a waiver of the sanctions and it was denied.” Iranian state TV said Eslami and a delegation “took a regular flight to Vienna on Saturday, but were blocked on the way because of obstructions by the United States”. Behrouz Kamalvandi, a senior official from Iran’s nuclear agency, accused the US of “bullying political pressure” and said the bloc set a precedent that would affect everybody. The Austrian foreign ministry said it had requested an exemption for Mohammad Eslami, who is covered by a UN travel ban, but that the Security Council rejected it “due to a lack of consensus”. A diplomatic source in Vienna had said earlier that US pressure was behind the entry refusal. Eslami was due to attend the annual general conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN’s nuclear watchdog, which runs until Friday. Eslami attended last year’s event and delivered a speech there on behalf of Iran, a member state of the IAEA, despite the sanctions against him already being in place. Tehran summoned Austria’s charge d’affaires in response to the decision to bar Eslami. “The Austrian government’s refusal to issue visas to the delegation of the Islamic Republic of Iran is a completely unjustified decision,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said at a press conference in Tehran attended by AFP. “It is clear to us that this incident occurred under American pressure, but that does not absolve the Austrian government of responsibility.” The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. For decades, Western powers have accused the Islamic republic of seeking nuclear weapons, a claim that Tehran categorically denies.

title: Cloudy with a chance of Big Macs: McDonald’s and Meituan launch drone route in Shanghai
description: Fast-food orders will soar through the Shanghai sky, quickly reaching designated kiosks along the West Bund, offering a new way to collect meals.
content: Shanghai’s bustling riverfront has become the latest testing ground for urban logistics technology, with McDonald’s and Chinese food-delivery giant Meituan joining forces to launch the country’s first catering brand-exclusive drone-delivery route. Commencing operations last week, the new service allows visitors strolling or exercising along the scenic West Bund area in Shanghai’s Xuhui district to have their fast-food orders ‘airdropped’ directly to designated kiosks, according to a recent statement by district authorities. The 3.1km (1.93-mile) flight path, originating from a McDonald’s restaurant in Xuhui, is designed to serve thousands of office workers in the area, as well as the large crowds of tourists who frequent the riverside, the statement said. The customised drones can handle a maximum payload of 2.4kg (5.29lbs) and complete waterfront deliveries in as fast as 10 minutes, according to an official Meituan statement. The move reflects how China is doubling down on its so-called “low-altitude economy” as a new engine for tech innovation. The Shanghai route offers a glimpse into how airborne logistics can play an increasing role in the fiercely competitive food delivery industry. Meituan has been expanding its drone business in recent years, seeking to maintain an early-mover advantage over domestic competitors like Alibaba Group Holding and JD.com in the race to dominate next-generation urban logistics. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Meituan’s commercial drone delivery orders have surpassed 900,000, the company told Chinese media in May. Meituan is likely to see its drone business achieve large-scale “front-end profitability” in the next two to three years, Meituan vice-president Mao Yinian was quoted as saying. The new route is part of a broader “aerial delivery network” planned by Meituan to connect landmarks in Xuhui. It also marks the food-delivery giant’s second “systematic urban aerial network”, following its first in Shenzhen. The Shanghai network hosts nearly 20 catering brands, and Meituan said it expects that number to surpass 40 by the end of the year. Wei Qijun, who is in charge of national commercial management for Meituan’s drones, was cited by the district government as saying that the aircraft maintained a “99.999 per cent safety factor” – a metric he attributed to the company’s nine years of research and testing. The drones can operate normally in moderate rain and snow, as well as in Force 6 winds, Wei said. On the Beaufort scale, Force 6 indicates strong winds of up to 49km/h (31mph). Wei added that the system would automatically ground the fleet, after completing active orders, if the weather turned extreme.

title: Buyer’s bonus or brazen theft? The legal fight over HK$30 million Mark Six prize
description: Lawyer says 14 government employees must launch civil proceedings to recover their shares after a colleague allegedly kept the prize money.
content: Fourteen Hong Kong government employees can only recover their shares of a HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) Mark Six lottery windfall through civil legal proceedings, a lawyer has said, after a colleague allegedly refused to split the prize, went missing, and was later arrested. Vitus Lawyers principal partner Vitus Leung Wing-hang told the South China Morning Post on Monday that retrieving the money would not be easy for the victims, who worked at the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. Leung added that the 36-year-old colleague, arrested on Friday on suspicion of theft, would still face criminal charges even if he returned the disputed funds. “If that person is found guilty, the bank account doesn’t belong to the other 14 people. So the bank will not release the money immediately,” he said, adding that the victims would “have to go to civil court”. The dispute centres on the suspect’s failure to reach a consensus with the 14 victims over his claim to a larger share of the windfall. He reportedly argued he deserved more because he bought the tickets and decided the strategy, even though all 15 had contributed to a pooled fund. The group won the prize in the September 5 draw, which was part of the record HK$228 million “snowball” jackpot marking the 50th anniversary of the Mark Six lottery, organised by the Hong Kong Jockey Club. Following a deadlock during a meeting over how to divide the winnings, the suspect reportedly vanished from work for five days. His disappearance prompted a 53-year-old colleague to file a police report, leading to the man’s arrest on Friday for alleged theft. Police subsequently froze the suspect’s bank account and the HK$30 million prize pending further investigation. Leung said the victims could not simply ask the bank to hand over the money even if the suspect were convicted of theft. The bank would not release the funds immediately because the frozen account belonged to the suspect and might also contain his personal cash mixed with the prize money, he said. He compared the civil recovery process to online fraud cases, where victims who transfer money into a third party’s account must sue the account holder to retrieve their funds. The group would need to hire lawyers to initiate civil proceedings to recover their shares from the frozen account, Leung said. Leung added that the bank account might have “monies more than that amount to be released to the 14 people”, so the victims would need “another civil procedure” to get the funds back. Leung emphasised that possessing a winning lottery ticket did not automatically confer full legal ownership of the prize money. He said the law carefully distinguished between the person holding the ticket and the true beneficial owners of the asset. Although the arrested man held the ticket and the funds in his bank account, all 15 contributors remained the beneficial owners of the prize, he added. With any property, including land, the legal title might be in one person’s name, but the beneficial owner could be someone else, Leung said. To avoid similar disputes, Leung advised members of lottery syndicates to establish clear terms before buying tickets, suggesting that even a basic written record would suffice. “Just put it in a simple message in a WhatsApp group,” Leung said.

title: Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan royal crisis deepens amid claims of grave disloyalty to ruler
description: The customary council says an April proclamation purporting to remove Tuanku Muhriz Munawir was invalid from the outset.
content: Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan royal crisis escalated on Monday after the state’s customary council said six men behind the latest attempt to remove ruler Tuanku Muhriz Munawir could be regarded as having committed grave disloyalty to the monarch. The ruling deepens a months-long struggle over Malaysia’s only elective monarchy, where a rival group of traditional chiefs has sought to depose Muhriz and install another royal in his place. The dispute helped bring down the previous state government and trigger a snap election, only to resurface weeks after a new Umno-led administration took office. The Dewan Keadilan dan Undang said after a special sitting on Sunday that an April 19 proclamation purporting to remove Muhriz was invalid from the outset. “No such investigation was ever carried out,” the council said, referring to the constitutional requirement for a “full and complete” inquiry before the four territorial chiefs, known as the undang, could ask the ruler to step down. It said Muhriz had never been given notice or an opportunity to answer the allegations of misconduct, while three of the four men who signed the April proclamation were not legally holding office as undang at the time. The council also said a later document publicised on September 5, bearing the signature of Chief Minister Ismail Lasim, could not revive the April proclamation. “There cannot be a successor so long as the office is lawfully occupied,” it said, reaffirming Muhriz as the legitimate Yang di-Pertuan Besar, the title used for Negeri Sembilan’s ruler. The council said the actions of six signatories to the September document could be considered derhaka under adat law, using the Malay term for grave disloyalty or defiance towards a ruler. It accused four of them of using offices they did not hold, trying to remove the ruler without the required inquiry and issuing invalid directions to government officials. The council ordered its secretary to lodge a police report and told state officials not to act on instructions arising from the disputed proclamation. It also rejected the state government’s proposal for a reconciliation committee, saying customary matters assigned to the council under the state constitution could not be delegated. Negeri Sembilan differs from Malaysia’s eight other royal states because its ruler is elected by four undang under adat perpatih, a matrilineal customary system with roots in Sumatra. Article 10 of the state constitution allows the undang to seek a ruler’s abdication, but only after a full inquiry and through a formal proclamation. The crisis began in April when four chiefs declared Muhriz removed and named a replacement. The council rejected that move on July 31. The political fallout contributed to the dissolution of the state assembly and an August 1 election, after which Ismail was sworn in before Muhriz on August 2. Ismail later acknowledged signing another proclamation to remove Muhriz on August 3 but said he did so “against my will and under duress”. He filed a police report and called the document “invalid, unconstitutional and unenforceable”. Lawyers for the rival chiefs denied coercion, saying Ismail signed voluntarily after being briefed and while accompanied by his own lawyer. Police have opened an investigation into Ismail’s allegation. Constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said the council’s use of derhaka should not be read as a criminal treason charge. “The Malaysian Penal Code doesn’t have a ‘treason’ offence per se,” Lim told This Week in Asia, adding that provisions covering waging war against or intending death or hurt to a ruler did not apply here. “So I don’t think anyone is envisioning criminal action.”

title: China’s inbound tourism revenue projected to reach US$470 billion by 2040: UBS
description: Country’s inbound travel revenue forecast to double share of economy and capture 15 per cent of global holiday market, Swiss bank says.
content: Revenue from inbound travel to China is forecast to reach US$470 billion by 2040, more than doubling its current share of the economy and helping offset weak domestic demand, according to UBS. Tourism from outside mainland China would expand to 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) on a compound annual growth rate of 8.9 per cent from 2025, the Swiss investment bank estimated. China’s inbound travel revenue would represent 15 per cent of the world tourism market by around 2040, said Chen Xin, head of China leisure and transport research at UBS, in a special report summary on Friday. “Amid weak domestic demand, policymakers increasingly see inbound tourism as an incremental consumption driver,” the report said. China, aiming to stimulate its economy, has opened visa-free travel in stages since 2023 to about 50 countries including Australia, Russia, Singapore and most of Europe. The list of visa-free countries had expanded by 188 per cent compared with pre-2023, UBS said. International flight capacity for China trips could increase by about 150 per cent from last year through 2040. China offered “competitive travel costs”, the bank said. UBS expected a “spending mix upgrade” among inbound arrivals, with accommodation, catering and shopping at an estimated 78 per cent of their spending by around 2040, up from 51 per cent in 2019. Tax-refund “optimisation” and stronger domestic brands should drive more shopping among foreign tourists, alongside a growing supply of mid- to higher-end hotels and a broader calendar of international events, UBS said. We see the clearest read-through for airports, hotels, premium malls and online travel agencies, where incremental foreign traffic can support topline growth UBS report “A key investor debate is whether the opportunity is large enough to move domestic consumption and travel-related earnings,” the report said. “We see the clearest read-through for airports, hotels, premium malls and online travel agencies, where incremental foreign traffic can support topline growth and international travellers’ per-passenger spending is likely to be higher than that of domestic tourists.” The report said China appeared “structurally well positioned to capture a larger share of global travel spending, supported by its rich tourism resources, competitive travel costs and improving accessibility”. UBS forecast a 4.7 per cent compound annual growth rate for the number of inbound travellers by 2040, with per-capita spending growth at 4 per cent. Domestic travel is expected to grow at 4.8 per cent annually from 2025 through 2040, it forecast. Local consumption has come under pressure in China from a prolonged downturn in the property sector and a tough labour market.

title: Reacher star Alan Ritchson splits from wife Catherine after 20 years – what to know about her
description: They share three sons and collaborated on the 2017 short film Tree House Time Machine, starring Emily Alyn Lind, before their recent separation.
content: Reacher star Alan Ritchson, who plays the hit Amazon Prime Video show’s titular character Jack Reacher, recently announced his split from his wife Catherine. The former couple, who were married for 20 years, announced the news in a joint Instagram post. “After 20 years together, Cat and I have decided to end our marriage and continue alongside one another in a different way,” the statement read. “We grew up together. We built a life and a family together. And we are raising three incredible boys who will always be the center of our world.” They added: “The best gift we can give one another – and our boys – right now is friendship, grace and a commitment to becoming the strongest co-parents we can be.” Here’s everything you need to know about Alan Ritchson’s wife, Catherine Ritchson. What does Catherine Ritchson do? Born in March 1989, Catherine Ritchson is a writer and producer who worked on the 2017 short film Tree House Time Machine, written and directed by her husband. The film also stars Emily Alyn Lind, the lead actress in We Were Liars. According to IMDb, Catherine is also the writer and producer of the comedy project Employee 665, although there is little information about it as it is still in development. How did Alan and Catherine Ritchson meet? Catherine first met Ritchson during their secondary school years when they were both doing ballet. “I thought she was a college student, so I was afraid to talk to her,” the actor told The Hollywood Reporter in a 2024 interview. “I figured there was no point because she’s going to be older than me, but I found out she was doing the exact same thing that I was. We finally spoke and then did a play together that summer,” the Runner star said. During an appearance on Today, Ritchson told hosts Hoda Kotb and Jenna Bush Hager that Catherine would bring him cookies before his stage performances. “Of course I fell in love,” he said. They share 3 sons Ritchson and Catherine tied the knot in 2006 and have three sons – Calem, Edan and Amory. Catherine has supported her husband throughout his career, serving as his plus-one at several red carpet events. In 2023, Catherine penned a sweet Instagram post celebrating their 17-year wedding anniversary: “Something I’ve learned over our 17 years of marriage: Real love is not found in star charts, flirtation, or charming manipulation. In fact, real love isn’t found at all.” “As the days, months, and years pass you look around and realize you’ve built a kingdom. Some parts will lay unfinished; others may have been knocked down and need to be rebuilt. But the important part is that you both keep building by tenderly place each brick with dedication and honor in your heart for one another,” she continued. While the announcement of their split is recent, Page Six reported that Ritchson quietly filed for divorce in December last year. Court documents uncovered by TMZ revealed that the pair had reconciled in March before eventually calling it quits in September.

title: Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions blocked by a second judge
description: The decision comes as Trump’s ‌Republicans battle to retain control of both houses of Congress in the ‌November 3 midterms.
content: A second federal judge late on Sunday moved to block President Donald Trump’s administration from implementing a new ‌US Postal Service (USPS) rule that would tighten mail-in voting requirements, though the US Supreme Court is still weighing the administration’s request to overturn a separate order blocking the rule. Washington-based ⁠US District Judge Carl Nichols’ decision comes as Trump’s ‌Republicans battle to retain control of both houses of Congress in the ‌November 3 midterms. Trump, who falsely claims that ⁠his ⁠2020 presidential election defeat was the result of widespread voter ‌fraud, has for years called for restrictions on voting by mail. Nichols ‌granted ‌a request from the Democratic Party for ‌a preliminary injunction blocking the rule, which the ⁠party called an unlawful intrusion by the federal government ⁠into election administration. The judge, who was appointed by Trump during his first term in the White ⁠House, wrote that the new rule could make it harder for some people to vote by mail and that the new regulation exceeded the Postal ‌Service’s authority. “No statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts ‌of the rule,” ‌wrote the judge, who was appointed by Trump during his first term in the White House. Neither the Justice Department nor the Postal Service immediately responded to requests for comment. In a separate case, Boston-based US ‌District Judge Indira Talwani blocked the rule on September 4 at the behest of Democratic-led states and voting rights groups. The administration ⁠swiftly asked the Supreme Court ⁠to pause that order so the USPS could implement the new rule, meaning the final decision on whether the restrictions can proceed likely rests with the nation’s top court. The rule would ‌require states to submit a list of voters eligible to receive mail ballots to the USPS and to place unique barcodes on outbound and return ballot envelopes. The USPS would be empowered to refuse ‌to ‌deliver ballots to voters who do not appear on the lists or in states that do not comply with the new standards. In urging Nichols ‌to block the USPS rule, the Democrats in an August 25 court filing wrote that the US Constitution assigns the role of administering elections to the ⁠states with congressional oversight, not the president and executive branch agencies. The Democrats said the rule risked disenfranchising eligible voters. “Congress has enacted nothing to empower USPS ⁠or the President to interfere with States’ decisions about who should receive a mail ballot or how mail-ballot envelopes should be designed,” the Democrats wrote. Justice Department lawyers, representing the administration, said the USPS was not seeking to “seize control” of ‌federal election administration. The lawyers said states ‌would retain control over who was eligible to vote. “The rule does not displace a single state election law. And it need not and should not prevent a single voter from voting by mail,” the lawyers said in a September 4 filing. All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting. Of those, 29 states allow voters to ask to cast ballots by mail without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely by mail.

title: Japan eyes quantum sub-hunting drone sensors as China extends undersea reach
description: Feeling the pinch from cost and personnel pressures, Tokyo’s defence planners aim to unlock potential in uncrewed systems.
content: Japan is looking to develop submarine-detecting quantum sensors for aerial drones, the latest move in a growing undersea competition pitting China against the United States and its allies across the Indo-Pacific. Released in late August, Tokyo’s defence budget request for fiscal 2027 includes research into a smaller, more capable quantum magnetic sensor, a technology that uses the properties of atoms to detect tiny changes in magnetic fields that could reveal a submarine. The project is one of numerous initiatives submitted ahead of Japan’s planned year-end security strategy revisions, with funding to be decided during budget compilation. The Nikkei newspaper reported on Thursday that the defence ministry aimed to develop the sensor by fiscal 2031. It would be mounted on low-cost drones flying near the sea surface and operating from warships. The move towards uncrewed search comes as Japan faces growing cost and personnel pressures. Masashi Murano, a defence specialist with the Washington-based Hudson Institute, said crewed anti-submarine warfare was “extraordinarily expensive per unit of ocean searched”, and while unmanned systems could bring down the cost of persistent coverage, the difficulties of detection remained. “My understanding is that magnetic sensors are limited in detection range and are not suited to wide-area searches,” Murano said. But Chinese submarines must pass through straits to reach the Pacific, making low-cost sensors useful around chokepoints, he added. “Even if the detection range of each individual sensor is short, mounting them on cheap unmanned systems that can be fielded in large numbers makes this far more efficient than doing the same job with a crewed P-1 patrol aircraft,” he said. Chinese researchers are also pursuing this technology, reporting last year that they had already tested a drone-mounted quantum magnetic sensor system at sea. Beijing has also unveiled a host of new anti-submarine capabilities, including the Y-9Q patrol aircraft, the shipborne Z-20F helicopter and a Wing Loong X drone variant designed to drop sonobuoys. In tandem, Beijing is building ocean sensor networks linking satellites, buoys, underwater gliders and seabed listening arrays – elements sometimes described as the “Underwater Great Wall”. The surveillance build-up is unfolding alongside an expanding Chinese submarine fleet. According to the Pentagon, China could have 80 subs by 2035 as construction capacity expands. Against this backdrop, Washington and its allies are also investing in detection and attack systems. In January, drone maker General Atomics said it had tested an MQ-9B SeaGuardian carrying a larger sonobuoy load, while the US Navy last month sought industry input on Silent Anvil, a compact air-launched torpedo for a wider range of crewed and uncrewed aircraft. Under the Aukus partnership, Australia, Britain and the US are developing payloads and supporting systems for uncrewed underwater vehicles, including for anti-submarine warfare. Japan has also joined the three in testing underwater acoustic communications for maritime autonomous systems, while Australia’s future Mogami-class frigates will carry Japanese towed-sonar technology. These developments point to a widening contest over the ability to detect, track and attack opposing undersea forces. Murano said that while anti-submarine warfare competition was “certainly accelerating”, it was “not a symmetric arms race”. Instead, he described it as “a collision of two mutually reinforcing requirements”. “For the first time, China has a sea-based nuclear-armed force worth protecting,” Murano said. Its growing fleet of nuclear-powered attack submarines also needed to get beyond the first island chain, he added, giving Beijing a stronger incentive to invest seriously in anti-submarine warfare and undersea surveillance. The US and its allies, meanwhile, needed the undersea domain because it was “the only place they can operate persistently inside China’s weapons engagement zone”, the area exposed to Chinese long-range sensors and weapons. “Both sides now have to hide and hunt at the same time,” he said. Against this backdrop, Murano said advances in data processing were just as important as the sensors themselves, because computers could combine many weak signals that might reveal little on their own. “What is new is less the sensors than the ability to make them mean something together,” he said. In this context, retired Australian vice-admiral Peter Jones of UNSW Canberra pointed to artificial intelligence, saying it had been used in Ukraine to identify targets “among the mass of picture clutter”. Jones also said that submarine detection could occur at ranges of only “a couple of thousand metres or less”, making more sensors especially valuable. “The proliferation of all these sensors will make it more difficult for submarines to conduct their ops covertly,” he said, particularly where sensors were concentrated. “This will only make the submariner’s life harder.”

title: Hyrox Beijing athlete who soiled herself says ‘win is a win’ as faecal row rages
description: Joanna Wietrzyk continued despite unfortunate accident, and officials have done little to dampen resulting furore or defuse growing backlash.
content: An elite competitor who soiled herself during Hyrox Beijing and then went on to win has defended her actions saying “go hard or go home...a win is a win”. In a now-deleted Instagram story, Joanna Wietrzyk thanked everyone for their support and said she would be back soon. Wietrzyk’s actions this past weekend have sparked furious debate among the Hyrox community, with others asking how she had been allowed to continue, and organisers facing criticism for their response to the incident. A spectator, identified only as Ms Zhai, told local media that Wietrzyk started her race at 2.40pm on Saturday and that faecal matter was visible on the track 30 minutes later, causing several runners to slip. “Think about how disgusting it is, especially when we use the exact same track,” another participant racing the following day said. Competitors also raised questions over perceived double standards. Under Hyrox rules, littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose on the floor incurs a two-minute penalty. Splashing water on one’s body to cool down is also banned “to avoid slip hazards for others”. The incident resulted in foreign matter contaminating the track, sledge pads, rubber flooring, and station areas. Spectators reported that event officials alerted competitors to bypass affected spots but failed to stop Wietrzyk or halt the event, leaving more than 1,000 subsequent participants to compete on the contaminated surface. Zhai said a domestic competitor had been penalised simply for splashing water on her face, while Wietrzyk continued unpunished, ultimately winning the women’s solo event. On Monday, Hyrox World released a statement acknowledging the organisational lapses while defending the athlete. “In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood,” the governing body wrote. While acknowledging that community concerns were “legitimate,” the organisation praised athlete resilience, stating: “That courage, resilience and refusal to give in are precisely what makes elite athletes so extraordinary.” Addressing the growing online backlash, Hyrox said it drew “an important line” against harassment, and said anyone doing so would be “permanently banned from all Hyrox events”. Officials in China previously said staff had immediately isolated affected areas, performed comprehensive disinfection through the end of the day, removed impacted equipment, and scheduled a carpet replacement after the event wrapped up. That did not stop the backlash on Chinese social media, with users condemning local organisers as “arrogant”. “Athlete incontinence is an accident, nothing to mock,” one commenter wrote. “But continuing to run after doing so, contaminating the track and making subsequent athletes step on it and staff clean up after, I really cannot understand what kind of ‘sportsmanship’ this is.” Another asked: “Does this mean more people will now have an excuse to relieve themselves in the venue under the guise of perseverance?” Later on Monday, Hyrox China admitted the global rulebook lacked provisions to penalise an athlete in these circumstances and said referees had relied solely on Elite 15 experience and failed to intervene, revealing “deficiencies in the establishment of competition rules”. “Safeguarding the experience of every participant and maintaining venue public hygiene and safety is Hyrox China’s primary baseline,” organizers said, while adding they had submitted a proposal to introduce rules governing track management, race intervention, and result determination under scenarios of “extreme physical distress and venue public health risks”. Organisers also pledged that future events would include third-party sanitation testing alongside dedicated teams sanitizing equipment “during intervals between different athletes’ use”.

title: Finland to join France’s forward nuclear deterrent
description: France’s initiative would extend its nuclear deterrent to other European countries through joint exercises.
content: Finland has decided to join France’s forward nuclear deterrence initiative, extending the measure to a country sharing a long border with Russia, the two countries said in a joint statement on Monday. France is extending its nuclear deterrent to European allies as the continent reassesses its security in the wake of US President Donald Trump’s shake-up of Nato. “Finland has decided to join forward deterrence,” the two countries said. “A nuclear steering group will be set up in the coming months to begin implementing this cooperation.” Finland is the 10th European country to agree to join the plan to access France’s nuclear stockpile to bolster security on the continent. Eight countries were initially on board: Britain, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece and Denmark. Norway then joined in May. Monday’s announcement came as part of a new strategic partnership between Finland and France, due to be signed by the countries’ foreign ministers later in the day in Helsinki. Finnish President Alexander Stubb confirmed the decision on social media, saying it was “first and foremost about strengthening European security”. He stressed that the French nuclear deterrent would not “replace or overlap” with Nato’s. “Finland’s foremost priority is to act as part of Nato and the European Union,” he added. France’s initiative would extend its nuclear deterrent to other European countries through joint exercises and allow participating countries, for the first time, to temporarily host French nuclear-armed aircraft. Paris would retain national control over its nuclear arsenal, with the final decision on its use remaining with the French president. Finland abandoned decades of military non-alignment when it joined Nato in 2023, following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its parliament voted in June to lift the country’s blanket ban on nuclear weapons, allowing them to be brought into, transported through, supplied or possessed in Finland when required for the country’s defence.

title: 9 movie locations in Prague you may recognise, from XxX to Van Helsing and Amadeus
description: Prague has served as the backdrop for a number of films, from Mission Impossible to Amadeus and Casino Royale. Here are 9 locations.
content: Tom Cruise tearing through the Old Town alleyway Zelezna towards the Estates Theatre; Mozart conducting an opera – these are just a couple of scenes from the many classic films shot in Prague, in the Czech Republic. Beyond the Cruise spy thriller Mission: Impossible (1996) and Amadeus (1984), winner of eight Oscars, recent films include Blade Runner 2099 and A Place Called Home. Then there are the television shows, says Hedvika Petrzelkova, a public relations officer at the Czech Film Commission. “There are around 30 to 40 film and TV series projects each year,” she says. Prague is a city popular with producers and film crews, and the place to go for film fans who like city breaks. Petrzelkova spells out why the Czech capital is popular as a film location: “The historic city, with its Gothic, Renaissance and baroque architecture, is in good condition. What’s more, it’s not as expensive to film here as it is elsewhere. And the Czech film crews have ‘golden hands’, as they say here. They’re known for being able to sort anything out.” Compare films with reality and you will recognise Prague straight away – even if it doesn’t always play itself, but stars as Paris, Vienna or London. Here are nine must-see stops for a trip to Prague. 1. Old Town Square Prague’s most significant square, the Old Town Square (Staromestske namesti), exudes history, smells of the horses from the carriages, and is flanked by ornate facades and the twin-towered Tyn Church. That was Notre-Dame in the 2004 film Van Helsing,” says Eva Kupr, who offers film-themed tours for visitors. The Old Town Square also served as a backdrop in US action films xXx (2002), starring Vin Diesel, and Bangkok Dangerous (2008), starring Nicolas Cage. 2. Charles Bridge Where crowds surged across the Vltava, Tom Cruise sprinted ahead as agent Ethan Hunt – and Oscar-winner Jon Voight plunged into the river. In Mission: Impossible, neither of them had time to appreciate the city’s beauty. In the 2006 remake of the horror film The Omen, Father Brennan (Pete Postlethwaite) delivered shocking news to the protagonist Robert Thorn (Liev Schreiber) beneath the bridge. A little further on, in the park on Kampa Island, Matt Damon’s character tried to get some sleep on his first night in Zurich in The Bourne Identity (2002). 3. Rudolfinum Within sight of the Charles Bridge stands the neo-Renaissance Rudolfinum. A grand staircase, flanked by garlands of lanterns, leads up to it. Classical music resonates through the concert hall. This is the home of the Czech Philharmonic Orchestra. The magnificent building featured as a location in The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen (2003), starring Sean Connery, and Hannibal Rising (2007). 4. Bluelight Bar To the west, the Charles Bridge stretches towards the Mala Strana district, where the Bluelight bar is bathed not in blue but in orange light. In marital drama Endstation Prague, Danish film star Mads Mikkelsen takes a seat at the bar and listens to a live performance by a young Czech woman with whom he is having a brief affair. Bartender Anna Vechtikova is not familiar with the 2006 film, but years ago she played herself in an episode of a German crime series. However, when she saw the results, she was disappointed. The scene was over in a flash, she says. “They’d been filming all day, and I was absolutely knackered.” 5. National Museum “Bond. James Bond.” Yes, he was here too, played by Daniel Craig. In Casino Royale (2006), we see the museum’s vast, elegant foyer on Wenceslas Square – replete with arches, runners and diminutive lanterns – starring as a hotel lobby. It has worn many guises, from the US embassy in Mission: Impossible, and as a medical school in From Hell (2001), which starred Johnny Depp. Otherwise, the National Museum – Narodni muzeum – is the No 1 destination when it comes to the country’s natural and cultural history, with the neo-Renaissance building itself playing a part in that storied past. 6. Prague Castle The sprawling complex of Prague Castle – Prazsky hrad – a Unesco World Heritage site and now the seat of the president of the Czech Republic, has featured in numerous films. You may have seen it in The Brothers Bloom (2008), starring Rachel Weisz and Adrien Brody, or Shanghai Knights (2003) with Jackie Chan, where the Matthias Gate was cast as the entrance to Buckingham Palace. Equally striking is the neighbouring Hradcany Square (Hradcanske namesti), which came to life in Les Misérables (1998). Meanwhile in Amadeus, a masterpiece by director Milos Forman, house No 7, represented Mozart’s Vienna home. Visitors can still marvel at the wooden portal and the door fittings there. 7. Strahov Monastery Visitors can still sense Strahovsky klaster’s mysterious aura today when they approach the barriers to the baroque monastery library, split into two sections. Surrounded by ceiling frescoes and tens of thousands of books, the library stood in for the Vatican in The Omen and the British House of Commons in Casino Royale. 8. The Saints Cyril and Methodius Cathedral This Orthodox church is a unique spot where reality and cinema blend together as nowhere else. During Operation Anthropoid in 1942, resistance fighters who assassinated Nazi leader Reinhard Heydrich took refuge in the crypt, but their hiding place was betrayed. In Anthropoid (2016), Cillian Murphy starred as one of the assassins. Petrzelkova says the original church was blended with a replica at the Barrandov Film Studios in Prague, a move often adopted by productions to protect fragile sites from damage during action shots. 9. Riverbank area Petrzelkova describes a scene: “Ana de Armas arrives in a boat and walks through the round glass entrance into the Avoid Café, but in the film that was the entrance to a hotel.” This is from the 2025 action thriller From the World of John Wick: Ballerina. “Some scenes for Ballerina were also filmed a little further down the river on the (A)Void Floating Gallery with Keanu Reeves,” barman Emil Obsluha says. Recently, he and his colleague Michael Kadlec got to meet another Hollywood star up close: Orlando Bloom, filming a beer ad at the “Avoid Café”.

title: Chinese dining chain drops ‘Stir-Fried Pork King’ title amid award scandal
description: ‘Nowadays, everyone seems to be a master or an expert. These titles no longer carry the same weight,’ says a commenter.
content: A Hunan restaurant brand from China has become a sensation in the US, yet faces scrutiny at home regarding its once-esteemed title of “Stir-Fried Pork King.” Founded in 2003, Chef Fei has evolved into one of China’s most recognisable Hunan restaurant chains, celebrated for its fiery flavours and signature stir-fried pork dish. The brand now operates over 200 outlets nationwide and reports having served more than 100 million customers in China by 2025. On August 29, Chef Fei launched its first US outlet in San Diego, California. For many diners, the allure extended beyond a mere plate of chilli pork; it embodied the cultural experience that accompanied it. As staff serve the signature dishes, the dining room resonates with a rhythmic introduction inspired by guankou: “Ni hao, ni hao (hello in Chinese). China’s King of Stir-fry. Enjoy Chef Fei’s stir-fried beef with peppers.” Guankou, a technique from Chinese Xiangsheng, involves performers delivering lengthy passages in a rapid, uninterrupted flow. To cater to local preferences, Chef Fei modified its signature stir-fried pork into a beef version, priced at US$32.79. In a US market historically dominated by adapted versions of Chinese cuisine, Chef Fei offers more than just flavourful dishes: it provides a curated encounter with contemporary Chinese dining culture. Online, some American diners embraced the restaurant as a more authentic alternative to Western adaptations of Chinese food, such as orange chicken. One customer described the food as “delicious,” noting that it tasted just like the dishes they had enjoyed in China. For some Chinese students in the US, hearing a foreign server say “ni hao” was enough to justify hours of travel. However, the reception back home has been much more complicated. The controversy surrounding Chef Fei surfaced after the China Cuisine Association announced in July that previously issued honorary titles, including “master” awards and related certificates, would no longer be recognised. In August, the Chinese government further clarified that social organisations should not host unapproved competitions offering honorary titles that include terms like “national.” Online users traced Chef Fei’s “National Stir-Fried Pork King” title to a 2020 online competition organised by the association, where dishes were evaluated through submitted photos, videos, public voting, and professional reviews. The revelation sparked criticism from consumers, who questioned whether a dish’s taste and quality could truly be assessed solely through images. In response, Chef Fei removed the title from its promotional materials and replaced it with a new slogan: “Selected black pork, cooked by professional chefs.” According to Jiemian News, founder Fei Lianghui expressed his support for the new regulations in an internal notice to employees. Fei’s personal journey has long been integral to the brand’s identity. He began learning to cook from his father at 16 and became a head chef by 20, later earning the China Cuisine Association’s “Chinese Golden Chef Award.” In China, the brand’s signature chilli pork dish has historically been priced between 60 and 70 yuan (US$9 and US$10). However, its rapid domestic expansion seems to have slowed. Chef Fei reportedly opened 46 new restaurants last year, in contrast to just 16 this year. The chain has also faced a series of consumer complaints in recent months, including failed food safety inspections and reports of foreign objects found in dishes at several outlets. “Nowadays, everyone seems to be a master or an expert. These titles no longer carry the same weight,” remarked one online commenter. Another quipped: “I only hope Chef Fei will lower its prices now that it has lost the title.”

title: Hong Kong’s HK$500b silver economy by 2034 offers ‘blue ocean’ prospects: Paul Chan
description: Finance chief urges elderly care industry to employ AI and robotics technology, while exploring what bay area has to offer.
content: Hong Kong’s silver economy is set to become a HK$500 billion (US$63.8 billion) market by 2034, the city’s finance chief has said, urging the elderly care industry to deploy technology and explore cross-border opportunities. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Monday that Hong Kong’s ageing population presented both a challenge and a “promising blue ocean” market opportunity for the city, which could serve as a model for other regions. In a speech at an event to mark the 30th anniversary of the Senior Citizen Home Safety Association (SCHSA), Chan noted that expenditure by individuals aged 60 and above in Hong Kong could grow by 47 per cent from around HK$340 billion in 2024 to nearly HK$500 billion by 2034. “The growth of the silver economy is not merely about increasing products and services, but also about offering better lifestyle choices for seniors with different capabilities and needs,” Chan said. He said that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) had enabled innovative applications in elderly care services, including medical diagnosis and daily living care, while robots could share the load of household chores and assist with physical tasks such as patient transfers. “The direction of using technology to boost caregiving efficiency and relieve carer burden is very clear, and Hong Kong has the right conditions to take the lead in this field,” he said. The city had advantages – including world-class life and health research capabilities, a concentration of funding, talent and start-ups – and was building an international medical innovation centre, Chan said. “The key is to connect these strengths to propel research outcomes into practical and commercially sustainable services,” he said. The Greater Bay Area also offered new opportunities as new demands had emerged for care service referrals, health information sharing and cross-boundary support arrangements, Chan noted. “If we can establish a safe, reliable and seamless service model, there will be opportunities to replicate and promote this model to benefit more seniors,” he said. “This may well be a promising blue ocean worth exploring.” At the same event, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the city had become a “super-aged society” as the median age of Hong Kong’s population was currently 49 years, with nearly a quarter of the population aged 65 or above. Sun said the government’s promotion of senior-friendly technology had raised public awareness and attracted more investment through the HK$2 billion Innovation and Technology Fund for Application in Elderly and Rehabilitation Care. He added that gerontechnology would advance rapidly in the next five years and that it was crucial to cultivate seniors to learn and use it as early as possible, but authorities had to tackle cost and privacy issues. “Another issue the government needs to address is the legal concerns of the public, including how to resolve privacy issues at home and how to ensure that data does not stray from its proper scope,” he said. Joyce Ho Mei-yee, tech enablement director at the Hong Kong Council of Social Service, said the city could consider importing gerontechnology products developed in mainland China, which offered high cost-performance advantages. “Bringing mainland products to Hong Kong involves localisation, which is adapting technology and language for our elderly users,” she said during a panel discussion. However, Ho said popularising these products would be a major challenge moving forward as the localisation process was difficult. Law Chi-kwong, former chairman of the SCHSA, said he expected future developments in gerontechnology to proceed at double the speed compared with the past. His association introduced an emergency alarm system three decades ago when 30 elderly people died during a cold spell at Chinese New Year. Elderly residents living alone can press a button and call a 24-hour support system for immediate help. Law, a former welfare minister, said he envisioned the system growing into an intelligent robot which could see and move in the future. “This kind of service will integrate various aspects of care and companionship with robotics,” he said. “Technology is neutral, but the question is how we design the service to achieve a ‘human-centric’ approach, keeping genuine care at the very core of the service.”

title: China rejects calls for ‘pacing’ on AI development, fearing it would entrench US tech lead
description: Chinese researchers say a slowdown would protect established US incumbents while freezing latecomers out of the market.
content: Calls by US tech leaders for a voluntary slowdown in artificial intelligence development have run into sharp pushback from Chinese researchers and state media, who question whether the proposal is a genuine push for responsibility or an effort to entrench America’s technological lead. The debate intensified on Monday when OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined a growing chorus of Silicon Valley leaders demanding industry-wide “pacing”, warning that competitive pressure must not override safety as AI advanced rapidly. “The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened,” Altman wrote on social media platform X. “Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.” His comments followed a call on Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for frontier labs to slow down development of their most powerful models – a stance also endorsed by xAI founder Elon Musk. In a post on his personal website, Amodei also called for “worldwide pacing of the frontier”, but admitted this would be “much harder to achieve.” “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” he said. Industry leaders and observers are urging a slowdown in AI development after a series of recent safety incidents where experimental models in testing phases hacked into real-world systems. In China, however, the sudden pivot towards self-imposed restraint has been met with scepticism. Some Chinese researchers argued that a blanket slowdown disproportionately protects established US incumbents while freezing latecomers out of the market. “Those who already possess resources can afford a pause. Those who are still building their careers cannot,” said Zhang Xuanming, a researcher with Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen team, in an article on X on Friday. For market leaders, a slowdown was a precaution; for rising players, a “blanket pause” threatened to “close the frontier” before they could compete, he wrote. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Other Chinese engineers echoed that frustration. “When we try to accelerate you tell me to slow down? OMG [oh my God] …” Lin Junyang, a former lead researcher on Alibaba’s Qwen models, wrote in an X post on Sunday, calling on US executives to “stop pretending” they needed permission to operate. Ronny He, an engineer at Shanghai-based AI firm MiniMax, wrote on social media on Sunday, “Yesterday, the mission was AGI. Today, we’re told to slow down. Why do you always get to define the game – and change the rules?” AGI, or artificial general intelligence, refers to software that matches human-level reasoning across a variety of tasks. Concerns have also surfaced in Chinese state media. In a commentary on Sunday, state-owned tabloid Global Times accused Anthropic’s Amodei of proposing a “quiet AI Cold War” to widen America’s technological lead “through technological barriers and regulatory monopolies” while excluding China from global AI governance. In his essay, Amodei called on Washington to tighten restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips, while cracking down on “distillation” – using AI outputs from more advanced models to train cheaper rival models – and the theft of proprietary “model weights”, the underlying code and data that power AI systems. “If we execute these measures well, I believe they would slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead significantly over the next three to five years,” Amodei wrote. Beijing and Washington push ahead The call for caution faces resistance not only in China, but also from the White House. US President Donald Trump dismissed calls for a pause over the weekend, warning that halting progress risks ceding America’s technological edge to China. “Whoever wins with AI wins,” Trump told reporters, writing off safety concerns as the work of “negative forces”. Meanwhile, Beijing is framing AI as a key national security domain. Writing in a journal published by the Cyberspace Administration of China on Sunday, state security minister Chen Yixin labelled AI a primary arena for superpower rivalry, urging robust security frameworks and global governance to manage rising threats. Rather than slowing down, Chinese AI players are accelerating their development timelines. Z.ai, known in China as Zhipu AI, said on Sunday it had raised 33.5 billion yuan (US$5 billion), earmarking 60 per cent of the funds to develop its next-generation GLM model and advance a “fully self-training” system. Last week, prominent researchers – including Zhou Bowen, head of the Shanghai AI Lab, alongside engineers from ByteDance – submitted a paper outlining a five-stage road map towards systems capable of autonomously improving their own code.

title: Meet Ian Bohen, the Yellowstone actor playing operative Grady in Season 3 of Lioness
description: First collaborating with Taylor Sheridan in 2011, the actor has built a career with credits including Teen Wolf, The Dark Knight Rises and Superman & Lois.
content: Fans of Oscar-nominated writer Taylor Sheridan, creator of hit series including Yellowstone and Lioness – which launched its third season on Paramount+ last month – are accustomed to seeing recurring actors across his screen universe. Joining an A-list ensemble led by Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman, and Morgan Freeman, Ian Bohen boards Lioness for Season 3 as US Army Delta Force operative Grady. The drama draws on a real-life military unit of undercover female agents fighting terrorist organisations. The 49-year-old actor began working with Sheridan long before the showrunner became famous for his Western dramas. So who exactly is the “Sheridanverse” star, Ian Bohen? What is Ian Bohen’s background? Ian Bohen, who plays ranch hand Ryan in Yellowstone, was born in September 1976 in Carmel-by-the-Sea, California. As a child, Bohen spent his summers at his grandfather’s ranch, where he learned skills that would come in handy for his Yellowstone role, including horse riding, he told Wide Open Country, an online media outlet covering country music, lifestyle, and entertainment, in 2022. Bohen began acting in 1992 in the sitcom The Torkelsons. He has since amassed over 56 screen credits, starring in projects such as Teen Wolf (both the television series and the film), The Dark Knight Rises (2012) and Superman & Lois (2022). When did Ian Bohen join the ‘Sheridanverse’? Bohen first crossed paths with Sheridan when he was cast in the director’s 2011 horror film Vile. In 2018, Bohen returned to the Sheridanverse as Ryan in Yellowstone. The actor told People that well before Season 3, he had expressed interest to Sheridan about joining Lioness, but was unable to do so due to filming commitments on Yellowstone. Thankfully, the opportunity came up when Bohen wrapped filming Yellowstone’s finale and received a call from Sheridan. “I got a phone call saying, ‘Would you like to come?’ I think the [exact] words were, ‘Would you like to come play with us?’ And of course, those are the magic words,” Bohen recalled in his interview with People. “Yellowstone concluded gloriously, and then I had the opportunity to come and be with these guys. Yeah, it’s great timing.” Who is Ian Bohen dating? Bohen appears to be single at the moment. In the past, he was rumoured to be dating his Yellowstone co-star and on-screen love interest, Lainey Wilson – who married former NFL quarterback Devlin Hodges this May.

title: Forms Syntron draws Hong Kong’s next-gen tycoons in HK$940 million IPO
description: Business heirs are moving beyond property into cutting-edge tech and digital finance companies as the city’s IPO market rebounds.
content: Hong Kong’s younger generation of tycoons is becoming increasingly active in the city’s initial public offering market through family offices and private investments. But their investments extend beyond the property and traditional financial sectors associated with their predecessors, into technology and digital finance. Prominent business leaders Cheng Chi-heng of New World Development and Peter Lee Ka-kit of Henderson Land participated as cornerstone investors in Shenzhen Forms Syntron Information’s HK$940 million (US$119.8 million) Hong Kong listing, according to the company’s official filing on Monday. In exchange for guaranteed share allocations and a mandatory commitment to hold the stocks for at least six months, Cheng and Lee agreed to buy HK$40 million and HK$39.6 million worth of shares, respectively. They were joined by private investment firm Thalassa Capital and Hong Kong-listed LCD manufacturer Yeebo International Holdings. Lee has been particularly active in Hong Kong’s IPO market in recent years. Through his wholly-owned private investment vehicle, he has served as a cornerstone investor in several high-profile debuts, including XtalPi in 2024 – the first specialist technology company to list under Hong Kong’s Chapter 18C rules designed for innovative firms in hi-tech industries. As the city’s broader IPO market stages a robust recovery in 2026 – with total funds raised surpassing HK$340 billion in the first eight months – tycoons and family offices are drawing renewed market attention. Forms Syntron said it met these high-profile investors through business connections, introductions by corporate partners and global offering underwriters during its regular business and investment activities. The financial technology service provider, which caters to the banking industry, has started taking investor orders for its Hong Kong listing and expects its trading debut on September 22. It is offering 58.9 million shares at a maximum price of HK$16 each, according to its listing document. The price marks a 40 per cent discount compared with the 23.02 yuan (US$3.43) closing price of its Shenzhen-listed shares on Friday. The company plans to channel the capital raised into research and development, operational capabilities over the next three to five years, international sales expansion across mainland China and overseas markets, and potential strategic technology acquisitions. Although headquartered in mainland China and already listed in the A-share market, Forms Syntron has strong ties to Hong Kong. Founder and chairman Chow Chi Kwan grew up and was educated in the city, earning a bachelor’s degree in social science from the Chinese University of Hong Kong in 1995. He also serves as a non-official member of Hong Kong’s Digital Economy Development Committee. Founded in 2003, Forms Syntron provides fintech software development, consulting and systems integration services to banks, regulatory authorities and financial institutions across mainland China and Hong Kong, supporting their digital transformation. The Hong Kong market now accounts for more than 80 per cent of the company’s total revenue. Its client base mainly comprises financial institutions and non-bank financial firms, with its top five customers contributing 89.1 per cent of revenue in 2025. The company recorded revenue of 630 million yuan (US$93.9 million) last year, down from 740 million yuan in 2024. Full-year net profit rose 10.3 per cent year on year to 74 million yuan. The company won 221 new projects in 2025, compared with 297 in 2024.

title: Ozempic-maker Novo Nordisk slims down to ‘Novo’
description: It will keep the full Novo Nordisk as its legal corporate name, using Novo and an updated version of its bull logo for its packaging.
content: Danish pharmaceuticals giant Novo Nordisk, maker of weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy, announced on Monday a name change to just Novo, hoping it will be more “memorable and relevant” for clients. The rebrand comes ahead of a strategic presentation on September 21, when executives are to lay out their plan for “a faster, more competitive and increasingly consumer-driven market”. The company is battling fierce competition in the anti-obesity sector, where its hugely successful Ozempic and Wegovy treatments have spurred rivals to catch up. It released a new tablet form of Wegovy in the United States in January, and the pill was recently approved for use in Europe. It will keep the full Novo Nordisk as its legal corporate name, using Novo and an updated version of its bull logo for its packaging. Chief executive Mike Doustdar told Denmark’s TV2 television the rebrand was part of an effort to “reinvent the company”. “People who use insulin are only considered as patients,” he said. “But over the past four or five years, we’ve seen the emergence of a bigger and bigger group that tells us, ‘I’m not a patient, I’m not sick. I just want to lose weight’.”

title: Shein shares drop to lowest since IPO amid ‘underperform’ rating, contact-lens recall
description: Jefferies says Shein’s ‘low-cost parcels, Guangdong’s supplier density, and supplier-funded experimentation’ will be more expensive.
content: Shein Global Holdings saw its shares plummet to their lowest level since listing two weeks ago, falling as much as 10 per cent in Hong Kong trading on Monday, slammed by an “underperform” rating from Jefferies and product safety recalls in Australia and New Zealand. Shein closed down 9 per cent to HK$36.40 on Monday, the lowest since its September 1 debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange. The high-profile stock has been on a downward spiral and is now 25 per cent lower than its initial public offering price of HK$48.56. The latest drop came a day after Jefferies initiated its research on the fast-fashion giant with an “underperform” rating, with a target price of HK$26, implying it has further room to fall. The company’s competitive moat was in its “industrialised newness” that feeds customers new items at a fast speed, but the advantages of “low-cost parcels, Guangdong’s supplier density, and supplier-funded experimentation” would become more expensive, Jefferies equity analysts including John Chou said in a Sunday report. The analysts projected a share price of HK$45 in an “upside scenario”, in which artificial intelligence reduced the cost to sustain newness while localising supplies outside China replicated the ecosystem in Guangdong, Shein’s biggest supply base. A downside scenario could drag its share price down to HK$16, the Jefferies report said. Meanwhile, adding to Shein’s woes were recalls of one of its contact lenses in both Australia and New Zealand, as both governments on Friday said that the products, for cosplay and make-up, may be contaminated with Burkholderia cepacia complex bacteria. “Exposure to this bacterium may pose a risk of eye infection or irritation and an incident was reported in the United Kingdom involving a user who developed an eye infection,” New Zealand’s Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment said on Friday. Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Listed two weeks ago in Hong Kong, Shein’s market capitalisation was HK$155 billion (US$19.8 billion) on Monday, a significant markdown from its peak valuation of nearly US$100 billion in 2022, as well as its Series D+ funding valuation of around US$64 billion in 2023. “Shein’s earnings power is materially exposed to the reset in low-value parcel rules in the US and EU,” Jefferies analysts said. Both regulators have imposed tariffs on low-value imports, “materially increasing the cost of Shein’s historical China-to-consumer model”, they added. As Shein expands its supply chains outside China, including Brazil and Turkey, costs have risen. “Recreating China’s apparel ecosystem overseas would require substantial investment in suppliers, manufacturing capabilities, and operational infrastructure, likely reducing Shein’s historical cost advantage,” according to Jefferies. The question was not whether the company could “continue generating newness”, but whether it could continue doing it “at the same returns”.

title: Hong Kong’s iPhone scam: how to protect your credit card from online fraud
description: In the wake of Hong Kong’s iPhone credit card scam, experts break down data security risks, 3DSecure and practical online shopping safeguards.
content: More than 700 Hongkongers were shocked to discover that their credit cards had been used to place unauthorised orders for Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro series handsets over the weekend. Although banks reassured victims they would not be charged as long as the cards were used with due care and the transactions were proven to be unauthorised, the incident still caused widespread concern over credit card security. The South China Morning Post asked information technology experts for practical tips on how to safeguard credit cards. 1. What happened? Over the weekend, many social media users in Hong Kong reported that their credit cards had been compromised to place orders for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro series, which opened for pre-order on Saturday evening. Police confirmed receiving over 700 reports involving HK$14.7 million (US$1.87 million) in unauthorised transactions. Experts and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) suggested that multiple-factor authentication might have been disabled by Apple to facilitate a smoother customer experience amid a surge in orders, creating a loophole for scammers to exploit. Major Hong Kong banks said victims would not be held liable, provided the transactions were proven unauthorised and cardholders acted with due care. Meanwhile, Apple said it was reviewing all its current orders to identify and cancel suspicious transactions. 2. What is 3D Secure? 3D Secure (3DS) serves as an extra security layer for online payments that helps authenticate the buyer’s identity. It is used by major credit card organisations, including Visa, Mastercard, American Express and UnionPay. With the latest version of 3DS, card issuers can determine transaction risks using information provided by the merchant, browser fingerprinting, and the user’s transaction history. While most legitimate transactions are completed seamlessly without requiring customer action, higher-risk purchases may prompt buyers to enter a one-time password (OTP) or approve the transaction via their mobile banking app. However, some merchants opt to disable 3DS through their payment gateways to streamline the checkout process. According to the HKMA, when merchants bypass 3DS authentication, they must bear full financial liability for any losses resulting from unauthorised transactions. 3. How was the credit card information exposed? Experts who spoke to SCMP believe the stolen credit card information had been leaked previously and held by fraudsters over time. The data was likely compromised during purchases on retail websites that were not obliged to submit regular audit reports to authorities, and therefore might not constantly review their security features, they added. “It is common for these retailers – or their processing platforms – to skip encryption when backing up the data. That is exactly how data leaks happen,” said Anthony Lai Cheuk-tung, director of cybersecurity firm VX Research. Even if the data was encrypted during transmission, that protection might still be dropped when it reaches the database or is shared with contractors for maintenance, leading to risks of breaches, he added. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, suspected some victims might have also used proxy purchasing services on concert ticket platforms, where users hand over full payment credentials to automated tools or agents to secure high-demand tickets. “The problem is that you’re giving them every piece of your information. It’s not just your credit card details – you’re handing over your phone number, home address, passwords, everything. Handing over all that data during the process is extremely risky,” he said. He warned that once details were leaked, credit card fraud could happen to anyone at any time. 4. What should I do if I spot an unauthorised transaction? According to experts, the immediate first step is to suspend the compromised credit card through the issuing bank and file a police report concurrently. Under a 2023 HKMA circular, all banks in Hong Kong are required to allow cardholders to instantly block cards via mobile banking apps. Alternatively, users can call customer service hotlines or visit a local branch. It is also important to screenshot the unauthorised transaction, along with any supporting evidence showing it was physically or logically impossible for you to make the purchase. For example, if someone uses your card to order a product in the United States, a screenshot showing a local Hong Kong transaction made just hours earlier can help prove your case, Fong said. He added that most unauthorised charges could be successfully charged back if reported to banks and police promptly. 5. How can I protect my credit cards? Both experts agree that consumers should refrain from using credit cards directly on retail websites, or storing their payment credentials on these platforms. Instead, buyers should use digital wallets such as Alipay, PayMe, or PayPal when making online purchases. Alipay is a payment tool by Alibaba Group, the owner of SCMP. Payment tools that directly link to credit cards, such as Apple Pay and Google Pay, were also safer than using the cards directly, as the websites would not have direct access to card information, Fong said.

title: Malaysian teen acquitted of murdering schoolmate Yap Shing Xuen
description: The court also ordered the boy, who was 14 at the time of the attack, to be sent to a psychiatric hospital for treatment.
content: A Malaysian teenager was on Monday found not guilty of murdering his 16-year-old schoolmate last year, after a high court ruled that he had been of unsound mind when he attacked the victim in their school, in a case that left the country reeling in shock and horror. The boy, who was 14 at the time of the attack last October, was arrested at his high school in Selangor state on the same morning that he had repeatedly stabbed Yap Shing Xuen in the school’s toilet. The victim, who was a year from finishing high school, had suffered at least 180 stab wounds to her body and died from injuries to her neck and chest, according to the forensic report. Judge Adlin Abdul Majid ruled during closed-door proceedings that the defence had successfully established a plea of insanity based on the testimony of forensic psychiatrist Dr Ian Lloyd Anthony that the boy suffered from severe schizophrenia. The boy’s condition was left untreated for several years before the fatal attack, leaving him “incapable of knowing the nature of his act, and, independently, incapable of knowing that it was wrong or contrary to law”, his lawyer Kitson Foong said. “The court held that, because of his illness, the child offender did not know the nature of what he was doing and did not know that it was wrong or against the law,” Foong told This Week in Asia. Earlier, Foong reportedly said that the boy’s condition was so bad that “he thought he was God and heard voices”. The court ordered the boy to be sent immediately to a psychiatric hospital for treatment, counselling and medication until he is assessed to no longer be a threat to society and ready for release, his lawyer said. The boy will be detained accordingly by the Sultan of Selangor. Any decision to release him will depend on periodic medical and psychiatric reports presented to the state ruler, Foong said. A lower court had in January ruled that that the boy was fit to stand trial and enter his defence, following a psychiatric evaluation. His case was later transferred to the high court where he was charged with murder, an offence that carries either the death penalty or up to 40 years’ jail and at least 12 strokes of the cane. During his arrest, police recovered two knives and a kerambit, a small curved blade traditionally used by Malay martial arts, from the boy’s bag. A handwritten note, allegedly written by the boy, was also found at the scene. The note, which later went viral on social media, read: “This world is fake. I have already won.” Police had initially pointed to unrequited love as among the motivations behind the grisly attack, besides “social media influence”. The victim’s mother, Wong Lee Ping, denied the claim, arguing that her daughter “did not know the boy, had never spoken to him and was not in any relationship with him”. “My daughter is already a victim. Please stop circulating fake stories about how she died,” Wong said, describing her daughter as a bright, disciplined and loving person. The killing happened at a time of heightened public scrutiny of student safety and child protection measures in schools, following a string of gang rape cases and the death of 13-year-old Zara Qairina Mahathir in July last year, allegedly linked to bullying.

title: Singapore is open to chemical castration, but what are ethical, health concerns?
description: Experts point to considerations on who receives the treatment, duration of the process and whether it is proportional to the offence.
content: Singapore’s openness to chemical castration for sex offenders has cast light on the ethical questions surrounding the treatment, with the discussion centred on whether it would fill any gap left by existing legislation. Experts point to how safeguards would be set regarding who receives the treatment, the duration of the process and if resulting medical consequences would be proportional to the offence. The debate comes after Senior Minister and Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam’s written parliamentary reply last week, where he said Singapore was open to considering chemical castration if there was clear evidence that the measure was effective in lowering crime rates. But Shanmugam stressed that evidence around the method remained inconclusive, pointing out that the country already had “heavy penalties” in place for such crimes. Chemical castration, also referred to as pharmacological anti-androgen treatments, involves the administration of drugs to reduce libido, compulsive sexual fantasies and capacity of sexual arousal, and is usually reversible. Singapore recently strengthened its framework for dealing with high-risk sexual and violent offenders. Rapists can be jailed up to 20 years, fined and caned. If the victim is aged under 14, the offender will be imprisoned for at least eight years and face a minimum of 12 strokes of the cane. Molestation is punishable with a prison term of up to three years, a fine and caning. The Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection, which took effect on July 31, allows courts to impose minimum detention periods of between five and 20 years on serious violent or sexual offenders assessed as posing a substantial risk of reoffending. Before release, offenders undergo an updated psychiatric assessment and can remain detained if they are still considered a public threat. Sexual drive and reoffending The existing framework already fulfilled the objectives of punishment and keeping convicted sex offenders away from society, said Chen Siyuan, a law professor at the Singapore Management University. Any push for chemical castration would then have to show additional benefits delivered, particularly for those deemed most likely to reoffend. “If the objective is to target the likeliest reoffenders, then one still has to balance it against proportionality, such as whether the punishment has undue permanent effects,” Chen said. He called for stronger medical evidence and research into whether the treatment actually served that purpose. Reported sexual offences are on the rise in Singapore – police figures showed 261 rape cases in the first half of this year, compared with 230 during the same period last year. Molestation cases rose to 762 from 739. But experts cautioned against assuming that suppressing sexual drive would necessarily stem reoffending. Mervyn Cheong, an associate law professor from the National University of Singapore, said the penalty had to be balanced carefully with the existing framework. “It raises real operational and policy questions of when it should be deployed instead of, or in addition to, present custodial measures,” he said. “Chemical castration does not map cleanly onto the four traditional pillars of deterrence, retribution, prevention and rehabilitation.” Cheong described the treatment as “controversial” due to its punitive nature as it continued to burden offenders physiologically even after release from prison. Medical professionals have similarly warned that although the effects of anti-androgen treatment are generally reversible, they can be substantial.
