Studies have linked such treatments to conditions including osteoporosis, depression and cardiovascular issues. Tan Kok Kuan, medical director at Dr Tan Medical Centre and a specialist in men’s health, said recovery after treatment could also depend on an offender’s age and how long the drugs had been administered. “If the patient is of advanced age when the treatment is stopped, fertility or bone strength may not return to 100 per cent,” he said. Cheong added that policymakers would also have to consider less easily measurable consequences, including whether compulsory treatment could generate resentment or grievance among offenders and undermine rehabilitation. For criminal lawyer Zachary Lim of IRB Law, these concerns mean any move to implement the treatment should have a far narrower threshold than simply applying chemical castration to broad categories of sexual offenders. If introduced, he said, its use should be discretionary, preceded by medical assessment and confined to the most serious cases. “A statutory threshold drawn any wider would be difficult to defend,” Lim said. Other Asian countries have moved to implement the penalty, although experts note that studies on its effectiveness have been limited. South Korea in 2011 approved its use on convicted paedophiles for a maximum period of 15 years, and later included sex offenders such as attempted rapists and offenders whose sexual crimes led to injury or the death of minors. In 2020, Indonesia’s then president Joko Widodo signed a regulation that required offenders who inflict or threaten sexual violence against those under the age of 18 to undergo chemical castration for a maximum of two years. In 2023, Thailand provided the treatment as an option to sex offenders in return for an early release from prison. Offenders are first evaluated by a psychiatrist and an internal medical specialist. Human rights activists have criticised such laws for being improperly coercive, voicing concerns that inmates may be forced to choose between staying in prison and undergoing treatment. Medical professionals have also expressed concerns about side effects, such as osteoporosis, and the ability of offenders to make informed decisions. US-based advocacy group Human Rights Watch has denounced chemical castration as a “cruel and degrading form” of corporal punishment. Public attitudes in Singapore, meanwhile, are considerably less hesitant. Singaporean content creator Athalie Yi, 33, said she believed medically supervised treatment should be considered if it lowered the danger posed by repeat offenders. “I think it’s fair to also consider whether a medically supervised treatment could help reduce the risk of reoffending, especially once someone returns to society,” she said. “The comfort and consideration afforded to convicted sexual offenders should never carry more weight than the safety and assurance we owe victims and potential victims.” But Lim acknowledges the risk of the treatment’s wider appeal to society overtaking evidence of what it can actually achieve. “A measure of this kind carries a symbolic weight well beyond its practical reach, and public expectations of what it can deliver should be managed carefully from the outset.”

title: Indonesia’s Prabowo appoints third finance minister in under 2 years
description: Suahasil Nazara takes over amid growing pressure on the budget, with analysts expecting a more cautious approach to fiscal management.
content: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto abruptly removed Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa on Monday after just over a year in the job, turning to veteran ministry technocrat Suahasil Nazara as his government grapples with mounting fiscal pressure and questions over economic policy coordination. Suahasil, who had served as deputy finance minister since 2019, becomes Prabowo’s third finance minister in less than two years, following Purbaya and his internationally respected predecessor Sri Mulyani Indrawati. No official reason was given for Purbaya’s removal, which came after a tenure marked by an aggressive push for faster economic growth and, more recently public friction over government finances and the management of state funds. The surprise nature of the reshuffle was underscored by Purbaya’s movements on Monday: he had been attending a parliamentary hearing when he left after receiving a phone call, shortly before Suahasil was sworn in at the presidential palace. “The priority is to run a credible state budget,” Suahasil said after taking office. He said Prabowo had instructed him to safeguard the health and credibility of state finances while pledging to keep the fiscal deficit below Indonesia’s statutory ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP. He also sought to portray his appointment as continuity rather than a sharp policy shift, pointing to his long tenure inside the finance ministry. Analysts said Suahasil’s extensive experience inside the finance ministry could help steady policy after a turbulent period. “To help restore market confidence and stabilise macro-fiscal management, President Prabowo finally made the decision to appoint Suahasil Nazara, an experienced internal fiscal expert, amid growing frictions over revenue targets, state budget implementation, and policy coordination – including debates over state fund transfers and contributions from Danantara,” said Harry Su, managing director at brokerage Samuel Sekuritas Indonesia. One of the most visible disagreements in Purbaya’s final weeks concerned state investment fund Danantara Indonesia. Purbaya said late last month that Danantara would contribute about 120 trillion rupiah (US$6.8 billion) to the state budget this year, describing the payment as a decision by Prabowo and saying the funds could provide an additional fiscal buffer as the government sought to contain its deficit. But Danantara chief executive Rosan Roeslani subsequently said the institution had not internally discussed such a 120 trillion rupiah payment, contradicting Purbaya’s account of the proposed payment. Bhima Yudhistira, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, said Danantara had mounted “strong protests” over the finance ministry’s proposal. “Purbaya’s internal coordination methods, including his communication style, have been deteriorating over time. He was also overconfident. That’s what led to his reshuffle,” Bhima said, although the presidential palace has not officially disclosed the reason behind the dismissal. Questions over Purbaya’s management style had also surfaced over tax refunds after businesses complained that delays were squeezing company cash flows. Purbaya said last week that he had instructed officials to increase scrutiny of tax refunds in the coal sector but acknowledged that implementation had apparently extended more broadly than he had intended and promised to investigate the problem. Bhima said the dispute reflected internal coordination problems involving tax and customs officials and had angered businesses whose refunds were held back. “This upset many business owners, as tax refunds were initially withheld for audits in the natural resources sector but they ultimately affected all sectors,” he said. The episode added to a reputation Purbaya had cultivated as an unusually outspoken economic policymaker. After replacing Sri Mulyani last year, Purbaya pursued a more expansionary approach aimed at accelerating an economy that has grown at roughly 5 per cent for much of the past decade, including moving large amounts of government cash into state banks to spur lending. He repeatedly said Indonesia could achieve growth of around 6 per cent, a target broadly in line with Prabowo’s ambitions but above the country’s recent trend. Bhima said Suahasil was likely to bring a markedly different tone to the job, with communications that would be “more careful, more credible” than what he called Purbaya’s “cowboy style” rhetoric. “He’s a veteran in the Ministry of Finance bureaucracy since the Sri Mulyani era and understands internal matters. He’s considered capable of moderating internal conflicts and relationships,” Bhima said. Suahasil is a former academic who headed the finance ministry’s Fiscal Policy Agency before becoming deputy finance minister in 2019, making him one of the most experienced officials inside the institution. But analysts said a calmer style would not remove the difficult fiscal arithmetic awaiting him. Indonesia’s 2026 budget deficit is forecast to widen to 2.85 per cent of GDP from an original projection of 2.68 per cent, bringing it closer to the legal 3 per cent ceiling as higher expenditure puts pressure on state finances. Dipo Ramli, a researcher at the Center of Reform on Economics Indonesia, said Suahasil’s biggest challenge would be navigating “limited fiscal space”, particularly for regional governments, while Prabowo continued to pursue ambitious spending programmes. “At the national level, [our financial situation] might still be considered safe, but we know that many regions have problematic [fiscal] situations,” Dipo said. Prabowo has made costly programmes – including free nutritious meals for schoolchildren and pregnant women and the development of tens of thousands of Red and White village cooperatives – central to his economic agenda. At the same time, his government is targeting growth of 6 per cent under its proposed 2027 budget while seeking to narrow the deficit, leaving the finance ministry with the task of reconciling faster expansion and heavy expenditure with Indonesia’s long-standing fiscal guardrails. The immediate market reaction to Purbaya’s removal was mixed. Jakarta stocks recovered most of an earlier sell-off to finish 0.1 per cent lower on Monday, while the rupiah weakened 0.33 per cent against the US dollar. This latest reshuffle follows Prabowo’s replacement of Sri Mulyani last year and the unexpected resignation in July of Bank Indonesia governor Perry Warjiyo, who has since been succeeded by Destry Damayanti. Dipo said frequent changes in such positions could signal to foreign investors that the administration was still “trying to find its groove”. “For foreign investors, the minister of finance and Bank Indonesia [governor] are usually considered stable positions. Replacing them is not a good idea, but considering our fiscal situation, I think adjustments are necessary,” he said. “It’s true that the market might not like it, and foreign investors might not like it, but given the numerous problems, I don’t think there’s a problem with replacing the minister of finance.” Additional reporting by Reuters

title: How an AI plot targeted Malaysia’s elections and exposed deep data risks
description: Anthropic’s discovery of an AI election campaign in Malaysia shows how weak data safeguards exacerbate the risk of political manipulation.
content: Anthropic’s discovery of an AI-powered election manipulation platform targeting Malaysia offers a glimpse into how the technology can exploit a country’s political vulnerabilities for sophisticated influence operations. The operation’s use of millions of voter records, fake social media accounts, a synthetic news site and fabricated dossiers pointed to a deeper risk, analysts said: weak data safeguards and entrenched ethnic and religious fault lines could allow political actors to target voters faster than regulators or platforms can respond. In a report released on Thursday, the US artificial intelligence firm said it had removed an account that used its Claude model to run what it described as a commercial election manipulation platform across Malaysia’s 222 parliamentary constituencies. Anthropic said the operators ingested census and electoral data to profile voters constituency by constituency, while using the platform to manage a network of fake accounts designed to inflate online support and avoid detection. “The platform managed a network of about a thousand fake accounts optimised to inflate engagement metrics and evade social media platforms’ detection systems,” Anthropic said in its threat intelligence report. The operation also used an AI rewriting system to run a fake news site called “Malaysia Pulse” and generated fabricated intelligence dossiers containing allegations against opposition politicians and civil society groups. While Malaysian political parties routinely combine government records with internal party data for voter targeting, analysts say the country is too lax on personal data protection. Benjamin YH Loh, a media studies lecturer at Monash University Malaysia, said that the country’s Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (PDPA) – the core law regulating personal data processing – has rarely been enforced regarding data leaks or abuse. “Unless the government changes its prerogative towards handling personal data, this is unlikely to change,” Loh said. Loh drew parallels between Anthropic’s findings and the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which personal data harvested from tens of millions of Facebook users was combined with voter records for targeted political profiling, including work connected to Donald Trump’s successful US presidential campaign in 2016. “After Cambridge Analytica, it should be all parties [held accountable] the moment the perpetrators sought to use these technologies to produce and distribute disinformation or propaganda,” Loh said. He added that while regulators bear some responsibility, platform owners must also be held accountable. “The onus is on them to report these instances as they occur, and with more transparency.” Professor Anwar Abdul Majeed, head of Sunway University’s Department of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, said the danger posed by AI is a “collapse in cost”, allowing operations that once required a war room to be run from a single subscription. Malaysia’s safeguards remain “mismatched to the threat”, Anwar said, pointing to gaps in the PDPA’s coverage and the absence of election-specific rules governing AI-generated content. “The real danger is linkage,” he said, warning that AI could fuse voter rolls, census information and leaked databases into constituency-level targeting capabilities that none of those datasets intended to enable. The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) has launched an investigation into Anthropic’s findings, seeking further information and clarification from relevant parties. “Based on the information and evidence obtained, MCMC will determine the appropriate follow-up action within its jurisdiction, including working with relevant authorities,” the agency said in a statement on Friday. Other analysts cautioned against viewing AI influence campaigns as an entirely new phenomenon, framing them instead as a new method of exploiting existing societal divisions. “The use of AI is just an incredibly powerful technological upgrade,” said Wong Chin Huat, a political scientist at Sunway University. Wong said AI-driven fake accounts were particularly effective at amplifying echo chambers and exploiting herd mentality on social media. “Fake accounts operated by AI can create a fake impression that certain opinions are mainstream, making targeted netizens feel empowered or disempowered,” he said. “More importantly, they can heighten partisan conflicts by provoking netizens into emotionally charged quarrels to harden their positioning.” Wong said the underlying strategy was unchanged: exploiting identity politics and escalating partisan behaviours to mobilise supporters or demobilise opponents. However, he was sceptical that legislation alone could contain the threat given the difficulty of defining where legitimate political expression ends and prohibited content begins. Malaysia has increasingly clamped down on online content touching on the sensitive “3Rs” – race, religion, and royalty – though the consistency and effectiveness of that approach is questionable. “The only way is through identification and removal of fake accounts, regardless of their content, like what Anthropic has done,” Wong said, adding that long-term resilience depended upon civic culture. “We need to build a healthier political culture where political parties and politicians would be sanctioned by each other and, most of all, the public, if they cross the line of decency,” he said. “If decency survives offline, the damage of anonymous fake operations online would be limited.”

title: Beijing hails Taiwanese scholar’s rare proposal on reunification
description: Detailed plan on how ‘one country, two systems’ could be applied to the self-ruled island sent to mainland platform on cross-strait issues.
content: Beijing has hailed a “one country, two systems” proposal by a Taiwanese scholar in a rare official statement on an issue regarded as politically sensitive on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. “We are pleased to see that more and more Taiwan compatriots are facing up to reunification, beginning to understand and discuss the specific content of a one country, two systems plan for Taiwan, and offering suggestions and proposals for such a plan through various means,” Chen Binhua, a spokesman for mainland China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said last week. Chen was referring to a detailed proposal by Li Ci-ze, an associate professor at Taiwan’s National Changhua University of Education, on how one country, two systems could be applied to Taiwan. Li submitted the proposal in late August to a mainland social media channel that has long focused on cross-strait issues. Despite Beijing’s long-held stance that it wants Taiwan to reunite with the mainland under one country, two systems, it has never discussed in detail how the island would be governed in the arrangement. Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2019 called for efforts to “explore a ‘two systems’ plan for Taiwan”, sparking a lively discussion among mainland media and scholars on ways to achieve reunification. In contrast, mainstream politicians in Taiwan either remained lukewarm or were vocal in opposing the call. Taiwan’s major political parties have yet to comment on Li’s proposal. Citing a series of previous mainland statements on the subject, Li wrote that Taiwan, after peaceful reunification, should be able to retain its direct elections for the island’s top executive official and legislature while “fully retaining” its opposition parties. He also proposed that, during the initial stage following reunification, the mainland should not permanently station troops in Taiwan. At the same time, Taiwan could pledge not to join foreign military alliances or deploy long-range weapons capable of threatening the mainland. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Citing Beijing’s previous statements, the proposal further said that Taiwan should retain an independent judiciary, the power of final adjudication and its monetary system. It did, however, state that Taiwan might have to give up its official name, the Republic of China. Li proposed that foreign affairs should be handled centrally by Beijing, while Taiwan should retain forms of international participation that did not imply sovereignty, such as in the World Trade Organization and the Olympic Games. The proposal has evoked considerable discussion on the mainland, with state-owned Global Times drawing public attention to it. A commentary posted to the newspaper’s website last Wednesday said that Li’s proposal set forth “the genuine concerns of Taiwanese society … way of life, continuity of institutions, judicial safeguards, fundamental rights and international functions”. “The core concerns of mainland society are also clearly identified: the one-China principle, national sovereignty, the risk of external intervention and common obligations after reunification,” it added. According to Zhang Wensheng, deputy dean of Xiamen University’s Taiwan Research Institute, such discussions are rare, and Beijing always welcomes them as long as they are premised on the one-China principle. “For a long time, there has been very little detailed discussion or envisioning of how one country, two systems could work in Taiwan,” Zhang said. “Under the [ruling Democratic Progressive Party], which leans towards Taiwan independence, engaging in such discussion comes with considerable pressure.” “Taiwanese society has long had concerns about one country, two systems. More public discussion may help eliminate prejudice and misunderstandings.” Since 2019, mainland academics have developed several versions of a Taiwan plan for one country, two systems, Zhang added, saying Li’s proposal shared many features with those versions and left considerable room for flexible negotiations while maintaining the position that the two sides should ultimately reunify. Yet, Li’s proposal highlighted a lack of trust in Taiwanese society over Beijing’s commitments and discussed ways to impose institutional constraints on Beijing’s ability to unilaterally alter commitments. Li argued the question of whether Beijing could renege on its promises was “the deepest structural problem in one country, two systems”. “If the two-systems arrangement is merely a policy that can be adjusted at any time, it will be impossible to gain the long-term trust of Taiwanese society,” he wrote. “The lessons previously seen in Hong Kong have already taught everyone this.” A 2024 opinion poll conducted by Taiwanese authorities found that more than 85 per cent of respondents opposed the one country, two systems concept. Even many leaders of the mainland-friendly Kuomintang, Taiwan’s main opposition party, have publicly rejected the idea and voiced support for maintaining the status quo. Zhang cautioned that if the island were reunited by force, then it would enjoy much less autonomy, a point already asserted by Beijing’s closest Taiwan policy advisers.

title: China, Kazakhstan plan QR payments, expanding yuan’s reach in overseas retail purchases
description: Planned launch follows existing cooperation between super apps Alipay and Kaspi.kz, letting travellers use home-country app at certain merchants without exchanging cash.
content: Kazakhstan plans to launch QR-code payments with China by the end of 2026 – a move that analysts say could expand the yuan’s use beyond trade and investment into everyday transactions while offering a “gentle yet substantive” alternative to the US dollar. The decision comes as Beijing is deepening trade and financial ties under China’s Belt and Road Initiative, while advancing the yuan’s use in cross-border transactions amid a broader de-dollarisation trend. The Central Asian country is preparing to introduce cross-border payment services with 11 countries, including China, India, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, according to comments on Friday from Binur Zhalenov, deputy governor of the National Bank of Kazakhstan. The payment system with China is expected to begin operating by year-end, allowing citizens of both countries to make payments using mobile QR codes while visiting each other’s countries, Zhalenov said at a fintech summit in Almaty, according to state news agency Kazinform. Systems with other countries are tentatively scheduled to launch from mid-2027. The move “signals that yuan internationalisation is extending deeper into everyday consumer transactions, moving beyond major trade settlements”, said Liu Feng, chief economist at the International Institute of Green Finance at the Central University of Finance and Economics. “Payment habits represent the most fundamental usage of a currency. When Kazakh residents can scan and pay as easily as [Chinese people], the network effect of the yuan begins to take root at the retail level,” Liu said, adding that this could help move the yuan from a settlement tool to a regional payment currency. Kazakhstan’s adoption could also give China an early foothold in establishing yuan-based payment standards in Central Asia, Liu said. “As a key hub of the Belt and Road Initiative, Kazakhstan’s adoption effectively embeds yuan payment standards into Central Asia,” he explained. “As neighbouring economies align with these systems, it creates a network effect and path dependency - offering a gentle yet substantive alternative to the dominance of the US dollar and euro.” The planned system builds on existing cooperation between the two countries’ payment platforms. In 2024, Kazakhstan’s all-in-one payments app, Kaspi.kz, partnered with Chinese payment app Alipay to enable Kaspi users to make mobile payments in China. Alipay is owned by Ant Group, an affiliate of Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post. The expansion comes as Beijing seeks to broaden the yuan’s global use amid a wider push to reduce reliance on the US dollar. “The internationalisation of the yuan is a continuous and steady process, and an irreversible trend,” Lu Lei, deputy governor of the People’s Bank of China, said at a press conference on Thursday. To support the yuan’s expansion, Lu said the central bank would expand cross-border use cases for the digital yuan and QR-code payments. “The building of a comprehensive ecosystem for yuan internationalisation is taking root,” said Zhang Danhong, an adviser at the Centre of Geopolitics for the Global South. She also said the development with Kazakhstan reflected the expansion of China’s efforts to internationalise the yuan “from central bank foreign reserves and trade settlement to capital markets, and now into consumer retail application”.

title: The View | Why Shanghai offers hope for China’s ailing real estate market
description: Pockets of resilience and growth in the city’s property sector could be the prelude to a broader recovery across the country.
content: Albert Edwards, head of global strategy at Societe Generale, is renowned for his bearish views on the global economy and stock markets. Weak domestic demand in China is grist to his mill. In a report on August 25, Edwards said the collapse in China’s credit impulse – the change in credit growth as a percentage of economic output – was the most underappreciated trend in global markets right now. Edwards singled out recent data on China’s housing market which Societe Generale analysts described as “hopeless”. It is true that the five-year market downturn has shown little sign of easing. Home sales by value in 70 cities contracted 13.2 per cent in annualised terms in the first half of this year while property investment plunged 19.2 per cent. As Nomura noted, “national property indicators have broadly worsened in recent months”. However, there are pockets of resilience in first-tier cities. Nowhere is this more apparent than in Shanghai. According to data from the National Bureau of Statistics, prices of new homes rose on a monthly basis for 12 of the last 13 months, the longest growth streak among first-tier cities. Moreover, prices of second-hand flats have risen for six straight months. In a report on July 17, Bank of America said China’s financial hub is leading the recovery in the secondary home market, recording the strongest growth in prices and the sharpest increase in transaction volumes. While Shanghai’s government has implemented measures designed to reduce oversupply, including policies that make it easier for non-resident buyers to purchase properties, the current rebound in prices and sales differs significantly from the one in late 2024, which was driven by major stimulus. “The latest improvement looks less like another pure policy bounce [and more like] a more genuine move towards market rebalancing,” Bank of America said. Second-hand home listings in Shanghai have fallen sharply since the end of last year and are down 28 per cent from their peak. The combination of a steep fall in listings and a strong recovery in sales suggests inventory is being absorbed as fewer owners feel compelled to sell amid expectations that a recovery is taking hold. In a report on September 8, JPMorgan said the stabilisation of the market was “an important first step of a likely long recovery journey, as Tier 1 cities (particularly Shanghai) often serve as the bellwether for the nationwide market”. It is not just Shanghai’s housing market that is showing signs of resilience. In the office sector, where rents have been declining since 2022 amid the acute supply-demand imbalance that has pushed up the average vacancy rate to more than 24 per cent, sharp divergences within the market have not received the attention they deserve. As is the case with Hong Kong, where rents for state-of-the-art offices in the Central business district are outperforming the rest of the market, the highest-quality buildings in Shanghai’s core central business district are performing much better than other grade A offices. In a report on August 18, JLL said that although rents for the grade A market as a whole continue to decline, premium grade A offices – top-tier buildings that are best in class in terms of design, amenities, location and sustainability – “have demonstrated exceptional resilience, outperforming the market and emerging as a core driver of Shanghai’s overall office market recovery”. In the first half of this year, rents for nearly 70 per cent of premium grade A offices were flat or growing slightly, with some buildings recording growth of more than 5 per cent. While the average vacancy rate for premium offices has increased to more than 10 per cent because of supply pressures, the performance gap between premium and regular grade A buildings has widened. Top-tier offices command a higher rental premium while the vacancy gap has increased since 2018 amid premium buildings’ stronger leasing velocity, underpinned by robust upgrade and relocation demand from leading corporate tenants, especially in financial and professional services. “The downturn has not been uniform,” said Neo Huang, head of office leasing advisory for Shanghai at JLL. “Premium grade A offices are showing clear value as the recovery emerges.” To be sure, sources of resilience in Shanghai’s housing and office markets need to be put into perspective. Despite the rebound in residential sales, there is little sign that homebuyers are taking on leverage, which points to “localised pent-up demand rather than the start of a broader, credit-reinforced upcycle”, Bank of America said. Furthermore, premium offices account for just 10-15 per cent of Shanghai’s grade A office stock. Although the rental divergence theme mirrors the trend in Hong Kong and other leading cities around the world, the leasing recovery is still too weak and narrow to stabilise the broader market. However, the green shoots should not be dismissed. Pockets of resilience and growth in Shanghai’s real estate sector could be the prelude to a broader recovery.

title: Should you walk your cat? Los Angeles pet owners and vets weigh in
description: From harnesses to strollers, owners are taking their pets outdoors for enrichment. But experts warn that cat walking is not for every feline.
content: Gnocchi sits attentively on a Beverly Grove pavement with his owner, Julia Luke. Gnocchi wears a pink collar with his name on it, an AirTag and a red harness with a leash. He observes the neighbours. He sniffs the grass. He watches bugs crawl in the dirt. “People know Gnocchi’s name before they know mine,” Luke says. But seeing Gnocchi stops strangers in their tracks. That is because Gnocchi is not a dog. “It’s a cat on a leash!” an unfamiliar neighbour exclaims, stooping to pet him. While walking cats may seem like a novelty, more pet owners in Los Angeles do it than you think. Many say they want to give their pets a fully enriched life, fearing that indoor-only cats miss out on the outdoors experience. Rather than subjecting free-roaming outdoor cats to dangers like cars and coyotes, some opt for supervised harness and pram walking. “I know [Gnocchi] is happier when he has exposure to more sensory things than being inside all day long,” Luke says of her domestic shorthair. “I think about how happy I would be if my whole entire life was inside.” In Highland Park, Hayden Freedman and her partner Kyle Smithers walk their cat Zephyr up and down their quiet street, usually once a week. Sometimes they bring their dog Ivy, who treats the walk more as a cool-down than a workout. In Silver Lake, Allison Nill walks her cats around the local reservoir in a pet stroller. Safely tucked beneath the pram’s netted covering, Lana – short for Lana Del Rey – a tabby, takes in the sights while Steve, an orange American shorthair and Abyssinian mix named after Stevie Nicks, lounges in the shade. “I call them our hot girl walks,” Nill says, pushing Lana and Steve in their stroller around the Silver Lake Reservoir. The sunset-hour routine helps relax her when she feels anxious. “Most nights, it’s just [Lana] and me.” Meanwhile, Beachwood Canyon residents David Atrakchi and Sophie Meister, both actors and producers, take their Bengal cat, Taita, for hikes near the Hollywood Reservoir, Bronson Canyon and even Joshua Tree. Taita prances along rock walls and rolls in the dirt, meowing with his tail held high. “When he has his tail up, he is happy,” Atrakchi says on a recent hike overlooking the reservoir. The practice comes with benefits and risks. Dr Kate Blair, a feline veterinarian at the Cat Hospital in Marina del Rey, says it comes down to knowing your cat. “For the right cat, I think it’s a great thing. That’s the key … not every cat will enjoy spending time outdoors on a walk,” Blair says. Confident, curious cats may do well, but cats who like predictable environments may be fearful. “It’s not something to force by any means.” Mental enrichment is the biggest health benefit “by far”, Blair adds. Understimulated cats may have an increased risk of obesity and urinary problems, and the ability to explore the sounds, scents and textures of the outdoors is one way to provide that enrichment. There’s also a small exercise benefit, but remember: you aren’t walking a dog, Blair says. “A very successful cat walk can be five minutes,” Blair says. “They go outside, they smell a bush, they look at some birds, they get to make a few choices on their own. You’re following their lead, and then you go back home.” That is what a walk looks like with Freedman and Smithers’ cat, Zephyr: a short, leisurely stroll up their street, with plenty of pauses for Zephyr to rest on the pavement or scratch a tree. “Are you ready to go back?” Freedman says on a recent evening, noticing Zephyr had turned around. “All right, well, he is ready to go back.” Rescues in LA tend to discourage cat walking, says Gwendolyn Mathers, executive director of Pasadena’s Tail Town Cats, a cat cafe and adoption centre that partners with Kitten Rescue Los Angeles, one of the city’s largest shelters. Tail Town Cats doesn’t exclude adopters who consider walking their cats. However, they advise caution due to the many uncontrollable factors that could spook a cat outdoors like cars, dogs and wildlife. “That’s what this is all about,” Mathers says. “What do you have control over?” If a cat panics, Mathers says, anything could happen, including losing the pet. “Anyone who has wrangled a scared cat knows it’s not just like picking up a dog and holding them,” Mathers says. “They are clawing you to get away because, to them, that is a life-and-death situation.” Nill, a digital creator and actor, got her first pet stroller in a brand deal about a year ago. After one walk, Lana was hooked. She would climb into the basket on her own, meowing, purring and rolling on her back. Steve isn’t as consistently interested in the ride as Lana, but if he makes his way to the stroller, Nill takes him along, too. Many of those who have walked their cat offered the same tips: start slow, don’t force anything and follow your cat’s lead. “We started outside our building, by the pool, by the gardens, then in the street, and then we went to here, on different hikes,” Atrakchi says. Every hike is at Taita’s pace: “Very slow,” Meister says. Be prepared: if you take your cat outdoors, they may expect it regularly. “It’s like Pandora’s box,” Atrakchi says. “Once you open it, you have to continue doing it, because they will want to go out.”

title: Hong Kong faces pressure to speed up trading hours review after South Korea’s move
description: Korea Exchange launches four-hour after-market in addition to regular trading, intensifying debate in Hong Kong over extending hours.
content: Hong Kong’s stock market is facing renewed pressure to accelerate its review of longer trading hours after South Korea’s main bourse extended its session by four hours on Monday, according to an industry player. The Korea Exchange, South Korea’s bourse operator, launched a real-time after-market from 4pm to 8pm in addition to regular trading from 9am to 3.30pm. It also signalled ambitions to expand to nearly 24-hour trading, following similar plans by Nasdaq and the London Stock Exchange. The extension means South Korea’s main stock market now trades 10 and a half hours on weekdays, almost double Hong Kong’s five and a half hours from 9.30am to 4pm with a one-hour lunch break. In July, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) separately told the South China Morning Post they were exploring longer hours but gave no details. The latest move by South Korea could prompt HKEX and the SFC to speed up consultation, said Tom Chan Pak-lam, honorary president of the Institute of Securities Dealers. “South Korea’s after-hours launch is another data point in the global lengthening of trading sessions and reinforces the case for Hong Kong to keep studying and potentially phasing in better accessibility for global investors,” he said. HKEX will make adjustments … based on the local market environment and actual demand … rather than solely looking at changes in other markets Kenny Ng, Everbright Securities International An HKEX spokesman said on Monday that the bourse “is committed to enhancing Hong Kong’s competitiveness as an international financial centre and regularly reviews opportunities to improve market accessibility to meet evolving investor demand”. He said further updates would be provided in due course. Echoing that stance, an SFC spokesman said the regulator was working with HKEX to explore various initiatives to enhance market competitiveness. “The SFC has had preliminary discussions with HKEX regarding possible enhancements to trading hours to assess their impact, and remains committed to working closely with stakeholders to strengthen the global competitiveness and attractiveness of Hong Kong’s capital market,” he said. Kenny Ng Lai-yin, a strategist at Everbright Securities International, said it was worth examining whether South Korea’s extension would boost turnover, which would be a useful reference for the HKEX. “HKEX will make adjustments on trading hours based on the local market environment and actual demand of the market, rather than solely looking at changes in other markets,” Ng said. Stockbrokers, however, have concerns regarding longer trading hours. “Whatever HKEX does, I believe they will need to get sufficient consensus and feedback from the market first instead of hastily launching it without taking into consideration the practical challenges of our markets,” said Robert Lee Wai-wang, a lawmaker for the financial services sector and chairman of Grand Finance Group. “Nonetheless, it is likely a good time to review holistically what benefits and challenges extended hours would bring to our markets and consult stakeholders for the way forward.”

title: China’s self-powered neural device helps stroke survivors walk naturally
description: Prosthesis developed by mainland China and Hong Kong team uses electrical current to flex the wearer’s ankle while walking.
content: Scientists have developed a lightweight, battery-free device that could help improve the mobility of people with difficulty walking, such as stroke survivors. Developed by researchers in Hong Kong and mainland China, the neural prosthesis uses energy generated by the wearer’s own movements to electrically stimulate their muscles, helping to flex their ankle and restore their natural walking pattern. This could prevent falls for stroke survivors, elderly individuals, and others living with mobility impairments. The researchers behind the device also said it could even be used by athletes during training. “Rather than relying on external sensors or battery-powered control, the device operates automatically during walking through mechanically coupled energy harvesting and stimulation delivery,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications on September 2. Requiring just a few steps to power up, the device helped to increase stride length and walking speed in stroke survivors during both indoor treadmill trials and outdoor walking tests. These improvements were “immediate” and were achieved without the need for a complex set-up, according to the team led by researchers from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong Polytechnic University. This includes a 67.3 per cent increase in walking distance and a 43.5 per cent increase in walking speed during outdoor tests. “The system operates without external batteries, integrates into standard footwear and requires minimal donning time, supporting pragmatic use beyond the laboratory,” the researchers wrote in their paper. Corresponding author Yang Zhengbao, an associate professor at HKUST, said on September 10 that the device had several advantages over existing therapies, including the fact that it took advantage of the “natural intelligence” of human walking patterns. The team said in the paper that while the device was not a replacement for all existing assistive devices, the benefits of supporting natural gait patterns rather than replacing or restricting them offered a distinct strategy for rehabilitation. Strokes are one of the leading causes of death and long-term disability worldwide, with one in four adults over the age of 25 predicted to experience one in their lifetime. Stroke survivors can face numerous complications, including brain injury, memory loss, speech impairments and motor issues. Foot drop, or the inability to flex the ankle and lift the front of the foot, is a common impairment that reduces the efficiency of walking, increases the risk of falling and limits quality of life, according to the team. Conventionally, rigid braces on the lower leg have been prescribed to help correct post-stroke foot drop. However, they work mainly by constraining the ankle joint rather than restoring flexion. This not only makes it difficult to walk naturally, but can also cause muscle atrophy with prolonged use. The field of robotic exoskeletons has been advancing rapidly. However, these devices can be challenging to use as mobility aids in real life due to their complexity, size and need for calibration. “Here, we addressed this translational gap with a discreet, daily-life-oriented self-powered neuroprosthesis designed to assist ankle dorsiflexion and thereby reduce foot drop during walking,” the researchers said. Pan Qiqi, a former postdoctoral fellow at Yang’s lab who is now a professor at the Huazhong University of Science and Technology, said that the design of the device was inspired by natural gait patterns. Humans typically walk in an alternating pattern. First comes the stance phase, when the leg is on the ground, followed by the swing phase, when the leg is lifted and moves forward. “This natural gait pattern aligns well with the needs of stroke patients, who typically have one healthy leg capable of normal walking while the other requires assistance,” said Pan, a lead author of the paper. The team’s device harvests mechanical energy from the movement of the less affected limb using a component embedded in the wearer’s shoe. This harvested energy then powers a lightweight neurostimulator secured around the calf of the weaker limb, which uses electrical current to help the wearer’s muscles contract. Pan said that unlike exoskeletons – which typically substitute or assist lost motor function rather than rehabilitate it – the team’s solution “actively stimulates the user’s muscles to facilitate the movement”. The paper said that while foot drop was not completely eliminated during outdoor trials, the device still significantly improved wearers’ gait. The researchers noted that their prototype still required optimisation, including more precise control of the stimulation to broaden its applicability for different patients. Pan said that study participants were “very eager to get appropriate rehabilitation products”. “Stroke patients often prioritise socialisation and community engagement. We therefore aimed to develop a wearable device that integrates seamlessly into their natural gait, encouraging them to socialise and engage with others.” He added that existing exoskeletons and functional electrical stimulation devices were complex and expensive, so he hoped their device could be “low-cost, easy to use and lightweight”. Yang said that further reducing the complexity of the design could help cut costs, which could allow people in low-income countries to benefit from the device. Very few companies want to develop products for this population, according to Yang, who encouraged more researchers and companies to create designs that could improve their quality of life. He said they had shown the device to a colleague who worked with elite Hong Kong athletes and they were interested in using the device for training purposes. The team is working on similar products for the knee and hip using different approaches, which Yang said could “generate positive impacts for the world”. The researchers are also hoping to incorporate the energy harvesting system into pacemakers, which could help reduce the devices’ size, much of which comes from the battery.

title: Probe launched after 2 brothers found dead in Hong Kong public flat
description: Security guard alerted authorities after detecting foul smell coming from flat in Tung Yip House at Lei Tung Estate.
content: Hong Kong police have launched an investigation after two brothers were found dead in a public housing flat in Ap Lei Chau. The police force said a security guard alerted authorities after detecting a foul smell coming from the flat at Lei Tung Estate’s Tung Yip House at around 2pm on Monday. Rescue personnel forced their way into the flat and discovered the bodies of the pair, aged 53 and 55. Paramedics confirmed their deaths at the scene. One brother was found in a bedroom and the other in the bathroom. Investigators said no suicide notes were found at the scene. Nothing suspicious was discovered during an initial probe. Police investigations into the incident are continuing.

title: NBA star Curry visits Hong Kong school, gives tips on dealing with self-doubt, pressure
description: Back in the city for the first time in a decade, four-time NBA champion Stephen Curry shares some tips for success with Tuen Mun children.
content: NBA superstar Stephen Curry made a quick trip to Hong Kong on Monday, and visited a local school where he told pupils that working hard and accepting that sometimes failure happens had helped make him a four-time champion. Appearing in the city for the first time in 10 years, Curry arrived at Shun Tak Fraternal Association Leung Kau Kui College in Tuen Mun to thunderous cheers from pupils, teachers and a crowd of more than 1,000 onlookers. The two-time MVP briefly watched a school game, before partnering with several players to take shots from five different spots on the court. Chatting with several students afterwards, Curry, who some NBA scouts believed was too short and too slender to succeed in the league, gave them tips on how to deal with self-doubt and external pressure. “You have to understand that’s part of life,” said Curry, who was drafted seventh overall by the Golden State Warriors in 2009. “People are always going to say that you can’t do this, you can’t do that. “But I just made sure that I had as much fun as possible, and I relied on my work ethic to get me through. I had big dreams, but I worried about just getting better every single day, and then eventually, hopefully, I could accomplish those goals.” Curry, who has earned a reputation for making crucial and often game-winning shots, also said “it’s OK” to be nervous. “I still get nervous because if you don’t, that means it doesn’t matter to you,” he said. “But I rely on all the times that I’ve shot the shots that I know that I’m about to go do on the court, and then I’m OK if I miss it, I’m not gonna be happy. “I know that failure is a part of it. You have to be able to accept what happens out there on the court. But I don’t shy away from those moments because I work really hard for them. Curry has his entire playing career remaining in the Bay Area, and he urged local pupils to work hard for their dreams. “You control the work that you put in. You control the energy that you put into whatever you’re doing, not just in sports, but in school, in life,” he said. “If you can control those things and step good things after each other and be able to put yourself in a position where you’re ready for anything, that is the stuff that people don’t get to see.” Hong Kong marked the final stop of Curry’s China tour, which started on September 9 and also included stops in Beijing, Dongguan and Shenzhen.

title: Himalayan ‘glacier bankruptcy’ threatens water security for 2 billion in Asia
description: Glacier mass loss is causing the region to approach ‘peak water’, the point when river flows stop rising and start declining.
content: The Himalayas are approaching a tipping point as glaciers melt faster than a decade ago, threatening water security as the region approaches “peak water” by mid-century, according to a study released this month. The findings come after the collapse of a Himalayan glacier in late August along the ‌Nepal-Tibet border, which caused cascading landslides and flash floods in the valleys below. At least 1,300 people have been confirmed dead and more than 5,300 are missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region. As glaciers retreat, they are leaving behind unstable glacial lakes held back by little ⁠more than loose rock and ice, above valleys where millions of people live, ‌the study found. The study was produced by Systemiq, a sustainability advisory firm, together with the Integrated Mountain Initiative, the International ‌Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, and India’s G.B. Pant National Institute of ⁠Himalayan Environment. Himalayan glacier mass loss has accelerated in recent decades, while only 21 glaciers were currently monitored on the ground out of an estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region, the study found. Close to 200 glacial lakes ‌in India had been identified as high risk, with 56 classified as “very high ⁠risk”, leaving millions exposed downstream. As the region nears “peak water”, the point when river flows stop rising and start declining, it will have profound implications for water security. Experts warn that the August 26 tragedy is “not the end, but the beginning”. As Himalayan glaciers continue to shrink, they say, an era of “glacier bankruptcy” is approaching – one in which permanent water shortages will spread across India and large parts of Asia. Permanent shortages Stretching roughly 3,500km (2,200 miles) from Afghanistan in the west to Myanmar in the east, the Himalayas are known as “Asia’s water tower” – supplying food, drinking water and energy to some 2 billion people. The data point to an alarming trajectory. According to a report released in March by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), headquartered in Kathmandu, the rate of glacier loss has doubled since the beginning of the 20th century. Between 1990 and 2020, roughly 12 per cent of the region’s total glacier area disappeared. Glaciers in the basins of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Indus – sources of some of Asia’s major rivers – shrank by 21 per cent, 16 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively. The findings are based on a comprehensive survey of around 63,700 glaciers across the Himalayas. The United Nations has likewise reported that global glacier mass has declined by more than 30 per cent since 1970, and has warned that glaciers across low- and mid-latitude mountain ranges could disappear entirely within decades. Global warming is also reducing the snowfall needed to replenish glaciers. An ICIMOD analysis found that snow persistence across the Himalayas in 2025–26 fell 27.8 per cent below the historical average, reaching its lowest level in more than two decades. Snow persistence refers to the length of time snow remains on the ground after falling without melting. The region has become locked into a vicious cycle: rising temperatures lead to less snowfall, remaining snow disappears earlier, and glaciers are increasingly unable to regenerate. The Himalayas underpin more than 20 per cent of India’s ‌GDP, making up a key piece of the country’s national economic infrastructure, upon which hundreds of millions of people depend. Though forming around 18 per cent of India’s land, the region accounted for roughly 35 per cent of the country’s natural disasters. Additional reporting by The Korea Times

title: Hong Kong consumer watchdog questions supermarkets’ buy one, get one free deals
description: Consumer Council urges shoppers to compare unit prices after finding some offers provide smaller-than-expected discounts or no savings at all.
content: Hong Kong shoppers may be saving less than expected – or nothing at all – with supermarkets’ buy one, get one free and bulk-buy promotions, a watchdog has warned, urging residents to compare unit prices rather than rely on promotional labels. The Consumer Council on Monday released the findings of a survey covering 222 products sold by Aeon, ParknShop and Wellcome between September 2025 and July this year. It found that the actual discounts offered in some promotional campaigns were less attractive than consumers might expect. During the period, 48 products at two supermarkets were offered under bulk-buy promotional campaigns, such as buy one, get one free, choose any two and get one free, and get one more for HK$1 (13 US cents). But for some of these products, the single-item price during the promotional period was higher than during non-promotional periods, meaning the actual discount fell well short of the about 50 per cent consumers might expect, the council said. The findings add to long-standing concerns over whether supermarket multi-buy promotions always offer the savings suggested by their labels. “We hope the supermarkets in Hong Kong and grocery stores can list their unit price on their offline or online shops to make it easier for consumers to choose the products they want,” said Alaina Shum Jiu-fai, the watchdog’s chief executive. “Hong Kong is a free market, and the merchants have the flexibility to adjust the prices any time, but it’s not a prudent move to adjust the price immediately before the promotion – it will affect the consumers’ confidence.” In one example, a 150-millilitre (5.1 US fluid ounces) bottle of sesame oil was sold under a buy one, get one free campaign at one supermarket for HK$20 or HK$22 per item, significantly higher than its pre-promotion price of HK$10 to HK$14. “After accounting for the promotion, the average price per item was HK$10 or HK$11, representing a maximum discount of only about 29 per cent compared with the pre-promotion single-item price, which might not align with consumers’ expectations that a buy one, get one free offer is equivalent to nearly a 50 per cent discount,” the council said. The same product was offered at a discount of up to 21 per cent under a choose any two and get one free promotion at another supermarket, the council said. “Under both promotions, the average price per item during certain periods was even about 10 per cent higher than the corresponding non-promotional prices, reflecting that bulk-buy promotions may not always offer better value than purchases made during non-promotional periods,” it said. Similar patterns were observed for other items, including a 410ml bottle of soy sauce for steamed fish, for which the effective discount was about 16 per cent, and a 280-gram (9.9 ounces) pack of rice vermicelli, for which discounts ranged from zero to 29 per cent, despite both being sold under bulk-buy schemes. The council also found that larger pack sizes did not necessarily offer better value. Of the 15 product groups compared by unit price, the larger pack cost of seven was found to be between 2 and 35 per cent more per unit than the smaller version during certain periods. The watchdog received 359 complaints about supermarkets in the first eight months of this year, up by 16.9 per cent from the same period last year. About 20 per cent concerned service quality at physical stores, followed by disputes over product quality and pricing. Consumers should compare products using their “unit price” and historical selling prices, rather than making purchasing decisions solely based on promotional formats or pack sizes, the council said. It also directed shoppers to its Online Price Watch platform, which provides shopping-budget calculations and target-price alerts for about 2,800 products across nine retailers.

title: Woman spared jail over forging PhD reference letter for Education University
description: Mainland Chinese student was ordered to perform 160 hours of community service after admitting she used an altered letter to secure admission.
content: A woman convicted of using a forged reference letter to gain admission to a Hong Kong doctoral programme has been spared jail and ordered to perform 160 hours of community service. Fanling Magistrate Kenneth Chan Ping-chau said on Monday that he had decided to “make an exception” for 31-year-old Li Zuer, who earlier admitted falsely claiming that a former teaching staff member at the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK) had written a reference letter for her in March 2024. The letter praised the mainland Chinese woman for demonstrating “exceptional academic performance”, but was actually drafted by a Shenzhen-based agent whom she had commissioned. The original letter, written by Li’s teacher Ho Wai-yip in 2021, noted that she still had room to improve her English proficiency. Li subsequently applied unsuccessfully for doctoral programmes several times. She was eventually admitted to the programme last year after submitting the altered letter. But when university staff conducted an inquiry, Ho confirmed that he had not signed the letter. Li pleaded guilty to one count of obtaining services by deception. In mitigation, her legal representative, Senior Counsel Edwin Choy Wai-bond, told Chan earlier that Li had committed the offence because she had “high hopes” for herself. She was determined to pursue a career in academia and “took the wrong turn” after making multiple unsuccessful applications to doctoral programmes, Choy added. Citing the background report, Chan said Li took a teaching position at an institution in Guangzhou after completing a master’s degree in Hong Kong. She had received outstanding performance evaluations as a teacher. Chan said the offence was serious because it had unfairly deprived other candidates of the opportunity to gain admission. “But considering her outstanding teaching performance and that she has always been law-abiding, she was only influenced by the agent and took the wrong turn. I decided to make an exception … and accept the community service recommendation,” he said in sentencing. Chan had told the lawyers at an earlier hearing that defendants living across the border could still perform community service, provided that the Immigration Department handled their visas accordingly.

title: Cosco Shipping arm readies China IPO to capitalise on global shipbuilding wave
description: Supply chain stress and transit detours boost China’s shipbuilding orders, setting stage for Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry’s listing.
content: The shipbuilding and maintenance arm of state-owned marine transport giant China Cosco Shipping has completed initial public offering (IPO) guidance registration, paving the way for a domestic listing to capitalise on a global shipbuilding boom. Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry finished its pre-IPO registration and preparations, according to information released on the China Securities Regulatory Commission website on Saturday. Specialising in cargo and container vessels, the unit offers construction, repair, conversion, maintenance and offshore engineering services. It is wholly owned by China Cosco Shipping, headquartered in Shanghai. Operating nine shipyards across Shanghai, Nantong, Dalian and southern China, Cosco Shipping Heavy Industry commands a dominant market share in repairing and converting ships into floating facilities for the offshore oil and gas industry. Operating revenue reached nearly 40 billion yuan (US$6 billion) in 2024, with profits of 3 billion yuan. Revenue for 2025 soared 22 per cent. Company data showed that in 2025 it secured new shipbuilding orders for 79 vessels worth 41.3 billion yuan and delivered 62 vessels totalling 6.31 million deadweight tonnes (DWT). Its order book stood at 216 vessels amounting to 24.77 million DWT at the end of 2025. The IPO is expected to ride a new upwards cycle in global shipbuilding despite prolonged disruption to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, as deliveries fail to meet robust demand. Global newbuilding orders in the first half of 2026 hit 137.4 million DWT, surging more than 125 per cent year on year, according to data from maritime consultancy Clarksons. Chinese shipbuilders continue to capture the largest market share on the strength of complete industrial chains, green technology adoption and efficient delivery. The order book of Chinese shipyards represented 66.8 per cent of the global total in 2025, according to the China Association of the National Shipbuilding Industry. For the first half of 2026, total orders for Chinese shipyards reached 363.25 million DWT, up 54.9 per cent year on year. New orders totalled 121.06 million DWT, a 173 per cent year-on-year rise, according to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. China continues to secure most new orders globally for the three mainstream vessel types: bulk carriers, container ships and oil tankers. Cosco Shipping executives said in May that the US-Israel war on Iran and operators’ strategy to bypass the Middle East chokepoint by using longer routes created additional demand for larger vessels and multimodal transport. Cosco Shipping, one of the world’s largest marine logistics firms, was formed in 2016 through a merger between Cosco Group and China Shipping Group. The expected listing aligns with Beijing’s broader push to form industrial conglomerates by consolidating operations to enhance global competitiveness. In 2025, China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC) absorbed China Shipbuilding Industry Corporation in a 115 billion yuan deal, creating a flagship listed entity, CSSC Holdings, which now has a market capitalisation nearing 300 billion yuan.

title: High pay, high peril: conflict-torn Indian Kashmir still attracts migrant workers
description: Despite militant killings and security patrols, half a million Indian labourers flock to the region every year for double their home wages.
content: Every spring, mason Mohammad Ghulam Sarwar boards a train to Indian Kashmir, seeking higher wages despite the risk of being targeted by militants in the disputed Himalayan region. Sarwar, 25, is one of an estimated half a million migrant workers who stream into the Himalayan region each year, forming the backbone of an economy increasingly reliant on labour from some of India’s poorest states. The dependence has endured despite decades of insurgency and a series of militant attacks that have made migrant workers vulnerable targets. Since 2019, at least 24 migrant workers have been killed in militant attacks across the territory, according to local media reports. More than 1,500 people were killed in the same period, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal, 219 of them civilians. The latest attack last month saw gunmen shoot dead two brick kiln workers from the central state of Chhattisgarh. But for workers like Sarwar, the rewards outweigh the risks. “Kashmir is a real paradise. I will keep coming every year for as long as I have the strength to work,” Sarwar, from the eastern state of Bihar, said. While millions of Indians seek jobs in the Gulf, some workers say Kashmir offers nearly comparable earnings without the costs and complications of overseas migration. Sarwar earns 1,200 rupees (US$12) a day in Kashmir, compared with about 700 rupees in Bihar for the same work, if he could find any at all. The Muslim-majority region, battling some of India’s highest unemployment rates, has become increasingly dependent on outsiders to perform jobs that many locals consider menial, including domestic work, agriculture and construction. Local businesses say they struggle to find workers willing or able to take up many jobs. “Outside the handicrafts sector there is not nearly enough local skilled labour available in Kashmir,” said Mohammad Ashraf Mir of the Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry. “We see a rising dependence on migrant workers, tending towards absolute dependence.” Each morning, groups of labourers gather at prominent squares in the main city of Srinagar, waiting to be hired. Most stay for about eight months before departing ahead of Kashmir’s harsh winter, when construction slows and agricultural activity dwindles. Muslim-majority Kashmir has been divided between India and Pakistan since their independence in 1947, while an insurgency against Indian rule that erupted in 1989 has claimed tens of thousands of lives. Although the rebellion has been largely weakened in recent years, sporadic attacks continue. Sarwar said he saw a barber from his home state shot dead by suspected rebels some years ago. While he was saddened by the incident, it failed to deter him. “Life and death are in the hands of God,” he said. “If I remain fearful, I will have nothing. But if I overcome, I will have everything.” Sarwar shares a building in Srinagar with around 200 other labourers. Some seven to 10 workers squeeze into tiny rooms, sleeping and cooking in the same cramped space while paying little more than US$5 a month each. Outside, security is conspicuous. Paramilitary troops, armoured vehicles and police special operations units patrol streets. CCTV cameras monitor the compound around the clock. “They have been soft targets for the terrorists in the past,” a senior security official said on condition of anonymity. “But security arrangements for them have become robust over time.” Police encourage labourers to live in clusters and avoid venturing out after dark. A labourer from West Bengal said many Hindu workers adopt Muslim-sounding names while in Kashmir, fearing that displaying their religion could make them targets. Rebel groups say they target migrant workers to avenge police harassment of their families. Many labourers are reluctant to discuss security concerns publicly. “I face no troubles here,” said Mohammad Iqbal, a 53-year-old painter from Uttar Pradesh state who has worked in Kashmir since before the insurgency began and is now accompanied by his son. “It feels peaceful.” Others are more candid. “I am afraid of terrorists here,” said Shahid Sofi, a 24-year-old mason from Bihar who previously worked in Delhi and Mumbai. “But overall working conditions here are good, the weather is good, and I like working in the wide, open spaces of Kashmir.”

title: Japan’s Chubu Electric bosses resign over quake data-tampering scandal
description: An independent panel report said management’s ‘reprimand’ over delays was one of the reasons behind the falsification of figures.
content: Two top executives at Japanese nuclear plant operator Chubu Electric Power would step down following a quake data-tampering scandal, the company said in a statement on Monday. President Kingo Hayashi and Chairman Satoru Katsuno would be replaced, the statement said, and the firm would withdraw applications to restart the Nos 3 and 4 reactors at Chubu’s Hamaoka nuclear plant. Japan is moving to revive nuclear power 15 years after an enormous earthquake and tsunami sent reactors at the Fukushima atomic plant into meltdown in 2011. Chubu Electric’s Hamaoka nuclear plant – located in an area of central Japan at risk of a potential “megaquake” – has been undergoing regulatory safety checks, with the aim of restarting two reactors. But in January, the operator said that it had submitted data to regulators that underestimated earthquake risks. A 250-page report by an independent panel, released on Monday, said the management’s “reprimand” over delays in the restart review had created pressure on staff, and was “one of the factors contributing to the misconduct”. According to the report, whistle-blower reports were made within the utility twice, in 2019 and 2021, but neither was handled appropriately. Chubu Electric said on Friday it had received the report from the committee. Hayashi and Katsuno judged that they should take responsibility after considering the report’s contents, sources said. Hayashi told a news conference on Monday that he felt “a heavy sense of responsibility and am deeply remorseful”. He said he felt “a profound sense of regret” that he was unable to “foster an organisational culture that prioritises compliance and safety above all else”. Hayashi has mainly worked in sales-related posts and became president in April 2020. Katsuno served as president for about five years from June 2015. The data falsification began around 2012 at the latest and continued while Katsuno was president. Nuclear restart Japan pulled the plug on nuclear power in the wake of the meltdown at the Fukushima atomic plant. However, the resource-poor nation now wants to revive atomic energy to reduce its heavy dependence on fossil fuels, achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, and meet growing energy needs from artificial intelligence. The world’s biggest nuclear plant, Kashiwazaki-Kariwa, restarted operations earlier this year. The estimate of maximum seismic ground motion is important for the earthquake-resistant design of nuclear plants. In September 2023 the Nuclear Regulation Authority approved Chubu Electric’s estimate of 1,200 gal, a unit of acceleration used to measure the intensity of quakes. But in February last year the authority received information about possible data fraud from a whistle-blower. It suspended its safety review process for the Hamaoka plant in late December. The plant is located in Omaezaki, Shizuoka prefecture, near a seismic fault line where a massive Pacific earthquake is expected to occur in the coming years or decades. In 2024, the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its first special advisory for a possible “megaquake” in the area, known as the Nankai Trough, before lifting it a week later. The utility has been hit by a series of scandals, including document falsification, disclosed in August, involving cost claims related to decommissioning work at the Hamaoka plant’s Nos 1 and 2 reactors, as well as the overcharging of customers for electricity. Chubu Electric is planning to appoint Minoru Yasui, a director of the utility, as Hayashi’s successor, sources familiar with the matter said on Monday. Yasui graduated from the University of Tokyo and joined Chubu Electric in 1988. After serving as a managing executive officer, he became a director in 2026. He is from Aichi prefecture, also in central Japan. Additional reporting by Kyodo

title: Handshake or arm-wrestling match? What China’s stock traders expect from Xi-Trump meeting
description: Hope for material results is slim, but investors remain wary of volatility as banks forecast ‘fragile detente’ will continue.
content: The coming meeting between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart Donald Trump is on the radar of market traders in mainland China and Hong Kong, as the results – whether smiling handshakes or a tense test of wills – could add volatility to an already unpredictable market. However, observers said current expectations for substantial results from the meeting are minimal – so much so that investors have placed the event low on their hierarchy of variables likely to jolt stocks. Many stock traders are paying less attention to the sit-down scheduled for September 24 in the US than they did to Trump’s state visit to China in May, even as signs of a flare-up of tensions between the world’s two largest economies are emerging. It is widely expected that the two leaders will extend the current trade agreement and sign some industry-specific pacts, while key structural issues and differences will remain unresolved. “Investors should not be too excited about Xi’s trip to the US, given we do not expect any outcome which is materially supportive for China’s or Asia’s equity markets,” said William Bratton, head of cash equity research for Asia-Pacific at BNP Paribas. “Our base case expectations for the trip are an ongoing commitment to ‘constructive strategic stability’, the finalisation of earlier agreed trade commitments and an extension of the [tariff] truce.” Stock reactions have been subdued in the run-up to the leadership summit. Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index has dropped nearly 4 per cent over the past month, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index has retreated 1 per cent, largely reflecting fears of monetary tightening in the US. The two benchmarks rose at least 3 per cent preceding the last sit-down in May. At the expected meeting in Washington during his three-day US visit, Xi may be accompanied by top business leaders in technology, electric vehicles and aerospace – matching the delegation of US CEOs Trump brought to China, the South China Morning Post reported last week. The top-level talks were expected to focus on trade, technology and geopolitics, with the aim of managing stabilisation beyond the tariff truce, keeping dialogues alive and stabilising relations before key political events such as the US midterm elections in November, according to Barclays. The offshore Chinese yuan strengthened by an average of 0.15 per cent against the US dollar one month before the Xi-Trump meetings during 2017 and 2026, it added. Tensions between Beijing and Washington have been lingering ahead of the meeting. The US is mulling a 7.5 per cent tariff on Chinese imports for alleged manufacturing overcapacity and a new rule to restrict China’s access to sophisticated artificial intelligence chips through data centres. At the G20 finance summit, China refused to endorse a joint communique after disagreement about the rhetoric on trade surplus. “Despite low expectations of a major breakthrough, we see a reinforcement of the current status quo of stabilisation following Trump’s earlier visit to China in May,” said UBS Global Wealth Management’s chief investment office. “While larger structural issues aren’t likely to be resolved, this would still mark a slightly positive outcome that shows the current framework is holding.” Offshore investors held a mildly upbeat outlook for Chinese stocks after the leadership summit, with 46 per cent of those surveyed expecting modest gains in the following month, according to a survey released by Goldman Sachs on Monday. “Our baseline remains that US-China relations are likely to stabilise rather than materially improve or deteriorate,” the investment bank said. “Both sides have incentives to avoid renewed escalation, but strategic competition over trade, technology, and national security is likely to persist.” Goldman expected a “managed, albeit fragile, detente”, with targeted agreements possible but a broader improvement of relations unlikely.

title: Beijing puts a total ban on drones in update to regulations after deadly tower crash
description: China’s capital will enforce the country’s toughest rules on UAVs from November 15 but a no-fly zone will be in effect from Sunday.
content: Beijing has introduced stricter drone regulations, banning all uncrewed flights as well as the possession and storage of existing devices, while detailing disposal methods for the first time in an effort to strengthen security in the capital. The new rules, which will take effect on November 15, follow an incident in June, when a small aircraft crashed into Beijing’s tallest building, the Citic Tower – also known as China Zun – leading to the death of the pilot. The newly revised regulations on the management of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were announced on Sunday on the municipal government website. They will apply across the city. The authorities will also establish a no-fly zone in the capital and its surrounding areas, effective from September 20, primarily restricting non-essential flights, official media in Beijing said on Sunday. Commercial aviation and emergency rescue operations will be exempt. According to the document, Beijing’s entire administrative area is designated as restricted airspace for UAVs. It is forbidden not only to fly drones but also to possess, store, transport or bring them and their core components into the city, except in exceptional circumstances. The new rules, which build upon the original framework approved in March, state that the revisions are to “adapt to the new situations, tasks and requirements” of UAV management and “to effectively fortify the capital’s security defences”. The city will “further tighten control measures and comprehensively investigate hidden safety hazards … to strengthen airspace security management”, the government notice said. For drone owners, the regulations eliminate any remaining loopholes regarding possession of the devices and are widely considered to be “the strictest to date”. One social media user commented: “From now on, drones in Beijing have been ‘reduced to zero’. Possession is completely prohibited, and existing ones must be ‘relocated out of Beijing’.” “In Beijing, drones are now being regulated like firearms,” the commenter added. Another online comment, from someone working in the media industry, noted that previously, registered drones could be stored. Following the new regulations, people can neither fly nor keep existing devices. This would affect their industry, as “aerial photography will be entirely out of the question”, the commenter said. The original regulations, approved by the municipal legislative body, formally came into force on May 1. They declared Beijing’s entire airspace a restricted zone, requiring approval for all drone flights before take-off. However, the revised regulations impose a blanket ban on all UAV flight activities, except for special safety or security operations. The earlier rules also permitted the establishment of storage facilities for UAVs and their core components outside Beijing’s sixth ring road. Once the new rules take effect, all organisations and individuals – unless otherwise specified by law – will be prohibited from setting up storage facilities anywhere within the municipality.
