The document also outlined disposal methods for the first time for existing drone equipment in the city. Owners must transfer their drones out of Beijing via the specified official channels before mid-November, it said. Aside from owners physically removing the devices themselves, the municipality is offering three disposal routes: on-site buy-backs, scrapping and recycling, or sending them outside Beijing via courier. The city will provide various subsidy schemes and postage fees will be waived for drones mailed out of the capital, the municipal authority said. Interviews and research by the South China Morning Post earlier revealed that nearly 20 of China’s biggest cities had put in place a blanket ban on civilian drone flights in central areas, with some changes implemented without policy announcements. The national capital is by far the most thorough and rigorous in its control of drones.

title: ‘Conscious unbossing’: China youth reject promotions to avoid intense corporate stress
description: Employees share scripts online on how to decline promotions, choosing better pay and recognition over career advancement.
content: A growing number of young Chinese employees are increasingly turning down promotions, challenging the traditional notion that career advancement is the ultimate marker of success. This trend has gained significant traction on mainland social media, where related posts have attracted over 40 million views. Workers have shared scripts online that highlight their decisions to decline promotions, often expressing gratitude, citing feelings of insufficient readiness, and seeking better compensation or recognition of their value in their current roles. One online user, known as June, has turned down promotions three times during her decade-long career. Her first declined offer occurred while she was working as a management trainee at an internet company, when she chose travel over accepting a new role. Later, after being promoted to lead a training centre at an education firm, she reverted to her previous position within two weeks, overwhelmed by escalating pressure. In April, she declined a third offer after realising that the promotion came without a significant pay increase. In an interview with the online media platform 36Kr, June remarked that managerial roles frequently entail heavy responsibilities that are not commensurate with financial rewards. For Zheng, a product manager at another internet company, a “senior” title felt more like a burden than a reward. Following her promotion, she found herself juggling multiple responsibilities alone while her boss described the resulting pressure as an opportunity to “develop the ability to work independently.” “When you look around and see no one in this company whom you aspire to emulate, it indicates that the environment is no longer conducive to your growth,” Zheng reflected. For many young Chinese workers, declining a promotion does not equate to abandoning ambition or choosing to “lie flat.” Instead, it reflects a desire to sidestep the intense pressures associated with middle-management roles, caught between senior executives and frontline employees. “After becoming a temporary team leader, I earned only 100 yuan (US$15) more per month, but whenever something went wrong, I was the one held accountable,” one user noted. This shift is not unique to China. British recruitment firm Robert Walters has identified the global trend as “conscious unbossing.” A 2024 survey by the firm revealed that more than half of Gen Z respondents do not aspire to become middle managers, while 72 per cent prioritise personal development over managing others. Lucy Bisset, director at Robert Walters North, a regional division of the firm, cautioned that the waning appeal of management roles could present challenges for employers. She urged companies to reimagine these positions by providing greater autonomy and clearer pathways for skill development. One widely shared comment in China encapsulated the dilemma many young workers face: “Be too easy to rely on, and you will find yourself overwhelmed with work; be too difficult, and you risk being sidelined. The challenge lies in figuring out where to draw the line.” Another mainland user commented: “Turning down a promotion does not equate to giving up on growth. Growth isn’t always about climbing higher; it can also involve internal development. I aspire to have a stable and manageable job that grants me more time for my interests and family.”

title: Huge gaps in sanitary pad absorption speeds, over half poorly labelled: watchdog
description: Among 36 products tested, one pad took 73 seconds to fully absorb simulated menstrual blood, exceeding 60-second standard.
content: Disposable sanitary pads sold in Hong Kong have shown wide discrepancies in absorption speeds, with more than half of tested products also lacking adequate labelling, the consumer watchdog has found. The Consumer Council revealed the test results for 36 winged sanitary towels on Monday, including a sample that took 73 seconds to fully absorb simulated menstrual blood – exceeding the mainland China national standard recommendation of no more than 60 seconds. “The council calls on suppliers to strengthen quality management and conduct regular testing to ensure product hygiene and safety, while improving product labelling so consumers can make informed choices,” it said. The samples were bought from personal care stores, supermarkets and online platforms, with prices ranging from HK$1 to HK$5.60 (12 US cents to 71 US cents) per piece. The tests were conducted in accordance with the national standard for sanitary absorbent pads. They examined deviations between the actual and stated values for length, weight, absorption speed, adhesive peel strength, moisture content, chemical balance and the presence of hidden preservatives. After grouping the products into four categories by length, the watchdog added five millilitres (0.17 US fluid ounces) of synthetic fluid simulating menstrual blood to each sample, recorded the time required for complete absorption, and calculated the average absorption rate based on five samples per model. Overall, 16 samples absorbed the test fluid completely within 10 seconds. In the group of pads 22cm to 25cm (8.7 to 10 inches) long, the watchdog found that the fastest and slowest models differed in absorption speed by a factor of about seven to 10. One of the fastest samples was a day-use pad from the popular brand Kotex, with an absorption speed of seven seconds. A Whisper product recorded an absorption speed of 11 seconds, while Laurier products in this group generally ranged from 36 to 45 seconds. Two pads – the WomenX Pad‑Pro Sanitary Pad and the LadiM Far Infrared Graphene Antibacterial Day Use Sanitary Napkin – took 57 and 73 seconds, respectively, with the latter failing to meet the national standard. Nineteen pads failed to label main ingredients or surface materials in Chinese or English, with some also omitting shelf life or supplier information. Thirty-one brands had moisture content under 10 per cent, reflecting “relatively sound management across production, packaging and logistics”, the watchdog said. The remaining five pads recorded moisture content ranging from 10.7 per cent to 12.8 per cent, although it could not be determined whether such levels exceeded 10 per cent when they left the factory. The council called on manufacturers to review their production and packaging technologies and strengthen monitoring throughout the supply chain to prevent product quality from being affected by moisture and to minimise the risk of microbial growth. All tested pads, meanwhile, recorded balanced acidity levels unlikely to cause skin discomfort and satisfied chemical safety requirements. In a response to the council, the sole distributor of LadiM napkins said a factory inspection test report submitted to the watchdog indicated its product met the requirements of the national standards, covering absorption speed and other parameters. The company added its tested samples belonged to the same production batch as the council’s tested samples. The watchdog urged consumers to carefully check the expiry date and packaging for damage before purchase, and to store products in a clean, cool and dry place to prevent moisture from affecting quality and safety. It advised manufacturers to perform regular testing to ensure product quality and safety, label main ingredients, and clearly state production dates, shelf life and expiry dates to prevent health risks.

title: Data from Greater Bay Area’s 88 million residents to help improve healthcare policy: GSK
description: Executive says pharmaceutical company is investing in shared data infrastructure.
content: British pharmaceutical company GSK is turning to patient data gathered from the 88 million residents of the Greater Bay Area’s 11 cities to speed up drug development in vaccines and cancer care, as officials push for closer cross-border medical cooperation. GSK Hong Kong and Macau general manager Nicholas Teo said patient data was very important because it could form “supplementary evidence” to support regulatory filings and potential label expansions, and also help to “discover benefits other than the medication itself”. Vaccines were one example, Teo said last week. While their effectiveness against target diseases such as flu, shingles and respiratory syncytial virus was well established, he said researchers were increasingly studying potential benefits relating to cardiovascular health and neurological outcomes, which might help generate additional evidence and insights for future healthcare decision-making. Teo said GSK’s expertise lay in vaccination and disease prevention, citing shingles and respiratory syncytial virus as key areas, with the viral liver infection hepatitis B another area of focus. He added that GSK also had a growing oncology and haematology portfolio. The bay area is a government scheme aimed at integrating Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in mainland China’s Guangdong province into a single economic and business hub. Their combined gross domestic product last year was more than US$2.23 trillion, according to official data. GSK signed a memorandum of understanding in September last year with the University of Hong Kong and the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute on a study to examine the long-term health effects of the shingles vaccine. Teo said GSK would provide financial sponsorship for the HKU-led study and was also investing in shared data infrastructure. The company could access patient data through the partnership, such as data coming from hospitals and government agencies, but pharmaceutical companies did not have direct access to it on their own, he added. The institute, based in the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone and set up by the Hong Kong government, enables the free exchange of researchers and data between the two cities. Better decisions are made after we have better data Nicholas Teo, GSK Hong Kong and Macau The director of its real-world study and application centre, Cheung Ching-lung, said at the Hong Kong International Biotechnology Conference and Exhibition on Thursday that the institute aimed to use real-world data to drive evidence-based decision-making through global collaboration. He said real-world data was patient data gathered during routine clinical practice at hospitals and clinics. HKU pharmacy professor Ian Wong said at the conference that cross-border research required “infrastructure that’s safe enough” as the first pillar, alongside government regulation, ethics and public education, before real-world data could be used effectively. Raphael Yeung, a senior pharmacist at Hong Kong’s Drug Office, said the city had multiple regulatory safeguards in place, including the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance. Teo said the value of data ultimately came down to better outcomes and better policy. “Better decisions are made after we have better data,” he said. “If we have data that tells you a certain medication or vaccine benefits a particular population, the government can take a decision on whether to make it available, subsidise it, or improve access.” Teo added that GSK wanted to help prove that the cross-border data pipeline could work at scale. “We hope to be part of potential pilot studies or collaborations that will prove this data flow is safe, secure and high quality between Hong Kong and mainland China,” he said.

title: Asian Games bracing for India, Pakistan animosity to hit cricket clashes in Japan
description: In latest snub, India’s women refuse to accept Asia Cup trophy from regional cricket council president Mohsin Naqvi.
content: India and Pakistan are likely to clash in the latter stages of the men’s and women’s Asian Games cricket this month, and officials are bracing themselves for the bad feeling between the two to spill over in Japan. On Sunday, India’s women refused to accept the Asia Cup trophy ⁠from Asian Cricket ⁠Council (ACC) president Mohsin Naqvi after beating ⁠Sri Lanka in the final in Dubai, repeating the stand made by their compatriots at the men’s tournament last year. Naqvi is the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) chairman and also his country’s interior minister, and the team’s decision to snub the trophy presentation reflects the poor political relations between the neighbouring states. The nature of the cricket competition in Japan means India’s women don’t enter until the quarter-finals, and the first time they could face their rivals would be in a battle for gold, or, more unlikely, bronze. In the men’s contest, the two sides have been kept apart in the group stages and would, again, not meet until medals are on the line. India and Pakistan engaged in a brief military conflict last year that almost escalated into full-scale war. They do not play each other bilaterally in cricket and only meet in ICC and ACC tournaments on neutral venues. India coach ⁠Amol Muzumdar told reporters the decision not to collect the trophy from Naqvi was ‌taken by the country’s cricket board. “We stand by it. For us, this tournament is over. We are the champions. That’s good enough,” he ‌said. “We are united … I am proud of every single person in this ⁠unit, including the ⁠sports staff and the players.” India also refused to accept the trophy from ‌Naqvi after beating Pakistan in the men’s final in Dubai in September last year. The presentation ceremony was delayed by ‌more ‌than an hour before being curtailed just before the trophy would have been handed ‌over. India’s women beat 2024 champions Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final of the ⁠biennial tournament at Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Sunday, winning the continental title for an ⁠eighth time in 10 editions. Indian players have also refused to shake hands with their Pakistani counterparts before or after matches, a policy continued by the ‌women’s team when they ‌beat Pakistan by seven wickets in the Asia Cup group stage earlier this month.

title: South Korean president’s cabinet reshuffle hits new snag as gender minister nominee quits
description: Yong Hye-in steps down following public backlash over her parliamentary seat refusal as President Lee’s approval rating hits 38 per cent.
content: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s 36-year-old gender minister nominee stepped down before gaining confirmation of her position amid a public backlash over her suitability for the job in the latest negative fallout from the president’s cabinet reshuffle. Yong Hye-in, a lawmaker of the minor Basic Income Party, pulled out of consideration for the position on Sunday after controversy erupted over her insistence that she would not give up her parliamentary seat while serving in the cabinet. Yong said the ruling Democratic Party had urged her to make a decision, citing the custom that lawmakers elected through proportional representation vacate their seats when taking a cabinet post. “A cabinet minister is expected to serve as a bridge between the government and the National Assembly and help foster cooperation. However, I concluded that it would be difficult to effectively fulfil that role when even the ruling party has expressed concerns,” Yong told reporters. Yong’s withdrawal is the latest setback for Lee following a hasty cabinet reshuffle two weeks ago that was aimed at freshening up his administration and stopping a slide in public support. Lee’s approval rating fell to a new low of 38 per cent, according to a Gallup Korea survey released on Friday. Among those who disapproved of Lee’s performance, 24 per cent cited housing while another 16 per cent pointed to the reshuffle. The poll showed 61 per cent of respondents viewed Yong as not qualified for the job while 13 per cent supported her. Yong earlier said she would retain her parliamentary seat because she was her party’s sole lawmaker and giving it up would leave the party without representation in parliament. Announcing her withdrawal from the nomination, Yong criticised the opposition for what she described as mockery of the difficulties faced by a minor party, and media outlets for publishing “malicious and distorted” reports. The presidential office said it respected Yong’s decision. “We believe the nominee made the decision to minimise the burden on state affairs and people’s livelihoods,” Lee’s spokeswoman, Kang Yu-jung, said in a statement. “The Blue House will make every effort in its vetting and selection process to ensure that future appointments meet the public’s expectations.” The surprise nomination was widely viewed as part of Lee’s efforts to win back approval from younger voters, a demographic that is showing an increasing drift away from the liberal president. A two-term lawmaker, Yong has been vocal about advancing gender equality, highlighting challenges facing working mothers. She brought her infant to parliament in 2021 and, two years later, held a press conference with her toddler calling for banning the so-called “no-kid zones” in South Korea. Yet critics questioned whether the lawmaker had sufficient experience to lead the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family, replacing the current minister, Won Min-kyong, who has worked in the field for decades. Lee’s abrupt reshuffle caught many by surprise, including ministers who were axed at short notice. But the revamp did not initially include Lee’s outspoken policy chief, Kim Yong-beom, a figure who attracted attention both for his influence on the president and his backing of policies that have drawn criticism, such as the introduction of leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds. Kim eventually stepped down following criticism that Lee’s initial overhaul did not add up to a meaningful shift in direction.

title: Malaysia haj fund scandal: ex-religious minister denies role in US$211 million transfer
description: Jamil Khir Baharom’s prosecution is the latest legal action to follow a release of a royal commission inquiry into Lembaga Tabung Haji.
content: A former Malaysian religious affairs minister pleaded not guilty on Monday to three charges involving more than 860 million ringgit (US$211 million) in transactions linked to the country’s state-run haj savings fund and a Saudi property group. Jamil Khir Baharom, 65, served as minister in the Prime Minister’s Department overseeing religious affairs from 2009 until 2018, when the government of former prime minister Najib Razak lost power. His prosecution is the latest legal action to follow a royal commission inquiry into Lembaga Tabung Haji’s management and operations between 2014 and 2020. The report, which was declassified in July, identified 14 troubled investments. Malaysia’s Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan told parliament last month that the investments had collectively led to nearly 13 billion ringgit in losses, with seven totally emptied out. According to the charge sheet, Jamil is accused of causing Tabung Haji to transfer 42.94 million ringgit to real estate company Al-Rawda in April 2015, followed by 288.17 million ringgit in December 2016, and 529.19 million ringgit in August 2017. Jamil claimed trial before Kuala Lumpur Sessions Court judge Rosli Ahmad. The court set bail at 300,000 ringgit and ordered him to surrender his passport after prosecutors sought bail of 1 million ringgit. Each charge was brought under Section 403 of the Penal Code, which covers dishonest misappropriation of property and carries a mandatory sentence of six months’ jail and whipping upon conviction. Offenders also could be fined. Jamil was detained by the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission on September 1 and initially remanded for five days before the detention was extended by another two days as investigators pursued matters raised by the inquiry. His lawyer, Hisyam Teh Poh Teik, said the defence would challenge the charges after studying documents to be handed over by prosecutors. “Everyone will see that he was charged under Section 403 simply for carrying out his duties as a minister,” Hisyam told reporters at the court. “We will defend him as best we can. God willing, we will prove that he is not guilty.” Tabung Haji, founded in 1963, is a government-owned Islamic financial institution that allows Malaysian Muslims to save in a sharia-compliant system for the haj pilgrimage to Mecca – one of Islam’s five pillars. It also manages investments and pilgrimage operations. Depositor savings stood at 93.4 billion ringgit in 2025, according to the Finance Ministry. The Al-Rawda investment recorded the largest loss among the 14 troubled ventures identified by the inquiry. Tabung Haji paid about 1.55 billion ringgit upfront between 2015 and 2017 for long-term leases on four hotels in Mecca and Medina, intended to house pilgrims. The fund proceeded without a bank guarantee and before due diligence was completed, relying instead on promissory notes backed by the company owner’s personal guarantee. Al-Rawda stopped making rental payments in 2019. Amir told parliament last month that the investment had generated 1.86 billion ringgit in losses by 2024. “This cannot be dismissed as bad luck in investments; this is clearly a multi-step failure,” he said. Jamil joins several people charged after the report’s release. Former Tabung Haji chairman and Umno politician Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim pleaded not guilty last week to abusing his position over a 193.5 million ringgit investment in construction firm Putrajaya Perdana. Two former officials at Tabung Haji-linked companies have also been charged with criminal breach of trust totalling about 72,000 ringgit, while Alam Maritim Resources chief Azmi Ahmad faces two cheating charges involving vessel charter rates.

title: Why France’s Louvre Museum is looking East to help fund its €1 billion transformation
description: To offset the costs of a major upgrade, Christophe Leribault, president of the Louvre Museum, would ‘love to have some sponsors from Asia’.
content: Christophe Leribault, president of the Louvre Museum, is encouraging Asian art lovers to help fund a more than €1 billion (US$1.2 billion) architectural overhaul aimed at easing overcrowding and transforming the visitor experience at the Paris landmark. Leribault arrived in Hong Kong on September 9, fresh from opening a Renaissance exhibition in Tokyo that featured Leonardo da Vinci’s rarely loaned La Belle Ferronniere (circa 1490). Speaking at the French consulate in Hong Kong, he outlined his strategy for leading the world’s most visited museum out of a crisis. Leribault took office in February 2026, after his predecessor, Laurence des Cars, resigned under intense pressure following a catastrophic heist in which thieves stole French crown jewels valued at around US$100 million from the institution in 2025. To help offset rising security, urgent repair and infrastructure costs, international tourists are already shouldering a heavier burden. In January, the Louvre introduced a controversial dual-pricing system, hiking admission fees for non-European Union visitors by 45 per cent, from €22 to €32. However, ticketing income and state funding will only cover 75 per cent of the monumental Louvre Nouvelle Renaissance project, Leribault said. The project was put into place by des Cars and officially launched by French President Emmanuel Macron in 2025, to raise the museum’s annual capacity from 9 million to 12 million. A €360 million funding shortfall remains even after a €300 million contribution from the licensing fee earned from the Louvre Abu Dhabi. Noting that 16 per cent of the Louvre’s visitors come from Asia – Chinese tourists made up the largest group – Leribault hopes regional philanthropists will step forward. “I’d love to have some sponsors from Asia,” he said. “You know, about 80 per cent of visitors to the museum are foreigners. So it’d be nice if we could have the participation [in the donation drive] of some.” Taking the helm amid severe scrutiny, Leribault’s immediate priority was to engage with museum staff. After union complaints and multiple walkouts in the past year over understaffing and safety concerns, Leribault said he spent his first months at the Louvre consulting widely “to understand better the sources of the crisis”. “We have to really talk to the guards, with the curators, with the art conservators, for example,” he noted, and added that close collaboration with the city of Paris is also essential since the new entrances will reconnect the Louvre with the city centre. The overhaul is desperately needed to fix severe bottlenecks. The museum currently operates under a daily cap of 30,000 visitors, with the 1980s glass pyramid designed by I.M. Pei and the Mona Lisa being primary choke points. The master plan will relocate da Vinci’s famed portrait to a purpose-built underground gallery. Visitors will pre-book specific time slots and enter the viewing room in groups of “no more than 20”, ending the chaotic scrums of the past. Furthermore, two new entrances designed by architect Annabelle Selldorf will open below the Colonnade, a 17th century facade. Leribault emphasised that the design will be “softer” and highly respectful of both the historic palace and Pei’s architectural legacy. Beyond structural changes, Leribault is rethinking the art displays themselves. He plans to overhaul the gallery hangings, “mixing painting, sculpture and drawings, to show more to the visitors how all those forms of art are connected”. He envisions a balanced Louvre that honours its dual audience. “It’s a priority to welcome the people … who have taken the plane,” he said, while stressing the simultaneous need to “save some space and quiet moments for the people who are living in the city”. Construction is scheduled to begin in 2028 and will take up to 15 years, with wings closing individually to keep the museum operational. Leribault said he looks forward to further exhibitions for Hong Kong and mainland Chinese audiences, reinforcing his belief that the Louvre is “not a nationalistic museum” but a universal sanctuary devoted to artworks from everywhere.

title: US-led Luzon corridor in Philippines faces growing scrutiny over real local benefits
description: Filipinos, especially Gen Z, are concerned that the corridor and other US-led projects are ‘more exploitative than beneficial’, analysts say.
content: While Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr was pitching the Luzon Economic Corridor to a 600-strong delegation of foreign investors and officials last week, protesters outside were clashing with police, accusing the US-backed initiative of exploiting the country’s resources. The backlash mirrored opposition against the Pax Silica AI supply chain drive – a separate proposal but again, American-led. It underscored mounting tension over the ambitious corridor, since expanded from a transport and logistics project into development plans for energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing. Analysts say the pushback does not necessarily signal a wider rejection of Washington in a country where public trust in the US remains relatively strong. But the latest stirrings point to scepticism over local benefit from such foreign investments. The inaugural Luzon Economic Corridor Investment Forum on Thursday and Friday at the Grand Hyatt Hotel in Bonifacio Global City was sponsored by the US Trade and Development Authority and co-hosted by the Philippines, the United States and Japan – countries that had announced the initiative during a summit in 2024. Tensions erupted outside the venue, with human rights group Karapatan claiming that over two dozen supporters were injured and five paralegals arrested while protesting against what the group called a “US-backed open house for the plunder of Philippine resources”. Initially envisioned as a project linking three main ports and two international airports across four cities on the main island of Luzon, the corridor is now also drawing investments in energy, digital systems, cybersecurity, shipbuilding and advanced manufacturing. Marcos said in his speech that it had drawn “wider support” from other like-minded nations. Canada, Australia, Denmark, France, Italy, South Korea, Sweden and the United Kingdom pledged support in May while Spain and the EU announced their participation at the forum. “This growing interest reflects confidence in the Philippines as a reliable partner and an attractive destination for long-term investment,” the president said. “Across all these sectors, our goal is not simply to attract investment. We want investment that strengthens our economy and expands Filipino capability.” The protesters also rallied against the proposed Pax Silica hub, a 1,620-hectare (4,000-acre) industrial zone that will sit in New Clark City, part of the Luzon Economic Corridor. Pax Silica is a US-led coalition aimed at countering Chinese dominance in critical supply chains such as AI and semiconductors. The Philippines and Singapore are the only Southeast Asian countries to join the 13-member bloc. It has seen online backlash due to concerns over resource extraction and the widespread displacement of farmers and indigenous communities. Younger dissent Net trust among Filipinos for the US, though, remains “good”, according to Pollster Social Weather Stations. The June survey of 1,200 Filipinos found that 60 per cent were still positive about the US compared with 18 per cent who voiced distrust. Dissent towards the two US-led projects likely came from Gen Z, experts said. Sonny Africa, executive director of Manila-based non-profit think tank IBON Foundation, called the backlash “extremely significant politically”. “They show that reported positive views of the US don’t translate into public acceptance of every US economic or military initiative, and that the public is receptive to seeing these for what they really are beyond predictably glowing US and Philippine government hype,” Africa said. “If this leads to greater understanding of US historical dominance of the Philippines and of worsening global US economic and military aggression today, the Pax Silica protests could eventually snowball into a generalised anti-American turn.” Online access allowed people to decide for themselves. “Reports on the displacement of indigenous peoples strengthen the sense that these projects are more exploitative than beneficial,” said Gino Trinidad, a political science instructor at Ateneo de Manila University. “It does not help that a considerable number of Filipinos – especially the youth – have had access to reports of how the building of data centres in the US and elsewhere have contributed to the depleting of natural resources and polluting of water.” A Momentum Research survey of 1,487 Filipinos from August 18 to 23 found that while 33.9 per cent decried the Pax Silica project, opposition was highest among Gen Z compared with others at 43.2 per cent, with adequate power and water supply for data centre operations topping their concerns. Gen Z Filipinos were also the most concerned about environmental effects and the displacement of farming and indigenous folk, the polling firm said. “For a country that has locations still facing problems of accessing potable water, the potential ill-effects of the initiatives become harder to ignore,” Trinidad said. While initiatives such as the Luzon Economic Corridor promise “1 million jobs” for Filipinos, their critics are sceptical that these would provide higher value for the country and offset resource exploitation. “My sense is that the main promise of these initiatives is job creation … Jobs will indeed be created, but what kinds and if these jobs are high-value are questions that must be addressed clearly,” Trinidad said, pointing out that Central Luzon was already in the top three regions for total gross domestic product. “The level and potential effects of the exploitation of the Philippines’ natural resources by these projects should be clearly addressed. Furthermore, the redistributive potential of such projects must be scrutinised. Will these projects really lead to a more equitable distribution of economic growth?” ‘Minor’ benefits Africa called the expected benefits for the Philippines “shallow, minor and incidental at best if the overriding logic of the initiatives is another country’s strategic purposes”. “There will be construction activity, some foreign-oriented infrastructure with limited domestic use, and perhaps some foreign-owned mineral processing aside from how the government can report additional exports, jobs and foreign investment,” he said. “However, there is not likely to be much in terms of the Filipino firms, technology, profits and strategic productive capacity that constitute real Philippine industrial development.” US desire for technological dominance in semiconductors and AI would result in the Philippines staying in its “subordinate role in US-led value semiconductor chains”, Africa said, adding that it had been the case for decades despite billions of dollars in investments by American firms. “There’s also the opportunity cost. Philippine infrastructure, minerals and public resources will be directed towards the requirements of US semiconductor, AI and military supply chains instead of the country’s own national industrialisation and development priorities.” He warned that increased economic dependence on the US “becomes another mechanism to reinforce strategic alignment with the US, while excluding potentially productive relations with countries the US seeks to isolate such as China”. “National industrialisation and development is difficult enough as it is without these major external constraints,” he said.

title: Are Chinese students learning English just to ‘tell China’s story’?
description: With revised textbooks focusing more on Chinese culture, critics worry students are losing sight of the broader world.
content: For generations of Chinese schoolchildren, English textbooks offered a glimpse of an unfamiliar world, from London’s Tower Bridge and Big Ben to American school life and Halloween traditions. Today, students opening an English textbook are more likely to encounter passages on late Qing dynasty (1644-1912) thinker Liang Qichao, the Dragon Boat Festival and China’s overseas aid projects. These changes are part of a nationwide overhaul of China’s primary and middle-school textbooks, which have shifted their focus towards Chinese culture and “telling China’s story” of national achievements, sparking debate over the purpose of English education in China. The revised textbooks – which have been introduced in stages since 2024 and were fully rolled out at the start of this year’s autumn semester – have dropped much of the content on foreign cultures found in older editions as Beijing seeks to align education more closely with national priorities, including strengthening patriotism and boosting China’s image overseas. The changes have been praised by some parents and teachers who argue they will boost students’ cultural confidence, while others worry that they will limit children’s exposure to the wider world and undermine their English proficiency. Integrating Chinese cultural content into English courses was a growing education trend, state news agency Xinhua wrote in April 2025. The changes are reflected throughout primary and middle-school textbooks. Lessons place a strong emphasis on traditional festivals, Chinese historical figures, archaeological discoveries and the country’s modern economic, social and technological developments, according to teachers and Chinese media reports. The textbooks also introduce contemporary government policies, such as the idea of a “new socialist countryside” and the goal of building a “community of a shared future for mankind”. “I’ve been waiting for this change for many years,” a veteran English teacher wrote on social media. “Learning a language has never been just about the language itself. It is about learning how to use it to engage with the world. In the past, we learned to ‘listen to others’. Now we are finally learning to ‘speak for ourselves’.” Many others questioned whether the shift had gone too far. “There’s simply too much Chinese culture, ideological content and local elements in today’s English textbooks,” said another English teacher with a decade of experience. “We all agree that building confidence in Chinese culture is absolutely a good thing,” the teacher wrote. “But at its core, language learning is about entering other cultures, understanding different ways of thinking and seeing a diverse world.” The teacher argued that the generations who grew up using the older textbooks were not “eroded” by foreign cultures. They added that without exposure to foreign cultures and customs, students could struggle to develop a sense of curiosity about the language. Without any novelty, they said, studying English could easily become dull and formulaic. Some teachers criticised the new textbooks for turning English lessons into nothing more than “exercises in translating Chinese culture into English”. They said China needed people who could use English to present its culture to the world, but using a foreign language to express ideas and content already familiar to students could undermine the point of learning it in the first place. Some also noted that parts of the new textbooks were in “Chinglish”, saying students were learning how to fit Chinese ways of thinking into English sentences rather than developing more natural ways of expressing themselves in English. But while teachers debate the impact on language learning, Beijing’s top leadership has made clear that political direction takes priority. The latest high-level signal on textbooks and ideology came last week when senior officials at a national conference called for building a “high-quality textbook system with Chinese characteristics”. Speaking at the conference last Tuesday, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang highlighted the “political, people-centred and strategic” nature of education and said textbooks should have the “correct political direction and value orientation”. The textbook overhaul is part of a broader national push to promote “cultural confidence”, a term used by President Xi Jinping to describe a belief in the value and vitality of Chinese culture. In 2016, Xi described the essential “Four Confidences” – confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The formulation was later added to the Communist Party’s constitution. The push to strengthen patriotic education and cultural identity building in schools has been solidified through successive policies. In 2020, the Ministry of Education announced a ban on foreign-published textbooks in primary and junior high schools. The approach was given legal backing in 2023, when the Patriotic Education Law required patriotic education to be incorporated into different subjects and textbooks, stressing the importance of preserving and developing China’s traditional culture. What kind of identity is being shaped by textbooks is especially sensitive in China’s ethnic minority areas. In 2021, the former head of the Xinjiang education department was handed a suspended death sentence for his role in writing and publishing a number of school textbooks that were deemed “problematic” by the local authorities for encouraging “separatist thoughts”. The education ministry began to revise textbooks in March 2022, following the release of a new national plan for the compulsory education curriculum. The new textbooks were rolled out in stages from autumn 2024, beginning with primary grade one and middle-school grade seven. The roll-out expanded in 2025 to primary grades two and three and middle-school grade eight, before covering all primary and middle-school grades this autumn. Supporters of the revisions argue that the shift is intended to correct a long-standing imbalance. “Over an extremely long period in the past, our foreign-language textbooks, including English textbooks, were seriously lacking in content on China’s fine traditional culture, revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture,” said Dong Hongdan, an education ministry official, according to the 2025 Xinhua report. English was particularly well suited to carrying out patriotic and cultural education, he said. “If we want Chinese culture to reach the world, we first need to use language and forms of expression that others can understand to tell China’s stories well,” he said. On social media, one teacher warned that a child who studied English without learning about the cultures of English-speaking countries might end up with “not cultural confidence, but a closed sense of self”. “English textbooks should first and foremost be a bridge,” the teacher said. “Students need to learn to understand the world before they can truly speak to it.” “Good English education,” they added, “is not about telling students what we already have, but showing them what else the world has to offer.”

title: In Focus | How one company’s choice – resignation or the factory – left China’s young workers floored
description: The outlook for China’s young jobseekers could worsen further, after an ugly fallout from Xingyu’s mass dismissal of university graduates.
content: Weeks after sparking a nationwide outcry over its mass dismissal of recent college graduates, Xingyu – a major automotive lighting maker in eastern China – has severely penalised four of its executives and promised to help the former employees find new jobs. Two of the firm’s top executives received salary deductions and two human resources managers were dismissed or demoted for their “misjudgment and hasty decision-making”, the company said in a lengthy statement detailing its recent “mistake” last week. The saga began in early August, when the Shanghai-listed company, whose clients include international carmakers such as Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, presented more than 370 fresh graduates – who had joined the company a month earlier – with a stark choice. They could either resign “voluntarily” and receive half a month’s salary, or stay and be reassigned from office-based technical roles to factory-floor work, including tightening screws. According to the firm, 107 chose the former option. But the uproar that ensued has placed the company firmly in the centre of a media firestorm, with Communist Party news organ People’s Daily calling the move “a blatant trampling of social trust” in a commentary late last month. The extensive public attention the incident aroused stood as a tangible reflection of corporate workforce contraction, youth employment pressure and growing incidents of labour disputes, phenomena occurring within a broader slowdown in the world’s second-largest economy, analysts said. While neither the firm nor local authorities specified any violation of labour law by the short-term manoeuvre, which coincided with its application for a listing in Hong Kong, its adverse effects were evident, the analysts warned. “The company’s planned Hong Kong listing is very likely to be blocked, because the negative impact is simply too damaging,” said Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing. As for the employment of fresh graduates – an increasingly sensitive issue for Beijing amid a tough job market – “the fact that this incident has escalated to such a degree is also highly unfavourable. Big companies will become very cautious in their future hiring”, he said. According to its statement, Xingyu had recruited more than 400 college graduates through campus hiring last autumn and this spring, while 372 formally joined the company in July. About one month into their employment, the company’s human resources department conducted one-on-one meetings with each of them, presenting the binary choice. The decision resulted from a workforce optimisation plan “based on the company’s order pipeline and staffing needs”, it said. The move sparked backlash from many former employees, who complained to domestic media that after being dismissed, they lost their status as fresh graduates and could only re-enter the job market as social hires with a termination record on their résumés. Within China’s institutional framework, losing this status stripped them of many competitive job-seeking advantages. The company and the municipal human resources bureau of Changzhou, where Xingyu is based, have so far arranged for 71 of those dismissed to join new employers, while an additional 22 passed interviews and received offer letters. The remainder were either undertaking interviews or planning to pursue postgraduate studies, Xingyu said last week. Previously, both the firm and the bureau responded with apologies and explanations over the incident but failed to quell widespread public scepticism. On August 25, the bureau confirmed the controversial lay-off – after media reports went viral – noting that the negotiation process was “overly rigid and simplistic, lacking full and effective communication”. Two days later, the firm issued a public apology, acknowledging “managerial errors in decision-making” and offering a package of remedies including three months’ worth of job-seeking living allowances, free dormitory accommodation and an additional six months’ salary compensation for those who remained unemployed. At its half-year performance briefing on September 2, the company’s chairwoman and general manager, Zhou Xiaoping, apologised and said the company was “properly implementing remedial measures” under government guidance. According to its earnings results, Xingyu posted revenue of 6.88 billion yuan (US$1 billion) in the first half of the year, up 1.87 per cent, year on year, with a profit of about 712 million yuan, down 7.78 per cent, year on year. Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard Nie Riming, Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law Its 2025 sales figures showed that it held an 11.6 per cent share of China’s automotive lighting market, ranking first in the country, and accounted for 4.6 per cent of the global market share, ranking seventh. Nie Riming, a researcher at the Shanghai Institute of Finance and Law, said the broader lacklustre job market was primarily why this incident generated such a huge response. “Behind this is the current macroeconomic environment – finding a job is just very hard,” he said. Another record-breaking army of university graduates – an estimated 12.7 million students – entered China’s job market this summer, up about 4 per cent from last year, according to official data. The youth jobless rate – covering those aged 16 to 24, excluding students – climbed to 17.9 per cent in July from 14.9 per cent in the previous month. Nie noted that Xingyu’s immediate cash compensation alone could compare favourably with statutory minimums in Germany, where labour protections are generally stronger. While China has relatively high-standard labour laws on paper, enforcement and compliance are uneven, especially among smaller firms, he said. Against this backdrop, listed companies like Xingyu – along with foreign-invested firms and state-owned enterprises – remain the primary sources of higher-quality jobs in China. However, these relatively “well-behaved” companies had been steadily reducing their headcount in recent years, and after this incident, such formal, regulated positions were likely to become even more scarce, he added. “For companies going forward, they will become increasingly cautious when hiring for compliant, formal positions,” he said. “They will lean more towards non-standard employment arrangements – such as outsourcing and dispatching – to offload their staffing responsibilities. That, in turn, would further reduce formal direct hiring and reinforce labour-market dualisation.” The most contentious issue remains fresh graduate status, as many recruitment policies, including those for civil service admissions, favour fresh graduates, he said. “The way graduates are regulated has yet to align with the job market, and this disconnect must be resolved before it causes further frustration,” he urged. As the economic slowdown persists in China, lay-offs have become a recurring theme in the workplace, and labour disputes are on the rise. Labour dispute mediation and arbitration bodies at all levels handled 4.54 million cases nationwide in 2025 – a 7 per cent increase from 2024, following a 10 per cent rise over 2023, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security’s annual statistical bulletin. Meanwhile, Xingyu’s lay-off controversy emerged after it refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July, sparking market speculation that it was a short-term tactic to pad the company’s research workforce and make it look stronger for its listing ambitions. Among the dismissed employees, about two-thirds held bachelor’s degrees, while the remainder held master’s degrees. The majority were assigned to research and development roles, as well as manufacturing and production positions, while a smaller number were allocated functional support roles, according to last week’s statement. However, legal experts and academics considered it unlikely that this was the company’s primary intention, given that such a move would offer limited substantive gain while exposing it to significant compliance and reputational risks. Such risks may soon materialise, such as hindering its listing progress, said Zhao Zhanling, a commercial lawyer from Beijing-based Javy Law Firm. “The stock exchange and its advisers are likely to demand clarifications on the mass lay-offs, labour law compliance and internal control mechanisms,” he said. “Adverse media coverage may also invite regulatory questions, causing delays – though not necessarily scuttling the IPO altogether.” The Shanghai Stock Exchange website showed that it issued a regulatory work letter to Xingyu on Wednesday, specifying regulatory requirements regarding the company’s “relevant matters”, without providing further details. The saga could also lead to a loss of business opportunities, according to Tang, the Beijing researcher. “It is possible that its international clients would respond positively to public outcry,” he said, “but that does not mean they would punish Xingyu – they may downgrade its supplier tier ... or impose more stringent supply conditions.” Volkswagen China said earlier this month that it had initiated an investigation into the matter following intense media coverage.

title: Number of suspicious credit card transactions involving iPhones surges to 1,209
description: Apple spokesman says all current orders are being reviewed before processing as total amount involved rises to HK$25 million.
content: The number of suspicious credit card transactions involving pre-orders for the latest iPhone models has surged to more than 1,200 in Hong Kong, involving HK$25 million (US$3.2 million), police have said, while Apple is reviewing all current orders. The force said the number of unauthorised transactions had risen to 1,209 as of 5pm on Monday, up from more than 700 the previous day. The total amount involved had also risen from HK$14.7 million. Over the weekend, many social media users reported unauthorised credit card transactions involving Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro series, which went on pre-order on Saturday. The cards had been issued by different banks. Police said they had immediately contacted the relevant banks and Apple to ascertain the situation. “Our preliminary investigations have also revealed that the online mobile phone pre-order transactions in question did not require a one-time password via SMS or any other form of authentication,” Chief Inspector Chan Lai-yu said. “Consequently, the payment process could be completed without the cardholder’s confirmation, allowing fraudsters to exploit this vulnerability.” Chan said investigators were now tracing the source of the credit card data breach, including analysing whether victims had previously submitted the compromised information on shared platforms or had fallen victim to phishing scams in the past. The force was also investigating the identities of those involved and their digital footprints to identify the individuals who used the stolen data to make online pre-orders, Chan added. The cases have been classified as “obtaining property by deception”, with the force’s cybersecurity and technology crime bureau investigating. An Apple spokesman said all current orders were being reviewed before processing. “We are working to quickly identify and cancel any fraudulent transactions that may have been placed,” he said. Legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong told a radio programme on Monday that Apple should ultimately be held responsible, while estimating that the actual losses would not be significant. He described the incident as “rare”, given the large number of victims and the involvement of a platform operated by a major company such as Apple. Ng said he suspected hackers might have stolen and stored the credit card details over time while waiting for an opportunity to use them. He added that Apple might have disabled multi-factor verification for credit card transactions to keep its website running smoothly amid heavy traffic, allowing fraudsters to exploit a loophole. “[With multi-factor verification], they will use more computing and network resources to process the exact same orders because of the extra steps in the process,” he said. “This also creates a problem with longer wait times; customers have to queue up and wait while trying to make a transaction. So, the overall customer experience will definitely take a hit.” Some users complained that they had placed a single order but found that multiple orders had been made. Ng said this was likely to have been because of glitches in Apple’s platform and did not involve compromised credit card details. In such cases, Apple should bear ultimate responsibility for any losses incurred, he said. But Ng estimated that the actual amount would not be significant because Apple had not yet delivered the products and banks should have withheld the funds involved. On Sunday, major banks in Hong Kong reassured victims that they would not be held liable as long as the transactions were proven to be unauthorised. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, reminded the public to remain highly vigilant against “secondary scams” that fraudsters might launch in the wake of the incidents. “As fraudsters may already have obtained victims’ telephone numbers, names and some credit card details, there is a high likelihood that they will impersonate banks, merchants or law enforcement agencies and proactively contact victims under the pretext of ‘processing refunds’, ‘verifying fraudulent transactions’ or ‘cancelling suspicious transactions’,” Fong warned.

title: Letters | Hong Kong’s universities must avoid ‘easy entry, guaranteed pass’ model
description: Readers discuss the need to ensure academic rigour in tertiary education, and university orientation camps.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong is rapidly evolving into an international education hub. With 22 local degree-awarding institutions – nine publicly funded and 13 self-financing – producing around 50,000 graduates annually, the quality of these degrees is cause for concern. The prevailing approach often prioritises enrolment over academic rigour. This is driven by the funding formula for government-funded universities, which allocates resources largely based on total student headcount. Consequently, institutions are incentivised to maintain high intake numbers rather than enforce strict standards or fail underperforming students. Universities may admit a small percentage of students under “flexible admission” policies. There has also been an increase in the non-local student cap from 40 per cent to 50 per cent of local places. While inclusive, this risks admitting candidates with insufficient preparation. Coupled with graduation rates near 100 per cent, the system creates a “guaranteed pass” culture that fails to incentivise high standards. Are employers truly satisfied with the competence of executive trainees, teachers and social workers? Complaints of graduates lacking English proficiency or pedagogical skills are not uncommon. To maintain global prestige, Hong Kong must enforce rigorous exit requirements that ensure absolute competency. Current quality assurance relies heavily on institutional audits and peer reviews. To prepare for future expansion, three additional measures are essential. First, institute a common exit assessment. “Graduate attributes” like critical thinking must be more than marketing buzzwords. The authorities should mandate an internationally validated cognitive skills test, similar to the US’ Collegiate Learning Assessment, for all final-year students. A minimum threshold should be required to achieve Level 5 of the Hong Kong Qualifications Framework. Anonymised cohort results published by the University Grants Committee would expose institutions failing to deliver value-added learning. Second, make internships mandatory. Many traditional programmes allow graduation with zero real-world exposure. A universal requirement of 500 hours of accredited work-integrated education should be enforced. Crucially, if an employer fails a student on workplace competency or ethics, the student should not graduate, regardless of their Grade Point Average. Third, introduce performance-linked funding. Universities are currently funded based on enrolment and staff performance, not alumni competence. A significant portion of recurrent funding should be tied to longitudinal metrics, such as employer satisfaction and career progression three to five years post-graduation. Institutions whose graduates consistently underperform should face enrolment quota cuts and funding penalties. The trend of “easy entry, guaranteed pass” is unjustifiable and unsustainable. The government must take proactive steps to uphold the highest standards, ensuring Hong Kong remains a prestigious global education hub. Dr John Tse Wing-ling, executive director, Hong Kong Initiative for Diversity Orientation camps should go back to basics Many first-year University students in Hong Kong look forward to orientation camps as a chance to meet new friends, blend into the university culture and, most importantly, to have fun after years of intense public examination preparation. Yet in recent years, reports of inappropriate activities and alleged sexual assault at such camps have emerged with worrying regularity. This year, people were shocked by a video circulating on social media showing an inappropriate disco night orientation event organised by a student society of a local tertiary institution. What is the fundamental cause of this troubling trend? It is undeniable that well-designed orientation events can help university freshmen adjust to university life. However, this may no longer be the primary purpose of many orientation camps. Instead, some appear to have become occasions for students to “go wild” and seek entertainment, with insufficient regard for safety, dignity and consent. The public and universities expect orientation camps to introduce freshmen to campus facilities, student societies and university services. Meanwhile, students may primarily see the camps as opportunities to meet new people and enjoy greater freedom after secondary school. Although orientation activities such as ice-breaking games, water games and campfires can encourage students to socialise, they can also create an environment in which peer pressure, alcohol consumption, sexualised behaviour or the abuse of senior students’ power are normalised. This difference in expectations of orientation camps between the public and the students is the crux of the issue. Orientation events should not be treated as an excuse for humiliating, indecent or unsafe activities. Universities must exercise stronger oversight over orientation camps organised by student societies and provide mandatory training for student organisers to avoid indecent activities. Organisers should also verify participants’ identities and ages, ensuring they are legitimate students of the university. More fundamentally, universities and student societies should discuss what orientation camps are intended to achieve. If the purpose of orientation camps is to help students begin university life, then fun and socialising should support that objective, not replace it entirely. Leung Wai-chun, Siu Sai Wan

title: South Korea’s ‘grey digital divide’ leaves seniors pleading for help
description: From baseball tickets to hailing taxis, rapid tech adoption has left 80 per cent of elderly South Koreans isolated from everyday services.
content: A little cheer rose for 79-year-old Hwang Sun-hee after she managed to place an online order at a training session in South Korea, which has one of the world’s starkest digital divides for seniors. Age gaps in digital literacy are a global concern, yet the gulf has widened massively in the hyper-connected and fast-ageing country, prompting national campaigns to bridge it. “You can’t do anything without smartphone apps or a kiosk machine ... It’s too much for old folks,” Hwang said at a senior community centre in Suwon, south of Seoul, during government-organised digital survival training. The so-called grey digital divide has provided some striking examples in the nation of about 52 million, home to world-leading smartphone and memory chipmakers. Last year, several baseball clubs began reserving a small number of tickets for on-site sales after reports that older fans, cash in hand, approached younger people at stadiums and pleaded with them to buy tickets from machines. Nearly 90 per cent of taxi drivers use ride-hailing apps, yet more than 80 per cent of South Koreans over 60 still hail cabs by hand, a survey showed. A 71-year-old retired public servant at the same training session as Hwang recalled spending over 30 minutes trying to flag down a taxi on a busy Seoul street. The cabs kept passing him to pick up younger riders just metres away who were using smartphone apps to hail their rides. “I felt utterly useless,” the man, who gave only his surname, Park, said. The digital divide can also pose a real threat, leaving older people vulnerable to hi-tech crimes such as online scams or limiting their access to medical services, experts say. A state survey last year found that 60 per cent of South Koreans over 60 struggle to use public and commercial services due to lack of digital skills – compared with just six per cent of those under 40. “The intergenerational digital divide [in South Korea] appears wider than elsewhere,” said Kim Jeung-kun, professor of senior business at Kangnam University in Seoul. He noted that the nation’s “intensely compressed” industrialisation happened in just a few decades, while it took centuries in many Western countries. South Korea – which had a gross domestic product per capita below US$100 in the wake of its 1950–1953 war – is now the world’s 15th largest economy, according to the IMF. “Many of our elderly grew up at a time when many had no electricity, landline phones or proper schooling,” Kim added. The nation’s older cohort is massive – South Korea is what the UN calls a “super-aged society”, where more than 20 per cent of the population is over 65. In response, South Korea’s public tech training for the elderly began in 2020, when businesses and services turned online during the Covid-19 lockdown. Hwang, echoing others in the two-hour class, said she had made it this far by relying on her children for daily tasks she once managed herself – including enrolling in her favourite dance class at the local community centre. “Before, I could easily do all of these just by calling or showing up in person,” Hwang said. Officials now provide nationwide training for the “digitally vulnerable” for using mobile devices, apps, and AI. Vans packed with tech devices and mock kiosks drive to community centres and regional festivals popular among the elderly. In 2025, over 65,000 sessions were held for some 650,000 people over 60. Hwang gathered along with 30 neighbours for a session in August, practising how to pay hospital bills at mock kiosks, patting a prancing robot dog, or asking their phones: “Gemini, tell me about tomorrow’s weather.” She has undergone similar training several times – and said the lessons helped her confidence – but noted she was “so envious of young people who can do all this so easily”. “I wish I had been born young in today’s world,” Hwang added.

title: North Korea tests weapons capable of striking South Korea: ‘huge destructive power’
description: The live-fire drill tested attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, tactical ballistic missiles and large-calibre multiple rocket launchers.
content: North Korea said on Monday it conducted a joint live-fire drill involving missiles, artillery and drones that it claimed showed “huge destructive power”. The official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said Saturday’s drill was meant to get familiar with the procedure for the operation of the integrated firepower control system. South Korea’s military earlier said it detected short-range ballistic missile launches from North Korea’s eastern coastal Wonsan area on Saturday morning. After observing the drill, Marshal Pak Jong-chon said the drill would “improve the level of specialisation to bring down the enemy’s armed forces organisationally and structurally once an order is issued”. He added that the weapons systems mobilised showed “the huge destructive power of concentrated fire”, according to KCNA. The “joint firepower attack drill” involved five army units and tested several weapon systems, including attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, tactical ballistic missiles, and large-calibre multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said. It is extremely difficult to independently verify North Korean claims on its weapons tests. South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said several missiles fired Saturday each flew about 250km (155 miles) towards North Korea’s eastern waters. The flight distances signal the weapons are designed to strike targets in South Korea. The firing drill marked North Korea’s first public ballistic missile launches in about three weeks. Calibrating tensions “This was not a test of a ‌single weapon system but a demonstration of an integrated strike network,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor ⁠at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies in Seoul. North Korea appeared to be showcasing ⁠its ability to coordinate drones, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and rocket artillery through a unified command-and-control system, he said. The absence of leader Kim Jong-un and the delayed ‌report suggested Pyongyang sought to ‌present the event as a “technical and practical military exercise” while calibrating tensions, Lim said. “North Korea is also collecting operational data for actual deployment and demonstrating tactics aimed at saturating South Korean and US missile defences through simultaneous attacks by weapons with different flight characteristics.” Last month, US President Donald Trump scaled back a major bilateral military drill with South Korea, citing what he called a good relationship with Kim. That is an apparent effort to revive diplomacy between them, but North Korea rebuffed Trump’s overture, saying that shortening the drill did not change its “provocative, aggressive nature”. Buoyed by his advancing nuclear arsenal and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts say Kim likely thinks he has greater leverage in possible diplomacy with the US than when he first met Trump in 2018–2019. Kim said earlier this year that he could return to talks if the US dropped its “hostile policy” against his country and respected what he called the North’s status as a nuclear state. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: 3 killed, 15 wounded in gunfire ahead of historic Philippine regional election
description: Bangsamoro, a region long marred by political violence and blood feuds, is voting for its first elected president on Monday.
content: Three people were killed and 15 others wounded as gunfire erupted hours before the polls opened on Monday in a semi-autonomous Muslim region of the Philippines set to choose its first elected parliament. The vote is the culmination of an on-off peace process that began in the late 1990s and established the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in the country’s far south. Cotabato police chief Jibin Bongcayao said the shooting took place just before midnight as members of rival political factions jostled for the right to cast their votes first. “It started as a struggle for position in the queue between two groups,” Bongcayao said of the shooting outside a school being used as a polling station in the regional capital. “It led to shoving, escalated into a fist-fight, and eventually gunfire broke out in a crowded area.” Bongcayao added that the men had belonged to rival parties that had emerged from the group that spent decades fighting for regional autonomy in the predominantly Catholic country, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. In a region long marred by political violence and blood feuds between powerful families, a peaceful election would be considered a successful one, party leaders recently said. Security has been stepped up across Bangsamoro in recent days, with more than 20,000 security personnel fanning out in voting areas and quick-response teams assembled to address potential violence. Last month, a motorcade carrying the region’s interim chief minister – an appointee of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr – was ambushed and peppered with bullets. In a separate incident, a man died in hospital in the early hours of Monday following an explosion near another polling station. Police are still investigating the cause. Poll instead of weapons Around 2.4 million people are eligible to vote to fill 80 parliamentary seats, including regional, district and sectoral representatives, which will be contested by over 600 candidates. Voting started at 7am and will end at 7pm, with the results to be known as soon as Monday evening. The autonomous region is composed of five provinces and three cities, and its current parliamentarians were appointed by Marcos as transitional leaders. Some of them, including the chief minister, are among those vying for seats on Monday. “Instead of picking up their weapons, they are now using the poll,” Marcos told foreign correspondents at a forum in August. “They are now involving themselves in the political process, which of course will bring peace and, hopefully, progress.” The parliamentary election was originally set for 2022 but was pushed back by then president Rodrigo Duterte to 2025 to allow for more time for transition. Marcos then postponed it to September this year, with the winners’ terms to run from October until June 2031, and an election to follow every three years after. A peaceful transfer of power would bolster confidence in Bangsamoro. The agriculture-driven economy grew 5 per cent to 267 billion pesos (US$4.25 billion) in 2025, outpacing the country’s 4.4 per cent uptick, government data show. But the region continues to grapple with poverty and outdated infrastructure. More than a third of Bangsamoro’s cities and towns posted poverty rates exceeding 40 per cent, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority. That is far above the national average. Marcos expressed confidence in the region’s economic potential in his remarks last month. “I joke with some of my friends from the area. I said, when I’m done being president, I’m moving to Mindanao simply because the opportunities are just incredible,” he said. “So, I’ll finally be a rich person. I’ll make a lot of money when I go back into business.” Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: New York Fashion Week 2026: Calvin Klein’s minimalist chic, Michael Kors’ polished glam and other highlights
description: Model Kaia Gerber walked in Khaite’s boudoir vision, while Emily Dawn Long showcased her collection with a tongue-in-cheek film.
content: New York Fashion Week always stands out for its diversity of offerings, from quintessentially American labels like Calvin Klein and Michael Kors to independent brands such as Diotima, Ashlyn and Collina Strada. This season also saw the debut of Henry Zankov at Diane von Furstenberg and the first New York show from London-based American designer Conner Ives. Indian designer Sabyasachi and American designer Thom Browne are among the designers showing later this week. Here are highlights from the shows so far. Michael Kors showed Michael Kors Collection, his high-end label, in the Sculpture Garden of MoMA (Museum of Modern Art) in midtown Manhattan. “Polished” is the first word that comes to mind when looking at the line-up of perfectly put-together outfits for perfectly put-together women. The designer’s fantasy of a version of America that exists in places such as the Upper East Side of Manhattan, the Hamptons and Palm Beach never gets old but it could do with a bit of a shake-up. Named Architectural Modernism, the spring/summer 2027 collection will certainly please Kors’ well-heeled clientele – whether they’re looking for a beautiful dress with an asymmetrical hem to wear for a fabulous night out on the town or for preppy separates like a crisp striped shirt. A series of looks with sequin embellishments beautifully stood out amid the sea of primary colours in a line-up that stayed true to the designer’s vision of all-American glamour. Calvin Klein Collection’s current creative director Veronica Leoni presented her fourth range for the label in a space filled with sculptural installations by American minimalist artist Walter De Maria. The venue provided the perfect backdrop to the clean lines of the garments: foundational pieces such as the slip dress, the pencil skirt and the fitted trouser that have always been at the core of Calvin Klein. While Leoni has been doing a perfectly fine job since she joined the brand a couple of years ago to revive its luxury line, her shows often leave you wanting more. With its huge global presence and recognition, Calvin Klein has a lot of untapped potential and a fascinating history, as the success of the Hulu series Love Story – about the romance and tragic deaths of John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette – recently demonstrated. Known for her impeccable personal style, Bessette famously worked at the house back in the 1990s, an era that is having a major moment among younger generations. Mining aspects of the label such as its groundbreaking campaigns from that decade would make it resonate with today’s consumers looking for more than a beautiful pair of well-cut pants or a tailored jacket. Designer Cate Holstein, founder of Khaite, has built a loyal following thanks to her ability to reinvent wardrobe staples that are not just another take on quiet luxury. Her reinterpretations of American classics such as the cowboy boot and the leather jacket have turned the brand into a global success story. For spring/summer 2027, Holstein offered her version of boudoir dressing. Model Kaia Gerber opened the show in a white bra paired with a leather skirt unzipped at the back. There was an undone quality to the clothes, with unbuttoned shirts exposing the skin and fastenings that unravelled to reveal hints of flesh. With their frizzy and unkempt hair, the models looked like they just got out of bed or like they were ready to go to bed after a night of debauchery. The collection is likely to surprise many of Khaite’s long-time fans but they still have plenty to covet, from pointy-toe pumps and peep-toe mules to sharply cut leather jackets. As always at Khaite, the set was mesmerising. The designer and her team turned an event venue in Brooklyn that was basically a black box into a churchlike space where powerful projections created a mesmerising series of light columns. Every season designer Joseph Altuzarra, founder of Altuzarra, leaves a book on each guest’s seat. Usually a novel, the book acts as a sort of mood board: flip through its pages and you’ll discover clipped visual references that inform the story behind the collection. For spring/summer 2027, Altuzarra picked a photography book showcasing men cross-dressing as women in the 1950s and 60s at Casa Susanna, a retreat in the Catskill Mountains in upstate New York. Those joyful images of trans women freely expressing themselves “became the emotional foundation of the collection”, according to the show notes. Closet staples like oversized worker jackets were paired with madras print skirts while elements from men’s suits appeared throughout the androgynous collection. Most looks were paired with Oxford lace-ups. High-waist jeans, leather pants, studded belts and other American wardrobe classics gave the range a western feel. Among the best outfits were feminine blouses featuring men’s shirt cuffs and worn with lovely pleated skirts with floral embroidery at the waist. A couple of animal print knit skirt suits also looked fabulous. The final looks, including a wrinkled golden dress and a series of lingerie-inspired gowns, were an unabashed celebration of feminine glamour. It was a beautifully told story from a thoughtful designer who always stays true to his sharp vision and stands out as one of the strongest voices in American fashion. Anna Sui is another designer who is confident enough to do her own thing, regardless of short-lived fads. In the show notes, the designer explained how, while looking for a Richard Avedon photo in an old issue of Vogue, she came across a painting by artist Howard Gardiner Cushing. The collection explores that same sense of wonderment and of unexpected discovery. As always at Anna Sui, embellishments reigned supreme, from crochet and lingerie accents to florals, fringes and plenty of prints. View this post on Instagram A post shared by EMILY DAWN LONG (@emilydawnlong) Buzzy designer Emily Dawn Long showed her latest collection with a fun screening at Bridges, a popular bar in Chinatown.
