Titled The Crack of Dawn and starring Meadow Walker and Sydney Lemmon of Love Story fame among other up-and-coming actors, the short video was a cool way to present the range. The name of the film was a reference to the many butt crack-exposing dresses. The back, unsurprisingly, was a focal point with low-cut pleated hems that exposed it in a sexy and nonchalant way. A skirt and a dress with trompe-l’oeil prints of folds and pleats also stood out and showcased the designer’s ability to make desirable clothes that look and feel very of the moment.

title: Tourism and technology may hold key to boosting China’s public image in the US
description: Survey by Sun Yat-sen University team also concludes that many people believe the country has played a positive role on the world stage.
content: China could improve its image in the United States by highlighting areas such as tourism and technology and positioning itself as a responsible major power, a survey has concluded. Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou said that although concepts such as “decoupling” and “de-risking” had been increasingly prominent in media coverage of China, this had not entirely wiped away positive impressions of the country. When evaluating China’s strengths on a scale of 1 to 5, the respondents placed global influence at the top with a score of 4.38, followed by achievements in science and technology at 3.59 and higher education at 3.56. The survey found many respondents believed China was contributing to global peace, stability and governance, prompting the researchers to argue that Beijing should reinforce its image as a responsible major power by highlighting its role in United Nations peacekeeping missions, in fighting climate change and providing aid. It also emphasised the need to directly address “misunderstandings” and “scepticism” in international media through greater transparency and openness. The researchers also noted that the American public had “a high level of interest” in issues such as Hong Kong, Taiwan and Tibet. While the paper, published in the Chinese-language journal Global Communication, did not elaborate on what topics interested them, Western media coverage of these areas typically revolves around issues such as human rights, separatism, the environment and cultural preservation. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of its territory and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The United States, in common with most countries, does not recognise the self-ruled island as independent, but opposes any attempt to seize it by force and is committed to supplying it with arms to defend itself. The researchers said more diverse perspectives on areas with large ethnic minorities should be put forward. “We should face up to the limitations in how the international community – particularly certain Western media – perceives China’s global role, strengthen the explanation and communication of China’s foreign policy and multilateral contributions, counter misreadings and biases stemming from external narrative constructions, and foster a comprehensive understanding of China’s international image [abroad],” the report said. The findings follow a survey carried out by the Pew Research Centre in the US earlier this year that found that the number of Americans with a favourable view of China was rising. While negative opinions remained dominant, the poll found that 27 per cent of respondents held a positive opinion of China – up 6 percentage points from the previous year and nearly double the level recorded in 2023. The Pew survey also found that respondents’ confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing regarding world affairs had also risen by 4 points over the past year, roughly doubling since 2023. The Sun Yat-sen University survey also found there was strong public interest in non-political areas. Science and technology topped the list of areas American respondents were most curious about in China at 58.2 per cent, followed closely by tourism and food, both tied at 56.6 per cent. The researchers said that international outreach efforts should focus on technology and tourism, and called for a greater focus on the human-interest stories behind scientific breakthroughs and their positive contributions to global development. “[This approach could] help break down the anxiety over tech competition hyped by some US media outlets, guiding the American public to pay attention to the global welfare generated by technological cooperation,” the study noted. For tourism, researchers called for high-quality promotional content on social media and said more influencers should be invited to experience daily life in China first hand. Last year, the popular American live-streamer IShowSpeed (real name Darren Watkins) toured several Chinese cities, marvelling at the advanced infrastructure and smart technology he saw. His live streams attracted around 10 million views combined and some of his followers commented that China was “on another level” – a moment widely taken as a soft-power win for the country. The Sun Yat-sen University’s online poll sampled 1,327 American adults with a mean age of 32.8 and a balanced gender ratio.

title: Hong Kong 5-year plan to stick with capitalism, uphold ‘one country, two systems’: John Lee
description: In opinion piece published in South China Morning Post, city leader stresses that blueprint ultimately aims to ‘enable citizens to flourish’.
content: Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan will not change the capitalist system and instead fully exploit its advantages to map the city’s long-term development, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has said. In an opinion piece published in the South China Morning Post on Monday, the city leader also stressed that the blueprint, in focusing on the economy, would ultimately “enable citizens to flourish” by creating employment opportunities and upward mobility. Lee will unveil Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan on Wednesday, alongside his annual policy address, to map out the city’s priorities and align with the national blueprint covering the country’s development between 2026 and 2030. In the article, he sought to address concerns that introducing the five-year plan, a practice in mainland China for over seven decades, meant the city was walking away from its long-hailed laissez-faire system. “I have also been asked whether formulating a five-year plan would change Hong Kong’s original system. The answer is no,” Lee wrote. “The five-year plan will uphold Hong Kong’s rule of law and capitalist system, implement the Basic Law and adhere to ‘one country, two systems’ without distorting Hong Kong. “It will also uphold its status as an international city, ensure the free flow of capital, people, goods and information, while giving full play to the flexibility and advantages of the capitalist market.” He stressed that the one country, two systems guiding principle had been acknowledged by Chinese President Xi Jinping as a “good system” on multiple occasions that “must be adhered to over the long term”. Lee said he and his team had studied the experiences of Macau and mainland cities, with the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau also visiting different places to learn from their experience, before devising Hong Kong’s first plan “under an exceptionally tight schedule”. The government had also adopted artificial intelligence to analyse public feedback after receiving more than 17,000 submissions during the two-month consultation period, with 80 per cent coming from individuals, he said. Lee recalled that a resident once asked him during the consultation sessions what the plan, which focused on major economic issues, had to do with ordinary citizens. “My answer then, as now, is direct: I want the people of Hong Kong – every one of you – to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment,” he wrote. He said while the plan’s proposals – such as boosting Hong Kong’s traditional strengths, accelerating the Northern Metropolis megaproject and building global cooperation – focused on the economy, its ultimate goal was to enable residents to flourish. “With better employment opportunities and more upward mobility for our youth, that can become a tangible reality, turning governance from measures into results,” he said. Lee said the five-year plan would map out the long-term blueprint and strategic direction for Hong Kong’s development with “far-reaching significance”, while the policy address would continue to serve as an annual report and lay out how the government would implement the plan in a given year. “In the coming years, the annual policy addresses will continue to implement the blueprint, introducing policies and setting measures according to changing circumstances and economic dynamics,” he said. The coming policy address will be Lee’s last in his current five-year tenure. On Sunday, Lee revealed that he would wear a tie and a lapel pin designed by the faculty and students of the Technological and Higher Education Institute of Hong Kong during his address. The blue pin bore the Chinese characters for “one” and “five”, representing the city’s first five-year plan, while the two overlapping squares symbolised Hong Kong uniting resources and diverse talent, Lee said in a social media post. The tie, which features intersecting tech-pattern lines, was inspired by the Northern Metropolis’ technological development and represented internal and external connectivity, he added. Separately, a study by the think tank Youth Ideas found that more than half of the roughly 600 respondents aged between 13 and 34 wanted the government’s blueprint to focus on improving livelihoods and happiness, followed by ensuring economic growth benefited all parts of society equally. The study also found divided youth opinion on the five-year plan’s benefits, with nearly 40 per cent of respondents feeling a lack of involvement and one-quarter being unsure about the opportunities it would bring. About a quarter of respondents said the plan increased their confidence in Hong Kong’s future and their trust in the government. A similar percentage said these sentiments decreased. More than 60 per cent also said authorities had failed to explain the blueprint’s significance sufficiently. Think tank member Manteo Chan Man-to said focus group participants found that the government’s publicity methods were relatively formal and one-sided, with content that was condensed and lacked warmth. “As a result, youths merely know that there is a plan, but feel that it is very distant and difficult to spark resonance among their peers,” he said. John Poon Tsz-fung, think tank convenor, called on the government to better engage younger residents in Hong Kong’s long-term planning and include a forward-looking strategic plan to invest in them. Poon said young people were key stakeholders in Hong Kong’s future and called for a special chapter in the five-year plan focusing on youth development, with resources earmarked to send a “clear signal” about investing in this group. He proposed forming a cross-departmental “Future Commission” to ensure young people could genuinely participate, offer concrete feedback, and receive actual responses and tangible solutions.

title: Qatar seeks stronger logistics ties with China as war disrupts trade routes
description: Qatar logistics firm says Chinese businesses need local infrastructure and operating partners as they move into warehousing, fulfilment and sales.
content: Qatar is stepping up efforts to attract Chinese companies as the US-Israel war on Iran disrupts trade routes in the Gulf, adding urgency to a broader push by Chinese businesses to diversify supply chains and establish operations closer to customers. “Diversification of supply chain is going ahead anyway, right across the world,” said Sheikh Khalifa bin Salman al-Thani, a member of Qatar’s ruling Thani family and chief executive of Qatar-based logistics solutions company WareOne. Chinese companies have expanded across the Middle East in recent years, with platforms including Shein, Temu and AliExpress growing alongside electric vehicle, technology and consumer businesses. As more companies move beyond shipping goods from China to holding inventory and selling locally, they face a more complicated operating environment. “China has the most developed supply chain in the world. The question is no longer whether goods can move [but] who operates at the other end, which is the GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council],” Thani told the South China Morning Post on Thursday. The six GCC markets have different regulations, taxes and product-registration requirements, while companies may need local entities, customs agents, warehouses, fulfilment centres and delivery networks, Thani said. That can mean committing capital before demand is proven. “You have to build a warehouse, buy your own trucks and hire drivers. It costs you money,” he said. That is where companies such as WareOne see an opportunity. It provides warehousing, customs clearance, fulfilment and last-mile delivery, connecting merchants with existing capacity rather than requiring them to build their own logistics networks. Its model is to use existing infrastructure and invest in its own facilities where it sees gaps. “There is capacity already that exists. So you can plug in to that capacity through companies like us,” Thani said. WareOne said it was connected with major e-commerce platforms including Noon and Temu. It also handles AliExpress returns in the Gulf through a partnership with a local Chinese logistics company, sending returned goods back to Hong Kong, he added. Last Thursday, Thani signed a memorandum of understanding at Hong Kong’s Belt and Road Summit with logistics start-up Nexx to provide warehousing and last-mile services for Chinese merchants in the Gulf. The deal comes as Hong Kong seeks to deepen its ties under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative and strengthen links with emerging markets. WareOne has grown to more than 25 employees and over 60 clients after about two years of operations, and has moved hundreds of tonnes of goods and more than 100,000 e-commerce parcels, according to Thani. The expansion comes as Gulf economies compete to attract more trade and investment from Chinese companies. Qatar has invested heavily in ports, aviation, roads and free zones while seeking to position itself as a base for companies serving the wider region. In June, Qatar Free Zones Authority chief executive Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad bin Faisal al-Thani met JD.com CEO Sandy Ran Xu in China to discuss logistics and supply chains. While Dubai remains a major regional logistics and commercial hub, Thani of WareOne said Qatar can play a complementary role, or the starting point, in the network. He compared Qatar with Hong Kong, saying they had similar roles as connectors to larger economies. “Why do people come to Hong Kong when the market is bigger in mainland China? Because of regulations, infrastructure and connectivity,” he said. “Similarly, Qatar has everything to offer to serve as the gateway for the GCC,” he added.

title: ‘Cannon fodder’ Asians tricked to fight for Russia spur calls for intervention
description: A group of Indonesians was duped into fighting for Russia, Ukraine says, with other ruses involving Filipinos and Indians.
content: A report that eight Indonesians were allegedly tricked into fighting for Moscow in its war on Ukraine may be just the tip of the iceberg, analysts warn, cautioning that Southeast Asia’s existing scam networks could already be a hunting ground for Russian fraudsters. Ukraine’s intelligence agency revealed on August 27 that the Indonesians had been lured with promises of well-paid civilian jobs. Jakarta has confirmed it is aware of the case. The agency said Indonesia had become the “latest example” of countries whose nationals were being tricked into filling the ranks of Russia’s depleted forces. “The scheme Moscow uses to seek foreign cannon fodder has already been tested in dozens of other countries,” it warned. The disclosure follows earlier reports that Moscow had lured Filipinos into combat roles. The Philippine military said in August it was still verifying reports that a Filipino fighting for Russia had been killed in action. The Philippines’ Bureau of Immigration said that same month that it had rescued 18 Filipinos from what it described as “fake job offers”, though it did not specify whether these were related to deceptive recruitment into the Russian military. In January, a Filipino identified only as “John Patrick” was named by Ukraine’s intelligence services as among those killed in the occupied Donetsk region. Manila said at the time that it was seeking to confirm the Ukrainian statement. This Week in Asia has contacted the bureau for comment. Learning from scam centres The Indonesian cases suggest Russian recruiters have taken a page out of Southeast Asian scam networks’ playbook, according to analysts, with economic desperation driving victims to respond to fake job adverts on social media. “My take is Russia preys on the types of men people would easily miss,” said security researcher Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow at Verve Research. Mustaffa said the pattern suggested many of those recruited from Southeast Asia had travelled to Russia believing they were taking up non-military work, unlike foreigners who signed up for the war voluntarily. Russian officials have denied recruiting foreign nationals under false pretences, dismissing the reports as “dangerous and misleading” propaganda. Jovana Jezdimirovic Ranito, a member of the UN Working Group on the use of mercenaries and a professor at the University of Twente in the Netherlands, said fraudulent recruitment tactics had evolved in recent years. “While previously recruitment was based on glorifying war, it is now more common to see deceptive job posts or scholarship opportunities to attract individuals to fight in foreign conflicts,” she said. Victims often had their passports confiscated and were saddled with heavy debts owed to their recruiters, Ranito added. “This has similarities with scam networks observed in Southeast Asia. Many components are comparable, including deception, elements of human trafficking such as coercion and the removal of documents from victims, and violence.” Oksana Pokalchuk, executive director of Ukraine-based human rights group Truth Hounds, said South Asia had previously been the main recruiting ground, but sources had since diversified – citing information from Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War. The Ukrainian agency had counted at least 44 recruits from Southeast Asian countries – including Indonesia, Vietnam, Cambodia, the Philippines, Malaysia and Myanmar – as of January, with the true number “definitely bigger” today. Truth Hounds has interviewed foreign fighters who described being misled by brokers in their home countries, only to be told upon arrival that they had effectively been sold to the Russian military. “The most important similarity is the architecture of recruitment itself,” Pokalchuk said. “A person is offered legitimate, usually well-paid employment abroad; their economic vulnerability is exploited; travel, visas or tickets may be arranged or facilitated; and after arrival, the actual conditions are radically different from what was promised.” She said job offers were circulated through social media, recruitment agencies, brokers and personal networks. Monthly salaries for foreign fighters ranged from around 180,000 to 320,600 roubles (US$2,136 to US$3,805), with one-off signing bonuses of between 200,000 and 1.9 million roubles, Pokalchuk said – sums that might have drawn victims in before they understood the nature of the “work” on offer. In addition to confiscating passports, recruiters take away foreign fighters’ mobile phones, cutting them off from their families. Beatings and imprisonment for perceived disobedience have also been reported. Call for state intervention After minimal training, recruits were dispatched straight to the front line, Pokalchuk said. “Twenty-eight people we interviewed had participated in assaults on Ukrainian positions – operations often referred to as ‘meat assaults’, with drones attacking them very intensely and dead bodies lying all around,” she said. “John Patrick” reportedly received just a week of basic training before being sent to the battlefield, where he was repeatedly used to draw fire from Ukrainian forces. While some foreigners joined the Russian military voluntarily, Pokalchuk said many others were deceived and typically escaped only by surrendering to or being captured by Ukrainian forces. Analysts say brokers working with Moscow play a central role in funnelling unwitting victims into the war, and are urging governments worldwide to do more to stem the flow. “In some cases, brokers routed men through Saudi Arabia and the UAE using religious or tourist visas and other established migration channels, with Russia ultimately becoming the destination and the Russian military the actual employer,” Pokalchuk said. She praised the government of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for bringing home hundreds of Indian victims and securing their release from the war, and said other affected states should follow suit. Ranito, meanwhile, urged governments to ramp up public education campaigns warning citizens of the dangers posed by illegal recruitment networks. “States have a responsibility to identify these networks and to make explicit in their regulatory framework provisions that criminalise recruitment networks and enable them to be held accountable in court,” she said.

title: Style Edit: Le Damier de Louis Vuitton’s 8 new pieces reimagine the checkerboard design
description: The Parisian maison expands its range of fine jewellery with a pendant, earrings and bracelets drawing on one of its most famous signatures.
content: The visual symbols of the grand maison of Louis Vuitton are some of the most recognisable icons in the world, from the LV logo to the four-petalled flowers with which it’s so often interspersed. But perhaps the motif most instantly associated with the legendary Parisian brand is the classic pattern of checks that has adorned its creations since 1888, when it was created as a marker of authenticity. Known as the Damier pattern, after the French word for “checkerboard”, it’s most commonly found on Louis Vuitton’s bags and on the trunks with which the house first made its name. Two years ago, fine jewellery was added to that list, in the form of the Le Damier de Louis Vuitton collection. Originally an assembly of a dozen stunning pieces, including rings, earrings and bracelets, it reimagined the pattern on a canvas of diamonds and gold, reinventing the checkerboard as a series of geometric displays of stones, offset by their precious metal backdrop, with the round diamonds handset in slightly oblique squares. Now, eight more pieces have been added to the collection: five pairs of earrings, two bracelets and a pendant. Together, they tease out more of the unmistakable Le Damier DNA while taking the collection in several bold new directions. Three of those pairs of earrings are supersized hoops, complementing the small hoops already available in the collection. In yellow, white or rose gold, they’re dripping with Le Damier de Louis Vuitton’s signature geometrically arranged diamonds: 96 in all, together weighing in at 1.34 carats. Adding a new dimension to the collection, they’re joined by two new pairs of ear cuffs, available in rose or yellow gold. These are complemented by a showstopping pendant necklace, its sinuous yellow gold chain mounted with a trademark two-row gold and diamond centrepiece. With its adjustable, sliding design, it can be worn at any number of lengths. A similar supple aesthetic extends to the chain bracelet in the collection, also in yellow gold and prominently showing off the same shimmering gold and diamond centrepiece. But for attention-grabbing charisma, the star of the show is the collection’s new cuff bracelet. This statement-making yellow gold sparkler, which measures 9mm wide, comes festooned with 120 diamonds, arranged in four rows and weighing in at 2.8 carats.

title: Style Edit: Masterpiece by King Fook showcases daring Cyrus timepieces
description: Crafted by Jean-François Mojon, the new models include a pale-blue iteration of the Klepcys Dice, the world’s first double independent chronograph.
content: A series of timepieces from Cyrus, available in Hong Kong at Masterpiece by King Fook, highlight this most original of Swiss luxury watchmakers’ spirit of boundary-pushing creativity and daring individuality. Founded in 2010, the independent manufacture handcrafts its watches in small runs, infusing every one with a distinctive character. That Cyrus’ watches break away from the herd with aesthetically and mechanically distinctive designs comes as no surprise when you learn that they’re the work of the legendary Jean-François Mojon, the founder of movement manufacturer Chronode. The hidden genius working silently behind the scenes to create the beating hearts of watches for many major brands, Mojon is a specialist in highly creative movements that forge new realms of horological possibility. It’s a level of expertise that’s comprehensively demonstrated in the Cyrus Dominion GMT. The star of the show here is undoubtedly the dazzling openworked dial, lit up by a dramatic upper bridge in the shape of a palm tree to create a starburst of thrusting lines, like a fairy-tale castle on a faraway planet. Above that bridge appears the retrograde dual-time function, offering supreme legibility: the local time is indicated by large open-worked black hands that point to Arabic numerals on a transparent disc, while the second time zone is indicated by a retrograde hand with a triangular tip on a matte opaline grey arc featuring alternating Arabic numerals and dots. There’s also a small seconds display at 6 o’clock, equipped with an innovative, propeller-shaped hand. The Dominion GMT comes in a round, 42mm case accessorised with sweeping curved lugs and a double crown. It’s available in gold and titanium versions, limited to 25 and 28 pieces respectively. It’s joined among Cyrus’ stand-out offerings by the Etheral Twin Orbital Tourbillon, with its extraordinary 3D moving dial, on which a jumping hours display, the minute indication and two flying tourbillons change position over time. The product of over six years of work, the Etheral Twin Orbital Tourbillon features a new hand-wound manufacture calibre CYR518-E – a movement that boasts three patents – and comes in a limited edition of 18 pieces. Lovers of horological maximalism, meanwhile, will flock to the Klepcys Dice Glacial Blue, a new pale-blue iteration of the world’s first double independent chronograph, first unveiled in 2021. Its 30-minute counter at 3 o’clock is balanced by a small seconds subdial at 9 o’clock.

title: Style Edit: How Chanel jackets evolved from Gabrielle Chanel to Matthieu Blazy
description: Reinterpreted across eras, the French maison’s signature jackets remain enduring staples designed for a life in motion.
content: A Chanel jacket is often recognised before the eye has registered much else: the neat, graphic outline; the textured cloth; the trim defining its edges. Yet its staying power has less to do with instant recognition than with a quality that still feels remarkably current – clothes that look poised while allowing their wearer to move freely. Gabrielle Chanel began developing that idea in the 1920s, when she decided to work with tweed, then a fabric associated almost exclusively with menswear. Drawn to textiles that offered softness and comfort, she transformed tweed into one of her signatures, making the fabric lighter and more supple. The resulting tweed suit, and particularly its jacket, challenged prevailing ideas of restrictive womenswear with a new kind of casual elegance: structured, yes, but made to be lived in. The apparent simplicity of a straight-cut Chanel jacket conceals a highly exacting construction. At Chanel’s Tailleur ateliers on Paris’ Rue Cambon, the front is mounted on the straight grain and made without bust darts, a decision that preserves the garment’s shape while increasing suppleness. The back is divided only by a central seam, while the sleeve sits high at the shoulder to optimise ease of movement. The inside is as carefully made as the exterior. The lining is divided into the same number of panels as the outer fabric, allowing the two to move together. A brass chain is sewn into the lining’s hem to give the jacket its precise fall. Braid traces the contours of the pockets, cuffs and edges, lending definition to the silhouette, while buttons – in galalith, resin or metal – can take the form of lion heads, sheaves of wheat, camellias or the double C motif. They function not only as fastenings but as miniature adornments. Karl Lagerfeld gave the jacket fresh relevance after becoming head of the house in 1983. He altered its proportions, length, volume and shoulders from collection to collection, and enlisted the house’s métiers d’art in new interpretations through Lesage-woven tweeds, elaborate braids and jewelled buttons. His 1985 pairing of a Chanel jacket with jeans and a striped top remains a useful lesson in the garment’s adaptability: formality loosened by an uncomplicated styling choice. Virginie Viard, too, drew on Gabrielle Chanel’s stylistic language to reinterpret the jacket with a gentler modernity. Under the creative direction of Matthieu Blazy, who succeeded Viard in late 2024, the garment continues to evolve as a wardrobe essential. In the fall/winter 2026 show, the jackets and suiting are given what the house describes as exceptional lightness and mobility in ribbed knits, classic tweeds and new fabrics. A playful mix of silhouettes, and colours ranging from natural to iridescent, bring a fresh sense of energy. The jacket – at once precise in construction and designed for ease of wear – is, of course, a natural expression of that vitality. It is a piece of precision designed not to constrain its wearer, but to accompany her: practical, poised and always in motion.

title: Opinion | How the 5-year plan can serve the nation and deliver for Hong Kong
description: The city’s new development road map mirrors national priorities, leveraging deeper integration to drive national progress while securing local livelihoods.
content: This year marks the opening year of the national 15th five-year plan. Faced with accelerating change globally and significant opportunities brought by national development, Hong Kong must better integrate into and serve the overall national development, enabling our economic progress to reach new heights while enhancing people’s livelihood and well-being. This February, I announced that the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government would formulate the city’s first five-year plan. I led the compilation work, with the Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs taking primary responsibility for implementation, and all principal officials and heads of departments participating. Producing Hong Kong’s first five-year plan carried significant responsibilities, including meeting Hong Kong people’s earnest expectations for the city’s long-term development. The five-year plan, with all its demanding tasks, was devised under an exceptionally tight schedule. It often takes mainland cities one to two years of preliminary research and discussion to construct their five-year plans. We had less than a year to complete Hong Kong’s first five-year plan from scratch. I am grateful to all policy bureaus and departments, and the individuals involved, for their outstanding efforts under pressure – a breakthrough in the Hong Kong government’s public governance capabilities. My team and I began by reviewing the five-year plan experiences of Macau and mainland cities. Officials from the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau visited mainland cities to learn from their experience. In April, I introduced a research and public-opinion gathering channel between the government and the Legislative Council. My thanks to all Legco members for organising multiple opinion-collection sessions based on professional and sectoral divisions, and for submitting research reports covering six major areas to the government. Working together, the executive and the legislature allowed the government to race against time while ensuring that the plan was representative and its scientific foundations remained solid. In June, the Hong Kong government published the consultation document, launching a two-month public consultation on the five-year plan. During this period, the government held over 100 consultation sessions. I personally hosted more than 30. I also visited communities to listen to Hong Kong people’s opinions on their city’s future development. Among the more than 17,000 submissions we received, 80 per cent came from individuals. Given the public’s overwhelming response, my government used artificial intelligence to assist with opinion analysis. The voice of the public is clear. Hong Kong people support creating the five-year plan and reinforcing our traditional advantages, including our international financial, trade and maritime centres and our aviation hub. They want the government to build an international innovation and technology centre, accelerate the Northern Metropolis’ development and boost their livelihood and well-being. I am firmly convinced that the plan, and its vision for economic and social development, will safeguard and improve people’s livelihoods A member of the public asked me: “The five-year plan talks about major economic issues. What does that have to do with ordinary citizens like us?” My answer then, as now, is direct: I want the people of Hong Kong – every one of you – to share in the dividends of development, and feel a sense of happiness and fulfilment. And I am firmly convinced that the plan, and its vision for economic and social development, will do just that – safeguard and improve people’s livelihoods. The plan’s proposals – boosting Hong Kong’s traditional advantages, developing emerging and future industries, accelerating the rise of the Northern Metropolis, deepening the Greater Bay Area’s development and building global cooperation – focus on the economy, but their ultimate goal is to enable Hong Kong people to flourish. With better employment opportunities and more upward mobility for our youth, that can become a tangible reality, turning governance from measures into results. I have also been asked whether formulating a five-year plan would change Hong Kong’s original system. The answer is no. The plan will uphold Hong Kong’s rule of law and capitalist system, implement the Basic Law and adhere to “one country, two systems” without distorting Hong Kong. It will also uphold its status as an international city, ensure the free flow of capital, people, goods and information, while giving full play to the flexibility and advantages of the capitalist market. As President Xi Jinping has pointed out on multiple occasions, one country, two systems is a good framework that must be adhered to over the long term. I will release Hong Kong’s first five-year plan on September 16, followed immediately by the publication of the 2026 policy address. This is designed to allow the public to read both documents together, giving people a better understanding of the close interconnection between the two. The five-year plan maps out the long-term blueprint and strategic direction for Hong Kong’s development, while the policy address serves as an annual report – the focus of that year’s governance in implementing the five-year plan. In the coming years, the annual policy addresses will continue to implement the blueprint, introducing policies and setting measures according to changing circumstances and economic dynamics. The five-year plan is a vastly ambitious initiative accomplished through collective planning, the participation of all sectors and the building of social consensus – a formidable task saddled with responsibility and far-reaching significance. As for the result, I am encouraged and confident, and look forward to the comments of the people of Hong Kong. With the strong support of our country, Hong Kong is on its way to opening a bold new chapter in its journey from stability to prosperity.

title: China grandma drains life savings on US$450,000 beauty fraud before daughter discovers it
description: Salon charged 10 to 20 times the market rate; a single multi-procedure lip tattooing session cost a staggering US$6,000.
content: A 75-year-old woman from Shanghai spent three million yuan (US$450,000) on beauty treatments in a salon, completely depleting her retirement savings before her daughter uncovered the situation. The elderly woman’s daughter recently sought assistance from a Shanghai television programme after discovering that her mother had exhausted all her savings on beauty services. The woman, surnamed Yu, had spent her savings at a branch of Yongqi Beauty and Hairdressing Company, as well as a medical beauty institution associated with Yongqi, dating back to 2016. Yu revealed that the beauty treatments she bought included skin tightening procedures, thread lifting, and meridian massage. Billing details obtained by Yu’s daughter from the two establishments indicated that Yu also underwent eyebrow and lip tattooing procedures at the salon. What raised concerns was the fact that the charges for these services were 10 to 20 times higher than the market rates. For example, a multi-procedure lip tattooing session was priced at 39,800 yuan (US$6,000). The bill also indicated that Yu had repeated the same procedure multiple times, which in the case of tattooing, is unnecessary. Yu stated that she did not pay attention to the costs because she believed she was affluent. The savings she had stemmed from the sale of her home. By the time her daughter discovered the situation, she could no longer afford rent for a flat and had to sell her jewellery. Staff at the Yongqi store had referred her to a medical beauty clinic named Rouyi, which charged her 300,000 yuan (US$45,000) for an “intimate care” procedure. Although Yu paid, she did not undergo the procedure, which the clinic later substituted with other skincare treatments. Rouyi’s invoices included items such as “happiness chair” and “space capsule,” which Yu could not explain. The SCMP attempted to contact Rouyi for comment, but the numbers listed on Rouyi’s invoices were non-functional. Yu’s daughter discovered that the clinic had billed Yu through Yongqi’s account. A Yongqi staff member insisted that it was Yu who requested the frequent procedures due to her “appearance anxiety.” They also claimed that all prices were clearly marked, and by making payments, Yu accepted their pricing. The store issued a partial refund of Yu’s advance payment as a compromise. The SCMP also reached out to the store’s management for further comments, but they stated that the case was resolved and declined to provide additional details. Yu did not pursue legal action. The Yongqi store continues to operate without any signs of official investigation or suspension. While the store used “clearly marked prices” as a defence, China’s Provisions on Clear Price Marketing and Prohibition of Price Fraud also mandate that business operators uphold principles of transparency, fairness, and honesty. “Elderly individuals have the same right to pursue beauty, but their desires should not be exploited by unscrupulous businesses,” one observer remarked. Another added: “Beauty shops rely on customers’ additional spending to survive. It’s crucial to be wary of their tactics.”

title: Embrace your uniqueness: why being original is your greatest strength
description: From fingerprints to personality, celebrate what makes you special and be confident in your individuality and shine.
content:
When you look at your fingertips, do you see all those tiny swirls and loops?
No one else on the entire planet has fingerprints exactly like yours – not your best friend, not your teacher, not even a single person in a crowd of billions. You are an original.
And it’s not just your fingerprints; many other aspects of your character and personality are completely unique.
Did you know that even identical twins, who look so similar, are not exactly the same?
They have different personalities, different laughs and different things that scare or excite them. They are like two copies of the same book, but with different stories written inside.
Your uniqueness is everywhere. It is present in your appearance – your smile, your freckles and the way your eyes sparkle when you’re happy.
You can see it in the things you like – maybe you love exploring dinosaur facts, painting picturesque sunsets or playing football. It is also in the things you excel at – maybe you’re a fantastic listener, a speedy runner or a brilliant puzzle-solver.
But there’s something even more special inside you: your character strengths. Are you brave, kind, funny or patient? That’s your inner superpower, and no one else has your exact mix of talents and heart.
Sometimes, we look at others and wish we could be like them; we might even try to mimic their style or latch onto the way they talk. But here is a secret to remember: an original is always worth more than a copy.
Striving to improve and finding inspiration in people you admire can help you grow. But make sure you don’t hide the amazing person you already are. When you celebrate what makes you different, something magical happens: you feel truly confident – not the loud kind of confidence, but the quiet kind that says, “I am enough, just as I am.”
So explore your hobbies, practise your strengths and be proud of your quirks . The world doesn’t need another copy.

title: Pupils use colours to identify and express emotions at this award-winning Hong Kong school
description: ICHK Hong Lok Yuen (Kindergarten & Primary) was one of two schools to win for Hong Kong at the AIA Healthiest Schools Competition.
content:
When pupils in one primary school in Hong Kong’s Tai Po district struggle with their emotions, they use colours to express themselves.
At ICHK Hong Lok Yuen (Kindergarten & Primary), the children were taught to use blue to point to sadness or tiredness. Green is for focus. Yellow is for worry. And red is for feeling out of control.
After identifying their emotions, pupils learn how to regulate them.
For example, a student might tell a teacher: “I think I’m in the yellow zone now. Could I have some time outside?”
This system was inspired by the “Zones of Regulation”. Principal Derek Pinchbeck said it gave students “a common language they can use to share their emotions”.
“To really self-use and internalise [the ‘zones’] is difficult for some ... [but] the general language is something that is easy ... to comprehend,” he said.
The primary school was honoured in July when it became one of the city’s champions in the AIA Healthiest Schools Competition. The two winning Hong Kong schools each received US$50,000 (HK$392,000) to support their well-being programmes.
The AIA Healthiest Schools Competition is open to primary and secondary schools across the Asia-Pacific region. It encourages physical health, mental well-being and sustainability. This includes healthy eating, active lifestyles and mental health awareness.
Hong Kong True Light College took the top spot in the Hong Kong secondary school category.
Both of the winning Hong Kong schools advanced to the final event in Thailand, where they had the chance to win US$100,000.
Indonesia’s SMP IL Kapten Fatubaa was crowned the winner for its “Huka Upcycling Project”. In it, students learned to turn banana peel waste into ice cream and fertiliser.
Secondary school Hong Kong True Light College won for its “Embrace Health, Empower Your Mind” programme.
Principal Tammy Law Chor-wan called it a “whole school approach ... [combining] mental health education, regular physical activities and student-led campaigns”.
The key was ensuring that every student found a programme they wanted to join.
The school aimed to create something for everyone, from student-teacher competitions and inter-class sports to cooking classes and latte art workshops.
“For dancing, we have traditional Chinese dance, but we also have K-pop dance. For singing, we have the choir, a cappella and pop singing,” Law said.
The school said the programme led to an overall increase in students’ mental health scores on an Education Bureau questionnaire.
Law said the grant would fund student short films about interpersonal relationships and healthy living.

title: Beijing’s ‘trust issue’ with Hong Kong and what the city can promise in its 5-year plan
description: Hong Kong’s openness is both a strength and a weakness, so it must build robust security frameworks to reap rewards of national development, experts say.
content: In the final instalment of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Natalie Wong and Matthew Cheng look at how national security spans areas such as finance and technology and what Hong Kong must do to earn Beijing’s trust. Read part one here, part two here, part three here and part four here. With the recent sentencing of former leaders of Hong Kong’s Tiananmen Square vigil concluding a key high-profile subversion case, it would be easy to assume the city’s national security agenda has been largely settled. Now would be the time to focus entirely on economic growth and downplay national security, some experts have argued, warning the issue could deter potential investors. But that would be an erroneous and narrow understanding of national security, overlooking how inextricably it is tied to economic development, other insiders familiar with the government’s thinking have said. Indeed, in the coming inaugural five-year plan Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu will announce on Wednesday, a full chapter will be dedicated to national security, the South China Morning Post has learned. The emphasis will be another clear rebuttal to detractors on why national security extends well beyond law enforcement or combating “soft resistance” efforts, and is the framework that ensures economic development can enhance value rather than expose vulnerabilities for the country. Authorities are expected to lay institutional safeguards across key areas – most notably finance and technology among China’s 11 critical domains – to shield Hong Kong in its path to better support the country’s growth and its navigation of geopolitical risks. For the Hong Kong government, strengthening safety nets in these domains in the next five years is seen as a prerequisite for the international financial centre to consolidate its position and develop further into a global innovation hub. Observers said success would hinge on how the coming blueprint, complemented by the policy address, could leverage Hong Kong’s strengths to effectively and safely align with the nation’s five-year goals of achieving technological self-reliance and pushing for renminbi internationalisation. They said gaining Beijing’s trust through robust security frameworks could open “new doors” for Hong Kong to pilot new services and frameworks as mainland China further opened up its economy. Finance: safeguarding yuan internationalisation With Hong Kong’s first government-coordinated blueprint, the city is on a steep learning curve to reorient its mindset: shifting from only serving local economic interests to also serving the country’s priorities amid geopolitical tensions. One key arena in superpower rivalry is China’s push to internationalise its currency within a global financial structure dominated by the US dollar. Hong Kong has played a vital role by offering offshore renminbi liquidity support and building a fixed income ecosystem. Finance sector lawmaker Ronick Chan Chun-ying, an adviser to Bank of China (Hong Kong), said that the initiative might prompt Washington to pressure belt and road, Asean and Middle Eastern economies to disrupt yuan flows outside China, so Hong Kong should act decisively to mitigate risks. While mainland renminbi investment in Hong Kong has been largely confined to designated channels such as the Stock Connect programme and Wealth Management Connect scheme, Chan urged the city to accelerate the diversification of offshore renminbi products and fast track the introduction of derivatives to attract global capital. He added that effectively clamping down on illegal investment channels and money laundering would be crucial to galvanising Beijing’s confidence for the expansion of schemes and creating more new financial products. “It is very important for us to demonstrate to Beijing that the growing market is well-regulated, rather than a channel for mainland residents or enterprises to move capital offshore,” he said. After mainland regulators imposed fines totalling more than US$330 million on three brokerage firms – Tiger Brokers, Futu Securities International and Longbridge Securities – to curb unauthorised offshore stock trading, Hong Kong authorities have worked to strengthen oversight. In May, the Securities and Futures Commission required brokerages to conduct internal checks to validate documents used to open accounts. The following month, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority told banks to require mainland customers opening accounts to declare that their funds originated outside mainland China. Chan also warned that emerging products, such as asset tokenisation and stablecoins, that rested on blockchain technology, could present security vulnerabilities. “If we fail to [strengthen the safeguards for the financial infrastructure behind trading systems], when quantum computing and technologies mature, they could break our traditional financial encryption systems, and that would expose us to very high risks,” he said. Technology: cross-border data flow security Beijing’s strategy for technological self-reliance – which top officials regard as an existential national security matter – is to take ownership in every layer of the country’s tech stack. To support this, tech entrepreneur-turned-lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong argued that Hong Kong should better leverage the technology park at the Lok Ma Chau Loop to pioneer secure and controllable cross-border data channels with high-level safeguards, allowing mainland data to circulate within the city with proper limitations. “We need to give the central government strong confidence that Hong Kong will not become a loophole,” Ng said. “We need to have a well-established platform where the data is stored securely, and it will not be leaked under uncontrollable circumstances.” He said a successful trial in the loop, which officially opened in December last year, could pave the way for cross-border data flows in other key schemes under the Northern Metropolis megaproject, such as the San Tin Technopole. On local critical infrastructure, Ng warned that some key transport and energy networks remained reliant on technology from countries hostile to the mainland – a weak link requiring attention. He said a more diversified sourcing strategy was needed to reduce security risks. “Sourcing from other places does not have to be limited to the mainland; it could be from relatively friendly European countries, belt and road countries, and even local suppliers can be considered,” he said. Biosecurity: safeguarding samples The government is also looking into measures to allow seamless cross-border flow of materials, including biological samples, within the Hetao Shenzhen-Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone. Henry Yau Kwong-chi, managing director of the University of Hong Kong’s clinical trials centre, said that national security was among the country’s top concerns, including whether DNA data from Chinese people would be leaked. Foreign pharmaceutical firms, for example, could make use of that DNA data to develop medicines that were more effective in treating Chinese people’s genome-related diseases, and then patent those treatments, he said. “China could then lose the patent, and become subject to foreign countries and have to purchase drugs from them.” A potentially more serious threat, Yau said, was that unfriendly foreign countries could develop viruses that only infected Chinese people. “How can we properly monitor those samples so they do not end up in places or in the hands of people who should not be there,” Yau said. He said a mechanism should be put in place to properly monitor the flow of such bio-samples once they left the mainland, including setting up a facility to store them, and deciding who should supervise the samples and handle problems when they arose. National security: building trust With the coming dual blueprints, Lee’s administration is expected to align immediate actions and long-term strategies across various policy areas, so Hong Kong builds momentum to achieve a higher level of growth. National security runs through all of Beijing’s developmental goals, with authorities convinced that an insecure nation cannot focus on economic success and the well-being of its citizens. Beijing had a “trust issue” with Hong Kong because the city, as an open economy, could not insulate itself from geopolitical tensions, and its openness was both an advantage and a potential weak link that hostile forces could exploit, said Wilson Chan Wai-shun, co-founder of the Pagoda Institute think tank. It was therefore important for Hong Kong authorities to assure Beijing that the city was fortified against security risks. “When [the mainland] further opens up, will it continue to place that new door in Hong Kong, or does it want to try other pilot locations, such as Shanghai? This is something Hong Kong must fight for,” Chan said. He said the city’s task was to establish frameworks that both Beijing and the West could trust, operating within Beijing’s national security principles while adopting rules that the West was willing to comply with. Citing the Hong Kong-based International Organisation for Mediation as a model case, Chan said: “How can we develop a language that the West understands and that can be a bridge to them, while at the same time serving as a set of operational principles acceptable to Beijing? “This applies whether in finance, data or other strategic areas, and this is Hong Kong’s role today.” Additional reporting by Elizabeth Cheung

title: A chef is learning from restaurants across Hong Kong
description: Mel Ng shares her journey to culinary school and gives advice for aspiring chefs.
content:
In the morning, Mel Ng rolled out dumpling wrappers and mixed the next day’s fillings before surviving the lunch rush at Ah Chun Shandong Dumpling.
The restaurant has been in Hong Kong for about 30 years. Ng was spending the day learning everything she could from their kitchen. This is called “staging”, when a cook takes a temporary unpaid shift in a restaurant to learn its techniques .
Ng, who comes from a background in French cuisine, has staged at more than 20 restaurants since last year.
“They’ve all been very interesting to me because I’ve tried out many different kitchens, like Indian cuisine [and] Japanese ... things that I never would have tried before,” said the 36-year-old, who also works as a consultant in the food and beverage industry.
“But I think the ones that I enjoy the most are the ones that are related more to Hong Kong local heritage, just because these are the things I grew up eating.”
Ng calls herself a “culinary wanderer”. Having staged in restaurants across Asia, she considers traditional Chinese cuisine her toughest challenge mainly because these cooks rely on feeling, rather than written recipes.
“A lot of the techniques were ... new to me. Working in a Cantonese kitchen meant using a wok, which I’d never done before,” she said. “But I always step into the kitchen with an open mind.”
Why is it important to “wander” as a cook?
“Experience is the best teacher. And chefs will respect your work ethic more than whatever diploma you hold,” Ng explained.
Ng grew up in Hong Kong before studying business at Northeastern University in the United States. After trying jobs in finance, accounting and insurance, she realised these industries were not exciting to her, and she wanted to find another path.
“In college, I started cooking a lot for my roommate [and] for my friends,” she said.
These casual meals eventually transformed into a dream to become a chef, and she started culinary school at the International Culinary Centre in New York.
The programme had six levels. By level three, students experienced what it is like to repeatedly cook the same dish in a restaurant.
“That’s when things started getting a bit more tough physically,” she said. Ng added that she had to pass written and practical exams to move to the next level.
While Ng took the traditional route of culinary school, she encouraged aspiring chefs to learn on the ground.
“There are a lot of new techniques that you can learn from actual kitchen experience,” she said.
For many older Hong Kong eateries, Ng noticed that they struggled to find staff, and it was even harder to find young people who want to learn the craft .
“Since Covid, we’ve seen a lot of restaurant closures. Even heritage brands that have been around for 20 [or] 30 years closed down,” she said.
While staging in different restaurants, she uses her business skills to help struggling eateries survive. She also posts videos of her staging on Instagram to show Hong Kong’s rich culinary tradition to more people.
No matter what she is doing, Ng’s daily mindset is focused on “mise en place”, a French term meaning “everything in its place”.
“In the kitchen, it means having all your ingredients and tools ready before you start,” she said. “Whether I’m doing consulting work for a client or working a shift in the kitchen, I always have a plan in my head, thinking about the end goal and mapping out every step to get there.”
