title: Letters from readers about favourite school subjects, hobbies and a trip to the Big Buddha
description: This week, students share the classes they enjoy, what they do in their free time and write about a visit to Lantau Island.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
My favourite subjects are physical education (PE) and English.
In PE, we play dodgeball and pickleball, which are very exciting games. I also like English lessons because my teacher is good and kind. She lets us play the spinning wheel game and Kahoot! quizzes. We really enjoy learning English through these games.
My hobby is lacrosse. I have joined competitions. My other hobby is playing the saxophone because I like its sound and performing with my classmates.
My favourite animals are my two cute cats, Whisky and Soda. They always play hide-and-seek at home. It is very funny.
My family likes playing board games after dinner and going to the park on holidays. In summer, we go to the beach. I love them.
My best friends are Nason and Pui-yu. We always play together, and they always help me when I have problems.
My favourite subject in school is writing. It’s useful because weaving stories with words brings people joy.
My favourite animal is a dolphin, and my favourite memory about it is watching them dive at Ocean Park when I was three years old.
If I could change something about Hong Kong, it would be the language, because I don’t understand Cantonese.
I enjoy reading poetry and books because each story is unique. I especially like rhyming poems and series because if I like them, I can read on until the end.
I also specifically like poems about the unfairness of ancient times and poems about nature.
I recently went to the Big Buddha with my cousins. I was a bit frustrated because we had to queue up for a very long time to get on the cable car.
The cable car gave us a very beautiful view. The floor was made of glass. I felt like I was flying when I lay on top of it.
When we were far away, the Buddha seemed small, like a toy, but close up it was colossal.
When we arrived, we had to walk a long way. On the way, we did a challenge where we had to stamp all the stamp spots in the book we got at the cable car station. If you collected all the stamps, you could have a go at the claw machine.
We had to walk 200 steps to reach the Big Buddha. But surprisingly, it was much easier than I thought.
Inside, I learned a lot of interesting things about Buddhism. After that, I ate scrumptious tofu pudding. I also saw a dog eating fried bones.

title: Advice: How can I ask to join a group project if I am too shy to speak?
description: On this page, you’ll find advice from our team of psychologists to help you through all the ups and downs of life.
content:
It’s great that you still want to join others on group projects even though you feel shy. This shows that you’re looking for chances to step out of your comfort zone!
When you’re feeling too nervous to ask, this might be your brain trying to protect you from rejection. Afterwards, the embarrassment might make you feel even more nervous next time. However, these are completely normal reactions to have when you’re feeling shy. Here are some tips.
You can start with tiny steps. Try giving a small compliment like, “I really like your presentation!” or “Your idea in class was great.” These are easier to say and often make the other person smile. It could even spark a conversation.
Stand in front of a mirror and say, “Hi, can I join your group for the project?” a few times. The more you rehearse, the easier it becomes in real life.
Do a few rounds of breathing exercises before or after the nervous moment. Breathe in slowly for four seconds, hold it for four and breathe out for another four. This exercise tells your body, “I’m OK; everything is OK. I just want to do this one thing. I can relax now.”
Most importantly, be kind to yourself. Even if a conversation does not go perfectly, you’re growing braver by trying.
This question was answered by James Pho, a counsellor at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: Fiji stars full of fire, Hong Kong leave it late, as ‘sisters’ put on WXV Global show
description: City team beat Brazil at the death while Fiji score comeback win over Spain as the WXV Global Series Challenger gets under way at Kai Tak.
content: It was watching Fiji shock South Africa in a 2021 Women’s World Cup pool match that steeled the 18-year-old Alfreda Fisher’s determination to play international rugby. Or more accurately, it was hearing her father telling his sons at full time that one day he would watch them on the global stage that really got Fisher ticking. “Yeah, that’s when I thought I’m going to play for Fiji,” Fisher said, at Kai Tak Youth Sports Ground after her team’s rousing 38-32 WXV Global Series Challenger victory over Spain on Sunday. “I thought, ‘women are strong and we can play rugby, too’. I knew then that he’d be watching me.” The six-team tournament has been introduced this year, alongside an elite WXV Global Series, as World Rugby seeks to “accelerate the growth of the women’s game”. And its masterminds could not have asked for a more compelling start. Hong Kong followed the Fiji drama with a grandstand finish of their own, being awarded a penalty try in the last play of the game to beat Brazil 29-24. It was the first time they had led. “There were 23 sisters right there, showing that if we work together, we can do a lot of cool things,” Lara Schats, the co-captain and player-of-the-match, said. It was decided to stage the competition over three weeks in a central location to minimise individual unions’ expenses, with the global governing body footing a large slice of operating costs. The next edition in 2028 will provide one ticket to the following year’s World Cup. With Fisher as captain, Fiji competed in a second straight World Cup last year and beat Wales, the team they have just dislodged from 12th spot in the global rankings. Fiji coach Mike Legge said the 22-year-old had been named skipper in England because of her “follow-me mentality”. Raised in the small village of Togo, where girls playing rugby was frowned upon and she had to sneak off for games of touch rugby next to the sea with the boys, Fisher is back in the ranks in Hong Kong for a trio of “massive” matches. “Most of these teams don’t have many opportunities to play tournaments like this one and it’s vital that we get game time,” Legge said. “It’s a big part of the journey we’re on to try to qualify for the World Cup. “It’s the same for Spain; we need these opportunities to develop in high-pressure situations, so we can push the bigger nations when we face them.” The smattering of fans inside the ground in time for Fiji’s fightback against a team ranked two places below them were treated to a battle of contrasting styles. The athletic and expansive Fijians hit the front with three minutes remaining when 20-year-old Adi Salote Nailolo skipped past a weak tackle and ran clear to score. With Spain tiring against physical opponents, and losing their “discipline and decision-making capacity”, Repeka Adi Tove went over for Fiji’s sixth try. Casting aside his disappointment, head coach Regis Sonnes said it was essential for his side to play against the likes of Fiji, Samoa and Brazil “so we can push our limits and see where we are”. A larger and noisier audience saw Tanya Dhar and Lee Ka-shun both score a pair of tries to keep Hong Kong in touch with Brazil, before the penalty-try drama allowed the hosts to recover from 24-22 down at the last. “Seeing such a big crowd was incredible, and we don’t take it for granted,” Schats, whose team next face Fiji on Saturday, said. “We’re making sure we go 100 per cent and leave [Hong Kong rugby] in a better place for when these young ones [watching] come and take it off our hands. “We want to create a better path for them, so by the time they get here, we have a full-time set-up, and we can become one of the better teams in the world.” In the last game of a triple-header, the Netherlands put Samoa to the sword in a 70-0 thrashing. Frenchman Sonnes had coached male teams in France and Ireland, including Toulouse, Union Bordeaux Begles and Brandon RFC, and the Spanish men’s national side, before he accepted his current post in November last year. “It’s a new experience, and exciting for me to look for solutions and to grow as a person,” he said. “Coaching women, it’s more social; you have to create a great atmosphere. I love their passion, they send me a lot of positive energy.” Five of the six challenger teams are coached by men – illustrative, perhaps, of the relative youth of the women’s game. Patricia Garcia Rodriguez, the Spain women’s sevens head coach, is Sonnes’ deputy. “My second job is to prepare her to be next,” Sonnes said. “I am trying to give her some information, and she’s here for it.” While Legge led a Fijiana Drua team to the grand final of this season’s Super Rugby Women, where they lost to New South Wales Waratahs, Sonnes said that the Spanish players were competing in a league that “is not the best championship in Europe”. “They don’t play many high-level games, so when they’re under pressure physically, sometimes their collective decision-making is wrong. “That’s why we wanted games like these: to travel together and to touch the best. It will show the girls how to train, and what they need physically and technically.” Pleased with Fiji’s “mental resilience and ability to pull through”, Legge said that successive World Cup qualifications had begun to change perceptions of women’s rugby in the country. “We still have certain pockets who think the women don’t belong, but that’s rapidly changing,” Legge said. “Four or five years ago, the Fijian rugby public thought it was a joke, pretty much. There’s been a massive turn, and the country is behind us.” Still, Legge acknowledged that it would take “a bit of work” for women’s rugby to obtain parity with its male counterpart. For Fisher, who combines playing for the world’s 12th best team with working as an ordinary seawoman in the Republic of Fiji Navy, the ultimate goal is for women’s teams to be “talked about like the Springboks and the All Blacks”.

title: China’s intelligence chief warns of risks from AI as ‘new arena for strategic rivalry’
description: State data, business secrets and personal privacy are at stake, State Security Minister Chen Yixin warns as he calls for stronger safeguards.
content: China’s top intelligence official has warned of rising national security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI), calling for robust risk prevention frameworks and stronger global governance of the emerging technology. The call from Chen Yixin, China’s state security minister, comes as Beijing seeks to play a leading role in global AI governance while criticising US restrictions. At the Brics summit in India over the weekend, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed an AI-powered initiative to drive new industrialisation and deepen supply chain cooperation in the emerging economies bloc. Chen underscored Beijing’s view of the technology as a key geopolitical battleground. AI has become “a new arena for strategic rivalry among major powers”, he wrote for China Cyberspace, a journal run by internet watchdog body the Cyberspace Administration of China. The article was published on the journal’s social media account on Sunday. Chen called for maintaining security boundaries while seizing new opportunities as he highlighted the risks of AI development. AI could have a systemic impact on ideological security, he warned, including being “leveraged by hostile forces” to generate rumours and mass-produce harmful information. The technology also posed serious risks to critical information infrastructure, Chen warned, arguing that advances marked by next-generation US-led models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could significantly lower the technical threshold and costs of executing cyberattacks. “Foreign intelligence agencies are heavily exploiting smart web crawlers, data mining and profiling technologies to harvest sensitive information, including critical state data, business secrets, and personal information,” he wrote. Chen also cautioned about widespread domestic data leaks caused by careless users processing sensitive information via foreign AI tools. Viral open-source AI agents like OpenClaw had structural vulnerabilities that could allow remote device control and sensitive data leaks, he noted. He further warned of the growing development gap caused by AI monopolies, accusing dominant tech powers of severing the global AI supply chain through methods such as entity lists, tech controls, monopolising industry standards, and building closed-source ecosystems. Although Chen did not name any countries, his comments pointed to the broader US-China power rivalry, where Washington has openly declared that it could not allow China to surpass it on AI development. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned just on Tuesday that if the US lost out in the AI race with China, “nothing else would matter”. As part of a spiralling tech war, the US has imposed restrictions on Chinese industry across multiple fronts, including chip supply, investment, market access limits and talent exchange. Chen also called for strengthening early-warning mechanisms and public advisories to expose foreign attempts to use AI for spying, theft of state secrets, disinformation campaigns and strategic containment targeting China. The world must “resolutely resist hegemonism, technological barriers, and exclusive blocs”, and set up a “fair and open international AI rules system”, he wrote. China is actively building multilateral platforms for global AI governance. In July, 29 countries – including Russia, Kazakhstan, Laos, Pakistan and Indonesia – signed a landmark agreement in Shanghai to establish the China-backed World AI Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Waico aims to help Global South countries expand technical capacity building and create a worldwide AI governance framework that respects national policy differences.

title: Man up, break down: unpacking the Philippines’ male suicide crisis
description: Filipino men rarely seek help for mental illness, despite making up 80 per cent of suicide deaths. Advocates say it’s time for change.
content: Richardson Mojica is no stranger to thoughts of ending it all. The 40-year-old university professor and mental health advocate was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder and depression in his early 20s. He finds fulfilment in his job, yet suicidal ideation has always lingered. “We call it passively suicidal – you don’t want to live, but you don’t want to stop everything,” he said, revealing that he had survived a self-inflicted attempt on his life months ago. Survival is a daily discipline: continuous medication, regular therapy, psychiatrist check-ins and a support network he has learned to lean on. But seeking help meant confronting stigma – first at age 23 following a panic attack at work, then for years afterwards as he kept his condition to himself. Eventually, he told his family, but he found it difficult. “I’m the eldest son, so it wasn’t easy for me to be vulnerable in front of them, to cry in front of them,” he said. Mojica’s experience is emblematic of a wider struggle among men in the Philippines. Around 80 per cent of the country’s suicide deaths are men, according to the World Health Organization, and two in five are among those aged 15 to 29. The Philippine Statistics Authority recorded 3,379 deaths from intentional self-harm in 2024, up from 3,133 in 2023. Studies consistently showed men were less likely than women to seek help for mental health concerns, said Kristine Faith Moral, a clinical psychologist at Ateneo de Manila University. “This is also reflected in the ratio of men vs women who inquire about my professional services,” she said. “Even more so among those who eventually push through with seeking help.” Rigid expectations around masculinity, such as being self-reliant, could act as barriers, Moral warned. If the expectation is that a man should be the one who solves problems, then asking for help can itself feel like a failure Kristine Faith Moral, clinical psychologist Mental health professionals say women actually attempt suicide more often, but more men die by suicide because they use more lethal methods. “This is one possible way of understanding what is sometimes referred to as the gender paradox in suicidology: women tend to report suicidal ideation and suicide attempts more frequently, while men are more likely to die by suicide,” Moral said. “This does not mean men necessarily experience less psychological distress. Rather, there may be differences in how distress is understood and expressed.” Yves Miel Zuniga, co-founder of civil society organisation #MentalHealthPH, agreed. “Suicide is a preventable public health issue,” he said. “But we should be careful about reducing it to the idea that it’s simply because men don’t talk about their feelings … there’s no single explanation for why someone dies by suicide.” ‘Boys don’t cry’ Cultural expectations rooted in gender norms shape how men perceive mental health, advocates say. Moral said this largely came down to how boys were socialised, reinforced by media depictions of masculinity. “From a very young age, boys may receive messages that discourage vulnerability, such as ‘boys don’t cry’ … they may be told to ‘suck it up’ or ‘man up’,” she said. Zuniga warned against treating Filipino men as “one homogeneous group”, noting that gender only added to the complexity of suicide. Supposedly “masculine” traits such as resilience and self-reliance only became problematic when they were interpreted to mean men should suffer alone, he said, adding that the affordability and accessibility of mental health services was another major issue. Moral argued that underlying stressors – financial difficulties, work pressures or relationship troubles – could be similar for both men and women. “Gender expectations can influence the meaning they attach to those experiences and the ways they believe they are allowed to cope,” she said. Much of that conditioning begins at home, according to Moral. “Filipino family expectations can be particularly potent drivers of behaviour,” she said, adding that many men were expected to take on the role of provider, protector and problem solver. “If the expectation is that a man should be the one who solves problems, then asking for help can itself feel like a failure to fulfil that role.” Losing a job could therefore become more than a financial setback, Moral said. It could challenge a man’s sense of self-worth “particularly when his identity is strongly tied to being a provider or someone who is supposed to have things under control”. Mojica knows that feeling of vulnerability, sharpened by the social stigma associated with mental health struggles. “As a man, I think what bothered me was saying it out loud, telling people that I have this condition and letting everybody know,” he said. “Being vulnerable in public, being vulnerable to a lot of people and showing that I am weak, for a certain period of time, when these things happen … when I need to breathe, I need to cry, it’s hard.” Where change begins Advocates advise against trying to lecture men out of their instincts, saying what they need instead are peer groups where they can speak plainly to others facing similar struggles. For Zuniga, a lot has changed in the Philippines over the past decade or so, but much work still needs to be done. Depression used to be “perceived as being dramatic” rather than a public health issue, he said – reflecting progress, even as stigma and problems with cost and access to care remained. Filipino culture was capable of silencing men, but also protecting them, Zuniga said. “Research on help-seeking behaviour among Filipinos shows social support is very important, and Filipinos frequently turn to friends or family before formally entering the mental healthcare system,” he said. “So the question is: how do we make sure we have a society where Filipino men feel safe enough to speak, and know they’ll be taken seriously?” Moral’s answer is not to strip away the values that men hold dear, but to build upon them. “For many Filipino men, being a provider, protector or someone their family can depend on can be deeply tied to their identity,” she said. The goal was “to show that being strong and dependable can also include knowing when to ask for help”, Moral added. “Allowing yourself to be cared for and being emotionally present … it needs to start somewhere.” If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Ancient English gardens under threat from climate change
description: Gardeners warn of lasting damage as trees struggle to survive rising temperatures.
content:
At Hampton Court Palace, head gardener Graham Dillamore strode across the burnt beige grass in the spectacular formal gardens southwest of London, laid out in the 17th century.
“If we have a summer like this next year, by God, it’s going to be a struggle,” Dillamore said.
The gardens of stately homes are among England’s top visitor attractions. But their ancient trees are being hammered by climate change.
Gardeners said the concern is for the long-term consequences and keeping the spirit of their gardens alive.
Mature trees that take decades to establish are drooping, and some have leaves turning brown in August in a reaction to excessive heat.
“Some of these trees have actually given up. They’re not going to come back; they’re finished,” Dillamore said.

title: Schoolchildren survive Nepal floods thanks to  quick evacuation by teachers
description: Pupils in Dhading escaped rising waters, but several schools were damaged, affecting education for thousands of students.
content:
In one of the areas worst hit by last month’s catastrophic floods in Nepal, a group of schoolchildren managed to survive when they happened to leave their classroom for their lunch break.
Children attending other classes at the school in Dhading also escaped because teachers told them to quickly evacuate their classrooms shortly before the waters came crashing in.
“The teachers said, ‘There is a flood, and you should leave bags and tiffins,’” said Lakshmi Shrestha, the mother of a student attending the school.
Shrestha was among those who returned to the school over the next few days to find their children’s belongings.
The school was coated in mud, and the courtyard was filled with sediment.
At least 69 schools in Nepal’s flood-devastated districts have been destroyed or damaged, putting the education of nearly 19,000 children at risk, according to the non-profit organisation Save the Children.

title: Why chef Mel Ng is cooking her way through Hong Kong’s restaurant kitchens
description: Coming from a background in French cuisine, Ng takes shifts at the city’s eateries to learn their techniques and showcase their heritage.
content:
In the early hours of the morning, former chef Mel Ng was tasked with rolling out dumpling wrappers and mixing the next day’s fillings before surviving the chaotic lunch rush at Ah Chun Shandong Dumpling.

Coming from a background in French cuisine, Ng has staged at more than 20 restaurants since last year: from the beloved Kamcentre Roast Goose and viral Vietnamese eatery Banh Mi Nem to Indian restaurant Leela.
“They’ve all been very interesting to me because I’ve tried out many different kitchens, like Indian cuisine [and] Japanese ... things that I never would have tried before,” said the 36-year-old, who also works as a consultant in the food and beverage industry.
“The ones that I enjoy the most are the ones that are related more to Hong Kong local heritage, just because these are the things I grew up eating.”
In other countries, staging is a way for aspiring chefs to gain experience. The concept is not common in Hong Kong, but restaurants welcomed the extra help.
“In Western kitchens, you can just knock on the door and ask to stage for a week to see if it’s a good fit,” Ng said. “It’s the best way to learn. But traditional Chinese kitchens have never heard of it.”
Ng calls herself a “culinary wanderer”. Having staged in restaurants across Asia, she considers traditional Chinese cuisine her toughest challenge yet, largely because these kitchens rely on intuition rather than written recipes.
“A lot of the techniques were ... new to me. Working in a Cantonese kitchen meant using a wok, which I’d never done before,” she said.
“It was a steep learning curve , but I always step into the kitchen with an open mind.”
Why is it important to “wander” as a cook?
“Experience is the best teacher. And chefs will respect your work ethic more than whatever diploma you hold,” Ng explained.
After growing up in Hong Kong, Ng studied business at Northeastern University in the US city of Boston before attending the International Culinary Centre (ICC) in New York to learn to cook.
During her undergraduate years, Ng joined a programme that allowed students to study while working full-time. By the time she finished her business degree, she had a year and a half of work experience.
“I spent a lot of my internships mostly at office jobs [and] desk jobs – finance-related or insurance-related or marketing-related. And I realised I wasn’t very excited about the normal office path. So I wanted to try and find something that excited me,” she shared.
“I started cooking a lot for my roommate [and] for my friends. That’s when I started learning how to cook on my own.”
These casual meals eventually transformed into a dream to become a chef.
Culinary school was challenging, Ng shared. But she loved how it brought together people from all walks of life: from college dropouts to tai tai , a Cantonese term for wealthy married women.
The programme was structured into six levels, beginning with basic culinary fundamentals like knife cuts, bases and sauces. By level three, students began to experience the repetition of a kitchen – continuously cooking the same foods.
“I was working in teams to cook those dishes. So that’s when things started getting a bit more tough physically,” she said, adding that she had to pass rigorous written and practical exams before she could move to the next level.
“By level three, you kind of know which people are in it for the long run and which people are ... there just to have fun.”
While Ng took the traditional route of culinary school, she also encouraged aspiring chefs to learn on the ground.
“Going to culinary school, yes, you get the foundations and fundamentals of the industry, but a lot of those things are very old school,” she said. “There are a lot of new techniques that you can learn from actual kitchen experience instead of through school.”
For many older Hong Kong eateries, Ng noticed that staffing was a recurring obstacle, and it was even harder to find young people who want to learn the craft.
“Since Covid, we’ve seen a lot of restaurant closures. Even heritage brands that have been around for 20 [or] 30 years closed down,” she said.
Her mission to stage in different restaurants isn’t just about honing her culinary craft, but also about using her business acumen to help struggling eateries survive.
“A chef might have a great recipe, but if the concept isn’t spot on, doesn’t fit the neighbourhood or ignores current trends, the business will struggle,” Ng said.
“But because I’ve been on both sides, I can kind of speak both languages. Nailing a concept means looking at everything from the price point for the location [to considering], is the brand story clear? Is the menu designed for kitchen efficiency?”
Ng also posts videos of her staging experiences on Instagram in hopes of showcasing the rich culinary tradition of Hong Kong’s restaurants to a wider audience.
For those looking to break into the culinary world, Ng’s advice is to get hands-on experience by staging.
“It’s not just about which restaurant – it’s also about whether you can survive in the industry because every kitchen is very demanding. Working long hours, you don’t get a social life. So, not everybody enjoys that,” she said.
“If you can find a restaurant to stage for like a month, I think that would give you a good taste of whether you like being in the industry or not.”
Ng’s daily mantra is “ mise en place ”, a French term meaning “everything in its place”.
“In the kitchen, it means having all your ingredients and tools ready before you start,” she said.
“Whether I’m doing consulting work for a client or working a shift in the kitchen, I always have a plan in my head, thinking about the end goal and mapping out every step to get there.”

title: ‘Dear You’ captivates global audiences with its tale of migration
description: The film, shot in the Teochew dialect, is now a global cultural export, showcasing the history of a little-known story.
content:
One of the most talked-about films in China this year was filmed mainly in a southern Chinese dialect. Most viewers in China need subtitles to understand it.
Yet Dear You has become the second-highest-grossing film in China this year. Now it is going to other countries as part of a broader trend in Chinese cultural exports.
Dear You was mostly filmed in Teochew, which is a dialect spoken in the Chaoshan area of Guangdong. The story is set in the Teochew immigrant community in Bangkok.
The film looks at the long history of Chinese people moving to Southeast Asia over many centuries. It has done a good job of making this little-known history clear to people.
The movie is becoming popular as Chinese culture gains attention.
This includes things like collectable Labubu dolls and a social media trend in which people from around the world enjoy and share aspects of the Chinese way of life.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong cements superconnector role with wave of belt and road deals
description: The city has become central to the Belt and Road Initiative’s evolution from infrastructure projects to digital and hi-tech connectivity.
content: The Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong last week is tangible proof that 13 years after the initiative’s launch, the city has become central to its evolution from infrastructure projects to comprehensive connectivity and hi-tech platforms. More than 6,000 participants from over 70 countries attended, signing upwards of 60 commercial agreements and memorandums of understanding exceeding US$3 billion. These are evidence of sustained confidence in Hong Kong’s unique capacity to bridge mainland China’s innovation and capital with emerging markets. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu correctly framed the city as a “two-way springboard” – linking mainland enterprises with overseas markets while connecting international firms to Chinese opportunities. His visit to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June yielded seven MOUs, while Hong Kong outlets signed eight additional agreements in Kuala Lumpur last month. These show how diplomatic groundwork translates into commercial partnerships. The summit showcased media institutions embracing their connector role. The South China Morning Post hosted the inaugural China Conference: Central Asia in Astana, Kazakhstan, this month, then co-organised Thursday’s Belt and Road Summit panel examining artificial intelligence adoption across participating economies. Lee’s coming policy address will continue government support for local media expanding into belt and road markets to expand readership beyond Hong Kong. This marks the second consecutive year such initiatives have featured in the chief executive’s blueprint, reflecting recognition that credible storytelling requires institutional capacity and international networks. Following Lee’s Central Asia trip, momentum is building for closer economic ties between the city and the region, with potential cooperation extending from finance to tourism, professional services, mining, agriculture and digital infrastructure. Hong Kong is well positioned as what IBM’s Sony Angel Han termed the “superconnector” linking mainland AI innovation with belt and road markets seeking governance standards. The city’s mature regulatory system offers validation: AI models that succeed here gain credibility for deployment elsewhere. Fano Labs’ Albert Lam Yun-sang noted the crucial transition businesses struggle to navigate – from proof of concept to proof of value. Hong Kong’s robust professional services sector and open-minded adoption culture can facilitate this shift, provided investment in AI literacy accompanies technology diffusion. Meanwhile, Kazakhstan’s MOU with Hong Kong’s transport authorities to establish a joint laboratory and explore low-altitude economy solutions displays practical cooperation. Bakhtiyar Mukhametkaliyev, Kazakhstan’s vice-minister of AI and digital development, articulated the strategic logic clearly: Kazakhstan seeks mainland technology expertise paired with Hong Kong’s financial tools to develop projects across Central Asia’s five-nation market. Separately, Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn has confirmed that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations supports Hong Kong’s accession to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership. As Hong Kong is Asean’s fourth-largest foreign investment source, that is a natural but significant endorsement. Kazakhstan offers land, electricity infrastructure and tax incentives; Asean commands the world’s largest free-trade zone. Both recognise Hong Kong as their indispensable platform. The city must now sustain the momentum generated to push for innovation beyond roads and ports into advanced AI and digital systems. Our challenge is converting institutional confidence into expanded market access and deeper technology-finance partnerships to deliver development outcomes. As geopolitical fragmentation tests global cohesion, connectivity platforms acquire premium value. Hong Kong offers regulatory credibility, deep capital markets and Greater Bay Area industrial depth. Last week’s summit reaffirms this advantage precisely when alternatives remain scarce, and when the world confronts urgent questions of resilient growth, connectivity and trust – questions that belt and road cooperation can answer in practical ways.

title: How this Hong Kong Gen Z coffee entrepreneur is filling market gap with her can-do attitude
description: Lactose-intolerant Nikita Kuwadekar, 23, couldn’t find canned oat milk coffee anywhere. Now her additive-free Busy Brew cans are finding fans.
content: Few would guess that Hong Kong’s first plant-based canned coffee brand, Busy Brew, is run by a 23-year-old. One might be tempted to see it as a Gen Z entrepreneur fairy tale: a student spots a gap in the market, builds a cult following for her canned oat milk lattes, lands incubation funding and watches the product fly off shelves in some of the city’s largest retail chains. But founder Nikita Kuwadekar, born and raised in Hong Kong, will be the first to tell you that the journey has not been easy. Behind the curated Instagram posts and the accolades lies a story of open-heart surgery, rejections, relentless hustle and trading the security of a nine-to-five job for the chaos that comes with building a brand from scratch. Kuwadekar was born with a congenital condition and needed open‑heart surgery while still in high school. Determined not to fall behind, she overhauled her diet, cutting dairy and sugar to accelerate her recovery. The physical benefits were immediate: her skin cleared and her energy returned. She also made a discovery that would eventually shape her career. “I realised I was lactose intolerant, and that like 90 per cent of Asians, and almost 68 per cent of the world, are too,” she says. “That’s nuts. Because everything around us is dairy: bubble tea, coffees, every canned coffee on the shelf.” Milking a market niche As a first-year student at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Kuwadekar noticed that the only grab‑and‑go coffee options were loaded with milk powder and sugar. The gap in the market became impossible to ignore. “If you look at the ingredients of what’s on the shelf, it’s actually pretty terrible in the market, between stabilisers and additives and preservatives,” she says. “Coffee should be accessible, and it should be healthy.” Faced with spending HK$50 (US$6.40) to HK$60 on an oat milk latte every day, she thought: “Why doesn’t this exist in a can?” Kuwadekar, who was 19 at the time, entered various university pitch competitions with her idea for Busy Brew, which helped bring in the brand’s first internal funding. Next came entry into an incubation programme by Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation – a governmental organisation set up in 2001 to foster innovation and technology development – which provided the resources to turn a dorm room experiment into a real company. Kuwadekar spent more than two years refining her recipe through relentless customer testing, eventually landing on her vanilla oat milk latte formula with zero additives. Now her drinks are stocked by Hong Kong chains such as City’super and Louder, and online retailer HKTVmall. On February 24, 2026, Kuwadekar won the Spirit of Youth Award at the 13th Spirit of Hong Kong Awards at the Conrad Hong Kong hotel. A lot of what we’ve done has been unconventional Nikita Kuwadekar, founder of Busy Brew She is part of a generation rewriting the rule book on climbing the career ladder – by not climbing it at all. For many young entrepreneurs, the appeal of starting a business is not simply about rebelling against corporate drudgery, but aligning work with personal values. Kuwadekar’s business is the product of her own health journey, and that authenticity bleeds into every interaction. “Anytime I see someone drinking it, I genuinely feel like I know them,” she says. “The community we’ve built is incredible.” The true measure of success Kuwadekar measures her success less by sales figures than by the messages she receives and the people who show up to events. “If we’re not getting crazy sales but we can have a community event, and people come from all over just to hang out and try the product? That, to me, is more meaningful,” she says. For Kuwadekar, one interaction – involving a young man wearing a mask that covered his entire face at a pop-up event – remains particularly memorable. “He said dairy caused his acne breakouts and had been looking for a product like ours everywhere – dairy‑free, convenient, not expensive like a cafe latte,” Kuwadekar recalls. “He bought a huge stash, boxes worth, and now promotes us everywhere. “In my head, this was just an idea I wrote on my laptop at 2am. The moment I realised other people actually wanted it too? That was everything,” she adds. That sense of connection and purpose, Kuwadekar argues, is something a conventional entry-level job rarely provides. She says the loose framework of her young company – which allows it to work with customers and actively adjust its flavours in line with their feedback – steered it in the right direction. “A lot of what we’ve done has been unconventional,” Kuwadekar says. “Most people would say, ‘Don’t do this or that.’ But we haven’t been in the industry, so we don’t necessarily know those rules. We work around them in ways that are more ideal for a start-up.” She believes this willingness to sidestep industry norms is one of the secret advantages of youth. “Everyone on our team is in their twenties,” she says. “Some have corporate experience, some don’t, but in a way that helps us.” ‘Let me learn’ Despite her brand’s success, Kuwadekar does not encourage everyone in their early twenties to quit their job to chase a founder’s dream. “We over‑glamorise this lifestyle,” she says. “Ninety‑eight per cent of it is moving boxes, packing orders, giving out free samples, getting rejected all the time. It’s not easy.” Her assessment of the anti‑nine‑to‑five rhetoric that floods social media is equally pragmatic. “There’s this idea online: ‘Quit your job, go all in on your dream,’” she says. “That’s not feasible for everyone. If you’re paying your rent, looking after your parents, it’s not a good idea.” Kuwadekar points out that many of the world’s most successful founders started in their forties and fifties after building capital and life experience. “We shouldn’t be telling everyone to quit their jobs,” she says. “It’s not always good advice.” Instead, she advocates a more strategic approach. She describes herself as “risk‑averse but calculated”. “Do your market research,” she says. “Make sure the product is actually good before you spend all your savings on one production run. Because I did that – and everything was riding on that one batch.” Kuwadekar also wishes someone had told her earlier that it is OK to be young and still learning. “When I started, I tried to hide my age,” she says. “I’d be in meetings where people would ignore me and turn to the man next to me and ask, ‘What do you think?’ And I’d say, ‘Actually, I’m the founder.’ Now I’m more confident saying, ‘I don’t know this yet – let me learn.’” As for the future, Busy Brew has a darker roast in development, as well as potential new product lines and partnerships with health‑focused Hong Kong brands on the horizon. Kuwadekar recently took her first full weekend off in two years. “I felt like I could see colour again,” she laughs. “You can get really stuck in the hustle culture – this idea that you don’t want it bad enough if you’re not working all the time, especially if you’re young and you’re starting from scratch.”

title: Hong Kong’s Farmacy brings healing through hydroponics and horticultural therapy
description: Urban farming experiences nurture mind and body through hydroponics, plant art and aromatherapy.
content:
When Linda Lee was young and living in the heart of Hong Kong’s urban metropolis, her father found peace in a small cluster of greenery in their flat.
He stood in the corner every day, tending to each pot. Lee’s father was a tough character. He did not talk much. But Lee saw his face relax whenever he tended to his “garden”.
Today, Lee works at Farmacy, an urban farming organisation that uses hydroponic technology – in which plants grow in a water and mineral solution rather than soil – to create mobile farms and farm labs in Hong Kong.
These spaces are usually compact, indoor, climate-controlled environments.
Lee leads urban farming experience days about once a month. It is a time when participants can set aside their usual worries and engage all five senses amid the greenery at Farmacy’s headquarters in Shau Kei Wan.
The list of hands-on activities includes plant rubbing – an artistic technique that captures the texture of different leaves by placing them under a piece of paper and shading over them with crayons or pencils – and seed art. Visitors can also try aromatherapy.

title: Hong Kong aims to scale its tech ecosystem and nurture more unicorns: HKSTP CEO
description: Innovation and technology hub is attracting global capital, supporting and fostering bigger and more mature investment deals.
content: Hong Kong is intensifying efforts to attract technology start-ups and nurture unicorns through expanded financial support via a key government-backed platform, leveraging the city’s booming fundraising activities and world-class financial infrastructure. Investors are displaying an increased appetite for the local tech scene compared with a decade ago – a trend that Terry Wong Ping-sau, CEO of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP), said was a positive sign for the city’s broader innovation and technology (I&T) ecosystem. “Traditional enterprises and family offices, in particular, are showing huge enthusiasm, driven by the transformation needs of the next generation taking over Hong Kong family businesses that traditionally ran conventional operations,” Wong told the South China Morning Post. “Many actively reach out to us. “As an ecosystem hub, we can provide them with insights on I&T developments and introduce various investment opportunities.” Compared with Hong Kong’s fundraising prowess – the city helped firms raise about HK$285.8 billion (US$36.4 billion) via new listings last year – Wong noted that there was still room to improve in early-stage financing. The HKSTP was established in 2001 as a statutory body to bolster the I&T ecosystem by connecting stakeholders, nurturing talent and providing facilities for research and development. I believe the next eight to 10 years will be a golden era for Hong Kong to produce more high-quality, large-scale tech enterprises Terry Wong Ping-sau, HKSTP Along with local fintech hub Cyberport, the HKSTP is a key I&T flagship that has nurtured more than a dozen unicorns – privately held start-ups with a current valuation of US$1 billion or more – such as SenseTime in artificial intelligence, Lalamove in logistics and Insilico Medicine in AI drug discovery, as well as 17 initial public offering cases, according to HKSTP’s 2024-2025 annual report. To maintain Hong Kong’s competitiveness in nurturing high-potential start-ups, Wong said the city needed to accelerate the commercialisation of products. “This is also the direction where we hope to achieve a major breakthrough in the medium term – nurturing more high-quality large enterprises, even unicorns, and driving their listings,” he said. “I believe the next eight to 10 years will be a golden era for Hong Kong to produce more high-quality, large-scale tech enterprises, as many current start-ups already show high potential.” The HKSTP has built a wide range of funding channels to attract more start-ups, including a corporate venture fund established in 2018 that has since raised more than HK$170 billion. Every HK$1 it invests attracts HK$13 from the private market, the corporation claimed, adding that it had more than 500 corporate partners and 210 active investors. In April 2025, the government-funded platform also launched Hong Kong’s first public-private partnership fund for I&T – the Co-Acceleration Programme – which has attracted nine corporate limited partners to co-invest. Wong said that, under the programme, companies receiving investment may not originally be based in Hong Kong, but after securing funding, they must set up operations at the Hong Kong Science Park. “This is an efficient and high-quality way for us to proactively find and bring overseas I&T companies with potential to Hong Kong to continue their research and development,” Wong added. Wong expressed confidence in the Hong Kong government’s target of boosting the number of locally based unicorn enterprises to 30 by 2032, as the park strengthens its positioning as an “ecosystem orchestrator” to proactively build the I&T ecosystem. A recent study, conducted jointly by the HKSTP and technology market intelligence firm CB Insights, found that Hong Kong companies showed the strongest growth momentum among Asian markets, followed by Taiwan and Singapore, and several companies in the HKSTP were ranked in the global top 10 per cent. At the same time, capital is concentrating on fewer, larger bets. Overall tech funding in Asia jumped 157 per cent, year on year, in the first half of 2026, while the deal count dropped by 22 per cent, according to the joint study’s findings. John Kelly, managing director and senior vice-president of client innovation at CB Insights, said the shift towards larger deals was a sign of a maturing capital market. Once the venture capital and private equity network matures, he said, “the capital returns from large deals will flow back into early-stage and seed-round investment”. Start-ups should improve information transparency and leverage data and AI evaluation tools to help global investors uncover their value, Kelly added.

title: Spark Deep Dive: Hongkong Post struggles to deliver financially
description: Eight years of deficits and few branches profiting appear to spell the end of the city’s postal service as it exists now.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Hong Kong’s postal service has been losing money for eight years, with only a few branches turning a profit
The city’s post offices have started ways to save money
On a weekday morning in August, the Repulse Bay post office was almost empty. It stands in one of Hong Kong’s wealthiest neighbourhoods. In an hour, only five customers had walked through the door, with two staff members serving them.
Customer Dicky Lo sent a parcel to Europe. He said the post office was more reasonably priced compared with private couriers.
“I come here two to three times a month, mostly to collect online shopping packages,” the 43-year-old freelancer said. “Not many residents use this branch, which is exactly why I like it.”
The Repulse Bay resident said that closing the post office would be inconvenient for him. He would have to travel 7km to Aberdeen for postal services.
“Post offices are still necessary. Besides sending parcels, residents can pay electricity, water and tax bills here … They are different from private courier services,” Lo said.
“Not every government service is profit-making, as they have to satisfy residents’ needs. We cannot judge them merely by profit and loss.”
The Repulse Bay branch was one of five post offices that recorded a productivity index below 50 per cent.
Since 1995, the government’s postal services department has financed itself. In 1997-98, it saw its peak profit of HK$1.23 billion. But for the past eight years, it has only recorded deficits .
In 2024-25, Hongkong Post had a record deficit of HK$821 million. The city’s post offices only made HK$277 million in revenue while spending HK$522 million. This resulted in a loss of HK$245 million, 8 per cent higher than in 2020-21.
The Legislative Council has approved a rescue plan to give HK$4.6 billion to support Hongkong Post’s operations for the next three years. The government has also pledged to propose a road map for reform by 2028.
To save money, the Hongkong Post said it would stop giving permanent civil service positions to new employees. Instead, it would offer them two-year contracts. The move was criticised by public servants.
As a band-aid measure , observers have called for a review of the city’s post office network. The latest figures revealed that 98 per cent of post offices in Hong Kong had been losing money.
In 2024-25, the number of loss-making post offices rose to 120, or 98 per cent of all branches. This is up from 118, or 95 per cent, five years earlier. In comparison, 10 years ago, 103 post offices were loss-making, or 81 per cent of all branches.
1. Which of the following statements are false, according to the information in the news? (1) Many people in Hong Kong find Hongkong Post services too expensive. (2) A review of the city’s post offices is being called for due to budget deficits. (3) Most post offices in Hong Kong cannot make ends meet. (4) The Repulse Bay post office is one of Hong Kong’s most profitable branches.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (4) only C. (2), (4) only D. (3), (4) only
2. Apart from sending letters, what other services are offered at Hong Kong’s post offices? Why do you think people are not using these services as much as they did in the past?
3. How has Hongkong Post responded to this financial crisis, and what are the benefits and consequences of the measure?
1. How many post offices made profits in the year 2024-25, and how does this compare to the number of profit-making post offices in 2020-21?
2. Is the post office in Repulse Bay a profit-making branches? Explain using the news and the glossary.
productivity index: a metric measuring the amount of mail handled per worker at each site over a period of time
deficits: amounts in which money spent or owed is more than money earned in a particular period of time
band-aid measure: a temporary, superficial fix that addresses a symptom rather than solving the underlying root problem
You can also send and receive parcels and even pay government bills like your electricity, water and taxes. Today, many people use other delivery services and pay bills online through portals and websites. You can also send emails or message on social media instead of posting letters.
Hongkong Post will stop giving permanent civil service positions to new employees. Instead, it will offer them two-year contracts. The move has been criticised by public servants. A benefit of this measure is that it will save the government money and effort by avoiding the hiring of brand-new full-time employees. However, a consequence is that the postal service’s quality may be affected as the role could be filled easily by someone who is not committed and will leave for a permanent role elsewhere.
Only two post offices made profits in 2024-25, which is four fewer than in 2020-21.
The Repulse Bay post office cannot be one of the two profit-making branches, as its productivity index – which measures the amount of mail and the manpower at an individual site – was among the five post offices with a productivity index below 50 per cent.

title: Turn your strengths into superpowers with these activities
description: Learn to identify your abilities and plan what your future self can do with these strengths.
content:
Have you ever looked at superheroes in a comic book and wondered what your power could be? Well, here’s a little secret: you don’t need to be Spider-Man or the Scarlet Witch to have amazing abilities.
Superpowers aren’t limited to just flying, invisibility and telekinesis. The following activities will help you discover your out-of-this-world abilities.
First, copy the table below. Then write down the names of three people you know and admire.
Go to the first person you listed and ask them: “What are five ordinary, everyday superpowers that you have?” For example, they could be: the power of organisation, staying calm, playing a sport or even being able to stand on one foot for a long time.
Write what they say in the table below. Then, repeat the process with the other people you listed.
When you’ve finished your interviews, it’s time for you to find your own superpower by reflecting on yourself.
Think about these questions: What have you struggled with in the past? How have you improved a skill over time? What makes you happy and proud of yourself? How do you help other people in your community? If you find answering these questions difficult, you can ask someone who knows you well to help.
Now that you’ve researched, reflected and discovered your superpowers, it’s time to plan what to do with them. Write a letter to your future self about your strengths and what you hope to achieve. Open the letter at the end of the school year to see how far you’ve come. To keep your powers in force, it’s important to reflect on your growth every once in a while.
How have you improved as a person and as a learner?
What skills have you developed that will help you in your goals?
What do you aspire to do this year? How do you want to help others?

Hongkong Post’s deficits reveal structural problems
Could splitting postal services be the way forward?
The expansion of e-commerce , rise of private delivery firms and decline in traditional mail have all contributed to Hongkong Post’s dismal financial situation. The city’s postal service handled 611 million mail items in 2024-25, a 38 per cent fall from 978 million in 2020-21.
A spokesman said that the department’s primary duty was to establish a convenient postal network rather than to generate profits.
Former postmaster general Tam Wing-pong highlighted the intense competition from private couriers, which operate on a large, global scale to drive down delivery costs, making it difficult for Hongkong Post to compete.
Hong Kong Postal Workers Union chairman Cheung Wai-kuen attributed the heavy losses to high rent costs.
In 2023-24, the department spent HK$92 million renting 63 premises from private property owners, an average of HK$1.46 million per site. It reduced this to HK$79 million in 2025-26, bringing the average cost down to HK$1.3 million.
Economist Simon Lee Siu-po urged Hongkong Post to consider closing some of its branches, arguing that it was unreasonable to use public money to subsidise services for a few residents.
Cheung proposed adjusting post offices’ opening hours to cover the evening peak. While most post offices currently close by 5.30pm on weekdays, he suggested opening later and extending evening hours.
“Our union conducted a review and found that there were very few customers between 9am and 10am in most post offices,” Cheung said.
He said the change could reduce administrative expenses and allow branches to handle more items, such as e-commerce parcels.
Another cause of Hongkong Post’s financial burden could be its staff costs. In 2024-25, staff costs stood at HK$2.1 billion, down from HK$2.3 billion in 2020-21.
The struggles of public postal services have been a global issue. Some countries are separating public services from their more profitable delivery operations.
The United Kingdom has consistently reformed its government postal system, including a 2012 move to split the network of branches for public services from its delivery arm, Royal Mail. This paved the way for the privatisation of Royal Mail.
Post offices in Britain continue to offer some Royal Mail services; however, this postal service and courier company is losing ground in the parcels market. Its market share dropped from 45 per cent in 2015 to 35 per cent in 2024.
Hong Kong lawmaker Lam Wai-kong said the government could continue to provide public services without requiring them to make a profit, while the commercial delivery side could operate under a different model.
He cautioned, however, against full privatisation.
Still, it remains uncertain how effective this split would be, as the department’s e-commerce revenue, which includes commercial delivery, fell from HK$1.01 billion in 2023-24 to HK$590 million in 2025-26.
1. Why are the city’s post offices struggling to generate revenue? Explain using News, Issue and Glossary.
2. Explain two of Hongkong Post’s major expenses mentioned in Issue. What is being done to try to lower these costs?
3. List the pros and cons of separating the public services of Hongkong Post from other operations. To what extent do you agree with this plan?
1. Describe how the number of civil servants has changed over the time shown in the chart. Using Issue, explain how costs have reduced during this time.
2. Do you think Hongkong Post’s move to stop offering permanent contracts is enough to address its deficits? Explain using News, Issue and your own knowledge.
productivity index: a metric measuring the amount of mail handled per worker at each site over a period of time
deficits: amounts in which money spent or owed is more than money earned in a particular period of time
band-aid measure: a temporary, superficial fix that addresses a symptom rather than solving the underlying root problem
e-commerce: the process of buying and selling goods and services over the internet; popular e-commerce platforms in Hong Kong include Taobao, Pinduoduo and HKTVmall.
Royal Mail: the United Kingdom’s national postal service and courier company responsible for universal mail collection and delivery
You can also send and receive parcels and even pay government bills like your electricity, water and taxes. Today, many people use other delivery services and pay bills online through portals and websites. You can also send emails or message on social media instead of posting letters.
Hongkong Post will stop giving permanent civil service positions to new employees. Instead, it will offer them two-year contracts. The move has been criticised by public servants. A benefit of this measure is that it will save the government money and effort by avoiding the hiring of brand-new full-time employees. However, a consequence is that the postal service’s quality may be affected as the role could be filled easily by someone who is not committed and will leave for a permanent role elsewhere.
Only two post offices made profits in 2024-25, which is four fewer than in 2020-21.
The Repulse Bay post office cannot be one of the two profit-making branches, as its productivity index – which measures the amount of mail and the manpower at an individual site – was among the five post offices with a productivity index below 50 per cent.
The expansion of e-commerce, the rise of private delivery firms and decline in traditional mail have all contributed to Hongkong Post’s financial situation.
Two major expenses are staff costs, which totalled HK$2.1 billion in 2024-25, and high rent costs for branch premises, which reached HK$79 million in 2025-26. To lower staff expenses, Hongkong Post has stopped offering permanent civil service positions to new hires, replacing them with two-year contracts to reduce long-term benefit liabilities. To cut rental expenses, the department has renegotiated lease terms and streamlined leased sites, bringing total rental costs down from HK$92 million in 2023-24.
Separating commercial delivery from public postal operations allows the commercial arm to adopt flexible, market-driven strategies to compete with private couriers, while ensuring essential public services remain affordable and accessible. However, the downside is that commercial delivery may still fail to achieve profitability given falling e-commerce revenues, while the government remains burdened with funding loss-making public branches without commercial cross-subsidies. I agree with this plan to a moderate extent, as structural separation protects core civic access, but it must be paired with branch closures and adjusted operating hours to meaningfully eliminate the deficit. (accept all reasonable answers)
The number of staff declined by 9 per cent from 4,027 in 2023-24 to 3,683 in 2026-27.
I do not think Hongkong Post’s move to stop offering permanent contracts is enough to address its deficits. While switching new hires to two-year contract terms offers greater workforce flexibility and helps manage long-term civil service pension liabilities, it remains a short-term, superficial fix that fails to solve the causes of the department’s financial crisis. Hongkong Post faces a severe structural deficit, suffering a record loss of HK$821 million in 2024-25 with 98 per cent of its branches operating at a loss. Staff costs, while significant at HK$2.1 billion, are only one part of the problem. The deficit is fundamentally driven by a 38 per cent drop in traditional mail volume, fierce competition from global private couriers, falling e-commerce revenue and exorbitant property rental costs. Ceasing permanent hires does not reverse the decline in demand for physical post, nor does it restore lost e-commerce revenue. Also, relying heavily on contract staff could cause issues by reducing job security, increasing staff turnover, and harming frontline morale, ultimately impairing service quality. To achieve true financial sustainability, Hongkong Post must combine staffing flexibility with far broader structural reforms, including restructuring underutilised post offices, adjusting counter opening hours, or thinking of new ways to compete with private couriers. (accept all reasonable answers)

title: How air conditioners can affect your health
description: These machines may keep you cool but could also dry out your skin and throat – or even spread irritants into your lungs.
content:
When temperatures are high, it can be tempting to crank up the air conditioning. It’s an effective way to stay cool. However, air conditioning can also have unexpected side effects.
Staying in air-conditioned rooms for a long time can dry out your skin.
“Air conditioning tends to remove humidity from the air, which makes us feel cooler. But it can increase the water loss from your skin,” said Dr Opel Baker. He is a doctor at Mayfield Clinic, a private medical practice in Britain.
“This can lead to dry skin, tightness and flaking. It might even lead to increased sensitivity, eczema or chapped lips,” he explained.
If you have dry or sensitive skin, air conditioning might make it worse.
“Your nose and throat are designed to be kept moist. If they get dry, they can become irritated,” Baker explained.
“This might lead to a sore throat, a blocked nose or a hoarse voice.”
“When your nose and throat dry out, you’re less able to clear mucus, which is an important part of our immune defence system,” Dr Lucy Hooper added.
She is a London-based doctor and the co-founder of Coyne Medical.
Some people might experience nosebleeds. According to Baker, air conditioning dries out the inside of your nose. When your nose is dry, it can crack easily. If you blow or pick your nose, it might start to bleed.
Baker explained that if air conditioners are not cleaned properly and regularly, they can spread dust, pollen and mould particles in the air. These particles can irritate your lungs and cause problems like asthma.
Hooper said it could also increase the risk of getting a respiratory tract infection. This is especially dangerous for people who have a lung condition. She explained that an infection could cause these individuals serious and long-lasting problems.

title: Listen Up: Nutrition apps’ risky gaming features
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Nick Dearman, the studio manager at SCMP’s Video desk, and Young Post deputy editor Esther Cheung.
Voice 1: Green means go. Red means stop. A good performance wins you trophies or confetti, and people who fall behind get nudged to do better. These brightly coloured engagement tactics jumped from smartphone games to online shopping a long time ago. So it should come as no surprise that many nutrition-tracking apps also use gaming features to keep users coming back.
Voice 2: But as nutrition apps proliferate, some researchers are raising alarms that gamification features may do more harm than good for some people. Isabella Anderberg is a psychologist researching digital dieting behaviour at Flinders University in Adelaide, Australia. She said calorie tracking can reinforce behaviours associated with body dysmorphia and disordered eating. Anderberg said not everyone would be harmed from using the apps, but certain factors might increase risk, making it important for users to approach them with caution.
Voice 1: Health professionals that Anderberg interviewed during her research reported that apps could be especially helpful as meal-planning tools for people managing chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes. Physical activity apps can help remind people to move their bodies. Many users report enjoying them, saying that they feel motivated by tactics like streak notifications.
Voice 2: Angela Drury is an English professor in the US state of Georgia. She began using an app called MyFitnessPal more than 10 years ago to track protein, fat, carbohydrate and calorie intake when she started CrossFit, which is a type of fitness workout. She has since cycled through several other apps, including Weight Watchers and Lose It. Now, she uses Nourish, which is paid for by her insurance and includes blood work and weekly meetings with a dietitian.
Voice 1: Drury said the apps helped her stay on track with fitness goals. She said they sometimes steered her away from high-calorie foods when she uploaded photos of meals she was considering eating. She feels a little boost when she gets a badge for continuing a streak of logging meals. But a notification that says she has not entered lunch has the opposite effect. Then, it felt like it was scolding her, she said.
Voice 2: In most apps, users enter height, weight, age and other information. Then, they set a goal. The app may say how many calories or macronutrients are needed to reach that goal, using game-like elements such as badges, streaks, rewards, points and notifications to encourage user engagement. Many nutrition tracking apps are free but offer premium versions that users must pay for.
Voice 1: The US Centres for Disease Control says that how many calories you need depends on many factors, including your age, gender and level of physical activity. The health agency provides a tool to calculate how many calories an individual needs. But critics warn that food databases are often inaccurate, with estimated portion sizes and calorie counts that vary widely.
Voice 2: Courtney Simpson is a behavioural psychologist who oversees eating disorders at the Evidence-Based Treatment Centres of Seattle. She said some apps encouraged people to set calorie goals that were far too low for any adult. That is not only unhealthy but can also set people up for failure. Simpson said the gaming features might keep people coming back to unrealistic goals, creating shame that could contribute to binge eating or other behaviours people are trying to change. She added that gamification itself is not bad – it’s about what it promotes.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): Japan’s cooling machine tackles scorching heat
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
[1] Warehouse worker Isao Tabuchi felt dizzy and unwell after cycling to work. It was a hot summer day in Japan. When he got to work, he headed for his company’s newest purchase: a refrigerator for humans.
[2] The phone booth-sized machine uses jets of chilled air to ensure ice-cold comfort. The machine was launched only this year, but has proved popular in a country that seems to be getting warmer. “I was really able to recover thanks to that. Once you use it, it’s very, very cool,” said Tabuchi, 51. He lives in the western industrial city of Higashiosaka.
[3] Trusco Nakayama is an industrial equipment distributor based in Tokyo. It said it has sold more than 300 units of the Do Hiemon Box since April. They cost 1.5 million yen (HK$74,600) each. Customers include construction sites, factories and warehouses. The company will expand in the future to include golf courses, said company sales agent China Yamamoto. Baseball stadiums may also be interested.
[4] Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events around the world. Japan saw its hottest summer on record in 2025. The weather office began using a new word – kokushobi, or “cruelly hot day” – when temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius. They urged the public to treat extreme heat as a natural disaster.
[5] Tokyo alone recorded almost 120 heat-related deaths in the month to mid-August. This summer, close to 63,000 people nationwide needed emergency care. The Do Hiemon Box can provide one line of defence. It operates from a standard power socket. It can also be wheeled around, and uses little power, according to its maker. It automatically shuts off after 20 minutes to prevent overuse.
[6] It is essential to invest in heat-countering measures, said Yutaka Kono from Konoe. He works at the same company as Tabuchi. It helps maintain the existing workforce and attracts new recruits. Kono said that conventional air conditioners and spot coolers offer some relief. However, his firm has many open areas where trucks and heavy equipment can operate.
[7] “I was really surprised by this new concept of putting people into a kind of refrigerator. I found it very appealing that by going inside that refrigerator, a person’s body can be cooled in an instant to a safe temperature,” Kono said. “That made me think, ‘We definitely want to install one of these’,” he said.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): What is overthinking, and how can you stop the loop of negative feedback?
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] You have likely experienced some form of the late-night mental loop: replaying a terse exchange with a classmate, wondering about a loved one’s subtle shift in tone or worrying about a symptom you googled. Overthinking has become a modern buzzword blamed for wrecking everything from your emotional well-being to personal relationships. It is an aimless loop driven by negative, repetitive thoughts that offer no resolution.
[2] “Overthinkers go over and over their negative thoughts and feelings, examining them, questioning them,” wrote the late Yale psychologist Susan Nolen-Hoeksema in Women Who Think Too Much , a landmark book on the subject. Questions lead to more questions, she said, causing negative thoughts to multiply and spread.
[3] Overthinking consists of two elements plus a process. Rumination is the most common form of overthinking; it involves pondering past events in a negative way. For instance, feeling anxious about a conversation in which you might have said the wrong thing to somebody is rumination. Worry, another cause of overthinking, involves obsessing over future events. Both must feature a process called repetitive negative thinking. The negative thoughts keep repeating over and over, are difficult to disengage from, and start to consume all of the thinker’s time and energy.
[4] Unlike constructive problem-solving, overthinking has no clear endpoint. “Overthinking does not lead to solutions or insight,” Nolen-Hoeksema wrote. Instead, she explained, it creates a distorted filter that draws our attention exclusively to what is going wrong in our lives while giving us the false impression that we are gaining clarity. She also wrote that overthinking warps our view of ourselves and our life, and can obscure the fact that things might actually be going quite well.
[5] Overthinking feeds on itself. One way psychologists have explained this is through associative networks. We do not store thoughts and memories as isolated items, but link them together by their meaning, emotion and experience. So, put simply, a thought can bring similar types of thought to mind.
[6] If a thought is negative, it can pull up other negative thoughts, leading to a worsening mood. That bad mood then makes more negative thoughts available, and the process continues. The result is a spiral – the more the mind runs negative thoughts, the more material it finds to keep the loop of negativity going.
[7] There are self-help techniques available. Just realising that you are overthinking – and naming what you are doing as such – is a good start, as labelling something can often distance you from it. Writing down your fears and concerns can be useful, as the writing process can feel like you are giving them away, removing you from them. They can also sometimes appear ridiculous when you see them written down.
[8] Distract yourself from the overthinking process by doing something you enjoy. If you find you simply cannot stop overthinking, schedule a time for it to take place. Many overthinkers find that when that time arrives, their compulsion to overthink disappears.
Source: South China Morning Post, August 15

title: Open Questions | Veteran investor Fang Fenglei on why the China ‘investibility’ debate is no debate at all
description: Influential financier who helped found CICC says arguments against China investment ‘do not hold water’.
content: Over the past three decades, investor Fang Fenglei has had a major role in shaping China’s capital markets. He worked with Morgan Stanley in the early 1990s to help create the country’s first joint venture investment bank – China International Capital Corp. Then, at the start of the millennium, he spearheaded the listing of state-owned giants in Hong Kong as CEO of Bank of China International, later chairing a China joint venture with Goldman Sachs. Now the chairman of Hopu Investments, Fang discusses China’s investment opportunities, the artificial intelligence race, diversification from US dollar assets and Hong Kong’s growth potential. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. There has been talk from abroad that China’s economy has peaked, and debates continue over whether China is still “investible”. What is your assessment of foreign investors’ sentiment? Given their different sectors, standpoints and risk appetites, alongside political, economic and cultural influences, institutions hold divergent views on China. On a practical level, multinationals can achieve stable operations in China through equity-related and governance-oriented arrangements with Chinese partners. Take Starbucks’ joint venture deal with Boyu Capital, for instance. Boyu holds a 60 per cent stake, while Starbucks retains a 40 per cent stake and keeps ownership of the brand’s intellectual property rights. For McDonald’s China, a Citic-led consortium holds 52 per cent, with McDonald’s owning 48 per cent. Foreign capital acts both as “distant water” and “living water” for China: “distant water” refers to its long-term nature, while “living water” indicates its role in stimulating market dynamism. Some investors with reservations about China often point to falling birth rates and weak domestic demand. These are actually global issues intertwined with multiple factors including trade protectionism, regional conflicts and shifts in the global industrial landscape. Growth rates cannot be assessed in isolation from the size of an economy. As the world’s second-largest economy, China’s pursuit of moderate, high-quality growth represents a healthy trajectory. Arguments claiming China has lost its investment merit do not hold water. Looking back to 1979, when the concept of a “moderately prosperous society” was first introduced, China’s per capita gross national product stood at less than US$300. Few at that time anticipated China would become the world’s second-largest economy. To understand China, one must not only look at statistics, but also look at its proven capacity to deliver on goals and drive economic transformation. China’s property adjustment, a widely watched issue among investors, stems from changing market conditions and proactive government efforts to deleverage, deflate bubbles and fend off systemic risks. The property sector has long carried high leverage. Its unique features have delayed market self-correction and kept resources away from other industries. Many developers used to rely heavily on offshore US dollar-denominated bonds. However, the US Federal Reserve rate hikes in 2022 sharply increased their debt servicing burdens. Such risks would only continue to accumulate and escalate without timely regulation. The adjustment has come with pain, yet it has also steered resources towards strategic emerging industries.
