According to the supplier, inspections at its factory carried out by authorities on Friday confirmed that the production and cooking processes “fully comply with food safety standards”. The official investigation and test results had yet to be released, the supplier added. Authorities deemed the “classroom on-site portioning” arrangement at the school “suboptimal”, given “the lack of professional cooking and heat preservation equipment on campus”, the supplier said. It said the students handled the portioning themselves, and, combined with waiting times before consumption, these were factors that could allow bacteria to multiply rapidly before eating. “When the insulated food containers are opened in classrooms for portioning, the exposed surface area increases dramatically, leading to rapid heat loss in a short period and pushing the food into a temperature danger zone [where bacteria can multiply],” the supplier said. It added that, from Monday, at the affected school it would fully transition to individual, food-grade safe polypropylene containers transported under hot-holding conditions to enhance safety and efficiency. It also cited results of school lunch sampling inspections on Wednesday, which recorded no abnormalities in appearance, odour, taste or hygiene. The company supplied lunchboxes and provided on-site portioning services to 71 schools and institutions last Wednesday, totalling 17,683 meals. No other schools reported similar symptoms after consumption, the company said. It added that, as advised by authorities, it would also temporarily suspend the supply of the food items involved in the incident from Monday. Food poisoning clusters involving school lunches were last recorded in January, affecting 39 students from two primary schools. In September 2024, a school in Tai Po reported 51 cases of diarrhoea and vomiting after food from its canteen was eaten. In a notable case in 2023, major lunchbox supplier Luncheon Star suspended operations for two days to deep-clean its production line amid safety fears, after several pupils reported falling ill after eating its products. A spokeswoman for the Education Bureau said it reminded schools that if they adopted the “on-site meal distribution” model, they had to ensure sufficient space, facilities such as food warming and dishwashing equipment, and manpower to maintain cleanliness, efficiency and immediate post-meal washing. “The bureau will continue to monitor school lunch arrangements following the start of the academic year and provide advice and input to schools in a timely manner,” she said.

title: Philippines holding historic election in Muslim autonomous region
description: Under a 2014 peace deal brokered by Malaysia, the Moro Islamic Liberation Front gave up its goal of a separate state in exchange for autonomy.
content: Voters in an autonomous southern Philippine region will cast their ballots on Monday in the region’s first parliamentary elections, seen as a crucial step in the quest for self-determination and lasting peace after decades of insurgency and violence. The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, or BARMM, covers five provinces, three cities and 63 villages across eight special geographic area clusters. It has nearly 2.4 million voters, with election officials aiming for an 80 per cent turnout after polling was postponed for several years. There are 80 seats at stake in the elections that will determine members of parliament on September 14. These include 40 political party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives. Unlike the direct voting under the presidential system of the national government, the region’s chief minister, who heads the executive branch, is not elected by voters. Members of parliament will choose the chief minister from among themselves by a majority vote during their first parliamentary session. Voters will choose one regional party, one district representative and six sectoral representatives. The 40 regional party-representative seats will be distributed to nominees based on a party’s vote share. History of strife Centuries of colonialism by Spain, the US and Filipino Christian settlers turned Muslims into a minority group in resource-rich Mindanao, the southern third of the Philippine archipelago from which the BARMM was carved out. The region has seen decades of intermittent but bloody conflicts over land, resources and political power. Since the 1970s, about 150,000 combatants and civilians have died in the southern Philippines, while development was stunted in the country’s poorest region. Western and Asian governments feared the tenacious insurgencies could help foster Islamic extremism in Southeast Asia. The presence of private armies and long-running clan wars has added to the violent mix. Under a 2014 peace deal brokered by Malaysia, the largest Muslim rebel group – the Moro Islamic Liberation Front – gave up its goal of a separate Muslim state in the south of the largely Catholic country in exchange for broader autonomy. The group’s 40,000 fighters would be “demobilised” and given livelihoods and other help to bring them back to normal life. The Bangsamoro region was established under the peace deal to replace a poverty-wracked five-province autonomous region with a larger, better-funded and more powerful area, which has been governed by former guerrilla leaders under a transition period that ends with the first regular elections on September 14. Regional challenges The Moro Islamic Liberation Front last year suspended the disarming of its remaining 14,000 fighters after claiming that the government has not fully complied with socio-economic commitments it made under the 2014 peace deal. Then presidential assistant David Diciano, who had been helping oversee the transformation of the Bangsamoro region, said in a statement at the time that the Muslim rebel front’s central committee had decided “to postpone the decommissioning of 14,000 of its combatants and 2,450 of their weapons.” The Institute for Autonomy and Governance, a non-profit policy and research centre based in the region, has noted that the incomplete decommissioning of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front’s combatants as well as the organisation’s split into two rival political parties vying in the elections pose a potential danger of violence that may affect voters’ confidence in going out to vote. More than 20,000 military and police personnel are being deployed to secure the elections, officials said. “We have just one goal: for them to be able to vote. All our preparations and efforts would be in vain if our fellow citizens couldn’t vote,” Commission on Elections Chairman Erwin Garcia said. Sustaining parliamentary democracy Michael Henry Yusingco, a senior research fellow of the Ateneo Policy Centre, said, “Without a party ethos that is rooted in collective responsibility, mutual respect, and orientation toward the common good, parliaments risk devolving into arenas of personal rivalries, factional disputes, or transactional politics.” He said it is the right time for regional parties to show they can embody such party ethos to sustain parliamentary democracy. “Clearly, the BARMM’s history of clan politics, electoral violence, and patronage-based loyalties presents formidable challenges.”

title: Does Beijing need AI talent in ‘public opinion war’ over South China Sea?
description: Think tanks, seen as a vital soft power tool by Beijing, have been urged to recruit more tech expertise to help sway international opinion.
content: A leading South China Sea analyst has urged Chinese think tanks to recruit AI talent for the “public opinion war” over the disputed waters. Wu Shicun, the founding president of China’s National Institute for South China Sea Studies, said Chinese humanities and social science research had traditionally operated in a “lone-wolf” fashion and lacked interdisciplinary diversity. “The situation in the South China Sea is likely to evolve into a complex, multilayered competition … Cognitive and public opinion warfare has become a primary battlefield,” he told a forum in Shenzhen on Saturday. He added that physical maritime power alone would not offset losing the narrative battle. Once an adversary managed to frame an incident as “a big power bullying a smaller neighbour”, a delayed counter-response made that perception nearly impossible to reverse, he said. “That is why we urgently need talent in this field.” He urged think tanks to employ more scientists and algorithm engineers, “moving beyond traditional scholars engaged in theoretical debate and replacing pure commentary with technical and engineering capabilities”. Several other Chinese think tanks have been looking to harness artificial intelligence (AI) to better monitor global public opinion and amplify China’s messaging overseas. Saturday’s event took place amid fresh tensions between China and the United States over AI, following accusations that Chinese AI companies were copying American models “on an industrial scale”. Think tank leaders at Saturday’s event said there was a need for rigorous researcher training and for AI use to be regulated to curb security risks and avoid breaking national red lines. The Shenzhen forum, which discussed the development of Chinese think tanks, was also warned that Western dominance in AI training threatened China’s “knowledge sovereignty”. Wu Zhiliang, the deputy director of the culture, historical data and studies committee on the country’s top political advisory body, said China’s modernisation “has not yet been fully transformed into internationally influential ideas, resources or computable, structured knowledge data sets”. China’s think tank sector had “many institutions, [but] little genuine wisdom”, he argued. “Repositioning think tanks in the AI era goes beyond updating tools and methods … It demands a complete overhaul of how knowledge is produced and how value judgments are framed,” Wu said. Over the past decade, Beijing has stepped up efforts to expand its think tanks as soft-power tools. China had 1,329, one of the world’s highest numbers, by the end of last year, according to the latest China Think Tank Report. Other speakers said think tanks should create their own custom models. Guo Hai, executive dean of the Institute of Public Policy at the South China University of Technology in Guangzhou, urged researchers to ground their work in first-hand findings and establish a traceable verification system for policy reports. “We should also deploy domain-specific vertical AI models tailored to our think tank’s operational workflows. This will improve data accuracy while addressing security and privacy concerns,” Guo said. The forum, on the development and transformation of Chinese think tanks in the AI era, came days after the US company Anthropic accused its Chinese rivals DeepSeek and Moonshot of re-routing customer requests to its Claude models. It said this had exposed sensitive customer data across the US, Europe and China, including details about a user “likely” affiliated with the People’s Liberation Army. Earlier this month, the US government claimed that six Chinese companies – including DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding – were engaged in an industrial campaign to steal US model outputs, “likely with Chinese government awareness”. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Beijing rejected these allegations, calling them an effort to suppress China’s AI industry, and threatened retaliatory measures. Both countries are preparing for their first dialogue on AI risks ahead of the planned presidential meeting between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington later this month.

title: Hong Kong teen battling rare disease creates AI avatar to ensure his story lives on
description: Chen Tsz-kin, 17, who suffers from muscular dystrophy, says that while life may come to an end, AI can allow his message of perseverance to continue.
content: A Hong Kong teenager with a rare muscle-wasting disease has created an AI version of himself, hoping the digital twin can continue sharing his life story and message of perseverance even after he is gone. Chen Tsz-kin, 17, unveiled “AI Tsz-kin” at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) on Sunday, weeks before his 18th birthday – an age the student said he had long feared reaching because he was once told it was the average life expectancy for people with his disease, Duchenne muscular dystrophy. “Life may come to an end, but through different means, AI can allow [my message] to continue,” he said. “Even if one day I am no longer here, I just hope people remember the spirit behind it.” Tsz-kin was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy when he was just 1½ years old. The progressive rare and deadly condition causes muscles to weaken over time, and he now uses a wheelchair, wears a back brace and relies on a breathing machine at night. Even so, he has spent much of his childhood pursuing experiences that might have seemed impossible, including travelling to the Kyrgyz highlands, completing a 100km desert expedition with support from volunteers, paragliding and diving. Tsz-kin’s health has worsened over the past year. He suffered pneumonia twice – after contracting influenza in January and respiratory syncytial virus in August – with the second bout leaving him frightened about whether he would survive. “For the first time since I was little, I broke down crying in front of my mum,” he said. The experience made him think more deeply about how his beliefs and experiences could live on, even as his physical strength declined. The artificial intelligence (AI) project began about 18 months ago with Hong Kong-listed visual effects and virtual human company Digital Domain. About 400 images of his face were captured to recreate his appearance, while recordings made over roughly six weeks were used to reproduce his voice and pronunciation. His life experiences and views were also fed into the system. At Sunday’s event, the avatar answered the audience’s questions about his travels, favourite foods, outlook on death and relationship with his mother. When asked what he would say to her, the AI Tsz-kin replied: “Thank you for always taking such good care of me and supporting me. I know it has been very hard for you, but your love is my greatest motivation.” William Wong, chairman of the board at Digital Domain Holdings, said the company wanted the avatar to feel more personal and conversational than virtual humans it developed for commercial clients. “We are not trying to replace Tsz-kin,” Wong said. “We hope technology can help him share his experiences with more people, while reducing some of the physical burden on him.” Tsz-kin, who hopes to study social work, stressed that the avatar could never replicate the emotional impact of a living person. But he said that was not the point. “If, when people face difficulties in the future, they remember something I once shared and remember not to give up, that is already enough for me,” he said. “Then I would have no regrets.”

title: My Take | US-Israeli failure to bomb Iran into submission was preordained
description: From Nazi Germany to Vietnam, history is rich with examples of countries that simply refuse to surrender to bombing.
content: Winston Churchill famously praised the resilience of the British people during the Blitz, describing the nightly bombings of London as a “cruel, wanton, indiscriminate” attempt by Adolf Hitler to break the spirit of a tough “island race”. He was not wrong about the toughness and courage of his fellow citizens. But as one of the United Kingdom’s greatest leaders and historical writers, he created a false impression of the uniqueness of the British wartime experience. Strategic bombing alone, without the reinforcement of ground troops, almost never achieves its purpose. British resistance was not the exception but the rule. The war launched by Israel and the United States against Iran is a case in point. As Trita Parsee of the Quincy Institute, a Washington-based think tank, told the South China Morning Post, “it’s safe to say that the [Iranian] government’s internal position is stronger than it was six months ago.” Just by surviving, Tehran is winning. He said that “the Iranians have really survived an attack that almost no other country in the region would be able to survive”. He added: “They have been attacked by two nuclear-weapon states and they have essentially come out on top… As a result, their deterrence [against] the other states has increased, and their leverage has increased internally.” That seems obvious. Yet leaders such as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump have boasted that they could bomb their adversary into submission and that its people would rise up to overthrow their government. In his latest escalation, Trump called on the Iranian people to rise up: “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” Aside from the criminality, that way of thinking seems absurd. When you bomb a people and a society mercilessly, they would not welcome your war and rise up to overthrow their government, however much they despise it. Instead, they would instinctively feel a deep sense of nationalism and solidarity. You have effectively re-legitimised their government, as we are witnessing in Iran today. I have never felt more Canadian than when Trump threatened to make Canada America’s 51st state and renamed, by executive order, Lake Ontario as Lake America. And he hasn’t even bombed Toronto yet. The Allied bombings of Germany were far more brutal and sustained than the Blitz. But German war production peaked between 1943 and 1944, and civilian resolve did not break until a two-pronged ground invasion from the west and the east by Allied forces. Between 1965 and 1975, Washington bombed Vietnam to smithereens, having dropped roughly 7.6 million tonnes of ordnance on Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia – the latter two countries were not even supposed to be in the war – compared with about 2.1 million tonnes of bombs dropped across both the European and Pacific theatres combined during World War II. Imperial Japan did surrender from aerial bombing but only because it was threatened with complete annihilation by the then-new atomic weapons. Since then, no nuclear-armed country has dared to deploy them in combat. Perhaps the closest contemporary comparison to the levelling by atomic bombs of Hiroshima and Nagasaki is the Israeli war on Gaza. In April last year, peace studies specialist and University of Bradford Emeritus Professor Paul Rogers made the plausible estimate that the Gaza bombing was “equivalent to six Hiroshimas”. He compared the 70 kilotonnes of ordnance dropped across Gaza to the 12 kilotonnes yield from the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. Most other estimates, however, put the equivalent TNT yields at 15 to 16 kilotonnes in Hiroshima and 25 kilotonnes at Nagasaki. Still, Rogers’ point holds. Robert Pape, a University of Chicago political scientist and an authority on the history of aerial bombing, has laid out the contours of the Iran war during a series of interviews with major American newscasters such as Fox News, PBS and CNN International. While precision air strikes easily achieve tactical goals such as destroying facilities and eliminating leaders, they do not guarantee the desired political or strategic outcome, he argues. Like invasion, foreign bombing changes the political equation on the ground, uniting the targeted public and the regime against an outside aggressor rather than encouraging rebellion. Instead of collapsing, regimes typically respond with increased aggression and/or are replaced by a more radical and nationalistic leadership. Far from encouraging rebellion or democratic uprisings, targeted citizens naturally consider the foreign power dropping bombs on their children their more immediate enemy. Churchill himself warned against relying too much on aerial bombardment alone at the dawn of militarised aviation, in 1917. That was long before strategic or carpet bombing was a thing. “It is not reasonable to speak of an air offensive as if it were going to finish the war by itself,” he wrote with great prescience. “It is improbable that any terrorisation of the civil population which could be achieved by air attack would compel the government of a great nation to surrender.” His insight is as true today as it was during World War I. However, being historically uninformed and strategically incompetent, Trump is mesmerised by unrivalled American air power and wrongly assumes it can deliver what his heart desires. You can’t say the same about Netanyahu, who reportedly talked Trump into going to war against Iran, something he had failed with every previous US president. Perhaps any war that militarily weakens Iran and destabilises the region at America’s expense is considered good for Israel’s regional expansionist ambitions. Netanyahu was willing to throw the dice. The unintended consequences of the war have come to haunt him and his country. More is yet to come.

title: China’s FAST telescope maps neutral hydrogen, the cosmic gas for making stars
description: Survey identifies more than 156,000 extragalactic sources, offering an unprecedented pool for studying the universe’s biggest questions.
content: China’s FAST telescope has compiled the world’s largest catalogue of neutral hydrogen beyond the Milky Way, replacing a long-dominant US survey as the main reference for mapping the gas that fuels the formation of stars and galaxies. The FAST All-Sky H I Survey (FASHI), conducted with the 500-metre (1,640-foot) radio dish in southwest China’s Guizhou province, released its second batch of data this week. It contains 156,411 extragalactic sources – nearly five times the number detected by the now-defunct Arecibo Telescope in Puerto Rico. The publicly available data gives astronomers worldwide an unprecedented pool of galaxies to investigate some of the universe’s biggest questions – from how the vast cosmic web took shape, to why some galaxies thrive while others fade away. Compared with ALFALFA – the landmark US survey carried out with Arecibo from 2005 to 2012 – FASHI covered about three times as much sky and detected galaxies that were much smaller, fainter and further away, a team led by researchers from the National Astronomical Observatories reported. The work established “a legacy data set that bridges the gap” between earlier surveys and the coming Square Kilometre Array – a massive international radio telescope now being built in Australia and South Africa, they wrote in a study published in the peer-reviewed journal Science China Physics, Mechanics & Astronomy this month. For more than half a century, Arecibo’s 305-metre dish was an icon of radio astronomy. Completed in 1963, it remained the world’s largest single-aperture radio telescope until FAST overtook it in 2016, and was behind a string of major astronomical discoveries before its giant observing platform collapsed in 2020. Built into a natural depression in the mountains of Guizhou, FAST’s 500-metre reflector gives it greater sensitivity, while its ability to observe 19 patches of sky at once – compared with Arecibo’s seven – allows it to scan large areas much faster. One of FAST’s key targets is neutral hydrogen, the basic form of the universe’s most abundant element and the raw material for making stars. Its atoms give off a distinctive radio signal with a wavelength of 21cm (8.2 inches) that can pass through cosmic dust, revealing vast reservoirs of gas otherwise difficult to see. FASHI began systematically searching for that signal in 2020. Its first data release in January 2024 catalogued 41,741 galaxies – already surpassing ALFALFA’s final tally of roughly 31,500. The new release, based on observations through July 2025, nearly quadrupled that number. The huge sample could shed light on some of the universe’s least visible mysteries, such as how ordinary matter was distributed within the invisible framework of dark matter. The first FASHI release quickly gained international attention, with its paper cited more than 100 times since 2024, according to the National Astronomical Observatories. The full second release is now open to researchers worldwide, allowing teams to mine the data for their own studies. It could also serve as a benchmark for the next generation of radio surveys, including those planned with the Square Kilometre Array. Passionate about science? title: On all fours or off to a wilderness retreat? How Hongkongers are reclaiming their calm
description: From animal flow to film therapy and journaling, residents are embracing movement, mindfulness and micro‑pauses to rebuild resilience in a fast-paced city.
content: In the final instalment of the Health Matters wellness series on Hong Kong’s growing wellness trends, Emily Hung examines alternative therapies helping residents restore their balance, as practitioners stress that small, conscious moments can make the biggest difference. For Hong Kong film practitioner Ngai Tsz-wai, peace of mind begins on all fours. The 40-year-old practises animal flow, a quadrupedal, ground-based movement system that blends elements of yoga, dance, gymnastics and martial arts. “Moving on all fours helps me train strength, flexibility and coordination while rebuilding the connection between body and mind,” Ngai told the South China Morning Post. “Just as water needs to flow, our body and mind need movement to create new possibilities … which is helpful for my creative work.” Ngai’s journey into wellness began a decade ago while producing a video for a local yoga studio, where an instructor encouraged him to try a class. He soon adopted yoga, later adding daily morning meditation, breathwork, journaling and retreats in nature to his routine. “Starting a new day with meditation keeps me clear-headed, bringing me back to my own world and helping me stay grounded against external influences, good or bad,” he said. Ngai is among a growing number of Hong Kong residents leaning into wellness routines to navigate high-pressure careers and restore emotional balance. From a five-minute desk doodle to an off-grid retreat in the Mongolian wilderness, local health and wellness practitioners explain how these diverse practices work – and how anyone can integrate meaningful pauses into daily life. Calm over chaos On the tranquil island of Peng Chau, a 30-minute boat ride from Central, Zero Chan launched Island Within in 2020, offering wellness retreats centred around a cosy studio, the shade of nearby trees and the shore of a small beach. A singing bowl therapist and mindful yoga instructor, Chan structures her retreat day as a three-stage progressive journey to help participants foster self-awareness. Participants begin with gentle yoga and qigong to build physical awareness, followed by a sound bath for deeper relaxation, then “inner exploration exercises” such as flower arrangement, calligraphy and reflection card games to unpack subconscious patterns. “Driven by a need for safety, we often overthink and react out of fear before anything happens,” she said. “However, when we become aware of this anxiety, we can pause and make a conscious choice to respond rather than react automatically, thus rewiring the neural pathways and saving ourselves.” Chan said her classes filled rapidly during the Covid-19 pandemic, allowing her to host two sessions a week. Although demand stabilised after the border reopened, she still hosts a session almost every week, alongside on-site retreats for companies and NGOs. “People continue to join retreats, though they could have visited Shenzhen for a nice massage, because they are looking for a lasting sense of spiritual grounding,” she said. “Out there, people rarely get the chance to catch their breath or vent freely without facing judgment or unsolicited advice … Deep down, they are looking to reconnect with who they truly are.” Nature as teacher For those seeking a more radical shift, stepping entirely out of controlled, urban environments and into raw nature can offer a profound lesson in letting go. Bhakti Wong, a somatic psychotherapist and yoga instructor with more than two decades of experience, has led retreats to Mongolia for three years and is planning another in Finland next year. Wong said she chose Mongolia because its pure, raw nature offered an unmanufactured retreat without traditional spa amenities, allowing participants’ whole systems to relax. The retreat typically lasts seven to nine days, costing around HK$25,000 to HK$30,000 (US$3,188 to US$3,826), excluding flights and insurance. Each group consists of around 10 participants, who stay with nomadic families at yurt camps with no Wi-fi, electricity or running water – but are well cared for. The itinerary is light, with typically one activity each day, such as horse riding, river rafting, archery or a shamanic ceremony, giving participants ample time to rest and reflect. Wong said she believed that taking time to observe an entirely different way of life helped participants return home with a broader, more open perspective. For example, she recalled how the nomads chose not to interfere when an injured baby goat fell behind the herd, as its fate was to feed the wolves – a “strangely harmonious” way in which life-and-death challenges were accepted and embraced. “A lot of the time we see things from our perspective and our world, and we forget to see the bigger picture that everyone has challenges,” she said. “When they see it in nature – whether it’s animals or the way the nomadic families live, and how they take on challenges – it gives them a direct experience of something very natural to someone else.” Let films do the talking When days-long retreats are not feasible for busy urbanites bound by tight schedules and budgets, cinema can offer an unexpected sanctuary. Jasmin Fong Ting, a counselling psychologist specialising in cinematherapy, said watching films was not only a cathartic experience but also a way to uncover underlying, unspoken needs. “Movies can act as an ‘affect bridge’, connecting us to emotions that we were previously unaware of or had suppressed subconsciously,” said Fong, who previously worked in the film industry. “Highly rational people might struggle to speak about their feelings directly, but immersing themselves in films can help bypass the rational thinking process and unlock core emotions through impactful scenes.” Unlike traditional film studies, cinematherapy focuses on the viewer’s “subjective reality” – how an individual connects a movie to their personal memories and values, regardless of whether they interpret the plot exactly as intended. While formal cinematherapy takes place in professional sessions or psychoeducation, Fong said people could use cinema as a tool for personal growth. To practise that, Fong suggested setting aside dedicated, quiet time free from distractions. Viewers should tune into their emotional reactions and jot down quick notes whenever a scene, dialogue or character moment triggers a strong feeling, saving analysis for after the credits. Afterwards, they can use the notes to reflect on four areas: the scene that stood out; the emotions triggered; the personal memories or values brought up; and practical actions to address those insights. Fong recalled watching the 2002 Hong Kong film July Rhapsody. Rather than focusing on the main plot about a midlife crisis, she was deeply struck by a single scene: a high school teacher sitting quietly at a reunion surrounded by loud, wealthy classmates. “I wasn’t a middle-aged man, but that scene captured my hidden anxieties about the future – will I become just as ordinary in 10 years if I become a teacher? – at that point, it connected directly to my own reality,” she said. Fong noted that cinematherapy worked best for film lovers with a capacity for self-reflection, rather than those experiencing acute distress, severe trauma or attention difficulties. Comparing mental resilience to a bank account, Fong highlighted self-awareness and emotional release as psychological capital that protected people from distress. “You need to be aware of your needs to know you have a choice … Our choices come from knowing what we need,” she said. Small pauses, big shifts If sitting down for a film feels like too much of a commitment, art might offer quick exercises that fit into even the busiest schedules, with no artistic talent required. “Just like physical resilience, we need to build mental resilience in our everyday lives – understanding our preferences, core values, boundaries … and sources of security – through constant daily self-awareness,” art psychotherapist Gigi Leung Ching-wan said. That practice can start at a desk with a five-minute micro-pause: leave the phone behind, place one hand on the heart, ask “How’s my day?” and write it down. While keeping a journal requires commitment, Leung noted that it remained one of the most accessible tools: “Journaling helps you build resilience by witnessing your own growth and learning from your past experiences.” Other low-barrier exercises that can happen at a desk include doodling – even just scribbling freely on a piece of paper to feel the stroke of the pen – and tearing magazine pages to make collages. Those who struggled with blank pages could try “automatic writing” – writing down word associations rapidly without logic for just a few minutes, she said. In an efficiency-driven city, Leung said taking time for these seemingly useless pauses provided essential breathing room, serving as an anchor back to the present moment to disrupt intrusive thoughts of inadequacy or isolation. “We need to practise returning to the present moment, focusing on ourselves right here and right now, rather than an anxiety about the future or depression from the past,” she said. “However, we should refrain from going all-or-nothing … if you try 5 or 10 per cent, that’s still a good trial. You don’t need to do 100 per cent to make it worthwhile.” It’s in the little things Clinical psychologist Dr Amos Cheung said wellness activities could increase the variety of daily life, though improving mental wellness did not always require grand gestures. “We often do not feel the many pleasant moments in our lived experiences because we spend quite a lot of time on mindless actions, such as scrolling endlessly on our digital devices,” he said. “Scrolling is a good distraction from everything troubling you, but at the end of the day, you feel a stronger sense of losing control rather than gaining control.” Those “pleasant moments”, for example, could be enjoying an ice cream, chatting with family members over a meal, or simply taking good care of oneself by listening to favourite songs or stretching for 15 minutes, he said. “Rather than thinking you have no choice, so you just buy baked pork chop rice, you could think that you actually feel like having baked pork chop rice, so you buy it for yourself. The result is the same, but you feel better,” he said. “These actions aren’t about chasing intense happiness, but having the conscious awareness to feel those subtle moments that make you feel good about yourself.” However, Cheung warned that if low mood or loss of interest persisted for weeks alongside deteriorating sleep, professional support should be sought. For film practitioner Ngai, building this ongoing self-awareness ultimately reframed his relationship with his craft. “I’ve learned to let go of the obsession with gains and losses,” he said. “We often become too goal-oriented because we want to be seen. But when we stop worrying about the outcome and start enjoying the process, the stress naturally dissolves.”

title: Review | Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom movie review – Aardman’s hilarious horror spoof
description: Aardman Animations’ latest is a horror-infused celebration of slapstick and sly film references sure to delight viewers of all ages.
content: 4/5 stars Shaun the Sheep turns mad scientist in his mischievous third big-screen outing, unleashing a hirsute horror that terrorises the sleepy farm community after an unconventional attempt to grow pumpkins. Realised in Aardman’s signature stop-motion and devoid of any spoken dialogue, Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom – the feature debut of veteran series directors Steve Cox and Matthew Walker – is a hilarious, horror-infused celebration of slapstick, sight gags and sly film references sure to delight audiences of all ages. In the run-up to Halloween, all the residents of Mossy Bottom Farm are getting into the spooky spirit. The Farmer (voiced incomprehensibly by John Sparkes) has tickets to Mossingham’s Halloween Hoedown but is reluctant to ask the Vet (Nina Sosanya) to be his date because of his receding hairline. Shaun (Justin Fletcher) and the rest of the flock, meanwhile, have been cultivating a secret pumpkin patch with an eye to fashioning jack-o’-lanterns. But when an altercation between the Farmer and his belligerent goat sees their crop destroyed, Shaun has to think fast. In the rundown windmill on the edge of the farmland, Shaun finds a book on “Homemade Science”. Following a night of frantic experimentation, the desperate sheep emerges with a potion that he decants into a discarded bottle of the Farmer’s hair tonic. After Shaun pours the mixture over some remaining pumpkin seeds, the transformation is swift and miraculous. Unfortunately, the Farmer’s trusty dog Bitzer returns the tonic to its owner, who applies some to his own polished pate with equally extraordinary results. Within its opening seconds, the film playfully references James Whale’s Frankenstein and Michael Jackson’s Thriller, setting the tone for an 80-minute love letter to classic horror films, albeit in the guise of a colourful children’s animation. But for every knowing reference to The Wolfman or Psycho, there are just as many organically grown gags poking fun at everything from social media influencers to slapdash mail couriers, as Shaun and his farmyard chums set off on another madcap adventure to rescue their bumbling yet beloved patriarch. That the film succeeds in delighting horror fanatics and restless toddlers in equal measure is a testament to the incredible writers and animators who have guided this franchise impeccably across the big and small screens since Shaun’s first appearance in 1995’s Academy Award-winning Wallace & Gromit short, A Close Shave. Even more astonishing is that The Beast of Mossy Bottom is not the first film this year to accomplish such a feat, as Minions & Monsters walked an identical line to equally winning effect earlier this summer. Anyone still claiming horror films are not for kids needs to pay a visit to Mossy Bottom this Halloween. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Sweden’s election too close to call as final votes are counted
description: Swedes await final tallies as left-leaning opposition holds a razor-thin lead in the race.
content: Sweden’s general election was too close to call early Monday, as the incumbent prime minister and the left-wing opposition leader both said they were ready to govern and the far-right was seen losing ground. With more than 90 per cent of votes counted, four opposition parties led by Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, held a three-seat majority in the 349-seat parliament over Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats. “For now, we are in the lead. And if that is confirmed, Sweden will have a new government,” 59-year-old Andersson, who was Sweden’s first woman prime minister in 2021-2022, told her supporters. But her party – which ruled the Scandinavian country for most of the 20th century and remains Sweden’s largest – also looked to be heading for its worst score in over a century with 28 per cent of the vote. Outgoing prime minister Kristersson, whose Moderate Party was credited with 19.9 per cent of the counted votes, meanwhile said that if the result stood, he would respect Andersson’s attempts to try to form a government with the three other parties on the left. But he noted that the four had irreconcilable differences, primarily between the Left Party and the Centre Party, and were unlikely to agree on a government programme. “I will therefore, even if tonight’s result stands, examine whether there are any possibilities within this non-socialist parliamentary majority to find some workable government constellation,” Kristersson told his supporters. “Which government is going to govern Sweden in the coming years is still an open question,” Kristersson declared. In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which entered parliament in 2010, lost support for the first time, garnering 17.6 per cent of the vote, down from 20.6 per cent in 2022. “We don’t yet have the full election result, but it’s obvious that we’ve lost a few percentage points compared with our result four years ago,” party leader Jimmie Akesson told an election night watch party. But he said it was a success that supporters were no longer afraid to show their support for the party long seen as a political pariah. “There are now so many more people around our country who no longer find it difficult to say that they are Sweden Democrats,” Akesson said. The final outcome might not be clear for a few days, several party leaders said. Municipal election authorities will start counting votes on Wednesday that had not reached their destination on election night. In Sweden, all votes are also automatically recounted by the regional county administrative boards, which establishes the final result. This process usually takes a week. Kristersson has headed a minority coalition backed by the Sweden Democrats for four years, giving the far-right influence over policy in exchange for support in parliament. Kristersson had promised the Sweden Democrats key cabinet posts if the right-wing won. Throughout the campaign, opinion polls gave a comfortable lead to the left-wing opposition, but the gap narrowed to a dead heat in the final days. Much of the campaign focused on healthcare and helping struggling households cope with rising costs. Andersson, the first woman to head Sweden’s government in 2021-2022, has pledged to raise taxes on banks and high incomes, cut healthcare queues, and improve declining school results. Kristersson meanwhile vowed to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives now that his government’s clampdown on organised crime and immigration was starting to show results. Deadly shootings and bombings by organised crime networks have fallen sharply in recent years, while asylum applications were at a record low. “We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people … to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson said before the vote, borrowing US President Donald Trump’s trademark slogan. Over the past two decades, far-right leader Akesson has steered the party with neo-Nazi roots into the mainstream. “Sweden is becoming safer, better, and more Swedish,” Akesson told a campaign rally on Saturday, surrounded by blue-and-yellow “Make Sweden Sweden Again” posters.

title: Hong Kong to deepen ties with Global South and Middle East, finance chief says
description: Financial Secretary Paul Chan says city will build ‘networked, institutionalised’ links with emerging economies, from green finance to research and development.
content: Hong Kong will deepen ties with emerging economies worldwide, expanding connections with the Middle East and belt and road countries, from finance to innovation and technology, according to the finance chief. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po also said the city aimed to build “networked and institutionalised” connectivity with the Global South – a broad term for developing less-industrialised countries, primarily located in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Belt and road countries are nations that have signed cooperation agreements or participate in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s plan to link global economies into a China-centred trading network. In his weekly blog post on Sunday, Chan cited the country’s 15th five-year plan, writing: “The nation’s steadfast and all-round support [for Hong Kong] forms the foundation for Hong Kong to accelerate its engagement with the Global South.” The 2026-30 national blueprint pledges support for Hong Kong to develop into an international innovation and technology centre, and to consolidate and enhance its status as a global hub for finance, shipping and trade. “A broader domain of cross-regional cooperation also includes green transition, which requires alignment of standards and rules,” Chan said. “Climate change exerts the most direct impact on the Global South, and the substantial financing gap in green transition demands credible standards that allow investors to deploy capital with confidence and precision.” He noted that green and sustainable bond issuance arranged in Hong Kong totalled US$20.2 billion in the first half of this year, ranking first in Asia for eight consecutive years. “Capital requires channels, technology requires application scenarios, and rules are the key elements that enable the two to connect. This is another contribution Hong Kong makes to the Global South,” he said. He stressed the cooperation was mutually beneficial. “The Global South brings more business opportunities, capital inflows and deeper market liquidity to Hong Kong, while Hong Kong provides substantive and essential support for their development,” he said. On closer financial ties with the Middle East, Chan noted that Sohar International Bank, the second-largest lender in Oman, had opened its first office outside the Middle East in Hong Kong, becoming the first bank from the sultanate to set up in the city. The Oman Investment Authority also announced plans to participate in the Hong Kong government’s Innovation and Technology Venture Fund. Chan highlighted that cooperation between Hong Kong and the Middle East was expanding from “finance into innovation and technology … elevating bilateral economic and investment relations into broader domains”. Chan also pointed to Hong Kong’s solid research and development capabilities, backed by the strength of the innovation and industrial chain of the Greater Bay Area. The cluster comprises Hong Kong, Macau and nine mainland Chinese cities. “For partners in the Middle East and Central Asia, this means that Hong Kong offers practical innovation and research capabilities, commercialisation pathways, and high-end industrial capacity. “When these strengths are combined with the advanced manufacturing capabilities and vast market of Greater Bay Area cities, the outcome is not only commercial returns but also high-quality development that benefits all parties.”

title: Japan’s WEGO fashion brand is latest firm to feel force of Chinese consumer backlash
description: WEGO scrapped a collaboration with an anime and manga franchise that triggered controversy with a perceived reference to wartime atrocities.
content: Japanese fashion brand WEGO has scrapped a plan to launch a new range in collaboration with the hit anime and manga franchise My Hero Academia after it triggered an angry backlash from Chinese consumers. The Tokyo-based company triggered an outcry on Chinese social media after announcing it would release an exclusive range of My Hero Academia-themed clothing. The franchise was widely condemned in China over a 2020 controversy about a character that conducted lethal human experiments – a topic which evoked memories of the notorious wartime Unit 731, responsible for the deaths of thousands of mainly Chinese prisoners. The character’s name, Maruta Shiga, added fuel to the fire, because maruta (or log) was a derisive name given to the subjects of the unit’s human experiments. Some social media users also suggested that the surname Shiga was a reference to the scientist Kiyoshi Shiga, who has a bacterium named after him. The proposed launch date for the line – September 18, the 95th anniversary of the 1931 Mukden Incident, which served as the pretext for Japan’s invasion of China – further inflamed tensions. The furore underscores the persistent grass-roots acrimony over Japan’s imperial history that continues to sour relations between the two countries. Tensions between the two governments have also been running high for months, and the controversy happened to coincide with a visit to China by Japanese lawmakers intended to ease tensions. WEGO, which is planning to open its first Chinese flagship store in Shanghai later this month, has been growing rapidly in Asia’s largest market. It proved its drawing power in 2024, when a pop-up store in Shanghai generated 4 million yuan (US$560,000) in sales in six days. Its store on China’s largest e-commerce platform Taobao – whose parent company Alibaba also owns the South China Morning Post – sells more than 300,000 items each year. The retailer’s Chinese subsidiary issued an apology on social media on Friday, saying it “respected [Chinese] public sensibilities”. It added: “This collaboration was planned and launched in Japan by our Japanese parent company, WEGO, solely for the Japanese market. We deeply apologise for our failure to exercise adequate due diligence in the content.” Meanwhile, the Japanese parent firm posted a one-sentence notice of cancellation citing unspecified “circumstances” on Saturday. There has been no comment on the current row from My Hero Academia, but in 2020 its creator Kohei Horikoshi promised to change the character’s name, saying he took the issue “very seriously”. Both the artist and Shonen Jump, the magazine that published the manga, said there had been no intention to make any historical allusions. Earlier this year, another popular manga franchise, Detective Conan, was boycotted at several Chinese comic conventions over a collaboration with the creators of My Hero Academia. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Tokyo and Beijing are at their lowest ebb in a decade. The current chill set in after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said in November that an attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan justifying military intervention. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Japan, in common with most countries, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. Beijing retaliated by freezing high-level ministerial dialogue, suspending imports of Japanese seafood and tightening export restrictions on dual-use goods and rare earths. Tourist numbers also dropped significantly, and in the past two months nearly a third of scheduled passenger flights from mainland China to Japan were cancelled. Both countries have also significantly increased visa fees for visitors. However, some Japanese politicians and trade groups have been trying to restore communication channels. On Sunday, an eight-member cross-party parliamentary delegation from the Japan-China Friendship Parliamentarians’ Union began a three-day visit to Beijing. The group, led by Masahiro Komura, a member of the ruling Liberal Democrats, is scheduled to meet officials from the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries and tour international trade exhibitions. Another parliamentary delegation led by Shinichi Isa, from the opposition Centrist Reform Alliance, also visited late last month. During a meeting with Chinese officials, they were told that the relationship between the two countries was facing “serious difficulties and the root causes are clear”. Meanwhile, a delegation from the Japan Association for the Promotion of International Trade headed by former foreign minister Takeshi Iwaya is scheduled to visit at the end of the month, according to Kyodo News. The body, which serves as a channel for trade and economic exchanges with China, visits nearly every year for high-level talks. Last year it met Premier Li Qiang and is now seeking to meet President Xi Jinping.

title: Chinese researchers extend future memory endurance 100-fold in semiconductor advance
description: Restricting nitrogen-vacancy movement in wurtzite ferroelectrics looks to improve the reliability of next-generation storage, scientists find.
content: Chinese researchers have developed a way to make an emerging type of memory chip much more durable, potentially overcoming a critical reliability barrier to its use in high-performance computing and future artificial intelligence systems as the AI boom drives demand for more advanced semiconductors. The team demonstrated more than 10 billion writing cycles in wurtzite ferroelectrics, a class of materials that can switch between two electric states to store data. The result was roughly 100 times the endurance previously achieved with the same material and could help advance a potential next-generation memory technology, according to an online report published on Saturday by local media outlet Xian Daily. The breakthrough looks to bring ferroelectric memory closer to practical use in future computing hardware. The research, led by scientists at Xian-based Xidian University in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong and Fudan University, was published on Thursday in the journal Science. In recent years, wurtzite ferroelectrics such as aluminium scandium nitride, or AlScN, have gained attention as promising next-generation memory materials because they offer rapid switching speeds and potentially low energy consumption. Crucially, AlScN is also compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes, potentially streamlining its integration into future memory devices. However, the material has faced a significant hurdle: deterioration after repeated electrical switching. Existing AlScN devices have typically failed after roughly 100 million writing cycles – far shy of the billions required for commercial application. Think of ferroelectric material as a neatly planted cornfield, with nitrogen vacancies representing spots where seedlings are missing Wang Ruiqing, Xidian University The researchers said they identified the accumulation of nitrogen vacancies – spots where nitrogen atoms were missing – as a key reason for the relatively rapid failure rate of ferroelectric chips, as the defects create paths for electricity to leak through the chip. Wang Ruiqing, a doctoral researcher at Xidian University and one of the paper’s authors, broke it down more simply for the Xian Daily. “Think of ferroelectric material as a neatly planted cornfield, with nitrogen vacancies representing spots where seedlings are missing,” Wang was quoted as saying. The core issue, Wang explained, was not simply the number of these defects, but their behaviour as the material was repeatedly switched. The nitrogen vacancies could move and cluster together, eventually forming pathways through the material that allowed electricity to leak and could lead to breakdown. “In the past, researchers knew that the devices failed and could observe some of the symptoms, but no one had been able to explain at the atomic scale what was moving, how they were moving and how that movement ultimately caused failure,” Wang said. The team addressed the problem by designing a layered structure that confined the movement of the nitrogen vacancies. By restricting the movement and accumulation of the vacancies, the researchers were able to significantly slow the material’s deterioration, allowing it to withstand more than 10 billion writing cycles, they said in the research. The findings, though still at the laboratory stage, point to a path towards making these materials more durable for dense, low-power memory chips – an advance that comes as the global AI boom continues to fuel demand for faster and more reliable chips.

title: China Porsche owner covers car with 90 missing-child flyers, successfully reuniting a family
description: On Chinese e-commerce platforms, some vendors sell missing-child flyers for about 3 yuan (45 US cents) each to help buyers raise awareness.
content: A Chinese Porsche owner covered his luxury sports car with 90 flyers of missing children, garnering significant attention online. Recently, a Porsche 718 from Kunming, in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, went viral on Chinese social media, with many residents posting about their encounters with the eye-catching vehicle. They filmed the car not for its luxury appeal, but for the striking sight of the flyers featuring missing children that adorned it from bumper to bumper. The owner, Du Lin, explained that his car displays information about 90 missing children, which he obtained from the charity website Baby Come Home. He personally designed the car wrap using the flyers, adding headshots because the version he downloaded from the website only contained text. The Baby Come Home website, founded in 2007 by volunteers Zhang Baoyan and her husband Qin Yanyou, aims to assist parents in searching for their missing children at no cost. Over the past two decades, more than 400,000 volunteers connected through the site have successfully helped 15,000 families reunite. Families seeking help from Baby Come Home include those who had to abandon their children due to financial hardships, as well as those whose children were abducted. According to a 2021 report from the Bureau of Crime Investigation, Ministry of Public Security in China, nearly 6,000 child abduction cases were reported in 2012, a number that dropped to less than 700 by 2020. Utilising missing children’s flyers on cars has become a common strategy among some parents and volunteers to increase visibility and improve the chances of locating lost children. One notable case involves Du Houqi’s father, Du Xiaohua, who was highlighted in the 2014 film Dearest; he is the only parent featured whose child remains missing today. Du covered his car with flyers for his son and for other desperate families. On Chinese e-commerce platforms, some vendors even sell missing children’s flyers for about three yuan (45 US cents) each. Porsche owner Du promptly registered his car’s new look with the local police to ensure compliance with legal regulations. The 27-year-old, originally from Hubei province in central China, observed others distributing flyers randomly to passers-by and found that approach inefficient. While some questioned his motives, suggesting he sought attention, Du clarified that increasing awareness was his primary goal. “The more attention the car receives, the better the chances for more people to see the information about missing children, leading to more reunifications,” Du stated. He also revealed that one individual featured in his 90 flyers has already reunited with their family. “This is the coolest car I have ever seen,” commented one online observer. Another added: “I wish more cars could display these flyers, as many children want to come home. I hope fewer cars will need to feature these posters, because that would mean more children have been reunited with their families.”

title: Chinese scientists develop new oil refining method that may cut energy use by 90%
description: The new process, which works at a molecular level, may also produce higher value end-products, ranging from petrol to plastics.
content: Chinese scientists say they have devised a new technique for refining oil that cuts the amount of energy consumed during the process by roughly 90 per cent. If the technology used in the study could be scaled up for industry, it would not only greatly reduce production costs and emissions, but also make the process more precise and boost product value. Crude oil cannot be turned directly into petrol or plastics. Instead, refineries must separate it into different parts before each one can be put to good use – one of the most energy-hungry parts of the process. The traditional way this is done is through distillation, which relies on tiny differences in boiling point and heating the mixture over and over so it vaporises and condenses – a process that uses a lot of energy and is relatively imprecise. The new process operates at the molecular level to select different compounds and send them to the production line that suits them best, thereby maximising the use of resources. The technique, described by the researchers from the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics as “molecular refining”, uses a chemical membrane to separate the different molecules found in crude oil. These metal organic framework membranes act as a kind of molecular sieve, with specially designed pores and surface properties to perform different tasks. The process, known as cascade membrane separation, starts by screening the molecules for size. Although the molecules look similar, their sizes differ by about 0.1 nanometre. A specially made membrane acts as a type of very fine sieve that separates the smaller straight-chain and single-branched alkanes that are used to produce ethylene. In the second stage, the remaining molecules are even closer in size, with differences of less than 0.01nm. This stage involves another membrane that uses its surface chemistry to “recognise” molecules and separate chemical aromatics, which are essential intermediates for making plastics, resins and fibres, from the multi-branched alkanes and cycloalkanes that are used to make petrol. The team used a tannic acid micro-etching method to continuously tune the membranes’ pore size and surface chemistry to perform the different sorting tasks. When the two membranes were used in series, the team tested a simulated light naphtha mixture containing 15 components. In the lab, it was separated into three groups of high-value products with a recovery rate of between 85 and 90 per cent, the study said. More importantly, because the oil no longer needed repeated heating, vaporisation and condensation, the process used around 91 per cent less energy than the traditional distillation process. In their paper, published last month in National Science Review, the researchers wrote: “The proposed graded sorting paradigm thus offers a novel platform for petrochemical refining, maximising value extraction while greatly improving energy efficiency.” Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes under the surface. Sign up for free now.

title: From injury fears to triumph, ‘everything aligned’ at US Open, Elena Rybakina says
description: The Kazakh beat holder Aryna Sabalenka little more than three weeks after ankle injury raised questions over whether she would even compete.
content: The stars aligned in Elena ⁠Rybakina’s favour for a US ⁠Open triumph the Kazakh never expected ⁠on Saturday, as she leaves New York the champion and new world No 1 despite an injury that almost derailed her campaign. Rybakina beat the twice defending champion Aryna Sabalenka for the trophy little more than three weeks after an ankle injury that forced her out of the ‌Cincinnati tune-up tournament, raising serious questions over whether she would even compete in New York. “I was so upset. I didn’t know actually how it’s going to be day by day. We arrived in New York. We did MRI. It didn’t look that great. We had to talk with a lot of doctors to get opinions [on] what we should do,” she said. “For seven days I was just going from ⁠my hotel room to the gym, three hours there spending, a lot of recovery, treatments.” Fears over her fitness slowly ‌melted away through a series of comprehensive victories, as she beat twice winner Naomi Osaka to get past the fourth round for the first time and overcame the 2023 ‌champion Coco Gauff in the semi-final. And she marched confidently into Arthur Ashe Stadium on Saturday, ⁠having already assured an ⁠end to Sabalenka’s 99-week run at the top of the rankings. “It’s tough to find words right now, honestly. I didn’t expect nothing like ‌this coming to this tournament,” said Rybakina, after collecting her third major title and second of the season. “Somehow everything aligned together.” The win marks the latest ‌chapter ‌in a prolific rivalry, the 18th meeting between the two players in a compelling cat-and-mouse saga. Rybakina beat Sabalenka ‌in the title match at the 2025 WTA Finals, before besting the Belarusian in the Australian Open final little ⁠more than two months later. Sabalenka took the momentum back – for a handful of weeks, at least – as she ⁠beat the Kazakh in the Indian Wells final and in the penultimate stage in Miami. “I don’t know what future will bring, but it’s always very difficult matches against Aryna, and I feel like ‌we push each other to ‌be better after such tough battles,” she told reporters. “I feel like not only with her, with also other players, top players. You always want to try something new, to change in your game, to be better. “I don’t know what the future is going to bring, but I hope success and some more wins.” Sabalenka, denied a third consecutive US Open title and toppled from the world No 1 spot, vowed to come back stronger after a season of disappointment. “I think overall I should be happy with the level I played, and there’s lots of things to take from this tournament,” said the 28-year-old Belarusian, who had looked more than capable of salvaging her grand slam season before she ran into the buzz saw of Rybakina. But for the first time since 2022, she will end the year without a grand slam title. Rybakina beat her in the Australian Open final, and she fell in the quarter-finals of the French Open before a fourth-round exit at Wimbledon. In fact, it has all been a slog for Sabalenka since she won the prestigious Indian Wells-Miami double in March. “As experience shows, I only come back stronger, and all of these lessons this season definitely already made me stronger, but definitely going to motivate me for the next year to do (a) better job.” And she’ll take pride in a reign at No 1, a place she has held for a total of 107 weeks – including the stretch of 99 straight weeks that will end on Monday. “Ninety-nine? Well, that’s amazing,” she said. “Let’s see if Elena can beat me in that.”

title: Chinese scientists find ‘extremely high-value’ underwater gold mine in Pacific
description: Survey team says the ores, formed when super-hot water shoots from the seabed, are richer in gold and silver than those found on land.
content: Chinese scientists say they have discovered a massive underwater mineral deposit in the western Pacific that is remarkably rich in gold and silver. According to a report by state broadcaster CCTV on Friday, the discovery was made during a joint scientific expedition involving several Chinese academic institutions. The ores within this seabed hydrothermal field – an area where hot, mineral-rich water shoots out from openings on the ocean floor – are exceptionally rich in precious metals. Silver, in particular, reaches more than 1kg (2.2lbs) per tonne of ore at its highest grade, while the average metal content exceeds that of typical terrestrial deposits. “The [large seabed mining area] has extremely high exploitation value,” said Song Shiji, vice-dean of the Institute for Ocean Engineering at Tsinghua University and one of the lead scientists on the project. The survey team also included researchers from the Qingdao Institute of Marine Geology and Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The expedition set sail from Shenzhen on August 10 aboard the Xiang Yang Hong 10, one of China’s first domestically designed and built giant oceanographic research vessels. The precious metals were discovered in a sprawling, high-temperature hydrothermal field, concentrated in what are known as “hydrothermal sulphide” ores. These multi‑metal deposits form when super‑hot, metal‑rich water jets out of the seabed and hits near‑freezing seawater. The sudden cooling makes the metals bind with sulphur and drop out as solid sulphide minerals – mostly copper, zinc and lead, but often with some gold and silver as well. The 18-day expedition featured seven deep-submergence dives. State media reported that the deposit was located in a “back-arc basin in the western Pacific” within China’s exclusive economic zone, though precise coordinates were not disclosed. According to the Shipxy marine tracking platform, the vessel sailed through waters north and east of Taiwan and north of the Philippines. Hydrothermal fields cover much of the western Pacific, extending from the Kuril Islands north of Japan to waters northeast of New Zealand, according to a 2016 paper published in the Journal of Jilin University by marine scientists in east China’s Qingdao. Before the expedition, the team conducted more than a dozen preliminary surveys in the area. CCTV reported that these earlier missions identified dozens of high-temperature hydrothermal vents at depths of 700 to 1,500 metres (2,300 to 4,920 feet), with fluid temperatures exceeding 315 degrees Celsius (599 degrees Fahrenheit). Building upon this earlier work, the team pinpointed a “new and very large” hydrothermal mining area within the basin. The associated deposit consists of three massive, cone-shaped sulphide mounds. Preliminary laboratory analyses indicate that the ore body is mostly composed of economically important minerals such as chalcopyrite, pyrite and sphalerite. The average gold and silver concentrations were significantly higher than those of land-based deposits, CCTV reported. Gold grades reach up to 15.4 grams (about 0.5 troy ounces) per tonne of ore, while silver peaks at 1.27kg per tonne of ore. Song also noted that the active field harboured unique biological communities adapted to deep-sea conditions, providing scientific insight into how life sustains itself in extreme environments.

title: Nepal flood survivor says rescue efforts must continue
description: Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water for 10 days while praying for rescue.
content: For 10 days, Nepali hydropower worker Sanjay Sah survived in darkness inside a flooded tunnel, drinking muddy water and losing all sense of time as he desperately prayed for rescue. When a disaster response team finally pulled him to safety on September 4, Sah’s first question showed how deeply the ordeal had disoriented him. “When I was rescued I first asked, how many days has it been?” Sah, aged 30, said in an interview, while on his way back home in Saptari district on Sunday. “He said that it has been 10 days. I thought it had been just a few days.” Sah was among hundreds of workers at a series of hydropower projects hit by the catastrophic August 26 flood, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border. Sah’s extraordinary survival was a rare ray of hope after a disaster that killed at least 1,429 people and left more than 5,640 missing, the majority in Nepal. Family, friends and neighbours celebrated Sah’s return with garlands and a cake, and his home was adorned with balloons and colours. His mother, Kapur Devi Sah, embraced him tightly as she cried, and later washed his feet for an auspicious welcome. “My son has returned, I am very happy,” she said. Struggling to hold back tears, Sah recalled how the disaster had struck with stunning speed. “I was on duty, and then suddenly an unthinkable flood hit us, with tsunami-like waves that were several metres tall,” he said. Workers had received warnings that floodwaters were approaching, but did not get enough time to escape, he said. “We did get information to stay alert, that a big flood is coming. As much as possible, we tried to be alert and evacuate our friends,” Sah said. “But the water did not give us much time … we shut down everything, and tried to rescue and evacuate our friends.” Within minutes, however, the tunnel was engulfed by raging waters. The sheer scale of the flood was unlike anything witnesses had seen before, with the government pointing the finger at the dire impact of rising global temperatures on Nepal’s Himalayan mountains. ‘Divine energy’ Separated from his colleagues, Sah found himself stranded with little idea whether anyone would ever reach him. His Hindu faith helped carry him through the days of darkness and isolation. “I survived because of my deep belief and confidence,” he said. “I was chanting Maha Mantra [Hindu prayers], and the divine energy I received because of that allowed me to not be scared or despair,” he said. “I was able to stay there.” With no clean water to drink, he survived on whatever he could find. “There was water, but it was muddy,” he said. “I only had that.” The darkness and isolation might have been overwhelming, but Sah was not entirely alone. Another trapped worker, Kabir Maharjan, 45, had survived nearby. “We were separated but speaking to each other.” The ability to hear another human voice offered a lifeline to Sah. Eventually, after days of excavation and painstaking rescue efforts, search teams broke through to the trapped men and brought them out alive. Sah’s wife, Lakshmi Kumari Sah, said she never gave up hope of seeing her husband again. “God has helped us, we had our hopes,” she said, holding her daughter in her arms. Sah, who spent several days recuperating in a Kathmandu hospital, says he has mixed emotions. “I am happy, but I feel sad too,” he said. “I was able to get a second life, to survive there. But many of our friends were there.” As rescuers continue searching through the tunnels, Sah urged authorities not to abandon the effort. One Chinese worker was rescued on September 5, the day after Sah – but no signs of life have been heard since. “I hope the government continues its search and rescue. It is possible there might still be someone alive,” he said. “Or they will be able to find bodies of friends who have passed away and hand them over to their families.”

title: Opinion | Mild-mannered Canada shows the world how to take the fight to Trump
description: When a nation as inherently moderate as Canada is driven to a trade war with its closest neighbour, the world should take note.
content: For anyone who has spent time living in Canada, the country’s default posture towards its southern neighbour has long felt almost hard-coded: polite, deferential, almost allergic to confrontation. I saw this first-hand as a visiting scholar in the country in the early 1980s, when I met locals who embodied the national stereotype of moderation in all things. Canadians preferred compromise even when they had a right to push back, treating their far larger ally as a partner to be accommodated, not challenged. This was not weakness but a deliberate choice rooted in geography, history and a belief that good relations with the United States were essential to Canadian prosperity. This is why Canada’s recent decision to walk away from talks and impose counter-tariffs on American goods landed like a thunderclap. On August 22, after the US applied 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would impose matching tariffs on American exports of the same scale. Canada sends nearly three-quarters of its merchandise exports to the United States, it shares a border of nearly 9,000 kilometres with it and it is deeply integrated with its military and security apparatus through the North American Aerospace Defence Command. Its choice to stand up to the US is more than a news story – it is a turning point. This rebellion of the reasonable carries three profound implications for the global order. For one, Canada’s stance should shatter any lingering illusions among US allies. The Trump administration’s treatment of Canada – including openly suggesting Canada should become the 51st state and reportedly demanding rollbacks of French-language and Quebec cultural protections – shows its nationalist world view respects no friendship, however old or intimate. Trump’s agenda has turned even the closest US allies into cornered opponents. Rather than partners to be respected, allies are being treated like assets to be leveraged. As this drama unfolds, those who were once close to Washington are asking if it is still a reliable partner. The European Union in particular should take note: if the US can treat Canada as a vassal state, no country is safe. The Trump administration’s demonstrated desire for Greenland means it must be watched closely. Second, Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs show that middle powers have options to defend themselves. For years, the conventional wisdom was that any smaller country dependent on a larger power for trade or security had no choice but to capitulate. Canada has changed that calculation this time round. By responding immediately with counter-tariffs of equal size, Ottawa has made it clear that smaller countries have options other than caving. Despite deriving most of its export revenues from the US market, it is proving that interdependence remains a two-way street. When the dominant supplier of primary aluminium to the US – providing more than half of the country’s consumption – refuses to absorb punitive tariffs quietly, it exposes economic nationalism as a bluff that allies no longer have to fear. Meanwhile, early reporting suggests that US business groups are expressing concern about the effects of Trump’s trade war, warning that the cycle of tariffs and counter-tariffs is raising costs for US businesses. Apparently, even the world’s largest economy cannot throw around tariffs without facing consequences at home. Finally, Canada’s resistance is a harbinger of a broader geopolitical realignment. For decades, countries have largely acceded to American demands. Canada is now the first major US ally to impose full, equal retaliation against Trump’s unfair trade policies. Its willingness to defend its own sovereignty deserves global commendation. The economic costs will be real, though. Ontario’s Financial Accountability Office previously projected that US tariffs could result in 68,100 fewer jobs in the province in 2025, with losses rising to 119,200 this year under a sustained trade war. Even so, the political cost of submission – sovereignty, self-respect and the precedent that Washington’s threats are cost-free – would be infinitely higher. When a nation as inherently moderate as Canada is driven to a trade war with its closest neighbour, the world should take note. This is not the impulsive anger of a habitual belligerent; it is the cold resolve of those who have been pushed too far. Canada’s hitting back heralds a broader shift: if US trading partners stop accepting exploitation and coordinate responses to US pressure, Washington will no longer be able to divide and conquer them one by one. For nations hesitating over how to respond to Washington’s coercion, the EU and Japan in particular, the message from Ottawa is clear: one does not have to surrender sovereignty to keep the peace. When Washington demands handing over one’s interests, one need not comply. More often than not, fighting back works.

title: Hong Kong artist Lau Wai looks at the unsettling future of humans and AI in solo show
description: Lau Wai’s solo multimedia exhibition ‘After Intelligence’ is a disturbing look at how the lines are blurring between humans and AI.
