content: Hong Kong artist Lau Wai has spent the past two months turning the De Sarthe gallery in Wong Chuk Hang into an open studio, building a new body of work that asks a question many are only beginning to grapple with: as artificial intelligence advances, what will be the ultimate role of humans? The answer, in the artist’s new solo exhibition “After Intelligence”, is not a comforting one. The exhibition, which runs until September 25, unfolds like a closed loop: humans undergo AI training while AI learns to mimic humans, blurring the line between what is human and what is artificial in this digital age. At the centre of the narrative is W.A.I., a digital avatar of Lau that first appeared in their work The Cast of the Invisible (2024), which won the Award of Distinction at the Prix Ars Electronica 2025. At De Sarthe, the character – made from motion and facial capture technologies – starts a new journey in The Morphing (2026), a seven-minute CGI video that takes place in an office full of employees with identical desks and no faces. Anxious about losing their job (the avatar uses they/them pronouns, as does Lau), W.A.I. follows a colleague’s recommendation and signs up for a “Human to AI” training course, framed as a system upgrade. Spoiler: they never get out. This work represents Lau’s first use of AI-generated footage, even if it appears only briefly at the end. Until that point, everything clearly takes place within a virtual world. Then it switches to a shot of a Hong Kong street. At first glance it appears to be a real clip, but the garbled, unrecognisable street signs soon give it away. The effect is deliberately unsettling. “It tricks you into thinking that is genuine,” Lau says. “But actually, when you look deeper, that is also fake. I think it works well with this story – the first half unfolds in this virtual world that’s mimicking reality, but you can tell it’s virtual because of the materials and textures. Then at the end, everything shifts – and then you realise that’s also fake.” In the exhibition’s second space, four video works from The Cast of the Proxy series (2026) feature more replicas of W.A.I., this time learning to do human things: run, clean, dance, perform kung fu. Their movements are not animated by hand but are based on motion data extracted from real robot footage found online. “I’m being fed all these robotic videos so often these days,” Lau says. “They’re trying to mimic humans, right? But their movements are still a little glitchy and random.” They fail at first, but the videos make clear that eventual success is a matter of when, not if. Lau’s fascination with motion capture actors has long been a driving force in their work. “When they are performing, this is the reality they see: the character with all the dots on the face, the virtual reality suit,” Lau says. “But we won’t be able to see that side of reality on the screen. In the final product, we see another character using their data.” For Lau, this layering is a metaphor for how we live now. “We are always situated in between reality and virtuality,” Lau says. “They always have to be in transitions between both worlds, but they are not completely in either world. I think they are neither situated in reality nor virtuality, but in between, and they require both worlds to have a complete presence.” In the exhibition’s final space, Duplicate.exe (2026) turns the visitor from observer into participant. In the single-player interactive work – a video game Lau created – the player controls W.A.I. and, depending on how it is played, the avatar returns to the physical world or is absorbed completely, becoming another W.A.I. in turn. Here, the exhibition’s central question stops being rhetorical. Someone has to decide what becomes of W.A.I. – and for now, that someone is human. Lau often references the 2017 book We Are Data: Algorithm and the Making of Our Digital Self, by University of Michigan professor John Cheney-Lippold, as a touchstone. “What we present every day could have different layers for people to perceive us,” Lau says. “All the information we put online – even this article – presents a fraction of me. All these different online personas don’t have to be connected with each other. We’re always taking from all these different presences of us to form a self that we think is us.” “After Intelligence”, De Sarthe, 2/F, Block A, Vita Tower, 29 Wong Chuk Hang Road, Hong Kong, Tue-Sat, 11am-7pm. Until September 25.

title: Bangladesh draws closer to China in ‘political chessboard’ to balance India ties
description: Dhaka’s pursuit of closer defence and trade cooperation with Beijing could further complicate its complex ties with New Delhi, analysts say.
content: Bangladesh’s tilt towards China has added a new dimension to security and trade in South Asia, signalling what observers see as Dhaka’s desire to be a strategic actor in the region and ease its overreliance on India. The hedging policy comes after the fall of Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League government in 2024 amid a student-led uprising. Under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, and then the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) after it came to power in February, the country’s diplomatic, economic and strategic ties with Beijing have deepened. Both sides are preparing to launch a “2+2” dialogue covering diplomacy and defence, adding a new layer to bilateral ties that already span infrastructure development and trade. Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs, announced the move after meeting Chinese Ambassador Yao Wen on August 30. Shafi Md Mostofa, an associate professor specialising in South Asian foreign policy at the University of Dhaka, said the dialogue carried regional diplomatic implications and reflected a deliberate effort by Dhaka to diversify its external partnerships. “China is indispensable for infrastructure, trade and defence modernisation, while Bangladesh also remains engaged with India and other partners,” Mostofa said. “This hedging strategy allows Dhaka to secure economic benefits and advanced technology from Beijing, while avoiding overdependence on any single power.” The move highlighted China’s growing footprint in South Asia, he said, potentially reshaping power balances and forcing other actors – including India and the US – to recalibrate their approach. “India’s role as Bangladesh’s immediate neighbour is undeniable, and Dhaka continues to cooperate with New Delhi on connectivity, energy, and security,” Mostofa said. “However, the procurement of Chinese fighter jets and deepening defence ties will heighten India’s sensitivities.” Complex balancing act Bangladesh has finalised an agreement to buy 20 to 24 Chengdu J-10CE 4.5-generation multirole fighter jets from China, valued at up to US$2.3 billion. Mostofa said Bangladesh’s challenge was to manage parallel relationships by leveraging Chinese economic and defence cooperation while sustaining pragmatic engagement with India. “For any Bangladeshi government, economic interests remain paramount, and China’s role in trade, investment and infrastructure makes it a critical partner,” he said. A rupture with India is not on the cards, according to Mostofa, even as Bangladesh shifts towards a “more complex balancing act” taking into account its ties with China. “Dhaka will hedge between the two, ensuring neither relationship undermines its sovereignty or development priorities,” he added. Since Hasina’s ousting, Dhaka and Beijing have rapidly expanded economic and defence cooperation, signing at least 15 new memorandums of understanding and agreements covering trade, investment and other areas. During Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June, 11 Chinese firms proposed US$9.21 billion in investment in Bangladesh. Umer Karim, a political science and international studies researcher at the University of Birmingham, said the strengthening of the Dhaka-Beijing relationship indicated Bangladesh’s desire to emerge as a strategic actor in South Asia. “Dhaka is looking to assert its strategic autonomy and to emerge as an actor in its own right on the South Asian political chessboard,” Karim said. “Engagement with China is relatively a safe bet, as Bangladesh can get high-end defence products and also foster economic engagement. The traditional reliance on India as a security provider is indeed beginning to change, and Dhaka is showcasing elements of balancing behaviour in its statecraft vis-a-vis India.” Diversified foreign policy Karim said Indian apprehensiveness over Dhaka and Beijing’s defence cooperation meant Delhi would view the 2+2 dialogue as another attempt by Beijing to encircle India, further complicating ties between Dhaka and Delhi. Relations between Bangladesh and India hit a nadir after Delhi allowed the exiled Hasina to remain in the country following her flight from Bangladesh. The new government in Dhaka is seeking her extradition for a court trial. Jon Danilowicz, a retired American diplomat who has served in Bangladesh, said Beijing had played its cards well since Hasina’s downfall. “Throughout the interim government period, China developed closer relations with all of Bangladesh’s political stakeholders, hosting delegations from all three major parties,” he said. “At present, there is a broad domestic consensus in Bangladesh about the importance of the China relationship.” He added that as the BNP government pursued a “Bangladesh first” foreign policy, strong ties with China would remain an important pillar of its diversified international relations. “No doubt, this strengthens China’s hand in the broader region, including those related to developments in Myanmar and the Indian Ocean region,” he said. While India’s economic, security and geopolitical influence remains strong, the knowledge that Bangladesh can count on support from China allows Dhaka to resist overt Indian pressure, according to Danilowicz. “It is up to India to decide whether it will seek to reassert its primacy in relation to Bangladesh or can accommodate itself to a more independent neighbour,” he said. Bangladesh was looking to strengthen relationships with traditional and new partners, including the United States, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, Danilowicz said. Nilanthi Samaranayake, a security analyst and adjunct fellow at the East-West Centre in Washington, noted that China was already the main supplier of military equipment to Bangladesh before Hasina was overthrown, pointing to the Bangladesh Air Force’s purchase of modern Chinese aircraft under an affordable package that included training support. Even so, antagonising India was not in Bangladesh’s interests, and Dhaka’s engagement with China was a constant source of concern for Delhi, including when Hasina was in power, Samaranayake said. “Yet Bangladesh needs to have as many partners as possible as it works to stabilise its economy and domestic politics after the turmoil of 2024, and to continue expanding its diplomatic and military presence in multilateral institutions,” she added.

title: Why Chinese shoppers are ditching supermarkets for small ‘community stores’
description: Young Chinese favour local grocery stores offering low prices and fast delivery, with some saying they haven’t been to a supermarket in years.
content: For Cindy Wang, the newly opened “community store” near her home in Guangzhou has been a godsend: the small outlet is cheaper than a traditional supermarket, but offers a bigger range of groceries than convenience stores like 7-Eleven. The 20-something now often stops off at the shop after work to pick up a few items. On an early September evening, she has bagged a bottle of milk for just 7 yuan (US$1), a 2.5 yuan beer and some mangoes priced at 10 yuan per kilogram. “It’s convenient and enjoyable, and I can still have a decent shopping experience without spending too much,” Wang said. Community stores like this one are becoming a major new battleground in China’s retail sector, as consumers ditch big-box stores in favour of smaller neighbourhood outlets offering low prices and instant delivery services. For shoppers, community stores offer a mix of advantages, analysts say. They offer a greater array of fresh groceries than convenience stores, but they tend to be easier to get to than supermarkets. Unlike pure e-commerce businesses, customers have the option to pick out their food themselves at community stores, but the outlets also offer delivery in about 30 minutes, according to Sherril Sheng, senior research director at JLL East China. China’s retail giants are rapidly scaling up their community store offerings. The outlet Wang frequents – named Happy Monkey – is part of a burgeoning nationwide chain under the Chinese food delivery giant Meituan. The e-commerce firm JD.com also has its own community store chain, while US retailer Walmart entered the market last year and has opened about 20 locations so far. Tech giant Alibaba Group Holding has been focusing on neighbourhood grocery stores since 2024 through its Freshippo NB brand, which now operates nearly 500 outlets nationwide. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The new wave of stores caters to consumers who spend cautiously amid China’s economic slowdown. Inflation has been soft in China for years, with consumer prices rising just 0.8 per cent year on year in August, according to official data. “Consumers are prioritising value for money,” Sheng noted, adding that when it came to shopping for daily essentials, shoppers wanted a balance of convenience, quality and affordability. Chinese families were also increasingly ditching the traditional weekly supermarket stock-up trip for high-frequency, small-batch purchases, Sheng said. A rise in smaller households is adding to that trend, as fewer shoppers need large packs of essentials, according to a July report by Qince Consumer Research. Chen Jinni, an IT engineer living in Shenzhen, has already made this switch. “I haven’t been to a shopping mall for several years,” said Chen, who instead stops at community stores on his way home from work to pick up roast chicken, ready meals, drinks and snacks. Now in his early 30s, Chen lives with his girlfriend, and the couple rarely cook at home. “We prefer to eat out or choose ready meal options and spend the time at home relaxing, like watching AI-generated animated dramas,” he said. “Only our parents’ generation still stocks up on big grocery items from the supermarket.”

title: Rise and fall of Hong Kong’s ‘shop kings’: how plunging rents, debt crushed their empires
description: Shop prices in the city have fallen more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, but they may not have hit rock bottom yet.
content: They were the “shop kings” of Hong Kong, owning dozens of properties in the same district and even the same street. But over the past few years many of these landlords have gone bankrupt, hit by the collapse in post-pandemic rents and tighter bank lending. Shop prices in the city have fallen more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, but they may not have hit rock bottom yet, according to Centaline Commercial. “There does not appear to be any clear sign of a turnaround today, nor any glimmer of hope on the horizon that might trigger a rebound,” said Stanley Poon, managing director at the agency. According to Colliers’ data, in the first three quarters of this year, the total value of loss-making transactions involving street shops priced at over HK$100 million (US$12.75 million) reached HK$485 million – surging 81.6 per cent compared with HK$267 million the same period last year. One of the highest-profile names in the sector was Tang Shing-Bor – known locally as “Uncle Bor” – who owned more than 200 properties that were once valued between HK$70 billion and HK$80 billion. Tang ranked 19th on the Forbes 2021 list of Hong Kong’s richest people, earning him the nickname “king of shops”. Originally a neon light repairman, Tang later became a real estate broker and started investing in commercial property in the 1970s. He later handed over management of the family business to his youngest son, Stan Tang Yiu Sing, who tried to expand into other sectors such as hospitality, food and beverage, and co-working spaces – often using high-leverage financing. Starting in 2021, the family was embroiled in loan defaults and lawsuits, with some creditors initiating legal action directly against the administrators of the estate seeking to settle outstanding debts. The elder Tang died in May 2021. Last week, an industrial building in Sai Kung owned by The Tang family for nine years was sold to the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology for HK$141 million, representing a decline of over 60 per cent from the original purchase price. Another so-called shop king is David Chan Ping-Chi, also known as Hong Kong’s “cassette king” because he built his fortune on making cassettes and compact discs. In the 1980s, Chan began shifting capital from his industrial business into the local property market, focusing on commercial buildings, retail shops and car parks. Chan reached the pinnacle of his investment career in 2017, but it was short-lived. After 2019, the commercial property market took a sharp turn downwards, and his “deal of the century” involving The Center in Central ended up as a loss-making investment. More recently, Chan faced a full-blown financial crisis. In addition to offloading a large volume of assets at a discount, his own luxury residence was repossessed by the bank, and he faced a bankruptcy petition filed by creditors. Andy Kong, director at Midland Shops, said some seasoned investors acquired retail premises in the past to generate rental income and benefited from capital appreciation, or they bought shops for owner occupation to support business growth when Hong Kong’s tourism and retail sectors thrived. “They then used the gains from asset appreciation to expand their investment portfolios, gradually accumulating a substantial portfolio of retail properties,” he said. When the central government launched the Individual Visit Scheme following the 2003 Sars outbreak, it triggered a massive influx of mainland tourists to Hong Kong. That turbocharged the commercial property sector. “Many major international brands spared no expense to open multi-storey flagship stores, pushing local mass-market retailers and restaurants to secondary streets, and driving up street shop rents across Hong Kong,” said Poon from Centaline Commercial. Investors did not solely rely on mortgages during the market’s heyday. They also utilised commercial loans or bridging loans offered by banks. This short-term financing – or standby lines of credit – operated on a “pay-only-when-used” basis, thereby giving investors highly flexible access to capital. “When investors bought these retail units, interest expenses were not a primary concern. They prioritised the property’s capital appreciation potential over immediate rental yields,” Poon said. “Investors leveraged the financial standing and audit reports of their property investment businesses to secure commercial loans. The amount they could ultimately borrow depended primarily on the individual investor’s relationship with the bank.” Hong Kong’s ultra-low interest rate environment persisted from late 2008 to mid-2022. Banks aggressively competed for mortgage and commercial loan business, making it easy for investors to secure financing. “When investors took out loans back then, the interest rate was roughly 1 per cent to 2 per cent,” Poon said. “Even a casual purchase of a retail shop for rental income could yield a return of 2 per cent to 4 per cent.” By 2014, the market had peaked, and starting from 2015 “rents began to quietly retreat”, according to Poon. The situation deteriorated after the onset of the first US-China trade war in 2018, followed by the large-scale social unrest in Hong Kong in 2019. The final blow was the pandemic that broke out in 2020, which led to a drastic change in consumer lifestyles and consumption habits. After borders reopened, the surge of Hong Kong residents travelling abroad and spending time and money on the mainland dealt a further blow to the retail property market. The property revaluations triggered a downward adjustment, with Poon estimating that the total volume of non-performing commercial real estate loans across Hong Kong could reach HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion. “Once market conditions reverse or prices for commercial, industrial, and retail properties plummet, banks will need to cut losses or mitigate risk,” he said. “There’s no point in negotiating over today’s foreclosed properties. It’s a case of having 10 buckets but only one lid - you simply can’t cover them all.” Thomas Chak, head of capital markets & investment services at Colliers Hong Kong, said banks still held portfolios of assets and non-performing loans (NPLs) that needed to be addressed. “I believe banks will continue to handle the repossessed commercial properties currently on their books over the next six to 12 months,” Chak said. “In particular, if interest rates rise, banks might accelerate the disposal process.” But Chak also said that foreclosed properties would not necessarily drive down market prices because they would adjust to a reasonable level that offered value to attract investors back to the commercial property market.

title: Teens go from struggling swimmers to trained coaches at Splash Foundation
description: NGO’s new apprenticeship programme is empowering recent learners to pass on life skills – and lessons.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
A new swim coach training course is creating waves. The “Youth Apprenticeship : Swim & Coach Development Programme” was launched this year by Hong Kong charity Splash Foundation.
It gives former students of the non-profit organisation’s free swim classes the chance to pass on the lessons they once learned there.
Stephanie Ching is the programme manager for kids and teens at Splash Foundation. She said the new apprenticeship would push teens to grow.
“For them to become a coach, it’s even more courageous because you need to put yourself [out] there,” Ching said. “[Teens] put themselves in a vulnerable position … and trust us to bring the best out of them.”
She said that the apprenticeship is a way for young people to take what they learned through the foundation and help the next generation of swimmers.
In 2015, Libby Alexander and Simon Holliday noticed many domestic helpers and residents could not swim. That is why they founded Splash Foundation.
The charity expanded to include people from low-income families and ethnic minority groups. There are also programmes for children with disabilities, including special educational needs .
The foundation offers lessons during the school year and a Splash Camp in the summer.
Ching explained how the former students would learn to become effective coaches. Apprentices are taught how to encourage new swimmers and give them feedback. They also work alongside an experienced coach.
“It helps them become more efficient and passionate coaches,” she said.
Sixteen-year-old Kenneth Li was nervous when he first learned to swim with Splash Foundation in autumn 2025. But during the programme, as Kenneth learned how to swim, he realised he loved it.
He recently completed the youth apprenticeship and has taught at the foundation’s summer Splash Camp.
“I have a younger sister, and I like to teach others. Teaching kids is so fun and it [gives] me a sense of accomplishment,” he said.
But that does not mean it’s smooth sailing , Kenneth explained, especially when you have to manage a class of eight to 10 kids.
“You need to look after all the students,” he said. “Safety is the most important [thing]. Sometimes, the kids may be naughty and splash around.”
Kenneth added: “Managing so many people is a little bit difficult for me … I think it’s a good way to improve my patience.”
Keisha Elorm, 16, also took part in Splash’s first apprenticeship programme. She used to swim frequently but stopped during the Covid-19 pandemic.
Joining Splash’s summer camp in 2025 allowed her to restart a sport she loved.
“It was my first time coaching this summer; I was really nervous. I would mess up – giving them the wrong instructions,” Keisha said. “Once I had guidance from my lead coaches, I learned how to teach properly, how to give instructions and how to keep them safe.”
Keisha said the experience improved her communication skills. It also helped her become less shy, especially when speaking her second language.
“It gave me more reason to speak Cantonese. Even though most kids in Hong Kong learn to speak English, some have a real difficulty understanding it. It boosted my confidence.”

title: Rising number of South Korean beauticians providing illicit services in Hong Kong
description: Woman who provided services during short visit arrested by immigration officers last week, months after country’s consulate issued warning.
content: Visiting beauticians from South Korea continue to offer illegal cosmetic procedures in Hong Kong, despite a warning issued by the country’s consulate earlier this year reminding them that working without a permit is a crime. At least two practitioners have been arrested by local immigration authorities this year, including one caught red-handed in Tsim Sha Tsui last week during an operation witnessed by the South China Morning Post. Last month, the city’s beauty industry warned that clandestine operations by visiting beauticians were hurting local businesses and raised safety concerns over the lack of aftercare for clients receiving services from short-stay visitors. In early February, an industry insider reported a case to immigration authorities, and subsequently learned that a South Korean make-up artist had been arrested on criminal charges. After the arrest, the South Korean consulate in Hong Kong issued a notice on February 25, urging its citizens not to provide unauthorised services in the city. “Driven by the recent popularity of ‘K-beauty’, there has been an increase in cases where beauty professionals attempt to provide short-term services abroad – such as make-up application, eyebrow tattooing and lip tattooing – without a valid visa. “These attempts often stem from information obtained through paid seminars that promote overseas service trips by highlighting higher profit margins compared with the domestic market,” the notice read. The consulate warned that performing beauty services in the city without relevant permits constituted illegal employment and violated local laws. “In Hong Kong specifically, such activities are classified as illegal employment under the Immigration Ordinance (Cap. 115) and are punishable by up to two years in prison and a fine of HK$50,000 [US$6,400],” it said. “We urge Korean nationals to take note of this notice and ensure they do not violate local laws,” it said. A beauty industry insider told the SCMP that many South Korean artists were lured by “fast money” in the city, capitalising on local demand for an authentic “K-beauty experience” without travelling to the country. Such artists could earn two to three times more per session in Hong Kong than in South Korea, where a saturated market has driven prices down to as low as HK$1,000 per session. “A lot of local [practitioners] have been reaching out to [us] to complain about this issue because of the damage to sales,” the source said. She added that while some beauticians publicly advertised open slots on social media, they operated covertly by disclosing their location only after receiving a deposit. Checks by the SCMP found that these visiting make-up artists provided a full range of microblading services including procedures for eyebrows, eyeliners, lips and hairlines. They charged an average HK$3,000 per session, similar to local rates. Microblading is a semi-permanent tattooing technique in which a fine blade is used to slice shallow cuts and insert pigment into the skin, typically to create fuller eyebrows or defined lips. Chen Pui-yan, a beautician and part-time make-up artist with 30 years of experience, noted that while these pop-up sessions have existed for several years, their popularity has surged alongside the K-beauty trend. “They are taking away customers from the local practitioners … It is unfair competition,” she said. Chen, who is also a member of the Hong Kong International Professional Trainers Association for aesthetics practitioners, raised concerns about the lack of aftercare by foreign beauticians, who leave the city without offering follow-up appointments or touch-ups. She warned that clients who accepted treatments by these visiting beauticians would not be able to hold them accountable should complications arise. On September 8 at 1pm, the SCMP followed a client who had made a booking with a South Korean beautician suspected of working illegally in a commercial building in Tsim Sha Tsui. According to the client, the beautician had arrived in the city just a day earlier and had set up a temporary station inside an eyelash extension salon, equipped with a single bed, a chair, and a trolley of visibly dusty equipment. The practitioner’s luggage was still in the room, the client said. At around 1.15pm, immigration officers arrived just as the beautician had applied numbing cream to the client. The SCMP saw at least five officers enter to execute the arrest. The client said the beautician was shocked and initially refused to show her passport to the arresting officers. In response to queries from the SCMP, the South Korean consulate declined to comment or confirm the arrest of its citizens for working illegally in the city, but stressed that it urged “strict compliance with local regulations”. “The consulate general fully recognises the importance of abiding by local laws and actively undertakes various preventive measures to ensure that our nationals do not violate local regulations while abroad,” it said. Despite the risks, demand for these pop-up services has persisted for years. Macy Poon*, a white-collar worker in her forties, had her eyebrows tattooed by a South Korean beautician who came to Hong Kong for a few days about three years ago. She attended the booking at a five-star hotel and met the beautician in a suite. Poon recalled that she was asked to lie down on a mat on the floor, where the treatment was conducted. “She was quite professional,” Poon said. “The effect [on my eyebrows] was good. I did not have to fly to Seoul to get a nice treatment, but it was not cheap at all.” The SCMP contacted the same beautician and learned that she had made a two-day trip to the city in August this year and was actively taking bookings for September. The Immigration Department said it would continue to strictly enforce the law to combat related offences. *Name changed at interviewee’s request.

title: Russia says Ukraine attacked trucks supplying fuel to Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
description: An official said the strike killed two Russian servicemen and endangered the nuclear power plant.
content: The head of Russia’s state nuclear energy corporation ⁠accused Ukraine on ⁠Sunday of attacking diesel fuel trucks, ⁠killing two Russian servicemen and deliberately jeopardising safety at the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine. Alexei Likhachev said the attack took place on Friday and also resulted in injuries to other ‌Russian soldiers. The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe’s largest with six reactors, was seized by Russian forces in the early weeks of the Ukraine war that broke out in February 2022. Each side has regularly accused the other of actions that endanger safety at the plant and increase the risk ⁠of a nuclear accident. Likhachev issued a statement saying Ukrainian forces had launched “a series ‌of combined strikes” on Friday on fuel trucks which deliver diesel to the station. “The strikes hit very close to ‌the perimeter of the station’s site,” he said. “Two servicemen were killed and ⁠a large ⁠number of Russian soldiers were injured, some seriously. They were all involved in supporting this purely civilian ‌mission.” Fuel is critically important for the plant as diesel generators provide power to keep nuclear fuel ‌in the ‌reactors cool when the plant’s two external power links are down. Both were ‌down for nearly three weeks in August and September. Ukraine has demanded ⁠that Russia abandon the station and hand its operation back to Kyiv, a ⁠demand rejected by Moscow. The fuel currently generates no electricity. The UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, has stationed an observer team ‌permanently at the station, ‌along with Ukraine’s three other working plants. The agency has repeatedly acted as an intermediary when disputes arise and last month helped arrange a local ceasefire to carry out repairs and restore external power links.

title: Over 700 cardholders report unauthorised iPhone pre-order charges worth HK$14.7m
description: Some report multiple transactions on their credit cards, while an expert says fraudsters may have exploited pre-order rush for Apple’s new iPhones.
content: Hong Kong police have received reports from more than 700 people about unauthorised credit card transactions worth HK$14.7 million (US$1.87 million) linked to pre-orders of Apple’s newest iPhones, prompting the force and major banks to launch investigations. A police spokesman said the force’s e-Report Centre received the reports on Saturday and Sunday from individuals who suspected that their credit cards were fraudulently used for online purchases of smartphones. The largest single case involved as much as HK$114,000. Following preliminary investigations, the cases have been provisionally classified as “obtaining property by deception”. No arrests have been made so far. One social media user on the Threads platform said she received a message on Saturday night that she had unauthorised transactions of HK$33,598 from Apple on her HSBC credit card. “When I called Apple customer service, they hung up on me immediately. What should I do?” she asked. It took her half an hour to reach an HSBC customer service officer to suspend her credit card, and she subsequently filed a police report. Another internet user said she had at least four unauthorised transactions with Apple of HK$11,499 each on her Hang Seng credit card. “Only after browsing Threads did I realise so many people had their credit cards stolen tonight to buy an iPhone 18 Pro on Apple … After seeing the posts and checking my own card, I realised I fell victim to it too,” she said. Similar incidents occurred to others with credit cards from different banks. Internet celebrity “Szetosifu” told the South China Morning Post on Sunday that he tried to pre-order an iPhone 18 Pro Max at 8pm on Saturday night. He said he tried many times with his Hang Seng credit card, but failed to secure one after entering the card security code. His orders were rejected by Apple and he did not receive any receipt. He eventually gave up, but after 10 to 15 minutes, he received 10 SMSs, each saying that he had used his Hang Seng credit card to pay HK$13,299 on Apple’s Hong Kong website. Szetosifu said he tried to call Hang Seng’s hotline but no one picked up after a 30-minute wait. Nonetheless, he was not worried because he believed the bank was withholding the transfers and he would visit a branch on Monday to clarify the matter. Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone, along with the new iPhone 18 Pro series last week. Pre-orders for the iPhone 18 opened at 8pm on Saturday, with sales starting on September 18. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, surmised that the Apple Online Store might have bypassed certain verification steps, including a process called 3D Secure, to ensure smooth traffic during the high-demand pre-order phase. He said fraudsters might have exploited the shopping frenzy to carry out real-time fraudulent charges using credit card details previously obtained through phishing websites or black markets. “Basically, Apple should take responsibility, and I believe they will. However, who will compensate? Is it Apple or the banks? I don’t know,” he said, adding that there should be sufficient time to cancel all the unauthorised transactions, as there was still a week before the actual delivery of the new iPhones. Fong also said there could have been duplicate transactions caused by network congestion during the pre-order rush. An HSBC spokesman said on Sunday that the bank would investigate and return unauthorised charges to customers under its card scheme rules where applicable. He added that 3D Secure could provide an extra layer of protection, but the responsibility of deciding whether to use the feature lay with merchants. “Customers who have used their credit card reasonably and with due care, and who report promptly, can rest assured that they will be guided through the refund process,” he said. He reminded customers to suspend their cards if unauthorised transactions occurred. Hang Seng Bank said that while the bank investigated, it would support affected customers and, like HSBC, initiate return payments where applicable. “We’ll fully support impacted customers who have used their credit card responsibly and with due care throughout the refund process,” the bank said. Standard Chartered said customers who discovered any unauthorised transactions should notify the bank to suspend their credit card and report the incident to police as soon as possible. The bank would investigate in accordance with established procedures and submit chargeback applications to the relevant credit card organisations where applicable, it added. If its investigation confirmed that a transaction was not authorised by the cardholder, the cardholder would not be held liable for the relevant amount charged. Bank of China (Hong Kong) said all its credit card customers were protected by a chargeback mechanism, and they were not required to bear any liability for transactions verified as unauthorised. A spokesman for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said merchants could choose not to use or temporarily suspend additional authentication arrangements due to operational considerations. In such circumstances, however, the merchant would bear the liability and financial losses arising from unauthorised transactions. The spokesman added that, generally, if a bank credit card account was used for unauthorised transactions but the cardholder had not engaged in any fraudulent or severely negligent behaviour, then the cardholder was not required to bear any liability for the unauthorised transactions. The SCMP has contacted Apple Hong Kong for comment.

title: Climate change’s damage to old trees in gardens of England’s stately homes
description: Because of the excessive heat this summer, mature trees are drooping, and their leaves are turning brown.
content:
At Hampton Court Palace, head gardener Graham Dillamore strode across the burnt beige grass.
The palace is in the southwest of London and was laid out in the 17th century.
“If we have a summer like this next year, by God, it’s going to be a struggle,” Dillamore said.
The gardens of stately homes are among England’s top visitor attractions. But their ancient trees are being damaged by climate change.
Mature trees that take decades to establish are drooping, and some have leaves turning brown in August in a reaction to excessive heat.
“Some of these trees have actually given up. They’re not going to come back; they’re finished,” Dillamore said.

title: Brics summit ends with Xi’s AI offer, Modi’s warning on critical minerals as weapons
description: Bloc united on US curbs but Xi Jinping’s open-source AI pitch and India’s warning on weaponised tech reveal internal friction, analysts say.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded his brief trip to India on Sunday with an offer to help Brics members develop open-source AI and smart manufacturing. Summit host Prime Minister Narendra Modi, meanwhile, warned against turning technology and critical minerals into economic weapons. Experts said the exchange captured the wider picture of the Brics summit. Two days of diplomacy produced a united front against US tariffs, sanctions and “America first” pressure with a joint declaration, while heads of institutions Washington once dominated sat at a Global South table. Concerns over minerals and technology, however, exposed clear limits to that unity. Speaking on the second day of the summit in New Delhi, Xi identified open-source AI and smart factories as two out of five key initiatives to promote economic growth and technological development in the Global South. He also said Beijing would offer to train young talent from other member states in advanced technology and innovation, according to state news agency Xinhua. The bloc has grown rapidly in recent years and is being increasingly seen as one of the strongest voices for the Global South, as the United States becomes increasingly assertive on the world stage. Against this backdrop, the Chinese leader also issued a rallying call for unity and cooperation within the bloc to counter geopolitical hostilities and disruptive forces that he warned were shattering the stability of supply and industrial chains. “A world without rules is like an intersection without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder would be inevitable,” he was quoted as saying by Xinhua. Global rules should be written jointly and applied equally to all countries without double standards, Xi added. “The logic of might makes right should have been discarded long ago.” Xi’s offer covered some of the key areas of the rivalry between the US and China, where control of resources and technology is vital. Open-source models and smart factories require magnets, batteries, chips and processing equipment, and the supply chain of the minerals needed to make them run overwhelmingly through China. But the US is the key gatekeeper when it comes to advanced chips and chipmaking equipment, and has imposed a series of export controls on the most advanced technology. That leaves many Global South countries caught between two forms of dependence. While Chinese support could be vital to helping Global South countries develop, many are worried about over-reliance on either Beijing or Washington. Modi, chairing Sunday’s session, marked that fear without naming either side. “The weaponisation of technology and critical minerals can hinder our shared progress. Therefore, we have emphasised inclusivity in the adoption of technology,” he said. India already has first-hand experience of how supply chains can be used to exert economic pressure. After the deadly 2020 border clash between Chinese and Indian troops, fertiliser clearances slowed and supplies of some equipment were held up. In 2025, when China put rare earth magnets under a global export-licence system during its tariff war with the US, Indian automotive production lines felt the impact immediately. Xi, who arrived in New Delhi early Saturday afternoon local time, skipped a gala dinner hosted by Modi for Brics leaders. Meanwhile, a social media video posted by Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday captured a relaxed exchange on the summit sidelines between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov and Araghchi himself. At one point, as Lavrov was speaking, Wang reached over to look at the badge pinned to Araghchi’s collar. Analysts said New Delhi’s aim at the summit was simple: preserve Brics unity without letting its internal tensions take centre stage. Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said divisions within Brics were natural – given differences in geopolitics, political systems, levels of development and national interests – and had become more pronounced as the group expanded. Those differences did not prevent cooperation, he argued, saying consensus and divergence shared a “symbiotic and dialectical relationship”. But geopolitical trust remained a major weakness, Liu noted, particularly between China and India, something he described as “the biggest problem within Brics”. While members had found broad common ground on development and economic issues at this year’s summit, disagreements over critical minerals reflected India’s efforts to raise issues with China that were difficult to resolve bilaterally, he said. “India is trying to maintain ties with both sides,” Liu said, citing its cooperation with China and Russia through Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation while avoiding a break with the US and the West. Liu said Brics cooperation could also give the Global South including China a greater say in shaping international rules in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI) and space. “Many of the current rules in these fields were shaped primarily by Western countries, with the Global South having limited influence over their formulation,” he said. If Brics members and other Global South countries worked together to develop new rules, Western countries would have to take their views into account because they represented “huge markets” and “huge numbers of users”, he noted. Despite US President Donald Trump’s threats of 100 per cent tariffs if Brics nations chose to “play games” with the dollar, the bloc pushed for local currency settlement and linked payment systems to keep trade moving if Washington were to use the dollar as a sanctions or tariff weapon. However, member states remain divided over how and how much to move away from the US currency. Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies, said differences were inevitable given the members’ varying relationships with Washington. “Such differences are a natural existence under the current circumstances, and they can only reach consensus through long-term interaction and mutual adjustment,” he said. Lin said the unanimous adoption of the joint declaration also reflected the impact of US policies. “The measures of the US government are certainly a very important external stimulus,” he said, citing tariffs, sanctions and the “America first” policy, which he said had “damaged the external environment for development across much of the Global South”. He said Brics had a role to play in emerging areas where the US and other Western countries were “reorganising” their approach, but its ability to shape new global rules remained limited by “the diversity of interests among member states” and their differences.

title: Tung Chee-hwa remembered for foresight in developing Hong Kong’s tech sector
description: Singapore’s Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also praises Tung for his ‘steady and visionary leadership’ in a condolence letter to Hong Kong.
content: Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, has been remembered by former colleagues for his foresight in advancing the city’s tech sector and for actively engaging with mainland China to boost economic development during his tenure, while Singapore’s prime minister hailed his leadership. Singapore’s Lawrence Wong praised Tung, who died last week, for his “steady and visionary leadership” in a letter to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu to extend his condolences to Hong Kong. “[Tung] steered the city through major challenges … with a deep sense of responsibility for Hong Kong and its people,” Wong wrote, citing the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the 2003 Sars outbreak. “His service paved the way for Hong Kong’s long-term development and prosperity in the years to come under the ‘one country, two systems’ framework,” Wong added, also calling Tung “an old friend” of Singapore. The letter, dated Thursday, was posted on the Facebook page of the Singapore consulate in Hong Kong on Saturday Local political heavyweights praised Tung on Sunday for anticipating developmental trends ahead of others, citing his decisions to establish the tech hub Cyberport and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation. “He proposed developing Cyberport very early on, allocating land specifically to attract innovation and technology talent. This is exactly what we are doing now,” Tam Yiu-chung, who was a member of Hong Kong’s top decision-making body, the Executive Council, during Tung’s tenure, told a radio show on Sunday. Tam, formerly Hong Kong’s sole deputy to the National People’s Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, China’s top legislative body, also credited Tung with foreseeing the need to engage the mainland closely to support the local economy, at a time when many were focusing solely on Hong Kong’s own development. Examples cited by Tam included Tung’s support for the Individual Visit Scheme for mainland residents and the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement, a free-trade deal between the two sides. “Both of these were proposed by Tung,” said Tam, now a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank. “And they offered instant relief to the Hong Kong economy [after the severe acute respiratory syndrome epidemic].” Tung died at the age of 89 in Hong Kong last Tuesday, and a state funeral will be held for him next Sunday. As the first chief executive after Hong Kong’s return to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, Tung navigated the city through the 1998 Asian financial crisis and the Sars epidemic in 2003. He also attempted to enact the national security legislation required under Article 23 of the Basic Law in 2003, but withdrew the bill after half a million people took to the streets to oppose it. Tung resigned from the post in March 2005, citing health reasons, and later became a state leader as a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top advisory body. Speaking on the same show, Fanny Law Fan Chiu-fun, who headed Tung’s office before his swearing-in, echoed Tam’s remarks on his push for science and technology. “Tung indeed possessed great foresight. He had a set of excellent concepts to implement,” she said. “As there were many other investment options, when real estate and finance were thriving, it was difficult to persuade others to invest in areas that took a long time to generate returns.” Elsie Leung Oi-sie, who served as the city’s justice secretary during Tung’s tenure, said his humility had helped mediate ideological conflicts in the early post-handover stage. Leung said that while Tung was criticised for being indecisive in his policies at that time, she understood that he was just trying to satisfy both the pro-establishment and the then opposition camps before implementation. “Many of the problems were new, things everyone had never handled before. It was a period of transition requiring mutual adaptation,” she said, pointing to the constitutional interpretation power of the NPC Standing Committee and right-of-abode issues as examples. “Without Tung’s support, these things simply could not have been done, because everyone was unfamiliar with these issues.” Tam added that future administrations could learn an important lesson from the fallout after Tung’s term. He noted that Tung’s ambitious long-term housing targets faced intense pushback from developers and property owners when the 1998 financial crisis triggered a wave of negative equity. “Views emerged calling to halt the construction of public rental and subsidised flats. The halt lasted for 10 years, which ultimately led to the housing shortage we face today,” Tam said, emphasising that reviewing Tung’s long-term vision offered valuable guidance for future policy work. Former financial secretary John Tsang Chun-wah said on social media that Tung was audacious in addressing established problems in Hong Kong, including high property prices and a lack of economic diversity. Tung’s approach led to plans to build more public housing and promote technological development, Tsang said. “But during such a period of transition and when everything warranted further realignment, Tung could not win cooperation from all sectors when he tried to implement these policies,” he said. Tsang also praised Tung for doing everything within his power to fully implement the principles of “one country, two systems” and “Hong Kong people governing Hong Kong”. He did this “while steadfastly upholding the dignity of the chief executive’s role. His efforts in these areas should not be erased”, Tsang said.

title: Forget low-calorie food, Chinese youth turn to tasteless, chewy snacks to lose weight
description: One individual even admits to chewing on dog chew sticks to help alleviate severe exam anxiety.
content: Young dieters in China are increasingly turning away from low-calorie foods in favour of a new trend: chewy snacks. On social media, they are sharing their new-found favourites, including beef jerky, frozen buns, and even baby teething biscuits – each characterised by their toughness and chewiness. Many prefer chewy foods as a way to keep their mouths busy and trick their brains into feeling satisfied, reducing the urge to eat more. For these dieters, taste is not the top priority; instead, the focus is on the toughness of the snacks. The harder to chew, the more effective they believe it is. One 37-year-old netizen from Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, using the handle @yigexiangmujingli, has taken to munching on dangshen, a root thought to bolster the spleen and lung in traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) – as her chewy snack of choice. She shared with the SCMP that while she maintains a workout routine, she struggles with self-control around food. Hence, she seeks chewy snacks that keep her focused at work without adding weight to her body. According to her, dangshen offers a mildly sweet taste, which she prefers over traditional meat-flavoured options. She sometimes indulges in additive-free beef jerky and sugar-free chewing gum as well. The rise of chewy snacks has also inspired some to explore traditionally hard-to-chew foods across China. One user sourced Zhoushan hard cake – originating from Zhoushan city in eastern Zhejiang province – known for being “as hard as a brick.” This sundried glutinous rice cake was historically preserved by ancient civilisations for military campaigns and sea fishing. Other traditional chewy snacks being rediscovered include fried rice cookies from Guangdong and pancakes from Shandong. For these young dieters, calorie counts have taken a back seat to the enjoyment of chewing while keeping consumption to a minimum. One individual even expressed his affection for dog chew sticks, which help alleviate his anxiety during exams. He reported spending up to two hours on a single stick, noting that it also aids in maintaining oral hygiene. Chewy snacks represent just one strategy among young Chinese millennials seeking to lose weight, alongside opting for commonly consumed low-glycaemic index foods or “human food” – essentially diced and frozen meat and vegetables. These approaches are seen as healthier alternatives to extreme dieting strategies, such as severely restricting food intake. Some studies suggest that chewing can alleviate mental stress, while TCM principles advocate for thorough chewing and slow eating as beneficial for digestive health, ultimately enhancing metabolism.

title: Beijing pushes AI-assisted chip design as part of self-sufficiency drive
description: Agentic AI is creating a ‘paradigm shift’ in semiconductor design, chairman of domestic EDA leader Empyrean Technology says.
content: Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly taking the wheel in designing China’s next-generation semiconductors, as Beijing and domestic technology firms accelerate efforts to integrate AI into chip design software to bolster national self-sufficiency. Empyrean Technology, China’s top maker of electronic design automation (EDA) tools, has been accelerating the chip design process by using AI-optimised algorithms and agentic tools, according to company chairman Liu Weiping. By applying an AI agent to its simulation and layout tools, the company slashed the time needed for a circuit layout task from four weeks to just one week, Liu said. Agentic AI has brought a “paradigm shift” to chip design, moving away from “humans operating tools” to “humans commanding agents”, Liu said at the 2026 International Integrated Circuit Innovation Expo in Shenzhen on Wednesday. This shift would also apply to the business model of the industry, which was changing from the traditional software licence model towards a new model based on token consumption with agentic EDA, Liu said. Empyrean was developing an agentic EDA platform, which the company considered core to its future strategy, that would allow its own agentic tools to work with its partners’ agents, according to Liu. EDA is the highly specialised software that engineers use to design and test microchips before they are manufactured. Developing a domestic alternative has become a top priority for Beijing because the global EDA market is dominated by Western players such as Synopsys, Cadence Design Systems and Siemens EDA. Empyrean’s moves came as Beijing seeks to leverage AI to supercharge its drive for self-reliance in core technologies including semiconductors. An action plan published by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Friday called for deeper integration between AI and software, including industrial software like EDA and computer-aided design tools, with the goal of moving up to “the high end of the global value chain by 2030”. The rise of AI was redefining traditional software and its development model, presenting a “historic opportunity to reshape the competitive landscape and leapfrog” rivals, MIIT official Wang Weiwei said at a press conference on Friday. The global EDA leaders have also been actively leveraging AI agents in their chip design tools. US giant Cadence in June introduced its ChipStack AI Super Agent, hailing it as the industry’s first “Level-5” autonomous agentic AI design engineer that is capable of independently executing complex chip design verification workflows.

title: Splash Foundation youth apprenticeship turns former students into swim coaches
description: NGO’s new programme empowers teenagers to teach, passing on the important life skill and lessons.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
A new swim coach training course offered by one Hong Kong non-profit organisation is making a splash. The “Youth Apprenticeship: Swim & Coach Development Programme”, launched this year by Splash Foundation, gives former beneficiaries of its free swim classes the chance to pass on the lessons they once learned there themselves.
Stephanie Ching is the programme manager for kids and teens at Splash Foundation. She said the new apprenticeship, sponsored by the Laureus Sport for Good foundation, would give teens a whole new challenge, pushing them to grow.
“For them to become a coach, it’s even more courageous because you need to put yourself [out] there,” Ching said. “[Teens] put themselves in a vulnerable position … and trust us to bring the best out of them.”
She explained that the apprenticeship is a way for young people to apply what they learned through the foundation to help the next generation of swimmers.
“In the past, we had a few teenagers come and go. A few of them did become a coach with us,” Ching said. “But there was never a proper training or pathway [to become a coach]. We realised the potential there.”
Splash Foundation was founded in 2015 by Libby Alexander and Simon Holliday after they noticed many domestic helpers and Hong Kong residents at local beaches could not swim.
The charity expanded to include those from low-income families, people with ethnic minority backgrounds and children with disabilities, including special educational needs. It offers lessons during the academic year and a summer Splash Camp.
Ching noted that the newest youth course would last about nine months from selection and training to job shadowing.
To become an effective coach, Ching explained, the apprentices would learn how to give feedback to new swimmers and how to use positive language to encourage and empower beginners.
Apprentices would also train alongside an experienced coach.
“I think the most important part of the training is actually having a mentor next to them,” Ching said. “It helps them become more efficient and passionate coaches.”
Kenneth Li was nervous when he first learned to swim with Splash Foundation in autumn 2025.
“I was really afraid of getting in the water,” the 16-year-old recalled. But during the programme, as Kenneth learned how to swim – he realised he loved it.
He recently completed the youth apprenticeship and has taught at the foundation’s summer Splash Camp.
“I like to teach others. At home, I play piano, and my younger sister will follow me to learn. [That is how] I found out that teaching kids is so fun and it [gives] me a sense of accomplishment,” he said.
But that does not mean it’s smooth sailing, Kenneth explained, especially when you have to manage a class of eight to 10 kids.
“You need to look after all the students,” he said. “Safety is the most important [thing]. Sometimes, the kids may be naughty and splash around.”
Kenneth added: “Managing so many people is a little bit difficult for me … I think it’s a good way to improve my patience.”
Keisha Elorm, 16, also took part in Splash’s first apprenticeship programme. She used to swim frequently but stopped during the Covid-19 pandemic. Joining Splash’s summer camp in 2025 allowed her to restart a sport she loved.
“It was my first time coaching this summer; I was really nervous. I would mess up – giving them the wrong instructions,” Keisha said.
“Once I had guidance from my lead coaches, I learned how to teach properly, how to give instructions and how to keep them safe.”
Keisha said the experience improved her communication skills and helped her become less shy, especially when speaking her second language.
“It gave me more reason to speak Cantonese. Even though most kids in Hong Kong learn to speak English, some have a real difficulty understanding it. It boosted my confidence,” she explained.
Her experience reflects Ching’s belief that skills learned through the camp are not limited to the pool.
“Swimming is just a vehicle for people to improve themselves,” Ching said.

title: Javelin star’s injury scare adds extra spice to China v Japan battle for Asian Games gold
description: Yan Ziyi has dominated much of the season, but ankle trouble left her trailing Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi at Ultimate Championships.
content: The women’s javelin at the Asian Games is expected to go down to a battle between China’s Yan Ziyi and Japan’s Haruka Kitaguchi, and fans were given a glimpse of the fireworks they might expect in Nagoya this month. Yan has dominated since the start of the year, throwing the second furthest distance of all time and regularly beating her rival, who took gold at the Paris Olympics two years ago. Facing off at the World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest on Saturday, Yan again appeared to be heading for victory with an opening throw of 68.05 metres. But the teenager showed visible discomfort in her right ankle when making her second attempt, and managed just 63.95m as her rhythm and power suffered as a result. Kitaguchi exploded for a 68.92m throw in the same round to storm to first place, and while Yan opted for a third attempt her first was good enough for silver. Flor Ruiz of Colombia claimed third with a last-ditch 64.84m throw in the final round. The Japanese star’s winning throw in Hungary not only surpassed her gold-medal performance of 65.80m by more than three metres, it also smashed her national record of 67.38m, which was set in 2023. “The competition was very hard as the girls have been throwing far this season,” Kitaguchi said. “I dream and believe I have a chance every competition, and I threw a national record today to win the ultimate title and it feels wonderful. It has just been an amazing day.” Coached by men’s record holder Jan Zelezny, Kitaguchi missed last year’s World Championships in Tokyo, but said her performance in Hungary showed she was back to her best. Yan, meanwhile, left the field in a wheelchair, although coach Lu Xiurong said the injury did not appear to be serious. “She’s fine, she’s all right,” Lu told Chinese media. “Her bones aren’t injured. The X-ray results are just out, and she’s OK. Thank you everyone for your concern for Yan Ziyi.” Before competing at the Ultimate Championships, the 18-year-old Zhejiang native had maintained a 100 per cent record in five outings in the Diamond League this year, including a 71.74m throw in Xiamen which smashed the under-20 world record as well as the Asian record in May. An Olympic champion and a former world champion, Kitaguchi said she knew her throw “would go so far” the moment the javelin left her hand. “To be honest, at the start of this season, I wasn’t in a position where I could even think about the Japanese record,” she said. “I don’t think I am perfect yet, so I want to aim even higher. “I will be competing next at the Asian Games in my home country so I need to save some energy for that. It will be hard but my confidence in throwing is rising and I hope to show it at home.” The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya run from September 19 to October 4, with the women’s javelin final set for September 27, at the Paloma Mizuho Sports Park, which will also be the venue for the opening and closing ceremonies.

title: France apologises for criticising US’ human rights record after backlash
description: France’s permanent mission to the UN expressed regret over a social media post questioning Washington’s commitment to human rights.
content: The French UN mission said it regretted an online post criticising how the United States voted during a UN General Assembly meeting, with US officials saying on Saturday that Washington appreciated the statement. France’s permanent mission to the UN published the apology on Friday, saying it regretted a social media post criticising the US’ commitment to human rights. “France and the United States recently took different positions on a vote at the United Nations General Assembly. This difference concerned one vote, and not the defence of human rights,” the mission said in an English statement on its website. “Public differences of opinion on one vote do not stand in the way of close dialogue with the United States, and do not call into question our historical alliance, nor our ability to work together to advance peace, stability and prosperity, including within multilateral forums,” the statement said. The mea culpa was well-received by Washington, which has been holding up the appointment of France’s next US ambassador as a result of the dispute. “We note and appreciate France’s statement and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests,” a US State Department official said on condition of anonymity. The US State Department has held up the approval of Aurelien Lechevallier, French President Emmanuel Macron’s choice as France’s next envoy to Washington, replacing Laurent Bili. Lechevallier is currently French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot’s chief of staff. US approval of a choice of French envoy is usually a formality but has remained in limbo since the dispute. On July 24, the US was one of 10 countries to vote in the UN General Assembly against extending Volker Turk’s term as UN human rights chief, joining the ranks of North Korea, Russia and Nicaragua, among others. “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not any more,” the French mission wrote in a social media post after the US strongly opposed another term by Turk, who has repeatedly questioned US policies under President Donald Trump. The criticism attracted immediate backlash from Washington, with the US representative walking out of a UN Security Council meeting days later when France’s ambassador took the floor, in protest against the comments.

title: India-Pakistan water row deepens after Hague court ruling
description: India spent decades casting Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker. A tribunal ruling handed Islamabad the chance to return the favour.
content: For 65 years, even as India and Pakistan fought wars, severed diplomatic ties and traded nuclear threats, one agreement held: the Indus Waters Treaty, which governs the river system sustaining roughly 300 million people across the subcontinent. That was until April last year, when New Delhi suspended the pact in the aftermath of a deadly militant attack on tourists in Kashmir that it blamed on Islamabad. Now, an international tribunal has ruled that it should have done no such thing – handing Pakistan an unexpected win in the two countries’ long and bitter rivalry. On August 31, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that Delhi had no legal basis for suspending the water-sharing agreement, adding that India must also limit construction on the Ratle Hydroelectric Plant being built in Kashmir. The court’s five-member panel was unanimous: none of the grounds India cited justified suspending or terminating the agreement. It was a clean sweep for Islamabad, which brought the case after Delhi froze cooperation on the Indus and its tributaries – vital rivers that irrigate Pakistan’s agricultural heartland. A role reversal India has long cast Pakistan as the region’s rule-breaker, accusing it of harbouring militants and flouting international norms. But last month’s ruling flips that script, observers say. “This is particularly attractive to Pakistan, as it turns a long-standing Indian tactic upside-down,” said Daniel Markey, a senior fellow with the Stimson Centre think tank’s South Asia programme, adding that the tribunal’s decision gave Pakistan “a diplomatic opportunity to exploit”. “Even if Pakistan is only partially successful, it will relish the chance to muddy the waters and claim some high ground,” he said, describing the ruling as another front in a rivalry now “playing out in different forums, including this tribunal”. Within hours of the ruling being issued, Delhi had rejected it outright, insisting that its decision to hold the treaty “in abeyance” would stand. Islamabad’s reaction was equally swift and considerably more triumphant, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar declaring on social media that the ruling “vindicates Pakistan’s consistent position that a binding international treaty cannot be unilaterally suspended or set aside”. Delhi disputes the court’s right to rule at all, however, calling it “illegally constituted” because the Indus treaty specifically requires both parties to agree on how an arbitration panel is formed. “India is challenging the authority of the mechanism,” said Uttam Sinha, a senior fellow at the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses in Delhi. Describing the stand-off as a contest over “sovereignty vs consent”, Sinha said India’s ambition was not to “turn off Pakistan’s water” completely but to finally exploit its own treaty rights on hydropower, storage, irrigation and the like. “For decades, India had treaty rights and provisions on paper but had not developed the infrastructure necessary to harness them fully,” he said. Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani political scientist and senior fellow at King’s College London’s Department of War Studies, said Delhi was trying to “hide behind a technicality”, having previously turned to the very same court when it suited its own interests – notably in the case of Kulbhushan Jadhav, an Indian national sentenced to death by a Pakistani military court on espionage charges in 2017. How can India now say that it will not comply? Politically, this will be very embarrassing Ayesha Siddiqa, political scientist “How can India now say that it will not comply?” Siddiqa asked. “Politically, this will be very embarrassing, though like the United States, it can refuse to honour the judgment.” India’s actions are certainly not without precedent on the world stage. Sriparna Pathak, an associate professor of international relations at O.P. Jindal Global University in India, points to the US’ 2019 exit from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty after Russia deployed a banned cruise missile system as one of several precedents for unilateral treaty suspension. “States routinely invoke countermeasures … when they judge the other party’s conduct has destroyed the treaty’s object and purpose,” she said, citing a legal principle under which a fundamental shift in circumstances can void an agreement. But Pathak is clear-eyed about what is really at stake. India has tied the treaty’s suspension to a demand that Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” end its support for cross-border militancy – a condition that is political rather than legal. “That is a political precondition, not a technical one,” she said. “Compliance with The Hague order would undercut that position.” It is a dilemma India has long tried to avoid by keeping bilateral disputes, especially over Kashmir, out of international forums altogether – wary that outside mediation legitimises exactly the kind of “internationalisation” Delhi has spent decades resisting. Weaponised water Behind the legal arguments lies the reality that water has become a lever for coercion. In June, India’s minister of water resources, C. R. Patil, vowed that “not a single drop” would flow to Pakistan – prompting Islamabad to accuse Delhi of “weaponising” a shared resource and to warn, as it had in April, that any attempt to block or divert rivers would be treated as an “act of war”. For now, at least, the threat is mostly rhetorical. India’s existing infrastructure cannot yet shut off Pakistan’s water supply, according to Markey, nor can it “single-handedly cause flooding”. But as Delhi expands its hydroelectric and water storage capacity, its leverage will grow – and so will the inherent risks. Bigger Indian dams and barrages would create “a more likely target for Pakistani military attacks in the event of future India-Pakistan hostilities”, Markey said. “A return to the negotiating table looks unrealistic at the moment, but it will be the wiser course of action over time,” he added. “Neither side will readily benefit from pulling water to the centre of their bilateral dispute.” Sinha, meanwhile, resisted the idea of a looming “water war”, preferring instead to describe what was happening as the “strategic securitisation of water” – a contest fought not with weapons but with infrastructure, data, timing and design. That contest is now unfolding across the Indus River system, a vast basin of Himalayan tributaries spanning China, India and Pakistan upon which hundreds of millions of lives depend – and the latest flashpoint in a deep-rooted, acrimonious rivalry.

title: ‘Authentic’: Chinese-Canadian director’s queer love story starring Joan Chen
description: Xiaodan He opens up on ‘Montreal, My Beautiful’, in which an immigrant Chinese wife falls in love with a younger Quebecoise woman.
content: Director Xiaodan He immigrated from China to Montreal, Canada, 24 years ago. While many of her previous film projects were filmed in China, she returned to the French-speaking city for her newest film, Montreal, My Beautiful (2025). “The decision was very simple: I just really wanted to shoot a film in Montreal because I hadn’t done so yet,” she says. “I think it feels very cinematic, and through my eyes, it would look very beautiful on screen.” The 51-year-old Chinese-Canadian filmmaker did not just write and direct Montreal, My Beautiful, but is also the founder of the film’s production company, Red Dawn Productions. The film follows Feng Xia – played by legendary actress Joan Chen – a 53-year-old Chinese immigrant running a small Montreal convenience store and trapped in a loveless marriage. Her quiet life begins to shift as she begins taking French language classes and falls in love with a younger Quebecoise woman. Towards the end of the film, Feng Xia must decide between returning to China or staying in Canada, and remaining in her marriage or being with her new lover. The film is, in many ways, a love letter to Montreal. It would have been an entirely different story were it set in any other Canadian city. “Even the title wouldn’t make sense – ‘Toronto, My Beautiful’ sounds a bit weird, right?” He says, laughing. In early September, Montreal, My Beautiful was screened at the 37th Hong Kong Lesbian and Gay Film Festival. It had previously been shown at several Canadian events, including the Festival du Nouveau Cinema in Montreal, the Toronto Reel Asian International Film Festival and the Windsor International Film Festival. Approaching life honestly through film After studying filmmaking at the Beijing Film Academy, He went on to study screenwriting at the Universite du Quebec in Canada. Channelling the stylistic influences of cinema luminaries such as Hou Hsiao-hsien, Krzysztof Kieslowski and Abbas Kiarostami, she infuses Montreal, My Beautiful with an observational, poetic sensibility. “Authentic” is the word she would use to best describe her film. “I didn’t want to beautify life or artificially overdramatise it,” she says. “I wanted to respect life, facing the story and all the characters as honestly and truthfully as possible.” Queer cinema can suffer from fetishisation and stereotyping. He’s way of avoiding doing either was to simply not think about such external labels while writing or shooting. She did not set out a checklist of things to avoid regarding the portrayal of a queer Chinese woman. Instead, she simply returned to the core of storytelling: respecting the character herself. “Whether she is a queer woman or not is secondary to her being a human being,” she says. “Love is love, and desire is desire, right?” Working with Joan Chen When writing Montreal, My Beautiful, He knew casting the lead role of Feng Xia would be a delicate challenge. She required a highly talented, professional actress who had personally lived through the Asian immigrant experience to authentically convey the character’s internal journey and cultural complexities. To find her lead, she turned to a trusted friend who had offered to pass the script to Chen – a powerhouse of a woman who starred in The Last Emperor (1987) and directed Autumn in New York (2000). The protagonist’s courage, later-in-life awakening and journey towards self-actualisation resonated deeply with Chen. But while shooting the film, the veteran actress had to undergo a lesson in surrendering control. Time and money are naturally constrained on any independent film production. This pressure briefly brought tension during a key scene shot in a park in which the fading afternoon light was running out and the crew had to switch angles from Chen to cover co-star Charlotte Aubin, who plays Camille. Chen, feeling she had not captured her performance perfectly yet, requested another take. But He had to put her foot down. “I told her, ‘Joan, looking at the monitor, you were truly wonderful,’” He says. “‘Please trust me … I’m sorry, this isn’t Hollywood. We don’t have that kind of time.’ “If a director lacks clarity, time gets wasted and actors are left waiting.
