Making quick, precise decisions under intense time pressure was my biggest challenge and growth exercise on this shoot.” The film also navigates unique territory by pairing a veteran actress with a non-professional actor: John Xu, a former engineer in his 50s who plays Feng Xia’s husband in his first film role. According to He, Xu’s own trajectory mirrored that of his character, in that he also immigrated to Canada and experienced underemployment. Funding and future plans The director says that making Montreal, My Beautiful would have been impossible without the funding of Canadian government-led cultural institutions such as the Canada Council for the Arts. She notes that while directors can be supported by public funding, films in Hong Kong, mainland China or even the US tend to rely on private investors. “For someone like me who is a bit lazy and doesn’t enjoy socialising … asking people for money all day long would be so exhausting and difficult for my personality. So Canada’s policy suits me well,” she says. Naturally, however, the process can be slow and bureaucratic, and competition for public funding is fierce. For He’s next film, which she teases as a “mother and daughter revenge film”, she hopes to return to China and film it in her father’s hometown in Yunnan province – also where she shot the 2020 documentary My Father’s Journey, which explored her father’s Naxi roots. Having been in the industry for decades now, He knows that a career in filmmaking is far from easy. But she offers simple advice to the next generation of filmmakers: live life earnestly. “Observe life, be a mindful person and experience all the big and small moments around you.”

title: US church co-founder took substantial payment from HKIS to end ‘bad marriage’: source
description: Parties’ ‘fundamental’ differences would have led to more litigation if their partnership had continued, insider tells South China Morning Post.
content: The US church group that co-founded Hong Kong International School (HKIS) accepted an out-of-court payment to end a “bad marriage”, a source has told the South China Morning Post, saying their differences would have led to more litigation if the partnership had continued. The source familiar with the settlement said the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod (LCMS), which sued the school for allegedly breaching its operating agreement last September, decided to part ways with the institution after finding that they had “fundamental” differences. He told the SCMP that the settlement might give the impression that the church had filed the lawsuit for pecuniary reasons but the LCMS regarded the payment as a necessary “penalty” the school needed to pay for a number of “breaches”. “They paid a very, very substantial penalty because they were not aligned with the Lutheran mission,” the source said. The church had accused the school of serving only the “rich and privileged few”, violating its mission and amassing a large amount of financial reserves. The school management countered that the LCMS’ legal action was financially motivated as the church had explored multiple options to develop part of the HKIS campus in Repulse Bay into a US$1 billion commercial project. A High Court writ earlier indicated that the plaintiff threatened to evict the school from its Repulse Bay campus, while also seeking an indemnity of US$1.75 million. The LCMS remains the current registered owner of the campus. The source also revealed that months after LCMS filed the court writ, the school board had suggested monetary solutions for the parties to settle their dispute out of court. “HKISAL [Hong Kong International School Association Limited] was making offers and asked if we could find some monetary way to settle this,” he said. Both parties declined to reveal the amount of the payout. HKISAL also declined to comment on whether it had initiated the offer of a payment to settle the case. The source described the partnership as a “bad marriage” between parties of very different natures, and said that their parting was better for the future governance of the school. The church was “conservative and very mission-motivated”, while the school board was “formed by a group of people with strong financial, elite and prestigious backgrounds”, the source said. “If you force somebody to make changes in their vision and the operation of the school that they really fundamentally disagree with, you will probably be back in court in three years’ time. And then three years later, you have another lawsuit.” Ike Kutlaca, a partner at King & Wood, the law firm representing the LCMS in the disputes, also said the differences between the two parties were “fundamental”. “This was not an ordinary corporate dispute. It involved fundamental questions of institutional identity, governance and direction that had developed over decades,” he said. “At its most basic, the [co-founder] and operator had different views about the future of HKIS.” The source revealed that it was the church group that had proposed inviting former Hong Kong chief justice Geoffrey Ma Tao-li to act as a mediator, describing him as “intelligent, articulate and impressive” during the mediation process. The insider said no agreement was reached after the initial mediation session in August but added the process was “valuable and productive”. “It was productive in that both parties did a lot of thinking about the possible exits,” the source said. HKIS was co-founded by the LCMS and a group of American business professionals in 1966. HKISAL was established in 1974 to manage the school according to an operating agreement with the LCMS. The relationship between the missionary group and the association soured in 2022, leading to rounds of disputes over the management of HKIS. The source said the filing of the lawsuit and the school management’s retention of interim school head Ron Roukema as provost were key “inflection points” that affected the negotiations. Roukema was appointed as provost in 2015 and as interim school head two years later. He stepped down from the latter role before the start of the 2026-27 academic year after the LCMS objected to his permanent appointment on the grounds that he was not a member of the church group, but continued serving as provost. The LCMS said in April that it would start the process of recruiting a new school head. According to the source, Roukema’s retention as provost convinced the LCMS that even if the court ordered HKISAL to comply with its demands, the school’s management would “find some way around” the order.

title: Asian Angle | Politics aside, young Vietnamese are warming to China
description: Hit dramas, trendy consumer brands and economic opportunity are drawing a new generation into China’s cultural orbit.
content: Vietnam is often held up as proof of China’s underwhelming soft power in Southeast Asia: a millennium of resistance against Chinese domination, a border war within living memory, unresolved maritime disputes and elite surveys that consistently show Vietnamese respondents’ deep distrust of Beijing. Yet beneath these strategic tensions, a quieter shift is under way. Young Vietnamese are warming to Chinese culture, language, lifestyles and economic opportunity. From crowds queuing for Labubu toys to a scramble for Chinese-language jobs, and from Chinese content going viral on social media to record numbers of Vietnamese students choosing to study at Chinese universities, China is being woven even more tightly into the everyday lives of young Vietnamese. Four converging forces underpin this shift: cultural attraction, new-media connectivity, facilitation by both governments and economic incentives. China’s cultural appeal rests on a mix of cultural familiarity and contemporary trendiness. Chinese dramas have long been a fixture of Vietnamese television and Vietnam is now among Asia’s largest markets for them, their reach amplified by digital distribution. Content from major Chinese streaming platforms such as iQiyi, Tencent Video and Youku is carried on Vietnamese platforms such as VieOn and FPT Play, delivering China’s entertainment industry directly into Vietnamese homes and onto Vietnamese smartphones. Meanwhile, some Vietnamese celebrities have found wider fame on Chinese reality shows, while hit Chinese formats have been adapted for Vietnamese audiences. China’s appeal has also spilled into Vietnam’s shopping and lifestyle. Many Chinese brands have won over young Vietnamese with trendy designs and affordable prices. Mixue, the Chinese ice cream and tea chain, had expanded to more than 1,300 Vietnamese outlets by late 2024, making Vietnam its second-largest overseas market. Chagee, Cotti Coffee, KKV and Pop Mart have followed suit, turning shopping centres in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City into showcases of “Made in China” cool. Algorithmic ambassadors None of this cultural traction would travel as far, or as fast, without new media. TikTok counts more than 70 million monthly active users in Vietnam, out of 460 million across Southeast Asia, and sits within a broader Chinese digital ecosystem that channels content on Chinese culture and daily life to regional audiences. Vietnamese-language content on TikTok and Facebook – including from Vietnamese influencers living in or travelling through China – offers viewers a window onto Chinese cities, landscapes and the rhythms of life and work in the country. This bottom-up, peer-driven pull is unfolding alongside a renewed official push for closer people-to-people ties. Since the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations and the designation of 2025 as the “Year of Vietnam-China Humanistic Exchange”, officials on both sides have promoted youth engagement. The joint statement during President Xi Jinping’s state visit in April 2025 invited Vietnamese youth to join “Red Study Tours”. More than 1,000 have done so, visiting sites commemorating the two countries’ shared revolutionary history – among them the former base of the Vietnamese Revolutionary Youth League in Guangzhou – alongside hi-tech hubs that showcase China’s modern development and technological achievements. Two-way travel has expanded too, supported by growing rail and air links. Since August, Vietnamese citizens have been able to transit China visa-free for up to 10 days, and the Vietnam–China Tourism Cooperation Years 2026–2027 initiative aims to further strengthen people-to-people ties. The numbers are impressive: Chinese visitor arrivals to Vietnam surged 41.3 per cent to 5.3 million in 2025, making China Vietnam’s largest source of tourists, while Vietnam had become China’s fourth-largest source market by mid-2026. Education diplomacy tells a similar story: the number of Vietnamese students in China has more than doubled, from 11,300 in 2018 to about 25,000 today – still trailing the numbers in South Korea (43,300), Japan (36,300), Australia (33,000) and the United States (31,300), but expected to climb further as Beijing promises at least 1,000 government scholarships and 1,000 Chinese-language teachers to Vietnam. Mandarin pays Underpinning all this is economic pragmatism. Vietnamese attraction to China rests not only on what China represents, but also on what engaging with it offers. As Chinese investment has poured into Vietnam, Mandarin has become a sought-after skill for young Vietnamese. Vietnamese recruitment platform Joboko reported roughly 13,000 openings for Chinese-speaking professionals in 2025, up 50 per cent on the year before, with fluency commanding better pay in industrial estates and Chinese-invested companies. LinkedIn, TopCV and VietnamWorks each list thousands of Chinese-language roles in Vietnam, with monthly salaries ranging from US$500 to US$2,000 – attractive pay by Vietnamese standards. Demand is such that Vietnam recorded the world’s highest number of registrations for the HSK Chinese-proficiency test in the first quarter of 2025. At some Vietnamese universities, Chinese-language programmes now post higher admission scores than English ones, reflecting surging youth interest. English remains the default foreign language taught from primary school and is moving towards compulsory status by 2030, while Chinese is increasingly picked up later for its practical economic value. But anecdotal evidence points to growing parental demand for early Chinese learning and Vietnam has said it will pilot Chinese, Japanese and Korean lessons for preschoolers to prepare for future workforce competitiveness. Young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities All this unfolds as Hanoi emphasises the more productive dimensions of its relationship with Beijing, while keeping long-standing South China Sea tensions in the background. This favourable climate may have helped, but young Vietnamese people’s growing embrace of China coexists with deep-rooted patriotic sensitivities. The 2025 boycott of Chagee after its app and website displayed China’s disputed “nine-dash line” and the removal of some Chinese dramas displaying the same map show how quickly those sensitivities can resurface. Yet such episodes have merely interrupted rather than reversed the broader trend. Chagee is back in Vietnam, just as bilateral ties have recovered from the turbulence of the 2010s, when the maritime dispute overshadowed the relationship. Whether this societal warming can cushion or withstand the next downturn in relations remains to be seen. Vietnam’s history suggests that affinity with China and resistance to its power have never been mutually exclusive. A younger generation is now living that old paradox on new terms: drawn more directly and intimately into China’s orbit of culture and opportunity, while retaining the instinct to push back when national interests collide. Hoang Thi Ha is a Senior Fellow and Co-coordinator of the Regional Strategic and Political Studies Programme, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. Pham Thi Phuong Thao is a Senior Research Officer at the Asean Studies Centre, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published on the institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

title: China bets on early port and power deals in Sudan to secure post-war economic edge
description: Lack of leverage by army-backed government in Khartoum may allow Chinese firms to secure favourable investment terms.
content: China is moving early to secure a role in Sudan’s reconstruction, pursuing port and power agreements with the army-backed government while the war continues and many Western countries maintain only a limited presence. One expert also said Beijing was using the prospect of future investment as a bilateral incentive to encourage warring parties to cease hostilities. Sudan signed an agreement with the China Harbour Engineering Company in July to upgrade existing ports and build new ones. Meanwhile, Siyuan Energy has agreed to assess damaged power stations and supply transformers and mobile substations, while Hunan Construction is considering hybrid power projects. “Sudan appears to [have] become the next test case for China’s peace-through-development approach,” said Tim Zajontz, interim professor of international relations at the University of Freiburg. Although many foreign embassies, including that of the United States, suspended operations after fighting began, China maintained diplomatic operations in Port Sudan. War broke out in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces, led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), commanded by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. The army now mostly controls Khartoum, while the RSF holds much of Darfur. Beijing has not formally mediated between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF, emphasising investment and reconstruction as part of an approach that links development with stability. Cameron Hudson, an independent political analyst and former US government official, said China was moving before regional and Gulf states began competing for reconstruction work. “By getting in on the ground floor ahead of the competition, Beijing guarantees its long-term interests in Sudan,” he said. Zajontz said the army-backed government’s lack of leverage could allow Chinese companies to secure favourable investment terms. “General Burhan’s regime and the Sudanese Armed Forces are in a pretty weak negotiation position and ready to accept investment terms that a peacetime civilian government is unlikely to sign,” he said. David Shinn, a China-Africa specialist and former US ambassador to Ethiopia, said the port agreement was preliminary and could take time to produce work on the ground. “China can be expected to move cautiously on all of these business initiatives, although Beijing has a track record of engaging in more risky projects than Western countries are generally willing to do,” Shinn said. Hannah Ryder, CEO of Beijing-based consultancy Development Reimagined, met Sudan’s ambassador to China, Omar Issa Ahmed, in Beijing in mid-August to discuss investment and deeper engagement. Ryder said Sudan hoped China could “be involved in several ways”, including through construction, diversifying the country’s trade and supporting development projects that provide livelihoods. “[Ahmed] was of the view that security had improved significantly, especially in Khartoum,” Ryder said. China’s role was therefore “not about ending hostilities, but more about finding a way forward”. Oil has been central to China-Sudan ties, anchored by China National Petroleum Corporation’s first major integrated overseas oilfields, pipelines and the Khartoum refinery, with Sudan supplying nearly 10 per cent of China’s imports in 2002. In 2011, South Sudan transferred about three-quarters of the former unified country’s reserves to its new state but remained dependent on Sudan’s pipelines and Red Sea terminal for exports. Oil ties weakened after independence, and in late 2025 CNPC sought to terminate its Block 6 production and pipeline agreements after fighting, looting and damage to facilities had stopped production. Zajontz, who is also a research fellow at the Centre for International and Comparative Politics at Stellenbosch University, said Beijing had sought to remain neutral and supported multilateral initiatives to end the war. Its bilateral approach rested partly on the hope that prospective investment might give the warring parties an incentive to stop fighting. “But it’s not that easy,” he said. “A key driver of the conflict is the very question of who gets to control the country’s economy.” Shinn said China had stayed out of the mediation effort, which was most recently led by the US, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates but had stalled. For Hudson, the conflict already involved too many outside parties. “China’s calls for non-intervention and respecting Sudan’s sovereignty would be the best political contribution it could make now,” he said.

title: Mainland Chinese HKUST student loses HK$1 million to scammer posing as official
description: Phone scammer accused her of being involved in criminal case and demanded ‘guarantees’ from her, Hong Kong police say.
content: A mainland Chinese university student in Hong Kong has lost about HK$1 million (US$127,500) in a scam after a fraudster accused her of involvement in a criminal case and demanded “guarantees”. Police said they received a report from a 19-year-old student at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) at 1.07am on Sunday. The force said the victim had earlier received calls from someone posing as a government officer, accusing her of being involved in a criminal case on the mainland and demanding that she pay around HK$1 million in “guarantees”. She made the payment but later realised she might have been deceived, prompting her to call police, the force added. The case has been classified as deception. HKUST said it was aware of the incident and had reached out to the student to offer support. “The university provides counselling and other assistance to students in need. HKUST will continue to work closely with police and other stakeholders to raise students’ awareness and support those affected,” it said. In the first three months of this year, 42 mainland students in Hong Kong fell victim to scams involving fraudsters posing as mainland authorities. Police also found that the losses incurred by mainland students in telephone deception cases were 2.9 times higher than those of local students, averaging around HK$690,000 and HK$176,000, respectively. Since last year, the force has run targeted anti-scam efforts for mainland students, including social media publicity, seminars and surveys. Major universities in Hong Kong, including HKUST, have mandated anti-scam training for new students.

title: Letters | Ensuring building safety in Hong Kong an uphill struggle
description: Readers discuss efforts to reduce shoddy work in building renovation, signs on expressways, and classic Hong Kong comedy films.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to the report, “Government still weighing decision on restricting proxy voters, Hong Kong official says” (August 22). The government should be commended for seeking to combat bid-rigging in large-scale, high-value procurement decisions and to enhance the democratic process of voting in owners’ committee meetings. However, if the ultimate goal is to reduce poor and shoddy work, this outcome may not be achieved. As a relatively new homeowner – and, more recently, a reluctant inductee to the management committee – I have discovered, unsurprisingly, that the bottom line for most homeowners is cost. Consequently, the tender offering the lowest bid is often the one chosen. Although this is not always the case, lower costs tend to be associated with hastier work, inferior materials and short cuts. Most owners adopt an “it won’t happen to me” attitude when it comes to safety. Unfortunately, I cannot think of a straightforward solution to this problem. Perhaps the government could assign reputable contractors to perform maintenance essential to keeping buildings safe, leaving aesthetics, design and convenience work to the discretion of owners. Alternatively, there could be a licensing scheme that maintains and publishes benchmark pricing for standard repairs. The government might also assist with group procurement and technical support for smaller buildings. Regardless, it is heartening to see the government taking a more proactive role in ensuring safety in the building management process. It is everyone’s hope that, despite Hong Kong’s ageing buildings, the city will remain a safe and hygienic place to live. Jean Lim, Tai Wai Signs about pedestrians on expressways a puzzle Over the last few months, I have noticed the frequent posting of a very strange message on digital message boards on expressways: “WATCH OUT PEDESTRIANS NO SPEEDING.” I have spotted this message on Route 8 on Stonecutters Bridge, Route 9 in the New Territories and other expressways across the city. First of all, why does the Transport Department believe that there are pedestrians traversing Stonecutters Bridge and other expressways? Pedestrians are not permitted on expressways. Second, if there are pedestrians strolling along expressways, are they likely to be of reasonable and sound mind to follow road signs? Third, which pedestrian is capable of running faster than 70km per hour? In their current form, the signs appear to be addressing pedestrians, not motorists. If the Transport Department wants to address pedestrians, the sign should read: “Watch Out Pedestrians, No Speeding”. If the sign is for the attention of motorists, it should read: “Watch Out For Pedestrians. No Speeding.” In any event, these completely redundant postings bring a smile to my face when I pass under them as clearly the person posting the message has more familiarity than me with pedestrians on our expressways. Simon Constantinides, Clear Water Bay Stephen Chow’s comedies stand the test of time As a millennial who grew up in Hong Kong in the 90s, Stephen Chow’s films are a significant part of my childhood memories (“How Curry and Pepper showed Stephen Chow’s genius before superstardom arrived”, August 7). I idolised Chow as a comedian, and his co-star in Curry and Pepper, Jacky Cheung Hok-yau, one of the “Four Heavenly Kings”, remains the Cantopop singer I like the most. I vividly remember watching Curry and Pepper on a VHS tape at the movie rental shop my uncle owned in a shopping centre. I received a formal induction into the world of mo lei tau comedy watching Chow’s character verbally spar with his frenemy Pepper. That afternoon, I laughed heartily, to the delight of my uncle, who had thought a visit to his tiny, claustrophobic shop would bore me. After the credits rolled, I borrowed the tape and replayed it several times at home before returning it to my uncle. As a result of this prolonged exposure to Chow’s comedy, I grew obsessed with all his subsequent films. Knowing by heart some of the legendary comedic lines delivered by Chow, I sometimes find them to be words of wisdom in the face of adversity. Three decades on, Chow’s comedies still stand the test of time. Jason Tang, Tin Shui Wai

title: Indonesia searches for 130 passengers after ship sinks in Java Sea
description: Rescuers evacuated 107, and 6 bodies were recovered, after the vessel travelling from Surabaya to Banjarmasin lost contact in bad weather.
content: Indonesian rescuers say about 130 passengers and crew are missing after a ferry carrying more than 240 people sank in bad weather in the Java Sea on Sunday. At least 107 people were rescued and the bodies of six passengers were recovered as the search operation expanded in waters around the vessel’s last known position. The ferry was travelling from Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan province, officials said. The vessel’s captain had earlier reported rough seas with waves up to 3 metres (10ft) before issuing a distress message, saying the ship was listing, said I Putu Sudayana, who heads the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office. Authorities later received information indicating the vessel had overturned and then sunk. The rescue agency in Banjarmasin said it received a report two hours after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 at about 2am on Sunday. The ship had departed from Surabaya, Indonesia’s second largest city, en route to Banjarmasin, a city on Borneo Island. “The ship’s operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather,” Sudayana said in a video briefing. In response, a rescue ship was headed to the Virgo Transport 8’s estimated last known position, he said, and authorities were deploying rescue teams supported by four vessels, including a navy ship and a helicopter, as the ferry was carrying a large number of passengers and crew. Survivors are rescued and dead bodies recovered Initial information indicated the vessel’s last known position was in the Java Sea, about 148km (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin. The ship’s manifest said it was carrying 243 people – 213 passengers and 30 crew members – although it is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest. Sudayana, who is coordinating the search, said the agency was working with maritime authorities and other relevant agencies while closely monitoring the weather in the area. Search teams, helped by nearby tugboats and other passing vessels, had rescued 107 people and recovered six bodies by Sunday afternoon, he said. The Japanese-built Virgo Transport 8 is designed to transport both passengers and vehicles. Distraught relatives await news Hundreds of relatives gathered at a command centre in Banjarmasin’s Trisakti port on Sunday, awaiting word on family members believed to be aboard the ferry. Many anxiously checked passenger manifests and rescue lists as authorities continued searching for survivors. “I was shocked when I saw my uncle’s name on the passenger list,” said a woman who goes by a single name, Bunga. “But I felt relieved after officials told me he had been rescued.” Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters happen regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed. Last month, at least 211 people were rescued from an Indonesian ferry that caught fire in rough seas near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, while one person was found dead and four others remain missing. The incident happened less than two weeks after another Indonesian ferry, the Mutiara Sentosa 2, caught fire in waters off the main island of Java, leaving at least five people dead. Sunday’s accident comes just four days after a fire that gutted a passenger ferry in the Philippines killed at least 76 people, with at least 10 others still missing.

title: On This Day | Hong Kong mourns Mao Zedong’s death in 1976 –  SCMP archive
description: Fifty years ago, Mao Zedong’s death sent shock waves around the world.
content: This article was first published on September 10, 1976. Sense of grief in Hongkong A deep sense of grief was felt by great numbers of the people in Hongkong yesterday (September 9, 1976) when radio and television stations flashed the news of the Chairman’s passing. The news brought a cloud of gloom over celebrations of the mid-autumn festivities. Flags at a number of major building and hotels, – including the Bank of China – were flown at half-mast within an hour of the announcement. Hongkong people first heard the news over both channels of Radio Hongkong and the English Channel of Commercial Radio at 5.08 pm – minutes after Radio Peking broadcast the official announcement from New China News Agency. The first television flash was broadcast by RTV’s English Channel at 5.17 pm followed by others two or three minutes later. Large crowds milled outside television shops to watch for more announcements. Our Macau correspondent reported that almost immediately after the news became known, local cinemas cancelled shows for the rest of the day to show their respect for the Chinese leader. The Professor of Political Science at the University of Hongkong, Professor P. B. Harris, said it would be difficult to gauge the political significance of the Chairman’s death. “But his passing will mean that we are entering a new era in which things are much less certain than they have been. “But we have been prepared for his death for the past few months. We are psychologically more prepared than, say, a year ago and therefore the impact is much less than a year ago. “Chairman Mao has taken China from the warlord stage to the nuclear age.” A school teacher for the past 18 years, both inside and outside China, Mr Tseng Man-kiu, was confident that Hongkong would not be affected in the near future. “But everything would have to rest and the dust to clear. And when a new leadership emerges a clear evaluation of the whole situation could be made.” His view was shared by many who were interviewed. The feelings of the world community could be best summed up in the expression of sorrow by members of the local diplomatic corps. The Deputy Consul-General for Japan, Mr Yoshiyasu Sato, said: “Personally, I am much grieved to learn of his death. We respect his achievements in Chinese history and revolution, and feel that he was not only a great leader of the Chinese people, but has contributed to the philosophy of current politics in general. We will miss him.” The Consul-General of the United Arab Republic, Mr Ayoub Sharara, said: “I have just learned of the Chairman’s death and it is a great shock to me. The whole world has lost a great genius and a most fantastic leader. We have lost with his death a very dear and a very great friend indeed.” Mr Sharara also commented on the very good relations which have developed recently between China and Egypt. The Consul-General of Sweden, Mr Dag Bergman, also expressed his sadness at learning of the death of the Chinese leader. “We have known for some time of his bad health. But the things which he did for China were very great indeed and he will always stay in the memory of the world. He has brought the name of his country to glory, to be known and respected everywhere. “We can only bow our heads in deep respect and sorrow.” Mr Bergman said he has sent his deep-felt condolences to Chinese friends in Hongkong. The Consul-General of Thailand, Mr Manaspas Xuto, expressed shock, saying: “It has come rather unexpectedly, even though we knew Chairman Mao was pretty advanced in age. We thought he might merely have been taking some rest. There was no indication that his health was that bad, and we are very shocked to hear it.” Representatives of both the Netherlands and Pakistan also called the Chairman’s death “a great and grievous loss to the Chinese people.” The Canadian Commissioner in Hongkong, Mr M. G. Clark said China had not only lost a great leader but a symbol too. He said the world and particularly Hongkong would now be going through a period of “wait and watch.” The Indian Commissioner, Mr A. Madhavan said: “We are deeply distressed to hear this news. Our sympathies go to the Chinese people and the Chinese Government.” New Zealand’s Commissioner, Mr B. R. Finny, said Chairman Mao and his associates had restored the Chinese people’s great dignity and pride. “One always regrets seeing great historical figures pass on. Chairman Mao is one of the great men in history,” he said. The Australian Commissioner, Mr H. D. White, said: “The world has lost an important leader.” The doyen of foreign correspondents, Richard Hughes, who was in the Foreign Correspondents Club when the news came through, said it was at first greeted with complete scepticism. “Then there was the feeling it was nicely timed to coincide with the full moon of the Mid-Autumn Festival,” Hughes said. “It was a nice time to arrange it. It proves again that the Chinese are Chinese first and communists second.” The Deputy Editor of the Far Eastern Economic Review, Russell Spurr, said the future of Hongkong could depend on China’s new political situation and the decisions that would be made. “We don’t know enough about China to be sure of anything,” Spurr said. “I am relatively optimistic, I don’t think there will be a radical change.”

title: Focus on jobs sees affluent Chinese families spend more on tutoring than overseas exposure
description: Survey finds that percentage of children who travelled overseas during summer break fell this year.
content: China’s upper-middle-class families are spending more on their children’s local education to help them compete in a tight domestic job market at the expense of summer programmes aimed at gaining admission to foreign universities, a recent survey found. A survey of 277 affluent Chinese families by Babazhenbang, a parenting and education platform with a database covering hundreds of schools preparing students for overseas study, found that 84.5 per cent of families paid for subject-specific tutoring during the July–August public school holiday, up from 80.7 per cent last year. The share of families spending more than 60,000 yuan (US$7,653) over the break doubled to 9.4 per cent, Babazhenbang found. It said maths, English and tutoring on preparing for exams remained the top choices, with average spending of 24,000 yuan. An emphasis on getting children ready for work in China reflected a tough domestic job market along with thinning interest in overseas education, analysts said. “Families that have given up the international route are putting the money into domestic tutoring instead,” said Kent Cai, founder of Zhejiang Newway, an international education consultancy. “Once they switch to the domestic education track, competition becomes even more intense, so parents are willing to spend more on tutoring to increase their sense of certainty.” Babazhenbang’s survey found that average spending on summer break education programmes fell to a three-year low of 61,100 yuan this year, from 69,000 yuan last year. The share of families spending more than 100,000 yuan on those activities was 12.5 per cent, similar to last year but sharply below 39.4 per cent in 2024 and 26.7 per cent in 2023. The survey also found also that 15.5 per cent of the families had spent less than 10,000 yuan on their children’s summer programmes, the highest proportion in recent years. The percentage of children who travelled overseas during the summer fell from 28.2 per cent last year to 19.8 per cent. Four per cent of families spent more than 60,000 yuan on overseas summer camps this year, down from 7.4 per cent last year. Summer programmes often correlate with family ambitions to send children abroad for university education, but just 570,600 students went abroad last year, down from a peak of 703,500 in 2019, according to Ministry of Education data. Chen Zhiwen, a member of the Chinese Society of Educational Development Strategy, a Beijing-based education research organisation, said he expected the decline to continue, though not in a “cliff-like” fashion. Chen said tighter Western visa restrictions, geopolitical tensions and the improving quality of China’s universities were reasons for families to shift direction. Younger Chinese, he added, had grown up with greater confidence in their own country, making them less likely to view studying abroad as inherently more attractive. International and bilingual schools in the Yangtze River Delta, including those in Shanghai, were also finding recruitment harder, said Kent Cai, founder of Zhejiang Newway, an international education consultancy. He said “expensive” summer programmes for pre-university students in Europe and the United States were also losing appeal among Chinese parents. While families on the international track still outspent their domestic-focused peers this summer – averaging 78,600 yuan compared with 43,600 yuan – Babazhenbang’s survey found the gap was narrowing as parents rethought education priorities. Children from the surveyed families, mostly from China’s major cities, were concentrated in their middle or high school years. Nearly 60 per cent were pursuing international education in China with the rest in the domestic education system.

title: Should cats be permitted in Hong Kong restaurants?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
According to the Hong Kong government, more than 100,000 households in the city had cats as of 2018, and that number is growing rapidly.
It’s safe to say that Hongkongers adore felines – organisers of the Hong Kong Cat Expo 2025 put the city’s annual cat economy at HK$2.4 billion. The city loves these cuddly creatures, which is why cats should be allowed in restaurants.
Many cat owners are hesitant to leave their pets home alone.
As empathetic and social animals, cats can feel stressed and lonely when left isolated for long periods. Over time, this can lead to irreversible behavioural problems and chronic depression.
The Spruce Pets, a publication that provides practical pet care advice from registered veterinarians, says cats do not need a significant amount of space, are non-disruptive indoors and are quieter than other pets. Moreover, cats are self-cleaning and extremely hygienic.
While there may be concerns about customers who are allergic to or afraid of cats, these issues can be easily avoided by creating cat-friendly zones or times.
Rules can also be put in place to ensure that cats are leashed and do not climb onto tables.
A study by the University of Hong Kong estimated that in 2007, only 14 per cent of Hongkongers were allergic to cats.
In addition, according to an article in the journal BMC Psychology, only a very small percentage of the global population suffers from ailurophobia – the fear of cats.
A recent government scheme permitted 940 Hong Kong eateries to allow dogs on their premises. Despite initial hygiene concerns, these restaurants have reported overwhelmingly positive customer feedback, according to The Standard.
Considering dogs are louder and larger than cats, this suggests there would be an equal or even more positive customer response if a similar programme were initiated for cats.
From a business angle, making a restaurant cat-friendly would likely boost sales by attracting a larger customer base.
As Hong Kong restaurants grapple with sky-high rents, these higher revenues are vital for business survival and growth. Eateries can further capitalise on this by offering cat-friendly gourmet dishes and accessories.
Hong Kong’s recent initiative to allow dogs in restaurants has raised a logical follow-up question: should cats be granted the same privilege? While felines are equally beloved companions, extending this scheme to include them would be a significant error.
The recent debate over dog-friendly dining in Hong Kong has prompted online videos showing dogs licking plates and sitting on tables. This highlights the hygiene risks of allowing animals into restaurants. While cats may not behave the same as dogs, they introduce an equally concerning threat: airborne and surface contamination from shedding.
Cats are prolific shedders, releasing microscopic dander and loose fur continuously into their surroundings. In an enclosed dining environment, these particles can easily become airborne and settle onto food-preparation counters, utensils, and even customers’ plates before a meal is served.
Unlike dog saliva, which can be partially mitigated by washing, cat fur and dander are difficult to eliminate, as they can drift across tables or cling to fabric seats and waitstaff uniforms.
This contamination not only violates basic food hygiene standards but also directly impairs the dining experience. Consequently, even without direct contact with food, a cat’s presence in a dining area poses a tangible risk to both public health and customer satisfaction.
In addition, as Nidirect, a UK government-affiliated public service, notes, cats are territorial and form strong attachments to familiar environments – even minor changes, such as rearranged furniture or unfamiliar scents, can induce significant stress.
A restaurant presents an overwhelming assault of stimuli – loud noises, crowded spaces, and a number of food aromas – that can easily overwhelm a cat’s sensitive nature.
This heightened state of fear does not merely cause discomfort; it can trigger unpredictable and uncontrollable reactions. These could include escape attempts or defensive behaviour towards nearby customers, such as biting and scratching.
Such incidents not only disrupt the dining atmosphere but also pose tangible safety risks to other patrons and staff. From flying fur to stress-induced behaviours that endanger others, allowing cats into restaurants is an impractical idea.

title: Shun US goods, buy local: Canadians ‘mad with America’ reshape grocery shelves
description: A deepening trade war and the change in sentiment towards the US have made Canadians more conscious of where their dollars go.
content: A growing consumer push to buy Canadian and boycott US products is ⁠reshaping supermarket shelves in Canada, forcing grocers to improve country-of-origin labelling and secure new sources of supply. In Ontario, the president of independent grocer Vince’s Market, Giancarlo Trimarchi, turned to social media to show customers that most produce on the shelves of his stores is Canadian after receiving angry emails and comments about the grocer stocking US produce. A bitter trade war between the United States and Canada has made consumers more conscious of where their dollars go. “Buy Canadian” movements started last year after US President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on Canadian goods. They have intensified in recent weeks after ‌trade talks broke down and Trump signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America. “It is a lot more aggressive this time around than last year,” Trimarchi said in an interview. Trump told reporters in Dublin on Saturday that Canada is eager to reach a trade deal with the US and that an agreement could come “fairly soon”, while repeating his complaints that Canada has treated US farmers unfairly and should remove tariffs. Trimarchi’s four stores, spread across the Greater Toronto Area, now have about 90 per cent Canadian produce. Trimarchi is now sourcing strawberries from Quebec instead of the US and said he has cut his advertising budget as the changes have pressured operating costs. “We were always put in a position where you had to balance quality versus price. Now it’s quality versus price versus country of origin,” Trimarchi said. Loblaw ⁠Cos, Canada’s largest food retailer, in August brought back large signs featuring a maple leaf in its produce and fresh-food sections after a brief hiatus to flag the Canadian origins of products. Loblaw also reintroduced a “T” tag to tell ‌customers which products are affected by tariffs and make Canadian products easier to identify. Metro, the country’s third-largest grocer, said it would continue to prioritise local Canadian products in the current context. “There has been a permanent change in the Canadian psyche,” said Gary Sands, senior vice-president of public policy and advocacy for the Canadian Federation of Independent Grocers. Canada is the ‌world’s fifth-largest importer of fresh vegetables by value. The US is still the biggest supplier of fresh produce, accounting for more than half of the imports, followed by Mexico. However, the share ⁠of Canada’s vegetable imports from the US fell to ⁠62.6 per cent in July, the latest government data showed, from 69 per cent in the same month of 2023, before Trump was elected. More than half of Canada’s fruit imports came from the US as of July. Trade talks broke down on August 21, spurring a new round of tariffs and ‌counter-tariffs. John Ambard, 27, a software engineer who lives in downtown Toronto, said he has tried to avoid buying American products when possible, preferring to support Canadian brands and businesses. Ambard said he checks product labels and researches companies online to identify Canadian-made goods. “I think, honestly, if ‌I can ‌support Canadian products and Canadian institutions through these tough times, I think that’s a way to help in my small way,” Ambard said. “I’m a little bit mad with America right now with how things are going. The attitude has ‌just not been that of a friend.” Canada’s harsh winters present a challenge for fresh produce, and grocers typically rely on greenhouses, stocked root vegetables or imports, which are usually more cost-effective. But the change in sentiment towards the US could push grocers to explore more local suppliers, experts say, while Canada invests in building a more self-reliant food system. The Canadian government is investing about C$3 billion (US$2 billion) over 10 years to build greenhouses to increase production during ⁠the harsh winter months. It is also trying to lower food inflation – among the highest in the Group of Seven developed nations – by increasing the domestic food supply. Gordon Dean, the owner of Mike Dean Local Grocer, which operates stores in rural Ontario and Quebec, said his stores are now selling more produce from countries such as Spain, Brazil and Honduras than they previously did. “There’s nobody running ‌back to the US supply chain because once the new supply ‌chains are established, they’re far more diversified. We’re in a safer position,” Dean said. However, Dean said restrictions and differing regulations between provinces have made it harder to move food products across Canada, leaving many grocers reliant on suppliers south of the border. “Nationalism is now trumping economics to a degree that might switch if the relationship improves,” said Mike von Massow, professor of food, agriculture and resource economics at the University of Guelph. He said the Canada-US relationship may never fully return to where it was, but a future easing of tensions, particularly under a new US administration, could prompt a shift back to American products because they are often cheaper than other alternatives.

title: Denisovan fossils in China reveal an ancient ‘hunting paradise’
description: Discoveries in southwest China’s Yunnan fill a geographic gap, uncovering how Denisovans lived as expert hunters of animals such as deer.
content: Denisovan remains discovered in southwestern China reveal that Yunnan province’s warm, biodiverse plateau was a “hunting paradise” for the hominins during a global glacial period, according to new research published in the journal Nature. Within the region’s coniferous forests and forest-steppe environments, this archaic human group established a stable subsistence pattern highly adapted to local resources through specialised hunting and the intensive exploitation of animals. The extinct Denisovans once roamed Eurasia, having diverged from modern humans (Homo sapiens) and Neanderthals several hundred thousand years ago. Since Denisovans were first identified in 2010, research has yielded only a handful of molecularly identified remains, leaving scientists with a limited understanding of the species. On September 9, two papers co-authored by researchers from institutions including the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and the Yunnan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology were published simultaneously in Nature. The two papers overlap in their study focus and some of the researchers are cited as authors on both papers. The studies detail Denisovan fossils, associated artefacts and subsistence strategies discovered in Bianfu Cave in Yunnan, shedding new light on the appearance, evolution and behaviour of this elusive human group. One paper, titled “Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from southwest China”, said the findings “establish Bianfu Cave as a Denisovan locality yielding the most abundant remains of this hominin group outside Denisova Cave in Siberia”. The authors noted that the findings “fill a critical geographic gap” in the documented distribution of Denisovans, refining understanding of their evolutionary history. Unlike the widely studied Neanderthals – who were likely to have been replaced or assimilated by early Homo sapiens about 40,000 years ago – Denisovans are a more recent addition to the human family tree. The first Denisovan skeletal fossil was discovered in Siberia’s Altai Mountains in 2008, and the group was formally named in 2010 after the sequencing of DNA from a finger bone revealed a lineage distinct from all known human species. That landmark study was also published in Nature. Among the authors were the 2022 Nobel laureate Svante Paabo, a Swedish geneticist, and his former doctoral student Fu Qiaomei, who is now director of the ancient DNA laboratory at the CAS Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP) in Beijing. Since then, scientists have gradually identified a collection of cranial, facial and dental remains across Asia, including a male Denisovan jawbone dredged from the seabed in the Penghu Channel of the Taiwan Strait. Up to 5 per cent of the DNA of modern Southeast Asian populations can be traced back to Denisovans. By contrast, the figure is about 2 per cent for populations in the Tibetan Plateau region and effectively zero in Europe. This led scientists to speculate that Denisovans once existed widely across Asia, particularly in the southeast – a hypothesis supported by the fossil evidence unearthed in Yunnan. In 2019, workers beginning an ecological restoration project at a quarry in the province stumbled upon bones and stone tools. That same year, systematic excavations of Bianfu Cave began, eventually yielding thousands of fossils. The site is in Yunnan’s Dali Bai autonomous prefecture at an altitude of 2,370 metres (7,775 feet), on the southeastern edge of the Tibetan Plateau and the southern edge of the Hengduan Mountains, according to the Yunnan Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology. For the research detailed in the ancient proteins paper, Fu’s team at the IVPP screened more than 60,000 bone fragments. They identified three Denisovan fossils – two parietal bone fragments and one proximal radial fragment – as well as two Denisovan teeth. These remains date back between 134,000 and 167,000 years. During this glacial period, the relatively warm climate and conifer-dominated forest-steppe environments around Bianfu Cave are likely to have provided a stable supply of mammals, according to the paper, transforming the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau into a “hunting paradise”. However, given the scarcity of data, the researchers noted they could not yet determine the specific genetic contribution of this Denisovan population to modern human genomes. In the second paper, titled “Denisovans from southwestern China and their subsistence strategies”, a team led by Chen Fahu from the CAS Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research analysed the remains alongside faunal records and associated archaeological materials, including more than 1,300 stone artefacts. Faunal and pollen records indicate that the Denisovans inhabited a forest-like environment dominated by coniferous trees. The study found that the cave’s inhabitants were highly skilled at hunting medium and large animals. When it came to their tools, they favoured a highly practical approach – quickly chipping stones into shape as needed and making widespread use of raw, unshaped animal bones. A Nature News article about the research said: “Evidence from the site indicates that Denisovans crafted bone tools similar to those made by their relatives, the Neanderthals.” The artefacts suggested that the Denisovans – who occupied the site for at least 30,000 years, and possibly up to 120,000 years – were skilled hunters of animals such as deer, the article said.

title: Next-gen wealthy Hongkongers drop property for higher returns in deposits and hedge funds
description: Property is losing its sparkle for next-generation investors who prioritise liquidity, easy succession and higher returns.
content: When Maria’s family moved out of their house in Hong Kong’s Southern district, one of the bigger jobs was packing her mother’s belongings, including the orange Hermes boxes that had accumulated in the family gym. Her 86-year-old father was reluctant to rent, while her mother – who had spent her life buying homes – initially insisted that if they were going to rent, she wanted a house rather than a flat. “I have never rented a home in my entire life,” she said. They eventually settled at The Repulse Bay, a seaside luxury complex long popular with expatriates and senior professionals who rent in Hong Kong for the flexibility to move on. Three generations of the family now live there in separate rented flats of about 2,500 square feet each. Maria – who asked that her family name be withheld – shares one with her parents, her brother rents another, and her sister is preparing to move into a third. When the next generation comes to us, they often say the same thing: financial assets are simply much easier to manage Clifford Ng, Zhong Lun Law Firm The arrangement keeps the family close, but for Maria the more important question is what happens to the capital that would otherwise be tied up in another home. Her father built the family fortune through a screen-printing business he started in Hong Kong in the 1960s, with the family accumulating property along the way. Maria recently took over management of the family’s investments. She said liquid and illiquid assets were roughly split, with the family still holding substantial residential and commercial property. “I want to liquidate everything,” she said. Among the properties Maria wants to sell is a commercial unit at The Centre in Central, the property she said she “hated the most.” Bought for more than HK$100 million (US$13 million) in cash and without leverage, Maria estimates it is now worth about HK$60 million. The family also owns multiple residential properties worth HK$20 million to HK$30 million each. “I’m holding a property, but I can’t use that money,” she said. “I would rather liquidate it and have it make more money for me.” For generations, that would have been an unusual calculation in Hong Kong, where profits from businesses were often channelled into flats, shops and offices that could generate rent, appreciate, provide collateral for further borrowing and eventually be passed to children. Maria no longer expects the same gains. “Before, HK$5 million could easily become HK$15 million,” she said. “Now, if HK$5 million becomes HK$5.1 million, you’d almost sell it.” She is redirecting proceeds into liquid investments, including long-short hedge funds, multi-asset strategies, and investments in artificial intelligence, biotechnology and robotics. Gabriel Chan, managing director and head of investment services at BNP Paribas Wealth Management in Hong Kong, said the calculation was becoming more relevant for wealthy clients who already held sizeable property portfolios, although he did not expect them to abandon real estate altogether. “A lot of people got rich through properties ... but that’s why they would like to diversify,” Chan said. “The incremental investment may not be in real estate again.” The trade-off had become more visible as Hong Kong residential rental yields of about 3 to 3.5 per cent compared with US dollar deposit rates above 4 per cent, Chan said. “Even a deposit is paying you better than residential properties,” he said. “That’s the trade-off. Everything is relative.” For Maria, the numbers make renting easier to justify. One of her US$5 million private banking accounts earning 5 to 6 per cent would already generate US$250,000 to US$300,000 a year, she said. “Isn’t that more than enough for rent?” she said. “You can buy 20 more orange boxes with it.” I’m not against property. But I just don’t see those multiples happening in real estate any more. It’s not happening, not in my lifetime Maria, next-gen investor To support her and her family’s lifestyle at The Repulse Bay, she budgets about HK$5 million a year for rent, management fees, rates, utilities and household expenses, arguing that returns on the capital she would otherwise have put into a home can cover the cost of living there while leaving the principal invested. The calculation is also tied to succession. Maria has no children, while her siblings do, and she plans to retain a few flats for the younger generation while selling the rest. “The easiest thing to divide is money,” she said. Clifford Ng, a lawyer who advises family offices at Zhong Lun Law Firm, said younger heirs were often less interested in taking on physical assets accumulated by their parents and grandparents. “When the next generation comes to us, they often say the same thing: financial assets are simply much easier to manage,” he said. That can be particularly relevant for Hong Kong families whose fortunes were built in manufacturing and trading, as some third- and fourth-generation members move overseas or decide not to continue the businesses that created the family wealth. The shift is taking place even as another pool of wealth is returning to Hong Kong property. Mainland Chinese buyers accounted for roughly 80 per cent of transactions involving homes worth HK$100 million or more in The Peak and Southern district in 2025, according to Centaline Property. For Maria, there is no contradiction in wanting to continue living in one of Hong Kong’s most expensive neighbourhoods while choosing not to own the home. The family has become accustomed to the convenience of The Repulse Bay, where three generations can live nearby and building staff handle maintenance and facilities. Her father, long accustomed to being a property owner, has since changed his mind about renting. Maria has not changed hers about property. “I’m not against property,” she said. “But I just don’t see those multiples happening in real estate any more. It’s not happening, not in my lifetime.”

title: Opinion | Warming cities can’t afford to sacrifice their urban parks
description: Green spaces lower urban temperatures and boost quality of life. Cities may be short of space, but trading parks for concrete is a bad bargain.
content: Some of my earliest memories of Bengaluru, where I spent my summer holidays, are of looking up in wonder at the towering canopy of trees in Cubbon Park. Even in the height of summer, Bengaluru could be cool enough to require a light jacket. Today, the iconic Cubbon Park, the pride of the city I now call home, is under threat. So is Lalbagh Botanical Garden, another of the city’s iconic green spaces, with roots stretching back more than 250 years. On a Sunday morning in Bengaluru last month, thousands gathered at Lalbagh Botanical Garden carrying a simple message: “Walk in Lalbagh. Walk for Lalbagh”. They were protesting against a new Karnataka law that allows up to 5 per cent of protected parkland to be used for public infrastructure. The provision could make as much as 12 acres of Lalbagh and 15 acres of neighbouring Cubbon Park available for such projects. This is not the first time Bengaluru’s citizens have defended these green spaces from infrastructure projects. Earlier campaigns opposed proposals to build a metro line through Lalbagh. Today, protesters are confronting both a tunnel road project and a legislative change that potentially makes protected parkland easier to use. The tunnel road project will pass through ecologically sensitive spaces and entails the felling of about 900 mature trees. The threat is particularly worrying as Bengaluru’s vegetation cover has shrunk dramatically since the 1970s. The loss has been accompanied by a sharp rise in land surface temperatures. The protests in Bengaluru are striking because they are not just about two well-known parks or the city’s green cover. They are part of a larger struggle unfolding in cities around the world as urban residents confront the same question: what happens when cities run out of space? In Mumbai, the Save Aarey movement has become one of the city’s longest-running environmental movements. Nearly four years of weekly protests have been held to protect the 1,300-hectare (3,212 acres) Aarey Colony urban forest from development. In Singapore last month, a plan to clear two-thirds of the Maju forest to build public housing faced a public outcry, with thousands rallying to save the green space. A report published in January by Campaign to Protect Rural England highlighted that more than 50 parks and green spaces in London are under serious threat from development and commercialisation. Although the locations are different, the underlying threat is the same: infrastructure projects. Many of these cities once preserved green belts for fields, forests and open spaces to prevent indiscriminate development, but as cities grow and land becomes sparse, urban green spaces are being sacrificed. The UN-Habitat World Cities Report 2024 found that the average share of green space in cities worldwide fell from 19.5 per cent in 1990 to 13.9 per cent in 2020. East and Southeast Asia experienced a particularly sharp decline, from 32.5 per cent in 1990 to 18.6 per cent in 2020. A more recent study by Portland State University of 33 US cities found that 72.7 per cent of them were losing greenery, particularly in the hottest neighbourhoods. China offers a striking counter-example to the trend of infrastructure coming at the expense of green spaces. This is not because its cities have escaped the global loss of urban greenery, but rather because some of its largest cities are now trying to reverse that trajectory. Shanghai has already created 1,000 parks as of the end of 2025 and aims to add another 1,000 in the next 10 years, taking it to 2,000 parks by 2036. In a city where land is already scarce and population density is high, conventional large-scale park construction is expensive. Instead, the city plans to convert urban spaces into pocket parks. Beijing is similarly expanding its green spaces under the Beijing Garden City Plan. By 2035, it plans to raise forest cover to more than 45 per cent, provide at least 17 square metres of park green space per person and ensure that more than 95 per cent of residents have access to a park within a 500-metre radius. Both Shanghai and Beijing are moving towards a model where green space is part of urban infrastructure. This matters because urban parks can improve quality of life and help cities cope with the increasingly severe impacts of climate change. Depending on the canopy structure of trees and the city’s climate, trees can reduce air temperature by about 0.5-5.8 degrees Celsius and surface temperature by 2-12 degrees. Evidence from both Beijing and Shanghai demonstrates this cooling effect. A study of 10 large Beijing parks found that they produced an average daytime cooling of about 1 degree and nighttime cooling of 3.63 degrees. The cooling influence extended more than a kilometre during summer nights. Research examining 24 parks in Shanghai found that average temperatures inside urban parks were around 1.46 to 1.66 degrees lower than in the main city. While creating new parks and planting trees has its clear benefits, a sapling can take years to develop into a mature tree with dense canopy. Therefore, preserving established parks is all the more important. Mature trees provide environmental and public health benefits that cannot be replicated by planting new trees. The cities of the future will need more roads, housing and public transport, but they cannot instantly recreate a mature urban ecosystem once it has been destroyed. While planting trees and creating new parks for the future is important, protecting the mature urban parks we already have might be even more urgent.

title: China influencer exposed over fake US$150,000 flood gift; Red Cross finds only 15-cent offers
description: If proven to have exploited a public welfare event for self-promotion or falsified donation documents, influencer could face legal consequences.
content: A Chinese influencer faced widespread criticism after a purported donation of 1 million yuan (US$150,000) to flood relief efforts was allegedly revealed as fabricated. Since July, typhoon-induced torrential rains have ravaged the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region in southern China, resulting in the deaths of 159 people, according to local reports. On September 7, internet users accused a RedNote influencer known as Anlan of fabricating a donation record for flood relief in Guangxi, sharing screenshots of the alleged receipt across comment sections. Anlan, whose gender and true identity remain undisclosed, posted an image claiming to show a 1 million-yuan donation to the Guangxi Red Cross on July 17, accompanied by a caption: “Offering a humble contribution to post-disaster reconstruction.” The post quickly went viral, garnering thousands of likes and commendation from internet users who celebrated Anlan’s “act of kindness.” The account amassed more than 31,000 followers within days. The SCMP contacted the Guangxi Red Cross, which stated that it had not received any single personal donation of 1 million yuan on July 17. However, the organisation’s records indicated several one-yuan (15 US cents) donations on that day. One donor’s first name matched the name shown in Anlan’s screenshot, but the bank account details did not align with those publicly disclosed by Anlan. They could not confirm whether Anlan was responsible for any of the one-yuan donations. The Red Cross further clarified that all donation records were publicly accessible on its official website. The social media platform subsequently suspended Anlan’s account. As of publication, Anlan had not responded to SCMP’s requests for comment. The Guangxi Red Cross informed the SCMP that it was continuing to monitor the situation and had no additional remarks at that time. Legal experts cautioned that fabricating donation records or falsely claiming charitable contributions could result in legal repercussions. Ma Junzhe, a lawyer at Guangdong Zheqing Law Firm, pointed out that public donation pledges may incur legal obligations and could be enforceable through legal action. Similar cases have surfaced in the past. In 2023, Chinese entrepreneur Wu You was sued by his alma mater for failing to fulfil an 11 million yuan donation pledge to its foundation. Wu was later classified as a dishonest debtor and faced restrictions on high-value spending. Lawyer Ma added that if Anlan’s actions are found to have exploited a public welfare event for self-promotion or involved falsifying donation documents bearing official seals, police could impose administrative penalties, including fines and possible detention. Online reactions highlighted concerns regarding the broader implications for public trust. One observer warned that such incidents might foster scepticism towards authentic charitable initiatives. “Society should raise the cost of fraud. Merely banning an account is insufficient; Anlan should face consequences,” wrote one internet user. “I am still a student, and my only income comes from tutoring, yet I donate 50 yuan every month to a rural children’s fund. True kindness does not require display,” expressed another user.

title: How to solve Hong Kong’s triple whammy: ageing population, baby dearth and job losses?
description: Experts say this week’s policy address should go beyond welfare provision, offering strategy for job creation and upskilling the workforce.
content: In the fourth of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Fiona Sun and Edith Lin analyse how to improve livelihoods in the city by tackling the impact of demographic changes and technological advancement. Read part one here, part two here and part three here. Twenty-eight-year-old Hong Kong resident Fong and his wife want to have a child but he knows they cannot afford one for now. He earns about HK$10,000 (US$1,275) a month as a construction worker and lives in a subdivided flat in Prince Edward, paying roughly HK$3,000 a month for the 100 sq ft space. His mainland Chinese wife, 27, remains in Guangdong province as she waits for a one-way permit to be in Hong Kong with him. With unstable working hours and wages, Fong said he struggled to make ends meet. The cost of raising a child in one of the world’s most expensive cities is too heavy a burden to bear for now. “If you bring a child into the world, you have to raise them. It’s not something to be taken lightly,” he said. “It requires real commitment and a good environment for the child to grow up in.” Fong is among the thousands of Hongkongers who are staying child-free as reflected in the city’s record-low births, with residents wrestling over their financial woes, housing constraints and concerns over access to education and the lifestyle trade-offs they have to make to have children. The government is under mounting pressure to tackle the larger issue of the city’s population targets as it grapples with not just declining births but also a rapidly ageing society. This double whammy creates a high age dependency ratio, where a small number of working-age people are supporting a much bigger population of elderly or the very young. At the same time, Hong Kong faces fiscal constraints, making the challenge that much harder to tackle, experts say, as they await measures to be announced in Wednesday’s policy address and the city’s first five-year plan. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu is expected to announce policies to improve livelihoods. Observers say the approach should go beyond welfare provisions, offering a holistic strategy that includes job creation and new industries for new vocations as old ones are absorbed by emerging technology. Upskilling the labour force, leveraging emerging industries for job creation and unlocking the hidden workforce were critical to resolving the deep-rooted problems without disrupting social harmony, they said. “Hong Kong’s labour force is facing impacts from an unstable exterior economic outlook, an unequal interior development, technological transformation and the government’s deficit and ensuing cut in public resources,” said Au Yeung Tat-chor, an associate professor in the department of sociology and social policy at Lingnan University. “As we are facing a hard-to-change trend of declining birth rates, it is time to think of ways to allow the local population that was originally marginalised or excluded from the workforce to re-engage in the labour market, which will benefit both society and the economy.” Official statistics showed that the city’s labour force stood at 3.79 million people between May and July this year, down from the 3.81 million recorded for 2025. Record-low births Hong Kong recorded 29,700 births between mid-2025 and mid-2026. It is the first time the city has had fewer than 30,000 births in its midyear population update since official records began in 1962. The number of births continued to shrink despite the HK$20,000 baby bonus, tax relief and public housing perks. Experts warned that increasing financial rewards was unlikely to work, even as others pointed to the Singapore government’s recent push towards more generous pro-family measures. The centrepiece is a new scheme that will provide almost S$70,000 (US$55,255) in direct financial support for each Singaporean child until age 17. “First, we cannot mechanically replicate the amount and second, we need to assess how many families could be incentivised and determine the threshold – how much is needed – for them to have children,” said Eric Fong Wai-ching, chair professor in sociology at the University of Hong Kong. He added that financial incentives tended to work mainly for the working class, while better-off households might be less responsive as considerations other than money carried more weight. Fong called for a review of existing pro-family measures, and urged a more comprehensive population policy as it would require other supporting measures to sustain the population and hence the economy. Nelson Chow Wing-sun, an emeritus professor at the University of Hong Kong’s department of social work and social administration, said the city should prioritise attracting those from the mainland – whether for family reunion, imported labour, study or work – an advantage the city held over other low‑fertility regions. “Hong Kong’s population growth has been driven by people coming from mainland China rather than birth rates,” he said. “This is something Singapore does not have.” But he cautioned that cross-border migration must be conducted in a well-planned and structured manner to avoid creating new problems. Official statistics showed that the city had approved more than 462,000 applications through various talent admission schemes since 2023, with about 340,000, or 73 per cent, from the mainland. To fill the labour shortages, the city has also approved more than 122,000 applications through various labour importation schemes since 2023. Imported labour to supplement, not to replace But the schemes have also come at a cost. Sze Lai-shan, deputy director of the Society for Community Organisation, argued that labour importation had compromised the jobs of low-income locals. Under the Enhanced Supplementary Labour Scheme, employers may apply to import workers for 26 low-skilled job categories, but they must first conduct local recruitment. Operators in most industries must complete a four-week local recruitment exercise and maintain a staffing ratio of two local workers for each imported labourer. From mid-June, the catering sector faces a tougher staffing ratio and a longer local recruitment exercise in a bid to force it to turn first to locals. Sze pointed out that the scheme had not set a cap for each industry, while operators also could cut local staff’s working hours and salaries. She proposed setting a quota and halting applications for industries with an unemployment rate of at least 4 per cent. Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation, a think tank, suggested extending tougher labour importation rules to sectors with high unemployment rates and high vacancy rates. “The public expects that imported labour is a way to supplement local labour, rather than replacing local workers,” he said. “When it is unbalanced, authorities can consider halting the labour importation or adjusting the mechanism to safeguard the local workforce.” Leveraging AI and emerging industries Beyond imported labour, rapid technological change also imposes challenges on local workers. Shui warned of the relatively high unemployment rate among the younger generation, who were generally educated but faced challenges of companies replacing junior positions with artificial intelligence (AI). Between May and July, the city’s unemployment rate stood at 3.8 per cent, but it reached 14.6 per cent for those aged 15 to 19 and 8.4 per cent for 20- to 29-year-olds. Shui struck a positive note about the long-term employment market, as technological advancement would not only replace jobs but also create new ones, just as programming occupations were created with the invention of computers in the past. It is the transition period that the government needs to be attentive to. “However, the market needs to adapt in the short term,” he said, noting that upskilling and AI education were the solutions. He urged the government to devise courses to upskill labour after studying industry trends and the impact of technology. Leonard Chan Tik-yuen, founding chairman of the Hong Kong Innovative Technology Development Association, said the workforce should boost its AI literacy, professional knowledge, and interdisciplinary and communication skills to embrace new job opportunities ahead. While technology had replaced occupations with repetitive duties, it created new roles in AI compliance and regulatory work, as well as technicians for automotive and advanced wearable devices, Chan said. Chan added that new roles for programming and managing machine operations had also emerged as AI was applied in manufacturing and new industries for quality assurance and customer service. The government has also promoted smart manufacturing and new industries such as microelectronics, new energy and new materials in recent years, which are expected to create new jobs. “The industries and the government should think about how to set rules, make data available and provide application scenarios that AI empowers people, rather than replacing them,” he said. “It is about using AI to shorten employees’ working hours so that they can manage [a greater number of] AI agents. Employees will be happier, while productivity will improve without affecting the budget.” He added that new application scenarios and occupations would take time to evolve, urging workers to develop comprehensive skills and engage in new paths as technology shortened their working hours.
