Unlocking potential labour Au Yeung from Lingnan University said the city’s five-year plan should focus on unlocking segments of the local labour force that remained underutilised, including older workers and women. According to the Census and Statistics Department, the labour force participation rate of women, excluding foreign domestic helpers, was 47.3 per cent in the second quarter this year. The figure for people aged 60 and above was 22.7 per cent, while that for those aged 65 and over was 13.5 per cent. A key hurdle to be removed, he noted, was raising the retirement age. He said the current policies encouraging older people to return to workplaces relied heavily on short-term allowances as incentives, which had limited effect. Instead, he called for a long-term strategy that combined financial support with services and training programmes to help older people build new skills and networks. “Hong Kong’s labour force participation rate among the elderly is low, compared with some neighbouring mature economies,” he said. He called on authorities to set key performance indicators aimed at raising the labour force participation rates for the elderly and women. To ease women’s caregiving burden and facilitate their return to work, more public childcare services should be provided – especially for toddlers aged under three – while a more flexible working environment tailored to their needs, such as additional parental leave, was also needed, he added. Lawmaker Lam Chun-sing, also the chairman of the Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions, urged the government to roll out extra subsidies and support for certain demographics, such as single parents, who are one of the three groups already targeted under its poverty alleviation policies. “Employment can help alleviate poverty. If single parents enrol in courses, you can offer extra subsidies to entice them to seek jobs. Meanwhile, the government has to strengthen childcare support, allowing parents to have more time for retraining and employment,” he said. “The city should aim to build a family-friendly working environment so residents can earn a living without affecting their family life.” If such conditions improved, workers such as Fong said they would be more motivated to have children. More cash allowances would help, Fong added, while affordable childcare would allow his wife to work and earn an income. “All we hope for is to provide a good life for our child,” he said.

title: Asian Games: meet the footballer with Japanese blood ‘ready to fight for Hong Kong’
description: Sohgo Ichikawa poised for prominent role in city team’s daunting opener against hosts and country of his birth.
content: Five days away from one of the biggest matches of his young life, it would have been understandable had Sohgo Ichikawa reined in his efforts when his club team, Lee Man, faced Eastern District. Instead, the 22-year-old buzzed about on Friday in the manner that has made him the outstanding young player of the early part of the Hong Kong Premier League season. He will step out for the under-23s’ opening Asian Games fixture against his birth country, Japan, next Wednesday cradling fresh memories of scoring both Lee Man goals in a 2-1 win against opponents who last season boasted the league’s stingiest defence. Ichikawa has already twice played against Japan: once on his senior Hong Kong debut, aged 17, as a late substitute in the 2022 East Asian Championship, then again off the bench when the city team lost 4-0 in the Games semi-finals three years ago. A technically superb, direct and dynamic wide attacker, Ichikawa expects that next week he will be “more involved and one of the main players”. “I’m more excited for this game [than the previous two], and I want to prepare myself to be as fit as possible,” he said. “Playing Japan is always much more meaningful for me. It gives me an extra boost to fight harder and perform better. “I also want to show that, although I have Japanese blood, I want to fight for Hong Kong.” His parents will travel to watch the match, while his grandparents, who he visits every year in Japan, will also be in the 45,000-capacity Toyota Stadium, health permitting. Born in Osaka, Ichikawa was just two months old when his Japanese mother and Chinese father moved the family to Hong Kong. By the age of 13, he was playing for Hong Kong under-15s and on the books of Kitchee, while also training with FC Vandore, a Japanese junior club. In December 2021, months after he turned 17, Ichikawa was given his league debut, coming on early for injured Kitchee striker Dejan Damjanovic and scoring in a 6-1 drubbing of BC Rangers. “It was really a good confidence boost, and a valuable step for me to keep pushing myself harder,” Ichikawa said. It was somewhat unfortunate that the game at Rangers was Kitchee’s last of a campaign ruined by the coronavirus pandemic. When football resumed nine months later, Ichikawa found a host of senior players blocking his first-team opportunities. “It was difficult for me to really showcase my abilities, or to get minutes and keep working hard,” Ichikawa said. “I think I could have been doing much more and, maybe, I could have gone out on loan earlier. “Also, tournaments and overseas games were cancelled during Covid, so there were quite a few missed opportunities, which wasn’t great for me.” Ichikawa moved in 2023, agreeing a season-long loan to Southern. The district club borrowed him again for 2024-25, a campaign Ichikawa crowned with a man-of-the-match display in a 4-0 Sapling Cup final hammering of Lee Man. Still, he was in and out of the team for two seasons, before joining permanently last term and becoming a mainstay. A former pupil at Kiangsu-Chekiang College in North Point, Ichikawa mastered English to the extent it is “my best language”. He speaks Japanese at home with his parents, while he has picked up Cantonese from teammates and coaches. Ichikawa’s parents supported his decision to quit full-time education at 16 because “they want me to reach the highest level possible”. He had a private tutor and studied alone for A levels in mathematics, psychology and business. His grades? “Average,” Ichikawa said. “Not having to study any more has allowed me to focus much more on off-field things like recovery and extra training,” he added. In 2024, Ichikawa had a salutary experience with Real Union, the Spanish club where Hong Kong’s Shanghai Shenhua left-back, Shinichi Chan, went on loan the previous year. “It was my first time with an overseas club, and it was very hard to adapt to a completely new environment and language,” Ichikawa said. “But Spanish football is top. The intensity and quality of every player, even the reserves, were really high. It was a good learning experience.” Much like his start with Kitchee fizzled out somewhat, Ichikawa’s early international recognition proved a false dawn. After that brief 2022 outing in 6-0 humbling by Japan, he waited three years to play 15 minutes of a dreary 0-0 draw with Nepal last June. In June this year, he came on for the closing stages of a 2-0 friendly defeat in Cambodia. Going back overseas and gaining regular Hong Kong selection are “things I aim to do”, although of more immediate concern to Ichikawa is becoming indispensable at Lee Man. Nineteen at the previous Asian Games, Ichikawa was limited to one start in a meaningless group game against Uzbekistan, and confined to a watching brief for the landmark knockout victories over Palestine and Iran. Tsang Chiu-tat, the Hong Kong u23 head coach, believes the “smart and technically brilliant” Ichikawa has sufficient talent to put himself in the spotlight this month, when his side will also play Thailand and Kyrgyzstan. “He’s very mobile in running and turning, and he provides good agility in attack,” Tsang, who is also Ichikawa’s club technical director, said. “His understanding has improved at Lee Man and I see him playing much better now.” Recalling his experience from three years ago, Ichikawa said: “The emotions and excitement were incredible, and I was really happy with the results, but I also really wanted to be on the field. “We showed we could compete, and that’s given us motivation, and the confidence that we can at least get out of the group this time.”

title: China’s anti-corruption law is going global. What does it mean for overseas firms?
description: Beijing’s draft legislation looks like its US precedent but with some far-reaching differences, analysts say.
content: China’s new draft law on combating cross-border corruption is as much a weapon against foreign interference as it is a tool against illicit financial flows, analysts say. The draft sets out ways to block extraterritorial investigations and to retaliate against foreign anti-corruption enforcement, drawing a firm legal boundary against foreign jurisdictions while establishing its own mechanism to police overseas assets. In doing so, legal specialists warn, Beijing is also creating a double-edged regulatory framework that will force multinationals and Chinese businesses operating in regional hubs such as Singapore to navigate data compliance dilemmas. The draft Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law was submitted to the country’s top legislature in late August for its first reading, and the public has until September 26 to give feedback. During panel discussions about the legislation, lawmakers said the measures filled a crucial statutory void. Wang Ke, a member of the National People’s Congress’ Standing Committee, said that in the past, provisions covering the area had been scattered across the Supervision Law and Criminal Procedure Law, complicating asset recovery and procedures for trials in absentia. However, the new draft was a “fundamental law” that integrated prevention, punishment and international cooperation “into a single chain”, Legal Daily quoted Wang as saying on September 1. The legislation will add another layer to the legal firewall that China has steadily erected over the past five years against perceived Western legal overreach. Ryan Mitchell, an associate professor of law at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, said “foreign-related factors in the fight against corruption are on the rise” and “the intertwining of domestic and overseas corruption is intensifying”, making the draft bill part of Beijing’s “overall push for intensifying ‘foreign-related rule of law’”. “The rising globalisation of major Chinese firms makes cross-border corruption an ever more significant issue for Beijing. International perceptions regarding the fairness of Chinese competition, or the benefits of [Belt and Road Initiative] projects, are also tied to such genuine concerns,” Mitchell said. The rising globalisation of major Chinese firms makes cross-border corruption an ever more significant issue for Beijing Ryan Mitchell, law professor To some extent, the draft law resembles some anti-corruption laws in the West, such as the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and Britain’s Bribery Act. All three extend anti-corruption jurisdiction beyond domestic borders to target overseas bribery and cross-border commercial misconduct, and put corporate compliance programmes, internal accounting integrity, and third-party due diligence at the centre of enterprise liability and risk management. However, the US act focuses on bribery of foreign public officials and accounting controls, while the British model establishes broadly framed bribery offences and a corporate failure-to-prevent offence, according to Wang Jiangyu, a law professor at City University of Hong Kong. “The Chinese draft is much more institutionally and politically integrated,” he said. The Chinese bill covers not only outbound bribery but also corruption involving Chinese public officials, state organs and state-owned enterprises (SOEs), overseas misconduct by Chinese public-sector actors, flight by suspected persons, cross-border transfers of corrupt assets, and certain foreign conduct producing effects in China. “Beijing is borrowing some internationally recognisable elements of modern anti-bribery law, but embedding them in a distinctly Chinese model combining punishment, prevention, asset protection, supervisory governance, international cooperation and resistance to what China considers abusive foreign extraterritorial enforcement,” he said. That Chinese model includes establishing a centralised mechanism led by the National Supervisory Commission, which comes under the Communist Party’s top anti-corruption body. The commission will coordinate with a dozen or so state bodies, ranging from public security and finance to cyberspace administration. “This is important because cross-border corruption cases rarely involve bribery alone. They commonly require the tracing of payments, corporate records, beneficial interests, electronic data and overseas assets,” Wang said. China’s decision to adopt a framework like the US act carries a touch of historical “irony”, according to Matthew Erie, an associate professor of law at the American University Washington College of Law. Erie said that in 2011, then US Department of Commerce general counsel Cameron Kerry advocated for China to adopt a law equivalent to the American legislation. Beijing responded by amending its Criminal Law that year to criminalise bribes paid to foreign officials, fulfilling its obligations under the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, he said. But those statutory provisions remained dormant for over a decade until October 2023, when a court in the southern city of Guangzhou enforced them in a landmark case, convicting two former executives of state-owned China Railway Tunnel Group of bribing a government official in Singapore, Erie said. It was a signal that China’s foreign bribery laws were being enforced. What started out as a US effort to encourage trade has become a state-led push to resist Western legal dominance and American long-arm jurisdiction. Behind Beijing’s legislative shift lies a decade of deep frustration with international legal cooperation. Before turning to a statutory extraterritorial framework, Beijing tried for years to combat cross-border corruption and repatriate fugitives through traditional bilateral diplomacy. At its height, China negotiated 59 bilateral extradition treaties, believing that formal international agreements could serve as the legal backbone for anti-graft campaigns such as Operation Fox Hunt and Operation Sky Net, which were launched between 2014 and 2015 and continue today. However, Western scepticism – which Chinese authorities view as an unreasonable double standard – blocked this bilateral framework from expanding where Beijing needed it most. Key Western destinations for fugitives, including the United States, Canada, Britain and Australia, either refused to negotiate bilateral extradition treaties with mainland China or left signed treaties unratified due to human rights and judicial concerns. That left China with only around 45 active extradition treaties in force globally, mostly with non-Western nations. This lack of an enforceable international framework turned Western capitals into safe havens for scores of high-profile fugitives well known for their corrupt activities. Denied a functional multilateral repatriation pipeline, Beijing was left with little choice but to pivot to a statutory mechanism – creating what is, in effect, China’s own version of long-arm jurisdiction to police corrupt assets and actors overseas. Now, Beijing appears to be summoning its full legislative powers to take a far tougher line than the US and Britain. Mitchell said that both the US and British acts were widely regarded as being underused, with foreign officials seldom pursued and convicted of bribery. That enforcement is only set to decline further. In February last year, US President Donald Trump issued an executive order pausing enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act before the Justice Department unveiled new guidelines in June restricting prosecutions to cases directly threatening American economic competitiveness and national security. “The Trump administration has reduced usage [of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act] to promote the ‘competitiveness’ of American companies,” Mitchell said. “In contrast, Beijing is continually making its own anti-corruption framework more strict and far-reaching. The draft law indicates that this process of increasingly tight regulation continues to be a major focus for the party.” Provisions such as Article 17, which establishes rewards and legal protections for whistle-blowers, were key legislative tools aimed at bolstering enforcement capabilities, Mitchell said. One of the major features of China’s draft law is its power to fight foreign scrutiny and retaliate against overseas enforcement. Erie said the draft was “a confluence of two reform trajectories: domestic anti-corruption concerns and foreign adversarialism”. In particular, Article 6 was a reaction to perceived “unlawful US extraterritoriality”. The article authorises retaliatory and blocking measures if foreign states use anti-corruption enforcement “as a pretext” or improperly apply extraterritorial laws to suppress Chinese interests. Article 26 also targets sovereignty, banning foreign entities and individuals from conducting anti-corruption investigations or gathering evidence within China without explicit state approval. And Chinese domestic entities cannot help foreign authorities without prior clearance. Wang said Article 26 was “particularly important” because it was “a strong assertion that cross-border investigations must proceed through authorised government channels”. If enacted, the law’s broad reach will be tested in key financial and trading hubs across Asia, such as Singapore, which hosts regional management, treasury functions, intermediaries, and holding structures for many Chinese enterprises. Because cross-border investigations often involve offshore bank accounts, corporate structures, trusts and professional intermediaries, Chinese enforcement efforts will frequently require data and assets located within Singapore. Wang said there was a “solid foundation” for bilateral cooperation, as both nations were signatories to the UN Convention Against Corruption and maintained formal channels for legal assistance and information sharing. But it may not be automatic or unilateral. Wang said that any requests from Beijing would have to navigate Singapore’s independent judicial process, where local authorities – such as the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau and the Attorney-General’s Chambers – process inquiries strictly according to Singaporean domestic law, evidential thresholds and procedural due process. This raises three potential points of friction. “The first is data disclosure, particularly where a company faces a Chinese demand to cooperate but is also subject to Singaporean confidentiality, privacy or regulatory obligations,” he said. “The second is asset restraint, because Singaporean authorities or courts would need an adequate domestic legal basis before freezing or confiscating property. “The third is competing investigations, especially where China and Singapore characterise the same transaction differently or both wish to prosecute.” The broad scope of the law has also raised concerns over definitions of certain behaviour. Bing Ling, a professor of Chinese law at the University of Sydney law school, warned that the text lacked statutory definitions of core terms in Article 3 such as “power rent-seeking” and “waste of state assets”. “In practice, these concepts will likely derive their meaning from Chinese criminal law and internal disciplinary practice rather than internationally recognised standards, creating significant uncertainty for foreign firms dealing with Chinese SOEs,” he said. Another area of ambiguity is Article 18, which authorises Chinese authorities to demand evidence and require foreign corporate cooperation in major cases based on “reciprocity”. Ling said the draft did not define “cooperation” or how reciprocity operated in practice. While international law prohibits unilateral enforcement on foreign soil without state consent, the provision’s open-ended language fuels concerns that Chinese enforcers might seek evidence outside formal channels. For foreign multinationals, parallel-enforcement risk could increase significantly where a China connection exists Will Wu, Chance Bridge Law Firm For businesses, the draft law transforms internal compliance from a voluntary corporate safeguard into an independently enforceable statutory obligation. According to Will Wu, a Shanghai-based partner at Chance Bridge Law Firm, the draft law reshapes cross-border risk for both foreign and Chinese entities in distinct ways. “For foreign multinationals, parallel-enforcement risk could increase significantly where a China connection exists,” he said. Under Articles 29 to 34, all enterprises engaged in cross-border operations – including domestic firms operating abroad and foreign multinational corporations operating within China – are legally required to establish “integrity compliance” management systems. Wu said multinationals must evaluate China-related risks from the start and align their evidence handling, legal privilege, disclosures and remediation strategies across all involved jurisdictions. For overseas Chinese enterprises, compliance duties would become far more direct and stringent, he added. Article 33 spells out third-party due diligence, while Article 45 makes compliance failures an independently punishable administrative offence. Companies failing to rectify control flaws would face business suspensions or licence revocations, even without proof of an actual bribe. And while a parent company would not be automatically liable for an offshore agent’s misconduct, weak third-party oversight could trigger direct penalties and, together with other evidence, help legally link the company to suspected bribery involving that third party. Additionally, offshore proxies or nominees used to transfer or hold illicit funds linked to suspected corruption across borders would fall directly under the law’s asset-tracing, restraint and recovery provisions, Wu added.

title: The US and China are racing to build ‘self-improving AI’. Here’s what’s at stake
description: Both sides view ‘recursive self-improvement’ as a game-changer in the AI race. But who will get there first – and will it endanger us all?
content: The US-China race for artificial intelligence dominance has entered a new phase: using AI to build better AI. Leading AI companies in the United States and China are increasingly focused on deploying advanced models to write code, design experiments, and develop training techniques that can be used to improve more powerful models. The ultimate goal is to achieve what the industry refers to as recursive self-improvement (RSI) – the creation of AI systems that can train themselves autonomously. RSI has the potential to be a game-changer for the AI industry. As AI systems contribute to building more capable successors, which in turn become better at improving the next generation, the process could create an accelerating feedback loop – propelling the evolution of AI onto a new trajectory. In a blog post last week, OpenAI said it aimed to build an automated AI researcher capable of advancing deep learning research, though it was still unsure “how to safely get all the way to aligned, full RSI”. The company described its GPT-6 Astra model, released in early September, as “the world’s most intelligent and aligned model”. Chinese developers are also working towards RSI. During an earnings briefing on August 31, Tang Jie, the founder of Beijing-headquartered AI firm Z.ai, said its next-generation GLM-6 model was heading in the direction of “self-evolution”. As both sides push for RSI, where does the race stand – and what risks are emerging? Who is leading the RSI race? The US remains ahead in using AI to conduct AI research independently, an important precursor to recursive self-improvement, according to analysts. Wei Sun, principal analyst for artificial intelligence at Counterpoint Research, pointed to Anthropic’s research in June as evidence of the US’ early lead. Anthropic said Claude models were already designing experiments, writing code and developing post-training techniques that could be transferred to larger models. Other US companies have moved in the same direction. Google DeepMind released its Gemini 3.8 Flash model on September 2 and said it was “engineered for long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents and complex enterprise workflows”. Google DeepMind researcher Yao Shunyu called the model “one giant leap for RSI” in an X post. OpenAI has reported reaching its goal of developing an automated research intern. The Astra model can independently run some research experiments that would “take a skilled researcher a few days”, according to a company blog post. The company’s newly formed Strategic Futures team has also made the impact of RSI a core research priority. “American companies still appear several months ahead of China and have access to more compute for deployment,” said Erich Grunewald, senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy. “Chinese researchers are very capable at squeezing performance from scarce hardware, but those compute constraints do still bite.” Still, analysts emphasised that neither country had demonstrated open-ended, fully autonomous AI self-improvement indicative of RSI. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said while AI could optimise chip design or code execution, fundamental breakthroughs in model architecture still depended on human expertise. How is China pursuing ‘self evolution’? Chinese labs are building their own path towards self-improving AI. At Z.ai’s August interim briefing, founder Tang outlined “full self-training”, the technical road map for GLM-6.0, under which the company aims for AI to autonomously manage the entire training pipeline from pre-training through post-training. One central challenge, Tang said, was model judgment: enabling an AI system to determine when training should stop and to correct its own mistakes. Other Chinese labs have similarly framed their work in terms of “self-evolution”. Researchers behind MiniMax 2.7 said in an article titled “Early Echoes of Self-Evolution” earlier this year that the model could update its memory and build complex skills while executing reinforcement-learning experiments, with the resulting experience feeding back into its learning process. DeepSeek last month developed an agentic “harness” that gives models greater autonomy to navigate multi-step tasks, execute code and interact with external software. However, experts caution that such capabilities do not constitute a true recursive improvement loop. Philipp Schmid, a staff engineer at Google DeepMind, argued in a blog post last month that highly autonomous AI agents like DeepSeek’s remained dependent on a separate human entity to determine whether a change represented an improvement. “Open-ended recursive self-improvement asks for more. The system would improve how it finds changes and how those changes are judged. It would strengthen the verifier without being able to game it,” Schmid wrote. “Public evidence for that remains thin.” What safety risks would RSI create? The race towards RSI has sparked safety warnings globally. On Tuesday, former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X that he had resigned from Anthropic, accusing both AI giants of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has warned that rapidly accelerating RSI in the near term might not be the “right collective action we should take as the research community”. Alarm is also mounting in Beijing. Earlier this month, Wang Lihong, deputy director of the Cybersecurity Coordination Bureau at the Cyberspace Administration of China, warned of “extreme out-of-control risks” after frontier models bypassed sandboxes to target live production environments. Analysts said training models with flawed predecessors risked compounding misalignment. “If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents,” said Ben Hayum, a research assistant on the technology and national security programme at the Centre for a New American Security. “These are national security threats to America, China and the globe.”

title: As Asia rapidly ages, who cares for the carers when they grow old?
description: Asia’s care economy is booming, but its biggest supplier nations are ageing too, raising fears of a coming carer shortfall.
content: Bessie* left the Philippines for Malaysia more than a decade ago to care for other people’s children. She stayed to look after their parents instead. Certified as a carer, she now freelances around Kuala Lumpur’s Klang Valley, earning up to 25 ringgit (US$6) an hour for round-the-clock shifts, with clients providing her meals, transport and housing. “My former employer was very understanding and offered to release me earlier so I could earn a higher salary as a caregiver,” the 50-year-old said. Her career path is, in miniature, the story of many of Southeast Asia’s carers. Malaysia is often a way station: a place to earn a certificate and some experience before moving on to better paid work, sometimes with a path to residency, in Japan, Canada or Europe. “A lot of caregivers from the Philippines come to Malaysia or Singapore to work for a while, before they relocate,” Bessie said, adding that, unlike so many others, she planned to stay put. The region’s wealthier economies are now competing for a workforce that is thinning out as it moves around. Taiwan employed about 225,000 migrant social welfare workers as of March, 186,000 of them Indonesian, while Japan reached the end of last year with 67,871 foreign nationals employed in its skilled nursing-care category. Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia are all scaling up recruitment just as two major source countries for carers – the Philippines and Indonesia – are themselves greying. . Over-sixties already accounted for more than 10 per cent of Filipinos in 2024 and almost 12 per cent of Indonesians the following year. The dilemma now facing Asean governments is how to combat a regional shortage of carers without simply offloading the problem onto poorer states. Ready buyers Malaysia illustrates the strain from the buyer’s side. The country has no dedicated immigration pathway for foreign carers, so most arrive as domestic helpers or on temporary work passes – the route Bessie took. That mismatch has consequences, according to Delren Douglas, president of the Association for Residential Aged Care Operators of Malaysia (Agecope). “Many of our members have had the Immigration Department coming in and deporting foreign caregivers for doing work that is different from their permit,” he said. In May, Agecope put the national shortfall at roughly 1,400 carers across some 12,000 nursing-home beds. Douglas said it had worsened since, although he gave no updated figure. “We are being left with carers not adventurous enough to travel abroad or who lack the education required to work elsewhere,” he said. Local nursing home operator Christine Yee sees the same churn from the training side: carers gain confidence and skills on the job, then leave for Singapore or beyond. “It’s already very difficult to recruit people who have the temperament, the patience and passion for this type of work, because taking care of the elderly is not easy,” she said. Money explains much of the drift. Carers in Malaysia start on around 2,000 to 2,500 ringgit (US$490 to US$615) a month, while Singaporean employers pay about triple that, between S$2,200 (US$1,740) and S$2,500. Singapore’s response, outlined in parliament in March, is to “diversify the sources of foreign recruitment” and secure bilateral labour deals, with talks on care-worker cooperation taking place between acting manpower minister Jasmin Lau and her Philippine counterpart Francis Tolentino last month. The city state estimates its healthcare workforce will grow by a fifth by the end of the decade, to about 156,000, on top of the 300,000 or so migrant domestic workers who increasingly provide care for the elderly. Thailand, meanwhile, is entering the bidding rather late. The International Labour Organization (ILO) projects that the country may need over 250,000 additional paid care workers by 2037, roughly 55,000 of them migrants, and has flagged “increased competition for Asean migrant care workers”. In January, Thailand’s then labour minister Trinuch Thienthong warned that demand for foreign workers could climb by more than half, adding that future labour-import policies “must be clearly defined”. They still have not been. ‘Brain waste’ Indonesia illustrates how the shortage travels. Of the 153,049 Indonesians placed overseas in the first half of this year, 30,514 were carers – the largest single occupational group. Ferry Efendi, a community health nursing professor at Airlangga University, attributed the outflow to a shortage of jobs at home. “Indonesia has more than 700 nursing schools graduating about 50,000 nurses a year, far beyond what the domestic health sector can employ,” he said. Some graduates inevitably ended up caring for the elderly overseas, despite their qualifications – creating “brain waste rather than brain circulation”, as Efendi put it. Indonesia has no national long-term care system or regulated care-worker profession for them to return to. Malaysia’s proximity and linguistic familiarity could continue to attract Indonesian carers despite lower wages, Efendi added. “A nurse with young children in Sumatra may rationally prefer Malaysia to Taiwan even at a lower wage. But Malaysia would have to recognise her nursing background rather than repeat Taiwan’s practice of hiring nurses as care attendants.” The Philippines faces a somewhat similar contradiction. Its skills authority certifies about 41,000 carers annually, according to paper from the Philippine Institute for Development Studies published in May. Yet Japan, under a bilateral economic partnership agreement, takes in only about 200 of them a year. Filipino carers had become an expensive “gold standard” that Japanese employers were increasingly abandoning in favour of cheaper alternatives from India, Nepal and Myanmar, the paper said. Jean Clarisse Carlos, the paper’s co-author, warned that a training pipeline built for export became a liability once it collided with realities at home, including “persistent vacancies and high turnover in local care services, rising unmet care needs among older persons and continued dependence on unpaid family caregivers”. Her paper calls for a national care and migration strategy to mitigate what it termed the “care drain”. An invisible workforce Behind all of this sits a regulatory blind spot. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ 2006 mutual recognition arrangement on nursing left licensing power with national regulators while entirely excluding carers – “where most of the movement is actually happening”, according to Efendi. Because so much care for the elderly happened behind closed doors, classified as domestic work rather than a profession, it was invisible to regional skills initiatives, Carlos said. When Asean labour ministers met in Bangkok on August 26, their published communique focused on skills certification, without once mentioning care. Today’s employment surplus should not be read as tomorrow’s care surplus Ferry Efendi, community health nursing professor The International Labour Organization said in a statement that there was “no comprehensive mechanism within Asean or at the global level” to stop wealthier countries outbidding poorer ones. If workers obtained the right to migrate, restricting where they could work raised “significant labour rights concerns”, it said. The agency advocates for fair recruitment, portable social security and skills recognition, but that still leaves unresolved the question hanging over the region: whether today’s labour-exporting countries will have any carers left to spare once their own citizens grow old. “Today’s employment surplus should not be read as tomorrow’s care surplus,” Efendi said. *Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

title: Houthis hit Saudi base amid renewed fighting with Yemen government forces
description: The rebels have cemented their hold on the Bab el-Mandab Strait, which has become a key route for oil exports after Iran’s Hormuz blockade.
content: Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces forced growing numbers of civilians to flee. The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media. The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh. On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the southwestern part of the country. “Air Force of the armed forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three air strikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said on Sunday in a social media post. US news site Axios also reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called US President Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected. The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab el-Mandab Strait at the sea’s southern entrance. The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh’s Red Sea ports. The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni “forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia” near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesman for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city. The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 air strikes” on areas under their control. Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July. Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration. On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted “in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings and vehicles”. The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes. The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based. One of the displaced, Abdulali al-Rajihi, said the Houthis “told us: ‘Leave, scatter, you have half an hour.’” “We fled wearing the clothes on our backs. And we took our children, as much as we could manage.” Saddam Ali escaped from Al-Waziyah with his 11 children and a few possessions crammed into a small pickup truck. He said he had not found a single free house in the city, “not even a shelter”. The UN’s migration agency said on Saturday that, since July, 76,000 people had fled the fighting, a figure that had quadrupled since last week. About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country’s minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday. The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides. Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also “called us and they don’t want to fight with us”. He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy” in the region. In 2025, the US conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war. That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel. More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. In Yemen’s capital Sanaa, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail.

title: Why sleeping less than apes helped humans become Earth’s dominant species
description: Sleep expert and anthropologist David R Samson sheds light on how human sleep evolved from apes to hunter-gatherers to modern societies.
content: For most people, bedtime is a routine matter of turning off the lights and hoping for eight hours of rest. For David R Samson, an associate professor of evolutionary anthropology, it often means venturing deep into the wild or far back in evolutionary time. Whether sleeping high in the forest canopy to study chimpanzees or joining the Hadza tribe in remote Tanzania, Samson’s Indiana Jones-style fieldwork exposes the ancient roots of human slumber. As director of the Sleep and Human Evolution Lab at the University of Toronto Mississauga in Canada, Samson studies how human sleep evolved – from our primate ancestors to modern life. His book, The Sleepless Ape: The Story of Sleep in Human Evolution, highlights this work. His chief argument is that humans evolved to need less sleep than other primates, and that was the foundation for humanity’s position as the dominant species on our planet. “My primary research question has been, ‘What has made humans unique?’” Samson says in a recent In Vivo podcast. Humans are unique in a lot of different ways, Samson notes in the podcast, pointing to our exceptionally large brains relative to our body size and our reliance on complex social cooperation. And despite lacking sharp claws or massive canine teeth, humans evolved into the planet’s dominant species and have managed to live, adapt and thrive in every natural environment and ecosystem on Earth. “One of the things that underpins … all of these sweet adaptive traits is our sleep,” he adds. “None of it could have happened without our sleep.” The ‘sleep epidemic’ myth Samson’s research leads him to go against the grain when it comes to the problems of modern sleeping. Much talk today centres on how our stressful urban lifestyles have led to a “sleep epidemic” in which no one is able to get enough shut-eye. But Samson observes that people who live in modern societies – where just under seven hours is the norm – actually get around 45 minutes more sleep than those in hunter-gatherer tribes. His study participants, tribe members who spend their days hunting game with poisoned arrows, say they easily get enough sleep. While the modern approach to good sleep – including going to bed at the same time every night and sleeping uninterrupted for seven hours – is beneficial, Samson says we have evolved to take a more flexible approach to bedtime arrangements if the need arises. The cause of poor sleep goes beyond sleep duration, Samson says. It is a disconnect with our circadian rhythms, governed by our body clock, a temporal system that has evolved over millions of years to regulate our sleeping and waking patterns. It is based on natural light. Artificial light sources, which have been useful for humanity’s progress, have disrupted our connection with it. We are living with an evolutionary time lag, Samson says. Human technological progress has vastly outpaced biological evolution, leaving our bodies and minds genetically primed for ancient hunter-gatherer life rather than modern urban living. Lessons from tree-dwelling chimps Extensive fieldwork rather than lab work led Samson to these conclusions. His early excursions included observing how chimpanzees sleep, before shimmying up tall trees himself in the Toro-Semliki Wildlife Reserve in Uganda. Sleeping high in trees protects chimps from ground predators, with branches woven into secure platforms and native ironwood leaves acting as natural insect repellents. Ancient human ancestors likely built similar platforms, making them perhaps the earliest form of human construction. Samson also embedded himself with the Hadza, a tribe of hunter-gatherers in Tanzania, to study how they slept. He admits that although they live as nomads, building temporary huts, foraging for berries and hunting big game, we cannot assume that they live the way their ancestors did – but it is a good starting point at which to scientifically analyse sleeping habits of the past. Community and vigilance around the campfire Samson learned that the Hadza sleep communally, with up to seven people sharing a sleeping space. This enhances security: differing circadian rhythms and sleep requirements of the old and young mean that someone is likely to be awake at any given time to be alert to animal predators. These arrangements also foster a sense of community. He also saw that the Hadza’s sleep periods were fractured and irregular – two big no-nos in modern sleep culture. The tribespeople would leave the campfire to sleep at different times during the night, waking up to socialise, tend fires and meet partners. Although Hadza members slept roughly 45 minutes less on average than the seven hours common in modern societies, all but one of the tribe members he interviewed said they felt rested and satisfied with their sleep. Fire, REM sleep and human intelligence Other primates sleep for much longer than humans. From field trips and additional lab research, Samson concluded that our human ancestors used to sleep for longer when they dwelled in trees, and evolved to sleep less when they started sleeping on the ground. Originally, our ancestors were likely nocturnal, as foraging under the cover of night helped them avoid daytime predators – and sleeping unprotected on the ground was far too dangerous during the day. The control of fire, perhaps humanity’s most groundbreaking discovery, changed everything. Gathering around a campfire – much like the Hadza do today – enabled early humans to sleep soundly on the ground at night. Fire not only kept them warm, but it also expanded their nighttime visibility and warded off dangerous predators. Over time, early primates shifted their activity to daylight hours. “As they embraced the day, many primates found safety in numbers, leading to the formation of larger, more cohesive social groups,” Samson writes in The Sleepless Ape. “The advantages were clear: more eyes to spot threats, more hands to gather food.” These larger communities working towards common goals laid the structural foundation for our species’ rise. Transitioning from tree canopies to the ground forced humans to sleep less overall, but our sleep became vastly more efficient. As total sleep duration shortened, more time was devoted to both deep sleep and REM sleep – the stage critical for memory, learning and knowledge consolidation. Samson suggests this evolutionary shift towards more REM sleep directly fuelled humans’ exceptional cognitive abilities and intelligence. Fix your light, not your hours The Sleepless Ape is not a self-help book, but the research does have relevance for modern sleepers. Poor sleepers should quit worrying so much about sleep duration and focus on exposing themselves to more natural light. “We have fetishised sleep,” Samson says, but our obsession with hours logged in bed targets the symptom rather than the cause. The real engine of rest is our circadian system: an internal clock that predates sleep by over a billion years. Rather than reaching for sleeping pills, Samson stresses that basic “light hygiene” is the most effective way to restore our sleep – by syncing our bodies with natural daylight. As with the Hadza, we have built-in resilience to fluctuations in our sleep duration and sleep quality, but we cannot control our circadian rhythms. If we can seek out natural light when we wake up – 10 minutes in the morning would be enough, he says – and expose ourselves to more natural light throughout the day, that will anchor our circadian rhythms and help us get a good night’s sleep. This, Samson says, is as true for us today as it was for our ancestors millions of years ago. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong astronaut can help propel the city’s science and tech ambitions
description: Lai Ka-ying’s achievement should serve as the launch pad of a sustained push that makes science and innovation the new engine of the city’s development.
content: China’s growing achievements in aerospace technology continue to instil pride and patriotism, even more so in Hong Kong with the city’s first astronaut now on board the orbiting Tiangong space station. The historic live interactive lecture by Lai Ka-ying and her fellow crew members on the “celestial palace” on Wednesday was more than a one-off occasion for students to catch a glimpse of life and research in space. Sustained by the right policy drive, the fervour can turn into a lasting trajectory in promoting science and innovation among the younger generation. Jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency and live-streamed to campuses and on television in Hong Kong and Macau, the 90-minute session between the crew and participants at Lai’s alma mater in Tsuen Wan was a shared moment that made science feel tangible and relatable. From cooking chicken wings and wringing out a wet towel in zero gravity to describing spotting Hong Kong and the country from orbit, Lai and her crew members offered a glimpse into a captivating journey that was unthinkable a few decades ago. Space missions have never felt more relevant. Some students said they were impressed and inspired. A Form Five student who studies physics, chemistry, biology and extended mathematics said the dialogue inspired him to explore science and that he hoped to take part in the country’s research one day. A Form Six student said she would study hard to contribute to the country, saying Lai was a role model. Lai’s message that she was “not born able to fly” resonates with many from humble backgrounds who have lofty ambitions. Her appeal for youngsters to embrace the “Lion Rock spirit” and the spirit of manned space flight by daring to surmount obstacles and chase their dreams reinforces the idea that pursuits like outer space ventures are not out of reach. The astronaut’s tale has boosted Hong Kong’s growing pride and patriotism. Her journey from a local public school to space has opened up a new horizon in a city where success traditionally comes from finance and business rather than science and innovation. This is not the first time that the soft power of Chinese astronauts has been harnessed for government patriotism and education drives. It is important that the momentum be seized and turned into the launch pad of a sustained, system-wide push that makes science, technology and innovation the new engine of the city’s next phase of development. The timing could not have been more opportune. The city is pivoting towards this path with a revamped science and mathematics curriculum for senior secondary students from 2029-30. The Education Bureau has asked schools to actively encourage students interested in science and maths to take two or more science subjects to create a synergistic effect, aligned with the strategy in the nation’s 15th five-year plan to “invigorate the country through science and education” and supporting Hong Kong’s development as an international innovation and technology centre. Earlier, a worldwide study of academic performance in secondary school put the spotlight on the standard of Hong Kong students. According to the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, local students ranked 17th for science, down from seventh place in 2022, the first time their ranking has dropped out of the top 10. The ranking in maths also dropped from fourth place to seventh, but remains well above the international average. The city earned sixth place in “learning in the digital world”, trailing Macau, Singapore, mainland China, Japan and Taiwan. Experts said the decline in science and maths was partly due to the post-Covid impact on study habits and learning motivation. There is no room for slippage in the increasingly competitive world of innovation and technology. Lai’s inspiring journey could go beyond enhancing national pride and identity and drive development if backed by long-term policy and measures. It is now incumbent upon the authorities, educators and the wider community to seize the momentum to build an environment conducive to growth and achievement. Hopefully, the city can propel itself into a higher orbit in the world of science and produce more success stories.

title: Write to Win: What was something you were scared to try but found fun once you did? (Round 2)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form .
Milky Way: I used to think that kayaking was one of the most terrifying activities I could try. I was hesitant because I was scared of sports and water-based activities. However, in 2023, a friend invited me to join a kayaking event. With encouragement from the coach, I decided to give it a try for the first time. To my surprise, it turned out to be one of the most enjoyable experiences of my life.
Mercury: I was terrified to buy a secret second SIM card because my parents strictly limit me to three gigabytes of data a month. I was afraid they would discover my transaction. Still, once I finally went through with it, I used the extra data to watch a series of science videos and scroll through reels without the anxiety-inducing “data warning” popping up. It was incredibly fun. The sheer freedom of using my phone without constantly checking the settings felt like a huge weight lifted off my shoulders. Plus, the thrill of hiding it from my parents made it even more exciting.
Jupiter: During the last academic year, my school held auditions for a drama production. I was interested but also nervous and doubtful about my acting skills. However, my friends encouraged me to go for the auditions anyway. To my surprise, my energetic audition impressed the directors, and I landed the main role. What started as fear turned into joy, making me realise that everything is new and intimidating only until you give it a try.
Earth: I used to find the idea of eating alone at a busy restaurant quite intimidating, feeling completely exposed without a friend to accompany me. However, I recently asked myself: does that really matter? After trying it, I realised that nobody was actually paying attention to me; they were all focused on their own meals. By tuning into the comforting background noise of the restaurant, I was able to relax and fully enjoy my food.
Venus: Standing in front of a crowd terrified me, but with my parents’ strong support, I decided to try public speaking. To my surprise, it wasn’t scary at all; in fact, I enjoyed the experience a lot! That single step gave me the confidence to join the debate team and participate in speech competitions, eventually winning several awards. What began as a daunting challenge became one of my greatest strengths.
Mars: I was always terrified of riding roller coasters, dreading the massive drops and dizzying loops. Last month, my friends finally convinced me to try one. As the train climbed, my hands shook with fear. However, during the sudden drops, I found myself laughing and screaming with joy instead of crying. It was incredibly thrilling, and now, I absolutely love roller coasters.
Neptune: I never thought jumping off a cliff would be exhilarating. It wasn’t a real cliff, but once I tried it, I could not stop. My parents took me to Aqua Splash once, and it was all fun and games until I had to decide how to get off the course: the slide or the cliff? The cliff was roughly two metres high, and the adrenaline rush was so intense that I could hardly move my legs. After a long queue formed behind me, I finally felt forced to jump. When I emerged from the water, I realised I missed the adrenaline rush and discovered just how fun jumping off a cliff could be.
Saturn: “I want to go home.” That was all I could think about as I stood atop a flume ride in Hong Kong. I had been dragged into this by my friends, but I finally took the plunge. As I raced down, my heart hammered against my chest. I felt a wave of weightlessness, and cold water splashed across my face. Surprisingly, an adrenaline rush surged through me, and my fear transformed into excitement! When the ride ended, I laughed, already eager to go again.

title: J.D. Vance group courted Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro over anti-China rare earth deal: report
description: Senator’s logo appears on a plan to trade rare earths and position against Beijing in exchange for support on his presidential bid.
content: A campaign document belonging to Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing front-runner in the presidential election to be held in Brazil next month, offered Washington a rare earths supply chain designed to weaken China’s grip, local news site Amado Mundo reported on Saturday. Written in English and dated March 19, the 22-page presentation was drafted by Andre Marinho, a close Bolsonaro ally who presented the plan to the Rockbridge Network, a group of wealthy conservative donors founded by J.D. Vance in 2019, Amado Mundo said. Marinho, who built a television career impersonating Flavio’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, and is running for governor of Rio de Janeiro, confirmed on Saturday that he wrote the document, but claimed it was “never shown to an American official and had nothing to do” with Flavio’s campaign. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves, and Washington and Beijing have spent the past year competing for them. Left-leaning President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has refused to choose, balking at any American US deal by citing a law restricting exports of unprocessed ore. American money has arrived without waiting for that law, however, starting with USA Rare Earth’s US$2.8 billion purchase of the Serra Verde mine in Goias in April. The Pentagon added US$750 million for the site in August, and Beijing has since offered Brasilia a partnership. A Rio de Janeiro senator and the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, the nation’s 2019-2023 president and an ally of US President Donald Trump, Flavio Bolsonaro has courted Washington throughout the campaign. His father is serving 27 years for plotting a coup, but polls this week left Flavio level with Lula before a first-round vote on October 4 – with one putting him narrowly ahead. The report dominated Brazilian headlines within hours, reviving questions over whether proven US-linked funding could cost his place on the ballot three weeks before the South American country is expected to choose its next leader. The document built its case on three main points, all of them aimed at countering Beijing. A Flavio Bolsonaro government would stop selling raw ore abroad, would not become “structurally dependent on Chinese processing chains” and would align with Washington behind a “parallel supply system”, it said. Lula’s foreign policy was dismissed as pro-China and guided by “deliberate geopolitical ambiguity”, the document added, with four more years of it leaving Brazil a “supplier of raw materials to Chinese industry”. And for the United States, the document promised less dependence on China and secure inputs for artificial intelligence, defence and the energy transition. Brazil would become “one of the three largest suppliers outside China”, drawing up to US$100 billion into its mines over a decade. “Lula hesitates, Bolsonaro executes,” the memo said. Its closing message, addressed to what the text called American interlocutors, said that the West had “an execution problem rather than a minerals problem”. The file carried the campaign’s branding on every page, including the cover, which read “Flavio Bolsonaro | 2026 Campaign”, with the senator’s logo above the slogan “Prosperity Partnership”. Marinho’s route into the Trump administration also runs through his family. His sister, the singer Giulia Be, is married to Conor Kennedy, son of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jnr. His sister’s father-in-law brokered a meeting he had with Vance in April. Nine days after the document was reportedly written, Flavio Bolsonaro told the Conservative Political Action Conference in Dallas that Brazil could be “the American answer to Chinese mineral dominance”. Renan Santos, a rival candidate who co-founded the Free Brazil Movement, also said this month that the Rockbridge Network had put money into Flavio Bolsonaro’s run. A governing-party lawmaker has asked federal prosecutors to examine the claim. “These people work with many things, among them rare earths,” Santos said, adding that the network had courted Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas first. “They entered Flavio’s campaign, naturally and illegally.” View this post on Instagram The two men Santos named as the network’s operators in Brazil, entrepreneur Tallis Gomes and tourism operator Pedro Sang, denied the claim, and Gomes filed a criminal complaint accusing Santos of defamation. “Not a single cent was ever transacted,” said Sang, who was introduced to Rockbridge by Marinho. Marinho confirmed on Saturday that he flew to Dallas at the network’s invitation in March to discuss opening a Brazilian arm of their group, but said he dropped the idea in May. The US embassy in Brasilia could not immediately be reached for a comment. Brazilian law bars companies and foreign entities from funding candidates and requires that all donations be declared on a portal run by the electoral courts. That platform shows no American money, listing 48.17 million reais (US$9.4 million), of which 95 per cent came from his own party. Proof of a foreign donation could cost him his registration and even lead to a criminal investigation. Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign has not commented publicly on the document or on the funding accusations. Rare earths were already a campaign theme before the memo surfaced, with Lula telling voters this month that “traitors wanted to hand the country’s reserves to foreigners”, without naming the US.

title: Celine Dion makes long-awaited return to stage in Paris
description: The singer wept as she opened her first full concert in six years, amid her battle with the incurable Stiff Person Syndrome.
content: Celine Dion wept tears of joy on Saturday as she fulfilled her dream of returning to the stage after years battling a rare neurological disorder, with a sell-out concert in Paris. The 58-year-old French-Canadian singer appeared visibly moved as she opened her first full concert in six years with her 1990s French-language ballad “On ne change pas” (“One Doesn’t Change”), singing to a crowd of 30,000 enthralled fans that one newspaper said included US former first lady Michelle Obama. “These are, of course, tears of joy. I’m so delighted to see you,” Dion said, blowing kisses to the audience at the packed Plenitude Arena on the western edge of Paris. Her return to the stage underscored a remarkable comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome, an incurable condition that causes stiffness and cramps, forced her to cancel shows and cast years of uncertainty over whether she would ever perform again. “The path was rockier than expected,” she said, speaking in French and English. “But I held on to a faint ray of light in the distance, deep in the mountains.” “Tonight, I want to sing for you, sing for myself, sing for life,” she added. The largely female crowd sported sequinned dresses and tops, glittered cheeks, and T-shirts emblazoned with the star’s image or nods to her biggest hits. “It’s unreal to be here!,” said Elisabeth Landry, a 38-year-old Quebecer who lives near the star’s hometown of Charlemagne. “I was convinced we’d never see her again, especially not embarking on a run of concerts like this.” French daily Le Parisien said the former first lady of the United States was “discreetly attending this first concert”. Just hours before, one of the bestselling singers of all time greeted admirers outside her luxury hotel a short walk from the Arc de Triomphe. Albertina Cabral, a fan from the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo, said she could barely put her feelings into words. “It’s unbelievable to stay here and to go to the concert and to see Celine so close,” she said. “And she’s feeling good, she’s happy.” Paris spared no effort in welcoming Dion, drawing thousands of fans from across the world, including some who flew in from as far away as the French Polynesian island of Tahiti. For days, Paris played host to costume contests, giant karaoke parties and tribute cruises on the Seine. On Friday, the iconic cauldron rose above the Tuileries Garden, echoing the diva’s surprise appearance up the Eiffel Tower to perform “Hymn to Love” by Edith Piaf during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics in 2024. A lyric from the song, “I’d go and fetch the moon if you asked me to”, along with the singer’s first name, was projected in big letters onto the balloon. The suburban railway station serving the arena has been temporarily renamed “Celine”. Chloe and Katy Rydquist, who travelled from London, had spent around £1,500 (US$2,000) on their tickets, saying Dion’s return to the stage justified the cost. “She’s a legend,” said Chloe. The star’s residency is projected to generate hundreds of millions of euros in economic benefits. She kicks off her 26-date run with 16 sold-out shows in September and October, before returning for another 10 in May. Fans who missed out on tickets have found other ways to catch a glimpse of their idol. Dion has regularly stepped outside the Royal Monceau hotel to greet waiting fans, at times breaking into song and dance with them well into the early hours. Over her four-decade career, Dion has sold around 260 million albums in English and French, with hits including “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now” and “Because You Loved Me”. Dion revealed in late 2022 that she had been diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome. She has described it as making her feel as though she is being strangled, with cramps so intense they have left her with broken ribs. Dion’s return to the stage comes after what she has described as years of training “like an athlete”, doing ballet and Pilates several times a week, as well as voice therapy.

title: This week in PostMag: a guqin revival, odes to Central Asia and a peek into Puyi’s last days as emperor
description: How Hong Kong connoisseurs are reviving China’s ancient seven-string zither, a look around the Bukhara Biennial, a trip to a Kazakhstan horse museum and the last months of imperial rule at the Forbidden City.
content: Even at more than 120 years old, there are still firsts for the South China Morning Post. One of them was this month’s anticipated debut of our signature China Conference business, trade and investment forum in Astana, Kazakhstan. In honour of that milestone, and the exciting developments brewing in this fast-flourishing region, the curation for this issue includes two tales from Central Asia. Hei Kiu Au saddles up for a journey to the Great Steppe, where a father and son have raised a monument to the horse and the ancient Botai people, tracing the origins of the human-equine relationship and its importance to Kazakh culture. Meanwhile, in neighbouring Uzbekistan, one of the oldest cities in the world is undergoing a cultural transformation. Aaina Bhargava takes us on a visual exploration of the artworks, installations and presentations of the inaugural Bukhara Biennial, where old meets new and preservation meets innovation, and the theme “Recipes for Broken Hearts” is interpreted through the rich imagination of international artists and local artisans. On the subject of creation, photographer and director Wing Shya – whose trademark moody, romance-tinged aesthetics and evocative stills, captured on the set of Wong Kar-wai films, made him a household name – tells Jing Zhang about returning to Hong Kong after university to save graphic design and Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing’s promise. Past and present collide in this week’s stories, with revival, reminiscence and resurgence woven into the narratives. Kamala Thiagarajan follows the soulful melodies of the guqin to a small group of players and makers in Hong Kong keeping the traditional teachings, practice, heritage and spirit of the instrument alive as the seven-stringed Chinese zither experiences a renaissance. Whether those showing an interest now will continue doing so after finding out that masters will put their disciples through three months of just learning how to string the guqin is a different matter altogether … Elsewhere, we have something for the bookworms. Paul French’s latest release transports us into the Forbidden City to witness a pivotal moment in history: the months before China’s last emperor and empress’ expulsion into the “Great Without”, in 1924. The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City is an intimate, nuanced portrait of the teenage royals living in sequestered limbo as the nation around them goes through major upheaval and regime change. Fionnuala McHugh talks to the British author to discover how one well-timed story – for this magazine, no less – led him to a gold mine of material for his tome. And just like that, we are fast approaching the Mid-Autumn Festival. With mooncake flavours promising to be more outlandish and outrageous with each passing year – so far, we have seen mushroom char siu, durian and whisky chocolate, not to mention the recurring Goods of Desire option that’s shaped like buttocks as a play on the “mooning” pun – we take a look back at simpler times, when good old lotus paste and salted egg yolk reigned supreme. Enjoy the read.

title: Meet ‘Choosin’ Texas’ singer Ella Langley’s parents, Jason and Heather Langley
description: Her hit track from Dandelion has topped the Billboard Hot 100 for 21 weeks and counting – but how much do you know about the country star’s family life?
content: Ella Langley is one of the biggest country music stars of the year. The 27-year-old has spent 21 weeks and counting atop the Billboard Hot 100 chart with her smash hit “Choosin’ Texas” from her second studio album Dandelion. It is the first-ever non-Christmas track to achieve this feat. Langley also conquered the UK’s Official Singles Chart for the first time with the same song, beating the UK’s longest-running No 1 single, “Rein Me In” by Sam Fender and Olivia Dean, which spent 23 weeks at the top, though not consecutively. Despite her meteoric rise to fame, Langley has remained close to her roots. So, who are her parents, Jason and Heather Langley? Ella Langley is the second eldest of 4 children Jason and Heather Langley tied the knot on April 18, 1998, and share four children, of whom Ella is the second oldest, according to People magazine. The singer’s older brother is Thomas, 35, and her younger brother is Stuart, 25. The youngest Langley is Katie, who is 19. According to Taste of Country, a country music news platform, Jason Langley is a businessman. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Ella Langley (@ellalangleymusic) The siblings grew up on a farm in Hope Hull, Alabama, and the coordinates of their childhood home are tattooed on Ella’s arm. She also has a bumblebee tattoo in honour of her mother, who calls her “Ella Bee”. Langley now owns a house in Montgomery, close to her parents’ place. Ella Langley called her parents’ marriage a ‘wild ride’ On the This Past Weekend w/ Theo Von podcast this May, Ella described her parents’ marriage as a “wild ride”, adding that they “stuck it out” despite having ups and downs in their relationship. Heather, who hails from Michigan, has never shied away from celebrating her marriage, often posting about relationship milestones on her Instagram. However, her account was private at the time of writing. They’ve supported Ella Langley’s music career The Langleys introduced their eldest daughter to music, per the Montgomery Advertiser. “If we were riding down the road, music was playing. So in my dad’s truck I heard a lot of big rock bands, old-school country and even disco,” she recalled, adding that her mother “played everything from Peter, Paul & Mary to 80s new wave to Pearl Jam”. Jason’s parents further nurtured their granddaughter’s musical talent. Both of them were singers, and Ella gushed on the God’s Country podcast that her grandfather could “play every instrument by ear”. She grew up singing with them, and later inherited her late grandfather’s guitar. When Langley wanted to drop out of Auburn University without completing her forestry degree, her parents supported her. Her mother, in particular, referred to her move to Nashville as her “schooling”, Ella told the Katie & Company podcast in 2024.

title: Macroscope | As US leadership proves unreliable, Asia needs to start focusing on itself
description: Asian policymakers should start laying the groundwork for a new organisation that has this region’s interests at its core.
content: The Group of 20 (G20) was launched in 1999 amid high hopes that Asia and other emerging regions of the world would gain a stronger voice in global economic and financial affairs. Things have not worked out that way. Instead, a world order led by the United States stumbled into the 2008 global financial crisis and appears to be on course for another one. This suggests there could be an opening for a new regional organisation – one that is more centred on China or Japan and which can bring the political, economic and financial stability the US under President Donald Trump is unable to provide. By the time the G20 was launched, the post-war Group of Seven (G7) nations – Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the US – had become increasingly unrepresentative of the global economy. Emerging economies wanted representation, and they appeared to get it in the form of a G20 whose membership includes the likes of India, China and Australia. The world has moved on, though, and US leadership of the G7 has proved unreliable and erratic under Trump. This seemed clear from the recent G20 pre-summit ministerial gathering in Asheville, North Carolina. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hosted the meeting, which ended in a lack of consensus. Nobel laureate economist and Columbia University professor Joseph Stiglitz wrote in a subsequent commentary: “Bessent was supposed to be the member with the most credibility. But he has now squandered it with his recent, failed attempts to steer the bond and currency markets.” The likes of the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, the World Health Organization and numerous other global bodies have proved to be too big, bureaucratic and politicised to effectively represent Asian and other regional interests. From this point on, the guiding principle in forming institutions must be that “small is beautiful”. The world needs something different today, and not another version of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum or other similar bodies. This organisation must be one which recognises that the global centre of trade – and consequently economic and financial power – has shifted from West to East. Whatever this new grouping is called, it must reflect this fact and have its leadership rotate accordingly between Japan, China and South Korea, with leading Southeast Asian nations also stepping up at some point. It must not strive to be all things to all people in the emerging global economy. It must also realise that Asia already has valuable experience in dealing with financial crises of one kind or another on a variety of occasions. The G20 has fallen short of its goals because it has tried to embrace the US, Europe, Britain, Africa, South America, the Middle East and more, bringing in members whose interests do not always align. What role might this new institution perform? The world of finance and international capital flows has become extremely complex and potentially risky in recent decades, bringing about various crises. The new grouping should focus on these risks and how to prevent or deal with them. It should also bear in mind that, beyond the US, Asia is the principal source of potentially destabilising international capital flows. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) was largely discredited among many Asian countries after the 1997 Asian financial crisis because of its one-size-fits-all approach in dealing with the crisis. It was heavily criticised for mistaking a crisis of capital accounts for a domestic financial crisis. That mistake has not been forgotten in this region, and even though a highly watered-down version of the IMF was established here eventually in the shape of the Chiang Mai Initiative, it has rarely been invoked. Its functions could be taken over as part of the remit of this new regional grouping. The global financial system is replete with problems these days. Its ailments include excessive lending and borrowing, overleveraging, overinflated valuations of financial assets, non-bank exposure to borrowers, conventional currencies being both overvalued and undervalued, trade imbalances, digital currencies, the threat from artificial intelligence and more. Some of these problems are prevalent outside Asia. However, Asia needs to focus on itself and deal with its own vulnerabilities rather than those of the world at large. After all, the Chinese yuan is becoming increasingly influential around the globe while the Japanese yen is suffering from its traditional overexposure to the US dollar. There are also other Asian currencies that have the potential to play a larger role in global finance. The global landscape is unlikely to change dramatically after the end of the Trump presidency, something which could happen sooner rather than later. Asian policymakers would do well to start laying the groundwork for a new organisation that has this region’s interests at its core.

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ wins Gold Lion at Venice Film Festival
