description: Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy was the only woman directing a feature film in the main 21-strong film line-up.
content: Danish filmmaker May el-Toukhy’s post-war drama Woman Unknown ⁠won the Golden Lion at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, with its star Mathilde Arcel also taking best actress honours in a rare double victory. El-Toukhy was the only woman directing a feature film in the main, 21-strong film line-up, a disparity that drew criticism during the festival and prompted renewed scrutiny of the barriers facing women in cinema. Set in the aftermath of World War II, Woman Unknown follows a housemaid played ‌by Arcel whose past relationship with a German soldier threatens to destroy her future. The film unfolds against the backdrop of a newly liberated Denmark, where women accused of fraternising with occupying German forces were often subjected to vigilante justice. “To me personally, Woman Unknown is about the female body as a battleground and a public matter. And at the same time, the film tells the tale of women who are invisible, unseen, and voiceless,” el-Toukhy said in her acceptance speech. South Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong took the runner-up Silver Lion award for Possible Love, while Russian-born filmmaker Ilya Khrzhanovsky won best director for DAU, a hugely ambitious ⁠project shot largely in Ukraine before the ongoing war that has attracted intense scrutiny and controversy. Khrzhanovsky, who has renounced his Russian citizenship and is a fierce critic of ‌Moscow, dedicated his prize to Ukraine. John Malkovich was named best actor for his performance as an ageing, maverick CIA agent in Martin McDonagh’s razor-sharp comedy Wild Horse Nine. “I am humbled to be chosen for this award which has been given to so many wonderful actors,” ‌said Malkovich, speaking via a video link from Canada where he is shooting a new project. The Venice festival marks the start of the awards ⁠season and regularly throws up big favourites ⁠for the Oscars. However, many of the big studio-backed contenders that once crowded the Venice schedule were absent this year as Hollywood reconsiders how to market its films and cut costs. In a change of ‌tone, the festival offered a programme steeped in global politics and social upheaval, including NAZA – a hard-hitting documentary by Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that won the Special Jury Prize. Based on anonymous interviews with 24 ‌Israeli intelligence officers ‌and soldiers, the film accuses the Israeli military of routinely approving mass civilian deaths when they target militants in the Gaza Strip. Israel has denied the charge. The ‌documentary received a record 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere on Thursday – the second year in succession that a film about Gaza has resonated in Venice after The Voice of Hind ⁠Rajab, a true-life account of the killing of a Palestinian girl during the war. “The Israeli intelligence officers we spoke with talked to us about how this mass killing ⁠is systemic, not by accident, but by design,” Abraham said on Saturday. “We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist.” Stephane Brize, Coralie Amedeo and Olivier Gorce received the screenplay award for their well-received French workplace drama A Good Little Soldier, while Malou Khebizi was named as best emerging ‌young actor for her role in another ‌well-received French production – A Place to Heal. Festival director Alberto Barbera has defended the male-dominated line-up this year, insisting that selection decisions were based on artistic merit rather than quotas, and urging the industry to do more to help women break into the business. El-Toukhy said women filmmakers continued to face greater difficulties securing financing, limiting budgets, casting opportunities and, ultimately, access to major festivals. The head of the main jury, US actor-director Maggie Gyllenhaal, also weighed in, telling reporters that female filmmakers often struggled to secure financing because the stories they want to tell were not seen as important.

title: From Hermès to Dior, double-finger ring designs are making a bold fashion statement
description: Jewellery houses everywhere, including Cartier, Rick Owens and Jean Paul Gaultier, are turning the design into a statement of scale and attitude.
content: The ring is extending its reach, with recent launches from Cartier to Hermès seeing the jewellery staple stretch across two, three and even four fingers. “A double-finger ring naturally changes the way a hand looks,” says Milka Karaagacli, founder and creative director of the fine jewellery label Kismet by Milka. “It feels stronger and more defined.” The finger-spanning style has a long history, its current trendiness notwithstanding. Multi-finger rings were worn in ancient Egypt, where they served as markers of power and protection, and in Hellenistic Greece and Rome, where they signified status. By the late 19th century, the style had found a place in fine jewellery. As an example, the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds a gold double-finger ring by New York jeweller Marcus & Co. Featuring two bezel-set rose-cut diamonds flanking a central rectangular cabochon-cut green gem, the piece dates to around 1895, and draws inspiration from Roman examples dating all the way back to the 4th century. The goal is always to create a design that looks sculptural but feels easy and natural to wear Milka Karaagacli, Kismet by Milka In the late 20th century, the double-finger ring resurfaced in hip-hop and punk subcultures. Bold, knuckle-duster designs from the likes of Rick Owens, Jean Paul Gaultier and Yohji Yamamoto, typically in brass or silver, followed. Hermès, meanwhile, has been producing double-finger rings for more than 20 years, courtesy of fine jewellery creative director Pierre Hardy. “Adding double-finger rings to any collection instantly makes it feel more editorial and fashion forward,” says Ritika Atwal, founder and designer of the fine jewellery brand Ritique, which offers several double-finger designs, including the Belle Amour ring from the brand’s Éden collection, inspired by French gardens and set with rose-cut and round diamonds. “Despite their bold appearance, our double-finger rings are actually very comfortable and easy to wear,” she says. “The design has to be thoughtfully created, keeping in mind that it cannot be overly structured, large or rigid. There needs to be flow within the design, along with open spaces that allow the piece to move naturally with the hand.” Kismet by Milka’s designs are crafted on the same principle. “Comfort is always essential for me, no matter how bold the design is,” Karaagacli says. “With double-finger rings, proportion and balance become everything. The spacing between the fingers, the weight distribution, the flexibility of the structure – every millimetre matters. The goal is always to create a design that looks sculptural but feels easy and natural to wear.” A chic example is the Crux ring, designed in Karaagacli’s signature Roslow (rose-yellow) gold as well as white gold, and sprinkled with teeny white diamonds. “Because it spans two fingers, [the ring] creates a much stronger line on the hand and changes the entire proportion of the silhouette,” she says. “With Crux, I wanted the design to feel sharp, confident and intentional from every angle. It has a presence that’s difficult to achieve with a classic single-band ring.” Last year’s Cartier Trinity collection included a two-finger ring in white, rose and yellow gold, set with no less than 428 brilliant-cut diamonds and accented with black lacquer, each of the three bands representing a different animal, from reptile-patterned white gold to tiger-stripe rose gold and panther-spot yellow. The Bee de Chaumet line plays on the house’s signature motif with a rose gold ring spanning four fingers, set with brilliant-cut diamonds. Hermès has explored the double-finger ring, meanwhile, with Chaîne d’Ancre Aléa II, which reworks the house’s anchor chain links in twisted, striped and beaded silver, while the brand’s Clou d’H double ring in rose gold set with diamonds extends the brand’s Médor pyramid stud across two fingers. The double-finger ring has also cropped up at New York-based Marli, whose Avenues Statement ring combines asymmetrical lines with multi-cut diamonds, and at Dior, in the brand’s newest Diorissima high jewellery collection as well as the Couture Dior and My Dior fine jewellery lines. Brazilian-Armenian designer Ara Vartanian came to the double-finger ring by studying what a conventional ring cannot do. “The double-finger ring came from an observation about the relationship between the stone and the hand,” he says. “By extending the structure across two fingers, the stone could rest more naturally, with a stronger sense of balance and proportion. It allowed the piece to feel more integrated with the body instead of simply sitting on top of it.” That relationship with the body is what interests him most. “It opens space for tension, asymmetry and scale in a way that feels very fluid and organic,” he says. “There is a boldness to it, but also a certain sensuality in how it follows the movement of the hand.” His most technically ambitious example is a two-finger ring at the heart of Ara x Mr Dean, his 2025 collaboration with Grammy-winning producer Swizz Beatz, whose surname gives the collection its name. First worn by Beatz and Alicia Keys at last year’s Met Gala, the collection blends the producer’s love of emeralds and rubellites with Vartanian’s sculptural aesthetic. “When developing the design [of the two-finger ring], I became very interested in movement, particularly the balance between strength and fluidity found in horses and equestrian structures,” Vartanian says. “What I find most interesting about the piece is the tension between engineering and elegance. Even though the mechanism behind it is quite complex, the final result feels effortless and instinctive on the hand, which is always something I look for in jewellery.” “For me, jewellery should feel alive on the body,” the designer adds. “The double-finger ring became a way to explore that idea more freely.”

title: Anthropic boss Amodei calls for AI slowdown, Altman and Musk agree
description: Researcher Jacob Coxon quit days earlier, saying that AI firms were ‘gambling with our lives’ in pursuit of self-improving models.
content: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems. His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement. OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who owns xAI, quickly chimed in to say they agreed with Amodei’s assessment, as pressure builds for improved oversight. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei said in a post on his personal website. “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way,” said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021. “But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence.” Amodei’s statement echoed another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development. Then in late July, Altman said developers might need to voluntarily tap the brakes to give society a chance to catch up. More than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies including Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”. OpenAI had revealed that during testing, AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code. In that incident and others, the blame was placed on AI agents, which are software programs that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on social media, as Altman said: “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier.” Earlier this week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pre-training AI models – first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach. Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a social media post. Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence. Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face incident should not be dismissed as a one-off. “A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand,” he explained. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” potentially generating hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, he added. The Anthropic CEO said his company would grant “employee-like access” to a team of “third-party evaluators” who would verify adherence to safety practices – and he called on all companies to follow his lead. Altman said he would commit to similar outside oversight, adding that he would have “more to share soon”. Amodei also suggested that companies work together to establish common safety standards, and said he supported some kind of government cooperation on the issue. In early August, the US government put in place a voluntary security review process for advanced AI models before their release, but the parameters of that programme remain unclear. Industry observers say they are not sure how effective it would be, as US President Donald Trump’s administration has thus far favoured a light-touch, deregulatory approach to most industries, including tech.

title: Bulgaria probes explosion at weapon storage site
description: The facility is run by a Bulgarian arms trader whose facilities have been alleged to be the ⁠target of attacks by Russian operatives.
content: Bulgaria is investigating the cause of a fire at a weapons storage facility operated by EMCO, including the possibility of sabotage and a link to a previous blaze at another of the company’s facilities in August, the interior minister said. No ‌injuries were reported in the fire, which broke out near the village of Tsareva Livada and lit up the night sky, according to videos broadcast locally. The incident came weeks after an explosion and fire at another EMCO weapons depot in western Bulgaria. Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told journalists on Saturday that the fire was under control and that an investigation was under way. “We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern,” he said. “We are not ruling out outside interference.” EMCO later said in ‌a statement that the fire was the result of sabotage, citing more than 10 similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, although it did not identify any suspects. “There is no reason to assume that ‌this case is any different,” the company said. EMCO is run by Bulgarian arms trader Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors have ⁠previously alleged was the ⁠target of attacks on his facilities by Russian operatives. In 2024, Bulgaria issued arrest warrants for six Russian citizens accused of involvement in the destruction of EMCO arms depots that ‌stored munitions destined for export to Ukraine and Georgia between 2011 and 2020. Prosecutors at the time said they had grounds to suspect links between the blasts in Bulgaria, an ‌attempted poisoning of ‌Gebrev in 2015, and munitions depot explosions in the Czech Republic in 2014. Moscow has dismissed the allegations. Slavcho Dimiev, manager of EMCO’s ‌production facilities, confirmed Saturday’s fire at the storage site, which he said mainly holds ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-calibre rounds. The company also ⁠accused authorities of failing to adequately protect defence facilities. “Not a single investigation into the more than 10 such incidents at the industry’s ⁠leading enterprises has been concluded,” the company said, adding that its warehouse has been inspected seven times since the beginning of the year, with the last one 20 days prior. Demerdzhiev expressed concerns about the security and the conditions under which explosives ‌are stored and the way ‌these facilities are guarded. The blast comes at a time of flux in Bulgarian politics after Prime Minister Rumen Radev came to power in April on a Kremlin-friendly ticket. But in June, the newly appointed defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, said Bulgaria would no longer provide arms to Ukraine and urged Moscow and Kyiv to sit down at the negotiating table to end the war.

title: 39 pupils and staff fall ill after eating school lunches in Sha Tin
description: Authorities are investigating a suspected outbreak of food poisoning at Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School.
content: Hong Kong health authorities are investigating an outbreak of suspected food poisoning that hit 39 pupils and staff members who ate lunch at a Sha Tin school earlier this week. Twenty-three boys and 14 girls, aged between five and 11, from Baptist (Sha Tin Wai) Lui Ming Choi Primary School and two employees, aged 34 and 38, were affected. They developed stomach pain and diarrhoea about eight to 22 hours after eating school lunches provided by a supplier on Wednesday. A spokesman for the school, located at 8 Yuen Chau Kok Road in Sha Tin, could not be reached for comment on Saturday night. The Centre for Health Protection did not name the supplier in a statement on Saturday. “Initial investigations of the [centre] revealed that the affected persons consumed the same type of lunchboxes before the onset of symptoms, pointing to food poisoning likely related to the consumption of marinated chicken leg and penne provided by the lunch supplier,” it said. Two pupils sought medical advice but did not require hospitalisation. They were in a stable condition. The others experienced mild symptoms and did not need to see a doctor. Meanwhile, officers from the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department inspected the lunch supplier, reviewing its food storage, cooking procedures and hygiene. It was ordered to suspend operations on Saturday for thorough cleaning and disinfection. Food and environmental samples were collected for testing. Officers, including personnel from the Centre for Food Safety and the environmental hygiene branch, also visited the school to conduct a joint investigation. “They examined the food storing and distributing processes and environmental hygiene at the school, and collected food samples at school for testing,” the statement said. “The officers also provided preventive advice against food poisoning to the school.” Health authorities have urged members of the public to maintain personal, food and environmental hygiene to prevent foodborne diseases. Last week, the health authorities also reported a series of suspected food poisoning clusters in which a total of 14 diners fell ill after eating buffet meals at a hotel restaurant in Yau Ma Tei.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors movie review – Lav Diaz’s brutal colonial epic
description: Director Lav Diaz’s latest film explores colonial terror, faith and resistance in a perilous 17th century jungle in the Philippines.
content: 3.5/5 stars Filmmaker Lav Diaz takes audiences into the jungles of the Philippines with Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors, a harrowing historical drama premiering out of competition at this year’s Venice International Film Festival. The premise here loosely evokes Henri-Georges Clouzot’s The Wages of Fear (1953), replacing the volatile nitroglycerine of that film with massive blocks of limestone. Set in the early 17th century, approximately a century after the events of Diaz’s 2025 film Magellan – which explored the Portuguese and Spanish colonial campaigns across Southeast Asia – the new feature continues the Filipino director’s fascination with the subject. The year is 1617, a period when churches were being erected across the Philippines, claiming countless indigenous lives as a result. For the past 15 years, a small place of worship has been under construction deep within the jungle. “It is the church that will build this island,” remarks Padre Enciso (Bart Guingona), a brutish Spanish friar dubbed a “curse” for his deviancy, sexually exploiting local widows at every opportunity. Striking fear into the locals (“Be afraid with the punishment of God”), Enciso forces his son, jungle-dweller Dungwen (Christian Bables), to transport the limestone for the church’s altar through hazardous terrain, promising him riches if he succeeds. The sheer effort of dragging huge blocks of stone through the jungle is enough to break anyone, but with Dungwen’s men terrified of an unseen predator named Bari-Bari, paranoia quickly consumes them. Shooting in stark black and white, Diaz ensures audiences feel every footstep of this arduous trek through highly inhospitable terrain. Eschewing studio backdrops for immersive location shoots, he captures everything from mudslides to cacophonous insect noise. This “hellish pathway”, as Enciso calls it, recalls both Francis Ford Coppola’s Vietnam war saga Apocalypse Now (1979), which was also shot in the Philippines, and Werner Herzog’s Fitzcarraldo (1982) in the Peruvian jungles. Clocking in at 151 minutes, Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors is practically a short film by the standards of Diaz’s famously sprawling filmography. While one could never call the pacing rapid, his usual adherence to “slow cinema” is less pronounced here. Most of the horrors are kept off-screen – the jungle’s creatures, for example, are curiously absent – but for Dungwen and his crew, Diaz still has some surprises in store, including one twist that will leave viewers stunned. The sheer will required of Diaz – who also edited, shot and designed this filmmaking feat – is admirable. Though the journey’s gruelling nature makes it a tough watch, the director clearly and cleverly outlines the horrors of Western colonialism perpetrated in the name of religion, superstition and fear. title: Farage’s Reform UK gets second record £36 million donation in 48 hours
description: The donation comes as the veteran Brexit campaigner’s party is confronting allegations about irregularities in its funding, which it denies.
content: Cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne said on Saturday he had donated £36 million (US$49 million) to Britain’s anti-immigration Reform UK, matching an already record contribution to Nigel Farage’s party a day earlier as it prepares for the next election. The donation gives the veteran Brexit campaigner’s party £72 million from two donors in ‌less than 48 hours at a time when it is confronting allegations about irregularities in its funding, which it denies. The figure exceeds what either the governing Labour Party or the opposition Conservatives spent during last year’s election campaign, according to Electoral Commission figures. The funds will help Reform, whose lead in opinion polls has slipped over the funding allegations, win over voters before the next election, which is due by 2029. Harborne, already Reform’s biggest donor, disclosed the contribution in a Telegraph newspaper article, saying fellow crypto investor Ben Delo’s pledge a day earlier had inspired him to match it. “What do I ⁠expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government,” Harborne wrote in the article. Delo’s donation ‌on Friday had already dwarfed the previous record of £10 million that British businessman John Sainsbury, who died in 2022, had left to the Conservatives, according to the Electoral Commission’s online database. Reform has said that if it comes to power, it would propose a ‌law to boost crypto adoption, including by cutting capital gains tax for digital assets and creating a bitcoin reserve fund at the ⁠Bank of England. The donation ⁠comes little more than a week after Reform was hit by allegations that two senior aides to Farage had helped arrange for a foreign donor to fund political polling, claims which the party ‌denies. Earlier in September, Reform said head of policy James Orr and Farage adviser Dan Jukes had stepped down pending an internal investigation after an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 alleged the party had broken ‌electoral law by ‌arranging for a US company to pay for polling commissioned by the party. Reform has denied any wrongdoing, saying it had been targeted in a hoax by ‌climate activists. Farage has said the party had “broken no laws” and had not taken any improper donations. Labour has asked police to investigate possible offences linked to the ⁠allegations. Police said they were assessing information provided to them, while the Electoral Commission said it was considering the claims and was in contact with law enforcement. On Friday, ⁠Delo, the British co-founder of cryptocurrency trading platform BitMEX who was convicted of a US Bank Secrecy Act violation and later pardoned by President Donald Trump, said he would donate £36 million to Reform UK. Delo said he wanted the party to spend less time fundraising and more time preparing ‌for government, arguing it needed resources to compete ‌with Britain’s two established parties, Labour and the Conservatives. Farage welcomed the backing from both men on Saturday. “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne have shown such confidence in Reform,” he said in a statement. “Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election. Thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field.”

title: Quality concerns prompt further tests on concrete used in 3 public housing blocks
description: Main contractor on Tung Chung estate, Able Engineering, is also part of a joint venture involved in scandal-hit lift installation work.
content: The quality of concrete used in three blocks of a public housing estate under construction in Tung Chung requires further testing and review, Hong Kong’s Housing Authority has revealed. According to official documents, the main contractor on the project is Able Engineering. The same company is also involved in a scandal over defective lift installation work at an expansion project at Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam. The authority said on Saturday that regular checks had uncovered issues with the quality of concrete used in three blocks of the estate at Tung Chung Area 42 on Lantau Island between late August and early September. “The Housing Authority’s engineering team discovered during routine concrete cube strength tests between late August and early September that the quality of concrete used in certain structural components of blocks 3, 4 and 5 at the Tung Chung Area 42 public housing estate required further review and testing,” a spokesman said. The estate, with a total site area of about four hectares, comprises six residential blocks, providing more than 6,000 public housing flats for a planned population of 16,611. The project’s cost was estimated at about HK$5.4 billion in 2023. The authority said it had instructed the contractor to extract additional concrete core samples for compressive strength testing in accordance with contract standards to assess whether the concrete strength met the design and contractual requirements. The contractor was also required to submit a detailed report, along with a rectification and repair plan, and to replace the concrete supplier immediately, the authority added. The authority, the biggest supplier of public housing in Hong Kong, warned that if an investigation confirmed any fault by the contractor, its performance would be penalised under official scoring mechanisms, directly affecting future tendering opportunities. If the situation was severe, the authority would consider taking harsher regulatory action, including suspending the contractor’s eligibility to tender, it said. It would closely monitor the progress and quality of the project, with the goal of completing the development by the original contractual completion date. Last month, widespread installation defects were revealed at the new block of Queen Mary Hospital, which had delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, prompting deep concern over project oversight and civil service accountability. The main contractor on the project is a Paul Y-Able joint venture, with the lift subcontractor being Anlev Elex Elevator. Lawmaker Scott Leung Man-kwong noted that the concrete issue was proactively uncovered by the authority during routine inspections. He said it showed that existing monitoring mechanisms for public housing estates were functioning effectively as an early warning system to manage risks during construction and safeguard structural integrity. “The initial impact on overall public housing supply appears limited for now,” he said. Pending the outcome of further concrete retesting and investigation, unaffected works on site, such as non-structural construction, could continue, he added. Leung also expressed hope that the department could reallocate resources and adjust construction schedules to minimise delays and prevent disruption to housing supply. Regarding public concerns over accountability, he noted it was premature at this stage to assign ultimate responsibility.

title: Why PLA’s laser-equipped Type 19 vehicle could matter in a Taiwan conflict
description: Images appear to show amphibious platform adapted with energy weapon and extra sensors for counter-drone defence.
content: The People’s Liberation Army may be seeking to give its frontline mechanised units mobile protection against the kind of drone-saturated battlefield that could emerge in a Taiwan conflict. Unverified images posted on mainland Chinese social media on August 29 show a new variant of the Type 19 amphibious 8x8 combat vehicle featuring a turret-mounted laser weapon and extra sensors alongside its standard autocannon. Janes, an open-source defence intelligence provider, reported in 2023 that vehicles from the Type 19 family had entered service with the 73rd Group Army under the Eastern Theatre Command, which includes amphibious brigades expected to play a major role in a potential Taiwan landing operation. Assuming the new variant retains the base platform’s amphibious capability, it could accompany frontline units in a possible landing operation, providing defence against uncrewed surveillance and loitering munitions. Timothy Heath, founder of defence consultancy Perceptum and a former senior China analyst at Rand Corporation and for the US military, said it was difficult to know without more technical data whether the modifications affected the Type 19’s amphibious performance, but he believed operating the laser system while afloat “should be possible”. The added weight could potentially be offset by reducing the crew size or other equipment, although the system would also need to be protected from salt water, he said. Heath said that if those challenges could be overcome, the laser-based counter-drone system could be “very useful in a Taiwan conflict” in which Taiwanese forces might use drone swarms to target amphibious vehicles coming ashore. The laser system’s low operating cost could make it particularly useful against such attacks, Heath added. The development comes as Taipei moves to field drones on a much larger scale and expand the role of uncrewed systems across its military. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. On September 3, the island’s cabinet proposed a new NT$145.7 billion (US$4.6 billion) supplementary defence budget that includes more than 600 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, and more than 40,000 coastal attack drones. The package still requires legislative approval. Days earlier, lawmakers approved a separate six-year NT$240 billion framework for domestically produced drones after rejecting a competing government plan. Taiwan has also reorganised parts of its military around drone warfare. The army finalised drone battalions across three operational combat zones in April, while its marine corps had earlier established a drone battalion as part of a restructuring that included disbanding tank and self-propelled artillery battalions. During the island’s Han Kuang 42 exercise in August, Taiwanese aerial drone units carried out battlefield surveillance and reconnaissance, intelligence transmission and attack missions, according to the defence ministry. For PLA forces trying to establish and expand a foothold on the island, the threat would extend beyond direct drone attacks. Uncrewed aircraft could also expose troop movements and positions and help cue artillery, missiles and other weapons against exposed forces. Heath said the new Type 19 variant was consistent with lessons from the Russia-Ukraine war, where drones had proved effective against tanks, artillery and other frontline targets, increasing the value of mounting counter-drone systems directly on individual platforms. He said the PLA had “almost certainly” drawn similar lessons from earlier fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan, where drones had shown an ability to bypass traditional air-defence systems. These lessons appear to be shaping a broader PLA effort to protect troops and vehicles from drones, using everything from added armour on tanks to lasers, microwave weapons and conventional guns or missiles. The new Type 19 variant could represent a further step in that evolution: integrating sensors and different counter-drone systems onto an armoured platform capable of keeping pace with frontline mechanised formations. Similar vehicle-mounted concepts are also emerging elsewhere, although the specific configurations remain at the prototype stage. Heath pointed to Hanwha’s Tigon 8x8 armoured vehicle, unveiled this week with a 50-kilowatt counter-drone laser, and AeroVironment’s 20kW-class Locust system mounted on US Army Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. Hanwha has built a prototype and plans serial production by the end of 2027, while JLTV-mounted Locust systems were delivered to the US Army in December under a prototyping programme. But laser weapons also have limitations. Their effectiveness can be reduced by weather, smoke and dust, while power and cooling requirements are another constraint. Keeping the autocannon could therefore provide another option when conditions make the laser less effective. While Janes assessed the newly seen vehicle as a Type 19-based counter-drone variant, it is not clear whether it is operational, undergoing trials or serving as a technology demonstrator.

title: Iran, UAE leaders discuss de-escalation as oil supply worries spike
description: President and crown prince meet for first time since tensions intensified after Iran hit back at US allies following US-Israeli strikes.
content: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and the crown prince of Abu Dhabi met on the sidelines of the Brics summit in New Delhi on Saturday, marking the highest-level meeting between the two sides since the Iran war began. The bilateral meeting came as the fallout of the war in Iran widened, with Saudi Arabia shutting its key East-West oil pipeline after it was attacked by drones on Friday. The closure of the pipeline stretching across the Arabian peninsula has heightened global concerns over more oil supply disruption. The meeting, confirmed by the Iranian embassy in New Delhi, brought the Iran and UAE leaders face to face months after bilateral frictions intensified sharply in late February, as US-Israeli strikes saw Tehran hit back at American allies in the region. The crown prince, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, said in a social media post after the meeting that the two sides discussed regional and international issues, “along with the importance of supporting de-escalation efforts, reducing tensions, and achieving stability in the region”. Retaliatory strikes across the Gulf region saw Iran launch sustained ballistic missile and drone attacks against the United Arab Emirates that damaged energy infrastructure, ports and commercial facilities across Dubai and Abu Dhabi. Meanwhile, escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have led to strikes on commercial vessels, including oil tankers operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. Relations reached a breaking point last month after two Iranian ballistic missiles splashed down in waters near the UAE coastline, prompting Abu Dhabi to enact a comprehensive, indefinite embargo. The UAE suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran, cutting off the banking and transshipment channels that Tehran has historically relied upon to bypass international isolation. As Iran’s second-largest trading partner after China, the UAE has long been an indispensable commercial hub for the Iranian economy, providing roughly 30 per cent of its imports and access to foreign currency, banking networks, and global shipping. At the Brics foreign ministers’ meeting in May, Iranian top diplomat Abbas Araghchi clashed with Emirati representatives, accusing the UAE of providing bases, airspace, territory, intelligence and other facilities to the US and Israel during the attacks on his country. But India successfully bridged the divergence on Saturday, steering member states towards the formal adoption of the joint Delhi Declaration. The declaration condemned the imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law, including economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, and called for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Gulf conflict.

title: Will Malaysia’s Umno pull the plug on coalition partner PH?
description: Umno has been buoyed by recent state victories and growing talk of a new alignment to consolidate the Malay vote.
content: The political impasse in Malaysia’s government has regressed to a game of chicken, experts say, with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and the former ruling Umno party trading barbs and dares as pressure grows for snap polls with more than a year left to term. Relations between Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition and erstwhile rivals Umno have hit its lowest point since the two sides cut a deal to form a unity government in 2022, after a series of recent state polls that saw PH all but decimated at the hands of Umno. The lopsided victories in Johor and Negeri Sembilan over the past two months have since emboldened Umno to demand that a general election be held immediately. At the closing of the party’s general assembly on Saturday, Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said it was now up to Anwar to decide whether he wanted the government to remain in political limbo or seek a fresh mandate to rule. “There are only two choices. One, get a fresh mandate through a general election; second, formally remove us [from government] and hold a confidence vote in parliament,” Zahid said as over 6,000 party delegates chanted “dissolve, dissolve” at the party headquarters in Kuala Lumpur. “Do you dare? If you have the guts, do it quickly!... remember, the unity government was formed because of Umno. The prime minister became prime minister because of Umno’s support,” added Zahid, in some of his most pointed criticism of Anwar since being appointed his deputy over three years ago. Ties between the reformist PH and Malay-nationalist Umno deteriorated quickly over the past two months, triggered by a landslide victory by Umno in the Johor state election in July that left PH with just a handful of seats. The feud worsened a month later when Umno joined opposition Islamist party Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) to depose PH in the Negeri Sembilan state polls, even after Anwar approved the release of a royal commission of inquiry report detailing dubious dealings – mostly during Umno’s past rule – that led to well over 1 billion ringgit (US$245.7 million) in losses at state-run pilgrim’s fund Tabung Haji. The long-time rivals had come together to form the government after a deeply split national election in 2022, following a decree by then-king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah appointing Anwar as prime minister on condition that he create an administration that includes both supporters and opponents. But Anwar’s dependence on Umno, which provides much-needed representation for the country’s Malay-Muslim majority in his administration, has driven a deep wedge in his own coalition as it struggles to regain the faith of its own supporters angered by PH’s failure to push much of its promised reforms. “In almost any other government, a deputy prime minister openly challenging the prime minister in this manner would risk being sacked,” Asrul Sani, associate vice-president with strategic advisory and business consulting firm The Asia Group, told This Week in Asia. “That Zahid can do so underscores both Umno’s leverage and the political constraints facing Anwar.” The two leaders have been taking media potshots at each other on Friday, after Zahid borrowed the catchphrase “guru, hentikan, guru” (stop, teacher, stop) popular on Malaysian TikTok to needle Anwar over what he described as inconsistent economic policies that only confuse the public. Anwar later responded on social media, urging his “student” to learn from “guru” on how to conduct diplomacy when announcing his arrival in New Delhi for the Brics leaders’ summit. Both leaders notably used Gen Z terms like “slay” and “flex” in their messaging, in a clear attempt to engage a voter base that will increasingly decide the fate of political parties. Youths aged between 18 and 30 account for almost 6.4 million or 28.8 per cent of eligible voters nationwide, according to the latest Election Commission data. “They form a substantial segment of the voters, so it’s important for politicians to connect with them. But politicians need to do more than parroting Gen Z lingo to win their votes,” said Adib Zalkapli, managing director at geopolitical and public affairs firm Viewfinder Global Affairs. For all the bluster, it does not hide the fact that Anwar is in a difficult position. Voters have rejected his ruling PH coalition in three state contests now, starting last November when they were all but wiped out in the Sabah state election. The result was a major red flag for the Democratic Action Party (DAP) – the largest member of PH – which forced its leaders to revert to campaign tactics from their days in the opposition to try and staunch the bleeding support. Anwar’s People’s Justice Party (PKR) saw four senior leaders quit so far, including his daughter and party deputy Nurul Izzah, as criticism mounted over his alleged favouring of Umno over his own allies and at the expense of their decades-old reform pledges. “Holding the 16th general election now would be a suicidal move for the prime minister,” said Mazlan Ali, a political analyst at the University of Technology Malaysia. Umno could very well force snap polls if it quit government and withdrew support for Anwar, but doing so would paint it as a saboteur and only gain public ire, experts say. Until and unless Umno makes such a bold move, Anwar still has time to reclaim PH’s support base before the elections, which do not need to be held until early 2028. The first real test will come soon, with Anwar scheduled to table his 2027 budget in October. “The speeches we heard are just political theatre for now. They only mean anything if the Umno MPs collectively resign from the government and vote against the 2027 budget,” said Adib of Viewfinder Global Affairs.

title: Under Trump’s shadow, Brics takes step towards de-dollarisation
description: New Delhi Declaration pushes for cheaper and faster payments system and takes aim at sanctions and unilateral tariffs.
content: Brics countries agreed on Saturday to expand trade and payments in local currencies, making another step towards de-dollarisation as the bloc seeks to counter an assertive United States. Facing pressure from Washington, the member nations found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits. The pledges were part of the “New Delhi Declaration 2026”, adopted unanimously on the opening day of the 18th Brics summit. After a closed session, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi emerged to say that no member had “objected” to the text. The 45-page declaration said the group’s Payment Task Force had studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and held talks on using local currencies for “trade settlements and investments”. The task force was told to keep working on payments that were “fast, low cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe”. But the leaders were also clear about just how far they were prepared to go. The declaration said there was “no one-size-fits-all approach”, and that national priorities must be respected. That caution matters in Washington. US President Donald Trump has threatened the bloc with 100 per cent tariffs if it “plays games with the dollar”. In his opening remarks on Saturday, Modi said that Brics was “not against anyone”. The declaration also does not name Trump or the United States, but it does criticise unilateral tariffs, sanctions and protectionist measures of the kind he has used. It voiced “serious concerns about the rise of unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures which distort trade and are inconsistent with World Trade Organization rules”, and warned that “indiscriminate” increases in tariffs and protectionism “under the guise of environmental objectives” threatened global trade and supply chains. It also condemned “unilateral coercive measures”, including “unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions”, calling them contrary to international law and demanding their elimination. A separate line opposed “unilateral, punitive, discriminatory and protectionist measures”, including carbon border taxes – carbon fees imposed on imported goods. Trump’s shadow also hung over one of India’s biggest diplomacy tests of the summit: Iran and the United Arab Emirates are both Brics members, and on opposite sides of the Middle East conflict that began in February. Sherpas worked into the early hours of Saturday to find wording that all members could live with. “The New Delhi Declaration adopted today gives a clear direction to our shared resolve. It is now our responsibility to translate these commitments into tangible results,” Modi said, describing the day’s meeting as “productive” and “creative”. Observers said the calibrated language reflected the fine line India was walking as it pushed for greater strategic autonomy without turning Brics into an explicitly anti-US bloc. Farwa Aamer, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, said India had positioned itself as the voice of the Global South and was challenging the international order that excluded those parts of the world. At the same time, it was not pursuing an anti-West agenda. “It has an interest in not letting China establish sole dominance in the region and within the Brics, and despite recent strain, it continues to engage with Washington,” she said “India’s balancing act is a delicate one but with Brics consensus, it succeeds in asserting its own strategic autonomy and ensuring that its effectively hedging interests.” Aamer described the language on the West Asia conflict as “a very balanced and somewhat restrained position”. “Perhaps that was the only way to reach a consensus, not supporting any single national interest over the other,” she said. Manoj Kewalramani, chairman of the Bengaluru-based Takshashila Institution’s Geostrategy programme, called the declaration a “compromise document, which underscores how far the interests of Brics members diverge”. He noted that without naming the US, the text criticised it over protectionism, unilateral sanctions and the conduct of states in international institutions, including withholding assessed contributions. It also confirmed Brics’ goal of revising the international order in favour of greater representation for emerging and developing economies. However, he added, “the pathway to that goal ... is far less clear than the goal itself, and the reason is the divergence of interests within the group”.

title: Xi tells Modi China and India bear ‘significant responsibilities’ as Global South powers
description: Leaders meet on sidelines of Brics summit in New Delhi; Indian statement says they reaffirmed that ‘differences should not become disputes’.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”. Xi said that although the countries had different national circumstances, “there is ample scope for us to learn from each other’s strengths, offer mutual support, achieve shared success and pursue common development”. “Over the past two years, Prime Minister Modi and I have met twice, guiding the relationship from a ‘fresh start’ to a ‘new level of advancement’,” Xi said, according to a readout from Xinhua. “Institutional exchanges between the two countries have gradually resumed, the list of cooperative initiatives has steadily expanded, and the volume of bilateral trade has hit a new high. This situation was hard-won and deserves to be cherished.” On the border issue, Xi said that both sides should maintain peace and tranquillity in boundary areas and commit to “parallel development and mutual promotion of bilateral relations and border issues”. The two sides have sparred repeatedly along their ill-defined border, including the 2020 Galwan Valley clash in which at least 20 Indian and four Chinese soldiers were killed. Even the length of the border is not agreed upon, with India recording it at around 2,160-miles (3,476 km) while China puts it at less than half that. Xi looks to ‘future of humanity’, ‘well-being of our people’ The two leaders met on the sidelines of the Brics summit in New Delhi, where trade, investment, the long-running border dispute and the normalisation of ties took centre stage. “We must keep the future of humanity and the well-being of our people at heart, join hands to drive high-quality cooperation within the expanded Brics framework, advocate for an equal and orderly multipolar world and an economic globalisation that is universally beneficial and inclusive,” the Chinese leader said. Xi also called for both sides to inject greater positive energy into promoting global peace, stability and prosperity. The Chinese president acknowledged that the two countries, with their combined 2.8 billion people, are in “different” economic and geopolitical positions. But he said they could “learn from each other’s strengths”, offer mutual support, prosper and pursue common development. China’s economy is currently four times larger than India’s in nominal GDP terms, compared with rough parity in 1987. Xi outlined a vague four-point plan for future China-India relations that was short on specifics, in keeping with many of Beijing’s foreign policy initiatives. He called on the neighbours to align on “objective and rational” strategy; engage in “win-win” cooperation; overcome differences through “political wisdom” and mutual understanding; and collaborate to bolster the global good in part by working together in multilateral groupings. “China and India are partners rather than rivals, and present opportunities for each other’s development rather than threats,” he said, according to Xinhua. Xi, Modi address lingering China-India border questions The meeting began at 5.45pm, with Cai Qi, a close aide to Xi and China’s fifth-ranking official, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi taking part. India was represented by National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and Vikram Doraiswami, India’s ambassador to China. The two countries have been trying to turn their fragile diplomatic thaw into a broader reset following years of military tensions, frozen political engagement and sharply curtailed economic and people-to-people links. New Delhi’s statement on the meeting said the two leaders “reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long-term perspective of their ties”, and that “differences should not become disputes”. Modi “emphasised that peace and tranquillity in the border areas remains an essential basis for the continued development of bilateral relations”, underlining “the need for both sides to observe existing agreements and understandings on border-related issues”. “The two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable, and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question proceeding from the political perspective of their overall bilateral relations and the long-term interests of the two peoples,” the statement read. According to China’s version, India also said it “adheres to an independent foreign policy” and its relationship with China is “not influenced by third parties”, an apparent reference to any role by Washington. Beijing further noted that India’s policy and stance regarding Taiwan and Tibet-related issues “remain unchanged”, adding that New Delhi “does not permit any forces to engage in anti-China activities on Indian soil”. More than 70,000 Tibetans live in India, including the 91-year-old Dalai Lama. Xi arrived in New Delhi around midday on Saturday leading about a 70-strong delegation. He is scheduled to attend Sunday morning’s Brics summit session before leaving the country. A separate Chinese business delegation is also visiting, underscoring the economic dimension of the trip. The meeting is taking place amid tight security, and Chinese personnel were spotted in New Delhi ahead of Xi’s visit. Deadly Galwan clash colours China-India relations The optics of the visit are significant. Xi’s last trip to India was in October 2019, when he held informal talks with Modi. His first trip as leader took place in 2014, and he also took part in the 2016 Brics summit in Goa. But high-level engagement between the two countries came to a near-standstill after the deadly Galwan confrontation. The incident led to a multi-year military stand-off along their disputed frontier, with direct flights and several official dialogue channels being suspended. Pilgrims were also barred from travelling from India to sacred sites such as Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar in Tibet. The first major political opening came in October 2024, when Modi and Xi met on the sidelines of the Brics summit in Russia after the two sides reached an understanding on disengagement along the border. The two leaders also met on the sidelines of last year’s Shanghai Cooperation Organisation meeting in the Chinese city of Tianjin. Meanwhile, direct flights have resumed and pilgrims have been permitted to travel to the sacred sites. The Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination and the Special Representatives’ Dialogue on the Boundary Question have also resumed. Last month, after the latest border talks between Wang and Doval in Beijing, the two sides issued a rare joint statement, signalling an effort to build momentum ahead of Xi’s India visit. They also produced an eight-point consensus that included commitments to keep the frontier quiet, create new working groups, add military communication channels and continue talks on pilgrimages, border trade and rivers. The next round of boundary talks will be held in India in 2027. The bigger test now may be whether the diplomatic thaw can translate into an economic reset. Saturday’s Indian statement said the two leaders also agreed to intensify people-to-people exchanges and pledged to address concerns regarding market access, trade imbalances and supply chains, points echoed in China’s version. Two-way goods trade has continued to grow, exceeding US$150 billion in the latest full-year figures, according to publicly reported customs data. But the economic relationship remains heavily skewed and politically sensitive. For Beijing, a stable relationship with India could help restore one of its most consequential Asian economic partnerships. For New Delhi, the question is whether greater economic engagement can take place while it has concerns over market access, trade imbalances, investment and national security. “India appreciates China’s support for its hosting of the Brics summit and pledges full support for China’s Brics chairmanship next year,” according to China’s readout. “India is ready to coordinate and cooperate closely with China to strengthen Global South cooperation, promote a multipolar world and economic growth and serve as a force for stability and progress in a turbulent world.”

title: US-China decoupling could benefit other countries, China trade war game suggests
description: The study suggests a complete severing of trade ties would hurt both superpowers while bringing temporary gains elsewhere.
content: Chinese researchers have modelled a war game scenario suggesting that a complete economic decoupling between the US and China could, unexpectedly, yield dividends for most other nations. Using a quantitative trade model – a data-based economic framework that estimates how changes in trade affect economies – two researchers based in southern China’s Guangdong province found that if the world’s two largest economies were to sever trade relations entirely, a number of other countries, including nations in Southeast Asia, would actually see an increase in overall economic welfare. “These favourable changes are attributable to the fact that, in the process of global supply chain restructuring, these countries have partially taken over trade and production activities previously carried out through US-China cooperation,” the authors wrote. However, the simulations carried an important caveat: any spillover benefits would be fragile. If those economies were subsequently to cut their own economic ties with China, their initial welfare gains would quickly turn into losses. The study, co-authored by researchers from the Guangzhou Geological Survey Institute and the Bay Area International Business School at Beijing Normal University, was published in the peer-reviewed South China Journal of Economics. Seeking to quantify the macroeconomic fallout from aggressive tariff policies, the researchers simulated the shocks to China’s economy under various decoupling scenarios. In their model, “complete decoupling” was defined as an extreme scenario in which the two sides imposed reciprocal tariffs of 10,000 per cent – effectively cutting off bilateral trade. The findings showed that a China-US rupture would cause significant economic welfare losses for both superpowers, while potentially bringing temporary gains to other economies. Cambodia, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Mexico were among those projected to benefit most. Vietnam – buoyed by relatively low labour costs and an expanding manufacturing base – was projected to benefit significantly. This, the authors noted, was probably because the country managed to “attract part of the production processes or orders previously located in China”. Mexico’s gain was driven by its geographical proximity to the United States and integration into the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), a trilateral free-trade pact, which would enable the country to efficiently absorb industrial activities tied to the near-shoring or reshoring of North American supply chains. However, the study also found these nations to be among the economies most exposed if they later decoupled from China. In the case of Vietnam, the authors noted that the country was deeply integrated into a China-centred East Asian production network, its key export industries – particularly electronics and textiles – relying heavily on intermediate goods imported from China. The study found that decoupling from Beijing would rupture these supply lines and bring “devastating damage” to the country’s manufacturing sector. The researchers extended their simulations to assess the impact of China completely decoupling from its other major trading partners, including the European Union, Japan, South Korea and members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. “The welfare losses arising from a China-EU decoupling are the largest,” the paper noted, citing the “extensive and deep two-way dependence” between the two sides, particularly in high-end manufacturing, capital goods and technology-intensive products. By comparison, the model suggested that China could partly cushion the economic shock of a US-China decoupling by replacing some US imports – including agricultural commodities, energy products and standardised industrial goods – with supplies from other countries or domestic production. China is the EU’s second-largest trading partner after the US. However, trade friction, geopolitical rivalry and economic competition are increasingly dominating the narrative between Brussels and Beijing. A European Commission delegation has recently been locked in talks with Chinese officials in Beijing, as both sides seek a diplomatic off-ramp from a potential trade war before an October deadline set by Brussels.

title: French police probe if sabotage derailed train and injured 44
description: A fragment of rail was found on the track, with the possibility of a malicious act that resulted in 44 people injured.
content: Investigators suspect that a train derailment in northwest France which injured 44, one gravely, was the result of sabotage, a police source said on Saturday. A fragment of rail was found on the track, with the possibility of a malicious act being treated as the main line of inquiry as a result, the source said. Carrying 186 passengers, the train was running between the Normandy cities of Rouen and Caen when it derailed around 7.45pm local time on Friday close to Renault’s factory in the town of Cleon. Authorities activated a mass-casualty response plan, with 130 firefighters, five medical teams and 80 vehicles drafted in. An AFP photographer saw a mass of railway staff working around the train on Saturday morning. Rouen prosecutor Sebastien Gallois said 44 people were injured including an 18-year-old woman evacuated “in a critical condition”, while tests for drugs and alcohol on the train driver had come back negative. “Suddenly there were a few jolts, and then after about three seconds it got stronger and stronger,” one of the passengers, Louis, 24, told ICI Normandie radio. “I couldn’t stay in my seat any more,” he said. “The windows partially shattered, the stones from the track came into the carriage. It was really shocking. I’m still shaking.” Those who escaped unharmed were taken to a room made available by Cleon’s mayor, according to the authorities. SNCF Reseau, which controls the French rail network, said that traffic on the line had been suspended and power to the tracks cut to allow emergency services to operate. According to SNCF, the accident caused “major disruptions” to rail traffic between Rouen and Caen and between Caen and Le Havre in both directions. A spokesperson for SNCF Reseau said on Saturday morning that services had resumed. On the Rouen-Caen line, which usually sees 10 return services per day and six at weekends, a replacement bus service has been set up, SNCF Voyageurs said. According to the spokesperson, the train will only be lifted off the line once the public prosecutor allows it, with investigations into the cause of the derailment still ongoing. SNCF insisted that it would offer “full cooperation in complete transparency” to the inquiry.

title: A year after lawmakers veto equality bill, LGBTQ Hongkongers still hope for change
description: A year after Legco votes down bill protecting rights of same-sex couples, LGBTQ people remain in limbo as government mulls ‘administrative’ solution.
content: When Hong Kong’s Legislative Council vetoed a government bill that would have granted limited recognition to the city’s same-sex couples, 51-year-old Isaac Yick said he was “disappointed but not surprised”. Yick was born and raised in Hong Kong before moving to Canada, where he eventually met and married his husband. They returned to the city together in 2013. He said there was initially a sense that things were changing for the LGBTQ community in the city, citing victories in court that conferred some rights for same-sex couples, including one landmark case from 2019 involving spousal benefits. “It would still have to go through all the courts, which was unnecessary, but once the decision was handed down, we saw the change,” he said. So when the Court of Final Appeal ruled in 2023 that the government had a positive obligation to recognise same-sex partnerships in the city, there was reason for optimism. But by the time the government’s bill made its way to Legco two years later, Yick had the feeling legal recognition was not going to happen. In the year since the bill was rejected, the pace of change had slowed considerably, he said. “I think it’s still progressing but, since the veto, the speed has slowed down quite significantly. There’s more uncertainty,” he said. As the government continues to mull over how to “administratively” protect the rights of same-sex couples after the bill was vetoed, members of the city’s LGBTQ community told the South China Morning Post they remained stuck in limbo and were awaiting signs of a path forward. “It has been one year and we still haven’t heard anything from the government,” said Jerome Yau, chief executive of the NGO Aids Concern, who also previously co-founded the advocacy group Hong Kong Marriage Equality. “Until such time the government announces what it intends to do … I guess we are sort of in a holding pattern.” The bill was the government’s response to a 2023 ruling by the Court of Final Appeal, which gave authorities two years to draw up laws to set out “core rights” for same-sex couples. The legislation would have allowed couples who had a valid same-sex marriage, partnership or civil union registered in a jurisdiction outside Hong Kong to have their relationship recognised in the city under a proposed registration mechanism, but it was rejected by 71 out of 87 lawmakers. The veto marked the first time a government bill had failed to be greenlit by Legco since Beijing overhauled the city’s electoral system in 2021 so that only “patriots” could hold public office in Hong Kong. According to some lawmakers, their reasons for voting against the bill included a lack of public consensus on the issue. Immediately after the bill was vetoed, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau would look at how to “administratively” protect the rights of the LGBTQ community, including those related to healthcare and property. In a response to a detailed list of questions from the SCMP, the bureau said the government had performed its duty by proposing the Registration of Same-Sex Partnerships Bill last year, and that it respected lawmakers’ votes and Legco’s final decision. “As directed by the chief executive, we are now exploring administrative measures to provide appropriate protections for same-sex partners in relevant areas. The relevant work is in progress,” the bureau said. It did not provide an exact timeline for when such measures would be announced, nor any examples of what rights they might include. Yau said he had doubts administrative measures alone would be enough to satisfy the requirements of the court’s ruling, and he was hopeful the government would go further than the proposed bill to confer rights to same-sex couples. “Ideally, it would go further than that because what was covered in the original bill was really basic,” he said. The proposed legislation would have granted rights related to medical and after-death matters. While the LGBTQ community has gained some rights over the years through a series of court victories, many gaps remain. A report released earlier this year by global law firm A&O Shearman, commissioned by the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s gender studies programme, found 21 areas in which a person might be treated differently due to their relationship status, including those relating to children, housing and public welfare. The report also noted inconsistencies within the same legal domain, as only certain parts of the law were successfully challenged. As an example, it noted that while a same-sex spouse might have first priority to “inherit on intestacy” – when someone dies without a will – they might have lower, or even no, priority to administer the estate under existing grant rules. Lawyer Azan Marwah, who has handled numerous cases pertaining to LGBTQ rights, said he believed administrative measures could help same-sex couples in certain legal areas. However, there were still many areas where the lack of legislation would run up against existing laws that were partial to straight married couples, he added. “We are not going to have a true or complete solution,” he said. Forty-year-old Hongkonger Mandy, who asked to be referred to only by her first name, travelled to Australia – where citizenship is not required for marriage – in 2019 to marry her wife surrounded by friends and family. She said it was important to get married, even if it was abroad, as a commitment of love and to show those who remained closeted about their sexuality that it was safe to be themselves. Despite the lack of legal recognition for her marital status in Hong Kong, she held out hope that things would eventually change. “I hope in the coming future, our marriage [will be] legally recognised here,” she said. “We deserve to be recognised.”

title: China’s newest tennis star Sun facing familiar foe in third junior grand slam final
description: Sun Xinran into girls’ singles final at US Open, where she will face Anna Pushkareva, who beat her at Wimbledon.
content: The newest tennis star in China said she wanted to be like Zheng Qinwen and hoped she could play against the Olympic champion on the professional tour one day, after reaching the US Open girls’ singles final. Sun Xinran beat Chukwumelije Clarke of the United States 7-5, 0-6, 6-1 to reach the final, where she will face fifth seed Russian teenage girl Anna Pushkareva. New York is the third grand slam final for Sun this year, after reaching the last two at the French Open and Wimbledon, but she has yet to win a title. The Chinese star lost to Pushkareva in London two months ago, despite being a set up. “I have no expectations any more. I’ll just play as if I’m going to lose,” Sun, the top girls’ seed, said. “I’ve already lost twice already, and tomorrow’s opponent is the same one I lost to at Wimbledon. “I know her very well. She plays exceptionally well too. So I’ll just try my best to play my best tennis and see if I can do better than last time.” Sun, who is 16 and started playing tennis a decade ago because her mother loved the sport, possesses a maturity beyond her age. Trailing 5-4 and facing a set-point in the opening set against host player Clarke in the semi-final, Sun saved the set-point and broke the American to draw level, before winning the next two games to steal the first set. “I was really nervous but I told myself, if she could hit the ball across the field, so could I,” Sun said. “That’s how I steadied myself; I believed I am stronger and better than her, and that I could hold on for one more shot than her. “I was under a lot of pressure today. I even cried a few times, but that’s something all tennis players have to go through, so I tried to focus on the next point and not think about what happened in the previous point.” A 6-0 score in the second set did not crush Sun as the Shenzhen native found footing – despite the landslide loss – and bounced back from the start of the deciding set. “I didn’t have a great start in the second set, and felt like I was crashing late in the set,” she said. “But all I was thinking about back then was, ‘How am I supposed to have a good start in the third set’? “That’s why at 5-0 down and it was Chukwumelije’s service game, I was still trying to perform the way I wanted myself to in the next set, so that I would be in a better form for the final set.” Sun added that she tried not to think about the score in the last set despite her solid lead, and “I just focused on my tactics”. Sun said she was portraying her resilience and mentality after compatriot Zheng, who twice fought back from the brink of losing this week, before levelling her career-best US Open result, exiting in the quarter-final after throwing away her lead against Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan. “Whenever I am down 3-0 or 4-1, I feel like I can still catch up,” said Sun, the first Chinese player to reach the US Open girls’ singles final since Wang Xiyu triumphed in the metropolis in 2018. “I’ve always aspired to be as resilient as Zheng Qinwen. I’m a fan of hers; she’s amazing. “She was trailing 5-0 [against Madison Keys and Iga Swiatek] in both matches, but I always believed she could turn things around because I know she has an incredibly strong mentality. I want to be a player like her and hope to one day play against her.” While Sun, the U-18 women’s singles winner of the Orange Bowl International Tennis Championships last year, had publicly admitted to admiring both Zheng, as well as Chinese tennis legend Li Na, a random Weibo thread with the hashtag “Sun Xinran surpasses Zheng Qinwen’s junior grand slam record” appeared to have sparked a debate online. Zheng has previously reached the girls’ singles semi-finals at the French Open and the US Open in 2019. “That was because Zheng turned professional when she was only 17, there was no need for her to pick on the younger opponents,” said one commentator. Other commentators said it was commendable for young players to achieve excellent results, but there was no need “to use such a hashtag to deliberately compare with or criticise” the other players. “Junior achievements are just the starting point of a tennis journey; the real tests lie in senior tour tournaments and grand slam main draws,” said another commentator. “Zheng Qinwen has weathered countless tough battles, and repeatedly broken through her limits to write new chapters for Chinese tennis with her tenacious performance. “Young players need to grow steadily and practically, instead of the others creating conflict or inciting arguments with such headlines.”

title: Meet Moshe Levi, who is dating Apple Martin, the daughter of Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin
description: They have reportedly been a couple since their days at Vanderbilt University and were recently spotted sharing a kiss in the Hamptons.
content: Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin’s daughter, Apple Martin, was recently spotted enjoying a weekend in the Hamptons with a “mystery man”. Apple was seen sharing an embrace and a kiss with her beau, whom Page Six has identified as her long-time boyfriend, Moshe Levi. Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin’s daughter Apple Martin appears to have a new romance. 💕 The 22-year-old was spotted passionately kissing a mystery man during a shopping trip in the Hamptons — seemingly the same guy she was seen cuddling in an Instagram Story back in May.… pic.twitter.com/b5vUkosXmD — HouseOfVanity (@HouseOfVanity88) September 9, 2026 While the 22-year-old grew up in the media spotlight and has recently been making headlines for her red carpet appearances, Apple rarely offers a glimpse into her romantic life. He is a philanthropist View this post on Instagram A post shared by MOSHA (@moshaperu) Levi’s family launched a non-profit organisation called Mosha in 2019. I’m sorry, but you are just another narcissist that wants everyone to like ya.”

title: Rescue operation launched after boat begins to sink at Hung Hom
description: Police and firefighters alerted by fisherman, but divers who sweep recreational vessel find no one aboard.
content: A rescue operation was launched in Hung Hom in Hong Kong on Saturday afternoon after a recreational vessel began taking on water and sinking. Emergency services were alerted at around 1.36pm when a man fishing nearby spotted the pleasure boat gradually submerging off the Hung Hom Promenade. Police and firefighters rushed to the scene, and fire service divers swept the vessel. Following a search of the submerged hull, rescue personnel confirmed that no one was on board. It is understood that the vessel had been anchored at the location for about a month. It was not immediately clear why the vessel began to sink.

title: Brics members find common ground on AI, trade and alternative payment expansion
description: Xi Jinping also tells the event in New Delhi that the bloc should play a ‘due role’ in bringing peace to the Middle East.
content: Brics members agreed in New Delhi on Saturday to continue the push to expand trade and payments in local currencies to counter US pressure. The member nations also found enough common ground to overcome some of their biggest diplomatic splits. In addition, Chinese President Xi Jinping used his address at the Brics summit to deliver a thinly veiled critique of US policies, calling on members to deepen cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence. Xi proposed an initiative on “AI-empowered new industrialisation” designed to deepen collaboration on industry and supply chains, according to state news agency Xinhua. The call came as the bloc was celebrating its 20th anniversary, having grown from a small economic framework into what Xi calls “the most influential cooperation platform for emerging markets and developing countries in today’s world”. At the same time, the gathering is being held against a backdrop of regional and global turmoil, from the war in Ukraine and the Middle East conflict to protectionism and tariff tensions. And its unity is being tested by divisions such as Iran’s repeated attacks on fellow members, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Xi’s attendance at the summit is the latest in a flurry of diplomatic activities preceding his trip to the United States, efforts that are expected to give him the upper hand in his meeting with his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
