Brics, a bloc of developing nations, has increasingly been viewed as a counterweight to Western-led institutions and a platform for building an alternative international order. Part of that push includes cross-border payments. The group’s Payment Task Force had studied “cross-border interoperability of payment and messaging channels” and would keep working on payments that were “fast, low cost, more accessible, efficient, transparent and safe”. But the leaders were also clear about just how far they were prepared to go as the declaration said there was “no one-size-fits-all approach” and that national priorities must be respected. As well as the host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, other high-profile attendees include Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian. For China, Brics is also seen as a platform to advance Beijing’s vision of a multipolar world and cement its standing as a leader of the Global South. In that vein, Xi said Beijing was willing to work with Brics countries to play a “due role” in bringing peace to the Middle East, calling on the group of emerging economies to oppose bloc confrontation and the “infringement upon the sovereignty of other countries and interference in their affairs”. His call for AI cooperation also highlights Beijing’s efforts to advance its own framework, the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico), widely seen as its answer to Washington’s Pax Silica Initiative. The two countries are vying for AI dominance and Pax Silica is Washington’s approach to secure AI and semiconductor supply chains among allied nations. Xi invited all Brics countries to join Waico to shape global AI governance and development. “China stands ready to work with all parties to jointly produce more research and development and application outcomes, and to deepen cooperation across industrial and supply chains,” he said. “Facts will prove that ‘decoupling and severing supply chains’ cannot hinder our development process, and ‘small yards with high fences’ will only confine oneself and fragment the world,” Xi said, in a veiled swipe at the US. “We must firmly … strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence, encourage open source and collaborative sharing and push practical cooperation to new heights.” Xi said the Global South was growing stronger and urged Brics countries to “firmly stand on the right side of history” and lead the international order towards a more just and equitable direction, away from unilateralism and power politics. Member nations unanimously adopted the 45-page “New Delhi Declaration 2026” on the opening day of the summit, with Modi saying that no member had objected to the text. In a thinly veiled challenge to Washington’s stance, Xi urged the Brics members to criticise protectionism and unilateralism, calling on emerging economies to defend international institutions such as the United Nations and the World Trade Organization against tariff threats, treaty withdrawals, and efforts to carve out exclusive global trade alliances. “We must oppose withdrawing from organisations, breaking treaties, and starting anew by setting up separate mechanisms,” Xi said. Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said Xi’s call for Brics to become “a vanguard for peace and stability” was especially relevant, given India’s efforts, as the group’s chair, to avoid being drawn into geopolitical conflicts. Xi urged Brics countries to pursue “common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security”, reject cold war thinking and bloc confrontation, and oppose violations of sovereignty and interference in internal affairs. He also called for constructive efforts to resolve regional hotspots, saying China was ready to work with Brics partners to “contribute to peace and stability in the Middle East and Gulf region”. Liu said the political and security dimension, part of the three pillars of Brics cooperation, had become increasingly important as global tensions intensified. “In today’s turbulent global environment, the political and security pillar is especially critical. As Xi emphasised, Brics should play a constructive role in mediating and easing regional tensions to advance global and regional peace.” Modi, who chaired the opening session, said the voice of developing economies could not remain “a courtesy” and that emerging countries had to write the rules of global governance. Brics, he said, was “not against anyone” but instead was for everyone. “The current structure of global governance resembles a pyramid,” he added. “Power and decision-making sit at the top. Those who live with the consequences sit at the bottom, they are affected by every decision, excluded from every one of them.” China will assume the organisation’s rotating chair next year. In a sit-down after the summit, Xi told Modi that China and India, as the world’s most populous nations and key members of the Global South, bore “significant responsibilities” in an international landscape “fraught with turbulence and change”. The grouping first took shape in 2006 when Brazil, Russia, India and China began informal talks before it was officially established in 2009. South Africa joined in 2010, turning the bloc from Bric to Brics. The grouping has undergone two expansions since, adding Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025. Brics now covers nearly half the global population and about a third of the world’s GDP. Over the years, the bloc has evolved into a political platform for intergovernmental cooperation in areas ranging from finance and trade to culture and justice. It has also become increasingly vocal about overhauling global systems, including proposing alternatives to US dollar-based payment systems, a suggestion that prompted warnings from Trump. But its expansion has also brought fresh challenges to the bloc, with analysts suggesting that there are now more competing voices which have slowed its progress and made it harder to reach a consensus on issues. Additional reporting by Orange Wang, Nayan Seth, Alyssa Chen, Shi Jiangtao and Victoria Bela

title: China urges US to ‘stop all spying’ or face retaliation, slams ‘gangster logic’
description: Commerce ministry retort follows CIA official’s defence of spying on China’s AI and chip sectors just weeks ahead of US visit by Xi.
content: Beijing has urged the United States to “immediately stop all espionage activities” targeting Chinese companies, warning that it had “firm resolve and abundant means” to retaliate after a senior CIA official defended spying on China’s artificial intelligence (AI) and chip sectors. The call from China’s Ministry of Commerce comes just two weeks ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, where AI and advanced technologies – the new battleground in the US-China rivalry – are expected to be high on the agenda. The ministry’s remarks late on Friday were in direct response to statements made earlier in the week by Michael Ellis, the deputy director of the US Central Intelligence Agency. In a rare public speech on Tuesday, Ellis revealed that the CIA was expanding its intelligence work on China, suggesting that Chinese companies were “legitimate targets” for espionage in areas such as AI, semiconductors and biotechnology. Friday’s brief Chinese ministry statement said the US had “exposed its gangster logic of hegemony in broad daylight”, which China firmly opposed. Economic competition was a regular commercial activity, and those in advantage relied on technology, talent and innovation, said the statement, which was attributed to a ministry representative. “The US has blurred the lines between competition and security and even framed economic competition as a so-called ‘threat’,” the representative said. “This is, in essence, a zero-sum, Cold War mentality at work.” The statement noted that the US had issued a directive in 2014 saying intelligence activities should not be used to collect foreign private commercial information or trade secrets for the purpose of giving US companies a competitive advantage. However, Washington had ignored its own rules, it said. Moreover, the US routinely accused other trading partners of collecting intelligence while defending its own actions as reasonable, the representative said, calling it a “blatant double standard”. “China has firm resolve and abundant means at its disposal,” the ministry warned, adding that Beijing would “take all necessary measures to punish legal violations and resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises”. As the US-China technological rivalry intensifies, economic espionage has turned commercial sectors into national security battlegrounds. At a congressional hearing in June, David Shedd, former acting director of the Defence Intelligence Agency, alleged that China had “orchestrated a highly strategic, highly accelerated and multifaceted effort to steal commercial and technological secrets” from the United States and other Western countries. The testimony came amid growing scrutiny over Beijing’s ability to collect vast amounts of data from Americans and US firms. The Chinese embassy in Washington said at the time that the accusations of industrial espionage were baseless, steeped in Cold War mentality and amounted to “malicious slander”. A month before Shedd’s hearing, experts warned the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission about shortcomings in countering Beijing’s data-collection drive.

title: Profile | Who is Nana, the K-pop idol and star of Netflix K-dramas The Scandal and Mask Girl?
description: Nana’s rise in the industry has been a journey of talent, resilience and reinvention, going from singer and model to bona fide actress.
content: Following her head-turning role in Climax earlier this year, K-pop idol turned actress Nana is back on screens this month in the hotly anticipated Netflix period drama The Scandal. A new adaptation of the famed French novel Les Liaisons Dangereuses, the series sees Nana share the screen alongside Son Ye-jin and Ji Chang-wook. A native of Cheongju in central South Korea, Nana was born in 1991 and first came to national prominence in 2009, when she stepped onto the stage as a model and debuted in the girl group After School. She later featured in the subgroups Orange Caramel and A.S. Red. Although After School effectively disbanded more than a decade ago, Nana returned to the music scene last year to launch her debut digital single, “Seventh Heaven 16”. These days, Nana is far better known as a screen actress. She has steadily built up a portfolio of striking performances and grown from strength to strength with each new challenge. Before beginning her acting career in earnest, she appeared in a few projects in brief cameo roles – generally as herself – such as in the 2011 K-pop-themed horror film White: The Melody of the Curse. Why we love her Once Nana made the leap from music to acting, she picked up credits and experience in China, where she was cast in two 2015 projects: the big-screen romantic comedy sequel Go Lala Go II and the fantasy romance television series Love Weaves Through a Millennium, a remake of the 2012 K-drama Queen In-hyun’s Man. Nana was an in-demand model early in her career, often appearing in fashion shows, magazines and ad campaigns. She is also one of the rare idols to hold an official make-up artist licence and is a registered member of the Makeup Artists Association in Korea. Beyond her looks and screen roles, Nana has popped up in the news for a variety of reasons and has cultivated a reputation as a formidable figure. Occasionally she has stoked controversy, most notably for openly showing her tattoos during press events for the 2022 film Confession – something almost unheard of for K-pop celebrities. She later had most of the tattoos removed, which she had got as a means of coping during what she described as a difficult emotional period. In 2025, Nana once again made the news dramatically when she and her mother subdued an intruder who broke into their home and attempted to rob them. The attacker then tried to sue Nana for bodily injury, but Nana’s actions were ruled legitimate self-defence. The star-making roles Nana’s first major role after her Chinese projects was the Korean remake of the hit American television series The Good Wife. Playing an investigator at a major legal firm working alongside a lawyer played by series lead Jeon Do-yeon, Nana received praise for her performance and scooped the rookie actress award at the 2016 Asia Artist Awards. Shortly after The Good Wife, she shared the screen with Jang Ki-yong in Kill It (2019), a noir action drama in which she played a dogged detective with a chequered past who goes head-to-head with a compassionate assassin. The iconic parts Nana joined the ranks of streaming leading performers when she was cast in the 2022 Netflix series Glitch, playing a vocal member of a group that believes in aliens. She helps Jeon Yeo-been’s protagonist track down her missing boyfriend, whom they suspect was abducted by extraterrestrials. A year later, she returned in the acclaimed drama-thriller Mask Girl, featuring as an insecure office worker who begins a clandestine life as a masked celebrity influencer, only for the walls of her fabricated life to begin collapsing around her. The unheralded performances Following a five-year absence from the big screen, Nana returned to theatres in 2022 with the well-received Confession, a mystery-thriller based on the 2016 Spanish film The Invisible Guest. Unfortunately, likely because it was released during the pandemic, the film opened to little commercial fanfare. Nana plays Kim Se-hee, the mistress of a successful tech entrepreneur. When she is one day found dead in a locked room, the entrepreneur – played by So Ji-sub – becomes a suspect in her murder and engages the services of a top lawyer. Tomorrow’s turns Following Glitch, Mask Girl and The Scandal, Nana is yet again taking on a leading role in the Netflix original series Materesa. Nana plays the titular character, a cold-blooded criminal psychologist who investigates murder cases with the help of characters played by Kim Dan (The Winning Try) and Jung Gun-joo (Mercy for None). Materesa is directed by Jang Young-woo (Queen of Tears) and co-written by Kwon So-ra and Seo Jae-won, who penned this summer’s period horror series The East Palace.

title: A symbol of harmony: Chinese scientists discover earliest dragon-phoenix pairing in ancient tomb
description: The two mythological creatures represent the peaceful balance created when opposing forces come into union.
content: It sometimes guards kingdoms and empires; other times, it hoards treasures within a hidden cave. The dragon frequently symbolises power, strength, and good fortune. In contrast, its counterpart, the phoenix, meets its end in a pile of ashes only to be reborn at the pinnacle of its beauty, symbolising grace, beauty, and rebirth. Individually, the dragon and phoenix are iconic figures in Chinese mythology. Together, these contrasting creatures embody a yin-and-yang that serves as an important emblem of harmony in Chinese history. At its height, the dragon-and-phoenix image functioned as the state emblem of the Republic of China from 1913 to 1928, appearing on coins minted during that period. It was ultimately replaced when the Kuomintang came to power under Chiang Kai-shek. However, the dual imagery of the dragon and phoenix reaches much further back in Chinese history, nearly to the dawn of China itself. In mid-August, a group of scientists unveiled the discovery of the oldest known pairing of the dragon and phoenix, dating back about 4,300 years. According to the Global Times, the symbols were positioned as clay statues about the size of a human body, placed beside the deceased in a grave located in Inner Mongolia, northern China. The dragon was positioned to the right of the body, with its head aligning closely with the human skull. The phoenix, on the left, was depicted as soaring upwards. The scientists believe the body likely belonged to a person of means, as dental analysis indicated a diet that included more meat than was typical for the population of that era. “[The discovery] pushes back the materialised representation of the dragon and phoenix to the Longshan era,” stated Sun Jinsong, the head of the Inner Mongolia Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, in an interview with the Global Times. These statues also provide significant evidence of the development of a remarkably complex society in northern China towards the end of the Neolithic period. The gravesite indicates that dragon and phoenix imagery emerged before the establishment of the unified state we envision today. While this is the oldest known example of the dragon and phoenix being represented together, it is not the first image of either mythological creature to appear in China. The earliest dragon imagery was discovered in a 5,000-year-old tomb, also in Inner Mongolia, crafted from jade. Known as fenghuang, the phoenix predates this, first emerging in central China’s Henan province, dating between 6000 BC and 7000 BC. The Chinese phoenix was originally divided into the feng, the male figure, and the huang, the female. Over time, this gender distinction faded, and the fenghuang is now typically depicted as a unisex mythological creature. The images of dragons and phoenixes gained popularity as burial objects during the Shang dynasty (1600 BC–1046 BC) and continued to become popular in art during the Warring States period (475 BC–221 BC), notably in the acclaimed piece, the Silk Painting of Human Figure with Dragon and Phoenix. Together, these two mythological creatures illustrate the natural harmony that arises from the blending of polar opposites. Their integration into funerary practices is fitting, as the imagery seeks to honour how seemingly conflicting forces can create the balance essential for a fulfilling life. The Longshan era (3000 BC–1900 BC) is renowned for its pottery, often referred to as the “black pottery culture” due to its highly polished, deep black ceramics. It was also characterised by a notably diverse populace, with historians recognising that “Longshan” serves as a broad term encompassing communities that varied significantly from region to region.

title: Meet Candace Cameron Bure’s daughter Natasha Bure Perry, who is expecting her first child
description: The eldest child of the Full House star is expecting her first baby with husband Bradley Steven Perry – but who is she and why is she setting boundaries online?
content: Candace Cameron Bure’s daughter, the singer and actor Natasha Bure Perry, is expecting her first child with Good Luck Charlie star Bradley Steven Perry. She is determined, though, to keep her journey to motherhood under wraps, for now at least. The 28-year-old was recently accused of hiding the birth of her child for social media engagement. She denied the rumour in a recent TikTok video, where she showed her baby bump, proving she was still pregnant. Calling the internet a “creepy, parasocial space where people feel entitled to information about your life”, Bure Perry clarified that her decision to experience major life events privately before sharing them online is not a monetisation strategy. So, who is Natasha Bure Perry? She is Candace Cameron Bure’s eldest child Natasha Valerievna Bure was born on August 15, 1998, to Full House star Candace Cameron Bure and her husband, former NHL player Valeri Bure. She is the eldest of three, with younger brothers Lev, 26, and Maksim, 24. Bure Perry was born in Los Angeles, but spent her early childhood in Canada while her father played for the Calgary Flames. Bure Perry also grew up in South Florida, per the author bio for her book Let’s Be Real: Living Life As an Open and Honest You (2017). What does Natasha Bure Perry do? Bure Perry grew interested in her mother’s profession when she was only six or seven years old, per A Worthy Conversation Podcast. She caught the acting bug after taking up musical theatre as a child, according to her IMDb, and started acting in commercials, per Parade. “I felt like, for me, school was always the enemy,” she told the outlet, citing the pressure to maintain good grades for a worker’s permit to act. In 2016, Bure Perry appeared on The Voice Season 11 and was eliminated early, but she called it a “good growing experience” on the Conversations with Olivia Jade podcast. She has since acted in Faith, Hope & Love (2019) and starred opposite her mother in Aurora Teagarden Mysteries: Haunted by Murder (2022) and a 2020 episode of Fuller House. “I would say that I work for everything that I get, and I’m hustling on my own, and I have a completely separate life from my parents,” Bure Perry told People. When did she marry Bradley Steven Perry? The Perrys keep their romance largely private. They reportedly got engaged in April 2025 and married that September at Malibu’s Calamigos Ranch, per Just Jared. “There is nothing better than marrying your best friend,” the couple told People. In May this year, they announced they were going to be parents.

title: Hong Kong Police College becomes first government unit to roll out degree course
description: Police chief Joe Chow says force hopes Bachelor of Policing (Honours) (Security and Criminal Investigation) course can start by year-end.
content: The Hong Kong Police College has become the first government department to offer a bachelor’s degree programme, with the force set to roll out the course for rank-and-file officers by the end of this year. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming announced the development on Saturday, after the Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications approved the college’s Bachelor of Policing (Honours) (Security and Criminal Investigation) programme last month. “We hope that the programme can start by the end of this year. Students will take around three to four years to complete it. With this bachelor’s degree, they can sign up for master’s courses if they are interested,” he said after attending a passing-out parade at the college in Wong Chuk Hang. He said the programme, which is free, would target rank-and-file officers. The curriculum will cover foundation and criminal investigation training, internships including frontline patrols, and language courses. Students will also be expected to complete a thematic report before graduating. “The Police College has become an institution that can confer a bachelor’s degree, and it is also the first government department that is qualified to do so,” Chow said. According to the Education Bureau’s website, the programme is a part-time in-house training course valid from last month until August 2031. Established in 2006, the college was originally founded as the Police Training School in 1948. It provides various types of training, including a foundation programme for recruits and specialised and generic competency courses for serving officers. Chow said police had so far recruited 30 probationary inspectors and 362 police constables in the 2026-27 financial year. The police force began a recruitment drive at local universities this month. The force has struggled to meet its recruitment targets since 2020. It has scrapped the minimum height and weight requirements, while candidates can wear glasses or contact lenses when taking eye tests. Applicants who failed public examinations can also take a new Chinese- and English-language written test to qualify. As of March 2025, the force’s vacancy rate was 17.4 per cent. It aimed to recruit 130 probationary inspectors and 1,140 police constables in the 2025-26 financial year. Lawmaker and former police officer Joe Chan Cho-kwong hailed the programme. “It not only helps equip our police officers with the knowledge to cope with new challenges in the new era, it also provides a promotion pathway for frontline officers,” he said. “The force has been eager to upgrade the general quality of its members. Society has changed. Policing must also change to address new technological, social and structural realities. “We need a new generation of effective officers and visionary leaders to meet the challenges that are faced in a 21st century community.” Chan, who sits on the Legislative Council’s security panel, encouraged serving officers to take the course whenever practicable and said he believed it would be popular. “If our officers only like to stay on patrol and do field work, rather than upgrade themselves or seek promotion to take up senior or managerial roles, I don’t think they are the people the force wants,” Chan added. The minimum academic requirement for a police constable is level 2 in five subjects in the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education Examination (HKDSE). Recruits with a degree usually opt to apply to become inspectors. The force used to train recruits and officers at the former Police Training School. Courses focused heavily on practical field skills, discipline and the basic legal knowledge required for beat and station duties. After the school was upgraded to a college in 2006, its courses were revised to cover leadership training and also provide a pathway for frontline officers to pursue further studies. The force partnered with the then Open University of Hong Kong, now Hong Kong Metropolitan University, to deliver modules in the foundation training course for police constable recruits.

title: Elderly couple found dead in Ma On Shan flat after foul odour reported
description: Police say firefighters found bodies of man, 72, and his wife, 74, in flat’s living room, with source adding no signs of foul play found.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating the deaths of a couple in their seventies after their bodies were discovered inside their home in Ma On Shan. Police said officers were alerted at around 8pm on Friday to a strange odour emanating from a flat in Heng Yat House at Heng On Estate. Firefighters forced entry to the flat, discovering a 72-year-old man and his 74-year-old wife lying in the living room, police said, adding the couple were pronounced dead at the scene. No suicide note was found, and the cause of death was awaiting autopsy results, the force said. A source said on Saturday that the couple had a good relationship, and had one daughter and two sons, who lived separately after getting married. The couple suffered from high blood pressure, diabetes and hyperlipidemia, while the wife had also been living with dementia for five years, the source added. Both required regular medical appointments at Prince of Wales Hospital in Sha Tin. According to the source, a man had noticed a foul smell coming from the couple’s flat since Monday and had made several complaints to the estate management. After staff found nothing suspicious, the man escalated his concerns to police. Officers found the flat’s door and windows were locked, with no signs of ransacking or a struggle, while an examination of the bodies revealed no suspicious injuries, the source said. Neighbours told officers that the couple had a good relationship and were not involved in any feuds or disputes over debts, the insider added. Surveillance footage showed the pair returning to the building at 11.13am on August 31, and they were not seen again afterwards, the source said. A forensic examiner found no signs of foul play and estimated the time of death to be about three to four days earlier. Following a preliminary investigation, police classified the case as dead body found, with the force’s Sha Tin district following up, the source said.

title: Bodies from Philippine ferry arrive at port after fire killed at least 76
description: There were 43 survivors among the 132 people on board.
content: Rescuers retrieved more remains from a passenger ferry in the Philippines that was gutted by fire, bringing the death toll on Saturday to 76 with 13 missing. Forty-three people survived the fire on Wednesday night among the 132 on board. The ferry sailed from the capital, Manila, and was off the village of Turda some 39km (24 miles) from its destination, the Port of Coron, when the fire was reported on Wednesday evening. The cause of the blaze has not been determined but a survivor said it may have started from the cargo hold. The survivor recounted hearing a blast, with smoke and fire quickly spreading, fanned by the winds, officials said. Tents were put up in the Port of Borac in Coron, Palawan province, where body bags will be brought down from a ship that transported them from the burned ferry. The coastguard said the bodies will be turned over to the local government, with police officers assisting in identifying the charred remains. Commodore Noemie Cayabyab, the coastguard spokesperson, said authorities are looking for the ship’s captain, who reportedly survived but is not listed among the survivors. The multi-agency maritime safety and criminal investigations will look into all angles, and the possible liability of the captain and crew, she added. Cayabyab said survivors recounted the incident had happened quickly, with no time to get life jackets. A tarpaulin that shielded the open areas of the ship from the rain “may be a possible contributing factor but we can’t determine now if they were trapped inside”, she added. Investigators will also check if fire emergency procedures were followed, including if the captain sounded an alarm or gave a warning and instructions, and if the crew assisted the passengers. Images provided earlier by the coastguard showed the charred interior of the ship and what appeared to be human remains, ashes and burnt metal, including a car. Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva, a survivor who recounted the chaos inside the ferry after the fire quickly spread, told a local news outlet that he could not get a life jacket as people were in a panic and stepping on him. Lira Daco, whose 20-year-old daughter is missing, said she was pained by the thought that her daughter could have burned alive, and by the difficulty of identifying her among the charred remains found in the ship. According to the manifest, 134 people were on board, with 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. The 53m (174-foot) vessel had a capacity to carry 306 passengers and 27 crew. Two passengers listed in the manifest reported to authorities that they failed to board, the coastguard said. Two of the survivors were tourists from Chile, according to Rachel Conserman, a staffer of the ship’s owner Atienza Interisland Ferries. The coastguard said the foreigners have left Coron and authorities have coordinated with their embassy. The shipping company said in a statement it was assisting those who were on board and their families while coordinating with the coastguard and maritime officials to locate the missing passengers and determine the cause of the fire. Coron is a popular tourist destination known for clear blue waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations. Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces. In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker in the central Philippines, killing more than 4,300 people in the world’s deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.

title: Hong Kong’s ethnic minority groups can play key role in belt and road, summit hears
description: Speakers at Zubin Foundation summit highlight multicultural advantages of local youth in helping mainland Chinese firms expand overseas.
content: Hong Kong’s ethnic minority communities can leverage their multicultural backgrounds and language skills to play an “important role” in the city’s efforts to build ties with belt and road countries, the labour minister has said. Other speakers at the Zubin Foundation’s Ethnically Diverse Youth Leadership Summit on Saturday also highlighted the advantages these historically marginalised communities possessed in helping mainland Chinese companies go global. In his opening remarks, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han told an audience of about 300 young people from ethnic minority backgrounds that they had a role to play as the city pursued deeper ties with countries under the Belt and Road Initiative. “When looking ahead, we are building and forging much closer collaboration with countries from the belt and road,” Sun said. “Here in Hong Kong … we have a locally grown talent [pool]. They speak the language, they know the culture … while they know so much about Hong Kong. “So I think you do have a very important role to play in the years to come.” Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative aims to improve trade and economic integration across multiple continents, and includes a number of countries where Hong Kong’s ethnic minority groups trace their roots, including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. Excluding foreign domestic helpers, Hong Kong is home to more than 300,000 members of ethnic minorities, making up about 4.1 per cent of the total population, according to the 2021 census. Many of those with South Asian and Southeast Asian backgrounds have ties to the city that span generations. Despite progress in recent years, many members of ethnic minority groups continue to face challenges climbing the socioeconomic ladder, including low incomes, poor career opportunities and a lack of Chinese-language proficiency. Saturday’s summit focused on identifying the opportunities available to them. Others taking part included government officials, business leaders, entrepreneurs and community representatives. “Too often, discussions about our communities focus on barriers and challenges,” Shalini Mahtani, founder of the Zubin Foundation, said in her own opening remarks. “We created this summit because we wanted to focus on something equally important – opportunity, leadership, aspirations and the future.” Mahtani said many of the young people in the audience were “far more talented” than members of her own generation. “You’re multilingual, you are truly globally connected across belt and road countries and beyond … and you are ambitious,” she said. Nicholas Ho Lik-chi, Hong Kong’s commissioner for belt and road, said the trend of Hong Kong and mainland companies looking to expand overseas gave the city’s ethnic minority communities a “huge advantage”. “The major issue, apart from finance and trade, that Hong Kong and Chinese mainland companies face … to go global is talent,” he said. “They can’t find the right talent to help them access these markets. “And [ethnic minority] youth have a huge advantage, because your mindset is more culturally diverse – you have both your community advantage [and] the Hong Kong advantage. You are a product of multiple cultures.” Ho also said that young members of ethnic minority groups had a greater role to play as the city continued to attract top talent and students from belt and road countries to its universities. He noted that many of those coming to study in Hong Kong faced challenges, including building local connections and finding jobs after graduating. “What we hope for is that the belt and road youth and our community here are ready to engage and work closely together,” he said. Young members of ethnic minority groups should view their future as not only in Hong Kong but in the entire belt and road, Ho said, citing the rapid growth in trade and people-to-people connectivity with the city.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong’s contemporary artists deserve a bigger stage in its museums
description: Now that other Asian societies are taking their artists more seriously, it is time for M+ and HKMoA to give our living artists major solo exhibitions.
content: There has been much hyperventilating over two recent controversies at M+, Hong Kong’s museum of visual culture. The first was a series of mahjong social nights charging museum members and patrons up to HK$2,500 (US$319) for a package including an exhibition tour, a meal and social tile-shuffling in the members’ lounge. Mahjong may have had a Chinamaxxing makeover in the West, but in Hong Kong, the game is still considered a tad unwholesome for a museum even when no money changed hands. Frankly, if M+ wants to hold pai gow tournaments or caai mui drinking games in its fabulous but underused members’ lounge to build community and generate revenue, let it. As for the “private club” claim, the HK$300-600 membership fee it charges for year-round admission and lounge access doesn’t exactly grant elite status. The second incident was the last-minute cancellation of a performance by singer-songwriter Wong Hin-yan – who has a history of supporting local protests – in an evening music programme. This is more worrying as it bore the hallmarks of an opaque blacklisting of Hong Kong creative talent since the introduction of the national security law. M+ has not provided any explanation; Wong has taken to social media to say it was not his decision to cancel. As Wong posted, “it is what it is”, and it may not be something the M+ team would necessarily have control over in the current political environment. Meanwhile, there is a little-discussed scandal that plagues both M+ and the government-run Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA), and one the institutions can fix. That is their chronic, baffling resistance to mount major, academically rigorous solo exhibitions for Hong Kong’s living contemporary artists – something that became painfully clear to Hong Kong visitors at the recent Seoul Art Week. Rarely do you see Hong Kong shine the spotlight on individual local artists to help elevate them to the global stage. The two museums have had group shows of Hong Kong art, and M+ will have a major show on local cultural influences since the 1970s next March, but these do not go deep enough to allow for a proper appreciation of each artist’s practice. And while M+ in particular has presented solo shows of Hong Kong artists at the Venice Biennale, these are, alas, relatively small, stand-alone projects. Consider where some of Hong Kong’s brightest are securing their landmark museum shows in recent years. Kong Hong-chuen (also known as Kongkee) debuted his dazzling “Warring States Cyberpunk” at San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum in 2022, managing only a smaller version at Tai Kwun two years later, co-curated by Kwok Ying, then senior curator for Tai Kwun Contemporary. Last year, Jaffa Lam landed a major museum show at the Sea World Culture and Arts Centre in Shekou, Shenzhen, while Samson Young staged his highly praised “Pavilion” at the New Taipei City Art Museum. This year, Ellen Pau’s survey, titled “She Moves”, opened at the SculptureCenter in New York, and Leelee Chan had her first institutional exhibition at the He Art Museum in Shunde, Guangdong province. Contrast this with the ecosystem in South Korea. There, you will find Do Ho Suh’s massive retrospective at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art – half of which, plus some new works, will travel to M+ next year; Yang Ah Ham’s expansive three-floor show at the Art Sonje Centre and Youngeun Kim’s staggering spatial audio triumph at the National Asia Culture Centre – which, incidentally, includes Hong Kong-born, Switzerland-based composer Alice Yeung Hoi-ching as a collaborator. Also in South Korea, Singapore’s Ho Tzu Nyen is making waves for his curation of the main exhibition at this year’s Gwangju Biennale. Already celebrated for his artistic practice, he is demonstrating remarkable curatorial rigour and sensitivity that he said was fuelled by the momentum of a massive, exhausting mid-career survey hosted by the Singapore Art Museum in 2023-24. Coincidentally, Ho and Wong created a piece together last year to present a multisensorial experience of time at M+, highlighting the deeply unsettling ambiguity of red lines for Hong Kong artists. As Hong Kong artists are demonstrating in other cities, they are capable of producing large-scale, engaging and internationally relevant exhibitions. Now that the rest of Asia is taking their artists more seriously, it is time for the two Hong Kong museums – with their unparalleled expertise and collections – to stop outsourcing the validation of Hong Kong artists to overseas peers and smaller local institutions such as Tai Kwun and the Centre for Heritage, Arts and Textile. Technically, Hong Kong contemporary art is more HKMoA’s turf, but Kwok – formerly of Tai Kwun – has recently joined M+ as head of visual art. Given the many years that she has been immersed in the Hong Kong art scene, it really would be a travesty if M+ doesn’t hold a Hong Kong solo show under her watch.

title: Review | Pianist Eric Lu brilliantly reflects Chopin’s genius in HK Phil concert
description: Lu’s terrific rendition of Piano Concerto No 1 in E minor was bookended by Yao Chen’s panda-themed waltz and Stravinsky’s Firebird Suite.
content: Given their proportions and lack of upright agility on their hind paws, the very notion of giant pandas dancing a waltz sounds, dare I say, absurd. So going by its title alone, any chance of a cheeky lilt in 3/4 time or a nostalgic nod to the Strauss clan in Yao Chen’s panda-themed Waltz of the Rolling Giants, the opening piece in the Hong Kong Philharmonic’s “Chengdu Pre-Tour Concert: Eric Lu Plays Chopin”, seemed slim. Thankfully, though, Chen’s waltz – an HK Phil world premiere written especially for the orchestra’s coming China tour, which begins, coincidentally, in Chengdu, the home of pandas – neither spiralled into a clumsy “polonaise for polar bears”, as musicologist Donald Tovey famously dubbed the finale of Sibelius’ Violin Concerto, nor ended up as an awkward romp among the bamboo shoots. As it turned out, it was the spiralling and moments of playful whimsy that ultimately saved Chen’s waltz from such a fate, offsetting any tendency to layer the orchestral texture too densely along the way. With resident conductor Lio Kuokman at the HK Phil’s helm, Chen’s fragments, which stem partly from a Sichuan mountain song and a Cantonese melody, were lent a buoyant character, soon morphing into a quasi “panda motif” – an idea Chen took from Wagner, drawing inspiration both from the “giants” of his operas and from the composer’s use of distinct leitmotifs. For all its spinning and sliding, not to mention the addition of two extended rainsticks for extra effects, Chen’s “Waltz 2.0” packed a great deal of musical material into a piece lasting less than 10 minutes. Eric Lu delivers Whether Chopin really had the chops – pardon the pun – to orchestrate his Piano Concerto No 1 in E minor remains a bone of contention. Though most post-premiere reviews were overwhelmingly favourable, many still consider the concerto’s orchestration dry and dreary – this author included – while musicians such as the Russian pianist Mikhail Pletnev even see a need to revise Chopin’s orchestral parts. Indisputably, however, the piano part does reflect Chopin’s true genius, and that was clearly front and centre in Massachusetts-born pianist Eric Lu’s thought-provoking rendition at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre Concert Hall on Wednesday evening. Lu won the First Prize and Gold Medal at the 2025 International Chopin Competition, wowing the judges and clinching the deal with a brilliant performance of the Polish master’s Piano Concerto No 2 in F minor. Here, too, the young, unassuming Berlin- and Boston-based soloist delivered technical brilliance and tonal sheen of the highest quality, presenting his more hushed utterances, free of pretension, with whiffs of ethereality as they unfolded. Lu’s gentlest keyboard poetry, notably in the Romanze-Larghetto slow movement, was nothing short of angelic as it floated effortlessly over a still, sensitive orchestral landscape. As staid as some passages of the concerto’s opening tutti may sound, dreamlike dialogues between Lu and the wind soloists Benjamin Moermond (bassoon), Andrew Simon (clarinet) and Michael Wilson (oboe) unfolded with inspired phrasing. Slick and compelling Stravinsky The transition to the colourful and dazzling orchestration of Stravinsky’s vibrant Firebird Suite (1919) after the interval was both a welcome and poignant paradigm shift. Lio, who had memorised the rhythmically challenging score, showed considerable skill and agility with the baton. With second associate concertmaster Wang Liang by his side in the “hot seat” – that is, the concertmaster’s chair, which is still officially held by the seldom-seen violinist Jing Wang – things were rhythmically slick and compelling. Of Stravinsky’s three versions of the suite, all written after the resounding success of his complete ballet score, the second has long been a staple for orchestras worldwide. The versions were produced primarily as a means for the composer to earn money after the original publisher was effectively put out of business by the 1917 Bolshevik revolution in Russia. With the suite’s mortal and supernatural elements, distinguishable through a system of leitmotifs, the HK Phil players flaunted their extended techniques to the max with a bevy of finely honed effects. These included ponticello (raspy-sounding effects played on or near the string bridges), col legno (a percussive sound in which the wooden part of the bow is used to tap the strings), glissandi (spooky and seductive slides) and some brilliant examples of flutter-tonguing in the winds. Striking, too, were the atmospheric rumbles in the introduction, as well as the rich, sensual bassoon playing from Moermond in the berceuse section (music with a swaying motion like a lullaby), accompanied by Woojin Lee’s alert and ever-sensitive harp plucks and strums. A startling whip-crack signalled the evil King Kashchei’s “Infernal Dance”, leading ultimately to his death by exhaustion. Snarling brass terrified with much acerbic bite, while the suite’s glittering “Finale” provided a grand culmination of events, befittingly depicting all the glitz and glamour associated with the prince’s timely marriage to his dancing princess. “Chengdu Pre-Tour Concert: Eric Lu Plays Chopin”, Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, Hong Kong Cultural Centre Concert Hall, 10 Salisbury Rd, Tsim Sha Tsui. Reviewed: September 9

title: How AI tools are reshaping stock trading, investment research in China
description: For China’s 250 million individual investors, AI is helping them make money from one of the world’s most volatile stock markets.
content: When Ryan Lei has an investment idea, he no longer has to spend days writing code and trawling through historical data to corroborate it. The 27-year-old quantitative trader in Hong Kong now delegates much of the grunt work to artificial intelligence. For a recent bet tied to a major technology initial public offering, Lei deployed Futu’s AI agents to collect data on similar listings over the past decade and parse their post-debut performances. The AI-assisted research informed a short position that eventually earned him several thousand US dollars. AI can rapidly complete workloads that used to take days or even weeks, according to Lei, who has nine years of investing experience and co-manages a seven-person proprietary quantitative trading team. Lei’s case highlights the extent to which AI could change the behaviour of traders and even reshape the landscape of the financial and asset-management industries. In the US, brokerages such as Robinhood and Webull are integrating AI into their tools to help clients, mostly individual investors, buy and sell stocks. In Hong Kong, Futu Securities – one of the city’s largest online brokers – launched an agentic feature called “expert mode” in July, allowing clients to conduct investment research and place orders for stocks, options and exchange-traded funds using natural-language instructions. Daily queries to Futu’s AI tools jumped about 50 per cent month on month in August after the introduction of the new feature, according to the company More than half of user queries now focus on individual-stock analysis, including company fundamentals, earnings and technical trends, while derivatives and quantitative strategies have emerged as the second largest use cases, the company said. The path is more cautious in mainland China, where retail investors mostly use AI tools for information gathering, data analysis and stock-price monitoring, rather than directly making or executing investment decisions. That is because mainland regulations prohibit stock recommendations by individuals and entities not licensed by the securities regulator. When the South China Morning Post asked for stock recommendations from Doubao, the popular AI chatbot run by ByteDance, it answered that investors should be held accountable for their own decisions, and only offered general advice such as “using idle money” and assessing stocks by “corporate fundamentals”. Still, AI is rapidly being adopted by the investment and financial community. More than 80 per cent of mainland Chinese brokerages have deployed AI in their trading apps, helping investors glean and parse data, according to domestic media. Leading brokerages are also pressing ahead with integrating AI into research and development, replacing the manual work of information collection, data processing and translations of research reports. For China’s 250 million individual investors, AI can help them make money from one of the world’s most volatile stock markets. Jacky Jia, a 48-year-old investor in Shanghai, has realised a return of about 5 per cent from stock picking so far this year. His frequently-used AI tools are Doubao and Baidu’s Ernie chatbot, which he uses to analyse financial results and business prospects of target companies, as well as conduct technical analysis on where stocks would meet resistance. “AI can be wrong sometimes and you need to make decisions on your own,” Jia said. “But it’s great at gathering information. I will keep using it for stock trading in the future.” Jia’s portfolio, which is concentrated in tech stocks, managed to beat the benchmark CSI 300 Index that has declined more than 2 per cent this year. For Lei, the quantitative trader, AI has become embedded in almost every stage of his team’s workflow, from collecting and analysing data to generating strategies and writing code. He estimated that AI now helped produce about 99 per cent of the code used by his team. Still, there is one task that remains in human hands. While Lei’s team uses AI for research and strategy development, it leaves the final execution of trades to a conventional rule-based quantitative trading system. “Quantitative investing needs to be rigorous, while AI still has a certain degree of randomness,” Lei said.

title: Chinese men warned over bridal scams as ‘marriage squeeze’ drives wife search in Africa
description: Authorities clamp down on cross-border matchmaking schemes as lonely Chinese men look overseas after failing to find a bride at home.
content: A young Malagasy woman was stopped at Madagascar’s Ivato International Airport last month as she prepared to travel to China for a proposed marriage, according to local media reports citing police. She had reportedly been promised 10 million ariary (US$2,300) once she arrived and married a Chinese man. The case led police to investigate a suspected network involved in arranging similar marriages. Four people were detained, and police reportedly recovered false stamps, documents and 10 Malagasy passports. Investigators said several women might have already travelled to China through the network. These arrangements are often marketed as a solution for Chinese men struggling to find a partner at home. Men are told they can travel abroad, pay a matchmaking fee and bride price, then return home with a wife. But recent cases reported in Malawi and Madagascar show that Chinese men can face fraud, extortion and criminal investigation, while women recruited as brides can face deception, coercion and human trafficking. Such cases have prompted warnings from Chinese embassies and raised questions about whether they are isolated incidents or part of a broader, emerging pattern. Cai Chen, a doctoral researcher in anthropology at the Universite libre de Bruxelles in Belgium, said Africa was a newer destination in a longer history of Chinese men seeking wives abroad. Cross-border matchmaking had previously involved women from Southeast Asia, Pakistan and former Soviet countries, while more recent cases have emerged in African countries including Egypt, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. “One important reason is … the ‘marriage squeeze’ in China,” Chen said. Many men from rural or disadvantaged backgrounds struggle to marry because of the need for a high caili – a sum of money paid by the groom-to-be to the bride’s family as a way to secure the marriage and show wealth – and expectations that they should own a home and often a car. This particularly disadvantages men with little money or insecure jobs. Meanwhile, men who remain unmarried involuntarily could face increasing pressure from their families and communities to marry and continue the family line as they grow older. “For some economically marginalised Chinese men, marrying in Africa may therefore appear more affordable than marrying in China or even through matchmaking networks in Southeast Asia, where agency fees, bride wealth and other costs can also be high,” Chen said. Wei Wang, a University of Amsterdam postdoctoral researcher who has studied marriages between Chinese men and Ethiopian women, said services offering foreign wives might sell an “imagined geographical solution” to men who struggled to marry in China. “Someone who feels relatively ‘unmarriageable’ at home may be told that his nationality, income or ability to pay will make him more desirable elsewhere,” Wang said. About a month after the Madagascar airport case, the Chinese embassy in Malawi warned citizens not to trust advertisements promoting “marriage by purchase” or the idea of “buying a wife”. In a statement published on its social media account on September 7, the embassy said several Chinese citizens had recently fallen victim to marriage scams overseas after trusting cross-border matchmaking services and paying large bride prices. However, it did not say where the cases occurred. “Paying large sums to purchase a marital relationship can easily create legal risks involving human trafficking, financial extortion and threats to personal safety,” the embassy warned. Chinese law prohibits international marriage introduction services or making a profit from such activities. Similar cases were reported in Malawi in October last year, when the Chinese embassy said several citizens had paid intermediaries and bride prices before facing extortion and threats. It warned that such arrangements could lead to human trafficking investigations, imprisonment and financial loss. In a separate case in May 2023, Malawian police stopped two Chinese men from leaving the country with two local women after they obtained marriage certificates without waiting the required 21 days. The men and a Chinese female accomplice were convicted of human trafficking and sentenced by a Lilongwe court to six years in prison in February 2024. Malawian women have also reported being deceived or forced into marriages after reaching China. A 2023 investigation by Malawi’s Platform for Investigative Journalism documented the case of Ethel Moyo, who said she was sent to China at 17 for an arranged marriage. Moyo alleged that agents changed her age to 25, instructed her to claim she was travelling to study and sent her to Shaanxi province, where she married a 33-year-old Chinese man. She said an agent later pressured her to remain in the marriage. Moyo’s present circumstances could not be confirmed. In Madagascar, China’s embassy said in March last year that Malagasy public security authorities had uncovered a human trafficking case linked to cross-border marriages and arrested several Chinese citizens. Wang’s research in Ethiopia and southern China’s Guangzhou showed that some marriages often grew from work, migration and social connections rather than paid matchmaking. Being Chinese did not automatically make men attractive husbands, and African women did not necessarily see China as a desirable place to live, Wang said. Chen said the cases in Malawi and Madagascar should not be dismissed as completely isolated incidents, but cautioned against overstating the scale of the phenomenon. “They appear to be part of a broader, emerging pattern,” Chen said. “But it is still too early, and there is too little reliable evidence, to claim that brokered marriages – or the abusive practices sometimes associated with them – are widespread across Africa.”

title: No ‘red line’ for approving assemblies but security threats remain: police chief
description: Hong Kong’s police commissioner warns national security risks remain despite landmark conviction and imprisonment of Tiananmen vigil organisers.
content: There is no “red line” for approving public assemblies, Hong Kong’s police chief has said, while warning that national security risks persist despite the landmark conviction and imprisonment of organisers behind the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil for inciting subversion. The government on Saturday also strongly condemned Western countries, anti-China media, overseas organisations and politicians for launching “malicious attacks” over the trial of the disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which concluded on Friday. Former alliance chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months behind bars, respectively. Former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, who pleaded guilty ahead of the trial, was sentenced to five years and two months. They were convicted last month after three High Court judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including the annual June 4 vigil, which was the only large-scale public gathering on Chinese soil to remember the 1989 crackdown in Beijing. Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming warned on Saturday that national security risks persisted despite the sentencing. “The public may think that society appears peaceful after a major national security case has concluded. But as always, undercurrents are everywhere. We cannot state that there are no other risks. There are undercurrents and soft resistance,” Chow said after attending a police passing-out parade. He cited the recent example of a small group of residents who gathered outside Prince Edward MTR station on the night of August 31. They chanted slogans and conducted “so-called commemoration activities” to mark a 2019 protest flashpoint “without any evidence” of abuses by authorities, Chow said. Three people, including former Kowloon City district councillor Virginia Fung King-man, were subsequently arrested. “Obviously, a small number of people are still eager to incite others’ hatred against the central government and the local government through unreasonable slander. We cannot afford to let our guard down,” Chow said. Asked whether organisers of public assemblies and demonstrations would find it more difficult to secure a green light from the force, Chow said police would assess the overall situation, such as national security risks, public safety and order, public rights and the impact on other residents. “I do not think there is a red line here,” he said. The police chief noted that alliance leaders Lee and Chow intended to appeal their sentence and acknowledged their right to do so. Separately, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok declined to comment on the case in a television interview on Saturday, but said he was aware of criticisms of the court’s ruling by foreign countries. Lam dismissed those criticisms as “slogan-like accusations”, saying they were unjustified. “If you look at our past cases – whether they involve national security – all cases strictly follow the process of a fair and open trial,” he said. “Every defendant is given ample opportunity to present their arguments. When delivering a verdict, the judge also provides a detailed explanation of the reasons and grounds behind their decision. “These are the objective facts we should use to judge whether the rule of law is being respected. I really do not see any aspect where the methods or procedures we used failed to align with the spirit of the rule of law.” In a separate statement, a government spokesman said certain individuals had exploited national security cases to attack Hong Kong’s rule of law and human rights, and fabricated “lies and scaremongering remarks”. “In recent years, Western countries have continuously generalised the concept of ‘national security’, intimidating individuals and enterprises engaging in legitimate activities, and suppressing dissidents using various means,” the spokesman said. “The relevant governments and politicians have failed to reflect on their own actions, and their local organisations and media have turned a blind eye towards such acts. “Yet, these external forces adopt double standards to attack the government for fulfilling its duty to safeguard national security in strict adherence to the principle of the rule of law. This is complete hypocrisy and a despicable political manoeuvre.” The spokesman said authorities would spare no effort in preventing, suppressing and punishing acts and activities that endangered national security. During the passing-out parade, Deputy Commissioner of Police Andrew Kan Kai-yan, also the force’s national security director, urged officers to be cautious as national security challenges became more invisible, complex and volatile. He noted that external forces had not stopped interfering in Hong Kong, while people with ill intentions used different soft resistance measures to smear the government. Kan said officers should not only fight against traditional crimes but also guard against ideological infiltration and shoulder the responsibility of safeguarding national security. Chow praised the deputy police chief, who is set to retire soon, for his contributions to the force and the city.

title: Probe launched after body of mainland Chinese woman found in sea off Lamma
description: Body spotted floating in ocean near Lamma Power Station, and police found no suicide note, but recovered mainland identity card.
content: Hong Kong police are investigating after the body of a 53-year-old mainland Chinese woman was found in the waters near Lamma Island on Saturday morning. Police received a report at 10.19am after a body was spotted floating in the ocean near the Lamma Power Station. Firefighters were deployed to the scene to recover the woman from the water, and she was pronounced dead at the scene. Officers found no suicide note, but recovered a mainland identity card from the body. The cause of death will be determined by an autopsy. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial or message via WhatsApp 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: How a lunch break saved lives at a school hit by China-Nepal floods
description: Children in other classes at the school in the Dhading district in Nepal also escaped just in time.
content:
Last month, dangerous floods struck a border crossing between China and Nepal. But in one of the areas worst hit, a group of children survived when they happened to leave their classroom for their lunch break.
Children in other classes at the school in Dhading also escaped because teachers told them to quickly leave their classrooms before the waters came crashing in.
“The teachers said, ‘There is a flood, and you should leave bags and tiffins,’” said Lakshmi Shrestha, the mother of a student at the school.
Shrestha was among those who returned to the school over the next few days to find their children’s belongings.
The school was coated in mud, and the courtyard was filled with dirt.
At least 69 schools in Nepal’s flood-devastated areas have been destroyed or damaged. This puts the education of nearly 19,000 children at risk, according to the non-profit organisation Save the Children.

title: Police freeze HK$30 million in bank account of man who refused to share Mark Six prize
description: Hong Kong police chief says investigation not directly connected to Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, although suspect is member of staff.
content: Hong Kong police have frozen HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) held in the bank account of a 36-year-old man who was arrested on suspicion of theft after he allegedly refused to split a winning Mark Six jackpot with his colleagues. The arrest was made on Friday after a 53-year-old man reported to police on Wednesday that he was one of 15 colleagues who had chipped in to buy the winning ticket for the draw last week, according to a source. The group reportedly included some staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD). “The case is being investigated by the Western district crime support team. A 36-year-old man was arrested yesterday, and the relevant funds in his bank account have been frozen,” said Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming on Saturday. “Regarding communication with the FEHD, the report was made by another person, so we do not see a direct connection to the department itself.” The suspect bought the ticket and received the payout into his personal bank account, but he refused to split the cash equally among his colleagues, according to the source. A 30-minute meeting in Aberdeen on Wednesday evening failed to resolve the dispute, as he allegedly insisted on keeping the money, the insider added. Fearing he would make off with the winnings, a colleague filed a police report at around 10pm that night. The 36-year-old suspect reportedly skipped work for five days before being arrested. The FEHD said it was cooperating with the police investigation. The dispute involves prize money from the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s September 5 Mark Six 50th anniversary snowball draw, which featured a record HK$228 million jackpot. The first prize pool paid out HK$63.3 million per winning unit across 3.5 units.

title: Alarm as Syria plans private jet hub on former torture site
description: Rights groups warn turning Mezzeh airbase into a VIP airport could destroy mass graves and evidence of Assad-era atrocities.
content: Syrian government plans to turn a former military airport in Damascus into a ⁠hub for private jets are raising alarm among rights groups and residents who say redevelopment could disturb suspected mass graves and override private land claims. Syria’s civil aviation authority said last week it was preparing to reclassify Mezzeh military airport for limited civilian use, focused on private and executive aviation, to complement Damascus International Airport. Rubble removal and infrastructure upgrades had already begun, said a report on Syria’s state news agency, Sana. The project is emerging as a test of how Syria’s new authorities balance a drive to attract investment and redevelop state assets with two ‌unresolved legacies of the Assad family’s rule: the fate of tens of thousands of missing Syrians and property rights clouded by decades of expropriation. Under ousted ruler Bashar al-Assad and his father Hafez, Mezzeh housed key branches of the powerful Air Force Intelligence Directorate, as well as numerous detention facilities where suspected government opponents were tortured, executed and subjected to enforced disappearance. Parts of the airbase were used for presidential and other official flights. Air Force Intelligence (AFI) documents recently obtained by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre (SJAC), a US-based Syrian-led human rights group, showed that senior Syrian military officials approved Mezzeh in 2012 as a site for carrying out executions of detainees sentenced to death by military field courts. One document proposed moving executions from Sednaya – the country’s most notorious prison at the time – to ⁠Mezzeh because it was a “closed security compound” close to Damascus. Subsequent correspondence discussed a firing range and later a hangar beside the runway as execution sites. The documents, which highlight the central role of Mezzeh in the Assad-era security system, ‌show officials ordered construction of a platform at the hangar, requested nylon rope and directed that the work be carried out under AFI supervision “in utmost secrecy”. A 2025 investigation by SJAC identified two suspected gravesites linked to people who died in detention at Mezzeh, where it said more than 1,150 detainees died, some by execution and others from torture ‌or maltreatment. In a July 2025 letter, SJAC provided Syria’s National Commission for Missing Persons with the coordinates of the two suspected graves inside the airport, urging authorities to prevent ⁠construction or excavation until the sites were investigated. The commission told ⁠SJAC at the time that there were no construction or refurbishment plans for Mezzeh, SJAC said. SJAC wrote to the commission again on September 8 after the redevelopment plans emerged, warning that excavation, rubble removal or other works could damage human remains and evidence crucial to identifying victims, ‌according to a second letter. SJAC said it had not yet received a response to its second letter. Amer Matar, founder of the Syria Prisons Museum, a Germany-based NGO documenting detention facilities including those at Mezzeh, said the planned works showed a lack of respect for Syrian families who ‌still have ‌no answers on the fate of loved ones detained under Assad. “To construct a business airport on a site that may contain mass graves, without a thorough prior investigation, without site protection, without searching for the missing and their remains ‌and without preserving evidence, is an act of extreme recklessness and disregard,” Matar said. The Syrian civil aviation authority, Syria’s National Commission for Missing Persons and Syria’s defence ministry, which has been operating the airport, did not respond to questions ⁠about suspected graves and land claims. Sana cited the civil aviation authority as saying that Mezzeh’s refurbishment would take into account the surrounding urban area and relevant legal and social issues, but did not specifically ⁠mention the graves or land rights. It is unclear who will develop the airport. The dispute over the land on which airport facilities were built is decades old. Under the Assads, private land was regularly expropriated for government projects, often without compensation. Mezzeh airport was built on land belonging to hundreds of private citizens across 2.76 sq km (1.1 square miles), according to land records from the ‌Moadamiya municipality. A former municipal official, who asked ‌not to be named, said that expropriation decrees retroactively justified the government’s use of those lands when the airport was built in 1956, and that compensation had not been paid. Residents demonstrated in Moadamiya a day after the redevelopment plans were announced. “We welcome investment, but we should be sitting at the table and discussing our share with investors, not the state,” said one protest organiser, who gave his name as Abu Khaled. “We have a documented right to this land.” The dispute comes as Syria faces calls to address Assad-era property seizures. On September 2, United Nations land rights experts appealed to Syria’s government to suspend and repeal laws they said had enabled systematic property dispossession under Assad, and to either establish mechanisms to return properties to their legitimate owners or provide adequate compensation.

title: US wants Taiwan to ‘serve as cannon fodder’ against mainland China: state media
description: CCTV warning follows comments by de facto US ambassador that the island did not need to show it could win a war outright to deter an attack.
content: “Separatists” and the United States are putting Taiwan in greater danger, mainland China’s state broadcaster has warned, days after Washington’s de facto ambassador to the self-ruled island said it only needed to convince a potential adversary that landing forces would be very difficult. “Taiwan doesn’t need to demonstrate that it can win a war outright,” Raymond Greene, director of the American Institute in Taiwan, said in a keynote address at the 2026 Taipei Security Dialogue on Wednesday. He added that Taiwan had unique strengths that could deter an attack, including uncrewed systems, mission command and societal resilience. The island had collaborated with American companies to develop drones, battle-tested autonomous systems and other equipment, Greene noted. “It simply needs to convince an adversary that it would struggle to successfully land a large ground force in heavily urbanised, mountainous terrain and sustain it across 90 miles [145km] of open, turbulent waters. “It is hard to imagine a more difficult and complicated operation, even for a combat-experienced military force.” A CCTV commentary published on its website on Friday said: “The subtext of Greene’s speech is clear as day: he said that Taiwan does not need to win, which means the US doesn’t care whether it wins or loses. “It meant that Taiwan’s mission is to serve as cannon fodder in confronting and containing the mainland. It’s meant to turn Taiwan into a battlefield capable of wearing the mainland down over the long haul.” According to the Chinese state broadcaster, Taiwan’s No 2 leader Hsiao Bi-khim responded to Greene’s speech by saying that Taipei “must strive to achieve” its goal of raising defence spending to 5 per cent of gross domestic product. But Greene warned that it was still not enough. The commentary also said Greene’s speech was a public projection of US strategy. President Donald Trump has previously said he was not “looking” to send the US military “9,500 miles to fight a war”. The piece further cited comments by Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon undersecretary for policy, that “Taiwan is very important to the US … but not an existential interest”. It added that Hsiao and Taiwan’s leader William Lai Ching-te were using the island as a pawn to “curry favour” with the US, save themselves and provoke conflict. Accusing the pair of pursuing a separatist agenda, the commentary said: “We hope that our compatriots in Taiwan will see through the schemes and tactics of Taiwan independence separatists and external interference forces and resolutely oppose them.” US policy towards Taiwan has come under fresh scrutiny ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington this month. Trump recently threatened to sue the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office, Taiwan’s de facto embassy in the US, as part of a campaign against the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning think tank. Trump included the office in a list of foreign donors to the centre, saying he was “strongly considering” including them in a US$5 billion lawsuit over a report disputing his claims about National Guard deployments in US cities. Meanwhile, US hawks have been pushing the White House to forward a US$14 billion arms package for Taiwan to Congress. During his state visit to Beijing in May, the US president described the package “a very good negotiating chip” with Beijing. Acting navy secretary Hung Cao later said the deal had been paused to ensure enough weapons were available for the Iran war. Xi told Trump in May that the Taiwan issue was the “most important” one in the US-China relationship and mishandling it could lead to conflict. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The US, like most countries, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with weapons to defend itself.

title: 330-gram premature Chinese baby defies the odds to reach 2.5kg in 105 days, heads home
description: His skin is as thin as a cicada’s wing, tiny blood vessels visible beneath surface, soles of his feet are smaller than an adult’s thumb.
content: A premature baby in southern China, weighing just 330 grams and measuring as large as an adult’s palm, was discharged from the hospital in good health after a 105-day stay. The newborn baby boy was born on May 20, when his mother was only 23 weeks and four days pregnant, at Shenzhen Maternity and Child Healthcare Hospital, as reported by the South Daily. Nicknamed Little Zebao, he is recognised as the lightest premature baby in Guangdong province. His skin was as thin as a cicada’s wing, with tiny blood vessels visible beneath the surface. The soles of his feet were smaller than an adult’s thumb, according to the report. Doctors discovered that the baby’s intestinal tract was as thin as a piece of hair and his immune system was not yet developed. Upon birth, the baby was immediately transferred to the neonatal intensive care unit, where he received dedicated treatment and care from the hospital’s medical staff. On September 1, Little Zebao was discharged from the hospital, having gained weight to 2.5kg and declared healthy. “At first, to be honest, we did not expect the baby to survive. Now he is fine and discharged from the hospital. I am truly thrilled!” the baby’s mother, whose name has not been disclosed, told the media. The couple sent the hospital a red pennant emblazoned with Chinese characters praising the exceptional skills and kindness of the medical team. The baby was delivered much earlier than the due date because his mother, age undisclosed, suffers from chronic hypertension and developed severe pre-eclampsia, a pregnancy complication resulting from high blood pressure. Continuing the pregnancy posed significant health risks for the mother. Therefore, doctors devised a meticulous plan to enhance the foetus’s chances of survival. Medical staff prepared thoroughly before the birth by preheating the incubator, checking equipment, and organising medications. Within one minute of the baby’s birth, doctors intubated him due to weak breathing. They also wrapped his skin in films to maintain warmth and minimise moisture loss. In less than half an hour, nurses connected an indwelling needle to the umbilical artery, allowing medication and nutrients to be delivered to the baby. “We have helped him overcome numerous challenges,” Dr Huang Zhifeng, a senior doctor at the hospital, was quoted as saying. A critical moment occurred on the third day following Little Zebao’s birth when his heart rate and blood oxygen saturation suddenly plummeted. An ultrasound examination revealed that fluid had accumulated in the cardiac sac, a situation that could potentially lead to sudden cardiac arrest. Doctors swiftly performed a puncture to remove the fluid, averting danger in just over 10 minutes. “What a medical miracle!
