I wish this baby grows up healthy,” one internet user commented. “Doctors and nurses have done a great job. They possess immense compassion!” another remarked. This is not the first instance in which the Shenzhen hospital has saved extremely premature babies. In October 2023, a baby of undisclosed gender was born at the hospital when the mother was only 21 weeks and four days pregnant. That infant received treatment for 143 days before being discharged. As a result of this case, the Shenzhen hospital set a record for saving the youngest gestational age premature baby in China.

title: Need a break from screens? These yoga poses help you switch off, stretch out
description: After spending too much time on your phone, try these 4 exercises to restore your posture, deal with neck pain and refresh your eyes.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
It is hard to imagine life without our smartphones and tablets, but our favourite devices might be wearing us down.
If you have ever noticed tight shoulders after hours of scrolling, you have experienced “tech neck”.
In an article published in the Postgraduate Medical Journal in 2025, researchers analysed data from seven past studies involving a total of 10,715 adults. They found that people who overused their smartphones had a significantly higher risk of neck pain.
These findings show that smartphone usage is a crucial health issue.
But neck pain is not the only problem. Poor sleep and eye strain are also some of the many negative effects of our screen-dominated world.
Striking a healthy balance with technology is important. To help fight the harms of screen time, take a break from your devices and try these yoga exercises.
Sit down and find a nice tall posture by rolling your shoulders back and down and imagining your spine lengthening upwards. Tilt your chin slightly down towards your throat. Turn your head in a clockwise direction, as though you are drawing circles with your nose. Choose a speed that feels good to you.
Do five rounds and then repeat in an anticlockwise direction for five rounds. Remember to breathe deeply as you do this.
This is a great movement for opening up the front of your neck, chest and shoulders.
Standing up, clasp your hands behind your back. Lift your clasped hands away from your body and hold them at a level that feels comfortable. Tilt your head to look upwards. Stay here for three breaths.
Give your eyes a rest from digital devices with this soothing eye exercise. Before you start, clean your hands, and if you wear glasses, be sure to remove them.
From a seated position, rub the palms of your hands together to create some heat. Close your eyes and cup the palms of your hands over your eyes, without applying pressure to your lids. Stay here for five breaths.
This yoga pose stretches the front of the body, helping to counteract the rounded posture you have when using a phone or sitting at your desk using a computer. This supported version of the bridge pose uses a pillow, which makes it easier to hold the position.
Get a pillow and lie on your back. Bend your knees and bring your feet towards you, keeping them on the ground. Make sure there is a hip-width distance between them. Lift your hips and place the pillow horizontally underneath your lower back. Lower your hips down and stretch your legs out.
Stretch your arms out to the side and bend your elbows, with your hands pointing to your head and your palms facing the ceiling. Stay here for five deep breaths.
To come out of this pose, bend your knees to lift your hips and slide the pillow out from beneath you. Lower your hips to the ground before turning to one side and pushing yourself up with your hands.

title: Hong Kong to table cooling-off period bill for beauty, fitness deals by mid-2027
description: Commerce chief Algernon Yau says both sectors supported seven-day cooling-off period but differed on exemption thresholds.
content: The Hong Kong government will table a bill at the Legislative Council in the first half of 2027 to introduce a statutory cooling-off period for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts, the commerce chief has said. Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah revealed the timeline on Saturday, two weeks after the government concluded a two-month consultation on the policy proposal to address limitations of the Trade Descriptions Ordinance on August 31. “We hope to table the amendment bill in the first half of 2027 and queue to amend the ordinance,” he told a radio show. “However, its schedule is subject to whether the government has other bill amendments. We hope to move forward as quickly as possible.” The administration suggested rolling out a statutory seven-day cooling-off period and a 14-day refund window for prepaid beauty and fitness contracts. It also proposed exempting lower-value contracts to minimise disruptions, with the threshold ranging from HK$3,000 (US$382) to HK$15,000 or above. Yau said that while the two industries supported a seven-day cooling period – a common policy in other economies – representatives from both sectors held different views on the contract threshold. “They are two different industries and have very different contract amounts. We will make amendments based on the views collected from the industries. We hope the threshold facilitates their businesses while safeguarding consumer benefits. We have to strike a balance,” he said. “It is possible that the threshold will be different between the fitness and beauty industries.” Yau said the threshold would depend on the nature of the contract and the services, and authorities would need to study it in detail. To protect consumers, the government planned to forbid operators from splitting a single service contract into multiple documents to evade regulation, he said. He noted that some operators suggested that authorities could first implement the cooling-off period without setting a contract threshold, and added that the government was open to all suggestions. He added that the sectors expressed concerns over potential financial harm to businesses if contracts were cancelled during the cooling-off period. Yau said the government suggested allowing traders to deduct an administrative fee, which was up to 2 per cent of a one-off card payment and up to 5 per cent of an instalment payment plan. He noted that authorities still had to discuss with banks and industry players how to handle and speed up the refund process, as banks might refund prepaid transactions to customers directly. Yau said the government would focus on regulating the beauty and fitness sectors first and consider other industries later if needed. The government’s proposal also included imposing a two-year limit on contract duration, and giving the Customs and Excise Department powers to handle cases involving the wrongful acceptance of payment. The proposed measures would apply to contracts offered by fitness centres – including access to exercise equipment and training in fitness, bodybuilding and weight control – as well as beauty parlours providing treatments, cosmetic procedures and hair restoration services. Premises to be exempted included those managed by public hospitals or clinics, education institutions, charitable organisations, national sports associations, and clubhouses at hotels and residential properties. In 2024, the Consumer Council, which has long advocated for a statutory cooling-off period, recorded 2,929 complaints regarding beauty services, involving HK$93 million. Almost half of the cases stemmed from contracts of the Physical Fitness chain that abruptly closed that year.

title: Unvaccinated children, elderly face much higher risk of major flu complications: official
description: Hong Kong director of health cites data showing unvaccinated children and elderly are four to five times more vulnerable than vaccinated individuals.
content: Unvaccinated children and elderly people are four to five times more likely to face serious complications or mortality from flu infections than those who receive vaccinations, a Hong Kong health official has warned, as influenza cases in the city continue to rise. Director of Health Ronald Lam Man-kin issued the warning on Saturday as he pointed out that Hong Kong’s influenza infections had been increasing since June. “Up until last week, the number of flu infections still remained at a high level,” he told a radio programme. He said 13 per cent of laboratory samples tested positive for flu viruses, up from 12 per cent during the same period last year. “The rate of seeking medical treatment or being hospitalised in public hospitals due to influenza was 0.83 cases per 10,000 people, significantly higher than 0.27 cases per 10,000 people over the same period last year. Among them, about 80 per cent of cases were caused by influenza A,” he added. So far this year, 19 severe cases of influenza among children were recorded, including one death, he said. Eight cases involved children aged five or younger who were unvaccinated. Lam urged the public, particularly the vulnerable groups, to actively get vaccinated as the government’s seasonal influenza vaccination programmes would begin next Thursday, one week earlier than in the previous year. “For unvaccinated children, our data, including overseas data, shows they have five times greater risk of having complications or serious infections than those who got jabbed,” he warned. “For the unvaccinated elderly aged 65 or above, they face four times greater risk of having serious infections or even mortality than their vaccinated counterparts. So the protection of vaccination is really strong.” Some government programmes fall under the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme (VSS), which offers subsidised doses to vulnerable groups such as children, residents aged 50 or above, pregnant women and adults with chronic diseases. Other schemes include the outreach vaccination programmes for schools and residential care homes. Lam said he expected that all students vaccinated under the school scheme would receive injections before mid-December. Authorities have also strengthened a pilot scheme that helps private doctors procure vaccines under government contracts by tripling the supply and expanding the criteria for eligibility. Private doctors who registered with the scheme will provide free jabs to the public.

title: Foie gras, puppies, water parks: North Korea gets a glow-up
description: Kim Jong-un wants his middle class to splurge and is funding a splashy leisure boom to soak up their excess cash.
content: Coffee bars. Water parks. Retail therapy. ⁠North Korea – a country few would associate with leisure or pleasure – is experiencing an ⁠unlikely outbreak of fun. Leader Kim Jong-un, himself no stranger to indulgence, is orchestrating new ways for his citizens to spend ⁠their wealth. North Korea’s imports of massage equipment have surged 40-fold over the past decade, according to Chinese customs data. Treadmill shipments jumped over 600 per cent. Pianos and even bumper cars are pouring in, too. The consumption drive extends to luxury malls, beach resorts and ski destinations that are popping up around North Korea, according to a review of trade statistics and state media reports, and interviews with five recent visitors and two defectors. It’s not just about expanding access to life’s little luxuries, analysts say. By channelling personal spending through state-controlled leisure and retail networks, Kim strengthens government control of commerce, squeezes informal markets and unlocks new sources of revenue and growth for the nuclear-armed country. The strategy drew “the production, distribution and capital flows concentrated in the markets into an official economic space managed by the state,” said ‌Kang Seong-hyeon, a research fellow at the Seoul-based Hyundai Research Institute think tank. Avenues for consumption have proliferated even as North Korea faces heavy UN sanctions – including on luxury goods, energy and mineral trade – designed to impede Kim’s weapons programme. North Korea’s economy grew 3.5 per cent in 2025, a third consecutive year above 3 per cent, the South Korean central bank said in July. The glow-up has attracted the attention of outsiders. After visiting Pyongyang in May, Singapore’s foreign minister Vivian Balakrishnan called the capital’s progress “remarkable”, saying it resembled “any modern city” in East Asia. Residents drink cappuccinos and browse home appliances at the Rangnang Aeguk Kumgang Service Complex, a luxury shopping centre in Pyongyang that opened last year, according to social media videos verified by reporters. A hard-earned thirst can be quenched at the Hwasong Taedonggang Beer Restaurant, a two-year-old drinking den celebrated in state media. In April, Kim toured a new pet shop with his daughter, Kim Ju-ae, who was drawn to the kittens and puppies. Pyongyang’s leisure blitz is bankrolled by revenue streams including cryptocurrency heists, the deployment of North Korean troops to fight for Russia in Ukraine and exports of coal and other minerals, according to South Korean researchers. The United States and other foreign officials and cybersecurity experts have repeatedly tied crypto theft to North Korean state-sponsored ⁠hackers. The Seoul-based Institute for National Security Strategy, a South Korean government-funded think tank, estimates North Korea earned up to US$14.4 billion from its involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war between August 2023 and December 2025. The influx of cash trickles through North Korea’s economy, where many have also made money from informal trade. But accumulated wealth created a problem: “a ‌middle class of roughly 8 million people with savings and nowhere to spend them”, said Ruediger Frank, a professor of East Asian economy and society at the University of Vienna. Consumption was Kim’s answer, Frank said: it reduced frustration, channelled money away from bidding up prices of essentials such as rice and generated growth through domestic demand. With its fortunes uplifted, North Korea has less need for sanctions relief and fewer incentives to restart nuclear negotiations with Washington, analysts have said, despite US President Donald Trump’s stated desire for another ‌meeting with Kim. North Korea’s embassy in Beijing did not respond to questions about the domestic-consumption drive. Russia’s foreign ministry and the White House also did not comment. China’s foreign ministry said it maintained trade and cooperation with North Korea while implementing UN Security Council resolutions, adding that sanctions should not ⁠affect the country’s livelihood. Mentions of tourism, leisure and cultural life in ⁠North Korean state media have increased since 2022 as attractions have been opened or refurbished, a review of more than 1,200 articles found. These developments include the Wonsan Kalma beach resort, which launched in the summer of 2025; five luxury hotels that opened in December in Samjiyon, on the Chinese border; a ski resort under construction nearby; and a water park and yet-to-be-finished equestrian club in the northeast. State media coverage of a heatwave ‌in August showed the Wonsan beach resort packed with domestic visitors. “One local contact even told me that when taking his family there, several members had to share a twin room because everything else had already been booked,” said Rowan Beard, co-founder of travel operator Young Pioneer Tours. Wonsan Kalma received more than 300,000 domestic visitors in the latter half of 2025, according to China’s embassy in Pyongyang, which mentioned the figure in a February ‌post about its ‌ambassador’s visit. Saunas, pools, video-game arcades and sports centres had also sprung up in northeastern Rason city, said a Chinese businessman who gave his surname as Cui. As part of a regional development plan, Kim is also building leisure complexes containing libraries, restaurants and cinemas across the country, with at least two dozen completed or under construction, ‌according to state media. But the most lavish additions are in Pyongyang. State media has described a new housing district containing a gaming arcade, car showroom and a barbecue restaurant that serves salmon belly and foie gras burgers. The range of goods available in North Korea also has expanded, according to three recent visitors. At Ryugyong Golden Plaza, ⁠which opened in 2023, shops display the logos of watchmakers including Rolex, Omega and Herbelin, and an electronics store features Huawei branding, according to social media footage verified by reporters. Rolex and Huawei declined to comment. Omega and Herbelin said they had no official retailers or distributors in North Korea. North Koreans shop online using mobile ⁠apps, according to images published by Beard and NKTechLab, an analysis project of the US-based Stimson Centre think tank. Beard, who visited Pyongyang in May, said mobile app payments were used “everywhere” and for “anything available for sale”. Trade statistics show how the leisure drive encompasses both personal goods and state-led infrastructure. Chinese customs data reveal surging shipments of pianos, watches and amusement equipment – including merry-go-rounds, rollercoasters and waterslides. North Korea imported more than 3 tonnes of bumper cars from China, worth more than US$20,000, between January 2025 and July this year. Trade with China has rebounded broadly since the Covid-19 pandemic. A ‌flourishing car culture has even emerged in Pyongyang, fuelled by Chinese imports. After North Korea’s famine in the 1990s, semi-legal markets flourished as the state could not supply residents. Attempts to close them early this century failed because the state lacked the distribution infrastructure to replace them, according to Jung Chang-Hyun, director of the Peace Economy Research Institute in Seoul. Now, Kim’s consumption gambit served that purpose: building state commercial infrastructure that could compete with and eventually undermine private markets, he said. Payment and delivery apps also enable official scrutiny of private spending, analysts say. In 2023, Pyongyang passed a law requiring every bank and store to accept electronic payments. Not everyone benefits from the consumption boom. Yang Il-cheol, who worked as a driver in Pyongyang before defecting to South Korea last year, said people like him had little access to the new restaurants and leisure facilities. While cellphones had become ubiquitous in the capital, many North Koreans distrusted the government and preferred cash payments, Yang said. Frank, the professor, said Kim’s campaign to boost domestic spending appeared to be paying off – for now. “Consumption buys time,” he said. “It does not buy loyalty forever.”

title: Hong Kong wants to be Asia’s next fashion hub. This event could help make it happen
description: Hong Kong Fashion Fest 2026 highlights local talent as well as the challenges they face as the city seeks to cement its place in fashion.
content: Can Hong Kong realise its ambition as a premier fashion hub in Asia? The answer may have lain in this year’s Hong Kong Fashion Fest. The annual festival’s third edition – organised by the Cultural and Creative Industries Development Agency under Hong Kong’s Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau – runs from September 1 to 14, featuring independent designers, international labels, retailers, manufacturers and sustainability advocates. Centrestage, one of Asia’s premier annual fashion showcases and trade platforms, was a highlight of the festival, bringing together some 270 brands from 24 countries and regions at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, in Wan Chai, from September 2 to 5. It featured Hong Kong fashion label Zidi and designers Mountain Yam, Angus Tsui and Kit Wan. “Hong Kong is a mix of East and West,” says Yam, who has independently operated his label for 12 years and showed on the Hong Kong Dopamine catwalk at Centrestage. “We have international exposure, but we also understand the Chinese market. I feel hopeful, especially with brands helping each other to get more awareness to the mass audience.” Elsewhere, Virtuose: The Artistry of Couture, held at the Hong Kong Palace Museum on September 1, showcased Hong Kong couture labels Vivian Luk Atelier and Tigerstrolling alongside Spain’s Guillermo Decimo and Vietnam’s Phan Huy in an evening of glamour attended by influencers and fashionistas from around the world. Home-grown futuristic looks Perhaps the most persuasive display of confidence and outlandish creativity came from Kit Wan on the Centrestage Elites catwalk. The Hong Kong-born designer and visual artist presented more than 30 new looks in front of a glass wall that looked out over Victoria Harbour. “Emotions are high, especially as a designer walking out after this huge output of love, resources, joint creativity,” Wan says after the show. “It’s a human reaction of pride and gratitude to all those who shared in this moment with the studio.” Wan made his name creating weird and wonderful stage costumes for Hong Kong pop stars including Miriam Yeung Chin-wah, Hins Cheung, MC Cheung Tin-fu and Panther Chan, with his made-to-order outfits even being worn at the Grammy Awards and Eurovision. His sci-fi-style silhouettes offered a futuristic vision of Hong Kong fashion this time – a fantastical zone between fashion, armour and collectable art. Not many of the outfits would survive a commute on Hong Kong’s MTR, but practicality was hardly the point. “It seems like the Hong Kong cultural branches are hard at work to promote all the fabulous creatives in this great city,” Wan says. “I can say as a visual artist, it’s important to fund and support the arts; it makes for a more cultured society.” At Virtuose, Guillermo Decimo, Phan Huy, Tigerstrolling and Vivian Luk Atelier sent 40 ensembles through four culturally inspired entrances. The setting was unapologetically grand, although the true spectacle lay in more intimate details: embroidery, boning, hand-draping, wiring and exacting fabric manipulation. “This is not fashion to chase, but to appreciate,” says Bonita Cheung, Virtuose’s conceptual and project director. “[It is] a celebration of the human hands behind the creation, where couture’s true power lies in the artistry of its application.” While Hong Kong is not a world couture capital in the same way as Paris, it has the opportunity to become an Asian couture nexus point where designers can reach wealthy buyers, retailers and VIPs. Sustainability beyond slogans The Redress Design Award for sustainable fashion design injected the fest with a sense of urgency. The eight finalists transformed discarded leather, army canvas, deadstock jersey, industrial waste and unwanted furniture, while other competitors explored fruit leather, non-animal wool and recyclable knitwear. “Around the world, the legislative hammer is coming down on the polluting fashion industry,” says Dr Christina Dean, founder of Redress, the non-profit organisation behind what is among the world’s leading sustainable fashion awards. “Despite the complexity, the fashion industry is screaming for circular design solutions.” The competition is important because garments made from waste – such as those seen in Jon Liesenfeld’s winning collection – can provoke urgent debate in an industry responsible for massive amounts of waste and carbon emissions. “While the fashion industry faces serious challenges … it is catastrophically still on its wasteful, runaway train wreck,” Dean says. “Circularity is flatlining despite circular textile business models being estimated to generate US$700 billion in economic value by 2030 … while clothing waste skyrockets, exacerbated by global dominance of ultra-fast fashion brands.” Liesenfeld adds: “My generation of designers won’t be judged just on aesthetics.” Circularity begins at the design stage, where choices about materials, longevity and disposal are made. Redress is leading that charge, joined this year by sustainable-fashion delegations from Austria and Australia. Circularity emerged as a major theme at forums across Hong Kong. On September 3, Fashion Summit (HK) brought together companies, environmental groups and technology specialists under the theme “Code the Fashion Forward”, while Fashion Asia Hong Kong’s separate Fashion Challenges Forum examined regional cooperation, retail and brand building. South Korea was Centrestage’s partner country, and creatives from the East Asian nation took part in insight sessions. The Australian Fashion Council pavilion, meanwhile, underlined Hong Kong’s potential as a commercial gateway to Asia. Marianne Perkovic, the council’s executive chair, says that the United States’ biting tariffs have “most certainly changed our strategy and vision to expand Australian fashion into new markets”, adding “Hong Kong is a strategic priority”. Perkovic says she was encouraged by the potential partnerships forged during the packed 180-meeting schedule in Hong Kong. The elephant in the changing room Fashion Fest showed Hong Kong lacks neither creativity nor regional draw, and its consumers remain hungry for fashion – even if many are still drawn to global fast-fashion names and Western luxury houses. The question is not whether Hong Kong can produce innovative brands, but whether the market can sustain them. Established brands such as Shanghai Tang and Vivienne Tam have combined their cultural identity with the commercial instincts needed for international success. Then there is the elephant in the room: Hong Kong’s high rents and production costs. These make it difficult for independent companies to open permanent stores, pushing them towards temporary spaces and online retail. Before the Covid-19 pandemic, Yam’s 112 mountainyam had three boutiques in the city; it now operates from a studio-store at PMQ in Central and also sells goods on its online store, on RedNote and at pop-ups. “The challenge is the costs,” Yam says. “Rent and production are quite expensive in Hong Kong. But I believe that Hong Kong people are flexible and we always find a way.” This highlights a harder truth: fashion-week visibility means little if customers cannot find the clothes – or designers cannot afford to remain visible throughout the year. The government already supports the events under the Fashion Fest banner. The two-week festival showcased the city’s creativity, manufacturing expertise, international reach and institutional backing. Yet the overlapping names, organisers, agendas and formats can still be confusing. Uniting the catwalks, trade shows and forums under one recognisable Fashion Fest banner should help define a coherent fashion identity. A stronger connective structure emerged this year, boosting prospects for home-grown talent such as Mountain Yam, Kit Wan, Zidi, Vivian Luk Atelier and Tigerstrolling – and giving international buyers more reason to pay attention. The spotlights are the easy part. The real test begins when the lights go off.

title: State funeral for Hong Kong’s first chief executive Tung Chee-hwa set for September 20
description: State leaders and central government officials expected to join funeral committee for Tung, source says.
content: The state funeral for the city’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, is scheduled for next Sunday, the South China Morning Post has learned. A source confirmed on Saturday that the service would take place on September 20, with details being arranged. State leaders and central government officials are expected to join the funeral committee, in line with previous practice. The SCMP reported earlier that a state funeral would be accorded to Tung to honour his legacy as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework. “Preparations were under way” and were being coordinated by the city government after Tung’s death on Tuesday at the age of 89, a separate source told SCMP previously. The government’s Administration Wing said on Thursday that it would announce relevant arrangements in due course. Since the 1997 handover, only two other local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Both held the rank of vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), a position that Tung also held. Tung and Fok served as two of the eight pallbearers at Ann’s funeral after he died of heart complications at 88. The other pallbearers at the time included both mainland Chinese and local officials, including Leung Chun-ying, who would later also serve as city leader, as well as the late entertainment tycoon Run Run Shaw and two of Ann’s longtime business partners. The service started at 9.30am and lasted 100 minutes, with mourners standing in silent tribute. A committee comprising 74 leading mainland and Hong Kong figures oversaw the funeral arrangements for Fok in 2006, when he died at age 83. Headed by CPPCC vice-chairman Wang Zhongyu, the panel had four deputy directors: Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office director Liao Hui, head of the United Front Work Department Liu Yandong, Tung and chief executive Donald Tsang Yam-kuen. As Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung played a pivotal role in implementing the then-untested and novel “one country, two systems” model, under which the city would be administered after the end of British colonial rule in 1997. After his death on Tuesday, Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’” and a “renowned patriot”. Despite facing major challenges during his tenure, including the first and ultimately unsuccessful attempt at passing national security legislation required under Article 23 of the Basic Law, Tung oversaw deeper economic integration between Hong Kong and the mainland. The city and Beijing signed the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement, giving Hong Kong preferential access to mainland markets, while the Individual Visit Scheme opened the door for more residents from over the border to travel independently to the city. Both measures helped revive Hong Kong’s hobbled tourism sector and economy as it battled to recover from the Sars epidemic in 2003. They continue to be vital to the city’s economy more than two decades later. After resigning as chief executive in March 2005, citing health reasons, Tung went on to assume a prominent role at the national level and increasingly came to be regarded as an elder statesman, serving as a CPPCC vice-chairman.

title: Bhutan banks on high-altitude hazelnuts to remake mountain farming
description: It takes years for trees to yield, but growers say stopping mudslides and landing better prices makes the long wait worth it.
content: Farmer Pema Dema had never even heard of hazelnuts when she was first recruited to begin growing them on her land in Bhutan’s Thimphu region. “I wondered what sort of a nut it was,” the 58-year-old said with a laugh, looking out over the deep valley and terraced rice fields that unfold below her farm. Now she has more than 140 hazelnut trees on the steep slope overlooking her home, and incorporates them into Bhutan’s traditional salted suja tea when guests visit. Pema is one of thousands of Bhutanese growing hazelnuts as part of a social enterprise hoping to help subsistence farmers develop a high-value crop. Mountain Hazelnuts began in 2009 as Bhutan’s first 100 per cent foreign direct investment project in the agriculture sector. More than 40 per cent of Bhutan’s workforce is employed in agriculture, but production remains largely subsistence-based and is complicated by the country’s mountainous terrain. Steep slopes can be impossible to plough and prone to topsoil washing away in heavy rain. Hazelnuts seemed to offer a solution. They grow well at high altitudes and on mountainsides, require no ploughing and their roots can fix soil in place. Hazelnuts are also a high-value crop with a growing market and the trees can produce for decades. That was what attracted Pema, who has been farming for 40 years. “I thought hazelnuts would be better in terms of fetching a better price,” she said. “I hoped that it would benefit us in the future.” Mountain Hazelnuts distributed its first saplings in 2011: more than 145,000 plants to 800 growers. Each recruit’s land was assessed for suitability and to ensure the crop was not displacing anything. Growers can only use land that is fallow or degraded, with the goal of increasing Bhutan’s overall farming output and improving the country’s soil. Dawa Dhendup, 82, was keen to put the trees on a steep stretch of his farm where he had struggled to grow potatoes. “It was hard annual labour. But once the hazelnut trees are planted, it’s permanent.” In sunglasses to protect his eyes after cataract surgery, he cut a sprightly figure as he harvested nuts from his 1,400 trees. The company said it now had around 9,000 families growing hazelnuts on 6,000 acres (2,400 hectares) of land across Bhutan. But in some ways, the project is only just getting off the ground after a series of setbacks and learning curves. A mismatch between production and polliniser saplings in early planting delayed fruiting and had to be solved by mass grafting of polliniser plants into orchards. The pandemic struck another blow, cutting farmers off from outreach officers who advise them on tending the crop. And then there was climate change. The hazelnut variety the company initially distributed needs around three months of cool temperatures to develop properly. But climate change meant trees at lower altitudes were getting as little as six weeks of colder temperatures. The company again turned to grafting, using stock from Georgia that required fewer “chill-hours” for plants growing between 1,600-2,400 metres (5,250-7,870 feet). In a best-case scenario, hazelnut trees take several years to fruit, and the various setbacks and extended waiting time meant that some farmers simply abandoned the project. But both Pema and Dawa said neighbours who had given up were now reconsidering. “I’m harvesting and the price is increasing, and they’re regretting their decision and feeling envious,” Dawa said. Still, like most growers, he does not yet generate significant income from the nuts. The company has said it will be increasing the price it offers growers, and with trees reaching maturity and yields expected to increase, income should start to rise. Investors have ploughed US$36 million into Mountain Hazelnuts so far and for now the company is reliant on what CEO Sean Watson calls “patient capital”. It hoped to be “cash flow positive” by 2031 and reach 10,000 tonnes of production, Watson said – a long way from the current 30 tonnes But “fruiting is starting to really kick in” and production was expected to at least double each year, Watson added. Seated next to flat baskets full of drying hazelnuts, Pema said she had already benefited because the trees have stopped soil from sliding onto her home during heavy rain. “Every year the yields are increasing,” she said. “If I had more land, I would have planted more.”

title: Hyrox boss says event is not a fad, believes it will survive where others failed
description: ‘Hong Kong has been, and will continue to be, a special destination for Hyrox and one in which we want to keep investing,’ executive says.
content: Hyrox executives and coaches believe the indoor fitness competition will not follow in the footsteps of gym trends that have briefly captured the imagination before fading from view, in part because its universal format gives it global appeal. While competitions such as CrossFit, HIIT and a variety of outdoor obstacle races have largely struggled to build on their initial popularity, Hyrox has become one of the fastest-growing fitness competitions in the world. Founded in November 2017 by Olympic field hockey champion Moritz Furste and Christian Toetzke, the first Hyrox event was held in Hamburg, Germany five months later. On its Hong Kong debut, Hyrox attracted around 700 competitors, next year the world championships will bring more than 6,000 athletes to the city. This week, the sport’s global success resulted in Furste and Toetzke buying back a majority stake in the company in a deal reportedly valued at €600 million (US$698.28 million). Gary Wan, managing director of Hyrox in Asia-Pacific, said the sport’s success lay in the fact it was easy to understand while also being “closely aligned with the running and strength training millions of people already do to remain active and healthy”. “Hyrox is also genuinely accessible, with no required finishing time,” he added. Wan also pointed to a network of training clubs and official gym affiliates that embedded the sport within local communities and gave people a place to train together throughout the year. And then there was Covid, which Hong Kong-based coach Clayton Law Chun-yip said had contributed to people taking up running when other exercise was not available. “The most fun part is the vibes, all the cheering from the spectators,” Law said. “The most challenging part is how you prepare for the race, all the training and the time you put in before stepping onto the start line.” Today, there are more than 130 official training clubs and performance coaches in Hong Kong, within a network of over 2,400 across Asia-Pacific that is growing by around 120 to 150 clubs each month. Wan said he knew from the start that the region had strong potential. “I believed from the beginning, given the region’s growing appetite for goal-based and collaborative fitness following the pandemic,” he said. “The pace and scale of the growth, however, have exceeded what anyone would have reasonably predicted. “Fewer than 1,000 people took part in our first APAC race in Hong Kong in 2022, while our most recent Hong Kong race welcomed nearly 20,000 participants. Across APAC, nearly 200,000 people have already competed this year.” Hyrox is popular not only in the city and the surrounding region, but also globally. There are events in more than 35 markets and 95 cities worldwide. Over 1.5 million people have competed so far this year, and this number is expected to reach 1.7 million by the end of the year. The frequency of events around the world has also opened up new opportunities for Hyroxers. “Race weekends are increasingly becoming a reason to travel, bringing athletes, supporters and spectators into host cities and creating a wider impact across hotels, hospitality, retail and tourism,” Wan said. Law, 33, who competed at an event in Beijing this week, said he aimed to race overseas at least once a month “to keep my motivation and momentum going”. “We see participants shaping holidays around Hyrox races and travelling with friends, family and training partners, creating connections across borders as well as within individual gyms,” Wan added. While cautious, Wan is confident about the future of Hyrox although acknowledges that “no sport or fitness movement can take continued growth for granted”. “Sustaining that momentum requires us to keep evolving and reinvesting in the experience for participants, spectators and fans,” he added. “Participation growth alone is not our objective; ultimately our goal is to create an experience people want to return to. With Hong Kong hosting its sixth Hyrox event since its debut in 2022 in January, Wan believes the consistent progress suggests there is no need “for a second bloom” in the city. “Its growth has not been a single spike; our biggest focus now is to deepen that relationship while continuing to raise standards,” he said. “The biggest challenge is ensuring that Hyrox’s growth in Hong Kong remains sustainable and never impedes the race experience. “As for the world championships, it is expected to have a global viewership of over two million; we have an exciting opportunity to showcase both the world’s best Hyrox athletes and Hong Kong as an international sporting destination.” And according to Wan, Hong Kong’s status within the sport is unlikely to change. “It remains firmly within our long-term plans,” he said. “Our participation has grown steadily, reflecting the strength and commitment of the city’s fitness community. “We want to build on the momentum already established here, continue elevating the Hyrox experience and ensure the city remains a key destination on our calendar for years to come.”

title: Hong Kong is lagging in the AI race – can it raise its game, and how?
description: As Singapore pulls ahead, experts say Hong Kong must overcome risk aversion and refine its governance frameworks to boost adoption.
content: In the third of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Leopold Chen and Theodora Yu look at how the city can raise its game and expand the adoption of artificial intelligence. Read part one here and part two here. Spotting bags of construction waste illegally dumped near a temporary refuse collection point in Hong Kong’s Southern district last year, former lawmaker and resident Michael Tien Puk‑sun immediately dialled the government’s 1823 hotline to file a complaint. Days later, he saw the bags at the same spot. The hotline had not recorded his complaint at all, he said, as he went on social media to lambast the authorities’ lack of action. “The problem comes down to the hotline simply saying it had never received the initial report,” Tien told the South China Morning Post. Soon, residents’ grievances about the government’s inefficient handling of public complaints will be addressed differently as the government pledged last month to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into public services, including the hotline. The expanded adoption of AI is expected to take centre stage when Hong Kong unveils its first five-year plan and its latest policy address on Wednesday. Experts say significant challenges remain as the government has been slow to embrace AI. They have urged authorities to boost their risk appetite, refine data governance frameworks and ensure that local tools remain internationally compatible if the city is to raise its game in an environment where privacy concerns still loom large. In July, the government introduced three AI tools – HKChat, HKPilot and HKMeeting – on its private cloud service to enhance civil service efficiency. The tools assist government workers with smart searches, document drafting and meeting transcription respectively. But Hong Kong’s roll-out lags behind those of regional peers. Singapore launched its Pair smart search chatbot for public officers in 2023, which now reaches over 80 per cent of its civil servants, boasting 73,000 monthly active users and more than 7,700 agency-tailored bots. The city state also equips officers with SmartCompose to draft responses to public inquiries and Transcribe for speech-to-text recording, while making chat.gov.sg available as an all-in-one public inquiry AI chatbot for citizens. In February, Singapore set up the National AI Council, chaired by Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, to formulate strategic directions for the country’s AI development agenda. Hong Kong has a similar Committee on AI+ and Industry Development Strategy, chaired by Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, which held its first meeting in late June. Hong Kong’s Digital Policy Office, under the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau, is mainly responsible for driving changes across government departments. The office is planning to introduce a public-facing chatbot on the iAM Smart digital identity portal later this year. It also pledged to integrate AI into 1823 to transcribe calls and generate case summaries, freeing frontline staff to handle more complicated cases. The measure is one of its 30 initiatives using the technology to enhance public services efficiency. “Nowadays, the government has placed the adoption of AI across different industries and using the technology to facilitate future development as a top priority,” said Duncan Chiu, lawmaker for the innovation and technology sector. “We must maintain such a positioning as AI will bring significant change to our life, work and future.” But Chiu, also deputy leader of the government’s AI efficiency enhancement team, noted that a legal framework heavily focused on privacy had historically made it difficult for different units to share resident data with one another. Chiu said the government had long lived in a risk-averse culture that hindered broader AI adoption. “Authorities should refine their AI governance. In the past, when AI had some level of risks, they would refrain from using it entirely,” he said. He called for a risk-based, tiered classification mechanism for application scenarios within the civil service over the next five years, encouraging officials to be bolder in applying new technologies to lower-risk situations while remaining cautious in high-risk areas. “In the first five-year plan, what is bigger for us is how to establish more legal regulations around data,” Chiu said. “Once you have a proper data governance framework, how AI moves forward under it becomes much clearer.” Professor Ray Cheung Chak-chung, associate provost in digital learning at City University (CityU), noted that while Hong Kong could leverage a “latecomer’s advantage”, it faced key bottlenecks in digital literacy and risk appetite. He urged the government to establish a clear “trial-and-error” policy to encourage AI experimentation. “As long as you maintain close communication with stakeholders while doing it, even if you make a mistake or the results are not ideal, you will not stray too far off track,” said Cheung, an electrical engineering professor. Cheung argued that after careful operational analysis, the government should prioritise funding for “quick wins” that deliver immediate relief to residents, with 1823 being one example. “In the use of AI, the government naturally takes up a demonstration role,” he said. “When more people benefit [from AI-powered public service], society’s support for AI adoption will increase.” Accelerating AI adoption is also a core policy priority for Beijing. In China’s 15th five-year plan, research into AI chips and the application of the technology in different scenarios were identified as key policy directives to promote the country’s technological self-reliance. Hong Kong, meanwhile, is positioned as an innovation and technology hub under the blueprint. Last year, the State Council stipulated that the penetration rate of next-generation smart terminals and AI agents across priority sectors should surpass 70 per cent by 2027 and reach more than 90 per cent by 2030. Both Chiu and Cheung agreed that Hong Kong should draw on mainland China’s approach by establishing concrete adoption goals. Cheung added that Hong Kong must also introduce a unique indicator for internationalisation to set itself apart. “Take languages as an example – different regions have different linguistic environments. On the mainland, AI is largely Chinese-centric, whereas in Western countries, AI is predominantly English-focused,” Cheung said. “Can Hong Kong set policy benchmarks to track whether our AI adoption and content can seamlessly cater to both languages?” he added, noting that Hong Kong must outperform regional competitors such as Singapore in bilingual execution to maintain its edge. Hong Kong has also taken the initiative to expand AI adoption in the education sector to facilitate teaching and learning, while enhancing digital literacy among students. In June this year, authorities rolled out the Blueprint for Digital Education Development in Primary and Secondary Schools, requiring teachers to undergo digital education training and schools to integrate AI education strategies into their annual development plans. Earlier in 2023, the Education Bureau also introduced an AI curriculum for junior secondary students, covering basic concepts, ethical issues and social effects of the technology. Major universities in Hong Kong have also launched AI literacy initiatives for students, with some institutions making completion of such programmes a graduation requirement. Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said allowing students to learn about AI as early as primary school would be “a positive step” to foster talent and drive widespread AI adoption. He said it was crucial to update the curriculums and teach students from an early age how to gather information with AI, frame appropriate questions and address its underlying limitations and biases, as well as to fact-check and exercise independent decision-making rather than relying on generated answers. For Cheung, although these measures offer some policy guidance on promoting digital education, clearer operational indicators – such as how to approach execution and who is held accountable – must be set out. He added that more resources should be devoted to training people rather than mere hardware upgrades, while an integrated AI education framework should be introduced to bridge classroom learning and real-world application. Despite these shared goals, a policy debate remains over whether Hong Kong needs a dedicated strategy. A recent Legislative Council research report noted that nearly 70 economies globally had promulgated stand-alone AI development strategies – a document currently absent in Hong Kong. Instead, the government identified AI as a strategic priority under its broader Innovation and Technology Development Blueprint in 2022. The report also cited an International Monetary Fund report in 2024 that Hong Kong ranked 20th out of 174 economies in overall AI preparedness, trailing many regional markets including Singapore, Japan and South Korea. All experts agreed that keeping AI at the top of Hong Kong’s policy agenda would be essential to closing the regional gap, with Cheung calling for a stand-alone strategy under which a dedicated cross-bureau task force was formed to drive overall AI development and use. Shui supported the idea of devising a comprehensive AI development blueprint in the city. He said the committee chaired by finance minister Chan could help formulate the plan, which shall establish medium- to long-term plans alongside quantifiable key performance indicators. “For instance, there could be specific targets to boost AI adoption rates, measure how much AI should contribute to GDP growth, or define target figures for increasing the supply of AI talent – for Hong Kong as a whole or for specific industries,” Shui said, adding that having clear objectives enabled regular progress reviews and adjustments. He also agreed that refining data governance would be helpful in reassuring residents in handing their data over to government-managed AI, so as to enhance the use of AI in public services. In response to the South China Morning Post’s inquiries, the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the authorities had been promoting the wider and deeper application of AI in public administration to enhance operational efficiency and provide more convenient public services. The bureau added that it had also launched various subsidy schemes to promote digital transformation across different industries. “These multidimensional AI policies and specific measures are not only in line with the national ‘AI+’ initiative but also highly coherent with the global development path of AI,” it said. CityU’s Cheung said Hong Kong did not need to compare itself with other places. “As the Chinese saying goes, ‘those who start later can still arrive first and overtake’,” he said. “What I care about most is whether Hong Kong is making progress and whether we have the determination to press forward in this direction.”

title: Is the yen carry trade starting to unravel as Japan’s currency strengthens?
description: The trade relies on borrowing cheap yen to invest in higher-returning assets overseas, but analysts say the strategy faces mounting pressure.
content: The Japanese yen has climbed from multi-decade lows, driven by shifting policy expectations and returning domestic capital, putting the yen carry trade – a popular global investment strategy – back in the spotlight and raising questions about its long-term viability. Having strengthened by more than 3 per cent since the start of the month to about 153.5 against the US dollar, the currency is trading near a seven-month high and above levels reached after a rare joint US-Japan market intervention in July. Matteo Giovannini, senior finance manager at Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, attributed the strengthening to a mix of factors: the possibility of a narrowing US-Japan yield gap, some scaling back of short-yen positions and growing expectations of a Bank of Japan (BOJ) rate hike. “A stronger yen and greater expectations of BOJ tightening make the carry trade less attractive because the cost of funding positions in yen is rising while the risk of exchange-rate losses increases,” Giovannini said. Markets have priced in a 0.25 percentage point rate hike at next week’s BOJ meeting, which would lift Japan’s benchmark interest rate to 1.25 per cent – its highest level since 1995. That could help narrow Japan’s wide interest rate gap with the United States, which has historically fuelled the yen carry trade by allowing investors to borrow cheaply in yen to finance investments in higher-yielding assets overseas. While Giovannini expects investors to reduce their leverage and exercise more caution, he said the trade was unlikely to disappear as long as a significant yield gap remained between Japan and other major economies. Carlos Casanova, a senior economist at Union Bancaire Privee, noted that while the carry trade’s risk-reward profile had worsened, it was still supported by a US-Japan policy rate gap of about 2.75 percentage points. “Expectations of further Fed [US Federal Reserve] tightening mean that this differential is not expected to narrow materially in the immediate term, which should allow the yen carry trade to remain broadly intact,” Casanova said. Although the Fed was previously expected to hold rates steady for the rest of the year, persistent inflation data has increased the likelihood of a rate hike at its meeting next week. But risks to the carry trade, Casanova warned, could emerge if markets began anticipating a faster pace of BOJ tightening relative to the Fed over the coming year. Investors, he noted, were currently interpreting the BOJ’s forward guidance as increasingly hawkish, pricing in an additional 0.75 to 1 percentage point tightening over the next six months and a terminal policy rate of about 2 per cent. “For now, however, this remains a market expectation rather than an explicit signal from the Monetary Policy Board,” Casanova said, expressing scepticism over aggressive market assumptions and noting that coming central bank meetings would provide greater clarity. Competition for capital is already intensifying among major Japanese institutional investors. Tang Yuxuan, head of Asia rates and FX strategy at JP Morgan Private Bank, noted that institutional repatriation – the return of capital to home markets – had also helped drive the yen’s recent rally. “Higher domestic yields and increasing urges from policymakers are improving the incentives for large foreign asset holders to rebalance towards domestic assets,” Tang said, citing movements by major investors including Japan’s US$1.8 trillion Government Pension Investment Fund. In a note published on Tuesday, Tang added that returning domestic capital could offer a more sustainable source of support for the yen than repeated, direct market interventions by authorities. But she said such allocation shifts were likely to be gradual, serving to stabilise the yen rather than drive a lasting rally against the US dollar. “Durable FX market stabilisation ultimately requires the BOJ to meaningfully accelerate rate hikes,” she said.

title: China targets ‘toxic’ traffic as viral sensations upend daily life and public services
description: From content creators to organised fan groups, state media and local authorities urge greater awareness of boundaries and restraint.
content: Authorities in China are taking content creators, fan groups and online platforms to task as their aggressive pursuit of online traffic upends lives and public services across the country. State media and local authorities have called on these parties to exercise restraint and stop attention-seeking behaviour from getting out of control. The warnings followed a wave of public attention that hit a 75-year-old man and his wife in Shaoxing in eastern Zhejiang province this month. Crowds of visitors, live streamers and photographers descended on the couple’s home to see seven gourds growing on their balcony, a scene reminiscent of Calabash Brothers, a popular Chinese animated series released in 1986. The series follows seven magical brothers born from gourds and raised by their grandfather. Videos and images of the couple in Shaoxing and their gourds quickly went viral, with internet users dubbing the man “Grandpa Calabash”. However, as more visitors began gathering outside the home, taking photographs, live-streaming, calling out “grandpa” and knocking on the door, what began as an expression of affection increasingly disrupted the couple’s daily life, eventually leading them to cut down all the gourds last Saturday. The incident showed a need to maintain boundaries between public attention and private life, wrote People’s Daily, a Communist Party mouthpiece, in a commentary published on Tuesday. “Without boundaries, even genuine kindness can change its meaning; care without restraint can become a burden that others can hardly bear.” It cited other similar cases, including a tree in a wheat field in Xian, Shaanxi province that became an online sensation earlier this year for its scenic view. Visitors thronged the field and damaged crops, prompting a villager to cut the tree’s crown to protect the crops. And in Wuhan, Hubei province, in 2022, a man dubbed “Grandpa Sugar Water” had to close his stall after his low-cost sugar-water business of 17 years went viral and questions surfaced about its hygiene. The Zhejiang provincial publicity department made a similar point in a recent commentary, saying that once ordinary people were thrust into the spotlight by algorithms, “their lives could hardly completely belong to themselves”. Posted on the department’s social media account, the commentary said traffic came with its own “cruel logic” and that the online world often left little room for ordinary people who did not seek fame to make a “dignified exit”. The commentary called on local authorities to be more discerning in how they responded to online traffic, rather than embracing every burst of attention as a way to boost local tourism. Viral attention could bring short-term tourism benefits, but private spaces should not simply be turned into tourist attractions and online popularity did not necessarily create lasting value for tourism, it said. In recent years, a number of places in China had become overnight online sensations, drawing waves of visitors, the commentary said, describing them as having brought excitement and tourism revenue as well as congestion, higher prices, and disruptions to residents’ daily lives. “Traffic cannot simply be regarded as a gift that brings benefits without harm,” it said. The tension between online attention and offline capacity has extended to public services. In Xuzhou, in eastern Jiangsu province, nearly 49,000 complaints were filed with a government public service platform over a 10-day period in late August, mostly regarding concerts by a boy band, as rival fan groups argued over the staging of performances. Most of the submissions came from fans of the band, with a small number of parents of fans also involved, said “Xuzhou 12345”, a social media account affiliated with the official public service platform, in an article published on September 1. The surge forced the Xuzhou 12345 hotline to activate an emergency response mechanism, with staff working round the clock to handle and follow up on submissions. According to the article, all service operators were mobilised, while the number of night-shift operators was increased from 15 to 43 to cope with the spike in requests. The article was taken down after it drew online attention. In a September 4 article, People’s Daily said citizens had the right to use the channel to express legitimate concerns but lamented that the mass mobilisation of fans had turned a public service into a “battleground for fandom disputes”. “This was far more than simple fan enthusiasm,” the commentary said of the Xuzhou incident, calling it “an aggressive intrusion of toxic fan culture into public spaces”. On September 2, popular Chinese microblog service Weibo reported that accounts involved in mobilising fans to use government hotlines to pressure authorities over disagreements had been muted. “Public resources are not a ‘wish pool’ for individuals or certain groups but a limited social ‘first aid kit’,” People’s Daily said. The newspaper also warned that repeatedly or excessively occupying public hotline resources without legitimate reason could incur legal liability. It urged greater public awareness and further discussions of the boundaries for using public resources.

title: When Indonesia burns, these women run towards the fire
description: Meet the all-female volunteer brigade risking their lungs and lives to fight Indonesia’s devastating wildfires.
content: Irma smells the fire before she sees it: a column of thick, yellow-tinged smoke rising above the tree line near her small wooden home. She pulls on heavy rubber boots, checks her equipment and drives straight into the impenetrable smog emanating from wildfires devouring the peatland and ancient forests of Borneo. “I am terrified that the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous,” the 39-year-old mother told This Week in Asia, moments before disappearing into the murk that has settled over the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan. Irma, who like many Indonesians only goes by one name, is one of roughly 150 Muslim women who make up Power of Mama, an all-female volunteer firefighting unit that heads out every day during the dry season to battle blazes smouldering deep beneath the island’s peatlands. They fight fires lit, deliberately or otherwise, by the agricultural burning of poor farming communities clearing land the cheapest way they know how. This year, those fires arrived earlier and burned harder than most can remember, fuelled climate anomalies and drought conditions. “We are the ones who feel its effects most,” said Irma, who is the group’s coordinator, explaining that it was women who were left to care for housebound children through increasingly long stretches of the year. “The haze causes the airports and schools to close, and it makes our community ill. I thought I had to do something about it.” Indonesia has an estimated 206,000 square km (79,500 square miles) of tropical peatland, making up about 10.8 per cent of its total land area and the most carbon-dense store of its kind anywhere on Earth. When the peatlands burn, they release thousands of tonnes of greenhouse gases into the air, fuelling a vicious cycle that drives global warming and worsens each year’s drought. Smog from the wildfires then drifts over Singapore, Malaysia and further afield – poisoning the air and damaging lungs as it does so. Peatlands are normally waterlogged, but most of Borneo has not seen heavy rain since late June. Decades of deforestation and drainage for palm oil plantations and other intensive agriculture have helped create a wildlife crisis that each year consumes vast tracts of the country, destroying the last natural habitat of some of the world’s rarest species, from orangutans and hornbills to pangolins. From her village in Ketapang regency, Irma has witnessed the damage first-hand. “We used to see wild boars, deer, muntjacs and even sun bears; we had hornbills, but now it seems as if they have disappeared,” she said. Authorities say more than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) of Indonesia burned between January and July – an area nearly twice the size of Hong Kong. The Sipongi monitoring website of Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry had recorded 8,638 hotspots across Kalimantan by the end of August. Ketapang, where Irma lives, accounted for about one in five of those fires, placing her volunteer group right on the front line. Hard hats and hosepipes Wearing hard hats or motorcycle helmets over their jilbabs, the Power of Mama volunteers haul long hosepipes into singed forest and fields, their bright red uniforms the only splash of colour against the scorched earth. Most wear thin surgical masks or cloth coverings for protection while they carry out their gruelling, unpaid work. The small creeks and rivers that once served as natural firebreaks had been drying up since June, Irma said – forcing the volunteer firefighters to linger at the edge of forests or plantations as they try to douse the flames wherever they can. The group was formed in 2022 by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), the local affiliate of global non-profit International Animal Rescue. Translating to the Indonesian Nature Rehabilitation Initiatives Foundation, YIARI operates with a mandate that extends well beyond firefighting. “This isn’t just about putting out fires,” YIARI founder and CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said. “It’s about seeing these women become more confident and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.” Members are trained to fly surveillance drones and lead community outreach as well as fight the fires, which can be very difficult to put out. “You can’t see the flames,” Sanchez explained. “But the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.” Back on patrol, Suriati, 32, and Ratinah, 56, both of whom also go by a single name, pick their way along a narrow track towards the edge of the forest. “We often fall off our motorbikes,” Ratinah said. “Particularly during the rainy season when it’s slippery and muddy.” Fire is not the only obstacle. In a conservative, male-dominated society, the women’s authority is regularly tested by the neighbours they are trying to protect. “Sometimes they won’t accept it,” said Suriati, a housewife who runs a small grocery stall alongside her firefighting duties. “They feel that we are being patronising. They say ‘what do housewives know’? With the older people in particular, we cannot simply forbid them … we have to treat them gently.” When the rains finally do arrive, the volunteers will turn to advising farmers on controlled burning and nitrogen-restoring alternatives to slash-and-burn agriculture, rehabilitating degraded mangroves and teaching schoolchildren about how to steward the land their parents have been setting alight. The night shift For Ely Marlina, 46, the fires are personal. She joined the volunteers after the 2019 fire season, when Ketapang regency alone logged more than 1,000 hotspots and doctors reported an alarming spike in chronic breathing conditions among children. By day, Ely teaches at a junior high school. By night, she fights fires. It was already dark when word reached her of a recent blaze less than 3km (1.86 miles) from her home in Sungai Awan Kiri village, West Kalimantan. “Some of the residents’ houses were about 100 metres away and the distance to the densely populated residential area was only about 200 or 300 metres,” she recalled. At the scene, she climbed onto a fire truck to rig water pumps, hosepipes and portable tanks, then joined the other members of her team hauling the equipment towards the flames. “The area was peatland,” the 46-year-old said. “The ground was very dangerous. My leg even slipped and sank half a metre into the peat.” Hours later, the fire was finally extinguished – a small victory for Ely and her exhausted team, in a battle that begins again with every sunrise. “Like it or not we have to stay on guard during the dry season,” she said. “The people depend on us.”

title: Letters | Let’s protect Hong Kong’s children from social media ourselves
description: Readers discuss how the city should shield children from social media’s harmful effects, and the public healthcare system.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Meta Platforms has agreed to pay up to US$18 billion to settle the social media harm case brought by US state attorneys general, and to implement default protections for teens, including a two-hour daily limit. A company does not agree to a sum like that over a misunderstanding. In Hong Kong, the company has started helping parents protect teenagers online. While it deserves credit for both moves, they don’t undo what has already happened. Litigation was needed to change a handful of settings and there has been no settlement outside the United States. The harm of the past decade was not reversed last month, and our students are still carrying it. Dr Lam Ching-choi, chairman of the Advisory Committee on Mental Health, has said that prevention is always better than cure, and that the first tier of a proposed three-tier mental health support model must be broad. The Education Bureau’s digital education blueprint requires schools to write digital education into school development plans. The blueprint appears to focus more on artificial intelligence than social media, though social media platforms shape students’ lives just as much. Schools need not wait for a policy covering social media. In my view, the work of preventing harm to children’s mental health starts with us adults using our own phones less frequently in front of them. Next come clear boundaries, set by schools rather than left to individual teachers, between when these tools help students learn and when they stand in the way. In the 88 primary schools we work with, we have found that what protects children is relationships. A child who has one adult at school who knows them, and classmates they can be honest with, needs no screen to feel worthy. The term began on September 1. Use these first weeks to tell students they are valued and loved. A child who is understood at school is less likely to be looking for a chatbot at midnight. Raymond Yang Sze-ngai, co-founder and executive director, Just Feel Public hospital service delivery needs improvement It appears that the Hospital Authority prefers to stay silent on my grievance about the treatment I received at a public hospital (“Cardiac patient decries wait times”, August 6). In September 2024, I was referred by a private doctor to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital for the treatment of left ventricular hypertrophy – a condition I had not heard of before – after it was detected by an electrocardiogram. After waiting 20 months, it was finally my turn to see a public doctor in July this year. The doctor simply told me that I needed another ECG as well as an echocardiogram. I was then scheduled to do the former in January 2027 and the latter in October 2030. Given resource constraints, I understand the need to queue for a public doctor, though a 20-month wait for an initial consultation appears excessive. Nevertheless, I am deeply disappointed that I have to wait six months for one diagnostic test and more than four years for another. Furthermore, I have yet to be advised of the implications of my condition, let alone a treatment plan. My case is by no means an isolated one. If what I experienced is the norm, there must be something seriously amiss within our public healthcare system. The more-than-four-year wait for a diagnostic test makes a mockery of our healthcare authority’s recent emphasis on shifting healthcare priorities from curative treatment to disease prevention and early diagnosis. It also runs counter to the spirit of our chief executive’s oft-cited motto: “People’s livelihood is no small matter.” To ensure that our healthcare policies and services are truly user-centred, it is high time our government considered initiating a public consultation exercise to gather feedback from all key stakeholders – with a particular focus on patients’ perspectives – on how to address the flaws of current healthcare arrangements and improve service delivery. It might be wishful thinking on my part, but I earnestly hope to see this initiative considered for inclusion in the chief executive’s coming policy address. S.B. Lai, Chai Wan

title: What is AGI? How China’s AI firms are catching up as OpenAI Astra sparks debate
description: A primer on what AGI means, where top Chinese AI developers stand, and how Chinese policymakers view the technology.
content: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s declaration that artificial general intelligence (AGI) has arrived following the release of OpenAI’s latest model, Astra, has ignited debate over whether AI’s holy grail is now reality. As China races to close the gap with the US, leading Chinese AI companies are declaring their ambitions to pursue AGI, even as Beijing appears to maintain a cautious stance towards the concept. Here is a primer on what AGI means, where top Chinese AI developers stand, and how Chinese policymakers view the technology. What is AGI? There is no single definition for AGI, though it broadly refers to systems that match or surpass human-level intelligence. First coined by US physicist Mark Gubrud in 1997, the term was popularised in the 2000s by computer scientists Ben Goertzel – author of the book Artificial General Intelligence – and Shane Legg, co-founder of Google DeepMind. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have triggered new efforts to define it. A widely cited paper in December by researchers – including Dan Hendrycks from the Center for AI Safety and Dawn Song from the University of California, Berkeley – defined AGI as AI matching the “versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult” across 10 cognitive components, such as reading and reasoning. Google DeepMind researchers argued in March that existing definitions “failed to cover the full breadth of human cognition”, proposing a 10-faculty framework evaluated against human perception, problem solving, social cognition and other abilities. Has AGI been achieved? Experts remain sharply divided. While scholars like University of California, San Diego’s Eddy Keming Chen and Mikhail Belkin argued in February that current LLMs already displayed the flexible, general competence characteristic of human thought, many view Huang’s declaration as premature. Researchers including Hendrycks noted that while current models were “far smarter” at specific tasks, they lacked essential cognitive capabilities. Critical prerequisites such as long-term memory and continuous learning remained missing in deployed systems, according to Alvin Wang Graylin, digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centred AI. “Jensen Huang’s declaration tells us more about Nvidia’s order book than the state of the AI industry,” Graylin said. Technology analyst Ben Thompson wrote out on Tuesday that models still did not continuously self-learn. Are Chinese AI labs pushing for AGI? Top executives across China’s leading AI firms have made AGI their explicit objective. DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng told potential investors in a private meeting in May that “increasing the probability of achieving AGI” was his top priority, citing “keeping costs low for users” as a key strategy for reaching that goal. Z.ai founder Tang Jie pledged in an internal letter in July to prioritise AGI over near-term commercialisation, defining AGI as the “aggregation of all human intelligence”. MiniMax founder and CEO Yan Junjie vowed in July to forgo his salary until the company achieves AGI. In a podcast discussion in 2024, Moonshot founder Yang Zhilin framed AGI as a high-stakes “moonshot” goal, while Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – said last year it saw an “increasingly clear trajectory” from AI agents to AGI and superintelligence. How does Beijing view AGI? While China’s 15th five-year plan published in March mentioned “exploring development paths for general artificial intelligence”, analysts have cautioned against equating Beijing’s terminology with Silicon Valley’s definition of AGI. Kyle Chan, a fellow at Brookings Institution, noted in a February article that Chinese authorities used the term to mean “general-purpose AI” rather than human-surpassing autonomous intelligence. “Policy is organised around technology diffusion, open-source weights and sovereign compute,” Graylin said. AGI was “not the North Star for the AI community in China the way it is in Silicon Valley”, Jacob Stokes, senior fellow at the Center for a New American Security, wrote in a report last month. Beijing’s focus remained on risk mitigation and state control. At the World AI Conference in Shanghai in July, President Xi Jinping reiterated that AI must be safe, secure and under human control.

title: Your Voice: Munsang College’s centenary musical, fast fashion crisis, elder scam awareness
description: This week, students write about preparing for a school performance, the impact of fast fashion, scam awareness tips for the elderly and being kind online.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
“When do you think this musical will come together?” I placed my neatly stapled script of Munsang College’s centenary musical, PHILO・SOPHIA , down and directed the question at our director. We were weeks into production, surrounded by piles of costumes and the echoing chords of the piano, yet the finish line felt miles away. With a knowing twinkle in his eyes, he laughed and replied, “We don’t get to control it. It’s like … kindling catching fire. When the moment comes, it will all come together and set the stage ablaze.”
At that time, his words felt like an abstract promise, contrasting sharply with our chaotic reality. As the assistant director, I served as the primary liaison among the creative teams, the backstage crew and the actors. My daily routine was a relentless cycle of communication – balancing logistics, interpreting the artistic vision and piecing together the various moving parts. From this central viewpoint, I witnessed the transformation unfold.
The journey began quietly in the rehearsal room, where hesitant voices blended as they searched for their pitch. However, sparks flickered in the actors’ eyes as they dedicated themselves to memorising the complex harmonies, refusing to be held back by the challenging scores.
That same determination carried over to the dance floor, where exhausting sessions left everyone breathless. Even in moments of fatigue, specks of light swayed to the music, gradually transforming awkward choreography into fluid, synchronised storytelling.
The dramatic scenes presented a different kind of challenge – a frustrating process of trial and error. Yet, glow-worms sparkled the moment the cast finally understood their characters, breathing authentic life and vulnerability into the script.
