Meanwhile, a chaotic dance was unfolding backstage. The crew initially navigated a maze of heavy stair units and misplaced props during early scene changes. However, over time, they began to master the transitions with stealthy precision, and the atmosphere crackled with energy.
Nearby in the dressing rooms, the repetitive tasks of pinning, measuring, and sketching designs faded away the moment the ensemble slipped into their vibrant costumes, lighting up the space with bright flashes of colour. In the orchestra pit below, the atmosphere was equally charged. What began as a chaotic blend of tuning instruments and complex rhythms soon transformed into a harmonious collaboration. As the musicians beautifully aligned their melodies with the singers on stage, a brilliant energy ignited, uniting the entire production.
As May approached, these isolated sparks began to drift towards one another.
With over 600 students, teachers and alums working hand in hand and united in spirit, the stress of preparation transformed into pure energy, leading to seamless performances. When the final curtain fell and a thunderous round of applause erupted, I looked around and saw our team shedding tears of joy. In that moment, I realised that the fire had truly ignited within us all.
The journey of PHILO・SOPHIA is too bright to keep to ourselves. You can visit Munsang College’s website to experience our show completely free of charge.
Penelope Hoad, Hong Kong International School
When you walk through any shopping district in Hong Kong, you’ll find racks of clothes that are popular online, often sold at tempting prices. New styles emerge almost overnight, prompting people to stay up to date with the latest trends.
However, beneath this ongoing cycle of fashion lies a more profound story with significant environmental, social, and cultural impacts.
Fast fashion has transformed how people buy and wear clothes. Brands like Zara, H&M and Shein release new collections at a rapid pace, making it easy for customers to stay fashionable without spending much.
In Hong Kong, shopping is not just a necessity; it is a lifestyle. The availability of affordable and trendy clothing promotes a culture of frequent consumption.
Fast fashion allows people to access affordable clothing easily, but this convenience comes at a high cost. The environmental impact of fast fashion is substantial. The production of clothing requires a vast amount of water, energy and chemicals. Additionally, synthetic materials like polyester and nylon shed microplastics when washed, which eventually pollute our waterways.
As a coastal city, Hong Kong is especially vulnerable to marine pollution. Furthermore, the city is grappling with a major waste crisis, as textile waste puts added pressure on its limited landfill space.
This issue goes beyond just environmental concerns. Many garments are produced in factories where workers are paid low wages and often face unsafe working conditions. Every time you make a purchase, it can overshadow someone else’s right to work in a safe environment.
Fast fashion fosters a “throwaway” mindset, where clothing is often worn just a few times before being discarded. This occurs either because items are no longer trendy or because the low-quality materials cause them to wear out quickly.
Despite the challenges, Hong Kong is making strides towards change. Some local designers are adopting eco-friendly practices. Second-hand shops and clothing swap events are gaining popularity, offering alternatives to the constant cycle of buying new clothes.
Additionally, various organisations are promoting sustainable fashion through educational initiatives and design competitions. You can contribute to this change by making simple choices, such as buying fewer items, opting for higher-quality clothing, supporting ethical brands or recycling old garments.
While fast fashion may provide convenience and affordability, its hidden costs are too significant to overlook. For Hong Kong, the challenge lies in moving towards a future where style, sustainability and responsibility coexist harmoniously.
Chan Yin-tung, Po Leung Kuk Ho Yuk Ching (1984) College
It is not uncommon for elderly people in Hong Kong to fall victim to phone scams. Elderly individuals often suffer from isolation. Many of them spend significant time alone or without support, making them vulnerable to scammers.
Scammers frequently adopt a friendly demeanour to gain the trust of the elderly, exploiting their desire for companionship and attention.
They also often have low digital literacy. This lack of familiarity with technology can make them vulnerable to scams. For instance, when they receive suspicious links, they may open them without hesitation.
To address the root of the problem, several suggestions can be considered. The government should raise public awareness about elderly phone scams. By using advertisements and billboards, the government can alert the community to the seriousness of these scams affecting the elderly.
Young people can also play a crucial role in educating older adults on how to use their phones safely. Given their higher digital literacy, young individuals can help combat scams by teaching them to avoid potential pitfalls.
In conclusion, it is clear that both the government and young people can contribute to solving this problem. So why not take action starting now?
In an age when nearly everyone is connected to the internet, it is concerning to see how easily technology is used to harm others rather than unite us.
When we use social media or messaging apps, it is easy to forget that there is a real person on the other side of the screen. This can lead people to say hurtful things they would never say in person. The anonymity of the online world may give some a sense of power, but in reality, it’s a cowardly way to treat others.
Online harassment can result in loneliness, anxiety and depression.
A person who is targeted online may feel like they have nowhere to escape the abuse. Their phone, which should serve as a tool for connection, becomes a source of fear. It is distressing to know that someone is trying to damage your reputation, and it is worse when that abuse seems to follow everywhere you go.
Too often, people simply stand by and watch when someone is being bullied because they are afraid to get involved or do not want to become the next target. When we observe any form of harassment, we must take action. This means standing up, reporting the behaviour and supporting the victim.
The internet has the potential to be a place for learning, creativity and friendship. It is up to us to ensure it remains that way.

title: Trump says Irish unification would be ‘a  fantastic thing’
description: Trump made the comment on the way to visit his luxury resort in Doonbeg on Ireland’s west coast to watch the Irish Open golf tournament.
content: US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he would “love to see” a united Ireland, wading into a politically sensitive subject as he embarked on a two-day Irish visit that blurs the lines between his presidency and personal business interests. After meeting Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland – split for over a century – would be “a fantastic thing”. “The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now,” he told reporters, adding though that “the UK will have something to say about it, obviously”. The island of Ireland has been split between the Irish republic in the south and Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom, since 1921. Under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland that killed about 3,000 people, a referendum can be held if the UK government determines a majority there is likely to favour joining the Republic of Ireland. The people of the Republic of Ireland would also have to vote in favour for reunification to occur. The United States has previously adopted a position of neutrality on the issue. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted last month that a unity referendum was “off the table”, drawing a sharp response from the pro-unity party Sinn Fein. “As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic,” Gavin Robinson, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, said on social media in response to Trump’s comments. The US president touched down at Dublin airport in his Qatari-gifted plane shortly before 8.25am local time under a security operation dubbed one of the largest ever mounted in Ireland. At least 4,000 police and other personnel, including snipers, are mobilised for the visit, which will see Trump fly to his luxury resort in Doonbeg on Ireland’s west coast to watch the Irish Open golf tournament. He inspected a military guard of honour after being received by left-wing President Catherine Connolly, an outspoken critic of the US leader. He then met Martin, when the Iran war and US tariffs on EU pharmaceuticals and immigration were on the agenda. Ireland and the United States have long been close allies, partly because of their common ancestral ties. But the Irish government’s politics diverge sharply from those of the Trump administration on many issues, with Ireland being one of Europe’s most pro-Palestinian countries. Ireland is among several countries, including Spain, the UK and France, that have announced a trade ban targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. After a brief visit to the US embassy, Trump was due to fly to his Doonbeg resort – a remote, coastal site in County Clare that the Trump Organisation bought in 2014. His attendance at the Irish Open adds an extra layer of complexity to a security effort that is reportedly costing Ireland €20 million (US$23 million). It comes with the country already grappling with a massive policing operation for its six-month presidency of the EU. Some 40,000 fans are expected at the tournament over the weekend, with six-time major winner and current world number two Rory McIlroy the main draw. McIlroy, who has played golf with Trump, told the BBC this week that the tournament will feel “different” with the US president on site, but that the players will just “keep our heads down and play”. The 80-year-old billionaire has promoted his family’s golf business unabashedly since returning to the White House for his second stint as president in January 2025. Last summer, he welcomed then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer and European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen to his plush resort at Turnberry on the west coast of Scotland. Trump then inaugurated another golf course bearing his name in the town of Balmedie, near Aberdeen on the northeast Scottish coast. The golf-mad president – whose relaxed relationship with the game’s rules was documented by sports journalist Rick Reilly in the 2019 book Commander in Cheat – may even award the trophy on Sunday. “He’s really just visiting the golf resort he owns and dropping into Dublin for a courtesy visit,” Daniel Geary, a US history professor at Trinity College Dublin, said. “He sees little difference between his private interests and his role as president.”

title: US declares end to lettuce parasite outbreak that killed 2
description: Nearly 13,000 people fell ill across 21 states in the nation’s largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak.
content: US health authorities on Friday declared the ⁠nation’s largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak ⁠over, after contaminated iceberg lettuce sickened thousands, though ⁠the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it was still investigating how the parasite entered the food supply. The outbreak, which federal investigators linked to lettuce from central Mexico sourced by Taylor Farms, prompted one of the largest food recalls in recent years and renewed scrutiny of food-safety controls for imported produce. It also rattled consumer confidence, with some ‌shoppers avoiding raw fruits and vegetables as well as dining out, hurting foot traffic at restaurants such as Taco Bell, Sweetgreen and Chipotle. According to data from the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 12,883 people across 21 states fell ill after consuming contaminated lettuce. The outbreak resulted in 570 hospitalisations and two deaths, and accounted for more than half of the 19,595 laboratory-confirmed US cyclosporiasis cases reported since May 1. At the peak of the outbreak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections ⁠were reported in a single day. In August, infections had fallen to fewer than two per day on average, the CDC said. “I ‌don’t think that we have the necessary tools and technologies to stop outbreaks like this in the future,” said Donald Schaffner, a professor and extension specialist in food science at Rutgers University. Schaffner called for ‌better strain-tracking tools and sustained funding for parasite research to prevent such outbreaks. The FDA said on Friday it was ⁠confident that all recalled iceberg ⁠lettuce linked to the outbreak was off the market. The CDC said best-by dates for all products linked to the outbreak had passed and the lettuce would ‌no longer be available in shops or restaurants. Taylor Farms recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 17. The FDA also said it had completed on-site ‌inspections and collected ‌samples from lettuce farms and the processing facility in Mexico, with analysis pending, and would continue working with US, Mexican and ‌state partners. “Our facility in central Mexico remains closed while the investigations by the FDA, our team, and independent experts are being completed,” ⁠Taylor Farms said in a statement. Retailers Walmart, Whole Foods and restaurant chains Taco Bell (Yum Brands), Chipotle Mexican Grill and Sweetgreen did ⁠not respond to requests for comment. Target declined to comment. Michigan, the state hardest hit by the outbreak, reported more than 14,000 cases and two deaths linked to the parasite, according to federal and state health officials. Ohio ‌and Missouri also saw thousands of ‌infections tied to contaminated lettuce from Taylor Farms. Unusually high case totals from Michigan were attributed to a large backlog of reports processed in August, highlighting the strain on a system weakened by federal funding cuts under the Trump administration. Before 2026, the largest US cyclosporiasis season on record was reported in 2019, when roughly 4,700 illnesses were documented nationwide.

title: Philippines bets big on rail, but can it fix a broken transport network?
description: A US$4.8 billion transport budget will not end Manila’s gridlock unless bus and jeepney services also improve, analysts say.
content: A two-hour commute for a 14km (8.7-mile) journey. For Julius Dalay and millions of other Filipinos, this is just how public transport works in Manila: a mishmash of jeepneys, trains and buses that commuters are left to figure out for themselves. Dalay, an environmental planner, is resigned to the chaos. Reaching his destination usually involves hailing a jeepney, then cramming into a packed train and enduring a slow bus crawl along the capital’s main thoroughfares. “You either wait the jeepney out, or you pray to God that the vehicles aren’t packed,” he said. The Philippine government now says it wants to change that, with the roll-out of its biggest transport spending plan in years. President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s administration is proposing to more than double the transport department’s budget to 300.96 billion pesos (US$4.8 billion) next year, as it races to push forward major railway projects meant to transform mobility across the congested capital and its surrounding provinces. The Philippines was ranked Asia’s most congested country in the 2025 TomTom traffic index, with Manila placed 14th among the world’s 492 metropolitan areas and Davao City faring even worse, at 11th. But transport planners and commuter advocates warn that money alone will not fix Metro Manila’s problems. The bigger challenge, they say, is making sure existing buses, jeepneys and other modes of public transport are not neglected while costly new projects – still years in the making – get built. For Dalay, the daily commute has turned into even more of a headache since state-owned operator Philippine National Railways suspended services to make way for the North-South Commuter Railway, a 147km (91-mile) link that is slated to connect New Clark City to Calamba in Laguna province by 2029. Services between Malabon in the northwest and Alabang in the south were paused two years ago, pushing commuters onto other rail lines and forms of transport – despite their partial resumption this June. Dalay, who founded the advocacy group Commuters of the Philippines, called the budget increase “necessary”, but warned against putting all the government’s financial eggs in one basket at the expense of other transport systems. He points to the EDSA Carousel, a dedicated bus rapid transit system running along the capital’s main expressway, as a case in point. “Some projects, like the carousel, are getting zero budget – this is detrimental. We can’t neglect the existing systems for the sake of future ones, simply because people need transport now,” Dalay said. Creating a transport ecosystem in which different forms of transport compete for funding rather than complement one another was a “major shortcoming” of the government, said Patricia Mariano, director of AltMobility PH, an advocacy group for pedestrian and commuter rights. “Every mode serves a specific purpose and meets different mobility needs,” she said. Rail baggage The Marcos administration’s decision to sharply increase transport spending comes as the government faces mounting costs for major railway projects, many of which rely on a mix of internal funding and substantial foreign loans. Rail projects in the Philippines could take years to move from planning to operation, said Manuel Jose Camagay, a mechanical engineer and transport, urban and logistics specialist. The Metro Manila subway was one such example, he said, with the project delayed partly because the capital’s development had for decades been planned around roads and private vehicles rather than rail infrastructure. “All developed economies, especially in Europe and Japan, prioritised rail or mass transit as the effective solution to development instead of single-car driving,” he said. Camagay suggested that the proposed budget increase might reflect pressure to accelerate railway construction before Marcos leaves office in 2028. Transport researcher Sandy Mae Gaspay, an associate professor at UP Diliman Institute of Civil Engineering, said financing would still be a challenge given the nature of the loans involved. “It is the Philippines’ obligation to provide the counterpart funds for these loans,” she said, adding that railways were “disproportionately more expensive to build compared to other transport projects”. Gaspay warned that projects such as the North-South Commuter Railway and the Metro Manila Subway could not meet the transport needs of the wider capital region on their own. “They don’t replace the need for a genuinely networked system across Metro Manila and its surrounding regions,” she said. “That network shouldn’t be understood as rail alone. Buses and jeepneys still carry the bulk of daily trips and will continue to for the foreseeable future, so a real network has to integrate rail with these other modes.” Camagay said commuters would eventually benefit from the railway projects, but argued that bus rapid transit systems could deliver faster gains in urban mobility in the meantime, without the need for extensive construction. Corruption was also a concern, he added, warning that simply building infrastructure would achieve little if public works were compromised by dishonest practices. Mariano said the government should also look beyond the capital’s transport demands to other parts of the country. “Considering the rapid growth we’ve been seeing, investments and road space would be best allocated to rail or other mass transit … rather than roads and highways,” she said, adding there was “a strong case for mass transit in other metropolitan cities like Cebu and Davao.” A new hope Even with the Philippines’ chronic public transport issues, analysts welcomed the sheer scale of the projects now under way as a positive shift away from piecemeal infrastructure planning. “What gives me optimism is that there are many ongoing initiatives that are leading to a more integrated outlook,” Gaspay said – though she added that weak coordination between government agencies and local authorities remained a major obstacle. “I’m always hopeful that better days are coming,” said Gene Lambert Giron, an assistant professor on land-use planning at the University of the Philippines Open University. “But the big question is when?” Even Laos, a country which is not as economically prosperous as the Philippines, has long-distance railway infrastructure Gene Lambert Giron, urban planning specialist Giron contrasted the Philippines’ progress with that of other countries in the region. “Imagine, years ago, the economy and infrastructure of Vietnam were behind us. Look at Vietnam now,” he said. “Even Laos, a country which is not as economically prosperous as the Philippines, has long-distance railway infrastructure. Indonesia, also an archipelago, has a functioning long-distance railway infrastructure.” A study published last year by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies found that the country’s public transport system seriously lagged behind that of its Southeast Asian neighbours. Manila’s ambitious transport agenda would only succeed if it stayed focused on the seamless movement of both vehicles and people, Mariano. “Our hope is for the administration to dream bigger: to pursue a mobility renaissance, with a greater focus on the needs of the nearly 90 per cent of Filipinos who rely on public and active transport in their daily lives,” she said.

title: Internal splits threaten to slow Brics’ progress as bloc looks back on 20 years of growth
description: The grouping has emerged as a strong champion of the Global South, but analysts warned that major challenges still lie ahead.
content: Leaders from some of the world’s largest emerging economies are gathering in New Delhi this weekend for a summit marking the 20th anniversary of Brics, a fast-expanding group of developing nations. Chinese President Xi Jinping, along with his Russian and Iranian counterparts Vladimir Putin and Masoud Pezeshkian, are among those meeting in the Indian capital for one of the group’s most closely watched gatherings in years. Brics can point to some achievements over that time, with analysts highlighting its growing influence and role as a champion of the Global South. But serious challenges lie ahead, including major splits on issues such as the best approach to handling the United States and what one observer described as a “bottleneck” impeding its development. The grouping first took shape in 2006 when Brazil, Russia, India and China began informal talks before it was officially established in 2009. It expanded in 2010 to include South Africa, turning it from Bric to Brics. Then Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates joined in 2024, with Indonesia following a year later. A further 10 countries have been brought in as partner nations. Its early focus was on economic cooperation and reforming Western-dominated financial institutions such as the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, which have been widely criticised for not representing the interests of the developing world. But the bloc’s growth means that it has been increasingly seen as an attempt to build an alternative international order. “Brics has not only grown stronger over the past 20 years but it has also achieved some successes,” said Lin Minwang, vice-dean at Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies. He pointed to financial collaborations such as the New Development Bank, which bankrolls infrastructure and development projects in member states, as some of the bloc’s main achievements. Qian Feng, a senior research fellow at the National Strategy Institute at Tsinghua University, said the expanded Brics still had “a lot to offer”, with the grouping now representing over 40 per cent of the world’s population and GDP. He said Brics had established a “new multilateral paradigm”, as a voluntary and non-binding partnership that did not require a formal alliance. Qian added that the bloc had also stepped into gaps left open by existing global institutions of global governance, without trying to overthrow the international order. “Brics is now widely recognised as the leading force in the Global South, which significantly enhances the Global South’s voice and influence on global governance issues,” he said. The grouping had also expanded its scope to include issues such as counterterrorism, cybersecurity, innovation and artificial intelligence, he added. But observers were blunt about the challenges facing the bloc, arguing that its expansion had brought in more competing voices, which slowed its progress and made it harder to reach a consensus. Jiang Shixue, a distinguished professor at Hangzhou Normal University, said the 11 members “cannot speak with one voice on many issues”. Jiang, who is also vice-president of the Expert Committee of the China Think Tank Council for Brics Cooperation (China), added: “The only solution is to continuously strengthen political consensus.” Lin said the expansion had widened divisions within the bloc and had “brought many conflicts into the mix”. “The biggest challenge is the lack of consensus among members on the direction of development [of the Brics], especially since the start of the strategic competition between China and the US,” he said. “Although Brics itself has not said that it is challenging or opposing the United States, some countries remain sceptical.” Qian also pointed to divisions over its stance towards the West, adding that Iran and Russia were the most openly anti-Western members. He also said the bloc was experiencing “growing pains” and even when member states proposed new ways to cooperate, practical outcomes had often been limited. He said that despite its push to reduce the US dollar’s dominance by settling more transactions in local currencies, these only accounted for 20 per cent or so of intraregional deals. This attempt at de-dollarisation has also drawn the ire of US President Donald Trump, who has threatened 100 per cent tariffs if the bloc creates a rival currency. Analysts also pointed to organisational problems within the bloc, such as the lack of a permanent secretariat, which Qian said left it heavily reliant on the coordination capacity of whichever country holds the rotating chair. Lin made a similar point, saying Brics nations had proposed various initiatives but there had been little follow-through. “Because there’s no broad strategic consensus, most of its initiatives have not been implemented,” he said. As a result, it had reached a “bottleneck in its development” with member states only looking for development opportunities on the margins. But observers said there was still much to cheer as the grouping marked 20 years of cooperation. Beijing, for one, has praised Brics as a “key platform for solidarity and cooperation among emerging markets and developing countries”. “Brics countries have been committed to upholding multilateralism, defending fairness and justice, and pursuing common development ever since the grouping was formed. Today, Brics has grown into a real force standing at the forefront of the Global South,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Friday. Qian said the summit this weekend was particularly important given the current turmoil in global affairs. “As the leading group in the Global South, the Brics countries should voice their support for multilateralism and oppose bloc confrontation,” he said.

title: As I see it | Tung Chee-hwa had a clear vision for Hong Kong
description: The city’s first post-handover leader had strategic instincts to spare, but not the tactical and political skills needed for execution.
content: The death of Tung Chee-hwa at age 89 has prompted a necessary reckoning with the legacy of Hong Kong’s first chief executive. Two decades after his resignation, the question endures: was Tung a hapless administrator overwhelmed by crisis, or a prescient leader constrained by circumstance and an unforgiving political environment? The contrasting assessments of political scientist Sonny Lo Shiu-hing and former Central Policy Unit head Lau Siu-kai frame this debate sharply. Their divergent analyses reveal not merely different judgments of one man, but fundamental disagreements about governance, legitimacy, and vision in the post-handover era. Lo’s critique is unforgiving; some consider it unfair. In his 2001 book, Governing Hong Kong: Legitimacy, Communication and Political Decay, he documents systematic institutional deterioration under Tung’s watch – weakened administrative capacity, executive-legislative paralysis, and the erosion of the once-vaunted civil service. Tung was chosen by a 400-member committee rather than universal suffrage, in accordance with the Basic Law. His administration depended entirely on performance-based credibility. When the Asian financial crisis struck months after the handover, followed by a property market collapse that plunged homeowners into negative equity, that fragile foundation crumbled. The ambitious pledge to build 85,000 housing units annually – intended to address affordability – instead became a political albatross when it collided with economic reality. Lo further indicts Tung for his paternalistic leadership style and dismal political communication skills. The administration’s handling of public sentiment culminated in the catastrophic miscalculation over Article 23 national security legislation. Against a backdrop of economic malaise and lingering anxieties from the Sars (severe acute respiratory syndrome) epidemic that killed 299 people, an estimated 500,000 Hong Kong residents took to the streets on July 1, 2003. The proposed legislation was the trigger, but the mass protest was really caused by a combination of social grievances and the economic downturn. The government’s subsequent withdrawal of the bill was a humiliating climbdown. By December 2004, even Beijing was expressing concerns. His resignation three months later, ostensibly on health grounds, surprised no one. By contrast, Lau Siu-kai rates Tung highly, praising his strategic foresight and even considering him a visionary. Lau argues that Tung, unburdened by civil service orthodoxy, recognised early that Hong Kong’s over-reliance on finance and property posed structural risks. He pushed economic diversification and the development of innovation and technology – priorities that now dominate government policy. Tung’s attempts to move beyond the colonial-era philosophy of “positive non-intervention” towards a more proactive government role presaged current approaches. His introduction of the Principal Officials Accountability System during his second term sought to inject political responsiveness into an entrenched bureaucracy resistant to change. Few leaders could have survived unscathed, in quick succession, the Asian financial crisis, the Sars and bird flu outbreaks and collapse of the Hong Kong property market. The trajectory of several Tung initiatives lends credence to this revisionist view. Cyberport, once derided as property development masquerading as technology policy, has evolved into a genuine innovation hub. The Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement (Cepa) and Individual Visit Scheme, introduced after the 2003 protests, laid the foundations for closer mainland integration that current leaders continue to build upon. Even the Article 23 legislation – politically toxic in 2003 – was finally enacted in revised form in 2024, vindicated by changed circumstances and public attitudes. Hong Kong’s current chief executive and his successors can learn from both Tung’s insights and his failures Tung was both a visionary and an inadequate leader – a leader whose strategic instincts often outpaced his tactical abilities and political acumen. His recognition of Hong Kong’s need for economic diversification, closer mainland ties, and a more interventionist government proved prescient. These were genuine insights into the city’s structural challenges. Yet foresight was one thing, execution another. His administration was hemmed in by the pan-democrats – some of whom we now know from court testimonies were under foreign influence – and entrenched business and property interests. What reconciles the conflicting perspectives is recognising that Tung operated in an impossible environment: implementing an untested “one country, two systems” framework during severe economic turbulence; managing Beijing’s expectations while navigating fierce local opposition; and steering a bureaucracy whose morale and loyalty were severely tested in the early years of post-handover Hong Kong. Vision and implementation must go hand in hand. Hong Kong’s current chief executive and his successors can learn from both Tung’s insights and his failures. His economic diversification agenda and push for innovation were correct. But the city requires leaders who can combine strategic foresight with the political dexterity to build consensus and maintain public trust. As Hong Kong mourns its first post-handover leader, the fairest judgment may be that Tung saw clearly where the city needed to go, but struggled to bring it there. That is a tragedy of governance. History will likely remember him as a visionary whose vision was compromised by the extraordinary challenges of his era.

title: China teen’s Hong Kong concert trip costs family government subsidies, sparking mixed reaction
description: Girl’s entertainment expenditure, despite being self-funded, contradicts the fundamental intent of the subsidy scheme, says lawyer.
content: A teenage girl in mainland China travelled to Hong Kong to attend a concert of her idol, resulting in her family losing their government living allowances due to her actions being classified as a form of “high-end consumption.” This incident has sparked intense debate in China and has divided public opinion since it was reported by the mainland news portal, The Cover. According to a social media post shared by the girl’s cousin in early September, the girl is a technical secondary school student from Ganzhou in eastern Jiangxi province. She attended a concert in Hong Kong several weeks ago. Her parents, struggling to make a living due to health issues, depend on the city’s living allowance subsidy scheme designed for low-income households, which provides 2,000 yuan (US$300) per month. The girl, whose surname is Huang, informed her family that she could finance her trip to Hong Kong independently. She saved her pocket money and took part in manual labour during the summer holiday, amassing between 3,000 and 5,000 yuan by late August. The identity of her idol has not been disclosed. Before her trip, local community officials cautioned her multiple times that travelling to Hong Kong would result in her family losing their eligibility for government living allowances. This is because self-funded travel abroad is classified as “high-end consumption” behaviour, an official noted, with Hong Kong being regarded as an overseas region. Despite her parents’ repeated attempts to dissuade her from going to Hong Kong, their efforts ultimately proved ineffective. Upon Huang’s return to Ganzhou, the local civil affairs authority informed her family that they would cease their subsidies, as her travel records had been detected by the extensive database, triggering a review process. “Her parents are lamenting that ‘the sky has fallen.’ They are uncertain about what they will do in the future without the government’s aid,” the girl’s cousin wrote in the viral post. “My parents are reassuring her parents and her grandmother. I’m unsure how to comment on her actions. Perhaps she was naive, perhaps she didn’t realise that Hong Kong is considered overseas, or perhaps she was unaware of the potential consequences,” said the cousin. The standards for the living allowance subsidy scheme vary across regions in China, with local authorities modifying these standards annually. Huang’s cousin deleted her post after it gained widespread attention online. On September 7, the government of Ganzhou’s Economic Development Zone, where Huang’s family lives, issued a statement affirming that they are reviewing the case. The statement clarified that the qualification for Huang’s family to receive subsidies has not yet been revoked, and that her cousin posted seeking assistance out of concern for potential repercussions. Li Su, a lawyer from Beijing Huicheng Law Firm, explained that China’s regulations governing social assistance mandate scrutiny of families receiving government subsidies in a “dynamic manner.” If their spending exceeds set standards, the government is empowered to terminate financial aid. “This girl’s entertainment expenditure, even though self-funded, contradicts the intent of the subsidy scheme. Moreover, officials had warned her in advance. Thus, it is justified for the authorities to review and potentially revoke their eligibility,” Li was quoted as saying. “However, I recommend that the authorities carefully assess the extent of subsidy cessation applicable to the family. If the family contests the government’s decision, they have the right to request an administrative review or even file a lawsuit to protect their rights,” the lawyer added. “The government’s subsidy is intended to ensure basic living standards. If you can attend a concert, it indicates that your living conditions exceed the minimum threshold. Therefore, your quota should be allocated to those who are truly in need,” one internet user commented. Conversely, others expressed support for the girl, with one remarking: “She earned the money herself, without resorting to government aid. Her parents’ allowance should not be impacted.”

title: North Korea launches missile salvo after US-South Korea-Japan drills
description: The ballistic missiles, which flew about 250km, were fired despite Donald Trump’s recent push for talks with Kim Jong-un.
content: North Korea fired several short-range ballistic missiles ⁠from the Wonsan area towards the sea off its east coast, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said on Saturday. The missiles were launched at around 5.20am and flew about 250 km (155 miles), the JCS said in a statement, ‌adding that South Korean and US authorities were conducting a detailed analysis of their specifications. South Korean and US intelligence authorities had tracked and shared information on the launches from the outset, while information on the ballistic missiles was also shared with Japan, the JCS said. “South Korea’s military is closely monitoring North Korean activity and maintaining the capability and readiness to respond overwhelmingly to any ⁠provocation under its combined defence posture with the United States,” the JCS said in a statement. South Korea’s ‌presidential National Security Office convened an emergency security meeting involving the defence ministry, the JCS and other relevant agencies following the launch, the presidential office said. Officials reviewed the ‌government’s response, assessed the impact of the launches on South Korea’s security and examined necessary ⁠measures, the presidential office ⁠said. It urged North Korea to immediately stop ballistic missile launches, calling them a serious violation of UN Security Council resolutions. Separately, ‌US Pacific Command said it was aware of the launches and was consulting closely with allies and partners. It said the launches, based ‌on its ‌current assessment, did not pose an immediate threat to US personnel, territory or allies. “The United States ‌remains committed to the defence of the US homeland and our allies in the region,” it said ⁠in a post on social media. Last month, North Korea launched more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles and ordered its ⁠military to maintain full readiness during South Korea’s ongoing joint exercises with the United States. Saturday’s launch came a day after South Korea, Japan and the US concluded their joint military ‌drills to test readiness against North ‌Korea’s missile and nuclear weapons threats. Separately last month, US President Donald Trump abruptly scaled back military drills, which he described as hostile to Pyongyang, and said he expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong-un later this year.

title: Taobao’s ‘ugly’ goods find a growing market among China’s young consumers
description: Items that might have once been seen as unmarketable are going viral online as shoppers embrace quirkiness and novelty over conventional aesthetics.
content: Products widely considered “ugly” or “bizarre” have gone viral online in China as millions of young consumers embrace the items’ quirky humour and distinctive character. Cumulative sales of such products on Taobao – an e-commerce platform of Alibaba Group Holding – have surpassed 230 million yuan (US$34.3 million) since 2020, when Taobao launched its so-called Uglies Award to celebrate creatively unusual goods, the platform said recently without specifying exactly what constitutes an “ugly” product. This year also marks Taobao’s second Treasured Uglies Art Exhibition, themed “Ugly, But Mine”, in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, where the company is based. The exhibition, which covers an area nearly twice as large as last year’s inaugural event, will be open from Saturday to September 27. “Consumers are not just buying oddly shaped goods, but the emotions, stories and self-expression they carry,” said Hu Yu, project lead for the Uglies Award. “Some keep these items on their work desks, while others wear them to show their personal styles. “These offbeat designs help consumers connect with similar people and express who they are.” On Taobao, small, medium and micro enterprises account for 85 per cent of all products, and the broad range of non-standard offerings, combined with a large base of young consumers, helps niche aesthetics find an audience, according to the platform. For instance, legendary figures from ancient cave murals in Dunhuang, Gansu province, have been brought into 3D form. The Dunhuang Academy, which oversees the Unesco World Heritage site, has reimagined them as collectable figures. A winged figure – inspired by an ancient mural and launched last year – has sold more than 70,000 units through online and offline channels, according to the store. “To engage younger consumers with traditional culture, a history lesson is not always the best starting point,” said Huang Sijia, operations lead for the project. “Sometimes, all it takes is a character that feels relatable, friendly and full of delightful surprises.” Meanwhile, the provocatively named Hot Nipples Club, a women’s wear store on Taobao, has nearly 100,000 followers and mainly sells quirky dresses. Its founder, known as Sister Shao, who declined to disclose her full name, quit her job and started the business in 2021. Rather than designing for mainstream aesthetics, the store uses humour, irony and even rebellion to respond to consumers’ emotions. Shao said she expected that her customers would be mostly young people from subcultures, but store data showed that the shoppers have included office workers and civil servants. “People who appear conventional also want to step outside mainstream norms temporarily and show another side of themselves,” she said. Another shop, Out Side Window, sells small, unconventional goods. Its owner, Xia Weiyi, born in 2001, handles both design and sales. She created an apron printed with a guitar, inspired by a moment while cleaning during the Spring Festival, when she imagined a broom as a guitar. Priced at 12 yuan (US$1.79), the apron has sold more than 2,000 pieces. “Some buyers wore the apron to music festivals, K-pop fan-signing events and concerts by Danish rock bands,” Xia said. “Ugly” is not the opposite of beautiful, and this is not about replacing one standard with another, said Liu Tian, the exhibition’s curator and a professor with the School of Intermedia Art at the China Academy of Art in Hangzhou. “It is a move away from a single aesthetic order, making room for individual differences, chance, and humour alongside mass production and consumption,” Liu said. Alibaba owns South China Morning Post.

title: Exclusive | Senior civil servant asked to resign over defective lifts at Queen Mary Hospital
description: But Architectural Services Department, where Tuesday Li served as a chief project manager, says her departure didn’t involve ‘forced resignation’.
content: A senior Hong Kong government officer who oversaw faulty lift installation work that stalled the launch of a new block at Queen Mary Hospital was asked to resign and left her post last month to take responsibility for the defects, the South China Morning Post has learned. But the Architectural Services Department (ASD) denied any “forced resignation” was involved in a reply to the SCMP on Saturday night. The officer tendered her resignation for personal reasons and gave three months’ notice, leaving the civil service in the middle of last month, it added. Complaints about the malfunctioning lifts extend back to last year, soon after the block opened. Experts have criticised the authorities’ handling of civil service management missteps, which bypassed the established disciplinary mechanism, saying it lacked transparency. Multiple sources said that Tuesday Li Pak-yee, a chief project manager at the ASD who oversaw the multibillion-dollar development at the hospital in Pok Fu Lam, left her directorate pay-level post in August. The SCMP has reached out to Li for comment. Li’s departure came shortly before media scrutiny began mounting over defective work at the largest hospital on Hong Kong Island, which left 24 of the 28 lifts in the new 34-storey clinical block unfit for use. “[Li] was advised by the Architectural Services Department to resign,” a government insider said. “Such a departure is extremely rare within the civil service framework.” Another government source said the department regarded Li, who served as the main official liaising with contractors and overseeing the hospital project’s execution, as possibly having made “management missteps” over the delay, and that it tried to resolve the matter internally rather than initiate formal disciplinary proceedings. The source added that other projects she had supervised had been delayed. Widespread installation defects, revealed last month, have delayed the full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block by up to a year, prompting deep concern over project oversight and civil service accountability. The delay has prevented medical departments from moving into the block, although a blood bank and restaurants remain open. Construction of the building began in 2018 and was mostly completed last year. Health authorities earlier said hospital staff had started using the building but it had not yet formally been taken over from the department. Clinical services had originally been expected to start relocating there from the end of last year. Li held a directorate pay scale point one post, which carries a monthly salary of up to HK$183,015, according to information in the public domain. Information on LinkedIn shows that Li is an architect by profession and is currently “open to work”. She had served as the chief project manager since April 2022. Her former supervisor at directorate pay scale point two has taken on her responsibilities alongside his existing duties – an arrangement an insider described as “unusual”. The source said that typically when an officer left a post or took extended leave, the vacancy was filled by someone of equivalent rank, such as from another division. The ASD said last month that the main contractor, a Paul Y-Able joint venture, and lift subcontractor Anlev Elex Elevator would be required to bear all costs of remedial work. However, on September 4, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said that her bureau had also directed the ASD and the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department – both of which it supervises – to submit internal review reports evaluating their handling and supervision of the project. The Health Bureau said it was not in a position to comment on “technical details” as it was the end user of the facility. Insiders, meanwhile, noted that under existing protocols, once the Legislative Council had approved funding and the ASD awarded the tender, the department would advise the Hospital Authority on revised completion dates and conduct joint site inspections. Sources said the workflow meant the authority should have been told about any lift issues in advance. On the existing disciplinary mechanism, an insider said the current protocols had made it extremely difficult to dismiss administrative staff. The insider noted that if a supervisor wished to dismiss an employee, they had to prepare a year in advance, documenting the staff member’s performance issues while providing coaching. The process required regular, documented face-to-face meetings and extensive justification for the dismissal, which consumed a significant amount of time and involved numerous procedures, the source added. Even though the government had recently proposed revamping the civil service’s appraisal system, the changes might only shorten the timeline rather than simplify the requirements, and still demanded substantial time and effort, he said. In its reply to the SCMP, an ASD spokesman said Li had resigned for personal reasons and had given the required three months’ notice under established protocols. The department said it would hold relevant companies and individuals accountable, whether currently employed or not, based on the findings. Lawmaker Rebecca Chan Hoi-yan said major issues such as lift malfunctions should be caught well before a building was handed over by project managers. This was especially so in the Queen Mary Hospital case, since incidents such as staff being trapped in lifts dated back to last year. “Under normal circumstances, for a standard engineering project, you would not wait until handover or building acceptance to discover these issues,” she said. “It is impossible for the Hospital Authority to be unaware that its employees had raised questions about the lifts … every department involved must have its own issues that led to today’s situation.” Chan suggested the government launch a formal investigation into the matter. John Burns, an emeritus professor of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong, said that if the allegations about keeping the situation secret were true, it would be damaging for the government. “To keep it internal and not reveal what’s going on is very damaging – very damaging to the reputation of those involved,” he said. “Whoever tried to keep it internal and keep it secret, [made a] huge mistake. And that person’s behaviour should be investigated, also. In fact, we need outside parties doing the investigation.”

title: Reflections | Amid Trump’s ‘Lake America’ stink, the Chinese emperor whose renaming campaign backfired
description: Two thousand years ago, Wang Mang’s renaming of places, peoples and titles fuelled rebellions that ended both his regime and his life.
content: I suspect many Americans are embarrassed by their president’s recent actions. On August 27, Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” following the collapse of trade talks between the United States and Canada. The change applies only in the US, while Canada and the rest of the world continue to call it Lake Ontario. Doug Ford, premier of the Canadian province of Ontario, has put up a sign declaring “Lake Ontario Now and Always”. The lake, meanwhile, remains impressively indifferent. This is not the first time Trump has renamed something. In January 2025, he renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America”. The rest of the world, and many in the US, have ignored the change. His recent attempt to rename The John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts “The Donald J. Trump and John F. Kennedy Memorial Centre for the Performing Arts” was thwarted when a judge ruled the change illegal. Nearly 2,000 years ago, a Chinese ruler took renaming to an altogether more ambitious – and absurd – level. In AD9, Wang Mang replaced the Western Han dynasty (202BC-AD9), which he had served as an official and whose imperial family he was related to by marriage, with his own. As emperor of the Xin – literally “New” – dynasty, he then embarked on what might be described as a massive government rebranding exercise. More than 90 of the empire’s roughly 100 first-tier local administrative units, including the capital, underwent name or structural changes. Below them, around 700 districts were renamed. Almost all the titles of members of the imperial family, nobles and officials were changed. Name changes were also used to express political hierarchy. Neighbouring peoples and states were given names intended to convey submission or inferiority. Like the US under Trump, Wang Mang used place names to make an international political statement. While Trump’s motivation for his name changes is a distorted sense of America’s – and his own – greatness, Wang Mang’s inspiration was antiquity, particularly Confucian classics such as the Rites of Zhou, which describes institutions dating back around 1,000 years before Wang Mang’s time. He believed that the ideal political order lay in the distant past, and that restoring its institutions and their names would restore that order. For names of things not found in ancient texts, Wang Mang chose words that suggested peace, order, security, beauty and good governance. The empire was to be surrounded, at least linguistically, by all things good and wonderful. There was, however, a small practical difficulty: people had to remember all the new names. Officials struggled to keep track of the changes. Ordinary people were even less enthusiastic about abandoning names they had used all their lives. The renaming became so confusing that government documents sometimes had to include the old names alongside the new ones simply to explain where or what the government was talking about. Wang Mang eventually discovered that reality was considerably less cooperative than the ancient books. Economic problems, administrative confusion and armed rebellions helped bring down his regime. In AD23, rebels, led by members of the fallen Han imperial family, captured the capital and killed Wang Mang. They eventually restored the Han dynasty, known in history as the Eastern Han (AD25-AD220). Wang Mang’s “New” dynasty had lasted only 14 years. Wang Mang offers a useful example to any ruler tempted to believe that changing a name amounts to changing reality. Names can proclaim power or legitimacy, but they cannot, by themselves, make anything great again. Trump may have the authority to call Lake Ontario “Lake America” on US government documents. He may even force some American maps to follow suit. But the rest of the world is unlikely to pay any heed to such hubris.

title: Dodging deer and scary, sodden descents: inside Hong Kong’s Asian Games time trial quest
description: Chloe Leung and Vincent Lau poised to begin city’s medal challenge in Japan following daring reconnaissance mission with coach Herve Dagorne.
content: After a flying reconnaissance visit to Japan, where they dodged deer and navigated treacherous, rain-sodden descents, the daredevil cycling pair of Chloe Leung Wing-yee and Vincent Lau Wan-yau have equipped themselves with the smarts to launch Hong Kong’s Asian Games campaign in grand style next week. If it is a bugbear of Herve Dagorne’s that each delegation is allowed only one rider in the individual time trial races that get the Games cycling programme under way next Sunday, then in Leung and Lau, who claimed time trial bronze in Hangzhou in 2023, the head coach believes he has the perfect duo for a glory bid. A bronze medallist in the discipline in 2018, and fourth three years ago, Leung has impressively rebounded from the gut punch of being controversially overlooked for the Paris Olympics two years ago; delivering a succession of notable performances that included a pair of fine rides in last year’s UCI Road World Championships. An archetypal mountain goat, she claimed Asian Road Cycling Championships time trial silver earlier this year on a flat route in Saudi Arabia that was entirely unconducive to her climbing and technical strengths. But for a self-confessed mental wobble when she realised she was ahead on the road, Leung would have won. “It required no skill,” said Dagorne, who is rubbing his hands together over a course in Nagoya that is “in the middle of nowhere, with super narrow roads”. “There are lots of leaves, moose running around and it’s very slippery,” Dagorne added. “The technical aspect is going to be really important.” Having already taken Leung and Lau to the Games venue for a trial run earlier this year, and spent time with Leung in the Spanish city of Girona to allow her to practice in conditions similar to those she will encounter next week, Dagorne travelled with the two riders for a mini-camp back in Japan from Saturday to Monday this week. “We wanted a technical rehearsal, and to test different materials,” he said. “It’s still the rainy season and we needed to choose their tyre pressures. I wanted them to make the choice and feel comfortable, not be stressing two days before about what they’re doing.” After what he saw from Leung when a bright morning last Sunday gave way to torrential downpours, Dagorne is praying that the heavens open on race day. “I was filming and my assistant was driving, and it was hard to follow her downhill in the rain,” Dagorne said. “The work we did in Girona gave her confidence. “She’s really good at downhill cornering and, like in Formula 1, you see the talent of the pilot when it’s raining. Honestly, I was scared watching her, but she’s doing really well. The same with Vincent, he’s making good progress, too.” After finishing 22nd and 39th in last year’s world championships time trial and road race, respectively, Leung, 29, has buried her frustration over being forced to skip the 2026 edition in Montreal because of its direct clash with the Asian Games. Leung would have fancied her chances of bettering those results from 12 months ago, when she was the first Asian home in the time trial, after a year when the 29-year-old was also part of the Hong Kong mixed relay time trial team that stunned overwhelming favourites Kazakhstan to win Asian Road Championships gold. Working with a sports psychologist for more than three years, Leung said, had allowed her to “believe I can do it”. “It’s not good for an association when you can’t go to a world championships, but she’s not thinking about Montreal,” Dagorne said. “Her focus is the Asian Games, and we’re talking about Olympic qualification.” On that note, Dagorne said next year’s Hong Kong National Road Championships would be upgraded to Group A status and double their Olympic qualifying points offering. Organisers reversed the Asian Games schedule from three years ago to stage the road events before the four-day track programme, which starts on September 29: a switch that has also given the continent’s cyclists little time to prepare for the UCI Track World Championships in Shanghai from October 14. “It’s not helping the Asian countries, it’s doing a disservice to them,” said Dagorne, who is still vexed over the decision to allow teams only three riders in the Games road races, which will happen on September 22 and 23. Dato’ Amarjit Singh Gill, the Asian Cycling Confederation president, told the South China Morning Post that the Asian Games road events were being held during Japanese public holidays “to minimise the impact of [temporary traffic restrictions] on economic activity and the daily lives of citizens”. “Rubbish,” Dagorne said. “I saw three or four cars in two days driving there. The road is silent, apart from moose. When it was raining at 3pm, it was dark because we were in a forest.” Poised to announce his Asian Games squad on Monday, Dagorne had to finalise selection at the start of June. “It was hard to manage, but we’re a small team,” he said. “Some riders were not happy, and I understand, but the names we have correspond with who I would pick today”. One rider certain of a seat on the plane is Ceci Lee Sze-wing, who claimed two silvers and one bronze from the Games in 2023, albeit she is set to channel her efforts entirely into the track and, primarily, a golden bid in the blue-riband omnium event. After competing in a series of Italian races in July, Lee and her fellow endurance riders staged an altitude camp in mainland China province Yunnan, while the sprint contingent continued preparations in Sydney under coach Anthony Peden and hired-help, Eddie Dawkins, the New Zealander who claimed team sprint silver from the 2016 Olympics. Dagorne, who also sent a number of his male riders to last month’s five-day China Xizang Trans-Himalaya race, will have a streamlined staff in Japan. “It’s the same as the Olympics, where the numbers are limited,” he said. “I remember [as a competitor in the 1988 and 1992 Games] waxing my helmet and helping the mechanics. “The SF&OC [Hong Kong Sports Federation and Olympic Committee] have been very helpful. Along with the cycling association, they’ve fulfilled nearly all of my requests, so I can’t complain.”

title: Up in smoke: why Southeast Asia failed to halt the haze
description: Asean was going to eliminate transboundary haze by 2020. What happened?
content: Dr Asma Zafirah doesn’t need satellite images to know when Kalimantan is burning. She sees it in the watery eyes and laboured breaths of the patients at her clinic in Sarawak, and the children who are kept home from school to protect them from the toxic air. Southeast Asia’s transboundary haze crisis was meant to have been brought under control six years ago. But Borneo is once again belching out dangerous emissions, as fires in the peatlands and forests of Kalimantan – Indonesia’s section of the island – send a wall of pollutants across Malaysia’s Sarawak and on to the wider region. Repeated, prolonged exposure to haze wreaks havoc in the human body, triggering inflammation, asthma attacks and other respiratory problems. “That is already a signal that their body is not simply being irritated,” Asma said. “It is having a clinically significant response to the exposure.” Left unchecked, that exposure can scar lungs, cause cardiovascular illness and lead to cancer, as PM2.5 particles small enough to cross into the bloodstream spread the damage far and wide. In Sarawak, the Air Pollutant Index (API) Malaysia uses climbed as high as 519 this week, surpassing a level so hazardous it triggered a state of emergency in the Bornean state’s Serian district that was lifted only once the air was clear enough to breathe. Singapore, which had gone three years without air quality breaching unhealthy levels, restarted daily haze alerts and in the Philippine capital, more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) from the wildfires, schools were forced to shut their doors. Climate experts warn of a meteorological double-whammy conspiring to make this the hottest year on record for Southeast Asia. “Super El Nino” – a massive warming of the Pacific Ocean that chokes off regional rainfall – is being stacked on top of a developing positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which cools regional waters, further cutting off moisture. Together, they act as a force multiplier, fuelling droughts, heatwaves and wildfires from Indonesian Borneo and Sumatra to the Mekong nations of Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar. Extreme weather is only part of the story, however. The fuel for the fires is the land cleared, year after year, for palm oil, pulpwood, corn and sugar cane, on plantations that drain water from the region’s peatlands until they become as dry as tinder. It’s agribusiness vs the atmosphere, observers say – and for now, agribusiness is winning, despite decades of Asean pledges, a real-time satellite-powered fire-detection system and US$1.5 billion in funding to tackle the crisis that has yet to be raised. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, facing an electorate once again struggling to breathe, called on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to take action. “Asean ministers must seriously look at it”, he told reporters, “because it is affecting lives, particularly of children and babies”. The crisis is also decimating some of the world’s greatest stores of biodiversity. Pitiful photographs from Kalimantan of rescued pangolins curled into defensive balls and orangutans with their fur singed orange-black have refocused the world’s attention on the issue. But climate advisers warn against a convenient narrative taking hold: that this is simply the fault of this year’s “super El Nino”, rather than the businesses making billions from the burning. “El Nino and dry conditions are risk multipliers, not the root cause,” said Renard Siew, a climate change specialist at the Centre for Governance and Political Studies in Kuala Lumpur. “We cannot govern El Nino away,” he added. “But we can manage land better, prevent fires, enforce regulations and reduce the underlying vulnerability. Climate change is effectively making the consequences of weak governance more severe.” History repeats By far Southeast Asia’s worst haze offender is its most populous nation and largest economy. Indonesia’s peatland fires began alarmingly early this year, with hotspots detected way back in January – months before the typical dry season burn. More than 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) have burned so far and police have named 138 arson suspects, including eight companies implicated in forest and land clearance. But arrests are of little comfort to the families forced to live under a cloud of toxic haze. Lina Rose, a mother of four in Sarawak, has had to keep her children indoors for most of the recent school holidays. “I’m worried about my child who has asthma,’’ she said. “The sky looks so gloomy that you think it’s going to rain, but then it doesn’t.” Residents hark back to 2015, when Indonesia’s worst haze crisis in decades – fuelled by the same slash-and-burn clearance for palm oil and pulpwood – released thousands upon thousands of tonnes of carbon into the atmosphere and blanketed tens of millions of people, from Sumatra to Singapore, in choking smog for months on end. Jakarta, faced with international fury, labelled that year’s crisis a “crime against humanity of extraordinary proportions” and belatedly signed on to an Asean road map promising haze-fire skies by 2020. But that deadline came and went – and still the haze continued. A second road map followed in 2023, with a new target year of 2030. Yet few believe this new framework will be any more effective than the first. The reason comes down to Asean’s modus operandi: consensus and non-interference are not conducive to policing environmental crime across borders, analysts say. Meanwhile, the palm oil, pulp and paper conglomerates whose business models depend on cheap land clearance have every incentive to keep enforcement weak. “The fundamental shift has to be from ‘managing haze’ to preventing the conditions that create it,” Siew said. “That means stronger land-use governance, better fire prevention and peatland management, clearer accountability across supply chains and much greater investment in local capacity.” To its credit, the newer haze-control road map does “contain something its predecessor lacked”, according to Dominique Nicky Fahrizal, a legal expert and researcher at Indonesia’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies – namely, measurable indicators, “including zero days at the highest alert level for two consecutive years”, as well as pledges to reduce burned area by 10 per cent and hotspots by 5 per cent, with a midterm review due in 2028. But the mechanisms for holding anyone accountable remain weak. “The consensus principle and the related ‘Asean Way’ approach have led to the creation of mechanisms that are ambitious but have been described as toothless,” said Helena Varkkey, an associate professor of political ecology at the University of Malaya. “This is because the mechanisms often lack strong operationalisation or punitive measures.” Sanctions would not work, Fahrizal said, as Asean members would never agree to impose them on one another, adding that the latest road map “is not a binding instrument” with reporting done by member states themselves. Asean’s consensus-based approach has allowed Jakarta to commit to haze-free targets with no penalty attached to missing them. After 2015, it did impose a moratorium on peatland clearance and created an agency to restore affected areas, eventually rehabilitating some 1.6 million hectares (6,177 square miles). But Indonesia also produces more than half the world’s palm oil and its industry has found ways to adapt, securing permits for “sustainable” farming on the one hand while surreptitiously clearing protected areas on the other. The peatland restoration agency, for all the good it did, was dissolved last year. Fahriza said the most “realistic” option for enforcing anti-haze measures was to employ independent, third-party verification of data that could be reviewed collectively to impose “consequences for reputation and access to financing”. Absent that, Asean’s credibility – and relevance – would “ultimately be judged by the citizens breathing the smoke, not by the number of documents signed”, he said. Patchwork fixes Advocacy groups are done waiting for another of the bloc’s road maps to fail. On Monday, Asean Parliamentarians for Human Rights called for the region’s latest haze crisis to be treated as a “human rights emergency”, urging Asean member states to use an October summit in Vietnam to close enforcement gaps and hold corporate offenders to account by forcing companies to publish fire and land-use information for independent scrutiny. Some smaller-scale bilateral cooperation has also emerged. Thailand and Laos signed a data- and resource-sharing agreement on Wednesday aimed at pre-empting wildfires before they spread, echoing a similar arrangement Bangkok struck with Myanmar last month. External pressure is building too, with mixed results. The European Union’s threatened ban on palm oil linked to deforestation has been delayed to 2027, after Indonesian objections and Brussel’s own need to lock in a new trade deal amid rising US tariffs. Then there are the built-in weaknesses in Asean’s own crisis-response tools: under the bloc’s latest haze agreement, accepting emergency firefighting help from abroad remains entirely voluntary. “At the moment, the arrangement exists, but ultimately it cannot function without the explicit invitation of the host country,” Varkkey said. “This should be a scientific decision, when the haze is bad enough to warrant external help, not a political one.” Singapore perhaps best captures the tension between profit and public safety: its companies are heavy investors in Kalimantan’s palm oil sector, yet its people – the region’s wealthiest – no longer tolerate haze imported from beyond their borders. The city state’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014 lets it prosecute companies for haze pollution regardless of where the fire was lit, a legal reach that was tested after the 2015 pollution crisis when six companies, including Indonesia’s Asia Pulp & Paper Group, were investigated – a move Jakarta called an affront to its sovereignty. As of 2021, four of the cases remained open, Singapore’s environment minister told parliament. There has been no public confirmation of their closure in the years since. Meanwhile, Singapore still wheezes whenever Borneo burns. Wildlife photographer Eddie Vanderloot, 47, has learned to recognise a tight chest and itchy eyes as unmistakable signs that the air has turned. “Constantly planning activities around the air quality gets tiring and it’s hard not to feel worn down by it,” he said. “Even with all the windows closed, a mask on, an air purifier and air conditioners switched on, the haze still affects me for hours.”

title: Hong Kong film festival celebrates 37 years of queer cinema
description: Asia’s longest-running international LGBTQ film festival invites Hong Kong audiences on an emotional, cinematic ride, with a revamped programming featuring six distinct ‘moods’.
content: The global landscape for LGBTQ culture has shifted dramatically since the Hong Kong Lesbian and Gay Film Festival (HKLGFF) debuted in 1989. Over the past 37 years, queer art and media have stepped out of underground venues into a vibrant scene, immortalised locally by icons such as Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing. The festival’s enduring run attests to the community’s resilience, proving how the transformative power of cinema continues to push the envelope while creating a sanctuary for generations to come. For its 37th edition, HKLGFF rolls out its largest line-up in years – 37 features and 38 shorts – while spotlighting a new generation of local queer filmmakers. Opening the festival are two titles: RuPaul’s campy disaster comedy Stop! That! Train!, a wild ride packed with outrageous gags and a star-studded drag cast including Jujubee, Ginger Minj and RuPaul as president of the United States; and He Xiaodan’s award-winning Montreal, My Beautiful, starring Golden Horse “Best Actress” Joan Chen as a repressed immigrant mother set on a path of self-discovery after meeting a free-spirited younger woman. Breaking from traditional genre categories, the festival organises its line-up around six refreshingly emotional “moods”: “Love” explores heartfelt queer romance; “Laugh” celebrates queer humour; “Reflect” looks back at queer identity and history; “Thrill” offers adrenaline-fuelled passion and suspense; “Pride” takes the social pulse of pride across the world; and “Remember” pays tribute to German queer cinema legends Rosa von Praunheim and Monika Treut through a retrospective in partnership with the Goethe-Institut. In doing so, the festival hopes to foster deeper connection and mutual understanding across the queer community and among audiences. Programme highlights include closing-title duo Tiger, set in Ni-chome, Tokyo’s hub of gay subculture, and ZsaZsa Zaturnnah, an adult animated feature adapted from the iconic queer Southeast Asian comic-book superhero. Centrepieces Maspalomas and The Education of Jane Cumming share the spotlight with special presentations Test and horror stand-out Leviticus. Seven themed short-film showcases will further spotlight local creative voices. Judging this year’s Short Film Jury Award is a panel featuring screenwriter Kate Reilly, director Doris Yeung and art director Kary Kwok. Concurrently, the 5th Chinese-language Short Film Screenplay Competition offers rising local writers mentorship from industry icons including William Chang Suk-ping, Tracy Choi, Felix Tsang, Cheung Shuk-fong and Ray Yeung. Rounding out the celebration, HKLGFF presents its prestigious Prism Award to Gigi Chao – co-founder of Hong Kong Marriage Equality and founder of the Faith in Love Foundation – honouring her exceptional leadership and dedication to LGBTQ advocacy. Thirty-seven years on, HKLGFF continues to put queer stories front and centre, celebrating the universal spectrum of human emotions. So, what are you in the mood for? The 37th Hong Kong Lesbian and Gay Film Festival. Until September 20. Various venues. Tickets from HK$80

title: Editorial | Brics summit could emerge as milestone in bloc’s unity
description: The expected meeting between the leaders of China and India on the sidelines of the multilateral summit bodes well for stability in Asia.
content: India’s public preparations for this weekend’s Brics summit in New Delhi are not to be compared with the spectacular display for the Group of 20 summit three years ago. The low-key approach to the meeting of leaders of emerging major economies and developing countries from the Global South can be misleading. What Brics may lack in pomp it makes up for in substance, such as the landmark in relations between the world’s two most populous nations. The occasion marks the first visit to India in close to seven years by Chinese President Xi Jinping. It includes a summit between Xi and his host, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, expected on Saturday on the sidelines of the formal proceedings. Coming less than two weeks ahead of Xi’s expected visit to the United States on September 24 for a summit with US President Donald Trump, the Xi-Modi meeting will be closely watched from Washington to Moscow. The US is India’s biggest export market while Russia is a major arms and energy supplier. The Brics grouping was formed 20 years ago by Brazil, Russia, India and China – they were soon joined by South Africa – as a counterweight to the Group of Seven of rich, developed nations. It has become a credible voice for the Global South, having expanded into a group spanning Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. It includes energy exporters, manufacturing powers, emerging economies and countries with sharply divergent relationships with Washington and Beijing. The Delhi summit is ultimately a test of whether Brics can mobilise all this diversity for the common good. It has never had the clear leadership of the kind to be found, for example, in the G7, and needs to find more common ground and forge greater cooperation. That said, Brics has still achieved extraordinary development, all things considered. The significance of the Delhi event is that it is likely to emerge as a milestone in unity of the bloc. Its members increasingly realise they need to band together to fend off geopolitical risks, including a more aggressive and assertive US, and navigate a geopolitically unstable environment. In that regard, the summit has a particularly apt official theme: “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. For many years Brics has been troubled by the relationship between China and India, including border conflicts amid prevailing tension. By attending the Brics meeting and holding bilateral talks with Modi, Xi is trying to improve relations and narrow differences. There is a positive message there for the bloc at large, which stands to emerge in a stronger position in terms of enhanced regional stability. As part of China’s strategy to maintain a stable regional environment, Xi has undertaken a month of diplomatic travel leading up to the expected summit with US President Trump. First, he visited Kyrgyzstan for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, then – for the first time in 10 years – Egypt, before this weekend’s visit to India. This contrasts with the earlier part of the year, which saw Xi mainly staying in Beijing and hosting a succession of visiting foreign leaders.
