The positive signals of stability in Asia being sent will help China undertake negotiations with the US from a position of strength. For India and China, this weekend’s multilateral and bilateral summits will be a good opportunity for Modi and Xi to consolidate the reduction of border tension. The two sides have gradually come to an understanding on de-escalating and disengaging in the disputed area. From time to time, however, there are still reports of outbreaks of tension. Hopefully Xi’s visit will help the two sides institutionalise the agreement reached after the conflict and gradually improve relations. On the economic side, India is facing persistent outflow of foreign capital on top of US tariffs and a trade deficit with China. An improved bilateral diplomatic relationship could pave the way for India to seek better economic relations with China and also encourage more Chinese investment in India. The Brics summit is shaping up as a significant occasion for the Global South and beyond.

title: Famous Chinese women in folklore, from Hua Mulan to a consort who brought down a dynasty
description: These women have inspired countless poems, books, movies and TV shows over the centuries, but what are their stories and why do they endure?
content: Women are vastly under-represented in ancient Chinese literature. The few who appear, often in myth or semi-fiction, serve primarily to reflect that era’s moral expectations for women. From filial warriors to patriotic seductresses and femmes fatales, these women have one thing in common – they all trade personal autonomy for survival in a man’s world. Here are three fictional women in Chinese history and what makes their names live on to this day. 1. Hua Mulan The only historical record of Hua Mulan is the Ballad of Mulan, a melodic 332-character folk poem believed to have been written during China’s Northern Wei dynasty (386-535). The poem begins with a melancholic Hua: “The sound of one sigh after another / As Mulan weaves at the doorway / No sound of the loom and shuttle / Only that of the girl lamenting.” It goes on to recount how Hua’s ageing father is drafted into the army because her family does not have an adult son and one man from every family must serve. But instead, Hua decides to disguise herself as a man and fight in her father’s place. She serves on the battlefield for over a decade, her skill and bravery helping her rise through the ranks while maintaining her male disguise. Upon victory, the emperor offers her lavish rewards, but Hua refuses and asks only for a horse to take her back to her family. Upon arriving home, she changes out of her battle cloak and puts on her old female clothing and traditional make-up. Her comrades-in-arms are astounded to learn she has been a woman all along. The poem concludes with her saying: “The male hare has heavy paws / The female hare has dreamy eyes / When the two hares run side by side / How can you tell whether I am male or female?” By risking treason to spare her father, Hua becomes the embodiment of both filial piety and loyalty – to the throne and her family. Her legend was retold and embellished over the next 1,300 years. It is believed that Ming dynasty playwright Xu Wei came up with the surname Hua, gave her bound feet – which is historically inaccurate, but reflected 16th century Chinese norms – and ended her story with an arranged marriage to a scholar-official selected by her parents. A real love interest for Hua Mulan only materialised in 20th century screen adaptations, from pre-World War II productions to Disney’s 1998 animated feature. In 2020, controversial mainland Chinese actress Liu Yifei starred in a live-action remake of the 1998 feature. 2. Diaochan Diaochan’s tale is also one of self-sacrifice. The fictional character is based on a real-life maidservant referenced in the third-century historical compilation Records of the Three Kingdoms, who had dangerous affairs with two warlords, Dong Zhuo and his adopted son, Lu Bu, both of whom lived during the late Eastern Han dynasty (25-220). Although the maidservant who inspired Diaochan’s character existed, she is not known to have deliberately driven a wedge between the father and son. It was only in the 14th century that Luo Guanzhong’s novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms cast her as the adopted daughter of rival politician Wang Yun. In the book, Diaochan, a beautiful and patriotic manipulator, sets a honey trap to destroy the tyrannical Dong by seducing both him and Lu. Wang secretly betroths her to Lu, then later presents her to Dong as a concubine. Diaochan tells the two warlords different sob stories, casting herself as a victim and pitting the two against each other. Lu’s loyalty to Dong diminishes, and he eventually joins forces with Wang to orchestrate Dong’s assassination. That is as far as Diaochan’s story goes in Romance of the Three Kingdoms, but in some later folk adaptations, she has an interesting dynamic with another military general, Guan Yu. Depending on the story, Guan Yu either marries her or executes her for what she has done or may do with her beauty. In lesser-told versions, Diaochan kills herself or becomes a nun after Lu’s death. In the last 100 years, the story of Diaochan has been told in at least 11 films from Hong Kong, mainland China and Japan, and 16 Chinese TV shows. The character has mostly been portrayed as an attractive, pious patriot with two powerful men wrapped around her finger. 3. Daji Hua Mulan was chaste, while Diaochan used her womanly charm to get what her adopted father wanted. Daji, on the other hand, was never viewed as selfless. Still, her stories mirror how the ancient Chinese perceived morality and female sexuality. Daji’s legend has been largely passed down through word of mouth. She is widely imagined as the debauched favourite consort of Di Xin, the last king of the Shang dynasty (c. 1600BC-1050BC). She is said to have been a noblewoman whose father had to marry her off after losing a battle. The earliest written references to Daji are in early Zhou dynasty (c. 1046BC-256BC) texts criticising Di Xin for the outsize influence he allowed Daji to have over him. Centuries later, Han dynasty historian Sima Qian (145BC-86BC) blamed Daji’s sadism and influence on Di Xin for the fall of the Shang dynasty. In Records of the Grand Historian, he noted that her corruption led to extravagant spending, neglected governance and heavy taxes, ultimately justifying King Wu of Zhou’s successful rebellion. In fact, Daji’s emperor-husband, Di Xin, was described in historical texts as a cruel ruler who liked to “indulge in wine” and “favoured women”. Still, that does not change the view of some ancient Chinese writers that Daji was an evil temptress who led Shang to ruin. The 16th century novel Investiture of the Gods famously casts Daji as a thousand-year-old fox spirit sent by a goddess to ruin the Shang dynasty. She succeeds in corrupting Di Xin, but spin-off texts reveal she was ultimately punished for surrendering to human temptations. Of the numerous film and TV adaptations of Investiture of the Gods, the portrayals of Daji by Irene Wan Bik-ha in the 2001 Hong Kong TV series Gods of Honour, and by Fan Bingbing in League of Gods (2016), remain among the most memorable. Real women were largely erased from Chinese history, but fictional archetypes – including virtuous, helpless or sexually weaponised women – served as essential cultural tools for defining morality, womanhood and power.

title: Ex-Canada PM Jean Chretien tells US: ‘never mistake our generosity for weakness’
description: His pointed message was issued in Gander, the Canadian town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks.
content: Standing in the town that sheltered thousands of stranded Americans after the September 11 attacks, former Canadian prime minister Jean Chretien marked the 25th anniversary on Friday with a pointed message for the US: “Never mistake our generosity for weakness.” The 92-year-old former leader, who was prime minister at the time of the attacks, drew a standing ovation after telling his “American friends” that Canadians might be tolerant and kind but “we bow to no one”. US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra rose afterwards and hugged him. “I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another,” Chretien said. “Friends need to be honest with each other.” The unusually blunt remarks came during a solemn ceremony honouring the nearly 3,000 people killed in New York, at the Pentagon and aboard Flight 93, and remembering Gander’s extraordinary response to the attacks. Gander, Newfoundland, opened its arms to nearly 6,600 airline passengers diverted there when the US government shut down airspace during September 11. The remarks came at a striking moment in Canada-US relations. The long-time allies are embroiled in a trade war under US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st US state. Chretien recalled how Canada rallied behind the US after the attacks, when Americans were “our neighbours, our closest friends under attack”. “It was a day when we saw the worst of humanity and the very best,” he said. Some of the very best, he said, happened in Gander. On September 11, 2001, 38 planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers and crew were diverted to the small Newfoundland town after the US shut its airspace. The arrivals nearly doubled Gander’s population. Residents in Gander and surrounding communities turned schools, churches and meeting halls into shelters, supplied food and medicine and welcomed strangers into their homes. The stranded travellers became known locally as the “plane people”. American passenger Raphael Fusco, who was 17 when his flight from Milan to Newark was diverted to Newfoundland, said Gander left him with a different memory of September 11. “So while the rest of the world was seeing these horrific images, we saw something very different,” he said. “We saw extraordinary kindness.” “They also opened their hearts,” Chretien said. “Because that is what I call the Canadian way. When our friends are in trouble, we don’t hesitate. We act.” Hoekstra also received applause as he thanked Gander and Canada for standing with Americans then and in the years since. “Thank you to the people of Gander. Thank you for your friendship,” he said. Hoekstra called those who responded 25 years ago “extraordinary people doing extraordinary things”. “Beds? Check. Food? Check. Medicine? Check. Roof over their head? Check,” he said. “You stood up. You did what was needed to be done.” His warm reception was notable because Hoekstra’s participation had itself generated controversy. Gander officials defended inviting him after criticism of his planned appearance, saying his attendance did not amount to an endorsement of the Trump administration. “September 11 is bigger than politics, personalities or titles,” the town said. The story of what happened in Gander inspired the hit Broadway musical Come From Away, and passengers and residents have continued returning for reunions. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney used a campaign stop in Gander last year to say his nation was mourning “a friendship lost” with the United States. Canada-US trade negotiations collapsed last month after Carney rejected proposed terms he said threatened Canadian sovereignty and key industries. Washington imposed steep new tariffs, Canada retaliated this week and the Trump administration responded with additional restrictions on Canadian goods and access to US government contracts. Against that backdrop, Chretien said Canada’s willingness to help should not be misread. “Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination,” he said. “And never, never mistake our kindness for softness.” “Building a country like this, with this climate and this geography, is a sign of toughness, not of weakness,” Chretien said. He recalled Canadians and Americans fighting together in Afghanistan after the attacks and the long history of the countries standing beside one another. Chretien noted that 165 Canadians died in Afghanistan, including 158 members of the Canadian Armed Forces. “We embrace our friends and we help them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one,” Chretien said. “And the more we are insulted, threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united.” Hoekstra, whose parents were liberated in the Netherlands by Allied forces that included Canadians during World War II, also invoked the countries’ history of shared sacrifice. “We stood side by side,” he said. Chretien ended not by rejecting that friendship but by calling for its restoration on terms Canada could accept. “Respect, friendship and good neighbours,” he said. “Long live the United States and long live Canada.”

title: Chinese AI firms shunned US delegation over sanctions fears, commission says
description: Members stress value of Washington-Beijing dialogue as both sides prepare for dedicated talks on AI governance.
content: A US congressional advisory body on China said on Friday that leading Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) firms declined to meet its members during a recent Beijing visit over concerns that doing so could expose the firms to US sanctions. But members also underscored the importance of the coming AI dialogue between Washington and Beijing. “We were told, ‘You guys are a really scary commission, and you do hawkish anti-China things, and they’re afraid if they meet with you, they might be put on the entities list,’” said Randy Schriver, the chairman of the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC) during a panel discussion at Johns Hopkins University. “And we said, ‘Aha, actually meeting with us, we can help you get off the entities list.’ But [they] didn’t seem to buy it.” A bipartisan USCC delegation travelled to Beijing, Hangzhou and Shanghai in July for its first visit to China in seven years. The commission called the trip a fact-finding mission and said what it learned would inform its ongoing work, including its annual report to Congress on China’s military, economic and technological developments. Created by Congress in 2000, the USCC examines the national security implications of US-China economic and trade ties. During the visit, the delegates met Chinese government officials, think tank experts, diplomats and business representatives to discuss AI, advanced technology, biotechnology, economic security and regional issues. But not the AI firms. Schriver added that the delegation had requested meetings with companies including Alibaba and DeepSeek during its trip to Hangzhou but was not allowed to visit them. “I think there’s a little bit of a contradiction that we observed: the confidence expressed by the government officials, particularly around AI; a reluctance to allow us to meet with any of their labs,” said Chris Slevin, a USCC commissioner who was part of the delegation. “Sometimes it’s really telling what you don’t get,” Schriver added. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The Chinese embassy in Washington said that Beijing’s AI development “comes from greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology”. “As two major powers in AI, China and the US should step up cooperation and earnestly act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang told the SCMP. While the embassy welcomed the USCC’s recent visit to China, Beijing has repeatedly criticised the commission’s annual reports and other research. In November last year, China condemned the USCC’s annual report that called for additional sanctions on Hong Kong over alleged “dismantling” of the city’s autonomy and the “erosion of fundamental freedoms”. “We urge the relevant US politicians to stop fabricating so-called annual reports and immediately cease interfering in Hong Kong affairs and China’s internal affairs,” the Chinese foreign ministry’s arm in Hong Kong said at the time. Despite differences, Schriver said he saw value in maintaining dialogue between Washington and Beijing, especially on AI, and was “moderately optimistic” about the coming talks. “I think that’s a recognition that both sides understand the risk, understand the dangers, and know that to achieve a better state, dialogue is necessary,” he added. “I think it’s better to have it than not have it.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lead the US side in bilateral negotiations with his Chinese counterparts on AI governance ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month. Both sides are preparing for dedicated talks on AI, even as Washington and Beijing remain divided over the scope of the discussions, with China seeking a broader conversation and the US pushing to focus on AI safety, sources told the SCMP. The Treasury Department said in August that the administration was looking forward to “using our position as the global leader in AI to share our expertise with the world’s number two”. The two countries agreed to launch formal talks on AI governance after US President Donald Trump’s May meeting with the Chinese leader in Beijing.

title: Exclusive | AI fight shadows final preparations for Xi Jinping’s White House visit to meet Donald Trump
description: Chinese side is said to view US requests as limiting both harmful outcomes from AI and Beijing’s ability to develop its own capabilities.
content: Rising tensions over artificial intelligence are shaping the final preparations for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States. Washington and Beijing are discussing the possibility of folding a long-awaited AI dialogue into a broader economic meeting in the days before Xi meets US President Donald Trump, according to several people familiar with the arrangements. The two leaders agreed in Beijing in May to launch an intergovernmental dialogue on AI. For months, that channel was treated separately from the trade talks led by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, with both sides struggling to make progress in the dialogue. Sources now say Bessent is expected to handle the two issues in one meeting. Bessent is the American lead on both the AI talks with Beijing and the economic talks. The sources said that holding a second high-level meeting so close to the summit was becoming difficult to arrange. Development of AI in China has always been part of He’s portfolio, as the Chinese vice-premier is in charge of the National Development and Reform Commission, China’s powerful economic planning agency overseeing industrial development in the country, including AI. The arrangements are similar to the ones in May, when Bessent and He met in Seoul days before Trump sat down with Xi in Beijing. Officials have not confirmed the exact date or venue for the coming session, but it could happen just days ahead of the Xi-Trump handshake. A person familiar with the discussions said He and Bessent were likely to cover all three economic initiatives: the Board of Trade, the Board of Investment and an AI working group, though only the Board of Trade was expected to yield a deliverable in time for the summit. Beijing and Washington have invested heavily in making the reciprocal visit happen. According to another person familiar with the discussions, officials on each side say “strategic stability benefits both sides and will be better defined by this visit” and both sides see it as an important opportunity before major political events in both countries: US midterm elections for Trump, and for Xi, a Communist Party plenum next month and a party congress next year. Both sides were trying to “manage expectations and clarify red lines periodically”, the person said, as competition between the two countries, especially in AI, was “very intense”. Trump and Xi were described as “having to manage opposition inside their own systems to ensure the visit does not go off course”, the person added. The decision to hold the AI conversation in the Bessent-He session is being presented in private as a scheduling fix. It would take place in a harsher political climate than when the AI dialogue was first proposed. Several people following the talks said the concern was that a stand-alone dialogue could shift away from risk reduction and towards semiconductor chips, model access and export controls. One person said the Chinese side was unhappy with how the US was approaching the AI dialogue, viewing American requests as aimed at limiting harmful outcomes from AI as well as constraining China’s ability to develop its own capabilities. One person familiar with the Chinese assessment of the process said a combined session was understandable on logistics alone. Beijing was not given a clear picture of which US agencies would sit on the American side of an AI table until late July, the person said, and with Bessent leading that track as well as trade, asking him to appear twice so close to the leaders’ meeting created an obvious clash. Another source said the AI file now spanned semiconductor controls, distillation and intellectual property, safety rules, cybersecurity and military constraints. With such a broad spectrum and amid divergent expectations, they did not expect much from this round. AI security, they said, was the one area where some overlap looked possible. Such is the context in which American AI companies have been “aggressively lobbying” the White House for a harder line, according to a person following the talks, while the Chinese side was expected to resist any US attempt to “impose a global ban on Chinese AI models”. Earlier this week, Bessent warned that “nothing else would matter” if China pulled ahead in AI. That same day, American agencies accused six Chinese firms, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and Alibaba, of industrial-scale distillation of frontier US models since late 2024, likely with “Chinese government awareness”. On Thursday, US-based Anthropic alleged Alibaba alone ran more than 151 million Claude exchanges between May and July, while Moonshot and DeepSeek routed tens of millions more queries, in some cases exposing sensitive military and government data. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Beijing rejected the claims, calling them groundless and accusing Washington of trying to suppress competition. Beijing said it was still willing to hold “constructive and professional discussions” under the dialogue as the two leaders agreed in May. According to Sourabh Gupta of the Institute for China-America Studies, the wide range of issues in the AI file suggested the track should ideally run in parallel to, but separately from, the broader trade, technology and economy channel. “[If He] is indeed Bessent’s counterpart on the AI track, it makes more sense to conduct the AI conversation at the same time and venue as the broader trade, tech and economy discussion without necessarily merging the two tracks together,” Gupta said. Denis Simon of the Quincy Institute, a Washington think tank, said that if the AI discussion was folded into the Bessent-He economic track, “it would constitute a modest downgrade in institutional status but not necessarily a substantive abandonment of AI risk reduction”. Simon said that a stand-alone AI session would give officials a protected block of time for issues that rarely survived a ministerial agenda: military applications, autonomous cyber operations, accident notification, frontier model evaluation, and the relationship between AI and nuclear command and control. Folded into a Bessent-He economic meeting, AI would compete with tariffs, overcapacity, rare earths, farm purchases, investment rules and summit deliverables, he added. “Those issues are politically immediate and economically quantifiable,” Simon said, adding that “nuclear AI risk reduction is neither. In bureaucratic terms, it is therefore especially vulnerable to being pushed towards the end of the agenda”. Bessent himself had simultaneously cast AI as something Trump and Xi should discuss, he said, “but that does not make Treasury the natural institution for sustained military AI or nuclear command discussions”.

title: Meet Sandra Bullock’s children, Louis and Laila, who appear in Practical Magic 2 ‘in voice and in spirit’
description: The Blind Side actress’ adopted son and daughter make a surprise cameo in her first film since 2022, which co-stars Nicole Kidman, Joey King and Maisie Williams.
content: Sandra Bullock may be one of the biggest stars in Hollywood, but there’s no role she takes more seriously than motherhood. The 62-year-old actress has a son, Louis, 16, and a daughter, Laila, 13 – both adopted. She has been sharing rare glimpses into their lives while promoting Practical Magic 2, which marks her first appearance on the silver screen since 2022’s The Lost City. Her teenage children also make a surprise cameo in the film. So, what do we know about Louis and Laila? When did Sandra Bullock adopt them? The Miss Congeniality star adopted Louis Bardo Bullock in 2010, when he was three and a half months old, according to People. He was born in New Orleans. Bullock told InStyle he was “wise and kind” and had a “spiritual bigness to him”. Shortly after his adoption, the attention around Bullock’s divorce from Jesse James due to his infidelity became so toxic that she had to hide the newborn child in a hockey bag to escape the paparazzi, she revealed to Jennifer Aniston for Interview Magazine. In 2015, two-and-a-half-year-old Laila Bullock became part of the actress’ family. She was previously in foster care in Louisiana, per People, but it was Louis who “spearheaded the whole journey” of bringing her home. Bullock raised her children with her long-time partner, photographer Bryan Randall, alongside his daughter from another relationship, until his death in August 2023 from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). What are their interests? In 2022, Bullock described her son as a “crazy foodie” on Live with Kelly and Ryan, revealing his interest in cooking and mixing drinks. Watching his mother’s films is “not his cup of tea”, she said on Jimmy Kimmel Live!, adding that he has “really good taste”, which includes Spider-Man and anime. The Oscar-winning actress also shared on The Tonight Show that Louis enjoys basketball and fashion while calling Laila a “government hacker”. She once told People that the little girl is set to be the president of the United States. More recently, on Kylie Kelce’s Not Gonna Lie podcast, Bullock talked about Laila’s interest in racing cars. Their subtle cameo in Sandra Bullock’s new film On The Tonight Show, Bullock revealed that her children appear “in voice and in spirit” in Practical Magic 2. Their voices come to her character, Sally Owens, after her magic is “unblocked” in the sequel. “The first thing I hear, always, are my babies,” she said, explaining the decision to “chronologically play [her] kids as much as we can up to a certain age”. Bullock further revealed to Interview Magazine that the film is a “love letter to Laila”, noting her daughter’s similarity to her on-screen daughter, Kylie, played by Joey King.

title: Saudi pipeline that bypasses Hormuz shut after attacks
description: The kingdom said the East-West pipeline was targeted by drones launched from Iraq, causing several injuries.
content: Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline after the vital oil conduit came under aerial attack in the widening Middle East war. The world’s largest crude oil exporter temporarily closed the pipeline after a drone attack that both Baghdad and Riyadh said had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate. Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday in response to the attack. The 1,200km (745-mile) pipeline running across the Arabian Peninsula had helped Saudi Arabia to bypass a shipping logjam in the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic has slowed to ‌a trickle due to the war between the US and Iran. The Saudi energy ministry said it had shut the pipeline as a precaution. The line has been moving 4 million to 5 million barrels per day in recent months, amounting to 4 to 5 per cent of global supply, according to ship tracking companies and analysts. The attack comes as Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen tightened their grip in the Red Sea, which combined with the Strait of Hormuz disruptions has put an energy squeeze on both sides of the Arabian peninsula and sent global oil prices back above US$100 per barrel. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Iran was probably responsible ‌for the attack. “I think ⁠they are, probably they are,” Trump told reporters in ‌Dublin when asked if Iran was responsible for the attack on the vital ‌oil conduit. Trump also said that ⁠he ⁠had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom ‌he described as a “good friend”. Trump added that Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis had ‌called ‌his administration and indicated they did not want ‌the US to become directly involved in ⁠the conflict. Four Yemeni government sources said that Houthis had seized the strategic island of Perim on Friday at the mouth of the Red Sea, in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The dual attacks reported on Friday – on the pipeline and Perim island – could represent a dangerous escalation while diplomatic efforts to end ⁠the war have stalled. Saudi Arabia had asked Washington for military help with the Houthis, sources said, at a time when higher fuel prices during the war have already exacted a political toll on Trump and his ‌Republican Party ahead of November congressional elections. The East-West pipeline was hit on Thursday morning in Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh and Medina regions, the Saudi energy ministry said. It was not immediately clear who was responsible for the strikes. Satellite images showed black smoke rising from an area of the pipeline south of Medina. The attack resulted in some injuries and damage that was being assessed, ‌the Saudi foreign ministry said without detailing the impact on exports. The dismissed Iraqi military commander had led operations in Maysan province, according to Saturday’s statement by the Iraqi prime minister’s office. Maysan ⁠province, which borders Iran in southeastern Iraq, has long been ⁠regarded as an area where Iran-backed Shiite militias operate and maintain influence. Saudi Arabia had opted against retaliation so far following a request from the Iraqi prime minister, the Saudi foreign ministry said in a statement, while adding the kingdom reserved the right to “take all measures necessary” to protect its interests. ‌Iraq’s government condemned attacks. Saudi crude supply fell to the lowest levels in more than three decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due to attacks on ships transiting Bab el-Mandeb by Houthi-linked groups. Iraq responded by ordering the closure of the Shalamcheh border crossing between Iraq and Iran as a precautionary measure, ‌two security ‌sources told Reuters. The crossing serves as one of the main routes for imports to Iraq of vegetables and other food supplies from Iran. The two sources said a wide-scale operation was under way to find those responsible for ‌the pipeline attack. Counter-attack planned If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, their backer Iran could gain a critical advantage in its war with the US. Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthis – ⁠mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi air strikes during Yemen’s civil war – in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline. The dramatic Houthi advance down Yemen’s Red Sea coast reportedly came with direct ⁠guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. Iran describes the Houthis as an ally but publicly denies giving them military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”. The Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to ‌a previously announced ban. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed ‌bin Salman called Trump at least twice on Thursday to request US military help in fighting the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter said on Friday, confirming an earlier report by Axios. Washington told Riyadh it was not willing to take direct military action for now but would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, the two sources said. The White House did not address a question about any phone calls between the two leaders, but a senior administration official speaking on the condition of anonymity said Washington was in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government.

title: US boy, 15, rescued after clinging to capsized boat for days in Alaska’s Bering Sea
description: The teen’s brother and cousin died after the small skiff flipped, and their bodies were recovered after he was hoisted to safety.
content: A 15-year-old boy survived on top of an overturned skiff in Alaska’s frigid Bering Sea for roughly two days, losing his older brother and then his cousin to the ocean after the boat capsized while they were out fishing. The teen, identified by a relative as Derek Parker Aghnaanga, was finally hoisted to safety Monday by a fishing boat near St Lawrence Island – a remote Alaskan island closer to Russia than it is to the US. The bodies of his cousin and brother were also recovered. The cousin had held onto the overturned boat for a while too, but did not survive until the rescue, the teen told one of the rescuers. The captain of the fishing boat that came to his aid said Aghnaanga clung to the skiff through darkness and water temperatures around 10 degrees Celsius (50 degrees Fahrenheit). “That’s one tough kid,” Adam White, captain of The Northwest Explorer, told KTUU-TV in Anchorage. “Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff,” White said. “And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away.” US coastguard planes and helicopters began searching for the skiff on Monday morning after family members reported the three missing the night before. The group left the village of Savoonga on St Lawrence Island on Friday and planned to return early on Sunday, the coastguard said. Halibut fishing is a part of the culture and important to survival in the village where there are about 800 residents and jobs are hard to come by, said Collen Walker, an aunt of the two brothers. Residents often share their catch with family and neighbours, she said. “That’s how we do it in our community. We take care of one another,” she said on Friday. “We still live a traditional way of life even if the world is changing.” Aghnaanga, the teen rescued, often went fishing with his 35-year-old brother, Sidney Kulowiyi, and looked to him as a father figure ever since their own father died when they were younger, Walker said. She described Kulowiyi, a commercial fishing captain, as a humble and loving “provider for people in the village”. She did not want to release the name of their cousin who died, saying he also came from Savoonga. Their skiff capsized on Saturday night far out in the ocean, she was told. The coastguard said one of its aircrews spotted the boy on Monday morning and deployed a raft and supplies before contacting The Northwest Explorer. Aghnaanga’s mother was listening to a radio transmission of the rescue Monday while other family members huddled around a speakerphone, Walker said. “We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, ‘We found a kid, he’s alive, he’s alive,’” she said. “Then we asked, ‘Where’s the rest of them?’” Video of the rescue shows Aghnaanga in a bright yellow jacket kneeling atop the overturned skiff. The boat’s crew tosses him a line, tugging the skiff closer until they can pull him into a rescue basket. He was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he got onto the boat, the coastguard said. The fishing boat crew warmed him with blankets and hot packs, its captain said.

title: Luxury bar soap revival: how Chanel, Jo Malone, Diptyque and Aesop elevated everyday cleansers
description: With sustainable packaging and modern skin-friendly formulations, high-end beauty houses are transforming soap bars into sought-after items.
content: For most of the 2000s, the body wash industry did a convincing job of making bar soap feel like something only your grandfather used. Sleek bottles, foaming textures and a lot of vocabulary around “moisturising complex” pushed the bar quietly to the back of the shelf, where it sat next to nothing in particular. Then, sometime in the past few years, it had a glow-up. It wasn’t one thing that brought it back into the fray. The slow beauty and sustainability conversation started picking away at single-use plastic packaging and suddenly a paper-wrapped bar looked like the more considered choice. At the same time, the shower started being treated as a ritual rather than a chore, which meant everything in it became an opportunity for intention (and aesthetics). Which is probably why Chanel’s No 5 bath soap, a creamy bar scented with the floral notes of the iconic fragrance, now sits on bathroom shelves alongside things like candles and curated ceramics. Chloé’s Atelier des Fleurs line translates the maison’s single-note fragrances into logo-engraved bars finished with its signature pleating. And Claus Porto, the Portuguese house that’s been producing elaborately illustrated soaps since 1887, has made a collector’s item of its Deco collection slabs. But the most interesting part of the bar soap story is what’s changed inside. Traditional bar soaps were alkaline, usually landing somewhere between pH 9 and 10, while your skin’s natural surface sits at a slightly acidic 4.5 to 5.5. “That alkalinity strips away the skin’s natural oils and disrupts the acid mantle, the protective film that keeps moisture in and irritants out, and it can take your skin hours to recover its natural balance afterward,” says John Blount, biochemist and president and CEO of Pure & Gentle. So that tight, dry feeling most people associate with bar soap was really the skin’s acid mantle struggling. Modern bars are engineered to a different standard. Blount points to three main advances in the best of them: gentler surfactants that lift dirt without over-stripping; barrier-supportive ingredients like ceramides, fatty acids and humectants including glycerine; and what formulators call deposition technology. “Smart ingredients cause a conditioning film to actually stick to your skin as you rinse, rather than washing straight down the drain,” he says. “Without that, adding moisturising ingredients to a rinse-off product is largely pointless.” Many of the better bars on the market now are what the industry calls syndet (synthetic detergent) bars: think of them as liquid body wash that’s had the water removed and been pressed into a bar, with the same pH balance and the same skin-friendly logic. Dove’s classic Sensitive Skin Beauty Bar is probably the most recognisable example, and it’s lasted this long for exactly the same reasons the format is having a moment now. “High-quality bar soaps often contain fewer preservatives and unnecessary additives compared to some liquid cleansers,” says Dr Anna Andrienko, dermatologist and aesthetic doctor at Dr Ducu Clinics in London, which means a well-formulated bar can actually be a gentler option for reactive skin than an elaborate body wash full of fragrance and emulsifiers. She also notes that formulation matters more than format. “While traditional soaps were often criticised for being harsh due to their alkaline pH, modern bar soaps are frequently enriched with humectants and emollients such as glycerine, plant oils and butters,” she adds, all of which support the skin barrier, reduce moisture loss and keep skin hydrated after washing. So how do you tell which bars are doing what they are intended for, versus the ones that are mainly beautiful to look at? Blount says to look for glycerine reasonably high in the ingredient list, and check whether the formula includes ceramides, fatty acids or humectants. “These ingredients help replace what washing takes away,” he says, and in a rinse-off product, where they sit in the formula matters as much as whether they’re there at all. Dr Andrienko’s guidance is similarly practical: “ingredient quality and pH balance remain key considerations”, particularly for dry or sensitive skin types, and she’d add fragrance to that list too, since scenting agents are some of the most common triggers causing irritation in cleansers. The category has also spread wide enough that the bar you reach for depends entirely on what you’re asking it to do. If the goal is simplicity, Dr Bronner’s Pure-Castile Bar Soaps, made from saponified plant oils and barely anything else, is about as minimal as a cleanser gets. For those dealing with body texture or congestion, a soap like Soft Services’ Buffing Bar takes the format in a more targeted direction, combining physical and chemical exfoliants in a bar that functions closer to a treatment than a basic cleanse. And for something that sits between the functional and the indulgent, L’Occitane’s Shea Butter Extra-Gentle Soap offers a more fragrance-forward approach, without being aggressive and still gentle enough for daily use without a second thought. Luxury bar soaps operate on a different logic, and at this end of the category, the premium goes into the scent experience as much as anything else. A Chanel No 5 soap, a Jo Malone Pomegranate Noir bar or a Diptyque Eau Rose is a way of wearing a fragrance you love in a format that’s also practical. Brands like Aesop have taken a different approach, treating bars less as fragrance vehicles and more as counter objects, with formulations that are just as popular as anything else in their range. And for those who want the scent experience and the formulation to match, Malin+Goetz’s triple-milled, glycerine-enriched bars are a good middle ground. None of which means we have to choose between a bar that performs and one that we actually enjoy using, and that’s really what’s shifted: not the format itself, but the scrutiny we’re bringing to it. The same ingredient-reading energy that transformed the skincare aisle has finally arrived in the shower. As Blount puts it, “The real question is always what’s in the formula, not what shape it comes in.”

title: Americans mark 25 years since 9/11 attacks amid enduring grief, reflection
description: Nearly 3,000 people were killed on the day that has shaped US society for decades, influencing its foreign policy and domestic politics.
content: Twenty-five years ⁠after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims, many carrying pictures of their loved ones, joined Vice-President J.D. Vance and four former US presidents at ground zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s ‌North Tower. Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that lasts for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001. Other moments of silence followed, marking when the other three planes crashed and the two towers collapsed. For the first time, a seventh moment of silence was set to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterwards. Gregory Carafello attended the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise ⁠that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.” At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, where American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building’s west flank, killing 184, US President ‌Donald Trump chronicled some of the stories of those aboard who perished in the crash: a woman pregnant with her first child, a family of four headed to Australia, three sixth-graders on a field trip. The president and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who also delivered remarks, both used their speeches to make the case for the Iran war, which they have defended as necessary to prevent Tehran from acquiring ‌nuclear weapons. “We salute our first responders and law enforcement, and we love them,” Trump said. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s No 1 sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic ⁠of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.” Mourners were also ⁠gathering in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington. The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes ‌towards security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families and friends, first responders and rescuers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes ‌before striking ‌the North Tower. Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him to her father’s grave last week and attended a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday. “This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing ‌that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian aid, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. “We owe it to my father and all ⁠the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added. A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them. The attacks initiated the “war on terror”, which led to the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the Iran war. At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and ‌patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the ‌attacks. At the same time, however, Muslim-Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found September 11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. Zohran Mamdani, New York’s first Muslim mayor, faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected. Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescuers who spent weeks or months at the site afterwards, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of September 11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone.

title: Man arrested after allegedly refusing to share HK$30m Mark Six jackpot with group
description: Insider says 36-year-old refused to evenly divide prize money with 14 others who shared ticket, prompting group member to make police report.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a 36-year-old man suspected of having fled with a Mark Six jackpot worth around HK$30 million (US$3.8 million) that he should have shared with 14 colleagues. A source said on Friday that a 53-year-old man had reported to police on Wednesday that he was one of 15 colleagues who had chipped in to buy a Mark Six ticket for the draw on Saturday. The group reportedly comprised some staff members of the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD). His colleague, a 36-year-old man, bought the ticket and held the account into which the winnings were paid, the source said. After the ticket won, the 36-year-old refused to evenly divide the prize money among the group, which prompted a dispute, the insider said. A meeting was held on Wednesday evening in Aberdeen to try to resolve the dispute, but the source said the ticket-buyer allegedly insisted that he would not split the winnings during the roughly 30-minute negotiation. Worried that the 36-year-old intended to keep the entire prize and disappear, the 53-year-old man filed a police report at 10.06pm the same day. The 36-year-old reportedly did not go to work for five days. Police said on Friday night that a man, 36, had been arrested on suspicion of theft. He remained in custody. Officers from Western police district are handling the investigation. In response to South China Morning Post queries, the FEHD said it noted that police were investigating the case and would cooperate with their probe. “As the police investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate for the department to comment on the details at this stage,” a department spokesman said. The September 5 draw was a “Mark Six 50th Anniversary Snowball” draw, held by the Hong Kong Jockey Club, with a record jackpot of HK$228 million. According to the club’s website, the first prize pool had 3.5 winning units, each paying HK$63.3 million.

title: Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro under investigation over alleged corruption
description: The probe stems from questions over an investment Bolsonaro allegedly solicited from Daniel Vorcaro, owner of failed lender Banco Master.
content: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in next month’s election, is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering tied to failed lender Banco Master, according to court documents unsealed on Friday. The probe into the senator, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, was opened in July by Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee who has recently been hailed ‌as a hero by many on Brazil’s right, including Flavio Bolsonaro himself. The development could further shake an already volatile presidential race, with multiple opinion polls showing Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula statistically tied in a simulated second-round run-off. The judge opened the probe at the request of federal police as part of a broader investigation into the failed bank. But details of the investigation only became public after Chief Justice Edson Fachin ordered the proceedings related to the Banco Master case unsealed late on Thursday. Mendonca complied with Fachin’s request, releasing thousands of pages of court records. Further details and the broader implications of the newly unsealed documents were not immediately clear, as parts of the case, including details of ⁠the investigation into Senator Bolsonaro, remained under secrecy as police actively investigate. Brazil’s institutions have been shaken by the fallout from the expanding probe and alleged ties between banker Daniel Vorcaro and central ‌bank officials, senior government members, opposition politicians and Supreme Court justices. The investigation into Flavio Bolsonaro stems from questions over an investment he allegedly solicited from Vorcaro, owner of Banco Master, to help finance Dark Horse, a film about his father that stars US actor Jim ‌Caviezel. Questions about the film’s financing emerged in May, prompting the senator to acknowledge seeking financial backing from Vorcaro, while denying wrongdoing. The disclosures cost him support in ⁠opinion polls at the time. The unsealed ⁠documents show the federal police then requested an investigation, authorised by Justice Mendonca, to examine whether Senator Bolsonaro committed money laundering, illicit foreign exchange and corruption. Police cited donations made by Vorcaro, who was arrested in March, to the film ‌as grounds for seeking the probe. The senator has repeatedly said his dealings with the banker were strictly private and unrelated to the matters under investigation by the federal police. The new developments intensify a crisis rattling Brazil as voters head ‌into ‌an unusually tight election campaign in which any major development could tip the balance in favour of either left-wing Lula or Bolsonaro. Fachin has sought to resolve a public clash between ‌justices Mendonca and Alexandre de Moraes, who has also been mentioned in the Banco Master probe, that thrust the court into one of its most severe internal crises in decades. Mendonca made public ⁠documents from the investigation earlier this month, including dozens of messages that police say Vorcaro sent to Moraes. The disclosures prompted calls for an unprecedented investigation into a sitting Supreme Court ⁠justice over allegations that Moraes acted as an adviser to the banker. Moraes, in response, accused Mendonca of abusing his authority. Fachin scheduled a full-court session for Tuesday, when the court’s 10-member bench is expected to discuss allegations regarding Moraes’ relationship with Vorcaro. Flavio Bolsonaro’s supporters have attempted to link Lula to Moraes, who pursued ‌former president Jair Bolsonaro over a 2023 coup plot ‌and secured his conviction last year. During Independence Day rallies in Sao Paulo on Monday, a giant inflatable balloon depicting Mendonca towered over crowds gathered to support Bolsonaro’s campaign. Seeking to distance himself from the crisis at the court, Lula publicly supported unsealing the investigation hours before Fachin’s decision. “Whenever there is an allegation involving the judiciary or politics, it should be made public so everyone knows what is happening,” he said in an interview with SBT TV on Thursday. “Investigate everything, disclose everything, regardless of who it hurts.”

title: Review | Venice 2026: A Bit of Light movie review – Iranian drama strikes a melancholic chord
description: Ali Asgari’s Tehran-set drama about an aggrieved doctor who decides to end it all as war looms is well acted but never fully bursts into life.
content: 3/5 stars Set against the backdrop of recent protests and looming war, Ali Asgari’s on-the-nose drama illuminates the grim reality of everyday life in modern Iran. Receiving its world premiere in competition at the Venice International Film Festival, A Bit of Light is Asgari’s sixth feature film and comes after 2025’s Divine Comedy. He co-wrote the screenplay of his latest film with Shadmehr Rastin, who previously collaborated with Jafar Panahi on the Cannes-winning It Was Just an Accident. Set in Tehran, A Bit of Light opens in the wake of nationwide protests against the Iranian government in December 2025 over mounting economic hardship. The shadow of war looms as “this Trump guy” threatens to bomb the country, prompting residents to stick gaffer tape in an “X” shape over their windows to prevent the glass from shattering. At times, Asgari flirts with black comedy. “War is a very strange thing; it gives you crazy ideas,” one character remarks, adding that he would not mind a missile striking his old house if it meant saving on demolition costs. At the centre of the narrative is Arash (The Seed of the Sacred Fig’s Missagh Zareh), a kindly doctor who has reached the end of the road. After he treated wounded demonstrators, he saw his practice shut down and ransacked, while his medical licence was revoked. In Iran, Arash reasons, when you wake up, you never know whether you will make it to the end of the day. Consequently, he has decided to end his life. With 20 years of medical experience, he notes, “I know how to end it painlessly.” Rather than simply killing himself, he decides to put his affairs in order – from distributing his plants and finding a home for his cat to telling his brother, two sisters and mother of his intentions. If only Arash, a gentle soul, could open his eyes to how beloved he is by his family and by the patients who rely on him for medicine and comfort. At the heart of the film is a soulful turn from Zareh, whose sad eyes speak volumes. It is a deeply human performance, full of warmth and humour – such as when he tells his mother he is 10kg overweight after she claims he looks thin. Unfortunately, even his sensitive portrayal cannot propel a film that is sluggishly paced and lacks the desired emotional impact. A Bit of Light is a respectable work, made partly in Tehran under challenging conditions, but it remains a character study that never fully bursts into life. There are quietly contemplative scenes – not least a moment of small joy as the family tucks into bowls of watermelon – but, set against the great works of Iranian cinema, A Bit of Light strikes only a minor melancholic chord. title: Sweden heads into final stretch before key election
description: The results could see either the centre left take back power or the far-right enter government for the first time.
content: Sweden’s party leaders campaigned on Friday in the final stretch of a close election race that could see either the centre left take back power or the far-right enter government for the first time. Outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was hoping for a renewed mandate to “make Sweden great again”, he told Agence France-Presse on the sidelines of a campaign rally, in a nod to US President Donald Trump’s catchphrase. While Europe is dominated by right-wing governments, opinion polls in Sweden have for months shown the opposition left-wing bloc holding a strong lead ahead of Sunday’s general election, although this has narrowed considerably in the final days of the campaign. “The most important thing is that the right-wing wins, to continue what they have started,” pensioner Kurt Flodin, 79, said of Kristersson’s outgoing government. He said he wanted Kristersson to continue focusing on curbing the organised crime plaguing the country. For their part, the centre-left Social Democrats – which governed for the better part of the 20th century and remain Sweden’s biggest party – have pledged to help struggling households pay bills and bolster the welfare state. Jenny Larsson, a theatre worker who turns 54 on election day, said these issues mattered. She said she was unhappy with politicians “blaming immigration for things that are not caused by immigration” – and feared the far-right Sweden Democrats would be allowed into government if the right-wing bloc won. The anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, long viewed as political pariahs, caused shock in the 2022 election when they overtook Kristersson’s Moderates to become Sweden’s second-biggest party, on 20.5 per cent. Kristersson responded by making an unprecedented deal with the extreme-right party so his minority coalition could form a government. He gave the Sweden Democrats significant influence over government policy – especially on crime and immigration – in return for far-right support in parliament. He has now gone further, promising the Sweden Democrats cabinet posts if he is re-elected, a pledge whose significance he downplayed on Friday. “There’s nothing dramatic in that,” he argued. “Everybody can see that we have been cooperating successfully for the last four years.” An Indikator opinion poll published on Friday credited the four opposition parties – the Social Democrats, Greens, Centre and Left – with 50.8 per cent of voter support. The right-wing bloc – Kristersson’s Moderates, the Sweden Democrats, the Christian Democrats and the Liberals – garnered 47.6 per cent. Party leaders took part in a flurry of televised debates in the final days of campaigning. “Fewer and fewer Swedes are able to realise their dream of owning their own home. Life has become too expensive,” Social Democrats leader and ex-prime minister Magdalena Andersson told a debate on Thursday. “We’ve had four years of rising unemployment, with a salary that pays for less and less,” she said. Kristersson retorted that “two normal salaries should be enough to buy a small house”, saying people needed “economic growth and tax incentives” so they could do so. The debate focused on the housing shortage, plummeting education scores, jobs, the climate and security. Fearful of deteriorating security in Europe following Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Sweden has massively rearmed and boosted civil preparedness. So recent allegations of the far-right’s ties to Russia caused a stir. Extremism watchdog Expo revealed that a Sweden Democrat civil servant in parliament had shared pro-Russian propaganda for years. “On Monday, we could wake to a government where the keys to the defence ministry will be handed over to the Sweden Democrats … revealed to be infiltrated by friends of Putin,” Andersson warned in Thursday’s debate. “Don’t take that risk,” she urged voters. While the four opposition parties hold a slim lead, they are splintered ideologically and thorny negotiations would be needed to form a government even if they hold a majority.

title: In Focus | No pit stops: Chinese coal mine makes big upgrade with autonomous electric trucks
description: The deployment of self-driving vehicles, now past the pilot stage, has improved safety, efficiency and operating costs, mine manager says.
content: In north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region, home to the country’s largest coal reserves, a vast open-pit mine cuts deep into the earth, shrouded in clouds of dust. Winters here are long and brutal, with temperatures plunging to as low as minus 40 degrees Celsius (minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit). In older, more traditional days, hundreds of truck drivers, bundled in heavy winter gear, had to brave icy roads and the risk of frostbite as they hauled loads through the pit. When dense fog and snow rolled in, visibility could fall so low that drivers had to stop work for fear of a fatal crash. Today, however, an observer at the edge of the same pit could see a convoy of electric mining trucks rumble deep into the mine. A closer look would reveal something remarkable: no one behind the wheel. This is the scene in Yimin – one of the five largest open-cast coal mines in China – which launched the world’s first large-scale fleet of cabless, electric autonomous mining trucks in May last year. More than a year on, the performance of the 100-vehicle fleet offers a chance to assess how the technology has fared beyond the pilot stage – and whether it can be scaled up further to help upgrade China’s traditional energy sector. “The autonomous electric trucks have helped us cut operating costs, improve safety and increase efficiency,” said Zhao Yaozhong, deputy manager for technology at the mine. Beyond easing recruitment difficulties caused by harsh working conditions, the deployment has – more importantly – improved safety by reducing the scope for human error, analysts and industry insiders said. This consideration takes on particular importance amid renewed scrutiny of mine safety following a spate of recent accidents. The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment Zhao Yaozhong, deputy mine manager for technology at Yimin Custom-built by heavy machinery maker Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group to withstand extreme cold, the self-driving trucks operate over a 5G network and Huawei Technologies’ cloud-based AI dispatching system, allowing them to navigate the mine and optimise routes in real time, according to the companies. Automated swapping stations replace depleted batteries in about six minutes, while a dedicated solar microgrid supplies electricity, allowing the fleet to achieve zero-carbon status and run constantly. “The trucks don’t need to eat or rest, so they can work around the clock, while we just monitor the health of the equipment,” Zhao said. He noted that many mining accidents over the years had been linked to human factors, such as emotions or failures to follow operating procedures. Zhao contrasted this with the autonomous trucks, which he said executed commands precisely once given instructions to haul coal or overburden – the layer of rock and dirt covering a mineral deposit. Coal mine safety has fallen back under the regulatory microscope in China following a gas explosion in May at the Liushenyu Coal Mine in Shanxi province. The blast killed 82 people, making it the deadliest coal mine disaster in more than a decade. Aside from safety, the autonomous solution also offered cost savings, Zhao said, remaining cheaper to operate than conventionally driven trucks even after factoring upfront investments in the vehicles, battery-swapping stations and 5G cloud platform, as well as maintenance costs. The savings have come mainly from lower labour and fuel costs, with the deployment replacing a crew of nearly 270 truck drivers with a smaller maintenance and support team – equivalent to about 220 fewer positions – and saving an estimated 13,300 tonnes of diesel. Zhao said operating costs for the autonomous trucks were about 6.5 yuan (US$0.97) per cubic metre for hauling coal and overburden, compared with roughly 12 to 14 yuan per cubic metre for conventional haul trucks – almost half the cost. Since the fleet was deployed in May last year, it has hauled about 28 million cubic metres (988.8 million cubic feet), saving nearly 200 million yuan (US$29.8 million) in operating costs, he added. Coal has long been the backbone of China’s energy system, powering the country’s rapid industrialisation and still accounting for more than half of its energy consumption. Its dominant role has also helped cushion China from this year’s global energy shock, which saw a rapid increase in oil prices triggered by the US-Israel war with Iran. Wang Hongzhi, head of the National Energy Administration (NEA), said at a press conference in June that “coal is our biggest source of confidence in maintaining a stable energy supply”, saying China should build up its major coal production bases in line with its national circumstances. Meanwhile, upgrading and transforming the traditional energy sector has also become part of Beijing’s broader energy strategy. A blueprint released by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA for China’s “new energy system” during the period covered by the country’s 15th five-year plan called for a “modern coal supply chain”, with wider adoption of green mining practices and the development of smart mines tailored to local conditions. In another blueprint intended specifically for the coal industry over the period, the two agencies set a target to further advance smart mining across the sector and raise the share of production capacity at smart mines to 75 per cent by 2030. Analysts from Citic Securities said regulators’ focus on ensuring a safe and stable coal supply amid energy security concerns was driving smart mining, which could also help address labour shortages and cut costs for coal companies. “The industry’s development is therefore driven not only by central policy coordination and local development plans, but also by coal companies’ own willingness to upgrade,” the analysts said in a report on smart mining last year. They estimated that smart upgrades could reduce mine staffing by 20 to 30 per cent, with the investment potentially paying for itself in about seven to eight years on labour savings alone. Since its deployment in May 2025, the Yimin fleet has moved beyond the pilot phase, taking on more demanding operations as the mine prepares to add 200 more trucks by the end of this year. Initially used to haul topsoil and rock on the surface, the trucks began hauling coal in November, Zhao said. The mine also relocated its battery-swapping stations into the pit to test whether the trucks could navigate more challenging terrain, such as the confined spaces of the coal-preparation plant. “We need to verify the system’s stability, because we plan to deploy 200 more trucks by the end of this year,” he said. For Yimin, the experience suggested that technology was no longer the main barrier to wider adoption. But replicating the model across China’s coal mines was another question, with differences in geology, infrastructure and power supply likely to determine how quickly it can scale. “The technology behind autonomous electric mining trucks is ready for nationwide deployment, but the biggest challenge is whether individual mines have enough power infrastructure to support them,” Zhao said. Yimin, China’s first coal-and-power integrated project, has an advantage in electricity supply, with the mine able to draw power directly from the affiliated Yimin power plant. “For other mines, such as those in [the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region], the biggest issue is whether they have enough power supply,” he noted, adding that government efforts to encourage mines to develop microgrids combining solar and wind power with energy storage could offer a potential solution. Developing smart microgrids in mining areas that coordinate power generation, grids, electricity demand and energy storage is also listed in the coal industry’s five-year plan, which calls for the integrated development and operation of solar and wind power, coal-mine gas generation, energy storage and smart control systems. According to the Citic Securities analysts, autonomous trucks at open-pit mines and mining robots for underground operations were among the two most mature applications combining artificial intelligence with mining hardware in China, while home-grown large language models for mining provided the technological foundation for such integration. “We expect … mining-specific large models to incorporate generative AI, further enhancing data analysis and decision-making capabilities while improving safety and energy efficiency in mining operations,” the analysts said.

title: UK lawmakers reject bill to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales
description: The bill had proposed allowing adults with fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death, subject to approval.
content: UK lawmakers on Friday voted down legislation to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives. The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was opposed by 286 members of parliament, while 270 voted for it. The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in parliament about assisted dying. On two previous occasions in 2024 and 2025, the elected House of Commons had backed the bill, but it did not become law because it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the revising House of Lords chamber. The bill had proposed allowing adults in England and Wales, with fewer than six months to live, to apply for an assisted death subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel. The government took a neutral stance, saying it was a matter of conscience. The new UK leader, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, did not vote because he said he did not want to “unduly influence the debate”. Opponents branded the bill unsafe and unworkable, citing concerns around potential coercion of vulnerable people and a lack of safeguards for those with disabilities. Lawmaker and cancer surgeon Dr Zubir Ahmed also noted uncertainty around a doctor’s prognosis. “I have to be honest with you,” he said. “When I am asked to prognosticate as to whether someone has six months to live or not, I am as often wrong as I am right.” Proponents of “assisted dying” – sometimes referred to as “assisted suicide” – had hoped it would mark the biggest change to social policy in the United Kingdom since abortion was partially legalised in 1967. The intention was to put an end to the practice of those near the end of their lives going to other countries, such as Switzerland, for an assisted death. Assisted suicide – where patients take a lethal drink prescribed by a doctor – is legal in countries including Australia, Belgium, Canada, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, Switzerland and parts of the United States, with regulations on qualifying criteria varying by jurisdiction. In July, French lawmakers backed a similar bill to allow adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. However, it has not become law, because there will be a review to determine if it complies with the French constitution. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Pillar of Shame sculptor to ask Denmark to negotiate for artwork’s return
description: Hong Kong officials rebut Jens Galschiot’s claims of ownership, note sculpture previously given to alliance challenging Communist Party.
content: The creator of a sculpture commemorating those killed in the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown will ask Danish authorities to negotiate with Hong Kong for its return, with city officials disputing his claims of owning the confiscated artwork. The fate of the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture has come back under the spotlight after the High Court on Friday handed jail sentences to three former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China at the end of a high-profile national security trial. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Danish artist Jens Galschiot said he intended to ask his government to officially declare the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) sculpture a work of art and part of his country’s cultural heritage so it could be returned to “its rightful owner”. He revealed he had raised the issue with the Danish parliament’s foreign policy committee, adding that a cross-party group of the European Parliament and the European Union’s Hong Kong office had also followed up on the matter. “For me, the issue is quite simple: the Pillar of Shame is my sculpture,” Galschiot said. “It was never given away. It should not be confiscated or destroyed because of its political symbolism or because it commemorates the victims of the Tiananmen Square massacre.” In its verdict last month, the court found the now-disbanded alliance had incited supporters to undermine the Communist Party’s leadership by advocating the group’s operational objective of ending “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China. The three presiding judges found the alliance had organised various public events to achieve that aim, including the annual cleaning of the sculpture at the University of Hong Kong campus. The court has adjourned a decision on the sculpture’s disposal, pending the hearing of further arguments. Chief Superintendent Steve Li Kwai-wah of the force’s national security department rejected Galschiot’s claim of ownership on Friday and said the sculpture belonged to the alliance, whose properties were now under the official receiver’s jurisdiction. Without mentioning the sculpture by its name, Li said “this pillar” was closely linked to the alliance’s attempts to incite others to undermine the Communist Party. “I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” he said. Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung added that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated. Former alliance vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung, who was sentenced to seven years and three months in jail on Friday, had demanded that the sculpture be returned to Galschiot. But the court said she might not be in a position to comment since she did not act on behalf of the alliance during the trial. The judges nonetheless invited Chow to make written submissions on the matter, but added she should also include reasons why she was a relevant party. The alliance was best known for organising annual candlelight vigils to mark Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters on June 4, 1989. The event used to be the only large-scale commemoration of the incident on Chinese soil.

title: US consumer prices pick up in August, bolstering chances of interest rate increase
description: In the 12 months through August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4 per cent after rising by the same margin in July.
content: US consumer prices accelerated in August as the cost of petrol rebounded after two straight monthly declines, bolstering financial market expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates next week. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.4 per cent last month after edging up 0.1 per cent in July, the Labour Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics ‌said on Friday. In the 12 months through August, consumer inflation advanced 3.4 per cent after rising by the same margin in July. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI increasing 0.4 per cent over the month and climbing 3.4 per cent year on year. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI rose 0.3 per cent last month after gaining 0.2 per cent in July. The so-called core CPI increased 2.4 per cent year-on-year in August after rising 2.5 per cent in July. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price indexes for its 2 per cent inflation target. The government reported on Thursday an increase in the Producer Price Index ⁠in August, with strong rises in several key components that feed into the calculation of PCE inflation. That added to last week’s robust employment report for ‌August in boosting rate increase prospects next week. The odds of a rate increase had diminished following comments by Fed Governor Christopher Waller last week that he was inclined to argue in favour of keeping rates ‌steady if data confirmed inflation pressures were cooling. Oil prices climbed back above US$100 a barrel on Thursday, while diesel costs are at record ⁠highs, suggesting inflation was set to ⁠remain elevated and broaden out. Some economists saw price pressures persisting because of tariffs on imports, most recently against Canada, one of the United States’ top trade partners. Frustration over ‌higher prices, especially for petrol and food, has led to a sharp erosion in President Donald Trump’s approval ratings and could cost his Republican Party control of the US Congress in the November midterm ‌elections.
