After Thursday’s ‌PPI data, economists’ estimates for August’s core PCE price index ranged from as low as a 0.15 per cent gain to as high as a 0.28 per cent increase. ‌Core PCE inflation rose 0.2 per cent in July. Estimates for the year-on-year increase in core PCE inflation ranged from 3.2 per cent to 3.3 per cent. Core PCE inflation advanced 3.3 per cent in ⁠the 12 months through July. The August PCE inflation report will include changes to the methodology, which some economists say could lower the core inflation rate by ⁠a couple of basis points. Ahead of the CPI report, financial markets priced in a roughly 70 per cent chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase at the Fed’s policy meeting next week, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. The Fed’s benchmark overnight interest rate is currently in a 3.50 per cent to 3.75 per cent ‌range. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh last month said ‌the central bank would “have work to do” if policymakers did not get the confidence needed that inflation was declining to 2 per cent. But Trump is pressuring the Fed to cut rates, posting on social media last week to “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. Economists have blamed what they called political intimidation for the surge in yields on long-term US government bonds. Some expected the Fed to tighten policy next Wednesday to underscore its independence.

title: Study reveals link between Tibetan Plateau heat  and record rain in California
description: The discovery could transform winter forecasting and explains why severe floods hit the US west coast when dry weather was expected.
content: Abnormally high temperatures across the Tibetan Plateau in early winter can trigger catastrophic rainstorms in California, according to a new study revealing a previously unidentified climate connection. In the winters of 2016-2017 and 2022-2023, record-breaking rain swept across the US state and surrounding areas, causing billions of dollars in damage and several deaths during years when drier weather was expected in the region. A study led by researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) found that these rain events happened shortly after periods of unusually high land surface temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau in early winter. As the planet heats up and the world braces for what could be a record-strength El Nino event, understanding climate and weather connections over long distances could be the key to better weather forecasting and preparedness. The record rain caused “extraordinary damage and severe societal impacts”, according to the paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances on Wednesday. Rainfall in the winter of 2016-2017 effectively ended California’s five-year drought, with property damage reaching around US$2 billion. Heavy precipitation in the winter of 2022-2023 brought severe flooding, killing several people and causing around US$4.6 billion in damage. These winter events happened during La Nina years – the cold phase of the El Nino-Southern Oscillation (Enso) global climate pattern, when California typically experiences less precipitation. The extreme flooding that occurred during both seasons was not forecast in advance, nor was it recreated by computer simulations after the storms happened, according to the researchers from institutes in the US, China, France and India. “With more similar, though less severe, events occurring in recent years and drawing widespread public concern, it has become imperative to adequately address this scientific challenge,” they said. Using Earth system models, the team found that anomalous early winter heating over the Tibetan Plateau helped drive the extreme precipitation across the Pacific Ocean. The study was part of an international collaboration called GEWEX/LS4P that aims to study how land surface temperature and snowpack affect precipitation predictions. Xue Yongkang, study author and a distinguished professor at UCLA, said that through the collaboration, researchers were working with major meteorological institutions to integrate their findings into forecasting systems. “Because our paper presents a breakthrough discovery, it will take some time for relevant agencies to formally adopt it,” Xue wrote in an email on Wednesday. The Tibetan Plateau, which lies mainly in southwestern China and is the largest and highest plateau in the world, has been heating up rapidly in recent years as a result of climate change. The world is bracing for what has been dubbed a “super El Nino” – a particularly strong warm phase of the Enso cycle. The event, which could be the strongest on record, has raised concerns about the impact on land and ocean temperatures, as well as the potential for extreme weather events. Xue said the underlying mechanism of the Tibetan Plateau-California connection was “driven by general dynamic and physical principles, rather than depending specifically on Enso”. “Historically, general statistical relationships suggest that an upcoming strong El Nino should bring increased rainfall. However, a past El Nino event was paradoxically associated with an extraordinary California drought,” Xue said. “While we wait to see how the current event unfolds, we must also closely monitor early winter surface temperatures on the Tibetan Plateau.” Before 1980, there was no statistically significant relationship between early winter Tibetan Plateau temperatures and late winter precipitation in California. Xue said this was “largely because extreme hydroclimate events were far less frequent”. “However, the rise of unprecedented extremes in recent decades points to a shifting climate dynamic that warrants further investigation. Quantifying the exact scale of these future changes will require targeted, rigorous research.” Xue said early warning systems could be improved by shifting to a comprehensive, multi-variable approach that integrates data from the Tibetan Plateau. This could fill a critical gap in winter forecasting for the US west coast, which has traditionally relied heavily on sea surface temperatures. It would also improve winter preparedness by giving more weight to land temperature and extending warning windows. “Tracking Tibetan Plateau surface temperatures in early winter allows meteorologists to enhance early warning systems. This gives west coast communities vital extra time to prepare for devastating atmospheric rivers,” Xue said, referring to narrow bands of highly concentrated water vapour high in the atmosphere that can release large amounts of rain or snow when they make landfall. In control simulations, the team found that the models initially failed to reproduce the link between the Tibetan Plateau and California, leading to the need for model adjustments. Xue said that all weather forecast models used in the GEWEX/LS4P project, including those from the world’s major weather prediction centres, struggled to accurately simulate land temperature anomalies on the plateau and the link with California. “While we are working to enhance simulations in these areas, achieving substantial improvements will take time,” he said.

title: Chinese investors snap up government bonds amid global market jitters over US Treasuries
description: From social media tips to long queues at banks, buyers in China are rushing to secure government debt amid a global sell-off of US Treasuries.
content: While US Treasuries remain at the centre of a global bond sell-off despite efforts by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to calm the market, investors in China are rushing to buy domestic government debt. After China’s Ministry of Finance issued a fresh batch of savings bonds worth up to 55 billion yuan (US$8.2 billion) on Thursday, domestic buyers took to social media to share tips on how to secure them and voice frustration at how quickly the allocations had run out. “Those government bonds went so fast,” one user wrote on China’s popular lifestyle social media platform RedNote on Thursday. “I even set an alarm specifically to get them, but they were completely sold out within two minutes. The speed caught me by surprise.” Another user shared a screenshot showing the bonds had sold out within just five minutes of their launch, commenting: “The savings bonds were gone in seconds. Who am I competing with to get them?” The buying frenzy also spilled over into bank branches. The state-run Shanghai Securities News reported on Thursday that a Bank of China outlet had sold out of its three- and five-year savings bonds by about 10am amid long queues. Cliff Zhao, chief economist at CCB International in Hong Kong, noted that several overlapping factors were driving the demand. He cited declining bank deposit rates, which have made savings bonds more attractive; a shortage of alternative investments offering safe and predictable returns; and a broader shift among households towards wealth preservation and securing a steady income stream. This strong domestic appetite contrasts sharply with conditions in major developed bond markets, as the sell-off in US Treasuries ripples through global markets. Yields on sovereign debt have climbed amid persistent anxiety over US fiscal sustainability and persistent inflation, with the 30-year US Treasury yield reaching its highest level since 2007 and the 10-year yield nearing 5 per cent. Yields continued to rise even after the US Treasury Department said on Wednesday it would buy back up to US$6 billion of long-dated debt – a move widely seen as an effort to support the market and ease pressure on longer-term yields. Against this backdrop of global market strain, Zhao offered a measured assessment of the potential role of Chinese government debt in international portfolios. “As volatility in US Treasuries increases, Chinese government bonds can offer diversification benefits in global portfolios, but they should not be directly compared with US Treasuries,” he said. Zhao explained that while US Treasuries remained a core global reserve asset backed by deeper liquidity and a wide range of investment instruments, Chinese government bonds faced structural hurdles. In the near term, he said, currency-hedging costs and lower secondary-market liquidity would limit their role to supplementary assets rather than a direct substitute for US government bonds. Despite these constraints, data released by the People’s Bank of China’s Shanghai branch last month showed that overseas institutions held 2.02 trillion yuan (US$301 billion) in government bonds at the end of July, marking a third consecutive monthly increase.

title: As Singapore weighs joining China-led AI body, does it risk US retaliation?
description: Joining the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation gives Singapore influence, but may affect its Pax Silica role, analysts say.
content: As Singapore considers joining a China-led body on artificial intelligence, analysts say membership would give the city state a bigger say in global governance matters related to the technology but may invite an unfriendly response from Washington. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo revealed in parliament earlier this week that Singapore had received an invitation to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico). Singapore would consider the proposal alongside its broader engagements with China and other international AI cooperation initiatives, she added. Launched in July, the Shanghai-based bloc aims to build cooperation in areas such as AI governance, technical standards and development strategies. Responding to a parliamentary question on Singapore’s strategic positioning between Waico and the US-led Pax Silica initiative, Teo said on Wednesday: “Whether we participate in any particular initiative depends on its objectives, the substantive areas of common interest, how it complements our existing engagements, and Singapore’s overall interests. “It is therefore less meaningful to make one-to-one comparisons between individual initiatives.” The Pax Silica initiative aims to help partners strengthen supply chains for minerals essential to AI. Singapore was among seven signatories that agreed to collaborate during its launch last December. The government said the initiative aligned with its approach of pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation with international partners and reflected a “shared commitment to advance prosperity, technological progress and economic security”. Teo added: “What matters most is the overall relationships we have with each of our partners, and how we can continue to work with them in ways that advance Singapore’s interests and contribute constructively to international cooperation on AI.” ‘Less about China’ Joining the China-led bloc would, in principle, be in Singapore’s interests by providing a platform to shape AI governance. But an intensifying superpower rivalry over the fast-evolving technology might complicate decision-making, analysts said. Beijing has positioned Waico as a way to advance “AI for good and for all”. William Heidlage, senior director of technology at strategic advisory firm BowerGroupAsia, said Singapore was likely to evaluate Waico membership based on whether it would have a say in AI issues. “For Singapore, joining Waico is less about China and more about whether it can shape emerging AI governance from inside the room,” he said. Teo said on Wednesday that it was in Singapore’s interest to ensure AI interoperability, noting that diverging international standards would pose difficulties for companies based in the city state. Heidlage said the objectives of Waico and Pax Silica were complementary rather than contradictory for Singapore. “One seeks to prevent fragmentation in governance and the other seeks to prevent concentration in capability,” he said. Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said accepting Beijing’s invitation could give Singapore a larger say in shaping governance standards. “This could be useful for Singapore if the organisation ends up being substantive and independent.” Miguel Alberto Gomez, a senior research fellow at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, noted that joining Waico would give Singapore greater access to AI technology that could not be developed domestically, while reducing the risk of over-dependence on the United States and its partners. But analysts cautioned that the decision could not be viewed independently of broader geopolitical friction. Growing competition between Washington and Beijing made the invitation “less straightforward than before”, said Chong, suggesting that dual membership could prompt the US to impose restrictions that Waico’s benefits might not offset. The invitation comes as countries face escalating pressure to choose between both superpowers in the AI race. While Pax Silica does not explicitly target China, its objective to reduce “coercive dependencies” is widely interpreted to reference China’s dominance and rare earths. Reuters reported last month that Washington was preparing to tell a dozen countries to pick sides, warning they would be excluded from Pax Silica if they were to sign up for the Chinese framework. Kazakhstan is the only nation so far with membership in both initiatives. Beijing, however, has said it firmly opposes forcing countries to take sides or creating bloc confrontation in AI. Joining Waico might also limit Singapore’s ability to engage with parties leaning strongly towards either AI bloc, Gomez said. “This is not a novel situation for Singapore, and ultimately it must prioritise its own strategic interests.” The city state, which has long maintained a stance of non-alignment, had to prioritise its own strategic interests while maintaining cordial relations with both powers, Gomez said. “I do not think this reality is lost on both the US and China. Moreover, I would think both are aware of the value of having Singapore on side in the long run, especially in this region.” Unified Asean position? While a collective Asean position on Waico and Pax Silica would give the 11-nation bloc greater bargaining power, analysts said a consensus among its members would be unlikely due to diverging national interests. Teo confirmed on Wednesday that the Association of Southeast Asian Nations had no position on either organisation. Chong said Asean members could wield greater influence in shaping regulations and norms for AI initiatives if they used their collective weight. “It could also have the option of setting its own standards, given the accumulated economic, population and geographic size of Asean,” he said. However, reaching an agreement would be challenging for a bloc operating on the principle of consensus. Tensions arising from competing AI frameworks could further strain internal cohesiveness, Chong added. Singapore and the Philippines are the only two Asean members in Pax Silica, which is widely perceived as an effort to isolate China from key technology supply chains. Five other Asean members – Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia and Myanmar – were among the 29 original signatories at Waico’s launch. A consolidated Asean position would require members to navigate competing interests and priorities, said Elina Noor, a non-resident scholar in the Asia programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “In theory, it’s possible for Asean to form a common or consolidated position, but in reality, its members compete with each other on both the supply chain and governance fronts,” she said.

title: ‘Lone warrior’ travels to Poland to fulfil promise to watch China at U20 Women’s World Cup
description: ‘When the players entered the pitch and ran to the centre to warm up, I felt it was all worth it,’ 23-year-old football fan Li Zijian says.
content: A “lone warrior” watched on as China’s football team started their 2026 U20 Women’s World Cup with an emphatic 5-0 victory over New Caledonia in Poland. Li Zijian was the sole Chinese fan in attendance at Sosnowiec Arena, his solitary cheers spurring on the team during the match. And his presence did not go unnoticed. At the end of the match, captain Liu Chen led her team hand in hand towards an almost empty stand, bowing deeply to the 23-year-old earlier in the week. Li was also in attendance to watch China play out a 0-0 draw against Nigeria in Poland on Friday, leaving them second in the group. According to Chinese media reports, Li, a former member of the military from Beijing currently studying Spanish as an exchange student in Navarra, Spain, travelled more than 7,000 kilometres to fulfil a promise he made in April. 🇨🇳 Zhou Xinyi China 3-0 New Caledonia pic.twitter.com/9VzocIDj6T — CHINEMEREMMA ACTIVE 🦅 (@CHINEMEREMMA993) September 7, 2026 After China secured their World Cup berth with a 2-1 comeback victory against Uzbekistan in Thailand at the U20 Women’s Asian Cup, Li shouted “See you in Poland” alongside fellow supporters. Four months later, Li made the journey alone. Flying from Beijing with the U20 team to Frankfurt, he travelled to Barcelona, took a train to Navarra to handle university affairs, returned by train to Barcelona and finally flew to Poland. He funded the trip using part of his military retirement pay, spending around 20,000 yuan (about US$2,900) on flights and hotels after previously spending over 10,000 yuan to watch the team in Thailand. “After the World Cup ends, this under-20 team will belong to history,” Li said. “I wanted to watch them complete their final matches.” Arriving three hours before the 3pm kick-off on matchday, Li found himself sitting alone in the stands, confirming he was indeed the only Chinese fan at the game. During the opening match, when Huang Jiaxin scored her first goal, Li shouted her name from the stands, and she waved back. Other spectators occasionally turned to give him a thumbs-up or record him on their phones. When the team approached the stands after the match, Li broke down in tears, thinking of players who were cut at the last minute after taking part in intensive training and the Asian Cup. 五球大胜开门红！U20女足世界杯开幕，中国球迷“一个人的远征”获“铿锵玫瑰”集体谢场，看台唯一中国球迷李子剑激动落泪。 在波兰工作生活的中国人这么少吗？下一场多去几个。虽然这一个球迷也挺有气势的，但还是多点更有氛围😁 pic.twitter.com/NOfvuLTq5N — 田字格 (@tianzige4) September 10, 2026 “They worked so hard for so long, only to stop at the final step right before standing on the World Cup stage,” he said. With a voice already hoarse from shouting throughout the match, Li called out to the players, “Great job!” “I was deeply, deeply moved, and tears of excitement fell,” Li said. “Actually, our women’s players have it very, very hard. They deserve more support and attention.” Photos and videos of Li went viral on Chinese social media after the match, with netizens dubbing him the “Lone Warrior.” Li deflected the praise, stating: “I shouldn’t be the protagonist, the players are.” When asked if the arduous journey was worth it, Li remained firm. “When the players entered the pitch and ran to the centre to warm up, I felt it was all worth it,” he said. “I just wanted to see our under-20 players at the World Cup.” Writing on social media, Li added: “This U20 women’s team is a team I love to my core, so I don’t care about whatever I gave up for them. I just want to do my best to give them more support.” Li began watching football in 2014, but shifted his focus heavily to women’s football in May 2025, after watching Wuhan Jiangda ACF win the Asian Champions League final in a penalty shoot-out, where substitute goalkeeper Chen Chen saved consecutive penalties. Following that match, he started devoting more time to the Chinese Women’s Super League as well as the U20 and U17 national teams. “The atmosphere within the domestic women’s football community is actually very good. Fans of different teams have almost no disagreements or barriers, and we mostly encourage each other,” Li said. He noted, however, that the sport lacks a dedicated fanbase. “Whether it is Women’s Super League clubs or the national team, there is a severe lack of diehard fans compared to the Chinese men’s national team or Super League teams.” Li recalled travelling to Guangxi to support Beijing Women’s FC, where only three travelling fans were present, with similar tiny turnouts for Zhejiang and Guangdong away matches. “For a men’s match with 50,000 spectators, having one more or one fewer fan makes no difference, but women’s away matches are different,” Li said. “I want to give them a little more motivation so they know someone is always in the stands cheering for them.” At the end of Friday’s match against Nigeria, the players once again ran towards Li’s section of the stadium. This time, however, he was joined by three fellow Chinese supporters waving the national flag.

title: ‘Key pillar’: the 5-year powerhouse plan for China’s car industry
description: Beijing’s outline calls for boosting domestic market and innovation while controlling capacity to avoid involution effects.
content: China is set to secure its place among the global automotive powerhouses by 2030 through further efforts to boost domestic sales and foster technological innovation, while a capacity alert mechanism will be introduced to guard against disorderly competition. The ambitious targets and actions are laid out in the country’s 15th five-year plan for the development of the intelligent connected new-energy-vehicle industry, unveiled on Thursday by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and eight other ministries. The new-energy category comprises both battery-powered electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid models. According to the plan, China would further shore up its complete industrial supply-chain strengths in the sector and prepare for the large-scale roll-out of vehicles equipped with automated driving functions. “[By 2030] the automotive sector will solidify its standing as a key pillar of the national economy,” the plan stated. “The timing for rolling out this five-year plan is well judged,” said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). “The auto industry is undergoing structural transformation; total domestic sales are declining, as market leadership shifts from gasoline-powered passenger vehicles to electric cars.” Data from the CPCA showed around 1 million electric passenger vehicles were sold domestically in August, down 10.1 per cent from a year earlier. Total sales in the January-August period fell 12.1 per cent year on year. Cui said that exports currently served as the biggest pillar for China’s carmakers. But the new plan emphasised the domestic market, which was expected to fuel future growth. To hit its targets, the five-year blueprint lays out concrete milestones. By 2030, new-energy passenger vehicles and new-energy commercial vehicles should make up 70 per cent and 40 per cent of new vehicle sales within their respective segments in the domestic market, it said. Data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) showed that for the first eight months of 2026, the respective ratios stood at 58.6 per cent and 33.9 per cent. The plan also sets a goal to lift overall labour productivity by 15 per cent by 2030 compared with 2025, backed by wider deployment of digital and smart production lines. China’s rapidly growing automobile sector has sparked alarm in Europe and elsewhere over its potential to affect local industries. Critics have accused Beijing of industrial overcapacity, a sentiment that has intensified and evolved into the “China Shock 2.0” theory. Proponents of the concept have pointed to Beijing’s record-breaking trade surplus of nearly US$1.2 trillion in 2025, riding a surge of low-cost, hi-tech exports like electric vehicles. Thus the blueprint will further intensify pressure on established automotive powerhouses such as Japan and Germany, according to analysts. But fostering growth is only one element of the strategy, with curbing industry involution standing as another key objective. Unlike the plan for 2021 to 2025, this round incorporates the “capacity alert” mechanism. “Strict criteria will apply to new stand-alone new-energy-vehicle projects,” the plan said. “Legally compliant mergers, acquisitions and cross-regional integration of auto manufacturers will be stepped up.” Oversight and capacity alerts for battery manufacturing would also be strengthened, it added. Data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed that the auto sector’s capacity utilisation stood at 70.8 per cent in the second quarter, a 0.5 percentage point rise from the first quarter. Seventy-five per cent or above is usually regarded as healthy. The CPCA’s Cui said the capacity alert was “a key lever” in the development of the auto industry, shifting anti-involution efforts “from rhetoric to institutional practice”. “The plan can prevent haphazard construction of new plants while lifting capacity utilisation rates,” Cui said. “The early warnings covering both the auto-making and battery sectors will help avert price wars and foster a more balanced, rational pace of investment.” According to the CAAM, China’s auto industry posted total revenue of 5.19 trillion yuan (US$773.5 billion) in the first half of this year, 1.8 per cent higher than a year earlier. Yet total profit tumbled 19.5 per cent as price-cutting ate into profit margins.

title: Opinion | Beijing can rewrite China’s property rules, but it can’t undo the damage
description: A narrower supply pipeline, industry consolidation and years of balance-sheet repair are inevitable as China seeks stability, rather than a perpetual housing boom.
content: Financial markets are notoriously prone to mistaking a fundamental institutional shift for a temporary liquidity crisis. The futurist Roy Amara is often credited with the observation that people tend to overestimate the short-term effect of a transformation while underestimating its long-term impact. China’s real-estate sector is furnishing a textbook case of an analogous dynamic. On August 28, Chinese housing authorities and financial regulators announced a package to overhaul the commercial housing sales system. The measures include a gradual shift towards sales of completed homes, tighter supervision of presale escrow accounts, new project-based financing arrangements and extended mortgage terms. The announcement initially sparked excitement among global financial centres eager for another round of sweeping property stimulus. Equity markets quickly delivered a far more complicated verdict. When trading resumed on Monday, shares of major property developers plummeted. China Jinmao and Greentown China dropped by more than 10 per cent; China Resources Land and other major builders also suffered losses. This whiplash – early optimism followed by a punishing sell-off – underscored a disconnect between policy intentions and investor expectations. The market initially misinterpreted Beijing’s intent, only to reprice as the reality of structural deleveraging set in. Global investors often evaluate Beijing through a simple binary lens, expecting either aggressive credit expansion or policy neglect. The recent regulatory actions reveal a more deliberate objective. By reshaping the architecture of project sales and commercial credit, Beijing is not attempting to revive the speculative boom of past decades. It is rewriting the institutional rules for an industry that has entered a mature, lower-growth era. For over two decades, real estate expanded through a high-leverage feedback loop. After the 1998 housing reforms that ended state welfare housing allocation, rapid urbanisation created immense demand. Municipal governments relied heavily on land sale proceeds for revenue, while state commercial banks provided abundant credit. Developers acquired land with borrowed capital, sold flats long before completion, used presale proceeds to clear debt and buy more land, and repeated the cycle. That expansion produced vast urban infrastructure but also built a financial system dependent on rising land values, high leverage and rapid inventory turnover. Once housing prices softened, the machine operated in reverse. Declining sales compressed corporate cash flows, inventory valuations fell and debt defaults spread across private developers. Municipalities lost critical land revenue while households watched their primary asset come under sustained pressure. The downturn was never merely a surplus of physical flats; it was a balance sheet crisis. Policy responses have evolved accordingly. Early regulatory interventions focused on curbing corporate leverage and containing systemic financial risk. Subsequent measures prioritised project completion to protect homebuyers from developer insolvencies. Now, the regulatory focus is shifting towards stabilising broad demand and restructuring the sector. As the Communist Party theoretical journal Qiushi noted, real estate is not merely a utility for shelter, but a key component of household wealth. Because residential property accounts for roughly 70 per cent of Chinese household assets, stabilising real-estate value has become a prerequisite for restoring consumer confidence. The push towards completed home sales represents a consequential structural pivot. Under the traditional presale framework, buyers effectively funded project construction, assuming operational and financial risks for developers. Transitioning to sales of completed units removes that risk from families, placing financial accountability back where it belongs. Institutional reform inevitably introduces operational friction. Selling completed homes requires developers to commit substantial equity capital throughout the construction cycle. Capital turnover slows, project timelines lengthen and the balance-sheet threshold for entering the market rises. This shift protects homebuyers while raising capital requirements for builders, which is likely to produce a consolidated industry with fewer active developers and new housing starts. That contraction does not imply a policy failure. China no longer suffers from an absolute shortage of residential space. Per capita housing floor space in cities like Shanghai has roughly quintupled since the early reform era, rising from single digits to the high thirties in square metres – narrowing, though not closing, the gap with the world’s densest global cities. The primary challenge today involves matching modern housing standards with genuine demand while managing a vast stock of homes. A smaller, more disciplined supply pipeline may ultimately prove far healthier for long-term economic stability. Real estate remains inherently capital-intensive, requiring substantial upfront funding for land acquisition and construction. The structural issue has never been the use of credit, but whether that leverage is transparent and properly supervised. Establishing a sustainable financial model requires absorbing accumulated losses from the past. The performance of China Vanke illustrates the scale of this adjustment. Vanke reported a first-half revenue of 70.2 billion yuan (US$10.5 billion), down by over 30 per cent from a year earlier, and a net loss of nearly 15 billion yuan. Despite repeated backing from its state-owned shareholder, Shenzhen Metro Group, Vanke continues to negotiate debt extensions and manage asset impairments. State support can forestall a sudden liquidity failure, but it cannot erase the structural losses embedded in the old business model. Investors appear to be pricing in a prolonged period of balance-sheet repair. Real estate can no longer serve as the primary engine of national expansion. Policy capital is flowing towards advanced manufacturing, artificial intelligence and green technology. Yet these emerging sectors cannot quickly reproduce the employment, municipal revenue and consumption effects that property once generated. Beijing therefore faces two tasks simultaneously: settling the accounts of the past and constructing the rules of the future. The boom cannot be rewritten, but an economy of 1.4 billion people does not need a perpetual property miracle. It needs a foundation built to endure.

title: ‘Rest in eternal peace’: veteran horror actor, filmmaker Simon Loui dies at age 62
description: Long-time friend, fellow actor Frankie Ng reveals to reporters on Friday that Loui lost his battle with gastric cancer earlier this week.
content: Veteran Hong Kong actor and filmmaker Simon Loui Yu-yeung, better known to fans as the “King of Ghosts” for his prolific work in horror films, has died at the age of 62. Long-time friend and fellow actor Frankie Ng Chi-hung revealed to reporters on Friday that Loui’s wife, TV and radio personality Ma Li, had confirmed the filmmaker had died in a hospital in Guangzhou on Monday after losing his battle with gastric cancer. “The family hoped to stay low profile. There was no big announcement,” Ng said. “May he rest in eternal peace, free from all pain and sickness in heaven.” Ng said he had known of Loui’s previous struggles with gastric cancer, which had been treated, but later learned the condition had come back in recent years. Loui was born in 1964 and enjoyed an entertainment career spanning more than three decades across TV, radio and film and included his work as a filmmaker. After finishing an artist training course at free-to-air broadcaster TVB in the late 1980s, he started with appearances in TV dramas and variety shows before moving to the film industry in the early 1990s. The jump saw him quickly become a familiar face among fans of Hong Kong’s horror and comedy genres. Loui appeared in nearly 100 films over the course of his career, with notable credits including the comedy dramas Play with Strangers (2000) and Headlines (2001). But the entertainer earned his title as the “King of Ghosts” for his appearances in the long-running comedy horror series Troublesome Night, starring in numerous instalments throughout the late 1990s and early 2000s. Loui also co-wrtote the action-thriller The Replacement Suspects (2001). Aside from TV and film, he tried his hand at radio. During the 1990s and 2000s, he also hosted a series of late-night horror programmes on Metro Radio and Commercial Radio. But the performer had largely stepped back from the limelight since marrying mainland Chinese personality Ma in 2012. The couple had a son together and settled in Guangzhou, with Loui rarely returning to Hong Kong.

title: Fresh photos offer clearest view yet of China’s ‘WZ-X’ spy drone
description: Analysts say the stealthy aircraft appears to be designed for reconnaissance deep inside contested airspace.
content: Fresh clues are emerging about a new type of Chinese drone being developed as a long-range intelligence and surveillance platform intended to operate deep inside contested airspace. New photographs circulated on Chinese internet forums earlier this month that appear to show the massive drone in the air, offering much clearer views of its wing shape than earlier images. The original source of the photos and exactly where they were taken have not been independently verified. Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist on Chinese military aviation, said the photographs showed the clearest view yet of the aircraft’s serrated trailing edge – a sawtooth-like shape along the rear of the wing characteristic of stealth design. He added that the aircraft appeared to have been flown in daylight, suggesting such flights might have reached a degree of normality. Rupprecht said he was “100 per cent certain” the photographs showed what military aviation watchers have dubbed the “WZ-X”, citing its dimensions, proportions and other visible details. Beijing has not publicly confirmed the aircraft’s designation, purpose or specifications. The aircraft was first publicly identified by US defence website TWZ in satellite imagery from May last year showing the Chinese air force’s Malan test facility in Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. Its estimated wingspan of around 52 metres (170 feet) is comparable to that of a US B-2 stealth bomber. Rupprecht said the aircraft was designed as an intercontinental high-altitude, long-endurance (Hale) intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drone – a platform intended to operate deep inside defended airspace and function as an advanced communications relay node. He likened its probable role to that of the RQ-180 – a secretive US high-altitude stealth flying-wing drone believed to be designed for reconnaissance inside defended airspace – describing the Chinese aircraft as an “RQ-180 XXL”. He stressed that the comparison was about the expected mission and likely sensor role rather than proven performance, saying it remained unclear whether the WZ-X’s larger airframe translated into greater altitude, range or endurance. Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said the WZ-X was likely intended as a strategic high-altitude reconnaissance platform. Compared with smaller medium-altitude, long-endurance drones, large Hale aircraft could offer advantages in speed, survivability and capacity for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance payloads, according to Bosack, a former US Air Force drone maintenance unit commander who worked on MQ-9 Reaper strike-capable drones. “The speed comes from the larger engine and allows the aircraft to get to its target faster,” he said. “The survivability comes from its ability to fly higher than traditional air-defence systems can detect and reach.” He added that the WZ-X’s airframe appeared to be shaped to minimise its radar signature. Its high operating altitude could protect it from many conventional air-defence threats, he said. Bosack said a practical challenge would be shelter and maintenance, since keeping it out of satellite view would require sufficient hangar space. But he cautioned that size and design alone would not determine whether the aircraft became operationally useful. “Airframes like this are meaningless without the systems they carry,” Bosack said. “However, if they can achieve the right flight profile and carry the most useful ISR equipment, then they can stay operationally relevant for decades.” “Simply put, until we know what sensors or other payloads the Chinese will put into the aircraft, we cannot really determine how useful it will be.” Other key details remain uncertain, including the aircraft’s inlet configuration, engine count, sensor fit and whether more than one airframe has been built. Bosack said the drone’s ability to contribute to real-time operations would depend on whether China could move large amounts of sensor data quickly and securely across the battlespace. Without that, he said, the aircraft could be more useful for collecting intelligence for later analysis than directly supporting fast-moving combat operations. He also considered a strike role unlikely, arguing that weapons would detract from its more useful reconnaissance mission. Tate Nurkin, founder of OTH Intelligence Group, also sees the WZ-X mainly as an intelligence and communications platform rather than a strike aircraft, pointing to its potential for wide-area maritime surveillance, target identification and tracking, as well as data relay. The WZ-X could fit into a broader People’s Liberation Army effort to expand and integrate specialised uncrewed reconnaissance systems. Last month, Chinese state media showed the new GJ-3A armed reconnaissance drone operating alongside WZ-10 and WZ-7 systems, with the three drone types described as providing intelligence support across the PLA. “Everything points towards networking, joint and inter-service interoperability,” Rupprecht said, adding that the WZ-X could initially complement and eventually replace the WZ-7 and WZ-10 while performing similar missions in more demanding environments. Open-source research has linked the Malan facility in far western China to the PLA Air Force’s 178th UAV Brigade and identified it as a major testing and training facility for unmanned aerial vehicles. Rupprecht described Malan as the Chinese air force’s principal drone test centre, saying the WZ-X’s presence there clearly showed the programme’s importance. Western China, which falls within the PLA’s Western Theatre Command and includes the frontier with India, could serve both as a testing area and as an early environment for evaluating the drone in scenarios involving India, according to Rupprecht. He said operations around Taiwan were unlikely to be a priority for the WZ-X, given the island’s proximity to mainland China. “For Taiwan you don’t need such a range and endurance – it’s almost on the doorstep,” he said. Given the WZ-X’s likely reach, Rupprecht said the South China Sea, waters around Japan and the Korean peninsula, and potentially the eastern Pacific were other possible operational theatres for the drone. Nurkin placed greater emphasis on the western Pacific, arguing that the aircraft appeared to be tailored for the “longer ranges, better air defences, [and] more complex maritime environment” of a broader regional conflict. He noted that while Taiwan itself was nearby, a crisis over the island could expand “north to Japan, east to Guam, and south to the Philippine Sea and South China Sea”. In such a contested environment, a stealthy uncrewed aircraft capable of long-range operations could bolster China’s existing surveillance network. For now, the WZ-X is known mainly through imagery and analyst assessments rather than official information. Its significance may depend less on size than on the sensors and communications systems it ultimately carries.

title: Exclusive | Beijing freezes plant approvals for energy-storage  batteries amid overcapacity fears
description: ‘Dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,’ analyst says.
content: Beijing has put a freeze on new approvals of production facilities for energy-storage batteries amid worries about excess supply and vicious price competition, according to industry officials. Companies had not been allowed to add new capacity since May, as key regulators like the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) stepped in to curb a construction spree that risked creating severe overcapacity despite rising demand from renewable-energy projects around the world, the sources said. The temporary ban could be lifted if the supply-demand balance changed, they added. “The decision to suspend construction of new ESS [energy-storage system] battery factories was made because dozens of new projects in the pipeline sparked policymakers’ fears about redundancies,” said Ivan Li, a researcher at Loyal Wealth Management in Shanghai. “The ministry-level authorities apparently looked to take pre-emptive measures so that sustainable growth could be achieved.” Energy-storage systems, comprising batteries along with battery management, power conversion and control equipment, store excess energy generated from renewable sources like solar and wind farms while providing backup power during outages and helping stabilise electricity grids. The MIIT, which is mainland China’s top economic planning agency, the National Development and Reform Commission and provincial-level regional governments are jointly responsible for drafting policies about ESS projects. An official with an advisory firm that serves some of the battery firms said the suspension was seen as “window guidance”, and new approvals would be granted if additional manufacturing capacity was needed. Window guidance is used by Chinese authorities to deliver verbal or written instructions to companies or local authorities on government policies. This form of guidance is not officially announced or published and can be adjusted swiftly. The MIIT did not respond to a request for comment on Friday. Data from the China Industrial Association of Power Sources, a government-backed industry syndicate, showed that more than 100 battery factories passed through all relevant approval procedures in the first seven months of this year. These facilities could churn out a combined 2,600 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of batteries a year and required a total investment of 447 billion yuan (US$66.65 billion). The planned production capacity between January and July represented a 48 per cent increase from the total output of 1,755GWh by Chinese manufacturer in 2025. Technically, 2,600GWh of ESS batteries could be used to support renewable energy projects with an installed capacity of 1,300 gigawatts (GW). One GW of capacity can supply around 750,000 households for a year. The boom in artificial intelligence has been driving demand for renewable energy, and the ESS infrastructure supporting these projects created huge demand for batteries. Chinese battery companies also revved up new plant building after the global energy shock arising from the Iran war further spurred demand for alternative energy. China dominates the global ESS battery industry, with mainland companies accounting for more than 80 per cent of the market. According to Seoul-based SNE Research, global ESS battery demand rose 79 per cent year on year to 550GWh in 2025. The regulators aimed to avoid “involution” in the ESS battery sector, according to the sources. The term refers to intense price ­competition that erodes sustainable growth and makes profits elusive.

title: Death toll from Philippine ferry fire jumps to 35
description: Rescuers recover 30 bodies on Friday after managing to gain access to the vessel, which had caught fire on its way from Manila to Palawan.
content: Philippine rescuers recovered ⁠30 bodies from a burned-out ferry on Friday, raising the death toll from the blaze to 35, authorities said. Firefighters found the remains after they gained access to the vessel for the first time, having extinguished a fire that had hampered search and rescue efforts since Wednesday night. Responders in protective suits were seen carrying black body bags from a small boat onto a coastguard vessel, video footage released by the coastguard showed. Thick smoke and extreme heat had ‌earlier prevented rescuers from entering the ferry, which was carrying more than 130 people when it was engulfed in flames. As families waited for news of missing relatives, some expressed frustration at the lack of information they were receiving. It was not immediately clear how many people remained unaccounted for, but authorities had reported 84 missing before Friday’s recovery of 30 bodies. The number of rescued stood at 43 as of Friday morning. Images released by the coastguard showed the destruction caused by the fire inside the ferry, with rows of accommodation berths reduced to twisted metal and ash. One image showed what appeared to be skeletal remains amid charred debris in a heavily damaged section of the vessel. Another photograph appeared to ⁠show a burned vehicle. “We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident. Rest assured that operations are carried out with utmost respect for the deceased and their bereaved families,” coastguard spokeswoman Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said. Richard Marceliano, one of the survivors, told GMA News he saw a small amount of smoke that quickly turned into a raging fire and spread through the ferry within seconds. He said he and other passengers spent nearly two hours floating in the sea before they ‌were rescued. The fire is the latest in a string of deadly maritime accidents in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands where millions rely ⁠on ferries and small boats to travel between ⁠provinces and islands. In January, more than 60 people died when a passenger vessel, carrying more than 300 people, sank en route to the southern province of Sulu. As the search continued, stories of those still unaccounted for ‌began to emerge. A trip meant to celebrate a renewal of wedding vows instead brought grief and uncertainty for Jonnsban Tibay, 60, who fears his wife, Eden, was among those trapped on the ferry. He had not accompanied her, and the couple were ‌on a ‌video call as the fire broke out. “She said, ‘We’re leaving now.’ I told her not to hang up and that we should keep the video call going. I was about to ask ‌her to join our prayer when the call suddenly cut off,” he said. Tibay does not believe his wife was able to escape. “I’m 100 per cent certain she didn’t jump. She must have been trapped,” ⁠he said. “She was diabetic and physically weak. She was no longer as agile as before.” “It hurts so much,” Tibay said. “My two children can’t stop crying.” At a port in Coron, Myra Bilan, ⁠whose sister and brother-in-law are missing, sobbed. Bilan, 47, said the couple had been travelling to Palawan on business to deliver beds. “I hope our government takes action. So many people have died,” she said. “I hope they don’t turn a blind eye to poor families like us.” Outside the office of shipowner Atienza Inter-Island Ferries in Manila, frustrated relatives ‌waited for information about their loved ones. The ferry company ‌has said it is fully cooperating with government authorities investigating the incident. It remained unclear what started the blaze, which broke out as the ferry neared the end of its more than 20-hour voyage to Coron, a popular tourist spot in northern Palawan. A statement from the Maritime Industry Authority, citing survivor accounts, said two successive explosions were heard from within the ship, triggering the fire. The ferry, with capacity for 330 people, was also carrying five motorcycles, an electric vehicle, a forklift, a pickup truck and other cargo, according to the coastguard.

title: Chinese optical transceiver makers dodge US ban for now as FCC updates rules
description: The devices are emerging as central to artificial intelligence race, and China’s suppliers hold key market position.
content: The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has published its final decision on updates to its equipment authorisation rules, easing market anxiety over potential bans on Chinese optical transceivers. The rule, adopted in July and finalised on Friday, tightens authorisation requirements for devices containing certain hardware components made by entities on the Covered List – a US blacklist of foreign technology equipment and service providers deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to national security. Optical transceivers, devices located within data centres that facilitate the transmission of data, were not targeted by the ruling, which calmed market speculation after a Reuters report in August said that the Trump administration was drafting measures to block new Chinese models from entering the US market this year. Zhongji Innolight, a leading producer of optical transceivers used in data centres, ended the day up about 4 per cent in Shenzhen and 4.37 per cent in Hong Kong, as peer Eoptolink Technology gained nearly 3 per cent. Suzhou TFC Optical Communication fell 2.62 per cent in Shenzhen. Why are optical transceivers at the centre of the AI race? The regulatory scrutiny comes as optical communications is becoming increasingly important in global artificial intelligence infrastructure, a domain where Chinese suppliers hold a commanding market position. As clusters expand, electrical connections become harder to scale efficiently because of limits in bandwidth, distance and power consumption, making optical links necessary. “The competition is no longer simply about the computing power of a single card,” said Man Jiangwei, director of Huawei Technologies’ advanced optoelectronics laboratory, in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Thursday. “It is increasingly about the scale of the whole cluster.” This shift is accelerating both market growth and technical adoption. The global optical interconnect market was projected to soar from US$24.8 billion in 2025 to US$111 billion by 2030, according to industry research firm LightCounting. While traditional telecoms optical transceiver generations evolve every three to five years, data centre cycles can now churn in less than two years, InnoLight chairman Liu Sheng said during a Goldman Sachs event last week. Goldman Sachs expected global shipments of 800-gigabit-per-second (Gbps) optical transceivers – currently a mainstream specification for large AI data centres – to reach about 45 million units this year and 49 million in 2027. Shipments of the faster 1.6-terabit-per-second (Tbps) generation, meanwhile, are forecast to jump from roughly 33 million units this year to 71 million in 2027, overtaking 800Gbps transceivers within a year. The next 3.2Tbps generation is expected to begin ramping up in 2027. Why is China favouring NPO architecture while US leaders push CPO? To keep pace with rising data rates, the industry is moving optics closer to silicon to tackle electrical bottlenecks between switch chips and optical modules. However, a regional split in technical focus has emerged. Preferred by Chinese players like Huawei, Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings, near-packaged optics (NPO) keep optical engines in separate packages, placed close to the switch chip, shortening electrical connections while leveraging existing manufacturing ecosystems. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Pursued by US leaders like Nvidia and Broadcom, co-packaged optics (CPO) integrates optical engines directly onto the same substrate as the switching silicon. Nvidia’s Spectrum-X Ethernet Photonics CPO switches are already in production for its Vera Rubin platform, alongside several generations of CPO Ethernet switches from Broadcom. Engineers at Alibaba and Tencent acknowledged that CPO offered the best performance, but argued that NPO was more practical and cost-effective today because it tapped into the mature, pluggable module supply chain, according to LightCounting. Huawei’s Man noted that this divergence stemmed from the companies’ current strengths, rather than geography. Chinese firms excelled at optical module manufacturing, making NPO a natural evolutionary step, whereas CPO relied more heavily on advanced semiconductor packaging and silicon integration dominated by US vendors. Does China really dominate the global optical transceiver market? By volume and headline revenue, China appears dominant. Chinese firms supplied nearly two-thirds of global transceivers by volume and accounted for 60 per cent of optical datacom transceiver revenue in 2025, according to Counterpoint Research. However, that dominance is strongest at the module level and does not extend across every part of the upstream supply chain. High-end optoelectronic parts remain heavily reliant on overseas suppliers. Investment bank Nomura noted that foreign companies continue to dominate critical components like 200Gbps EML laser chips used in 1.6Tbps transceivers, keeping global supply tight. Optoelectronic and electronic chips, including lasers and DSPs, typically accounted for over half of the material cost of a mainstream high-speed transceiver, according to China Insights Consultancy data from Innolight’s Hong Kong initial public offering prospectus published in July.

title: Why Sweden, once one of Beijing’s most outspoken critics in Europe, has changed its tune
description: Driven by geopolitical shifts and critical industrial needs, Stockholm is expected to pivot towards Beijing to shield its economic future.
content: Millions of Swedish voters head to the polls on Sunday to elect a new parliament. Whatever the outcome, analysts say, the country is likely to look more towards Beijing for its technology edge and to diversify away from an increasingly unreliable Washington, despite persisting challenges in China-EU trade. “Many factors right now suggest that relations between Sweden and China will change in the long term – not necessarily directly linked to the elections – because I see more Swedish businesses [realising] that they rely on Chinese technology for their competitiveness,” said Paulo Silva, founding partner of New Republic Public Affairs and a former adviser at the Swedish Finance Ministry. The increasingly uncertain geopolitical environment was also likely to push Swedish political leaders and the business community to be more pragmatic and diversify, he said. The US under the Trump administration was increasingly being seen as a real threat, according to Silva, citing episodes such as his demand to annex Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark, which has close ties to Stockholm. In Gothenburg, they sort of looked at it and said, ‘China is one of the good guys, because they provide job opportunities’ Niklas Swanstrom, Institute for Security and Development Policy The percentage of Swedes holding a positive view of the US collapsed to 19 per cent in 2026 from 55 per cent in 2023, while those holding a positive view of China increased to 27 per cent from 12 per cent during the same period, according to a Pew Research report published in July. Meanwhile, the rise of far-right nationalist political forces in Germany and France, the two core European Union states, has raised concerns about the bloc’s future. “There are worries in the business community here. What does it mean? Because Germany is the most important market for Sweden … will we have the European Union and the internal market as we have had now?” Silva said. On the official front, ties between Sweden – once one of Beijing’s most outspoken critics in Europe – and China have warmed in recent months after years of strain. Ties soured in the late 2010s over Beijing’s detention of Hong Kong bookseller Gui Minhai, a Chinese-born Swedish citizen. Gui Congyou, China’s ambassador to Sweden from 2017 to 2021 who is seen as one of Beijing’s best-known “wolf warrior” diplomats, added to the friction. Sweden eventually gained visa-free access to China last November – the only two other EU countries excluded are Lithuania and the Czech Republic, both of which have clashed with Beijing over Taiwan – and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited Sweden in July, becoming the first Chinese foreign chief to visit the country in more than 20 years. “Sweden’s attitude towards Chinese companies is warming up,” said a senior Chinese executive in Sweden, who chose to remain anonymous to speak freely. During Wang’s visit, he met with Jacob Wallenberg, a leading member of the Wallenberg family that wields considerable influence over Swedish business – a positive signal, the executive said. Compared to countries like Germany, which has turned more defensive in the face of a widening trade deficit with China, Sweden was also better shielded, analysts said. “We do not compete necessarily on the same terms with China as the Germans do … the economic impact is greater on Germany,” said Niklas Swanstrom, director of the Institute for Security and Development Policy in Stockholm. Sweden’s steel companies produce niche, green steels that compete in different markets than Chinese steel, and Volvo Cars – Sweden’s automotive crown jewel – is owned by Chinese group Geely, which has been praised for its stewardship. “In Gothenburg, they sort of looked at it and said, ‘China is one of the good guys, because they provide job opportunities’,” Swanstrom said. Nevertheless, challenges remained for future economic ties, as Sweden needed to align with EU trade policy and politicians increasingly focused on security concerns in Chinese activities, according to Frederic Cho, vice-chairman of the Sweden-China Trade Council. “There’s a discrepancy between what politicians say and what the business world wants and expects the government to help them with,” he said. Cho added that Beijing’s stance on Russia’s invasion of Ukraine had led politicians to view China increasingly through a security lens, a concern he said was felt more sharply in Sweden than in southern Europe for geographical and historical reasons. Sweden has also passed “one of the most stringent” foreign direct investment regimes in Europe in recent years, according to Cho, making Chinese investments in certain sectors challenging. Pressure from Chinese competition is also playing into Sweden’s domestic debates. The next major round of wage talks begins at the turn of the year, with industry negotiating first and setting the benchmark for the rest of the labour market. The Confederation of Swedish Enterprise argued in an April report on the second China shock that “the assessment of the scope for wage increases ahead of 2027 needs to take greater account of global competitive pressure and the value of a stable, internationally competitive industry.”

title: Beijing lodges diplomatic protests over Taiwan official’s visit to Italy
description: European Parliament official says conference attendance by Hsiao Bi-khim was kept confidential to safeguard her participation.
content: Beijing has strongly condemned a visit to Italy by senior Taiwanese officials and lodged formal diplomatic protests with both Rome and Brussels. Criticising the visit on Friday, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Beijing had submitted “serious representations against Italy and the European Union” following reports that Taiwan’s No 2 official, Hsiao Bi-khim, had arrived in Italy to attend an international forum. “[Taiwan’s] Democratic Progressive Party authorities and individual politicians have spared no effort to seek attention everywhere, attempting to pursue independence under the guise of democracy and freedom,” Mao said. “Their moves are truly despicable, and futile.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Italy, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Italy, like most countries, has no formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan. Mao said Beijing firmly opposed any official interaction between Taiwan and nations that maintained formal diplomatic ties with Beijing. Beijing says such visits violate the one-China principle. She said the one-China principle was a widely recognised norm in international relations and the fundamental political foundation for Beijing’s relations with both Italy and the EU, calling on relevant parties to observe it through concrete action. Hsiao is visiting the Italian island of Ventotene, off the coast of Naples, to attend the Second European Conference of Ventotene for Freedom and Democracy, which runs from Thursday to Saturday, alongside Taiwan’s foreign affairs head Lin Chia-lung, according to Taiwanese media reports that quoted local authorities. Confirming the visit, Pina Picierno, a vice-president of the European Parliament, said on social media on Thursday that Hsiao’s presence “was kept secret until her arrival to protect her participation” in the conference. “No one can determine who can be hosted on European soil, what voices can be heard and what presences must be hidden,” Picierno wrote. In November, Hsiao spoke at the annual meeting of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China at the European Parliament in Brussels, drawing strong criticism from Beijing and representations against the EU. In June, Beijing banned four New Zealand lawmakers for one year over their trip to Taiwan, saying the visit in May sent “wrong signals” to the island’s ruling party and “Taiwan independence” forces, and constituted “interference in China’s internal affairs”.

title: Man dies in fall from scaffolding in 19th fatal construction accident this year
description: Police say they received a report of a construction worker discovered lying on podium along Yu Chau Street in Sham Shui Po.
content: A construction worker has died after falling while erecting scaffolding, marking Hong Kong’s 19th fatal accident in the construction industry and second to involve truss-out platforms this year, according to police and a concern group. The force said it received a report at 11.39am on Friday that a male worker had fallen and was found lying on a podium along Yu Chau Street in Sham Shui Po. The man was rushed to the nearby Caritas Medical Centre, where he was later declared dead. Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, with the exact cause of death to be determined by an autopsy. The Labour Department said it had immediately deployed staff to the scene upon receiving the report, adding that it was investigating the cause of the incident. The department also issued suspension notices to involved contractors, halting the erection, alteration, dismantling and use of scaffolds on the building’s external wall until the relevant risks were addressed. Fay Siu Sin-man, chief executive of the Association for the Rights of Industrial Accident Victims, said the victim was a 50-year-old sub-subcontractor who had worked as a scaffolder for many years. The man arrived at the site at around 8am and was putting up his second set of scaffolding when a support bracket was suspected to have come loose, causing him to fall, she said. She added that the building had suffered from water leakage, and that the scaffolding was being erected to allow for inspections and repairs. Siu said the man left behind two adult children – a son who was a student and a daughter who was unemployed. “I feel grief about the accident, but it also reflects just how severe and frequent workplace accidents have become,” she said. Siu noted that it was the 19th fatal accident in the construction industry this year and the second such incident to involve truss-out scaffolds. The first such accident occurred in February, when a 57-year-old worker fell to his death while setting up scaffolding on the exterior wall of a Maxim’s Group food factory in Tai Po. The case was also classified as an industrial accident. The association at the time urged frontline workers to ensure their own safety and said employers should also provide suitable equipment, such as safety belts, and monitor employees working at height to ensure they used the gear properly. Siu said on Friday that she hoped the employer, the main contractor and the subcontractor involved in the latest case could make proper arrangements to support the family. She also urged the man’s employer and the relevant authorities to seriously review how to prevent such accidents.

title: Singapore and mainland China top global student assessment as OECD scores hit record low
description: Latest survey of 15-year-old students across 91 countries and economies included new computational problem-solving module for AI era.
content: Singaporean and Chinese students led the world in educational performance in 2025, according to an assessment by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, as average scores across OECD countries reached a record low. The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment comprised 760,000 15-year-old students across 91 countries and economies, including OECD members and partners. This edition of the survey was the largest since the OECD first administered the triennial assessment in 2000. In the report that OECD released on Tuesday, Singapore outpaced mainland China in reading with 535 points against China’s 527. The city state also posted strong results in mathematics and science with 563 and 560 points, respectively – second only to China. Students from mainland China led globally in maths with 612 points and science with 597 points, vastly outperforming the OECD averages of 463 and 482 points, respectively. The surveyed students from mainland China hailed from the country’s four eastern education powerhouses: the cities of Beijing and Shanghai, and Jiangsu and Zhejiang provinces. Mainland China is not an OECD member and did not take part in the OECD’s previous assessment because of coronavirus pandemic-related disruptions. The 2025 edition expanded beyond reading, maths and science to debut a computational problem-solving module. It tested students’ ability to use programming tools, run experiments and design digital products. Macau, a special administrative region of China, topped the new digital module with a score of 572. Singapore came second at 563, edging out mainland China’s 560 and well above the OECD average of 500. Traditionally, Singapore and mainland China place a premium on strong school discipline, academic achievement and perseverance. Both are relatively strict in controlling digital distractions in the classroom compared with many Western systems. Other top-performing education systems included Macau, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Estonia, Hong Kong and Britain. In contrast, American students posted mixed results. They scored 490 in reading – down 14 points from 2022 – and 463 in maths, similar to the 465 tallied three years ago. US science scores rose modestly to 502, with computational skills at 513. At a global level, the results looked bleak. Compared with 2022, average OECD scores slid across the three mainstay subjects to varying degrees. “The overall performance of OECD countries declined, with the lowest average levels of performance ever observed,” the report said. Across the OECD, one in five 15-year-old students is now a low performer in science, maths and reading, up from 16 per cent in 2022, according to the report. Long-term data showed reading had declined since peaking around 2012, while maths fell sharply after 2018. Science performance has dipped more gradually over the past decade. The report also highlighted a drop in skills critical for the artificial intelligence (AI) era, such as evaluating information, synthesising multiple sources and thinking critically. And the proportion of “hasty readers” – students who rush through texts and give quick but incorrect answers – nearly doubled between 2018 and 2025. Digital distraction in classrooms was identified as a major driver of the slump, with more than a quarter of OECD students reporting that peers were distracted by electronic devices during science lessons. Meanwhile, the link between AI usage and academic performance was nuanced. The 2025 data revealed that students who used AI for specific tasks such as drafting, summarising or research performed worse in science than non-users. However, those who used AI for general learning and received AI literacy training at school scored slightly higher. Mathias Cormann, OECD’s secretary general, said the data showed that “reversing declines in student performance is urgent”. Technology and AI must be used purposefully rather than as “a substitute for attention, effort and understanding”, he added.

title: Yemen’s Houthis reach strategic island in Bab el-Mandeb Strait
description: The move potentially tightens the militants’ grip on a vital shipping route, further increasing the threat to energy markets.
content: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis reached the strategic island of Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Friday, four Yemeni government sources told Reuters, moving to tighten their grip on a vital global shipping route in the widening Middle East war. Earlier, two sources from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised Yemeni government said its forces had pulled out of Perim and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, which faces the island. If the Houthis gain control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is ‌on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz, it could give their backer Iran a critical advantage in its war with the US, reducing supplies through a second major transit corridor and sending oil prices surging. Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter and a close US ally, has relied on the Red Sea route since the Iran conflict effectively closed Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil used to flow. In the wider war between Iran and the United States, the two sides have carried out a wave of tit-for-tat attacks this week on shipping in the Gulf, while President Donald Trump has jacked up economic pressure on Tehran. Diplomacy is largely stalled. Iran confirmed on Friday that its representatives and those of Iraq and the Gulf Arab states would meet in Oman on Monday to resume discussions on safe commercial shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The Financial Times originally reported the planned meeting. In a further potentially significant development for Riyadh, satellite imagery showed smoke on Thursday in the vicinity of Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, which has become a vital means for the kingdom to divert its crude exports from ‌Hormuz. There was no confirmation from Saudi Arabia of any incident in the area. The Saudi government media office and state oil giant Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the smoke visible in the imagery verified by Reuters. Aramco has used the East-West pipeline to ramp up crude flows from Saudi Arabia’s eastern coast to the Red Sea after US-Israeli air strikes on Iran began six ‌months ago, prompting Tehran to effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi crude supply fell 2.3 million barrels per day on the month in August to 6 million bpd, the lowest level in more than three ⁠decades, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, partly due ⁠to the targeting of ships transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by groups linked to Yemen’s Houthis. Global oil prices were on track to end the week above US$100 a barrel for the first time since mid-May. Vessels recorded transiting the Strait of Hormuz fell to seven on Thursday from 11 the previous day, preliminary ship-tracking data ‌showed on Friday, well below the 10-day average of 10. The Houthis’ military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said on Telegram that maritime navigation remained safe for all shipping except Saudi vessels subject to a previously announced ban. “We will continue to enforce blockade for blockade and escalation for escalation until the aggression stops and the blockade on our people is ‌lifted,” he ‌said on Friday, referring to Saudi attacks on Yemen. Yemeni government forces indicated they would try to retake areas captured by the Houthi militants in their lightning offensive this week along the Red Sea coastline. They announced they would deploy ‌weapons and aircraft to eliminate any movement of the “terrorist” Houthi militias in strategic areas, including the road leading to the coastal city of Mocha, which the militant group captured on Thursday along with the Red Sea islands of Hanish. Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nazili called ⁠on civilians to avoid using the route between the city of Taiz and Mocha and steer clear of equipment belonging to the Houthis, mountain fighters who withstood years of devastating Saudi air strikes during Yemen’s civil war. Reuters reported on Thursday that the dramatic Houthi advance ⁠down Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week came with direct guidance from Iran’s Revolutionary Guards seeking to open a new front in Tehran’s war with the US, according to Yemeni government, Iranian and regional sources. Iran told the Houthis last week to escalate their attacks on Saudi Arabia and promised more funding, weapons and senior officers to help them do so, two Iranian sources said. While Iran describes the Houthis as an ally, it publicly denies giving them ‌military direction, saying they are “not a proxy”. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump twice on Thursday and urged him to launch strikes against the Houthis, Axios reported, citing two US officials. Trump rejected the request, and US officials said the administration did not intend to take direct military action against the Houthis at this time, the report said. Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report. A regional source said Trump was considering what actions to take and that the US was helping with targeting the Houthis. According to Axios, Washington is worried about the rapidly escalating conflict in Yemen and is stepping up support for Riyadh while seeking to avoid direct military involvement.

title: Why Marcos’ Brics trip is ‘low-risk opportunity’ for Philippines to make new friends
description: The president, attending in his capacity as Asean chair, should not miss the opportunity to diversify ties beyond the US, analysts say.
content: President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr is set to be the first Philippine leader to join the Brics Summit in New Delhi this weekend – presenting him with the perfect “low-risk opportunity” to engage the grouping as Manila continues to diversify its ties, analysts say. “The president seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel said in a press briefing on Wednesday. “This participation is a strategic opportunity to monitor emerging economic frameworks and to represent the priorities and perspectives of the region, while directly engaging leaders of major emerging economies.” Brics, an international organisation formed in 2009 of emerging economies, currently counts Brazil, Russia, India, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates among its members. While Marcos is attending the event in his capacity as Asean chair, he is also scheduled to meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and business executives on the sidelines. Issues to be discussed include the progress of the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership, a review of the implementation of an action plan for 2025 to 2029, and a follow-up with business leaders on the US$5.8 billion investment pledges Marcos secured during a state visit to India in August last year.
