Analysts say the summit is Marcos’ chance to engage Brics members and diversify beyond its traditional ties with the US amid geopolitical tensions with China. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also expected to be attending, marking his first trip to India in seven years. “The Asean chairship provides President Marcos with a relatively low-risk opportunity to engage Brics more closely without necessarily signalling that the Philippines is already moving towards membership or changing its broader strategic orientation,” said Enrico Gloria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman. The engagement was “not particularly unusual” given that Association of Southeast Asian Nations members already have varying degrees of ties with Brics, he said. Indonesia is a full member and Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam are partner countries. “For the Philippines, this is less as choosing another geopolitical camp and more as a way for it to continue diversifying its partnerships.” ‘Friends to all’ Marcos’ attendance reflected his “friends to all and enemy to none” stance on foreign policy, said Chester Cabalza, founder and president of the Manila-based think tank International Development and Security Cooperation. Under Marcos, the Philippines has signed defence pacts with countries such as Japan, Canada, New Zealand and France. “Marcos should not ignore this opportunity, not only because he represents Asean, but also due to India’s benevolent acts to the Philippines. The Philippines has India to thank for the Brahmos missiles,” he said. “The growing economic potential of Brics is unprecedented in terms of its energy and AI global outputs.” For a smaller power such as the Philippines, “expanding the number of countries and institutions it can work with increases its room to manoeuvre”, Gloria said. Last year, Marcos said he was open to considering Brics membership for the Philippines. But this visit appeared to be “exploratory rather than preparatory”, Gloria said, adding it was not “evidence that Manila is already moving towards a formal plan of accession”. There is an important difference between being open to something and having made it a foreign-policy objective. Marcos himself framed it last year largely in terms of giving the Philippines more options, rather than announcing an intention to join,” he said. This is a good chance to re-engage China and India amid uncertainties from the global oil crisis, according to Cabalza. “Manila should learn from India’s non-alignment policy even as Delhi experienced a territorial rift with Beijing in 2000,” he said. “Navigating this tedious diplomatic stunt is important for a country that needs to bring home barrels of oil, employment through investments, and latest AI protocols.” Despite the finalisation of the code of conduct in the South China Sea remaining an Asean priority, it was unlikely that Marcos would tackle China on maritime issues, he added. “He is going to India as Asean chair, so Marcos’ policy recommendations and contributions to the conversation must attribute to the needs of Asean. He is a statesman from Southeast Asia and not only of the Philippines in that summit.” Beyond India One of the most consequential goals of Marcos’ visit would be a deepening engagement with India, both analysts said. “⁠Following up on the Indian investment commitments should certainly be one of the most tangible objectives of the visit,” Gloria said. “A meeting with Prime Minister Modi offers an important opportunity to assess how much of that potential can actually move towards implementation.” Manila can also explore further partnerships with India – especially as it looks to strengthen its position as a hub for diversified supply chains. One possibility is the multi-country Pax Silica initiative to secure global supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and critical minerals. “This could help move the conversation beyond individual investment pledges towards a more strategic discussion of how Philippine-Indian economic cooperation can contribute to more resilient and diversified regional supply chains,” Gloria said. Predicting that India would be the “future second-largest economy of the world”, Cabalza said it would be good to “enhance our ties to secure investments in agriculture, business process outsourcing, medical and spaceport ventures”. However, Gloria cautioned that the Philippines should not focus solely on India as the forum presented a chance for Manila to develop a diverse range of partners beyond traditionally aligned states. “One weakness of Philippine foreign relations historically has been the concentration of our diplomatic emphasis and economic attention on a relatively small number of major partners. A more multipolar world requires the Philippines to develop a multipolar diplomatic portfolio as well,” he said. “As the current Asean chair, the Philippines is poised to leverage that institutional power not just for the region but for its own interests as well to diversify existing partnerships.”

title: Profile | How Cantopop lyricist Wyman Wong pushed Hong Kong’s LGBTQ, style and emotional boundaries
description: Songwriter for the stars, fashion journalist, LGBTQ activist – Wong’s impact on modern Hong Kong culture cannot be overstated.
content: This is the 85th instalment in a biweekly series profiling major Hong Kong pop culture figures of recent decades. For lovers of Cantopop music, Wyman Wong Wai-man is a pre-eminent architect of modern Hong Kong’s emotional landscape. Through the classic songs he has written for top singers from Eason Chan Yick-shun to Miriam Yeung Chin-wah, the 57-year-old has chronicled the loves and heartbreaks of a generation. Yet to define him strictly as a lyricist is to ignore a sprawling, multi-hyphenate career. Born on May 21, 1969, Wong showed a remarkable linguistic proficiency from an early age and consistently achieved high marks in literature. As a teen he started writing freelance fashion and lifestyle columns for newspapers and magazines – work he continued even as a social science student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. “Writing is an instinct to me,” he told HK Magazine in a 2008 interview. “I sit down and I write. It’s not a hard job for me.” In his final year at university in 1991, he won a Commercial Radio Hong Kong pop quiz contest, impressing producers who offered him a part-time DJ role on the spot. Upon graduating, he transitioned directly into a full-time radio position, marking the beginning of a new era for Cantopop. Wong made his debut as a lyricist in 1993, working with the popular rap duo Softhard. In 1995, he gained significant recognition for his biting, raw emotional lyrics for Amanda Lee Wai-man’s breakout hit “(You Will Not Have) A Happy Ending”. In 1998, he received the best original film song honour at the 17th Hong Kong Film Awards for Leo Ku Kui-kei’s megahit “Enjoy Yourself Tonight”, which he wrote for the film Cause We Are So Young. Shaping the sound of a generation That same year, Wong left full-time radio to devote himself to songwriting, fashion journalism and acting. Over the following decade, he cemented his status as one of Cantopop’s top two lyricists, alongside Lin Xi (or Lam Chik, real name Albert Leung Wai-man), with the press dubbing them “The Two Wai-mans”. Wong has gone on to write more than 1,500 songs, including career-defining hits for many of Hong Kong’s major singers. These include “Bike” (2001) for Eason Chan, “Pain Love” (2001) for Joey Yung Cho-yee, “Wild Child” (2001) for Miriam Yeung and “Wedding Invitation Street” (2008) for Kay Tse On-kay – songs that would come to symbolise 2000s Hong Kong pop culture. Beyond stand-alone hits, Wong became celebrated for constructing interconnected thematic narratives across different artists, most notably the tragic “Trash Quartet” – which included “Vortex” (2000), a duet by Cass Phang Ling and Anthony Wong Yiu-ming, and “Trash” (1998) by Candy Lo Hau-yam. His trophy cabinet grew steadily and culminated in the rare feat of receiving both the best lyricist and hall of fame lyricist awards at the 2013 Chinese Music Media Awards. Subverting the norms At the same time, Wong was building an equally influential career as a fashion journalist and cultural commentator. From the late 1990s, he wrote long-running style columns for a wide range of publications that were later compiled into essay collections. He is widely credited with introducing high-fashion concepts into compelling narratives using local Cantonese slang, humour and pop-culture analogies, bridging the gap between the rarefied world of Parisian catwalks and the everyday aspirations of Hong Kong fashion enthusiasts. Wong has long been a front-row regular at Paris, Milan and London fashion weeks, attending as an industry commentator and respected voice in those circles. Underpinning all of this is his legendary personal archive, a collection of rare designer fashion built over three decades. In his 2008 interview with HK Magazine, Wong traced his fashion obsession back to his childhood, noting his mother was a tailor who frequently performed impromptu catwalk shows at home. “Gender is a social stereotype, and that concept is outdated in modern society,” he added. “Sure, in ancient times there was a clear division of labour, so men and women were assigned certain personality traits. But now we don’t need that kind of differentiation. Just let it be!” This philosophy heavily permeated his lyricism. Wong was instrumental in subverting gender norms and pushing LGBTQ visibility within mainstream Cantopop, writing queer anthems such as Denise Ho Wan-see’s “Rolls. Royce”. While he never hid his sexuality on the personal front, he made a rare formal tribute to his partner of over a decade, psychiatrist Dr Stephen Ng Wai-man, during his remote acceptance speech at the ViuTV Chill Club Music Awards on January 1, 2023. Spectacle on stage and screen Wong’s glamorous style extended far beyond the page. Styling Cantopop stars, including Denise Ho and Joey Yung, for their tours and residencies, Wong brought the avant-garde catwalk directly onto concert stages, music videos and album covers. The crowning achievement in this realm came in February 2012 with “Concert YY”, his six-night songwriting showcase at the Hong Kong Coliseum, which he transformed into a live catwalk. Wong personally coordinated haute couture looks for more than 40 guest performers who sang 84 of his songs, turning a retrospective of his musical career into a visual spectacle. Though Wong is selectively private, he and Miriam Yeung – once close creative partners – experienced a publicised falling-out in the mid-2000s. The painful end of their friendship inspired Wong to write Eason Chan’s 2006 hit “Best Bad Friend”, but in 2012, Yeung made a surprise, heavily pregnant appearance at “Concert YY”, making peace before a sold-out crowd. Meanwhile, Wong maintained a prolific acting and hosting career that spanned from 1995 through the mid-2010s. Characterised by his stout physique, shaved head and witty delivery, he frequently played eccentric sidekicks or sharp-tongued friends in films such as 2002’s Love Undercover and The Lion Roars. He also hosted several television programmes, famously spending HK$500,000 on designer outfits for his role fronting ATV’s game show 1 vs 100 in 2006. Advocacy and the ‘Cantopop Multiverse’ Yet beneath this flamboyant showbiz persona, Wong was becoming an increasingly outspoken advocate amid Hong Kong’s shifting sociopolitical landscape. His vocal support for civil rights, local culture and free expression during Hong Kong’s 2014 and 2019 social movements resulted in several of his songs being quietly pulled or censored on mainland Chinese streaming platforms. During the debate over Hong Kong’s controversial 2014 copyright amendment bill, Wong granted full permission for netizens to parody his copyrighted lyrics. Accepting lyricist of the year at the Ultimate Song Chart Awards on January 1, 2016, he sarcastically remarked that if the law passed, he might be spending his next award season in prison for making parodies. In late 2021, Wong relocated to London. He established an overseas base while continuing to write full-time, providing lyrics for new Hong Kong singers such as Mirror members Keung To and Edan Lui Cheuk-on, Gareth. T (Tong Ling-shan), and Cloud Wan Ho-ying. The move did nothing to diminish his influence; if anything, it broadened his perspective. Between 2020 and 2025, he won the Ultimate Song Chart Awards’ lyricist of the year title for six consecutive years. In both 2022 and 2023, he claimed the ViuTV Chill Club Music Awards’ lyricist of the year title. During his remote acceptance speech in 2022, he introduced his philosophy of a “Cantopop Multiverse”, describing a global Cantonese music community that transcended geographical boundaries. Although Wong maintains a tight-knit circle of long-time friends in Hong Kong and remains one of the city’s most influential lyricists and fashion figures, his legacy across the mainland China border remains highly contested. While Wong’s name is sometimes scrubbed from mainland Chinese broadcasts and music platforms – reduced to a mere “Anonymous” – this stark attempt at erasure only echoes louder, paradoxically underscoring his enduring cultural weight in his home city.

title: Yoon Suk-yeol acquitted in case linked to South Korean marine’s death
description: The court ruled it was unclear whether Yoon deliberately intended to disrupt the investigation into the death of the marine.
content: Former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol was acquitted on Friday in a case related to a marine’s drowning death in a rare reprieve in one of the criminal cases brought against him following his ousting for imposing martial law. The independent counsel’s indictment had alleged Yoon deliberately appointed former defence minister Lee Jong-Sup as his ambassador to Australia to help him leave the country and evade a criminal investigation into the death of Corporal Chae Su-geun, who drowned during a search-and-rescue operation for flood victims in 2023. But the Seoul Central District Court ruled it was unclear whether Yoon’s appointment was intended to disrupt the investigation. Yoon said he appointed Lee as ambassador to promote military cooperation with Canberra, and his lawyers welcomed the court’s verdict while calling on prosecutors not to appeal. Yoon’s former justice minister and presidential security director were among other defendants also acquitted of charges that they colluded with Yoon to help Lee sidestep the investigation. Prosecutors did not immediately say whether they would appeal against Friday’s verdict. A separate indictment alleges Yoon and other officials tried to cover up and manipulate the investigation into Chae’s death, which sparked a public uproar after it emerged that military commanders had ordered soldiers to conduct search operations without life vests and other safety equipment. An early investigation by the marine corps held a division commander and seven other people responsible for Chae’s death. But Yoon expressed fury over the commander’s inclusion, prompting senior presidential and defence ministry officials to pressure the marine corps to revise the report to exclude the commander, according to prosecutors. Prosecutors said the then head of the marines’ investigation team, Park Jung-hun, defied the pressure and sent the report to police and that Yoon subsequently ordered officials to retrieve the report from police and dismiss Park, who was investigated for insubordination. Yoon was formally removed from office in April 2025 and has faced multiple criminal trials after President Lee Jae Myung approved special investigations into his martial law imposition and several other matters, including Chae’s death. He has appealed against the conviction and life sentence for rebellion, which was the most serious charge stemming from his brief imposition of martial law in December 2024. Yoon’s martial law decree lasted only hours, after a quorum of lawmakers managed to break through a blockade of heavily armed soldiers and voted to revoke the measure, forcing his cabinet to lift it.

title: China’s young investors embrace risk. Why are their portfolios so safe?
description: Despite high risk tolerance, millennials and Gen Z invest in safer assets due to a combination of factors, a study shows.
content: Young Chinese investors may be just as willing to take risks as their global peers, but their portfolios remain more conservative against a backdrop of years of relative underperformance in China’s stock market, a prolonged property downturn and deflation, according to a senior researcher at the CFA Institute Research and Policy Centre. The disconnect between their willingness to take risks and their actual investment choices illustrated what the institute called an “aspiration-implementation gap”, said Rhodri Preece, senior head of research at the institute. “They want to retire early. They’re willing to take risks, but yet their portfolios [show] the most commonly cited investments are more conservative investments like wealth-management products and money-market funds,” Preece said in an interview on Thursday. The findings were based on the institute’s latest survey of 400 affluent investors in mainland China conducted in December, with its main analysis focusing on 300 Gen Z and millennial respondents. Some 72 per cent of Chinese respondents held cash or cash equivalents and 62 per cent owned bank or trust wealth-management products, the survey found. By comparison, cryptocurrencies and mutual funds were the two most commonly owned investments among young investors globally, at 67 per cent and 64 per cent, respectively. Yet the institute found no clear difference between young Chinese investors and their global peers in their attitudes towards risk, Preece said. He attributed the divergence in their portfolios partly to differences in product availability and the market environment in which young Chinese investors have come of age. China’s equity market has underperformed global benchmarks over much of the past several years, although it staged a strong recovery in 2025. The Shanghai Composite Index gained about 18 per cent last year, compared with a 21.6 per cent return for the MSCI World Index. The mainland benchmark had fallen 3.7 per cent in 2023 after dropping 15.1 per cent in 2022. Alongside the equity-market weakness, the prolonged property downturn had further narrowed investment options, while deflation had made cash and cash-like products relatively more attractive by boosting their real returns, according to Preece. “If I want to preserve wealth and I’m a US investor, holding cash is not a good way to preserve wealth, because inflation will eat away at the value of my cash,” he said. “It’s different in China,” he added, referring to the country’s deflationary environment. Product availability provided another explanation for the different portfolio mix, according to Preece. Cryptocurrencies had become an entry point into investing for many younger retail investors in markets including the US, UK and Canada, Preece said, but are restricted in mainland China.

title: I’ll write romance novels if AI solves all maths problems, Chinese Fields winner jokes
description: As AI models prove they can push the boundaries, mathematicians are grappling with the threat that they could become obsolete.
content: Deng Yu, the 37-year-old Chinese mathematician who won the 2026 Fields Medal, has a backup plan if artificial intelligence puts him out of a job. On Tuesday, he wrote on social media that “if AI can solve all maths problems, I’ll go home and write my yuri novel”. Deng is known to be a big fan of yuri, a genre of Japanese novels and comics that depicts intimate friendships and romantic relationships between women. In the post, which was later shared on another Chinese social platform, Deng wrote that AI has created “an atmosphere of restlessness and impatience” in mathematical circles. “Once this wavefront passes in the next year or two, the situation will gradually become clear. Mathematics will naturally adapt slowly, and a new ecosystem is gradually taking shape.” Deng told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday that he was “not currently writing a yuri novel. That statement was entirely in jest.” “I don’t believe AI can develop to the point of solving all mathematical problems, at least not those I mentioned in my post,” he added. Nevertheless, uncertianty is brewing in some parts of the maths world over AI’s impact on the field. On September 8, OpenAI said it had used one of its models to solve the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem – one of the major questions at the frontier of mathematics. Seven mathematical challenges were named Millennium Prize Problems by the US-based Clay Mathematics Institute on May 24, 2000. Each problem comes with a US$1 million prize for its solution. In 2003, Russian mathematician Grigori Perelman solved one of the problems – the Poincaré conjecture – but declined the prize and the Fields Medal he was subsequently awarded. And now, a second Millennium Prize Problem may have been solved – but not by a human. The Navier-Stokes equations are widely applied in fluid mechanics, yet our understanding of them remains limited. A successful proof would greatly advance humanity’s overall comprehension of mathematical physics. According to OpenAI, the proof was generated using OpenAI’s unreleased next-generation model, which worked for 88 hours and consumed 130 billion output tokens worth millions of dollars. However, a mathematician also working on the problem claimed that OpenAI began its efforts only after hearing of his progress towards a solution. According to a report by Scientific American on September 8, the night before OpenAI announced its proof, New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster posted on social media that he and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpoge had proven the Euler equations. The Euler equations are widely regarded in the field as a crucial step towards tackling the Navier-Stokes problem. Buckmaster said that he and his collaborator had used several AI models to solve the equations, including those from OpenAI. In a statement on Monday, Buckmaster claimed that OpenAI learned of the mathematicians’ progress the week before and adopted the approach they were using to solve the entire problem. OpenAI later clarified on social media that it had independently proven the Euler equations, but did not completely deny it had drawn on ideas from other mathematicians. “We did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly – in particular, no specific user data was accessed to solve this problem,” the company said. “De-identified data from their use of our products may have helped improve our models.” The American Mathematical Society said on Tuesday that while Alpoge and Buckmaster had made breakthroughs “assisted by new technologies”, the mathematicians at OpenAI had completed the final proof. “The purpose of mathematics is human understanding, and this achievement, and the process that led to it, will bear fruit for a long time to come,” the society said. This is not the first time that AI has been used to overtake human mathematicians. For instance, OpenAI researcher and University of Pennsylvania Wharton School statistics and data science professor Su Weijie said on September 4 that he had used AI to make progress in one of the field’s biggest problems – the twin prime conjecture. In 2013, Zhang Yitang proved that there are infinite pairs of consecutive prime numbers whose gap is bounded by a finite number. He proved that this gap was no more than 70 million. This was one of this century’s most important mathematical breakthroughs. The following year, the “Polymath8b” project, led by Terence Tao, proved that the gap was just 246. Over the next 12 years, this value remained unchanged. On August 31, Austrian mathematician Julia Stadlmann uploaded a 34-page preprint to arXiv. She proved that there exist infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes whose difference does not exceed 240. The paper does not mention the use of any AI tools. According to an interview with China Science Daily on September 7, Su began working on the twin prime conjecture on August 15 and quickly advanced. “I used an internal version of [OpenAI’s] GPT-6 Astra to first improve from 246 to 240, then quickly advanced it to 188, and after a period of exploration, finally reached 186,” Su said. “In this proof process, my role was auxiliary. I only gave the AI simple prompts. The AI’s mathematical proof capabilities are far from reaching their limit,” Su told China Science Daily. Tao, who won the Fields Medal in 2006, said in a September 6 social media post that “if AI had emerged 20 years earlier, Zhang would still be working as an adjunct lecturer, and Maynard would have switched out of analytic number theory to a different topic of study”. James Maynard was the recipient of the 2022 Fields Medal.

title: Chinese milk tea chain sparks heated debate over ‘military-style’ onboarding programme
description: Lawyer warns that forcing new hires into humiliating onboarding tasks can expose organisations to severe legal risks.
content: A Chinese milk tea chain has ignited a debate about workplace culture and employee autonomy after reports of its military-style onboarding training garnered public criticism. Frontline employees at Chayanyuese, also known as Modern China Tea Shop, recently voiced their concerns on mainland social media, alleging that the company’s “Cornerstone” induction programme infringes on personal boundaries. Headquartered in Hunan province, Chayanyuese is one of China’s most recognisable milk tea brands, with annual revenue reportedly around 3 billion yuan (US$447 million). A user on RedNote, with the handle @unmeaning, shared photos depicting strict dining rules at the training base, including a 30-second limit to collect meals, enforced rigid postures while eating, and a prohibition against chewing food while standing. Another employee, identified as @Xigua, claimed that recruits were required to surrender their phones, adhere to military-style dormitory rules, and fold their quilts into the precisely squared “tofu block” shape. They also alleged that during a military posture drill, a trainee collapsed and required hospitalisation, but the company refused to cover medical expenses. Moreover, several recruits interviewed by Sina Finance reported they were mandated to memorise corporate values and scripted service phrases, with failure to meet these standards potentially jeopardising their positions. Some online commenters defended the approach, contending that, as a customer-facing service business, milk tea chains require consistent standards for employee behaviour, appearance, and communication. Conversely, others expressed discomfort with what they described as “militarised management” extending beyond workplace training. Chayanyuese later asserted that such operational standards existed in its stores but declined to provide details about its internal training programme. He Bo, a lawyer at Sichuan Henghexin Law Firm, informed the SCMP that measures such as phone restrictions and dining protocols generally fall within employers’ management rights if employees are informed in advance and the requirements are reasonable. However, he cautioned that unsafe physical training or humiliating activities could breach legal boundaries. From traditional manufacturers to modern food and beverage brands, military-style training has increasingly emerged as a strategy for Chinese companies seeking to shape the behaviours of new employees. Mary, who has worked for a home appliance manufacturer in Guangdong for a year, recounted her experience in an induction programme for fresh graduates that included a gruelling 50km hiking challenge. “We walked through the night until morning. It was exhausting, especially in the heat. The activity also operated on a penalty system – if someone dropped out halfway, their team would lose points, making people feel they were letting everyone down,” she recalled. The programme also incorporated military-style exercises, including army songs and marching drills, alongside job-related training. Mary noted that she understood the rationale behind such programmes: helping “undisciplined” graduates shed their campus habits and adapt to professional life. “Ultimately, it could also be viewed as a test of obedience,” she reflected. Nonetheless, some corporate onboarding programmes have faced even harsher criticism. In 2024, China Philanthropist reported on an intensive induction programme organised by food company Jinmailang, where 77 employees were required to complete 80 push-ups, carry weighted equipment on a 60km hike, and participate in a “stress test” involving asking strangers for money and dining at their homes. The company stated that the training aimed to challenge employees’ mindsets, unlock their potential, and help them overcome psychological barriers. In July, livestock giant Muyuan Group faced backlash after reports that employees were required to read aloud and memorise a “pig worship text” praising the spirit of selfless contribution among pigs. While the company clarified that the exercise intended to promote respect for life and appreciation of the industry, critics accused it of fostering unconditional sacrifice. Lawyer He added that forcing employees to ask strangers for food could be deemed humiliating and expose companies to legal risks, including penalties or civil claims. He noted that employees are entitled to wages and rest rights during training. For many online observers, the controversy raises broader questions about how companies cultivate loyalty. “Companies invest considerable effort trying to foster employee loyalty, but for workers, the issue is straightforward – when compensation reflects the effort they put in, employees will invariably feel more motivated and loyal,” one user wrote.

title: Shattered pelvis, existential crisis and butterflies all part of Lai’s Asian Games journey
description: Hong Kong rider Jacqueline Lai once feared her first Games appearance would be her last, now she’s ready for a fifth and eyeing loftier goals.
content: When she shattered her pelvis in 2011, Jacqueline Lai Jing-man wondered if the music had stopped on her athletic career after one Asian Games experience just months earlier – 15 years on she is ready for her fifth. Part of the team jumping quartet that claimed Hong Kong’s first Games equestrian medal, it was soon after she won bronze in Guangzhou in 2010, that her mother, the former actress Ellen Ng Ha-ping, revealed she had spent more than HK$10 million (US$1.3 million) on helping Jacqueline and her sister, Jasmine Lai Zin-man, become “good riders”. At the time, Ng said she had also “moved from a big house of 3,000 sq ft overlooking Victoria Harbour to a small flat of 400 sq ft in Causeway Bay”. That all that sacrifice, effort and commitment could have been taken away following one horrible training fall in Denmark, where Lai based herself after leaving Chinese International School in 2009 to prepare for the following year’s Games, gave the now 35-year-old “an understanding of how much I loved what I did”. “It was pivotal for me, and it gave me a new sense of appreciation for being physically strong and able-bodied,” Lai said. “It enhances your understanding and empathy for people going through injury, and people with disabilities. “It was tough coming back, but luckily, I was young and I had good support.” Now living with enough metal in her pelvis to sell for scrap, Lai’s injury sidelined her for around eight months. In 2013, 2½ years after the accident, she won individual jumping silver at the National Games, having claimed team bronze at the 2009 edition. Lai acknowledged that today her all-consuming sport had become “pretty much a lifestyle”. Based in the Netherlands, she “misses coming home at the weekend, having a family meal and talking about things that are not horses”. “But being over there gives me the chance to be really focused and tuned in,” Lai said. “Ultimately, that’s what it takes for someone coming from a background that has nothing to do with horses. We have some catching up to do, and that takes us doing it full-time.” Born in America but raised in Hong Kong, Lai’s best Asian Games individual jumping result was the 15th place she managed three years ago. In the team event, the city quartet’s highest finish since 2010 was the sixth place they managed four years later. Comparing herself today with the rider and person who made her Games debut, Lai said: “I consider myself a professional athlete now, whereas in 2010 I’d just come out of school. My mum bought me my first horse [Capone 22] at that level. “Since then, I’ve been having to train my own horses. The sport requires a deep knowledge of horsemanship, and I’ve tried to understand more every year. I’m better now at supporting my teammates and dealing with the pressure of competing at bigger Games.” Unlike their well-supported elite horse racing counterparts, leading equestrians, Lai said, are “an all-in-one”. “We clean the boxes, we plan the vet visits, the farriers,” she said. “We’re riding the horses and competing on them. You’re in charge of your own game as an equestrian.” Still, Lai said the ceaseless demands had taken no physical or mental toll, and that the sport was “enriching, because it’s what I love to do”. Nonetheless, an athlete who in 2013 raised more than HK$480,000 from a crowdfunding campaign to sustain her career, Lai said that “over the past few years, I’ve experienced an existential dilemma”. “A lot of riders in our region drop out at a certain level, because we go to Europe as consumers of sport horses, training programmes and competitions,” said Lai, who without that cash boost 13 years ago would potentially have reverted to her original plan to go to university in America, the path her sister took. “[In those circumstances], when our horses retire or get injured, how do we keep going?” Lai has started to become a “supplier in the industry”, developing more stock with the intention of “building my own horsepower”. “It might take a few years, but I hope it opens doors for the younger generation of riders from our side of the world,” she said. Despite the shift in emphasis, Lai has “not considered quitting” riding competitively, on the contrary, she has designs on “competing at the highest level.” “That requires a lot more than just the day in, day out,” Lai said. “It takes a lot more long-term planning and working with horse owners. “A horse that’s ready to compete at five-star today will cost you €1 million [US$1.16 million]. “If you want five of those, you have to start with them when they’re young. Even then, there’s no guarantee they’ll reach the top, or be your ride.” Unusually in sport, Lai has time on her side. In 2016, Nick Skelton won Olympic individual jumping gold at 58. Silver in 2024 went to 42-year-old Steve Guerdat. Months after turning 60, Roger-Yves Bost won this year’s Longines Hong Kong International Horse Show grand prix. “I have people on board who want to go that way with me and, hopefully, in six or seven years a few of my young horses will have come up, and I can enjoy the sport at a higher level,” Lai said. More immediately, Lai said an individual Asian Games medal on board “relatively green” nine-year-old Kalina’s Way was not realistic. Still, after the Hong Kong team finished third in last year’s Asian Championships, Lai said that as a foursome “medals are always on our mind” when it comes to Japan. She will channel the butterflies she expects to experience next month into a force for good. “You have to accept the nerves,” Lai said. “We only get them because we care. Working with horses helps you control your emotions. They don’t understand when a competition is a deal breaker. “They feel most comfortable when you have the same mindset as when you train. You have to breathe and keep as steady-headed as possible.”

title: Meet Blake Griffin’s fiancée, Francesca Aiello, who founded Frankies Bikinis
description: Linked to the former NBA player after his split from Kendall Jenner, the swimwear founder has collaborated with stars including Sydney Sweeney and Pamela Anderson.
content: Wedding bells might be ringing for former NBA star Blake Griffin and his fiancée, Francesca Aiello, who reportedly spent a grand weekend in Porto Ercole, Italy, celebrating with friends, says TMZ. The couple looked loved-up and were even photographed sharing a kiss. Guests included Griffin’s supermodel ex, Kendall Jenner, whom he reportedly started dating in August 2017 but split from after a few months, per People. While it has been speculated that Griffin, 37, and Aiello, 31, may have tied the knot on their European getaway, neither the former power forward nor his entrepreneur partner has confirmed the news. The pair announced their engagement in January 2025, less than a year after he retired from the NBA. So, what do we know about Francesca Aiello? Read on to find out. What is Francesca Aiello’s background? Aiello hails from Malibu, California, where she was born on March 16, 1995. She spent her summers working as a junior lifeguard in the mornings, surfing in the afternoons and practising water polo at night, she said in a 2024 interview with VS Insider, a blog run by Victoria’s Secret. Aiello is close to her mother, whom she calls her inspiration. Growing up, she was friends with Gigi Hadid, and they remain close. How did Francesca Aiello launch Frankies Bikinis? Aiello was in secondary school when, inspired by a woman wearing a bold bikini bottom on the beach, she started designing her own bikinis. “My mom encouraged me to bring my design ideas to a seamstress, and eventually all my friends were asking for my custom bikinis, too,” she recalled to VS Insider. Eventually, the Instagram page @frankiesbikinis was born, and it started gaining traction, even catching the eye of supermodel Candice Swanepoel. In 2012, 17-year-old Aiello and her mother, Mimi, founded Frankies Bikinis. At 19, she became the youngest designer to debut a collection at Miami Swim Week. She has collaborated with stars like Gigi and Bella Hadid, Sydney Sweeney and Pamela Anderson, and has expanded into ready-to-wear and beauty. Aiello even made Forbes’ 30 Under 30 in 2022. “I want girls to look at our brand and feel inspired and confident, not body shame themselves or question their appearances,” she told Forbes. Her relationship with Blake Griffin Aiello was linked to the former Los Angeles Clippers and Boston Celtics player in June 2018, shortly after he and Jenner broke up, per People. In August 2020, Griffin told Entertainment Tonight he was single, indicating a brief split. Three years later, Aiello and Griffin were spotted on holiday and were said to be back together. Griffin – who shares son Ford, 13, and daughter Finley, 10, with his ex-fiancée, Brynn Cameron – seemingly popped the question to Aiello in 2024, and later told Us Weekly that wedding planning had been “pretty chill”.

title: Emma Bonino, Italian politician who fought for abortion rights, dies aged 78
description: Bonino was a passionate advocate for social justice and gender equality who deliberately courted controversy to advance her many causes.
content: Emma Bonino’s life in politics began with a crime. In 1974, at a time when abortion was illegal in Italy, ⁠she travelled to a clandestine clinic in Florence ⁠to terminate an unplanned pregnancy. “Coming back by train at night, I ⁠decided that never, never, never again should anyone have to suffer this humiliation,” she later recalled. A year later, determined to drag abortion out of the shadows, she handed herself in to police, turning her private “offence” into a public act of defiance. The arrest made headlines, fuelling a campaign that eventually led to the legalisation of abortion in 1978. It also launched Bonino into parliament with the Radical Party, a small but relentless force for civil rights. Direct and diminutive, ‌Bonino was a passionate advocate for social justice and gender equality who deliberately courted controversy to advance her many causes at home and abroad. “I have been fighting for rights all my life, warning people to defend them, because they don’t last forever,” she told state broadcaster Rai in 2024. In a dynamic career spanning five decades, Bonino won repeated election to both the Italian and European parliaments and served as a foreign minister and European affairs minister in Rome. She was also a high-profile European Commissioner in Brussels. She remained in frontline politics well into her 70s, overcoming lung cancer despite refusing to give up smoking. Underscoring her high standing in Italy, and belying Roman Catholic disapproval of her stance on ⁠abortion, the then Pope Francis made an unusual trip outside the Vatican in November 2024 to visit her in her home after an acute health scare. She died on Friday aged 78, ‌her spokesperson said. On Monday, Bonino was hospitalised in a serious condition, but was taken out of intensive care on Thursday and transferred to a private clinic. Founded by Bonino’s mentor, Marco Pannella, the Radical Party helped redraw Italian society, promoting an array of causes through ‌acts of civil disobedience, hunger strikes and dozens of referendums. Some battles they won, such as banning nuclear power. In other campaigns, including a push to legalise ⁠cannabis, they fell short. To widespread surprise, Bonino ⁠was appointed to the European Commission in 1994, thanks to the backing of the then Italian prime minister Silvio Berlusconi. There she took charge of a disparate group of dossiers that no one else had claimed – fisheries, consumer policy and the ‌European Community’s humanitarian office. She was the first woman ever to wear trousers at a meeting of the male-dominated Commission, and proved herself to be one of the most colourful politicians in an often grey Brussels. Accomplished and confident before the television cameras, she ‌quickly drew ‌media interest by riding Spanish fishing boats on the high seas during the EU’s “fish war” with Canada. Not one to mince her words, she accused Canada of piracy, which that country’s ‌government denied. In 1997 she was briefly detained by Taliban militia during a visit to Afghanistan after people in her party took pictures in a women’s ⁠hospital – an offence under Taliban regulations. She condemned the international community’s silence over the fate of Afghan women under the Taliban but told Reuters in 1996 that she did not see ⁠herself as a traditional feminist. “I do not want and I do not think that we women are a category,” she said. “If we think we are a category to be protected, I think we will lose our fight.” After her stint in Brussels, she pursued a broad mix of causes, including the campaign against female genital mutilation, ‌pension equality in Italy and migrant rights. She also ‌promoted closer integration across the European Union, founding the +Europa (More Europe) party in 2017. While she herself regularly scored well in popularity polls, her new party fared poorly at the ballot box, failing to win any seats at the 2019 and 2024 European parliamentary elections, while picking up just two seats at the 2022 national polls. Bonino, who was born in northwest Italy in 1948, never married and did not have children. “I didn’t have them out of choice,” she told Io Donna magazine in a 2018 interview. “You need a lot of courage [to have children]. With a child you need to say ‘for ever’. I never managed that.”

title: Ant to let AI agents shop via 10 digital wallets, from AlipayHK to Starryblu to KakaoPay
description: With open-source release of Agentic Mobile Protocol and deals with credit-card giants, company bids for key role in global standards.
content: Ant International, the overseas affiliate of Chinese fintech giant Ant Group, is making a major bid to power the next phase of mobile payments: letting autonomous artificial intelligence agents handle your electronic wallet to make purchases. The company on Friday open-sourced its Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP) on GitHub, effectively putting it forward as a potential global technical standard for how AI agents securely pay for real-world goods. AMP was built onto Ant International’s existing Alipay+ cross-border network, which connects to 10 major Asian digital wallets serving 1.5 billion consumer accounts for an initial phase, according to the company. The protocol’s release would “enable agents to enter existing mobile payment systems as trusted actors”, allowing platforms like Alipay in mainland China, AlipayHK in Hong Kong, Starryblu in Singapore, and KakaoPay or Toss in South Korea to accelerate their AI strategies, said Yang Jiang-ming, Ant International’s chief innovation officer. Beyond Asia, Ant International on Thursday also announced a joint effort with credit card giants Visa and Mastercard on a so-called know-your-agent (KYA) framework, an effort to establish standardised identity verification for AI agents across card networks, digital wallets and online marketplaces globally, the company said. The launches come as tech firms increasingly focus on autonomous AI agents capable of carrying out end-to-end commercial tasks. Speaking at a conference in Shanghai this week, Ant Group CEO Cyril Han Xinyi said that many Chinese merchants still struggled to adapt their services into formats AI agents could navigate, limiting their participation in the emerging agent economy. Spun off in 2024, Ant International aims to build the world’s largest agentic AI payment network. Its Alipay+ network, launched in 2020, has connected more than 150 million merchants to over 2 billion user accounts across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Latin America. In July, Ant International raised about US$1.2 billion to accelerate international growth in its first known funding round, with existing backers Ant Group and Alibaba Group Holding – owner of the South China Morning Post – taking part. To address consumer privacy and security risks tied to automated spending, the company said AMP included an AgentSafePay feature, which offered merchants a money-back guarantee to cover potential losses related to agent-initiated transactions. The protocol also established “clear boundaries of permissions” so consumers could retain ultimate control over their accounts, the company said.

title: Over 60% of new dentists join Department of Health after mandatory internship
description: A consultant dental surgeon says the 46 new recruits have helped ‘significantly ease’ department’s manpower crunch.
content: About 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s first batch of dental graduates who underwent mandatory internship training have joined the city’s Department of Health, a move that has helped “significantly ease” the manpower crunch. The development followed a controversial amendment to the Dentists Registration Ordinance in 2024, requiring all dental graduates in Hong Kong to complete a 12-month internship before obtaining a full licence starting in 2025. The measure aimed to enhance hands-on clinical experience in real-life settings. Dr Kitty Hse Mei-yin, consultant-in-charge of the department’s dental services, said on Friday that the government had recruited 62 per cent, or 46 of the first batch of 75 interns. The rest went on to work at the Prince Philip Dental Hospital’s teaching facility, at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), in non-governmental organisations or in the private sector. “While students have learned a lot from their six-year undergraduate training, the internship allowed them to put what they learned in books into practice in the real world, meeting different kinds of patients in different roles under the support of experienced dentists,” Hse said. “During the internship, they never know what kind of problems will be brought into the room by the next patients, which is different from their clinical training at school … that could enhance their clinical judgment and independent thinking skills.” Under the internship, all students were rotated to four clinical settings – general and emergency dental service, public hospital, teaching hospital, and school or community dental service – with each rotation lasting for three months. Participants were subject to ongoing assessments by veteran dentists. After completing the internship, students were issued with a certificate of experience by the Dental Council of Hong Kong on August 31, followed by full registration the following day. All students passed the internship, except for one who was suspended from duty in January for accessing the digital medical records of 16 patients without consent. Hse said the department would build on the experience and continue the rotational arrangement in the future, while increasing their exposure to different specialities and their safety awareness when using the digital health record systems and social media. In an anonymous online survey that covered about 70 per cent of dental interns in July, more than 80 per cent said they were satisfied with the internship arrangement. Reasons cited included the constructive and prompt feedback they received from senior dentists, alongside opportunities to enhance their communication, clinical and time-management skills. Patients also gave positive feedback to those interns. Dr Sharon Lee Siu-man, a consultant dental surgeon at the department, said that while the purpose of the new rule was never intended to fill vacancies in the public sector, the manpower crunch had been “significantly eased”. “We will continue to run the internship programme, ensure sufficient roles for them to complete the internship, and that is not related to our manpower situation at all.” HKU, the city’s sole dental school, supplies about 70 new dentists each year. But most graduates tend to join the private sector, which offers better pay and hours. Health authorities earlier predicted that Hong Kong would be short of 180 dentists by 2030 and 120 by 2035, before seeing a surplus of 20 by 2040. Dr Jason Yip, a graduate who just completed the internship and joined the department as a dental officer, said the undergraduate training had already equipped graduates with certain skills. “Throughout the six years of studies, we started clinical internship by the end of year two, and many more treatments were performed in the third year … we needed to meet a certain number of [teeth treated] to graduate in the first place,” he said. Yip added that the internship taught him that being a dentist was not just about performing treatments, but also “perfecting the details”. He recalled an elderly lady with acute tooth pain who requested removable dentures, but wished to keep them discreet so people around her would not know. He struggled to find a solution until a veteran specialist guided him, and the patient was happy with the result.

title: Chinese regulators unleash power of cost accounting to tackle price war problem
description: At same time, State Council issues guidelines on avoiding delays in payments to small and medium-sized enterprises.
content: China’s years-long fight against the cutthroat price wars plaguing key industries has prompted the deployment of a more powerful tool – cost accounting – as the authorities also renew efforts to help small businesses receive delayed payments. The country’s top economic planning agency – the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) – and the State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) publicly released a notice on Thursday on tackling “low-price disorderly competition” in important industrial products. It contained specifics of the cost accounting required to determine if products are priced below cost. “Current price law contains only broad-strokes measures and there is a need to clarify cost accounting requirements … market players should compete on quality and innovation, not just pricing,” the NDRC said in a related questions-and-answers document. It added that “superior quality should command a premium price”. The notice said cost accounting should be based on costs incurred during production, using industry averages as a reference, and they should be calculated by industrial associations and reviewed by the NDRC and SAMR. Cost calculations should also use audited accounting records or properly documented bookkeeping provided by producers. Industry average costs could be determined through a census or sampling approach, the two agencies said, adding that for industries with regional disparities, calculations could be conducted on a regional basis. They said monitoring would be stepped up to focus on price changes in key industrial goods – which they left undefined – so that issues could be promptly identified. Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank, said while the regulators’ intent in fighting price wars was commendable, such work was easier said than done. “Counting the cost of products is complex given constant price changes,” he said. “While broad product categories have benchmark prices, companies have different supply chains, sources of inputs and sales channels. “It’s difficult to pin down the exact cost or to track discrepancies between costs and end prices.” He said the government could rely on industrial associations and statistics departments to monitor prices to save administrative costs and avoid undue interference. Both the NDRC and SAMR said they would carefully steer clear of intervention. “Market-determined pricing serves as the critical lever for resource allocation,” they said. “Businesses’ autonomy in pricing decisions must be respected … regulators will only go after disorderly acts to uphold fair competition.” Both agencies also vowed to avoid a one-size-fits-all enforcement approach, and said they would also consider capacity utilisation and actual operating conditions. Cost-accounting is a measure contained in a dedicated law on pricing practice that was promulgated in 1997. SAMR is now working on an amendment. Cutthroat price wars, also known as involution, remain widespread in the world’s second-largest economy – from the electric vehicles sector to daily consumer goods – crimping business margins. The Communist Party’s top leadership has called out the practice in recent years, describing it as a race to the bottom that threatens to derail market order. In October, the party Central Committee’s fourth plenum listed tackling involution as a key economic task. Business contracts should be treated more seriously and law enforcement must be stepped up Tang Dajie, China Enterprise Institute Also on Thursday, the State Council, China’s cabinet, published guidelines on addressing delays in payments to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), many of which are privately owned. Key measures included industry-specific rules on maximum payment periods, more robust payment supervision of big companies and a recommendation that cash payments be made to SME suppliers and partners within 60 days of the delivery of goods or services. All government procurement will be settled through cash payments, as will purchases from SMEs made by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) under the central government. Large enterprises abusing dominance to withhold payment will face government actions, according to the guidelines. Tang said it was correct to focus on SOEs because some lacked a good track record in making prompt payments to smaller upstream suppliers, but he also urged that more significance be attached to contracts and rule of law. “Rather than another State Council document, business contracts should be treated more seriously and law enforcement must be stepped up to fundamentally address delayed payments,” he said. Separately, the NDRC convened a meeting with private sector representatives on Thursday and heard complaints about investment barriers. The agency also published a new batch of 36 recommended projects spanning railways, logistics, water conservancy and energy that are expected to seek a total of 15.6 billion yuan (US$2.3 billion) in private capital. The NDRC said it would maintain close contact with private firms and optimise support services in funding and land supply. Private investment in China fell 9.4 per cent year on year in the first seven months of this year.

title: Mainland Chinese investors to drive Hong Kong wealth boom despite new tax rules: report
description: The city will continue to serve as a vital platform linking mainland China with international capital, Hong Kong Association of Banks says.
content: Hong Kong banks expect the contribution of mainland Chinese investors to the city’s wealth management business to continue to grow through 2030, presenting opportunities despite Beijing’s tightened cross-border tax rules. Mainland China’s share of local assets under management was projected to reach 68 per cent from 59 per cent within five years, according to a report released by the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB) and Deloitte China on Friday. The report surveyed 147 member banks in the first half of 2026 and offered 37 recommendations on the sector’s development as Hong Kong prepares to unveil its first five-year plan. “Hong Kong has become the world’s largest cross-border wealth management centre [and] will continue to serve as a vital platform linking mainland China with international capital,” said Stephen Chan, acting chairman of HKAB and deputy CEO of Bank of China (Hong Kong), at a media briefing on Friday. Surveyed banks considered wealth management to be the biggest growth driver, said David Wu, Hong Kong financial services industry leader at Deloitte China. Rising demand from mainland investors for international diversification, intergenerational wealth transfer and the expanding family office sector were the primary factors, according to the report. Banks that integrated portfolio construction, family governance, succession planning and digital asset custody would be best positioned to capitalise on this growth, HKAB and Deloitte said. To seize opportunities from mainland China, lenders urged the Hong Kong government to enhance the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect Scheme by gradually relaxing investor eligibility, easing sales and promotion rules, raising quotas and broadening product ranges to include medium-risk and higher-return options. Wealth Management Connect, launched in 2021, is currently open only to Hongkongers as well as mainland residents in the Greater Bay Area, an economic region that includes Hong Kong, Macau and nine mainland cities in southern China’s Guangdong province. Eligible mainland investors should have at least two years of investment experience as well as a minimum of 1 million yuan (US$150,000) in net financial assets and 2 million yuan in household financial assets. Banks also advised the government to deepen financial linkages with mainland China by adding a long-awaited connect scheme for initial public offerings. They urged accelerating the inclusion of a yuan counter in Stock Connect, enabling mainland investors to subscribe to new listings in the city while boosting yuan internationalisation. The recommendations came as Beijing tightened taxation on cross-border gains of mainland residents and beneficiaries from offshore trusts and insurance, sparking concerns over Hong Kong’s financial industry. However, Beijing has backed Hong Kong’s role as an international asset and wealth management centre, enshrined in the country’s latest five-year plan through 2030. Beyond wealth management, the lenders also highlighted the integration of the bay area corridor and artificial intelligence deployment as two other pillars for the next five years. They suggested promoting yuan usage in Belt and Road Initiative projects to drive the internationalisation of the currency and establishing a quantum computing strategy to secure Hong Kong’s long-term competitiveness.

title: Surrounded by war, Turkey more than triples defence spending
description: Most of the 229 per cent budget increase will fund domestic arms production as Ankara seeks to cut reliance on the West.
content: Turkey has unveiled plans to more than triple its defence spending over the next three years, driven by regional conflicts and a desire for a greater security footprint across Europe and the Middle East. Rather than ramping up its purchases from Western allies, Nato’s second-largest military power will direct most of its 229 per cent budget increase between 2027 and 2029 towards expanding domestic production. Announcing the plan on Sunday, Vice-President Cevdet Yilmaz said the aim was to ensure Turkey “develops its own technologies in the defence industry, can meet its own needs and produces high added value”. Outlining the rationale behind the increase, Yilmaz added: “Where there is no security, there can be neither development nor democracy. We are shaping our budget accordingly.” Bill Park, a senior lecturer in defence studies at King’s College London, said Ankara had long been building towards greater defence self-sufficiency. This shift came partly from Turkey having “not enjoyed dependency on Western allies who have sometimes proved unreliable”, as well as a “more general desire for greater autonomy”, Park said. Turkey had also taken into account the reality of its “multidimensional security situation”, as reflected by the mutual defence pact it signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in early August, he said, adding: “It isn’t just about Nato these days.” Omer Ozkizilcik, an Ankara-based non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank in Washington, said Turkey – with Ukraine to the north, Iran to the east and Israel to the south – was surrounded by active conflicts, alongside its long-running dispute with Greece to the west. Moreover, Washington’s stated desire to reduce its Middle East commitments had “demonstrated that states need to rely more on themselves, rather than the umbrella of an American defence architecture alone”, Ozkizilcik said. Turkey’s overseas military presence in countries including Libya, Qatar, Somalia and Syria was one of the largest among so-called middle powers and required further upkeep, he said. Park pointed to the unpredictable nature of surrounding crises as a major motivation for the spending increase. The Russia-Ukraine war has increasingly spilled into the Black Sea, where drone, mine and missile attacks on commercial shipping reached record levels in August. This is a major concern for Turkey, which controls the Bosphorus and Dardanelles straits connecting the Black Sea to the Mediterranean under the 1936 Montreux Convention. The region also forms transatlantic security alliance Nato’s southern flank, where Turkey’s military power acts as a deterrent against Russian acts of sabotage targeting alliance members Bulgaria and Romania – such as last week’s attempted drone strike on Leipzig airport in Germany. Uncertainty also looms over the future of Iran, in light of its war with the US and Israel and the involvement of the Arab world. Meanwhile, Israel’s growing assertiveness in Syria and its expanding security ties with Greece were “significant factors in Turkey’s security calculus”, Park said. Tensions over Syria escalated last month when Israel bombed an airbase near the Turkish border, claiming it was acting to prevent Ankara from deploying additional troops – a premise rejected by Ankara, Damascus and US special envoy Tom Barrack. Barrack said the surprise attack could easily have led to an air battle with Turkish warplanes patrolling the border. Military tensions have also spread into the eastern Mediterranean. Turkish naval destroyers recently approached an Israeli missile boat near Cyprus before withdrawing, according to Israeli media. The incident followed a €3 billion (US$3.48 billion) deal signed on August 31 for Israeli firms to supply air defence systems to Greece. Responding to these developments on Monday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan warned: “We will not watch from the sidelines hostile steps aimed at encircling our country in our region.” “Those who are disturbed by our country becoming stronger and by our efforts to establish peace and stability in our region cannot turn us back from our path,” Erdogan said after a cabinet meeting in Ankara. With security in Europe and the Middle East looking increasingly fragile, “Turkey expects, and will be expected by others, to play a greater role”, Park said. Ozkizilcik agreed, noting that European allies had also shown a growing appreciation for Turkey’s role since the war in Ukraine began. Furthermore, as Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen continued to pose a threat to Saudi Arabia – Turkey’s partner in the newly formed Mecca Defence Pact – “one can expect Turkey’s security role in the Middle East to grow even further”, he said. Rather than strengthening the overall capability of the Turkish military, the budget increase will have a bigger impact on the country’s fast-growing defence industrial base – a sector largely formed in response to past Western military sanctions. Turkey now develops a wide range of hardware, including tanks, submarines and drones that have been used in Ukraine and other conflicts. Following a recent diplomatic thaw with Washington, the US committed to supplying engines for Turkey’s indigenous fifth-generation Kaan stealth fighter jet. Prospective customers for the aircraft include Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. “Turkey has turned from a defence consumer to a defence provider, and the increase in defence spending reflects the perspective to continue progressing on this path,” Ozkizilcik said. Park expected much of the new funding to focus on “drone warfare, air defence and electronic warfare” – capabilities proven critical in the Russia-Ukraine and US-Iran wars. Turkey would seek to strengthen its abilities in these areas while establishing itself as an exporter of such military technologies, he said.

title: From Pakistan to Uzbekistan: how China’s J-10CE is widening its overseas reach
description: Fighter jet is becoming an appealing option for a growing number of foreign operators, potentially providing insight into its performance.
content: Battle-testing modern weapon systems can come at a steep price: a country must send its forces to war. But for China’s 4.5-generation J-10CE fighter aircraft, exports have opened another route. Pakistan provided the aircraft’s first major combat test during its four-day conflict with India in May 2025, when Islamabad’s J-10CEs were used in an air battle. Two US officials told Reuters that at least two Indian aircraft were downed, including a French-built Rafale – though the precise losses, weapons and circumstances remain disputed. That combat validation raised the jet’s foreign sales prospects, and it also set the stage for a wider overseas footprint. As export deals materialise, each new operator could expose the fighter to different climates, basing conditions, combat doctrines and potential adversaries far beyond the East Asian environment for which it was originally developed. This could give China growing operational insight into the aircraft’s performance without having to deploy its own forces. The fighter jet’s overseas reach is already widening. Uzbekistan has become its second confirmed foreign operator, introducing the J-10CE into a Central Asian air force long reliant on Soviet-designed aircraft, while Bangladesh has moved ahead with plans for a possible purchase, with a draft proposal submitted for government approval. What began as China’s effort to develop a modern fighter for its own air force is gradually becoming a higher-end option for a small but growing number of foreign operators. The J-10CE traces its roots to China’s J-10 fighter programme, which dates back to the late 1980s. The aircraft was developed by Chengdu Aircraft Corporation (CAC), part of state-owned aerospace giant Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC). Its first flight was back in 1998. Early J-10As relied on Russian AL-31FN engines, but successive variants saw the aircraft’s sensors, avionics, weapons and propulsion progressively upgraded. The J-10B introduced a redesigned intake, infrared search-and-track sensor and upgraded avionics. The J-10C then added an indigenous active electronically scanned array radar, improved networking and electronic systems, newer PL-10 and PL-15 air-to-air missiles, and eventually China’s WS-10B engine. That provided the foundation for the J-10CE, the first J-10 variant designed specifically for export. Li Jun, the aircraft’s chief designer at AVIC’s Chengdu Aircraft Design and Research Institute, has said it can be customised for different operating environments and mission requirements, with optional payload packages. That flexibility also extends to the wider support package. China offers the fighter together with its own weapons, training, maintenance and support, while the domestically produced WS-10B engine reduces reliance on Russian suppliers for a critical component. Pakistan became the J-10CE’s first foreign operator in March 2022, adding it to a fleet already built in part around the lighter, lower-cost JF-17 jointly developed with China. Islamabad presented the acquisition as a response to a shifting regional balance of air power after India introduced Rafale fighters, with then prime minister Imran Khan saying the J-10CE would help address a “security imbalance” in the subcontinent. According to the Pentagon, Pakistan ordered 36 J-10CEs, with 20 delivered by May 2025. The International Institute for Strategic Studies called the delivery a “step change” for Chinese fighter exports, marking a shift from ageing designs that it said “did not compare favourably” with Western or Russian aircraft towards a modern fighter equipped with advanced sensors and weapons. In a 2020 assessment for the Royal United Services Institute, air-power specialist Justin Bronk called the J-10 a “rough equivalent” to the US-made F-16 and Sweden’s Gripen, matching most single-engine fighters while being “significantly cheaper to acquire”. While Bronk noted it has less range and lower performance at high altitudes than bigger twin-engine jets, its lower price could appeal to states seeking effective fighters without the political ties attached to Western suppliers. The jet’s appeal, however, rests on more than price. Its radar allows it to detect and track targets, while data links allow it to exchange target information with other aircraft and supporting platforms, helping it use long-range weapons such as the PL-15E missile more effectively. Public estimates of the PL-15E’s range vary considerably. Display specifications at the 2021 Zhuhai air show listed the range at 145km (90 miles), whereas a Xinhua military report in January said the PL-15E’s maximum range could exceed 200km (124 miles). Separately, Reuters reported that Pakistani officials put the May 2025 Rafale engagement at around 200km, while Indian officials said it was even farther. The Indian officials said their pilots had believed the export missile’s range was around 150km. Actual combat range can vary considerably depending on factors such as launch altitude, airspeed and the target’s manoeuvres. More broadly, the clash with India offered only a partial test of the J-10CE. In a separate assessment in January, RUSI noted that the engagement provided “useful, albeit incomplete, insight” into Chinese aviation and missile capabilities. The fighter’s performance demonstrated clear operational credibility, but the outcome ultimately depended on a broader kill chain – the sequence of detecting, tracking, targeting and engaging an enemy aircraft. For Beijing, the episode provided rare operational evidence of how an export package built around Chinese sensors, weapons and data links performs in high-intensity combat involving modern Western-designed fighters. That battlefield credibility could further strengthen the J-10CE’s commercial appeal by adding operational credibility to advantages China already offers on procurement terms. A 2025 Pentagon report noted that Beijing could offer developing nations weapons that were “less expensive than Western systems”, with financial incentives and flexible payment options.

title: ‘The more, the better’: Hong Kong won’t cap talent scheme passes, labour chief says
description: Minister addresses concerns about policy’s impact on population, saying renewal criteria ensures arrivals ‘contribute meaningfully’.
content: Hong Kong will not cap the number of admissions under its talent schemes, with the labour minister saying “the more, the better” amid a global race for skilled workers, despite rising concerns over whether the city can absorb the influx. Wrapping up a five-day visit to Hong Kong by overseas innovation and technology (I&T) specialists, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said on Friday that no quota would be set for the two main categories of talent passes – one for professionals with job offers and the Top Talent Pass Scheme – but renewals were conditional on holders being employed or having set up companies in the city. “Such requirements ensure arrivals contribute meaningfully to the economy. The more talent that comes to Hong Kong, the better,” he said. Experts have raised concerns about whether the city can absorb the influx of non-local talent without putting strains on its population. Hong Kong has rolled out a suite of talent schemes since late 2022, including the Top Talent Pass Scheme for top earners and graduates of leading universities, the points-based Quality Migrant Admission Scheme, and channels for professionals with job offers and technology specialists. Authorities have approved 126,942 applications since 2023, with 94.5 per cent, or 120,009, involving candidates coming from mainland China. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu is expected to give an update on the city’s talent hunt when he delivers the 2026 policy address and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan next Wednesday. The government is reportedly moving to add professions related to artificial intelligence (AI), and plans to incorporate related qualifications into existing entries to ease an anticipated shortage of interdisciplinary AI experts, with such efforts slated for completion in the first half of 2027. A delegation of 20 overseas tech specialists organised by Hong Kong Talent Engage (HKTE), a government office under the Labour and Welfare Bureau, concluded a five-day visit from Monday covering Hong Kong, Qianhai in Shenzhen and Nansha in Guangzhou. The tour aimed to familiarise participants with the region’s I&T ecosystem and support measures. The group comprised winners of a hackathon co-organised by HKTE and Germany’s EuroTech Federation in June, as well as federation representatives. They toured major tech hubs including Cyberport, the Hong Kong Science Park and the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, in addition to the Northern Metropolis. During the trip, they visited local research institutes, enterprises and start-ups to explore opportunities in AI, robotics, smart transport and biotechnology. Cem Deniz Araz, a German doctor and chief executive of heal.health, a preventive healthcare start-up, said he was impressed by the Greater Bay Area’s hi-tech infrastructure. His company, which is still in early development, was exploring opportunities to expand in Hong Kong and mainland China. “What impressed me most was the self-driving technology – I never saw that in Germany,” he said. “Hong Kong also has great potential for my AI healthcare business, as the city is dealing with an ageing population.” Aleksandr Gorbunov, a Russian co-founder of muunai, an AI start-up focused on automating clinical documentation for medical practices, said he was struck by the scale of robotics manufacturing on the mainland, and hoped to explore opportunities there in the future. “We got to visit biotech, AI and robotics at the forefront of development in China,” he said. “At one robotics company, they showed us what their robots can do, and seeing that as a human was truly remarkable.”

title: Opinion | What Ukraine has that Japan and Taiwan lack
description: Ukraine’s former defence minister is launching a new venture that could offer more than drone technology. Asia should take notes.
content: On September 1, former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced that Alex Karp, CEO of artificial intelligence and data analytics firm Palantir Technologies, would become the lead investor in a new defence technology company he is building. This confirmed what Fedorov had only gestured at two days earlier in an interview with the Financial Times: that what he was selling investors was never really drones. In that interview, he also suggested he was ready to trade drone-warfare know-how for Patriot interceptors to get Ukraine through winter, essentially exchanging battlefield knowledge for one of the world’s most sophisticated air-defence weapons. Six weeks before Karp’s name entered the picture, Fedorov had been Ukraine’s youngest-ever minister. The day after his July dismissal, Italy’s defence minister invited him to Rome as an adviser. Karp, whose firm is worth US$440 billion, reportedly soon called him to discuss working together. Neither was calling for Ukrainian hardware. What they presumably wanted was harder to manufacture: what Fedorov had learned running the system that produced that hardware. That system was a loop: battlefield, failure, feedback, redesign, test, back to the battlefield. Brave1, the defence-tech cluster that was essentially Fedorov’s brainchild, is known for fast procurement – more than 500 grants in two years, prototypes certified in weeks. However, speed alone wasn’t the asset. Rather, the asset was the rapid feedback loop of real-world experience, which included soldiers dying when a tactic failed. Military theorist John Boyd argued that combat is won by whoever cycles through observing, orienting, deciding and acting faster than the enemy can adapt. Ukraine didn’t just build weapons faster, it closed the loop between failure and correction faster than Russia could exploit the failure. Covid-19 exposed a civilian version of the same mechanism: emergency conditions compressed vaccine development from years to months by running trials, manufacturing and regulatory review in parallel because immediate human costs were moving faster than ordinary institutions could tolerate. In Ukraine, that loop was hard to contain within a conventional chain of command. An organisation built for rapid experimentation and discretionary procurement can collide with institutions built for command and accountability, even in a country fighting for survival. Federov’s dismissal in July was reportedly the result of irreconcilable differences with Ukraine’s top military commander Oleksandr Syrsky and of his ministry procuring at its own discretion rather than as requested by the general staff and the military. Ukraine’s fastest learning system remained, in the end, answerable to a chain of command it had been built to outrun. Some of these dynamics may be visible in Taiwan too.
