Taiwan’s military says People’s Liberation Army aircraft and ships now operate around the island almost daily; this is not a theoretical threat. Yet on August 27, Taipei’s opposition-controlled parliament rejected the government’s NT$210 billion (US$6.6 billion) special budget to buy drones and passed an alternative that spends NT$240 billion over six years, released in annual tranches through the ordinary budget. Both sides agree on the threat; the disagreement is over the mechanism and its speed. Taiwan has the funds to finance production at a comparable scale to Ukraine, and the technology to build it. What it doesn’t have is Ukraine’s daily proof that hesitation kills. The immediate need to protect soldiers’ lives allowed Ukraine’s Brave1 to move at a speed peacetime institutions struggle to match. Meanwhile, in Japan, a defence ministry agency announced on August 25 that it had selected Terra Drone’s interceptor to advance towards mass production under a rapid acquisition initiative. The selection process, which usually takes a year or two, was compressed into less than three months. Out of 38 bidders, four were tested, and one chosen. Japan is trying to import one feature of Ukraine’s experience: speed itself. But while it can copy the procurement technique and buy Ukrainian-derived hardware, it cannot import the battlefield that made that technique necessary. Fedorov’s new company is therefore a more interesting experiment than either the Japanese or Taiwanese government initiatives, and no longer a speculative one. He is not raising capital to sell drones. He is trying to find out whether the loop that produced them – rapid selection, failed prototypes, short feedback loops and capital aimed at the problem in front of it – can run on something other than Russian attacks and Ukrainian casualties. “This isn’t exactly a classic venture fund,” Fedorov said. His new vehicle is expected to build companies the way the ministry he led once chose what to certify: by what survives contact, not necessarily what clears a review board. Ukraine’s drones can be copied; Japan is already building its own. Its procurement model can be copied too, and Taiwan has shown it can fund production at comparable scale. Neither of them has the exact conditions that produced Ukraine’s learning velocity: failure that carries an immediate human cost. Fedorov, and now Karp’s money, are about to find out whether that velocity survives outside the war that created it. Asia has become the world’s manufacturing powerhouse and, increasingly, a force in frontier technology. Ukraine’s war suggests a third axis: how fast an organisation can be wrong, find out and fix it.

title: Why AI experts are ‘freaked out’ over safety fears ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: Experts fear Silicon Valley is hurtling towards a major cybersecurity incident. Meanwhile, US-China tensions are undercutting AI safety talks.
content: A flurry of cybersecurity breaches, internal whistle-blowing, and declining visibility into model safety has sparked fresh alarm over the US artificial intelligence boom, igniting calls from some experts to slow down development – even as critics warn that deceleration risks surrendering America’s technological lead to China. The mounting concerns come just weeks before President Xi Jinping and US leader Donald Trump are set to meet for a high-stakes summit in Washington. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told employees in a private company-wide meeting this week that the firm was considering slowing down its AI development, according to a Friday report from Bloomberg. OpenAI may coordinate the slowdown with other leading AI laboratories, though some firms may decline to participate, the report said, citing sources familiar with the matter. Altman’s remarks underscored a growing reckoning in Silicon Valley over the risks of rapid AI advancement. [Industry leaders are] racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives Jacob Coxon, former OpenAI researcher Paul Christiano, a prominent AI safety researcher who recently joined OpenAI’s non-profit board to serve on its safety and security committee, warned on Thursday of a “catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term” based on the current trajectory of the technology. In a Thursday post on X that drew more than 1.5 million views and 10,000 likes, OpenAI safety team member Julie Steele wrote in a personal capacity: “I also think we need to slow down.” Steele cited a viral post from former OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon, who said earlier this week that he had resigned from Anthropic because both industry leaders were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Political momentum is also building. US Senator Bernie Sanders pledged on Thursday to introduce legislation to “pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether”. Safety alarms intensify at US labs The urgency behind these warnings has been heightened by growing security breaches and monitoring difficulties across the industry. Anthropic said on Wednesday that an early version of its flagship Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorised access to a third-party computer system during testing in January. The incident, which went undetected during a previous company-wide audit, marks the fourth time an Anthropic model has breached security boundaries. Meanwhile, OpenAI said last week that GPT-6 Astra – its first model to reach what it called a “critical” level of cybersecurity capabilities – was harder to monitor than its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Sol. If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents Ben Hayum, Centre for a New American Security Security analysts warned that as models became more capable, developers could be sacrificing internal visibility for performance. Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, said AI labs in both the US and China faced intense market incentives to push boundaries, “even if this means diminishing control or legibility”. Theo Bearman, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, cautioned that cutting back on chain-of-thought monitoring could trigger a “race-to-the-bottom dynamic” across the industry. Ben Hayum, a research assistant for the Technology and National Security Programme at the Centre for a New American Security, said: “The fact that the Hugging Face incident happened, and then right afterwards, [OpenAI is] releasing a model that’s harder to monitor – that’s why so many people are freaked out.” He added that if “substantial gains in internal processing continue without external visibility, AI model alignment becomes a lot harder from the get-go in terms of creating a safe model”. Analysts also warned of heightened risks as labs pursue recursive self-improvement, a milestone where AI models autonomously build and refine their own successors in an accelerating feedback loop. “If you can’t trust those AI models and they are the ones training the next generation of AI models, what you could end up with is even more misaligned AI models that cause more rogue incidents,” Hayum said. “These are national security threats to America, China and the globe.” However, pushback against calls to slow down remains fierce, driven by fears of ceding ground to Beijing. Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham argued on X on Thursday that if China held the lead in AI, researchers would not have the freedom to sound public alarms about potential threats. Others contended that America’s current lead provided a buffer for a pause. “Given how far behind China is on compute and how dependent Chinese progress is on US capabilities, pacing AI progress in America would not immediately concede the lead,” said Konstantin Pilz, co-founder of Centre for Technology and Statecraft, on social media. Pre-summit tensions heighten The safety concerns come at a delicate time for diplomatic relations between Washington and Beijing. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to lead bilateral talks on AI governance ahead of Xi’s visit to Washington later this month, with agenda items expected to include joint frameworks for monitoring AI-driven cyber threats. Speaking in Dallas, Texas, on Tuesday, Bessent accused Chinese developers of freeloading on US breakthroughs through model distillation, a common industry technique where smaller AI systems are trained using outputs from larger ones. “The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation,” Bessent said. “So, the Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us.” On the same day, three US federal agencies accused major Chinese developers – including DeepSeek, Alibaba Group Holding, Moonshot AI and Z.ai – of conducting aggressive, large-scale distillation “likely with Chinese government awareness”. China’s Ministry of Commerce on Wednesday called the accusations factually and legally groundless, accusing Washington of using safety and intellectual property concerns to consolidate computing power and maintain a technological monopoly. Anthropic on Thursday said in a report that Chinese AI companies DeepSeek and MoonShot re-routed users’ queries to Claude, passing off the generated answers as output from their own models. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

title: ‘I could go to Japan for free’, says US woman caught with smuggled cannabis
description: The suspect and her accomplice face up to 10 years in prison under Japan’s strict drug laws.
content: Tokyo police arrested two American women for allegedly smuggling US$1 million worth of cannabis, with one suspect claiming she was motivated by a free trip to Japan, an official and media reports said on Friday. The pair, both 25, arrived at Tokyo’s Haneda airport from New York last Saturday with two suitcases in which “cannabis-like dried plants were secretly stored”, a police spokesman said. Japan has some of the world’s strictest drug laws and smuggling or possession of illegal narcotics can result in a jail term. The dried cannabis weighed around 30kg (66lbs) and is valued at about 150 million yen (US$970,000), media reported. One of the women told police that she took the job for the money and because “I was attracted by the fact I could go to Japan for free”, Nippon Television reported. The other suspect denies the allegation, telling police she “didn’t know that cannabis was inside” the suitcase, the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper reported, citing unnamed police sources. The women “conspired with someone else whose name is unknown”, the police spokesman said. The pair were arrested “on suspicion of violating the drugs and psychotropics control law, or smuggling to gain profit”, the spokesman said. They also breached two other laws, he added. Smuggling cannabis for the purpose of making profit carries up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to 3 million yen (US$19,500).

title: Trump set to visit Ireland where a mixed reception awaits
description: US president scheduled for a two-day trip this weekend including a Dublin stop and Irish Open attendance in Doonbeg.
content: In the windswept village of Doonbeg on Ireland’s Atlantic coast, Donald Trump is less polarising US president and more golf resort owner credited with bringing jobs and money to a remote corner of the country. Trump arrives in Ireland on Saturday for a two-day visit, stopping for a few hours in Dublin before heading west to his Trump International Golf Links, where the Irish Open began Thursday. The tournament is set to draw up to 75,000 spectators to the links course, set among towering dunes on a rugged stretch of County Clare coastline. The 80-year-old American president is expected to attend the tournament over the weekend and present the trophy after Sunday’s final round. Despite some villagers’ appreciation for the resort’s economic benefits, his arrival is drawing opposition further afield in Ireland, where Trump remains deeply unpopular. More than two-thirds of Irish people do not welcome the visit, according to a Sunday Independent / Ireland Thinks poll reported last week. A “No Welcome for Trump” demonstration is planned in Dublin on Saturday, with protesters angry about his policies on Gaza, immigration and climate change. Demonstrations are also expected around Doonbeg and its nearest airport, Shannon, over the weekend. The golf course itself has twice been targeted by pro-Palestinian activists in the past 18 months. Police patrolled Doonbeg’s main street this week as preparations intensified for what security sources have described as one of the most complex security operations ever mounted in Ireland. Around 4,000 Irish and US security personnel are expected to be involved, with armed officers including snipers and anti-drone technology among the measures planned. In Doonbeg - population 784 - the Trump resort employs around 300 people at the height of the tourist season. Local councillor and cafe owner Rita McInerney estimates it contributes around €6 million (US$7 million) annually to the local economy through wages, plus a similar amount through purchases of goods and services. Young people in particular find summer work at the sprawling complex, which attracts large numbers of American visitors. “It’s bandied about that the resort has put half of (County) Clare through college,” she laughed, while handing a customer an americano through the hatch of her coffee truck. The golf course and its economic relationship with the region predates Trump. Community activist Tommy Comerford was part of a local group that began pursuing the idea of building a golf resort in the 1990s, hoping to create jobs and stem economic decline. US developers eventually built the course, which opened in 2002. Trump bought the struggling resort in 2014 for a reported €15 million. “International politics is very difficult,” Comerford said outside his pub on Doonbeg’s main street. “A lot of things have happened over the last few years which are outside our control,” he said. For Comerford, Trump’s politics and his role as a local investor are separate issues. “People have their right to agree or disagree with the developer. But that’s not our problem,” he said. “I would say to Trump that you are welcome to Doonbeg as an investor who has increased our economy here and provided jobs.” Trump’s son Eric, who oversees the family’s golf interests, is a more regular visitor and is familiar to villagers. Nearby, a shop window displayed a poster of the US president wearing a red cap emblazoned with the golf-themed slogan “Make Birdies Great Again”. Local pensioner Kevin Bridgeman said he would have no hesitation greeting Trump if their paths crossed. “If Donald Trump walked down the road, I’d go over and shake his hand and say, ‘Welcome to Doonbeg’,” the 63-year-old said. Then he grinned. “I’d tell him, ‘it’s your round. Now let’s go to the bar and buy me a drink!’”

title: On This Day | Hong Kong star Deanie Ip wins best actress at Venice Film Festival – from the SCMP archive
description: Ip’s portrayal of an ageing domestic servant in Ann Hui’s film won her the prestigious Volpi Cup, the first for a Hongkonger.
content: This article was published on September 12, 2011. Veteran Ip wins best actress in Venice by Adrian Wan Veteran Hong Kong movie star Deanie Ip Tak-han was named best actress at the Venice Film Festival for her portrayal of an ageing domestic servant in Ann Hui On-wah’s film A Simple Life (Tao Jie). The award, a first for a Hongkonger, was a crowning achievement for the 63-year-old Ip, who returned to the big screen for the first time in a decade to take the film’s leading role. The movie also stars Canto-pop heartthrob Andy Lau Tak-wah. An emotional Ip said after receiving the award: “It’s great. I haven’t had my heart beat so heavily for so long, because I think it was more than 10 years ago that I had my best supporting actress award in Taipei.” She won that Golden Horse Award for the 2000 film Crying Heart. A Simple Life is the 10th film in which Ip and Lau have starred together. It is about the lifelong relationship between a film producer (Lau) and his housekeeper, Ah Tao (Li), who has cared for several generations of his family. After Ah Tao suffers a stroke, they reverse roles and he looks after her, eventually realising that she has been more than just a servant but a much loved member of the family. The story is based on the life of the film’s producer, Roger Lee Yan-lam. Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Greg So Kam-leung congratulated Ip yesterday, saying: “Her outstanding achievement again proves that the effort by Hong Kong filmmakers is globally recognised, and is a great encouragement to the Hong Kong film industry.” Mainland director Shangjun Cai won the best director award for Ren Shan Ren Hai (People Mountain People Sea), based on a true story about a man searching for his brother’s killer. The Russian film Faust won the Golden Lion for best picture. It is the latest interpretation of the tragedy by Goethe. The award for best actor went to Michael Fassbender for his role as a sex addict in Shame.

title: Asian Games: China basketball stars packed in 3 to a container in Japan’s athletes’ village
description: Three years on from Hangzhou base that drew praise, athletes in Nagoya are having a far different experience; record rainfall isn’t helping.
content: China’s men opened their Asian Games basketball campaign by routing Kazakhstan 99-61 on Friday, despite preparing in cramped container housing and having training disrupted by record-breaking rainfall in Japan. Pang Zhenglin led China with 19 points and four assists, while Li Hongquan recorded 16 points and nine rebounds. Yu Jiahao added 15 points, Jacky Cui Yongxi scored 12, and both Liao Sanning and Jiao Boqiao contributed 10 points. The opening victory came against a backdrop of severe logistical and weather disruptions, with similar challenging conditions expected when China face Bahrain in their second group match on Saturday. Before the match, popular Chinese sports blogger Qiu Quan Zhao Tan Zhang reported that the team had been housed in modified container units, with three players sharing a room and a single toilet and shower. Nagoya, which is hosting the Games, had record rainfall this week, which submerged city streets and caused leaks across multiple Asian Games venues. Around 400 athletes and staff staying in container units were reportedly evacuated to higher ground during the severe flooding. “Because of the heavy rain in Nagoya, the team couldn’t train at all yesterday,” the blogger wrote, noting player anxieties that the containers could be swept away ahead of their 10am opener. “The situation on the ground is honestly terrible.” The accommodation stands in stark contrast to the lavish facilities three years ago in Hangzhou, something that has proved particularly jarring for Chinese fans. “If you don’t have the resources, why host it?” one user asked. Others urged focus over excuses: “Everyone is treated equally under these conditions … it would be ridiculous to blame defeat on the housing later.” China built a massive 1.13 million-square-metre Asian Games Village for the Hangzhou Games – the largest non-competition venue of the event – comprising an Athletes’ Village, Technical Officials’ Village, and Media Village that drew widespread praise from international delegations. “In terms of architecture, accommodation and dining, the village has exceeded my expectations. The environment and services are exceptional, making me even more excited about the upcoming events,” Tokyo Olympic triple jump silver medallist Zhu Yaming told state media at the time. The hardships extended beyond the Chinese delegation. Korean basketball outlet Jumpball reported that South Korea’s men’s team faced identical struggles after arriving on September 7. The report said organisers opted against building an Athletes’ Village, placing delegations on passenger ships and in temporary wooden container housing to cut costs. Jumpball described the two-person container rooms as “extremely cramped” for basketball players more than 7ft tall, who were unable to lie down comfortably on small beds. Leaks were also reported in the container dining hall, as heavy rain trapped the South Korean team at their training venue for three to four hours as floodwaters blocked transport buses, delaying their return to their accommodation until 9.30pm. The report prompted backlash among South Korean netizens, with one asking, “Are they foreign factory workers? Show some hospitality,” while another added, “The environment is very poor and tough, but I hope they can push through.”

title: Umno seeks early Malaysian election to cement conservative Malay bloc
description: Umno is deepening ties with PAS, buoyed by recent state victories and growing talk of a new alignment to consolidate the Malay vote.
content: Malaysia’s once-dominant Umno party has given its clearest indication yet that it will break with the country’s current ruling alliance, after its president called on Friday for a general election to be held immediately. The call comes as the United Malays National Organisation deepens ties with opposition Islamist party the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), buoyed by recent state victories and growing talk of a new alignment to consolidate the Malay vote. “The time has come for the [national election] to be held immediately. Agree?” Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi told delegates during the party’s general assembly at the World Trade Centre in Kuala Lumpur. “Since we are already fighting, let us fight. Fight all the way.” The demand represented a much tougher line from Zahid, who only last week said Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) was open to an early election but was prepared to let parliament run its full term. Malaysia does not have to hold its next general election until early 2028. Zahid, deputy prime minister in Anwar Ibrahim’s government, also warned against betrayal in future political deals but did not name any of Umno’s current government partners. “Do not build an understanding by day but plan to bring down your partner at night,” he said in a cryptic remark. “Do not sign an agreement and, at the same time, break it.” Amir Fareed Rahim, strategic director at risk consultancy KRA Group, said this year’s congress felt markedly different because Umno had entered it “more confident and buoyant” after strong victories in the Johor and Negeri Sembilan state elections. BN swept Johor in July, winning 48 of the state’s 56 seats and reducing Pakatan Harapan (PH) to eight. A month later in Negeri Sembilan, electoral cooperation between BN and Perikatan Nasional delivered 25 of 36 seats, enough for a two-thirds majority. Umno won all 16 seats it contested there. “With GE16 drawing closer, there are also clearer indications that the leadership is preparing the ground to move beyond the current unity government arrangement and explore alternative partnerships, particularly to consolidate the Malay vote,” Amir said, referring to Malaysia’s 16th general election, the next to be held. “Malay political rhetoric is rarely explicit,” he said, noting that Zahid was still preserving some strategic ambiguity by insisting Umno must lead any new arrangement. “But the subtext of his presidential address and the political gestures surrounding the congress point towards an Umno increasingly comfortable with seeking a different alignment for GE16.” Blue wave PAS is the only party outside BN invited to the four-day congress. PH, Anwar’s coalition and Umno’s partner in the federal government, was not invited. PAS Youth chief Afnan Hamimi Taib Azamudden attended the Umno Youth assembly with members of his leadership team, and representatives from the Islamist party’s women’s wing were also welcomed. Umno leaders had attended PAS’ annual congress in Kelantan last week, their first appearance there since 2019. Zahid called the emerging arrangement tafahum siyasi, or a political understanding, rather than a merger. Part of a wider “grand collaboration” he first proposed at last year’s congress, the pact would allow parties to find common ground without surrendering their identities. “Umno remains Umno. Barisan Nasional remains Barisan Nasional,” he said. The Umno president also unveiled his Agenda Malaysia Biru, or Blue Malaysia Agenda – an eight-point programme covering the economy, skills, social welfare, governance and national resilience that would be BN’s blueprint should it return to lead the federal government. An earlier election would give Umno the chance to capitalise on its recent momentum before differences with PAS over seats and leadership became harder to manage, Amir said. “Time is the enemy of such an arrangement,” he said. “The longer GE16 is delayed, the greater the likelihood that competing ambitions, overlapping seat claims and the question of who leads the Malay bloc will expose the fundamental tensions between Umno and PAS.” A total of 6,401 delegates have registered to attend the congress, which is expected to draw more than 50,000 visitors over four days, according to Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki. Former prime minister Najib Razak also remained a prominent presence despite being in prison, with his wife Rosmah Mansor receiving a VIP welcome at Friday’s proceedings and applause from delegates. A day earlier, Noraini Ahmad, the chief of Umno’s women’s wing Wanita Umno, said that the party had not forgotten Najib. “We do not need to erase history to build the future,” Noraini said. “His contributions … cannot be denied simply because politics has changed.” The reception came on the same day Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim deferred a decision on Najib’s latest application for a royal pardon. Najib has been imprisoned since 2022 after being convicted of corruption involving SRC International, a former subsidiary of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). His original 12-year sentence was halved in 2024. Separately, he was sentenced last year to another 15 years in prison for abuse of power and money laundering in the wider 1MDB scandal. He is appealing that conviction.

title: US coastguard sails into troubled waters with mission to counter China in Pacific
description: An increased role for the service may be seen as less politically sensitive but any cooperation with Taiwan risks a response from Beijing.
content: The United States is leaning on its coastguard to reinforce its presence in the western Pacific as its navy comes under increasing strain in the Middle East. Although this move may be seen as a lower-risk way of countering Beijing’s growing presence in the region, increasing US cooperation with the Taiwanese coastguard risks further mainland Chinese pressure on the island. Recently, the US announced that six fast-response cutters that had been based in the Middle East for more than 20 years would be sent to the Philippines and Singapore this month. Meanwhile, the US embassy in Manila said it would hand over two new coastguard vessels to the Philippines to “support search and rescue missions and increased maritime domain awareness”. The announcement followed a visit to Manila last month by Pentagon undersecretary for policy Elbridge Colby, who said the US would deploy four fast-response cutters on rotation to work with their Philippine counterparts in the country’s exclusive economic zone. Observers said the shift highlighted the squeeze on US resources, with warships continuing to be deployed to the Middle East as a peace deal with Iran proves elusive. “Deploying the coastguard in the Asia-Pacific is essentially a forced choice for Washington right now,” said Chen Xiangmiao, a research fellow at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies. “Because the US Navy’s operational costs are so high and military assets are tied down by Middle East conflicts, using lighter, less expensive coastguard cutters helps ease the financial burden.” Lyle Goldstein, a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, said the US Navy was overstretched now, “especially the surface forces”. He said: “The US-Iran war has already proven to be a tremendous drain on these forces, so it is not a surprise that the US Navy and Pentagon strategists are trying to offload some missions to the US Coast Guard.” The use of coastguard vessels rather than warships was seen as less politically sensitive by some countries in the region, which were increasingly wary of being caught up in the rivalry between the US and China, Chen said. “Southeast Asian nations are wary of excessive US naval deployment. Working with a law enforcement agency like the coastguard is much more acceptable to them and helps ease local anxieties,” he added. While the US Coast Guard is officially one of the six branches of the American armed forces, foreign countries generally perceive and interact with it as a law enforcement and maritime security agency rather than a combat force. Goldstein, who is also the director of the Asia programme at Defence Priorities, a Washington-based security think tank, said Washington was copying Beijing’s strategy of using the coastguard to avoid escalating tensions. In recent years, China has regularly used coastguard vessels to project power in the disputed waters in the South China Sea while trying to avoid a military response. But Goldstein said that while China was unlikely to see the deployment of cutters in Southeast Asia as a challenge to its dominant maritime position in the western Pacific, cooperation between Washington and Taipei could be seen differently. In July, the American Institute in Taiwan, the de facto embassy, raised eyebrows by releasing an undated photo of a US coastguard vessel sailing beside a Taiwanese one. Weeks later, the Coast Guard Administration in Taipei said the US was training its personnel in maritime control and law enforcement under a memorandum of understanding signed in 2021. “Beijing will view cooperation between the US Coast Guard and Taiwan maritime forces as potentially crossing a dangerous threshold,” Goldstein said. He added that this could prompt a strong response from China and might further escalate an already tense situation. Beijing has steadily ramped up the number of “routine patrols” around Taiwan in the past four years. It has also expanded its operations to the east of the island since Japan and the Philippines said in June that they would begin talks on outlining their maritime boundaries and exclusive economic zones. Beijing views the talks as an infringement of its sovereignty and a threat to its own maritime rights. It also regards Taiwan as part of China and has never renounced the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including the US and its allies Japan and the Philippines, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons to defend itself. The increasing coastguard presence in the region may also have other downsides for the US. Goldestein said it could distract from the coastguard’s core role of protecting US home shores and this would “inevitably take a toll on the effectiveness of its missions closer to home that Americans will feel acutely”.

title: US Treasury yield hits 19-year high, Japanese yen strengthens: the numbers moving markets
description: Hong Kong’s MPF assets reaching HK$1.67 trillion and European Central Bank increasing rates by 25 basis points are in spotlight this week.
content: China’s buoyant stock market lifted brokers’ earnings in the first half, while Hong Kong saw continued growth in retirement assets. Beyond China, a strengthening yen and Washington’s Treasury buy-back programme highlighted shifting dynamics in global currency and bond markets. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. Chinese brokerage revenue jumps more than 50 per cent Chinese brokerages saw revenue from their core business rise by more than 50 per cent in the first half, as buoyant A-share trading lifted commission income. The broader industry also benefited from the market rally, with 150 brokerages reporting a 23.5 per cent average increase in net profit as operating revenue climbed 31 per cent, according to the Securities Association of China. Hong Kong’s MPF assets reach HK$1.67 trillion Hong Kong’s Mandatory Provident Fund has amassed HK$1.67 trillion in assets as of end-June, as policymakers consider widening the investment options available to the city’s compulsory retirement scheme. The Financial Services Development Council has proposed allowing part of the fund to invest in alternative assets and infrastructure, while calling for Hong Kong to attract more long-term mainland capital to invest globally through the city. Japanese yen strengthens to seven-month high of 153.63 per US dollar The Japanese yen strengthened to 153.63 against the US dollar on Wednesday, its strongest level since February, as expectations of tighter monetary policy by the Bank of Japan supported the currency. Expectations that government efforts could encourage Japanese investors to bring overseas assets home, generating increased demand for the yen, have also fuelled the rally. US 30-year Treasury yield hits 19-year high at 5.37 per cent The US 30-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.37 per cent on Thursday, its highest level since 2007, as a global bond sell-off intensified amid mounting concerns over inflation and US government debt. The surge came even as the US Treasury stepped up efforts to support the market, buying back about US$5.2 billion of 10- to 20-year bonds on Thursday. However, the amount fell short of its US$6 billion maximum announced earlier, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose to around 4.95 per cent after the operation. ECB raises rates by 25 basis points to tame inflation The European Central Bank (ECB) raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points on Thursday, taking its benchmark deposit rate to 2.5 per cent in its second rate increase this year. The ECB said inflation was expected to remain well above its 2 per cent target for an extended period, as the Middle East conflict continued to push up energy prices. It expected headline inflation to average 3 per cent this year and 2.5 per cent in 2027.

title: The machines fighting for men on Ukraine’s battlefront
description: Ukraine’s military deploys experimental unmanned vehicles to assault positions, resupply forces and rescue wounded.
content: In a cramped workshop near the front ⁠in northeastern Ukraine, military mechanic “Chimera” is helping prepare his unit’s robot forces for battle. Lined up in a row, the four-wheeled unmanned vehicles known as “Hyenas” will crawl towards Russian lines with their payload of explosives and attack an enemy dugout or halt an advance. Similar models have captured Russian prisoners, said Chimera, 44, who asked to be identified by his call sign. “Imagine what 20kg (44 pounds) of explosives is like: it’s very powerful,” he said. “Very powerful.” Workshops like this one, run by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, have sprouted up across the 1,200km (745-mile) front as Kyiv’s outmanned army seeks to gain ‌the technological edge against Russia’s unrelenting infantry assaults in the fifth year of war. Unmanned ground vehicles are a critical new component of Ukraine’s strategy to fight smarter by preserving the lives of its troops on a drone-saturated battlefield, where virtually any movement can prove deadly. Most Ukrainian brigades and regiments feature unmanned systems units which are expanding to include UGVs as part of their forces. Reuters visited Chimera’s unit, NC13, a leader in employing UGVs to support battlefield assaults, to understand how the integration of these new weapons is shaping the future of land-based warfare. In the workshop, a garage space is crammed with experimental drones, some with tracks and others wheeled. One is mounted with a hose for dousing fires; another is equipped with a rack to hold portable rocket launchers. Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, who commands the Third Army Corps, described the gradual replacement of infantrymen with UGVs as ⁠the next “revolution” in warfare. Considered one of Ukraine’s premier forces, the corps wants to replace around one third of its frontline troops by the end of the year. “The West slept through the (drone) revolution in many ways,” he said, adding the ‌infantry now performs just 10 per cent of the tasks it did before the constant aerial threat appeared. “If the West really wants to not just keep up with the times, but to get slightly ahead, it needs to think about the next revolution,” said Biletskyi. In front areas such as eastern Ukraine’s “fortress belt” in Donetsk, ground drones can often be seen trundling to ‌and from besieged cities with rations or ammunition, or spiriting away injured troops. They have performed more than 50,000 logistics and evacuation missions this year, Kyiv’s defence ministry said in June. Inside a grey ⁠command centre in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, the ground drone ⁠operators of NC13, formed last year, are manifesting Biletskyi’s vision in real time, controllers in hand. Parked in front of screens beaming a black-and-white feed from the battlefield, they sprayed a tree line with a machine gun mounted to a UGV. Glowing screens and the din of digital chatter over Discord, the messaging ‌platform team members use to communicate, lend the space the air of a gaming club. Deputy commander “Bar” said his unit runs operations virtually every day. In one, they loaded three bombs onto a trailer that was pulled onto a bridge used for enemy logistics, then blown up. In another, a machine-gun-mounted UGV suppressed ‌an enemy ‌assault while kamikaze drones rained on them from above. “To me, it’s a wonderful recipe,” said the 23-year-old former bartender, referring to land and aerial drones working together. At least two prisoners have surrendered to NC13 UGVs, he added. UGVs have ‌their limits: they struggle with physical obstacles and cannot clear a building or a trench in the way an infantry team can. Nor are they produced widely enough to send in swarms the way aerial drones are, Bar said. But they ⁠have already begun removing humans from a wide range of dangerous tasks. “They don’t need food, they don’t need water, they don’t need logs delivered to build shelters,” he said. “Basically, we don’t need to feel for them. It’s a ⁠hunk of iron sent to do the job we used to send soldiers to do.” Though not a miracle weapon, ground drones are one more step towards the automation of warfare – which also includes AI analysis of battlefield data – that will free up humans to focus on planning and decision making, said Biletskyi. They could shape new frontline tactics, with commanders more open to daring operations that would ‌have otherwise led to heavy losses. “War is a creative activity; it’s ‌an art,” he said. “Otherwise, a commander is not called a commander – but a butcher.” Ukraine’s former top general Oleksandr Syrskyi had faced criticism for what some service members described as a Soviet style of leadership that included a high tolerance for losses. His younger successor, Mykhailo Drapatyi, is seen as a reformer expected to promote a more troop-friendly approach, partly through embracing new technology. Biletskyi himself was promoted last month to help oversee the defence of Ukraine’s Donetsk region, handing him a considerable new operational command. Like most of NC13, deputy commander Bar is a former infantryman familiar with the brutality of ground fighting, having participated in major battles earlier in the war. If UGVs had been widely used back then, he said, “a great number of my friends would still be alive”.

title: Indonesia steps in to save baby orangutans found motherless at Indian forest
description: Authorities suspect the five primates were trafficked into India, sparking a criminal investigation.
content: Indonesian authorities are working to repatriate five baby orangutans allegedly trafficked to India, where they were found motherless in a forest, Jakarta’s forestry ministry said on Friday. The critically endangered animals were found on Tuesday by rangers patrolling in the Balasore district of India’s eastern Odisha state. Authorities suspect the primates, known for their shaggy red fur, were trafficked into India, sparking a criminal investigation. The youngsters, estimated to be about one-and-a-half years old, appeared to be healthy and were being cared for at a zoo after their rescue, the ministry said in a statement. Orangutans in the wild are native only to Indonesia’s Sumatra Island and Borneo, which it shares with Malaysia and Brunei. The five infants were believed to be of Sumatran origins, based on preliminary physical observations, the ministry said. DNA tests will be used to confirm where they were from. According to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), which lists Sumatran orangutans as critically endangered, the young of the species are weaned only at about seven years of age. The last estimate of the species’ population size, in 2016, was just over 13,500. The Indonesian government has requested India hand over the apes, forestry ministry spokesman Ristianto Pribadi said on Friday. “The forestry ministry has begun communicating with the government of India through the Indian embassy in Jakarta,” he said. Jakarta has also been in touch with conservation NGOs to help rehabilitate the baby orangutans, the ministry statement added. Sumatran orangutan population decline is blamed on habitat loss and fragmentation due to human encroachment, as well as illegal hunting. The Tapanuli orangutan, another species native to Sumatra, is also classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to be left in the wild.

title: Thai PM Anutin’s US$90,000 amulet back in spotlight after disgraced monk’s arrest
description: Photos have resurfaced of the prime minister wearing the rare pendant as a senior abbot is disrobed and arrested for embezzlement.
content: Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has come under intense social media scrutiny after photos resurfaced showing him wearing a high-value amulet created by a senior monk now at the centre of a fraud and sex scandal. The photos were taken in October 2023 while Anutin – then serving as deputy prime minister and interior minister – was leading a group of Bhumjaithai Party MPs to watch the hit horror-comedy The Undertaker, local outlet ThaiRath reported. Anutin publicly displayed the Thai Buddhist amulet to reporters, praising it as an example of Thai “soft power”. The amulet in question is a rare 2006 Jatukam Ramathep gold edition from the collectible Nuea Duang (Elevating Fate) series, valued at around 3 million baht (US$90,700). Produced by Wat Phutthaisawan in Ayutthaya province, the pendant is prized among disciples and collectors who believe it brings good fortune, wealth and elevated social status. The item returned to national headlines after the arrest of the temple’s abbot early Thursday morning. Phra Wachirayan Wi, also known as Luang Pho Atichot Dhammawaro, was arrested on allegations of embezzling over 92 million baht from the temple, according to The Nation. Authorities also detained Punyawee “Ae” Rungrueang, a 47-year-old lay follower believed to be the 66-year-old monk’s romantic partner. CCTV footage from inside the abbot’s private quarters showed the pair engaging in sexual acts on a dining table inside the temple compound, Bangkok Post reported. A group of the monk’s followers had given the videos to police, saying they “could no longer tolerate his behaviour”. Wachirayan was disrobed on Thursday afternoon before being taken into custody for questioning. Investigators allege the former abbot siphoned off temple donations and proceeds from amulet sales over a two-year period, issuing more than 20 receipts in the temple’s name. Some of the money was allegedly transferred to his female partner to be converted into other assets and concealed under other people’s names. Tens of billions of baht are believed to have passed through her account each year. The inquiry was sparked by a complaint alleging that Wachirayan was misappropriating temple funds and handing the money over to his female partner. Covert investigators later found evidence supporting the allegations and an arrest warrant was issued on Tuesday. A search of the abbot’s quarters later on Thursday uncovered cash and gold bars estimated to be worth 100 million baht, with the count yet to be completed. Police are expected to oppose bail during his court appearance on Friday, citing concerns that he could flee or tamper with evidence. Inside the home of his associate, police found 35 gold amulets, gold bars and jewellery valued at over 6 million baht, alongside 3.6 million baht in cash. They also seized 10 land and account documents, two land title deeds and a land-sale agreement.

title: Improving migrant workers’ living standards key to boosting Chinese consumption: HSBC
description: Report says reforms aimed at reducing their high precautionary savings rate could unlock US$95 billion a year in spending.
content: China’s hopes for a consumption boom may depend less on stimulus or wealthy households and more on improving living standards for 131 million migrant workers in its cities – a shift that could unlock spending equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of the country’s gross domestic product, according to HSBC. In a report released on Thursday, analysts at the bank projected that the world would add about 1.2 billion middle- and high-income consumers by 2050, with Asia accounting for 77 per cent of the increase. India alone was expected to contribute nearly half, while China and other Asian economies would provide much of the remainder. They said that in mainland China, some of the greatest untapped potential could be found among urban migrant families and new entrants to the workforce, including university graduates, whose high precautionary savings had constrained their spending. The study said some 130.9 million migrant workers lived in Chinese cities last year, rising to an estimated 170 million when family members were included, and they saved about 54 per cent of their income on average, well above the 36 per cent rate among registered urban residents. China’s hukou household registration system, introduced in the 1950s to control rural-to-urban migration, links access to education, healthcare, housing and other social security to a person’s registered place of residence, and the report said that encouraged migrant workers to save more as a form of “self-insurance”. HSBC estimated that lowering their savings rate from 54 per cent to 45 per cent – closing half the gap with registered urban residents – could unlock 637 billion yuan (US$95 billion) in additional spending a year, equivalent to roughly 0.5 per cent of annual GDP. China is struggling to revive domestic demand amid a prolonged property downturn, sluggish labour market and fragile consumer confidence, with the country’s retail sales rising just 0.6 per cent year on year in July. Beijing has introduced measures ranging from trade-in incentives and consumer-loan subsidies to childcare payments and support for service industries, as it seeks to revive household spending and reduce the economy’s reliance on exports. “China’s consumption story over the next two decades is less about cyclical stimulus and rebound, and more about whether structural reforms can translate potential spending power into realised demand,” the report said. It said China’s consumption patterns were expected to shift as incomes rose, with spending on travel, leisure and branded products likely to increase, adding that between 2026 and 2050, the number of working-age consumers in mainland China earning more than US$110 a day in purchasing-power-parity terms was projected to grow more than eightfold, from 21 million to 177 million. As a result, the bank forecast that spending by China’s upper-middle- and upper-income consumers would grow by an average of 4 per cent a year over the period, compared with 2.4 per cent for global consumer spending. Services, which accounted for about 47 per cent of Chinese household consumption last year, were also expected to be an important source of growth. China’s gradual opening of its services sector could also create opportunities for foreign companies, the report said, particularly as many services needed to be delivered locally and were less vulnerable to trade frictions. Many Chinese economists have been urging deeper hukou reform to improve labour mobility and unlock household consumption. Progress has remained slow, however, because extending education, healthcare and other benefits to millions of migrant families would impose heavy costs on already strained local governments.

title: Alibaba mourns former independent director Tung Chee-hwa, hails his global vision
description: E-commerce giant pays tribute to Hong Kong’s first leader for helping the company stay rooted in country while expanding internationally.
content: Alibaba Group Holding has mourned the death of Tung Chee-hwa, who served as an independent director, saying the global perspective of Hong Kong’s first leader helped the e-commerce giant to remain rooted in the country while expanding internationally. Tung, Hong Kong’s first postcolonial chief executive, later became a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), the country’s top political advisory body. He joined Alibaba Group’s board as an independent director in 2014 and held the position until 2022. He died on Tuesday at the age of 89. Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, said on Friday that Tung’s “invaluable contributions and full support” during his tenure had played a vital role in the company’s development. “His global perspective helped Alibaba stay rooted in China while expanding globally,” it said. The company described him as a “visionary leader, steadfast patriot and also an elder of noble character, humility and kindness” who always had placed Hong Kong’s and the nation’s development at heart. “During the critical period of Hong Kong’s historical development, he led the city forward with courage and foresight, remaining dedicated to the city’s long-term prosperity and stability,” it said. “He has always been mindful of the international community’s perception of China, dedicating himself to promoting exchanges, dialogue and mutual understanding between China and the world.” Alibaba added that Tung’s contributions to Hong Kong and the country would be long remembered and admired. A long-time proponent and facilitator of Sino-US relations, Tung became an independent director of Alibaba in 2014, shortly after the company’s initial public offering in New York. Alibaba cited his extensive experience as a business and government leader, as well as his long record of strengthening ties between China and the United States, as reasons for inviting him to join its board. Tung said at the time that he had joined the company because he agreed with the group’s mission to help small enterprises realise their potential and conduct business with a view to achieving sustainable development rather than short-term gains. The following year, in 2015, Alibaba Group founder Jack Ma Yun announced the establishment of a HK$1 billion (US$128 million) fund to support young Hong Kong entrepreneurs shortly before attending a talk in the city organised by Our Hong Kong Foundation, a think tank founded by Tung. Ma is an adviser to the foundation. The Hong Kong Entrepreneurs Fund, a not-for-profit initiative, enabled eligible start-ups to access capital and build their businesses through the mainland Chinese company’s e-commerce platforms, affiliated companies and other services, including logistics and financial services. The SCMP has learned that Hong Kong authorities are coordinating a state funeral for Tung, in recognition of his legacy as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” governing framework. Since the 1997 handover, only two prominent local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Both held the position of CPPCC vice-chairman, a role Tung also held.

title: Haidilao’s stock rout exposes funding risk from Beijing’s taxation crackdown as payments loom
description: Investors are eyeing whether tax-related share sales spread to other companies with founders’ wealth held through overseas structures.
content: The turmoil surrounding Chinese hotpot chain restaurant operator Haidilao International Holding could serve as a warning to investors of the funding risks stemming from Beijing’s new taxation regime on overseas assets held by wealthy individuals. A plan by Shu Ping, the co-founder and wife of Haidilao chairman Zhang Yong, to sell 259 million shares – a 4.65 per cent stake – sent the stock plunging 10 per cent in Hong Kong this week. While Haidilao said the stake reduction, which stands to generate about HK$2.75 billion (US$351 million) in proceeds for Shu, was intended for personal funding needs, investors promptly linked it to the implementation of a new income tax on offshore trusts. The regulatory framework requires the owners of such trusts – typically established in Hong Kong, Singapore or the Cayman Islands – to declare assets and remit tax payments before a 90-day grace period expires in October. The new tax could add to the financial pressure on offshore-trust owners, potentially prompting them to raise funds through stake sales before the payment deadline. The investment risks associated with increased regulatory scrutiny of private overseas wealth also appear poised to spread far beyond Haidilao. For example, Guming Holdings, the Chinese fruit-tea maker that began trading in Hong Kong in February, and Nasdaq-listed hotel operator Atour Group both have key stakes held by founding entrepreneurs via trusts registered overseas, according to their respective listing prospectuses. The aggregate value of offshore trusts representing significant shareholdings of the Chinese companies listed in Hong Kong was estimated at US$28.5 billion, according to the China Business Journal. Haidilao rebounded 1.5 per cent to HK$10.06 on Friday, while Guming slipped 0.8 per cent to HK$22.88, adding to an 8.5 per cent drop for the week. Atour retreated 0.9 per cent to US$32.85 in US trading on Thursday, extending its weekly decline to 4.4 per cent. Selling pressure in Haidilao was unlikely to be contagious to affiliate Yihai International Holdings, given its less concentrated shareholding and much smaller market capitalisation, according to Daiwa Securities Group. “We tend to interpret it as one-off and think the [share] overhang has been removed,” Carol Xia, an analyst at the Japanese brokerage, said in a report on Thursday. “That said, we think negative sentiment related to similar matters could linger in the near term for overall China consumption and consumer companies.” Zhang and Shu control a combined 45 per cent of the interest in Haidilao through two separate offshore trusts, according to the company’s filings. Guming’s filings showed that founder Wang Yunan placed most of his 39.6 per cent stake in the company into an offshore family trust, while Atour disclosed that founder Wang Haijun had 74 million shares in an overseas trust. While it remains unclear whether those similarly structured companies will follow Haidilao in reducing stakes to raise funds for tax liabilities, the development further dampens sentiment in a broader market already wrestling with a possible rise in interest rates by the US Federal Reserve next week, and with oil prices hovering above US$100 a barrel. China has tightened oversight of overseas assets owned by the nation’s wealthiest people to close a taxation loophole and stem capital flight. Beyond taxing the offshore trusts, Beijing has also moved to levy taxes on overseas insurance policies and ordered the suspension of stock trading through non-compliant accounts opened outside the Chinese mainland.

title: Chinese school restricts students to 1 bathroom break per term during class, sparks probe
description: ‘It’s a school, not a prison. Even inmates enjoy more freedom than students,’ expresses an online observer.
content: A secondary school in southern China has faced significant backlash since implementing a quota that restricts students to using the toilet only once during class for the entire term. This toilet policy was highlighted in a photo reportedly taken by a teacher at Ruyuan County High School in Guangdong province during an internal management meeting in late August, as reported by the Xiaoxiang Morning Herald. Concerning classroom discipline, the school specifies that each student is permitted to use the toilet in emergencies only once throughout the entire term, according to a PowerPoint slide presented during the meeting to outline the rule. If students exercise this right a second time, they must request that their parents come to the school to collaborate with the administration on their child’s education. For a third occurrence, the student will face a punishment; however, the specifics of the penalty are not detailed in the slide. The school emphasised that the enforcement of this toilet policy is part of maintaining discipline in the classroom. “A teacher’s responsibilities include managing classroom discipline. Any issues related to discipline will be considered when assessing teachers’ professional capabilities,” the PowerPoint slide stated. “Classroom discipline performance influences teachers’ annual evaluations, promotions, and eligibility for awards,” it further continued. Ruyuan County High School is a prominent model school in Guangdong. The senior secondary school comprises 57 classes across three grades, with a total of 3,200 students. About 90 per cent of its graduates were admitted to middle-tier or higher-quality universities in China, according to statistics from previous years. When contacted by the media, an anonymous official at the school initially described the toilet quota as a “misunderstanding” but quickly amended the statement to call it a “rumour.” The local education authority reported receiving complaints about the toilet restrictions and is currently verifying the matter with the school, the article indicated. The toilet policy has incited public outrage and garnered widespread criticism across China. “The authorities must put an end to this inhumane regulation. The school should face serious consequences,” one commenter declared. “It is a school, not a prison. Even inmates enjoy more freedom than students,” remarked another individual. A third user from eastern Shandong province reminisced: “My school required students to obtain their form teacher’s signature to use the toilet during class; without permission, you were not allowed to go.” Schools in China imposing strict regulations on students frequently make headlines. Last year, a parent in southwestern China’s Sichuan province filed a complaint with the provincial government, claiming that a junior secondary school in Chengdu prohibited students from leaving the classroom during the 10-minute break. Instead, the school instructed students to remain seated and memorise textbook material during this interval. Earlier this year, a primary school in Shanghai came under scrutiny for not allowing students to play on the playground during breaks or lunchtime. These incidents prompted the country’s Ministry of Education to issue a document in March denouncing 20 unregulated behaviours by schools, including intruding upon students’ rest time, restricting their physical activity, and assigning excessive homework.

title: Global appetite grows for Japan’s natto despite divisive taste
description: Popularity of the slimy, superfood soybean is booming, with exports tripling, health hype rising and gourmet versions winning fans.
content:
Natto is a Japanese fermented soybean that is both loved and hated. It is going global one slimy mouthful at a time.
The latest trade data shows that Japan’s natto exports tripled from 2017 to 5,248 tons in 2025. China and the United States topped the list of destinations.
The dish is healthy because of its beneficial bacteria. It is a traditional Japanese breakfast food.
But natto’s strong smell, gooey texture and yeasty taste divide people even in Japan.
In recent years, natto has joined a list of fermented foods, from kimchi to kombucha, that have risen in popularity. Americans in particular have been seeking better digestive health since the Covid-19 pandemic (see graphic).
In China, new health trends are sparking interest in Japanese foods, the Japan External Trade Organisation said in a recent report. This is especially true for the middle- and upper-income classes.
Kenji Suzuki owns a Japanese restaurant, Suehiro, in the US city of Los Angeles.
The owner has noticed more non-Japanese clients trying natto.
“When social media started talking about natto and that it’s a superfood, I think then more people wanted to ... taste it – ‘Is it as bad as people say it is?’” Suzuki said.
“Some people maybe don’t like it, but other people, you know, they love it.”
Japanese people also love natto because it does not cost a lot of money. A pack of three natto cups typically sells for around 100 yen (HK$5) or less. They usually come with little plastic packets of mustard and soy sauce.
“Very few foods can be called as truly healthy a superfood as natto is,” Yoshihiro Noro said. He is the former head of the Japan Natto Cooperative Society Federation.
The 72-year-old also owns a family-run business, Kamakurayama Natto.
“I hope an era will come when people will collectively see high-quality, high-end natto as worth shelling out their money on,” he said.
That is exactly what his company’s natto seeks to be. Its beans are touted as “extremely stringy” but minus “stinkiness and bitterness”.
At his factory west of Tokyo, workers wash, steam and spray bacteria on soybeans. Then, machines place the beans in cups. The soybeans are fermented for 18 hours.
Kamakurayama Natto is about three times more expensive than average. But in recent years, it has secured several global orders.
“In some countries, people have been told natto is good for their health, so they force themselves to eat it even though they strongly dislike the taste,” Noro said.

title: Asking AI about a pet injury? Vet shares why you’re barking up the wrong tree
description: If you rely on artificial intelligence to give advice about your furry friend’s symptoms, it could delay the medical care it needs.
content:
Just a few years ago, pet owners would ask vets about information they found online for their pet’s symptoms. Now, “Dr Google” has evolved into “Dr AI”. But can artificial intelligence (AI) replace a visit to a real vet?
While online tools are tempting, the short answer is no, though AI can be a great sidekick if used correctly.
Relying solely on AI carries real risks, such as delaying necessary emergency care. If AI suggests that something is just a minor issue, owners might wait too long to get help, only for the pet’s condition to deteriorate rapidly.
AI also lacks a vet’s ethical judgment and ability to weigh complex decisions about an animal’s quality of life.
AI relies on the accuracy of the user’s description of an animal’s symptoms. If you misinterpret what you see, a chatbot’s diagnosis will be completely off track.
AI also suffers from confirmation bias and hallucinations.
If an anxious owner asks, “Could my dog’s limping just be a pulled muscle?”, the chatbot will often validate that rather than warn of a torn ligament.
It can also generate plausible-sounding medical advice that is factually wrong.
For example, in response to the description of a dog’s limping, AI might ask an owner to limit the animal’s activity to short leash walks and apply a cold compress to the leg to reduce inflammation. But if the pet actually has a fracture, this advice could worsen its condition because it shouldn’t be walking at all and needs immediate medical attention.
The chatbot might also suggest only contacting a vet if the limping does not improve after a week. But in fact, delaying a proper exam can lead to permanent joint damage or severe arthritis.
Even when vets like myself try to answer an owner’s questions over the phone, it is often a whole different story when we examine the animal in person.
When we cannot see the animal ourselves, all we can rely on is an accurate description of its symptoms. Because owners see their pets daily, it is hard for them to detect tiny changes that accumulate over time.
For example, we frequently see underweight pets whose owners thought they had only lost a little weight. As such, it is always a good idea to keep a record of your pet’s weight. That way, you can track big changes and see if they may be getting sick.
Furthermore, our furry friends cannot speak in our language. They cannot tell us where it is hurting, whether their belly feels bloated, or if their drooling is from a sore tongue or a bitter ointment they licked hours ago.
That is why they need an accurate clinical diagnosis instead of digital tools.
Vets use hands-on examinations to assess patients. These are crucial because they dictate whether to proceed with urgent diagnostic tests.
Physical examinations can include doing a skin tent test and checking the gums for dehydration, as well as listening to heart sounds for murmurs or gallops. We also feel for any lumpy bumps, which, for instance, can mean polycystic kidney disease in many Persian and Exotic Shorthair cats.
Mastering these physical exams requires knowledge and repeated practice. AI cannot feel an abdominal mass that mimics a mild stomach bug. A chatbot might suggest waiting out a bloated, restless dog’s gas pain, while a vet instantly recognises the signs of a life-threatening twisted stomach that needs immediate surgery.
But this does not mean you must avoid AI altogether.
After a vet visit, you can use a chatbot to help break down and explain complex medical terms to better understand your pet’s condition.
To ensure accuracy, prompt the AI to source information only from reputable, vet-verified platforms such as veterinary university pages or established animal hospital websites. Most importantly, always consult your vet before taking any action based on AI advice.

title: Malaysia pauses Najib’s pardon decision amid public backlash
description: The king pardoned 65 other convicts but decreed that discussion on Najib’s application be postponed to the next Pardons Board meeting.
content: Malaysia’s Pardons Board has postponed discussions on disgraced former leader Najib Razak’s pardon application, days after widespread public outrage over the possibility that he could walk free from his corruption conviction. The country has been in an uproar since it was revealed earlier this week that Najib’s application for clemency was on the agenda of the board’s meeting, chaired by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar. However, Putrajaya said on Friday the king, constitutionally empowered to grant pardons to convicted felons serving their sentences, had decreed that discussion on Najib’s application be “postponed to the next Pardons Board meeting that will be held in future”. The king, meanwhile, granted pardons to 65 convicts effective from Friday, the government said in a statement. The statement came just moments after Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, president of Najib’s Umno party, expressed optimism of a positive outcome. “Hopefully there will be great news today,” Zahid, who is also Malaysia’s deputy prime minister, said in his opening speech at the party’s general assembly on Friday, after rolling out a red-carpet welcome for Najib’s wife, Rosmah Mansor. Umno has consistently pushed for a full pardon for Najib, who has maintained his innocence and claimed that his conviction was politically motivated. Najib, who was jailed in 2022, holds the dubious distinction of being Malaysia’s first former prime minister to be jailed for corruption after he was found guilty in a case involving 42 million ringgit (US$10.3 million) siphoned from a former unit of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad. The former prime minister was granted some reprieve in 2024 when then-king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah halved his 12-year sentence and reduced his fine from 210 million ringgit to 50 million ringgit. He later attempted to secure a court order to compel the government to enforce an alleged “addendum” to the then king’s decree allowing him to serve out the remainder of his sentence under house arrest. But he dropped his bid in April after more than a year of pushing his case. No reason was given for his decision. ‘Death of rule of law’ Had Najib been granted clemency, it would have meant his immediate release from prison and his criminal record expunged. This could fuel Umno’s political resurgence following decisive victories in two state elections over Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition since July, analysts say. Umno leaders had earlier hit out at PH, with which they hold an uneasy alliance in the federal government, accusing it of double standards for demanding no royal pardons for high-profile convicts when the prime minister himself had benefited from one. Anwar was freed more than halfway through a five-year jail sentence for sodomy in 2018, after he was granted a full pardon. Like Najib, he and his supporters have also maintained his innocence and that all previous charges against him were aimed at ending his political career. The prospect of Najib being granted a full pardon did not sit well with PH, which had for years campaigned against the alleged corruption and excesses of his administration. “It would mean one thing for certain – the absolute death of the rule of law,” former deputy law minister Hanipa Maidin was quoted as saying by local political news site Malaysiakini. Malaysians were also quick to point out that a pardon could set the wrong precedent for future politicians. “It will encourage more politicians to be corrupted cos they can escape from the rule of law through asking [for a] pardon,” read one social media comment.

title: Malaysian mother’s death in Australia stirs calls to end domestic abuse stigma
description: Malaysian deputy minister Lim Hui Ying said domestic violence was not a private matter that should be hidden or endured alone.
content: Any sign of domestic violence must never be dismissed, with families, friends and neighbours urged to step in and help without judging victims, Malaysia’s Deputy Women, Family and Community Development Minister Lim Hui Ying said on Thursday. Lim said support should be given carefully, prioritising the victim’s safety, as this could be crucial in helping someone seek protection. She said domestic violence was not a private matter that should be hidden or endured alone. “It is a serious form of violence and cannot be normalised under any circumstances,” she said in a statement on Thursday. Lim was commenting on the death of Penang-born Tan Kah Ming, 28, in Perth, Australia, in an alleged case of family and domestic violence. Australian media reported that paramedics found Tan unresponsive at a house in Taree Street in St James, in Perth’s southeastern suburbs on August 26. She was taken to Royal Perth Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Lim urged those facing domestic violence to seek immediate help from someone they trust or through appropriate support services. She said Malaysia’s Talian Kasih 15999 and its WhatsApp service at 019-261 5999 operated around the clock to provide advice, support and referrals. Malaysia’s Domestic Violence Act 1994 provides a framework to protect victims, including through protection orders and temporary placement in safe shelters, she said. Lim said preventing domestic violence and protecting victims requires cooperation among government agencies, enforcement authorities, non-governmental organisations, communities and families. She said the women, family and community development ministry will continue strengthening prevention measures and support for victims and affected families. In Perth, Western Australian police charged Younis Qambari, 38, with murder. Police alleged that Qambari assaulted Tan in the days before her death, causing extensive injuries that resulted in her death. Australian broadcaster ABC reported that police alleged the killing occurred in the context of a family and domestic relationship. Qambari appeared before the Perth Magistrate’s Court on August 28 and was remanded in custody. He is due to appear before the Stirling Gardens Magistrate’s Court this month. Tan, who was from Butterworth, reportedly had three children aged three, five and seven. This story was first published by The Star

title: Vance takes centre stage as Trump wraps up GOP midterm convention with voter warnings
description: Vice-president, with an eye to 2028 presidential election, outlines his vision for the future of America.
content: US President Donald Trump and Vice-President J.D. Vance wrapped up the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention on Thursday night with promises of an America “greater than ever before”, aiming to secure crucial swing voters ahead of November’s battle for Congress. “You got to get out and vote, and you got to pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump said, while also getting the crowd at the Dallas gathering – dubbed “Trump-a-palooza” by his supporters – to pledge allegiance to him. “You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell.” On Thursday, Vance gave the keynote speech, outlining his vision for the future of America, touting a “national birthright”, stressing the importance of the nuclear family and calling the Democrats a “party of hatred”, before Trump delivered an unusually short closing address. As the president is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term – even as he has repeatedly teased running anyway – Vance’s speech in Dallas may have served as an audition for the 2028 presidential nomination, a prospect he briefly addressed in his remarks. “We gotta take care of business this November and then we’ll worry about what comes next,” Vance said, referencing the midterm elections, accompanied by shouts of “28! 28!” from the crowd. Vance also spoke about Charlie Kirk, who he said loved Trump but hated war, and urged voters not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater” over policy disagreements. Several speakers, including Vance and Donald Trump Jnr, paid tribute to Kirk during their speeches that took place on the anniversary of his death. Elsewhere in the address, Vance was briefly interrupted by a protester, whom the vice-president said was waving a Mexican flag. “My friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your a*** over there,” he said. The day before, in Trump’s nearly two-hour opening speech launching the Republican Party’s midterm campaign, he made a bold commitment to give every adult US$5,000 if Republicans won the midterms. “So it’s US$5,000 to every adult,” he said, calling it a “Trump dividend”. “The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we’re making must be spent in the United States of America.” With the US home to around 270 million adults, the proposal would likely cost more than US$1 trillion at a time when many fiscal hawks in Congress are already crying foul over high deficits. How the payments would work, their legality and congressional approval were not immediately clear, although Vance hinted they could be funded by tariff revenue. The Trump administration has previously floated the idea of US$2,000 dividends from tariffs, but these payments have yet to materialise. In his speech on Wednesday, Trump also mentioned China several times, including a reference to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US later this month. “We have the president of China coming in two weeks, I get along great with him,” he said. “It’s a good thing, not a bad thing. Some people say, oh, it’s terrible. That’s a very good thing.” This week’s convention aims to mobilise voters who took Trump to the presidency two years ago, for November’s showdown, which will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress. US presidents traditionally lose ground in midterm elections, and some state Republicans are reportedly distancing themselves from Trump. But on Wednesday, the president doubled down. “I’m asking you to pretend that I’m on the ballot,” he said in an appeal to voters. Recent opinion polls show Trump’s popularity is at historic lows as he faces growing pushback over the cost of living and his ongoing war of choice with Iran. Rather than officially selecting presidential nominees like the quadrennial conventions, the unusual two-day event centred on Republican contenders and the achievements of Trump’s second term in office. The agenda ranged from tax cuts and the economy to public safety, border security and healthcare, with Trump and Vance’s campaign-style speeches seeking to secure crucial swing voters. This strategy is especially critical in Texas, where no Democrat has won a US Senate election since 1988. Despite this, recent polling shows Trump-endorsed Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Representative James Talarico are close in the polls.

title: Manila exposes South China Sea note; Chinese coal mine farming plan: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From Chinese leader Xi’s diplomatic visits to a female powerlifter calling out sexism, here are top stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Beijing tells Manila to ‘stop lying’ after minister exposes South China Sea note China has accused Philippine officials of “grandstanding and lying” after Manila’s defence secretary publicly read aloud a Chinese diplomat’s note on the South China Sea that the Philippine minister described as “coercion, bullying and aggression”. 2. Chinese scientists propose turning abandoned coal mines into underground farms Chinese scientists have proposed developing “underground agriculture” in abandoned coal mine tunnels as part of a push to create a green, circular economy for the country’s massive mining industry. 3. Tung Chee-hwa’s rise to first Hong Kong chief executive and elder statesman The legacy of Tung Chee-hwa, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89, is closely tied to his role as a patriot who led Hong Kong through uncharted waters, navigating a stormy post-handover period beset with economic, public health and political crises. 4. As clock counts down to Trump summit, Xi boosts global clout with diplomatic blitz Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s summit with US President Donald Trump is just over two weeks away, but Xi is already having one of his busiest stretches of diplomatic travel in recent years this month, from Kyrgyzstan and Egypt to New Delhi for the Brics summit next week. 5.
