Hong Kong restaurant prosecuted after live newborn rat found in takeaway food Hong Kong food safety authorities have prosecuted a restaurant after an investigation into claims that a newborn rat was found wriggling inside one of its takeaway lunchboxes uncovered unsatisfactory hygiene conditions. 6. Malaysian woman who stabbed boyfriend to death over sex demand gets 12 years A Malaysian court has nearly doubled jail time for a woman who stabbed her boyfriend to death for demanding sex after ruling that the sentencing court had been “over-sympathetic” towards the accused. 7. Indian powerlifter won silver at world meet but says focus was on her looks Twenty-one-year-old Indian powerlifter Keyaa Kunal Banerji, who won a silver medal at a world championship, has spoken out after being targeted with online harassment and objectified for her looks, calling the ordeal “sexism at its finest”.

title: Chinese swimming prodigy Yu Zidi ‘excited’ for Asian Games debut, eyes Olympic glory
description: Some in the swimming world have questioned the mental and physical impact of high-level training and competing on the 13-year-old schoolgirl.
content: Yu Zidi made history last year aged 12 when she became the youngest-ever medallist at the swimming world championships. Now a teenager, she headlines China’s bid for Asian Games domination and has Olympic glory in her sights. The 13-year-old schoolgirl with a pixie haircut stunned the sporting world last year with a series of eye-popping times. At the 2025 World Aquatics Championships in Singapore she helped China reach the 4x200m women’s freestyle relay final. She did not swim in the final but China came third, earning Yu a historic bronze for swimming in the heats. Yu just missed out on medals in the 200m and 400m individual medley events and the 200m butterfly, coming fourth in all three races. In November at China’s National Games, having just turned 13, she clocked a blistering 2:07.41 in the women’s 200m medley for what was then an Asian record. While training with the China team in Beijing, she told local media this month she was “excited” for her Asian Games debut. “Train well, don’t slack off. Demonstrate the level of your training and work hard to break past yourself,” she said, according to state news agency Xinhua. The Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan open on September 19. A coach, Ha Sinan, once described Yu with a Chinese saying that translates as “a newborn calf fearless of tigers”. But the teenager has spoken of struggling to deal with the heavy load placed on her. Yu grew up in the city of Baoding, about 90 miles (150 kilometres) south of Beijing. She started swimming aged six and since then has juggled schoolwork with training. “Being in class all day and still having to train was really tiring,” she said in January. “Sometimes I was so tired I could fall asleep even while eating,” she said at an event celebrating Hebei province’s National Games wins. Yu said she “never considered quitting” and always dreamed of being a national champion. But during the tune-up to last year’s National Games she said the pressure of wanting to win the 400m medley nearly became too much. “It was like a big stone that weighed on me and made it hard to breathe,” she said. Yu eventually told her coach she wanted to do anything other than train. Her coach told her to persevere and “believe in yourself”, she said. Yu went on to win four medals at the National Games. Some in the swimming world have questioned the mental and physical impact of high-level training and competing on Yu at such a young age. Under World Aquatics rules, the minimum age for international championships is 14 but exceptions can be made for younger swimmers if – like Yu – they are fast enough. It seems certain that Yu will compete at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, when she will be 15, and on current trajectory will be a major medal threat. She is aware that her success for someone so young has made international headlines. But she knows hard work outweighs innate talent. In June she won the women’s 400m medley in 4:30.79 at China’s national championships, a time which would easily have earned her silver at the Paris Games in 2024. “Although talent determines where you start, going further and standing taller is dependent on perseverance and effort day after day,” Yu said at the January event. “There is still a long road ahead,” she added. “I will keep holding fast to my original dream, drawing strength from my team, to stand on the Olympic podium.”

title: South China Sea: Manila says flares fired at aircraft near Subi, Mischief reefs
description: Philippine coastguard releases footage, accuses PLA of targeting the unarmed plane as it flew over Spratly Islands on Monday.
content: The Chinese military appeared to fire flares near a Philippine aircraft operating close to the Subi and Mischief reefs, according to the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), as tensions continue to spread to other South China Sea hotspots. The coastguard released video clips on Thursday of footage that it said had been filmed from the aircraft on Monday. PCG spokesman Jay Tarriela said on social media that the unarmed plane was on a maritime domain awareness flight over part of the Spratly Islands when Chinese forces fired multiple flares at it. Beijing has not responded to the claim. The footage appears to show flares being fired from land as the aircraft approaches the artificial islands. In one clip, a lighthouse visible in the background appears to match the structure China built on Subi Reef in 2016. Other visible facilities include airfields, aircraft hangars, radar installations, harbours and other infrastructure of the type that are known to have been built on Subi and Mischief reefs. According to the PCG, Chinese forces first challenged the aircraft by radio as it flew over Subi Reef and then discharged flares. The same actions were repeated over Mischief Reef, it said. The aircraft subsequently landed at Thitu Island, which is occupied and administered by the Philippines, where it is known as Pagasa. The PCG also claimed in April that Chinese forces fired flares at its aircraft over Mischief and Subi, calling it “a clear and deliberate act of bullying”. Subi Reef – known as Zhubi in China and Zamora in the Philippines – lies in the western part of the Spratly Islands, just 26km (16 miles) southwest of Thitu and 120km northwest of Taipei-controlled Taiping Island, also called Itu Aba. China has reclaimed about 4 sq km (1.5 square miles) of land on Subi, making it the second largest of the Chinese artificial islands among the Spratlys. Mischief Reef, known as Meiji Reef in China and Panganiban Reef in the Philippines, lies in the southeastern Spratlys. It is the archipelago’s largest artificial island, with more than 5 sq km of reclaimed land. Beijing carried out large-scale reclamation at both reefs from 2014-15, building runways that can accommodate large passenger planes as well as aircraft hangars, radar and communications facilities, missile positions, harbours and other military infrastructure. The People’s Liberation Army maintains personnel at both outposts. Both reefs are claimed by the Philippines as part of its Kalayaan Island Group, while China claims the Spratlys as the Nansha Islands. The two countries also have competing claims in other parts of the South China Sea, such as Scarborough Shoal. Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea and are occupying some of its features. Taiwan, which Beijing sees as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if needed, also has overlapping claims with other claimants. Most countries, including the United States, do not see Taiwan as an independent state, but most are opposed to any change of the status quo by force. Tensions between Beijing and Manila have escalated in recent years, with frequent confrontations reported around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal.

title: This Leslie Cheung 70th birthday exhibition offers an intimate look at the Cantopop star
description: The Hong Kong Heritage Museum exhibition features never-before-shown stage outfits and offers rare insights into Cheung’s private life.
content: For those too young to have attended a live concert by Hong Kong Cantopop icon Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing, who died on April 1, 2003, appreciation often relies on recordings of his performances and exhibitions dedicated to his career and legacy. While many retrospectives over the years have celebrated Cheung’s achievements and influence in film and music, the Hong Kong Heritage Museum’s latest offering, “Miss You Much. Leslie 70th Birthday. Exhibition”, offers a much more intimate and rare look at his private life and his relationship with fans. Cheung would have turned 70 on September 12. Running from September 9 to May 10 next year to commemorate Cheung’s 70th birthday, the showcase features more than 300 exhibits lent by his long-time partner Daffy Tong Hok-tak, his manager Florence Chan Sock-fun and Cheung’s industry friends, alongside items from the museum’s own collection. Among the expected items are vinyl records, classic stage costumes, film posters and stills, music trophies, and pop culture memorabilia. At first glance, these items may give visitors the impression that it is just another show about Cheung’s stardom, but a closer look reveals that they have been selected and curated to present him not just as an idol, but as a genuine friend and creative artist. The entrance to the exhibition features a giant origami crane sculpture against a butterfly backdrop. This transports visitors back to the 10th anniversary of Cheung’s death in 2013, when local and overseas fans folded and collected 1,900,119 – later updated to 1,956,912 – paper cranes in his memory for a showcase at Times Square in Causeway Bay, setting the Guinness World Record for the world’s largest paper crane exhibition. “Suddenly, there was a butterfly circling above me and the fans at [Times Square] before it landed on the screen,” Chan recalls of that day. “It was as if Gor Gor [Cheung’s affectionate Cantonese nickname] was coming back to see us.” The items on display Two decades after his death, Cheung remains a deeply cherished part of Hong Kong’s collective memory. Joseph Chow Chi-lim, the museum’s assistant curator, shares that the team received an overwhelming number of exhibits from fans across the city. “We received more than we could fit in this exhibition,” he says. A selection of items on display for the first time includes a portrait of Cheung by local movie poster artist Yuen Tai-yung, and a birthday card made by members of his fan club, Les FANmily, on his first birthday following his death. Cheung’s rise to fame in the music and film industry began in 1977 when he placed second in RTV’s Asian Singing Contest. His major musical breakthrough arrived in 1983 with his smash-hit single “Monica”, which revolutionised Cantopop by introducing energetic, dance-oriented music and defining an era of local pop culture. In tandem with his music career, Cheung established himself as an actor. He gained critical acclaim in the late 1980s for his roles in John Woo’s action classic A Better Tomorrow (1986) and the romantic fantasy A Chinese Ghost Story (1987). “A lot of our display items, such as film posters, were produced in multiple languages, including Japanese and Korean,” Chow says. “Gor Gor’s influence was not confined to Hong Kong. He was a global pop culture icon.” A visionary pop culture icon While many of his contemporaries focused on more conventional paths to stardom, Cheung fearlessly blurred the boundaries between traditional masculinity and fluid femininity on screen and on stage in the 1990s and 2000s. From his ethereal, gender-defying portrayal of Cheng Dieyi, a Peking opera dan (female role) actor, in Farewell My Concubine (1993) to the androgynous wardrobe for his 2000 Passion Tour featuring long flowing hair and feather accents, Cheung’s bold embrace of gender-bending aesthetics made him a visionary pop culture icon who was far ahead of his time. The exhibition features outfits and shoes from Live in Concert 97, including the pair of sparkly red high heels he famously wore during the show. These were originally white shoes that Cheung had spotted in a boutique in New York. “He wanted them in red, so the shopkeeper taught him how to dye them,” Chan says. “Then he had them decorated with glittery red gems, creating one of his most iconic concert looks.” She adds that he gifted them to his close friend and renowned Hong Kong film producer Shi Nan-sun after his performances. “As well as his extravagant, feathered robes and glittery heels, he also wore a dressing gown on stage, which was rather unusual at the time,” Chow says, pointing to the costumes and photographs on display. “I want to highlight the message in his very own song, ‘I Am What I Am’.” Another corner of the hall recreates for the first time several interior settings from his former residences on Kadoorie Avenue in Ho Man Tin and at Turtle Cove in Tai Tam, featuring both original pieces and faithful copies of his furniture. “We can show people his tastes in his private life beyond his music, film and TV careers,” Chow says. “Performance was such a central part of his life that he would sometimes bring his home furniture on stage.” That includes designer Ron Arad’s stainless steel mesh recliner with undulating curves, which Cheung used on stage in 1997. Bittersweet memories Perhaps the most poignant detail is the photograph hanging above the recreated living room, in which Cheung is absent. It was taken at Cheung’s birthday party in 2003, five months after his death. “A lot of industry friends – Tsui Hark, Shi Nan-sun, Lydia Shum [Lydia Sum Tin-ha] and others – were very worried about Daffy,” Chan says, tearing up as she recalls the moment. “This was the first birthday without Gor Gor, so we all got together to accompany Daffy. We were all smiling in the photo, but of course our hearts were not.” That same sentiment still resonates today. As Chan prepares the birthday celebrations – which, apart from the exhibition, also include a new album of Cheung’s songs with Universal Music (formerly Polydor, the record label under which Cheung published his music), fan gatherings and music performances – she feels both bittersweet and heartened. “I am touched to see that decades after Gor Gor passed away, we still remember him so fondly,” she says. “These projects are a gift to him, and I wish to share his warmth with everyone so that his fans will form great memories of him for the next 10 years, or even longer.” “Miss You Much. Leslie 70th Birthday. Exhibition”. Until May 10, 2027. Hong Kong Heritage Museum, 1 Man Lam Road, Sha Tin. Free admission. For more information, visit heritagemuseum.hk

title: Hong Kong police arrest 2 tourists over graffiti on MTR Corp train carriages
description: Australian and American suspects arrested at the airport after allegedly breaking into Chai Wan depot and spray-painting carriages.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested two tourists at the airport on suspicion of criminal damage after they allegedly broke into an MTR Corporation depot in Chai Wan and spray-painted graffiti on the exterior of two carriages. The force said on Thursday evening that it had received a report at about 2pm the previous day that two men had forced their way into the depot by cutting sections of barbed wire at the top of its walls. They allegedly spray-painted each of the carriages with a five-metre-by-one-metre (16.4-by-3.3-foot) graffiti design in green, yellow and pink. “By going through vast amounts of CCTV footage … and intelligence analysis, police successfully arrested two suspects in the restricted areas of the airport who were waiting to board at around 8pm on the same day, six hours after the report,” Chief Inspector Chan Chi-leung said. The force identified the suspects as a 34-year-old Australian who said he worked in e-commerce and a 30-year-old American who said he worked in construction. Both remained in custody as the investigation was ongoing. Officers said the pair left behind nine cans of spray paint, a wooden ladder and two high-visibility vests as they fled after being spotted by staff. They allegedly scaled a three-metre-high wall before running off towards Shing Tai Road. The force reminded the public that criminal damage was a serious offence under the Crimes Ordinance, punishable on conviction by up to 10 years’ imprisonment. Trespassing on or entering railway premises was also illegal. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, a United States consulate spokesman said: “We are aware of the detention of a US citizen in connection with the graffiti case. The Trump administration takes its commitment to assist US citizens abroad seriously and is monitoring the situation.” The SCMP has contacted the Australian consulate and the MTR Corp for comment.

title: In snack-crazy India, global brands find looming warning labels unappetising
description: Firms resist front-of-pack labels on unhealthy packaged foods as India prioritises nutrition over taste amid rising diabetes cases.
content: India’s proposal to put ⁠health warning labels on some food products has sparked a nationwide debate over how the country came to rely on cheap packaged food while companies sold more nutritious versions of the same brands in other markets. With an income per household well below the global average, Indians are keen consumers of cheap food products such as Nestlé-owned Maggi instant noodles and Coca-Cola Co’s Thums Up – giving big food manufacturers a huge market with little pressure to apply the food standards they adopt in many other countries. Until now. In a setback to the industry, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Thursday it could introduce tougher red warning labels on ‌food that exceeds government-set limits on added sugar, salt or saturated fat in one go, after Supreme Court judges raised questions about FSSAI’s initial plan for a phased introduction. High sugar content is a particular risk in India, which accounts for about a quarter of all global cases of diabetes, which health experts have blamed partly on processed food. More than 101 million people in India are living with diabetes, while another 136 million have prediabetes, Danish drug maker Novo Nordisk said in July. India’s packaged food market grew to US$137.25 billion in 2026, from US$129.18 billion in 2025, and is projected to reach US$238.83 billion by 2034, according to research firm IMARC Group. Around 6 billion meals eaten in Indian households and on street corners every year are Maggi 2-minute masala noodles, made by Swiss food giant Nestlé. Maggi launched India’s first brand of instant noodles in 1983, targeting newly working mothers and children as a fast evening snack with print ads featuring kids slurping bowls of Maggi noodles “after school, ⁠after play” and saying “Mummy, I’m hungry”. The product’s success strengthened Nestlé’s foothold in what is today the company’s fastest-growing region, where all variants of Maggi are made with palm oil, whereas many versions sold in Britain use pricier sunflower oil. Similarly, Nestlé’s KitKat bars in India have ‌less cocoa in them than Australian versions. “It plays on national pride – why is it that India is getting short-changed? Why do companies make the call on my behalf that I can’t afford better ingredients?” said Shashank Mehta, a former marketing manager at Unilever’s India unit. Higher quality ingredients are also more expensive and could prompt price increases in a cost-conscious market, a former senior Nestlé executive, who declined to be ‌named, said. Nestlé said in a statement that its recipes are developed taking into account consumer expectations, local taste preferences depending on the food culture, availability of ingredients and climatic conditions. Recipe variations do not affect product quality, ⁠Nestlé said, adding that it has more than 10 regional ⁠KitKat recipes globally. The company said it complies with all Indian food safety laws and that ingredients are clearly declared on packs. India has debated front-of-pack warning labels for years to flag high content of sugar, salt and fat, like those implemented in Chile and Mexico, but faced industry opposition, with businesses specifically worried as many ‌traditional Indian products are high in sugar or fat. Chile’s 2016 food labelling law, which puts separate black octagons on a pack for each high nutrient, was followed by a 23.7 per cent decline in purchases of sugary drinks, researchers have said. The All India Food Processors’ Association says 80 per cent of packaged food could be flagged in India as having high fat, sugar ‌or ‌salt content under the proposed labelling rule. Pressure in India for stricter labelling has intensified recently from health advocates and social media influencers among others. The food safety regulator’s proposal came amid public anger after India’s government yielded to industry lobbying in ‌March when Coca-Cola and groups backing Nestlé and PepsiCo opposed having warning labels on the front of food and drinks packaging. Western packaged food giants have been in India for about a century. Nestlé started to sell sugary condensed milk in 1912 to what was ⁠then a British colony with an extremely poor local population. Unilever began selling dalda – a hydrogenated vegetable oil formulation – in India in 1937. It provided a very affordable alternative to expensive traditional ghee and quickly became a staple in lower-class kitchens, restaurants and sweet shops. Foreign ⁠corporations quickly began producing locally to keep prices low. “Many recipes in India were designed decades ago for a very cost-conscious consumer, and those recipes have simply been carried forward,” said Parul Sharma, a former executive at Mondelez’s India unit who oversaw supermarket sales. “For the longest time, Indian consumers never really questioned brands.” Coca-Cola Co’s Thums Up – a cola moulded over decades to suit local tastes – has grown into a more than US$1 billion brand that is sold in India and ‌exported to the Indian diaspora. Thums Up looks similar to Pepsi ‌and Coca-Cola but tastes different. Coca-Cola Co bought the brand for about US$60 million in 1993 to slowly phase it out and replace it with its own flagship drink. But Indian shoppers were so loyal to the taste that Coke decided to keep it. Coca-Cola’s traditional cola is also a cultural mainstay, sold on street corners with a healthy dose of spices as “masala coke”. Coca-Cola did not respond to a request for comment. A Unilever spokesperson said that in the last five years the company has “made significant progress in reducing both sugar and salt across the portfolio, reflecting our support towards healthier diets”. “We have a long-standing commitment to improving nutrition, guided by rigorous science-based standards.” Former Mondelez executive Sharma said taste entrenchment is one of the biggest deterrents for large companies to modify recipes. “You can’t change a recipe overnight without risking the loss of a very loyal consumer base,” Sharma said.

title: Kazakhstani firms eyeing Hong Kong, mainland China urged to take long-term view
description: Managing director of Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund also says rail operator KTZ aims to list in Hong Kong by end of year.
content: Kazakhstan’s businesses should prioritise long-term fundraising ambitions rather than quick wins in Hong Kong and mainland Chinese markets, a managing director of the Central Asian country’s sovereign wealth fund has said. Saltanat Satzhan, managing director for development and privatisation at Samruk-Kazyna, said she also aimed to have state-owned rail operator Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) listed in Hong Kong by the end of the year. KTZ, wholly owned by the government through the fund, has filed listing applications in Hong Kong, London and Astana. The planned listing would mark the first company under Samruk-Kazyna to go public in Hong Kong. Satzhan stressed that KTZ was much more than a domestic railway, describing it as a vital geopolitical stabiliser connecting China with Europe. “If you invest in Kazakhstan’s national railway, you’re not just investing in the domestic operator, but in the connectivity of the companies that connect China and Europe,” she said during a panel discussion at the Astana Finance Days forum on Thursday. “That’s why we are hoping we can go public by the end of this year, and we are anticipating this transaction.” According to the company’s prospectus, facilitating the “high-quality development of the Belt and Road Initiative” is among the reasons for choosing Hong Kong as a listing venue. “Given all the geopolitical conditions, given what’s happening in the world right now, everyone needs a very resilient [route] to connect China to Europe,” Satzhan said. The belt and road scheme is Beijing’s plan, launched in 2013, to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Africa and Europe. Commenting on her country’s capital market links with China, Satzhan said Kazakhstani companies should aim to build a long-term presence in the neighbouring nation, rather than treating it simply as a convenient fundraising venue. She said some of the sovereign wealth fund’s strategic companies, including national oil and gas company KazMunayGas and national rare metals and uranium producer Kazatomprom, already had deep-seated economic ties with China. Satzhan also said Kazakhstan’s capital market activities could further leverage the country’s existing ties with China. The total value of “panda bonds” – yuan-denominated debt issued by foreign entities in the Chinese market – offered by the sovereign wealth fund has already reached 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) this year. “If you want to go to China, don’t go just to get cheap money, attractive financing terms; go there earlier, not just when you need money,” Satzhan said. “Go there to build relationships, to tell your story and to have this long-term presence with our great neighbour.” In the same discussion, panellists from Hong Kong underscored the importance of the city’s bourse going global by attracting firms from beyond the mainland. Johnson Chui, managing director and head of global issuer services at stock exchange operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), said the city could offer Kazakhstani companies broad international exposure to investors from both the mainland and beyond. “Whether it’s in technology, finance, transportation or infrastructure, there are just so many sectors that Hong Kong and Kazakhstan could partner in,” Chui said. HKEX signed a memorandum of understanding with the Astana International Financial Centre – a regional financial hub and special economic zone – during Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s trip to Kazakhstan in June. The agreement establishes a framework for collaboration related to carbon markets, green finance and sustainable development. Denise Jong, a partner at law firm Reed Smith, who has advised on cross-border transactions and listing-rule reforms in Hong Kong, said an underlying factor for the exchange’s growth would be to attract listings from around the world. “It’s no longer about looking into your backyard to China. We need to look at connectivity across the globe,” she said. Jong urged regulators to remain open-minded about emerging markets, arguing they should no longer assume firms from emerging markets needed to list in Hong Kong to improve their corporate governance, as entities such as Samruk-Kazyna already maintained robust standards. “We’ll take care of the legal stuff, but the more exciting thing is to be led by the business case, and I think that also applies to the exchange,” she said.

title: Data centres sprouting in Thailand fuel fears of public health impact
description: The discovery of a data centre in Bangkok that was illegally storing 200,000 litres of oil prompted authorities to close a legal loophole.
content: At a market in Bangkok, stallholders say they had no idea initially about a boxy structure covered in gunmetal grey panels that was quickly built and installed opposite their stalls. According to them, nauseating oil began to waft through the area, where a hospital is also located, several months ago along Rama XI, an arterial road in the heart of the Thai capital, prompting complaints that led to the revelation that a new data centre might have been set up. More worryingly for the stallholders, the facility was later found to have stored 200,000 litres of oil without a permit. The revelation last week spurred Thai authorities to carry out inspections and close a legal loophole – the energy- and water-guzzling facility could not be registered as a data centre and instead could only be classified as a warehouse or a factory. For the people who have worked in the area for years, the discovery has fuelled concerns that the country is welcoming big investments such as data centres too fast without proper consultation and explanation. “I don’t know much about what this data centre is for. But it’s frightening that even the oil could leak into our drainage,” said Yui, a stallholder in her 60s, giving only a nickname. “I heard that it could generate a lot of heat too. Where will all the heat go? I can’t even get permission to modify my house, but these guys can just build this massive data centre right in the middle of our community? They didn’t even need a permit.” Across Southeast Asia, billions of dollars of investments in data centres are pouring in as tech giants build infrastructure at breakneck speed ahead of demand. The BKKO1 data centre inspected by the authorities was linked to a US$1 billion investment by Dubai conglomerate DAMAC in Thailand in collaboration with a local partner. When DAMAC announced the investment in 2024, the company said it chose Thailand to be a Southeast Asia gateway and to have access to chips, printed circuit boards and other infrastructure needed to power the data centre and “hyperscale” it once operations were scheduled to begin this year. Bangkok authorities appear to have been caught flat-footed about the facility’s existence. Anti-pollution officials found oil residue had leaked into a nearby canal from a spill. Authorities have not given the facility’s operator permission to store large quantities of oil for the data centre. If convicted, the operator could face a 200,000 baht (US$6,000) fine for illegally storing the fuel. Dozens of other data centres that have been built, are under construction and are being planned in Bangkok have triggered fears over public safety and pollution, as the facilities are located around populated urban areas. The issue has revealed tensions and disconnect between Thailand’s pursuit of billions of dollars in tech investments and regulators who have been slow to catch up. Last Friday, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul called on data centre operators to pause their construction until his government could make “airtight” laws to reclassify the facilities and protect public safety. “Thailand is attracting interest from both local and foreign investors … we need to ensure alignment with laws, standards and the national interest,” he told reporters. Bangkok Governor Chadchart Sittipunt said the issue arose because of regulatory gaps. “The term ‘data centre’ has never been defined in the law. When permit applications are made, they are filed in the form of warehouses,’’ he told reporters. “As a result, under urban planning regulations, they are not subject to EIA requirements and do not require industrial factory permits. Therefore, there must be a review of the law to bring it more in line with the urban context,” he added, referring to environmental impact assessment. Critics say the data centre rush is another example of vast inflows of foreign capital from businesses using Thailand and its resources as a base, while providing few jobs and long-term benefits for ordinary Thais. Cautious of upsetting their wealthy neighbours running the BKK01 data centre, stallholders at the nearby market did not want to identify themselves to This Week in Asia but expressed concerns about the massive investments flowing into the city without proper checks. “Before the authorities came to clean the drain, the smell of oil was so strong it gave me headaches,” a long-time stallholder said. “It’s better now. But the people who did this only have to pay a 200,000 baht fine for this. That is one baht for every litre.”

title: Chinese film ‘Dear You’ shares a story about Teochew migrant history
description: The story is set in Bangkok, Thailand and was filmed mainly in Teochew, a southern Chinese dialect.
content:
One of the most talked-about films in China this year was filmed mainly in a southern Chinese dialect. Most viewers in China would need subtitles to understand it.
Still, Dear You has become the second-highest-earning film in China this year.
Dear You was mostly filmed in Teochew. This is a dialect spoken in the Chaoshan area of Guangdong. The story is set in the Teochew immigrant community in Bangkok.
The film looks at the long history of Chinese people moving to Southeast Asia over many centuries. Many migrants came from the Guangdong and Fujian provinces in southern China.
The plot revolves around qiaopi , letters used by Chinese immigrants to send money and news back home. Many workers who could not write Chinese relied on scribes to compose the letters.

title: Letters | Hong Kong has changed. So should its marketing message
description: Readers discuss the city’s evolving appeal, unleashed dogs in public places, and former chief executive Tung Chee-hwa.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong is still marketed as a low-tax, global financial centre. However, if we listen to what people actually say about daily life – especially retirees struggling to afford household staples – the picture that emerges is quite different. Hong Kong has become more affordable through scale, competition and connectivity. The retail sector has grown more competitive since major mainland e-commerce platforms entered the city. More supply channels mean more choice, and more choice means less pricing power for any single seller. The result is not only lower costs for households but also a clearer signal to businesses: the city’s consumer ecosystem can adapt quickly when distribution and procurement become more efficient. However, affordability is not just a retail story. It is increasingly a workforce story. Hong Kong benefits from an inflow of students through overseas recruitment and mainland study pathways, as well as from talent schemes that help graduates transition into local employment. When more highly educated and skilled workers enter the pipeline, employers gain a broader base of talent, supporting hiring and improving productivity. This is how Hong Kong can convert openness into economic momentum: smoother talent matching, faster capability building and stronger long-term investment confidence. Finally, Hong Kong’s competitiveness needs a structural foundation. The Northern Metropolis offers that opportunity. By developing additional land for housing, offices and industrial buildings, the city can reduce the cost pressures that constrain both households and businesses. In a world where companies evaluate not only taxes and wages but also overhead, logistics and operational costs, land supply is an economic policy lever. Therefore, InvestHK should sharpen its message. Yes, the financial system and tax environment matter, but Hong Kong can now credibly promote a second brand of strength: a liveable, competitive city powered by rapid consumer supply, expanding talent pipelines and growing land for economic activity. If we package this narrative well, Hong Kong can attract more global partners – not just because it is convenient to do finance here, but because it is increasingly efficient to live and operate here. Joseph Chan, partner and principal director, Oriental Patron Financial Group Action needed against unleashed dogs I am writing to draw urgent public attention to an ongoing safety concern along the seaview promenade on Beach Road, Repulse Bay. Despite clear legal requirements, a number of dog owners consistently walk large dogs completely off-leash in this heavily frequented public space. When politely reminded of the law and asked to leash their pets, these individuals show complete disregard for courtesy and public safety, simply shrugging and walking away. This lack of responsibility has already caused real harm. A few months ago, a large, unrestrained dog charged towards my friend; startled and fleeing the animal, my friend tripped and suffered a painful fall onto the road. Despite multiple complaints submitted to the authorities, no visible enforcement or corrective action has been taken. The lack of active monitoring has only emboldened these repeat offenders, leaving pedestrians, including children and the elderly, to navigate a public walkway at their own risk. Public promenades should be safe for everyone to enjoy. I urge the authorities to initiate regular patrols and strictly enforce local leash regulations along Beach Road before a more severe injury occurs. Pradip Agarwal, Mid-Levels Recalling Tung Chee-hwa’s dedication to education Learning of former Hong Kong chief executive Tung Chee-hwa’s passing vividly reminded me of a special day in 1997 at Government House. Having recently arrived from the mainland and having scored seven distinctions in the public exams, I was invited to a tea party hosted by the chief executive for high-achieving students. When Mr Tung asked about our future plans, I shared my intention to study in the United States because of its four-year degree system, contrasting with Hong Kong’s three-year model at the time. Years before Hong Kong’s 2012 academic reform, the chief executive listening directly to a young newcomer was unforgettable. As a university educator today, I deeply appreciate how his early dedication to education and talent integration laid the foundation for Hong Kong as a global education hub. Dr Simon Wang, lecturer, Hong Kong Baptist University

title: Hong Kong sees alarming rise in suicide rates among young people under 15
description: Experts urge schools to bolster mental health support systems; link spike to social media, academic pressure and digital distress signals.
content:
The suicide rate for individuals under 15 in Hong Kong reached its highest level in ten years in 2025, countering an overall trend of decline. Research from a local university indicates a strong connection between social media usage and incidents among youth.
The Hong Kong Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention at the University of Hong Kong also took advantage of World Suicide Prevention Day on Thursday to urge educational institutions to enhance their support for students, especially in light of a recent increase in suicide attempts at the beginning of the school year.
“As we pursue academic excellence, we should also look after the mental health of young people,” Professor Paul Yip Siu-fai, the centre’s founding director, said.
“It’s been just a while since the school year started, and we have already seen a few student suicides. Here I would like to call on schools to give pupils more time and space to build rapport with their teachers and schoolmates, strengthening their support system.”
Using data provided by the Coroner’s Court, the centre estimated that there were 976 suicide cases, or 13 per 100,000 residents, last year – a slight decline from 2024.
While rates declined across nearly all age groups, the figure rose among under-15s to 2.9 per 100,000, the highest since 2016.
A further breakdown of data for that age group showed the suicide rate for boys was four per 100,000 and 0.4 for girls.
The centre noted that among the boys under 15 who died by suicide last year, most had experienced academic and interpersonal stress. All of the cases occurred at home, and all suicide notes or expressions of suicidal ideation were in digital form, Yip added.
Yip said the rise in the number of young people taking their lives was not unique to Hong Kong, and the priority of prevention work was to identify those at risk more precisely, consistently, and effectively, rather than only concentrating on those with a diagnosis.
There is limited data on suicide rates of the under-15 demographic around the world.
An April study found that the suicide rate for children aged 10 to 14 is generally between 0.2 and 0.8 per 100,000 across most members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
The rates were 0.3 in the United Kingdom, 0.9 in the United States and 1.2 in South Korea.
Yip stressed that while authorities had put in place a three-tier emergency mechanism covering prevention and intervention for students, it was important their academic lives were fulfilling in the first place.
“I do not think students will take their own lives just because they struggled to adapt to school life,” he said. “It’s part of a bigger problem such as awareness of and attitude towards mental health, willingness to seek help and the accessibility of those supports.”
He suggested that at the start of the academic year, schools could hold only morning classes in the first week, spend the afternoon on bonding among students and arrange fun activities and events such as having an ice-cream truck visit the campus.
Yip said the figures would be subject to further adjustment next year due to time lags in Coroner’s Court reports.
The centre used artificial intelligence (AI) to help analyse suicide cases among under-15s between 2022 and 2025, finding that more than 30 per cent of the students were studying at Band 1A schools.
The term refers to top-tier institutions under the three-band, nine-subgroup ranking system.
The analysis found that 24 per cent of cases were enrolled at Band 1B schools, another 12 per cent at Band 1C and the rest at Band 2 and 3 institutions.
Researchers at the centre also collaborated with the Hong Kong Press Council to investigate the relationship between suicides, traditional media and social media.
As part of the collaboration, the centre and council tested how traditional media reports and social media content about suicide related to the number of cases.
The results showed that while traditional media reporting does not directly predict the suicide rates of people aged below 35, social media platform activity was strongly linked to cases.
Social media could act as a conduit, turning traditional media coverage into higher rates of youth suicide and attempted suicide, researchers found.
“Social media and traditional media are not independent of each other, as the information often comes from the latter. If traditional media could do better, they could influence social media activities too,” Yip said.
“When news about suicide pops up, we strongly encourage people not to like, comment on or share it. Just taking a quick pause before reacting can go a long way in stopping the story from spreading so widely.”
The centre also conducted an AI-assisted review of news reports on suicide cases by six local Chinese-language media outlets and found that most of the stories failed to comply with coverage guidelines issued by the World Health Organization.
The ignored guidelines included sharing information on suicide warning signs or risk factors and avoiding detailed descriptions of the incident locations.
If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial or message via WhatsApp 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline.
You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Israel destroys Hezbollah tunnel network in Lebanon, triggering tremor
description: USGS records 4.1 magnitude tremor after a massive blast on the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge.
content: Israel said Thursday it demolished key tunnels built by the Iran-backed Hezbollah group beneath the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge in southern Lebanon, triggering a 4.1 magnitude tremor. Agence France-Presse journalists in the area heard several explosions. In a video shared by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, a huge fireball can be seen rising into the night sky. The explosion comes a few days after Israeli authorities claimed to have taken control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, saying that the pro-Iranian Hezbollah had dug numerous tunnels there, allowing it to attack Israel from this mountainous area. Israeli troops occupy part of southern Lebanon, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he wants to establish a “security zone” to prevent any attacks on the north of his country. “This is strategic terrorist infrastructure that was built over two decades, with Iranian funding and planning,” Netanyahu and Katz said in a joint statement. הבטחנו וקיימנו. המחבלים חוסלו ומנהרות עלי טאהר הושמדו. כל הכבוד לצה"ל 🇮🇱 https://t.co/yd9n4KjqGH — ישראל כ”ץ Israel Katz (@Israel_katz) September 10, 2026 The destruction “completes the achievement of operational control over the Ali al-Taher ridge – above and below ground”, the statement added. The United States Geological Survey reported a 4.1 magnitude tremor in the area, after Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that Israel carried out a “massive explosion” on the Ali al-Taher ridge in the Nabatieh region, “causing tremors and a powerful rumble”. “We were sitting there and everything shook,” Joelle Fares, who recently moved to Majayoun, said. Israel announced last week that it had captured the Ali al-Taher ridge. The Israeli army said the Hezbollah infrastructure extended for more than 2km (1.2 miles) and contained “dozens of Iranian-made rockets, missiles, and UAVs (unmanned aerial vehicles), as well as machine guns, dozens of anti-tank missiles, and hundreds of mines and explosive devices”. The underground compound also included a command centre of Hezbollah’s “Badr” unit, the army added. A military official said that some of the militants that had operated in the area of the ridge had abandoned it, while others were “eliminated by aerial strikes and artillery fire”. The official said Hezbollah members had dug eight underground routes to move safely beneath the ridge, and several dozen explosive drones and hundreds of mines were seized by the Israeli army. In March, Hezbollah dragged Lebanon into the Middle East war in support of its backer Iran. There had been a lull in violence after the understanding reached between Iran and the United States in June, followed by an agreement between Lebanon and Israel. But strikes have increased in intensity in recent days. During negotiations, the United States, which sponsored the talks, proposed that the Lebanese army take control of the Ali al-Taher ridge, but Hezbollah refused, a source close to the parties said. Beirut authorities say Israeli strikes have killed more than 4,300 people in total since March, and Israeli forces continue to occupy a so-called “security zone” in the south.

title: New York Fashion Week 2026: Tory Burch brings vibrant spring collection to Isamu Noguchi’s Sunken Garden
description: Celebrating the joy of getting dressed, the runway showcased rich textures and vivid colours, with Amanda Seyfried and Sandra Ng in attendance.
content: Designer Tory Burch couldn’t have chosen a more mesmerising location for her spring/summer 2027 show: Isamu Noguchi’s Sunken Garden, located deep below a pedestrian plaza smack in the middle of Manhattan’s financial district and surrounded by towering skyscrapers. Made of natural stones imported from Japan interspersed with water fountains, the garden was inspired by Ryōan-ji, the famous imperial garden in Kyoto. Attended by actress Amanda Seyfried, singer Ravyn Lenae, Korean actress Gong Hyo-Jin and Hong Kong actress Sandra Ng, the show was about “the joy of getting dressed”, Burch explained in the notes. With plenty of embellishments, textures and patterns, the show was an ode to opulence. Jewel tones dominated a vivid palette where bright hues were beautifully paired with each other. The colour combinations – clashes, you may call them – were a joy to behold. The knitwear was outstanding: a series of cardigans with flower embroidery paired with pencil skirts stole the show, as did a couple of pleated dresses in pastel hues that will look great on any red carpet this award season. Bags and shoes – both categories at which Tory Burch excels – included a shopper version of the Lee Radziwill handbag and kitten-heel slingbacks in woven leather. Unexpectedly, the last look was a simple black coat that was the definition of a palate – or palette, in this case – cleanser. While it all sounds like a lot, the decorations never overwhelmed the clothes, which were some of the best the American designer has shown in recent years.

title: Yuen Kee Food enters final stage of Hong Kong IPO after HKEX approval, sources say
description: The dumpling chain is likely to list in October following three funding rounds.
content: Yuen Kee Food Group, the owner of well-known restaurant brand Yuen Kee Dumpling, has cleared its listing hearing with the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), aiming to raise between HK$300 million (US$38.3 million) and HK$400 million, according to people familiar with the matter. The conclusion of the hearing marked its initial public offering (IPO) plan entering its final stage, and the company planned to kick off the offering in October, the sources said, who asked not to be named because they did not have permission to speak publicly about the matter. Ahead of its IPO, Yuen Kee completed three funding rounds, bringing in BA Capital – a China-focused consumer sector investment firm which had previously backed Pop Mart and Heytea. Huatai International and GF Securities are serving as joint sponsors. The final amount fundraised would depend ⁠on the company’s valuation and investor demand, and the timing and size of the offering could still change, one source said. As of late May, Yuen Kee operated 4,773 outlets globally, covering more than 250 mainland Chinese cities, primarily through franchised stores. The group officially entered the Hong Kong market in 2018 and has since opened over 40 stores locally. The company is expanding into overseas markets such as Singapore, Britain and Thailand, operating 41 overseas stores. It operates a franchising business model under the Yuen Kee Dumpling brand, known for serving hand-wrapped and freshly cooked dumplings, wontons and related products in both ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook formats, with a standardised supply chain. Similar to beverage giant Mixue, the bulk of its revenue stems from selling food and providing management services to franchisees. This asset-light model enables rapid, low-capital expansion, though top-line growth remains heavily reliant on maintaining a steady pace of new store openings. The company recorded operating revenue of 2.7 billion yuan (US$402.3 million) in 2025, and about 1.3 billion yuan in the first five months of 2026, up 39.8 per cent year on year, according to the filing materials. Adjusted net profit for the first five months this year was 185 million yuan (US$27.6 million), a significant increase from 69 million yuan a year earlier.

title: Israeli film on AI-backed Gaza killings gets 25-minute Venice ovation
description: Oscar-winning directors premiere ‘NAZA’, featuring military whistle-blowers detailing automated target selection.
content: A chilling new documentary about Israel’s AI-powered mass killing of civilians in Gaza from two Oscar-winning Israeli filmmakers received a 25-minute ovation at its premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday. The audience clapped continuously for Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor after the screening, setting what is thought to be a record in Venice after a 23-minute ovation for another film about Gaza last year. In their film NAZA, Abraham and Szor used conversations with 24 different Israeli military or intelligence whistle-blowers who spoke on condition that their identities be protected. “We are letting the soldiers and the officers speak about what they did,” Abraham told Agence France-Presse. “The goal was very simple: we wanted to hear in as much detail as possible, how the systems of killing in Gaza looked like, how they operated.” The 80-minute film left many audience members stunned, with interviewees describing how they felt like they worked in a killing “factory” or a lethal video game. NAZA draws its name from a euphemism used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that are expected to be killed in an air strike. It was described as an “urgent, gut-punch” by film magazine Screen, while The Hollywood Reporter said it inspired “outrage … indignity as well. Most certainly disgust, on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime”. Israel’s bombardment of Gaza has left around 73,500 Palestinians dead and 174,500 wounded since October 2023, according to Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the United Nations deems reliable. The pounding of the territory followed an attack on Israel by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, that resulted in the death of 1,219 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official figures. The men and women featured in NAZA, with their voices and faces digitally altered, detail an AI-powered system known as “Lavender” that was used to identify people for assassination. “It was done on a mass scale, like a factory,” one says, filmed like all of them at night on a roof terrace with an eerily quiet Tel Aviv as the background. “Lavender” uses data from the mass surveillance of Gaza, where the entire telecommunications network is monitored by Israel, to identify targets based on their phone calls, movements and interactions. “The system’s parameters are so complex, it’s hard to understand,” one interviewee, who said he worked on the system, told the filmmakers. Others describe the systematic destruction of civilian homes, the disregard for war and humanitarian laws, and a “general atmosphere” of “hatred” towards Palestinians. “It’s like a video game because everything is done remotely,” one interviewee involved in identifying targets says at one point. Another describes it as “insanely fun”. The result of a nearly three-year investigation, NAZA is the only documentary in competition at this year’s Venice Film Festival, which wraps up on Saturday. Ovations can be easily manipulated and are seen as an imperfect measure of a film, but they do give an indication of the impact on festivalgoers and critics. Along with Palestinian peers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, Abraham and Szor won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank. Their latest movie has been produced by Britain’s Jim Wilson with help from Jonathan Glazer – the team behind Auschwitz-set Oscar winner The Zone of Interest – as well as Britain’s Guardian newspaper. The war in Gaza retains broad Israeli public support, but Abraham and Szor said they hoped it would encourage Western nations to drop their backing for Israel and apply pressure through sanctions. “Those of us inside Israel and Palestine trying to fight for change, need it,” Abraham said. “You are weakening the people inside who are supporting human rights and a political solution by refusing to act.” Israel denies deliberately targeting civilians in Gaza, accusing Hamas of hiding among the population of the densely packed and besieged enclave where around 2 million people lived before the war. Last year, The Voice of Hind Rajab, a docudrama about the killing of a five-year-old Palestinian girl by Israeli forces, picked up second prize at the festival after receiving a 23-minute standing ovation at its premiere. Increasing numbers of top entertainment figures are openly criticising the Israeli government, as part of a shift in public opinion in Western countries against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies. Foreign journalists have been prevented from reporting from Gaza since the start of the conflict, except under tightly controlled conditions with the Israeli military.

title: Tiananmen vigil leaders jailed for up to 7 years, group fined HK$1.5 million
description: Hong Kong High Court judges jail three vigil organisers and fine their disbanded alliance over calls to end one-party rule in China.
content: Three former leaders of the now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil have been sentenced to up to seven years and three months in jail under the national security law for inciting subversion by calling for an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China. Three High Court judges on Friday also ordered the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China to pay a HK$1.5 million (US$191,300) fine in three months, as they brought the high-profile trial at West Kowloon Court to a close. The alliance, former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted last month after the judges found they had incited public hatred towards the Communist Party and advocated the group’s illegal agenda through various public events, including what used to be the only large-scale commemoration on Chinese soil of Beijing’s crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in 1989. Lee, 69, and Chow, 41, were sentenced to seven years and seven years and three months behind bars, respectively. Former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty ahead of the trial. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the rule of law could only be upheld by imposing severe penalties on the accused. “The law never allows anyone to blatantly harm their country and compatriots under the guise of promoting human rights, democracy and freedom,” he said. Central government authorities in Hong Kong hailed the tough sentences as a manifestation of the city’s rule of law, while warning “external forces” against smearing the court’s decisions. A spokesman for the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said the alliance and the defendants “had long incited public hostility, hatred and disaffection towards the state regime”, adding that their offences had seriously challenged the constitutional order of Hong Kong and gravely violated the city’s national security law. “They must be severely punished in accordance with the law,” the spokesman said. The foreign ministry’s arm in Hong Kong said the alliance had undermined the central government’s authority “at both ideological and practical levels”. Beijing’s liaison office said the defendants deserved severe penalties for attacking the party’s leadership, while the country’s Office for Safeguarding National Security in Hong Kong described the ruling as “widely supported” by society. Ho is expected to complete his sentence in April 2028, assuming he is not granted a one-third reduction by prison authorities on the basis of good conduct during his incarceration. Lee Cheuk-yan may be released in September or October 2029, whereas Chow may have to serve her sentence until early 2030. The pair intend to lodge an appeal. Lee’s wife, Elizabeth Tang Yin-ngor, said the sentences did not only punish the alliance and its former leaders, but also those who subscribed to the group’s beliefs or previously attended its annual vigil at Victoria Park in Causeway Bay. “I think free speech is already a thing of the past,” she said. “They were given such heavy sentences even though they had never resorted to any unlawful means.” Chow’s mother, Medina Chow Lau Wah-chun, said her daughter had only intended to “speak the truth”. The elder Chow added that she was not free to speak her mind because of a police investigation against her. Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Jong-herng and Anna Lai Yuen-kee said the case was serious and warranted five to 10 years’ imprisonment under a two-tier sentencing regime of the national security law. They noted the offence lasted for 14 months after the law took effect on June 30, 2020, during which the defendants persisted with their offensive conduct on social media and during public events at a time when Hong Kong remained “turbulent and unsettled”. “Despite the defendants’ belief that their agenda of ‘ending one-party dictatorship’ might be in breach of the [Chinese] constitution and the national security law, they recalcitrantly pursued their course of conduct and strenuously promoted their agenda. This was a premeditated act,” the judges said in a 19-page written ruling. The European Union said about the sentencing: “This ruling undermines confidence in the rule of law and harms Hong Kong’s reputation.” The United Nations Human Rights Office said the jailing of the trio highlighted the ever-increasing restrictions on civic space in Hong Kong, including harsh measures taken against civil society actors, since the National Security Law was passed in 2020. The office’s High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk called for these sentences to be quashed. Meanwhile, the court adjourned handling the prosecution’s request to confiscate the “Pillar of Shame” sculpture, created by Danish artist Jens Galschiot, pending further arguments. Galschiot has repeatedly demanded that the eight-metre-tall (26-foot) artwork be returned to him since it was seized by police’s National Security Department in 2023. Steve Li Kwai-wah, the department’s chief superintendent, argued the sculpture belonged to the alliance and was used to incite others to undermine the party. “I think the rationale is very simple. You created something and gave it to someone else. Can you ask to take it back any time you want?” Li said. Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung said that any item relevant to the commission of an offence should be confiscated. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Galschiot said he intended to request his government to take diplomatic action so that the sculpture could be returned to “its rightful owner”. Former trade union leader Carol Ng Man-yee, who was released from prison last year after serving 45 months for a subversion offence, and former alliance standing committee member Tang Ngok-kwan were among those who attended the brief hearing on Friday. Ng said she felt relieved the three defendants finally got to know when they might be released, but said she was still saddened by the outcome. Tang Ngok-kwan urged the public to continue to honour those who died in the 1989 crackdown in a “reasonable and lawful” manner. The alliance organised annual candlelight vigils in Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to commemorate the event and called for democratic reforms across the border and the end of one-party rule. Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.

title: Can John Lee untie the 4 knots choking the tech loop in Northern Metropolis?
description: What measures will the chief executive take to facilitate the flow of personnel, capital, data and materials into the hi-tech cooperation zone?
content: In the second of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Elizabeth Cheung and Vivian Au drill down on what’s holding back the Northern Metropolis. Read part one here. For employees of surgical robotics company Yuanhua Tech, travelling between their Shenzhen base in Nanshan district and its Hong Kong office in the Science Park means a two-hour commute. And when the hi-tech firm sends money to Hong Kong for operations, the process can take up to two months. “The procedures required for transferring funding from our Shenzhen headquarters to Hong Kong headquarters are very complicated … sometimes when we are urgently in need of money, there could be delays,” said Max Meng Qinghu, the company’s chief scientist. But the Hong Kong office will move into the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park at the border with mainland China, part of the wider Hetao cooperation zone at the Lok Ma Chau Loop, by the end of this year. By then, those challenges could be addressed. All eyes will be on the measures city leader John Lee Ka-chiu announces in the city’s first five-year plan and his policy blueprint next Wednesday to facilitate the flow of personnel, capital, data and materials, such as biosamples, across the border within the zone. Experts stress that the timely movement of the four elements is critical to the park’s success. Major streamlining in these areas could resolve current bottlenecks in research, recruitment and operations, unleashing the full potential of hi-tech companies and boosting the zone’s overall appeal. With the barriers removed, Meng expected travel time between the company’s offices in the Hetao area and Shenzhen to be cut by half. “This could raise efficiency … and would be very favourable to staff who need to commute daily,” he said. Currently, the company relies more on mainland talent, as it requires workers with engineering backgrounds, hospital experience and a deep understanding of robotics. But Meng said the benefits went far beyond convenience for staff. The company, founded by his wife Lily Meng Li Aili in 2018, planned to set up a manufacturing base in Hong Kong, while the supply chain for parts used to produce surgical robots would remain in Shenzhen. “With a base in Hetao, closer to Shenzhen, we have faster access to the supply chain, with higher efficiency,” he said. While Shenzhen offers cheaper components and greater efficiency in research and development, the company hopes that a manufacturing presence in Hong Kong will make it easier for its products to enter international markets. The national 15th five-year plan, released in March this year, called for accelerated development of emerging strategic industries and new drivers of economic growth. It covers artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technology, biotechnology, robotics, aviation and aerospace, and new energy, while stressing the need for translational applications. The six pillar industries selected for the Hong Kong park in the cooperation zone – life and health technology, AI and data science, new energy, new materials, microelectronics and robotics – dovetail with the national plan’s goals. The park is also slated to become the first test bed for the seamless cross-border flow of the four elements. Beijing’s top official on Hong Kong affairs, Xia Baolong, visited the park in June, underlining the central government’s determination to make it a success. As home to the new innovation park, the Northern Metropolis aims to diversify Hong Kong’s economy through technology. Beyond driving the next stage of development, the megaproject will create skilled jobs and learning opportunities for youth while improving quality of life with larger homes. Last week, the park attracted six bids from five conglomerates and technology firms specialising in cutting-edge technologies in its first land tender. Sources said the bids involved AI, quantum technology and semiconductors. The number inevitably drew comparisons with the two bids received in July for the Hung Shui Kiu logistics hub, another zone within the Northern Metropolis megadevelopment. The better-than-expected response is seen as a key milestone and a bellwether for the megaproject, which aims to diversify the city’s economy by establishing a major innovation and technology (I&T) industry. The megadevelopment is expected to accommodate 2.5 million people with more than 900,000 flats and provide about 634,000 jobs. Professor Tim Cheng Kwang-ting, vice-president for research and development at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), said Hetao’s competitive edge would rest on seamless cross-border integration of the four key elements under the “one country, two systems” governing framework. He added that while Hong Kong provided an international environment, common law protection and global financial connectivity, Shenzhen offered an unrivalled supply chain, rapid prototyping capabilities and massive industrial scale. “If Hetao can establish the policy framework to unlock the free flow of talent, capital, data and technology, it offers a unique, irreplaceable advantage that no other innovation hub in the world can replicate,” he said. He noted that establishing the right policy framework to blend international talent, facilitate the free flow of capital into the region and enable seamless cross-border data transfers would be the most critical catalysts for the park’s near-term success. Players in the biomedical sector, one of the strategic areas to be developed in Hetao, also envisaged how research in Hong Kong could prosper if the four flows were approved. Professor Ian Wong Chi-kei, of the University of Hong Kong’s department of pharmacology and pharmacy, expected research into rare diseases and genomics, as well as clinical trials, to benefit if biosamples and data from the mainland were made accessible to the city. He said given the mainland’s vast population, its pool of patients with rare diseases would be larger than Hong Kong’s, providing valuable research data. For example, Hong Kong researchers could collect blood samples from mainland patients taking part in clinical trials and examine how an experimental drug affected cells in their blood, he said. “This is the first step to enhance our power to conduct this research … as well as clinical trials,” he said. “Hong Kong will benefit more than the mainland.” Lawmaker Johnny Ng Kit-chong, chairman of the innovation and technology panel in the Legislative Council, said the free flow of data could also benefit AI development. “The three main components for AI are computing power, algorithm and data. Without data, it’s useless to have just computing power,” he said. “If mainland data can be used in the Hong Kong park of Hetao, training of large language models could be possible … this will add to Hong Kong’s uniqueness.” He added that the city also lacked middle-tier engineers, including those involved in software and AI development. The free flow of talent would allow companies in Hetao to recruit experts from Shenzhen. Another bottleneck, according to lawmaker Duncan Chiu, is that some components required for robotics could take several months to clear Hong Kong procedures before they could be transported from the mainland to the city. The lengthy process involved the registration and safety inspection of parts required by Hong Kong authorities, such as the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department, he said. Chiu, who represents the technology and innovation sector, said a “green channel” could provide streamlined arrangements for transporting such materials across the border. But he stressed that a mechanism was also needed to guard against illegal activities. “You have to be careful that some people would make use of the ‘green channel’ to smuggle materials. So there should be a mechanism to prevent illegal activities,” he said, adding that authorities could consider monitoring the frequency and quantity of cross-border materials. The lacklustre interest among local developers in the megadevelopment more broadly is also a growing concern, as insufficient capital investment could hold back I&T development. Colliers head of research and retail Kathy Lee, who is also a planner, said the Northern Metropolis must not rely on a one-size-fits-all model. “Instead, execution strategies must remain flexible, tailoring specific demands of developers for different land parcels,” she said. Lee noted that the coming large-scale land parcels in the megaproject would require participation by a wide range of consortiums, given their sheer scale and complex infrastructure needs. Asked whether the reluctance of local developers to participate could slow the megaproject, Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said the government and developers should both take the plunge, even as they continued to explore the most suitable development models. Two years ago, at a meeting with Xia, 85 business heavyweights pledged to participate in the mega development after he called on them to take part in wider reforms and help the city navigate global changes. “It is inevitable that the government and the private sector must take on some development risks and share the venture [to take the project forward],” Lau said.

title: On This Day | 25 years ago, America faces ‘darkest hour’ as 9/11 terror attacks unfold – SCMP archive
description: Two hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Centre on September 11, 2001, leaving thousands dead and a nation in shock.
content: This article was first published on September 12, 2001. America’s nightmare by Greg Torode in Washington President George W. Bush this morning (September 12, 2001) told the United States that thousands had lost their lives after two hijacked airliners destroyed New York’s World Trade Centre and another smashed into the Pentagon in the most brutal terrorist attacks in the nation’s history. Mr Bush, in a televised address to the nation, condemned the “despicable” attacks, saying: “These acts shattered steel but they cannot dampen the steel of American resolve”. But as his top security team put the nation on a war footing from secure crisis bunkers, officials denied the US was responsible for what initially appeared to be missile strikes on Kabul, the capital of Afghanistan, early this morning. The first hijacked plane struck the World Trade Centre early yesterday (September 11, 2001) and then millions around the world watched in horror as a second struck it just 18 minutes later. Within 30 minutes another airliner had smashed into a wall of the Pentagon, America’s defence headquarters. A fourth airliner went down near Pittsburgh, raising fears that it was being flown towards Camp David, the presidential retreat outside the capital. Officials declared states of emergency in both New York and Washington. They warned it could be days before the full death toll was known. Pressure to retaliate intensified as Mr Bush flew into Washington, his helicopter flanked by three fighter jets. Vice-President Dick Cheney and National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice worked from the situation room deep beneath the White House as America’s military and most sensitive agencies were placed on full alert. Lawrence Eagleburger, secretary of state under former president George Bush Snr, demanded immediate strikes against nations that sponsored terrorism, saying the President must declare “war on terrorism”. “We need to be prepared to act as if we are at war,” he said. Senator John Warner, fresh from security briefings, said yesterday’s attack represented America’s “darkest hour”. He urged Americans to treat terrorism as a “common enemy” for all. Officials said radical Muslim terrorist Osama bin Laden remained the main suspect. Senator Orrin Hatch claimed intelligence agents had already detected his followers boasting that they had hit “two targets”. Bin Laden is thought to be in hiding in Afghanistan but Pentagon officials insisted reports of missiles hitting Kabul were probably linked to the civil war. Both the World Trade Centre’s 110-storey towers - the workplace for about 40,000 people - collapsed in a cloud of fire and rubble that engulfed downtown Manhattan two hours after they were struck by the two airliners shortly before 9am yesterday, New York time. Workers were seen leaping from windows before the collapse. New York’s hospitals were jammed with hundreds of burns victims and the city’s firefighting union said it feared 200 firefighters had been killed. America’s two largest airlines - United and American - each confirmed they had lost two aircraft to hijackers. A total of 266 people were on the planes. All other commercial flights across the US had been grounded. International flights were being diverted to Canada. In his initial response, President Bush vowed retaliation but urged calm. “Make no mistake, the United States will hunt down and punish those responsible for these cowardly acts - freedom will be defended. Our military at home and around the world is on high-alert status and we have taken the necessary security precautions to continue the functioning of your Government”. All sensitive military and government installations in America and overseas were on full alert, from the Los Alamos nuclear laboratory in New Mexico to the giant National Security Agency outside Washington. Extra security forces were deployed. The White House, the Pentagon, the Supreme Court and Capitol Hill were all evacuated, except emergency bunkers, including the White House’s underground situation room. The Federal Reserve vowed to pump more money into the banking system to keep America’s financial system working. The New York Stock Exchange was shut for two days amid fears the strikes could push the global economy into recession. The Red Cross was calling for emergency blood donations while National Guard volunteers were being summoned in Washington and New York. Large areas of both cities were shut down and roads leading away from them were jammed with traffic. Even before investigations could begin, government sources linked the attack to bin Laden. Some sources suggested America’s vast intelligence community may have had some idea that an attack was being planned. Some leaders urged calm, insisting that Americans must not panic. Others described the situation as “war”. Joseph Biden, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, urged Americans to show calm so that their system remained “strong, secure and united”. Senator Chuck Hagel, a Nebraska Republican, declared the attacks “our generation’s Pearl Harbour”. Sandy Berger, national security adviser to ex-president Bill Clinton, warned America would respond to what appeared to be a creative and orchestrated attack. “Their footprint is large enough - we are going to find someone who is responsible”. New York Governor George Pataki said: “This is an attack upon the whole concept of our way of life”. Chris Yates, an aviation expert at Jane’s Transport in London, said: “This is perhaps the most audacious terrorist attack that’s ever taken place in the world. It takes a logistics operation from the terror group involved that is second to none. Only a very small handful of terror groups is on that list. I would name at the top of the list Osama bin Laden”. Barbara Olson, a commentator for CNN, was on board an American Airlines 767 that was hijacked from Dulles airport in Washington and telephoned her husband to say all the passengers and crew had been herded to the back of the plane. She said the hijackers were armed only with paper cutters and knives. The plane crashed into the Pentagon, killing all on board.
