Governments around the world tightened security at US embassies and public buildings, and planes bound for the US were recalled. Hong Kong police stepped up security outside the US Consulate-General. Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa expressed his condolences to the families of the victims to US Consul-General Michael Klosson. President Jiang Zemin was among many world leaders who expressed horror at the attacks and extended sympathy to “Mr Bush, the US Government and people for the disastrous attacks against the US”. However, some Palestinians in the West Bank celebrated the news, and Iraqi television played a patriotic song that began “Down with America”. Terrorist bombers struck the World Trade Centre in February 1993, killing six people and injuring more than 1,000 others.

title: ‘Cross-party voting’: how Chinese-American voters are bucking the trends
description: New data challenges common perception that the United States’ Asian communities form a reliable voting bloc for Democrats.
content: A survey of potential Chinese-American voters suggests a significant gender gap in party affiliation as well as a high level of willingness to vote across party lines, according to results released on Thursday. The data – from the Committee of 100 (C100), a civic group of prominent Chinese-Americans, and a University of Chicago polling firm – challenges the common perception that these citizens form a reliable voting bloc for the Democratic Party. Recently naturalised immigrants were more likely to vote Republican than the average among long-term US residents, the survey report added. “The findings should make both parties want to engage with Chinese-Americans, a fast-growing community that could make the difference between victory and defeat in close races,” Paul Cheung, the C100 president, said. The survey results, released on Thursday, were part of continuing research by C100 to spotlight the Asian community and highlight the stereotypes and challenges it faces. According to the report, 54 per cent of Chinese-Americans identify as Democrats compared with 28 per cent as Republicans. Drilling down, however, 38 per cent of Chinese-American men consider themselves Republicans, compared with 18 per cent of women. “Partisanship among Chinese-Americans does not appear to constrain vote choice as much as among other groups, and we see cross-party voting down the ballot as well,” said Nathan Chan, an assistant professor at Loyola Marymount University and a lead author on the study. On other fronts, 11 per cent of Chinese-American Republicans voted for Democrat candidate Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, crossing party lines at a higher rate than any other racial or ethnic group. The study found even higher rates of Republicans voting for Democrats in state and local races, compared with around three per cent of Chinese-American Democrats saying they voted for Republicans. The results also found that the length of time respondents had lived in the United States had a significant impact on party identification. Some 71 per cent of Chinese-Americans born in the US identified as Democrats. That was nearly twice as high as the 38 per cent of recent Chinese-American immigrants since 2010, while more than a third of those who immigrated to the US in the past 15 years identified as Republican. C100’s results roughly dovetail with other surveys on the fast-growing Chinese-American community. A survey last month by civic group Asian and Pacific Islander American Vote found that 90 per cent of Asian-American and Pacific Islander registered voters expected to vote in the 2026 November midterm elections, up from 84 per cent in 2022 and 86 per cent in 2018. A total of 71 per cent say they are absolutely certain they will vote. The dominant issues most cited in their selection were the cost of living and inflation. On those issues, 44 per cent said they trusted Democrats to do a better job compared with 18 per cent who voiced trust for Republicans.

title: Japan’s Sapporo Snow Festival rebrands as snowfall dwindles
description: Warming winters and military labour shortages are forcing the world-famous Hokkaido event to pivot towards sustainability.
content: Japan’s hugely popular Sapporo Snow Festival is shifting its focus towards protecting the environment and sustainability, with a climate expert warning that global warming and reduced snowfall across Hokkaido will make it increasingly difficult to stage the event. In August, organisers unveiled a new logo, official mascot and revised concept for the 77th snow festival, an eight-day event running from February 4 next year. The updated branding expresses appreciation for the annual snowfall the northern Japanese city receives. The new concept – “A festival of gratitude for snow: blessed by the snow” – accompanies the debut of Saporon, a yeti-like mascot with hair twisted into an “S”. “This rebranding project embodies our desire to shift the perspective that ‘snow is a nuisance’ and evolve the event into a festival where everyone can once again share in the value of snow and express our gratitude,” organisers said in a statement. “We aim to deepen our collaboration with citizens, visitors and businesses who share our vision, and to create diverse connections, thereby evolving into a sustainable event that will continue into the future.” The festival has faced mounting challenges in recent years, including rising temperatures and shortages of snow. Since 1955, the local Ground Self-Defence Force (SDF) garrison has transported snow from outside the city to construct two of the largest sculptures at the Odori Park venue. But their trucks now have to travel much further to collect snow. In addition, strains on the military – including personnel shortages – mean the SDF will build only one statue from next year. Other recent challenges include rising prices and labour costs across the three primary festival sites. While the local economy benefits enormously from the influx of domestic and international visitors, murmurings about overtourism are growing. “I used to go quite a lot, but there are a lot of tourists there now and the whole city centre gets very busy,” said Yoko Tsukamoto, a Sapporo resident and academic. “I also agree that it is too much to ask the SDF to do so much every year,” she said. “They have to bring in snow from a long way away ahead of the festival and then compact it before it can be carved. On top of their regular duties, that is too much of a burden. I’m happy they will only be making one statue next year.” Signs of the changing conditions have been apparent for years. During the 2012 festival, a three-metre (9.8-foot) ice statue in Odori Park collapsed onto a tourist, breaking her pelvis. City officials blamed the accident on the base of the statue melting. In the 15 years Tsukamoto has lived in Sapporo, she has noticed some big differences in the region’s weather. “The snow is definitely starting later than in the past and ending earlier,” she said. “Last year we seemed to get a lot of snow, but it came in a shorter period and, because it was generally warmer, turned to slush more quickly.” Tsukamoto pointed out that the city gathered snow from streets every winter and trucked it to a single collection site. Historically, that snow had lasted until mid-June, but she said it melted away by mid-May this year. Data from the Japan Meteorological Agency shows Sapporo’s average February temperature was minus 1 degree Celsius (30.2 degrees Fahrenheit), with average lows around minus 11 degrees. In February 2000, the monthly average was minus 3.8 degrees, with temperature drops dipping close to minus 15 degrees. “It was not that long ago that we would get minus 10 degrees regularly through the winter, but we rarely get that any more,” Tsukamoto said. Takahiro Oyama, a researcher at the National Institute for Environmental Studies’ Centre for Climate Change Adaptation, said the Japanese archipelago was undergoing major shifts in weather patterns. And while he said parts of northern Japan had experienced “disaster-level” snowfall in early 2026, it was unlikely to become the norm in Hokkaido. “Generally, snowfall is decreasing year on year,” Oyama said, adding that in a large city like Sapporo, the “heat island effect” also led to elevated temperatures. “I can imagine a time when Sapporo cannot have a snow festival because it has become too warm,” he said. “Already they are having to import snow from areas around Sapporo for the statues.” Traditional festivals across Japan are facing similar pressures, with several summer events postponed to cope with extreme heat, while Kyoto’s month-long Gion festival – with its massive wooden float processions and evening street parties – has had to contend with increasingly unpredictable seasonal weather patterns.

title: Japanese natto gains global fame as a health-conscious superfood trend
description: Diners embrace the fermented soybeans despite their polarising taste and aroma.
content:
Natto, the Japanese fermented soybean superfood that people either love or hate, is becoming popular worldwide one slimy mouthful at a time.
The latest trade statistics indicate that Japan’s exports of the highly nutritious gooey beans tripled from 2017, reaching 5,248 tons in 2025, with China and the United States as the top destinations.
The dish, rich in beneficial bacteria, is a traditional Japanese breakfast staple, but its strong aroma, thick texture and yeasty flavour can be divisive, even in Japan.
In recent years, natto has become one of several fermented foods, including kimchi and kombucha, that have gained popularity worldwide. This trend, especially prominent in the US, is driven by a growing interest in better digestive health following the Covid-19 pandemic (see graphic).
In China, too, the “trend towards health-consciousness, especially among the middle and upper-income classes,” is igniting interest in Japanese foods, the Japan External Trade Organisation said in a recent report.
In the US city of Los Angeles, at Japanese restaurant Suehiro, owner Kenji Suzuki has noticed more non-Japanese clients taking the plunge.
“When social media started talking about natto and that it’s a superfood, I think then more people wanted to see what it is, wanted to taste it – ‘Is it as bad as people say it is?’” Suzuki said.
“Some people maybe don’t like it, but other people, you know, they love it,” said the second-generation owner.
Aside from its supposed health benefits, natto – dubbed the “star student of pricing” – has long been loved in Japan for its stunning affordability.
A pack of three natto cups, each weighing 40 to 50 grams, usually sells for around 100 yen (approximately HK$5) or even less at supermarkets. Each pack typically includes small plastic sachets of mustard and soy sauce.
“Very few foods can be called as truly healthy a superfood as natto is,” said Yoshihiro Noro, former head of the Japan Natto Cooperative Society Federation. The 72-year-old is also the owner of his family-run business, Kamakurayama Natto.
“I hope an era will come when people will collectively see high-quality, high-end natto as worth shelling out their money on.”
And that is exactly what his company’s Kamakurayama Natto, touted as “extremely stringy” but minus “stinkiness and bitterness”, seeks to achieve.
At his factory west of Tokyo, workers wash, steam and generously spray the soybeans with bacteria, which then undergo 18 hours of fermentation.
Kamakurayama Natto is around three times the average price, but it has recently secured international orders from places like Hong Kong, Shanghai, Singapore and even Norway.
“I’ve heard that in some countries, people have been told natto is good for their health, so they force themselves to eat it even though they strongly dislike the taste,” Noro said.
“But keep eating it, and you will definitely get hooked.”
First, soybeans are sorted and washed. Next, they are soaked in water to double their weight. This can take between seven and 18 hours, depending on the season. The process takes longer during the winter.
The soaked beans are steamed in a pressure cooker to kill bacteria and soften them.
Pure natto yeasts are sprayed onto the hot beans, which are then packed loosely into containers to allow air to pass through.
The beans ferment in a room at a temperature between 38 and 42 degrees Celsius for about 16 to 24 hours.
Afterwards, they are cooled and then placed in a refrigerator at 5 degrees Celsius to mature before being prepared for shipment.

title: New York Fashion Week 2026: Tommy Hilfiger brings preppy SS27 collection to The Plaza Hotel
description: The legendary American designer reflects on living at The Plaza Hotel, shooting with Travis Kelce and Jisoo, and bringing ‘youthquake’ energy to NYFW.
content: Tommy Hilfiger’s spring/summer 2027 show took place at The Plaza Hotel, where the designer and his wife Dee lived for more than a decade. The historic New York property, overlooking Central Park, was also the backdrop for the brand’s fall/winter 2026 campaign, starring ambassadors such as Gigi Hadid, who opened the show, Travis Kelce, Jisoo and Peggy Gou, all clad in the brand’s “prep made current” separates. The designer is not new to New York City’s landmarks – he once showed a collection at Grand Central Terminal’s Oyster Bar – but The Plaza obviously has a special place in his heart, as he explained in an interview before the show. What he recalls most fondly about his decade spent living there is the proximity to Central Park. “It was like living in the country,” he said. The spring/summer collection, however, wasn’t a direct homage to the hallowed grounds of The Plaza. Youthquake and the energy of New York City were the running threads in a fun showcase of the preppy separates that have always been the bread and butter of Tommy Hilfiger, from navy blazers to rugby shirts and pleated skirts. Jisoo, along with the likes of Girls’ Generation, Kate Moss and Lucien Laviscount, attended the show, which ended with a performance by American singer-songwriter Slayyyter. Here are highlights from our pre-show conversation with the legendary designer. How did the decision to show at The Plaza come about? I lived here for over a decade, and I wanted to bring people home to my home. And I thought that it would be an incredible contrast to what we’re showing, and so many people have come through these revolving doors, over the years, all different personalities, all different people, different styles of clothes, families, celebrities, people from Hollywood, and I thought, what a great place to show. Is there a memory you cherish from the 10 years you lived here? Yeah, Central Park. It was, like living in the country, because you would look out and just see the green, nature. At the same time, it is an iconic epicentre of the world. Was the actual collection inspired by the actual place? Mainly by New York, and the youthquake in New York. It is full of energy, full of creative people, full of, literally, anything and everything you want. From Broadway theatre to sports events, to concerts, to Chinatown, Little Italy. There’s just so much in the city that is so inspiring. And if you’re a curious person or if you like to experience something different, you come to New York. You also shot a campaign starring many of your ambassadors like Travis Kelce and Jisoo here at The Plaza. It’s about Travis checking into the hotel and bumping into a number of different people, from Jisoo to Peggy Gou, Carmelo Anthony, Gigi Hadid, Frances Tiafoe, the tennis player, and it’s really the heart of New York. He arrives in New York, is walking through the halls of the hotel, and says hello to everyone, meets them in the elevator, and all that energy and the excitement.

title: Enflame shares soar 179% in Shanghai debut as Nvidia challenger taps investor fever for AI
description: Tencent-backed company valued at US$25 billion, highlighting its role in Beijing’s push for domestic chips amid US export restrictions.
content: Enflame Technology, one of the major challengers to Nvidia in China, saw its share price surge 179 per cent in its Shanghai trading debut on Friday, giving the Tencent Holdings-backed artificial intelligence chipmaker a market capitalisation of 170.9 billion yuan (US$25.5 billion). The Shanghai-based company opened at 410 yuan, up from its issue price of 142.18 yuan. It surged as much as 234 per cent to 475 yuan during the day, before closing at 397 yuan. The performance reflects continued investor appetite for domestic AI chip champions, with Enflame being the last of China’s “four little dragons” in the sector to go public. Enflame’s gains stood out against the broader market on Friday. The Star 50 Index fell 1 per cent, while the benchmark CSI 300 Index dropped 0.8 per cent. Enflame raised about 6.12 billion yuan by selling 43.04 million shares. The offering valued the firm at about 61 billion yuan before trading began, making it one of the largest tech listings in mainland China this year. The retail portion of its initial public offering (IPO) was oversubscribed by 4,073 times, with about 7 million online investors submitting orders for 42.1 billion shares. The allocation rate for individual investors was just 0.025 per cent, one of the lowest on the mainland market this year. The strong market response highlights Enflame’s role – alongside peers Moore Threads, Biren Technology and MetaX Integrated Circuits – in Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency as the US restricts exports of advanced chips from global leaders such as Nvidia. Early stakeholders saw their paper wealth soar following the blockbuster debut. The stake of Tencent, Enflame’s largest institutional backer, rose 20 per cent to nearly 35 billion yuan. Other prominent investors include memory chipmaker GigaDevice, smartphone and electric vehicle maker Xiaomi, chip packaging firm Tongfu Microelectronics, and telecommunications giant ZTE. Enflame’s first-day performance trailed its peers MetaX and Moore Threads, which were among the first domestic AI firms to list in a wave that started last year. Driven by the global AI frenzy, the two companies saw first-day pops of 693 per cent and 425 per cent, respectively, in their debuts on the tech-focused Star Market in December. Founded in 2018, Enflame has rapidly scaled its business on surging domestic demand for AI computing power. Unlike Nvidia and its three domestic peers – which focus on general-purpose graphics processing units (GPUs) capable of handling a wide range of workflows – Enflame has staked its future on domain-specific architecture (DSA), which the company said is an advanced evolution of application-specific integrated circuits. The company expected revenue to reach between 2.3 billion and 3 billion yuan in the first nine months of 2026, a year-on-year jump of up to 455 per cent, according to its prospectus. However, Enflame remains unprofitable as it continues to pour capital into research and development. Chairman Zhao Lidong said the company was on track to turn a profit as early as this year. “Considering our orders on hand, product delivery schedules, staff cost budgets and R&D planning, we expect to achieve consolidated profitability in 2026 or 2027,” Zhao said during the company’s IPO roadshow earlier this month.

title: Foreign carmakers offer steep discounts on petrol-powered cars in cutthroat Chinese market
description: With more consumers switching to electric vehicles, companies including VW and Toyota are slashing prices on lower-tech offerings.
content: Foreign carmakers have been slashing the prices of petrol-powered cars they make in China by more than 20 per cent to survive in a cutthroat market amid weakening consumer demand. Last month, big international marques including Volkswagen and Toyota offered average discounts of 23.4 per cent on cars powered by internal combustion engines, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). That compared with an average discount of 23.7 per cent in July. “Because their new cars were priced at a particularly low level, the strong promotional efforts have persisted over the past months, which resulted in a small sales increase,” the association said in a report released this week. It said that, in comparison, the average discount in 2023 was about 13 per cent. The accelerating electrification seen on mainland China’s roads over the past decade has eaten into international car brands’ market share in the world’s largest automotive market due to their slow transition to electric vehicles (EVs), according to analysts. They said the global energy shock arising from the Iran war had exacerbated the foreign carmakers’ bleak sales outlook as more budget-conscious consumers opted for battery-powered vehicles to save fuel costs. Last month, EVs’ share of vehicle sales on the mainland hit an all-time high of 65.2 per cent, according to CPCA data. However, overall car sales slumped 23.6 per cent year on year. Increasing EV penetration will pressure foreign brands to further lower their petrol vehicle prices Steve Shi, Juchen Auto Trade It said foreign brands commanded a 34.4 per cent share of the mainland auto market in the first seven months of this year, 5.4 percentage points less than in the same period last year. Most international marques operating in China focus on petrol-powered vehicles. “Increasing EV penetration will pressure foreign brands to further lower their petrol vehicle prices to lure customers,” said Steve Shi, a manager at Juchen Auto Trade, a China-based car service firm. “Overall weak consumer demand and consumers’ increasing interest in EVs will cause some of the international petrol brands to exit the market in the near future.” At the end of June, global consultancy AlixPartners forecast that weak sales could fuel a deeper price war in China’s auto market during the second half of this year. Among the nearly 30 Chinese ­carmakers that solely produce EVs, only BYD, the world’s largest EV builder, Stellantis-backed Leapmotor and premium EV assembler Nio were profitable in the first half of the year. Foreign brands dominated the Chinese automotive market in the first two decades of this century, with their market standing at 63 per cent in 2015, CPCA data showed.

title: Opinion | Why China is steering clear of the US’ ‘exorbitant privilege’ model
description: Beijing is decoupling the internationalisation of the yuan as a transactional currency from the role of an unconstrained global reserve store of value.
content: The Chinese export juggernaut shows no signs of slowing, rising by a quarter year-on-year in August and putting the nation well on track for another record annual trade surplus after becoming the first in history to surpass the US$1 trillion mark last year. While much of the world remains preoccupied with debating China’s so-called overcapacity, an equally consequential phenomenon is frequently overlooked: the profound impact of Beijing’s trade strategy on the internationalisation of the yuan and the broader global financial system. China is now the world’s top trading nation, accounting for roughly 15 per cent of global exports – a milestone last reached by the United States during the mid-20th century. Historically, such trade dominance often led to a financial paradigm shift. As American industrial power crested in the early-to-mid 1900s, New York eventually supplanted London as the world’s financial capital, and the US dollar superseded the British pound as the primary global reserve asset after World War II. Yet China is carving out a fundamentally different path. Both the British pound in its prime and the US dollar today have functioned simultaneously as the default medium of exchange for global trade and the ultimate store of value as reserve currencies. Beijing, by contrast, is aggressively encouraging its trading partners to adopt the yuan for cross-border settlements while maintaining its stringent capital controls. We are consequently witnessing a deliberate decoupling: the internationalisation of the yuan as a transactional currency but explicitly not as an unconstrained global reserve store of value. This strategy bypasses the classic structural trap that redefined Anglo-American finance. Under the traditional dollar framework, supplying the world with liquidity requires open capital accounts and deep financial markets that attract global capital inflows – a dynamic that pushes up the currency’s real exchange rate and routinely leads to current account deficits. While proponents label the ability to borrow cheaply in one’s own currency an “exorbitant privilege”, it can systematically hollow out a nation’s manufacturing base over time. Chinese leaders are firm believers in the hard power of industrial capacity. They have no intention of following that script. Beijing’s policy of separating the yuan’s medium-of-exchange role from its store-of-value function also stems directly from a core policy principle: financial stability and absolute state control over capital. Standard economic doctrine dictates that creating a global reserve currency requires opening capital accounts, floating exchange rates, and granting foreign institutions unfettered access to domestic financial markets. The Chinese leadership views that model as an unacceptable risk to its financial governance. The uniqueness of Beijing’s approach becomes clear when contrasted with history. When West Germany and Japan ran massive trade surpluses in the 1970s and 1980s, their central banks actively suppressed the global adoption of the deutsche mark and the yen out of fear that currency appreciation would destroy their export competitiveness – though market forces eventually pushed both into global reserves anyway. China, conversely, is intentionally driving global yuan settlement, not to replace the dollar as a universal store of value, but to reduce its dependence on Western financial rails, insulate itself from potential sanctions – such as disconnection from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) global messaging system – and deepen trade ties across the Global South. In short, Beijing wants global adoption of the yuan, but strictly on its own terms. Instead of relying on trade deficits to export liquidity, Beijing uses its capital account controls to engineer a state-directed monetary loop, particularly through Belt and Road Initiative partner nations. Under this framework, China injects yuan abroad through denominated loans, outbound direct investment and bilateral central bank currency swap lines. By financing infrastructure, manufacturing and supply chain hubs across Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa, China supplies its currency directly to recipient nations, who then spend it on Chinese capital goods, engineering contractors or debt service. Hong Kong plays a vital role in this machinery: through regulated corridors like the Southbound Stock Connect and Bond Connect schemes, Chinese institutional investors channel capital outward, supplying offshore markets with yuan liquidity without compromising mainland capital controls. Hong Kong can help partially mitigate the yuan’s weak store-of-value function by expanding offshore yuan investment options, but this cannot fully solve the core problem without liberalising the onshore capital account. Developing an isolated, offshore yuan market creates a functional “sandbox” but cannot resolve the fundamental constraints that limit how strong a store of value that currency market can provide. Where the traditional dollar framework invites the world to acquire the currency through American consumption and store that wealth in open US capital markets, China supplies yuan through state lending while strictly capping foreign access to its onshore assets. Whether Beijing can sustain this balancing act against credit risks abroad and capital controls at home remains to be seen – but watching this novel macroeconomic experiment unfold from a ringside seat here in Hong Kong as a journalist is nothing short of fascinating.

title: New York Fashion Week 2026: Coach celebrates 85th anniversary with festive SS27 show
description: Stuart Vevers delivered a party-ready runway of sequins, party hats and archival bags, with Elle Fanning and Troye Sivan in attendance.
content: Last month Coach owner Tapestry reported that it achieved annual revenue of US$8 billion in its fiscal year ending in June 2026, driven largely by Coach. The label has been on a roll, growing into a roughly US$7 billion business, according to a recent report in trade publication WWD. Its ability to connect with Gen Z consumers and the accessible price points of its bestselling handbags are behind its success, but the buzzy collections of creative director Stuart Vevers also play a key role. The British designer was in a party mood for the spring/summer 2027 collection, a celebration of the brand’s 85th anniversary. The show began with a series of monochrome – almost drab-looking – looks: oversize jackets worn with nothing underneath and matching pants were paired with scuffed white tennis sneakers, while shrunken tank tops in distressed leather came with front pockets in the shape of the label’s signature kisslock bags. That forlorn parade of very stylish street urchins – an archetype that has become a recurring theme in Vevers’ work for Coach – didn’t last long. The rest of the collection was a fun birthday party. Sequinned dresses in bright hues such as pink were accessorised with cone-shaped party hats and crowns while models’ arms and hair were covered in glitter and confetti. Some of the outfits looked like actual presents: made of shiny fabrics, they were laden with bows, ribbons and whistles, as well as birthday cards and gift boxes made of leather. As always at Coach, there were plenty of desirable bags – from new versions of bestsellers such as the Brooklyn and a very sparkly Tabby to the new Turnlock Tote, inspired by an archival design from 1970. Bright young things like Elle Fanning, Troye Sivan, Sherry Kong and Gigi Yim were among the celebrities who attended the show and the after-party that followed.

title: Chinese man, 106, embraces ‘reverse schedule’, celebrated alongside wife as ‘model couple’
description: Regarding his remarkable longevity, Wang cites a positive outlook on life, strong family values, and an enduring passion for work and learning.
content: A 106-year-old man in eastern China has inspired many online with his unconventional lifestyle and enduring marriage. Wang Dinggao, from Rui’an in Zhejiang province, remains remarkably independent despite experiencing some hearing loss, according to the mainland media outlet Daxiang News. In contrast to most people, he adheres to a “reverse schedule”: sleeping around 4 or 5pm, waking at 1am, enjoying breakfast at 3am before embarking on his morning walk. His son has adapted to this unusual routine, rising early each day to prepare breakfast, while the family continues to honour Wang’s long-established habits. Additionally, Wang maintains a high level of independence, managing his own laundry, bathing, and even skilled sewing tasks. His diet is simple and unrestricted; he enjoys seafood, particularly river crabs, and occasionally shares a meal along with a glass of baijiu (Chinese liquor) with his son. When asked about his longevity, Wang attributes it to a positive mindset, strong family traditions, and a lifelong passion for work and learning. Although he received only four years of formal education, Wang’s curiosity and perseverance enabled him to acquire knowledge and skills that far exceeded his schooling. He was appointed village cashier at a young age. Beyond his official duties, he learned by observing fellow villagers and eventually mastered cooking, bamboo weaving, and rice sculpture. Wang and his wife, Hong Ailan, shared an extraordinary 80 years of marriage and raised a son, with their family now spanning four generations. To their neighbours, they were regarded as the village’s “model couple.” When conflicts arose between families, residents frequently sought their guidance in resolving disputes. Their son revealed a contrast in their personalities: his mother was quick-tempered, while his father was calm and gentle. When his wife became upset, Wang never argued. Instead, he would quietly offer her a cup of warm water and say with a smile: “Have some water first, then you can continue being angry.” This simple gesture often diffused the tension. After Hong’s death, Wang became withdrawn and struggled physically, but he gradually regained his strength with his son’s support. The date of her passing has not been publicly disclosed. Though his wife is gone, her presence lingers in their home, from the cherished photographs Wang treasures to the handmade handrail she left behind. One online commenter suggested that “a happy marriage and a kind, tolerant nature” may be among the secrets behind Wang’s longevity. Another remarked: “My father is 86 and stays up late watching short videos every day. Maybe I should start respecting his habits.” China’s seventh national population census in 2020 recorded 119,000 centenarians, making the country home to the world’s largest population of individuals aged 100 and above.

title: Can a US$6 trillion South Korea-Japan economic bloc succeed?
description: A South Korean tycoon’s proposal could create the world’s fourth-biggest economic bloc, if both countries put history behind them.
content: A fraying global economic order could push South Korea and Japan towards deeper trade integration, with business leaders and analysts saying the two neighbours stand to benefit from such a partnership despite lingering historical wounds. The two countries could draw closer as the era of relatively open global trade gives way to tit-for-tat tariffs and supply-chain disruptions due to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. SK Group chairman and Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry chairman Chey Tae-won has in recent weeks proposed building a shared economic community between South Korea and Japan. In an interview with Japan’s Asahi newspaper published this week, Chey said connecting the two countries more closely could create an economic bloc valued at US$6 trillion annually, ranking fourth globally after the United States, the European Union and China. Lee Won-deog, a professor at the Institute of Japanese Studies at Kookmin University, called Chey’s proposal “bold” and said: “Korea-Japan economic integration is the spirit of the time as the global trade order fragments, superpower rivalry grows and regional blocs strengthen.” Japan and South Korea could learn from France and Germany, whose post-war reconciliation began with cooperation in industries such as energy and steel and helped lay the foundations for the EU, he added. With South Korea’s gross domestic product per capita and exports having reached levels comparable to Japan, Seoul could engage Tokyo on an equal footing, according to Lee. South Korean companies are competitive in batteries, shipbuilding and advanced manufacturing while their Japanese counterparts are strong in chemicals, energy technologies, machinery and finance, he added. The intensifying US-China rivalry is making it more difficult for South Korea and Japan to rely solely on global markets. Their economies also face major structural challenges including rapidly ageing populations and low birth rates. “They should step up their economic integration and expand this merger into other countries,” Lee said. South Korea and Japan have held discussions in recent months to boost their supply chain cooperation. In March, they signed a partnership covering supply-chain disruptions, critical minerals and other areas. Last week, the two sides met again in Tokyo to discuss ensuring stable supplies of liquefied natural gas, crude oil and petroleum products during times of crisis. They also discussed cutting carbon emissions to meet EU requirements for imports entering the bloc. Lee said closer energy cooperation could benefit South Korea and Japan as they were among the world’s major oil and gas importers and could gain better terms through joint procurement. At the corporate level, some companies from the two countries are seeking to cooperate and boost their competitiveness. To meet surging demand for AI-related memory chips and reduce manufacturing costs, SK Hynix – an affiliate of Chey’s group – is considering partnering with Japanese NAND flash producer Kioxia to build a memory-chip facility in Japan. On artificial intelligence, Chey has identified NTT and Tokyo Electron in Japan as potential partners for South Korean companies, with both sides collaborating on AI data sharing, developing global standards and increasing cross-border investments in start-ups. ‘Political sandwich’ Pak Seong-bin, a Japanese affairs expert at Ajou University, said South Korea and Japan faced similar trade risks as manufacturing powerhouses heavily dependent on international supply chains. They are caught in a “dual geopolitical sandwich”, with dual pressures from the US-China rivalry adversely affecting global supply chains and security tensions in Northeast Asia, according to Pak. The energy sector held potential for strong bilateral trade cooperation, whereby Japan could procure crude oil for South Korea to refine and export it back to its neighbour, Pak said. With the emergence of more international trade standards, South Korea and Japan could work together and have greater say in the process, according to Pak. He cited the EU-led hydrogen certification rules as an area where the two East Asian economies could coordinate their positions in areas ranging from extraction, supply and transport to consumption. Another possibility was combining Korean technology with Japanese planning and finance to undertake large, high-risk infrastructure projects in third countries, Pak said. However, Cho Jin-goo, a professor at the Japan Research Centre at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said prospects for a South Korea-Japan economic community were low for now given their historical baggage. The two countries remain divided over issues arising from Japan’s 1910-45 brutal colonial rule over the Korean peninsula, including compensation for victims of wartime forced labour, as well as the territorial dispute over the Liancourt Rocks, known as Dokdo in South Korea and Takeshima in Japan. Nonetheless, a strong economic partnership between South Korea and Japan could not only benefit them at the bilateral level but also influence China to join hands with them to deepen global trade networks, Cho said. “Cooperation in trade and technology [in East Asia] will hopefully set a good example for the rest of the world as the global trade order fragments.”

title: Hong Kong sport ‘setting bar low’, enabling mediocrity with cash handouts, coach says
description: Triathlon coach Andrew Wright laments lack of ‘high-performance thinking’, as city sports institute asks to be judged on more than medals.
content: As a whopping 580-strong Hong Kong squad prepares to go to this month’s Asian Games on the taxpayers’ dime, one of the city’s leading coaches has said that cash is being squandered on athletes who have no right to generous financial backing. While not pointing the finger in any specific direction, Andrew Wright, the Hong Kong triathlon head coach, said sports bodies in the city “set the bar pretty low … which breeds a non-high performance environment”. “What also frustrates me is the amount of money people are given that they haven’t earned,” he said. “It’s enabling in a way.” Underlining that cash does not necessarily buy ambition, a Hong Kong Sports Institute (HKSI) spokeswoman said that in a “highly competitive” sporting world “while medals are a natural aspiration, success is defined more broadly”. An elite athletes development fund that was established in 2012, using HK$700 million (around US$89.2 million) of taxpayers’ money, funnelled HK$982 million to HKSI for the 2025-26 period, a 4.3 per cent increase on the amount gifted in the previous 12 months. John Lee Ka-chiu, the Hong Kong chief executive who last week challenged the city’s athletes in Japan to improve on their record 53-medal haul from the 2023 Games, is likely to cover sports development in the city in his annual policy address next week. “Delivering the best possible performances, demonstrating the results of athletes’ training, and achieving personal breakthroughs in competitions are equally important [to medals],” the HKSI spokeswoman said. Greg Koenig, the mastermind behind Cheung Ka-long’s two Olympic golds and a key driver of Hong Kong’s fencing revolution, said that on arriving in the city eight years ago he discovered a mindset of “if we perform well in Asia, it’s perfect”. “I said, ‘come on, guys, you have the potential to reach world-class level’.” Koenig related that when he began fencing in his native France he had to pay to join the national programme. “Only with hard training and great, great results, do you find a way to make money,” he said. “It makes you really strong in your training. “With money, some athletes might take profits from the system and just control their ranking. I’m happy that with my group of fencers now we don’t have this issue.” Another coach from a successful national association said that athletes in Hong Kong are “really well helped compared to anywhere else in the world”. “It’s difficult to say if there’s too much help, but individual situations are different,” they added. The prominent sports of tennis, athletics and gymnastics will all be fighting to retain their precious HKSI backing in Japan. Carrying the racquet sport on his back, Coleman Wong Chak-lam has theoretically been given the unenviable task of sparing it from the chop. Tiffany Yue Nga-yan delivered the long jump of her life to win Asian Games bronze and preserve athletics’ status back in 2023, but the sport in Hong Kong is on life support after a barren three years. Gymnastics is indebted to the now retired Stone Shek Wai-hung’s 2024 Olympic qualification for their ongoing backing. Wright oversaw a 2023 Asian Games triathlon mixed-relay bronze, and his athletes delivered two medals from last year’s National Games. Nonetheless, he said he routinely feels like he is “bashing my head against a brick wall” in his quest to turn the city’s triathlon programme into a world leader. Frustrated that “not much high-performance thinking goes on in Hong Kong”, Wright said: “We get more money than any [triathlon] training programme in the world, and we should be doing much better than we do. We have amazing facilities. We have all this money, and the population is very talented. The problem is that the system in place [across a number of sports] does not develop athletes.” Wright said he had not been asked why Hong Kong is failing to rear triathletes who challenge for global honours. “I don’t think people in Hong Kong see [the ability to compete on the world stage] that way, and it’s almost impossible to change their opinion on it,” he said. “The bar is set pretty low … so that’s what everybody is aiming for and what everyone’s expecting. “It breeds a non-high performance environment, which just makes it difficult for those who are trying to do it properly.” The city men’s 4x100m relay quartet in 2012 were the last Hong Kong track and field athletes to qualify for an Olympics by right, while athletics returned empty handed from last year’s National Games. Christy Yiu Kit-ching, in 2016, and Ching Siu-nga four years later, secured Olympic spots in marathon and race walking, respectively. Still a Tier A sport, athletics has 57 “elite” performers pocketing between HK$35,450 (US$4,500) and HK$41,740 (US$5,300) per month from HKSI. Including juniors, 193 track and field athletes enjoy HKSI support. Simon Yeung Sai-mo, senior vice-chairman of the Hong Kong, China Association of Athletics Affiliates (HKAAA), said he felt the HKSI funding criteria were “objective enough”. The latest HKSI grant period will expire on March 31 next year. To retain Tier A backing, a sport must in the previous four years have either qualified an athlete for an Olympics, obtained a World Championships or Asian Games medal, or won National Games gold. Asked whether more should be demanded from the city’s track and field competitors, Yeung said: “In Asia, we have the likes of China, Japan, South Korea and India. They are very strong even by international standards, so winning an Asian Games or Asian Championships medal is not very easy.” Nonetheless, looking towards the forthcoming Games, Yeung said there was “always pressure to win a medal”. “It’s best if we win one, if not we must focus on qualifying for the Olympics on our own merit,” he added. According to the HKSI, tennis is currently serving an “observation period” and will supposedly have its funding axed if it fails to conjure an Asian Games medal. Rules were bent last year to keep the sport behind what one coach called HKSI’s “golden gates”, and in the event that they flop in Nagoya it would be no surprise, given Wong’s climb into the world’s top 100, if the same happened again. Unless they manage a Games podium finish, athletics and gymnastics would enter a similar two-year internal review period, which essentially amounts to a second chance after four years of underperformance, from January 1 next year. They would have until April 1, 2029, halfway through the next four-year grant cycle, to save their skins. Hong Kong gymnastics has mustered only two Asian Games medals, vault golds for Shek in 2014 and 2018. A HKSI source said that gymnastics, a Tier A sport with 13 “elite” athletes on full-time HKSI retainers, and another 15 juniors receiving support, “needs good results”. Regarding Wright’s accusation that too little is expected of the city’s athletes, and too many are given too much too soon, Albert Ng Tsz-kin, executive director of the Gymnastics Association of Hong Kong, China, said he had “no comment”. Shek, now coaching the Hong Kong women’s team, did not reply to a request for comment. Wright certainly did not have rugby in his crosshairs when he took aim at the city’s sporting culture. Hong Kong’s men’s sevens team claimed Asian Games gold in 2018 and 2023, while the women scooped bronze three years ago. Nonetheless, why the seven-a-side sport needs 72 athletes contracted to HKSI, and 28 more on junior grants, is a legitimate question. Paul John, the head of Hong Kong sevens rugby, had “nothing to say” about those numbers. Hong Kong marathon runner Chong See-yeung used the chicken and egg idiom to address the question of whether athletes were handed too much on a plate. “For some athletes, if they don’t have that kind of support, how can they achieve great results?” he said. “They can’t achieve great results the moment they receive support.” Wright acknowledged that athletes of the “right calibre” would thrive at HKSI. “The issue is finding the right level of athlete,” he said. “Somewhere in Hong Kong, there is a potential Olympic champion triathlete.” Koenig, whose leading foilists, Cheung, Ryan Choi Chun-yin, Harris Ho-shing-him and Leung Chin-yu are expected to vie for Games honours this month, said his athletes were “a little bit surprised” back when he spelled out their global potential. “After a few good results, they understood they could do it,” he said. “Once your A team can do it, your B team fights hard to reach their level. “Harris Ho is 17 and when he was 11 he watched Cheung Ka-long win Olympic gold on his television. He thought, ‘I’m from Hong Kong, I can do it, too’. “When you have this mindset, you work harder and don’t limit yourself to Asian competitions. HKSI helps athletes in the best way in the world, there are lots of good coaches and no reason to not succeed.” The HKSI spokeswoman added that “athletes are fully backed to train and pursue excellence on the international stage, ensuring they have the environment needed to achieve breakthroughs and success”. Wright said he planned to stick around to keep trying to instigate change from within. “We make it so difficult for ourselves and it’s hard to be around that sometimes,” he said. “Some days it really feels like you’re just at a massive loss, and there’s no way that we can improve or get the job done. Other days, like when I see my six Asian Games athletes thriving and improving, give you a glimmer of hope that we can do it. “There are definitely athletes doing a very professional job. Dealing with Hong Kong athletes is unique, and I don’t think there’s anybody else in the world more suited to the position that I’m in.” Additional reporting: Mike Chan

title: Hong Kong guqin devotees embrace the ancient zither’s history, philosophy and craft
description: A renewed appreciation of the seven-stringed zither is as much about understanding ancient Chinese culture as it is enjoying the music.
content: When civil servant Jackel Wan Chak-kui, 28, first heard a guqin being played, he was a young boy wandering through Chi Lin Nunnery, in Diamond Hill. He remembers being entranced by the instrument’s music, at once subtle and comforting. It seemed to envelop him like a warm embrace, complementing the natural beauty of the gardens, melding with stone, water, wood and stillness. Years later, as a student at Baptist University, Wan chanced upon the sound again, while scrolling through YouTube. He delved deeper this time, yearning to learn more. He ordered his first guqin from Taobao (“Not a good one, but at least I could have a touch [of the instrument],” he says) and taught himself from scores found in the university library, learning where to place his fingers on the seven silk strings. A seven-stringed zither, the guqin (“ancient stringed instrument”) was once the preserve of noblemen and royal courts, poets and scholars, and has been part of a musical tradition that has existed for more than 3,000 years in China, played in small, elite gatherings. Since Unesco first recognised guqin music as part of humanity’s intangible cultural heritage in 2003, the seven-stringed zither has become more widely appreciated, with the instrument itself having been inscribed on China’s National List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2006. Virtuoso Chen Leiji played a specially composed piece on the guqin during the opening ceremony of the 2008 Beijing Olympics, reaching millions of viewers worldwide, and today, it’s commonly seen being played in concerts and online videos, with younger musicians being drawn to the instrument. In Hong Kong, the guqin’s renaissance goes beyond simply renewed popularity, say scholars and players, many of whom construct their own. What they want to preserve are not just the rich sounds of an ancient instrument, but also a traditional way of life. When it comes to the instrument and its music, “the guqin may be more accessible than before, but true revival is not just about more people playing it. It is about whether people understand its inner life: its craft, philosophy, subtle sound, cultural memory and intensely personal mode of expression”, Wan explains. “Because the more you understand Chinese culture, the more you realise that the guqin goes beyond music to explore other cultural aspects, such as Taoism, philosophy and history.” A player’s understanding of those references can shape their interpretation of the music. Wan gives as an example the piece Li Sao (“Encountering Sorrow”) – a lament to Qu Yuan (circa 339BC-278BC), the poet-politician whose exile, grief and moral idealism are central to one of the great works of Chinese literature, also titled Li Sao. To perform such a piece properly, Wan says, it is necessary to enter the emotional and philosophical world behind the notes, rather than just play them. “It is like the first-, second-, third-person thing – the player might perform as if they are Qu Yuan, or they could be a storyteller, telling the story of Qu Yuan. Or [they could] consider themselves as humming the Li Sao prose,” says Wan, explaining that “to acquire these perspectives, one must cultivate not just the musicality, but also the culture, in a broad sense, of the qin”. He continues, “It is a good mix of understanding traditional culture and the current situation of ourselves.” Players should learn to develop an appreciation for the guqin’s silences, too, says John Yiu Shek-on, an art historian and the deputy director of the Jao Tsung-I Petite Ecole academic research and cultural centre, at the University of Hong Kong. “It has so much void – the space between the musical notes,” he says. As a child in Hong Kong, Yiu played Western instruments, including the piano, but was later drawn to the guqin through its cultural and literary presence. “I didn’t start with the music,” Yiu admits. “I actually started from writing about it, because it is a very revered instrument in Chinese poetry.” He notes that the music’s silences remind him of “negative space”, referring to the intentionally untouched areas of silk or paper in Chinese paintings, which are not so much empty but alive with suggestion. In 2005, he began learning to play the guqin and was soon appreciating the lingering pauses before notes, as part of the music’s emotional landscape. He found himself drawn not only to the instrument’s sound, but also to its refusal to overwhelm the listener – a quiet invitation to slow down and listen inwardly. Unlike many old-school qin players, Yiu says, both private enjoyment and public performance matter to him. “I enjoy playing just for myself […] and actually, just last year, I had a concert with my teacher in Shanghai.” Yiu is a member of the Deyin Qin Society, founded in 1998 by disciples of Tsar Teh-yun (1905-2007), a guqin master, poet and calligrapher who relocated to Hong Kong from Shanghai in the 1950s. “She is widely regarded as one of China’s last great literati,” says Yiu, whose own teacher learned from her directly. Tsar was born in Huzhou, Zhejiang province, into what Yiu describes as a scholar-gentry family. She received an education in traditional arts, poetry and Kunqu – a polished, flowing style of singing that originated in Suzhou more than six centuries ago – and spent around 30 years teaching in Hong Kong. “Importantly, she did not teach for a living, and treated her students like friends. Many of her students later became established scholars or successful professionals. What united them was not only musical ability, but a temperament suited to the guqin; they’re all quite low-key people,” says Yiu. Nowadays, the Deyin Qin Society has fewer than 80 members but “we hold regular, semi-private yaji [‘elegant gathering’] salons every two months. We also do public concerts sometimes”, at venues such as the Xiqu Centre and Hong Kong City Hall. Appreciation of the seven-stringed zither is passed on through other intimate circles as well. Wee Lian-hee is a professor at the Academy of Language and Culture at Baptist University, and his initial encounter with the guqin came in the 80s. Living in Singapore, he read about the seven-stringed zither while researching Chinese instruments, but struggled to find much information. It wasn’t until the early 2000s, while pursuing a PhD in linguistics in the United States, that he learned of Choi Chang-sau (1933-2025), the third-generation owner of Hong Kong’s Choi Fook Kee Musical Instrument Factory, a producer of Chiuchow and Hakka instruments, as well as violins and guitars. Choi was a foremost expert in crafting, restoring and preserving the guqin. Established players choose their disciples with care. When Wee visited the master’s workshop, expressing an interest in learning how to make the instrument, he was advised to return after he had settled in Hong Kong. In 2001, Wee moved to the city for work but, preoccupied with his career, postponed his guqin studies. In 2012, he sought out Lau Chor-wah, an esteemed guqin musician and philosopher, and a founding member of the Deyin Qin Society. Lau refused to teach him for two years, a test to see if he was worthy and genuinely interested. Eventually, he proved his dedication, and she agreed. Her teaching was strict and rigorous, says Wee, requiring weekly attendance at a fixed time, and the first three months were dedicated solely to learning how to string the instrument, a process that requires enormous focus and patience, and can take a novice hours. Precision and gentle finesse are required to maintain the correct tension on each silk string if the right pitch is to be attained. With a recommendation from Lau, Wee was accepted by Choi as a student, although the master insisted that, to become a maker, one must first be an accomplished player. “Both playing the guqin and crafting it are equally fulfilling,” says Wee. He views both as integral to developing a connection to the instrument. Of the 50 or so students who studied under Choi, as many as 10 are still making guqin in Hong Kong, among them Sou Si-tai, chairman of the Deyin Qin Society. A guqin’s body is traditionally fashioned from thoroughly seasoned wood, typically that which has been dried in the shade for about a century. Wee explains that a range of wood is used for different parts of the qin: “The top board is typically paulownia or cedar, the bottom board is more varied and the inlaid parts may be various kinds of hardwood.” After careful selection, the wood is hollowed and shaped before layers of ash and lacquer are applied, polished and adjusted. Constructing a guqin usually takes more than 200 person-hours, spread over nine painstaking steps that must be planned according to the season. Every detail affects the sound: the thickness of the boards, the curve of the body, the placement of the bridges, the tension of the strings and the way the surface responds to a player’s touch. “Historically, the guqin is a niche instrument,” says Wee. “Sudden popularity has led to commercialisation and changes that should raise discussion.” One area of contention is the use of metallic strings, which are louder, more stable and less expensive, but alter the instrument’s sound dynamics and are harsh on the fingers. Unsurprisingly, they are not favoured by purists. Wee is unsure how many guqin he owns, with several still under construction. Although he appraises and repairs antique guqin for friends and collectors, he says he would never consider selling one of his own creations, as they are “my personal explorations into creating the sounds for my music”. Says Wee, “It takes me an average of three years to make a guqin, so even if I were to imagine selling it, I wouldn’t know how to price it. I usually lend my instruments to like-minded friends and musicians for their playing pleasure.” For his wife, he carved a guqin from the beam of a 200-year-old school in Yuen Long that was demolished, and decorated the instrument with a symbol representing his name, inlaid in sheep bone. Using material found in the vicinity of his village, in the Lau Fau Shan area, Wee fashions many of his guqin in memory of deceased pets. In one instance, the ashes of their dog Lily were incorporated into the guqin he made for his wife, an instrument that bears a carving of one of Lily’s paws. Wan recently made his first qin, an undertaking he estimates took more than 200 hours. He shares that the process demanded a different kind of attention than that needed for playing. It meant learning to understand the instrument not only through sound, but through wood, lacquer, strings and touch, and to consider how small changes in shape, tension and surface alter the way it resonates. “Both crafting and playing [the guqin] are a means of connecting with nature, to the world around you,” says Wan. “I’d say it’s a way of life.”

title: Help! I’m shy and find it hard to make friends at school
description: Each week, we respond to a question from our readers and give advice and resources they can turn to.
content:
Do you have a personal question you’ve been too afraid to ask? Whether it is about school, family or your social life, you can share it with us through this form . Don’t worry, you’ll remain anonymous.
I am very shy at school, and I find it hard to make friends. When we have group projects, I want to join my classmates, but I am too nervous to ask. When I do ask, I start to stutter , and it is embarrassing. Please help me.
Being shy at school and finding it hard to make friends is something many young people go through, even if others might not show it. You’re not alone in feeling like this, and it’s completely OK to be nervous.
It’s great that you still want to join your classmates on group projects even though you feel shy. This shows that you are looking for chances to step out of your comfort zone .
When you’re feeling too nervous to talk to someone or when you start stuttering, this might be your brain trying to protect you from rejection . That can make your heart race and your voice shaky. Afterwards, the embarrassment might make you feel even more nervous next time.
But these are completely normal reactions to have when you feel shy. It will take time and repeated practice before you feel more confident when making friends. Here are some ideas to help you along the way.
Try giving a small compliment to a classmate like, “I really liked your presentation!” or “Your idea in class was great.” These can make the other person smile and could even spark a conversation.
Stand in front of a mirror and say, “Hi, can I join your group for the project?” a few times. You can also try other questions you’ve been thinking about asking in school. The more you rehearse, the easier it becomes in real life. You can also make it fun by practising in front of a stuffed toy or imagining that you are speaking to your favourite character.
When you feel nervous, breathe in slowly for four seconds, hold your breath for four seconds and exhale for another four. This exercise tells your body, “Hey, I’m OK. Everything is OK. I just want to do this one thing. I can relax now.”
They may be feeling just as nervous and might be hoping someone else reaches out first. You don’t need to become the most talkative person in class to find friends, and friendships can start from short compliments or quiet moments working with others.
Most importantly, be kind to yourself. Even if a conversation doesn’t go perfectly, or you find yourself stuttering, you’re becoming braver by trying. Shyness doesn’t disappear overnight, but don’t let it stop you from trying again the next day. You are already doing well by trying.
This question was answered by James Pho, a counsellor at Your Relationship Clinic.

title: In Focus | What’s a Northern Metropolis-like project doing in Malaysia? Lessons for Hong Kong?
description: Development of Malaysia’s Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis offers case study on mutual learning.
content: Deep in the southern border zone of Johor, Malaysia, separated from Singapore by a narrow strait, a steady flow of commuters moves seamlessly between the two sovereign neighbours. Beyond the immediate checkpoints, a short 30-minute train ride connects visitors to regional hubs such as Kulai, where a vastly different dynamic comes into view – one defined by the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure. Inside YTL’s sprawling Green Data Centre Park, massive operational blocks stand beside numerous others under construction. The park supplies high-performance computing power and artificial intelligence (AI) chips to global technology giants, sitting squarely within the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ), a landmark 350,000-hectare (865,000-acre) project officially established in January 2025. Covering an area more than four times the size of Singapore, the JS-SEZ aims to generate 260 billion Malaysian ringgit (US$63.9 billion) for Johor’s regional economy by 2030 and create more than 20,000 high-skilled jobs, anchored by the coming 4km Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link designed to slash travel times and cement cross-strait integration. For Malaysia, the early trajectory of Hong Kong and Shenzhen remains the foundational blueprint. Lee Ting Han, Johor’s state executive councillor for investment and trade, told the South China Morning Post that despite distinct political frameworks, the wealth gap between Singapore and Johor mirrored the historic economic disparity between Hong Kong and Shenzhen. “Similarly, it is pretty much like the early days of Hong Kong and Shenzhen, where the economic disparity between the two regions was so wide … what we are trying to do now is see whether there’s a way for us from a business standpoint to make it more integrated from trade relationships to investment culture,” Lee said. He acknowledged that building the JS-SEZ presented unique regulatory challenges because Johor and Singapore operated as sovereign nations without an overarching central authority such as Beijing to coordinate rules. However, Johor is studying how Shenzhen strategically transitioned over decades from labour-intensive assembly to capital- and technology-intensive hubs by leveraging Hong Kong capital to build home-grown tech giants in the same vein as Huawei Technologies and DJI. As Asia’s premier financial and technology centres construct massive border-spanning growth corridors, Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis and Malaysia’s JS-SEZ offer a compelling case study in mutual learning. While Malaysia looks to emulate Hong Kong’s long-standing success in frictionless border flows and joint state-directed planning, the city stands to learn key lessons from Johor’s aggressive strategy in nurturing talent pipelines and deploying state-backed infrastructure to secure a low-cost, high-reliability energy grid for power-hungry tech industries. Key to Johor’s rapid rise is its approach to energy, an area where Hong Kong could draw valuable operational insights. Highlighting the power requirements of data centres, Lee noted that Malaysia’s utilities were largely state-backed. This allows the government to take a long-term, strategic view by investing heavily in power infrastructure upfront, insulating critical digital hubs from the short-term profit pressures faced by purely private, commercial utility entities. Malaysia adopted a forward-looking approach by making heavy infrastructure investments ahead of the cycle. Chew Chong-sin, a former Mengkibol state assemblyman who has analysed the region’s economic integration, noted that by combining Singapore’s global financial and connectivity hub status with Johor’s land, energy, and industrial capacity, the zone aimed to mirror Shenzhen’s early evolution into a technology powerhouse. However, he cautioned that significant operational hurdles persisted – most notably easing severe bottlenecking at the world’s second-busiest land checkpoint and resolving head-on competition in ports and logistics – even as the coming RTS Link aimed to streamline cross-border mobility by 2027. Crucially, the zone was positioning itself to absorb global supply chain diversification, offering a neutral, disaster-free base for multinationals and mainland Chinese enterprises looking to de-risk, Chew said. He added that this momentum had already drawn increased interest from Hong Kong firms, including sustainable aviation fuel producers and hospitality enterprises. As Malaysia and Singapore finalise a comprehensive 10-year master plan, he said that the zone’s ultimate success would depend on maintaining the strict execution discipline needed to translate high-level blueprints into lasting economic integration. To spur investment ahead of its full master plan launch in late 2026, authorities introduced sweeping tax incentives starting January 2025. Firms deploying at least 500 million ringgit in high-growth fields such as AI, quantum computing and aerospace enjoy a 5 per cent preferential corporate tax rate for years, paired with stamp duty waivers. These incentives have caught international attention. A representative from a Mexico-based construction and information technology enterprise, who did not wish to be named, confirmed to the SCMP that the company would visit Malaysia to explore data centre sites, citing the country’s strong connectivity within Asean, widespread English proficiency and attractive tax environment. Following stops in Kuala Lumpur and coming visits to Johor, he commended Malaysia’s proactive tech push. Turning to Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis, however, the representative observed that while the city retained distinct institutional advantages, its position within China imposed inherent geopolitical limitations when manufacturing high-end, sensitive semiconductor chips. The Northern Metropolis has been touted repeatedly as a top priority for Hong Kong’s administration, capped most recently by a visit from Xia Baolong, director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office, who underscored Beijing’s call to accelerate construction. The megaproject aims to transform 30,000 hectares into a major housing hub and an economic growth engine. Both the Northern Metropolis and the JS-SEZ are strategically positioning themselves as multifaceted growth engines that integrate international education hubs, hi-tech innovation corridors and vibrant ecotourism circles. Joining the call for deeper integration, Kathy Lee, head of research and retail consultancy at Colliers Hong Kong, said the city could take reference from Johor as a benchmark for cross-border development by aligning its land-grant policies with Shenzhen and leveraging universities to spearhead innovation. She noted that Johor’s experience showed how robust research and technology ecosystems relied heavily on close synergies with academic institutions. To build a sustainable tech ecosystem, Lee urged authorities to synchronise housing and talent policies with project completion timelines, anticipating a resurgence in demand as new infrastructure came online. Given the intensive energy requirements of advanced technology and data centres, she recommended that the government initiate joint feasibility studies with mainland Chinese authorities on cross-border electricity supply to secure a reliable, green power source for the city’s tech sector. Echoing the push for seamless integration, former lawmaker Edward Lau Kwok-fan argued that Hong Kong should draw inspiration from the JS-SEZ by speeding up the implementation of bespoke legislation for the Northern Metropolis to unlock the fluid movement of people, goods, capital and data. He also called on higher education institutions to take greater initiative. “I feel universities have not done enough yet. In the future, universities could evolve towards an industry-oriented development path,” said Lau, a member of the Advisory Committee on the Northern Metropolis. “Universities need to reflect. There is a need to rethink course offerings and review academic programmes going forward.” In response, Hong Kong’s Development Bureau said that the Northern Metropolis operated as a strategic cross-boundary hub under the “one country, two systems” governing principle, utilising coming Hetao-specific legislation to facilitate fluid cross-border resource sharing within the Greater Bay Area. The bureau highlighted that by pairing the city’s five global top-100 universities and a planned 1,000-hectare university district with Shenzhen’s industrial scale, Hong Kong provided a platform, backed by common law, capable of rapidly converting lab discoveries into mass production. The Education Bureau also said in a reply that it was encouraging University Grants Committee-funded universities to revamp their academic offerings, backed by a fund launched in 2023 to drive digital teaching reforms. The Chinese University of Hong Kong said in a reply that it offered AI degree programmes across its engineering and science faculties, which delivered structured training to foster AI talent equipped for real-world innovation and academic research. The SCMP also reached out to the University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. Under the 2025-28 triennial planning cycle, local universities were introducing 27 new undergraduate degree programmes tailored to STEAM fields, the bureau said. STEAM refers to an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths. Addressing Hong Kong’s internal bottlenecks, lawmaker Aaron Bok Kwok-ming, a former president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers (HKIE), stressed that the city had to aggressively tackle its ongoing engineering talent shortage similarly to Malaysia. To supply future high-value talent for the JS-SEZ, the Johor Talent Development Council acts as a centralised talent engine by partnering with universities, institutions and agencies to deliver industry-aligned upskilling, matching programmes and specialised training. Bok called for targeted manpower forecasts, particularly in electronic engineering, to pinpoint exact deficit areas as Hong Kong advanced its innovation ambitions. He urged government leaders to conduct official, comprehensive surveys rather than relying on industry estimates, while establishing structured pathways to entice overseas Hong Kong engineers back home and expanding domestic university training. According to a manpower forecast report by Hong Kong’s Construction Industry Council released in 2023, the sector is expected to face a shortage of about 6,000 to 6,500 professionals by 2027, with civil, mechanical, structural and environmental engineering listed among the most severely affected specialisms. Drawing on the forecast report, the HKIE noted in 2023 that the city would face a shortfall of about 3,000 professional engineers over the five years through 2027, stressing that engineers played an indispensable role in supporting the government’s push for new industrialisation and biotechnology. This deficit is already affecting local businesses. Some tech companies previously said that while they struggled to find veteran talent, such as experienced electronics engineers, locally in Hong Kong, they could easily recruit skilled professionals on the mainland. Addressing these industry concerns over projected workforce shortages, including the estimated shortfall of 3,000 engineers, engineer and former technology minister Alfred Sit Wing-hang said that emerging technologies such as AI, robotics and building information modelling required more sophisticated technical expertise rather than diluted entry criteria. Sit added that as Hong Kong’s economic landscape underwent a structural shift towards advanced manufacturing and technology-driven industries, local universities and professional bodies were actively overhauling their training frameworks. AI had increasingly become a core component of undergraduate engineering curricula, while new certification programmes were being developed to upskill mid-career professionals in fields such as smart industrial engineering and automation, he said. On the energy front, lawmaker and energy sector expert Chan Siu-hung noted that Hong Kong already possessed top-tier infrastructure for data centres and computing hubs, but suggested the government could accelerate the roll-out of power infrastructure blueprints to match coming industrial investments. On the city’s digital expansion, he noted that major development zones such as the Lok Ma Chau Loop and the San Tin Technopole were well positioned, with strong power supply nodes. Responding to queries on energy security, the Environment and Ecology Bureau said that the government had signed Scheme of Control Agreements (SCAs) with the city’s two power companies. Under these agreements, the suppliers are obliged to support the development of Hong Kong including the Northern Metropolis, by providing, operating and maintaining sufficient electricity-related facilities to meet the needs of various industries. Chan stressed that actual energy demand would ultimately depend on incoming corporate investments. “To ensure long-term energy security, Hong Kong’s two power suppliers need to finalise power agreements with mainland supply, securing cross-boundary supply options while advancing low-carbon energy goals,” he said. “Officials should provide clearer and earlier timelines for these infrastructure plans to give operators certainty.”

title: Moonshot, DeepSeek secretly routed user requests to Claude, Anthropic claims
description: AI giants accused of cloning American models by funnelling real Chinese user queries to them via network of intermediate platforms.
content: American artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has accused its Chinese AI rivals DeepSeek and Moonshot on Thursday of covertly routing customer requests to its Claude models, then showing users the responses as if they were from their own models. The new allegations mark a further escalation in US criticism of China’s AI industry practices. Earlier this week, three US government agencies, including the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), claimed that six Chinese companies were engaged in an industrial campaign to steal US model outputs, “likely with Chinese government awareness”. Beijing on Wednesday rejected those allegations, describing them as actions by Washington to suppress China’s AI industry and threatening retaliatory measures. While US companies OpenAI and Anthropic have repeatedly accused their Chinese counterparts of “stealing” their outputs to improve their own models in a process known as “distillation”, Anthropic’s latest claims mark the first time it has accused Chinese companies of re-routing users directly to Claude, which would expose Chinese users’ information and activity to the American company. “[These] findings raise concerns about the misuse of user data by PRC AI labs,” the company said in its 154-page report released on Thursday. According to the report, Kimi model developer Moonshot secretly showed its users Claude model outputs and passed them off as Kimi’s, then used those exchanges to improve their own models. In one 10-day window, Moonshot allegedly routed 300,000 requests to Claude through 5,380 fraudulent accounts, most of which appeared to be located in Singapore and Japan. The Beijing-based company has emerged as one of China’s leading AI champions following the success of its K3 model release in July, with its models surging in popularity globally. The company’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – is expected to reach US$1 billion by the end of the year, doubling since mid-2026, according to Nomura Securities. However, Anthropic said that the diverted traffic allowed it to see sensitive data belonging to Moonshot’s customers in the US, Europe and China, including a user “likely” affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army who thought they were using Kimi to analyse CCTV footage of a targeted person in Chengdu, Sichuan province. It claimed to have also accessed data from “high-profile” Chinese tech companies, without specifying which ones. DeepSeek is also accused of diverting user requests to Claude, although Anthropic did not say how large the Hangzhou company’s operation was. Moonshot and DeepSeek did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
