The report accuses five other Chinese companies of distilling their Claude models since February 2026, including Qwen developer Alibaba Group Holding, GLM developer Z.ai, MiMo developer Xiaomi and M model developer MiniMax. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. None of the companies responded to requests for comment during China’s non-working hours. Distillation is a widely used technique in the AI industry that uses the outputs of larger AI models to train smaller ones. However, Anthropic said in its latest report that Chinese firms are engaged in a form of “illicit” distillation because of the “industrial” scale of their efforts to access the outputs of Anthropic’s models, which the company does not permit to be used in China, through fake accounts and stolen credit cards. Joe Khawam, managing director of legal and AI policy at the Law Reform Institute in Washington, said that the Anthropic report highlights new data privacy concerns surrounding Chinese companies’ distillation practices, which could violate both US and Chinese laws. “I would think that Chinese law could potentially be implicated as well here,” he said. “There are details here that are potentially legally relevant.” Khawam, a former US Department of State lawyer, also noted the timing of the two reports as a potential signal that the Trump administration will raise the issue of Chinese companies’ distillation practices at the coming US-China AI talks this month. “It’s clear that the US government is digging much deeper into this issue and beginning to develop what the [distillation] campaigns entail,” he said. “I think all of that is putting the US government in a position to diplomatically engage with the Chinese government on this issue and see if they could achieve their objectives quietly without having to resort to other tools.”

title: Police say 5 dead, 40 injured in tour bus crash in Switzerland
description: Coach carrying 45 passengers overturns in Alpine canton of Graubuenden, police say.
content: Police say five people have died and 40 others were injured after a Dutch tour bus slammed into a roadside crash barrier and overturned in eastern Switzerland. The bus, with 45 people on board, overturned Thursday afternoon in a construction zone between the villages of Susch and Zernez in the Alpine canton of Graubuenden. Seven rescue helicopters and 13 ambulance crews took part in the rush to evacuate the victims, police said. Three people remain in serious condition in hospital. Images from the scene showed crews in fluorescent suits cutting into the overturned bus with power saws overnight. Prosecutors and police were investigating what led to the accident, though no other vehicles were believed to be involved. Oad, a travel agency behind the trip, said in a statement that it was “deeply shocked and devastated by the tragic bus accident” and its thoughts were with those involved and their loved ones. Swiss President Guy Parmelin, writing on X, vowed that Swiss authorities would ensure a “comprehensive and thorough investigation” of the case. Dutch King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima, in a statement posted on social media, said: “Our hearts go out to the next of kin, to everybody who is now living in fear for the fate of loved ones and to the injured”.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong is building a two-way global education highway
description: The inaugural Global Education Summit highlighted the city’s efforts to align with the nation’s goals and consolidate its position as a global education and talent hub.
content: Thanks to the favourable global rankings of its universities and its unique linkage with mainland China and the world, Hong Kong is well positioned to upgrade itself into an international education and talent hub. Under the incumbent administration’s drive, more ambitious measures are being rolled out to burnish the “Study in Hong Kong” brand, and rightly so. The inaugural Global Education Summit held in the city over the weekend provided clarity on the way forward. Co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier, the two-day event drew more than 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents from around the world to discuss regional talent development, artificial intelligence integration and evolving academic pathways. Among the attendees were principals and admissions officers from more than 40 leading secondary schools and universities, including the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. Addressing the summit, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin posed a thought-provoking question. “We don’t just care about rankings on a piece of paper. In an age dominated by artificial intelligence, fast-changing global markets and evolving career landscape … are we truly preparing our next generation to thrive?” she asked. The answer is in the affirmative. It is encouraging that the government has clear targets on further boosting education quality. With the concrete goal of lifting STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics) enrolments to 35 per cent of undergraduates by 2026-27, and a broader range of study programmes, Hong Kong is no longer just nurturing local talent or preparing students to study overseas. It is doubling down on a decisive shift towards building a two-way global education highway. There have been long-standing concerns about skill mismatches, especially when the local economy pivots towards innovation, technology and re-industrialisation. The education minister’s pledge to pair programme growth with efforts to better connect education, research and industry is reassuring. In the 2025-28 triennium, universities are launching 27 undergraduate programmes related to STEAM, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, creative industries, sustainable development and data science. The expansion of the Northern Metropolis university town project, from the original 60 hectares to some 300 hectares, along with the surrounding technology paths, industry zones and vibrant communities that span more than 1,000 hectares in the New Territories, underlines the recognition of the links between academic research and real-world applications. The ambitious drive by the government comes as study preferences and talent flow are being reshaped by intensifying geopolitics across the world. The city’s advantages stand out in this respect. With proximity to the mainland market, a bilingual environment, strong research tradition, and a global outlook that appeals to international institutions and students, local universities have proved to be magnets for aspiring students overseas in recent years. The 2025-26 academic year logged 30,400 non-local students from over 100 countries and regions, a 30 per cent increase over two years. The figures speak volumes about Hong Kong’s ability to provide a safe and promising pathway for academic and career development. Under the nation’s latest development goals up to 2030, the city has an important mission: to consolidate its position as a global education and talent hub. With the city’s first five-year plan, which will align with the national strategy, to be announced next week, the Hong Kong government is expected to double down in this direction with more concrete policies and measures. Precisely, this means stronger efforts in coordinating the expansion of the Northern Metropolis university town, enhancing visa policies and affordable accommodation for international students as well as converting innovation and research outcomes into viable products and services. Nurturing a comprehensive and conducive environment for world-class education and research requires strong leadership and strategic focus. The soon-to-be-released five-year plan will hopefully inject fresh impetus into the city’s drive to seize opportunities and enhance the Study in Hong Kong brand.

title: Hong Kong home prices headed for 15% gain this year, Midland forecast says
description: As the market digests uncertainties, new property launches are accelerating and buyers are returning to the market, executive says.
content: Hong Kong’s home prices will end the year 15 per cent higher than a year earlier, but still 16 per cent below their high-water mark in 2021, according to local property agency Midland Realty. Underpinning the positive forecast, the city’s banks were not likely to follow an increase in US interest rates by the Federal Reserve if one occurred this year, executives from the agency said at a press conference on Thursday. Dave Ma Tai-yeung, CEO of Midland (Residential), said that as the market gradually digested geopolitical and external economic uncertainties, new property launches were accelerating and buyers were returning to the market. “With the improved market sentiment, developers will accelerate the launch of new projects, and the residential market is expected to further recover,” Ma said. First-hand residential property transactions, after falling for two consecutive months to just over 800 units in June and July, rebounded to 1,100 units in August, while second-hand residential transactions were also gradually stabilising, according to Midland’s data. Ma said that first-hand property transactions in the final quarter would increase by 50 per cent quarter on quarter to 5,100 units, while secondary market transactions would rise by 10 per cent to 12,700. “With residential rents hitting new highs one after another, there is room for property prices to catch up,” Ma said. Benny Sham, research analyst at Midland Research Centre, said developers would continue to offer attractive prices when they launched new home sales, drawing buyers away from the secondary market. “However, based on past experience, strong sales of new properties can boost the housing market and indeed help support transactions and prices in the second-hand residential property market,” he added. Regarding interest rates, Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services, said that even if the US raises rates, Hong Kong banks were not guaranteed to immediately follow suit, or could raise their prime lending rates only slightly. Under a currency peg known as the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong’s monetary policy has moved in lockstep with Fed policy since 1983, so the base rate set by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority always follows the US lead, but commercial banks can decide when and how to adjust their prime and savings rates. With Hong Kong’s latest policy address by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu coming next week, market sources suggested that the government could lower the stamp duty threshold for super-luxury homes. “Although the stamp duty on super-luxury homes was increased in the February budget, as we have consistently stated, demand for super-luxury homes remains very robust,” Sham said. “We’ve seen first-hand residential property transactions exceeding HK$100 million [US$12.8 million] remain active since the stamp duty adjustment in February.” More than 80 first-hand residential property sales exceeding HK$100 million had taken place this year, he added, surpassing the total for the entire previous year in just over eight months, reflecting a market that had already absorbed the stamp duty increase.

title: Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ up for auction for first time in decades
description: Iconic Christina Stambolian gown is estimated to reach US$300,000 at Sotheby’s sale in New York.
content: The “revenge dress” worn by the late Princess Diana in 1994 is up for auction at Sotheby’s for the first time in nearly three decades. The black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian is estimated to fetch as much as £220,000 (US$298,110) when it goes on sale on December 9 during Sotheby’s Luxury Week in New York, the auction house said on Thursday. Diana wore the dress in June 1994 as she arrived at the Serpentine Gallery in London for a fundraising dinner. It gained notoriety because the then Prince Charles – from whom she had been separated for nearly two years but not yet divorced – was widely expected to say in a national television interview broadcast that same evening that he had been unfaithful to her. According to a later documentary, her decision to wear the dress was a last-minute one after initially setting aside a more traditional Valentino outfit. “She wanted to look a million dollars,” her former stylist Anna Harvey said on the programme, according to Vogue. “And she did.” “On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life,” said Morgane Halimi, head of fashion at Sotheby’s. It “gave licence to anyone, but especially women, to use fashion beyond adornment and much more intentionally and meaningfully: as a shield, a weapon or both,” she added. Stambolian’s off-the-shoulder dress features an asymmetric hemline and chiffon train. It will make its first public appearance at Sotheby’s in London during Fashion Week in September, before further exhibitions in Hong Kong and Geneva before it goes to New York for the auction. The dress was previously sold at auction in 1997, according to Sotheby’s, without giving details. In 2023, a black, ballerina-length velvet gown owned by Diana was sold at Julien’s Auctions in Hollywood for US$1,148,080 – 11 times its estimated price. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Maduro’s wife seeks release from US jail, citing worsening heart condition
description: Lawyers request home confinement in New York for former Venezuelan first lady Cilia Flores ahead of June trial.
content: Venezuela’s former first lady wants to be let out of jail while she and her husband await trial on US drug-trafficking charges. Cilia Flores, the wife of ex-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, “deserves the opportunity to await her trial while on home confinement” while dealing with a heart condition that has only got worse since she has been in jail, her lawyers wrote in court papers filed on Wednesday. The lawyers, Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez, asked a judge to allow her to leave a Brooklyn federal jail for a home within the Manhattan federal court district where she and Maduro are scheduled to stand trial next June. There, the lawyers said, she would be under 24-hour-a-day armed surveillance and would only be allowed to see visitors approved by the court and federal prosecutors. The home would be monitored by video and her calls recorded, the lawyers said. Federal prosecutors have yet to file a response. A spokesman for the US attorney’s office in Manhattan declined to comment. The judge, Alvin K. Hellerstein, has yet to rule on Flores’ request. Flores, 69, and Maduro, 63, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since US forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York City. Both have pleaded not guilty to charges alleging that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the US. In a separate court filing, they recently asked that their indictment be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country. Flores’ lawyers said that she has lived for years with a mitral valve prolapse but has not received a monthly injection she needs to manage the ailment since her arrest and subsequent incarceration at the Metropolitan Detention Centre in Brooklyn. Instead, Donnelly and Sanchez said, she has been prescribed baby aspirin, a statin, diltiazem and nitroglycerine as needed for chest pains. She has continually suffered from reflux and gastritis, has lost two molars and shed more than 11.3kg (25 pounds). Flores has been advised by doctors that she should undergo cardiac catheterisation, which could lead to further heart procedures, her lawyers said. If that happens, they said, she “will need adequate time to recover from any procedures in a setting conducive to restoring her health”. Staff at the jail “have been extremely respectful toward her and her husband” and Flores “does not dispute that she has received excellent care from medical professionals” at the jail and hospital, Donnelly and Sanchez said. But, they argued, “a detention centre lacks the conditions needed for such a recovery”.

title: Exclusive | Tech, EV and aerospace executives likely to join Xi’s US trip to mirror Trump team
description: Sources say business leaders are expected to travel to Washington, but the plans may be ‘more about optics’ than concrete results.
content: Beijing is weighing plans to send a group of top tech, electric vehicle and aerospace executives to accompany Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington later this month, as the two sides race to finalise details for the closely watched visit. The South China Morning Post first reported on August 28 that Chinese and US officials were negotiating whether business leaders would join Xi’s delegation to the US. However, details about who might be included have not been previously reported. According to sources, while specifics of the delegation are still being ironed out, China has approached the selection with the aim of modelling the American CEO delegation that followed US President Donald Trump to China earlier this year. This meant that the Chinese delegation was expected to comprise business leaders from the tech, finance, EV and aerospace sectors, they said. One source familiar with the matter said China had yet to formally commit to bringing any business leaders to Washington with Xi. But both Beijing and Washington were treating every aspect of the visit as a matter of reciprocity, including the composition of the business delegation. When Trump travelled to Beijing in May, more than a dozen top American CEOs joined him, including the heads of Tesla, Apple, Nvidia and Boeing. Another source said that top Chinese tech executives would be on the list, with a networking event for business leaders on the agenda during Xi’s visit, which is planned to run from September 23 to 25. According to that source, several Chinese tycoons expected to be part of the delegation have yet to be granted US visas, with Beijing urging Washington to expedite the approval process. The sources, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly comment on the issue, said a Chinese delegation accompanying Xi would be “more about optics than concrete deliverables”, pointing to friction over Chinese investment in the US. The summit will be Xi’s second with Trump this year, but expectations for a breakthrough remain low. The meeting comes amid escalating tensions between the two powers over artificial intelligence (AI), with Washington scrutinising how Chinese firms gain access to advanced chips and accusing Chinese developers of copying leading US models. Beijing has firmly rejected US allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation as groundless and warned that it will retaliate if Washington uses the claims as a pretext to curb China’s development of the technology, which is closing the gap with the US. The two rival economies have also traded tit-for-tat measures in recent weeks, with the US Federal Communications Commission banning the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters, sectors in which China is a global leader. Washington also added more than 40 Chinese companies to its Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act entity list the same month. Beijing retaliated by tightening export controls on drones and sanctioning seven American firms. Negotiations on pending issues could go down to the wire. The sources said Beijing and Washington were planning a meeting between Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in the coming days, shortly before Xi’s trip. That would reflect the timing of the pair’s last meeting, held in Seoul just days before Trump landed in Beijing in May. Bessent and He used those talks to work through thorny economic and trade issues, widely seen at the time as a prelude to the Xi-Trump summit that followed. The sources said that this time, He and Bessent were expected to discuss key deliverables of the May summit: an artificial intelligence dialogue and the Boards of Trade and Investment, mechanisms to manage commercial flows and investment access. They added that while there might be some progress on trade negotiations, talks on the Board of Investment had stalled amid strong pushback from Washington. One source said Beijing had hoped Washington would draw up a list of industries open to Chinese investment, but Washington favoured a case-by-case review. The source said that both Beijing and Washington viewed Xi’s reciprocal visit to Washington very seriously, seeing it as an important opportunity to stabilise relations. Another source said that only the Board of Trade was likely to produce a deliverable. The SCMP reported last month that efforts to get the trade board up and running were in the final stages, focusing on identifying non-sensitive sectors and products eligible for tariff-reduced trade capped at US$30 billion for each side. Citing sources, the report added that Beijing and Washington were also working towards extending a trade truce reached in Busan in October 2025, but that both sides disagreed over how long that extension should be. A separate SCMP report said the Board of Investment was unlikely to be among the deliverables for the Xi-Trump summit in Washington as neither side was ready for discussions with the private sector. Analysts have attributed the lack of progress to differing views in the Trump administration and Congress on the benefits and risks of more Chinese foreign direct investment in the US. Last month, when Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met David Perdue, the US ambassador to Beijing, he said the US-China relationship faced risks and challenges and called on both sides to “remove disruptions and overcome obstacles for high-level exchanges”. Asked about that meeting on Thursday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun stressed that head-of-state diplomacy played an “irreplaceable strategic guiding role” in US-China relations, adding that both countries had maintained communication regarding arrangements for exchanges between their leaders this year.

title: China rebuts top US diplomat Marco Rubio over ‘Communist Party-backed projects’ in Peru
description: Embassy in Lima defends US$30 billion investment stock and takes aim at visa curbs as Fujimori joins Trump’s Shield of the Americas.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks in Peru on Thursday on countering Beijing’s growing footprint around the strategic Chancay megaport, drawing a sharp response from China’s embassy in Lima, which defended its investments and took aim at Washington’s strict visa rules. Rubio met President Keiko Fujimori at the Government Palace, where she confirmed Peru would join the Shield of the Americas, a US-led coalition against organised crime. The Peruvian capital was the last stop of a three-day tour that also took him to Colombia and Ecuador. Fujimori, a conservative who took office in July, has courted Washington on security while protecting its trade with China, which buys 35 to 38 per cent of Peruvian exports. “Projects backed by the Chinese Communist Party bypass Peru’s legal frameworks and pose risks to transparency and data security,” Rubio wrote in the Peruvian newspaper El Comercio ahead of the visit. In its statement on Tuesday, the embassy said China had “never interfered in the internal affairs of other countries” and “never demanded that other countries take sides”. “The western hemisphere is nobody’s backyard,” it added. The embassy borrowed the “western hemisphere” terminology repeatedly used in the Trump administration national security strategy that revived the 19th century Monroe Doctrine last year. That document vowed to deny rivals from outside the region control of “strategically vital assets” there. A separate post took a backhanded swipe at US immigration policy even as it reminded Peruvians they had been able to visit China without a visa for up to 30 days since June last year. “China opens its doors and welcomes the Peruvian people with open arms,” the embassy wrote. “So why do Peruvians, when applying for a visa to a certain country, have to undergo rigorous checks and even face threats that the visas of their entire family will be cancelled?” The post did not explicitly name the United States, which has barred officials across the region who have dealings with Beijing. The exchange has turned Peru into a test case for the Trump administration’s campaign against Chinese influence in Latin America. The country is the second-largest destination for Chinese investment in the region. . In February, Rubio revoked the visas of a Chilean cabinet minister and two other officials over a proposed undersea cable to Hong Kong. Their immediate families were also barred from entering the US. Rubio’s op-ed singled out Chancay, a US$1.3 billion deep water port 80 kilometres (50 miles) north of Lima that opened in November 2024. Chinese state-owned Cosco Shipping holds 60 per cent, with Peruvian miner Volcan owning the rest. Scrutiny of the port intensified in February, when a Peruvian court limited the regulator’s oversight of the terminal. The US State Department warned at the time that “cheap Chinese money costs sovereignty”. In April, Maria Elvira Salazar, the Republican who chairs the House subcommittee on the western hemisphere, said the port had “dual usage” potential and urged Peru’s next government to “take it back”. Rubio also flagged the power sector, where state-owned China Southern Power Grid and China Three Gorges control all electricity distribution in Lima, home to about 10 million people. He presented American investment as the alternative, citing a critical minerals agreement signed in February and US$5 million from the US International Development Finance Corporation for Peruvian mining. This week, the two governments also signed a memorandum on artificial intelligence, while Lima is weighing a purchase of 12 F-16 fighter jets worth about US$2 billion. The embassy’s reply began with a defence of the party itself, which it said worked “for the well-being of the Chinese people” and “for the progress of humanity”. It described Chinese investment in Peru as “transparent and in accordance with the law”, put its stock at more than US$30 billion and said the projects carried “not a single cent of debt”. According to the embassy, China has been Peru’s largest trading partner for 12 consecutive years. Peru has built up a US$52 billion surplus with China since their free-trade agreement took effect in 2010. Senators question US ties as Fujimori joins Shield of the Americas Fujimori’s courtship of Washington has drawn criticism from lawmakers on both the left and the right, including members of her own Popular Force party. At a Senate hearing on Monday, Popular Force senator Juan del Aguila described China as “Peru’s main ally in the Asia-Pacific axis”. He told Foreign Minister Carlos Espa that closer ties with the United States must not come at Beijing’s expense. Leftist senators questioned the terms of Peru’s entry into the Shield of the Americas. Some also doubted the independence of Espa, who spent 15 years as a communications director at the US embassy in Lima. The minister argued the US-led coalition would make Peru far more effective against criminal gangs. Fujimori formalised Peru’s membership of the coalition of more than 15 countries on Thursday, after meeting Rubio at the Government Palace. She said it would give her government tools and information against organised crime and welcomed Trump’s “political decision to look towards Latin America”. Rubio, who called transnational criminal and terrorist groups “the region’s main threat”, pledged US help to confront them. He did not mention China, even when a reporter asked whether Peru would deepen its partnership with Washington despite Chinese investment in Chancay. Rubio focused instead on events in the hemisphere having a direct impact on the United States. Fujimori, on the other hand, did mention Beijing, noting that Peru, the US and China all belonged to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. Lima would “keep selling its minerals, fish and farm products to Asia, Europe and other markets”, she said.

title: Opinion | The Global South cannot afford to let its maritime border disputes fester
description: Cambodia’s compulsory conciliation with Thailand under UN sea law shows how international law can deliver peaceful outcomes before tensions boil over.
content: The ocean looks like peace from afar and truth up close, they say. But beneath the waves, the map of the world’s oceans is far less settled than it looks. Today, dozens of sea borders remain unresolved. Like so many conflicts, they owe their origins to complicated questions of where one country’s territory ends, and another’s begins. Many involve overlapping claims to areas rich in resources; and a disproportionate number concern the waters of the Global South. Africa’s coastline is a stark example. The continent has the highest number of unsettled sea boundaries. These disputes are liabilities, and at the worst possible time. The conflict in the Middle East has shaken energy markets around the world but nowhere has been more exposed than the Global South. This vulnerability is why governments in these regions can no longer afford to leave these borders unsettled. As future chokepoints preventing much-needed resource development, they also risk confrontation and create grey zones ripe for illegal fishing. Global conflicts are not just disrupting energy markets, but the legal order that maritime security, and much else, depends on. The need for governments to engage with these disputes has rarely been more urgent, and there is no better time for the Global South to show how international law can and should provide solutions. Lessons can be drawn from recent developments in the Gulf of Thailand. In May, Thailand withdrew from a 25-year-old memorandum of understanding with Cambodia to resolve their maritime boundary and peacefully develop undersea energy resources valued at over US$300 billion. Rather than escalate, Cambodia initiated compulsory conciliation proceedings under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). Thailand accepted the offer in June, and a commission of international legal experts has now formed to hear the dispute and peacefully work towards a resolution. Cambodia, the smaller nation of the two and in open conflict with Thailand months ago, has secured a hearing on a dispute it could never have won by force. Sceptics will say that any recommendation from the commission will be non-binding on Thailand. This is correct, but not the point. Conciliation produces recommendations, not verdicts. Its value is not in a guaranteed outcome. It is a guaranteed process. One that builds a framework for compromise rather than capitulation, producing a result that can be negotiated rather than imposed. Compulsory conciliation under UNCLOS has only been used once before. Cambodia’s case should send the signal to every other disputing nation that these mechanisms are available and ready to use. And every time they are used adds important weight to a system being undermined by conflict and unilateralism. Invoking legal proceedings against a neighbouring country can appear like an escalation that pre-empts diplomacy. A court verdict might settle the map, but often the relationship between the parties remains volatile. This is a known risk, but the force of the law always remains superior to the law of force. And while it might be tempting to conclude that international law is too blunt to use to settle disputes in sensitive contexts, this view fails to appreciate the richness of the system and range of tools at a government’s disposal. Conciliation is consensus-building by design. Independent conciliators help both sides reach agreement rather than declaring a winner. It preserves the relationship that the dispute threatens by giving a recommendation rather than a ruling. Both parties are then free to take that recommendation forwards. This is not an argument against the courtroom altogether. The virtues of litigation have been shown. Ghana and Ivory Coast welcomed the ruling by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in 2017 that settled their maritime boundary, giving finality to both nations and energy companies operating in the Atlantic Ocean. Litigation is one tool among many, well suited to some contexts and poorly suited to others. And it can be a complementary, rather than exclusive, option. Think of these tools as instruments for different problems, or stages of the same problem. A government can look to conciliation to keep a relationship intact for negotiating issues such as shared resources, but might turn to international courts if unlawful activity is ongoing or presents an urgent risk. These tools are not new. But the persistence of global instability now provides the ultimate incentive to use them. Cambodia did not wait around after its bilateral process collapsed with Thailand. Ghana took its maritime dispute with Togo to UNCLOS arbitration in February, rather than leave it to fester indefinitely – although the process is more adversarial than conciliation, it still signals a reach to the broader toolkit international law offers. And they were not under any illusions about the system they are engaging with. These states have good reason to doubt the fairness of an order they did not design and have been largely disenfranchised from for decades. But it is precisely these states that depend on its functioning. Watching that order fray in the Strait of Hormuz is an argument for reinforcing it at its edges, not abandoning it. Dozens of economies are under a chokehold because of frozen borders, precisely at a moment a conflict has shown what happens when the law of the sea goes unenforced. They need the investment a settled boundary unlocks, and the world also needs proof that international law remains a viable route. Cambodia’s conciliation with Thailand offers a glimpse of what that proof could look like: a boundary being settled at the table rather than by force.

title: Switzerland publishes 200-page dossier on Nazi doctor Mengele, known as ‘Angel of Death’
description: The war criminal was infamous for carrying out horrific medical experiments on inmates at Auschwitz.
content: The Swiss federal intelligence service on Thursday published a 200-page dossier on the notorious Nazi war criminal Josef Mengele, the German doctor known as the “Angel of Death” for conducting horrific medical experiments on prisoners at Auschwitz. During World War II, Mengele served at the Auschwitz extermination camp in Nazi-occupied Poland, where about 1.1 million people were killed, around 1 million of them Jews. He became infamous for carrying out brutal medical experiments on inmates, including children, under the guise of scientific research. After the war, Mengele obtained a Red Cross travel document under a false identity, allowing him to leave Europe. Like many former Nazi officials, he spent years in hiding in Latin America while being pursued internationally for his crimes. He drowned in 1979 while swimming on the coast of Brazil. The documents released by Swiss authorities include material provided to police suggesting that Mengele may have returned to Switzerland after initially fleeing Germany, or may have been planning to enter the country under a false name, according to the German news agency dpa. Historians seeking to establish whether Mengele spent time in Switzerland while being pursued as a war criminal, without Swiss authorities catching him, had long sought access to the files. Swiss authorities had maintained that the documents should remain sealed until 2071 on security grounds and to protect individuals named in them. Historian Gerard Wettstein successfully challenged those restrictions before the Federal Administrative Court, leading to the online publication. Some sections have been redacted to protect sources and the personal data of third parties, authorities said. The dossier was compiled by the police service of the federal prosecutor’s office, a predecessor of Switzerland’s federal intelligence services, and transferred to the Federal Archives in 2001.

title: Canada unveils US$254 million air defence package for Ukraine
description: Kyiv is ‌running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors, as Russia steps up its ballistic missile attacks.
content: Canada ⁠has agreed to a C$350 million (US$254 million) aid package for Kyiv to acquire air defence interceptors, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, after meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Kyiv is ‌running critically low on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of stopping Russia’s ballistic missiles at a time when Moscow is stepping up its attacks. “As Russia escalates its barbaric aerial warfare indiscriminately targeting civilian populations, Ukraine’s air defences are critical,” Carney told reporters in ⁠Calgary. “Earlier today Canada and Ukraine finalised an agreement to deliver critical ‌air defence interceptors … this C$350 million equipment package will help protect Ukraine’s people, infrastructure, and skies,” he said. He ‌did not give details of which interceptors would be delivered ⁠or when ⁠the aid would start flowing. The weapons will be provided through a US programme ‌that allows third-party nations to quickly buy and supply weapons such as Patriot missiles to ‌Ukraine. “I thank ⁠you for this ⁠package. It’s of [the] utmost importance, especially now,” Zelensky said. Canada, ‌one of Ukraine’s most vocal defenders, has committed more than C$25.5 ‌billion in overall aid since Russia invaded in February 2022, including ⁠C$8.5 billion in military aid. Carney also said Canada aimed to ramp ⁠up drone production to be able to produce millions of units within the next two years. A third of those ‌would go to ‌Ukraine, he said. Zelensky said Ukraine needed more technology and funding to produce enough drones to fend ⁠off mass Russian attacks. Canada is home to an estimated 1.3 to 1.4 million people of Ukrainian descent, forming one of the largest Ukrainian diasporas in the world. As part of the ‌deals signed on Thursday, Canada will provide nearly C$435 million in new loan guarantees to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to support energy security in Ukraine, especially during the winter.

title: Chinese scientists boost hydrogen fuel cell power fourfold with new design
description: The proton-transfer breakthrough could improve hydrogen vehicles and space systems, while reducing the use of costly platinum.
content: Chinese scientists have developed a way to generate a fourfold increase in power output of hydrogen fuel cells, an advance that could broaden their use from road vehicles to space missions. Hydrogen is widely viewed as a promising clean energy source for a low-carbon future. Fuel cells convert the chemical energy in hydrogen directly into electricity, producing water as their only exhaust. In a study published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on Thursday, researchers at the Beijing Institute of Technology reported a major advance in proton-exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), the type already used in many hydrogen-powered vehicles. Li Jie, assistant professor with BIT and one of the paper’s authors, said on Thursday that, with the new tech, the “power stack of a fuel cell vehicle can be made smaller and lighter, and the vehicle can get stronger continuous output and a longer driving range”. PEMFCs operate at relatively low temperatures, generally between 60 and 80 degrees Celsius (140 to 176 degrees Fahrenheit). They can convert about 50 to 60 per cent of the energy in their hydrogen fuel into electricity. The process is straightforward: at the anode, hydrogen molecules give up electrons and become protons. While the protons pass through an electrolyte membrane to the cathode, the electrons flow through an external circuit, generating electricity. At the cathode, the protons, electrons and oxygen combine to form water. The bottleneck lies in the speed at which protons can move through the catalyst layer, the part of the fuel cell where chemical reactions take place. For years, industry-standard materials such as Nafion – a synthetic polymer commonly used as a proton-conductor – have tended to form tightly packed structures at the nanoscale when mixed with catalysts. This can slow proton transport and limit the cell’s efficiency. The Chinese team took a different approach, designing a new interface that works like a relay race. Instead of travelling directly to the catalyst surface, protons hop between intermediate “islands”. This arrangement – known as a Brønsted acid-Lewis base interface – greatly speeds the movement of protons. Laboratory tests found that the new material increased proton diffusion tenfold, improved proton conductivity by a factor of 6.5, and more than halved activation energy – the energy barrier protons must overcome before a chemical reaction can occur. Under standard operating conditions, the new fuel-cell design produced four times as much power as conventional designs. It achieved 0.75 watts per sq cm at 0.7 volts while using only a small amount of platinum, the expensive precious-metal catalyst commonly needed in hydrogen fuel cells. Measured by platinum use, the device delivered 6.9 kilowatts of power per gram of the metal, outperforming present state-of-the-art fuel-cell technology. After 30,000 cycles of accelerated stress testing – a repeated charge-and-discharge routine that speeds up ageing – it retained 63 per cent of its initial peak power, compared with just 30 per cent for conventional systems under identical operation conditions. This composite material is well suited for mass production. “In the lab right now, they can make about 100 grams in three days. That’s enough for 10 100-kilowatt-class stacks,” Li Jie said. The researchers said the improvements could be especially valuable in demanding applications such as space missions using liquid oxygen, where fuel-cell efficiency depends heavily on how effectively protons move through the device. “Our technology addresses how to generate power with higher efficiency and higher power density inside a smaller stack volume. This matches what aerospace energy systems need,” Li Jie said. The breakthrough comes as China’s hydrogen sector expands. By the end of 2025, the country’s hydrogen production capacity exceeded 51 million tonnes a year, while China accounted for 53 per cent of renewable-energy-powered hydrogen projects based on electrolysis. According to China Electric Power News in August, more than 130 fuel-cell power plants were operating in the country by 2025, with combined installed capacity exceeding 30 megawatts. More than 20 long-distance hydrogen pipelines are also planned nationwide. China’s 2026 government work report named hydrogen a “new growth point” for the first time. Passenger fuel-cell vehicles remain far less common than battery-electric cars, but official backing remains strong. The country had about 32,000 fuel-cell vehicles on the roads at the end of 2025. In March 2026, three central government ministries set a target of 100,000 such vehicles by 2030. They also called for cutting the retail price of hydrogen from more than 30 yuan (US$4) per kilogram to below 25 yuan. That is considered the point at which hydrogen-powered heavy trucks would become cheaper to operate than diesel models over their full life cycle, including purchase, fuel and maintenance costs. However, substantial hurdles remain. Researchers will need to show that, outside the laboratory, the technology can be manufactured at industrial scale, kept affordable, and validated for long-term safety and reliability. “Fuel cell vehicles don’t need to copy battery EVs. Battery EVs fit short trips. Fuel cells fit heavy trucks, long hauls, and cases that need quick refuelling and long range,” Li Jie said. “Next, the team will build and test high-performance fuel cell stacks for different scenarios. We’ll also scale up the related materials and technology – and turn them into real-world products,” she added.

title: US existing home sales hit weakest pace in over a year
description: Contract closings slipped 2 per cent to an annualised rate of 3.98 million in August, as would-be buyers wait for relief on mortgage rates.
content: Sales of previously owned homes in the United States slowed last month to their weakest pace in more than a year, as would-be buyers waited for relief on mortgage rates before purchasing. Contract closings slipped 2 per cent to an annualised rate of 3.98 million in August, data released on Thursday by the National Association of Realtors showed. Last month marked one of only two times since the autumn of 2024 that sales have dipped below 4 million. The disappointing figures reflect a housing market in desperate need of a catalyst. Home price growth has cooled off from the pandemic era, when annual increases ran into the double digits, but affordability concerns remain a material headwind for buyers. The median sales price rose 1.6 per cent from a year ago to US$429,100, extending a streak of annual price increases dating back to mid-2023. Mortgage rates, now at their highest levels in more than a year, also provide a disincentive to move, especially for people who refinanced a few years ago at borrowing costs less than half that. Nationwide, less than a quarter of outstanding mortgages have rates above 6 per cent, according to a recent housing report from Apollo Global Management. “Mortgage rates and home sales move in opposite directions, so it’s not surprising to see a mild dip in home buying activity due to high mortgage rates,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. Even so, buyers were “not falling apart” amid rising mortgage rates, Yun said on a call with reporters, noting that job and wage gains were helping to support demand. Yun suggested mortgage rates could soon touch 7 per cent, however. One positive sign for the market was the rising number of homes for sale. In August, the supply of previously owned homes on the market reached the highest level since November 2019, increasing 5.9 per cent from a year ago to 1.62 million, the NAR report showed. At the current sales pace, that would equate to 4.9 months of housing supply – the most in more than a decade. The group’s housing affordability index, which measures whether a typical family earns enough to qualify for a mortgage for a median-priced home, also improved. The gauge rose 3.5 per cent from a year ago, though remains historically depressed. Previously owned home sales in the south, the nation’s biggest home-selling region, dropped 1.6 per cent in August to an annualised 1.84 million, the weakest in a year. Sales in the midwest and northeast both fell, while sales in the west were unchanged. First-time buyers accounted for 30 per cent of sales in August, compared with 29 per cent a month earlier.

title: Mainland Chinese pay tribute to Tung Chee-hwa for opening door to Hong Kong
description: Solo-travel scheme introduced in 2003 opened city to millions, shaping unforgettable memories for generation of mainland visitors.
content: Mainland Chinese have paid tribute to Hong Kong’s first chief executive, the late Tung Chee-hwa, for introducing a solo-travel scheme more than two decades ago that opened the city to millions of travellers and created indelible memories for middle-class families. The Individual Visit Scheme has grown from a handful of cities in Guangdong province in 2003 to its current 59 spanning the country as far west as Urumqi in Xinjiang, contributing to a more than fivefold increase in the number of mainland arrivals to Hong Kong. Henry Tang Ying-yen, who served as financial secretary in 2003, framed the scheme as part of a broader effort to align with the mainland’s reform and opening-up while fostering understanding between residents on both sides of the border. “It was introduced in the post-Sars era when cross-boundary exchanges were seriously impeded,” he told the South China Morning Post on Thursday, referring to the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome. “Individual visitors from the mainland contributed to our economy.” Tung, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89, played a key role in getting the central government to approve the scheme by incorporating it into the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement (Cepa), the free-trade deal Hong Kong negotiated with the central government. Soon after travel restrictions were relaxed in four Guangdong cities in July 2003, the Tung administration coordinated with Beijing to broaden the scheme’s scope. Within a month, it was expanded to include the capital and Shanghai. Under the scheme, mainlanders can visit Hong Kong solo for up to seven days each time. According to the government’s yearbook, Hong Kong received 6.83 million mainland visitors in 2002. Last year, the number hit 37.8 million, representing a 453 per cent increase. “I definitely appreciated [Tung]’s efforts in facilitating more mainlanders to travel to Hong Kong,” 24-year-old tourist Jackie Zhu from Liaoning province said, adding that he had travelled to Hong Kong four to five times under the scheme. Zhu said he first visited Hong Kong around 2013 and was impressed by the city’s “sense of age” – old people, old buildings, old streets – along with how international the city felt, with foreigners visible everywhere. “I am very willing to visit Hong Kong as a tourist,” he added. An influencer from the mainland, known as Shou Lou Chu, also paid tribute to Tung in a video that was widely circulated on WeChat, She said the scheme had allowed an ordinary mainland household to eat a bowl of fishball noodles in Mong Kok, buy a phone in Causeway Bay and watch a concert at the Hong Kong Coliseum. “The memories about Hong Kong in our generation were all from there,” she said. Secretary for Culture, Sports, and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui, recalled her time working at the Trade and Industry Department when Tung was negotiating Cepa with mainland authorities. Law said on Wednesday that the solo-travel scheme was incorporated into the deal at the last minute, and she only learned of Tung’s efforts in proposing it to revive Hong Kong’s economy after the agreement was implemented. She said the scheme helped fuel the much-needed rebound in the city’s retail, catering and tourism sectors following the Sars outbreak. Law also recalled joining the Tourism Commission in 2010 and spending the following six years helping expand and manage the scheme, describing it as a “cornerstone” of Hong Kong’s tourism industry. “Mr Tung’s deep love for Hong Kong, and his vision and foresight, continue to benefit the city profoundly to this day,” she said. However, researchers have recently urged Hong Kong to shift its focus from boosting visitor numbers to increasing tourist spending, as mainland arrivals rebound but switch to more selective consumption habits. A joint study by Polytechnic University and consultancy Think China, released in late April, showed mainland visitor arrivals had recovered to about 88 per cent of pre-pandemic levels in 2018. However, high-income travellers are spending less and becoming more value-conscious. Same-day travellers, mainly from the Greater Bay Area, visit more frequently but spend less, with median spending of about 1,000 yuan (US$149) per trip.

title: ICAC charges ex-HKEX vice-president over alleged failure to declare assets
description: Geoffrey Tong faces a count of failing to comply with a notice issued under the Prevention of Bribery Ordinance, Hong Kong’s corruption watchdog says.
content: A former vice-president of Hong Kong’s stock exchange operator has been charged by the city’s corruption watchdog with allegedly failing to comply with a statutory order to declare his assets during a probe. Geoffrey Tong Po‑hang, 39, former vice-president of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), faces a count of failing to comply with a notice issued under the Prevention of Bribery Ordinance, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said on Thursday. He was released on bail pending his plea at Eastern Court on Friday. ICAC officers served Tong with a notice in September last year requiring him to furnish a statutory declaration detailing property, expenditures and liabilities over the preceding three years. It extended the deadline to March this year on Tong’s request. Prosecutors allege Tong, without reasonable excuse, failed to comply with the March 12 deadline by neglecting to provide information on 30 cash deposits totalling more than HK$2.1 million (US$153,017) made to his bank account. Under the ordinance, if there are reasonable grounds to suspect a person of committing a corruption offence, investigating officers may apply to the Court of First Instance for an order requiring the individual to submit a statutory declaration detailing their property, expenditure and liabilities. An ICAC spokesman described corruption as “a highly insidious crime” and stressed that its legal powers under the ordinance were designed to ensure effective investigations. HKEX has pledged its full cooperation with the ongoing probe, the spokesman added.

title: Huawei racketeering trial in US enters second day of testimony
description: Prosecutors allege a 20-year ‘culture of crime’, while defence says Huawei’s success was built on innovation, not theft.
content: Key witnesses are expected to testify in Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies’ landmark criminal case on Thursday in Brooklyn, New York, as it enters its second day of testimony. It comes after a US government lawyer told federal jurors on the opening day that Huawei engaged in criminal activities to achieve “growth at any cost”, while a lawyer for the company said that Huawei employees deemed to have broken company policies were punished for their actions. Brian Heberlig, of US law firm Steptoe, also said on Wednesday in his opening statement that the 2021 admission of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou to violating US sanctions on Iran should not be viewed as a “confession” as Meng did not admit to deliberately deceiving any government officials or banks, or that anyone else at Huawei acted with criminal intent. The admission was part of a “negotiated statement of fact” reached with the US government, the defence lawyer said. The remarks were a response to the opening statement by the federal prosecution, which highlighted Meng’s admission made “under oath” as key evidence that Huawei became one of the world’s leading telecoms companies through “theft, lies [and] cover-ups”. Justice Department lawyer Taylor Stout told jurors that a “culture of crime” had existed at Huawei for over 20 years, stemming from the top leadership including founder Ren Zhengfei and his daughter Meng. Meng, Huawei’s chief financial officer, spent almost three years under house arrest after being arrested in Canada in 2018 on suspicion of violating US sanctions on Iran and bank fraud. In 2021, she reached a deal with the US government that saw her agree to sign on to a "statement of facts", which included admission of some wrongdoing, and prosecutors withdrawing their extradition request, allowing Meng to return to China. Stout said that Huawei had been run as a criminal enterprise for decades, stealing technology from US companies such as T-Mobile and Cisco, violating US sanctions by doing business in Iran and lying to international financial institutions including HSBC. He told jurors that they would soon see evidence in court showing that Huawei employees were following company policy as they engaged in “a pattern of criminal activity lasting 20 years”, including video of a Huawei employee stealing a robot part from T-Mobile and testimony from former Huawei employees. However, Heberlig accused prosecutors of “cherry-picking” isolated incidents to label Huawei as a long-running criminal enterprise when in fact its success is based on “competition not conspiracy” and “innovation not theft”. “[The prosecution] will ask you to infer a grand plan based on disconnected incidents, but the evidence won’t show that,” he told the courtroom in the Eastern District of New York, where the case is being heard. Huawei has been charged with 14 criminal counts including bank fraud, money laundering and racketeering conspiracy, with the alleged criminal activity dating back as early as 1999. Meng’s 2021 deal with the US government is expected to be a major flashpoint in the trial as prosecutors look to present it as key evidence of Huawei’s top-down criminal culture, while the defence seeks to minimise its importance. How Meng’s admission may be used in evidence in the trial was a major subject of debate in the pre-trial litigation between the two legal teams, with US District Judge Ann Donnelly ultimately allowing those earlier admissions to be used in the trial. Heberlig said on Wednesday that Huawei merely “adopted” that statement, including through a press release released after Meng was allowed to return to China in 2021 that said the company would continue to defend itself against the US government’s charges. Prosecutors said in a pre-trial court filing that they sought to call Meng to testify at the trial with a guarantee that she would not be detained during her stay in the US, though she is not expected to testify at the trial.

title: Ex-China volleyballer Wang Yunlu says missing Paris Olympics made her feel like a ‘failure’
description: Outside hitter breaks her silence on being dropped by head coach Cai Bin just before the 2024 Games, a decision that sparked public backlash.
content: Former China national volleyball player Wang Yunlu tearfully confessed, in an in-depth video interview released on Wednesday, that her career felt like a “failure” after being dropped from the Paris Olympics roster at the last minute. Wang spent more than two years as an indispensable starter during the Paris Olympic cycle, stepping up when stars Zhu Ting and Zhang Changning were sidelined with injury. However, she was left off the final squad following the return of key veterans and roster constraints, the decision triggering fierce public backlash against head coach Cai Bin. Speaking candidly about her omission in the interview hosted by Shen Qunqi, a presenter for Shanghai Radio and Television’s sports channel, Wang struggled to hold back tears. “Failing to make it to Paris, I still feel that I am a failure,” she said. Despite the painful outcome, Wang harboured no resentment towards Cai, emphasising that she remained deeply grateful for his mentorship after he revived her international career. Born in 1996, Wang rose to prominence early by winning best outside hitter at the World Youth Championship. However, after years away from the national team during her peak, she was recalled before the Paris cycle. Initially a bench player behind Li Yingying and Jin Ye, Wang eventually earned a starting spot through her dependable service reception and out-of-system scoring, playing a pivotal role as a supporting player in China’s silver-medal finish at the Volleyball Nations League. Recalling her final conversation with Cai before leaving the team, Wang said she could feel the coach’s reluctance to let her go. “There are too many things in life beyond one’s control. It is not your fault,” Wang told him at the time. “No matter what position you put me in, I will do my job well. “In the end, I feel I fully delivered on that,” Wang added. “Then he sincerely said to me, ‘Thank you’, and my tears just flowed.” Wang pointed to her crucial contributions in helping China secure Olympic qualification, notably during the Nations League leg in Rio de Janeiro, shortly before her departure, where she helped the team beat the United States and Serbia. “If we had lost those two matches, we wouldn’t have made it to the Paris Olympics,” Wang said. “I believe that if I didn’t bloom here, I will bloom somewhere else in the second half of my life. Gold will always shine.” Yet the heartbreak of missing the Olympics continues to linger. Wang revealed that she still seeks reassurance from her mother. “Even now, I still ask my mother if my volleyball career was quite a failure,” Wang said. “She tells me, ‘No, you are very successful. So many people couldn’t achieve what you have’.” When asked if she would choose the same path given another chance, Wang did not hesitate. “Of course I would join the national team,” she said. “For anyone who plays volleyball, the ultimate goal and highest ceiling is the national team. That is the direction you have to strive for.” As clips from the interview went viral and rekindled online criticism against team management and former teammates, Wang issued a statement on social media on Thursday to clarify her intentions. “My main intention in participating in this interview was to share my volleyball journey with fans and spread positive energy to younger players,” Wang wrote. “I do not want my interview clips taken out of context, and I especially hope people will not cyberbully my former teammates. “I have never implicitly targeted anyone in the interview,” she added. “I believe most fans are rational, and I hope everyone continues to support the Chinese women’s volleyball team.”

title: US producer inflation tops expectations as energy costs jump amid Iran war
description: The Producer Price Index was up 5.4 per cent year-on-year last month, a significant acceleration from the 4.8 per cent rise in July.
content: US wholesale inflation picked up more than expected in August, government data showed Thursday, driven by higher energy costs in the month – particularly for diesel – as the US war with Iran continued. Rising prices at the pump are squeezing US households and businesses weeks ahead of key midterm elections, pressuring President Donald Trump’s administration, as average diesel costs hit new highs. The Producer Price Index (PPI) was up 5.4 per cent year-on-year last month, the Department of Labour said. This was a significant acceleration from the 4.8 per cent rise in July and above the 5.3 per cent that economists expected in a consensus forecast published by MarketWatch. On a month-on-month basis, PPI rose by 0.4 per cent, in line with analysts’ expectations published by MarketWatch. Energy costs jumped by 4.2 per cent over the month, notably boosted by the cost of diesel fuel, which surged 24.1 per cent, the Labour Department report said. The costs of regular petrol and diesel in the United States have risen since US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran in late February prompted Tehran to choke off the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation. The waterway is a crucial route for global energy transit. The price of diesel, the fuel needed for road hauling and agriculture, has rocketed to a new record in the United States this week. It now stands at a national average of US$5.98 per gallon, significantly up from the year-ago average of US$3.71 per gallon, according to the AAA motorists’ association. While Trump has vowed that oil prices would cool as soon as the US wins the war, the conflict has hit an impasse more than six months after it started. The US leader is under pressure to end fighting as the November midterm elections approach, with his supporters – including farmers – growing increasingly frustrated. Steeper costs for the diesel used to fuel farm equipment has added to expenses over the fall harvest season. On Thursday, government data showed that costs for petrol, jet fuel, home heating oil, alongside confectionery and nuts, also rose. Also Thursday, the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond climbed to 5.35 per cent, hitting its highest level since 2007. All eyes are now turning to the Consumer Price Index, a key gauge of consumer inflation due to be released on Friday, for the overall bearing these figures may have on US interest rates. The Federal Reserve’s rate-setting committee is due to meet next week and high inflation could push policymakers towards raising rates. Airfares, hospital care and doctor services all grew more expensive last month, with airfares jumping 4.2 per cent. Those measures are all included in the Fed’s preferred gauge and their increases could make a rate increase more likely. With wholesale inflation “still looking relatively hot, the Fed seems likely to hike this year even if it doesn’t pull the trigger this month”, wrote Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics. Already, the CME Group’s FedWatch tool puts the likelihood of a 25 basis points rate increase at nearly 70 per cent for next week’s meeting. “It is likely to be a close call on whether the FOMC decides to raise rates next week,” said Nationwide senior economist Ben Ayers, referring to the Federal Open Market Committee. “Headline producer prices were pushed higher predominantly by the jump in diesel fuel costs over August,” Ayers said. “But the Iran war and resulting supply chain disruptions also continue to add pressure to goods costs beyond energy and food,” he added in a note. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: US Navy plans compact Silent Anvil torpedo as China’s submarine fleet surges
description: The weapon is expected to be air-launched and suitable for use across a range of platforms.
content: As China expands its submarine fleet, the US Navy is looking to develop a compact air-launched torpedo that could enable more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to attack submarines from farther away. The US Naval Air Systems Command issued a request for information – a step towards development – to industry in late August for the Silent Anvil Air-Launched Torpedo (SAA-LT). While air-launching a torpedo from stand-off range is not new – the US Navy already has the High Altitude Anti-Submarine Warfare Weapon Capability (HAAWC) – the SAA-LT would be much smaller. HAAWC adds a glide kit to a Mark 54 lightweight torpedo and can be launched by P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft from altitudes of up to 30,000 feet (9,140 metres). According to the request for information, the navy wants the new weapon to weigh up to 268lbs (122kg) while measuring up to 70 inches (178cm) long and 7.5 inches (19cm) in diameter – dimensions intended to broaden the range of aircraft that could carry it. The requirements also envisage that Silent Anvil would be compatible with aircraft carrier storage and handling systems, potentially allowing carrier-based platforms to field the weapon. The US Navy said it was considering two approaches: a new integrated weapon designed to glide into the water before homing acoustically on its target, or a glide kit fitted to an existing torpedo. The glide system could receive targeting updates during flight, helping it to release the torpedo closer to the submarine’s expected location. Once in the water, the torpedo would use its own acoustic sensor to find and attack the target. The document does not mention China, nor does it name any potential adversary. But it comes as Beijing expands and modernises its submarine fleet amid intensifying US-China military competition in the western Pacific. Peter Jones, a retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral and an adjunct professor with the Naval Studies Group at UNSW Canberra, said Silent Anvil could potentially enable many more crewed and uncrewed aircraft to serve as delivery platforms for weapons. “The overall effect will be a more responsive anti-submarine capability,” Jones said. “For an adversary submariner, it means that any air platform could be a weapon carrier.” But Jones said the Silent Anvil’s usefulness would also depend on whether the weapon could be produced cheaply enough to be widely deployed, while the aircraft carrying it would still rely on air, surface and underwater systems to find submarines. Lyle Goldstein, director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities, said spreading the mission across more platforms could be particularly valuable because specialised US anti-submarine warfare aircraft such as the P-8 were few in number. Large, slow anti-submarine warfare aircraft could struggle to operate in the vast and highly contested airspace of the Asia-Pacific, potentially increasing the value of drones operating from “very remote locations under austere conditions”, he added. While separating detection platforms from those that attack submarines could make better use of resources, it could also complicate operations, Goldstein observed, citing the enormous distances involved, attempts to jam communications and attacks on logistics nodes. James Holmes, a professor of maritime strategy at the US Naval War College who was speaking in a personal capacity, said that while the Silent Anvil concept “shows a lot of promise”, its effectiveness would have to be shown in practice. “The difficulty here is ensuring connectivity among elements of the force,” Holmes said, especially as China’s “systems destruction warfare” concept involved disrupting the networks that allowed an adversary’s forces to operate together, including through electronic warfare. The push to broaden US options for attacking submarines comes as Beijing rapidly builds up its undersea fleet. Rear Admiral Mike Brookes, head of the US Office of Naval Intelligence, told a congressional commission in March that China could have up to 80 submarines by 2035, roughly half of them nuclear-powered – a major shift for a force that has historically relied heavily on conventionally powered boats. The build-up is not only about numbers. China is also developing new submarine designs. The South China Morning Post reported in July that satellite imagery and expert analysis indicated a previously unidentified attack submarine at Shanghai’s Jiangnan Shipyard. Its propulsion type remains uncertain. Meanwhile, another next-generation nuclear-powered design has been spotted at Bohai Shipyard in Liaoning province, northeast China. According to Goldstein, China’s newer nuclear-powered attack submarines could pose a growing challenge by operating farther into the central and eastern Pacific. “As this challenge grows, the US will be forced to devote more effort to the anti-submarine threat.” Holmes observed that the undersea competition could increasingly resemble the Cold War rivalry between the navies of the US and the then Soviet Union, particularly in relation to a potential conflict involving Taiwan. He compared the first island chain – an arc of islands from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines that underpins the US security strategy in the region – to the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap, a key Cold War passage for Soviet submarines entering the Atlantic. Holmes described both as geographic barriers to a wider ocean. “We are back to the future,” he said. According to Holmes, the Luzon Strait and the Bashi Channel south of Taiwan are obvious routes for People’s Liberation Army Navy submarines seeking access to the western Pacific. The depth and underwater conditions of these waterways would make them difficult places for submarine hunters, while frequent rough weather could further complicate operations above the surface, he said. If successfully developed, Silent Anvil would be “highly relevant” in such a scenario, in his view. “Any system that would help seal up the PLA Navy’s access to the western Pacific would help the US and its allies stiffen a ‘denial defence’,” Holmes said. Goldstein said he expected the US Navy to be closely coordinating potential anti-submarine operations with Australia and especially Japan, including through sharing technology and tactics. Any conflict could require large stocks of anti-submarine weapons at forward bases in those countries, he said, but those bases and logistics nodes could be vulnerable to Chinese missile and drone strikes. Companies have until September 29 to respond to the request, which calls for a complete system demonstration within 18 months of a development agreement, followed by production of about 180 prototype weapons over the following three years.

title: Record China-US gap in bond yields unlikely to trigger capital flight: Marsh Investment
description: Executives say dollar dominance remains intact as borrowers diversify funding and use offshore yuan bonds to help manage elevated US financing costs.
content: The widening yield spread between Chinese and American government bonds is unlikely to trigger catastrophic capital flight from China, according to investment executives at Marsh Investment, who attribute the record spread to the United States’ fiscal pressures and global macro trends rather than a structural retreat for Chinese assets. The spread between benchmark 10-year US Treasury bonds and equivalent Chinese sovereign bonds hit a record 3.17 percentage points this week. Yields on US Treasury bonds rose to 4.85 per cent – their highest level since 2023 – while China’s 10-year yield held at 1.68 per cent. While the expanding gap has raised fears that higher US returns could siphon capital away from Chinese assets and weigh on the yuan, executives at Marsh Investments – formerly known as Mercer – downplayed the risk during a media briefing on Thursday. “In the pantheon of things driving broader moves in the dollar and US rates, we do not see [capital flight] as a major impact compared with other forces at play,” said Niall O’Sullivan, global chief investment officer at Marsh. O’Sullivan attributed elevated long-term US yields to global supply-demand imbalances, expanding US national debt and heavy corporate borrowing – particularly across the tech and artificial intelligence sectors. The unusually wide yield gap has also fed broader debate about whether the combination of high US borrowing costs and mounting government debt could eventually weaken the dollar’s dominance in global finance. To become the replacement reserve currency, a huge amount of plumbing has to go into the system Niall O’Sullivan, Marsh Investment Addressing market speculation that the yield divide could accelerate “de-dollarisation” or erode the dollar’s reserve status, O’Sullivan expressed scepticism. Reserve-currency status, he said, required decades of financial infrastructure to build. He compared it with the way the British pound remained a reserve currency long after the United Kingdom’s trading dominance faded. “To become the replacement reserve currency, a huge amount of plumbing has to go into the system,” O’Sullivan said, adding that no alternative yet matched the dollar’s liquidity and scale. Mike Sebastian, global head of multi-asset at Marsh, agreed that talk of de-dollarisation was “a bit overblown” in the near term, with no dramatic shifts expected in the foreseeable future. Rather than fleeing mainland assets outright, global borrowers and tech “hyperscalers” were adapting to high US borrowing costs by diversifying their funding bases, according to the investment team. This includes increasing the issuance of offshore yuan “dim sum” bonds to lower overall capital costs. The executives’ comments came as Chinese authorities step up oversight of cross-border transactions and offshore earnings to curb capital leakage. Despite the recent scrutiny, Marsh expects cross-border flows to remain resilient over the long term. While policy tightening has generated “some concern” over near-term cross-border flows, fundamental demand will continue to support the market once temporary market noise subsides, according to Graham Elliot, the firm’s Asia head of investments and retirement. “I think the feeling is that this will play out,” said Elliot, who has operated in Hong Kong for a decade, adding that fundamental cross-border demand would evolve and continue to underpin the regional market.

title: Lives ‘at serious risk’ as Gaza’s hospitals, homes battle fuel shortages
description: Doctors say hospitals have resorted to rotating power cuts between buildings, putting patients in ‘severe danger’.
content: As power cuts cascade through one of Gaza’s largest functioning hospitals and patients wait for treatment in sweltering wards, doctors warn that shortages of engine oil and spare parts are causing generators to seize up, putting lives at risk. The crisis is spreading beyond hospitals, where soaring costs for oil and diesel are making electricity from neighbourhood generators increasingly unaffordable for families that depend on it. Gaza has been without grid electricity since the start of Israel’s military offensive in the territory, launched in response to the ‌Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023. Israel halted electricity supply and restricted the import of fuel as well as engine oil, describing them as measures to punish Hamas. Those restrictions have continued despite an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire that brought an end to full-scale fighting but has failed to halt Israeli attacks, secure Hamas’ disarmament or relieve Gaza’s humanitarian and energy crises. Ahmed Al-Nabris, an internal medicine specialist at Nasser Hospital, said shortages of fuel, engine oil and spare parts had forced the hospital into an austerity plan that includes rotating power cuts between buildings. “Patients are in severe danger, because any power cut puts their lives at serious risk,” said Nabris. One of the hospital’s four generators is now out of service, and the largest two of ⁠the remaining three are under strain, he said. Normally, engine oil in generators should be changed every 250 operating hours, but shortages have forced technicians to extend that interval to around 1,000 hours. Al-Nabris ‌said the hospital’s electrical system had suffered repeated damage since an Israeli military raid in early 2024. A solar energy system was destroyed and never replaced, while both a main and backup generator were lost. Israel has accused Palestinian militants of using Gaza hospitals as bases. Fatima Abu Taima, a patient at ‌Nasser Hospital who suffers from pulmonary fibrosis, says those needing to be hooked to a ventilator or nebuliser have to wait as electricity is rotated among departments. “We keep waiting, ⁠counting down the seconds and minutes,” she said. “You ⁠have to wait for the electricity to come back.” The mother of four said her condition had worsened since the outbreak of war in 2023, forcing her to move into the hospital. Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said in a statement in ‌August that thousands faced greater risks of illness and death because restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts were undermining hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps and water trucks. Dwindling supplies had forced humanitarian groups to turn to the local market, it said, ‌where locals ‌say prices have surged to US$1,300 per litre from about US$3 before the war. Israel’s COGAT military agency, which controls access to Gaza, said in a statement that a mechanism coordinated with the international community facilitates ‌the entry of engine oil, generator spare parts, ambulances and other hospital equipment into Gaza under monitoring and oversight. COGAT said that mechanism was “aimed at preventing advanced equipment from falling into the hands of Hamas and ⁠ensuring that such equipment reaches the population directly”.
