Beyond hospitals, the shortage has hit Gaza’s network of private and neighbourhood generators that provide homes with a few ⁠hours of electricity a day. Palestinian and UN records showed earlier this year that at least two-thirds of Gaza’s population of about 2 million were still living in more than 1,000 displacement sites across the territory, with severe shortages of water and electricity. Residents say only a tiny portion can afford to pay for private generators. Yasser Ashour, who sells electricity ‌from generators he owns, said that despite the pressing ‌need for steady power supplies – especially for those with medical conditions or serious injuries – staying in business had become increasingly difficult as prices for engine oil, diesel and spare parts had soared. The shortages had driven up the cost of electricity supplies to homes around 20-fold in the past months, residents said. Still, many have little choice but to pay. Alaa Al-Hourani, 65, who suffers from liver fibrosis and low oxygen levels, said his struggles to secure costly food and water sometimes left him unable to afford electricity. “It is suffocating and agonising, but there is nothing we can do. We have nothing but cardboard to fan ourselves,” he said.

title: AI bottleneck-breaker: China’s Huawei touts high-speed optical module
description: Company claims it has the industry’s first 7.2-terabit-per-second NPO module, as firms race to set next-generation AI infrastructure standards.
content: Huawei Technologies has unveiled a high-speed optical module designed to eliminate bottlenecks in artificial intelligence infrastructure, staking an early claim in the race to set standards for next-generation data centre connections. The Shenzhen-based tech giant showcased what it called the industry’s first 7.2-terabit-per-second (Tbps) near-packaged optics (NPO) product at the China International Optoelectronic Exposition (CIOE) in Shenzhen this week. The technology replaces traditional copper wiring with light-based signals to shuttle vast amounts of data between AI processors at higher speeds and lower power consumption than current systems. As AI clusters grow to include thousands of interlinked processors, conventional copper connections are hitting physical limits in bandwidth, transmission distance and power efficiency. NPO aims to solve this by bringing optical components closer to network switching chips, shortening electrical connections and reducing signal loss and power consumption. Huawei’s module combined 36 channels operating at 200 gigabits per second each, giving it an aggregate bandwidth of 7.2Tbps, according to Man Jiangwei, director of Huawei’s advanced optoelectronics laboratory. The capacity puts the module among a new generation of high-density optical interconnect products emerging for AI systems, alongside 6.4Tbps optical engines developed for co-packaged optics by US chipmaker Broadcom. “We have already fully entered the product development stage,” Man said in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Thursday. “Once the whole supply chain and manufacturing system is in place, I believe it won’t be long before we can move quickly into volume production.” Despite technical progress, a lack of unified industry standards remains a major hurdle to commercialising NPO at scale, as component makers, equipment suppliers and chipmakers currently use different designs. “The biggest bottleneck is getting everyone to speak the same language,” Man said. Huawei is stepping up efforts to shape these emerging specifications. While standard-setting typically took 18 to 24 months, strong industry participation was accelerating the process, Man said. The company expected 3.2Tbps NPO modules to start seeing real-world deployment this year, with 7.2Tbps versions gaining traction over the next two years as supply chains matured, he said. Chinese manufacturers dominate the global optical transceiver supply chain. Domestic firms supplied nearly two-thirds of global optical transceivers by volume and accounted for around 60 per cent of optical data communications transceiver revenue in 2025, according to data released last month by Counterpoint Research. Domestic rivals including InnoLight and Eoptolink also displayed next-generation optical engines at CIOE.

title: Indonesia rescues 6 orangutans from forest fires in a week
description: The apes were saved from plantations in West Kalimantan province, where they got stuck after fires cut off access to their forest home.
content: Six orangutans including two nursing infants have been rescued from fires raging on Borneo island in the past week, Indonesian authorities and rescuers said on Thursday, bringing the total to 15 in a month. The apes were saved from plantations in deep rural West Kalimantan province, on the Indonesian part of the island, where they got stuck after fires cut off access to their forest home, according to the forestry ministry and the YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation. A large fire was burning just 200 metres (656 feet) from where the group of critically endangered primates were found, the ministry and YIARI said in a joint statement. “This situation left the orangutans without a safe route back to their habitat; they could only move from one plantation to another,” the statement said. “In addition to facing the threat of flames and smoke, the orangutans’ movement among plantations also has the potential to increase interactions and conflict with [human] communities.” Four orangutans were rescued on Friday, with the help of residents and plantation workers, followed by another mother-infant pair on Tuesday. Rescuers had to anaesthetise the animals to minimise stress and the risk of injury. All six were taken to YIARI’s rehabilitation centre in the town of Ketapang. Orangutans are endemic to Borneo and Sumatra islands – two of the places hardest hit by wildfires that have destroyed vast swathes of land and spewed putrid haze that has spread as far as Malaysia and Singapore. The Indonesian government said more than 202,000 hectares of land burned countrywide between January and July. Figures for August have yet to be released. The Nusantara Atlas project has put the number at closer to 300,000 hectares, and on Thursday gave an estimate of 895,657 hectares, which includes August. Last week the European Union’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service said the haze emitted by the fires was the worst for any month of August in 24 years. Indonesia’s dry season typically runs from July to October, made worse this year by a strong episode of the El Nino weather phenomenon. Wildfires emit dangerous levels of PM2.5 particles so small they can enter deep into the lungs and even the bloodstream, with potentially dire consequences for health. According to Greenpeace estimates using government data, some 35 million people in Indonesia are exposed to toxic haze. Some 43,000 firefighters were deployed to combat the blazes, national disaster mitigation agency spokesman Berton Panjaitan told reporters in Jakarta on Thursday. He said a Japanese navy ship had arrived in West Kalimantan with three helicopters to aid water-bombing efforts.

title: Disney+ K-drama Made in Korea season 2: Hyun Bin returns for dark 1980s political thriller
description: South Korea’s history continues to be explored in the series, as Hyun Bin’s Ki-tae navigates the 1979 assassination of leader Park Chung-hee.
content: Lead cast: Hyun Bin, Jung Woo-sung, Woo Do-hwan Over the past several years, the allure of South Korea’s dark modern history – particularly the men who stalked the corridors of power – has become one of the country’s most reliable sources of prestige entertainment and commercial success. This September, viewers can flock to cinemas to catch the big-budget period thriller The Assassin(s), which chronicles the 1974 attempt on South Korean president Park Chung-hee that killed his wife, first lady Yuk Young-soo. They can then stream the second season of Disney+’s Made in Korea, which opens with a fictionalised account of his 1979 assassination. Several major films have covered this turning point in Korean history before. In 2023, Made in Korea co-star Jung Woo-sung featured in 12.12: The Day, which chronicles the coup d’état that followed in the wake of Park’s death. The assassination has been depicted in films such as Im Sang-soo’s The President’s Last Bang (2005) and The Man Standing Next (2020), from Made in Korea filmmaker Woo Min-ho. This makes Woo the first director to depict the incident twice on screen, raising the question: have filmmakers returned to this well once too often? As seen with its slick first season, Made in Korea is a curious amalgam of dark political history and thrilling entertainment. It builds a fabricated tale of greed and crime around real-life events, though the characters based on real figures have had their names changed. This approach is not entirely new. We can look back on the ambitious prosecutor saga The King (2017) – once again featuring Jung – which follows fictional characters playing power games around real events over several decades, or the 2025 Netflix series Aema, which colourfully reimagines the making of a landmark 1980s erotic drama. However, Made in Korea is more brazen than its predecessors. It hews much closer to real historical events while filtering them through a distorted dramatic lens that reframes the narrative. Season one opened with the 1970 hijacking of Japan Airlines Flight 351 by Japanese communists and introduced Hyun Bin’s fictional Korean Central Intelligence Agency (KCIA) operative Baek Ki-tae, who smuggles drugs on the plane yet becomes the hero of the day by saving everyone on board. The new season opens nine years later, by which time Ki-tae has risen through the ranks and brings in massive profits with his drug operation. Park, the president, looks favourably upon Ki-tae and seems poised to elevate him to director of the KCIA, until the fateful events of October 26, when Ki-tae’s superior – the current KCIA director – rashly kills the president. Ki-tae’s reaction to the incident prompts him to orchestrate the aftermath of the assassination, leading to the outcome that history has already taught us – just not for the same reasons. Jung’s character, Jang Geon-young, a dogged and oddly kooky prosecutor, sits out the start of the season after being beaten by Ki-tae and jailed at the conclusion of season one. He returns near the end of episode two, and it remains to be seen what part he will play in the story. Stepping up in a larger capacity this season is Woo Do-hwan as Ki-tae’s principled younger brother, Ki-hyeon, a military officer who is forced to investigate his own sibling in the wake of the assassination. While the socio-historical intentions of Made in Korea remain somewhat opaque, there is no denying this second season is an even more impressive affair than the first. The pacing is swift, the performances are frosty and controlled, and plenty of set pieces give the season an exciting start. Following his alignment with the Park administration of the 1970s, it will be interesting to see how Ki-tae’s character trajectory dovetails with the terrible events that punctuated the 80s under the Chun Doo-hwan regime. Social unrest around the edges is already pointing towards the Gwangju massacre, which took place only a few months after Chun’s rise to power. Ki-tae is the suave anti-hero who soared to the top and beat the man investigating him at the end of last season. However, given the democratic future ahead for South Korea, one imagines the coming episodes may chronicle his reverse trajectory as he falls from grace and, perhaps, finally has a change of heart. Made in Korea season two is streaming on Disney+.

title: Investment surge in Central Asia drives calls for expanded use of Chinese yuan
description: Use of the currency can cut risks and costs for infrastructure firms active in the mineral-rich region, according to speakers on an investment panel.
content: Expanding use of the Chinese yuan in fast-growing Central Asia, where China is a top investor, can reduce risks and costs for infrastructure firms, part of a broader trend that sees the currency gaining ground wherever commercial flows create demand for it, according to speakers on an investment panel in Hong Kong on Thursday. Smoother access to the yuan would lower risks inherent in currency exchanges, particularly when the more internationalised US dollar is trending strong, and bring down the costs of exporting equipment from China, speakers said during a discussion on yuan internationalisation at the Belt and Road Summit. “The internationalisation of the renminbi is particularly important to us because most of our equipment is manufactured in China and shipped over,” said Long Jisheng, chairman and CEO of the Shanghai-based waste management firm SUS Environment. In the infrastructure industry, where margins are razor-thin, exchange-rate fluctuations could wipe out profits entirely, he noted. To resolve this, Long said that Chinese enterprises needed a closed-loop financial system fully denominated in yuan, spanning investment, financing, procurement and returns. This financial strategy is becoming increasingly critical in the five-country Central Asian region, which has captured global attention in recent years because of untapped mineral resources. According to the Yorktown Institute, more than 11,000 enterprises with Chinese capital operate there. SUS is one of them. “Many of these countries are small, and it’s difficult to achieve complete domestic production there due to their limited scale,” Long said. “Therefore, internationalisation allows us to reduce our financing costs and mitigate exchange-rate risks. We are very much looking forward to this.” Panellists pointed to use of the yuan in Southeast Asia and Africa as proof the Chinese currency, though unconvertible in much of the world, had a role where there was demand. “How the adoption develops really depends on the corridor and reflects commercial flows,” said Karen Ng, global head of yuan engagement with Standard Chartered. “For example, in Southeast Asia, adoption is largely driven by the supply chain, manufacturing and procurement needs, [while] in the Middle East and parts of Africa … commodities, energy and infrastructure also provide the practical entry points.” Hong Kong, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates are now among the top offshore spots today for circulating the yuan. The most successful yuan internationalisation “models” around the world hinged on actual commercial flows, expansion beyond a single transaction method and local and international “connectivity”, Ng said. Looking ahead, Long predicted the “biggest catalyst” for wider yuan adoption in Central Asia would be successful benchmark infrastructure projects. Managing a project’s “full life-cycle” with stable returns would boost local regulators’ confidence, transitioning the currency’s use from “isolated cases to normalised development”, he said. Kazakhstan, a key partner in China’s Belt and Road Initiative, also sees growing demand for the currency. Timur Onzhanov, deputy management board chairman of Baiterek National Investment Holding – a state-owned body supporting Kazakhstan’s economic growth – said that local companies shifting towards exporting “processed goods” needed “sophisticated renminbi settlement trades”. He urged better connectivity between Chinese and Kazakh financial platforms, suggesting that investors should have access to suitable equity and insurance products, and that overall export support should be strengthened. “It’s time to connect these platforms and also help them to enable a suitable financial means between China and Kazakhstan,” he said. Several large Chinese banks operate in Kazakhstan, the largest Central Asian country by population and land area. In June, a 70-person delegation from Hong Kong and mainland China to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan generated 96 deals worth US$1.65 billion.

title: Trump threatens Taiwan’s representative office, sparking debate over island’s US policy
description: Ahead of expected Xi-Trump summit, some in Taiwan question whether Taipei’s funding of American think tanks has become a political liability.
content: Taiwan’s representative office is among a list of entities US President Donald Trump has threatened to sue as part of his crusade against a progressive American think tank, triggering debate about the island’s US policy ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month. Trump named the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office (Tecro) in a social media post on Monday attacking the Centre for American Progress, a prominent left-leaning Washington think tank, over a report disputing his claims about the effect of National Guard deployments on violent crime. Trump called the think tank a “radical left scam” and threatened to seek US$5 billion in damages, adding that he was “strongly considering” including some of its donors in the lawsuit. He named Tecro – Taiwan’s de facto embassy in the US – alongside the Japanese embassy, the Korea Foundation and the embassy of the United Arab Emirates as foreign supporters of the think tank. The remarks have raised questions in Taiwan about whether Taipei’s funding of US think tanks has become a political liability under Trump, particularly ahead of his expected summit with Xi. Chen I-hsin, head of the culture and communications committee of the Kuomintang, Taiwan’s main opposition party, described Trump’s remarks as an “unusual diplomatic warning”. He questioned the value of using taxpayers’ money to support an institution strongly critical of the US leader, only for Taiwan to be singled out by Trump. “[Taiwan’s] foreign ministry must immediately explain how much taxpayer money is still being provided to CAP since Trump returned to the White House,” Chen said. He acknowledged that Taipei’s cooperation with US think tanks across the political spectrum predated the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) return to power in 2016, but said “diplomacy required adjusting to political changes”. Chen said that if the DPP government continued providing substantial funding to institutions closely associated with US Democrats and strongly critical of Trump, it raised questions about whether Taipei’s diplomatic strategy had become unbalanced. “Taiwan-US relations must not pay the price for the DPP’s misguided political bet,” he said, adding that the government should explain the situation to the public. Taiwan’s foreign ministry defended the practice, saying it and its overseas missions had long worked with major US think tanks and academic institutions across the political spectrum. It said the cooperation supported research into Indo-Pacific security, supply-chain resilience and critical technologies, while improving Americans’ understanding of Taiwan and the island’s ties with the US. “Such cooperation does not involve Taiwan in US local politics and should not be turned into an issue for political manipulation in Taiwan,” it said. The ministry added that Taipei would continue deepening cooperation with the Trump administration on the basis of mutual respect and mutual benefit. Taiwan has funded prominent Washington think tanks for years as part of efforts to build support in the United States. A 2020 investigation by The American Prospect magazine identified the Centre for American Progress, Brookings Institution, Centre for a New American Security, Centre for Strategic and International Studies and Hudson Institute as recipients of Taiwanese funding. The report questioned whether researchers adequately disclosed their institutions’ Taiwanese funding when advocating stronger security and economic ties between Washington and Taipei. Taipei later rejected suggestions that its funding influenced research, saying it respected academic freedom and that such programmes promoted scholarly exchanges and expert discussion. Data from the Washington-based Think Tank Funding Tracker showed Taiwanese entities provided about US$6.77 million to 25 American think tanks between 2019 and 2024. International relations and strategic studies scholar James Yifan Chen said Taipei still needed relationships with US think tanks given its reliance on Washington’s support, but should ensure its outreach was politically balanced. “For over a decade, the DPP has relied heavily on US support … and often seeks partnerships with American think tanks that share similar values,” Chen said, adding that such an approach risked unsettling Trump and his Republican allies. “Without formal ties, Taiwan must adopt a more balanced approach, building bipartisan relationships to avoid future embarrassments,” he said. Chen added that Taiwan should cultivate ties across the US political spectrum and allocate its resources more strategically. “Taiwan must avoid actions that could complicate the situation in the lead-up to the Trump-Xi summit,” he said. Chen said he believed the planned September 24 meeting in Washington was “unlikely to provide much room for transactional bargaining” between Trump and Xi. Instead, Xi was likely to seek to stabilise relations and offer incentives that aligned with Trump’s desire to strengthen the US economy ahead of the midterm elections, he said. Dennis Lu-chung Weng, an associate professor of political science at Sam Houston State University in Texas, said Taipei should focus less on whether funding the Centre for American Progress was right or wrong and more on whether the broader political atmosphere in Washington was shifting ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting. He said Trump’s decision to name Tecro was “not a positive development” because the US leader appeared to be ramping up the pressure from attacking the think tank’s work to drawing attention to those supporting the institution. “For Trump, negotiations often begin well before anyone sits down at the negotiating table,” Weng said. “Public statements, legal threats and even naming the other side’s supporters can themselves form part of the negotiating process.” There was no evidence Trump would take action against Tecro, Weng stressed, but if the list was not random, being named could be a political signal that Taiwan had entered his field of vision. The real concern would be if the island were incorporated into Trump’s broader political calculations over US-China relations, Weng said. “That would not be something that could simply be resolved with money.” Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. The United States, like most nations, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but is opposed to any forcible change to the status quo and is committed to providing arms for its defence.

title: Tottenham should be awarded 2017 Premier League title after Chelsea broke rules: Pochettino
description: The Blues should be stripped of title after admitting to, and being punished for, breaching competition rules, says former Spurs manager.
content: Mauricio Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of their 2016-17 English Premier League title ⁠and it should be handed ⁠to his former Tottenham Hotspur side following ⁠the Blues’ record fine for rule breaches earlier this year. Chelsea were fined a record total of £10.75 million (US$14.56 million) in March for historical breaches of the Premier League’s regulations after voluntarily reporting in 2022 that they had evidence of a potential breach of the rules relating to third-party payments ‌and financial reporting. The Premier League established that between 2011 and 2018, undisclosed illicit payments by third parties associated with Chelsea were made to players, unregistered agents and other third parties. Spurs, who last won the top-flight title in 1961, finished with 86 points when Pochettino was in charge in 2016-17 – a record for the club. “We should win one Premier League, we should have been awarded it,” said Argentine Pochettino, who now ⁠manages the United States national team and last month signed a contract extension to remain in position until the 2030 World Cup. “If that [Chelsea breaking rules] was true, then we deserve to be champions that year, for sure. ‌They were punished, they admitted it? So that’s it. The title should be for the team that was second. “We can say that they scored goals, they won games. But ‌it’s completely fair to say that we didn’t compete before the start of the season with the ⁠same card. “Maybe with the ⁠same rules, we could have signed some players that would have made the team better or scored more goals.” Chelsea have been contacted for comment. Managed by Antonio Conte, Chelsea won the title with 93 points that season, largely thanks to 16 goals and five assists from Eden Hazard – one ‌of seven players signed using payments made to unregistered agents. “I have no doubt, and I’m not scared to say ‌the truth. The Chelsea fans will be upset with me,” added Pochettino, who also managed Chelsea in the 2023-24 ⁠season. “But if we were at Tottenham and broke the rules, I’d admit the same: ‘We don’t deserve the title because ⁠we broke the rules’ … For everyone, it needs to be the same rules and then you have the capacity to create the best team. “I don’t say that Chelsea didn’t play well, that Conte was ‌not great. I don’t want ‌the message to be twisted. But if you broke the rules then ciao – you need to give it to another team.” Chelsea, who were hit with a one-year first-team transfer ban, suspended for two years, plus an immediate nine-month academy transfer ban, accepted the punishment and said they would pay the full costs of the league’s investigation. Chelsea were initially given a suspended six-point deduction along with the fine but the points penalty was replaced by the suspended transfer ban. Pochettino left Tottenham in 2019. He went on to coach Chelsea in 2023-24, leaving by mutual consent after a troubled campaign in which he failed to secure qualification for the Champions League.

title: Exclusive | Hong Kong policy address to continue push helping local media go global
description: City leader to offer support for second straight year to assist local news companies in building global networks, source says.
content: Hong Kong’s policy address next week will continue with measures to help local news outlets expand overseas and build global networks, the South China Morning Post has learned. A source said on Thursday that Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s “go global” initiative would assist local media, which report in Chinese and English, in reaching readers beyond the city. The industry could offer media services particularly in countries that came under the umbrella of the Belt and Road Initiative, the insider added. “The government will continue to assist local media in expanding their networks outside Hong Kong and telling good Hong Kong stories,” the source said. “This marks the second consecutive year that the chief executive has incorporated support for local media network expansion into the policy address.” The insider noted that the chief executive pledged last year that the initiatives would not involve any interference with media operations. Lee is scheduled to present his policy address and the city’s inaugural five-year plan on Wednesday. In last year’s policy address, the initiatives for the media fell under the chapter “integrating into the overall national development”, which laid out ways to further turn Hong Kong into a platform for overseas expansion to create business opportunities and economic returns. The media measures align with the latest national five-year plan, which calls for building China’s international discourse and improving communication effectiveness to present a “reliable, admirable and respectable” image of the nation. The source said that Hong Kong could leverage its fact-based journalism to attain this goal, adding that the move to go global could also create new revenue for media companies and enhance their international profile, including through hosting conferences. Other than government support, media sector players needed to strengthen their offerings locally and abroad, such as through marketing, public relations, event planning and social media, so they could seize opportunities, the source said. Lee led a delegation to Central Asia in June that included the chairwoman of the Newspaper Society of Hong Kong, Tammy Tam, who is also the SCMP’s publisher. “During the visit, Hong Kong media organisations signed seven memorandums of understanding with government departments, mainstream media, financial institutions, technology parks and telecommunications enterprises in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan,” the source said. The SCMP then hosted the inaugural China Conference: Central Asia in Astana, Kazakhstan’s financial and commercial hub, on Monday. The conference was co-organised by the Astana International Financial Centre. Central Asian countries are core economies under the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s strategy to boost global trade and infrastructure connectivity. Last month, Director of Information Services John Tse Chun-chung led local media executives to the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union’s Kuala Lumpur headquarters, witnessing the signing of eight memorandums of understanding with regional peers, think tanks and production firms to expand international operations. The agreements aim to facilitate and support visits to Hong Kong by media professionals from association member organisations to promote dialogue and understanding. A source told the SCMP that the association would organise two international conferences in Hong Kong next year. Meanwhile, Tse said on Thursday night that the government’s Information Services Department had helped facilitate a panel discussion at the Belt and Road Summit earlier that day that was co-hosted by a Hong Kong media company and the event organiser. He added that such facilitation underlined Hong Kong media’s ability and professionalism in organising global events. The panel, titled “From Innovation to Implementation: Hong Kong’s AI Advantage in Belt and Road Initiative”, was co-organised by the SCMP.

title: Malaysia to charge former minister over haj fund corruption
description: Ex-religious affairs minister Jamil Khir Baharom is the highest-ranking figure to be implicated in the Tabung Haji scandal.
content: A former Malaysian minister overseeing religious affairs will be charged with corruption next week, the country’s anti-corruption agency has said, as authorities close in on once-powerful figures believed to have stolen from the nation’s haj pilgrim fund. The Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) confirmed on Thursday that Jamil Khir Baharom – who served as religious affairs minister under disgraced former prime minister Najib Razak – would face three charges on Monday for misappropriation of assets linked to the multibillion-dollar Tabung Haji fund. The charges relate to alleged dubious dealings involving the leasing of hotels in Saudi Arabia, which manages access to Mecca where millions of Muslims from around the world gather annually for the haj pilgrimage. “This proves our commitment in handling corruption, leakages and abuse of power,” MACC chief commissioner Abdul Halim Aman told reporters at a media briefing. “We conduct our probes regardless of an individual’s background or affiliation.” Jamil was arrested and remanded earlier this month after the MACC launched a crackdown following the release in July of a royal commission of inquiry report into alleged corruption and misappropriation at the fund. If found guilty, he faces up to five years in prison. Jamil would be the highest-ranking person charged in connection with the scandal. His prosecution follows that of former Tabung Haji chairman Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim, who pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to abusing his position to secure a lucrative corporate post and influence a 193.5 million ringgit (US$47.6 million) investment by the fund. Abdul Azeez faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of at least five times the value of the bribes if found guilty. MACC chief Abdul Halim said they were investigating at least five more cases linked to Tabung Haji involving entities in Saudi Arabia and Singapore. “This will take a bit more time to get the documentation and cooperation from overseas parties … investigations are still ongoing,” Abdul Halim said. Tabung Haji, set up to help Malaysian Muslims save for the pilgrimage to Mecca, held 93.4 billion ringgit in savings deposited by 9.7 million Muslim account holders at the end of 2025. The royal commission report highlighted more than a dozen questionable investment decisions made between 2014 and 2020 – spanning Najib’s Barisan Nasional administration and successive governments following its historic 2018 election defeat. The inquiry identified political interference, governance failures and problematic investments that resulted in losses exceeding 1 billion ringgit over that period. The report’s release came after a landslide victory for Najib’s party, the United Malays National Organisation, in the Johor state election in mid-July and ahead of their win over Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan coalition in the Negeri Sembilan state polls a month later.

title: Macroscope | Why the global economy and markets continue to defy doomsayers
description: Despite rising energy prices and bond yields, economic growth has been resilient and equity markets have been performing strongly.
content: There is no shortage of reasons to worry about the outlook for the global economy and markets. On September 9, Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, surpassed US$100 a barrel in response to the intensification of hostilities in the Middle East. Bank of America warned that a renewed escalation in the conflict between Iran and the United States would prove more damaging to a global economy which “would no longer have the oil inventories buffer as it had early in the year”. Another threat is the recent surge in yields on long-term government bonds. The average yield on long-dated debt across the Group of 7 advanced economies has risen to its highest level since 2000, according to Bloomberg data. In the US, the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds is approaching the 5 per cent level beyond which higher yields start to hurt stocks. These two threats add to the persistent uncertainty caused by US President Donald Trump’s reckless trade tariffs, which are designed to hurt America’s friends more than its foes. The onslaught of protectionism has damaged US alliances around the world and contributed to the erosion of confidence in US assets. Yet despite all these risks, the global economy and markets have held up remarkably well. In fact, the most compelling narrative since the beginning of last year is not the succession of shocks but the unexpected resilience of growth and the strong performance of equity markets. In a report on September 3, George Saravelos of Deutsche Bank noted that global economic data has beaten expectations for the longest period on record, excluding the 2009-10 liquidity-fuelled rebound from the 2008 global financial crisis. Citigroup’s global economic surprise index, which shows whether economic data releases are beating or falling short of analysts’ expectations, is at its highest level since April 2023. According to a gauge of global manufacturing and services sector activity compiled by JPMorgan, output last month rose to a nearly 30-month high, reaching a level consistent with annual growth of 3.1 per cent. Meanwhile, the MSCI All-Country World Index, which tracks global stocks, stands at an all-time high. JPMorgan notes that non-US equities are on track to outperform the US for the second straight year, underpinned by stronger growth in corporate earnings. The findings of Bank of America’s latest global fund manager survey on August 18 showed that allocations to global stocks stood at their highest level since November 2021. Only 4 per cent of respondents expected a “hard landing” for the global economy, compared with 49 per cent just after Trump unveiled his sweeping “Liberation Day” tariffs in early April 2025. While the optimism is excessive, it is not entirely misplaced. First, the artificial intelligence boom (AI) has been a counterweight to geopolitical shocks, spurring a dramatic increase in capital spending on digital infrastructure, boosting investment in the US and generating positive spillover effects across global supply chains, especially in Asia. Moreover, Trump’s protectionist and nationalist policies have forced other big economies to become more self-sufficient. Investments in rearmament, critical goods production and new energy infrastructure have provided additional stimulus. Saravelos credited the resilience of growth to “a big, global capex cycle in AI (private capital) and a buildout of strategic autonomy (public capital) in defence, energy and supply chains.” Second, although the energy shock has driven up consumer prices, inflation expectations have not become unmoored. Financial market measures of long-term inflation expectations are well-behaved. The five-year, five-year forward inflation break-even rate – a gauge of long-term inflation expectations – stands at 2.3 per cent, slightly above the US Federal Reserve’s 2 per cent target. “The Fed has not lost credibility in the bond market. At least not yet,” Barclays said. Third, the reason for the rise in bond yields is as important as the rise itself. Although there is debate over the determinants of higher yields, stronger-than-expected growth and the consequent need for higher interest rates are undoubtedly key factors. Furthermore, it is important to put things into perspective. While the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield is close to its highest level since 2007, this seems high only because central banks kept yields artificially low for more than a decade following the 2008 financial crisis. “The low rates that too many people had come to view as ‘normal’ were symptoms of deep social pathologies,” said Matthew Klein, publisher of The Overshoot newsletter. Finally, Trump’s reckless policies have injected volatility into the US dollar and Treasury bonds, undermining their role as safe havens. Despite the succession of geopolitical shocks, the dollar has fallen, keeping global financial conditions looser than they would otherwise have been. This has contributed to the relative resilience of emerging markets. While the global economy and markets face acute challenges, from the threat of a more severe and prolonged energy shock to a disorderly unwinding of the AI trade, their resilience has been underappreciated.

title: SHKP posts 4.6% profit rise amid Hong Kong’s property recovery
description: Hong Kong’s biggest developer reported underlying profit of HK$22.85 billion, as the city’s property market continues to recover.
content: Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHKP), Hong Kong’s biggest developer by market capitalisation, reported its underlying profit for the year ending June rose 4.6 per cent to HK$22.85 billion (US$2.91 billion), excluding investment property revaluations. Meanwhile, its reported profit increased to HK$21.43 billion, backed by a HK$1.38 billion net revaluation gain versus a HK$742 million loss last year, according to its filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange on Thursday. “For the year under review, Hong Kong’s residential property market continued its recovery, underpinned by improved economic conditions, an active financial market, and a relatively accommodative interest rate environment,” said Raymond Kwok Ping-luen, the company’s chairman and managing director, in the filing. “The sustained inflow of talent and students contributed to a steady rise in residential rents, reinforcing homebuyers’ confidence,” Kwok said. “Primary residential projects with premium amenities and convenient transport links continued to receive encouraging sales responses.” Contracted sales during the year amounted to HK$38.1 billion in Hong Kong, with major contributors including the Sierra Sea of Sai Sha Residences and Cullinan Sky and Cullinan Harbour in Kai Tak. For the rest of the year, the group said it planned to launch Sierra Sea phase 2C and phase 1A of the Tung Shing Lei project in Yuen Long. In the first half of 2027, new launches are expected to include a new project in Tai Wai, phase 1 of the Kwu Tung North project, a project near MTR City One Station in Sha Tin, and phase 1B of the Tung Shing Lei project. The group’s annual results reflected the improved prospects of Hong Kong’s residential property segment, which shook off a three-year slump in 2025 as lived-in home prices jumped 3.59 per cent, according to data from the Rating and Valuation Department. The developer also emphasised its support for Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis project. “The group’s commitment is demonstrated by the development of eight projects in the area, providing around 10,000 residential units and essential commercial and transport amenities that facilitate the development of the Northern Metropolis into an area ideal for living, working, learning and tourism,” Kwok said. “These developments are located across different areas in the Northern Metropolis, including those adjacent to future MTR stations such as Kwu Tung and Hung Shui Kiu.” Meanwhile, the group’s gross rental income across its portfolio in Hong Kong, including contributions from joint ventures and associates, edged up by 1 per cent to HK$17.7 billion, with overall occupancy remaining “stable”, the disclosure said. “Driven by active IPO and financial market activities, the two IFC towers in Central achieved an occupancy of close to 100 per cent,” Kwok said. “ICC in West Kowloon maintained a high occupancy of about 92 per cent, supported by new leases from multinational and mainland corporates, as well as in-house expansion from wealth management firms.” For the coming year, SHKP said it expected mainland China’s economy to “stay resilient”, adding that Hong Kong had “also been growing steadily, driven by robust trade performance and resilient domestic demand”. “Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, which serves as a strategic blueprint for its economic development, is expected to strengthen the city’s position as a leading offshore renminbi (yuan) hub and wealth-management centre, while further reinforcing its role as a ‘superconnector’ and ‘super value-adder’,” Kwok said. SHKP declared a final dividend of HK$2.93 per share for the year, to be paid on November 19. Along with the interim dividend of 98 HK cents per share, the dividend for the full year will be HK$3.91 per share, an increase of 4 per cent from the previous year.

title: MTR Corp warns of prosecution as tour guide identified in fare evasion probe
description: Rail operator working closely with police and Travel Industry Authority to gather evidence for further follow-up and possible prosecution.
content: Hong Kong police have identified a tour guide suspected of helping members of a travel group evade fares at an MTR station last month, the city’s rail operator has said, warning that anyone found in breach of the rules could face prosecution. The MTR Corporation said on Thursday that police had identified the guide involved in the incident at Tsim Sha Tsui station, and that it was working closely with the force and the Travel Industry Authority to gather evidence and information for further follow-up and possible prosecution. The operator said it “strongly condemned” fare evasion and stressed that passengers who failed to pay the correct fare or otherwise evaded payment could face a surcharge or prosecution under MTR by-laws. The incident took place at about 11pm on August 23, when a tour guide was suspected of helping fellow members of a travel group improperly exit Tsim Sha Tsui station, with several passengers allegedly failing to pay the correct fares. Footage circulating online appears to show groups of passengers tailgating through an exit gate after a woman, believed to be their guide, taps her card. More than 30 people are estimated to have passed through without tapping their own cards. The MTR Corp earlier reported the incident to police. The force said on Tuesday that it had classified the case as a “miscellaneous incident” and handed it to the rail operator for follow-up under the Mass Transit Railway By-laws. The corporation said it would continue inspections, enforcement and public education efforts, and urged passengers who witnessed suspected fare evasion to alert station staff immediately. Meanwhile, the force told the South China Morning Post it had no further comment on the matter.

title: Wall Street Journal publisher convicted for blocking reporter’s bid to lead union
description: Court rules company broke labour laws by preventing Selina Cheng from running for chairmanship in Hong Kong Journalists Association election.
content: The publisher of the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) has been found guilty of violating Hong Kong’s labour laws by illegally preventing a former reporter from running for the chairmanship of a local press union. However, Eastern Court on Thursday cleared Dow Jones Publishing Co (Asia) of unlawful termination of Selina Cheng Kar-yue’s contract, finding her dismissal could have been the result of a broader restructuring exercise as the American newspaper shifted its Asian headquarters from Hong Kong to Singapore. The court ruled that Dow Jones had illegally deterred Cheng from exercising her right of association by requiring her to seek prior approval for her involvement in the Hong Kong Journalists Association’s leadership race in June 2024. The defendant, a subsidiary of the company that hires WSJ employees in the region, faced a fine of up to HK$100,000 (US$12,750) under the Employment Ordinance. Sentencing is expected early next year. In his verdict, Principal Magistrate David Cheung Chi-wai found that Dow Jones’ prior-approval requirement for employees was a “wrongful and unjustified” application of its code of conduct. He said the arrangement had placed the newspaper’s management above the law and left workers at the mercy of the wishes and arbitrary exercise of power by its senior executives. “By imposing the requirement for getting prior approval before election, the only irresistible inference to be drawn from the full facts is that the defendant intended to prevent [Cheng] from exercising her right to take part in activity of election of [the association],” Cheung said. The magistrate rejected the defence’s assertion that Cheng’s legal action was driven by greed after the publisher snubbed her offer to settle a separate civil claim for HK$3 million. He accepted that Cheng genuinely wished to hold her former employer liable for breaking the law and was not using the case as leverage in settlement negotiations. Cheng, who eventually won the press union’s leadership race and is now an independent journalist, praised the verdict as “meticulous and fair to all parties”, while urging authorities to take firm action against future violations of workers’ rights to join trade unions. “The outcome today speaks for itself,” she said. “That being said, I’d still have preferred if the government had prosecuted instead of me, as not many ordinary workers or employees have the resources to bring private prosecutions. “If it costs millions of dollars just to assert one’s basic right, that right is in effect no longer guaranteed by the law.” A Dow Jones spokesman said the firm disagreed with the ruling and would evaluate its next steps. “The Wall Street Journal has a long and proud history as an employer in Hong Kong,” he said. “Throughout that time, we have remained deeply respectful of its labour laws and supportive of our employees’ rights, while publishing excellent, impartial journalism about the region.” The association has come under intense pressure since the 2019 anti-government protests, with pro-Beijing media asserting that the group colluded with anti-China forces to stir unrest in the city. Security minister Chris Tang Ping-keung has consistently accused the association of lacking credibility and legitimacy. He also slammed the union for defending former media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying and warned that authorities could crack down on the group if it committed a national security offence. In late 2024, Cheng initiated private prosecution proceedings – a right derived from the city’s common law tradition – against her former employer after the Labour Department decided not to act on her complaints. The Department of Justice previously said it would not intervene in the proceedings. Cheng said her then-supervisor and Dow Jones’ human resources department had asked her to pull out of the association’s election, saying her role as the union’s chief would be incompatible with her job and that she had failed to obtain the company’s green light. Her employment was terminated on restructuring grounds on July 17, 2024.

title: Hong Kong can become AI literacy hub, industry leaders say
description: City can also help build trustworthy AI, experts tell panel discussion co-organised by the SCMP at the Belt and Road Summit.
content: Hong Kong can become an educational hub for artificial intelligence literacy and help build trustworthy AI by leveraging the city’s strength in professional services, industry leaders have said. Speaking at the Belt and Road Summit on Thursday, Ellen Lau Sin-tung, executive director of technology training company Preface AI, highlighted a significant gap between corporate leadership and frontline staff during digital transformation efforts. She noted that corporate leaders often expressed frustration over AI adoption as employees were often held back by the fear of being replaced by AI. “Even though the company is trying to find the best engine for its staff, if they do not have the literacy to adopt it, they might not be able to do that [transformation],” Lau told an audience at a panel discussion, titled “From innovation to implementation: Hong Kong’s AI advantage in Belt and Road Initiative”, co-organised by the South China Morning Post. The belt and road scheme is China’s plan to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Europe and Africa. AI literacy was important to help people differentiate between various AI models and understand AI agents, she said. Lau said that senior management needed to work hand in hand with frontline staff and tell them: “We are actually also navigating the change in the world as senior leaders. So I am learning myself. You are also learning with us.” She added: “We have to be so humble to learn about all the unknowns and the changes in the market, but we are also very bold to try out different new things.” Lau told the forum that different AI firms visited Hong Kong to promote their new AI models and companies in the city were open-minded about trying them. “Hong Kong is definitely a hub where everybody is trying new things and trying to have regulated practices as well,” she said. “We will bring the best practices to everywhere around the world.” Sony Angel Han, head of strategy and value advisory at IBM Consulting Hong Kong, said there was no lack of enthusiasm for AI adoption in the business world. However, he noted that many companies focused too much on the proof-of-concept stage to improve the technology, but faced questions and challenges on business value. He advocated a shift from proof of technology to proof of active value. Han also said that, in terms of AI build-up, there was a strong track record of infrastructure in the Belt and Road Initiative market, including data centres and electricity supply. Hong Kong could be a “superconnector” for the application layer to build trustworthy AI models. Han noted that there was a potential, emerging international standard to determine what a safe, well-regulated and well-governed AI looked like, and Hong Kong could make use of its strong professional services industry to help companies build trustworthy artificial intelligence. Albert Lam Yun-sang, chief research officer of Fano Labs, agreed that Hong Kong could be a superconnector to help bring AI models from mainland China to other countries as the city had a very open and mature legal system and regulatory framework. “If we can show that [an AI model] works well in a highly regulated system like Hong Kong, then people will feel comfortable using your system in other markets,” he said. Lam also said Hong Kong had all the hardware and the environment to help companies bridge the gap from the proof-of-concept to the proof-of-value stage, and the same model could be adopted in other countries as well.

title: China says yuan’s global rise is ‘irreversible’ – and has a strategy to back it up
description: From bilateral swaps to keeping premier tech firms on mainland exchanges, Beijing details the blueprint to build a financial powerhouse.
content: Chinese financial authorities have pledged further steps to expand the yuan’s global use amid a broader de-dollarisation trend, while vowing to make listing on mainland stock exchanges the “primary” choice for top-tier domestic companies. “The internationalisation of the yuan is a continuous and steady process, and an irreversible trend,” said Lu Lei, deputy governor of the People’s Bank of China (PBOC), at a press conference on Thursday. To meet growing demand from market participants seeking more diverse currency options, the PBOC had steadily strengthened the yuan’s global monetary functions and international standing, Lu said. To support this expansion, he said China would increase bilateral currency swap agreements and local-currency settlement while improving the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System – a Chinese alternative to Western-dominated settlement networks such as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, or Swift. The central bank would also expand cross-border use cases for the digital yuan and QR-code payments, Lu added, while it planned to optimise market access schemes – including Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Swap Connect – to further open up China’s onshore financial markets. Authorities also pledged to reinforce Hong Kong’s role as the premier offshore yuan hub, while supporting tailored, differentiated market development in London, Singapore and Dubai. Shanghai’s growth as a global hub for yuan asset allocation and risk management would be further enhanced, Lu added. “The yuan has become China’s top settlement currency for cross-border receipts and payments, the world’s second-largest trade finance currency and the third-largest payment currency, holding the third-highest weighting in the IMF’s Special Drawing Rights currency basket,” Lu added. The pledges align with Beijing’s new five-year plan framework to transform the country into a “financial powerhouse”. At the same press conference, Li Chao, vice-chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), said authorities would push to make the A-share market the primary listing destination for leading domestic companies. Historically, many prominent Chinese technology firms have opted to go public in New York or Hong Kong first, where listing rules are generally viewed as more flexible. However, amid tightening scrutiny of overseas listings and persistent geopolitical tensions, Beijing is actively seeking to retain home-grown tech leaders on mainland exchanges. The CSRC would “accelerate the development of world-class exchanges to comprehensively enhance overall strength and global competitiveness” of the domestic capital markets, Li said. Addressing international concerns, Lu reiterated that China had neither the need nor the intention to deliberately weaken the yuan to make its exports cheaper. He said Chinese companies’ bargaining power and their ability to manage exchange-rate risks had steadily strengthened in recent years, making trade less vulnerable to currency movements. “At the same time, foreign trade enterprises are increasingly utilising exchange rate hedging tools, and the rising share of the yuan in trade settlements has further reduced the sensitivity of trade to exchange rate fluctuations,” he noted.

title: France’s Macron urges Europe to ‘assert its ambition in crewed space flight’
description: French president says Europe must step up efforts to boost its space sector and sets out a series of milestones for the next decade.
content: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday called on Europe to develop its own crewed space flight capability within a decade as part of a broader push to strengthen the continent’s space sector. Macron made the call during an international space summit held in Paris this week, which was shown the cold shoulder by several US companies including SpaceX and Blue Origin. “We want Europe to assert its ambition in crewed space flight,” he said. “Our European space programme remains fragile and we must step up our efforts.” His call follows that of European Space Agency (ESA) chief Josef Aschbacher who late on Wednesday appealed to ministers and dignitaries in a closed-door meeting for more resources to develop an independent European space sector. “Will we be passengers or pilots?” Aschbacher asked, in a copy of his speech provided to Agence France-Presse. Aschbacher pointed to the rapid development in space technology by countries around the world from satellite development to the exploration of the Moon and Mars. “In this emerging context, Europe must position itself as an indispensable partner, with its own capabilities,” he said. Europe has in recent years sought greater independence in space but has never sent a manned mission, instead relying on the rockets and capsules of Russia and the United States. The French president on Thursday laid out a series of milestones he wants Europe to reach over the next decade. “In two years’ time, I want to see the first European cargo capsule, Nyx, dock with the International Space Station; in five years’ time, the first European lunar lander, Argonaut, land on the Moon’s surface,” he said. “And in 10 years’ time, the first European manned capsule take off from Kourou with European astronauts and those from other nations on board,” he added, referring to Europe’s spaceport in French Guiana. Developing the sector comes with a significant price tag. Aschbacher estimated it would require an investment of around €1 billion (US$1.16 billion) per year for the next decade. Remaining reliant on other partners is also costly, however, he added. “Buying flights for European astronauts from foreign providers would cost €5 billion over 10 years,” he had said, pointing out that those funds would support foreign sectors rather than Europe’s, losing out on the opportunity to create local jobs and build technological capacities and autonomy. ESA member states are expected to meet for a ministerial meeting in December to decide how to move forward. Last year, the ESA secured a record budget of €22.1 billion to fund its programmes for the next three years.

title: Hong Kong’s first leader Tung Chee-hwa to be honoured with state funeral
description: City government coordinating arrangements to honour Tung as deputy national-level leader and his contributions to ‘one country, two systems’ framework.
content: Hong Kong authorities are coordinating a state funeral for the city’s first chief executive, the late Tung Chee-hwa, the South China Morning Post has learned, honouring his legacy as a deputy national-level leader and his contributions to the “one country, two systems” framework. A source familiar with the matter said “preparations were under way” and were being coordinated by the city government after Tung’s death on Tuesday at the age of 89. Responding to queries from the SCMP, the government’s Administration Wing said on Thursday that it would announce relevant arrangements in due course. Since the 1997 handover, only two prominent local figures have been granted state funerals: industrialist Ann Tse-kai in 2000 and tycoon Henry Fok Ying-tung in 2006. Both held the rank of vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), a position that Tung also held. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said that as a deputy leader at the national level, Tung could have a funeral comparable to Fok’s. He expected central government officials to be appointed to a funeral committee and attend the service for Tung, with state leaders sending wreaths. Veteran China watcher Johnny Lau Yui-siu also believed Tung would be accorded a state funeral in line with convention. He said the funeral’s arrangements and scale could be similar to those of Ann and Fok, and would be coordinated by the central government. He noted that Tung’s status as the city’s first chief executive gave him special standing in Beijing, meaning his funeral could be greater in scale than past state funerals of local figures. “Ann and Fok were not [Hong Kong] government leaders, whereas Beijing highly recognised Tung’s contributions to one country, two systems and his work,” he said. “Beijing spoke highly of Tung, so we have to observe whether [Beijing] will consider these factors.” The state funerals of Ann and Fok were coordinated by the central government, with committees chaired by a CPPCC vice-chairman. They were attended by senior mainland officials, including the director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO), with coffins draped in the national flag and state leaders laying wreaths in tribute. Fok’s funeral in 2006 was attended by then CPPCC vice-chairman Wang Zhongyu, then HKMAO director Liao Hui, and then head of the United Front Work Department Liu Yandong. Both Ann and Fok were appointed CPPCC vice-chairmen in 1993. Ann, a textile entrepreneur, was regarded as one of a handful of capitalists who had the ear of Chinese President Deng Xiaoping in the early 1980s, and held key positions in major bodies Beijing formed to prepare for the handover. Fok was widely seen as Beijing’s most trusted person in the city and played a vital role in China’s reform drive through major investments on the mainland. Alibaba Group on Friday mourned the death of Tung, who served as an independent director of the company from 2014 to 2022. “During his tenure, his invaluable contributions and full support played a vital role in Alibaba’s development. His global perspective helped Alibaba stay rooted in China while expanding globally,” the e-commerce company, which owns SCMP, said. The company described Tung as a “visionary leader, steadfast patriot and also an elder of noble character, humility and kindness”, who led Hong Kong with courage and foresight and dedicated himself to promoting exchanges, dialogue and mutual understanding between China and the world. Tung joined Alibaba Group’s board as an independent director shortly after the company’s initial public offering in New York in 2014. At the time, Alibaba cited his extensive experience as a business and government leader, as well as his long record of strengthening ties between China and the United States, as reasons for inviting him to join the board. A day earlier, Adriel Chan, chairman of Hang Lung Group and subsidiary Hang Lung Properties, paid tribute to Tung for his lifelong contribution to the city and the country, for facilitating US-China relations and for leading Hong Kong out of several rounds of difficult times. “Mr Tung was a steadfast and resolute leader dedicated to the people and deeply committed to Hong Kong; his spirit and exemplary character will always remain in the hearts of Hong Kong people,” he said. The Hong Kong Shipowners Association, which he chaired in the 1970s, praised his foundational contribution to the maritime sector. Its chairman Richard Hext said Tung helped build shipping companies that later became giants in the industry, adding that his “energy, wisdom and determination” earned wide recognition when he became chief executive. “We are very grateful for his dedication to the shipping industry, to Hong Kong, and to the nation, which greatly changed our lives for the better,” Hext said. Shipping firm OOCL - which was founded by Tung’s father and later acquired by China’s state-owned Cosco Shipping in 2018 - described him as a “renowned shipping pioneer and trailblazer” with a global vision and a deep sense of patriotism. “Mr Tung assumed leadership at a critical moment and guided OOCL through a major restructuring, restoring its foundations for future development,” the statement said. “[He] recognised the opportunities of a changing era and worked closely with industry peers to promote the deeper integration of Chinese shipping into global trade, helping to chart the course for the industry’s development.” Fred Lam Tin-fuk, chairman of the Airport Authority, said Tung strengthened Hong Kong’s position as a global aviation hub and praised his devotion to serving the nation and Hong Kong. The authority said Tung strongly believed air transport played a vital role in driving Hong Kong’s economic and social progress, and that his support laid a strong foundation for the growth of the city’s aviation industry. Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park Limited also praised Tung for laying the groundwork for the city’s governance and the development of its innovation and technology sector.

title: Does North Korea’s Kim Ju-ae have a younger sibling? Seoul thinks so
description: Seoul’s spy agency says it believes the daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has a ‘younger sibling of unknown gender’.
content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s daughter and apparent successor is believed to have a younger sibling, South Korea’s spy agency has said, offering a more detailed view of the ruling family’s line of succession. Seoul’s spy agency previously said Kim was thought to have three children, but some uncertainty remained on the number of offspring as well as the order of their birth. The Kim dynasty is now in its third generation ruling the closed-off nation, and the current leader’s children would be potentially poised to take over one day. Kim’s daughter, Kim Ju-ae, was first introduced to the public in 2022 when she accompanied her father to the launch of an intercontinental ballistic missile. Seoul had initially indicated that Kim and his wife Ri Sol-ju had their first child, a boy, in 2010, and that Kim Ju-ae was their second child. But in 2023, Seoul’s unification minister said that the government was “unable to confirm” the existence of the son. The child described on Thursday by South Korea’s spy agency would be the youngest. “The National Intelligence Service [NIS] currently assesses that Kim Ju-ae is being groomed as the successor and understands she has a younger sibling of unknown gender,” the agency said, reaffirming its conclusion on succession. North Korea tightly controls information about its leadership and ruling family, leaving even basic details about Kim Jong-un’s children difficult to verify. The NIS added that it was continuing to examine whether Kim Ju-ae had an older brother, but believed that “even if he exists, he is not in a position to become the successor”. The age or even the gender of the children could be secondary to their potential as successors to their father, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University. “Kim himself inherited power as the third-generation leader despite not being the eldest son. In the same context, he would consider which of his children has the greatest potential to carry on his legacy and further develop his achievements,” Lim noted. “So we can assume that he assessed Ju-ae as having the greatest potential to become his successor.” Since 2022, Ju-ae has appeared at a number of major political events with the North Korean leader, including a high-profile visit to Beijing. North Korean state media have also referred to her as “the beloved child” and a “great person of guidance” – hyangdo in Korean – a term typically reserved for top leaders and their successors. Before 2022, the only confirmation of her existence had come from former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who reportedly made several visits to the North between 2013 and 2017. Kim Ju-ae has drawn attention for her taste in luxury fashion, appearing in Gucci sunglasses and wearing a Cartier watch. At other times, she has mirrored her father’s distinctive style, wearing matching leather jackets and dark glasses.

title: ‘Worth zero’: why stolen Renoir paintings have little black market value
description: Two paintings stolen on Tuesday have a combined estimated value of US$10.5 million, but the thieves’ chance of profiting is ‘extremely low’.
content: Two Renoir paintings stolen from a small French museum on September 8 have yet to be recovered, but if the thieves are hoping to cash in on the artwork, they will be hard-pressed to find a buyer. Selling well-known, stolen art is impossible to do at an auction house or through other public channels without raising eyebrows. Even under the table, the value plummets. And unlike other eye-catching artefacts such as jewels, paintings cannot be chopped up and sold for parts without losing their entire worth. Art crime experts stress that most buyers simply do not want the liability. In short, the reality looks nothing like the films. “People always think that there is this kind of Dr No type from the James Bond movie,” says Arthur Brand, a private art detective based in the Netherlands. “But that’s Hollywood. In the real world, there are no collectors like that.” Brand, who has investigated art crime for about 20 years, explains that often “nobody will touch” stolen art, particularly high-profile work. Sometimes that means paintings valued at millions of dollars are effectively “worth zero” once they are outside the museum, he added, if not a small fraction of the price. The theft at the Renoir Museum – the converted last home of painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir – in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a French Riviera commune near Nice, marks the latest high-profile art crime targeting collections around the world, and experts warn there could be more. A ‘get out of jail free’ card Cagnes-sur-Mer’s mayor, Bryan Masson, says a group of “well-equipped” burglars stole four Renoir paintings from the museum. But they dropped two of them – Renoir’s Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895) and Coco Reading (1905) – in the museum garden before they fled, the prosecutor’s office said in a statement. Police are still searching for the perpetrators. In the meantime, Renoir’s Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Young Woman at the Well (1886) remain missing. Masson estimated the value of the combined Renoir works stolen at €9 million (US$10.5 million). But the probability of profiting from such a theft is “extremely low”, says Erin Thompson, an art crime professor at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice in New York. And in cases that end in arrests, the common takeaway is that “thieves are people who are good at stealing things and bad at thinking through the consequences”, she adds. Some may try to make money from heists in other ways, such as through demanding a ransom or looking for an insurance payout. But Thompson explains many museums do not have insurance because it is too costly. That is why the practice is so rare in the US, for example, and it would be difficult to negotiate with insurance companies elsewhere without the thieves incriminating themselves. As a result, if not surrendered or otherwise recovered, stolen paintings may remain hidden – or, in some cases, eventually destroyed to get rid of evidence, Thompson says. Brand, who collaborates regularly with law enforcement in his art crime investigations, says that he has still seen limited cases of stolen paintings “floating around in the underworld” – perhaps as partial payments for products like drugs. And depending on country-by-country laws, he notes that the promise of returning the art has led to reduced sentences for other charges. “Some more savvy criminal will acquire it as a ‘get out of jail free’ card, sort of a bargaining chip,” adds Christopher Marinello, a lawyer and founder of Art Recovery International. “So if some drug dealer ever is arrested, he can bargain with the prosecutor and say, ‘Listen, give me a lesser sentence, and I’ll show you where these Renoirs are.’ And that has always worked, and it will work again.” Why jewels are worth more than art Stolen paintings are much more difficult to profit from than museums’ other crown jewels – literally. Jewelled and metal goods have increasingly become theft targets because they can be melted down or broken down into parts. Last year, a handful of experts warned that this could be the fate of the stunning theft of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris, for example – noting that, if done successfully, smaller pieces could later go up for sale as part of a new necklace, earrings or other jewellery without turning too many heads. But of course, such pieces would lose their historical worth and, if sold, likely only go for a fraction of their original value. Experts also warn that it is far from a simple process overall – and gems may still be identifiable by characteristics like clarity, for example. Apart from an emerald-set imperial crown found outside the museum the day of the October 2025 theft, the stolen jewels remain unrecovered. Paintings, in contrast, do not have the same commodity value that can potentially be parcelled off. “It’s a canvas with some old oil paint on it,” says art theft expert James Ratcliffe, of the Art Loss Register. “You can’t touch it up. You can’t resell it other than for what it is.”

title: Japan’s AI satellites and other space ambitions ‘a serious threat’, China warns
description: State broadcaster CCTV says satellite plan is a cornerstone of Tokyo’s broader space militarisation strategy.
content: Japan’s plan to develop tactical satellites equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) would boost its long-range offensive strike capabilities and pose a serious threat, Chinese state media has warned. The Japanese Nikkei newspaper reported last week that the planned AI-equipped satellites would be capable of analysing surveillance intelligence in space. The aim is to speed up targeting decisions and strengthen the country’s “counterstrike capability”, such as missile guidance. According to the report, the defence ministry will develop a prototype satellite with domestic companies and conduct ground tests in the coming years, with space launches expected from the 2030 financial year. Funding for the project has been included in Japan’s draft defence budget request for the 2027 financial year, although the exact amount has not been disclosed. While traditional reconnaissance spacecraft send raw images to the ground for processing, these devices will collect data from other satellites and process the information in orbit. By only sending the AI-generated analysis results, the Japanese project aims to significantly reduce the time for space-to-ground communication, according to the Nikkei report. The AI-assisted satellites will support ground command’s rapid decision-making by identifying enemy forces’ locations in space and predicting the movements of mobile targets, such as warships approaching Japan’s remote islands. They would also be able to provide real-time target information to Japan’s long-range missiles, helping to update their guidance and improve strike accuracy, the report said. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said on Tuesday that the AI satellites served as a cornerstone of Japan’s broader space militarisation strategy, as Tokyo upgraded its Air Self-Defence Force to an Air and Space Self-Defence Force – officially designating space as an operational domain. According to military commentator Shao Yongling, the technology could compress the intelligence cycle from tens of minutes or hours to minutes or even seconds, enabling Japan to track time-sensitive mobile targets more effectively. Additionally, sending processed intelligence rather than large volumes of raw imagery could reduce the satellite’s exposure to electronic surveillance and jamming. If ground stations were jammed, the AI satellites could even directly guide strike units, she noted. Shao said that Japan’s development of tactical AI satellites was intended to reduce its reliance on US intelligence for long-range strikes and establish a space-based intelligence and kill chain under its own control. “The purpose is … to independently complete target detection, identification and coordinate generation, to reduce the risk of being restricted by the US chokepoints and secure greater operational autonomy within the alliance,” she said. According to Nikkei, the AI for the satellites is expected to be domestically developed, while the information processing system will come from a US company that has taken part in projects for the US Space Force. The report did not name the companies involved. Last year, US start-up Starcloud successfully tested in-orbit AI training and inference using a satellite powered by an Nvidia chip. Google has also announced its Suncatcher space-based AI data centre project – aiming to launch two prototype satellites equipped with its own chips by early next year. China has also been developing its own space-based AI capabilities. The first batch of 12 satellites for the Three-Body Computing Constellation was launched in May 2025, with plans to deploy up to 100 by 2027. The constellation is reported to be the largest operational space-based computing system to date, with a capacity of 5 petaflops – each petaflop equals one quadrillion floating-point operations per second. The constellation carries AI models that are specialised in areas including Earth remote sensing, astronomy and weather forecasting.

title: Exclusive | Senior Pentagon official for China to lead US delegation to Xiangshan Forum
description: Cynthia ‘Xanthi’ Carras to attend Beijing’s largest annual high-level security and defence conference.
content: The American delegation to the Xiangshan Forum, a major Chinese security conference in Beijing, will be led by Cynthia “Xanthi” Carras, the principal director for China, Taiwan and Mongolia at the Department of Defence, the South China Morning Post has learned. This year’s Xiangshan Forum, the 13th edition of the event, will be held in Beijing from next Tuesday to Thursday. Carras’ attendance marks a higher level of American participation than last year, when Washington sent a defence attaché from the US embassy in Beijing. The forum is often seen as Beijing’s counterpart to the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, Asia’s premier security forum. It comes weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to pay a state visit to Washington, following US President Donald Trump’s trip to China in May, when the two sides sought to stabilise bilateral relations. At the forum’s opening ceremony on Wednesday, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun is expected to deliver a keynote speech on China’s security position. It remains unclear whether higher-level Chinese officials will attend this year’s edition, which marks the 20th year since the forum launched in 2006. Dong skipped the Shangri-La Dialogue this year for the second year in a row.
