Beijing has viewed the Singapore gathering as Western-led, amid long-standing criticism of mainland China’s positions on issues including the South China Sea and Taiwan. Carras attended the Xiangshan Forum in 2023. A year later, the US sent a higher-ranking official, Michael Chase, the US deputy assistant secretary of defence for China, Taiwan and Mongolia. Carras’ attendance comes as Sino-US military relations appear to have improved. The two countries ended a two-year hiatus in theatre-level military contact, with a meeting earlier this month in Canada between the senior People’s Liberation Army commander overseeing the Taiwan Strait and his US Pacific counterpart. Chinese General Yang Zhibin, commander of the Eastern Theatre Command, and US Admiral Samuel Paparo met for the first time at the Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence Conference in Victoria, British Columbia. The PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command has the main responsibility for operations facing Taiwan, the East China Sea and Japan. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. At this year’s forum, organisers have scheduled an event at which Chinese and American representatives will discuss “constructive strategic stability” in Sino-US relations.

title: Yemen’s Houthis close in on strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait in new threat to shipping
description: Yemeni government sources say the Houthis have reached the Red Sea ⁠islands of Hanish after capturing the coastal city of Mocha.
content: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi militants have ⁠reached the Red Sea islands of Hanish after capturing the coastal city of Mocha, two Yemeni government sources said, in a dramatic strategic shift that could threaten the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes. Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified in recent days, with the militant group shifting its focus to control over Yemen’s long coastline instead of just the north, putting them in a stronger position to disrupt maritime trade. Despite concerns over possible new problems for global shipping from the Middle East turmoil, a Houthi spokesman said freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remained safe and operations were limited to specific ‌targets. But they would only stop when the “aggression” against Yemen ended, added Mohammed Abdulsalam, in a post on social media. The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Coordination Centre, set up to liaise between Houthi forces and commercial shipping operators, said navigation in the Red Sea was safe for all shipping companies, except Saudi vessels, which remained subject to a previously announced ban. The group had launched attacks on Hanish, pushing government forces and their allies south to Dhubab, which sits directly on the strait across from the island of Perim, the Yemeni sources told Reuters on Thursday. Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said. The escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia’s Yemeni allies in the internationally recognised government and the Houthis has created a second theatre of war in the Iran conflict that threatens global energy and commodity supplies. Houthi militants earlier seized control of the historic port city of Mocha, four government military sources said. Brent crude prices hovered above US$100 a barrel on Thursday as supply routes through both the Strait ⁠of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted. To avoid the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has been loading millions of barrels of oil a day from its Yanbu port, which lies further north on the Red Sea coast. Houthi control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait ‌risks further disruptions to the flow of the kingdom’s oil supplies to Asia. The militant group has already declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter. A UN-brokered truce in Yemen in 2022 largely halted years of war but has not led to a lasting settlement, with the latest fighting threatening a return to full-scale conflict. Bab el-Mandeb, or the Gate of Tears, named for its perilous navigation conditions, is ‌the southern outlet of the Red Sea, between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast, making it a major prize for the Houthis, who control Yemen’s most populous areas and much ⁠of the north. It is one of the world’s most important ⁠routes for crude oil and fuel from the Gulf bound for the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, or the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline on Egypt’s Red Sea coast, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil. A military leader allied with Yemen’s government forces said on Thursday that he directed his group on the west coast to establish ‌an alternative command centre in a safe location, the Al-Jumhuriya television channel linked to him reported. The instructions from Tarek Saleh, nephew of assassinated Yemeni president Ali Abdullah Saleh, were another sign that the Houthis were pushing his National Resistance Forces from the west. A group of Houthi fighters armed with rifles and chewing qat, a green leaf narcotic that dominates life ‌in Yemen, celebrated ‌their advances at a security directorate building in the Hays district south of Hodeidah, chanting: “Death to America, death to Israel” in a video verified by Reuters. Pakistan had delivered a Saudi warning to Iran to rein in its Yemeni Houthi allies after they stepped up attacks ‌on the kingdom, Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources said, in the hope of preventing the conflict from spiralling. A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message to Tehran on Tuesday and its response was that “Iran does not control the Houthis”. However, two Iranian sources said Tehran told ⁠the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising additional funding and weapons, while several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks. The Houthis disrupted Red Sea shipping in 2023, saying they were acting in support of Palestinians ⁠during Israel’s war in Gaza. Those attacks on Red Sea shipping, as well as on Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States’ war on the Houthis’ close ally Iran. The Houthis said on Wednesday that Saudi strikes hit the Yemeni provinces of Al Jawf, Marib and Saada, bordering the kingdom, as well as Taiz in the south and Hodeidah city along the Red Sea coast, a Houthi stronghold used as a base for their broader campaign ‌of attacks on shipping in the waterway. Saudi Arabia did not confirm ‌the strikes. Saudi Arabia said Houthi attacks on the kingdom in recent days have wounded 73 people, including women and children, after targeting civilian and economic sites in the south. In 2014, the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa, driving the internationally recognised government south towards Aden. Fearful of growing Iranian influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in 2015. The resulting civil war triggered one of the world’s biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of bitter fighting and devastating air strikes by Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners. With Iranian support, the group’s leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, turned his faction of mountain fighters into a force of tens of thousands that demonstrated significant missile and drone capabilities, attacking oil installations and vital infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in the conflict.

title: China ‘living Buddha’ honoured for US$9 million donation after saving every cent for charity
description: Wang is leaving no inheritance to his children, having informed them that his wealth will continue to be donated even after his passing.
content: A 98-year-old man in eastern China has garnered widespread praise for his remarkable philanthropy, which includes donations totalling 60 million yuan (US$9 million), while leading an exceptionally frugal life himself. Wang Chunwen, a resident of Ninghai county in Zhejiang province, has been honoured with the China Charity Award by the Ministry of Civil Affairs, the highest accolade in the country to recognise significant contributions to charitable efforts. In early September, Wang’s son travelled to Beijing to attend the award ceremony and accept the award on behalf of his father, who has chosen to refrain from travelling due to his advanced age, as reported by the Ningbo Daily. Wang is the founder of Xinghua Industries, a manufacturer of plastic and steel products. Since 2001, he has donated 60 million yuan to the Ninghai Charity Foundation. Before that, he engaged in a myriad of charitable activities over several decades. Wang faced significant challenges in his early life, losing his father at the age of 13, which forced him to leave school and work as an apprentice. Reflecting on those difficult times, Wang recalled witnessing the struggles of others who lacked basic necessities such as food and clothing. This experience instilled in him a commitment to help the less fortunate if he ever achieved wealth, as he believed “other people’s pain was also my pain.” He established Xinghua Industries in 1984, and a defining moment occurred when he accidentally fell into a well while visiting a client, only to be rescued by a passer-by just in time. “After this incident, my sole wish has been to engage in charity and do good,” Wang stated. In 1988, he donated 1.5 million yuan to construct a bridge and road in his hometown. Over the next decade, he supported the development of a power network in a village, built a sea wall, and opened a kindergarten in the county. Additionally, he funded an old age home that accommodates 900 senior citizens in the region. Despite his wealth, Wang has never bought a car or a villa for himself, opting instead to live in a modest flat. “If I were to drive a car to deliver money to those in need, they would see me as superior. But if I ride a bike, they will see me as their equal,” Wang explained. “I would rather use the money I could spend on a villa to help those in difficulty, and this choice brings me peace. Living in a villa would not provide me that same sense of relief,” he added. Wang’s frugal lifestyle includes wearing a coat for 36 years and sleeping on a wooden bed for 80 years. He typically wears cloth shoes made and repaired multiple times by his late wife, Chen Jijin, who died in 2021, and supported his charitable endeavours throughout their marriage. Wang has expressed that he does not intend to leave any savings to his son or daughter, believing that they should be self-reliant. “I donate while I am alive; I will continue to donate after I die,” he stated. According to his daughter, the nonagenarian visits his company monthly to review the accounts. “He is not concerned about how much money we make but wants to ensure we are donating promptly,” she shared. Wang’s inspiring story has sparked a wave of admiration across mainland social media. “He has engaged in good deeds for such a long time. He deserves our respect and salute!” remarked one internet user. Another added: “He has made tremendous contributions to children, the elderly, and those in need. The old man is a living Buddha!”

title: China presses France to drop ‘protectionist’ anti-fast fashion law
description: Beijing is also holding talks with French companies over whether they received subsidies that may have partly benefited their Chinese operations.
content: China’s Ministry of Commerce (Mofcom) said on Thursday it had held talks with French companies operating in China and reiterated calls for France to stop using its “anti-fast fashion law” to undermine the rights and interests of Chinese enterprises. According to ministry spokesperson Huang Ling, public reports suggested some French companies had received subsidies from the European Union and its member states, and that this support might have been “partly passed through to their Chinese-based entities”. The discussions with French companies were aimed at “seeking information and requesting explanations” to “assess the impact”, Huang noted. The ministry also addressed recent French legislation aimed at regulating “ultra-fast-fashion” companies, urging Paris to halt its implementation immediately. The rules, it said, had “clear trade protectionist traits”, despite being promoted as measures to protect the environment and promote sustainability. The law uses “plainly targeted standards and parameters to discriminate against and suppress Chinese cross-border e-commerce operators. The rules would severely distort fair competition”, Huang said. Under the French legislation, clothing qualifies as “ultra-fast fashion” based on two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and garment repair costs relative to the retail price. The per-item fee will vary on a set scale based on how each product scores on both standards. Shein, known for its ultra-low prices and rapid turnover of apparel, recently made a muted debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange after earlier plans for initial public offerings in New York and London were derailed, according to media reports. Separately, Mofcom said on Thursday that Chinese and US trade teams were working to deliver on commitments made during US President Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing in May. The statement comes just two weeks before President Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington. The two sides are currently holding talks on a framework for reciprocal tariff reductions, aiming to roll out the measures soon. Beijing and Washington agreed to establish a board of trade, along with a board of investment, following Trump’s Beijing visit, targeting tariff relief on about US$30 billion worth of goods on each side.

title: Hong Kong watchdog investigates Cloudbreak Pharma for ‘rigged’ IPO, suspends its shares
description: Regulator cites ‘serious concerns’ about ‘artificial impression of demand’ in US-based company’s US$78 million listing in 2025.
content: Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has directed the stock exchange to suspend trading of US-based biotech firm Cloudbreak Pharma pending an investigation into its US$78 million initial public offering (IPO) last year. “The SFC has serious concerns that Cloudbreak’s initial public offering may have been rigged to create an artificial impression of demand for Cloudbreak’s shares,” the SFC said in a statement on Thursday. The regulator considered the suspension “necessary or expedient to maintain an orderly and fair market” for the firm’s shares and to “protect the interests of the investing public”, it added. Cloudbreak, a biotechnology firm focused on treatments for people suffering from eye diseases, raised HK$611.88 million (US$78.45 million) in its IPO in late June 2025. The IPO’s retail portion was oversubscribed by 77 times, attracting 29,007 retail investors. Its international offering tranche, however, was not popular, with only 168 investors subscribing to an amount equal to 89 per cent of its offering, according to the company’s announcement at the time of the listing. The company’s share price dropped 39 per cent on the first day of trading, and has lost more than 90 per cent from its IPO price of HK$10.10, closing at HK$1.19 on Wednesday. The shares were suspended at 9am on Thursday, before the market opened. Cloudbreak’s founder and CEO Ni Jinsong formed the company in California in 2015 after some 20 years working for pharmaceutical giants Pfizer and Allergan, according to the company’s information. The company’s Hong Kong listing came under it Chapter 18A rules, which are designed for pre-revenue biotech companies. Introduced in 2018, the rules have helped Hong Kong become one of the world’s biggest fundraising hubs for biotech firms. Under Hong Kong securities regulations, the SFC has the power to direct the stock exchange to suspend trading of a listed company’s shares when the regulator alleges any materially false or misleading information issued by the companies, or if it finds a suspension is necessary to maintain orderly and fair trading and to protect investors.

title: Wildfires threaten Indonesia’s new capital as carrier ordered in
description: The president has ordered water-bombing drones and an aircraft carrier to Kalimantan as 400 hectares burn near Nusantara.
content: Indonesia’s wildfires are creeping towards Nusantara, the country’s new capital under construction on Borneo island, challenging its promise of becoming an eco-friendly “smart forest city”. The Southeast Asian nation is battling what officials call its most intense wildfire season in 11 years. Nearly 202,000 hectares (499,000 acres) of forest and peatland have been razed nationwide from January to June, according to Sipongi, the Indonesian forest ministry’s monitoring platform. Sipongi data shows more than 14,000 hotspots were recorded between August 1 and September 9 – up from 1,033 over the same period last year. Fires have been detected across more than 400 hectares of the land earmarked for Nusantara in East Kalimantan, which is surrounded by some of the hardest-hit areas. Nusantara sits on 252,000 hectares of land, only a quarter of which will host governmental offices, civil service housing and commercial infrastructure. The fires near the site drew direct intervention from President Prabowo Subianto, who instructed officials on Monday to deploy assets to stop the spread. These included water-dropping drones and the use of the country’s first aircraft carrier, the Giuseppe Garibaldi. The ship was donated by Italy and is set to arrive on September 17, the Indonesian Navy said on Tuesday, as cited by state news agency Antara. Buffer zone blazes Myrna Asnawati Safitri, the deputy for environment and natural resources at the Nusantara Capital City Authority (OIKN), said that fires were confined to the surrounding development area, roughly 35km (22 miles) from the main construction zone. “There are currently no hotspots or fires detected in the core governmental area. Air quality has been generally good since July,” Myrna said. The 199,000-hectare development area was designated as an “environmental buffer and [for] food security”, she said. As OIKN was focusing on building in the centre, “there is no infrastructure development” in the areas affected by the wildfires, Myrna said. OIKN conducted aerial water bombing operations on Saturday with support from the National Disaster Management Agency and the Indonesian Air Force. Ground efforts are being spearheaded by a rapid response unit made up of OIKN personnel, the Forestry Ministry, local authorities, universities, private firms, NGOs, volunteers and security forces. Severe drought driven by El Nino conditions had made the fires worse, Myrna said, but human activity also played a major role. “The main cause of land and forest fires is land clearing by burning,” she said, adding that OIKN had issued strict prohibitions and provided training for 100 local farmers on land management techniques that avoided burning. Legal action is also under way. Officials have launched criminal prosecutions against one person suspected of illegal burning in Nusantara and sanctioned a plantation company found to have started a fire, requiring the firm to restore the damaged land. Three mining companies operating on the boundary between Nusantara and East Kalimantan province were also reported to the Environment Ministry. Nationwide, the ministry has temporarily suspended operations for 30 companies across seven provinces whose concessions suffered fires between January and early September. Flammable foundations Environmental activists say the crisis was entirely predictable given the site’s location on an area of sensitive wetlands and peatland. “As an essential ecosystem, it has a crucial hydrological function,” said Wahyu Perdana, a campaigner at peatland restoration NGO Pantau Gambut. “If damaged, two things will happen. During the rainy season, flooding becomes very common. During the dry season, especially during the current extreme El Nino, it becomes very flammable.” Hotspot counts in neighbouring districts have surged. In Penajam North Paser, hotspots rose from 6 in July to 136 in August, Wahyu said. In Kutai Kartanegara, numbers climbed from 86 to 1,188 over the same period. Relying solely on water bombing to douse peatland fires was ineffective, Wahyu said, because water sources were limited and the fires smouldered underground. “Water bombing burning peat once or twice will actually increase the potential for the haze to become thicker,” he said. Urban planning experts like Nirwono Joga of the Urban Studies Centre in Jakarta advocate for large-scale infrastructure solutions to safeguard the site, such as constructing massive hydrological barriers. “Small retention ponds won’t be enough. When we talk about Nusantara … it must be at minimum the size of lakes or reservoirs, or even large-scale dams,” Nirwono said, noting Kalimantan’s rolling terrain was well suited for artificial reservoirs. For OIKN, long-term success hinges on strict regulatory enforcement alongside technical mitigation. “We must strengthen our disaster management system, especially regarding forest and land fires,” Myrna said. “El Nino is currently very strong, so [mitigation] efforts must be more intensive. We will continue to strengthen prevention efforts, including transforming farming practices to zero-burn agricultural land management. To ensure a deterrent effect, law enforcement is non-negotiable. We are consistent in this.”

title: China’s Xi Jinping to make first trip to India in 7 years for Brics summit
description: The visit is yet another stop in a busy month of diplomacy for the president, who will be in Washington in a fortnight.
content: China has confirmed that President Xi Jinping will travel to New Delhi for the Brics summit this weekend, his first visit to India in close to seven years and the latest leg of the Chinese leader’s busiest run of summitry in years. China’s foreign ministry said Xi would attend the summit at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Xi is expected to have a sit-down with Modi on the sidelines of the summit. The Chinese president’s visit to India follows closely on a packed diplomatic travel schedule that first took him to Kyrgyzstan for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, and then to Egypt last week for his first state visit there in a decade. He is expected to travel to Washington later this month to meet US President Donald Trump. Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also be in Delhi for the Brics meeting, as will Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. Xi’s visit to India comes as the two Asian neighbours work to improve ties that soured after a deadly border clash in 2020 triggered a years-long military stand-off. The two sides have taken steps to strengthen relations, including resuming direct flights last October and restarting border trade last month. The two sides also held boundary talks in Beijing in August, with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi describing China and India as important neighbours and saying that the development of China-India ties served the interests of the two countries as well as the Global South. The boundary talks between Wang and Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval produced a series of consensus points, including commitments to keep the frontier quiet, create new working groups, add military communication channels, and continue pilgrimage, border trade, and river talks. The next round will be held in India in 2027. Xi’s trip comes as Beijing puts greater emphasis on developing ties with its neighbours and emerging economies. Like the SCO, Brics is often viewed as a platform for Beijing to advance its ambitions for a multipolar world and cement its position as a leader of the Global South. But it also comes hard on the heels of a recommendation from India’s Serious Fraud Investigation Office for a detailed investigation into Chinese tech company Xiaomi. Asked about the recommendation on Thursday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China-India economic and trade cooperation was mutually beneficial in nature. He also urged India to provide “a fair, just, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment” for companies. India tightened scrutiny of Chinese investments in 2020 under its Press Note 3 policy, which requires government approval for investments from countries sharing a land border with India, widely seen as targeting Chinese capital. Several Chinese firms have faced tax, foreign exchange and compliance investigations in recent years.

title: Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr begin AFC Champions League bid as Saudi clubs chase 3rd straight title
description: Saudi Pro League teams have spent more than US$2 billion on foreign players since 2023, with Al-Ahli lifting the trophy the past two seasons.
content: What could be Cristiano Ronaldo’s last chance to win a first AFC Champions League Elite title for his Saudi club will get under way next week. Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr are one of five Saudi Pro League teams in the tournament. Combined, they have spent more than US$2 billion on foreign players since 2023, with Al-Ahli lifting the continental trophy in each of the past two seasons. Al-Ahli captain and goalkeeper Edouard Mendy is hoping to make it three in a row in the 32-team tournament. “This is the biggest club in Saudi Arabia and Asia, and we will do everything to win,” Mendy, who signed from English Premier League club Chelsea in 2023, said. “Last year, we won the Champions League and we will have to use all the things we did then to be successful this time, too. We are building year after year.” One competition, two zones The tournament is divided into two geographic zones until the playoffs, with the top eight teams from each progressing to the round of 16. Al-Ahli start their defence against Pakhtakor of Uzbekistan in the western zone. Saudi league champion Al-Nassr’s roster contains 41-year-old Ronaldo and his Portugal teammate Joao Felix, the domestic league player of the season. Al-Nassr was a finalist in the second-tier continental championship last season. Felix, who joined the Riyadh club in 2025 for a fee of around US$60 million, is determined to win a major title under new coach Ange Postecoglou. “We have a really good squad, a deep squad; our goal is to win every competition we can,” Felix said. “We want to win the league, the cup and the Champions League – everything. We don’t play to dream – we play to win.” Riyadh rival Al-Hilal have won a record four Asian titles. After spending more than US$200 million in the summer on English Premier League stars and three internationals – Ollie Watkins of England, Brazil’s Gabriel Martinelli and Crysencio Summerville of the Netherlands – Al-Hilal will be dealing with high expectations. Al-Ittihad, winners in 2004 and 2005, are aiming for a third continental crown. Al-Qadsiah, under former Liverpool and Celtic boss Brendan Rodgers, are making a first appearance in the competition. The Saudi teams have avoided Iran’s two representatives – Esteghlal of Tehran and Tractor – in the group stage. With tension high because of war in the region, the Iranian clubs are set to host home games in neutral countries. Esteghlal will host Al-Sadd of Qatar in the Iraqi city of Basra in the opening round. Tractor will travel to the United Arab Emirates to face Shabab Al-Ahli in Dubai. Eastern zone contenders Clubs from Japan have lost the past two finals to Al-Ahli. And Japan, like Saudi Arabia, has five representatives in the tournament. Of them, only Gamba Osaka and Kashima Antlers have lifted the trophy before, in 2008 and 2018 respectively. South Korea is the most successful nation in terms of combined Asian titles. South Korean hopes will rest with three-time champions Pohang Steelers and two-time winners Jeonbuk Hyundai Motors this season. Shanghai Port and Beijing Guoan are China’s representatives in the tournament. Thailand has three teams for the first time: Buriram United, Port and Ratchaburi. Australia’s hopes rest on Newcastle Jets, making just a second appearance in the group stage.

title: Meet Frankie A. Rodriguez, who plays mascot Danny in Chad Powers
description: Before his role in the Glen Powell-led comedy, the actor appeared in Modern Family and starred opposite Olivia Rodrigo in High School Musical: The Musical: The Series.
content: Following a wildly successful debut run, Hulu released the complete second season of Chad Powers on September 3. In the show he co-created with Michael Waldron, Powell plays Russ Holliday, a disgraced quarterback who decides to revive his American football career by creating a new persona, Chad Powers, and joining a struggling college football team: the South Georgia Catfish. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chad Powers (@chadpowershulu) Early in Season 1, the Catfish mascot Danny, played by Frankie A. Rodriguez, discovers Chad’s real identity. The two form an unlikely friendship, and Danny goes on to protect Chad’s real identity to the best of his abilities throughout the show – which ultimately doesn’t go so well. With all six episodes of the new season available to stream, here is what to know about the 27-year-old actor behind the mascot suit in Chad Powers. What is Frankie A. Rodriguez’s background? Frankie A. Rodriguez was born in July 1999 in Sanger, California and is of Mexican descent. His love for the stage was evident during his years at Sanger High School, where he took part in several school productions. “I completely found my people when I joined theatre,” Rodriguez told Out magazine in a recent interview. “I never had trouble making friends at school, but I always had trouble relating to them. When I did theatre, I found my people. We all just want to sing and dance. It has shaped everything I’ve done in my entire career.” He worked with Olivia Rodrigo Rodriguez made his acting debut in 2015 when he landed a recurring role in the comedy web series Raymond & Lane. He also appeared in two episodes of the beloved television sitcom Modern Family in 2019. But Rodriguez’s Hollywood breakthrough didn’t come until he landed the role of Carlos, a student choreographer, in Disney’s High School Musical: The Musical: The Series. The mockumentary, based on the popular franchise, also starred Olivia Rodrigo. After that, the actor booked a role in Mindy Kaling’s The Sex Lives of College Girls before joining the Chad Powers cast. Who is Frankie A. Rodriguez dating? Rodriguez is openly gay and is engaged to fellow actor Joe Serafini. The couple met on the set of High School Musical: The Musical: The Series, in which they play an on-screen couple – one of the first queer couples in Disney history. Rodriguez and Serafini reportedly began dating in 2019 and announced their engagement via an Instagram post in August this year.

title: Meet Lane Kiffin’s ex-wife Layla, who is supporting him amid LSU expulsion threat
description: The daughter of late NFL star John Reaves has three children with the LSU Tigers coach and opened her own fitness centre in Baton Rouge this year.
content: American football coach Lane Kiffin has been making headlines in the past weeks as his team, the Louisiana State University (LSU) Tigers, await a verdict on whether they will be expelled from the collegiate Southeastern Conference (SEC). Leaders from schools in the conference are planning to meet on Thursday to discuss expelling LSU amid a dispute over the team’s push to add players who spent time on NFL teams. On Tuesday, the SEC amended a lawsuit filed last week to request a temporary restraining order so the school can’t interfere with a meeting where a “potential termination” of its membership will be discussed. The conference would need a two-thirds majority to approve LSU’s removal, according to the filing. A spokesperson for LSU declined to comment. The SEC said Tuesday’s filing is necessary to preserve its ability to govern competition among its members. “The SEC and its member universities have the right to establish, through agreed-upon governance procedures, the rules under which they voluntarily compete and to expect those rules to be followed,” the SEC said in a statement. “A commitment to those rules, and to the core principles of the Southeastern Conference, is an essential element of SEC membership.” The dispute revolves around the eligibility of players who Kiffin, LSU’s first-year head coach, wanted to add to his team. It also continues the blurring of lines between college and professional sports, following a US Supreme Court decision in 2021 that opened the door for collegiate athletes to be compensated. Yahoo Sports writer Ross Dellenger posted on X that the university’s expulsion was “no longer expected to be an agenda item during Thursday’s SEC presidents meeting”, citing unnamed sources. Meanwhile, sports news website ClutchPoints reported that the federal lawsuit remains pending and LSU still faces other potential penalties. Just days earlier, Kiffin and his family, including ex-wife Layla Kiffin, celebrated the LSU Tigers’ victory against Clemson Tigers on September 6. While they originally split in 2016, Kiffin and Layla seemingly reconciled last year. She has since shown her support for her ex-husband’s career via Instagram posts and more. Here’s everything you need to know about Lane Kiffin’s ex-wife, Layla Kiffin. What is Layla Kiffin’s background? Layla Reaves Kiffin was born in January 1974. Her late father, John Reaves, was a celebrated quarterback who played in the NFL for 11 years, per ESPN. He died in 2017 at age 67. Little information is available about Layla’s mother. According to EssentiallySports, Reaves reportedly raised her and her stepbrothers, Stephen and David Reaves, alone. Layla attended the University of Florida, where her father played American football. She was a member of the Zeta Tau Alpha sorority, per People. How did Layla and Lane Kiffin meet? According to EssentiallySports, Layla worked for the special events department at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Florida after graduating from university. During her time there, she met Kiffin, who was a quarterback for the team. Kiffin’s father, Monte, was their defensive coordinator. The couple began dating in 1999 and married in 2004. They have daughters Landry and Presley and a son, Knox. Their divorce and reconciliation The couple divorced in 2016 with Kiffin announcing the news via a statement. “After a lot of careful thought and consideration, Layla and I have mutually decided to divorce,” he said in a statement. “We are fully committed to our kids’ future being our No 1 priority. We will maintain an amicable relationship with respect for each other as we raise these three wonderful children,” the statement read. However, nearly a decade later, the couple were spotted spending time together again. In January 2025, Kiffin shared a photo of himself hugging his ex-wife and wishing her a happy birthday. Since then, Layla has been spotted at Kiffin’s games to support him. Outside of her family, Layla is also a businesswoman and founded Livin Studio, a fitness centre that provides infrared-heated yoga classes in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, this May. With additional reporting from Bloomberg

title: Far-right AfD party won big in Saxony-Anhalt. Will it affect Germany’s approach to China?
description: In the wake of a key state election, observers say Germany’s economic pressures will persist, no matter who is in power.
content: With its sweeping victory in a key state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany is putting pressure on the ruling federal coalition and could nudge Berlin towards a more pragmatic approach to China, analysts said. By securing 43.8 per cent of the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt – more than double its 2021 result – the AfD sent shock waves and piled further pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party. In the state it has governed in coalition since 2002, the CDU’s vote plummeted from 37.1 per cent in the previous election to 17.2 per cent. The AfD, which calls for expelling immigrants, cutting aid to Ukraine and repairing diplomatic ties with Moscow, looked unlikely to form what could be Germany’s first far-right state government since World War II, because it fell short of a majority and appears unable to form a coalition with other parties. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said in Berlin that the party was aiming for 40 per cent in the 2029 general election, up from its current first-place polling of 28 per cent. Analysts say the results in Saxony-Anhalt will have an indirect effect on Germany’s China policy. “The AfD’s electoral rise will make Merz more cautious on China,” said James Downes, director of the Europe-Asia programme at the US-based Centre for Explanatory Research and Scientific Prediction. “However, weaker exports and pressure on German industry still favour targeted, gradual measures to reduce economic dependence on Beijing.” The AfD’s “economy-first” message was gaining ground among “some industrial voters and business constituencies”, Downes said, but its main effect was likely to be indirect, shaping public debate and the rhetoric of the CDU/Christian Social Union in Bavaria coalition, rather than determining federal policy. Ding Yifan, a senior fellow with Renmin University’s Institute of Global Governance and Development in Beijing, said China was monitoring the political shift in Germany with a wait-and-see attitude after having “changed its previous policy of avoiding contact with far-right parties”. “If the AfD comes to power, it will prompt Germany to return to rationality and reconsider its relations with Russia and China,” Ding said. He said that addressing Germany’s economic difficulties would be key to the party’s ability to win public support. “If the AfD and National Rally, a French far-right political party, come to power, they will influence the direction of EU policy,” Ding said. “They will weaken the European Commission’s decision-making power and make greater use of the European Council, where leaders of countries friendly to China will have more say.” Beijing has so far offered a cautious response to the AfD’s victory. On Monday, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning called the Saxony-Anhalt election “Germany’s internal affair” and said “Beijing’s position on developing China-Germany relations was consistent”. The AfD’s rise has brought its more China-friendly economic messaging into greater focus, even as Merz seeks to revive growth in Europe’s biggest economy through reforms and greater spending. Ahead of Merz’s visit to Beijing in February, the AfD’s Bundestag group published an article saying “China is not an enemy, but a partner”. In a separate article in December, “EU tax on China is a sign of weakness”, Peter Felser, parliamentary managing director of the AfD parliamentary group, urged Berlin to “advocate in Brussels for better coordination and a genuine dialogue with our Chinese partners”. According to Jonathan Lehrer, a China specialist at the German foundation Koerber-Stiftung, the AfD’s approach to China may appear pragmatic, but is “actually rather chaotic”. “There is currently no clear policy on China to anticipate,” Lehrer said. “Of course, the AfD wants to strengthen ties with China, and compared to other German parties, it is the least China-hawkish.” But even if the AfD entered federal government, which Lehrer said was unlikely in the near future, it would “face the same structural problems with China’s economy as any other party”, including securing inputs, markets and the position of German companies in China and Europe. “It is a competition over industrial supremacy and the AfD, with its very simplistic economic concepts, is not well equipped to help Germany win it,” Lehrer said.

title: Palace plot in Malaysia’s Negeri Sembilan entangles Umno leaders
description: Umno president has questioned a fellow party member’s statement that he was forced to sign a document to remove the state’s ruler.
content: Malaysia’s Umno has been drawn deeper into a royal row in Negeri Sembilan, after the president of the dominant Malay nationalist party denied attending a meeting reportedly linked to a bid to remove the state’s ruler. The controversy has put the new Umno-led state government under pressure barely six weeks after taking office, reviving the same royal crisis that helped bring down its predecessor and force a snap election in August. The episode is particularly sensitive for Umno, which has long cast itself as a defender of Malaysia’s Malay rulers. State monarchs retain important constitutional powers, including in the appointment of chief ministers. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, also Malaysia’s deputy prime minister, said late on Wednesday that he was not present when his fellow party member Ismail Lasim, the head of Negeri Sembilan’s government, signed a purported proclamation seeking the removal of ruler Muhriz Tuanku Munawir. “I was not there. Ismail himself has denied this,” Zahid told reporters at Umno’s annual general assembly in Kuala Lumpur. He also rejected speculation that Ismail had quit. Zahid said Umno would “not dirty our hands” in the dispute and questioned Ismail’s claim that he was forced to sign the proclamation. “Who forced him? He says he was forced, that is what he said,” Zahid said, adding that lawyers present at the signing should verify Ismail’s comments. Zahid was expected to meet Ismail later on Thursday to discuss the controversy, according to local media reports. Ismail acknowledged in a statement on Wednesday that he signed the proclamation on August 3, one day after he was sworn in as chief minister before Muhriz at the royal palace in Seri Menanti, but said he had done so “against my will and under duress”. He lodged a police report on Monday and maintained that the proclamation was “invalid, unconstitutional and unenforceable”. He also pledged his “full support and unwavering loyalty” to Muhriz. Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said the episode had left Umno with little room to manoeuvre and could be used by its rivals to destabilise the state government. “It is going to be very difficult for him [Ismail] to manoeuvre this particular issue, and also very, very difficult to be the chief minister when [Muhriz] is the Yang di-Pertuan Besar,” Azmi told This Week in Asia. “The state government must have a good relationship with the monarchy,” he said. “Whether the chief minister signed under duress or not, it is an awkward position” not only for Ismail but also for Umno’s leadership. The Singapore-based Straits Times had earlier reported, citing sources, that Zahid, Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki and information chief Azalina Othman Said were present at the August 3 meeting in Port Dickson. All three have denied attending. “I don’t know, I wasn’t there when he [Ismail] signed it. I really wasn’t,” Azalina told reporters. Asyraf also denied any involvement, saying he was not part of the Negeri Sembilan leadership. Throne trouble The dispute began on April 19, when four men claiming authority as Negeri Sembilan’s traditional territorial chiefs, known as the undang, declared Muhriz removed and named Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar as his successor. Negeri Sembilan has Malaysia’s only elective state monarchy. Muhriz is one of the country’s nine state monarchs, who together form the Conference of Rulers and elect Malaysia’s federal king. Unlike Malaysia’s hereditary state monarchies, Negeri Sembilan’s ruler, known as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar, is chosen by four undang representing Sungai Ujong, Jelebu, Johol and Rembau under adat perpatih, a customary system with roots in the Minangkabau traditions of Sumatra. The chiefs also have constitutional powers to require the ruler to temporarily withdraw or abdicate under certain circumstances. Two currently recognised undang, representing Sungai Ujong and Rembau, said the proclamation bearing Ismail’s signature could not be enforced. They said the state’s highest customary council had already ruled on July 31 that the April attempt was void and that three of the chiefs behind it no longer had authority to act in those positions. The royal dispute brought down the previous state government in April, when all 14 lawmakers from the Umno-led Barisan Nasional withdrew support for chief minister Aminuddin Harun, ending his Pakatan Harapan-led administration and forcing the August 1 election. BN subsequently won 18 of the state’s 36 seats and formed a government with Perikatan Nasional, which took seven seats. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan won the remaining 11.

title: DeepSeek says new Flash AI model beats Kimi K3 on cyber, coding benchmarks
description: Developer’s V4.1 Flash launch highlights China’s AI battle, where efficiency and speed drive competition amid chip curbs.
content: DeepSeek has released its V4.1 Flash model, claiming it outperforms its previous flagship while cutting inference costs and boosting speeds – the latest salvo in China’s aggressive price-and-performance war. The Chinese artificial intelligence developer said on Thursday that V4.1 Flash used a new “Causal-Encoder-Decoder” architecture. While built on a massive 552 billion-parameter framework, it relies on a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) design. In traditional AI, every query runs through the entire system. An MoE system routes tasks only to the specific subnetworks best suited for the job. By activating just 8 billion parameters to process inputs and 16 billion to generate responses, DeepSeek said it significantly reduced the computing power needed per request. DeepSeek described V4.1 Flash as the smallest model in its new series, with native multimodal visual understanding. The model outperformed V4 Pro on benchmarks evaluating coding, cybersecurity and autonomous agent tasks, the company said. The launch comes as tech giants and pure-play AI developers lock horns in a fierce battle to commercialise AI across China. With rising hardware costs and foreign chip export curbs tightening compute constraints, Chinese players are racing to offer efficient models that deliver high-end reasoning at fraction-of-a-cent operational costs. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, which tests AI on real-world compute tasks, V4.1 Flash scored 90.6, surpassing OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 at 88.3, and DeepSeek’s own V4 Pro at 87.9. On Cybergym, a benchmark that tests AI models on cybersecurity tasks, V4.1 Flash scored 88.1, ahead of V4 Pro at 83.3, Kimi K3 at 80, and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol at 84.5. V4.1 Flash narrowly edged out Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 on software engineering benchmark DeepSWE v1.1, though the US model retained leads on other tests. A main breakthrough of the new architecture was memory optimisation, according to DeepSeek. The company said it reduced the model’s key-value (KV) cache – the temporary memory storage an AI uses to remember earlier parts of a conversation. By shrinking this memory footprint to 890 bytes per token, down from 3,514 bytes in the previous Flash version, the company said it significantly lowered inference costs for AI agents. DeepSeek slashed its application programming interface rates to as low as 0.02 yuan (0.003 US cents) per million cached input tokens during off-peak hours. “Given that the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model comprehensively surpasses the V4 Pro in all metrics … it would not be appropriate to provide DeepSeek users with the originally underperforming V4 Pro model at a higher price,” said Cui Tianyi, head of DeepSeek’s Harness team, on social media platform X on Wednesday. DeepSeek would temporarily route all V4 Pro requests to the cheaper Flash model until its more powerful V4.1 Pro was ready, the company told users in a notice on Wednesday. The release underscores a growing trend among Chinese developers, which are competing on “Flash” variants to win over clients. Last month, Z.ai unveiled its GLM-5.3-Flash – previously code-named Ox Alpha – which selectively activates just 18 billion of its 320 billion parameters. Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, launched Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, activating just 6 billion of its 125 billion parameters.

title: 25 dead after fire on board foreign-flagged cargo ship in China’s Qingdao
description: The vessel was docked for repairs, CCTV report says, as President Xi Jinping orders preventive measures tightened.
content: Twenty-five people were killed after a fire broke out on Thursday morning aboard a foreign-flagged cargo ship at China’s eastern port of Qingdao. The vessel with 42 people on board was undergoing repairs at the state-owned Qingdao Beihai shipyard, according to state broadcaster CCTV. The blaze, which started at around 11.15am, was put out by 2.30pm, the report said. Twelve people were evacuated safely while five others had to be hospitalised. President Xi Jinping earlier gave orders to step up search and rescue efforts, according to CCTV, a rare instance of instructions from the top leadership accompanying an accident report. He also called for a swift investigation into the cause of the fire and to ensure prompt follow-up and victim support, the report said. All regions and relevant departments must “draw profound lessons from the blaze”, tighten preventive measures and “resolutely curb major accidents to safeguard lives and property”, Xi was quoted as saying. A photo released by state news agency Xinhua suggests the ship is the Liberia-flagged bulk carrier Ocean Melody. According to the MarineTraffic website, the vessel is moored in Qingdao. Premier Li Qiang had ordered emergency teams to “focus on rescuing trapped personnel and treating the injured”, while “preventing secondary disasters”, the CCTV report said. According to Xinhua, he has also directed the country’s top work safety authority to thoroughly identify workplace risks and take concrete steps to prevent major accidents. CCTV said the Ministry of Emergency Management had sent a working group to the scene to guide rescue and investigation efforts, while provincial authorities in Shandong had mobilised resources to manage on-site operations. Qingdao Beihai is a major shipyard managed by the China State Shipbuilding Corporation. It specialises in commercial shipbuilding, ship repair and offshore engineering. The facilities are spread across 330 hectares (815 acres) along 9km (5.6 miles) of coastline. Calls to the shipyard went unanswered. Data from vessel tracking platform Ship Value Visualisation shows that the Ocean Melody arrived for repairs in Qingdao on August 31, after sailing north from Taicang port in neighbouring Jiangsu province. It was scheduled to depart on Sunday. The bulk carrier’s registered owner is a Chinese company Huili Shipping, managed by Yuyangkunpeng Shanghai Ship Management, according to maritime data platform Rynda. This is China’s second fatal shipyard accident within a month. On August 13, an explosion following a blaze on a vessel at the Century Huahai (Fujian) shipyard in Fujian province left one firefighter dead. Following Thursday’s blaze, multiple provincial authorities reposted an emergency management ministry cautionary note urging heightened safety precautions during ship repair and maintenance work. Additional reporting by Carol Yang

title: Hong Kong to strip logos and branding from cigarette packs starting in March
description: Only brand and variant names in prescribed font will be permitted, printed in standardised plain brown on packs under changes to existing law.
content: All logos, colourful designs and branding will be stripped from cigarette packs in Hong Kong under new rules that take effect in March next year as part of a fresh push to reduce smoking rates. The Department of Health announced on Thursday that subsidiary legislation would require all retail packs of cigarettes, long cigarette boxes and specified cigars to drop brand logos and advertising elements. Only brand and variant names in a prescribed font will be permitted, printed in standardised plain brown on the pack. Manufacturers will have until December next year to ensure their products meet the new rules. Dr Manny Lam Man-chung, head of the Tobacco and Alcohol Control Office, said the measure would reduce the appeal of tobacco products, citing a 2023 Chinese University of Hong Kong study in which 79.8 per cent of smokers surveyed said plain packaging made cigarettes less attractive. “The measure will weaken brand effects, stop consumers underestimating health risks and make the graphic health warnings more prominent and effective,” he said. Lam said 27 countries and regions, including Australia, Canada and France, had adopted standardised packaging. An Australian study found attempts to quit rose from 20.2 per cent to 26.6 per cent within a year after standard packaging was introduced in 2012. “We believe Hong Kong will achieve similar deterrent effects, though smoking reduction is driven by other measures as well,” he said. The rules will take effect on March 1, 2027, with full enforcement beginning on December 1, 2027 after the nine-month transition. The new regulation under the Smoking (Public Health) Ordinance were tabled in the Legislative Council on Wednesday and will be gazetted on Friday. The government will also replace the 12 graphic health warnings depicting smoking-related diseases and their impact on daily life, in use since 2018, following World Health Organization advice that warning content be rotated regularly to maintain its long-term deterrent effect. Cigarette packs sold in Hong Kong currently carry one of 12 government-designated health warning images covering at least 85 per cent of the packaging. Tar and nicotine content labelling will be removed from packs and cartons, to prevent smokers from wrongly believing that products with lower levels are less harmful, reducing their motivation to quit. A duty-paid cigarette label system will be introduced at the same time. Every pack must carry a label with physical and digital anti-counterfeit features so that duty-paid products can be distinguished from illicit ones. Anyone who breaches the standardised packaging requirements faces a maximum fine of HK$50,000 (US$6,375) upon summary conviction. Henry Tong Sau-chai, chairman of the Hong Kong Council on Smoking and Health, said the council fully supported the law, believing it could effectively deter teenagers from being attracted by colourful displays and promotional slogans. “Our council always targets youth smoking prevention, and we often see at retail outlets that the packages are colourful with slogans like ‘fresh experience’ and ‘new legend’, which appeal to teenagers,” he said. Hong Kong ramped up its anti-smoking measures earlier this year, doubling the fixed penalty for smoking in no-smoking areas from HK$1,500 to HK$3,000 in January, and extending the ban to public transport queues and areas within three metres (9.8 feet) of specified entrances and exits. It is now illegal for individuals to possess vapes and heated tobacco products. Hong Kong’s smoking rate fell to 8.5 per cent last year, missing an ambitious target of 7.8 per cent, but down from 9.1 per cent in 2023.

title: Thais take to streets in rare protest against Israel: ‘not for sale’
description: The protest follows months of complaints about illegal landholding, cultural disrespect and proliferation of Israeli religious houses.
content: Hundreds of Thais, led by a veteran political activist, rallied outside the Israeli Embassy in Bangkok on Thursday in a rare public protest against a group of foreign nationals. The protest follows months of complaints about illegal landholding, disrespect towards local culture and proliferation of religious houses for Israelis, echoing those made by some locals in the Philippines and Sri Lanka. Israelis have been flocking to Thailand since the war on Gaza that followed the October 7 Hamas assault on their country. Many are service personnel from the Israel Defence Forces seeking respite from a war that has killed over 70,000 Palestinians and left around 2 million more stranded on the strip without food and water. In a country with hair-trigger sensitivities over sovereignty, allegations that swathes of prime Thai land have been sold illegally to Israelis have raised uproar. Disputes between Thais and Israelis – mainly on the islands of Phangan and Samui and the mountain retreat of Pai – over non-payment of bills, public misbehaviour and pro-Palestine flags at some Thai businesses have gone viral, adding to the tensions. Thursday’s protest – which saw an angry crowd waving a sea of Thai tricolours and banners saying “Save Thailand”, “Thailand Is Not For Sale” and “This is Not The Promised Land”, alongside some plainly antisemitic placards – was led by firebrand Sondhi Limthongkul. The controversial 78-year-old former media mogul and conservative “Yellow Shirt” hardliner, who was at the crux of Thailand’s long and bloody years of street politics, can still draw a large crowd. Thailand has a long-standing tradition of “extending warm hospitality to foreign visitors”, he said. “However, let it be clearly understood by the embassy and the government of Israel that generosity must never be mistaken for weakness.” Accusing Israelis of wanting to “occupy our country, building your own community”, he added: “Hospitality does not equate to submission to exploitation, and courtesy is not an open licence for anyone to act with impunity on our sovereign soil.” “Widespread grievances” committed by Israeli residents and tourists “include violations of domestic law, public disturbance, disrespect towards local traditions and culture as well as recurring payment default and service-related fraud”, he added. “The patience of the Thai people has reached a limit.” Sondhi’s return to frontline protest is a significant development in a country where street politics and hyper-nationalism have helped topple governments, shape policy pivots and fanned conflict with neighbours over the years. He gave a letter to the embassy and called on the Thai government to take “concrete actions” to root out illegal businesses and end what he described as a culture of “disdain towards their [Thai] hosts”. His campaign, called “Take Thailand Back”, would continue with another protest against alleged “grey” businesses in the country, he said. Other leading nationalist figures joined the rally, uniting in a show of patriotism that pointed to the widening rancour. ‘Not looking to invade’ Ahead of the protest, Israel’s ambassador to Thailand Alona Fisher-Kamm tried to assuage anger by addressing what she said was misinformation driving some of the viral episodes that have enraged Thais. A small minority of Israeli visitors had behaved badly, she acknowledged, but insisted there was no attempt at “colonisation”, suggesting outside instigators were brewing up hostility against Israeli nationals. “The vast majority of Israeli tourists are good tourists, they don’t provoke and there is no conflict and they are well welcomed by Thais,” she told PPTV on September 3. “We see cases of misunderstanding or of Israelis who might be badly behaved because they don’t understand the culture, or do not know the law as well.” She said Israelis were briefed on dos and don’ts before arrival in Thailand and inside the country, insisting the embassy was “not going to protect anyone” found to have transgressed Thai laws. The core allegation among many of Thursday’s protesters is that Israeli nationals used nominee relationships to secure Thai-only land. That loophole, now closing fast after a string of scandals, has seen foreign nationals buy majority shares in land restricted to Thais by paying locals to be silent partners. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sarwar Sohel (@nomadicsohel) Across the southern islands of Samui, Phangan and Phuket, Thais complain that the speed and scale of this action are freezing them out of their own territory. One protester, who asked to remain anonymous, said “corrupt Thais had sold off the country, but that doesn’t mean we have to take the insult of Israelis who treat us like we are dirt”. The Israeli ambassador, however, refuted the idea of nominee holdings as “an Israeli phenomenon”. “Singling out Israelis or saying that the vast majority of cases are Israelis that have nominees or have any kind of illegal business, I think it is misleading,” Fisher-Kamm said. “Everything in Thailand is Thai territory, it has nothing to do with Israeli territory, Israelis are not looking to invade Thai territories.” On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow met Fisher-Kamm for what he described as “frank” discussions and warned that ties between the countries could become strained if more flashpoints between Thais and Israelis occurred. “Visitors must understand and respect Thai culture and traditions,” he told reporters after the meeting. But he also urged the public not to hold the actions of the few against all Israelis. There were around 31,000 Israeli nationals in Thailand as of March, the Immigration Bureau said. A total of 420,202 Israelis visited the country last year, most of whom left after a short stay, it added.

title: Opinion | Cop31: Forget climate pledges, countries like Nepal need actual cash
description: No payout from the loss and damage fund has reached vulnerable nations. Cop31 must focus on delivering the money already promised.
content: Every climate summit now runs on the same illusion: the next pledge will be the one that finally saves us. It will not. The money the rich world has promised the poor world is not coming at anything like the scale advertised, and pretending otherwise has become the main business of climate diplomacy. Barely nine weeks before the UN climate summit Cop31 opens in Antalya, Turkey, the honest task is not a bigger pledge. It is to make the finance that already exists reach the people drowning in the consequences. Nepal is the test sitting in plain sight, and the system is failing it. Late last month, a melting glacier gave way on the edge of the Himalayas and sent a wall of rock and water down the valley, burying whole settlements and leaving a country in national mourning. Nepal then did everything the system asks. It went through the proper channel, the UN Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, and framed its request as a matter of liability rather than charity – the correct framing for a country that emits less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gases. The reply has been procedural. The fund has not released a single dollar since its creation and its first decision is only due in December. Even its own board has asked for an emergency meeting. Set that against how quickly everything else moves. In the same few weeks, the calendar filled with gatherings: a climate finance week in Istanbul, a week of chief-executive meetings in Baku, Azerbaijan, and a Pacific leaders’ summit in Palau. There is no shortage of mobilisation, only not the kind that moves money from one account to another. A fund that cannot send US$20 million to a grieving country in the time it takes to hold three high-level meetings is not yet a fund. It is a promise with a letterhead. The rich world pledged US$40 billion a year in adaptation finance and reached only about US$26 billion, then answered the shortfall at Cop29 in Baku by lifting the target to at least US$300 billion a year and a hoped-for US$1.3 trillion. The gap between what is pledged and what arrives now runs into hundreds of billions a year, and chasing a larger pledge is a way of looking busy while it widens. The more useful question is why so little of the money that exists ever moves. Much of what has been committed sits in the approval pipelines of intermediary institutions, waiting on conditions that small and poor countries cannot meet. Finance that flows straight to national and local bodies, rather than pooling in the middle, reaches communities faster and at lower cost. But it is simply not what the architecture is built to do, because it was built to reassure donors, not to reach victims. Antalya must resist the pull towards another pledge to celebrate and quietly miss. The work of an implementation summit is unglamorous. Accountability for money committed. Direct access, so a grieving country does not need consultants to reach a fund created for it. An end to the debt conditions that force vulnerable states to choose between climate investment and loan repayment. Antalya will be judged on whether it turns commitments into concrete, verifiable action. The implementation era means nothing if no one is accountable for implementing anything. The cost of getting this wrong is not hypothetical. Pakistan rebuilt from its 2022 floods largely by borrowing, and now services debt on a catastrophe it did not cause. That is the quiet cruelty of the present arrangement. It converts climate injustice into sovereign debt and files the paperwork as relief. When help arrives as loans rather than grants, the victim pays twice. The disasters will keep coming, faster than the pledges and far faster than the payments. The glaciers that failed above Nepal will fail again somewhere else, and the fund meant as an answer will still be scheduling meetings. What the world needs from Antalya is not a bigger promise. It is proof that the promises already made can reach the ground. Turkey is pleased to host, and its hoteliers expect the summit to stretch the season towards 150,000 visitors. Those are fair rewards for a host. But the worth of the climate summit will not be the money it brings into Turkey. It will be the money it finally moves to the people burying their dead. The world knows how to gather in a conference hall. In nine weeks, it has to prove it still knows how to pay.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, September 11-13
description: From a craft beer festival to an introspective art exhibition and a soundwalk to Tomorrowland’s fashion pop-up, there’s a lot on this weekend.
content: The peak summer heat is finally easing in Hong Kong, and a lot is going on in the city in the coming days. Whether you are in the mood to check out cool art, browse exclusive fashion pop-ups or go on a forest soundwalk, here are five things to do in Hong Kong this weekend. 1. Chilai Howard at the Goethe-Institut Hong Kong interdisciplinary designer and artist Chilai Howard’s solo exhibition, “A Self-Portrait: The Process of Erasing” is running at the Goethe-Institut Hongkong until October 6. The introspective showcase explores themes of memory, personal objects and the self. Howard takes objects associated with different stages of his life and coats them in a thin layer of metal. Instead of destroying the objects, he strips them of their everyday function, sealing their original surfaces and transforming them into relic-like forms. While the physical item survives, key fragments of its past identity are now forever hidden. For more information, click here. Goethe-Institut Hongkong, 14/F, Hong Kong Arts Centre, 2 Harbour Road, Wan Chai 2. Soundwalk at Upper Shing Mun Reservoir Find solace in nature while contributing to a good cause this weekend with a soundwalk hosted by Hong Kong mental health clinic Sacred Space Therapy and Wellness in celebration of International Forest Bathing and Soundwalk Weekend. The event is scheduled for this Saturday, September 12, from 2pm-4pm. Hikers can meet at Tsuen Wan MTR station beforehand. The soundwalk will be led by an Association of Nature and Forest Therapy-certified guide. The small-group session, capped at 10 participants, invites attendees to slow down, practise deep listening and reconnect with nature among paperbark trees and local wildlife. The event doubles as a charity fundraiser, with 100 per cent of the net proceeds going to Direct Relief’s Nepal Flood Relief Fund. The suggested donation is HK$350 to HK$500. Click here to sign up for the event. Upper Shing Mun Reservoir, Tsuen Wan 3. Flockfest at PMQ Flockfest 2026 is a three-day craft beer festival hosted by Hong Kong’s Black Kite Brewery at PMQ, in Central, from September 11 to 13. The event honours craft and culture by fusing Japanese precision with Hong Kong’s dynamic creative energy. Attendees can experience beers from eight cult-favourite breweries – four each from Japan and Hong Kong, including DD4D, Far Yeast Brewing, Deadman Brewery and, of course, Black Kite Brewery. There will be 20 taps, including eight event-exclusive collaboration brews. Beyond the beer, the festival will feature performances by 15 top Hong Kong indie music acts such as post-punk band Biascut, jazz-folk musician Reggie the Leaf and surf rock band Black Lodge Cabaret. Entry to the festival is free. More information can be found here. PMQ, 35 Aberdeen Street, Central 4. Tomorrowland x Juice pop-up Tomorrowland offshoot festival The Magic of Tomorrowland is returning to Shanghai in October following the success of its China debut in 2025. This Saturday, September 12, electronic music fans can celebrate at a pop-up event in Hong Kong’s Causeway Bay. The official apparel line of Belgium’s Tomorrowland brand will be available at fashion store Juice on Cleveland Street. Visitors can browse limited-edition festival wear, graphic tees, hoodies and lifestyle accessories. Beyond shopping, the event recreates a festival atmosphere with live in-store DJ performances, including by mainland Chinese techno DJ Meguru. Juice, Shop A, 9 Cleveland Street, Fashion Walk, Causeway Bay 5. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East Writer-director Wen Muye’s bombastic anti-war drama arrives in Hong Kong having already grossed a whopping 2 billion yuan (US$298 million) at the mainland Chinese box office, delivering a message of peace and diplomacy through the appreciation of authentic Chinese cooking. Lambasting both sides of an unnamed Middle Eastern conflict – the United States’ 2003 invasion of Iraq in everything but name – this latest effort by the Dying to Survive filmmaker addresses a parade of wartime atrocities, from devastating shock-and-awe strikes to black-site prisons, radicalised child soldiers and suicide bombings. This is filtered through the perspective of an opportunistic yet affable Chinese chef (played by Shen Teng), whose mouth-watering cuisine is the only thing uniting the warring factions. Read the full review here. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East opens in cinemas on Friday.

title: Hong Kong teams up with 50 partners to set standards for low-altitude aviation
description: Key MOUs related to low-altitude economy exchanged with mainland partners at Belt and Road Summit.
content: Hong Kong has secured support from more than 50 organisations to develop common standards for the low-altitude economy, as the city seeks closer integration with the national strategy for the sector. The announcement was made on Thursday at a low-altitude economy forum attended by Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan. The low-altitude economy covers commercial activities involving drones and electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft. “No single city can establish a global standard alone,” Chan said. “That is why we are joining hands with all the stakeholders, with different cities, and our [Greater Bay Area] partners to proactively reach out to jurisdictions across the group that recognise the potential of [low-altitude economy] development.” She said Hong Kong’s common law system, internationally respected aviation expertise and status as an international financial and commercial hub made it ideal for real-world testing. Supporting organisations included mainland Chinese low-altitude economy and telecommunications firms such as AutoFlight, EHang Intelligent Equipment, China Telecom Global and China Unicom Innovation Research Institute. Chan also said the government had expanded its regulatory testing framework. “Building on this foundation, we are redoubling our efforts in launching the Regulatory Sandbox X to tackle even more advanced and more complicated scenarios for low-altitude economy applications [such as] cross-boundary logistics operations and unconventional aircraft, including those for carrying passengers,” Chan said. A sandbox is a space where software or new technology can be tried out in a pilot scheme or test environment. Earlier on Thursday, the government exchanged two memorandums of understanding (MOUs) related to the low-altitude economy with mainland partners at the Belt and Road Summit. The agreements comprise a bilateral sandbox with Nansha in Guangdong and a pact with a partner in central mainland China. Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the Nansha agreement would combine the Greater Bay Area’s production and testing capabilities with Hong Kong’s strengths in research and standards setting. “The agreement will leverage the strength of our [bay area] partners in testing environment and industrial production capability, and Hong Kong’s strengths in standards setting, as well as research and development,” Wong said. He added that the agreements would “facilitate the harmonisation of common standards and promote commercialisation of innovative [low-altitude economy] applications.” The annual summit promotes business among countries taking part in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network. Wong said the government was pressing ahead with a regulatory scheme to test advanced aerial projects. Hong Kong aims to align with the overall national strategy of developing the low-altitude economy in urban areas. He said more than 140 applications had been approved for commercial services, including deliveries, infrastructure surveillance and materials lifting. A further 33 complex projects involving partners had been selected for testing under Sandbox X. Wong also said that, two weeks earlier, he had witnessed the inaugural flight of an unmanned eVTOL aircraft at Cyberport in Hong Kong’s Southern district. “Hong Kong’s role as a superconnector and super-value-adder extends naturally into the field of low-altitude economy,” Wong said. “The challenges we are addressing domestically, including safety standards, airspace coordination and infrastructural support, are similar to those facing many of our belt and road partners.” He added: “We believe Hong Kong’s world-class legal system, well-recognised aviation regulatory expertise, and strength as an international financial and trade centre together put us in a strong position to provide an effective platform to serve enterprises across belt and road partner countries.” Wong also highlighted a recent regional delegation led by lawmaker Elizabeth Quat, which visited Malaysia and Indonesia to secure new business opportunities and forge long-term partnerships.

title: UBS pulls plug on fund sales on a wealth platform in China amid stiff competition
description: Change is part of ‘business integration plan’ aimed at ‘optimising’ the wealth-management business, Swiss bank says.
content: UBS plans to shut down its fund-distribution business on one of its mainland China wealth-management platforms, as it faces intense competition. As part of a “business integration plan”, UBS Fund Distribution (Shenzhen), known as UBSFS, would cease its fund sales business, including fund subscription and fund switching, at the end of September, the Swiss bank said in a statement to the South China Morning Post. UBS added that it remained “committed to China” and would “continue to invest strategically”, as the country was still a key market. The confirmation came after reports that WE.UBS, a wealth-management platform operated by the Shenzhen unit, was facing operational challenges and would be shut down. The move resulted from fierce competition in fund sales from rivals in mainland China, including those who were “originally built on online channels”, said two people familiar with the matter. UBS was giving up on the WE.UBS platform, and began the adjustment a few months ago, with redemption of funds to clients still taking place, one source said. Some of the employees affected would be transferred to other UBS entities in mainland China, the source added. The platform’s assets under management were relatively low, and the closure was expected to have a limited impact on the bank’s mainland wealth-management business, said another person familiar with the matter, adding that two other UBS entities in mainland China also distributed funds and served high-net-worth individuals. In the statement, UBS said that UBS Securities – its brokerage unit in mainland China – was “exploring opportunities to further strengthen its wealth-management presence in the Greater Bay Area”. “With the vision to become the leading international wealth manager in the Chinese market, UBS will integrate its relevant businesses and resources in China, including optimising the wealth management-related business structure and enhancing synergies,” the bank said. Assets from the Greater Bay Area – an economic area comprising Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in Guangdong province, including Shenzhen – accounted for nearly one-third of UBS’s total assets under management in Asia, the bank said in May. Launched in October 2022, WE.UBS was regarded as China’s first digital-led wealth-management platform operated by a global wealth manager. The bank touted its ability to get new clients on board in only three minutes via a mobile app. UBS said that 90 per cent of the funds offered on the WE.UBS platform achieved positive performance last year. The platform’s service accounts on WeChat have not published new posts since December 19. UBS is not alone in adjusting its mainland business in recent years. Citigroup, for example, sold its retail wealth-management portfolio in mainland China to HSBC in 2023.

title: China’s global expansion offers German firms opportunity, but they see window narrowing
description: German chamber notes how some members see ‘golden window to partner up’ with Chinese companies as competition, trade tensions and possible EU measures raise risks.
content: While German companies operating in China increasingly view the global expansion of local firms as a chance to collaborate, the window of opportunity is narrowing as Chinese firms rapidly develop the expertise needed to expand overseas on their own, according to a new report. The internalisation of Chinese companies has emerged as the most frequently cited business opportunity for German firms in China, selected by 36 per cent of survey respondents and up from 20 per cent in 2022, according to a report published on Thursday by the German Chamber of Commerce in China. Engagement takes several forms, with nearly half of surveyed German businesses supplying products or services to Chinese companies operating abroad, while a quarter help those companies meet international standards.
