But the report – which drew on findings from the chamber’s 2025-2026 business-confidence survey of 627 member companies, as well as interviews with 11 executives between April and June this year – noted that these opportunities to collaborate would not last indefinitely. “The broader finding is that Chinese companies are rapidly developing overseas experience themselves,” Oliver Oehms, executive director and board member of the German Chamber of Commerce in northern China, said at a press briefing in Beijing on Thursday. “They are developing their own local networks or ecosystem, and obviously, they are quick learners, and they are getting familiar with the respective standards in the target market,” Oehms said, adding that German capabilities presenting partnership opportunities were becoming less distinctive over time. Oehms noted that one executive from an automotive supplier called the next 18 months a “golden window to partner up”. Once that window closes, Chinese companies may have gained enough operational experience to expand globally on their own, the executive warned. Another executive at an automotive joint venture said that some Chinese standards had already surpassed German benchmarks in certain technology segments, even as the Chinese entity still lacked the expertise to manage intellectual property internationally. At the same time, the global expansion of Chinese companies is increasing competitive pressure on German businesses. Chinese firms sometimes operate with faster decision-making, lower costs, and a willingness to prioritise market share over short-term profitability – a strategy that many German firms struggle to replicate – according to the report. Chinese companies are increasingly looking to overseas markets for new growth opportunities and to escape from sluggish demand and intensifying competition at home. But these ambitions – together with China’s massive trade surplus – have heightened tensions with the European Union, which is considering tougher measures on China ahead of an October deadline for demonstrable progress in resolving the economic dispute. While Berlin has historically been more reluctant to impose overly aggressive trade measures against Beijing, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shifted course amid growing domestic industrial pressures. The German chamber warned in its report that geopolitical tensions could affect German businesses’ strategies, as companies collaborating with Chinese firms may face greater political scrutiny. “It’s not a deal breaker yet, but considering the possible consequences, it’s a very important variable that must be factored in … before business decisions are taken,” Oehms said. The best-case scenario for German businesses for October would be for the EU to avoid broad tariffs on Chinese imports while reaching an agreement with Beijing over its restrictions on rare earth exports, he said. Executives interviewed for the report also called for trade protections covering entire supply chains rather than isolated production stages. Narrowly targeted measures could drive up input costs and erode the export competitiveness of European manufacturers, they warned.

title: SOTY 2025/26: Best Improvement category winner is a champion of change
description: Shiny Poon’s journey from academic setback to sports enthusiast highlights her resilience, leadership and passion for coaching young athletes.
content:
From the moment Shiny Poon Suen-man first picked up a badminton racquet in kindergarten, she realised that sports would be more than just a pastime.
“I quickly realised I had a natural talent for it,” the 19-year-old recalled.
When her secondary school years at Good Hope School opened new opportunities – an invitation to join the athletics throw team and the launch of a handball squad – she did not hesitate.
“I decided to jump at the opportunity, which sparked my multi‑sport commitment,” she said.
Poon developed a passion for a variety of sports, including badminton, athletics, basketball and handball.
“Playing different sports showed me how fascinating it is to master distinct rules, techniques and tactical mindsets, and I fell in love with the variety of each sport and challenge of it all,” she said.
While Poon excelled on the court, she encountered setbacks academically.
“My major turning point happened in Form Three when I had to repeat the year,” she said.
“It was tough. I could feel the negative stereotypes from those who didn’t know me well.”
Rather than accept that label, she used the experience as fuel.
“Deep down, I knew I wasn’t a ‘bad student,’ and that setback pushed me to transform my mindset. I committed to proving who I really was,” she said.
“By Form Six, my growth and effort led to me being named captain [of my sports team]. That opportunity ignited a deep passion to give back to my school and my teams,” she shared.
Leading the badminton and handball teams taught Poon that effective leadership relies on open communication rather than mere commands.
“As a captain, I focused on ... acting as a bridge between the coach and the team,” she explained.
“Whenever teammates felt discouraged or misunderstood the coach’s feedback, I stepped in to comfort them and translate that advice into constructive motivation.”
Poon noted that handball taught her the importance of selflessness. Initially, she pursued personal achievements, but over time she learned to set her ego aside for the team’s benefit.
“I learned to trust my teammates and distribute the play equally,” she said. “Passing up an individual shot to [instead] empower a teammate has completely transformed our collective offensive chemistry and pushed our team forward.”
To balance sports and studies effectively, Poon understands that small, intentional choices accumulate over time.
“Managing multiple sports means every day brings a different training focus,” she explained.
“On those double‑session days, I would complete a two‑hour badminton practice right after school, then head off‑campus for another two‑hour handball session. It was physically exhausting, but I learned to optimise my recovery.”
Travel time is treated as rest time, and meals are scheduled to provide the necessary fuel and support recovery.
“Discipline for me means making every minute count, whether training, travelling or resting,” she said.
When competitions, practices and exams collide, Poon’s solution focused on efficiency and concentration. She admits that early on she was easily distracted, but her breakthrough came with the technique of compartmentalisation.
“I needed a complete mental shift: when it is time to study, I focus 100 per cent on studying; when it is time to train, I am fully locked into practice,” she said.
This ability to separate her focus allows her to manage overlapping pressures without experiencing burnout.
Poon’s journey was recognised as one of the winners in the Best Improvement category at the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club. This month, Poon started a bachelor’s degree in media and communication at City University of Hong Kong.
After completing her university entrance exams, Poon began coaching children in badminton and discovered a new passion.
“That experience was an eye‑opener – I realised coaching requires a completely different skill set than being an athlete,” she said. “My goal is to combine my experience across multiple sports with effective communication strategies to build strong, resilient and inspired young athletes.”
Poon’s story is one of consistent reinvention: a student who transformed setbacks into momentum and now a young coach ready to share the lessons she learned.

title: Indonesia orders Netflix to pay US$4.3m in music royalties or face shutdown
description: Netflix has agreed to pay music royalties it owed in South Korea and faces a tax demand on its income in Australia, media reports say.
content: Indonesia is demanding that Netflix pay an estimated 75 billion rupiah (US$4.3 million) in royalties accumulated since its launch in the country or risk being shut down. The National Collective Management Organisation (LMKN), a government-supported agency overseeing the country’s royalty system, said the streaming platform had not paid music royalties since entering the Indonesian market 10 years ago, the Jakarta Globe reported. “The amount is estimated at around 75 billion rupiah, which Netflix must settle for the period since it opened access to its commercial digital service in Indonesia in 2016,” LMKN secretary general Bigi Ramadha Putra said in a statement on Wednesday. Netflix is required to pay royalties under Indonesia’s 2014 copyright law, a 2021 government regulation on the management of song and music copyright royalties, and a 2025 regulation by the Law Ministry, according to Bigi. “Netflix, as a digital platform conducting commercial activities in Indonesia, is required to respect copyright regulations and fulfil its obligations to rights holders,” he said. Should the platform continue to drag its feet, LMKN plans to take the matter to the Law Ministry and the Communications and Digital Affairs Ministry. “If an obligation has been established but remains unfilled, then we must pursue the legal mechanisms available to us,” Bigi said. “If the regulations are not complied with, we will propose that access to Netflix in Indonesia be shut down.” LMKN representatives have already met Netflix informally in London over the issue, according to Bigi. Based on information received by LMKN, Netflix had paid royalties to the Philippines and Thailand amounting to hundreds of billions of rupiah, he added. That claim could not be verified but what has been reported is an agreement by Netflix to pay five years’ worth of music royalties it owed to South Korea. Under the licensing contract signed with the Korea Music Copyright Association, the streaming platform agreed to pay for songs used in shows and films from 2021 to 2025, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported on August 27. An earlier deal signed in 2018 covered usage from 2016 to 2020. Music royalty rates for streaming platforms in South Korea, set in December 2020, started at 1.5 per cent of sales and rose to 1.9 per cent this year. Netflix also faces new demands on its income from Australia. On Friday, the Australian Taxation Office ruled that income earned from cloud or streaming services would become taxable for the first time, the Financial Review reported. As there was a copyright or intellectual property element included in the service fees, they should be taxable as a royalty payment, the office said.

title: Why is surrogacy in China proving so difficult to ban despite the crackdown?
description: Undercover investigation leads to allegations of two labs operating illegally, despite the nation’s tough stance against the practice.
content: Two laboratories in central China have been shut down for alleged surrogacy activities, an underground practice that persists despite repeated crackdowns. On Wednesday, the health bureau in Changsha, Hunan province, said six people were detained after a tip about a “laboratory that illegally uses assisted reproductive technologies”, according to state news agency Xinhua. A day earlier, the Wuhan Municipal Health Commission, in neighbouring Hubei province, announced that an illegal lab had been shut down and eight people detained. Police are investigating and will “severely punish any illegal activities”. A long-time anti-trafficking activist and whistle-blower, who uses the pseudonym Shangguan Zhengyi, was responsible for both tips, according to his posts on social media this week. He wrote on Wednesday that he had gone undercover for eight months, finding that the Changsha lab was operated by a surrogacy agency. Operations started at around 11am, with cars and staff circling the area on lookout, he added. On Tuesday, Shangguan Zhengyi alleged that the Wuhan lab was equipped with a surgery room and embryo incubator. The doctor who operated at the facility came from the Hubei Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, he claimed. The activist also alleged that the surrogacy agency had previously been reported to authorities but only halted operations for a few days before opening up again. According to China’s medical laws, assisted reproductive technologies can only be performed by permitted medical institutes for married couples suffering from infertility, and only for medical purposes. Medical institutes that apply these technologies for surrogacy can be fined or charged criminally. Xia Ying, a criminal lawyer at the Beijing-based BZW Law Firm, pointed out that the laws only governed medical facilities. A lack of direct regulations on surrogacy was a contributing factor to repeated offences, she said. “There’s no specific criminal offence for surrogacy activities,” Xia said, adding that in these cases, the rulings took a “patchwork form”. “Rather than directly passing judgment on surrogacy, the authorities break down the commercial surrogacy industry chain and fit each activity into a matching, existing offence,” Xia said. “For example, some could be charged for illegal medical practices, or abducting and trafficking women and children, others for buying and selling state-issued certificates, abandonment, infringement of personal information and fraud.” According to Xia, charges in the newly reported cases would be determined by what exact activities the detainees were accused of carrying out. Chinese authorities are adamant that surrogacy activities in any form are prohibited. In 2021, when National People’s Congress deputies suggested allowing legal surrogacy to prevent repeated illegal operations, the National Health Commission (NHC) replied that “surrogacy severely harms women’s health rights and interests”. The practice “objectifies women and gives rise to a string of grave social problems, including human trafficking, and can cause ethical crises within the family and society”, it said. The commission’s response also noted that, since 2015, the NHC had joined forces with the police in a series of crackdowns on illicit collection and supply of human sperm and eggs, as well as surrogacy. Despite the crackdown, the activities became more covert. In May 2025, media reported that undercover investigations had revealed two illegal surrogacy agencies in Changsha, with more than 10 women a day driven by car for operations. The local authorities fined the agencies more than 130 million yuan (US$19.3 million) and suspended the certificates of doctors and nurses involved. One reason that cases are continuing to be uncovered is that demand for surrogacy still exists. According to Xia, the lawyer, many of the clients of these operations are unable to have children themselves. National Business Daily reported in 2022 that, according to surrogacy agencies, their clients were couples who could not give birth and families who had lost their only children, followed by single people and members of the gay communities. According to NHC data, in 2021, about 7 to 10 per cent of people in China were suffering from infertility-related conditions. The cases have also sparked discussion in the media about the social issues that arise from surrogacy, including whether the resulting children can obtain household registration, a necessity for education and other social benefits.

title: Hong Kong under-15 suicides hit decade high as social media comes under scrutiny
description: Rate for age group hits 2.9 per 100,000, with boys far higher at four compared with 0.4 for girls, University of Hong Kong research finds.
content: The suicide rate among under-15s in Hong Kong rose to a decade-high in 2025, defying an overall downward trend, with social media activity strongly linked to cases among young people, according to research from a local university. The Hong Kong Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention at the University of Hong Kong also used World Suicide Prevention Day on Thursday to call for schools to strengthen support for students in light of a spate of suicide attempts around the start of the academic year. “As we pursue academic excellence, we should also look after the mental health of young people,” Professor Paul Yip Siu-fai, the centre’s founding director, said. “It’s been just a while since the school year started, and we have already seen a few student suicides. Here I would like to call on schools to give pupils more time and space to build rapport with their teachers and schoolmates, strengthening their support system.” Using data provided by the Coroner’s Court, the centre estimated that there were 976 suicide cases, or 13 per 100,000 residents, last year – a slight decline from 2024. While rates declined across nearly all age groups, the figure rose among under-15s to 2.9 per 100,000, the highest since 2016. A further breakdown of data for that age group showed the suicide rate for boys was four per 100,000 and 0.4 for girls. The centre noted that among the boys under 15 who died by suicide last year, most had experienced academic and interpersonal stress. All of the cases occurred at home, and all suicide notes or expressions of suicidal ideation were in digital form, Yip added. Yip said the rise in the number of young people taking their lives was not unique to Hong Kong, and the priority of prevention work was to identify those at risk more precisely, consistently, and effectively, rather than only concentrating on those with a diagnosis. There is limited data on suicide rates of the under-15 demographic around the world. An April study found that the suicide rate for children aged 10 to 14 is generally between 0.2 and 0.8 per 100,000 across most members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The rates were 0.3 in the United Kingdom, 0.9 in the United States and 1.2 in South Korea. Yip stressed that while authorities had put in place a three-tier emergency mechanism covering prevention and intervention for students, it was important their academic lives were fulfilling in the first place. “I do not think students will take their own lives just because they struggled to adapt to school life,” he said. “It’s part of a bigger problem such as awareness of and attitude towards mental health, willingness to seek help and the accessibility of those supports.” He suggested that at the start of the academic year, schools could hold only morning classes in the first week, spend the afternoon on bonding among students and arrange fun activities and events such as having an ice cream truck visit the campus. Yip said the figures would be subject to further adjustment next year due to time lags in Coroner’s Court reports. The centre used artificial intelligence (AI) to help analyse suicide cases among under-15s between 2022 and 2025, finding that more than 30 per cent of the students were studying at Band 1A schools. The term refers to top-tier institutions under the three-band, nine-subgroup ranking system. The analysis found that 24 per cent of cases were enrolled at Band 1B schools, another 12 per cent at Band 1C and the rest at Band 2 and 3 institutions. Researchers at the centre also collaborated with the Hong Kong Press Council to investigate the relationship between suicides, traditional media and social media. As part of the collaboration, the centre and council tested how traditional media reports and social media content about suicide related to the number of cases. The results showed that while traditional media reporting does not directly predict the suicide rates of people aged below 35, social media platform activity was strongly linked to cases. Social media could act as a conduit, turning traditional media coverage into higher rates of youth suicide and attempted suicide, researchers found. “Social media and traditional media are not independent of each other, as the information often comes from the latter. If traditional media could do better, they could influence social media activities too,” Yip said. “When news about suicide pops up, we strongly encourage people not to like, comment on or share it. Just taking a quick pause before reacting can go a long way in stopping the story from spreading so widely.” The centre also conducted an AI-assisted review of news reports on suicide cases by six local Chinese-language media outlets and found that most of the stories failed to comply with coverage guidelines issued by the World Health Organization. The ignored guidelines included sharing information on suicide warning signs or risk factors and avoiding detailed descriptions of the incident locations. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial or message via WhatsApp 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Exclusive | Kimi maker Moonshot AI to explore dual Hong Kong and Shanghai IPOs to boost capital: sources
description: Moonshot’s exploration of dual listings may stem in part from the weaker performance of AI stocks in Hong Kong, the sources said.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up Moonshot AI, developer of the popular Kimi K3 model, may explore options for dual listings in Hong Kong and Shanghai in pursuit of greater capital and exposure, according to two people familiar with the matter. Since a meeting with its financial backers in July, when the Beijing-based company negotiated detailed arrangements for an initial public offering in Hong Kong, it has hinted at options to also list on a mainland bourse afterwards, one source said. On the mainland, Moonshot was likely looking at the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s tech-heavy Star Market and may soon begin negotiations, according to the other source. The Star Market has attracted many Chinese technology stars recently, including ChangXin Memory Technologies and Unitree Robotics, while awaiting other big names like DeepSeek and Yangtze Memory Technologies. Moonshot’s exploration of dual listings may stem from the weaker market performance of AI stocks in Hong Kong, and because too many firms had applied to list in the city, the sources said. Moonshot did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. The firm has already filed confidentially for a Hong Kong IPO, targeting a listing as early as the first quarter of 2027. Meanwhile, it has undertaken a final financing round ahead of the IPO, which could value it at around US$50 billion, the South China Morning Post reported last week. Shares of rivals Z.ai and MiniMax have fallen in recent weeks. Both firms are in the process of separate listings on the Star Market. A key procedure before Moonshot’s IPO is to unwind its offshore structure, known as a variable interest entity, or VIE. It informed shareholders in May it would start the process, the SCMP reported at the time, but it had not been completed, the first source said. The IPO and financing plans signal an accelerated fundraising pace as global competition heats up in frontier AI models. Moonshot made headlines in July with the release of its Kimi K3 model: the world’s largest open-weight AI model, with more than 2.8 trillion parameters. As of Thursday, it ranked as the second-best Chinese model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, behind Z.ai’s GLM-5.3. But they both trailed over 10 closed-source systems from American labs Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta Platforms. Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – has been growing. The figure was expected to reach US$1 billion by the end of the year, doubling from an estimated US$400 million to US$500 million as of mid-2026, according to a research note published by Nomura Securities in July. For comparison, Z.ai’s ARR had reached US$1.6 billion by the end of August, and MiniMax’s hit US$800 million last month. Moonshot was also exploring a revenue share deal with overseas cloud service providers including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, under which the platforms could share up to 30 per cent of revenue from services hosting its Kimi K3 model, according to a Reuters report last month.

title: Women’s Basketball World Cup: China reach last 8, but fans worry over squad depth, fatigue
description: Han Xu leads way again in win over Puerto Rico but now faces two New York Liberty teammates in tough French team – with only 19 hours of rest.
content: China’s 75-72 victory over Puerto Rico in Berlin on Wednesday secured a fourth consecutive Fiba Women’s World Cup quarter-final berth, sparking a wave of relief on domestic social media alongside growing fan anxiety over squad depth and fatigue ahead of a daunting clash against France. WNBA star Han Xu produced a dominant 21-point, 11-rebound double-double – her third in a row – to lead China through the qualifying play-in. Yang Shuyu scored 15 points, while 2.21-metre (7-foot-3) centre Zhang Ziyu added 13 points on 5-for-6 shooting. With the game tied at 66-66, Han sank a go-ahead three-pointer with 2:56 remaining. A minute later, Luo Xinyu hit another shot from deep to extend China’s lead to six points. Puerto Rico’s Arella Guirantes cut the deficit to 72-70 with 25 seconds left, but Yang sealed the victory by making two free throws eight seconds later. Trinity San Antonio led Puerto Rico with 24 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, while Imani Stafford-McGee added 16 points as Puerto Rico’s tournament ended one round earlier than in 2022. The result sets up a last-eight clash on Thursday against world No 2 France. China won silver at the 2022 World Cup after beating France 85-71 in the quarter-finals, though France routed China 82-50 during the Paris Olympic qualifiers earlier this year. “We are a young team, but they were No 2 at the Olympic Games,” Han said of France. “They’re so tough and they are winning games by a lot, but we are not afraid. We just play 100 per cent and hope we can learn a lot from this game.” Han will also face New York Liberty teammates Marine Johannes and Pauline Astier. “For one day we aren’t friends. After that we are friends again,” Han joked. China head coach Gong Luming acknowledged the stern test ahead. “France are Olympic silver medallists, and their defensive style is very tough,” Gong said. “We hope to learn from them and play to our strengths, combining our inside and outside play better. We want to cherish these opportunities against strong teams to refine, train and improve ourselves for future Olympic Games.” On Chinese social media, fans widely praised Han as the sole “world-class” pillar steering the team through a rebuilding phase. “Han Xu is the only world-class player on the Chinese team,” one fan wrote, with another comparing her to male basketball legend Yi Jianlian for “fighting a lonely battle”. A popular joke online read: “Coach Gong: ‘There were too many people around just now; now that we’re in private, Sister Han, let me kowtow to you a few times.’” However, supporters voiced sharp criticism over weak guard play, high turnover rates and a lack of offensive creation. “We are in a guard drought now. Nobody can take over from Wang Siyu, whose form has dropped severely,” one online user noted. Another added: “The current national team guard line is failing even by Asian standards … Why can’t China produce a few elite guards? Both the men’s and women’s teams have this issue.” Fans also lamented the absence of key stars Li Yueru, reportedly sidelined because of passport issues, and winger Li Meng. “If we had Li Meng and Li Yueru, we could even challenge world No 1 USA,” one user commented. Compounding fan anxiety is a punishing schedule that leaves China with just a 19-hour turnaround after Wednesday’s qualifying match, compared with three days of rest for France as group winners. “Back-to-back against France tonight – this schedule is completely unreasonable. Han Xu barely got any rest last night,” one user complained. Despite the hurdles, most fans viewed reaching the top eight as a satisfactory outcome. “France is in a different weight class,” one commenter noted. “Losing by a small margin is a win!”

title: 2 men jailed for up to 38 months over pro-independence group’s secession plot
description: Judge says pair, acting as advisers, devised ‘full plan’ to advance goals of Taiwan-based group calling for Hong Kong’s independence.
content: Hong Kong’s District Court has sentenced two men with autism to up to three years and two months in prison for their involvement in a pro-independence group seeking to separate the city from Chinese sovereignty. District Judge Ernest Lin Kam-hung on Thursday found that courier Chan Tai-sum, 27, and waiter Ng Chi-tung, 25, had been deeply involved in the Taiwan-based Hong Kong Democratic Independence Union between November 2024 and July 2025. He said the pair had jointly devised a “full plan” to advance the group’s objectives, although it had not been carried out. Founded by a fugitive, the union advocates Hong Kong’s “liberation” from mainland Chinese rule, seeks international recognition for a self-proclaimed “Hong Kong Parliament” and calls for the establishment of an army to “restore and defend” the city. Both defendants had earlier pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit secession. Judge Lin said the pair had served as advisers within the organisation. Chan was responsible for designing promotional materials, establishing ties with foreign organisations and compiling personal data on police officers and their families. Ng advised on policy matters, including proposals for a new “national flag” for Hong Kong, a ban on certain media outlets and the execution of government officials. “If such behaviour is tolerated, it could trigger an uncontrollable chain reaction that might plunge Hong Kong back into the unrest of 2019,” Judge Lin said. Defence lawyers said in mitigation that the pair had been diagnosed with autism and had difficulty socialising in real life. They said the disorder had influenced them when they committed the offence. When the defendants were arrested in July 2025, police searched Ng’s home and seized 19 flags bearing slogans associated with separatist movements in Tibet, Xinjiang and Guangdong province. Lin noted that Ng’s developmental condition did not appear to have reduced his active participation in political activities, as evidence showed that he knew such advocacy was illegal. Although Ng told police that he had joined the scheme “out of curiosity”, while sharing the group’s pro-independence views, the judge rejected the claim that he was merely curious. Chan served a one-year prison term in 2022 for sedition and incitement. His defence counsel said he had felt ostracised by society after his release and had struggled to move on. The judge described him as a repeat offender who had failed to learn his lesson. “Apparently, the previous sentence bore no deterrent effect on him,” he said. Lin imposed a heavier sentence on Chan than on his co-defendant. After granting sentence reductions for their timely guilty pleas, he sentenced Chan to 38 months in prison and Ng to 36 months.

title: Apple enters a crowded foldable smartphone market in China – can it beat Huawei?
description: The new iPhone Duo flagship handset is trending on Weibo but faces fierce domestic competition and local hurdles.
content: Apple’s long-awaited entry into the foldable smartphone market, the iPhone Duo, has drawn immediate attention in China over its eye-watering price tag and exclusive dual-eSIM design, as the American tech giant targets entrenched domestic rivals Huawei Technologies and Xiaomi. Unveiled on Wednesday, the iPhone Duo – Apple’s thinnest and most expensive flagship model yet – captured the attention of Chinese consumers with its smooth transition between inner and outer displays. By Thursday morning, the hashtag #iPhoneDuoFoldAnimationIsPerfect had surged to second place on microblogging platform Weibo. Tech blogger Weibusi, who has 1.6 million followers on Weibo, praised the device’s redesigned interface for extending the familiar iPhone experience across folded and unfolded modes, rather than simply replicating iPadOS. Despite the positive initial reception, however, some argued adoption in China could hit a wall over connectivity issues. Tech and gaming commentator Wang Weichen, who has 1.3 million followers on Weibo, applauded the model’s “user-friendly interface”, but said the lack of a physical SIM tray could “turn away a lot of buyers”. Unlike many international markets where digital eSIM profiles can be transferred seamlessly online, carriers in mainland China enforce strict real-name user registration. Activating or migrating an eSIM requires consumers to complete time-consuming in-person identity checks at bricks-and-mortar stores. Despite those potential consumer hurdles, financial markets welcomed the announcement. China is likely to be the most demanding market for the iPhone Duo Francisco Jeronimo, IDC Shares of component maker Lingyi iTech jumped over 5 per cent in both Hong Kong and Shenzhen on Thursday morning. The supplier provides Apple with precision hinge components, screen support plates and ultra-thin heat spreaders for the iPhone Duo, according to a source familiar with the matter. Even so, in a fiercely competitive smartphone market, consumer adoption could ultimately hinge on the retail price tag. Tech influencer Technology Xiaonai, who has 1.2 million Weibo followers, pointed out that the 256GB base model starts at 15,999 yuan (US$2,384), well above domestic rivals such as Huawei’s Pura X Max and Xiaomi’s 18 Fold, both priced from 10,999 yuan, and Samsung Electronics’ Galaxy Z Fold8, which starts at 12,999 yuan. However, the iPhone Duo undercuts Huawei’s new premium trifold handset, the Mate XT 2, which was unveiled on Monday with a starting price of 19,999 yuan. Apple’s pricing was a “bold move” amid rising memory costs, said Liz Lee, associate director at market intelligence firm Counterpoint Research, noting that the device commanded only a US$100 global premium over Samsung’s flagship. “It will leave consumers eager and waiting early on, especially if supply is much tighter than expected,” she said. Apple’s debut foldable was unveiled during an unusually crowded week of launches in China, with both Huawei and Xiaomi – which launched its 18 Fold on Monday – introducing new devices in the segment. “China is likely to be the most demanding market for the iPhone Duo,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president for worldwide client devices at IDC. He observed that while Huawei dominated the domestic foldable phone market with a 79 per cent share, Apple’s latest entry “just handed Chinese buyers their first genuinely compelling reason to reconsider”. The US firm, Jeronimo noted, could end up leading the category by value, provided the device offered enough differentiation in design, durability and software utility to justify switching. To appeal to niche users, Apple included Apple Pencil compatibility – a feature highlighted on Thursday by Goldman Sachs analysts led by Allen Chang. By contrast, Samsung recently removed S Pen support from its latest Fold series. Neil Shah, vice-president of research at Counterpoint Research, said Apple’s arrival in the segment had “immediately put the category in the spotlight”. This was despite foldables accounting for just 2 per cent of the broader smartphone market, Counterpoint said in a report last week. In that same report, Counterpoint projected that Apple would ship up to 6 million iPhone Duo units this year, capturing a 25 per cent global market share to rank second behind Samsung at 38 per cent and ahead of Huawei at 22 per cent. Additional reporting by Iris Deng

title: High-quality, natural audio: listen to SCMP articles with improved narration
description: The South China Morning Post has relaunched its text-to-speech feature, leveraging next-generation AI models.
content: The South China Morning Post has relaunched its “listen to article” text-to-speech feature, taking advantage of improved artificial intelligence (AI) models to provide subscribers more compelling and natural narration. Audio functionality has also been added to SCMP Plus, our premium reader product, letting readers listen to eligible Plus articles. The previous SCMP audio feature was launched several years ago, but with AI models rapidly improving every few months, the decision was made to rebuild the entire text-to-speech platform and replace external providers with a proprietary solution. We also took on board reader comments, which gave us invaluable insight into where improvements could be made. The cross-team project – which spanned several months – set out to enhance voice narration quality and technical performance, including intonation for easier listening. The result is an integrated, in-house AI text-to-speech platform which provides custom, scalable, high-quality voice synthesis and article narration. Along with SCMP Plus, the text-to-speech feature has been rolled out across all SCMP products, including our student publication Young Post. The much-improved feature now lets all SCMP subscribers keep up with our journalism on the go, whether it’s catching up with headlines while commuting or enjoying the latest opinion pieces, totally screen free. To experience our text-to-speech feature, click or tap on the “Listen” button in the header of any eligible article, whether on desktop, mobile web or the SCMP app. We hope SCMP readers enjoy this upgrade and welcome your feedback. Let us know what you think of the feature, or what else you would like to see from us, by commenting on this article.

title: Mainland Chinese shoppers lose trusted Hong Kong veggie tag as customs revamp hits shelves
description: Change sparks concern among consumers, with the Hong Kong label having long served as a selling point for high quality.
content: Mainland Chinese supermarkets, including US warehouse retailer Sam’s Club, have dropped the Hong Kong-bound vegetable label under new customs rules. The change has triggered widespread concern among consumers, as the label had long served as a selling point for high quality amid frequent mainland food-safety incidents. The removal stems from new rules by the General Administration of Customs. From September 1, registration will no longer be required for growing farms, and only food-processing firms need to register. Before, I just looked for the Hong Kong-bound label. Now I must check the details myself Consumer This means vegetables grown on the same farms that supply Hong Kong can no longer carry the Hong Kong-bound label when sold in mainland supermarkets. “Before, I just looked for the Hong Kong-bound label,” said a female consumer in a post this week on Chinese social media platform RedNote. “Now I must check the details myself, and that’s the change.” Hong Kong-bound labelled lettuce was once a bestseller at Walmart-owned Sam’s Club on the mainland, drawing middle-class shoppers who trusted its quality. Given its high popularity, the retailer added a tag on the product to explain the new customs rule. The 600-gram pack, still priced at 12.90 yuan (US$1.90), uses the same packaging and supplier from China’s northwestern Ningxia Hui autonomous region, distinguished only by the new “Dali lettuce” label. The retailer found a way to retain a hint of Hong Kong appeal. Dali lettuce is what Hong Kong people know as Chinese lettuce, a broad-leaf Italian variety, and the Cantonese pronunciation for “Italian” sounds similar to “Dali”. This has sparked heated discussion online. Many shoppers said the new Dali lettuce did not measure up, and some complained it lacked the crunch and moisture of the old version. Others said merchants could still claim unchanged quality, and shoppers would struggle to pursue legal claims if the vegetable failed to meet old supply standards, according to RedNote posts. Constrained by limited land and industrial layout, Hong Kong imports over 90 per cent of its food. The mainland was its top supplier of fresh produce, providing 94 per cent of fresh pork, 92 per cent of vegetables and 66 per cent of eggs consumed locally, according to the Environment and Ecology Bureau in Hong Kong. To meet Hong Kong’s food-safety requirements, mainland food bound for the city saw steady quality improvements. Supply farms for Hong Kong became a priority for regional agriculture and a way to boost added value. Such sites are usually located in pristine and low-pollution areas.

title: J-50 designers reveal leapfrog tech for China’s next-gen stealth fighters
description: The aircraft are expected to have futuristic systems for self-flying and large-scale drone wingman squads.
content: China’s next-generation combat aircraft will be able to fly by themselves if a pilot loses consciousness, navigate without satellite signals and operate in self-reorganising large drone formations. That is the plan laid out by researchers from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, a top Chinese military aircraft design organisation, in a paper last month. The institute is associated with the development of the Chinese next-generation aircraft commonly referred to as the J-50, which first appeared in flight-test imagery in December 2024, although the paper does not mention the J-50 by name or confirm that the aircraft will incorporate any of the described technologies. China’s future fighters, including the J-50 and J-36, are considered rivals to the US Air Force’s sixth-generation main fighter programme, the F-47, being developed by Boeing. The lead researcher is chief flight-control designer Zhang Dong at the institute, and his team’s paper – rare for its public details – was published in a peer-reviewed journal Aircraft Design in August. China’s next-generation stealth fighter programmes were undergoing a “leapfrog transformation from being able to fly steadily to being able to win in combat”, wrote Zhang and his colleagues. Zhang’s study presents a future of pilots handing over control during periods of extreme workload or incapacitation, quantum navigation technologies supporting operations in satellite-denied environments and crewed fighters coordinating attack, reconnaissance and protection missions with reconfigurable wingman drones. The team’s institute is part of the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China, which oversees much of the country’s aircraft research and development. Its subsidiary, Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group, is also developing the J-36 fighter, widely regarded as another candidate for China’s next-generation sixth-generation combat aircraft. In 2025, an investigation by defence news website, The War Zone, using satellite imagery found that the Chengdu J-36 and the Shenyang J-50 aircraft were both based at an experimental military airfield near Lop Nur, a highly secretive site for aerospace test flights that has often been compared to the United States’ Area 51. Their simultaneous presence at the same base suggested that China’s military was actively supporting the parallel development of the two programmes. Zhang’s paper presents a rare technological road map for future combat aircraft, describing a fundamental restructuring of the flight-control system from a device concerned mainly with flight quality into a core enabler of collaborative engagement, intelligent manoeuvre and mission effectiveness. The change reflected what the authors described as three successive eras of air combat. In the earlier “energy manoeuvrability” era, victory depended heavily on physical manoeuvring performance in close-range combat, while flight-control systems were largely closed and centralised, with specialised hardware and software designed mainly to keep the aircraft stable, controllable and responsive to pilot inputs. The rise of long-range radar, stealth shaping and precision-guided weapons shifted combat towards “information manoeuvrability”, where detecting, tracking and attacking an opponent before being detected became increasingly important. Fifth-generation aircraft such as the F-22 and J-20 use full-authority digital fly-by-wire systems and increasingly integrate flight control with fire-control and propulsion systems through high-speed data links. The authors argued that the next phase was “cognitive manoeuvrability”, in which artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and distributed networking allowed air combat to move from platform-versus-platform competition towards system-level contests involving manned-unmanned formations. This changes what flight control is expected to do. “The functional positioning of the flight control system is undergoing a fundamental restructuring – from a platform controller merely pursuing flight quality to a core enabler of collaborative engagement management, intelligent manoeuvre decision-making and closed-loop mission effectiveness,” Zhang and his co-authors wrote. The first major capability is autonomous flight control. Instead of making pilots constantly turn high-level battle plans into precise stick movements, the new system would let on-board intelligent algorithms do that job automatically, translating tactical orders into smooth, continuous flight actions while keeping the aircraft safely within its physical limits, even during extreme manoeuvres. The aircraft would constantly monitor its own health by fusing data from sensors such as inertial navigation, airspeed indicators, control-surface positions and engine performance. This would allow it to assess its flight state, estimate remaining manoeuvrability and detect potential problems before they develop into emergencies. The system could then automatically adjust control settings and redistribute on-board resources while strictly enforcing safety boundaries to avoid stalls, loss of control or stuck control surfaces. In particularly stressful situations, the aircraft could take over from the pilot. The paper proposes allocating control authority between humans and autonomous systems so that pilots can spend less effort on low-level aircraft handling and more on battlefield assessment and tactical decisions. During periods of excessive workload or if a pilot loses the ability to control the aircraft, the system could take control and continue executing the intended tactical task while prioritising flight safety. The second major change concerns navigation. Future combat aircraft may need to operate when satellite navigation is jammed, disrupted or unavailable, prompting the researchers to identify quantum inertial navigation, visual navigation, geomagnetic navigation and terrain matching as potential technologies for passive autonomous navigation. The paper proposes combining data from various sensors to reduce errors and prevent failures caused by the degradation or loss of any single sensor under severe electromagnetic interference. Quantum inertial navigation is therefore presented as part of a broader effort to give aircraft an independent sense of movement and position, rather than as a replacement for GPS. The study framed these technologies as areas requiring further engineering research and implementation, rather than saying a quantum navigation system had already been deployed on a Chinese fighter. The biggest shift, however, may come from the way multiple aircraft work together. Future formations could pair crewed fighters acting as command nodes with uncrewed wingmen assigned to reconnaissance, attack and protection roles. Flight-control systems would coordinate their positions, routes, electromagnetic spectrum use and weapons-launch windows while dynamically allocating tasks between aircraft. The authors saw this as more than a traditional formation controlled by a single leader. If an aircraft suffered a malfunction or combat damage and left the formation, the remaining aircraft could automatically reorganise, replace the missing node and redistribute its unfinished tasks. The system used consensus-based coordination and a dynamic “virtual leader” replacement mechanism to maintain autonomous operation without relying on a permanent central node. Zhang and his team said single-aircraft autonomous control guaranteed survival in complex environments, while swarm coordination delivered multiplied combat effectiveness. The paper pointed towards a more heterogeneous air-combat network rather than a simple arrangement of one crewed fighter and several identical drones. It further highlighted large collaborative wingmen alongside various aircraft and autonomous platforms, suggesting a future architecture in which crewed fighters, larger unmanned aircraft and smaller autonomous systems could perform different functions within the same network. Aircraft such as the Chinese Y-20 transport aircraft, the J-20 fighter and even the H-20 stealth strategic bomber, which is believed to be under development, could potentially form part of such a combat network. However, Zhang and his team did not say whether the “combat group”, or the crewed “lead aircraft” and unmanned wingmen, would consist mainly of large numbers of drones or a combination of the larger aircraft described above. The Shenyang Aircraft Corporation and the paper’s authors did not respond to a request for comment. Based on the paper’s publicly available discussion, the researchers suggested retaining conventional systems engineering as the safety backbone while using intelligent tools for tasks such as parameter optimisation, test expansion, automated testing and defect detection, with early trials conducted on lower-cost uncrewed platforms before broader adoption in major aircraft. But the researchers do not advocate handing the aircraft’s most safety-critical functions directly to artificial intelligence (AI). Instead, they identified a basic engineering conflict between intelligence and flight safety. Data-driven algorithms can be difficult to explain and verify, and they might not apply in every situation, especially in extreme scenarios. Applying such systems directly to the innermost control loops could therefore introduce unpredictable risks. The proposed solution was a layered architecture. “Engineering practice widely adopts a hybrid architecture with a closed core and open periphery,” the team wrote, allowing high-reliability, real-time functions to remain tightly controlled while more flexible software functions could be upgraded and connected across different platforms. Under this model, the inner loop would retain conventional, highly deterministic controls for functions such as attitude stabilisation, control-surface actuation and hard flight-envelope protection. AI would operate mainly in the outer loop, handling tactical decision-making, trajectory optimisation, multi-aircraft coordination and payload adaptation, while rigid safeguards would constrain its commands so that its recommendations remain inside a safe operating envelope. The researchers called for further work on open layered architecture, verifiable intelligent flight control and cross-domain cooperative control, supported by large-scale simulation and flight-test data to improve the robustness and verifiability of intelligent models.

title: Singapore MPs back ministerial pay rise, but agree money alone won’t lure talent
description: PM Wong defended the new salary structure for leadership renewal while Workers’ Party chief Pritam Singh sought more modest increases over time.
content: While Singapore’s officials are among the highest-paid in the world, money alone cannot attract the brightest leaders to public service, lawmakers have said during a debate on the increase in ministerial salaries – a move supported by both opposition and ruling party MPs. The parliamentary discussion on Thursday, which saw MPs share their personal reflections on stepping into public office, followed an announced rise in ministerial salary, which Prime Minister Lawrence Wong insisted was necessary for leadership renewal and to keep pace with the private sector. Benchmark salaries of Wong’s cabinet will be increased by more than 60 per cent, ranging from S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) to S$3.6 million annually. Ministers will receive a one-off rise of up to 9 per cent next month, with subsequent increments subject to individual performance and responsibilities. Singapore last adjusted the salaries of political holders in 2012, slashing wages by more than 35 per cent. A recommendation to increase the pay following a 2017 review was not adopted. “If too many capable people conclude that political service asks for sacrifices which are just too great, then over time we will have fewer people prepared to step forward,” Wong said as he rounded up the debate that lasted over 3½ hours. “Eventually, the quality of our leadership will suffer and Singapore will suffer the consequences.” He called it a “mistaken framework” that the purpose of the salary structure was to entice people into politics with money since “motivation to serve” and “responding to the call” had to come first. “We have to persuade good people that Singapore needs them, that the work matters, that they can make a difference. Then, if someone is prepared to step forward, remuneration becomes a practical consideration,” Wong said. Earlier, opposition Workers’ Party chief Pritam Singh questioned if the city state’s high earners in the private sector were deterred from politics by lower pay or whether the issue was political responsibilities. He argued that most of Singapore’s cabinet continued to be fielded from the public sector, while “only a small handful” chose to leave the private sector for politics. “For some, it would not be out of order to suggest that no amount of money will persuade them to trade their suits and ties for grass-roots activities and to immerse themselves in municipal concerns and the rough and tumble of politics,” he said. Singh in parliament reiterated his party’s view that ministers’ salaries should be a multiple of an MP’s allowance instead of pegged to the median wage of the top 1,000 earners in Singapore, with a discount. The approach of WP – the only opposition party in parliament – would have resulted in more modest increases over time, he said. Wong argued that the WP’s formula would arrive at a similar figure and if the salary was benchmarked with inflation, a higher sum would be derived. “For all intents and purposes, within this term of government, we agree on the implementation approach. Beyond that, we will have to consider the circumstances then,” Wong said, noting that another independent review would be done in five years. Wong also countered the argument that Singapore’s office holders were among the highest earners in the world, saying political office holders in many countries were given pensions, allowances, housing and other benefits beyond their official salary package. As prime minister, Wong’s salary would be increased from S$2.2 million to S$3.6 million. He pledged to donate the increment to good causes for five years and said on Thursday that he would not keep the tax benefits from his donation. Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry) Tan See Leng, a former doctor and medical entrepreneur, shared his personal experience of giving up his career as group CEO and managing director of IHH Healthcare to enter politics in 2020, at the age of 55. Tan said on Thursday that he made the move after a “growing inner realisation” that his experience in the private sector could be put to good use to give back to the country. He added that no realistic level of ministerial salary could have matched what he was earning in the private sector. On attracting future talent, Tan said: “If we make entry into the public service come at too high a personal cost for too many capable Singaporeans, then over time we will indeed narrow the pool from which our country can draw its leaders and, members of the House, that would be a far greater cost than any salary debate.” Singapore’s ministerial salary model ensured that its leaders were “not incentivised to look elsewhere” and act with citizens’ best interests in mind, said Christopher de Souza, a lawmaker from the ruling People’s Action Party. Prolonged wage stagnation may lead political office holders to view their time in office as a stepping stone for their professional careers, he said, citing examples of state leaders from the United States and the United Kingdom who earned large sums from assets and corporate deals after leaving office. “If politicians know that their future careers may depend on relationships built while in office, the public will inevitably wonder whether today’s decisions are made solely in the national interest, or whether tomorrow’s opportunities are also at the back of the minds of their leaders,” he said. Several MPs raised concerns regarding negative public sentiment over ministerial pay increases and some asked for more information to be made public on how ministers’ performances were reviewed. Wong said he understood the concerns, but there was never going to be a “politically convenient time” to adjust salaries. “If every difficult circumstance becomes a reason not to act, then we will keep putting the issue off, and there will come a point where restraint ceases to be prudence and becomes neglect,” he said, adding that leadership renewal was urgent. On how ministers’ performance bonuses were distributed, he cautioned against the assessment being made into a public popularity contest and said the cabinet was a team that Singaporeans should judge based on how the government as a whole performed. “If we fall short, Singaporeans can choose another team to govern. That is the final accountability in our system,” Wong said. The pay bump reignited a long-standing debate on the thorny issue, with opposition parties voicing swift criticism. Some pointed out ongoing economic uncertainty and rising unemployment rates, while others criticised the salary framework. Chong Ja Ian, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, said the argument of recruiting and retaining talent was justifiable from a human resource perspective. He said the amounts would, however, appear “eye-watering” to the public and raise questions about “other forms of inspiration” to serve the people. “Even without the pay rises, political appointees still earn more than enough to afford a very, very comfortable standard of living.” He suggested that indicators such as total fertility rate and progress on climate issues be included in the assessment for compensation for political office holders. Currently, ministers’ salaries include a national bonus, which is linked to socio-economic indicators such as the growth rate of residents’ median income and Singapore’s real gross domestic product.

title: Grab Singapore apologises over microdrama ad that raised passenger safety fears
description: The ride-hailing giant admits insensitivity over the romcom series following complaints that it trivialised driver harassment.
content: Grab Singapore has apologised after a new promotional series formatted like popular Chinese microdramas raised concerns over personal boundaries and passenger safety in the city state. Titled I Fell In Love With My Grab Driver, the video campaign stars local actress-model Regina Lim as Emily, a widow stretched thin by the demands of her children and mother. The campaign’s trailer, released on Friday, shows Emily meeting Grab driver Henry – played by Singaporean actor-singer Glenn Yong – when he picks her up as she is running errands. After the car hits a bump, Henry stops to check on her, causing Emily to realise he is not the middle-aged “uncle” she expected. He then begins popping up throughout her daily routine: delivering food to her door, catching her mid-fall K-drama style, and rescuing her from an abusive boss. The campaign’s tagline asks: “What if your Grab driver becomes the love of your life?” Six of the planned 12 episodes were published on Grab Singapore’s official YouTube account before the backlash intensified. It is unclear whether the tech giant will release the remaining episodes. Reactions on social media were swift and divided. Some users praised the brand’s creative direction as innovative, saying they “can’t wait” for the release. “Finally, a fun ad! We need this,” one said. Others, however, were critical of the message, especially against a backdrop of complaints against ride-share drivers for inappropriate behaviour. “This is so weird,” one user said. “There are countless people who had feedback and complaints about drivers being inappropriate. People go lengths to cover up and make sure that your drivers behave well. This microdrama just enables all their actions.” “It is absolutely ridiculous that the biggest ride-hailing company [in Singapore] would green-light a microdrama with this boundary being crossed. What are you trying to tell your drivers? That it’s OK and possible to have something with your passenger?” another said. There have been a number of complaints against ride-hailing drivers in Singapore recently. On July 12, content creator Sarah Lim posted a video on social media of her conversation with a driver. In it, the driver can be heard asking what ethnic group Lim is from. When she says she is “a bit of Canto”, the driver says: “I love Cantonese girls. They are so good looking.” He then adds that Cantonese was a “sexy language to learn”. A day later, another passenger said on social media she filed a police report against her driver for allegedly making inappropriate and sexually explicit remarks towards her – including asking for a threesome – during the ride. Addressing the online backlash, Grab Singapore issued a statement on its social media accounts on Tuesday prioritising safety standards. “We completely agree that safety, clear boundaries and respect in everyday interactions should never be compromised,” the company said. It added it had set out to “create a fun, fast-paced series for the ‘sandwich generation’ juggling parents, children and careers” using a microdrama soap opera-style format to tell a “cheesy romcom story that includes a hidden identity, a love triangle, and heightened family drama”. “In hindsight, we should have been much more thoughtful with how the title came across, as it understandably raised concerns about safety. We are sorry for causing any discomfort and alarm. We want to be clear that inappropriate actions or conversations are never acceptable – whether from or towards our passengers, or our driver and delivery partners.” Good or bad, the reactions sparked by the microdrama have given Grab the buzz it wanted. When the trailer was first unveiled, analysis by media intelligence firm Carma found that 40.25 per cent of mentions were positive, compared with 7.21 per cent negative, Marketing-Interactive reported. “We see real potential in entertainment-led storytelling as a way to build genuine relevance, so it’s a space we’re keen to keep exploring,” Mindy Yap, head of regional brand and Singapore country marketing at Grab, told the news and intelligence platform. “This first series has taught us a lot – including from the conversations it’s sparked – and we’ll take these learnings into whatever comes next.”

title: Man, 61, dies in hospital after collapsing on board Hong Kong train
description: MTR Corp says morning train services along Tsuen Wan line were disrupted to allow passenger to receive urgent medical aid.
content: A 61-year-old man died in hospital on Thursday after collapsing on board a Hong Kong train earlier in the morning. Police said they received a report at 7.39am from passengers who found the man collapsed on a Central-bound train as it arrived at Cheung Sha Wan station. The incident temporarily disrupted MTR services along the Tsuen Wan line. The force added that firefighters and paramedics had arrived and found the man unconscious. He was rushed to Caritas Medical Centre in Sham Shui Po and later died at 8.47am. The MTR Corporation said that rail services along the line were affected between 7.35am and 8.40am as a result of the incident. “Train service on the Tsuen Wan line was disrupted on September 10 because of a passenger on a train requiring urgent medical help at Cheung Sha Wan station,” the rail operator said.

title: Chinese cousins in their 50s redesign, revitalise ethnic fabric, model, sell clothing globally
description: Pair faced criticism from family for their modelling videos, with one relative telling them to ‘act their age’.
content: A pair of Chinese cousins in their 50s have redesigned ethnic brocade and promoted it by cross-dressing in women’s clothing made from the fabric, despite facing objections from their family. Uncle Yang, 56, hails from Fujian province in southeastern China, while his older cousin, Uncle Song, is from Heilongjiang province in northeastern China. Although they grew up separately, they reunited for their shared passion for fashion in the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. Videos of them wearing women’s attire crafted by Yang from Zhuang Jin, an ethnic brocade unique to Guangxi and one of China’s “Four Famous Brocades”, went viral on social media. Yang’s account has attracted hundreds of thousands of followers across various domestic and international platforms. In addition to numerous orders from China, they have also received requests from customers in Japan and the US. However, their fashion career has faced significant challenges. Song, who began selling clothes on the street at the age of 17, invited Yang, who started designing at a factory at the same age, to Guangxi in 2008 to collaborate on their own fashion brand. At their peak, they owned 106 stores in the region, but unfortunately, all were shut down during the Covid-19 pandemic. Following this setback, Yang fell ill and his weight dropped to less than 50kg. Song took on a job as a security guard to make ends meet. Their wives suggested a trip to help alleviate their stress. During this journey, Yang discovered the beauty of Guangxi Zhuang brocade. It became clear to them that the Zhuang brocade was less recognised than the other three famous brocades: the Yun brocade from Nanjing, the Shu brocade from Chengdu, and the Song brocade from Suzhou. Determined to incorporate the traditional Zhuang brocade into his neo-Chinese clothing designs, Yang faced challenges in hiring a suitable female model. To promote their brand more effectively, he convinced Song to try on the finished women’s attire he created. Song recalled that Yang initially asked him to wear the clothing “to help me see its effect.” From being hesitant to wear the garments in public to confidently walking the runway on the street, Song garnered admiration from many netizens, who noted that his posture “highlights the grandeur of the Zhuang brocade and Uncle Yang’s design.” At times, Yang also modelled his own creations. They mentioned that their family still struggles to accept their modelling videos, with one relative criticising them for “not acting your age.” Additionally, Song’s daughter refused to contact him for six months. Despite the challenges, the cousins remain committed to their promotional approach, with the ultimate goal of preserving traditional culture and raising awareness of the beauty of Zhuang brocade. Earlier this year, they were invited by an international luxury brand to an event in Shanghai, which they viewed as a significant achievement in their promotional efforts. “Hats off to the cousins, who are both not from Guangxi but dedicate themselves so fully to the Guangxi brocade,” commented an online observer.

title: Meet James Wilkie Broderick, son of Sarah Jessica Parker and Matthew Broderick
description: The eldest child of the Sex and the City star has quietly taken on acting roles, including in the Natalie Portman-led miniseries Lady in the Lake.
content: It’s not every day Hollywood parents can keep their children out of the spotlight and give them relatively “normal” childhoods. But long-time married couple and proud parents, Matthew Broderick and Sarah Jessica Parker, have raised their three children largely outside the public eye – until now. In recent years, 23-year-old James Wilkie Broderick, the pair’s eldest child, has quietly made his on-screen debut and, most recently, starred in the 2026 short film Altar Egos. Here’s everything you need to know about Sarah Jessica Parker’s son, James Wilkie Broderick. How was James Wilkie Broderick raised? James Wilkie Broderick was born in October 2002 and is an older brother to twin sisters Marion Loretta Elwell and Tabitha Hodge. Despite her bona fide Hollywood status thanks to Sex and the City, Parker’s upbringing wasn’t a glamorous one. In 2008, she told Parade magazine: “I think that if I had been raised a child of privilege, I wouldn’t be the working person I am today. I have a great appreciation for work.” The actress said she therefore refrained from raising her children in a life of excess and luxury, adding: “I think it’s incumbent on my husband and me to really stress and to show James Wilkie by example what it means to owe your community something and that he is not entitled to the benefits of our hard work.” Parker also shared that she was dressing her son (who was five years old at the time) in hand-me-downs from her older nephews and in her brothers’ clothes that her mother had saved. “I don’t think I’ve ever bought him any clothes,” the actress disclosed. “I do buy him shoes, because everybody’s feet are different.” In fact, Parker and Broderick often talk about their parenting styles in interviews. She talked to People about the importance of having conversations as a family, saying: “Sometimes I just sit on the stairs because they’re all in the kitchen, eating all the food, and I listen. And I’m so charmed by their conversation. I’m so happy with the young man he’s becoming,” she added, referring to James. The doting mother of three also said she was proud “that our children talk to us in the way they do.” She added that they are “curious people”, and that her son has “this great friend group”. He has plenty of different hobbies While iconic for her role as Carrie Bradshaw, and known as the face of several fashion and beauty brands, Parker revealed to Entertainment Tonight that her children don’t really talk to her about her work. Instead, conversations at home seem normal, like those in other households. “It’s school and interning and soccer, and conversations about university and how to spend time, and where’s everyone’s stuff that’s missing?” the actress said. James’ Instagram shows a mix of interests, including playing football, reading, and hanging out with close friends, who also tag him in photos ranging from proms to art gallery exhibits. He graduated from Brown University last year and previously labelled himself a “musician/band” on his profile, signalling a possible career path. He was brought up in a religious household In the same interview with Parade, Parker spoke about the different religions her son James Wilkie has been exposed to. The actress is Jewish, while her husband comes from both a Jewish and Catholic background. At the time of the interview, Parker said their babysitter was a devout Catholic, and that “she’s had some influence on James” and “says prayers with him”. Parker herself also says prayers with her son. “He’ll probably end up a Unitarian,” she added. He remains low-profile … for now James has hit a few red carpet events, including the premiere of And Just Like That in 2021. He also supported his father’s film, No Hard Feelings, at the New York City premiere in 2023. In 2017, he and his siblings attended the Broadway opening of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. Since then, James has made his acting debut in a minor role as a valet in an episode of the 2024 television miniseries Lady in the Lake, starring Natalie Portman. He also appeared in an episode of Elsbeth and starred in two short films. This June, James made headlines after he shared black-and-white portraits of himself flexing his muscles for a photo shoot. “Ah handsome. And happy. Xxx, mama,” Parker commented under the post. The photos were snapped by photographer Brad Walsh for his book Fella: Images of Men, Walsh said in an Instagram post. He explains that the book’s “subjects include many types of men – mostly ordinary people – peppered with actors, singers, models and other cultural figures”. Additional reporting by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Jewellery shops shut down as Chinese consumers switch focus to gold bars and coins
description: High prices and decline in marriages cited as reasons for one-third drop in jewellery sales in first half of year.
content: Most of the gold jewellery shops that once lined the main commercial street in Biyang, Henan province, have closed as gold prices hover at high but volatile levels and a decline in marriages dents demand. “Gold jewellery used to be very popular in our small county,” said 25-year-old kindergarten teacher Yu Qian, who described herself as a frequent buyer of gold jewellery. “There used to be more than 20 gold shops operating here, but I’d estimate that over two-thirds of them have already closed down.” Jewellery retailers across China have been closing stores as demand weakens. In recent corporate disclosures, Chow Tai Seng reported a net reduction of 473 stores across the country, while Lao Feng Xiang said it had closed 342 outlets in third- and fourth-tier cities. China Gold cut 323 locations in the first half, and Chow Tai Fook logged a net loss of 258 mainland China stores in the second quarter of the year, primarily driven by franchise contraction. Fred You, a Guangdong-based business development manager at a national jewellery brand targeting lower-tier markets, said small jewellery shops were now under heavy pressure. Consumers were buying less gold by weight, while shop owners still had to carry inventory, pay rent and bear other operating costs, he said. “The willingness to pay a high brand premium for decorative appeal has largely evaporated,” You said. In a report released in July, the World Gold Council said Chinese gold jewellery demand had fallen 28 per cent year on year in the second quarter to its lowest level for that quarter since 2004, with elevated, volatile gold prices and cautious consumers weighing on demand. In a consumer insight report released last year, it said declining marriages and births were exerting longer-term downward pressure on China’s gold jewellery market. Over the past five years, gold prices have tracked upwards despite periods of sharp volatility. After climbing from around US$1,800 a troy ounce in 2021 to a record high of US$5,200 early this year, bullion dropped to US$4,170 before rebounding to its current level of around US$4,400. Yu said she believed high gold prices had even dented people’s marriage plans. “A lot of young people here are reluctant to get married now,” she said. “Gold jewellery and the bride price have both become heavy financial burdens for young couples getting married.” China recorded 3.275 million marriage registrations in the first half of this year, down 7.46 per cent from the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Civil Affairs. Yu and others said economic headwinds, high living costs and employment uncertainty had led young people to delay or forgo marriage. China’s gold market is now increasingly split between higher-margin jewellery and investment gold. The World Gold Council said in July that consumers had adapted to the market by exhibiting preferences for lighter-weight jewellery, old-for-new exchanges and lower-premium investment products. Data from the China Gold Association showed that jewellery demand plunged 33.88 per cent year on year to 132.1 tonnes in the first six months of this year, while demand for safe-haven gold bars and coins rose 28.42 per cent to 339.3 tonnes. Total gold consumption increased by 1.23 per cent. For some middle-class investors, the caution extends beyond gold. Guangzhou-based gold investor Vicky Liu, a doctor, said sharp swings in the US dollar, US Treasuries, Chinese stocks, gold, commodities and property had made it harder to identify safe places to put money, with one gold investment she made earlier this year still mired in loss. “Whatever you invest in can lose money now, so people are becoming much more cautious,” she said.

title: Asian Games: Japan men’s gymnasts facing race to be fit for home tournament
description: Shinnosuke Oka, who won gold in the all-around, team and horizontal bar events at the 2024 Paris Olympics, has a lower back injury.
content: Japan men’s gymnastics team for their home Asian Games this month include multiple Olympic and world champions, but serious injuries have clouded their chances. Shinnosuke Oka, who won gold in the all-around, team and horizontal bar events at the 2024 Paris Olympics, is facing a race to be fit after suffering a lower back injury last week. The Games begin in Nagoya and the wider Aichi area on September 19, with the men’s gymnastics competition getting under way two days later. Former junior world champion Tomoharu Tsunogai is also nursing a serious ankle injury, while lower back pain for Shoma Tsukiyama means three of Japan’s five-man team are carrying injuries heading into the competition. Oka did not take part in a team practice on Wednesday but told reporters afterwards that he still intended to compete in Nagoya. “I’m looking forward to it and I think a switch will flick in me,” the 22-year-old said. “I’m at the level now where I can only do the bare minimum but I don’t want to give up on aiming for gold.” Japan are the reigning Olympic team champions but China won the Asian Games title on home soil in Hangzhou in 2023. Japan’s team for this year’s competition also includes reigning world and former Olympic all-around champion Daiki Hashimoto, as well as Kiichi Kaneda. Japan team boss Kensuke Murata said he would assess his team’s fitness and decide on any changes before the September 16 deadline. Murata said that Oka would perform less difficult routines if he does compete. Oka and Hashimoto are also set to be part of Japan’s team for the world championships in Rotterdam next month. Oka said he hurt his back in training and that “the pain was different to the kind of pain I usually feel”. “I went to the hospital and it wasn’t a herniated disc, but it was something serious,” he said. Hashimoto, the all-around Olympic champion in Tokyo in 2021 and a three-time world all-around champion, said he was not worried by Japan’s injury woes. “I think the athletes themselves understand their situation better than anyone,” the 25-year-old said. “As long as they’re thinking about what they can do and what they should do, I’m not worried because they have already put in an incredible amount of training.”

title: Can Hong Kong stocks contend with wild swings without help from state hands?
description: State buying appears to quash panic selling in mainland China-listed shares, but Hong Kong’s unsettled market can’t expect government intervention.
