content: As concerted state buying puts a floor under mainland China’s onshore stock market amid Beijing’s stabilisation measures, investors in Hong Kong worry about coping with high volatility at a delicate time, with multiple market-roiling factors. These include geopolitical tensions, sluggish earnings growth, a stumbling artificial intelligence trade, possible US tightening and a looming supply glut from expiring share lock-ups. Investor worries also grew after renewed military strikes in the Middle East sent oil prices above US$100 a barrel, while Washington’s latest initiative to buy up to US$6 billion worth of long-end Treasuries failed to stem bond-market sell-offs. A possible unwinding of the Japanese yen-financed carry trade may also weigh on Hong Kong stocks, which remain vulnerable to overseas flows, after heightened expectations that the Bank of Japan would accelerate interest-rate increases. The shift could trigger sell-offs in assets bought with borrowed cheap Japanese currency. “State intervention may iron out volatility and provide liquidity to stabilise [mainland] stocks, at least in the near term,” said Dai Ming, a fund manager at Huichen Asset Management. “The Hong Kong market is now to some extent marginalised, because of poor liquidity.” The Hang Seng Index fell 1.3 per cent at the close on Thursday, tracking global caution over risk assets amid elevated Treasury yields and crude prices. It marked the benchmark’s biggest decline in more than two weeks, while mainland equities reacted more mildly, with the CSI 300 Index edging 0.5 per cent lower. Beijing’s regulatory effort to talk up stocks alongside at least 60 billion yuan (US$9 billion) of state buying seems to have temporarily eased panic selling, with a key tech gauge recouping some lost ground last week after sliding into bear-market territory in July. With the China Securities Regulatory Commission repeatedly stressing stability to prevent sharp ups and downs on stocks, the cost of defying the state support would be high for any investor. In contrast, Hong Kong stocks were on the back foot, as performance largely hinged on how the AI trade evolved and whether the US Federal Reserve embarked on a new tightening cycle, according to analysts. A majority of Hong Kong-listed firms are from mainland China, including state-owned banks, energy firms and industrial giants. Some of them are already echoing Beijing’s stabilisation call to buy back yuan-denominated, mainland-listed stocks, known as A-shares, or increase their stakes. State support is one reason cited by investment banks including Morgan Stanley for favouring A shares over Hong Kong shares. The Hang Seng Tech Index has trailed the mainland’s peer benchmarks this year, partly because of its limited exposure to AI hardware companies. Direct government intervention is rare in Hong Kong except in extreme turmoil. During the Asian financial crisis in 1998, the Hong Kong government spent about HK$120 billion (US$15.3 billion) buying key members of the Hang Seng Index, as well as index-futures contracts, to contain contagion risk arising from the currency market. Like in other developed markets, Hong Kong’s support for stocks is mainly via indirect means, such as interest-rate cuts and liquidity injections into the financial system. Given Hong Kong’s status as a global financial hub and its high level of institutional participation, direct intervention could expose the Hong Kong government or Beijing to criticism for the possible moral hazard of insulating investors from downside risks and encouraging them to take excessive bets, analysts said. Such intervention, however, may have its place in the mainland market, where foreign ownership is low, at around 4 per cent of total market value, and a colossal army of individual investors tends to amplify swings.

title: ‘Too fast’, ‘too low’: pilot pressed on with landing despite warnings in Miami crash
description: NTSB releases transcripts of recordings from Amazon cargo plane that skidded off runway, killing five.
content: One pilot of the Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that crashed in Miami on Sunday cautioned they were flying “too fast” just over a minute before touching down on the runway they overran, the National Transportation Safety Board said. The pilot continued to comment on the plane’s speed while automated warnings sounded in the cockpit. However, the other ‌pilot did not give a clear verbal response, according to the cockpit voice recording detailed in an investigative update on Wednesday that did not identify the speakers as the captain or first officer. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 operated by 21 Air overran the runway by some 396 metres (1,300 feet) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground, killing five people and injuring another five. Before the plane touched down, “sink rate sink rate” rang out twice in the cockpit as the aircraft at one point descended 400 feet in just four seconds, based on the information ⁠released by the NTSB. That was followed by five warnings of “too low terrain”. “The big question is, why did they continue their approach?” said Anthony Brickhouse, an aerospace ‌safety consultant. “They had several cues that their approach was not stable, but they continued instead of going around.” Fifteen seconds after touching down, one of the pilots called for aborting the landing and the engine throttles were increased to a value consistent ‌with go-around thrust, the NTSB said. At this point the plane was nearing the end of the runway but still travelling at ⁠120 knots (222km/h), according to data from ⁠Flightradar24 based on initial NTSB disclosures. But four seconds later, the throttles were reduced to idle power and there were then sounds similar to the plane departing the runway’s paved surface, the ‌NTSB said. The board said on Tuesday there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed to help slow the plane. Miami-based 21 Air did not respond immediately ‌to a ‌request for comment on the information released by the NTSB. Safety experts say most plane accidents are caused by multiple factors that need to be thoroughly ‌investigated. “From what I’ve seen so far, there was definitely a breakdown in crew resource management,” Brickhouse said, referring to training pilots receive to communicate clearly and coordinate ⁠decisions in the cockpit. When a pilot ignores cues that something is wrong, “unfortunately, bad things happen,” he added. “So as an investigator, I want to know ⁠with that many cues available, what was their motivation? What was their thought process? Why did they continue that approach instead of going around?” NTSB investigators spent much of Wednesday interviewing the captain and first officer before releasing details from the cockpit voice recorder. The Amazon cargo ‌plane was on its third flight of ‌the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It had flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan earlier on Sunday before the crash at 1.53pm. The captain, 55, received his type rating for the 767 in May and has 7,145 hours of flight time, while the first officer, 37, received his type rating on the 767 in April 2025 and has 2,655 flight hours, the NTSB said on Tuesday.

title: 4 Chinese nationals charged over Singaporean man’s Malaysia airport kidnapping
description: If convicted, the suspects, including a woman, face a prison term of between 30 and 40 years.
content: Four Chinese nationals, including a woman, claimed trial at the Sessions Court in Balik Pulau, Malaysia’s Penang state, on Thursday to charges of kidnapping a Singaporean man. The accused: Liu Ting Jun, 46; Huang Jin, 39; Wang Hao Yu, 32; and Guan Siqi, 24, pleaded not guilty after the charge was read to them in Mandarin before Sessions Court Judge Ahzal Fariz Ahmad Khairuddin. According to the charge sheet, the four are alleged to have acted jointly to abduct and wrongfully confine 72-year-old Singaporean Quek Aik Teng at Penang International Airport in Bayan Lepas at around 4.15pm on July 26. They were charged under Section 3(1) of the Kidnapping Act 1961, read alongside Section 34 of the Penal Code. If convicted, the offence carries a prison term of between 30 and 40 years, as well as caning. Deputy public prosecutor Ikmal Affendi Zulkifly prosecuted, while lawyer Edward Ng represented Liu. Counsel Azizul Hilmi Zulkifli appeared for Guan, Huang and Wang. Ikmal strongly urged the court to withhold bail, emphasising the gravity of the offence and the overriding public interest. He added that the suspects’ passports were still undergoing verification with the immigration department. Pleading for bail, Ng argued that his client had fully cooperated with police during detention and had a distant relative living and working in Malaysia who was willing to act as a surety. Similarly, Azizul submitted that his three clients were willing to surrender their passports, report periodically to a local police station and abide by any strict conditions imposed by the court. Judge Ahzal denied all four bail applications after hearing arguments from both sides. The court fixed October 15 for document submission. The arrests follow an August 7 police operation to rescue two kidnapping victims at a residence in Taman Amira, Alor Setar. Two foreign suspects were killed in a shoot-out with police during the raid, while six others were subsequently detained to assist in ongoing investigations. This story was first published by The Star

title: How Hong Kong chef Tiffany Lo picked herself up after closing her beloved French bistro
description: Following Jean May’s closure, Tiffany Lo is back as a consulting chef in a new kitchen – but still dreams of opening a restaurant of her own.
content: Tiffany Lo is still heartbroken. Starting in 2020, the chef poured herself – emotionally, mentally and physically – into running Jean May, her beloved little French bistro in Wan Chai on Hong Kong Island. In 2026, after years of trying to keep the business afloat, Lo finally decided it was time to say goodbye. On March 22, she and her team held their final service. The closing still weighs on her, but the chef knows it is time to move on. Soon after Jean May closed, a friend introduced her to Rajeev Bhasin, managing director of the Silver Spoon Restaurants group. Now, they have partnered to open a casual Parisian eatery, Bistrot’s Suzette, in Kai Tak’s Cullinan Sky Mall. The two were aligned over the idea of doing a traditional French restaurant, says Lo, who has taken up the role of consulting chef. “There are no surprises, just standard dishes that you would get in any Parisian bistro,” she says. That means French onion soup, duck confit, beef bourguignon, salade Nicoise, steak frites and more. For variety, she also included some interesting Mediterranean-inspired entrées such as warm zucchini, feta and mint tart, and aubergine and couscous. For Lo, who loves making classic charcuterie, highlights include the house-made chicken liver pâté and pâté de campagne. While the dishes are traditional, she still includes little twists. “One dish not many people order but I really love is panisse,” she says, referring to the classic dish of fried chickpea flour fritters. Hers are made with the addition of briny black olives. “Also, we do a lighter version of the beef bourguignon,” she adds. “Actually, overall we use very little butter in the whole menu.” The restaurant is also named for the signature French dessert, crêpes Suzette; Lo’s version is more of a crêpes soufflé Suzette, where the egg whites are whipped up to give the pancakes more height and lightness. Bhasin reveals that Lo would often show up in the kitchen hours before she was required to help prep dishes and ingredients, and make sure the line cooks could replicate the dishes properly. “After I decided to close Jean May, in my mind I thought I was going to take a rest, but I haven’t,” Lo says. “I have actually been doing collaborations and events, offering classes, workshops and consultancy work. I realise that I really am a bit of a workaholic. And probably I have been avoiding thinking about Jean May.” For now, Lo is keeping the relationship casual. Her role is only as consulting chef, but the experience has been positive – so who knows if this will be more of a lasting relationship than just a short fling? “As consultant, my scope of work is to come up with the menu, the recipes and to pass on their execution to the team,” she says. “But when I am in the kitchen, I am working like it is my own place. I still try to put as much care and commitment into it.” That includes organising the kitchen to make sure processes run smoothly, and to minimise errors. She is doing a bit of training for the staff, mainly suggesting how to keep on top of the prep. I still hope to have my own place again, although I’m very scared Chef Tiffany Lo Working within an operation where commercial consideration takes as much precedence as culinary choices has been a learning curve for Lo. Instead of a seasonally driven menu and kitchen like at Jean May, the process is now about smoothing out routines so efficiency and consistency can be maintained year-round. “At Jean May, I actually discouraged my team from looking at recipes,” Lo says. “I wanted them to cook instinctively. But with the number of people in this kitchen here, I felt I could not do that. As a consultant, I want to make sure everything is as straightforward as possible, so there is a guideline to follow for recipes. “Personally, I do prefer cooking intuitively, but I do realise that for a busy operation, and to ensure the success of such a restaurant as this, it is important to take away as much uncertainty and have as much control as possible.” Jean May, named for her maternal grandmother, was always a heartfelt and sentimental affair. A health scare earlier in her working life was what made her switch careers from investment banking to something she loved – cooking. But the challenge of maintaining a struggling restaurant in Wan Chai proved insurmountable. Still, surviving six years in a difficult economy – and a pandemic – is hardly an utter failure. But Lo is now gun-shy about starting again on her own. “I still hope to have my own place again, although I’m very scared,” Lo says. “A part of me wants to do it, but another part of my brain is saying, ‘It’s going to fail again.’ “A lot of people say, ‘Find someone to do the accounts and bookkeeping.’ Although I would really appreciate it if someone could help, I still prefer to do it on my own. “One of my biggest struggles was social media, and then having to cook, deal with human resources, call people to fix the toilet, fix the phone line. I was doing everything, which meant other things fell behind and I had already spent 20 hours in the kitchen. If I do it the same way, what is going to prevent me from failing again?” Part of Lo’s issue is that she is painfully shy, she admits; she is far happier staying in the kitchen, unlike some big-ego chefs who crave adoration and validation. “Many times, I wanted to come out of Jean May’s kitchen after cooking and cross into the dining room, say hello and talk to guests,” she says. “But eight times out of 10, I just turned back because I was so scared.” With Bistrot’s Suzette, Lo only has to worry about what is happening in the kitchen. Everything else is handled by the Silver Spoon Restaurants team. In a way, being a culinary hired gun seems an ideal role for Lo. The thing is, it is not her own personal restaurant, so she is not cooking nightly at Bistrot’s Suzette. But it just might be the rebound gig she needed. “It is nice to work with other people who have been in the industry for so long and have their own take on how to sustain a good restaurant,” she says. “Working in this new way, I have learned that every single person, from manager to chef, has to be on the same page. Because even if one person does not pull their weight, it is really tough. “No one person can do everything alone. That is one of my biggest lessons.”

title: China rejects US claims of ‘industrial scale’ AI model distillation, warns of retaliation
description: The commerce ministry says distillation is ‘neutral’ and widely used by companies around the world, including American firms.
content: China has rejected US allegations of “aggressive, malicious” AI distillation as groundless, warning that it would retaliate if Washington used the claims as a pretext to contain the country’s rapidly advancing artificial intelligence sector. China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Wednesday that US allegations of Chinese AI companies copying American models “on an industrial scale” lacked factual and legal grounds, accusing Washington of using the allegations to assert technological dominance, monopolise computing power and suppress competition. The response came after the US government on Tuesday accused six Chinese companies – including DeepSeek and Alibaba Group Holding – of conducting “aggressive, malicious and targeted” distillation of advanced American models on an industrial scale, allegedly with the Chinese government’s awareness. Model distillation is a technique in which a smaller AI model is trained on responses generated by a more powerful system, reducing the computing power, time and expense needed to develop a competitive product. The commerce ministry described distillation as a neutral and widely used industry practice employed by companies around the world, including American firms. It accused Washington of using national security agencies to interfere in normal commercial activity and protect US dominance in computing power and data. “If the US takes action to contain or suppress Chinese AI companies in the name of combating distillation, China will certainly take resolute measures in response,” the ministry said. The latest confrontation comes as Washington and Beijing prepare for a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI safety expected to be on the agenda. “The two leaders have agreed to establish an intergovernmental dialogue on AI,” the ministry said. “China stands ready to hold constructive, substantive talks with the US on the basis of equality and mutual benefit.” China’s foreign ministry also urged Washington on Wednesday to stop making “groundless accusations” against Beijing, saying China’s AI advances were driven by its own technological capabilities and innovation. “China and the US are both leading AI powers and should work more closely together,” ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press briefing. On Tuesday, the FBI, National Security Agency, and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued a joint cybersecurity advisory alleging that the six companies had used outputs from models developed by Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk’s xAI to train their own products more quickly and cost-effectively. The agencies alleged that Chinese developers routed requests through multiple channels and shared bulk purchases of premium subscriptions to gain unauthorised access and circumvent the US companies’ terms of use. On the same day, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an event at Southern Methodist University’s Cox School of Business in Dallas that China could “never get ahead” of the US in AI. “The Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us,” Bessent said. Bessent also projected that the US would account for 80 per cent of global computing power by 2028, compared with about 15 per cent for China and 5 per cent for the rest of the world combined. The dispute marks an escalation of earlier accusations by US officials and technology companies. Anthropic previously alleged that Chinese developers had used thousands of fraudulent accounts to generate millions of exchanges with its Claude model, while the White House said in April that Chinese entities were conducting “industrial-scale” distillation campaigns. In June, Anthropic further alleged that operators linked to Alibaba and its Qwen AI unit used nearly 25,000 fraudulent accounts to conduct more than 28.8 million exchanges with Claude between April 22 and June 5. Alibaba did not immediately respond to the allegations at the time. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: Mouthing Off | Join my dinner club, where the sole purpose is to share food, not network or socialise
description: For hungry singletons and couples who want to gorge on giant feasts, Andrew Sun proposes grouping up – just forget the chit-chat.
content: Indian food is always frustrating for my partner and me. We often crave it, and our neighbourhood curry house has a huge menu. The vexing part is that there are so many dishes we greedily want to order, but it is just the two of us. We all know many Indian dishes can be heavy and filling. Their dense proteins, cooked in ghee and cream, with starchy carbs like flatbread and basmati rice expand exponentially in the stomach. Although we want to devour the whole menu, reason dictates we settle on one curry, one tandoori dish, one naan and a biryani rice. These alone usually result in leftovers to take home. It is a family-style sharing cuisine better suited for bigger groups, similar to dim sum and Chinese banquets, which typically demand a table of 10 for the proper multi-course experience. A Thanksgiving turkey dinner for two is kind of pathetic. The same goes for a barbecue. All the prep work with charcoal to grill just two hamburger patties would be sad. Anyway, my point is that sometimes it is just impossible to gather enough friends to eat together. Even when you find people, too many are overly picky eaters or vegans, or have allergies, intolerances or self-imposed dietary restrictions that make life less fun. If your food selfies take too long, especially with dishes meant to be eaten hot, you will be photobombed by our utensils digging into the plate I know group dinner is a popular format for social matchmaking and singles-dating events. But some of us simply want a higher headcount to fully indulge in an entire roast goose, a big king crab and the spectacle of a giant winter melon soup. This smorgasbord of dishes is impractical to partake in when it is just a party of two. Perhaps the time has come for a new dinner club for hungry singletons, hermits and Dink (double income, no kids) couples who want to binge and gorge on ginormous feasts. It will not be about socialising, networking or mingling. The sole purpose of getting together will be for the sake of gluttony. Participants do not even have to engage in chit-chat or small talk. You can comment on the food, but no attention-hogging soliloquies and no one is required to respond. In short, be civil, friendly and show enough social etiquette and manners to prove you were house-trained. In my dinner club, you are responsible for declaring what you cannot or will not eat, but we will not accept guilt-tripping the rest of the group from ordering whatever we feel like. Food pics are allowed, but complicated lighting set-ups are discouraged. And if your food selfies take too long, especially with dishes meant to be eaten hot, you will be photobombed by our utensils digging into the plate. Perhaps my rules sound harsh, but I think real gourmands will have no issue and find these guidelines reasonable. And like-minded appetites would appreciate and relish such a feast. Alternatively, I guess my gal and I can just go on our own to Indian lunch buffets when we feel a little more than just peckish.

title: Toddler with heart and brain conditions dies after being found unresponsive in bed
description: The 23-month-old girl was found without a pulse in a Hong Kong flat and was later certified dead in hospital.
content: A 23-month-old girl born with heart and brain conditions has died after her parents found her unresponsive in their Hong Kong flat, the South China Morning Post has learned. Police said they received a report from the infant’s mother at 5.30am, saying her daughter had passed out at their public housing flat at 20 Olympic Avenue in Kai Tak. Paramedics arrived shortly afterwards and found the girl unconscious, with no pulse. She was taken to Kwong Wah Hospital in Yau Ma Tei, where she was certified dead at 6.51am. A source told the SCMP that the girl had been diagnosed with cardiac and cerebral conditions at birth and had attended regular follow-up appointments at the hospital. According to the insider, the 39-year-old father and 27-year-old mother had checked on the girl before going to sleep at 2am and noticed nothing unusual. The baby slept in their bed between them, the source added. At about 5am, the father found that she was cold to the touch, prompting the mother to alert emergency services. The girl was last admitted to the hospital for a medical check-up on August 30 and was discharged last Friday with medication prescribed by her doctor, the source said. Following her discharge, she continued to suffer from diarrhoea and vomiting, the insider added. The Sau Mau Ping district crime unit is investigating the case.

title: Letters | Suicide prevention in Hong Kong: let’s normalise reaching out for help
description: Readers discuss how the community can work together to prevent suicides, sentencing in cases of sex crimes, and responsible pet ownership.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10 is a timely reminder that suicide prevention cannot begin only at the point of crisis. Hong Kong needs strong clinical services and emergency response, but we also need to make help-seeking simpler and more socially acceptable long before a person reaches breaking point. For many people, the hardest step is the first one: admitting they are struggling and reaching out. Stigma, fear of judgment, and the belief that they should “handle it themselves” can delay that first call. This is particularly concerning during periods of heightened stress, including the back-to-school season for students and times of sustained pressure in many workplaces. That is why clear, responsible public messaging matters. When support information is placed in everyday spaces where people already are – on commutes, in estates and in community settings, it lowers the psychological barrier to seeking help. Messages should be practical and non-sensational: you are not alone; talk to someone now; here is a direct way to reach a trained listener. One practical step is ensuring people know where to turn in the moment. The Samaritans’ 24-hour hotline (2896 0000) is staffed by trained volunteers who provide non-judgmental listening support. Just as importantly, friends and family members who are worried about someone also need clear guidance on how to start a conversation and what to do next. In addition, prevention requires better support around the person. Teachers, managers and other frontline gatekeepers need training, time and clear referral pathways so they can respond calmly and appropriately to signs of distress, without blame or panic. Suicide prevention is not only a medical issue. It is a community responsibility, and it is also about culture: whether someone feels safe enough to speak up early. This World Suicide Prevention Day, let us invest in crisis services and build everyday environments that normalise reaching out for help. Cedric Cheung, chief operating officer, The Samaritans Hong Kong Defendant’s background shouldn’t affect sentencing I refer to the report, “RTHK editor sentenced over upskirt video” (August 27). After the 57-year-old defendant pleaded guilty to one count of the unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts of a woman, he was sentenced to 160 hours of community service. Such lenient sentencing raises questions about our society’s and our legal system’s attitude to victims. The defendant, described as married with two sons and the family’s sole breadwinner, was seemingly shielded by his status. He had also argued that the crime was “a momentary lapse of judgment driven by sexual impulse”. In South Korea, the legal system has a tendency to go easy on men who commit sex crimes. Inebriation has historically been used as a legal defence for assault, or the judge might say a harsh sentence would ruin a young man’s future prospects and that the court ought to go easy on him. The implications of such an approach are profound, as they suggest that potential damage to the defendant’s reputation can overshadow the irreversible harm done to the victim. Upskirt recordings and harassment are violations of privacy and have long-lasting effects on victims. The legal system must prioritise the experiences and rights of the victim, and we must advocate for a legal framework that emphasises accountability, regardless of a defendant’s status, as we are all equal under the rule of law. Sennett Shi, Tung Chung Education on responsible pet ownership needed I am writing in response to the letter, “Dog owners have a duty to protect the community” (August 26). Two shocking cases have made headlines recently. An unleashed large dog in Yuen Long killed two small pets, and it had attacked another dog a month earlier. Tragically, a woman lost her life after being bitten by a large dog at a pet‑boarding facility in Ta Kwu Ling. These incidents show that the problem cannot be overlooked. It is important to understand that dogs themselves are not born dangerous. Most risks come from irresponsible owners who fail to train, supervise or leash their pets in public. No resident should feel afraid in parks, pavements or housing estates. Besides strict enforcement of existing rules, heavier penalties are necessary for negligent owners. Meanwhile, public education, easier channels for reporting dangerous dogs and more special exercise grounds for dogs can encourage responsible pet-keeping. I love animals, yet human safety must come first. With firm law enforcement, widespread education and higher owner accountability, we can build public spaces safe for both people and pets. Andy Yiu Chi-hang, Kwun Tong

title: August was hottest month ever recorded globally, scientists say
description: UN warns of ‘spiralling price’ of fossil fuels after Earth’s record-shattering summer temperatures.
content: The EU’s climate monitor said on Thursday that August was the hottest single month ever recorded globally, with ocean temperatures also reaching unprecedented highs as western Europe capped its warmest summer. In response to the assessment by the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the UN warned that until humanity weaned off fossil fuels, the planet would only push deeper into uncharted territory. Copernicus observations go back to 1940 but other evidence – such as ice cores, tree rings and coral skeletons – allow scientists to place today’s climate against a much longer historical context. “Humans haven’t seen temperatures as hot as today for, arguably, at least the last 100,000 years,” Samantha Burgess from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, which oversees Copernicus, said. Global average air temperatures in August were 16.96 degrees Celsius, Copernicus said – surpassing by 0.01 degree the previous all-time monthly record set in July 2023. Copernicus said it considered the two months joint highest given the narrow difference. Scientists say that human activity – primarily the burning of coal, oil and gas – has warmed the planet by roughly 1.4 degrees since pre-industrial times and increased the severity and likelihood of extreme weather. Yet heat-trapping greenhouse gas emissions rose to new highs in 2025. “The evidence is irrefutable: this is the spiralling price of humanity’s fossil fuel addiction, and the global climate crisis it is fuelling,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said of the Copernicus report. Global sea surface temperatures also set a new daily high and tied equal-hottest for August, extending a three-month streak of record-breaking warmth across the world’s oceans. More than 90 per cent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gas emissions has been absorbed by the oceans, sparing land from warming but at severe cost to marine life, reefs and coastal communities. Records tumbled in overheated basins like the Atlantic and Mediterranean and also the tropical Pacific, where the strongest El Nino weather pattern in the modern era is fast accumulating strength. These events are marked by unusually warm Pacific waters but raise the odds of wild weather thousands of kilometres away, from floods in Peru to droughts in Africa and wildfires in Australia. The warmer phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino episodes usually deliver a temporary spike in global temperatures already elevated by long-term background warming. Scientists expect records to keep falling in the months ahead as this “super” El Nino approaches peak intensity around December and for 2027 – and maybe even 2026 – to become the hottest years ever observed. “Climate change makes every El Nino hotter, and until we stop burning coal, oil, and gas these record-shattering months will simply keep on coming,” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist from Imperial College London. Copernicus also said that August “marked the end of western Europe’s warmest summer” that surpassed the long-standing record set in 2003. The June to August season was defined by severe, back-to-back heatwaves that shut schools, dried up rivers and primed the land for devastating wildfires. Between mid-July and mid-August, the continent’s EuroMOMO monitoring platform estimated that Europe saw more than 32,000 excess deaths. Scientists from the World Weather Attribution network concluded that a particularly strong heatwave in June would have been “virtually impossible” without the influence of climate change. But extraordinary heat was felt around the globe. On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said the contiguous United States has endured its hottest summer on record. And regions home to around 900 million people lived through the hottest July ever observed, according to Agence France-Presse analysis of Copernicus data. “We’ve had an exceptional summer – not only in Europe, but other parts of the world where records that have existed for close to a century have fallen,” said Burgess, an ocean scientist and strategic lead for at ECMWF. The climate would “continue to get more extreme unless we turn off the tap to global emissions”, she added.

title: Trump touts ‘most successful’ presidency, promises US$5,000 to citizens in speech
description: The US president spoke for nearly two hours at the launch of the Republican Party’s unusual midterm convention in Texas.
content: US President Donald Trump kicked off the Republican Party’s midterm campaign season in Dallas on Wednesday night, headlining the opening of a highly unusual convention aimed at rallying voters ahead of November’s high-stakes battle for control of Congress. “This has been the most successful two years financially and every other way in the history of the presidency,” he said, as the crowd chanted “USA! USA!” In the almost two-hour-long speech, Trump also made a bold promise to give every adult US$5,000 if Republicans win the midterm elections, calling it a “Trump dividend”. He said the money would have to be spent in the United States. “So it’s $5,000 to every adult,” he said. “The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we’re making must be spent in the United States of America.” Unlike quadrennial conventions that formally nominate presidential candidates, the two-day gathering – dubbed a “Trump-a-palooza” by Republicans – has no nominating business. Instead, it is focused on showcasing Trump’s second term record and promoting candidates. Trump’s speech focused largely on domestic issues but he also spent considerable time discussing tariffs and the trade war, the Iran war and his immigration policies. “I said tariff is my favourite word and the fake news went crazy. They said, ‘what about love? What about wife? What about God, religion, family?’ So I moved tariff down to fifth,” he said. Trump also mentioned China several times, including while he was discussing record foreign investment in the US and the visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping in a few weeks’ time. “We have the president of China coming in two weeks, I get along great with him,” he said. “It’s a good thing, not a bad thing. Some people say, oh, it’s terrible. That’s a very good thing.” He also touted the White House ballroom, whose construction has sparked controversy, saying it would be better than Beijing’s Great Hall of the People. “When I was in China, they have a building. It’s called the Great Hall of China. It’s a serious hall. This is a very large hall, but we’re going to top it. You know, we’re going to top it,” he said. Trump also repeated his criticism of previous presidents for allowing the semiconductor industry to move to Taiwan. The convention’s agenda centres on tax cuts, the economy, border security, public safety, healthcare and medicine costs, as well as education and cultural issues. Trump is scheduled to return to the event on Thursday for the closing speech. Vice-President J.D. Vance, several Cabinet officials, congressional leaders and candidates are also taking part. Todd Blanche, the newly confirmed head of the Justice Department, spoke earlier and struck a forceful tone on public safety and immigration enforcement, saying that 2.6 million “criminal aliens” had been removed from the US so far. “To evil men and women in this country, know this: President Trump will hold you accountable,” he said. “Americans, thank you for choosing to make our country safe again.” Democrats have criticised the gathering as a Trump-centred political spectacle, accusing Republicans of pursuing what they called a reckless agenda, including the administration’s policies on Iran and tax cuts for wealthy Americans. Texas itself is home to one of the most closely watched Senate races of the midterm cycle. The Trump-endorsed Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democratic state Representative James Talarico in November. The race has drawn national attention, with recent polling showing the two candidates in close position. No Democrat has won a US Senate election in Texas since 1988.

title: AIIB eyes new platform to pool private capital for Asia’s US$1.7tr infrastructure needs
description: The bank is building a pooled-capital platform to draw insurers, pension funds and other investors into Asia’s infrastructure debt.
content: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is developing a new platform to pool capital from institutional investors, aiming to roughly quadruple the private capital it mobilises for infrastructure projects across Asia, according to a senior officer. The mechanism will allow insurers, pension funds, and other institutional investors to co-invest in infrastructure debt alongside the bank across its 111 member countries on a programmatic basis, rather than negotiating deal by deal. Kim-See Lim, AIIB’s chief investment officer, described the initiative as being at a very early stage, with further details expected within six to nine months. She spoke to the South China Morning Post following a joint private capital mobilisation conference co-hosted by the AIIB and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority on Tuesday. The Beijing-headquartered multilateral bank has mobilised around US$17.5 billion in private capital, both directly and indirectly, from its inception through the end of 2025 – a base Lim wants to grow far faster through the new platform. “It needs to be done faster and ... on a greater scale,” she said. “What we will do is reach out to a group of like-minded investors to try to come up with a set of common terms on how we can invest in infrastructure as an asset class together.” The need is there, and the opportunity is there. We just need to make these projects happen so investors will come in Kim-See Lim, AIIB The push comes as Asia’s infrastructure shortfall remains stark. The Asian Development Bank in a 2017 report estimated that the region required US$1.7 trillion in annual infrastructure investment through 2030, with Lim pointing to a persistent shortfall of up to US$700 billion a year. Lim cited “bankability” as the biggest obstacle. She said 55 to 65 per cent of projects still required government or multilateral support to move ahead. Citing International Renewable Energy Agency data, she added that about 45 per cent of projects submitted to its Energy Transition Accelerator platform were rejected for being poorly prepared. Foreign-exchange risk was another common deterrent, Lim said, since infrastructure projects typically earned revenue in local currency while investors sought hard-currency returns. AIIB has raised about US$66 billion across 20 currencies since 2019 to help hedge that exposure for its partners. Hong Kong, Lim said, was well placed to help close the gap. The city topped global rankings for initial public offering fundraising in 2025, hosted around 200 environmental, social and governance funds alongside a similarly sized private equity industry – both potential conduits for channelling capital into infrastructure. AIIB has already tested that model through the Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation, anchoring three rounds of its infrastructure loan-backed securities, which repackage bank loans into rated tranches for investors with different risk appetites. AIIB confirmed in November it would open a Hong Kong office – its second outside mainland China after Abu Dhabi – in the coming months. Looking ahead, Lim named project preparation, foreign currency volatility, and interest rate trajectories as the main hurdles to accelerating private capital flows, though she expressed strong confidence in Asia’s economic trajectory. “Asia is still the fastest-growing region by GDP [gross domestic product], with young, tech-savvy demographics,” Lim said. “The need is there, and the opportunity is there. We just need to make these projects happen so investors will come in.”

title: Rubio defends US strikes on boats, warns of drug cartel ‘cancer’
description: US Secretary of State pledges continued military operations against suspected drug traffickers in Latin American waters.
content: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended controversial strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats during a visit to Ecuador on Wednesday, arguing Latin American cartels would “eat these countries alive” if left unchecked. Hailing a new generation of conservative leaders emerging across the region who are allied with President Donald Trump, Rubio said Washington was finding partners willing to be “very aggressive” against criminal groups. Since Trump returned to power, the United States has embraced air strikes against vessels plying known trafficking routes in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific. According to Pentagon figures, the operations have killed more than 200 people. Rights groups, fishermen and their relatives have questioned the campaign, alleging vessels were targeted without sufficient evidence of links to trafficking. Experts have also questioned whether they do anything to curb the flow of cocaine and other drugs to the United States – the world’s largest consumer. Speaking after talks with President Daniel Noboa in Quito, Rubio said the operations would continue. “If you don’t confront these groups, they will eat these countries alive,” he warned. “It’s like a cancer that continues to grow until you don’t literally have a state any more.” “I’m glad that we have leaders in this region that are serious about going after these groups, because if we didn’t, we would have failed country after failed country.” In recent weeks there have been signs of a shift in tactics, with joint US-Ecuador patrols removing crews from at least six boats before sinking the vessels. Rubio said decisions were made case by case and depended on the threat posed by a vessel, its location and local laws. “When you’re conducting a joint operation in territorial waters, you have to reach an understanding as to how those operations are going to occur,” he said. Asked whether vessels would continue to be destroyed, Rubio replied: “Well again, it depends, and we still blow up ships”. Later Wednesday, the US military’s Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said American forces executed a “lethal kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean”. The operation “killed three narco-terrorists,” SOUTHCOM posted on X along with black-and-white footage of a ship exploding in the water and bursting into flames. In Ecuador alone, more than 25,000 people have been murdered in the last three years as drug gangs have vied for control of trafficking routes. “We are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” Rubio said. While in Quito, he announced the designation of one gang, Los Tiguerones, as a “terrorist organisation” and sanctions against seven Ecuadorian former officials. The Tiguerones made international headlines in early 2024 when masked gang members stormed a TV studio during a live broadcast, firing shots and forcing terrified crew to the ground. After visiting Colombia and Ecuador, Rubio late Wednesday landed in Lima, where he will meet Peruvian leaders on the last stop of a tour to shore up right-wing allies and bolster US influence across the region. In Colombia, Rubio pledged to restore “natural relations” with Bogota after years of leftist rule. He had less warm words for leftist-led Mexico, which he said was stepping up the cartel fight “but it is still not nearly enough”. “There are territories, vast territories in Mexico that are not governed by the state,” he said. “That threat will have to be confronted one way or the other.” His last stop is in Peru, which has been led since July by conservative President Keiko Fujimori. There, he was expected to advance the “Shield of the Americas” initiative, a US-backed security partnership.

title: Resurgent Zheng Qinwen takes positives from storming US Open run
description: Chinese star beaten by new world No 1 Elena Rybakina in three sets but poised for top 60 return following New York exploits.
content: Zheng Qinwen’s storming run through qualifying to the US Open quarter-finals has the 2024 Olympic gold medallist finally feeling like a force on the court again. The Chinese star fell in three sets to Elena Rybakina on Wednesday, but her time in New York was a leap in the right direction for the former world No 4. After her lengthy recovery from elbow surgery last year was followed by a string indifferent results, Zheng’s ranking dropped so low that she had to come through three qualifying rounds to make the US Open main draw: tough on her ego but apparently positive for her game. “I think the good thing is I know how to compete better than at the beginning of the year,” Zheng said. “I was a bit out of tournament rhythm, and, obviously, this tournament helped me to find myself little by little.” Zheng’s run to the last eight included a remarkable third-round comeback victory over 2025 Australian Open champion Madison Keys, who held a 5-0 lead in the final set only for Zheng to win the last seven games for a 1-6, 7-6, 7-5 triumph. Zheng saved a match point in that contest, and in her next put together another seven-game run in the opening set as she stunned six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3. “I think tennis gives me a lesson all the time that [as long as] the match is not over, you just have to keep fighting,” she said. “Second thing is, I think there is so much more I still have to improve.” Those were the positives Zheng said she was taking despite her disappointment in the wake of her loss to Kazakhstan’s Rybakina, who is set to end Aryna Sabalenka’s 99-week reign as World No 1 after booking a semi-final date with 2023 champion Coco Gauff. “There were some decisions in important moments I [didn’t get] right,” Zheng said of the Rybakina contest. “It was also very physical match for me. “I could take some positive things, and the rest I could go back and [see] what I could do better.” Currently ranked world No 121, Zheng is projected to break into the top 60 on the strength of her New York showing, just in time for the WTA Tour’s Asian swing, which features four tournaments in China, including 1000 level events in Beijing and Wuhan. “I’m always so excited to play in China, especially coming from qualifiers at the US Open [to the quarter-finals),” Zheng said. “That was a really, really difficult journey for me. Playing at home, I’m always more motivated, and also carry some pressure, because I really want to do well there. “I just want to keep calm and train day by day, focus match by match, [and] focus on the present.”

title: After Apple’s launch of its foldable iPhone, what are the caveats for Chinese buyers?
description: Apple is attempting to break into China’s foldable phone market, the world’s largest and most competitive, dominated by Huawei Technologies.
content: Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first-ever foldable smartphone, at its annual product launch event on Wednesday in Cupertino, California, following months of mounting anticipation. Presented by CEO John Ternus, the sleek, passport-style device stole the spotlight at the Apple Park event. Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1, said the handset would “redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”. Starting at US$1,999 – or HK$17,499 (US$2,231) if bought in Hong Kong – Apple’s most expensive iPhone to date comes in cheaper than industry estimates, despite soaring component costs. In mainland China, the device starts at 15,999 yuan (US$2,384), rising to 26,499 yuan for the top-tier model. “[The] iPhone Duo … is Apple’s attempt to frame foldability as a complete premium experience, rather than an experimental hardware feature,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president for worldwide client devices at IDC. “Apple showed up years after everyone else … [but it] set the price and the standard every rival will now be measured against.” Here is what you need to know about Apple’s landmark product launch, and the caveats facing buyers in mainland China. What sets the iPhone Duo apart? Featuring a wide-fold design, the iPhone Duo pairs a 5.4-inch outer screen with a 7.6-inch inner display that expands into a passport-sized tablet. Ternus said that rival foldable models felt like “two phones awkwardly stuck together,” highlighting Apple’s focus on a larger canvas that felt “as natural and intuitive as an iPad”. The device is powered by the A20 Pro, the same 2-nanometre chip used in the new iPhone 18 Pro series, complemented by an advanced thermal management system to sustain peak performance, according to Apple. What hurdles face mainland Chinese buyers? While mainland China is slated for the initial launch wave, with pre-orders opening October 16 ahead of an October 23 release, availability hangs in the balance. Apple’s official Chinese website notes the model “will go on sale once regulatory approval is granted”. One obstacle is the device’s eSIM-only design. Mainland regulators require strict reviews of eSIM technology due to anti-fraud and cybersecurity concerns. A similar hurdle caused a weeks-long delay for the iPhone Air last year. It remains unclear whether Apple can secure approval over the next six weeks before its target retail debut. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside normal US business hours on Thursday. The stakes are critical for Apple in China, the world’s largest and most competitive foldable market. Domestic titan Huawei Technologies controls nearly 80 per cent of the segment. However, Jeronimo said the new device could disrupt the status quo: “Apple has just handed Chinese buyers their first genuinely compelling reason to reconsider [other brands of foldable phones].” Software presents additional headwinds. Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, key features of the new line-up of phones, remain unavailable in mainland China. Despite Cook confirming in July that Apple was working to roll out Apple Intelligence locally, the event offered no update beyond confirming support for simplified Chinese language. Meanwhile, Apple Reference Image, an opt-in feature on the iPhone 18 Pro that uses a new sensor to verify whether photos have been edited by artificial intelligence, would also be omitted in China at launch due to regulatory restrictions. What else debuted at the event? Alongside the foldable iPhone, Apple also introduced the flagship iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, featuring upgrades in AI, performance, battery life and camera technology. Driven by rising memory prices, both models saw a US$100 price jump from last year, starting at US$1,199 and US$1,299 respectively. Apple also updated its wearables ecosystem with the AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

title: Philippines races to find survivors of ferry fire that killed at least 5
description: The MV June Aster had departed from Manila and was near a tourist hotspot in Palawan province when the blaze started.
content: The Philippines has deployed coastguard, military and civilian vessels in a race to find survivors on a smouldering passenger-and-cargo ferry off the western island of Palawan, after ‌a fire on board killed at least five people and left more than 80 missing. Drone footage released by the coastguard showed the blackened ferry surrounded by clear blue-green waters, with the vessel still generating smoke hours after the fire broke out on Wednesday night. Coastguard spokeswoman Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said thick smoke continued to billow from the vessel, while extreme heat and the risk of explosions prevented rescuers from boarding. So far 43 people, including two Chilean nationals, have been rescued from the ferry, ⁠which was on a voyage from Baseco in Manila to Coron, a popular tourist destination in Palawan known for its diving sites and ‌island-hopping attractions. Cayabyab said the coastguard had deployed two 44-metre vessels and three smaller craft, while army rescue boats, local fishermen and private resort owners had joined the search since Wednesday night. One military aircraft ‌was also on standby, she said. At least one survivor reported hearing a loud explosion from the cargo hold before the ⁠blaze spread rapidly through ⁠the ferry, Cayabyab told a press conference, adding that the survivor described it as a powerful blast, but authorities had yet to determine what caused it. Cayabyab said some survivors ‌pulled from the sea were not wearing life jackets, suggesting passengers could have jumped overboard as the fire spread. According to the vessel’s manifest, the ferry was ‌carrying 117 passengers ‌and 17 crew members and had a maximum capacity of 330 people. Cayabyab said the vessel had passed safety inspections. It was also ‌carrying five motorcycles, an electric vehicle, a forklift, a pickup truck and mostly cargo goods, she said. The coastguard would conduct a ⁠comprehensive investigation into the fire, Cayabyab said. Asked whether authorities were looking at possible sabotage or a terrorist attack, she said it was ⁠too early to draw conclusions and that the investigation was ongoing. The vessel’s owner, Atienza Inter-Island Ferries, said it was fully cooperating with government authorities investigating the incident. “We are working around the clock and have mobilised all available resources to manage this ‌crisis,” the company said in a ‌statement, adding it was committed to transparency as the investigation progressed. Ferry travel is a common mode of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands, where millions of people rely on boats to travel between provinces. The country has a patchy maritime safety record, and many previous ferry disasters have been linked to overcrowding, rough weather and lax enforcement of safety regulations.

title: Is the Philippine military ‘massively underfunded’?
description: Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr has warned there could be no military recruits next year due to budget cuts.
content: The Philippines’ military modernisation road map is set for delays over budget constraints, with critics calling out what they say is President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s “lip service” approach and questioning his commitment to the ambitious project. In 2024, Marcos approved a revised 1.9 trillion Philippine pesos (US$30 billion) plan to acquire newer military assets until 2034, aiming to enhance the capability of the military to project power in parts of the South China Sea that Manila considers its territory, in line with the emphasis on archipelagic defence. In his State of the Nation Address in July, Marcos vowed to “do all that is necessary to continue upholding” the 2016 arbitral award, under which a tribunal’s ruling in The Hague negated China’s nine-dash line, which overlaps with the Philippines’ claims in the contested waterway. Defence and security analyst Manuel Mogato called Marcos’ promise “mere lip service”, adding that the yearly budget should be at least 100 billion pesos to achieve military modernisation by 2034. During the House budget committee hearing last week, Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr gave lawmakers a graph that showed the Department of National Defence’s proposed modernisation fund for next year amounted to 126.97 billion pesos. But the Department of Budget and Management reduced it to 50 billion pesos. Mogato said: “He [Marcos] promised to prioritise modernisation. But he did not give any money [for new military hardware] for next year.” Meanwhile, the Department of Budget and Management allocated 324 billion pesos in its 2027 expenditure plan for the military and the Department of National Defence, about 43 per cent less than the 572.79 billion pesos budget that Teodoro had proposed. The allocation prompted Justin Baquisal, a security analyst with local think tank FACTAsia.org, to call it a “massively underfunded” military budget. Mogato referred to the 50 billion pesos set aside for modernisation next year, saying that the lower budget might not even be enough to pay for military hardware previously bought on credit under a multi-year scheme, which allows the military and the Department of National Defence to buy equipment with a down payment followed by multi-year repayments. Teodoro showed in the hearing that the repayments due under the scheme next year totalled 56 billion pesos, more than the 50 billion pesos allocated for modernisation. He said he was discussing with Budget Secretary Kim Robert De Leon to release an additional 50 billion pesos. Teodoro appealed to the lawmakers to help raise the military’s budget, as a shortfall would affect its modernisation. Due to the budget cuts, there could be no recruitment for the military and the Department of National Defence next year, Teodoro warned. As such, military personnel could be stretched to the limit and have “no time” for rest and recreation and troop rotation, he added. While the military is slated to receive US$100 million from the US Congress next year, the sum “will not be transferred to our treasury because it’s in the nature of foreign military financing”, according to Teodoro. The priority for this sum would be to finance assets in areas such as coastal defence, maritime security and integrated air defence, he added. Teodoro said that his department was moving ahead to build a dockyard inside an industrial estate in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental province on the island of Mindanao, run by the Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority, an entity with links to veterans and retirees from the Philippine military. He said that the construction was delayed due to land title and right-of-way issues. The dockyard would replace the existing naval base in Sangley Point, Cavite on Luzon Island, which would be abandoned since it was now “extremely shallow, extremely small”. When asked at the hearing if the dockyard could become part of the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement, under which US forces could have access to designated Philippine military bases, Teodoro said the US Navy could potentially use the site for its ships. However, he added that with the new Philippine naval assets coming in, the place would be “crammed” and he did not foresee any space for expansion to accommodate US warships.

title: Style Edit: The Longines Master Collection gets a 2026 redesign and a new monopusher chronograph
description: The line’s star-studded campaign features the watchmaker’s ambassadors of elegance, including Jennifer Lawrence, Henry Cavill and Kate Winslet.
content: Since it was introduced in 2005, the Longines Master Collection has consistently embodied a particularly smart and dressy interpretation of the watchmaker’s trademark aesthetic. Now, for 2026, the collection has been completely redesigned – and its new retro look has made it even more handsome than ever. With the introduction of new models, including the first monopusher chronograph in the collection, this dramatic reinvention is being supported with a campaign that shines appropriately brightly with celebrity wattage, bringing together six of the brand’s ambassadors of elegance. The Master Collection is a tribute to Longines’ storied history, drawing on and honouring design codes from the manufacture’s nearly two centuries of watchmaking. The development of the collection over the past two decades has been marked by a growing array of complications – and that continues today with the new Chrono Monopusher. The watch is distinguished by a complication of which Longines has long been a master: the monopusher chronograph. Most chronograph watches feature two pushers, one to start the timer and the other to stop it. In a monopusher chronograph, the start, stop and reset functions are all united in a single pusher. Longines released its first monopusher chronograph watch as long ago as 1911, and just two years later introduced Calibre 13.33Z, the first compact chronograph movement. These early chronographs even helped expand the range of human exploration, as the watches of choice of legendary aviators such as Amelia Earhart and Richard Byrd. Now, Longines has incorporated its mastery of the monopusher chronograph into the Chrono Monopusher, where it appears alongside a round, polished 41mm stainless case, paired with a concave bezel and a dial of peerless, classic good looks. That dial is distinguished by features that include a smart barleycorn finish, available in either warm silver opaline or icy frosted blue; engraved sub-dials; and the collection’s distinctive applied Arabic numerals, inspired by the Longines Weems Second-Setting watch of 1928, which here, come either rhodium plated and polished or 5N rose plated, and are joined by matching hands. Appearing around the edge of the dial is the other distinguishing characteristic of the Longines Master Collection Chrono Monopusher: a pulsometer scale. This unusual feature allows the wearer to easily calculate the number of heartbeats per minute without a full minute needing to elapse. Timepieces equipped with a pulsometer scale were originally known as doctor’s watches, and functioned as an early form of heart-rate monitor. The beating heart of this particular watch, though, is the manually wound Calibre L799.5, developed exclusively for Longines. It offers a 68-hour power reserve and powers a chronograph subdial at 9 o’clock and a 30-minute counter subdial at 3 o’clock. The watch comes with a choice of leather straps, in black anthracite or brown with an Oxford finish. The new Chrono Monopusher is joined in the latest iteration of the Master Collection by new three-hand models and moonphase chronographs. The brand’s Home of Elegance campaign sees these eye-catching new additions worn by celebrities Longines refers to as its ambassadors of elegance. They represent a formidable constellation of stellar acting talent, including Academy Award winners Kate Winslet and Jennifer Lawrence; Eddie Peng, star of acclaimed films including 2024’s Black Dog; Zhao Liying, whose presence represents a seal of quality in Chinese TV shows; Yosh Yu (Yu Shi), best known for his performances in the Creation of the Gods trilogy; and even Superman himself, Henry Cavill. Together, they constitute the perfect smart set to showcase watches of unmatched elegance and sophistication.

title: China’s Communist Party quietly signals social stability push with new high-level body
description: Central Committee social governance group, while not formally announced, has been operational for a while, provincial reports indicate.
content: China’s ruling Communist Party has signalled a renewed push for social stability by quietly setting up a high-level party group about a year ahead of its 21st national congress. The creation of the Leading Group for Social Governance of the party’s Central Committee underscores the growing focus on internal security and grass-roots governance ahead of the next five-yearly congress, expected to be held in autumn 2027. Beijing has never officially announced the formation of the body, nor disclosed who leads it. However, a trail of local government reports in recent months has offered quiet evidence of the group’s active operations. The latest hint came on Monday, in an online post from the social works department of Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia autonomous region. The city authority said that it had convened a meeting to “convey and study” the spirit of “the fifth plenary meeting of the Central Leading Group for Social Governance” alongside that of its regional counterpart in Inner Mongolia. The report came in the form of a statement posted to the department’s official social media but appears to have since been taken down. The statement showed that the high-level social governance group had been active for a while – having recently held its fifth meeting – and that a network of provincial counterparts had also been set up. In recent months, similar official statements had surfaced across Zhejiang, Henan and Jiangsu provinces, detailing local meetings to study the instructions from the same central leading group and their corresponding provincial bodies. Those posts are also no longer available online. In China’s tightly managed top-down party-state hierarchical system, the ruling party often uses “leading groups”, or lingdao xiaozu, as authoritative, cross-ministry steering mechanisms designed to cut through bureaucratic silos and project the priorities of the top leadership. Such groups are usually led by members of the Politburo – China’s top decision-making body. Since taking the helm of the party in 2012, President Xi Jinping has established and chaired numerous such party groups, each focused on a specific policy area. Grass-roots governance has gained higher policy priority over the past three years. In a restructuring plan rolled out in 2023, Beijing announced the creation of a Central Social Work Department directly under the party’s powerful Central Committee, seeking to consolidate its control over all non-public sectors and grass-roots organs. A key responsibility of the department is to “coordinate and guide” the handling of petitions from the public and the soliciting of public opinion, according to the reform plan. It is also tasked with leading the work of industry federations, improving the governance of grass-roots communities in urban and rural areas, and setting up party organs in private companies and other social organisations. A key priority for the group is expanding the party’s reach among China’s around 84 million gig economy workers – including food delivery riders, couriers and ride-hailing drivers – as well as firms behind major internet platforms and tech start-ups. The department has lately also partnered with the party’s disciplinary watchdog to crack down on misconduct within national trade associations and social organisations, targeting corrupt practices and governance abuses. A high-level social governance conference held in Beijing last November underscored directives from Xi that hold up social governance as “crucial to the party’s long-term governance and the country’s long-term stability”. Xi’s chief of staff and Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi presided over the conference. A Guangdong official familiar with related affairs said that provincial deputy party secretaries – whose job it is to assist their party chiefs – were heading their respective regional social governance leading groups. The official spoke on condition of anonymity as they are not authorised to speak to the media.

title: Nepal floods: How a principal saved 900 students from devastation
description: Rajendra Dawadi’s quick thinking and evacuation to high ground saved hundreds from floods that have killed over 1,350 and left 4,900 missing.
content:
Rajendra Dawadi was inside his school near Nepal’s Trishuli River with around 900 students on August 26 when a colleague delivered an urgent warning.
“My accountant came to the school and said, ‘The flood is coming, the flood is coming’,” the school principal said in a recent interview. Dawadi quickly ordered an evacuation, and teachers hurried hundreds of students from classrooms to higher ground.
Minutes later, the 47-year-old watched the Trishuli Bazaar Secondary School in Nuwakot district, which he had run for years, collapse into a raging torrent.
“If the information were wrong, we would lose a day of schooling,” he recalled of the morning. “But if it was true, we were going to lose our lives.”
Students panicked, Dawadi said, and one girl fainted. Bus drivers bringing in other students were asked to turn back, including one driver who had just entered the school grounds. The timely evacuation saved some 900 lives.
Standing above the scarred river banks weeks after the disaster, Dawadi described himself as “a principal without a school”.
The tsunami-like wall of water, ice and debris unleashed by a massive glacial and rock collapse along the Nepal-China border has killed at least 1,398 people and left more than 5,510 missing across both countries.
Outside the school, five students, a teacher and a security staff member died in the flooding.
Authorities in Trishuli Bazaar had not provided an evacuation plan, Dawadi said. Some residents tried to cross the bridge but were swept away. Others took refuge on higher ground.
“When I looked back, the school was standing there like the finest of buildings,” Dawadi recalled. “In five minutes, everything collapsed ... It’s also the school where I studied. There was nothing left.”
Santoshi Dotel, 17, was in an accounting class when Dawadi’s evacuation order came. At first, she struggled to comprehend the danger:
“We never would have thought the flood could reach such a scale,” Dotel said. She initially went down to the river with her friend to try to cross and reach her family home.
“The bridge was swept away,” she said. “I started to cry because I thought I would never get home and that there was nothing we could do.”
Her friend pulled her up the hillside as the flood roared below.
Santoshi broke down as she recalled the anguish of not knowing whether her parents had survived. It was only days later that a helicopter reunited her with her family.
Her mother had feared the worst: “Seeing the river in flood, I had lost all hope that my daughter had survived.”
According to figures cited by Save the Children, at least 69 schools were destroyed or damaged, disrupting the education of nearly 19,000 children.
Dawadi said the disaster was “far worse” than the earthquake that hit Nepal in 2015: “This time, we’ve lost the land and the building. We need a school again. But first, we need somewhere safe to build it.”

title: Opinion | Social media must join the fight against teen suicides
description: The causes are complex, and home and school problems are major factors, but the digital environment is a significant amplifier of distress.
content: As we observe World Suicide Prevention Day on September 10, the global community reflects on a sobering reality: suicide remains a leading cause of death among young people. Every year, more than 720,000 people die by suicide – each life a story cut short, a family shattered, a community left to grapple with unbearable loss. In Hong Kong, the Jockey Club Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention (CSRP) at the University of Hong Kong estimates last year’s suicide rate at 13.0 per 100,000 in the population – a slight improvement from 13.8 in 2024. But let me be clear: this is no cause for complacency. The rate among our young people, particularly boys, remains stubbornly high, and that is where my deepest concern lies. We can no longer afford to ignore the role of social media in the mental health crisis facing our teenagers. Social media has become the landscape of modern adolescence. In the United States, reports indicate that up to 95 per cent of adolescents use social media, with over one-third reporting near-constant use. For young people, these digital spaces are not merely entertainment – they are where identities are formed, relationships are navigated and self-worth is measured. Their impact on mental health deserves attention. For decades, my team at the CSRP has tracked the data, studied the patterns and advocated for evidence-based solutions. The evidence is overwhelming. Excessive use of social media is correlated with poor mental health and deteriorating family relationships. The causes of youth suicide are complex – home and school problems are major, intertwined contributors – but the digital environment has become a significant amplifier of distress. We have long known that irresponsible media reporting can trigger the Werther effect – where sensational coverage of suicide leads to imitative behaviour. Social media has made this problem exponentially more complicated. A single post, whether a careless comment or misguided “awareness” message, can reach thousands of vulnerable young people instantly. Specificity in describing methods or locations – even when framed as a warning – drives contagion risk. Yet the responsibility does not rest solely with individuals. The platforms design their algorithms to maximise engagement, often at the expense of well-being. The recent US$18 billion settlement by Meta Platforms – agreeing to examine its algorithm design to improve mental health among young users – should be a wake-up call for the industry. The tragic case of American Sophie Rottenberg, who ended her life after months of confiding in a ChatGPT therapist, illustrates the dangers of unregulated digital environments. In our work on chatbot development, we have observed that overly empathetic responses can inadvertently reinforce a user’s negative thoughts, create a dangerous feedback loop and validate harmful ideation. For years, we have partnered with local media to promote safe reporting practices. But the landscape has shifted dramatically. Passive audiences have become content creators. The old guidelines were not designed for this reality. That is why, with the support of The Better Hong Kong Foundation, we worked with the Hong Kong Press Council to produce an updated 2026 edition. For the first time, we have incorporated targeted guidance for social media alongside traditional recommendations. So, what does responsible social media use look like? First, pause before posting. If your post describes methods, means or locations in specific detail, do not share it. Do not speculate on causes or spread rumours. Always obtain consent before sharing someone else’s experience with suicide. Second, promote hope, not despair. Whenever suicide is mentioned, attach help-seeking resources. These can make a tangible difference. Share recovery stories that highlight coping strategies and resilience. Third, use mindful language. Avoid phrases that frame suicide as noble, peaceful or an act of empowerment. Such framing normalises it for at-risk individuals. Describe the pain, not the act. But individual action is not enough. We must hold platform operators accountable. With their sophisticated algorithms, these companies have the ability to identify at-risk users – the same algorithms that deliver personalised advertisements can be repurposed for early detection and intervention. Platforms worry that intervening might affect traffic volume. But we cannot accept profit motives as a justification for inaction. Platforms should detect and remove harmful content using automated tools, but they must route flagged items to human moderators before removal to avoid overreach. They should deprioritise borderline high-risk content in recommendation feeds while reserving outright restriction for clear violations like content that promotes suicide methods, pacts or graphic acts. They must act swiftly against cyberbullying, which remains a major class of harmful content. And they should pin help resources prominently alongside sensitive posts. I am pleased Meta has suggested a two-hour daily limit for young users and content filtering for children under 15. These are potentially effective measures. But we need systemic change. Our government has committed to continuing the three-tier system to support mental health in secondary and upper-primary schools. That is welcome. However, I must highlight a critical point often overlooked: by our estimates, about 75 per cent of suicides occur among those who do not have depressive symptoms. By focusing solely on depression, we are missing most of those at risk. This is a central reason our suicide rate remains stubbornly high despite increased mental health awareness. To truly move the needle, we must think beyond clinical interventions. We must promote a healthy lifestyle: a balanced diet, regular exercise and adequate sleep are all essential. We must make schools and homes safe places where young people feel valued and supported. And we must give them something to look forward to – a meaningful future, hope and a strong support network. There is no silver bullet to solving the suicide problem among teenagers. The path forward is difficult and requires coordinated effort across families, schools, governments and technology companies. But it is not impossible. We have seen progress: the rate has come down from 13.8 to 13.0. That shows our efforts are working. We just cannot afford to ease up. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: China wife exposes husband’s US$1.5 million insurance-buying affair involving 180 hotel stays
description: Husband sent ‘I miss you’ texts and numerous 520-yuan transfers, a number that phonetically means ‘I love you’ in Chinese.
content: A Chinese man’s seven-year affair with an insurance agent has ignited a legal dispute, revealing dramatic details uncovered by his wife.
