Guo, from Liuzhou in Guangxi province, southern China, is married to Zhen, with whom he shares a two-year-old daughter, according to Hongxing News. In 2017, Zhen discovered flirtatious messages exchanged between her husband and Li, an insurance agent eight years his junior. These texts included “I miss you” and multiple transfers of 520 yuan (US$77), a figure widely associated with “I love you” in Chinese due to its phonetic similarity. Years later, while hospitalised in 2024, Zhen discovered that Guo had bought medical insurance policies for her and their daughter. This revelation raised suspicions that Guo and Li had continued their relationship. Zhen later calculated that Guo had transferred over 3 million yuan (US$447,000) to Li over the course of the seven years. Insurance records indicated that he had acquired more than 50 policies through Li, paying over 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) in premiums. During this period, Li was promoted to manager in her insurance firm. Zhen subsequently filed a lawsuit against Guo, Li, and the insurance company, seeking a refund of the premiums. She alleged that Guo had used marital assets for these purchases and that Li had unduly influenced them. Additionally, she demanded the return of the 3 million yuan transferred to Li and filed a separate claim against Li’s husband, arguing that he should share liability for the repayment. Li denied having an affair with Guo, stating that there is no legal prohibition against meeting in hotels for business discussions. She claimed that it was Guo who sought a refund due to an inability to afford the premiums and had joined forces with his wife to recuperate the funds. Nonetheless, a police report indicated that Guo confessed to staying in hotels with Li over 180 times. Guo also stated that he owned more than a dozen properties and faced no financial difficulties. The court determined that Guo and Li had engaged in an improper relationship and ordered Li to return about 900,000 yuan in inappropriate gifts to Zhen, along with interest. Li’s request for a retrial was subsequently denied. The insurance company contended that Guo’s extensive purchasing history represented “rational decisions consistently reaffirmed over time” rather than purchases made under pressure or impulse. Guo, however, acknowledged that his relationship with Li played a significant role in his decision to acquire multiple policies. The dispute regarding the insurance contracts remains under review. The case quickly went viral on mainland social media, amassing over 100 million views on related posts. One online observer remarked: “Guo called it business with his wife, love with the agent, and an investment in himself. In the end, he gained nothing but a lawsuit.” Another commented: “Money given to an affair partner may be reclaimed, but insurance is a different story. The purchase itself was legally valid and should not simply be cancelled.” A third added: “According to Li’s perspective, she may have viewed the affair less as romance and more as a business opportunity.”

title: Over 65% of cars sold in China are now EVs as Iran war drives electric shift
description: China’s electric vehicle adoption rate has hit yet another record high, as rising fuel prices accelerate the pivot away from petrol cars.
content: China’s electric vehicle (EV) adoption rate has hit an all-time high, as the Iran war drives motorists to shift away from petrol cars despite a sluggish automotive market. A record 65.2 per cent of the 1.54 million cars sold in mainland China last month were either pure electric or plug-in hybrid vehicles, data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed. The figure broke the previous record of 65.1 per cent set a month earlier. “Consumers are convinced of EVs’ advantages now that range anxiety has been largely eased,” said Zhao Zhen, a sales director at Shanghai-based auto dealer Wan Zhuo Auto. “Higher penetration rates can be expected as more drivers shun petrol cars.” The pivot to electric cars comes as overall vehicle sales in China slump amid an economic slowdown. Last month, petrol car sales plunged 40 per cent year on year, while EV deliveries fell by a more modest 10.1 per cent, according to CPCA data. The Iran war appears to be accelerating the electrification shift, as rising fuel costs prompt more Chinese consumers to shun petrol vehicles. Another factor has been the debut of hundreds of new EV models in recent months featuring advanced driver-assistance systems and other new technologies, which have helped convince millions of buyers to splash out on a new vehicle, according to car dealers. Global oil prices remain far higher than pre-Iran war levels, with Brent crude hovering at around US$97 per barrel on Wednesday, 34 per cent above the price in late February, when the conflict erupted. If oil prices remain at around US$90 a barrel, Chinese petrol car drivers will see their annual fuel costs rise by roughly 2,000 yuan (US$298) compared with pre-war levels, according to an estimate by UBS in March. Meanwhile, China has pushed forward with a massive charging infrastructure buildout. The country had 5.1 million public EV charging stations as of the end of July, up 21.3 per cent from a year earlier, according to the China Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Promotion Alliance. Household charging piles had reached nearly 18.6 million, up 48.8 per cent year on year. The EV penetration rate has continued to rise even as Beijing rolls back purchase subsidies and tax incentives for electric cars. Buyers of a 100,000 yuan electric car in mainland China now receive a subsidy of 12,000 yuan, down 40 per cent compared with last year. They are also now required to pay a 5 per cent vehicle purchase tax, whereas previously EV purchases were exempt. Between January and August, Chinese carmakers delivered a total of 6.67 million EVs to domestic consumers, down 11.6 per cent from a year earlier, according to the CPCA.

title: In Focus | Softer focus on national security in Hong Kong’s 5-year plan? Why it won’t happen
description: Experts expect John Lee’s policy address to set ambitious governance agenda on various social and economic issues, but security will underpin them all.
content: In the first of our series of previews on the five-year plan and policy address, to be announced on September 16, Natalie Wong and Matthew Cheng look at the key political issues and the city leader’s hopes for a second term. When Hong Kong’s leader John Lee Ka-chiu steps up to the Legislative Council podium next Wednesday, he will break from decades of political tradition. Lee’s coming policy address will summarise his four years in office while setting out what is expected to be his most ambitious and forward-looking governance agenda to date, as it will serve as an execution document to complement the city’s inaugural five-year plan to be delivered on the same day. Observers are closely watching where the two blueprints will take Hong Kong, and whether the synergy of high-level strategic planning will be used by the 68-year-old leader to build momentum for securing a second five-year term next July. Pressure is mounting on him to deliver on the Northern Metropolis near the Shenzhen border, with some political experts saying a key challenge is getting businesses to commit to the megaproject that could take up to 20 years to complete. Beyond policy initiatives, they said Lee’s future in the job also hinged on issues of political accountability arising from the Tai Po fire, Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze in decades, which occurred on his watch. An independent committee’s findings are set to be published in late October, after months of evidential hearings earlier this year. In the remaining nine months of his tenure, Lee also faces pressure to address long-standing societal problems such as housing affordability while showing how his administration will execute its expanded vision. Analysts said some quick wins would be vital. While economic and technological developments will occupy a significant portion of the five-year plan, the South China Morning Post has learned that national security will also be a critical aspect of the blueprint, reflecting Beijing’s stance that security and economic development are mutually reinforcing – and inseparable – goals. Caution over Northern Metropolis Topping the consultation agenda for the five-year plan is the Northern Metropolis, which has been viewed as the mother of all engines to power Hong Kong’s economic transformation. While the flagship project has received widespread verbal support from Hong Kong businesses, they remain cautious when it comes to making substantial investments. The hesitation was evident when the government rolled out its first “zone development” public-private partnership pilot in the Hung Shui Kiu New Development Area. The HK$16.8 billion (US$2.1 billion) logistics and residential package was awarded to a consortium comprising five mainland Chinese state-owned and private conglomerates, alongside just one local player, Sino Land. It was one of only two bids received for the megaproject. Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, chairman of the board of directors of the Hung Shui Kiu Industry Park Company, said limited local participation at this stage was not surprising as Hong Kong developers’ past success was built on traditional real estate rather than tech-driven innovation. Lam, who is also a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, argued that as the government had already established a new public-private development model after overcoming significant policy hurdles, mainland companies’ commitment could pave the way for local businesses to take part in the next stages after the primary infrastructure matures around 2028. “One can’t say they threw out the money to ‘test the waters’, as this is serious investment,” he said. “In projects of this scale, infrastructure must take the lead. Those participating in the first stage are inevitably large corporations. Once completed, you’ll see plenty of small businesses move in.” He added that, from his observations, companies from various countries were also keen to invest in the megaproject, citing Hong Kong’s unique role in connecting them to the vast mainland market. Lawmaker Rock Chen Chung-nin, who also serves as an independent non-executive director at Sino Land, urged the government to attract leading technology companies, such as firms comparable to Nvidia, to establish a presence in the megaproject as a “ballast”. He said this would be essential for building an ecosystem by drawing upstream and downstream companies to the city. He stressed that the government must deliver results in the next few years, citing a trillion Hong Kong dollars in expected investment, and called for more favourable policies, including tax incentives and lower land prices, to attract foreign businesses. Lee’s 4 years: progress versus unfinished business Since taking office in 2022, the former security chief, who characterised his government as “results oriented”, has fulfilled major mandates in security, including the enactment of Article 23’s Safeguarding National Security Ordinance in 2024, which had dragged on for more than two decades due to fears of renewed public backlash. On the economic front, Hong Kong experienced a heady resurgence in initial public offerings (IPOs) of companies seeking funding and was placed second globally in a competitiveness ranking in June. The administration also spearheaded high-profile missions to explore non-traditional markets in the Middle East and Central Asia, while rolling out measures to deepen integration with mainland China. But there were some areas where it had been slow to act, observers said. Lawmaker Peter Douglas Koon Ho-ming said the city’s rapidly ageing population could become a political time bomb if the problem was not comprehensively addressed, as the long-term population decline would affect residents’ healthcare and welfare, among other livelihood issues. In 2025, about 1.78 million residents were aged 65 or older, accounting for a quarter of the total population. The figure is projected to rise to 36 per cent by 2046, a trend some scholars had previously described as alarming and unsustainable, with a shrinking labour force compounding the problem of the growing older population. “This is a top priority … This problem will hold you back in the long run as it will affect development, when one-third of the population [is elderly],” Koon said. “If the government does not address the issue, it will definitely be criticised … It needs to do scenario planning for what problems will arise in the worst-case situation.” John Burns, an emeritus professor of politics and public administration at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), said the city’s economy had grown but the gains had been uneven, with some sectors, such as retail, food and beverage, and small and medium-sized enterprises, performing poorly. Burns argued that the pace of civil service reforms was “incredibly slow” despite Lee’s campaign pledge to change the mindset across the bureaucracy. The effectiveness of a review of the accountability system for heads of departments had yet to be seen, he noted. Whether Lee could secure a second term would depend on Beijing’s top priority for Hong Kong over the next five years, but Lee’s performance in safeguarding national security had been outstanding from the central government’s perspective, he added. “From the economic perspective, if we were talking about this government, the results have been mixed,” Burns said. He also cited the Tai Po fire, which occurred under Lee’s watch. The catastrophic blaze tore through the Wang Fuk Court housing estate last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents. A subsequent investigation exposed oversight failures across multiple departments, including systemic issues surrounding bid-rigging in building maintenance. The findings of an inquiry by a judge-led independent committee are set to be released in late October. National security ‘integral part’ of 5-year plan Despite calls from parts of the business community to shift the city’s focus towards economic growth, the SCMP has learned that national security will remain an integral part of the five-year plan, reflecting Beijing’s view of the close link between security and economic development. This perspective aligns with commentaries reposted by the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office that described development and security as “two wings of a bird” or “two wheels of a car” – analogies that state in no uncertain terms how both are critical to the city’s progress. The commentaries warned of persistent “severe threats” to Hong Kong, with anti-China forces devising new forms of “soft resistance”. Such forces would “use disasters” like the Tai Po fire to disrupt Hong Kong, and also “glorify violence” by presenting flowers to released political prisoners, the essays warned. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant to the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said tackling subtle forms of “soft resistance” without inviting Western political attacks was a test of Lee’s political acumen. “Maintaining vigilance against unconventional national security threats is important. But on an operational level, they should avoid triggering unnecessary concerns. What matters is reassuring foreign capital that Hong Kong remains an open, profitable international hub,” he said. Lau also warned of other threats, such as cybersecurity, financial security and geopolitical tensions surrounding Hong Kong’s role as an offshore renminbi centre, amid the city’s increasingly fraught relationship with the West. He said Beijing expected Lee to deliver the twin blueprints to help Hong Kong navigate the shifting global environment and better serve the country’s needs, and urged authorities to quickly adapt to cope with increasingly unpredictable threats. Lau added that security was a core metric of the administration’s performance, not only for Lee’s second-term prospects, but also because Beijing viewed national security and effective governance as inextricable. “If the government does not govern well, accumulating social grievances will be exploited to destabilise Hong Kong and fuel anti-government sentiment … That would threaten stability which Hong Kong cannot afford,” he said.

title: US firms’ confidence in China has soared amid Xi-Trump trade truce: survey
description: US businesses in China are feeling more upbeat than at any point since 2021, as bilateral relations become more stable, survey finds.
content: Profitability and business confidence among US companies in China have rebounded to the highest levels in years, as Beijing and Washington work to stabilise bilateral trade relations, according to a new report by a prominent business chamber. The survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai (AmCham Shanghai) logged a marked upswing in confidence among its members compared with last year’s report, with the proportion of US firms feeling optimistic about their five-year outlooks in China soaring 17 percentage points to 58 per cent. That is the highest level recorded since 2021 and breaks a run of four years in which confidence fell to record lows, according to the findings released on Thursday. Meanwhile, only 16 per cent of respondents reported feeling pessimistic about their prospects, the lowest figure since 2021. US firms’ profitability in the Chinese market has also hit a post-pandemic peak, according to the survey, with 78 per cent of firms reporting a profit last year – the highest level since 2019. The improvement has coincided with an easing of last year’s US-China trade war, with both sides working to stabilise bilateral ties, though frictions over trade, technology and security persist. High-level engagement between the two powers has also picked up in recent months, with US President Donald Trump visiting China in May and Chinese President Xi Jinping expected to travel to the United States later this month. “Members have clearly noticed government efforts to improve the regulatory environment, and this year those gains are reinforced by steadier US-China relations,” said Jeffrey Lehman, chair of AmCham Shanghai. “We urge both countries to build on the momentum of recent engagement and lock in a stable, transparent framework that is conducive to cross-border trade and investment.” The survey, conducted in June, collected responses from 262 companies, according to AmCham Shanghai. Nearly 90 per cent of the firms had been operating in China for more than a decade, and 63 per cent of them had been based there for more than 20 years. For the first time since 2022, businesses did not point to US-China tensions as their top challenge, according to the report. Instead, competition from domestic Chinese firms emerged as the top obstacle for US firms, with 68 per cent naming it among their biggest three issues – up 5 percentage points from a year earlier. “Local firms continue to lead on speed to market, and foreign companies are now losing ground in areas where they once held clear advantages, like product development and quality,” the report said. By comparison, 53 per cent cited US-China tensions among their top three challenges, down 13 percentage points from a year ago. “That has probably a lot to do with the recent improvement of the bilateral relationship,” said Eric Zheng, president of AmCham Shanghai. “Our member companies are more comfortable with the current state of the US-China relationship.” The report also noted a clear improvement in perceptions of China’s business environment, with 55 per cent of surveyed firms saying they felt it was transparent – the first time this figure had risen above 50 per cent since 2020. Investment confidence also recovered, although a “wait-and-see” approach prevailed, the report said. About 28 per cent of respondents increased their investment in China last year, the highest level in four years, while 17 per cent cut spending. AmCham Shanghai said its members were “betting on China-based innovation but with boundaries”, with half of surveyed firms with China-based research and development operations planning to increase spending this year, up sharply from one-third in 2025. Yet 46 per cent of those firms reported headquarters-imposed restrictions on China-based R&D, up 6 percentage points from a year earlier, amid tighter global technology controls and greater strategic caution around sensitive innovation, according to the report.

title: Japan’s protest over Russian soldier statue aggravates ‘summer of tension’
description: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is under pressure from conservatives to take firm action, including helping Ukraine in its war against Russia.
content: Russia has rebuffed a strongly worded complaint from Japan over a statue in the city of Khabarovsk depicting a Soviet soldier smashing an imperial-era border marker bearing the Japanese emperor’s emblem, with analysts predicting bilateral relations will stay chilly. The 15-metre granite monument, commemorating the Soviet Union’s victory over Japan in 1945, shows a soldier using the butt of his rifle to shatter the border post – a replica of the markers once installed along the 50th parallel on Sakhalin Island, which divided Japanese-controlled southern Sakhalin from the Russian-held north. The Soviet Union seized control of southern Sakhalin near the end of World War II, and Japan renounced its claims to the territory in 1951. A 16-petalled chrysanthemum motif, the imperial symbol, is depicted on the statue. Its unveiling last week went ahead despite Tokyo’s requests through diplomatic channels for changes, prompting Japan’s foreign ministry to call it “extremely regrettable”. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she had also requested the statue’s removal, adding in a statement on Saturday: “The Chrysanthemum Crest is widely recognised as a symbol of Japan, and it is completely unacceptable to erect a monument depicting its destruction.” Speaking in Moscow on Tuesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov made clear that Tokyo’s protests would be ignored. “It is difficult to say what they have forgotten and what they remember in Tokyo, but at least we have not forgotten,” Tass news agency quoted him telling a press conference. “We have not forgotten Japanese militarism and the victory we achieved over it.” James Brown, an international-relations professor specialising in Russian affairs at the Temple University’s Tokyo campus, described “a summer of real tension between Japan and Russia”. Ties took a nosedive after Tokyo imposed sanctions on Russia in 2022 over its invasion of Ukraine, with relations deteriorating further this year after Japan accused a former Russian trade delegation official of espionage. This was followed by Russian warships and aircraft operating near Japan, including joint exercises with Chinese units. Russian President Vladimir Putin also visited Iturup, north of Hokkaido, in August – a trip Japan’s foreign ministry and Takaichi both criticised. Iturup is one of the four southern Kuril Islands that Tokyo calls its Northern Territories, seized by Soviet forces after Japan’s 1945 surrender. The territorial dispute has prevented a peace treaty ending the countries’ wartime hostilities. “This is especially awkward for Takaichi,” Brown said. “She is supposed to be a nationalist, a hawk, but Putin has visited what she sees as sovereign Japanese territory. Now a statue has been unveiled showing the smashing of the imperial chrysanthemum, and she is not able to respond in a meaningful way.” Takaichi’s room for manoeuvre is partly constrained by energy concerns, according to Brown. With conflict in the Middle East pushing up oil prices, Japan wants to preserve access to energy supplies from Sakhalin, despite its diversification efforts. “There have been complaints through diplomatic channels, but nothing further,” Brown said. “It’s just empty rhetoric.” Conservatives were infuriated by Putin’s island visit. Kiyofumi Iwata, former military chief of staff, denounced it in an opinion article published by the right-wing Japan Institute for National Fundamentals as “an outrageous action designed to justify the former Soviet Union’s entry into the war against Japan … and its illegal occupation of the Japanese territories after the war”. Iwata was equally scathing about Takaichi’s response, which he said had been “limited to verbal protests” despite Russian “openly trampl[ing] on Japan’s sovereignty and public sentiment”. He called for “deterrence through action”, urging Japan to “make Russia feel pain” – including by supplying Ukraine with air defence weapons and jointly developing drone technology. Ben Ascione, an assistant professor of politics and international relations at Waseda University in Tokyo, said mounting criticism from allies, the opposition, the media and the public could push Takaichi towards a tougher stance. “The statue showing the imperial chrysanthemum being smashed is extremely provocative,” Ascione said. “The emperor and the imperial family are held in very high regard here. Conservatives expect her to be tough on territorial issues and protect the dignity of the imperial family, and we have had two hot-button issues in a short space of time.” Failing to take a firmer line could push supporters towards the more hardline Sanseito party, denting her standing and electoral prospects, he added. Andrei Lankov, a Russian-born professor of history and international relations at Kookmin University in Seoul, said both leaders were being driven by domestic political concerns, with Putin facing a legislative election later this month. “Both leaders need to please a domestic audience. Pushing a line that a leader is tough is always popular, especially when it does not cost the taxpayer anything,” Lankov said. “I do not think there is any amount of protest that Japan can make that will change how Russia represents World War II. That is especially the case now as Russia emphasises victory over Japan at the same time as it is improving relations with North Korea and China.” Brown added that hopes of joint development of the southern Kuril Islands – as appeared possible when former prime minister Shinzo Abe met Putin repeatedly a decade ago – had vanished. “This must be a major disappointment to Russia because even this year it had hoped that it would be able to make progress on this issue with Takaichi, in part because she was Abe’s protege,” he said. “But as is so often the way with Russia, they pushed harder when they detected softness and that very quickly killed off any engagement on the issue.”

title: Indian powerlifter won silver medal at world meet but says internet focused on her looks
description: Keyaa Kunal Banerji calls out ‘sexism at its finest’, saying her feat of lifting more than three times her body weight was downplayed.
content: An Indian powerlifter who won a silver medal at a world championship has spoken out after being targeted with online harassment and objectified for her looks, calling the ordeal “sexism at its finest”. Keyaa Kunal Banerji, 21, showed remarkable strength early in her career at the 2026 IPF World Sub-Junior and Junior Classic Powerlifting Championships in Sun City, South Africa, late last month. Weighing 45.7kg in the Junior Women’s 47kg category, Banerji pulled 140kg in the dead lift, more than three times her body weight, to claim second place in the individual dead lift event and secure a silver medal. However, after a video of her performance went viral online, the promising young athlete was forced to navigate unwelcome internet fame as public discussion quickly shifted away from her athletic achievement and towards her physical appearance. According to Indian news agency ANI, Banerji faced cyberbullying, attacks from fake accounts, photo misuse, and thousands of unauthorised AI-altered images generated using her likeness. Meet Keyaa Kunal Banerji, a 21-year-old from Haryana who just deadlifted more than 3x her own bodyweight on a world stage. At the 2026 IPF World Sub-Junior and Junior Classic Powerlifting Championships in Sun City, South Africa, Keyaa stepped up weighing 45.70kg and pulled… https://t.co/Tejn9spILX pic.twitter.com/oDugZnEBZH — Vaibhav Bodana (@VaibhavSpace) September 3, 2026 “I think it was just sexism at its finest. I don’t think I can put it any other way. The way I was treated, men would never have to face this, like after winning a championship or something like that; a male athlete never has to face something like this,” Banerji said. “Most of the conversation revolved around my appearance. All people would talk about was my appearance, and I think that really bothered me because I had accomplished something so big for myself and I had done something so big in my sport,” she added. Despite the distress caused by the sudden viral focus, Banerji said she was grateful for the opportunity to do news interviews and speak about her passion for powerlifting. “So, I’m over it. I’m definitely over it. But it was a little bit hard in the middle,” she said. Banerji originally had no plans to become a professional athlete, hitting the gym merely for personal fitness before a friend introduced her to powerlifting. That friend was a world-class powerlifting coach who had previously won a gold medal for India. “So, I felt extremely inspired and felt very curious about how this works,” she said. As her numbers in the squat, bench press and dead lift steadily improved, her curiosity gradually transformed into competitive ambition. Despite the unwanted online attention, Banerji remains firmly focused on the sport that has played a central role in her life. “My sport is something that really helped me in my life. During my college times, I used to look forward to training. Sometimes I would have to train at night, sometimes I would have to skip classes to train, but it’s something that never really bothered me. It’s always something I really enjoyed,” she said. During the world championship event, Banerji also logged a 90kg squat and a 50kg bench press, finishing with a 280kg total that placed her fifth overall in her weight class. Banerji, who recently earned a BSc in Psychology from Ashoka University, is considering pursuing a Master of Business Administration.

title: Q&A | Logan Horne on upcycling Hermès and Celine scarves into shirts and homeware
description: Loved by celebrities like Travis Kelce and Dwyane Wade, J. Logan Home now offers a curated selection of reworked pieces at Beaureguards in Rosewood Hong Kong.
content: Former fashion buyer and celebrity stylist Logan Horne has been making quite the splash with his latest venture, J. Logan Home, known for its vibrant cabana shirts, accessories and homeware made from upcycled luxury scarves. It may come as a surprise, then, that the designer himself – who prefers to be called a fashion “artist” – is colour blind. “That gives me a unique eye when it comes to pattern, colour and all that,” Horne said in a recent interview in Hong Kong, where a curated selection of his pieces is now available at the Rosewood Hong Kong’s luxury boutique, Beaureguards. “I really see things outside the box.” That’s exactly why J. Logan Home has become a hit with male style stars like Taylor Swift’s new husband, American football player Travis Kelce, and basketball player Dwyane Wade, among a host of other celebrities. The Florida-born Horne shares how he went from styling in Los Angeles to working in New York to running a farm in his home state and eventually launching his brand in Palm Beach. How did J. Logan Home get started? During the pandemic, I was doing a lot of online shopping, especially pre-owned. That’s when I started to notice just how many scarves were out there. I saw an influx of Gucci pocket squares on The RealReal, all brand new with tags. These aren’t vintage – this is an overproduction problem. Obviously they’re trying to find new ways of offloading this inventory. I got a good price on cool scarves from the Alessandro Michele era, so I made my first [item], The Block, my stool/ottoman ‘futon,’ whatever you want to call it. From there I started collecting larger scarves, looking for unique prints and stories, to give these a new life – speaking to the greater trend I saw in menswear of scarf print shirts. There are so many because brands are still producing them at such a rate. I don’t think about waste as just excess inventory. I see pre-owned as waste too. [J. Logan Home] was always meant to be an homage to these brands I’ve adored since I was a kid, when they weren’t as accessible as they are now. When I bought my first Louis Vuitton piece, we had to go to Europe. Now there’s a Louis Vuitton in every mall in America. Upcycled homeware is what makes J. Logan Home unique. How did that come about? I’ve always been interested in upholstery. I’d been living in a one-bedroom apartment in New York and didn’t have a lot of room for seating, so my idea was creating this modular piece you could stack in the corner. [J. Logan Home] truly was born from boredom. If it hadn’t been for the pandemic, I don’t think I would’ve gone down this road. How did connections help when it came to launching your brand? I [styled] Gossip Girl star [Leighton Meester], and she put me on the map. That was a very fashion-centric show, so I had all the brands at my fingertips – getting to go to Paris Fashion Week in my early 20s. I was always trying to find new brands. I remember being one of the first stylists to put Charlotte Olympia shoes on an American actress. Emilio de la Morena, all these big UK designers, even Christopher Kane in the early days. US stars were not wearing those brands on the red carpet. I began my fashion career in retail and worked my way up to being a buyer when I was still in high school, having appointments at St John [Knits] and Missoni. My plan was to move to New York and go to fashion school, but I pulled the plug and moved to LA. I was intrigued by Hollywood and [those were] the early days of paparazzi pictures – Perez Hilton. In the early 2000s, the coolest brands were coming from Los Angeles: Juicy Couture, 7 [for All Mankind] jeans. My first job in LA was [at] Miu Miu and that’s where I got introduced to styling, in the time of Rachel Zoe. I assisted top Hollywood stylists on nights and weekends, whenever I wasn’t working retail or going to school. Then I learned LA wasn’t the place for high fashion – I went to FIDM, where Lauren Conrad went. There was this influx of kids who just wanted to be on MTV! That’s when I moved to New York. I worked for several high-profile publicists and designers: Kelly Cutrone, Tara Subkoff. All those experiences informed where I am now. Why did you launch your brand in Florida? I got stuck there during the pandemic, living with my parents. I found a local job [at] an aquaponic farm in my hometown, a very small sustainable operation. The woman who hired me actually quit a month after, so I inadvertently ended up running a farm I knew nothing about, growing micro radish and arugula, distributing to local restaurants and organic markets. That, too, was part of what led to this brand because I [thought], if I can do this – I built them an e-commerce platform, saved [them] during a really tough year – then I can do anything I want in fashion. I was going to go to business school, then when the pandemic didn’t seem like it was going anywhere, I just [decided] to start my brand. What unexpected challenges did you face? We got a cease-and-desist [letter] from Chanel a few years ago. I didn’t think about intellectual property and thought if I buy it and own it, I can do whatever I want. I ended up writing a letter to the CEO and that resonated with them. I agreed to stop using their products, but we never went to court. I’m very lucky because they do come for people all the time. That was two years ago and came on the heels of a lot of press after Travis Kelce started wearing my brand. Having been in this industry for 20 years and having deep ties to a lot of brands helped my case. I was never trying to create a Chanel garment and pass it off as my own. Speaking of Travis, has menswear been a big source of business for you? Men are taking way more fashion risks than they used to. Once a trend happens, you see the brands fall in line. Travis and other athletes are the ones really having fun with fashion, wearing non-gendered clothing and rocking handbags. Even more than Hollywood stars – you see pretty straightforward menswear on the red carpet. Travis found my brand shopping at The Webster in Miami. That’s [also] how Future, 2 Chainz, [other] rappers, NBA players and NFL stars found me. The Webster picked me up when [my brand] was barely five months old. They sold out of my first collection in the first week. I’ve never had to gift anyone anything. I can’t, as a small brand. My costs are very high. I’m working with really rare materials; I make everything in Florida. I don’t have the freedom to do large giftings like private equity[-funded] brands. It’s to their detriment. They end up on Poshmark. Have you learned anything else about running a small business? I’ve been a supporter of Thom Browne since the early days, and I discovered him at Barneys, the fashion mecca as far as I was concerned as a teenager. He candidly gave me [the advice to] “go slow”. Brands have a little bit of success and start showing at fashion week, and it really is a rat race. If it’s too big too fast, it becomes hard to sustain. Where else is J. Logan Home available? We found most success in these niche multi-brand boutiques, [and] a lot of upscale hotel properties that have [experiential] retail: the Four Seasons, Rosewood, specialty stores. E-commerce is not my world. I got picked up by FWRD, which is great, but I get lost in the shuffle. Why we’ve had so much success at hotels in particular is because people are on vacation. They want something to take home that’s sentimental, that’s unique. The Webster is my biggest retailer. I’m in all 11 stores [across the United States]. I’m spread pretty thin because I don’t make that much product.

title: How urban farming helps Hongkongers plant seeds of peace
description: Farmacy uses hydroponic technology to create mobile farms and farm labs in Hong Kong, bringing the joy of cultivation to city dwellers.
content:
When Linda Lee was young and living in the heart of Hong Kong’s urban metropolis, her father found peace in a small cluster of greenery in their flat.
He stood in the corner every day, tending to each pot. Lee’s father was a tough character. He did not talk much. But Lee saw his face relax whenever he tended to his “garden”.
Today, Lee works at Farmacy, an urban farming organisation that uses hydroponic technology – in which plants grow in a water and mineral solution rather than soil – to create mobile farms and farm labs in Hong Kong.
These spaces are usually compact, indoor, climate-controlled environments.
Lee leads urban farming experience days about once a month. It is a time when participants can set aside their usual worries and engage all five senses amid the greenery at Farmacy’s headquarters in Shau Kei Wan.
The list of hands-on activities includes plant rubbing – an artistic technique that captures the texture of different leaves by placing them under a piece of paper and shading over them with crayons or pencils – and seed art. Visitors can also try aromatherapy.

title: Indo-Chinese cuisine in Hong Kong: a delicious dialogue of cultures and flavours
description: At a moment when diplomats are talking about rebuilding trust between India and China, two chefs in Hong Kong are already finding common ground in spice, smoke and fire.
content: On September 12 and 13, world leaders and ambassadors are due to gather in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, with President Xi Jinping expected to be among them – his first visit to India since 2019. It is a moment of cautious optimism in a relationship that has see-sawed between tension and thaw for the better part of a decade, marked by such events as the 2017 Doklam (Donglang) stand-off and the 2020 clashes in the Galwan valley. But as politicians cook up deals and diplomacy, two chefs in Hong Kong would rather let the food do the talking. In July, chef Palash Mitra of Prince and the Peacock and chef Theign Phan of Grand Majestic Sichuan fired up their tandoors and woks, trading notes on the almost 2,000-year-old conversation their cuisines have been engaged in, long before anyone put it on an agenda. Growing up in Kolkata, the capital of West Bengal state in eastern India, Mitra never thought of Chinese food as a separate cuisine. It was simply stitched into the city’s culinary fabric. He remembers the Chinese food carts his family would visit on special occasions, and “Shubhon”, the man behind the wok, whose real name was Chen Shiobin. By day, Shubhon worked at a rifle factory; by night, he sold street bites, peddling in fluent Bengali, bargaining at the market in Bengali, laughing in Bengali. “He was as much a part of Kolkata as the tram lines and the Durga Puja pandals. He was simply one of us,” says Mitra. It’s easy to think of Indian and Chinese gastronomies as detached empires. But beneath the surface, a dialogue has been under way for more than a millennium. On ancient maps, the two are interwoven through the maritime lanes of the spice trade and the mountain passes of the Silk Road. It is believed that India initiated the exchange, sending black pepper to China during the first two centuries AD. Later, the favour was returned: China dispatched cassia bark and star anise along the same routes. By the time Hakka and Cantonese settlers arrived in Kolkata – then named Calcutta – more than 200 years ago, and adapted their woks to local ingredients to give birth to a composite cuisine now beloved across the subcontinent, Chinese and Indian communities had been using food as the language of negotiation for generations. “Indo-Chinese is not a hybrid that belongs nowhere,” Mitra asserts. “It belongs specifically to Kolkata, a city that has always absorbed the world and made it its own.” Global trade had shaped Kolkata for centuries. Portuguese merchants brought chillies, potatoes and cashews in the 1500s, and the English East India Company followed in the 1600s, chasing the spice trade. By the time the city was established, in 1690, other settlers, such as Armenians, had already brought their own kitchens and their own gods. Kolkata’s Chinese community, concentrated in Tangra, the “new” Chinatown, peaked at 40,000 around the time of World War II. Settlers had arrived in waves, starting in the late 18th century, first making a home in Tiretta Bazaar, the “old” Chinatown, and then again throughout the 19th century and early 20th century, fleeing war and invasion. Many worked in the tanning industry, a profession that higher-caste Hindus considered “polluting”, leaving a niche that the Hakka filled. As tanneries in the Tangra neighbourhood closed or relocated over the years, the community increasingly turned to food to sustain their livelihoods. Like many new immigrants, the Chinese adapted their cuisine, adding more chillies, more garlic and more ginger to suit Indian palates, while keeping the non-negotiables – wok, high heat and soy sauce – close to the hearth. A menu at an Indo-Chinese restaurant is what Mitra calls “gloriously Calcuttan”. While early Kolkata institutions such as Eau Chew pioneered the genre in the 1920s, the now-classic Hakka wheat noodles dish was later popularised by the grass-roots, family-run kitchens of Tangra. In 1975 came chicken Manchurian, invented at the Cricket Club of India, in Mumbai, when the Kolkata-born chef Nelson Wang paired the Indian trinity of ginger, garlic and green chilli with soy sauce and cornflour instead of garam masala. Chilli paneer – cubes of firm cheese fried with peppers and green chilli – emerged in the late 20th century as a vegetarian adaptation of familiar Indo-Chinese poultry recipes. Mitra carried those memories with him when he arrived in Hong Kong. “It was only when I was dining at Luk Yu Tea House that I realised chilli chicken did not exist in China,” he says. “[Chicken] Manchurian was an Indian invention. Hakka noodles, as we knew them, did not belong to any province on a map [of China]. Instead, I found dim sum and Cantonese broths.” It was the culinary equivalent of an American landing in Hong Kong and discovering fortune cookies were never Chinese to begin with. “Looking back, I laugh, because I had unknowingly grown up loving a cuisine that bore very little resemblance to the Chinese food I encountered in Hong Kong. Living on both sides of that divide has been a rare gift,” he reflects. Phan speaks that same dialect of living between cultures – born in Malaysia, raised in Singapore, now cooking Sichuan food in Hong Kong. She recalls a childhood of tucking into roti prata at hawker centres, fish-head curries with her father and banana-leaf meals where she learned to eat with her hands. “[Indian food] was always bold, flavourful and communal,” she says. “It was only after I started cooking professionally and travelling that I realised how incredibly diverse Indian cuisine is. What I knew growing up was just a small glimpse.” Phan’s father is Hakka, so learning about the Kolkata community resonated with her. She had seen the same dynamic play out in Peranakan cuisine, born from Chinese-Malay intermarriage. “Neither cuisine was created because people wanted to invent something new; they developed naturally because communities settled in a new place and began cooking with what was around them, while holding onto parts of their own identity,” she says. At a time when a quick scroll on social media can (virtually) transport you to a Chongqing hotpot joint, it’s easy to forget the ingredients themselves have already travelled farther. While huajiao (Sichuan pepper) is native to Sichuan province, chilli peppers arrived from Mesoamerica. It took centuries of seafaring and cross-continental trade to bring them together in a single pot. Mala, one of Sichuan’s most famous flavour profiles, is defined by the chillies that hit the tongue first, delivering a building burn that lingers, and the huajiao that numbs the tongue, a tingling that feels almost electric. It’s a dialogue between two different kinds of fire, connected through ancient routes. But just as it would be a mistake to generalise Indian food as “curry” – a British catch-all for a whole universe of Indian cooking – it would be equally reductive to sum up Sichuan cuisine, which has 24 official flavour profiles, such as the sweet, sour, salty, savoury, spicy and numbing guaiwei (“strange flavour”) and the fish-free yuxiang (“fish-fragrant”), as just mala. With such vast and layered traditions on both sides, how do two chefs even begin to find common ground? “Both cuisines understand the importance of balance,” says Phan. “Even when a dish is spicy, it’s never just about heat. You’re looking for aroma, depth, acidity, texture and fragrance all working together.” In Indian cookery, this plays out in the methodical blooming of whole spices in oil before adding aromatics and garam masalas. In Sichuan fare, the same instinct runs through layers of aromatics and the slow heat of chillies and peppercorns. Both traditions also share a deep understanding of fermentation – the funky depth of doubanjiang (fermented broad-bean paste) meets the sharp tang of Indian pickles and kasundi (fermented mustard). More importantly, they are unafraid of fire. “Whether it’s a tandoor or a blazing wok, both cuisines rely on high heat to create smokiness, caramelisation and complexity,” Mitra adds. When the two chefs travelled through India together earlier this year, these parallels became tangible, and the trip became the foundation for two four-hands dinners at Prince and the Peacock and Grand Majestic Sichuan. In Mumbai, Phan ordered crab cooked two ways and found herself naming Sichuan flavour profiles: garlic paste and fragrant-spicy. “I could taste cardamom, peppercorns, cassia bark, coriander seeds – not just chilli, but layers of dry spices working through the sauce,” she says. In hotel restaurants across the country, the international menus told the same story: Sichuan stir-fried vegetables, triple Sichuan fried rice (an Indo-Chinese dish with “Manchurian” gravy), kung pao prawns, mapo tofu. “It really shows India’s love of Sichuan food – the flavours have been embraced so naturally,” says Phan. For Mitra, the trip was also a homecoming: “I probably ate Hakka noodles almost every day we were in India.” Mitra’s cravings naturally found their way onto his four-hands menu – but with a twist. During recipe trials in Jamnagar, in Gujarat state, he was making a bowl of Hakka noodles when a leftover Goan xacuti spice blend caught his eye. He added a little without thinking and found that “the coconut rounded everything out, while the stone flower brought an earthy note that worked surprisingly well with the soy [sauce] and chilli” – and so the spice blend stayed. Both flavours are products of migration and adaptation; xacuti carries Portuguese influence into Goa, while Hakka noodles carry Chinese technique into Kolkata. Chilli paneer was another classic discussed from the start. “We always knew we wanted chilli paneer on the menu because it’s such an iconic Indo-Chinese dish,” Mitra says. But Prince and the Peacock doesn’t have the kind of set-up that produces wok hei (“breath of the wok”), so he turned to the grill. Paneer hits the hot metal with a hiss; onion and capsicum blister and pop as the skewers turn. “It still tastes recognisably like chilli paneer, but the grill gives it a different character,” he says. It’s the same spirit that built Tangra’s kitchens: when you don’t have the right tool, you invent a new way to use the one in front of you. At Grand Majestic Sichuan, Phan had the woks to spice things up. In Mumbai, she had a Bombay duck chilli fry and thought about how to translate its fragrant heat, sweetness and savouriness through a Sichuan lens for the collaboration, eventually landing on the flavours of kung pao. What emerged keeps the crisp-fried fish and the punchy chilli of the original, but reroutes it through the sweet-sour-nutty dialect of kung pao. Other dishes in their four-hands collaboration, such as the chilled soup of chaas and tangerine peel, look forwards, rather than backwards. Chaas, a spiced buttermilk drink meant to cool the palate, takes on a faint bitterness and citrus fragrance from the dried tangerine peel, a combination Mitra and Phan describe as “completely new”. It is a dish that requires both chefs in the same kitchen, with no particular interest in staying inside the lines. “Sharing a meal creates a different kind of connection,” says Mitra. “Food has always travelled more freely than politics.”

title: Iran likely to reverse-engineer captured US underwater drone
description: The loss represents ‌a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington’s efforts to project technological superiority.
content: Iran’s capture of a US military underwater drone gives Tehran an opportunity to study and potentially reverse-engineer the vessel, delivering a setback for the Pentagon and drone maker Anduril. The US military and Anduril have downplayed the significance of the drone falling into Iranian hands. The vessel, a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle designed for long-range surveillance and other undersea missions, is among a new ‌generation of military drones intended to operate for days with little human intervention. Washington has previously treated the loss of advanced drones to Iran as a serious matter. After Iran captured an RQ-170 Sentinel stealth reconnaissance drone in 2011, then US President Barack Obama publicly asked Tehran to return the aircraft. Iran later claimed it had reverse-engineered the drone and subsequently unveiled domestically produced models that appeared to draw heavily on its design. More recently, the US military moved swiftly to prevent Iranian forces from taking possession of uncrewed maritime technology. In 2022, a US Navy patrol ship and MH-60S Seahawk helicopter were deployed after an Iranian naval vessel attempted to tow away ⁠a Saildrone surface vessel in the Gulf, according to the Navy. Analysts say Iran is unlikely to gain a decisive military advantage from the captured drone, but the episode nonetheless represents ‌a propaganda victory for Tehran and an awkward setback for Washington’s efforts to project technological superiority. Iranian embassies around the world have mocked the US for losing its drone. Iran’s embassy in Ghana, in a social media post, boasted about picking the submersible up ‌in “a strait controlled by people who can hear a shrimp sneeze”, adding that: “Our guys picked it up like a plastic bottle in a fishing ⁠net. Fully intact. Still blinking like an ⁠idiot. Condolences to whoever was holding the joystick.” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins of US Central Command said the “defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Anduril ‌did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “Of course Iran will take every opportunity as a propaganda win,” said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. “It can help the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] ‌make ‌better versions of their own designs.” Iran will almost certainly try to pry open the drone’s hardware, but the drone’s software carries built-in defences, said Bryan Clark, a senior fellow ‌and director of the Centre for Defence Concepts and Technology at the Hudson Institute. Iranian engineers “could definitely reverse-engineer the mechanical systems”, he said, pointing to Tehran’s track record with captured American ⁠aircraft. “Unboxing ceremony by our reverse engineers, tomorrow morning!” Iran’s embassy in Hyderabad wrote on social media. The incident has also highlighted a disconnect between the messaging of Anduril and its ⁠customer, the US Navy. Navy officials said the Dive-LD was an older-model vehicle that suffered a malfunction and was recovered by Iranian forces after being left “dead in the water”. Anduril has promoted the Dive-LD as “the most reliable and flexible” large autonomous underwater vehicle available, saying it is capable of operating for up to ‌10 days in demanding conditions. In addition to ‌its use by the US Navy, the Dive-LD was the test bed vehicle for the development of Australia’s new Ghost Shark large underwater drone. “This is something that Iran has proven very adept at exploiting for its own benefit in terms of seeking to frame the narrative as one of US, in this case, ineptitude and their ability to sort of retain control over the Strait of Hormuz,” said Mona Yacoubian, director of the Middle East programme at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

title: Editorial | Tung’s legacy continues to inspire city under ‘one country, two systems’
description: Hong Kong’s first chief executive navigated the uncharted waters of an unprecedented governance formula and helped lay the foundations of the city’s future success.
content: As Hong Kong’s first post-handover leader, Tung Chee-hwa was destined to go down in history. From steering the city through its uncertain early years after its return to Chinese rule to laying the foundations for its later momentous growth, the shipping magnate-turned-inaugural chief executive will be remembered not just for navigating the uncharted waters of “one country, two systems” but for his foresight in maintaining the city’s unique strengths as it integrated with the country for better development. Thanks to Beijing’s trust, his extensive mainland and international ties, and his strong commitment to the country and city, the political novice was plucked out of his business empire to lead Hong Kong in 1997. Essentially, he was tasked with proving that the unprecedented governance formula for the city was practicable and the best way forward, and that the freewheeling financial centre left behind by the British could do even better under Chinese rule. He inherited a population of 6.5 million not quite certain about the future and about how Hong Kong’s capitalist system would function under “one country” as well as a bureaucracy that often made reforms two steps forward, one step back. He also faced growing pressure to tackle an array of deep-seated problems. While Tung was eager to introduce reforms on fronts ranging from education to government efficiency, there was resistance from various sectors and his considerate character was seen by some as being too cautious sometimes. As much as Tung wanted to resolve Hong Kong’s notorious housing problem, the Asian financial crisis which hit the city’s property market hard forced him to shelve the target of building 85,000 housing units a year. Nevertheless, he was the first leader to realise the importance of handling the housing problem and its link to Hongkongers’, especially young people’s, sense of belonging to the city. He later introduced the city’s very first accountability system to boost government efficiency. A major challenge was the severe acute respiratory syndrome outbreak and the July 1 mass protest that led to the shelving of the national security bill under Basic Law Article 23 in 2003. With Tung’s efforts, the central government agreed to allow mainland tourists to visit the city and later approved the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement for Hong Kong. Tung was attacked by opposition activists, but he was determined to do what he believed was good for Hong Kong. His legacy extends beyond his commitment to the implementation of one country, two systems. He is credited for his foresight in innovation, education and care for the elderly and disadvantaged. His push for closer integration with the mainland, including cross-border transport links, positioned Hong Kong as a gateway between China and the world. Tung was also a patriot in the truest sense. His famous maxim – “If Hong Kong is good, the nation is good; if the nation is good, Hong Kong will be even better” – encapsulated his belief in the intricate relationship between the city and the country. This continues to guide successive administrations. He fully understood that Hong Kong’s success depended on its ability to contribute to China’s development while maintaining the attributes that made it unique. Even after stepping down midway through his second term in 2005 on health grounds, Tung remained deeply engaged with Hong Kong and national affairs. He established a think tank dedicated to policy research aimed at addressing the city’s long-term challenges. He spoke out at key moments to defend Hong Kong’s interests, urging dialogue and understanding between the city and Beijing. The work he continued to do reflected a genuine love for the city and the country. Tung did not stop contributing to Sino-US relations, using his own money as seed funding to set up a foundation and leveraging his stature and experience to foster dialogue, including people-to-people exchanges. In an era of geopolitical friction, his efforts to maintain channels of communication were invaluable. He recognised that Hong Kong’s role as a bridge between East and West depended on stable Sino-US ties. Tung’s legacy offers a reminder that Hong Kong’s future lies in its ability to play to its strengths as a bridge between China and the world. His vision, patriotism and unwavering commitment to both Hong Kong and the country continue to inspire.

title: Inside Cantopop singer Jude Tsang and property investor Kevin Yeung’s Hong Kong home
description: Three generations live in harmony in Peak home that weaves faith, family and Fujian heritage into the design.
content: When patriarch Yeung Wing-wah was thinking of renovating his long-time family home on The Peak, he had a vision. Younger son Kevin Yeung Iat-seng and wife Jude Tsang Yeuk-wa had returned from living in Britain and planned to start a family of their own. Why not make it a spiritual sanctuary where three generations would live together? The couple were instantly on board. “I grew up in this apartment with my brother and sister,” says Kevin Yeung, a property investor, who, with Cantopop singer-songwriter Tsang, welcomed their firstborn in 2025. “Now that my child is also growing up here, I feel the home carries a sense of passing down through generations, making moving back even more meaningful.” Built in the 1960s, the 2,500 sq ft (232 square metre), three-bedroom apartment offered elevated city and harbour views that provided an inspirational canvas for Soil Studios co-founders OJ Miu Ka-kei and Alexander Ho Lik-shan, both of whom had been introduced to the family by a mutual friend. The goal, Ho says, was to build a haven that connected with nature and carried family memories forward, accommodating both Buddhist faith and multigenerational needs. Paying homage to the classical Minnan architecture of Fujian, the family’s ancestral homeland in mainland China, the designers replaced existing dividing walls with three timber-framed arched portals as the new “spine” of the home. As Ho explains, the gentle curves are a contemporary translation of the sequenced archways and intricate joinery found in traditional homes and buildings in the Minnan region in southern Fujian. In this apartment, their presence restores order and rhythm to a previously disconnected floor plan while also solving a design problem by concealing structural columns. Beneath the first, smallest arch by the foyer, an auspicious “three rams bringing bliss” sculpture symbolises the intergenerational make-up of the household. “The sheep serve as an emotional anchor in the spatial narrative, embodying family metaphors and the close bonds among its members,” Ho says. The medium and largest arches span the living and dining zone, the social heart of the home, where a life-size wooden sculpture of Guanyin, the Goddess of Mercy (commonly known as Kwun Yum in Hong Kong), is given pride of place. Having been in the family for many years, it now holds special meaning for the young couple. On a trip to Putuo Mountain in China’s Zhejiang province, a sacred site dedicated to Guanyin, Kevin and Jude prayed for a baby. “After our return, we found out we were expecting our son,” Kevin says. “We do believe in a higher power, and that somehow Guanyin helped us. Every time I walk past that statue in our living room, I say, ‘Thank you.’” In subtly defining functional zones, the three progressive arches allow spaces to interpenetrate so that even when family members are in different areas, they can still see each other. “Fluted glass partitions in key areas [the study and kitchen] maintain a sense of transparency while ensuring privacy,” Miu says. “They also ensure that every main space can engage in dialogue with the view outside, letting the scenery become the most precious artwork on display.” One of these screens encloses a multifunctional third bedroom that can take on various roles as needed, pivoting from band practice studio for Jude, to home office for Kevin, to occasional guest room or nursery. Curves in the ceiling, walls and custom-made furniture continue as a unifying theme, complemented by tactile finishes in timber and stone, and a nature-inspired neutral palette. The two main bedrooms have en suites and a corner chair each for quiet time. In one, bedlinen in cobalt blue not only complies with feng shui requirements (being calming and meditative) but also echoes the deep hue of the harbour view. Above the bed hangs another spiritually meaningful design feature: a calligraphy work bearing the Buddhist saying “free from attachment”. From big picture to small details, every design element has purpose. With the safety of the elder and younger generations in mind, the designers avoided sharp corners in the bathrooms. And at every turn, windows frame different pictures of nature, the shifting shades of light and colour reflected on the matt terracotta walls of the apartment’s airy interior. For Ho and Miu, this project was a rare and deeply moving experience. “When the family first shared their story – their Fujian roots, their Buddhist practice and their wish to bring three generations closer – we knew this wasn’t going to be an ordinary design project,” Ho says. “It became a quiet dialogue between past and present. “The three portals, for instance, emerged from conversations about the grandparents’ childhood memories and a desire to gently frame, not divide, how the family moves through the home. Seeing those timber arches take shape felt like weaving their ancestry into the very bones of a modern apartment. We came away not just as designers, but as people who’d been taught something about what home really means.” For Kevin and Jude, the happiness imbued in the home is an enduring legacy of the renovation. “The apartment feels more gentle, more organic – almost like it’s breathing with you,” Kevin says. “It’s a blessing from my father to be sharing this beautiful environment with Jude and our baby. I feel like I am following in his footsteps.” Living room The life-size Guanyin sculpture has been in the family for decades. Sofa from Edra. Armchair from Baxter. Coffee table designed by Soil Studios. Artwork from Douguya Hatcharea. Textured ceiling and wall paint from AKK. Valletta Oak Nature flooring from Joyful Sky. Sofa from Edra. Armchair and coffee table designed by Soil Studios. Artwork and “three rams bringing bliss” sculpture (in small niche) from Douguya Hatcharea. Bedroom Bed, side tables and writing table all designed by Soil Studios. Calligraphy (“free from attachment”) from Kevin’s father. Bedside lamps from Audo Copenhagen. Custom-made bedroom chair and television console designed by Soil Studios. En suite bathroom Cabinetry designed by Soil Studios. Gessi tapware from Colour Living. Multifunctional room Sliding doors in fluted glass, display shelving and table all designed by Soil Studios. Three arches Inspired by Minnan, the traditional architectural style of Fujian, arched portals were designed by Soil Studios and lined with oak veneer. Kitchen Kitchen, in woodgrain laminate with quartz composite benchtops, from Arclinea. Dining room Dining table, chairs and pendant light all designed by Soil Studios. Tried + tested Even with a voice as polished as Jude’s, not everyone wants to listen to constant musical practice. That is why Soil Studios specified sound-absorbing materials for the multifunctional band room, which multitasks as a third bedroom and study. Polyform Eos Prism acoustic wall covering from Texdecor is a polyester faux-suede textile on a polyurethane foam backing. According to the company, the acoustic absorbency of this wallcovering range varies from α 0.15 to 0.30 depending on the desired thickness of the foam (7mm and 5mm), which equates to absorbing 15 to 30 per cent of sound energy that hits it. A curtain for the glass sliding door that encloses the music room – Pico Cookie thick pile polyester velvet from Villa Nova, supplied by Wallpaper+ – provides another layer of sound absorbency. To any parent of a rising star, and their neighbours, you are welcome.

title: US says China ‘on track’ to fulfil farm purchases ahead of Xi’s Washington visit
description: Trump administration trade official says ‘China is ramping up their purchases’ and business is progressing well between two countries.
content: The Trump administration on Wednesday said that China is on track to meet its agricultural purchase commitments, with the sector expected to feature prominently in the deliverables for US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping’s talks in Washington later this month. “China is ramping up their purchases,” said Luke Lindberg, the US Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs at the US Department of Agriculture (USDA). “We’re seeing that progress happen.” Speaking at a Council on Foreign Relations event, Lindberg added that China is on track to buy US$17 billion worth of US agricultural products this year, in addition to soybeans, which he said would bring annual sales to US$30 billion. He noted that China had already met its commitment to buy 12 million metric tonnes of US soybeans in the 2025 season and is “on track right now” to meet the agreed-upon target of 25 million metric tonnes this year. In the run-up to Xi’s visit, USDA flash reports show a rise in soybean exports to China, crossing 700,000 metric tonnes in the first nine days of September. The USDA said later: “President Trump secured another strong deal for American farmers and ranchers with China. “While China has work to do to fulfil its promises to the United States, we are pleased to see China meeting its commitment on soybeans and remain hopeful that it will follow through on its commitments across other US agricultural products.” The soybean deal was a key outcome of the trade truce reached in Busan, South Korea, last year and was expanded after another leaders’ meeting in May in Beijing to include China’s promise to buy at least US$17 billion worth of US agricultural products annually for the next three years. The commitments fell well short of the US$40 billion in agricultural exports to China recorded in 2022. The loss of a large share of the Chinese market, coupled with rising fuel and fertiliser costs linked to the US war in Iran and President Trump’s tariff policies, has deepened the crisis facing US farmers. Uncertainty remains over US farm incomes and exports The squeeze has added to uncertainty over farm incomes and exports, prompting the administration to step up efforts to help producers find alternative markets for their crops. However, Lindberg asserted that soybean farmers are “very happy” with their China sales and are not interested in going “much higher” than current levels, given their focus on “diversification” of export markets. John Bartman, an Illinois-based fifth-generation soybean farmer, disputed the claim and termed the administration’s farm policies “all buffer and no results”. “The American soybean farmer used to have 50 per cent of China’s soybean market, and now we’re lucky if we have 20 per cent of it,” he said. Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, also said soybean sales had not picked up and pointed to weak beef exports to China, even though purchase promises were another key outcome of the Beijing agreement. “Sale of beef from the last meetings is nearly impossible because we are simply, as a country, importing beef products just to keep up with domestic demand,” he said. China’s renewal of licences for US meat plants has yet to revive beef exports, with higher US prices and weaker Chinese demand weighing on shipments. As in May, agricultural purchases are expected to be a key outcome for the coming Trump-Xi summit. “We expect that we will probably have some more announcements on agriculture and non-tariff barriers related to agriculture to incentivise American sales into China,” US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in an interview with Fox News last week. In July, the Chinese embassy in Washington said agriculture and aviation were among the sectors selected for tariff-reduced trade, adding that the two sides had “set a guiding objective of expanding two-way agricultural trade” and agreed “in principle” to include agricultural products in a framework for reciprocal tariff reductions. The SCMP also reported last week that the Busan trade truce was likely to be extended, along with the operationalisation of the US-China Board of Trade. However, these agreements are unlikely to move the needle for US farmers. Bartman highlighted rising input costs, calling them a “self-inflicted wound” resulting from Trump’s policies, including the war in Iran and tariffs. “We are still operating at below break-even costs,” he said. Question remains whether US is reliable trading partner On government efforts to find export markets beyond China, he said buyers in new markets no longer have assurance that the US is a “reliable trading partner any more”. “They don’t know what things are going to cost because, from day to day, he changes the tariff rate,” he added, referring to Trump. Jeff Winton, a dairy farmer in upstate New York, also said that farmers are under “historic stress and pressure” due to higher costs, tariff policies and a “diminishing labour force” as a result of an immigration crackdown. “There is a growing mistrust among American farmers about anything coming out of Washington now,” Winton said.

title: Susquehanna latest to pick up larger office space in Hong Kong’s Central, sources say
description: The US-based firm is set to rent space in Cheung Kong Center II as the Central district leads office rental market recovery in the city.
content: US investment firm Susquehanna International Group has agreed to lease more than 4,808 square metres (51,762 square feet) of office space at the Cheung Kong Center II, a prime office skyscraper developed by CK Asset Holdings in Hong Kong’s main business zone of Central, according to market sources. Neither Susquehanna nor CK Asset immediately replied to the South China Morning Post’s requests for comments. The new space would span three floors of the property, according to the sources. Susquehanna’s current listed address in Hong Kong is at the AIA Central on Connaught Road Central, close to Cheung Kong Center II on Harcourt Road. The group moved to its current address in 2021, leaving Three Garden Road, also in Central, “with a significant cost savings”. Hong Kong’s office property market is currently seeing a gradual recovery with Central leading the upswing, according to analysts, with one citing the record-setting lease by trading firm Jane Street in the district last year as an example. “We are seeing increasing demand from financial institutions such as Jane Street for high-quality office space in Central as it remains Hong Kong’s premier business district,” said Alex Lam, executive director and head of Hong Kong Island for office services at Colliers. Vacancy rates in the central business district fell to 10.2 per cent as of the end of the second quarter from 14.5 per cent a year ago, on sustained occupier demand, data tracked by the property consultancy showed. As of August, empty office spaces in the district further declined to 10 per cent, Colliers said. Meanwhile, rents in Central rose 1.9 per cent quarter on quarter, it added. “Central remains the preferred location for many finance, asset management and wealth management firms because of its concentration of capital markets activity, clients, professional services and talent, creating a unique ecosystem,” Lam said. In the second half of the year, Colliers forecast that despite a completion of about 111,484 square metres (1.2 million square feet) of new office supply, broad-based office rental corrections were unlikely as “the market has largely priced in the new supply.” Colliers also upgraded its forecast for Central and Admiralty rents to an increase of 10 per cent this year.

title: Tate brothers lose bid for release from US jail pending extradition fight
description: In denying bail, the judge cited the influencers’ wealth and frequent international travel as making them ‘quintessential flight risks’.
content: Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate lost their bid for release from a Miami jail on Wednesday as they contest extradition to Britain, where they are wanted on rape charges. In denying bail for the Tate brothers, Miami-based US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis said the brothers’ wealth and frequent international travel made them “quintessential flight risks”. “While [the brothers] may not ‌in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction,” Louis said. In a statement, the Tates’ lawyers said they would “continue to defend themselves against the allegations they face and engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction”. In court filings, their lawyers had previously argued their “extraordinary public visibility” would make it impractical for them to flee, and described social media posts in which the brothers touted their wealth as “theatrical” and “grandiose”. Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18 after ⁠Britain requested their extradition to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. The Tate brothers, who have dual US and British citizenship, have denied ‌any wrongdoing. The arrests marked a new phase in the legal troubles for the former kick-boxers, who have built a large online following promoting their views on masculinity and wealth. Andrew Tate has previously described himself as a misogynist. Prosecutors with the Miami US Attorney’s office argued there was a strong presumption in favour of detention in international extradition cases. ⁠They said the brothers could pose a ⁠danger to the public if released, citing British allegations that they strangled victims during forcible rapes. The Tates recruited dozens of women to work for a webcam pornography business starting in 2014, and ‌later ran online courses called “Hustler’s University”, prosecutors said in an August 10 court filing. At an August 27 hearing in Miami federal court, prosecutors showed the court a video of Andrew Tate saying “slap, slap, grab, choke, shut ‌up b****, ‌sex”. At the hearing, both Tate brothers testified they were playing characters online when they made crude remarks. Louis wrote on Wednesday that the nature of ‌the allegations against the Tates indicated they posed dangers to the community. The brothers have also been under investigation on charges including human trafficking since 2022 in Romania, where ⁠they were mainly based since 2017. Romanian prosecutors officially indicted Andrew Tate on Friday on charges of trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor and witness tampering. ⁠Tristan Tate was indicted for complicity. A Romanian lawyer for the Tates said they rejected the allegations. The legal process for determining whether the Tate brothers may be extradited to Britain could take months. Britain has until September 16 to submit its full extradition ‌request to the State Department, US court records ‌show. The impetus for the brothers’ arrests in Miami was new charges brought by Britain’s Crown Prosecution Service relating to alleged offences involving four alleged victims between July 2010 and August 2017. They had previously faced rape and human-trafficking charges in Britain related to three alleged victims, the CPS said. A British judge issued a warrant for their arrests in 2024. They have not appeared in British court to enter a plea to those charges. Britain is seeking to extradite the brothers to face both sets of charges.

title: Exclusive | Once sidelined, China stands ready to broker fourth Trump-Kim handshake
description: Beijing seeks role as central player in Korean peninsula diplomacy but wants a guarantee Washington has clear goals, source says.
