content: China is willing to help broker a possible meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, sources have said just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected in Washington for a bilateral summit. Multiple people familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post that Beijing was stepping up to play an “active” and “constructive” role in reviving US-North Korea diplomacy, underscoring its resolve to remain a central player in negotiations on the Korean peninsula as Trump seeks to reignite engagement with Pyongyang. According to two sources, Beijing will support all credible efforts that could lead to resumed dialogue. But they argued that Kim was likely to demand a high price for returning to the negotiating table, given his strengthened ties with Russia – which affords Pyongyang greater diplomatic and military leverage – and China, as well as Kim’s disappointment from past meetings with Trump. One source said Kim was likely to insist on sanctions relief and US recognition of its nuclear status before agreeing to another meeting with Trump. However, a second source added that China would seek to clarify whether Washington had defined potential concrete outcomes ahead of any planned summit. One person familiar with the issue said China was particularly keen to broker a Trump-Kim meeting, seeing Pyongyang as leverage against Washington, but that Beijing would only push the two leaders together if its own interests were protected. Another source said there had been discussion of a Trump-Kim meeting being held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen in November, although nothing has been confirmed. One more person familiar with the matter said Trump was now all but certain to attend Apec. An envoy was sent in mid-August to scout both Shenzhen and Hangzhou in what was described as a preparatory trip for a potential meeting with Kim. The source said the planning gathered pace after Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May. Trump has sent multiple public feelers to North Korea in recent days, expressing his desire to resume the high-profile personal diplomacy that produced three largely inconclusive meetings during his first term. But communication between Washington and Pyongyang is limited at best, according to multiple sources. Trump’s recent comments on North Korea were an effort by his administration to both revive diplomacy with Kim and distract global attention from the Iran war, one source added. Last month, Trump halved the duration of annual joint military exercises with South Korea to just five days and described his relationship with Kim as “very good,” while criticising South Korea for not joining the US in the “denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran”. Trump said the exercises sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, which, in his view, “has been unthreatening and respectful”. He floated plans to meet Kim and last month, when asked by reporters whether he expected to meet the North Korean leader before the end of 2026, Trump said: “Yeah, I will be.” “I know Kim Jong-un very well, and he’s going to be fine as long as we have a smart president,” he said. Publicly, North Korea has not responded to Trump’s offer with much enthusiasm. Kim Yo-jong, the North Korean leader’s influential sister, said Washington’s “hostile policy” towards North Korea had not changed and Pyongyang still regarded the military exercises – although curtailed – as provocative. “If the US side is trying to tout its decision as some kind of an ‘act of goodwill’, they will not get the response that they want,” she said in a statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency last month. North Korea also test-fired more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles, prompting South Korea’s presidential office to convene an emergency security meeting. Trump held three meetings with Kim during his first term, starting with a summit in Singapore in June 2018, followed by a meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, in February 2019. Both engagements failed to bridge their differences on sanctions relief for North Korea and its nuclear programme. In Vietnam, Trump cut his meeting with Kim short after both leaders failed to agree on removing sanctions, ending the summit without a deal. The two met again in June 2019 at the demilitarised zone separating North and South Korea, where Trump became the first sitting US president to step onto North Korean soil. China played a crucial role in the Trump-Kim summits, both behind the scenes and in more visible ways. Beijing provided Kim with an Air China Boeing 747 for his trip to Singapore and after the meeting, Kim visited Beijing where he met Xi. Beijing also made elaborate logistical and security arrangements for the North Korean leader’s 60-hour train journey from Pyongyang to Hanoi via mainland China. Three sources added that the North Korean leader remained displeased with the lack of outcomes from previous meetings, especially the Vietnam summit where Trump walked away from the discussions. The embarrassment of Kim, who had travelled for more than two days for the talks, remained a challenge, one source said. There has been a shift in the geopolitical landscape since their last meeting in 2019. In addition to North Korea’s stronger ties with Russia, China has also strengthened its relationship with North Korea. In June, Xi visited Pyongyang where both sides vowed to deepen strategic cooperation in several sectors. In a congratulatory message to Kim on Wednesday to mark the 78th anniversary of the founding of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, Xi said China was pleased by North Korea’s development achievements. Xi said their countries were friendly socialist neighbours that stood by each other and shared prosperity and adversity, according to the message released by Xinhua. China’s president said he was ready to work with Kim to promote the development of the two countries and peace and prosperity in the region.

title: US sanctions Chinese-language Xinbi Guarantee marketplace over cyber scams
description: Washington also seizes Telegram channels and US$52 million in cryptocurrency linked to the platform’s alleged illicit operations.
content: The Trump administration sanctioned Chinese-language marketplace Xinbi Guarantee on Wednesday, along with two affiliated organisations, as part of a wider crackdown on transnational cybercrime. The US Department of Justice also announced it had seized Telegram channels and cryptocurrency wallets tied to the platform, which has over 650,000 users, freezing more than US$52 million in potentially laundered funds in just one day. “This is not a distant overseas crime story,” said Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, at a press conference. “It is an industrial extraction of American savings run by Chinese transnational criminal enterprises and platforms.” Wednesday’s operations were conducted by the US Department of Justice’s inter-agency Scam Centre Strike Force, alongside the Department of the Treasury. Xinbi Guarantee, which runs on the encrypted messaging app Telegram, is accused of enabling scam centres to buy and sell illicit services that target Americans, acting as a central node connecting syndicates with merchants. Singapore-based SafeW Technology Co and Cambodia-based Anwen Technology Co were also hit by the sanctions over allegations that they provided applications supporting Xinbi’s operations. “Xinbi’s platform is used by scam centre operators to purchase goods and facilitate transactions in support of cyberscam and cybercrime operations, including various types of financial fraud,” said the US Department of the Treasury in a press release. “Since its inception around 2022, Xinbi Guarantee’s marketplace has processed the equivalent of over US$24 billion in digital assets and fiat currency through its marketplace and via its platforms, primarily facilitating transactions in countries located in Southeast Asia.” The government also announced it had deployed teams to Madagascar to assist in taking down 13 scam compounds, which it said were Chinese-run. The Chinese embassy in Washington said its government requires Chinese citizens overseas to abide by local laws and regulations and refrain from criminal activity. “The Chinese government has always taken a zero-tolerance approach to telecom fraud,” added embassy spokesman Liu Chang. “China looks forward to joining hands with all parties to jointly combat these crimes.” While many scam compounds are located in Southeast Asian countries, including Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar, investigators and US officials have linked myriad operations to Chinese transnational crime groups. Wednesday’s move is part of a push by the second Trump administration on the issue. US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March seeking to combat cybercrime, fraud and predatory schemes against American citizens. The government also formed the Counter-Scams Contact Group with 12 other countries, aiming to coordinate enforcement, seizures and information sharing. China is not a member. The United Kingdom, which is part of the group, imposed sanctions against Xinbi in March. Beijing has also conducted its own crackdown on online fraud, collaborating with Southeast Asian governments and police to raid compounds and repatriate scam workers to China. Southeast Asia’s cyberscam industry has grown rapidly in recent years, with syndicates initially targeting Chinese speakers before expanding globally. Analysts said that criminal syndicates increasingly turned from targeting Chinese nationals to targeting Americans after Beijing’s 2023 crackdown in the region. The sanctions come after a number of US government reports examining the financial damage to Americans from Southeast Asia scams linked to Chinese criminal organisations. In a March report, the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Americans lost at least US$10 billion to Southeast Asia-based scams in 2024, with 2025 figures projected to be higher. Chinese criminal organisations are moving quickly to stay ahead of crackdowns by embracing advanced tech and exploiting crypto, according to the commission. The House Select Committee on China also released an investigation in May that found that the scam centres concentrated in Southeast Asia, particularly in Cambodia and Myanmar, were part of a criminal ecosystem linking cyber fraud, human trafficking and money laundering. “Rather than direct state control or any state-backed conspiracy, the report concludes that Chinese governance and enforcement patterns have enabled the growth of these criminal networks,” the Select Committee said. While America has strong enforcement mechanisms such as the strike force, it has also reduced funding for local civil society and investigative journalism, which are often vital for gathering on-the-ground evidence, said Jacob Sims, a visiting fellow at Harvard’s Asia Centre at an Asia Society Policy Institute event in July. After Trump returned to office in 2025, his administration effectively dismantled the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), formerly the world’s largest aid agency, including terminating nearly all USAID counter-trafficking projects. This was a huge blow since in Asia alone, USAID had obligated about US$164 million to such projects from 2001 to 2020.

title: US drone ban proposal to combat China’s dominance concerns American police, farmers
description: Fears in US surround banning of Chinese drones used for non-military purposes such as search and rescue, factory inspections and farming.
content: Greg Reverdiau, an Arizona-based drone trainer, said he saw something highly unusual for politically polarised America when he waded through public comments on a US government proposal to restrict foreign-made drones: a consensus. Reverdiau, the founder of Pilot Institute, which helps aviators obtain licences, said he reviewed over 3,800 comments submitted to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and estimates that about 98 per cent opposed the proposal or raised concerns about it. “Those numbers are pretty damning for the FCC as to what they’re trying to propose,” Reverdiau said. “I hope that they’re going to be making changes.” In July, the FCC outlined a plan prohibiting the continued importation and marketing of previously authorised foreign-produced drones, also known as unmanned aircraft systems, and critical components that meet a new definition of “military-grade”. The proposal, which the commission said was intended to address national security risks, comes amid a broader US effort to reduce reliance on Chinese drone technology and strengthen domestic supply chains. During the six-week public comment period, which ended in early September, a wide range of stakeholders spoke out against the rule, including law enforcement agencies, farmers, utilities and other commercial drone operators. The vast majority urged the federal government to alter, narrow or delay the proposal, warning it could have significant consequences for their operations. The key conflict is the breadth of the proposed definition of “military-grade”. Among the categories are drones equipped with thermal imaging or Lidar – technologies that sense heat and measure distances to objects using infrared and laser signals, respectively – widely used for non-military purposes, including search and rescue, factory inspections, mapping, and farming. The proposal reflects a central dilemma in Washington’s effort to counter China’s dominance of the commercial drone market: technologies with military applications are also increasingly embedded in everyday civilian operations. Public comments can shape a final rule by forcing agencies to address significant concerns, but the process does not require an agency to adopt commenters’ recommendations. With the Trump administration pursuing an aggressive regulatory agenda amid intensifying US-China rivalry, it remains less clear how much weight the FCC will ultimately give the unusually broad opposition to its proposal. Chinese companies, particularly DJI, have long dominated the US and global commercial drone market, offering relatively inexpensive and widely available aircraft. Some popular DJI drones commonly used by American operators can cost several hundred dollars or up to US$1,500, while comparable alternatives can be far more expensive and harder to obtain. The US government has increasingly sought to curb that dependence, first by placing foreign-produced drones on the FCC’s Covered List in December 2025, and then by proposing to restrict the continued import and marketing of previously authorised models that meet its new military-grade criteria. But the pushback has been substantial. Law enforcement, farmers speak out over proposed ban Among those commenting on the latest proposal was the National Sheriffs’ Association (NSA), which represents more than 3,000 county law enforcement officials across the US. The association raised concerns about public-safety agencies that already have drones and critical components that could fall under the FCC’s proposed definition of foreign-produced military-grade systems. Sheriffs increasingly use drones for search and rescue, crime-scene documentation, disaster response and other missions, the association said. It asked the FCC to clarify the rule’s scope and improve access to alternative equipment. It also sought an exemption for law-enforcement agencies if adequate alternatives are not available. “NSA recommends that the FCC add a carve-out for state, local, tribal, and territorial law-enforcement agencies,” the association said. A proposed weight threshold of 55lbs (25kg) was one particular concern, which the association said was useful for search-and-rescue operations, particularly when covering a large area. Other law-enforcement agencies, from the New York State Police to small-town departments nationwide, submitted similar comments. Farm groups raised similar concerns. The Agricultural Retailers Association and California Agricultural UAS Association were among those who defended drone use for spraying pesticides and other chemicals, reducing the need for larger aircraft or ground equipment. Other groups that might not immediately appear to have a stake in the debate included the American Mosquito Control Association, citing public-health purposes, and Reuters News & Media for newsgathering. DJI’s long fight with US government The comment record also included legal objections from Chinese drone manufacturers DJI and Autel Robotics, arguing that the FCC lacked statutory authority to impose the restrictions. The dispute is part of a broader and increasingly complicated legal battle between DJI and the US government. The FCC placed foreign-produced unmanned aircraft systems and critical components on its Covered List in December 2025. The designation blocked new models from receiving the FCC approval generally required before electronic devices can be imported, marketed or sold in the US, while allowing previously authorised drones to remain in use. The latest proposal would go further by cutting off the continued import and marketing of some previously authorised models. DJI has challenged the underlying FCC action in court. In the latest filing, DJI said the Covered List designation will cost the company US$1.5 billion annually. In August, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia gave DJI another opportunity to challenge its separate designation on a Pentagon list of companies allegedly linked to the Chinese military. DJI was first placed on the Pentagon’s Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies in 2022. The FCC’s drone restrictions are separate from the Pentagon designation, but the cases are part of a wider US effort to restrict Chinese technology on national-security grounds. Beijing has spoken out against Washington’s series of moves, calling them “discriminatory” targeting of Chinese businesses and an “overstretching” of the concept of national security. Supporters of proposal make voices heard Not everyone opposed the FCC proposal. The Washington-based Foundation for Defence of Democracies (FDD) argued that foreign-produced drones with military-grade capabilities pose a distinct national-security threat, particularly when they combine advanced sensors, heavy payloads, resilient communications or autonomous capabilities. The conservative think tank specifically pointed to agricultural drones, including DJI’s Agras T100, arguing that their ability to carry large payloads and dispense pesticides shows how civilian systems can have potential military applications. FDD also argued that thermal imaging and Lidar should be considered military-grade capabilities, saying they can provide valuable military intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities even when used in civilian settings. The FCC did not respond to a request for comment. The commission could issue a final decision any time after reviewing the comments. For Reverdiau, the consequences could extend well beyond large drone manufacturers. He said small businesses, including operators doing wedding and real-estate photography, could be particularly vulnerable if they can no longer purchase or replace the drones they currently rely on. “They would not have a drone available to purchase, which means that, well, they can close businesses,” he said.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong must plan for the population it wants to have
description: As the population ages, becomes more mobile and welcomes more non-locals, data-based planning is needed to inform and improve urban planning.
content: What kind of population is Hong Kong planning for? That is the question the chief executive’s policy address must tackle as the Northern Metropolis begins to take shape. Much more than just another new town, the Northern Metropolis is Hong Kong’s most consequential project for its next phase of development, expected to house 2.5 million residents and provide 650,000 jobs. The numbers are well known, but they are not the story. This population of 2.5 million will be like no other. The Northern Metropolis’ deep integration with Shenzhen and the Greater Bay Area means its residents will live, work, study and access services on both sides of the border. As Hong Kong’s population becomes increasingly dynamic and mobile, the Northern Metropolis should serve as the starting point for developing a citywide population strategy that aligns public policies with the realities of a cross-boundary lifestyle. Hong Kong’s demographic profile is undergoing substantial changes. Fertility remains exceptionally low, at 0.7 to 0.8 births per woman. Residents 65 years and older now account for about 24 per cent of the population. Meanwhile, the number of residents aged 15 to 34 years fell from 1.747 million in 2018 to 1.461 million last year – a decrease of 285,900 people, or 16.4 per cent, in seven years. At the same time, talent admission schemes since 2022 have brought a more varied population to Hong Kong. According to the latest Immigration Department figures released in March, the government has received about 600,000 applications and approved more than 410,000 as of end-February. Of these, about 300,000 approved cases involved mainland talent and nearly 110,000 involved holders of non-mainland passports. Many have entered finance, innovation and technology, information and communications technology, trade and other professional fields. These individuals should not be viewed merely as inputs into the labour market. They are new Hongkongers. They are parents considering where their children should study; they are tenants or potential homebuyers; they are users of medical, childcare, transport and community services. Their degree of commitment to Hong Kong will depend not only on the job or investment opportunities, but also on the quality of life the city offers. A researcher may work in the Northern Metropolis, collaborate with a laboratory in Shenzhen, and choose to live in a mature district such as Kowloon Tong, closer to family, established amenities or an international school. An entrepreneur from overseas may choose to establish client-facing or regional headquarters functions in Central while locating back office, research or technology operations in the Northern Metropolis, and choose to make West Kowloon home, attracted by the convenient access to high-speed rail services, the West Kowloon Cultural District and a more established urban living environment. These permutations show why Hong Kong’s planning must adapt to patterns of living and working that differ markedly from the traditional model of a relatively stable population concentrated on large housing estates. Our housing, education, healthcare, transport and community services must become more responsive to a population that is older yet more diverse, and increasingly mobile across districts and borders. Take education for example. Falling birth rates have put pressure on government and aided primary schools: public schools have been cutting Primary One classes for several years, including a record 126 cut in the 2026-27 school year. Yet enrolment in private and international schools has risen, to 87,220 in the 2025-26 year, up 12 per cent from three years ago. This does not mean Hong Kong should weaken its commitment to public education. It means the city must manage the increasing demand for private schools. The same is true of housing. Hong Kong must continue to meet the needs of lower-income households and public-housing applicants. But it must also provide a broad mix of housing types, locations and living environments to retain young families, skilled professionals and entrepreneurs. A city that attracts talent but cannot offer suitable homes, schools, healthcare and community facilities risks becoming a temporary stopover rather than a long-term home. Urban renewal in established districts is equally important. Hong Kong should continue to invest in our city’s liveability. Hong Kong needs a dynamic population policy planning mechanism that monitors, analyses and projects changes in population size, composition and behaviour. It must use these insights to inform urban planning decisions on land use, housing, education and other public services. If Hong Kong gets this right, the Northern Metropolis will not simply create opportunities for young graduates, professionals and investors. Under “one country, two systems”, it can also become the catalyst for a more liveable, inclusive and internationally competitive city – one designed not merely to accommodate people, but to keep them.

title: Brazil scraps tax on small parcels as Chinese platforms lose US and EU access
description: Congress cleared the measure days before it expired, handing Shein, Shopee and AliExpress a tariff-free lane into Latin America’s largest economy.
content: Brazil on Wednesday eliminated its federal import tax on small overseas parcels, moving in the opposite direction from US and European Union efforts to close a loophole that saw such Chinese retail giants as Shein and Temu expand rapidly. The elimination will hurt the country’s tax base, but the levy on lower value shirts, electronics, toys and kitchen gadgets ultimately proved too unpopular among Brazilians ahead of the October 4 presidential election, forcing Brasilia to back down. In an apparent attempt to minimise media exposure over a domestic scandal involving a bank recently closed by local authorities, which has implicated several of his allies, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has opted not to hold a signing ceremony for the legislation negotiated over weeks with Congress. But in a video posted by his campaign on social media last week, he commented on the initiative, stating that its approval was a matter of social justice. “The upper-middle class travels abroad, spends 2,000 dollars, and pays no tax. Why is it that when a person from the favelas … buys something for 50 dollars, they want to tax them?” “It is simply a matter of justice … so that the Brazilian people can buy the things they need without anyone bothering them,” the president said. Favelas are dense informal urban settlements often built on steep hillsides. The country received 28.36 million international parcels in June, the highest figure on record and 118 per cent more than a year earlier, according to the federal tax authority. June was the first full month without the tax, against a monthly average of 15.4 million in the first four months of the year. The law will effectively end a 20 per cent charge on orders worth up to US$50. Consumers have not paid it since May, when Lula scrapped it by provisional measure, an instrument that takes legal effect on publication but expires unless Congress ratifies it. The Senate approved the text on September 3 in a symbolic vote, hours after the lower house and five days before the deadline. Known in Brazil as the taxa das blusinhas, or the little-blouses tax, and abroad as de minimis, the nickname came about because the charge fell hardest on cheap clothing, phone cases and household goods bought by poorer consumers. The levy applied to orders placed on platforms certified under Remessa Conforme, a voluntary scheme whose members collect all taxes at checkout in exchange for faster customs clearance. Its largest members are the Asian-owned platforms Shein, Shopee and AliExpress. The South China Morning Post is owned by Alibaba, which also owns AliExpress. However, removing the federal charge does not make the parcels tax-free, because state value-added tax of 17 to 20 per cent still applies to every international order. The exemption also stops at the threshold, as orders between US$50.01 and US$3,000 still pay a federal rate of 60 per cent, with a US$30 discount on the tax owed. That means consumers pay US$30 in federal tax on a US$100 shipment: US$60 at the 60 per cent rate, minus the US$30 discount. Washington closed its door, Brasilia opened one The United States ended its US$800 de minimis exemption for goods from mainland China and Hong Kong in May last year, then suspended it for all origins in August. The European Union has moved to bring forward removal of its own 150 euro (US$175) threshold. The effect on the platforms was immediate, with Temu’s monthly users in the United States falling 30 per cent and Shein’s 12 per cent in the weeks after the change, according to Sensor Tower. In the second quarter of last year, 90 per cent of Temu’s 405 million monthly users were outside the United States, HSBC found, with growth concentrated in poorer markets including Latin America. Brazilian industry groups have argued for more than a year that inventory shut out of the United States would be rerouted to markets that stayed open. Customs authorities publish parcel volumes but no breakdown by origin, so the Chinese share of the June surge cannot be established officially. Brazil created the charge in August 2024, after retailers argued that untaxed parcels undercut local production. It raised about US$925 million in its first full year. Lula reversed course on May 12, five months before a presidential election in which he is seeking another term. The tax reached the statute book as an amendment to an unrelated bill on green vehicles, pushed by retail lobbies. Lula opposed it in public but signed the law in June 2024 without vetoing that clause, after his government negotiated the rate down from the 60 per cent Congress had wanted. Former finance minister Fernando Haddad said the president never wanted the tax and had threatened to veto it. The finance ministry estimated the exemption would cost about US$360 million this year and close to US$1.8 billion by 2028, at a time of fiscal weakness. Retailers say the field is tilted A joint congressional committee approved a report by Senator Leila Barros on September 2, adding the oversight industry had demanded as the price of passage. Barros contrasted the levy with the tax-free allowance of up to US$1,000 for returning travellers, saying that taxing parcels heavily while preserving it for inbound passengers protected wealthy consumers and burdened the poor. The finance ministry must assess the policy in November and every six months after, covering employment, competitiveness and revenue. Platforms must also trace foreign sellers and flag under-invoicing and the artificial splitting of orders. The National Confederation of Industry, which had lobbied Congress to reject extension of the under US$50 exemption measure, said the change favoured foreign manufacturers over Brazilian producers. The heaviest impact would fall on small firms, it said. The Brazilian Textile and Apparel Industry Association called the repeal deeply flawed. “It is unacceptable that Brazilian companies bear a heavy tax burden, very high real interest rates and regulatory costs,” it said, while foreign competitors were given better access to the same market. About 80 per cent of garments sold in Brazil fall below the US$50 threshold, it estimates. By the calculation of that association and the Brazilian Textile Retail Association, taxes levied at every stage of a domestic garment’s journey from factory to shop floor can reach 90 per cent of its value. Asian platforms selling the same item now remit only the 17 per cent state tax, the two said in a joint statement. AliExpress countered in May that the repeal broadened access to brands unavailable at home. Shein said it was updating its systems and Shopee said it was following the law. Temu has not commented at any stage. The Chinese embassy in Brasilia did not respond to a request for a comment. Brazil’s tax reform will bring the parcels back into the federal net from 2027, through a new contribution on cross-border purchases of any value. The exemption approved this week therefore has a defined end date.

title: South Park creators ‘rename’ show to ‘South America’ in jab at Trump
description: The US president has a penchant for renaming things, including a recent suggestion to call New Mexico ‘New America’ instead.
content: The creators of the long-running and enthusiastically insolent television show South Park aren’t known to be huge fans of US President Donald Trump. However, they’ve decided to adopt one of his ideas – in a way. They’re changing – at least for the moment – the name of the popular series, which just won the Emmy for outstanding animated programme. In a statement posted on the show’s social media page, creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone say they are “changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA”. The statement comes as Trump, escalating his trade war with Canada, has declared he’s renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States. The move by the two satirists, a week before the 29th season premiere of South Park – er, SOUTH AMERICA – also takes aim at Apple and Google, which have adopted Trump’s changes, as well as the show’s own parent company. Apple has relabelled Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, following cartographic competitor Google. “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA. We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount – a Skydance Capitulation.” The hugely successful South Park airs on Paramount-owned Comedy Central. Parker and Stone have taken aim at Paramount’s merger with Skydance. But in July 2025, Paramount announced a five-year renewal deal with Parker and Stone, including streaming rights for previous South Park seasons on Paramount+. During his second term, Trump has also signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” even though parts of it lie in international waters. Apple and Google maps also followed suit in that case. Also in line with Trump’s enthusiasm for renaming things – after America, or after himself – he suggested this week that New Mexico be renamed “New America”, though it was uncertain whether that was serious. He also arranged for the Kennedy Centre to add his name to its building, a move that has triggered much controversy. The decision to rename the show is not the only jab Parker and Stone have recently taken at Trump. “You finally got your Emmy,” the show posted on social media along with a cartoon depiction of the president – with his trousers down, surrounded by the show’s characters. A recent storyline on the show depicted Trump as romantically involved with Satan. Canada, too, has not gone unnoticed by the show. In 1999, its foray onto the big screen, South Park: Bigger, Longer and Uncut, depicted Canadians as scapegoats of a national parental movement to stop children from swearing – which they blamed on comedians from Canada named “Terrance and Phillip.” The movie was structured like a Broadway musical, and one of the key “show tunes” it presented was called “Blame Canada”. Its overall point: people can find a way to blame anyone for anything. “It seems that everything’s gone wrong since Canada came along,” one character sang. Other targets of the show’s sharp parody over the years have been Saddam Hussein, Tom Cruise, the soft drink Prime and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.

title: Ukraine, Moldova play down Norwegian claim Zelensky’s plane ‘almost hit’ by drone
description: Officials clarify airspace closure delayed Ukrainian leader’s flight to Oslo following Russian drone intrusion.
content: Ukraine and Moldova on Wednesday played down claims from Norway’s prime minister that a plane carrying President Volodymyr Zelensky was almost hit by a drone as it flew to Oslo. Jonas Gahr Store told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK that Zelensky’s plane was “almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova”. But a source in the Ukrainian presidency described the claim that Zelensky was at risk as “exaggerated”. “It was an alert in Moldova when a Russian (drone) entered Moldovan and Romanian airspace,” the source told Agence France-Presse. In Chisinau, government spokesman Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon just after 4.30pm local time due to a Russian drone that entered from the direction of Ukraine. “The airspace was closed to protect aircraft flying over Moldova at the time: three departures and four arrivals were delayed as a result,” he added. “After 1720, the authorities confirmed that the drone had come down and exploded … some 160km (100 miles) from Chisinau International Airport. “Flight restrictions were then lifted. For the same reason, the plane of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky took off … later than scheduled.” Zelensky arrived in Oslo on Tuesday evening and held talks with Store, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide on Norwegian military aid, including air-defence support, and civilian assistance. On Wednesday, he joined a host of other foreign dignitaries at the funeral of Norway’s King Harald, who died on August 28, aged 89. Zelensky left Norway afterwards, headed for Canada and talks with leaders there, Store told NRK.

title: Trump offers new timeline on Iran war: end after US midterm elections
description: US president claims Tehran is trying to influence vote as he warns against activity at underground nuclear site.
content: US President Donald Trump said he expected the war with Iran to end after the November US midterm elections and threatened again to attack a site associated with the Islamic Republic’s nuclear programme after the two sides launched their biggest wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the six-month-old war. Tensions in the region were high, with Saudi civil defence authorities on Thursday issuing emergency alerts in ‌the southwest city of Khamis Mushait for the fourth time in 24 hours, as clashes flared with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis. Brent crude prices hovered above US$100 a barrel as supply routes through both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea remained heavily disrupted. Iran said it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers, the latest in a series of tit-for-tat strikes that have signalled scant chance of an imminent end to hostilities. The war and subsequent increase in fuel prices have helped drive Trump’s popularity to record lows. The president said Tehran was trying ⁠to influence the November US midterm elections, which will determine whether his Republican Party retains control of Congress. “I think war is going to end immediately after the ‌election because they can’t hold out any longer. They’re desperate to try and affect the election,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. Trump has previously set deadlines for the war to end and repeatedly threatened escalations while leaving room for talks. In a social media post in August, he declared “Mission Accomplished” in Iran - a statement echoing former president George W. Bush’s premature 2003 declaration regarding the Iraq war. The Wall Street Journal reported later that top White House advisers, including Vice-President ‌J.D. Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, have privately warned Trump that the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency, ⁠which ends in January 2029. Reuters could ⁠not immediately verify the report. Trump also said the US may hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes near Iran’s damaged Natanz uranium enrichment facility. “We notice there’s a little ‌activity at Pickaxe. I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard,” Trump said in a speech at the midterm Republican convention. Trump has been threatening strikes on ‌Pickaxe Mountain since ‌at least mid-July. The US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February partly due to concerns over Tehran’s nuclear programme. Iran says its nuclear activities are ‌for peaceful purposes. In recent weeks Washington had cited increasing success guiding tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of oil supplies before the ⁠war. But a resumption of fighting this month appears to have set back any such gradual reopening. Just seven vessels transited the strait on Wednesday, half the 10-day average, ⁠preliminary ship-tracking data showed on Thursday. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen has also escalated in the past few days, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East. At least 73 people were wounded in four southern Saudi cities, including Khamis Mushait, ‌in recent Houthi attacks on the world’s ‌largest oil exporter, the Saudi-led coalition said on Tuesday. The militant group said it attacked an airbase in the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait and oil infrastructure in nearby cities in one of the biggest attacks on Saudi Arabia since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in February. Saudi civil defence authorities issued an all-clear on Thursday following another emergency alert declared in Khamis Mushait. Additional reporting by Tribune News Service

title: Nuclear agency board refers Iran to UN Security Council for first time in 20 years
description: IAEA remains blocked from key sites damaged during June 2025 military strikes by the US and Israel.
content: The UN atomic watchdog’s board on Wednesday reported Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years, citing it for failure to cooperate in a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites. Western officials suspect that the traces could provide evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Iran says that it is not pursuing nuclear weapons, and that its programme is entirely peaceful. Reporting Iran to the Security Council opens the country to possible sanctions and asset freezes, though such punitive measures are unlikely because Iran’s allies Russia and China hold veto power on the panel. Twenty-three countries on the International Atomic Energy Agency’s 35-member board of governors voted for Wednesday’s resolution at IAEA headquarters in Vienna. China, Russia and Niger opposed it, while eight countries abstained and one did not vote as it was in arrears, according to diplomats who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the outcome of the closed-door vote. The resolution was put forward by the United States, Britain, France and Germany. The diplomatic move has been under consideration since June 2025, when the IAEA board found Iran officially in non-compliance with its non-proliferation obligations because of Tehran’s lack of cooperation in the investigation. Iran’s ambassador to the UN in Vienna, Reza Najafi, rejected the resolution, describing it as a “political tool” and saying that it ruined confidence in the IAEA’s “independence, impartiality and credibility”. He suggested that compliance with any obligation to allow UN inspections of nuclear sites inside Iran was, in any case, impossible at the moment because of the country’s continuing war with the US and Israel. The US this week destroyed five Iranian oil tankers and Tehran hit back at American targets in Jordan, the latest burst of back-and-forth strikes that have lurched the sides back towards open hostilities in a more than six-month-old war. The draft resolution, which was seen by Associated Press, requested IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to report the agency’s concerns “to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations, in accordance with the relevant provisions of the IAEA Statute”. The resolution also reiterated its call upon Iran “to urgently remedy its non-compliance” with previous agreements and to take steps deemed necessary by the IAEA to assure “the non-diversion of nuclear material”. Since Israel and the US struck Iran’s nuclear sites during the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran has not given IAEA inspectors access to nuclear sites that were affected by the strikes. The IAEA also has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the June bombing. Najafi said that air strikes by the US and Israel made safe access for inspectors to Iran’s nuclear sites “materially impossible”. He said that Iran has “neither stopped nor suspended its safeguards obligations”, adding that “performance is currently impossible under continuing military operations and persistent threats”. Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi echoed that sentiment in an post on X. “They attack Iran’s safeguarded nuclear facilities, disrupt the normal verification process, and then use that very disruption as a pretext to pass a resolution at the IAEA Board of Governors,” he said. According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9kg (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60 per cent purity – a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent. That stockpile could allow Iran to build as many as 10 nuclear bombs, should it decide to weaponise its programme, IAEA chief Grossi warned in an interview last year with AP. He said that it does not mean that Iran has such a weapon.

title: Trump gave US$45,000 cash to close aide Natalie Harp and others
description: The payments raise ethics concerns because federal employees are ‌generally barred from receiving compensation beyond their salaries.
content: US President Donald Trump gave tens of thousands of dollars in cash gifts last year to executive assistant Natalie Harp and three other close aides working in the West Wing, according to financial disclosures released by the White House. The payments raised ethics concerns because federal employees are ‌generally barred by statute from receiving compensation beyond their government salaries. Harp, communications adviser Margo Martin and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris each received US$45,000, described in their disclosures as “Cash Gift for Holidays”. The payments were equivalent to roughly one-third of the aides’ federal salaries of US$150,000 per year, according to the White House annual personnel report to Congress. Walt Nauta, another aide who works as the director of Oval Office operations, received US$20,000 in cash, the disclosures show. His annual ⁠compensation is US$175,000. The Washington Post first reported the gifts on Tuesday. “A White House staffer is not your Fifth Avenue doorman,” Richard ‌W. Painter, a law professor who served as the chief White House ethics lawyer between 2005 and 2007 under President George W. Bush, said in a social media post. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said the gifts complied with ethics rules. “The president has a long-standing ⁠practice of giving Christmas gifts ⁠to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector,” Ingle said in ‌a statement on Wednesday. “The gifts at issue here have nothing to do with any of these individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal ‌and ethical standards.” Harp ‌and Nauta are among Trump’s most trusted aides, with near-constant access to the president during long days on the road ‌or at the White House. Harp drew public scrutiny last month when The Washington Post reported that she and Nauta were ⁠in a catering truck that secretly moved Trump to a flight he took in July from Turkey to the UK ⁠amid concerns about potential threats from Iran. Harp exercises control over Trump’s Truth Social account, posting on his behalf and helping draft social media statements, according to a person familiar with her role. Colleagues sometimes call her the “human ‌printer” as she provides often favourable news ‌coverage to Trump from a portable printer that she carries. Nauta, a former White House valet, faced accusations from federal prosecutors of helping Trump hide top-secret documents that the Republican president took when he completed his first term at the White House in 2021. Nauta pleaded not guilty, and the case was dropped after Trump returned to office.

title: AI researcher quits Anthropic over superintelligence fears: ‘gambling with our lives’
description: Jacob Coxon says he and others building AI believe it could ‘kill us all by the end of the decade’, as firms race to build advanced models.
content: An artificial intelligence researcher who left OpenAI to join Anthropic has decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop AI models capable of self-improvement. Jacob Coxon, 27, spent the past three years pretraining AI models, first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach. Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data. “Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said on Tuesday. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a social media post. “This is not a marketing stunt,” he added. Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence. Anthropic safety executive Evan Hubinger backed up Coxon. “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” he said on social media, adding that he estimated that risk at more than 10 per cent over the next decade. Hubinger said Anthropic is “trying its best”, but does not yet have a plan to ensure an AI system that surpasses human capabilities would obey its creators. He said there was a “low” risk of that happening with current models. Coxon’s resignation comes as Anthropic prepares for its market debut, following a summer marked by unauthorised hacks carried out by AI tools during testing. The two companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. AI leaders say so-called “recursive self-improvement”, a stage where AI systems could essentially design and train the next generation of AI with little human involvement, is drawing near. Coxon considers Anthropic’s efforts genuine but said he believes no company can responsibly develop an AI that surpasses humans without government intervention or a coordinated slowdown. “At Anthropic, the stakes are well understood, but they are locked in a race to get there first – they believe no one else will act responsibly, so they must do it themselves, despite the risk,” he said. In February, Anthropic removed a pledge from its safety charter to halt the development of its models if it failed to control their risks. It argued that if it unilaterally paused its work, its less cautious rivals would dominate the industry, making it less safe overall. At the end of July, more than 1,000 tech industry employees, including Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei, called on Washington to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems. OpenAI halted training of its latest models for two weeks in August before resuming it under tighter controls. On Sunday, OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, called for “extreme caution”. “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world,” he said in a blog post. AI models are not regulated by federal law in the US. In September, Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic congressman Greg Casar introduced a bill seeking to suspend AI development until a federal regulator is created.

title: Tributes flow in as Hong Kong mourns Tung Chee-hwa, pioneering first leader
description: Former business magnate faced difficult crisis during tenure, but officials and former colleagues praise his compassion and ‘brave leadership’.
content: Hong Kong is mourning the death of Tung Chee-hwa, the city’s first leader after its return to Chinese sovereignty and a respected elder statesman, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89. Tung was surrounded by his family when he “passed away peacefully” at 9.57pm, according to state news agency Xinhua. Tributes and messages of grief poured in on Wednesday from across Hong Kong and mainland China, as well as from overseas, with top officials, politicians, business leaders and others praising his pioneering role as the first steward of the “one country, two systems” policy under which the city would be administered after the end of British colonial rule in 1997. They remembered him for steering the city through its uncertain transitional years and laying the groundwork for its post-handover prosperity, and hailed his later role as an elder statesman who worked tirelessly to help improve US-China relations. Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong issued a statement, describing Tung as a “close friend of the Communist Party of China”, an “outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’” and a “renowned patriot”, while the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office sent a condolence message to his wife, Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping. The offices said Tung had made “major historic contributions” to Hong Kong’s smooth return to China, while crediting him with tackling complex political, economic and social challenges during the formative years of the special administrative region. They also highlighted his work after leaving office, saying he had continued to support successive chief executives and governments, promote closer ties between Hong Kong and the mainland and use his extensive international connections to foster exchanges between China and the rest of the world. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said Tung’s leadership had made “exemplary contributions” to Hong Kong’s smooth return to Chinese rule and the implementation of the governing principle, as well as the Basic Law. “With visionary foresight, he instituted mechanisms to promote economic and trade ties and coordinated development between Hong Kong and the mainland, laying a solid foundation for Hong Kong’s enduring competitiveness,” he said. Tung’s other successors also paid tribute to his role in shaping post-handover Hong Kong. Former chief executive Carrie Lam Cheng Yuet-ngor said Tung had led the city into a new era with “deep patriotism, vast international experience, and a humble approach to governance”, describing his contribution as historic and enduring. Leung Chun-ying, Lam’s predecessor as city leader, said Tung had overseen the establishment of the special administrative region and its government, leading to “Hong Kong people administering Hong Kong” with a high degree of autonomy. “Mr Tung was benevolent and won people over with reason, serving as a role model for our generation,” he said. Donald Tsang Yam-kuen, who succeeded Tung in 2005, remembered him as an approachable and broad-minded leader with vision, saying he had worked relentlessly to guide Hong Kong through its transition after the handover. Tung, who was a shipping magnate before he entered politics, was picked to be Hong Kong’s first chief executive in 1996 after securing 320 votes from the 400-member Selection Committee, defeating former Chief Justice Ti-liang Yang and businessman Peter Woo Kwong-ching. He was officially appointed by the State Council and took office on July 1, 1997. The city’s stock and property markets were bullish at the time, only for the Asian financial crisis to strike months later and send asset prices tumbling as unemployment rose. Tung’s tenure was marked by difficult policy choices and successive crises, with former officials saying some of his decisions then had taken on a different significance with the passage of time. Tung’s ambitious pledge to build 85,000 homes a year became one of the most controversial policies of his administration, drawing opposition from property developers. Amid a worsening fall in home prices and the Asian financial crisis, the target was quietly dropped. In the wake of the crisis, Tung’s administration took the extraordinary step in August 1998 of intervening directly in the stock and futures markets, using HK$118 billion from the Exchange Fund to buy blue-chip shares and counter speculative attacks on the Hong Kong dollar and equities. The move was fiercely debated because of Hong Kong’s traditional commitment to free-market principles, but officials later credited the intervention with helping restore financial stability. The government subsequently launched the Tracker Fund of Hong Kong in 1999 to progressively dispose of the shares it had accumulated. Political pressure intensified on Tung in the middle of his second term in 2003, when Hong Kong faced an outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) and the government attempted to press ahead with national security legislation required under Article 23 of the Basic Law. The bill was eventually shelved after an estimated 500,000 people marched on July 1 that year, amid opposition concerns about suppression of civil liberties and mounting dissatisfaction over livelihood issues. But 2003 also marked the beginning of a much deeper phase of economic integration between Hong Kong and the mainland. The city and Beijing signed the Closer Economic Partnership Arrangement, giving Hong Kong preferential access to mainland markets, while the Individual Visit Scheme opened the door for more mainland residents to travel independently to the city. Both measures helped revive Hong Kong’s hobbled tourism sector and economy as it battled for recovery from the Sars epidemic, and continue to be vital to Hong Kong’s economy more than two decades later. Tung later acknowledged the shortcomings of his administration. In January 2005, two months before his resignation, he said the government had at times failed to sufficiently understand public concerns and had been indecisive in responding to emergencies. But several former officials and political figures said on Wednesday that his record deserved to be judged over a longer horizon. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said Tung showed “brave leadership” during the Asian financial crisis, while former executive councillor Bernard Chan said he hoped history would give Tung “a fair assessment”. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Tung was a compassionate and upright person whose kind-hearted image often won over public sentiment and facilitated a smooth handover. As head of the Central Policy Unit under Tung’s administration, he also said Tung had a strategic mind and made many long-term development proposals, with the Principal Officials Accountability System the most significant among them. “Because he was in the shipping business, he travelled around the world and was acquainted with many foreign political figures. This broadened his vision and enabled him to approach issues with strategic thinking,” Lau added. However, he noted that Tung’s business background often diminished his ability to secure public support for his policies. “On many occasions he was unable to build social consensus, could not withstand the pressure from opposing forces, and lacked sufficient backing within the civil service,” he said. After resigning as chief executive in March 2005, citing health reasons, Tung went on to assume a prominent role at the national level and increasingly came to be regarded as an elder statesman in Hong Kong, serving as a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top political advisory body, and remaining involved in exchanges between Hong Kong, the mainland and the international community. He founded Our Hong Kong Foundation in 2014, bringing together figures from different sectors to conduct policy research and promote areas including innovation, culture and Hong Kong’s integration into the country’s national development. Tung also founded the China-United States Exchange Foundation in 2008, through which he promoted dialogue between Beijing and Washington, building on relationships with senior American political figures developed over several decades. He was known to have close ties with the family of former US President George H.W. Bush, and was credited with helping to mediate tensions between Beijing and Washington over the years. The George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations offered its “sincere condolences”, saying Tung’s efforts to deepen understanding between the two countries “was a cause that was very personal” that showed “in his warmth, graciousness, magnanimity, optimism, boundless energy and indefatigable spirit”. Tung largely withdrew from public view in his final years. He was last seen publicly in July 2021, when he attended the premiere of a film marking the centenary of the founding of the Communist Party of China. His office confirmed in October that year that he had undergone surgery for an undisclosed condition and was recuperating at home. Among Tung’s best-known sayings was his belief that Hong Kong’s fortunes were inseparable from those of the country: “If Hong Kong is good, China will be good. If China is good, Hong Kong will be even better.” More than two decades after he left the city’s top job, the breadth of tributes on Wednesday reflected the enduring place he had come to occupy in Hong Kong’s political history, as the man tasked with leading the city through the uncertain first years of a new era.

title: Police widen criminal probe into Reform UK over foreign funding claims
description: The party has denied wrongdoing and says it will ‘fully cooperate’ with the police investigation.
content: British police said on Wednesday a criminal investigation into the populist Reform UK party would be widened to include allegations made in a documentary that officials planned to break electoral law on foreign funding. Reform, led by veteran Brexit campaigner Nigel Farage, denied any wrongdoing ‌and a spokesman for the party said it would “fully cooperate” with the investigation. Farage, under investigation by a parliamentary watchdog about earlier donations, was forced to sack two of his closest aides last week, after the undercover investigation was aired. It showed two senior officials in Reform – then head of policy James Orr and Farage’s former right-hand man, Dan Jukes – speaking about funding with a supposed US businessman and his British-based son, including ⁠conversations about a payment for three opinion polls commissioned by the party. On Friday, Reform launched an internal investigation ‌and denied the allegations, saying the party had been the victim of a hoax. Farage described some of the comments as little more than “loose pub talk”. London’s Metropolitan Police said in a ‌statement its detectives had assessed a number of “reports relating to donations and polling involving a political ⁠party” and had decided “there are ⁠potential offences requiring investigation”. “The potential offences are similar in nature to matters already under investigation by the Met’s Special Enquiry Team relating to donations ‌made to the same political party. As a result, these matters will form part of that ongoing investigation.” London’s police said in July they were investigating ‌Reform for potential ‌offences under laws governing donations to political parties, which could include concealment of the source of funding or ‌giving false information to the treasurer of a party. The widening of the criminal investigation piles pressure on Reform, ⁠whose commanding lead in opinion polls has faltered over the funding allegations, including a £5 million (US$6.77 million) gift to Farage, focus ⁠of the parliamentary probe. Reform’s annual conference last week, when Farage wanted to set a vision for the party’s first 100 days in power if it wins the next national election, was overshadowed by the ‌undercover probe, conducted by investigative group ‌Verbatim. Instead of talking about a national election, which must be held by mid-2029 at the latest, Reform spent almost equal amounts of time either vigorously denying the accusations or trying to ignore them. “We won’t be commenting further while a live investigation is under way,” the Reform spokesman said.

title: Indonesia’s wildfire emissions surge to world’s highest, data shows
description: The country is battling what authorities say is its most intense wildfire season in 11 years.
content: Indonesia is facing ⁠a surge in emissions from wildfires burning through parched stretches of forest and peatland on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, with carbon dioxide readings currently the highest in the world, data has shown. Fire emissions from Indonesia from September 1 to September 7 reached 19.7 million metric tons, overtaking Russia this week and making up more than a third of the global total, according to Fire Emissions Watch, a portal developed by the European Union’s Copernicus climate ‌monitoring service, on Wednesday. Indonesia is one of the world’s most fire-prone countries, but as “super-El Nino” weather conditions drive up temperatures and cause punishing droughts, the country is battling what authorities say is its most intense wildfire season in 11 years. “We do expect to see some fires across the region at this time of year, but with El Nino, it clearly just gives a big enhancement to them,” said Mark Parrington, senior scientist at the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service in Bonn. “It’s much drier, it’s hotter, and when there’s ignition, these fires burn in a far more extreme way.” From September 1 to 7, fire emission intensity exceeded 1,500kg/sq km, more than 10 times the ⁠Russian level, with the highest concentrations in Kalimantan in Indonesia’s part of Borneo and eastern parts of Sumatra, Copernicus data showed on Wednesday. Emissions were 273 per cent higher than the seasonal average, though still ‌lower than the 21.7 million tons emitted in the same week of 2015, when Indonesia was battling similarly intense El Nino conditions. Among the hardest hit areas has been the city of Pontianak in West Kalimantan, where the air quality index was 394 on Wednesday, according to Swiss air ‌quality monitoring firm IQAir. A reading of 300 is considered hazardous. Indonesia’s environment ministry told Reuters in a statement that it viewed the hazardous air quality readings ⁠in Kalimantan and elsewhere “with concern”. It said it ⁠was monitoring Copernicus’s data, but added it “does not directly reflect air quality conditions in a specific area”, and other factors needed to be taken into account. From January to July this year, fires burned ‌around 202,000 hectares (780 square miles) of Indonesian land, about a third the amount over the same period in 2015, said Nisa Novita of the environmental group YKAN, which helps communities tackle fires. “However, August data are estimated to show a significant increase ‌of around ‌600,000 hectares, particularly in Kalimantan, Sumatra and South Papua,” she said. Indonesia lost a total of 2.6 million hectares to fire in the whole of 2015, an area bigger than Wales. The ‌number of recorded hotspots from August 1 to September 8 reached 13,443, compared with 9,454 over the same period of 2015, according to Indonesian forest ministry monitoring platform Sipongi, based on ⁠data from Nasa’s Terra and Aqua satellites. A record monthly high for hotspots was recorded in October 2015, Sipongi data showed. Fire Emissions Watch uses satellite observations to estimate concentrations of particulate ⁠matter, volatile organic compounds, greenhouse gases and other fire-fuelled pollutants, but Parrington said it could actually be underestimating the extent of the problem. “One of the aspects with peat fires is if they’re burning at low temperatures or underground, they’d be below the detection limit of the sensors, which means we’re not actually seeing them,” he said. Studies ‌have shown that fires in Indonesia in ‌2015 produced more emissions per day than the whole of the EU, and caused more than 100,000 excess deaths throughout Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. “We have to remember that this is still the beginning of the season, and we expect the fires to continue and the emissions to keep increasing, potentially through to the end of October, which is what we saw in 2015,” Parrington said. “In two months we’ll know how extreme this year has been, but the early indications are that it is at pace, if not slightly above those previous El Nino years.”

title: Tung Chee-hwa hailed as visionary leader who helped build US-China relations
description: US consulate, the George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations and former city leader Donald Tsang highlight his pivotal diplomatic legacy.
content: Hong Kong’s first chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, who died on Tuesday, has been lauded as “one of the greatest movers in China-US relations”, with a foundation established by Neil Bush, a former American president’s son, praising Tung’s “profound contributions” to deepening ties between the two nations. The US consulate and former city leader Donald Tsang Yam-kuen also praised Tung’s work in strengthening ties between the United States and Hong Kong, paving the way for deeper business links and high-level dialogue in the early years following the 1997 handover. In response to the South China Morning Post’s queries, the George H.W. Bush Foundation for US-China Relations on Wednesday issued a statement extending sincere condolences over Tung’s death and commending his “decades of visionary leadership” in Sino-US relations. The statement highlighted Tung’s warmth, graciousness, magnanimity, optimism, boundless energy and indefatigable spirit. “Mr Tung will be sorely missed, but his deep and positive impact on the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship will long endure,” the statement read. The US Consulate General in Hong Kong and Macau noted that Tung “played a pivotal role in strengthening the relationship between the US and Hong Kong during a period of profound transition, both before and after the 1997 handover”. “His contributions to that relationship leave a lasting legacy, and he will be remembered for his dedication to Hong Kong and its people,” it said in a statement. Tsang, who served as chief secretary under Tung, said his predecessor drew on his deep network of contacts in American political and business circles to open new opportunities for bilateral trade and high-level official dialogue between Hong Kong and the US. Tung, who cultivated notable relationships with several former American presidents, remains the first and only chief executive to meet a sitting US leader in Washington, and for many years served as a vital bridge connecting Beijing, Hong Kong and Washington. Just two months after the city’s return to Chinese sovereignty, Tung visited the US and was received by then-president Bill Clinton. He later arranged Clinton’s visit to Hong Kong in 1998, still the only instance of a sitting US president visiting the city. In 2001, Tung led another delegation to the US to meet then-president George W. Bush. The connection between the two families stretches back to the seventies, when Tung’s father, shipping magnate Tung Chao-yung, formed a personal friendship with George H.W. Bush, then America’s de facto ambassador in Beijing. At the time, the younger Tung actively lobbied American political and business leaders in support of China’s accession to the World Trade Organization. The SCMP previously reported that Tung also worked behind the scenes to support Beijing’s successful bid to host the 2008 Olympics by encouraging the US to maintain a neutral stance. Three years after leaving office in 2005, Tung founded the China-United States Exchange Foundation (CUSEF), a Hong Kong-based non-profit organisation aimed at helping Beijing and Washington recognise and develop areas of common interest. As a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, the country’s top political advisory body, between 2005 and 2023, he remained a prominent figure in exchanges between Beijing and Washington. In 2012, when China’s leader Xi Jinping was still vice-president, Tung took part in events surrounding Xi’s visit to the US, including meetings with former senior American officials. In 2015, he was invited to the White House state dinner during Xi’s state visit. Tung’s deep relationship with the US began early in life. After graduating from the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom in 1960, the 23-year-old moved to America to work for General Electric in Massachusetts. In 1965, Tung joined the New York office of his family’s shipping business before returning to Hong Kong in 1969. James Chau, president of the CUSEF, noted that those formative years in America laid the foundation for the wide networks Tung later developed across politics, business, academia, civil society and journalism on both sides of the Pacific. More importantly, Chau said, they gave Tung a deep understanding of the country. “He got married there, he started his family there, he had his first job there. In a sense, he went from being a young person to a young man in America. It was that place where he really transitioned into the person that he became,” he said. Chau said Tung long believed that Hong Kong’s distinctive value lay in its close links with the US and other economies, and such a consequential relationship could not be sustained alone through formal diplomacy. Under Tung’s leadership, Chau said the CUSEF brought together global figures including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates and former US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, to engage with Chinese counterparts. The foundation proposed measures later adopted by Beijing, including 10-year multiple-entry travel visas for Americans and the establishment of intellectual property courts, steps Chau described as having a profound impact on Sino-US relations. “I do not know anybody who comes close to him, yesterday, today, or even tomorrow,” Chau said. “He was one of the greatest movers in China-US relations.” Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, highlighted Tung’s contributions through “Track 2 diplomacy” – unofficial exchanges involving non-government figures from both sides – in improving Sino-US relations. He said Beijing valued Tung’s extensive American and global connections and appointed him to the CPPCC leadership in part to strengthen people-to-people exchanges. He added that the CUSEF consistently supported research and diplomatic dialogues intended to constructively influence US policy on China.

title: Japan’s China-facing military build-up confronts labour, budget and political limits
description: Amid ambitious transformation driven by risk it could be drawn into a Taiwan conflict, Tokyo tackles tough obstacles at home, analysts say.
content: The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the third of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines the various challenges confronting Japan in its bid to expand its military. Driven by the growing risk that a conflict over Taiwan could draw Tokyo into a high-intensity confrontation with Beijing, Japan is pursuing its most ambitious military transformation since World War II. Tokyo is acquiring long-range missiles, embracing drones and expanding defence partnerships stretching from Canberra to London. Yet, analysts say some of the toughest obstacles to the transformation may lie at home. As Tokyo prepares to revise its strategic security documents by year’s end, its historic military build-up must contend with growing constraints. These include a shrinking pool of military recruits, an ageing population, mounting fiscal pressures, an industrial base struggling to expand and lingering questions over how far the Japanese public would support the use of its ascendant military power. Together, the pressures raise a fundamental question about the next phase of Japan’s transformation: not simply how much military capability Tokyo can acquire but whether the country has the economic, human and political resources to sustain it, especially if a prolonged regional conflict were to erupt over Taiwan. According to Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, acquiring the hardware is only one part of building an effective force. “Japan may acquire increasingly sophisticated weapons without necessarily developing the manpower and institutional capacity required to operate them effectively,” Matsuoka said. She warned that the mismatch could create a “hardware-capability gap”, with sophisticated equipment outpacing the ability of Japan’s Self-Defence Forces (SDF) to translate it into operational capacity. Understaffed, outdated The first test is therefore whether Japan can find enough people to operate the force it is building. The country’s declining birth rate is shrinking the pool of potential recruits while a tight labour market forces the SDF to compete with private employers. Recruitment improved in the 2025 financial year, but the SDF still had only 217,701 personnel against an authorised 247,154 at the end of March – a staffing rate of 88.1 per cent. Defence ministry projections released in February suggested that, without corrective measures, personnel numbers could fall from about 220,000 to about 130,000 by 2045. Tokyo is responding with better pay and working conditions as it turns to uncrewed systems and automation to do more with fewer personnel. But the ministry itself acknowledges that strengthening recruitment and retention alone will not be enough. The shortages could become particularly consequential in a contingency over Taiwan. Japan’s southwestern islands lie close to the potential conflict zone and the SDF could face demands to defend Japanese territory while maintaining operations under sustained pressure. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Filling the ranks, however, is only part of the problem for Tokyo. The force itself may also have to change. Rintaro Inoue, a research fellow specialising in Japanese defence strategy and industry at the Institute of Geoeconomics as well as a PhD candidate at Keio University, said the challenge went beyond recruitment. “In order to deter China from initiating a conflict in the region, the [Japan Self-Defence Force] will need to significantly change its force composition,” he said. For instance, preparing for high-end warfare could require Japan’s Maritime Self-Defence Force to shift resources from some existing vessels and crewed patrol aircraft towards Aegis destroyers, uncrewed vessels and sensors, Inoue said. Meanwhile the Ground Self-Defence Force may need to reduce its reliance on infantry, tanks and artillery as it expands missile forces, he added. Internal organisational politics, resistance from local governments concerned about the economic impact of base closures and continuing demand for disaster-relief operations could make such changes difficult. The structural problems are emerging even as the amount of money Tokyo is committing to defence keeps climbing.
