The defence ministry has requested a record ¥8.9 trillion (US$55.7 billion) for the financial year 2027 – its 15th consecutive annual increase in defence requests. In addition, officials have indicated that the figure could ultimately rise to about ¥10 trillion once the revision of Japan’s three main security documents is completed by the end of the year. But spending more does not necessarily mean Japan can buy proportionately more military capability. Matsuoka said the financial burden should not be measured merely by the initial cost of acquiring weapons. New systems bring long-term spending on personnel, maintenance, training, ammunition, infrastructure, upgrades and eventual replacement. Once incorporated into the SDF, such capabilities could also become politically and strategically complicated to give up, potentially locking Japan into “a long-term cycle of defence spending that is increasingly difficult to sustain”, she said. Japan says it has already reached its goal of spending about 2 per cent of gross domestic product on defence ahead of schedule. But sustaining that level, let alone substantially exceeding it, could prove harder. High debt, weak yen Darren Tay, head of Asia-Pacific country risk at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said the 2 per cent level itself was affordable but would become more difficult to sustain as Japan’s enormous stock of government debt was refinanced at higher interest rates. National debt servicing is budgeted at ¥31.3 trillion in financial year 2026 and, under one finance ministry scenario, would reach ¥41.3 trillion by financial year 2029. Tay identified debt servicing as the biggest economic constraint on Japan’s defence ambitions, ahead of demographics or procurement inflation. BMI expects the government’s effective borrowing cost to rise to about 2.4 per cent by 2035 as older, near-zero-yield bonds mature and are refinanced at higher rates. That would force defence, social-security spending and interest payments to compete for the same government revenue, Tay said. At the same time, the weak yen is eroding the defence budget’s purchasing power. Much of the equipment Tokyo buys from the US is priced in dollars, meaning depreciation raises its cost in yen. According to Tay, procurement planning underpinning the five-year build-up had assumed an exchange rate of about ¥108 to the dollar. Moving towards defence spending of 3.5 per cent of GDP would therefore be of a “different order of difficulty”, Tay said, while reaching 5 per cent would require painful trade-offs with other public spending and was unrealistic without an acute geopolitical crisis directly involving Japan. Fiscal constraints could thus force Japan to scale back what it can afford to buy. “The more likely outcome is not a further rise in the budget but quietly accepting what is effectively a smaller defence budget,” Tay added. “Japan ends up buying less rather than paying whatever it takes.” Inoue framed the dilemma differently. Given Japan’s security environment, Tokyo might have little choice but to spend more, he said, making the question whether the country was willing to bear the cost. Sustaining a prolonged conflict The Sanae Takaichi administration has sought to ease the burden by promoting a “virtuous cycle between defence and the economy”, including investment in dual-use technologies and expanded weapons exports that could lower unit costs. Inoue described the objective as optimistic, saying the actual savings were likely to be limited. Even if Tokyo finds the money to buy the force it wants, sustaining it through a prolonged conflict poses another challenge. Japan’s defence industry has historically been structured to supply the SDF in relatively small quantities rather than replenish weapons at wartime rates. Companies have withdrawn from parts of the sector, while limited production runs have contributed to high unit costs and made it harder to maintain suppliers and skilled workers. Tokyo is trying to reverse that decline by improving conditions for contractors, attracting new entrants and expanding weapons exports, potentially increasing production volumes and spreading costs across larger orders. Nevertheless, Tay said, the economic benefits would be “real but modest” this decade. “The bigger pay-off is keeping Japan’s industry technologically capable and its equipment supply secure”, rather than substantially relieving pressure on the defence budget, he added. Japan is also expanding ammunition production, shoring up supply chains and pursuing joint production with allies and partners. Still, the defence ministry has acknowledged shortcomings in its ability to sustain operations, prioritising ammunition, fuel, equipment availability and hardened facilities. Building stockpiles before a crisis is one challenge; replacing missiles, repairing damaged equipment and maintaining production as fighting continues is another. And while hardware can be manufactured, public resolve cannot automatically be assumed. Matsuoka cautioned against equating a growing public acceptance of a stronger SDF with a willingness to fight. “There is an important distinction between support for strengthening defence in principle and support for actually using military force,” she said. Acceptance of higher defence spending and new weapons would not necessarily mean the public would accept Japanese forces taking part directly in a war, suffering casualties or conducting operations that could expose Japan to retaliation, Matsuoka added. “The build-up has therefore shifted the debate away from the traditional question of whether Japan should possess military power towards the more consequential question of how and under what circumstances that power should be used.” The distinction is particularly important regarding Taiwan. Japan’s stated mission is to defend its own territory rather than Taiwan itself, but its proximity to the island, the presence of major US bases and the strategic importance of its southwestern islands mean a cross-strait conflict could force Tokyo to make decisions on how far and under what legal circumstances the SDF should be involved. Regional reactions Takaichi brought the question directly into the Taiwan debate last November when she said a contingency involving mainland Chinese warships and the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation”, a legal designation that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence under certain circumstances. The prime minister’s remarks drew a strong reaction from Beijing, which called them a violation of Tokyo’s Article 9 – the war-renouncing clause of Japan’s constitution that constrains the use of military force. Beijing could raise the cost of Japan’s transformation through tighter controls on rare earths and dual-use materials, Inoue said. However, such pressure could reinforce Japanese threat perceptions and accelerate efforts to reduce Tokyo’s economic dependence on China. Other than the reaction from Beijing, Japan’s transformation also depends on regional acceptance of its growing military role. Inoue said Japan enjoyed considerable support, pointing to renewed military training with South Korea and wider defence cooperation with Southeast Asia. Matsuoka was more muted, describing the receptivity as “conditional rather than unlimited”. “We should distinguish between welcoming Japan as a security partner and welcoming Japanese military expansion,” she said. Southeast Asian states may welcome Tokyo’s security assistance without necessarily supporting unrestricted military expansion. Furthermore, historical concerns could become more salient if Tokyo’s posture were perceived as increasingly autonomous or offensive, she said. Despite such constraints, Matsuoka said Japan’s defence transformation was becoming more difficult to reverse. Institutions, budgets, procurement programmes and alliance arrangements were being built around a particular conception of the regional security environment, she noted, giving the transformation a structural staying power that could extend beyond any single government. But threat perceptions themselves are mutable. A major improvement in Sino-Japanese relations, shifts in US policy, economic pressure, domestic political change or declining public willingness to bear defence costs could all alter the trajectory, she said. The opposite outcome is also possible: a self-reinforcing cycle in which Japanese capabilities intended to bolster deterrence reinforce Beijing’s perception of Japanese militarisation, prompting Chinese responses that further strengthen Tokyo’s perception of threat. “Japan’s challenge is not only to strengthen deterrence but also to avoid a security strategy in which military expansion becomes the default answer to every deterioration in the regional security environment,” Matsuoka said.

title: Josh Kerr ready for US$150,000 Ingebrigtsen battle, but Scot not planning to chase paydays
description: Josh Kerr and Jakob Ingebrigtsen will renew their rivalry at the World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest.
content: From the football bosses seemingly hellbent on creating a year-long product, to a tennis calendar that Carlos Alcaraz this week called impossible, sporting administrators have been accused of roundly abandoning the concept of less is more. There was also the case a couple of years ago of Chinese table tennis pair Fan Zhendong and Chen Meng withdrawing from the world rankings in protest at the fines being imposed on overworked players for skipping events. Given the steady uprising of athletes against schedules foisted on them that risk physical and mental burnout, it was strange to hear Jakob Ingebrigtsen accuse Josh Kerr of “ruining” track and field after the brilliant Scottish middle-distance runner opted out of last month’s European Athletics Championships. Poised for a humdinger of a 1,500m battle with Ingebrigtsen at this week’s inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, Kerr said he “felt tired” just thinking about a year that could have included the European Championships and many more Diamond League outings than his single appearance in London. Kerr’s relative inactivity has contributed to his 1,500m world ranking tumbling to No 84. As such, he required a special exemption to compete in the Ultimate Championships, where race winners will win US$150,000. “I’ve heard that people are frustrated with the invite [but] I didn’t ask for it,” Kerr said. “I’ll either be in trouble for not going, or I’ll be in trouble for taking an invite I don’t deserve. Just pick your frustrations with me. But I’ll be ready to race.” The 28-year-old declined an offer to “take a spot from someone who deserved it” for the Europeans, having missed June’s UK Athletics Championships, which served as qualifiers, to focus on his world-record attempt. In July, he drew a capacity 60,000 crowd to London Stadium to roar him to the world mile record; the triumphant culmination of “Project 222”, Kerr’s quest to cover the distance in three minutes and 42 seconds. Not the act of a man wrecking his chosen profession. The following month, he won Commonwealth Games gold in the same discipline, having become world indoor 3,000m champion back in March. “I’m not a robot,” he said. “Three championships a year is the maximum I can do.” “It’s an individual sport and we’re not forced into specific racing strategies,” Kerr said. “Every athlete is different in the way they approach the season. I circle two to four big dates and work my way around those. “I’m not short sighted and I’m not going to get greedy.” Among a 16-strong support crew that includes his physiotherapist mother, Jill, a personal chef and a chiropractor, Kerr employs mental coach Jose Maresma to aid a mind he once said contained some “deep weaknesses”. Before a race he keeps to himself and thinks athletes who go looking for their friends are worried about what’s to come. “I think people do that when they’re nervous,” Kerr said. “They try to find another nervous individual to share thoughts and feelings with, and that’s not really how I roll. “I’m not seeing the call room as a networking event, but some athletes seem to think it is.” Equally, Kerr was not shy when it came to talking up his mile world record bid, nor of saying the day before the attempt that he felt the odds were “in my favour, for sure”. After Kerr finished in 3:42.66, becoming the first person to complete a mile quicker than 3:43.00, his assistant coach, Julian Florez, said: “I hope more athletes become more vocal … People can call it cocky, but it’s confidence and I think that confident characters bring eyes to the sport. “I hope more athletes have this rhetoric and aren’t afraid to really call their shot.” In assembling his expansive team, Kerr “took inspiration from individual sports [where athletes] get paid a lot more money than we do”. “So tennis, golf, mixed martial arts, boxing,” he said. “I broke down how they did it and created a situation as close as possible to that for myself.” Having family members on board, with Larimar another in the support circle, helps “cut expenses”, but his outgoings partially explain why Kerr was miffed to be awarded the same US$50,000 bonus for his mile feat as previous record holder Hicham El Guerrouj was given 27 years ago. With inflation, that US$50,000 from 1999 would be worth a tick above US$100,000 today. At the time, Kerr called the prize money “appalling”. Speaking nearly two months later, he said: “It’s ridiculous, but I haven’t properly spoken to anyone about it. It was just a comment, nothing came of it. “I haven’t received it yet, so that’ll be a good time”. On a call with reporters to preview the Ultimate Championships, which is delivering Kerr back to the Hungarian city where he became world champion three years ago, he was met with incredulity. “Really, you’ve not had your money?”, he was asked. “Of course not,” Kerr said. “We don’t get paid for ages in this sport. But that’s a whole separate issue.” The 2015 European Junior 1,500m champion, Kerr said his world gold was especially important, because “I hadn’t won a lot and it was starting to really p*** me off”. Winning again at the scene of that “pivotal moment” would “cement my love and feeling for Budapest”, and Kerr vowed that he would be competing for more than the bounty on offer. “I was caught chasing paydays early in my career and it doesn’t lead to long-term success,” he said. “There are not many things left that I want to achieve ... but those things aren’t going to get closer with going after dollars and pounds in the short term. Racing against the best athletes in the world is important to me. I have to perform and win because it’s another tick on my side of the sheet.” Beginning on Friday, the Ultimate Championships will be staged across three three-hour evening sessions. They boast an athletics-high prize pot of US$10 million, while Mondo Duplantis, the two-time Olympic pole vault champion, wrote and sang the event anthem, “Gold”. He will perform it on the closing night, soon after Kerr and Ingebrigtsen do battle. “Running is going through a boom,” Kerr said. “Running stores are seeing a boom in shoe sales, and that gets filtered into the athletes, and into the next marketing route. “We’re seeing progress. US$150,000 is a lot of money [for winning a race]. It’s not as much as in other sports, but they’ve earned that through years of pushing their marketing. We’re moving in the right direction with these championships.” While Kerr is careful to manage his diary, he believes those athletes who pack their days fall into distinct categories. “You can do it if you’re young, but you’ll have long-term injury problems,” he said. “Others do it but have inconsistent results, which is not something I’m looking to do. And then there is the grey area of drugs.” Kerr’s dad, John, was a professional rugby player who won the 1996-97 Scottish Inter-District Championship with Caledonia Reds. Elder brother Jake, 30, is a retired one-cap Scotland rugby international, who played as a hooker for Leicester Tigers and Bristol Bears. Josh and Jake began running to gain rugby fitness, before the younger sibling joined Edinburgh Athletics Club at eight years old. Now the owner of a hybrid Scottish and American accent, Kerr moved to the USA at 17 to major in exercise science at the University of New Mexico, while competing in the country’s famously cutthroat collegiate system. On the day he arrived, he met his wife, Larimar, who was a budding 400m runner. The couple, whose Las Vegas wedding ceremony last year was overseen by an Elvis Presley impersonator, have a house 6,000ft above sea level in their university city of Albuquerque, allowing Kerr to train at altitude. Straight out of education in 2018, Kerr joined the Brooks Beasts Track Club in Seattle, where he began working with Danny Mackey, the coach who guided him to Olympic 1,500m bronze in 2021 and silver three years later. The pair will be together again this weekend, when Kerr looks to add to his legacy, and, when officials get around to it, his bank account.

title: 14 killed as explosion rocks Syria arms depot: authorities
description: The marks the second deadly blast in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province this month, after a car carrying ammunition exploded, killing five.
content: An explosion at an arms depot in Syria’s northwestern Idlib province killed 14 people on Wednesday, the local health department said, without specifying the cause of the blast. “The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada … registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count,” the Idlib health department said. The Syrian defence ministry’s media department earlier told state television that several of the ministry’s personnel had been wounded in the incident. Syrian media broadcast images showing large columns of smoke rising from the site of the blast, while rescuers rushed to the area. The incident marks the second deadly blast in Idlib this month, after a car carrying ammunition exploded, killing five in the city of Binnish. A government source told Agence France-Presse at the time that the car was owned by a weapons trader, while authorities did not announce the cause of the blast. There have been sporadic blasts in Idlib involving ammunition-laden cars or arms depots. The province was a key stronghold of armed anti-government factions during the country’s more than 13 years of civil war, before long-time ruler Bashar al-Assad was toppled in December 2024.

title: Far-right election win in Germany adds uncertainty to shaky China-EU relations
description: Outcome could harden Berlin’s stance towards Beijing ahead of an October deadline for trade rebalancing, analysts say.
content: The landslide victory of a far-right party in a German state election has raised doubts about whether a politically weakened Berlin can remain a driving force behind the European Union’s increasingly tough approach to Beijing amid mounting trade tensions. During the weekend election in the country’s eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) took 43.8 per cent of the vote, according to preliminary results, achieving its best state-level result but falling short of securing an absolute majority. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU) saw their share more than halved to 17.2 per cent. The result came as the European Commission considers tougher trade measures on China ahead of an October deadline for Beijing to show “tangible results” on imbalanced trade. Germany, as the largest economy in the bloc, is expected to play a “pivotal role” in the decision-making process, analysts said. While AfD co-leader Alice Weidel appeared to be friendlier in her stance towards relations with Beijing, the election outcome could reinforce Berlin’s increasingly tough stance on trade with China, rather than softening it, analysts argued. However, Germany’s domestic political turmoil could leave Berlin too distracted to lead the bloc’s strategy against Chinese industrial competition, they added. “The EU is entering the most consequential period in its relations with China in many years,” said Noah Barkin, senior adviser at Rhodium Group. The election result sent shock waves across the bloc, drawing responses from national leaders and EU officials. Speaking at a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, EU trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic warned against “national-only solutions” and stressed the need for unity in negotiating with major powers such as China and the US. Though AfD’s state-level victory would not directly change Berlin’s foreign policy, it could create cracks within the country, as the party stands apart from Germany’s political mainstream on many issues, analysts said. “What [AfD] wants is a Germany for Germans,” said Shi Shiwei, a Berlin-based professor at the University of International Business and Economics who specialises in the German economy and China-Germany relations. The party’s state platform breaks with Berlin and Brussels on trade and energy alike, calling for halting wind power, continuing the use of coal, restoring cheap Russian gas, stripping powers from the EU and putting German interests first in external economic relations. On China, the party’s leaders remained relatively friendly and pragmatic, Shi said, adding that co-leader Weidel had spent years working in China and the AfD had opposed some of the EU’s protectionist measures. Nevertheless, analysts cautioned against assuming that the AfD’s rise would pull Berlin closer to Beijing. The party’s gains were probably driven partly by fears of industrial decline and job losses, said Juergen Matthes of the Cologne Institute for Economic Research, whose work identified Chinese competition as a major driver of Germany’s deindustrialisation. If social unrest grew, he said, the AfD itself could turn to a more robust China policy. “It is a populist party, after all,” he said. That could find support among German voters, who are becoming Europe’s most hawkish electorate when it comes to China. A survey by the European Council on Foreign Relations last month found 49 per cent of Germans saw Beijing primarily as a rival or adversary, the highest share among 13 countries polled. In Brussels, however, the concern is less about an immediate shift in Germany’s China policy than about Berlin’s ability to act in Europe. “Merz has broken with his predecessors in backing a tougher stance [towards Beijing],” Barkin said. “He has been the driver of this major policy shift.” If Merz made way for a new chancellor weeks before the October summit, he added, it would introduce “a huge amount of uncertainty” into the process. Even if Merz were to stay, the result would increase the risk that he would be too distracted and constrained by domestic politics to provide European leadership, Jeremy Cliffe and Jana Puglierin of the European Council on Foreign Relations wrote on Tuesday. With France, Italy, Poland and Spain all entering election seasons, “a Germany riven by internal drama cannot be the anchor that Europe needs”. “Other European capitals should curb their expectations of German leadership,” they wrote, adding that leaders including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen would need to depend less on Merz to advance ambitious proposals.

title: Singapore’s DBS sued for US$1 billion in alleged 1MDB-linked claim
description: DBS has rejected the claim and says it will ‌fight it vigorously, but that the company has made no ⁠provision ⁠for the lawsuit.
content: Singapore’s DBS Bank is being sued for an estimated S$1.298 billion (US$1.03 billion) in damages linked to the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal, Southeast Asia’s largest lender DBS Group has said. The claimants include the liquidators of four companies: BlackRock Commodities (Global), Platinum Global ‌Luxury Services, Affinity Equity International Partners and TKIL Global Investments. The liquidators confirmed in an emailed statement that they ‌had filed and served a damages claim of more than US$1 billion against DBS Bank. DBS on ⁠Wednesday rejected the claim and said it would fight ⁠it vigorously, adding ⁠that the company had made no provision for the lawsuit. The bank did not ‌provide any more details on the allegations it faces. The lawsuit is the latest among wide-ranging ‌efforts ‌to recover money belonging to 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB), from which US investigators ‌say about US$4.5 billion was stolen between 2009 and 2014 in a ⁠complex, globe-spanning scheme. All this time, there was no claim against DBS, ⁠according to the lender’s statement. In July last year, liquidators trying to recover money from 1MDB sued Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, ‌alleging it enabled fraud ‌that led to more than US$2.7 billion in financial losses between 2009 and 2013. Shares of DBS closed 0.8 per cent lower at S$77.50 earlier in the day.

title: US scrambles to match China’s air-breathing hypersonic missiles with Darpa programme
description: US defence agency launches next-generation weapons project a year after PLA unveiled pioneering hypersonic missiles in military parade.
content: A year after China unveiled the world’s first operational air-breathing hypersonic missiles, the United States is launching a programme to double down on developing similar weapons. The US Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency (Darpa) will bring contractors together later this month to lay out what it wants from the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile, with air-breathing propulsion at the heart of the project, according to the agency’s website. Unlike rocket-powered missiles, air-breathing weapons draw oxygen from the atmosphere instead of carrying all they need on board, freeing up weight for fuel or payload. China put that technology on public display at a massive military parade in Beijing last year, when it unveiled the YJ-19 anti-ship missile and the much larger, road-mobile CJ-1000. Both are believed to use air-breathing scramjet engines and were presented as operational weapons in service with the People’s Liberation Army. The YJ-19’s distinctive air intake was visible during the parade, while the CJ-1000 is designed for much longer-range strikes against targets on land, at sea or in the air, according to Chinese state media reports. Darpa has made clear it is looking for more than an upgrade to existing technology. In an industry request issued last month, the agency called for radically new propulsion, fuels, boosters and systems to cope with the extreme heat of hypersonic flight. The new missile could come in varied sizes, from weapons carried by tactical aircraft to much larger systems launched from bombers or the ground. Darpa has asked contractors to consider flight tests over distances ranging from about 250 to 2,000 nautical miles (460 to 3,700km). Hypersonic weapons travel at least five times the speed of sound, but air-breathing cruise missiles work very differently from boost-glide weapons such as China’s DF-17. Both need a rocket to get up to speed. But a glide weapon is then released and coasts towards its target without an engine, while a hypersonic cruise missile switches to an air-breathing engine that continues to propel it through the atmosphere. That combination of extreme speed, sustained propulsion and the ability to manoeuvre can make such missiles particularly difficult to detect and intercept, according to Darpa. The US has already proved that the technology can work in flight. The Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept, a joint Darpa and US Air Force project, flew experimental scramjet-powered vehicles above Mach 5 and for more than 300 nautical miles, but the programme ended in 2023 without producing an operational weapon. Russia has also claimed its Zircon missile, in service since 2023, is a scramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missile. However, analysis of debris recovered after its use in Ukraine has cast doubt on that description, suggesting Zircon may instead use solid-fuel rockets and operate more like a quasi-ballistic missile.

title: EU plan aims to help cities crack down on Airbnb, holiday rentals
description: The European Commission’s Affordable Housing Act lays out conditions under which local authorities can limit short lets.
content: European cities will gain more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb under new EU plans that aim to bring down housing costs in tourism hotspots. The European Commission laid out conditions on Wednesday under which local authorities can limit short lets, under a proposal seeking to address Europe’s “housing crisis”. “Short-term rentals are a part of the problem in many cities,” Dan Jorgensen, the 27-nation bloc’s housing commissioner, told a press conference in Brussels. Though hugely popular with visitors, short-term lodgings are blamed by residents in many popular travel destinations for depriving locals of flats for long-term rental and pushing up prices – something holiday-let providers dispute. Cities from New York to Tokyo and Barcelona have imposed or considered restrictions on tourist flats in recent years. But curbs have often been met with court challenges, resulting in legal uncertainty. The commission’s Affordable Housing Act – which still has to be negotiated with lawmakers and EU countries – aims to provide cities with legal cover, clarifying when authorities can take action without falling foul of the bloc’s single market rules. “They shouldn’t fear that they can be dragged into court,” Jorgensen said. Tech lobby group CCIA, whose members include Airbnb, said the rules marked a “clear improvement over the restrict-first-ask-later approach taken by cities to date”. But it complained about the lack of enforcement mechanisms. “With little provision for independent scrutiny or effective redress, disproportionate restrictions could still be imposed unchallenged and remain in place for years,” it said. Cities and other relevant authorities would be allowed under the plans to limit holiday rentals as well as the purchase of property for short-term letting purposes in areas deemed “under housing stress”. The definition applies to districts where the price of an average size home is at least eight times that of locals’ disposable per-capita income. Before introducing restrictions, authorities must show short-term rentals have had a significant adverse effect on housing affordability or availability for at least three years. Measures must be non-discriminatory, proportionate and limited to five years. The legislation will not affect landlords who rent out their own primary residence for short periods, nor rules cities had previously brought in. More than half of EU city dwellers told a 2025 survey housing affordability was “an immediate and urgent problem”. Property prices in the bloc have surged by 60 per cent in a decade, while rents have climbed 20 per cent, Brussels says. This is mainly driven by insufficient housing supply, but short-term rentals – which grew 93 per cent across four major platforms between 2018 and 2024 – added pressure, the EU says. Short rentals account for only about 1.2 per cent of the European Union’s total housing stock but can reach 20 per cent in popular tourist districts, EU data shows. Residents had been “crowded out of their homes” leading to “totally unacceptable” price increases, Jorgensen said. “Over the past 10 years, rents have gone up by 59 per cent in Berlin, by 75 per cent in Madrid, by 103 per cent in Lisbon. This means that normal people with normal jobs – nurses, schoolteachers, police officers – are not able, very often, to live where they serve,” he said. Yet rental providers deny holiday lets are to blame. In a letter to the commission, the CCIA said that in some cities with restrictions, both local rents and hotel prices had risen regardless, noting that Lisbon recently overturned some of the curbs it had previously imposed. Airbnb warned the EU’s plan as drafted would “not add homes, while creating increased regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities”. Short-term rentals generated some €40 billion in tax revenue and more than 2 million jobs EU-wide in 2023, it said. George Mavros, Airbnb’s head of EU government affairs, said making housing more affordable required a focus on “construction, renovation, and the homes standing empty across Europe today”.

title: More than 1,000 children dead in Bangladesh measles crisis
description: The South Asian nation of 170 million has recorded 1,002 deaths and 187,484 infections among children since March.
content: The death toll from measles in Bangladesh topped 1,000 children since March, health officials said on Wednesday, admitting that failures in a vaccination drive could have fuelled the outbreak. The South Asian nation of 170 million has recorded 1,002 deaths and 187,484 infections among children, making this year’s outbreak the country’s deadliest in decades, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS). Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught. Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems. Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable. The disease has kept spreading in Bangladesh even as health authorities rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak. DGHS spokesman Zahid Raihan said more than 18 million children had been vaccinated so far, and teams were searching for those who had missed inoculations. “We couldn’t achieve herd immunity,” Raihan said. Official figures show that about 4 million children were left out of the campaign, leaving pockets of vulnerability that experts say have fuelled the outbreak. “Measles cannot be eradicated and the aim was to reduce casualties. We will keep vaccinating our children,” Raihan said. Controlling the outbreak, however, required more than vaccinations, Raihan said, pointing to the need to tackle chronic malnutrition among children – a factor that can worsen the disease’s impact. The mounting measles crisis is also stretching an already burdened healthcare system as authorities grapple with a simultaneous surge in dengue fever cases. “Hospitals with the capacity to handle 50 dengue patients are now dealing with 500,” Raihan said. Nine people died from dengue on Tuesday alone, while 1,571 patients were admitted to hospitals, according to health department data. Since January, Bangladesh has recorded 45,475 dengue cases and 130 deaths. In 2023, there were 321,017 cases of the mosquito-borne disease – the highest figure recorded in the country. Junior Health Minister MA Muhit warned that dengue cases could rise further in the coming weeks. “If we take measures to keep our surroundings clean, we may see a lower incidence of dengue,” he said at a seminar on Wednesday. “Otherwise ... dengue may take a dangerous turn in the last week of September and early October.” Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to inaugurate a three-month nationwide anti-dengue campaign on Saturday.

title: Buildings Department files 259 charges over work at fire-ravaged Hong Kong estate
description: Charges against two firms, four individuals relate to alleged use of substandard materials and failure to properly supervise repairs.
content: Hong Kong’s Buildings Department has filed 259 charges against two companies and four individuals over repair works at the inferno-ravaged Wang Fuk Court, after investigations found non-fire-retardant materials were used and safety obligations were not met. The department said on Wednesday that the charges included allegedly permitting or authorising to be used in the carrying out of building works materials which are defective or did not comply with the provisions of the Buildings Ordinance, as well as failing to properly supervise repair works, among other offences. The two companies charged are the project’s consulting firm, Will Power Architects, and main contractor, Prestige Construction & Engineering. The four individuals are Will Power director Wong Hap-yin and registered inspector Ng Yeuk, together with Prestige directors Ho Kin-yip and Hau Wa-kin. In June, both firms, the four individuals and three others were charged by police and the Independent Commission Against Corruption with offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, money laundering, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion. The Labour Department also laid 25 charges on Wednesday against related parties – the contractor, the project consultant and an individual – under the Factories and Industrial Undertakings Ordinance, in connection with the deaths of five contractors’ staff during the fire. A Buildings Department spokesman said the department and the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit “spared no effort in conducting investigations into the major repair works at the estate” following the Wang Fuk Court blaze. The investigation found that the registered inspector employed by the consulting firm did not properly supervise the prescribed repairs and failed to ensure the buildings were safe, he added. The two companies were also suspected of having permitted or authorised the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding netting, canvases and foam boards to cover windows during the work, and of removing fireproof windows on emergency staircases to create easy access to the scaffolding, which were then sealed with non-fire-retardant materials. These actions caused the fire to spread rapidly and obstructed residents’ escape, which ultimately resulted in 168 deaths and 79 injuries, the spokesman said. The department reiterated that contractors and building professionals must properly supervise inspections and construction work in accordance with the ordinance, subsidiary regulations, and relevant codes of practice to ensure that the materials used are appropriate and that the work is carried out safely for the project. Under the Buildings Ordinance, any person directly concerned with minor works who permits or authorises to be incorporated in or used in the carrying out of works any materials which are defective or do not comply with the provisions of the ordinance commits an offence. A person who carries out, authorises or permits minor works to be carried out in such a manner that causes injury to any person or damage to any property faces a maximum penalty of HK$500,000 (US$63,765) and 18 months’ imprisonment. A registered inspector who fails to supervise the carrying out of the prescribed repair that is minor works properly is liable to a fine of up to HK$150,000, while a registered inspector or registered general contractor who fails to ensure a building, for which they are appointed to supervise or carry out the prescribed repair that is minor works, is safe or has been made safe faces a maximum fine of HK$500,000 and 18 months’ imprisonment. The fire, which broke out in November, was one of the deadliest in the city’s history, tearing through seven of the eight blocks of the Tai Po estate, killing 168 people, including a firefighter, and injuring 79 others. Nearly 5,000 residents were left homeless. The estate’s high-rise towers were wrapped in scaffolding for renovation when a piece of safety netting covering the lower floors of Wang Cheong House, one of the eight blocks, caught fire. Concerns over possible bid-rigging also emerged after the estate’s renovation budget more than doubled from a preliminary estimate of HK$152 million in September 2023 to HK$336 million in 2024, when the most expensive option was adopted.

title: Beijing boosts Taiwan-facing firepower with brigade-level 155mm howitzer deployment
description: Upgrade for Eastern Theatre Command’s 71st Group Army streamlines PLA’s firepower across land and sea as US artillery programmes lag.
content: Beijing has reinforced its military firepower facing the Taiwan Strait by deploying more 155mm PLZ-05 self-propelled howitzers, according to state media reports. Replacing its older 122mm artillery, a heavy combined-arms brigade under the People’s Liberation Army’s 71st Group Army has been equipped with a batch of the 155mm self-propelled howitzers over the past two months and conducted its first live-fire test of the weapons, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Sunday. The 71st Group Army belongs to the Eastern Theatre Command, which has the main responsibility for operations facing Taiwan, the East China Sea and Japan. This marked the first time the PLZ-05 had been assigned at the brigade level. The powerful artillery system was originally operated at the group-army level as a long-range suppression weapon. “For us, receiving 155mm self-propelled howitzers for the first time has significantly improved our overall combat effectiveness,” brigade officer Sun Xialong said. Painted in brown desert camouflage, the batch of tracked howitzers appeared to have been relocated from the Western Theatre Command, which has instead received lighter, wheeled PCL-181 155mm self-propelled howitzers better suited to the plateau and mountainous terrain it covers. The PLZ-05 is equipped with an autoloader that enables a maximum rate of fire of eight to 10 rounds per minute, with the crew always staying inside. It can fire advanced 155mm ammunition, including the BeiDou-guided WS-35, which has a maximum range of up to 100km (62 miles). The 71st Group Army is considered a frontline unit that always maintains a high state of combat readiness for a Taiwan contingency. In an amphibious assault scenario, the firepower of its 155mm artillery would be capable of effectively destroying coastal defensive fortifications and enemy firing positions. Once landed, the tracked self-propelled vehicles would also provide off-road mobility and deliver suppression-fire support in depth. While the PLA is modernising its artillery forces through increased deployment of PLZ-05 and PCL-181 howitzers, the US Army’s efforts to replace its ageing M109-series tracked 155mm self-propelled howitzers with a new generation of systems have faced repeated setbacks. In the wheeled 155mm artillery category, the US Army in August awarded Hanwha Defence USA, a subsidiary of South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace, a US$100.3 million contract for six wheeled 155mm K9A2 Mobile Howitzers, with an option for 12 more systems that could bring the total contract value to US$262.9 million. The PLA Navy has also been testing a 155mm naval gun aboard an experimental ship, which was seen going on trials at sea earlier this year. If formally adopted and made compatible with the Chinese army’s existing 155mm ammunition, the weapon could streamline the PLA’s logistics and allow the Chinese navy to draw on the ground force’s established inventory of advanced 155mm munitions. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: Hong Kong Medical Council rejects proposal on time frame for handling complaints
description: In written submission to Legislative Council, watchdog also rejects proposed reforms to its disciplinary sentencing, supervision and membership.
content: Hong Kong’s medical watchdog has said a target time frame for handling complaints will not be necessary as it presented its rebuttal against a government proposal that includes major reforms to its operations, disciplinary sentencing, internal supervision and membership make-up. The Medical Council on Tuesday presented its views on the government’s proposed amendments, which were first laid out in late June and aimed to speed up the watchdog’s process and accountability in handling complaints. In a written submission to the Legislative Council’s bills committee on the medical registration amendment bill, dated Tuesday and uploaded to the Legco website the next day, the Medical Council’s chairwoman Professor Grace Tang Wai-king said a dedicated working group had been established to study the details of the bill and assess its implications for the watchdog’s operations. Among the government’s proposed amendments was requiring the watchdog to make public the target time frames for specific steps in its complaints procedure, and set up milestone dates for submissions of documents and inquiries. “There is no need to stipulate the requirement for the Medical Council of Hong Kong to set target time frames for specific steps in the law,” the council stated in the submission. “Instead, this can be handled administratively by [the council] as [has been] the practice of government departments and other statutory bodies.” Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau previously said that the reform could help cut down the inquiry process from an average of 42 months to an estimated 29 months. The suggested changes to the watchdog’s operations followed a 15-year delay in its handling of a complaint against Dr Sit Sou-chi, who was accused of a blunder that left a boy permanently disabled in 2009. The case was terminated last year on the grounds that the procedural delay prevented a fair hearing, but the council made a U-turn and resumed the inquiry in April following a public outcry. Under the proposal, the government also planned to overhaul the disciplinary system for medical professionals, including replacing suspension orders for doctors. But the council thought otherwise. “It is suggested to retain the option of a suspension order … to cater for professional misconduct in certain situations,” the watchdog said, adding that the arrangement could be applicable to cases that did not involve patient safety. The watchdog also strongly objected to a proposal to specify its supervisory role in overseeing its secretariat’s performance. “The chairman and members of the Medical Council of Hong Kong who are working on part-time and voluntary basis are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to deal with every detail of the work and performance of the secretary [or] secretariat,” the watchdog said, quoting a member who “strongly questioned” the government’s proposal. On the proposed changes to the council’s membership, including the addition of three directly appointed seats to expand the number of members to 35, the watchdog said “the operation of [the council] might be adversely affected if the government appointed ‘strangers’ who were not familiar with the roles and functions of [the council] to fill the seats”. Instead, the watchdog said those three seats should be filled by doctors from different organisations. The government had previously proposed adding three lay members who were healthcare professionals other than doctors, appointed by Hong Kong’s chief executive, to “promote multidisciplinary collaboration”. The watchdog also expressed doubts about including the government’s commissioner for primary healthcare in the council, saying that its functions were focused on the registration and regulation of doctors rather than the formulation of healthcare policy. The legislature is scrutinising the government’s amendment bill related to the reforms to the council, with the next meeting expected to be held in late September.

title: Malaysia’s ruling PH restates anti-corruption pledge as Najib’s potential pardon looms
description: The Pardons Board is set to meet this week to discuss clemency for Najib, who is in jail for corruption, according to media reports.
content: Malaysia’s ruling Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition has doubled down on its pledge to stamp out corruption, as all eyes turn to the country’s Pardons Board, which is reportedly set to discuss the possible release of disgraced former leader Najib Razak at a meeting this week. The Pardons Board, chaired by the country’s king, is expected to meet on Friday to discuss potentially granting Najib clemency from his ongoing jail sentence for corruption linked to the multibillion-dollar 1MDB scandal, according to local news reports. The revelation adds a fresh spin to the drama surrounding Najib’s earlier attempt at securing a court order to complete his sentence in his home after his 12-year jail term was halved and his fine reduced from 210 million ringgit (US$51.6 million) to 50 million ringgit following a decision by former king Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah in 2024. Should the pardons board, led by current king Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, grant Najib a full pardon, it would mean his immediate release from prison and his records wiped clean of all existing criminal records, similar to when Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was freed from a sodomy conviction in 2018. In an apparent response to a news report on the Pardons Board meeting by local Chinese daily Sin Chew Daily, the PH secretaries’ council said the coalition continued to reject corruption and abuse of power, and that any individual found guilty of such offences, especially in high-profile cases, “must complete their sentences in full”. “Pakatan Harapan was built on the support of Malaysians … who placed high hopes on our Reform agenda and the creation of a country that is clean, with integrity and responsible,” the secretaries’ council said in a statement on Wednesday. “This trust demands that we continue to be consistent in upholding principled positions, even if we face challenging situations and pressure from various angles,” the statement added without naming any individual. The Sin Chew report claimed that PH’s presidential council was briefed on Tuesday evening on the timing and agenda of the Pardons Board meeting by Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh, who sits on the board by virtue of her ministerial post. When contacted, Yeoh’s press secretary Ahmad Fazli Mohd Yadi denied that the minister had met with the presidential council or briefed its members on the matter, but could not confirm if a Pardons Board meeting was scheduled for Friday. The National Palace did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Sources close to the matter said that Najib’s clemency application was on the agenda for the Pardons Board meeting this week, according to a report by local English news site FreeMalaysiaToday, though it was not clear whether a decision would be made. It was never confirmed publicly whether Najib had filed an application for clemency this year. In April, the former prime minister dropped his legal bid to compel the government to carry out an alleged addendum to Sultan Abdullah’s 2024 decree that he said allowed him to serve the remainder of his jail term under house arrest. No reason was given for his decision. A full pardon would deal another blow to the already battered credibility of Anwar’s ruling coalition, which experts say is facing a crisis of confidence among its supporters angered over its failure to deliver substantive reforms. “Of course, the government can detach the accountability and put the decision-making cleanly with the royal institution. And that will likely be the messaging if it happened,” Aziff Azuddin, research director at think tank Iman Research, told This Week in Asia. “But the public would still read this as something that happened under the Madani government’s watch,” Aziff added, referring to Anwar’s government tagline, which roughly translates to civilisation. A royal pardon for Najib – who remains deeply popular among his Malay-majority support base – would also boost the growing momentum of his former ruling Umno party, which has enjoyed a resurgence with decisive victories over its federal partners but electoral rivals PH in two state elections over the past two months. In a response to PH’s statement, Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki accused the coalition partner of double standards by demanding that all convicted felons complete their jail terms when Anwar had received a royal pardon previously. “Their latest action indirectly reveals the ‘true colours’ of PH who have repeatedly made light of and disputed the Institution of Malay Rulers for their own political interests,” Asyraf said in a statement. Azmi Hassan, senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said that with national polls due in a little over a year, the stand-off over Najib’s royal pardon would drive a wedge further between the two uneasy partners. “It is already a full-blown war between PH and BN,” Azmi said, referring to the Barisan Nasional coalition led by Umno.

title: Chinese AI firm DeepSeek taps underwriters including Citic Securities for IPO: sources
description: Start-up aims to begin the IPO process this year to list on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star market, sources say.
content: Chinese frontier artificial intelligence lab DeepSeek has hired underwriters including Citic Securities in preparation for a domestic initial public offering (IPO), according to two people familiar with the matter. Citic Securities was one of the four underwriters tapped by the Hangzhou-based firm, which aims to begin the IPO process this year to list on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s Nasdaq-like Star market, the people said, asking not to be identified as the information was private. DeepSeek and Citic Securities did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside normal business hours on Wednesday. The progress towards an IPO comes as the company is moving to complete a pre-IPO round of financing that could value it at about 500 billion yuan (US$74 billion) before investment. DeepSeek is pursuing its listing alongside Beijing-based Moonshot AI, which confidentially filed last week for a Hong Kong IPO early next year, the South China Morning Post reported last week. Moonshot, developer of the Kimi K3 model series, was also raising a final round of financing that could value it at around US$50 billion before the IPO, in which it aims to raise US$3 billion to US$5 billion, according to a report by Bloomberg, citing sources. In their push for funding and IPOs, the firms are following in the footsteps of Beijing-based Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, and Shanghai-based MiniMax, which went public in Hong Kong earlier this year. The two were among the world’s first pure-play AI model developers to tap public market capital to fund their expansion, although their valuations lag their US counterparts. OpenAI and Anthropic could be valued at US$1 trillion and US$2 trillion, respectively, in their coming IPOs, while Z.ai and MiniMax’s market capitalisation stood at HK$425 billion (US$54 billion) and HK$112 billion as of market close on Wednesday. DeepSeek’s funding push comes amid a hiring and infrastructure buildout spree. The company on Tuesday embarked on an “unprecedented” recruitment move to overhaul back-end systems that have been severely strained by booming user demand, the SCMP reported. The company was also in talks with local data centres to add computing capacity.

title: Tung Chee-hwa remembered as kind, approachable Hong Kong leader
description: People who worked closely with Tung praise him as ‘kind-hearted’, ‘exceptionally hard-working’ and inspired others to take up public office.
content: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first leader following its return to Chinese sovereignty, has been remembered as a “kind-hearted man” who mentored others and inspired some to take up public office. As tributes poured in for Tung, who died on Tuesday aged 89, people who worked closely with him shared touching anecdotes about the man they said cared deeply about Hong Kong even in the years after he stepped down as chief executive in 2005. Bernard Chan, chairman of the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority board, described Tung as an approachable leader who often reached out to find solutions to Hong Kong’s deep-rooted problems even after his retirement. “I still remember there was a year during the ‘two sessions’, he asked to meet me over lunch,” Chan said, referring to the annual plenary meetings of the National People’s Congress and the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. “When I got into his hotel room, there was only a sandwich and we jumped right into the issues he was concerned about.” Chan said Tung had asked for his views about the city’s development and young people’s future. “It was very intense. He kept taking notes. After that, he said he would take a quick nap and rush to attend the closing ceremony of the two sessions,” Chan said. “He’s a person who truly believed in working to resolve problems. He worked so hard despite his age. Why should I be complaining? He motivated me.” Ex-financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung described the former chief executive as his “mentor”, saying he was grateful to Tung for entrusting him with major responsibilities. Leung said Tung was exceptionally hard-working and demanding of himself, but never a harsh leader who publicly reprimanded others. “He woke up at 5am every morning to read documents and called as early as 7am to discuss government business,” he said. “Meticulous and thorough in everything he did, I truly witnessed the heavy weight of the word ‘responsibility’ through him.” Hong Kong Trade Development Council chairman Frederick Ma Si-hang, who served as secretary for financial services and the treasury in the Tung administration, described the late leader as the man who brought him into public service. “Mr Tung was a kind-hearted man who always led by virtue,” he said. He recalled that he would not have joined the government without Tung’s invitation. “Back then, Antony Leung introduced me to him, but it was Mr Tung who decided to invite me into the government. In that sense, he was my benefactor for entering public service, and I feel deep sorrow at his passing,” Ma said. He praised Tung’s love for the country and Hong Kong, as well as his foresight and vision for the city. “He put forward many proposals for Hong Kong; some succeeded, some did not, but no matter what, his heart was always with Hong Kong,” he said. During his time as chief executive, Tung needed not only to implement the then-untested and novel “one country, two systems” governing model, but also to steer the city through major crises, including the 1997 Asian financial crisis and 2003 Sars outbreak. But there were also a number of failed policies, including his swiftly abandoned pledge to build 85,000 homes a year and the city’s first, ultimately unsuccessful, attempt at passing national security legislation as required under Article 23 of the Basic Law. Henry Tang Ying-yen, who was a member of the government’s key decision-making Executive Council beginning in 1997, described Tung as an outstanding leader who made a great contribution to the city’s stability and prosperity. Praising Tung’s visionary leadership in economic development, arts and culture, and innovation and technology, Tang said many of Hong Kong’s achievements today were rooted in policies introduced during Tung’s tenure. James Chau, president of the China-United States Exchange Foundation, which was founded by Tung, recalled his first interaction with the former leader as a journalist covering the then-chief executive’s visit to the US in 2001. “I was at the back of the queue because I was sitting in economy … And he suddenly came through with Mrs [Betty] Tung, guided by airport security,” Chau said. “No matter how many times the airport authorities tried to get him onto the aircraft, he said, ‘No, I’m going to wait at the back’ and insisted on waiting at the back of the queue and standing for quite a long time.” It was then that staff members assumed they were travelling together and placed Chau’s hand luggage in the business-class cabin. “One of the business-class passengers was very annoyed with me because he was wondering why my bag was in the cabin that he paid a higher fare for,” Chau said. “Mr Tung saw what was happening, stood up and said to the gentleman, ‘I am very sorry,’ and made him feel better.” “He always had a way to find a solution. He always had a way to moderate.” Lawmaker Simon Hoey Lee, who once worked closely with Tung as deputy executive director of Our Hong Kong Foundation, recalled how he and the former city leader clashed over research studies on the 18 districts. But after 10 minutes of a tense atmosphere, he said Tung comforted him and ultimately adopted his proposal. “This showed his meticulous care, deep affection and unwavering support for young people,” Lee said.

title: Norwegians bid final farewell to King Harald V, ‘grandfather of the nation’
description: Foreign dignitaries in attendance include Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Britain’s Prince William.
content: Norway bid farewell on Wednesday to King Harald V in a funeral reflecting his open and unifying nature, and attended by dignitaries including Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky and Britain’s Prince William. After a procession through the streets of Oslo packed with crowds and a funeral service at Oslo’s Lutheran cathedral, the king’s casket was transported to the Akershus Castle church where it was to be placed in the royal crypt. Until his death on August 28 at age 89, Harald was the oldest reigning monarch in Europe and hugely popular among Norwegians, despite the scandals that dogged his family towards the end of his reign. Some 48,000 people lined the streets for the procession, police said. “He was our rock,” said Inger Elise Kolsto, a 63-year-old accountant. Carried on an artillery carriage, the king’s casket, draped in the red royal banner, was transported along the city’s main avenue, followed on foot by his son and heir King Haakon VIII, members of his family, and dozens of other dignitaries. Only Harald’s widow, 89-year-old Queen Sonja, and the new Queen Mette-Marit, who underwent a lung transplant in June, followed the procession in a car. Among other guests were Scandinavia’s royal families, royal couples from Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands, the crown prince of Japan, the presidents of Finland and Germany, and the French and Thai prime ministers. The church service began at 1pm local time with a nationwide minute of silence. “He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth,” Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. “He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.” Marius Borg Hoiby, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship who is under house arrest pending the appeal of a rape and assault conviction, had been granted permission to attend the funeral. At the end of the service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in formation, as the casket made its way to the Akershus Castle. There, after a private ceremony with the family, the casket was to be lowered into the crypt of the royal mausoleum, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents. He was to be laid to rest in a US$2 million sarcophagus whose design remains secret. On the throne since 1991, Harald had always ruled out abdicating, despite mounting health woes towards the end of his life. Seen as embodying an open and tolerant Norway, Harald made a deep impression by celebrating diversity in a 2016 speech. “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other,” he said, adding: “Norwegians believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing.” In that vein, several religions were represented at Wednesday’s funeral service. A representative of Norway’s indigenous Sami community also held a eulogy to the king in the Sami language. Once the funeral was over, flags across the country, which were lowered to half mast after Harald’s death, were once again raised and church bells rang for an hour. From the balcony of the palace in central Oslo, the royal family then waved at the cheering crowd that had gathered. The funeral took place under high security, with almost 3,000 police deployed. The square in front of the palace has been covered with flowers, drawings and candles for days as Norwegians honoured the man they dubbed “the grandfather of the nation”. “He was like the beloved grandfather of a family, who embraced all his children and grandchildren, regardless of their appearance or beliefs,” said student Arthur Fosheim. “He truly embodied that spirit of inclusion and a multicultural Norway.” Almost three out of four Norwegians, 72 per cent, said they supported the monarchy, up by eight percentage points from a previous survey in May, in an opinion poll conducted after the king’s death and published last week. Support had dropped to its lowest level in February, to 60 per cent, when the royal family was embroiled in a series of scandals. Mette-Marit in particular was under heavy criticism for her past ties to the late convicted American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son’s legal troubles. While Haakon VIII, 53, is very popular, opinions on the new queen, also 53, remain deeply divided.

title: China’s robotic lawnmower industry sets its sights on EU amid bare domestic market
description: Once a niche market, sales of robot mowers in Europe have more than doubled in the past five years.
content: At least nine Chinese brands launched new robotic lawnmowers at this year’s IFA, Europe’s largest consumer electronics show, as the industry commits to continued expansion in the EU, despite an ongoing anti-dumping investigation by Brussels against their products. Chinese lawnmower makers turned one hall at IFA in Berlin – which ran from Friday to Tuesday – into a patchwork of artificial gardens, with brands setting up demonstrations on their respective turfs. “Everyone came in over the past two years,” said Ryan Kong, Segway Navimow’s general manager for Europe. Robotic lawnmowers, a category with almost no market in China, have become a new export frontier for Chinese makers. IFA had no shortage of loud newcomers. Robot vacuum makers Dreame and Roborock, plus pool-robot maker Aiper, have all entered the market since 2024. Mova, a Dreame brand, hired a DJ, as five mowers waved fans with robotic arms in time with the music to draw visitors. Chinese makers have been drawn by the growth potential of what was once a niche market. Annual sales of robotic lawnmowers in Europe have risen from about 800,000 units in 2021 to roughly two million, and could reach three to four million, Kong estimated. Navimow’s growth has mirrored the market. Launched in 2021, the company said global sales rose from 3,000 units in its first full year to about 300,000 last year. Its operating entity earned 269 million yuan (US$40.1 million) in the first half, according to the interim report from its parent company Segway-Ninebot. The market has already drawn scrutiny on both sides of the Atlantic. The US Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made advanced robots, including lawnmowers, to its Covered List on July 28, barring new models from sale in the country. The European Commission, meanwhile, opened an anti-dumping investigation into Chinese robotic lawnmowers in November. Several people in the industry said they expected any final EU duty to exceed 20 per cent – one person put it at above 40 per cent. The sources asked not to be named because of the sensitive nature of the matter. Even so, none of the Chinese companies at IFA showed any signs of pulling back from Europe. An anti-dumping investigation could raise the barrier to entry, but may not dissuade companies with deep pockets, other businesses to fall back on and a complete supply network, said Guan Ruhang, marketing head of the new-category business unit at Roborock. Roborock, which began selling mowers in Germany in March, is pushing into authorised specialist dealers, Amazon and the building materials chain Bauhaus. Mammotion said it had about 1,000 employees, large for a company in the sector, and was still hiring in sales and engineering. The threat of steep anti-dumping duties was also prompting several Chinese makers to redraw their supply chains. Mova said it and other companies were considering plants in Southeast Asian countries such as Vietnam to guard against potential duties. Yet regulatory pressure is only one challenge. As more Chinese firms pile into the market, their fiercest competition is not from Swedish brand Husqvarna or other established European makers, but from one another. Price has become the new battleground. Entry-level machines now sell for as little as 400-500 euros (US$465.2-US$581.6), as newer entrants chase market share. Several industry insiders who spoke with the South China Morning Post said the competition over pricing was squeezing margins to unsustainable levels. That price war leaves the cheapest models most exposed to any duties from the EU investigation, which must conclude by January 2027. The SCMP has previously reported on the industry view that machines priced above US$800 were less vulnerable and smaller players could be forced out. “We have to do everything at once,” Kong said of the challenges, from global manufacturing to deeply localised sales and marketing.

title: Opinion | Delhi’s test: make Brics work without making it work against India
description: Success for India isn’t replacing the West or empowering China – it’s walking away with more strategic choices and leverage.
content: When leaders of the Brics group of emerging economies meet in New Delhi on September 12-13, India will confront an awkward paradox: the grouping has never been bigger or harder to make coherent. What informally began as a four-member bloc comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China in 2006 has expanded into a grouping spanning Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America. Its members include major energy exporters, manufacturing powers, emerging economies and countries with sharply different relationships with Washington and Beijing. That makes Brics a more credible voice for the Global South. It also makes consensus much harder. For India, the Delhi summit is therefore less a test of whether Brics can become an alternative to the Western-led order than whether it can turn its diversity into something useful. The answer will depend heavily on how New Delhi manages its most obvious contradiction: China. India wants Brics to give emerging economies greater influence over global institutions and reduce their vulnerability to Western-dominated financial systems. However, it has no interest in replacing dependence on the US dollar with dependence on China. That tension will shape the summit’s biggest ambitions, particularly de-dollarisation, cross-border payments and supply chain cooperation. A common Brics currency remains an attractive political slogan but a distant economic prospect. There is a more concrete economic prize at stake. The bloc accounts for around 40 per cent of global GDP and half of the world’s population. If Brics members can make national currency settlements easier, connect payment systems and reduce transaction costs, an Indian exporter could potentially receive payment from a Brazilian, Emirati or Indonesian buyer without routing every transaction through dollar-based intermediaries. Such linkages could give companies alternatives when geopolitical shocks disrupt established routes. That makes Brics economically relevant even without a common currency or a break with the US dollar. The bigger opportunity for India is to turn the grouping into a network that makes trade, investment and payments easier among its members. Even so, Delhi must protect its own interests first. It wants Brics markets and investment while simultaneously seeking Western capital, technology and export opportunities. It cannot afford to let de-dollarisation become a campaign against the US-led financial system, and neither can it accept digital or financial infrastructure that increases dependence on China. This is why India’s strategic dilemma is sharper than simply balancing East and West. It wants Brics to dilute the dominance of Western financial and trade systems, but it does not want China to emerge as the dominant power inside the alternative. India needs Chinese manufacturing and Brics markets while simultaneously trying to reduce its dependence on Chinese imports and deepen supply chain ties with the United States, Europe and Japan. It wants more trade in national currencies, but not a financial architecture that gives Beijing greater leverage. Delhi’s strategic autonomy works only if India retains multiple options. That is why India’s best strategy might be to make Brics more useful, not more ideological. Delhi can push for practical cooperation on payments, trade, energy, critical minerals and supply chains while resisting demands for a common currency or a unified geopolitical line. Brics has no binding collective foreign policy or obligation to act as a bloc. Its members have different relationships with the US, China and each other, and their interests can diverge sharply. That clarifies what it is: a forum where countries with different political systems and strategic priorities can coordinate when their interests overlap and push for greater influence over institutions that still reflect an older distribution of global power. India should build on that reality rather than fight it. The real measure of the Delhi summit should be whether members can agree on practical mechanisms that survive beyond the summit: easier cross-border payments, more resilient supply chains, greater trade in national currencies, stronger cooperation among businesses and a louder collective demand for reform of global institutions. If Brics can deliver even on a few of these, its expansion will look like strength rather than sprawl. India’s test in Delhi is whether it can make the grouping work for Indian interests without becoming captive to anyone else’s agenda. For India, a successful Brics is not one that replaces the West or empowers China. It is one that leaves India with more choices, more leverage and fewer dependencies than it had before.

title: Ex-Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa worked to bridge US-China divide even in final years
description: In one of his final public engagements, Tung visited SCMP headquarters in Causeway Bay in 2020 to deliver keynote speech at China Conference.
content: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive who died on Tuesday at the age of 89, kept a low profile in the final years of his life, making only a few public appearances but continuing to help bridge the China-US divide. Wearing a face mask and accompanied by his wife Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, Tung visited the South China Morning Post’s headquarters in Causeway Bay on December 1, 2020, to deliver a keynote speech at the China Conference organised by the company. Tung spoke in his capacity as a vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, a role he stepped down from in 2023. The conference was held online for global and local audiences and themed on ties with the United States, asking: “Can unravelling relations be reversed?” Tung was a long-time proponent and facilitator of Sino-US relations, with his views partly informed by the decade he spent in the country. He and Betty married in New York in 1961. At the SCMP conference, Tung called for the US to cast aside its hostility and misconceptions about China so the two nations could come up with solutions to the challenges facing the world, including the Covid-19 pandemic. He also noted that Hong Kong, along with Xinjiang and Taiwan, had become one of the biggest sticking points in Sino-US relations and China’s ties with other Western powers. Tung underscored that “Beijing would never want to destroy” the “one country, two systems” governing principle. Weeks later, on December 17, he spoke at an online conference organised by Our Hong Kong Foundation, the think tank he co-founded in 2014. Tung’s final public appearance was in July 2021 when he attended the premiere of a film marking the centenary of the Communist Party of China.

title: Man in Singapore gets protection order against wife who sent AI obscene images
description: The court found the act of sending of fake images and videos of the man and his sister engaging in sexual acts amounted to family violence.
content: A family court has granted a man a personal protection order (PPO) against his wife, who had abused him emotionally or psychologically with text messages about him having sex with his sister. The court found that the sending of fake images and videos of the husband and his sister engaging in sexual acts, generated by artificial intelligence, amounted to family violence. The man had sought the PPO alleging that his wife had inflicted emotional or psychological abuse on him by accusing him of having sex with his sister. The wife had an acrimonious relationship with her husband’s sister, according to a judgment published on Wednesday. The man said what sparked the saga was that he had agreed to contribute S$100,000 (US$79,120) towards his father’s medical bills. He also informed his wife that he had transferred about S$65,000 to his sister. Magistrate Soh Kian Peng said the wife’s angry response was to send messages that were “hideously offensive and vile”, and that the man was evidently “tormented and distressed” at trial. He found that the man had proved both requirements for protective orders in the familial context – establishing that the wife had committed family violence on him, and that an order was needed for his protection or personal safety. Soh said there were 90 pages of screenshots from the husband showing not only the texts sent to the husband by the wife, but also explicit fake images and videos of the man and his sister. The wife did not dispute sending these messages to her husband. She said she had used a free application to produce the obscene images and videos. Soh said it was “abundantly clear” that the messages and shots sent had inflicted emotional or psychological abuse on the man. He gave what he described as “but a small excerpt” of the text messages, with the woman describing her sister-in-law in sexual terms. The husband had lost weight “precipitously”, the magistrate noted. He found that there was a high risk of the wife continuing to inflict family violence on her husband by sending such messages, noting that she had stopped when her husband made the court application. The magistrate said the conflict between the couple concerning the sister-in-law remained unresolved, noting that it was hardly possible and there could not be any expectation that the husband cut off all contact with his sister to avoid conflict with his wife. Soh added that while the wife might have had her own grievances and frustration with her husband, she did not have a healthy way of expressing these emotions. Besides granting the PPO to the man, the magistrate also ordered the couple to go for counselling. This story was first published by CNA

title: Hysan courts fintech office portfolio as ZA Bank commits to new Causeway Bay headquarters
description: As landlords navigate soft office demand, tech and digital enterprises are stepping in to capitalise on falling rents and more favourable terms.
content: Digital bank ZA Bank is taking 45,000 square feet (4,181 square metres) across four upper floors at Hysan Development’s Lee Garden Eight for its new headquarters, adding to a wave of financial and technology companies reshaping Causeway Bay’s commercial landscape.
