The move comes as landlords across the district grapple with a changing property market marked by excess office space. The bank is scheduled to move into Tower 3 in 2027, coinciding with Hysan and partner Chinachem Group completing the delivery of about 1.1 million square feet of commercial space to the district in the fourth quarter of this year. The leasing push comes as Causeway Bay and Wan Chai continue to absorb office supply, with demand recovering more slowly than in Central. Grade A office vacancy in the two districts stood at 9.8 per cent in August, according to property consultancy JLL. Hysan’s office portfolio was 93 per cent occupied at the end of June, down from 94 per cent six months earlier. Office turnover fell 1.3 per cent in the first half to HK$694 million (US$88.5 million), while rental reversions remained negative, according to interim results published in August. To offset these trends, Hysan has targeted more fintech and other digital economy tenants for Lee Garden Eight. Over the past few years, ample supply and cheaper rents have prompted some companies in the district to move to Central. “The new economy tenant portfolio is becoming stronger,” said Ricky Lui, Hysan’s executive director and chief operating officer. Leasing activity, he noted, had picked up recently, with the current tenant mix roughly split among financial services, professional services and co-working operators. “The pre-leasing is progressing well,” Lui added, saying Lee Garden Eight had reached double-digit occupancy. “The project is definitely one of the choices tenants consider when they look for a new location, and we are very confident about that.” For ZA Bank – which began operating in 2020, surpassed 1 million users last year and now has about 400 to 500 employees – the expansion would support continued hiring, said CEO Calvin Ng. “We have been staying in our previous office for quite a long time, so we want to upgrade both the hardware and software,” Ng said at a welcoming ceremony on Wednesday. “We also want a workplace that is more comfortable and convenient for employees, including better options for social gatherings and dining,” Ng noted, citing Causeway Bay’s mix of offices, restaurants and other amenities as an important factor in the bank’s decision. ZA Bank has no immediate plans to open a physical branch. The broader shift is also visible at street level. Causeway Bay was once one of Hong Kong’s main luxury shopping districts, with international brands paying some of the city’s highest retail rents. As rents have fallen, financial and technology companies have started taking prominent retail space. EleBank, another licensed digital bank, is taking a 1,640-square-foot ground-floor shop in Causeway Bay for about HK$500,000 a month, according to market sources. That stood at about 76 per cent below the HK$2.1 million monthly rent paid by Fossil for the shop at its peak in 2012, according to Midland Realty.

title: Beijing tells Manila to ‘stop lying’ after minister exposes South China Sea note
description: At Seoul Defence Dialogue, Gilberto Teodoro Jnr brands China’s handwritten memo on arbitration ruling as ‘coercion and bullying’.
content: China has accused Philippine officials of “grandstanding and lying” after Manila’s defence secretary publicly read aloud a Chinese diplomat’s note on the South China Sea that the Philippine minister described as “coercion, bullying and aggression”. “We urge certain people in the Philippines to stop this grandstanding and lying, and to protect China-Philippine relations and the peace and stability in the South China Sea,” Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said. Mao was responding to a question regarding the remarks of Gilberto Teodoro Jnr who – while speaking at a Seoul Defence Dialogue session on Tuesday – received a note reiterating China’s position on the South China Sea arbitration. Teodoro read out parts of the handwritten note, which included Beijing’s rejection of the arbitration and a statement that the award in 2016 denying most of China’s claims in the South China Sea, was “illegal, null and void”. The forum organiser later said the note came from a military attache at the Chinese embassy in Seoul, who passed it to a forum staff member and asked that it be given to Teodoro, according to South Korean news agency Yonhap. Teodoro said the move was impolite to their South Korean hosts. “How can you deal with a country in an international forum beyond the question asked to me?” he said. “Disrespecting the organisers of this forum, how do you expect to deal with it civilly?” Teodoro said the note also showed disrespect for international law. “So, perhaps basic decency and behaviour is what China needs to do … This is actual coercion, bullying, and aggression,” he said, adding that he would keep the note as a “memento of how desperate China is”. On Wednesday, the Philippine foreign ministry weighed in, with assistant secretary and spokeswoman Analyn Ratonel saying in Manila: “We respect the statement and views of Secretary Teodoro.” Tuesday’s episode came amid heightened tension over the disputed waters in the South China Sea, where confrontations – and sometimes clashes – between coastguard and naval vessels from China and the Philippines have prompted concern of a military escalation that could draw in the United States, a treaty ally of the Philippines. In June, in a rare move targeting a sitting senior foreign official, Beijing announced sanctions on Teodoro for what Beijing said were erroneous remarks against China that undermined China’s legitimate interests and damaged bilateral relations.

title: Young Argentines’ mounting debt struggles test support for Milei
description: Nearly half of Argentina’s 45 million people owe money, and more than 5 million are behind on payments, according to a non-profit group.
content: At 18, Martin Taborda began studying law at Argentina’s prestigious University of Buenos Aires, hoping to become the first in his family to graduate. Just two years later, that dream has slipped out of reach. Unemployed and US$1,300 in debt, he can no longer afford the bus fare from his suburb or the books he needs to keep studying – even at a tuition-free university that has helped generations of Argentines climb into the middle class. He’s not alone. Nearly half of Argentina’s 45 million people owe money, and more than 5 million are behind on payments, according to the Centre for City Studies, an Argentine non-profit that tracks debt using central bank data. Borrowers under 25 have the highest delinquency rate of any age group, at 37.6 per cent. “There’s hardly any work for anyone in this country right now,” said Taborda, who borrowed the equivalent of just over US$100 through a mobile payment app in 2024 for education expenses. His debt swelled tenfold as interest accrued on missed payments. Forced to rely on others, he said, “You start to feel like a parasite.” A new wave of household debt is testing support for President Javier Milei among the young Argentines who helped elect him, and offering the nation’s fragmented opposition an opening to rally disillusioned voters ahead of next year’s presidential election. Opposition lawmakers have called a special session of Congress for Wednesday to consider interest-rate caps and other measures to help Argentines renegotiate their debts. Labour unions and debtors planned to protest outside the building during the debate, which strikes at the heart of Milei’s free-market experiment as voters increasingly look beyond his success in taming inflation to bigger concerns about jobs and wages. “Households took on debt to survive and now cannot repay it,” left-wing lawmaker Nicolas del Cano and fellow sponsors wrote in their legislative proposal, describing it as “an emergency measure to address the crisis”. Milei has rejected calls for government relief, arguing that unpaid debts are a private matter between borrowers and lenders rather than a symptom of wider economic distress. Economy Minister Luis Caputo promised at a recent press conference that banks were easing repayment terms, although he added, “We shouldn’t confuse empathy with public policy.” On a recent afternoon, Taborda joined a few dozen other students in a classroom at his university’s economics school to discuss the emotional toll of their debts. The gathering followed confidentiality rules similar to those of Alcoholics Anonymous. A moderator asked for a show of hands: Who bought groceries in instalments? Who borrowed through payment apps to make ends meet? Who took on debt to repay old loans? Most hands went up. Since assuming office in late 2023 promising to break with a discredited political establishment, Milei has slashed the budget deficit and brought annual inflation down from a peak of 289 per cent in early 2024 to about 34 per cent in July. The greater macroeconomic stability has encouraged banks to lend more, while steep cuts to subsidies for petrol, electricity and transport have pushed bills up faster than incomes, forcing many Argentines to borrow just to get by. In the past, wage increases meant to keep pace with runaway inflation could gradually ease the burden of fixed loan payments. Now, slower inflation means smaller pay rises, while borrowing costs remain sky-high under the government’s tight monetary policy. Digital payment apps require less paperwork than banks but often charge much higher interest because of the greater risk, with annual rates reaching triple digits. “There was a time when people took out loans to buy a house, an apartment, a car,” said Vanesa Bittoco, a spokeswoman for Organised Debtors, an advocacy group that campaigns for repayment plans tied to workers’ incomes. “Now people take out loans to buy food to make it to the end of the month.” At the anonymous debtors’ meeting, students described feeling trapped, ashamed and increasingly powerless over their futures. The distress extends beyond campus: More than 80 per cent of adults surveyed in Buenos Aires and its suburbs in April said economic problems had a major impact on their psychological well-being, according to the university’s Applied Social Psychology Observatory. Experts warn that Argentines’ mounting debt struggles could erode Milei’s support among young voters as he seeks a second term in the 2027 presidential election just 14 months away. “Clearly, the economic model is hitting young people much harder than other Argentines,” said public opinion consultant Ana Iparraguirre, a partner at Washington-based strategy firm GBAO. “If this continues, Milei is putting his re-election at risk with the same electorate that helped him win.” Milei has offered little sympathy for struggling Argentines, blaming the surge in delinquencies on irresponsible spending. “They bought TVs to watch the World Cup and figured they’d decide later whether to pay,” he told investors in the port city of Rosario last month. “Well, now they haven’t paid.” The debt squeeze comes as Milei’s broader support has weakened. A recent online poll of 1,500 people by well-known Argentine pollster Zuban Cordoba put approval of Milei’s administration at 33 per cent, down from 49 per cent in December 2025, with most respondents saying they are worse off financially than when Milei took office. The survey, conducted from July 22 to 26, reported a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. “They’re going to have to provide a solution,” Bittoco, the advocate, said of the government. “Otherwise, they’re the ones who will have a problem.”

title: Court acquits brother of incest, citing failure to prove teen knew it was wrong
description: Man was 11 to 14 years old at the time of alleged offences, while his sister, now 20, was between seven and 10.
content: A Hong Kong court has found a 24-year-old man not guilty of committing a spate of sexual offences against his younger sister a decade ago, ruling that prosecutors failed to prove the defendant knew what he did as a teenager was seriously wrong. A High Court jury of five men and two women acquitted the defendant on Thursday of four counts of incest and three of indecent conduct towards a child under 16. The verdict came at the direction of the presiding judge, who concluded that the charges could not be legally established. The man, identified in court only by his initials LHCN, was accused of committing grossly obscene acts against his younger sibling at the family’s home in Sha Tau Kok between September 2013 and July 2016. He was 11 to 14 years old at the time of the alleged offences, while his sister, now 20, was between seven and 10. Following his arrest in 2021, the defendant admitted engaging in sexual acts with his sister and expressed deep regret. In a police interview, he insisted that he did not rape his sister, while claiming his elder brother had also committed obscene acts against her. According to the defendant, the girl resorted to self-harm and attempted suicide after failing to cope with the blame and guilt of engaging in sexual acts with her blood relatives. She eventually disclosed the incidents to a social worker who later informed her parents. The Juvenile Offenders Ordinance stipulates that no child under the age of 10 can be held liable for a crime. Common law also presumes that a child aged between 10 and 13 is incapable of breaking the law, unless the prosecution can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the child knew their act was so seriously wrong that it went beyond mere naughtiness or childish mischief. Prosecutors argued the 24-year-old man showed “a clear degree of maturity beyond a child of similar age” based on the language he used towards his sister. But Madam Justice Susana D’Almada Remedios said the prosecution failed to show why the common law presumption of a child’s criminal responsibility should not be applied in the present case. She said that while the prosecution attempted to show the defendant’s knowledge of sex by calling two teachers from his schools to testify, neither witness could show that he understood the gravity of his actions. Remedios also noted that the accused had only admitted engaging in sexual acts with his sister during the police interview. “Proof of the act itself that comprises the offence is not evidence to prove that the defendant knew what he did was wrong, or seriously wrong; therefore knowledge that the act was wrong or seriously wrong cannot be presumed from the mere commission of the act,” the judge explained. The siblings’ 48-year-old father, identified only as LWD, is scheduled to be sentenced on Wednesday after pleading guilty to perverting the course of justice by asking his daughter to drop her allegations against her two elder brothers.

title: Review | 54 horses dazzle at Cavalluna’s Hong Kong debut, despite cliché story
description: Cavalluna’s Asian debut stunned the city with its spectacular horsemanship, but plain and flawed storytelling was a fly in the ointment.
content: Hong Kong is no stranger to equine sports, hosting both horse racing and world-class equestrian events such as the Longines Hong Kong International Horse Show, where elite showjumpers compete. But Cavalluna – Gate to the Otherworld, an equestrian spectacle from Europe that combines high-level horsemanship, dance, acrobatics and theatre, takes equestrian experience and entertainment to another level. The production, which is presented by the Hong Kong Jockey Club and runs until September 13 at Kai Tak Arena, features 54 horses of various breeds, sizes and colours. They are cast as characters in a fantastical tale about the sorceress Meerin and her journey from losing her magical powers to rediscovering faith in herself. But Cavalluna – a name derived from caballo and luna, the Spanish words for horse and moon – is far more than a simple display of beautiful horses. The evening at the arena featured both breathtaking and thrilling moments that highlighted the riders’ skills and their extraordinary partnership with the animals. In one scene, an evil wizard rides a galloping white horse hands-free. Set against Emmy-nominated composer Klaus Hillebrecht’s soul-stirring score, it looked as though the wizard – with a giant crystal ball floating above – was magically flying across the arena. In another, the ponies won over the audience with adorable jumps, kicks and humorous, intentional disobedience as one lay on the ground like a puppy refusing to heed its trainer’s call. The performances also featured dramatic special effects, with two riders flicking a rope that was ablaze. Meanwhile, other horses and riders wore light-up costumes in the pitch-black arena, appearing like sci-fi phantoms. The most heart-stopping moments belonged to a troupe of acrobats who balanced upside down on galloping horses, riding backwards, performing splits and stabilising themselves along the sides of the horses through pure core strength. When one rider fell, he was quick to remount for a triumphant second attempt. The production also incorporated Bollywood dance, step dance and aerial acrobatics into its narrative. While the story itself can feel a bit cliché, with plot points that leave the audience unconvinced – a sudden romance out of nowhere, or a king far too gullible to change his mind – the nearly three-hour show is not really about storytelling anyway. Showcasing remarkable athleticism and hair-raising feats, the horses and their riders were the true stars of the night. “Cavalluna – Gate to the Otherworld”, Kai Tak Arena. Reviewed: September 8. For more information, visit cavalluna.com

title: Hong Kong astronaut inspires pupils across city’s school halls in historic live lecture
description: City’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying and crewmates offer glimpse into their lives and experiments in space, inspiring youngsters in Hong Kong and Macau.
content: Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying has conducted a live lesson for students of her alma mater from the Tiangong space station, showing them how chicken wings are cooked in zero gravity and how she locates the city’s lights from the darkness of space. In a livecast to teachers and students of Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College on Wednesday that was also streamed at other campuses across Hong Kong and Macau, Lai offered a glimpse of life in orbit and the experiments her team conducted. She also encouraged students during a question-and-answer session to build a solid foundation in maths and science, telling them to “keep pushing and never fear hardships”. “My education background, research and development experience, and my career have laid critical foundations for me to seize this opportunity. I hope students can constantly equip themselves and be brave and proactive as opportunities come along,” she said. Lai and her crewmates, mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan, joined the “Tiangong class” at the school, jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency. The 90-minute session was streamed on campuses across the city, broadcast on television and aired to students in Macau, with youth, and innovation and technology representatives and a visiting Macau delegation also in attendance. Lai opened the lesson by spinning a top, echoing the gyroscope that opened China’s first Tiangong class delivered by astronaut Wang Yaping. Colonel Zhu introduced the station’s three modules and showed how recycled water also helped to produce oxygen. Lai then gave a tour of her sleeping area, which is decorated with her children’s drawings, family photos, models of Hong Kong street food and the police force’s anti-scam mascot. “When we pass over China, I always look for the Greater Bay Area. Although Hong Kong is small in size, it has bright lights at night,” she said. Speaking at the school, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the government was planning an astronomy-themed popular science education campaign, and urged the public to take part in the activities. “I also hope that the younger generation will take astronauts as their role models, strive to equip themselves, have the courage to pursue their dreams, and use their wisdom and hard work to contribute towards building the nation into a strong nation in space and opening a brilliant new chapter for the Chinese nation,” he said. Before the class, Lai’s former teachers recalled her school days. Principal Lau Sui-yee described her as a diligent student and active student union member, while university supervisor Chow Kam-pui remembered her as a team player with strong analytical skills. Students raised questions about AI and experiments in orbit. Lai said the station had begun trials of AI and robots that documented the crew’s tasks and inspected narrow ventilation ducts. The crew also described some of their experiments, involving animals such as zebrafish and mice, that examined how zero gravity affected living organisms. Lai also shared the toughest challenges she endured before the space mission, from desert survival exercises and a 72-hour sleep deprivation test to six days of cave training. She lifted off aboard Shenzhou-23 in May 2026, becoming Hong Kong’s first astronaut and China’s first female payload specialist. One student asked how maths and science had helped her to become an astronaut. “Take mathematics and science seriously and learn how to connect the dots between different fields to put your knowledge into practice in the future,” Lai replied. Lai also responded to letters from students and briefly spoke with city leader Lee before concluding the lesson at about 11.30am. “My presence in space has shown how the nation supports and attaches importance to Hong Kong. We are very lucky to experience an era of a strong and thriving nation,” she said. Form Five student Chan King-lam, who studies physics, chemistry, biology and extended mathematics at the school, said the dialogue inspired him to explore science and that he hoped one day to take part in the country’s research. “How Lai sacrificed family time for this career really earns our respect and makes me want to improve on my science studies,” he said. He said he was awed to see Lai demonstrate textbook physics principles in zero gravity during the broadcast. “What impressed me most was watching them cook chicken wings and cakes. It really shows how difficult preparing fresh food is in space,” he said. Without gravity, heat cannot circulate through air as it does on Earth, so Lai said they relied on special equipment such as forced-air ovens instead of microwaves to make their meals. Form Six student Chan Tsz-ki said she was proud to see an alumna of her school become an astronaut and saw Lai as a role model as she pursued her science studies. “I feel very close to her as we are using the same campus, the same facilities and some teachers are still the same,” she said. “I will also study hard to contribute to the country.” Lai, a former Hong Kong police superintendent with a doctorate in computer science, was selected in 2024 as part of China’s fourth batch of astronauts. Before her selection, Lai was attached to police’s technical services division and was later transferred to the Security Bureau. Lai grew up in Tsuen Wan and attended Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College in the 1990s. She enrolled at the University of Hong Kong in 2001, where she majored in computer science and information systems and later completed her doctorate.

title: China GT bosses ‘grossly negligent’ over fiery crash, team says; staff pay rumours swirl
description: Leaked recruitment screenshots show security jobs paying as little as US$8.50 for daily-wage workers to ‘watch the site and maintain order’.
content: The organisers of the China GT Championship in which British driver Ollie Millroy almost died have been accused of “gross negligence” amid claims some track staff were gig workers being paid just 60 yuan (US$8.50) a day. Millroy’s car burst into flames after a three-vehicle collision at the Shanghai International Circuit, and he was pulled from the burning wreckage by 23-year-old Dutch driver Loek Hartog with fire marshals and stewards nowhere to be seen. According to his Instagram account, the 36-year-old Englishman sustained six broken ribs, a broken collarbone, a broken hand and a punctured lung in the accident, which took place on the seventh lap of Saturday’s race. He underwent a four-hour operation in a Shanghai hospital to insert plates and screws into the broken bones. Doctors also inserted a drain line into his abdomen to release gas and fluid leaking from his lung. “I am still alive tonight, entirely thanks to one man. Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight and risked his own life to get me out of the car,” Millroy wrote on his Instagram account. “I don’t remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and 1 hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life.” 吴彦祖批评 GT China不负责任，草菅人命。 pic.twitter.com/hKlwJlwYQS — 卓野Joey (@LMDC5288) September 7, 2026 Yang Baijie, of 610 Racing, was one of the drivers involved in the crash and claimed on social media that emergency workers had “dropped their fire extinguishers out of fear and fled”, while an ambulance took 15 minutes to arrive at the scene. The Chinese racer was particularly angry that the first reaction from stewards was “to try to shift the blame to us, asking if we could direct public opinion towards us to reduce their negative impact”. In a long statement, Millroy’s team, AAI Motorsports, attacked the conduct of organisers and said they would not race in China until there had been a “comprehensive investigation” and the results made public. “The event organiser was grossly negligent in its emergency response and safety rescue arrangements, with serious deficiencies in the rescue response that nearly resulted in a tragedy,” the team wrote. “Even more outrageously, during the live broadcast of the accident, event staff failed to verify the on-site situation and hastily reported that the driver had left the wrecked vehicle on his own. In fact, the driver of our No 91 car was pulled out of the burning car by Loek Hartog, driver of the No 79 car of Phantom Team who risked his own life to carry out the rescue.” 60 RMB a day. That’s ~US$8–9. Not per hour. Per full day. That’s what track marshals were paid at China GT Shanghai. No wonder they dropped the extinguishers and ran when the Ferrari caught fire. You don’t risk your life for a rate that barely covers lunch and the metro. A… https://t.co/zGlsrLGYfK pic.twitter.com/Z9I3ddSTiW — The Great Translation Movement 大翻译运动 (@TGTM_Official) September 8, 2026 Yang also said he was permanently withdrawing from China GT, adding that an onboard camera had captured the incident, and he would take legal action if organisers did not take responsibility for the issue. His version of events was supported by actor and driver Daniel Wu, who had retired after crashing in a race the previous day. During a live stream, Wu said it had taken between 30 seconds and a minute for race officials to issue a red flag, while marshals were “bungling around, [and] clearly did not know what they were doing or did not know what to do in a situation like this”. “Not sure why the fire truck took so long to get there, but clearly mistakes were made all along the way. For Chinese motorsport to be better, these organisers need to be better,” Wu added. The accident and its aftermath triggered widespread outrage on Chinese social media, exposing the extensive use of multi-tiered subcontracting, known locally as waibao, for event security and emergency staff. In China, labour dispatching is common for large events, where budgets pass through main contractors, subcontractors and intermediaries, leaving frontline workers with minimal pay. Leaked recruitment screenshots showed security posts paying as little as 60 yuan for daily-wage workers, with job descriptions limited to “watching the site and maintaining order”. “What do you expect a 60-yuan-a-day security worker to do? His daily wage isn’t even worth as much as the fire extinguisher,” one social media user noted. Another worker claiming to have checked tickets at the same event posted that ticket checkers earned 180 yuan a day, while security personnel received 200 yuan for shifts lasting from 7.30am to past 5pm. Organisers claimed an initial review showed event staffing met national standards, and promised a comprehensive post-race review. “According to our preliminary review, the event’s overall staffing and resources met the standards required for a national-level motorsport event, although there remains room for improvement in detailed operational management,” organisers wrote. “We will conduct a further review and investigation into the accident and develop more comprehensive plans to address shortcomings in race organisation, support arrangements, emergency response, rescue operations and medical services.”

title: Indonesia has new food safety rules for free meals. Why are students still falling ill?
description: In three days last week alone, close to 2,000 students suffered from food poisoning after eating meals from Prabowo’s flagship programme.
content: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s flagship free nutritious meals programme is facing renewed scrutiny after yet another wave of mass food poisoning that affected more than 2,000 students, raising questions about why safeguards on paper fail to translate to food safety on the ground. A series of illnesses were reported in Java, Sumatra, and Sulawesi in the past week. The latest was on Tuesday in Rembang, Central Java, where 200 students of an Islamic school showed symptoms of food poisoning such as vomiting and diarrhoea after eating meals from the programme. Between September 1 and 3, a total of 1,961 students suffered from food poisoning across the country, many requiring medical treatment. In the case in East Java’s Sidoarjo on Thursday, at least 730 students of Manbaul Hikam Islamic boarding school fell ill after lunch. Sudaryono, head of the National Nutrition Agency (BGN), which supervises Prabowo’s initiative, chalked up the incident to “deliberate negligence”. Last month, BGN issued new safety protocols to prevent mass food poisoning – a recurring problem since the US$15.2 billion programme was launched in January 2025. At least 43,000 children had suffered from food poisoning linked to the programme by the end of August, according to data from the Network for Education Watch. Prabowo’s administration promised reforms to fix the initiative, following the arrest of BGN’s former head and top officials for alleged mark-ups and corruption in June. Fake information Among the new protocols is a mandatory requirement for meals to be consumed within four hours of cooking, with expiry labels to be placed on all food trays. In the Sidoarjo case, the expiry labels bore false information and were plastered on one food tray, instead of all trays, Sudaryono said on Thursday, as cited by Detik. “Preliminary investigation shows that the food was cooked at 5am, so it should be consumed before 9am … However, the label showed that it was cooked at 8am … and not all food trays were labelled,” he said. “The food … was delivered to the school after 11am. The students ate it only after 12pm, resulting in food poisoning.” Sudaryono said in a video posted on his Instagram account on Tuesday that he had fired the head of the kitchen responsible. Since August 3, BGN has sacked at least 137 heads of kitchens in various regions due to lax food safety. BGN has forbidden students to bring the meals home, as food quality could decrease the longer it is left uneaten. Last month, it said it would introduce a test kit in each kitchen to detect spoilage. Each kitchen partner is also required to obtain a Certificate of Hygiene and Sanitation Suitability from the Ministry of Health. Those without certificates will be shut down. Sudaryono said on Tuesday that the agency had temporarily closed 1,999 out of the 27,022 kitchens in the programme for failure to be certified. Nutrition expert Tan Shot Yen said the latest wave of food-poisoning cases underlined a lack of effective monitoring and enforcement, which could render BGN’s new food safety measures futile. “There are now regulations regarding [the food safety] in the programme, but is there monitoring? That’s what’s important. In Indonesia, people have a driving licence, but they still get hit by trains because they want to rush ahead. Law enforcement is always an issue in Indonesia,” Tan said. She also questioned whether each kitchen examined the health status of their food handlers, especially when meals are garnished with raw vegetables such as lettuce or tomatoes. Sudaryono and BGN did not respond to This Week in Asia’s requests for comments. Tighter focus Jimmy Daniel Berlianto, a senior researcher at the Centre for Indonesian Policy Studies, said the new cases showed that “governance” remained a “fundamental issue” in the free nutritious meals programme. “The change we hope for is for the [programme] to transition to a locally-driven approach, driven by community actors such as schools and public health facilities,” Berlianto said. “Regional governments, along with local communities, should also be empowered to adjust the programme according to their respective problems and needs.” BGN currently manages all aspects of the programme, from granting kitchens’ operational permits to monitoring their operations. Both experts said that the programme’s beneficiaries, currently at 63 million, could be trimmed down to include only children in remote, underdeveloped and frontier regions. Prabowo aims to distribute the meals to nearly 83 million schoolchildren, toddlers, breastfeeding mothers, and pregnant women to prevent stunted growth and malnutrition. But the programme is not the only way to achieve these goals, according to the experts. To address stunted growth, Tan suggested the government pledged more funds to the existing supplemental feeding programme offered by health centres across Indonesia. Under the initiative, toddlers and pregnant women were given meals “cooked under the supervision of nutritionists” for up to 90 days, she said. As for malnutrition, Berlianto said that officials should focus on delivering the meals to children from poor families. “The free nutritious meal programme still has a positive impact if implemented in a targeted manner,” he said. “Many studies in other countries show that free school meals could improve nutritional status and educational participation for those with high levels of vulnerability, such as children from poor households.”

title: Power of Siberia 2 pipeline talks stall over China-Russia price dispute: sources
description: Moscow-Beijing negotiations over pipeline have halted as ‘no progress’ made on bridging a big gas price gap, sources say.
content: China and Russia’s negotiations regarding the construction of the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline have stalled, according to multiple sources who have knowledge of the issue, as both sides cannot bridge a big gap over gas price expectations. “China hopes to secure a price comparable to Russia’s subsidised residential rate, around US$50/thousand cubic metres, or at least the domestic industrial rate of about US$120-130/thousand cubic metres,” said one source, who asked for anonymity due to the sensitivity of the issue. But Russia has a different expectation, as it wants to reference the price of the existing Power of Siberia 1 pipeline, which is about US$250-260/thousand cubic metres, the source added. China’s current average gas import price via Power of Siberia 1 is about US$258/thousand cubic metres, the source noted, while Russia’s selling price to Europe before the Ukraine war was over US$420/thousand cubic metres. “It seems to me that Gazprom and CNPC (China National Petroleum Corporation) are preparing to begin supplying Russian gas to China via the Far East route and are discussing projects to expand and increase supplies along this route,” said a second source, who also asked to remain anonymous. “The same is happening with the Power of Siberia 1 – we see that they are also working to increase physical supplies.” The planned 2,600km (1,553 miles) Power of Siberia 2 pipeline is expected to carry 50 billion cubic metres of gas per year ‌to ⁠China via Mongolia from the Arctic gas fields of Yamal, which is also assumed to serve as a complement to Power of Siberia 1 or the China-Russia Far East Gas Pipeline. Sources confirmed that both sides had halted the decades-long negotiations for Power of Siberia 2 due to “no progress on price”. The first memorandum on the project was signed back in 2006. Russian energy minister Sergei Tsivilev announced during the Eastern Economic Forum in early September that Russian President Vladimir Putin had renamed the pipeline to “Power of Baikal”, without further explanation. China’s customs database only showed China’s monthly import volume of Russian natural gas through pipelines up to 2021. Last year, China’s import value of Russian pipeline gas rose 17.2 per cent year on year to US$9.4 billion, customs data showed. Russia’s deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said that Russia planned to deliver 50 billion cubic metres of natural gas to China in 2026, up from 38 billion cubic metres in 2025. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin were expected to discuss the Power of Siberia 2 project in a meeting in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, held between August 31 and September 1. However, the official readout did not mention such discussions. The announcement of Russia’s renaming of Power of Siberia 2, after the SCO Summit and during the Eastern Economic Forum, was “mostly a PR move for the domestic audience, which was pre-coordinated with both Beijing and Ulaanbaatar”, said Munkhnaran Bayarlkhagva, a former official at the National Security Council of Mongolia. The way Mongolia’s new prime minister, Uchral Nyam-Osor, framed the country’s intent regarding the Power of Siberia 2 pipeline as “potentially serving the principles of mutual benefit”, added Bayarlkhagva, implied that the previous articulation of Soyuz-Vostok – the connecting part of the pipeline in Mongolia – did not fully serve its interests. “In other words, Ulaanbaatar did not want to commit to ‘the Power of Siberia 2 [or] Soyuz-Vostok configurations’,” he explained. Aleksei Chigadaev, associate fellow at New Eurasian Strategies Centre, noted that China’s negotiating position was “becoming stronger by the day”, and there was little reason for Beijing to rush a decision over the construction of Power of Siberia 2. “The US factor should not be overlooked either,” added Chigadaev, pointing to the future meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump. Both sides could discuss the impact on energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, which could become yet another factor shaping China’s negotiating strategy towards Russia.

title: Alibaba sends AI ‘digital employees’ to work in rival apps from ByteDance, Tencent
description: QoderWake tool now lets users create assistants that can function within office communication platforms from rivals, as well as Alibaba’s.
content: Alibaba Group Holding is giving users the ability to put artificial intelligence-powered “digital employees” to work within rival office platforms, opening a new competitive front against ByteDance and Tencent Holdings in enterprise AI. The latest version of the QoderWake tool, launched by Alibaba Cloud on Tuesday, allowed users to generate fully functioning workers using a single-line description of the required role, the company said. These digital workers could then be put to work within any of China’s three major workplace communication platforms: Alibaba’s DingTalk, ByteDance’s Feishu and Tencent’s WeCom. QoderWake’s digital workers could “operate seamlessly” within the three workplace platforms, autonomously absorbing context from shared documents, calendars and group chats, Alibaba said on Tuesday. The move reflects how domestic tech giants are aggressively pivoting their costly AI models towards lucrative business-facing applications capable of executing complex enterprise workflows. Meanwhile, they are open to incorporating rival products at the application layer, shifting away from their traditional “walled-garden” approach. Beyond customised roles, QoderWake also had 10 ready-to-use roles, including product manager, data analyst, user interface designer and front- and back-end developer, the company said. These roles had been fine-tuned using data from top-tier industry teams, allowing them to undertake real-world tasks without requiring additional training, it added. Since its initial release in April, QoderWake had deployed nearly 100,000 digital employees, executing around 2 million tasks across real-world enterprise scenarios over the past three months, the company said. China’s office AI agent sector experienced a major catalyst in early 2026, when overseas agents like Claude Cowork created massive market buzz, prompting domestic tech companies to release more than 20 competing products within six months, according to a recent report by iiMedia Research. Tencent also accelerated its enterprise AI push this month by launching an open platform for its WorkBuddy assistant, backed by partnerships with more than 100 hardware and software developers to broaden its ecosystem. ByteDance last month launched Doubao Work, which it said could autonomously break down tasks, deploy tools and execute complicated workflows. Alibaba’s enhancements to QoderWake follow the recent global roll-out of the international version of QwenWork, the firm’s all-in-one AI productivity platform. Targeting fast-growing markets across Asia, the Middle East and Latin America, the international edition combines AI agents with multimodal capabilities. Without writing any code, users could prompt QwenWork to build web applications or generate audio, video, and office documents in a single workflow, according to the company. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: More schools close in Indonesia as haze worsens
description: Schools in Palembang switch to remote learning as haze from forest and peatland fires pushes air pollution to unhealthy levels.
content: Schools in the capital of Indonesia’s South Sumatra province switched to remote learning on Wednesday as worsening haze from forest and peatland fires pushed air pollution to unhealthy levels, adding to disruptions that had already affected more than 1.4 million students across the country, officials said. Indonesia has been plagued by forest and land fires for decades but an intensifying El Nino pattern and a prolonged dry season made the impact of the fires especially dire this year. Toxic haze and smoke have spread far beyond Indonesia’s borders in Southeast Asia, creating a regional health crisis. The smoke has drifted as far as the Philippines, more than 800km (500 miles) away, and breached Malaysia’s emergency-level threshold, forcing authorities to declare an emergency last week in a town in Sarawak state on Borneo Island. In Palembang, the capital city of South Sumatra province, schools from kindergarten to junior high were ordered to start conducting classes online on Wednesday under an emergency measure. Mayor Ratu Dewa said the thickening smoke posed health risks to children, including acute respiratory infections. “Students’ health and safety remained the government’s priority,” Dewa said. Teachers were also asked to avoid excessive assignments during the period of remote learning, he added. The policy, affecting more than 250,000 students at 1,030 schools in Palembang, would be reviewed regularly, and in-person classes will resume once conditions improve, he said. About 12,800 schools across Sumatra and Borneo islands remained closed as dangerous air quality persisted, according to government data. Save the Children, a leading international non-government organisation, said haze from wildfires, intensified by El Nino-driven dry conditions, had forced more than 1.4 million students into online learning in affected areas in Indonesia. “The Earth, our home, is on fire, and children, including here in Asia, are being left to bear the consequences,” said Arshad Malik, Save the Children’s regional director for Asia. “This is not just a health or an environmental crisis, it is a child rights crisis.” Large fires have burned thousands of hectares in Indonesia’s Kalimantan and Sumatra regions, including areas of Borneo, the world’s third-largest island shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. The wildfire crisis has been centred in Indonesia’s Kalimantan region on Borneo, where thousands of hectares have burned. Satellite Environment Ministry data on Wednesday showed that Central Kalimantan remained the country’s wildfire hotspot, with 2,459 hotspots detected. South Sumatra recorded 1,445 hotspots, the second-highest number nationwide, while West Kalimantan ranked third with 928 hotspots. Indonesian authorities have escalated firefighting efforts in several provinces as they seek to contain the blazes. The efforts have involved aircraft provided by countries in Southeast Asia and beyond, including Japan, the United States, Russia, Australia, Canada and Ukraine. Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry recorded more than 202,000 hectares of burned land between January and July, almost three times Singapore’s size.

title: How Silk Road as East-West melting pot turns Central Asia into culinary destination
description: Far more than a simple trade route, ancient network was a vibrant hub of cultural exchange that shaped modern culinary landscape, say scholars.
content: Imagine it is the height of the Tang dynasty (618–690, 705–907), and the imperial court awaits a gift of pure opulence. The exotic luxury would not have been a golden statue or precious gem; those were easy enough for high royalty to procure. Rather, it was a humble peach, specifically, the “golden peach of Samarkand,” which symbolised the allure and mystery of a faraway land. Originating in what is modern-day Uzbekistan, the luscious peach shows how food spread along the Silk Road and how Central Asia often served as a centre for cultural blending, particularly in spreading ingredients both East and West. “In many ways, Central Asia is a forgotten land, and few people in East Asia or Europe are familiar with the many names of prominent empires that rose and fell in this vast region,” said Dr Robert N. Spengler III, the director of the Paleoethnobotany Laboratories at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History in Germany. He pointed out that Central Asia sat at the crossroads of the Silk Road, and that foods like rice, chicken, and melons came from China, while items like wheat, lentils, cattle, and fava beans spread from Southwest Asia. All of them travelled through Central Asia. “However, few people acknowledge that domesticated plants originated in Central Asia, including the apple, walnut, pistachio, and quince,” said Spengler, whose team found in 2022 that pistachios were cultivated in Central Asia at least 2,000 years ago before spreading westward. As these ingredients spread, people would have used them to experiment with foods already in their diet. Dr Peter Frankopan, a Professor of Global History at Oxford University and author of the book Silk Roads and its follow-up, The New Silk Roads, said Central Asian plov is “a glorious example of how cooking seasons rice with meat.” “Fruit and spices spread not only across this region but into India and South Asia, where it is called biryani,” he said. “There are also samosas, pastries stuffed with minced meat, nuts, and other savoury ingredients, which again spread across vast distances. And of course, noodles and pasta are the signatures of the Silk Roads.” But did these ingredients explode onto the scene like any food fad? Or were the changes gradual, slowly integrating into people’s daily lived experience? Spengler said he tends to believe culinary changes were gradual. “But it is hard to parse them out in the archaeological record. Elite commodities, such as spices, likely only spread into the culinary tradition of commoners long after they were established in the broader economy.” Spengler told the SCMP that, 2000 years ago, rice was a luxury commodity in Central Asia, an idea that would be anathema today. Part of what made Central Asia such a melting pot was that merchants almost never travelled the entire length of the Silk Road, and goods were typically relayed across Asia as they made their way to the final destination. Frankopan pointed out that, for most people, the trade hubs were the point: “The Silk Roads were studded with marketplaces, towns, and cities. If you could match supply and demand, you could make serious money – not just from silks, textiles, ceramics, and technology, but from food too,” he said. Clara Wang, a food journalist who wrote about how the Silk Road created Asia’s first food diaspora, wrote that the “forces of global history blew certain foods across the desert.” She pointed to the huge varieties of dumplings that have developed across Asia. Chinese jiaozi are cousins of Korean mandu, which are vaguely similar to the Nepalese momo, reminiscent of a mantuun buzz in Mongolia. And so on, and so forth. The point is, as Frankopan, Spengler, and Wang all described, the Silk Road was far more than a trade route for imports and exports; it was a vibrant centre for cultural blending that laid the foundation for the food we still eat today. And, as any fan of food would know, our modern world’s constant cultural exchange and food experimentation are surely building the bedrock for future cuisines we cannot yet comprehend. “The evolution of food is constant, and food is a dynamic thing. Even the most traditional dishes – like spaghetti and meatballs, or risotto, or dumplings, or La Bian – something that seems sacrilegious to change in a culture, is in fact the product of constant dynamic friction between cultures,” said Wang.

title: Merging air, land and sea swarms – the next frontier in China’s drone technology
description: CETC says mature formations of similar drones are the foundation for a combat network linking uncrewed assets across domains.
content: If mastering drone-swarm technology were not difficult enough, China is now tackling the more complex task of integrating uncrewed land, sea and air platforms, according to the country’s leading developer in the field. In an article posted on China Electronics Technology Group Corporation’s (CETC) social media account on Sunday, the company’s Intelligent Technology Research Institute said drone-swarm technology was not merely “many drones flying together”, but an intelligent, distributed combat system in which aircraft communicated, coordinated, made local decisions and collectively generated capabilities. China had made advances in developing and deploying swarm systems made up of similar drones, the institute noted. The country’s longer-term goal, however, was a combat network capable of coordinating different uncrewed platforms across the entire operational area and in multiple domains. “Drone swarms are a key force for adapting to complex, intelligent future warfare and for driving changes in how modern wars are fought,” the article’s authors wrote. The disclosure is the latest indication of China’s advances in drone-swarm technology. In January, state media released footage showing one of the country’s most advanced drone-swarm systems in operation, with a single soldier reportedly able to control up to 200 drones. The institute said large-scale field tests had shown that drone swarms could autonomously reconfigure their networks, close gaps in formation and continue missions under extreme conditions, including the loss of individual units in combat, communications disruptions and intense electromagnetic interference. Work is continuing on technologies to improve the survivability of heterogeneous swarms – comprising different drone platforms – during long-range operations in heavily contested environments. On cognitive capability, the institute said its swarms could combine sensor data from multiple drones, enabling them to detect and make sense of more of their surroundings than any individual drone could alone. The article said drone swarms could autonomously screen targets, detect camouflaged objects and pinpoint their locations. They could also build a comprehensive picture of the battlefield in complex environments, enabling high-precision sensing across a wide area and in multiple domains. But the article said further improvements were needed in the ability of drone swarms to detect and identify small, concealed objects with weak sensor signatures amid heavy background clutter and intense interference. On planning and decision-making, the institute said China had fully mastered key technologies for coordinating and controlling large drone formations. The drones could be launched from various types of platform, it said, and could autonomously change formation, plan routes, avoid collisions and dynamically allocate tasks. More advanced capabilities – including tactical innovation by swarms operating in complex, unfamiliar battlefields against a capable adversary – remained at an early stage of development, it said. The article said drone swarms could be rapidly deployed and launched in large numbers within seconds. Such systems could support the full operational cycle, from all-domain reconnaissance and electromagnetic suppression to precision strikes and battle-damage assessment. But it said China still faced challenges in coordinating different types of drones and uncrewed systems across the air, land and sea, and integrating them into joint operations involving different branches of the military. China’s swarm AI could adapt to a degree, the institute said, but fully autonomous real-time learning and tactical innovation had yet to mature. As for future development, the institute said China would continue refining swarms made up of the same type of drone before pursuing technological breakthroughs that would allow different drone types to operate in mixed formations. The final stage would be the integration of all systems across all domains.

title: Houthi offensive on Bab el-Mandeb Strait threatens new Red Sea shipping crisis
description: Rebel strikes in Saudi Arabia and fierce fighting in Taiz risk choking global maritime traffic and undoing 4 years of peace.
content: A battle for control of Yemen’s coastal plains overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, launched on Friday by Iran-aligned Houthi rebels, is rapidly intensifying into an all-out war with Saudi-backed government forces. A wave of Houthi missile and drone strikes launched against four cities in southern Saudi Arabia early on Tuesday, injuring 73 civilians, may prove to be the tipping point in the conflict, analysts say. Coinciding with an escalating battle of attrition between the United States and Iran for control of the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi air strikes are widely viewed as a precursor to a parallel conflict with Saudi Arabia for dominance over the Red Sea. As with Hormuz, the intense fighting in Yemen’s Taiz and Hodeidah governorates is expected to strangle maritime traffic using the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Indian Ocean to Europe via the Suez Canal. A Houthi embargo imposed in July on Saudi shipping transiting the strait has forced the kingdom to divert oil exports from Red Sea ports to Asia around Africa, adding thousands of kilometres and associated costs to tanker voyages. “We are looking at both the return of Houthi cross-border attacks into Saudi Arabia and the resumption of the group’s efforts to bring a virtual halt to Red Sea shipping,” said Adam Baron, a veteran Yemen analyst and fellow with the future security programme at the Washington-based think tank New America. The economic and political fallout of this escalation risked “further shaking the wider region”, particularly as it effectively underlined the potential capacity of the Iran-led axis of resistance to “squeeze US-aligned Gulf states from both sides of the Arabian Peninsula”, Baron said. Analysts said it was unclear how much of a role Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps played in the Houthi push to decisively change the balance of power in Yemen following four years of relative peace. According to Baron, the escalation instead underlined the extent to which it remained in the Houthis’ interests – both as an autonomous force and as part of the axis of resistance – to “maintain a demonstrable capacity to shut down Bab el-Mandeb”. Particularly in light of the situation in Hormuz, “this remains a key point of leverage for Iran’s wider regional network”, he said. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed no such doubts about Tehran’s involvement. “The Houthis, in many ways, are agents and proxies of the Iranians,” Rubio told reporters in Washington on Tuesday. “I think behind some of this is clearly the Iranian hand.” Speaking in Moscow on Tuesday, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Farhan bin Faisal refrained from directly pointing fingers at the Islamic Republic, but warned the Houthi militia that it had embarked on a course of action whose consequences “it will not be able to handle”. While Farhan reiterated the kingdom’s openness to a negotiated political settlement in Yemen, he stressed that Saudi Arabia “will not hesitate to defend ourselves and we will not hesitate to protect our interests”. The strident tone of his remarks led many Saudi analysts to conclude that Riyadh was preparing to ditch its long-standing policy of containment in Yemen in favour of establishing military deterrence against Houthi aggression. Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political commentator reputedly close to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said he expected the kingdom to “respond aggressively and continue its strong support of the Yemeni government forces”. Analysts note that the competing factions making up the internationally recognised government forces were currently at their strongest since Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year after Houthi rebels seized swathes of northern and western Yemen, with the conflict ending in stalemate in 2022. The UN-sponsored political road map agreed upon at the time failed to produce the desired settlement, despite lengthy mediation efforts by neighbouring Oman, because of incessant jockeying for position between the Houthis and rival elements within the Yemeni government camp. Southern separatists backed by the United Arab Emirates went on the offensive in southern and eastern Yemen late last year, leading to the UAE’s expulsion from the country in December – and an unprecedented rift between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi. Since then, Riyadh has worked to consolidate anti-Houthi groups under a unified command. This force benefits from Saudi intelligence, better weaponry and advanced drones that have proven especially effective in repelling recent rebel ground assaults. Pro-government forces have responded to the Houthi offensive in Taiz and Hodeidah by counter-attacking at strategic points across multiple fronts – a tactic aimed at drawing Houthi forces away from the Red Sea coast. On the other hand, the Houthi offensive may be intended to prevent operations against Houthi-controlled areas along the western coast, according to Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, a Brussels-based non-profit organisation focused on conflict prevention and resolution. Amid widespread rumours of a government offensive to retake the key Red Sea port of Hodeidah, Houthi operations could pull government forces away from their coastal positions and reinforce Houthi defences in the mountains overlooking the western coast. In an advisory published by the International Crisis Group on Tuesday, Nagi said the Houthis appeared intent on seizing high ground on the western coastal plain and areas near Mokha port and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This would expand their control over terrain overlooking the coast, putting them in a stronger position to target transiting shipping. By staging this ground assault alongside cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia and maritime operations against Saudi-linked shipping, the Houthis were “seeking to demonstrate the ability to operate simultaneously across multiple fronts”, Nagi said. They also hoped to project an image of strength after suffering losses to government-aligned forces using advanced drones in recent weeks. Nagi warned the scale of reinforcements in weapons and manpower on both sides suggested the current battle “may well morph into a prolonged confrontation”. Continued escalation could open additional fronts. In particular, the Yemeni government, with Saudi support, “may see an advantage in expanding military operations” to force the Houthis to disperse their forces and stretch their capabilities, rather than allowing them to concentrate their resources on the Taiz and western coastal fronts. With both sides eyeing momentous territorial gains, Baron described the line between brinkmanship and aiming to make decisive gains as “quite thin”. Both the Houthis and their adversaries now “broadly assess that a return to fighting is in their interest”, he said.

title: Meet Wynn Everett, who plays Tricia Yeager, the ‘Gus Fring’ of Chad Powers
description: Glen Powell and Michael Waldron, who co-created the Hulu series, recently compared Everett’s character to Breaking Bad’s main antagonist – so who is she exactly?
content: Hit Hulu series Chad Powers returned for its second season on September 3, following the wild success of its inaugural run. Led by Glen Powell, the show follows Russ Holliday (Powell), a disgraced quarterback who decides to revive his football career by creating a new persona, Chad Powers, and joining a struggling college football team: the South Georgia Catfish. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Chad Powers (@chadpowershulu) With all six episodes of the new season available for streaming, fans will see Wynn Everett, who plays the show’s primary antagonist Tricia Yeager, take a villainous turn. Powell and Michael Waldron, who co-created the show, even compared Everett’s Tricia to Breaking Bad’s calculating and terrifying villain Gus Fring (played by Giancarlo Esposito) in a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter. Here’s everything you need to know about the 47-year-old actress, starring as Tricia in Chad Powers. What are Wynn Everett’s credits? Wynn Everett was born in October 1978 and was raised in Atlanta, Georgia. She grew up as a theatre kid and fell in love with the characters she portrayed. In secondary school, Everett was a lead in a production of Children of a Lesser God, for which she won Georgia State best actress, per IMDb. The actress has also credited a teacher in Atlanta with sparking her love for acting. “She taught me that empathy, curiosity, is the way into the lives of a character, finding that human connection, creating from a space of love,” Everett told Mastermedia in 2020. What roles has Wynn Everett played? Everett graduated from Auburn University in Alabama, where she majored in communications and minored in theatre. During her time at Auburn, Everett spent a summer interning for ABC’s Good Morning America in New York and landed a job at the show’s green room after graduating. “I worked 4am to 10am every day,” she told the university’s publication in 2017. “I did that for five years. It was a wonderful time for me because the schedule was brutal, but I would be out by 10am, so I would have my days free to do New York and audition and get back into theatre. It was great.” Everett landed her first on-screen role in the television sitcom Hope & Faith. She went on to star in major shows including Supernatural, Bones and Grey’s Anatomy. The actress is also a part of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, where she plays supervillain Whitney Frost, aka Madame Masque, in the drama series Agent Carter, and voiced the character in the animated series Avengers Assemble. Who is Wynn Everett married to? Everett married writer and entrepreneur Michael Albanese in 2004. They share two daughters, Asher and Georgia.

title: Hong Kong targets biomedicine powerhouse status in debut 5-year plan
description: Tied to the national strategy, the city’s first five-year blueprint doubles down on Greater Bay Area medical tech and healthcare cooperation.
content: Biomedicine is set to feature in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, due to be unveiled next week, as the city’s top officials signal closer medical cooperation across the Greater Bay Area. Lending weight to those ambitions, global pharmaceutical company GSK emphasised its interest in expanding its role in the region’s biotech development on Wednesday, at the fifth Hong Kong International Biotechnology Conference and Exhibition (BIOHK). Speaking at the event, Hong Kong Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said the city’s first five-year plan would align with the national blueprint, which had designated biomedicine as “one of the emerging industries of strategic importance”. “Biotechnology is ... a national and regional imperative. And Hong Kong is answering that call with conviction and speed,” Lo said. The city, he noted, served as a “superconnector” and “super value-added” hub for biotech and manufacturing capacity in the Greater Bay Area – the integrated economic and business hub linking Hong Kong and Macau with cities in Guangdong province. The region, home to 88 million people, generated a gross domestic product of more than 15 trillion yuan (US$2.23 trillion) in 2025, official data showed. Hong Kong’s first-ever five-year plan is expected to be unveiled on September 16 at a Legislative Council meeting, followed by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s 2026 policy address. The 15th five-year plan is the country’s blueprint for economic, social, technological and political development for 2026 to 2030. To streamline approvals, the health secretary Lo said Hong Kong would establish its own Centre for Medical Product Regulation by the end of this year, with the goal of becoming “an internationally recognised regulatory authority”. Meanwhile, Jonathan Symonds, GSK’s chair, said the company was changing its strategy in China. “We no longer want to be an asset-heavy company that is building physical assets in China,” he said. “We want to be an integrated collaborator with all of the assets that exist in this country.” GSK employs more than 4,000 people in China and has five regional hubs, including in Beijing and Guangzhou. The company has also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Hong Kong government, the Greater Bay Area International Clinical Trial Institute and the University of Hong Kong. Looking ahead, Symonds noted that preventive healthcare would become increasingly important as ageing populations and rising chronic disease added to the economic burden. Prevention refers to early intervention aimed at slowing or stopping disease risk factors before they progress into full-blown illness. Symonds pointed to the Hetao Shenzhen–Hong Kong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone as providing the physical space and regulatory framework needed to develop the field. “One of the big suppressors of both economic growth and productivity is health,” he said. Also speaking at BIOHK on Wednesday, Leung Chun-ying, the vice-chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, highlighted Nansha’s role in Guangdong-Hong Kong cooperation, noting that the district was just 45 minutes from Kowloon by high-speed rail. The partnership, Leung said, was targeting “cell and gene therapy and high-end medical devices”, with the goal of “accelerating the gathering of leading enterprises and various innovative elements at home and abroad”.

title: Purity of China quartz deposit ‘highly similar’ to US Spruce Pine standard: study
description: Geologists identify Xiaohuaguo site in central Hubei, unlocking potential silica resources for solar panels and semiconductor production.
content: Geologists say they have identified a new deposit in central China that can yield high-purity quartz comparable to the quality produced at a critical world-leading mine in the United States. The quartz from the Chinese deposit is described as having “highly similar” properties to the resources produced at North Carolina’s Spruce Pine, which is crucial to the global production of solar panels and semiconductors. In the US, there is a growing call from the industry to use high-purity quartz as a weapon against China’s rare earths export ban. Chinese researchers say the newly explored deposit near Shiyan in Hubei province is the latest in a string of quartz discoveries that could help the country cut its reliance on US imports. “This discovery of the Xiaohuaguo high-purity quartz deposit provides a new prospective area for the exploration of hydrothermal vein-type high-purity quartz resources in China,” the team wrote in a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language journal Earth Science last month. “Furthermore, the particle size, morphology and residual fluid inclusion characteristics of the purified quartz sand were highly similar to those of Unimin’s IOTA-CG type high-purity quartz sand, demonstrating significant potential for application in high-end technology fields.” Researchers from the China University of Geosciences, the Wuhan Centre of China Geological Survey and the Hubei Geological Bureau conducted the exploration and purification of the Xiaohuaguo quartz. While quartz is the second most abundant mineral in the Earth’s continental crust, high-purity quartz is a rare form characterised by silica purity above 99.9 per cent. Due to its properties of high temperature and corrosion resistance, high insulation and low thermal expansion, the Chinese team said high-purity quartz was “an indispensable material in hi-tech fields such as semiconductors, fibre optic communications, new energy, and aerospace”. In particular, it is used to produce fused quartz crucibles and other materials to manufacture semiconductors and solar panels. The IOTA high-purity quartz sand line, now produced by Sibelco, is considered an industry benchmark for the material. The Quartz Corp also produces quartz from Spruce Pine. Despite China being the largest producer of hi-tech products, it relies heavily on high-purity quartz imports – mostly from the US – to meet manufacturing demands. “This excessive dependence on imports, coupled with foreign export restrictions and technological blockades, poses a significant challenge to the secure supply of high-purity quartz in [China],” the team wrote. But recently, several deposits capable of producing ultra-high-purity quartz have been found in the country, including in Henan province and the Tibet and Xinjiang Uygur autonomous regions. According to the Chinese team, vein-type quartz deposits – one of the potential sources for high-purity quartz – are rarely reported in China. Besides Spruce Pine, other important sources of high-purity quartz include the Tysfjord region in Norway and the Kyshtym deposit in Russia. In their study, the Chinese team investigated the potential to prepare quartz from the Xiaohuaguo deposit in the Wudang uplift of the South Qinling mountain belt, a few kilometres from Shiyan. They found that the total impurity content of the purified quartz was 11.98 micrograms per gram, which is below the threshold of 50 micrograms per gram required to define high-purity quartz. The team said this impurity level was also below the 20 micrograms per gram threshold required for use in the inner layer of solar quartz crucibles. The total content of 17 trace elements in the purified material was also less than the upper limits specified for high-purity quartz. Although they did not conduct deep drilling during this survey, they determined that the deposit was likely to be of a medium size and had potential for hi-tech applications. According to an article by US recycling company Quest Metals, the US and its allies could exploit Beijing’s high-purity quartz vulnerabilities and squeeze its supply to try to diminish its strategic advantages amid China’s export ban on certain rare earth metals. This could include restricting advanced purification and mining technologies and leveraging sanctions against high-purity quartz entities to try to hamper China from upgrading its own domestic quartz processing facilities, Quest Metals said in June last year.

title: Hong Kong, Kazakhstan sign MOU on transport lab, discuss low-altitude economy
description: Kazakh vice-minister Bakhtiyar Mukhametkaliyev says his country envisions connecting mainland tech companies with Hong Kong financial tools.
content: Kazakhstan has signed a memorandum of understanding with Hong Kong’s transport authorities to establish a laboratory and discussed low-altitude economy initiatives to help manage traffic jams. Bakhtiyar Mukhametkaliyev, Kazakhstan’s vice-minister of artificial intelligence and digital development, told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday about discussions with the team of Hong Kong’s Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan on the sidelines of the Belt and Road Summit in the city. “In Hong Kong, I signed the memorandum agreement about launching the … laboratory with the [Transport and Logistics Bureau] of Hong Kong,” Mukhametkaliyev said. “We discussed the low-altitude economy … we tried to exchange knowledge about the management of traffic jams.” He noted that Hong Kong was actively implementing low-altitude economy initiatives, such as drone deliveries. Mukhametkaliyev added that Kazakhstan aimed to connect mainland Chinese technology companies with Hong Kong financial tools. “Hong Kong has good financial tools, good experience,” he said, adding that if Kazakhstan cooperated with mainland big tech firms, for example, the country could use Hong Kong’s financial tools to develop projects in Central Asia. “Because in Central Asia we’re the leader, it’s not just only one country; it’s a Central Asian market.” Mukhametkaliyev said that Kazakhstan wanted to work with mainland artificial intelligence companies including DeepSeek, Alibaba and Huawei Technologies, after two supercomputer clusters were launched in the country last year. Alibaba owns the SCMP. The organisers of the summit – the government and the Trade Development Council, said the event brought together global political and business leaders to explore Central Asia cooperation and emerging market opportunities. The Belt and Road Initiative is a global trade, infrastructure, and economic connectivity strategy launched by China in 2013. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led the city’s first business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June to open up bilateral trade opportunities. Mukhametkaliyev said Kazakhstan could offer land, electricity infrastructure and a flexible tax regime to attract technology investors. He said he met a robotics company in Hong Kong in April, which built a plant in the country in September. “We give the land, we give the conditions, we give the special tax regime. No problem,” he said. Mukhametkaliyev added that Kazakhstan had adopted a digital code and launched more than 1,300 government services online. “It’s like your official document, your driving licence, your passport. It’s only online,” he said. Meanwhile, Kao Kim Hourn, secretary general of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), said the 11-member economic bloc advocated for Hong Kong’s accession to the world’s largest free-trade agreement, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP). Kao noted that Asean advocated for the accession because of its long-standing trade and investment cooperation with Hong Kong, which ranked as the bloc’s fourth-largest source of foreign direct investment. Kao added that the accession required all member states to reach a consensus. “I am very confident that Hong Kong, China, will be able to join [RCEP] in the future,” he said.

title: In a bid to boost births, Shanghai waives out-of-pocket expenses for maternal care
description: The city’s fertility rate last year was just 0.66 – well below the 2.1 needed to ensure a stable population.
content: Shanghai, grappling with one of China’s highest rates of ageing and lowest rates of fertility, has made maternal care completely free in its latest move to encourage childbirth. The city government rolled out a pioneering policy on Tuesday that waives all out‑of‑pocket expenses for maternal care, from pregnancy screenings through childbirth to postnatal follow‑ups. The policy builds on – and goes beyond – a central government commitment to make basic services for hospital delivery free to all patients across the country by the end of this year, part of a push to raise birth rates amid a looming demographic crisis that threatens the country’s long-term economic prosperity. From October, all female participants in the city’s medical insurance scheme will be entitled to a maternal care allowance of 4,500 yuan (US$671), the municipal healthcare bureau announced, adding that if their bills exceed that amount, maternity insurance would cover the rest. Costs for prenatal check-ups, hospital delivery and postpartum recovery within 42 days after delivery would also be reimbursed in full, the bureau said. Last year, the central government pledged the nationwide roll-out of a policy of zero out‑of‑pocket costs for giving birth, but it has yet to materialise in all corners of the country. “Shanghai’s move is a step forward towards zero‑cost childbirth,” said Yuan Xin, a professor of demography at Nankai University in Tianjin. “But like traditional Chinese medicine, these policies are a slow burn – they take time to take effect and will never deliver quick fixes.” The fertility rate among women of childbearing age with Shanghai household registration was 0.66 last year, meaning each of them only had that number of children on average, according to data from the city government. A value of 2.1 is widely viewed as the minimum to maintain population stability. In addition, by the end of last year, the population aged 65 and above with Shanghai household registration was 4.67 million, accounting for 30 per cent of the total. The World Bank has set its threshold for qualification as a super-aged society at 20 per cent. Chinese demographers have estimated that last year’s national fertility rate was about 1.0, and official figures showed the share of those aged 65 and above was 15.9 per cent. Vowing to create an environment that is friendly to new parents, governments at the central and local levels have implemented a series of measures to encourage childbirth in recent years, ranging from childcare subsidies to longer maternity leave. But Yuan said such incentives may be less effective in affluent regions like Shanghai than in less-developed areas, where financial burdens played a bigger part in people’s decision to have children. Tianmen in the northern province of Hubei has become a closely watched case study, bucking national trends after offering strong financial support – worth up to 220,000 yuan per child – for childbirth and childcare.
