The city saw its number of newborns surge by 17 per cent year on year after the policy was introduced in 2024. The increase has continued since, though at a slower pace, with the rate standing at nearly 2 per cent last year and 1.8 per cent in the first seven months of this year, government data showed.

title: Caught between US and Iran, South Korea weighs Hormuz role
description: Seoul is sending a fact-finding mission to the UAE as it balances Washington’s security requests with warnings of Iranian retaliation.
content: South Korea is inching closer to a potentially risky military role in the Strait of Hormuz after sending a fact-finding team to the Middle East, with Seoul weighing US pressure to contribute against the threat of Iranian retaliation. The mission underscores the dilemma Seoul faces over supporting a major security ally and avoiding being dragged into a conflict it did not start. Observers argue that any deployment should be delayed, limited and conducted through a broader coalition rather than under American command. The South Korean team left for the United Arab Emirates over the weekend and was reportedly assessing operational conditions for a potential deployment. Seoul’s Ministry of National Defence maintained that the mission “is not being conducted on the premise that an actual deployment would take place” and denied reports that Washington had requested troop deployments by November. Addressing the potential deployment, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei wrote in Korean on social media on Monday: “The military presence or operational participation of other nations in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz would inevitably be viewed as direct support for the party committing acts of aggression, and would lead to serious consequences.” The UAE hosts military forces and support facilities operated by the US and other allied countries. If approved, South Korean forces are expected to use a UAE base as their main operating hub. The fact-finding team is expected to return to South Korea as early as this week to report to the National Security Council (NSC), according to local media. Any official decision would require deliberations by the NSC and the cabinet, presidential approval and parliamentary authorisation – a process observers say could take up to a year. Yu Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, said the mission should be viewed as an independent evaluation to determine whether deployment is necessary. Yu said Seoul could scale back the troop deployment, adjust the mission or choose an alternative form of contribution. However, some security experts warn that excessive hedging carries its own costs for Seoul. A former defence vice-minister told This Week in Asia that delaying a decision could backfire: “Taking an ambiguous stance due to domestic political reasons does not benefit mid-to-long-term national interests centred on the ROK-US relationship. A clear position must be stated, and the public must be persuaded if necessary.” From Washington’s perspective, the transactional nature of US alliance politics adds leverage to the request. Rob Rapson, a former acting US ambassador to South Korea, said Seoul’s deliberation made “perfect sense” amid rising US pressure. “I think they have been gaming this out for some time now,” Rapson told Yonhap News Agency. “Given the highly transactional nature of Trump 2.0 and its clear willingness to leverage any and all other elements of the alliance to get its way, I believe the South Korean government can find a way forward to oblige President Trump’s demands, at some level, without necessarily compromising core Korean national interests and legal requirements.” Proceed with caution Cho Yong-kun, a military-science professor at Kyungnam University’s College of Public Services, said that while South Korea had a track record of agreeing to US requests for overseas troop commitments, it should proceed with extreme caution in this case. “This is a high-stakes question – how should we navigate the situation between US pressure and the threats from Iran? It is clear that we must act, but the crucial questions are when and how we should proceed,” he said. South Korea sent about 320,000 soldiers to the Vietnam war, making it the second-largest foreign military force there after the US. Since then, Seoul’s overseas deployments have largely focused on humanitarian and peacekeeping operations, including sending 600 doctors to southern Iraq in 2003 and the 3,600-strong Zaytun Division to northern Iraq in 2004 for non-combat reconstruction work and medical support. A better idea could be for Seoul to join the multilateral coalition proposed by the UK and France once a ceasefire was reached, according to Cho. “My primary concern is that, given the current situation where the US is attacking Iranian oil tankers and Iran is targeting oil tankers and merchant vessels, deploying troops now carries a high risk of casualties.” Aside from the Vietnam war, South Korea has not suffered combat casualties during overseas deployments. “We should wait,” Cho added, emphasising that public opinion could give the government leverage to delay. “We cannot enter the Strait of Hormuz right now, even if a truce holds, even if it is fragile. We should delay the timing. When we go there, we must enter as part of a multilateral coalition led by the UK and France.” Cho also stressed the importance of maintaining an independent command structure, citing General Chae Myung-shin’s operational authority during the Vietnam war as precedent. Military authorities are reportedly considering scaling back any potential deployment. Initial plans included the navy’s new logistics support ship, the ROKS Soyang, and roughly 150 personnel. But concerns over the Soyang’s large crew size and its role in directly supporting US naval vessels – which could escalate tensions with Iran – have shifted preferences towards specialised assets, such as P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and Explosive Ordnance Disposal teams. Cho Han-bum, a senior analyst at the Korea Institute for National Unification, warned that Tehran would “definitely retaliate” if Seoul joined US forces in military action. “From Tehran’s perspective, South Korea’s involvement would encourage other Asian nations like Japan and Australia to follow suit,” he said. “Iran would go to great lengths to stop it right from the start.”

title: Gunman shoots and kills kindergarten teacher in Thailand
description: The shooting occurred at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten in Chonburi province. Three other teachers and 44 students were evacuated safely.
content: A gunman shot and killed a kindergarten teacher on Wednesday inside a school building in eastern Thailand, where 44 children and three other teachers were evacuated safely, authorities said. The shooting took place around 11am inside a building at the Nongplalai Municipal Kindergarten in Chonburi province, about 150km (93 miles) southeast of the capital Bangkok. All 44 students were unharmed and evacuated along with the other teachers after the shooting, according to the Chonburi provincial government. The shooter, who is believed to be the victim’s husband, fled the scene. His house was surrounded by police, officials said. Thai media reports identified the suspect as a police officer at the nearby Bang Lamung station. The Chonburi Provincial Police office said the matter was still under investigation. Chonburi Governor Narit Niramaiwong ordered the school to be closed and mental health experts to be available to support the students and school staff, his office said. Sayan Klomaon, chairman of Nong Pla Lai subdistrict council, said the gunman came to the school at about 10.30am and talked to his wife before shooting her. No students saw the incident, as it happened outside the classroom, he said, adding that the gunman then left to go home, and since then all the children had been picked up. School safety and gun violence in Thailand have come under scrutiny after a 14-year-old student opened fire at his high school and family home in August, killing eight people and injuring more than 20 before apparently taking his own life. Earlier this month, a 14-year-old student was arrested after he fired several shots but failed to injure anyone at his school in Kamphaeng Phet province, 200km north of Bangkok. Calls for tighter controls on firearms have intensified and the national government has ordered a review of gun regulations, including suspension of new permits to purchase firearms and a review of existing permits. Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia despite fairly restrictive gun laws. While mass shootings are still rare, the country has seen an uptick in high-profile attacks in recent years. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Insurers Prudential, Manulife seal tech alliances amid Beijing’s tightened tax rules
description: Among cross-sector tie-ups, Prudential partners with Alibaba Cloud, Manulife works with Ant Health and BOC Life joins hands with Deloitte.
content: Several Hong Kong insurance companies, including Prudential, Manulife and BOC Life, are racing into cross-sector alliances from artificial intelligence underwriting to healthcare tie-ups to strengthen capabilities and efficiency amid China’s tightened cross-border tax rules. Prudential announced a partnership with Alibaba Cloud to launch an AI underwriter, designed to help financial consultants make preliminary decisions based on a client’s financial situation, medical record, occupation and residential profile. Collaboration would be a trend, as insurance companies alone could not cope with the new technology, said Lawrence Lam, CEO of Prudential Hong Kong, in a media briefing on Wednesday. “AI underwriting allows our financial consultants to identify client needs and deliver preliminary results within minutes instead of days,” he said. Ethan Yuan Zhiming, vice-president of international business and regional general manager of Hong Kong and Macau at Alibaba Cloud, said the partnership combined Prudential’s insurance expertise with Alibaba Cloud’s AI capabilities to provide faster and better service. Insurers which can best use AI technology to develop their businesses would be the winners Lawrence Lam, Prudential Hong Kong Alibaba Cloud in June also signed a strategic partnership with Manulife Hong Kong to develop AI solutions to enhance customer experience and operational effectiveness. Alibaba Cloud is the AI and cloud computing services unit of Alibaba, owner of the South China Morning Post. On Monday, Manulife and AHA Healthcare Technology signed a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration in health management and cross-border healthcare services and insurance technology. The collaboration comes as more Hongkongers seek medical treatment at lower cost on the mainland. AHA is the Hong Kong unit of Ant Health, which provides online hospital appointment booking and payment services for patients in mainland China. “Working with partners that offer complementary strengths allows us to explore ways to create a simpler, more connected and customer-centred healthcare experience,” said Steve Finch, president and CEO of Manulife Asia. “We believe cross-sector collaboration can play an important role in addressing the often fragmented cross-boundary healthcare experience, where customers have to make multiple inquiries and coordinate different stages of their healthcare journey.” BOC Life last month teamed up with Deloitte Private to capture growing demand from high-net-worth individuals and wealthy families for succession planning and wealth advisory services. “With high-net-worth clients seeking increasingly sophisticated asset management and legacy planning, cross-sector expert collaboration has become pivotal,” said Wilson Tang, CEO of BOC Life. The partnerships come as Beijing enforces new tax rules on cross-border investment. Visitors from mainland China were leading buyers of Hong Kong life insurance products, accounting for about one-fourth of all sales, according to data from insurers. In July, China brought income generated through offshore trusts under its ­personal income tax regime. Early last month, several major mainland cities, including Shanghai, began collecting a 20 per cent levy on gains from offshore insurance policies. Prudential’s Lam said insurance companies needed partners to adopt AI. “Insurers which can best use AI technology to develop their businesses would be the winners,” he said. “Establishing a partnership with a trusted technology partner would be the best way forward.” Lam added that insurers should embrace AI to enhance their competitiveness, regardless of policy changes. “Demand for mainlanders buying insurance policies in the past few months has been similar to that before the recent enforcement activities from mainland China drew wider attention,” he said. “Customers are seeking more information, but they still need to buy insurance in Hong Kong to get protection for their families.”

title: Opinion | Governance must be the new competitive edge for China’s global firms
description: A compliance case involving a key Chinese auto supplier highlights a growing vulnerability ambitious manufacturers can no longer ignore.
content: Chinese manufacturers have long understood overseas barriers in visible terms: tariffs, market access, technical standards and geopolitical restrictions. The controversy surrounding Changzhou Xingyu Automotive Lighting System points to a quieter threat: a governance failure at home can follow a company into global markets. Online, the dispute has been cast as a story of young employees fighting back. According to media reports, Xingyu recruited 440 graduates but asked 107 of them – just over a month after they joined – to sign immediate resignation agreements stating that they were leaving for personal reasons. They were offered half a month’s salary in compensation. Several then lodged complaints with European carmakers and the Hong Kong stock exchange. On September 1, Volkswagen confirmed it had begun an investigation into the dismissal of the 107 graduate recruits. The carmaker said that basic values and rights must be protected throughout its supply chain and that it would take “appropriate steps” after completing its review. Volkswagen described the inquiry as standard procedure. A dispute that began inside a human resources department in Changzhou has entered the compliance system of a global carmaker. Xingyu is no marginal supplier. In its July Hong Kong listing application, it described itself as China’s largest automotive lighting supplier by 2025 revenue and the seventh-largest worldwide. It operates 12 manufacturing plants in China and Serbia and has 16 research and development centres. Its customers include Volkswagen, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota, Nissan and Honda. Its products, customers, production footprint and financing ambitions have become increasingly international. Its employment practices, however, appear to have remained within the narrow orbit of a local human resources department. The controversy exposed a fundamental mismatch: Xingyu’s business radius expanded faster than its governance radius. More Chinese companies entering global markets will face the same test. There are precedents for what can happen when labour management failures enter a customer’s compliance system. In 2014, Samsung suspended its business with Dongguan Shinyang Electronics after evidence of suspected child labour was found at the Chinese parts supplier. In 2020, Apple placed its supplier Pegatron on probation after finding that the company had misclassified student workers at its Shanghai and Kunshan facilities, required them to work prohibited night shifts and overtime, and falsified records. Until corrective measures were completed, Apple barred Pegatron from receiving new business. Neither case depended on a court ruling against the supplier. The customer’s purchasing power turned its code of conduct into an enforceable business requirement. For Xingyu, the more realistic European exposure therefore runs through customers rather than Brussels. European rules first bind large manufacturers, which then transmit those requirements down the supply chain through procurement contracts, supplier codes, audit rights, corrective action plans and decisions over new vehicle programmes. Germany’s Supply Chain Due Diligence Act already requires large companies to identify and address certain human-rights and environmental risks across their global supply chains. Mercedes-Benz, for example, says complaints submitted through its Business & People Protection Office may be assessed, investigated and followed by corrective action. A supplier that refuses to implement an agreed improvement plan could ultimately face suspension or termination of the business relationship. A Chinese supplier might never face a European regulator directly. However, it could still be asked to produce evidence, undergo an audit, implement corrective measures or explain allegations that affect its supplier rating. A complaint does not need to become a legal case before it becomes a business problem. Tariffs are measurable; they appear as a line on a cost sheet. The erosion of trust is more diffuse. It might take the form of more frequent audits, slower approvals, tighter contract terms, fewer invitations to bid or a future project quietly awarded elsewhere. Its cost is harder to see but can be more enduring. This trend will strengthen as the EU Forced Labour Regulation and corporate sustainability due diligence directive are phased in. Global customers do not buy components alone. They also buy assurance that a supplier will not create an avoidable compliance or reputational liability. The Xingyu case points to a deeper shift in the foundations of Chinese manufacturing competitiveness. Quality, cost and delivery helped Chinese manufacturers enter global supply chains. Staying there will increasingly depend on a fourth capability: verifiable governance. A company might manufacture automotive lights in Changzhou and sell them around the world, but its labour relations no longer stop at the factory gate. Once it enters global supply chains and international capital markets, a local employment decision could be examined simultaneously under Chinese labour law, customer compliance rules, European supply chain requirements and Hong Kong disclosure standards. For Chinese manufacturers going global, an avoidable breach of trust can become an export barrier with no tariff code or formal ban – and it could ultimately cost more than either.

title: Carlos Alcaraz says ‘I leave with a smile’ after epic US Open loss to Ben Shelton
description: Dethroned Spaniard comes away ‘proud’ in defeat, while American’s win boosts hopes of a first hometown male grand slam winner since 2003.
content: At the end, when five riveting sets and one agonisingly tight tiebreak were over – and when the latest-finishing match in US Open history had concluded – Ben Shelton was not the only player smiling. Carlos Alcaraz, the player Shelton had just defeated in an entertaining, spine-tingling marathon, was smiling too. The dethroned defending champ grinned as he walked to the net to hug Shelton. And he did so again a few minutes later when he stood in a hallway surrounded by reporters, reflecting on a night that seemed to have taken every ounce of his strength to endure. “I leave the court happy,” Alcaraz said. “I leave the court with a smile. I am proud of myself, how I fought.” There was probably not a single person in Arthur Ashe Stadium who would have disagreed. Though many of the thousands of fans who remained until the 3.33am conclusion – yes, you read that time right – cheered for Shelton, the top-ranked American who now meets compatriot Frances Tiafoe in the semis, there were plenty who cheered for Alcaraz, one of the most charismatic players of his or any generation, and one of the most naturally gifted players ever born. “Ole, Ole, Ole, Ole,” Alcaraz’s fans chanted, and “Vamos Carlos!” – competing with shouts of “USA, USA” or just “Let’s Go, Ben!”. Most importantly, Alcaraz said he was leaving healthy. That had been a real concern going into this US Open after a four-month break due to a wrist injury. “As I said before the tournament began, my expectation was to go there, compete, play these kinds of matches, be healthy,” he said after his 6-7, 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 defeat. “I mean it was close, it really was close, so I was disappointed I didn’t get the win in the end, but I’m just happy … physically I was really tired, but I found a way to push myself.” The Spaniard also had nothing but praise for Shelton, who played the match of his young career to defeat the seven-time grand slam champion. “Shelton played a very complete, very mature match,” Alcaraz said in Spanish. “He knew exactly what to do at every moment. And, physically, he’s a beast. It seemed like he had no weaknesses whatsoever.” Shelton on his part said the match “was a war”. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions of our sport,” he said. “It was the most enjoyable match I’ve had in my career, for sure.” Alcaraz had arrived at the US Open with much uncertainty as to how much of a liability his wrist injury remained. But he seemed healthy from the start, and said he felt better than expected. In his first four rounds he lost only one set. “It feels like I’ve been competing the whole time,” he said of his extended break. “I surprise myself the way that I’m feeling, and the way that I’m recovering after every match. “I’m just really happy about it,” he had said after advancing to the fourth round, “that I’m able to perform at my best after every match.” Alcaraz also said he would be taking more long breaks in the future, since he did not need to depend on a rhythm or to play a lot of tournaments. And he was so relaxed, he did not even know, after handily defeating Tommy Paul in his fourth-round match, who he would be facing next. Former US Open champ Andy Roddick, a commentator for ESPN, let him know. Then came Tuesday’s (and Wednesday’s) quarter-finals, and Shelton. After Alcaraz won the first, tight set, Shelton started playing out of his mind. He took the next two sets. Alcaraz rallied for the fourth, and then the two traded games in a nerve-racking fifth. Shelton’s match-up with compatriot Tiafoe boosts home hopes of a first American men’s grand slam ‌champion since 2003. “For me it’s always about the people in the crowd,” Shelton said in explaining how he got through the gruelling ⁠contest. “Whether it’s my coaches and my team there, all my family and friends here, or the city of ‌New York that showed up tonight till 3am with the USA chants until the very end. “That’s what kept me going, and that’s what got me ‌this win tonight. “It’s incredible. I always say that this is the greatest sports city in ⁠the world. I say ⁠that this is the greatest stadium in the world.” Shelton added: “I’m hoping that my best friend and my sister up there ‌don’t have to be at ‌work in three hours. “It would be huge from their employers to let them have the day off today. “To be here in front of you guys tonight is an absolute honour. Sharing the court with Carlos is an absolute honour, and I cherish every moment I have out here.”

title: Review | Once Upon a Time in the Middle East movie review: Shen Teng leads bombastic anti-war drama
description: Full of roaring action and heart-wrenching tension, this mainland China hit delivers a message of peace through Chinese cooking appreciation.
content: 3.5/5 stars Writer-director Wen Muye’s bombastic anti-war drama Once Upon a Time in the Middle East arrives in Hong Kong having already grossed a whopping 2 billion yuan (US$298 million) at the mainland box office, delivering a message of peace and diplomacy through the appreciation of authentic Chinese cooking. Lambasting both sides of an unnamed Middle Eastern conflict – the United States’ 2003 invasion of Iraq in everything but name – this latest effort by the Dying to Survive filmmaker addresses a parade of wartime atrocities, from devastating shock-and-awe strikes to black-site prisons, radicalised child soldiers and suicide bombings. This is filtered through the perspective of an opportunistic yet affable Chinese chef, whose mouth-watering cuisine is the only thing uniting the warring factions. China’s latest go-to everyman, Shen Teng (Pegasus), stars as Xu Fu, an accomplished chef who travels to the fictional city of Bahata in 2002, hoping to pay off his debts. He is introduced as a haggard and battle-scarred old man being questioned by immigration officials over an old terrorism charge on his record. Although the US cleared him years earlier, local authorities want more answers. Xu recounts how he got a job at the busy Dragon Restaurant owned by Zayd (Sherif Sobhy), a government official, where he works alongside Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), a fellow countryman who has lived in the region for many years and speaks the language, and whose fiancée (Naira Al-Qasim) teaches at a nearby orphanage. Soon after Xu’s arrival, the US military bombs the city, destroying the orphanage. Xu gives the children shelter in return for labour and takes one boy, Seif (Omar Sherif), under his wing. When American troops arrive, the Dragon Restaurant becomes their preferred hang-out, and Xu meets Tony (Aarif Rahman), a troubled Chinese-American soldier. After Zayd is accused of masterminding the bombing of a US checkpoint, Xu falls under suspicion by association. Charting an increasingly desperate chain of events over several years, the film lets audiences witness – via Xu’s wavering neutrality – how a seemingly peaceful nation is ravaged by an unfocused and unnecessary conflict. There are numerous early digs at the Americans, from the poor quality of their Chinese food to their violent disregard for the civilian population. However, the screenplay does not shy away from how this anger is manipulated into weaponised religious rhetoric, especially when Xu’s clan of orphans is swept into the maelstrom. In terms of sheer spectacle, the film delivers plenty of thunderous action and heart-wrenching tension, while the editing occasionally echoes Christopher Nolan’s penchant for emotive, crescendoing montages. The messaging is never subtle, inevitably urging Xu to return to the safety of his homeland, but as blockbuster entertainment, Once Upon a Time in the Middle East is genuinely exceptional.
