title: Australians question US commitment to Aukus submarine deal in crowdfunded inquiry
description: Under the Australia-UK-US security pact, Canberra will get eight nuclear-powered submarines at an estimated cost of up to US$266 billion.
content: Dissent voiced in an ongoing inquiry into Australia’s most ambitious nuclear submarine pact has laid bare growing uncertainty over US commitment, amid questions about the clarity of Canberra’s explanation of the Aukus deal to citizens. Under the trilateral security pact between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, Canberra will get eight nuclear-powered submarines at an estimated cost of up to A$368 billion (US$266 billion). Three used Virginia-class nuclear submarines will initially be bought from the US and delivered from between 2032 and 2038. Australia will also work with the UK to build the new Aukus submarines locally, with the first delivery expected in the early 2040s. At an Aukus public inquiry in Canberra last week, one of Australia’s leading submarine experts, retired Rear Admiral Peter Briggs, called the plan “flawed and undeliverable”. Australia scrapped an agreement for France to supply Attack-class submarines in favour of the Aukus sale in 2021. Briggs said the French deal was the better option, arguing that US shipyards, already struggling to meet the domestic demands, could not deliver the promised nuclear-powered submarines on time. At the same inquiry, former civil servants dealing with national security Michael Keating and Jon Stanford said joining Aukus meant Australia was significantly more likely to be dragged into a conflict with China and potentially targeted with nuclear weapons. Australia had “sacrificed considerable sovereignty” to the US while leaving the country vulnerable without a guaranteed security safety net, they said. Canberra has said that, apart from protecting Australia’s vast ocean trade routes, acquiring such capability is also aimed at countering China’s growing military presence in the region. The 12-week inquiry, which ended on Thursday, was crowdfunded as Canberra refused to hold a formal parliamentary inquiry. It was led by former ministers, parliamentarians, senior officials, public servants and retired military officers. Demand for the inquiry showed the lack of transparency and public debate surrounding Aukus, according to Manoj Harjani, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies. “Uncertainty regarding the US’ commitment to Aukus, particularly since Donald Trump took office, has been a thorny issue,” he said. “This will not be the last time you hear about a review of Aukus. It is a substantial commitment in more than monetary terms and deserves the level of scrutiny it is receiving.” Questions about US commitment to the pact stem mainly from the slow pace of production in US shipyards and American policy reviews questioning if transferring high-end military assets abroad aligns strictly with US interests. Explanation needed Troy Lee-Brown, a research fellow at the University of Western Australia’s Defence and Security Institute, said with the strategic environment in the region deteriorating, Canberra should do a better job in explaining Aukus to Australians. Aukus, he said, was delivering results. The Submarine Rotational Force-West, an Aukus initiative where Australia will host a rotational presence of UK and US nuclear submarines at HMAS Stirling near Perth in Western Australia, will start operations next year. “But the timeline of the Aukus project is measured over multiple decades, with the eventual delivery of SSN Aukus from the early 2040s,” he said. The inquiry was long overdue, said Nishank Motwani, senior fellow at The Alliance Futures Institute think tank in Washington. Since Aukus was launched in September 2021, there has not been a public debate about the pact and its wide-ranging effects on the economy, workforce, waste management and use of taxpayers’ money. “If one word captures why the Aukus public inquiry is taking place now, it would be ‘frustration’,” he said, adding that government information so far had been “top-down, drip-fed, and highly controlled”. One reason why Canberra did not want to open Aukus up to public debate was the fear of backlash, he said. A public inquiry would “expose [the government] to hard questions, legitimate concerns, and difficult choices they are unprepared to meet because in some ways, Aukus is billed as ‘too big to fail’”. The inquiry attracted significant interest across Australia. Over 700 written submissions were made and all the public hearings were reportedly packed. Last week’s hearings in Canberra even had to be extended by a day due to strong interest. “It will be hard to ignore the momentum the inquiry has generated,” Motwani said. In the longer term, it could harm future governments if they dismissed the inquiry and its recommendations. “It exposes the reality that the inquiry is doing the job the government should have done all along: explaining Aukus to the Australian people in a trusting, transparent and accountable manner,” he said. This was an opportunity for the government to learn about public thinking on Aukus, without having to put political stakes on the line, he said, adding that “sidestepping or dismissing the inquiry’s findings would be costly for the government, as these represent real voices it has not yet reached”. In a written statement to the inquiry on August 31, Motwani recommended the appointment of an Aukus special envoy with decision-making power. “The appointment must sit within the national security apparatus, reporting directly to the prime minister, with an explicit mandate to drive Pillar I and Pillar II delivery against defined timelines, public accountability measures, and counter threats,” he wrote. Pillar I is the delivery of the nuclear-powered submarines to Australia while the second pillar refers to the sharing of advanced technology and capabilities among the three allies. The inquiry, Harjani said, should be seen as an example of the challenges facing defence policymaking regarding major acquisitions. “Who should ultimately decide, and whose opinions should be given weight to?”

title: US firm used AI to hijack WeChat account, spurring call for cyber cooperation with China
description: The flaw allowed for remote account takeovers without user interaction, prompting Tencent to patch the problem after Calif cybersecurity team flagged it.
content: US cybersecurity researchers have demonstrated how artificial intelligence could help hijack WeChat accounts via unanswered voice calls, intensifying concerns about AI-driven cyber threats and prompting renewed calls for bilateral cooperation between the United States and China. US security firm Calif said on Tuesday that its AI system identified a critical flaw in Tencent Holdings’ widely used messaging and payments app in July. In just a little over a week, researchers developed WeWorm – an experimental exploit that could allow an attacker to take full control of a target’s WeChat account via a simple voice call, without the victim ever picking up the phone. Tencent patched the bug in late August, according to Calif, which alerted the Chinese tech giant. A Tencent spokesperson confirmed on Wednesday that a server-side fix was deployed, requiring no user action, and noted there was no evidence that the vulnerability was ever exploited in the wild. Tencent added that it was “grateful to the researchers for bringing this to our attention and working with us”. The experiment underscores the speed at which AI is accelerating cyber threats. A worm of this complexity previously required months of work from larger engineering teams, but Calif researchers noted that “AI can already do most of the work here”. The findings left some analysts alarmed. Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, described the incident as “extremely serious”, adding that neither Washington nor Beijing was prepared for the rapid escalation of AI-driven risks. “Now, more than ever, it’s important for both sides to keep an open channel of communication,” he wrote on social media. On Tuesday, Calif researcher Thai Duong also urged bilateral collaboration: “The US and China disagree on plenty, but keeping billions of people safe online shouldn’t be one of them.” Also commenting on social media, Duong added: “AI gives us a chance to find and fix these bugs faster than ever.” The push for a security dialogue comes ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month, though official rhetoric remains combative. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, expected to lead upcoming bilateral AI talks, said on Tuesday that China “can never get ahead” of America due to China’s “central planning” model. On the same day, three US agencies accused six leading Chinese AI firms – DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, StepFun, Z.ai and Alibaba Group Holding – of distilling knowledge from American AI models to train their own. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Last month, Yuyuan Tantian – a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV – accused US AI firm Anthropic of trying to dictate industry rules and criticised Washington for weakening safety standards to “maintain technological hegemony”. Calling frontier-model safety a “crucial topic” for the upcoming summit, the outlet urged industry stakeholders to distinguish genuine security threats from technological competition.

title: PAS slammed in Malaysia for linking heaven to support for party
description: Malaysian politicians criticise the comment, saying PAS is implying that Muslims who do not vote for it are ‘condemned to hell’.
content: Malaysian politicians have slammed a Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) party leader for claiming that those who join the Islamist party would “certainly” go to heaven. Among them, Amanah vice-president Mahfuz Omar, said in a social media post on Tuesday: “PAS’ office is not an immigration counter for the afterlife, where you get a ‘heaven’ stamp upon showing your membership certificate and ballot vote.” During the PAS assembly over the weekend, secretary general Takiyuddin Hassan said party supporters were guaranteed entry into paradise, according to news portal Free Malaysia Today. People who died defending Islam became martyrs and were rewarded with divine blessings in the afterlife, he said. “Joining PAS in that way, God willing, we can enter heaven when we die. That is certain, ladies and gentlemen.” Takiyuddin’s remarks drew immediate condemnation from Muslim lawmakers in the country. “Entry into heaven is not from political party votes but because of Allah’s mercy,” former religious affairs minister Mujahid Yusof Rawa wrote on social media on Sunday. “Will a political party that declares fellow Muslims to be disbelievers and labels those who do not align with it as hypocrites and the like invite Allah’s mercy or His calamity?” Mahfuz, who is Mujahid’s party mate, likewise countered Takiyuddin’s words. “PAS can ask the people to support or vote for it. But PAS has never been given the mandate by Allah to determine who will enter heaven. Heaven does not belong to PAS but to Allah,” he said. “PAS should not act as though it is the gatekeeper of heaven – those who vote for PAS are allowed through the gates, while those who do not are told to wait outside.” Mahfuz argued that a ballot paper was not a “passport” to the afterlife. “If voting for PAS is a ticket to heaven, how about Muslims who do not vote for PAS? Does that mean Muslims who are not members, do not vote for and do not support PAS will be condemned to hell?” Mujahid also criticised PAS’ behaviour, saying: “How can PAS’ attitude of slandering and lying for the sake of power invite Allah’s mercy and lead to paradise?” The former minister sued PAS in 2022 over a social media post linking him to the LGBT community. The case was settled out of court last December. PAS leaders are no strangers to making controversial remarks. On Monday, leader Abdul Hadi Awang was contacted by police for his explosive allegation that the United States once offered to help his party topple the government – an allegation Washington has flatly dismissed as false. Hadi sparked outrage and ridicule last month with unproven claims linking religion to dishonesty, suggesting that Muslims were less corrupt than non-Muslims.

title: Chinese energy firms warn policy volatility complicates long-term expansion abroad
description: Sungrow, EVE Energy say bans, probes and shifting rules abroad expose the fragility of their long-term energy investments.
content: Chinese energy firms have called for policy stability in overseas markets as their global investments face mounting geopolitical risks amid headwinds from the oil crisis. The call came from Sungrow Power Supply and EVE Energy executives, who said policy stability topped their expectations at an event in Hong Kong on Tuesday. Both companies have come under fresh pressure in the US market in the past two months. Sungrow, the world’s second-largest energy storage system maker, was hit by a US import ban targeting foreign-made inverters, while EVE, the seventh-largest electric vehicle (EV) battery supplier globally, is being probed by the US International Trade Commission over a patent complaint filed by South Korea’s LG Energy Solution. “Geopolitics can, in fact, be rather irrational at times and there are often misunderstandings regarding companies like ours which are entirely privately owned,” said Cai Zhuang, general manager of product business at Hefei-based Sungrow, at a BloombergNEF event. “The truth is that we ourselves do not know what ‘ghost software’ is,” added Cai, pushing back at claims that inverters – a key component in modern grid networks and energy storage systems – could act as spyware. After firms like us have injected about [US$1.5 billion] into the local market, we can’t quit Yuan Huagang, EVE Energy Talk against inverters, more than half of which were manufactured in China in 2024, began circulating in 2025. The European Union and the US initiated formal bans on foreign-made grid equipment in May and July, respectively, citing national security and supply chain risks. Sungrow’s Shenzhen-listed shares have plunged over 40 per cent since media reports about a US ban surfaced in late June. At the same event, EVE senior vice-president Yuan Huagang stressed the importance of policy consistency in local markets, noting that overseas investments such as battery plants required a minimum depreciation period of 20 years. Yuan cited EVE’s Hungary investment, which faced uncertainties and public pressure after a change in government. “After firms like us have injected about 10 billion yuan [US$1.5 billion] into the local market, we can’t quit,” Yuan said. “I think we need stable expectations and respect for business ethics.” Hungary has been a key hub for Chinese companies expanding in Europe. But after a new administration came into power this year, battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited and Semcorp, the world’s biggest producer of lithium-ion battery separator film by volume, were recently forced to halt operations due to health and pollution concerns. To handle shifting policies, Cai and Yuan said their companies would continue strengthening compliance. Albert Cheung, CEO of BloombergNEF, said energy security concerns had grown worldwide, boosting the importance of energy transition to reduce the reliance on imported fuels. Cheung said “clustering” – consumers imitating neighbours by buying EVs or installing rooftop solar panels – was a bigger driver of transition than rising oil prices. Cheung added that near-term uncertainties, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and doubts over the profitability of artificial intelligence, would curb investor appetite for key commodities like oil and copper. Brent crude prices could exceed US$100 per barrel again if the Middle East conflicts escalated further and affected key shipping infrastructure around Kharg Island and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, said Catherine Li, Middle East and global energy analyst at Chinese brokerage Haitong International. Brent rose 1.63 per cent to US$99.50 per barrel on Tuesday.

title: Japan’s Nagoya reels from record rain, stranding commuters and flooding city
description: The weather chaos injured 41 people, damaged 200 vehicles and forced 1,600 residents to take shelter at evacuation centres.
content: Nagoya in central Japan said on Wednesday that it has decided to provide emergency relief across the city where at least 41 people sustained minor injuries after a linear rain band formed, pounding the Tokai region with record rainfall the previous day. Many commuters and students were stranded for the night in Nagoya after transport was paralysed due to the rain. Around 1,600 people had taken shelter at evacuation centres as of 7pm on Tuesday and 200 vehicles had been damaged by the rain as of 4am on Wednesday, local authorities said. In the vicinity of Nagoya Station on Wednesday morning, many people headed to work looking exhausted after being unable to go home, including a 23-year-old woman from neighbouring Kasugai who spent the night at a karaoke venue near the station with a friend. The Japan Meteorological Agency warned on Wednesday of continuing heavy rain across wide swathes of the country through Thursday due to an active front, urging vigilance for landslides, flooding and rising rivers. In areas including the Tokai region, even small amounts of additional rain could heighten disaster risks due to loosened ground. According to the agency, a front is stretching across the Pacific coast of eastern and western Japan, while a tropical depression, following the downgrading of Typhoon Krovanh, is moving northward south of the island of Shikoku. Warm, moist air is flowing towards the active front, which is expected to shift slightly southward and remain south of the main island of Honshu on Thursday. The agency said linear rainbands, capable of bringing localised torrential downpours over prolonged periods, could also form over Tokai and other areas on Wednesday. In the 24 hours through 6am on Thursday, up to 200mm (seven inches) of rain is forecast for Tokai as well as western Japan’s Kinki region and 150mm for Shikoku in the west. Up to 120mm is expected in Kanto-Koshin, including Tokyo and Hokuriku, with 80mm in Tohoku in the northeast.

title: China-Nepal floods; arthritis drug restores alopecia patients’ hair: 7 science highlights
description: From Beijing’s bid to stop US AI dominance to impact of China-Nepal floods, here are some highlights from SCMP’s recent science reporting.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on science from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. China’s radar satellites capture sharp images of glacier collapse site in Nepal Within hours of a devastating glacier collapse on the China-Nepal border, a Beijing-based satellite company had already redirected six of its satellites to survey the disaster zone. 2. Chip expert Chen Ye joins China’s Zhejiang University – as it overtakes Harvard Chen Ye, a semiconductor quality control expert with more than 16 years of industry experience in the United States, has been appointed as a Qiushi Distinguished Professor at Zhejiang University’s College of Integrated Circuits, the university has announced. 3. Arthritis drug restores 100% hair on 1 in 5 alopecia patients in global trial For many, losing hair isn’t just a cosmetic worry – it is a deeply personal struggle that can chip away at confidence, social life and mental health. Now, a surprising candidate is offering new hope: a pill originally designed to treat arthritis. 4. China-Nepal floods: first research shows no one could have outrun debris flow Not even the world’s fastest sprinters could have outrun the devastating floodwaters that struck a border crossing between China and Nepal last week, according to one of the first peer-reviewed assessments of the disaster. 5. China will never allow any country to achieve AI dominance: Victor Gao China will thwart US ambitions for global artificial intelligence (AI) dominance, the vice-president of the Centre for China and Globalisation has said, while warning that Washington’s military-focused strategy was pushing towards “AI for evil”. 6. The ‘Asian water tower’ is starting to wobble, computer simulations show “Asia’s water tower” is heading towards a more unpredictable and unstable future, according to a new study measuring the Tibetan Plateau’s stability. The study, published on August 21 in Nature Communications, examined the entropy of the region to gauge how much chaos or disorder was building up in a complex system. 7. Chinese coastguard has 0.3% chance of using weapons in disputed waters: study A Chinese coastguard ship is shielding a cluster of fishing boats when several small, fast vessels begin circling – sometimes darting closer, sometimes backing off. Are they just curious fishermen? Or are they probing for a weak spot, trying to lure the patrol ship into a trap?

title: Meet Jelena Ostapenko, the fiery Latvian tennis star making headlines over US Open drama
description: The 2017 French Open winner, who defeated Aryna Sabalenka at last year’s Stuttgart Open final, was once a national-level ballroom dancer.
content: Latvian tennis star Jelena Ostapenko and her Taiwanese partner, Hsieh Su-wei, missed out on the US Open women’s doubles semi-finals after losing to Elise Mertens and Diana Shnaider on Tuesday. Leading up to the match, Ostapenko was at ⁠the centre of another ⁠heated US Open exchange on Monday, confronting an opposing coach after reaching the women’s doubles quarter-finals with Hsieh. The fourth seeds beat Australian-Taiwanese pair Maya ‌Joint and Chan Hao-ching 6-4, 6-4, but tempers flared after Ostapenko took exception to the behaviour of their opponents’ coach. Hsieh had approached the umpire during a changeover and Ostapenko pointed towards the opposing team’s coach, urging the official to intervene. The ⁠Latvian said the coach had been clapping and shouting after their ‌mistakes and sarcastically praising their shots in Chinese, which Hsieh translated for her. “They do this because they ‌know they cannot beat us,” Ostapenko told the umpire, calling ⁠the behaviour “very ⁠disrespectful” and asking for the presence of a Chinese translator. After the umpire agreed ‌to deal with the situation, the pair returned to the court and turned up the ‌heat ‌to seal the straight-sets win. Ostapenko then celebrated by roaring towards ‌the opposing box while Hsieh and Chan did not shake hands ⁠at the end of the fiery encounter. Ostapenko, the 2017 French Open ⁠singles champion, has been involved in several on-court disputes. At last year’s US Open, she accused Taylor Townsend of having “no ‌class” and “no education” in ‌a verbal confrontation with the American. Ostapenko later apologised, saying her choice of words during the exchange had been misunderstood because English was not her first language. Here’s everything you need to know about Jelena Ostapenko. What is Jelena Ostapenko’s background? Jelena Ostapenko was born in June 1997 to parents Jelena Jakovleva and Jevgenijs Ostapenko. Both of Ostapenko’s parents are former athletes. Her late father was a professional Ukrainian footballer who played for FC Metalurh Zaporizhzhia, per EssentiallySports. He was 43 years old when he passed away in 2020. According to her interview with Latvian Public Service Media, Ostapenko’s mother, a former tennis coach, introduced her to the sport when she was only five years old. The now 29-year-old has previously revealed that she prefers to go by the name “Alona”, which was the preferred name her parents chose when she was born. They ended up legally naming her “Jelena” as the name “Alona” did not appear on the Latvian calendar – in Latvia and several other European countries, there is a tradition of celebrating “name days” where locals celebrate names associated with the days of the year as listed on their calendar. “Everyone who knows, they call me Alona,” Ostapenko told The New York Times in 2017. “I don’t like when people call me Jelena if they know.” She gave up professional dancing for tennis When Ostapenko started playing tennis, she was introduced to ballroom dancing around the same time and would go on to dance at the national level for seven years. “I chose the tennis because I liked it more and I had better results,” she told AFP in 2016. The tennis prodigy won the junior Wimbledon singles title in 2014 and her ITF junior ranking peaked at No 2 in September that year. She has since won nine WTA tour-level titles, including her recent victory against world No 1 Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus at the Stuttgart Open final in 2025. She was coached by her mother through major parts of her career, including when she won her first grand slam at Roland-Garros in 2017, becoming the first Latvian to do so. Who is Jelena Ostapenko dating? The tennis star was previously linked to Latvian football player Arturs Karasausks, but she has moved on and has been sharing couple snaps with her new beau on Instagram. There is little information available about Ostapenko’s new partner, who uses the Instagram handle @kriossss and keeps his profile private, while attaching a link to Ostapenko’s website in his account bio. With additional reporting from Reuters

title: Malaysia arrests second pilot linked to Jakarta Ecstasy pills smuggling
description: Police said the suspect was in charge of handling the proceeds of the drug sales.
content: A second pilot has been arrested in the ongoing investigation of a drug trafficking case involving a Malaysia Airlines pilot arrested in Indonesia for allegedly smuggling drugs worth 45 million ringgit (US$11 million). Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Commissioner Hussein Omar Khan said the latest arrest was made two days ago and that the suspect was believed to be in charge of handling the proceeds of the drug sales. “He was caught in the Klang Valley area and is in his 30s. He was involved in the handling of the money, specifically in the transferring of money,” Hussein told reporters on Wednesday. “Drug tests conducted showed that he tested negative for drugs. So this arrest brings the total arrests to seven as of now.” It is believed that the suspect worked for a different airline from the first pilot who was arrested in Indonesia. Previously, six suspects were arrested based on information obtained during the questioning of the first pilot by a team of NCID officers sent to Jakarta from August 11 to 15. The suspects are believed to be suppliers and couriers who provided drugs to the first pilot, who was detained at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport after arriving from Kuala Lumpur on Malaysia Airlines flight MH727 in late July. Indonesian customs officers found 14 packages containing 70,114 Ecstasy pills weighing about 25kg (55lbs) in his luggage, as well as 4 grams of methamphetamine in his carry-on belongings. According to Indonesian police, the co-pilot had allegedly been promised 50,000 ringgit to transport the drugs to Jakarta, where they were to be collected by another individual from a hotel. This story was first published by The Star

title: GBA integration may help mainland China’s philanthropy sector learn from Hong Kong
description: City’s experience could ‘drive a major upgrade’ of the philanthropic landscape, experts tell Jockey Club forum.
content: Urgent priorities for advancing China’s philanthropy sector include fostering a favourable legal environment and overhauling the nation’s social service industry, according to leading policy experts at a forum in Hong Kong on Tuesday. Mainland charitable organisations could learn from Hong Kong’s experience to increase their professional expertise, while the Greater Bay Area city cluster plan could be leveraged as a catalyst to boost the sector, they said. The panel discussion – part of the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s Philanthropy for Better Cities Forum – examined China’s philanthropic landscape, with each speaker outlining their priorities for the sector over the next decade. “We need to create a more favourable legal and policy environment for the development of charity organisations – that is good laws and sound governance,” Jin Jinping, associate professor at Peking University law school, told the panel. Wang Zhenyao, a former senior official who spent more than 22 years at the Ministry of Civil Affairs, said Beijing should draw on Hong Kong’s mature philanthropy sector to “drive a major upgrade of the entire social service sector”. Wang is the founding dean of the China Philanthropy Research Institute at Beijing Normal University. Philanthropy is undergoing a profound transformation in China, where historically it has been viewed mainly as an emergency relief tool for natural disasters or basic poverty alleviation. Over the past decade, Beijing has explicitly redefined philanthropy as an integral component of national social governance, tasked with bridging public welfare gaps and delivering social services. This elevated status has come with heightened state oversight, domestic economic headwinds, squeezed corporate margins and changing public expectations. “All of which are driving a broader structural reshaping of the sector,” said Wang Xiangwei, the panel’s moderator. The senior visiting scholar at Harvard Kennedy School is also a former editor-in-chief of the South China Morning Post. As corporate budgets tighten amid economic uncertainty, Chinese businesses are fundamentally rethinking their philanthropic approach, moving beyond cash donations towards leveraging their operational strengths to address social challenges. “For logistics firms, for instance, it is more effective to deploy their well-established logistics systems to build supply chains for disaster-stricken areas rather than simply donating money,” Jin said. Companies were increasingly adopting a sustained approach to social issues, with pharmaceutical firms making the conquest of rare diseases a core objective, while consumer technology companies treated elderly care challenges as potential business growth opportunities, she added. According to Jin, this shift reflects an evolution in corporate thinking – from passive compliance to active corporate social responsibility, and now towards rethinking the fundamental social value of businesses. “Only when money is tight can the companies’ true spirit of volunteer service and social value really shine through,” she said. Wang Zhenyao echoed Jin’s view, stressing that modern sustainable business success required a deep alignment with societal needs. “For enterprises to truly thrive, they must closely integrate with society … and with the objective needs of national welfare and people’s livelihoods,” he said. Looking ahead, the experts regarded cross-border collaboration in the Greater Bay Area – the integrated economic and business hub linking Hong Kong and Macau with cities in Guangdong province – as the main driver for the sector’s transformation. Hailing Hong Kong’s “irreplaceable strengths” – including its mature social work systems and advanced infrastructure – Wang Zhenyao suggested that cross-border integration could catalyse “a new social service industry employing millions of people, with an output value in the tens of trillions of yuan”. However, the panel acknowledged that there were practical hurdles to the proposal under China’s Foreign NGO Law, the main regulatory framework that governs cross-border philanthropy. The legislation requires overseas non-governmental organisations to secure a government or government-affiliated sponsor – known as a professional supervisory unit – to establish a permanent representative office on the mainland or partner with a domestic entity for temporary activities. The law – which also prohibits foreign NGOs from raising funds publicly or recruiting Chinese citizens as members, while subjecting them to stringent financial oversight – had created practical friction for Hong Kong organisations, Jin said. These included what she described as difficulties in securing mainland supervisory units and restrictions on cross-border fund transfers. To overcome these roadblocks, the panellists advocated leveraging the city cluster of the Greater Bay Area to connect Guangdong in southern China with Macau and Hong Kong as “a policy sandbox”. Wang Ming, founding dean of Tsinghua University’s Institute for Philanthropy, said Hong Kong delegates to the political advisory body and national legislature should propose targeted relaxations or special arrangements, rather than pushing for statutory changes. Jin agreed, noting that pilot schemes could also serve cross-border integration. “Starting with the GBA to test and refine these regulations through public participation channels is feasible,” she said.

title: Hong Kong students’ Pisa science scores drop out of top 10 for first time
description: Covid-19 and assessment changes impacted results, but pupils excel in digital learning, highlighting strong STEAM education efforts.
content:
Hong Kong secondary school students’ performance has declined in an international assessment covering three core subjects, marking the first time in the history of the study that their science scores have fallen out of the global top 10.
Experts noted that this drop in scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) can be attributed, in part, to the effects of Covid-19 on students’ study habits and motivation to learn.
Held every three years, Pisa is a worldwide study by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) that tests 15-year-old students on reading, mathematics and science.
The latest study, which ranked 91 countries and economies, was conducted from May to July 2025.
Each cycle since 2012 has also featured an “innovative domain”, which refers to a rotating test topic that measures real-world skills.
The 2025 results, announced by the University of Hong Kong’s education faculty, showed that the city’s students ranked 17th for science, with a mean score of 496, down from seventh place in 2022.
In comparison, the mainland Chinese municipalities and provinces of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang collectively ranked first, scoring 597.
Hong Kong ranked seventh in maths after scoring 522, down from fourth place in 2022, but remained well above the international average of 463. The mainland’s top regions held first place with a score of 612.
In terms of mother-tongue reading literacy, Hong Kong’s score dropped to 480, bringing it down from 11th place in 2022 to 15th. Singapore topped the ranking, netting a score of 535.
The latest study’s literacy portion placed greater emphasis on navigating multiple digital sources and judging online information.
Hong Kong’s Education Bureau, which commissioned the university to conduct the assessment, noted the OECD report partly attributed the decline in overall performance to the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.
The bureau also noted a gap between the latest scores and the education sector’s observations of students’ abilities, with reasons for the disparity including pupils’ psychological state and concentration levels during the test.
Lam Wai-Ip, an associate professor of the faculty and co-project leader for the study, also said the drop in domain subject scores was part of a global decline.
She said that the current cohort had experienced pandemic-related disruptions and grown up in a highly digital environment with rapidly consumed, fragmented online content.
“The pandemic has affected student study habits and learning motivation,” she said.
“The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development found that curiosity, persistence and the ability to integrate and process long or complex texts have dropped since 2022.”
Professor Nancy Law Wai-ying, a member of the study team, said the drop in the city’s science score was related to a shift in the assessment framework, which had moved beyond rote-learning knowledge and now required students to research, evaluate and use scientific information to justify decisions in uncertain contexts.
But Hong Kong students managed to achieve a strong score in the latest assessment’s special topic, “Learning in the Digital World”, with the city ranking sixth and scoring 545, far exceeding the international average of 500.
The assessment tested computational problem-solving through two 30-minute units, one focused on programming and the other on computational modelling.
The framework measured their ability to solve problems using computational tools, conduct experiments, analyse data and debug artefacts, all while exercising self-regulated learning.
The test results showed that 43.1 per cent of Hong Kong students had high levels of proficiency in digital learning, compared with a global average of 25.7 per cent.
Meanwhile, 12 per cent of Hong Kong students had low levels of proficiency, nearly half the global average.
In response to the results, the bureau said: “The outstanding performance in Learning in the Digital World shows the tangible results of our STEAM promotion.”
STEAM learning is an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths.
It also promised to continue focusing on artificial intelligence education, developing curriculum frameworks, supporting teacher training and strengthening students’ digital literacy.
Frederick Leung Koon-shing, an emeritus professor with the faculty and the study’s leader, stressed the importance of enhancing student agency to ensure future readiness.
“Excellent performance in Learning in the Digital World shows many students possess key competencies for developing agency, and the next step is to transfer these strengths to core domains,” he said.
Hong Kong was also found to have maintained strong educational equity in the latest assessment, with 15 per cent of disadvantaged students among top performers, above the OECD average of 12 per cent.
According to the report, Hong Kong students also reported strong teacher support, with 81 per cent saying teachers showed genuine interest and 82 per cent receiving extra help with their studies until they understood subject matter.
The city also scored 497 in digital and environmental adaptability, against an OECD average of 480, with nearly 80 per cent reaching baseline proficiency.
The latest assessment marks Hong Kong’s ninth cycle of taking part in the study. The 2025 sample covered 239 secondary schools, with 230 institutions and 6,445 students included in the final data set after quality assurance checks.
The participating students comprised 52 per cent boys and 48 per cent girls.

title: Chinese stock recovery faces US Fed and oil pressures in September, says top fund manager
description: Strong corporate earnings may cushion stocks, though US rate and oil risks threaten to weigh on sentiment, according to a leading asset manager.
content: Chinese stocks are likely to trade sideways through September, as resilient earnings growth is weighed down by concerns over potential monetary policy tightening in the United States, according to a recent strategy report by China Asset Management, the country’s second-largest mutual fund firm. Mainland-listed companies posted double-digit profit growth in the first half of the year, providing a cushion that is expected to keep a floor under stock prices. But a hawkish tone from the US Federal Reserve and elevated oil prices were likely to cap equity gains, said the money manager, which oversees 2.2 trillion yuan (US$328 billion) in assets. A faster pace of initial public offerings in the third quarter was also expected to squeeze market liquidity, it added. “While the rebound is still getting under way, expectations for returns should be lowered in a rangebound market environment,” the firm stated in the report, as it advised investors to navigate the sideways market by buying on dips rather than chasing rallies. Chinese equities have been recovering from a sharp sell-off in July that hit technology companies especially hard. The chip-heavy Star Market 50 gauge rebounded with a 3 per cent gain in August after plunging 26 per cent the previous month. Still, markets weakened heading into September, approaching July lows after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh signalled that curbing inflation could remain the central bank’s top priority, followed by a hotter-than-expected August jobs report. Rates traders had priced in a 58 per cent chance that the Fed would raise interest rates by 25 basis points at its policy meeting next week, according to CME Group on Wednesday. At the same time, crude oil prices rising to nearly US$100 a barrel after escalating strikes between the US and Iran have further fuelled expectations of monetary tightening. Higher global borrowing costs could unwind heavily crowded trades in the tech sector, where stretched valuations are coming under pressure while funding costs for artificial intelligence investment are rising. To manage this uncertainty, China Asset Management recommended a balanced portfolio approach known as a “barbell strategy”, which splits investments between high-growth technology shares and more stable, defensive sectors like coal production and banking. The asset-management firm projected an increase of up to 15 per cent in full-year earnings for listed companies outside the financial and petrochemical sectors, adding that the market had not yet fully priced in that growth. Corporate profit growth reached 14.1 per cent in the first half, up 1.9 percentage points from the first quarter, the firm said. Technology companies led earnings growth in the first half. Firms trading on the Star Market recorded a more than fourfold surge in profit, driven by strong demand for domestic alternatives, according to data from the China Association for Public Companies. China Asset Management currently manages more than 500 fund products, with stock-focused funds making up about one-third of its total assets, according to data compiled by Wind. Citic Securities is its largest shareholder, with a 62 per cent stake.

title: Amid China’s AI shift, JD.com bets on 3 million robots to automate logistics
description: The firm plans to retrain frontline workers for more technical roles, including maintenance of robots.
content: Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com is accelerating its push into robotics with a sweeping plan to automate its nationwide logistics network, while promising to retrain its vast workforce of couriers for technical roles as machines take over frontline duties. At an event in Beijing on Wednesday, the company’s logistics arm unveiled its industrial Wolf Robot series. Over the next five years, JD Logistics aimed to procure 3 million robots, 1 million unstaffed vehicles and 100,000 delivery drones to create a fully automated supply chain, according to Cao Peng, the chairman of the company’s technology committee. Designed to take up repetitive, labour-intensive tasks and operate in challenging conditions, the Wolf Robot system would pick, sort, transport and deliver goods with minimal human intervention, said Liu Lige, head of embodied intelligence robots at JD Logistics. The line-up included specialised units capable of operating in cold environments down to minus 20 degrees Celsius, automated pharmacy dispatchers and delivery drones, Liu said. The rapid shift towards automation comes as JD and its ecosystem companies continue to employ some 700,000 delivery and logistics personnel. To address job displacement concerns, founder Liu Qiangdong outlined earlier this year the company’s so-called Nirvana Plan, an initiative to retrain couriers and warehouse staff for technical roles like robot servicing and maintenance, ensuring frontline workers were retained as automation spread. Beyond hardware, JD was betting that its major advantage in embodied artificial intelligence would lie in data collection. Training general-purpose embodied AI models requires vast data sets. Global stockpiles of quality collected interaction data for embodied AI stood at about 500,000 hours as of early this year, far short of the tens of millions of hours required, according to a report in June by SWS Research. Leveraging its physical footprint across warehouses, retail stores and pharmacies, JD planned to gather more than 10 million hours of real-world operational data, Cao said. The company also aimed to establish more than 80 RoboBase hubs across China dedicated to robotics research, pilot production, data annotation, equipment upgrades and maintenance. To support the heavy computational demands of this ecosystem, JD signed a deal on Wednesday with Chinese chip designer Moore Threads to build a computing cluster powered by 100,000 domestic chips. The cluster would be used to train and run AI models, as well as embodied AI applications, and to help JD integrate domestic chips into an AI development pipeline that spans data collection, model training, simulation and deployment, according to the two companies.

title: Thailand probes clinic linked to UK influencer’s penile filler death
description: Igho Ubiribo’s death from a penis enlargement procedure at a Bangkok clinic has sparked medical tourism safety concerns in Thailand.
content: Thai authorities said on Wednesday they are investigating a Bangkok clinic where a Nigerian-born British businessman and influencer underwent a penis enlargement procedure that led to his death. A coroner in London last month ruled that the March 6 death of Igho Ubiribo, 43, in the Thai capital was caused by the hyaluronic acid injection he received hours earlier. The case has reignited debate about medical tourism, with Thailand a leading destination for visitors from abroad seeking healthcare, including aesthetic procedures. Ubiribo, reportedly known as “Tiny” and “Ego”, had 185,000 followers on Instagram, regularly posting pictures with his wife Danielle enjoying a luxury lifestyle. Thailand’s health ministry ordered an investigation into his death and officials on Monday visited the central Bangkok clinic where Ubiribo was treated. Authorities are looking into whether it holds a valid licence and followed health and safety protocols, a health ministry official said. He was having a massage after receiving the filler when he complained of chest pains and collapsed, according to an August report from the UK coroner, which formally determines cause of death. He was taken by ambulance to hospital, suspected of having a pulmonary embolism, but lost consciousness before he could have a CT scan. Doctors tried to resuscitate him for over 100 minutes but he was declared dead around 1am. “Postmortem examination and toxicology determined the cause of death to be due to the hyaluronic acid injection,” the report said. Senior Bangkok police official Utit Soodjai said his officers were also investigating. “When it comes to medical procedures, we advocate for the highest level of caution,” Thai Health Minister Pattana Promphat told reporters. The investigation was intended “to ensure fairness for everyone and to reassure both local and international patients that they are receiving safe, high-standard and valuable care in Thailand”, he added in a statement. According to the health ministry, the clinic’s managers said Ubiribo had been a regular patient since 2024 and had undergone five penile enlargement injections. The first four procedures took place in 2024 and 2025, while on his fifth visit on March 5, he received 40 millilitres of filler. The doctor had recommended splitting the procedure into two sessions, but Ubiribo requested that the entire amount be injected in one session, clinic management told investigators. Hyaluronic acid fillers are widely used in aesthetic medicine, considered minimally invasive and relatively low risk. Thailand has a reputation for excellent healthcare and has long been a centre for medical tourism, while the aesthetic market is booming. As of 2024, official figures showed it had 7,000 aesthetic clinics, including 2,000 in Bangkok, and forecast a market worth US$7.51 billion in 2027 – three times the size in 2020.

title: Record rain forces hundreds of Asian Games athletes to evacuate accommodation
description: There is no dedicated athletes’ village, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden containers and hotels.
content: Hundreds of Asian Games athletes in Japan were briefly evacuated from their accommodation as record rainfall lashed host city Nagoya, with competition starting on Thursday. Rainwater also leaked into some competition venues, with more wet weather forecast for the coming days. The Asian Games officially begin on September 19 but several events, such as basketball, get under way before that. About 104mm (four inches) of rain fell in an hour in Nagoya on Tuesday, prompting municipal officials to issue an evacuation order for parts of the city. Cars were forced to plough through heavily flooded roads, causing huge traffic jams, while water streamed into subway stations. Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of weather events in Japan and elsewhere. There is no dedicated athletes’ village at this year’s Asian Games, with organisers instead relying on a cruise ship, temporary wooden containers and hotels. An official with Nagoya Port Authority said that “hundreds” of athletes staying at the city’s Garden Pier area, where the wooden container huts are located, were told to move to safety. The athletes returned after the evacuation order was lifted about two hours later. Rainwater was found in several competition venues but Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said the facilities were not seriously affected and that events would go ahead as scheduled. “There has been limited impact like rainwater leaking from the roofs of some buildings, but the situation is not so serious that the opening [ceremony] on the 19th is in jeopardy for now,” he said. “Given the current circumstances, I believe there will be no obstacles to holding the Asian Games.” Subway and bus services in Nagoya were temporarily halted on Tuesday and the Japan Meteorological Agency issued its highest flood warning for a major river in the area. Television footage showed rainwater pouring onto a railway line like a waterfall from elevated ground. In another part of Nagoya, an abandoned car sat on a pedestrian pavement Wednesday. “Traffic congestion is terrible because cars that can’t move any more are here and there, blocking the roads,” Hitomi Terada, who works at a hotel in hard-hit Chigusa district, said. “Most of our 25 guest rooms were filled with guests who were unable to go home because of traffic congestion,” the 44-year-old said. “Some of our hotel employees couldn’t come this morning for work because of traffic problems.” Japan’s weather agency issued further warnings Wednesday for heavy rain and landslides, with rainfall expected to continue intermittently through Thursday in many areas of the country, including Aichi prefecture that is hosting the Asian Games. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are expected at the Games – a bigger number than the Olympics.

title: As China embraces AI, only 24% of US pharmaceutical execs bet on it for innovation
description: Survey finds drug companies planned to scale AI or had already done so, but few anticipated a ‘wholesale revolution’ from the tech.
content: Pharmaceutical companies have embraced artificial intelligence in drug research almost universally, yet few company executives expect AI to actually make drugs succeed, according to a Citi survey released on Tuesday. “The biggest risk to the AI-powered drug discovery thesis is not that AI fails to accelerate discovery,” said John Yung, head of Asia healthcare research at the US investment bank. “The stronger risk is that acceleration does not translate into better drugs or higher probability of success.” “It’s only through that translation that companies can turn AI-driven speed into profit, and patients into real beneficiaries,” Yung added. Some 72 per cent of respondents said their companies were either “scaling” or had “fully scaled” AI across research and development, and no company reported having no plans to adopt the technology, the survey found. Citi Research polled 50 US-based executives responsible for technology strategy in pharmaceutical research and development in June 2026. Yet that enthusiasm comes with a caveat. Only 24 per cent of respondents expected AI to deliver a significant improvement in drug success probability, while 56 per cent expected only a moderate uplift, “not a wholesale revolution,” according to the survey. Another 34 per cent said human biology, clinical judgment and execution will remain as bottlenecks, regardless of how much AI is deployed. The findings suggested “executives are genuinely optimistic [with AI], but they are not naive about the complexities of biology”, the survey noted. Executives saw the biggest near-term payoff in early-stage discovery rather than in the clinic. Target identification and validation was cited by 70 per cent of respondents as an area where AI was expected to improve success rates, followed by lead optimisation and hit identification and screening. Most respondents expected double-digit budget increases for AI-related R&D spending over the next 12 months. Shortening discovery timelines was the leading commercial reason companies sought outside AI partners, with 84 per cent surveyed engaging with external AI companies, the survey found. Business consulting and market research firm Frost & Sullivan estimated AI could save the industry US$26 billion globally at the drug discovery stage and a further US$28 billion in clinical research – about half of current spending in those phases. Unlike many US companies in the sector that remain loss-making, several Chinese leaders, such as Shanghai-listed DNA-encoded-library maker HitGen and Hong Kong-listed AI drug researcher Xtalpi were already profitable, according to Citi. They “should see earnings accelerate as robust demand translates into stronger utilisation and operating leverage”, Yung said. However, valuations paint a different picture. Leading Chinese AI drug discovery companies trade at a median price-to-sales ratio – a measure of how much investors are paying for each dollar of a company’s revenue – of 19 times their projected 2026 sales, a steep discount compared with the 93 times commanded by their US peers, according to Citi.

title: Chinese grandparents let court jail granddaughter for stealing US$3,000 to teach her a lesson
description: Traditional Chinese values emphasise family as a collective, where parents typically share wealth with children, regardless of age.
content: An elderly Chinese couple reported their granddaughter to the police after she took 20,000 yuan (US$3,000) and a gold bracelet from their home without permission, igniting intense discussions online. The woman, identified by her surname Chen and hailing from northwest China’s Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, received a six-month jail sentence for theft, along with a fine of 2,000 yuan, according to the Legal Daily on September 1. Chen had taken the money and jewellery from her grandparents while her grandfather was napping at home. Subsequently, she sold the gold bracelet for over 27,000 yuan and squandered the entire amount. Even during her trial, she maintained that she should be acquitted of all charges, stating: “It is my grandparents’ money that I took. They will forgive me and won’t hold me accountable. This is our family matter.” However, the elderly couple opted not to grant her forgiveness. They said that they had indulged their granddaughter, whom they described as lazy and always wanting to “reap without sowing.” Previously, she had taken other valuables from their home, each time of greater worth. Consequently, they decided to utilise legal measures as a means to educate her. The sentence Chen received sparked passionate discussions on Chinese social media. “She must have repeatedly stolen their money and ultimately disappointed them,” commented one observer. “The grandparents acted appropriately. This isn’t solely about the money; it’s an opportunity for her to completely reform,” remarked another. Some believed the elderly couple had overreacted. “They could have resolved the issue privately, but instead, they chose to push her into a corner and jeopardise her future,” remarked an online commenter. Traditional Chinese values regard the family as a collective, where parents often share their wealth with children, regardless of their age. For instance, Chinese parents typically cover their children’s educational expenses even as they pursue advanced degrees. It is also common for young couples buying property to tap into the so-called “six wallets,” referring to pooling their savings alongside those of their parents and in-laws. In recent years, another term, “full-time children,” has emerged to describe this traditional Chinese familial dynamic, wherein more young adults live with their parents and function as household carers in exchange for monetary support. For parents with substantial pensions who can financially support their children, this “salary” is perceived by some as a new form of pocket money generously provided to alleviate their children’s financial burdens. Echoing the Chinese ethos of shared wealth, another commenter backed the grandparents’ decision: “You can ask me for money, but you cannot steal from me.” According to Chinese Criminal Law, individuals who steal considerable amounts of public or private property, or who commit repeated theft, face imprisonment of up to three years. While stealing from family members or close relatives is generally not classified as a crime if forgiveness is obtained, offenders may still receive leniency if pursued for criminal liability.

title: Horoscopes: what’s your luck like in September 2026, the Fire Rooster month?

September is traditionally the month of communication and commercialism. It is the Fire Rooster month. This month is all about letting go and clearing emotional and physical clutter. In traditional Chinese culture, the rooster’s energy is glamorous and detail-oriented. Associated with communication, renewal, and commerce because of its metal element, the Rooster signifies opportunities, making this a great month to make changes that may have been delayed until now. Driven by a keen sense of justice, the Rooster values equality and advocates for those who struggle to speak up for themselves with conviction and clarity. Naturally honest and passionate, Roosters can be both an asset and a hindrance depending on communication conditions – sometimes coming across as blunt and argumentative, yet if you have a Rooster on your side, you can count on coming out on top! Ideal career choices for Roosters include anything that brings colour and action into their life, like tourism, education, the fashion and beauty industry, charity work, politics and the music business. Famous Roosters include Dolly Parton, Hans Zimmer, Jo Brand, Melanie Griffith, Stephen Fry, Gloria Estefan, Spike Lee, Gwen Stefani, Ariana Grande, Harry Styles, Beyoncé, Matthew McConaughey, Matthew Perry, Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bob Marley, Yoko Ono, Roger Federer, Aung San Suu Kyi and Helen Mirren. The Rooster is compatible with the Dragon, Ox and Snake. Challenges occur with those born in Rabbit years. The Rabbit is the nemesis of the Rooster (they are astrological foes), a difficult match, as the Rooster can be too “loud” for the quiet nature of the Rabbit. Their communication is their weakest point, which can be determined by the pair holding opposite directions of east and west. What does September 2026 hold for your astrological sign? Health gains strength, making it a great month to move forward with confidence in any collaborations that have been slow to come to fruition. Your previous efforts will be richly rewarded, with the chance to secure an important position. Play to your strengths, Tigers. X Rabbit – wealth luck is good Your clash month of the year brings a busy period, but your efforts will still be proportional to your rewards, gaining traction and recognition from key figures who can open doors for you. Wealth luck is good; hard work brings a substantial income, so be willing to consider some financial planning. A busy month suggests you may be consumed by work, leaving your partner feeling neglected. Be aware of how important communication is this month, and take time to listen to them. Balance work and rest to avoid a weakened immune system due to overwork. √ Dragon – seriously consider any self-investment Be willing to rub shoulders with the right people, as strong connections make all the difference in the last quarter of your year. Wealth luck is rising, and investments in learning and upskilling will be well spent. Do seriously consider any self-investment. Health and harmony appear smooth, and your partner may share learning goals that enhance your mutual understanding. You appear astute, enjoying clarity and a positive mindset, which supports learning and thinking. ∞ Snake – time management is key Your workload increases as business picks up, and your income matches the effort you are willing to put in. Your star power is undeniable, and you may be asked to take on even more; if so, be willing to step up, take the lead, and pursue your most ambitious targets. Time management is key to making the best of the energy surrounding you; maintain a regular sleep schedule to avoid burnout and disharmony with loved ones. You may suffer from skin and respiratory issues; the good news is that overall, your health appears strong, so keep your immune system in good shape to maintain your energy and output. ∞ Horse – avoid major changes The Rooster should help you get back in the saddle and back on track with any previously stalled projects that may have a chance to restart. Things should run smoothly under your control. Avoid major changes or anything that might upset the status quo and delicate balance this month. Wealth improves slightly, but cautious management may still be necessary. Health appears better, but as the seasons change, be aware of internal dampness, which can affect the lungs and upper body. Ears are susceptible at this time of the year. ∞ Sheep – avoid being too outspoken Take everything presented to you this month with a grain of salt, as the surrounding energy indicates the potential for loss – such as misplacing personal items or losing wealth through ATM or credit card transactions. You may have to contend with some rivalry, so it’s best to lie low, even regarding your quiet successes. Avoid being too outspoken; focus on producing your best work. This will go a long way towards rewarding previous efforts, allowing both your status and reputation to improve quietly. It may be a sociable month, so ensure you are in good health to enjoy some fun moments. ∞ Monkey – wealth luck appears stable As you share the same astrological location as the Sheep, you may also encounter some strong competition in the workplace where others may try to take credit for your work. So, play your cards close to your chest to avoid conflict and petty individuals. If you can keep your head down, you may be rewarded with some kind of partnership opportunity. If so, take your time to evaluate it carefully, and avoid being deceived by others and their fancy schemes. Wealth luck appears stable, as long as you safeguard what you have already built and keep a close eye on spending. Support the body with enough rest to reduce stress and tension. ∞ Rooster – beware of some rivalries September is your astrological month when female benefactors may offer their support; any previous difficulties are resolved, and work will be busy, ushering in new developments. This benefactor brings wisdom and experience, and may also present financial opportunities. You may be in the limelight; beware of rivalries fuelled by jealousy, and avoid heated discussions at all costs. Prioritise your mental well-being by delegating whenever possible. If you have recently met someone new, allow the relationship to evolve at its own pace. X Pig – be vigilant and patient Energy may remain low this month, making it harder to keep up your usual pace. Prioritise your most important tasks and let the less important ones wait. Be vigilant and patient, especially with interpersonal relationships. Keep operations steady and avoid taking on any new or potentially stressful ventures, focusing on maintaining what you have already achieved this year. Rest well and avoid overexertion; if anything feels amiss, see a doctor early. The good news is that a windfall may be on the way.

title: Umno heavyweight charged in Malaysian haj fund scandal as party eyes comeback
description: Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim is the highest-profile politician to be charged so far in the fallout from a royal inquiry into Tabung Haji.
content: Former Malaysian pilgrimage fund chairman Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to abusing his position to secure a lucrative corporate post and influence a 193.5 million ringgit (US$47.5 million) investment by the fund. Azeez, 60, a veteran Umno Supreme Council member, is the highest-profile politician to be charged so far in the fallout from a royal inquiry into the state-run savings fund Tabung Haji. Wearing a purple police lock-up uniform and handcuffed as he stood in the dock, Azeez said: “The allegation in this corruption case is completely untrue, and I ask to be tried.” The Kuala Lumpur Sessions Court appearance comes as the former ruling party opens its annual congress after recent state-election gains. Azeez is accused of using his position as Lembaga Tabung Haji head in August 2014 to become chairman of construction company Putrajaya Perdana. The post, which paid 690,000 ringgit a year, came with a BMW 7 Series and a full-time driver. Prosecutors allege he instructed then Tabung Haji chief executive Ismee Ismail to nominate him as the fund’s representative at Putrajaya Perdana and persuaded its board to approve an investment of up to 193.5 million ringgit, about 30 per cent of its existing issued share capital, despite having an interest in the deal. The charge, under Section 23(1) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) Act, carries a penalty of up to 20 years in prison and a fine of at least five times the value of the gratification involved, or 10,000 ringgit, whichever is higher. Earlier on Wednesday, Azeez and two former senior Tabung Haji officials were remanded for two days in a separate police investigation into alleged fraud involving the fund’s profit distributions to depositors. His lawyer said the other two were the former chief executive and group chief financial officer. Azeez returns to the dock four years after the High Court acquitted him of nine unrelated corruption and money-laundering charges involving road projects in Perak and Kedah. He was fully cleared in December 2022, three months after receiving a discharge not amounting to an acquittal. Past baggage Tabung Haji helps Malaysian Muslims save for the haj pilgrimage. It held 93.4 billion ringgit in depositor savings at the end of 2025, with 9.7 million depositors nationwide. A royal commission report released in late July examined Tabung Haji’s management from 2014 to 2020, spanning Najib Razak’s Barisan Nasional government and the administrations that followed its 2018 defeat. It identified political interference, governance failures and problematic investments, and proposed 25 reforms. The commission also found that Tabung Haji had resorted to “creative accounting” while paying profit distributions beyond its financial capacity. Had Malaysian accounting standards been fully applied, the fund would have recorded a 1.4 billion ringgit loss in 2017, instead of the 3.4 billion ringgit profit it reported. Among the failings identified was the appointment of active politicians to Tabung Haji’s leadership, Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Hasan told a special parliamentary sitting last month. “We must never again allow Tabung Haji to become a victim of the abuse of power and political interests,” he said. The MACC said last week it had opened 14 investigation papers linked to the inquiry, detained 18 people and remanded 11. Former religious affairs minister Jamil Khir Baharom was separately remanded over a inquiry into Tabung Haji hotel leases in Saudi Arabia and released on bail on Tuesday. Two Tabung Haji subsidiary officials have also pleaded not guilty to criminal breach of trust charges, while former chief operating officer Adi Azuan Abdul Ghani is due in court on September 24. Less than two weeks ago, former prime minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob, another Umno veteran, pleaded not guilty to failing to declare millions in local and foreign currencies and gold bars. The legal pressure comes as Umno tries to convert its recent state election gains into momentum for a broader federal comeback. Party president and Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi is also calling for the next general election to be held earlier than February 2028. Zahid has described the party’s recent momentum as a “blue wave” towards Putrajaya. Umno began its four-day annual assembly on Wednesday after Barisan Nasional, the coalition it leads, scored strong victories in Johor and Negeri Sembilan. James Chin, a scholar of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania, said Azeez’s prosecution “complicates the party comeback narrative” but was unlikely to shake Umno’s core support. “Umno is of the view that this really doesn’t matter as long as they can get the votes of [Malay] supporters,” Chin said. “Most people associate Umno with grand corruption … people are not surprised,” he said. “It’s not going to affect the core Umno votes at all.”

title: Ex-Hong Kong lawmaker William Wong’s bail extended on 4 traffic offences
description: He was arrested on suspicion of crashing his car into two parked vehicles while under the influence of alcohol on the CUHK campus.
content: Former Hong Kong lawmaker William Wong Kam-fai, who resigned after an alleged drink-driving incident, has been given two months to consider his plea on four traffic offences. Wong, 66, was not required to enter a plea during his first appearance at Sha Tin Court on Wednesday. Defence lawyer Paul Tse Wai-chun, also a former legislator, sought a nine-week adjournment to allow time for legal advice. Magistrate Raymond Wong Kwok-fai set the next hearing for November 11. A computer scientist by profession, Wong became the first Legislative Council member to resign over personal conduct since Beijing overhauled Hong Kong’s electoral system in 2021 to restrict public office to those deemed “patriotic”. He was arrested in the early hours of June 30 on suspicion of crashing his car into two parked vehicles while under the influence of alcohol on the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) campus in Sha Tin the previous day. According to a charge sheet available for press inspection, Wong’s breath-alcohol concentration was 45 micrograms per 100 millilitres – more than double the statutory limit of 22 micrograms. He is also alleged to have failed to stop after the accident and to have failed to report it to police within 24 hours. Wong faces four charges: driving with an alcohol concentration in breath above the prescribed limit, dangerous driving, failing to stop after an accident and failing to report an accident. The court extended Wong’s HK$5,000 (US$638) bail, previously granted by police, but barred him from driving or contacting prosecution witnesses. He was ordered to surrender his driving licence and to report to police once every two weeks from September 23 upon his return from a business trip. Following his arrest, Wong apologised for “causing inconvenience” to Legco. CUHK suspended him from his administrative duties as an associate dean of its engineering faculty. Wong is a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), the nation’s top political advisory body.

title: China needs monkeys: lab animal shortage could hinder biotech growth
description: As fundraising and out-licensing deals in China grow, so does demand for monkeys and other primates for testing.
content: China’s biotechnology market has “significantly” driven up the demand for primate experimental models as the market recovers, tightening the supply of laboratory monkeys, according to a leading biotech firm. The continued recovery of fundraising and out-licensing deals in innovative drugs in China this year has led to significant growth in the demand for primate experimental models, contract research firm Joinn Laboratories (China) said on Tuesday. Primate experiments typically use monkeys and other non-human species to test the safety and efficacy of a drug under development before clinical trials on humans. As global pharmaceutical giants continued their buying spree for China’s cheaper innovative drugs, the price of a lab monkey has climbed as high as 200,000 yuan (US$29,802) in July, compared with only about 50,000 yuan in early 2025, according to Chinese media. Over US$110 billion worth of Chinese-developed drug candidates were traded in 81 out-licensing deals in the first half of the year, equivalent to 80 per cent of the full-year value in 2025, data from China’s National Medical Products Administration showed. Joinn added that the price increase resulted from the tightened supply of non-human primates for experimental use in China, as their breeding rate has remained relatively stable. Shanghai Medicilon, another global contract research organisation, also told investors in July that the overall supply of lab monkeys had contracted amid the biotech industry’s recent recovery. The shortfall of lab monkeys in China was projected to range between 15,000 and 20,000 from 2026 to 2028, according to a note by Zheshang Securities in March. Dubbed the “Mao-tai of lab monkeys”, Joinn has significantly benefited from China’s biotech boom, with its Hong Kong-listed shares skyrocketing over 150 per cent since 2025. In the first half of the year, Joinn reported a net profit of 747.5 million yuan, an 11-fold growth year on year, primarily citing the paper gains of “biological assets”. Joinn said it owned over 20,000 non-human primates used for breeding and non-clinical research as of December 2025. In its interim results report, the firm said its inventory grew steadily from January to June, though did not divulge specific figures. In 2022, Joinn spent 1.8 billion yuan to acquire two companies in China’s southwest with a combined inventory of nearly 20,000 non-human primates. WuXi AppTec, another Chinese biotech giant, acquired a Suzhou-based company for about 804 million yuan, with one of its acquired entities holding about 20,000 macaques. US pharmaceutical giant Charles River proposed in January to acquire K.F. (Cambodia), one of its monkey suppliers, for US$510 million to secure the non-human primate supply chain. Laboratory monkey reserves and stable supply had become a core factor in the competitiveness of preclinical contract research organisations, according to Orient Securities analysts. Demand for the animals would continue to grow, as more Chinese-developed drugs were in the pipeline, they said in a note on August 31, adding that applications for pre-market drug candidates increased by 33 per cent year on year to 627 cases in the first half of 2026. “In the medium to long-term, the home-developed drugs will account for more share in China’s pipeline of innovative drugs for overseas markets, further increasing the demand for macaques,” the analysts said.

title: Vegan dim sum, salads, Indian: where a Polish marketing manager eats in Hong Kong
description: Jakub Lewandowski of The Mira Hong Kong reveals his top vegan dining spots, from custom salads to Chinese dim sum and Indian buffets.
content: Jakub Lewandowski is the PR and marketing manager of The Mira Hong Kong in Tsim Sha Tsui, and a vegan. He spoke to Andrew Sun. I was born in Krakow, the royal capital of Poland. My family house was blessed with a garden and mini orchard, with seasonal fruit, berries and vegetables. As on every Polish table, there would be plenty of meat. Baked home-made rabbit pâté was a thing for us. When I was 12, my sister and I were invited by our half-Scottish, half-Filipino relatives to stay for a summer in Kalimantan – the Indonesian part of Borneo. There, I was exposed to a bewildering choice of exotic fruits. Later, I met a partner who opened my eyes to healthier and cleaner eating. In 2008, we switched to a vegan lifestyle. For a treat, I head to Treehouse (Shop S28, B/F, Heath, 36-44 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 6180 6396). My regular order is a custom salad box. I am addicted to the roasted cherry tomatoes and kimchi that go so well with the mixed grain rice and greens. The sweet potato fries and chocolate brownie are hard to resist, too. I am not into Chinese vegetarian buffets where dishes are often fried or excessively oily. Everyday (Diamond Court, 10-12 Hillwood Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2570 2266) is an exception, with serene organic vibes that contrast with the area’s hustle and bustle. There are times when office life calls for a birthday lunch. Luckily, my teammates are thoughtful enough to select somewhere with at least one veggie option. Coucou Hotpot-Tea Break (various locations including B124, K11 Art Mall, 18 Hanoi Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2347 2028) proved a fun surprise. It offers a coconut water broth as an alternative, served in its own mini hotpot so I can avoid cross-contamination. Another time, we went to the vintage establishment Tai Ping Koon Restaurant (40 Granville Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2721 3559). The single vegan item on the rich menu, curried vegetables, was hearty and spicy enough to call for white rice on the side. I loved the 1950s ambience and seeing people enjoy the signature Swiss chicken wings and XXL soufflé. I heard great things about Gaylord Indian Restaurant (5/F, Prince Tower, 12A Peking Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2376 1001), so we tried their affordable lunch buffet. I would return for dinner as the setting is very comfortable. For more casual dining, Rue du Liban (Shop A, 22-26 Hillwood Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2310 2922) is an established Middle Eastern hotspot with a nice ambience and some fully plant-based mezzes. I also feel privileged to dine at Cuisine Cuisine (3/F, The Mira Hong Kong, 118-130 Nathan Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2315 5222) for work. Chef Ringo Wong’s art of dim sum is really another level. The delicate handmade wild mushroom and vegetable dumplings reign supreme among all guests, not just vegetarians. A more rough-around-the-edges but authentic Cantonese dim sum lunch is Veggie Kingdom (7/F, VIP Commercial Centre, 120 Canton Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 2366 0336), which really impresses with textures and flavours. My personal benchmark of what plant-based cuisine should be is Hum Central (VNPT Building, Nguyen Van Binh Street, W. Saigon, Ho Chi Minh City. Tel: +84 89 918 92 29), which is locally inspired, fresh and delicious, and set in one of the city’s most eye-catching buildings.
