The square deep-fried spring rolls are mouth-watering, with one sheet of rice paper holding a generous mushroom stuffing. A healthy alternative is the chargrilled wild mushroom rolls in doi dat leaf with its distinct aroma. The crunchy Dien Bien sticky rice with wild Sapa mushrooms is a stand-out.

title: Trump slams Australia’s social media crackdown as ‘extortion’
description: The White House warns Australia over its proposed algorithm opt-out bill, as Anthony Albanese defends national sovereignty.
content: US President Donald Trump has condemned Australia’s recent moves to clamp down on social media – predominantly run by American tech companies – as “a form of extortion”, hinting at more threats to come. “President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector,” White House economics spokesman Kush Desai said on Tuesday night, as reported by news.com.au. “The administration remains committed to raising these issues with our trading partners.” Under the new “My Feed, My Way” initiative announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Tuesday, Australians would have the option to opt out of powerful social media algorithms. Draft legislation introducing a mandatory “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to parliament this week. “We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC on Monday. “There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” added Wells, who led Australia’s world-first social media ban for children under 16. “Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards.” On Wednesday, Wells told News24 Australia that US officials had not contacted her office over the proposed law, and ‌rejected the suggestion that her government’s social media reforms amounted to “extortion”. If passed, the law requires firms including Meta Platforms, Google and TikTok to protect younger users from damaging material – such as content promoting harmful behaviour or causing serious mental distress – while offering users over 16 control over their social media curation. “We’ll require social media platforms provide user empowerment tools that give people over the age of 16 genuine and enduring choice about what they see in their feeds,” Albanese said, according to news.com.au. “We have an opportunity to shape technology for the better rather than let it shape us. That is what our reforms are all about.” Under the proposal, social media platforms will be required to send notifications giving users a choice over their default feed, according to US public broadcaster NPR. Users can opt to have personalised content recommended by an algorithm or a chronological feed showing only posts from people they follow. Digital services, including online games, apps and AI chatbots, will also be required to ensure children are shielded from design features promoting harmful behaviours such as addiction. Companies that fail to comply could face fines of up to A$100 million (US$65 million), according to Wells. However, a media analyst has questioned whether users will take advantage of the option. “The government has handed Australians a switch. Whether anyone flips it is another matter,” Lisa Harrison, a lecturer in communication and media at Flinders University, told Agence France-Presse, citing a 2025 survey across six countries where only one in five people said they would switch off personalised recommendations. “The algorithm is good at its job, and the minority who do opt out will find a feed of friends and creators feels quieter than the one they left,” Harrison said. The move is the latest in Canberra’s broader campaign against big tech firms. Last month, Australia passed the News Bargaining Incentive to compel major digital platforms to fund local journalism – a measure the White House similarly called extortion. The National Foreign Trade Council, a US business association, raised concerns last week after the Australian Tax Office reclassified cloud computing and streaming revenue as royalties, subjecting them to higher tax rates. “Australia has become more and more aggressive on the tax front, and a less and less hospitable environment for investment across the board,” Anne Gordon, the council’s vice-president for international tax policy, told The Sydney Morning Herald. Trump and Albanese are set to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York later this month. Asked if he expected pushback from the US president, Albanese said: “We’re a sovereign nation; we decide our policies based upon the Australian national interest. But my relationship with the US president is indeed very good, and I look forward to seeing President Trump in New York in a couple of weeks’ time.”

title: Hong Kong a ‘2-way springboard’ between mainland China and world: John Lee
description: Speaking at Belt and Road Summit, chief executive says city is taking structured approach to new markets in Southeast Asia, Middle East and Central Asia.
content: Hong Kong will continue to serve as a gateway linking belt and road economies with mainland China and global markets, the chief executive has said, underscoring the city’s role in bringing together capital, talent and businesses to advance the national initiative. Speaking at the opening of the annual Belt and Road Summit on Wednesday, John Lee Ka-chiu said more than 60 government and business agreements and memorandums of understanding (MOUs) would be signed during the event, with the total value of projects and deals exceeding US$3 billion. “In a world struggling with unprecedented change and geopolitical fragmentation, connectivity, cooperation, and consensus are essential. That’s precisely what the Belt and Road Summit offers,” he said. “The Belt and Road Initiative is not a map of the past, but a shared blueprint for the future. And Hong Kong is where we realise that future: where East meets West, where capital, talent, businesses and opportunities converge.” Lee described Hong Kong as a “two-way springboard” for mainland enterprises seeking to expand overseas and international companies looking to access the mainland market. He said the city would serve as a global gateway for belt and road businesses to raise capital, citing recent examples such as Kazakhstan’s national railway company applying to list on the city’s stock exchange. Lee said Hong Kong had adopted a strategic and structured approach to exploring new markets, strengthening ties with regions including Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Central Asia following visits he made to them. “Our regional focus is structured. Our reach remains flexible. Our drive stems from meeting the needs and interests of the business community,” Lee said. “[The visits] underline Hong Kong’s long-standing focus on opening new markets, forming new partnerships and advancing regional cooperation.” He highlighted his visit to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June, which aimed to create an interconnected network of hubs and had already produced tangible results. The South China Morning Post organised the inaugural “China Conference: Central Asia 2026” in the Kazakh capital Astana on Monday. Lee also emphasised efforts to promote cultural and educational exchanges with belt and road countries, noting that the government’s scholarship scheme had supported more than 830 students from the nations, while about 600 had taken up internships in Hong Kong. The two-day summit, themed “Advancing high-quality development, embarking on a new journey”, promotes business among nations participating in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network. For the first time, a dedicated “Go Global Chapter” will support mainland firms expanding overseas. Speaking at the summit’s keynote lunch, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said Southeast Asia had a huge young population, a rapidly expanding middle class and market, and was an important partner in technological advancement and industrial upgrading. He stressed that Hong Kong could leverage its strengths to help the region better capture economic and technological gains. “By building on our respective strengths and working together, we can turn these assets into greater progress and shared prosperity across the region,” Chan said. “Hong Kong is ready to play its part: connecting innovators with global markets, mobilising patient capital and providing a place where talent from across the region can thrive.” Chan cited the city’s leading position in global initial public offerings last year, with a growing number of listings from Southeast Asian and other belt and road economies. He also highlighted the Greater Bay Area’s unique advantages, which offered businesses a vast consumer market and a concentration of frontier research and industries within easy reach, with the Northern Metropolis megaproject deepening cross-regional collaboration. He added that the city continued to attract outstanding overseas scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs, thereby bringing in more long-term investors and patient capital. Frederick Ma Si-hang, chairman of the Trade Development Council, the summit’s organiser, said belt and road initiatives aimed to turn potential into opportunity that benefited the world, with momentum coming from high-growth regions such as Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America. He noted that this year’s summit had introduced dedicated Central Asia and Middle East zones to help attendees expand their networks with business communities from those regions. He added that Hong Kong was ideally positioned to connect belt and road businesses, citing its strength as a global financial centre, a hub for trade and logistics, a pool of top international talent and recent advances in innovation and technology. More than 6,000 government leaders and professionals from over 70 countries are attending the summit, which Ma described as a “powerful testament” to Hong Kong’s unique role. “Today’s presence of so many distinguished guests and leaders from around the world is a powerful testament to the value of connecting, which leads to tangible action and, eventually, results,” Ma said. “It is also a powerful testament to Hong Kong as a viable commercial platform for the Belt and Road Initiative.”

title: Asian Games: Hong Kong football boss left with little time to prepare for Japan test
description: Only appointed in July, Tsang Chiu-tat will not work with his full squad until 24 hours before opening fixture against hosts.
content: He has a degree in accountancy but Tsang Chiu-tat can rarely have encountered a calculation as complex as the one of trying to help the Hong Kong under-23 team compete in this month’s Asian Games. Appointed in July after predecessor Darren Arnott quit to become Football Club head coach, Tsang will work with his full 23-man squad for the first time on the eve of next Wednesday’s opening fixture against hosts Japan in the 45,000-capacity Toyota Stadium. This week, those players in the city have gathered in the afternoon following morning sessions with their clubs. The Hong Kong Premier League contingent will play for their teams this weekend, with those involved in Sunday’s two matches flying to Aichi prefecture on Monday, 24 hours after the rest of the squad. Hong Kong face Thailand and Kyrgyzstan in their other two group games on September 20 and 23, respectively. “It’s not easy [to prepare] because we have limitations,” Tsang, 37, said. “We have to train when players are very tired, so we need to take precautions.” During a roughly 90-minute session at the Jockey Club HKFA Football Training Centre, Tsang repeatedly urged his players to slow to walking mode as soon as they had completed short and sharp pattern-of-play drills. “We are trying to do as much as we can in tactical and conceptual terms,” Tsang said. “I’ve told the players it’s a privilege to play in this tournament, and to be part of the Hong Kong team. They have an opportunity to compete with one of the best sides in Asia and to show themselves. The keys in this preparation period are going to be our attitude and mentality.” A former right-back, Tsang took charge of Yuen Long, the club where he finished his career at the tender age of 27, in 2016. Less than two years later he led them to the Senior Shield title. A role at Lee Man took in a title win in 2023, before a poor start to the following season cost him his job. Back with the top flight side as technical director since the middle of last year, Tsang recently obtained his AFC Pro Licence. “It was an honour and a privilege to be asked to help the Hong Kong team,” Tsang said. “I think I’ve improved as a coach [since leaving Lee Man] but in reality everything depends on performances and results, so I leave it to others to decide if I have.” An excellent training ground communicator in English as well as Cantonese, having pursued his accountancy qualification at City University of Hong Kong, Tsang has a hard act to follow after Jorn Andersen led the city team to the semi-finals three years ago. That 2023 competition was a very different beast from the 2026 edition, however, with the city team given a free pass out of their group after losing twice to Uzbekistan, before shocking Palestine and Iran en route to a semi-final defeat by Japan. “People have expectations, but we can’t control how others think of us,” Tsang said. “The most important thing is that we show the values of the Hong Kong team, and I am demanding that everyone gives their best in the tournament.” Midfielder Wu Chun-ming, 28, an overage player in 2023, is reprising that role this year. The three-man quota is completed by 28-year-old Qingdao Hainiu midfielder Ngan Cheuk-pan, and Helio Goncalves, the 40-year-old defender who was a Citizen teammate of Tsang’s around 15 years ago. “The older players need extra care, and I’ll tell [Goncalves] that if he needs rest and to not train, it’s OK, I’ll accept it,” Tsang said. “We have good communication and he brings a lot of value to the team.” The owner of 38 senior Hong Kong caps, Goncalves refers to himself as a “coach on the field” for current club Eastern District, but Tsang said the centre-back would be only one of 23 leaders in his squad. “I demand that everyone thinks for themselves and makes their own decisions, so they are all coaches,” he added. The mainland-based pair of Ng Yu-hei and Timmy Ma Hei-wai, and Jeremy Tsang Lok-to, who plays and studies in America, will link up with the squad this weekend. Meanwhile, on Tuesday, Hong Kong named a 48-man squad for the “September to October Fifa window”, without any reference to the Fifa Asean Cup the city is supposed to be hosting this month. Despite announcing in June that they would stage the second-tier Challenge Division of the new tournament, the Football Association of Hong Kong, China (HKFA) did not specify in their latest release who or when their representative team would be playing. The world governing body has listed group fixtures for Hong Kong against Laos and Brunei at Kai Tak Stadium on September 27 and 30, respectively, having previously removed them from its website. The South China Morning Post has been told that the HKFA expects the tournament to go ahead. Wu and Ngan are among 10 players from the Asian Games squad included in the provisional senior party. Local Premier League club Eastern have parted company with head coach Manu Torres and the Spaniard’s backroom staff Juan Serrano, Javier Benavent and Roberto Diaz. Cristiano Cordeiro, the assistant boss, has been appointed acting head coach “until further notice”. Eastern lost their opening two league fixtures but Torres appeared to have bought himself some breathing space following a 4-0 win over Kowloon City on Saturday.

title: Inside Post Malone’s holy grail watch collection, from Rolex to Richard Mille
description: Many of the musician’s most prized timepieces, including a gem-set Patek Philippe Nautilus also owned by Drake and Kylie Jenner, are rarely seen in public.
content: Post Malone is someone who’s always been hard to define, whether you’re talking about his genre-blurring music or his approach to collecting luxury watches. The singer-songwriter, musician and businessman has built a multimillion-dollar fortune over a decade-long career, making him one of the bestselling artists of his generation. In recent years, he has leaned further into pop and country, supporting Taylor Swift on “Fortnight”, teaming up with Morgan Wallen for the chart-topping “I Had Some Help” and embracing Nashville on his country album F-1 Trillion. View this post on Instagram His tastes have evolved offstage, too. Earlier in his career, Malone was almost as famous for his extravagance as for his music, flashing diamond-encrusted chains, grills and a luxury watch collection easily worth over US$2.5 million. These days, however, the Richard Milles, Rolexes, Patek Philippes and Audemars Piguets don’t seem to make quite as many public appearances. That may fit with a broader shift in Malone’s life. After a close call with burglars and a relocation to Los Angeles for a quieter life in Utah, the once relentlessly blinged-out star has embraced a somewhat more low-profile existence. He hasn’t completely lost his taste for expensive collectibles, though: in 2023, he famously paid US$2 million for the ultra-rare Magic: The Gathering One Ring card. And as for those watches? Malone has said in interviews that he views his collection as investments, some that he could eventually pass down to his children. So while his million-dollar timepieces may not see quite as much daylight these days, there are likely at least a few treasures tucked away in Post Malone’s vault. Here are some of the watches he has collected over the years. Rolex Sea-Dweller Deepsea One of Malone’s earliest luxury watches was a Rolex Sea-Dweller Deepsea, given to him by his manager Dre London for his 21st birthday. The caseback is engraved with a birthday message to “Austy” (Malone’s real name is Austin), giving this otherwise rugged dive watch plenty of sentimental value. Estimated at around US$15,000, it is among the least expensive timepieces in Malone’s collection, yet one he is likely to never part with. Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Another watch Malone has said he’ll hold onto forever is an Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, a gift from 21 Savage, his collaborator on the 2017 hit “Rockstar”, after the pair toured together in 2019. Malone’s ref. 15400ST is a relatively restrained choice by his standards, pairing the Royal Oak’s signature stainless-steel case and integrated bracelet with a dark black-grey Grande Tapisserie dial, rather than the more coveted blue. It retails for around US$17,000, but as watch fanatics know, a Royal Oak can easily resell for more than US$50,000. Hublot Techframe Ferrari Tourbillon Chronograph Malone has a confessed soft spot for Hublot, praising the brand’s “tacticalness” and describing its watches as well suited to everyday life in rugged Salt Lake City. That increasingly outdoorsy, cowboy persona feels fitting for the star raised in Texas, though this particular Hublot probably isn’t the one he takes out on the trails. His rare Techframe Ferrari Tourbillon Chronograph was one of just 70 white gold pieces created with Ferrari to celebrate the carmaker’s 70th anniversary in 2017. Made from 18-karat white gold with sapphire components, the tourbillon chronograph originally cost around US$179,000. Hublot Spirit of Big Bang Moonphase This Hublot hints at Malone’s more playful side – fittingly, he wore it while escorting Jimmy Fallon to his first-ever Olive Garden meal for a 2018 The Tonight Show segment, with the pair arriving in a pink stretch limo. Released in 2017, the Spirit of Big Bang Moonphase is an oversized pink explosion for the wrist, pairing a 42mm tonneau-shaped titanium case with an open-worked skeleton movement visible through a translucent pink quartz dial, matching strap and a bezel set with 48 pink sapphires. At around US$20,000, it’s also relatively affordable – at least by Malone’s standards. Rolex Rainbow Daytona This is another colourful timepiece that watch spotters love to see in the wild. The Rolex Rainbow Daytona is a kaleidoscopic take on the brand’s legendary chronograph. Its signature feature is a bezel set with 36 baguette-cut sapphires arranged in a rainbow gradient, with more gems decorating the dial and case. With famous collectors including John Mayer and Cristiano Ronaldo, the Rainbow Daytona is hands down one of the most coveted modern Rolexes, notoriously difficult to secure even if you have the cash (upwards of US$350,000 on the secondary market). Malone, who wore this on The Tonight Show in 2019, clearly has both the connections and the funds. Patek Philippe Nautilus Another serious grail watch in Malone’s arsenal is the Patek Philippe Nautilus. While just about any Nautilus would qualify as a flex, the musician opted for one of the collection’s biggest statement pieces: the gloriously iced-out ref. 5719/10G, a favourite among VVIP collectors and A-listers, with Mark Wahlberg, Drake and Kylie Jenner also known to own one. Crafted from 18-karat white gold, the watch is smothered in an extraordinary 1,343 diamonds across its case, dial and bracelet. Unsurprisingly, the timepiece comes with a heavy price tag, valued at upwards of US$500,000 on the secondary market. Richard Mille RM 27-01 Tourbillon Rafael Nadal If there’s one watchmaker Malone seems to especially love, it might be Richard Mille. He owns at least three of the brand’s famously expensive creations, including the RM 27-01 Tourbillon Rafael Nadal, which he has been spotted wearing everywhere from celebrity birthday parties to playing Magic: The Gathering. Designed for the tennis legend to actually wear on court, the watch features appropriately extreme engineering: weighing less than 19 grams including its strap, it was billed as the world’s lightest tourbillon when released, yet engineered to withstand the immense forces generated during professional play. This supercar of a watch was limited to just 50 pieces and reportedly retailed for around US$740,000. Richard Mille RM 052 Tourbillon Skull ‘Asia Edition’ Last but certainly not least – in fact, this is handily the ultimate piece. With a seven-figure price tag, Malone’s Richard Mille RM 052 Tourbillon Skull “Asia Edition” is the most expensive watch he has publicly revealed in his collection. Already one of Richard Mille’s most outrageous creations, the Skull takes its macabre motif beyond a stylistic choice: the skull itself forms part of the movement’s architecture, with its jaws cradling the ruby of the tourbillon cage at 6 o’clock and four bridges extending outward like the crossed bones of a pirate flag. Malone’s all-black version makes an already rare watch even more exclusive. Created specifically for the Asian market, this particular configuration was limited to just six pieces and combines hi-tech materials including black-coated titanium, ceramic, carbon and zirconium. Malone has said he paid US$1 million for his, calling it both his most expensive watch and one of his favourites.

title: Taiwan waits for its new F-16s, still stuck in Hawaii after a fortnight’s delay
description: No official reason has been given for why the initial two aircraft are yet to leave the Pearl Harbour-Hickam base.
content: The first two F-16 Block 70 fighters bought by Taipei from the United States have yet to reach Taiwan, after spending more than two weeks in Hawaii for reasons that remain unclear. The aircraft, which were expected to arrive at Taiwan’s Chihhang Air Base in late August, were spotted preparing for departure at Joint Base Pearl Harbour-Hickam on Monday, raising expectations that the fighters were finally about to resume their journey. But the two single-seat F-16Cs, numbered 6727 and 6728, apparently did not leave Hawaii, with witnesses saying they taxied towards the runway before returning to the apron. It was the latest twist in the long-awaited delivery of the aircraft, which arrived in Hawaii on August 21 after leaving the continental United States with aerial refuelling support from US Air Force KC-135 tankers. The pair had been expected to continue to Guam after refuelling and servicing before making the final leg to Taiwan. Instead, they have remained at Hickam, with reports suggesting an earlier attempt to leave Hawaii was also aborted. Neither the US side nor Taiwan’s air force has publicly explained why the aircraft have been held up for so long, fuelling speculation among military and aviation enthusiasts that technical problems might have emerged. Some local reports have cited military sources as saying the aircraft encountered “minor problems” that required adjustments in Hawaii. Poor weather along the trans-Pacific route and around Taiwan has also been cited as a possible factor. Neither explanation has been officially confirmed. Michael Bosack, a former US Air Force officer and director of the Parley Policy Institute, said maintenance, tanker problems, aircrew health or weather could have caused the delay, but a maintenance issue was the most likely explanation. Even a routine warning could force an aircraft to return for inspection, he said. If a more serious defect was discovered, repairs would have to be followed by further checks and a post-maintenance safety flight before the aircraft could continue. “All it would take is one of the aircraft to be ‘hard broke’ … to stop the transit,” Bosack said, adding that problems could emerge even in newly delivered aircraft once they had been flown for some time. Another possible factor was aerial refuelling, with a maintenance problem involving the designated tanker or limited tanker availability potentially disrupting the flight plan, Bosack noted. Aircrew health could also have played a role, particularly if one or more pilots became unwell, he said, adding that he considered weather to be less likely as it would take “extreme conditions” to prevent the flights. However, Taipei-based military analyst Erich Shih said weather could have been a significant factor, with Hurricane Lowell bringing heavy rain, strong winds and high waves to Hawaii and conditions along the westbound route remaining unstable. “Monday may have offered the only recent window for the ferry flight, as conditions in Hawaii were barely acceptable and Taiwan’s weather had improved after days of heavy rain,” Shih said. But US commanders might have decided not to take any risks, he said, adding that this might explain why the two fighters entered a taxiway connecting Hickam with Honolulu airport before being recalled and the mission cancelled. One military enthusiast questioned why two newly built aircraft would require such a lengthy stay in Hawaii if only routine adjustments were involved. “The point now is not when they will fly back, but why newly delivered aircraft have encountered problems and what kind of defects would require such a long time to fix,” the enthusiast said. Other disappointed military fans have also complained about the repeated delays in the programme, which has already fallen well behind its original delivery schedule. “Taiwan has spent a huge amount of money buying so many aircraft, but has yet to receive even one, while [the military] keeps asking for more money,” one online commenter wrote. Others were more cautious, noting that ferrying fighter jets across the Pacific was a complex operation involving weather, aerial refuelling, maintenance and coordination between several bases. Flight safety should take priority over meeting a delivery date, they said. Taiwan’s air force has declined to give a firm arrival date, saying the arrangements remain subject to notification from the US side. “We are waiting too,” an air force official said on Monday when asked about the delivery, while thanking the public for its interest. Mounting delivery pressures The uncertainty comes as the entire F-16 Block 70 programme faces mounting pressure over its delivery schedule. Washington approved the sale of 66 newly built F-16 Block 70 fighters to Taiwan in 2019, for more than NT$247.2 billion (US$7.6 billion). The order comprises 56 single-seat F-16Cs and 10 twin-seat F-16Ds, which will mostly be stationed at the Chihhang base in the eastern county of Taitung and operated by the air force’s Seventh Tactical Fighter Wing. Deliveries were originally scheduled to begin in 2023, with all 66 aircraft due by the end of this year. But production line relocation, Covid-19 supply-chain disruptions, software issues and more recent flight-testing problems have pushed procurement well behind schedule. Wellington Koo Li-hsiung, the Taiwanese defence minister, said earlier this year that US contractor Lockheed Martin was producing 46 single-seat and 10 twin-seat F-16V Block 70 fighters for Taiwan. He did not give an update on the remaining 10 aircraft. Koo later acknowledged that the original completion target would not be met but has stopped short of saying whether all the remaining aircraft could be delivered by next year or 2028. The new fighters will significantly expand an F-16 fleet that is at the centre of Taiwan’s air defences as the People’s Liberation Army increases aerial operations around the island. Once all 66 fighters are delivered, they will join 139 older F-16A/B Block 20 aircraft that Taiwan has upgraded to the F-16V standard, giving the island more than 200 F-16s and making it one of the world’s largest operators of the type. The Block 70 aircraft are also fitted with conformal fuel tanks, giving them greater range and endurance than Taiwan’s older F-16s. Even so, moving fighter aircraft across the Pacific remains a complex undertaking, requiring careful coordination of weather, aerial refuelling and servicing, as well as stopovers. Based on Taiwan’s previous F-16 deliveries, the new fighters are expected to stop in Guam before continuing to Taitung. The Hawaii-Guam leg takes about eight hours and 20 minutes, while the flight from Guam to Taiwan takes roughly four hours and 40 minutes. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force for reunification. The United States, like most nations, does not recognise Taiwan as an independent state but is opposed to any forcible change to the status quo and is committed to providing arms for its defence.

title: Singapore police question 5 over racist comments on Nepal floods, Air India investment
description: Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam had denounced the remarks as ‘shameful and totally unacceptable’.
content: The police have identified and interviewed five people over online comments relating to the Nepal floods and discussions surrounding Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India. Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday that the police were looking into “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the Nepal-Tibet disaster and SIA’s investment in Air India. In response to media queries, the police on Wednesday confirmed they received police reports and are investigating certain online comments related to both matters. Five people, aged between 29 and 66, have been identified and interviewed in connection with these comments, police said. “We will continue to investigate and identify those responsible for these online comments,” they said. The police said they take a serious view of conduct that may wound racial feelings or incite hostility and ill will between different racial groups. As investigations are ongoing, the police are unable to comment further on the specifics of individual cases, they added. Shanmugam on Saturday gave several examples of racist remarks made online about the missing Singaporeans, including “No they are not our own”, “I only see Indian faces here. Skip. Rescue cut.” and “All ABNNs look the same, how to AI?” He noted that “ABNN” is a derogatory term for Indians. More than a thousand people had died and Singaporeans remained unaccounted for, he said, yet such remarks continued to circulate online. News that Air India is seeking fresh equity from shareholders, including SIA, also sparked a new wave of “anti-Indian, racist ranting” online, such as “references to snakes, curry, prata, black magic”, Shanmugam said. Shanmugam said on Saturday that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines. “The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security. This story was first published by CNA

title: Cyberattack ruled out as UK air travel chaos deepens
description: Nearly 300 flights cancelled a day after an air traffic control problem disrupted travel across Britain.
content: UK air travellers faced more misery on Wednesday with nearly 300 flights scrapped across the country, as Britain’s air traffic control service scrambled to recover from a technical glitch which it ruled out as a cyberattack. After 1,746 flights were cancelled on the first day of the outage on Tuesday, another 291 were axed on Wednesday – the majority to and from London Heathrow, the United Kingdom’s biggest and one of Europe’s busiest airports – according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. “We ended up sitting on our plane for just over five hours,” said Matt Ernster, 28, who was returning to Boston via Heathrow from his honeymoon in Paris on Tuesday. When they were finally allowed to disembark from the plane, “it turned into a gigantic, chaotic scene”, Ernster said. The baggage collection “felt like an apocalyptic situation”, and there were no hotels available in a two-hour radius. “It was the worst travel experience I’ve ever had.” The head of the National Air Traffic Services (NATS), Martin Rolfe, said “we have at this point ruled out cyber” activity as a cause. “We don’t believe it was a cyberattack,” he told BBC Radio. Rolfe said NATS would be doing a “very, very thorough” investigation into what exactly caused the incident. National carrier British Airways said it had to cancel more than 190 flights during the incident, which it said affected “tens of thousands of our customers”. The air traffic chaos followed a technical glitch in July last year that saw scores of flights to and from the UK cancelled, prompting anger from airline chiefs. Britain suffered its worst air systems failure in years in 2023, with more than 700,000 passengers affected after hundreds of flights were delayed or cancelled. UK news outlets reported that British Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander had summoned Rolfe to a meeting with her. Alexander said on social media that she was “seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job”. Rolfe told Sky News he accepted “full responsibility” but declined to say if he was considering quitting his job. Neal McMahon, chief operations officer at Irish no-frills airline Ryanair, called for Rolfe to be fired, accusing him of having “failed UK travellers”. Heathrow said late on Tuesday that departures had resumed, after the “technical issue” forced the airport to suspend arrivals, while warning that “disruption is expected to continue.” Caught up by the glitch, healthcare worker Josie Donoghue endured “an absolute nightmare” at London’s Gatwick airport, having had to disembark her flight to Ireland after three hours stuck on the runway. “Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz,” she told Britain’s domestic Press Association. Susie Senahe, 55, who was travelling back to Accra in Ghana after visiting her daughter in the UK, had been rebooked onto a Friday flight. She said on Wednesday she was planning to sleep at the Heathrow terminal until then. Another woman travelling to the US, who did not want to be named, said she slept in the airport on Tuesday night because nearby hotels were “fully booked”. Manchester, Birmingham and Edinburgh airports were also affected, while Dublin airport said it had cancelled dozens of flights. Ryanair said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted with 50 of its flights cancelled. English football club Arsenal, due to play Napoli in the Champions League on Wednesday in the southern Italian city, was forced to cancel a news conference after the team’s flight was delayed.

title: Letters | Belt and Road Initiative is more than a trade and investment platform
description: Readers discuss how far the belt and road framework has come, the use of AI in official translations, and the start of the school year.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The Belt and Road Initiative Summit taking place in Hong Kong on Wednesday and Thursday marks 13 years since the framework was launched. As the summit returns, I feel both continuity and renewed momentum. I attended early sessions when the initiative was still taking shape, and I have watched how the initiative has evolved alongside a rapidly changing global economy. One of the most visible changes over the past decade has been the rising global stature of the renminbi. The renminbi is now a major currency in global trade and financing and plays a growing role in international payments. More importantly, currency diversification reduces systemic risk created by overreliance on a single dominant currency, offering investors, central banks and companies additional options for financing, reserve management and cross-border transactions. But currency progress is only one aspect of the Belt and Road Initiative’s value. The initiative is more than a trade and investment platform: it is a connectivity bridge that combines practical economic cooperation with people-to-people engagement and cultural dialogue. Long-term development depends not only on moving goods across borders, but also on mutual understanding that supports genuinely win-win partnerships. In the post-pandemic era, Chinese firms have accelerated their overseas expansion, seeking new markets and stronger industrial resilience amid geopolitical and supply-chain uncertainty. At the same time, China’s cultural reach continues to grow. Chinese short-form dramas and online content are gaining viewers abroad, helping everyday audiences connect with Chinese stories, language and modern life. Personal experiences show this soft-power impact. During a trip from Frankfurt to Manchester last year, I met a British student who practised Chinese characters daily and was eager to study abroad in Xian. An American expat interviewed by CNBC, who has lived in Shenzhen for several years, described how everyday public services and high-quality living have shaped his family’s decision to stay and build a future. Sustaining the Belt and Road Initiative’s momentum will require continued innovation. Beyond infrastructure, cooperation should deepen in areas such as advanced technology, artificial intelligence, digital systems and cultural creativity, while promoting fair competition and upgrading manufacturing through robotics and smarter production. As the summit convenes, the world’s urgent questions remain: how to keep growth resilient, strengthen connectivity and rebuild trust amid fragmentation. These are precisely where belt and road cooperation can offer practical solutions – from trade and infrastructure to cultural respect and mutual learning. Tseung Cheukyee, Sai Ying Pun Smarter language can improve China’s image I refer to the report, “AI can make China’s political language sound threatening, professor warns” (August 30). Professor Li Yan’s discussion of artificial intelligence possibly making China’s political language sound threatening brought to mind some phrases commonly used in China’s public announcements. Two of these are “correct their mistakes” and “doomed to fail”. As a Westerner who has lived here since 1970, I take a keen interest in how China is viewed abroad. I believe these phrases tend to make China sound dictatorial and inflexible. Instead of “correct their mistakes”, it could be better to say those who criticise China should “look for the facts” or “discover the truth”. “Doomed to fail” might perhaps be rendered “cannot succeed”. Such seemingly small changes might make Westerners begin to feel that China speaks the same way as they do. They will begin to think of the pronouncements not as propaganda but rather meaningful statements. There is huge value in being perceived in a normal or even positive way by one’s detractors, and every effort should surely be made to achieve this. Sensitive, expert translators should at all times supersede AI in the generation of good messages for world consumption. David Gwilt, Sai Kung Schoolchildren bring Shakespeare to mind There is no better example of how the writing of Shakespeare remains relevant today. As the new academic year commences, the streets of Hong Kong are filled with children and their “shining morning face, creeping like snail. Unwillingly to school”. It is beautiful to behold. Mark Peaker, chairman, Shakespeare4All

title: 12 years after surviving breast cancer, a new health scare tests an American journalist
description: This Gynaecologic Cancer Awareness Month, US-based author and filmmaker Amy Wu shares her experience of dealing with cancer – twice.
content: The symptoms started a little before my 50th birthday in December. I pride myself on healthy living, and my gauge of good health has always been consistency: are sleep, eating, digestion and period cycle regular? Now the clockwork was off, if only slightly. My hypervigilance was born more than a decade earlier in Hong Kong, where I lived from 2009 to 2013 while working as a journalist. In 2013, at age 37 with no family history, I was treated for stage 0 breast cancer – the earliest detectable form. I kept my breasts and have had clean annual screenings since, but the scare left behind an inner antenna. Now back in the United States – in Connecticut, north of New York – that familiar paranoia returned as I began navigating a new medical crisis. As I write, I am recovering from a total hysterectomy following a diagnosis of precancerous uterine changes in January. In the dizzying reality of medical statistics, there was a 40 per cent chance that cancer already existed, and a more than 50 per cent chance it would advance to full-blown uterine cancer within a few years if left untreated. Today, I am celebrating a clean pathology report: no cancer was found. My diagnosis was a stark reminder of how common these issues are. Uterine cancer includes any cancer originating in the uterus. In the universe of women’s reproductive cancers in Hong Kong, the most common is endometrial cancer, says Dr Karen Chan Kar-loen, chair and professor at the University of Hong Kong’s department of obstetrics and gynaecology. “Endometrial cancer [which begins in the uterus’ inner lining] usually presents as bleeding after menopause and tends to be diagnosed early,” she says. “Early endometrial cancers can be treated by surgery, and the prognosis is good. Recently, immunotherapy has been introduced for advanced disease.” Risk factors include obesity, early menstruation, not having given birth, late menopause, and tamoxifen, a medication commonly used in breast cancer patients. An ultrasound sheds some light Mysterious signs came after I recognised something was “off”: bloating, constipation and a marathon period so heavy I told a friend, “It looks like I’ve been shot.” After plugging the symptoms into search engines, I convinced myself it was ovarian or colon cancer. My paternal family tree noted four members who had succumbed to cancer, including an aunt who died of oesophageal cancer at 43. I started speed-dialling doctors. When I scored a rare Saturday appointment with OB-GYN Dr Anita Chait in New Jersey, I jumped on it. She ordered an ultrasound, which returned a clue: my uterine lining was five times thicker than normal for a woman of my age. The next step was a D&C – dilation and curettage, the gold standard for uterine cancer screening. Under general anaesthesia, the uterus would be cleaned out and cells examined. When the fog of anaesthesia lifted, I caught Chait’s silhouette. “It’s a good thing you came to see me,” she said. The images were concerning. Polyps are usually round and smooth; some of mine had jagged edges like mountains and craters. A week later, the report came back with a little alarm symbol. “Atypical complex hyperplasia,” Chait said matter-of-factly. Precancerous cells in the uterine lining. “Cancer again?” I thought. “Not me.” You’re going to be fine. You’re going to live another 50 years Dr Peter Dottino, OB-GYN oncology surgeon Ovaries – to keep, or not to keep My case eventually landed at Smilow Cancer Hospital and Yale Cancer Centre at Yale New Haven Health, in Connecticut, in the hands of Dr Peter Dottino. An OB-GYN oncology surgeon with a brash, unfiltered demeanour, Dottino drew out my fate on paper, explaining how erratic perimenopausal hormones can cause the uterine lining to thicken – a condition called hyperplasia. In rarer cases, cells become abnormal. I was at stage three of this four-stage sequence, making radical preventive surgery my clearest option. “You’re an outlier,” Dottino said. “Sometimes there are no answers.” The diagnosis typically hits women who are overweight; I was not. There were options, but none that fit me. A total hysterectomy was the path. Then came the ovary question. Because I was not yet in menopause, removal was elective. If I kept them, I would face a 1.3 to 2 per cent chance of ovarian cancer, one of the deadliest gynaecologic cancers because symptoms often surface late. If I removed them, I would be thrown into surgical menopause: hot flushes, dry skin, insomnia and a diminished sex drive. The medical team reminded me that removing the Fallopian tubes alone cuts ovarian cancer risk by half. “You can tell me the day of [the surgery] what you decide,” Dottino said. “But make sure you’re 100 per cent certain, otherwise your recovery is going to be tough.” He added: “You’re going to be fine. You’re going to live another 50 years.” Support in a sisterhood The weeks that followed were a whirlwind of searching for reassurance and answers. I spoke with medical professionals and a doctor’s assistant with deep knowledge of menopause who briefed me on hormone replacement therapy. I reconnected with a high school classmate who had recently had a hysterectomy, and friends introduced me to others who shared their experiences, including what to expect and what to buy – leaving me with enough yoga pants to last a lifetime. Joining online support groups, I found support in a vast sisterhood of women navigating the same path. I dug into the research. A genetic test I had in 2023 showed no cancer-linked genes. A friend with osteoporosis recommended a bone-density test, which showed I had osteopenia, pre-osteoporosis. After weighing everything, I decided to keep the ovaries – at the doctor’s suggestion, both of them. Since my breast cancer diagnosis, I had watched young friends lose their battles with the disease. Now, a friend undergoing treatment for advanced cancer offered a perspective that stilled my fear. After I shared my health crisis, she said: “Well, at least they can do surgery and cut it out.” While my friends’ losses weighed heavily on me, my own condition offered a clearer path forward. Unlike many silent reproductive diseases, endometrial cancer often gives early warnings – even if it lacks a routine screening test, as Dr Jacqueline Lee Ho-sze, a consultant in gynaecological oncology at Hong Kong Baptist Hospital, notes. “Many cases are still diagnosed early because symptoms of vaginal bleeding frequently prompt women to seek medical attention,” she says. The D&C remains the standard diagnostic tool, though newer options – including detection through cervical scrapings – are emerging. Taking care of yourself and staying vigilant – that’s what matters Dr Anita Chait, OB-GYN Endometrial cancer is highly treatable: a 90 per cent five-year survival rate for stage 1, and 73 per cent for stage 2. On February 27, at dawn, I went in for surgery. About a week later, the pathology report arrived earlier than expected. “No cancerous cells observed,” the nurse said. After a happy dance and fireworks, a six-week recovery followed – slow, steady steps back to driving, swimming, jumping rope and a new perspective. I had the chance to thank Chait, who had uncovered my diagnosis and is herself a breast cancer survivor. “People sometimes ignore things because life isn’t easy and things get in the way,” she said. “But taking care of yourself and staying vigilant – that’s what matters.” Finding a way forward Below is a snippet from the thank-you note I wrote to loved ones who supported my recovery: “While we may not be able to change the size of the dining table we’re given, we can rearrange what’s on it – making space to prioritise our health and well-being. Without that, it becomes more challenging to care for our loved ones. “In a world that is often stressful and constantly changing, this experience has reinforced how important it is – especially for women – to put ourselves first. We can’t push through and dismiss warning signs as the usual fatigue of busy lives.” My final visit to Dottino fell on Earth Day, April 22. “You look good – very good – as good as when we first met before the surgery, only without the worry,” he said. I asked about ovarian cancer. “It’s untrue that there are no signs,” he said. “Maybe your pants are a bit too tight, or you feel bloated. Don’t listen to others who say you’re just getting old. Get it checked out. Your body is very smart. Don’t ignore it. Just like you did this time – you listened.” My decision to keep the ovaries was the right one, he said. I was given a clean bill of health and asked to return annually. “Adios,” Dottino said, waving. “I hope I don’t see you again. Now you have another 50 years!” Life rarely moves in a straight line, though. By late summer, as I celebrated starting a new job, getting married and returning to open-water swimming, a routine vision check brought a new alert: an atrophied optic nerve, a mystery, as I have had no stroke or eye trauma. As I wait for appointments with a neurologist and a neuro-ophthalmologist to learn more about the damage in the nerve that carries impulses from my eye to my brain, I feel the familiar anxiety of the unknown. Yet while rattled, I remain hopeful. I have been in this waiting room before, and I know the way back. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: US, China trials suggest a single nanodrug shot might stop bad cholesterol forever
description: Separate trials using CRISPR and base editing to silence lipid genes show drastic drops in LDL-C without daily medication.
content: Imagine swapping your daily cholesterol pill for a single injection that keeps “bad” cholesterol under control for a year, a decade – or even a lifetime. Two clinical trials, one in the United States and another in China, suggest that this one-and-done approach could become a reality. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), better known as “bad” cholesterol, is a major driver of heart disease – the leading cause of death worldwide. Triglycerides, another type of blood fat, add to the risk. For millions of people, the standard fix is a daily statin pill. Research led by the Cleveland Clinic in the US and carried out in Australia, New Zealand and Britain, tested a gene-editing nanodrug called CTX310 on 15 volunteers. The therapy uses tiny particles to carry a CRISPR gene-editing tool straight into liver cells. Its target is a gene named ANGPTL3, which helps control how much fat circulates in the blood. Some people are born with a natural mutation that inhibits ANGPTL3. They have extremely low cholesterol and triglycerides, and they rarely develop heart disease. CTX310 is designed to mimic that genetic switch. The results, published in The New England Journal of Medicine on August 28, were dramatic. One year after a single intravenous injection, the four volunteers who received the highest dose saw their ANGPTL3 levels fall an average 78.6 per cent, according to the paper. Their bad cholesterol dropped by 52.5 per cent and triglycerides fell by 47.8 per cent. Even more encouraging, the edited liver cells kept producing new, healthy cells with the same cholesterol-lowering edit – suggesting that the effect might be permanent. It follows the publication of a paper by Chinese scientists at Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Renji Hospital in Nature Medicine in March, which focused on patients with an inherited form of dangerously high cholesterol called familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH). People with FH are born with faulty cholesterol-clearance machinery and face a heart attack risk 10 to 20 times higher than normal, often requiring lifelong medication. The Chinese team used a different gene-editing tool called an adenine base editor to target the PCSK9 gene which – when overactive – destroys the liver’s ability to remove bad cholesterol from the blood. By “switching off” PCSK9, the nanodrug lets the liver clean house again. Like the US trial, the numbers were encouraging. In the high-dose group, LDL-C fell by an average of 52.3 per cent after 24 weeks – nearly double the effect of typical statins. The team reported that the PCSK9 protein levels had dropped 74.4 per cent without creeping back up. The teams behind both trials said their research showed the treatments to be safe. In the Chinese study, participants were reported to experience mild, temporary side effects such as fever, muscle aches or slight liver enzyme changes. In the US study, one patient died suddenly 179 days after receiving the lowest dose. Investigators concluded the death was unrelated to the drug, according to the paper. No other serious events were reported. Gene editing, which has aided patients battling cancer, is now being rolled out to help fight chronic diseases because many genes that helped our ancestors survive famines or malaria have become health hazards in the modern world. During a famine, genes that could raise blood sugar and lipid levels were advantageous but in the modern era, these genes can lead to severe metabolic problems. Similarly, while a single thalassaemia gene continues to protect against severe malaria, inheriting severe thalassaemia leads to life-threatening anaemia. A single nanodrug jab could rewrite those genetic instructions. Clinical trials on hyperlipidaemia in both the US and China are still under long-term continuous observation. “The therapy is being assessed in separate cohorts of patients with specific lipid disorders,” Cleveland Clinic cardiologist and corresponding author Steven Nissen said at the end of the American paper. The Chinese team, when interviewed in March by the Liberation Daily outlet in Shanghai, said it would conduct long-term follow-up research up to 15 years for patients in its clinical trials to monitor treatment effects, and would also seek to improve the lipid nanoparticle formulation.

title: Chinese court guidance aims to smooth developer bankruptcies, reassure creditors
description: Framework from Supreme People’s Court aims to end judicial inconsistencies across regions, aid flow of capital for construction continuation.
content: China’s Supreme People’s Court has issued the country’s first systematic judicial guidance governing bankruptcy proceedings for property developers, in an effort to end inconsistencies that have slowed disposals and deterred capital in recent years. The framework called for timely reorganisations of viable developers and prompt liquidations of those lacking sustainable value, according to a statement by the Supreme People’s Court on Monday. It also said asset-management companies and institutional investors should receive higher priority for continuation-of-construction repayment when taking part in stalled project continuations and reorganisations, according to the statement and an analyst. “This will significantly boost creditor security and help draw more social capital to actively participate in home delivery guarantees and the revitalisation of existing projects,” said Yan Yuejin, vice-president of the E‑house China Research and Development Institute, a Shanghai-based property consultancy. Now five years into the China Evergrande crisis, the country’s property downturn has spurred regulators to roll out a series of measures to help stabilise the market and streamline bankruptcy proceedings. The guidance comes as courts continue to work through the fallout from major developer failures, including the acceptance of a liquidation petition against Evergrande’s main onshore unit Hengda Real Estate on August 21, a day after its founder Hui Ka-yan was sentenced to life in prison. When a property developer was going bankrupt, and a residential sales contract was terminated because delivery became impossible, with no realistic prospect of completion, priority repayment should first go to homebuyers for their paid purchase amounts and outstanding personal mortgage loans, the statement said. The guidance also seeks to make stalled projects easier to revive, allowing courts to approve feasible construction plans before the first creditors’ meeting. New financing for resumed construction should generally be treated as common-benefit debts, while projects that could not be salvaged should generally be sold in their entirety to maximise value, the court said. As property developer bankruptcy cases involve massive debt volumes, multiple stakeholder groups and intricate creditor claims, inconsistent judicial interpretations across regions have slowed down disposal efficiency in past cases. To unify the application of legal standards and support a steady market, the Supreme People’s Court convened a national symposium in Beijing in December. With officials from multiple departments, participants deliberated and agreed on core issues that shaped the new guideline. The resulting guideline also calls for further refining the normalised mechanism for government‑court coordination and issue resolution in bankruptcy cases, under which the government leads risk control and administrative coordination, while courts oversee judicial proceedings. Regulators including financial watchdogs, natural resources authorities, housing and urban-rural development agencies, market regulation departments and tax authorities would jointly work to address bottlenecks and pain points in market-based investment and financing, asset disposal, tax relief and credit repair, the court said.

title: ‘Keep pushing, never fear hardships,’ Hong Kong’s first astronaut tells students
description: Students ask about AI, robots and animal tests in space as Lai Ka-ying, and crewmates Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan take part in ‘Tiangong Class’.
content: Hong Kong’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, will deliver a live lesson from space to students and teachers at her alma mater on Wednesday morning, with the 90-minute event broadcast to campuses across the city and streamed live on television. Lai and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members – mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan – will take part in the “Tiangong Class” at Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College. Representatives from the youth sector and innovation and technology community, as well as a visiting delegation from Macau, will also attend. The session will also be broadcast to students in Macau. Jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency, the event will feature an expert lecture, in-orbit demonstrations and a question and answer session designed to showcase the space environment. Astronaut alumna inspires young minds Form Five student Chan King-lam, who studies physics, chemistry, biology and extended mathematics, said the dialogue inspired him to explore science and he hoped to one day join the country’s research ranks. “How Lai sacrificed family time for this career really earns our respect and makes me want to refine my science studies,” he said. He said he was awed to see textbook physics principles demonstrated in microgravity during the broadcast. “What impressed me most was watching them cook chicken wings and cakes. It really shows how difficult preparing fresh food is in space,” he said. Form Six student Chan Tsz-ki said she was proud to see an alumna of her school become an astronaut and would take her as a role model in pursuing science. “I feel very close to her as we are using the same campus, the same facilities and some teachers are still the same,” she said. “I will also study hard to contribute to the country.” Lesson ends with Lai encouraging students The 1½-hour space lesson ended before 11.30am, with Lai briefly interacting with Chief Executive John Lee. Lai also offered words of encouragement as she responded to letters written by Hong Kong and Macau students. Lai said she often felt lonely and found the training and her mission hard, but she never thought about giving up, given the expectations of Hong Kong and Macau residents. “My presence in space has demonstrated how the nation supports and attaches importance to Hong Kong. We are very lucky to experience an era of a strong and thriving nation. Our motherland has provided us many precious opportunities, I am confident that the youth of Hong Kong and Macau are full of potential,” she said. “Living in such a great time, you must keep pushing and never fear hardships. Your future selves will thank you for the perseverance and hard work you put in today. You should hold the nation in your heart, and use your knowledge to give back to society and contribute to our motherland.” She added that the nature of the city’s “Lion Rock spirit” and manned space flight spirit were the same, as they required courage and perseverance amid hardships and pursuit of dreams. Be brave, Lai tells students A Form Six student, who studies at Lai’s alma mater, asked Lai how maths and science subjects helped her to become an astronaut. Lai said maths taught her how to analyse data, identify patterns and make judgments, while science taught her to observe, raise questions and use evidence to find out the answers. She stressed that the space mission was not only about the two subjects, as she also held a doctorate in computer science and dealt with different fields. She added that the mission also required good communication skills and teamwork. “I hope students take mathematics and science seriously, establish a solid foundation in language, expose themselves to different subjects, and learn how to connect the dots between different fields to put your knowledge into practice in the future,” she said. Lai urged students to be courageous as they chased their dreams. “My education background, research and development experience, and my career have laid critical foundations for me to seize this opportunity. I hope students can constantly equip themselves and be brave and proactive as opportunities come along,” she said. ‘Cherish everything’ During the 30-minute question and answer session, students asked Lai about life in space, her training and how she decided to apply to become a payload specialist. Lai shared some of the toughest parts of her astronaut training. Among the most demanding were desert survival exercises, in which she had to work with teammates under extreme conditions. She also had to stay focused during a 72-hour sleep-deprivation test and complete a six-day cave training exercise, which she called a major physical and mental challenge. “Every time I return to normal life after completing these high-intensity training sessions, I feel like I was as if in another lifetime and I should cherish everything I have,” she said. “These training sessions have also made me realise that astronauts do not rely on themselves alone. What is even more important is discipline and teamwork. Only by helping and reminding each other can we accomplish the mission together.” Lai added that becoming an astronaut was not her childhood dream, but she seized the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity when China opened selection to a candidate from Hong Kong. Even after preliminarily confirming she was eligible for the mission, she said the decision was not easy. “I can temporarily put down my job [in Hong Kong], but I have three young children. I felt uneasy about not being able to accompany them for a few years if I were selected. However, my family showed full support. Therefore, I decided to join the selection process,” she said. AI, robots and animal tests After a 30-minute tour inside the space station, the three astronauts shared details of their mission in about 25 minutes as representatives from several primary schools and secondary schools, and a University of Hong Kong student put questions to the crew. In response to a question about whether they use AI in their missions, Lai said the station had begun trials and studies using AI and robots. The robots could help document the crew’s work and navigate narrow ventilation ducts. She added that she expected more powerful AI systems to be deployed in the future to help astronauts complete their missions. Responding to a question on animal tests in space, Zhang said such trials could help scientists understand how a zero-gravity environment affected living organisms and provided important data for future exploration and for safeguarding astronauts’ health. Zhu described how the crew prepared for earlier extravehicular activities, including checking their spacesuits and practising with the equipment, when a student asked him how they felt while performing them. He said the mission was “very exhausting” in the heavy suits, but the crew was moved by the view of Earth and felt a deeper sense of purpose in their work. Lai’s sleeping space During the dialogue, Lai showcased her sleeping zone, which is decorated with her children’s drawings and clay art, family photos, depictions of Hong Kong street food and Hong Kong police’s anti-scam mascot. Lai said that she could observe the Earth from a window at her sleeping zone, while she also wondered what her family was doing as the space station passed over China. “When we pass over China, I always look for the Greater Bay Area. Although Hong Kong is small in size, it has bright lights at night,” she said. Lai also explained the operation of a small vegetable garden inside the space station, while Zhu demonstrated watering the plants and tasted lettuce grown in space. The pair also played table tennis with a ping-pong ball made of water. Tour of Tiangong space station Zhu and Lai talked about their lives in space and introduced equipment inside the Tiangong space station, including devices for scientific research. According to Lai, the astronauts enjoy balanced meals with rice, noodles, bread, vegetables and meats. The space station is equipped with cooking devices that can warm food and even bake a mini cake that makes Lai recall her favourite street food, Hong Kong-style egg waffles. Lai told the students that astronauts had to exercise for one to two hours daily, as she demonstrated wearing a vest to stabilise herself on the running machine. She further demonstrated wringing a towel in space, where water droplets do not stream down in a weightless environment. Space dialogue begins with address, demonstration The space dialogue began with the astronauts’ addressing the pupils, with Lai greeting the students and Chief Executive John Lee in Cantonese. As part of the space lesson, Lai showed a spinning top, following the traditions of China’s previous space lectures, in which astronaut Gui Haichao and crewmates used everyday objects to explain physics in orbit. Lee urges younger generation to make astronauts their role models Speaking at the college, Chief Executive John Lee said the government would begin an astronomy-themed popular science education and promotion effort, urging the public to actively participate in the activities. “I also hope that the younger generation will take astronauts as their role models, strive to equip themselves, have the courage to pursue their dreams, and use their wisdom and hard work to contribute towards building the nation into a strong nation in space and opening a brilliant new chapter for the Chinese nation,” he said. Lee added that the China manned space delegation’s visit to Hong Kong in 2023 had sown seeds of national pride, space exploration and pursuing dreams, while Hong Kong’s participation in the space exploration mission had demonstrated the growth of such seeds. Space experts and Lai’s former teachers get lesson going Before the live dialogue begins, Professor Wu Bo from Polytechnic University, Professor Su Hui from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and Professor Yao Zhonghua from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) shared knowledge and their projects with students at Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College. According to Su, the Multi-Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory, a greenhouse gas monitoring instrument spearheaded by HKUST, has been assembled and tested in orbit by Lai Ka-ying. Su said her team was currently analysing the data and would unveil the results as soon as possible. Lai’s former teachers also shared their interactions, including Chow Kam-pui, an honorary associate professor at HKU. Chow, who guided Lai through her master’s degree in cryptography and subsequent PhD in digital forensics from 2004 to 2011, said Lai was a team player and had strong analytical ability. Lau Sui-yee, the school’s principal, said Lai was diligent and focused in class, and her former teacher remembered her as an active member of the student union where she handled external affairs. Both teachers said Lai set an example for students to follow and explore the world beyond the classroom. ‘No doubt she can overcome any challenge’ Leaving her family behind was the most difficult part for Lai Ka-ying when she blasted off on May 24 for her six-month mission, according to her elder sister, Lai Ka-man. According to the elder Lai, her sister’s three children were still in primary school when she chose to become a payload specialist in 2024. They are now being cared for by both sets of grandparents and other family members. Ka-man attributed her sister’s strong will to their father, who taught both daughters to scrutinise every matter carefully and make thorough preparations in advance. “I have no doubt she can overcome any challenge,” she said, citing her sister’s self-discipline, resilience and impressive composure, as well as her attentiveness and ability to listen well. Unlocking quantum potential in orbit Chow Kam-pui, Lai’s supervisor at HKU, said in May that computer science could support space exploration. “For example, experiments in the space station will generate a lot of data. This would require the continued development of data science,” he said, noting data transmission as another key area to explore. He added that further down the road, scientists were also interested in seeing how quantum computing performed in orbit, as the machines faced many limitations on Earth. “The nature of quantum computers in space remains entirely unknown, with many new fields for exploration,” he said. What is Lai doing in orbit? During Lai’s time on the space station, the Shenzhou-23 crew will conduct more than 100 new scientific studies, including research involving zebrafish, mice and artificial embryos to examine reproduction in space. They will also test aerospace medicine and a new energy-storage battery for use in space, and explore the effects of the space environment on new materials, such as rare earth permanent magnet alloys. As a payload specialist, Lai’s duties include conducting on-orbit electroencephalogram tests and research into human adaptation to space. She has also taken part in rendezvous and docking training and equipment maintenance in the Wentian laboratory module. The path to space Lai’s path to becoming an astronaut began among about 120 applicants from Hong Kong when China opened its fourth batch of astronaut recruitment in late 2022, marking the first time applications were accepted from Hong Kong and Macau. By May 2023, more than 10 candidates from the two special administrative regions had passed the preliminary screening round, including Lai. The following month, as she and the other Hong Kong finalists prepared to travel to Beijing for the second round of the selection process, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu met them at Government House. She was then selected for training in 2024 as part of China’s fourth batch of astronauts. Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying, then a Hong Kong police superintendent with a doctorate in computer science, was selected in 2024 as part of China’s fourth batch of astronauts. Before her selection, Lai was attached to the police force’s technical services division and was later transferred to the Security Bureau. Lai grew up in Tsuen Wan and attended Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College. She enrolled at the University of Hong Kong in 2001, where she majored in computer science and information systems, and later completed a doctorate there. She lifted off aboard Shenzhou-23 in May 2026, becoming Hong Kong’s first astronaut and China’s first female payload specialist.

title: ‘Flying doctor’ helicopter crash in Malaysia kills 5 people
description: Search ⁠operations at the crash site in Sarawak were complicated by hazy conditions, with rescuers barred from using ‌air services.
content: Five people, including medical ⁠staff, died after a “flying ⁠doctor” service helicopter crashed in Malaysia on Tuesday, authorities and state news agency reports said, as haze from wildfires complicated search efforts. Health Minister Dzulkefly Ahmad in a statement ‌said initial information showed a pilot and four ministry staff were aboard the chopper that crashed near Sarawak state’s Long Lellang short take-off and landing airport. Among them were a medical officer, an assistant medical officer and two nurses on official duty, he said. A disaster management committee official in Miri, Sarawak, confirmed to state news ‌agency Bernama that all five aboard died in the crash. A flying doctor service typically uses aircraft to provide medical ‌care, emergency transport and clinical services to rural or isolated ⁠regions. Search ⁠operations on Tuesday had been complicated by hazy conditions, with rescuers barred from using ‌air services, Sarawak police commissioner Mohamad Zainal Abdullah said in a statement. The crash site was ‌in a ‌remote area that required a 10-hour journey by road, he ‌added. The civil aviation authority said the transport ministry’s air accident investigations ⁠bureau was investigating the incident. Sarawak, on Borneo island, has been hard-hit ⁠by haze arising from forest fires in neighbouring Indonesia, with many areas recording unhealthy air quality levels, government data showed on ‌Wednesday. Malaysia declared an ‌emergency last week in Sarawak’s Serian district after air pollution rose to hazardous levels, though the declaration was later lifted following improvements in air quality.

title: China’s factory-gate price growth picks up in August as Iran war fuels energy volatility
description: Producer price index rises 3.8 per cent, beating economists’ projections amid war-driven oil surge and weak domestic demand.
content: China’s factory-gate price growth accelerated in August, while consumer inflation picked up again, amid volatile energy and commodity costs linked to the US-Israel war on Iran. The producer price index rose 3.8 per cent year on year last month, up from 3.5 per cent in July, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on Wednesday. The reading beat a 3.6 per cent projection from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. Meanwhile, the consumer price index (CPI), a crucial gauge of inflation, rose 0.8 per cent year on year, rebounding after two months of slower growth. That figure improved upon July’s 0.5 per cent rate and was broadly in line with Wind’s projection of a 0.78 per cent rise. “Rising international prices for crude oil and non-ferrous metals drove up prices in related domestic sectors,” said Dong Lijuan, a senior NBS statistician. Dong noted that coal mining prices surged 26.6 per cent year on year in August, while non-ferrous metal processing rose 20.8 per cent. Prices in the oil and gas extraction industry climbed 10.5 per cent. Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, said he expected higher input costs to continue supporting reflation. “The inflation data shows a clear sector-by-sector split, mirroring the broader economy’s uneven momentum,” Song said. Factory-gate prices have been rising since March, as higher energy and input costs resulting from the US-Israel war on Iran broke a spell of deflation stretching back 41 months. After a brief respite when oil touched a wartime low amid a temporary truce in early July, Washington and Tehran resumed retaliatory strikes, keeping the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping lane effectively closed. Despite higher prices, the world’s second-largest economy is struggling to meet its annual CPI target of about 2 per cent, with domestic consumption weighed down by a prolonged downturn in the property market and a trying labour landscape. Dong said sharper rises in energy prices contributed 0.28 percentage points to the year-on-year rise in CPI in August, but falling food prices offset gains, with lower pork prices subtracting 0.22 percentage points. Pork prices, however, rose 1.3 per cent month on month in August, hinting at recovery. Xing Zhaopeng, senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said he expected the rebound in pork prices to support CPI in the second half of the year, with concerns over the El Nino weather cycle reinforcing expectations of higher food inflation. Core inflation, excluding volatile food and energy prices, rose 1 per cent year on year in August. Consumer goods prices were up 0.8 per cent, service prices rose 0.8 per cent and food prices fell 1.4 per cent. Song said he expected CPI to rise around 0.9 per cent year on year in 2026 – below Beijing’s target – but added the figures would be unlikely to sway monetary policy. Xing similarly noted that the rebound in inflation reduced the urgency of a near-term rate cut. “For China to escape from long-term deflation, the government is expected to lean on supply-side measures, such as the anti-involution push and reforms in public service pricing,” Xing said.

title: Iran says captured US underwater drone in Strait of Hormuz
description: Pentagon plays down the seizure, saying it was an older unmanned vehicle that had malfunctioned.
