content: Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday it had captured a ‌US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, offering a rare glimpse into how underwater drones are being used in military operations. Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defence firm Anduril. The 5.8-metre (19-foot) submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering ⁠and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said. “We trapped ‌one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This ‌submersible is equipped with the latest technologies,” the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in ⁠a statement carried by ⁠Iranian state media. In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had “malfunctioned more than a day ago”. “It ‌was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data ‌nor ‌carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” the spokesperson said. Anduril confirmed ‌the loss ‌of one of its vessels, but played down the significance of the incident. “Dive-LD is an ‌attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss ⁠of the vehicle is an expected possibility,” a company spokesperson said. The US military is investing heavily in unmanned naval systems, including ⁠underwater and surface vessels, as it seeks cheaper ways to monitor vast areas of ocean, gather intelligence and track adversary ships and submarines without putting sailors at ‌risk. According to Anduril’s website, ‌Dive-LD can operate for up to 10 days without returning to base and is designed to dive to depths of as much as 6,000 metres (19,700 feet). Dive-LD units cost about US$2.5 million each, US military news site DefenseScoop reported in 2024.

title: Humble leader and role model for a generation: Hong Kong’s Tung Chee-hwa mourned
description: Tung, hailed as a ‘close friend of the Communist Party of China’ and credited with working to improve China-US relations, died on Tuesday.
content: Tung Chee-hwa, Hong Kong’s first chief executive who oversaw the city’s 1997 return to Chinese rule, has died. According to a statement from his office issued in the early hours on Wednesday, he died on Tuesday at the age of 89, surrounded by his loved ones. It is understood that he died at the Hong Kong Sanatorium & Hospital. Tung was also a vice-chairman of China’s top political advisory body, the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference. In this live blog, the South China Morning Post details how people from all walks of life remember Tung.

title: Oman’s No 2 bank Sohar International to open representative office in Hong Kong this week
description: The new office, located at Cheung Kong Center II in Central, marks the first time the bank has expanded outside the Middle East.
content: Sohar International Bank, Oman’s second-largest bank by total assets, will open a local representative office in Hong Kong this week, according to sources, underlining the city’s role as a stable financial hub amid Middle East conflicts. CEO Abdulwahid Mohamed Al Murshidi will visit Hong Kong for the office’s opening ceremony on Thursday morning, according to a source, who requested anonymity as the information was private. The new office, located at Cheung Kong Center II in Central, represents the first time the bank has expanded outside the Middle East into the international market. Donald Chia will serve as chief representative of the office, according to a source. Sohar International did not immediately respond to a request for comment about its Hong Kong plans on Tuesday. The bank announced in April that it had received approval from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to establish a representative office in the city. The move reflected “endeavours to internationalise its business” and would help serve clients active in the broader Asian market, the bank said in a LinkedIn post at the time. In a blog post on Sunday, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the city was increasingly cementing its role as a long-term capital “landing point” and a platform for Asia-Pacific business expansion. Sohar International was founded in 2007 as Bank Sohar and rebranded in 2018. Its 2023 merger with HSBC Bank Oman solidified its position as the country’s second-largest bank, according to Sohar. The institution operates 74 domestic branches and has expanded into Saudi Arabia, offering retail, corporate, Islamic, and investment banking services, while investing in digital transformation and ESG initiatives. According to HKMA data, five Middle Eastern banks currently operate in Hong Kong, out of around 200 registered institutions.

title: Young Chinese turn to Mao Zedong for life advice, 50 years after his death
description: A new generation is embracing Mao’s teachings to cope with modern pressures, but analysts say the trend gives Beijing reason to be wary.
content: When you are denied a pay rise, when you feel anxious about your children’s education, or when you are alienated by colleagues, Chairman Mao can help. At least, that is what China’s online influencers and their hundreds of thousands of followers believe. Wednesday marks the 50th anniversary of the death of Mao Zedong, founding father of the People’s Republic of China. Chinese authorities have not announced any plans to mark the date, as former state leaders are usually commemorated on the anniversaries of their birth. The only special arrangement in place is at the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall in Beijing, which will open for an extra three hours on Wednesday. Visiting slots for the week are fully booked. Despite the official silence ahead of the anniversary, it is hard to ignore the quiet comeback of Mao’s popularity in the country. In recent years, younger generations of Chinese have rediscovered Mao as their life coach. They organise online book clubs devoted to his works, spread the gospel through artificial intelligence-narrated videos, and affectionately refer to him as jiaoyuan, or “teacher”, a title Mao himself once said he preferred. His views are regularly cited in times of US-China tensions. Last year, when the Trump administration imposed a 104 per cent tariff on Chinese goods, social media users searched for the term jiaoyuan, described imperialism as a “paper tiger” – one of Mao’s best-known slogans – and quoted his collection of speeches, On Protracted War. While much of this youthful sentiment aligns with China’s official narrative about Mao as a symbol of national independence, especially in the face of US-led international pressure, experts say Beijing is also wary that Mao’s teachings could feed into scepticism about the country’s economic policies and its interpretation of Marxism. Mao in youth culture For Mao’s most vocal online admirers, the former state leader is a symbol of resilience, courage and dedication to the common people. One blogger on the arts and culture forum Douban praised Mao’s selflessness, especially the fact that he sent his own son to the battlefield. “He stood with us, the people, at all times,” she wrote. The 29-year-old blogger, who asked to be referred to only by her surname Liu, describes herself as an “ordinary company worker”. She said she had read most of Mao’s works and applied them to her own life. “Don’t regard a mistake as merely a disgrace; see it as an asset,” she said, quoting the late leader. She added that this perspective had taught her not to criticise herself too harshly. I believe [Mao’s] spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals Li Muqi, Chinese university student Young people can also be spotted paying tribute to Mao at a giant monument in Changsha, Hunan province. Li Muqi, a second-year student at Hunan Normal University, has made a habit of visiting the enormous statue before final exams to pray for good luck. “I believe his spirit in heaven can bless young students like us, help us make progress and achieve our ideals,” Li said. According to public data, the number of annual visitors to the site has more than tripled in about a decade, from 5.88 million in 2016 to 19 million last year. It is hard to estimate the number of Mao’s young followers in China today, but a glimpse is possible through growing library loans and merchandise sales. At Beijing’s prestigious Tsinghua University, the Selected Works of Mao Zedong topped the library loan list last year, open records show. On Taobao, one of China’s largest online shopping platforms, a shop selling enamel mugs with Mao’s portrait sold more than 20,000 units in the past year. Wealth gap and nationalism The deeper reason for the interest in Mao is that young people are becoming increasingly disillusioned by today’s China and cannot achieve their aspirations, according to analysts. In June 2023, the official urban unemployment rate for young people aged 16 to 24 hit a record high of 21.3 per cent. Fearful for their futures, university graduates have started joking that they have to “degrade themselves” and consider blue-collar jobs with low pay. “I think a lot of people have realised that this isn’t something that could simply be solved with the cake being made bigger,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University in Australia. He said that Mao’s theories on class struggle and conflict were still relevant today, as young people facing immense pressure, a wealth gap and few employment opportunities sought an explanation or simply comfort. This has been accompanied by a rise in nationalism in recent years. Many admire Mao for his foresight in areas such as the development of nuclear weapons, satellites and the industrialisation of inland provinces – achievements that have helped China compete and defend itself against outside forces. During recent US-China tensions, members of the public have regularly cited Mao’s teachings. For example, a Baidu blog post from last year stated that thanks to the former leader’s strategy, China “holds the ace” for winning the trade war. Despite tariffs, China has developed its domestic industry chain, made alliances with other countries and used rare earths to counterstrike – all moves out of Mao’s playbook on protracted war, according to the blogger. An April commentary in the Monthly Review, a New York-based independent socialist magazine, said Mao’s legacy offered a “powerful counternarrative to the Western-centric story of globalisation”. “He represents the possibility of an alternative path to modernity, one that does not require submission to the economic and political dictates of Washington.” Mao reimagined Rana Mitter, S.T. Lee Chair in US-Asia Relations at the Harvard Kennedy School, noted that young people’s interpretation of Mao’s teachings generally did not include the violence of the Cultural Revolution. When asked about the Cultural Revolution, Douban blogger Liu said she had mainly read Mao’s works to see the logic of his writing, how he worked and his attitude towards life, and she had not done “systematic research on historic events”. Rebecca Karl, professor of history at New York University, said that for young people, the Cultural Revolution “reads as a liberatory moment”, rather than the “doom and gloom that we know from mainstream narrative convention and state repudiation”. One reason young people have an incomplete view of Mao is due to censorship. The Mao era came to an end with his death in 1976. In the years that followed, his legacy was officially defined by the Communist Party. A 1981 party resolution under Deng Xiaoping, China’s leader at the time, established the basic framework: Mao was credited with major achievements and with laying the foundations of modern China, but his later rule was heavily criticised, particularly for the Cultural Revolution, which was described as a “catastrophe”. Under President Xi Jinping, the emphasis has shifted towards more recognition of Mao’s achievements. Xi argued in 2013 that Mao’s three decades of rule “could not be repudiated” by the reform era. Tiptoeing around Mao Chinese authorities are prepared to tackle anyone who deviates from the official assessment of Mao’s legacy, and the government censors those who openly criticise him. But at the same time, Beijing has been careful not to let Mao-related discussions get out of hand, especially those concerning his more radical ideas and the Cultural Revolution. Analysts said that while the Mao revival among young people would not grow into a larger movement, it would persist as a form of self-expression. “His return signifies that the fundamental questions he posed about China’s path are not relics of a bygone era. The questions of class, of social justice, and of who truly holds power in society have not been resolved by decades of market reforms … The revolutionary agenda, it seems, remains unfinished,” the Monthly Review commentary said. Gao, the professor of Chinese studies, said the trend was a collection of mixed feelings mostly confined to the digital realm, and it would not be allowed to develop into something larger. However, facing the problems of today, young people turn to Mao because “there’s no new path to take”, according to Gao. “When the entire world is changing – and even chaotic – there’s no alternative narrative,” he said.

title: Deutsche Bank sees supply chains driving yuan’s rise in global trade
description: Europe’s first foreign RMB clearer says Chinese firms’ overseas expansion is strengthening the currency’s role in cross-border commerce.
content: The global rise of the renminbi, the Chinese currency also known as the yuan, is being driven by shifting supply chains rather than a campaign against the US dollar, according to a senior Deutsche Bank executive, following the German lender’s appointment as Europe’s first non-Chinese renminbi clearing house. Konrad Haunit, Deutsche Bank’s head of multinational corporate coverage for the Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa, said the yuan’s use had grown steadily over the past five years. “It’s been a gradual shift, as business models and supply chains have evolved,” he said. “As our clients diversify their operations across the region and beyond, they have continued to increase their use of renminbi globally.” His comments follow the People’s Bank of China’s decision last month to name Deutsche Bank as Europe’s first foreign yuan clearing bank. The appointment gives the lender direct clearing and settlement capability for cross-border yuan transactions in Frankfurt, adding to its existing offshore yuan operations in Hong Kong, Singapore and London. Haunit called the appointment “hugely important” for the bank, saying it would support the long-term growth of the offshore yuan ecosystem. Asked if the yuan could broadly replace the US dollar, Haunit urged caution. He said yuan adoption was being driven by established commercial practices in specific trade corridors, rather than a sudden global shift, citing European industrial giants in China that had invoiced in renminbi for more than a decade. Haunit traced the deeper shift to the Covid-19 pandemic rather than geopolitics. When lockdowns, border closures and shipping disruptions interrupted the flow of goods, companies could no longer rely on supply chains built mainly to minimise costs. They began prioritising flexibility – including alternative suppliers, production sites and trade routes – so they could keep operating when one link failed. Tariff volatility had also reinforced that logic, prompting manufacturers to redirect goods across markets as trade conditions have shifted, Haunit said. The relevance of Chinese innovation, Chinese goods and Chinese supply chains is just going to keep increasing Konrad Haunit, Deutsche Bank “Ten years ago, it was all about maximising price efficiency,” he said. “Now clients value more than that. Flexibility and resilience are also key considerations.” This shift, he noted, had expanded trade corridors beyond China’s traditional links with Europe and the US, deepening connections with emerging trade markets, including Southeast Asia and the Middle East – most of them carrying goods and components sourced from China. Trade between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations reached 4.34 trillion yuan (US$646.3 billion) in the first half of 2026, up 18.2 per cent from a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. Trade in intermediate goods – parts, components and other production inputs – climbed even faster, up 24.5 per cent. Haunit pointed to electric vehicles, batteries, pharmaceuticals and construction work as examples of industries where clients follow China’s growing manufacturing scale. In this evolving ecosystem, Hong Kong would function as a crucial liquidity anchor rather than merely a payment hub, Haunit said. Multinationals would rely on the city’s deep offshore yuan pool to manage cross-border cash flows and hedge currency exposure as their regional operations spread, he added, describing Hong Kong as a “key gateway”. Yuan deposits in Hong Kong rose 2.9 per cent in July to 1.13 trillion yuan, while cross-border renminbi trade settlement handled in the city increased 8.3 per cent to 1.38 trillion yuan, Hong Kong Monetary Authority data released in late August showed. Despite this momentum, the yuan remains a relatively small player in global payments. According to the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication messaging network, the currency ranked fifth in global payments in July with a 3.1 per cent share, compared with the US dollar’s more than 50 per cent dominance. As supply chains stretch further into emerging markets and Chinese manufacturers continue to expand overseas, Haunit said he expected yuan usage to gain further ground. “Our clients generally do whatever makes the most sense for their business, whether it’s efficiency, growth, resilience or innovation,” he said. “The relevance of Chinese innovation, Chinese goods and Chinese supply chains is just going to keep increasing.”

title: As I see it | Britain should accept a Hong Kong-style handover of the Falklands
description: Argentina has history, geography and justice on its side. The 1984 Joint Declaration offers a clear precedent for a peaceful, negotiated transfer of sovereignty.
content: Argentine President Javier Milei has every right to reassert his country’s territorial claims over the Falkland Islands. His proposal to use the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration as a template for resolving the Falkland Islands dispute merits serious consideration as a pragmatic framework for bringing this long-standing territorial conflict to a peaceful conclusion. Argentina’s claim to what its citizens call the Islas Malvinas rests on solid foundations. Upon independence from Spain in 1816, Argentina inherited sovereignty over the islands under territorial succession. Argentina arguably exercised governmental authority over the archipelago between 1820 and 1833, appointing officials and raising its flag. The islands lie 480km (300 miles) from the Argentine mainland, while sitting 13,000km from Britain – a relic of empire sustained by military might rather than natural association. International legal scholars Marcelo Kohen and Facundo Rodriguez have together articulated the standard legal arguments for Buenos Aires. Milei is, in fact, repeating them, especially by citing the Joint Declaration. Their arguments invoke uti possidetis juris – asserting Argentina inherited Spanish sovereignty upon independence and characterising Britain’s 1833 expulsion of Argentine authorities as illegal usurpation. They reject self-determination for current islanders, deeming them a “transplanted” colonial population rather than indigenous people. While Britain emphasises the islanders’ overwhelming 2013 referendum supporting British sovereignty, Argentine jurists frame the dispute as territorial integrity versus colonial occupation – a fundamentally irreconcilable doctrinal clash. Argentina’s diplomatic protests since 1833 prevent acquiescence to British rule. In January 1833, British naval forces expelled Argentine authorities and settlers by force, an act Argentina immediately protested and had never recognised as legitimate. For almost two centuries, successive Argentine governments have maintained this claim with unwavering consistency. The United Nations had recognised the dispute’s legitimacy in Resolution 2065 in 1965, inviting both parties to negotiate a peaceful settlement. That invitation remains unanswered. Milei’s invocation of the Hong Kong handover references a tested diplomatic precedent. Under the Joint Declaration signed in 1984, the UK transferred sovereignty while preserving Hong Kong’s prevailing social systems for 50 years. The arrangement acknowledged historical claims while respecting established ways of life – precisely the compromise needed for the Falklands. The roughly 3,600 islanders could retain their governance structures, British cultural identity, and economic arrangements under Argentine sovereignty, mirroring the “one country, two systems” framework. Britain’s counter-argument centres on self-determination, citing the March 2013 referendum in which 99.8 per cent of islanders voted to remain a British Overseas Territory. Yet this principle cannot operate in isolation from competing legal frameworks. If demographic preference alone determined sovereignty, every colonial power could simply plant settlers and claim perpetual legitimacy – a formula incompatible with the UN’s decolonisation mandate that placed the Falklands on its list of non-self-governing territories in 1946. Moreover, self-determination was selectively applied in Hong Kong, where residents were granted no referendum on their return to Chinese sovereignty. The precedent exists because the international community recognised that historical claims can outweigh preferences of transplanted populations. This does not diminish the islanders’ views – any settlement must protect their interests – but such sovereignty questions involve balancing multiple, often conflicting legitimate principles. Britain handed back Hong Kong to China not from weakness but from a recognition that historical realities evolve The shifting geopolitical landscape strengthens the case for negotiation. US President Donald Trump’s statement that Washington is “reviewing” its historically neutral stance; American support can no longer be taken for granted. The late Ronald Reagan was Margaret Thatcher’s soulmate, but Trump is Milei’s best pal. Britain today faces demographic decline and diminished global influence, making the islands’ defence 13,000km from home increasingly difficult to justify, let alone carry out. Milei has explicitly rejected military solutions, stating Argentines “do not believe in war” and seek a “consensus solution” – a marked departure from General Galtieri’s reckless adventurism in 1982. Britain should reciprocate this good faith rather than hiding behind the referendum result. The path forward requires compromise from both sides. Argentina must guarantee the islanders’ way of life, property rights and governance autonomy. Britain must acknowledge that historical wrongs and geographical absurdities cannot be perpetuated simply because they have endured nearly two centuries. The Joint Declaration offers a proven mechanism: a negotiated timeline, explicit guarantees of autonomy, and recognition that sovereignty can transfer while preserving identity. Here, Chinese diplomats can offer assistance to the Argentines. The alternative is indefinite confrontation – militarily impossible for Argentina, politically untenable for Britain, and wholly unnecessary for a dispute that diplomacy could resolve. Britain handed back Hong Kong to China not from weakness but from a recognition that historical realities evolve. The same recognition should now guide London’s approach to an archipelago that geography, history and justice place within Argentina’s natural sovereignty. Milei has extended a rational olive branch. Britain should grasp it.

title: Chinese sisters’ 86-page expose accuses PhD supervisor of affair with dad, academic misconduct
description: Document further alleges that Fu and Zeng misused university research funds for personal gain, calls into question Zeng’s academic integrity.
content: A pair of Chinese sisters, aged 20 and 15, have exposed a decade-long affair between their father, a former professor at the prestigious Wuhan University, and his student, who is now a professor at the same institution. Recently, they published an 86-page expose of this affair online, sparking heated discussions across social media platforms. The sisters are targeting their father, Fu Lei, a 47-year-old former professor and doctoral supervisor at Wuhan University’s College of Chemistry and Molecular Sciences, who currently serves as the vice principal at Anhui University and is a member of the Party Committee’s standing committee. According to circulating materials, Fu’s former doctoral student, 35-year-old Zeng Mengqi, has been involved with Fu since 2016. The sisters experienced a shocking revelation about their father’s affair in 2018 when they discovered the online avatars he and Zeng used from the popular Japanese anime Detective Conan, while they were aged 12 and 7. Fu allegedly used the character Conan as his avatar, while Zeng portrayed Ai Haibara. In the expose, the authors noted: “Ai Haibara is a fictional character, but the family that Zeng destroyed is real.” The online document claims that Fu was always prompt in responding to Zeng’s requests, even during family holidays. The sisters also witnessed provoking messages sent by Zeng to their mother. Moreover, despite Zeng marrying her university colleague in 2023, she reportedly continued her affair with Fu. Two years ago, Fu left the family, prompting their mother to manage the mortgage and care for her two daughters alone, resulting in a weight loss of 15kg. The older sister confronted Fu at a university leadership meeting, compelling him to sign an agreement to provide monthly child support of 5,000 yuan (US$750). Notably, Fu’s annual salary exceeds one million yuan (US$150,000). The expose also accuses Fu and Zeng of misappropriating university research funds for personal use and questions Zeng’s academic integrity. Zeng graduated with a PhD in 2018, became an associate professor in 2020, and advanced to professor a year later. She has also been recognised among the Young Talent of the National High-Level Talent Special Support Programmes. Additionally, Zeng has been accused of depriving other students of first authorship on publications or using Fu as a ghostwriter for her articles in leading journals, including Nature Materials and the Journal of the American Chemical Society. As of now, neither Fu nor Zeng has publicly addressed the accusations. The SCMP reached out for comments but did not receive a response by the time of publication. On September 3, Wuhan University officially announced that it had received the whistle-blower material on August 19 and would conduct an investigation into the matter. A representative from Anhui University confirmed that they have also initiated an investigation regarding Fu. Both institutions vowed to share the results of the investigation once completed. No parties have been suspended from their positions. While many sympathise with the suffering endured by the two young daughters over the past decade, some suspect that the expose may have been written by Fu’s wife in her daughters’ voice, given certain phrasing used in the document. Lawyer Zhou Zhaocheng from Beijing Anjian Law Firm noted that if the universities find evidence of professional ethics violations or academic misconduct, Fu and Zeng could face removal from their positions or even dismissal. Conversely, if the material is deemed to exaggerate the facts, the whistle-blower may be held liable for defamation.

title: Hong Kong agencies warn of lingering Jakarta flight delays after volcano eruption
description: Employment companies hold off booking flights for Hong Kong-bound helpers as airlines struggle to clear backlog after Indonesian volcano eruption.
content: Some Hong Kong employment and travel companies have warned that air traffic in Jakarta could continue to face disruptions even after the Indonesian capital’s international airport reopened following a volcanic eruption that spewed ash into the sky, as airlines work through a backlog. GLC (Manado) Employment Service founder and director Chu Shek-yin told the South China Morning Post that he would not rush to book an air ticket for his client’s helper despite the resumption of operations at all eight airports in Indonesia on Tuesday. Chu said the helper was scheduled to receive a work visa for Hong Kong around this week but the string of flight cancellations meant the helper’s arrival would be delayed by a week or more. “I won’t book an air ticket until Jakarta’s airport operations stablilise. Otherwise, my heart will beat like a roller coaster,” he said. He recalled an “upsetting” experience over a year ago when a sudden airport closure due to another volcanic eruption left a helper stranded and he had to share some of the losses with his client by buying another air ticket. Chu said an employment agency typically charged about HK$18,000 (US$2,296) to bring over an Indonesian helper, including for a one-way air ticket that could cost roughly HK$1,800 for an indirect flight. Domestic helper agencies had earlier revealed up to 200 Hong Kong-bound helpers had been stranded by the eruption, including new employees and workers returning after their holidays. The eruption of Mount Anak Krakatoa on Saturday unleashed a stream of lava and a towering plume of volcanic ash. Eight airports suspended operations over the weekend, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded. Moon Yau Moon-yee, assistant general manager at Sunflower Travel Services, said the eruption had so far had a limited impact on the company’s business because Bali, the main Indonesian destination for Hong Kong holidaymakers, remained served by direct flights operating normally. But travellers whose destination was Jakarta or who needed to transit through the capital were more seriously affected, he said. “Although Jakarta’s airport has gradually reopened, airlines are likely to need some time to rearrange flights and clear the backlog of stranded passengers following the large number of cancellations over the previous two days,” Yau said. “Airport operations also remain highly dependent on the weather, with wind direction, weather conditions and the latest movement of volcanic ash creating uncertainty over the coming days.” The Hong Kong International Airport’s website showed that three of the four flights scheduled to arrive from Jakarta on Tuesday had been cancelled. Chu said he had another client whose helper flew out just in time on Saturday before the Jakarta Soekarno-Hatta International Airport suspended flights the following day. “By God’s grace, she changed flights in Singapore for Hong Kong, so she arrived at Hong Kong on time,” he said. “I normally choose either Singapore or Malaysia for layover, these places are less vulnerable to any natural disasters.” Hong Kong Observatory satellite images captured the eruption with ash reaching heights of 50,000 feet (15,000 metres). The local forecaster said volcanic ash could travel thousands of kilometres and as high as plane cruising altitudes, posing a serious threat to aviation safety.

title: Trump bans some Canadian goods, raises tariffs on others as trade war escalates
description: White House targets alcohol, dairy, and consumer goods while Ottawa defends US$20 billion in retaliatory duties.
content: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday escalated his trade war against Canada, banning imports of alcohol and various products and raising tariffs on others, with the conflict showing no sign of abating. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney stood firm, acknowledging that reducing economic ties with the United States would come at a cost but saying the benefits would outweigh the pain. A range of Canadian products, from mattresses to motorboats and golf carts, would be subject to a 50 per cent surcharge beginning September 15, according to Trump’s executive order issued late Tuesday. The import ban, which targets various alcoholic beverages as well as some dairy products like whey, would come into effect on September 29, according to other executive orders issued at the same time. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect earlier Tuesday, applying to C$27.6 billion (US$20 billion) in US imports, including steel and aluminium products and dairy goods such as cheese, in response to duties announced by Washington on August 22. Canada has “everything we need to pivot and prosper,” Carney said in a video address. “That pivot will come at a cost. There’s always a cost to action. But it doesn’t come close to the cost of standing still.” Responding to the latest Canadian levies, Trump pledged to restrict Canadian companies from securing US government contracts. In a social media post earlier Tuesday, Trump said he was directing officials “to REMOVE Canadian-origin products from GSA’s Multiple Award Schedules,” referring to a General Services Administration programme for long-term contracts. Contracts through such schedules account for more than US$50 billion a year, Trump added. On Monday, Trump threatened to try to block sales of Canada’s Bombardier Aviation unless the Quebec-based plane maker moves manufacturing to the United States. In response, the aerospace company pointed to its creation of tens of thousands of jobs across the United States, with direct employment in more than 20 states, including Kansas, Texas, Arizona, and California. The two Republican senators representing Kansas said they had conveyed their concerns to the White House. “I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s more than 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Senator Roger Marshall posted on X, with similar comments posted by Senator Jerry Moran. US tariffs pose a modestly negative risk to Canada’s overall economy, but analysts note that they have a sharper impact on central Canada’s manufacturing sector. “I don’t believe in escalating the conflict. That’s not constructive,” Carney said in his video statement Tuesday. “But our tariffs are necessary to protect our workers, protect our companies, and protect our communities. “This is about who we are as Canadians.” Reacting to Trump’s move, Canada’s minister in charge of trade with the United States, Dominic LeBlanc, said late Tuesday that Ottawa was “assessing the latest tariff measures”. Negotiations between the two sides broke down on August 21 after days of meetings in Washington. At the time, Carney said US negotiators had introduced restrictions on Canadian trade deals with other countries at the eleventh hour, as well as unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture”. Ottawa and Washington have not resumed talks since. On Sunday, Trump posted an illustration of himself towering over Carney as they played ice hockey, with Trump saying: “Get up, governor”, a reference to his determination to turn Canada into another US state. Trump also signed an order in August to rename Lake Ontario, on the border with Canada, as “Lake America”, sparking fury in Canada amid a broader wave of patriotism triggered by the US president’s hostility. Although Carney is backed by Canadian public opinion, his country remains reliant on its neighbour. Nearly 60 per cent of Canada’s imports come from the United States, and about 70 per cent of its exports go to the US market. To help businesses and workers, Canada’s government has unveiled an aid package worth C$7.5 billion (US$5.4 billion).

title: After stint in snake ward, rugby opponents hold no fear for Hong Kong’s fly-in fullback
description: Sabay Lynam balancing veterinary technology degree from University of Queensland with burgeoning international career.
content: On the first placement of her veterinary technology degree, Sabay Lynam found herself patrolling the “domestic reptile ward”. “There were lizards, turtles and snakes,” she said. “Lots of snakes.” Slight of stature, Lynam is a fast and fearless fullback for the Hong Kong women’s 15s team. She is home from Australia, the country she left for Hong Kong at four, and where she now studies at the University of Queensland, for the WXV Global Series Challenger tournament. In the battle for a World Cup spot in 2029, nothing about Sunday’s opponents Brazil, nor Fiji or Samoa, Hong Kong’s opponents over the following fortnight, is likely to frighten Lynam, who has been playing for Wests Bulldogs in Queensland Premier Rugby. Going into the “snake ward”, however, she had to “put on my brave face”. “I was a bit scared of snakes,” Lynam said. “But they’re such amazing creatures. The main reasons people don’t like them are the way they look, and the way they strike. But if you learn to respect them, keep your distance and don’t poke them, they’re fine. They’re just like anyone else.” Having studied part-time to accommodate rugby, Lynam will soon have to commit to a full timetable for her “big placement year” working alongside a veterinary surgeon. She is talking to her university counsellor and international coaches to design a plan that stops her losing ground in the sporting sphere. Lynam’s parents, Glen and Susanna, brought their young family to Hong Kong from Australia 18 years ago. “They were working for an NGO based in China, and my mum was flying there every couple of weeks,” Lynam said. “She had four little kids at the time, so they decided to relocate. “They originally said, ‘We’ll go for a year and see how it goes’, but they loved it.” As a pupil at YMCA of Hong Kong Christian College, Lynam played “a bit of football” and competed over 200m, 400m and in the long jump. Still, after beginning to play for Flying Kukris in Tuen Mun around the age of eight, the oval ball took precedence. “Whenever I told people I played rugby, they’d say, ‘Oh, that’s a bit of a rough sport’, but my parents were very supportive,” said Lynam, who will turn 23 on September 15. “They loved us getting into rugby, and I really enjoyed it, so I never bothered about people’s opinions on that.” While older sister Christina played volleyball but now focuses on her job in education, and older brother Callan, a musician, is a lapsed rugby player, younger sister Ella has also embraced rugby and could make her Hong Kong debut against Brazil. “It’s amazing that we can play together; it never happened when we were growing up because she was the year beneath me,” Sabay Lynam said. “We’ve always been competitive, but in rugby we’re very supportive of each other. It’s a blessing in disguise that we play the same position; we help each other out with what we’re missing.” A dinner table argument over who is the most talented member of the family could extend until daybreak. Lynam’s mother, Susanna, is a children’s author and teacher librarian at International College Hong Kong. Performing under the name Glen Alfred, her father is a solo musician who last year toured Europe and is now poised to travel to America to record his next album. In Sabay, Glen and Susanna chose an exceptionally rare name for their third child. “My mum was visiting the grave of a relative [in Australia] and she saw the name on a gravestone,” Lynam said. “There was a picture of the lady, and my mum said she was beautiful. She thought it was a pretty name, so she kept it in her mind.” The star local turn at last year’s Cathay/HSBC Hong Kong Sevens, when she top scored with five tries in the hosts’ successful Melrose Claymores campaign, Lynam “always strove for the highest [in rugby] but never saw myself playing at this level”. “I was keen on going to university, but I got this opportunity and loved it,” she said, having joined the Hong Kong sevens programme straight out of school. “I enjoyed going in so young, and I had a lot of friends around me I’d played with since youth rugby.” It was to the more seasoned contingent that Lynam turned for advice as she began to grapple with juggling rugby and studying on another continent. “The biggest challenge is being away from the team, but some of the older girls who’ve done the same told me that, with our support system, it would be fine,” she said. “I chat all the time with the strength and conditioning team about what they’re doing in Hong Kong and I mirror that in Australia as best I can. They get updates about what I’m doing with my rugby over there, and they’re happy with it.” In the Queensland competition, Lynam has encountered “bigger bodies and girls who play quickly”. “It forces me to be better and compete with others in my position who might be bigger,” said Lynam, who is deliberating over whether to add some bulk to her wispy frame. “With balancing university, it’s hard to manage your weight if you want to fill out,” she said. “In my position, as long as you’re fast and able to make your tackles, your size doesn’t matter. It doesn’t faze me; I’m comfortable with how I am.” A non-passport holder, and therefore ineligible for this month’s Asian Games, Lynam has been in Hong Kong for more than two weeks preparing for the forthcoming matches at Kai Tak Youth Sports Ground. “Showing up for the team is a big thing that gets me going,” she said. “I see girls who show up to train after eight hours at work. They’re doing their conditioning and reviews, and getting their fuel in. That really motivates me to want to become better for them.” Keen to begin her veterinary career in a wildlife hospital, Lynam expects to stay down under immediately after graduation, with a medium-term plan to relocate to Hong Kong. Rewinding to her first “hands-on” placement, Lynam recalled the new experience of having an animal’s “life in your hands”. “The degree teaches you the right way to do things, but the first time you monitor a patient by yourself, or put an animal under, it’s nerve-racking,” she said. “The first thing I did was to give medications to wild birds: to magpies, cockatoos, rainbow lorikeets. I’ve treated koalas, possums and kangaroo joeys. My parents always had animals and, from very young, I knew I wanted a career helping them.”

title: No foreign soldiers: Japan shuts down proposal to fix military shortfall
description: Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi rules out non-nationals in uniform, even as a report warns personnel levels could fall to 130,000 by 2045.
content: By 2045, Japan’s Self-Defence Forces (SDF) could shrink to 130,000 personnel – nearly half today’s strength. But Tokyo has already ruled out one think tank’s controversial fix: recruiting foreign nationals. The proposal formed part of a report written by a panel of senior former defence bureaucrats and military chiefs, released by the Sasakawa Peace Foundation on September 2. It attracted widespread comment, both supportive and critical, before Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the government’s position clear on Friday, stating he was “not considering” hiring foreign nationals for the armed forces. He acknowledged that “securing human resources is a major challenge in the context of the declining birth rate and ageing population”, but said the government was instead drawing up plans to address personnel shortfalls by improving conditions and facilities for serving members and their families, offering more support after they had left the armed services and expanding the use of technology such as AI. Employers across Japan are struggling to find workers and analysts say the military holds little appeal for many young people. While other countries allow non-nationals to serve – Britain, for example, recruits Commonwealth citizens – Japan has shown far greater reluctance to follow suit, a stance that coincides with hardening public opposition to immigration more broadly. “There are just too many reasons, from the military, the government and the public, why this suggestion is not going to work,” a government adviser on national security told This Week in Asia. “All arms of the SDF are understaffed at the moment and they are having problems retaining trained people. But this [proposal] has alarmed people.” In military and government circles, officials argue that hostile countries could exploit the policy to infiltrate their own nationals into the SDF to obtain military secrets or defence plans, or even carry out sabotage and distribute propaganda, said the expert, who declined to be named. Screening prospective recruits “would be a huge headache” for the Ministry of Defence, he added, and revive the wider debate over foreign nationals and naturalised citizens serving in the civil service or running for the Diet. Opposition to foreigners defending Japan mirrors a broader rise in hostility towards their presence. A University of Tokyo study released last month found that 56.3 per cent of Japanese opposed allowing more foreigners to settle permanently, up 20.7 percentage points from a similar study in 2024. The shift was most notable among young people and those expressing a belief that “there is no hope for Japanese society”. Given that sentiment, the timing of the Sasakawa report’s release was unfortunate. It was written by a panel that included Tetsuro Kuroe, a former vice defence minister; Koji Yamazaki, a former chief of staff of the Joint Staff; and Yutaka Murakawa, a former chief of staff of the Maritime Self-Defence Force. It noted that current policy required Japanese nationality for public servants involved in “the exercise of public authority and the formation of national will”, but argued that certain SDF roles fell outside this definition – pointing to Britain, the US and Australia as countries that had successfully integrated foreigners into the military. The report also warned that Japan’s demographic decline was becoming more of an issue. As the population shrinks, the number of 18- to 32-year-olds eligible to apply to the SDF has fallen to less than 40 per cent of the total three decades ago. Recruiters are falling short of annual targets and the Ministry of Defence estimates that, if current trends continue, personnel levels could fall from 220,000 today to around 180,000 by 2035 and just 130,000 by 2045. Garren Mulloy, an international-relations professor at Daito Bunka University and a specialist in military affairs, said it was “unfortunate” that Japanese media had focused almost exclusively on the foreign-recruitment proposal, which accounted for just two pages of the 38-page report. Japan needed to seriously confront the future of its armed forces, he said. “Young people are not joining in the numbers required to keep levels up, the junior ranks are particularly short of personnel and the average age of the troops is increasing,” Mulloy said. He noted, however, that scope might still exist for recruiting foreign nationals into support roles such as logistics, medical care, weapons development at government-affiliated research institutions, or work at private defence technology companies. Mulloy also suggested that recent measures making it harder for foreigners to settle in Japan – including stricter visa rules and higher fees – were partly designed to reassure voters at a time when far-right parties such as Sanseito were stoking public anxiety about foreign nationals. Social media commentary has been overwhelmingly supportive of Koizumi’s rejection of the proposal. “In Japan’s case, the hypothetical enemy is China,” read one comment under a Yomiuri newspaper report on Friday. “But the largest group of foreigners in Japan are Chinese nationals, so … the majority of the candidates would inevitably be Chinese.” Another commenter put forward a proposal that could prove just as contentious: “Japan should be protected by Japanese people. I believe the solution to the personnel shortage is to revive conscription like other countries.”

title: Must-see fall 2026 exhibitions and a new museum on our radar, from Monet to George Lucas
description: Explore a spaceship-like cultural centre co-founded by the Star Wars creator, the historic Bayeux Tapestry, designs by Geoffrey Bawa, and more.
content: From medieval embroidery to Impressionist masterpieces, the cultural calendar this autumn is packed with unmissable exhibitions. Here are eight stand-out shows to see from around the world – from the Bayeux Tapestry on display in London to the opening of George Lucas’s ambitious new museum in Los Angeles. Lucas Museum of Narrative Art The most high-profile museum opening of the year comes courtesy of none other than George Lucas, the legendary director behind film franchises such as Star Wars and Indiana Jones. Located in Los Angeles’ Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, which opens later this month, is housed in a 300,000-square-foot spaceship-like building designed by Ma Yansong of Chinese architects MAD, along with US-based architecture firm Stantec. The museum’s collection, amassed by Lucas over 50 years, includes important works by the likes of Diego Rivera, Robert Capa and Gordon Parks, as well as movie posters, props and other film memorabilia. Viktor & Rolf. Spectrum Self-proclaimed “fashion artists” Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren, the Dutch duo behind the label Viktor & Rolf, are the subjects of an exhibition at Milan’s 10 Corso Como Galleria. Displaying 20 haute couture displays looks in pairs, echoing the designers’ focus on duality in their work. Named “Viktor & Rolf. Spectrum”, the exhibition is a full immersion in the creative world of what they call their “creative marriage”. From September 25 until November 22 Night Maurizio Cattelan, the conceptual artist behind the banana installation that went viral at Art Basel Miami in 2019, is the subject of an exhibition at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. The show, named “Night”, features some of his most famous works, including seminal pieces such as Him (2001), Novecento (1997), La Rivoluzione Siamo Noi (2000), as well as newer commissions. One of the most influential artists working today, Cattelan has never been afraid to tackle topics such as religion and politics in his often satirical and controversial work. From September 10 to March 7, 2027 Es Devlin: Other Worlds British artist and designer Es Devlin is the subject of an exhibition at London’s Design Museum. “Es Devlin: Other Worlds” explores her work across disciplines ranging from sculpture to stage design and even music. Devlin began her career working in theatre more than three decades ago and has since developed a remarkable body of work that defies easy categorisation, just one reason to check out the show. From October 2 to April 4, 2027 Herzog & de Meuron: In Focus Architects Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron – founders of the firm Herzog & de Meuron, established in Switzerland in 1978 – are behind some of the most striking buildings in the world, from the National Stadium in Beijing to Prada’s Epicenter Tokyo in Aoyama. Hong Kong’s M+, also designed by the duo, is celebrating its fifth anniversary with an exhibition, “Herzog & de Meuron: In Focus” showcasing their projects in China that include the Tai Kwun complex in Central – through models, drawings and other objects. From September 12 to January 2027 Bayeux Tapestry Depicting the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings and the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, the Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the wonders of medieval art. Measuring more than 70 metres long, the monumental embroidery is part of the permanent collection of the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux in Normandy. While the museum is closed for renovation until next year, the work will be on display at London’s British Museum, one of the city’s most visited cultural institutions. From September 10 to July 11, 2027 Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses Exhibits including drawings and artworks, models, furniture, historic footage and photographs are part of an exhibition at the Vitra Design Museum in Germany showcasing Sri Lankan architect Geoffrey Bawa’s remarkable work. Although he trained in the West and was influenced by Western modernism, Bawa created his own style, informed by his Sri Lankan roots, later known as Tropical Modernism. Titled “Geoffrey Bawa: Architecture for the Senses”, the exhibition also sheds light on Bawa’s close connections with Sri Lankan artists and craftspeople. From September 26 to February 28, 2027 Monet, Peindre le Temps To mark the centenary of Claude Monet’s death, the Musée d’Orsay and the Musée de l’Orangerie in Paris are organising a series of exhibitions and events dedicated to the artist. Opening at the Musée de l’Orangerie this month, “Monet, Peindre le Temps” (Monet, Painting Time) explores the painter’s way of depicting the passing of the hours and seasons. Besides the suggestive paintings of the celebrated Impressionist master, the exhibition also features an immersive VR experience showcasing his famous Water Lilies. From September 30 to January 25, 2027 Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Go with the flow of these 6 swimming-related idioms for every wave of life
description: These expressions can enhance the way you communicate about adapting to challenges.
content:
Summer is the perfect time to dive into the cooling waters of new idioms.
Most humans are used to living life on land, and swimming is something we have to learn. This selection of phrases shows how swimming can be an apt metaphor for navigating life’s challenges and adapting to new situations.
Meaning: to be in a situation that you cannot control; to struggle to understand something because it is too difficult
Example: The maths class is too hard for me. I’m out of my depth.
Meaning: to go against what most other people are doing, often involving making a choice or taking a stance that opposes what others believe
Example: While my teammates supported taking this short cut, I voiced my concerns, swimming against the tide of their enthusiasm.
Meaning: to be relaxed and do what others are doing because it is the easiest thing to do
Example: I decided to go with the flow and joined my friends on a last-minute hike.
Meaning: to succeed or fail based on your own efforts or abilities, often in a challenging situation
Example: When my team had just one more day before the deadline, I knew it was time to sink or swim, and I had to step up my efforts.
Meaning: to manage to survive during tough times, especially when you are having financial problems
Example: Our family’s shop is losing customers, so we’re doing everything we can to keep our heads above water.
Meaning: to start a task or challenge that is difficult or new without preparation or prior experience
Example: When I started my new job and had to learn everything about it on my own, it felt like I was jumping in at the deep end.

title: Trump transport chief blasts Ford’s business deals with Chinese firms
description: CEO Jim Farley hit back, saying the letter urging him to cut ties with firms like China’s CATL, Geely and BYD was ‘wrong-headed’.
content: The Trump administration on Tuesday blasted Ford Motor’s business partnerships with Chinese companies, saying they posed national security concerns. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a letter ‌to Ford CEO Jim Farley sent on Tuesday said the carmaker’s dealings with Chinese battery maker CATL and Chinese carmakers Geely and BYD raised “profound concern”. He urged Ford to cut ties with major Chinese companies. Duffy said USDOT was “deeply alarmed” by Ford’s reliance on licensed technology from Chinese battery manufacturer CATL at its plant in Marshall, Michigan, and noted that CATL is on the Pentagon’s list of companies accused of ⁠ties to China’s military. He also criticised the company’s decision not to move production of the Lincoln Nautilus from China ‌to the United States until 2030, as it left the company reliant on Chinese manufacturing for several more years. Ford, in a statement, said Duffy’s “letter is a wrong-headed attempt to ‌capture headlines”. The company added that “while others continue to import Chinese batteries, Ford is investing to build ⁠batteries here in ⁠America” and added that “Ford owns the plant, controls the operation and employs the workforce”. US President Donald Trump is set to meet with Chinese ‌President Xi Jinping later this month. Duffy’s comments come as Congress is pushing to tighten a ban on Chinese vehicles in the United States. Major carmakers ‌last week ‌urged Congress to pass the ban before the end of the year – and expressly urged lawmakers to bar ‌BYD and other Chinese carmakers from receiving waivers to sell vehicles in the United States. Duffy also questioned ⁠Farley’s pitch in January to administration officials at the Detroit vehicle show “to facilitate Chinese joint ventures on United States ⁠soil”. The Chinese embassy in Washington, CATL, BYD and Geely did not immediately respond to requests for comment. “When a company intentionally chooses to deepen operational dependencies on strategic competitors, it fails to act ‌as the reliable partner the American ‌public and this DOT require,” Duffy said of Ford. Ford’s deal with Geely faced criticism in July, with the chair of the US House select committee on China, congressman John Moolenaar of Michigan, saying the “partnership with Geely will further enable China’s decimation of auto markets in Europe”. It has also faced criticism for its partnership with CATL.

title: How Chinese investment is driving Central Asia’s green energy boom
description: The Belt and Road Initiative, with its massive investments in wind, solar and nuclear power, is quietly reshaping the region’s energy future.
content: When President Xi Jinping announced the launch of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2013, the sprawling network of new railways and highways branching out from China across Eurasia was just imaginary lines on a map. This year, the total volume of China’s BRI investments reached US$1.3 trillion, with a 257 per cent spike in Central Asia compared to last year, and many of those lines are no longer imaginary. The five Central Asian states of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan constitute a vital node on this “New Silk Road”. But while much of the world’s attention is on China’s investments in transport and logistical undertakings in the region, Beijing has also been growing its investments in green energy projects. This shift is primarily driven by domestic necessity in Central Asia. There, governments face severe energy supply shortages and mounting ecological challenges. That is why by 2030, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan aim to increase the share of electricity generated from renewables to 15 per cent and 50 per cent respectively. According to the International Energy Agency, in 2023, 49 per cent of Kazakhstan’s energy supply came from coal and 79 per cent of Uzbekistan’s from natural gas. In both cases, renewables accounted for around just 2 per cent. Across Central Asia, public trust is closely tied to the reliable delivery of basic services. Water shortages, winter blackouts and natural disasters therefore carry more than just environmental consequences, according to Dr Akbota Karibayeva Meyer, a Washington-based Central Asia analyst. The threat of such disruptions has helped move the green agenda from “symbolic gesture to genuine priority” and spurred demand for outside capital, including China’s. According to the Center for International Private Enterprise, over the period of 2003-2024, Beijing’s cumulative investments in Central Asia reached US$44.4 billion. Though short of the US$50.6 billion the US invested in the region, China supported 175 projects compared to 135 by American firms. Renewable power projects form the backbone of this expanding footprint. In southern Kazakhstan, the 100MW Zhanatas Wind Power Plant has been operational since 2021. Built at a cost of US$140 million, the project was co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, and the Green Climate Fund. Currently, China Power International Holding holds an 80 per cent stake through its subsidiaries. Cooperation in Uzbekistan has also accelerated. Tashkent recently signed agreements with Chinese firms to construct a 100MW energy storage system in the capital, alongside a 500MW wind power plant in Bukhara, where China Southern Power Grid had already invested US$240 million in two existing wind projects. Sany Renewable Energy also initiated a US$1.2 billion wind farm project in Karakalpakstan. Clean mobility and aviation are following suit. At the 5th Tashkent International Investment Forum, China’s Sinopec Engineering Group signed a US$6.1 billion contract with Allied Biofuels to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) domestically, supporting Uzbekistan’s ambitions to become a key Eurasian transit hub. Simultaneously, Chinese electric vehicles are reshaping local automotive markets. Long nicknamed “Chevrolistan” due to the ubiquity of Chevrolet vehicles, Uzbekistan saw BYD secure an 8.6 per cent market share – a twofold increase from the previous year that saw Chevrolet’s dominance drop from 82.6 per cent of the market down to 79.3 per cent. The green transition that drives demand for wind turbines and EVs means an urgent demand for the raw materials that make them possible. Every Chinese wind farm erected and every BYD sold depends on minerals that Central Asia possesses in abundance. The region holds 38.6 per cent of the world’s manganese ore, 30.1 per cent of chromium, 20 per cent of lead, 12.6 per cent of zinc, 8.7 per cent of titanium, 5.3 per cent of copper and cobalt, and 5.2 per cent of molybdenum. All are essential components for batteries, electric vehicles and wind turbines. If successful, Central Asia will be a model for developing countries looking to transition into green energy Bruce Pannier, Turan Research Center For China, investment in the region represents a practical move to build robust supply chains for key minerals. China controls around 90 per cent of global rare earth processing capacity and relies heavily on Central Asian mineral exports. “For the Chinese, proximity to the assets is a defining factor, along with the fact that most well-established export logistics run east or north into China,” says Kamal Aubakirov, an independent critical minerals analyst based in Almaty. While Western states are increasingly interested in Kazakh mining opportunities in particular, structural barriers limit their entry. “Before anything else, you have to look at economics,” Aubakirov says. “If a Western partner has not been in the region before, it adds extra cost for their firms just to understand the due diligence behind an asset.” Surging power demand from expanding urban areas and data centres has accelerated global interest in nuclear energy, with the World Nuclear Association expecting global capacity to more than triple by 2050. According to International Atomic Energy Agency estimates, nuclear capacity in Central and Eastern Asia is set to increase 15 per cent by 2030 and 45 per cent by 2050. Central Asia sits at the centre of this “nuclear renaissance”. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan rank as the first- and fifth-largest uranium producers globally, with Kazakhstan contributing 39 per cent of global uranium mining production. Beyond resource extraction, technical nuclear partnerships are deepening long-term regional integration. After selecting Russia’s Rosatom to construct its first nuclear power plant, Kazakhstan announced that China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) would subsequently build the next two HPR-1000 (Hualong One) reactors. Because nuclear partnerships require decades of workforce training, technical assistance, and maintenance, the project cements long-term structural alignment between Beijing and Astana. Daniyar Ashimov, a nuclear expert and former deputy director of the Agency of the Republic of Kazakhstan for Atomic Energy, shares that while sourcing uranium is the foundation of Beijing’s engagement with Astana, geographic proximity also creates opportunities for cooperation across more of the nuclear fuel cycle. “China offers scale, financing capacity, reactor technology, and a very large long-term market,” Ashimov explains. “Kazakhstan’s economy, to some extent, is relying on China. And perhaps, the vast majority of Central Asia is too.” If these large-scale energy projects succeed, Central Asia could establish a blueprint for other developing regions. “If successful, Central Asia will be a model for developing countries looking to transition into green energy. They will have the know-how,” says Bruce Pannier, a senior fellow at the Turan Research Center, a US think tank interested in modern developments in the Turkic and Persian worlds. Astana’s choice to engage both Moscow and Beijing for its nuclear energy buildout highlights a broader “multi-vector” foreign policy framework governing Central Asian diplomacy and foreign investment. “Rather than aligning with a single foreign partner, they deliberately cultivate good working relationships with everyone so that no one becomes indispensable – and use the resulting competition to extract the best terms for their national interest,” noted Karibayeva Meyer. “In this context, engagement with China on infrastructure and energy is driven by domestic necessity and pragmatism.” How long Central Asian states can continue their multi-vector approach is uncertain. China’s infrastructure and economic presence is likely to grow not only because of aligned energy priorities with its regional partners but because of a strategic longevity that contrasts with ever-shifting political cycles in the West, if not Russia. “Over the past 35 years since independence, Central Asian governments have learned that partnerships with the US are tied to the interests of who is in the White House,” Pannier observes. “China’s footprint is not just getting bigger, it is permanent. It is lasting.”

title: Editorial | For Hong Kong and Central Asia, the real work lies ahead
description: Building on the success of Chief Executive John Lee’s June trip, both sides must now build a durable commercial architecture.
content: Hong Kong’s expanding engagement with Central Asia represents more than a commercial drive. It signals a strategic recalibration that, if pursued with discipline and realism, could position the city as an indispensable bridge between East and Central Asia at a moment when traditional corridors of trade and exchange face mounting strain. Both sides must now move beyond aspirational declarations to overcome challenges constraining regional commerce. The concrete outcomes Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu reported at the South China Morning Post’s China Conference in Astana this week already indicate initial success. They were tangible follow-through on the trip Lee led to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June – a mission that produced 96 deals worth US$1.65 billion. Over 300 business leaders from the region attended the conference, marking the first time a Hong Kong media outlet organised a major event in Kazakhstan and demonstrating how the media industry can actively facilitate the city’s “superconnector” mission. The SCMP signed a memorandum with Nazarbayev University, Central Asia’s top-ranked institution where President Xi Jinping first announced the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013. Within the framework of this infrastructure programme, Jiaxin International Resources’ successful August 2025 dual listing – in Hong Kong and Kazakhstan – served as a pioneering effort. The tungsten miner invested in Kazakhstan for over a decade before raising HK$1.2 billion (US$154 million) through Hong Kong’s capital markets. Kazakhstan’s national rail operator, KTZ, is preparing for a triple listing in Hong Kong, Astana and London. Hong Kong is deepening connectivity, with Kazakh students forming the largest undergraduate cohort from Central Asia. Direct flights launching on January 9 are expected to boost tourism and professional services. Cultural and financial institutions are actively exploring new collaborations, including potential exhibitions and market opportunities in legal services, food processing and water treatment. Our city and Central Asia must now build on the momentum to sustain capital flows and achieve genuine investment and cooperation. The strategic logic underpinning this initiative is unassailable. The region’s five republics sit at the geographic heart of the Belt and Road Initiative. Kazakhstan, the region’s largest economy, can serve as a critical node connecting Chinese production networks to European markets. Hong Kong’s merchandise trade with Central Asia increased 27 per cent between 2020 and 2025. The city brings distinct advantages to this relationship as the world’s most sophisticated offshore renminbi financial ecosystem, encompassing foreign exchange, bonds and liquidity pools where the Central Asian economies can diversify trade and currency exposure. Kazakhstan’s Development Bank issued Central Asia’s first dim sum bond worth 2 billion yuan in Hong Kong last September – a transaction demonstrating complementary capabilities. The broader geopolitical context cannot be ignored. Hong Kong’s engagement unfolds against intensifying global protectionism and strategic competition between major powers. For Kazakhstan, Hong Kong’s unique status under “one country, two systems” allows engagement as a separate customs territory while benefiting from a strategic alignment with China. The Astana International Financial Centre’s governor, Renat Bekturov, has identified the imperative: making conditions practical for investors by removing regulatory frictions over the next two to three years. This prosaic work will ensure successful outcomes. Hong Kong has competitors for capital flows and regional connectivity. Our edge rests on specialisation where legal certainty, capital mobility and China access converge. Central Asia offers a proving ground for whether Hong Kong can leverage these strengths in emerging markets lacking established relationships. Lee has aptly described Hong Kong as a “trusted partner” in financing sustainable growth. The latest initiative builds on the success of the June mission. Hong Kong’s relevance depends on execution. Both sides must now build a durable commercial architecture for a bright future along the new Silk Road.

title: Chinese matcha’s rapid rise and the Hong Kong couple stirring up the UK tea scene
description: A mission to bring Chinese tea culture to Britain unexpectedly turned Hong Kong couple Raphael Chow and Joyce Ding into matcha entrepreneurs.
content: A trip to Puer in China’s Yunnan province changed the way Hongkongers Raphael Chow and his wife, Joyce Ding, thought about tea. Home of its namesake fermented brew, the city is widely regarded as the ancient birthplace of Camellia sinensis – the plant from which most of the world’s tea is made. The London-based couple not only fell in love with the region’s teas, but also with its communal tea-drinking culture. Upon returning to the UK capital, they founded their own fine loose leaf tea company, Brut Tea, in 2024. Despite their long histories, many of Britain’s most-established tea brands continue to frame tea through a colonial narrative, Chow says. He recalls visiting the Twinings flagship store in London’s West End, where he felt the only obvious reference to China was a pair of sculptures of Chinese sailors employed by the British Empire that sat above the entrance, while Chinese tea itself received little attention. “You’ll go in and see this very colonial display where they feature [India’s] Assam and Darjeeling, which of course is where their [Twinings] plantations were,” he says. “Then there will be a very small footnote when you reach the end of the shop saying, ‘Oh, there’s this little thing called Puer tea and we have some of that in the corner over there.’” By sourcing their teas directly from Yunnan’s oldest tea-growing regions, Chow and Ding set out to show a new generation of British tea drinkers the history behind their usual “cuppa”. At a time when Gen Z is beginning to embrace aspects of Chinese culture – a movement that has manifested as “Chinamaxxing” on social media – they also hoped to spark curiosity about tea’s Chinese origins and complex preparation rituals such as gong fu tea. But when they began approaching cafes across London, they were met with a different response. One conversation they kept having again and again was whether they could supply the cafes with matcha, the powdered green tea that has taken over social media. The UK has become Europe’s fastest-growing matcha market, valued at US$40.1 million in 2025 and projected to rise to US$77.5 million by 2033. From independent coffee shops to major cafe chains and even unassuming local fish and chip shops, a strawberry matcha latte is now as likely to appear on the menu as a flat white. Between 2024 and 2025, the number of cafes in the UK serving matcha tripled from 365 to 1,096, according to data reported by the Financial Times. Britain’s matcha mania has even begun eating into coffee’s dominance, as sales growth of flat whites, cappuccinos and lattes all fell into negative territory for the first time in 2025, having last outpaced matcha’s growth in 2022. The shift has been fuelled in part by younger consumers, many of whom have embraced matcha through social media where, in addition to its pleasing aesthetics, it is being touted as a wellness drink for its slower-release caffeine and high antioxidant content. Growing interest in travel to Japan, combined with the nation’s comparatively weak currency, has also introduced more British visitors to matcha first-hand. This new-found thirst is only part of a growing global trend. Demand for Japanese matcha from around the world has tripled over the past decade, according to Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, placing unprecedented pressure on Japanese farmers and suppliers and resulting in a nationwide shortage. “We’re out of stock … our suppliers can’t get any to us … they’ve tripled the price,” Chow heard repeatedly from cafe owners across London. He realised Brut Tea needed to get in on the green rush if it was to succeed. But instead of looking to Japan, where they would have to compete with established brands for scarce supplies, they decided to return to China, where they were familiar with its loose-leaf “teascape” and curious about whispers of an emerging matcha industry. “We used the same approach as we did with our loose leaf teas: going back to the historical heart and soul of matcha,” Ding says, recounting the couple’s trip to Jingshan mountain in Zhejiang province. “We did that with Puer … and we did it again with matcha.” It was here, according to historical accounts, that some of the earliest forms of powdered green tea emerged during the Tang dynasty (618-907). Tea was pressed into bricks for easy transport, and pieces were broken off and ground before drinking. This ritual flourished during the Song dynasty (960-1279), becoming high art. China was also where Japanese Buddhist monk Eisai is believed to have encountered powdered tea while studying Zen Buddhism. He later brought it back to Japan, where it was refined over centuries to become a core component of Japanese culture. Although enlightened by their history lesson, the couple remained sceptical of China’s modern matcha industry. Japan had spent centuries refining the craft, while China had abandoned it almost 700 years ago in favour of loose leaf tea after China’s Ming dynasty authorities banned tea bricks in 1391. But a deeper look into Zhejiang’s tea farms – and later the Yun-Gui Plateau, an elevated tea-growing region spanning Yunnan and Guizhou provinces – changed their perspective entirely. A visit to Guizhou’s vast matcha production facilities was particularly eye-opening, as they were informed that one giant factory alone would soon have the capacity to produce around 10,000 tonnes (11,023 tons) of matcha powder annually – more than Japan’s total production of around 6,000 tonnes. “After China gave up matcha centuries ago, they didn’t really know how to cultivate it, but in recent years, they’ve addressed it and fixed it,” Chow says. He points to China’s rapid investment in matcha production over the past decade, with expansion accelerating in recent years as provinces including Shandong, Hubei and Sichuan begin developing their own matcha industries. Chow and Ding were also able to track down skilled producers capable of crafting premium matcha powder across a diverse range of terroirs, with different cultivars producing new and exciting flavours. Many of these also possessed a bolder character that they felt was particularly well suited to British consumption habits. Unlike the delicate notes prized in premium Japanese matcha, designed to be served plain with hot water, the Chinese samples were able to retain their flavour when paired with milk and syrups, making them especially suitable for the matcha lattes that dominate the UK’s matcha scene. But their discovery had them wondering why British suppliers and cafe owners, who had been involved in the matcha space for far longer than themselves, appeared unaware of China being the world’s largest producer of matcha – especially as they struggled to secure supply from Japan. Upon returning to the UK, they found that British wholesalers often stocked premium Japanese matcha powder alongside cheaper, lower-grade Chinese green tea blends, with nothing in between. “It became clear that a lot of people had only experienced Chinese matcha through this low-quality category,” Chow says. “They hadn’t actually seen what China was capable of producing.” In 2025, Brut Tea introduced its own premium Chinese matcha sourced from farms they had visited in Guizhou and Zhejiang. They now supply 60 cafes across the UK and schedule regular pop-ups. “Through Brut Tea,” says Katy Soto, founder of London’s Soto Coffee, “we were introduced to a Chinese matcha that tasted great, worked beautifully in the drinks we serve and gave us an opportunity to offer something a little less expected. We were also drawn to how passionate Joyce and Raphael are about Chinese tea and about giving the quality and history behind it the recognition it deserves.” Ding has since started hosting matcha workshops where she uses matcha to introduce customers to the wider history of tea, and invites them to try and compare matcha from China, Japan and Korea, while exploring its Chinese origins. “I was happy to see that people were going on TikTok after attending our workshops to express their new-found knowledge that matcha originated from China,” she says. As the market matures, the couple expects consumers to move beyond novelty and develop a deeper interest in provenance, cultivation and flavour, similar to the evolution of coffee culture over the past 20 years.
