For Chow, this represents an exciting opportunity to explore an even wider range of flavours shaped by China’s vast and diverse terroirs. Although Brut Tea’s matcha sales have eclipsed those of its original loose leaf teas, the couple remain committed to its identity as a fine tea brand. They see matcha as the viral gateway they never knew they needed to introduce British tea drinkers to the wider world of tea, and to fulfil the mission they had set out from the beginning. “Matcha isn’t going anywhere,” Chow says. “But hopefully it can also help people discover where the story of tea really began.”

title: Macau kingpin’s former ‘love nest’ finally sells for HK$81m in cut-price deal
description: The Mid-Levels flat – once owned by Alvin Chau’s former mistress – is the latest luxury property to sell for a steep paper loss in Hong Kong.
content: The luxury Hong Kong flat once owned by Mandy Lieu – the former mistress of Macau gambling kingpin Alvin Chau Cheok-wa – has finally been sold at a steep loss for just over HK$81 million (US$10.3 million), according to market sources. The flat on the 38th floor of the Argenta development in Hong Kong’s Mid-Levels West changed hands on Monday for HK$81.2 million – a price that is over 10 per cent lower than the amount Lieu reportedly paid to acquire the property 12 years ago. Lieu, a renowned model, bought the flat under her own name for HK$91.3 million in mid-2014, paying the full amount upfront in cash, according to previous media reports. She reportedly shared the property with Macau “junket king” Chau. Following Chau’s downfall in late 2021, Lieu mortgaged the property and then put it up for sale at an asking price of HK$120 million. However, the flat failed to sell, even after she lowered the price to HK$105 million. After the mortgage fell into arrears, the property was formally repossessed by the creditor, Melco Resorts (Macau) Limited, which appointed an agency to list the flat for sale as a foreclosed property in October 2023. The asking price was lowered once again to HK$95 million. The three-bedroom apartment with views of Victoria Harbour eventually sold for substantially lower even than that figure. The final price worked out at about HK$37,200 per square foot, based on the flat’s listed saleable area of 2,182 square feet. According to Land Registry records, the new buyer is Atlas Worldwide Holdings Limited, a company registered outside the local jurisdiction. The firm’s ultimate beneficiary remains unknown. The more than HK$10 million paper loss on the flat reflected current market conditions in Hong Kong’s luxury property market, with the repossessed apartment having been on the market for a considerable time, according to Tommy YT Chow, senior principal district sales director at Centaline Property. “With a total price exceeding HK$80 million, finding suitable buyers for such high-value transactions is more challenging than in the past,” he said. “While there is continued demand for second-hand luxury properties in Mid-Levels West, buyers will only consider them if the pricing is attractive and closely aligned with bank valuations.” According to data from Centaline Property, a total of about 80 secondary residential transactions were recorded in Mid-Levels West in August, with a combined value of about HK$1.14 billion and an average price per saleable square foot of around HK$21,600. Chau – the founder of Suncity Group, now known as LET Group Holdings – was sentenced to 18 years in prison by the Court of First Instance of Macau in November 2023, after being convicted on 162 charges, including founding and leading a criminal syndicate and engaging in illegal gambling operations. Lieu began a high-profile relationship with Chau in 2014, maintaining a long-term extramarital affair with three daughters and a son, but the couple broke up in 2019.

title: Hong Kong universities power Belt and Road Initiative through strategic ties
description: Tertiary institutions such as PolyU, EdUHK and HKUST are establishing lasting academic and industry partnerships across the world.
content: Hong Kong has been actively advancing links with Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) countries in trade, finance and professional services. Similarly, the city’s local universities have been developing innovative programmes and exchanges to strengthen ties, share knowledge and promote long-term cross-border collaboration between academia and industry. A prime example is the Hong Kong Polytechnic University’s (PolyU) Belt and Road Advanced Programme in Power and Energy. This year’s cohort of 45 professionals from countries including Brazil, Argentina, Indonesia, the Philippines, Russia and South Africa focused on the ways that AI technologies are enabling new power systems. “Running the programme takes persistence and belief,” says Professor HC Man, dean of the Faculty of Engineering. He notes that over 900 professionals from 44 BRI countries have taken part since 2018. “What we have done,” continues Man, “creates impact by introducing participants to the latest technology and learning, which they then take back home.” This ripple effect is tangible. For instance, last year three attendees from Chile were so impressed that they subsequently sent a team of professors to PolyU to initiate ongoing collaboration. Furthermore, the workshops and visits have provided industry partners with valuable exposure and opportunities to forge new business connections in BRI markets. By leveraging both consular and academic networks, PolyU has also established new contacts with overseas universities renowned for their strong power and energy departments. According to Ir Wilson Kwok, dean of the HK Electric Institute, the PolyU programme has become an effective international platform for advancing collaboration, talent development and innovation in the energy sector. He believes it has fostered dialogue and meaningful exchanges, helping to build capacity and lead the transition to a low-carbon future. “We share our experience of power system planning, operations and asset management with the participants,” Kwok says. “We also offer them valuable insights into the best practices and challenges associated with operating a highly reliable electricity network and show how the latest engineering concepts are applied in real-world settings.” For example, this year the programme introduced next-generation grid maintenance technologies, including a 3D digital twin for distribution substations. Participants were also shown an in-house AI model for proactive cable diagnosis to anticipate possible risks and optimise network health. “New technologies are fundamentally shifting the power sector from reactive or time-based maintenance to automated, predictive and intelligent grid management,” Kwok adds. At the Education University of Hong Kong (EdUHK), a key initiative is the one-year, full-time MA in Belt and Road Business Communication and Administration, launching in the 2026-27 academic year. The programme has already attracted thousands of applications. It is taught in Putonghua, a strategic choice that has drawn significant interest from candidates in mainland China and positions it to serve the needs of enterprises expanding along the Belt and Road. “The aim is to leverage Hong Kong’s unique advantages as a ‘superconnector’ in both higher education and international business,” says programme leader Dr Leo Liu Jindong. “We are nurturing talent who can contribute to BRI developments and are building partnerships with leading universities in key countries such as Kazakhstan and the United Arab Emirates.” Dr Liu anticipates that networks, opportunities and the overall landscape of the BRI will evolve rapidly, which has prompted EdUHK to invite industry experts for guest lectures and explore new collaborative pathways. Meanwhile, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) Business School is taking a different approach. Dean Professor Frederik Anseel is currently leading a week-long study tour to Kazakhstan for the mid- and senior-level professionals of the Kellogg-HKUST executive MBA programme. A key part of this mission is for delegation members to explore ways their companies can expand, verify business assumptions and determine what it takes for international businesses to succeed in the region. Anseel will also use the opportunity to strengthen ties with Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Business, a partner with HKUST in launching Asia’s first undergraduate BBA in Eurasian business, where students divide their time between both campuses for an immersive cultural and academic experience. “As a university, we are very strong in AI, fintech, cybersecurity and robotics – areas that companies in BRI countries are eager to learn about,” Anseel explains. To avoid spreading resources too thinly, HKUST is concentrating on Central Asia and the Middle East, and is actively recruiting former executives with experience in these regions as adjunct faculty. These three universities demonstrate the multifaceted role Hong Kong plays in the BRI. Whether importing talent for training (PolyU), exporting talent for management (EdUHK), or building strategic partnerships (HKUST), they are collectively forging a new, people-centric model of international collaboration that extends far beyond Hong Kong’s traditional strengths in trade and finance.

title: Kazakhstan’s privatisation push offers new IPO opportunities for Hong Kong
description: The city’s deep capital markets and SOE listing expertise offer Central Asia’s largest economy a proven pipeline to global investors.
content: In the almost 35 years since leaving the Soviet Union, Kazakhstan has been gradually privatising its numerous state-owned assets. The pace of change has been uneven, but the political will seems to be there – and this desire to attract foreign capital could provide Hong Kong with a huge opportunity. The economies of Kazakhstan and China have long been intertwined. The sprawling Central Asian nation to China’s northwest was once a vital node on the ancient Silk Road, and today it plays an equally pivotal role in the Belt and Road Initiative. It was no coincidence that President Xi Jinping chose Kazakhstan’s capital Astana from which to announce the formation of the terrestrial Silk Road Economic Belt in 2013. Though it is the world’s ninth-largest country, Kazakhstan has a population of only about 21 million and an economy dominated by industries such as oil, gas and minerals. It is the world’s largest producer of uranium and a leading producer of many other important minerals including chromium, copper, lead, zinc, iron, silver, gold, bauxite and manganese. Astana’s drive to attract foreign investment is gaining swift momentum. Kazakhstan’s public sector has long been anchored by two core pillars: sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna and development finance institution Baiterek. While Samruk-Kazyna’s holdings cover gas, electricity, aviation and mining, Baiterek focuses on lending to SMEs, housing and infrastructure. Together, their economic footprint accounted for roughly 40 per cent of national GDP in 2024, according to estimates by the International Monetary Fund. Seeking to transform this public sector landscape, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov announced in May 2025 that 475 state-backed enterprises will be privatised, merged or liquidated in phases leading up to 2030. Realising this ambitious goal will require overcoming persistent historical hurdles. Previous privatisation drives, including a major initiative launched in 2016 following a recession, frequently fell short of expectations. Landmark IPOs have faced repeated delays, and the “People’s IPO” boom of the early 2010s resulted in only 21 out of 106 planned assets being auctioned off by late 2014. “For decades, Hong Kong has successfully guided massive Chinese state monopolies through the complex process of modernising corporate governance Professor Darwin Choi, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology According to Dr Yifei Zhang, senior lecturer at the University of Hong Kong Business School, previous attempts suffered from poor execution. “Their assets were corporatised, put on international accounting standards and given proper boards before sale. They also used tough foreign exchanges to prove their companies could handle global disclosure,” he says. “On the other hand, they counted how many small assets were sold while keeping the big ones. They sold monopolies without first creating regulators or allowing [market] entry. Some direct sales were opaque.” Linda Cai, inbound and outbound head of China corporate finance for PwC, adds that previous rounds of state-owned enterprise (SOE) privatisation often lacked transparency and undervalued high-quality state assets. In the future, Zhang argues that Kazakhstan should establish regulatory frameworks before selling; commit to a fixed calendar run by a body with its own reputation at stake; disclose all beneficial owners; and price initial deals attractively for global investors. The country has two stock exchanges – the more established, Almaty-based Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), and the newer Astana International Exchange (AIX). The latter is part of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), partly owned by the Shanghai Stock Exchange and Nasdaq, and the focus of Belt and Road Initiative-related activity. AIX signed an MOU with Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) in June to work together on cross-border listings. Hong Kong should represent an ideal destination, offering a proven bridge between international capital and emerging-market SOEs. Professor Darwin Choi, associate head of the Department of Finance at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, emphasises that Hong Kong’s history with mainland China provides a ready blueprint. “For decades, Hong Kong has successfully guided massive Chinese state monopolies through the complex process of modernising corporate governance, aligning with international compliance standards and successfully floating on global markets,” Choi says. Such experience “is highly relevant” and “this blueprint is directly applicable to Samruk-Kazyna, as it seeks to modernise and privatise its portfolio companies”, he adds. Eddie Wong, capital markets leader for PwC Hong Kong, says Hong Kong offers several advantages for companies looking to list. “It has a well-established regulatory and market infrastructure, a deep and liquid capital market and extensive experience in supporting the listing of large state-owned enterprises and leading companies from a wide range of industries. “For Kazakh SOEs operating in sectors such as transport, energy, minerals and infrastructure, Hong Kong also offers access to investors who understand emerging markets, commodities and cross-border infrastructure themes. As Kazakhstan continues to strengthen its economic ties with Asia, Hong Kong presents a platform through which Kazakh issuers can broaden their investor base and diversify their sources of capital,” Wong says. Kazakhstan has already begun implementing reforms to enhance the effectiveness of competition policy, strengthen supervision over monopolistic markets and improve antitrust regulation, says Cai of PwC. “The prospect of Kazakh companies listing in Hong Kong will largely depend on the government’s reform strategy and the readiness of target companies. Hong Kong investors care about earnings visibility, corporate governance, valuation logic and liquidity – areas where prospective Kazakh SOEs will need to focus their preparation efforts.” HKEX leadership has actively engaged with Kazakh issuers to build connections and share expertise. “Supported by a highly liquid market, broad international investor base and one-of-a-kind connectivity with the Chinese mainland, HKEX enables issuers to tap both global and Chinese mainland capital,” says Johnson Chui, head of global issuer services at HKEX. “During recent visits to Kazakhstan, we engaged with a range of companies and market participants and were encouraged by their interest in learning more about Hong Kong’s capital markets, international investor base and fundraising ecosystem.” A spokesperson for the Astana International Financial Centre adds: “Over time, this could support greater access to investment opportunities, facilitate cross-border activity and contribute to the development and internationalisation of both markets.” If successful, Cai believes this privatisation programme could be transformative. “It can open high-quality assets to domestic and foreign investors, attracting capital to key sectors such as energy, logistics, infrastructure and telecommunications, while diversifying the economy and market participants. Strategic investors bring technology, governance expertise, risk control systems and financial support, helping enhance the international competitiveness of enterprises.”

title: Hong Kong’s Belt and Road cultural exchange builds ties beyond railways and ports
description: Beyond physical trade routes, the city’s museums, universities and orchestras are cultivating the personal relationships needed to sustain international cooperation.
content: When the Belt and Road Initiative is discussed, the imagery is often concrete: ports, railways, motorways and transmission lines. But across Hong Kong, a parallel form of connectivity is playing out in galleries, concert halls, classrooms and studios. At the Hong Kong Palace Museum, visitors have been encountering thousands of years of Chinese art and history alongside “Ancient Egypt Unveiled: Treasures from Egyptian Museums”, which brought 250 objects from Africa to West Kowloon. In September, the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra will present “Belt & Road: Zitong Wang Plays Chopin” – billed as “a river of sound flowing across Asia and Europe”. Meanwhile, in November 2025, 35 designers and professionals from 30 regions took part in “Threads of Unity: Belt and Road Fashion Show” at Hong Kong Polytechnic University (PolyU). These are not just exercises in soft-power projection or cultural window dressing for a programme focused mainly on hard infrastructure. They create personal, professional and institutional relationships – the less tangible links that can determine whether cross-border cooperation endures. “Hard infrastructure gets you a port or a railway. Cultural exchange gets you trusted people – the kind who pick up the phone five years later when a deal hits a snag,” says Professor Michael Jinghan Zeng, head of the Department of Public and International Affairs at City University of Hong Kong. Zeng argues that the benefit of such exchange is dependent on it being more than propaganda or soft-power projection. “The healthier frame is mutual intelligibility,” he notes. “If you treat cultural institutions as instruments, you kill the very thing that makes them attractive abroad – their credibility.” For Dr Louis Ng Chi-wa, director of the Hong Kong Palace Museum, the institution embodies mutual intelligibility. It has worked with partners including Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, the Museum of Islamic Art in Doha and museums in mainland China, and its forthcoming exhibition “Cultural Exchange and Buddhist Art along the Silk Roads” will combine works from the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris with material from Chinese museums. Underpinning these exhibitions is a conviction, as Ng puts it, that civilisations develop through encounters rather than isolation. “Chinese art and culture is not a closed system,” he points out. He says that openness to trade, religion, art and ideas has “energised the development of civilisation”. That perspective is at the heart of the Palace Museum’s approach. Rather than presenting Chinese and overseas collections separately, they are put in dialogue. Ng cites displays that ask visitors to compare objects made in Beijing and Paris, or works from Mughal India and Qing China, displayed side by side, prompting thoughts of how taste, techniques and ideas have travelled. Beyond the public galleries, the value is also institutional. Building an exhibition with overseas partners requires curators, conservators and educators to work through different professional practices and cultural assumptions. “The final process may be the exhibition, but we enjoy the [planning] process very much,” Ng says. “From every project, we learn something.” Fashion can make the same cultural exchange immediate and tactile. PolyU’s “Threads of Unity” featured 70 outfits by designers from Asia, Europe, the Americas, Africa and Oceania. It combined a runway presentation with an exhibition, a lecture on Silk Road trade and Buddhism, and a natural-dye workshop. “The vision was to leverage fashion, textiles, and education as a platform for international cultural exchange, mutual learning and cross-border innovation,” says Professor Joanne Yip, associate dean of PolyU’s School of Fashion and Textiles. Hong Kong, she adds, can act as “a dynamic bridge and test bed for international innovation”. The long-term aim should be enduring partnerships rather than isolated events, Yip explains, pointing to the potential for joint research on heritage textiles, student mobility, touring craft exhibitions and co-designed collections. “Infrastructure connects physical trade routes, but cultural initiatives build human connection and mutual respect.” Music offers another avenue. For Bernhard Fleischer, chief executive of the Hong Kong Philharmonic Orchestra, East-West exchange is key to his work. “What we are doing is a constant Belt and Road,” he says. Infrastructure connects physical trade routes, but cultural initiatives build human connection and mutual respect Joanne Yip, Hong Kong PolyU The orchestra’s September recital, led by Chinese conductor Yuan Ding and featuring Chinese pianist Zitong Wang, will include Chinese and European pieces. The players’ international make-up reinforces the point: according to Fleischer, the HK Phil has musicians from 16 countries. Fleischer argues that culture must travel alongside commerce. “If you do good trade, you have to bring interesting culture and cultural exchange with it. Otherwise, it’s cold and empty,” he says. Music, he adds, can emphasise common ground: “There are so many similarities between different cultures.” Yet as this cultural programming expands, the challenge becomes distinguishing substantive exchange from mere photo opportunities. Zeng suggests looking beyond visitor figures and social media reach. The better tests, he says, are whether scholars publish together years later, institutions co-commission new work, students choose Hong Kong because of earlier exchanges, and staff remain long enough to sustain relationships. His advice is to invest less in flagship festivals and more in artist and curator residencies, fellowships, student mobility and translation. “That’s boring, unsexy work,” he says, “but it’s the actual bedrock of sustained intellectual exchange and it’s chronically underfunded.” In other words, a physical road may connect places on a map, but it is a deeper human infrastructure that ensures people, ideas and institutions keep using it.

title: How China’s Belt and Road Initiative is shifting to green energy and private investment
description: Beijing has moved past its Covid-era mantra, pivoting from large sovereign loans to green tech investments, but execution bottlenecks and risks remain.
content: Five years after President Xi Jinping urged planners to prioritise “small and beautiful” projects under the Belt and Road Initiative, the value of the average Chinese overseas deal is the highest on record. Chinese investment across 150 Belt and Road countries reached US$49.8 billion in the first half of 2026, alongside US$76.5 billion in construction contracts – marking the strongest first half since the Initiative’s 2013 launch, according to research led by Christoph Nedopil, founding director of the Green Finance & Development Center at Fudan University. More than 30 deals topped US$1 billion, up from 29 a year earlier, including an US$8 billion rail contract in the United Arab Emirates. According to the Green Finance & Development Center report, the pandemic-era “small and beautiful” motto is now officially “bygone”. Nedopil clarifies that while smaller deals are still signed, the slogan no longer propels the Initiative. “The motto is not the main driving force of the [Belt and Road],” he says. Instead, the campaign’s chief remaining characteristic is its focus on sustainability. These days it is less the size of the cheque than who writes it, what it buys and how it is structured. Top-down sovereign lending by state policy banks has contracted significantly. China Development Bank and the Export-Import Bank of China extended just 28 overseas sovereign loan commitments worth US$10.5 billion in 2020 and 2021 combined, as mounting host-country debt burdens limited capacity for new borrowing. Instead of direct project finance, China has pivoted to co-financing through foreign development financial institutions, establishing joint equity funds and leveraging private capital. Data from Nedopil shows that private Chinese companies grew their share of Belt and Road engagement from 12.5 per cent in 2020 to 47.7 per cent in the first half of 2026. While state-owned enterprises continue to dominate heavy civil construction, private firms now lead direct investment. This capital realignment changes the nature of foreign engagement. “A private company invests very differently. It sets up joint ventures with local partners. It builds factories and supply chains, not railways,” says Miguel Latorre, founder and managing partner of Kynsen Advisory. “A private solar manufacturer going into Indonesia with a local partner has nothing in common with a policy bank funding a port.” The financial pivot aligns with Beijing’s broader sustainability goals. In July, the China International Development Cooperation Agency reiterated China’s ambition to help “developing nations in green infrastructure, clean energy … enhancing capabilities to address climate change”. China’s green energy and hydropower engagement roughly doubled year on year to about US$20.1 billion in the first half, with renewables accounting for 56 per cent of total energy engagement – a record in both absolute and relative terms. Investment in green energy and technology hit new highs too, with strong buildout of solar and battery manufacturing and “particularly strong engagement” in Africa, according to Nedopil. Fossil fuel deals also rose, if more slowly. However, translating high-level targets into utility-scale infrastructure faces operational hurdles. “The paperwork is the easy part,” Latorre says. Rebecca Ray, a senior academic researcher at the Boston University Global Development Policy Centre, describes the transition as directional rather than complete. “The composition of financing of the [Belt and Road] has clearly shifted from brown to green energy, but we haven’t seen green energy rise to take the place of fossil fuel energy yet,” she says. Ray highlights a major bottleneck: a shortage of pre-feasibility studies for grid-scale renewable projects, particularly across Africa. Lacking utility-scale grid connections, the energy transition in many receiving nations has become bottom-up, with individual households and private businesses purchasing Chinese solar panels and battery storage units directly for off-grid use. Joint equity funds may, over time, help bridge this gap by seeding utility-scale project pipelines, depending on local government priorities. This evolving deal structure introduces new risk dynamics. On one hand, shifting from sovereign debt to foreign direct investment reduces national debt service burdens for recipient countries while facilitating technology transfer. On the other hand, importing clean technology still requires foreign exchange reserves, and countries with lingering repayment schedules from earlier mega-projects now face negative net financial transfers. The composition of financing of the [Belt and Road] has clearly shifted from brown to green energy, but we haven’t seen green energy rise to take the place of fossil fuel energy yet Rebecca Ray, Boston University Global Development Policy Centre Nor is small automatically safe. “Smaller projects were supposed to be safer,” Latorre observes. “In my experience they carry their own risk. They don’t get the senior attention the big projects get, so problems stay hidden until they become expensive.” Looking ahead, analysts agree there are few signs of China reverting to major direct project finance. “It is in China’s interest to increase affordable investment in the Global South,” Ray says, “in order to bolster markets for China and to secure alliances in an increasingly geopolitical world.” Ben Simpfendorfer, a partner at Oliver Wyman, says the initiative had become more targeted around supply chains, connectivity and technology – a result of market rather than governmental forces. “A less capital-intensive Belt and Road should also be a more financially sustainable one,” he says. “Think fewer standard-gauge rail projects and more EV factories, solar projects and technology solutions.”

title: How the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway is reshaping Eurasian trade
description: The challenging Belt and Road Initiative project offers a vital Middle Corridor route – linking China to Europe while bypassing Russia.
content: When the groundbreaking ceremony for the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway took place in December 2024, it marked the end of a nearly 30-year-long diplomatic journey. First discussed in Paris in 1997, the project had languished for decades, a symbol of unrealised potential in a disconnected, landlocked region. Now finally under construction, it is one of the most audacious projects in China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). The CKU promises economic transformation in an underdeveloped part of the world but carries profound risks. It is a high-stakes gamble to drive a railway line over and through such notoriously mountainous terrain: will it reshape Central Asia or turn into a financial black hole? Forging a fresh path Since the unveiling of the BRI in 2013, there have been more than 100 projects in Central Asia, with railway lines often making the biggest headlines. These have included development of the new 5,420km (3,367 miles) Xining-Balkan route, linking China’s western Qinghai Province to the Balkan region of Turkmenistan, and the short but technically demanding Angren-Pop line in Uzbekistan and Vahdat-Yavan line in Tajikistan. The CKU is intended as a capstone for these projects, providing a so-called “Middle Corridor” to Europe, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR). This alternative to the “northern route” through Russia has become strategically vital for China and Central Asia, as sanctions on Moscow, due to the invasion of Ukraine, have forced a search for more reliable trade routes. Freight traffic on the TITR’s new railway line, running from the Chinese-Kazakh border through Kyrgyzstan to Uzbekistan, will be quicker compared to the current Khorgos line. Experts expect it will cut shipping times to Europe by 7-8 days and reduce costs by as much as 30 per cent. Kyrgyzstan, the primary beneficiary, expects the railway’s ultimate freight capacity to be up to 15 million tons, thereby more than doubling the country’s 2025 capacity. Such numbers have fuelled tremendous optimism. Kyrgyz deputy prime minister, Edil Baisalov, claimed the route could generate over US$300 million annually, “even under the most pessimistic scenarios”. This economic incentive is driving a new era of regional cooperation. “I’ve watched this railway move Kyrgyz-Uzbek relations from friction to cooperation,” said Akramjon Nematov, first deputy director of Uzbekistan’s Institute for Strategic and Regional Studies. “And I measure progress not in words, but in cubic metres of earth moved.” Beyond Central Asia, the CKU is viewed as a critical component of a larger Eurasian network. “Central Asian and Caucasian states all want to capitalise on Russia’s isolation to secure their role in [the Middle Corridor],” notes Nicholas Castillo, a recent reporter for CivilNet in Armenia and an MA student at Harvard’s Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies. Challenges ahead Despite the fanfare, optimism is tempered by numerous complications that risk delays and added costs. The primary obstacles, as they have been since the 1990s, are “financing and geography”, according to Yunis Sharifli, a PhD researcher at Istanbul University. “Kyrgyzstan’s mountainous terrain makes railway construction technically difficult and expensive. The route requires extensive construction of tunnels, bridges and other infrastructure through challenging terrain.” Most of the route through Kyrgyzstan, passing through Torugart, Makmal and Manas, is mountainous and completing the route necessitates constructing 50 new bridges and 29 tunnels, including Naryn No 1, Kosh-Dobo and Fergana, each of which is at least 12km long. This geographical challenge is compounded by mechanical incompatibility. China uses a standard rail gauge of 1,435mm, while Central Asian states use the wider Russian gauge of 1,520mm. This discrepancy necessitates the construction of a costly transshipment station in Makmal to shift containers between different bogies (the undercarriage framework that includes the wheels and suspension), adding another layer of logistical friction and expense. These complications have fuelled hesitancy about the CKU, and concerns over loan repayment challenges, corruption, transparency and ethical local hiring practices are long-standing. While BRI-funded projects like the Tazara line, which connects Zambia to the Indian Ocean, and the Boten-Vientiane railway in Laos offer compelling success stories for landlocked countries, the scale of the CKU’s challenges is unique. The current goal to complete just 5 per cent of the railroad by the end of 2026 is an indicator of the immense size of the task ahead. Eyes on the prize To understand China’s determination to proceed, one must look past the mountainous terrain of Kyrgyzstan to the economic anchor at the line’s end – Uzbekistan. The number of Chinese companies operating in the country has almost tripled since 2022, making the nation an increasingly vital hub for Chinese industry. “Andijon [in Uzbekistan] is one of the core recipients of Chinese companies,” Frank Maracchione, an ESRC postdoctoral fellow at the Department of Politics and International Studies of SOAS University of London, told the SCMP. “It’s one of the core regions that has had a really strong cultural and historical connection with the region of Xinjiang and the Chinese empire before. It’s a core of Chinese industry in Uzbekistan. The development is sensible given the context of the growing relationship between China and Uzbekistan.” This underscores a crucial point that often gets lost in the discussion of the Middle Corridor. Although the project’s role is often discussed as a conduit to Europe, an equally essential purpose is bolstering China’s economic relationship with a rapidly growing Central Asian market. “Overall, it’s important to not only imagine a project like this as a connection from China to Europe, but also as a connection to Central Asia,” says Maracchione. “This project contributes to both the BRI and the Middle Corridor, and it should start to shape how we view the connection from China to Central Asia as an important region and trade partner rather than just a corridor.” For Kyrgyzstan, a country where in the first 30 years after independence from the USSR no new rail tracks were laid, the completion of this project will be a litmus test. The next big challenge will be to link the two halves of its fragmented rail system together. Plans are already being discussed to extend the existing rail line that ends in Balykchy westwards to maximise the CKU’s benefits. Construction on the CKU is finally under way, three decades after it was first envisaged. The question is whether its momentum is unstoppable this time. If it succeeds, it is likely to be transformative, unlocking the economic potential of Central Asia, diversifying China’s trade routes and solidifying its influence in the heart of Eurasia. If it becomes mired in delays and cost overruns, its legacy may yet be a cautionary tale about the limits of infrastructure diplomacy.

title: In Focus | How Japan is digging in to deter – and withstand – a conflict over Taiwan
description: A planned Hiroshima defence hub highlights how Tokyo is accelerating preparations to sustain its military should a Taiwan crisis reach Japan.
content: The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the second of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Tokyo is building military resilience within its territory. Japan’s recent purchase of a former Nippon Steel site to build a sprawling new defence hub points to a deeper shift in Tokyo’s preparations for a potential Taiwan conflict: it is increasingly planning not only for how to deter a war, but also for how to sustain the fight if deterrence fails. The planned complex in Kure, Hiroshima prefecture – already home to one of Japan’s major naval bases – is intended to combine military facilities, logistics and defence production, concentrating several of the functions Tokyo would need to sustain its forces during a prolonged conflict. Four years into a sweeping defence build-up, experts say that emphasis on endurance reflects a grim conclusion taking hold in Japanese defence planning: preparing for a Taiwan crisis increasingly means preparing to defend Japan itself. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made that concern unusually explicit last November, saying a Taiwan contingency involving warships and the use of force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan – potentially allowing its Self-Defence Forces (SDF) to act even if Japan itself had not come under direct attack. The geopolitical stakes far exceed the 110km (68 miles) separating Taiwan from Japan’s westernmost territory. Taiwan lies along vital Japanese sea lines of communication and at the centre of the first island chain, close to Japan’s southwestern islands and key US military installations. Should Beijing gain control, it could significantly strengthen the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) operational position around Japan and its access to the western Pacific. But the more immediate concern is what could happen during a war over the island. Beijing sees Taiwan as a breakaway province to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not see Taiwan as a sovereign state but are opposed to any forcible change to the cross-strait status quo. US forces operating from bases in Japan could play a central role in a Taiwan conflict, potentially placing those facilities – and Japan itself – in Beijing’s crosshairs. For a country whose post-war security policy has been built around constitutional pacifism and an exclusively defence-oriented posture, preparing to absorb and fight through such attacks marks a profound shift in military thinking. That pivot is likely to shape revisions to Japan’s National Security Strategy, National Defence Strategy and Defence Buildup Programme, which the government has brought forward to this year, just four years after the present documents were adopted. The timing shows how quickly Japan’s defence transformation is moving. Tokyo is updating its three strategic documents a year ahead of schedule in response to what Takaichi described as “new ways of warfare” and a growing need to prepare for protracted conflict – developments she said were “accelerating across multiple domains”. That shift is also reflected in successive increases in military spending. The defence ministry is seeking 8.9 trillion yen (US$55.7 billion) for fiscal 2027, which would mark another record defence budget. The request identifies “sustained response capabilities” as one of three main pillars, alongside responding to “new ways of warfare” and strengthening the foundations of defence capability, including the defence production and technology base. Yet Tokyo draws an important line around what those preparations are intended to achieve. Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo and a former Japanese defence ministry official, said the strategic review was intended to strengthen Japan’s ability to defend its own territory, “not to promote an active Japanese role in a contingency over Taiwan”. But Japan’s stated mission is different from the question of what kind of war its Self-Defence Forces are preparing to fight. Analysts say the capabilities being assembled suggest Japanese planners expect bases and communications to come under attack while forces must remain operational as ammunition, fuel and equipment are depleted. Ogi said that because of Taiwan’s proximity and the strategic importance of Japan’s southwestern islands, a cross-strait conflict could spill over into an armed attack on Japan, depending on Beijing’s decisions. Japan’s concern over Taiwan is not new. Masashi Murano, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said Tokyo had been shifting its military centre of gravity southwest since issuing its 2010 National Defence Programme Guidelines. What had changed were its assumptions about how a conflict with Beijing would unfold. Murano said Japanese bases, ports and radar sites would probably come under large-scale missile attack in the opening phase of a conflict, while the PLA’s ability to strike US and Japanese forces and bases across the region could hamper US efforts to reinforce Japan. The more resilient those sites became, however, the harder it would be for Chinese planners to assume an opening barrage could quickly suppress Japan’s ability to fight or support US operations. By raising the prospect of a longer and costlier conflict, that resilience itself becomes a form of deterrence. This calculation is driving Tokyo towards weapons that can survive, disperse and impose costs despite the PLA’s numerical advantage. Uncrewed systems could also help offset Japan’s manpower constraints. Murano said SDF personnel numbers were likely to decline, making affordable systems essential for fielding forces in greater numbers. The remote southwestern Nansei Islands are central to that strategy. For Murano, they are both territory to defend and positions from which dispersed surveillance systems, anti-ship missiles and one-way attack drones could threaten People’s Liberation Army forces moving through chokepoints between the East China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean. “Southwest island defence, long-range fires and Japan-US integration should be understood not as separate elements but as a single structure,” Murano said. Michael Bosack, founder and director of the Parley Policy Institute in Melbourne, said Taiwan’s proximity to Japan would become even more significant as relatively cheap uncrewed systems proliferated. In a conflict, such systems could threaten ports, supply lines and commercial shipping – a particular vulnerability for trade-dependent Japan. Japan’s emerging Shield – Synchronised, Hybrid, Integrated and Enhanced Littoral Defence – concept reflects similar thinking, combining longer- and shorter-range missiles with large numbers of unmanned systems to target enemy forces at different distances as they approach Japan’s remote islands. Murano cautioned against relying too heavily on lessons from Ukraine, noting Beijing’s large missile arsenal and expanding bomber force. For Japan, he said, “the far more serious problem is the lack of an effective capability to counter PLA bombers” – particularly given vulnerable Japanese airfields and the PLA’s numerical advantage in combat aircraft. But denying access to a rival force is only part of the challenge. Japan is also preparing to keep fighting after taking losses. The defence ministry has acknowledged shortfalls in the availability of ammunition, fuel and equipment for sustained operations, which is why Tokyo is expanding stockpiles and hardening facilities, including by moving key command centres underground. The Ground Self-Defence Force is also reorganising its logistics system to centralise the management of ammunition, fuel and other supplies, enabling their more flexible distribution in a contingency. Bosack said that combining concealment, dispersal and hardening – hiding assets, spreading them across sites and reinforcing facilities against attack – could frustrate Beijing’s operational planning, but warned that “Japan’s transparency in its security practice introduces additional risk”. PLA planners could glean information about new ammunition, fuel and weapons storage simply by following defence ministry engagement with local communities, he said, helping them update potential target lists. For Murano, Japan’s stockpiling, acquisition of affordable uncrewed systems and pursuit of force survivability are “all premised on a protracted war of attrition lasting months”. But he cautioned that preparing for a prolonged war would require more than stockpiling – Japan would also need a “defence innovation cycle” that rapidly fed battlefield lessons back into weapons and tactics, rather than treating sustainability simply as a question of how much ammunition had been stockpiled beforehand. Tokyo is already experimenting with faster equipment procurement. Less than three months after seeking interceptor drones in June, the defence ministry’s procurement agency selected Terra Drone’s Terra B1 and signed a mass production contract for delivery to the Maritime Self-Defence Force. Joint operations Surviving PLA strikes would mean little if the SDF could no longer coordinate its operations, however. This realisation is driving changes in how Japanese and US forces plan to command operations during a potential crisis. The Japan SDF Joint Operations Command (JJOC), established in March 2025, created a permanent headquarters for joint operations, while Washington is turning US Forces Japan (USFJ) into a more operational “warfighting” headquarters. USFJ commander Lieutenant General Stephen Jost said in July that about 215 personnel had been added since the transformation began, including around 100 recent arrivals working to develop bilateral command procedures with the JJOC. The expanded headquarters now had enough personnel to sustain round-the-clock operations across key functions, Jost said. Tokyo is also investing in space capabilities, cyberdefence and resilient communications networks to maintain its ability to detect targets and transmit information should infrastructure and command nodes come under attack. Murano said Japan should develop greater independence in the “kill chains” – systems used to find, track and strike targets – supporting its long-range weapons, rather than relying entirely on US systems. With the SDF becoming more dependent on unmanned platforms, he said, resilient space-based communications would become particularly important. That emphasis on resilience extends beyond the military. Tokyo is developing shelters in parts of the southwestern islands and plans its first field exercise next year to practise evacuating residents from remote Okinawan islands, including Yonaguni, in a military contingency. The measures underline how planning for a Taiwan conflict encompasses not only keeping the SDF in the fight but protecting civilians if hostilities reach Japanese territory. And Japan’s ability to remain operational would have consequences beyond the defence of its own territory. Murano cautioned that the phrase “a Taiwan contingency is a Japan contingency” did not mean the SDF would necessarily be assigned a mission to defend Taiwan. But Japan would be a critical platform for US forces that did. If Japanese military infrastructure were disabled or Tokyo were coerced into dropping out early, Murano warned, the US would struggle to effectively support and defend Taiwan. The PLA’s ability to strike Japanese and US targets across the region could therefore serve not only to physically disrupt their operations but also to exert “psychological coercion” aimed at making Tokyo drop out early – “before the war begins, if possible”, Murano said. That makes the line between preparing to defend Japan and preparing for a Taiwan conflict increasingly difficult to draw. For Bosack, planning around a scenario in which Japan remains untouched makes little sense. “There may only be one scenario where Japan makes it through unscathed, and a thousand where it doesn’t,” he said. Preparing for those scenarios requires more than making the SDF itself resilient. A prolonged conflict could rapidly consume missiles, drones and ammunition, while damaged equipment would need repair or replacement. That brings Tokyo’s acquisition of the Kure site back into the equation. The defence ministry signed the contract with Nippon Steel in late August to acquire the former Setouchi Works site, where the planned hub is intended to combine equipment maintenance and manufacturing, logistics and operational facilities. The ministry has said integrating those functions will help increase the sustainability of SDF operations. The development comes as the Japanese government is also considering a greater state role in defence production, including government-owned facilities operated by private companies. The approach reflects a problem that stockpiling alone cannot solve: a prolonged conflict would require Japan to replenish weapons and ammunition, and repair damaged equipment. Tokyo increasingly describes its defence production and technology base as “defence capability itself”. Beijing, however, sees the transformation very differently. Responding to Japan’s 2026 defence white paper last month, the defence ministry in Beijing accused Tokyo of hyping the “China threat” to justify easing post-war restraints on its military, pointing to the accelerated revision of the three strategic documents, rising defence spending and longer-range strike capabilities. Chinese officials have repeatedly described Japan’s trajectory as “remilitarisation” and warned of a revival of militarism, while accusing Tokyo of interfering in Beijing’s internal affairs over Taiwan. Tokyo rejects that characterisation, maintaining that the capabilities it is acquiring are intended to deter attacks and defend Japanese territory. For Ogi, the central task of the review is organisational rather than conceptual: integrating the missiles, drones and other capabilities envisaged in Japan’s 2022 defence strategy documents into how the SDF is structured and fights. Tokyo may insist its military is not being built to defend Taiwan. But its preparations suggest that a war over the island could force Japan to withstand missile attacks, disrupted communications and months of high-intensity attrition simply to defend itself. Stronger Japanese capabilities would in turn make Beijing “more hesitant to expand a conflict into Japanese territory”, Ogi said, and indirectly, make a successful PLA takeover of Taiwan more difficult. For Bosack, that is ultimately the logic behind Japan’s preparations. “At best, it deters China,” he said. “At worst, it prepares Japan for a conflict that will inevitably impact the country in significant ways.”

title: Albania protests against Trump-linked development turn violent after 100th day
description: Dubbed the ‘flamingo revolution’, the demonstrations seek to halt the massive project over the environmental damage it could cause.
content: Police in Albania blocked protesters from reaching parliament on Tuesday as the latest rally against a luxury development linked to US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, turned violent The march was staged as parliament resumed from a summer recess and after the demonstrations marked their 100th day on Monday. They challenged a police cordon in the centre of the capital, Tirana, pelting officers in riot gear with eggs and tomatoes. Cars transporting lawmakers to the parliament building were confronted by the crowds and were hit with plastic water bottles before police intervened to let them through. Dubbed the “flamingo revolution” for protesters’ signs depicting the pink bird that could be harmed by the coastal development, the anti-government protests have rocked Albania. Although Albanian officials have avoided giving details of Kushner’s role in the project, Trump’s daughter, Ivanka, has spoken about her family’s involvement in the venture, describing it as an “incredible project”. The protests are aimed at stopping the massive project that critics say would cause environmental damage and limit public access to the coast. The nightly Tirana protests initially only focused on the development but have since grown into a major challenge to the country’s long-ruling Socialist government. Prime Minister Edi Rama – a target of the demonstrations – strongly supports the investment project, arguing that it would help modernise a country that spent decades in Communist isolation. “We are here because we want change. Young people are struggling. Life is getting harder, and the government is not listening. We believe Albania can do better,” protester Elidon Mehmetaj said. “We are not asking for much. We are asking for a better future – for Albanian citizens, for our country, for our future,” he said. Demonstrators chanted “Arrest Rama!” during the clashes, as police escorted lawmakers to and from the parliament building. Several protesters were detained, but it was not immediately clear whether any arrests had been made.

title: Iran, US engage in wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping
description: The attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz sent oil prices surging, as Tehran says it also fired ballistic missiles at a US base in Jordan.
content: Iran said on Wednesday it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers, in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat attacks on shipping by both sides since the start of the six-month-old war. The attacks sent the price of oil surging, with benchmark Brent crude futures breaching US$100 a barrel for the first time since July. At least one seafarer aboard a tanker was reported killed and another listed as missing. Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a ‌base used by US forces in Jordan. Attacks by both sides since the end of August have shattered a month of relative calm, with the US and Iran hitting military, shipping and energy assets. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said they would sharply escalate their response to any further attacks, hitting 20 targets if the enemy struck two or three. Iran would soon release maps of a new, enlarged off-limits zone at sea that would extend as far as Chabahar on the far reaches of Iran’s coast near Pakistan, the IRGC said. Recent days have also seen an escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, a second theatre of war that threatens global energy supplies from the Middle East. The Americans said they destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, releasing video of ships ablaze before they sank. The US military’s Central Command called its attacks a response to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeting a US Navy ⁠warship twice with ballistic missiles over the previous two days. No Americans were harmed, the US said. Washington has announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers in retaliation for fire that threatens its warships, and says it has hit 10 so far over ‌the past week. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters during a visit to Colombia. Iran said it fired on two US ships and eight tankers in response. One seafarer was killed aboard the oil products tanker Hercules Star while at anchorage ‌off Dubai and another crew member was missing, said the vessel’s charterer, Peninsula. Maritime security sources said it could have been hit by a drone. The British maritime security agency UKMTO described a vessel in the ⁠vicinity that was listing, possibly taking on water after being struck ⁠by a projectile. Reuters could not immediately determine whether this referred to the same ship. Two Iraqi port officials said a tanker carrying 2 million barrels of fuel oil, the New Andros, had caught fire after being struck by a drone in Iraqi waters. There were no reports of casualties among the 22 crew. ‌The Iraqi government confirmed the incident and said the tanker had been used for storage. The UKMTO said it had received reports of several merchant ships struck by disabling fire in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman, on either side of the strait. Iran also threatened oil tankers in Kuwaiti and Bahraini ports, according to a statement ‌carried ‌by state media. A maritime security source reported a liquefied natural gas tanker was damaged in the Emirati port of Khor Fakkan. The IRGC also said on Wednesday it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces near Al Azraq, ‌in eastern Jordan. Jordan said its air defences had intercepted 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, with two falling harmlessly in unpopulated areas. A US official said Iran’s strikes in Jordan were ineffective and all American troops were accounted for. In recent weeks ⁠Washington had boasted of increasing success guiding tankers through the strait, which carried a fifth of oil supplies before the war. But any such gradual reopening appears to have been set back by a resumption of fighting this month. Claudio Galimberti, chief economist ⁠at consultancy Rystad Energy, said flows through Hormuz had fallen back as low as 2 million barrels per day, having reached as high as 8 million to 9 million bpd in the week before fighting resumed on August 30. Even more severe than the rise in crude prices has been a surge in the cost of the fuels refined from it. The politically sensitive average retail price of US diesel hit a fresh all-time high on Wednesday ‌above US$5.94 a gallon. Petrol is also more expensive than ever at ‌this time of the year. Escalating combat between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement that controls most populated parts of Yemen has created additional uncertainty for energy markets. On Tuesday, the Houthis launched an attack on four cities in Saudi Arabia, causing huge fires visible from space at oil installations. Saudi authorities said 73 people were wounded. The Saudi Press Agency released footage showing homes damaged and injured patients in hospital. Saudi authorities announced alerts on Wednesday in two of the cities hit the previous day, but later said the threat had passed. A Saudi-backed government based in the south of Yemen has launched a multipronged assault on areas controlled by the Houthis, who have threatened Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

title: Nicaragua hands gold concession to sister firm of US-sanctioned Chinese miner
description: Three months after Washington blacklisted Xinxin Linze Mineria, the Nicaraguan government granted its executives a gold concession.
content: Nicaragua has granted a Chinese-owned company linked to one sanctioned by Washington the right to prospect and dig for gold across 262 sq km (101 sq miles) of rainforest, about a quarter the size of Hong Kong. The 25-year concession over the block, named Jade, went to Linze Excelente Mineria, a company that appeared in Nicaragua’s mining registry only last year. The block is in a corner of the country where prospectors first struck gold in 1880. Corporate filings list Lijun Dong as legal representative of both Linze Excelente and Nicaragua Xinxin Linze Mineria Group, a firm the United States blacklisted in April. Shiliang Yang, who signed the Jade title, also appears as a lawyer for the sanctioned company. The US Treasury sanctioned Xinxin Linze in April, saying it had received tens of thousands of acres from the Nicaraguan government and shipped more than US$25 million in gold to the United States in the first half of 2025. Gold is one of the few sources of hard currency left to Daniel Ortega, who has governed Nicaragua for most of the past four decades and now rules alongside his wife Rosario Murillo. Washington has sanctioned the family and its business network since a 2018 crackdown that killed hundreds of protesters, and Managua has turned to Beijing in response, breaking with Taiwan in 2021 and implementing a free-trade agreement in 2024. American buyers take most of the metal, which is why the Treasury has gone after the companies digging it rather than the trade itself. Because Linze Excelente carries no designation of its own, American banks may still process its payments and refineries may still buy its metal. Washington officials also claimed that the mining sector had been reorganised since 2020 into a web of front companies built to generate hard currency and launder assets already under sanction, with proceeds from one Managua exporter probably paying for pro-government paramilitary groups. Linze Excelente was assembled by that route, receiving 10,592 hectares from its sanctioned affiliate in July 2025, its only holdings until this week. Neither the Chinese embassy in Managua nor the Nicaraguan lawyer general’s office responded to requests for comment. Concession granted after the sanctions Linze Excelente applied for the block on June 26 and had its title three days later, accepting the terms on July 13. The transaction sat unpublished until it surfaced in the official gazette on Monday, and several news agencies reported this week that the concession had been granted that day. The paperwork shows the decision was taken in late June, 10 weeks after the affiliate was blacklisted. A concession hands over the exclusive right to explore and extract minerals, which the holder may later sell, split or lease with the ministry’s approval. Villagers already panning gold by hand keep that right, though the company may not dig within 100 metres (328 feet) of a house, a well or a church without written permission from the mines directorate. Chinese firms now hold Nicaraguan concessions covering 1.28 million hectares, close to a 10th of the country, according to an atlas published in July by the environmental group Fundacion del Rio. The group’s president, Amaru Ruiz, stripped of his citizenship and living in exile, calculated that 84 blocks had been granted to 22 Chinese companies since 2021, of which 62 overlap indigenous and Afro-descendant territories. Those blocks also hold copper, cobalt, nickel and uranium, the survey found. Gold pays for everything in the meantime, analysts say, earning Nicaragua US$1.97 billion last year and 22.7 per cent of all export revenue, even despite tough sanctions imposed by the US and other Western countries. Linze Excelente will pay the Nicaraguan state 25 US cents per hectare in its first year on the Jade block. That comes to about US$6,550 for ground larger than Lantau Island, or less than the price of 50 grams of gold.

title: Opinion | Trump’s Venezuela oil deal: why China can wait and watch
description: Beijing’s response reflects a calculation that the deal’s fragility will soon show. Energy dominance is not seized by executive order – it is earned through capital, technology and time.
content: When US President Donald Trump announced on August 28 that the United States had secured majority control over some 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil through a private company, the North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), he called it “the biggest oil deal in history”. The White House fact sheet provided the details: NABEP’s 100-year concessions on 17 oilfields with 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, a 35 per cent Pentagon stake, a 20 per cent State Department offtake at cost with right of first refusal, and a Washington veto over the appointment of board members, the majority of whom must be US citizens. Reuters quoted an unnamed US official as saying, “We are opening up the United States as the market for this oil, which was previously being sent to China.” Rather than sanctions, this is the forced displacement of a strategic competitor’s energy operators in a third country through a US government-controlled proxy. Call it the Venezuela template. This first full implementation of a new doctrine of indirect expropriation should be understood alongside the administration’s “economic D-Day” against Iran. Trump’s claim of 65 billion barrels is real, but it is not what it sounds like. Venezuela holds an estimated 303 billion barrels in the ground – about 17 per cent of the world’s supply – yet the country currently produces just over 1 million barrels per day, or about 1 per cent of global output. Rystad Energy estimates that restoring production to 3 million barrels per day would require US$183 billion in capital across 15 years, an amount far beyond NABEP’s pledge of up to US$100 billion. Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodriguez projects US$209 billion in royalties and taxes over 25 years; the White House puts the figure at around US$200 billion. Having visited Venezuela’s oilfields and worked in Alberta – the geological twin of the Orinoco Belt – I can say: developing extra-heavy oil is a multi-decade undertaking. Three constraints make the rosy projections implausible. First, break-even costs for key Orinoco Belt heavy oil projects exceed US$80 per barrel Brent – above the US$50-60 threshold operators typically require to approve projects. Second, Venezuela’s heavy, high-sulphur crude trades at a steep discount to benchmark prices and requires expensive diluting agents and upgraders, so even with West Texas Intermediate prices near US$91, the profit per barrel to the producer is far thinner than the headline price suggests. Third, the US$183 billion that Rystad says is needed dwarfs the US pledge. Alberta’s oil sands have been in development since the 1960s and still produce approximately 3.1 million barrels per day. The notion that 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan “proven reserves” will soon flow to US refineries is a political narrative, not an engineering reality. The NABEP structure is the real innovation. When Washington could not sanction Iran without sanctioning China – the buyer of an estimated 90 per cent of Iran’s oil – yet targeted only “teapot” refineries and terminal operators, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s “economic D-Day” became a charade. So the Trump administration pivoted to a deniable, privately held vehicle – one that provides the US government with equity, board control and procurement guarantees while maintaining the appearance of a private commercial transaction. This is expropriation of state capital, not a commercial transaction. Six of the 14 newly granted NABEP contracts were previously operated by foreign companies: five by Chinese companies – two by China Concord Resources, one by Sinopec, one by China National Petroleum Corporation, and one by an unnamed Chinese firm – and one by a Russian firm. Their contractual rights are simply being overridden. China’s response was measured. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on September 1: “China-Venezuela cooperation is protected by international law and the laws of both countries. China’s legitimate rights and interests in Venezuela must be guaranteed.” He did not name NABEP for criticism or threaten retaliation. This is strategic calibration, not weakness. Beijing understands three things. First, the Maduro government is gone and Rodriguez’s interim regime is fully dependent on Washington. Second, Venezuela’s constitution declares oil and gas resources are state-owned and not for sale. Harvard economist Ricardo Hausmann called the deal “unconstitutional”. Third, the NABEP structure is theatre. The Pentagon’s 35 per cent stake requires no taxpayer money, delivering a domestic political narrative at zero cost ahead of the November midterm elections. Beijing’s response reflects a calculation that the deal’s fragility will show within months. Venezuela’s production will not surge. The US$100 billion in pledged investment will not materialise while the interim regime’s legitimacy is in question. And China’s existing contracts, protected by international law, remain a legal sword. China remains Venezuela’s most important Asian oil customer and creditor. Though physical crude flows to China were disrupted this year, Beijing’s more than US$60 billion in oil-for-loan financing since 2007 creates debt obligations that survive the change in field operators – and China’s economic leverage ensures its interests cannot be erased by a 100-year concession granted to a US proxy. The Venezuela template carries an unmistakable message to every non-US investor in the Global South: once installed, a US-backed proxy could void your contractual rights overnight. However, while Washington can redraw subsurface rights, it cannot change the physics of extra-heavy oil production nor the geography of global energy demand. Energy dominance is not seized by executive order – it is earned through capital, technology and time. On all three counts, the NABEP mirage falls short. Trump’s deal is not the “largest in history” but rather the largest admission that when sanctions fail, Washington grasps what it cannot hold.

title: China ‘can never get ahead’ of US in AI, Bessent says in advance of Xi’s visit
description: Trump’s treasury secretary accuses Chinese artificial intelligence firms of ‘stealing and copying’, weeks before leadership summit in Washington.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent claimed that China “can never get ahead” of America in artificial intelligence, in part due to its “central planning”, as three government agencies accused Beijing of maliciously copying technology from its leading firms. “The technical word for stealing and copying American AI models is distillation. So, the Chinese distil our models and they can never get ahead of us,” he said on Tuesday during a discussion at the Southern Methodist University’s Cox School of Business in Dallas. “It’s kind of like if you’re looking over someone’s shoulder, copying their homework, you can never get a higher grade than they do.” Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which a smaller model learns from the output of larger ones. The remarks came weeks before Bessent is expected to spearhead US bilateral talks on AI governance with his Chinese counterparts ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington later this month. The rhetoric from Bessent is in sharp contrast with recent remarks from President Donald Trump, who last week said he was excited about the Chinese leader’s visit. “By the way, we have the president of China coming on the 24th. That’ll be very exciting. Great, love to have him. A lot of good things to discuss, very, very productive things to discuss with President Xi,” Trump said. “AI is going up, and we’re leading China in AI very substantially,” he added. Also on Tuesday, three US agencies accused leading Chinese AI companies of engaging in “aggressive, malicious and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale”. They alleged that the practice was carried out “likely with Chinese government awareness”. In a jointly released advisory report, the National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI named six leading Chinese AI companies: DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI. The report claimed that the firms extracted “billions of tokens across millions of exchanges/requests from US frontier AI models, including variants of Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok, since at least late 2024”. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The Chinese embassy in Washington rejected US allegations and termed the Trump administration’s distillation concept a “deliberate attack on China’s development and progress in the AI industry”. “We urge the US to respect facts, discard bias, stop its containment on China’s sci-tech development and choose the course of action conducive to sci-tech exchanges and cooperation between China and the US,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang told the SCMP. “Such actions will only stifle global AI advances and serve no one’s interests.” As Chinese companies have narrowed the capability gap in frontier AI models, US firms and Trump administration officials have increasingly accused Beijing of stealing and copying American technology to speed up the development of its own systems. Bessent also contrasted China’s approach with the US strategy. Beijing relied on “central planning on AI”, which would “never work” because the government would not “turn over enough control”, he argued. According to Bessent, Chinese leaders fear that AI could eventually threaten the Communist Party if technology developed by its leading companies became powerful enough to “bring their regime down”. “Whereas in the US, we want to make sure things are safe, and we want to make sure that AI serves the American people,” he added. Both sides are preparing for dedicated talks on AI later this month, even as Washington and Beijing remain divided over the scope of the discussions, with China seeking a broader conversation and the US pushing to focus on AI safety, sources told the SCMP. The Treasury Department said in August that the administration was looking forward to “using our position as the global leader in AI to share our expertise with the world’s number two”. The two countries agreed to begin formal talks on AI governance following the Trump-Xi May summit in Beijing. The bilateral discussions are planned amid competing US and Chinese approaches to shaping the global AI landscape. The US is advancing its Pax Silica supply chain initiative, while China is promoting the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation. US under secretary of state for economic affairs Jacob Helberg, architect of the 24-member Pax Silica, said in July that he hoped dialogue with Beijing on AI governance would help create areas for “constructive engagement” despite intensifying rivalry between the two countries. “Our goal is to pursue these engagements in good faith and work to restate our views and hear Chinese views,” Helberg told the SCMP in an exclusive interview.

title: White House pulls ‘Build the Wall’ game after warning from Tetris
description: Arcade game removed amid copyright review and sharp criticism over racist themes and anti-immigrant tropes.
content: The White House on Tuesday pulled a Tetris-style game called Build the Wall from its new online arcade, four days after a warning by the classic game maker that it takes copyright infringement seriously. The block-stacking game, subtitled Zombie Border Siege, told players to “protect the border from the coming horde”. It was no longer available on the website on Tuesday. The White House did not immediately respond to a request asking why it was removed. The Tetris Company said on Friday that it played no part in the game’s creation. “The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of Build the Wall and did not authorise or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game,” it said, adding that it was “currently reviewing the matter” when asked whether it was weighing legal action. “At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” the company wrote on social media. “P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously,” the post continued. The arcade, launched on Thursday on the White House website, drew condemnation for racist themes and questions about potential copyright violations. The games and the promotional clips the White House posted on social media borrowed imagery resembling that of Sega, Microsoft-owned Xbox and the Flappy Bird Foundation. In one clip, the letters of the Sega logo morph into Maga, the acronym for US President Donald Trump’s Make America Great Again slogan. Other games remained playable, including Flappy Bill, in which a bald eagle dodges columns against a backdrop resembling Washington, and Rio Run, a Snake-style game themed on deportations. “This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the president’s many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said Thursday in a statement. Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has moved aggressively to conduct deportations.

title: US Secretary of State Rubio arrives in Colombia to clarify China ties, sign minerals deal
description: Washington’s top diplomat lands in Barranquilla on first leg of three-country tour, with critical minerals, civil nuclear deals to be signed.
content: United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Colombia on Tuesday to meet President Abelardo de la Espriella, sign agreements on critical minerals and civil nuclear cooperation and take up the country’s ties to China, in the first visit by a cabinet-level US official since the Colombian leader took office a month ago. Colombia’s participation in the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and Chinese investment in critical infrastructure were on the agenda for the meeting, a Colombian official who was not authorised to speak publicly told the South China Morning Post. “We have a lot of common interest with them, both taking on regional transnational criminal terrorism and also economic engagements,” Rubio told reporters before the trip. “It’s part of a trend that you’re seeing in the Western Hemisphere of alignment with US and US interests.” The New York Times first reported that trade relations with China would be on the agenda, citing two people familiar with the trip. The Chinese embassy in Bogota and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Colombia holds coal, nickel and copper deposits and has been mapping reserves of the metals used in batteries and electronics, a supply chain China dominates worldwide. Neither government said in advance which minerals the agreement covers. The two leaders were scheduled to meet alongside Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar at an army base in Barranquilla. In this Caribbean port city, De la Espriella has set up a second presidential office away from the capital, Bogota. Bula Escobar said in a video released on Tuesday that the visit opened “the beginning of the reconstruction of a strategic alliance” with the United States, which he called Colombia’s main partner in the region. Colombia is the first stop on a three-nation trip that will also take him to Ecuador and Peru. From Barranquilla, the tour runs on to Quito, where Chinese money built a major hydroelectric dam, and then to Lima, where the megaport at Chancay has given Peru a Pacific gateway to Asia. Rubio was to meet Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa and Keiko Fujimori, sworn in as Peru’s president in July.
