US State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott said in announcing the trip that Rubio would discuss cooperation against narcoterrorism; American help after the earthquake that killed 331 people in western and central Colombia in August; and “the benefits of deeper commercial relationships between our countries”. The statement did not mention China. Rubio also planned to deliver a message from US President Donald Trump to “eradicate cocaine and dismantle trafficking groups”, pressing the Colombian leader to destroy hundreds of square miles of coca crops and to target the finances of armed groups, according to The New York Times, which said the two would also discuss military capabilities, migration and deportations. De la Espriella was expected to ask Washington to suspend the 12.5 per cent tariff on Colombian goods including cut flowers, one of the country’s biggest exports to the US, to soften the economic damage from the quake. From Petro’s BRI accession to alignment with Washington Under former president Gustavo Petro, Colombia spent years deepening relations with Beijing. In 2025, the South American country signed a BRI cooperation plan, the first time Bogota committed to the Chinese infrastructure and trade programme, two years after the relationship was raised to a strategic partnership. Petro’s foreign ministry called the accession “a historic step” but stressed that the plan was not a treaty and created no binding obligations. But his successor campaigned on a security alliance with the United States, won an endorsement from Trump, and has not said publicly whether he intends to keep Colombia in the programme or withdraw. Beijing congratulated De la Espriella after he won the second round of the election in June by a narrow margin, when foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China was ready to work with the incoming government and viewed the relationship “from a strategic height and long-term perspective”. Chinese ambassador to Colombia Zhu Jingyang made obvious the chillier turn in relations within days of the earthquake, writing on X that Beijing hoped the government would “immediately” name the official and the channel to coordinate international assistance for the victims. Colombia turned down or left pending offers of rescue teams from China, Mexico, El Salvador and the United Nations, and took US aid instead. De la Espriella called the accounts of a rejection false. China involved in largest infrastructure project in Colombia Chinese state builders are already running the largest infrastructure project in Colombia, the first line of the Bogota metro, and reconstruction after the quake will put more public works out to tender. Zhu told a congress of Colombian exporters last week that Chinese appliance makers and other companies had come to the embassy looking to invest or build plants there. “Everything depends on Colombian policy towards China, on how we manage to maintain this pragmatic spirit of continuing to work together, and on the way Colombia handles its relationship with the United States and China in a balanced manner,” the ambassador said. The ambassador cited De la Espriella’s commitment to keep the metro line going, a US$4.3 billion contract held by a consortium led by China Harbour Engineering Company and Xian Rail Transit Group. Chinese direct investment in Colombia has been marginal according to its central bank’s records, which registered a net outflow of US$99.8 million last year and 0.14 per cent of all foreign investment in the first quarter of this year. The United States supplied 29.7 per cent of the total last year. The figures track equity stakes rather than the engineering contracts through which Chinese firms have entered the market, the metro among them.

title: Putin and Trump discuss Ukraine in ‘extremely frank’ call
description: The hour-long talks focused on ‘the issue of a settlement’, the Kremlin says, as the US leader called for a speedy end to the fighting.
content: Russian President Vladimir Putin and US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday discussed the Ukraine conflict in an “extremely frank” and constructive hour-long phone call, the Kremlin said. It came after US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend in an attempt to kick-start long-stalled US efforts to end the fighting. Washington has been pushing for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv. Kyiv says the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was “too early” to discuss a venue or dates. During their call on Tuesday, Putin and Trump “focused on the issue of a settlement in Ukraine”, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters. Trump called for a speedy end to the fighting, Ushakov said, while Putin presented an “objective and detailed analysis” of the frontline situation. Putin has routinely said his troops are advancing across the entire front, with the capture of the entire eastern Donbas region a matter of time. Putin “pointed out what the Americans could realistically do to bring the hostilities to a swift conclusion” and stressed that Russia had “no aggressive plans” towards Europe, Ushakov added. Trump and the White House did not provide an immediate readout of the call. Russia has intensified aerial attacks on Ukrainian towns and cities in recent months. After announcing a brief ceasefire to coincide with Witkoff and Kushner’s visit to Kyiv, Moscow resumed strikes on the Ukrainian capital overnight, killing at least five people, according to Ukraine’s rescue services. Reporters in Kyiv heard fresh explosions in the early hours of Tuesday, triggering fires and sending locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter. Zelensky, meanwhile, said Russian, Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this month for talks on finding an end to the war. “If all sides agree, we also want to hold it in the autumn. If September works out, then it would be great. The earlier, the better,” he said. Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kyiv have shifted their positions. “The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said. “His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.” Russia said it had carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centres in Kyiv and its suburbs. Locals said they ran for cover as the attack started. “It was very terrifying, we barely managed to run into the parking lot. The parking lot was shaking all over too,” Nina Kimova, 55, said, adding that her car had been “burned to ashes”. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s offensive, according to statistics verified by the United Nations. In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people. Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the US was pushing for a de-escalation before winter and that Putin did not want to annoy Trump before the US midterm legislative elections in early November. Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since launching its offensive in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20 degrees Celsius (-4 Fahrenheit). The two sides appear no closer to agreeing on how the war should end. Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support. Kyiv has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

title: Huawei goes on trial in US for racketeering after nearly decade of litigation
description: Chinese tech giant accused of engineering a racketeering conspiracy to steal American technology and unfairly gain an industry advantage.
content: Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies went on trial on Tuesday in Brooklyn, New York, on criminal charges after eight years of legal wrangling with the US government. The Shenzhen-based company has pleaded not guilty to all 14 counts, including bank fraud, wire fraud, trade secret theft, and racketeering, with the alleged criminal activity dating back to 1999. Jury selection began on Tuesday, local time, with US District Judge Ann M. Donnelly of the Eastern District of New York instructing potential jurors to strive to be as “fair and impartial” as possible. “China and the Communist Party … are not on trial,” she said, also noting that the ongoing US-Iran conflict should not influence jurors’ judgment. Federal prosecutors said in court documents filed with the Eastern District of New York that Huawei carried out a decades-long racketeering scheme to grow its worldwide business. They accuse it of engaging in intellectual property theft, violations of US sanctions on Iran and deceiving major banks about its Iran ties, all of which the company denies. Huawei said in a statement that the US government’s “overarching narrative is demonstrably false” and that the company’s recent successes, including US$126 billion in global sales revenue last year, its best performance in nearly five years, were achieved through its own research and development efforts. “Long-term investment in innovation, backed by the utmost respect for intellectual property, has been the driving force behind Huawei’s business success,” a Huawei spokesperson said. On September 4, the prosecutors dropped two counts of sanctions violations, according to a pre-trial filing, while proceeding with the remaining 12. If convicted, Huawei faces fines and forfeiture of proceeds gained during the alleged criminal activity, potentially one of the biggest ever US corporate fines. The US government first charged Huawei in 2019 during the first Trump administration, when Huawei chief financial officer Meng Wanzhou was accused of misrepresenting Huawei’s relationship with Skycom Technologies, a Hong Kong corporation that provided telecoms infrastructure and services in Iran. The indictment sparked a years-long effort by the US government to extradite Meng from Canada, where she was arrested, causing a sharp downturn in both China-US and China-Canada relations. Meng’s legal case concluded in 2021 when she admitted to lying to US financial institutions about Huawei’s business activities in Iran, as part of a deal with the US government that saw it drop its extradition request and allow Meng to return to China. In June, Judge Donnelly ruled that Meng’s admission could be used as evidence in the coming trial after Huawei’s lawyers sought to have it excluded. Prosecutors said that they have sought to call 25 China-based Huawei employees, including Meng, the daughter of Huawei founder Ren Zhengfei, to testify at the trial. Huawei is being represented by US law firms Jenner & Block, Sidley Austin and Steptoe. Margaret Lewis, a law professor at Seton Hall University, said that the complexity of the case means that the prosecution is likely to “take some time” to get its points across to jurors. “This case is unusual in that the charges span … close to a decade,” she said. “And the factual allegations underlying the case span more than a quarter century.” Nick Turner, a Washington-based partner at Akrivis Law Group, said that the two parties could still reach a settlement during the trial. “It is atypical for large companies to fight all the way to trial,” he said. Prosecutors and Huawei previously engaged in settlement negotiations, but they reached an “impasse”, according to a US Department of Justice filing with the court in 2024. Founded in 1987, Huawei has grown to become the world’s biggest telecoms equipment maker and a major smartphone manufacturer. The company was added to the US trade sanctions Entity List in 2019, which restricted its access to cutting-edge American technology. However, the company has emerged in recent years as a central player in China’s tech industry, including artificial intelligence, where it is a key software and hardware provider with its Ascend semiconductor chips and Compute Architecture for Neural Networks (CANN) open-source ecosystem. The prosecution told the court on Tuesday that it expected to conclude its case by November, while the defence said it would need around a month.

title: Singapore man Malone Lam pleads guilty after massive US bitcoin heist and spending spree
description: The 22-year-old helped launder the stolen funds, then used the money to buy sports cars, rent mansions and spend millions at nightclubs.
content: A 22-year-old man pleaded guilty on Tuesday to teaming up with friends to steal nearly a quarter-billion dollars in bitcoin from a Washington resident – one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in US history – and then embarking on a wild spending spree with the laundered proceeds. Malone Lam, an eighth-grade dropout who came to the US from Singapore, faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years after pleading guilty to a federal racketeering conspiracy charge. US District Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly did not immediately schedule Lam’s sentencing hearing in Washington. Lam was an organiser for a network of young men who carried out a string of cryptocurrency scams starting in 2023, prosecutors said. He is one of 18 defendants charged in the case and is the 11th to plead guilty, but his conviction marks a breakthrough for the Justice Department’s investigation. In August 2024, Lam and others used “social engineering” techniques to dupe the Washington man out of bitcoin worth over US$245 million. Two of Lam’s alleged co-conspirators posed as representatives of Google and the Gemini cryptocurrency exchange to manipulate the man into giving them access to his Google Drive and revealing security codes that allowed Lam to siphon off over 4,100 bitcoin, according to prosecutors. Lam helped launder and convert stolen cryptocurrency into cash that he used to buy a fleet of sports cars, rent mansions in Miami and spend millions at nightclubs, including US$569,000 in one evening at one Los Angeles club, authorities said. The spending spree lasted a month before FBI agents arrested Lam in Miami. An off-duty law enforcement officer had tipped off Lam that authorities were on their way to arrest him, the indictment says. “We always talked about what it would be like if I were to go down, but never thought it would be this crazy,” Lam told associates from jail on a recorded call, according to his indictment. Lam’s purchases included a US$2 million watch and over 30 cars, including custom Porsches, Lamborghinis and Ferraris, according to the FBI. When Lam indicated that he bought most but not all of those vehicles himself, the judge asked him if he remembers which ones he personally bought. “I would need some time,” he told the judge.

title: Leaders ‘lied’ about New York’s 9/11 toxic air, Mayor Mamdani says
description: City releases 170,000 documents revealing officials hid health risks around ground zero to limit liability.
content: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Tuesday the release of tens of thousands of documents showing the city did not disclose all it knew about air toxicity after 9/11. The release comes ahead of the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, attacks that killed 2,977 people in the United States, mostly in the collapse of the Twin Towers in New York. In the years since, more than 9,400 have died from illnesses linked to their exposure to the area, according to a federal medical monitoring programme. “These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around ground zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability,” the mayor told a news conference following the online release of 170,000 pages of documents on health concerns, air quality and the city’s response to the attacks. The release is part of an agreement with 9/11 Health Watch, a victims’ advocacy group that had taken legal action to compel the city to make the documents public. “For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as City officials continued messaging to the public that the air was ‘safe and acceptable’,” the group’s director Benjamin Chevat said in a statement. After the initial dust cloud that followed the collapse of the World Trade Center, months of pollution and lingering dust ensued, causing cancers that thousands of New Yorkers still suffer today. When asked about the names of officials who had withheld information from the public, Mamdani said, “this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted”. “People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air.” Roughly 173,000 documents released Tuesday, and additional ones which will be published online in waves over the next 12 months, could implicate two former New York mayors. They are Rudy Giuliani, in office at the time of the attacks, and then Michael Bloomberg, mayor from January 2002 to December 2013. Some concern discussions Giuliani’s administration had at the time about its legal liability and health risks, New York City’s chief counsel Steven Banks said Tuesday. Giuliani’s spokesman did not return a request for comment. Another document highlights information provided by Congressman Jerry Nadler during Bloomberg’s tenure regarding concerns from residents of Lower Manhattan about the quality of the air they were breathing. Bloomberg’s team declined to comment. On September 11, 2001, hijackers seized control of two planes that struck the two World Trade Center towers. A third hijacked jet smashed into the Pentagon, and a fourth, which seemed to be headed for the Capitol or the White House, crashed in woodland near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back and seized control.

title: US targets Iran’s airlines with sweeping new sanctions
description: The US Treasury is aiming to ground Mahan Air and other firms in a sharp escalation of Trump’s economic pressure campaign.
content: The US on Tuesday issued 36 ⁠fresh Iran-related sanctions targeting Iran’s aviation sector and other companies as part of a broad push to escalate economic pressure on Tehran as the war in the Middle East entered a seventh month. The US Treasury Department said the action was aimed at grounding Iran’s Mahan Air, already sanctioned by the US and the European Union, and all other Iranian airlines. The sanctions also ‌took aim at covert front companies, foreign intermediaries and deceptive transshipment routes that Washington says Iran relies on to obtain US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology. The Treasury also issued an alert asking financial institutions to report any procurement networks supporting Iran’s aviation industry, while designating firms based in Turkey and the United Arab Emirates that it said helped Tehran procure US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control also suspended three Iran-related aviation authorisations that allowed overflights and permitted non-US airlines to fly US-origin or US-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran. Tuesday’s actions marked a sharp escalation ⁠of the Trump administration’s renewed push to squeeze Iran’s economy and pressure Tehran to loosen its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. A US naval blockade ‌and tougher sanctions are curbing oil exports, restricting access to foreign currency and exposing growing strains in the economy. The Treasury said any foreign firm or individual aiding Iranian airlines through aircraft transfers, cargo services or general sales agent support would face ‌serious consequences. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week had warned that the Trump administration was eyeing airlines as possible sanctions targets ⁠along with digital assets and the ⁠maritime industry. “Under Operation Economic Outcast, we promised severe consequences for those providing financial lifelines to the Iranian regime,” Bessent said in a statement on Tuesday. “Let this be a warning to anyone doing ‌business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.” The US Treasury has repeatedly targeted global networks supporting Mahan ‌Air. In ‌July, Treasury designated six entities and individuals in China, India, Russia and Iran, including several firms that act as sales agents for the US- ‌and EU-sanctioned airline. Washington first sanctioned Mahan in 2011 over support it provided to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. In 2020, Washington imposed sanctions on a China-based company ⁠it accused of acting on behalf of Mahan Air. On Tuesday, Treasury designated 27 Iranian airlines, as well as several firms based in Turkey and ⁠the United Arab Emirates, for helping Mahan Air secure at least three Boeing B-777 aircraft this summer that had been retired elsewhere. It also hit UAE-based Egyptian citizen Ibrahim Ali Mohamed Mohamed Mahran, the chief executive of ECT Aviation Support, as well as the British unit ‌of the firm. OFAC also imposed sanctions ‌on two firms based in Turkey and Malaysia that it said had serviced Mahan Air’s international flights and coordinated cargo shipments. As a result of the sanctions, all property and interests of the designated firms and individuals that are in the US will be blocked and must be reported to OFAC. Violations of sanctions can result in criminal and civil penalties.

title: Tung Chee-hwa’s rise to first Hong Kong chief executive and elder statesman
description: Shipping tycoon steered city through stormy post-handover era of economic and health crises before helping improve US-China ties.
content: A shipping tycoon who was thrust onto the international stage as Hong Kong’s first chief executive and went on to become an elder statesman and consummate diplomat, Tung Chee-hwa will be remembered as a defining figure of the city’s modern history. The legacy of Tung, who died on Tuesday at age 89, is closely tied to his role as a patriot who led Hong Kong through uncharted waters, navigating a stormy post-handover period beset with economic, public health and political crises. With his Shanghai roots and extensive international connections, Tung was also known as a key backchannel envoy between China and the United States, working as an elder statesman to enhance people-to-people ties between the two superpowers. Seeking to offer reassurances about the “one country, two systems” governing framework, he famously said: “If Hong Kong is good, China will be good. If China is good, Hong Kong will be even better.” That reassurance was critical in the years after the 1997 handover from British to Chinese rule, when anxiety was rife about Hong Kong’s future and the transition was being scrutinised globally. In his inaugural speech as leader that July 1, Tung declared: “For the first time in history, we, the people of Hong Kong, will be masters of our own destiny.” He added: “The SAR government is fully committed to preserving the Hong Kong way of life, maintaining Hong Kong’s free economic system, upholding the rule of law and building a more democratic society.” Just two months later, Tung travelled to Washington to meet US president Bill Clinton to show how Hong Kong was moving forward smoothly. Milestones as leader Dubbed the “7-11 Chief Executive” for keeping long working hours, Tung enjoyed a brief honeymoon period after taking office, with his popularity rating peaking at 70.4 marks in September that year. But within months, the Asian financial crisis struck, subjecting the local currency to attacks by international hedge funds aiming to break the Hong Kong dollar’s peg to the US dollar. Tung’s administration deployed HK$118 billion to buy local shares and defeat the currency speculators, protecting the financial system from collapse. At the time, financial secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen recalled Tung’s unwavering support for his decision which appeared to go against the city’s free-market philosophy. “I cried two or three times because I didn’t want to lose taxpayers’ money and because it was against my fiscal philosophy,” Tsang said. “When I asked Mr Tung about this, he agreed to it in half an hour.” Tung was also credited with ensuring Hong Kong Disneyland became Asia’s second Disney resort, spearheading the development of the Cyberport tech hub and laying the groundwork for the West Kowloon Cultural District. He is also remembered for overhauling the civil service system in 2002 when he started his second term. The Principal Officials Accountability System, which he introduced, transformed bureau heads into political appointees answerable for major policy failures. Public health and political crises His leadership faced strain during the severe acute respiratory syndrome (Sars) outbreak in 2003, which claimed nearly 300 lives in the city. Pressure escalated that year when his administration tried to pass controversial national security legislation under Article 23 of the Basic Law, the city’s mini-constitution. The push, coming amid the post-Sars economic downturn, livelihood problems and a negative equity crisis, sparked a mass protest of about 500,000 residents, forcing him to shelve the bill. Following the demonstration demanding his resignation, Tung defended his choice to remain in office: “If I decide to step down, it would be an easy decision. But to stay is difficult; it requires courage and greater commitment.” Tung eventually resigned in March 2005, citing health reasons. From shipping tycoon to leader Tung was born in Shanghai on July 7, 1937, the son of Tung Chao-yung, who founded Orient Overseas Container Line (OOCL). The family’s roots in Shanghai shaped Tung’s formative years and helped later align him with the Beijing leadership. Jiang Zemin was surrounded by elites associated with Shanghai when he rose to the pinnacle of the country’s leadership. The family moved to Hong Kong in 1947, and after graduating with a degree in marine engineering from the University of Liverpool in 1960 and working in the United States, Tung returned to Hong Kong in 1969, taking the helm of OOCL following his father’s death in 1982. Tung was appointed a member of the Basic Law Consultative Committee in 1985 and was given a seat on the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) in 1992. During a Preparatory Committee meeting in 1996 where Tung served as vice-chairman, Jiang famously gave him an extended handshake in front of the press, which was interpreted as a sign of Beijing’s endorsement. On December 11, 1996, Tung was chosen by a 400-strong selection committee to become the first chief executive of Hong Kong with 320 votes, beating former chief justice Ti-liang Yang and businessman Peter Woo Kwong-ching. Elder statesman and US-China envoy Tung remained active in public life after he stepped down in 2005. Serving as a vice-chairman of the CPPCC, he leveraged his extensive ties with American leaders to encourage dialogue between China and the United States. He is one of the few Hong Kong politicians to have officially met two US presidents, Bill Clinton and George W Bush. He founded the China-United States Exchange Foundation in 2008 to encourage dialogue between the two nations and started a think tank, Our Hong Kong Foundation, in 2014. In 2015, Tung joined Chinese President Xi Jinping’s official state visit to the US to meet president Barack Obama, playing an important role in behind-the-scenes talks. He arrived ahead of the delegation to act as a senior envoy. Concerns about his health began to grow in March 2021 when Tung fell over at the end of the National People’s Congress meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Tung was last seen in public in July that year, attending the premiere of a film to mark the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China. Months later, his spokesman said Tung had undergone an operation for an undisclosed condition and was resting at home. Tung is survived by his wife Betty Tung Chiu Hung-ping, whom he married in 1961, three children and nine grandchildren.

title: Review | Practical Magic 2 movie review: Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reunite for dull sequel
description: Joey King, Maisie Williams and Lee Pace also feature in this boring follow-up that falls short of the spellbinding 1998 original.
content: 2/5 stars Whether Practical Magic 2 was genuinely conjured into existence by fan demand – as its PR campaign claims – or is simply the result of Hollywood scraping the intellectual-property barrel and mining anything with a vague following, this long-delayed sequel to 1998’s Practical Magic is a disappointment. Ultimately, this reunion with the magically inclined Owens family from Massachusetts is anything but spellbinding. Once again, we meet the central coven of witches: Sally (Sandra Bullock), her younger sister Gillian (Nicole Kidman) and their eccentric aunts, Frances (Stockard Channing) and Bridget (Dianne Wiest). While Gillian remains resolutely single, Sally has raised her daughters Kylie (Joey King) and Antonia (Maisie Williams) to be blissfully unaware of their extended family’s magical powers or the curse that led to the loss of their father. As we are told early on, “Any man who loved an Owens woman was marked with tragedy.” And so it goes for Kylie’s boyfriend Gideon (Xolo Mariduena), who falls into a coma after a traffic accident. Only then does Kylie discover the truth, a revelation that sends her on a trip to the UK to try and break this haunting spell. This is where the film really starts to plummet, as Susanne Bier – who directed Bullock in the far more intriguing 2018 film Bird Box – takes us on a whistle-stop tour of tourist hotspots, from the Tower of London to a chocolate-box English countryside village complete with a red telephone box. In pursuit of Kylie, Sally and Gillian soon run into Lee Pace’s rugged, inked-up hunk (or “Professor Tattoos” as Sally calls him, in one of the more amusing lines), an academic who studies magic and soon becomes a slightly forced love interest. The big issue with Practical Magic 2 – aside from a deathly dull plot cooked up by original writer Akiva Goldsman along with Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel – is the sorcery itself. Setting the film in the land of Harry Potter was, arguably, not the smartest move, since it automatically invites comparisons. And while the first Practical Magic arrived before J.K. Rowling’s books were turned into a hugely successful movie franchise, this sequel feels uninspired next to the epic scale of the Harry Potter films. Cast-wise, the underappreciated Pace injects something fresh, and it is a genuine pleasure to see Channing and Wiest back on screen. Bullock is always watchable, but Kidman’s flighty, flirty performance is something of a turn-off. Maybe this witchy reunion is what fans wanted, but after nearly three decades, viewers will be left wishing for something far more magical. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Singapore ‘open’ to using chemical castration for sex offenders if proven effective
description: Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam says the evidence on whether such measures are effective in reducing crime rates is so far ‘inconclusive’.
content: Singapore remains open to considering chemical castration as a measure to tackle sex crimes if there is clear evidence that it is effective in reducing crime, Home Affairs Minister K. Shanmugam has said. However, the evidence so far was inconclusive, he said in a written parliamentary reply on Tuesday. “We remain open to considering measures including pharmacological anti-androgen treatments, also known as chemical castrations, if it is clear that such measures are effective in bringing down crime rates. So far, the evidence is not conclusive on that,” Shanmugam said. Shanmugam, who is also the coordinating minister for national security, was responding to a question from Member of Parliament Gerald Giam on whether the Ministry of Home Affairs had evaluated such treatments or a sex offender register as additional measures to deter crime and reduce reoffending. Giam also asked whether statutory penalties for major sexual offences against children and young people would be reviewed in light of recent increases in reported cases. In response, Shanmugam said the government took a serious view of sexual crimes and imposed stiff penalties, particularly when the victims were minors. Rape, or penetrative sexual assault, involving a minor under the age of 14 without consent carries a mandatory jail term of at least eight years and up to 20 years, with a minimum of 12 strokes of the cane. Outrage of modesty against a minor under the age of 14 is punishable with up to five years’ jail, fine and caning. If the minor is hurt or restrained during the offence, the offender faces a mandatory minimum jail term of three years, which may extend up to 10 years, and mandatory caning. “These are heavy penalties, which send a strong signal to deter such offences,” he said. Shanmugam also pointed to legislative amendments over the years, including the Sentence for Enhanced Public Protection (SEPP), which commenced on July 31. Under the SEPP, offenders who have committed serious violent or sexual offences and who pose a substantial risk of reoffending will be detained for a minimum term of between five and 20 years, as determined by the court, and will only be released if the Minister for Home Affairs assesses that person no longer poses a threat to the public. Responding directly to Giam’s question of a sex offender register, Shanmugam said police already maintained a non-public record of people convicted of serious offences, including sexual offences. The records are shared with selected agencies, including the Ministry of Social and Family Development and the Ministry of Education, when screening people who apply for roles involving sustained contact with children and young people. “This approach balances the need to safeguard our children and the rehabilitation and reintegration efforts of ex-offenders,” Shanmugam said. He added that the government had been considering expanding such screening to cover more types of roles involving contact with children and young people. This included considering whether voluntary screening could be introduced for unregulated sectors, Shanmugam said, adding that the government would share more details when ready. This story was first published by CNA

title: Endangered Sumatran tigers born in Greece as zoos build safety net
description: Three two-month-old Sumatran tiger cubs receive identification microchips and their first vaccinations at a zoo near Athens.
content: The world’s most endangered tigers have started a family in Greece, offering hope for a predator rapidly vanishing from the wild. Three two-month-old Sumatran tiger cubs received identification microchips and their first vaccinations on Tuesday at a zoo near Athens, as part of a global effort to build a backup population. The Sumatran tiger, classified as critically endangered, is found only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, which is slightly larger than Sweden. As few as 400 are believed to remain in the wild, mainly because of aggressive forest clearing. It joins the South China tiger and the Malayan tiger in the category of severe risk. “The Sumatran tiger is one of the most threatened tiger species in the world, and among felines in general,” said Theodoros Babilis, head keeper of cats and monkeys at Attica Zoological Park. Zoos in Europe and elsewhere were maintaining a safety population, he said, “so that in the future there can be potential reintroductions of this species into the wild”. The Sumatran tiger is the smallest tiger species in the world, but males can still grow up to 2.55 metres (8.4 feet) long and weigh as much as 140kg (309 pounds). Skilled swimmers and climbers, they use their dark stripes – unique to each animal, like a fingerprint – to hide in the dense forest as they hunt deer, wild pigs and smaller mammals. Even at two months old, Babilis said, the cubs had already developed sharp claws and teeth that made handling them a challenge. The cubs were born in early July to Toba, their mother, and Argos, their father, who has since died of cancer. The surviving cubs are expected to take names from characters in Homer’s The Odyssey, according to zoo staff. Two males and one female, the cubs were restless during Tuesday’s vaccination. Veterinary staff needed help to complete the procedure, ferrying the animals back and forth in carriers on electric buggies. Caring for the animals is demanding work, according to Dr Arsenoi Psaroudaki, a zoo and wildlife veterinarian. “The tigers don’t like to be handled. They’re very wild,” she said, explaining that staff had to work quickly to limit stress. The cubs received microchips logged in a shared database, plus a vaccine similar to one commonly given to cats that protects against three diseases. For Psaroudaki, the work is also rewarding because it offers “some hope for safeguarding these really rare cats”. She added: “It’s very humbling to be able to work with the rarest tiger species in the world.”

title: Asian Games organisers in final push to boost sluggish ticket sales for football, baseball
description: Repeated schedule changes have sparked widespread frustration among athletes and spectators, with some complaining on social media.
content: Asian Games organisers announced they were making a final push to boost sluggish ticket sales for sports such as women’s football and baseball ahead of the opening ceremony in less than two weeks. There was, however, better news for other sports, with Aichi governor Hideaki Omura announcing at a press conference on Tuesday that more than 60 per cent of tickets have been sold across 31 of the 41 sports. While overall sales figures for the opening and closing ceremonies were not disclosed, 17 sports, including table tennis, badminton and volleyball, have sold more than 80 per cent of tickets, according to Japanese news outlet the Okinawa Times. “I hope as many people as possible will come to the venues and enjoy the intense competition of these international matches,” Omura said, adding that organisers planned to release additional seats for sold-out events on a rolling basis whenever they became available. Although organisers initially announced a planned release of 2.75 million tickets across the Asian Games and Asian Para Games in Japan, the Okinawa Times also reported that insider estimates revealed only 700,000 to 800,000 tickets had been sold by late August. Official ticketing data showed that tickets had sold out for unique events, such as kabaddi and sepak takraw, as well as select dates for women’s volleyball and almost all dates for badminton. Matches featuring Japanese athletes and finals have also sold particularly well. In contrast, ticket sales for sports held in larger venues, such as baseball, judo and women’s football, remained weak, particularly for weekday qualifying rounds. Attracting spectators to venues outside Aichi prefecture, including those in neighbouring Shizuoka and Gifu, also remained a major challenge. Compounding the ticketing difficulties, repeated schedule changes have sparked widespread frustration among athletes and spectators. On August 19, one month before the Games, organisers announced schedule changes for several high-profile athletic events, including the women’s 100-metre hurdles and men’s high jump, while also reducing the men’s water polo field by one team. Under official ticketing rules, refunds are granted only if an entire event is cancelled, leaving spectators unable to refund or exchange tickets affected by schedule changes. Local media reported that the policy triggered a backlash on Japanese social media, with fans complaining that the situation was akin to “buying a baseball ticket only to end up watching football”. Hurdler Hitomi Nakajima, who set multiple Japanese records in the women’s 100m hurdles in August, publicly apologised on social media to fans who bought tickets early. “I am so sorry to those who bought tickets early … I’m deeply sorry, but there’s nothing I can do about it.” Runner Reiri Nakashima previously emphasised the shared responsibility of sporting events in an interview. “Sports are created jointly by organisers, athletes and spectators,” he said. Writing on social media, Nakashima condemned the ticketing rules, calling the lack of refunds “an utterly absurd situation”. “Unlike baseball or soccer, different track and field events are practically different sports entirely,” he wrote. “If the specific event you are interested in is moved, the entire purpose of going changes … Honestly, what they are doing is crazy.” The organising committee explained that the schedule changes resulted from entry fluctuations following the July 1 deadline, stating the adjustments were made “to ensure an environment where athletes can compete in peak condition”. The Games run from September 19 to October 4, bringing together more than 15,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions. Overseas contingents have already started arriving in Japan, local media reported, including Jordan’s men’s basketball team and South Korea’s sailing team on September 6, with most arrivals expected three to four days before the opening ceremony.

title: Hong Kong students drop in global rankings for maths, science and literacy
description: City’s students drop out of global top 10 in Pisa’s science section – the first time since Hong Kong joined international assessment.
content: Hong Kong secondary school students’ performance has fallen in an international assessment focused on three core subjects, with their science score dropping out of the global top 10 for the first time in the study’s history. Experts said on Tuesday that the decline in Hong Kong scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) was partly due to the post-Covid impact on study habits and learning motivation. Held every three years, Pisa is a worldwide study by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) that tests 15-year-old students on reading, mathematics and science. The latest study, which ranked 91 countries and economies, was conducted from May to July 2025. Each cycle since 2012 has also featured an “innovative domain”, which refers to a rotating test topic that measures real-world skills. The 2025 results, announced by the University of Hong Kong’s education faculty, showed that the city’s students ranked 17th for science, with a mean score of 496, down from seventh place in 2022. In comparison, the mainland Chinese municipalities and provinces of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang collectively ranked first, scoring 597. Hong Kong ranked seventh in maths after scoring 522, down from fourth place in 2022, but remained well above the international average of 463. The mainland’s top regions held first place with a score of 612. In terms of mother-tongue reading literacy, Hong Kong’s score dropped to 480, bringing it down from 11th place in 2022 to 15th. Singapore topped the ranking, netting a score of 535. The latest study’s literacy portion placed greater emphasis on navigating multiple digital sources and judging online information. Hong Kong’s Education Bureau, which commissioned the university to conduct the assessment, noted the OECD report partly attributed the decline in overall performance to the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic. The bureau also noted a gap between the latest scores and the education sector’s observations of students’ abilities, with reasons for the disparity including pupils’ psychological state and concentration levels during the test. Lam Wai-Ip, an associate professor of the faculty and co-project leader for the study, also said the drop in domain subject scores was part of a global decline. She said that the current cohort had experienced pandemic-related disruptions and grown up in a highly digital environment with rapidly consumed, fragmented online content. “The pandemic has affected student study habits and learning motivation,” she said. “The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development found that curiosity, persistence and the ability to integrate and process long or complex texts have dropped since 2022.” Professor Nancy Law Wai-ying, a member of the study team, said the drop in the city’s science score was related to a shift in the assessment framework, which had moved beyond rote-learning knowledge and now required students to research, evaluate and use scientific information to justify decisions in uncertain contexts. But Hong Kong students managed to achieve a strong score in the latest assessment’s special topic, “Learning in the Digital World”, with the city ranking sixth and scoring 545, far exceeding the international average of 500. The assessment tested computational problem-solving through two 30-minute units, one focused on programming and the other on computational modelling. The framework measured their ability to solve problems using computational tools, conduct experiments, analyse data and debug artefacts, all while exercising self-regulated learning. The test results showed that 43.1 per cent of Hong Kong students had high levels of proficiency in digital learning, compared with a global average of 25.7 per cent. Meanwhile, 12 per cent of Hong Kong students had low levels of proficiency, nearly half the global average. In response to the results, the bureau said: “The outstanding performance in Learning in the Digital World shows the tangible results of our STEAM promotion.” STEAM learning is an educational approach that combines science, technology, engineering, the arts and maths. It also promised to continue focusing on artificial intelligence education, developing curriculum frameworks, supporting teacher training and strengthening students’ digital literacy. Frederick Leung Koon-shing, an emeritus professor with the faculty and the study’s leader, stressed the importance of enhancing student agency to ensure future readiness. “Excellent performance in Learning in the Digital World shows many students possess key competencies for developing agency, and the next step is to transfer these strengths to core domains,” he said. Hong Kong was also found to have maintained strong educational equity in the latest assessment, with 15 per cent of disadvantaged students among top performers, above the OECD average of 12 per cent. According to the report, Hong Kong students also reported strong teacher support, with 81 per cent saying teachers showed genuine interest and 82 per cent receiving extra help with their studies until they understood subject matter. The city also scored 497 in digital and environmental adaptability, against an OECD average of 480, with nearly 80 per cent reaching baseline proficiency. The latest assessment marks Hong Kong’s ninth cycle of taking part in the study. The 2025 sample covered 239 secondary schools, with 230 institutions and 6,445 students included in the final data set after quality assurance checks. The participating students comprised 52 per cent boys and 48 per cent girls.

title: China’s Xi Jinping urges deeper UK ties in first call with PM Andy Burnham
description: Xi asks to ‘transcend differences’, while British leader speaks of will to restore ties to ‘highest historical level’, Xinhua reports.
content: President Xi Jinping on Tuesday called for deeper cooperation between “major technological powers” China and the UK as he held his first official call with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Xi congratulated Burnham on his appointment as the country’s leader, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua, emphasising that the shared interests of China and the United Kingdom outweighed their differences in social systems. “Both sides should respect and trust each other, transcend differences, seek common ground while reserving differences, and expand mutually beneficial cooperation,” Xi was quoted as saying. “Both China and the UK are major technological powers with abundant resources in education, culture and sports. They should maintain an open and forward-looking approach and strengthen exchanges and cooperation in various fields.” Xi also urged the UK to work with China as a fellow major economy and permanent member of the UN Security Council, in backing multilateralism and free trade, and pushing for an “equitable and orderly multipolar world”. Burnham took office as prime minister on July 20, after succeeding Keir Starmer as leader of the Labour Party. Tuesday’s call took place at Burnham’s request, Xinhua said. A statement from Beijing released in the evening did not say if the wars in Iran and Ukraine were part of the talks. According to Xinhua, Burnham told Xi that the UK was willing to maintain “the continuity of its China policy”, build a “long-term stable strategic partnership”, hold high-level exchanges and “restore bilateral relations to their highest historical level”. He also referenced the two countries’ UN roles, saying: “In the current turbulent and complex international landscape, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, Britain and China should promote dialogue to resolve international hotspots, jointly address global challenges such as climate change, and work together to maintain global stability and prosperity.” A Downing Street statement about the meeting said the two leaders discussed the importance of “pragmatic cooperation” in advancing their interests and addressing shared global challenges. Issues raised by Burnham included the Ukraine war, Hong Kong and human rights, the statement from No 10 said. He also pledged to engage “frankly and constructively” on matters affecting both countries. Britain began to seek warmer ties with China under Starmer, following a frosty period marked by contentious issues ranging from security concerns to China’s human rights record. Britain banned Chinese telecoms giant Huawei from its 5G networks in 2020 and sanctioned Chinese officials a year later over alleged rights abuses relating to the Uygur minority group in Xinjiang. Beijing retaliated by slapping counter-sanctions on British lawmakers. But London pursued deeper trade ties with Beijing during Starmer’s two years in office from 2024. In January, he became the first British prime minister to visit China since 2018, leading to an agreement between the two nations to build a “long-term, stable comprehensive strategic partnership”. They also agreed to cut tariffs on Scotch whisky and signed a raft of trade and investment deals.

title: South Korea sends fact-finding team to assess Strait of Hormuz conditions
description: The defence ministry says the move ‘does not presuppose an actual deployment’.
content: South Korea said on Tuesday it had sent a fact-finding team to assess the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, stressing no decision had been made about potential troop deployment to the strategic waterway. Traffic through the vital shipping route has been virtually paralysed since the US-Iran war began on February 28, disrupting global energy markets. The South Korean defence ministry said it had “dispatched a fact-finding team to assess conditions on the ground in the Strait of Hormuz”. “The team was sent to examine the regional situation and security conditions, and its mission does not presuppose an actual deployment,” it said. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pressured ally South Korea to provide help for the war in the Middle East, but Seoul denied that Washington had asked it to deploy troops by a specified deadline. “No decision has been made regarding the deployment of troops,” the South Korean defence ministry said. The fact-finding team left for the United Arab Emirates over the weekend and was assessing operational conditions for a potential deployment, Yonhap news agency reported, citing officials. The team was expected to return to South Korea as early as this week, the report said. Contacted by Agence France-Presse, the defence ministry declined to comment on the report. Iran and the United States have been at war since February 28, with Tehran largely controlling the Strait of Hormuz – a vital shipping route linking the Gulf to international waters. South Korea said on Friday it was considering “contributions” to US security efforts along the strait, while stressing that no decision had been made. Tuesday’s announcement followed a warning from Tehran a day earlier that any South Korean military contribution to the conflict would have “serious consequences”. “Any military deployment or participation in operations by other countries in the Persian Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz can only be regarded as direct support for the party responsible for that aggression and will have serious consequences,” Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a Korean-language post on social media. He warned Seoul against succumbing to what he called “US pressure and intimidation”. Negotiations between Iran and the US have stalled as they vied for control over Hormuz, which normally carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas exports.

title: China’s HQ-17AE Shorad system to boost Pakistani drone defence as India tensions simmer
description: Successful integration with other foreign systems by Pakistan would strengthen China’s export case ‘considerably’, analyst notes.
content: Pakistan has unveiled a newly acquired Chinese-made short-range air defence system that analysts say could boost its ability to counter Indian drones and low-altitude threats in a future conflict. A social media video posted by the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) on Sunday confirmed for the first time that it was operating the HQ-17AE short-range air defence (Shorad) system. The HQ-17AE is an export version of China’s HQ-17A air defence system – a wheeled variant of the original HQ-17 that was reverse-engineered from the Russian Tor-M1 missiles. The HQ-17AE has an operational range of up to 20km (12 miles) and a flight altitude of up to 10km. It is designed to engage with low-altitude and short-range threats such as unmanned aerial vehicles, helicopters, cruise missiles, guided munitions and aircraft. It is known that it has been exported to Saudi Arabia, Serbia and Tajikistan. Pakistan’s revelation makes it the fourth foreign operator of the Chinese-made system. Sunday’s video sought to promote the PAF’s multidomain operational skills, as deployed in the border conflict with India in May last year. Apart from the HQ-17AE, air defence systems showcased included the also Chinese-made HQ-9P long-range surface-to-air missiles, as well as the Turkish-made Korkut self-propelled anti-aircraft gun and Sahin counter-unmanned aircraft system. These systems are part of Pakistan’s new “layered integrated air defence system” designed to counter a range of modern aerial threats, including drone swarms. The layered network deploys the HQ-9 for long-range aircraft and missile defence; the LY-80 – the export variant of the Chinese-made HQ-16 – against medium-range threats; and the HQ-17AE to counter short-range penetrators, complemented by the Turkish systems targeting drones and low-flying threats. Jagannath Panda, head of the Stockholm Centre for South Asian and Indo-Pacific Affairs, Institute for Security and Development Policy, said Pakistan was likely to view the HQ-17AE mainly as a mobile battlefield and point-defence system. “More importantly, Pakistan appears to be filling a vulnerability at the lower end of its layered air-defence architecture,” Panda said. “Its acquisition also reflects changes in warfare. Pakistan cannot economically use expensive long-range interceptors against every drone or loitering munition. The HQ-17AE gives it another layer for dealing with increasingly dense, low-altitude aerial threats.” Panda added that the important question was whether the Pakistani military could network sensors, command systems and engagement procedures into a coherent layered architecture. Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said anti-drone defence was likely to be a key mission for the HQ-17AE in Pakistan but not its only one. “However, it is probably less cost-effective against very small commercial drones than systems such as Korkut or Sahin,” she added, noting that the Turkish systems were “specifically optimised” to counter unmanned aerial systems. China remains Pakistan’s top arms supplier and, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, accounted for 80 per cent of its total weapons imports between 2021 and 2025. Pakistan’s acquisition of the HQ-17AE reflects the increasing use of low-cost, low-flying threats – such as drones – in modern warfare, given that border tensions with India continue to simmer. Chinese-supplied platforms played a major role in Pakistan’s brief border conflict with India last year, when a J-10CE shot down an Indian Rafale fighter jet. Pakistan claimed to have downed four of the French-made 4.5-generation combat aircraft in the May 7-10 war. This marked both the first reported combat kill by the Chinese fighter jet and the first-ever downing of a Rafale. Odgaard said a successful integration of the HQ-17AE with Turkish systems by Pakistan would strengthen China’s export case “considerably”, by proving that Chinese systems could operate within mixed-vendor architectures. “[It] makes Chinese short-range air defence solutions more attractive to countries already using Nato or Turkish equipment,” Odgaard said. But the real test lay in actual combat, she pointed out. “Export success will depend less on technical compatibility alone and more on whether Pakistan can demonstrate effective real-world performance against drones, cruise missiles and saturation attacks. “Combat credibility remains the strongest advertisement for any air defence system.” Panda said the HQ-17AE could “matter” in any future India-Pakistan confrontation, which was “increasingly unlikely to be dominated simply by manned fighter aircraft”. “The 2025 confrontation reinforced the significance of stand-off weapons, drones, electronic warfare and layered air defence. The HQ-17AE is designed precisely for this increasingly crowded lower-altitude battlespace,” Panda said. The HQ-17AE’s successful integration into the Pakistani military indicated a denser layered air defence network intended to “raise the risks and costs of Indian stand-off and low-altitude strikes”, Panda added. “The more consequential trend is therefore not one particular missile system, but Pakistan’s attempt to construct an increasingly integrated anti-access and air-denial architecture combining Chinese long- and short-range missiles with Turkish counter-drone and gun-based systems,” he said. “That could gradually make the aerial offence-defence competition between India and Pakistan more technologically intensive.”

title: UK, France, Canada block imports from Israeli West Bank settlements
description: Foreign Minister Ed Miliband says Britain refuses to be ‘bystanders to further suffering and to the destruction of the two-state solution’.
content: Britain, France and Canada on Tuesday moved to block imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, while a wider group of Western countries signalled they may take further steps to defend the two-state solution amid mounting concern over settlement expansion and violence in the territory. The trade measures are the latest in a series of actions targeting Israel’s settlement policy and underscore its growing diplomatic isolation among some of its traditional allies. British ‌Foreign Minister Ed Miliband said Britain could no longer simply “call out” injustice and suffering, but had to act to oppose the expansion of settlements, which he said threatened the viability of a Palestinian state. A Reuters report published on Tuesday found Israel’s government is financing some of the West Bank’s most radical settlers, who use illegal outpost farms to displace Palestinians. Ahead of the announcement, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee criticised the planned British sanctions, while two Israeli ministers called for retaliatory measures against London. France, also introducing a ban on West Bank products, cited the “frenzied expansion” of settlements there and a “flare-up of violence” as the reasons for it taking action. Given the small volume of exports from the settlements, the trade bans are largely symbolic, and will not dent ⁠larger bilateral trade flows, but are part of wider efforts to reinforce support for the two-state solution, just as Israel announced plans for 1,000 new West Bank homes on Tuesday. Britain, France and Canada were ‌joined by the foreign ministers of 10 other countries, including Denmark, Norway, Poland, Spain and Sweden, in a statement reaffirming support for a negotiated two-state settlement. “Together, we are resolute: the two-state solution must be protected, and we will take action in pursuit of a just and lasting peace,” they said. Miliband, who became Britain’s foreign ‌minister in July, went further, saying the UK believed that there was ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank. “Today we refuse to be bystanders to ⁠further suffering and to the destruction of the ⁠two-state solution,” Miliband said, referring to Britain’s long-held support for the two-state idea, which Israel opposes. Speaking as “a proud British Jew”, Miliband said he remained grateful to Israel for providing refuge to his grandmother after his grandfather and 60 family members were killed by ‌the Nazis. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the British ambassador in Israel to be expelled, while national security chief Itamar Ben-Gvir said he had asked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, which is accredited to the Palestinian Authority in ‌the ‌West Bank. Both Israeli ministers are sanctioned by Britain. Israeli President Isaac Herzog meanwhile accused Britain of interfering in Israel’s coming elections, due in late October. The focus of recent concerns is Israel’s E1 settlement project ‌in the West Bank not far from Jerusalem, which would cut across land the Palestinians seek for a future independent state. The United Nations, Palestinians and most countries regard settlements as illegal under international law. Israel ⁠disputes this. Israel-UK relations have become increasingly strained in recent years with London criticising Israel’s conduct in Gaza, the expansion of West Bank settlements and rising settler attacks on Palestinians. Britain in 2025 joined other countries to ⁠recognise a Palestinian state as a means to promote the two-state solution, and had already issued sanctions in relation to West Bank settlements in June. France’s ban on goods from Israeli settlements comes amid growing frustration among some European Union member states that have pushed for a bloc-wide response to settlement expansion, but have so far failed to secure the qualified majority needed for ‌EU action, largely because of opposition from countries including ‌Germany. West Bank settlements’ main produce is agricultural, including dates, citrus fruits, herbs and wine, and makes up only a tiny fraction of Israel’s total exports. Miliband said the new legislation would be in place in six to nine months, but added he was also immediately sanctioning a number of extremist settlers who he said had supported acts of violence. Recognising the threat to Israel from Iran, Miliband added that he would sanction Hezbollah-run financial institution Al-Qard Al-Hassan and would reimpose economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

title: Elon Musk says Tesla has a rare-earth-free motor. Should China be worried?
description: Elon Musk says Tesla’s new Cybercab motor has no rare earths, but analysts saw the move as only a slight step towards reducing industry reliance – or China’s leverage.
content: As Tesla CEO Elon Musk touted the motor of his company’s Cybercab – which, he claims, contains no rare earth elements – debate has emerged over whether the technology could mark a meaningful shift in electric vehicle (EV) supply chains, or undercut one of China’s trump cards in its protracted trade conflict with the US. While the move has been viewed as an effort to reduce the EV industry’s reliance on rare earths – an essential component in the permanent magnets that power electric motors – analysts said it would be difficult to meaningfully weaken China’s leverage, given the challenges of scaling the technology and the minerals’ widespread use across other industries. Their comments followed a social media post from Musk on Friday saying the motor of Tesla’s new self-driving Cybercab used no rare earth metals while maintaining the same range, a progress he described as “extremely hard to achieve”. David Zhang, general ­secretary of the Shanghai-based International Intelligent Vehicle Engineering Association, said that Tesla’s rare-earth-free motor remained largely a “commercial concept”, and it was still not certain whether the vehicle’s engine could match the efficiency and performance of conventional motors containing rare earth permanent magnets. “Musk’s recent claim reflects Tesla’s efforts to strengthen supply chain security as the US and China use advanced chips and rare earths, respectively, as leverage against each other,” he said. Zhang noted that Tesla initially used rare-earth-free AC induction motors before adopting rare earth permanent-magnet motors in mass production with the Model 3 in 2017, which offered improved performance. “I believe rare earth permanent-magnet motors will remain the mainstream solution for new-energy vehicles globally over the next five years, and Tesla’s rare-earth-free motor is unlikely to replace them at scale.” Rare earths such as neodymium and dysprosium are critical to the permanent magnets used in many EV motors, helping them deliver greater power density and efficiency. China is the world’s leading producer of rare earth elements, accounting for about 70 per cent of global rare earth mining and 90 per cent of global processing capacity, which gives its EV industry an advantage through access to a deeply integrated domestic supply chain, from raw materials and components to EVs. Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting, noted that while the move carries importance amid “geopolitical tensions over rare earths and US efforts to reduce dependency on China”, it would be hard to meaningfully reduce the EV industry’s reliance on rare earths. “Rare earths go into much more than motors in a typical EV, including in sensors, infotainment systems, displays and other electronics,” he said. “So even a rare-earth-free motor wouldn’t remove rare earths from EV supply chains; it would just narrow where they show up.” Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, also said it was “too early to call this a defining moment” or say that China had lost its “rare earths trump card”. Even if Tesla fast-tracks the technology’s application, other carmakers could face intellectual-property barriers to accessing the technology, he noted. Beyond the challenges of reducing the EV industry’s reliance on rare earths at scale, analysts pointed to their use across other key industries, suggesting China’s leverage in the sector would be difficult to erode. “Musk’s technology may overcome the bottleneck of permanent magnet motors, but there’s the uncertainty whether the same solution can be applied elsewhere, say defence equipment,” Xu said. Montufar-Helu expressed similar views, saying, “Rare earths are used across a wide range of industries and China dominates not just the supply of key rare earths but their processing as well. “That leverage will continue,” he added. Last month, China’s rare earth exports fell by 18.25 per cent year on year by volume, according to customs data released on Tuesday, as Beijing maintained tight control over shipments of the critical minerals.

title: Women’s Basketball World Cup: Han Xu stars again as China seal second spot in group
description: WNBA centre scores second double-double in two days as teen sensation Zhang Ziyu chips in to set up quarter-final qualifier with Puerto Rico.
content: Chinese WNBA player Han Xu scored a second consecutive double-double as China beat Italy 71-51 to secure second place in their group at the Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup. China’s 7ft 3in (2.33m) teenage sensation Zhang Ziyu scored eight points with perfect shooting from the field as her team established an 18-point lead at one point, while New York Liberty centre Han led the team with 19 points and 10 rebounds. Han had powered China to the comeback win against the Czech Republic the previous day, with 22 points ‌and 14 rebounds to get their campaign back on track. Against the Italians, Yang Shuyu added 15 points, five rebounds and four assists in a team-high 33 minutes, while Wang Siyu contributed five points, five rebounds, six assists and two steals. China, who lost to group winners the United States in their opening Group D match, will face Puerto Rico in a play-off for second- and third-placed teams on Wednesday. The winners will advance to meet France in the quarter-finals on Thursday. After running the US close the night before, Italy struggled to find the same energy levels in their defeat to China in front of a raucous crowd at the Max-Schmeling-Halle in Berlin. Matilde Villa led Italy with 15 points and acknowledged the game against the US on Sunday took a toll. “We spent a lot of energy, mentally and physically, and I think we felt it,” Villa said. “But yes, we didn’t approach the game in the right way, and this has to be a lesson for us. Now we will take a day off, recover, and then we will think about the next game.” Italy, back in the tournament after a 32-year wait, next face Australia on Wednesday for a place in the quarter-finals, where the winner will meet Spain. The US bounced back from their scare the night before with a 105-64 rout of the Czechs. Breanna Stewart had 19 points, seven rebounds and six assists to help the Americans win their 33rd match in a row in the tournament. The four-time defending champions now have two days off but await the winner of Tuesday’s Hungary v Japan tie. The other qualifier for the quarter-finals match sees Germany take on South Korea on Wednesday, with the winner then facing Belgium on Thursday.

title: Could China sanction US for illegal international seabed mining? A study says yes
description: But issue is said to create tension for Beijing between defending the multilateral system and protecting its own access to critical minerals.
content: For decades, the United States has used economic and financial restrictions as major foreign policy tools. But as China and other countries gain greater economic and technological strength, they are also acquiring more ways to push back against US actions, with deep-sea mining possibly becoming a testing ground for that shift. China could join other countries in taking coordinated countermeasures, including sanctions against companies, if the US proceeds with seabed mining in violation of international law, according to Bian Yongmin, a professor of international law at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing. “[However,] if the United States insists on ignoring international law, it would indeed be difficult to restrain them,” said a Beijing-based international law expert familiar with the proposal who asked not to be named, citing the sensitivity of the matter. Bian’s analysis was published in the June issue of the peer-reviewed China-based Pacific Journal. The US remained bound by customary international law governing global seabed resources, despite not being a party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), the professor wrote. The Donald Trump administration has been moving from policy to concrete preparations for seabed mineral development after issuing an executive order in April last year promoting offshore critical-mineral extraction and subsequently advancing proposed lease sales in Pacific waters. On July 16, the Marine Minerals Administration, an agency within the US Interior Department, published a proposed leasing notice for a potential mineral lease sale offshore American Samoa, with a proposed sale date of November 19 this year. On August 17, the agency issued another proposed leasing notice for potential mineral leases offshore the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, with a proposed sale date of December 16. Even though the US was not a member of Unclos did not mean Washington had a free hand on the international seabed, Bian wrote. Several principles contained in Part XI of Unclos had developed into customary international law, she added, including the principle that the international seabed was the “common heritage of mankind”, the obligation to protect the marine environment and the requirement that benefits from seabed mineral resources be shared internationally. In addition, the US’ own past conduct could weaken any argument that it had consistently rejected those rules, Bian said. In 1970, Washington voted in favour of a UN General Assembly declaration recognising the seabed beyond national jurisdiction as the common heritage of mankind. It later supported arrangements recognising benefit-sharing from deep-sea mineral development. Bian argued that the US could not, therefore, simply invoke its non-party status to Unclos to escape customary rules it had previously accepted. The legal question is likely to hinge on how US-authorised mining is ultimately carried out, including whether it appropriates international seabed resources, causes serious environmental harm or allows mining operators to retain benefits that should be shared, according to Bian’s study. The Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a mineral-rich seabed area in the northeast Pacific, covers about 4.5 million sq km (1.74 million square miles) and is estimated to contain about 21 billion tonnes of polymetallic nodules rich in nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese. The Metals Company, a Canadian firm, has an American subsidiary that applied this year for a US deep-sea mining permit to operate in the zone. The zone lies on the seabed of the high seas, and companies and organisations holding exploration licences there have agreed to follow mining rules set by the International Seabed Authority, according to Bian’s research. The deep ocean is particularly sensitive because polymetallic nodules can take millions of years to form, and experimental mining has been found to leave lasting ecological effects. For China, the issue creates a tension between defending the multilateral system and protecting access to critical minerals, with Beijing already deeply involved in international seabed development. “If the United States starts mining first, China may follow,” the unnamed expert said, adding that this was an industry view rather than a personal one. That said, China’s response would not necessarily mirror the US’ approach, according to Bian’s analysis. China could conduct seabed mining while continuing to work with the International Seabed Authority and following existing multilateral principles on the common heritage of mankind, benefit-sharing and environmental protection, Bian wrote. China has multiple exploration contracts in the international seabed area and capabilities in deep-sea equipment, mining machinery and mineral processing, with Chinese participants including China Minmetals Corporation and the China Ocean Mineral Resources Research and Development Association. Other countries are pursuing their own approaches, although they differ in scope and legal circumstances. According to Bian’s research, exploration licences in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone are also held by Belgium’s Global Sea Mineral Resources, Norway’s Loke and Green Minerals, Germany’s Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources, France’s French Research Institute for Exploitation of the Sea, Kiribati’s Marawa Research and Exploration Ltd, South Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and UK Seabed Resources. “If the United States unilaterally authorises mining, it cannot take the zone, part of the zone or other areas of the international seabed for itself or improperly prevent other countries from legally mining in the area,” Bian wrote in her study. The unnamed expert said that “Japan and the United States have already signed an agreement to develop rare earth resources on Japan’s continental shelf, which I think is an attempt that faces relatively fewer legal obstacles”. “The European Union, because of environmental concerns, may not begin deep-sea mining in the foreseeable short term,” the expert said, adding that “India’s technology is not up to it”, when asked about the South Asian country. But the most immediate response to a US breach would still be negotiation and consultation, the professor said. Coordinated action could follow if diplomacy failed. Bian wrote that countries firmly committed to upholding the multilateral mechanism for deep-sea mining could at least refuse to cooperate with American mining companies. They could also avoid buying deep-sea mineral products sold by American deep-sea mining companies and their processed products, she wrote. “Companies such as Apple, Google, Microsoft and BMW have promised not to purchase deep-sea minerals in their supply chains.” And even if American companies obtained permission, mining could not begin immediately. “Seabed mining is highly risky,” Bian said. “Even if American companies obtained permission, it could not be implemented immediately. I estimate that environmental impact assessments and other procedures will take a lot of time.” She also said environmental impacts could affect market demand for seabed minerals. “If the environmental impact is really significant, this kind of mineral may be resisted to a certain extent by the market,” Bian added. “People are reluctant to be associated with problematic products, just as they resist forced-labour products.”

title: 12 South Koreans arrested in Thailand scam centre crackdown
description: Police say the alleged scammers entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and rented a luxury house south of Bangkok.
content: Thai authorities arrested 12 South Koreans and a Chinese national accused of running a scam call centre from a high-end rented house south of Bangkok, police said on Tuesday. The alleged scammers “entered Thailand from a neighbouring country and were hiding in Samut Prakan province, renting a luxury house”, Thai police said in a statement, without naming the country. Cambodia and Myanmar, which border Thailand, have become hubs for criminal groups operating fake romance, investment and other schemes that defraud victims around the world of billions of dollars each year. But authorities in both nations have also raided scam compounds in recent months, pushing some scammers to set up elsewhere in the region.
