Inside the house in Thailand, authorities found a call centre set-up with 13 workstations equipped with Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) phones and other equipment, including dozens of computers, mobile phones and scripts allegedly used in online scams. Police also discovered a list of South Korean victims and forged documents falsely claiming to be official letters from the South Korean prosecutor’s office. “The perpetrators targeted victims in South Korea, impersonating prosecutors or South Korean government officials and making threatening phone calls,” the Thai police statement said. “The perpetrators falsely claimed to be involved in a criminal investigation and tricked victims into transferring money to them.” Thai and South Korean authorities had investigated organised criminal groups that illegally entered and hid in Thailand since last year, the statement said. Around 40 suspects accused of call centre scams, including South Koreans and Chinese, have been arrested in Thailand since 2015. The multibillion-dollar cyberscam industry has ballooned in Southeast Asia in recent years, with organised criminal groups initially mostly targeting Chinese speakers before widening their reach and targeting victims globally. They recruit and traffic scammers from around the world, with individuals from at least 80 countries and territories found in scam compounds across the Mekong region, according to a UN report.

title: Qatar’s PM vows to prioritise China’s energy supply amid Middle East tensions
description: Meeting in Beijing concludes official state visit as two sides stress importance of unimpeded maritime traffic through Strait of Hormuz.
content: Qatar on Tuesday vowed to prioritise China’s energy supply and safeguard shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, as both countries coordinated efforts to de-escalate Middle East tensions. During a meeting in Beijing, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani stressed the importance of unimpeded maritime traffic through the waterway. Sheikh Mohammed affirmed Doha’s “support for all diplomatic efforts and endeavours aimed at a solution that ensures freedom of maritime navigation and paves the way for reaching a comprehensive agreement that achieves sustainable peace in the region”, the Qatari foreign ministry said in a statement. They also examined key regional developments and the diplomatic efforts under way to de-escalate tensions and promote security and stability there, as well as reviewed strategic bilateral relations and how to expand cooperation, the statement said. According to a separate read-out by China’s foreign ministry, Sheikh Mohammed said Qatar “would overcome difficulties, prioritise China’s energy supply and work hand in hand with China to create a more brilliant next ‘golden decade’ for bilateral relations”, noting Beijing was Doha’s largest trading and energy partner. Wang said Beijing had always prioritised relations with Qatar in its Middle East diplomacy and that in recent years bilateral strategic partnership had yielded considerable progress, with growing mutual political trust and deepening mutually beneficial cooperation. “China is Qatar’s most reliable and longest-term partner in its development process,” Beijing’s top diplomat added, calling for consolidating and expanding cooperation in traditional and new energy, investment, advanced technology and people-to-people exchanges. Noting that China firmly supported Qatar in safeguarding its national sovereignty, independence, security and stability, Wang asserted that Qatar would continue to offer firm support on issues concerning China’s core interests. He also expressed appreciation for Qatar’s “long-term commitment to mediating hotspot issues” and its contributions to easing disputes and seeking peace, saying Beijing stood ready to maintain communication and coordination with Doha on international and regional affairs. Sheikh Mohammed also met on Tuesday with founders, chairpersons, and executives of a number of Chinese companies on the meeting’s sidelines, where they discussed cooperative relations, along with a number of topics of common interest, the Gulf Times reported. The foreign minister-level talks followed Monday’s meeting between Chinese Premier Li Qiang and Sheikh Mohammed, who was on an official two-day visit to Beijing aimed at bolstering bilateral ties. Li pledged to deepen cooperation in energy, investment, artificial intelligence and diplomatic efforts to ease Middle East tensions. The Chinese premier described Qatar as an important strategic partner in the Gulf and voiced support for Doha’s role mediating regional disputes. On Tuesday, Wang elaborated on Beijing’s vision for a “new regional security architecture”, echoing a four-point proposal put forward last week by Chinese President Xi Jinping during his state visit to Egypt. Xi urged regional countries to become “masters of their own destiny”, reject external interference and place economic development at the heart of “regional common security”. Wang said current tensions in the Middle East and Gulf were seriously affecting the security of regional countries, as well as energy, shipping and supply-chain stability. “Pressure through the use of force is not the way forward. Dialogue and negotiation are the only viable path.” Without naming Iran or other Gulf states, Wang said the sovereignty and security of regional countries should be fully respected and the legitimate concerns of all parties properly addressed. “China is willing … to strengthen communication and coordination with Qatar and other regional parties, support regional countries in taking their future and destiny into their own hands, restore regional peace and stability as soon as possible, and establish a fair and reasonable new regional security architecture,” he added. Sheikh Mohammed said Qatar appreciated China’s “objective and impartial” position and supported Beijing’s initiatives on promoting Middle East security. Qatar was willing to strengthen coordination with China to safeguard the security of global energy channels, restore regional peace and stability at an early date, and explore a security architecture that reflected the independent spirit of regional countries, he added. The discussions took place against the backdrop of continuing regional tensions and diplomatic efforts to keep the Strait of Hormuz open. The push to secure the strait is critical for both countries’ energy security. Qatar’s LNG exports supply nearly one‑third of China’s demand for liquefied natural gas, while the strait remains a vital chokepoint for global energy flows. Since 2020, China has been Qatar’s largest trading partner and top export destination, with bilateral trade rising from US$10.6 billion in 2014 to US$24.22 billion in 2024, according to Cao Xiaolin, China’s ambassador to Doha. In recent months, Qatar has positioned itself as a mediator, maintaining channels with Iran while hosting a major US military presence. The meetings with Li and Wang highlight the careful balancing act Gulf states continue to perform as they deepen economic and political engagement with Beijing alongside long-standing security ties with Washington.

title: Opinion | Openness must not be sacrificed in US science and tech policy on China
description: It’s not engagement vs security. The challenge is smart openness: protecting what matters without hurting a great US scientific strength.
content: When President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his planned September 24 visit – his first state-level visit to Washington in more than a decade – artificial intelligence is expected to be near the top of the agenda. Both administrations are preparing for their first formal dialogue on AI. Washington has framed much of that conversation around the need for tighter controls on sensitive technologies. That framing is the problem. For much of the debate over US science and technology policy towards China, Washington has been stuck on a false choice between engagement (scientific exchange, international students and collaborative research) and security (export controls, research restrictions and visa limits). The real choice is between indiscriminate restriction and disciplined risk management. The security concerns are genuine. Some advanced technologies have clear military or intelligence applications. Universities must take seriously undisclosed affiliations, conflicts of commitment and improper technology transfer. Federal research security policy already requires extensive disclosure of appointments, foreign support, affiliations and potential conflicts of interest and commitment. Advanced computing, semiconductors, quantum science, biotechnology and AI all raise legitimate national security questions, largely because so much of the work is dual-use[end optional trim. But acknowledging those risks does not require treating every interaction with China as equally dangerous. The challenge is to protect what truly matters without damaging the openness that has long been one of America’s greatest scientific strengths. Smart openness starts from a simple premise: technologies are not equally sensitive and not every Chinese institution carries the same risk. Military-relevant quantum sensing is not cooperation in basic mathematics or astrophysics. A researcher who conceals ties to a defence laboratory has little in common with a Chinese graduate student studying theoretical chemistry. Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing. Policy too often blurs those distinctions. Once national security becomes the primary lens for nearly every scientific interaction with China, agencies and universities turn deeply risk-averse. Restrictions spread, compliance burdens grow and institutions abandon perfectly legal activities because they look politically risky. The result can be self-defeating: measures meant to protect American technological leadership can erode elements of the research system that produce it. Research Caroline Wagner and I conducted for the Quincy Institute has argued that a more sustainable approach would distinguish genuine security risks from ordinary international scientific collaboration, rather than treat broad categories of China-related activity as inherently suspect. American pre-eminence in science was built in substantial part on imported knowledge and talent. The National Science Board reports that foreign-born workers accounted for 43 per cent of the US science and engineering workforce at the doctorate level in 2021; among foreign-born science and engineering workers, China is one of the two leading countries of origin. Chinese students and researchers have made tangible contributions to American science and technology. China has also gained substantially from its access to the US research ecosystem, and concerns about technology transfer are well founded. Policy has to hold both facts at once. Washington should begin by defining critical technologies more narrowly and updating those definitions regularly. Controls should focus on identifiable capabilities with plausible national security consequences, not on sprawling categories like “AI” or “biotechnology.” A “small yard, high fence” approach works only if the yard stays small. The government should also build a genuinely tiered framework for international research collaboration. The most sensitive technologies, and institutions closely tied to China’s military and security apparatus, warrant heightened scrutiny or outright prohibition. Dual-use research should proceed under disclosure rules, access controls and institutional review. Fundamental research outside those categories should remain open. Washington should move away from nationality-based screening as well. Visa and research-access decisions should turn on affiliations, research fields, access to controlled information and disclosure records – not on citizenship or country of birth. A Chinese passport is not evidence of a security threat. Universities receiving substantial federal funding should maintain serious research-security capabilities, conduct due diligence on sensitive collaborations and enforce disclosure requirements. In return, universities need clearer and more consistent federal rules. Institutions should not be punished after the fact because a government assessment shifted. Washington also needs a firmer distinction between disclosure violations and espionage. Researchers who hide material foreign affiliations or funding should face consequences. But a disclosure failure is not by itself proof of illicit technology transfer. The United States should treat talent attraction as a national security asset. Foreign students who earn advanced American degrees in important scientific and engineering fields deserve clearer pathways to stay, subject to appropriate screening. It makes little strategic sense to educate exceptional people, then push them to build their careers elsewhere. The importance of this talent pool is particularly evident in advanced science and engineering: more than half of doctorate-level computer and mathematical scientists and engineers working in the US were born abroad. In the competition for scientific talent, the ability to attract and retain such researchers is one of America’s most important structural advantages. Finally, major restrictions should face a competitiveness test. Policymakers should ask not only what a measure prevents China from obtaining, but what it costs the US in lost talent, weaker collaboration, slower innovation and incentives for other countries to reduce their dependence on American technology. That calculation is too often missing. The competition runs deeper than technology. It is a contest over where the world’s best scientists, engineers and entrepreneurs choose to build their careers, and openness remains a decisive American advantage. Access to China’s talent pool has real strategic value. The US does not have to choose between security and openness, though it does have to get better at both. A good place to start is by re-energising the US-China Science and Technology Cooperation Agreement, revised and extended for five years in December 2024. The amended agreement already comes close to the model we need: it limits government-to-government cooperation to basic research while adding stronger safeguards concerning national security, intellectual property, transparency, data reciprocity, and researcher safety and security. Rather than retreat from scientific engagement, Washington should build on it, drawing sharper lines around genuinely sensitive technologies while preserving room for collaboration where the risks are manageable. The measure of a successful China policy is not how many doors America can close. It is whether the country can protect what needs protecting without sacrificing the openness, international talent and collaboration that have long been among its greatest sources of strength.

title: Thousands of Ecuadorians flee their homes as gang violence worsens
description: Ecuador recorded 9,216 violent deaths last year, a homicide rate of 51 per 100,000 inhabitants.
content: For one grandmother, it was when bullets began hitting ⁠the rooftops of her neighbourhood that she decided she would have to leave the housing development ⁠where she had lived for nearly 20 years. A sharp rise in fighting between gang factions in Ecuador has prompted thousands of families to flee and abandon their homes to the gangs, who strip the houses for drug money or use them to hide kidnapping victims, according to residents and police. One of the areas that has been the site of the heaviest bloodshed is the Nueva Prosperina district in the coastal city of Guayaquil, where fighting between factions of the Los Tiguerones gang last year killed 22 people. Among those who fled was a 66-year-old woman, who, like other residents of the district Reuters spoke to for ‌this story, asked not to be identified for fear of reprisals from the gangs. Armed groups were targeting people indiscriminately, assuming that anyone entering the neighbourhood belonged to a different gang, she said. She worried that if she had stayed, her daughter, who commutes to work on a motorcycle, could be killed or her teenage grandson recruited. “It was a terrible situation. Bullets were hitting the rooftops and that made me leave,” she said. The woman and her family are among more than 300,000 people in Ecuador who have left their homes over the past three years because of violence, including death threats, extortion, recruitment by criminal groups or the murder of relatives, according to the UN Refugee Agency and the Ombudsman’s Office, though advocates say the true figure could be higher. Ecuador, once considered a relatively safe part of Latin America, now has the region’s third-highest level of internal displacement behind Haiti and Colombia, according to the Norwegian Refugee Council. Displacement has ⁠been driven by a sustained rise in nationwide violence, says the Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights in Guayaquil. President Daniel Noboa took office in 2023 vowing a crackdown on the violence, which derives from Ecuador’s increasing role as a drug transit ‌hub. But Noboa’s security strategy had not curbed the violence and could even have worsened it, said the Guayaquil human rights committee. Killings and arrests of criminal leaders have caused many groups to splinter into rival factions fighting over territory. Ecuador recorded 9,216 violent deaths last year, a homicide rate of 51 per 100,000 inhabitants, some eight times higher than its rate of a decade ago and well ‌above rates of 21.4 in Mexico and 25.8 in Colombia reported last year by authorities in those countries. Noboa’s government says its strategy is nonetheless systematically diminishing criminal groups and killings fell 8 per cent between January and July ⁠this year compared with the same period in 2025. Most ⁠of those killed are linked to gangs, the government says. ‘Free inside our homes’ Criminal gangs use extortion as a systematic means of control in neighbourhoods across the country, according to police and the Ombudsman’s Office. Half of the families living in Nueva Prosperina have suffered some form of extortion, according to projections by local ‌police. “A WhatsApp message has almost the same impact as a bomb,” said the Norwegian Refugee Council’s Francesco Volpi. “It is indiscriminate extortion.” One 45-year-old shopkeeper said he fled Nueva Prosperina after his children received death threats by gangs seeking to recruit them and after intimidation by people he identified as police officers. Nueva Prosperina police chief Gino Pillajo said several people ‌in the district had been arrested for impersonating police officers. Many cases of extortion were unreported because of fear, making them difficult to investigate, he added. According to Pillajo, police work with community leaders to gather information about extortion and post QR codes in local ‌shops to allow people to report anonymously. Officers also accompany residents when they leave, to provide security and to allow them to map where owners are absent. The violence and displacement are not confined to Guayaquil. Chachi Indigenous communities near the Colombian border ⁠have temporarily abandoned their territory because of threats from illegal miners, according to the Ombudsman’s Office. In Babahoyo, in Los Rios province, businesses close early as a self-protection measure, while in the Amazon province of Sucumbios families are abandoning their land to prevent criminal groups ⁠from persuading young people to join them, according to cases reported by the Norwegian Refugee Council. Government officials Reuters spoke to acknowledged the problem but said they did not know which agency was responsible for dealing with forced displacement. Noboa’s press office did not respond to a request for comment. “There is no legal recognition of internal forced displacement caused by violence, and that means the phenomenon is not discussed, no action is taken to protect victims, ‌and no mechanisms are created to monitor and assist affected communities,” said ‌Billy Navarrete, the head of the Guayaquil human rights committee. That complicates the delivery of assistance to victims of displacement, many of whom end up staying with family in other neighbourhoods or even moving cities. Other families – hamstrung by lack of resources or support networks, or fear of abandoning their belongings – are forced to live alongside the gangs. “We have to stay silent. We are silent accomplices. We can’t say anything because our lives are at risk,” said a Nueva Prosperina resident. She said gangs used the neighbourhood to hide kidnapping victims, hold banned community events, and inspect residents’ cellphones to make sure they did not belong to rival gangs. “We are free inside our homes, but outside we are prisoners,” said the 49-year-old woman. “They make the rules. If they don’t want you there, they throw you out.”

title: HKU launches wealth management academy to boost city’s role as hub for ‘new money’
description: Cross-border wealth in Hong Kong reached US$2.95 trillion in 2025, compared with Switzerland’s US$2.94 trillion, according to BCG.
content: Hong Kong’s first university-led wealth management academy was launched on Tuesday, as the city’s rapidly expanding private-wealth industry competes for professionals capable of serving increasingly sophisticated and international clients. The Wealth Management Academy, established by The University of Hong Kong Business School, aims to bring together policymakers, financial institutions and academics to train professionals for the wealth management, asset management and family-office sectors. It seeks to connect “policy, industry, academics and research”, with talent development as its overarching objective, according to HKU. “The quality of human capital ultimately determines how well financial capital is managed,” said Christopher Hui, Hong Kong’s secretary for financial services and the treasury, during a keynote speech at the academy’s inauguration ceremony on Tuesday. Hui said Hong Kong’s connections with mainland China and the wider world gave the city a “distinctive role”, and that the wealth management industry increasingly required professionals capable of handling investment, succession, governance and cross-border issues. The launch comes amid rising demand for wealth management professionals and talent as Hong Kong seeks to consolidate its position as a global wealth hub. The city has overtaken Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth management centre. Cross-border wealth reached US$2.95 trillion in 2025, compared with Switzerland’s US$2.94 trillion, according to Boston Consulting Group. “Switzerland is mostly [about] old money from the West, and Hong Kong needs to do new money from the East,” said Hongbin Cai, dean of HKU Business School. Hong Kong could attract new wealth not only from mainland China but also from emerging markets in the region, he added. The academy builds on HKU’s existing wealth-management education programmes. The university launched its undergraduate asset management and private banking programme in 2017, followed by a master’s programme in wealth management and family wealth management in 2024 and 2025, according to a handout from HKU. The academy will focus on research, talent development and industry engagement, while organising activities including scholarships, forums, company visits and practitioner dialogues, according to the handout.

title: Tour industry protests over Taiwan’s new mainland China travel registration rules
description: KMT politicians accuse ruling DPP of turning cross-strait exchanges into an election issue ahead of year-end local polls.
content: Taiwan’s opposition and tour operators have hit back at new registration rules for travellers heading to mainland China, with politicians accusing the ruling Democratic Progressive Party of trying to fan cross-strait fears ahead of local elections. Since September 1, travellers to the mainland, Hong Kong and Macau have been required to register details of their trip, including the purpose of their visit, contact information, travel dates as well as the numbers of their passports and mainland travel permits. Travel agencies handling mainland-bound inspection visits, exchanges and privately organised groups must submit the information on behalf of their clients or face fines of between NT$10,000 and NT$50,000 (US$330-US$1,650). The move came ahead of new mainland entry and exit regulations taking effect on September 15, which Taipei has warned could increase risks for Taiwanese visitors. But travel operators questioned why they should be held responsible if travellers refused to register or give their details. “Working in the travel industry now feels like selling drugs. We have to operate on the sly, and if we’re caught, we get fined. Are they really trying to force us out of business?” Taipei-based tour operator Lan Hsueh-hua said. Another operator, Chen Chien-chin, said agencies could find themselves caught between personal data protection requirements and penalties for failing to register travellers. “A travel agency might make only NT$300 or NT$500 from selling an air ticket. What have we done to deserve this?” he said, adding that seven or eight independent travellers had already cancelled planned trips because of the controversy. Tourism industry leaders called the policy unreasonable and urged the sector to challenge it. “Do the administrative authorities have sufficient legal grounds to require travel agencies to register the information and penalise those that fail to comply?” said Hsiao Po-jen, chairman of the Taipei-based Taiwan Straits Travel Development Association. He argued that such obligations and penalties required “explicit statutory authorisation”. Critics have also questioned whether the rules are meant to reinforce negative perceptions about mainland travel at a politically sensitive time. Hung Mong-kai, a legislator with the main opposition Kuomintang (KMT), accused the DPP of “turning cross-strait exchanges into an election issue”, suggesting that the policy was an attempt to revive the DPP’s “resist China, protect Taiwan” campaign strategy before voters elected mayors and county magistrates later this year. Fellow KMT lawmaker Weng Hsiao-ling said the DPP was “turning back the clock” by restricting the freedom of movement it once promoted. Weng said that under Taiwan’s constitution, Taiwanese had the right to travel overseas without government interference. People are voting with their feet Lee Chi-yuen, High Quality of Travel Association She also questioned the repeated warnings by Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) about the dangers of mainland travel, arguing that Taiwanese could face even tougher scrutiny when entering the United States. The government, however, has insisted the registration is intended to protect travellers rather than restrict them. MAC spokesman Liang Wen-chieh said registration would enable the authorities to identify and help Taiwanese during emergencies. Liang said that travellers who refused to register “would not be forced to do so”, although he did not clarify whether agencies could still be fined if their customers did not comply. He also pointed to Taiwanese reported missing, questioned or suspected of being detained on the mainland as evidence of the risks. According to the MAC, 426 Taiwanese were reported missing, detained for questioning or suspected of having their personal freedom restricted on the mainland between January 2024 and August 27 this year – figures that Beijing dismisses as exaggerated. Despite those warnings, the number of Taiwanese travelling to the mainland has continued to rise. Taiwan’s Tourism Administration recorded 1.85 million cross-strait visits in the first half of this year, making the mainland the second-most-popular overseas destination after Japan for Taiwanese travellers. Mainland figures put the number substantially higher at 2.85 million, up 24.9 per cent year on year. Lee Chi-yuen, chairman of the Taipei-based High Quality of Travel Association, said the trend suggested that Taiwanese were making their own assessment of the risks. “The government has repeatedly used various means to tell the public that travelling to the mainland is dangerous, but the number of people going there has continued to increase every year,” he said. “People are voting with their feet.” Beijing has also accused the DPP of exaggerating the dangers to discourage cross-strait exchanges. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. Washington opposes any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to providing it with the means to defend itself.

title: Copper rally sets record price on LME as US tariff fears fuel ‘scramble’ for stockpiles
description: Inventories of the metal are diverging across major exchanges as AI infrastructure build-up spurs demand and potential trade restrictions keep prices elevated.
content: Copper prices have surged to an all-time high on the London Metal Exchange (LME) amid anticipations of potential US tariffs and a tightening supply crunch, with analysts expecting prices to remain elevated in the short term. Benchmark three-month copper futures closed at US$14,510 a tonne on Monday, after rising to a record high of US$14,533 a tonne earlier in the session, surpassing the previous record set in January. The rally came with the market widely expecting the United States to expand tariffs to imports of refined copper starting next year, analysts at China Asset Management wrote in a note on Tuesday. “This expectation has prompted American buyers to stockpile before restrictions take effect,” the analysts said, triggering what they described as an early “transpacific and transatlantic scramble for copper”. This has driven a sharp divergence in global inventories, according to the note, with inventories on New York’s Commodity Exchange (Comex) rising significantly, while LME inventories have fallen to a near five-month low. Inventories in Shanghai Futures Exchange warehouses have also dropped to their lowest level since 2024. The surge of shipments to the US is also driven by price differentials between New York and London contracts, with elevated premiums on Comex futures creating a lucrative arbitrage window. “As long as the [US’] refined-copper tariff policy is not finalised, the Comex-LME price spread will continue to offer event-driven trading opportunities,” Cinda Futures analysts Lou Jiahao and Ma Ziyao wrote in a research note on Tuesday. They noted, however, that elevated Comex inventories were providing a buffer against future demand, and that subsequent stockpiling by US buyers might experience slight, phased fluctuations. A key material used in a broad range of industries, including electronics and clean energy, copper has seen its price increase by about 16 per cent on the LME this year. Amid an artificial intelligence boom, the global roll-out of related infrastructure – including data centres and power grids – has strengthened demand. The rally has continued in the two months since the US Department of Commerce was due to submit a report to the White House on whether to proceed with previously proposed tariffs of 15 per cent on refined-copper imports starting in January, rising to 30 per cent from 2028. Meanwhile, supply constraints in Chile, the world’s largest copper producer, have also pushed prices higher. Chilean state copper agency Cochilco last month noted that the country’s production of the metal was expected to fall 2.6 per cent this year to 5.27 million tonnes. Exports from the country last month fell 14 per cent in value terms from July and were down 3.2 per cent from a year earlier, according to data from the Chilean central bank. Extreme weather in the last two months has disrupted mining operations and shipping in South America, although outbound volumes have since begun to recover, according to the analysts from Cinda Futures. Low inventories and expectations of a peak season through October were set to keep the copper supply tight in the short term, Lou and Ma said. Beyond October, support for prices was expected to weaken marginally, as interrupted mining operations resume and US stockpiling demand moderates slightly, the two noted. “In the long term, insufficient global capital expenditure on copper mines and declining grades at older mines will keep supply elasticity low over the next one to two years, while emerging demand – from power grids, energy storage, new-energy infrastructure, and AI data centres – remains in an expansionary cycle,” they said.

title: Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou retains crown as world’s top innovation hub
description: Hong Kong government says ranking by UN body reaffirms Greater Bay Area’s ‘outstanding innovative capacity’ and strong financing ecosystem.
content: A cluster comprising Hong Kong and two mainland Chinese cities has been ranked the world’s top innovation hub for the second consecutive year by a United Nations body. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster retained its crown in the 2026 Global Innovation Index released by the World Intellectual Property Organization on Tuesday. Tokyo-Yokohama, San Jose-San Francisco, Seoul and Beijing followed in the rankings. A government spokesman welcomed the ranking, saying it reaffirmed the Greater Bay Area’s “outstanding innovative capacity” and its strong financing ecosystem for innovation and technology (I&T). He said the city would “proactively align with the national 15th five-year plan to strengthen its strategic positioning” as an international I&T centre. The government would also deepen collaboration across the bay area – which refers to Beijing’s initiative to turn Hong Kong, Macau and nine mainland cities into an integrated hi-tech economic powerhouse – to help build a modern industrial system and support national technological self-reliance, he said. The ranking identifies local concentrations of world-class innovation activity using three key metrics: international patent filings via the organisation, scientific publications and venture capital deals. For 2026’s ranking, the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster filed 2,259 patent applications, published 4,060 scientific articles and had 138 venture capital deals per 1 million inhabitants over the last five years. Huawei Technologies was the top patent applicant in the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster, while Sun Yat-sen University in Guangzhou was the leading publishing organisation, the report showed. Mitsubishi Electric and the University of Tokyo led patent filings and publications in Tokyo-Yokohama, while Google and Stanford University topped those categories in San Jose-San Francisco. Samsung Electronics stood out as the top patent filer in four economies: Seoul, Bengaluru, Moscow and Warsaw. China ranked first globally with 25 innovation clusters, followed by the United States with 20. Germany had seven, while the United Kingdom and India each had four. The report also published an Innovation Intensity Ranking, in which San Jose-Francisco topped the list with a total innovation intensity share of 1.836 per capita. Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou ranked 44 with a score of 0.278, up one spot from 2025. The government spokesman said authorities remained committed to enhancing the I&T ecosystem, continuing to develop the original grant patent system and introducing the patent box regime, which offers tax breaks on intellectual property income to promote innovation. The number of start-ups rose from over 1,500 in 2015 to more than 5,200 in 2025, while Hong Kong Science Park and Cyberport have collectively produced about 20 unicorns – privately held companies valued at over US$1 billion – to date, he said. More than 100 technology enterprises and institutions had signed leases and begun moving into the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park, which opened in December 2025, the spokesman said, adding that the San Tin Technopole Company was also established in June 2026 to press ahead with the development of 210 hectares (519 acres) of I&T land in the zone. The spokesman said Hong Kong had a vibrant private equity market with assets under management close to US$250 billion, adding that the government was boosting venture financing to support start-ups at every stage – from university research and early seed funding to expansion, commercial launch and global growth. Victor Kwok Hoi-kit, deputy research director of Our Hong Kong Foundation, noted that venture capital deals per 1 million inhabitants saw only a modest increase, rising from 135 last year to 138 in 2026. “There is still room for improvement in financing activity,” Kwok said. “If we can better leverage our role in private capital, we can further transform our strength in scientific research and development into industrial and capital results.” He added that as an international financial centre, Hong Kong should leverage government-guided funds and international venture capital networks to attract more global investment both to the city and the wider bay area. Francis Fong Po-kiu, honorary president of the Hong Kong Information Technology Federation, said the city played a bridging role within the Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou cluster. Amid rising geopolitical tensions, marked by US tariffs and sanctions, Hong Kong should capitalise on its status as a dual gateway, serving as an entry point for foreign businesses into the mainland and a launchpad for enterprises from over the border expanding globally, Fong said. He also said the cluster’s relatively lower per capita innovation intensity ranking was primarily due to its massive population base and noted that it continued to close the gap with the US across various fields of technological innovation.

title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats, Moscow vows ‘painful’ response
description: Budapest says the envoys had acted in ways incompatible with their status, but stresses the decision does not mean cutting ties with Russia.
content: Hungary ⁠expelled 10 Russian diplomats on ⁠Tuesday, saying they had acted in ways incompatible with their diplomatic status, in a stark reminder that the pro-Russian years of former prime minister Viktor Orban are over. Russia’s foreign ministry ‌said it would retaliate and its response would be painful for Hungary, local media reported. “The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” said foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. Orban, swept from power in Hungary in April after 16 years in office, had kept close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin even after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February ⁠2022. Under him, Hungary continued buying Russian oil and gas, held up European Union ‌sanctions on Russia and blocked a €90 billion (US$97 billion) EU loan to Ukraine. After Russia invaded Ukraine, many European countries expelled ‌dozens of Russian diplomats, while Hungary expelled none. Until Tuesday, it ⁠had not ⁠sent any home publicly since 2018. Those kicked out “were engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable ‌for diplomats under the Vienna Convention”, Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban, who is not related ‌to the former ‌prime minister, said in an emailed statement on Tuesday. “This decision … does ‌not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue ⁠the necessary dialogue,” the statement added. New Prime Minister Peter Magyar and his ⁠centre-right government have repeatedly said that Hungary’s main alliances are the EU and Nato and that the government aims to rebuild trust ‌eroded under Viktor ‌Orban. In a parliamentary hearing in May, Anita Orban said Russia would “remain a partner” but the relationship could not be based on “one-sided dependency”, adding that Moscow’s policies posed a security challenge to Hungary and Europe. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Hong Kong Ballet takes on China’s Mogao Caves in Dunhuang: In Search of Light
description: Choreographers Ricky Hu and Mai Jingwen reveal their new production for Hong Kong Ballet inspired by the Mogao Caves in Dunhuang.
content: When Hong Kong Ballet’s resident choreographer Ricky Hu Songwei and his wife, fellow choreographer Mai Jingwen, were assigned to create a new production inspired by Dunhuang for the company, they had what they describe as “an immediate headache”. Dunhuang, in northwestern China, is known for the Mogao Caves, a Unesco World Heritage site on the ancient Silk Road featuring more than 1,000 years of Buddhist rock art. Over the years, its murals and statues have inspired numerous dance productions across China, all bringing the site’s wall paintings to life by blending classical ballet techniques with Dunhuang dance movements. “There are so many dance dramas based on Dunhuang themes already, so how could we create something different from theirs?” Mai says. Audiences often arrive with fixed stereotypes of the murals or feel they need academic preparation, she adds. “That’s why we were bashing our brains to find a story that would genuinely resonate.” The two, with the Hong Kong Ballet team, visited the caves in October last year to look for inspiration for Dunhuang: In Search of Light, set to premiere on October 16 at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre. The show is co-commissioned by the Greater Bay Area International Theatre Festival, which will run until December, and is co-produced by the China Arts and Entertainment Group. Plans to run Dunhuang: In Search of Light in the rest of the Greater Bay Area have yet to be announced. Not what they anticipated Hu and Mai expected to be stunned by grand sculptures lit by floodlights and surrounded by intricate, elaborate wall paintings. To their surprise, the grottoes – which number in the hundreds – were kept pitch dark to protect the murals from degrading. They could not see a thing until the guide used a flashlight. “We felt deeply shaken, not so much by the visual impact, but by the quiet dedication of these painters who settled down calmly inside a dark grotto to paint for an entire lifetime,” Hu says. Hu and Mai spent another week studying classical Dunhuang dance in Lanzhou, the capital city of Gansu province. While figures like the Nine-Coloured Deer and the Flying Apsaras – recurring art motifs in the caves – will feature in their new production, the pair chose not to merely replicate traditional styles, focusing instead on a spiritual journey. Hu says one of the most memorable grottoes was Cave 158. “We went through a narrow path to arrive at the famous, massive reclining Buddha and its murals. This cave depicts the Buddha’s Parinirvana,” he says, referring to the Buddhist state of final liberation and release from the cycle of rebirth and suffering. “This reminded us of Hermann Hesse’s 1922 novel Siddhartha, which we read a long time ago. In the story, set in India, a man looks back at the different moments of desire, separation and suffering in his life just as he is about to reach ultimate fulfilment.” Their ballet production is a contemporary adaptation of Siddhartha merged with their own experience of “enlightenment” in Dunhuang. “Perhaps, for the Dunhuang painters, their ultimate purpose in life was artistic pursuit,” Mai says. “For us choreographers, our journey is about evolving from pursuing box-office successes to pushing our creative boundaries. “I hope our audiences can be inspired to find their own journey of enlightenment after watching our show.” She adds that seeking one’s purpose in life is a universal topic that resonates across time and cultures. “It is paramount, perhaps even more so today, that urban dwellers with hectic lifestyles take time to reflect on what they truly want and need.” Telling stories through ballet The project brings the pair full circle. Having begun their training in Chinese folk dance before transitioning to choreography, they found their foundational muscle memory gave them an edge in mastering the specific demands of Dunhuang dance. In ballet, they explain, movements stretch the body upwards, whereas in Chinese dance, the body tends to sink downwards. In Dunhuang dance specifically, dancers bend their limbs and fingers to form angular postures that mimic the characters depicted in the murals. “For a ballet dancer, this presents significant challenges,” Mai says. Instead of constantly blending the styles, the choreographers prefer to present the two genres in distinct scenes based on what works best aesthetically on stage. Mai and Hu have previously worked on several ballet productions telling traditional folk stories, such as the classic Chinese love story The Butterfly Lovers for Hong Kong Ballet in 2024 and Magpie Bridge – also known as Love Bridge, based on the Chinese myth of the Cowherd and Weaver Girl – for Suzhou Ballet Theatre in 2025. “Through these productions, we’ve gradually found our unique voice for telling stories through ballet and our identity as choreographers,” Mai says. Compared to their award-winning The Butterfly Lovers, the new production relies on abstract emotion rather than concrete plot. For Mai, this contemporary approach offers immense creative freedom. “True cultural preservation isn’t about blindly repeating the past,” she says. “It’s about tracing your roots to illuminate your own journey.” Dunhuang: In Search of Light, Hong Kong Ballet, Grand Theatre, Hong Kong Cultural Centre, 10 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui. October 16-18. For more information, visit hkballet.com.

title: China’s highest court sets out new AI red lines with rules on deepfakes and privacy
description: New guidelines provide a broader legal framework for everything from privacy breaches and sexual content to fraud and consumer protection.
content: China’s top court has issued new guidance on how judges should handle civil cases involving artificial intelligence, setting out rules on liability for deepfakes, voice cloning, hallucinations and violations of personal rights. Although Beijing has yet to pass a dedicated AI law, the guidelines expand the country’s legal framework governing the technology. The Supreme People’s Court’s 24-article opinion, released on Monday, instead provides guidance for handling AI-related disputes under existing laws, including the Civil Code, Cybersecurity Law, Copyright Law and Personal Information Protection Law. The rules were the first of their kind and aimed to “draw clear legal red lines” while supporting innovation and development, the court said, aligning itself with the current national policy. A major focus of the opinion was the use of AI to create deepfake images and videos, clone people’s voices and digitally “bring the dead back to life”. The court said this could infringe legal protections covering aspects of a person’s identity and elements such as their image, voice and reputation. Si Yanli, deputy director of the Supreme People’s Court’s research office, told a press conference that using AI without consent to generate and publish an identifiable digital likeness of someone could infringe their rights. Using a person’s voice as training data without consent to generate a recognisable synthetic voice by imitating their timbre, tone and speaking style could also be an infringement. The top court also cited media reports about “one-click undressing” tools used to create sexualised images of people, saying victims could apply for an injunction if failing to stop the spread of sexualised material could cause irreparable harm. Courts could also order people to stop spreading sexualised material or require internet platforms and AI service providers to act to prevent further harm, the guidelines said. The court said the damage from such abuse was difficult to reverse because AI-generated content could be produced at low cost and spread rapidly. “The traditional approach of seeking redress through litigation after the fact is not conducive to providing timely and effective protection for victims’ legitimate rights, making the proper application of personal-rights injunctions particularly important,” the court said. It also warned that the serious misuse of deepfake technology, including for fraud, defamation, personal-information violations and the production or distribution of obscene materials, could result in criminal liability. The guidelines also set out when generative AI providers could be held responsible for content that damaged people’s reputations or breached their privacy. They would not be expected to screen every prompt and output in advance, but could be held liable if they failed to act after being notified of infringements. Meanwhile, users who deliberately used AI to generate such content could also be held liable. Other areas covered in the guidelines include consumer disputes, such as “big-data price discrimination”, where algorithms are used to offer customers different prices and terms for the same products, and AI-generated impersonations of celebrities in live-stream sales. Consumers will be able to seek punitive damages when such impersonation constitutes fraud. The guidelines were less clear on copyright disputes and did not rule on whether AI-generated content could itself qualify for copyright protection or whether using copyrighted works without permission to train AI models constituted infringement. Instead, courts were instructed to consider factors including the type of AI service, the source of training data, the parties’ participation and measures taken to prevent infringement when determining liability in such cases. Wang Liming, a vice-president of the China Law Society and a professor at Renmin University, wrote in an article published by the official People’s Court Daily on Tuesday that China should adopt a different approach to both the European Union and the United States. He said the EU’s approach prioritised security and strong regulation, while the US placed greater emphasis on development and lighter regulation. “China should avoid the constraints of both models and seek a balance between AI development and security,” he wrote. He said the court’s guidelines reflected a distinctly Chinese approach to AI judicial governance, which made support for innovation and development a fundamental principle. In contrast, the latest additions to the EU’s AI Act, which came into force last month, will oblige tech firms to make AI-generated content identifiable. Meanwhile, those using deepfakes will also be required to disclose that the content is artificial.

title: Indonesia knew a volcano was erupting. Could it have prepared better?
description: An expert advises Jakarta to take steps such as announcing evacuation routes and releasing maps following a pre-eruption alert.
content: The eruption of Anak Krakatoa in Indonesia has tested the country’s disaster preparedness, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights carrying more than 340,000 passengers as volcanic ash spread across the region. Authorities say they are monitoring the volcano, which remains under the country’s second-highest alert status. According to scientists, the event’s exceptional scale makes its impact hard to anticipate. The eruption has renewed debate on whether Indonesia’s monitoring and disaster planning can be strengthened. On Friday, the volcano, situated on the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra, started its 25-hour “continuous” eruption, according to the Geological Agency. The agency this week said the probability of further eruptions from Anak Krakatoa in the near future “remains high”, as the volcano could eject “incandescent rocks accompanied by heavy ashfall” as well as “lava flows”. Volcanic ash reached as high as 50,000 feet (15,240 metres) on Monday, meteorological agency BMKG said. Jakarta’s principal airport Soekarno-Hatta resumed operations on Tuesday, alongside seven other air hubs whose operations were previously halted due to volcanic ash. As of Monday afternoon, a total of 2,961 flights and 341,000 passengers were affected by the halted airport operations, including 622 international flights, according to Indonesia’s Transport Ministry. Indonesians have taken to social media to vent frustration over what many perceive as a sluggish official response. The Geological Agency had placed the volcano under siaga, or alert level 3, the second-highest warning status, since early July. In a viral social media post on Sunday, a user pointed to the alert and said: “So if you say that it can’t be predicted, that’s clearly a big mistake.” Many were also frustrated by skyrocketing prices for protective N95 masks on major e-commerce platforms, which officials have recommended using as thick volcanic dust settled over cities like Jakarta and Bandung. According to one social media user, the price of a box of 35 N95 masks, usually priced at 34,500 rupiah (US$2), has increased to 120,000 rupiah. President Prabowo Subianto said in a statement on Sunday that the government “continues” to monitor the situation and would “provide the necessary protection and assistance to the community”. “To people affected by volcanic ash, [I urge] them to wear masks or respiratory protection, reduce outdoor activities if the ash is thick enough, and follow the instructions of health officials and local governments,” he said. ‘Easier to predict than earthquakes’ Disaster mitigation experts suggest that robust contingency plans should be activated well before ash clouds paralysed Indonesia’s key transport hubs. “If the status is at ‘alert’, preparations must be made to assess what to do if an eruption occurs. These include evacuation routes, maps, signs, and even drills. We should be able to estimate which communities will be affected and to what extent,” said Dwikorita Karnawati, a professor in earth sciences and geology at the Gadjah Mada University. “Volcanoes are easier to predict than earthquakes. We can’t predict when, what month, or what year an earthquake will occur. But with volcanoes, we can predict [the eruption] from the increase in magmatic activity. Anak Krakatoa has erupted many times. We should already have empirical information about it.” Dwikorita said officials’ response to Anak Krakatoa eruptions “could be improved”, including by installing better “technology and human resources” to monitor the volcano’s activities. Erma Yulihastin, a climatology and climate change expert at the National Research and Innovation Agency, however, said that scientists could not map out the extent of volcanic ash before eruptions. Anak Krakatoa’s eruptions this time were also considered “larger and far more extensive” than previous eruptions, she said. “Satellite data showed the volcanic ash column reaching into the tropopause, with ash plumes spreading west, up to 841km [522 miles], which is the distance between the Sunda Strait and Surabaya,” Erma said. Erma suggested that once a volcano’s status was increased to level 3, “monitoring of its activity should be increased more frequently, such as once every three hours, up from the standard once every six hours”. Titan Roskusumah, a spokeswoman with the Geological Agency, did not immediately respond to questions sent by This Week in Asia. Japan’s example Dwikorita, a former head of BMKG, said Indonesia’s multi-agency approach posed a hurdle in the country’s general disaster response, including during the Anak Krakatoa eruptions. “In Japan, their disaster characteristics are similar to those of Indonesia’s, which are volcanoes, earthquakes, and tsunamis. But in Japan, a single agency manages all of it under the Japan Meteorological Agency,” Dwikorita said. In Indonesia, disaster monitoring is split across multiple units. Volcanic activity is monitored by the Centre for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation under the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources’ Geological Agency, while seismic or tsunami hazards are monitored by BMKG. According to Dwikorita, as of 2024, inter-agency data sharing had been plagued by technical problems, including incomplete situational data and locational points. “It would be easier if the agency managing volcanoes was unified with the one handling earthquakes and tsunamis, like in Japan. There wouldn’t be issues of waiting for data to arrive because it would be managed together,” she said. Erma urged officials to improve the country’s multi-hazard maps, a protocol recommended by the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction to map out various types of hazards or natural disasters in a particular area. “In Indonesia, multi-hazard maps are typically fixed, but they need to be updated every six months and completed with risks that a region could face, in terms of human and ecological loss, when a disaster strikes,” Erma said. Officials could follow the example of the Japanese government, which had created multi-hazard maps for each region, including using leaflets with large images, “making them easy to read for the elderly or those who aren’t internet savvy”, she said.

title: US port pledge ups China rivalry in Pacific but island nations stick to own course
description: Washington commits millions of dollars at last week’s regional leaders’ forum in Palau, but experts say it will not be that simple.
content: The United States is stepping up its presence in the South Pacific with new funding and a reinforced diplomatic footprint, as its competition with China intensifies across the region. Yet the effectiveness of the push is tempered by Washington’s deep cuts to its main overseas aid agency, leaving doubts about the consistency of US commitment among Pacific leaders, according to analysts. The Pacific island nations are unlikely to frame their foreign relations as a simple choice between the two. Instead, they are expected to navigate the great power rivalries with a strategic flexibility consistent with their long-held practice of hedging, according to observers. At the 55th Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in Palau last week, the US and Australia announced a combined US$580 million package for the region. Washington’s pledge of US$150 million included US$60 million to help island nations through the energy crisis with expanded fuel storage and stronger power grids. The remainder, from Australia, will mainly be used to combat drug smuggling through greater aerial surveillance and law-enforcement training. In a parallel move, Washington and Wellington pledged US$50 million and NZ$17.5 million, respectively, to upgrade a former World War II port in the Cook Islands. In response, Beijing said that cooperation should “safeguard regional peace and stability”. Washington is expanding its diplomatic footprint in a region that has seen Beijing deepening infrastructure and security cooperation in recent years, and where Australia remains the largest traditional donor. The US reopened its embassy in the Solomon Islands in February 2023, opened another in Tonga later that year and established a mission in Vanuatu in July 2024. It has also been seeking to open a diplomatic headquarters in Kiribati. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the latest US-Australia package reflected both a response to China’s growing influence and a broader adjustment of Washington’s Pacific strategy. “The US and Australia are increasingly trying to combine traditional development assistance with security issues,” Sun said. He also pointed out that the Cook Islands port project with New Zealand underscored “how the US and its allies are using infrastructure to re-establish a strategic foothold in the Pacific”. But the Washington push comes after the Trump administration slashed USAID’s global budget, leading to a global aid freeze and the cancellation of up to 83 per cent of the agency’s programmes. The cuts have disrupted health, climate and disaster-preparedness initiatives in the Pacific – areas that island leaders describe as existential threats as sea levels rise and extreme weather intensifies. “The impact of USAID cuts on US credibility does exist in the short term, and recovery is not simply a matter of adding another sum of money,” Sun said. “Pacific island countries place a high value on continuity and predictability. If a country’s aid policy fluctuates significantly with a change of government, island nations will naturally reassess its reliability.” But Pacific island nations have largely resisted framing their relationships with Beijing and Washington as a binary choice. Their governments had instead sought to extract benefits from competing powers while retaining room to manoeuvre, analysts said. According to Graeme Smith, deputy director of the Coral Bell School of Asia-Pacific Affairs at Australian National University, that strategy is likely to continue. “While there’s a spectrum of Pacific island countries – with Palau the most pro-US, and Kiribati and Nauru vying to be the most pro-China – all Pacific countries will continue to hedge, as they have always done,” he said. “It is not in their interests to choose one or the other, as neither the US nor China can provide everything for countries that are the world’s most remote.” The Solomon Islands example shows how diplomatic alignment in the Pacific is rarely permanent. Honiara signed a security pact with Beijing in 2022, after terminating 36 years of formal relations with Taiwan in 2019. It also later denied a US coastguard vessel a port call. But Prime Minister Matthew Wale’s government has since sought to rebuild ties with Washington, signing an agreement in July allowing US coastguard vessels to patrol its waters with local police officers on board. Military developments have also complicated relations with Beijing. A Chinese nuclear-powered submarine launched a ballistic missile into international waters in the South Pacific in July, prompting criticism from the US, Australia and New Zealand over the lack of transparency and short notice. At last week’s forum, the leaders expressed concern over the test and called for greater transparency and advance notification of at least 24 hours. But Nauru dissented from the communique, underscoring the difficulty of forging consensus within the group. According to Smith from the ANU, China’s growing engagement has nevertheless given Beijing greater room to offer a broad model of development, from infrastructure and poverty alleviation to policing and engineering standards. Tsinghua University’s Sun said that China’s cooperation with Pacific island nations was mainly driven by development needs and the expansion of diplomatic relations, noting the region’s practical demands for infrastructure, healthcare, climate resilience, fisheries and training. But influence would not ultimately be determined simply by filling a vacuum left by another power, Sun observed. “It would depend on project quality, debt sustainability, local employment and respect for island states’ autonomy,” he said.

title: MTR Corp reports mass fare evasion after video goes viral, vows more patrols
description: Groups of people evade fares by following paying passengers through turnstiles, with no station staff intervening.
content: Hong Kong’s rail operator has reported a suspected mass fare evasion incident to police after online footage showed more than 30 people tailgating through barriers at Tsim Sha Tsui station, with no station staff seen intervening. A viral video last week appeared to show a woman, believed to be a tour guide, tap her card at an exit gate in Tsim Sha Tsui station. As the gates opened, several men and women following her passed through in single file without tapping their own cards, causing the gate indicator to flash red repeatedly. Multiple groups used the same method, with an estimated 30 or more people exiting without paying. In one instance, as many as six people trailed behind a person who made a single card tap to leave the station fare-free. No MTR Corporation staff were seen intervening throughout. The incident sparked outrage on social media, with users expressing shock at the apparent lack of staff response to the fare evasion. The MTR Corp said it strongly condemned the behaviour, had reported the matter to police and would step up station patrols and remain vigilant. It said the incident occurred at around 11pm on August 23. “The company strictly reminds passengers that failing to pay the correct fare or any other form of fare evasion constitutes a violation of the MTR by-laws. MTR staff perform ticket inspections within the railway premises from time to time,” a company spokeswoman said. She warned that violations could lead to enforcement action, including a surcharge or prosecution. She stressed that the MTR Corp would continue to remind passengers to pay the correct fare and use valid tickets. “Passengers who observe any suspected violations of the by-laws should notify station staff as soon as possible for immediate follow-up,” she added. Police confirmed on Tuesday they received a report on Saturday from MTR Corp staff. The case was classified as a “miscellaneous incident” and handed to the MTR Corp for follow-up under the Mass Transit Railway By-laws, the force said. Passengers who fail to pay their fare could face a maximum fine of HK$5,000 (US$638) or up to three years’ imprisonment.

title: Why China’s sugar stockpiles may blunt an El Nino-fuelled global supply crunch
description: The major sugar importer is expected to lean on strong domestic supplies amid soaring international prices.
content: China is expected to slow sugar imports for the rest of the year as concerns grow over a global supply crunch and higher prices, with Thailand – the world’s second-largest exporter – facing a sharp drop in production. The world’s second-largest economy relies on imports for about a third of its sugar supply, though high domestic stockpiles are expected to cushion the impact. Analysts estimated only moderate increases in local prices for the sweetener, which is considered a strategic agricultural commodity under Beijing’s food security agenda. Thailand’s sugar production was projected to drop by at least 17 per cent for the coming 2026 to 2027 season, largely because of El Nino-driven dryness, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The Thai Sugar Millers Corp. anticipated total output to fall below 10 million tonnes, down from 12 million tonnes the previous season. The forecasts follow a steady rise in global sugar prices over the past month amid persistent supply concerns. Niu Zhe, an analyst at bulk commodity consultancy Sublime China Information, noted that China’s import policy for the sweetener had already shown signs of tightening during the 2025 to 2026 crushing season. “With domestic production expected to remain strong in the 2026 to 2027 season and the cost of importing raw sugar from Brazil and Thailand continuing to rise, the out-of-quota import window has completely closed, and the pace of imports is likely to slow markedly in the second half of the year,” he said. China applies a 15 per cent tariff on sugar imports up to 1.945 million tonnes, with a steeper 50 per cent duty on any volume above that threshold. Official data showed that national sugar output for the 2025 to 2026 crushing season reached 12.95 million tonnes, up 16 per cent year on year and a 12-year high. Industry association data from Yunnan province and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, China’s two main sugar-producing regions, also showed industrial sugar inventories had risen sharply year on year by the end of July and remained elevated. “Overall domestic supply will remain relatively ample, so the rise in domestic sugar prices is expected to be far smaller than that in the international market, with limited pass-through to everyday consumer prices,” Niu said. In a report released last week, the International Sugar Organisation projected a global supply shortfall of 200,000 tonnes for the 2026 to 2027 season. The UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) also reported last week that its global sugar price index had jumped 11.9 per cent last month, raising the broader benchmark index for international food commodity prices. The FAO attributed the increase to several factors. “The surge reflected expectations of lower sugar beet yields in the European Union due to adverse weather, concerns over the impact of El Nino on production prospects in key producing countries in Asia, lower sugar production in Brazil, and India’s announcement of duty-free raw sugar imports,” it said. In August, India – the world’s third-largest sugar exporter – authorised the import of 1 million tonnes of sugar for the first time in a decade. The policy shift came amid expectations of lower domestic sugar cane production, driven partly by reduced rainfall linked to El Nino conditions.

title: Uber to apply for Hong Kong licence by end of October as Macau rides surge
description: Ride-hailing giant prepares application under new rules while Hong Kong users fuel fivefold trip growth in gaming hub.
content: Ride-hailing platform Uber will submit its operator’s licence application in Hong Kong by the end of October, its local general manager has revealed, as the city government moves to regulate the service. The platform also said on Tuesday that Hong Kong residents accounted for the largest share of its non-local users in Macau, months after it relaunched in the gaming hub in February following a nearly decade-long absence. “We’re putting our best foot forward, making sure we can comply with the government requirements and we have continued communication with [the government],” Estyn Chung, general manager of Uber in Hong Kong, said. The new regulations require ride-hailing platforms to fulfil nine key requirements, including a proven track record of providing lawful services in cities with populations of more than 7.5 million and handling more than 100,000 daily orders in at least two locations. A spokeswoman for the United States-based Uber said the company had continued efforts to support drivers, with financial aid for exams and tests, one-on-one consultations and information sessions to ensure service quality during the transition period. Separately in the Macau market, Uber said it was working with nearly 1,000 metered taxi drivers each month on average, with the number of completed trips in July surging more than five times compared with its launch in February. “During periods with important events, Hong Kong riders could account for up to one-third of Uber taxi’s business in Macau,” Chung said. “This goes to show that the operations in Macau serve not only its residents, but also Hong Kong visitors, as well as tourists from other areas.” The other leading source markets for non-local riders were Taiwan, the United States, South Korea, mainland China, Japan and the United Kingdom, he noted. Uber said 23 per cent of its customers in Macau were from Hong Kong, with the peak single-day share reaching 37 per cent when Hong Kong singer Keung To held three concerts in the gaming hub in June. In anticipation of the October “golden week”, Uber also announced the launch of its WeChat mini programme feature for the Macau market, allowing mainland Chinese travellers to call a taxi without having to download a separate app. “We know that mainland visitors make up over 70 per cent of tourists in Macau, and we observed that there has been a fast uptick in their use of our app, which is why we’re launching the feature,” Chung said.

title: Will Malaysia’s potential Huawei AI deal risk clash with US trade pact?
description: The reported move, tied to a US$494 million sovereign AI project, underscores Kuala Lumpur’s superpower balancing act.
content: Malaysia’s reported move to use chips from Chinese tech giant Huawei in its 2 billion ringgit (US$494 million) sovereign AI project could test the export-control commitments it signed with Washington last year, analysts say. The move could complicate Kuala Lumpur’s long-running effort to work with both American and Chinese technology firms, particularly as Washington pushes US AI systems across Southeast Asia. Bloomberg reported on Monday that Malaysia was seriously evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C accelerators as the backbone of its sovereign AI initiative, citing people familiar with the matter. State-linked Telekom Malaysia was selected as the key operator after a public tender, while officials from Malaysia’s National Security Council are expected to travel to Washington later this month to discuss the issue, the US-based news agency reported. A separate tender that could give US chipmakers such as Nvidia a more direct opportunity to compete was also under discussion, the report said. Trade pact clash Asrul Hadi Abdullah Sani, a political analyst and associate vice-president at strategic advisory firm The Asia Group, said proceeding with Huawei would raise questions over how Malaysia intended to reconcile the move with assurances it had given Washington on export-control enforcement. Article 5.2 of the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade signed by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and US President Donald Trump last October says Malaysia will, through its domestic regulatory process, “align with all unilateral export controls” imposed by Washington and ensure Malaysian companies do not undermine them. It also calls for cooperation on restricting transactions involving companies on the US Commerce Department’s Entity List, where Huawei has been listed since 2019. The trade agreement remained unratified by both countries as of July, according to Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani, who said lawmakers would be briefed before Malaysia decided whether to proceed. This Week in Asia contacted Johari for comment on the reported Huawei plan but had not received a response by the time of publication. It would create real friction with Washington Asrul Hadi Abdullah Sani, political analyst The US Commerce Department warned in May 2025 that using advanced Chinese computing chips – including Huawei’s Ascend 910C – risked violating US export controls and could expose companies to enforcement action. “It would create real friction with Washington,” Asrul said. “A government-backed decision to use Huawei chips for the sovereign AI project would reinforce the perception in Washington that these are not isolated commercial choices, but part of a broader shift by Malaysia towards the Chinese technology ecosystem.” Malaysia’s Digital Ministry proposed the 2 billion ringgit sovereign AI cloud project under the 2026 budget to underpin secure AI infrastructure, protect national data and enable large-scale AI applications. Anwar has framed the project partly as a response to concerns about foreign jurisdiction over Malaysian data, citing the US Cloud Act, which can compel American technology companies to produce data stored overseas, as a reason Malaysia needed a sovereign cloud for “critical security and personal data”. Huawei already plays a major role in Malaysia’s digital infrastructure. Telecoms operator U Mobile selected Huawei and ZTE in April 2025 to supply equipment for the country’s second 5G network, while the first nationwide network, run by Digital Nasional, was built with Swedish equipment maker Ericsson. Anwar also launched Huawei’s AI Lab and Innovation Centre in April, and in July witnessed an agreement between Huawei and Malaysia’s National Cyber Security Agency, covering cybersecurity, cryptology, AI security and digital sovereignty. Dual-stack dilemma Asrul said Malaysia could frame Huawei as a sovereign commercial choice based on “cost, availability and control over national data”, but Washington would inevitably view it through the lens of the wider US-China tech war. Washington launched the US-Asean AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting the American AI stack for public-sector use. A study by Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute published last month found that Malaysia was increasingly hosting a “dual-stack” digital ecosystem, with significant US and Chinese workloads onshore and greater exposure to geopolitical pressure over export controls. Hafidzi Razali, chief executive of policy advisory firm Strategic Counsel, said “whether it leads to a US policy retaliation would depend on the full extent of the scale, usability and whether it actually happens”. Whichever choice Malaysia made was its right, he added, but it would have to be weighed against “all tangible and intangible possibilities” involving both the US technology sector and Huawei. Adib Zalkapli, managing director at geopolitical advisory firm Viewfinder Global Affairs, said the Huawei move “could potentially test Malaysia’s balancing act with the US, given ongoing tech rivalry and export controls”. Whether the deal happened would depend on how the US responded to the reported negotiations, he added. The US was Malaysia’s largest source of approved foreign investment in the first half of 2026 at 33.1 billion ringgit. On Tuesday, Nvidia-backed Firmus announced a multi-year deal with OpenAI to supply computing capacity from two data centres in Malaysia. Malaysia’s Digital Ministry declined to comment when contacted by This Week in Asia. The Prime Minister’s Office, Telekom Malaysia and Huawei had not responded by publication time.

title: Hong Kong Jockey Club to offer computer training to more children in Cambodia
description: Club’s charities trust signs MOU with Cambodian authorities to expand computational training programme to cover early childhood learning.
content: The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Cambodian education authorities to expand a computational training programme to cover early childhood learning in the Southeast Asian nation. The MOU, which builds on an agreement signed last year to roll out the club’s CoolThink@JC programme in the country’s primary schools, was signed at the PBC (Philanthropy for Better Cities) Forum on Tuesday. The programme was launched in 2016 and originally focused on providing quality computational thinking education to primary students across Hong Kong. It was co-created by the Jockey Club, the Education University of Hong Kong, City University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The framework combines computer programming with logical thinking, problem-solving and other areas. Hong Kong’s Education Bureau formally introduced the programme to publicly funded schools in 2023. It was also adopted in mainland China through a “sister school” initiative launched in 2025. Last year, the trust signed an MOU with Cambodia’s Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport to bring the programme to the country’s primary schools. It was officially rolled out earlier this year. Under the initial agreement, the programme’s curricular materials are being introduced across 100 public schools in Cambodia between 2025 and 2028, reaching an estimated 30,000 students.
