The latest MOU focuses on expanding the programme to cover early childhood education as well. At Tuesday’s ceremony, the new agreement was described as “laying the groundwork for strengthening collaboration on early years support” and “marking a fresh chapter of cooperation and shared dedication to safeguarding the positive development of children everywhere”. Kim Sethany, the permanent secretary of state for Cambodia’s Ministry of Education, Youth and Sport, signed the MOU alongside Gabriel Leung, the Jockey Club’s executive director for charities and community. Sethany said that the initial roll-out of the programme had already surpassed expectations, noting that about 600 teachers were utilising the scheme in the first six months of implementation, despite the ministry initially estimating only 500 would take part between 2025 and 2028. The programme is currently active in 40 schools nationwide, reaching about 16,000 students. She added that she was especially proud that girls made up most of the students benefiting from the scheme. “Watching these young girls collaborate, write code and confidently lead group projects proves that when we provide equal access to quality tools, gender barriers fade away and [their] potential shines through,” Sethany said. The Jockey Club’s two-day forum brought together about 2,000 delegates from philanthropy, sports, government, business and academia to the city’s West Kowloon Cultural District. During the event’s closing panel, former NBA star Yao Ming touched on what he described as the “athlete’s spirit” and how it exists in everyone. He was joined on stage by top local athletes, including former Olympic swimmer Yvette Kong Man-yi, rugby sevens player and two-times Asian Games gold medalist Cado Lee Ka-to, and equestrian Jacqueline Lai Jing-man. “‘Athlete’ is a spirit that lives in your mind,” Ming said. “Obviously the training will help you … but an athlete is not only [someone] that plays on the sports field. When you study hard, when you work hard, when you are passionate about something … that is athlete spirit too.”

title: Record US$1.3 trillion pours into Hong Kong investment products
description: Record investor numbers drive 63 per cent surge in sales of non-traded products, led by collective investment schemes, FICC offerings.
content: Sales of non-exchange-traded investment products in Hong Kong surged to a record HK$9.9 trillion (US$1.3 trillion) in 2025, marking a 63 per cent year-on-year increase, according to the latest joint survey by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). A significant expansion in market participation drove the record-breaking performance. The number of investors completing at least one transaction rose 33 per cent to a record at more than 1.6 million, while the number of licensed corporations and registered institutions engaged in product sales grew 9 per cent to 452. Reflecting this broader industry scale, the number of large firms – categorised as those recording significant transaction volumes – increased 27 per cent to 128. “The strong growth captured in this year’s survey is a clear testament to investor confidence in Hong Kong’s asset and wealth management industry,” said Kenneth Hui, the HKMA’s executive director for banking conduct. Collective investment schemes emerged as the top-selling product category, with sales surging 85 per cent to overtake structured products for the first time since 2020. Within this segment, money market funds accounted for 88 per cent of the top five sales reported by large firms, up 80 per cent in 2024, according to the survey results released on Tuesday. Fixed-income, currency and commodity (FICC)-related offerings remained central to investor asset allocations, as market participants prioritised liquidity and income-generating assets. The new records of sales and market participation reflect global investors’ confidence in Hong Kong as a leading international financial centre Eric Yip, SFC Notably, currency-linked product sales increased by 50 per cent year on year to HK$698 billion. Debt securities continued on a solid growth trajectory, driven by a 138 per cent jump in sovereign bonds and strong interest in corporate bonds from mainland Chinese issuers, illustrating Hong Kong’s vital role as an offshore fundraising hub. The aggregate transaction amount for debt securities reached HK$929 billion, representing 9 per cent of total market volume. Equity-linked products continued to dominate structured product sales, rising 58 per cent to HK$2.7 trillion, which accounted for 70 per cent of structured products. Eric Yip, the SFC’s executive director of intermediaries, highlighted the city’s evolving role as an up-and-coming FICC hub. “The new records of sales and market participation reflect global investors’ confidence in Hong Kong as a leading international financial centre,” he said. “The SFC will continue to collaborate closely with stakeholders to drive the quality growth of Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem.” The survey also highlighted the industry’s digital transformation. Online platforms accounted for 21 per cent of the total transaction amount in 2025, up from 17 per cent in 2024. The number of firms distributing products online increased by 17 per cent to 122, with collective investment scheme products making up 84 per cent of online sales, as firms continue to adapt to changing distribution models.

title: Hong Kong seizes HK$1.4b suspected drugs over summer as traffickers target students
description: Customs says 150 people aged between 18 and 68 arrested and 6.1 tonnes of suspected drugs seized between May and August.
content: Hong Kong customs has smashed an international drug trafficking network over the summer, seizing 6.1 tonnes of suspected narcotics worth more than HK$1.4 billion (US$178.5 million) and arresting 150 people as syndicates actively recruited students during the holiday period. Acting head of the Customs and Excise Department’s drug investigation bureau Wong Ngar-lun said on Tuesday that real-time intelligence exchanges with overseas law enforcement agencies helped dismantle complex, multilayered smuggling routes before the narcotics could reach local or global markets. “During the summer break, many students travel abroad after sitting for public exams or during their school holidays. Criminal syndicates take advantage of this period to exploit and mislead young people, particularly students, into cross-border drug trafficking,” Wong said. “In response, Hong Kong customs launched a joint operation with various mainland and overseas law enforcement agencies between May and August this year, targeting syndicates that attempt to smuggle drugs in and out of Hong Kong via air passenger and cargo channels.” Wong said the operation uncovered 424 cases – 118 involving passengers and 306 through cargo – and led to the seizure of 6.1 tonnes of suspected drugs. Cannabis accounted for almost 60 per cent of the haul, or 3.6 tonnes, followed by 2.2 tonnes of ketamine, which made up 36 per cent. The remainder included cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and Ecstasy. The drugs had a total estimated market value of more than HK$1.4 billion. A total of 150 people aged between 18 and 68 were arrested. About 80 per cent of them were Asian, 16 per cent European, 3 per cent from the Americas and 1 per cent African. Wong said 104 of those arrested, or about 70 per cent, were aged between 18 and 40, indicating that syndicates deliberately targeted young adults for these illicit activities. Chan Kim-sau, divisional commander of the Airport Command’s airport apron division, said a 23-year-old local woman arriving from Brazil via Turkey was caught carrying 3.4kg of suspected cocaine valued at HK$2.7 million. Officers discovered the narcotics concealed inside two white statues placed within gift boxes and wrapped in clothes. In another case, a 40-year-old mainland Chinese man arriving from Kuala Lumpur was found with a suitcase that remained unusually heavy after its contents had been removed. Officers subsequently uncovered 2kg of suspected ketamine, valued at HK$800,000, hidden beneath a wooden board at the bottom of the suitcase. Wong stated that the operation brought airport drug seizures to 3.3 tonnes, an 80 per cent increase compared with the same period last year, while the number of arrests rose to 134, representing a nearly twofold increase. “The investigation revealed that the drug syndicates sought to exploit Hong Kong’s comprehensive aviation network, sourcing drugs from places with a lower market value and exporting them to lucrative overseas markets through Hong Kong, so as to generate massive illicit profits,” he said. “However, through intelligence analysis and risk assessment, we successfully intercepted the transnational drug supply chain at the airport, preventing the narcotics from reaching global markets.” In one case that involved 50kg of suspected cannabis with a market value of HK$10 million, the authorities not only made one arrest locally, but also alerted multiple law enforcement agencies overseas. The intelligence led to the interception of an additional 2.4 tonnes of drugs worth HK$500 million in six countries and regions across Central Asia, Europe and Africa. Wong warned that drug trafficking could lead to life imprisonment and a HK$5 million fine upon conviction, vowing to continue deepening international collaboration to crack down on cross-border drug smuggling activities.

title: Nicaragua accuses Germany of ‘multiple violations’ of law in Gaza genocide case
description: Nicaragua says Germany has breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention with its support, notably arms shipments, for Israel.
content: Nicaragua on Tuesday accused Germany of “multiple violations of international law” at the United Nations top court, as it pressed its case that Berlin was complicit in what it described as genocide in Gaza. The Central American country has dragged Germany to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, accusing Berlin of breaching the 1948 UN Genocide Convention with its support, notably arms shipments, for Israel. “Nicaragua invokes Germany’s responsibility in connection to multiple violations of international law, particularly in respect of the odious scourge of genocide and international humanitarian law,” ambassador Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez told the court. Gomez said Nicaragua’s claims “involve the most serious breaches of obligations arising under … general international law”. The court – which rules on legal disputes between countries – has already thrown out a request by Nicaragua to impose emergency measures on Germany, notably to stop arms exports to Israel. The case continues however and Germany is now seeking to have it thrown out completely, arguing that judges do not have jurisdiction and that Nicaragua’s case does not hold water. On Monday, the first of four days of hearings, Germany’s representative Julia Monar noted her country’s “unwavering support for the existence and security of the State of Israel” but also said it was one of the world’s largest bilateral donors to the Palestinian Territories. “All German exports of military technology and equipment to Israel – as to any country – are subject to strict licensing requirements which exceed international requirements,” she said, adding that Nicaragua’s statements “create an inaccurate and distorted picture”. It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases. The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered “on the merits” in more detail. This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies. The ICJ’s rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them. For example, it has ordered Russia to stop its invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin.

title: ‘Time waits for no man’: Chinese man’s 33-year, US$1.5 million world trip inspires many
description: Chen draws a parallel between running a business and exploring the world – both require perseverance through challenges.
content: A Chinese man has recently achieved his ambitious goal of travelling to 233 countries and regions around the world, sharing the life wisdom that “time waits for no man.” Chen Jinwei, 53, returned to his hometown in Zhuji, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, after a remarkable 33-year global tour that ended when he returned from Peru after visiting various corners of the world. Reports indicate that only about 70 individuals in China have previously travelled to 233 countries, territories, and regions. As the owner of a machinery company, Chen invested a total of 10 million yuan (US$1.5 million) into his journeys. His international adventures began in 1993 with a trip to Singapore, Malaysia, and Thailand. At that time, the internet was still not widespread, and Chen felt a strong desire to learn “what the other side of the world looks like” – not through books or hearsay, but through his own firsthand experiences. Chen integrated his world tour with his responsibilities of managing his business and family, often alternating between spending one month at home and one month on the road. He strategically chose to start with challenging destinations, including the polar regions. His quest to reach Antarctica required two separate journeys. In November 2015, he made his first attempt aboard the French expedition cruise ship Le Boréal, but he had to abandon the trip when the vessel lost power, emitting black smoke on the third day. In January 2016, he set out again for the South Pole, successfully reaching his destination. Chen identified Tokelau, a small island territory of New Zealand, as his greatest challenge. In 2019, despite meticulous preparations and navigating complex procedures, he arrived in New Zealand only to be forced to cancel his Tokelau trip due to a public health emergency. This year, he attempted the journey again and finally set foot on the atolls of Tokelau, expressing that he was “incredibly excited.” Throughout his travels, Chen encountered many unconventional and challenging experiences, including contracting malaria in Africa and enduring an earthquake in Greece. He said these challenges empowered him to become more adaptable: “When faced with a problem, first stay calm, then think about solutions.” He emphasised that his journeys were about more than simply “checking off tourist attractions.” At each stop, he aimed to stay as long as possible and immerse himself in the local culture. He collected currencies from 198 countries and donated them to the Xu Xiake Memorial Hall. Xu Xiake (1587–1641), a renowned geographer and explorer from the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), can essentially be regarded as China’s earliest travel blogger. Chen remarked that travelling and running a business share fundamental similarities. “Regardless of the ups and downs, joys and sorrows, just persevere in whatever you do.” For those eager to explore the world but often lamenting their lack of time or money, he offered straightforward advice: “Don’t wait. Time waits for no man.” Now, Chen aims to spend more quality time with his children and parents. He also plans to interview 100 leading figures in the outdoor and tourism industry, documenting their life stories. An online observer commented: “To achieve such a goal as Chen’s requires both time and money, which are luxuries for most ordinary people.”

title: Meet Perry Mattfeld, who plays Ricky in Chad Powers alongside Glen Powell
description: Married to ex-NFL quarterback Mark Sanchez, the actress has appeared in Shameless and worked with Selena Gomez on Wizards of Waverly Place.
content: Following a wildly successful first season, the Glen Powell-led Hulu show Chad Powers is back on our screens with a second instalment, which premiered on September 3. The sports-comedy series follows Russ Holliday (Powell), a disgraced quarterback who decides to revive his football career by creating a new persona, Chad Powers, and joining a struggling college football team: the South Georgia Catfish. Towards the end of Season 1, fans saw that Chad’s real identity had been discovered by two people, one of them being Perry Mattfeld’s character Ricky Hudson, who is an assistant coach for the Catfish. While Ricky is not the first to learn Chad’s secrets – the team’s mascot Danny discovers his real identity early on in the season – it complicates their will-they, won’t-they chemistry. Here’s everything you need to know about 32-year-old Chad Powers actress Perry Mattfeld. What is Perry Mattfeld’s background? Perry Mattfeld was born in March 1994 in Long Beach, California. She started dancing ballet when she was only five, per her IMDb profile. Having always known she wanted to work in entertainment one day, Mattfeld took classes with Debbie Allen and regularly took part in community theatre, according to People magazine. One day, one of her friends’ mothers asked Mattfeld’s mother if she wanted to take the aspiring actress to an American Girl tour audition. Intrigued, Mattfeld and her mother decided to check it out, and Mattfeld ended up landing the roles of Kirsten Larson and Kit Kittredge in the American Girl Dolls musical tour – a live theatre production of the popular Mattel doll franchise. How did Perry Mattfeld kick-start her career? After working with Mattel for almost three years, Mattfeld fell in love with acting and went on to star in various television shows, including Disney’s Wizards of Waverly Place, led by Selena Gomez. Despite landing various roles, Mattfeld decided to take a break from acting to complete her education. “I let my agents and manager go and just did college for four years. I told them I want to go to school, I want to be in a sorority, I want to ride my bike to get food, I want to carry my books, I want to go to football games, I want to be a cheerleader, I wanted all of that. And looking back, I have no regrets,” the actress told Her Campus in 2020. Mattfeld returned to the industry after graduating from the University of Southern California with a bachelor’s degree in fine arts. She was cast in television shows such as Shameless opposite Emmy Rossum and Jeremy Allen White, and in films like The Idea of You, starring Anne Hathaway and Nicholas Galitzine. Who is Perry Mattfeld married to? Mattfeld is married to Fox Sports analyst and former NFL star Mark Sanchez. The couple met via a mutual friend in 2017 and tied the knot in 2023, per People. They welcomed twin daughters in March 2025. Mattfeld is also the stepmother to Sanchez’s son, Daniel, from a previous relationship.

title: Chinese AI firms Z.ai and MiniMax could remain loss-making until 2030, Macquarie says
description: As both firms mature beyond early growth, an analyst says the industry is looking for a better metric for valuations.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence companies Z.ai and MiniMax could remain loss-making through 2030 even as their revenues surge, underscoring the enormous cost of competing at the technological frontier, according to Macquarie Group’s head of Asia internet and software research Ellie Jiang. One reason cited was the expense required for the computing power to train and run frontier AI models. Jiang told the South China Morning Post on Tuesday that China’s compute crunch was two to three times more acute than the wider global shortage, as domestic developers struggled with US restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced processors. Speaking on the sidelines of the Macquarie Asia Technology Conference 2026, Jiang said that the investment bank was “still modelling loss-making into 2030” for Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and MiniMax. “We are trying to be a bit more conservative in our estimate,” she added. Macquarie’s relatively conservative outlook comes despite expectations for rapid growth in annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – as Chinese AI developers attract more paying users and businesses increase their use of generative AI. “The flip side of that story is, we also assumed a much higher ARR growth,” said Jiang. The Macquarie analyst said Z.ai had planned for ARR of around US$2.4 billion by the end of the year, while Macquarie’s estimate was closer to US$3 billion. Last week, Z.ai disclosed during its first-half earnings that its ARR had reached US$1.6 billion by the end of August. By comparison, MiniMax CEO Yan Junjie stated last month that his firm’s ARR hit US$800 million in August. For now, both companies are loss-making. The results have fueled growing scepticism about the long-term competitiveness of both AI labs. Jefferies analysts said in a note on Monday that they viewed China’s large language model industry as “overcrowded” and favoured full-stack cloud service platforms, such as Alibaba Group Holding and ByteDance over standalone AI labs. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. These cloud giants had advantages in computing power and data, strong balance sheets to fund AI investment and multiple ways to monetise AI, according to Jefferies. MiniMax’s Hong Kong-listed shares closed down 5.59 per cent on Tuesday, while Z.ai took a 10.02 per cent dive. The widening gap between revenue growth and profitability highlights the large amounts of money that frontier AI developers must continue to pour into model training, computing infrastructure and research and development to remain competitive. Investors have so far been willing to tolerate those losses while the market remained in an early stage of adoption, Jiang said. Still, Jiang said prolonged losses should not be mistaken for an inability to monetise AI models. Monetisation was improving, including among Chinese companies developing open-weight models, challenging the assumption that giving users broad access to model weights prevented developers from making money. People are trying to find a more predictable, more reliable figure [than ARR] to build the valuation on Ellie Jiang, Macquarie Group Companies could still generate revenue through application programming interface (API) usage, enterprise deployments and commercial licensing arrangements, while greater usage could also provide valuable real-world data for improving subsequent versions of their models, she added. “But it’s not to the point that it completely justifies all the spending,” Jiang said. “That’s where we’re at now, but it doesn’t mean that it won’t justify in the future.” In an interview last week with Qiushi, the official journal of the Communist Party, Z.ai’s co-founder Tang Jie said that computing capacity remained a major challenge for the company, with an “expanding range of application scenarios” creating a severe shortage of computing power. In an analyst note last month, HSBC analysts wrote that MiniMax must ramp up investment to stay competitive, noting that any revenue upside hinged on securing sufficient computing power. Jiang said that the industry was trying to find alternative metrics to ARR. “The fact is we’re so early to the adoption cycle that only ARR makes sense because things are just growing,” the analyst said. “It’s month over month, week over week, we’re seeing this exponential growth.” But the market is also beginning to look beyond ARR, a metric widely used by rapidly growing software and AI companies to annualise recurring sales. “People are trying to find a more predictable, more reliable figure to build the valuation on,” said Jiang, adding that it could include metrics like price-to-sales ratios and gross profit.

title: New China badminton chief vows to fight corruption, ‘purge chaos’ after predecessor removed
description: Former president of the CBA has not been seen for months after being accused in April of ‘serious violations of discipline and law’.
content: China’s new badminton chief has vowed to crack down on corruption and “purge industry chaos” after being appointed to replace two-time Olympic gold medallist Zhang Jun. Zhang Jun, the former president of the Chinese Badminton Association (CBA), has not been seen for months after being accused in April of “serious violations of discipline and law”. On Tuesday, the CBA said Zhang Xin – an official from China’s General Administration of Sport – would be the new president. The governing body would, Zhang Xin said, “resolutely carry the fight against corruption through to the end, [and] draw lessons from these cases”. He also said the CBA would “simultaneously advance the goal of ensuring officials do not dare, are not able, and have no desire to be corrupt”. Last week, CBA vice-chairman Xia Xuanze and former vice-chairman and secretary-general Wang Wei were placed under investigation on the same day. Xia, an Olympic bronze medallist in 2000, was placed under investigation for suspected “serious violations of the law”. And just as Zhang Xin came in Tuesday, Xia was removed from his post. In the statement announcing Zhang Xin’s appointment, the CBA also said it would “purge industry chaos, purify the industry ecosystem, reshape the industry image, continuously improve the sports integrity system and create a clean and upright environment for the development of badminton”. Under Chinese President Xi Jinping there has been a widespread crackdown on officials, extending into sport. China are a badminton superpower and consistently the most successful country in the sport at the Olympics. With the next Games in Los Angeles less than two years away, the CBA said it would focus on the “central task” of preparing for that event and “build a team capable of fighting well and possessing an excellent work style ... and contribute greater strength to the development of badminton and the building of a sports power”.

title: Hong Kong gaining lustre as bridge to China’s tech sector: HKEX CEO
description: Hong Kong remains a top IPO destination for Chinese tech start-ups seeking to connect with global investors, Bonnie Chan Yiting says.
content: The Hong Kong stock exchange’s initial public offering (IPO) pipeline remains strong, as the city benefits from its unique role as a connector between mainland Chinese tech start-ups and global investors, according to the bourse operator’s CEO. Bonnie Chan Yiting, CEO of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX), said mainland Chinese companies’ interest in listing shares on the bourse was growing as a wave of firms looked to go global. “More and more mainland firms are choosing Hong Kong as an important platform for international development,” Chan told the HKEX China Conference in Shanghai on Tuesday. “Those companies not only look to obtain financing support in Hong Kong, but hope to connect with global capital, customers and business partners via Hong Kong so as to accelerate their expansions in overseas markets.” Her remarks came after a string of blockbuster IPOs on the mainland’s A-share market, which is being bolstered by investors’ voracious appetite for shares in Chinese tech champions such as chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). But unlike in Hong Kong, mainland stock exchanges are still mostly off-limits to foreign investors due to China’s capital controls. Only select foreign institutional investors can buy mainland-listed shares through the qualified institutional investor schemes, while traders in Hong Kong can access the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges through the Stock Connect programme, though the scheme is subject to an investment quota. With global investors becoming increasingly keen to invest in China’s tech sector, Hong Kong’s reputation as a fundraising destination was gaining additional lustre, according to Chan. “We have seen positive changes in HKEX’s investor structure,” she said. “More international institutional investors are participating in Hong Kong IPOs to get involved in the development of innovative Chinese companies.” As international institutions diversified their investments, actively chasing Chinese technology firms amid their low valuations, the HKEX could become the runner-up in IPO fundraising this year, trailing only the United States’ Nasdaq market, said Paul Uren, JPMorgan’s Asia-Pacific investment banking head, in May. Chinese tech firms in fields ranging from artificial intelligence and robotics to biotechnology are attracting interest from global investors due to their strong research and development capabilities and cost advantages in production, according to analysts. Several major Chinese players in strategic industries have gone public on Shanghai’s Star Market in recent months, including CXMT and humanoid robot maker Unitree Robotics. Chinese regulators have also accepted a listing application from the chipmaker Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation. Hong Kong was the world’s top destination for IPO fundraising last year, reclaiming the number one spot for the first time since 2019. The city’s IPO market has continued to boom this year, with total funds raised jumping 92 per cent to HK$210.2 billion (US$26.8 billion) in the first six months of 2026, data from LSEG Data & Analytics showed. But the city was still overtaken by the Nasdaq, after Elon Musk’s SpaceX completed its US$75 billion IPO in June.

title: Philippines wants to be a global semiconductor giant by 2030. Can it get there?
description: An ‘ambitious’ road map aims to more than double annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030.
content: The Philippines has launched a five-year road map to expand its share of the global semiconductor and electronics sector, but capacity challenges and political stability are potential stumbling blocks, analysts say. The Philippine Semiconductor and Electronics Industry road map, launched by the Philippines’ Semiconductor and Electronics Industry Advisory Council (SEIAC) on September 2, aims to grow annual exports of chips and electronics to US$110 billion by 2030, and move beyond manufacturing and assembly into higher-end operations. SEIAC chief and executive secretary Ralph Recto said the goal was to transition to chip design, engineering, research and innovation to boost regional competitiveness. One target is raising the Philippines’ share of global assembly, testing and packaging – already the country’s top semiconductor activities – from 4 per cent to 7 per cent by 2030. Other goals include growing the country’s share of the global electronics manufacturing services market from less than 1 per cent to 4 per cent and building an integrated circuit design sector that generates US$2 billion to US$3 billion in annual exports. This expansion would translate to opportunities beyond factories, including jobs in engineering, research, design and other highly skilled fields, Recto said. Over 60 per cent of the Philippines’ current merchandise exports are from the semiconductor and electronics industry, which generates over US$45 billion annually. The industry is also being eyed as a major driver of the Luzon Economic Corridor, a US-Japan-Philippines infrastructure initiative and economic hub. “Whether we act or not, this industry will continue to expand. And we must grow with it. That is the direction President [Ferdinand] Marcos Jnr has set for us,” Recto said. The SEIAC chairman said the government would focus on removing barriers – such as skilled worker shortages, gaps in power, water and logistics infrastructure, slow permitting and regulatory bottlenecks. All technical working groups would be held to specific targets and timelines, he said. “A road map is only as good as its execution. We have enough good plans in government. What the industry needs from us now are results.” Explicit strategy Josef Yap, a senior research fellow at the Ateneo School of Government, said the road map turned previous recommendations into a “much more explicit industrial upgrading strategy”. It addressed a larger portion of the value chain and connected semiconductor policy to related sectors such as AI, data centres, consumer electronics, clean energy, infrastructure corridors, economic zones and international partnerships. “This makes the road map more ambitious as an instrument of economic transformation,” he said. Lawrence Dacuycuy, a professor of economics at the De La Salle University, said the US$110 billion export target was “possible but highly ambitious”. Electronics exports in 2025 hit US$49.64 billion – meaning a compound annual growth of over 17 per cent for five years would be needed to reach the mark. The most “credible” target would be raising its global assembly, testing and packaging (ATP) share, due to its established base, he said. But here, the Philippines faces stiff competition from neighbours Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and India. “Achieving 7 per cent would require the Philippines to outperform the current forecast and expand faster than global ATP capacity growth … This is especially challenging because Vietnam is projected to increase its share from 1 per cent to 8 per cent, and Malaysia from 7 to 9 per cent,” Dacuycuy said. “The key is to strengthen the country’s supply chains … and design an investment architecture that would support upgrades, advanced manufacturing, diversification and financing.” Though not the first, the road map was the Philippines’ “most ambitious and sophisticated one yet”, said Lianne Angelico Depante, a doctoral researcher at Tokyo’s National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies. Its strength lay in recognising the need to build infrastructure such as national laboratories for design, advanced packaging and lab-scale fabrication. “The focus on building capabilities is an important shift in the way we think about industrial policy compared to before,” he said. But the real test would be “whether we can actually implement it effectively and consistently,” he said. “This is where the Philippines has historically struggled.” Bigger picture To succeed, Manila should take a “whole-of-government” approach by developing related sectors and exploring more holistic financing, the analysts say. Instead of being dependent on foreign direct investments, the industry should look to “embedded reciprocity”, Yap said. “The central policy question is not simply how to attract foreign investment, but how to convert the presence of [multinational corporations] into domestic … capabilities.” State funding, such as sovereign wealth fund Maharlika Investment, could potentially play a role, particularly for projects that private capital may consider too risky or long-term, according to Depante. “But ultimately, this will depend on whether the government has the risk appetite … because, in an industry like semiconductors, the willingness to take calculated risks is what determines whether a country remains in low-value activities or successfully moves up the value chain,” he said. Krista Danielle Yu, an economics professor at the De La Salle University, said the government should prioritise talent development. “Without talent, investors will not come. The road map looks at the talent pipeline in the higher education part, when in reality, it should start as early as elementary school.” She also stressed the importance of developing stable and cheaper sources of energy. The Philippines’ power rates are the highest in Southeast Asia, according to the Department of Energy. “Industrial water costs about three times what it does in Malaysia. Logistics is also more expensive compared to other Asean countries,” she said. To move up the value chain, the focus had to go beyond semiconductor firms, Depante said. “We also need to develop the industries that support them, from chemicals, metals, equipment, logistics and power to other upstream and downstream activities.” Clark, a central hub in the Luzon Economic Corridor, could potentially play that role, concentrating all forms of support around it, he said. Most importantly, the survival of the road map will depend on how it weathers leadership changes, according to Depante. Launched with less than two years in the Marcos administration, the road map could be disrupted by shifting priorities under the next presidency. “If we genuinely believe that semiconductors and electronics can be a strategic industry for the Philippines … then we need to build institutions and a policy consensus that can survive beyond any single administration.”

title: Museum brings back Leslie Cheung exhibition to mark late star’s 70th birthday
description: The ‘Miss You Much. Leslie 70th Birthday. Exhibition’ runs from September 9 this year to May 10, 2027, at Hong Kong Heritage Museum.
content: The Hong Kong Heritage Museum is reviving its tribute to late singer-actor Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing three years after its first iteration, marking what would have been the Cantopop icon’s 70th birthday with rare items from private collections, stage costumes and other exhibits. The “Miss You Much. Leslie 70th Birthday. Exhibition” runs from September 9 this year to May 10, 2027, at the museum in Sha Tin. Admission is free for the event, which is being presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department. Cheung, affectionately known to fans as “Gor Gor” – Cantonese for “big brother” – rose to stardom during Cantopop’s golden era in the 1980s and 1990s. Returning on a “much grander scale” than the 2023 showcase, the exhibition features more than 300 items, including vinyl records, film posters and other pop-culture memorabilia. In addition to the museum’s own collection, the exhibition includes items loaned by Cheung’s long-time partner, Daffy Tong Hok-tak, and former manager Florence Chan Sock-fun, among other loved ones, fan group Les FANmily and independent artists. The exhibition marks the first time many of these objects will be displayed publicly. Highlights include 11 costumes worn during Cheung’s live acts, notably the cloak he wore for his performance of “For Your Heart Only” at his Final Encounter of the Legend show in 1989, as well as his gold jacket, sequinned top and purple-striped trousers from Live in Concert 97. For the first time, the museum has recreated the interior of Cheung’s former residence in collaboration with his original interior designer. The display includes a photograph of his friends gathering at his house after his death. Six of Cheung’s films will also be screened at the museum during the event. “[The exhibition] will give a fuller picture of Gor Gor on and offstage, and hopes to share his warmth with the public,” said Chan, who is also a guest curator for the exhibition. Brian Lam Kwok-fai, museum director, said that about 370,000 people visited the 2023 exhibition, noting that many came from Japan, South Korea and parts of Southeast Asia, among other places. He expected that the exhibition would draw large crowds, especially on September 12, Cheung’s birthday. Visitors would be allocated time slots for entry to improve the viewing experience on busy days, he said. “We hope this exhibition allows us to once again pay tribute to Gor Gor’s significant contribution to Hong Kong’s popular culture, and to showcase our city’s pop music and performance techniques on the international stage and promote Hong Kong’s popular culture,” Lam said. Cheung’s career began in 1977, when he became first runner-up in the Asian Music Contest with his performance of Don McLean’s “American Pie”. He went on to release more than 40 albums and appear in 56 films. His breakthrough film role came in the 1986 hit A Better Tomorrow, followed by starring roles in acclaimed titles such as Farewell My Concubine, Days of Being Wild, Ashes of Time and Happy Together. Cheung plunged to his death from the Mandarin Oriental hotel in Central in an apparent suicide in 2003. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Cambodia’s scam gangs; Filipino-Americans decry ‘xenophobia’ games: 7 Asia highlights
description: From Japan warships attracting US interest to viral clip of Blackpink’s Jennie, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Southeast Asia’s scam gangs regroup after Cambodia’s crackdown Cambodia says it has flushed out a scam industry estimated to have stolen tens of billions of US dollars last year alone, but a string of arrests in recent days suggests the gangs behind it may have simply changed address. 2. Filipino-Americans rattled by Trump’s anti-migrant ‘xenophobia’ games The recent release of classic arcade games on the White House website, which allow players to deport migrants and build a border wall, has stoked more fear and anger among Filipino-Americans, as observers call out the “xenophobic” tactics in US President Donald Trump’s widening immigration crackdown. 3. What a viral Jennie clip reveals about South Korea’s deepfake struggles For a few seconds during Blackpink member Jennie’s headline set at Tokyo’s Summer Sonic festival last month, it looked like something had come undone. 4. New Zealand ‘must never be seen as a proxy’, former PM Helen Clark warns Calling the US Pacific strategy a “game of bluff”, Clark urges Wellington to defend its independent foreign policy tradition. 5. Bangladesh’s talk of joining an ‘Islamic Nato’ raises red flags in India Bangladesh’s potential entry into a defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan could give Dhaka fresh leverage in its dealings with India, but observers warn the move risks fracturing its long-standing strategic neutrality and alarming a hawkish New Delhi. 6. US wants foreign warships for its navy. Japan is hoping to be picked Japan’s Mogami-class warship is turning out to be a hot item among global navies. Australia is buying 11, New Zealand is considering putting in an order – and now, even the United States is showing interest. 7. Malaysian heritage site caught in row over non-local staff Images of a migrant worker apparently guiding visitors around one of Kuala Lumpur’s best-known heritage sites have triggered a backlash in Malaysia, with critics asking why locals were not hired instead.

title: Brent crude stares down the barrel of US$100 barrier as global frictions raise supply risk
description: Geopolitical tensions and strikes on energy infrastructure are tightening supply expectations, threatening to push oil higher and curb China’s appetite for imports.
content: Heightened geopolitical tensions are pushing global crude benchmarks towards the critical US$100-a-barrel threshold, and investment banks have lifted their end-2026 price forecasts, dampening import appetite in China – the world’s largest net crude importer. Saudi Aramco oil installations at Jizan, home to a 400,000-barrel-per-day refinery, were attacked on Monday, the Financial Times reported, with authorities assessing the damage. Iranian-backed rebels had yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack, according to the report. In the wake of the report, global crude markets saw renewed bullish momentum on Monday. Brent futures surged past US$98 a barrel during intraday trade. The benchmark edged higher in Tuesday afternoon trading, reaching its highest mark since June and getting close to the US$100 barrier. Ongoing conflicts, as well as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, have provided additional support for elevated crude prices. “Neither the US nor Iran has the willingness or capacity to escalate the existing conflicts, meaning negotiation channels will reopen,” said Zhao Xuyi, analyst at Shanghai-based Guotai Junan Futures. “Yet, talks can only de-escalate conflict intensity – they cannot resolve disputes over control of the Strait of Hormuz or other underlying frictions.” She added that under such conditions, the “ceasefire – negotiations – renewed conflicts” cycle will persist, keeping price volatility high. Analysts appear to be converging on the outlook for crude prices. Goldman Sachs lifted its year-end Brent forecast by US$5 – to US$85 per barrel – on Monday. Analysts at the bank, led by Daan Struyven, wrote that the revision reflected “our new assumption that Middle East shipping disruptions continue into 2027”. The investment bank also mapped out extreme scenarios in which Brent could surge above US$120 a barrel if the average Gulf output in 2027 remains well below pre-war levels, while intensified Hormuz and Red Sea shipping attacks were the most likely trigger for further price gains. Elevated crude prices pushed “price-sensitive” China to continue reducing crude oil imports in August, the bank’s analysts said. Chinese customs data showed that the country imported roughly 37.92 million tonnes of crude oil last month, a year-on-year decline of 23.4 per cent. For the January-August period, total imports fell 14.6 per cent from a year earlier. Goldman Sachs said that this trend was likely to persist while oil prices remain elevated. “China crude demand should remain price-sensitive because investment in electric [vehicles] and coal-based petrochemical plants has increased flexibility to switch away from oil without much pressure on economic activity,” the bank’s analysts noted. Meanwhile, they estimated that China’s visible crude stocks were sitting well above 1.1 billion barrels, with volumes “even higher when invisible stocks are included”.

title: Hong Kong reserves right to seek compensation over faulty hospital lift work
description: Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn says contractors must cover remedial costs after lift defects delay Queen Mary Hospital’s new block.
content: Hong Kong authorities have reserved the right to seek compensation from contractors over faulty lift installation work that has delayed operations at Queen Mary Hospital’s new block, the development minister has said. Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Tuesday that the main contractor, a Paul Y-Able joint venture, and lift subcontractor Anlev Elex Elevator would be required to bear all costs of remedial work, ensuring public expenditure on the project would not increase. Both firms were suspended from tendering for public works last month. The full commissioning of the hospital’s new HK$13.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) block has been delayed by up to a year after serious defects left 24 of its 28 lifts unfit for use. The delay has prevented medical departments from moving into the facility, where a blood bank and restaurants remain open. “Since deficiencies in the construction work have been identified, the relevant works departments will, in accordance with the contract, reserve the right to pursue claims for compensation,” Linn said. “The costs of all these remedial measures will definitely be borne by the responsible main contractor and subcontractors. “Therefore, the occurrence of these issues will not result in any increase in public expenditure for this project.” Linn said the departments had not publicly disclosed all the problems at this stage to avoid legal disputes with the contractors that could affect the government’s position and rights in pursuing future claims. Construction of the 34-storey building began in 2018 and was completed in 2025. Clinical services had originally been expected to start relocating there from the end of last year. The new block is designed to accommodate the accident and emergency department, emergency medicine and inpatient wards, the diagnostic radiology department, a perioperative centre, cardiac catheterisation laboratories and intensive care units. Linn’s pledge came after Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said on Monday that he was disappointed by the delay. “As healthcare workers, we feel a bit disappointed, and we expect rectification in the project to be carried out as soon as possible,” Lo said. Hospital Authority Chief Executive Libby Lee Ha-yun said current hospital services had not been affected but stressed that redevelopment projects were intended to meet medium to long-term needs. “We have not yet received the building for the time being, so we are still evaluating the impact on our future development,” she said. Linn said on Tuesday that relevant public works departments had found poor installation workmanship in some lift components, as well as dimensional deviations in the lift shafts. “If there is a dimensional deviation, it will result in insufficient clearance when installing the lift, leading to the lift not running smoothly,” she said. She added that the Development Bureau had asked the Architectural Services Department and the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department to submit reports reviewing their handling of the project. “Beyond this particular project, it also raises the question of whether there are aspects of the existing system that need to be tightened or strengthened,” she said. “These are precisely the areas that the Development Bureau is currently involved in.” Linn said the bureau would review the reports to determine whether the system for supervising and accepting works could be improved, while the Health Bureau and Hospital Authority would assess how the delays had affected hospital services. She added that the departments were confident the problems could be fully resolved by the fourth quarter of this year. All 28 lifts had received permits from the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department by July last year after it reviewed the subcontractor’s testing reports and conducted on-site inspections. Anlev Elex Elevator is a subsidiary of ATAL Engineering Group, founded by Otto Poon Lok-to, the husband of former justice secretary Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah.

title: Hong Kong’s first astronaut to give live space lecture to students on Wednesday
description: Lai Ka-ying will take part in ‘Tiangong Class’, which will feature expert lecture, in-orbit demonstrations and question-and-answer session.
content: Hong Kong’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, will deliver a live lecture from space to students and teachers at her alma mater on Wednesday morning, with the session also to be broadcast to pupils across the city and neighbouring Macau. According to an Education Bureau notice sent to all primary and secondary schools on Tuesday, Lai and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members – mission commander Colonel Zhu Yangzhu and Zhang Zhiyuan – will take part in the “Tiangong Class” at Tsuen Wan Public Ho Chuen Yiu Memorial College. The 1½-hour event, which will begin at 9.50am, will also be attended by representatives of the youth sector and innovation and technology community. A delegation from Macau will visit Hong Kong to attend the lecture in person. The government said it encouraged primary and secondary school teachers and students to watch the broadcast on campus. The event will also be streamed live on the Information Services Department’s website and Facebook page, as well as on local television channels. Jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency, the event will feature an expert lecture, in-orbit demonstrations and a question-and-answer session designed to showcase the space environment. The notice said the “rare dialogue between space and Earth” would be a valuable aerospace science education activity that could enhance students’ knowledge and stimulate their interest in learning. It added that the session would help build students’ aspirations, encourage them to be daring in their exploration, further cultivate their patriotism and strengthen their sense of national identity. The mission carrying Lai was launched in May. The 43-year-old police superintendent and mother of three is serving as the mission’s payload specialist. She is expected to help conduct more than 100 scientific studies aboard Tiangong, ranging from biomedical experiments involving mice and artificial embryos to materials testing and new energy-storage systems. One crew member will remain in orbit for a year to study the long-term effects of space flight on astronauts’ health and improve in-orbit medical support, while the other two are scheduled to return in November.

title: The View | To match China’s economy, India must accept its investment
description: Border rivalries shouldn’t block Chinese capital, just as wartime history never stopped Japanese investment from powering East Asia.
content: Although President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared a brief exchange last week at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the real action will unfold later this week at the Brics summit when Xi arrives in New Delhi with an expected delegation of 400 officials. China is one of India’s top trading partners, yet it remains unclear whether Chinese companies are welcome as investors in India. The two countries’ trade and investment relationship has diverged starkly. Between 2016 and 2025-26, bilateral trade between China and India more than doubled from US$71.5 billion to US$151.1 billion. However, China’s investments in India have fallen from a height of US$705 million in 2015 to a mere trickle of US$6.5 million last year. The two trends are related. Fuelled by its growing economy, India buys more from China, particularly capital goods. These expanding imports are driven by a lack of domestic alternatives which could have been established by Chinese investments. Restricting Chinese investments has only exacerbated the growing trade deficit with China. The pathway towards greater economic sovereignty for India lies not with restricting but expanding foreign direct investment from China. After all, FDI is how China became the manufacturing powerhouse it is today. The subdued level of Chinese FDI into India is a result of India’s choices. In the wake of their border dispute, India curtailed the level of investment from China, a chill that has only recently begun to thaw. However, even lifting all of India’s investment restrictions will not suddenly turn the country into an attractive destination for manufacturing. While software and services are the dominant targets for FDI into India, the pharmaceuticals sector – one of India’s most competitive exports – receives only about 4 per cent of inbound investment. Potential investment in India’s manufacturing sector is hampered by a range of structural shortcomings, from regulations to infrastructure. China offers useful lessons. As a socialist economy, China faced greater regulatory challenges at the start of its economic reforms. Deng Xiaoping overcame these challenges with the introduction of special economic zones. China’s collaboration with Singapore on the China-Singapore Suzhou Industrial Park provided significant impetus in attracting FDI to Suzhou. To overcome cumbersome regulations, India could emulate such models for tech zones, potentially in partnership with Singapore and China. China’s manufacturing growth has evolved along with its improving infrastructure. As a leading developer of green energy and high-speed rail around the world, there is no better partner for India to upgrade its infrastructure than China. Imagine the progress India would have made if China were its primary partner in building high-speed rail. FDI has been a key driver behind East Asia’s economic development. The rise of post-war Japan could not have been as rapid without American investment. The massive casualties Japan suffered during World War II did not stand in the way of its deep economic ties with the United States. The industrialisation of South Korea and Taiwan was also accelerated by Japanese investment. Pragmatism overcame nationalism despite their colonial history under Imperial Japan. Now that Taiwan and South Korea have surpassed the per-capita GDP of their colonial overlord, wasn’t leveraging Japan to catch up with Japan the right choice for the long-term dignity of their peoples? While China broadly used investments from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Europe, it did not exclude Japan, which played an important role in China’s economic rise. China suffered tremendously under Japanese atrocities during World War II. Despite its many options, China did not let its deep-seated animosity towards Japan stand in the way of Japanese investment. China’s industrial prowess has surpassed that of the rest of the world. China now leads the world in sectors from electric vehicles to robotics. While the US and Japan still hold the commanding height in the semiconductor ecosystem, their advanced technologies are perhaps not India’s highest priority now. Even as two of India’s leading investors, the US and Japan are not investing in India at the scale they once did in China earlier this century. Developing nations aspiring to industrialise suppress FDI from China at their peril. This is particularly true for a nation the size of India. If India wishes to achieve broad-based economic development that lifts the bulk of its people, it cannot stray too far from the proven East Asian model – open economies which effectively leverage FDI for industrialisation towards export competitiveness. Compared to the profound historical enmity of Korea and China towards Japan, the border dispute between India and China is a mere disagreement. Letting a lingering trace of British colonial cartography dictate India’s development trajectory exacts a disproportionate price. Can Washington or Tokyo match Beijing’s speed and hunger in contributing to India’s nation-building? India might hedge deftly in a multipolar world, but its future must be written in Asia.

title: The making of Hope, Na Hong-jin’s sci-fi spectacular and most expensive Korean film ever
description: The director talks about tension, timelines, sequel potential and a clash of tastes at Cannes as Hope gears up for US and Hong Kong releases.
content: With a budget reported to be closing in on 100 billion won (US$74.3 million), Hope, a white-knuckle action spectacular from South Korean genre specialist Na Hong-jin, is the most expensive Korean feature ever produced. The filmmaker first came to prominence with 2008’s serial killer thriller The Chaser and later cemented his reputation as one of his homeland’s most significant auteurs with crime drama The Yellow Sea (2010) and horror sensation The Wailing (2016), which, like Hope, also premiered at the Cannes Film Festival – one of the most prestigious events on the cinematic calendar. “Hope is completely different from my previous works,” the director tells the South China Morning Post at the recent Summer International Film Festival in Hong Kong. “While my past films focused on building up narrative, this time I wanted to make a film that maximises the visuals and audio.” If that was indeed his primary goal, Hope – Na’s first full-length film in a decade – easily eclipses its predecessors. It delivers a breathless two-and-a-half-hour roller coaster of relentless thrills and jaw-dropping surprises, as the residents of a small, isolated community scramble to survive when a pack of giant otherworldly entities attacks their sleepy enclave. A town under siege Hwang Jung-min, Korean cinema’s favourite exasperated everyman, plays Bum-seok, the ill-prepared police chief of Hope Harbour, a tiny coastal community close to the country’s hotly disputed demilitarised zone. When reports come in of a possible tiger attack, Bum-seok investigates, only to discover that the threat is far larger, stranger and infinitely more dangerous. The film’s bravura hour-long opening set-piece follows Bum-seok as he sets off in pursuit of his marauding quarry, backed by a trigger-happy mob of residents that includes the more than capable rookie officer Sung-ae (Squid Game star Jung Ho-yeon), the chief’s hunter cousin Sung-ki (Zo In-sung), and an army of gun-toting pensioners, who have seemingly been prepping for a confrontation like this since the 1950s. Na keeps the creatures hidden for the entire first act, so the tension ramps up through an incredible combination of suggestion, reaction and bone-shaking sound design. “I wanted to increase the density of every single shot through visuals as well as sounds,” he says. When the threat is finally revealed, the locals discover that giant anthropomorphic aliens have invaded their home, each one with its own unique appearance and personality. To play these intriguing extraterrestrials, Na enlisted an impressive cast of Hollywood actors, including Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander, Taylor Russell and Cameron Britton. While Na’s stature as a filmmaker is significant, one wonders what convinced such high-profile performers to sign up for these curious roles, which are realised entirely through digital performance capture and receive relatively little screen time. A story chopped in half As he reaches for a pad of paper and excitedly scribbles a diagram of the film’s timeline, Na explains that originally he created a single script where the whole story took place over the course of just one day. “But after writing it, I felt the story was moving way too fast … so I essentially chopped the script in half.” Hope definitely ends on something of a cliffhanger, with the fate of the characters, the community and the rest of the world left hanging in the balance. Should this first instalment prove successful at the global box office, there is plenty more of Hope left to be told. “I felt like the density was dropping too much – the movie wasn’t allowing each scene to grow,” Na says. “So I decided, let’s just take this first half and make a complete movie out of it.” By this stage, the sheet of paper in front of Na is a mass of lines, shapes and arrows that – in the moment, at least – make perfect sense to both of us. “When you look at the ending, you start wondering how these aliens will move next, how the humans will react and what will unfold once the sun finally sets,” he continues. “The next part starts exactly from there, and it also reveals the history of the aliens.” A clash of tastes at Cannes When Hope made its debut at Cannes back in May, it notably premiered in the main competition. This meant Na’s blood-spattered, adrenaline-infused roller coaster was competing alongside a selection of comparatively highbrow and muted dramas from the likes of Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu. Even with countryman and fellow genre stylist Park Chan-wook headlining the jury, Hope’s inclusion seemed a little out of place. “I felt this movie didn’t fit a place like Cannes,” Na acknowledges. “I literally thought to myself, ‘This isn’t an art-house film, so why are we even going?’” Unsurprisingly, Hope left the festival empty-handed, after receiving some rather colourful and mixed reviews. While critics were largely unanimous in their praise of the film’s breakneck opening salvo, the effects work was lambasted by many. Clarence Tsui, reviewing for the SCMP, labelled Hope “a high-octane, low-on-substance spectacle weighed down by a half-baked premise and bad CGI”, and he was not alone. While some other critics praised the film, Na’s frustrations were understandable. Perhaps the refined, intellectually inclined tastes of Cannes’ critics and jurors were not the most appropriate test audience for his monster-sized crowd-pleaser. Na has gone on record to state that since Cannes, he has tinkered with the film’s maligned digital effects while amplifying its sound design, removing a couple of short scenes and adding others. Despite how this might look to observers, he insists that these changes were not a response to the film’s initial reception. “No, that was not the problem,” Na says, returning to his scrap of paper. He scrawls “JULY” on the page in large letters. “We had a deadline of the beginning of July, but suddenly we had to go to Cannes in May. So I had to push the film to Cannes first.” Box office triumph and beyond Whatever unfolded behind the scenes, the results of Na and his crew’s tireless efforts are on the screen. In the eyes of this writer at least, the current version of the film stands as one of the year’s very best – something the public reaction appears to reflect. Since opening in South Korea on July 15, Hope has taken more than US$35 million from 4.5 million admissions, making it the third-highest-grossing domestic release of the year. Opening this week in the United States in some 1,500 cinemas (marking the widest release for a Korean-language film in that market since 2019’s Parasite), as well as Hong Kong and several other territories, it should have no difficulty finding a large and appreciative audience, paving the way for the franchise to continue – at some point. “Right now, I want to do a different movie first,” Na clarifies. “I want to make the kind of film where I can capture a specific actor with extreme density and focus. Since I just finished doing a massive project like this, I don’t really have the desire to jump straight into the sequel right this second.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Malaysian woman who stabbed boyfriend to death over sex demand gets 12 years
description: An appeal court nearly doubled the woman’s jail term, calling the initial sentence ‘over-sympathetic’.
content: A Malaysian court has nearly doubled jail time for a woman who stabbed her boyfriend to death for demanding sex after ruling that the sentencing court had been “over-sympathetic” towards the accused. The Court of Appeal increased the prison sentence for the woman, identified only as Shy to protect her identity, from the six and a half years imposed by the Johor Bahru High Court to 12 years, Free Malaysia Today news portal reported on Tuesday. Evrol Mariette Peters, one of the three judges in the panel, said in the grounds for judgment that the state court had placed too much emphasis on Shy’s age while failing to give sufficient weight to the seriousness of her actions. Shy was 19 at the time of the incident. According to court papers, she and her then boyfriend, 29, checked into a hotel near Jalan Austin Heights in Johor Bahru on September 20, 2022. The couple had been going out for about a year. In the room, Shy’s boyfriend asked for sex but she refused, saying she was menstruating. The boyfriend pulled out a knife and threatened her with it. She fought to take the weapon away from him and, in the struggle, stabbed him multiple times in the chest. An autopsy later found 28 stab wounds on his body. Upon her surrender, Shy was initially charged with murder. However, this was later amended to culpable homicide not amounting to murder after her lawyer made representations to the court. Shy pleaded guilty to the lesser charge and was sentenced to six and a half years’ jail. The prosecution appealed the sentence. The appellate court agreed with the prosecution, saying that the sentence did not take into account the seriousness of the crime. Peters said the high court had erred in treating Shy’s loss of young defender status as a mitigating factor. As she was 22 when convicted, she had aged out of the statutory limit of 21. The high court had also taken into account the struggle. “This was not a single impulsive stab. The multiple injuries demonstrate a sustained violent attack,” Peters said. While acknowledging Shy’s youth, guilty plea, remorse, lack of previous convictions and psychiatric condition as mitigating factors, Peters said these had to be balanced against the 28 injuries, the use of a knife, the targeting of the chest and the loss of a man’s life. “She is young, remorseful and traumatised, and for that, she deserves leniency. But she owes a debt, not to Shylock, but to the memory of the deceased and his grieving family,” the judge said, referring to a character in William Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. Twelve years was proportionate and necessary in the public interest, the court ruled, with the sentence to take effect from the date of Shy’s arrest. The maximum sentence for culpable homicide is 30 years.

title: A year on, Nepal remembers 76 lives lost in protests that ousted government
description: The commemoration came as the country continues to mourn the vast loss of life from devastating floods two weeks ago.
content: Dozens of young people congregated at Nepal’s burnt-out parliament building on Tuesday to mark the anniversary of deadly anti-corruption protests that toppled the former government. The gathering in memory of those who died in the demonstrations came as the Himalayan nation continues to mourn the vast loss of life from devastating floods two weeks ago. The rallies on September 8-9, 2025, were initially sparked by anger over a brief government ban on social media but were driven by deeper frustration over economic hardship, corruption and entrenched political practices. The unrest caused the deaths of 76 people and the torching of the parliament building in the capital, Kathmandu, as well as the prime minister’s office and other government buildings. It also led to the downfall of the administration of KP Sharma Oli, setting in motion a series of events that culminated with the election of youthful Prime Minister Balendra Shah in March. “The loss of life was of course terrible. But the impact on politics was worth it, we have seen changes,” said former protester Aastha Shrestha, 23, on the grounds of the ruined building. “It feels like the [current] government values the sacrifice we made,” she said next to a stack of burnt vehicles. Banners bearing photos of people killed in the protests were hung in the parliament grounds. Shah said on social media that he hoped the anniversary would “inspire us all to move forward towards building a fair, transparent, and opportunity-filled Nepal”. Sushila Karki, who led Nepal as interim prime minister after Oli’s government was overthrown, paid tribute to “all the brave individuals who lost their lives”. “Let us all perform our duties honestly, responsibly and vigilantly … so that a situation never arises again in which people are forced to take to the streets once more for good governance and change,” she said in a social media post. An inquiry commission set up to investigate the violence submitted its report in April and recommended further investigation against several officials including Oli. Most victims – 51 people – were shot dead, many in the head or chest, according to the report. But there has been little genuine accountability, said Anish Acharya, 19, who came with flowers to pay his respects. “Why did we sacrifice our lives, what did we get? There is no hope that change will come. Oli was arrested the next day but what then? The culprits are out and walking free,” he said. “The government has not valued our sacrifices and demands.” Shah’s administration is facing its toughest challenge since taking power as it leads rescue and recovery efforts following cataclysmic glacial floods on the country’s border with China. The August 26 disaster killed at least 1,399 people in the two countries, including 1,356 in Nepal, according to official tolls. A total of 5,500 people are still missing in Nepal and China.

title: China rallies Central Asian police chiefs on terrorism threats, energy and trade
description: Security ministers from five nations back Beijing initiative targeting extremism, border order and telecoms fraud.
content: China’s top police officer has pledged deeper cooperation with his Central Asian counterparts to crack down on terrorism, separatism and extremism, while strengthening measures to protect Belt and Road Initiative investments. Presiding over an informal meeting of the China-Central Asia Public Security and Interior Ministers’ mechanism in Beijing, Chinese Public Security Minister Wang Xiaohong on Monday urged his counterparts from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan to jointly combat the “three evil forces”. The “three evil forces” is a term used extensively in Beijing’s security doctrine and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) framework to refer to perceived interconnected threats to national sovereignty and political stability posed by terrorism, separatism and extremism, according to state news agency Xinhua. For decades, Beijing has used the term to refer to the ideas behind terrorist attacks in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region. The security talks followed the SCO summit a week ago where Chinese President Xi Jinping said security was a “key goal” and called for the SCO to foster “an environment of common security”. With Central Asian energy corridors and transport routes vital to China’s economic and strategic interests, Beijing has prioritised intelligence sharing, joint law enforcement training and the defence of infrastructure to ensure stability at its western border and beyond. Wang called for the ministerial mechanism to serve as a benchmark for regional security governance when he met his Central Asian counterparts. He said China sought expanded practical cooperation in areas including transnational crime, managing immigration, protecting overseas interests, building law enforcement capacity and securing belt and road projects. Delegates from the five Central Asian nations expressed support for the mechanism, committing to implement its outcomes and strengthen security ties towards improved regional stability and economic development, according to Xinhua. During the meeting, officials held a video unveiling ceremony for the newly established China-Central Asia Law Enforcement Training Base, a facility intended to boost joint operational and technical capabilities. Wang also presented the “Golden Great Wall Commemorative Medal” – an honour awarded by China’s Ministry of Public Security to recognise contributions to bilateral security ties – to Kazakh Interior Minister Yerzhan Sadenov and Uzbek Interior Minister Aziz Tashpulatov, according to Xinhua. On the sidelines of the event, Wang held discussions with Kyrgyz Interior Minister Ulan Niyazbekov and Kazakhstan’s Sadenov. Wang stressed to Niyazbekov the importance of maintaining political security, port-of-entry order and joint counterterrorism efforts, while Niyazbekov voiced support for a Chinese initiative to establish an international alliance against telecoms and network fraud, Xinhua reported. In talks with Sadenov, Wang called for stronger legal frameworks and exchange channels between the Chinese and Kazakh police forces, culminating in the signing of new bilateral cooperation agreements, according to the Chinese state news agency.

title: Thieves steal art worth millions from Renoir Museum in France
description: Suspects abandon two artworks during their getaway after early morning break-in in Cagnes-sur-Mer.
content: Police were on Tuesday hunting for two thieves who escaped with two Renoir paintings from a museum in southern France, after abandoning two others in its garden as they fled, a mayor said. The heist is the latest in a string of such robberies in France, including the daylight theft last year of crown jewellery valued at around US$100 million from the Louvre in Paris. Bryan Masson, the mayor of the southern town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, said the duo appeared “well equipped and well informed” about the museum housing works by French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir. “They were equipped with a metal saw and cut through the pistons that held the frames of Renoir’s works,” he said. But “the museum and police sirens forced the burglars to hurry, stealing only four works from the Renoir Museum”, he added. Of those four, two were “left behind in the gardens of the Renoir museum”, added the far-right official, whose office earlier estimated the value of the stolen works at €9 million (US$10 million). They made off with a portrait titled “Madame Colonna Romano” and the depiction of a woman at a well called “Jeune femme au puits”, his office said. The paintings retrieved include “Madame Pichon” and “Coco lisant”, a portrait of Renoir’s young son Claude reading. The Renoir Museum lies a half-hour drive from the southern city of Nice, in Renoir’s last home before he died aged 78 in 1919. Its collection comprises nine paintings by Renoir, according to its website. It also includes several sculptures by him, as well as objects and furniture that belonged to the painter, such as his easel and wheelchair. Some of his more famous works are on display at the Musee d’Orsay in Paris, as well as in London and New York. The mayor urged the culture ministry to earmark substantial funding to better protect France’s museums. “It is the heritage of all French people that has today become the target of gangs,” he said. A spate of heists at French museums, including at the Louvre, has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets. The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the jewels they are accused of grabbing in the seven-minute heist have still not been found. Italian police in August said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth over US$10.4 million that were stolen in a three-minute heist from a museum in March. In one of France’s most high-profile art thefts, in 1911, Leonardo da Vinci’s famed “Mona Lisa” was stolen from the Louvre Museum in Paris. The robber turned out to be an Italian glazier who helped frame the museum’s paintings. He was caught two years later when he tried to sell the artwork.

title: Philippine ex-speaker stashed billions of pesos ‘he could no longer hide’: prosecutors
description: Ex-House speaker Martin Romualdez is accused of buying mansions and shares in an attempt to hide ill-gotten gains.
content: Martin Romualdez, a cousin of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, accumulated so much wealth over the past three years that he had to convert it into mansions and shares to avoid scrutiny, the Office of the Ombudsman alleged on Tuesday – a day after filing a plunder case against the former House speaker. The Ombudsman filed the case on Monday against Romualdez, former House appropriations committee chairman Zaldy Co and two others, accusing them of accepting at least 7.44 billion pesos (US$118 million) in commissions, shares, kickbacks, “commitments” and other financial benefits. Prosecutors said the money was funnelled from contractors and other individuals with interests in government-funded projects, including flood-control and infrastructure works, between 2022 and 2025, the Philippine Star reported. The country’s anti-corruption court, known as the Sandiganbayan, found probable cause and issued arrest warrants the same day, with no bail recommended.
