Romualdez was arrested that evening at Cardinal Santos Medical Centre in San Juan City, where he was already being treated for what Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla described as a “cardiovascular event”, unstable blood pressure and an anxiety attack, the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported. ‘He could no longer hide’ Romualdez’s true wealth over the three-year period reportedly ran far higher than the amount with which he was formally charged – between 56 billion and 57 billion pesos, Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano told ABS-CBN on Tuesday. The former House speaker had converted much of this into assets “because he could no longer hide the money”, Clavano alleged. “He bought so many mansions and acquired so much in shareholdings – all just to avoid keeping the cash on hand,” he said. “He needed to immediately convert his money into actual assets, yet we never saw these reflected in his [financial declarations].” The Ombudsman’s own charge sheet separately alleges Romualdez and Co engaged in “concerted and coordinated acts” to amass roughly 56 billion pesos in ill-gotten wealth over the same period. Court filings say the money was “specifically traced and laundered” through shell and dummy corporations. The Ombudsman’s office alleges aides of Co made at least 15 cash deliveries – of around 2 billion pesos a month – to properties “owned by, occupied by, or associated with Romualdez” between September 2022 to 2025, and that nearly 5 billion pesos went towards setting up dummy companies used to buy property and other assets, including houses in the upmarket Forbes Park gated community. No special treatment Remulla said Romualdez would be transferred to New Quezon City Jail, where other suspects in the flood-control corruption scandal are being held, once he received medical clearance. “We will check every day until he is well enough to be presented to the court,” Remulla said. “We assure you, he cannot hide behind his wealth. No matter how rich he is, he cannot pay the law to allow him to stay in a place of this calibre.” Romualdez’s lawyers have separately asked the court to let him remain in hospital, citing a documented history of cardiac problems, diabetes and hypothyroidism. Plunder is a non-bailable offence in the Philippines carrying a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, along with the forfeiture of any wealth found to be ill-gotten. Romualdez has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Ade Fajardo, said in a statement that his client “will face the allegations against him in accordance with law”. “We recognise the public interest surrounding this case. But ultimately, criminal liability must be determined by the evidence presented in court, under the rules and safeguards of our justice system,” Fajardo said. “Representative Romualdez asks for no special treatment. He asks only for the same due process and fair hearing guaranteed to every Filipino.” Malacanang Palace said it respected the Ombudsman’s decision to press charges against the president’s cousin. “For the president, whoever is accountable should be held to account,” presidential press officer Claire Castro said at a briefing on Monday. “Whether it is a relative, an ally or an opponent in politics, whatever the evidence reveals should be disclosed.” Romualdez stepped down as House speaker last year after contractors alleged he and other lawmakers had received kickbacks from public works projects.

title: Australian group calls for ties with US ‘war machine’ to be severed
description: The group linked to the ruling Labor Party argues that the US has ‘led Australia into wars of aggression’ for 50 years.
content: A grass-roots group associated with Australia’s ruling Labor Party has called on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s government to break from “the American war machine” and pursue an independent defence policy for the future. Traditional security allies Canberra and Washington have deepened their military ties in recent years, including through troop deployments and the trilateral Aukus pact, which also involves the United Kingdom. ⁠Some American defence personnel are also stationed at a naval base in Western Australia, where four ‌US-commanded Virginia-class submarines are scheduled to be stationed starting next year. Last week, the two sides “agreed to accelerate force posture initiatives at Australian bases, bolster cooperation in combined logistics and build greater interoperability through joint exercises”, following a meeting between Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles and his US counterpart Pete Hegseth in Washington. “We need to be ensuring that we build deterrence, that we build balance, so that we can provide for the peace and stability of the region in which we live,” Marles said. “Collaboration through the alliance with the United States is fundamentally important to that.” That renewed cooperation – along with a report detailing how US military and arms manufacturers control or access 110 facilities on Australian territory – has rattled the Labor Against War group, which said Washington had “led Australia into wars of aggression” for 50 years. “The latticework of US bases and facilities across our continent should alarm anyone that values Australia’s independence from the American war machine,” said Marcus Strom, the organisation’s national convenor, according to a report by The Guardian. “Labor Against War calls on the Albanese government to chart a new course for Australia’s foreign and defence policy that is suited to the future, not clinging to the fading guarantees of the past,” Strom said. He also demanded that the government cancel the Aukus agreement aimed at countering China’s growing military footprint in the Pacific. Beijing has warned the deal could trigger a regional arms race. Despite the disquiet in the ruling party over the military ties with the US, Foreign Minister Penny Wong defended the alliance in parliament on Monday, saying it “contributes to Australian sovereignty”. Wong was responding to Greens senator David Shoebridge, who asked her why “Labor signed Australia up to the next US war”. The minister added that “everything the government is doing is working to deter and avert conflict”. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Eager capital prompts IPO plans for more Chinese makers of brain-computer interfaces
description: Arfysica and Neuracle aim for Star Market listings amid what a Morgan Stanley analyst calls the ‘early stage of a multi-year IPO upcycle’.
content: A handful of home-grown Chinese companies involved in brain computer interfaces (BCIs) are moving towards initial public offerings (IPOs) on onshore markets, taking advantage of the sector’s status as a new darling of private capital. The trend fits into a broad pattern of hi-tech firms flocking to list on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s Nasdaq-style Star Market. Among the BCI hopefuls, Shanghai-based Arfysica Innovation is the latest to register for IPO coaching for a Star Market listing, according to a filing with the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC). The company, which develops products for central nervous system injuries and disorders of cognition, hired Huatai United Securities as its sponsor. BCIs aim to allow brain signals to control external devices, such as computers or robotic limbs. Elon Musk’s Neuralink is a prominent company developing the technology. Founded in 2015 with registered capital of 100 million yuan (US$15 million), Arfysica is controlled by founder Wang Wei, who holds a combined 51 per cent stake and serves as the company’s legal representative, according to the CSRC website. Wang earned a bachelor’s degree from Tianjin University before completing a PhD in biomedical engineering at the University of Southampton in the UK in 2006, and later worked at Siemens Healthcare, according to her LinkedIn profile. The company raised an undisclosed amount of capital in its latest financing round in February. Its earlier round in January raised 160 million yuan from investors including the state-owned National SME Development Fund, according to company database Crunchbase. Another IPO candidate, Shanghai-based Neuracle Medical Technology, signed an IPO coaching agreement with Citic Securities on February 4, according to a filing with the CSRC. The company won China’s first-ever regulatory approval for an implantable BCI system designed to help patients with spinal cord injuries regain hand movement. It has raised 72 million yuan across five rounds of investment, counting HSG, Tsinghua Holdings Capital and Baidu Ventures among its investors, according to Crunchbase. Its legal representative, Xu Honglai, graduated from Tsinghua University in biomedical engineering, according to the university’s website. At least two other Chinese BCI companies are pursuing onshore IPOs, according to local media reports. Further along in tapping capital markets is BrainCo, one of Hangzhou’s so-called six little dragons – a group of tech firms that have gained global recognition in AI, robotics and other frontier fields. BrainCo has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO, Bloomberg reported on January 12. The company is working with China International Capital Corp and UBS Group on the share sale, though the deal size has not yet been disclosed. BrainCo has partnered with a hospital affiliated with Beijing’s Capital Medical University to develop BCI products for screening depression, according to the company. This year’s crop of listing candidates was “hardcore in innovation”, with higher strategic value, stronger capital backing and higher “intensity” in research-and-development spending than those that went public just four years ago, Morgan Stanley said in an August 28 report. The market is “still at a very early stage of a multi-year IPO upcycle”, said Huang Chiyao, an equity analyst with the Wall Street bank, in the report. Some 72.6 per cent of this year’s IPO firms could be categorised as having domestic leadership in innovation, Morgan Stanley found, even as many still trailed the global frontier. A total of 106 companies listed on the Star Market between June last year and mid-July of 2026, raising about 281 billion yuan.

title: Hong Kong’s MTR Corp wins bid as part of group to build new Sydney station, properties
description: Rail giant and subsidiaries of Malaysian engineering firm Gamuda Berhad win bid as joint venture, in deal reportedly worth A$880 million.
content: Hong Kong rail giant the MTR Corporation has won a bid as part of a consortium to design and build an underground metro station and develop property in Sydney’s second central business district. The company said on Tuesday that it and its two partners – both subsidiaries of Malaysian engineering firm and developer Gamuda Berhad – won the bid as the joint-venture Riverside Link Consortium, with Australian media reporting the deal to be worth about A$880 million (US$635 million). The deal is a major part of the Sydney Metro West project in New South Wales. It will be key to the growth and development of Parramatta, a commercial and financial centre located 24km (15 miles) west of Sydney and regarded as the city’s second central business district. “The project provides an opportunity for the MTR Corp to apply our experience in integrating transport infrastructure with residential, commercial and community development opportunities to create well-connected, vibrant and people-focused urban precincts,” David Tang Chi-fai, the rail giant’s managing director for property and international business, said. The joint venture will be responsible for designing and building the Parramatta metro station by 2032. The facility is expected to cut train travel times from Parramatta to Sydney’s city centre to about 20 minutes. The development also covers offices, retail and residential properties at and around the new station, which will be completed in stages following the opening of the railway. Tang said the joint venture would leverage the MTR Corp’s proven “rail-plus-property” business model of developing commercial and residential real estate above stations to raise non-fare revenue and diversify financing sources. Gamuda Engineering Pty Ltd Australia, the lead partner of the joint venture, is also building the Western Tunnelling Package, another part of the Sydney Metro West project, developing 9km of twin metro rail tunnels between Westmead and Sydney Olympic Park. “This is more than just another station award. It’s the first time all three partners have joined forces on one integrated transport-oriented development for Parramatta,” Ewan Yee, the company’s CEO, said. Michael Tien Puk-sun, a former chairman of the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation, said the MTR Corp’s winning bid showed Australia was interested in the rail-plus-property model, calling the approach successful and highly profitable. “The MTR Corp’s rail-plus-property model has proved to be highly profitable through the development of property atop rail projects, as shown by strong gains of HK$7.7 billion [US$982 million] in the first half of this year from property development. That’s why it won the Australia contract,” he said. “With the right to develop the property above the station of the Sydney Metro West line, the project will surely generate a sizeable profit and stimulate the business district’s economic activities. The MTR Corp has proved to be a global enterprise now.”

title: Live newborn rat found in takeaway lunchbox at Hong Kong restaurant
description: Food safety officials have prosecuted the business for unsatisfactory hygiene conditions after diner finds live baby rat covered in beef noodles.
content:
Food safety authorities in Hong Kong have prosecuted a restaurant after an investigation into claims that a newborn rat was found wriggling inside one of its takeaway lunchboxes uncovered unsatisfactory hygiene conditions.
The lunchbox came from Wa Jer Restaurant, located in the Wah Sing Industrial Building on Wah Sing Street.
A customer reportedly bought a HK$44 (US$5.60) set meal that included satay beef rice noodles, a ham omelette and a drink.
When opening the takeaway box, she discovered a live baby rat covered in satay sauce and moving among the noodles.
The customer uploaded the footage to a social media platform, where it quickly went viral and sparked heated online debate over the source of the creature.
The diner preserved the meal box intact and immediately filed a complaint with the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department.
A department spokesman said it received the complaint on Monday, seized the food for testing and found hygiene conditions in parts of the premises to be unsatisfactory.
He added that the operator was prosecuted under the Food Business Regulation and ordered to make immediate improvements.
“Regarding the suspected discovery of a baby rat in takeaway food, the department is conducting an investigation covering various aspects including food preparation, packaging, storage, and delivery,” he said.
“At this stage, it is inappropriate to jump to conclusions as to when and how the baby rat got into the food based solely on online video clips or the finding of a suspected baby rat in the food.”
The department said it had invited the complainant to provide further information and make a formal statement, but the individual had declined.
The South China Morning Post has also contacted the customer but she declined to elaborate.
The restaurant’s operator told media he was baffled by the incident but did not want to speculate on whether it was a prank.
He explained that the business had been operating for just over a year and had never received complaints about rats or insects in takeaway meals.
He acknowledged that the restaurant was located in an industrial area where rodents occasionally appeared, and said monthly deep cleaning and disinfection had been carried out.
He stressed his wish to contact the customer directly to understand the situation and pledged to step up pest control.
The restaurant will close on Tuesday for a day of cleaning.

title: DeepSeek embarks on ‘unprecedented’ hiring spree as it overhauls back end systems
description: The company cited a rapid surge in user demand for AI and increased complexity of its computing systems.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up DeepSeek is embarking on what it calls an “unprecedented” hiring spree to overhaul back end systems severely strained by booming user demand and compute-heavy AI agents. Cui Tianyi, a former quantitative trading expert who joined DeepSeek in March to lead its Harness team, said in a social media post on Monday evening that the Hangzhou-based company was seeking to recruit around 150 senior back end engineers. According to Cui, the push was driven by rapid surges in data volumes, machine numbers, training workloads and active users. “In computing, once anything scales up in quantity, it leads to a massive increase in complexity,” Cui wrote, noting that DeepSeek’s current back end infrastructure was reaching its limits and must be extensively upgraded, maintained and rewritten to support new technical directions. The sharpened focus on infrastructure engineering signals a strategic maturation for DeepSeek. As the open-weight champion transitions from a research disrupter into a high-volume platform, it is boosting the underlying engine required to deliver reliable, enterprise-grade commercial services. The expansion comes as the company continues to scale aggressively. In June, DeepSeek announced plans to “at least double the size of every department”, opening 33 distinct roles across research, engineering and product management. Financial momentum is also building. DeepSeek recently raised its Application Programming Interface (API) access prices amid a fierce price war among domestic AI rivals. It is also nearing the completion of a funding round, valuing the firm at about 500 billion yuan (US$74.5 billion) before investment, ahead of a potential listing on Shanghai’s Star Market, the South China Morning Post reported late last month, citing sources familiar with the matter. Operational pressures remain high as autonomous AI agents gain traction. Unlike standard chatbot queries, a single agentic task triggers repeated model calls and requires isolated computing environments. This forces DeepSeek to sustain heavy capital expenditure on servers, networking and software, even as it works to keep its API pricing competitive against Western rivals. In an apparent move to address these bottlenecks, the 150 new positions are targeted across two core technical areas. The first centres on server-side development across large-model research platforms, agent frameworks, internal research and development infrastructure, public API maintenance, online services and data engineering. The second focuses on elastic computing infrastructure, split between agent platform maintenance and lower-level system optimisation, to keep dynamic compute workloads fluid. The hiring spree was announced the same day the company said it had begun beta testing for a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model, a new version coming months after the original V4 series was first previewed in April. In a notice posted to a WeChat user group, the company said the V4.1 Flash features a new model architecture with native support for multimodality. “It’s stronger in capability, and faster and cheaper,” the company said in the notice, urging users to test the model and share their feedback. Additional reporting by Ben Jiang

title: Expand Hong Kong’s MPF investment choices, lure mainland pension funds: financial council
description: Official think tank urges broader retirement-fund investments, more mainland institutional capital and reforms to boost listings, bonds and corporate restructuring.
content: Hong Kong should consider allowing the Mandatory Provident Fund to invest in more asset classes, and lure more long-term patient mainland capital, such as pension funds, to invest globally through the city, the Financial Services Development Council (FSDC) said in a report on Tuesday. The MPF, the city’s compulsory retirement scheme, now has total assets of HK$1.67 trillion (US$213 billion) and invests in stocks, bonds and deposits. The FSDC suggests allowing a portion of the funds to be invested in alternatives and infrastructure. FSDC executive director Rocky Tung Yat-ngok said mainland patient capital, including insurance companies and pension funds, had strong interest in investing overseas to diversify risk and achieve higher returns. “There is an appetite for this patient capital to invest via Hong Kong in different currencies, including the yuan,” Tung said during a media briefing on Tuesday. “It would be important for Hong Kong to develop more long-term fixed-income products and other investment choices to meet the demand of the insurance and pension funds.” The council also urged the city to implement further reforms to reduce the time and costs associated with new listings and other fundraising activities, and to introduce a corporate rescue plan to help troubled companies restructure. These are among the core recommendations issued by the FSDC in a report that collected views from more than 600 market participants on how to further promote the Hong Kong capital market. The report was released ahead of Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s anticipated release of the city’s first five-year plan on September 16. The FSDC, a government-backed think tank, conducts research to strengthen the city’s position as an international financial centre. Many of its recommendations have previously been adopted by the government and regulators. Andrew Weir, vice-chairman of the FSDC, said the report was an execution road map focused on enhancements in five areas, which he called the “five I’s”: issuer, investor, intermediary, instrument and infrastructure. “With an open and interoperable ecosystem that supports companies, investors and intermediaries across the entire market spectrum, we can turn Hong Kong’s superconnector advantage into a global capital nexus,” Weir said in the same media briefing. Elevated global uncertainties are driving investors to look for opportunities that combine growth, market stability and risk diversification Benjamin Hung Pi-cheng, FSDC Other recommendations in the report include widening the Wealth Management Connect scheme and ETF Connect, as well as promoting the issuance of more Hong Kong-dollar and yuan-denominated bonds. It also called for a review of the definition of professional investor to recognise digital-asset holdings kept in custody with Securities and Futures Commission-licensed platforms. Weir said that the council also wanted to help the city’s roughly 600 brokerage firms develop further, and that it would organise activities to support them. The report is a sequel to one released in December that called for the city to attract more international listings, as more than 90 per cent of new listings are from mainland companies. Benjamin Hung Pi-cheng, chairman of the FSDC, said Hong Kong needed to implement further reforms to capitalise on opportunities arising from geopolitical tensions. “Elevated global uncertainties are driving investors to look for opportunities that combine growth, market stability and risk diversification,” Hung said in a statement. “Hong Kong is one of the few places in the world that can offer these features.”

title: Vietnam’s To Lam visits Russia and France amid South China Sea tensions
description: Visiting Moscow and Paris in succession allows To Lam to rally support for Hanoi’s maritime stance without taking sides, analysts say.
content: Vietnam’s president and Communist Party chief travels to Russia and France this week, on a trip analysts say is designed to do double duty: shore up support for Hanoi’s claims in the South China Sea and help bankroll its bid to become a high-income economy by 2045. To Lam’s itinerary encompasses talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before flying to Paris to meet French President Emmanuel Macron and attend an International Space Summit from Wednesday. By engaging two opposing powers back to back, observers say Lam is putting his country’s signature “bamboo diplomacy” on display for a global audience. Alexander Vuving, a professor at the Asia-Pacific Centre for Security Studies in Honolulu, said Lam would likely use the visits to try to convince both Moscow and Paris to take “Vietnam’s side” on the South China Sea. Both capitals formally maintain neutrality in the territorial dispute. Late last month, Vietnam lodged strong diplomatic protests against China over new infrastructure developments and land reclamation at Antelope Reef and Yagong Island, the latter of which Hanoi calls Ba Ba Island. China rejected the protests, saying the work fell within its sovereign rights. Vuving said the Russian leg of Lam’s trip, from Monday to Wednesday, would mainly focus on energy and defence cooperation, with major projects including a nuclear power plant in central Vietnam and hydrocarbon exploration in the South China Sea. “Lam will try to elevate hi-tech to a major area of cooperation between Vietnam and Russia, as well as France,” he said, adding that science, cybersecurity and digital transformation would also be among the areas emphasised. The two leaders might also discuss ways to overcome payment difficulties stemming from Western sanctions on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, Vuving added. Valeria Vershinina, deputy director of the Asean Centre at MGIMO University in Moscow, said Hanoi’s push to build its digital economy and turn Vietnam into a developed country hinged on technology transfer and skilled workforce training – “areas where Russia can offer experience”. Vietnam’s upcoming turn as country coordinator for the Asean-Russia Dialogue Relations from 2027 to 2030 will also be discussed, according to Vershinina. “The role gives Moscow a useful channel for deepening ties with Asean through Vietnam, a partner that understands Russia’s positions well while still keeping the association’s own interests and priorities.” Russia saw clear practical value in Vietnam’s extensive network of partnerships across Asia and Europe, she said. “[It] gives Moscow an indirect channel for advancing its own regional initiatives and for building closer links with Asean and other Southeast Asian groupings where Russia’s institutional presence is limited.” Nguyen Khac Giang, a political scientist and visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute’s Vietnam studies programme in Singapore, said Russia played a key role in helping Vietnam secure oil and gas supplies and advancing its nuclear ambitions. Vietnam would continue to rely on Russia for maintenance, spare parts and technical support “for years” despite diversifying its defence partnerships away from Moscow, Giang said – further noting that the pair’s two-way trade, modest at under US$5 billion, was unlikely to grow much in the current climate. “Visiting both countries illustrates Hanoi’s determination and ability to work with competing powers while preserving its own room for manoeuvre,” he added. Visiting both countries illustrates Hanoi’s determination and ability to work with competing powers Nguyen Khac Giang, political scientist In France, analysts say the focus will be on enhanced cooperation with Airbus, French appetite for Vietnam’s railway and defence projects and the space summit itself. The visit would build on a comprehensive strategic partnership signed in 2024, said Ha Hoang Hop, chairman of VietKnow, a Hanoi-based political think tank. Vietnam and Russia elevated their ties to that level in 2012. But he warned that visiting Russia before France amid the Ukraine war “carries optics risk and may invite scrutiny from Western partners”, despite Hanoi’s insistence that it remained neutral. ‘Personal diplomacy’ This week’s visits to Moscow and Paris form part of a longer itinerary for Lam. He heads to the United States and Canada later this month, with a UN General Assembly speech expected, and to Brussels next month for talks with European leaders. Since taking ⁠power in 2024, he has visited more than two dozen countries and hosted a parade of foreign leaders in Hanoi, including Myanmar’s Min Aung Hlaing last weekend. Giang said Lam saw “personal diplomacy” as an effective way to mobilise capital, technology and partnerships for his domestic economic agenda – an “era of national revival” centred on 10 per cent annual growth, a pivot away from low-cost manufacturing to a knowledge economy and a target of reaching high-income status by 2045. Hop attributes the travel blitz to Lam’s “authority to drive foreign policy directly” as Vietnam’s general secretary and president – a dual role he reassumed in April, having previously held both posts temporarily from August to October 2024 before military general Luong Cuong served a stint as president. “This near-continuous travel … suggests a leader building a personalised diplomatic brand,” Hop said, helping position Vietnam as a potential “indispensable interlocutor” to major powers. Vuving said Lam’s frequent overseas trips reflected Hanoi’s hedging and multi-alignment strategy amid global volatility, as well as his “effort to boost his domestic legitimacy by enhancing Vietnam’s international prestige and standing”.

title: Hong Kong stocks face double threat: US inflation and yen carry-trade risks
description: Investors are bracing for higher borrowing costs and further volatility as US and Japanese rate expectations shift.
content: Hong Kong and mainland Chinese stocks face a high-stakes week as investors navigate US inflation data, a strengthening Japanese yen and looming monetary policy decisions by two of the world’s most influential central banks. Friday’s consumer price index in the United States will take centre stage, with the report arriving just ahead of the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting next week. With Fed Chair Kevin Warsh already signalling a strong emphasis on curbing inflation, market analysts believe a higher-than-expected reading could heighten the chances of a benchmark rate increase. Meanwhile, the Japanese yen has appreciated to its strongest level against the US dollar in seven months, clouding the outlook for global equity markets. The shift is weighing on the “carry trade” – an investment strategy where traders borrow yen at low interest rates to buy higher-yielding foreign assets. At its rate-decision meeting next week, the Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise benchmark borrowing costs. For stocks in Hong Kong and mainland China, these pressures could compound existing challenges, including elevated US Treasury yields and lingering volatility in hi-tech sectors. Higher interest rates in the US and an unravelling of the yen-funded carry trade could put further pressure on the two markets, hitting Hong Kong stocks particularly hard because of their greater sensitivity to overseas capital flows, according to market analysts. “In the event of an interest-rate increase, US Treasury yields will remain elevated,” said Chen Meng, an analyst at Soochow Securities. “That will hold back a rebound in Hong Kong stocks.” The August inflation figures could determine the Fed’s next steps, with Warsh’s closely watched remarks at the central bank’s annual symposium in late August suggesting policymakers would remain guided by incoming data. Major financial institutions offered varying forecasts. Bank of America projected a 0.22 per cent month-on-month rise in core consumer prices, keeping expectations for a rate increase alive. But Citigroup estimated only a 0.18 per cent increase, a slower trend that could prompt the central bank to pause further tightening. Meanwhile, CME Group projected a 58 per cent probability for a rate increase of 0.25 percentage points next week. The strengthening yen is also introducing broader risks across global markets. Trading at 153.3 against the US dollar on Tuesday – its strongest level since February – the currency has gained momentum from expectations of monetary tightening and government initiatives encouraging the repatriation of overseas investments. According to Guosen Securities, a stronger yen could prompt a broader re-pricing of global assets, with the unwinding of carry-trade positions potentially hitting artificial intelligence-related trades. A rate increase in Japan would also roil global bond markets by driving yields higher and weighing on risk-oriented assets, the brokerage said. “The market is staring down a Fed hike, a live inflation debate, oil near triple digits, the risk of further Japanese tightening, possible capital repatriation back to Japan,” said Stephen Innes, a managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “Looming behind all of that is what could become a fairly brutal purge in risk assets.”

title: Chinese scientists propose turning abandoned coal mines into underground farms
description: Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, mining tunnels could offer agricultural advantages amid climate change, scientists say.
content: Chinese scientists have proposed developing “underground agriculture” in abandoned coal mine tunnels as part of a push to create a green, circular economy for the country’s massive mining industry. A team of researchers from Shanxi, a major coal-producing province in central China, described the idea late last month in the journal China Mining Magazine. An estimated 15,000 abandoned mines in China are expected to close by 2030. Insulated from surface weather and natural disasters, these subterranean spaces offer unique advantages. The researchers, based at the Shanxi Province Coal-based Resources Green and High-efficiency Development Engineering Centre, suggested that existing tunnels, power grids, ventilation systems and groundwater at these mines could be repurposed to support agriculture. “With climate change intensifying globally, the stability and sustainability of traditional land agricultural systems are facing severe challenges,” they wrote, adding that there was a lot of practical value in developing “closed-environment farming”. The paper assesses whether critical factors – including light, temperature and water – could support these farming operations. While the former mines lack natural sunlight, their ample space and robust power infrastructure would allow for the installation and calibration of artificial lighting, according to the paper. Subterranean temperatures are also largely immune to seasonal fluctuations. Geothermal energy could provide a sustainable heat source for crops, significantly curbing greenhouse gas emissions, the researchers added. Transforming decommissioned mines into farmland could also aid in the treatment and use of polluted mine water. Following a mine’s closure, residual pollutants such as lubricating oils and hydraulic fluids become potential contamination hazards. These can spread through geological faults, fissures and poorly sealed boreholes, ultimately threatening surface bodies of water. The authors said that establishing underground agricultural laboratories could “indirectly promote research, treatment and utilisation of mine water”. For instance, mine water bearing high concentrations of sulphates and heavy-metal ions could undergo treatments – such as adsorption and membrane separation – before being used to irrigate acid-tolerant crops such as rapeseed and tea plants. The researchers emphasised that the main goal was not large-scale crop production, but rather the creation of an “agricultural engineering experimental platform”. This would allow scientists to study the behaviour of key environmental factors – light, heat, water, air and carbon – deep underground and address cultivation challenges. The research could eventually support deep-space exploration, laying the groundwork for stable food production and ecosystem maintenance in extraterrestrial environments. Between 2010 and 2019, China shut down around 12,000 abandoned mines. As more facilities are decommissioned, the volume of usable underground space is projected to reach around 7.2 billion cubic metres (254 billion cubic feet) by 2030. Similar scientific trials are already under way in subterranean facilities in China and Britain. In Daye, a county-level city in Hubei province, researchers operating 245 metres (804 feet) below ground inside an abandoned copper mine are growing butterhead lettuce using artificial lighting, intelligent cultivation systems and low-carbon energy, according to Chinese news reports. Meanwhile, in Britain, researchers in North Yorkshire have established the world’s deepest underground farm more than 1,000 metres below the surface. They are running trials for a project that “could transform UK food production”, according to a report in The Guardian last month. That operation is housed within a science facility at a working mine that produces polyhalite, a mineral used as an agricultural fertiliser. The concept has been gaining traction for years. As early as 2018, Saffa Riffat, president of the World Society of Sustainable Energy Technologies, championed underground farming in old coal mines as a cost-effective method to meet growing global food demand. The idea gained support from some British mine owners, while the Chinese government also expressed interest, according to a BBC report at the time.

title: China targets fourfold boost in AI computing capacity by 2030 in major tech push
description: The nation’s intelligent computing capacity hit 2,185 eflops at the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, according to MIIT.
content: China plans to deploy artificial intelligence computing clusters containing 100,000 accelerator cards and sharply expand the country’s intelligent computing capacity over the next five years, as Beijing steps up investment in the infrastructure underpinning its AI ambitions. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), in a five-year industry plan released on Monday, set a target of 9,800 eflops of intelligent computing capacity by 2030, and called for 3.8 trillion yuan (US$532 billion) in cumulative information infrastructure investment over the 2026-2030 period. The plan calls for the “orderly deployment” of intelligent computing clusters with 10,000 graphics processing cards or those using 100,000 or more cards, alongside inference computing facilities tailored to different applications. It also calls for greater efforts to adapt infrastructure to home-grown computing chips. The targets extend a rapid expansion already under way. China’s intelligent computing capacity had reached 2,185 eflops – short for exa floating-point operations per second – by the end of June, up 177 per cent from a year earlier, and the country had built 52 intelligent computing facilities each equipped with more than 10,000 accelerator cards, according to MIIT. That means China would need to more than quadruple the June level to reach the 2030 target. By the end of July, capacity had already risen to about 2,450 eflops, according to the National Data Administration, an agency overseen by the National Development and Reform Commission. The expansion builds on the “East Data, West Computing” project launched in 2022, which seeks to shift power-intensive computing workloads from densely populated eastern regions towards western areas with cheaper land and abundant energy. China has since formed a network centred on eight national computing hubs, 10 data-centre clusters and three regions focused on coordinating computing facilities with power supplies. China is also linking previously fragmented computing resources across regions. By the end of the first quarter, a government-backed platform had aggregated about 316 eflops of intelligent computing capacity from 155 companies and 578 resource pools, including roughly 720,000 graphics processing units, according to MIIT. More than 80 per cent of the country’s intelligent computing capacity was concentrated in the eight national hubs. The expansion is being driven by a sharp increase in AI workloads. Average daily token usage in China rose from about 100 billion in early 2024 to 140 trillion in March this year, according to National Data Administration figures. Chinese-designed AI chips accounted for 41 per cent of domestic shipments in 2025, according to Sinolink Securities. The brokerage said broader adoption was still constrained by fragmented software ecosystems and compatibility issues. Beyond computing infrastructure, the plan also sets out China’s priorities for the next generation of communications networks. It calls for commercial 6G services to be launched “at an appropriate time”, deeper integration of 5G with the BeiDou satellite navigation system, and wider use of embedded SIM cards, or eSIMs. It also encourages technologies that allow communications without conventional network coverage, while calling for research into space-based computing. The targets come after years of heavy investment in 5G. China had about 5.1 million 5G base stations by the end of June, accounting for roughly 69 per cent of the global total, according to the Telecommunication Development Industry Alliance. With nationwide coverage largely in place, operators are increasingly shifting from large-scale base-station construction towards network upgrades and 5G-Advanced deployment. China Mobile’s 5G-A network, for example, had reached more than 330 cities. Preparations for 6G are also moving into the standards and testing stage. China approved the use of the 6GHz band for 6G trials in May, while standards body 3rd Generation Partnership Project, known as 3GPP, has formally started work on Release 21, the first global 6G standard, which is scheduled to be finalised in 2029.

title: Chinese grandma who struggles with Mandarin sings in 6 foreign languages
description: Most of Li’s family members were initially hesitant about her pursuit of singing English songs, considering it unconventional for a woman her age.
content: A 62-year-old woman from southern China, who cannot speak standard Mandarin or recognise the English alphabet, has gone viral on social media for singing over 100 songs in six different languages. Li Deru, known online as @Auntie Ru, boasts 800,000 followers and has garnered millions of likes across both domestic and international social media platforms. In addition to English, Li performs songs in Korean, Japanese, Thai, Hindi, and Italian. In her videos, Li, always elegantly dressed, confidently sings English songs, albeit with a strong accent, while walking slowly and calmly in parks or scenic locations. Over the past three years, she has shared more than 100 English songs, all popular hits among young audiences. The songs Li has covered include Poker Face, Jar of Love, Taylor Swift’s Love Story, and Justin Bieber’s Baby. Li’s rendition of APT, a massive global hit by South Korean singer Rosé and American pop star Bruno Mars, has received 1.6 million likes, even earning praise from Rosé herself. “I admire her for memorising those long English lyrics despite apparently not knowing English. She is truly an inspiring role model!” remarked one internet user. Another individual praised Li, stating: “I am the same age as Auntie Ru and know several foreign languages, yet I wouldn’t dare sing in front of the camera. She is brave and confident. Well done, Auntie Ru! Keep going.” “You are amazing. Keep being yourself,” commented a foreign online observer. A different foreigner added: “What a delightful grandmother she is!” Li lives in a village in Shantou, Guangdong province. Like most locals, she struggles with Mandarin and primarily uses the Teochew dialect in her daily interactions, as reported by News Weekly. Despite having only completed four years of primary school and never having studied English, she shared that she has always enjoyed listening to English songs and watching English-language films. Li married at 21 and, alongside her husband, opened a factory in her village. After her son and daughter had children, Li dedicated her time to caring for her grandchildren. Six years ago, she retired, passing the factory to her son, and no longer needed to look after her nearly grown grandchildren. The first thing Li did was enrol in a vocal training class. Since then, she has consistently attended two classes a week. Initially, nearly all her family members opposed her pursuit of singing English songs, believing it was inappropriate for a woman of her age. Only her son supported her, encouraging her to follow her passions. Li learned music from Cai Xiuqin, a mainland Chinese singer skilled in English songs, who operates a studio in Shantou. Cai told the media that Li initially struggled to pronounce any English words correctly. To overcome this, Li developed a unique phonetic notation method, marking Chinese characters beneath English words, and pronounced them according to their Teochew dialect pronunciation. Li made her public singing debut in January 2023 at her village’s gala event. Supported by the audience’s applause, she began sharing videos of her performances on social media. This year, she made a brief appearance in the blockbuster Dear You, a film celebrating Chaoshan culture, and toured various domestic cities with the cast for promotional events. Earlier this year, Li was invited to perform at a gala show in Macau, where she sang in front of an audience of 10,000. “I have more than realised my dream. I am happy and grateful,” Li was quoted as saying. “My fans give me confidence. I will continue to work hard and pursue my passion for music,” she added.

title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia ignite fires at oil facilities, wound dozens
description: Operations halted at southern facilities as Iranian-backed rebels target border cities in a major escalation.
content: The Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group in Yemen launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, wounding more than 70 people and igniting fires at oil facilities and utilities in the kingdom, authorities said. The attack was a major escalation in renewed fighting between an important US ally and the Iranian proxy group. It also threatened to further destabilise a region rocked by nearly three years of wars and deliver a new blow to the global economy. Weeks of clashes have added pressure to limited global oil supplies as the Houthis target a shipping route Saudi Arabia has used to transport oil to world markets while the Strait of Hormuz is throttled due to the US-Iran war. Tuesday’s attacks hit Saudi oil facilities connected to the alternative route, the Bab el-Mandeb, a strategic waterway off the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The conflict between Saudi Arabia, one of America’s closest Mideast allies, and the Houthis, a Shiite militant group armed and trained by Iran, goes back years. The new fighting has threatened to reignite the country’s civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and much of northern Yemen and forced the government into exile. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year to try to restore the government to power. Fighting has greatly died down since a truce was reached four years ago. The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed the country to the brink of famine. The Houthis are part of a network of Iranian-backed proxies across the region that have stepped up attacks on regional shipping and Israel and neighbouring countries in recent years in response to Israel’s wars in Gaza and Lebanon, and more recently during the US-Israeli war against Iran. The Houthis often act in coordination with Iran but also have carried out operations independently to promote their own interests. The attacks early on Tuesday hit “civilian and economic facilities” in the Saudi cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, said Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen. Al-Malki said the attacks wounded 73 people, including women and children. He did not provide further details. The attacks ignited fires at several oil facilities and utilities in Saudi Arabia’s southern region, the kingdom’s Energy Ministry said. Operations at the oil facilities and utilities were temporarily suspended, it added. The southern region houses major oil facilities, including a 400,000-barrel-per-day oil refinery in Jazan, which is one of Saudi Arabia’s largest. The Houthis previously attacked the Abha airport. The ministry said firefighters were battling the fires on Tuesday morning. Al-Malki called the attacks a “serious escalation” and vowed retaliation. In a pre-recorded video statement, Brigadier General Yahya Saree, the rebels’ military spokesman, said they fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at oil and economic facilities, as well as an airbase in southern Saudi Arabia. He said they targeted Jazan City for Primary and Downstream Industries, a major industrial and logistics hub on Saudi Arabia’s southwestern Red Sea coast. The rebels also aimed at Aramco facilities in Najran and Abha, as well as King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait. Saree blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation, warning that “every aggression against our country and people will be met with a firm response”. The attacks came hours after the rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for an air strike that hit a prison in Yemen’s northern province of Jawf. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others were wounded. The latest escalation stemmed from a Houthi attempt in July to fly a plane from Tehran to Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, challenging a decade-long air and naval blockade by the Saudi-led coalition. A coalition air strike struck the runway of the Sanaa airport, preventing the landing of the flight. The Houthis responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, and attacks on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, ending a 2022 truce that had largely halted fighting. The rebels also launched attacks on Saudi-allied forces inside Yemen, prompting government forces to respond with attacks on the Houthis across Yemen’s west coast and elsewhere in the country. Government forces have reclaimed territory from the Houthis in the provinces of Hodeida and Taiz, and attacked the rebels in the northern province of Jawf as well as the central provinces of Marib and Bayda. The flare-up has displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida in southwestern Yemen, further pressuring communities in southern Taiz and the West Coast, according to the International Organization for Migration. “Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it’s safe to go back,” said Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen’s chief of mission. “Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before.”

title: Beijing sends record 16 Hong Kong civil servants for UN positions
description: Officers sent under UN Junior Professional Officer scheme come from 13 grades and departments, topping earlier deployments in 2019 and 2023.
content: Beijing has recommended the largest-ever cohort of civil servants from Hong Kong for roles at United Nations agencies this year, expecting the deployments to broaden their global perspective and strengthen the city’s position as a bridge between the country and the international community. The 16 officers sent under the UN Junior Professional Officer (JPO) scheme represent 13 grades and departments, including customs, police and the anti-corruption agency. This marks a steady increase from the five officers sent in 2019, when Hong Kong joined the programme, and the 12 sent in 2023. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu on Tuesday said previous cohorts had excelled in fields spanning anti-drug operations, climate and resource coordination, trade and transport, and intellectual property protection. “Previous batches contributed across fields, from drug enforcement to climate coordination. They earned high praise from the UN, with nearly half seeing their tenures extended at the organisation’s request,” he said. “This affirms [the capabilities of] Hong Kong youth and strengthens our resolve to contribute to the international community.” Lee said Hong Kong’s first five-year plan, set to be unveiled Wednesday next week, would align with the nation’s 15th five-year blueprint, and that dispatching young civil servants to the UN was part of the city’s effort to serve national diplomacy and meet global commitments by leveraging its professional strengths. The UN JPO Programme provides young professionals with hands-on experience in international development and multilateral cooperation, with positions funded directly by sponsoring member governments. The latest batch of officers will take up posts at the UN headquarters in New York, as well as in offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi, this month. Cui Jianchun, commissioner of China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Hong Kong, said sending the city’s young public servants to UN agencies reflected Beijing’s efforts to leverage the “one country, two systems” governing framework by broadening their international exposure. “Hong Kong’s young people are proficient in two written languages and three spoken languages, possess both Chinese and Western cultural backgrounds, and have unique advantages in professional capabilities and international perspective. They are valuable talent for the nation as it participates in global governance,” he said. “As unilateralism and protectionism rise, the UN needs more talent to tackle global challenges. Hong Kong’s strengths in finance, intellectual property, anti-corruption and meteorology mean it is well placed to contribute more to global governance.” Assistant Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Felix Yung Yik-ho, who will serve in the Department of Operational Support in New York, said he hoped to gain global governance experience and apply what he learned to the city. “Working in Hong Kong as the international financial centre, we used to look at the world from a Hong Kong perspective. Now joining the UN will allow me to look back at China and Hong Kong from an international perspective,” he said. Cindy Ho Pui-ha, an acting chief investigator with the Independent Commission Against Corruption, served at the UN Office on Drugs and Crime in Vienna as part of the 2023 cohort. She said she shared the city’s anti-corruption expertise while learning skills in multilateral cooperation. “While Hong Kong has in recent years been smeared and misunderstood by some international media, serving in the UN gives me a chance to tell the story of Hong Kong and China,” she said.

title: Minister defends Singapore Airlines’ Air India stake amid scrutiny, racist rants
description: Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said the carrier funded investments from its own balance sheet, urging it to grow overseas to expand further.
content: Singapore’s transport minister on Tuesday defended Singapore Airlines’ investment in Air India, saying the city state’s flag carrier must grow overseas because there is a limit to how many people will fly to or from Singapore. Responding ‌to a question in parliament, Minister Jeffrey Siow said the flag carrier was a listed company that funded investments from its own balance sheet and it had not sought further capital from shareholders. The airline is majority owned by Singapore state investor Temasek. Singapore Airlines’ 25.1 per cent stake in Air India has weighed on its earnings and been subject to political scrutiny as the Indian carrier’s losses widened during a multibillion-dollar turnaround that could take up to a decade. Air India is also seeking about US$1.5 billion in fresh equity from its owners, Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines. “Many ‌overseas investment returns will not necessarily emerge immediately. Whether its specific investment in Air India proves valuable is for [Singapore Airlines] and its shareholders to answer,” said Siow, adding the current assessment was ‌that the airline’s ability to serve Singaporeans was not adversely affected. “Singapore Airlines has not sought further capital from ⁠its shareholders, and if it ⁠were to do so, that would be a commercial matter between the company and its shareholders,” he said. Singapore Airlines said in a statement on Tuesday that investments ‌in India have been and will continue to be funded through the flag carrier’s internal resources, subject to board approval and a disciplined capital allocation framework. It ‌said Air ‌India’s transformation was a complex, multi-year programme that was not expected to be linear, and the flag carrier’s investment in ‌the airline was a long-term strategic commitment aligned with its multi-hub strategy. News of the funding request had prompted Kenneth Tiong, ⁠a lawmaker from Singapore’s opposition Workers’ Party, last month to urge that Temasek’s funds not be used to shore up ⁠the Indian carrier and submit the question answered in parliament on Tuesday. On Saturday, Singapore’s Minister for National Security K Shanmugam said that as a shareholder of Singapore Airlines, Temasek expects the company to make responsible investment decisions and that ‌such decisions are for the company to ‌make. He also asked police to examine what he described as racist comments about the Air India investment debate. “That news has given rise to a whole series of anti-Indian, racist ranting online,” Shanmugam said over the weekend, adding that Temasek’s CEO and senior management had been attacked over their ethnicity.

title: Singapore ministers set for pay rise with entry-level pay up to US$1.4 million
description: First pay update since 2012 aims to ensure political salaries do not ‘fall further behind’ market rates, the prime minister says.
content: Singapore’s ministers will receive gradual pay increases following a 60 per cent jump in their baseline salary benchmarks, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has announced. The entry-level ministerial salary benchmark will rise to S$1.8 million (US$1.4 million) from S$1.1 million, while the prime minister’s pay benchmark will increase to S$3.6 million from S$2.2 million, in line with recommendations made by an independent committee. Wong said during a ministerial statement in parliament on Tuesday that he would donate the increase in his salary to “suitable good causes” but did not expect other political office holders to follow suit. “Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue. The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely and why many feel strongly about the matter,” he said. Wong said as the prime minister he held “ultimate responsibility” for the salary framework. “So I want to be clear about how I will personally handle the increase and why I am taking these changes forward, because I believe they are in Singapore’s interests.” The review was conducted by an eight-member committee formed in January, after a deferment amid geopolitical uncertainty arising from the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. The review, which is held once every five years, was initially set for 2023. Wong said the government had accepted the committee’s recommendations, but it did not intend to implement them all at once. The recommendations will take effect on October 15, starting with a one-off increase of up to 9 per cent, depending on factors such as performance and past adjustments. Subsequent increases will be made based on individual performance and responsibilities. Wong said the S$1.8 million benchmark was not a target for every minister, projecting that most junior ministers’ pay would fall at the lower end of the range – at about S$1.35 million – by the end of this term. Starting October 15, members of parliament will also see their monthly allowances rise to S$18,500 (US$14,600) from S$13,750. Following Wong’s announcement, Coordinating Minister for Public Services Chan Chun Sing explained that the adjustment accounted for inflation. He said in a statement that it was a “practical update to ensure that MPs are adequately supported in discharging their duties on the ground”. The salaries of Singapore’s political office holders, among the highest in the world, have long stirred public debate. About 35 per cent of a minister’s salary consists of variable components, including an individual performance bonus and a national bonus. The national bonus is linked to socio-economic indicators, such as the growth rate of residents’ median income and Singapore’s real gross domestic product. US President Donald Trump reportedly draws US$400,000 a year while in office, whereas the British prime minister makes around US$235,000. Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu takes home HK$452,200 (US$57,680) a month, as reported by his office in 2022, bringing his annual salary to more than US$690,000. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi earned 36.4 million yen (US$233,000) last year, local media reported, citing parliamentary reports. Singapore benchmarks ministerial pay against its top 1,000 highest-earning citizens, based on the premise that the qualities and abilities of the cream of the crop “reflect the desired calibre of the people whom Singapore needs for good government”, according to the Public Service Division. Following the 2011 general election and simmering public discontent, then prime minister Lee Hsien Loong appointed an independent committee to review ministerial salaries. Political office-holders’ salaries were last adjusted after a 2012 review, slashing politicians’ pay by more than 30 per cent. Lee’s salary of US$3 million was cut to US$2.2 million. These were reviewed again in 2017, but remained unchanged despite the committee recommending an increase in line with rising benchmark salaries. The government has long maintained that hefty pay cheques are necessary to attract talent and deter corruption seen in countries in the region. If the personal and financial sacrifices become too large, many capable people will simply choose to do something else Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong Wages in the public and private sectors had risen over the years, Wong said, causing ministerial salaries – which were last adjusted in 2012 – to “fall further behind”. Some permanent secretaries were now earning more than ministers, he added. On Tuesday, Wong reinforced the importance of selecting individuals of the right calibre to join the cabinet, noting that other countries often struggled to find such talent. He said leadership renewal was among his top priorities, recalling that there had been a lack of younger ministers to succeed their senior counterparts when he first took the helm. Before last year’s general election, Wong said he had tried to recruit multiple chief executives and senior business leaders, but was turned down by all of them. “The reduction in political salaries in 2012, followed by 15 years without adjustments to the benchmark, did not make the task any easier,” he said. “Politics must remain a calling to serve our fellow citizens. But if the personal and financial sacrifices become too large, many capable people will simply choose to do something else.”

title: From BYD cars to DJI drones, Guangdong showcases tech prowess ahead of Apec summit
description: As Shenzhen prepares to become the third Chinese city to host the Apec meeting, its province has set up media visits to tech firms.
content: As China’s southern tech hub Shenzhen gears up to host November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, its province, Guangdong, is making sure its technological prowess is also receiving global attention. At Saturday’s Asia-Pacific Media Forum, a major media gathering before the summit, a hall was packed with hi-tech products from the province, including a BYD car, DJI drones and Tencent Holdings’ artificial intelligence products, as well as smartphones from Honor and Vivo. Before the main forum, media representatives joined two-day tours across six cities in Guangdong, visiting the headquarters and factories of provincial poster children including BYD, electronic appliance maker Midea Group and smartphone giant Oppo. The South China Morning Post took part in the visit to BYD, the world’s top electric car maker in terms of deliveries, in eastern Shenzhen. The company showcased its latest new energy and automotive technology, charging a Denza Z9GT premium sedan to a range of 700km (435 miles) within about six minutes at minus 30 degrees Celsius (minus 22 degrees Fahrenheit). Outside the office building, a Yangwang U9 super-coupe showcased its quad-motor all-wheel-drive system by rotating 360 degrees on the spot. Other firms in Shenzhen and neighbouring cities – including Midea in Foshan and Oppo in Dongguan – displayed the digitally enabled smart features of their products. The province’s Communist Party secretary Huang Kunming said at Saturday’s forum that the province had benefited from the “unique advantage” of its closeness to Hong Kong and Macau as it faced the Asia-Pacific region, becoming a “vanguard” of China’s reform and opening-up. In the first half of this year, Guangdong’s trade with other Apec economies surged 21 per cent to nearly 3.6 trillion yuan (US$536.3 billion), accounting for 65 per cent of its total imports and exports, according to official data. Shenzhen will become the third Chinese city to host an Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, following Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. Preparations for the summit, scheduled for November 18 and 19, are proceeding apace, with slogans including “Shenzhen in action” and “Let’s gather in Shenzhen for a prosperous Asia-Pacific Region” a regular presence in city scenery. The event may see a trilateral meeting between President Xi Jinping, United States President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, according to Yuri Ushakov, a key foreign policy adviser to the Kremlin. Putin confirmed his intention to attend the Apec meeting four months ago, but Trump has not yet done so.

title: Nepal’s flood survivors face economic ruin as migration beckons
description: With homes and savings washed away, survivors of last month’s devastating floods in Nepal are seeking work abroad.
content: Taradevi Tamang’s village exists on official maps, but on the ground, it looks as though it was never there at all. Two weeks ago, raging floodwaters ripped through her village in central Nepal’s Nuwakot district, sweeping away Tamang’s tin-roofed home alongside the modest savings and gold jewellery she had accumulated over the years. The Trishuli River also washed away her family’s main source of income: 265 piglets and 34 wild boars. Tamang, 50, is among roughly 3,500 people currently sheltering in government-run facilities across the three worst-hit districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading. Having lost their homes, land and life savings, survivors now face an uncertain future, haunted by the daunting task of rebuilding from scratch. “We lost our house during the earthquake but still had the land to rebuild with aid,” Tamang said tearfully at a shelter in Nuwakot, referring to the devastating quake that hit Nepal in 2015. “We thought our lives would improve, but it’s just one stress after another. My heart gets heavy thinking about what to do. We don’t have anything to hold on to now.” The swollen Trishuli River has receded since August 26, when the floods killed more than 1,300 people and left over 5,000 missing. But outside an army camp in Bidur, where helicopters ferry relief materials, the search continues. Relatives arrive carrying photographs of loved ones, looking for a wall to post fliers, hoping someone might recognise a face. A short distance away in Dhunge Bazaar, entire settlements have been reduced to rubble. The ground beneath them still feels unstable as the river roars past, while mud stains three storeys high on buildings far back from the bank reveal how high the water rose. On a sweltering Sunday afternoon, passers-by stopped to photograph the destruction while displaced residents picked through the mud to salvage what they could. Salina Nepali and her father walked away with just two bags of clothes – everything else was gone. The family’s clothing shop vanished overnight, taking with it cash stored in a cupboard and 1.2 million rupees (US$7,700) in new stock, which had been delivered just one day before the flood. “This is nothing,” said 20-year-old Nepali, holding up her small bag. “We don’t know where we’ll go now. Maybe we have to find work and rent a room somewhere. Everything is uncertain.” Mental health workers warn that this uncertainty is deepening the psychosocial trauma across affected communities. Thousands of people searching for missing relatives are hanging between hope and despair, unable to find closure. Children are especially vulnerable. Save the Children, an international non-profit organisation providing psychological support, temporary learning centres and play areas in shelters, has warned that “the need for mental healthcare is growing”. At a Nuwakot sports hall converted into a shelter, 46 of the 164 residents are children, several of whom lost both parents. While play areas keep them occupied, counsellors assess their condition. Achitra Thing, a counsellor with Transcultural Psychosocial Organisation Nepal, said many children had not yet processed their loss. Some brought to Nuwakot from Rasuwa also faced a language barrier, speaking only the local Tamang language rather than Nepali. “When this seven-year-old boy sees a helicopter, he thinks his parents are being brought back, even though he saw both of them swept away,” Thing said. “The body of his 18-month-old brother has been found. We should prioritise more psychosocial support in all shelters.” Adults are suffering quietly, with few receiving formal counselling. Some men have turned to heavy drinking to cope, creating added safety concerns for women and children in shared spaces. Suchita Joshi said her 64-year-old mother suffered from recurring nightmares. While the elderly woman had survived alongside two sons and an 18-month-old grandson, she lost her two daughters-in-law and grandchildren, aged five and seven. “My mother sometimes breaks down completely,” Joshi said while tending to her wailing nephew. “The child keeps looking for his mother since he’s breastfeeding. We have not shown her photograph to him because we don’t know how he might react.” Joshi’s family lost their home and kitchen utensils shop in Trishuli Bazaar, across the river from Dhunge Bazaar. The flood destroyed the property, carrying away their inventory and their silver and gold jewellery. “My brothers are extremely stressed since they have nothing left,” she said. “They have lost hope. How do you start over after losing everything you worked for all your life?” With the economy already constrained by limited domestic opportunities, thousands of Nepalis leave the country every month to work overseas. Observers expect the disaster to accelerate this outmigration as families look for other ways to survive. Kopila Tamang, 20, had planned to study hotel management in Japan. But after the flood killed her mother and destroyed her home, her family can no longer afford the tuition. Karan Tamang, 17, lost both parents and is unsure whether he will be able to sit his secondary education examination, a crucial milestone for students in Nepal. “I just don’t have the courage now,” he said. “I dreamed of living with my parents. Maybe I’ll go abroad for work.” Others are determined to keep what remains of their families together. Taradevi Tamang is intent on keeping her 13-year-old son at home. She said her brother had already spent 13 years in India and she did not want her family to be separated again. “My son should study as much as he can,” she said. “I hope the government gives us land in a safe area so we can rebuild. We don’t want to go back near the river.”

title: Up to 200 Hong Kong-bound helpers stranded in Indonesia after volcano eruption
description: Employment agencies association expresses concerns but says ‘contingency plans in place’ if Mount Anak Krakatoa erupts again.
content: Up to 200 Hong Kong-bound domestic helpers remain stranded in Indonesia despite the reopening of several affected airports, as the city’s employment agencies association braces for possible further closures due to volcanic ash. Indonesian transport authorities said Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport resumed operations on Tuesday after being shut for several days, following the eruption of Mount Anak Krakatoa on Saturday, which affected thousands of travellers. Cheung Kit-man, chairman of the Hong Kong Employment Agencies Association, said the stranded travellers included 150 to 200 helpers heading to Hong Kong, including new employees and workers returning after their holidays. Some were expected to fly out on Wednesday as operations resumed, but agencies remained concerned flights could be suspended again if further eruptions occurred, he said. “Of course we are worried, because it is a natural phenomenon and [the volcano] can erupt at any time. No one can predict it,” Cheung said. “If it does erupt again, we already have contingency plans in place.” He said that some workers had been diverted to depart from Surabaya, Indonesia’s second-largest city, located east of Jakarta and currently unaffected by the eruptions. Agencies had also liaised with airlines to place the stranded helpers on a priority standby list, he added. Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Overseas Domestic Helpers Association, said the delay had disrupted arrangements for some families. “Families, of course, do not want this situation. Especially for those who have to go to work and need [helpers’] care for the elderly, they hope the helpers can arrive as soon as possible … the impact on them is the greatest,” she said. “We just hope air travel [resumes normally] quickly so that it can help the families in need.” The Hong Kong International Airport website showed that out of four incoming flights originally scheduled from Jakarta on Tuesday, three were cancelled. Mount Anak Krakatoa, located about 150km (93 miles) from Jakarta, erupted on Saturday, spewing a fountain of lava and a plume of volcanic ash. Eight airports halted operations over the weekend after ash was detected in their airspace, disrupting nearly 3,000 flights and leaving more than 340,000 passengers stranded. On Monday alone, more than 240 domestic and international flights were cancelled or delayed at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, affecting nearly 30,000 travellers.

title: Why China’s Unesco-listed Kaiping watchtowers are best discovered on two wheels
description: Many of the ‘diaolou’ can be reached only by farm tracks and quiet paths, making cycling the ideal way to explore them.
content: Imagine a classic Chinese landscape of bamboo forest, rice paddies and lotus-filled waterways, dotted with villages that seem untouched by time. Now add to that scene hundreds of castle-like watchtowers, their turrets rising unexpectedly against the skyline. This is Kaiping in Guangdong province, just a couple of hours from Hong Kong by direct high-speed train from West Kowloon Station. It is one of mainland China’s lesser-known Unesco World Heritage sites and home to more than 1,800 distinctive structures called diaolou. Dating back to the Ming dynasty – though most were built in the 1920s and 30s – the diaolou were part fortress, part family home and part status symbol, protecting against bandits and flooding while projecting wealth and prestige. This brings five other cyclists and me to Kaiping for a weekend cycling trip organised by travel specialists Bike Aways. Scattered across the flat countryside, many of the diaolou can be reached only by farm tracks and quiet paths, making cycling the ideal way to explore them. With Bike Aways founder Bruce Foreman and local guide Winson leading the way, the riding is easy-going. They take care of the logistics and navigation, time our visits to avoid the crowds, and encourage us to stop often to sample local specialities. Foreman has a simple philosophy: “I see the bike as a passport rather than the main event. It lets us venture into places buses and cars can’t reach. I like taking people down forgotten back roads, through villages they might otherwise miss, and stopping for the sort of food locals actually eat. It’s less about how far you ride than how much you see and the experiences and encounters you have along the way.” We ride around 50km (31 miles) on Saturday and 25km on Sunday. The pace is relaxed, with regular breaks. The emphasis is on the journey rather than the mileage, but you do need the confidence and fitness to comfortably cover the distances and cycle along everything from country lanes to occasional sections of busy main roads. Our ride starts early on Saturday morning in the town of Tangkou, where we stay at the family-run Diaomin Tribe Boutique Hostel. It is a charmingly quirky place, spread across a maze of old buildings filled with curios, and though a little rough around the edges, it is clean, comfortable and welcoming. Bikes, helmets and chilled water bottles are waiting for us outside, and our first destination is breakfast at a friendly dim sum restaurant a 20-minute ride away. After ordering too much and overeating, it is time to get back on the bike. Throughout the morning, we pass dozens of tumble-down diaolou, regularly stopping to take a closer look. At their peak, more than 3,000 diaolou stood across Kaiping. Those that survive today are mostly abandoned, derelict or slowly crumbling back into the countryside. Four of Kaiping’s historic village areas – Jinjiangli, Zili, Majianglong and Sanmenli – form part of the Unesco World Heritage site. Their diaolou have been carefully restored and protected, their interiors preserved and open to visitors with an admission ticket. From the late 19th century onwards, Foreman explains, generations of Kaiping residents left for the goldfields, railways and trading ports of America, Canada, Australia and Southeast Asia. They sent money, letters and photographs home before returning with new ideas and the means to bring them to life. The result was an unprecedented period of diaolou construction, with no two looking alike. Roman arches and Greek colonnades rise above traditional Lingnan roofs, while baroque decorative flourishes and art deco details create a style that is unmistakably Kaiping. We spend our first morning exploring two of Kaiping’s four Unesco-listed diaolou village areas: the Majianglong Village Cluster and Jinjiangli. Majianglong lies hidden among dense forest. As we follow shady paths, the watchtowers gradually appear through the banana trees. The only sounds are the creak of bamboo and the steady hum of cicadas. It is easy to imagine how bandits once approached unseen. These diaolou have been lovingly restored, and the original hand-carved wooden furniture, decorative tiles and stained-glass partitions remind us that these buildings were not just fortified watchtowers but the grand homes of prominent families. Only when Foreman points them out do I notice the gun ports, iron shutters and overhanging rooftop “swallow’s nests” from which defenders could fire on attackers below. In an era when raids were a constant threat, these affluent and isolated villages were frequent targets. By lunchtime, dark storm clouds are chasing us, and we reach Jinjiangli just as the heavens open.
