We are welcomed into the home of an older couple, who serve nong jia cai – generous family-style country cooking that has become a favourite with visitors seeking authentic rural flavours. After a chicken is plucked and prepared, lunch is served at the kitchen table. Winter melon and fish soup, stir-fried chicken, a mountain of garlicky broad beans, beef with ginger, and bowls of rice arrive one dish after another. By the time the rain eases, we have shared the sort of lunch you are unlikely to stumble across on your own – and one I’ll remember for a long time. Just around the corner is Ruishi Lou, the tallest surviving diaolou in Kaiping, rising 28 metres (92 feet). The climb up nine storeys is hot work, but it is one of the best places to photograph the surrounding countryside, with balconies, arches and a circular window framing the view. After descending, we cycle the 20km back to our guesthouse along the banks of the Tan River and sections of the Guangdong Greenway, a network of traffic-free cycling and walking trails. During the evening, I wander around Tangkou, a small rural town quietly reinventing itself through a growing number of creative heritage projects, including a branch of Librairie Avant-Garde, one of China’s best-known independent bookstore chains, housed in a former grain depot. Dinner is a five-minute moonlit cycle ride away at Tangkou Wenyuan Restaurant. We eat outside in the courtyard of a restored diaolou, ordering the local specialities of Magang goose and eel claypot rice. On Sunday morning, our coffee stop is an unusual one: Hainongdao Jiangyuan Kafei, a traditional soy sauce brewery. In the courtyard, soybeans ferment in rows of large, squat earthenware pots beneath conical lids that look like hats. The signature soy sauce coffee may sound like a gimmick, but it is surprisingly good – subtly salty, gently sweet and strangely moreish. We continue on to Zili, another of the Unesco villages. Spread across an open plain, it has the greatest concentration of residential diaolou anywhere in Kaiping and is a highlight of the trip. The setting is especially pretty, with wooden boardwalks crossing meadows and ponds filled with lotus flowers. The towers are some of the best-preserved. One building displays movie posters and photographs documenting Kaiping’s long association with cinema. Many films have been shot among the diaolou, including Jiang Wen’s Let the Bullets Fly, Wong Kar-wai’s The Grandmaster and Lau Kar-leung’s Drunken Master II. Our last stop is Li Yuan, Kaiping’s grandest garden estate, a 20,000-square-metre (215,000 sq ft) complex built in the 1930s. Italy-inspired pavilions, elegant archways and manicured gardens unfold around a network of canals, culminating in the estate’s unmistakable golden birdcage pavilion. As our adventure draws to a close, it feels fitting to end by watching a short documentary in the small cinema at Li Yuan’s Kaiping Diaolou Museum. It brings everything together – in many ways, the perfect ending to a journey full of history and culture. Upcoming trips will run September 18-20, October 23-25 and November 27-29. The package includes bike hire, local guides, accommodation, meals and admission tickets. For more information and bookings, visit Bike Aways.

title: Zheng Qinwen says return to form ‘painful process’ after win over Iga Swiatek at US Open
description: ‘I think, for me, these past three or four months have been basically the worst period of results in my career,’ former world No 4 says.
content: Zheng Qinwen has described her slow return to form as a painful rebirth that left her questioning herself and led to “uncomfortable conversations” with her parents and coaches. After months of struggling on the tour, the Chinese star has returned to form at the US Open, and produced a second thrilling win in a matter of days on Monday in New York, battling back from 5-0 down to beat Iga Swiatek in straight sets to reach the quarter-finals. The former world No 4 has been in such poor form for the past year, that she had dropped to 125th in the rankings and needed to come through qualifying just to reach the main draw. Now the 23-year-old is the first qualifier to reach the last eight since Emma Raducanu came through from nowhere to win the tournament in 2021. “I think the process of rebuilding myself is a very painful one, especially when I constantly have to face failure: OK, it’s not just one loss, the next match, OK, you lose again, and you have to ask yourself why all the effort you put in seems useless. And then comes the next match,” Zheng said in an interview with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV. “I think, for me, these past three or four months have been basically the worst period of results in my career. Even when I talk to myself, [I] find it unbelievable: why did it turn out like this? Is it simply because I was injured for so long without touching a tennis racquet, and my muscle memory was so slow to return?” Before rolling through the likes of Swiatek and Madison Keys, who she beat after fighting off match point in the fourth round, Zheng’s best result this year was reaching the quarter-finals at the Athens Open in July. And there had been little to suggest a change in fortunes was in the offing, with the Olympic champion losing to Thailand’s Lanlana Tararudee in the first round of qualifying at the National Bank Open in Toronto at the start of August. In fact, there were even fears last year’s elbow surgery had left Zheng without the powers that took her to the final of the Australian Open in 2024, and into the elite of the women’s game. “Even when I got injured as a kid, I was out for maybe a month at most. But this time, it was three, four, or even five months where I barely touched a racquet,” Zheng said. “When I came back after that, it felt ... I often describe it as completely losing all my form, and then having to rebuild step by step from scratch. “So, I often tell myself that this is a process of rebirth. Even now, looking back, I don’t really want to recall that period. Whether it was my parents or the team around me, we all went through a lot of uncomfortable conversations. I was also waiting to see when I could return to form. That’s why these recent victories are truly important to me, they are immensely encouraging.” After her most recent win on Monday, a 7-5, 6-3 triumph over Swiatek, Zheng said she had even forgotten “the score in the first set”. “It shows how focused I am. I guess to come back last time is not lucky,” Zheng added. While Swiatek, who fell to Zheng in the gold medal match in Paris two years ago, left the Arthur Ashe Stadium in tears, her Chinese opponent revelled in being back on centre court. “I just really appreciate being here in the Arthur Ashe Stadium,” she said. “It has been a while that I didn’t beat any top 10 player, so I’m just happy to win this match. It’s not easy.” Next up for Zheng is second seed Elena Rybakina, who cruised past Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4 in just 66 minutes, and the Chinese star said she would approach the match with the same attitude as she has done for the past week and more at Flushing Meadows. “I would say right now, the most important challenge for me is to keep this humble and be there, fight like I have nothing,” Zheng said. “The reality is you are just 125 [in the world], so you are not the top 10 you were before. Don’t treat yourself so high. You are here as everyone else. You start from the ground, so stay there and keep fighting.”

title: Hong Kong a boon to Kazakhstan’s advanced manufacturing ambitions, ties to Europe: expert
description: Sabr Yessimbekov says some projects in MOUs signed between Kazakhstan and Hong Kong-mainland China delegation in June already under way.
content: Hong Kong firms could look to Kazakhstan as a base for advanced manufacturing and as a gateway to Europe, while the city’s robust capital markets could attract businesses in the Central Asian country, a diplomat and business adviser has said. Sabr Yessimbekov, adviser to the chairman of the presidium of the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of the Republic of Kazakhstan, told the South China Morning Post on the sidelines of the inaugural China Conference: Central Asia 2026 that some projects in MOUs signed during Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s trip to Kazakhstan in June had already got under way. “We are talking about processing of raw materials and industrial production. There are some companies from Hong Kong and they have already started investing,” he said on Monday. The firms included tungsten miner Jiaxin International Resources, which became the first company to be dual-listed on Hong Kong and Astana’s bourses last year. In June, Lee led a 70-strong business and professional delegation from Hong Kong and mainland China to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to establish new trade corridors amid global geopolitical tensions, resulting in 96 agreements worth US$1.65 billion. On Monday, Lee said during a virtual appearance at the conference that a bank in that delegation had since backed the Development Bank of Kazakhstan with US$785 million in financing. Kazakhstan’s national rail operator, KTZ, had also filed to list in Hong Kong, while a local family office had signed an agreement with the Central Asian country’s authorities to strengthen cooperation in sustainable energy, he added. Yessimbekov noted that the successful dual-listing of Jiaxin had also boosted Kazakh firms’ interest in listing on the Hong Kong stock exchange. To his knowledge, some private investment funds from the Central Asian state were also starting to explore the city’s capital markets. “Now they understand, so they have a taste for the Hong Kong market, and everybody understands that it’s very well-connected to mainland China,” Yessimbekov explained, adding that the city’s connections with the rest of the world were also part of its appeal to Kazakh businesses. The adviser, who is also a career diplomat, said Chinese business interest in his country had surged after China and five countries in Central Asia – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan – signed a multilateral treaty last year. “The main change is that international businesses are no longer discussing why Central Asia, but rather which specific projects can be implemented here?” Yessimbekov said. He added that Kazakhstan could serve as a platform for manufacturing, the processing of raw materials, logistics, technology and as a gateway to other markets. However, Kazakh businesses were also looking to develop joint production operations with international partners, rather than passively receiving investment. “Kazakhstan’s business mission is to move along this production chain,” Yessimbekov said. For the resource-rich state, the aim was to move beyond mining to processing its raw materials – oil and gas, minerals, rare earths and other metals such as copper, titanium and uranium – into usable components, and manufacturing finished products for export. The role of Hong Kong in this process, according to Yessimbekov, will be to facilitate the building of industrial plants, materials production and exports to both China and Europe via the city’s expertise in financing and its access to the mainland market. “Hong Kong can act as a financial and professional bridge between Central Asia, mainland China and international capital markets,” the adviser said. The business opportunities Hong Kong presented to Kazakhstan were also bolstered by the city’s links with the mainland, he added. “So, in broader terms, China can be the market and industrial partner, Hong Kong is a financial and professional connector, and Kazakhstan is a production and a regional platform,” Yessimbekov said.

title: Chinese PLA aircraft to headline Egypt air show in display of export potential
description: No official word on which equipment will feature, but event comes just days after the end of a joint drill between the armed forces.
content: Fresh off a joint air drill, China will for the first time showcase several PLA Air Force aircraft overseas at an air show this week. The featured aircraft were selected for the air show in Egypt to demonstrate the air force’s integrated combat abilities and export potential, according to a military analyst. China’s armed forces on Tuesday posted pictures of Z-20, J-16, YY-20, and KJ-500 with its social media postings about the El Alamein International Airshow. The PLA Air Force said the involvement would “increase friendship and mutual trust, and strengthen diversified military cooperation between the two armed forces”. The event gets under way on Tuesday and runs until Thursday. It follows the China-Egypt Eagles of Civilisation joint training exercise, which began in late August and ended earlier this month. According to Egypt’s State Information Service (SIS), China sent six J-16 fighters, two YY-20A aerial-refuelling tankers, two Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, one KJ-500 early-warning and control plane, and two Z-20K helicopters for the exercise. SIS also posted photos of the J-16 and KJ-500 in statements about the air show. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military commentator and former People’s Liberation Army instructor, said all this equipment was expected to be displayed at the air show. “This is a breakthrough. It is to fully demonstrate integrated combat capabilities,” Song said. He added that among those with export potential were the KJ-500, Y-20, YY-20 and Z-20. “This equipment can be exported because China’s production capacity can be further expanded, not just fulfilling its own needs, but also meeting the demands of the international market,” he said. For the first Egypt air show in 2024, China sent seven J-10 aerobatic aircraft from the August 1st Aerobatic Team and one Y-20 transport aircraft. Fu Qianshao, a Chinese military analyst and former air force officer, said this should be the first time the J-16, KJ-500 and Z-20 had been seen at an overseas air show. The participation was also unusual for the number of aircraft that will be on show. “Half the time, only a mock-up is displayed,” Fu said. But both analysts said China was unlikely to export the heavyweight J-16. It is not certain whether China will put the J-16 on display at the Zhuhai air show in December, which is a prime event for weapons exports. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, China sold an unknown number of KJ-500s to Pakistan last year but they have yet to be delivered. Pakistan is also one of two foreign operators of its medium-weight J-10CE fighter jets. Uzbekistan is the other and Bangladesh is set to become the third.

title: Russia resumes deadly strikes on Kyiv after pause for Trump envoys’ visit
description: Explosions rock Ukrainian capital after expiration of a three-day halt for Witkoff and Kushner visit.
content: Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city. Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend. Fresh explosions early Tuesday triggered fires and sent locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter. “The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media. “His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.” Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s re-engagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people were trapped in a residential building after the strikes. Russia’s army said it had carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centres in Kyiv and its suburbs. Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s invasion, according to statistics verified by the United Nations. In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people. The strikes came hours after Witkoff touted “substantive progress” in the discussions with Ukraine and Russia, raising the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II. “President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace,” he said on X. Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday, before holding separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in their first official trip to Kyiv. The Kremlin announced Monday that it did not rule out three-way talks, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters “it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage”. Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing to de-escalate the conflict ahead of the long winter. Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20 degrees Celsius. Zelensky has said the weekend talks included US proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Tuesday appeared to rule out a Turkish proposal for a truce on strikes in the Black Sea, saying it was “unrealistic” and “impossible to monitor”. The two sides appear no closer to agreeing on how the war should end. Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support. Kyiv has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

title: Letters | Why Hong Kong’s medical schools should phase in their Cantonese requirement
description: Readers discuss language prerequisites at the city’s medical schools, and the promise of AI.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Hong Kong has long distinguished itself through world-class universities, an internationally respected healthcare system and a reputation for excellence that attracts talent from across the globe. If the city is serious about being an international education and innovation hub, it must ensure its medical education policies are aligned with that vision while upholding the highest standards of patient care. Recently, the University of Hong Kong (HKU) revised its admission criteria to require a good working knowledge of Chinese, rather than Cantonese specifically. Cantonese remains essential in clinical practice because it enables trust, understanding and accurate diagnosis. However, requiring full Cantonese proficiency before admission to medical school risks excluding international students who have the academic ability, dedication and potential to contribute to Hong Kong’s healthcare and research ecosystem. HKU has said that it will provide language support to help those who lack Cantonese proficiency when admitted. A phased language integration model where applicants are admitted on the basis of academic excellence and aptitude for medicine while being required to achieve professional Cantonese proficiency before undertaking significant clinical responsibilities seems reasonable. Rather than lowering standards, this would simply change when the standard must be met. Medical education is already structured in stages. The first years of most medical programmes are devoted largely to preclinical sciences, where instruction is predominantly delivered in English. This provides a window during which universities can offer intensive, mandatory medical Cantonese training tailored to patient communication and clinical interactions. By the time students begin extensive patient contact, they would be expected to demonstrate the language competence necessary to communicate safely and effectively. Such a model would allow Hong Kong to compete for international talent while safeguarding patient welfare. Importantly, modern medicine extends beyond direct clinical practice. By attracting highly capable students from around the world, Hong Kong can help address future healthcare workforce needs and enhance its research capacity and innovation ecosystem. Universities and teaching hospitals can support this transition through structured language programmes, supervised clinical placements and additional communication support during the early stages of training. These would ensure patient safety remains paramount while helping talented students integrate into Hong Kong society and healthcare settings. At a time when cities worldwide are competing for the brightest minds, Hong Kong should remain confident, ambitious and open. A phased language pathway would reinforce the city’s international outlook, strengthen its medical schools and research institutions, and ensure Hong Kong continues to attract the talent needed to thrive. Ahmed Ashfaq, Tsim Sha Tsui What relationship should humans and AI have? I am an enthusiastic user of artificial intelligence (AI). Over an extended period, I have used AI as an interlocutor while conducting academic research. What has impressed me is not simply its ability to provide information or answers but the usefulness of the developing conversation: questioning assumptions, suggesting connections and challenging conclusions. AI has enhanced rather than replaced my thinking. However, this experience also makes me concerned about a public debate which concentrates heavily on which occupations AI can automate, which human capabilities it can equal or exceed and what economic gains might result. We are neglecting a more fundamental question: what kind of relationship between humans and AI should we create if AI is to augment human thinking rather than substitute for it? This in turn leads to a broader question: how can society obtain the benefits of the cognitive transformation by AI without people surrendering their intellectual, economic and political agency? I am particularly interested in whether the answers look different when considered from China and East Asia. Recent reports concerning protection of China’s labour market from AI disruption, automation designed around human workers and humans continuing to provide AI’s purpose and moral compass raise an intriguing question: do different societies have different conceptions of the relationship between technological progress, human agency and social legitimacy? Transformative technologies require legitimacy as well as effectiveness, but different societies can attach different meanings to agency, social cohesion and legitimacy. Perhaps augmentation is broadly desirable across societies, while the meaning of agency – and therefore the conditions under which AI transformation is considered legitimate – varies substantially. Whatever those differences, AI could become an extraordinary instrument of human empowerment. It need not be an artificial mind to which we progressively surrender our thinking but a capable interlocutor through which we learn to think better ourselves. These questions deserve a wider public conversation. The objective should be not merely more capable AI but more capable human beings. David Backinsell, Rickmansworth, UK

title: In Gyirong Port, small items speak of the human cost of the China-Nepal disaster
description: In the ruins of a bustling border crossing, the search goes on for signs of the lives that were swept away on that devastating day.
content: “I do not want to stop [searching]. If I pause, I start thinking about my brothers and sisters and all the moments of my life here.” Gui Xinwei, deputy chief of the Gyirong Border Inspection Station, was speaking to Chinese state broadcaster CCTV from the ruins of his workplace, seven days after the devastating mudslide erased the port crossing where China and Nepal meet. “I just don’t want to stop.” Gui was away on holiday on August 26 when a glacier collapsed in Nepal, triggering a massive mudflow and floods that travelled 22km (14 miles) in just seven minutes, flattening the entire Gyirong Port area. Many of his colleagues were lost in the disaster. Returning to the site, Gui found the 20-metre (65 feet) port building that had survived previous heavy floods as well as strong earthquakes completely gone. It was as if he had been thrown into “a parallel universe or a nightmare”, he said – until a pine tree on the mountain ridge reminded him that this was the very place where he had worked for more than 20 years. “Every single thing I dug up, a piece of clothing, jewellery, cosmetics or just tiny items – even a charging cable or a phone case – I don’t know if they belonged to my brothers and sisters,” Gui told the reporter. “But I know for sure that these things belonged to someone. They definitely belonged to someone.” The report, which aired on Sunday, detailed the heroic search and rescue efforts carried out in extreme circumstances: blocked roads, thick mud, falling rocks, torrential rain, precarious barrier lakes and the looming risk of secondary flooding. Firefighter Yang Qiqiao, from the closest city, Shigatse, was among the first rescuers to reach the site, after bushwhacking through rain-soaked forest, thousands of metres above sea level. They struggled for 12 hours to advance just a few kilometres on the map. “It felt like the mountains had no top and no bottom … It was just one mountain after another,” Yang said. “All we could think about was to keep pushing and breaking through, so we could get to the site as quickly as we could.” When they arrived, Yang and his team found the area blanketed by thick silt. They immediately began searching through the metre-deep mud, calling out into the silence for survivors. “The truth is, no one answered. It was truly heartbreaking,” Yang said. The rescuers spent the first two nights in small caves, taking shelter from the rain. They were forced to evacuate once, when a barrier dam breached and triggered new flooding. Although there was dim hope of finding anyone alive, Yang and his fellow dozens of rescuers continued their search. They were instructed to also look for any personal items that could help to identify the missing, such as ID or clothing. “Yesterday we found an immigration police officer’s vest. The sight was devastating. When the immigration officers came to check, they were deeply grieved,” Yang said. Engineers and construction crews have been working tirelessly to repair a 1.8km stretch of the G216 road which was destroyed and buried by debris, blocking access to the port site. Excavators operated in a narrow line between unstable cliff walls on one side and fast-flowing floodwaters on the other. In a series of safety measures, the cab doors were removed, the operators were given life vests and escape ladders were hung from the cliffs. “In case of an emergency, they can jump out immediately … and climb to safety,” said Li Hongjun, commander of the construction team. Huang Xun, operator of the first excavator in the line, found his track submerged most of the time. With no way of knowing the conditions beneath the water, he drove blindly, “relying solely on feel”. “Because once I drove in, the second and third excavators followed right behind me. A whole string of them came in. If I delayed, I’d hold up the entire line. The faster I moved forward, the sooner we could all get in,” Huang said. The repairs to the road were finally completed and heavy machinery was able to enter the site on September 2. As of Saturday, the Chinese side has counted 43 deaths while 519 people were still missing, including 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries. Rescuers have recovered 993 items from the debris. State media has reported that more than 60 forensic experts are working across three laboratories to identify the victims. On the Nepalese side, by Monday morning the death toll had risen to 1,355 with an additional 4,996 missing.

title: China’s export machine strengthens in August as US critiques trade imbalance
description: While Western officials still name China’s trade surplus as an area of concern, analysts said the 2026 surplus is on track to beat last year’s record.
content: China’s exports continued to beat expectations in August, buoyed by strong demand for tech products and pre-Christmas orders that offset severe weather disruptions, though analysts warned the country’s widening trade imbalances remained a concern among Western policymakers. The country’s exports rose by 25 per cent year on year to US$401.44 billion last month, according to Chinese customs data released on Tuesday. The reading was above a forecast of 21.93 per cent growth from economists polled by financial data provider Wind. That compared with 23.9 per cent growth in July. China also saw imports grow by 28.2 per cent last month to US$282.36 billion, slightly above the Wind poll’s projections of 28.07 per cent growth. That brought China’s trade surplus to US$119.09 billion last month, up from US$112.5 billion in July. This marked the fourth consecutive month the surplus had stayed above US$100 billion. China’s export sector has remained resilient this year, as the global artificial intelligence boom and energy security worries linked to regional conflicts – including the US-Israel war on Iran – have driven up shipments of goods as well as prices. Exports have also benefited from seasonal pre-Christmas orders, though a series of typhoons last month caused widespread delays at Shanghai’s two major container ports. Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research, said that demand related to AI offset the effects of adverse weather, with high-priced tech shipments boosting export figures, while tariff uncertainty continued to front-load US import demand. However, looking ahead, Xing said he expected overall export growth to slow later in the year due to a higher base, noting exports may be close to their peak and fourth-quarter growth “may not be so strong”. Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING, also noted that tech-related export categories outperformed in August. “The trade data came in broadly in line with expectations, and illustrates that external demand remains strong.” He added he expected China’s balance of trade to keep growing, with another record trade surplus likely by the end of this year. The cumulative surplus had already reached US$805.51 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up about 3 per cent from the same period last year, customs data showed. That figure, which hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year, has drawn intensified scrutiny from the West and prompted trade restrictions over Beijing’s industrial policy. Speaking publicly after a meeting of Group of 20 finance ministers last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called China’s current account surplus “unsustainable” and cited opposition from Beijing as the reason the group failed to issue a unanimous statement. As China continues to rely on exports to support the economy, trade imbalance has become an area of discussion among policymakers, said Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management. He added that while the recent appreciation of the Japanese yen and South Korean won had built up pressure on the yuan to appreciate, exchange rate adjustment would likely be modest this year, with limited impact on trade imbalances. President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington later this month, with trade, AI and the Iran war expected to be high on the agenda. In August, China’s exports to the United States rose 34.4 per cent year on year, against a low base for the same period last year. Exports to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, China’s largest trading partner by bloc, rose by 30.21 per cent year on year, while shipments to members of the European Union increased by 6.61 per cent. The world’s second-largest economy is taking steps to further boost trade with Southeast Asia. The 134km (83-mile) Pinglu Canal is set to open to navigation next week, linking south China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region to Vietnam and other countries in the region via the Gulf of Tonkin, also known as the Beibu Gulf. Meanwhile, the EU’s trade deficit with China has become a point of contention for Brussels. Amid marathon trade talks with their Chinese counterparts at the end of June, the bloc’s trade officials set a three-month deadline for the two sides to make “tangible progress” in disputes spanning several areas. EU policymakers and business leaders have expressed fears that cheap Chinese imports – aided by hefty state subsidies – are helping to deindustrialise swathes of the continent’s manufacturing economy. Separated by product category, the data showed tech-related exports continued to rise as automobile exports slowed. Shipments of integrated circuits fell by 7.92 per cent year on year in volume terms last month but surged by 129.83 per cent in value – driven by higher prices amid a memory chip shortage fuelled by a global AI infrastructure buildout. The pace improved upon July’s 116.57 per cent growth, as well as June’s 121.9 per cent growth rate. Outbound shipments of automatic data-processing equipment and related components also jumped last month, growing by 76.52 per cent year on year. Export growth for automobiles, however, was 43 per cent in value terms, down from the 60 per cent rate recorded in July. China’s rare earth exports fell by 18.25 per cent year on year by volume, as Beijing continues to exert tight control over shipments of the minerals, which are essential to the production of a range of hi-tech products. Meanwhile, imports came in a little softer than expected, Song said. Both the import volume and value of automobiles dropped in August, falling by 50 and 32 per cent, respectively. “China’s import profile is undergoing a clear structural shift in autos, where heavy domestic competition has also driven a sharp drop in demand for foreign imports,” Song said. The country’s crude oil imports reached US$22.72 billion last month, down 8.85 per cent year on year in value terms, while shipments fell by 23.36 per cent. Among emerging economies, China’s imports from Africa slowed to just 3.7 per cent year on year compared with a 25 per cent surge in July. Last week, Xi paid a state visit to Egypt, his first in 10 years, aimed at boosting economic and trade ties.

title: Hong Kong emerges as leading Asian study destination for Kazakhstani students
description: Hong Kong universities attracting growing number of students from Central Asian country, with enrolment up by 408 per cent in eight years.
content: Kazakhstan has recorded the largest student population and fastest enrolment growth at Hong Kong’s public universities among Central Asian countries in recent years, according to official data, while students from the country say the city is the most preferred regional higher education destination in Asia among their peers. Among Hong Kong’s tertiary education institutions, City University (CityU) enrolled the largest share of Kazakhstani students. CityU council chairman Michael Ngai Ming-tak told the South China Morning Post that students from Kazakhstan were among the university’s top-performing undergraduates and that the country’s government was committed to educating its young people. According to University Grants Committee (UGC) figures, Kazakhstan accounts for the largest number of students studying at Hong Kong’s publicly funded universities among the five countries that make up Central Asia. The number of Kazakhstani students at the universities rose from 97 in the 2017-18 academic year to 493 in 2025-26, an increase of 408 per cent – the highest growth rate among Central Asian countries. CityU enrolled 203 Kazakhstani undergraduates this year, a record 49 per cent rise from 135 the previous academic year. Assem Kanabek, a third-year chemistry undergraduate at CityU, said Hong Kong’s proximity to her hometown, its Asian culture and the quality of its universities had prompted her to choose the city. The 20-year-old is also the recipient of a CityU Entrance Scholarship, which covers full tuition fees and provides a living allowance. “For me, I’ve always wanted to stay in Asia, closer to home. I know a lot of people from my cohort of high school students wanted to apply to the Ivy League or America or the UK. But I always felt like Asia is just a closer culture, would be a closer culture to me,” she said. Kanabek said she had considered South Korea and Japan as well, but believed Hong Kong had Asia’s best universities, particularly for her subject. She added that Hong Kong was also a popular destination in Asia among her peers. “For my cohort of high school students, we had a countrywide group chat where a lot of people were applying for universities … there was specifically a group about Asian universities,” she said. “In that group, maybe about 60 per cent plan to or are already seniors in Hong Kong.” She added that the growing Kazakhstani community in Hong Kong had also made the city more attractive to people in her hometown. “Out of all the places in Asia, Hong Kong is the most popular choice,” she said. “There’s also a lot of support from Kazakh people who might have already graduated, who work here, who study here. We’re all really tight-knit, and we all like to try to support each other. We are growing, but we’re still a small community.” Third-year computer science student Islam Seitzhanov, also 20, said the prospect of a scholarship and the popularity of his programme at the university were among his main reasons for choosing Hong Kong. “From my childhood, I wanted to stay in Asia a lot. I had three top destinations. They were at the same level for me – Korea, Hong Kong and Singapore … I decided to stay in Hong Kong because CityU offered me a scholarship,” he said, referring to the university’s Entrance Scholarship. He added that most Kazakhstani students at the university studied computer science, and that career opportunities in the city were another reason young people from the country chose Hong Kong. “They think Hong Kong is a very rapidly growing city and it’s also a business centre in Asia. That’s why they think that they have a lot of opportunities here,” he said. “We have students who have graduated [in Hong Kong] already. They talked to high school students and recommended it because they find that this is a really great space to flourish.” CityU council chairman Ngai said the first sharp rise in Kazakhstani student admissions had come after the university signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Central Asian country in 2023 to promote academic exchanges, talent development and research. That agreement was followed by various other partnerships and collaborations. “We can see that the government has the ambition to grow and also to train the young generation,” he said. Ngai said students from the country were among CityU’s strongest academic performers. “We have done statistics on the performance and the results of our students. The best performers in our university, on average, are Kazakh students,” he said. He added that having the students learn in Hong Kong was a win-win situation. “The government and the companies in Kazakhstan told us that the bottleneck for its growth is talent development. So that’s why they are sending students and professionals to Hong Kong,” he said. “Hong Kong’s status as a finance centre will also benefit from the arrival of the students and professionals from Kazakhstan.” The four other Central Asian countries – Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan – have also continued to send students to Hong Kong in recent years, according to UGC figures. The number of Uzbekistani students at Hong Kong’s public universities rose from one in 2017-18 to 29 in the most recent academic year. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) and the University of Hong Kong had the largest number of Uzbekistani students, with nine each in 2025-26. Kyrgyzstan also had nearly 50 students in Hong Kong. Enrolment rose from nine students in 2017-18 to a peak of 102 in 2021-22 before falling to 47 in 2025-26. CityU had the highest number of students from the country. Tajikistan had a comparatively small student population in Hong Kong. Its total peaked at 11 in 2020-21 and then steadily declined to four in 2025-26. Turkmenistan had only two students studying in Hong Kong in 2025-26, both at HKUST. Central Asia is a strategic region for China’s Belt and Road Initiative, the global infrastructure and trade strategy announced by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2013. The Hong Kong government has awarded dedicated scholarships to 833 students from 57 belt and road countries over the past decade for undergraduate and research postgraduate studies in the city. Indonesia and Malaysia have produced the largest numbers of recipients, with more than 100 students from each country benefiting since 2016-17. The annual quota for the scholarship was gradually raised from an initial 10 places to 150 for 2024-25. In total, 833 students from the 57 countries have received the scholarship. The SCMP signed an MOU with Nazarbayev University in Kazakhstan on Monday to promote knowledge exchange between East and Central Asia, and expand Hong Kong’s media presence in the region. The MOU was signed in Astana ahead of the SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026, which also examined Kazakhstan’s higher education sector and its collaboration with universities in Hong Kong. The strategic partnership formalises links between the SCMP and Nazarbayev University – Central Asia’s top-ranked higher education institution – through academic dialogue and knowledge-sharing, and connects the city’s capital and media reach with the region’s tech and resource ecosystem.

title: Huawei’s new Kirin chip puts LogicFolding to the test, with bigger ambitions in AI
description: New smartphone processor is a crucial test of the firm’s attempt to route around US-led curbs on the most advanced chipmaking technology.
content: Huawei Technologies’ latest flagship mobile processor is serving as a high-stakes test of whether the company can bypass US technology sanctions by layering circuits on top of each other to boost performance, according to analysts. The Shenzhen-based firm on Monday launched the Kirin 9050 Pro, the first commercial chip employing its LogicFolding architecture. The new strategy aims to squeeze greater computing power out of semiconductor designs without relying solely on the circuit-shrinking provided by the world’s most advanced lithography equipment, which remains blocked by US export controls. Powering Huawei’s new Mate XT 2 trifold smartphone, the Kirin 9050 Pro delivers a 42 per cent leap in overall performance over its predecessor alongside improved power efficiency, according to the company. For global chipmakers with access to leading-edge manufacturing equipment, stacking components – or 3D integration – is typically a supplementary tool used alongside transistor miniaturisation. Constrained by trade restrictions, however, Huawei has instead made advanced packaging and architectural workarounds its main strategy. While existing 3D techniques simply stack largely self-contained dies, Huawei’s LogicFolding splits core computing functions across two active layers designed to operate as a single unit. “LogicFolding is first and foremost a compensatory route – a choice born of external constraints,” said Leslie Wu, CEO of semiconductor consultancy RHCC, in a research note. Wu said the approach came at a cost. Bonding two active silicon layers requires complex manufacturing steps – including precise wafer thinning and microscopic vertical wiring – that can weigh on factory yields. For global companies that can simply print smaller transistors on a single layer, the economics of LogicFolding may be less compelling. While the Kirin 9050 Pro debuted in a consumer handset, industry observers saw the mobile chip as a trial run for Huawei’s long-term artificial intelligence ambitions. In a research paper published in May introducing Huawei’s “Tau Scaling Law,” He Tingbo, head of the company’s HiSilicon semiconductor unit, outlined plans to eventually bring LogicFolding to its Ascend AI accelerator line. Huawei has said it expected to rely on more established technologies like 3D stacking through the rest of the decade before deploying LogicFolding on its flagship Ascend 990 AI chip around 2030. Smartphone processors offered “a far gentler starting point” than AI chips, said Venkat Somala, a researcher at Epoch AI, in a report on Friday. Somala noted that smaller smartphone chips made production losses easier to manage, while lower power consumption reduced thermal challenges. High smartphone sales volumes would also give Huawei’s assembly lines crucial opportunities to mature before tackling AI chips, he added. Scaling LogicFolding to AI would be considerably harder, given the larger sizes of Ascend chips and their intense heat output, Somala said, adding that mastering the technology would nevertheless be “key to Huawei’s competitiveness beyond 2030”. The architectural push comes as Huawei seeks to expand its presence in international AI infrastructure. Malaysia is evaluating Huawei’s Ascend 910C processors to power a 2 billion ringgit (US$494 million) sovereign AI project, Bloomberg reported on Monday. The Southeast Asian nation was considering the older 910C over Huawei’s more advanced Ascend 950, which remained in limited production, the report said.

title: Style Edit: Breguet’s tourbillon legacy and its enduring role in watchmaking history
description: From Abraham-Louis Breguet’s 1801 patent to 2025’s Expérimentale 1, the tourbillon remains at the heart of the maison’s ongoing horological innovation.
content: There have been moments in watchmaking when a problem as fundamental as gravity became the starting point for an entirely new chapter in horology. For Abraham-Louis Breguet, that moment came at the turn of the 19th century. In the pocket watches of his era, the balance and hairspring were particularly vulnerable to the effects of gravity with the watch remaining in a vertical position for extended periods. His solution was not to fight gravity, but to keep the regulating mechanisms moving through it. On June 26, 1801, Breguet was granted a patent for his tourbillon regulator. Its ingenious principle was to place the escapement and regulating organ inside a rotating cage, continuously changing their position relative to gravity. By averaging out positional errors, the mechanism could improve the consistency of the watch’s timekeeping. That cage would become one of the most recognisable signatures of mechanical watchmaking – and a surprisingly fertile area for experimentation. The original construction was made from materials very different from those used today. Breguet’s modern interpretations employ titanium for the cage, reducing its weight and therefore the energy required to keep both cage and balance in motion. Even seemingly minute details have been reconsidered: the contemporary Tradition Tourbillon, for example, uses a three-arm cage rather than the two-arm construction described in Breguet’s original patent, improving stability and resistance to shocks. The most compelling expression of that philosophy is seen in the Expérimentale 1. Here, Breguet returns to the same fundamental question that occupied its founder – how can the precision of a mechanical watch be pushed further? The answer is radically contemporary: a 10Hz tourbillon combined with a constant-force magnetic escapement. The high frequency allows the regulating system to recover rapidly from disturbances, while controlled magnetic interactions help maintain a consistent impulse to the balance. Breguet’s first tourbillon was an attempt to neutralise one of nature’s most persistent forces. Nearly 225 years later, the maison is still experimenting with ever-more refined solutions – only now, gravity is joined by the effects of magnetism, the need for shock resistance and the demands of increasing precision. The cage keeps turning. The question remains the same: how far can mechanical timekeeping go? 5 things you may not know about Breguet 1. The tourbillon took years to reach the public Breguet patented it in 1801, but the first commercial examples did not appear until 1805. Between 1796 and 1829, just 40 finished tourbillons were produced. 2. Precision was behind many of Breguet’s inventions Before the tourbillon, Breguet patented a constant-force escapement in 1798. More than two centuries later, both principles have been brought together in the Expérimentale 1. 3. The maison was once the watchmaker of royalty Marie Antoinette and Napoleon Bonaparte were among Breguet’s celebrated patrons. Breguet was the inventor of the first tact watch in 1799, as part of the Souscription series for Napoleon’s wife Josephine Bonaparte. 4. Breguet had serious credentials at sea He produced 78 marine chronometers, and his instruments accompanied some of the great scientific voyages of the 19th century. 5. The tourbillon has a modern comeback story Breguet revived the complication for the contemporary era with Ref. 3350 in 1989, helping propel the tourbillon back into the spotlight of haute horlogerie.

title: Style Edit: Richard Mille revs up vintage elegance at 3 racing events
description: The Swiss watchmaker champions classic racing through partnerships with the Richard Mille Cup, Le Mans Classic and Rallye des Princesses.
content: No other Swiss luxury watchmaker constantly pushes back the boundaries of the possible quite like Richard Mille. The high-performance worlds of motorsport and sailing share a similar passion for mechanical mastery – and it’s an affinity that leads naturally to collaboration. Richard Mille is partner to a trio of sporting events, covering sailing, road racing and rallying, that celebrate the brand’s fondness for precision machines that blend supreme beauty with peerless technical sophistication. While today’s streamlined, super-speedy racing yachts are certainly impressive, the elegant yachts of a century ago glide across the waves with an unmatchable élan. That golden age of sailing was celebrated with the return of an event that brings together a selection of the most beautiful vintage yachts, which battle it out over an equally spectacular course – the Richard Mille Cup. This was the third edition of the cup, contested every two years in the challenging waters surrounding the UK. But while the first two editions saw competitors sail between the south coast of England and France, this one moved the action much farther north, to the choppy waters of the Firth of Clyde, off the west coast of Scotland. There, a fleet of 12 classic yachts fought it out over 10 days in June, kicking the race off at the fairy-tale Culzean Castle to the south of the firth. The location might have been sublime, but it was also fiendishly challenging, with turbulent seas demanding a combination of sailing skill and steely resilience. Among the much-loved vintage vessels joining the battle for the beautiful silver trophy made by British jeweller Garrard were Kismet (1898), Moonbeam (1903), Mariquita (1911), Moonbeam IV (1920) and Saskia (1931). Just as the Richard Mille Cup celebrates the most gracious of vintage racing yachts, so does the Le Mans Classic tip its hat to their terrestrial counterparts. The race pits vintage racing cars against each other over the legendary 13km Circuit de la Sarthe in northwestern France, the same course used for the 24 Hours of Le Mans. The Le Mans Classic is likewise contested over 24 gruelling hours, with cars dating from the 1920s to the 1980s divided into six eras. Richard Mille has partnered with the race since its debut in 2002, creating a special watch in the event’s colours for every race since 2008. This year marked a major milestone in the history of the Le Mans Classic, with the race reborn as the Le Mans Classic Legend and moving from biennial to annual. Attracting nearly 160,000 spectators, the 2026 edition featured 350 cars on the track and 3,200 vehicles on display. Classic cars were given an even broader canvas to strut their stuff at another event celebrating motorsport history: the Rallye des Princesses Richard Mille. Held since 1999 and inspired by the Paris-Saint Raphaël Féminin Rally of 1929, the race sees all-female teams take to the roads of France over five days of rallying. They are at the wheels of vehicles dating from 1946 to 1991, and the race, rather than a contest of pure velocity, is a regularity rally, where the aim is to complete the course while remaining close to a target average speed. The 25th edition of the Rallye des Princesses Richard Mille, in May, was contested by 97 teams. They started at the Place Vendôme in Paris, guiding their cars 1,700km down some of France’s most beautiful roads to finish in the iconic seaside town of Saint-Tropez on the French Riviera. En route, they took in gems including the beautiful medieval town of Troyes, the charming spa town of Vichy, the stunning forested lakeside location of Aix-les-Bains and the ancient city of Nîmes, renowned for its perfectly preserved Roman monuments. Won by Véronique Lagache and Anne Sampeur, driving a vintage Porsche 911 3.2, the race was a unique combination of peerless mechanical excellence and effortlessly distinctive style – which made it the perfect fit for Richard Mille.

title: Australia nears treaty with Solomon Islands in bid to limit China’s influence
description: Canberra has pledged US$708 million in extra funding for Honiara as part of the deal expected to be signed in the coming weeks.
content: Australia is in the process of finalising a treaty with another Pacific island nation, with the national broadcaster reporting that Canberra has struck an “in-principle” agreement with the Solomon Islands. The two nations will work to sign the deal in the coming weeks, Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported, citing unidentified government officials. The news comes after Solomons Prime Minister Matthew Wale saw off a challenge to his leadership from within his cabinet, with the rival withdrawing over the weekend. Australia has pledged A$980 million (US$708 million) in extra funding for the Solomon Islands’ government, according to a leaked text message from the Australian ambassador that was also reported by the ABC. Once finalised, the deal would represent a significant diplomatic victory for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s government. The Solomon Islands shot to geopolitical prominence in 2022 when then-prime minister Manasseh Sogavare signed a security pact with China, provoking alarm in Canberra and Washington. Albanese was first elected prime minister just weeks after the Solomons-China agreement was revealed, and has worked over the past four years to both reverse that deal and rebuild ties with the archipelago nation. Since Wale came to power in May, he has shifted his government’s diplomatic focus back to Australia and the US, breaking with previous administrations’ tilt towards Beijing. Wale’s first overseas trip was to Canberra in June, with Albanese then reciprocating in July, when he travelled to Honiara and announced the start of the negotiations for the treaty. That meeting came a day after Albanese signed two new deals with Fiji, including a military alliance, which New Zealand has also expressed an interest in joining. Those talks are all part of a web of security and policing agreements that Australia has established with nations including Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Nauru, Indonesia and others as it seeks to limit Chinese influence in the region. Canberra is also strengthening security ties with Japan, including plans to buy Japanese-made naval vessels. China’s test of a submarine-launched nuclear-capable ballistic missile in the Pacific region in early July also focused regional leaders’ attention on the risks of growing US-China strategic competition. Australia, Palau, New Zealand and others immediately condemned the test. While Pacific nations were initially unable to agree on a joint response to China’s move, at the Pacific Islands Forum last week in Palau, all but one of the 18 member nations signed on to a statement calling out the firing of the missile and demanding proper advance notification and transparency.

title: Can Japan, South Korea move past the ‘comfort women’ issue?
description: The issue is set to continue rattling ties between Tokyo and Seoul even as they seek to find common ground on security and trade issues.
content: South Korean citizens’ groups have called for the abuse of wartime “comfort women” to be recognised by Unesco, as analysts say the ongoing feud between Seoul and Tokyo threatens to upset recent improvements in their relations. They also suggest that the two nations would benefit from working together at a time of unprecedented regional and global security and economic challenges, although they admit that may be impossible. On Sunday, a coalition of South Korean citizens’ groups called on the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation to move forward with the listing of documents about wartime comfort women on its Memory of the World Register. The request was made at a press conference in Seoul more than a decade after groups from eight countries first requested that Unesco collate and preserve victims’ testimonies and other paperwork related to the sexual slavery of women from across Asia imposed by Japanese troops. It comes after the Korean Supreme Court on August 12 dismissed an appeal by Japan’s Nippon Steel against a lower-court ruling in South Korea that ordered the company to pay 80 million Korean won (US$59,528) to the family of the late Min Moon-sik for forced labour in 1942. The previous month, Unesco passed a resolution at its World Heritage Committee meeting in Busan insisting that Japan present the “whole history” of forced labourers – including more than 1,500 Koreans – who worked during Japan’s colonial era at a mine on the Japanese island of Sado. More than 80 years after the end of the second world war, it is unlikely that the two nations will see eye-to-eye on their shared history – and particularly the years of Japan’s often brutal occupation of the Korean peninsula in the early decades of the last century, according to analysts. “I do not think it will ever be possible to have a bilateral alliance in the usual sense between the two nations,” said Toshimitsu Shigemura, a professor of politics at Tokyo’s Waseda University. “Friendship might be possible, but even that will not be easy.” Japan was at fault for failing to apologise to the nascent Korean nation immediately after its surrender in 1945 and for not immediately offering to provide compensation for its 35 years of colonial rule, Shigemura said. It was not until 1965 that the two countries normalised diplomatic relations and Tokyo paid US$300 million in compensation to Seoul. “Japan should have reflected more carefully on its behaviour sooner after the war and emphasised that we were adopting a constitution committed to peace,” he said. “But on the other hand, I think there are still many people in Japan who consider themselves to be superior to Koreans and that we actually helped to modernise their society.” Equally, some in Korea blamed Japan for virtually all the nation’s problems and to this day insisted that Tokyo intended to expand its military so it could invade and reoccupy the Korean peninsula again, Shigemura said. “There have been failures on both sides, and that is why I am not optimistic that the relationship will ever be really strong.” Robert Dujarric, co-director of the Institute of Contemporary Asian Studies at the Tokyo campus of Temple University, likened the relationship to the similarly troubled ties between England and Ireland. The two countries have had disagreements over past sectarian violence in Northern Ireland, which is part of the UK, and Dublin calling for a vote to allow the Northern Irish to decide on reunification. “I do not think Japan and South Korea will ever be able to have what I would call ‘normal’ relations,” he said. “There will always be irritants, so the question is how the two governments control those situations to make sure they do not degenerate.” Dujarric said he hoped that the Japanese government would not comment on the Unesco documents request, although he expressed concern that conservative groups in Japan would be unable to let go of the opportunity to criticise their neighbour. Criticising the request and becoming embroiled in debates on the other historical issues would only escalate the rivalry and potentially return the relationship to the lows it experienced in 2018 and 2019, when the row over the sovereignty of Korean-held Dokdo island came to the fore, and a Korean warship locked its radar onto a Japanese maritime patrol aircraft. On the trade front, Japan imposed new restrictions on exports of key materials critical to South Korea’s semiconductor industry in 2019, triggering a swift boycott by Korean consumers of Japanese goods before the end of the same year. Political leaders in both capitals have in subsequent years worked hard to smooth ruffled feathers, a task arguably made easier by the worsening security situation over North Korea and their separate deepening trade disputes with the US. In 2019, then-president Moon Jae-in also angered Japan when he reversed the December 2015 “final and irreversible” agreement to settle the comfort women dispute, under which Japan made a formal apology and acknowledged the suffering of the women. Tokyo also paid 1 billion yen (US$8.3 million) that was meant to be disbursed to the former comfort women through a foundation. “China and North Korea are security problems that both Japan and South Korea have to face up to, but that situation has been made worse by questions over their alliances with this US administration and the trade tariffs that Washington has imposed on its two most important Asian allies,” Dujarric said. “Seoul and Tokyo are not short of challenges and enemies, so it would clearly be in their best interests to work together,” he said. “Relations are OK at the moment, but there is always potential for something to happen that upsets that – like a Japanese politician going to the Yasukuni Shrine.” Yasukuni is the last resting place of Japan’s nearly 2.5 million war dead and is controversial because it also honours the memories of 14 Class A war criminals. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi most recently visited the shrine on August 12, the anniversary of Tokyo’s surrender at the end of the war. “I hope they can continue to muddle through,” Dujarric said. Yuji Hosaka, a professor of political science at Korea University in Sejong city and an adviser to the South Korean government on Japan relations, is also pessimistic about the relationship and fears that Tokyo is going to be disappointed if it is holding out hope that the comfort women issue will come to a natural end when the last surviving victim dies. “There are many groups in South Korea that were not satisfied with the 2015 comfort women agreement, and one of the survivors, Lee Yong-soo, is still very active in promoting their campaign,” said Hosaka. “I met her recently, and it is clear that she has great power to push the citizens’ movement forward,” he said, pointing out that there were just five former comfort women alive today. “I recently met another woman who told me that her mother was also a victim, and she said she was committed to continuing the movement even after the last of them has died,” he said. The South Korean government of President Lee Jae Myung was presently “quiet” on the issue of historical issues with Japan, Hosaka said, but behind the scenes they were being “very helpful” to victims of Tokyo’s colonial rule.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong aviation success today means more than just adding routes
description: Success was once measured by how far local airlines could fly. Now, it’s about how effectively global networks intersect here to power the wider economy.
content: When Cathay Pacific Airways announced direct flights to Almaty starting next January, the significance went beyond adding another destination. The service will be Cathay Pacific’s first to Central Asia and the only non-stop passenger connection between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan. Another announcement pointed to Hong Kong’s growing aviation reach from a different direction. Qatar Airways Cargo relocated its regional office to Hong Kong and agreed with the Airport Authority to increase frequencies and develop new routes through the city. The airline already operates around 56 cargo flights a week via Hong Kong. Taken together, these developments offer an interesting glimpse of how Hong Kong’s aviation map is evolving. As Cathay celebrates its 80th anniversary this year, Hong Kong also finds itself entering a new era for its airport. The three-runway system and Skytopia development signal ambitions that extend well beyond aviation. Hong Kong International Airport is no longer being positioned simply as one of the world’s best to arrive at or for transit, but as an integrated destination for tourism, business and entertainment. In this year’s budget, the government reaffirmed the Airport City development as a strategic economic initiative. Hong Kong’s airport handled some 63 million passengers in the year ended March 31, nearly 15 per cent more than in the previous year, while remaining the world’s busiest cargo airport. Yet these developments also pose an important question. If Hong Kong’s ambitions for its airport have evolved, has our thinking about what makes a successful aviation hub kept pace? For decades, success was measured largely by how far Hong Kong could reach. That made perfect sense. As an outward-looking economy, our city depended on international connectivity. Long-haul routes linked the city to financial centres, attracted multinational businesses and reinforced its position as one of Asia’s leading gateways. Those connections remain essential. But the map around Hong Kong is changing. Almaty is interesting because it does not fit neatly into the traditional division between the established long-haul markets in Europe and North America, and the familiar short-haul destinations within Asia. It opens another direction towards Central Asia, with which Hong Kong seeks deeper economic and tourism ties. Qatar Airways Cargo’s decision shows another dimension of connectivity. Hong Kong’s value as a hub also depends on whether international carriers see the city as a useful place from which to connect their networks. This matters as the Airport City takes shape. Hong Kong once judged aviation success by how far its airlines could fly. Tomorrow’s measure may increasingly be how effectively networks intersect here and the value they create for the wider economy. Regional travel remains an important part of that equation. The International Air Transport Association expects the Asia-Pacific to account for over half of global passenger growth over the next two decades. More affordable fares and denser regional networks are also making shorter, repeat trips increasingly common. For Hong Kong, this creates a different opportunity. A regional visitor returning several times a year can generate recurring demand for hotels, restaurants, retailers and attractions. Frequency deserves to be considered alongside spending per trip. The objective should not be merely to attract more arrivals, but to give nearby travellers compelling reasons to return. This is why Hong Kong’s conversation about aviation may need to become broader. When Cathay acquired HK Express in 2019, much discussion centred on competition in the regional low-cost market. Today, the two airlines can increasingly be viewed as complementary. Cathay connects Hong Kong with established global centres while opening up emerging markets such as Central Asia. HK Express, meanwhile, may quietly be becoming one of Hong Kong’s more important tourism assets. Its growing network of secondary Asian cities encourages frequent regional travel and brings different visitor segments within easier reach of Hong Kong. Viewed alongside international carriers such as Qatar Airways, a broader picture emerges. Hong Kong’s strength need not come from one type of connectivity. It can combine Cathay’s global reach, HK Express’ regional accessibility and international airlines feeding their own networks through Hong Kong. Events in the Middle East reinforce why such diversity matters. Airspace disruptions temporarily altered passenger flows and highlighted how quickly established travel patterns can change. The lesson is not that Hong Kong should seek to benefit from difficulties facing other hubs. Rather, aviation resilience increasingly depends on having multiple strong gateways and routes available when circumstances change. Hong Kong should aim to be one of those indispensable intersections. That requires looking beyond the old aviation map in which Hong Kong primarily connected China and the rest of Asia with Europe and North America. The opportunity today is more multidirectional: stronger links within Asia, connections to emerging markets such as Central Asia, access to the Greater Bay Area and partnerships that plug Hong Kong into the networks of other global carriers. Skytopia adds another dimension. If the airport becomes not just somewhere to change planes but also somewhere to spend time, do business and be entertained, every additional flow of passengers creates opportunities beyond aviation. The objective should not simply be more routes. Hong Kong should ask what each connection adds to the wider network, what markets it opens and whether it gives travellers another reason to arrive, connect, stay or return. Cathay’s first 80 years helped Hong Kong become one of the world’s great gateways. The opportunity now is bigger than connecting East and West. It is to make Hong Kong the place where an increasingly diverse set of routes, regions and travellers meet.

title: Chinese woman sues son for US$54,000 in childcare fees after 15 years, sparking debate
description: ‘Grandparenting fees’ disputes are not aimed at commercialising family relationships, but serve to clarify responsibilities, legal experts stress.
content: A woman in eastern China took legal action against her son, seeking more than 360,000 yuan (US$54,000) in compensation for her role in caring for his daughter. This dramatic case has ignited a nationwide debate concerning evolving perspectives on grandparental childcare responsibilities. In April, a Shanghai court disclosed details of a case from last year involving Xu, a woman in her 60s, who sued her son, surnamed Liang. Years after divorcing her husband, Xu had been living with her son. Following Liang’s divorce in 2014, when his daughter was just four years old, Xu assumed most of the responsibility for raising the child. This included covering her living expenses, medical bills, and educational costs, according to a report by Xinmin Evening News. In the lawsuit, Xu accused her son of lacking a “sense of family responsibility” and failing to fulfil his duties as a father. Liang contended that he had supported his daughter to the best of his ability, given his modest monthly income of only 3,000 yuan (US$450) at that time. The conflict escalated after Liang remarried and moved out with his new wife, leaving his daughter in Xu’s care. After 15 years of caregiving, Xu expressed that she could no longer continue due to financial pressures and sought compensation from her son. This dispute is emblematic of a broader debate in China surrounding “grandparenting fees.” In a separate case disclosed by a Beijing court, grandparents who supported their granddaughter’s expenses since she was one year old later sued their son and daughter-in-law for 320,000 yuan (US$48,000) in childcare costs Other cases have highlighted the challenges faced by elderly carers. In August, a 59-year-old woman in Hunan province in southern China was diagnosed with anxiety after losing 20kg while assisting her son in caring for his child for six months. Such situations have sparked discussions on whether grandparental childcare should be regarded simply as a family obligation or acknowledged as unpaid labour. Traditional Chinese families have long honoured multigenerational support, with Confucian values emphasising mutual obligations between generations. However, urbanisation and shifting lifestyles have altered these dynamics significantly. As rural workers migrate to cities, grandparents have increasingly become the primary carers for left-behind children. In urban areas, the rise of dual-income households and limited childcare options have also compelled many grandparents to step in. Once perceived as a natural expression of selfless devotion, grandparental childcare is now increasingly recognised as valuable caregiving labour. Improved pensions and changing retirement lifestyles are reshaping older adults’ expectations, as noted by Zhang Liyong, a social work scholar from Hubei province, in an interview with the SCMP. “Compensation can take various forms,” Zhang remarked. “Families can share living costs and engage in more open communication, while society should work to expand public childcare services.” Legal experts have emphasised that disputes over “grandparenting fees” are not about commercialising family relationships; rather, they seek to clarify responsibilities. Liu Gui’e, a lawyer at Shanghai Shentong Law Firm, stated in mainland media Nanfeng Chuang that parents remain primarily accountable for raising their children, with grandparents stepping in only when parents are unable to provide care. Some online observers contend that the issue underscores deeper inadequacies within China’s childcare system. “If China aims to promote higher birth rates, it requires a stronger childcare infrastructure, readily accessible services, and supportive policies, rather than relying on older generations to bear the burden,” one internet user suggested.

title: Jiaxin’s Hong Kong-Kazakhstan listing paves way for mining peers, official says
description: Jiaxin’s ‘proof of concept’ should lead to more such listings, governor of Kazakhstan’s Astana International Financial Centre says.
content: The Chinese mining firm that carried out the first Hong Kong-Kazakhstan dual stock exchange listing after a tough start in the industry could motivate many more initial public offerings (IPOs) by peers who are keen on the Central Asian country’s extensive mineral deposits, a financial official said on Monday. The dual listing of Jiaxin International Resources Investment last year established a “proof of concept”, said Renat Bekturov, governor of Kazakhstan’s Astana International Financial Centre, a regional financial hub and special economic zone. To encourage more listings, Bekturov said at the SCMP China Conference Central Asia 2026, the financial centre was aligning its regulatory framework with international practices while increasing efficiency and transparency. He anticipated momentum within two years. “The institutions are there,” he said. “The capital is there. Now the task is scale. Our job is to make the exceptional ordinary.” Jiaxin became the world’s first company to make a dual primary listing in both Hong Kong and the lesser-known exchange in Astana, capital of Kazakhstan. The move raised more than US$150 million for Jiaxin, which is backed by state-owned Jiangxi Copper, and provided a blueprint for mineral companies in Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, to reach capital from China and beyond in a single transaction. The Kazakhstan operation, Jiaxin’s only asset, also ranked last year as the world’s largest open-pit mine for tungsten, a crucial raw material with industrial uses ranging from aerospace gear to common cutting tools. Commercial production began in 2025, and expansion is expected next year. As testament to wider interest in mining in Kazakhstan, a record 96 cooperation agreements and memorandums of understanding worth more than US$1.65 billion were reached during Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s visit to the country in June. The work ahead was clear-cut, some in the mining business said on Monday. Mining investors were demanding transparency on the details of newly discovered deposits and fairness in issuing licences for those sites, said Ruslan Baimishev, Kazakhstan Chamber of Mines president, during a separate conference panel. “Otherwise, investors will leave,” he said. Around 4,000 licences had been issued in Kazakhstan to date, he said, and those operators should “report publicly”, avoiding any market speculation. Kazakhstan’s investment environment also should ensure work for smaller local companies, regardless of how much capital poured in, Baimishev said. “If [an] exploration is successful, then a larger, medium-sized investor comes in,” he said. “Those projects can then be consolidated by medium-sized players and eventually moved into production. After that, global companies with plants and processing capacity may acquire those projects.” Increasingly on the radar of foreign mining investors, the country is the world’s largest uranium producer, the third biggest in titanium production, seventh in zinc, eighth in lead and 11th in gold, according to the US International Trade Administration. Jiaxin’s board chairman and executive director Liu Liqiang advised his peers at the conference to stick through hard times, keep their word and follow international laws. The operator got started in Kazakhstan more than a decade ago with an outlay of US$400 million but only sparse discoveries of its target mineral, tungsten. Liu said the company explored extensively anyway. “For me, the most important thing was to believe in ourselves,” he said during a fireside chat. “We saw huge potential.” Miners entering a foreign market should “pay close attention to compliance” including syncing with international laws, Liu said, adding that “if you start by violating certain rules or laws, the cost of the project will increase”. “You need to have a tangible plan, a clear route, and a road map for the further implementation of projects, especially when we are talking about projects that are important for the further development of the country,” he said. When in Kazakhstan, he added, investors should keep their word. “If you say something, you need to fulfil that obligation,” Liu said. “That is why, when you are in Kazakhstan, you need to be very precise about what you say.”

title: Hong Kong celebrity Jeffrey Ngai splashes out on US$16,000 rental home
description: The singer and actor recently moved into a Mid-Levels duplex near his friend, singer Tyson Yoshi, market sources say.
