content: Hong Kong singer, actor and model Jeffrey Ngai Tsun-sang recently moved into a luxury residence in Mid-Levels East with a monthly rent of HK$130,000 (US$16,581), highlighting strong demand in the high-end segment, according to market sources. The luxury residence was a duplex, where Ngai, 28, would be neighbours with his close friend singer-songwriter Ben Cheng Tsun-yin, known as Tyson Yoshi, the sources said. Joseph Yan, senior principal district sales director at Centaline Property, said that the luxury residential rental market was buoyant, with a total of 141 rental transactions recorded in The Peak and Southern district in August. Flats with monthly rents of HK$80,000 to HK$150,000 were the most sought-after, with the majority concentrated in the Repulse Bay area, Yan said. Ngai’s market value rivalled that of the Hong Kong boy band Mirror, according to entertainment industry insiders, with his standard fee for advertising endorsements starting at over HK$1 million. He also commanded an appearance fee of at least HK$500,000 for brand events, and his annual earnings were expected to exceed HK$10 million, they said. Summer is traditionally a peak season for Hong Kong’s luxury property rental market, as families hunt for homes in neighbourhoods with good schools. According to agents, rental transactions of luxury properties tended to be more active in the second half than in the first half. Last month, local media reported that Commercial Radio DJ Bonnie Wong Ching-yi nicknamed Ah Jeng – a close friend of Ngai – had moved into the prestigious Kadoorie Hill neighbourhood, an area traditionally favoured by the wealthy, at a monthly rent of HK$70,000. This made her a neighbour to Hong Kong superstars such as Andy Lau Tak-wah and Kelly Chen Wai-lam, even though she later stated that the rent was not as high as reported.

title: Should Chinese schools demote English as a core subject?
description: A teacher’s call to end ‘worshipping foreign things’ reignites debate over the language’s role in schools.
content: Calls to reduce English’s status as a core subject in China’s education system have resurfaced after an internet-famous maths teacher urged the country to end “worshipping foreign things”. The controversy has revived a long-running debate over the role of English in Chinese schools. The argument came to life again after Tang Jiafeng, a maths teacher known for coaching students through the national postgraduate entrance exam, said on social media that children, parents and schools had devoted disproportionate amounts of time and resources to English, a subject he argued had little relevance to the jobs most people eventually did. “I publicly call for English to be stripped of its status as a core subject,” Tang wrote on Saturday. “No country in the world places English in such a supreme position as we do.” He argued that Chinese children were being pushed to cram in English before they had even mastered their own language, despite the country’s thousands of years of civilisation. “English is just a tool. It is enough to know how to use it,” Tang said. “The history of Chinese people worshipping foreign things and fawning over foreigners should end!” His remarks came after history was reduced in weight as a subject in local exam reforms, a decision he said left him “heavy-hearted”. History lessons helped students remember the hardships of earlier generations and develop sound values, Tang said, adding that if any subject deserved to be assigned less weight, it should be English rather than history. At present, English is a core subject in China’s basic education system, alongside Chinese and mathematics. In the traditional 750-point structure of the gaokao, the national college entrance examination, each of the three subjects is worth 150 points. While the weighting and assessment of other subjects have been reshaped in recent years as part of reforms to the gaokao and the zhongkao – the national high school entrance examination – the three subjects have stayed central to China’s exam-oriented education system. Meanwhile, history has seen its prominence diminished in some recent local reforms, with fewer and fewer students choosing to study it as a gaokao elective. Not everyone agreed with Tang. Former Global Times editor-in-chief Hu Xijin said those who denounced English learning as “worshipping foreign things” and sought to remove it as a core subject were “extreme”, “narrow-minded” and using nationalist rhetoric to portray their position as patriotic and morally justified. Also taking to social media on Saturday, Hu said English should remain a core subject because it could give students access to international knowledge and opportunities across a range of fields. Weakening English in basic public education could undermine educational equality, he added, saying that wealthier families would still be able to pay for private English education while students from less privileged backgrounds would lose access to the same opportunities. “Basic education should leave everyone room to advance as far as they possibly can,” the former editor said. “This is not about ‘worshipping foreign things’; it is about educational equality at the starting point of real life.” English’s global dominance reflected the West’s historical lead in modernisation, Hu said, and Chinese would naturally gain influence as the country kept ascending. He warned that trying to “accelerate that shift through administrative measures” or nationalist rhetoric could backfire and stir “unnecessary ideological controversy”. Calls to cut English’s weight in the gaokao have surfaced in recent years. In the past few editions of the “two sessions” – China’s largest annual political gathering – some political advisers and lawmakers have proposed reducing English’s score in the exam, dropping its core-subject status and making it an elective. The debate has intensified alongside growing confidence in China’s economic and technological standing. Supporters of demoting English often invoke growing “cultural confidence”, saying the expanding global use of Chinese, combined with advances in AI translation, reduce the need for such intensive English-language education. Others question the effectiveness of China’s heavily exam-oriented approach to English teaching, saying students could spend years memorising vocabulary and grammar for tests without developing an ability to communicate confidently in real-life situations. The phenomenon is often described in China as “mute English”. The 2025 EF English Proficiency Index, an annual ranking of adult English skills based on test results in 2024 from more than 2.2 million people worldwide, placed China 86th out of 123 countries and regions – in the “low proficiency” category. The content of English teaching itself has also shifted, according to some critics, with Chinese textbooks and classrooms placing greater emphasis on Chinese history, culture and domestic achievements, and less on Western society and international culture. The changes undercut one of the original purposes of learning a foreign language, which was giving students a window to the outside world, they said.

title: Exclusive | AI, chip firms among bidders for flagship Northern Metropolis tech hub at border
description: Source says tender results for four parcels at Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park could be expedited to as early as November.
content: Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub at the border with mainland China received bids from firms specialising in cutting-edge fields such as chips, artificial intelligence and quantum technology, the South China Morning Post has learned. The government last week said that it received an “enthusiastic response” to the tender for four land parcels in the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (HSITP), with a better-than-expected six bids submitted. The sites are earmarked for laboratories and talent accommodation, with a combined gross floor area exceeding 76,000 square metres. “The Loop Hong Kong Park Company is considering advancing the announcement of the tender results, as it aims to speed up the hardware developments of the park to draw crowds and build up popularity,” a government insider said on Monday. According to the source, five companies submitted six bids. Of these, three specialise in cutting-edge technologies including chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology. The remaining two are conglomerates with AI, data and medical research departments or subsidiaries. While the government said in August that tender results would be revealed by year-end, the timeline could be accelerated to November at the earliest, according to the insider. HSITP is located in the Hetao cooperation zone proposed by Beijing in 2017, comprising two parks on either side of the Hong Kong-mainland border. The project is part of the Northern Metropolis mega development, which aims to diversify the city’s economy and is expected to be a highlight in Hong Kong’s first five-year plan. According to the company, the vetting mechanism will apply a weighted “two-envelope” scoring system, allocating 70 per cent to technical proposals and 30 per cent to financial offers. The framework encouraged developers to submit forward-looking blueprints that bridged scientific research with commercial applications across the entire supply chain, the firm added. Successful bidders will be responsible for the design, construction, financing and management of the relevant sites, including the accommodation facilities. According to the tender documents obtained by the South China Morning Post earlier, bidders must deposit a bank-backed, on-demand “construction bond” of HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) as a financial guarantee upon signing the agreement as security for fulfilling contractual obligations. The construction must also be finished within 30 months of signing the sublease, with a “long stop date” final target set for April 1, 2030. A second tender exercise for the hub, involving three sites for labs and one for talent accommodation, is expected to end by October 20. Lawmaker Duncan Chiu said many emerging tech and intelligent equipment companies had a huge demand for cross-border research and early-stage testing. For example, quantum technology companies needed to move data between Hong Kong, where the research was conducted, and mainland facilities to complete related research, he said. “After the two tenders are completed, I think there are still quite a few plots in the HSITP that can be put forward for similar tenders,” Chiu said. “I’ve seen that the demand is fairly significant – both from scientific research-related companies and from what we call ‘emerging tech’ companies.” Legislator Elizabeth Quat said the companies would play an anchoring role in showing how cross-border flows worked and in helping to attract more advanced firms to Hong Kong. Quat added that the global technology competition was a “race against time”, and she hoped authorities could go beyond construction and coordinate across departments to expedite approvals for water and electrical facilities. The first tender followed closely after a large-scale land sale for another Northern Metropolis pilot project at Hung Shui Kiu, which drew only two bidders in July. The tender eventually went to a consortium, comprising China Merchants Land, China Resources Land (Overseas), China Overseas Land & Investment, Sino Land, CTG Investment and mainland e-commerce titan JD.com, which won the tender for HK$1.03 billion, with total investment projected at HK$16.8 billion.

title: In Singapore, malls for shopping only are going out of style
description: Marina Square’s future revamp typifies the rise of mixed-use developments incorporating retail, office, residential and other components.
content: While the announcement last week of the closure of a 40-year-old mall in Singapore’s Marina Bay district for redevelopment has caused an outpouring of sentiment among shoppers and tenants, experts say the prime real estate has to be updated into a mixed-use site to survive in the city state. Last Monday, property developer Singapore Land Group (SingLand) said in a statement that Marina Square, which was completed in 1986, would close on March 31 for a redevelopment that would include features such as luxury residences, serviced apartments and offices with a gross floor area of more than 360,000 sq m. The revamp, slated for completion in 2031, will have a 304-key hotel that will place guests close to the Marina Bay area, and Marina Square will be refreshed into a four-storey shopping centre offering a wider variety of food and drink options and pet-friendly environments, according to SingLand. Three new towers will be integrated into the site, including a 49-storey residential tower hosting 204 luxury homes, while offices will occupy eight floors of a new mixed-use tower, providing around 13,000 sq m of lettable space. Local media reported that the news of Marina Square’s closure came with disappointment from shoppers and tenants alike. Parents lamented the loss of the shopping centre known for its indoor playgrounds and children’s retail outlets, while tenants said they were shocked by the short notice. Retail experts point out that consumers today are increasingly seeking experiences, community and connection, and this shift is fuelling the growth of mixed-use developments around the world. Speaking to This Week in Asia, Tina Qiu, partner and head of Southeast Asia and China at PLP Architecture, the development’s master planner and lead designer alongside local firm DP Architects, noted that the current Marina Square mall was built in the 80s, before much of the iconic Marina Bay precinct had come into existence. “It was really quite unique of its time because it was the only object there. But in the last 40 years, everything around it to the south of the bay has really been developed,” said Qiu. Marina Bay was built through a decades-long land reclamation and water management project that transformed open sea and docking points into a modern downtown financial and lifestyle district. The iconic Marina Bay Sands building was opened in 2010. Qiu noted Marina Square was built in an “introverted” way since malls were then designed to keep shoppers inside the building and the focus was internal attractions like department stores, bowling alleys and cinema complexes, without much connection to pedestrians walking on the street. “It remained quite by itself, tucked away. Meanwhile, it holds this massive jewel [of being] in the centre of this bay front,” Qiu said. Without any rejuvenation, the mall would have struggled to keep up with everything else happening around Marina Bay, and there was a need to prepare for the next 40 years to stay relevant, she added. The revamped mall will have better wayfinding, sports facilities like padel courts, a botanic loop, gardens, covered bridges linking it to other buildings in the area like the coming NS Square and places for members of the public to sit. Marina Square is the latest example in Singapore of a shopping centre being redeveloped to offer a wider range of amenities. Union Square along Havelock Road is slated to become a mixed-use landmark with offices, retail, and luxury residences, while Tanglin Shopping Centre near Orchard Road is slated for a similar transformation. These projects are being upgraded with support from the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s (URA) Strategic Development Incentive (SDI) Scheme, which encourages the rejuvenation of older commercial buildings in some areas into innovative developments that will transform the surrounding urban environment. The scheme allows developers to apply for customised planning parameters, including higher density allowances to the gross floor area and gross plot ratio, permission to change land use, like introducing residential or hotel components into commercial areas and greater flexibility for taller or distinct architectural building profiles. Experts noted that such upgrades in Singapore reflected a global shift to mixed-use developments for shoppers, homeowners and office tenants to enjoy a more diversified experience. Seshan Ramaswami, an associate professor of Marketing Education at Singapore Management University, called the redevelopment of Marina Square “another little chipping off of the traditional bricks-and-mortar shopping model”, which was based on large malls, department stores as anchor tenants and a huge array of specialty stores. In recent years, several major department stores in Singapore, including John Little, Robinsons and Metro, have either ceased or wound down their operations due to evolving lifestyle trends. Ramaswami likened modern retailing to a real estate business where a developer would build what would generate the greatest value in returns over the long term. “Increasingly, all physical retail is facing very powerful competition from e-commerce outlets across the world. And then, in Singapore, there is also the proliferation of physical malls built up over the last decades. Some estimate that over 50 new malls have been developed in Singapore since 2000,” Ramaswami said, noting that every town in Singapore had its own mall with similar offerings. “The attractiveness of centrally located malls in the Orchard and central business district area has reduced considerably consequently,” he added. Sona Aggarwal, managing director and head of retail sales and strategy in Asia-Pacific at Cushman & Wakefield, noted that for asset owners too, mixed-use developments offered the added advantage of diversified income streams and greater resilience across market cycles. “By integrating retail with residential, office and hospitality components, these developments can generate consistent footfall throughout the week, benefiting retailers while enhancing the overall appeal and long-term value of the asset,” said Aggarwal. She noted that across Asia, many of the most successful retail destinations were now part of large-scale mixed-use developments that integrated retail, offices, hotels, residences and public spaces into a single, connected precinct. These included Bangkok’s IconSiam and One Bangkok, Omotesando Hills in Tokyo and Taikoo Li in Shanghai, which combined retail with lifestyle, cultural and public space elements to create vibrant urban precincts, Aggarwal noted. She pointed out that particularly in land-scarce Singapore, mixed-use developments enhanced land productivity and created stronger and more consistent footfall. “As consumer preferences continue to change, the modern mall is no longer just a place for commercial transactions, but a destination for community, connection and shared experiences,” Aggarwal said. Sulian Tan-Wijaya, executive director and head of retail at Savills Singapore, noted that what made Singapore unique was the “level of government orchestration”. “Through precise planning incentives like the SDI scheme, Singapore’s URA pushes developers to think about urban renewal, sustainability and community placemaking much faster than market forces alone would dictate,” Tan-Wijaya said. She also noted that the Marina Square example showed redevelopment no longer meant demolition since the plan was to retain the existing retail podium structure, which would minimise the project’s carbon footprint. “It shows that cities can radically reinvent themselves for the next century without erasing their architectural heritage or destroying the environment,” said Tan-Wijaya. Alice Tan, head of consultancy at Knight Frank Singapore, noted that what made projects like Marina Square particularly interesting was that they were no longer being repositioned solely as real estate projects but increasingly being planned as urban ecosystems. “Marina Square’s proposed redevelopment is significant because it signals a broader shift in how ageing city-centre assets may be renewed. Rather than relying on periodic upgrading works, owners may increasingly pursue deeper repositioning strategies that respond to future patterns of living, working and consumption rather than past success,” Tan said. Helen Kuan, a regular at Marina Square, said she had been going to the mall since it opened, when it was the largest shopping centre in the country. With about 59,000 sq m of retail space at the time, it was said to be the largest shopping complex in Southeast Asia. Kuan, a retired regional human resources director, recalled family outings at the mall when her children were young. “Now that it will be redeveloped, I’m going to miss it but it’s for the good of the future and its expansion. I’m looking forward to seeing the new Marina Square,” said Kuan.

title: Ma Ning hopes to ‘pass torch’ to next generation of Chinese referees after second World Cup
description: Only the second official from the country to take charge at a Fifa World Cup, Ma says next step is encourage others to follow in his footsteps.
content: Chinese referee Ma Ning hopes to “pass the torch” to the next generation of football officials in the country, and encouraged them to show the world what they are capable of. Ma became only the second official from the mainland to take charge of a game at the Fifa World Cup when he oversaw Curacao’s goalless draw with Ecuador this summer – and the first to serve at two different tournaments. While he does not know if he would want to stand at a third, he said he would gladly do so if his country were to ask. In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post on Monday, Ma also said he believed it was essential for any newcomer to genuinely love the game, and while mistakes would always happen, anyone hoping to follow in his footsteps should be devoted to minimising them. “Coming back from the World Cup, I feel my physical condition and competitive status remain at a very high standard,” said Ma, ahead of his appearance in a panel discussion at the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust’s Philanthropy for Better Cities Forum. “I am OK, and it would not be impossible for me to carry on until the next World Cup. But personally, I am sure I would not participate in the nomination process or compete for a spot at the next World Cup.” Ma, however, said it would not be his choice alone, and there would be more discussions with Fifa, the Asian Football Confederation, and his bosses at home before any final decision was made. “The General Administration of Sport of China and the Chinese Football Association created multiple platforms for me, so that I could stand on the stage of the World Cup,” said the 47-year-old, who became only the second Chinese referee to officiate at a World Cup match. “Any decision of mine could not be a reflection of just my personal feelings. If I need to carry on for a few more years, then I would, but the most important reason [for me to not continue] was that I wish more Chinese referees would climb the ladder, and that the world would be able to witness them.” Growing up as a football fan and playing as a goalkeeper as a child and young adult, Ma said he had volunteered to referee at pre-university level, even though he had not been trained, years before he became a professional in 2007. “My knowledge about refereeing was from the coaches, my seniors at college, or even football commentators when I watched football on television,” the Liaoning native said. “It wasn’t until my first year at Shenyang Sport University that I truly came into contact with professional football. “Whether that was tactics or rules, that was when I first learned about professional football and refereeing rules. I was shocked to discover that what I had learned previously was different, if not significantly wrong. “That sparked my interest because I felt that, as a football lover or a professional in the industry, I first needed to understand the rules thoroughly, meaning I need to study them in-depth.” He also saw the similarities between being a goalkeeper and a referee on the pitch, as both were prone to errors. “Even a superstar can miss a penalty kick; players, coaches, referees, everyone can make mistakes,” Ma said. “If it is a technical mistake, it is unavoidable. “What we need to do is minimise these mistakes or errors. It’s impossible for them to not happen, but we can, through our efforts, improve the accuracy rate of judgments from 90 per cent to 95, 97, 98 or 99 per cent, bringing us close to achieving 100 per cent accuracy. “Even computers can hang; so I think all we can do is try our best to solve our problems, and make ourselves better and better.” Ma, who began his international career in 2011 and has since taken charge at the Asian Cup and Fifa Club World Cup, is now the only official from his country who has served at two World Cups, after working as a fourth official in a group match in Qatar four years ago. He said the World Cup, being the “highest palace of football”, has to be very important to anyone who associates with the sport. “It’s a chance and a stage for me to demonstrate my ability to the world,” Ma said. “I think the biggest takeaway for me this summer was that I can officiate well at the World Cup, and show the world that Chinese referees can stand on the World Cup stage.” Looking back on his 20-plus-year career as the man with ultimate authority on the pitch, the two-time Chinese Super League best referee award winner, in 2016 and 2017, said it was not easy to hold on for two decades. “It’s always about your original aspirations: how we first got to know the sport of football and how we understand football referees, this is important,” he said. “Do we truly love football from the bottom of our hearts? Because only then can we treat it as a career. So, staying true to our original aspirations and persevering, I believe we will be able to realise our ideals and dreams.” Speaking about the time it took for a second Chinese referee to make it to the World Cup, Ma said there were a lot of factors contributing to that, but urged others to first consider things from their perspective. “We have an old Chinese saying: ‘To forge iron, one must be strong oneself’. You will be discovered if you truly possess the strength and ability,” said the veteran referee. “This is what we need to think about, and act upon, so that we can consistently provide Chinese referees to the World Cup. “It was truly through the efforts of several generations of Chinese football referees that I was able to step onto the World Cup stage. “And after two World Cups, we’ve summarised some experiences on how to become a World Cup referee and know which direction to strive towards. Now we have a goal and know how to achieve it. The next step is to discover and select better young referees.” Ma believes that bringing back experience from the World Cup was not only about finding the next Chinese referee capable of officiating at the highest level of football matches. “The World Cup is quite different from other competitions, after all,” he said. “We also hope to learn from these World Cups and apply what we’ve learned to our own matches and the future development of Chinese referees. This is something we need to do next.”

title: Songmont, Bosideng and other Chinese fashion brands taking Eastern aesthetics global
description: From Paris flagships to viral social media debuts, Chinese creators are leveraging quiet luxury design, direct-to-consumer strategies, and rich cultural resonance to build international footprints.
content: The Chinese have always been major consumers of international luxury brands, but it wasn’t until the Covid-19 pandemic that the demand for domestic brands began to flourish. While fashion labels were among the first to benefit from this new wave, shoppers began to broaden their horizons, driving growth in unexpected categories including outerwear, jewellery, leather goods, footwear, and fragrance. “I believe this evolution is fundamentally driven by a cultural awakening and a growing sense of cultural confidence. My generation grew up in a time when our aesthetic sensibilities were largely shaped by the West, but over the past decade, I’ve witnessed a significant shift,” says Shen Li, co-founder of the Chinese luxury fragrance and lifestyle brand To Summer. “People are no longer satisfied with being passive consumers of Western aesthetics; they are actively seeking out and embracing expressions that resonate with their own heritage.” As a result, today’s Chinese brands have come a long way from predecessors like Shang Xia, Chow Tai Fook or Shanghai Tang. According to a recent report by Bain & Company, their success has been driven not only by innovative, desirable products but also by original branding and storytelling, strong cultural resonance, digital-first direct-to-consumer strategies and exceptional quality at lower price points than international brands. Interestingly, these factors have also made these brands more appealing to a global audience, who have started to view their products as desirable and on par with their Western counterparts. “Chinese brands today are no longer competing only on speed or value, but increasingly on relevance, design and cultural fluency,” says Judy Liu, co-founder of agency Trinity Asia. “Chinese founders are also bringing a much more sophisticated sense of taste and brand-building, thinking not just about product or price, but about design language, customer emotion, retail experience and long-term positioning in a much more integrated way.” Take the Chinese jewellery brand Laopu Gold, which is known as the “Hermès of gold” across social media. Its products blend Chinese history and traditional craftsmanship, including motifs such as gourds and Buddhist symbols transformed into pieces with modern details like precious stone embellishments and matte finishes. Elsewhere, niche fragrance brands Documents and To Summer are making waves with their Eastern-inspired scents crafted using local botanicals and ingredients. These can be experienced in a series of retail spaces that mirror each brand’s philosophy while showcasing cool architectural and heritage design details. Aesthetics aside, many of these brands are also winning when it comes to quality. Ready-to-wear label Icicle – which also has a presence in Paris – has amassed a cult following with its stealth wealth essentials such as hand-finished double-face cashmere coats and lightweight knits that are not just sustainable and luxe but also reasonably priced. Minimalist leather goods brand Songmont has also gone viral thanks to its high-quality yet accessible designs, placing it alongside other international favourites like Polène. With their originality, superior craftsmanship and growing global profile, the rise of Chinese brands has only just begun. 5 Chinese brands with global appeal Bosideng Outerwear brand Bosideng isn’t exactly new – it was founded in 1976 – but it has been trending since the brand hired hip British designer Kim Jones. Jones, who previously held high-profile roles at brands like Dior and Louis Vuitton, is now the permanent creative director for their luxury label Areal, which blends high fashion couture tailoring with technical, high-performance outerwear. Its signature down jackets, including a must-have trench style, remain bestsellers and have been worn by celebrities like ambassador Eileen Gu, Kendall Jenner and Nicole Kidman. Icicle Founded in 1997 by husband-and-wife duo Ye Shouzeng and Shawna Tao, this eco-conscious label championed sustainability – and quiet luxury – long before they became fashion buzzwords. Known for its refined, minimalist aesthetic, its collections feature high-quality natural fabrics such as Mongolian cashmere, linen, wool, silk and cotton crafted into versatile, everyday essentials. Earlier this year, luxury conglomerate Kering acquired a minority stake in the brand to help expand its international footprint, proving that it’s one to watch. Pane At any given time, the lines outside Pane’s mainland stores could easily rival those at international luxury brand boutiques. In just four years, the Shanghai-based sneaker brand has become a cult favourite with locals and foreigners alike thanks to bestselling styles including the Aria ballet-sneaker hybrid and the viral GAT (German Army Trainer) light training shoes. The brainchild of designer Chen Ning, it is known for its minimalist, retro-inspired designs, cool details and superior comfort. To Summer To Summer became a fragrance pioneer by rejecting Western perfume norms to create scents that embrace Chinese collective memory and lifestyle. Each composition tells a poetic story about Chinese culture while showcasing authentic Chinese ingredients that are rarely used in global fragrances such as osmanthus, white magnolia, camellia, bamboo and Pu’er tea. Other initiatives, such as its independent editorial platform and collaborations with local master glassmakers and ceramicists, also promote Chinese craft. Songmont Songmont was born out of necessity. Unable to find a stylish bag to carry her laptop, founder Fu Song asked her seamstress mother and traditional artisans in her native Shanxi province to make her one. Since then, the brand has become known for its high-quality, understated designs that celebrate versatility and adaptability, including the bestselling Luna, which can be worn as a shoulder bag, crossbody or clutch. Each design pays tribute to elements of Chinese culture – be it traditional architecture, lunar phases or natural landscapes – through subtle design details.

title: Hong Kong students urged by top UK universities to prioritise curiosity
description: Officials assert academic resilience is key at education summit, advise pupils to explore subjects beyond school for admissions success.
content:
Top British universities are focusing on real curiosity and the ability to overcome challenges instead of strict test preparation and “perfect personal statements,” said leading admissions officials at an education summit in Hong Kong.
Representatives from top universities, such as the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge and King’s College London, spoke on the second day of the Global Education Summit, which was organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier.
The discussion was about studying abroad. About 11,000 people attended the two-day summit.
“At the heart of the admissions process at Oxford is a passion for the course that you want to study,” said Samina Khan, director of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Oxford, during a panel curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm.
“Whether you’re doing an A-level or a Hong Kong diploma, don’t just stick to what you’re being taught in school. You should be researching, you should be reading, listening to TED Talks to expand your knowledge.”
Admissions leaders emphasised that high grades represented only a starting baseline.
Sarah Hales, senior regional manager in admissions and access at the University of Cambridge, said the university selected candidates with genuine intellectual drive.
“Last year we welcomed students from around the world, including over 140 countries. But students from Hong Kong have always been and will remain just valued students at the university,” Hales said.
Hales noted that artificial intelligence (AI) was expanding beyond traditional technical majors into the humanities.
She highlighted growing engagement with fields such as digital humanities, adding that while course choices remained stable, the modules students selected were evolving.
To distinguish top applicants, Cambridge evaluates how students handle small-group academic discussions during interviews, which mirror the university’s core supervision teaching model.
“It’s not always the students with the top grades,” Hales said. “Sometimes it’s those students that want to go beyond that. It’s quite often the ones that might question what a teacher says.”
She added that interviewers looked for students who constantly investigated and challenged assumptions, as this demonstrated genuine excitement for the subject. During these sessions, the university tested motivation by working through complex problems with the applicant.
Khan stressed that successful Oxford candidates had to demonstrate academic resilience and a deep, self-driven interest in their subject that extended beyond the classroom.
She noted that the university was moving to standard UAT-UK admissions tests for the first time, retiring its long-standing in-house assessments.
Applicants for 2027 entry must sit these standardised tests during the October 2026 window. Oxford is also aligning its testing platform with Cambridge to simplify the application process for international families.
“The admissions tests help us understand who has the academic ability and who will perform really well in an intensive environment,” Khan said, noting that candidates must adapt to Oxford’s rigorous weekly tutorial system.
Meanwhile, British Council research shows that six in 10 Hongkongers are considering the UK as a study destination.
More than 16,000 students are currently enrolled in British universities, according to Andrea Hales, acting director for Hong Kong and head of English and exams at the British Council.
While families seek assurance that higher education will yield better career outcomes, driving peak interest in engineering and data science, the report stressed that top employers increasingly look beyond technical knowledge.
Mandy Zhang, head of East Asia for the global student recruitment and admissions directorate at King’s College London, highlighted that top British universities prioritised authentic personal reflection in applications.
“We’re not looking for a sort of shocking list of things that the student has done. The most important thing is to relate those activities to the course that you are applying for,” Zhang said.
She noted that students did not need costly external education consultants to build a competitive file.
“We want students to show real stories and competencies, developed either inside the classroom or externally using free online and in-person resources. You don’t have to pay for services to apply or write a personal statement,” Zhang added.
Sarah Hales from Cambridge also cautioned against generic introductions, urging applicants to explain exactly what sparked their interest and how they explored the subject outside school through extra reading or personal research projects.
“We don’t want to hear that ever since I was a child I’ve been interested in this subject,” she said.
“We’re interested to know what got you interested in this subject. What did you do outside school to explore that subject? Was it extra reading? Did you challenge yourself to do a personal research project?”

title: Foreign, mainland students flock to Hong Kong, sparking property demand in education sector
description: City to attract around 200,000 extra students, requiring international schools, university campuses to expand, as incentives lure wealthy migrants.
content: Hong Kong’s bid to become a global education hub is likely to transform the sector as a sustainable source of property demand, with the city tipped to see around 200,000 non-local students by 2035, according to CBRE. The city’s international schools are estimated to require enormous additional real estate to accommodate nearly 30,000 to 40,000 non-local students, as the institutions would need to set up 40 to 50 new school campuses. This could mean up to an extra 1.11 million square metres (12 million square feet) of gross floor area, a study released by the consultancy on Monday showed. At the tertiary level, with a projected inflow of 150,000 students, universities were likely to expand their academic space by 1.39 million to 2.14 million square metres (15 million to 23 million square feet). Currently, Hong Kong’s 12 institutions that award degrees occupy around 4 million square metres of gross floor area. Moreover, the student accommodation segment would also need more than 70,000 additional beds to provide living space for these students in about a decade. “Hong Kong’s education sector is undergoing a structural transformation,” said Marcos Chan, executive director and head of research at CBRE Hong Kong. “Historically, education demand was closely linked to local demographics, but future growth will increasingly be driven by non-local students, talent migration and the city’s position as an international education hub.” The trend “will establish education as one of the most important long-term demand drivers for Hong Kong real estate, creating sustained requirements for campuses, academic facilities and student accommodation”. The sector’s expansion is underpinned by support from the government, which launched the initiative to attract more international students in 2024, as well as programmes to lure wealthy immigrants and professional talent to Hong Kong, with many bringing dependants including school-aged children. Mainland Chinese students were expected to be the main source of inflow of new students into Hong Kong, given the current geopolitical concerns over studying in the West, while the city’s universities have also placed prominently in various rankings. CBRE noted that Hong Kong was home to five universities featured in the QS World University Rankings for 2027, with the University of Hong Kong and the Chinese University of Hong Kong both ranked among the Global Top 20. In Asia, Hong Kong boasts five universities within the Top 10 of the same rankings. Additionally, eight universities from Hong Kong were included in the Times Higher Education Asia University Rankings for 2026, with five making it into the Top 20 list. Between January 2025 and August this year, CBRE tracked about 49,000 square metres (527,432 square feet) of new spaces leased by education groups and property acquisitions worth HK$845 million (US$108 million). Meanwhile, during the same period, the agency said there were 4,500 student bedrooms expected to become available, in addition to the 9,500 already in place. For investors, the future requirements of the education sector could be a huge opportunity given that many of the city’s neighbourhood malls struggle amid a narrow-based recovery of the retail sector. Retail podiums, typically the lower floors of a residential estate, were particularly favoured as current regulations bar high-rise buildings as venues for academic facilities for schoolchildren. “We are seeing a lot of transactions where international schools are buying or leasing retail podiums and we believe this trend will continue because of the rising demand,” Chan said. The record real estate demand of the education segment has been driving investor appetite for Hong Kong’s property assets, including those coming from overseas, said Frederick Lai, senior director for capital markets at CBRE. “We know of at least 500,000 square feet (46,45 square metres) of demand for space, whether it’s from existing schools in Hong Kong or new groups trying to set up a campus here,” he said.

title: In pictures: from factory floors to AI – the evolution of innovation in Hong Kong
description: A visual journey through the city’s industrial evolution, from 1960s textile factories to AI pioneers such as SenseTime and DJI.
content: From bustling 1960s workshops to next-generation AI labs, Hong Kong’s industrial landscape has undergone a remarkable evolution. In the mid-20th century, the city established itself as a global light-manufacturing hub, driven by crowded factory floors where textiles, plastics and consumer electronics were produced by hand. As production migrated across border to the mainland cities of the Pearl River Delta, Hong Kong pivoted towards finance and trade while keeping its inventive edge. Home-grown breakthroughs in the 90s – such as Group Sense’s handheld translators and the ubiquitous Octopus card – revealed a knack for practical tech long before smartphones redefined daily life. Industrial high-rises were retrofitted and government-backed hubs such as the Hong Kong Science Park took shape to facilitate research. Today, enterprises such as SenseTime and Lalamove carry that legacy forward, alongside robotics giant DJI, which traces its roots to research at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, before its headquarters and manufacturing facilities were established across the border, in Shenzhen. Here is a look at how South China Morning Post photographers have captured this dynamic evolution over the decades.

title: Trump posts US Space Force uniforms based on movie’s Nazi-inspired outfits
description: ‘Next generation’ gear inspired by Starship Troopers, whose director explicitly aimed to mimic Nazi propaganda.
content: US President Donald Trump posted an image of dark “next generation” US Space Force uniforms on Sunday that the text claims were “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform” – a design the director of the 1997 film Starship Troopers said was directly meant to evoke Nazis. Trump also posted an AI-generated image titled “Space Force” of himself in a spaceship as two nuclear mushroom clouds detonate on Earth behind him, part of a frenzy of Truth Social postings over the weekend that also included AI images of himself in a decorated military uniform and pondering changing “New Mexico” to “New America”. The “next generation” uniforms, the image text stated, were “modernised for the Guardians of the space domain”. The Space Force, which Trump signed into law in 2019, had already announced new service dress uniforms for their Guardians last year. But Trump’s post was of black boots, black shirts and “midnight black” collars, seemingly evoking the villains in a science fiction film – which is what they were. Paul Verhoeven, the Dutch director of the 1995 film based on Robert Heinlein’s 1959 novel about a space military fighting giant alien insects, said his film was about “fascists who aren’t aware of their fascism”. “I borrowed from the films of Leni Riefenstahl to show that these soldiers were like something out of Nazi propaganda,” he wrote in the Guardian newspaper in 2018. “I even put one in an SS uniform. But no one noticed.” That character, played by Neil Patrick Harris, wears a black uniform very similar to the “next generation” Space Force uniforms posted by Trump. “If I tell the world that a right-wing, fascist way of doing things doesn’t work, no one will listen to me,” Verhoeven said in a 2014 interview. “So I’m going to make a perfect fascist world: everyone is beautiful, everything is shiny, everything has big guns and fancy ships, but it’s only good for killing … ” The Space Force has bases in California, Colorado and Florida, including Patrick Space Force Base in Brevard County. Florida’s congressional delegation recently pushed for a new Space Academy to be located in the state.

title: Editorial | China’s Xi sends a strong message before his US visit
description: Xi’s month of travel signals that China is playing a key role in South-South cooperation amid a tariff war and geopolitical instability.
content: President Xi Jinping has begun a month of travel expected to lead to the United States and a summit with President Donald Trump. That contrasts with the earlier part of the year which saw Xi hardly going anywhere but staying in Beijing. Instead, he hosted foreign leaders who flocked to meet him, including those of middle powers such as Britain, Germany, Canada and Spain, as they looked beyond an unpredictable American president and mixed signals from Washington. This reflects the growing importance of China’s economic power, the potential of its vast market and latest technological advances. Now, ahead of his proposed visit to the US on September 24, Xi has launched a diplomatic offensive. First he visited Kyrgyzstan for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, then – for the first time in 10 years – Egypt. This weekend he goes to India for the summit of Brics (Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), an organisation now of 11 members designed to counterbalance Western-led global governance. China is sending a strong message that it is playing a key role in South-South cooperation amid a US-China tariff war and mounting geopolitical instability, as wars disrupt shipping routes, drive up energy prices and – together with extreme weather – deepen threats to global food security. At the SCO summit, Xi said that the 10 member countries should “prioritise security” and prevent external interference in the affairs of other nations. He also announced initiatives including a new centre for international artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation. Xi said the Eurasian bloc should take on a bigger global role in technology and security. A key lesson from the bloc’s 25 years of cooperation was “finding the right way to coexist without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”. “Its most significant achievement has been its steady growth into a new type of regional cooperation organisation that now spans the widest territory, encompasses the largest population and holds the greatest development potential in the world,” Xi said. However, the world was at a crossroads, with rivalries between dialogue and confrontation, win-win cooperation and zero-sum competition, and multilateralism versus unilateralism. Xi said countries had to “prioritise security and create a universally secure environment”, and prevent external forces from interfering in the internal affairs of other countries to safeguard regional stability. In Cairo, where Xi held talks with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi, he presented a four-point proposal for peace and a new security architecture in the Middle East, which reflects Egypt’s influence in the region. It encourages regional countries to take charge of their own security by resolving differences through dialogue, promoting a vision of security combining development and peace, focusing on economic growth and regional cooperation as a bedrock for stability, and supporting the United Nations and respecting national sovereignty. Analysts said Xi’s journey from Central Asia to Egypt highlighted Beijing’s efforts to strengthen alternative trade, energy and manufacturing networks across Eurasia and Africa, as wars and tariffs expose a reliance on vulnerable supply routes and overseas markets. Xi’s latest visits will also consolidate the Belt and Road Initiative, and promote a world order of multilateralism in contrast to US-led unilateralism. While Trump has said Xi will visit on September 24 and that a formal state banquet will be hosted in his honour, the conflict and rivalry between the two major powers remain real. It remains to be seen how much common ground the two can find, ultimately, on AI governance, as well as trade, Taiwan and many other thorny issues. Xi’s diplomatic charm offensive promotes China’s vision for world peace and global collaboration. It reflects a consistent foreign policy of multilateralism and mutual respect for sovereignty and core interests. Meanwhile, it is to be hoped a Xi-Trump summit will have concrete outcomes. It is reported that Xi will also lead a big Chinese business delegation to the US, paving the way for agreements on enhanced trade and economic ties that should be positive for bilateral relations, though differences will remain.

title: How Hong Kong artisan perfume house Floriography bottles memories and the city’s vibes
description: Floriography’s perfumes are inspired by environments and experiences, from old bookstores to Hong Kong’s chaotic street smells.
content: Can you capture and bottle something as ephemeral as a vibe, a memory, an atmosphere? Floriography promises to do just that. For the past eight years, Jo Shaw, the 35-year-old founder of the Hong Kong-based artisan perfume house, has been creating niche fragrances that emulate concepts such as old bookstores, the earthy scent after rain and a chaotic urban jungle smelling like metal, temple smoke and steamed rice. “When I started, there weren’t any brands – at least in Hong Kong – selling fragrances that reminded you of an environment or an experience,” Shaw says. “The perfumes available were very literal and not very imaginative.” Her scent awakening came in 2013 when she studied abroad for a year in Milan during her finance degree. She recalls that the Italian city’s arts heritage opened her eyes “in the realms of fragrance and how I see the world”. This marked the start of her dive into flowers and scents, as she picked up her first books on extracting and distilling essential oils from botanicals. Upon her return to Hong Kong, she progressed from experimenting with DIY essential oil blends to sourcing professional fragrance materials and blending her own perfumes. In 2018, she released her first bottle, Old Bookstore, with notes of pine, spruce, wood, musk, vetiver and vanilla to “remind people of walking into a vintage bookstore”. It was also partly inspired by the Bodleian Library, the main research library at the University of Oxford in England – the second-largest library in the country and one of the oldest in Europe. “It was my first attempt at [creating] a fragrance,” she says. “Practice makes perfect with this kind of skill, so I just kept on blending fragrances every day or whenever I had free time.” Growth and her flagship scent As she gradually expanded her collection, Floriography began to take off, especially during the Covid-19 pandemic when “people were bored and shopped online a lot”, she says. Business boomed when normality returned, and she quit her full-time corporate job in 2024, dedicating all her time and energy to her studio in an industrial building in Kwun Tong. By this point, Floriography had already signed with retail stockists in Hong Kong and consignment stockists in Taiwan. Old Bookstore is now her flagship scent and the foundation of her Frames collection, which she explains as “an easier and simpler entry point” into her perfumes. It is also her most prolific line, currently with 23 scents. One of the more popular bottles is After Rain Earth, which, as its name suggests, produces a lingering fragrance reminiscent of an airy, scenic walk after rain has soaked the earth beneath. A customer told Shaw that it evoked the memory of running up a hill with their dog. “It reminds people of different things,” Shaw says. She adds that Floriography uses “a lens-based perspective”, and the Frames line represents her attempts at taking momentary “snapshots of everyday scents and environments”. Hong Kong scents And what is more photogenic than Hong Kong? Her subseries, titled 852, draws from the streetscapes and everyday cultural elements of her hometown and currently features three fragrances: Concrete, Roasted Chestnuts and Orchid. The first, Concrete, is a more universal Hong Kong experience: a stroll down a bustling street as the smell of something metallic, jasmine rice and sandalwood incense hits your nose. Shaw says it is a favourite perfume of its illustrator, Manila-based Ross Du, who designs the drawings on all of Floriography’s bottles. Roasted Chestnuts harks back to many a childhood memory for those who have grown up in Hong Kong, where, in the winter, street hawkers sell snacks such as chestnuts and quail eggs from a cart with an open wok. Similarly, Orchid reminds Shaw of the perfumed air when old women sold white jade orchid bulbs on the streets. Floriography’s other main collection, Flow, is an in-depth and cinematic experience with a bit more storytelling. Take Tatami and Sweet Koji, for example. Unlike regular fragrances with just a few notes, the former oozes sun-dried igusa grass, lavender, hay, Aglaia, tonka bean, vetiver, sandalwood, balsam, musk and earth. The latter – inspired by a koji fermentation class that Shaw attended – blends citrus, fresh sake, lemon zest, sweet pea, orange blossom, rose, soft musk and sake lees (sake residue). Rather than evoking memories that resonate with consumers, Flow scents envision movie scenes or perhaps fully constructed film sets. “It’s still through a lens, but it may be more complicated with more layering and has a longer and bigger transition from the top note to the mid and base. I created Flow to challenge myself and go beyond what sells, to hone my skill and do scents that people have never heard of.” A flowing aesthetic To accompany this philosophy, Shaw designed the bottles herself. Instead of using a regular flat base as most fragrance brands do, she wanted a flowing aesthetic – in a wide umbrella-like shape – that “conveys the idea of a scent flowing from one note to the next”. “Ninety-nine per cent of the time you see a curved bottle, it’s flat at the base,” she says. “This doesn’t have a flat base at all and is very difficult to balance, but it can stand upright. It took me a year to really design and refine the shape, but I think it’s paid off because a lot of people have commented on it.” Shaw says that running an independent perfume house in Hong Kong is challenging as many Hongkongers tend to look for big European or US brands. Customers more intrigued by Asia tend to be those in the West. But she has her own unique way of staying afloat. Aside from a perfume pop-up in four bookstores in Taipei and Kaohsiung, which wrapped up in August, she often collaborates with brands that may seem completely unrelated to fragrance. In 2022, she made a paddy-field scent for Taiwan’s Rice Heaven Tianzhong Marathon, and in 2024, she created a Valentine’s Day perfume inspired by blue cheese and apples for Hong Kong pizzeria chain Jacomax. Both collections have since sold out. “Making perfume is a very one-person project – you’re doing it in a confined space by yourself, and there aren’t many people you can share it with because there aren’t that many perfumers in Hong Kong,” Shaw says. “Working with people from different backgrounds has helped me gain perspective in my scents. I really appreciate these collabs because I feel like I’m not just selling fragrances. I’m recording day-to-day experiences.”

title: Flights restart in Indonesia as airports reopen after volcanic eruption
description: Hundreds of thousands of travellers have been stranded since late Friday’s eruption of Mount Anak Krakatoa.
content: Indonesia had planes flying again on Tuesday after a volcanic eruption forced the country’s major airports to close for days, with authorities saying that flights would resume gradually. The disruption, caused by the eruption of Anak Krakatoa, halted nearly 3,000 flights and stranded more than 340,000 passengers. Ash from Anak Krakatoa, which sits halfway between ‌Java and Sumatra islands, has blanketed Jakarta and some surrounding areas since its initial eruption late on Friday. The country’s main airport serving the capital Jakarta and four other airports reopened early on Tuesday after authorities cleared volcanic ash from critical infrastructure. Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi told reporters it would take time for flight schedules to return to normal. Dudy said there were around 178 aircraft at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, Jakarta’s main air travel hub. “We will be operating these aircraft, but before we do so, we want to ensure their airworthiness. So, it may take a bit of extra time,” he said. “We ask for a little patience from passengers and the public, as we will be carrying out inspections to ensure that these aircraft are fit to fly,” he added. The transport minister said three flights departed shortly after the airport reopened, including two commercial flights to eastern Indonesia. Airport operator Angkasa Pura Indonesia said in a statement that volcanic ash had been cleared from the runway and other areas to ensure the facilities were safe for flights. Alvin Pratama Putra, 31, who arrived at Soekarno-Hatta on Sunday ‌to travel to South Korea for work, said his cancelled flight had now been rescheduled to Thursday. “What can you do? It’s the nature. It’s dangerous ‌for the plane if you force it,” he said, adding that he had been sleeping ⁠on a bench at ⁠the airport. Nozomi, a Japanese tourist who only gave one name, said the airport closure left her confused because authorities had not provided clear information. “I hope things stay like this, no delays, no closing airports. I hope everyone can go where they want to go,” said the 37-year-old homemaker who came to Indonesia for a family holiday. Bayu Sutanto, secretary general ⁠of the Indonesia National Air Carriers Association, said the delays put strain on airlines’ finances, losing revenue from cancelled flights and facing higher operating expenses. Bayu said airlines would have to ‌incur various expenses such as extra fuel costs from route diversions, aircraft parking, or crew-related costs, adding that a delay of one plane at Soekarno-Hatta could affect the next three or four ‌flights using the ‌same aircraft. Airlines could lose up to 19 billion rupiah (US$1 million) a day during such a disruption, Bayu said. Anak Krakatoa erupted again three times on Tuesday morning, the ‌volcano monitoring agency said. While smaller than the earlier eruptions, there was still potential for flight disruption depending on ash ⁠height and wind direction. “So far, the impact is not as big as the previous eruptions, but we’ll continue to monitor,” ⁠Lana Saria, head of the geological agency, said. Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatoa killed 429 people and displaced thousands. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Labubu meets LVMH: Pop Mart to open flagship store in Paris amid cooling overseas sales
description: With Pop Mart’s overseas revenue share slipping in 2026, the firm remains focused on boosting international retail presence.
content: Chinese collectible toymaker Pop Mart International is pushing forward with a global retail expansion amid slowing overseas sales, and will open its first European flagship store in Paris’ Boulevard Haussmann, the same street as iconic department stores Galeries Lafayette and Printemps, according to the company. Last week, Pop Mart founder and CEO Wang Ning travelled to Paris ahead of the brand’s coming store opening. While in Paris, Wang met Bernard Arnault, chairman and CEO of luxury goods multinational LVMH, gifting him a Pop Mart Labubu doll. This follows another high‑profile meeting at Apple’s Cupertino headquarters in July, when Wang met Tim Cook and then‑incoming Apple CEO John Ternus. They discussed creative design, digital ecosystems and global consumer trends, Pop Mart said. Also present at the meeting in Paris were Delphine Arnault, CEO of Dior and Arnault’s eldest daughter, and Pietro Beccari, CEO of Louis Vuitton. “We think the business ties between Pop Mart and LVMH are underpinned by potential collaborations around Pop Mart’s major IPs [intellectual properties],” said Jeff Zhang, an equity analyst at Morningstar. “Following Labubu’s partnership with Moynat last year, we view Wang Ning’s visit as mainly raising the profile for Pop Mart, but the co-branded premium products should not boost the firm’s overseas revenue significantly,” Zhang said. Further cooperation between the two companies was under way, with Pop Mart IPs likely integrating with some of LVMH’s luxury offerings, he added. In October last year, Hong Kong-born artist Kasing Lung, the creator of Labubu, met Bernard Arnault in Paris, and in December, Wu Yue, president of LVMH for Greater China, took on a non-executive director role at Pop Mart. “We think Wu’s joining has paved the way for Pop Mart to diversify into non-toy businesses, mirroring the playbook of legacy peers, including Disney and Sanrio,” Zhang said. “Given Wu’s experiences in the luxury sector, there should be more collaborations between luxury brands and Pop Mart.” Zhang added that he expected these collaborations to further contribute to Pop Mart’s licensing income. Following its interim results release in August, the company’s management said it no longer expected to hit this year’s 20 per cent revenue growth target, given last year’s high comparative base. International expansion has long been one of Pop Mart’s priorities. Its overseas revenue reached 4.97 billion yuan (US$740.1 million) in the first half of this year, down 11.1 per cent year on year. The firm’s overseas revenue share of its total revenue slipped to 29 per cent, compared with 40.3 per cent in the same period a year earlier, according to its interim results. After strong overseas growth fuelled by Labubu IP last year, Wang described 2026 as “a year of adjustment”. He emphasised that Pop Mart would focus on strengthening fundamentals and optimising its global channel layout instead of pursuing short-term expansion. As of June, Pop Mart ran 676 physical stores globally, including 419 in mainland China, 36 in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, 90 in the Asia‑Pacific region, 86 in the Americas and 45 in Europe and other markets, according to the company.

title: Black boxes recovered from Amazon cargo plane that overran Miami runway
description: NTSB investigators inspect ‘utter devastation’ at crash site where Boeing 767 struck two vehicles, killing five people on the ground.
content: Investigators with the US National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday they had recovered the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder from an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran the runway and crashed while landing in Miami on Sunday, killing five people ‌on the ground. NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the two devices, commonly referred to as the black boxes, were being returned to the agency’s headquarters in Washington on Monday night for evaluation. The 32-year-old Boeing 767-33A, operated by Miami-based 21 Air LLC, overran the runway by some 396 metres (1,300 feet) and crashed into two vehicles on the ground: an Econoline van on the airport grounds carrying seven people from an airline cleaning crew and a Toyota SUV that was driving on a road beyond the perimeter fence. The two people aboard the ⁠plane, the pilot and co-pilot, survived and had yet to be interviewed, Homendy said in a press conference. Five people were injured, three of them ‌critically, officials said on Sunday. Homendy, leading a team of 32 investigators at Miami International Airport, briefed reporters on the early stages of the investigation but said a probable cause of the accident would not be determined until the end ‌of the investigation. The NTSB was still recovering and recording evidence, and crews were still removing jet fuel from the ⁠scene and aircraft, keeping two ⁠of the airport’s four runways closed. Although the airport halted all flights immediately after the crash, flights had resumed by Sunday evening. Asked to describe the scene, Homendy responded: “Utter devastation”. “You can ‌see on the paved surface tyre marks that continue through the grass. There’s debris everywhere. The Econoline van is torn apart,” Homendy said. “The SUV, you can see airbags, the surrounding airbags. You ‌can ‌see components from the vehicles, both passenger vehicles and the aircraft.” Photos showed the jet with its nose on the ground and tail ‌tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks. Homendy did not offer details on who was killed ⁠in the crash, but said they were from the two vehicles struck on the ground. The van contained a team from Professional Ocean ⁠Service Corp, which provides cleaning services for airlines, and the SUV beyond the airport perimeter fence was travelling on Northwest 67th Avenue, she said. The Amazon cargo plane was on its third flight of the day, coming from San Juan, Puerto Rico. It ‌had flown from Cincinnati to Miami, and ‌from Miami to San Juan, earlier on Sunday before the crash at 1.53pm EDT, Homendy said. Part of the NTSB investigation will examine the significance of the lack of runway material designed to stop runaway aircraft. Not every US airport has an Engineered Materials Arresting System, or EMAS.

title: Burnham risks friction with Trump over Israeli West Bank settlement sanctions
description: Downing Street targets West Bank trade while attempting to reassure White House over symbolic impact.
content: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government is expected to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday as he seeks to adopt a stronger policy on an issue that is important to his governing Labour Party but may anger US President Donald Trump. A new sanctions regime targeting Israel but limited to Jewish settlements in the West Bank will be announced by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, according to people familiar with the matter. Burnham and Trump spoke by phone on Monday, according to a readout from 10 Downing Street, which said the two leaders discussed a two-state solution for Israel and the Palestinian territories. That suggests Burnham used the call to notify Trump that the sanctions on Israel were coming. Downing Street and the Foreign Office declined to comment. The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Bloomberg first reported that Britain was drafting the sanctions package last month as it sought to raise pressure on Israel over its decision to advance home-building in a strategically important part of the West Bank. Proposals under consideration included a new sanctions regime including measures to prevent the exchange of goods and services with Israeli settlements. Miliband has also looked at expanding existing human-rights sanctions to cover the obstruction of aid, which has been blamed for exacerbating the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. The foreign secretary has also been looking at explicitly endorsing the International Court of Justice’s non-binding 2024 opinion that Israel’s occupation of territory that Britain now recognises as the state of Palestine is unlawful. UK officials are nonetheless concerned that the announcement may provide an early setback for Burnham’s relationship with Trump. British diplomats have privately told the US that the sanctions are largely symbolic and will have no material impact on the UK’s wider relationship with Israel on trade or security, in a bid to soothe the Trump administration’s response, people familiar with the matter said. The proposals were drawn up in the wake of Israel’s decision to open a tender for the construction of 1,200 settlement homes in one section of the West Bank. Disputes between Israeli settlers and Palestinians have further flared in recent months as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a tough battle to keep his job in a general election slated for October 27. Burnham was joined by the leaders of Canada and five European governments, including France, Germany and Italy, in a statement condemning the housing plan as “unacceptable” and urging Netanyahu to withdraw the tender. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz separately denounced Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir’s call for nightly assassinations in Gaza. Burnham is eager to show Labour early on that he takes a more critical view of Israel than his predecessor, Keir Starmer. Although Starmer toughened his stance towards Israel over his two years in office, including formally recognising the state of Palestine, his early refusal to demand that Netanyahu halt his military campaign in Gaza split the left. That helped drive down Labour’s standing in the polls and fuelled Green Party election gains across the country. Burnham, whose return to parliament forced Starmer’s departure last month, apologised for Labour’s stance on Israel’s military action in Gaza under his predecessor, saying the party “didn’t get it right”. Last month, Burnham’s new defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who faced stiff competition from a Muslim independent candidate in his own northeast London constituency at the last general election, said Israel had “fallen short” of international standards.

title: US private-equity firm close to buying controlling stake in fitness brand Hyrox
description: Sources say L Catterton values the brand at about US$700 million, and may bring in global partners including from Asia to co-invest.
content: Private equity firm L Catterton is close to buying a controlling stake in Hyrox in a deal that may value the fitness competition brand at about €600 million (US$697 million), according to people familiar with the situation. L Catterton, which is based in Greenwich, Connecticut in the United States, is also considering bringing in global partners including from Asia to co-invest, the people said, as Hyrox quickly gains popularity in places such as mainland China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Tokyo. An agreement may be reached soon, they added, asking not to be identified because the information is not public. A representative for L Catterton did not respond to request for comment. Hyrox is owned by Switzerland-based marketing firm Infront Sports & Media AG, which counts Chinese conglomerate Dalian Wanda Group Company as a backer. A consortium led by Boyu Capital was in talks to acquire Infront last year, Bloomberg News reported in October. A representative for Dalian Wanda declined to comment. Hyrox and Infront did not respond to requests for comment. Launched in 2017 in Hamburg, Germany, Hyrox has become one of the fastest-growing mass-participation sports, featuring competitors alternating between runs and workout stations. Hong Kong is hosting the 2027 World Championships, the first time it will be held outside Europe or North America. Sky News reported in June that L Catterton was in talks to buy a Hyrox stake. L Catterton last year invested in L.A.B. Golf, a maker of hi-tech putters, while its other consumer and sports-related assets include Equinox fitness clubs and Hydrow, which makes rowing machines.

title: In Focus | How Tokyo is widening regional defence ties to complicate Beijing’s Taiwan calculus
description: Tokyo is strengthening partnerships across the Indo-Pacific and beyond, possibly bolstering its ability to withstand a prolonged armed conflict.
content: The risk of a conflict over Taiwan is shaping Japanese defence planning, with Tokyo shoring up security at home and abroad for a potentially prolonged fight. But there are economic, demographic and political constraints on how far its military transformation can go. In the first of a three-part series, Gabriel Dominguez examines how Japan is building a network of partnerships to strengthen its strategic endurance. Japan is rapidly building a web of defence partnerships spanning the Indo-Pacific and beyond, a move that may bolster its ability to withstand a prolonged armed conflict over Taiwan and complicate Beijing’s calculations. The push was on display in Australia last month, where Tokyo and Canberra moved to deepen cooperation, ranging from defence planning and advanced weapons development to the construction and sustainment of Japanese-designed warships. But the deepening relationship with Australia is only part of a much broader shift. With Taiwan increasingly shaping its defence planning, Japan is connecting regional military ties with defence-industrial and technological partnerships across North America and Europe. The United States is Japan’s only treaty ally and security cornerstone, and Tokyo is looking to other countries to complement that relationship: from operational and logistical cooperation with Australia and the Philippines to weapons production, intelligence and more secure supply chains farther afield. Analysts say the aim is not to create a Nato-style coalition committed to fighting alongside Japan but to give Tokyo greater capacity to sustain a prolonged crisis. For Beijing, that could mean having to calculate not only Japan’s own military strength in a Taiwan conflict but also the wider network of countries that could help keep its forces supplied, its economy resilient and its defence industry running. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. According to Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, Tokyo’s growing defence partnerships could make it harder for Beijing to “isolate or exhaust Japan” in a Taiwan contingency, even though European partners would be unlikely to fight the People’s Liberation Army directly. “A wider network of partners could give Japan more options and make it harder for China to pressure Japan into accepting an early settlement,” Matsuoka said. The question of how much support Japan could draw upon has become more salient since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said last November that an attack by Beijing on Taiwan involving military force could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” – a legal designation that could allow Tokyo to exercise collective self-defence under certain circumstances. Beijing said the remarks implied possible “armed intervention in the Taiwan Strait” and demanded they be retracted, contributing to a sharp deterioration in Sino-Japanese relations and renewed attention to Tokyo’s potential role in a conflict. Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at Warwick University, described Tokyo’s approach as a three-layered strategy: strengthening Japan’s own capabilities, integrating more deeply with the United States and building complementary ties with like-minded American allies and partners. The first two remain at the core, Hughes said, meaning the blossoming relationships with regional partners and Nato member states are not intended to replace the US alliance. Celine Pajon, head of Japan research at the French Institute of International Relations, echoed that analysis. “Japan is not trying to replace the US alliance,” Pajon said. “It is trying to make itself less dependent on any single partner.” For decades, the region’s US-led security architecture followed a “hub-and-spokes” model, with Washington at the centre of separate alliances with Japan, Australia and the Philippines. Tokyo is now connecting those spokes through bilateral and minilateral arrangements while building ties beyond the traditional US alliance system. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi referred to the shift at the Shangri-La Dialogue in May, describing Japan’s ambition as turning individual security relationships from “points into lines, and from lines into planes”. Koizumi said this went beyond military access and exercises. Asking what would happen if “necessary items run short and logistics are cut off” during a crisis, he called for partners to cooperate more closely on defence production, maintenance and sustainment. That thinking is reflected in work on the coming revision of Japan’s three main security documents. Defence ministry planning material calls for a “multilayered web of cooperation” spanning bilateral and minilateral frameworks, including the US alliance, Japan-US-Australia-Philippines cooperation and the Global Combat Air Programme.
