Such convergence is particularly advanced in Japan’s relationship with Australia, where cooperation increasingly spans operations, defence planning, advanced technology, production and sustainment. Under a defence coordination framework established in December, the countries have deepened cooperation across operations, intelligence, technology and industry. On August 18, they agreed to let Japan use Australian ranges to test next-generation long-range precision-strike and autonomous systems, including those linked to its hypersonic missile programme. The talks also highlighted successful field trials under Boobook, the countries’ first jointly funded defence research project, involving laser technology. Meanwhile, Australia’s decision to acquire Japan’s upgraded Mogami-class frigate is creating plans to build and sustain the warships locally. The tempo of cooperation has also accelerated sharply. Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles said he and Koizumi had met seven times over the past 12 months, while bilateral exercises were increasing “at a really significant rate”. The relationship is also becoming a platform for wider regional partnerships. Japan, Australia and New Zealand launched trilateral defence-ministerial talks in May, while Japan, Australia and Indonesia held their first trilateral defence ministers’ meeting on August 26, agreeing to advance three-way cooperation across the Indo-Pacific. Japan is also widening its operational ties with India, with the Japan Air Self-Defence Force set to deploy F-2 fighters there in September for the first time, following earlier Indian Air Force deployments to Japan for joint exercises. In addition, Tokyo and New Delhi are expanding defence-industrial cooperation, adding another dimension to their deepening security relationship. But it is in the Philippines, which is also embroiled in a territorial dispute with Beijing, where Tokyo’s push intersects most directly with the geography of a potential Taiwan conflict. The Philippines’ security calculations have become entwined with Taiwan, with Manila quietly expanding unofficial security contacts with Taipei. The country’s geography, US alliance and economic interests could make remaining outside a major US-China conflict difficult. At the same time, Japan, the Philippines and the US have been deploying missile systems close to Taiwan along the first island chain, creating what some analysts describe as a tacit “division of labour” that could constrain the PLA in a conflict over the island. For instance, Japan is strengthening its Type 12 missile capabilities across its southwestern islands while the Philippines has deployed BrahMos anti-ship missiles and US forces have fielded systems including NMESIS and Typhon. Taiwan sits at the geographical centre of this increasingly distributed architecture. Those capabilities are being accompanied by agreements aimed at deepening operational and logistical ties. A Japan-Philippines Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement that entered into force in August enables reciprocal logistical support during joint operations and exercises. It builds on a reciprocal access agreement that makes it easier for Japanese forces to train in the Philippines and conduct rotational deployments, alongside expanding defence equipment and sustainment cooperation. Beijing views the trend differently. For Beijing, the significance goes beyond more Japanese forces exercising overseas. Access, logistics and complementary capabilities could help dispersed forces operate across the first island chain, forcing mainland China to account for threats from several directions during a Taiwan contingency. Responding to Japan’s participation in the Balikatan exercises and growing defence relationship with Manila, Chinese defence ministry spokesman Senior Colonel Jiang Bin accused “certain politicians in Japan and the Philippines” of stepping up “military collusion” and criticised Tokyo for “instigating bloc confrontation and building ‘small circles’”. Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo, said the emerging minilateral frameworks were intended to help deter Beijing while expanding Japan’s regional security role, amid growing concern about Washington becoming distracted by crises elsewhere. According to Maslow, the network has three broad objectives: to offset the US’ eroding security role, deter China and expand Japan’s security footprint in the region. But broadening operational ties across the Indo-Pacific is only one dimension of Japan’s internationalisation. Tokyo is also seeking industrial and technological depth through Europe, Canada and other partners that could help it sustain a prolonged crisis. Nato has become one avenue for that expansion, with Japan deepening cooperation with the alliance on cyber defence, hybrid threats, technology and defence industry while strengthening bilateral relationships with individual member states. Japan, Britain and Italy are developing a next-generation fighter under the Global Combat Air Programme, which Canada joined as an observer in July, while France and Germany have expanded bilateral defence cooperation and military engagement with Tokyo. “GCAP is about much more than building a fighter,” said Pajon, referring to the programme. “It is Japan learning to build defence capabilities internationally.” But the potential wartime relevance of industrial cooperation extends beyond sophisticated platforms. Hughes said these links could help Japan maintain a technological edge over China in some areas while reducing overdependence on the US, which has sometimes been less willing to export or license particular technologies. European partners could also work with Japan on less “exquisite” but militarily useful systems, he said, including massed deployments of drones – equipment they might be able to supply during a regional contingency. That trend is already visible in rising foreign interest in developing and producing drones and other defence technologies with Japanese industry. Japan’s liberalisation of defence exports reinforces the process. Tokyo has increasingly treated equipment transfers, joint development and industrial cooperation as instruments of security policy, particularly in Southeast Asia, where they can create long-term relationships involving training, maintenance, parts and upgrades. Japan’s Official Security Assistance programme extends that approach by helping strengthen the capabilities of strategically located partners whose territory, waters or surveillance capacity could shape the wider regional environment during a Taiwan contingency. Recipients have included the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia. Economic security is another component. Tokyo is seeking to reduce vulnerabilities including foreign weapons supplies that could be stretched by competing conflicts and dependence on China for critical materials and components. Maslow said this reflected a broader conception of national security in Tokyo, with supply-chain resilience, trade and investment increasingly forming part of Japan’s strategic competition with China. Pajon said that ultimately Japan’s expanding partner network was making China’s strategic environment “more complex and less predictable”, while Maslow similarly argued that Tokyo’s efforts had “complicated China’s security planning”. In a Taiwan contingency, this means Beijing would have to factor in not only Japan’s own military capabilities but also Tokyo’s access to outside sources of technology, production, intelligence, economic support and political backing as a conflict continued. Matsuoka described the broader objective as an attempt to build “strategic endurance”, giving Japan greater capacity to withstand the political, economic and military pressures accompanying a prolonged confrontation. However, there are significant limits to what this network could deliver if deterrence failed. Hughes said Japanese policymakers were “relatively clear-eyed” about European capabilities, adding that their defence commitments to the Indo-Pacific remained “quite limited and not to be relied on in a potential conflict over Taiwan”. European submarines or aircraft carriers that sometimes sail to the region might play some role, he said, but more realistic contributions could include economic pressure or European navies assuming greater responsibility in the Indian Ocean, freeing US forces to concentrate on Japan or Taiwan. Pajon likewise said Europe’s strongest contributions would probably come through diplomacy, sanctions, cyber and information operations, intelligence, capacity-building and selected military deployments rather than large-scale combat operations. “The real value therefore lies in deterrence through a broader network of capable partners, not in assuming that Europe would provide large-scale military support if deterrence failed,” Pajon said. Tokyo thus does not need every partner to fight the PLA for its growing network to have strategic value. Sharing intelligence, producing components, repairing equipment, protecting shipping routes, imposing economic costs or assuming security responsibilities elsewhere could all help Japan sustain a Taiwan contingency. But that distinction may carry little weight in Beijing, which already regards Tokyo’s expanding security relationships as a form of bloc-building. China’s foreign ministry said in April that Japan had been “interacting frequently with Nato” in an effort to bring the “non-regional military organisation” into the Asia-Pacific, accusing Tokyo of “provoking confrontation”. And for most of this year, Chinese state media and spokesmen have lashed out frequently at Japan’s defence push, comparing it with the country’s pre-World War II military build-up. The perception gap between Tokyo and Beijing risks intensifying an already deepening security dilemma. “The same network that makes Japan harder to isolate could also deepen the regional arms race,” Matsuoka said. “From Japan’s perspective, these measures are largely defensive and intended to strengthen deterrence. From China’s perspective, they may look like Japan is becoming part of a wider military coalition.”

title: Meet Naomi Osaka’s mother, Tamaki, who’s gone viral for her US Open outfits
description: From courtside ties to statement minidresses, the Hokkaido native who worked tirelessly to fund her daughter’s career is now stealing the spotlight in New York.
content: Naomi Osaka is known for bringing her A-game in both fashion and tennis whenever she steps onto the court. In the past week, however, it’s Osaka’s mother, Tamaki Osaka, whose striking fashion choices have been stealing the spotlight. At Naomi’s recent US Open match against Katerina Siniakova on September 3, Tamaki was spotted sitting courtside in a fashionable white dress shirt and a silver-grey jacket, paired with a matching grey tie and white fingerless gloves. A few days earlier, she turned heads in an eye-catching red minidress with black gloves, sunnies, and a bold red lip while watching her daughter during her US Open practice session. Here’s everything you need to know about Naomi Osaka’s fashionable mum, Tamaki Osaka. What is Tamaki Osaka’s background? Tamaki grew up in Hokkaido, Japan, and met her husband, Leonard Francois, when she was graduating from high school and he was a university student in Japan, per People. The pair dated for several years, keeping their relationship secret until Tamaki’s father tried to set her up for an arranged marriage. Tamaki and Francois, who is from Haiti, later relocated to Osaka together after Tamaki’s father disapproved of their relationship. They welcomed their two daughters, Mari and Naomi, in 1996 and 1997 respectively. Tamaki and Francois decided to give their daughters Tamaki’s maiden name “Osaka” for practical reasons while living in Japan. The family later relocated to the United States to give their daughters better tennis training opportunities, according to People. Naomi Osaka credits her parents for her tennis success Francois was inspired by Serena and Venus Williams’ father, Richard Williams, and decided to coach his daughters in tennis despite having no experience in the sport himself. Naomi has repeatedly credited her parents for their support and sacrifice throughout her career and mental health journey. “Growing up, I dreamed about winning grand slams and becoming No 1 in the world,” she told People in 2021. “While it was not easy, my family was dedicated to helping me get the access I needed to reach my goals. But unfortunately, not all girls have the same opportunities that I did.” “I came from a mom that worked for basically my entire childhood to put me through tennis,” she said of her mother in a 2022 interview with CBS News. “Tennis is an expensive sport. So, just to put two kids through that and just, I guess, believe in them so much is something that – I always call my parents a bit crazy.” In another interview with InStyle, Naomi revealed that her mother would work overtime and sometimes even sleep in her car to support her tennis career. Tamaki Osaka became a grandmother in 2023 Tamaki became a grandmother in 2023 when Naomi welcomed her first child, daughter Shai, with her then-boyfriend, American rapper Cordae.

title: Opinion | Japan must reckon with how it views foreign workers
description: As Japan raises fees for residence permits and tightens the requirements for permanent residency, the effect on long-term settlement warrants attention.
content: Japan will substantially raise its fees for residence permits next month. Depending on the period of stay applied for, renewing or changing one’s residency status could cost as much as ¥75,000 (US$480). The application fee for permanent residency will rise to ¥200,000 from ¥10,000. The government is also tightening the requirements for permanent residency. Applicants are already expected to be able to support themselves. New criteria proposed include an above-average household income, sufficient projected pension benefits, Japanese-language proficiency, and an understanding of Japanese institutions and rules governing daily life. The changes go beyond a simple revision of administrative fees. Japan is becoming increasingly dependent on foreign labour. Faced with a shrinking, ageing population and labour shortages, successive governments have expanded the channels through which foreigners can enter and work, while refraining from describing Japan as an immigrant society. Last year, the number of foreign workers hit another record high, reaching 2.57 million at end October. Although they accounted for only about 3 per cent of the labour force, the Bank of Japan estimates that foreign workers represented more than half of the labour force increase between 2023 and 2024. Official data showed that last year, manufacturing employed 24.7 per cent of foreign workers, followed by the service sector at 15.2 per cent, wholesale and retail at 13.3 per cent, accommodation and food services at 12.4 per cent, and construction at 8 per cent. The burden of the higher fees may not be evenly distributed. According to Japan’s 2020 population census, male foreign workers were considerably more likely than Japanese men to be in non-regular employment. Among male employees, excluding company executives, the proportion was about 15 per cent for Japanese nationals, compared with about 53 per cent for Brazilians, 45 per cent for Indonesians and around 40 per cent for Vietnamese, Nepalese and Peruvians. For foreign workers on low incomes or in unstable employment, fees of several tens of thousands of yen add to the financial burden. Those granted shorter periods of residency may need to renew their status more frequently, increasing costs over time. If employers choose to cover some or all of these costs, the higher fees become an additional recruitment and employment expense, particularly for smaller firms. If they do not, foreign workers will bear the cost. Either way, the effects may be felt most strongly in sectors already struggling to recruit and retain workers. The effect on long-term settlement also deserves attention. Japan’s number of permanent residency approvals peaked in 2007, the year after the available data series began. It subsequently declined and, despite some recovery, has remained at roughly 30,000 to 40,000 annually in recent years. Neither the number of approvals nor the approval rate has risen in step with the rapid growth of Japan’s foreign workforce. The higher fees and stricter criteria could influence both the willingness of foreign workers to remain and Japan’s ability to attract workers. There are already signs Japan faces challenges in maintaining its attractiveness as a long-term destination for foreign workers. A 2026 Mynavi Global survey found that, among foreign residents who expressed a desire to continue working in Japan, the proportion hoping to do so for at least five years fell by 15 percentage points from the previous year, to 62 per cent. The government says the additional revenue will help fund immigration administration and measures supporting coexistence with foreign residents. As foreign nationals are being asked to bear higher costs, it will be important to ensure they and their families have access to essential support, particularly as recent opinion polls indicate increasingly restrictive public attitudes towards foreign nationals. Japan has long promoted the principle of tabunka kyosei, or multicultural coexistence. In practice, however, the support available to foreign residents and their families can differ across regions. A clearer national framework is needed so access to help does not depend heavily on where a person lives. Support should also extend to employers that recruit, train and help foreign workers settle into their workplaces and local communities. There is a tension at the centre of Japan’s foreign labour policy. The country is expanding recruitment to address demographic decline and labour shortages while increasing the costs and requirements associated with long-term residence and permanent settlement. The question is not simply how much the government should charge for residency procedures. It is whether Japan views foreign workers primarily as temporary labour or recognises that many are becoming long-term members of society. Recognising this reality would require linking the expansion of foreign labour with more effective integration policies and clearer pathways to long-term settlement.

title: Netanyahu’s main election rival accuses Israeli PM of prioritising survival over security
description: Former general Gadi Eisenkot unveils candidate slate for Israel’s October election, alleging premier ducked accountability after October 7.
content: Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accused the sitting premier of looking merely after his own political survival and not the country’s security at a rally in central Israel on Monday. Unveiling the candidates of the Yashar party for the October 27 election, the former military commander said nothing about how he would handle the Palestinian question or the wars against Iran and Lebanon launched by Netanyahu, but accused him of ducking responsibility in the nearly three years since the massive Hamas attack. A relative newcomer to politics, his party Yashar (Hebrew for “Upright”), founded a year ago, has surged in the polls in recent months, with many voters seeing him as a viable candidate to replace Netanyahu, thanks to his military background. At Monday’s rally in a hall in the central Israeli city of Rosh Haayin, Eisenkot vowed to put an end to the divisions that have plagued the country since October 7, 2023 over Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza, where dozens of Israeli hostages were held, and on other fronts. “In the face of the great rift that opened on October 7, and in the face of the immense challenges before the State of Israel, I believe we need a leadership that knows how to rise to the magnitude of the hour, that knows how to unite and bring unity around what we share, and to fundamentally restore the principles of stateliness and Zionism,” Eisenkot said. Eisenkot also touched on other hot-button issues in the coming election, such as the exemptions and benefits granted to ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. “Will we go on for more years under a government that promotes evasion of duty without shame?” he said. “A government that hands out billions of shekels to those who neither serve nor work?” According to a poll by Israel’s public broadcaster Kan published on Sunday, Yashar is expected to win 23 Knesset seats out of 120, slightly ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud at 20. The anti-Netanyahu bloc is projected to win 51 seats, while Netanyahu’s Likud and its coalition partners are polling at 52 in total. That means that neither bloc would have the 61-seat majority needed to govern, unless it secures support from unaligned parties, including two Arab-majority lists that together account for 13 seats. Eisenkot appeared confident that his party would be able to draw away votes from Likud, the historic political home of the Israeli right. “I meet many people who have been voting for the same party for decades. They tell me how hard it is to vote differently,” he said. “I reply: just as you trust me, I trust you to make the courageous and right choice for Israel.”

title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs take effect as Trump threatens Bombardier sales
description: Ottawa targets US$20 billion in US goods after trade talks collapsed, with both sides digging in and analysts warning of further escalation.
content: With the well-telegraphed arrival of Canadian retaliatory tariffs on US products on Tuesday, importers, exporters and trade officials waited to see which side would blink first with billions of dollars at risk in one of the world’s largest trading relationships. At midnight, Canadian tariffs of up to 50 per cent took effect on C$27.6 billion (US$19.9 billion) worth of steel, aluminium, apparel, farm equipment and other American goods, escalating an economic stand-off that saw negotiations break down and US President Donald Trump announce sweeping duties on Canadian products. Hours before Canada’s tariffs took effect, Trump opened a new front by threatening to block sales of Bombardier aircraft in the US unless the Quebec-based plane maker moved its manufacturing there. By Tuesday afternoon, Trump had extended his list of grievances to the dairy industry and government procurement. “Canada has been ripping us off for years,” he wrote in a lengthy social media post. “That is not reciprocity, it is a Canadian Trade Scam.” Bombardier responded by highlighting the tens of thousands of US jobs it supports through its operations and supply chain. Analysts held out hope that the two could find common ground in their US$900 billion trade relationship. “Clearly, at this point each side does not want to look too anxious to re-engage in fear of looking weak,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president at the Asia Society Policy Institute. “But importantly, [Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney] he has not closed the door to talks.” Both sides are doing their sums and assessing their vulnerabilities even as the clash tests the ability of smaller economies to counter US intimidation and as Canada reaches out to China, India and Europe to diversify its trade structure. The Canadian economy is around 8 per cent the size of its southern neighbour’s and far more interdependent. Nearly 60 per cent of its imports come from the United States and some 70 per cent of exports go to the US market, with Carney’s popularity likely to ebb in a protracted clash. On the US side, the pain will fall disproportionately on several key US battleground states ahead of the November US midterm elections, including Michigan, North Carolina and Pennsylvania. “Nobody in Ottawa picked this list out of a hat,” said Kyle Peacock, principal with Peacock Tariffs Consulting. “Whether that moves the White House is another matter.” Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed slammed Trump’s tariff policy on Monday. The trade war is “a war on Michigan because we have to pay the price every day for goods that shouldn’t cost as much as they do”, he said. The fight also comes as Trump’s popularity hits new lows, affordability is a major election issue and his agricultural base is already hurting from his other tariffs. “Our farmers are really taking it on the chin, the back, the kidneys,” said Nicole Bivens Collinson, managing principal with law firm Sandler, Travis and Rosenberg, formerly with the Office of the United States Trade Representative and the Commerce Department. “There are clear aces that Canada holds.” Betting market Kalshi on Tuesday gave 19 per cent odds that a deal would be reached before November 1, 50 per cent before December 1 and 30 per cent before January 1. In classic Trump fashion, the president released a meme depicting himself as a dominating hockey player looming over Carney and telling him to “Get up, Governor”, one of several barbs issued by the president and his administration. This followed a social media post by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth that appeared to mock the physical appearance of a Canadian soldier. Trump also signed an order in August directing US federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” and has previously said that Canada should become the 51st US state. These remarks were “beneath their office” and “not constructive”, Carney said, adding that both sides can return to negotiations “when the Americans stop doing memes” and start being serious. Canada’s duties of 15 per cent, 25 per cent and 50 per cent apply to 629 US tariff items, including aluminium products, appliances, cheese and other dairy goods, although Canada removed some seafood products from its initial list. This followed Trump’s imposing 50 per cent tariffs on a similar amount of Canadian products involving Washington termed “discriminatory treatment” against the US alcohol, automobile and dairy industries. In breaking off US-Canadian negotiations on August 21, Carney said the US terms were unacceptable, accusing Washington of adding onerous terms at the eleventh hour while the US countered that it was Canada that acted in bad faith. The two sides have not resumed negotiations since. But analysts expressed measured optimism that a breakthrough will eventually be found, with the caveat that the Trump administration tends to embrace unpredictability, which it sees as a source of leverage, and massive threats that the US leader often walks back. “This stand-off is likely to end in the coming weeks and months as targeted economic pain caused by the tariffs is felt in both economies,” said Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator. “The big unknown now is whether, how and when the administration may take further escalatory measures.” But a long showdown could mean a lot of pain for importers and exporters. “Tariffs on today will persist potentially for months,” said Henrietta Treyz, economic policy director with consultancy Veda Partners. “And we caution that escalation from here appears more likely than de-escalation.” Others agreed. “Long haul – plan for that and treat a reversal as a bonus,” said Peacock. “The reason isn’t politics, it’s plumbing.” When the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s use of emergency tariff powers in February, the administration rushed to replace that authority with more deliberative sections 232, 301 and 338 of trade law. “Those take process to build, which means they take process to unwind,” added Peacock. “I expect de-escalation one sector at a time, metals and autos first, not a clean return to duty-free trade before the midterms.” Trump’s announced crippling auto tariff increases are not set to go into effect until the beginning of the new year. “US and Canadian companies have little choice but to buckle their seat belts and get ready for further escalation,” Cutler added.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Arrested Memory movie review – Ethan Ruan leads Sabu’s muddled crime thriller
description: Ethan Ruan plays a detective with memory issues investigating a kidnapping case in this action-packed if confused police procedural.
content: 2/5 stars Premiering out of competition at this year’s Venice International Film Festival, this latest effort from Japanese writer-director Sabu, in which a Taipei detective battles amnesia, is an underwhelming twist on the police procedural that never truly feels like it knows, or even cares, what it wants to be. Taiwanese actor Ethan Ruan Ching-tien (The Pig, the Snake and the Pigeon) stars as Detective Lee, a formidable policeman who oversees a loyal crew of men with nicknames like “Wolf”, “Bear” and “Smallfry”. After a sting operation goes disastrously wrong due to his brain fog, Lee realises something is drastically amiss. “Stress-induced amnesia,” suggests the doctor, but it is not enough to see Lee take some time off. Instead, hiding his memory issues and clad in a stylish white suit and black shirt, he barrels headlong into the next case: the kidnapping of a five-year-old boy whose abductors seek a fortune for his safe return. The boy is the son of Hatta (Shinichi Tsutsumi), the Japanese head of a furniture company, who lives in luxury and certainly doesn’t suffer fools. Lee’s erratic actions don’t help, with the intolerant Hatta soon believing the officer has gone on the run with the ransom, as an increasingly muddled plot descends into a mass of shouting and shoot-outs. Since his 1996 debut, Dangan Runner, Sabu has developed a trademark mix of black comedy and thrills, and it is not hard to see him straining to do that with Arrested Memory. Only here he presents a real head-spinning hodgepodge, from full-on dance routines to a meth addict, Mad Dog Luke (Akira Huang Guan-zhi), who is something akin to the fool in King Lear. True, some moments of physical humour work well, not least the effortlessly executed stunt when Ruan kicks one fellow out of a hotel room window. Yet as Lee’s attempts to foil the kidnap plot become more chaotic, the film’s tone sways violently and the comedy rarely gels with the action. One such occasion sees Lee speak on his mobile phone in an attempt to arrange a drop-off for the ransom. The joke, if that is what you call it, is that he is standing right next to the kidnappers, who are blissfully unaware he is in the vicinity. At least the cinematography, by Hong Kong’s Jai Ip Siu-ching, lends the film some lived-in authenticity, and there is something appealing about the burnished red and gold interiors, conjured by production designer Chen Po-jen, where much of the later action takes place. For the most part, though, you probably will not want to strain your brain and remember Arrested Memory. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: New Panama Canal chief says El Nino could force further transit cuts
description: Daily vessel limit may be lowered to 29 as falling reservoir levels strain key shipping route.
content: The number of ships sailing through the Panama Canal could be cut further due to drought caused by the El Nino weather pattern, the new administrator of the waterway said on Monday. Panama has declared a nationwide emergency over El Nino, a phenomenon developing over the Pacific Ocean that is affecting worldwide weather patterns and pushing up global temperatures. This year’s El Nino is expected to be the strongest since record-keeping began four decades ago. Panama’s restrictions come even as use of the canal has risen: shippers are seeking an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has blocked in retaliation for the war launched by the United States and Israel. The interoceanic Panama Canal – which handles 5 per cent of global maritime trade – has already reduced the maximum number of ships allowed through daily, from 36 last month to 32 by mid-September. It operates using rainwater that collects in two reservoirs, whose levels have dropped due to the onset of El Nino. Without water, the locks that lift and lower ships at the start and end of their crossing cannot function. Ilya Espino de Marotta, who took over as head of the Panama Canal Authority on Monday, told Agence France-Presse that further measures may be implemented if the drought does not subside. “We do not rule out the possibility that in February or March we may have to lower the limit – probably not to 24 slots per day, but it could be reduced to 29 or something similar,” she said. Each ship requires about 200 million litres of water, which is then discharged into the sea. In 2023, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits from 38 to 22 due to the dramatic reduction in reservoir levels. Espino de Marotta, the first woman ever to head the US-built canal authority, stated, however, that she does not expect restrictions to reach the levels seen that year. Apart from reducing the number of vessels, canal authorities have also reduced their maximum draft, from 15.2 metres to 14.6 metres. The draft is the vertical distance between the waterline and the lowest point of a ship’s hull. It is a measure of how much water is needed for a ship to float safely without running aground. Experts have warned that long-term restrictions on canal crossings could lead to higher shipping costs and longer waiting times for deliveries. The United States and China are the main users of the canal, which is the fastest maritime route between the east coast of the United States and China. The canal connecting the Atlantic and Pacific handles around 40 per cent of US container traffic. The Iran war has pushed up traffic through the channel. With shipping at a standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, the Panama Canal has become a fallback route for energy shipments.

title: Trial opens in Mexico over alleged murders of Australian, US surfers
description: Three men face court over the 2024 killings of the Robinson brothers and their American friend in Baja California.
content: The suspected murderers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot went on trial Monday, two years after their killings in a suspected robbery. Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state. They had been camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft several days after they went missing. They bore gunshot wounds to their heads. Three men are on trial over their killings. The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the proceedings. Bereaved mother Debra Robinson stared at the accused before bursting into tears in the courtroom. “It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” her partner Martin Robinson earlier told reporters. “We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said. Authorities say the men were murdered during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was found burned near their bodies. Three witnesses appeared before the court on Monday, including the stepson of one of the defendants, who described his stepfather as violent. Testifying from an adjoining room with his face concealed, he said he accompanied the accused to the crime scene, waiting nearby when the “commotion” began. “I heard a lot of noise,” he said, explaining that he had run away but rejoined the group after they called him. He said they warned him that “the same thing that happened to the gringos would happen to him” if he said anything. The girlfriend of the witness’ stepfather was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery in order to steal the pickup’s tires. Ary Gisell Silva told a court that she had urged her boyfriend and two other men to rob the surfers, noting they had “good phones and good tyres”. The crime sparked outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, where the surfers’ friends and families galvanised a major search on social media for their bodies. Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the United States. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was set to marry. Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn’t usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were murdered in 2015 while travelling through the northwestern state of Sinaloa in the northwest. Their bodies were later burned.

title: UN demands accountability after 23 die in US immigration custody in 2026
description: Human rights chief voices alarm over rising detention fatalities and reported ICE plans to deploy electric shock gear.
content: The United Nations rights chief on Monday demanded accountability for swelling numbers of deaths in US immigration custody, and urged Washington to halt deportations to places where people face “irreparable harm”. Speaking before the UN Human Rights Council, Volker Turk highlighted that “four more people have died in US immigration custody since my last update to this council” in June. That meant there had been “a total of 23 deaths in 2026 alone”, he said, insisting that “there needs to be accountability for these deaths”. US President Donald Trump has made combating illegal immigration a top priority of his second term, with authorities rounding up thousands of people and expanding detention centres. A joint report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights in June said the rate of people dying in ICE custody has reached its highest level in over a decade amid Trump’s crackdown. The UN rights chief on Monday also called out a range of other US immigration enforcement practices, including forcing migrant returns to dangerous places and to countries they had no connection to. “I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries,” he told the council. The UN rights chief also voiced alarm at the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s reported plans to “equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves”, warning this would “increase the violence associated with their operations”. The plan to purchase the shock gloves, which was first reported by Associated Press, calls for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the ICE parent agency, to spend up to US$20 million on what are described as “distraction and de-escalation” devices. ICE has come in for criticism for a series of fatal shootings during enforcement operations, including those of two American citizens in Minnesota in January who were involved in anti-ICE protests. Critics have focused on the forceful tactics used by ICE agents in rounding up migrants and on an alleged lowering of the standards of training for new recruits.

title: King Charles clarifies Harry and Meghan’s status after UK return
description: Palace letter confirms couple will not use royal titles or receive state-funded security for private work.
content: Britain’s King Charles has reiterated that Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, remain non-working members of the royal family following their return to the United Kingdom. A letter sent on behalf of the king to senior government officials said the couple will continue to refrain from using their royal titles as they have done since stepping back from official royal duties in 2020. Any charity work the couple undertakes will be carried out in a private capacity and operational security decisions are matters for the relevant police agencies, the letter adds. The letter was sent by the Lord Chamberlain, the most senior official in the royal household, to senior officials in the government and military, as well as lord lieutenants, the king’s personal representatives around the country. “To help avoid doubt or confusion, The King has directed that [this] information be shared,” the letter says. While the communication simply confirms that Harry and Meghan’s status remains unchanged, the decision to send the letter and release it publicly shows the concern among some palace observers that the couple’s status could allow them to become a sort of parallel royal court, competing with working members of the royal family. The security question is particularly sensitive because Harry has fought a long-running battle with the government for the restoration of publicly funded police protection, which was cancelled when the couple gave up their royal roles. The decision about whether to restore the couple’s round-the-clock police protection is a matter for a government panel known as RAVEC, or the Royal and VIP Executive Committee. “Any specific questions from official and State organisations about the courtesies which should be extended to the Duke and Duchess, and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace,” the Lord Chamberlain said in his letter.

title: Sweden buying US-made Himars for long-range strike capability
description: New Nato member spends US$730 million on Lockheed Martin artillery while deepening defence ties with Finland.
content: Sweden’s government said on Monday that the country would spend 7 billion kronor (US$730 million) to buy US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (Himars) rocket artillery for its military. The government said in a statement that the acquisition would “enable the Swedish Armed Forces to operate over larger areas, and with greater long-range capacity than with current systems”. Defence Minister Pal Jonson told reporters that the deal covered about 10 trucks equipped with launchers and a large quantity of ammunition, news agency TT reported. The first deliveries of the artillery system made by US defence giant Lockheed Martin were set for 2027, according to the government. “In light of the security situation, rapidly available capabilities are needed that complement conventional artillery systems,” such as the Swedish-made Archer artillery system, the government said. Sweden also announced a joint declaration with Nordic neighbour Finland about deepening cooperation on the countries’ rocket artillery systems. The Swedish government noted that Finland uses the Multiple Launch Rocket System (MLRS), which uses the same munitions and components as Himars. Sweden has been racing to boost its defences after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Both Sweden and Finland dropped decades of military non-alignment and joined Nato in the wake of the invasion.

title: Kazakhstan aims to become education hub, but experts say jobs must match skills
description: Experts on panel at SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026 say collaboration with Hong Kong and mainland universities is in the pipeline.
content: Kazakhstan is aiming to become an education powerhouse in Central Asia but efforts must also ensure young people have sufficient access to opportunities that match their skill sets amid the country’s rapid economic transformation, experts have said. Educators and advocates added that further collaboration with Hong Kong and mainland Chinese universities was in the pipeline, with growing demand for specialists who understood the business environments of both Kazakhstan and China. The comments were made at a panel discussion at the South China Morning Post’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026 in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana. The session addressed how the region – which has a young population, with an average age below 27 years – was building the talent needed to match its ambitions. Nazarbayev University in Astana was strengthening its position as a leading research institution in Central Asia, president Professor Waqar Ahmad noted, just as Kazakhstan was working towards its goal of becoming a regional education hub. He stressed the importance of building a broader ecosystem that could keep talent at home. “If you look at education hubs, whether it’s London, New York or the UAE [United Arab Emirates], it isn’t just quality education. It’s the broader ecosystem,” he said. “Are there opportunities for [students] to take a job there, even for a short period of time, to enhance their skills before they go back to their home countries? I would say that Hong Kong is there, Kazakhstan is working towards it, and [mainland] China is somewhere in the middle.” Ahmad said Kazakhstan was “working very hard” to attract foreign students and had managed to draw nearly 40,000, beating its original target. He added that Nazarbayev University had been expanding strategic partnerships with leading global institutions, including a dual-degree programme with Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), and was holding negotiations with Polytechnic University and other leading universities. Ahmad said 88.2 per cent of the university’s graduates worked in Kazakhstan. “That doesn’t happen accidentally. It doesn’t happen because they don’t have options; they’re highly, highly employable. It happens because they see a future for themselves and their families inside Kazakhstan,” he said. Katarzyna Wawiernia, the UN Development Programme’s resident representative in Kazakhstan, said the country needed education that provided young people with the skills matching where it was heading, along with meaningful economic opportunities. “A young population does not automatically become an economic dividend,” she said. “It becomes a dividend when education, skills, investment and productive job creation move together – and when young women and men, including those outside the major cities, can actually access those opportunities.” She said women and rural communities should not be left behind as Kazakhstan bred the new generation of artificial intelligence and tech talent. “That means investing not only in digital infrastructure, but in local skills ecosystems – connecting universities and colleges, employers, local government, entrepreneurs and young people,” she said. Dr Chan Young Bang, founder and president of KIMEP University in Almaty, argued that quality education was the best investment for the country. The university was set up in 1992 during Kazakhstan’s transition to independence to train leadership and business professionals for the modern market economy. He said the private university, which teaches fully in English, had recruited highly qualified faculty members and had trained graduates ranging from former prime ministers to deputy provincial ministers. “The return on investment is the highest. [The graduates] are the backbone of Kazakhstan. They are going to lead in Kazakhstan,” Bang said. Gulnar Shaimergenova, founder and CEO of the China Studies Centre in Kazakhstan, meanwhile, highlighted the immense opportunities for locals as the collaboration between the country and China grew. With growing demand for such talent, she said people should not only master the language but also learn how to understand and deal with the systems on both sides.

title: New York Fashion Week 2026 preview: CFDA’s Steven Kolb on Made in America and rising designers
description: As the spring/summer shows kick off in New York, the council chief breaks down domestic garment production, an unpredictable luxury market, and why US heritage labels are thriving.
content: New York Fashion Week kicks off this Wednesday with the spring/summer 2027 Ralph Lauren and Coach shows. Coach, which celebrates its 85th anniversary this year, has become one of the success stories of American fashion. Led by British designer Stuart Vevers, Coach has thrived thanks to its well-designed and accessibly priced products, and its involvement in pop culture phenomena like last summer’s hit series The Summer I Turned Pretty. Unlike their European counterparts that have been alienating aspirational luxury consumers with constant price increases, US labels such as Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Tory Burch have stayed relevant by catering to customers who are becoming more mindful when it comes to luxury purchases. Their success, however, belies a polarised market where top brands reign supreme while many independent designers often struggle to make ends meet and have to rely on collaborations with sportswear giants or prize money from industry awards to keep their businesses afloat. Steven Kolb, CEO and president of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) – a non-profit that serves as the governing body of the US fashion industry – agrees that bigger brands have always dominated the industry but adds that smaller businesses have their own ways of cultivating customers. “I don’t think there’s anything new about more established brands like Coach or Ralph Lauren, which everybody is talking about in American fashion as a model of success and even as an example for some of the European houses that have been struggling,” says Kolb in an interview. “They’ve been in business a very long time. Success comes with age and experience. There’s a trajectory of success from where you are and how you build a brand. Is it harder to start and build a brand today than it was 40, 50 years ago or 20, 30 years ago? Certainly. There are different circumstances that influence how one builds a brand: the number of designers and brands in the space, the access to knowledge and information on the consumer level, how she’s going to shop, where before maybe she only knew certain brands, but now there’s such great awareness and a lot more choice.” Designers these days can reach clients by staging pop-up shops or by holding trunk shows, without having to rely on fickle department stores and online luxury retailers, which back in the day represented a lifeline for independent labels. Kolb mentions Amir Taghi and Emily Dawn Long as examples of how to build a business without adhering to tried-and-tested formulas that are not relevant any more. Taghi, for instance, recently opened a summer store in Aspen, the high-end resort in Colorado, while Dawn Long works from a very cool space in the Lower East Side that also functions as her showroom. She will present her spring/summer 2027 collection with a film, reveals Kolb, adding that both designers are finalists of the CFDA Vogue Fashion Fund, a competition that provides winners with financial support and a mentorship programme. The fashion industry is rife with awards for emerging designers, not only in the US but around the world – from the Paris-based LVMH Prize to Qatar’s Fashion Trust Arabia. Kolb is a firm believer in the vital role these initiatives play but explains that young designers should prioritise building a strong foundation rather than relying too heavily on them. “There are a lot of awards and programmes that young designers can apply to and I encourage every designer to apply to every single one of them,” he says. “If there’s money that they can access, and if it’s mentorship that they can gain, why wouldn’t they go for it? But what happens to some is that they build their business based on applying for programmes versus really focusing on building a business based on product and design. That’s just a catch that I think a designer has to be very careful about. You can’t sustain a business by just winning prize after prize after prize after prize, no matter how talented you are. You really have to learn how to build, price, sell, and grow and produce. So I would say that is definitely just a caveat to be careful about. I think the prizes are good. I think they bring visibility. The 10 designers who are currently in Fashion Fund, I don’t think there’s one of them that would tell you that the experience so far hasn’t been great. I see the ones from the past all the time and all of them tell us that it was a turning point for them in their careers. All of a sudden, they were just at a different level.” While the CFDA Vogue Fashion Fund and the CFDA Fashion Awards are the most high-profile initiatives under the remit of the CFDA, the entity has also been trying to revive New York’s garment industry with projects that predate the current pivot to Made in America of the US government. “We do a lot of work in that space,” explains Kolb. “I think the misconception of Made in America is that production is going to onshore or come back in a mega way but you’re never going to make things like T-shirts or [sneakers] here. That’s just not in our future. But as a kind of development for small batch quantity or [high] quality, that’s kind of where we at CFDA have been able to support designers.” He brings up the Local Production Fund, in partnership with the New York City Economic Development Corporation, and the Fashion Manufacturing Initiative as examples of the CFDA’s efforts. These programmes offer stipends to brands and grants to factories that base some of their production in New York. As someone who has attended countless fashion shows in New York and around the world, Kolb says that not every designer needs to invest in one to present their collections. He can’t deny, however, the appeal of a well-staged runway, like the theatrical productions of Thom Browne, the New York-based designer who also acts as chairman of the CFDA. Although Browne often shows in Paris and more recently Milan – his brand is owned by the Zegna Group, based in Italy – he is closing New York Fashion Week this season. He is one of a handful of US labels that have managed to build a loyal following in the luxury sphere. Khaite, founded by Catherine Holstein, is another high-end brand that never fails to please editors and buyers with directional collections that are quintessentially American yet have global appeal. Kolb, who has one of the busiest schedules during New York Fashion Week and makes an effort to attend almost every show, singles out a few other labels he’s looking forward to checking out this season. Kallmeyer, Sandy Liang, Christian Siriano and LoveShackFancy demonstrate the diversity of offerings of New York Fashion Week while London-based, American designer Conner Ives and Sabyasachi, India’s leading luxury label – both showing in New York this season – are examples of the global outlook of the New York shows. Calvin Klein and Michael Kors, two brands that have become synonymous with American fashion and have been undergoing some changes in recent years, are also on the calendar as is DVF, another very New York brand where designer Henry Zankov will make his debut. Editors’ favourite Marc Jacobs is not on schedule: Jacobs, whose brand was recently sold by LVMH to a joint venture formed by WHP Global and G-III Apparel Group, showed his latest collection in June. “Clearly, tariffs, the economy, the war in the Middle East, all of that continues to be a thorn in the side of the businesses but there’s a lot of excitement,” Kolb says, adding that you can’t dismiss the importance of the US market. “The truth is America is a huge market, gigantic. There’s a reason a lot is shown in New York, there’s a reason Gucci showed here.” Kolb certainly has a point. In recent months, Chanel, Moncler, Gucci, Louis Vuitton, Dior, Zegna and Hermès have all held shows in locations ranging from snow-capped mountains in Aspen to an abandoned underground subway station in Manhattan. Their US counterparts will get the chance to shine in the spotlight as New York Fashion Week kicks off a month of back-to-back shows and presentations that will end in Paris next month.

title: Kazakhstan, Hong Kong ‘can build biotech unicorns by linking talent and capital’
description: Top academic tells SCMP event there’s real opportunity to connect capital, ideas and state support across the two regions.
content: Kazakhstan and Hong Kong could partner to build biotech unicorns – private start-ups valued at US$1 billion or more – by linking the Central Asian country’s strong tech workforce with the city’s global financial network, a top academic has said. Huck-Hui Ng, dean of the school of medicine at Kazakhstan’s Nazarbayev University, said the nascent biotech sector in the country has already produced several start-ups in areas including artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health, and could build a “substantial” ecosystem with the right policies and government support. Ng made the remarks on Monday at the South China Morning Post’s inaugural “China Conference: Central Asia 2026” in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana. “There is a real opportunity to connect entrepreneurs with capital, ideas and government support across the two regions,” Ng said during a panel. “If we can bring those elements together, I believe many things can happen.” Kazakhstan is pushing to become a regional healthcare hub, with the nation’s drug regulator in April becoming the first in Central Asia to win World Health Organization certification for meeting global standards. The country has also attracted manufacturing investments from overseas drug makers, including companies in China, and it is rolling out AI to help with diagnosis at clinics nationwide. The broader Kazakhstani tech sector can already point to one unicorn, Higgsfield AI, a developer of AI-generated video tools for marketing and social media. The company, founded in 2023, was valued at US$1.3 billion in a fundraising round in February. Hong Kong offers lessons for Kazakhstan and beyond in developing the biotech sector, including the importance of support at the university level, such as research funding, said Fariza Zhorabek, another panellist at the event. Zhorabek, who grew up in Kazakhstan before attending university in Hong Kong, is now research and development lead at Allegrow Biotech, a biotech spun out of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST). Beyond funding, Allegrow received support from HKUST’s entrepreneurship centre in areas such as intellectual property management and establishing facilities, Zhorabek said. Further help came from an incubation programme at Hong Kong Science Park tech hub at Pak Shek Kok. Kazakhstani companies could also tap into Hong Kong’s large pool of “patient capital”, as the city boasts experienced biotech investors who understand that the sector is a long-term and high-risk bet, she said. There was also potential for collaboration between Hong Kong drug developers and Kazakh manufacturers, she added. The Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park at Lok Ma Chau Loop was also helping to form connections between Kazakhstan and Hong Kong technology firms, said Anita Chau, director of ecosystem development at the park. This included a “close relationship” with Astana Hub, an innovation cluster in Kazakhstan, she said. The technology park supports companies from around the world, helping them roll out new products more quickly and aiding in the creation of production capabilities in the city through developments such as a manufacturing lab, she said. “This is another example of how an ecosystem can support technology companies, help them move faster and create greater value for the industry,” she said. Chinese drug makers investing in Kazakhstan include Sinopharm, Sinovac and Kangtai Biological Technology, all of which signed up for new production facilities in the country in January as the government seeks to boost local drug production.

title: UN expert warns evidence of Israel’s ‘atrocity crimes’ risks being removed
description: Francesca Albanese says rubble in Gaza is ‘material record’ of war, and implications of Israel’s large-scale debris removal are ‘profound’.
content: A UN expert has warned that large-scale rubble removal in parts of Gaza under Israeli control risks erasing traces of “atrocity crimes”, and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains. Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement on Monday that the implications of Israel’s “ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza” were “profound”. “Gaza’s rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide,” she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remained buried under the debris in the war-ravaged Palestinian enclave. The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of “deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble”. In the devastated, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, “rubble is not just construction waste”, the expert insisted. “It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years.” Israel’s full-scale war on Gaza – which began after a Hamas attack inside Israel on October 7, 2023 – reduced much of the Palestinian territory to rubble. The relentless Israeli bombardment and ground offensive has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including more than 1,330 since a ceasefire agreed last October, according to Gaza’s health ministry, which is under Hamas authority. Hamas’ October 7 attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Many of the Palestinians killed in Gaza are children. Albanese insisted on Monday that the possibility of recovering human remains in Gaza was far from theoretical. She pointed to the burial last month of 112 members of one extended civilian family whose remains were recovered from under Gaza City buildings destroyed by Israel in November 2023. “The remains of 41 others killed in the same strike were never located,” her statement said. “It is vital that before decisions are made on displacement or crushing by the occupying army or its allies, the recovery and dignified identification of human remains, systematic documentation of sites and materials, preservation of potentially relevant evidence, and an unbroken chain of custody under independent oversight must take place.” The expert called for international criminal investigators to oversee the evidence gathering, and to warn countries and companies involved in any removal that they “could incur international criminal responsibility” if they destroyed evidence of international crimes. “Destroying evidence of atrocity crimes is illegal,” she stressed. “It is unacceptable that the reconstruction of Gaza is conditioned upon the erasure of its past and the evidence required to secure justice for its victims.” Israel did not respond immediately to a request for comment on Albanese’s statement. The United States, a major ally of Israel, imposed sanctions on Albanese after she criticised Washington’s policy on Gaza.

title: How can Hong Kong, Central Asia build momentum on growing ties and go beyond MOUs?
description: Tourism, professional services, mining and digital infrastructure prospects discussed at SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026.
content: About three months after Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu visited Central Asia, momentum is building for closer economic ties between the city and the region, with potential cooperation extending beyond finance to tourism, professional services, mining, agriculture and digital infrastructure. Government officials and senior figures from the industrial, investment and financial sectors discussed the prospects at the South China Morning Post’s inaugural China Conference: Central Asia 2026, held in Kazakhstan’s capital, Astana, on Monday. Business leaders said the real test over the next 12 to 24 months would be whether the agreements and enthusiasm generated by Lee’s visit would translate into projects and lasting commercial relationships. Nicholas Ho Lik-chi, Hong Kong’s commissioner for Belt and Road, said interest had increased on both sides since Lee’s visit in June. “We are getting more and more inquiries, not just from Kazakh companies or Kazakh organisations looking to use Hong Kong as a hub for finance and trade,” Ho said. “We’ve also seen Hong Kong and Chinese mainland companies wanting to use Hong Kong as a hub to access Kazakhstan and the Central Asian market.” Lee led Hong Kong’s first business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June. The trip yielded 96 agreements and memorandums of understanding (MOUs) worth more than US$1.65 billion across sectors including investment, finance, aviation, technology and education. At Monday’s conference, participants identified a broader range of opportunities, with improved connectivity seen as an important condition for expanding trade and investment. Ho said direct flights expected to debut in January between Hong Kong and Almaty, Kazakhstan’s most populous city, would reduce the journey to about six to seven hours. “That would dramatically increase not just business travel, but also tourism,” he said. “We strongly believe that Almaty would be a great tourist destination, not just for Hong Kong people but also for travellers from Greater Bay Area cities.” Dr Li Kouqing, deputy director of the CAREC Institute, an intergovernmental organisation, said nearly US$60 billion had been mobilised for regional cooperation in Central Asia over the past 25 years, with about 70 per cent going to transport infrastructure. “For a long time, it was very, very difficult to reach this region,” Li said. “But following this huge investment, we now see easier access to Central Asia and closer connections between the region and the rest of the world.” Sabr Yessimbekov, an adviser to Kazakhstan’s Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs, said the country was seeking to move beyond its traditional image as merely a supplier of natural resources and a transit corridor. “Investors increasingly see Kazakhstan as a platform for manufacturing, raw-material processing, logistics and technology, with access to several major markets,” he said. Yessimbekov also identified water infrastructure and food processing and packaging as promising areas for cooperation. Kazakhstan wanted to move further up the agricultural value chain by exporting more finished products rather than relying on sales of raw meat and grain, he said. In the mining sector, Johnson Chui, managing director and head of global issuer services at Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing, highlighted the stock exchange operator’s Chapter 18, a listing regime designed for mineral and mining companies ranging from exploration and early production projects to more established operations. Artificial intelligence and data-centre infrastructure were also identified as potential areas for investment, although electricity shortages in Kazakhstan could constrain large, energy-intensive projects. Yessimbekov said the priority over the coming years was to move “from memorandum-based relations to real, industry-based and project-based results”. Joshua Chang, senior director of investment at the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, identified information gaps as another obstacle, saying Kazakhstan offered many potential opportunities but that “an information disconnect” made it difficult for investors to identify viable projects.

title: North Korea, Russia open first road bridge in ‘new symbol of friendship’
description: The bridge can allow up to 300 vehicles to cross every day and will be linked ‌to Russia’s federal road network, says PM Mikhail Mishustin.
content: North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge on Monday in a carefully choreographed display of friendship. The structure, which crosses the Tumen river, has been cast by both sides as an important milestone ‌in their deepening strategic partnership. The first flag-adorned trucks trundled across the 1km (0.6-mile) long two-lane bridge as Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korea’s Premier Pak Thae Song tuned in by video link to address workers and government officials from both countries. Construction of the new bridge, which had been under discussion for years, began in April last year after the project was agreed during a visit by President Vladimir Putin to North Korea in 2024. There are already direct air ⁠and rail links between Moscow and Pyongyang, but until Monday there had not been a proper road link. Instead, since 1959 and by ‌special arrangement, planks had been placed on the nearby rail bridge – for decades the sole border crossing point – in order to move vehicles across the border between the two countries. “I am convinced that the ‌expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological ⁠and cultural cooperation,” said Mishustin, who ⁠said ties between Moscow and Pyongyang were “at an unprecedented high level” and called the opening of the bridge “a genuinely historic event”. The construction of the bridge was not ‌merely an engineering project, he said, but “a new symbol of friendship”. Mishustin said up to 300 vehicles would be able to cross every day and that the bridge would ‌be linked ‌to Russia’s federal road network and have easy access to the transport corridor which runs from the far eastern city of ‌Vladivostok to St Petersburg. Trucks would begin to use the bridge immediately to transport cargo, the Russian government said. At the end of this ⁠year, the bridge would be fully operational and could be used for passenger traffic too. The bridge was built near an existing “Friendship ⁠Bridge”, a rail bridge which was commissioned in 1959 after the Korean war. Symbolically, the new bridge is named after Yakov Novichenko, a Red Army soldier who Pyongyang credits with protecting the life of North Korea’s first leader Kim Il ‌Sung in 1946 by intercepting a ‌grenade thrown at him and others. Ties between the two countries have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022, with Pyongyang sending thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help repel a 2024 Ukrainian incursion there. Mishustin made a reference to that in his speech on Monday, referring to “the Korean heroes who, only recently, fought shoulder to shoulder with our soldiers and defended Russian soil”.

title: Diving into a new life: Olympic champion Zhang Jiaqi defends choices on reality TV show
description: Following retirement last year, 22-year-old former diver gives viewers a look at her unapologetic love for anime and casual living habits.
content: As the best athletes prepare to perform on the region’s biggest stage at the coming Asian Games, Zhang Jiaqi, a Chinese Olympic diving champion, was making headlines for a different type of performance. The 22-year-old former diver, who won gold at the 2018 Asian Games and the Tokyo Olympics, recently appeared on the reality television show My Little One, providing viewers with a look at her unapologetic love for anime, casual living habits and desire to break free from the state sports system. Alongside Zhang, the current season features actresses Michelle Chen, Chen Yao and Huang Cancan. The show highlighted that Zhang’s current situation was very different from her gruelling childhood in the national team. Following her retirement in 2025 at 21 years old, Zhang declined a stable, state-arranged job, opting instead to rent a modest flat in Shanghai and start an e-commerce live stream. When asked why she turned down state employment, she said: “The bigger the storm, the more expensive the fish,” implying a preference for high-risk, high-reward ventures. On the show, Zhang revealed that she earned 810,000 yuan (US$120,000) when she was just 13 years old, a revelation that quickly topped Weibo trending topics. Asked when she made her “first pot of gold”, Zhang replied: “I got my first pay cheque in 2014 when I was 10. It was probably around 4,000 to 5,000 yuan.” When pressed about her largest source of income to date, she said: “Prize money. The biggest bonus was from a competition in 2017 when I was 13. It was 810,000 yuan.” The prize money likely stemmed from her breakout performance at the 13th National Games in Tianjin in 2017. Representing Beijing, Zhang swept the women’s individual 10-metre platform and the synchronised 10m platform, beating Olympic champions and drawing praise from state media as the future of Chinese diving. She later partnered with Chen Yuxi to win synchronised gold at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, her only Olympic appearance before the rise of Quan Hongchan and the physical challenges of adolescence relegated her to a backup role. Selected by the Beijing diving team before she turned six, Zhang spent her youth confined to training halls, cafeterias and dormitories. She revealed on the show that her daily schedule was strictly micromanaged, from diet and sleep to weight control, leaving her fewer than 30 days a year to visit home. In contrast, the reality show featured her sitting cross-legged on the floor of her small, cluttered Shanghai flat, binge-watching television while eating crisps. Food delivery boxes were piled up in the corner, cat hair covered the furniture and the refrigerator only had half-eaten apples and snacks. Netizens were divided. Some called it a “pity” that an Olympic champion lived like that while others defended her, with one commenting: “This isn’t messy; this is the first time in her life she is living exactly the way she wants.” Zhang admitted on the show that she now frequently replaces meals with snacks, achieving a “snack freedom” she never dared imagine. As for physical activity, she was blunt: “I don’t exercise right now. I just don’t want to.” The show also highlighted the complex bond between Zhang and her mother, an emotional distance shaped not by personal conflict, but by years of forced separation during her time in the national team. Viewers were particularly shocked by her mother’s hyper-critical parenting style, especially the relentless criticism over the mess, poor cooking skills and snacking habits, including a candid admission that she wished Zhang was more like another person on the show, Chen. Zhang, who spent most of her young life diving, once told her mother: “I wasn’t raised by you; I was raised by the team.” Despite her family’s concerns about the instability of live streaming, Zhang remains resolute. When she started, her audience numbered in the hundreds until her former teammate Quan Hongchan joined a chat, sparking accusations that Zhang was using her compatriot’s fame to boost her own name. Zhang addressed the criticism directly. “I admit that some of my fans came from Quan Hongchan, but I don’t want to consume her popularity. I want to prove myself with my own abilities,” she said. Rather than regressing, fans and commentators suggest Zhang is simply “making up for lost time” for the life skills and autonomy she missed while winning medals for the country. “Being successful in diving doesn’t mean I’m successful in my entire life,” Zhang said. “New life is like this: one difficulty appears after another, and I go solve them. Once I solve them, I feel like I’m awesome and I’ve made progress again.”

title: As clock counts down to Trump summit, Xi boosts global clout with diplomatic blitz
description: Beijing leverages Eurasian and Middle East ties to show Washington it has alternatives.
content: His summit with US President Donald Trump is just over two weeks away, but already this month Xi Jinping has had one of his busiest stretches of diplomatic travel in recent years. First he wrapped up the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and then he made a state visit to Egypt. Xi is expected to head off again later this week to visit New Delhi for the Brics summit before he travels to Washington. Beijing has not yet confirmed those two trips, in line with its practice of making official travel announcements at the last minute. Observers say the flurry of diplomatic activity is not only about making progress on bilateral ties but also an effort to strengthen China’s negotiating hand with the United States. Sun Chenghao, a fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said the summit with Trump was important but Xi’s diplomatic sequencing emphasised that China’s foreign relations did not “revolve around a single axis centred on Washington”. “What Bishkek, Cairo and New Delhi truly offer is a demonstration to Washington that China possesses substantial space for strategic manoeuvre and a broad network of international partners,” Sun said, adding that the diplomatic itinerary highlighted Beijing’s emphasis on multilateralism and global governance. This was echoed by Julian Gewirtz, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s school of international and public affairs. “Xi appears to see an opportunity to show that China has friends and options around the world at precisely the moment Washington is alienating many of its allies,” Gewirtz wrote in a Substack post on August 28. The SCO summit – which brings together key Central Asian nations and powers such as Iran, Russia and India – is widely viewed as a platform for Beijing to project its strategic influence outside Washington-led institutions. In a veiled swipe at the US military alliance system, Xi praised the SCO at the summit for charting a path of peaceful coexistence “without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”. And, without naming the US or Israel, the leaders issued a joint statement condemning military strikes on Iran for violating international law and posing “serious risks to international peace, security and stability”. They also backed the right of Iran as an SCO member state to a peaceful nuclear programme under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. Trump has repeatedly insisted Tehran abandon all nuclear capabilities, a demand Iran has rejected. Gewirtz said Beijing’s diplomatic whirlwind was intended to show China could build an “international ecosystem less centred on Washington while managing – and extracting benefits from – Washington itself”. “Xi will spend September cultivating institutions and relationships meant to expand Beijing’s influence across Eurasia and the Global South, then fly to Washington to be welcomed by an American president eager to celebrate their relationship. “For Xi, that sequence is not a contradiction. It is the point.” Sun, of Tsinghua University, noted that the diplomatic tour, which covered vital pillars of China’s diplomacy, could also improve Beijing’s strategic environment when negotiating with Washington. China’s deepening energy and infrastructure ties across Eurasia yielded tangible leverage which Washington could not ignore if it expected Beijing’s cooperation on issues regarding Russia, Iran, critical minerals and global supply chains, he said.
