He pointed out that the diplomatic blitz created a posture “with greater room for imagination” for his US visits, as Xi would arrive in Washington not merely as a leader defined by the US-China rivalry, but one fresh off a series of major multilateral and bilateral diplomatic engagements. “What truly enhances China’s negotiating power is not how many countries take its side diplomatically, but whether China can convince the US that even if bilateral negotiations run into trouble, China still retains sufficient economic partners, diplomatic manoeuvring space and policy options,” Sun said. Last week, during his first visit to Egypt in a decade, Xi urged Middle Eastern countries to build a self-led security model and “independently take charge of their own future”, nudging them to cut reliance on Washington without positioning Beijing as an alternative security guarantor. The trip took place as tensions flared again over the US-Israel war with Iran, which has prompted regional US allies to rethink their strategic ties with Washington. China and Egypt also deepened their defence cooperation, conducting their second joint air force exercise from mid-August to early September. Jesse Marks, founder of Middle East consultancy Rihla Research and Advisory, said Washington would see this as a potential risk given that Cairo had historically been a primary recipient of US defence aid, although bilateral relations had been strained in recent years. Zhang Chi, a senior researcher at the University of Hong Kong’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said that while China and the US aimed to stabilise their ties, Beijing’s risks and challenges remained and it needed to “unite all viable forces to rally momentum behind leading ‘true multilateralism’”. He said polls from this year showed a broader trend of China’s global favourability outpacing that of the US. “Capitalising on this strategic window – particularly converting favourable public sentiment into [other countries’] positive China policies – will be a major task for Beijing,” Zhang said. While some view the coming Brics summit in Delhi as a diplomatic opportunity for India to ease tensions with the US and expand China-India cooperation on global conflicts, Marks doubted the outcomes from Cairo and Delhi would be “sufficient to tip the scales away from Washington”. “China and its ties with Pakistan are still India’s largest regional concern, and SCO ties do not resolve that. China may want to wedge between India and the US, but that can only go so far,” he said. “Same with Cairo, because Cairo’s largest regional concerns will not be solved by China, but they will be directly shaped by the US.”

title: Review | Venice 2026: Look Back movie review – Hirokazu Koreeda explores childhood manga dreams
description: A deep, intense friendship between two schoolgirls is explored in Hirokazu Koreeda’s adaptation of a manga by Tatsuki Fujimoto.
content: 4/5 stars Unveiled in competition at the Venice International Film Festival just three months after he took the somewhat disappointing Sheep in the Box to Cannes, Hirokazu Koreeda’s Look Back – in which a childhood friendship shapes an artistic dream – is an elegant work that once again underlines the Japanese director’s preternatural skills at working with young actors. The film is full of surprises and beautifully rendered, much like the manga at the heart of the story. Adapted from Tatsuki Fujimoto’s work – which was turned into an equally charming animated feature of the same name in 2024 – Koreeda’s film begins as Fujino (Furi Nanase) is encouraged by her teacher to reach out to fellow fourth-grade pupil Kyomoto (Rokka Okada), a reclusive girl who, like Fujino, loves to draw. At first, she is a little upset when she overhears someone say that her artwork looks “kind of average” next to Kyomoto’s. But whatever jealousy she feels washes away when she meets the shy Kyomoto, who later explains she “stopped going to school” because she got “scared of people”. Ignoring her sister, who warns her that in middle school she will be seen as a “creepy manga nerd”, Fujino is a driving force who dreams that one day her and Kyomoto’s work will be turned into anime. Koreeda seamlessly advances the narrative in time to when the girls are a little older. Now played respectively by Natsuki Deguchi and Aju Makita, Fujino and Kyomoto have made good on their collaboration, publishing under the pen name Kyo Fujino. Their first effort is good enough to impress an editor, who cannot believe that two teenagers have managed such dexterity on the page. With Fujino full of ideas for further manga (including Shark Kick, about a vengeful shark that takes on humans), her dream seems set. But the story’s final third takes a very unusual turn, one that shows childhood fantasies can sometimes be crushed by unanticipated realities. Handled with Koreeda’s usual warmth and accompanied by a soaring score, the film finds one of its greatest pleasures in watching the girls at their desks, drawing, shading and sketching. Paying great attention to their surroundings (in the wintry north of rural Japan) and their clothing (Kyomoto’s green cardigan and bright yellow coat really pop), Koreeda delivers a film awash with childhood memories, both sad and special. While the film emerges as something akin to Lukas Dhont’s Close (2022), which also detailed the intense friendship of two youngsters, it is a shame that the finale of Look Back slightly loses its way. Brisker editing might have helped by cutting back on some of the dreamier sequences. This flaw is certainly not enough to derail the film, but it perhaps stops a very respectable work from becoming a masterful one. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Hong Kong restaurant prosecuted after live newborn rat found in takeaway lunchbox
description: Food safety officials uncover unsatisfactory hygiene conditions after diner finds live baby rat covered among beef noodles.
content: Hong Kong food safety authorities have prosecuted a restaurant after an investigation into claims that a newborn rat was found wriggling inside one of its takeaway lunchboxes uncovered unsatisfactory hygiene conditions. The lunchbox came from Wa Jer Restaurant, located in the Wah Sing Industrial Building on Wah Sing Street. A customer reportedly bought a HK$44 (US$5.60) set meal that included satay beef rice noodles, a ham omelette and a drink. When opening the takeaway box, she discovered a live baby rat covered in satay sauce and moving among the noodles. The customer uploaded the footage to a social media platform, where it quickly went viral and sparked heated online debate over the source of the creature. The diner preserved the meal box intact and immediately filed a complaint with the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department. A department spokesman said it received the complaint on Monday, seized the food for testing and found hygiene conditions in parts of the premises to be unsatisfactory. He added that the operator was prosecuted under the Food Business Regulation and ordered to make immediate improvements. “Regarding the suspected discovery of a baby rat in takeaway food, the department is conducting an investigation covering various aspects including food preparation, packaging, storage, and delivery,” he said. “At this stage, it is inappropriate to jump to conclusions as to when and how the baby rat got into the food based solely on online video clips or the finding of a suspected baby rat in the food.” The department said it had invited the complainant to provide further information and make a formal statement, but the individual had declined. The South China Morning Post has also contacted the customer but she declined to elaborate. The restaurant’s operator told media he was baffled by the incident but did not want to speculate on whether it was a prank. He explained that the business had been operating for just over a year and had never received complaints about rats or insects in takeaway meals. He acknowledged that the restaurant was located in an industrial area where rodents occasionally appeared, and said monthly deep cleaning and disinfection had been carried out. He stressed his wish to contact the customer directly to understand the situation and pledged to step up pest control. The restaurant will close on Tuesday for a day of cleaning.

title: Hong Kong’s Nepalis gather for prayers on 13th day of flood mourning
description: At community hall in Yau Ma Tei, attendees light candles, lay flowers, and leave messages of condolence to honour the dead.
content: Hundreds of Nepalis in Hong Kong gathered on Monday to pay tribute to thousands of victims of the flash flood in their homeland, marking the traditional 13th day of mourning since the disaster struck. The hour-long programme, organised by local community groups with support from the Nepalese consulate, coincided with a national day of mourning in Nepal on September 7. Addressing the crowd, Satish Gurung, the acting consul general for Nepal in Hong Kong, said it was a “very difficult time” for the country. “The flash flood disaster of August 26 in Nepal, Tibet and China was a terrible tragedy with unfathomable cost to human lives. As of today, the death toll stands at 1,355, with an additional 4,996 still missing,” he said. Gurung noted that the disaster was driven in part by “global warming in the mountains” and called for support to Nepal not only through aid and charity, but also through climate justice. Climate justice frames global warming not just as an environmental problem, but as a human rights issue where the burden of change falls on the world’s biggest polluters. At a community hall in Yau Ma Tei, attendees lit electric candles, laid flowers, and left messages of condolence to honour the dead. About half a dozen participants had families affected by the floods in Nepal, and they received counselling from the Hong Kong Red Cross. Amar Tamang, a Hong Kong resident for seven years, said he feared the worst for his 75-year-old grandmother, who lived in the flood-hit Trishuli Bazaar area. “Her whole house was flooded and covered in mud,” Tamang said in Nepalese, tearing up. The 42-year-old said he hoped the government and non-profit organisations would help recover her body. Yau Tsim Mong district councillor Aruna Gurung said the programme marked the final day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period, during which prayer rituals are held to honour the dead. Nepal is a Hindu-majority nation. She previously told the South China Morning Post that 60 Nepali residents in the city hailed from the devastated Trishuli River region, and two had lost their lives in the disaster. Gurung said she and the local community would try their best to help those with families affected by the floods. “We hope to serve as a bridge to pass messages on behalf of those who lost contact with families in Nepal, or by providing supplies and emotional support, not just today but in the days ahead,” said Gurung, whose office was one of the event’s co-organisers. Rabina Joshi, a Nepali clerk who has lived in Hong Kong for 19 years, came to offer condolences straight from work in Hung Hom. “We cannot do much but contribute by being here to show support to families and friends,” Joshi said. Separately, Black Sheep restaurant group has raised more than HK$225,000 (US$28,700) through donations to support disaster relief efforts in Nepal. With one-fifth of the group’s hospitality staff from the Nepalese community, it aims to raise HK$500,000 and has extended the closing date for donations to September 13.

title: China’s Xiaomi unveils folding phone with home-grown chip as it takes on Apple, Huawei
description: Introduction comes on same day as Huawei launches its latest foldable, with Apple expected to enter the fray on Wednesday.
content: Xiaomi unveiled a series of new products on Monday – from a flagship foldable phone featuring proprietary chips to new models of its premium Skynomad SUV – underscoring the Chinese giant’s intensified push to compete against rivals including Tesla, Apple and Huawei Technologies. Beijing-based Xiaomi launched the 18 Fold, a foldable phone featuring a 7.58-inch inner display, a proprietary Xring O3 system-on-chip (SoC), and LPDDR6 memory chips from ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), said Lei Jun, founder and CEO, at an event held in Beijing. Lei said the 18 Fold was built for durability with a new hinge structure to protect the inner display, a high-strength aluminium frame and strengthened cover glass. He also touted the phone’s performance gain thanks to adoption of its Xring O3, an AI processor packed with 24 billion transistors, a 26 per cent increase from its predecessor Xring O1 launched last year. Lei said the Xring O3’s CPU performance was 60 per cent higher than that of O1, while power consumption in certain tasks was reduced by 25 per cent. The Xiaomi 18 Fold will sell from 10,999 yuan (US$1,639), with sales kicking off at 10am on Thursday. While acknowledging challenges it faces in its chip push, Lei said that Xiaomi had a long-term plan for making its proprietary chips, with a total of 50 billion yuan earmarked for the initiative. The company’s overall research and development was also growing, with 105.5 billion yuan invested in the past five years and a plan to invest a further 200 billion yuan over the next five years, Lei said. The 18 Fold’s launch comes amid an unusually busy week for foldable smartphones, as global major smartphone vendors double down on the growing segment. Huawei earlier on Monday unveiled the Mate XT 2, its latest trifold handset powered by its in-house developed Kirin 9050 Pro SoC, the first to feature the company’s new LogicFolding architecture. The model sells from 19,999 yuan. Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s Consumer Business Group, said at the unveiling that Huawei’s trifold series had sold more than 1 million units globally. US tech giant Apple is scheduled to hold its annual product event on Wednesday in California, where it is expected to introduce its first foldable iPhone, reportedly to be called the iPhone Ultra. The Apple device could sell from US$2,099 to US$2,299, according to estimates by market researcher TrendForce. The intensified competition comes as the overall smartphone market faces a difficult year. A global shortage of memory chips has driven up component costs, forcing manufacturers to raise prices, trim lower-end product lines or absorb pressure on margins. The squeeze has been particularly acute for budget phones, as price-sensitive consumers delay upgrades or turn to refurbished devices. Market research firm Counterpoint said in February that global smartphone shipments would decline 12.4 per cent this year, making it the market’s sharpest annual contraction on record. Foldables are a rare bright spot. Counterpoint said in a research note on Monday that the global foldable segment would hit over 100 million cumulative shipments by the end of the year, a milestone since the category first emerged in 2019. Apple’s market entry and releases from vendors including Samsung and Huawei would further boost demand for foldables, it said, adding that global shipments were poised to rise 37 per cent year on year in 2027, with the next 100 million foldables shipping within the next three years. “Foldables are still a very small part of the overall smartphone market, so there is room for the category to grow well beyond current volumes,” said Tarun Pathak, a research director at Counterpoint, in the note. Xiaomi also unveiled various models for its new extended-range Skynomad SUV series, which the company first made public in late July. Extended-range vehicles can travel more than 1,000km on a single charge, using a small petrol engine to recharge the battery rather than drive the wheels. Xiaomi has priced its Skynomad models at a discount to US carmaker Tesla’s Model Y L SUV, which starts at 339,000 yuan. The five-seat N70 Pro under the Skynomad series would sell from 209,900 yuan, while the seven-seat N90 Max would start at 269,900 yuan, Lei said at the event. Among the other products unveiled on Monday was the Xiaomi Pad 9 Pro Max tablet, which also uses the Xring O3 chip and starts at 4,799 yuan.

title: War criminal Ratko Mladic buried with military honours in Serbia despite EU warnings
description: Thousands of mourners gather to attend his funeral in Belgrade, defying EU warnings against glorification of war criminals.
content: Ratko Mladic, the Bosnian Serb commander who died while serving a life sentence for war crimes, was buried on Monday with military honours and crowds attending as Serbia defied European Union warnings against allowing public homage to the man found guilty of the continent’s first case of genocide since World War II. Thousands of mourners started arriving early at the small Serbian Orthodox Church of St. Luke in Belgrade to honour Mladic as his body lay in state. Mladic is still viewed as a hero by many Serbs. His military officer’s cap and sabre rested on the coffin, which was flanked by men in fatigues. The head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, led the funeral service while Serbian army soldiers carried Mladic’s flag-draped coffin at the cemetery as mourners clapped and a military orchestra played. Pro-government media broadcast the ceremony live. Bosnian Serb nationalist leader Milorad Dodik and the Russian ambassador in Serbia, Alexander Botsan-Kharchenko, were among those present at the funeral. Mladic died aged 84 on August 27 in The Hague, the Netherlands, where he was serving a life sentence. He was sentenced in 2017 for orchestrating the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica in 1995; the years-long siege of the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo; and other war crimes, including setting up concentration camps for detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers. Since Mladic died, his nationalist admirers have held vigils, painted a series of murals in Belgrade with his image and lit flares in his honour. On Sunday evening, football fans displayed a huge image of Mladic and chanted his name at a match in Belgrade. In Bosnia, the Mothers of Srebrenica group that gathers relatives of the victims urged the EU to react, saying that Mladic’s funeral “threatens to become the biggest fascist gathering in Europe in the last 70 years”. “The glorification of genocide is not honour, it’s a shame,” they said on social media. A UN “safe haven” for Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims), Srebrenica ended up being overrun by Serbs who forced men and boys to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves. The EU’s foreign service said in a statement that “any glorification of war criminals, genocide denial and revisionism contradict the most fundamental European values and have no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries”. “We are standing in solidarity with all victims, survivors and their families who suffered from war crimes in countries of former Yugoslavia,” the statement said. For Milan Dobric, a mourner who travelled from Kosovo for the funeral, Mladic “was a man who gave everything in his life for the Serbian people”. Dobric was “glad that this morning people are coming to pay special respect”. While the funeral arrangements were formally made by Mladic’s family, the Serbian government also sent a plane last week to bring his remains to Belgrade, and soldiers carried his coffin wrapped in the national flag. A military commemoration was held on Saturday at an official Serbian army venue. Populist President Aleksandar Vucic, a former extreme nationalist who supported Serbia’s expansionist policies during the war, described the funeral as an “emotional outpouring” that “has nothing to do” with whether the Serbian government approved it or not. Serbia is a candidate nation for EU membership and has faced strong criticism for honouring Mladic after his death. Marta Kos, the enlargement commissioner for the bloc, cancelled a coming visit to Serbia in protest, arguing that “the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built”. Serbia, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war, remains defiant over its wartime role and accuses the West of anti-Serb bias. Vucic said that “we [Serbs] have been persecuted and harassed for 30, 40 years … always guilty whatever happens”. He added that “people just won’t take it any more”. Vucic, who is not attending the funeral, previously has accused Kos of lying. The Serbian president has stepped up his anti-Western rhetoric ahead of an early parliamentary election expected next month. A number of other European officials joined the criticism of Serbia, along with regional leaders and relatives of Mladic’s victims from the war in Bosnia. The conflict left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless before it ended in 1995 in a US-brokered peace agreement.

title: PLA Rocket Force highlights ‘major danger signal’ from Japan in nuclear terror study
description: Study by a rocket force medical team also warns there is a risk of attacks on cities ‘driven by geopolitical or religious conflicts’.
content: Chinese cities must brace for a potential nuclear attack, a new study has warned, singling out Japan for “sending a major danger signal” to the world. The report, from a People’s Liberation Army medical team, said the likelihood of a large-scale global nuclear war was relatively low. “However, the possibility cannot be ruled out that small or medium-sized nuclear-armed or potentially nuclear-armed states, driven by geopolitical or religious conflicts, could carry out a single nuclear-weapon terrorist attack on neighbouring countries or on key cities of major powers,” they wrote. The study, from the PLA Rocket Force Characteristic Medical Centre, was published last Friday in the peer-reviewed Chinese Journal of Radiological Health. The researchers specifically named Japan as a major concern. They said Tokyo had yet to accede to the first legally binding international agreement to ban nuclear arms, signed in 2017, and was considering a change to its long-standing policy, known as the “three non-nuclear principles” of not possessing, not producing and not permitting the introduction of nuclear weapons. “Japan has still not acceded to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, and the current Japanese government is even openly considering revising the principle of ‘non-introduction of nuclear weapons’ within its ‘three non-nuclear principles’, sending a major danger signal to the international community,” the report said. In January 2022, the five United Nations Security Council permanent members – China, the United States, Russia, Britain and France – issued a joint statement affirming that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”. But the PLA study warned: “Once certain countries or terrorist groups take such a risk, the possibility that Chinese cities could suffer a nuclear terrorist attack cannot be ruled out.” The study modelled a scenario in which a major Chinese city was subjected to a single, low-yield nuclear terrorist attack – using smaller-scale tactical weapons. Drawing on historical data from the 1945 Hiroshima bomb and simulations carried out around the world, they said medical teams would face a range of challenges after an attack, ranging from hazardous conditions and widespread social disorder to complex injury patterns. Beijing has already established an emergency rescue network comprising more than 30 bases to treat casualties from a nuclear attack. The researchers argued that China should further expand its treatment capacity with more resources and specialised training. They also suggested that local authorities should stockpile sufficient emergency supplies – including antibiotics and radiation-protection equipment – and ensure they were kept in a state of “combat readiness”. Society as a whole must also strengthen public education on nuclear and radiation safety, rescue protocols and protective measures to minimise irrational behaviour and panic in the event of an emergency, the study added. Compared with the emergency medical response to a civilian nuclear facility accident, even a low-yield nuclear terrorist attack would cause heavy casualties and complex, multi-trauma injuries. Such an event would pose a “huge test” for the medical capacity of any city or country, the authors wrote, urging China to “prepare for a rainy day”. Beijing has repeatedly accused Tokyo of pursuing “remilitarisation” and has long held suspicions about its nuclear ambitions. An official report released in January alleged that Japan “may already have produced weapons-grade plutonium in secret” and possessed “the technological and economic capabilities to achieve nuclear armament in a short period of time”. It added that the country had “established a comprehensive nuclear fuel cycle system and possesses robust nuclear industrial capabilities”. Fears of a renewed global arms race are also escalating. The end of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty – the last remaining cap on US and Russian nuclear arms – has only amplified these concerns. In April, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres warned that the momentum behind nuclear proliferation was building. “For too long, the treaty has been eroding. Commitments remain unfulfilled. Trust and credibility are wearing thin. The drivers of proliferation are accelerating,” Guterres said during a gathering to review the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.

title: Zhang Ziyu, China’s towering teenage basketball World Cup sensation, ‘just a little girl’
description: Teammate Han Xu’s view echoed by WNBA star Caitlin Clark, who says 19-year-old is a ‘wonderful player’ and there is more to her than her size.
content: Chinese teenage basketball player Zhang Ziyu stands 2.23 metres (7 feet 4 inches) and towers over opponents at the Women’s World Cup – but off the court she’s “just a little girl”. That was the assessment of the giant 19-year-old by teammate Han Xu after China’s 74-70 overtime win over the Czech Republic on Sunday in Germany. The teenage centre scored three points in just over 10 minutes on court against a physical Czech side, having been more of a threat against reigning champions the United States in a 94-61 loss to start the tournament. After that defeat, US superstar Caitlin Clark had warm words for Zhang, saying: “I’ve never played against a woman of that size and she obviously presented some challenges for us. “I think she’s a wonderful player and you see how young she is. “You can tell she’s still growing and learning how to play and how to leverage her advantage, which is her size. “There’s not much you can do to stop her when she gets it really close to the basket.” Zhang’s height is listed at 223cm on the website of world governing body Fiba, making her already taller than NBA great Shaquille O’Neal, and even in a sport where height matters, she stands out in women’s basketball. Zhang might be destined for the WNBA, but Clark and Han warned against placing too many expectations on the teenager. “In life she’s just a little girl,” said Han, who top-scored for China with 22 points against the Czechs. “I always want to give her good energy … she can finish to the rim and protect the paint. “I think she is a great player and we just keep thinking [about] how to use her better and hope she can be more aggressive.” The official website for the Women’s Basketball World Cup describes Zhang as “epically tall”, noting she first came to international prominence when she was crowned MVP at the U18 Women’s Asia Cup two years ago. Footage and images of Zhang looming over her opponents have gone viral online, but Clark said there was more to her than just that. “She’s still a very young player, but to be this young and to be in a World Cup and to go up against the top players is only going to help her continue to grow,” Clark said. “So I think if she continues to develop, then there’s definitely a place for her.”

title: Rare drone film of suspected dumping spurs Chinese agencies into investigation
description: Authorities mount inquiry in wake of new rules holding officials responsible for life for serious environmental damage.
content: Authorities in central China have joined forces to investigate suspected industrial dumping on the Yangtze River following the release of rare drone footage of the activity. The environment bureau in the Hubei city of Wuhan said on Monday that it had launched the inquiry in association with police and transport authorities. The announcement comes less than two weeks after Beijing revised performance assessment rules for officials, holding them accountable for life for serious environmental damage on their watch. The investigation was spurred by the release of drone footage online on Sunday showing barges discharging an unknown black substance into the river near Tianxingzhou, an islet in the Wuhan section of the Yangtze. Tianxingzhou is home to a facility that supplies about 3,000 tonnes of water daily to roughly 800 residents, according to 2024 data from Hubei’s water resources department. In the footage posted on the account “Fishing and Hunting Brother Qi”, a barge stops in the middle of the river and dumps its load within about 10 seconds, leaving a dark plume several times the length of the vessel. The black discharge fans out across the surface in a whale-tail shape roughly as wide as three barges. The vessel then turns before another barge carrying a similar material approaches a little while later. The footage also showed crew members hosing down the deck after dumping, sending the run-off straight into the water. The person who posted the material said he saw three vessels carry out dumping operations in 90 minutes. The Yangtze is China’s longest river, stretching from the Tibetan Plateau to the East China Sea. Wuhan, the capital of central Hubei province, lies along its middle reaches. The video sparked widespread outrage online, with users highlighting the Yangtze’s role as the main source of drinking water for tens of millions of people. The incident comes amid heightened central government scrutiny over environmental damage. Late last month, the Communist Party and the State Council released amended regulations tying green metrics directly to officials’ promotion prospects. Under the rules, cadres remain liable even after being transferred, promoted, or retired. It is part of a broader national effort to repair and protect the environment, a priority laid out in the present five-year plan. President Xi Jinping has also sought to frame environmental protection as a source of economic value.

title: China unveils plan to revamp ‘classic products’ in bid to boost sluggish consumer spending
description: Heritage is the latest sector targeted by authorities, following similar efforts in the sports, winter tourism and nightlife industries.
content: China is leaning on its cultural heritage to jolt sluggish domestic spending, rolling out a push to modernise industries ranging from silk and tea to liquor, ceramics and traditional Chinese medicine. Authorities laid out plans to cultivate 50 leading enterprises in heritage industries, each with a scale of at least 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion), by 2028, according to a statement released on Monday by six government departments. “Many classic products are perceived as somewhat outdated and struggle to capture the attention of young people,” said Xie Yuansheng, vice-minister of industry and information technology, at a press conference in Beijing on Monday. The goal is to make heritage products “trendy” and appealing to both young people in China and abroad, Xie said, adding that officials would support collaboration between these industries and prominent designers, brands and fashion companies. The push comes as policymakers seek new levers to stimulate household spending, which remains constrained by a battered property sector and soft labour market. Retail sales grew just 0.6 per cent in July, missing forecasts and coming in lower than the 1 per cent recorded in June. Heritage products are the latest in a line of sectors targeted by authorities, following similar policy efforts in the sports, winter tourism and nightlife industries. Early efforts to modernise traditional sectors so they appeal to younger consumers already look promising. In recent months, bars across China serving traditional Chinese medicine-infused beverages – where drinks are sometimes customised following pulse-reading consultations – have gone viral on social media. Some ceramic and woodcarving products have also seen rising popularity following the release of the blockbuster video game Black Myth: Wukong in late 2024. Meanwhile, these products are also beginning to garner attention abroad. Driven by social media trends like “China-maxxing” – where international users adopt Chinese lifestyle habits ranging from drinking hot water and tea to practising traditional qigong exercises – visibility for Chinese heritage has grown significantly. “[Heritage products] meet material needs while also bringing emotional resonance, cultural enrichment and aesthetic enjoyment,” Xie said. Under the latest plan, authorities pledged to support scenic spots and shopping districts in setting up creative markets and interactive exhibitions, and encouraged live-streaming and short-form video platforms to market heritage industries and drive sales. Officials will also promote expansion into duty-free stores, and appoint prominent figures as overseas brand ambassadors to raise the profile of Chinese heritage goods abroad.

title: UN rights chief warns AI could pose ‘existential’ risk to humanity’
description: Volker Turk calls for ‘cast-iron guarantees’ to secure AI against risks that his office says includes disruptions to critical infrastructure.
content: UN rights chief Volker Turk warned on Monday that artificial intelligence could pose a threat to humanity, and pledged to press AI firms to reduce risks that his office said included disruptions to services, communications and democratic systems. He called for “cast-iron guarantees” to secure AI in a speech ahead of the start of his unprecedented second term, in which he also demanded accountability over ‌deaths in US immigration custody and condemned Russia’s reported use of autonomous drones. The wide-ranging address was his first to the 47-member council since he won the four-year term in July in the face of opposition from Moscow and Washington. “I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity,” Turk told the body in Geneva. “I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late.” Turk did not elaborate on the nature of ⁠the risks but a spokesperson for his office said failures involving powerful AI systems could disrupt critical infrastructure and democratic institutions. She referred to the “dangerous agent-training behaviours” in July’s ‌so-called Hugging Face incident where a swarm of OpenAI agents hacked an open-source platform, saying it suggested that frontier AI capabilities are advancing faster than the safeguards. Turk warned that just a handful of men held “almost unlimited power over AI” without naming ‌any. Top AI companies include Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. “At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its ⁠supply chains to come together around ⁠agreed red lines,” he said. The council is meeting until October 7 to discuss the Iran war, Sudan’s civil conflict and a string of other crises. The Trump administration disengaged from the council ‌last year, accusing it of anti-Israeli bias. Turk called for accountability for 23 deaths he said had taken place in U.S. immigration custody so far this year and added that he was concerned about plans ‌to ‌equip agents with electric shock gloves. The Department of Homeland Security has previously said it was committed to ensuring a “safe, secure and humane” environment in detention. Its inspector ‌general is examining deaths in custody since October 2021. The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Turk condemned Russia ⁠for its intensified attacks on Ukraine, and Iran for the rising numbers of executions. He also voiced “horror” at reports that Russia had used fully autonomous drones in ⁠Ukraine, allegedly killing three people in August. “I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement,” he said, referring to talks in Geneva. Reuters has not independently verified these reports. Russia’s diplomatic mission did not immediately respond to a request for ‌comment. With more than 60 wars around the ‌world involving at least one state – the highest since World War II – Turk set out ideas for ways to promote peace, pledging greater scrutiny of the businesses and economic interests that are fuelling conflicts. “We will not shy away from exposing the shadow players and calling for accountability,” he said. Later this month, the UN human rights office is due to publish a list of businesses operating in Israeli West Bank settlements the global body deems illegal – a charge dismissed by Israel.

title: Japan’s Shinjuku to ban more than half of holiday rentals
description: The policy will only apply to existing rentals, an official says. It is likely to result in the closure of about 2,000 properties.
content: Japan’s tourist hotspot Shinjuku will impose a ban on more than half of its holiday rentals, including homes on Airbnb, after a surge in complaints about visitors, an official has said. Known for its buzzing commercial and entertainment district in the Japanese capital Tokyo, Shinjuku has about 4,000 short-term rentals, according to the ward’s official website. That is nearly 10 per cent of the country’s total. But its large residential population has become increasingly exasperated with tourists who fail to properly dispose of rubbish, smoke where they are not supposed to and make too much noise. A Shinjuku official supervising holiday rentals said on Monday that the district was “planning to revise the current ordinance … to ban private lodging” in residential zones and areas near schools. “As the number of private lodging businesses has risen, complaints and troubles around them have increased,” the official said on customary condition of anonymity. More than 50 per cent of short-term rentals in Shinjuku faced a ban under the new rules, he said, adding that the plan would formally be announced by the Shinjuku mayor on Tuesday. The policy would only apply to existing rentals, the official said. It is likely to result in the closure of about 2,000 properties, including an unknown number on Airbnb. Japan aims to attract 60 million foreign tourists by 2030, up from 42 million in 2025, but overtourism has emerged as a major challenge. Residents of Japan’s former imperial capital Kyoto and other hotspots have expressed annoyance at selfie-taking crowds as well as traffic congestion and soaring land prices. In Shinjuku, the number of complaints over holiday rentals increased by about 40 per cent in the financial year to March, the official said. “Many complaints are about the violation of trash disposal rules while others include smoking and trespassing,” he said. American tourist Luke Jemison, 24, said the rules “make sense, because of noise”. Masaru Sato, a Shinjuku resident in his 70s, said “many foreigners, including operators of private lodgings, don’t follow local rules”, adding that “this area gets dirty because the way they dispose of trash is very messy”. Agence France-Presse has contacted Airbnb for comment but several hosts in Shinjuku declined interviews. In July, the Japan Tourism Agency gave municipalities the right to regulate short-term lodgings if “a tranquil living and educational environment” is under threat or if they “hinder the maintenance of a permanent population and local community”. Kyoto is also considering a ban on short-term lodging, but only for new rentals within residential and industrial areas. Other global cities have cracked down on private lodgings available through online rental platforms. That is partly due to overtourism concerns, but also because some residents say home-sharing websites for tourists deprive locals of flats for long-term rent and push up prices for homes remaining on the market. Barcelona, one of Europe’s most-visited cities, aims to ban flat rentals to tourists by 2029 to ease a housing shortage. Under rules introduced in 2023, New York prohibits rental periods of less than 30 days unless the host lives in the property.

title: China vows deeper cooperation with Qatar in energy, AI and Middle East de-escalation
description: Li Qiang makes pledge during meeting with Qatari prime minister visiting on official two-day state visit in Beijing on Monday.
content: Chinese Premier Li Qiang pledged to deepen cooperation with Qatar in energy, investment, AI and diplomatic efforts to de-escalate Middle East tensions. Li delivered the remarks during a meeting on Monday in Beijing with Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, who is on an official two-day visit to China aimed at bolstering bilateral ties. His visit came as Beijing and Doha sought to navigate an increasingly volatile regional security environment and ensure international navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for China’s energy imports and Qatar’s LNG exports, which supply nearly one-third of China’s demand for liquefied natural gas. Iran on Monday said talks with Oman on a temporary safe passage through the strait were in their final stage, with the agreement expected to be registered with the International Maritime Organisation in the coming days. Tehran also confirmed that a Qatari delegation’s visit on Sunday was part of regional de-escalation efforts. “China stands ready to work with Qatar to strengthen communication and coordination, firmly support each other and deepen cooperation in energy, investment, artificial intelligence and people-to-people exchanges,” a Chinese foreign ministry statement quoted Li as saying. Calling Qatar China’s important strategic partner in the Middle East, Li also called for enhanced multilateral coordination between the two countries to help build “a more just and equitable global governance system”. The Chinese premier said Beijing supported Qatar’s mediating and brokering role regarding the situation in the Middle East, adding that Beijing was ready to work with Qatar, other Gulf states and the broader international community to “restore peace and tranquillity to the region at an early date”. Sheikh Mohammed said Qatar was willing to work with China to strengthen exchanges at all levels, deepen cooperation in trade, high technology and advanced manufacturing, and jointly usher in the next “golden decade of bilateral relations”, according to the Chinese statement. In a statement published on social media, Qatar’s foreign ministry said the talks focused on expanding cooperation in the economy, investment, trade, energy and technology, as well as boosting existing partnerships in areas of mutual interest. The two sides also discussed key regional developments, it said without elaboration. Since 2020, China has been Qatar’s largest trading partner and top export destination, with bilateral trade volume rising from US$10.6 billion in 2014 to US$24.22 billion in 2024, for a 128 per cent increase over the decade, according to Cao Xiaolin, China’s ambassador to Qatar. Majed bin Mohammed Al Ansari, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesman, told the Qatar News Agency on Sunday that Sheikh Mohammed’s visit would address “major regional developments and diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions,” while strengthening bilateral relations “across various fields” and emphasising “the need to ensure the security and freedom of international navigation in the Strait of Hormuz”. During his state visit to Egypt last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping unveiled a four-point proposal for a new Middle East security architecture, urging regional countries to become “masters of their own destiny”, reject external interference and place economic development at the heart of “regional common security”. Last Wednesday, Xi told Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that China stood ready to work with countries in the region to safeguard the security of international shipping lanes, advance development cooperation and eliminate the breeding grounds for conflict. Qatar hosts a major US airbase while maintaining open channels with Iran and has been a mediator in the Middle East. Its position is widely seen as complementary to Beijing’s preference for dialogue and economic leverage rather than military involvement. In late August, Sheikh Mohammed visited Tehran to mediate between Washington and Tehran, focusing on keeping the Strait of Hormuz open and identifying a framework for resuming US-Iran dialogue. The Qatari foreign ministry said the talks addressed de-escalation efforts and a proposed Iranian-Omani framework for managing navigation through Hormuz, a major conduit for global energy supplies through which about 20 million barrels per day of oil pass, with roughly 80 per cent destined for Asian markets. In March, during a phone call with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, Sheikh Mohammed said Qatar appreciated Beijing’s mediation efforts and hoped it could play a greater role in bringing about a ceasefire. This week’s meeting in Beijing underscores the complex balancing act Gulf states face amid the intensifying US-China rivalry. The states continue to rely on deep security and military partnerships with Washington, even as they expand energy and investment ties and political engagement with Beijing, which offers cooperation without security guarantees or alliance obligations.

title: China and Russia launch first sea ice survey aboard Xuelong 2 as Arctic tensions swell
description: Beijing and Moscow are stepping up cooperation in the polar region, drawing Washington’s attention as climate change opens new sea routes.
content: China and Russia have conducted their first joint on-site sea ice survey in the Arctic Ocean aboard the Xuelong 2 research icebreaker, as tensions continue to rise over economic opportunities in the rapidly warming northern region. Two researchers from Russia’s Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute boarded Xuelong 2 as part of China’s 16th Arctic Ocean Expedition, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV on Saturday. According to Lin Long, captain of the Xuelong 2 sea ice team, this joint observation has been more “practical” than previous Chinese Arctic voyages. During the mission, they visually observed ice conditions along the ship’s route, recording details about the concentration, thickness and type of sea ice, snow cover, atmospheric factors and large animal sightings. “By taking part in this joint observation, we were able to learn from the Chinese team’s experience in sea ice observation and draw on the valuable aspects of their observation methods,” CCTV quoted Evgeniy Kozlovskiy, a lead engineer at the Russian institute, as saying. The observations could complement satellite remote sensing, improve scientists’ understanding of climate change, and lay the foundation for more international cooperation, according to the report. Moscow and Beijing have stepped up cooperation in the Arctic, and Washington is closely watching their activities in the region. Rapid melting as a result of climate change has opened up new Arctic shipping routes, drawing the attention of Russia and the United States, but also China – which sees itself as a “near Arctic” nation. In August 2024, Chinese Premier Li Qiang and his Russian counterpart Mikhail Mishustin signed a joint communique to develop Arctic shipping routes. China has funded research and exploration for the establishment of a “Polar Silk Road”. In an interview with Russian tabloid Komsomolskaya Pravda on Friday, Russian political scientist Vasily Kashin said that China’s interest in the Northern Sea Route “has grown significantly” despite challenges to Arctic cooperation, including Western sanctions. A few years ago, China had diversified partnerships, including major investment projects in Iceland, Greenland, Norway and Canada, according to Kashin, director of the Centre for Comprehensive European and International Studies at Russia’s Higher School of Economics. “Now, under US influence, the Chinese are being squeezed out of these Arctic partnerships. Therefore, today they are interested in collaborating with us, and we are interested in collaborating with them,” he said. But some warn that Russia has mixed feelings about China’s increasing activities in the Arctic. According to a policy brief by analyst Patrik Andersson for the Danish Institute of International Studies in July of last year, Moscow views the Arctic as a core national interest and remains wary of China’s long-term ambitions to become a great polar power. The Sino-Russian partnership in the Arctic is “constrained by diverging priorities”, and their dynamic could “intensify underlying frictions” even as the two neighbours draw closer, according to the brief. The negatives of a warming Arctic are likely to outweigh potential economic benefits. The downsides include the rapid thaw of permafrost, which threatens Arctic infrastructure, and climate feedback loops that drive further warming. China’s 16th Arctic Ocean Expedition, which includes the research icebreakers Xuelong, Xuelong 2 and Jidi, departed from the port city of Dalian in Liaoning province in early July and is expected to end in early October. The Xuelong 2 icebreaker conducts surveys in the Arctic and Antarctic in their respective summers. The current expedition, which also includes the research ship Tansuo 3, was organised by China’s Ministry of Natural Resources to survey and monitor the Arctic Ocean’s sea ice, ecosystems, and water and atmospheric conditions. In July, state media reported that China would also collaborate with scientists from Germany and other countries on the expedition to respond to global climate change and its impacts. On August 20, China and Russia launched their fourth joint Arctic expedition aboard the research vessel Akademik M.A. Lavrentyev. It is scheduled to last 62 days and cover regions between the northwest Pacific and the Arctic Ocean, including the Chukchi Sea, which lies between Russia and Alaska.

title: China warns against ‘third party’ interference after reports of US pressure on Mexico
description: Beijing pledges to help maintain Mexican sovereignty and security during a meeting between the countries’ foreign ministers.
content: Relations between China and Mexico should not be influenced by outside powers, Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday, following reports that the United States was pressuring its neighbour over its ties to Beijing. “China-Mexico relations are not directed at any third party, nor should they be influenced by any third party,” Wang told his Mexican counterpart Roberto Velasco Alvarez. He added that China supported Mexico in maintaining its independence, safeguarding its sovereignty and security and opposing external interference, according to the foreign ministry. Velasco, making his first official visit to Beijing since taking office in April, said both nations had a shared respect for sovereignty and equality. He added that Mexico was willing to strengthen high-level exchanges, advance bilateral mechanisms and deepen pragmatic cooperation, according to a Chinese statement. “I hope that today we can identify new areas of understanding and cooperation between our nations, for the benefit of our people, and lay the foundations for a joint work agenda for the coming years,” Velasco said, according to Mexico’s N+ news agency. Velasco also said Mexico would host the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in 2028, an event that he described as “a historic opportunity” to project Mexico’s leadership as a bridge between the Americas and Asia, according to the report. The two sides also exchanged views on international and regional issues of mutual concern, the Chinese foreign ministry said. Wang said China and Mexico shared similar positions on many international and regional issues, adding that Beijing was willing to strengthen strategic coordination with Mexico on multilateral platforms to safeguard their respective legitimate interests and jointly promote the unity and strength of the Global South. Mexico also used the visit to highlight the opening of a new consulate in the southwestern megacity of Chongqing. Velasco’s trip comes as Mexico is in talks with the US to lock in bilateral deals before the two countries enter three-way talks with Canada. Trade negotiations between Ottawa and Washington collapsed last month, in part because of reported US demands to limit Canada’s trade deals with third countries. The restriction was widely seen as an attempt to target China. Mexico may face similar pressure, with Bloomberg reporting in July that Washington was pushing the Latin American nation to mirror its trade barriers on Chinese steel and aluminium. Mexico appears to be taking steps to ease Washington’s anxieties. At the end of last month, the administration of President Claudia Sheinbaum submitted a proposed reform to the Senate to amend the country’s Foreign Investment Law. The amendments would subject foreign acquisitions in sensitive sectors such as energy, artificial intelligence and semiconductors to national security reviews.

title: Philippine tennis sensation Alexandra Eala looking forward to having ‘fun’ at Asian Games
description: World No 18 says she loves the Games environment, will be favourite in Aichi-Nagoya in absence of China’s Zheng Qinwen, Japan’s Naomi Osaka.
content: Philippines sensation Alexandra Eala said she cannot wait to experience the “really fun environment” of the Asian Games after a battling defeat in the third round of the US Open. The rising 21-year-old will be favourite to win women’s singles gold when the Games begin in Japan on September 19. At the previous edition of the Games, in 2023 in China, Eala went home with bronze medals in singles and mixed doubles. Much has changed for Eala since, last month becoming the first player from the Philippines to win a WTA singles crown and now ranked 18 in the world. Her groundbreaking exploits have made her a superstar back home. “I love playing and competing with the Philippines team,” Eala said after her agonising three-set loss to United States teenager Iva Jovic in New York on Saturday. Proud Filipino Eala has been a regular at the Southeast Asian Games, winning singles gold last year, and she added: “I think it’s a really fun environment, and I love being with the team, especially this last SEA Games in December; I had such a great time. “I think they are really memories that stick with me.” China’s Zheng Qinwen won Asian Games singles gold three years ago on home turf. She will not defend her title in Aichi-Nagoya. Also not involved will be Japan’s four-time grand slam champion Naomi Osaka, who will be in action at the China Open in Beijing. Eala will miss Beijing knowing that gold at the Asian Games would seal an automatic berth at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Eala is set to play at the Singapore Open on September 21-27, with the Asian Games women’s singles starting the same day that Singapore ends.

title: Opinion | AI titans’ ‘circular deals’ are starting to look like ‘daisy chains’
description: It’s time to ask how much of the industry’s extraordinary growth is being financed by the same companies benefiting from it.
content: The “circular deals” among AI titans increasingly resemble the “daisy chains” of the 1980s savings-and-loan crisis. Forty years ago, interconnected transactions obscured the dangers, multiplied systemic risks and helped inflate asset values before roughly a third of US thrift banks failed. Today’s financial engineering – an incestuous ecosystem of interlocking multi-year commitments to provide financing, buy semiconductors, secure gigawatts of power and lease data centres – could meet a similar fate, especially if revenue fails to outpace costs or a black swan event eviscerates artificial intelligence (AI) trajectories. OpenAI has struck deals with Nvidia, CoreWeave and others ahead of an initial public offering planned for next year while competitors Anthropic and xAI have pursued similar agreements. Anthropic’s US$35 billion cloud-computing deal with provider Lambda is the latest example. Last month, the AI developer signed a US$45 billion arrangement with another Nvidia-backed neocloud, Nscale, to rent data-centre capacity. Nvidia is involved in more than US$750 billion worth of AI investments, financing deals and partnerships, according to PitchBook. Demand from AI labs receiving Nvidia financial support will account for roughly a quarter of the company’s business next year, CFO Colette Kress said. The rash of AI investments is unprecedented in scale – 4.5 times the level three years ago, according to Bank for International Settlements data. This raises a question: how much of the industry’s extraordinary growth is being financed by the same companies benefiting from it? Meanwhile, hidden risks are colliding with a borrowing binge well under way. The five largest hyperscalers carry roughly US$1.65 trillion in debt through special purpose vehicles and other off-balance-sheet structures, exceeding the US$1.35 trillion they report directly, according to Nikkei. Circular transactions can reinforce valuations and revenue expectations that, in turn, justify still more investment. Financing creates demand, demand supports valuations, valuations facilitate more borrowing, which finances still more demand. To be clear, however, they are not fraudulent “round-trip” transactions using sham trades. For China – with an estimated 30 per cent of the global market for legacy chips and plans for a five-fold increase in advanced chip output – the fallout could be enormous. Tech giants like Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post, have ramped up AI spending to match global buildout trends, leading to plunging profits and negative free cash flow. In 1980s America, undercapitalised savings and loan associations (S&Ls) traded junk bonds within a mutually supportive “chain”, creating an illusion of liquidity, solvency and market stability. Deceptive accounting hid losses and manufactured profits on paper. But when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates to then-historic highs to combat inflation, S&Ls were trapped. They held old mortgages with low, fixed rates while their deposit costs skyrocketed. Today’s “virtual flywheels” differ in crucial respects. Hyperscalers are solvent, generating unparalleled revenue growth amid extraordinary global demand. Interest rates have yet to play a role. No regulator has alleged fraud. And Wall Street offers many financing tools. Yet some of the dynamics that made the thrift-era daisy chains so dangerous are reappearing. Circularity is mutually validating asset values with correlated counterparties. By recycling capital among interdependent parties, circular deals can blur where risk ultimately sits, the Bank of England warns, while concentrating risks unevenly across the chain. A hyperscaler could lose twice: first, when demand falls for its products and services, and again when its equity investment declines. As long as demand and valuations rise, the flywheel accelerates. But if one critical link fails, the virtuous circle turns vicious. The same financial links that magnified growth can transmit distress throughout the ecosystem, turning one company’s losses into another’s impaired investment, unpaid contract or stranded asset. Nvidia president and CEO Jensen Huang has said the deals are “not circular because obviously they do their own business and we do our own business”. Demand for compute power is high, with Nvidia claiming at least US$1 trillion in back orders through 2027, total financial commitments represent a small portion of expected free cash flow, and infrastructure can be reallocated, Huang maintains. He may be right. The AI boom could generate sufficient revenues to make today’s commitments look modest in hindsight. But that assumes demand keeps compounding, computing costs keep falling and the infrastructure remains productive long enough to repay the debt financing it. The lesson of the thrift crisis is not that AI’s virtual flywheels are destined to collapse. It is that interconnectedness – the combination of circularity, leverage, interdependent counterparties and assumptions that mutually validate one another – can transform an unexpected setback into something much larger. A breakthrough requiring dramatically less computing power, a collapse in AI pricing or another unforeseen shock could abruptly rewrite today’s economics. We had a taste of that when China’s DeepSeek and Moonshot AI made breakthroughs. The flywheel that accelerates investment on the way up can just as easily shift into reverse.

title: Taiwan sets up US-backed cyber unit to hunt hidden military threats
description: Taiwanese defence minister says exchanges with the US are ‘even more extensive than you might imagine’.
content: Taiwan’s military plans to step up its cyber defences against mainland China with a new threat-hunting team and foreign expertise as it deepens cooperation with the US. The Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command has earmarked NT$95.93 million (US$3.03 million) in its proposed 2027 budget to establish the team and bring foreign experts and instructors to Taiwan for advanced training. According to the budget plan, which still needs legislative approval, the programme would focus on “proactive cyber threat hunting”, moving the military beyond conventional defences, such as firewalls and post-attack remediation, towards actively searching networks for hidden threats. Taiwan’s defence ministry did not identify where the foreign instructors would come from, but local media reports suggest they would mainly be from the United States. The instructors are expected to introduce realistic adversarial training comparable to the US military’s Cyber Flag exercises, according to the Taipei-based Liberty Times. Like detectives following clues, team members would be trained to search military networks and critical infrastructure during peacetime for hostile hackers bypassing existing defences and concealing themselves inside systems, the outlet said. The Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command is an independent branch of Taiwan’s military specialising in digital warfare, with responsibilities that include cyber operations, electronic warfare, military communications resilience and the protection of critical infrastructure. The planned threat-hunting team would identify and eliminate hidden intruders and back doors before an adversary launched an attack, while bringing Taiwan’s cyber capabilities more in line with international practices, according to the report. The plan comes as Taipei and Washington expand military exchanges well beyond arms sales, with American military personnel, civilian defence officials and contractors increasingly involved in advising, training and observing forces from the island. Taiwanese Defence Minister Wellington Koo Li-hsiung acknowledged the extent of that cooperation ahead of last month’s Han Kuang exercises – the island’s largest annual war games – saying that exchanges with the US were “even more extensive than you might imagine”. Personnel seen observing Taiwanese exercises represented only a small part of the relationship, Koo said, adding that exchanges with the US Indo-Pacific Command were helping Taiwan improve its defensive capabilities. US personnel involved in such activities have become colloquially known in Taiwan as “American English teachers”, reflecting the sensitivity that has traditionally surrounded the presence of American military personnel on the island. Taiwanese media estimates that more than 100 foreign instructors and observers were present during this year’s Han Kuang exercises, watching activities that ranged from reserve mobilisation and coastal operations to drills in Taipei’s metro system. Their roles are largely advisory and do not amount to the deployment of formed US combat units. US personnel involved in defence-related activities in Taiwan include active-duty service members, civilian defence officials and contractors, with assignments ranging from short training visits to longer-term postings. Their work includes specialist exchanges, observing exercises, providing training assistance and advising on the operation and maintenance of US-supplied weapons. American personnel have also worked with Taiwanese forces on special operations, satellite communications, target acquisition and fire coordination. Beijing, which regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary, has repeatedly opposed US military cooperation with Taipei. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state. Washington opposes any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to providing it with the means to defend itself. Chieh Chung, a research fellow at the Association of Strategic Foresight, a Taipei-based think tank, said US personnel had reasons to observe Taiwanese forces first-hand because Taipei had increasingly adopted American recommendations in areas such as training, kill-chain modernisation and special operations. “Observation during exercises allows the US side to assess whether its recommendations are working and identify shortcomings that could be addressed in subsequent training,” he said. During the Han Kuang drills, US influence was also reflected in Taiwan’s greater emphasis on realistic and unscripted training, decentralised command and allowing lower-level commanders to make decisions when communication with higher headquarters was disrupted. The military introduced the US-style “backbrief”, in which subordinate commanders explain to their superiors how they understand the missions and orders – a practice intended to strengthen independent decision-making in combat. Cyber operations were another major element of Han Kuang. The Information, Communications and Electronic Force mobilised more than 100 civilian cybersecurity specialists to work alongside military cyber personnel to test vulnerabilities and conduct offensive-defensive exercises involving critical infrastructure. The force also tested mobile microwave communications and backup power supplies to maintain command-and-control networks after simulated enemy attacks. Analysts said the proposed threat-hunting team would take that approach further, training personnel to sift through vast amounts of network traffic and system logs to uncover advanced persistent threats that penetrated military networks without triggering conventional security alarms.

title: Cross-sector push needed for youth facing ‘paradox of AI fluency’: minister
description: Labour chief Chris Sun says higher education alone no guarantee of job success, while Singapore’s trade minister calls for ‘continuous learning’ mindset.
content: Hong Kong’s labour secretary has called for greater cross-sector efforts to help young people gain job experience amid disruption caused by artificial intelligence (AI), while Singapore’s trade minister has urged embracing a “continuous learning” mindset. Speaking at the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s PBC (Philanthropy for Better Cities) Forum 2026 on Monday, the city’s Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said that higher education alone was no longer enough to ensure career success in the age of AI. “If you look at what’s going to make a success in a career, the task usually is that you invest in higher education,” Sun said. “It’s almost a guarantee as a passport to a good career. “Right now, this is not a recipe for success any more.” Sun added that success today required AI fluency, trade-specific professional skills, and soft skills such as communication and the ability to “win people over”. While young people typically exhibited the highest AI fluency, they faced difficulty getting opportunities to be tested in real-world work environments, he said. “So for me, this is like a paradox of AI fluency without a platform,” he said. “I think here we need a concerted effort between the government, employers and also philanthropy, to help provide a better transition for young people to be really tested in the workplace as soon as possible.” People working in clerical jobs were also at a high risk of losing their jobs, Sun said. During the panel discussion, Sun outlined measures the government was implementing to help residents with social mobility and retraining. He highlighted plans to upgrade the Employees Retraining Board under the rebranded moniker Upskill Hong Kong, and proposals to launch a social welfare project-matching platform later in the year. Sun said the government’s coming manpower forecast would also outline which jobs were more likely to be lost to AI. “We need to tell people which jobs are more AI-proof [and] which jobs are more prone to AI destruction,” he said. The Jockey Club’s two-day forum brought together about 2,000 delegates from philanthropy, sports, government, business and academia to the city’s West Kowloon Cultural District. Held under the theme “Leaping for Impact”, it marked the fifth edition of the forum, which was first held in 2016. Speaking on the same panel, Singapore’s Minister for Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said his country’s approach to AI was like taking “a bull by the horns”. “We are pushing AI fluency and literacy to as broad a base of our population as possible,” said Tan, who formerly served as the country’s minister of manpower. “We nudge all of our Singapore workers to go on to these AI courses, which are heavily subsidised ... We hope to make [AI fluency] as widespread, as pervasive as possible.” He also highlighted Singapore’s upskilling programmes such as SkillsFuture Credit, which provided citizens with subsidies for approved training courses. First introduced in 2015, the programme was recently updated to include a mid-career “top-up” for those aged 40 and over. He added that the country’s Skills and Workforce Development Agency had worked with universities and other higher education institutes to connect undergraduate students with internships and traineeships. In the current economic climate, attaining a skills-based training certificate or degree was just the beginning of the learning process, Tan said. “With the way the technology is moving, the job cycles are becoming shorter and shorter and shorter. So we need to embrace this mindset of continuous learning,” he said.

title: University of Hong Kong suspends professor over past sexual misconduct in Canada
description: University of Hong Kong confirms that Peter Tanuseputro was asked to work from home after it became aware of professional misconduct ruling against him.
content: A professor at Hong Kong’s oldest medical school has been suspended from clinical work and face-to-face teaching after the university discovered he was temporarily disqualified from practising in Canada following past sexual harassment allegations. The University of Hong Kong (HKU) confirmed on Monday that Peter Tanuseputro, a clinical professor in the department of family medicine and primary care, was asked to work from home after the university became aware of a professional misconduct ruling against him. “After learning of the incident, HKU’s faculty of medicine immediately suspended all of the professor’s clinical work and face-to-face teaching activities, and arranged for him to work from home,” the university said in response to an inquiry from the South China Morning Post following a whistle-blower’s complaint. Tanuseputro, who obtained his medical practice certificate from the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario in 2010 and joined HKU in 2024, was found by the Ontario Physicians and Surgeons Discipline Tribunal on April 8 to have “constituted conduct that was disgraceful, dishonourable or unprofessional and conduct unbecoming a physician”. He was reprimanded, and his certificate of registration in Canada was suspended for eight months from April 9. He was also ordered to pay C$6,000 (US$4,335) in costs to the college. The tribunal heard that in 2018, while working for the University of Ottawa and holding two research positions at hospitals, Tanuseputro made sexual comments to a female research assistant after a social gathering and engaged in unwanted touching. Between September 2020 and October 2021, Tanuseputro was accused of making inappropriate comments to another woman who worked for him, and sexually harassing her by unwanted touching and kissing, on two occasions. On one occasion, he was accused of grabbing and kissing her hand, hugging her and kissing her hair. Text messages revealed that he admitted to the second woman – whose graduate studies he was supervising – that his conduct was “crazy” and “totally belligerent”. According to the tribunal’s finding, the doctor did not contest that his conduct towards the two women was “in breach of their employer’s workplace policies and related legislation prohibiting sexual harassment”. The tribunal concluded that Tanuseputro had “abused his power” as the two women were considerably younger and held junior positions. “We have found that Dr Tanuseputro engaged in repeated boundary violations with two junior colleagues,” the tribunal stated. The ruling body added that his actions were contrary to the college’s policy on professional behaviour, violated workplace policies and related legislation. Tanuseputro’s main research focus is on frail, older and marginalised populations, as well as on public and population health. HKU said on Monday that while all applicants for clinical professor positions were required to declare all criminal convictions and findings of professional misconduct, Tanuseputro did not make the declaration as he had not been found guilty of misconduct when he joined the institution. “The medical faculty was unaware whether he was undergoing a disciplinary hearing at the time,” HKU added. According to records of the Medical Council, which handles registration and disciplinary regulation of doctors, Tanuseputro holds a limited registration licence in the city. His three-year licence, which specifically requires employment by HKU, began on June 27, 2024, and is valid until June 14, 2027. HKU said that the doctor had reported the case to the medical watchdog. “The medical faculty will review the professor’s work arrangements in due course, according to procedures and circumstances, and in accordance with the results of the disciplinary inquiry by the Medical Council of Hong Kong,” the university stated. In a reply to the SCMP, the council said investigations into misconduct by registered medical practitioners were conducted in private and that it was not in a position to answer or confirm specific enquiries relating to Tanuseputro. It added that, in general, any registered practitioner who had been the subject of adverse findings in disciplinary proceedings by another regulatory body would be required to report them to the city’s medical watchdog within 28 days. According to the Medical Registration Ordinance, a doctor on limited registration in the city has to be registered with a medical authority outside Hong Kong, among other requirements.

title: Germany urges UN’s top court to dismiss Gaza genocide case
description: Berlin says judges lack the jurisdiction to rule on the case and dismisses Nicaragua’s accusations as ‘inaccurate and distorted’.
content: Germany on Monday urged the United Nations’ top court to throw out a case against it by Nicaragua, which has accused Berlin of “facilitating genocide” in Gaza with its support of Israel. Julia Monar, representing Germany at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), said judges lacked the jurisdiction to rule on the case and dismissed Nicaragua’s accusations as “inaccurate and distorted”. Nicaragua has dragged Germany before the ICJ in The Hague, arguing that its backing of Israel, notably in terms of arms exports, contravenes the 1948 UN Genocide Convention. Opening four days of hearings, Monar told ICJ judges that “the conditions on which this court’s jurisdiction is based are not met in this case”. “For the first time in the history of this court, it is being asked to adjudicate a case that is twice removed from a classic bilateral dispute,” Monar told the court, which rules on legal arguments between countries. “Neither Nicaragua nor Germany is a party to the conflict that forms the real subject matter of this case, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” Monar noted. This meant that the court should declare itself incompetent to rule on the case, she said. The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel’s offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment. The court threw out Nicaragua’s request in April of that year, saying “the circumstances, as they now present themselves” did not justify emergency orders. The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule on the case or that Nicaragua’s argument does not stack up. Berlin has filed “preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims” presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement. Addressing that “admissibility”, Monar said: “Nicaragua’s factual statements are not only inapposite at this stage of the proceedings, but also create an inaccurate and distorted picture. All German exports of military technology and equipment to Israel – as to any country – are subject to strict licensing requirements which exceed international requirements.” Monar noted Germany’s “unwavering support for the existence and security of the State of Israel”, but also said it was one of the world’s largest bilateral donors to the Palestinian Territories. Germany sought a “lasting peace” in Gaza, a goal Monar said was shared by Nicaragua. “However, Germany has serious doubts that the case brought to your court by Nicaragua would in any way bring us any closer to this shared goal,” she said. “By way of consequence, Germany respectfully requests the court reject Nicaragua’s claims,” Monar concluded. During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was “pathetic” to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons. Nicaragua’s ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court at that time: “Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide.” The court will hold four days of hearings at the Peace Palace where the court sits, with Nicaragua responding on Tuesday. It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.
