The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered “on the merits” in more detail. This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies. The ICJ’s rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them. For example, it has ordered Russia to stop its invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin.

title: Hong Kong customs seizes 200 crickets, 13kg of cockroaches at border checkpoint
description: Man and woman intercepted at Lo Wu border in separate cases involving HK$5,900 worth of illicit feeder insects.
content: Hong Kong customs officers have intercepted two travellers in separate cases at the Lo Wu border checkpoint for allegedly importing live insects commonly used as reptile feed. On Saturday, officers stopped a 71-year-old local man at the arrival hall and seized 200 crickets from his baggage, valued at about HK$2,000 (US$255). The following day, officers intercepted a 66-year-old local woman at the same checkpoint carrying 13kg (28.6lbs) of dubia roaches, worth about HK$3,900, in her baggage. Both individuals were arrested. The cases have been referred to the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for follow-up investigation. Cockroaches and crickets are commonly used to feed reptiles and other insect-eating pets.

title: Why Tencent is swapping Bilibili equity for debt, and what AI has to do with it
description: The deal allows Tencent to release capital from a legacy asset to support AI projects while retaining downside protection as a debt holder.
content: Tencent Holdings’ pivot from a core shareholder to a major creditor in Bilibili offers a clear window into how China’s Big Tech players are rebalancing portfolio risk while funding expensive artificial intelligence initiatives. The shift, executed through Bilibili’s proposed US$700 million convertible bond package announced on Friday, allows Tencent to lock in capital flexibility without severing ties with one of China’s largest online video platforms, according to analysts. Here is a look at Tencent’s strategic move. What does the capital restructuring involve? Bilibili plans to issue US$700 million in convertible senior notes maturing in 2031, according to a filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange. Under the deal, Tencent’s subsidiary, Huang River, would subscribe to US$200 million of Bilibili’s convertible bonds. At the same time, Tencent would sell about 26.4 million Bilibili shares via a secondary placement at HK$115.38 per share, generating nearly US$400 million in gross proceeds. Bilibili would allocate proceeds from the bond issuance to buy back US$200 million in shares directly from Tencent, alongside an additional US$100 million public buy-back to cushion market dilution. By restructuring Tencent’s equity sell-down into a convertible bond transaction, the deal helps cushion Bilibili’s share price against sudden volatility. Shares of Bilibili fell as much as 2.7 per cent in early Monday trading in Hong Kong as investors digested Tencent’s stake reduction, before rebounding to close up nearly 2 per cent at HK$123.80. For Bilibili, the proposal removed a major market “overhang” on share disposal by Tencent, Jefferies analyst Thomas Chong wrote in a research note on Friday. It represented a “win-win transaction” for both parties, Chong said, adding that Tencent’s decision to hold Bilibili’s convertible bonds reflected its long-term confidence in the video site. How does this fit into Bilibili’s AI road map? Net proceeds retained by Bilibili would primarily go towards strengthening its AI model capabilities in content comprehension, recommendation and creator tools to drive user retention, the company said. The move reflects a broader trend among Chinese tech companies expanding capital expenditure to keep pace with accelerating AI deployment across consumer-facing platforms. Why swap equity exposure for convertible debt? The transaction allows Tencent to release capital from a legacy portfolio asset to support its own AI projects while retaining downside protection as a debt holder. While the tech giant’s sprawling global portfolio spans mobile gaming, e-commerce and consumer goods, its AI strategy has rapidly accelerated. The company has been quietly reallocating capital away from legacy internet assets, including trimming its long-held stake in short-video sharing platform Kuaishou Technology. Tencent chief strategy officer James Mitchell noted during an earnings call with analysts in May that the company was “accelerating the process” of liquidating portions of its broad investment portfolio to meet evolving capital priorities. Still, Tencent’s exit strategy from Bilibili remained “uncommon” compared to standard secondary share sales, according to Ivan Su, an analyst at Morningstar. “A firm in immediate need of cash would typically sell out entirely rather than retain the convertible bonds,” Su said on Monday. “Only a company like Tencent, backed by strong cash flows from its core businesses and ample access to lending facilities, can afford this kind of gradual, staggered sell-down.”

title: China hits critical Japanese chipmaking chemical with steep anti-dumping measures
description: The preliminary ruling targets a vital material that Chinese manufacturers have historically imported from Japan and comes amid continued bilateral friction.
content: China will impose provisional anti-dumping duties of up to 99.2 per cent on Japanese dichlorosilane, a critical chemical used in chipmaking, after an eight-month investigation found that dumped imports had harmed local manufacturers. The Ministry of Commerce announced the preliminary ruling on Monday, saying importers of dichlorosilane originating from Japan would be required to pay corresponding cash deposits from Tuesday. Shipments from Denal Silane, a manufacturer of semiconductor speciality gases, will be subject to a lower cash deposit rate of 80.8 per cent. Other Japanese companies, including Shin-Etsu Chemical – a major global supplier of semiconductor silicon wafers and electronic chemicals – will face the maximum rate. “China has consistently applied trade remedy measures in a prudent and restrained manner, remaining firmly committed to safeguarding fair and free trade,” the ministry said in a statement on Monday. “Moving forward, we will continue the investigation in compliance with the law, fully guarantee the rights of all interested parties, and make an objective and impartial final determination based on the investigation findings,” it added. Dichlorosilane is mainly used in thin-film deposition processes in semiconductor manufacturing and plays an important role in producing various types of chips. Beijing launched the anti-dumping investigation in January. Japan dominates production of the chemical. The world’s top three producers – Shin-Etsu, Nippon Sanso and Sumitomo Seika – are all Japanese, while the largest Chinese producer, Tangshan Sunfar Silicon, ranked fourth by market share back in 2023, according to an industry report published by QYResearch. China has traditionally relied heavily on imports for its domestic supply. Japanese products represented 72 per cent of China’s domestic market for the chemical between 2022 and 2024, according to Sunfar, the company that filed for the anti-dumping investigation. The announcement comes as bilateral relations between China and Japan continue to cool, after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi angered Beijing in November last year by suggesting that a hypothetical attack on Taiwan could constitute an “existential threat”, potentially warranting a military response under the limitations of Tokyo’s pacifist constitution.

title: Golden opportunity: can China lure European central bank gold reserves from US?
description: Geopolitical tensions and US dollar concerns have seen Shanghai and Hong Kong step up efforts to build gold storage infrastructure.
content: Amid persistent geopolitical strains and growing concerns over the weaponisation of the US dollar, European central banks have continued shifting gold reserves away from US vaults – with the latest move announced by the Netherlands – and analysts say China could take it as an opportunity to draw more bullion flows into custody hubs in Shanghai and Hong Kong. De Nederlandsche Bank, the Dutch central bank, said in a news release on Wednesday that it had transferred 86 tonnes of gold from vaults in the United States and Canada to London between March and August. Following the relocation, the share of Dutch gold held in New York fell 12.8 percentage points to 18.5 per cent. The bank linked the move to “increasing geopolitical unrest” and said it would “strengthen its crisis preparedness”. “A more balanced distribution of the gold stock between North America, the United Kingdom, and the Netherlands helps to spread risks,” it said. European central banks appear united in re-evaluating their offshore gold holdings. In results disclosed in April, the French central bank said it had sold 129 tonnes of bullion held in New York before repurchasing equivalent high-standard gold bars in Europe. Serbia and Germany have pursued similar courses of action in recent years. “There has been a fundamental shift in how countries view the security of their sovereign assets, and this shift will not reverse in the short term regardless of whether geopolitical tensions ease or escalate,” said Liang Yonghui, deputy secretary general of the China Non-Ferrous Metals Industry Association’s gold and silver branch. She said the earliest catalyst for the shift could be traced back to 2022, when the Ukraine war broke out. “That year, some of Russia’s gold reserves held in overseas markets were frozen, which overturned many countries’ long-held perceptions over the safety of overseas reserve assets,” Liang said. The World Gold Council’s Central Bank Gold Reserves Survey 2026, which was published in June, revealed an increase in central banks’ vault-location adjustments. Of the 76 central-bank respondents, 10 per cent said they had diversified their overseas storage locations in the preceding 12 months – which the council described as “a notable uptick” from the 2 per cent in the 2025 survey. Seven per cent of respondents said they planned to boost domestic gold storage in the coming 12 months, while 9 per cent intended to diversify overseas storage locations – up from 2 per cent in last year’s survey. “Drawing on the examples and influence of European central banks, more countries are expected to re-evaluate their overseas reserve assets,” Liang said. Against that backdrop, China has accelerated its push to build more gold custody infrastructure, with Shanghai and Hong Kong at the forefront. Shanghai laid the groundwork in 2021, when the municipal government issued policies supporting Pudong’s high-level reform and opening-up. One provision explicitly called for developing “a large national-scale precious-metals depository”, a task assigned to the Shanghai Gold Exchange. Few official updates on the project have emerged since. An executive at the exchange, who requested anonymity, said the work remained under way, with the aim of attracting gold reserves from overseas central banks. Meanwhile, Hong Kong is positioning itself as a regional gold trading hub, with plans to expand its vault storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years. As part of that push, the city recently launched a trial gold clearing and settlement system involving 11 Chinese and international banks. “The financial framework ensures China’s gold reserves – whether stored onshore or offshore – operate independently of foreign institutional systems,” Yan Zeyang, a researcher at the Beijing-based China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, wrote in an article published in January. “Meanwhile, it can provide secure vaulting alternatives for other central banks. “Amid heightened dollar-sanction risks, China is poised to draw gold reserve inflows into Shanghai and Hong Kong, which will further strengthen China’s influence within the global gold market.” At the end of August, following 22 straight months of central‑bank purchases, China held over 2,300 tonnes of gold reserves. Authorities do not disclose how much of that is stored overseas.

title: Hong Kong landlords accuse banks of deepening shop slump with reluctance to lend
description: Pressing owners to repay loans amid falling values while turning away new buyers could prolong wider economic drag, advocacy group says.
content: Hong Kong landlords and property industry figures are accusing banks of deepening the city’s shop slump by pulling back from commercial mortgages, leaving more potential buyers unable to secure financing even though property values have fallen sharply. Shop buyers were increasingly being turned away, even though Hong Kong’s residential market had gained momentum this year and banks were competing for mortgage borrowers, they said. Shih Wing-ching, founder of Centaline Property, said banks tended to be positive with prospective buyers initially, but financing often became difficult once deals reached the approval stage. “It takes a long time,” Shih said at a press conference organised by advocacy group Momentum 107 on Monday. “A considerable number of clients end up unable to get financing at the last minute … If it weren’t for this, there would be many more shop transactions.” Raymond Ho, convenor of Momentum 107, said the sharp decline in shop values over the last few years had rapidly eroded the pool of available capital, weighing on investment and consumption. Banks were pressing owners to repay loans amid falling property values while also refusing to provide mortgages to new buyers, which discouraged both users and investors from entering the market, further reducing transactions. Banks’ tougher stance comes as lenders face growing pressure to address troubled commercial-property loans as falling valuations make it harder to justify extending debt. “The situation now is that when banks hear it is a shop, they do not do the mortgage,” Ho said, creating a vicious cycle in which lenders’ actions were reinforcing the market downturn. Raymond Tsoi Chi-chung, founder of Asia Property Agency, said shop mortgage lending was at about 20 per cent of its peak right now. Many people he knew in banks’ loan-approval departments had failed to complete even a single shop loan recently, he added. Tsoi attributed some of the banks’ caution to losses in their mainland China businesses, but said Hong Kong commercial-property loans were generally backed by collateral. “It’s not right to lose money in mainland China and then blame Hong Kong,” he said. Many shop investors are business owners who used leverage to build their property holdings during the boom, but some are now facing severe financial pressure, including forced sales of luxury homes. The financing squeeze comes after years of weakness in the retail-property market. Average monthly transactions have plunged to about 60 from around 600 at the market’s peak, according to Midland Realty. Shop prices have fallen more than 40 per cent from their 2018 peak, and the vacancy rate reached 12.5 per cent at the end of 2025, a 40-year high, according to Momentum 107. The impact extends beyond property owners. Tony Kwok Tak-leung, chairman of the Guangdong Hong Kong Macau Greater Bay Area General Chamber of Real Estate, said neighbourhood areas such as Kowloon West had unusually high numbers of vacant shops. “Some people don’t need to borrow, but when they see banks taking such a negative view, they decide not to buy,” Kwok said. “Having collateral and still not getting a loan is absurd.” John Wong, president of the Federation of Hong Kong Brands, said businesses wanted lower rents, but shop values and rents had become increasingly disconnected. Landlords were already offering concessions including rent-free periods and renovation subsidies of as much as HK$1 million, he added. Industry representatives called for higher commercial mortgage loan-to-value ratios, faster approvals and more objective valuations, while urging banks to handle loan calls case by case. “If commercial and retail properties do not recover, Hong Kong’s economy will not recover,” Tsoi said.

title: Cathay Pacific, Google scale up AI tests to reduce aviation’s climate impact
description: Second-phase trials with Contrails.org will target ultra-long-haul Asia and transpacific routes, building on early tests that reduced contrail warming impact by about 40 per cent.
content: Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways and Google are expanding AI-powered flight trials designed to steer aircraft away from contrail-forming zones in the Asia-Pacific region, using the data to inform broader sustainability decisions. Condensation trails, or contrails, formed when aircraft flew through cold, humid patches of air, trapping atmospheric heat and accounting for roughly one-third of aviation’s climate impact, Kemal Armada, product manager for climate and AI at Google, said on Monday. He said the second phase of trials would include non-governmental organisation Contrails.org as a partner. A randomised controlled trial on ultra-long-haul flights across Asia and transpacific routes would be conducted. “With this, we are going to expand our partnership into its new phase, where we are going to do a much larger trial that is going to include ultra-long-haul flights,” Armada said. Cathay became the first commercial airline in the Asia-Pacific region to test the technology in live operations and the first globally to test contrail avoidance on ultra-long-haul routes, said Michael Yue, managing director and general manager at Google Hong Kong. “It gives us a great opportunity to use predictive AI and to find cost-effective, scalable ways to mitigate the impact of contrails on the overall climate impact,” Yue said. Cathay said AI deployment would complement other initiatives such as fleet modernisation, operational efficiency improvements and the use of sustainable aviation fuel to cut emissions. Tony Pringle, line operations manager and an Airbus captain at Cathay Pacific, said operational flight plans to avoid contrail-forming conditions were delivered directly to pilots through an iPad application, with data updated every hour during flight. “It’s completely scalable within our operation at this point,” Pringle said. Grace Cheung, general manager of sustainability at Cathay Pacific, said coordination among international policymakers was important in shared airspace because contrails would still form if aircraft from other airlines flew through the same atmospheric zones. “So, really, international coordination of the policymaker with the rise of technology, data availability to really move forward together is very important,” Cheung said. AI models would be used to address broader climate problems beyond contrail mitigation, said Lawrence Fong, director of digital and information technology at Cathay Pacific. “So this is just a start, just a beginning,” Fong said. Pascal Siu, senior research manager and head of green and sustainability research at think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said that while avoiding contrails did not reduce carbon emissions, it prevented the formation of heat-trapping clouds and cost far less than sustainable aviation fuel in terms of climate benefit per dollar. “[Sustainable aviation fuel] cuts the actual carbon coming out of the engine – that’s the long-term fix and there’s no way around it,” Siu said. However, sustainable aviation fuel currently accounted for only about 0.3 per cent of global jet fuel, Siu noted. “So the answer is that contrail avoidance is a cheap, immediate add-on you can do with today’s aircraft, not a substitute for [sustainable aviation fuel],” Siu said. The potential of contrail avoidance was substantial because condensation trails represented the single largest non-carbon dioxide warming effect caused by flying, Siu added. “Because only a small share of flights hit the right cold, humid conditions, adjusting the altitude of a small number of flights could remove a significant amount of that warming, at an extra fuel cost of only about 0.2 per cent to 0.3 per cent across the whole fleet,” Siu said.

title: PAS chief to face Malaysian police over claims US would help ‘topple’ government
description: The US has rejected Abdul Hadi Awang’s claim that it offered help to change Malaysia’s political leadership during Obama’s visit in 2014.
content: Malaysian police have contacted Islamist opposition leader Abdul Hadi Awang over his explosive claim that the United States once offered to help his party topple the government – an allegation Washington has flatly dismissed as false. The controversy erupted after Hadi told thousands of delegates at the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) congress in Kelantan on Saturday that American representatives had approached party leaders when Barack Obama visited Malaysia in 2014. Hadi’s political secretary Syahir Che Sulaiman told This Week in Asia on Monday that federal police headquarters Bukit Aman had contacted the PAS president following several police reports over remarks he made at the party’s annual congress. “Hadi has been informed and is ready to give the police his full cooperation,” Syahir said, adding that a date and time would be fixed “in the near future”. Bukit Aman criminal investigation department chief M Kumar said in a statement late Monday that police were investigating the case under Section 505(b) of the Penal Code, which covers statements that may cause public alarm, and Section 233 of the Communications and Multimedia Act for improper use of network facilities or services. Police had received 12 reports on the issue and recorded statements from 12 witnesses, Kumar said. Hadi’s statement would be taken “in the near future” to complete the investigation. If convicted under Section 505(b), Hadi could face up to two years in prison, a fine or both. Section 233 carries a maximum fine of 500,000 ringgit (US$120,000), up to two years in prison, or both. During his winding-up speech at the 72nd PAS annual congress on Saturday, Hadi said several party leaders had been invited to the US embassy during Obama’s visit to Malaysia. “We were invited to meet at the US embassy,” Hadi said. “They wanted to discuss it, they were prepared to help topple the government and take over the government. America was prepared to help.” Malaysia was then governed by Barisan Nasional under Najib Razak, while PAS belonged to the now-defunct opposition Pakatan Rakyat alliance alongside Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s People’s Justice Party (PKR) and the Democratic Action Party (DAP). Hadi said senior PAS figures Takiyuddin Hassan, Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar and Mustafa Ali had attended the meeting. He claimed a US ambassador later asked to meet him directly and wanted to know whom PAS would support as prime minister. “He asked, ‘Who does PAS propose as prime minister?’” Hadi said. “I said, ‘Who does America agree with?’” Hadi said he later told former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad about the exchange, and Mahathir told him it had been a “good response”. But the US embassy rejected Hadi’s account. “The United States has never sought to decide Malaysia’s political leadership,” chargé d’affaires David H. Gamble Jnr said on Sunday. “Any account to the contrary is false.” Obama’s April 2014 trip was the first visit to Malaysia by a sitting US president in nearly half a century. He met Najib and upgraded bilateral ties to a comprehensive partnership, while also publicly raising human rights and political freedoms. Obama did not meet Anwar during the visit. Three PKR officials lodged police reports at Cheras police station on Sunday, according to state news agency Bernama. One of them, PKR Bandar Tun Razak branch vice-chief V. Jonathan, said the reports were intended to ensure that any alleged attempt to overthrow or weaken Malaysia’s government and parliamentary democracy through unconstitutional means would be investigated. Cheras district police chief Mohd Rosdi Daud confirmed receiving the reports at about 5pm on Sunday and said they would be referred to Wangsa Maju district police headquarters. Why ‘overreact’? PAS has since turned the row back on Anwar’s governing coalition, accusing Pakatan Harapan figures of “overreacting” even though Hadi had not accused them of involvement. “What interest do they have in this issue? Why suddenly overreact and make police reports?” PAS information chief Ahmad Fadhli Shaari wrote in a statement shared on social media on Monday. “Did the PAS president link anyone from Pakatan Harapan to this issue? Not at all. So why are they overreacting? Or are they actually connected?” The argument carries an added political charge because Anwar has long had publicly documented links with American democracy organisations, including the congressionally funded National Endowment for Democracy. NED’s former president Carl Gershman said in 2019 that he had first met Anwar in Washington in 2005 after his release from prison. Anwar later delivered NED’s annual Seymour Martin Lipset Lecture on Democracy, speaking on “Confronting Authoritarianism”. PAS and Anwar were themselves allies when the alleged approach took place. Pakatan Rakyat won about 52 per cent of the popular vote in Malaysia’s 2013 general election but failed to take power. The alliance collapsed two years later after increasingly bitter clashes between PAS and DAP over the Islamist party’s push to enforce hudud criminal law in Kelantan.

title: Huawei unveils new trifold smartphone powered by Tau Scaling Law-based Kirin chip
description: Coming just ahead of new models from Apple and Xiaomi, the device highlights a fierce battle in the high-end foldable market.
content: Huawei Technologies has unveiled its first smartphone powered by a next-generation mobile processor based on the company’s proprietary Tau Scaling Law, continuing its push to boost chip performance while reducing reliance on advanced foreign semiconductor equipment. Speaking at a launch event in Guangzhou on Monday, Richard Yu Chengdong, chairman of Huawei’s consumer business group, described the Kirin 9050 Pro as the company’s “most powerful Kirin chip ever”. The processor is based on Huawei’s newly established Tau Scaling Law, which seeks to improve semiconductor performance by reducing signal delays. One technology developed under the new approach, LogicFolding, is designed to shorten signal paths and ultimately pack more transistors into a smaller space. The chip is used in the Mate XT 2, a new trifold smartphone unveiled on Monday starting at 19,999 yuan (US$2,980). Huawei’s Yu stated that the chip improved overall performance by 42 per cent compared with the previous-generation Mate XTs model released last year. The launch comes as competition in the foldable phone sector heats up. Chinese rival Xiaomi is set to announce a new foldable model later on Monday, while Apple’s first-ever foldable is expected to be revealed on Wednesday. Global shipments of foldable phones grew 18 per cent last year, according to Counterpoint Research on Monday, which projected growth to accelerate to 24 per cent this year and 37 per cent in 2027. The Mate XT 2 is also the first device to run on the updated HarmonyOS 7, the latest version of Huawei’s self-developed operating system. Initially released to developers in June as a beta version featuring AI coding agents, the software began rolling out to existing Huawei phones on Monday. The wave of new hardware and software releases underscores Huawei’s continued drive for innovation despite strict export controls that have severely limited the company’s access to advanced American chips and semiconductor equipment, and cut it off from Google’s proprietary Android services. The Kirin chip, mentioned in a research paper in July under the code name “Kirin 2026”, is based on Huawei’s Tau Scaling Law. The company has said the approach could help it achieve transistor densities equivalent to those of a cutting-edge 1.4-nanometre process by 2031 – without requiring advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which are subject to United States-led export restrictions on sales to China. In a paper published last week, Huawei reported that the chip ran cooler than its predecessor, packed 55 per cent more transistors per square millimetre, and cut power use by up to 66 per cent on some critical tasks. The paper, out on ChinaXiv, has not yet been peer-reviewed. When presenting the Tau Scaling Law in May, He Tingbo, chairwoman of Huawei's Scientist Committee and president of the company’s semiconductor business department, said the firm had used it to design and mass-produce 381 chips over the past six years. The heavy investment in chip development, coupled with rising component costs, has weighed on the company’s profitability. Research and development spending jumped 25 per cent year on year to 121.4 billion yuan (US$18 billion) in the first half of the year, while net profit fell 36 per cent to 23.8 billion yuan. However, revenue still grew 9.6 per cent during the period to 467.8 billion yuan, helped by a strong rebound in smartphone shipments and accelerating demand for Huawei’s AI processors. Huawei also led the Chinese smartphone market with a 22.6 per cent share in the second quarter, driven by a 19.4 per cent jump in shipments, according to data from research firm IDC. Beyond smartphones, Huawei continues to benefit from wider adoption of its Ascend AI chips as a domestic alternative to China-restricted Nvidia products. A growing list of AI firms, including DeepSeek and Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, are looking to deploy Huawei chips and accelerators to run and even train their AI models. Huawei and other domestic chip suppliers were expected to capture nearly 80 per cent of China’s AI server market this year, further squeezing global rivals such as Nvidia, according to TrendForce data in June. Additional reporting by Howard Liu

title: Tesla offers rare China inventory discounts to fight sliding Shanghai production sales
description: The discounts underscore Tesla’s sliding output and fading demand, as analysts warn of intensifying EV price battles.
content: Tesla China has launched discounts on its Shanghai-made cars for the first time since the end of 2024, responding to falling deliveries in the world’s largest market for electric vehicles (EVs). Prices of Model 3 vehicles in inventory would be reduced by 5,000 yuan (US$745) each, while buyers of the Model Y could enjoy a discount of 10,000 yuan per unit, the US carmaker announced on Monday. The promotions would run until the end of September, Tesla China said in a statement. “Tesla has been refraining from cutting prices on its cars while resorting to subsidies for car insurance purchase or interest-free loans to drive up sales in China,” said Eric Han, senior ­manager at Shanghai consultancy Suolei. “The discounts it is offering this time are likely to trigger a fresh round of price competition amid weak consumer demand.” A 5,000 yuan price reduction translates into a 2.1 per cent discount to the 235,500 yuan retail price for a basic Model 3. An entry-level edition of Model Y, sold at 263,500 yuan, sees a price drop of 3.8 per cent after the 10,000 yuan discount. Tesla is also offering each buyer of its Shanghai-made vehicles an 8,000 yuan cash subsidy for insurance purchases. In the first seven months of 2026, Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory – its largest production hub worldwide – delivered 266,204 vehicles to Chinese buyers, down 12.4 per cent from a year earlier, according to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). In August, Tesla’s deliveries fell 7.9 per cent month-on-month to 86,166 units, including both domestic sales and exports, CPCA data showed. Overall retail sales of EVs on the mainland slumped 3.9 per cent in July, extending their decline to a seventh consecutive month as fading government incentives and weaker consumer demand weighed on the market. Between January and July, Chinese carmakers delivered a total of 5.67 million EVs to domestic customers, down 12.5 per cent from a year earlier, according to the CPCA. At the end of June, global consultancy AlixPartners said China’s slowing car sales would fuel a brutal price war in the second half of 2026, as the mainland’s overall automotive industry remained profitable. Among the nearly 30 Chinese ­carmakers that solely produce EVs, only BYD, Stellantis-backed Leapmotor and Shanghai-based premium EV builder Nio were ­profitable in the first half, according to the CPCA.

title: Meet Jonathan Steinberg, ex-Fox News anchor Maria Bartiromo’s multimillionaire husband
description: The veteran TV presenter and close ally of Donald Trump has disputed her sudden dismissal, as attention turns to her Wall Street financier husband.
content: Long-time Fox News anchor Maria Bartiromo has been abruptly sacked by the network, with the channel saying her firing was “effective immediately” in a September 3 statement. “We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 and a half years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” the statement read. In response, Bartiromo’s lawyer Bryan Freedman issued a statement on September 4 denying that she had been fired: “The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false.” “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses, and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise,” he added. Bartiromo’s ousting came as a shock to many, including US President Donald Trump, who took to Truth Social to write: “I can’t believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business.” Bartiromo has long been a vocal supporter of Trump and is considered one of his closest allies in the network. While Fox News did not explain the reasoning behind Bartiromo’s departure, CNN pointed to her close ties with Trump and her alleged “disclosure of confidential information to the Trump White House”. The Maga leader was even said to have considered Bartiromo for vice-president, according to Politico reporter Alex Isenstadt’s book Revenge: The Inside Story of Trump’s Return to Power, published in 2025. Isenstadt claims Trump was “dead serious” about the then-Fox Business anchor as his running mate at least until the assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. “She was great with the big-donor Wall Street types and she knew how to do TV, Trump told his team,” Isenstadt wrote. Ultimately, Trump’s campaign team, led by chief of staff Susie Wiles, decided they had “no time to vet Bartiromo” and picked J.D. Vance instead, according to the book. Bartiromo, nicknamed “the Money Honey” from her days on the New York Stock Exchange floor as a CNBC reporter, is evidently quite the celebrity in the financial sphere, per Forbes. Over the years, she’s enjoyed dinners with Trump at Mar-a-Lago and defended his positions and policies on air. But besides her association with Trump, another man in her life who has drawn significant interest is her husband, Jonathan Steinberg. Here is what we know about him. What is Jonathan Steinberg’s background? Jonathan Steinberg is the son of late magnate Saul Steinberg and his high school sweetheart, Barbara Herzog. Per New York Magazine, Steinberg Sr was a Wharton School graduate who launched the company Leasco Data Processing Equipment in his twenties and took over Reliance Insurance in 1968. He also attempted to bring Disney and Chemical Bank into his fold but failed. While Jonathan attended Wharton like his father, he had difficulty with reading and did not graduate, per The New York Times. What is Jonathan Steinberg’s net worth? Jonathan Steinberg is the founder and CEO of WisdomTree, a global financial company offering exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and other investment products. The company was founded in 1988, before which Steinberg worked for the now-defunct investment firm Bear Stearns. In 2015, he won EY’s Entrepreneur of the Year New York award. As of Monday, Steinberg’s net worth is estimated at US$230 million, per GuruFocus. How did Maria Bartiromo and Jonathan Steinberg meet? Steinberg and Bartiromo met in 1990, when she had just completed journalism and economics studies at New York University, per The New York Times. The pair tied the knot in 1999 in Quogue, New York. They have no children. According to Success, the couple lives in a five-floor Manhattan town house, and per the Los Angeles Times, they also own a beach house in Westhampton, New York. Additional reporting by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: China ‘Snakeaholic’ dedicates life to studying, protecting snakes despite losing finger
description: After an IUCN listing, black-market prices for the viper soared past US$150,000 each, but Chen refused all offers to sell them.
content: Despite being bitten nine times and losing a finger to its venom, 77-year-old “Snake Doctor” Chen Yuanhui remains on the front lines of researching and protecting the Mangshan pit viper, the rare species he discovered 37 years ago. Originally from southern China’s Guangdong province, Chen graduated from a clinical college in central China’s Hunan province at the age of 19 and worked at a snakebite research centre. The centre was discontinued in 1982, but Chen chose not to pursue a conventional career in the city. Instead, he settled as a snakebite doctor deep in the Mangshan mountain. In 1984, Chen treated a forestry worker bitten by a strange venomous snake. Nicknamed by locals as the “little green dragon,” the snake was described as “yellow and green all over, with a white tail and patterns that look like squares when viewed from above and triangles from the side.” Sensing that it might be a species that had never been officially recognised by the scientific community, Chen began searching for it. After five years of searching, Chen heard that a worker had captured a nest of 23 snakes that matched the description of the “little green dragon.” Hiding it from his wife, he used the money his family had saved for three years to buy a refrigerator to purchase the snakes. After consulting with snake experts in China and the US, in 1990, Chen officially announced the discovery of China’s 50th venomous snake and named it the “Mangshan pit viper (Protobothrops mangshanensis).” When discovered, only about 200 Mangshan pit vipers existed. For the next three decades, Chen dedicated his life to studying and protecting the species. He and his family never left their 51-square-metre bungalow. He also artificially bred the species at home. In 1994, he successfully bred the Mangshan pit viper in captivity for the first time. In 2017, he successfully incubated 10 snakes under simulated natural conditions. Up until 2022, Chen had bred 160 Mangshan pit vipers, all of which were released into the mountain’s nature reserve. To this day, Chen said there are still fewer than 600 Mangshan pit vipers. The species has been listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species since 2011. The rare species endemic to China is also nicknamed “the giant panda of snakes.” After its listing on the IUCN, the price of the Mangshan pit viper in the black market reportedly soared to over one million yuan (US$150,000) each. Chen declined many tempting offers and even moved the snakes he bred into his own home after a snake dealer stole one from his pit. His wife also quarrelled with him many times and even threatened to divorce him, but gave up the idea after witnessing his unwavering passion for snakes. Chen was bitten nine times by the Mangshan pit viper. He wrote his last words just in case after being bitten eight times, and he lost a part of his left middle finger after being bitten the ninth time. On the ninth occasion, he chose to photograph the bite marks for scientific records instead of applying first aid during the first critical minutes. He was unconscious for three days and nights, and fortunately ended up with just a loss of a finger. Despite this, Chen said he never regretted the path he chose. His passion for snakes earned him the nicknames “Snake Doctor,” “Snake Immortal,” and “Snakeaholic.” Chen’s remarkable work was brought to the spotlight after the National Zoological Museum of China denounced a man for encouraging his two children to play with a specimen of the Mangshan pit viper, causing it to be damaged. Chen, who donated the specimen, said he was heartbroken and confused why adults would let children play with such precious specimens as toys. He believed the parent was fully responsible for the damage. “Children don’t understand, but adults should,” he remarked.

title: Rare Beijing spy series highlights real-life intelligence drama with Taiwan
description: TV series backed by Ministry of State Security and depicting espionage across Taiwan Strait proves ratings hit at its launch.
content: A television drama produced by Beijing’s top counter-espionage agency has put the spotlight on real-life cases in the high-stakes intelligence battle between mainland China and Taiwan. Over the past decade, mainland Chinese spy dramas have rarely touched on contemporary espionage across the Taiwan Strait but on Sunday state broadcaster CCTV began airing a 40-episode television series about such intelligence efforts from 1998 to 2018. Overseen by the Ministry of State Security, The Long Watch delves into two decades of attempts by both sides of the Taiwan Strait to turn each other’s operatives, plant agents and carry out assassination and protection missions. “Subject to confidentiality requirements, the production team made repeated visits to the front line of national security agencies to conduct immersive field research,” state news agency Xinhua reported last Tuesday. Screenwriter Wang Xiaoqiang told mainland media that the drama was adapted from archival material relating to more than 20 real-life declassified national security cases. On Sunday, The Long Watch topped television ratings in its time slot. Its storyline makes a reference to controversial remarks in 1994 by then Taiwanese leader Lee Teng-hui during an interview with Japanese journalists. Lee at the time voiced sorrow over “being born a Taiwanese and not being able to do anything for Taiwan”. His comment was widely seen as expressing that a distinct Taiwanese identity existed separately from China, triggering intense anger in Beijing. In the storyline, tensions heighten across the Taiwan Strait following the remarks, prompting both sides to begin seeking spies and intensifying efforts to infiltrate each other. The first two episodes, broadcast on Sunday, depicted the exposure of a covert source in Taiwan’s intelligence agencies working for the mainland. A mainland protagonist is tasked with protecting the agent, but the mission ultimately fails. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Mainland China’s patriotic films and television dramas have long celebrated Communist Party secret agents, but relatively little has been disclosed about espionage operations across the Taiwan Strait. Now, Beijing appears to have shifted on this point. The television drama Silent Honour, released in September last year, broke ground by becoming the first dramatic production to document and commemorate Communist Party espionage operations in Taiwan. The operations began in the final months of the Chinese civil war in 1949, when the defeated Kuomintang retreated to Taiwan. The emergence of the two television dramas comes amid escalating tensions across the strait, with espionage being a point of mutual accusation. Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te, from the independence-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), has called Beijing a “hostile foreign force” and proposed 17 security measures to counter Beijing’s alleged infiltration efforts. Last year, at least four people close to senior DPP officials were under investigation or detained for reportedly leaking classified information to mainland Chinese intelligence. They included aides to Lai and Joseph Wu, secretary general of Taiwan’s National Security Council. Between 2020 and April 2026, 202 people were indicted for allegedly engaging in espionage for mainland China, according to Taiwan’s National Security Bureau. Beijing has denied the allegations.

title: UK minister slams ‘thuggish’ anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth
description: The gathering was the second anti-migrant demonstration in two days, after masked men disrupted traffic in the port of Dover ‌on Saturday.
content: British minister ⁠Emma Reynolds has condemned hundreds of ⁠protesters who blocked streets in the ⁠English coastal city of Portsmouth late on Sunday to try to stop the arrival of migrants from France, calling them “thuggish”. The gathering was the second anti-migrant demonstration in two days, after masked men disrupted traffic in the port of Dover ‌on Saturday, chanting “Stop the boats”, a reference to the vessels carrying asylum seekers across the English Channel. Both groups appeared to be led by Daniel Thomas, an ally of veteran far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, better known as Tommy Robinson. “Perhaps the scale of the protest was something that we hadn’t seen before, but the police have brought this under control,” Reynolds, who is chief secretary to the Treasury, told Sky News on Monday when asked about the protests in ⁠Portsmouth. Successive British governments have faced accusations from opposition parties and anti-migration activists of failing to curb ‌the numbers of asylum seekers coming to Britain, often in overcrowded, inflatable boats. Reynolds said the numbers had fallen sharply to about 17,000 from January ‌1 to September 1, down 43 per cent on the same period last year. The protesters, ⁠who were responding to calls from some far-right groups believed to be using messaging systems including Signal and Telegram, ‌were reacting to the arrival of 140 migrants who had crossed to England. “This is thuggish and intimidating behaviour,” Reynolds said. When asked ‌about how ‌the protests seemed to be organised very quickly, she said that was “a concern”. Donna Jones, ‌police and crime commissioner for the area, said while the protesters were mostly peaceful, the ⁠large size of the gathering meant the local force had to draft in officers from other regions ⁠to help. The arrival of small boats in Portsmouth represents a change from the usual route taken by the dinghies which tend to come ashore further east near ‌Dover, where there is ‌a large facility to receive migrants. “Portsmouth and other parts of southern England are not set up to be able to take and deal with, not just the public order, but also the processing of these people coming into Britain illegally,” Jones told BBC Radio. Britain’s Maritime and Coastguard Agency said lifeboats, a coastguard helicopter and a plane were involved in the operation to bring the migrants to shore. Additional reporting by Associated Press

title: Will China’s US$54b capital injection be enough to ease financial strains?
description: Capital boost strengthens buffers of financial institutions, but stronger fiscal support is needed to reignite credit demand, observers say.
content: Beijing’s planned 360 billion yuan (US$54 billion) capital injection into eight state-owned financial institutions is a step in the right direction, but further fiscal support is needed to revive credit demand and ensure the fresh capital is put to better use, analysts say. They noted that the move extended a recapitalisation drive since 2025 that had largely focused on banks, now widening to insurers and other financial institutions, reflecting a broader effort to strengthen capital buffers across the financial system. Raymond Yeung, chief Greater China economist at ANZ Bank, said the low-interest-rate environment was “weighing on both insurers and banks” by reducing insurers’ investment returns and narrowing banks’ net interest margins. “The capital injection is aimed at safeguarding financial stability, particularly amid persistent concerns over banks’ non-performing loans,” he added. Analysts led by Xiong Yuan, chief economist at Guosheng Securities, said in a note on Monday that the move was mainly aimed at strengthening financial institutions’ capital as low interest rates had slowed their ability to build capital, making it harder for them to maintain sufficient capital buffers. Their comments came after eight major state-owned banks and insurers – including Agricultural Bank of China (ABC), Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and China Life Insurance Company – announced plans on Sunday to raise a combined 360 billion yuan in capital, with 300 billion yuan from the Ministry of Finance and an additional 60 billion yuan from the tobacco sector. The move followed a 500 billion yuan special treasury bond injection in 2025 that recapitalised four major state-owned banks: Bank of China, China Construction Bank, Bank of Communications and Postal Savings Bank of China. The analysts at Guosheng said injections into banks were largely expected, but the inclusion of insurers surprised the market, which had anticipated their replenishment at a later stage. Faster fiscal spending would be needed to generate demand for credit, with monetary and credit policy playing a supporting role Ding Shuang, Standard Chartered They said insurers were facing greater pressure to match assets with liabilities amid lower returns, while expansion and increased investment in equities and other risk assets would continue to raise their capital needs. “Capital injections are therefore needed to strengthen their capital base, improve solvency and create more room for long-term investment,” they said. However, analysts said that the capital injection alone would not be enough to ease the pressures facing financial institutions. Ding Shuang, chief economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered, said that while the injection would give banks more room to lend amid falling net interest margins, the recapitalisation itself would not be enough to boost lending. “Weak credit demand, rather than banks’ lending capacity, remains the bigger constraint,” Ding said. “Faster fiscal spending would be needed to generate demand for credit, with monetary and credit policy playing a supporting role.” China’s new yuan loans fell 340 billion yuan in July, data from the People’s Bank of China showed. The decline was the largest on record, according to financial data provider Wind. The capital injection did not translate into an immediate boost in market reaction for ABC and ICBC on the Shanghai Stock Exchange, with the banks falling by 2.16 per cent and 1.97 per cent respectively on Monday. Both banks are dual-listed in Shanghai and Hong Kong. “It is one step in the right direction,” said Chen Zhiwu, chair professor of finance at the University of Hong Kong. “But this is not enough, and more will be needed given the many accumulated bad loans and bad investments that have been made by these banks and insurance companies.” Additional reporting by Julie Zhang

title: Hong Kong plans to grow STEAM education, boost global talent development
description: Initiatives aim to attract international students and adapt curriculum for an AI-driven future.
content:
The government of Hong Kong is set to enhance education in science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) and plans to provide additional land for higher education institutions. This initiative aims to shift the conventional study-abroad trend from a “one-way street to a two-way global highway”, as stated by the education secretary.
Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin delivered the remarks at the inaugural Global Education Summit, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier.
“We have set a clear goal. By the 2026-27 academic year, 35 per cent of all undergraduate students at our government-funded universities will be enrolled in STEAM disciplines,” Choi said.
The event brought together more than 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents from around the world to discuss regional talent development, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and evolving academic pathways.
Attendees at the two-day summit included principals and admissions officers from more than 40 leading secondary schools and universities, including the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford in the UK.
Elaborating on the targets, Choi noted that the drive to expand relevant degree programmes was matched by a broader effort to build the infrastructure needed to connect education, research and industry.
“To support this, in the 2025-28 triennium, our universities are launching 27 undergraduate programmes related to STEAM, including AI, cybersecurity, creative industries, sustainable development and data science,” Choi told the summit at the Grand Hyatt Hong Kong hotel in Wan Chai.
“These are not theoretical courses,” she said, detailing plans for the flagship Northern Metropolis University Town (NMUT).
“We drastically increased the reserved land for the campus area of the NMUT from the initial 60 hectares to approximately 300 hectares. When integrated with surrounding technology paths, industry zones, and vibrant communities, the broad and macro area of the NMUT spans more than 1,000 hectares.”
She said the project would follow a “one town, five elements” model integrating education, technology, talent, industry and urban development.
Choi noted that Hong Kong had welcomed 30,400 non-local students from more than 100 countries and regions in the 2025-26 academic year, a 30 per cent increase over two years.
SCMP publisher Tammy Tam said Hong Kong’s role as a regional hub gave it distinctive strengths in attracting international talent and strengthening its long-term competitiveness.
“Hong Kong is uniquely positioned with our open society, international outlook, and deep global connections, most of all with the special governing formula of ‘one country, two systems’, to serve as that elite gateway to the world,” she said.
“Hong Kong’s future relies on talent. Nurturing, re-skilling, and attracting bright minds is fundamental to our city’s continued vitality.”
A panel, curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm, featured leaders from Hong Kong’s leading universities and explored how local institutions could help shape the future of education.
The discussion brought together Professor Jay Siegel, vice-president and pro-vice-chancellor for teaching and learning at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), Professor Irwin King, pro-vice-chancellor for education at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) provost Professor Yike Guo.
The panellists discussed how higher education must adapt to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce.
“In the next phase of this AI era, universities must integrate more skills and the right attitude into their curriculum,” said King, advising parents not to focus solely on traditional academic performance.
He added that CUHK had recorded a 75 per cent increase in non-local student intake last year, attracting applicants from more than 100 countries.
“We’re looking for great students who are passionate about what they do. And sometimes the passion is not inside your GPA, but in the extracurricular things that you do and the things that you’re involved with,” he said.
Siegel, speaking about early childhood development, warned against exposing young children to AI tools too soon. He said excessive reliance on technology at an early age could impede cognitive development and affect long-term mental health.
“If we think that AI is going to turn three- to eight-year-olds into geniuses, then we’ve lost the lesson of child development,” he said.

title: How fashion houses are building branded residences as demand for ‘ultimate luxury’ booms
description: From Thailand to Turkey, labels like Etro and Karl Lagerfeld are wooing wealthy buyers looking to do more than just wear their brands.
content: The world of high-end luxury is witnessing a global boom in branded residences, with heritage fashion houses partnering with property developers to build immersive homes in prime locations. Fabrizio Cardinali, CEO of Italian luxury fashion and lifestyle brand Etro, has identified the “home” category as a primary engine for growth – and a return to the company’s roots. Its portfolio includes Etro Residences Istanbul and Etro Residences Phuket, which are scheduled for completion in late 2026 and 2027, respectively. “Etro’s innate lifestyle DNA [was] deeply rooted in the brand from the beginning, when interior textiles were among its earliest expressions,” says Cardinali, who joined Etro at the end of 2021 following more than a decade at Dolce & Gabbana. “This authenticity allowed [Etro] to enter the real estate sector both legitimately and swiftly, as it was a coherent extension of their history rather than a forced marketing play.” Immersive environments are now essential to the luxury experience, he adds. Fashion house Karl Lagerfeld has also expanded into key destination markets with branded villas in Marbella, in Spain, and Dubai, alongside an upcoming residence project in Lisbon and The Karl Lagerfeld Macau hotel. Caroline Lebar, Karl Lagerfeld’s senior vice-president of image and communications, says authentic properties require complete experiential consistency. “Design, service and atmosphere all work together to express the house’s values and Karl’s vision,” Lebar says. “Every detail is carefully considered, from the architecture and interiors to the materials, artwork, music, scent and the way guests experience the space. The objective is not simply to place a logo on a building, but to translate Karl’s creative universe into a living environment.” The Savills Branded Residences Annual Report for 2024-25 found that the branded residence sector had expanded by more than 180 per cent over the previous decade, led by fashion houses such as Armani, Versace and Karl Lagerfeld. According to the report, developers actively pursue these alliances because a luxury brand name can command a price premium of around 30 per cent compared with non-branded luxury developments. The movement extends beyond fashion brands into world-class hospitality concepts. Hong Kong’s award-winning Upper House hotel recently broke ground on a new residence development in central Bangkok slated for completion in 2030. “Globally, demand for luxury residences associated with highly regarded hospitality brands continues to grow,” says Casey Au, co-managing director of City Dynamic, a joint venture between Thai property developer City Realty and Hong Kong’s Swire Properties. “Buyers are looking beyond location, size and finishes. They increasingly consider how a residence will support their everyday life over the long term through design, wellness, service, sustainability and the quality of ongoing management.” For Etro Residences Phuket, which comprises just eight luxury apartments, the Italian brand has teamed up with the Gardens of Eden development near Bang Tao Beach. Shortly after the project’s sales launch in January 2026, two three-bedroom apartments sold for US$5.5 million each. High-net-worth individuals from Russia, China and Europe now account for nearly 60 per cent of luxury residence transactions in Phuket, prioritising lifestyle holiday homes complete with wellness retreats and bespoke concierge services, Cardinali says. The broader Gardens of Eden estate – developed by Amal Development and backed by a Dubai-based real estate investment group – features six pools, eight restaurants and various spas and kids’ clubs. The ultimate luxury is … the home away from home you never want to leave Fabrizio Cardinali, CEO of Etro A key challenge for fashion-branded residences in destination markets is balancing distinct house aesthetics with local surroundings. For the tropical setting of Phuket, Etro adjusted its signature maximalism. “We opted for lighter, more harmonious interpretations, maintaining our signature elements such as patterns, textures and crafted details, while translating them into a palette and mood that truly converse with the surroundings,” Cardinali says. He believes this ability to adapt from urban settings such as Istanbul to lush tropical landscapes gives Etro a competitive edge. He adds that his confidence in leading Etro into the branded residence market stems from believing that the brand can transcend fashion while remaining authentic to its narrative and aesthetic language. As the high-end market continues to evolve, the line between fashion brand and lifestyle concept is vanishing. “It is about refining the potential of a brand that was born in the world of textiles and is now transitioning into a way of life,” Cardinali says. “For the elite global traveller, the ultimate luxury is no longer about having access to exclusive locations – it is the home away from home you never want to leave.”

title: SCMP partners with top Kazakh university to deepen Hong Kong’s Central Asia ties
description: Memorandum of understanding with Nazarbayev University signed ahead of SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026 in Astana.
content: The South China Morning Post has signed an agreement with a leading university in Kazakhstan to foster the exchange of knowledge between East and Central Asia while extending Hong Kong’s media presence in the region. The memorandum of understanding (MOU) was signed on Monday in Astana, just ahead of the SCMP’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026, a flagship event making its debut in the region. According to the agreement, the strategic partnership formalises links between the SCMP and Nazarbayev University – Central Asia’s top-ranked higher education institution – by fostering academic dialogue and knowledge-sharing as well as “connecting the city’s capital and media reach with the region’s tech and resource ecosystem”. SCMP publisher Tammy Tam said the agreement represented a vital bridge between leading academic research and global media excellence. “As a premier voice on China and Asia, the South China Morning Post is proud to collaborate with Kazakhstan’s flagship university to elevate cross-border storytelling, foster deeper cultural and educational exchange, and illuminate Eurasia’s critical role in shaping the future of global connectivity and building a talent pool for the region,” she said. Professor Waqar Ahmad, president of Nazarbayev University, said the partnership would bring the institution’s academic expertise and research to a much wider international audience, adding its studies could also provide the newspaper with new perspectives on the region. “The partnership also creates new opportunities for our students to access knowledge and perspectives from a leading international media organisation, while bringing our academic communities closer together,” he said. “Building meaningful international partnerships of this kind is an important part of our journey towards becoming a world-class university.” The full-day conference, co-organised by the Astana International Financial Centre, brought together policymakers, institutional investors and corporate delegates from more than 100 companies across the wider region, including mainland China, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia. A high-level delegation led by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in June also visited Nazarbayev University, where Chinese President Xi Jinping first announced the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013. The Education University of Hong Kong and Polytechnic University signed separate partnership agreements with Nazarbayev University at the time to boost cross-border research and student exchanges, with the city leader saying the moves would help deepen academic collaboration and strengthen social bonds.

title: Chinese firms’ green-tech expansion hinges on Hong Kong, senior bankers say
description: Offshore yuan liquidity makes city a ‘superconnector’, but finding projects with strong returns is now the challenge, senior bankers say.
content: Hong Kong is poised to play a bigger role in financing Chinese green-technology companies’ expansion into emerging markets, as geopolitical fragmentation and high funding costs reshape how capital is deployed in the global energy transition, according to senior banking executives. The city’s deep sustainable-finance market and offshore yuan liquidity could help channel capital into green and climate-resilience projects across developing economies, executives from Bank of China (Hong Kong), DBS, HSBC and Standard Chartered said during a panel discussion at a forum on Monday. The annual forum organised by the Hong Kong Green Finance Association and the Greater Bay Area Green Finance Alliance brought together policymakers, financiers and industry leaders to discuss sustainable investment amid rising geopolitical, trade and economic uncertainty. Chinese companies in solar power, wind energy, batteries and other green technologies are increasingly taking their solutions overseas, particularly to the Global South, and Hong Kong could play a larger role in financing these companies as they expand into developing markets, said Wang Huabin, deputy CEO of Bank of China (Hong Kong). “Hong Kong has also led Asia in sustainable finance for years … [and it] is well positioned as a bridge for Chinese green technology going global,” Wang said, adding that the city’s sustainable-finance market, offshore yuan liquidity and professional services could be combined to provide financing and professional support for Chinese companies investing abroad. Natalie Blyth, HSBC’s global head of sustainable finance and transition, said that mainland Chinese companies have some of the “most dynamic low-carbon technologies” globally. Accelerating their deployment overseas at scale could make a significant contribution to tackling climate change, she added, and Hong Kong could be an “essential superconnector” for this. HSBC launched a US$4 billion dedicated facility a few months ago to support mainland companies expanding through Hong Kong into overseas markets, she added. The key challenge now was no longer the availability of capital, but whether enough projects could generate returns at acceptable levels of risk, particularly in developing economies, according to the speakers. “Capital is never constrained,” said Kelvin Wong, chief sustainability officer at DBS Bank. “What’s constrained is the pipeline projects.” He pointed to renewable energy, alternative fuels and cross-border power infrastructure as areas of investment opportunity in Asia. Marisa Drew, chief sustainability officer at Standard Chartered, said the challenge in the transition process had evolved from “mobilising capital” to “mobilising investibility”. Higher funding costs, currency risks and other challenges would make projects in emerging markets “unbankable” even when similar investments would be viable elsewhere, Drew said, adding that targeted government support and financial innovation could help lower those barriers and mobilise more private capital.

title: Nepal’s US$2.5 billion flood bill puts UN climate fund to its biggest test yet
description: Nepal has petitioned the UN Loss and Damage Fund to ‘respond rapidly, directly and effectively’ after its worst natural disaster in decades.
content: Nepal is seeking financial aid following the catastrophic flood that killed hundreds of people and caused billions of dollars in economic losses, tapping a global financial mechanism established to address the impacts of climate change in developing countries. Kathmandu has formally requested the UN-backed Fund for responding to Loss and Damage to “respond rapidly, directly and effectively” amid the country’s worst natural disaster in decades. In a letter signed by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Environment Minister Gita Chaudhary, officials said early action by the entity would signal a capability to respond “with humanity, flexibility and solidarity when climate-vulnerable countries face loss and damage beyond their capacity to address alone”. The August 26 tsunami-like flooding – triggered by a rock-ice avalanche along the Nepal-China border – has killed more than 1,300 people, with roughly 5,000 others still missing. On Friday, the Nepal Army rescued two local workers trapped inside a hydropower tunnel for nine days, while a Chinese national was pulled out the following day. “What Nepal is doing by submitting the request is genuine and right,” Raju Pandit Chhetri, executive director of the environmental non-profit Prakriti Resources Centre, told This Week in Asia. “The support that Nepal might get may be minuscule, but it will send a significant message symbolically and set a precedent for other countries.” Following decades of negotiations, nations agreed to establish the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage at the 2022 UN Climate Change Conference (Cop27) in Egypt. The fund was operationalised the following year at Cop28 in Dubai, laying the groundwork to assist developing nations. The fund relies mainly on government contributions. Of the money pledged so far, US$250 million has been allocated for its initial 2025–26 funding phase, with at least 50 per cent earmarked for small island developing states and least developed countries. Governments from climate-vulnerable countries and climate activists have long called on the world’s biggest emitters to take greater responsibility for the damage caused or exacerbated by climate change, including providing financial aid to countries bearing the heaviest burden. The World Bank estimates that Nepal contributes only 0.01 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. However, development organisation Germanwatch’s Climate Risk Index 2026 ranked the Himalayan nation as the sixth most affected country globally for extreme weather impacts in 2024. [] “We desperately need climate reparations,” global environmental activist Greta Thunberg wrote in a social media post demanding climate justice for Nepal. “Stop calling it aid. Stop calling it generosity. What is owed to Nepal is climate debt: money that is due because of harm that was caused. Not a gift that so-called developed countries get to decide whether or how much to give.” However, analysts cautioned that the mechanism did not involve legal liability or forced compensation, but rather relied on cooperation and facilitation. The fund is not intended to finance adaptation, resilience building or early warning systems, but rather rehabilitation, recovery and reconstruction in the aftermath of a climate event. “This unfortunately means that the fund is not a reparations or compensation fund,” said Sneha Pandey, a climate diplomacy and policy analyst at Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute. “The fund is meant to finance activities that come after the immediate humanitarian response, and to assist particularly vulnerable developing countries in responding to both economic and non-economic loss and damage.” Nepalese officials estimate economic losses at 400 billion rupees (US$2.5 billion), with recovery costs nearing US$5 billion – almost one-tenth of Nepal’s economy. The hardest-hit areas are in the northern and central districts of Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot. Climate change link Experts also say that Nepal must establish that the disaster was directly linked to climate change while providing a detailed loss assessment to support its claim. Pandey said that monetising non-economic losses was complex and raised ethical concerns. However, she noted it remained feasible, as costs for psychosocial services, restoration of cultural sites and support for bereaved households “do not try to put an oversimplified number on the loss itself, but quantify the response to such losses”. “This is a huge gap because it understates what was lost and the scale of the response required,” Pandey said. “COP31 [in November] is an opportunity to make the case at the highest level for mobilising more finance for climate-induced loss and damage.” Last week, Prime Minister Balendra Shah told parliamentarians that the Himalayan region faced increasing risks from rising temperatures, emphasising that Nepal must urgently present a strong global case regarding climate impacts. Shah is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York later this month during his first official foreign trip since assuming office in March. “We have to give a clear message to the international community that Nepal alone cannot fight the impacts of climate change, and this is the result of inaction from the global community,” Chhetri said. “Whatever has been committed under conventions to provide financial and technical capacity needs to be swiftly provided. We’re not begging, but asking for what was promised.” On Wednesday, board members and alternates representing African, Asia-Pacific and least developed nations formally wrote to the fund’s leadership, urging the entity to “act as swiftly as possible” to support Nepal. The Loss and Damage Fund Secretariat did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication. Chhetri said the entity must respond to Nepal’s request while also establishing procedures to handle similar claims, as there are no established guidelines governing such claims. “This will also be a test of the fund itself,” he said. “The ball is in their court now.”

title: Philippine president’s cousin charged with plunder over US$118 million flood scandal
description: Ombudsman vows ‘no sacred cows’ as former House speaker faces life imprisonment over bogus project scheme.
content: Philippine prosecutors filed a criminal charge on Monday against a lawmaker and cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr over his alleged involvement in a massive corruption scandal involving bogus flood-control projects. The case came more than a year after Marcos put the so-called “ghost” infrastructure projects, believed to have cost Filipino taxpayers billions of dollars, centre stage in a public address. Several construction firm owners, government officials and politicians have been accused of pocketing funds from the projects. On Monday, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said the plunder case against Martin Romualdez, the Philippine president’s congressman cousin, involved a total of 7.4 billion pesos (US$117.9 million) in alleged bribes, anomalous budget insertions and project allocations. Investigators earlier alleged that Romualdez, former lawmaker Elizaldy Co and other personalities conspired to unlawfully accumulate 56 billion pesos in ill-gotten wealth from public funds. Romualdez has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Plunder is a non-bailable offence referring to large-scale corruption punishable by life imprisonment. “We don’t pick and choose, there is no name here that we’re trying to avoid. Everything here is based on evidence,” Remulla told reporters. “This case proves that there are no sacred cows.” Remulla said prosecutors intended to file additional cases against Romualdez and others implicated in the flood-control scandal. Romualdez’s co-respondents include Co and several others accused of conspiring to unlawfully accumulate wealth through government funds. In a statement to reporters, Romualdez’s lawyer, Ade Fajardo, said his client would face the allegations through the courts. “We respect the courts and the legal process,” Fajardo said. “[Romualdez] asks only for the same due process and fair hearing guaranteed to every Filipino. Truth, evidence, and a fair process must prevail.” The court filing comes as Marcos faces mounting pressure from the public seeking accountability for the stolen funds intended for flood mitigation projects. Monsoon rains and typhoons in recent weeks have severely flooded numerous areas, killing 43 and prompting 58,000 to take shelter in evacuation centres, according to government data. Business and consumer confidence have taken a hit while government spending slowed after Marcos exposed the corruption issue last year, sinking the Southeast Asian nation’s economic growth to the slowest since 2009, excluding the pandemic. Public officials, including a senator, have been arrested on corruption charges. “Those who ought to be held accountable must be held accountable – whoever they may be: a relative, a friend, an ally, or a political opponent,” Presidential Communications Office Undersecretary Claire Castro said on Monday. Marcos, during his national address in July, said the government had conducted extensive investigations, and he was leaving the prosecution to the Ombudsman. “I am not the president of my family. I am not the president of my friends,” he said. “I am the president of the Philippines, and my duty is to you – my fellow Filipinos.” In September last year, Romualdez resigned as speaker of the House of Representatives after his name surfaced in the widening investigation. At the time, he said stepping down would allow investigators to perform their work without “undue influence”. He remains a member of Congress. Corruption has long been a problem in the Philippines’ brand of freewheeling democracy, and accounts for much of the massive poverty in the Southeast Asian nation of 112 million people. Additional reporting by Bloomberg

title: The View | China’s new property presale rules risk prolonging sector downturn
description: Beijing is putting homebuyers first, but only by transferring financial risks to to developers already under severe strain.
content: More than two decades after China’s central bank recommended that developers be forbidden from selling flats before they are completed, the government has called time on the presale financing model that contributed to the excesses of the property boom and shattered homebuyers’ confidence in the market. On August 28, Beijing announced a package of measures designed to rebuild trust in the completion and handover of pre-sold homes, stimulate demand and put the country’s ailing residential market on a firmer financial footing. HSBC said “policy alignment” among regulatory bodies and government ministries suggested the policies were “a concerted step towards a new and healthier long-term housing market model”. The most important measure was the reform of housing finance. A notice jointly issued by housing and financial regulators raised the threshold for presales to topping out the main structure of the building. It also stipulated that mortgage proceeds would be deposited into supervised escrow accounts that will not be available for use until the project is completed. In a report on August 29, Nomura said “deferring the release of funding after home completion effectively dismantles the financing function of presales”. Standard Chartered said in a report on August 31 that “the new rules emphasise project-based financing, shifting away from developer-based credit”.
