At a time when global investors barely give China’s economic data a second look, it is important to recognise that Beijing is addressing one of the underlying causes of the housing bust. At the peak of the boom in 2020-21, presales accounted for nearly 90 per cent of residential floor space sales. Over-reliance on presales contributed to excessive leverage and amplified the liquidity crisis in response to the government’s imposition of limits on borrowing by developers, known as the “three red lines”. By prioritising the sale of completed homes, Beijing is putting the interests of homebuyers first. As S&P Global Ratings noted in a report on September 1, “developers will be more responsible for their own financing instead of shifting the investment burdens to homebuyers through presales”. The reforms could mark a turning point for domestic demand in China. S&P went on to say that “authorities are attempting to strengthen the trust of homebuyers, a key ingredient to improve consumption growth”. This does not necessarily fix the problem, though. By transferring financing risks from homebuyers to developers, policymakers are trading one problem for another. Already under severe financial strain as the five-year downturn shows little sign of easing – home sales in 70 cities contracted 13.2 per cent in annualised terms in the first seven months of this year while property investment plunged 19.2 per cent – developers will now be saddled with higher upfront funding requirements and longer cash conversion cycles. Bank of America believes the new financing rules will delay developers’ cash inflows by up to two years, further crimping housing starts and investment. “Developers used to get the proceeds from presales six months after they purchased the land,” said Lulu Shi, director of corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings in Shanghai. Although equity and bond markets are expected to play a stronger role in financing home builders, longer lags in the realisation of cash inflows will limit land acquisitions, weighing on sales. Local governments can no longer expect a rebound in revenue from land sales, while banks will have to hold property loans on their books for a longer period, increasing their exposure to real estate risks. In its report on the new rules, Citigroup said they would benefit stronger developers with a higher percentage of completed new home sales and Beike, an agency business for second-hand properties. Nomura took a bleaker view, warning that some private developers “might be too financially stretched to transition smoothly to the new model”. However, the higher bar for presales will curb new supply as developers focus on destocking completed homes and accelerating the delivery of projects currently under construction. This will help reduce the excess inventory that has been a major impediment to the stabilisation of China’s housing market. Furthermore, the reforms will underpin green shoots of recovery in the sector. Prices for second-hand flats in Tier 1 cities, which have shown positive growth across much of the past six months, are likely to benefit from tighter supply. “The market for well-located second-hand flats in first-tier cities will gain the most,” Shi said. The new rules also underscore Beijing’s strong preference for structural adjustment over large-scale stimulus. Housing policy is an appendage of the government’s self-sufficiency drive in which constraints are imposed on stimulus as China transitions towards new growth engines. However, the transition is a long and painful one. Structural reforms cannot compensate for the growth drag from the collapse of a residential property sector that contributed as much as 2 percentage points to economic output as recently as 2018. The new housing finance regulations, while designed to reassure homebuyers, could prolong the drag further.

title: What North Korea’s new warship reveals about Kim’s moves to secure surrounding waters
description: Kim’s promised ‘important plans’ that will deepen the ‘concerns of the enemies’ are likely to be nuclear, observers say.
content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un’s promise to unveil more projects in eight months’ time at the launch of the country’s second modern destroyer hints at another major strategic military asset, according to experts. “The nuclearisation of our navy is being realised, making it increasingly suited, diversified and practical for the use of our deterrent,” Kim said while commissioning the Kang Kon in the southeastern port of Wonsan on Sunday. Kim was accompanied by his daughter and potential successor, Kim Ju-ae, his wife, Ri Sol-ju, his influential sister, Kim Yo-jong, and other senior officials “We must make the practical operation of our nuclear combat systems more diverse and effective, and our military activities for maritime defence and war deterrence more explicit, by making our powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent more clear,” he said. “Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened.” North Korea was currently carrying out “important plans to strengthen our naval forces”, Kim said without elaborating. “I will demonstrate them to the world once again eight months from now.” This specific time frame suggests that North Korea could unveil another large-scale asset, such as a submarine capable of carrying submarine-launched ballistic missiles or a nuclear-powered submarine, according to observers. It could be a “disclosure of progress in the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine, a third destroyer or additional naval bases”, said Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies. Other possibilities included “nuclear torpedoes designed for use by destroyers or improved versions of strategic cruise missiles”. The commissioning of the Kang Kon came roughly 15 months after the vessel was damaged during its launch in May 2025, and 75 days after the first modern destroyer of the same class, the Choe Hyon, was put into active service in June. The Choe Hyon is operating in the Yellow Sea off North Korea’s western coast, while the Kang Kon has been deployed in the Sea of Japan off the eastern coast. Both are the North’s most advanced 5,000-tonne destroyers and are equipped with nuclear-capable missiles. Sovereignty exercise The back-to-back commissioning of the two destroyers underscored North Korea’s efforts to develop a more diversified and operationally credible naval nuclear deterrent, Kim said. “This is a clear reality that allows us to measure the speed at which our navy is changing,” he said. The North Korean armed forces’ duty was to “safeguard the absolute security of the state, maintain strategic stability and the balance of power in the region, and deter geopolitical threats”. The commissioning ceremony came as the United States, South Korea and Japan kicked off their five-day Freedom Edge exercise on Monday in waters off South Korea’s Jeju Island, in a demonstration of their commitment to deterring North Korea’s nuclear and missile threats. “The fact that the Kang Kon is being officially commissioned into the maritime force of the East Sea, and the information that naval bases are being built in the East Sea, sends an unmistakable signal to our enemies,” Kim said. “Now is the time to exercise our sovereignty directly at sea and underwater as well.” The East Sea is the name used by both Koreas for the Sea of Japan, off the eastern coast of the Korean peninsula. Yang said the move appeared to serve multiple purposes: “addressing North Korea’s relatively weaker defensive posture in the East Sea, responding to Japan’s recent moves to strengthen its military capabilities, countering the presence of US aircraft carriers, and potentially taking into consideration expanding maritime military cooperation with Russia”. Although North Korean state media did not explicitly mention Ju-ae in its report, photographs showing her accompanying her father underlined her position in the hierarchy, Yang said. “Her attendance may be intended as part of her military education and exposure to high-level defence and naval affairs as a potential future successor.” The commissioning of the Kang Kon, and North Korea’s broader effort to nuclearise its navy, could also be intended to portray the country's ability to secure the Kim family’s bloodline, according to Yang. “Kim Ju-ae’s visible participation in events alongside senior party, government and military officials may be intended to strengthen her public image and cultivate familiarity and personal affinity, thereby indirectly building support for the future leadership succession,” he said. Addressing the Kang Kon’s crew, Kim described the destroyer as “one means and capability incorporated into the state nuclear response system”. “If the adversaries attempt to use force against us, I will order you comrades to use absolute power that will be most lethal to the enemy. You must deliver a devastating retaliatory strike against the enemy at any moment that order is given.” ‘Nuclear for nuclear’ Those remarks amounted to a public declaration that North Korea was “moving towards the operational deployment of a sea-based nuclear response system”, said Lim Eul-chul, a political-science professor at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies. They also signal efforts to make the country’s maritime nuclear deterrent more practical and diversified, including through the deployment of tactical nuclear-capable cruise missiles, according to Lim. “This suggests that the vessels are intended to be operated as launch platforms for tactical nuclear-capable multipurpose cruise missiles, or submarine-launched cruise missiles,” Lim said. “In particular, by designating the East Sea as a major security threat area and forward-deploying the Kang Kon there, North Korea appears to be pursuing an Anti-Access/Area Denial, or A2/AD, strategy aimed at directly deterring South Korean, US and Japanese naval exercises and the deployment of their nuclear assets within the destroyer’s operational range,” he said. The East Sea is a key approach route for US Navy aircraft carriers and strategic ballistic-missile submarines. “By explicitly referring to the construction of a blue-water fleet and expansion into distant waters, North Korea is signalling that it intends to continue building larger warships and expanding its naval capabilities,” Lim said. In his speech, Kim singled out the East Sea as North Korea’s greatest security threat. “Nowhere else on Earth can you find waters surrounding any country where warships of the opposing side constantly appear, carrying out the movement and deployment of nuclear assets and joint warfare demonstrations without any restrictions, and using them as a stage to track and deter even the legitimate exercise of self-defence,” he said. “We must respond thoroughly to these threats with highly professional and overwhelming force, possessing the will and sufficient capability to use it.” By openly declaring the nuclearisation of its warships, Pyongyang was making clear the concept of a “nuclear-for-nuclear” confrontation and showing its intention to directly counter the deployment of US naval forces with a sea-based nuclear deterrent, according to Lim. “North Korea also sent a strong A2/AD message by saying it would ‘strictly constrain’ US naval forces and force them to make a ‘strategic retreat’. This indicates that Pyongyang does not recognise the maritime superiority that the United States has enjoyed in the East Sea and intends to challenge it,” he added. The risk of close encounters and accidental clashes with South Korean, US and Japanese vessels is higher now that North Korea is expected to increase patrols and show of force in the Sea of Japan, according to Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification. “As the East Sea is also a contact zone with the Russian Pacific Fleet, attention must be paid to the possibility that it could become a channel for accumulating open-ocean operational experience through future joint North Korea-Russia naval activities or port calls,” he added.

title: China’s Moonshot and Z.ai bring AI model subscription race to Tmall’s retail shelves
description: By packaging tokens and coding plans like everyday retail goods, AI labs are opening a new front in their push for sustainable revenue.
content: China’s artificial intelligence developers are competing for paying users on a new consumer front: Alibaba Group Holding’s Tmall, where AI subscription plans are now being sold alongside smartphones, skincare and luxury fashion brands. Moonshot AI, developer of the Kimi K3 model, and MiniMax were in talks to open official flagship stores on the e-commerce platform, people familiar with the matter told the South China Morning Post on Monday. The move comes as AI developers look for new channels to convert soaring user numbers into recurring revenue. Beijing-based Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, kicked off the trend last week by opening an online storefront selling subscriptions to its GLM Coding Plan. A day later, Tmall launched an “AI Space Station”, a central marketplace where users can buy AI subscriptions, top up tokens and purchase specialised packages from Alibaba Cloud, Z.ai, MiniMax and DeepSeek. Early market signals have been positive. Within 48 hours of Z.ai opening its storefront, transactions involving AI tokens and subscription products across Taobao and Tmall jumped by more than 160 per cent, a Tmall spokesperson told the SCMP on Monday. The digital marketplace packages cutting-edge AI services in a familiar consumer format, similar to topping up a prepaid mobile phone plan. While Alibaba Cloud and Z.ai run their own storefronts, packages for Kimi, MiniMax and DeepSeek are currently sold through third-party vendors. By putting access to models on digital retail shelves, Chinese developers are turning software subscriptions into everyday retail products and could become less reliant on direct website sales. Poe Zhao, a China technology analyst and founder of Hello China Tech, said Tmall gave developers a more efficient channel to acquire paying users, but with a trade-off, as it made them “more dependent on traffic controlled by the platform”. “Competition will probably intensify through distribution,” Zhao said. “Once several AI plans appear on the same shelf, search ranking, discounts and shopping festivals become competitive tools.” Zhao added that direct price comparisons between AI models remained difficult because core metrics – such as tokens, usage limits and underlying capabilities – “are not standardised”. The push into e-commerce comes as China’s top AI labs seek to build sustainable business models amid rapid revenue growth. Z.ai last week reported revenue of about 953.89 million yuan (US$142 million) in the first half of 2026, up about 400 per cent from a year earlier, while still recording a net loss of about 2 billion yuan. Meanwhile, Moonshot has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong initial public offering, sources familiar with the matter told the SCMP. The company is looking to undertake a final financing round ahead of the IPO, which could value it at about US$50 billion, according to the sources. Nomura Securities estimated in a research note published in July that Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue could top US$1 billion by the end of this year, about double its US$400 million to US$500 million level in mid-2026. MiniMax last month reported first-half revenue of US$116.6 million, up 283 per cent from a year earlier, driven by a 700 per cent surge in its enterprise business. But top-line growth remained below the pace needed to meet full-year analyst forecasts. Its adjusted net loss more than doubled to US$293 million during the period, even as its total loss narrowed 11 per cent to US$358 million. Alibaba owns the SCMP.

title: China’s brokers expected to continue robust performance with blockbuster IPO offerings
description: Active A-share market trading boosts investment firms’ top line by 50%, as mega IPOs predicted to fuel underwriting and sponsorship growth.
content: Chinese brokers delivered strong profits in the first half of the year, driven by active trading in the A-share market that boosted brokerage revenues by over 50 per cent, while the blockbuster initial public offerings (IPOs) are expected to make underwriting and sponsorship business a key growth engine in the second half. The industry also recorded a robust first-half performance, with 150 brokers posting an average of 23.5 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit, driven by a 31 per cent surge in operating revenue, according to the Securities Association of China (SAC). The revenue increase was fuelled primarily by a 51 per cent jump in brokerage income, as heightened market activity boosted commission earnings. Investment advisory services also emerged as a stand-out, with net revenue soaring 57.24 per cent – the fastest growth among all business segments – reflecting rising demand for research reports and wealth management advice. Wall Street investment bank Citibank was positive towards the sector’s outlook. In a research note last week, the bank forecast that covered Chinese brokers would achieve a return on equity of about 11 per cent in 2026, supporting a price-to-book ratio above 1x. This implies an average of 36 per cent upside for H-share brokerage stocks. Industry concentration remained, with top players Citic Securities and Guotai Haitong collectively generating 96.9 billion yuan (US$14.4 billion) in first-half revenue – nearly 30 per cent of the industry total – and 44.9 billion yuan in net profit, accounting for 32.4 per cent, according to SAC. Citibank also sees underwriting and sponsorship as a key growth engine for the second half, predicting robust equity fundraising momentum will extend into the third quarter, supported by mega IPOs. Recent blockbuster debuts include ChangXin Memory Technologies, which raised around 60 billion yuan, and Unitree Robotics, which raised 6.1 billion yuan. Looking ahead to the second half, Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp’s listing application has been accepted by the China Securities Regulatory Commission, with plans to raise 33 billion yuan, while Tencent Holdings-backed Shanghai Enflame Technology has opened its blockbuster IPO, recording 4,073 times the subscription and raising 6.12 billion yuan. “With more AI-related start-ups and model developers listing in A-share markets, the tech sector will continue to provide a vital pipeline for IPOs, supporting brokers’ investment banking business,” said Stevan Tam, associate director at Fulbright Financial. While steady-to-weak A-share performance may moderate second-half brokerage income, and tighter regulatory scrutiny on new accounts and margin trading adds pressure, Tam expects the regulatory impact to emerge gradually without disrupting overall industry stability.

title: Malaysia lifts haze emergency in Sarawak, but warns pollution risks remain
description: King Sultan Ibrahim revokes the emergency status after rain lowers air pollution levels in Serian district.
content: Malaysia called off a haze emergency in Sarawak state on Borneo island on Monday but said very unhealthy levels of air pollution remained as a result of forest fires in neighbouring Indonesia. Sarawak has been heavily affected by fires in Indonesia’s Kalimantan, with the haze forcing school closures in some parts of the state. Kuala Lumpur on Friday activated the emergency after obtaining royal consent when pollution levels reached critical levels in Serian, about 65 kilometres (40 miles) south of the Sarawak capital, Kuching. King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar “today approved the termination of the declaration of emergency”, the prime minister’s office said on Monday. The decision was based on advice from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Sarawak Premier Abang Johari Openg, as well as reports from government agencies showing that air quality readings in Serian were no longer at a hazardous level. “The haze situation in Sarawak has not yet fully recovered, and the air pollution index (API) reading in several areas ... particularly Serian and Samarahan districts, is still at very unhealthy levels,” it said in a statement. The federal government and the Sarawak state government will continue to closely monitor the situation, and residents in affected areas are advised to limit outdoor activities and to always comply with instructions from the authorities,” it said. API figures in Serian passed the critical threshold of 500 on Friday, peaking at 519 with the town cloaked in a thick cloud of smoke. Under Malaysian guidelines, API levels above 300 are classified as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency. Rain in Serian on Friday night and Saturday morning – believed to have been the result of cloud seeding – brought some respite, with API levels dropping back below hazardous levels to 222 on Monday, according to environment department data. Toxic haze has shrouded parts of Indonesia and Malaysia for weeks as Jakarta struggles to contain fires that have scorched large tracts of Borneo and Sumatra, with the smoke drifting into neighbouring Malaysia, Singapore, and Brunei. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: China’s leading EV battery makers’ profits nearly double that of industry’s carmakers
description: Leading electric vehicle battery makers’ profits by far outpace the industry’s carmakers in first half.
content: China’s electric vehicle (EV) battery makers saw their combined net profit in the first half of the year nearly double that of the country’s major carmakers, widening the profitability gap amid weakening domestic demand for EVs. Seven major battery manufacturers, including Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL), recorded a net profit of over 50 billion yuan (US$7.4 billion) during the January-June period, up 49 per cent year on year, according to the companies’ exchange filings. However, China’s 11 major EV makers, from BYD to Great Wall Motor, saw their combined interim net profit shrink by 19 per cent over the same period to 28.8 billion yuan. The combined net profit of the seven battery makers was 75 per cent higher than that of the 11 listed EV makers in the first half, compared to a minor lag of 4.56 per cent for the same period one year ago. The increase in battery makers’ profits comes as China’s retail EV sales declined 14 per cent year on year to about 4.7 million units in the first half of the year, dragged down by the sharp decrease in budget vehicles amid a subsidy pullback, according to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). “Profits have diverged sharply between upstream and downstream sectors,” said Cui Dongshu, secretary general of the CPCA, in his social media post on Friday. “This reflects how price wars are severely squeezing downstream’s room to operate, while profits along the supply chain are highly concentrated among leading upstream companies.” Notably, three out of six smaller EV battery players, EVE Energy, CALB Group and Gotion High-Tech, reported three-digit profit growth in their first-half net profit. This is faster than CATL’s 42 per cent profit increase, though the Fujian-based giant contributed over 85 per cent of the combined net profits. High battery technology barriers and robust EV exports helped cement the pricing power of the leading EV battery makers like CATL, said Yale Zhang, managing director at the consultancy Automotive Foresight in Shanghai. “[Chinese] carmakers need to pay more attention to the safety of battery packs, as any quality issue would affect their global reputation,” said Zhang. “It could weaken the bargaining power of carmakers a bit further.” Morgan Stanley estimated that China’s EV exports in 2026 would jump 95 per cent year on year to 4.88 million units and 55 per cent to 7.57 million units in 2027, according to a report published on August 24. In July, CATL dominated the China EV battery market with a share of 42.33 per cent, followed by BYD at 19.23 per cent, CALB at 6.95 per cent, Gotion High-Tech at 6.29 per cent and EVE Energy at 6.05 per cent, data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance showed. But CATL’s dominance also triggered EV makers’ efforts to seek cheaper alternatives, including building in-house battery capabilities and strengthening partnerships with tier-two players. Improvement of product quality by smaller battery makers might create a more competitive EV battery market and narrow the profitability gap for EV makers, said Zhang. On the other hand, battery makers like CATL are expanding into new businesses, including the power sector and energy industries like robotics, diversifying their revenue streams, said Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics. “The few big battery makers can probably maintain their position and technological lead,” said Zhang of WaterRock. “So they should continue to have good pricing power.”

title: Chinese naval scientists fall in love with the ‘big guns’ on Trump-class warship
description: Military researchers suggest large-calibre weapons firing fragmenting shells from battleships could neutralise low-cost drone swarms.
content: US President Donald Trump’s vision of new warships bristling with huge-calibre guns – widely mocked as a billionaire’s vanity project and a throwback to the battleship era of the second world war – has received an unexpected nod from military scientists in China. In a paper published last month by the Chinese peer-reviewed journal Command Control & Simulation, the authors suggested that large-calibre naval guns could have a critical role in future warfare by countering the growing threat of cheap drone swarms. According to Wang Lei and his team from the People’s Liberation Army’s Dalian Naval Academy, these guns could fire prefabricated-fragment shells that would explode near a drone swarm, creating a high-speed cloud of fragments capable of damaging multiple targets within an area. The Trump-class battleship, announced in December as part of the president’s proposed “Golden Fleet”, is designed to combine an extensive missile capacity with nine large naval guns and other electromagnetic weapons. The proposal has raised questions from experts and social media commenters alike about whether concentrating so much firepower on a single, extremely expensive platform makes sense in an era of long-range missiles and unmanned weapons. One US online commenter ridiculed the plan as “designed by a rich moron with no concept of practicality or functionality”, while another joked that the ships would be “quite literally gold-plated”, in a mocking reference to their perceived wastefulness and extreme cost. Another post described the concept as a “Swiss army knife” that tried to do everything but was “useless at everything”. Criticism has also come from military analysts, with the privately owned US website Military.com arguing that battleships have long been vulnerable to aircraft, submarines and missiles. Phillips O’Brien, a strategic studies professor at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, said the Trump-class plan appeared designed more to produce a “scary-looking vessel” than to address changing maritime threats. The cost of the programme is another concern, with the US Congressional Budget Office estimating in August that the first nuclear-powered battleship could cost about US$23.4 billion and that a 15-ship programme could reach roughly US$275 billion. According to the paper, which appeared online on August 18, rather than modelling a shell as a single projectile that must hit one drone, the PLA naval scientists used a statistical model commonly used to describe fragment-size distributions, together with a projection of how fragments spread through space. In their example, the swarm consisted of 30 Russian-made Lancet-3 loitering munitions, each with a maximum take-off mass of about 12kg (26lbs) and a payload of up to 3kg. The researchers assumed that one shell would produce 2,000 fragments, of which 1,589 would exceed the mass threshold required to cause damage. Under the model’s assumptions, which included a 15 metre (49ft) fragment-cloud kill radius, the calculated probability of damaging an individual drone was 3.95 per cent – or about 1.19 drones per shell in the 30-drone swarm, according to the paper. The researchers said the approach would still depend heavily on accurate detection and tracking, fire-control systems and programmable fuses, and suggested integrating the guns with electronic warfare, lasers and command-and-control systems. But their proposal also faces opposition from China’s defence community, with one Chinese weapons and equipment specialist dismissing the study. “It is just a lousy paper written for promotion.” The specialist, who asked not to be identified because of the sensitivity of his affiliated institution and a potential conflict of interest, said he did not believe the paper provided convincing evidence that large-calibre guns would be effective against a drone swarm. The naval research team has not responded to a request for comment. The debate therefore remains unresolved, particularly over the cost and complexity of deploying such weapons on a giant warship. The US Navy says it plans to order 15 Trump-class battleships between 2028 and 2056, although funding and industrial feasibility remain uncertain. Funding for the programme was removed from a pending Senate appropriations bill, while US shipyards face severe labour shortages and questions remain over whether the industry can deliver the ships on schedule. title: Future filled with gold for China’s teen javelin star Yan after historic Diamond League win
description: The 18-year-old finishes ahead of Paris Olympic gold medallist Haruka Kitaguchi in final in Brussels and ends season undefeated over five events.
content: Javelin star Yan Ziyi’s sweet tooth almost cost her a place in the history books in Brussels on Sunday, as it was she joined a very select group of Chinese athletes. The 18-year-old said she ate so many desserts during lunch that she made herself sick, but it still wasn’t enough to stop her from becoming the youngest female champion in Diamond League Final history, beating Paris Olympic gold medallist Haruka Kitaguchi. Yan won the women’s javelin gold with a meeting record throw of 68.42 metres to end the season undefeated over five events and earn her first Diamond League trophy. Victory made the teenager just the fourth Chinese athlete to win a Diamond League Final title, following shot putter Gong Lijiao, javelin specialist Lu Huihui and discus star Feng Bin. The path to success was not smooth, however, with the tasty treats causing a rare dip in form during the final. She fouled on her first and third attempts while registering a modest 62.21m on her second throw – far below her usual standard. She recovered on her fourth attempt with a 64.95m throw to move into first place, before sealing the win with 68.42m. Japan’s Kitaguchi finished second with a season-best 65.44m on her final attempt. Addressing her shaky start after the event, Yan revealed that eating too many desserts at lunch had caused nausea and physical discomfort. “I was completely out of form,” Yan said. “Fortunately, my coach gave me the greatest support and encouragement immediately, helping me quickly adjust to regain my rhythm.” She said these setbacks actually proved to be a valuable experience. “This is my first true world major title, and my journey in senior world-level competition really begins today,” she added. Yan noted that she would prepare more thoroughly for future events, while adding with a laugh: “Javelin is a highly technical event, and state of form cannot always be online. If I perform poorly in the future, I hope everyone won’t criticise me too harshly.” In a single season, Yan has established herself as a dominant force in international women’s javelin. Following this victory, she is scheduled to compete in the World Athletics Ultimate Championship before heading to the Asian Games, which starts on September 19. Born in 2008, Yan turned 18 in May and was then allowed to compete at top-tier World Athletics competitions. She won all four Diamond League events she entered this season – Xiamen, Oslo, Paris and Monaco – recording winning throws above 67m in each one. In Xiamen, she set a personal best of 71.74m, coming within 54 centimetres of Czech star Barbora Spotakova’s 18-year record of 72.28m. Currently ranked world No 1, Yan earned the nickname “One-Throw Yan” among fans for frequently securing victory on her first attempt. As the peak age for female javelin throwers typically ranges between 25 and 35, the teenager is just starting her career, and her Asian Games debut will be widely watched. Her victory drew widespread praise on social media, where fans applauded her composure under pressure. “It feels like her era has arrived,” one netizen wrote. “An 18-year-old athlete pushing through a tough start to overturn the pressure and break her limits throw after throw, the future is bright.” Others highlighted her potential longevity while emphasising physical health. “If her peak lasts until 36, her reign could extend as long as her entire life so far,” another user noted. “I just hope she manages her health and avoids major injuries, as there is still time before the next Olympics,” one fan said.

title: Make home ownership a 5-year plan goal, Legco president says
description: Starry Lee says reviving Tenants Purchase Scheme and reserving subsidised flats for young, middle-class families could help achieve target.
content: Hong Kong authorities should make raising home ownership a goal of the city’s first five-year plan, Legislative Council president Starry Lee Wai-king has said, following a visit to a public estate with the housing minister. Lee also said the goal could be achieved by reviving a scheme that allowed public housing tenants to buy their flats and reserving subsidised homes for youth and middle-class families. She made the remarks after inspecting Oi Man Estate in Ho Man Tin with Housing Bureau and Housing Department staff on Monday. “I suggest gradually raising the home ownership ratio among local residents as a mid- to long-term policy goal. This would build a clearer housing ladder for citizens,” she said in a Facebook post after the inspection with Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin. Lee said she had presented her recommendations on the city’s first five-year plan and housing policy to Ho during the visit. While the Legco president said she agreed with the government’s direction of continuously increasing housing supply, she proposed additional measures to boost home ownership. The proposals included reintroducing a refined Tenants Purchase Scheme at certain estates to help eligible public housing tenants buy their flats. Lee also suggested increasing the supply of flats under the Home Ownership Scheme (HOS) and other subsidised sale properties, reserving a specific quota for young people and middle-class families, and optimising allocation mechanisms. “This offers hardworking residents a realistic hope of home ownership,” she said. During the inspection, Lee exchanged views with Oi Man Estate residents and raised their concerns to Ho and the visiting government staff. The concerns covered estate management, environmental hygiene, facility maintenance, drainage improvements, greening and landscaping, barrier-free access and support for the elderly. They also discussed longer-term issues such as electric vehicle charging infrastructure, smart housing management systems and future community planning following the redevelopment of Ma Tau Wai Estate. Anthony Chiu Kwok-wai, executive director of the Federation of Public Housing Estates, said that while the Tenant Purchase Scheme would raise the home ownership rate, the government should also consider increasing the proportion of subsidised flats for sale in newly built public housing. “The ratio of rental public housing to subsidised sale flats should be adjusted from the current 7:3 to 5:5, so residents can buy more affordable housing,” he said. Lawmaker Chan Hok-fung, who sits on the Legislative Council’s housing panel, backed Lee’s call to raise the home ownership rate to strengthen social stability and residents’ sense of belonging. However, he said the rental-to-sale ratio should remain unchanged for now, as the average waiting time for public rental housing had yet to reach the government’s target of 4.5 years. “The Tenant Purchase Scheme has always been an important means to help raise the home ownership. Public housing turnover is low, with only a small number of tenants each year buying HOS flats, passing away, or moving out,” he said. “With so few flats being freed up, it is better to sell them to sitting tenants, allowing the government to gain revenue while residents move up the housing ladder.”

title: Hong Kong a ‘trusted partner’ to drive Central Asia growth, city leader says
description: Central Asia offers immense potential for global businesses, John Lee reveals as SCMP’s China Conference debuts in Astana.
content: Hong Kong is committed to being a “trusted partner” in driving Central Asia’s emergence as a global growth engine, according to the city’s leader, who hailed the substantial outcomes achieved since his landmark mission to the region. In a virtual appearance at the South China Morning Post’s China Conference: Central Asia 2026 held in Astana on Monday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said that a bank in his June delegation had since backed the Development Bank of Kazakhstan with US$785 million in financing. Kazakhstan’s national rail operator, KTZ, had also filed to list in Hong Kong, while a local family office had signed an agreement with the Central Asian country’s authorities to strengthen cooperation in sustainable energy, he said. Lee underscored that Central Asian countries – all important economies in the Belt and Road Initiative – possessed immense potential and opportunities for global businesses seeking to diversify their activities and strengthen international connections. The Belt and Road Initiative refers to a plan rolled out by Chinese President Xi Jinping in 2013 to grow global trade. “As we look ahead, the promise of Central Asia as a global growth engine is not to be missed. Hong Kong stands ready as your trusted partner, connecting markets, financing sustainable growth and driving seamless cross-boundary trade,” Lee said. In June, Lee led a record 70-strong business and professional delegation from Hong Kong and mainland China to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to forge new trade corridors amid geopolitical tensions, resulting in 96 deals worth US$1.65 billion. The city leader said on Monday that many enterprises in the delegation had successfully built strong rapport with their partners in Central Asia and had already commenced cooperation projects. Cheng Kefan, charge d’affaires ad interim at the Chinese embassy in Kazakhstan, said Hong Kong would play a unique role in the nation’s cooperation with Central Asia following Lee’s visit to the region earlier this year. He said China’s cooperation with the five Central Asian states – Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan – had drawn on deep historical ties and fast-growing investment. Even amid rising protectionism and geopolitical instability, Cheng said China’s engagement with Central Asia remained focused on a shared goal of high-quality development for a modernised region, driven by high-level strategic alignment and deeper collaboration in natural resources and the digital economy. “This type of collaboration, from shared ideals, values and stances, would exceed the traditional framework of geopolitics to establish a new model for international relations,” he said. Renat Bekturov, governor of the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), said at the conference’s opening that there was significant potential to deepen financial and investment ties with China, one of Kazakhstan’s key strategic partners. “Through the AIFC and Astana International Exchange, we seek to connect Chinese capital and expertise with investment opportunities in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia, while opening new pathways for Kazakhstani businesses to access Chinese markets,” he said. He pointed to stronger hub-to-hub links between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan over the past 12 months, saying his office would now work to make conditions more practical for investors over the next two to three years by removing regulatory frictions to cross-border transactions. The AIFC governor said his organisation would deepen ties with Chinese legal institutions and push the Astana International Exchange to expand collaboration with counterparts in Hong Kong and on the mainland. “Our job is to make the exceptional ordinary, and to turn the Astana-Hong Kong route into a genuine market,” Bekturov said. The conference, co-organised by the AIFC, marked the debut of the SCMP’s flagship event in Central Asia. The event brought together policymakers, institutional investors and corporate delegates from more than 100 companies across the wider region, including the mainland, Hong Kong and Southeast Asia. Former city leader Leung Chun-ying, now a vice-chairman of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, said Central Asia was a key region in the Belt and Road Initiative. He was confident that bringing the conference to Astana would identify opportunities for broader economic and professional collaborations between China and Central Asian countries, particularly through Hong Kong’s role as a “superconnector”. SCMP publisher Tammy Tam said the publication served as a premier catalyst for global understanding and strategic intelligence, just as the city functioned as an irreplaceable bridge for business and trade. “We are uniquely positioned to bridge markets, foster high-level cross-border dialogue, and connect Central Asia’s rising dynamic with global capital and influence,” she said, calling the region “an extraordinarily promising market”. “In this gathering, we bring that vision directly to Astana – convening leaders across sectors to exchange insights, challenge perspectives and unlock transformative growth across macroeconomics, financial markets, mining and regional infrastructure.”

title: China has 1.4 billion mouths to feed. How vulnerable is it to a global food crisis?
description: El Nino fears and disruptions to Ukraine’s grain exports are driving up global crop prices, but China’s robust supplies temper the impact.
content: A surge in global agricultural prices has sparked fears of a global food crisis in recent weeks. But China’s limited reliance on staple grain imports and robust domestic reserves should cushion the blow of any external shocks, analysts said, though unpredictable weather, geopolitics and US-China trade tensions could still pose risks. The assessment comes as Beijing steps up efforts to diversify grain trade with other countries. On Saturday, China and Kazakhstan launched a grain trading platform in Changsha, Hunan province. The head of China’s National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, Liu Huanxin, said the platform was crucial to ensuring regional food security. Global grain prices have risen sharply in recent weeks, with Chicago corn, soybean and wheat futures reaching multi-year contract highs in late August and early September, according to CME Group. Meanwhile, the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation’s food price index climbed to 131.1 points in July, its highest level since January 2023. The rally was driven by a combination of factors. The escalation of the Russia-Ukraine war has disrupted grain exports via the Black Sea, while the US-Israeli war on Iran continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. An El Nino cycle projected to be one of the strongest in decades has also raised worries over the stability of global grain supplies. Argus, an international energy and commodity price assessment agency, said disruptions in the Black Sea had been the main driver of the recent rally. Daily exports through Ukrainian ports have plunged to about 20,000 tonnes, down from more than 180,000 tonnes under the former Black Sea Grain Initiative, according to the agency. The initiative began in 2022 to ease grain exports through the sea but collapsed the following year. The disruptions came during the peak export season from July to September, forcing buyers in Europe, North Africa and the Middle East to seek alternative supplies from North America, South America and Australia, and pushing up prices globally. Those higher global prices have also begun to reach China. The cost-and-freight price for November shipments of US Gulf corn to China had reached US$330 per tonne on Friday, up more than US$30 per tonne from early August, according to Argus assessments. However, analysts said the impact on China’s broader food market would remain limited, particularly compared with more import-dependent economies. “China is relatively well insulated from a global food-price shock compared to import-dependent Asian economies because it produces most of its staple grains domestically and maintains sizeable reserves,” said Sheana Yue, an economist at Oxford Economics. Argus said the direct supply impact on China appeared relatively limited, as China did not rely heavily on Black Sea corn imports. “While higher international prices may influence domestic market sentiment, price transmission into China is likely to be more moderate and potentially shorter lived than in some other markets.” That resilience is underpinned by China’s large domestic grain harvests. Argus said current market indicators suggested domestic grain availability in China remained relatively comfortable. “Based on currently available weather data, conditions across key growing regions have generally been favourable, reducing the immediate need for additional overseas purchases,” the agency said. China’s summer grain harvest exceeded 150 million tonnes for the first time this year, while early rice output remained above 28 million tonnes for the sixth consecutive year, official data showed. But China’s insulation is far from absolute. One key area of exposure is soybeans, with China relying on imports for more than 80 per cent of its consumption. Yue described soybeans as the “bigger vulnerability”, saying a sustained rise in global soybean prices would be more likely to “feed through indirectly via livestock-feed costs and meat prices than through a sharp increase in staple food inflation”. In addition, “domestic weather disruptions remain an additional risk, particularly for corn and soybeans”, Yue said. Argus said market participants would be closely watching September’s weather patterns as China’s corn harvest progressed. Attention would also focus on developments surrounding the Black Sea grain corridor, while changes in China-US trade policy, including tariffs, could influence import purchasing decisions for feed grains, the agency said.

title: Can gold hit US$5,000? Wall Street turns bullish despite US job growth fuelling rate fears
description: Record buying spree by central banks offsets Fed tightening fears, pushing gold towards US$5,000 by year-end, investment banks forecast.
content: Gold will probably test US$5,000 an ounce by the end of 2026, as demand from central banks diversifying their foreign reserves remains strong, countering fears of US monetary tightening after strong labour data and a hawkish tone from the Federal Reserve, according to investment banks. RBC Capital Markets is the latest to join the bullish camp, forecasting US$4,929 by year-end and US$5,296 in 2027. That aligned with Goldman Sachs and State Street Investment Management, which predicted that gold would climb to US$4,900 and US$5,000, respectively. The projections implied at least a 10 per cent gain from current levels. Gold is back in favour among investors even as expectations mount for higher US interest rates, which traditionally weigh on the non-yielding metal. The inverse correlation between the yellow metal and borrowing costs is breaking down amid concerns over fiscal discipline and relentless bond sales by the Trump administration, fuelling the so-called debasement trade. This is a fiscal spending backdrop that potentially favours gold allocations as a strategic monetary hedge Aakash Doshi, State Street Central banks are ramping up gold purchases to hedge against US Treasuries, whose long-end yields rose to multi-year highs last month. “In this case, it does not appear to be above-trend GDP [gross domestic product] growth or corporate margins driving higher long-term interest rates,” said Aakash Doshi, a strategist at State Street. “This is a fiscal spending backdrop that potentially favours gold allocations as a strategic monetary hedge.” Gold slipped 0.7 per cent to US$4,444 on Monday, with a rally from last month slowing after an August US jobs report exceeded expectations and Fed chairman Kevin Warsh delivered a hawkish tone at the annual policy symposium in Jackson Hole. The odds of a quarter-percentage-point rate increase this month stood at 58.4 per cent, according to global commodity marketplace CME Group. The metal surged nearly 10 per cent in August, its biggest monthly gain since January, buoyed by central-bank buying and the flushing out of speculative positions. Central banks could buy 750 to 900 tonnes of gold this year, the World Gold Council estimated. That compares with an average annual purchase range of between 400 and 500 tonnes. Sovereign buying surged 62 per cent from a year earlier to 289 tonnes in the second quarter, the highest for a three-month period in four years. The enthusiasm contrasts with a recent rout in US Treasuries, with the 30-year yield rising to a level not seen in nearly two decades on unease over US government debt amounting to a record US$40 trillion. Gold could find support at around US$4,000 amid near-term rate headwinds, a level that would spur acceleration of central-bank buying and institutional inflows, according to Goldman. “They are diversifying reserves, reducing exposure to assets that can be politically frozen, and buying insurance against the increasingly uncomfortable mix of fiscal risk, geopolitical fracture and policy uncertainty,” said Stephen Innes, managing partner at SPI Asset Management. “For now, gold is caught between a near-term rates headwind and a structural bid that has not gone away. The first can be violent. The second is much harder to dislodge.”

title: More Chinese pet owners choose TCM for chronic pet illnesses using herbs, bee stings, acupuncture
description: Growing popularity of TCM – noted for being milder and having fewer side effects – is largely driven by ageing pet population.
content: An increasing number of Chinese pet owners are turning to traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) to address chronic diseases and provide hospice care for their senior pets. On one social media platform, the hashtag #petTCM has amassed over five million views, reflecting a growing willingness among people to share their experiences with TCM treatments for their pets. A pet owner from Beijing took his dog, Iron Man, a seven-year-old mix of a border collie and golden retriever suffering from severe gastrointestinal issues, first to a Western veterinary clinic. The veterinarian there diagnosed Iron Man with inflammatory bowel disease and prescribed medication; however, his condition failed to improve. Seeking alternatives, the owner decided to explore TCM to “give it one more try.” The TCM practitioner assessed Iron Man by taking his leg pulse, examining his tongue, eyes, and mental state, and inquiring about his medical history, past treatments, daily diet, and activities. The doctor then prescribed Chinese patent medicine pills and dietary therapy. To the owner’s astonishment, the new treatment regime proved effective, as Iron Man’s persistent watery diarrhoea stopped after just three days. Another pet owner, caring for her 17-year-old Chinese native dog, ground Chinese herbal tonics into powder and mixed them with his favourite meat after observing a decline in energy and overall functionality due to age. After a month of administering the supplements, she noted a significant boost in her dog’s energy levels and physical strength. The owner, surnamed Zhang, likened the treatment for her dog to yang sheng – the traditional Chinese practice of holistic wellness. “I understand that this method cannot rejuvenate my dog, but it can certainly enhance his quality of life,” she stated. This belief is also why many owners seek out TCM practitioners for their elderly pets. In another case, a pet owner in Guangzhou brought their 17-year-old poodle diagnosed with cancer to a TCM clinic for bee sting therapy. Doctor Chen Jiayan performed the stinging, a traditional method believed to alleviate pain and swelling. Chen explained that the owner opted for this gentle approach, mindful of the dog’s advanced age. Other popular TCM treatments for pets include massage, moxibustion, and acupuncture. According to statistics released during this year’s Pet Fair Asia in Shanghai, around 20 million dogs and cats in China are over seven years old, indicating that they are entering their senior years. Last year, there were 126 million pet dogs and cats in urban areas, meaning about one in six of these pets were elderly. Shi Dayou, director of the Small Animal Medicine Sub-Association of the Guangdong Association of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Medicine, told the Guangzhou Daily that the increasing popularity of TCM, noted for being milder and having fewer side effects, is largely driven by the ageing pet population. Moreover, industry surveys reveal a growing willingness among pet owners to invest in the long-term well-being of their pets. A Beijing veterinarian who practises TCM, identified only by his surname Zhang, referred to his clinic as a “nursing home” characterised by a slow-paced lifestyle and compassionate care. “We cannot guarantee full recovery for pets, but we can offer them peace and dignity in their later years,” Zhang said. In fact, TCM veterinary medicine is not a new field; it has existed since ancient times when Chinese people first treated livestock. Currently, only six universities in China offer undergraduate programmes in TCM veterinary medicine, though some vocational colleges also provide this course of study. Shi noted that the most significant difference between TCM for humans and animals is that pets cannot communicate verbally, and their anatomical structures differ from those of humans. This reality necessitates a high level of professionalism in this field. This year, the Chinese Veterinary Medical Association published its first guidelines on acupuncture for dogs and cats, along with an action plan for promoting the development of TCM veterinary medicine over the next three years. This initiative is viewed as an important step towards the professionalisation of the industry.

title: Iranians recount horrors of suspected US missile attack on first day of war
description: Missiles that struck the southern city of Lamerd on February 28 dispersed tungsten fragments, killing at least 21 people.
content: Thirteen-year-old Mohammad Reza Barfar remembers the free kick more clearly than almost anything else on February 28 when the US-led attack on Iran began. The football-loving schoolboy went to a local field after classes for a match between his village and another team. He scored from a free kick and his brother captured the goal on video. Hours later, Mohammad Reza was lying wounded amid smoke and debris after a series of explosions struck Lamerd, an industrial city in Iran’s southern Fars Province. “This was the last time I touched the ball,” Mohammad Reza told Kyodo News, as he showed the video of the goal. Four pieces of metal struck his body, according to his family and medical treatment records, mangling the sole of his right foot and the heel of his left, and injuring his head and right arm. Damage to a bone in his left leg has left him dependent on a wheelchair. After the match, Mohammad Reza went to his family’s flower shop and he was resting there when a powerful explosion shook the ground. “Shortly after, I heard a loud whistle, then an explosion,” he recalled. “I felt someone grab me and then throw me to the ground.” Brown smoke filled the area so thickly that he could not see or breathe. Then he felt intense burning in his feet. “It was like burned charcoal was on my skin,” he said. Unable to stand, the boy crawled back into the room until his older brother found him. He spent 28 days in hospital and underwent 16 major surgeries on his legs. His mother, Zeynab Mortazavi, was also struck by shrapnel and still has difficulty walking after surgery. “We were a normal family living our lives,” she said. “I cannot understand why the US attacked us.” Mohammad Reza says he still wants to become both a doctor and a professional football player, but worries about returning to school. “Other kids might step on my leg. I might get hurt again,” he said. A few kilometres away, another family is living with a loss that cannot be treated. Helma Ahmadizadeh was just days short of her 10th birthday when she went to volleyball practice that afternoon. Although Tehran had come under attack that morning, her parents believed Lamerd was far from the fighting. Before practice, Helma tried on three different outfits and asked her father, Ali Ahmadizadeh, which one looked best. “She was very happy, cheerful and laughing,” he recalled. He dropped her at the Shahid Naimi sports complex shortly before 4pm. Soon afterwards, Helma called him. “Would you please come pick me up?” she asked. “Definitely, I will come, my love,” he replied. It was their last conversation. As Helma’s parents prepared to pick her up, they heard explosions. As they drove towards the sports complex, they could see black smoke rising. “The closer we got, the less hope we had,” Ahmadizadeh said. They rushed from the damaged gymnasium to the hospital. According to an official medical report, a small tungsten projectile had entered Helma’s upper left chest and penetrated her heart, causing fatal internal bleeding. She had no vital signs on arrival. “We don’t dare to recall those scenes or describe them,” said Ahmadizadeh. Her parents remember Helma as an energetic girl who loved sports and singing and led her school choir. “She was always laughing and happy,” her father said. A local investigation based largely on security-camera footage concluded that four missiles struck Lamerd beginning at 5.12pm, according to a report cited by Iran’s official IRNA news agency and confirmed to Kyodo News by local authorities. The blast sites – including near the flower shop and near the sports complex – were found to be at least several hundred metres from the city’s only known Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps post, which is not publicly known as a major missile base or command centre. A New York Times visual investigation published in March concluded that videos of the Lamerd attack showed characteristics consistent with the US Army’s newly developed Precision Strike Missile, or PrSM. The newspaper said the missile’s shape, flight characteristics and damage pattern were consistent with the weapon, which can detonate above a target and disperse high-velocity tungsten fragments. A US official also told The New York Times that the missile used was the PrSM. The PrSM, made by Lockheed Martin, is a new long-range weapon capable of strikes beyond 499km and can be programmed to detonate in the air. The missile used in Lamerd is believed to have dispersed large numbers of tungsten fragments, while Iranian authorities say the attack killed 21 people and wounded more than 150. But the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the US forces did not carry out any strikes in Lamerd or within 30 miles (48km) of the city. For Mousa Mousavi, a veteran surgeon and lawmaker representing Lamerd, he recalls how the “situation was chaotic and critical”. Mousavi was in the city when the explosions occurred and joined medical teams treating the wounded. Patients arrived with serious injuries to the head, neck, spine, abdomen and chest, while children, women and men crowded the hospital. “I had only seen such a scene on the front lines of the Iran-Iraq War,” he said. He said lawyers are gathering evidence for possible international legal proceedings and that, based on what he witnessed at the hospital, those killed and wounded were civilians. For Helma’s father, no compensation or court judgment can bring his daughter back. Mohammad Reza’s wish is simpler. “I wish the war was over forever,” he said.

title: 2 Hong Kong travel agencies, guide stripped of licences over ‘coerced shopping’
description: Travel Industry Authority says agencies failed to stop coercion of mainland Chinese tourists, while guide used threats to encourage purchases.
content: Hong Kong’s tourism watchdog has revoked the licences of two travel agencies and a guide after finding they failed to protect members of mainland Chinese tour groups from “coerced shopping”. The Travel Industry Authority said on Monday that the licences of Go Go Ming Travel Services, Grandee Travel Company and guide Sun Kwun-ying had been revoked with immediate effect. “The authority adopts a zero-tolerance approach towards coerced shopping and any conduct that damages the reputation of Hong Kong’s tourism industry,” it said. The watchdog said the decision stemmed from two cases involving mainland tour groups handled by the agencies in February and April. Investigations found the companies had failed to take all reasonable steps to ensure tour participants were not subjected to coerced shopping, while Sun had made threatening remarks to pressure visitors into making purchases, it said. The authority added that it would step up inspections with other law enforcement agencies ahead of the mainland’s National Day “golden week” holiday, when the city is expected to receive an influx of visitors from across the border. Lawmaker Nixie Lam Lam, a member of the Legislative Council’s economic development panel, welcomed the decision and said the penalties would serve as a warning to the industry. “Severely punishing industry practitioners who operate in breach of regulations will help reinforce visitors’ confidence in travelling to Hong Kong and uphold the city’s image as a quality tourism destination,” she said. Lam urged the authority to work alongside customs and police to conduct more inspections of tourist attractions and shops registered to receive tour groups during the holiday period. She also called for stronger professional training and compliance education for frontline tourism workers to prevent coercive shopping at its source. “The vast majority of Hong Kong’s tourism practitioners are dedicated to serving visitors, but a small number of bad actors can cause serious damage to the city’s reputation,” she said. Monday’s announcement marks the third time this year that the authority has revoked licences over coerced shopping, following similar actions against a travel agency and two guides in April and June. It also suspended Kaiser Jewellery International from receiving inbound tour groups for 30 days from August 26 after finding the retailer had failed to stop a guide from pressuring mainland visitors to shop there. The cases have renewed concerns over ultra-low-priced tour packages that rely heavily on commissions from designated shopping stops and revenue from paid add-on activities. An investigation by the South China Morning Post earlier this year found one-day Hong Kong tours advertised on mainland online platforms for as little as 1 yuan (15 US cents). A reporter who joined one such tour found that guides repeatedly promoted optional activities and said the initial tour fee was insufficient to cover operating costs. Participants were also taken to an outlet in Tsim Sha Tsui selling health supplements, jewellery and souvenirs, where some tourists who did not buy anything were reprimanded. Industry sources have said such packages cannot cover their costs without shopping commissions and revenue from optional activities. Under the Travel Industry Ordinance, licensed travel agencies, guides and tour escorts are responsible for ensuring participants are not harassed, coerced or improperly influenced into entering or remaining in shops or making purchases. Breaching licence conditions is a criminal offence. Travel agencies face a maximum penalty of a HK$100,000 (US$12,800) fine and two years’ imprisonment, while guides and tour escorts can be fined up to HK$50,000 and jailed for one year. The authority urged visitors who encountered coercive shopping or other unfair treatment to contact it or seek help from police.

title: Woman found dead in submerged car in Japan amid record rainfall
description: Authorities warn of landslides after more than 480mm of rain fell on Niijima Island, the largest amount since local records began.
content: Heavy rainfall hit eastern Japan and elsewhere on Monday, with the weather agency urging maximum vigilance against landslides on Niijima and Oshima islands, south of Tokyo, and a woman dying in Iwaki in the northeast after her car became submerged. The Japan Meteorological Agency issued a special landslide warning for Niijima after more than 480mm (19 inches) of rain fell there over 24 hours, the largest amount since local records began. Heavy rain also hit eastern Japan including Tokyo from the early hours of Monday, disrupting train services and forcing some school closures. The weather agency issued a Level 4 landslide alert on its five-point scale for parts of Chiba and Saitama prefectures, neighbouring the capital. The agency also warned that rainbands capable of bringing localised torrential downpours over prolonged periods could develop in the northeastern Tohoku region as a seasonal rain front moved north. A woman in her sixties was declared dead after being found unresponsive in a submerged car at an underpass in Iwaki, Fukushima prefecture, according to the local fire department. Two people suffered minor injuries after falling amid the heavy rain in Chiba, the prefectural government said. The central government has set up a liaison headquarters at the prime minister’s office to assess potential damage and streamline emergency responses. The weather agency is warning of more rainfall in wide areas facing the Pacific as warm and damp air approaches the rain front stretching along the main island of Honshu.

title: Meet LaMonica Garrett, who plays Tucker in Taylor Sheridan’s Lioness
description: Named after former Oakland Raiders quarterback Daryle Lamonica, the actor worked as a FedEx driver before landing roles in hit television series such as NCIS and Suits.
content: It has been more than a month since Taylor Sheridan’s spy drama Lioness debuted its third season on Paramount+ on August 2. Inspired by a real-life unit of undercover female agents fighting terrorist organisations, the show boasts an A-list cast led by Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman and Morgan Freeman. The Oscar-nominated writer who created Yellowstone is renowned for working with a recurring ensemble across his projects – a phenomenon dubbed the “Sheridanverse” by fans. Many viewers were already familiar with LaMonica Garrett, who plays Quick Reaction Force operative Tucker in Lioness, long before the show premiered in 2023. So, who is the 51-year-old actor, and which other Sheridanverse titles feature his work? What is LaMonica Garrett’s background? Born in San Francisco in May 1975, LaMonica Garrett was named after former Oakland Raiders quarterback Daryle Lamonica – a nod to his parents’ favourite player, according to his 2017 interview with Muscle & Fitness. Garrett grew up with ambitions of playing American football, inspired by his father, who played semi-professionally in Chicago. When he failed to sign with the NFL, he pivoted to acting – a field in which he had always held a keen interest, he told the fitness magazine. How did LaMonica Garrett break into acting? Per Muscle & Fitness, Garrett worked as a FedEx driver to support himself and pay for acting classes. In the meantime, he also started playing SlamBall – a basketball hybrid game involving trampolines. As fate would have it, the teen drama series One Tree Hill was filming a storyline involving SlamBall, so Garrett landed an audition and appeared in one episode. After that, the actor appeared in shows such as NCIS, Suits, and Designated Survivor. Garrett made his Sheridanverse debut as Thomas in Yellowstone’s prequel 1883 in 2021. In 2023, he returned as Tucker in Lioness. In an interview with TV Insider in August, Garrett expressed his interest in being in Sheridan’s gritty Texas oil rig show, Landman, starring Billy Bob Thornton and Demi Moore. “It’s active, and I consider myself an action guy, so put me on Landman out there with the sun on my back and a big wrench, and have me fix one of these wells or whatever’s going on,” Garrett said. “That would be something that I can get down with.” Who is LaMonica Garrett married to? Garrett has been married to property agent Mina Ivanova since 2017. The couple welcomed their first child together, a son, in 2019. Ivanova also appears to have an older daughter from a previous relationship, according to her Instagram posts.

title: Singapore’s Wong warns racist remarks over Nepal,  Air India risk ‘pulling us apart’
description: The prime minister said racist views expressed online did not represent Singapore as a whole and warned against dismissing them as harmless.
content: Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong warned against a recent spate of racist comments being made online, saying prejudice should not be allowed to become normalised in the multiracial city state. Wong said in a social media post on Sunday that an “uglier side” had emerged in recent online discussions, including remarks about Singaporeans caught in deadly floods in Nepal and debate over Singapore Airlines’ potential investment in Air India. “We can and should have robust debates,” he said. “But we should never use seemingly legitimate arguments as a cover to fuel prejudice against any community or hostility towards foreigners.” The prime minister said racist views expressed online did not represent Singapore as a whole and warned against dismissing them as harmless. “If such behaviour goes unchecked, it can become normalised, deepen mistrust between communities, and pull us apart,” he said. Wong’s comments followed remarks by Senior Minister K. Shanmugam on Saturday, who said police had been asked to look into the matter and would ask online platforms to remove comments that breached rules. In June, authorities ordered social media platforms to block access to 14 online posts that targeted the Indian community in Singapore. Shanmugam said there had been more racist remarks directed at Indians in Singapore recently, including attacks on senior executives at Temasek Holdings over their ethnicity. The senior minister said the state-owned investor, a majority owner of Singapore Airlines, did not account to the government for its individual investments. The government would not interfere in any decision to invest in Air India, saying such decisions should be made on commercial grounds, Shanmugam added. Air India is close to securing 100 billion rupees (US$1.06 billion) in aid from its owners Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines, as the carrier grapples with the fallout from a turbulent year, according to people familiar with the matter. The money was conditional on reaching certain performance milestones and would be paid out in instalments, they said. The support would be proportional to shareholding, they said, with Tata Sons owning 74.9 per cent of Air India and Singapore Airlines, the remainder.

title: Hundreds killed in deadliest Yemen fighting since 2022 truce collapsed
description: Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed forces fight over control of a key Red Sea gateway.
content: The toll from days of fighting between government forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in southwest Yemen climbed past 300 on Sunday, as hundreds of families fled their homes to escape the violence. Two military officials with the Saudi-backed government forces said that 84 of their troops were killed between midday Saturday and early Sunday morning, mostly in missile attacks. Four Houthi military sources said 57 rebel fighters were killed in the same period. The two sides have been fighting for days over control of a gateway to the Red Sea, in the deadliest flare-up in the Arabian Peninsula’s southernmost country since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July. Families fleeing fighting in Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi in Taiz governorate in Yemen’s southwest took refuge at Al-Bareen camp for the internally displaced on Saturday. And on Sunday, Agence France-Presse journalists saw displaced people with mattresses, livestock and other belongings setting up shelters in another camp in the area. “The shooting came at us from above and from below,” said Rawdhah Hasan, a woman displaced from Maqbanah. “They surrounded us from every direction, we fled with our children without even putting on our shoes,” she added. The Houthis launched an offensive on Thursday aiming to cut off the government-held port city of Mokha, under fire for weeks, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandab strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. A military official within the government said that the rebels had succeeded on Saturday evening in “cutting off the road linking Taiz to Mokha”. According to an Agence France-Presse tally compiled using various military and medical sources from both sides of the conflict, more than 300 combatants and some civilians have been killed since the start of the Houthi assault. The UN agency for humanitarian coordination OCHA said on Friday that an estimated 1,790 households had been displaced following “intense shelling and clashes” in Maqbanah and Jabal Habashi districts. A spokesman for UN chief Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the ongoing military clashes”, warning of “devastating political, economic and security ramifications for Yemen and its people”. One military official with the internationally recognised government based in Aden said fighting had subsided in the early hours of Sunday morning. The official said government “forces were able to establish positions for themselves north of Hays after advancing in the area”, referring to a frontline district less than 30km (18.6 miles) inland from the Red Sea coast. But the official added the Houthis had advanced west of Taiz, south of Hays, in their push towards the Bab al-Mandab. With Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships, the Bab al-Mandab chokepoint has gained importance as a transit route, connecting Asia to Europe via the Suez Canal. In July, a fragile truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government fell apart after the rebels welcomed an Iranian plane to the capital Sanaa, setting off a spate of attacks. The Houthis have also announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and have begun targeting its ships and territory.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Primetime movie review – Robert Pattinson catches predators in blunted satire
description: Robert Pattinson plays a fictional version of TV producer and paedophile hunter Chris Hansen in this drama that lacks substance.
content: 3/5 stars The latest entry in the journalism movie category that includes the likes of Network, Nightcrawler, Shattered Glass and Spotlight, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime turns the lens on Dateline NBC, the US news magazine show, and in particular the work of Chris Hansen, the presenter of To Catch a Predator – a disturbing segment that began in 2004. The show aimed to sniff out and expose internet paedophiles who attempted to lure underage children into meeting them. Played with oil-slick excellence by Robert Pattinson – who also serves as a producer – Hansen is a suited-and-booted showman who steps in once predators are caught on camera with a decoy. “What you’re doing matters,” a fellow plane passenger tells him. But in truth, he seems to care little about keeping the streets free of deviancy and is simply out to win the ratings war. Premiering in competition at this year’s Venice International Film Festival, the film sways between Hansen and Dan Plumb (Skyler Gisondo), a 23-year-old would-be actor whose babyish looks make him ideal bait. Recruited by Hansen’s team, run with ruthless efficiency by producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever), Plumb is delighted at first. But a growing queasiness emerges as he confronts these predators – including one who drops his trousers and sprays whipped cream on his manhood. Inspired by real-life events – in particular, a sting operation that went disastrously wrong – Oppenheim’s film asks us to consider the ethics and dangers of such crusading TV shows, and how complicit we might be as an audience howling for justice. Unfortunately, it never achieves this in a meaningful way, with the film’s second half – and its ominous crashes of thunder – lurching into an unsatisfying melodrama. Skating the surface of its subject, the execution feels rather superficial – a thriller with no thrills, its satire blunted. Moreover, Hansen remains too opaque, with the writing never quite getting under the character’s skin. Notably, a subplot involving the National Enquirer chasing him over alleged extramarital activities goes nowhere. As for the predators on the show, they are simply carted off by the police, never to be seen again. The film features some strong cameos, among them Wes Anderson regular Tony Revolori as an abuser, and singer Phoebe Bridgers – baseball cap firmly wedged over her head – as one of Hansen’s decoys voicing both boys and girls. But despite a wonderful seed of an idea, Primetime fails to fully blossom. “Let’s get some justice on camera,” we are told. Adding some substance might also have been a good idea.
