title: Badminton star An Se-young claims hat-trick of China Masters titles ahead of Asian Games
description: South Korean did not drop a game in the tournament, while India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty win men’s doubles.
content: Badminton world No 1 An Se-young sent a warning for the Asian Games as she clinched her third China Masters title in a row in ominous fashion. South Korea’s reigning Olympic and world champion will defend her crown when the Asian Games begin on September 19 in Aichi-Nagoya in Japan. The 24-year-old will be overwhelming favourite after winning the China Masters on Sunday with a ruthless 21-17, 21-6 demolition of Tomoka Miyazaki in Shenzhen. An did not drop a game all week on the way to her seventh title of the season. “I’m so proud of myself. I’m really pleased with the result and I feel so happy,” An said. Despite being the undoubted dominant force in women’s badminton once more this year, An said: “There are many players coming up and challenging. “I don’t think any match can be taken lightly.” The men’s singles final was surprisingly an all-Hong Kong affair, with world No 32 Jason Gunawan defeating Lee Cheuk-yiu 21-9, 21-16. In the men’s doubles, India’s Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty beat home duo He Jiting and Ren Xiangyu in a three-game battle. Shetty and Rankireddy will defend their Asian Games men’s doubles title in Japan. “Going into the Asian Games winning a title definitely reassures us what we are working on is heading in the right direction,” Shetty said. “We will go back home, push ourselves to the limit, train for the next 10 days and go all guns blazing in Japan. We want to go out there and have some fun.” China’s Feng Yanzhe and Huang Dongping won the mixed doubles while Sumire Nakade and Miyu Takahashi of Japan clinched the women’s doubles crown.

title: A not so ‘Dissident Chorus’? Busan Biennale 2026 makes some political noise
description: This year, South Korea’s oldest biennale explores politics through sound, performance and art, but does it truly challenge the status quo?
content: Politics has had a habit of barging into art biennales of late, from the current Gwangju Biennale in South Korea to the Venice Biennale earlier this year. However, at the Busan Biennale, political noise is not an unfortunate sideshow: it is the whole curatorial premise. The curators, Bahraini-Singaporean artist Amal Khalaf and Brussels-based writer Evelyn Simons, have called their edition of South Korea’s oldest biennale, “Dissident Chorus”. The biennale seeks to move away from “the ruins of speech” – a breakdown of trust and the divisiveness of conventional communication – echoing Cameroonian-Swiss curator Koyo Kouoh’s title for this year’s Venice Biennale, “In Minor Keys”. In Busan, the focus on sound is meant to be literal, as is the curators’ intention of bringing politics into the exhibition. Collective acts of listening can create solidarity and political agency, they say, pointing to the 20th century’s history of aural activism – using sound to drive social change. In the 1990s, American electronic music duo Drexciya used music to create an empowering Afrofuturist myth. Their album art, designed by American artist Abdul Qadim Haqq, is displayed prominently in Space OneZ, a former port warehouse and one of the Busan Biennale’s three venues. The House of Korean Protest Songs – an archive preserving the music behind modern social movements – occupies the lobby of the Museum of Contemporary Art Busan (Moca Busan) during the exhibition. Current members of Ultra-red, a sound art collective founded in 1994 by Aids activists in the US, are exhibiting in the former Busan Nam High School and holding workshops designed to generate ideas for political action and community organising. In this vast complex – recently vacated and wonderfully desolate – I had Pink Floyd’s “Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2” playing in my head (“We don’t need no education / We don’t need no thought control”) as I looked at Ultra-red’s upended desks and chairs; Filipino-Australian Bhenji Ra’s 31-screen educational videos on transferring knowledge from the transgender, indigenous and queer communities; and Mongolian artist Jantsankhorol Erdenebayar’s classroom makeover with horns, faux fur and knick-knacks from a flea market. With some works, sound does draw you in, namely Heaven Baek’s score as part of her piece Grass-Grown Corps Over the Sea and the Mountains, and fellow South Korean Hyunsung Park’s pulsating intervention in the kitchen area. One of the raisons d’être of biennales is to commission ambitious artworks, and Moca Busan’s more conventional galleries feature some exceptional pieces. Joshua Serafin’s three-channel film Whispering Pleas of the Eternal Echoes, which sprang from the Filipino’s discovery of a Japanese great-great-grandfather and the questions that arose for Serafin’s family, is a profound visual poetry about the afterlife. The multidisciplinary artist, who uses the pronouns they/them, performs for the first time with their mother in an intimate collaboration that is not the self-indulgent documentary-as-art mode this kind of biographical premise often adopts. South Korean artist Sungsil Ryu’s Ten Thousand Dreams – 12 ghostly dummies in school uniform singing from a scissor lift – is made with the same acerbic humour as seen in her video works, and the sadness and anger about the heavy expectations placed on children is certainly something many visitors can sympathise with. Chinese artist Shuang Li’s work, Alliance (Heart Loop), draws intriguing parallels between tornadoes and media storms, and Belgian artist Tom Hallet’s hand-drawn monumental scroll with 3D prints, XXX, blurs boundaries magnificently. South Korean artist Dew Kim’s site-specific installation, The Stage – After God, moves across the venues in three acts. “Act 1: The Stage of Blood”, at Moca Busan, consists of an altar without a deity, where the historic martyrdom of the queer and nonconforming is revealed, and where pain and pleasure are inseparable. “Act 2: The Empty Center” – a religious ritual ruin – and “Act 3: The Revealed Constellation” follow at the school, the latter of which sees a glass-roofed corridor turned into a stained-glass chamber, where metal hands hold up K-pop light sticks against a techno chorus – not in supplication to a god, but as an independent collective finding its own path. We Carry Our Pain Like a Language, by the Palestinian artist and writer Yazan Khalili, is a circle of baseball cap stacks, each embroidered with a fragment of a poem that can only be read in its entirety when displayed in order. They are for sale to raise money for Palestine-focused initiatives and thus designed to be dispersed. A continuation of his 2025 work Against Total Meaning, it makes us think about the events in Gaza and the West Bank while also raising questions about the commodification of art and, to return to the curators’ phrase, the ruins of speech. Burmese artist Moe Satt brings his project Body, Face and Fingers, a performance and installation exploring how we communicate without words, and the late Pakistani women’s-rights campaigner Lala Rukh’s works based on Hindustani classical music are on display. However, for a biennale about dissidence, it is disappointingly safe. Little truly resonates with how people in this particular region live in an unsettling political climate, apart from Korean documentary maker Lee Dong-keun’s multimedia account of the legacy of Japanese occupation on the Busan island of Gadeokdo, as well as conflicts in places such as Okinawa and Taiwan, and the continuing influence of larger powers. The biennale is not so much a dissident chorus but one that is in accord with the values frequently championed by the contemporary art world today, therefore taking few risks. Another concern is the uneven quality. In some cases, artist’s biographies seem to be used to prolong presentations beyond what the works themselves can sustain. None of this detracts from Khalaf and Simons’ contagious conviction that art can still make a difference, but “Dissident Chorus” is most persuasive when it is not simply presenting the correct politics. Busan Biennale: Dissident Chorus continues until November 1, 2026

title: Australians could opt out of social media algorithms under proposed law
description: The government’s digital duty of care bill forces big tech to offer chronological feeds, but the opposition raises doubts over enforcement.
content: Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said on Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week. It would require firms like Meta Platforms to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste. “A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” Communications Minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm – but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice,” she said “We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds.” Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Under the broader duty of care, tech giants could face fines exceeding A$100 million (US$72 million) for directing users towards “harmful content” through algorithmic recommendation systems, according to local news channel News24. Australia’s opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told ABC that the coalition had not seen the Labour government’s bill. “I am deeply sceptical. I fear that this is going to be an attempt by the government to censor social media, but as I say, we haven’t seen it. Let’s see what the government comes forward with,” he said. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in December, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”. The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under 16s in Australia were increasing their use of social media applications such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban. Additional reporting by SCMP’s Asia Desk

title: Ride-hailing giant Didi Chuxing to apply to test driverless vehicles in Hong Kong
description: Government adviser says mainland Chinese company plans Tseung Kwan O pilot project, with room to expand if business model proves viable.
content: Mainland Chinese ride-hailing giant Didi Chuxing will apply to test autonomous vehicles in a Hong Kong urban area this year, a government adviser has revealed, with the trial runs potentially being expanded later on to cover more new development areas. The announcement followed a visit to Didi’s Beijing headquarters last Wednesday by Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan and a group of lawmakers. Gary Zhang Xinyu, a member of the Transport Department’s working group for promoting autonomous vehicle applications, said on Monday that the company would apply for an autonomous vehicle pilot licence in Hong Kong this year, with initial trial runs planned for Tseung Kwan O. “Tseung Kwan O itself is large and diverse – the town centre, Lohas Park and the industrial estate all have different road conditions,” he told a radio programme. “The industrial estate is a more suitable place to start because the roads are wider, the traffic volume is lower, and the overall environment is relatively simple.” Didi is also recruiting autonomous vehicle test drivers for Tseung Kwan O roles at HK$21,000 to HK$22,000 (US$2,678 to US$2,805) a month, according to a job posting. The listing states that drivers will need to operate vehicles on open roads, as well as record conditions and system performance to ensure safety. Candidates must have held a Hong Kong driving licence for at least five years, with no traffic convictions in the past five years and have experience driving on the mainland. Zhang said testing could be expanded to new development areas such as Tuen Mun’s So Kwun Wat if a viable business model emerged. “In a few years, you will see autonomous vehicles in many places across Hong Kong, and this is something expected to happen,” he said. He added that commercialising autonomous ride-hailing services would require only technical amendments to existing ride-hailing licence frameworks, with the taxi industry already showing strong interest in integrating the technology. From September 2 to 5, transport chief Chan led Legislative Council transport panel members on a duty visit to Beijing, touring Didi’s headquarters and its autonomous driving test facilities in Yizhuang. The delegation inspected the government regulator’s real-time big data centre as part of research into Hong Kong’s coming ride-hailing and autonomous vehicle regulations. Ben Chan Han-pan, chairman of Legco’s transport panel and a fellow delegation leader, said riding in driverless vehicles in the Yizhuang autonomous driving zone showed the technology was highly mature, operating smoothly without a safety driver on board. He noted Hong Kong’s route-based testing differed from the mainland’s zone-based model and that local roads were less complex. “We welcome capable companies to test here because they bring technology and talent, but they must meet our legal requirements, and we will not lower standards,” Chan said. Baidu received Hong Kong’s first pilot licence for autonomous vehicles in November 2024, launching tests in North Lantau the following month. The Transport Department has since issued nine pilot licences covering 69 vehicles across areas including West Kowloon, Hong Kong International Airport and the University MTR station.

title: Prabowo-Putin payoff: can bond between Indonesian, Russian leaders translate to gains?
description: Good relations with Russia show ‘our president can work with all sides across the geopolitical divide,’ an analyst says.
content: The rapport between Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto and his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, was evident when the two met during the 11th Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok last week. “My profound apologies for missing this important event due to urgent matters I needed to attend to back home but I’m now here to repay my debt,” Prabowo told Putin on Wednesday, referring to a missed invitation earlier to be the guest of honour at Russia’s National Day celebration on June 12. Putin in turn referenced their “continued personal contact” and “strategic nature of the relationship between Russia and Indonesia”. The EEF is an annual event to encourage investment and development in Russia’s far east. Delegations from some 50 countries such as China and Myanmar also attended, with Prabowo and Mongolian Prime Minister Nyam-Osoryn Uchral the two highest-ranked officials representing their countries. But bonhomie aside, observers are divided on whether the Prabowo-Putin camaraderie will result in tangible results. “Prabowo has raised Indonesia’s international profile abroad by undertaking various foreign visits, pushing to advance our interests,” said Bawono Kumoro, a researcher at Jakarta-based pollster Indikator Politik. “Good relations with Russia are proof that our president can work with all sides across the geopolitical divide, and are in line with his motto, ‘One thousand friends are too few, one enemy is too many.’” Prabowo’s visit showed the opportunity for bilateral growth, said Dipo Satria Ramli, an economist at the Centre of Reform on Economics. “In theory, the trade structure between Indonesia and Russia is complementary and its underdeveloped state means there are a lot of areas that could be worked on,” he said. Trade between Indonesia and Russia last year was valued at US$5 billion, a mere 1 per cent of Jakarta’s total foreign trade. Last December, Indonesia signed a free-trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union – which includes Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Russia. It was ratified by the Indonesian parliament and signed into law by Prabowo earlier in July. During a panel discussion at the EEF, Prabowo was asked why he had signed the deal, despite what he claimed to be “overwhelming pressure from Washington”. He insisted on Indonesia’s neutrality when dealing with great powers. “We don’t belong to any military alliances and economically we are also independent,” he said, stressing his desire to work with all countries. “This was very clear from day one. In all our negotiations with our partners, they know this from the beginning.” Prabowo’s friendship with Putin “may be testing the limits of our non-alignment policy but as long as he doesn’t commit to any military alliance, it’s no violation”, Bawono said. ‘Budding relationship’ Radityo Dharmaputra, a foreign policy analyst and lecturer at the Centre for European and Eurasian Studies at Surabaya’s Airlangga University, however, challenged the strategic value of attending events such as the EEF. “It’s relatively unimportant and more about Russia’s interest rather than Indonesia’s.” Prabowo might have been star-struck by Putin, he suggested. “Prabowo appears to view Putin as one of his references of what a great and strong leader should be and Putin knows this.” This, he added, would explain why Putin had extended several personal invitations to Prabowo. The Indonesian president first visited Russia for the June 2025 St Petersburg International Economic Forum. Both leaders met again in Moscow five months later for bilateral talks. In April, Prabowo reprised his visit to the Russian capital, where he signed an agreement to buy 150 million barrels of Russian oil. “Their budding relationship will be a driving factor for stronger Indonesia-Russia relations, but the problem lies with implementation,” Radityo said, pointing to the oil refinery project in Tuban, East Java as an example. The refinery, worth US$24 billion in investment, was set up in 2017 as a joint venture between Indonesia’s PT Pertamina and Russia’s Rosneft. It is projected to be able to refine 300,000 barrels of crude oil a day when completed. Its status, however, is currently in limbo due to delayed funding from Rosneft as a result of ongoing Western sanctions against the Russian energy sector. “One possible avenue for closer cooperation would be education and cultural exchange,” Radityo said, noting that Russia had started a significant roll-out of scholarships for Indonesians and signed strategic partnerships with Indonesian universities. “Russia has also been growing its soft power in Indonesia through working with our local and youth NGOs, including sponsoring exchange trips to Russia.” Indonesia-Russia trade ties, though, are insignificant, according to Radityo. “Russia wants Indonesia to buy more of their fertilisers but Indonesia can switch to other producers, such as China. They also want to sell more wheat to us but they are hardly the only option,” he said. “Even in the military sphere, Orruda [the joint exercise between the Indonesian and Russian navies] is puny compared to the Super Garuda Shield.” While Prabowo was rubbing shoulders with Putin in Vladivostok, around 5,000 troops from Indonesia, the US and 13 other nations were engaged in the joint military exercise Super Garuda Shield 2026 on Indonesian soil and waters. The simultaneous events reflected a somewhat “incoherent” foreign policy by Jakarta, he said. “If Prabowo’s focus was financial and economic investment, he would go to China and the Middle East more often, rather than Russia, France or the UK,” Radityo said.

title: HSBC-backed platform drives green transition capital to emerging markets amid global risks
description: World may need up to US$20 trillion over five to eight years to build or upgrade renewable energy facilities, HSBC executive says.
content: HSBC has teamed up with partners to launch a non-profit platform to help emerging markets in upgrading their technology and shifting from oil and coal to renewable energy, according to a senior executive at the lender. The Green Accelerator Programme, rolled out on Monday with backing from HSBC, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Silk Road Fund and others, will channel private capital into feasibility studies and due diligence for emerging-market companies and governments adopting green technology. “Geopolitical disruptions such as those in the Strait of Hormuz have accelerated demand for resilient, alternative energy sources,” said Julian Wentzel, chief sustainability officer at HSBC, in an interview with the South China Morning Post. HSBC has seen an increase in demand for green financing since the US-Israel war on Iran started in late February, which has driven up oil prices and prompted global companies to seek cheaper, more stable energy supplies. Wentzel said such a trend presented huge opportunities for the banking industry, as companies and governments would need to raise funds to finance up to US$20 trillion in global expenditure over the next five to eight years to establish or upgrade their facilities to use renewable energy or other clean energy. This included global corporate transition spending, currently estimated at US$2.3 trillion per year and expected to increase to US$3.6 trillion per year by 2030. It is probably the most significant and fastest scale of deployment of capital I have seen in my over 30 years in banking Julian Wentzel, HSBC The growing demand for energy to support artificial intelligence infrastructure would require an additional US$5 trillion in expenditure over the next five to eight years, he said. “It is probably the most significant and fastest scale of deployment of capital I have seen in my over 30 years in banking,” Wentzel said. HSBC in 2025 offered US$102 billion in sustainable finance and investment, bringing the total to US$495.6 billion since 2000, he said. This puts the bank on track to meet its target of offering between US$750 billion and US$1 trillion in sustainable finance and investment by 2030. The increasing demand for renewable energy technology and low-cost energy will benefit both Hong Kong and mainland China. “China is very much leading in high-quality, low-cost renewable energy equipment,” Wentzel said. “China accounts for nearly 70 per cent of the technology and equipment in this transition economy, ranging from turbines, photovoltaic cells and battery technology.” Hong Kong, with its active capital market and high disclosure standards, has become a hub for mainland companies and other international firms to raise funds to finance their green projects. “Hong Kong is a leader in green finance as it serves as a critical capital hub and a conduit between China and the rest of the world for renewable technology investment,” he said. “The city provides deep capital markets through green bonds, sustainable bonds, transition-labelled instruments, and project finance.” Investors were interested in investing in green bonds or other green finance projects as they could provide good returns, Wentzel said. He pointed out that renewable energy offered a faster time-to-market compared to traditional power plants, with solar plants potentially being deployed in 18 months while traditional power plants may need several years to establish.

title: How China’s green tech is undercutting Trump’s ‘drill, baby, drill’ oil strategy in Africa
description: Record photovoltaic additions and major infrastructure deals allow developing nations to bypass fossil fuel price shocks.
content: In the US, the push is on to “drill, baby, drill”. In China, the national strategy is to “walk towards the light”. Two energy behemoths, two contrasting approaches to energy. For African countries working out which way to go, the deciding factor is cost and, with China’s advances in solar generation and battery technologies making acquisitions cheaper, a consensus is coalescing across the continent around renewables. “Africa’s solar revolution is here,” said Sonia Dunlop, CEO of the Global Solar Council (GSC). “Growth is spreading to new markets across the continent, and rooftop and distributed systems are putting power directly into the hands of households and businesses.” Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East had delivered “two major fossil fuel supply shocks in four years” that “exposed the brutal cost of energy dependence”, Dunlop noted. But cheap solar and improved battery storage had enabled the rapid replacement of fossil fuels with solar power across Africa, she said. Africa’s solar additions surged a record 54 per cent in 2025, according to the GSC, adding as much as 4.5 gigawatts in new photovoltaic power. With the US-Israel war on Iran causing the biggest disruption in oil and gas supply in history, this year’s installations are expected to set another record. Across Africa, China has been involved in developing several renewable energy projects including hydroelectric, wind and solar. Among them is the 1.8GW Benban Solar Park in Aswan, Egypt, completed in 2019 and involving state-owned China Energy Engineering Corporation and TBEA, a green energy equipment manufacturer. Ethiopia’s Adama I and II wind farms, with a combined capacity of 204 megawatts, were funded by the China Exim Bank and built by HydroChina and the CGCOC Group in 2015, which marked the start of the country’s journey towards tapping wind power potential of up to 1,300GW. Together with the 5,150MW Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, the country is working towards complete reliance on green power supply and streets filled with electric cars. South Africa’s De Aar wind power project, offering a capacity of 244MW, was developed and is run by China Longyuan Power Group and China Energy Investment Corporation, serving more than 300,000 homes in the country’s Northern Cape province. South Africa is the continent’s biggest importer of solar-related power products, enough to generate 3GW of power annually, according to official trade figures. Morocco hosts China’s most ambitious green footprint in Africa, leveraging its position as a bridge to Europe to build a manufacturing and export hub – including a US$1.3 billion electric vehicle gigafactory and battery component facilities capable of powering 1 million EVs annually. China has also supported renewable energy development across several African countries. In Kenya, it built a solar plant to bring clean power to rural communities previously dependent on diesel, while in Zambia and the Ivory Coast it has funded and constructed major hydroelectric projects. In Nigeria, the continent’s most populous nation, significant developments illustrating “both the urgency and the opportunity” to cut fossil fuel demand are unfolding, according to the GSC. With barely seven hours of grid supply daily, Nigerian households were forced to rely on some 22 million petrol- or diesel-powered generators, costing about US$12 billion a year to run, according to the 2025 “Connecting the Sun” study produced by GSC. These generated eight times more power than the national grid, the study noted, but came with high environmental and health costs. A surge in solar installations in the country since the Ukraine war began is curbing this fossil fuel demand. “High fuel costs are the real accelerant” for renewable energy adoption across Africa, said Cheta Nwanze, a partner and analyst at SBM Intelligence, an economic research firm based in Lagos, Nigeria. “Cheap Chinese panels simply made the alternative viable.” Under a policy change announced in April, the Nigerian government adopted a decentralised grid system to tap into the excess power generated from homes while enabling the establishment of off-grid power and interconnected mini-grids – all reliant on solar power. New business models in real estate, power supply and distribution are emerging to take advantage of the decentralised regime. Given Africa’s rapid population growth and burgeoning middle class, the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, or Opec, projects that oil demand on the continent will continue growing, doubling to 9.2 million barrels a day by 2050. It is an estimate now challenged by rising oil and gas prices and increased adoption of renewable alternatives. With 60 per cent of the world’s best solar resources, Africa needs annual investments of US$190 billion between 2026 and 2030 to achieve a transition to clean energy, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The IEA projects that Africa’s solar power deployment this year will surpass last year’s. The agency noted in a report that 15 major African markets imported more than US$400 million worth of solar panels in the first quarter of this year alone, compared with US$600 million for all of 2025. Moreover, as the retreat from crude oil gathers pace in Africa and other parts of the world, global oil producers may be heading towards an oversupply trap, according to analysts. Oil producers, including the US, face the double-edged risk of “price wars from oversupply” and renewable energy taking away their customers, according to Nwanze. “Trump is expanding supply into a market where China is exporting the technology that erodes long-term demand for that supply.”

title: Letters | Are we preserving the Hong Kong tourists come here for?
description: Readers discuss the new tourism campaign, and construction schedules in an era of climate change.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The Tourism Board’s new “Only in Hong Kong” campaign gets something right. Rather than leaning on mega-events and headline attractions, it turns its attention to Hong Kong experiences that are authentic and distinctive: tram rides, neighbourhood streets, dai pai dong, wet markets and scenes that visitors are more likely to remember long after they leave. That approach reflects how travel is changing. Increasingly, people are looking for a sense of place rather than another skyline to photograph. What stays with them is often not a landmark but the atmosphere around it. If Hong Kong wants to market itself through feeling and experience, it needs to preserve more of the things that create that feeling in the first place. The reaction to the filming of Highlander on Peel Street was a good reminder. The production recreated a Hong Kong streetscape with neon signs and hawker stalls, drawing hundreds of onlookers. While Henry Cavill helped attract the crowds, the fascination with the setting was hard to miss. Part of the appeal was the familiarity of seeing a streetscape that felt unmistakably Hong Kong, even though it had been reconstructed for a Hollywood production. None of this is an argument against development. Hong Kong should continue to build public spaces and neighbourhoods, but another polished mall, however impressive, is unlikely to be what visitors remember most. What gives the city its identity is often less spectacular: the layers of old and new, formal and informal, polished and improvised that have accumulated across its districts. Neon is perhaps the greatest example. It remains one of the visual signatures of Hong Kong in films and tourism advertisements, even though far less of it survives in the streets. Where modern safety standards can be met, more old signs should be retained and restored, while new neon should not just be confined to museums. The same principle should apply more broadly to wet markets, dai pai dong, hawker stalls and the everyday street life that gives neighbourhoods their identity. That is the opportunity that should be created by “Only in Hong Kong”. If the campaign is right that what makes a destination memorable is how it feels, the city should apply that same thinking beyond advertising and make sure the character it sells to the world can still be found in its streets. Adam Kwong Wing-hoi, Clear Water Bay Planning practices should change with the climate Our city is facing record-breaking weather, with more hot nights and increasingly extreme weather, so protecting outdoor workers is a pressing challenge. I welcome the government’s recent revision of the Heat Stress at Work Warning system, which recognises the risks faced by workers who spend long hours outdoors. However, I believe there is room for a broader policy discussion. Rather than focus only on how people work during extreme heat, we should also consider when certain types of work are performed. For non-emergency outdoor public works, especially those requiring prolonged exposure to direct sunlight such as road works and infrastructure construction, the government could plan and concentrate these activities between October and June. Temperatures are generally lower and there is a reduced risk of disruption from heat, heavy rain and typhoons. This would help safeguard workers’ health, improve productivity and reduce weather-related delays. To offset any impact on project timelines, the government could consider limited relaxation of noise restrictions, for example, allowing half-day shifts on bank holidays with appropriate controls and community consultation. If the public sector leads, hopefully the private sector will soon follow. This would not be a novel approach. Around the world, construction schedules are adapted to local climate conditions. India plans projects around the monsoon season, while Norway often limits concrete pours during winter because of operational difficulties. Building a climate-resilient city also means protecting our outdoor workers while balancing economic needs and the efficient delivery of public works. As the climate changes, our planning practices should evolve too. Henry Yau, Tai Po

title: Inside the Bulgari Kaleidos exhibition celebrating vibrant high jewellery in Shanghai
description: The immersive show, designed by Sanaa and Formafantasma, also features two installations by Chinese artists Liang Manqi and Zhang Ding.
content: Bulgari is the jeweller that perhaps, more than any other, is known for its bold and unexpected colour combinations – chromatic clashes, you may even call them – but the house’s love affair with vivid hues only began in the mid-40s and truly blossomed in the 50s. During World War II, when platinum had to be mainly used for weaponry, Western jewellers turned to yellow gold. While Bulgari’s French counterparts – based in Paris’ Place Vendôme – returned to platinum after the conflict, the Italian maison continued its predilection for yellow gold, which looks best when paired with coloured gems, Gislain Aucremanne, Bulgari’s heritage curator director, explained in an interview in Shanghai. Established in 1884 in Rome by Sotirio Bulgari, a Greek silversmith, the house – which was acquired by luxury group LVMH in 2011 – is one of the crown jewels of Italian savoir faire. While many know Bulgari for its Greek and Roman heritage and its Serpenti snake motif, the maison is also deservedly praised as the master of colours, as an exhibition currently on view at Shanghai’s Power Station of Art illustrates in depth. Titled “Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts” and named after the Greek words kalos (beautiful) and eidos (form), the exhibition, which first debuted in Tokyo last year, celebrates the power of colours not just from an aesthetic point of view. It also tackles topics such as colour theory and the way shades ranging from red to green affect humans, both from a scientific and an emotional perspective. Aucremanne aptly describes Bulgari’s use of colours as “a proper language of its own”. While most jewellers have always gravitated towards classical coloured stones like rubies, sapphires and emeralds, Bulgari has never been afraid to experiment with semi-precious stones. Amethyst, topaz, garnet, rubellite and coral are just some of the gems used by the Bulgari ateliers in Rome to create painterly chromatic compositions. “I always compare Bulgari to a painter, with pigments on a palette but with gemstones,” says Aucremanne. “These colours are put together to speak to the world, create a design which is recognisable, identifiable as Bulgari, and the stones are selected because they have a soul, a certain something.” Displaying more than 300 items, the exhibition is divided into three chapters: The Science of Colours, Colour Symbolism and The Power of Light. Designed by Japanese architecture firm Sanaa alongside Italian design studio Formafantasma, the immersive show also features two installations by Chinese artists – Liang Manqi and Zhang Ding – who were given carte blanche to interpret the theme and offer their takes on it. The Shanghai version of the show, which will travel around the world and make a stop in Dubai next, also pays homage to its location with a section devoted to the Chinese Five Elements system (Wu Xing). An entire gallery is dedicated to jade creations dating back to the early days of Bulgari, when the Rome boutique on Via Condotti featured a jade gallery displaying original pieces from China reworked into Bulgari creations. A necklace in gold with coral, onyx and diamonds, for instance, features as its centrepiece a pendant decorated with an engraved jade medallion, a perfect example of this dialogue between China and Italy, East and West. Rather than taking a chronological approach, which Aucremanne believes would feel too didactic and fall flat with today’s audiences, he and his team wanted to highlight what makes the house special, focusing on an aspect unique to Bulgari but also very universal. “Fortunately, and finally, jewellery is today considered a form of art,” he says. “It’s an art you transmit. There are a lot of personal emotions [and memories] from your grandmother or grandfather. It’s precious and [linked to] the past and it’s three-dimensional and sculptural. It’s an amazing human craft, made from anonymous hands.” “Bvlgari Kaleidos: Colors, Cultures and Crafts” is on view until October 31, 2026 at Shanghai’s Power Station of Art

title: Philanthropic giving in Asia forecast to hit US$1.5 trillion over next decade
description: Corporate giving makes up the largest share of philanthropic spending in Hong Kong, report says.
content: Philanthropic giving in nine Asian jurisdictions is projected to hit US$1.5 trillion over the next decade, while corporate contributions play a larger role in Hong Kong than in many regional peers, according to a new report released at a Jockey Club forum. The Commission on Asian Philanthropy released its interim report on Monday. In a separate report, the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust said the club had generated economic value equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of the city’s gross domestic product (GDP) in the 2024-25 financial year. Both reports were released on the opening day of the Jockey Club’s PBC (Philanthropy for Better Cities) Forum 2026, which marked the event’s 10th anniversary and brought together about 2,000 delegates from across philanthropy, sport, government, business and academia. Organisations taking part in the two-day forum included the Gates Foundation, founded by American tech pioneer Bill Gates and his ex-wife Melinda French Gates, and the Yao Foundation, the non-profit charity founded by former NBA star Yao Ming. At the opening ceremony, Jockey Club chairman Martin Liao Cheung-kong said the forum had given Hong Kong an opportunity to “showcase its credentials” as a global hub, while reinforcing its role as a bridge between East and West. “We are gathering at a critical time,” he said. “Philanthropy is growing in importance because governments are no longer alone in confronting the world’s most profound challenges. “Today, communities, businesses and civic society are all grappling with ever more complex social needs, demographic shifts, technological disruption and the pressing realities of climate change.” Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Hong Kong’s No 2 official, said the government was fully committed to turning the city into a global centre for philanthropy. “Under the ‘one country, two systems’ principle, and as a bridge between East and West, we are uniquely positioned to deploy global capital for the greater good,” he said. Helen Clark, New Zealand’s prime minister from 1999 to 2008, delivered the event’s keynote address, highlighting philanthropy’s role in addressing challenges during a time of geopolitical turbulence. “My overall message is that we should not be without hope and agency that we can bring about better times, and that philanthropy has a vital role to play in that as others falter,” she said. The Commission on Asian Philanthropy, which launched at the previous forum in 2024, comprises 13 charitable organisations from 10 jurisdictions across the region, including the Jockey Club Charities Trust. Taken together, the 10 jurisdictions – which include Hong Kong, mainland China, Singapore, Japan, and Saudi Arabia – account for 70 per cent of Asia’s population and 80 per cent of its GDP. Excluding the United Arab Emirates, whose data is not readily available, the commission’s interim report noted philanthropic giving across the other nine jurisdictions amounted to US$109 billion in 2024. When accounting for “organic growth” based on GDP projections, the commission estimated that such giving could reach as high as US$1.5 trillion over the next decade. The report identified an additional US$189 billion in monetary resources over the next decade if each of the surveyed jurisdictions were able to achieve “upside opportunity”. The metric reflects philanthropic models in each jurisdiction that are considered to have more room to grow and innovate. The commission also found that across the surveyed jurisdictions, individuals overall accounted for about 50 per cent of charitable giving, followed by companies at 25 per cent and state-led contributions at 21 per cent. Ultra-high-net-worth individuals contributed 4 per cent, it noted. In Hong Kong, however, corporate giving made up the largest share of domestic philanthropic spending, at 43 per cent, while individual giving was the second lowest, at 39 per cent. Giving by high-net-worth individuals was also the second highest among the jurisdictions surveyed, at 10 per cent. It was behind only Saudi Arabia, where such giving made up 12 per cent of the total. Separately, the Jockey Club Charities Trust released an inaugural report quantifying the impact of the philanthropic body’s work in Hong Kong for the first time. Citing an independent study by KPMG Advisory, the Jockey Club said it had contributed about HK$55.4 billion (US$7.07 billion) in economic value to Hong Kong during 2024-25, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of the city’s GDP. It also supported 52,000 full-time equivalent positions – a standardised metric based on working hours – representing 1.4 per cent of total employment in the city during the period. In a foreword to the report, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said the Jockey Club’s “value creation model” had helped the city to become a philanthropic hub, calling it “distinctive, truly made-in-Hong Kong innovation that has stood the test of time”. “Most importantly, this is an excellent adjunct to Hong Kong’s growing role as a wealth management hub for family offices, adding momentum to the initiatives the government has strongly promoted and where excellent progress has been achieved,” he said. Among a slew of announcements on Monday, the Jockey Club said it had approved a HK$134 million donation through its charities trust for the five-year Jockey Club Hoops Connect Community Basketball Programme. It said the programme would help enable more young people to learn how to play basketball while aligning with the nation’s 15th five-year plan, which called for the acceleration of China into a leading sports nation. Meanwhile, the Jockey Club remained Asia’s top corporate giver and the eighth-largest globally in the latest rankings by non-profit consultancy Bridgespan Group, with its annual average spending between 2020 and 2024 reaching US$774 million. When measured by institutional philanthropic giving – including private foundations, corporate foundations and state-linked entities focused on philanthropic work – the Jockey Club ranked 11th globally.

title: Armed man arrested after charging towards Ohio governor candidate
description: Democratic nominee Amy Acton was unharmed in the incident after suspect carrying pistols was tackled.
content: An armed assailant charged towards the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people before he was stopped by troopers, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said. The Ohio State Highway Patrol said in a statement that a man it identified as Patrick Havas, 38, forced his way through a crowd, knocking over multiple members of the audience as he moved towards Acton, the state’s former public health director. He had a taser and two pistols, the statement said. The Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after his arrest, and “no weapons were ever brandished or even removed from their holsters”. Havas was taken to the county jail and booked on charges of disorderly conduct and two counts of assault, the highway patrol statement said, adding that no other details were available pending an investigation. Republican Governor Mike DeWine said in a statement that the man “tried to forcefully push himself” towards Acton as she was speaking at the fair in Canfield, in northeastern Ohio. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable,” he added. The attempted attack is the latest political violence to roil the United States. And the Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most high-profile races this year as the campaigns enter the final six weeks of campaigning before the election in November. Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticise Acton. Ramaswamy’s campaign called the incident Sunday unacceptable. “Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement. Addie Bullock, communications director for Acton’s campaign, said in a statement that the suspect “lunged” at Acton. She said the Democratic candidate “will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another”. The incident brought condemnation from Ohio Republican Senator Jon Husted, who said on X that he and his wife were “disturbed by the attempted attack on Amy Acton today at the Canfield Fair. We are grateful for law enforcement’s quick response. There is no place for this kind of behaviour, and it must never be tolerated”. The country has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade. That includes the 2017 shooting at a Republican congressional baseball team practice in Alexandria, Virginia; the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of Democratic then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California; the 2024 assassination attempt on Trump at a Pennsylvania rally during his presidential campaign as well as another on the president at this year’s White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations last year of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk in Utah.

title: How generative AI helps SenseTime turn a profit even as Chinese peers struggle
description: The AI firm has managed to become profitable by carving out a niche involving one-person firms and productivity tools, company executives say.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence pioneer SenseTime is carving a unique path to profitability by steering away from a blind chase for model size, focusing instead on helping clients complete enterprise tasks, executives from the firm told the South China Morning Post. Speaking after the firm reported a net profit of 617.3 million yuan (US$92.0 million) for the first half of 2026 last week, executives including CEO Xu Li and chief financial officer Wang Zheng outlined how a pivot towards AI productivity tools and solo entrepreneurs had helped SenseTime create a sustainable business model. The performance – SenseTime’s first-ever first-half profit under International Financial Reporting Standards since its 2021 Hong Kong listing – marks a stark turning point for the company. Revenue rose 23.4 per cent year on year to 2.91 billion yuan. It also stands in sharp contrast to high-flying domestic peers. While fellow Chinese AI champions MiniMax and Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, both reported triple-digit revenue growth for the same period, they also logged net losses of US$358 million and 2.07 billion yuan (US$308 million), respectively. SenseTime’s core capabilities – spanning models, a token factory and an agent-harness system – have each formed “an independent commercial closed loop”, Xu said. “Among pure-play AI companies, we are one of the very few whose overall business trend is clearly moving in the direction of profitability,” Wang added. Central to the turnaround is the rapid monetisation of generative AI, which contributed 2.33 billion yuan, accounting for nearly 80 per cent of total group sales. For the first time, SenseTime disclosed its recurring revenue, which surged 124.4 per cent year on year to 1.14 billion yuan, representing nearly 40 per cent of sales. According to Xu, fresh momentum was stemming from a shift in user demographics. Rather than relying solely on traditional corporate IT procurement, SenseTime’s AI agents were penetrating frontline business units and “one-person companies” – solo entrepreneurs leveraging automated workflow tools. This aligned with a broader industry transition away from charging for raw computing power towards pricing for finished tasks delivered by AI agents or apps. “Frankly speaking, the token maximisation seen in many current projects looks more like paying tuition out of fear of missing out,” Xu said. “What we pursue is final value, priced by tasks ... . When you can charge by task, you truly penetrate the value of the production process ... and the gross margin of tasks is definitely high.” Gross profit margin for the first half exceeded expectations at over 41 per cent. Wang expressed confidence that the financial improvement was sustainable, forecasting that SenseTime would maintain profitability on an adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation basis while likely pushing full-year operating cash flow into positive territory. To support surging demand, SenseTime said it served a daily average of 2.4 trillion tokens in July. The company was partnering with the Hong Kong Science Park to build what it described as the city’s largest domestic AI computing centre, targeting 40,000 petaflops of compute capacity by 2030. Wang said SenseTime was expanding its infrastructure using a flexible mix of asset-heavy and asset-light models, adding that its investment strategy may lean slightly more aggressive moving forward given “quite ideal” returns on compute, although he did not specify an exact target. Looking ahead, Xu dismissed short-term market anxiety, emphasising that SenseTime remained focused on breaking through limits in model intelligence rather than simply expanding parameter scale. “If you look at the AI market today, as long as you can achieve a breakthrough at that critical point, you will always have a seat at the table,” he said.

title: North Korea’s Kim launches second nuclear destroyer as US-South Korea-Japan drills start
description: ‘Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened’, Kim says at the commissioning of the Kang Kon, just 75 days after the Choe Hyon.
content: North Korean leader Kim Jong-un commissioned his second naval destroyer and called for building a more reliable nuclear deterrent, state media reported on Monday, as the US, South Korea and Japan began a trilateral military exercise he views as a security threat. The development comes as North Korea dials up pressure on the US after rebuffing President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back a major military drill with South Korea in a conciliatory step towards Kim. Observers say North Korea wants to wrest bigger US concessions. The destroyer Kang Kon was commissioned into North Korea’s navy in the eastern port city of Wonsan on Sunday at a ceremony attended by Kim and teenage daughter Ju-ae, whom South Korea’s spy service calls his likely heir. Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) photos showed the girl dressed in a white dress and blazer walking alongside her father on a red carpet, touring the warship and posing with sailors together. The ship and the Choe Hyon, commissioned in June, are both 5,000-tonne destroyers equipped with nuclear-capable missiles, making them North Korea’s most advanced warships. In a speech at the ceremony, Kim said the destroyers’ back-to-back commissioning instilled fear in the enemies as the nuclear armament of North Korea’s navy made it possible to exercise its nuclear deterrent in a more diversified, practical manner. “Concerns of the enemies will be surely deepened,” Kim said. “We must establish more clearly a powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent, to put into practice the diverse and effective operation of our nuclear combat systems and further strengthen our military activities for maritime defence and war deterrence.” KCNA did not specify ‌what weapons systems might be deployed on the Kang Kon, but said it had ⁠the same systems as the Choe Hyon. A previous KCNA report said Choe Hyon-class destroyers ⁠could carry a range of weapons, including missiles that analysts said were capable of carrying a nuclear payload. Kim said he would demonstrate another ‌stage of North Korea’s naval ‌build-up in eight months, KCNA reported, without giving details. He also said the construction of naval bases on North Korea’s east coast was under way and that the country would create new naval units and build different classes of warships. Military drills On Monday, the US, South Korea and Japan were set to kick off their five-day Freedom Edge exercise in the waters off South Korea’s southern Jeju Island. South Korea’s military recently said the exercise was defensive in nature and was meant to respond to North Korea’s nuclear threats. Last week, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused the US of more clearly expressing its confrontational posture against the North. It cited the Freedom Edge exercise and US officials’ reported comments that the US remained committed to the complete denuclearisation of North Korea. On August 21, the US and South Korean militaries ended their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise six days earlier than originally planned, after Trump said he ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” the drill. Trump cited what he described as a good relationship with Kim, who views the drill as an invasion rehearsal. But Kim’s sister and senior official, Kim Yo-jong, shrugged off Trump’s outreach, saying just shortening the drill would not change its “provocative, aggressive nature”. North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea, apparently delivering on its previous threat to respond to the US-South Korean drill. Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the US dropped its “hostile policy” against North Korea and respected what he called North Korea’s status as a nuclear state. Kim and Trump’s earlier diplomacy collapsed in 2019 due to disputes over how much economic benefit North Korea should get in return for a limited denuclearisation step. Now with his advancing nuclear programme and deepened ties with Russia and China, experts say Kim has greater leverage than before. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: In Focus | China’s ‘Tesla imitators’ have a new mission: build affordable humanoid robots for consumers
description: Robotics has supply chain synergy with smart EV production because key components like cameras and radar, as well as software, are in both.
content: When Nio CEO William Li outlined earnings prospects for the Shanghai-based carmaker in March, he could not help but liken the automotive business to the development of robots. “I think robotics will represent a natural extension of our carmaking capabilities and business acumen,” Li told reporters at a media briefing after Nio posted its first-ever quarterly profits for the three months ending December. “Don’t you think that every car we produce in the future will actually be a robot? Its perception, decision-making, and execution will all be based on artificial intelligence.” While Li has adopted a “latecomer” strategy in robotics to avoid potential big losses in early-stage investment, he is convinced that robotics and carmaking have synergistic benefits. The premium cars Nio is building already embody perception, decision-making and control systems – similar to those of robots. That perspective on the future of mobility, buoyed by rapid growth of physical AI, is typical of the more than 10 Chinese manufacturers of intelligent vehicles that have ventured into robotics. These players, from BYD – the world’s largest electric vehicle (EV) maker – to Stellantis-backed Leapmotor, are once again being labelled as Tesla imitators because the US carmaker is accelerating commercialisation of its humanoid robot Optimus. Some of the Chinese firms – with clear-cut time frames to begin production and deliveries of self-developed robots – could compete against Elon Musk’s Tesla on an equal footing in robotics, buoyed by government support, an integrated supply chain and consumer willingness to embrace new technologies, according to analysts. “AI’s enhanced role in cars provides a catalyst to automotive companies’ diversification into robotics,” said Qian Kang, owner of a vehicle circuit board factory in eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “More importantly, Tesla’s business scope and model is inspiring Chinese companies to explore embodied AI.” The robotics sector has supply chain synergy with smart EV production because key components like cameras and radar, as well as software, are needed for both. Other key parts, from motors to heat control systems, are strongholds for automotive firms but also actively sought after by robot builders. Chinese EV maker Xpeng and autonomous driving technology developer Baidu got off to an early start in building robots. Five years ago, they offered a sneak peek into their vision of the future of mobility, underscoring the role of robotics technology. In August 2021, when Baidu founder and CEO Robin Li Yanhong unveiled a prototype “robocar”, he said that in the future “a car will be equivalent to a robot”. The two-seat vehicle looked like something out of a science fiction movie. It had no steering wheel or pedals, featured two retractable doors, and the cockpit was dominated by a large curved intelligent display and a control pad. A month later, Guangzhou-based Xpeng announced its plan to release a four-legged robot pony for children, banking on its design and manufacturing capabilities to churn out robotic products equipped with power modules, motion controls, intelligent navigation, and emotional interaction capabilities. Today, Chinese carmakers are viewed as strong rivals to Tesla as they meld the latest AI technologies with mobility, industry officials and analysts said. In December, Musk endorsed Xpeng’s Iron humanoid robot on social media while predicting Chinese companies would ­dominate the global robotics market alongside Tesla. Tesla has yet to sell any of its Optimus humanoid robots, and Musk is now transforming the EV maker from a hardware-centric business into a ­physical AI firm. Tesla has halted production of its Model S and Model X cars at its plant in Fremont, California, and instead will build humanoid robots in the facility. In April, Tesla’s China president, Allan Wang Hao, said the company’s Shanghai Gigafactory had the potential to produce humanoid robots, taking advantage of the mainland’s complete supply chain and advanced manufacturing techniques. The contest between Chinese carmakers and Tesla in humanoid robots takes on broader importance in the context of the heated China-US tech rivalry. The two countries are battling for supremacy in a number of fields, with humanoid robotics one of the key areas where Beijing and Washington hope their companies can establish global dominance. Thanks to the country’s diverse supply chain and large production scale, upstream Chinese suppliers could make high-quality, cost-efficient and innovative components for various types of robots, including humanoids, according to Lu Hancheng, former director of the Shenzhen-based Gaogong Robot Industry Research Institute. Mainland China was now home to more than 150 humanoid robot makers, according to the National Development and Reform Commission. They delivered 97 per cent of the total humanlike robots on the global market in the first half of the year, according to Morgan Stanley. Early this year, the US bank predicted that the global humanoid market would achieve US$7.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2050. Morgan Stanley also forecast in July that China’s humanoid robot shipments could hit 446,000 units by 2030, jumping nearly ninefold from about 50,000 units this year, spurred by competition to reach deployment scale and to close the real-world data feedback loop. Among the Chinese carmakers diversifying into robotics, BYD and Xpeng are now under the spotlight due to their development and manufacturing heft as their mass production plans draw near. At the end of July, BYD said in a statement to the South China Morning Post that its first humanoid robots would debut in August at the firm’s Di Space experience centres, but that timetable has now been delayed. In June, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice-president, predicted that China would become the first market to “see full commercialisation of humanoid robots”. However, automotive giants do not just see themselves as just making robots to sell on the open market. They also aim to achieve a high level of automation in production by gaining experience in embodied AI technology. In late July, BYD formed a strategic partnership with Chinese robotics start-up PaXini Tech to deploy robots in manufacturing. The carmaker will create real-world industrial environments for the robots, generating operating data to help train embodied AI models. Xpeng’s robotics subsidiary Dogotix received US$900 million in its latest round of financing last month, which valued it at US$6.3 billion. The fundraising, which attracted Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the SCMP, and IDG Capital, marked the biggest single private-equity deal involving a Chinese robotics maker. The company said it planned to begin producing its Iron humanoid robots at the end of 2026, targeting an initial volume of 1,000 units, to be deployed as sales assistants at its domestic showrooms. Iron runs on the firm’s Vision-Language-Action 2.0 AI model. Unlike older systems that translate images into text-based code before executing a movement, the newer model allows the robot’s neural network to convert visual data directly into motion, improving task efficiency and reducing information loss. Xpeng CEO He Xiaopeng said in November that the company aimed to sell 1 million robots annually by 2030, when costs would be brought down to a level to make the products affordable for household use. Rivals Li Auto, Xiaomi and Leapmotor have all ramped up the development of humanoid robots, which are expected to perform tasks such as factory work and elderly care. Since early 2024, Chery Automobile has been working with AI company Aimoga to develop Mornine, a humanoid robot capable of understanding natural language and interpreting human intentions. At the World Robot Conference in Beijing last month, the industry’s mindset had firmly pivoted towards real-world application ramp-up, Goldman Sachs said. “While demonstrations of locomotion and entertainment still attract interest, discussions are now centred on quantifiable metrics such as task performance, success rates, throughput, and payback periods, reflecting a healthy maturation of the sector,” the bank said in a research report. “Logistics sorting has emerged as one of the most visible early commercialisation directions.” Shao Yu, chief economist with the Sci-tech Innovation Centre at Fudan University’s School of Management, said tech industries, propelled by government support and an influx of private capital, were acting as the major growth driver for the Chinese economy. Shao added that tech sectors, from advanced semiconductors to embodied AI, would sustain their strength over a period of time despite worries of an AI-generated bubble. “With the trend of innovation, more investment will be made to those hi-tech areas to reflect the K-shaped structure of the Chinese economy,” Shao said. “The crux point is how to leverage hi-tech companies and products to benefit society as a whole.” A K-shaped divergence refers to China’s economic structure, where hi-tech manufacturing and exports are thriving while consumption, property and traditional industries are experiencing slower growth. But Xu Mingqi, a researcher at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, threw a wet blanket over investors’ expectations for quick returns from investing in physical AI. Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly Xu Mingqi, Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences “No AI technology with material impact on people’s lifestyle has been in sight yet,” he told reporters in a media briefing this month. “Real benefits from AI won’t be achieved quickly and it will still turn out to be a long drawn-out process.”

title: Style Edit: 45R brings masterful yarn-dyed indigo to Fair Isle and Cowichan knits
description: The Tokyo atelier channels its passion for textiles into a collection inspired by classic knitwear designs from Scotland and Canada.
content: 45R has remained a cult favourite for nearly half a century with good reason. Founded in 1977 in a small studio in Tokyo’s Daikanyama district, the Japanese label, named after the rotational speed of a seven-inch vinyl record, has built its reputation on a philosophy of nai monozukuri, meaning creating things that don’t exist, but feel like they should. Indigo is the brand’s heartbeat. Unlike conventional dyeing methods that stiffen yarn, 45R’s approach is very precise: the yarn is dyed before a single loop is formed. This preserves the natural bounce and elasticity of the fibres, allowing the fabric to breathe and age with a living patina that deepens over time. The August IDG (Indigo) Knit collection embodies that spirit, reinterpreting heritage techniques from Scotland to Canada with a distinctly Japanese sensibility. The Fair Isle pieces, for instance, draw on the century-old Scottish tradition of intricate, multicoloured geometric patterns. But here, they are rendered in 45R’s signature pre-dyed indigo yarn, creating deep, multi-tonal shades that feel both nostalgic and entirely new. A relaxed henley and a flared bolero are among the standouts, their motifs blooming in soft, textural knits. The craftsmanship becomes even more personal with the hand-knitted vests. Artisans build the houndstooth and herringbone designs stitch by stitch, carefully managing needle tension to create thick, architectural pieces that feel almost sculptural. Then there is the Cowichan series, inspired by the heavy, graphic knits of Canada’s Vancouver Island. Rendered in chunky, hand-knitted yarns, each item – from the statement vest to the hairbands – carries the unmistakable warmth of human hands. What ties it all together is the brand’s outstanding commitment to yarn-dyeing. By infusing each strand with colour before knitting, 45R ensures that the indigo does not merely sit on the surface but becomes part of the fabric’s soul. The result is knitwear that moves with you, softens with wear and tells a story of time, place and the quiet alchemy of Japanese craftsmanship.

title: How 60-year-old model Christina Chung and her daughter, Shiro, defy fashion norms
description: From Miu Miu to Chanel, Chung has turned heads on the runway – now three of her seven children are following in her footsteps.
content: Looking at Christina Chung on set, you can tell right away that the 60-year-old is a seasoned pro. Between shutter clicks, she moves easily from one pose to the next as she and her daughter, Shiro, model outfits from luxury brands, each accessorised with jewellery from Chow Tai Fook. Instinctive and entirely at ease, it is hard to believe that Chung only began modelling seriously at 56. “My first show was for Miu Miu almost two years ago,” she says. “After that, I was invited to walk in Chanel’s haute couture show and it was like a dream come true.” Chung made waves when she appeared in Matthieu Blazy’s first haute couture collection for Chanel, shown in Paris in January. Since then, she has walked in four more shows for the house. “I felt really honoured,” says the Hong Kong model. “I wanted to show my own experience, my richness, my grace – everything. I want models of every age to be seen genuinely.” At 1.8m, with a lean frame and defined contours, Chung has been approached by photographers and modelling scouts since her teenage years. “I was pretty stylish. You know how girls are, we love beauty,” she says. The instinct for personal style, it seems, runs in the family. “Shiro was born with so much talent,” Chung says, turning towards her daughter. “She always dresses so cool and has such a strong fashion sense. In the old days, she used to steal my clothes, but now we’ve switched.” Chung’s relationship with her daughter could not be more different from the one she had with her own parents. Born into a Chiu Chow family that settled in Hong Kong in the 1940s, Chung was the youngest daughter among eight siblings – four girls and four boys. She had a tumultuous relationship with her father, who favoured her brothers. On one occasion, he even doused her in kerosene and tried to set her alight; fortunately, the flame went out. Fearing for her daughter’s safety, Chung’s mother urged her to run away in the middle of the night – she was 16. In her early twenties, Chung began modelling to make ends meet and even appeared in an American Express commercial. But after attending her first catwalk lesson, where someone propositioned her for sex, she became frightened and disillusioned with the industry and left modelling behind. A career, two marriages and seven daughters later, it was Shiro who inspired her mother to return to the business in her fifties. “It was a journey of reinvention,” Chung says. She had always wanted to establish herself as an individual beyond her roles as wife and mother. When her youngest daughter turned 17, and all seven girls had grown up and become independent, Chung returned to modelling, initially taking on smaller projects before French photographer Kin Coedel scouted her. “I wanted to step up and inspire other women, especially mature women. We all have potential. We cannot just sacrifice ourselves to our family or our job, we should not limit our ambition. So when the opportunity to become a model came, I took it.” When asked whether she felt anxious about beginning a modelling career at an age when many people retire, Chung responds without hesitation. “Absolutely not. I’m still very youthful in my heart, and I never doubted starting at this age. It’s never too late. Time is not your enemy, your unlived potential is your enemy.” Walking one of fashion’s most anticipated runways may have come naturally to Chung, but the mother of seven – three of whom are models – admits that it is her daughter Shiro she is most eager to impress. “I feel like the bond between us is a bit different from the one between me and her siblings,” Chung says. Her comment earns an immediate “Ew” from Shiro, 30, who until now has been sitting quietly beside her mother. At this point, Chung leans towards her daughter with a mischievous smile, “I breastfed you, by the way.” Satisfied with the grimace on Shiro’s face, Chung turns back to the question. “Anyway, I’m always in love with this daughter. Sometimes I find myself wondering whether she likes what I do, whether she approves of my style or likes what I’m saying.” While she has her mother’s approval, Shiro says she was bullied for her appearance when she was younger. “I think we have such rigid beauty standards, especially in East Asia. I had all the features that were deemed unattractive – unruly hair, big lips and freckles – and I was bullied.” She remembers running to her mother for comfort. Then, at 18, shortly after graduating from secondary school, Shiro was scouted as a model while attending a protest. “I have your genes to thank,” she tells her mother, who seems pleasantly surprised – it’s not every day your 30-year-old daughter compliments you. Given her own early experience of the modelling industry, Chung admits that it was not easy to watch her young daughters enter the business. “I’m always supportive of what they want to do, so I observed their modelling careers very closely. I always knew what was going on, even if they didn’t know I was spying on them,” she says, laughing. “The industry seems to have changed a lot. That’s why I have no worries. I trust my girls’ judgement. They know how to distinguish between what’s good and bad, and what the right thing to do is.” While her mother is defying the status quo in an industry that has long favoured youth and perfection, Shiro is carving out a space of her own. Covered in tattoos, she is one of relatively few heavily tattooed women working in fashion. A trained tattoo artist, she began learning the craft at 17. “Maybe that gave me an edge,” Shiro says. “You don’t really see many fully tattooed girls, and back then I think I was the only fully tattooed model in Hong Kong signed to an agency.” But carving out a niche came with its own limitations, and Shiro realised she was being typecast. “I would refuse jobs for lingerie or very gothic styles. I wanted to bring more dimensions to people who look this way.” On set, the contrast between mother and daughter is clear. Chung carries herself with the self-assuredness of a woman who has spent a lifetime becoming herself, while Shiro carries the independent and maybe even a little rebellious spirit of someone determined not to be reduced to a single image. title: Style Edit: Audemars Piguet to host hands-on watchmaking masterclass in Macau
description: The maison brings the craftsmanship of Le Brassus to AP House Macau, giving guests a rare opportunity to assemble its signature Calibre 4302 movement.
content: This October, Audemars Piguet will invite guests in Macau to experience watchmaking not from across a boutique counter, but from the watchmaker’s bench. Hosted at AP House Macau – the largest AP House in Greater China – the new masterclass transforms the intricate mechanics of haute horlogerie into an intimate, hands-on encounter. Created for seasoned collectors and curious newcomers alike, the programme brings the manufacture’s tradition of passing knowledge between generations from Le Brassus to one of Asia’s most dynamic luxury destinations. The experience begins with a quietly ceremonial gesture: slipping into a traditional watchmaker’s coat. Participants then enter a dedicated setting conceived to evoke the calm, concentrated atmosphere of Audemars Piguet’s ateliers in Switzerland’s Vallée de Joux. At the heart of the programme is “The Path of Mechanical Energy”, a two-part exploration of how a mechanical watch comes to life and is refined. During the first chapter, guests work with Calibre 4302, the self-winding movement found in selected Royal Oak and Code 11.59 by Audemars Piguet models. Comprising 257 components, it operates at four Hz and delivers a 70-hour power reserve. Under expert guidance, participants assemble the elements that generate, transmit, distribute and regulate energy: the barrel, gear train, escapement and balance wheel. The exercise reveals a world in which fractions of a millimetre matter, and where reliability depends upon exceptional precision. The second chapter turns from mechanics to artistry. Guests practise traditional decorative techniques, including satin brushing, circular graining and polishing. These meticulous gestures demand patience, control and sensitivity – qualities that distinguish fine watchmaking from industrial production. Each participant also creates a personalised horological keepsake. After the workshop, the immersion continues within AP House Macau, an elegant hospitality-led space inspired by the landscapes and character of Le Brassus. Here, watchmaking, contemporary culture and conviviality converge in a distinctly Audemars Piguet expression of luxury. The masterclass is available by appointment from October 1 to 17. Each session welcomes up to eight participants aged 16 and above. The workshops are offered in English and Chinese and cost MOP3,200 (US$396) per person.

title: Opinion | Hong Kong’s local schools should not have to brace for the worst
description: The government must seriously reflect on the rising enrolments at international and private schools even as local schools struggle to keep primary one classes filled.
content: The vast majority of Hong Kong’s students are back in school now. With traffic expected to be horrendous last week, it was good that the government sounded the warning early, urging residents to allow more time for their morning commute. The government did more than that, actually. The Emergency Transport Co-ordination Centre was working at its highest operational tier at 6.30am on September 1 to monitor and coordinate public transport and traffic flow. Deployment of staff on the ground ensured that conditions were reported in real-time. Preparedness wins the day and the government deserves good marks for its efforts. It wasn’t raining when Noah built the ark, but it was on our first day of school. For those averse to change, the start of the school year can be comforting because it can be counted on to bring the same disruptions. Traffic is one thing, but parents of school-going children know that the first week means suffering from information overload, wading through an avalanche of notices and filling out paperwork into the wee hours. The certainty extends to the news cycle. Bad behaviour at university orientation camps almost always makes headlines every year. For those of us who have had our share of wild days in our youth, the video of a shirtless young man carrying a young woman wearing a bra and shorts at an orientation camp this year may not seem too troubling.
