But a former university student is on trial facing multiple charges of rape and indecent assault. Predators have no place in our educational institutions. Youth can never be an excuse. With couples in Hong Kong increasingly reluctant to have children, the dismal birth rate is no longer news. And so just as the sun rises in the east, we can count on the shutting of Primary One classes in recent years. This academic year, 126 Primary One classes have been wiped out, an 8 per cent decrease year on year. The worst, according to a primary school principal, is yet to come. Whether our government has given up on boosting the birth rate will be revealed in time, with the chief executive delivering his policy address on September 16. We’ll know then whether baby bonuses will be continued and whether the HK$2,500 (US$318) annual student grant will be resuscitated. If there are no efforts beyond handing out money, we will know our government is out of ideas. Hopefully, that won’t be the case. International and private schools have experienced a surge in enrolment amid an overall drop in the city’s student population. The English Schools Foundation is offering through-train admission programmes starting in preschool and new international schools like YK Pao School have opened. They are obviously filling a need. These schools are not just reaping the benefits of the government’s talent schemes. Ruth Benny, veteran consultant for international school admissions, bluntly points out that the rise in international and private school admissions “reflects a persistent demand from affluent local families opting out of the local curriculum”. This should be keeping our education authorities up at night. Our local schools are scrambling to enrol students and educators are stressing about their institutions being shut down. A persistent trend away from local schools demands that we look hard at our local system. Our public universities have admitted a record number of applicants outside the local exam system – nearly 30 per cent of the 15,000 government-funded places, representing a 63 per cent surge over seven years. This will exacerbate the problem. Government-funded schools – the tuition-free schools that our education minister denied were a factor in our low birth rate – only offer the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE) option. Non-DSE routes are offered at international, private independent and Direct Subsidy Scheme schools. Non-DSE schools can be expensive; families who enrol their children in them have the resources to help them obtain good scores. This, in effect, perpetuates a socio-economic divide. An education system that makes it harder for those with less economic means to advance is fostering educational inequity. Preparedness must mean more than bracing for worse to come. Our education authorities must look at ways to make local free education truly attractive to families with children. Equitable education in Hong Kong must be defended and prioritised at all costs. Maybe then, we will see more couples willing to roll the dice on having children of their own. Signing notices at ungodly hours at night may be an annual ritual for parents, one that can even be enjoyed. Government efforts to remove obstacles to children thriving would save parents a lot of sleepless nights.

title: Ancient roots: China pioneering sex therapist warns of rise of ‘relationship blind’ phenomenon
description: Tong recalls a client whose single father advised her to ‘wear more clothes’ after she faced school sexual harassment.
content: Behind many sexual difficulties lie questions that extend far beyond the confines of the bedroom. After years of assisting clients in navigating issues of intimacy and relationships, one of China’s pioneering sex therapists has observed how gaps in education and communication shape individuals’ most private struggles. Originally from Taiwan, Tong Songzhen began her career as a nurse before attaining a doctorate in sexology from Shu-Te University. Since 2016, she has established sex therapy practices in Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenzhen. Tong shared with the SCMP that most of her clients are between the ages of 30 and 50, with men comprising about 80 per cent of her clientele. While male clients often seek help for sexual dysfunction, women typically experience greater insecurity in intimate relationships. Her clientele has included two PhD holders who lacked fundamental sexual knowledge and mistakenly believed that pregnancy could result merely from sharing a bed. She also worked with an 80-year-old man who, after enduring the effects of a stroke for two decades, sought to rekindle physical intimacy with his partner. “Sex is never solely about sexual organs. It encompasses an entire system that involves the body, psychology, and social relationships,” she emphasised. Tong uses an integrative approach that combines bodywork techniques with medical and psychological support, aiding clients in addressing sexual health and relationship challenges through non-pharmaceutical and non-surgical methods. However, her profession has long faced misconceptions and stigma, with some critics dismissing her work as “another form of sex work.” Notably, discussions around sexuality have not been entirely absent from Chinese society. As early as the pre-Qin period (221–206 BC), fangzhong shu, or Arts of the Bedchamber, comprised a foundational body of sexual knowledge, addressing intimacy, reproduction, and sexual health while incorporating Taoist concepts of physical cultivation and longevity. The pre-Han (202 BC–220) text Su Nü Jing documented dialogues between the Yellow Emperor and Su Nü, a folk goddess linked to sexuality and music, concerning intimacy and reproduction. This text regarded sex as an integral part of the natural order. In ancient China, sexual manuals were even included in some brides’ dowries as valuable guides for married life. Modern sex education, however, has taken a different trajectory. Initially promoted for national continuity and population growth, it later evolved to encompass women’s rights and personal wellbeing. China officially incorporated sex education into school curricula in 1988, yet the subject remains sensitive, with terms like “puberty education” often employed to mitigate “discomfort.” In recent years, the internet has broadened public discourse around sexual rights, while AI technologies have introduced new forms of intimacy through virtual companions. Tong has noted another cultural shift within Chinese society. “We used to refer to people as ‘illiterate,’ then ‘aesthetically blind.’ Now, I believe we are witnessing a new phenomenon: being ‘relationship blind,’” she observed. She argues that many relationships today lack authentic intimacy. Although trust and openness are fundamental to closeness, some individuals find it easier to express their feelings to strangers rather than to those nearest to them. Years of treating sexual difficulties have revealed to Tong that many issues stem from systemic deficiencies in sex education, communication, and relationship-building. Tong recounted a female client, raised by a single father, who was told after experiencing sexual harassment at school: “Just wear more clothes.” This young girl later pushed her weight to nearly 100kg, believing that becoming physically stronger would protect her from further harm, all while lacking basic knowledge of intimate hygiene. She sought Tong’s help only after developing feelings for someone yet grappling with fear. Tong believes that sex is still frequently conflated with pornography in certain contexts, which restricts young people’s access to accurate and comprehensive sexual knowledge. “Sex education should not merely dictate to young people what they can or cannot do. It must also empower them to understand their bodies, respect others, establish boundaries, build trust, comprehend consent, and cultivate healthy relationships,” she remarked.

title: Hong Kong’s yuan pool is growing. Can it turn liquidity into global demand?
description: Regulators want banks to channel more offshore yuan into global markets, as the city pushes to deepen the currency’s role in international finance.
content: Hong Kong’s top financial regulators have urged local banks to make greater use of the city’s growing pool of offshore yuan liquidity, while also flagging the need to prepare for a coming wave of autonomous AI systems used in the financial sector. Speaking at the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB) Distinguished Speaker Luncheon, Eddie Yue Wai-man, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), called on lenders to leverage their international networks to expand the Chinese currency’s global reach. “We want your bank to use your global network to help us channel all this renminbi liquidity to the world,” Yue said. Regulators, he added at the Friday luncheon, were prepared to scrap the funding cap on Hong Kong’s yuan liquidity facility altogether if demand continued to grow. The specialised facility, which provides commercial banks with yuan funding that can then be lent to customers, currently operates under a 500 billion yuan (US$74.5 billion) quota, expanding from the previous 200 billion yuan in July. “There will not be any cap to it,” Yue said, adding that the facility’s quota could be expanded as demand increased and existing capacity was well used. He also urged lenders to report operational problems and difficulties faced by clients so the system could be refined. The push comes as yuan-denominated transactions accounted for about 30 per cent of China’s total trade settlement last year, up from 13 per cent in 2019, Goldman Sachs found in May. The shift has coincided with rapid growth in dim sum bonds – yuan-denominated bonds issued in Hong Kong – as well as offshore Chinese government bonds. However, Hong Kong’s Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) chief executive Julia Leung Fung-yee cautioned that wider international use of the yuan could stall unless financial institutions developed a deeper suite of yield-bearing and risk-hedging products. “If the renminbi that foreign companies obtain from trade is just swapped back into US dollars immediately … there’s no point of internationalisation,” she said, calling for “a broader and deeper renminbi ecosystem”. Leung said the SFC was technically ready to extend Hong Kong’s dual-counter stock trading model to Southbound Stock Connect flows – a change that would allow mainland investors using the scheme to buy and settle Hong Kong-listed shares directly in yuan. She also pointed to HKEX’s five-year China Government Bond futures contract, launched in August, as a new hedging tool. The panel, moderated by HKAB chairman and Bank of China (Hong Kong) chief executive Sun Yu, also discussed how AI and other financial technologies were reshaping the sector. Sun said developments in fintech and Beijing’s “AI Plus” initiative – elevated to a top national priority under the 15th five-year plan – were driving major changes across the city’s wealth management and capital markets. Leung cited January’s back-to-back Hong Kong listings of Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, and MiniMax as early evidence that the city’s markets were benefiting from the sector’s growth. She disclosed that the SFC was weighing further regulatory guidance for financial firms deploying “agentic” AI systems – software capable of executing complex, multi-step tasks with limited direct human intervention. On the banking side, HKMA chief Yue said the monetary authority was co-developing an AI explainability toolkit with the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub, the United Kingdom’s Financial Conduct Authority and the Saudi Central Bank. Testing is due to begin next quarter.

title: Embrace the new school year with confidence and curiosity
description: Young Post interns share their top tips for students: get organised, explore passions and embrace new experiences for growth.
content:
Every year, students feel anxious on the first day of school. Take a deep breath and remember that it is another opportunity for growth and to learn about yourself.
How do you plan to challenge yourself this year? To help you transition into the new term, some of Young Post’s summer interns have shared their advice for finding your unique groove .
As we begin the new school year, I want to highlight my unique ability: organisation. While this skill is often emphasised in schools, it does not come naturally to everyone.
When I started middle school, I struggled with a large number of papers scattered everywhere – some were here, others there, and many were simply missing.
I discovered that when I knew exactly where everything was, I felt more at ease and experienced less mental stress. Therefore, I encourage you to organise all your papers neatly in designated folders. This way, when you receive additional papers to take home, you will feel much more confident in your learning environment.
Treat this new year as a chance for personal exploration. Keep a weekly “passion journal”, join niche school clubs and volunteer for challenging projects.
For younger students just starting their school journey, the key lesson is that mistakes are stepping stones. Each error in maths or writing represents real brain growth.
It is also important to share ideas with classmates to improve your work and strengthen friendships. On the first day, a simple “Hi!” can make a big difference and help you connect with more friends on campus.
The best way to discover your unique abilities is to keep an open mind and be willing to try new things. I have explored a variety of activities – from sports like basketball, ping-pong and golf to musical endeavours such as dancing, singing and playing the guitar.
Over time, I discovered my talent for singing and playing instruments, realising that I have a natural gift for music. It was my curiosity and willingness to take risks that helped me uncover this skill.
So, I encourage you to seize every chance to explore the world and step into the unknown – you never know what you might learn about yourself.

title: Hongkonger shares tips for confident, sustainable fashion
description: Fashion expert Dianne Gupta explains how to explore colour psychology, low-cost style hacks and self-expression through clothing.
content:
When you don’t have to wear your school uniform, how do you decide what to put on?
For Dianne Gupta, who shares sustainable styling tips on her Instagram account, @dianneisdressed, fashion is less about following rules and more about discovering who you are.
“I think [fashion] is an important way to tell yourself and the world who you are,” said the 29-year-old fashion content creator.
In fashion and psychology, the concept of “enclothed cognition” suggests that the clothes we wear can affect our mindset, mood and behaviour. Gupta noted that people would often gravitate towards certain colours to reflect the emotions they want to feel.
“Students can use [colours] to their advantage when they need to trick their brain into feeling something,” she said. For example, you could slip into brighter colours when you need to put a little pep in your step .
As you get older and begin to figure out your identity and style, fashion can become a low-stakes way to experiment.
“Before I found my personal style, I wore a lot of neutrals. I wasn’t fully happy or confident. I felt too scared to take up space,” Gupta shared. “My style now feels very unapologetic .”
Rather than overhaul your wardrobe overnight, Gupta suggested taking small steps when trying a new style – for example, pair a bold piece that feels intimidating with a staple that you are already comfortable wearing.
Gupta shared three easy tips to help you develop your own style without spending a lot of money.
First, add a pop of colour to a simple outfit to enhance balance and contrast. Gupta said that a bright bag or a pair of colourful shoes could make a big difference.
Second, play with the small details of your outfits: roll up your sleeves, tuck in part of your shirt or even replace plain buttons on a shirt with colourful ones. Tweaking the subtle details of your clothes can refresh an outfit without buying anything new.
Finally, give old clothes a second life by borrowing from family members or swapping clothes with friends.
Gupta emphasised that you should not worry about looking perfect – instead, create a personal style that boosts your confidence.
“Being comfortable in your own skin and being unapologetic about how you wear [something] is part of having a personal style,” she said.

title: Exclusive | European chamber chief in Hong Kong heads to Brussels to ‘reset city’s image’
description: Johannes Hack says Hong Kong remains ‘fundamentally’ different from mainland cities amid growing trade tensions between Beijing and EU.
content: The head of the European Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong (EuroCham) aims to “reset” perceptions about the financial hub during the organisation’s first-ever “door-knock” mission to Brussels, emphasising that the city remains “significantly, fundamentally” distinct from its mainland Chinese counterparts. With Hong Kong set to unveil its first five-year plan on September 16 – the same day the mission begins – chairman Johannes Hack told the South China Morning Post that the city lacked a clear narrative to sell opportunities in the Northern Metropolis and the Greater Bay Area to European firms. Hack also highlighted data security concerns as one of the biggest challenges for foreign firms looking to do business in Hong Kong, leading to “missed opportunities” for collaboration. While planned months in advance, the door-knock comes during a particularly fraught period, as tensions between Brussels and Beijing ratchet up ahead of an October deadline to prevent a trade war over China’s record trade surplus with the bloc. The perception of Hong Kong also remains bruised since the enactment of the national security law in 2020, with the European Union continuing to speak out on the alleged erosion of political freedoms in the city – assertions local officials routinely reject as unfounded. “I think for a very long time the tagline for Hong Kong was that it was really this completely unique place that existed essentially on its own, and it was vibrant and exciting … and then clearly there was this somewhat abrupt shift,” Hack said. “So the key thing we are trying to achieve is to reset that tagline to once again focus on the [city’s] uniqueness and on the fact that it stands out. “Of course, [Hong Kong is] part of China. There’s no discussion around that. But it can be part of China and still be completely unique and valuable in that uniqueness.” EuroCham acts as an umbrella organisation, comprising 13 European Union (EU) member bodies, and those of Britain, Switzerland and Norway. During the trip, the delegation will meet officials from the European Commission – the EU’s executive arm – in Brussels and members of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Hack said he aimed to advocate for continued European engagement with Hong Kong. While he wasn’t expecting officials to agree with everything, he hoped they would listen to the chamber’s perspective and “give it weight”. “I think if you look at the totality of what we’re seeing, it’s still absolutely true that Hong Kong is significantly, fundamentally different from mainland Chinese cities,” he said, citing the city’s open society, government engagement and widespread use of English as some examples. He touted Hong Kong’s diverse talent pool and its financial and services sectors as key to the city’s success. Maintaining the city’s attractiveness for international talent and its distinctiveness from other mainland cities was beneficial for both China and the rest of the world, he added. Kicking off on September 16, EuroCham’s “door-knock” will coincide with the unveiling of the city’s first-ever five-year plan, where Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu is expected to chart a course for future development. The 30,000-hectare Northern Metropolis megaproject is expected to take centre stage in Lee’s address, as part of deepening integration with national development and the bay area – comprising Hong Kong, Macau and nine other mainland cities. Hack said the chamber was looking to the five-year plan to make both development projects something “people can feel”, adding that businesspeople in Hong Kong struggled to convince head offices back home of the opportunities in the city. “If I mention the word ‘Greater Bay Area’ in Brussels or Strasbourg, I’m pretty certain that out of 500 people, maybe one will have heard it,” he said. “For the Northern Metropolis, we’re still maybe five years ahead of that actual story. But both these things, for them to be attractive in our home markets, they need a story that we can tell.” Offering statistics on square mileage and infrastructure project specifications would not sell the vision, he explained. Instead, the city needed “clear-cut” success stories, such as a foreign drug maker using mainland blood samples to develop and market a product in the metropolis. When it came to the biggest challenge facing foreign firms in Hong Kong, Hack cited concerns surrounding data security. “The biggest hindrance is around data. In many Western countries, Hong Kong is getting lumped together with mainland China in terms of how data is treated,” Hack said. He described the lack of trust among both Western and mainland companies as a “lost opportunity” and a roadblock to development in the Northern Metropolis and cross-border collaboration. “The biggest opportunity will be in having trust in place,” he said.

title: Feature of the Week: Nip Wan-hei’s short story ‘Adventures of Snowball’
description: The seven-year-old from Po Leung Kuk Camoes Tan Siu Lin Primary School writes about a pearly-white kitten’s adventure in the garden.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your creative writing using this form .
A kitten named Snowball walked into the garden. There’s so much to explore, she thought. Snowball’s owner, Crystal, had just brought her home from the pet shop.
Just as Snowball walked to the flower beds, a neighbour had taken her dog for a walk. The dog ran off to the flower beds and scared the little white kitten.
Snowball took a few steps backwards and went inside. She stayed in the house for the rest of the day until she heard a purr from the garden.
Snowball slowly walked outside and found a beautiful yellow kitten in the bushes.
“Hello, I’m Belle. My mother died when I was young, and I learned to take care of myself and other things by myself.”
“Of course!” replied Belle. And from that day on, the two friends played together and protected each other. Crystal even adopted Belle.

title: Karlie Kong’s top pick: ‘Witchlings’ by Claribel A Ortega
description: The 9-year-old student from Kowloon Junior School shares why they love this book about three witches.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your recommendations using this form .
I recommend the book Witchlings by Claribel A. Ortega. It is about three witches: Seven Salazar, Thorn Laroux and Valley Pepperhorn.
These three witches are still witchlings, waiting to be placed into covens, where they will gain their powers and become witches.
Twelve-year-old Seven Salazar is waiting to be placed in the coven she has always dreamed of living in, House Hyacinth, along with her good friend, Poppy. But on the ceremony night, she isn’t placed in any group. That means she is still a witchling.
Seven meets other witchlings who were not placed in a coven, Thorn and Valley. Seven isn’t looking forward to being with them because she had hardly ever seen Thorn, and Valley is a bully. They are all disappointed because they do not want to remain witchlings for the rest of their lives.
But Seven is determined to do the impossible with Thorn and Valley: defeat the horrible, scary night beast. Read this amazing book to find out if they succeed.

title: Letters from readers about Hong Kong, favourite subjects and importance of fresh water
description: This week, students write about how Hong Kong can become a better city, why they enjoy maths and PE and why we must value clean water.
content:
Do you have something to share? Send us your letters using this form .
If I could change something about Hong Kong, the biggest thing I would want to change is the sheer, overwhelming intensity of the daily grind and the cost of living.
While the city’s convenience and energy are unmatched, many locals agree that the relentless pressure and high expenses make it tough to breathe and enjoy life.
I would transform some of the ultra-dense commercial space into more green community hubs and affordable social spaces.
By easing up the frantic pace, residents could actually relax.
My favourite subjects are maths and physical education (PE) because they are fun and easy. In maths lessons, we play treasure chest games. In PE, we go to the school playground and play dodgeball.
My favourite hobby is dancing. I started learning it when I was four years old. I love it because it is fun. I can stay healthy because I do a lot of exercise in class.
My family consists of my mum, dad, brother and cousin. I usually play computer games with my brother and my cousin. I play phone games with my mum. I talk to my dad every day.
My best friend is Eva. I usually play with her because she is kind and friendly.
We are very lucky in Hong Kong because there are lots of other places in the world that do not have access to fresh water.
In Hong Kong, I turn on my tap and get unlimited water, but in some places you cannot get fresh water immediately; you have to walk for many hours to get it, and it might not even be clean. We need to appreciate how lucky we are and try not to waste water.
Here are some ways to save water: turn off the tap when you are not using it. Do not take long showers. Tell an adult if you see a leak.
It is also important to drink a lot of water to stay hydrated.

title: Legendary Lessons: Helen Keller, disability rights advocate and social activist
description: After losing her sight and hearing at the age of one, this American activist fought to prove that people with disabilities could still live normal lives.
content:
“We are finding out what is wrong with the world. We are going to make it right.”
Imagine waking up in a world that is completely dark and entirely silent. No sight of the bright yellow sun, and no sound of your parents’ voices.
When Helen Keller (1880-1968) was just a baby in the United States, a severe illness left her both blind and deaf.
Because she could not see or hear, she communicated with her family using sign language. Still, when she realised that her family was speaking with each other using their mouths, she became frustrated that she could not join their conversations.
Everything changed when she met Anne Sullivan. A teacher, Sullivan knew Keller was brilliant and that she just needed a different way to communicate.
One morning, Sullivan held Keller’s hand under a cool, rushing water pump. As the liquid splashed over Keller’s skin, Sullivan quickly spelled the letters W-A-T-E-R on Keller’s other palm. Suddenly, Keller understood that the cool feeling had a name.
Learning was not easy. Keller had to practise spelling words on her hand thousands of times. Eventually, Sullivan took Keller to a school for the blind, where she learned Braille. Braille is read by touching raised dots. Keller also learned how to lip-read. She would gently touch her teacher’s lips and throat to feel the vibrations when words were spoken.
Can you imagine how much patience that took?
Keller went on to graduate from university, publish books and travel the world. She also gave inspiring speeches and wrote essays.
Keller spent her life helping other people with disabilities and fighting for the rights of women and workers. She also advocated against racism, segregation and war.
From a young age, Helen Keller knew the power of communication and connection. As she grew older and learned about society’s problems, she did not turn away. Instead, she used her platform to fight for the rights of other groups who were suffering in the United States. Her life shows us the power of compassion and activism.
Content provided by JEMS Character Academy

title: China marks major tunnel milestone for Central Asia railway bypassing Russia
description: Conceived in 1997, the 500km China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway will offer the shortest land route from China to the Middle East and Europe.
content: Fresh off Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, project officials have announced the successful drilling of a key tunnel along the long-stalled China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan (CKU) railway. This marks the first milestone for the flagship project under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, offering China a critical trade corridor bypassing Russia. The 210-metre (690-foot) tunnel was the first drilled through in the Kyrgyz section since full-scale work began in June 2025, China’s state broadcaster CCTV reported on Saturday. Overall progress on the section had reached 17 per cent, it said. The CKU Railway spans over 500km (310 miles), including about 305km in Kyrgyzstan alone. It runs from Kashgar in China’s western Xinjiang region through the mountains of Kyrgyzstan before terminating in Andijan, Uzbekistan. Once completed, it will form the shortest overland route from China to the Middle East and Europe, cutting transit times by up to eight days compared to the China-Europe Railway Express, all three main routes of which transit Russia or Kazakhstan. It will also provide a vital trade gateway for southern Xinjiang, according to CCTV. For landlocked Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, the line will secure direct overland access to Chinese and Asia-Pacific markets. Construction has begun on 27 tunnels, 43 bridges and 88 roadbed sections, while work on 20 railway stations is also under way, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. During Xi’s state visit to Kyrgyzstan last week, the two countries issued a joint statement pledging to guarantee the railway’s smooth construction. Conceived in 1997, the three-way joint venture has faced decades of delay due to engineering hurdles in difficult terrain, technical gauge disputes, and delicate geopolitical sensitivities. Being designed to bypass Russia, the corridor has reportedly raised concerns in Moscow over Beijing’s expanding footprint in Central Asia and the potential diversion of cargo from traditional transit routes through Russia and Kazakhstan. However, as the prolonged war in Ukraine weakens Russia’s strategic hold on Central Asia, Bishkek has increasingly prioritised securing alternative foreign capital, according to a Times of Central Asia report during Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov’s visit to Beijing in February last year. Meanwhile, Moscow’s economic ties with Beijing remain deep, with Western sanctions over its 2022 invasion of Ukraine having pushed Russia closer to China. Russian outlet Izvestia reported on Sunday that Moscow was expanding existing rail crossings and discussing new highways to accommodate growing bilateral trade. To overcome long-standing technical hurdles, the CKU railway project has adopted a dual-gauge compromise, according to CCTV. A 167.5km stretch from the Chinese border to Makmal in Kyrgyzstan will feature China’s standard gauge, while the remaining nearly 140km towards Uzbekistan will retain the Soviet-era broad gauge, supported by a transshipment hub at Makmal. “The significance of this arrangement is that China’s … standard gauge enters the heart of Central Asia for the first time,” Li Lifan, director of the Centre for Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Studies at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, told CCTV. China, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Russia are all members of the SCO bloc, which marked its 25th anniversary at a leadership summit in Bishkek last week. Xi Jihong, the project’s chief engineer, said the CKU railway was likely to be ready for operation by June 2031. However, Uzbekistan is pushing for a tighter timeline. Deputy transport minister Jasurbek Choriev said in June that they aimed to speed up work to complete the railway by 2028, local news outlet the Tashkent Times reported.

title: Pentathletes test American Ninja Warrior skills in Beijing as warm-up for the LA Olympics
description: Obstacle race will replace show jumping in modern pentathlon at 2028 Games, organisers say move will make sport ‘very exciting and very cool’.
content: Pentathletes used to need to know how to ride a horse as well as run, swim, shoot and fence. Now, they have to be able to swing from monkey bars, climb vertical walls and display the kind of skill contestants need on American Ninja Warrior. Obstacle racing will replace show jumping at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and as the discipline’s world championships finished at Universal Studios Beijing on Sunday, organisers are ready for what comes next. Like many other sports, modern pentathlon has had to evolve to keep up with the times. Athletics, for example, is debuting its Ultimate Championship in Budapest next week, featuring a distinctive lighting design in which the infield is predominantly black and only the active competition areas are illuminated. Fencing introduced a world league in April, while the International Swimming League, established in 2019, is returning to London in December after a five-year hiatus. Other new events include World Table Tennis, founded seven years ago, and the Ultimate Tennis Showdown, in the face of newer racquet sports such as padel and pickleball. In the case of modern pentathlon, making a change was a necessary move, according to the chief overseeing the development of the sport, which was created by Baron Pierre de Coubertin, the founder of the modern Games. “We recognise our heritage, and we respect it, but it’s not enough in today’s sports market,” Rob Stull, president of Union Internationale de Pentathlon Moderne (UIPM), said. “You have to innovate constantly. “The International Olympic Committee is looking for new audiences across all sports, and obstacle [racing] brings new audiences. That is important. We want to be part of their solutions in terms of new audiences, and new audiences create new revenue sources. “We have a sport that’s over 100 years old. It was created by the founder of the Olympic Games, but it has been reimagined for today’s audiences. It’s quite different and very exciting and very cool.” Having reportedly faced a boot from the Olympics more than a decade ago, modern pentathlon survived the chop following changes from within. These included holding all events in a single stadium, and replacing show jumping – which involved riding an unfamiliar horse – with obstacle racing. According to senior UIPM officials, the change ticked the boxes for “accessibility, participants and audiences”. “We have participants, we have audiences, and the sport itself is very accessible for everyone,” UIPM secretary general Shiny Fang said. “It’s just human nature to overcome the obstacles. The kids, they just cannot get enough of it. So with all this, and especially its competitiveness, I think that’s also very important for the Olympic elite sport.” Stull, a 65-year-old former Olympian and pentathlete, said that any changes were all about adapting to the world. “We don’t try to have the people adapt to us; we need to adapt to them,” said the American, who competed at the 1984, 1988 and 1992 Games. “People consume their sports differently; whether you watch it on television, on your phone, or however you’re getting your sports information, it’s different than when I did it when I was 35. “When I competed back in the dark ages, we had five days of competition. Now, a competition is 90 minutes, just like a football match, which makes it very convenient not just for broadcasters, but also spectators. “They come in, and don’t have to be there all day. It’s just like spending three hours with the family, including the drive time.” It was not only the sport that adapted; the pentathletes and the obstacle race had to do so as well. Reigning Olympic champion Michelle Gulyás triumphed in Paris, which was the last Games to feature show jumping as part of the modern pentathlon. The 25-year-old, who was born in London but represents Hungary, topped the show jumping table and won gold with a world-record number of points. Eight months later, Gulyás won the UIPM Pentathlon World Cup in Budapest, by which time show jumping had been replaced by the obstacle race. Originally designed as an outdoor sport, the obstacle race can also be held indoors or at iconic venues, Stull said. His aim was to make the event “suitable for every organiser in the world”, hinting that the UIPM was modifying its rules so it could be held in open water at the 2032 Brisbane Games. “If you have a lake, a sea or any other body of water, you’re not limited to a 25- or 50-metre pool,” he said. “You will have the open water options, so that can be attractive to any organiser. “I think we’re a sport for any organiser and any city and virtually any venue.” Stull also believed that the obstacle race aligned very well with the modern pentathlon narrative. “It’s a very demanding athletic discipline that helps to identify the complete athlete,” he said. “But it also has the modern relevance and popularity that is key to enhancing the value of the Olympic Games and bringing in new audiences. “We’re not fighting among the sports; we’re trying to get people active. Our enemy is video games, people staying at home and not being active. That’s the enemy.” The current UIPM Obstacle World Championships – offering the 100m and 400m as well as a 3km race – concluded on Sunday at Universal Studios Beijing, having moved from the National Olympic Sports Centre Stadium last year. “It’s an iconic marquee location, and they’re used to handling big crowds,” Stull said. “It’s like going from a baseball field in your hometown, then all of a sudden you walk onto a major-league baseball field, and it’s just night and day, the difference, in terms of the level. “The average daily attendance at Universal Studios is 60,000, and we’re here for five days; it exposes the sport in a great way.” The next two obstacle world championships will also be held in the Chinese capital, under a four-year partnership with the Beijing Capital Tourism Group, the Beijing Sports Bureau and the Chinese Modern Pentathlon Association. “Securing the four-year hosting agreement with Beijing was a no-brainer for us. China represents a massive market for our sport, and Beijing brings together a population of over 22 million, a thriving Asian obstacle scene and a world-class track record for hosting major sporting events,” Florida native Stull, who was also an épéeist at the Olympics, said. “Beijing is a double Olympic city. Hosting the world championships here is the perfect opportunity to elevate the sport – and tapping into a potential audience of 1.4 billion people offers incredible exposure.”

title: Nuclear waste plan for Japanese resort town sparks backlash: ‘not our problem’
description: Hitachiomiya weighs state handouts against lasting stigma as residents protest against a preliminary survey for radioactive waste storage.
content: The rural Japanese town of Hitachiomiya sprawls down the Naka River valley in northwest Ibaraki prefecture, surrounded by lush forests and overlooked by the picturesque Yamizo mountains. Just 140km (87 miles) from Tokyo, its golf courses attract weekend players, while onsen hot spring resorts in the surrounding hills keep local business steady year-round. The local tourism association’s website highlights traditional festivals, campsites, hiking and cycling routes, alongside unique sights – including a complex of cave tombs on Mount Raijin, an ancient cedar grove and centuries-old temples and shrines. Today, however, tourism representatives and municipal officials are more tight-lipped about the area’s attractions. This week, Hitachiomiya Mayor Sadayuki Suzuki accepted a request from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for his community to undergo a preliminary survey to determine whether the town’s geology is suitable for a repository to store Japan’s large – and growing – stockpile of highly radioactive nuclear waste. In a statement issued on Monday, Suzuki said the area showed a “relatively high probability of exhibiting favourable characteristics according to the scientific characteristics map”, adding that land was available “to install above-ground facilities for final disposal”. The mayor said that “local business leaders” had asked him to approve the initial review, known as a literature survey, which would scrutinise documents on the region’s suitability and examine, among other things, its history of seismic activity. Suzuki told constituents that he aimed to “contribute to national policy and promote the sustainable development of the region”. He stressed that agreeing to the initial assessment was not a commitment to building a permanent storage facility, further promising a series of town hall meetings with residents. “We will carefully listen to your opinions and consider what is best for the future of our city,” he said. While no official figure has been disclosed for Hitachiomiya, the towns of Suttsu and Kamoenai in Hokkaido each received up to 2 billion yen (US$12.8 million) in government subsidies after agreeing to similar literature surveys in 2020. If the first survey is favourable, two additional phases of on-site testing will follow, with a strong focus on seismic conditions. Seismic risk is a sensitive subject for Hitachiomiya, located just 110km from the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant that was devastated by the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. These subsequent phases come with further financial incentives, with large annual subsidies if a facility is finally built. Asked about the potential impact on tourism, both the local tourism association and city hall declined to comment. Local businesses were equally guarded, likely eager to avoid attracting unwanted attention. Kunitaka Yoshino, who runs the Santa No Yu onsen, said he was “not thinking about it much”, while an employee at the nearby Shikisaikan onsen echoed that sentiment, saying: “It’s not our problem.” Experts, however, warn that simply entertaining the proposal could inflict lasting damage. Kumi Kato, a professor in the faculty of tourism at Wakayama University, fears the association alone could ruin Hitachiomiya’s reputation. “The danger is that the town could be seen as an ‘unfortunate place’ where the government paid to dump nuclear waste,” Kato said. “Of course local people would get money from the government, but is that really going to be enough compensation?” Kato pointed out that 15 years after the Fukushima disaster, the prefecture still struggled to shake off negative perceptions. “Japanese people still ask if it is safe to visit Fukushima because there is quite low awareness of the situation there even today,” she said. Frequent news coverage of reactor decommissioning and off-site topsoil transportation continues to fuel public concern and online speculation – factors that could easily spill over to hit small tourism operators near Hitachiomiya. Hajime Matsukubo, secretary general of the Tokyo-based Citizens’ Nuclear Information Centre, said that while the local tourism sector might initially welcome a large influx of workers, the decade-long study period carried severe reputational risks. “The ryokan, restaurants and shops in town might think that constructing a storage facility will bring lots of workers to the community, encouraging them to support it. But these studies take at least a decade,” Matsukubo said. “In that time, people will link the name Hitachiomiya with nuclear waste and won’t want to go there. There is a huge contradiction here that will damage both the community and local tourism.” Public resistance is already surfacing. On Tuesday, a group of residents held a demonstration outside the city hall. In interviews broadcast by local network Tokyo MX, one protester said: “As a citizen, I am against it. We don’t know what kind of radioactive leak will occur.” Another added: “They say the council will decide whether to accept the investigation, but the citizens should be the ones to decide first. I want them to properly listen to our opinions.” The Japanese government and nuclear utility operators have spent decades searching for a permanent repository for the thousands of tonnes of highly radioactive waste produced since the country’s first commercial reactor opened in 1966. But communities have consistently turned down government subsidies, citing safety concerns over waste that experts say can take up to 100,000 years to decay to safe radiation levels. Pressure to find a permanent solution has intensified since the Fukushima accident, yet communities once swayed by lucrative state handouts are growing increasingly reluctant to take the gamble.

title: Standard Chartered ‘doubling down’ on China wealth opportunities despite tax pivot
description: Lender says it plans to add more luxury wealth centres, hire more talent and invest in technology platforms in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan.
content: Standard Chartered plans to increase its investment in wealth centres and hiring in Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan to gain more affluent clients, a senior executive said, adding that it doubts Beijing’s stricter enforcement of taxes on cross-border investment will hurt the wealth-management sector. “We are doubling down on Greater China wealth opportunity,” Judy Hsu Chung-wei, its CEO for wealth and retail banking, told a media briefing last week. “Greater China – Hong Kong, mainland China and Taiwan – is one of the world’s most important wealth corridors,” she said, explaining that this was why the London-headquartered lender aimed to set up more luxury wealth centres, hire more talent, and invest in technology platforms in the three markets to capture growth opportunities. Hsu said Hong Kong, Standard Chartered’s largest single market – contributing a third of its first-half pre-tax profit – was playing a key role in its expansion plan. Standard Chartered recently opened its seventh Hong Kong wealth centre in Causeway Bay, meaning a third of its wealth centres are in the city. Another third are in mainland China and Taiwan. “Hong Kong is our largest market and our leading cross-border wealth hub, connecting the region with global capital, investment opportunities and wealth,” she said. The lender has said it plans to invest US$1.5 billion in its wealth business between 2025 and 2029. Hsu said a large portion had been allocated to Hong Kong and Singapore, with “the Greater China corridor” to be its investment focus. Beijing has recently rolled out policies to enforce its tax rules on cross-border investment. China announced new rules in July that brought income generated through offshore trusts under its ­personal income tax regime. Early last month, several major mainland cities, including Shanghai, began collecting a 20 per cent levy on gains from offshore insurance policies. China has always had a global tax. Now they are clarifying and enforcing it Judy Hsu, Standard Chartered Hsu said some clients had queries about the tax issues, but she did not think they would hurt the long-term growth of cross-border investment. “We have not seen any change in our clients’ behaviours, and we are able to grow our wealth clients and net new money,” she said. “China has always had a global tax. Now they are clarifying and enforcing it.” The clarification was good because it meant customers could discuss the implications and compliance with their tax advisers, Hsu said. “Tax is a consideration, but it is not why the customers are setting up a trust,” she said. “The tax policy will not stop them from setting up a trust for succession planning or investing in the global markets.” Standard Chartered, which generates most of its business in Hong Kong and other markets in Asia, the Middle East and Africa, said its wealth-management revenue rose 38 per cent year on year to US$2.1 billion in the first half. Net new money for affluent clients – those with at least US$25,000 – increased to US$33 billion by the end of June. In the first half of the year, it booked 150,000 new affluent clients, while 150,000 existing ones put more assets under the bank’s management. Hsu said the bank would continue to invest in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and other Persian Gulf countries, even though US-Israel war on Iran was continuing. In an enhancement of its services, it was now offering a single-relationship-manager service for Priority Private clients who had at least US$1 million in assets under management in the UAE, and that banker could also help handle the client’s accounts in other markets such as Singapore or India. “We will continue to invest in the Middle East because there are still a lot of opportunities deep in the UAE,” she said. “We are not withdrawing, and we will continue to find good relationship managers to serve clients.” Hsu said she also supported moves by the Hong Kong and Singapore governments to introduce tax incentives to attract talent. In June, the Hong Kong government submitted a bill to lawmakers that would introduce a tax break on carried interest – the performance-based fees earned by hedge fund and private equity managers. A vote is expected to take place later this year. Singapore’s monetary authority and finance ministry also announced a package of measures last month aimed at enticing investment professionals to the city state, including tax exemptions on investment profits for managers of single-family offices and other qualifying funds. “Tax is important, but it is not the only reason why people move to a country,” Hsu said. “Both markets have done very well in creating a great place to live and a school system for their children to study in. “We are seeing more people moving here because the opportunities are here.”

title: From Ohio to Hong Kong: former NBA player Bryant Austin’s basketball journey
description: The American basketball star talks heroes, heading overseas and helping young players with his Hong Kong academy.
content: I WAS BORN in Lima, Ohio, a small city in the United States, to high-school sweethearts, in 1987. My childhood was split between the inner city and my great-grandparents’ farm: livestock, a wood-burning furnace, the whole thing. Although both my parents had been athletes, I never saw them in their prime. Instead, I watched my older sister. My parents split up when I was six or seven, and we moved to Columbus. My mum worked four jobs to support us. Money was tight, but there were constants: Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan films, and a meal at a Chinese restaurant as a reward when I did well at school. AT MY GRANDFATHER’S house, I’d sit for hours watching old VHS basketball tapes. There was Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan. One clip stayed with me – a young Kobe Bryant growing up in Italy, speaking Italian, playing basketball on the other side of the world (his father played for an Italian team). Something shifted in me. I started to dream of playing overseas. I was also quietly obsessed with Asia. I watched anime, drew constantly – it felt like a world I couldn’t explain to anyone in Ohio. Every year, our teacher asked us what our top three ambitions were. Mine never changed: professional basketball player, marine biologist, or lawyer. In that order. I was already manifesting it. MY SISTER IS two years older than me, and she was my hero before I knew what that meant. At school, she protected me from bullies, from older boys who wanted to jump me. When I was 13, a group of men broke into our home and held our family hostage at gunpoint for hours. While two of them left to move what they had stolen, one stayed behind. My sister – 15, maybe 16 then – wrestled the gun away from him. She shot him in the face. She saved all of us. I WASN’T AN immediate star. I have always been super-introverted, and had anxiety interacting with crowds and fans. I didn’t make varsity until my senior year. No one was knocking down my door offering scholarships. So, I started clicking through university websites, cold-emailing coaches. That’s how mundane it was. I ended up playing at Notre Dame College, then Columbus State and Indiana Tech. After graduating, I played in the professional minor leagues, but it wasn’t enough. MY TURNING POINT was a high-profile tournament in Portsmouth, Virginia, where I was up against players from Duke, Kentucky, North Carolina – the big blue-blood universities. I didn’t just hold my own; I dominated. There was a rage in me, the accumulated weight of being overlooked for years. My trainer and mentor, Greg “Radar” Williamson, spent two years helping me prepare for that moment. BY THE END, three NBA (National Basketball Association) agents were competing to represent me: Andre Buck, who worked with LeBron James; Sean Rooks, who had played alongside Kobe and Shaq (Shaquille O’Neal); and John Spencer, who had a past playing in Hong Kong’s A1 Division against Yao Ming and China’s national team. I signed with John. At the time, I didn’t realise how significant he would become to me. AT 25, I WAS drafted into the NBA Development League by the Fort Wayne Mad Ants. It was overwhelming. You’re meeting Magic Johnson and all these star players. So, on one side, you’re starstruck and on the other side, you’re thinking, “I’m supposed to be here.” I BROKE MY thumb the day before training camp. I decided to play through it without a cast because the NBA is so cutthroat, I couldn’t risk losing my shot. I also had a newborn son at home and no room for excuses. That season, I was also working as an overnight carer for disabled adults and as a substitute teacher. Three jobs, one broken thumb, a new baby. On the court, I was playing beside Khris Middleton, who would go on to become an NBA All-Star. I was proud, exhausted and watching every penny. AT THE END of that season, the team president, Jeff Potter, sat me down and was honest with me. He advised me to go overseas, build my profile and then come back, as I wasn’t getting much court time alongside so many more experienced players. John Spencer helped me get a contract in Israel. And when I landed in Tel Aviv (in October 2013), I was in heaven. I had an apartment right by the sea. The city was beautiful: new culture, new language, new food. Then came the blood clot. I PLAYED THROUGH what I thought was a severe calf strain for a month – it felt like my leg was being sawn off – but ego and pride refused to let me sit it out. I had developed a blood clot in my leg and then one in my lung and didn’t know it. The pain started in my chest, and nearly ended everything – not just my career, but my life. I WAS BACK home in the US (by December 2013), had almost died and was injecting blood thinners daily. The doctors told me I couldn’t play. I was depressed for six months. I didn’t talk to many people, I just retreated into myself and stopped training. I’d fought all those years to have my name on that jersey. Having it taken away so suddenly left me in a dark place. Then, a new drug, Xarelto, appeared and gave my cardiologist enough confidence to clear me. That same week (in April 2014), without knowing any of this, John Spencer called out of nowhere and asked if I’d go to Hong Kong. The league had been closed to American imports since the 2008 financial crisis, but had just reopened and the money was good. I call that timing a call from God. I STEPPED OFF the plane into the heat and humidity, and looked up at the skyline. Instantly, I fell completely in love. I saw bamboo scaffolding around glass towers and felt like I’d walked onto a Rush Hour set. Apparently, I was all over the local media. My American teammate, Reggie Johnson, had full culture shock; the density, the noise, strangers staring at two tall black guys on trains and in lifts. But I didn’t mind any of it. It felt like arriving somewhere I’d been dreaming of since I was a kid. THE BASKETBALL SYSTEM in Hong Kong is unlike anywhere else; it’s fast-paced and kind of chaotic. We won the championship with the Eastern Long Lions (now Hong Kong Eastern) team. I flew my mum over for the final and we celebrated with champagne. IN AUGUST 2014, I went to Bangkok to party for a week, to celebrate my Hong Kong championship with my close friend and NBA G League teammate, Tommy Smith, who works with me today. I asked to train with his team to stay sharp between nights out. They begged me to stay and I said yes. I played in the Thai Super League season, and then for an Indonesian team in Surabaya. INSTEAD OF GOING back to the US, I realised that life had a plan for me in Asia, and specifically in Hong Kong – it always drew me in. Now, I play forward and point guard for Chongde Flying Eagle here in the A1 Division. When I first got here, the Hong Kong fans were crazy, following me around, asking for autographs, photos. I just love that they love basketball as much as I do. I started a basketball academy with just five kids. I’d turn up in my jersey on the street courts of Southorn Playground, Nathan Road and Victoria Park, and ask to join games. Kids would clock who I was and ask if I coached. That’s how my academy, League MVP, started – organically. TODAY, OUR TEAM works with up to 150 local boys as well as international students here on holiday camps. We’ve worked with refugee children from Africa, India and Pakistan. One of the players I coached, Hong Kong-born David Muoka, became the first from the city to be drafted into the NBA. WHAT I WANT for Hong Kong basketball is more visibility, more opportunity. There’s talent here. It just needs investment, time and belief. Hong Kong is an underdog, but there are a lot of passionate players, and I want them to win. MY SON IS 13 now. Every summer, he comes over from Ohio. I wake him early – he hates it – and we’re in the gym by 5am. I never forced basketball on him, but once he chose it, I made it clear: no short cuts. We train hard, then we enjoy the city – Disneyland, Ocean Park, beaches, hotpot, the MTR. I push him to explore independently; this city is safe enough to do that. TWELVE YEARS AFTER I arrived, Hong Kong is home – not a posting, or a chapter. I’m 38, still playing, still growing my business, still up early doing weights – my life is kind of consumed by basketball. I’m manifesting my end game – the best is yet to come. And I know I want to be here when the next kid from a Hong Kong court makes it somewhere nobody expected, and gives the city another reason to believe. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

title: Why rare books, like Harry Potter first editions, are trending as investments
description: Bill Gates, Oprah Winfrey and Whoopi Goldberg are among today’s collectors of rare books, as buyers seek meaningful, tangible literary treasures.
content: Rare books are having a moment in the spotlight. In the past year, major auction houses have seen record-breaking sales for first editions, landmark historical texts and medieval manuscripts, including the almost £2.25 million (HK$23.7 million) realised by Christie’s in July for the Clermont-Tonnerre Grail, one of the earliest documents narrating the legend of King Arthur and his search for the Holy Grail. Antiquarian booksellers and bibliophiles are trending across social media while more celebrities are joining the likes of seasoned collectors Oprah Winfrey, Bill Gates and actresses Sarah Michelle Gellar and Whoopi Goldberg. A first edition of Edith Wharton’s classic novel The House of Mirth even became a storyline on the hit Apple TV series Your Friends & Neighbors. “As more of our lives become digital, physical books have become more desirable as objects in their own right. People are increasingly drawn to things that feel tangible, authentic and that endure,” says Pom Harrington, second-generation owner of rare book dealer Peter Harrington, which has stores in London and New York. Collecting rare books isn’t exactly a modern pursuit – it can be traced back to the 15th century, when royalty, scholars and aristocracy began amassing classical works and illuminated manuscripts. In modern times, the market has been primarily driven by wealthy educational institutions seeking to acquire prestigious titles and build auction-worthy catalogues. Now the industry is undergoing a shift as a new generation of collectors has come to the fore. “What’s particularly noticeable is the number of younger collectors entering the market. A decade ago, rare books were often associated with older, established collectors. Today, we’re seeing buyers in their twenties and thirties who have grown up in a digital world and are discovering the appeal of owning something physical with history, craftsmanship and permanence,” explains Harrington. Traditionally, first editions – the initial commercial printing of a title released by a publisher – are the most sought after. Their value is determined by several factors – in particular the item’s condition. For example, two copies of the same first edition can have vastly different values, depending on how well they have been maintained. “Condition and quality can vary. If there’s something wrong with one page in that book, or if there’s been any restoration done, it will affect the price,” explains Lorence Johnston, founder of Lok Man Rare Books in Hong Kong. “The binding can also make a difference as it is considered a craft in itself. In contrast, the value of modern books – typically from the 1920s and 30s onwards – is in the dust jacket, many of which feature vibrant artwork on the wrappers,” he says. Provenance also plays a vital role. A book owned, inscribed or gifted by a significant historical figure, or presented to someone famous or influential, can be considered a unique artefact. An author’s inscription or an original artwork can further elevate its value. Buyers should ultimately look for the right edition in the best condition, with the strongest story attached to it. “We have a book right now that was gifted by Salvador Dalí to his friend, Jack Warner, the co-founder of Warner Bros Studios. Dalí has also doodled a little sketch as part of the inscription. It’s that original artwork that makes that book desirable,” says Dan Whitmore, proprietor of Whitmore Rare Books in California. While iconic books and literary classics are still in demand, experts note that other categories are gaining popularity. Whitmore has noticed a growing interest in science fiction and fantasy, while Johnston highlights subjects including wine, food, coffee, finance and economics. “The strongest areas tend to be books that continue to resonate culturally. Modern literary first editions remain extremely popular, particularly titles that have shaped a generation of readers. We saw a big burst of interest in Frankenstein last year with the new film release. The interest in sci-fi peaks with each blockbuster release,” adds Harrington. This generation of book collectors is also being driven by emotional connections or personal sentiments. Unlike earlier generations, who bought books more often, today’s customers are seeking specific and meaningful titles as gifts for themselves or others. “It’s hard to highlight any market trend because customers are looking for books that are important to them. For example, it could be a title that inspired them to become a judge, or something that their mother used to read them when they were growing up. It’s about an emotional connection more than anything,” says Johnston. Booksellers anticipate continued growth in interest as aspiring bibliophiles can scour a variety of sources, including private collections, book fairs and auctions. While the latter can bring fresh material to the market, they often require independent expertise. Forgeries also exist, so finding a trusted dealer is crucial before making significant investments in a collection. “Collectors benefit from guidance and from building a long-term relationship with someone who understands their interests and collecting goals, and offers them material that they may not have considered or encountered elsewhere. Most importantly, dealers offer guarantees on what you buy,” says Harrington. Much like fine art, wine, or watches, the benefit of collecting rare books goes beyond personal enjoyment. Many even regard it as a potential asset class. While the industry has historically shown steady rather than speculative growth, there are rare occasions when a book’s price will increase exponentially, providing a lucrative opportunity for new investors. “There are examples of books – like the first printing of Harry Potter – that are something of an anomaly. It has experienced a meteoric rise in value from the time it was published until today,” says Whitmore. 5 tips for budding collectors 1. Start with books that have influenced your life, career or interests. 2. Don’t be limited by one subject or topic. 3. Choose first editions and buy the best condition you can afford. 4. Think about the story your collection is telling. The most memorable libraries reflect the personality and passions of the person who built them. 5. Find a trusted dealer. They are great resources and can help you vet potential purchases.

title: Imperial College London researchers create first biodegradable balloon
description: The ‘Bioloon’ fully degrades in nine months, protecting marine life and birds.
content:
Balloons are used around the world for celebrations, but they can harm the environment. They do not degrade and can hurt marine life and birds. Because of this, researchers in the United Kingdom are making balloons more eco-friendly.
Scientists at Imperial College London have created the first fully biodegradable balloon called the “Bioloon”. They hope to bring it to market in about two years.
Juliana Cumming is a PhD student at the university and co-creator of the Bioloon. She spent three years developing her biodegradable formula.
In a university laboratory, the 29-year-old showed a flask containing a precious yellow liquid. When it hardens, it turns into a soft, stretchy material that feels like a regular balloon. But it falls apart in nine months, unlike regular balloons.

title: Survey finds US teens’ critical thinking declines with AI dependence
description: Survey reveals that many students feel that using AI is hindering their original thought process and overall learning.
content:
A survey has found that American teens are not using their critical thinking as they depend more on artificial intelligence (AI).
The study was published by a United States media advice group called Common Sense Media. The survey involved more than 1,000 US students aged 13 to 17. It found that students were giving up on “critical thinking” as more classrooms use chatbots.
About 40 per cent of those using AI said these tools did not help them learn. They believe that depending on chatbots means that they come up with fewer ideas on their own.
Nearly six in 10 teens who used AI said they used it to get answers for schoolwork. A quarter did not change the answers. When schools block AI platforms, 59 per cent of pupils turned to personal devices to access chatbots.
Almost three-quarters of those surveyed said they have not been taught how to use AI safely.

title: Mental health awareness meets crafting and woodwork at A Collective Space
description: The women-led collective is tackling gender stereotypes and building human connection with conversation and carpentry.
content:
In a room, artisans carefully measure a wooden plank. Then, they chisel the surface with blades to shape the piece. This process delicately takes parts of the wood away and, along with it, the chance to “undo” any mistake.
This is woodworking at A Collective Space, stylised in all lower case. The collective was founded by Emmy Sandt and Sne Roy and runs crafting sessions that merge creativity with wellness.
For Sandt and Roy, woodworking is more than just making furniture. The craft also allows a person to embrace their missteps and blunders .
“In woodworking, some mistakes are irreversible. You can only start again,” said Roy, the director of programmes. “It’s OK to start over from scratch. It doesn’t mean I wasted my effort. It actually means I perfected my skill.”
Roy, 35, and Sandt, 33, officially launched the collective in 2023. Together, they are carving out a community through workshops and collaborations with schools and NGOs.
Sandt, head carpenter, was born and raised in Hong Kong to Finnish parents. She said woodworking helped her through a tumultuous time between 2019 and 2021.
“I found woodworking deeply therapeutic ,” Sandt said. “It was really my way to ground myself and to feel less dislocated from the world.”
Her partner Roy is originally from Kolkata in West Bengal, India. She moved to Hong Kong as a child and eventually worked in counselling.
Sandt introduced Roy to woodworking. They fondly recalled building Ikea furniture together. They even made home furnishings by upcycling discarded items.
Like Sandt, Roy found the process healing. And behind the wood grain, their relationship was changing. As they built together, the pair got closer: “We got to know each other at a different level,” Roy explained.
Sandt’s carpentry journey was influenced by her father. He enjoyed fixing and building things himself.
“It was always in my head that if you want to make something, it is possible,” Sandt said.
But becoming a female carpenter in Hong Kong was not simple. In Finland, Sandt said, it was no big deal to find women in male-dominated spaces and roles. In Hong Kong, there were “clear gender norms” in certain industries, she said.
Sandt’s abilities were often questioned. But years into her career, she is more than capable without a man’s help.
“One thing that I always kind of harp on about is that women can do physical things,” Sandt said.
Challenging gender stereotypes also extends to women taking on roles traditionally filled by men.
“Women’s leadership is sometimes considered to be more gentle and kind,” Roy explained. “Of course, we should be kind, but you … can be confident and forceful and that’s OK. That doesn’t make you aggressive.”
Every month, the collective organises two sessions of “Crafts & Yaps”. The informal gatherings bring about 10 people together to chat while they craft.
As they work with their hands, Roy guides the conversation. The questions are designed to help the group open up.
Roy and Sandt came up with the idea last year, after they found many people were hesitant to join formal events. They had “performance anxiety”.
“A lot of people said they would like to come but were too afraid to attend a public workshop,” Roy said. “I hope that they feel seen and heard while they are here.”
Some Crafts & Yaps participants have told the pair they stayed connected with others from their session.
Sandt said she hoped they were able to think back on the “one tiny little thing” they had made in the workshop.
“I can’t change [societal] pressure … but I can give you a space where you can laugh and just have fun,” Roy said.

title: Robots impress at World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing
description: From breaking human sprinting records to doing restaurant work, robots have shown their skills at the five-day event.
content:
The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games took place in Beijing last month. The event included competitions based on human sports and challenges to see how robots could perform in places like factories, restaurants and offices.
Two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 9.58-second world record in the 100-metre sprint. That was an improvement from 2025, when the winning robot’s time was more than 20 seconds. But braking was an issue, as the robots slammed into a mat placed after ‌the finish line.
Another humanoid ran 400 metres in 39.7 seconds. This is faster than South Africa’s Wayde van Niekerk, who has the world record of 43.03 seconds.
Robots also competed in restaurant work, emergency incident handling and hand-dexterity contests.
For Hua Rong, chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth, the real test is after the demonstration: “The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can really solve users’ problems.”

title: Editorial | Hong Kong must position itself as the bridge for China’s outbound funds
description: Demographic imperatives are driving the offshore expansion of Chinese pensions, handing the city an irreplaceable gateway role.
content: China’s National Social Security Fund (NSSF) has reached a pivotal inflection point. The doubling of its offshore investments to 580 billion yuan (US$86 billion) over three years – now comprising 15.23 per cent of its total assets – signals not merely an incremental shift in asset allocation, but also a strategic recalibration necessitated by demographic pressures and diminishing domestic returns. For Hong Kong, this transformation represents perhaps the most consequential opportunity to cement its role as the irreplaceable gateway for Chinese capital seeking global diversification. Stark realities are forcing this decision. China faces rapid population ageing that the International Monetary Fund projects will slow annual gross domestic product growth by 2 percentage points between 2024 and 2050, while pension spending could rise by nearly 10 percentage points of GDP. The NSSF generated a 13.2 per cent return in 2025, yet this performance was achieved against exceptional domestic stock market gains that cannot be sustained in an environment characterised by lower interest rates, property weakness and constrained growth. The fund’s managers recognise this reality, hence the systematic expansion of offshore allocations since 2022. This diversification imperative extends beyond mere yield hunting. Geopolitical tensions have rendered the traditional playbook – concentrating reserves in US Treasury bonds – increasingly untenable. No prudent sovereign fund manager can ignore the risks of over-dependence on a single economy or currency, especially when relations between Beijing and Washington remain fraught. Similar sovereign funds such as Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund and Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global demonstrate the wisdom of geographic diversification. Chinese pension managers are belatedly following this path. China’s belt and road strategy provides a natural avenue for such diversification. The nation’s deep relationships with Southeast Asian economies offer Chinese pension funds both superior growth prospects and institutional knowledge advantages. These emerging economies can generate returns that China’s ageing domestic market increasingly cannot. The combination of local expertise and genuine development opportunities positions Chinese capital to capture value that Western investors might miss. This is where Hong Kong’s competitive advantages become decisive. The city possesses the unique combination required to serve as operational headquarters for the trillions in outbound pension capital: rule of law, unrestricted capital flows, US dollar-peg stability, deep financial expertise, preferential tax treatment, and status as the world’s largest offshore renminbi hub. Hong Kong’s recent tax framework modernisation, expanding eligibility to pension funds, strengthens this proposition. When Chinese pension managers deploy capital globally, Hong Kong provides the legal certainty, financial infrastructure and talent base. The circular flow of capital presents a particularly compelling opportunity. As Chinese pension funds accumulate wealth abroad, capital controls necessitate repatriation through approved channels. Hong Kong stands ready to facilitate both the outward investment journey and the homeward return, earning intermediation fees at both ends. The Stock Connect scheme provides access to global products, while the city’s bond market attracted HK$239 billion in orders for recent government issuance. The infrastructure and the regulatory frameworks are proven. Foreign critics arguing that Hong Kong’s pre-eminence has peaked are mistaken; the city’s golden age lies ahead. The NSSF’s offshore expansion is not a temporary phenomenon but a structural shift driven by demographic and economic forces. Hong Kong must position itself as the indispensable platform for this transformation, investing in the regulatory frameworks, talent pipelines and financial products required by Chinese pension managers. The question is not whether trillions in Chinese pension capital will flow outward – this is certain – but whether Hong Kong will serve as the primary conduit. Seizing this opportunity will ensure that the city’s golden days truly lie ahead.

title: Why too much sugar early in life, even in the womb, could increase your dementia risk later
description: Hong Kong study finds links between lower sugar intake in utero and up to age two and reduced risk of dementia in older age. Experts explain.
content: This is the 97th instalment in a series on dementia, including the research into its causes and treatment, advice for carers and stories of hope. The seeds of dementia may be sown long before our first birthday – or even before we are born. New research shows that while risks such as high blood pressure and cholesterol compound over decades, early sugar exposure can harm the brain before we take our first breath. A study by the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) published in the journal Neurology in July 2026 suggests restricting sugar during pregnancy and in children up to age two could significantly protect the brain against future cognitive decline. “We were interested in whether nutrition during the first 1,000 days of life could influence brain health decades later,” says Dr Jiazhen Zheng, who was part of the research team at HKUST that examined medical records of almost 65,000 people from the UK Biobank. They compared data from people conceived and raised during World War II sugar rationing against those born immediately after the restrictions were lifted, when average sugar intake doubled. “The end of UK sugar rationing provided a rare natural experiment,” Zheng says. Sugar rationing began in 1940 and effectively limited everyone to between 30 and 50 grams of sugar a day – depending on whether they lived in the UK or the US. There are around five grams of sugar in a teaspoon. Sugar became widely available again in 1953, when average sugar consumption was estimated to have nearly doubled from roughly 41 grams to 80 grams a day. By comparison, today’s average sugar intake, which includes added, unseen sugar in ultra-processed foods, can be three to four times as much as people consumed during the rationing period. The news that limiting sugar early in a child’s life could protect their brain later confirms two things: how susceptible our brain is to high glucose levels and how early that vulnerability can impact us.
