The impact on the brain seemed to present in different ways. “Participants exposed to rationing had slightly greater grey-matter volume, fewer white-matter hyperintensities, and better performance in several cognitive domains later in life,” Zheng says. “Longer exposure was also associated with lower hazards of all-cause dementia and Alzheimer’s disease, and a delay in onset of up to approximately 2.6 years.” That is significant because brain volume shrinks with age as neurons and connections are lost. Since grey matter is made up of neurons and is where these connections happen, having more grey matter as we age is beneficial and suggests a younger-looking brain. White matter is the bundles of nerve fibres that carry signals between brain regions. On an MRI, “hyperintensities” are bright spots that indicate small areas of damage, usually from reduced blood flow, inflammation or general wear. They are common in older brains and are associated with things such as slower processing speed and higher dementia risk. So “fewer” hyperintensities means less damage – a marker of a healthier, younger-looking brain. Why might too much glucose – and a diet high in sugars – cause damage in the brain? There are several possible reasons. According to Zheng, heavy sugar exposure before and soon after birth hits the developing brain in two distinct phases. In the womb, high maternal sugar can trigger elevated blood sugar, insulin resistance and inflammation. This can impair placental function and disrupt early fetal brain growth. In early childhood, a high-sugar diet can interfere with how brain cells form connections (synapses), build protective nerve coatings (myelination), and build up “cognitive reserve” – the brain’s resilience against later decline. Zheng was eager to stress this was only a hypothesis, but given what we are learning about the effect of sugar on the brain, it makes sense. People with diabetes are known to be at higher risk of dementia than those without it. But it is not just high sugar levels that are bad for the brain; frequent episodes of low blood sugar are linked to risk of cognitive decline. The brain does best when blood sugar, or glucose, levels are neither too high nor too low. At the root of type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance – a condition in which cells become “numb” to insulin’s signals, forcing the pancreas to work overtime. This often leads to prediabetes, in which blood sugar levels are higher than normal but not yet at diabetic levels. Clinicians worry about prediabetes because it drives hidden vascular damage in the heart and brain even before a full diabetes diagnosis is made, according to Hong Kong-based general practitioner Dr Wong Sze-man. A typical Western diet – one with a much higher sugar content than during rationing years – causes blood glucose to run too high too often, which means insulin will, too. When that happens, you risk becoming insulin resistant. It is for this reason that some doctors recommend wearing a continuous glucose monitor – a device that tracks glucose levels round the clock, without needing repeated finger pricks. Originally designed for people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes to manage insulin dosing and avoid dangerous glucose highs/lows, in recent years people without diabetes have also started using them to see how their blood sugar responds to specific foods, exercise, sleep, or stress. You don’t need to wear a monitor to notice how sugar in your diet affects you, though, Wong says. Practical physical signs, such as fatigue, energy crashes and mood swings, are equally telling. Sweet cravings, dental issues, poor sleep and weight gain are other red flags. Having a sweet tooth as a child exposes a person to a lifetime risk of a taste for highly sugared foods. That is worrying in Hong Kong, Wong says, where clinicians are increasingly concerned about rising rates of diabetes, especially in younger people. Hidden sugars run high in the city’s popular iced teas, sweet dim sum glazes, bakery items and other popular foods. A developing fetus can taste flavours from its mother’s diet – including sweetness – by around the second trimester. According to the theory, called flavour-flow or prenatal/early flavour learning, repeated exposure to a flavour in utero and early infancy primes a preference for that flavour later. A high-sugar diet during pregnancy has been associated with children showing a stronger preference for sweet tastes and less acceptance of bitter ones, such as those of many vegetables, later in childhood. Moreover, if a mother has a sweet tooth, the diet in the home in which a child grows up is likely to be higher in sugary foods. Those with a sweet tooth – which may have developed because of their mother’s diet during pregnancy – can find ways to reduce sugar in their diet without feeling its deprivation, Wong says. She suggests “gradual sensory adaptation” to dial down the sweetness, for example, by reducing the sugar in your tea by a little every few days until you don’t notice how little is in it. Boost aroma by adding sweet-smelling spices to dishes – cinnamon, nutmeg, or vanilla extract. One easy hack to manage post-meal blood-sugar spikes is to eat the vegetables and protein on your plate before your carbohydrates. This also reduces later sugar cravings, Wong says. Take small and manageable steps rather than making drastic cuts to stand a greater chance of cutting sugar out for good, and safeguarding your brain. Like what you read? title: One in three kindergarteners in Hong Kong spends too much time on social media
description: A survey highlights excessive screen time among young children, prompting calls for better rules and parental guidance.
content:
One in three Hong Kong kindergarten pupils spends at least an hour a day on social media, a survey has found. Also, more than 80 per cent of arguments between parents and kids are about screen time.
The Hong Kong Institute of Family Education’s survey found that 34.7 per cent of kindergarten kids spend at least one hour a day on social media. The Department of Health says children ages two to five should have no more than one hour of screen time a day.
Sixty per cent of lower form secondary school students and 66.6 per cent of senior form students exceeded the global two-hour daily limit.
Tik Chi-yuen, the institute’s head, said kids in kindergarten mostly used screens to watch videos and talk to family using their parents’ accounts.
He said the trend was “not that worrying” because it was not common among these parents to use electronic gadgets to keep children quiet.
Tik urged the government to tighten regulation of children’s social media use, including restricting access for those under 16. He also asked schools and community groups to give more help to parents so they can learn digital skills and become better parents.

title: Hong Kong broadens sustainable finance taxonomy framework to boost transition capital
description: As Green Week kicks off, the HKMA expands its finance taxonomy to channel capital into projects that build climate resilience.
content: Hong Kong unveiled an expanded sustainable finance taxonomy as the city kicked off its annual Green Week on Monday, broadening the range of economic activities recognised as green or transition. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) launched a public consultation on the Phase 2B prototype of its Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance, adding 10 activities across transportation, manufacturing and waste management. Together with the reclassification of existing categories, the climate-mitigation framework now covers 39 activities, up from 25. The expansion brings battery manufacturing and recycling and other low-carbon technologies into scope, while providing transition pathways for hard-to-abate industries including aviation and steelmaking. Climate risks have become tangible financial risks Arthur Yuen, HKMA It also covers electric buses, minibuses and taxis, sustainable aviation fuel and green marine fuels such as methanol and ammonia. “Climate risks have become tangible financial risks,” Arthur Yuen Kwok-hang, HKMA deputy chief executive, said in an article published on Monday, adding that the market needed reliable assessment methods to channel capital into projects that genuinely strengthened resilience. The update coincides with the opening of the third Hong Kong Green Week, running from Monday to Friday, with around 60 events involving more than 100 local and international organisations, focusing on inclusive transition, climate adaptation and resilience. Phase 2B also strengthens the taxonomy’s climate-adaptation framework. The HKMA said the new phase introduced a five-step process-based assessment to account for location-specific climate risks, alongside 24 adaptation measures – 11 “white list” measures and 13 requiring case-by-case assessment. The initial focus is on shoreline protection and flood management. The framework is increasingly used in financing transactions. Projects aligned with the taxonomy this year included a HK$70 million (US$8.9 million) green loan for Hong Kong’s first public hydrogen refuelling station and a HK$200 million green loan for the purchase of electric buses, according to HKMA. “From the design stage, we have already taken market usage into consideration,” said Donald Chen, executive director for banking policy at the HKMA, at a media briefing on Friday. He added that the authority expected wider adoption as the taxonomy expanded to cover activities requested by market participants. Hong Kong arranged US$20.2 billion of green and sustainable bonds in the first half of 2026, up 3 per cent from US$19.7 billion a year earlier, while overall issuance in Asia remained flat, according to data provided by HKMA. The city accounted for 40 per cent of internationally issued green and sustainable bonds arranged in Asia in 2025, maintaining its top regional position for an eighth consecutive year, according to International Capital Market Association. The HKMA said it would develop practical guidance and survey banks on taxonomy usage, which could inform future consideration of whether to incorporate it into banking supervisory policy. The consultation runs until October 7.

title: Spark Deep Dive: Is Hong Kong’s GDP growth helping everyday workers and companies?
description: City’s economy seems to be doing well when it comes to its gross domestic product, but many workers and small businesses are struggling.
content:
Deep Dive delves into hot issues in Hong Kong and mainland China. Our easy-to-read articles provide context to grasp what’s happening, while our questions help you craft informed responses. Check sample answers at the end of the page.
Molly Lam lives in a public housing flat in Tsuen Wan. She worries about losing her job. She earns HK$12,000 a month. This is just enough to cover living expenses.
Lam believes news about Hong Kong’s economic growth means little to working-class people like her.
“The administration focuses heavily on high-end IT industries, which offer no safety net for low-skilled labourers like me,” she said.
Celeste Yeung is the co-founder and chief operating officer of a restaurant. She fears the city’s food and retail sectors are doing worse now than during the pandemic.
“[Our] cash flow is severely strained by weakened domestic spending, soaring rents, and many residents heading to mainland China or overseas during holidays,” said Yeung, whose business, Time To Gold, also supports the elderly by employing them.
After Covid-19, the city may have a stronger economy, but frontline workers like Lam and small businesses like Yeung’s feel they have not been part of the growth.
Gross domestic product (GDP) growth points to success but masks some struggles, industry leaders say. They suggest that the city must provide more immediate support to lower-income groups.
In the first quarter of this year, Hong Kong’s GDP saw its strongest quarterly growth in nearly five years. The growth was 5.9 per cent year on year.
“This macro-driven growth is expected to eventually stimulate local consumption, but the traditional retail and catering sectors are still facing severe hardships,” lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai said.
Retail sales rose only slightly between 2023 and 2025.
Shiu added that bricks-and-mortar industries such as retail and food and drink were being squeezed by a shift towards cross-border shopping, both via e-commerce and travel to the mainland. They would need time to adapt.
Amid the backdrop of US-China tensions and the US-Israel war on Iran, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has been trying to create new sources of growth.
He is pressing on with investments in innovation and technology, such as the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
Willian Chu, 65, is a logistics worker who lives in a subdivided flat in Sham Shui Po. He fears that the Northern Metropolis may result in smaller social subsidies for low-income groups.
Terence Chong Tai-leung is the executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance. Chong said the Northern Metropolis had yet to deliver real benefits to low-income workers, as it was still in development. Staff writers
1. Which of the following statements is false, according to the information in the news? (1) Hong Kong’s economy has become stronger after the pandemic. (2) The geopolitical tension between China and the United States is the only international issue holding back Hong Kong’s economic recovery in recent years. (3) This year, Hong Kong’s gross domestic product (GDP) had stronger growth than it did before 2021. (4) Hongkongers are heading to mainland China for holidays and weekends, causing challenges for the city’s shops and restaurants.
A. (1), (2) only B. (1), (3) only C. (2), (3) only D. (3), (4) only
2. How do workers like Molly Lam and Willian Chu feel about the government’s plans to invest in innovation and technology? Why do they feel that way?
3. What are some challenges that bricks-and-mortar industries are facing? Suggest ONE way to address the problem.
1. Note TWO observations about the growth of Hong Kong’s gross domestic product (GDP) from 2021 to 2026.
2. Do you think growth in the city’s GDP reflects how most people in Hong Kong are doing? Explain using examples from the news.
domestic spending: refers to the overall spending by households, businesses and government entities on goods and services within a specific country or region. In Hong Kong, people are spending less money in the city because many are going to mainland China for dining and entertainment.
gross domestic product (GDP): the total value of all goods and services produced by a place in one year
bricks-and-mortar industries: refers to traditional businesses that operate out of physical shops, including sectors for retail, hospitality, catering and entertainment
Northern Metropolis: a project that aims to transform 30,000 hectares of land along Hong Kong’s border with Shenzhen into a housing hub, a university town and an innovation-driven economic engine
They feel ambivalent or negatively about these plans because they think investment in innovation and technology will not have a positive impact on them and could even harm them by leading to a reduction in subsidies for low-income groups.
There has been a shift towards cross-border shopping, both via online e-commerce and travel to the mainland. The rent is also getting more expensive. The government can address this problem by capping rent increases for small and medium-sized businesses. This way, these businesses can have more room to offer deals that entice people to spend. (accept all reasonable answers)
The city’s GDP saw a severe downturn from 2021 to 2022 because of the Covid-19 pandemic. The economy has been recovering since 2023 but has not reached pre-pandemic levels. (accept all similar answers)
GDP only reflects the overall economy, but it can’t reflect how widely this growth is distributed among different industries and people with different income levels and jobs. For example, retail sales have only risen slightly while GDP has grown. Restaurants like Time To Gold are not getting enough customers. Many low-wage workers are still worried about having no safety nets. (accept all reasonable answers)

title: A Collective Space’s crafting sessions combine woodwork and well-being
description: The wellness-focused collective, run by Emmy Sandt and Sne Roy, is a rare women-founded initiative in the traditionally male carpentry world.
content:
Artisans carefully measured a wooden plank before methodically chiselling the surface with blades to shape the piece.
This is a type of woodworking found at A Collective Space, founded by Emmy Sandt and Sne Roy. The subtractive process involves some intention, as the delicate taking away of wood means there is little chance of “undoing” any mistakes.
The design and wellness collective had its own intention: to be a place where mindfulness and healing met creativity and crafts.
For Sandt and Roy, woodworking is more than a homeware-making art; it is also a process that allows one to embrace their missteps and blunders .
“In woodworking, some mistakes are irreversible. You can only start again,” said Roy, the director of programmes.
“And that is the very definition of resilience, right? You keep going … It’s OK to start over from scratch. It doesn’t mean I wasted my effort; it means I perfected my skill.”
Roy, 35, and Sandt, 33, officially launched the collective in 2023, carving out a community through tailor-made workshops and collaborations with NGOs.
It is all done with the intention of building connection and supporting well-being.
Sandt, the head carpenter, was born and raised in Hong Kong to Finnish parents. She then moved to Australia at 18 and spent six years building wooden theatre sets.
The temporary nature of the work came to frustrate her.
“I felt quite disheartened by the way you would build something and then you would throw it away at the end of the show,” Sandt said. “I wanted to have a bit more permanence in the stuff that we did.”
Sandt began to shift her focus to furniture. When she returned to Hong Kong, woodworking helped her through a tumultuous time between 2019 and 2021.
“I found woodworking deeply therapeutic,” Sandt said. “It was really my way to ground myself and to feel less dislocated from the world.”
Her partner Roy is originally from Kolkata in West Bengal, India. She moved to Hong Kong as a child and later worked in education and counselling.
Sandt introduced Roy to woodworking shortly after the pair met in 2017. They fondly recalled building Ikea furniture together and even making home furnishings by upcycling discarded items.
During the Covid-19 pandemic, Roy helped Sandt with different carpentry projects.
Like Sandt, Roy also found the process healing: “I soon realised that it was immensely therapeutic for me to do something so technical and [also] repetitive.”
And behind the wood grain, their relationship was changing. In the process of physically building something together, the pair were also getting closer.
“We got to know each other at a different level,” Roy explained.
The women also realised woodworking’s potential to offer others a respite from the city’s stressful, fast pace.
“In Hong Kong, we are not a very patient bunch. We are built for speed and efficiency,” Roy said. “[But woodworking could be] a pleasant surprise … It can take you days and weeks, sometimes months and years, to fulfil a project from start to finish.”
Sandt’s carpentry journey was influenced by her father, who enjoyed fixing and building things himself: “In my head, if you want to make something, it is possible to do it. You just need to put your head down.”
But becoming a female carpenter in Hong Kong was not so simple. In Finland, Sandt said, it was no big deal to find women in male-dominated spaces and roles. In Hong Kong, there were “clear gender norms” in certain industries, she said.
“It was definitely a challenge … Many, many times, I have faced ‘Where’s your boyfriend?’, ‘Where’s your husband?’, ‘There’s no way that you are doing this.’”
After years of experience – and without having to seek out or feel the need for a man’s help with her work – Sandt is solid in her career. Today, she runs her own furniture-making company, independent of the collective.
“One thing that I always kind of harp on about is that women can do physical things,” Sandt said.
And challenging gender stereotypes goes beyond carpentry for the collective’s founders. It also extends to women taking on roles traditionally filled by men.
“Women’s leadership is sometimes considered to be more gentle and kind,” Roy explained. “Of course, we should be kind, but you … can be confident and forceful and that’s OK. That doesn’t make you aggressive. It just makes you passionate.”
Every month, A Collective Space, stylised in all lower case, organises two sessions of “Crafts & Yaps”, informal hour-long gatherings of about 10 people.
The group chit-chats while working on a “mystery craft”, which is only revealed upon arrival. They work with their hands while Roy guides the conversation with questions designed to help them open up.
Roy and Sandt came up with the idea last year after they found that many young people were hesitant to join traditional, formal events because of “performance anxiety”.
“A lot of people said they would like to come but were too afraid to attend a public workshop,” Roy said.
The solution was to eliminate the need to be perfect. The pair envisioned a gathering where participants needed zero woodworking experience.
“You’re gonna fail. It’s gonna be ugly, and that’s OK,” Roy explained.
“When you are engaged in something else where you don’t feel the need to have intense eye contact with someone, you’re actually able to open up in a much deeper, meaningful way,” Sandt added.
In addition to the regular crafting and conversation sessions, the pair organise and host programmes at Hong Kong schools and universities that are tailored to desired learning outcomes. Roy said these workshops in particular showed her why their approach was important for young people today.
Crafts & Yaps participants have told the pair about staying connected with others from their session; some even regularly met up for board game nights and dinners.
Sandt said she hoped they were able to think back on the “one tiny little thing” they had made in the workshop, and the “peace and serenity” it may have brought them.
“I can’t change society. I can’t change the pressure … but I can give you a space where you can laugh and just have fun,” Roy said. “I hope that they feel seen and heard while they are here.”

title: Discover your one-of-a-kind traits with these two activities
description: Create a personal profile and explore fingerprint differences to celebrate individuality.
content:
Every person in the world is different, and that means you are, too. No one else looks exactly like you, likes the same things as you, or has your unique mix of great personality traits. Let’s have fun and find out what makes you special with these two activities.
Did you know that even identical twins have different fingerprints? This shows that nature never makes the same pattern twice – kind of like how everyone has their own unique personality.
Invite your parents, siblings or friends to be your fingerprint volunteers.
Have each of them gently press their thumb onto the ink stamp pad. Make sure their thumb is evenly covered in ink.
Press their inked thumb firmly down onto white paper. Lift it straight up carefully so the ink does not smudge. Write their name directly under the print.
Clean their thumb immediately with a wet wipe.
Lastly, place your own thumbprint right next to theirs.
Look closely at the prints. Notice how the tiny loops, whorls, curves and arch shapes look completely different for every single person.
Content provided by JEMS Character Academy

title: China get Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup campaign back on track as Italy give US a scare
description: Centre Han Xu leads way as China edge Czech Republic in overtime thriller, but fail to get most out of teenage sensation Zhang Ziyu.
content: China used their considerable height to battle past ⁠the Czech Republic ⁠74-70 in an overtime thriller ⁠at the Fiba Women’s World Cup on Sunday, with the New York Liberty’s nearly 2.13-metre-tall (7 foot) centre Han Xu’s double-double making the difference. In a later match, the United States survived their toughest test at the tournament in two decades with a 55-52 win over Italy, with Jackie Young scoring 10 points. Han powered China to the comeback win with 22 points ‌and 14 rebounds to get their campaign back on track, after a demoralising 94-61 opening defeat by the US. “I feel so proud of my teammates and coach,” Han said, after her team recovered from a five-point deficit with less than 30 seconds left on the ⁠clock to force the overtime. “Even in the last quarter, we lost six points but ‌we never gave up.” Han had put China level at 53-53 in the final quarter after her team had trailed for most of the game. Eliška Joklová put the Czechs 64-59 up with 27 seconds left only for Luo Xinyu to respond with a three-pointer and Yang Shuyu to level at 64-64 with three seconds to go – after Joklová missed two free throws. There was still time for Joklová to miss another chance to clinch the win. Yang also completed the scoring in overtime for China, which failed to get the most from 2.2-metre centre Zhang Ziyu. The 19-year-old sensation could score only three points in her second game after 13 on her World Cup debut against the US on Friday. “She has very great talent and we need to fix how we play together,” Yang said of the teenager’s performance. “Today everybody could see that we did not play so well with her, and we have to fix it.” China’s considerable height has astonished teams in Berlin and fans around the world, with Zhang providing one of the tournament’s early viral ⁠moments in her ⁠first call-up to the senior national team. “I feel like if me and her both go to ‌the court together I always want to give her good energy,” Han told reporters. “She’s the best ‌post player, ‌she can finish to the rim and she can protect the ‌paint.” Han will find herself across the court from her former Liberty teammate and ⁠close friend Lorela Cubaj when China play Italy in their final group-stage encounter ⁠on Monday. Meanwhile, the Americans’ win stretched their winning run to 32 games going back to a loss to Russia in the 2006 semi-finals. It was the fewest points the Americans had scored in a World Cup win since they beat Australia 42-38 in 1967. Italy trailed by 15 points early in the second quarter, but fought back through Olbis Andre and Cecilia Zandalasini as they cut the gap to six points before the break. Andre’s block on Caitlin Clarke before halftime brought a roar from the fans who increasingly got behind Italy, and Andre gave the Italians a three-point lead in the third quarter. The US trailed 50-48 with 4:29 left before going on a 7-0 run. Italy (1-1) had one last chance to tie it, but Zandalasini’s three-pointer was off at the buzzer. The tournament has provided plenty of ‌thrills so far, with ‌talent surging around the world, as Mali recorded their first win over a European team with an 82-73 Group A defeat of Spain, who had been widely expected to enjoy a deep run.

“This macro-driven growth is expected to eventually stimulate local consumption, but the traditional retail and catering sectors are still facing severe hardships,” lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai said.
Retail sales rose only slightly between 2023 and 2025.
Shiu added that bricks-and-mortar industries , such as retail and food and drink, were being squeezed by a shift towards cross-border shopping, both via e-commerce and travel to the mainland. They would need time to adapt.
Amid the backdrop of US-China tensions and the US-Israel war on Iran, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has been trying to create new sources of growth. He is pressing on with investments in technology and innovation, such as the Northern Metropolis megaproject.
Willian Chu, 65, is a logistics worker who lives in a subdivided flat in Sham Shui Po. He fears that the Northern Metropolis may lead to smaller social subsidies for low-income groups.
Terence Chong Tai-leung is the executive director of the Chinese University of Hong Kong’s Lau Chor Tak Institute of Global Economics and Finance. Chong said the Northern Metropolis had yet to deliver real benefits to low-income workers, as it was still in development. Staff writers

(1) Hong Kong’s economy has become stronger after the pandemic. (2) The geopolitical tension between China and the United States is the only international issue holding back Hong Kong’s economic recovery in recent years. (3) This year, Hong Kong’s gross domestic product (GDP) had stronger growth than it did before 2021. (4) Hongkongers are heading to mainland China for holidays and weekends, causing challenges for the city’s shops and restaurants.

2. Do you think growth in the city’s GDP reflects how most people in Hong Kong are faring? Explain using examples from News.
Despite the city’s investments in innovation, a biotech start-up describes the hurdles they still face
Traditional companies are also turning to technology in hopes of reducing their losses
Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce CEO Patrick Yeung Wai-tim said the city’s economic transformation would inevitably cause some pain during the process.
“Hong Kong is finding its direction of transformation, but success is not guaranteed, and everyone must work hard,” he said.
Sue Lam Wai-han is the chief operating officer of biotech start-up Pentide Therapeutics, based in Hong Kong’s Science Park. She felt the Northern Metropolis was strategically vital to the city’s development but said the emphasis was on attracting larger corporations and multinational pharmaceutical companies.
Lam, 49, said pharmaceutical start-ups such as Pentide needed clinical trial support, the capacity to manufacture their products to quality assurance standards and efficient regulatory and approval processes. The government has pledged to build an ecosystem for this.
“There are products and infrastructure, but there is a missing link in clinical trials,” she said. “We are desperate to start a clinical trial, which is crucial for a biotech start-up like us.”
Pentide focuses on developing innovative drug delivery methods, such as nasal sprays, to enhance treatment effectiveness.
To bridge funding gaps, they have tried to generate revenue by branching into health supplements while hoping the government will connect them with pharmaceutical factories.
“The road to success is very rough,” Lam said.
Sunny Lo Hoi-kwong, chairman of the fast-food chain operator Cafe de Coral Holdings, described last year as a period of restructuring to adapt to the city’s new spending patterns.
He said the group closed underperforming outlets, expanded into new residential areas and provided more discounts, offers and menu options. It also adopted digital tools and AI, improved efficiency and controlled overheads and rental expenses. Its workforce shrank by 8 per cent to 17,444 employees as of March 31, compared with a year earlier.
Lo said these measures helped Cafe de Coral recover some lost ground in the second half of 2025, but net profit still fell 29.4 per cent to HK$164.1 million in the financial year ending March 31.
“In tough times, a purely defensive strategy is not enough. After the setbacks of the first half [of 2025], we have regrouped and recovered – and are now ready to return to offence,” he said.
Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of Our Hong Kong Foundation think tank, said rapid AI transformation was opening new avenues for business survival. Rather than relying solely on top-line consumer growth , many firms were successfully deploying generative AI and automation to cut operating costs, optimise logistics and improve overall operational efficiency, he added. title: Tiny snails rescued from extinction on Deserta Islands in the Atlantic Ocean
description: Breeding programmes revive rare species as hundreds return to their natural habitat.
content:
Hundreds of tiny snails have been brought back to a rocky island in the Atlantic Ocean after a breeding programme was set up to save them.
The government of Madeira asked experts from Chester Zoo and the ZooParc de Beauval in France for help. Their job was to protect four types of snails found only on the Deserta Islands. These islands are part of the Madeira group of islands in the Atlantic Ocean.
A small number of snails were sent to different institutions, including 21 of the type called Geomitra coronula . These snails were believed to be the last remaining examples of their kind. They were found holding on under a single rock on Bugio Island.
More than 300 young snails that were raised at Chester Zoo have been sent back to live in the wild on the island. In addition, 270 snails from the species Discula lyelliana , which were bred by experts in France, have also been released into the wild.
Chester Zoo is now looking after all four species, Atlantica calathoides , Geomitra grabhami , Geomitra coronula and Discula lyelliana , in breeding pods similar to their natural environment.
“By the time the Madeira government contacted us for help, one of the species, Geomitra coronula, was so close to extinction that its entire global population could fit inside a single Petri dish … If we missed this chance, that was it – they were gone,” said Tamas Papp, who works at Chester Zoo.
Despite their small size, snails are important to the ecosystem (see graphic).
Over hundreds of years, people cut down many trees on the islands. They also brought in rabbits and goats. These animals ate the native plants, which stopped them from growing back.
At the same time, mice came to the islands. They used the snails for water because the islands are very dry. This made the snails disappear.

title: Listen Up: Taiwan’s ageing seaweed harvesters hope younger women wade in
description: Practise your English with our short listening exercises: play the audio and answer the questions in our quiz.
content:
Listen to the podcast and answer the questions in the quiz. If you’re still unsure about a question, read the script provided to help you.
This week’s podcast is voiced by Wasi Anjum Mirza, a production editor on SCMP’s digital desk, and Cathy Hilborn Feng, SCMP’s health and wellness editor.
Voice 1: Unfazed by the crashing waves, 72-year-old Wu Feng-chiao yanks fistfuls of brownish-purple seaweed to process into jelly. She is one of the last women in Taiwan keeping this marine harvest tradition alive. Wu said seaweed foraging on the rocky coastline at the edge of the Pacific Ocean could be arduous and dangerous. But her passion has kept her going for more than half a century.
Voice 2: Younger Taiwanese largely opt to live in the city rather than choose the island’s remote northeast. Once Wu’s generation of hainu – meaning “sea women” – is no longer able to carry on this seaweed harvesting tradition, she fears it could vanish completely.
Voice 1: Along the easternmost point of the coast, sea women stuff net sacks with “stone flowers” – as the algae is called in Taiwanese and Mandarin. They then lug heavy loads back home, spreading the seaweed out on the ground and snipping off residue. Absorbing sunlight, the seaweed takes about four days to fully dry before it can be washed several times and boiled to release the jellylike substance known as agar-agar.
Voice 2: Bobbing around the shore in goggles and a wetsuit, an energetic Wu recounted her decades of practising this tradition. She learned it from her father as a teenager. Wu said the seaweed grew around big rocks, which meant that when there were big waves, you had to move quickly. If a wave hit, you could get hurt.
Voice 1: Wu is a tiny woman, but she can confidently haul a single sack weighing 40 to 50 jin , which is around 20-25kg, over slippery rocks. Wu said this was tough work. The hardest part is carrying the seaweed back. She said it was heavy and her shoulders would ache afterwards.
Voice 2: Hainu , a vestige of the Japanese colonial era, shares some similarities with haenyeo, the centuries-old matriarchal tradition of free-diving in South Korea, although Taiwan’s sea women do not go underwater.
Voice 1: Wu said there were no more than four women in Magang, a fishing village in New Taipei City, who still regularly collected “stone flowers”. These women are all in their 70s or older. She hopes young people will come back and carry it on so that the tradition does not disappear.
Voice 2: Beyond the threat from demographic changes, the seaweed itself is also especially scarce this year, according to Wu, although she was not sure why. Developers have been encroaching on the peaceful coastal village, but Wu said the women were still resisting them. In 2018, residents created the Sandiaojiao Cultural Development Association to preserve Magang’s stone houses and keep the hainu tradition alive.
Voice 1: Despite the odds, Wu is by no means ready to give up. Even on days when she doesn’t plan to go into the water, she goes once she sees how calm the water is.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Challenger): Jakarta struggles to control stray cat population numbers
description: The story on this page has some tougher vocabulary words and questions to improve your reading and grammar.
content:
[1] Three flea-riddled kittens play near a food vendor at a busy railway station in Jakarta. The city is home to one of the biggest urban stray cat populations on Earth. There are about 1.5 million street cats in the Indonesian capital. Most people dote on them.
[2] “Cats are there to neutralise negative auras and to cheer you up,” 33-year-old vendor Saiful Faizin told Agence France-Presse. He gives the strays water and leftovers from his chicken porridge cart. He also plays with the little ones.
[3] There is no government department dedicated to domestic animal welfare. As a result, the number of stray cats in Jakarta has exploded over the years. They escape Jakarta’s traffic and depend on kind-hearted people for food and medical care. “There are too many cats here ... so they end up dying ... [in] incidents involving motorbikes,” said vendor Hilwa Tasya Sholehah, 25.
[4] Some residents welcome the free rat control. However, they also complain about smelly cat urine. There are also problems with noisy fights and property damage, such as scratches to motorbike seats. Jakarta has been free of rabies since 2004. This is because of mass vaccination of strays. However, cats can still give people other illnesses or bugs.
[5] “Some people don’t realise that giving the cats [food] without spaying or neutering them can cause another problem, which is overpopulation,” said Caolina Fajar. She works for the NGO Let’s Adopt Indonesia. “They keep mating, they keep having babies, and the population is increasing.”
[6] Let’s Adopt Indonesia spayed and neutered 2,274 cats in Jakarta last year. It receives money from private donors and overseas foundations to cover the costs. Estimates of the true number of strays in Jakarta vary wildly. One city official estimated the number at about 305,000. Another believed it could be five times that amount.
[7] Last year, the city sterilised 21,000 cats under a new programme. It budgeted 3.5 billion rupiah (HK$1.5 million) for the programme for 2026. However, the government needs much more money to achieve its goal. It aims to control the stray cat population by sterilising at least 70 per cent of strays. Jakarta’s top agriculture official is Hasudungan Sidabalok. He said the service did not have nearly enough official shelters, vets or paramedics to deal with cats in need.

title: Study Buddy (Challenger): ADHD fuels Hong Kong creator’s viral ChiQSinTV
description: This page is for students who want to take their reading comprehension to the next level with difficult vocabulary and questions to test their inference skills.
content:
[1] For Kenneth Lee, having attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) means he has always been interested in learning different things. “I took visual arts and history, and I learned Photoshop just so I could personalise the cards for the online game Game of Heroes: Three Kingdoms, ” recalled the 31-year-old product designer. Three Kingdoms was popular in Hong Kong during the 2000s and involved players being assigned a customisable historical character.
[2] Today, Lee expresses his creativity through ChiQSinTV, which translates to “crazy TV” in Cantonese, on Instagram and YouTube. He launched his Instagram account in April. By July 28, he had amassed 37,500 followers. His most popular content features him reimagining the Harry Potter film series with Cantopop idols or beloved characters from Hong Kong films like Young and Dangerous (1996).
[3] “It takes three days of locking myself in my room after work to make an episode,” Lee said. “The most frequently asked question in my comments section is whether or not what I do violates copyright law,” he added. “I’ve done some research, and as long as I’m not making money from the content, then it’s OK.”
[4] His love for Cantonese films and television stems from the death of Hong Kong icon Lydia Sum Tin-ha in 2008. “I remember watching ‘Dodo’ Cheng Yu-ling visibly tear up and wiping away tears on live television while hosting the TVB tribute special to [Sum]. I really felt that as these legends age and pass, we lose a bit of our culture,” he said.
[5] Lee was introduced to Harry Potter at the age of six, when his grandfather took him to the cinema to watch Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone . However, he did not pick up the book series until he was studying at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. “My father bought me the book in English when I was young, and I felt I had to understand every single word to appreciate the book, which brought on task paralysis ... so I never finished reading it,” he said.
[6] The idea to cross Harry Potter with popular Cantonese culture came about because of his curiosity in AI. “I started using ChatGPT when it came out, at first just to help me organise my thoughts and research, but as time wore on I felt I could create more.” He feels that ChiQSinTV is a culmination of his life experiences with ADHD. Meanwhile, Harry Potter showed him how a magical wizarding world could coexist with modernity, and his love for Hong Kong films led him to cast Chinese celebrities in the Harry Potter roles in his head.
[7] He wants people both with and without ADHD to know that whatever they spend their time on will not go to waste. “What doesn’t seem useful now might help you in the future,” he said. “Don’t be afraid of being curious.”
Source: South China Morning Post, July 28

title: Open Questions | Economist Lan Xiaohuan on the balancing act needed to boost China’s consumption
description: The bestselling author also discusses how recent geopolitical events are shaping China and makes the case for a social safety net.
content: Lan Xiaohuan is a professor of economics at China Europe International Business School. His book, How China Works: An Introduction to China’s State-led Economic Development, has sold millions of copies in China and has been translated into multiple languages. Here, he discusses the economic realities behind China’s record trade surplus, the case for a stronger social safety net, and how public data infrastructure shapes the artificial intelligence race with the United States. This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here. Since you wrote How China Works, the global and domestic environments have both evolved. What are the most critical shifts and developments for China? If you were to add a new chapter to the book to reflect these changes, what would be its central theme? I would not add a new chapter; I would write an entirely new book. It’s not that there aren’t new issues, but rather addressing them requires a new framework. Domestically, the decline of the real estate market and the rapid rise of manufacturing and technology are significant shifts. My new book would likely focus on China’s industry and technology. But actually, I think the most consequential changes are external: the impact of the pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war, the energy shocks regarding Iran, and shifting political dynamics in the United States. In comparison, China’s domestic baseline has remained relatively stable. How China Works explains to the world how to view China. I’ve also thought about writing a book explaining to Chinese people how to view the world. Historically, global world views have been dominated by a North Atlantic, Euramerican perspective. So what is the world from a Chinese perspective? In terms of economics, that would mean looking more closely at Southeast Asia, Central Asia and Russia, where we share closer relations but don’t yet have a systematic understanding of them. Amid a property market downturn, how can local governments secure new, stable streams of income? Fiscal pressure can’t be solved by money alone, nor by changing the development model alone; it needs both. Current policy adjustments – such as relaxing special local government bond quotas and easing bank credit – help refinance old debts with new ones to prevent defaults. This is meant to help buy time. Long-term fiscal sustainability is not only about increasing income – it requires aligning expenditure with income. Past local government spending was too high. It’s unrealistic to expect land revenue to support such a large amount of spending, or to expect other revenue sources to plug the fiscal deficit left by the property market downturn. There aren’t any long-term sustainable revenue sources that can directly replace land finance. Therefore, I think a reasonable approach is tax reforms in the long term, alongside spending cuts. Much of China’s core infrastructure – high-speed rail networks, urban undergrounds, major city expansions, and so on – has already been completed, so these kinds of local government expenditures will naturally decline. Local governments might still want to launch new projects, such as building airports, but their finances might not allow it. Investment remains a major engine of economic growth, but its share is not as large as before, nor should it be. For tax reforms, perhaps it’s not exactly about increasing local government revenue, but about making the distribution of the tax burden more reasonable, such as through adjustments to the value-added tax and consumption tax. But how exactly should they be adjusted? Even a fraction of a percentage point difference in tax rates carries major consequences. So while scholars have offered various opinions, these proposals mean little until implemented. Creating a strong social security system is what the government should do, and it shouldn’t be linked to consumption You mentioned that investment’s share as a growth driver must decline. Given the slow pace of rebalancing so far, what structural changes are needed for Beijing to boost domestic demand and bring household consumption in line with global benchmarks? There are two ways to increase income: raise wages, or raise property and asset income. In terms of wages, most citizens do not receive income from their labour from the state; they are employed by private enterprises. The state cannot simply mandate private sector wage hikes, it can only optimise the business environment in hopes that employment wages improve. For property and assets, this requires stabilising property values, improving financial asset performance and unlocking the latent value of rural land, such as through asset revitalisation. The main thing that the government can do directly is to step up social security and strengthen spending on education, healthcare and pension security. China’s current savings rate is relatively high, so hopefully these measures can help reduce the savings rate and increase consumption. But I hold a slightly different view from many economists on this issue, in that I think public welfare spending should be expanded regardless of whether it boosts consumption. Creating a strong social security system is what the government should do, and it shouldn’t be linked to consumption. Whether that triggers consumer spending is outside direct policy control, as citizens have a right to maintain a high savings rate even with a robust safety net. The transition to raise consumption is a long-term process. Household consumption currently accounts for around 40 per cent of GDP in China. In the United States, it accounts for around 70 per cent. But the number is so high because it is driven by housing, healthcare and education expenses. In China, healthcare and education – which form the bulk of service consumption – are not priced according to the market and are pretty affordable. In the US, healthcare and college tuition are relatively expensive. Do we really want to depend on this to drive consumption? I don’t think so. Germany and Japan are better international benchmarks, with household consumption at around 50 to 55 per cent of their economies. But if China raises its consumption share by one percentage point per year, the rebalancing will still take over a decade. Weak household consumption and industrial overcapacity have also driven China’s trade surplus to record highs. Beijing has signalled that it wants to rebalance these trade flows, but how successful can it be if demand remains anaemic? China’s trade surplus issue isn’t just about weak domestic demand and overcapacity – it also requires a willing buyer. China cannot force foreign markets to purchase its goods. One country’s exports and another country’s imports are two sides of the same coin. The surplus arises because foreign markets genuinely need these goods and demand is substantial. While foreign markets do want to restrict Chinese imports, what they really want is for China to set up factories there to sell the goods directly, while creating jobs and facilitating technology transfers. Trade barriers can’t restrict demand, they can only aim to take a cut of the profits and redistribute them. From China’s side, imports will surely expand, especially as the appreciation of the yuan makes foreign goods and services cheaper. But whether this expansion is driven by goods or services is still uncertain. Raising goods imports might be difficult. The things that China wants – such as graphics processing units and lithography equipment – others won’t sell. What else are we supposed to buy? American cars? That is hardly realistic. Customs data – including the US$1.2 trillion trade surplus – only represents trade-in goods and has significant limitations. Supply chains have become extremely complex. Many goods recorded as imports from Europe, Canada, Mexico and Southeast Asia might actually come from China, and vice versa. Goods that China imports that might not appear to come from the US or the European Union could actually be from these places too. Importing more services is possible, but it is difficult to calculate. For example, spending money while travelling overseas and sending children abroad to study count as importing services, but customs doesn’t track this. It can only be calculated through foreign exchange data. The current account surplus theoretically includes services, but service data is more complicated in reality. It’s hard to say who holds the trade surplus for services. China’s services imports have also been constrained by external political factors, such as strict visa policies or restricted access to certain educational programmes in the US. The fact that there are fewer Chinese students studying in the US now, that’s completely caused by the US themselves. Chinese people genuinely want to buy – previously goods, now services – but frankly, imports are severely restricted. Many people have noted that data has now become a new factor of production, with some comparing it to oil. What’s your view on this? Data as oil is just one analogy. I think it’s probably outdated now in the age of AI, though many data dispute rulings still work on the logic of this analogy. But data is different from oil. First, if you extract it, that does not stop me from extracting it too – oil does not work that way. If there is oil under a piece of land, your extraction precludes mine. Data does not have that problem; we can both use it. Second, oil is a natural resource – either you have it or you do not. Data availability, however, can be generated by policy. The data exists; it is simply a matter of whether you allow access. If you adjust usage policies – as Europe has done by relaxing certain rules – a vast amount of data suddenly becomes accessible. Therefore, the critical factor with data is what the law dictates: how much is recognised, what can be used, and under what restrictions. I think that regulatory boundary is the primary constraint. Oil is a very tangible resource, so ownership is easy to determine. If it is under my land, the oil belongs to me. Data ownership is not nearly as simple. How do we regulate this? A unified model has yet to emerge globally, and it is difficult to see how one will. There are other analogies to compare data to, and each one reveals different characteristics. For example, data is also inherently a product of labour. Let’s say you drive an electric vehicle. You’re constantly contributing your data to autonomous driving. The more you drive, the more data you contribute, but you don’t get paid for it – that’s frustrating. You continuously generate data for others to use, but you don’t receive corresponding compensation for the data generated by your actions, while others profit from this data. Frankly speaking, when it comes to the development path of artificial intelligence, only China and the United States are relevant right now How will this unique role of data affect the development of AI across different regions and their economies? Frankly speaking, when it comes to the development path of artificial intelligence, only China and the United States are relevant right now. Other countries lack foundational models. Europe has a presence but faces real structural headwinds, including strict data rules. The primary differentiator, then, boils down to who controls the data. In China, many core data assets are public property, meaning a wider variety of market participants can develop applications on top of them. In the US, however, commercial data holders always command a share of AI revenues. Take the legal sector as an example. In China, legal data repositories are provided directly by the government via the Supreme People’s Court, allowing anyone to access them. In contrast, the US market is dominated by two private data vendors, so data is more expensive to access. The two vendors are also developing their own AI tools, making it difficult for independent developers to enter the space. Similarly, Chinese municipalities and state-owned enterprises accumulate vast amounts of smart city and intelligent transport data. If held as private property, this data would be commercialised for profit. But if it is treated as basic infrastructure, the data owners do not extract direct profits from it. From the perspective of benefiting AI development, accessible, high-quality data – not completely free, but requiring just a nominal cost – is definitely more beneficial for applications. Think about the many companies in China developing autonomous driving systems: a significant reason is the relatively readily available underlying data, thanks to the infrastructure built by the government in the early stages. You don’t just need vehicle data, you also need various other data like road data and traffic light data. It needs to form a complete ecosystem, and I think you can’t do without public data. How close then is China to catching up with the US in the AI and tech race? In which areas is China leading, and where does it remain most vulnerable? Whether China catches up or surpasses the US in AI development is not important. What matters is which country can better utilise AI and leverage it for its own economy. The US leads in foundational models and computing power. But does this constitute a guaranteed advantage for the industry? Not necessarily. It also depends on electricity availability, data access, as well as the industry to which you apply it and the results it generates. For instance, the US excels in applications of AI in legal and financial fields. But for manufacturing, there are a few constraints. If a factory has not undergone digital transformation, or if its data is fragmented, practical application remains far off. AI models are universally applicable; the key is whether your infrastructure is ready – meaning whether your data is structured and your workflows are prepared. This is a new challenge for everyone, but I think China’s manufacturing sector has more application potential than the US. Cost is also a significant factor when it comes to widespread use for industry applications, and American models are considerably more expensive. Ultimately, the market will find a compromise in terms of cost-effectiveness. Some have voiced concerns that advanced tech sectors like AI and humanoid robotics are at risk of “involution” in China. What are your thoughts on this, and how can policymakers prevent these strategic industries from falling into the same hyper-competitive trap? Robotics are pretty competitive right now, but that’s not a risk yet. Humanoid robotics are still a long way off – the GPT moment for robots hasn’t arrived yet, so everyone thinks there’s still opportunities. Involution happens when the technological path is already set, and everyone rushes in. In the photovoltaic sector, for example, the playbook is clear. Companies expand capacity aggressively along established pathways while making incremental technical refinements. But for humanoid robots, the approach remains undefined. The industry is still in an exploratory phase. There’s no overcapacity now since robots aren’t widely used yet. Having hundreds of firms enter a sector at this stage is more of an exploration rather than involution. In contrast, I think AI large language models have already reached their limits in terms of competition. The “war of a hundred models” has consolidated because small firms cannot sustain the immense capital expenditures required for AI computing. The market has naturally winnowed down to a handful of players. Regarding policy guidance, I think these industries are still too young. Policymakers must understand what they are regulating. For instance, policies for the photovoltaic sector are relatively easy to formulate because the crux of the problem is already known. But right now, for sectors like humanoid robots, even some industry insiders cannot yet predict where the technology will land. While policymakers and entrepreneurs express optimism regarding technology, there is palpable public anxiety around AI, given stagnant wage growth and elevated youth unemployment. How worried should we be? I think worrying is pointless because we have reached a point of no return. AI is here to stay, and we simply have to accept it. While many economists argue that AI will cause unemployment but simultaneously create new jobs, I am sceptical of how this rebalancing will play out. There is likely to be significant demand for manual labour – which AI cannot replace for the time being – but displaced white-collar workers are probably unwilling and unable to take on these roles. And actually, even manual labour faces risks of displacement. I recently spoke with representatives from a major logistics company who shared that the number of delivery riders is falling as networks and systems are optimised with AI. If short-distance truck transport also becomes unmanned in the future, then another group of jobs will disappear. The immediate problem is university graduates, because entry-level jobs are increasingly hard to find. This is the case around the world. I don’t think China has reached a point where you can’t find work yet. There will always be work, even if it’s food delivery, but these are not the roles graduates seek. Or appropriate jobs may exist, but they are often not in first-tier cities or the graduates’ hometowns, which are usually the two preferred locations. Though at present, even with unemployment, basic survival is not threatened for most because general economic conditions have improved. Even if young people go home to “lie flat” and rely on their parents, they won’t go hungry. But I think the biggest and most important problem with AI is the erosion of a sense of purpose. Even if basic needs are met, people will begin to ask whether there is any meaning in this way of living. My imagination is limited, and I don’t know what new jobs will emerge. New types of demand will certainly appear, but I am sceptical that this will translate into a net increase in employment or successfully lower the unemployment rate on a macro level. How then should governments manage the risks that AI brings to employment? This brings us back to the same issue of social security. The issue is heavily discussed by academics around the world, but the shock has not yet reached a scale that forces major policy intervention in any country. In extreme scenarios, people have proposed a universal basic income, but that requires even greater fiscal expenditure. The AI economy cannot sustain itself if workers lose their incomes and can no longer consume. If everyone lost their jobs overnight, the solution might be clearer – universal basic income. The difficulty lies in the transition: many will lose their livelihoods while a small group becomes exceptionally wealthy. Taxing this wealth and creating alternative employment during this transition period will be difficult for any country. But we are not yet at that point, and you cannot mobilise state resources without an immediate crisis. And even if we were to reach that point, it will be a completely different world. It’s hard to imagine what that would look like – our relationship with AI, how to tax AI and robots, and so on. These will all change. But for that to happen, AI must enter the physical world. We need to see functioning, general-purpose robots first, and we are not there yet. While AI has progressed rapidly over the past six months, the marginal rate of development appears to be slowing. We have seen multiple cycles of AI optimism over the past half-century, but only recently did we see a breakthrough. It remains possible that artificial general intelligence or functional robotics will never truly materialise.

title: Spark Study Buddy (Explorer): Hong Kong hygiene authorities crack down on unlicensed hawkers
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Hong Kong’s hygiene authorities arrested 14 people in July. It was part of a crackdown on unlicensed hawkers. They took 600kg of food, some of which was expired. Food and Environmental Hygiene Department Chief Health Inspector Chan Sze-man is responsible for hawkers. She said the suspects were aged 38 to 76. They were arrested between July 17 and 28. All of the suspects held Hong Kong identity cards.
[2] Chan said the department is understanding of street sellers who do not have a licence. This is especially true if they are elderly or disabled. “But food safety is very important for public health. We cannot make exceptions,” she said. “We will never compromise.”
[3] Of the 14 arrested, 13 were also charged with obstructing public places. Two were also charged with selling restricted food without permission. The food officers took during the raids included cooked food, lunchboxes, bread, milk and expired items.
[4] Yuen Chiu-kit is a senior health inspector at Mong Kok District Environmental Hygiene Office. He said unlicensed hawkers were found at a footbridge on Tong Mi Road. Three people were arrested on suspicion of selling food from unknown sources. They were also charged with obstructing public places. Officers took about 83kg of food from unknown sources in Mong Kok.
[5] “Most of the food [taken] ... was cooked food from unknown sources,” Yuen said. He added that it was illegally sold in the open air. The sellers didn’t have proper refrigeration. They also didn’t have facilities to keep the food hot. “Food spoils easily and can breed bacteria in hot and humid weather. This kind of conduct seriously disregards public food safety and health.”
[6] Under the Public Health and Municipal Services Ordinance, only licensed hawkers are allowed to sell food. Offenders may face a maximum fine of HK$10,000 and six months’ imprisonment. Officers also learned that some residents had been collecting uncooked salmon from a food factory. In response, the department had provided information on proper hygiene. The factory later installed rubbish bins in appropriate locations. It began transferring waste directly to collection trucks. It also started using large rubbish bags to securely wrap up the waste.
Source: South China Morning Post, July 29

title: Study Buddy (Explorer): AI-designed burgers rival Big Mac in taste
description: Each week, this page tests your reading comprehension with an interesting story that we’ve adjusted to be more accessible for all English learners.
content:
[1] Researchers at Stanford University in California have developed an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that designs optimal burger recipes tailored to users’ preferences on taste, sustainability and nutritional content. This innovation was detailed in a study published in the scientific journal npj Science of Food.
[2] The AI-generated recipes also passed a real-world taste test with restaurant diners, the research team reported. “AI did not just generate plausible burger recipes – it created burgers that real people enjoy,” said Ellen Kuhl, a bioengineering professor at Stanford. “That may sound simple, but it means the model learned what makes food appealing to the human palate.”
[3] The modern hamburger originated in the late 19th century as a basic combination of minced meat and bread. Kuhl wrote in the journal Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering that although approximately 50 billion hamburgers are consumed annually in the US alone, the various combinations of burger ingredients are still largely unexplored.
[4] It is no surprise that the team estimates there are approximately 10 septillion possible burger recipes worldwide, which is a one followed by 43 zeros. To help organise these seemingly endless combinations, Kuhl and two colleagues developed a publicly accessible online tool called BurgerAI, which is trained on 2,216 recipes.
[5] The software calculates not only the taste of a burger using mathematical principles but also its texture, nutritional content, and sustainability for different age groups, genders, and consumer lifestyles. “For centuries, food design has been a matter of intuition, experience and trial and error,” Kuhl said. “We are beginning to show that AI can transform food design into a quantitative science with applications in other important fields.”
[6] The ultimate test involved a blind trial with 101 volunteers at a restaurant in San Francisco. Participants were served five AI-designed burgers, all professionally prepared, along with a Big Mac for comparison. According to the trio of researchers, the mushroom burger was more than 10 times more sustainable than the conventional product. In contrast, the bean burger had nearly double the nutritional value of its conventional counterpart.
[7] The AI burgers also held their own on taste. In terms of flavour, texture and overall verdict, they were at least on a par with the established burger classic, according to ratings on a seven-point scale. “We expected some trade-off between sustainability and consumer acceptance,” said lead author Vahidullah Tac. “But we found a burger with dramatically lower environmental impact could still compete with one of the world’s most successful burgers.”
[8] Food choices are among the most consequential everyday decisions people make, he stressed: “With one arrow, you can hit two targets – planetary health and personal health.”

title: Jamaica to petition UK king over slavery reparations in landmark legal test
description: Culture minister seeks Privy Council opinion on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade and UK liability for redress.
content: A Jamaican government delegation visiting Britain is set to file a petition addressed to King Charles on Monday, raising the question of slavery reparations, Kingston’s culture ministry said. Culture Minister Olivia Grange will lead the delegation “to advance Jamaica’s push for reparations for the African ancestors who suffered under hundreds of years of enslavement”, the ministry said in a statement. The petition asks the king, who is Jamaica’s head of state, to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to the Caribbean island’s highest court of appeal based in London. The delegation says it is the first time a Commonwealth country has used this legal route to pursue the matter of reparations. The British monarch has authority under the Judicial Committee Act of 1833 to refer legal matters to the London-based Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for an advisory opinion. Grange said it was “intended to ensure the long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured”. They want an advisory opinion on three questions: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress. A Buckingham Palace spokesman said: “We understand the Jamaican government is seeking a petition to be heard before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council,” referring to the London-based body. The king has “on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”, the palace added. Grange will also meet British Museum officials to discuss the return of colonial-era artefacts. King Charles and Queen Camilla are expected to visit the Caribbean later this year as part of a nine-day overseas trip which does not include Jamaica. An estimated 12.5 million Africans were forcibly taken by European nations from the 16th to the 19th century, and those who survived the trip across the Atlantic Ocean were enslaved on plantations in the Caribbean and elsewhere. In recent years, the UK has said it will not pay to make amends for slavery, while Caribbean leaders have called for a formal apology and various measures including debt cancellations. Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade that enriched their ancestors but have stopped short of a formal apology or any commitment to reparations. In a 2024 summit in Samoa, Commonwealth countries called on states including the UK to address the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade and open the door for dialogue on compensation. Additional reporting by dpa

title: Opinion | Heading to America to bridge the gap in US-China relations
description: In a year-long research across America, I hope to map where superpower friction ends, and where shared interest must begin.
content: Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case. I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side. As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here. Beginning this month, I take up a one-year appointment as a senior visiting scholar at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia at the Harvard Kennedy School. My purpose is straightforward to state and harder to fulfil: to sit down with American thought leaders across the political spectrum and ask them where they think this relationship is headed, and whether conflict is as inevitable as it now appears. To understand why this question matters so much, a brief look back is useful. The relationship began its current downward spiral in 2018, when the first Trump administration launched its opening salvo in the trade war. At the time, the confrontation felt sudden and jarring. It was not, in fact, sudden at all. Grievances had been quietly accumulating for decades across government, industry, trade, academia, science and technology. What changed in 2018 was that those grievances finally found their outlet. Layered on top were structural anxieties. In Washington, there is the perceived erosion of American primacy in manufacturing and superpower status. In Beijing, there is a mirror-image worry: that a declining but still-dominant America, unwilling to accept the reality of a rising China, is bent on containing its development, through tariffs, technology export controls and alliances built for that purpose. That mutual anxiety, in turn, fed less rational forces on both sides of the Pacific: incomplete narratives, hostile rhetoric, rumour dressed as fact, all doing damage to how each public sees the other. In Washington, there is a wry observation that American politicians agree on almost nothing except the need to get tough on China. In China, public sentiment towards the US has turned sour. The goodwill accumulated over decades of engagement has largely evaporated, replaced by mutual suspicion and precaution – of which my scrubbed phone is a small but telling example. None of this is to dismiss the seriousness of the moment. In the past fortnight alone, US Treasury officials have floated the possibility of sanctioning Chinese banks over their dealings with Iran, a suggestion that drew a sharp pushback from Beijing. Long Guoqiang, deputy director general of the Development Research Centre of the State Council, a leading government think tank, captured the prevailing mood in Beijing when he warned recently that the US remains “the biggest external source of uncertainty affecting China’s path to modernisation”. He argues that American containment of China will persist and intensify over the long run, notwithstanding the trade war truce. Long’s warning is not wrong. But a truce, however temporary, is also an opening. After their Beijing summit in May, President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are set to meet three more times this year: Xi is expected in Washington later this month, with further encounters likely on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 leaders’ meetings in November and December. Much of the coverage of these meetings will, understandably, focus on tangible deliverables – deals on trade, investment, technology. But Beijing and Washington might also use the moment to look at the bigger picture, along three tracks that receive far less airtime than they should. On global challenges, can both powers still cooperate on climate change and future pandemics, even if the current US administration shows little enthusiasm for the former? On engagement, law enforcement cooperation – against transnational crime, the booming scam-centre operations along China’s periphery, and the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals into North America – is a shining example. Quiet cooperation on precursor chemicals continued even through the worst of the trade war, proof that narrow, mutually beneficial arrangements can survive broader hostility when both sides see a direct interest in results. I am a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict And on global regulation, can the two governments find common ground in governing artificial intelligence, space and other emerging technologies? Right now, discourse in both capitals dwells overwhelmingly on the negative. Far less is said about where cooperation remains not just possible but necessary. That is what I intend to spend the next year finding out. I am, by long habit of observation, a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict. From Cambridge, I plan to reach beyond the think tanks most familiar to a China watcher, including into quarters not typically friendly to Beijing’s view of the world, setting aside my instincts and assumptions as best I can. What will I find by the time this fellowship ends? I do not know. But having spent three decades chronicling how perception so often diverges from reality in this relationship, I remain hopeful that reality, properly examined, still leaves room for two great powers to coexist – durably, and peacefully – for everyone’s sake.

title: Fireworks blast at Mexico festival kills 10, injures dozens
description: Explosion near church in Temascalcingo prompts investigation as rescue crews sift through debris.
content: Pyrotechnic material exploded during the festival for a patron saint in a town in Mexico State, collapsing a wall, killing at least 10 people and injuring another 64, Mexican authorities said. The explosion happened on Saturday night next to the Nuestra Senora de la Luz church in Temascalcingo, a municipality in central Mexico with 66,000 residents. Hundreds of them were preparing to watch a fireworks display that is part of a religious festival when the blast happened. The municipality is about 160km (100 miles) northwest of Mexico City. The cause of the explosion has not been determined and the Mexico State Attorney General’s Office has opened an investigation. A local bishop said two priests are among the injured. A video on social media shows the aftermath of the blast, with dozens of people walking through smoke and debris in search of survivors. Explosions involving pyrotechnics are common in Mexico, where fireworks are frequently used in street celebrations and religious festivals. Almost four years ago, a powerful fireworks explosion in a village in the municipality of Huejutla, in the central state of Hidalgo, left 17 people injured.

title: Amazon cargo plane overshoots runway at Miami airport, killing at least 5
