description: Boeing 767 overruns airstrip while landing at Miami International Airport, striking multiple vehicles on the ground.
content: An Amazon cargo plane barrelled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said. The aircraft overran the runway around 2pm after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and ploughed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalised with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference. It was not immediately clear if the pilots survived or those killed were all in vehicles when the plane struck. The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and co-pilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialised airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later. The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire. The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 48km/h (30 mph) were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service. The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24. More than 160 flights were cancelled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando International Airport, more than 320km north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate. Among the factors investigators are likely to consider is whether the plane flew too far before touching down, experts say. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 metres) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt. Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation. “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.” Sunday’s incident is not the first time an Amazon Prime Air plane has been involved in a fatal crash. In February 2019, Atlas Air Flight 3591, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating on behalf of Amazon Prime Air from Miami to Houston, entered a rapid descent and crashed into Trinity Bay, Texas, killing all three people on board. Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground, injuring 23 others. Miami, a major hub for trade with Latin America, is the third-busiest freight airport in ‌the US after Anchorage in Alaska and ‌Louisville in Kentucky, according to the Airports Council International. Freight shipments totalled nearly 3.5 million metric tons last year and passenger traffic reached 55.3 million, the eighth-busiest airport in the nation, according to the airport in June. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Iran plans new ‘exclusion zone’ outside Strait of Hormuz after ship attacks
description: Iranian security chief threatens sanctions on transit ships as US blockade and tanker strikes escalate tensions.
content: The new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council on Sunday said Tehran plans to announce an “exclusion zone” outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway. Mohsen Rezaei’s comments to Iran’s state broadcaster came with few details, a day after the US struck three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at US warships. Experts called the launches a dangerous escalation after Iran’s previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping. The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and “will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei said. “Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list.” It is not clear where Iran defines the location of the weekslong US blockade, which is aimed at Iranian ports and keeping Tehran from shipping out its oil. The US military has said over 20 warships are supporting the blockade, which as of Sunday had redirected 92 commercial ships and disabled three. The US has been introducing new measures to increase the economic pain on Iran after negotiations collapsed and no end to the intermittent fighting appears in sight. Meanwhile, Iran continues to attack some ships trying to transit the strait, which has become an important source of leverage for Tehran in the war that began February 28 with US and Israeli strikes. Iran earlier Sunday said it struck an unmanned US vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, a claim that the US military dismissed as a “total lie”. The United States and Iran resumed attacks last week, following a month of relative calm, with the Strait of Hormuz and areas along Iran’s southern coast again being targeted. At least five people were killed earlier in the week during a US bombardment that returned attention to the area where a school was hit in the war’s opening strikes. The Trump administration appears to have adopted a dual-prong approach to the conflict, responding militarily to attacks on the strait while going after foreign financial institutions that handle Iran’s money. But Tehran’s hardline new senior leaders including Rezaei have signalled a willingness to dig in after weathering decades of sanctions. Iran has found ways over the years to circumvent sanctions, and now the US blockade of its ports, and get its oil to buyers to help ease growing economic pressures. On the matter of the collapsed negotiations with the US, Rezaei on Sunday expressed wariness not only of the US but also of the mediators. The memorandum of understanding that the US and Iran signed in mid-June began to fall apart within days as each side accused the other of violations. “We had trusted our friends in Pakistan, Qatar or Oman, thinking that since they had stepped in as mediators, one of a mediator’s responsibilities is that if one side violates the agreement, they should stop them,” Rezaei said. “We are now pursuing diplomacy with guarantees.” The Strait of Hormuz is crucial to global oil and natural gas shipments and was seen as an international waterway before the war began. On Sunday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that on average, 9 million barrels of oil a day are getting through the strait, which should help to relieve pressure on energy prices. His estimate appeared to exceed average flows over the past 28 days through the strait, according to TankerTrackers.com and other sources. Wright told CNN that with oil also flowing through pipelines in the region, “we’re probably two-thirds or more of preconflict flows”. But those flows depend on the presence of the US Navy to help escort tankers and provide some protection against possible Iranian attack. Wright said he expected that other countries would eventually support the US Navy’s efforts. Meanwhile, Iran’s Rezaei in his interview with state TV claimed that “every day we are selling one million, one and a half million (barrels), as if Iran’s oil production and trade are continuing as usual”.

title: ‘We are family’: EU chief in Greenland to sign partnership deal
description: Brussels reinforces its support for the autonomous Danish Arctic territory coveted by Donald Trump.
content: The EU plans to deepen its cooperation with Greenland despite US President Donald Trump’s claims of control over the Arctic island, as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrived on Sunday for a two-day visit. Von der Leyen travelled to the resource-rich island, where a new EU-Greenland declaration is to be signed on Monday. Investment pledges running into the hundreds of millions are also expected. On her arrival, von der Leyen said the visit was about further cementing a unique partnership. “We are family,” she wrote on social media. Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark but is largely autonomous and not a member of the European Union. Von der Leyen was received at Nuuk airport by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen. At a brief joint press appearance, Nielsen said von der Leyen’s visit represented a very close friendship, a good partnership and something they wanted to build on further. He then set off with the Commission president and Frederiksen on a boat trip through the Arctic landscape as the first major item on the programme. The visit is politically charged because the US has been pressing claims on Greenland, citing security interests, and has sought to force a sale of the vast island to the United States. Trump has argued that Denmark cannot protect the world’s largest island from Russia and China. The territory, home to just under 57,000 people, is also of interest due to its extensive reserves of critical raw materials. Trump last renewed his claims on Greenland in July, linking them to an ongoing review of US troop deployments in Europe. He suggested the US could scale back its contribution to deterring Russia if no satisfactory agreement on Greenland’s future was reached. It remained unclear whether Trump still considers himself bound by an agreement brokered in January by Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte. That deal had been intended to guarantee Arctic security through joint allied action – in particular by the seven Arctic allies: the US, Canada, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland. According to sources within Nato, the US is also to be allowed to expand its military presence on Greenland and may receive a degree of co-decision rights over certain investments.

title: Sierra Leone ex-president Koroma returns after treason charges dropped
description: Ernest Bai Koroma returns from exile in Nigeria accompanied by foreign envoys ahead of 2028 election cycle.
content: Former Sierra Leone president Ernest Bai Koroma returned to his home country on Sunday, where authorities welcomed him after treason charges against him over an alleged coup attempt were dropped. Koroma had left for Nigeria in 2024, days after being charged with treason and other offences over a deadly 2023 army uprising. The former president, who led Sierra Leone from 2007 to 2018, arrived at the international airport in the capital, Freetown, accompanied by Nigerian ex-president Olusegun Obasanjo and Nigerian Foreign Minister Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu. He was welcomed by Sierra Leone’s Foreign Minister Mohamed Rahman Swarray and officials from Koroma’s party, the opposition All People’s Congress (APC). “Today I have come back home and I’m happy,” Koroma told journalists, smiling. Koroma had been cleared by Sierra Leonean authorities to travel to Nigeria for three months for medical treatment but ended up staying more than two years. In July, Sierra Leone’s justice ministry said it had dropped the charges against him, without giving a reason. On Friday, Vice-President Mohamed Jukdeh Jalloh told a gathering of local leaders and residents in Koroma’s stronghold, the central city of Makeni, that the former leader was returning home. His homecoming comes ahead of presidential elections set for 2028. The case against Koroma dated to November 2023, when armed attackers stormed a military armoury, two barracks, two prisons and two police stations, clashing with security forces. Twenty-one people were killed in what authorities deemed a coup attempt. Two dozen soldiers and Koroma’s former bodyguard were sentenced to prison terms ranging from 50 to 100 years by a military court for their alleged roles in the mutiny. Koroma had briefly visited Sierra Leone in July, after the charges were dropped, during a summit of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) at the invitation of current President Julius Maada Bio.

title: Lebanon president appeals for US help as Israeli strikes kill 7
description: Joseph Aoun condemns strikes on public buildings and hospital as Israel cites Hezbollah drone attack.
content: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun urged Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks, which killed at least seven people on Sunday despite a truce and a framework deal aimed at halting the violence. Israel said it had targeted Hezbollah operatives and sites in response to a drone attack a day earlier by the Iran-backed group on its troops in the vicinity of a strategic south Lebanon ridge. It reported no casualties but accused Hezbollah of a “blatant violation”. Israel last week said it had captured the Nabatieh-area Ali al-Taher ridge, which it considers part of its self-declared “security zone” in south Lebanon. Hezbollah, which has not claimed any attacks for weeks, has not commented on Israel’s declaration of control over the site. Aoun said Sunday’s strikes, which damaged government premises and destroyed an out-of-service hospital, were “a dangerous escalation … reaching Lebanese state institutions” and health facilities. He called on the international community – particularly the United States, which has sponsored direct Israel-Lebanon talks and a framework agreement between the sides in June – “to urgently act to stop these violations”. Lebanon’s health ministry said two people were killed in strikes on south Lebanon’s Nabatieh al-Fawqa, with two women also killed in nearby Arab Salim. It said 20 other people including several women and three children were wounded there, as well as in the city of Nabatieh and town of Kfar Rumman. The ministry later reported that a strike on a car park near Nabatieh killed three more people. The ministry said one of the strikes in Nabatieh al-Fawqa “totally destroyed” the out-of-service Ghandour hospital, decrying “another grave violation of international humanitarian law”. Israel’s army said it targeted Hezbollah operatives and infrastructure, including “weapons storage facilities and terrorist structures”, as well as “a Hezbollah command centre that had been established inside a building previously used as a hospital”. It had earlier issued its first evacuation notice in Lebanon in a month, warning residents near a building it called a Hezbollah facility in Arab Salim to leave ahead of an attack on the site. It did not issue warnings for other areas where strikes were reported. Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) said that after the Israeli warning for Arab Salim, “enemy warplanes launched a strike on another house, destroying it” and killing the two women. It said the Israeli military subsequently carried out a strike on the building threatened in the evacuation warning. At the scene of the second strike, an Agence France-Presse correspondent saw the ruins of a devastated villa, with large decorative columns lying on their side next to stairs littered with rubble. Haidar Haidar, the brother of the building’s owner, said that nobody had been living inside. At the other site in Arab Salim where the two women were killed, a mattress, furniture and other items including a Hezbollah flag were strewn among the rubble, while neighbouring buildings were also damaged. The NNA also reported a strike on a motorcycle in the Nabatieh area and said that another in the city itself targeted a historical building and damaged offices belonging to finance and agriculture authorities. An Agence France-Presse correspondent there saw rubble and extensive damage to nearby buildings, shops and cars, as heavy machinery cleared the road. Dust and debris covered chairs and desks in the regional ministry offices. Nabatieh Mayor Abbas Fakhreddine said “the Lebanese government must take action … and at the least defend its institutions”, adding that it was the second time the official buildings had been damaged by strikes. Lebanon was drawn into the wider Middle East war in March after Hezbollah attacked Israel in support of its backer Iran. Israel responded with air strikes and a ground invasion of Lebanon that Beirut says have killed more than 4,300 people. Violence has decreased since a US-Iran memorandum of understanding on the broader regional conflict in June and the Israel-Lebanon framework agreement later that month. Israeli forces are operating inside a self-declared “security zone” around 10km (6 miles) deep inside Lebanon along the border.

title: Germany’s Merz shaken as far-right AfD plots path to power after state election win
description: The German chancellor rules out working with the AfD even though he concedes its win in Saxony-Anhalt has upset his party’s foundations.
content: Chancellor Friedrich Merz ruled out working with the Alternative for Germany (AfD) on Monday after the far-right party surged into first place in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, but he conceded the result had shaken his party “to its very foundations”. The AfD is appealing to lawmakers from Merz’s conservatives to support its bid to rule the eastern state, in what would be the first time a far-right party takes power at state level in post-war Germany. The anti-immigrant, pro-Russia AfD won nearly 44 per cent of the vote, an outcome that underlined the deep unpopularity of Merz’s ruling coalition ‌and also triggered alarm among Germany’s neighbours, France and Poland, and elsewhere. However, the party – which wants to deport immigrants, halt support for Ukraine and restore ties with Moscow – fell short of an absolute majority in the state legislature, winning 39 of the 83 seats, and hopes to poach individual conservative lawmakers. The election result could test the long-standing refusal of Germany’s mainstream parties, including Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU), to work with the AfD, a policy known as the “firewall”. The AfD says this is undemocratic. “This shakes our party to its very foundations,” Merz said, according to the Bild newspaper. “We are all deeply shocked,” he added later at a press conference, describing the result as his party’s worst election result in decades. While sounding chastened, and vowing to try harder to connect with voters, Merz batted away suggestions that he might resign, saying he would broadly stick with his government’s reform agenda. Merz, whose own ⁠approval ratings have sunk to record lows, faces more state elections in the coming weeks and into next year, though he hopes his mix of reforms and higher spending in some areas will revive growth in Europe’s largest economy. Suggesting that ‌the AfD win was cheered in Moscow, Merz characterised the current political moment as a fight for the survival of Western values. He also defended a decision, taken last year, to borrow hundreds of billions of euros to spend on defence, saying the unity of the Nato alliance was at stake. “Giving up is not an option for me,” he said. The AfD’s ‌national co-leader Tino Chrupalla appealed to CDU lawmakers to make a “centre-right conservative majority” in Saxony-Anhalt possible. “Partisan games really ought to be a thing of the past,” he told German radio, referring to the ⁠firewall policy. Ulrich Siegmund, the party’s lead candidate in the state, said he would hold discussions with various parliamentary groups. Siegmund claimed voters had sent “a signal to Berlin” and took pleasure in mocking Merz, calling him “a very good campaigner” for the AfD. “It is a very clear government mandate,” Siegmund said. “It could hardly be clearer.” The only German party ⁠that has signalled readiness to work with the AfD is the populist left-wing BSW. The BSW shares the AfD’s hostility towards mass immigration, which it says undermines local workers’ rights, and also advocates for ending Germany’s support for Ukraine and restoring ties with Moscow. Both parties characterise sanctions on Russia as ‌needlessly self-sabotaging, denying German businesses access to Russia’s vast cheap energy resources on which Germany’s export-driven economy was able to thrive for decades. “Peace in Europe” was the second-biggest factor driving which way people voted in Saxony-Anhalt, according to numbers from the ARD broadcaster. But Merz told reporters that the AfD’s success was no reason ‌to ‌change course. “I will not deviate by even a millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom, especially now, against Russia,” he said. “If we stop supporting Ukraine, the situation will not improve by tomorrow, it will only ‌get worse. The Russian leadership aims to destabilise the system of values underpinning what we once called ‘the West’, a system of values that is non-negotiable.” During the campaign, the AfD tapped into growing disillusionment with established parties, which it characterises as tired and out ⁠of touch, offering instead a range of hardline policies, a promise of cleaner and safer streets and a revival of national pride. For some, there is also a nostalgia for life in the former communist-run East Germany. According ⁠to a breakdown of voters, the AfD was particularly popular among men, with 50 per cent voting for the party compared with 39 per cent of women. AfD voters also tended to be less economically secure and less educated. Saxony-Anhalt is a relatively small state, and one of the poorest in Germany’s former communist east, but Alice Weidel, the AfD’s other national co-leader, hailed Sunday’s result as a milestone and said her party aimed to win ‌at least 40 per cent in the next national election, due in 2029. The ‌AfD has been classified as right-wing extremist by the local office of Germany’s domestic intelligence service, but it dismisses accusations of extremism as scaremongering and an insult to the party’s millions of supporters. While far-right leaders in Europe welcomed the result as a mandate for change, and US billionaire Elon Musk cheered on the AfD from the sidelines, French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told RTL radio it “sends out a very, very worrying signal”. “This shows that we face a major challenge in the face of a populist wave which is spreading around the world today and which we must resist,” said Lescure, whose own country holds national elections next year that could see far-right veteran Marine Le Pen become president of France. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: Rewriting world history puts China’s image and ‘cultural security’ at risk: party journal
description: Article warns that claims ancient Greece was a hoax or the Industrial Revolution originated in China have already hurt the country’s image.
content: Radically rewriting world and Chinese history without solid proof could threaten China’s international image and national identity, a leading Communist Party journal has warned. There has been a growing trend to promote a less Western-centric view of history in recent years, while Beijing has also been keen to promote the idea that Chinese civilisation has a long and continuous history. But at the same time, the so-called pseudo-historical school – which has cast doubt on the origins of Western culture or claimed key scientific advances originated in China – has become increasingly popular in some circles. On Monday, the party’s theoretical journal Qiushi published an article criticising the trend. It warned that this could pose a threat to China’s own “cultural security and ideological security”. “The extreme pseudo-historical claims proliferating online continue to spread overseas and have already damaged our country’s ‘academic discourse power’ and cultural image abroad,” the article said. Some of the most eye-catching theories have cast doubt on key aspects of ancient Greek history, which risk damaging Beijing’s relationship with Athens and other governments. These include claims that Aristotle was a medieval hoax or that Greece’s mountainous terrain could not have supported a large population and advanced society. The Quishi article began with other examples of these “far-fetched and absurd narratives”, such as the argument that Mount Emei, a sacred peak in Sichuan province, “is the Alps” and “the Yongle Encyclopaedia gave rise to modern Western civilisation”. The Chinese names for Mount Emei and the Alps (A Er Bei Si) have some similarities in the way they are pronounced, and some have seized on this as evidence that Western civilisation originated in China. The Yongle Encyclopaedia, or Yongle Dadian, was commissioned by the 15th century emperor of that name. Many pseudo-histories claim that the achievements of the Industrial Revolution were copied wholesale from the work, arguing that calculus and the steam engine originated in China before being stolen by the West. The Chinese government has never expressed support for these pseudo-histories and the authorities have become increasingly wary about their growing popularity online. Last month, several official media outlets, including the People’s Daily website and a social media account run by Zhejiang’s provincial publicity department, ran articles criticising the trend. Continuing this theme, the Qiushi article said: “Some pseudo-historical narratives have ethnic separatist tendencies and could provide a theoretical basis for denying the unity of the Chinese nation.” It criticised proponents of pseudo-history for using the ethnic origin of rulers to determine whether a dynasty had the legitimacy to rule China. This often overlaps with a form of Han nationalism that regards the Manchu-led Qing dynasty (1644–1911) as an invading colonial regime after it overthrew the country’s Han rulers, the Ming (1368–1644). Both groups hold views that run counter to China’s official view of history. Han nationalists believe that China’s decline in the 19th century was due to Manchu rule, while the official line blames other factors such as stagnation and a lack of openness. The Communist Party also regards itself as the full successor to both dynasties with sovereignty over Xinjiang, Tibet and Taiwan. Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including Taiwan’s main international partner the United States, do not recognise the self-ruled island as independent. “The practical consequence of such claims is to deconstruct national identity, while the historical consensus underpinning the community of the Chinese nation risks being fragmented,” the article added. Beijing regards ethnic affairs as a key element in safeguarding China’s territorial integrity, development and stability, and President Xi Jinping has put the idea of “a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation” at the heart of this. Last year, China banned a series of influential social media accounts that promoted the pseudo-historical school and Han nationalism. Qiushi said that after those accounts were taken down, related content continued to spread in a more decentralised fashion. The article also said generative artificial intelligence was being used to mass-produce pseudo-historical content and this could erode the way the public, particularly teenagers, thought about history. It warned that “algorithms must not be allowed to become a megaphone for these narratives” and said the models used to recommend content to social media users should incorporate “mainstream values”.

title: Children among at least 25 killed in Cabo Verde bus crash
description: Such incidents are rare in the west African archipelago, where roads are generally in good condition.
content: At least 25 people, mostly children and teenagers, were killed in a bus crash on Cabo Verde’s Fogo Island, public radio network RCV said on Sunday. Several others were injured in Saturday’s accident, some of them seriously, the head of civil protection for Sao Filipe city, Jose Canuto, told reporters. Such incidents are rare in the west African archipelago, where roads are generally in good condition. Canuto and other local authorities said the bus, which was carrying 32 passengers, veered off the road and plunged into a deep ravine on the way back to Sao Filipe after an excursion to the Cha das Caldeiras village inside the Pico do Fogo volcanic crater. The dead include the bus driver, who organised the excursion to the unique site every year as a present for the pupils he drove to school during term time. Emergency personnel worked through the night to rescue victims trapped in the wreckage, which came to a halt in a rocky valley that is hard to reach. Seven were buried early on Sunday. The rest were set to be buried later in the day, according to RCV.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Possible Love movie review – Lee Chang-dong explores class in masterful drama
description: Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong play a rich couple opposite Sul Kyung-gu and Jeon Do-yeon’s have-nots in Lee’s sharp critique of Korean society.
content: 4.5/5 stars “Thou shalt not covet,” reads a title card at the beginning of Lee Chang-dong’s much-anticipated new film, Possible Love – alluding to the title of the 10th part of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s epic Dekalog. But covet what exactly? While Lee’s complex, nuanced drama features a modicum of sexual tension and a soupçon of envy, it goes much deeper. Issues of class and wealth bounce around like frenzied atoms in the Korean filmmaker’s first feature since his award-winning 2018 psychological thriller Burning. Possible Love, which is playing in competition at this year’s Venice International Film Festival before its autumn release via Netflix, has already been selected as South Korea’s official entry in the Academy Award race for best international feature. By putting two very different marriages under the microscope, it proves it will be hard to beat. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon, the star of Lee’s Secret Sunshine), who was born to a junk-dealer father and a mother who worked at a car wash, lives with her husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu, from Lee’s Peppermint Candy and Oasis) and their son Cheol. Ho-seok was laid off from his factory job, and this trauma has left him scarred in ways that only become apparent as the story unfolds. Already struggling with alcohol, he admits to feeling “like a dead phantom … no reason to go on living”. Much of this comes to light after his wife has a chance encounter with documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, Parasite) and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung, Hope), a successful businessman jokingly likened to Steve Jobs. Ye-ji is making a film about laid-off workers and wants to interview Ho-seok, who reluctantly agrees. “His eyes are so sad,” she says pityingly, although she doesn’t know the half of it. As Ye-ji gets closer to Mi-ok and her family, her enigmatic husband Sang-woo warns that she is very different from her subjects. “I’m trying to love those people,” she claims somewhat naively before inviting her new friends to Sang-woo’s family beach home for a summer holiday. Here, Mi-ok and her family truly get to see how the other half lives. Clocking in at 164 minutes, Possible Love channels a multitude of emotions, including bawdy humour – a drunken bathroom scene is a welcome moment of light relief – but never loses sight of its main focus. From workers’ rights to marital disharmony, it elegantly covers acres of ground. Of the main quartet, Sul is outstanding as the fragile Ho-seok, a maelstrom of raw emotion. Among the film’s many remarkable scenes, his envious gaze at a former colleague celebrating his child’s birthday lingers in the memory. Equally piercing is Ho-seok’s confrontation with cowardly former colleagues during a strike, as he decries their hollow slogans of “solidarity”, “resistance” and “unity”. Possible Love is a masterful work that cements Lee’s status as one of world cinema’s most important auteurs. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Hong Kong to review bookings for famous Sai Kung trail after high no-show rate
description: Only 1,560 registered and walk-in patrons arrived at Po Pin Chau on Saturday and Sunday, despite 3,230 people making bookings.
content: Hong Kong authorities will review a new reservation system for a Sai Kung trail famed for its dramatic volcanic rock columns after the National Day “golden week” in October, following large numbers of no-shows during the first two trial runs. Only 1,560 registered and walk-in patrons arrived at Po Pin Chau on Saturday and Sunday, despite 3,230 people having made bookings under the real-name reservation system. Lawmakers and a district councillor have called for more on-site quotas, clearer booking status information for walk-ins, and a penalty-points system to curb no-shows. In a response to the South China Morning Post Sunday, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) said it would step up visitor management, patrols and enforcement around the East Dam and Po Pin Chau area, while continuing publicity and educational efforts, including reminders to book in advance. “The department will conduct a comprehensive review of the effectiveness [of the trial] after the National Day golden week to assist in formulating long-term countryside management strategies,” a spokesman said. Golden week refers to mainland China’s week-long National Day and Lunar New Year holidays, as well as the five-day Labour Day break. Only 660 registered and walk-in visitors visited Po Pin Chau, out of 1,430 reservations made on Sunday. That mirrored Saturday’s no-show rates: about 1,800 bookings were made for the full day, but only around 900 showed up via prior bookings or by registering on site. The reservation system, which caps visitor numbers at 2,000 per designated day between 9am and 5pm for Po Pin Chau, was announced last month to tackle overtourism, largely driven by mainland visitors. Lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, who represents the southeast New Territories, said more data collected during the trial in the coming days – including October’s golden week when the city expects high footfall – could allow the AFCD to better gauge no-show rates and determine how many on-site quotas to release in future. He noted the AFCD released some on-site quotas at 10am on Saturday for unregistered visitors to sign up on the spot. Ip added the department could provide the public access to the daily booking status to help them make informed decisions about walk-in registrations. “A red indicator could mean the day is fully booked, ‘yellow’ could mean it is 70 per cent full, while ‘green’ could mean there is still plenty of availability … this can keep the public informed of the situation,” he said. Lawmaker Steven Ho Chun-yin urged the government to examine the underlying causes behind the high no-show rates for each time slot and make improvements accordingly. Ho noted that some visitors reserved the 9am slot Saturday, not knowing that minibuses departing from Pak Tam Chung bound for East Dam only start operating at 9.30am. Sai Kung district councillor Chris Cheung Mei-hung suggested the government implement a penalty points system similar to that used for booking government venues such as community halls, where repeated no-shows can lead to a temporary ban. “Setting a benchmark where a patron who fails to show up a number of times could deter people from abusing the mechanism when there is currently no cost for no shows,” Cheung said. The department previously said the system was put in place to protect the narrow trail from excessive wear and tear, prevent overcrowding and improve the visitor experience, adding that the quota would be further reviewed. The roughly 1km-long (0.62 mile) trail is within the Unesco Global Geopark at Sai Kung East Country Park and passes giant hexagonal volcanic rock columns dramatically jutting out from the sea, providing stunning views overlooking them.

title: China rolls out massive US$54b package for insurers, banks in financial powerhouse push
description: The rare capital boost of such magnitude seeks to shore up insurers and banks as solvency pressures mount and regulatory demands loom.
content: China rolled out a package of capital injections worth about 360 billion yuan (US$54 billion) on Sunday for the country’s largest state-owned insurers and state banks, marking a step towards Beijing’s long-flagged plan to build itself into a global financial powerhouse. The Ministry of Finance, which led the move, had rarely injected capital into financial institutions at such magnitude, according to analysts. China Life Insurance Company said it would receive 35 billion yuan to help strengthen its “ability to withstand risk”, according to its website. Among banks, the Agricultural Bank of China planned to raise up to 160 billion yuan through a private placement of new A shares to the finance ministry, China National Tobacco Corporation and related subsidiaries, an exchange filing showed. Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) was targeting up to 100 billion yuan from the same group of investors, according to an exchange filing. Recent top-level meetings have all called for more proactive fiscal policy to counter growth pressures, and capital injections into financial institutions are part of that fiscal toolkit Shen Meng, Chanson & Co The Export-Import Bank of China, a policy lender known as Eximbank, was set to receive 30 billion yuan to “significantly enhance its capacity to support the real economy and opening up, while reinforcing its resilience in risk prevention”, according to state news agency Xinhua. The People’s Insurance Company (Group) of China planned to issue new shares in onshore markets to raise as much as 15 billion yuan, with the finance ministry subscribing in cash, according to its filing with the Shanghai exchange on Sunday. China Export & Credit Insurance Corporation, known as Sinosure, announced a 10 billion yuan injection to replenish its core capital, aimed at improving its solvency adequacy ratio and expanding its capacity to meet insurance obligations. China Taiping Insurance Group was set to receive 7 billion yuan to help it withstand risk, according to the company’s website. China Reinsurance planned to issue new A shares, with the finance ministry set to subscribe in cash for a total of 3 billion yuan, according to its filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange. “Recent top-level meetings have all called for more proactive fiscal policy to counter growth pressures, and capital injections into financial institutions are part of that fiscal toolkit,” said Shen Meng, a director at Beijing-based investment firm Chanson & Co. “They not only reduce operational and regulatory risks for these institutions, but also stimulate broader investment and consumption through the multiplier effect of the financial sector.” Shen said the finance ministry had “rarely injected capital into financial institutions on such a scale, and that the few precedents were mainly aimed at repairing balance sheets and cutting risk”. The capital injections build on Beijing’s ambition to transform China into a financial powerhouse, a goal the central bank formally embedded in its first-ever stand-alone five-year plan this year, which pledges to expand the yuan’s global use and build a “strong central bank” to drive that vision. S&P Global Ratings has estimated China’s big four state-owned banks – ICBC, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China and Bank of China – faced a capital shortfall of as much as 3.7 trillion yuan by 2025 to meet total loss-absorbing capacity (TLAC) requirements. TLAC refers to a capital buffer international regulators require of the world’s biggest banks so they can absorb losses in a crisis without needing a government bailout. China’s six largest state-owned banks posted their first simultaneous increase in both first-half revenue and net profit since 2022 this year, driven by a tentative recovery in net interest margins – the gap between what banks earn on loans and pay out on deposits. That margin had steadily narrowed over the previous two years, dragging the industry average down to a record low of nearly 1.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026. Beijing’s push to fortify its state financial institutions dovetails with efforts to elevate Hong Kong’s role. Regulators have urged mainland insurers to invest in Hong Kong-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bolstering the city’s status as a global financial centre. Ping An, the country’s largest private insurer, had sought regulatory approval to expand into Hong Kong ETFs after posting 36 per cent profit growth in the first half of this year, according to the company’s board secretary. Mainland financial firms are also ramping up overseas fundraising to support yuan internationalisation. Last year alone, companies including China Pacific Insurance, ICBC and China Everbright Bank each raised between US$300 million and US$2 billion in Hong Kong and other offshore markets.

title: What China’s Lop Nur desert base expansion means for PLA stealth jets in race with US
description: Remote site is ideal for quiet testing of sensitive, next-generation aircraft, analysts say, as some forecast faster high-end PLA deployment.
content: China is rapidly expanding a flight-test facility deep in its western desert, satellite imagery has revealed, a push that analysts say could help fast track the development of its next-generation military aircraft as air-power rivalry with the United States intensifies. Latest satellite photos of the facility near Lop Nur, in China’s western Xinjiang region, show four large new hangars, new taxiway work, a circular pad believed to be an engine-run or turnaround area, and possible fuel-storage infrastructure, according to an August 28 analysis by defence website TWZ. The expansion comes as China pursues multiple advanced combat-aircraft programmes at once, potentially giving it greater capacity to test sensitive designs and conduct simultaneous flight-test programmes away from routine observation. Andreas Rupprecht, an aviation analyst and expert on the Chinese air force, said he was convinced Lop Nur would become the People’s Liberation Army’s new test centre for high-end next-generation aircraft. But another expert familiar with Chinese military aviation, who asked not to be named, cautioned against drawing firm conclusions until the base expansion was complete. The latest expansion began around August 2025, according to J. Michael Dahm, a retired US Navy intelligence officer and senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at the Mitchell Institute. That was when the large tailless sixth-generation PLA aircraft widely known as the J-36 was first observed there, Dahm wrote in an April assessment. Another next-generation design, commonly referred to as the J-XDS or J-50, was spotted 17 days later, Dahm noted. By February this year, China had added about 60,000 sq ft (5,570 square metres) of hangar space and more than 300,000 sq ft of other facilities, which Dahm said probably included test and evaluation facilities as well as personnel housing, effectively doubling the area of the base. The site already had a 5km (3.1-mile) runway and was linked to China’s reusable spacecraft programme as far back as 2020. Lop Nur’s remoteness is a key advantage, according to the experts. The base sits in a vast, sparsely populated expanse, offering ideal conditions for testing experimental aircraft away from populated areas and closer observation. It could also ease pressure on existing facilities. An additional base could help separate programmes, reduce scheduling conflicts and allow a higher testing tempo, the anonymous expert said. Multiple hangars could also support more than one flight-test programme concurrently, depending on aircraft size. Rupprecht said the location could allow combined manoeuvres involving advanced crewed and collaborative combat aircraft without the safety constraints associated with testing near major cities, while the anonymous expert said the environment could benefit sensor and electronic-warfare testing because of limited interference. “I don’t believe the new facility allows for anything that wasn’t already possible in Yanliang or Dingxin; it’s just that it’s even more remote, so you’re less likely to be observed,” Rupprecht said. Yanliang, in northwestern Shaanxi province, is home to China’s main flight-test establishment, while Dingxin in northern Inner Mongolia is used for military aircraft testing and exercises. Dahm has argued that infrastructure offers a clearer signal of China’s long-term investment in advanced aircraft rather than sporadic prototype sightings. The Lop Nur buildout is not happening in isolation. Dahm has documented major additions to manufacturing and testing infrastructure at Chengdu in southwest China, home of the J-20 and J-36 aircraft programmes, and a new production complex about 16km north of the existing plant in Shenyang, northeastern China, with around 4 million sq ft of manufacturing space. Timothy Heath, founder of defence research firm Perceptum and a former senior China analyst for Rand Corporation and the US military, said such investment mattered because developing an advanced aircraft involved much more than producing an impressive prototype. “The expanded flight test and development infrastructure is significant because it shows that China is refining and improving the quality of the aircraft that it manufactures,” Heath said. “Testing and development is essential for new aircraft to maximise their potential, and the expanded facilities show China intends to ensure its combat aircraft are effective and not just showy parade pieces.” Heath said appropriate infrastructure could shorten the time required for aircraft to become operational and improve their quality. “The concurrent development of military aircraft programmes shows China has the ambition and resources to build a large and technologically advanced air force,” he said. China and the United States are racing to develop a new generation of combat aircraft designed to operate alongside increasingly sophisticated uncrewed systems, sensors and long-range weapons. China has not disclosed the missions, specifications or formal designations of the J-36 and J-XDS or J-50. The Pentagon’s latest China Military Power Report described the two sixth-generation aircraft as being in the “nascent stages of development” and expected to become operational by 2035. The Lop Nur expansion has also revived speculation about China’s long-awaited H-20 stealth bomber, which has never been publicly unveiled and whose designation has not been officially confirmed. TWZ noted that three new hangars on the southern apron each measured about 80 by 40 metres (262 by 131 feet), large enough for any aircraft in the PLA’s current inventory, including the H-6 strategic bomber with its 33-metre wingspan. They are also considerably wider than typical tactical-aircraft shelters, potentially accommodating future aircraft with much larger wingspans. TWZ suggested that the hangars could be intended for the H-20, while stressing that this remained speculative. Rupprecht similarly said the scale of some facilities suggested “something big is on the way”, with the H-20 the most plausible candidate, although he said that designation could now be out of date.

title: New Delhi building collapse kills 3, traps dozens
description: Nine people were rescued, with five of them taken to a hospital in critical condition.
content: A building collapse in the Indian capital New Delhi killed at least three people on Sunday, local media reports said, as authorities worked to rescue those trapped in the rubble. The building, housing mostly students, came crashing down about midday in the southwestern Satya Niketan area of the city, with police and disaster response personnel cautiously lifting the rubble using heavy machinery. Three people died in the accident, according to The Hindu newspaper and other local media reports, quoting unnamed fire services officials. Nine people were rescued from under the rubble, with five of them taken to a hospital in critical condition, the reports said. The exact number of people feared trapped was not immediately known. An adjacent building has been vacated over fears it could also collapse. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the incident was “distressing” and offered “condolences to those who lost their loved ones”, according to a statement from his office. TV images showed rescuers pulling a young man out from the rubble and another trapped under a block of fallen concrete slab, with only his face visible. Delhi’s Chief Minister Rekha Gupta said she was “deeply concerned” by the incident. “Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped and provide immediate help to the affected families,” Gupta said in a social media post. The Satya Niketan area is home to hundreds of university students living in crowded, privately owned accommodation as paying guests. Building collapses are frequent in India, and illegal structures – often home to migrant workers and students – are common in big cities. Last year, at least 11 people were killed after a residential building collapsed in the northeastern district of the capital city.

title: Punching above their weight: how China’s AI giants stretch each dollar in compute race
description: Lower costs and faster growth rates let China’s AI firms narrow the divide, raising the question: does the spending gap still matter?
content: The massive gap in artificial intelligence spending between US and Chinese tech titans may not buy the advantage expected for American giants, as lower domestic costs and heavy state support allow Chinese firms to secure far more computing power per dollar, according to a new report by Moody’s Ratings. While US hyperscalers outspent their Chinese counterparts by a staggering margin, the physical gap in computing capacity was nowhere near as wide as those mega-budgets suggested, the report said. Lower buildout costs, targeted policy incentives and access to cheaper green energy meant Chinese tech firms were punching above their financial weight, narrowing the compute divide with American peers at a fraction of the price, Moody’s noted. The US retained a clear overall lead in cutting-edge semiconductor chips, but the findings suggested headline capex numbers tell only part of the story. Here is what you need to know. How wide is the spending gap between US and Chinese tech giants? Capital expenditure by China’s major tech companies was set to more than double to around US$140 billion this year – up from US$65 billion in 2025 – and reach US$165 billion by 2027, according to Moody’s. By contrast, five major US hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Oracle – plus AI cloud provider CoreWeave were projected to spend more than US$785 billion this year alone, approaching US$1 trillion by 2027. Why does China’s AI infrastructure cost so much less? China’s cost advantage lies in land, power and structural state backing. Under Beijing’s “East Data, West Computing” initiative, power-intensive workloads are routed to resource-rich inland regions like Inner Mongolia and the northwestern province of Gansu. By moving latency-tolerant AI training to hubs with abundant green energy and cooler climates – such as ByteDance’s expanding data centre footprint in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia – companies could slash power and cooling expenses while reserving valuable coastal capacity for real-time applications, according to BMI, a Fitch Solutions company. Government policy further tilted the scales through cheaper infrastructure, subsidies, fast-tracked approvals, and tax incentives, according to Moody’s. What is holding China back from overtaking the US? China’s cost advantage is concentrated mainly in non-chip infrastructure. Servers and accelerators accounted for the largest share of AI spending, while restricted access to leading-edge Nvidia chips remained a key constraint, Moody’s said. Domestic processors and software ecosystems continued to improve but still lagged Nvidia’s. There is also an efficiency trade-off. BMI said some Chinese semiconductor platforms consumed more electricity than Nvidia processors to perform equivalent computing workloads, meaning cheaper power and subsidies could only partly offset the higher operating costs of domestic hardware. At the system level, the trade-off is also stark. Semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis estimated that Huawei Technologies’ CloudMatrix 384 drew about 4.1 times as much power as Nvidia’s GB200 NVL72, while delivering nearly twice the computing performance, making access to abundant and relatively cheap electricity particularly important. Is China actually closing the compute gap? Measured by data centre capacity rather than pure dollar spend, the divide shrinks significantly. Installed US data centre capacity stood at 52 gigawatts (GW) at the end of 2025, compared with 28GW in China, according to International Energy Agency figures cited by Moody’s. By 2030, US capacity was forecast to reach 100GW, compared with 67GW in China. China’s capacity was expected to grow at an annual rate of 19 per cent, faster than the US rate of 14 per cent, narrowing the relative gap even as the absolute difference increased. While megawatt output does not directly equate to AI processing power, it shows that the capex gap overstates the physical capacity divide. China’s faster growth rate means it is steadily narrowing the relative gap even as the absolute difference expands. Model capabilities reflect this catch-up. Leading Chinese models – including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, and Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8 – now rank alongside top global open-weight rivals on benchmark platforms like Artificial Analysis and Chatbot Arena. Can Chinese tech giants turn these AI gains into revenue? Building compute is one thing; monetising it is another. Cloud platforms remained the main engine for AI revenue, but Chinese hyperscalers operated at a much smaller scale and in a more price-competitive market, Moody’s said. In their latest reported quarters, Microsoft generated US$59 billion in cloud revenue, Amazon US$42 billion, and Alphabet US$25 billion. Alibaba generated US$7 billion and Baidu about US$1 billion. US hyperscalers also benefited from larger enterprise customer bases, contracted cloud commitments and integrated software ecosystems, giving them clearer paths to recurring AI revenue. China’s lower-cost open-source models were driving adoption, but monetisation remained at an earlier stage, Moody’s said. There are signs the gap is beginning to narrow. Alibaba’s cloud business reported 45 per cent revenue growth in the June quarter – the fastest pace in 22 quarters – as demand for AI-related products accelerated. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.

title: ‘A victim’: American Bully dies in surgery, owners question fighting dog rules
description: Owners hope Monchiu’s death will ‘fight for the vindication and rectification of other Bullies in Hong Kong’.
content: The owners of an American Bully are challenging the authorities’ classification of “fighting dogs” after their pet, a breed strictly controlled in Hong Kong, died during neutering, a procedure they undertook amid a crackdown on non-compliance. Monchiu, a female, died under anaesthesia during the operation at a veterinary clinic on Friday, her owners said on social media late on Saturday. They said the dog, who suffered from vision and hearing impairment, as well as skin problems, was unfit for surgery but they proceeded out of fear she might be taken into the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department’s custody. The owners said the dog had been repeatedly reported since authorities stepped up checks, although they insisted she was obedient and posed no threat. “We were very afraid that it would be reported and taken to the department for detention. It had physical defects – it was born blind in one eye and could not hear, and had skin problems – and she could not survive such hot weather in the detention cell,” said the owners, who called themselves “dad and mum”. “Monchiu is a victim under the indiscriminate law enforcement of the department.” They questioned the classification of fighting dogs. “We hope that the departure of Monchiu could fight for the vindication and rectification of other Bullies in Hong Kong – Bully dogs are not fighting dogs and it is extremely risky for them to undergo forced sterilisation surgery,” they said. Concerns over the management of large and fighting dogs grew in Hong Kong after two attacks in mid-August. In the first incident, on August 17, two small dogs were mauled to death by a 60kg dog with genetic links to a mastiff in Yuen Long town centre. Days later, a 33-year-old woman was found dead near her pet training centre in Ta Kwu Ling after being attacked by a 30kg dog with traits associated with pit bull ancestry. Under Hong Kong law, four types of “fighting dogs”, the pit bull terrier, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa and fila Brasileiro, and their crossbreeds are banned from import or local breeding. They must be securely muzzled, kept on a leash no longer than 1.5 metres and wear a special collar when in public. Existing fighting dogs must also be neutered to be kept legally. The attacks prompted authorities to review the definitions of fighting dogs, and the department has strengthened inspection and enforcement. At least three dogs have been detained by the department on suspicion of being fighting dogs. On Wednesday, the department said the American Bully, alongside the American pit bull terrier and American Staffordshire terrier, was classified under pit bull terriers and therefore subject to fighting dog regulations. The department said the law regulated by “type” rather than “breed” and the three breeds had long been regarded as falling under the pit bull terrier type. It added that the three breeds had always been subject to the same strict regulations, and that the policy and definition of fighting dogs had not changed. In response to Monchiu’s case, the department said on Sunday that it had not received any inquiry or report concerning the animal, and had not classified it as a fighting dog. It said the determination of fighting dog types was the responsibility of the department’s veterinary officers, who would carefully observe the dog’s physical characteristics and external proportions, body structure, and related features to assess whether the dog truly possessed the high-risk traits characteristic of the fighting dog types, and thereby classify the dog. “This is the common international practice for identifying fighting dog types,” it said. The department said that if a classified fighting dog had not been desexed, it would escort the animal to a private veterinary clinic appointed by the dog keeper for desexing surgery. “The appointed private veterinarian will carry out a medical examination of the dog. If, on medical grounds, the veterinarian considers the dog unfit for surgery, a direction will be issued to the dog keeper allowing the surgery to be postponed until the dog’s health has been restored,” a department spokesman said. The department urged keepers to consult a registered vet before subjecting their dogs to any surgical procedures. Those who were worried that their pets could be fighting dogs should contact the department or a registered vet for verification, it said. The department also said that citywide special inspection and enforcement operations on the proper control of dogs on August 30 and this weekend had found three suspected cases where large dogs were not being securely held on a leash in public places. It added that its officers would follow up on these cases and institute prosecutions accordingly.

title: Dangling airport display back on after extra cables added, motion disabled
description: Airport Authority says inspections confirmed the five Terminal 2 screens met safety standards, following Saturday’s malfunction.
content: A dangling digital art installation at Hong Kong’s airport has resumed operation after technicians added extra support cables and disabled its motion system. The Airport Authority said on Sunday that inspections confirmed the five electronic displays suspended in Terminal 2 met safety standards and were cleared to restart showing content. Additional cables had been installed to secure the screens as an extra safety precautionary measure, the authority said. “Under the original safety design, two cables already provide sufficient assurance as fall-arrest mechanism. The additional cables will further ensure safety,” it said. “Upon resumption all screens will remain stationary” It added that while the screens were running in dynamic performance mode on Saturday morning, issues arose with the cables controlling their movement, and the mode had since been switched off to address public concerns. The incident occurred on Saturday morning when a circular overhead electronic display suspended from the ceiling of the departures hall in Terminal 2 suddenly dropped several metres and was left dangling in mid-air. The display came to rest eight metres above the floor after falling from its original height of 15 metres. Police said they were called at about 8.30am on Saturday over the incident involving the 1.5m-by-1.5m installation. Videos posted on social media showed some circular screens swaying, secured to the ceiling by two cables. No injuries were reported and the area was cordoned off. The authority said on Saturday that the installation “experienced a technical fault” but that its built-in anti-drop safety system engaged and prevented the device from falling further. Terminal 2 opened in late May as part of the Hong Kong International Airport’s HK$141.5 billion three-runway system upgrade. Passengers can check in, clear immigration and undergo security screening there before returning to Terminal 1 for departure. The digital installation was part of the upgrade to enhance the passenger experience, showcasing dynamic 3D visuals and ocean-themed content to create a relaxing atmosphere while offering photo opportunities for travellers. The screens were engineered to move independently or in synchronisation.

title: Opinion | Why China won’t ban housing presales outright
description: Popular as the move might be, Beijing is trying to unwind the debt-fuelled property growth model without inviting another financial crisis.
content: Late August marked something of a watershed moment for China’s embattled property sector, now in its sixth year of decline. It began with Chinese courts kicking off proceedings to liquidate the onshore business of China Evergrande Group – the collapsed property giant that came to epitomise China’s property debt bubble – and sentencing its founder Hui Ka-yan to life imprisonment over financial crimes. An unusually coordinated series of official announcements followed in days. The central bank, housing ministry and financial regulators each issued new rules governing how future property development would be financed. The choreography around these actions sent a message of its own: out with the old and in with the new. Beijing was moving to close the chapter on the property sector’s leverage-driven financing model while laying the groundwork for a healthier replacement, described by regulators as the “new property development model”. High on regulators’ chopping block were housing presales – the long-standing practice, now widely reviled by homebuyers, of paying for flats years before they are actually built. For China’s many property developers, the presale system offered an extraordinary source of cheap, upfront financing. Combined with years of lax restrictions on the use of those funds, it helped propel developers’ breakneck expansion – and ultimately fed into the sector’s financial reckoning. Closing financial loopholes was exactly what the latest policy salvo set out to do. Regulators promised tighter oversight of presale funds and, more importantly, to deny developers access to homebuyers’ mortgage money until project delivery. These provisions are aimed directly at the misuse of presale funds that has left projects unfinished and fuelled public anger in recent years, creating a source of financial instability and social risk Beijing clearly wants eliminated at the root. This raises the question of why regulators do not take the next step and abolish housing presales for good. After all, the idea of a clean fix has had no shortage of advocates among policy advisers since well before the property downturn, and today’s Chinese homebuyers hardly need any persuading. To Beijing’s credit, it has inched in that direction by tightening guard rails around presale permits and pledging to “vigorously promote” the safer alternative of post-construction sales. Yet for years, policymakers have largely repeated the same formula without quite committing to phasing out the old system. That caution stems from a policy dilemma: Beijing is weighing the financial risks of keeping presales against the macroeconomic cost of abolishing them too quickly. For all their flaws, presales remain a major source of working capital for developers, allowing them to fund construction with buyer payments long before projects are completed. Removing that funding channel outright would force already cash-strapped developers to rely much more heavily on bank credit or their own capital, both of which remain scarce. An outright ban on presales risks administering another liquidity shock to a sector still struggling to emerge from a years-long financing crunch. Deprived of a major source of working capital, weaker developers could once again find themselves unable to keep construction moving, recreating the very unfinished home problem Beijing is trying to fix. Firms with stronger cash flows might respond more defensively, shelving new projects and conserving cash at a time when property construction and fixed-asset investment are already under severe pressure. That retrenchment would travel further still: fewer new projects mean less demand for land, depressing land sale revenues and tightening the fiscal straitjacket on local governments already grappling with their own balance sheet stress. The policy bind therefore pushes Beijing towards gradualism rather than shock therapy. It cannot simply tear down the old property financing model and hope a healthier one emerges in its place. Instead, the transition must be carefully sequenced, starting with restoring developers’ access to more durable funding sources, then progressively reducing their dependence on presales and other high-risk financing practices. Seen in that light, the less headline-grabbing part of the latest policy package – meeting developers’ “reasonable” financing needs – could turn out to be the more consequential one. The policy rationale, as it implies, is that any major reform to the property sector requires first making it financially capable of surviving that reform. Meanwhile, markets could use a dose of sobriety and resist the urge to swing between two extremes: excitement that Beijing is finally ready to bring down the hammer on the old housing model, and disillusionment when the next policy package arrives in increments. China is trying to unwind and rebuild a property model of unparalleled scale while containing damage to its macroeconomy. That dual mandate all but guarantees a long and cautious transition.

title: Gunawan claims China Masters, beaten Lee hails ‘best day’ in Hong Kong badminton history
description: World No 25 Lee Cheuk-yiu loses to compatriot Jason Gunawan, who wins first Super 750 event after also beating world No 1 Jonatan Christie.
content: The city’s top player, Lee Cheuk-yiu, said he had witnessed the “best day in badminton history for Hong Kong” despite going down in straight sets to compatriot Jason Gunawan at the China Masters in Shenzhen on Sunday. World No 25 Lee, who had finished second at the India Open in 2024 and 2025, stormed to the final after eliminating the likes of fellow Hongkonger Angus Ng Ka-long, French duo Toma Junior Popov and Christo Popov, the world No 2, as he progressed. However, facing world No 32 Gunawan, who was playing in the first Super 750 event of his career, Lee failed to reproduce the form that saw him reach his first BWF World Tour final in 21 months. “Despite the results, today is the best day in badminton history for Hong Kong,” the 30-year-old Lee said. “I have the greatest pleasure to play with and witness the first 750 winner finally coming home, congratulations to Jason. “He played really well today. I probably had overexcitement clouding some of my judgment on the shots. I could have played better but I am still very happy to be on the podium again; it means a lot after so long.” Gunawan, who had beaten new world No 1 Jonatan Christie and Danish star Anders Antonsen, was dominant in the opening set. A 5-0 mini-run saw the 22-year-old extend his lead to 16-7 before he took the first set 21-9 at Shenzhen Arena. Facing an 8-1 deficit in the second set, Lee crawled back to trail only 12-11 at one point, but Gunawan kept his composure to seal the second set 21-16, adding to his previous world tour victory in India when he won the Syed Modi International, a Super 300 event, in November last year. The defeat meant Lee remained without a title since winning the Hong Kong Open on home soil in 2019, after losing four finals between 2023 and 2025. Up next for Lee and Gunawan will be the Asian Games, where they will compete alongside 18 others, eight men and 10 women. Lee and Ng will feature in the men’s singles and team events, while Gunawan will play only in the team event. “This definitely boosts my confidence and it’s a very good preparation for the Nagoya Asian Games, and thank you for all the home crowd support today,” Lee said.

title: Germany plans anti-sabotage shield after airport drone attack
description: A national ‘cyberdome’ would be established, with a network of digital sensors to detect and ‌intercept attempted hacking ‌attacks.
content: Germany is planning a broad package of measures to strengthen its defences against drone attacks, cyber intrusions and other forms of Russian sabotage after a failed airport drone attack ‌last month, an interior ministry spokesperson said on Sunday. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper, which first reported the plans, that Russia’s hybrid attacks had become a part of daily reality. “These attacks will increase, but we can ⁠defend and protect ourselves,” Dobrindt was quoted as saying. Russia has long ‌rejected allegations it is carrying out operations in western Europe and has denied involvement in the German airport attack, ‌with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying the accusations were “the start ⁠of a ⁠real war”, according to state news agency TASS. According to the ministry spokesperson, police mobile drone ‌defence capabilities would be expanded under the plan, with rapidly deployable counter-drone units stationed in ‌cities to ‌protect the airspace above critical transport hubs and government districts. Companies ‌operating critical infrastructure, such as power utilities and defence manufacturers, would ⁠be granted the legal authority to not merely detect drones but also actively ⁠fend them off. A national protective shield, or “cyberdome”, would be established, involving a network of digital sensors designed to detect and ‌intercept attempted hacking ‌attacks. The government also intends to expand the use of AI-supported technologies, biometric facial recognition and video surveillance, for example, at railway stations, to identify suspected attackers preparing acts of sabotage.

title: Huawei paper shows Tau Scaling Law chip solves overheating ahead of Kirin 2026 launch
description: The research directly counters claims that vertical stacking creates a thermal bottleneck, the tech giant’s paper says.
content: Huawei Technologies has released a new research paper showing its Tau Scaling Law-based semiconductor architecture can avoid overheating, which analysts view as a key technical hurdle for its anticipated Kirin 2026 smartphone chip. The paper, authored by He Tingbo, chairwoman of the Huawei Scientist Committee and president of the company’s semiconductor business department, rebutted scepticism that vertically stacking logic circuits would create an insurmountable thermal bottleneck. It was published on Friday on ChinaXiv, a publication platform for scientific papers that have yet to be peer reviewed. Despite heat being “the sharpest concern on Tau Scaling Law”, the company’s measurements for its new Kirin chip “turned that objection upside down”, He wrote. The paper said the Kirin 2026 chip ran cooler than its predecessor, while packing 55 per cent more transistors per square millimetre and cutting power use by up to 66 per cent on some key tasks. The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance Kaiyuan Securities The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance By vertically stacking active chip tiers, the design drastically shortened the physical distance that data signals must travel, cutting energy waste across neural processing units, graphics processing units, central processing units and digital signal processors – modules that dominate a smartphone chip’s thermal budget, the paper said. It also significantly boosted transistor density over last year’s Kirin 9030 Pro. Analysts said the findings guarantee performance for the coming launch of Huawei’s next flagship Mate series smartphones. In a research note to clients on Saturday, domestic brokerage Kaiyuan Securities said the new architecture balanced raw performance with power savings. Kaiyuan analysts said Huawei tackled this in two ways: it reduced source power density through folding to prevent localised high temperatures, while actively managing thermal layout during design by placing the most heat-intensive modules in positions with the clearest heat dissipation paths to achieve balance. “The new chip reduces power consumption while increasing transistor density, allowing it to flexibly switch between functional constraints and peak performance,” they said. Zheng Lei, chief economist at Samoyed Cloud Technology Group, said the method was “born out of necessity”, based on Huawei’s projections for its chip performance. While this method had limits, there was room for development, Zheng said, adding he believed the new Kirin chip would successfully resolve its overheating issues using this method. The paper is Huawei’s third since unveiling its Tau Scaling Law in May. The theoretical framework, presented by He, claimed its LogicFolding architecture could achieve transistor densities equivalent to the cutting-edge 1.4-nanometre processes by 2031 without access to advanced extreme ultraviolet lithography machines banned for sale in China due to US sanctions. In a second paper published in July, the company said its coming smartphone processor was on track for a 55 per cent density boost over the Kirin 9030 Pro, based on new production data. Analysts also expected Huawei’s progress on heat management to ripple across a few domestic players who could also potentially help Huawei address the thermal issues. Kaiyuan Securities suggested focusing on directions such as fabs, chip packaging and testing, and new chip equipment. Zhang Xinyuan, an analyst from Beijing-based think tank Kefangde, said the principle could spur innovations in areas such as new semiconductor materials and 3D heterogeneous integration technologies.

title: Why China is being urged to study Ukraine’s wartime PR blitz in the AI age
description: Study explores how Kyiv used a series of drone strikes on airbases deep inside Russia as part of its ‘information offensive’.
content: China has been urged to draw on the lessons from Ukraine’s communications as it looks at new forms of wartime messaging. A recent study concluded that in the complex modern information environment, possessing advanced technology was not enough because success would depend on “weaving” together the information strategy and military operations. It said such campaigns should try to shatter the adversary’s sense of security while strengthening domestic resolve and gathering international support. Beijing should prioritise “multi-actor coordination”, where government, think tanks and internet influencers are all used to deliver the message in sync, researchers at the National University of Defence Technology argued. They also called for layered storytelling tailored to different audiences and the aggressive use of generative AI tools to create, promote and defend its messaging amid “the complex landscape of international public opinion”. Their article, published in the Chinese journal Defence Industry Conversion, analysed the impact of Ukraine’s June 2025 operation, code-named Spiderweb, when more than 100 drones, hidden inside ordinary commercial trucks, attacked five Russian airbases deep inside the country. Ukrainian officials said they had destroyed 41 aircraft, while independent assessments put the figure at least a dozen. “The timing was deliberate, coming on the eve of a second round of peace talks. Within hours, the physical attack was joined by a carefully orchestrated information offensive that sought to rewrite the story of the war itself,” the article by Lin Jiawei and Yang Qingqing argued. China has repeatedly said that its relationship with Russia was not directed at any third party and that it supported a negotiated settlement to the war, which started more than four years ago. The researchers argued that Ukraine had constructed three interlocking narratives following the attacks. It first framed the strikes as legitimate self-defence against prolonged Russian aggression and then cast Ukraine as a restrained actor that was seeking to destroy the planes that had been bombing its cities, reducing civilian suffering. The third element was deterrence.
