By demonstrating the ability to hit high-value targets across multiple Russian regions and time zones, Kyiv was trying to force Moscow to recalculate the true cost of continuing the conflict and to puncture its long-standing claims of “absolute homeland security”. These messages moved through a deliberately diversified network – something, the authors argued, that had lessons for China. Global media and open-source intelligence outlets quickly turned Ukrainian official accounts into polished news packages. The story was also spread on social media by military influencers and eyewitnesses, with raw video footage and emotional commentary providing a grass-roots feel that state messaging often lacked. Ukraine’s use of surprise drone strikes and sophisticated information packaging had succeeded in placing cognitive pressure on Russia while sustaining domestic morale and Western support, the study said. “The result was a cascading amplification that reached Russian officials and the public, war-weary Ukrainians and Western decision-makers almost simultaneously,” it added. China has invested heavily in “intelligentised” warfare and the military uses of artificial intelligence (AI) in recent years. This ranges from autonomous systems to what it calls “cognitive domain operations” that are designed to weaken an enemy’s will to fight and disrupt its decision-making processes. Beijing is also closely monitoring ongoing wars and the use of technology as it seeks to improve its own strategies and battle readiness. Meanwhile, Beijing has doubled down on efforts to strengthen its messaging and screen information to weed out AI-generated deepfakes. The Ukraine war, the authors argued, showed how generative AI could be put to immediate practical use by producing high volumes of tailored content. They said Kyiv was also tailoring its messages to appeal to different audiences by matching text, images and audio to specific audience profiles, and enabling real-time monitoring of emotional trends so that messaging could be adjusted “within hours rather than days”. The study also pointed to ways that AI could be used to create a “narrative logic” that appealed to different groups – for example by strengthening the sense of national identity among a domestic audience or promoting ideas such as a “community with a shared future” internationally – and countered Western messaging. The study also stressed the need to counter disinformation and deepfakes, ensuring that the domestic information space remained controllable even as outward messaging became more agile. For a China intent on mastering the integration of AI across the military and information domains, the lesson was not merely to adopt new tools, but to orchestrate government voices, media, online influencers and ordinary citizens into a “coherent, adaptive system capable of shaping perceptions as decisively as any kinetic operation”, the authors concluded.

title: Man arrested over flag-day scam targeting animal charity donations
description: Man, 22, arrested after 14 people allegedly hired to act as volunteers to collect donations for Hong Kong Saving Cat and Dog Association.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested a man in connection with a scam in which at least 14 people were hired to “sell flags” for an animal concern group after they were spotted carrying fake donation bags and mixing with registered volunteers to collect money from passers-by. The rare street scam came to light during the group’s flag day on Saturday, a Social Welfare Department-approved fundraising initiative under which about 800 registered volunteers from the Hong Kong Saving Cat and Dog Association deployed across Kowloon from 7am to noon, the South China Morning Post learned. Flag days are a traditional fundraising practice in Hong Kong under which approved charities recruit volunteers to collect donations on the streets. Volunteers carry a designated donation bag and a sheet of small stickers, which replaced the traditional small paper flags that donors once pinned to their clothing many years ago. When passers-by drop coins into the bag or make a digital donation, the volunteer places a sticker on their clothing as a token of appreciation and recognition. The events are typically held on Saturdays, or occasionally on Wednesdays during school holidays. In Cantonese, flag days are called mai kei yat – or “flag-selling day”. Genuine volunteers reported on social media that a group of strangers had mixed into the crowd, openly displaying fake flag sheets and bags that were a different shade of blue. A police source said the complainant noticed individuals impersonating association staff near Langham Place in Mong Kok. Fourteen people carrying counterfeit bags were stopped. Investigations showed they had responded to a WhatsApp job advert offering HK$70 an hour for flag-selling work, and believed they were simply temporary workers. They were instructed to return the bags to a contact on Nelson Street at 12.30pm on Saturday, but the organiser never appeared. The fake bags were light blue, rather than dark blue ones used by the authentic volunteers, and bore a statement claiming the flag day had been approved by the department. The 14 recruits were taken to Mong Kok Police Station for questioning. On Sunday, officers arrested a 22-year-old man for deception, a police spokesman said. The case has been handed to the Mong Kok district crime squad for follow‑up action.

title: Curiosity beats perfect statements, UK elite universities tell Hong Kong students
description: Show real stories and intellectual drive, not just top grades or costly consultants, admissions chiefs say.
content: Elite British universities are prioritising authentic curiosity and academic resilience over rigid test prep and “perfect personal statements”, top admissions officials have told an education summit in Hong Kong. Representatives from the “golden triangle”, including the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge and King’s College London, spoke on day two of the Global Education Summit, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier. The session focused on studying abroad. Nearly 11,000 people in total attended the two-day summit. “At the heart of the admissions process at Oxford is a passion for the course that you want to study,” said Samina Khan, director of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Oxford, during a panel curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm. “Whether you’re doing an A-level or a Hong Kong diploma, don’t just stick to what you’re being taught in school. You should be researching, you should be reading, listening to TED Talks to expand your knowledge.” Admissions leaders emphasised that high grades represented only a starting baseline. Sarah Hales, senior regional manager in admissions and access at the University of Cambridge, said the university selected candidates with genuine intellectual drive. “Last year we welcomed students from around the world, including over 140 countries. But students from Hong Kong have always been and will remain just valued students at the university,” Hales said. Hales noted that artificial intelligence (AI) was expanding beyond traditional technical majors into the humanities. She highlighted growing engagement with fields such as digital humanities, adding that while course choices remained stable, the modules students selected were evolving. To distinguish top applicants, Cambridge evaluates how students handle small-group academic discussions during interviews, which mirror the university’s core supervision teaching model. “It’s not always the students with the top grades,” Hales said. “Sometimes it’s those students that want to go beyond that. It’s quite often the ones that might question what a teacher says.” She added that interviewers looked for students who constantly investigated and challenged assumptions, as this demonstrated genuine excitement for the subject. During these sessions, the university tested motivation by working through complex problems with the applicant. Khan stressed that successful Oxford candidates had to demonstrate academic resilience and a deep, self-driven interest in their subject that extended beyond the classroom. She noted that the university was moving to standard UAT-UK admissions tests for the first time, retiring its long-standing in-house assessments. Applicants for 2027 entry must sit these standardised tests during the October 2026 window. Oxford is also aligning its testing platform with Cambridge to simplify the application process for international families. “The admissions tests help us understand who has the academic ability and who will perform really well in an intensive environment,” Khan said, noting that candidates must adapt to Oxford’s rigorous weekly tutorial system. Meanwhile, British Council research shows that six in 10 Hongkongers are considering the UK as a study destination. More than 16,000 students are currently enrolled in British universities, according to Andrea Hales, acting director for Hong Kong and head of English and exams at the British Council. While families seek assurance that higher education will yield better career outcomes, driving peak interest in engineering and data science, the report stressed that top employers increasingly looked beyond technical knowledge. Mandy Zhang, head of East Asia for the global student recruitment and admissions directorate at King’s College London, highlighted that top British universities prioritised authentic personal reflection in applications. “We’re not looking for a sort of shocking list of things that the student has done. The most important thing is to relate those activities to the course that you are applying for,” Zhang said. She noted that students did not need costly external education consultants to build a competitive file. “We want students to show real stories and competencies, developed either inside the classroom or externally using free online and in-person resources. You don’t have to pay for services to apply or write a personal statement,” Zhang added. Sarah Hales from Cambridge also cautioned against generic introductions, urging applicants to explain exactly what sparked their interest and how they explored the subject outside school through extra reading or personal research projects. “We don’t want to hear that ever since I was a child I’ve been interested in this subject,” she said. “We’re interested to know what got you interested in this subject. What did you do outside school to explore that subject? Was it extra reading? Did you challenge yourself to do a personal research project?”

title: Zelensky warns Ukraine war is likely to continue into winter after US talks
description: US envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky both gave upbeat assessments of the talks but neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the war.
content: War with Russia “at the moment” looked likely to continue into winter, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday, after talks with US envoys visiting Kyiv. US envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky both gave upbeat assessments of the talks but neither announced any breakthroughs on ending the war with Russia. Witkoff, who is US President Donald Trump’s business ally, and Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, travelled to Kyiv a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow – the latest of several visits to the city. Sunday’s trip to Kyiv was their first visit to the Ukrainian capital, which has been hit by deadly Russian strikes for more than four years. Zelensky said: “We very much hope that we will be able to reach agreements with our American partners, and we are counting on the support of our European partners if the war continues in winter – and this is how it appears at the moment.” Zelensky also said Ukraine would hold talks with the US, France and Germany but did not elaborate. The Ukrainian leader, who has called for a meeting with Putin before, repeated his call that only a meeting between leaders could solve territorial issues. The US envoys brought new, possibly more workable proposals on ending the war and Zelensky is holding another meeting with them in a trio format, a senior Ukrainian presidential official told Agence France-Presse later on Sunday. “It’s not the same as it was before. This one now is more effective,” the source said adding: “They’re still talking. This is actually the most important part. There are three of them now.” Moscow occupies large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine and the Kremlin told the Americans on Saturday it was feeling “confident” it would advance more. Moscow has said it wants not just the territories it occupies but the land it claims as Russian to be recognised as its own – terms unacceptable to Kyiv. Witkoff said both sides would need to compromise. “We think we have the ingredients to get to that place,” he said. “We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.” Kushner added: “Hopefully this trip has come out with some new ways to advance forward. I think we’ve learned a lot from the trip.” Witkoff and Kushner travelled to the region hoping to revive the Trump administration’s push for peace in Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, after a summer of escalation. Another round of talks in the presence of British, French and German representatives was still continuing. Zelensky said he was grateful the Europeans were there, adding: “Here we are all on the same side.” Like all visiting officials, the American delegation had arrived by train, with “Peace Express” written on the platform at Kyiv Central Station. Zelensky said Kyiv had “prepared everything to make our airports operational” but Russian strikes had made arriving by plane impossible. Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Russia launched its invasion in 2022. Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other’s capitals during the US envoys’ trip. Moscow’s invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. A White House official said in a statement to Agence France-Presse that in Moscow the envoys had “discussed substantive plans which will be announced in the coming weeks”. Without elaborating, the Kremlin said the Americans had “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine, and Russia increased deadly strikes this summer. Since Putin launched the invasion in February 2022, the war has dragged on with no end in sight. In Kyiv, few people appeared to believe in a breakthrough. Nataliia Lipekh, 67, said it was “absolutely necessary [for them] to be here” and to see that “our land is already soaked with this blood and that we need some help”. “At the moment, I have no grounds for hope,” said 29-year-old Yaroslav, saying he had seen “far too many of these negotiation processes”. Putin on Saturday told the US envoys that Moscow would ensure their safety in Kyiv. Trump had said his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end the fighting. “We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating. Despite the ceasefire pledges for the capital cities, fighting continued elsewhere. Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked overnight with 108 drones and missiles, while Moscow said it had shot down 258 drones. Ukraine said on Saturday that 10 people were killed by Russian strikes, including an 11-year-old boy.

title: China will never allow any country in this world to achieve AI dominance: Victor Gao
description: China’s grip on rare earths will deny US any chance of using ‘AI for evil’, Centre for China and Globalisation vice-president says in Penang.
content: China will thwart US ambitions for global artificial intelligence (AI) dominance, the vice-president of the Centre for China and Globalisation has said, while warning that Washington’s military-focused strategy was pushing towards “AI for evil”. Addressing the Penang Peace Dialogue in Malaysia on Sunday, Victor Gao said the US was “weaponising and militarising AI”, and integrating the technology into systems ranging from drones and ballistic missiles to everyday software and hardware. This drive for hegemony posed a global risk, he argued. The Centre for China and Globalisation, a Beijing-based non-governmental think tank, is an influential institution that provides research on international trade, global governance and China’s foreign relations. “We should figure out a way to free us up from this attempted AI dominance,” Gao said, contrasting China’s open-source development to American closed-source strategies. “China will never allow any country in this world to achieve AI dominance. That is why China is so committed to push forward AI leadership,” Gao said. “China’s grip on rare earth control will deny the United States any chance of achieving AI for evil purposes,” he added. “China wants to break up that dominance. China wants to make sure that AI will be used for good, rather than be misused for evil.” The race for AI supremacy has emerged as a critical geopolitical fault line beyond commercial competition. Analysts at Sunday’s forum warned that the development could redefine global stability. They called for a shift towards multilateral cooperation and international AI governance frameworks to restrict the use of the technology for military purposes. [US] purpose is to militarise artificial intelligence at a maximal rate Jeffrey Sachs, Centre for Sustainable Development, Columbia University American economist Jeffrey Sachs, director of the Centre for Sustainable Development at Columbia University, described the US as a country led by “the military-industrial-digital complex because the companies of Silicon Valley are intimately connected with the Pentagon”. “The purpose is to militarise artificial intelligence at a maximal rate,” he said, echoing Gao. “The American view is that it is going to use that technological and financial leverage that comes from a dollar-based international trading system to maintain its dominance in the rest of the world.” Sachs dismissed this objective as a “delusion” that was “arithmetically, economically, financially and militarily impossible”. He said the US did not have the necessary dominance to achieve this goal and that the centre of gravity had returned to Asia – which accounts for more than half the global growth and population. Joanna Lei, chairwoman of the National Women’s League in Taiwan, cited mainland China’s top open-weight AI model Kimi K3 as a watershed moment that challenged the Western capitalist paradigm of technology development, even if it had yet to reach the cutting edge of US technology. “From the Western point of view, you put huge resources behind some cutting-edge technology, you build dominance, and in this entire ecosystem, you are the rule-setter,” she said. Citing the semiconductor industry as an example where top players dictated architecture, design and manufacturing standards, she said: “With that, you can tolerate high capital investment initially and even the deficit initially, because you will monetise later on.” “But Kimi K3 changed that whole equation in a massive way,” Lei added, noting that the AI competition was shifting from a race for the most powerful model to a race for deployment at scale, creating two increasingly distinct development paths. The Penang Peace Dialogue is a new annual international forum aimed at fostering peace and cooperation in a multipolar world. The two-day first edition that concluded on Sunday brought together roughly 200 academics, policymakers and business leaders from Asia and beyond.

title: ‘There are trade-offs’: how Hong Kong patients can use telemedicine wisely
description: Hospital Authority telehealth cases jump 33 per cent as private clinics tailor services for people with busy schedules.
content: In the fourth instalment of a five-part Health Matters wellness series on Hong Kong’s growing wellness trends, Lo Hoi-ying examines how telehealth is reshaping access to care, as practitioners warn it cannot fully replace in-person diagnosis. Hong Kong housewife Chan Ket-yee, nearly 60, has battled severe eczema on her neck and underarms for decades. Splitting her time between the United Kingdom and the city, Chan saw a dramatic improvement after visiting a Hong Kong public dermatologist, whose treatment plan proved far more effective than UK doctors who “just gave basic advice”. Telehealth allowed her to manage care seamlessly across time zones, with convenient, long-term support for her condition. In April, Chan attended a community event by WeDerm, a Hong Kong clinic specialising in integrated eczema care, where she learned about the link between skin and gut health. She took a gut microbiome test in Hong Kong before returning to the UK for the summer and completed an online follow-up with her nutritionist to review the results. “When the results came out, I was in the UK, so we communicated via WhatsApp video call,” she said. “He sent a list showing me the levels of gut strains I had and whether they were high or low. “He recommended a supplement brand available at Holland & Barrett in the UK, so I bought it and have been taking it for over a month now.” She regularly uses digital channels to ask questions and discuss diets: “If I have quick questions, I message my nutritionist on WhatsApp or comment on his Instagram posts about eczema and nutrition.” While demand for telemedicine in the private sector in Hong Kong has faded since the pandemic-era boom, online consultations remain an alternative for chronic patients needing regular check-ups, those with mobility issues, or residents studying or working abroad. According to Hospital Authority data, the number of patients using its telehealth service has increased steadily after the initial 2022 surge. Hong Kong’s public health system provided 175,384 telehealth cases in the past financial year, a 33 per cent increase from 2024-25. “The Hospital Authority has progressively implemented telehealth services in suitable services, including different specialist outpatient clinics, nurse clinics, allied health services and outreach services,” it said. Harrison Li Kin-cheung, co-founder of WeDerm, said telehealth benefited clients with busy schedules who might travel during treatment, which could last months. But he said interacting with patients in person was more effective for building trust and rapport. This was especially so with children and their parents, when reminding them about foods to avoid during treatment. “The first point of contact with a patient should be in person to build credibility. Virtually, it’s not as direct and convenient,” he said. Several traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) clinics in Hong Kong also provide online consultation services, with some tailoring offerings for clients in the UK. Yu Sheung-fung, medical director of the Yu Fung Chinese Medicine Group, said online consultations were popular among his younger customers, aged 30 to 50, who had busy schedules. “In Hong Kong, working professionals who are busy with work might find it hard to visit a clinic after office hours, making distance a problem,” Yu said, adding that online patients made up around 3 per cent of his total clientele. “They can schedule a teleconsultation during their lunch break and pick up their prescription at a clinic branch nearest to them after work.” He added: “It saves them time; the consultation itself only takes about 10 to 15 minutes, making it much easier for them to manage their schedule.” His clinic has a UK partner that delivers prescribed medication to local patients, an arrangement that began during the pandemic, which saw a boom in demand for such services. “Since the UK is a common destination for Hong Kong people – whether for studying or emigrating – the demand is there,” he said. “Some patients consult us for general health conditioning, like preparing for pregnancy. Others seek treatment for skin conditions like eczema, which worsened after moving to the UK, possibly due to changes in the climate. “Since they usually saw us in Hong Kong before, we did video consultations to treat their existing issues.” Lo Siu-luen, a Chinese medicine practitioner at Wing Fuk Tong, said there were “trade-offs” with online consultations. In TCM, practitioners perform clinical assessments through four diagnostic methods: inspection; listening and smelling; inquiring; and palpation. Lo said before the consultation, patients should ensure a stable internet connection, sufficient lighting and a quiet environment. “Other than pulse-taking, the rest can still be done through the camera lens, but patients have to make sure they have enough natural light so it won’t affect the doctor’s judgment,” he said. Another way his clinic uses telemedicine is for doctors to provide consultation without being physically in Hong Kong. “If a patient needs special attention for sleep issues, the senior doctor will join the consultation on a video call,” Lo said. “He will teach our practitioners some of his commonly used methods for acupuncture or manual therapies like massage, and our local doctor can perform them.” To test how the absence of pulse-taking affects consultations, the South China Morning Post booked an online TCM session with Wing Fuk Tong regarding the reporter’s irregular periods. The clinic arranged a same-day consultation via WhatsApp video call with TCM practitioner Kwan Yee-ha. Kwan quickly obtained an overview of the reporter’s physical condition by asking a series of questions about lifestyle habits and symptoms. After the reporter disclosed a habit of regularly consuming cold drinks and staying up late, Kwan determined that an excess of dampness had built up in the body, leading to swelling, congestion and a heavy physical sensation. To confirm her diagnosis of internal dampness, Kwan asked to inspect the reporter’s tongue, which revealed a white coating. She noted that cold hands and feet, combined with frequent dizziness, pointed to weak Yang energy and poor blood circulation. The practitioner also inquired about stool condition, appetite, sleep quality and stress levels. During the 20-minute session, Kwan deduced that high stress and late nights had weakened the spleen, causing dampness to accumulate while depriving the body of the energy required to circulate blood properly – ultimately resulting in a delayed period. Kwan advised going to bed early and avoiding cold drinks and greasy food, and prescribed five days of powdered Chinese herbs to be dissolved in hot water. Following the late-afternoon consultation, the prescribed medicine was delivered to the reporter’s doorstep by the next morning at a cost of HK$600 (US$76.50). Despite the convenience of telehealth, a 2025 Consumer Council study found a general lack of transparency in price and service information, including unclear fees, uncertain refund mechanisms and confusing service details. While telehealth was most commonly used for common cold and cough consultations, both surveyed practitioners and patients agreed that a major challenge was the inability to conduct physical examinations. The council found consumers had concerns about medical incidents or inaccurate diagnoses, and that services lacked transparent pricing, such as refund terms, and offered limited consultation time slots. Patients surveyed also said customer service was inaccessible and expressed concerns that sessions could be tracked and monitored. The council suggested a list of items to be included in guidelines for telemedicine in Hong Kong, including clinical standards, obligations and liability, disclosure for informed consent and the use of artificial intelligence (AI). While demand for private telehealth in Hong Kong has largely dwindled since the height of the Covid pandemic when the government enforced strict social distancing rules, online consultations now serve patients with specific needs for privacy and convenience. Li from WeDerm said it was difficult for telehealth to grow in Hong Kong as healthcare was easily accessible, but would be more popular in countries with a bigger urban-rural divide. Lo from Wing Fuk Tong agreed, saying demand for telehealth services at his clinic had dropped by more than 95 per cent since it was introduced during the pandemic. “If existing patients who usually see our doctors have chronic conditions that need management and it isn’t convenient for them to come to the clinic, they can choose teleconsultation,” he said. But one of telehealth’s strengths lies in the ease of set-up, allowing medical services to reach those in need in emergencies. During the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po last year, charity Light of Raphael was able to get TCM telehealth services up and running within a day. Founder Douglas Shum Hong-yuen first piloted the Clinic Without Walls telehealth project in 2022 during the height of the pandemic. By cooperating with Neighbourhood Elderly Centres, the clinic provided telemedicine support, including online consultation, dispensing and medicine delivery to elderly residents living alone and under quarantine. When the fire ravaged the housing estate, its team of TCM practitioners quickly set up online consultation services for Wang Fuk Court residents seeking shelter temporarily in three Sino Group hotels. “At that time, it was very urgent and we wanted to help them,” he said. “We thought about working with them since residents might have medical needs after moving in. For example, some might have inhaled thick smoke.” The medication was also delivered to the hotels, reducing the need for affected residents to commute while they settled in. Shum said that by partnering with the hotels, his team was able to set up the service within a day, while the hotels were preparing for residents to move in. “By the time residents moved in, they had already received a notice that they could contact us if they needed medical support,” he said. “There were quite a few cases of residents catching a cold, as some people were worried about their homes that day. “For these types of conditions, telemedicine could help them very quickly, making them a very suitable group of patients for us to reach out to at that time.”

title: Seoul Art Week 2026 sees galleries change tactics to woo buyers in a cooler market
description: Hosting over 300 galleries, Frieze Seoul and Kiaf leaned towards affordable art for collectors now that speculators have left the market.
content: Frieze Seoul’s fifth edition opened in a subdued art market, where prolonged uncertainty has made collectors more cautious and galleries more attentive to affordability. Held from September 2 to 5 at the Coex centre in Gangnam, the fair introduced new sections aimed at attracting buyers in a more austere market. Patrick Lee, director of Frieze Seoul, said the slowdown in the art market had been protracted, with established collectors taking a more measured approach amid broader macroeconomic uncertainty. He also noted that the influence of younger buyers had often been overstated. “There was a spurt of speculators, crypto investors and the like who generated a lot of activity during the pandemic,” he said. “And then they realised they couldn’t sell art like shares in the stock market.” Even so, he said, the four-day fair had attracted a curious and engaged new generation of collectors. Galleries, he added, had responded by diversifying their offerings and introducing more accessible entry points. The Korea International Art Fair (Kiaf) took place from September 2 to 6 on a different level of the same building as Frieze, with the two events sharing entry passes. With more than 300 galleries presenting across the two events, Seoul once again hosted Asia’s second-largest art fair week, after Hong Kong’s Art Basel week. Seoul’s fairs, however, remain less international in terms of gallery participation, with most exhibitors from Korea or the wider region. “The Korean market reached its highest volume in 2022 at around 1 trillion won [US$800 million], but by 2024, it had fallen 40 per cent to about 600 billion won,” said Lee Sung-hoon, president of the Galleries Association of Korea, which runs Kiaf. But like Patrick Lee, he said there were now signs that the market was returning to a more sustainable path. “The [hot] money receded, the speculators disappeared from the market, and real collectors remained,” Lee Sung-hoon said. The range of works sold on the first day of Frieze Seoul illustrated galleries’ need to cater to buyers with divergent budgets. White Cube’s opening-day sales included two works from Park Seo-bo’s “Ecriture” series, priced at US$300,000 and US$190,000, as well as a watercolour by Yoko Matsumoto at US$5,500. Thaddaeus Ropac sold Adrian Ghenie’s Figure with Funerary Stele for €1.1 million (US$1.3 million), alongside three paintings by young Korean artist Heemin Chung, priced between US$24,000 and US$33,000. Frieze Seoul’s new “Material Practice” section explored the intersections between art, craft and design. It featured Hong Kong gallery Soluna, which sold three porcelain works by Loewe Craft Prize 2026 winner Park Jong-jin for between US$6,000 and US$40,000. The gallery also sold two of Seungtaik Jang’s paintings on Plexiglas, each priced at between US$10,000 and US$15,000. Kyoto’s Yumekoubou Gallery brought bamboo master Tanabe Chikuunsai IV to Seoul. At the Frieze House art space, he wove a room-sized bamboo installation that withstood crowds of selfie-takers. A mini version, measuring two metres (6.5ft) across, was offered at the fair for US$69,300. Galleries also faced sharply higher shipping costs amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis. A heavily promoted exhibition of Gagosian artist Jonas Wood at Seoul’s Amorepacific Museum of Art was cancelled at the last minute because of the crisis. The museum instead assembled a large Sol LeWitt show in just one month, drawing on loans from across Asia and works that could be executed on site according to instructions. At the fairs, smaller galleries generally had less room to absorb disappointing sales. Fortunately for Hong Kong’s Double Q Gallery, the results of its first overseas fair exceeded expectations, according to co-owner Nick Chu. The gallery presented Serbian-French artist Djordje Ivackovic in the new “Spotlight” section, which was dedicated to solo presentations of overlooked 20th century artists. Chu said the works’ relatively accessible price range, from HK$50,000 to HK$150,000 (US$6,400 to US$19,100), helped attract buyers in the current market. Even if the costly participation did not generate a profit, he and co-founder Queenie Rosita Law regarded the fair as an investment in their longer-term efforts to promote Central European artists. Demand from museums and foundations in South Korea and the wider region remained strong at the top end of the market, said Marc Payot, president of Hauser & Wirth. Transactions were taking longer, he said, but South Korea’s strong institutional bases continued to grow their ambitious, world-class collections. Works by Do Ho Suh were everywhere. The South Korea-born artist had a solo booth at Lehmann Maupin, works on display at STPI’s booth at Frieze Seoul, and a 500-work retrospective at Seoul’s National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art. The exhibition is scheduled to travel to the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo and Hong Kong’s M+ in 2027. Georg Baselitz, who died this April aged 88, also loomed large. The German painter’s first posthumous retrospective in Asia opened at Seoul’s Sehwa Museum of Art, while Thaddaeus Ropac’s Seoul space presented his recent “Shadow” series. The gallery scene continued to grow at a “slow and steady” pace, Patrick Lee said. Although several galleries have closed recently, Gladstone Gallery has expanded its Seoul space, and Meyer Riegger has just established a Seoul presence jointly with Galerie Jocelyn Wolff. Hong Kong-based Pavilion also held the first edition of its art fair in Seoul during Frieze week, in a grungy, semi-open setting intended to further lower the barriers to buying art. Next year, Frieze Seoul will move from Coex to the Zaha Hadid-designed Dongdaemun Design Plaza. Design Miami Seoul held its second edition at the venue during the same week as the art fairs, underscoring the overlap between audiences for contemporary art and collectible design.

title: Hong Kong to propel belt and road market expansion, finance chief says
description: Paul Chan’s pledge comes ahead of 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this week.
content: Hong Kong will step up support for belt and road enterprises seeking to expand into new markets and tap regional growth, reinforcing its role as a pivotal business hub and platform for deeper exchanges, the city’s finance chief has said. In his weekly blog on Sunday, Paul Chan Mo-po also pointed to strong growth in emerging markets and developing economies in recent years, citing International Monetary Fund projections of a further 3.8 per cent and 4.5 per cent expansion respectively over the coming two years. “The gradual relocation of mainland China’s industrial chains towards belt and road regions is a response to this reality,” he wrote. Chan made the remarks ahead of the 11th Belt and Road Summit in Hong Kong this week. The annual event promotes business among participating nations in the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s project to build a China-centred global trading network. This year’s summit is being held under the theme “Advancing high-quality development, embarking on a new journey”. For the first time, there will be a dedicated “Go Global Chapter” to support mainland firms expanding overseas. Mainland firms have established around 58,000 overseas entities, creating more than 2 million local jobs annually, with an investment stock of US$3.4 trillion, nearly 90 per cent of which is in developing economies, according to Chan. “Market demand is clearly driving industrial-chain deployment, economic growth is attracting capital flows, and the momentum of trade and investment is unmistakable, characterised by vibrant two-way movement,” he said. “Hong Kong stands precisely at the intersection of this two‑way flow.” He said more than 100 belt and road firms with a combined market capitalisation exceeding HK$340 billion (US$43.6 billion) were now listed in the city and some Central Asian state infrastructure firms were also eyeing a debut on the local exchange. “We aim to further assist belt and road enterprises in market expansion, reducing transaction costs and unlocking regional growth potential,” Chan said. Hong Kong has signed double taxation agreements with 43 belt and road jurisdictions, while investment and free trade pacts cover 20 and 14 economies respectively, according to Chan. In bond financing, 82 listed bonds from belt and road regions had been issued in Hong Kong as of July, raising over HK$470 billion, Chan said. He noted that more governments, public institutions and enterprises from Southeast Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East had issued offshore yuan bonds in the city in recent years. As an example, Kazakhstan’s national oil and gas company issued about 3.5 billion yuan last month, the largest such offering by a Central Asian enterprise in Hong Kong, Chan said. “Whether attracting investment or supporting outbound expansion, Hong Kong serves as a pivotal hub and platform for accelerated development and deepened exchanges,” he said. The two-day summit on Wednesday and Thursday will also cover energy, artificial intelligence, the low-altitude economy and urban development, with on‑site visits. There will also be a climate-finance conference this week, co-hosted by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and the Dubai Financial Services Authority. This event, along with initiatives such as a green technology project accelerator programme and updated sustainable finance classification, showed the city’s commitment to driving regional growth through green technology and finance, Chan said. He added that Hong Kong would continue to leverage its unique advantages under “one country two systems”, from advancing hardware projects and aligning rules through soft connectivity, to fostering people-to-people bonds that bring communities closer together.

title: Chinese food vendor sparks ‘camera bullying’ debate after vloggers portray her as ‘evil granny’
description: Some content creators claim ‘there is no privacy in public places', lawyers clarify that people do not forfeit personal rights by being visible.
content: A 92-year-old snack vendor from southwestern China has sparked a debate over online exploitation after vloggers deliberately provoked her to produce sensational videos presenting her as an “evil granny.” This case mirrors a similar “camera bullying” incident last November, where tourists filmed an elderly woman from the Yi ethnic group in traditional clothing on a train, despite her apparent discomfort. “Camera bullying” refers to the act of filming individuals without their consent to garner online views, with critics highlighting the potential emotional damage it can cause. This issue transcends China’s borders. On TikTok, some teenagers have popularised the “flip the camera” prank, which involves pretending to ask strangers for help filming them before secretly turning the camera around to capture the passers-by’s awkward reactions. The recent controversy revolved around grandmother Xue, a vendor in Chengdu, Sichuan province, who sells egg-baked pancakes on the street after losing her son to illness. Her determination has garnered support from local residents. Xue often worked 15 hours a day during busy periods, with monthly earnings occasionally surpassing 20,000 yuan (US$3,000), as reported by local media. Nevertheless, she has also faced criticism. In 2019, some customers accused her of overcharging and having a poor temper, while others raised concerns about her food hygiene standards. While Xue mentioned that she does not own a smartphone or understand social media, she acknowledged that improving her attitude towards customers could be beneficial. However, some vloggers recognised that her controversial image could generate significant online traffic. They filmed her at her stall without buying any food, deliberately provoking her with comments to capture moments of anger or confrontation. Some even reportedly teased her by whistling or blowing smoke rings in her face. The resulting clips were edited with titles such as “evil granny” or “egg-pancake villain,” receiving thousands of likes. In several videos, Xue could be heard shouting: “Don’t film me,” and attempting to shield herself from the cameras, but the recording persisted. Some internet users criticised the videos as a form of “camera bullying,” arguing that her flaws do not justify public humiliation. “Xue may have shortcomings, but that does not mean she deserves disrespect,” one commenter wrote. “People provoke anger, profit from displaying it, and then label it as justice.” Another user expressed: “An elderly person of her age still relies on her own labour to make a living. Even if you dislike her, it is inappropriate to disturb her.” On August 27, Chengdu’s internet authorities shut down two social media accounts, citing violations of Xue’s reputation and privacy rights. This case has reignited discussions surrounding the boundaries of online content creation in China. While Chinese law protects citizens’ rights to privacy and personal image, lawyers noted that victims of camera bullying often find it challenging to seek redress due to difficulties in gathering evidence, limited legal awareness, and high litigation costs. Conversely, some content creators argue that “there is no privacy in public places,” but legal experts warn that this assertion is misleading, as individuals do not relinquish their personal rights merely by being visible to others.

title: How China’s youth job crisis is driving graduates to German vocational apprenticeships
description: Facing bleak employment prospects at home, some young Chinese workers are pursuing technical training abroad, but not all make it through.
content: Two years ago, Yuki Liu was a university student in the northern Chinese province of Hebei, studying traditional Chinese music and the pipa – a pear-shaped Chinese lute – weighing the usual paths considered by her peers: postgraduate degree or civil service exam. Today, her day begins at 1am in Germany. While many people sleep, she is already working as an apprentice at an industrial bakery in a small town outside Stuttgart in the country’s southwest, preparing the shop for the morning rush. The turning point for Liu came as she approached graduation and grew increasingly unsure about the path her studies could offer her in China. “With a music degree, your only option is to teach,” she said. “Otherwise you starve.” Liu came across Germany’s apprenticeship system almost by happenstance, discovering a path that the musician had never imagined: becoming a blue-collar worker in Europe’s largest economy. Liu is among a growing number of young Chinese turning to Ausbildung, Germany’s dual vocational training system, as an alternative to an increasingly competitive graduate job market at home and as a potential route to staying in Europe. Many applicants, like her, already hold university degrees or have worked for well-known companies. On Chinese social media, the pitch is straightforward: little upfront cost and the prospect of a job at the end. Apprentices are employed by a company in Germany and paid a training allowance while attending a state vocational school tuition-free. Most stay on as regular employees once they qualify. Back in China, there is a popular cultural refrain that students and degree-holders often use to describe how hard it is to find a job: “graduation means unemployment”. A record 12.7 million students graduated from Chinese universities this year, up 480,000 from 2025. Unemployment among people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, rose to 17.9 per cent in July – an 11-month high. For some, Ausbildung – literally translated as “education”, “training” or “apprenticeship” – offers more than a pay cheque. It is also one of the cheaper routes to relocating abroad, particularly for those looking to escape a working culture epitomised by a notorious “996” schedule – working from 9am to 9pm, six days a week. Social media has helped fuel the appeal. Liu recalled a video on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – featuring a philosophy postgraduate student who had dropped out and moved to Germany to train as a gardener, listing what he found different about working there: no rat race, no overtime and no office politics. The video drew thousands of likes, with viewers asking in the comments how they could follow a similar path. The financial incentives also blunt some reluctance towards blue-collar work. Workers in Germany with a recognised vocational qualification earned about €4,125 (US$4,800) a month before tax in April 2025, according to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office – roughly five times the average pay of production workers in China last year, data from the National Bureau of Statistics shows. “You can really feel it: far more people are talking about it than before,” said Emilie Xie, a former media worker in China who is now applying to become a carer in Germany. However, for some, reality often hits harder than the online pitch. Lin Chenxi runs a youth hostel in Hamburg and helps place Chinese apprentices with German employers, supporting them after they arrive. “Only about a third of the students we placed made it through,” she said. “The other two-thirds either got weeded out or lost heart and left.” The language, Lin said, can be the biggest hurdle. She explained how applicants need a B1 proficiency level in German – an intermediate stage in which they can handle everyday situations and communicate familiar topics – but many appear to have drilled their way through the German language exam in China, and they arrive unable to hold a conversation. I feel like a screw on an assembly line Yuki Liu The promise of plentiful jobs can also be misleading. Germany lacked enough qualified workers to fill 369,500 skilled jobs in 2025, according to the German Economic Institute, with nursing among the hardest-hit professions. Some of the roles that are more accessible to Chinese applicants are said to include care work, baking and kitchen jobs. “I feel like a screw on an assembly line,” Liu said, explaining how she spends about six hours every workday sorting deliveries and two hours making products. In nearly a year, she lamented, she had never taken a single item from raw ingredients to a finished loaf. Apprentices spend about three years on a training allowance that averages €1,238 a month before tax, according to the Federal Statistical Office, with smaller firms typically paying less. Liu takes home €873, of which €680 goes towards rent. She said she is already considering her next restart, possibly by pursuing another apprenticeship. Those realities may help explain the gap between the buzz on Chinese social media and the number actually taking the route. Germany counted 573 Chinese nationals in dual vocational training in 2024, up from 282 in 2020, according to the Federal Institute for Vocational Education and Training. The figures exclude nursing and other school-based programmes that attract many more Chinese applicants. Still, the overall number remains a fraction of China’s outbound workforce. For Emilie Xie, though, none of this has changed her mind. “A degree isn’t hard currency any more,” she said. “It has become consumption, not an investment.” Xie graduated from Hengshui High School – famed for its gruelling exam drilling – and went on to study at a university in Beijing. It was a path once seen as a ticket to a comfortable career. She worked in media before deciding to retrain herself. Xie said she deliberately chose care work: the sector is short-staffed, relatively easy to enter and – she believed – harder for artificial intelligence to replace. She said she knew the job meant changing adult diapers and cleaning up after people, but she said she was ready for it. For his part, Willie Wei had an advantage many other students lacked: he studied German as an undergraduate before dropping out of a journalism master’s degree programme in Beijing. He was hired by a large care provider for disabled people in Saxony on a regular employee contract, rather than an apprentice wage, with 32 days of paid leave and what he said was one of the better salaries in the sector. “Things are falling into place, step by step,” he said, revealing his plan to apply for German citizenship once he qualifies. Even so, looking back on his journey through the Ausbildung system, Wei said he would have preferred to have taken an academic path through a university – a route that he said he still may consider in the future.

title: Study that argued China’s solar policy hurt birds may have miscounted 2 billion egrets
description: Critics claim report in top US journal lacked quality control and used data suggesting one park had more than the entire global population.
content: A study in one of the world’s top scientific journals that concluded China’s policy-driven solar energy expansion was harming bird diversity has come under fire after allegations emerged that the analysis may have used observations of 2.1 billion little egrets in a single park – more than the entire global population of the species. It also brought up heated conversations on social media about negative narratives surrounding China’s green energy sector. The study in question – by researchers in China, Vietnam and the United States – published in Science magazine, a leading US peer-reviewed journal, on August 20. It compared the strength of China’s solar policy against changes in bird diversity from 2014 to 2023. The data used to plug into a bird diversity index was taken from the China Birdwatching Record Centre, the largest citizen-science platform for bird observations in the country. Late last month, a social media post from the China Ornithological Society warned of potential errors in the centre’s records, which it said may have influenced the paper’s conclusions. It pointed to a logged observation in 2015 of 2.1 billion little egrets in a wetland, and another in 2022 of 1.3 billion red-billed blue magpies in a park, both in Guangdong province. While there is no exact census for these species, historical estimates show that those numbers far exceed their entire global populations. A 2023 Wetlands International estimate placed the global little egret population at up to around 3 million. The society said that despite the data clearly exceeding “reasonable limits”, it was still included, pointing to a table in the Science paper where bird counts for certain subcategories – such as total resident birds – exceeded 3 billion. “This paper provides no information on birdwatching data quality control, making it impossible to accurately assess the reasonableness of the data used for analysis,” the society wrote, noting that checking for errors was required when using citizen science data. The society and others across Chinese social media have also criticised the methodology used in the study to quantify the strength of solar policy and diversity, including their use of a specific bird diversity index. “We believe that this paper has flaws in data usage and statistical bias, and cannot support the conclusion that China’s photovoltaic expansion policy has reduced bird diversity,” the society wrote. Meagan Phelan, the communications director for Science, said that “potential concerns related to this paper have reached our attention”. “We are evaluating them following our normal processes. We will reach the authors. If any adjustments are required, we will certainly make them,” Phelan said on August 27. The South China Morning Post has reached out to the China- and US-based corresponding authors of the study, as well as the China Birdwatching Record Centre, for comment. In the Science paper, researchers concluded that without meticulous spatial planning, policy-driven solar expansion can compromise bird diversity, including through a loss of breeding and foraging grounds. They argued that future solar development needed to be accompanied by stricter safeguards, particularly in non-desert and more economically developed regions, where they found bird diversity loss was more pronounced. In one e-letter – scholarly commentary submitted by scientists for Science papers – a researcher from Lund University in Sweden said the study’s design showed the impacts of county-level solar policies, but fell short of proving that physical solar development directly caused the observed bird changes. In another letter, researchers from institutes in mainland China and Hong Kong said the paper provided evidence that solar expansion reduced bird diversity, but they noted that translating this finding into policy required further evaluation. This included capturing more dimensions of diversity other than birds, accounting for system-wide effects beyond the local study sites and evaluating trade-offs within a broader social cost-benefit framework. The China Ornithological Society said that birdwatching data was increasingly being used to explore the impacts of environmental change on biodiversity. “However, we have also noticed that some academic papers, including this one, use birdwatching data in a less than scientifically sound manner, ignoring the limitations of this type of data and failing to conduct rigorous data quality control and preprocessing, resulting in flawed results and conclusions,” they wrote. The society said that while it encouraged researchers to use birdwatching data, they needed to understand the characteristics and applicability of such data, analyse and quality-check the data, and cross-validate with other sources.

title: World’s most powerful lightning-chasing satellite joins China-Nepal flood relief efforts
description: The Fengyun-4C’s storm-tracking abilities could provide vital early warnings about extreme weather events during the rescue operation.
content: China is using the world’s most powerful geostationary weather satellite to track severe thunderstorms over Nepal and deliver real-time intelligence as the two countries continue search and rescue operations following last month’s devastating glacier collapse. The Fengyun‑4C satellite – launched last December and now positioned 36,000km (22,000 miles) above the equator – carries a Lightning Mapping Imager (LMI) that captures 500 frames per second, sifting through 30 gigabits of data every second to pinpoint individual lightning strokes. That processing power, engineers say, is equivalent to playing 30 high-definition films a second and spotting every traffic light in each one. In the hours after the glacier disaster struck on August 26, Beijing set up a cross-border emergency monitoring observation mechanism, according to state news agency Xinhua. At the core of that response is the LMI’s continuous animation, which gives meteorologists a sharp, frame‑by‑frame view of lightning activity inside severe storms. Combined with the Fengyun‑4C series’ cloud animations, convective initiation data, rainfall estimates and precipitation measurements from the Fengyun‑3G satellite, the system allows forecasters to track regional rainfall and weather changes in real time. As the most obvious sign of extreme weather, lightning can reveal where storms are intensifying, how fast they are moving and when they might unleash flash floods, landslides or destructive winds. By tracking every bolt, forecasters can issue earlier, more precise warnings, which is especially critical during disaster relief when unstable weather can endanger rescue teams and already vulnerable communities. China’s National Satellite Meteorological Centre has also created a dedicated early warning channel for Nepal, feeding rapid‑scan imagery and lightning information directly to local authorities. The frequent updates and high spatial detail made the early detection of an intensifying storm possible, giving disaster managers a clearer picture of where the next flood, landslide or thunderstorm might strike, Xinhua reported. Fengyun‑4C is the newest member of China’s second‑generation geostationary weather fleet, with key technical capabilities two to three times better than its predecessor, the Fengyun‑4B, according to Xinhua. The two satellites now work in tandem, providing minute‑level rapid scanning, hyperspectral atmospheric sounding and round‑the‑clock lightning surveillance across the full Earth disk under their coverage area. They are able to monitor roughly one‑third of the planet’s surface and are currently watching over the whole Asia-Pacific region, including the disaster zone. Fengyun‑4C also carries extreme‑ultraviolet imagers and X‑EUV flux monitors that can detect solar flares and other space weather events before they reach the Earth, adding an extra layer of protection for the communication and navigation systems that provide vital support for disaster relief operations. The disaster on the border between China and Nepal nearly two weeks ago has killed at least 1,280 people and left more than 5,500 missing.

title: My Take | Why China’s shrinking population may be a blessing, not a curse
description: Research co-authored by Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu finds labour shortages can spur, rather than slow down, productivity and growth.
content: There is little in common between Daron Acemoglu and Xi Jinping. As a strong advocate of the Western model of liberal democracy, Acemoglu, co-recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics, may be considered the ideological opposite of the Chinese president. But on a crucial point about China’s future, the two may, strangely, be on the same page: an across-the-board introduction of cutting-edge technology may enhance productivity and maintain economic growth. It may counteract the negative impact of drastic population decline in the decades ahead. While that may be an emerging consensus among economists and other social scientists, it still runs counter to the popular narrative that a rapidly greying China is doomed. The official figures released in January, for example, set off alarmism. China’s population fell by 3.39 million last year to just over 1.4 billion – a fourth consecutive decline and the steepest so far. Births dropped by 17 per cent to 7.92 million, the lowest since records began in 1949. Roughly 323 million Chinese, close to a quarter of the population, are now over 60. The reaction was swift and familiar: China will grow old before it grows rich, its workforce will hollow out, its pension system will buckle, its ascent will end. Some concerns are warranted. If 2.1 children per woman is the population replacement rate, then those countries with the lowest birth rates – China at 0.63, Japan at 0.6, and South Korea at 0.46 – are projected by 2050 to experience population declines of 20-30 per cent relative to 2023; their share of the population aged 65 and over to reach 30-40 per cent; and older workers (aged 45 and over) to comprise 60 per cent of the labour force. But that’s not the whole story. In fact, much of it is missing, and the alarm has outrun the analysis. “What if the historical evidence tells us that collapsing birth rates, paradoxically, are good for the economy,” economist Joeri Schasfoort asks in his YouTube channel, “because they force companies to innovate?” He was referring to a groundbreaking paper, “Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy”, which was published in July by the National Bureau of Economic Research in the United States and has attracted widespread interest in academic and policymaking circles. The four economists – Acemoglu, David Autor, Keelan Beirne and Andrew Scott – studied seven decades of demographic change across more than 100 countries and 722 American local labour markets. They find that countries where birth rates fell earlier and further did not grow more slowly. Rather, they grew faster per head, and total output did not decline. Something is compensating for the missing hands. The authors argue that it’s technology “Contrary to the widespread expectation that these trends hamper economic growth, we find lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult across countries and higher wage growth across US commuting zones, with no negative impact on aggregate GDP or earnings,” they wrote. They found that these patterns could not be explained by educational upgrading and other likely factors. Rather, they reflected “the endogenous, labour-saving response of technology to the scarcity of younger workers”. The size of the effect is striking. A country with a birth rate one percentage point lower in 1950 saw income per working-age adult roughly a quarter higher 50 years later, or about half a percentage point (0.46 per cent) of additional growth every year, compounding across two generations. The same pattern appears in American regions, measured through wages. There is an obvious mathematical objection: the same output divided among fewer workers naturally produces a higher figure per worker. But the study finds no meaningful decline in total output either. Something is compensating for the missing hands. The authors argue that it’s technology. When young workers become scarce and expensive, employers buy machines. Economies with falling birth rates register faster productivity growth, heavier investment in equipment, a shift of employment from labour-intensive industries towards research-intensive ones, and more patenting in automation. The productivity gains are large enough to offset the lost labour entirely. The most persuasive test uses the second world war. Military casualties fell overwhelmingly on young men; civilian casualties fell across all ages. Fifty years later, countries that lost population to civilian deaths were poorer per head. Those that lost young men were measurably richer. It is not population loss that damages an economy, but the wrong kind of it. As the economists wrote: “Exploiting cross-country variation in WWII military and civilian deaths, we find that declines in younger population, rather than population size per se, drive our results [of productivity and growth].” China’s record is consistent with this. It does not have a labour shortage; rather the opposite. Youth unemployment reached 17.9 per cent in July as a record 12.7 million graduates entered the market. That is an argument for patience rather than panic: the cohorts that will genuinely be scarce are yet to come. Its factories installed 295,000 industrial robots in 2024 – 54 per cent of the global total – bringing the operational stock past two million units, the largest anywhere. Robot density rose 17 per cent in a single year, and Chinese manufacturers outsold foreign suppliers at home for the first time. That’s 166 robots per 10,000 employees, according to China’s statistics bureau. Robotics, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing sit at the centre of the 15th five-year plan. The economy grew by 5 per cent last year on a record trade surplus. None of these neglect genuine problems. The state pension fund for urban workers may be exhausted by the middle of the next decade. In 2023, 11 of 31 provinces were running deficits. But that is a question of who pays, not whether the wealth exists. If output holds steady while the workforce shrinks, the resources are there. Moving them from prosperous coastal provinces to depleted industrial ones is a political task, not a demographic one. The researchers themselves are cautious. The decline in China, they note, will be faster and larger than anything in their data, and their evidence for the technological mechanism is indirect. Or, as Schasfoort has observed, their findings describe the past and may not predict the future. However, that caution cuts both ways. The pessimistic case rests entirely on projections. The optimistic case rests on what has actually occurred across 70 years and most of the world. China now contemplates spending an estimated 180 billion yuan (US$26.76 billion) this year alone to lift the birth rate – subsidies, free preschool, funded fertility treatment. Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore have all tried variations of this, with more generous provisions and greater personal freedom. All have failed. The focus should be on preparing for a smaller, older, more automated workforce than trying to get women to have more babies when most other socio-economic factors cause them to have fewer or no children. Demography is not destiny. Beijing should focus on fighting the right war – advancing technology on all fronts.

title: Which overseas property markets will be the winners and losers if Fed raises US rates?
description: Fed chairman’s focus on inflation at meeting last month has heightened expectations of monetary tightening.
content: Comments by US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at its annual economic policy symposium in Jackson Hole last month have reinforced expectations of an impending interest rate rise in the world’s largest economy, which would have significant impacts on assets and investors around the world. While the Fed kept its target rate in the range of 3.5 to 3.75 per cent at its meeting in July, Warsh’s comments last month about it having work to do in controlling inflation have heightened expectations of monetary tightening. In the wake of Warsh’s comments, analysts said several property markets were more sensitive to higher interest rates in the United States and some stood to benefit. Hong Kong With the local currency pegged to the US dollar in a trading band of HK$7.75 to HK$7.85, property agents said any Fed movement would be mirrored by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), the city’s de facto central bank. “The HKMA’s base rate tracks the Fed’s moves and borrowing costs linked to Hibor [the Hong Kong interbank offered rate] follow suit,” said Pamela Ambler, head of Asia-Pacific investor intelligence at consultancy JLL. “With Hong Kong’s debt costs rising in contrast to China’s … that makes Hong Kong less attractive to southbound capital from mainland China.” Based on the frequency of pinyin surnames in purchase records, US-based investment bank JPMorgan Chase has estimated that mainland buyers have, in recent times, accounted for 29 per cent of home sales volumes in Hong Kong and 37 per cent of their value. And in the second quarter of this year, mainland-based investors were the second-largest non-local buyers of commercial property assets in the city, with purchases worth HK$1.23 billion (US$157 million), behind Singapore-based investors’ HK$3.37 billion, according to Colliers. Kingston Lai, the founder and CEO of Hong Kong-headquartered Asia Bankers Club, a direct investor sales company, said: “Markets that have leaned most heavily on cheap dollar liquidity will feel it first, and Hong Kong is very much in that camp, given the peg. “Any Fed hike flows almost mechanically into Hibor, so mortgage costs and cap rates here move in near lockstep with Washington, not with local fundamentals.” Australia, Canada, the UK and New Zealand Lai said other highly leveraged residential property markets, such as Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and New Zealand, where mortgages were mostly variable rate or reset on short cycles, also transmitted Fed moves to household balance sheets faster than in fixed-rate markets like the US. Although Australia and Canada have barriers that restrict foreign investment in residential property, Juwai IQI, a property portal with 7 million listings across 111 countries, said they were among the 10 markets that received the most inquiries from potential buyers from mainland China in the first half of the year. Thailand, Malaysia and Greece For investors who remained keen on buying overseas properties, there were several markets that remained a good bet, analysts added. “International buyers seeking second homes and holiday properties are zeroing in on Thailand,” said Kashif Ansari, Juwai IQI’s co-founder and group CEO. “Buyers seeking less expensive secondary school education for their children and a route to a good university education are looking at Malaysia.” Meanwhile, those seeking golden visas, which could pave the way for a long-term residency in Europe, were focused on Greece, Ansari added. Singapore Ambler said another option was Singapore – particularly its commercial real estate. “Singapore debt costs are influenced more by money market liquidity and global funding conditions than by central bank policies,” she said. “The MAS [Monetary Authority of Singapore] manages the Singapore dollar against a trade-weighted basket of currencies. A stronger Singapore dollar can help offset imported inflation, reducing the need for sharply higher domestic interest rates. This is one reason Singapore’s rate cycle may diverge somewhat from the Fed’s.” Japan Japan was also an option, she said, with its interest rates remaining among the lowest compared with other developed markets. “Japan’s fundamentals across sectors remain strong, on top of accommodative financing,” Ambler said. “Both domestic and cross-border investors have viewed Japan as a relatively stable yield market. Yen depreciation has made Japanese assets cheaper in foreign currency terms for overseas investors. The strong urbanisation trend continues, making Tokyo one of the most liquid office markets.” Lai said the Bank of Japan also “tends to move on its own path, separate from the Fed, so financing there is still comparatively cheap, and the weak yen gives buyers using [US] dollars or Hong Kong dollars real purchasing power”. The US Ansari said the US property market could also get a boost from international buyers despite higher interest rates. “We think the result will be lower home prices in the US,” he said. “That will create buying opportunities for cashed-up offshore buyers. That’s why we expect foreign buyer interest in US property to rebound and climb steadily over the next four to 18 months.” Lai said that if US interest rates did rise, investors flush with cash would have a good opportunity to snap up assets at lower prices. “When rates go up, it costs more to borrow, so fewer investors are buying, and that puts downward pressure on price in the markets that are more sensitive to rates,” he said. “And that is exactly when cash buyers have the most negotiating power, because they are not competing against people who need financing.”

title: Indonesia’s Anak Krakatoa volcano erupts, disrupting flights at 6 airports
description: The suspension of operations at the airports affected 209 flights and more than 22,000 passengers.
content: Indonesia halted operations at its main international airport outside Jakarta on Sunday after ash spewed from the Anak Krakatoa volcano more than 150km (93 miles) away, impacting thousands of passengers. Mount Anak Krakatoa erupted on Saturday, producing a fountain of lava and booming sounds that could be heard up to a few hundred kilometres away, the geology agency said in a statement. Two new eruptions were recorded on Sunday, the volcanology agency warned. Ash from the volcano was detected in the airspace surrounding Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, prompting authorities to initially suspend operations from 1.30am on Sunday to 5.30am. The suspension was extended three times, with the latest ending at 5.30pm on Sunday “due to increased eruptive activity”, the airport said in a social media post. Operations have been suspended at six airports including the Hussein Sastranegara airport in Bandung and Radin Inten II airport near Bandar Lampung on Sumatra, the country’s Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said. Several airports in cities, including Semarang and Surabaya, have been prepared as “alternatives for landing”, Dudy added. The disruption left some passengers scrambling to find alternative flights. Henny Yensan, 44, who had hoped to go back to her hometown with her mother, said “everybody was disappointed”. “No one flew into a rage, because after all, this is due to natural disaster,” the businesswoman, who had to reschedule her flight to Tuesday, said on Sunday. Samuel Guiberteau, a Danone executive on a business trip to Lombok since Friday, said by phone “nothing is certain for the moment”, as he searched for alternative flights back to the capital. More than 22,000 passengers have been affected by the suspension, the transport ministry said, adding that 209 flights were affected, in particular those to and from Singapore. Other affected international routes included Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. At least 16 domestic flights to and from Bali were also cancelled, local airport authorities said. Anak Krakatoa, which means Child of Krakatoa, sits in a strait that separates the islands of Java and Sumatra. Ships passing through the strait were asked to increase vigilance for possible disruption to navigation safety due to volcanic activities. The vessels are prohibited from approaching the exclusion zone of 3km radius from the volcano, local port authorities said in a statement. The volcano has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera that formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. That disaster was one of the deadliest and most destructive in history with an estimated 35,000 people killed. Geology agency head Lana Saria said “seismic activity indicates the movement or release of volcanic fluids within the volcanic system”. “However, the timing, magnitude and nature of the next eruption cannot be precisely predicted,” Lana added. Lana warned against approaching Anak Krakatoa, saying materials ejected from the volcano could endanger those within the exclusion zone. She said the most recent series of eruptions does not have the potential to trigger a tsunami at this time. A 2018 tsunami, triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatoa, killed 429 people and left thousands displaced. Indonesia, a Southeast Asian archipelago nation, sits on the “Pacific Ring of Fire”, where the meeting of continental plates causes high volcanic and seismic activity.

title: 5-year plan to boost livelihoods, policy address to set out concrete measures: John Lee
description: After two months of public consultation, city leader says five-year plan will focus on long-term well-being, policy address on immediate improvements.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has pledged to improve residents’ livelihoods through long-term strategies in the city’s first five-year plan, with concrete measures to be set out in the coming policy address. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Sunday that the administration would continue to uphold its people-oriented governance philosophy, focus on residents’ needs and push Hong Kong forward. Lee will unveil Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and deliver the annual policy address on September 16. Lee said the arrangement would help the public understand how the two documents complemented each other. “Hong Kong’s first five-year plan will enhance residents’ livelihoods and well-being through long-term development strategies. Meanwhile, the policy address will annually roll out concrete improvement measures on housing, livelihoods, medical care and other areas,” he said in a Facebook video. Lee added that the government had consulted the public on the two documents over the past two months. “We will consolidate views and incorporate them into our planning and policies to promote sustainable economic development, improve livelihoods, and join hands to create new opportunities in Hong Kong,” he said. The video on Lee’s social media page also featured interviews with residents, who shared how various government initiatives had helped their families. A subdivided flat tenant, surnamed Ng, who has used services at a community living room project, said the centre had helped her son, who has special education needs, improve his language skills and boost his confidence. According to the video, since the scheme launched in 2023, the city’s 16 community living rooms have served about 9,000 subdivided flat households and recorded close to 2.2 million visits. A working parent surnamed Cheung said the government’s School-based After-school Care Service Scheme had helped his daughter revise and take part in different extracurricular activities over the summer. The scheme was expanded after the government lifted the service quota cap in the 2025 policy address. In the 2025-26 academic year, schools taking part offered more than 10,000 places to families. A representative of ethnic minority care teams said members would proactively reach out to such families to share the latest government information and understand their needs. The video noted that the city had 12 ethnic minority care teams. They had contacted about 18,000 ethnic minority households and conducted around 10,000 family visits. Another resident shared how she had developed a habit of regular exercise and managed her high blood pressure through health initiatives. More than 260,000 residents have taken part in the Chronic Disease Co-care Scheme, which provides convenient screening services for eligible residents.
