Sze Lai-shan, deputy director of the Society for Community Organisation, said the coming policy address and five-year plan should prioritise poverty alleviation and protect employment opportunities for low-income residents. “The government focuses on rewarding those who are unemployed and subsequently find a job. It should also explore ways to help jobseekers,” she said. Sze suggested subsidising jobseekers and relaxing the asset limits for social security recipients to encourage the underprivileged to save. She also urged the government to continue expanding existing social services, such as widening the network and extending the operating hours of the School-based After-school Care Service Scheme to enable more parents to take up employment. Sze added that the administration could expand the community living room network by using communal centres or schools, while care teams should focus on identifying high-risk households, such as low-income seniors with serious illnesses and people recovering from mental illness. On Saturday, Lee said the two documents would promote steady economic development, attract more global firms to the Hong Kong park of a cross-border innovation and technology hub, and build the city into an international tertiary education hub.

title: Hong Kong open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease: labour chief
description: Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui also says revamped heat warning system would have triggered stronger alerts on two exceptionally hot days in August.
content: Hong Kong authorities are open to classifying heatstroke as an occupational disease, the city’s labour chief has said, acknowledging that the recently revamped heat warning system would have triggered stronger alerts on two exceptionally hot days last month. Commissioner for Labour Sam Hui Chark-shum said retrospective modelling showed the revised system would have issued a black warning on August 8 and a red alert on August 9, when the Observatory recorded 36.9 degrees Celsius (98.4 Fahrenheit) at its headquarters – the highest temperature since records began in 1884. “If we had applied the revamped Heat Stress at Work Warning system, we would have issued a red warning on August 9 and even a black warning on August 8,” Hui told a television programme on Sunday. The heat stress warning system has three levels – amber, red and black – and advises employers on rest arrangements for outdoor workers and those in indoor environments without air conditioning. Under the previous mechanism, only an amber warning was issued on August 9, prompting criticism from lawmakers, unions and meteorologists that the system failed to reflect the severity of the heat faced by outdoor workers. Amber signals significant heat stress and advises employers to arrange additional rest periods, while black is the highest warning level, under which workers performing heavy or very heavy labour should suspend work. The Labour Department subsequently revised the mechanism on August 28 by adding two triggers intended to make it more sensitive to extreme temperatures and strong solar radiation. Hui said authorities would continue studying the performance of the revamped system and consider whether further adjustments were needed before the next hot season. The labour chief added that the department was open to including heatstroke in the city’s list of prescribed occupational diseases, a move long demanded by unions seeking to make it easier for affected workers to claim compensation. “We have an open attitude towards the proposal, but there is work that needs to be done in between,” he said. “We have not reached a conclusion, but we believe this is an area worth studying.” Hui said heatstroke and heat exhaustion suffered during employment could already qualify for compensation as work injuries under existing legislation. But he acknowledged workers could face difficulties proving that their condition was caused by their job rather than underlying health problems, as classifying an illness as occupational requires an established medical link with a particular working environment or pattern. The department was exploring whether medical and pathological information from confirmed work-related heatstroke cases could be compiled as a reference database for healthcare professionals assessing future claims, he added. “If these methods can make the process faster and improve its accuracy, I think they may help workers in need,” Hui said, adding that there was no timetable for the proposal. Hui stressed that the issuance of a higher heat stress warning did not automatically require an entire construction site to suspend operations. Employers could maintain work by conducting risk assessments in advance and adopting measures such as providing cooling stations, ventilated clothing, fans, shade and rescheduling physically demanding work away from the hottest hours, he said. The department previously estimated that the revised mechanism could produce red warnings on four to seven days annually and black alerts on one or two days. Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said issuing red and black warnings more frequently would not necessarily result in work suspensions because the guidelines were not legally binding. “We believe there should be a mandatory rest mechanism when a red warning is issued and a work suspension mechanism when the warning turns black,” he said. Chau said construction work involved interdependent processes, meaning contractors that suspended operations voluntarily could delay other trades and be held responsible for idle labour costs or project delays without being entitled to an extension. “No one will stop workers from taking a rest, but they are still required to complete the day’s work,” he said. “The pressure is therefore shifted entirely on to workers, which is extremely undesirable.” He called on the government to give the heat warning system and its accompanying guidelines legal force, allowing contractors to suspend work and seek reasonable extensions without facing penalties. “This would ease the pressure faced by both workers and contractors and give workers a real opportunity to be protected,” he said.

title: Iran attacks naval drone near Hormuz after US strikes 3 oil tankers
description: The latest round of clashes, which began with US raids last week, comes amid a deadlock in the six-month war.
content: Iran said on Sunday that its forces attacked a US naval drone trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz, hours after targeting ships in retaliation for American strikes on three oil tankers. The latest round of clashes, which began with US raids last week, comes amid a deadlock in their six-month war. Iran has maintained its stranglehold on the strategic Strait of Hormuz while Washington continues a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Washington is also seeking to choke Iran’s economy, rolling out sanctions on entities with financial links to the Islamic Republic in a bid to force it into submission. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said on Sunday it “attacked an American military unmanned surface vessel” attempting to enter the strait, according to a statement carried by state television. Hours earlier, the IRGC said its naval forces “targeted three oil tankers on the unauthorised route of the Strait of Hormuz and three vessels affiliated with the child-killing America in other areas”. It warned ships not to attempt to transit by unapproved routes. On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the region, said it struck tankers linked to the Iranian Guards, accusing the most powerful arm of the Iranian military of unsuccessfully firing at American warships. “Following Iran’s failed attacks, CENTCOM permanently disabled the IRGC crude oil carriers M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask,” it said. “American forces also completely destroyed the unladen crude oil carrier M/T Kylo … in the Gulf of Oman, striking the vessel in multiple critical locations to render it inoperable after the crew was directed to abandon ship.” Video posted by CENTCOM showed large fireballs and billowing flames after projectiles slammed into the ships. The three vessels were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies”, it said. The Guards, meanwhile, claimed the two American warships they targeted had been “forced to retreat” after “suffering damage”, but CENTCOM said those ships successfully evaded Iranian attacks. CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper said after the operation: “If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost – taking out three of yours.” The Iranian foreign ministry hit out at Washington over the strikes on oil tankers, calling them “illegal and aggressive actions”. A correspondent for Iranian state television in Jask in the southern province of Hormozgan said one of the tankers was empty and the second was carrying oil. The crews were transported to shore on lifeboats. Another state television correspondent on Kharg Island said the attack there caused no casualties. Iran’s Khatam-al Anbiya central military command warned that if the US continued its attacks, then Tehran’s retaliation against US warships would be “more severe than before, and there is a possibility of their expansion”. The administration of US President Donald Trump has tried to downplay the significance of the six-month conflict, which has proven increasingly unpopular at home as the midterm election nears. US Vice-President J.D. Vance went so far as to say that he “wouldn’t call it a war”. Trump reiterated that view on Friday, calling the war “small potatoes” for Washington. Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned this week that the Islamic Republic had adopted a “new strategy” against Washington that “will shatter your foundations”. The US has been trying to step up pressure on Tehran in a bid to wrestle control of the Hormuz Strait, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed. A fragile ceasefire between the two sides collapsed in July after attacks on commercial ships in the strategic waterway. Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly threatened to claim sovereignty over the strait, even posting a map showing it as “new US territory”. Vance has insisted the US will not reopen talks with Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping in Hormuz.

title: Fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than double in first half of 2026
description: From ignoring lights to riding side by side, police flag common cycling offences driving rise in fatal accidents.
content: Fatal cycling accidents in Hong Kong more than doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with a year earlier, with nine deaths recorded, as police point to cyclists ignoring traffic signals and road signs. Overall, 59 fatal traffic accidents were recorded in the first six months of the year, killing 63 people, up more than 40 per cent from a year earlier. Fatal cases involving bicycles surged 125 per cent, accounting for nine of those deaths. “Most cyclists tend to ignore traffic signals and road signs, and ride without carefully observing surrounding road conditions,” a police spokesman said. “Combined with dangerous behaviours such as riding on the pavement, illegally carrying passengers and riding side by side, this largely increases the risk of accidents.” In response, the New Territories North police region launched a cycling safety campaign on August 1, combining street promotions, community lectures, interactive games and social media outreach to target high-risk behaviours and raise awareness of related laws and road safety. Officers then carried out a targeted enforcement operation on Friday and Saturday, after the education phase, issuing nine warnings and 159 summonses over the two days. “Bicycles have become a common mode of transport for many residents, but some riders showed weak awareness of road safety, with various offences risking serious accidents at any time,” the spokesman said. Police said they would continue the two-pronged strategy of education and enforcement, urging cyclists to strictly follow the Road Traffic Ordinance, stay alert to signals and road conditions, switch on front white and rear red lights at night, and avoid running red lights or riding against traffic.

title: Chinese military university urged to revise AI course to ‘educate for war’
description: Proposal sees mapping out defence scenarios as better preparation for future officers involved in intelligent warfare.
content: China’s military researchers have proposed a redesigned “AI principles and practice course” for graduate students with “educating for war” at its centre, embedding combat scenarios to better prepare future officers for intelligent warfare. Researchers from the National University of Defence Technology’s College of Intelligence Science and Technology outlined their proposal in the July issue of the journal Defence Industry Conversion in China. The initiative comes as China seeks to cultivate more military personnel with the technical skills to use artificial intelligence (AI) in future warfare. As global militaries explore the use of AI in planning, training and combat, the technology is also changing what the troops need to learn, with China aiming to train forces capable of applying emerging technologies to armed operations. The researchers said case studies in the existing AI course lacked sufficient “military flavour” and needed to be redesigned to better serve the practical needs of “educating for war”. The university introduced “Principles and Practice of Artificial Intelligence” as a tailored course for non-AI science and engineering graduate students in its 2022 autumn semester. It was intended to address differences in students’ AI backgrounds and help them find ways to combine the emerging technology with their areas of study, the researchers said. They propose building the course around a common uncrewed warfare scenario and using military operations as a thread to connect different AI concepts. Course topics would be mapped onto different stages of the military decision-making and targeting process: from observing and assessing a situation to making decisions and taking action, as well as finding, locating and tracking targets, engaging them and assessing the results. For example, a unit about reinforcement learning, in which an AI system learns through trial and error, could be taught through combat decision-making and war gaming, they said. Meanwhile, uncertainty reasoning, in which an AI system makes decisions with incomplete or unreliable information, could be illustrated through fault diagnosis in uncrewed systems and border intrusion warnings. The curriculum redesign could “enable students to gain a deeper understanding of the practical applications of course content in military settings and internalise theoretical methods as ‘intelligent thinking’ for solving specific problems in military scenarios”, the team wrote. One proposed exercise would ask students to train several simulated drones to work together to surround a high-value target. This would allow them to study how AI systems can coordinate their actions, communicate and make decisions when working as a group. The researchers said practical exercises should combine classroom theory with hands-on work, rather than simply asking students to run existing code. They proposed giving out clearly defined problems, data sets, algorithms and step-by-step tasks, along with questions that could challenge students to explore more advanced applications. The team has also developed an online simulation platform where students can design maps and scenarios, configure forces and missions, and train AI agents through mock combat exercises to build their understanding of reinforcement learning. The platform supports contests in which AI agents trained by different student teams compete against one another. The National University of Defence Technology is one of China’s leading institutions for military science and technology education. It is directly overseen by the Central Military Commission, the highest command body. The US Commerce Department added the university to its restricted trade list in 2015, alleging the use of American technology in supercomputers linked to nuclear explosive activities. Authors of the July paper also explicitly outline boundaries, emphasising that every exercise must reinforce a key principle – that AI serves strictly as a decision-support tool, while final command authority remains entirely human. They proposed debates on the “ethical and legal boundaries of autonomous weapons systems” to foster a “sense of responsibility”, while highlighting the weaknesses of AI – including data bias, environmental sensitivity and vulnerability to adversarial attacks.

title: Why artists are painting bird murals along Hong Kong’s trails
description: The Flock Project is spread across Lantau Island’s abandoned village homes and other hidden spots.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
When artist Dominic Johnson-Hill saw a blank wall in his garden, he wanted to add a splash of Hong Kong nature. So in 2024, he teamed up with British bird muralist Rob Aspire to paint a red-billed blue magpie on his wall.
Now, they have painted Hong Kong’s birds on many abandoned village homes and other hidden spots on Lantau Island. Their murals are known as the Flock Project. It has even inspired hikers to go on scavenger hunts looking for the paintings of birds.
“You’re making use of these abandoned buildings ... turning them into something that celebrates local wildlife,” said Johnson-Hill, 54.
“It’s given me an incredible purpose: celebrating all of these birds while exploring and learning about Hong Kong’s wildlife.”
Inspired by the 17 years he spent making art in mainland China, Johnson-Hill creates his work in lucky sets of eight. This is why the magpie was just the start.
“I told my wife, ‘I need to do another seven birds to finish the set,’” he explained.
To find his subjects, Johnson-Hill asked a local bird expert Paul Aston to make a list of the region’s most striking species.
According to Johnson-Hill, about 80 bird species are residents of Lantau Island. Hong Kong has more than 580 bird species. The city sits along the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, so it welcomes many migratory birds that are passing through.
“[Aston] told me these incredible stories about how most of the birds on Lantau just come and go,” Johnson-Hill said. “Some go to Africa, others to Myanmar and Vietnam. I love the fact that these birds are just so free ... They just move with the weather and the food.”
After finishing the first eight birds, he wanted to create his second series. So he raised about HK$22,000 through crowdfunding and selling T-shirts. The money allowed him to expand his project to other faraway parts of Lantau Island.
Last April, the project went viral when a hiking influencer mapped out a trail connecting the murals. Hikers began coming to Lantau for scavenger hunts, looking for the hidden art.
“Sometimes we’d have over 100 people following the route,” Johnson-Hill said. “It was wonderful because I started meeting all these lovely people.”
His third series is set to be finished in October, and he plans for his fourth series to be on Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and Lamma Island.
A post shared by Wang Tong Art | FLOCK Bird Murals HK (@wangtongart)
For Johnson-Hill, finding your passion is not about sticking to what you already know, but about trying what scares you most.
Public speaking terrified him as a kid, but he discovered his passion for it by challenging himself.
“Passions aren’t just things you naturally enjoy,” Johnson-Hill said. “Sometimes, they’re things you’re terrified of, hidden behind childhood anxieties. If you push through that fear, you find incredible skills.”
His creative journey began 20 years ago in Beijing. There, he opened a shop selling T-shirts featuring everyday Chinese objects. That leap of faith has shaped him into the artist he is today.
To him, true creativity is about being open to how the future might change.
“When you’re young, try as many things as you possibly can: be a barman, a waitress [or] a gardener. Enjoy the serendipity of life and take opportunities that don’t seem to make sense,” he said.
“If you want to go into the creative world, one of your greatest responsibilities is to go out, explore and enjoy life.”

content: Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s ex-husband lived an affluent lifestyle in mainland China allegedly funded by the model’s money and borrowed a car used to move equipment involved in her killing, a court has heard. The High Court heard on Monday that Alex Kwong Kong-chi used his former partner’s digital wallets to cover his expenses in Guangzhou while evading justice for his role in a HK$6.3 million theft case in 2015. The 31-year-old is standing trial alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, for allegedly murdering Choi on February 21, 2023. The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, is also contesting a charge of preventing the burial of the 28-year-old’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to the offence before the trial began last month. Herman Ng Deng-hao, Alex Kwong’s former business partner and friend, said in a written statement that the defendant appeared very wealthy while he was living across the border. He said Kwong used to stay at the luxurious Rosewood Guangzhou hotel and had a personal driver who would drive him around the province in either a Rolls-Royce saloon or Lexus seven-seater. But Ng noted that Kwong appeared to have used mobile payment apps authenticated under the abbreviated names “Fung” or “Tin-fung” whenever they met for meals. Ng, whose family was involved in property development in Guangzhou, said he first met Kwong at a gathering in September 2020. They later jointly invested in a real estate project, with Kwong contributing 3.5 million yuan (US$524,400) and earning a 10 per cent profit, the court heard. The witness said Kwong was forced to return to Hong Kong on June 10, 2022, after he told Choi that he had a girlfriend. According to Ng, the influencer was upset by her ex-husband “picking up girls” on the mainland while neglecting their two children in the city. He confirmed that Kwong had sought to borrow a car from him in January 2023 under the pretence that his own had a scheduled maintenance and that he needed one to drive his children to school. Ng later referred the defendant to his elder brother, who lent him a Toyota Alphard seven-seater. The defendants previously admitted that Kwong’s seven-seater car was never sent for repair in the lead-up to the model’s killing. Kwong Kau allegedly used the seven-seater car that his son borrowed to transport equipment specifically bought to dismantle Choi’s body to a 600 square foot rental flat in Tai Po’s Lung Mei village. Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains, including her head and legs, were discovered at the ground-floor flat on February 24, 2023. Senior government chemist Dr Tam Cheok-ning testified on Thursday that he found a cut mark on Choi’s remains that was consistent with the blade of one of two electric saws found in the flat. He also opined that the two plastic boxes found inside the premises were the same ones the defendants allegedly used to carry Choi’s body. In cross-examination on Monday, Kwong Kau’s lawyer Oliver Davies argued the box was “almost fully transparent” and that an observer could discern its contents from a distance. “It is not the kind of box that you would use to hide a body,” Davies said. Tam said he “did not consider” that possibility, but he agreed with the prosecution’s suggestion that the box’s contents would become much less clear if two stacked-up boxes were used and if they were seen from the side. The prosecution also called two school workers to testify about Choi’s failure to fetch her eight-year-old daughter on the day she was allegedly killed. Hui Siu-hung, then a senior executive officer at Malvern College Hong Kong, said Choi did not arrive to pick up her child at 3pm on February 21. She said the mother’s phone appeared to be turned off after she repeatedly tried to call her. Hui said she also failed to reach the girl’s paternal grandmother, Jenny Li Sui-heung, as she appeared to be talking to someone else on the phone at that time. College clerk Amy Yeung Wai-fun said Li eventually called back at 3.40pm and said she was caught in a traffic jam in Kwun Tong. The grandmother arrived to pick up the girl half an hour later, the court heard. The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

content: French President Emmanuel Macron promised on Monday that his government would announce a package of measures in response to weeks of street protests over a broad set of grievances, while acknowledging the risk of more unrest ahead. His prime minister, Sebastien Lecornu, is set to hold a news conference after a meeting with unions of high school students who want more resources ‌for the education sector and an overhaul of a university admissions process they say embeds inequalities. “I have … asked the government to respond to the legitimate demands that lie at the root of this social movement,” Macron told reporters in Marseille, where he travelled to inspect the damage from earlier protests. Macron repeated what Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said earlier, that more unrest is expected next weekend. The protests show little sign of easing after violence nine days ago engulfed dozens of cities, leading to fears the ⁠state had lost control of the streets. In response to the turmoil, the interior ministry deployed 70,000 police for Saturday’s protests, which unions called to denounce the ‌high cost of living and public services. The movement has grown far beyond initial student discontent, drawing in trade unions and “yellow vest” activists, known for their high-visibility jackets and mass protests against economic pressures including high fuel costs. Nunez said ‌the huge police presence prevented a repeat of violence seen earlier this month, but asked by BFM TV on ⁠Monday whether he expected further disturbances ⁠during protests planned for October 31, he replied: “Clearly, yes.” “Halloween evening is traditionally always a bit lively. We expect it to be complicated again,” he added. Nunez said 1,435 people were arrested ‌nationwide during Saturday’s protests and said police had also recorded a new phenomenon, with organised far-right gangs confronting far-left activists in several cities. “We knew there had been calls from numerous identity-based and nationalist movements ‌to ‌come out, officially, to defend businesses,” he said. “In a number of cities, such as Nice and Montpellier, these groups arrived in organised formations, mainly to ‌target the ultra-left movement.” The government sought to portray Saturday’s operation as evidence it had regained the upper hand, despite sporadic violence, especially in France’s three ⁠largest cities – Paris, Marseille and Lyon. “The state prevailed this weekend. The state was strong,” government spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told RTL radio. She said protesters had ⁠raised legitimate grievances that needed to be heard, but added that restoring calm was a prerequisite for meaningful negotiations. With his presidential mandate due to expire in April and public finances under severe strain, Macron has limited scope to defuse the crisis through the ‌costly concessions that helped quell previous waves ‌of unrest. Business leaders said the unrest was continuing to inflict heavy economic damage despite a calmer weekend. Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the CCI France network of chambers of commerce and industry, said many retailers had remained closed as a precaution after the violence of October 17, adding that sales had fallen by about 80 per cent. “We have shopkeepers who are tired and demoralised, and we are killing local commerce,” he told Radio Classique.

content: WuXi AppTec raised its full-year revenue guidance after its net profit surged 62.4 per cent in the first nine months of 2026, while revenue rose 38.6 per cent on strong demand for its drug development and manufacturing services. The Chinese pharmaceutical research services provider’s net profit reached 19.16 billion yuan (US$2.87 billion) for the nine months ended September 30, compared with 11.80 billion yuan a year earlier, a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange showed. Its revenue rose to 45.54 billion yuan from 32.86 billion yuan. The Shanghai-based company raised its full-year revenue forecast to 61 billion to 61.9 billion yuan, from 58.5 billion to 60.5 billion yuan previously projected, according to the filing. Revenue from continuing operations was now expected to grow 40 per cent to 42 per cent, compared with its previous forecast of 35 per cent to 39 per cent. Revenue from continuing operations rose 46.3 per cent to 45.54 billion yuan for the first nine months from one year earlier, while its backlog from continuing operations increased 36.4 per cent to 76.74 billion yuan during the same period. WuXi AppTec’s chemistry business, its largest segment, recorded year-on-year revenue growth of 51.5 per cent to 39.36 billion yuan in the first three quarters. Revenue from small-molecule drug development and manufacturing services rose 65.6 per cent to 23.58 billion yuan over the same period. Revenue from its testing business increased 32 per cent to 3.91 billion yuan year on year in the first three quarters this year, while its biology business grew 12.4 per cent to 2.19 billion yuan. WuXi AppTec said it had accelerated capacity planning to meet growing customer demand, including bringing a new site in Changzhou into operation ahead of schedule. It also raised its full-year adjusted free cash flow forecast to 14.5 billion to 15.5 billion yuan, from 13.5 billion to 14.5 billion yuan previously, while increasing its capital expenditure forecast to 8 billion to 8.5 billion yuan. The results come as the Chinese biotechnology firm faces scrutiny from Washington. The US Department of Defence added the company to its list of Chinese military companies in June, a designation the company challenged in court. A US federal court in August preliminarily barred enforcement of the designation, although broader US restrictions on dealings with Chinese biotechnology companies remain a potential risk. WuXi AppTec shares closed 1.2 per cent higher at HK$188.30 on Monday, before the release of its quarterly results.

content: Jordanian security forces arrested two brothers ‌and their brother-in-law after a shoot-out on Monday over a church attack that killed nine people, and the suspects appear to have no ties to other cells, senior government security officials said. “God willing, they only represent themselves,” Jordan’s Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah, said. Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East, and Friday’s attack on the Christian ⁠minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an “iron fist”. In a press conference, al-Maaytah and ‌Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism. “The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications ‌of any links between them and other cells,” al-Faraya added. Friday’s assault during a funeral at ⁠a Greek Orthodox ⁠church in the village of Hamoud, about 120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman, also wounded 34 others, alarming a Christian community. Witnesses ‌said gunmen opened fire for several minutes. The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. Reuters video footage showed ‌a building ‌pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate. Jordan’s Public Security Directorate ‌said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while hiding in an abandoned ⁠house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding ⁠them. No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects’ possession. There has been no claim of responsibility. “Terrorism has no place among ‌us,” the directorate said, adding that ‌the suspects had met their “just fate”. The Public Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups. Al-Faraya said the authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable any participants in the attack.

title: China’s next-generation KJ-3000 radar planes may have quietly entered production
description: China may have begun limited production of its next-generation KJ-3000 airborne early warning aircraft, with satellite imagery suggesting that three possible production examples were already parked at a factory as early as April, according to an imagery analyst. If brought into service, the aircraft could help the People’s Liberation Army to detect threats, track targets and coordinate air operations across the western Pacific, including during a potential conflict over Taiwan involving US and...
content: China may have begun limited production of its next-generation KJ-3000 airborne early warning aircraft, with satellite imagery suggesting that three possible production examples were already parked at a factory as early as April, according to an imagery analyst. If brought into service, the aircraft could help the People’s Liberation Army to detect threats, track targets and coordinate air operations across the western Pacific, including during a potential conflict over Taiwan involving US and allied forces. Satellite imagery captured on October 5 by US geospatial intelligence company Vantor showed four KJ-3000s at the Xian-Yanliang aviation complex in the country’s northwestern Shaanxi province, US defence media outlet TWZ reported last week. Three were parked near the Xian Aircraft Industrial Corporation (XAIC) factory and one prototype was parked at the neighbouring China Flight Test Establishment. Defence intelligence publisher Janes reported on May 15 that satellite imagery showed a fifth KJ-3000 airframe at Xian-Yanliang in April. An imagery analyst who requested anonymity said three of the five lacked the 78XX serial numbers carried by the two prototypes – the 7821 and 7822 – and could belong to an initial production batch. The three planes spotted at the factory appeared to have remained since April in an XAIC area normally used by aircraft awaiting delivery, rather than moving to the flight-test ramp, he said. The analyst questioned why China would need three additional prototypes when the KJ-3000 used the established Y-20B transport airframe. “They don’t need a tonne of prototypes when all they’re really testing are the systems as the airframe itself is mature,” he said. While prototype 7821 was absent from the October imagery, he said he had seen no evidence of KJ-3000s at operational PLA Air Force bases. The photographs therefore do not establish that deliveries have begun. Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist in Chinese military aviation, said factory-fresh aircraft usually remained at XAIC for months before delivery in batches, possibly while units prepared to receive them. Some could be awaiting additional systems, but the imagery could not establish why they had remained there. TWZ reported that J. Michael Dahm, a senior fellow at the US-based Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, believed serial production had started, but the media outlet cautioned that the imagery alone could not confirm this. The KJ-3000 could eventually replace China’s KJ-2000, a radar aircraft built on Russian-made Il-76 transports that was introduced around two decades ago. Only four KJ-2000s were produced, which TWZ attributed to a shortage of suitable airframes. The KJ-3000 instead uses the domestically produced Y-20B airframe and Chinese-made WS-20 engines, giving Beijing greater control over production and upgrades. But Rupprecht argued that the KJ-2000’s specialised strategic role, not Il-76 shortages, mainly explained why only four were built. China could have converted more Il-76s if needed, he said, but the large aircraft primarily served as command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance nodes, while smaller KJ-500s handled most tactical airborne early warning missions. He expected the KJ-3000 to serve as a similar node. For operations around Taiwan, further into the western Pacific and towards India, using the KJ-3000 would represent “a quantum leap in terms of being much more modern”, he said. Given the limited number possibly needed, he did not expect significant competition for production capacity with Y-20 transports and tankers. Janes reported in 2025 that markings on the prototype KJ-3000’s radar dome suggested two back-to-back antenna arrays, although its configuration and performance remain unconfirmed. A refuelling probe could extend its time in the air on operations. The Pentagon assessed in December 2025 that the aircraft would probably use digital radar with anti-jamming, passive-detection and target-identification capabilities. The KJ-3000’s potential military value extends beyond warning of approaching aircraft. In May 2025, Chinese state television reported that the Type 055 destroyer Lhasa had used data from an early warning aircraft to extend its detection range and engage targets without relying solely on the ship’s own radars. While the aircraft was not identified as a KJ-3000, the example illustrated how airborne sensors could extend naval strike capabilities. An April Mitchell Institute report, based on a war game of a hypothetical Taiwan conflict in 2035, identified KJ-3000s and KJ-500s as high-value targets because of their role in PLA long-range targeting. While the satellite imagery suggests KJ-3000 production may have begun, when the aircraft will enter operational service remains unclear.

content: US singer Chris ⁠Brown was spared an immediate prison sentence in Britain on Monday for attacking a producer with a tequila bottle in a London nightclub in 2023, with his fans cheering as the musician walked free from court. Brown, 37, was given an eight-month suspended sentence at London’s Southwark Crown Court ‌after he admitted a charge of affray over the attack on Abraham Diaw at the Tape nightclub in February 2023. Diaw was hit twice in the head with a bottle, which was then swung twice more at him in what prosecutors described as “a vicious and unprovoked attack”. The R&B star and his vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, pleaded guilty in July, having denied more serious charges of attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm and assault causing actual bodily harm. Judge Tony ⁠Baumgartner said: “This was serious, public violence. In your case, Brown, it involved the repeated ‌use ... of a bottle, including twice striking Diaw to his head.” Brown’s suspended sentence means he does not immediately go to prison unless he ‌commits another offence. Some of Brown’s fans queued outside court from around ⁠7am, about an ⁠hour before the building opened, and Brown thanked the judge before leaving the dock and nodding towards ‌his supporters in the public gallery. Brown, a two-time Grammy winner, was arrested in May 2025 having returned to Britain ‌for ‌the first time since the incident and was initially denied bail, throwing his ‌worldwide “Breezy Bowl XX” tour into doubt. But Brown was eventually released after promising to pay ⁠a £5 million (US$6.68 million) security fee, allowing the tour to go ahead. This court case is the ⁠latest involving Brown since he was charged with assaulting his then-partner Rihanna in 2009, with a photo of her bruised face making headlines around ‌the world. Prosecutor Heidi Stonecliffe ‌said Brown pleaded guilty to the 2009 assault of Rihanna and was sentenced to five years probation. He also admitted a 2013 assault on a fan he was accused of punching when he asked for a photograph.

content: A Singaporean woman pleaded guilty on Monday to conspiring with a friend and the friend’s boyfriend to abuse four-year-old Megan Khung, and helping to dispose of the child’s body after she died following months of abuse. Nouvelle Chua Ruoshi, 36, pleaded guilty to three charges, including conspiracy to commit child abuse, intentional disposal of a corpse and methamphetamine consumption, The Straits Times reported. Three further charges for conspiracy to commit child abuse will be considered when she is sentenced on November 13. During the court hearing, video clips showing Megan being abused, some filmed by Chua, were played in court. The judge warned that the footage was distressing and told those who wished to leave the courtroom could do so, CNA reported. Chua was arrested in July 2020 after Megan’s father reported concerns about his daughter’s whereabouts, according to the Singapore High Court’s written judgment in the cases against Megan’s mother, Foo Li Ping, and Foo’s then-boyfriend, Wong Shi Xiang. Megan endured 13 months of abuse before she died from a punch to the stomach in February 2020, the High Court judgment said. The couple were subsequently charged over their roles in the abuse and disposal of Megan’s body. Court documents showed that Megan was born to Foo and her then husband, Khung Wei-nan, on October 4, 2015. After their marriage broke down, Foo sent Megan to live with her maternal grandmother. Foo began a relationship with Wong in November 2018 and moved in with him in January 2019, while Megan continued living with her grandmother and stayed at the couple’s flat on some weekends. The abuse began during one of these stays in late February or early March 2019. Chua, who became close friends with Foo in 2019, also stayed at the flat with Megan. She witnessed and filmed some of the abuse, including incidents in which Megan was humiliated and physically mistreated. From January 2020, Foo and Wong increasingly deprived Megan of food. On February 21, 2020, after being starved throughout the day, Megan was punched in the stomach by Wong, causing her back to hit a wall with a loud thud. Chua arrived at the flat after midnight the following day and saw Megan lying on the bedroom floor, clutching her stomach and complaining of pain. Foo and Wong dismissed the child’s distress as attention-seeking, and Chua joined them in taking drugs in the living room. Several hours later, Megan was unresponsive. The three adults attempted to resuscitate her but did not call an ambulance. Foo feared that the abuse and their drug use would be discovered. A forensic pathologist with Singapore’s Health Sciences Authority said in October 2021 that possible causes of Megan’s death included septicaemia resulting from internal injuries, such as a ruptured intestine or abdominal bleeding, according to the High Court judgment. The three left Megan’s body in the flat while discussing how to dispose of it and conceal her death. On May 8, 2020, Chua accompanied Foo and Wong as they arranged to burn Megan’s body in a metal barrel. Wong later scattered the ashes at sea. Megan’s father reported her missing on July 20, 2020. Police brought the three suspects in for questioning, arresting Foo and Wong on July 23 and Chua the following day. Foo was sentenced to 19 years in prison in April 2025 for offences including child abuse, allowing the death of a child and disposing of a corpse. Wong was sentenced that month to 30 years in prison and 17 strokes of the cane for offences including culpable homicide, disposal of a corpse and drug-related offences. The case sparked public anger and renewed scrutiny of Singapore’s child protection system, with social media users expressing disbelief at the treatment of Megan and calling for stronger penalties for child abuse. “Cannot imagine a mother can be so cruel to her own daughter,” one user commented on social media. “May this be a strong message to everyone, especially those not prepared to be parents,” another said. In October 2025, a review panel convened by Singapore’s Ministry of Social and Family Development identified serious shortcomings across the agencies responsible for Megan’s welfare. That same month, Masagos Zulkifli, minister for social and family development of the city state, apologised for the lack of timely intervention by government agencies in Megan’s case. “As the lead for the national child protection system, I would like to say that we are sorry for the outcome,” Zulkifli said. “We will do everything possible to prevent the recurrence of such tragedies.” The ministry said in September that it had launched a new unit to gather relevant information from different agencies to detect potential cases of child abuse earlier and help professionals provide frontline support sooner. Chua’s case came shortly after another child-abuse case in Singapore, in which a couple were sentenced on October 21. Chloe Gan Ci Xuan, 23, and Neo Jia Ming, 27, were sentenced to 15 years and three months’ jail and 16 years’ jail, respectively, for offences related to the death of their eight-month-old son, Trevor Neo Yu Hin, CNA reported. Trevor suffered violence and suffocation at the hands of Gan and Neo over seven months, when the couple wanted him to stop crying. He died in September 2024 after Gan repeatedly smothered him. Gan and Neo were charged with causing and allowing the death of a child, respectively, as well as ill-treating Trevor, among other offences. Under Singaporean law, the maximum penalty for causing or allowing the death of a child under 14 years of age is life imprisonment and liability to a fine or caning. Meanwhile, the penalty for disposing of a corpse with intent to impede discovery, identification or criminal investigation is up to seven years’ jail.

title: Europe can still shape the rules of AI
description: In October, two technology executives offered Europe similar advice. In Turin, Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai urged European companies to use open-source models and their proprietary industrial data to build AI capabilities. In Berlin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang pressed German manufacturers to apply AI to factories, robotics and other physical industries. Both see opportunity in Europe’s engineering strengths, while their companies stand to benefit from supplying the technology. Recent...
content: In October, two technology executives offered Europe similar advice. In Turin, Alibaba Group Holding chairman Joe Tsai urged European companies to use open-source models and their proprietary industrial data to build AI capabilities. In Berlin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang pressed German manufacturers to apply AI to factories, robotics and other physical industries. Both see opportunity in Europe’s engineering strengths, while their companies stand to benefit from supplying the technology. Recent safety incidents and evaluations expose another dimension of the AI race: the difficulty of keeping increasingly capable AI agents under human control. During internal cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI agents bypassed isolation controls and accessed external systems beyond their intended scope. In September, Reuters reported on documented cases of Chinese-model agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot displaying deception or evading constraints in controlled tests. In October, Tencent Holding acknowledged unintended browsing behaviour by agents evaluating third-party models. These cases range from controlled experiments to real security lapses. They underscore the need for better evaluation before wider deployment. Europe should take this warning seriously as AI enters industrial systems, healthcare and public services. The same risks create a strategic opening. Countries lacking America’s and China’s frontier-model resources can still help establish the conditions under which these systems earn trust, gain market access and operate across borders. Europe’s regulatory framework is often presented as a handicap. The AI Act and data protection requirements raise compliance costs, create uncertainty and can slow adoption. The European Union acknowledged these pressures by simplifying obligations and extending deadlines as part of its omnibus legislative package. Yet regulation has also fostered expertise in risk classification, supervision, independent testing and sensitive-data management. These capabilities acquire strategic value if Europe can turn them into practical tools that other countries have reason to adopt. This opportunity extends to middle powers with different assets. The United States is organising secure technology and supply-chain partnerships through Pax Silica; China is expanding open-model adoption and development-oriented AI cooperation. The EU itself has joined Pax Silica while supporting UN-led governance discussions. Neither network gives other countries full control over their technological choices. Europe brings regulatory and industrial expertise; Singapore has developed AI testing tools; Gulf countries possess capital and energy resources; Switzerland offers international institutions and diplomatic networks able to connect different partners. Together, they could establish an international framework for evaluating AI agents across technological ecosystems. Rather than seek immediate legal harmonisation, the effort should start with practical tests: whether agents respect assigned permissions, report failed tasks, resist prompt manipulation and avoid unauthorised access to external systems. Results could follow comparable formats, with incident-reporting procedures and safeguards for sensitive information. Testing should cover advanced general-purpose agents alongside their deployment in manufacturing and other sensitive sectors. Shared technical assessments could reduce duplication, improve transparency and help regulators understand risks across jurisdictions. Each jurisdiction would retain authority over compliance and market access. Wider international adoption could also reward companies that have invested in safety assessment. Starting points exist. Singapore’s AI Verify initiative has developed testing tools. The International Telecommunication Union is working on standards for AI systems and agent identity. European regulators and laboratories could contribute sector-specific knowledge. A voluntary assurance pilot could bring these efforts together, publish evaluation methods and provide access to independent testing. China’s 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan supports international standards, AI safety and capacity building through multilateral institutions. The EU likewise advocates UN cooperation. These interests overlap on selected technical questions, even amid disagreements over surveillance, state access to data, political freedoms and national security. US companies and laboratories should participate too. Credibility requires technical independence, transparent governance and equal scrutiny of models from every country. Common testing cannot settle export-control disputes or eliminate advanced-AI risks. Its value is practical Developing economies face an additional challenge. Costly tests and imported compliance services can become barriers to AI adoption. Any partnership should fund shared laboratories, open evaluation tools and training, giving countries meaningful roles in setting priorities. Without such support, international safety standards could deepen existing divides rather than help poorer economies participate. The 2027 Geneva AI Summit offers a chance to turn discussion into implementation. This follows the UN’s inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva this July. It could convene regulators, researchers and companies around a funded pilot with measurable commitments. The UN can provide inclusive political discussion; technical organisations and national authorities must carry implementation forward after delegates leave Geneva. Europe still needs faster investment, more computing capacity, stronger domestic innovation and industrial adoption. Common testing cannot settle export-control disputes or eliminate advanced-AI risks. Its value is practical: making cross-border deployment safer, building shared technical evidence and keeping limited cooperation possible despite strategic rivalry. As Washington and Beijing compete to supply AI systems, other powers can influence how they are tested, trusted and deployed. Their leverage comes from organising capabilities the global market needs rather than replicating the American or Chinese technology stack. Europe’s regulatory experience could become one such asset by helping build institutions others have reason to use.

title: Death of former PM Yasuo Fukuda leaves void in fraught China-Japan relations

His passing comes as the relationship he spent decades nurturing faces its gravest test since diplomatic normalisation in 1972. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun offered...
content: Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who championed closer ties with China during his brief tenure and later served as a crucial diplomatic intermediary during bilateral crises, has died at the age of 90. Fukuda died of heart failure on Thursday at a Tokyo hospital, Japanese media reported on Monday. His passing comes as the relationship he spent decades nurturing faces its gravest test since diplomatic normalisation in 1972. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun offered condolences on Monday, praising Fukuda as someone who “made positive contributions to improving and developing China-Japan relations” and “held a correct view of history during his tenure”. Guo said Fukuda’s words “carried great weight”, reflecting the credibility and responsibility of Japan’s older generation of statesmen. Taking a swipe at Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, he added: “Those running the Japanese government should look inward and do serious soul-searching.” Guo’s comments laid bare how far bilateral relations had deteriorated since Fukuda’s era. Ties have been strained since November last year, when Takaichi suggested that a conflict in the Taiwan Strait might prompt military intervention by Japan. Wang Guangtao, deputy director of the Centre for Japanese Studies at Fudan University, who met Fukuda in person, described him as “modest and gentle” despite his political pedigree – his father, Takeo Fukuda, served as Japan’s prime minister from 1976 to 1978 – and credited him with playing an important role in bilateral ties at both official and unofficial levels. Wang called Fukuda’s death a loss that could not easily be replaced, warning that Tokyo now lacked figures with comparable credibility in Beijing. “We’ve witnessed a succession of Japanese statesmen who championed bilateral friendship pass away in recent years, when bilateral relations have entered an exceptionally challenging phase,” he said. Wang said Fukuda’s unique value was his credibility in Beijing, which few Japanese politicians could claim, earned through consistent engagement and a willingness to acknowledge historical facts. Finding another noteworthy politician to be trusted by Beijing like Fukuda would be “extremely difficult”, he added. Wang attributed that to Japan’s own political environment, saying domestic pressures had made engagement with China politically dangerous. “Any gestures of goodwill towards Beijing risk being portrayed as weakness at home,” he said. “This atmosphere intimidates politicians who wish to seek rapprochement.” Fukuda served as Japan’s 91st prime minister from September 2007 to September 2008, inheriting a bilateral relationship badly damaged by leader Junichiro Koizumi’s repeated visits to Yasukuni Shrine, which honours Class-A war criminals alongside Japan’s 2.5 million war dead, between 2001 and 2006. In December 2007, Fukuda made an official visit to Beijing, delivering a speech at Peking University that emphasised historical reflection and cooperation. Chinese state media hailed the trip as a “warm spring”, and Fukuda kept his commitment to never visit the Yasukuni Shrine. Arguably, Fukuda’s most consequential work came after he left office. When Japan in 2012 nationalised three of the disputed Diaoyu Islands, which Japan calls the Senkaku Islands, Beijing cut high-level contact with Tokyo. In July 2014, Fukuda made a secret trip to Beijing and met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The visit helped to broker a meeting between Xi and then Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum held in Beijing in November that year. Fukuda’s commitment to China-Japan relations was deeply personal. In 1978, when the Treaty of Peace and Friendship was signed, he served as his father’s political secretary, witnessing first-hand how Takeo Fukuda and then Chinese vice-premier Deng Xiaoping advanced bilateral ties in the negotiations leading up to the ratification ceremony. Thirty years later, in May 2008, when Yasuo Fukuda hosted then-Chinese president Hu Jintao for a state visit to Japan, the two leaders signed a document pledging to develop a “mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests”. The joint statement signed by Hu and Fukuda, alongside the 1972 Joint Communique normalising bilateral ties, the 1978 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, and the 1998 Joint Declaration emphasising future-oriented cooperation, formed the bedrock of modern China-Japan relations. The 1972 joint communique stated that Japan “fully understands and respects” Beijing’s position that Taiwan is an inalienable part of the territory of the People’s Republic of China, while the 1998 Joint Declaration reaffirmed Japan’s 1972 stance, reiterating that there was one China. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons. Throughout his post-premiership years, Fukuda repeatedly stressed that the jointly signed documents represented commitments that must be kept in mind and warned against backtracking on their principles. This approach to bilateral ties was built on the vision proposed by Abe, Fukuda’s predecessor. Abe’s abrupt resignation in 2007 left Fukuda to complete the task of cementing the relationship. After leaving politics in 2012, Fukuda led several delegations to China, with his last visit taking place in 2024. From 2010 to 2018, Fukuda served as chairman of the Boao Forum for Asia, widely referred to as the “Asian Davos”, promoting building consensus and cooperation in the region. In 2018, he toured the museum in Nanjing commemorating the victims of the Nanking massacre. Fukuda publicly stated that Japan’s diplomacy must properly handle historical issues, a flashpoint in Sino-Japanese relations, otherwise it would be isolated in the international community.

title: 14 Hong Kong civil servants sue colleague over HK$28.9 million Mark Six winnings
description: A Hong Kong civil servant has been sued by 14 colleagues for HK$28.9 million (US$3.7 million) after he allegedly refused to split a winning Mark Six jackpot. Health inspector Ling Chun-ting allegedly told his colleagues at the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) that they did not deserve a share of the HK$33 million prize drawn on September 5 because they had not physically bought the tickets themselves, according to a High Court writ seen by the South China Morning Post on...
content: A Hong Kong civil servant has been sued by 14 colleagues for HK$28.9 million (US$3.7 million) after he allegedly refused to split a winning Mark Six jackpot. Health inspector Ling Chun-ting allegedly told his colleagues at the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) that they did not deserve a share of the HK$33 million prize drawn on September 5 because they had not physically bought the tickets themselves, according to a High Court writ seen by the South China Morning Post on Monday. The 36-year-old, who has since been transferred to a different division within the department, allegedly promised to split the reward out of “good conscience” but failed to do so. “In fact, none of you knew which numbers I picked, so I could simply choose not to split the winnings with you guys,” the defendant was cited as telling his colleagues at their office on September 7. The writ said Ling also claimed that he would have fled with the prize money had he won the full jackpot, which was double the amount they had won. Police arrested Ling on suspicion of theft and froze his bank account after one of his colleagues filed a report on September 9, fearing he would flee with the entire prize money. The suspect has since been released on bail pending further investigation. The dispute involves prize money from the Hong Kong Jockey Club’s Mark Six 50th anniversary snowball draw on September 5, which featured a record HK$228 million jackpot. The first prize pool had 3.5 winning units, each paying HK$63.3 million. The writ said the 15 FEHD officers, who were at the time attached to a department division responsible for developing and renovating wet markets, agreed to pool their money for lottery tickets after a senior superintendent said it would foster team spirit. Although Ling was tasked with placing the bets and holding the tickets, all members shared a mutual understanding that any prize money would be distributed pro rata based on each person’s financial contribution, the filing said. The writ said the 14 plaintiffs each paid between HK$20 and HK$300 towards two HK$825 tickets for the draw, while the defendant allegedly contributed HK$210. The group won more than HK$33.1 million. Based on their distribution agreement, Ling was allegedly entitled to HK$4.2 million of that amount. The plaintiffs claimed that after learning they had won, Ling deleted messaging records that served as proof of purchase and informed them he was under no obligation to share the winnings. When the officers asked to see the physical tickets, Ling stated he was taking leave and requested to postpone discussions until September 13. “Nevertheless, the defendant did not make any distribution of the winnings pursuant to the agreement, or at all, to the plaintiffs up to date, despite repeated requests from the plaintiffs,” the writ said. The plaintiffs are suing Ling on grounds of breach of agreement, fraudulent representation, breach of trust, and unjust enrichment. They asked the court to restrain Ling from handling the HK$28.9 million, which they said represented their winnings, and to order him to pay damages.

title: 2 workers dangle more than 30 storeys up after Jardine House gondola fault
description: Firefighters rescued two workers left dangling on safety harnesses more than 30 storeys above ground outside a landmark skyscraper in Hong Kong’s Central district on Monday evening after their suspended working platform apparently malfunctioned and suddenly dropped. The incident occurred at about 6.16pm at Jardine House on Connaught Road Central, where the two workers, aged 25 and 47, were carrying out facade cleaning work from a gondola when it dropped and came to a stop a few metres above the...
content: Firefighters rescued two workers left dangling on safety harnesses more than 30 storeys above ground outside a landmark skyscraper in Hong Kong’s Central district on Monday evening after their suspended working platform apparently malfunctioned and suddenly dropped. The incident occurred at about 6.16pm at Jardine House on Connaught Road Central, where the two workers, aged 25 and 47, were carrying out facade cleaning work from a gondola when it dropped and came to a stop a few metres above the ground. One of the workers was left dangling for nearly 1½ hours before being rescued around 7.40pm. Another rescuer from the Fire Services Department’s High Angle Rescue Team brought the other worker to the roof of the 52-storey building at about 8pm. Both men were taken to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam for treatment, with the first worker suffering minor hand injuries. The suspended platform was suspected to have developed a fault and dropped, leaving the pair, who were wearing safety harnesses, dangling outside the 35th and 43rd floors, respectively. The pair stood on the building’s circular window frames to rest while awaiting rescue. Emergency crews rushed to the scene and launched a rescue operation. Two firefighters abseiled from the rooftop to reach them. An air cushion was placed at the foot of the building as a precaution. Earlier images from the scene showed the men stranded in mid-air outside the tower as rescuers prepared to bring them to safety. Landlord Hongkong Land said it had immediately launched an investigation into the incident and would cooperate with the relevant government departments on follow-up actions. Jardine House, Hong Kong’s first skyscraper, stands 178.5 metres (586 feet) tall and was completed in 1973. Formerly known as the Connaught Centre, it was also the tallest building in Asia when it opened. It held the local height record until it was surpassed by the 222-metre Hopewell Centre in Wan Chai in 1980. The landmark office tower is best known for its distinctive circular windows, numbering 1,748, and remains one of the most recognisable features of Hong Kong’s skyline and the Central business district.

title: Climate damage to Philippine ports could cost US$70b a year by 2100
description: The Philippines faces the highest climate-driven port damage costs in Southeast Asia, with annual losses projected to hit US$70.2 billion by 2100, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned. Analysts say the damage could cripple supply chains, drive up food prices and threaten livelihoods, urging Manila to adopt a more coordinated approach to flood protection rather than simply strengthening port infrastructure. In its latest report titled “Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the...
content: The Philippines faces the highest climate-driven port damage costs in Southeast Asia, with annual losses projected to hit US$70.2 billion by 2100, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has warned. Analysts say the damage could cripple supply chains, drive up food prices and threaten livelihoods, urging Manila to adopt a more coordinated approach to flood protection rather than simply strengthening port infrastructure. In its latest report titled “Asia-Pacific Climate Report 2026: Coastal Risks on the Rise – Actions for a Resilient Future”, the ADB said the Philippines could sustain US$20.6 billion in port damage under a moderate-emissions scenario, in which sea levels were projected to rise by 50cm to 80cm. A high-emissions scenario where sea levels could rise up to 1 metre could see annual port damages climb to US$70.2 billion by 2100. In the Asia-Pacific region, the Philippines only trails China, with projected annual losses ranging from US$82.2 billion to US$332 billion, while India’s projections are from US$70 billion to US$254 billion, which would be expected to include the cost of repairing damaged port infrastructure and losses from maritime trade disruption. Port damage can disrupt operations, delay shipments and interrupt supply chains that businesses and communities rely on for essential goods. “Because these networks link farms to markets, fishers to buyers, and households to health services and food supplies, their disruption cascades directly into livelihoods, nutrition, and well-being,” said the report, released last Wednesday. “The extent of exposed infrastructure is likely to increase as urban development increasingly puts these built assets in harm’s way.” In September, the Philippine Ports Authority (PPA), the agency tasked with regulating and managing the country’s seaports, said that it had embarked on efforts to strengthen its infrastructure, including climate- and disaster-resilient measures, to ensure business continuity and that ports could withstand typhoons and earthquakes and continue moving essential items in times of emergencies. “We continue to conduct drills, test different scenarios, strengthen coordination, and improve our infrastructure so that when a disaster comes, our ports can continue serving as safe and reliable lifelines for the country,” PPA general manager Jay Santiago said in a statement. This Week in Asia has reached out to the authority for comments on the ADB report. Manuel Jose Camagay, a transport, urban and logistics specialist, said the Philippines bore higher logistics costs than its neighbours in mainland Southeast Asia. “Ports are gateways to supply chains and natural disasters play the crucial villainous role of disrupting the normal flow of goods and people across the country,” he said. Ven Paolo Valenzuela, a research fellow at Singapore Management University’s College of Integrative Studies, said that when ports failed in an archipelagic country, the whole economy would stumble. “We’re very dependent on ports. Your food prices spike, your supply chain is severely disrupted, and post-typhoon relief cannot access devastated islands or coastal communities,” Valenzuela said. He echoed the report’s implications, adding that port damage created a compounding effect, from physical destruction to longer operational downtime. Valenzuela added that sea level rise was not the sole factor that could devastate ports, though it amplified other hazards such as coastal flooding from storm surges, powerful winds from intensifying tropical cyclones and coastal erosion in port areas. “Because of that, the disruption ripples across industries’ supply chains. You cannot move goods from Luzon to Visayas without going through a port,” he said, calling the problem a “big gap”. More than 20 typhoons hit the Philippines each year, affecting ports that dot its coasts. Typhoon Haiyan in 2013 showed “how storm surges can wipe out ports and the communities around them”, Valenzuela said. Camagay said that port damage was tantamount to trade and economic loss due to shipment delays and disruptions of basic commodities, losses of raw materials and equipment to continue operations, higher cost of goods and forgone income when deadlines were not met. He also called ports “employment magnets” given their appeal to flocks of migrant workers living in urban areas around these ports. Such communities were directly affected by port damage and coastal flooding, Valenzuela said, adding that Metro Manila’s main port complex, which handled the bulk of the country’s international and domestic container throughput, was vulnerable to storm surges, coastal flooding and knock-on effects of groundwater extraction. Other coastal hubs such as Iloilo, Cebu, Batangas, Subic, Davao and Cagayan de Oro were seeing rapid urbanisation in flood-prone zones that outpaced the building of drainage and other protective infrastructure, he said. Beyond port infrastructure Valenzuela said the Philippines lacked the means to protect its ports against climate change. “Technically, we know how to elevate and climate-proof ports – my own research in Japan proves it can be done sequentially without halting trade,” he said. “It’s easy to defend the port itself, but if the surrounding infrastructure isn’t planned as a system, it doesn’t matter how nice your defences are.” Valenzuela said that raising a port to address sea level rise would be “pointless” if drainage systems from the land were blocked and if the challenges of land sinking were not addressed. As for seismic risks, the Philippines cannot afford to ignore them, as it is a country prone to earthquakes, according to Valenzuela. Meanwhile, the Philippines could look to Indonesia and Singapore to learn how these countries had progressively upgraded their port facilities to mitigate climate impact without causing disruptions to cargo operations, he said. Indonesia had deployed floating piers, pontoons and logistics bases that could adjust to rising water levels, Valenzuela said. Singapore had been protecting its ports as part of its national efforts against rising sea levels, anchored by a multibillion-dollar coastal and flood protection fund, he added. Camagay said that at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations level, the bloc could also do its part to mitigate climate damage such as through its proposed adoption of green shipping operations, he added. “The goal is to reduce, if not eliminate, the carbon footprint not only from the sea vessels but also from the cargo, the packaging and the use of plastics and anything that impacts the environment.”

title: Pentagon chief Hegseth to visit Philippines to meet US allies at Asean events
description: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth will travel to the Philippines this week to meet regional allies, the Pentagon announced on Sunday. The visit comes amid a push by Washington to tighten security ties in the Indo-Pacific ahead of an expected meeting between the US and Chinese presidents in southern China. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has faced criticism from Democrats and some Republicans over his handling of the war against Iran, as well as concerns that the conflict could divert US...
content: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth will travel to the Philippines this week to meet regional allies, the Pentagon announced on Sunday. The visit comes amid a push by Washington to tighten security ties in the Indo-Pacific ahead of an expected meeting between the US and Chinese presidents in southern China. Hegseth, a former Fox News host, has faced criticism from Democrats and some Republicans over his handling of the war against Iran, as well as concerns that the conflict could divert US attention from the Indo-Pacific region. The Philippines is hosting the annual Asean summit in Manila next month, while the bloc’s defence ministers will meet with regional partners – including the United States – at the end of this month in Cebu. Manila is looking to use its chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations – which it holds under the bloc’s annual rotation system – to promote broader regional cooperation and strengthen ties with the US and its closest allies. The Pentagon said Hegseth would attend the defence ministers’ meeting and take part in several bilateral and multilateral engagements “to reaffirm America’s commitment to peace through strength in the Pacific”. The meetings aimed to “strengthen deterrence, advance key alliances and partnerships, and expand burden sharing across the region”, the Pentagon added. Last week, the South China Morning Post exclusively reported that US allies were planning to meet on the sidelines of the Asean summit in the Philippine capital. Hegseth’s visit will take place ahead of US President Donald Trump’s expected trip to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, where he is expected to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, for the third time this year. The trip also comes amid continuing tensions over Manila and Beijing’s competing claims in the South China Sea, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr taking a more assertive stance compared with his predecessor. The dispute has resulted in a series of confrontations between Philippine and Chinese ships near disputed features, prompting Manila to strengthen its relations with the US and other allies. Philippine Ambassador Jose Manuel Romualdez recently told the SCMP that meetings of the informal “Squad” grouping – consisting of the US, the Philippines, Australia and Japan – were likely to take place on the sidelines of Asean-related events in the Philippines. Romualdez also said the meetings might involve the countries’ defence ministers, adding: “If it’s an opportunity that is there, I’m sure that they will do it.” Meanwhile, Washington has confirmed that the Quad – a four-way gathering that includes India but not the Philippines – will also meet on the sidelines of the Asean summit. Hegseth will be attending a meeting between Asean defence ministers and eight dialogue partners – the US, China, Japan, India, Australia, South Korea, Russia and New Zealand – in Cebu this week. Neither China nor the Philippines has confirmed whether Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun – who attended the last two gatherings – would be present.

title: Do Hong Kong’s cardboard grannies have a future making just HK$30 for day’s work?

It is a laborious occupation that involves working long hours and travelling inconvenient distances, often in difficult outdoor conditions.
