content: The idea of collecting cardboard boxes and used paper in exchange for a few pennies was never something Kuang Su-ling thought she would have to do for a living. It is a laborious occupation that involves working long hours and travelling inconvenient distances, often in difficult outdoor conditions. But Kuang became a waste paper scavenger after she was diagnosed with diabetic eye disease seven years ago and lost her job as a cleaner. “I could not find any other work and I needed money to cover my medical expenses … at least I do not have to be a beggar,” said the 63-year-old, her small build cutting a stark figure against her large cart stacked with used cardboard boxes. On a sweltering Wednesday afternoon, Kuang, drenched in sweat, parks her cart in the shade near a Fanling market and greets the food and fruit store owners who keep their used boxes for her. Their relationship has been built on years of familiarity. “The job has become my spiritual anchor,” Kuang said. “Recycling is meaningful community work, and I treat the job as exercise to keep fit.” Living alone, Kuang said she found comfort in chatting with store workers and helping them recycle paper. But the rate paid by recycling firms had fallen to a measly 50 HK cents per kilogram of waste paper, and Kuang earned roughly HK$30 (US$3.80) a day, barely enough to scrape by on. “If the prices for waste paper continue to drop, I will have no choice but to stop collecting waste paper,” she said. After a new policy kicked in on October 1 to support developing Hong Kong’s only paper pulping facility in Tuen Mun and reduce reliance on waste paper exports, downstream recyclers have felt the pinch of falling prices. This has prompted calls from industry leaders to restore subsidies to support the sector and scavengers – known locally as “cardboard grannies” – such as Kuang. Another collector, Poon Chau-li, begins her day after an early breakfast and pushes her cart around her housing estate in Fanling, scavenging for waste paper. She takes meal breaks at home and sometimes works late into the night. The 73-year-old, who has lived alone since her children moved out, recalled that, just a few years ago, collectors were paid HK$1 per kilogram of waste paper and she could earn up to HK$200 a day. “I was much more driven to hunt for cardboard boxes back then,” Poon said with a grin. Her earnings recently dropped to around HK$70 per day due to the lower rate, and what little she earned she spent on groceries. While insisting that she remained in good health, Poon recalled a few occasions when she felt dizzy after physical exertion and had to sit down and suck on a piece of ginger to recover her strength. Poon said she would stop collecting waste paper if rates continued to drop. “What is all the hard work for? A day’s earnings will be gone after buying a few bottles of water,” Poon said. When the paper mill in Tuen Mun EcoPark commenced operations in July, the local waste paper recycling market underwent a structural shift, leading to price drops in October that affected upstream baling plants, corner recycling shops and frontline paper scavengers. In September, the environmental authorities announced that starting from October 1, rather than relying on exporting paper for recycling, Hong Kong’s waste paper would be handled by the centralised processing hub at the Tuen Mun facility, operated by Zhou Ji Paper Industrial Limited. The facility compresses waste paper into pulp before manufacturing it into reusable paper and will eventually handle 500,000 to 720,000 tonnes of waste paper annually. The move marks a “shift from past reliance on exporting waste paper” and supports the “development of a circular economy”, according to the Environmental Protection Department. It can take in more recyclable paper, expanding its range from traditional cardboard, office paper, newspapers, books and magazines to include paper boxes, paper roll cores, paper bags, as well as egg cartons and wrapping paper. Previously, more than 90 per cent of the city’s waste paper was exported, with the vast majority going to mainland China. But since late 2020, the mainland has banned the import of solid waste, including all waste paper. The ban rocked the local industry, with many concerned by plunging prices and wondering whether the city’s waste paper would simply end up in landfills. To support the industry, Hong Kong authorities struck an agreement with Beijing to retain some waste paper export quotas, sources told the South China Morning Post. But in September, recycling firms were informed that the export quota would be reduced to zero from October, meaning waste paper could henceforth only be processed at the Tuen Mun mill. At the same time, a monthly government subsidy launched in late 2020 – designed to ensure contractors offered a guaranteed minimum price to frontline collectors – also came to an end. To ensure frontline collectors receive a fair rate, the department mandates a minimum buying price for paper that meets quality standards, currently set at 65 cents per kilogram. Facility operators must also buy paper from collectors and recyclers at no less than a set minimum price of HK$1,295.51 per tonne. But some waste paper scavengers said they were paid a rate of 50 or 60 cents per kilogram. Those on Hong Kong Island were paid even less, as a percentage was deducted by upstream recyclers to offset operational costs. Jacky Lau Yiu-shing, chairman of the Recycled Materials and Re-production Business General Association, said the termination of the monthly subsidy – which covered transport costs for industry players – was the main cause of the price drop. “Overall, [the Tuen Mun facility] is a good thing for Hong Kong as we have an extra place for waste-to-energy conversion, but the question is how to address those small operational details first,” Lau said. Lam Kam-san, founder of Jinsheng Recycling, a corner recycling shop in Shau Kei Wan, said meagre margins from upstream recycling mills and high operational and transport costs might force his shop to stop collecting waste paper altogether. “We may as well just stop receiving waste paper from scavengers if we pay them such poor rates,” Lam said. “Worst case is we focus on other collectibles.” Kathy Hui, whose family runs Tak Lee Recycle Paper Collecting Co, a baling plant in Heng Fa Chuen, said the amount of waste paper collected has dropped by up to 40 per cent this month, with a loss of roughly HK$250,000 so far, equivalent to half of the facility’s monthly rent. She said the company previously handled waste paper exports to processing mills on the mainland, and the current situation was all the more grim as October to February was the industry’s peak season. In late September, Tak Lee was forced to let five staff members go. If losses continued to accumulate, Hui anticipated that the company would have little choice but to shut down in three to four months. “Even though we can technically export waste paper overseas, such as to Southeast Asian countries, oil prices now are too high,” Hui said. “Most of our waste paper was exported to clients in mainland China.” Both Hui and Lau urged the government to restore subsidies. According to data projections by the NGO Mission to New Arrivals’ Wastepicker Platform project in 2023, there were between 2,791 and 3,456 waste paper scavengers in Hong Kong, with many working seven days a week. The NGO’s officer Tang Wing-him suggested that the department meet more regularly with frontline workers and provide operational subsidies to recycling shops to ease their financial burden. The city’s total local waste paper recovery volume reached more than 410,000 tonnes from January to September, which was comparable to the same period last year, an Environmental Protection Department spokeswoman said. She noted that the previous government subsidy had been a “short-term support measure”, adding the government’s HK$300 million budget was now going to service fees for the pulp facility and to help “maintain long-term price stability and recycling volumes across the entire recycling chain”. The industry was currently in a transition phase and needed time to “adjust their business arrangements to adapt to the new environment”, she said. The department would step up support and maintain communication with sorting and baling yards to help them transition smoothly, she added.

title: Indonesia defends Singapore gas cuts, cites rising domestic needs and contractual limits
description: Indonesia has defended its decision to cut natural gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic electricity and industrial needs and arguing that the reduction remains within contractual limits. The cuts came days after Indonesia’s energy minister warned that his country could stop exports to nations that “did not respect” it. On Monday, Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia defended the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet per day in pipeline gas exports to Singapore, saying it represented about...
content: Indonesia has defended its decision to cut natural gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic electricity and industrial needs and arguing that the reduction remains within contractual limits. The cuts came days after Indonesia’s energy minister warned that his country could stop exports to nations that “did not respect” it. On Monday, Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia defended the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet per day in pipeline gas exports to Singapore, saying it represented about 8 per cent of the 409.55 million standard cubic feet supplied daily and remained within the minimum supply obligations under existing contracts. “On President Prabowo’s direction, our country respects contracts and rules, so don’t lecture Indonesia about its commitment to upholding and respecting contracts,” Bahlil said at a news conference in Jakarta, according to Indonesian broadcaster Metro TV. The cuts began on Saturday and affect supplies from the Natuna Sea and Sumatra, with Bahlil citing maintenance shutdowns and rising domestic demand, including the need to maintain reliable gas supplies for power generation. Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sunday that the country expected all parties to honour their commercial commitments, adding that its gas importer would take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under the contracts. “The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments, and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said at a People’s Action Party conference. Singapore generates about 95 per cent of its electricity using natural gas, with a significant portion of that coming from Indonesia, but the government has said alternative sources will help it manage the latest reduction. Singapore’s Energy and Industry Minister Tan See Leng said the reduction in supply amounted to 17 billion British thermal units per day over 18 days, or less than 2 per cent of the country’s daily power-sector gas demand, and that Singapore had sufficient replacement supplies, including liquefied natural gas. Tan said Gas Supply, Singapore’s gas importer, would engage its suppliers to determine whether there had been a breach of contract and pursue commercial remedies if one were established, according to the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry. The gas cuts come amid tensions over transboundary haze from fires in Indonesia’s Sumatra and Kalimantan regions, where land clearing and burning on peatlands have contributed to dense smoke drifting across borders. The haze has repeatedly pushed Singapore’s air quality into the unhealthy range in October, with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index reaching 230 on October 18, the highest of the season. In response, Singapore’s National Environment Agency issued preventive measure notices to 10 Indonesian companies over fires on land they owned or occupied in Sumatra and Kalimantan, requiring them to help extinguish or contain the blazes and take steps to prevent further fires. On Wednesday, President Prabowo Subianto criticised unnamed countries that he accused of insulting Indonesia over the haze, without identifying Singapore. The following day, Bahlil warned that Indonesia could review energy exports to countries that did not respect it. “I will conduct an evaluation. I will not hesitate to consider stopping exports to countries that do not respect Indonesia,” Bahlil said at an event in Jakarta. Neither official named Singapore, and Indonesian authorities have not publicly linked the gas cuts to the haze dispute. Before the recent export cuts, Bahlil had mentioned reviewing gas allocations to support domestic industries, including the petrochemical sector, as Jakarta seeks to expand downstream processing and make greater use of its natural resources at home. Indonesia and Singapore’s existing gas supply contracts run until the end of 2028, according to Singaporean officials. Both countries are also pursuing plans for cross-border electricity trade, but negotiations over pricing remain unresolved.

title: Why China’s new estimate on Greenland ice loss speed is 55% lower than America’s
description: Chinese researchers have created a new model to convert satellite surface elevation data for the Greenland Ice Sheet into a detailed estimate of how much ice it has lost in recent decades. Using satellite altimetry data covering 2002 to 2023, they found that the ice sheet lost an average of about 120 gigatonnes (264.5 trillion lbs) of mass per year. This figure is considerably lower than the widely cited figure reached by Nasa, which previously estimated Greenland’s annual loss to be nearly 270...
content: Chinese researchers have created a new model to convert satellite surface elevation data for the Greenland Ice Sheet into a detailed estimate of how much ice it has lost in recent decades. Using satellite altimetry data covering 2002 to 2023, they found that the ice sheet lost an average of about 120 gigatonnes (264.5 trillion lbs) of mass per year. This figure is considerably lower than the widely cited figure reached by Nasa, which previously estimated Greenland’s annual loss to be nearly 270 gigatonnes using satellite gravity data. The new figure is also lower than the Chinese team’s own estimate derived from the same data used by the US space agency. The lower number does not suggest Greenland’s melting is less severe than previously thought. Rather, the researchers said their study sought to refine elevation monitoring to provide a high-resolution map of exactly where the loss was happening. “A comparison between different satellite technologies reveals that satellite altimetry offers a significant advantage in spatial resolution over satellite gravimetry, enabling the identification of ice-flow channels in local glaciers,” the team said in a paper published in the Chinese-language Journal of Marine Information Technology and Application on October 19. Gravity-based data can offer a full picture of how much mass has been lost. Altimetry, or elevation data, can provide a more zoomed-in 1.9km (1.2-mile) resolution, but it needs to be converted into mass using density. The researchers from China’s Jiangsu Ocean University developed a dynamic conversion model that was able to identify glaciers experiencing the most rapid loss. This could help reduce uncertainties in estimates of ice sheet dynamics across space and time. The Greenland Ice Sheet covers about 80 per cent of the territory’s total land area and is the second-largest ice sheet in the world. The sheet stretches across 1.7 million sq km (656,300 square miles) and contains about 2.9 million cubic km (696,000 cubic miles) of ice, according to the US National Snow and Ice Data Centre (NSIDC). Since the mid-1990s, the sheet has been losing mass “in earnest”, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). This affects not only sea levels but also ocean circulation and properties, nutrient and sediment flux, as well as local ecosystems, contributing as feedback to future melting, NOAA said. The sheet’s maximum elevation reaches 3,673 metres (12,050 feet), and the sheet’s average thickness is about 1,800 metres. The sheet’s ablation or melting period typically occurs from May to August, according to the Chinese team. “Accurately estimating the spatiotemporal characteristics of the mass change of the Greenland Ice Sheet is of great scientific significance for understanding the complex feedback relationship between the polar ice sheet and the global climate system,” the team wrote. Precisely determining ice mass changes and where they are happening is also important for predicting future evolution and impact on sea level rise, they added. One of the primary methods to monitor long-term ice mass changes in the polar ice sheets is satellite gravimetry, which maps changes in the Earth’s gravitational field and can be used to determine mass loss. “Satellite gravimetry allows for the direct monitoring of relative changes in the total mass of an ice sheet, yet its spatial resolution is insufficient to capture fine-scale, localised variations,” the team said. Another method is satellite altimetry, which uses lasers or radar to track changes in the Earth’s surface elevation. This method offers the best resolution, but converting the data into mass can lead to estimation errors. Over the past few decades, satellites equipped with radar altimeters have been launched to track ice sheet elevation and monitor the ice sheets. In 2002, Nasa and the German Aerospace Centre launched two satellites as part of the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (Grace), which orbited until 2017, collecting data on the Earth’s gravity field. Its successor, Grace-Fo, was launched in 2018. Using data from Grace, Nasa estimated that Greenland lost 264 gigatonnes of ice per year between 2002 and 2025. According to the Chinese team, although there had been previous studies using altimetry data, these often focused on using the data to downscale or correct gravimetric results. There was a lack of systematic comparison between mass changes obtained from both methods, they said. In their paper, the team proposed a way to estimate mass changes using satellite altimetry data with the help of a climate model called Mar, allowing them to build a dynamic snow and ice density model. They evaluated mass changes from 2002 to 2023 using Mar to process surface elevation measurements. These measurements were derived from NSIDC’s multi-source satellite altimetry data, which incorporates measurements from Nasa’s ICESat. The researchers then compared this to the results from Grace-derived satellite-based mass concentration gravity data released by the University of Texas at Austin. The Chinese team found that the Greenland Ice Sheet “was in a state of continuous mass loss” between 2002 and 2023, with an annual loss of nearly 120 gigatonnes based on altimetry data. The melting rate of the ice sheet accelerated significantly after 2010. This meant a total loss of about 2,248 gigatonnes, contributing about 6.26mm (0.25 inch) to global sea level rise. Using the gravity-based data, the team estimated a total mass loss of about 2,830 gigatonnes over the same 22-year period. Thinning was most pronounced in the northwestern and southeastern parts of the ice sheet where the ice transitions into the ocean. They found that significant mass loss signals were seen in the coastal Jakobshavn, Helheim, Kangerlussuaq and 79N glaciers. In the hardest-hit basins, the altimetry data showed significantly less mass loss than the gravity measurements. This discrepancy suggests that melting may be occurring at the base of the ice sheet, or that ice and snow density was underestimated. According to the Chinese team, future research would seek to further refine density estimates by incorporating on-site density observations. “This integrated approach is intended to improve the accuracy of mass change estimates derived from satellite altimetry, provide more reliable data for analysing long-term trends in ice sheet mass and reduce uncertainties regarding the contribution of polar ice sheets to future sea-level rise projections,” they said.

title: In a global first, Hong Kong opens secondary trading for tokenised public funds
description: The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) on Monday approved the world’s first-ever secondary trading of tokenised public funds, reinforcing the city’s push to build the region’s leading ecosystem for tokenised finance. Investors can now trade two tokenised money market funds – the Hong Kong dollar and US dollar versions of the ChinaAMC Digital Money Market Fund – on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). “For retail investors, this marks a vital upgrade in time...
content: The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) on Monday approved the world’s first-ever secondary trading of tokenised public funds, reinforcing the city’s push to build the region’s leading ecosystem for tokenised finance. Investors can now trade two tokenised money market funds – the Hong Kong dollar and US dollar versions of the ChinaAMC Digital Money Market Fund – on an SFC-licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP). “For retail investors, this marks a vital upgrade in time sovereignty over fund management,” said Katie He, head of strategic business at China Asset Management (Hong Kong), noting that trading was now available around the clock, including weekends and public holidays. The initiative was jointly launched by ChinaAMC (Hong Kong), the local arm of one of China’s largest fund managers, and PantherTrade, a VATP backed by the fintech company Futu Holdings. “Together, we have proven that liquidity can be unlocked without altering the legal structure of public mutual funds or lowering investor protection standards,” He said. The SFC adapted existing regulatory frameworks governing VATPs and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which already support secondary-market trading, to enable trading of tokenised public funds. Previously, investors could access these funds only through primary dealing with a fund manager during conventional trading hours. He said the innovation extended “well beyond the product itself”, reflecting “Hong Kong’s institutional advantage in compliant digital financial innovation, as well as the execution capability of the overall market”. The regulator’s new framework added “an important building block – 24/7 trading capability – to Hong Kong’s evolving tokenisation ecosystem”, said Elisa Ng, executive director of investment products at the SFC, in a statement. The move comes as Hong Kong authorities and financial institutions step up efforts to expand the use of tokenisation, hoping to cement the city’s position as a fintech leader. HSBC, for example, on Monday launched HSBCnio, a platform that allows clients’ artificial intelligence tools to access authorised bank account and transaction information on a read-only basis, with the goal of integrating AI into treasury operations. Hong Kong’s Fintech Week x StartmeupHK 2026, which kicks off next week, expects to welcome more than 45,000 attendees from around the world.

title: Why China’s heritage-listed Dog-Carrying Festival honours canines as sacred lifesavers

content: In a remote Miao village in southwestern China, dogs are honoured as life-saving heroes. Every seventh month of the lunar calendar, residents of Jiaobang village in Jianhe county, Guizhou province, celebrate Tai Gou Jie, or the “Dog-Carrying Festival” – a unique folk tradition recognised as local intangible cultural heritage in 2015. During the festival, villagers select a dog. Traditionally, it was a white female, but today adult males and native Xiasi dogs may also be chosen. The honoured canine is dressed in traditional Miao attire, including a handcrafted tiger-head hat and a silver neck ring. Carried through the village on a bamboo sedan chair, the dog is accompanied by a ritual priest chanting ancient scriptures. The procession culminates in the surrounding fields, where villagers gather to perform drum dances and splash mud on one another. The rituals are intended to share blessings and pray for favourable weather and abundant harvests in the year ahead. The festival’s origins are rooted in two enduring legends. One ancient song recounts a time when a severe drought threatened the village with total crop failure. In a dream, a deity appeared to a village elder and revealed that praying with a dog would bring rain. The villagers followed the vision, rain fell, and the crops thrived. Another tale says that the early ancestors survived because a dog led them to a hidden water source in Guizhou’s karst landscape. Surface water in the region can quickly disappear into underground caves, making scarcity a serious challenge to survival. To the Miao people, dogs are miraculous heroes and lifelong companions. The festival helps pass core cultural values on to younger generations, teaching respect for all life and harmony with nature. Thanks to this tradition, Jiaobang village has earned the reputation of “China’s Village of Gratitude.” The celebration reportedly includes another heartwarming custom: unmarried young women carry puppies on their backs as they collect “hundred-family rice” from local households. A respected elder then distributes the food to young children in a ritual believed to promote their healthy growth. This reverence for animals reflects broader nature-worship beliefs in Miao culture, including the veneration of the “Butterfly Mother” – the mythical ancestor said to have emerged from a maple tree and laid 12 eggs from which humanity and animals were born. Another prominent example is the golden pheasant, which is credited with bringing millet seeds and saving the ancestors from a severe famine. In gratitude, the Golden Pheasant Miao created a traditional dance that imitates the bird’s graceful movements. The tradition also invites modern reflection. “The festival’s respect for animals is moving, yet dog-meat markets persist in a few areas of China. This reverence for life must take precedence over commercial interests,” one online user noted.

title: The Weeknd’s ‘Hong Kong’ captures nostalgia for bygone era, video director says
description: A new viral song by Canadian singer The Weeknd, “Hong Kong”, is a love letter to the city, the director of the accompanying video has said, adding that he believes nostalgia for the late 1980s and early 1990s era is the secret ingredient that has captured the hearts of many. US director Evan Larsen told the South China Morning Post exclusively on Monday that the video was produced in about a week, shortly before its debut at the singer’s concert at Kai Tak Stadium on Saturday as part of his 2026...
content: A new viral song by Canadian singer The Weeknd, “Hong Kong”, is a love letter to the city, the director of the accompanying video has said, adding that he believes nostalgia for the late 1980s and early 1990s era is the secret ingredient that has captured the hearts of many. US director Evan Larsen told the South China Morning Post exclusively on Monday that the video was produced in about a week, shortly before its debut at the singer’s concert at Kai Tak Stadium on Saturday as part of his 2026 Asian tour. Abel Tesfaye – the 36-year-old singer, songwriter, record producer and actor known as The Weeknd – fused Faye Wong’s 1993 Cantopop number titled “Seasonal Wind” into the song as a tribute to the era. “The Weeknd is a massive movie fan and loves Hong Kong cinema from the late ’80s and the early ’90s,” Larsen said. “He gave me a list of movies to check out before I arrived to get inspired by the city before I saw it in person. That definitely helped, and we wanted to lean into that.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Abel (@theweeknd) Larsen has toured with The Weeknd for the past four years and handles all the visuals. He said it was the first time the singer had asked him direct a project while on tour, “so this one was a little more hectic because we obviously had the shows”. He said the cinematography of the music video was heavily inspired by Hong Kong film director Wong Kar-wai’s Fallen Angels. Also on the film list were Wong’s Chungking Express and John Woo’s A Better Tomorrow and Hard Boiled. “Those were just some of the films that he was very into, had me watch, and we pulled a lot of inspiration from,” Larsen said. “I didn’t want to just shoot tourist locations. I wanted to find locations that would connect to people who have grown up here.” At the concert, The Weeknd performed “Hong Kong” against the backdrop of the video showcasing city landmarks and familiar sights, from the Victoria Harbour skyline and a red-sailed traditional junk boat to bustling alleys and red taxis. The montage also featured roasted chestnut hawkers, classic neon signs in Mong Kok, the circular footbridge in Causeway Bay, dim sum restaurants, the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront and The Peninsula hotel. Since the debut, Larsen said he had been flooded with messages that almost invariably conveyed how his piece brought back memories of those who lived in Hong Kong in the era. “It brought tears to their eyes. Reading these messages is exactly what we are going for … he loved the city, and he loves that era,” he said. “He really wanted to make the song but also the video a full-on love letter to the city. It’s amazing to see that it’s connected with so many people.” When asked how he recreated the vibe in his shoot, as the cityscape no longer resembles its iconic look from three decades ago, he said the team set out to secure occasions that connected with the bygone era while also capturing the city as it is today. “We weren’t necessarily wanting the video to feel like it took place in the late 80s or 90s. We wanted it to feel like it took place today, but paid homage to that era,” Larsen said in illustrating the creative process. Elaborating, he said half of the video was more produced, such as scenes featuring a vintage Ferrari, while the other half was more of a guerrilla-style shoot as the crew scouted for locations. “I loved Mong Kok, like that area is incredible … In the video, there’s a shot of the model just sitting on the staircase smoking, and that’s one of my favourite shots. We stumbled upon the staircase when we were in Mong Kok looking for a way to get to a rooftop area,” he said. “I was like, this staircase looks like something straight out of Fallen Angels. This is incredible.” Larsen said he was aware of online comments that the video was better at promoting Hong Kong than the Tourism Board’s efforts, but when asked if he would be open to selling the clip for that purpose, he said he would leave business decisions to the team. He stressed that the video would not have been possible without cinematographer Scott Postl and local Hong Kong producer Kiko Chu, who was “super helpful” in sourcing locations and bringing the vision to life. “It still feels like a dream,” Chu said in a social media post, adding that he had received a producer job referral last Saturday for an overseas crew coming to town to shoot at the weekend, which he agreed to as he was available. “Later, I contacted the director and studied his profile, only to find out it was for The Weeknd, not a weekend shoot. I was just lounging on the sofa, but I immediately sat up and changed my schedule for this week to start preparations,” Chu wrote. The Weeknd performed two concerts in Hong Kong on Saturday and Sunday, and will have another two this coming weekend, before heading to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, for the final leg of the tour. The tour also took in Tokyo, Jakarta, Singapore, Seoul and Bangkok.

title: AI chip surge lifts South Korea to record surplus, behind only China
