The current account measures a country’s trade and income with the world. It counts goods and services sold abroad, money earned on overseas investments and payments flowing the other way. A surplus means more foreign currency is coming in than going out. Surging demand for semiconductors...
content: South Korea earned US$116.63 billion more from the world than it spent in the second quarter of this year – exceeding the combined current account surpluses of Germany and Japan for the first time on record. The current account measures a country’s trade and income with the world. It counts goods and services sold abroad, money earned on overseas investments and payments flowing the other way. A surplus means more foreign currency is coming in than going out. Surging demand for semiconductors helped propel South Korea’s second-quarter surplus, with chip exports reaching US$113.89 billion in the three months to June, according to government figures – up 181.6 per cent from the same period last year. Prices for memory chips have jumped in recent months amid the global artificial intelligence boom. In June, US manufacturer Micron Technology reported that its prices had risen by as much as 80 per cent quarter on quarter. South Korea’s second-quarter surplus was second only to China’s US$193.72 billion among the 36 major economies tracked by the International Monetary Fund, according to data compiled by the Bank of Korea and released on Saturday. Germany recorded a surplus of US$52.28 billion and Japan US$50.62 billion, giving a combined total of US$102.9 billion, or US$13.73 billion less than South Korea. It marked the first time South Korea had surpassed the combined current account surplus of both industrial giants since comparable data became available in 1996. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung welcomed the news in a social media post on Sunday, saying “a great wave of opportunity is rising for our economy”, in a nod to a phrase popularised by late US president John F. Kennedy: “a rising tide lifts all boats”. Lee credited manufacturers, especially chipmakers, for the achievement and called for the gains to reach beyond corporate profits into jobs, income, investments and citizens’ quality of life. “South Korea is now moving beyond the role of a nation following in the footsteps of developed countries,” he wrote in Korean. “It is emerging as a leading nation that shapes the currents of the global economy.” A transient boom? Because South Korea’s surging current account surplus is mostly being driven by soaring chip prices, economists like Hur Jung of Sogang University have warned that it will “last only a few years at best”. Kim Sung-hyun, a professor in the economics department at Sungkyunkwan University, agreed with Hur’s assessment. “Semiconductor prices are likely to fall sharply in two to three years, as overseas competitors, including Chinese rivals, are going all out to expand semiconductor chip production,” Kim said. The record earnings being reported by South Korea’s chipmakers, defence industry and selected food companies had yet to spread to other areas of the economy, he added. Semiconductor prices are likely to fall sharply in two to three years Kim Sung-hyun, economics professor Meanwhile, the inflow of foreign currency has also pushed the won up against the US dollar, making South Korean exports costlier abroad. Hur said this would “put the won under mounting pressure to appreciate, dealing a blow to an economy greatly relying on exports”. Such a large surplus was also “likely to expose Seoul to the crosshairs of Washington”, which could use it to pressure South Korea to invest more in the United States, he said. The US and China are currently working flat out to secure their own memory supplies via domestic manufacturers such as Micron and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Kim Kwang-suk, head of economic research at the Korea Economic and Industrial Research Institute, said this was “raising concerns that South Korean companies could lose ground in the battle for market share”. Countermeasures would be needed, Kim added, particularly against changes that could cut chip exports to China. Yang Jun-sok, an economics professor at the Catholic University of Korea, warned that an early end to the global AI boom could deliver a severe shock to South Korea’s economy. “This year and next, when substantial amounts of money are flowing in, are the right time to carry out long-delayed restructuring, including the clean-up of marginal businesses,” he said. The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook projected a full-year current account surplus of US$421.95 billion for South Korea in 2026, behind only China’s expected US$863.2 billion and the world’s largest increase this year. South Korea’s surplus is especially striking given the size of its economy, which currently ranks 12th in the world. Its surplus is projected to reach 18.8 per cent of gross domestic product this year – the highest of any country since the IMF began tracking such data in 1980 – against Japan’s 4.6 per cent and Germany’s 4.5 per cent. The IMF forecasts South Korea’s GDP will exceed US$2.2 trillion this year, compared with about US$5.5 trillion for Germany and US$4.3 trillion for Japan.

title: China may well be the next big competitor for Asian migrant labour
description: For decades, China was one of the world’s largest sources of migrant labour. Its workers staffed factories at home and built infrastructure abroad. But demographic decline may eventually force China to contemplate a striking reversal: importing workers on a meaningful scale. That change is not imminent. China still has a vast labour force and substantial youth unemployment. It is investing heavily in industrial automation, extending working lives through a gradual increase in the retirement age,...
content: For decades, China was one of the world’s largest sources of migrant labour. Its workers staffed factories at home and built infrastructure abroad. But demographic decline may eventually force China to contemplate a striking reversal: importing workers on a meaningful scale. That change is not imminent. China still has a vast labour force and substantial youth unemployment. It is investing heavily in industrial automation, extending working lives through a gradual increase in the retirement age, and trying to move workers from regions with surplus labour to where employers struggle to recruit. Yet the direction of travel is becoming difficult to ignore. China’s population fell for a fourth consecutive year in 2025. The number of employed people declined to 725 million from 740 million in 2023. The problem is not simply that China will have fewer workers. It is that the composition and expectations of its workforce will almost inevitably have to change. The rural migrants who supplied the factories and construction sites are ageing. About 85 million migrant workers were already over 50 in 2022, almost twice the proportion a decade earlier. Meanwhile, younger Chinese are often reluctant to accept lowly paid, physically demanding or insecure jobs. China can offset part of this pressure through robotics and productivity gains. Automation, however, cannot easily replace carers, hospitality staff or every construction worker. Nor can it fully resolve geographic and skill mismatches. A country can have unemployment and labour shortages at the same time when workers do not live where vacancies exist, or lack the required skills or reject the conditions offered. China’s neighbours already confront that reality. Japan’s foreign workers hit a record high of 2.57 million last October. South Korea keeps expanding its Employment Permit System to recruit workers for smaller manufacturers, farms and other sectors. Singapore’s foreign workforce reached 1.91 million in June last year, supporting construction, shipyards, processing industries and domestic care. They show labour immigration usually begins not with a grand declaration that a nation has become an immigration society, but with programmes designed to solve specific workforce shortages. China could follow that path. The timing would depend on economic conditions. A prolonged slowdown could postpone shortages by reducing employers’ demand for labour while further automation could eliminate some repetitive jobs. But that merely changes which occupations encounter pressure first. As the working-age population contracts, Beijing will have to choose among accepting lower output, raising wages, automating more quickly, keeping people at work for longer and recruiting abroad. It will probably use all five. Beijing is already more willing to compete for elite talent. Its new K visa targets young foreign professionals in science and technology. But recruiting engineers and researchers is politically easier than admitting large numbers of carers, technicians, service workers or factory employees. The latter would require wider changes to work permits, social insurance, family rights and long-term residence. China remains an exceptionally small immigration destination relative to its population. The 2020 census counted only 845,697 foreigners. Public opposition to expanded permanent residence rules in 2020 showed how quickly immigration can become entangled with nationalism, race and perceptions of preferential treatment. These political sensitivities will encourage a gradual roll-out of foreign recruiting policies. China could initially sign bilateral agreements, allow employers in designated sectors or provinces to sponsor foreign workers, and describe the policy as a temporary measure. Care work may become an early pressure point. Such a system would fit Beijing’s preference for experimentation and administrative control. Pilot programmes could be expanded, modified or cancelled without presenting immigration as a permanent transformation of national identity. Yet temporary schemes often become durable when employers organise their business models around foreign labour, as the experience of other ageing Asian economies illustrates. If China enters Asia’s migrant-labour market at scale, the consequences would reach far beyond its borders. Japan, South Korea and Singapore already recruit heavily from Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines and other Asian countries. Chinese employers would be competing for many of the same people. China’s scale could increase wages and recruitment costs across the region. It could also strengthen the bargaining position of labour-sending governments, allowing them to demand better workplace protections, lower placement fees and stronger enforcement against abuse. Migrants would gain more ability to compare destinations according to pay, living costs, personal safety, family reunification and the possibility of remaining permanently. China would not automatically win this competition. Its geographic proximity and enormous labour market would be advantages, but language barriers, limited settlement pathways, internet restrictions and concerns about legal protection could deter. The immediate question is not whether China will suddenly embrace mass immigration. It is whether demographic decline will gradually make selective foreign recruitment less politically difficult than leaving essential jobs unfilled. China became an industrial power by mobilising hundreds of millions of workers from its countryside. Its next labour transition may require looking beyond its borders. If that happens, the country that once transformed global labour markets by exporting workers could reshape Asian migration by beginning to import them.

title: What Hongkongers need to know about the latest changes to the MPF scheme
description: Hong Kong employees will have better control over the management of their compulsory retirement savings under the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) starting from December 21. The new “full portability” mechanism comes after another major change in 2024, when the authority launched the eMPF platform, a centralised electronic platform to standardise, streamline and automate the administrative processes of the MPF scheme, marking the start of the MPF digital era. The South China Morning Post looks at...
content: Hong Kong employees will have better control over the management of their compulsory retirement savings under the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) starting from December 21. The new “full portability” mechanism comes after another major change in 2024, when the authority launched the eMPF platform, a centralised electronic platform to standardise, streamline and automate the administrative processes of the MPF scheme, marking the start of the MPF digital era. The South China Morning Post looks at the details of the latest changes and how they will affect employees. 1. What is MPF? The MPF System, set up in December 2000, is an important part of the city’s retirement protection framework, enabling residents to save up for retirement. Under the scheme, employees and employers are both required to make mandatory contributions of 5 per cent of the employee’s relevant income into the employee’s MPF account, subject to the relevant minimum and maximum income levels. Employers must make mandatory contributions to each employee from their own funds. They must also deduct the employee’s contributions from his or her income. For monthly paid employees, the current minimum and maximum relevant income levels are HK$7,100 (US$905) and HK$30,000 respectively. 2. What are the changes? Starting from December 21, employees will be allowed to move their entire MPF savings to a different provider once every calendar year. The arrangement, known as “full portability”, will allow eligible users to transfer both employer and employee contributions to their preferred MPF scheme. The current system follows a “semi-portability” arrangement, meaning only the employee’s portion can be moved. The new arrangement will be carried out in two phases. The first phase, starting from December 21, will cover employees who joined the workforce or changed jobs on or after May 1, 2025. The second phase, with the implementation date to be confirmed, will cover those who started their current employment before May 1, 2025. As employers’ MPF contributions can still be used to offset payments for long service or severance for the period before May 1, 2025, a legal amendment will be needed to enable “full portability” to be implemented for all employees. The government is expected to submit the legal amendment on the second phase of the arrangement in mid-2027. 3. How will employees benefit? According to Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority chairwoman Ayesha Macpherson Lau, the new arrangement will give residents better control over their MPF, encouraging them to manage their retirement savings more actively. Lawmaker Chau Siu-chung, who represents the labour constituency, said on Monday that staff would have the freedom to place their money with their preferred provider. “They can transfer their MPF savings to a trustee whom they deem to have lower administration fees, better service or higher returns,” he said. He added that individual trustees could lower their administrative fees if more competition was introduced for those services. 4. How can employees move their MPF savings to another provider? With the launch of eMPF, a centralised and digital system, employees can submit their transfer instructions via the platform. MPF derived from employees’ and employers’ mandatory contributions can be transferred to the same scheme, or to two different ones. Eligible employees who wish to transfer their MPF this year can make the transfer from December 21 to 31. Chau said the digital platform is expected to simplify the transfer process. Previously, employees had to visit the offices of service providers in person to handle the procedure. Since the launch of eMPF in June 2024, more than 2.3 million members have already registered to use the digital platform. 5. How many are eligible for the new change? About one million employees who joined the workforce or changed jobs on or after May 1 last year will be eligible for the first phase of the new arrangement when it starts on December 21. When the second phase is launched, a total of around 2.6 million employees could become eligible, according to a government document released last year. 6. How does ‘full portability’ affect employers? The authority says employers will not be affected. They do not need to be involved in the process of transferring MPF, and administrative arrangements under the scheme will remain unchanged. 7. What is the advice for employees? Lau reminded members to avoid “switching for the sake of switching” and refrain from transferring funds too frequently, as the MPF was a long-term investment. Before taking advantage of full portability, scheme members should weigh various factors, carefully compare fund choices, performance and fee levels of different MPF schemes, and make prudent decisions based on their stage in life, investment goals and risk tolerance, she said.

title: ‘Fed up’ Malaysian sultan rebukes scandal-hit pilgrimage fund, demands accountability
description: A Malaysian ruler is demanding accountability over the mismanagement of a pilgrimage fund, after a government rescue package, criminal proceedings against former officials and half-hearted reforms have fuelled concerns about political influence in an institution entrusted with the savings of millions of the country’s Muslims. Tabung Haji holds the savings of more than 9.8 million depositors and helps Malaysian Muslims finance and undertake the pilgrimage to Mecca, a religious obligation for...
content: A Malaysian ruler is demanding accountability over the mismanagement of a pilgrimage fund, after a government rescue package, criminal proceedings against former officials and half-hearted reforms have fuelled concerns about political influence in an institution entrusted with the savings of millions of the country’s Muslims. Tabung Haji holds the savings of more than 9.8 million depositors and helps Malaysian Muslims finance and undertake the pilgrimage to Mecca, a religious obligation for those with the means to make the journey. Its financial troubles required a government rescue in 2018, according to a royal commission of inquiry report released on July 29, which examined the fund’s management and operations between 2014 and 2020. Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah of Selangor expressed disappointment over the fund’s mismanagement in an interview marking his 25 years on the throne, published by state news agency Bernama on Sunday. “Likewise, there must be accountability and responsibility in managing funds meant for religious purposes,” he said, extending the principle to places of worship of all faiths and orphanages. The ruler said the abuses should not have occurred at an institution established to help Muslims save for their pilgrimage, while separately warning politicians against exploiting race and religion or drawing royalty into political disputes. “Like the rakyat, I am also fed up,” he said, using the Malay word for ordinary people, in remarks directed at excessive and unproductive politicking. “Politics should never come at the expense of racial harmony or religious understanding.” The inquiry identified political influence over profit distributions and pilgrimage charges, while also highlighting broad ministerial powers and conflicts of interest involving the fund’s subsidiaries. The government’s 2018 rescue package involved a state-owned company buying up troubled assets valued at 9.7 billion ringgit (US$2.38 billion) for 19.9 billion ringgit to plug the fund’s deficit, according to Tabung Haji. The institution has since maintained that its financial position is substantially stronger following years of recovery efforts. Former religious affairs minister Jamil Khir Baharom pleaded not guilty on September 14 to three charges of dishonestly causing the fund to dispose of 860.3 million ringgit to Saudi property company Al-Rawda between 2015 and 2017. He has maintained that decisions made during his tenure followed board recommendations and established procedures. Former chairman Abdul Azeez Abdul Rahim also pleaded not guilty on September 9 to abusing his position to secure a company chairmanship and influencing approval of a proposed 193.5 million ringgit investment. Shahelmey Yahya, a backbench MP belonging to the Barisan Nasional coalition, called for the removal of ministerial powers to issue general directions to Tabung Haji during a special parliamentary session on August 11. “An institution cannot achieve excellence when political influence is mixed into decision-making,” he told the chamber, according to Bernama. Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Hasan told parliament in an October 8 written reply that Tabung Haji had implemented 13 of the 17 inquiry recommendations assigned to it. The remaining four involved amendments to its governing law and oversight by the central bank and the Securities Commission. Raymon Ram, president of Transparency International Malaysia, said the outstanding reforms would determine who had the authority and responsibility to intervene when serious financial or governance risks were uncovered. “The 13 out of 17 recommendations represent progress, but governance reforms cannot be measured by completion percentages alone,” he said. “It should never again be possible for a serious warning to be raised without clarity over who must act.” He added that serious audit findings or regulatory warnings should automatically trigger a documented response with clear deadlines and assigned responsibilities. “We cannot have a system where everyone was warned, but ultimately no one was responsible.” Cynthia Gabriel, a partner at Malaysian law firm Halim Hong & Quek and founder of the Centre to Combat Corruption and Cronyism, said the sultan’s rebuke should be heeded, but added that the problems extended beyond Tabung Haji. “Institutional accountability is sorely lacking in our administrative system,” she said. “[Tabung Haji] is just one of many other scandals that point to poor governance, leakages, wastage and a deep-rooted problem of entitlement, entrenched with patronage and cronyism.” Gabriel argued that reforms must cover the wider network of government-linked companies (GLCs) rather than Tabung Haji alone. “I believe the GLC Act being mooted needs to clearly stipulate that political interference must be completely disallowed, in boards and in matters of business and finance,” she said.

title: Could new US investment curbs complicate China’s biotech licensing surge?
description: Chinese biotech firms face fresh headwinds in their global expansion as Washington’s proposed outbound investment restrictions threaten to disrupt deal structures, even though drug licensing agreements remain untouched for now, analysts say. The US Treasury Department’s draft rules released last week would “make it much harder for Chinese biotech firms to attract direct US investment or enter joint ventures”, according to David Zhang, an analyst at policy research firm Trivium China. US Treasury...
content: Chinese biotech firms face fresh headwinds in their global expansion as Washington’s proposed outbound investment restrictions threaten to disrupt deal structures, even though drug licensing agreements remain untouched for now, analysts say. The US Treasury Department’s draft rules released last week would “make it much harder for Chinese biotech firms to attract direct US investment or enter joint ventures”, according to David Zhang, an analyst at policy research firm Trivium China. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added biotechnology to an outbound investment screening programme, placing a broad range of transactions involving “countries of concern”, including China, under greater scrutiny. Restricted transactions included the acquisition of equity stakes and the formation of joint ventures, according to the Treasury Department. The proposals come as Washington grows increasingly concerned about the rise of China’s biotech industry, with the measures intended to “prevent our adversaries from using US investment to develop critical technologies that threaten US national security”, Bessent said last week. Chinese firms have assumed a growing role in the global biopharmaceutical industry in recent years. The value of out-licensing deals involving China-developed innovative drugs had reached US$130 billion this year, approaching the full-year total for 2025, according to China’s National Development and Reform Commission. The Treasury Department, as widely anticipated, stopped short of restricting conventional drug licensing deals, which Zhang said had been “a major driver of China’s biotech expansion in recent years”. With “commercial incentives remaining strong for US drug makers to rely on Chinese companies for promising new drug candidates”, the new rules were unlikely to lead to a “wholesale retreat from Chinese biotech”, he added. Instead, companies were likely to devote more effort to structuring cross-border deals in ways that avoided direct equity investment, Zhang said. Cross-border biotech deals had increasingly moved towards co-development arrangements and broader platform partnerships as Chinese firms’ resources and ambitions expanded, said Cui Cui, head of Asia healthcare research at Jefferies, in a note last month. Companies also face new biotech export control measures proposed by Beijing. Earlier this month, China’s Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology proposed export bans covering 14 technologies across sectors including artificial intelligence, biotechnology and photovoltaics. The restrictions would prohibit exports of certain cell and gene therapy platforms as well as small interfering RNA technology platforms. While both Chinese and US measures were “narrower than feared”, they would likely prompt companies in both countries to “recalibrate” and “protect” the flow of capital and core intellectual property, Cui said in a separate note on Friday. Morgan Xu, a partner at law firm Foley Hoag in Washington, described the latest moves by the US and China as “a curious symmetry” in an article on Sunday in Tonacea, a Chinese biopharmaceutical-focused publication. “Washington wants to restrict certain investments that could strengthen China’s technological capabilities; Beijing wants to retain control over certain foundational Chinese technologies,” Xu said. The Treasury Department’s proposed restrictions still face uncertainty, however, amid opposition from parts of the industry. “We cannot restrict our way to success … We need to ensure that we do not have an overly broad approach that would create uncertainty for innovators and investors, and that may unintentionally risk weakening US biotech competitiveness,” said John F. Crowley, president and CEO of the Biotechnology Innovation Organisation, in a statement last week after the Treasury Department unveiled the proposals. “But there’s also bipartisan political pressure for tougher restrictions, including even on licensing deals,” Zhang said. “I’d expect some version of the biotech restrictions to move forward. The bigger question is how far Treasury ultimately wants to go.”

title: Chinese video AI models beat US rivals in visual quality, but lag on safeguards: HKU study
description: Chinese AI video-generation models have surpassed leading US rivals in visual quality, but several fall behind in safety precautions, according to researchers at the University of Hong Kong. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 Pro took top spot in a ranking of 12 leading artificial intelligence video-generation models, scoring 3.84 out of 5 for visual quality. It outperformed Google DeepMind’s Veo 3.1, which scored 3.47, and OpenAI’s Sora 2 Pro, on 3.27, in a study led by Zhenhui Jack Jiang, professor of...
content: Chinese AI video-generation models have surpassed leading US rivals in visual quality, but several fall behind in safety precautions, according to researchers at the University of Hong Kong. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 Pro took top spot in a ranking of 12 leading artificial intelligence video-generation models, scoring 3.84 out of 5 for visual quality. It outperformed Google DeepMind’s Veo 3.1, which scored 3.47, and OpenAI’s Sora 2 Pro, on 3.27, in a study led by Zhenhui Jack Jiang, professor of innovation and information management at HKU’s business school. The ByteDance model also led in visual consistency, physical realism, aesthetic quality and instruction compliance, and maintained its lead when audio capabilities were factored in, scoring 3.86 against Veo’s 3.51 and Sora’s 3.35. Jiang said the ByteDance model’s performance was unexpectedly strong and “far ahead” of Chinese and American competitors. He said the primary reason for that success was likely to be ByteDance’s core business model because, as a company focused on short video, it possessed a massive volume of video training data that competitors lacked. Other Chinese models also demonstrated competitive visual performance. Vidu Q3 Pro, developed by Chinese start-up Shengshu Technology, scored 3.44 in visual-only performance and 3.49 in combined audio-video performance – ranking third in both as it narrowly trailed Veo but beat Sora. Kuaishou Technology’s Kling 3 tied with Sora for fourth place in visual-only performance at 3.27, though it slipped to sixth at 3.28 when audio capabilities were included. While the study underscored the rapid advances made by Chinese developers in a field increasingly contested by tech giants from the United States, it also revealed a gap between technical performance and content safety. The researchers found that some high-performing models generated legally prohibited visual content when presented with prompts involving extreme violence or unlawful behaviour, exposing weaknesses in safety filtering. Seedance ranked sixth among 11 models assessed for their ability to block harmful content, scoring 3.12 out of five. Vidu, with a score of 3.08, ranked seventh, and Kling, on 2.40, ninth. MiniMax’s Hailuo 2.3 – which ranked near the bottom in visual quality at 2.95 – emerged as the safest model tested, with a score of 3.63, narrowly beating Veo on 3.62 and Pika Labs’ Pika 2.2, which scored 3.52. The evaluation was conducted using 71 Chinese-language prompts covering text-to-video and image-to-video generation, with results judged by 20 human evaluators. The study assessed model versions available in April, excluding newer releases such as MiniMax’s H3. It also did not examine how differences between open-source and proprietary models could affect their safety, a growing concern as increasingly capable video-generation tools become more widely available. Jiang said high technical performance and robust safety guardrails were not mutually exclusive, adding that companies like ByteDance could strengthen safety standards without sacrificing performance. The findings come amid escalating competition and safety scrutiny across the global AI industry. Since the assessment in April, Chinese firms have rapidly upgraded their models. ByteDance launched Seedance 2.5 in July, while Kuaishou released Kling 4.0 this month, offering longer clips and better frame control. US tech giants have responded in kind, with Google launching its Omni model in May and releasing an Omni 1.1 Flash update in August. Safety remains a growing focus for developers on both sides of the Pacific. This month, ByteDance announced the creation of an alignment and preparedness team in its Seed research unit and launched a global recruitment drive for 10 researchers focused on AI safety. The move followed scrutiny sparked by Seedance 2.0’s unauthorised reproduction of copyrighted characters and celebrity likenesses. Meanwhile, OpenAI and Meta Platforms warned a US judicial panel this month that AI-generated deepfakes were becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic footage. OpenAI discontinued Sora in April, just months after its high-profile debut. ByteDance, Google, OpenAI, Shengshu, Kuaishou and MiniMax did not respond to requests for comment.

title: In Australia, Sydney’s second airport blows some passengers off course
description: Sydney’s new multibillion-dollar airport has already confused some travellers, with passengers mistaking the new facility for the Australian city’s existing airport and even booking flights to the wrong side of the country. Western Sydney International Airport, which opened at the weekend after decades of planning, is about 60km (37 miles) from the city centre, compared with just 8km for the existing Kingsford Smith Airport. The new airport operates around the clock, while most passenger flights...
content: Sydney’s new multibillion-dollar airport has already confused some travellers, with passengers mistaking the new facility for the Australian city’s existing airport and even booking flights to the wrong side of the country. Western Sydney International Airport, which opened at the weekend after decades of planning, is about 60km (37 miles) from the city centre, compared with just 8km for the existing Kingsford Smith Airport. The new airport operates around the clock, while most passenger flights at Kingsford Smith are banned between 11pm and 6am. Two Swedish students, both aged 23, discovered the difference the hard way after flying back from a weekend trip to Melbourne. Having read “Sydney West” on their boarding passes, they assumed it referred to another terminal at the familiar airport, they told broadcaster ABC in remarks published on Monday. It was only when they looked out of the window that they realised something was wrong. Their car was waiting at the other airport, almost an hour’s drive away. A traveller from New Zealand also misunderstood his destination, believing he had booked a flight to Perth in Western Australia after seeing the word “Western” on his ticket. By the time he realised his mistake, he was already heading to the new airport on Australia’s east coast. He took the mix-up in his stride, saying he was on holiday and could make the best of it. The A$5.3 billion (US$3.7 billion) airport, under construction since 2018, is intended to ease pressure on Sydney’s overcrowded aviation infrastructure. A planned rail link to the city is not yet complete, leaving passengers reliant on buses and shuttle services. Its first international flight, an Air New Zealand plane from Auckland, landed and soon afterwards flew out of the airport on Monday morning, launching a three-flights-a-week service to Sydney’s largely working-class western suburbs. “It’s not every day you get to be part of opening a brand-new international airport,” Air New Zealand chief operations officer Kate Boyer said. “Western Sydney is home to more than 2.5 million people and it’s a further gateway for Australian visitors to discover everything our country has to offer.” Qantas’ budget carrier Jetstar is now the main domestic carrier, flying to the Gold Coast, Melbourne and Brisbane. The airport says other international carriers are coming, including Singapore Airlines, Qatar Airways, Fiji Airways and VietJet. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the new airport marked a “wonderful new chapter” for Australia. It would also drive economic and jobs into western Sydney, an area often overshadowed by the city’s famed harbour and central business district, he said at the weekend. “For too long, Sydney has looked towards the harbour and the CBD. What this does is turn it around to where people live, to where jobs occur, to where investment occurs in western Sydney.” Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: 970 evacuated, 1 injured as fire breaks out at Hong Kong waste-to-energy plant
description: A fire broke out on Monday at Hong Kong’s waste-to-energy incinerator on an artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau, prompting more than 900 people to flee to safety and leaving one staff member feeling unwell from suspected heatstroke. The Integrated Waste Management Facilities Phase 1, or I·PARK1, located south of Lantau Island, also had to suspend operations following the fire. The blaze started at 12.43pm at the Integrated Waste Management Facilities Phase 1 and was upgraded to a No 3 alarm at...
content: A fire broke out on Monday at Hong Kong’s waste-to-energy incinerator on an artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau, prompting more than 900 people to flee to safety and leaving one staff member feeling unwell from suspected heatstroke. The Integrated Waste Management Facilities Phase 1, or I·PARK1, located south of Lantau Island, also had to suspend operations following the fire. The blaze started at 12.43pm at the Integrated Waste Management Facilities Phase 1 and was upgraded to a No 3 alarm at 1.24pm, according to the Fire Services Department. A No 3 alarm is the third of five levels, with five the most severe; higher alarm levels trigger the deployment of more resources. Firefighters deployed two water jets and two breathing apparatus teams to battle the flames. The fire was surrounded at 3.47pm and brought under control at 4.18pm. It was largely extinguished by 4.45pm. About 970 people were evacuated, while authorities said one staff member at the facility felt unwell because of the heat and was taken to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan. The employee, 60, suffered suspected heatstroke while helping with firefighting efforts, a police source said. Preliminary information indicated the blaze started on the roof of the area housing the third incineration module in the main incinerator building, the Environmental Protection Department (EPD) said. It said the contractor activated emergency response procedures, including notifying the Fire Services Department, deploying trained emergency personnel to contain the blaze, while evacuating about 970 construction workers and operational staff from the island. All major systems were also shut down. I·PARK1 temporarily suspended waste reception services. The department said it was reviewing the effects of the fire on the facility’s operations. Meanwhile, the department coordinated an extension of operating hours at the West New Territories Landfill Extension to ensure the city’s overall waste treatment services continue as normal. The police source said the fire broke out in a 14-storey building that was still under construction and contained building materials. Initial investigations suggested the fire started on the roof before spreading to lower floors. The EPD said the cause of the fire remained under investigation. It said it told the contractor to submit a fire incident report within seven days and would conduct a joint investigation with the fire department. It would also assess the extent of the damage and urge the contractor to carry out repair works as soon as possible. The waste management facility is the city’s first large-scale waste-to-energy plant. Built on a roughly 12-hectare artificial island off Shek Kwu Chau in Hong Kong’s southwestern waters, it is designed to handle up to 3,000 tonnes of waste a day. Costing HK$31.3 billion (US$4 billion) and taking more than seven years to build, the facility began operations in December last year as part of the government’s plan to phase out reliance on landfills by 2035. I·PARK1 comprises three incineration modules. The first module has commenced trial operations, while the remaining two modules began system testing and trial operations in the first quarter. Once fully operational, the facility is expected to process up to 3,000 tonnes of municipal solid waste per day and generate about 480 million kilowatt‑hours of surplus electricity annually for the city’s existing power grid, enough to meet the needs of 100,000 households.

title: Discovery of baby orangutans in India exposes booming illegal pet trade
description: The villagers who first spotted the five baby orangutans in a casuarina forest in India in early September were puzzled by their reddish hair and unfamiliar faces. The three males and two females, aged six to eight months – were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700km (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India. They are now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been...
content: The villagers who first spotted the five baby orangutans in a casuarina forest in India in early September were puzzled by their reddish hair and unfamiliar faces. The three males and two females, aged six to eight months – were left on a plantation in eastern India’s Odisha, over 2,700km (1,700 miles) from their native rainforests in Borneo and Sumatra, evidence of a growing illicit trade of apes being trafficked into India. They are now at an Indian zoo, where keepers reportedly have been playing classical music to soothe them. Wild orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, where they sustain rainforests by spreading seeds across vast areas, allowing trees to regenerate and store carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. The species is critically endangered, threatened by severe habitat loss. There are about 119,500 orangutans left in the wild, according to conservation organisation WWF. The global illegal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth US$34 billion annually, according to a 2026 study by National University of Singapore researchers, and India is emerging as an important market. Experts say seizures reflect a fraction of a booming trade in exotic or non-native animals sold to wealthy Indian collectors. India’s wildlife laws were mainly designed to protect native species such as elephants, rhinoceroses and tigers from being trafficked overseas. Gaps in controls on imported animals complicate efforts to trace the origins of exotic wildlife. In 2022, two juvenile Sumatran orangutans were found in boxes at a checkpoint between the northeastern states of Assam and Mizoram. Another was rescued in Mizoram in 2023, and a young orangutan was found in a flat near Mumbai in November 2024. At least 23 gibbons were seized at Indian airports in 2025, according to an analysis by non-profit Wildlife Trust of India. In May 2026, Egyptian authorities seized three India-bound, sedated baby chimpanzees. “India has become the No 1 destination for the live trade of primates,” said Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at the Orangutan Information Centre in Indonesia’s North Sumatra province. ‘Status symbols’ Wealthy collectors who prize rare animals as “status symbols” were driving the trade in trafficked animals from Southeast Asia, a regional hub for trade in species from elsewhere, said Uttara Mendiratta, a wildlife trafficking researcher in India. Expanding tourism has led to more direct flights to India through cities like Bangkok and Kuala Lumpur, giving traffickers routes that are faster, albeit riskier, than overland border crossings. “The profit margins are so high that they can afford to lose a few [animals] and still make a profit,” Mendiratta said. Questions also surround legal trade. Most commercial trade in orangutans is banned, but exceptions exist for captive-bred animals. India imported 41 orangutans between 2021 and 2024, according to CITES, the global treaty regulating trade in endangered wildlife. Sinan Serhadli, a wildlife trafficking expert at Indonesia’s Orangutan Information Centre, questioned whether the animals were legitimately bred in captivity. “It just shows the loopholes. And … corruption as well,” he said. The CITES Secretariat declined to comment, saying the matter was under review. Concerned about diseases spreading from animals to people during the Covid-19 pandemic, India allowed people to register their exotic animals in 2020 without proving their origins. They can report births, deaths and breeding of non-native species through an online portal. But the government lacks enough staff and expertise to adequately inspect collections and identify global species. The system also left room for trafficked animals to be misrepresented as registered ones, Mendiratta said. India tightened its wildlife laws in 2022, giving authorities clearer powers to seize illegally traded exotic animals and prosecute traffickers. But by then, it already had “opened the floodgates”, she said. India’s exotic pet trade “sits at the crossroads of biodiversity loss, unbridled community demand, and organised criminal activity”, said a 2026 report by Humane World for Animals India. India’s forest ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Return trip Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “active steps” to bring home the five baby orangutans found in Odisha, sending experts to verify their origins and assess their health. Their mothers were likely killed, traumatising infants that normally would depend on them for up to nine years. Conservationists have successfully returned orangutans to Indonesia from Thailand, but so far only one has been repatriated from India. When one orangutan was transferred last year to a private wildlife facility known as Vantara, run by billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s family, India’s federal wildlife officials and India’s CITES authority were not informed, a federal wildlife official in New Delhi wrote in a report. Officials concerned over the orangutan’s care at a local public zoo ordered it transferred to Vantara, which describes itself as a wildlife rescue and rehabilitation centre. The orangutan was treated for a respiratory infection and pneumonia before it was returned to Indonesia on October 19 after 19 months at the private facility. India’s CITES authority did not respond to a request for comment. Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) wildlife facility in western India, has over 150,000 animals and over 2,000 different species. It has faced international scrutiny over its animal acquisitions. In November 2025, CITES questioned shipments to Vantara that included snow leopards from Germany, a bonobo said to have been bred in Iraq and a gorilla reportedly from Haiti. The primates are not native to those countries. India’s Supreme Court cleared Vantara of wildlife trafficking and animal mistreatment allegations last year. In September, 27 wildlife conservation and animal welfare organisations issued a letter urging the facility to end imports of wild animals, raising concerns about endangered species and animal welfare. The groups said they had “never encountered anything comparable to the scale and diversity” of Vantara’s imports, citing more than 60,000 animals acquired in a short period. One controversial acquisition, according to Vantara’s 2024-25 inventory, is a Tapanuli orangutan, the world’s rarest great ape. Recognised as a distinct species only in 2017, it is only found in a small area of Indonesia’s Sumatra island, where 716 remain in the wild. “The Tapanuli orangutan is hovering just above extinction,” said Serhadli, whose organisation is one of the few that works with the species. The one at Vantara would be the only Tapanuli orangutan in captivity. CITES trade data shows that the animal left Indonesia in 2024 and arrived in India via the United Arab Emirates. “That can’t happen legally,” Serhadli said. Indonesia’s Ministry of Forestry said it was taking “seriously” reports that a Tapanuli orangutan might be outside the country. It said it could not confirm the animal’s species, origins or how it got to India. An investigation would require checking permits and transfer records, along with scientific testing, the ministry said. Neither Vantara nor Indonesia’s CITES authority responded to requests for comment.

title: Top bankers to gather in Hong Kong to learn how city has rethought ‘playbook’
description: Around 280 of the world’s top bankers, including 120 group chairmen and CEOs, will gather in Hong Kong next week to learn how the city has been rethinking its playbook as it moves forward, Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said on Monday. The financial luminaries include Morgan Stanley chairman Ted Pick, Goldman Sachs chairman David Solomon and...
content: Around 280 of the world’s top bankers, including 120 group chairmen and CEOs, will gather in Hong Kong next week to learn how the city has been rethinking its playbook as it moves forward, Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) chief executive Eddie Yue Wai-man said on Monday. This year’s summit will host the biggest number of group-level executives since its inaugural forum in 2022. The financial luminaries include Morgan Stanley chairman Ted Pick, Goldman Sachs chairman David Solomon and Blackstone president and COO John Gray, who will attend the fifth edition of the city’s Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit, Yue said. The summit is set to run from November 2 to 4. Titled “Rethinking the Playbook”, the summit takes place shortly after Hong Kong announced its first five-year plan to develop itself as a technology hub and a leading financial centre in September. “The leaders will also experience first-hand how Hong Kong has been rethinking its playbook to transform its economy through innovation and technology, and to stay competitive and forward-looking as an international financial centre,” Yue said in an article posted to the HKMA website on Monday. “We keep consolidating our strengths while continuing to push the frontiers that include the world’s leading offshore yuan hub with ever-expanding depth and reach, a more vibrant fixed income market, an enabling and resilient digital assets and payments ecosystem and new opportunities in gold and commodities business.” Besides presenting Hong Kong’s new development plans to the world’s top bankers, a panel of mainland Chinese financial regulators is expected to convene on November 3, but no names have been released yet. The attendance of high-level mainland officials or regulators has been a feature of the summit for some time. Yue previously said this was a highlight of the event, attracting global bankers to acquire first-hand information about government policies. Regular attendees such as HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery, Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters and BNP Paribas chairman Jean Lemierre will return, according to the programme. Other top bankers, including UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti, State Street chairman Ronald O’Hanley and JPMorgan Chase vice-chairman Daniel Pinto, will speak during the summit. Global financial markets have undergone multiple shock waves and tectonic shifts brought by the relentless advancement of technology Eddie Yue Wai-man, HKMA The welcome dinner on November 2 will take place at the Henderson in Central, while the main summit ­discussion on November 3 and 4 will be held at the Four Seasons Hotel. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu will address the main summit on November 3, while Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po will give a keynote speech the next day. The summit was launched in 2022 to signal Hong Kong was “back in business” after the Covid-19 pandemic. “Since the inaugural edition that marked Hong Kong’s recovery from Covid, the global financial markets have undergone multiple shock waves and tectonic shifts brought by the relentless advancement of technology,” Yue said. He recalled the past four years of summits had been held through challenging times, with regional military conflicts and trade war, as well as blockchain-based technology that had the potential to restructure global financial markets. “Yet the one thing that brings about the most impactful and enduring changes, I would argue, is AI,” Yue said, adding that the investments in artificial intelligence as well as the winners and losers across different industrial sectors will have a huge impact on labour and productivity that add uncertainties and risks in the financial markets. He said these changes underlined this year’s theme. “Over these three days, financial leaders will discuss key macroeconomic trends, financial market shifts and technological advances that are shaping emerging opportunities and risks across various sectors, asset classes and geographies,” Yue said.

To stay ahead, Samil PwC...
content: China’s expanding semiconductor industry is fuelling anxiety in South Korea, where a new report from PwC has warned local chipmakers to defend profitability as Chinese rivals scale up production and strengthen market share. Samil PwC, the South Korean member firm of the global consultancy, said in a report made public on Monday that Chinese competition would likely heat up first in the areas of conventional memory, mature-node manufacturing, and packaging and testing. To stay ahead, Samil PwC urged South Korean semiconductor companies to sharpen cost competitiveness in commodity memory while doubling down on cutting-edge sectors such as advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which are used alongside AI processors in a stacked configuration. China still lagged in these advanced segments, where customer validation and stable, high-yield mass production remained barriers, the report noted. The warning follows remarks earlier this month by SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won, who said Chinese rivals ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and Yangtze Memory Technologies Co (YMTC) were rapidly catching up. South Korea risked surrendering market share if Chinese competitors or US rival Micron Technology expanded capacity faster, Chey warned, according to Yonhap News Agency. He also cast doubt on the efficacy of US-led export restrictions, noting that CXMT and YMTC had made steady progress despite years of technology curbs. As pressure mounts, South Korea’s leading players are moving to protect their turf. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix were both upgrading their manufacturing facilities in China to produce more advanced NAND flash memory to counter YMTC and to meet AI-driven storage demand, Reuters reported last week. Samsung was retooling its Xian facility to fabricate 286-layer chips, while SK Hynix was preparing to produce chips with at least 240 layers at its Dalian plant, the report said, citing unnamed sources. Both companies said the upgrades were carried out in consultation with Washington. At the same time, Chinese memory specialists are pushing closer to the technological frontier. CXMT, the country’s leading producer of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), announced plans earlier this month to debut server memory using an advanced 4F² architecture by the end of this year. The space-saving design, which packs memory cells closer together to boost density, is also under development by Samsung and SK Hynix. Data showed that Chinese memory makers were already converting technical gains into commercial share. CXMT captured 10 per cent of global DRAM revenue in the second quarter, more than double the 4 per cent recorded a year earlier and enough to make it the world’s fourth-largest supplier, behind Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron Technology, according to Counterpoint Research. In flash storage, YMTC ranked third globally by NAND shipment volume in the second quarter, trailing only Samsung and SK Hynix, including its US-based Solidigm subsidiary. YMTC’s share of global NAND revenue climbed to 14 per cent in the first quarter of this year, up from 9 per cent a year earlier. Counterpoint projected earlier this month that YMTC’s server-related revenue could approach 39 per cent of its total sales by 2028 – up from virtually zero in 2024 – fuelled by an expansion into storage for AI data centres. MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint, said YMTC was benefiting from rising prices and stronger domestic order volumes, with enterprise storage presenting a lucrative channel to ride the AI wave. However, winning over international clients beyond China would remain a key test of YMTC’s ability to challenge Samsung on the world stage, he added.

title: Suspected murder of man at Malaysian underground gig raises safety concerns
description: The death of a 21-year-old delivery rider at an underground gig in Malaysia, now being investigated as murder, has highlighted concerns over crowd safety and regulatory flaws in the country’s independent live music scene, industry players say. Police reclassified the case on Sunday, four days after the man died from head injuries sustained at the gig in the southern state of Melaka, where the event was reportedly held without the necessary permits and local authority approval. The...
content: The death of a 21-year-old delivery rider at an underground gig in Malaysia, now being investigated as murder, has highlighted concerns over crowd safety and regulatory flaws in the country’s independent live music scene, industry players say. Police reclassified the case on Sunday, four days after the man died from head injuries sustained at the gig in the southern state of Melaka, where the event was reportedly held without the necessary permits and local authority approval. The reclassification followed an initial investigation into a charge of voluntarily causing grievous hurt using a dangerous weapon or means. Police detained 10 people aged between 18 and 25 on October 18 and 19 to help with the investigation, said Melaka Tengah district police chief Assistant Commissioner Halim Abas. The delivery rider was injured at the event in Kampung Jawa on October 17 and died at Melaka Hospital on October 21, local media reported. Halim said investigations revealed that the event had reportedly been held without a police permit or approval from local authorities. “Further investigations are ongoing,” he said in a statement. Kafe Tuju management, the gig’s organiser and a cafe operator, said on Friday that it was assisting police with the investigation and providing relevant evidence, including CCTV footage of the incident. “From the footage shown, it is clearly an unintentional incident where the victim was seen moshing in front of the stage when he and another person collided, resulting in the victim falling to the ground headfirst,” it said in a statement. The management said the show stopped completely when the incident happened, and other attendees and members of the organising crew helped the victim. “The victim was seen exiting the venue by himself without assistance, and we were told that he has been rushed to the hospital for further treatment.” The management told This Week in Asia that the incident took place in an event space behind its cafe in Kampung Jawa. “The event was not held at our cafe,” it said. Shamil Yusof, director of Neptunes Presents Malaysia, a concert promotion and live events company, said smaller independent gigs had long been central to the country’s local music scene, but some organisers operated without the necessary permits and licences. He said navigating licensing requirements could be particularly challenging for newer organisers, with permit costs and administrative procedures adding to the difficulties of staging smaller events. “However, it has remained somewhat guerrilla across the years, with [some] organisers not applying for the essential permits and licences for it,” Shamil said. Shamil, who has more than two decades of experience organising concerts, said the incident could lead to organisers reassessing the independent music ecosystem and improving support for smaller promoters, while encouraging authorities to streamline the permit approval process. He said event organisers bore the main responsibility for crowd safety, although newer promoters were not always familiar with licensing requirements and could struggle to navigate the regulatory process. “Perhaps down the line there could be methods to ease their [small organisers] journey and help them improve operations and safety and convenience of everyone in the industry,” Shamil said.

title: Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, known for seeking China ties, dies at 90

Following news of his death, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed “deep sorrow” when speaking to reporters in Tokyo, praising him as...
content: Former Japanese prime minister Yasuo Fukuda, who used ⁠his brief period ⁠in office to seek ⁠closer ties with Asian neighbours, particularly China, has died at the age of 90, according to the Nikkei business daily on Monday. The Japanese politician, the first son of a prime minister to become one ‌himself, died on Thursday from heart failure, the Nikkei reported. Following news of his death, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed “deep sorrow” when speaking to reporters in Tokyo, praising him as a leader who “worked to articulate Japan’s position on various international issues and enhance its standing in the international community”. Becoming prime minister on the sudden resignation of Shinzo Abe for health reasons in 2007, Fukuda lasted less than a year – a tenure even shorter than his father Takeo’s two-year stint. A graduate in economics from Tokyo’s prestigious Waseda University, Fukuda spent nearly ⁠two decades working his way up the ranks of an oil company – including ‌a two-year posting in the United States – before resigning to become a political secretary when his father became prime minister in 1976. Elected ‌to Japan’s more powerful lower house of parliament in 1990, Fukuda was ⁠chief cabinet ⁠secretary from 2000 to 2004, resigning as one of several cabinet ministers to admit not having paid into ‌the pension system. Known for his testy manner, the bespectacled Fukuda drew criticism in 2003 for off-the-record comments ‌in ‌which he suggested women who dressed provocatively were asking to be raped. When Fukuda ‌succeeded Abe, he joked he might have drawn the short straw in assuming ⁠office given the divided parliament and opposition parties’ ability to delay legislation. Frustrated with the ⁠stalled legislative process, Fukuda resigned in 2008, the second of six prime ministers to quit after only around a year in office. Fukuda made efforts to develop ties with China, carrying on the work by Abe, who had himself taken over from Junichiro Koizumi just a year earlier. Japan-China relations had been strained under Koizumi due to his repeated visits to Tokyo’s Yasukuni Shrine, which honours Class-A war criminals along with the war dead. Known as ‌a diplomatic dove, Fukuda visited China three months after becoming prime minister in September 2007 and invited then Chinese president Hu Jintao to visit Japan. Hu visited the country in May 2008, becoming the first Chinese head of state to do so in a decade. After leaving office, Fukuda ‌made several visits to China in an effort to improve often fraught relations. Fukuda leaves a son, Tatsuo, who is also a lawmaker and has been viewed as a potential future prime minister. Additional reporting by Kyodo

title: Hong Kong positioned as green gateway for belt and road firms: John Lee
description: Hong Kong is well-positioned to help companies deploy green services and technologies across belt and road countries, the city’s leader and a mainland Chinese official have said, with authorities set to provide training to at least five firms to promote green solutions overseas. Both officials made the remarks at the Belt and Road Green Innovation Conference, which opened in Hong Kong on Monday. It is the first time the event has been held outside the mainland, as the city seeks to act as a...
content: Hong Kong is well-positioned to help companies deploy green services and technologies across belt and road countries, the city’s leader and a mainland Chinese official have said, with authorities set to provide training to at least five firms to promote green solutions overseas. Both officials made the remarks at the Belt and Road Green Innovation Conference, which opened in Hong Kong on Monday. It is the first time the event has been held outside the mainland, as the city seeks to act as a bridge for expanding the global market for green technology. More than 400 officials and experts are expected to attend the conference. The Belt and Road Initiative is China’s plan to grow global trade. “From finance to green transformation, Hong Kong is well placed to serve as a superconnector and super value-adder, connecting people and opportunities and helping turn collaboration into concrete results,” Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said. “In building a greener, more prosperous and sustainable future, Hong Kong is your reliable partner. We look forward to continuing to collaborate, contribute and connect with you across the Belt and Road Initiative and beyond.” Lee added that green transformation was a shared endeavour and that multilateral collaboration could achieve more than a unilateral approach. He said the government attached great importance to sustainable development and the city would continue to promote green transformation and innovation. Lee said Hong Kong would “leverage its status as a centre for green and sustainable finance, and actively explore cross-boundary carbon trading, to support the country in building a carbon market of greater international influence”. China’s minister of ecology and environment, Huang Runqiu, echoed Lee’s remarks at the event. “Hong Kong has served as a major global financial and trading hub, a magnet for top international tech talent, and a springboard for China’s opening-up,” he said. “The city is expected to leverage its distinctive advantages to act as a green connector, advancing global policy exchange, knowledge-sharing and pragmatic collaboration.” Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan also said the government aimed to halve its carbon emissions while working with mainland partners and the city’s two power companies to develop new zero-carbon energy. In this year’s policy address, Lee announced the launch of the Green Technology Bridgehead Programme, which will bring together mainland and overseas technology companies using Hong Kong as a springboard to “go global” or “land” on the mainland. “By showcasing green solutions and technology applications through EcoPark, and taking advantage of Hong Kong’s legal, financial and environmental expertise, these companies can export green solutions to B&R countries,” Lee said in the blueprint released in September. As part of the drive, authorities also established a Belt and Road Sustainable Green Development Training Centre in Hong Kong in May to offer courses to personnel from countries along the route. According to authorities on Monday, at least five mainland and overseas companies are expected to join another programme next year and receive training to help them promote their green services overseas. The training will cover environmental protection technologies, green finance, legal frameworks and the compliance requirements for overseas expansion. As of last month, more than 100 belt and road firms with a combined market capitalisation exceeding HK$340 billion (US$43.6 billion) were listed in the city, while some infrastructure firms from Central Asian states were also eyeing a debut on the local exchange. The belt and road scheme, launched by President Xi Jinping in late 2013, aims to improve trade and economic integration across Asia, Europe and Africa. Meanwhile, the 21st Eco Expo Asia 2026 opened on Monday for a four-day run at AsiaWorld-Expo under the theme “Connecting the World for a Sustainable Future”. The event is jointly organised by the Trade Development Council and Messe Frankfurt (HK), and co-organised by the Environment and Ecology Bureau. More than 340 exhibitors from 15 countries and regions are taking part in the event, where government departments are also showcasing their innovative policies and measures in environmental protection and carbon neutrality. Among the exhibits, the Environmental Protection Department displayed four robots designed for different purposes, including environmental pollution detection and underground drainage system inspection.

title: China’s Communist Party opens fifth plenum with focus on discipline and loyalty to Xi
description: The Communist Party has started a key four-day conclave focused on party discipline and fighting corruption, as official media outlets say adherence to the party’s leadership under President Xi Jinping is key to the country’s success. The meeting – the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee – began in Beijing on Monday, according to state news agency Xinhua. It said the main agenda for the plenum included a work report by the Politburo to the Central Committee and the...
content: The Communist Party has started a key four-day conclave focused on party discipline and fighting corruption, as official media outlets say adherence to the party’s leadership under President Xi Jinping is key to the country’s success. The meeting – the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s 20th Central Committee – began in Beijing on Monday, according to state news agency Xinhua. It said the main agenda for the plenum included a work report by the Politburo to the Central Committee and the adoption of a document aimed at “deepening party self-governance”. Xinhua said Xi, who is also the party’s leader, delivered a work report to the plenary session and introduced the draft document. Discussions are expected to focus on internal party governance, discipline and political loyalty, with the outcomes to be released in a plenum communique on Thursday, the closing day of the event. As the party holds the plenum, its mouthpiece, the People’s Daily, published a long commentary under the byline Ren Zhongping that discussed the importance of “deepening party self-governance”. The byline means “Important Commentary of People’s Daily” in Chinese, suggesting the article carries particular weight. The commentary said that since the party’s 18th National Congress in 2012, Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building had provided guidance for the party’s self-governance. The doctrine was formally introduced in June this year. “In tackling corruption, the greatest threat facing the party, [it] has waged an unprecedented anti-corruption campaign with a sense of mission and responsibility to ‘offend thousands rather than let down 1.4 billion people’,” the state commentary said. It also outlined the party’s disciplinary demands on cadres, including “efforts to crack down on improper dining and drinking”, “cracking down on the acceptance of gifts in violation of regulations” and the pursuit of showy but ineffective projects intended to boost officials’ political achievements. The article noted that establishing obedience to the party’s central leadership had also been a top priority of party-building efforts under Xi. “Upholding the centralised and unified leadership of the party’s Central Committee is an important component of Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building and the supreme principle of party leadership,” it said. It noted that the anti-corruption campaign over the past decade had been successful. “The party has effectively resolved prominent contradictions and problems affecting its long-term governance, the country’s long-term stability and the well-being of the people, and eliminated serious hidden dangers within the party, the state and the military,” the commentary said. China’s military leadership has been severely shaken by a new round of anti-corruption investigations since 2022. Following the downfall of Central Military Commission vice-chairman Zhang Youxia and commission member Liu Zhenli this year, only two members remain on the seven-member commission, including Xi. The official commentary attributed these achievements fundamentally to the “Two Establishes”, establishing Xi as the core of the Communist Party and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as the party’s guiding ideology. Drawing parallels between the Long March and the potential crises facing China’s future development, the article stressed the need to continue strengthening party building, particularly upholding the authority of the party’s core. The commentary said the “Two Safeguards” – a phrase that means safeguarding Xi’s status and the party’s leadership – would ensure party stability amid crises and victories amid turmoil. It said Beijing’s handling of regional conflict and disruption to the global energy market were examples of success. The present 205-member Central Committee has been hit by an unprecedented wave of anti-corruption investigations. According to a South China Morning Post tally, 35 full members of the committee have either been placed under investigation or stripped of their seats in the national legislature, with many accused of disloyalty to the party’s central leadership. Some of the 35 are expected to have their removal from the Central Committee formally confirmed at this week’s plenum.

title: Cooler than Tokyo: Sendai named Japan’s most comfortable city amid record heat
description: As days of dangerous heat become more frequent in Japan, Sendai has emerged as the most comfortable city, with a climate that is “not too hot and not too cold”.
