Citing Japan Meteorological Agency data, the newspaper reported that Sendai had only 31 midsummer days and no midwinter...
content: As days of dangerous heat become more frequent in Japan, Sendai has emerged as the most comfortable city, with a climate that is “not too hot and not too cold”. The Miyagi prefectural capital, about 300km (186 miles) from Tokyo, has the best weather, according to the Asahi newspaper, with the lowest number of midsummer and midwinter days among 11 major cities in the nation. Citing Japan Meteorological Agency data, the newspaper reported that Sendai had only 31 midsummer days and no midwinter days between September 2025 and August this year. Midsummer days are logged when the temperature goes above 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), while midwinter days are when it falls below 0 degrees. Cities in the Tohoku region, which includes Sendai, generally did well weather-wise. Aomori had the second fewest extreme temperature days – 39 – in the same period, followed by Akita at 46 and Morioka at 48. Sendai’s mild weather makes it a comfortable city for living, the city government promotes on its official website. “It is my impression that there are many people planning to relocate to avoid the severe heat in Tokyo, and the pleasant climate is one of the reasons they choose Miyagi,” said Kuniko Isago, a counsellor at the Miyagi relocation support centre in Tokyo who helps those looking to relocate from the Tokyo metropolitan area. Tokyo had the fourth most midsummer days last year, at 71, behind Osaka, Nagoya and Fukuoka. It had no midwinter days. This year’s summer was the fifth-hottest ever in Japan, according to the weather agency. In April, after Japan experienced its hottest summer on record – 41.8 degrees in Isesaki, Gunma prefecture – the agency officially adopted the term kokushobi or “cruelly hot day” to describe days when the maximum temperature is 40 degrees or higher, according to nippon.com. From July to August, kokushobi were observed at 36 points across Japan, mainly in the Kyushu and Tokai regions. And while the heatstroke alert was issued 36 times in Tokyo and 27 times in Aichi prefecture this summer, Miyagi saw only three. Sendai’s average maximum summer temperature was 26.8 degrees, the lowest since 2020. The rainy season ended on August 4 in the southern Tohoku region, 11 days later than average, according to the Sendai District Meteorological Observatory. It was followed by cool winds from a high-pressure system. Meanwhile, Tokyo marked its hottest July 1 ever – at 36.8 degrees. Temperatures in the capital topped 30 degrees on Wednesday, the latest in the year a midsummer day had ever been recorded, Agence France-Presse reported. If the weather proves a draw, it would be good news for Sendai – especially after its population declined for the first time since records began in 1920. According to the 2025 National Census, released by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications on October 1, the population of Sendai City was 1,096,146 – a decrease of 558 from the previous census five years ago, national TV station TBS reported.

title: Saudi-led coalition hits Houthi missile sites after Riyadh targeted again
description: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis struck several of the group’s missile launchers and storage facilities, a spokesman said on Monday, while the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on Riyadh’s international airport. The coalition’s operation came a day after explosions rattled Saudi Arabia’s capital and authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a “hostile aerial threat” to the city, which has been heavily targeted by the Houthis in recent weeks. The...
content: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis struck several of the group’s missile launchers and storage facilities, a spokesman said on Monday, while the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on Riyadh’s international airport. The coalition’s operation came a day after explosions rattled Saudi Arabia’s capital and authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a “hostile aerial threat” to the city, which has been heavily targeted by the Houthis in recent weeks. The Saudi-led military coalition’s spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X on Monday that the operation had destroyed four ballistic missile launchers, as well as a missile depot and tunnels used by the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen. The operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control,” he added. The group has carried out waves of strikes on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. “Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” al-Maliki also said on Monday. The airport reopened and fights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target”. On Monday, the Houthis said once again they had attacked the airport “with a ballistic missile, striking the target with precision”, according to a post by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on social media. He said the Houthis had also struck oil pumping stations with drones. On Sunday, the Houthis had said they launched an attack on the airport in Riyadh, after the kingdom announced flights were resuming. The airport closure had been a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers. The Dakar Rally also joined a growing list of events that were cancelled, postponed or relocated in the fallout from the war. Saree had warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”. “The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport,” the spokesman said. Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider US-Iran war that erupted in February. As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and discussed a key air defence system. Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said. Greece has deployed a battery to operate the US-made Patriot air defence system in Yanbu, a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast. On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles. “The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning – may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait told Agence France-Presse on Sunday on condition of anonymity. The kingdom’s civil defence agency later said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles. Images released by the kingdom’s official press agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

title: In South Korea, jail time awaits Halloween police impersonators

Now, as Seoul prepares for its fourth Halloween since the disaster, police have launched a week-long nationwide crackdown on imitation police uniforms and equipment, aiming to stop any such confusion from happening again. The nationwide operation, announced by the National Police Agency on Sunday, runs until Monday next week. More than 4,500...
content: Four years ago, party-goers dressed as police officers were reportedly mistaken for the real thing amid a deadly crowd crush in South Korea’s capital. Now, as Seoul prepares for its fourth Halloween since the disaster, police have launched a week-long nationwide crackdown on imitation police uniforms and equipment, aiming to stop any such confusion from happening again. The nationwide operation, announced by the National Police Agency on Sunday, runs until Monday next week. More than 4,500 officers are also being deployed to Itaewon, Hongdae, Seongsu-dong, Myeong-dong and Ikseon-dong to ensure crowd safety, Yonhap reported. The crowd crush in Itaewon on October 29, 2022 killed more than 150 people. Confusion over imitation police uniforms hindered official rescue efforts, according to The Korea Times. Wearing or owning an imitation police uniform is a criminal offence in South Korea, with penalties ranging up to six months in prison or a fine of up to 3 million won (US$2,300). A separate law bars civilians from wearing military uniforms or clothing that could be confused with them. As part of this year’s crackdown, police are working with the Korea Online Shopping Association to monitor 54 major online retailers and block searches for terms such as “police uniform”, according to The Korea Times. Officers would also patrol popular Seoul party spots such as Itaewon and Hongdae to ensure compliance, the paper reported. A police official quoted by The Korea Herald urged party-goers not to wear Halloween costumes that could cause alarm or “stir unease”, including those that featured prop guns or knives. Police-themed outfits, even those that do not legally count as imitation uniforms, could be mistaken for genuine attire at night or in crowded areas, officials warned. Patrols have also been stepped up in Seoul to ease public anxiety after a series of stabbing attacks, The Korea Herald reported. The latest, at a shopping centre in Incheon on October 13, left eight people injured. Vehicle access to five of Seoul’s busiest districts will also be restricted from Friday to Monday as part of the police operation, according to Yonhap. Meanwhile, the National Fire Agency has announced a parallel crowd safety support plan covering 28 priority areas chosen by the Ministry of the Interior and Safety – Itaewon and Hongdae among them. A “Halloween situation task force” will oversee the national response to any mass casualty incident, according to local news outlet Chosun Biz, with 19 city and provincial fire headquarters setting up their own on-site task forces to monitor crowds in real time. Inspectors will check pinch points and bottlenecks, and ambulances will be pre-positioned in key areas, the outlet reported. “Protecting the public’s safety during the Halloween period, when crowds concentrate, is the most important duty of the fire service,” said Choi Yong-chol, commissioner of the National Fire Agency, according to Chosun Biz. “We will thoroughly block risk factors in advance, and in the event of any situation, we will do our utmost to protect the public’s lives and safety through proactive responses.”

content: A 26-year-old warehouse worker has been injured in Hong Kong after being chased by three dogs and bitten by one of them on his way to work. According to a source, police received a report at around 8am on Monday from the victim, surnamed Leung, saying one of the dogs had pounced on him as he was walking towards his workplace at a logistics company in Yuen Long’s Kam Pok Road. Paramedics arrived at the scene and found the victim with minor wounds. He was sent to Pok Oi Hospital in Yuen Long for treatment. The source said the man had been bitten on the left shin by a six-year-old, 1.2-metre-long (4-foot) female mongrel. The dog was captured by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department for inspection. The incident is the latest in a series of reported dog attacks in recent months. Last month, a pack of dogs was suspected to have attacked a 27-year-old woman, who was found unconscious beside a bicycle in Yuen Long and later died. Surveillance footage showed she had been chased by three canines. In August, a large unleashed mastiff-type dog fatally mauled two smaller pets in Yuen Long, leading to the arrest of its owner. A few days later, a 33-year-old woman who operated a canine training centre in Ta Kwu Ling, North district, was attacked by a dog at the facility and later found dead nearby.

title: ‘Passing down of the torch’ to young Asian Games winners bodes well for Hong Kong: John Lee
description: Chief executive proud of athletes who competed in Japan, notably those who contributed to record medal haul and produced ‘historic moments’.
content: Hong Kong’s athletes were praised for producing “a beautiful harvest of medals” at this year’s Asian Games, and the success of the delegation’s younger members bode well for the future, the city’s leader said on Monday. A first tennis, a rugby sevens three-peat, combined with success on the water, in the pool, and on the squash court all led to a historic tally of 54 medals and a record number of gold over a fortnight in Japan. While the rise of the city’s younger athletes was in many ways a continuation of the success achieved in Hangzhou three years ago, the number who medalled in Nagoya and beyond was not overlooked by Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu during a ceremony honouring the 580-strong squad, who competed across 15 sports. Addressing a host of officials and athletes at Kowloon Park Sports Centre, Lee said he was proud of all those who brought glory to the city, and highlighted several “historic moments” at the recent Games. “There was a historic men’s singles gold medal in tennis; the men’s rugby team completed a three-peat; we amassed our very first gold-and-silver tally in mixed doubles in squash, and rowing, sailing as well as windsurfing all reaped a bountiful harvest of medals,” Lee said. “I am also very happy to see many young talents emerging, and experienced seniors leading the newcomers to fight side by side, which reflects the passing down of the torch in sports.” He also took time to thank the teams behind the athletes, and hailed the efforts of the city’s Olympic Committee, Hong Kong Sports Institute and respective National Sports Associations, and reiterated his plans – as revealed in his Policy Address last month – that the government would continue to invest in providing training and support so that athletes could compete without worry. Of the Hong Kong medallists, many from most of the medal-winning sports, including cycling, fencing, karate, rowing, sailing, squash, swimming, table tennis, tennis, triathlon and wushu, were born after the millennium. One of those was fencer Harris Ho Shing-him, who won a men’s foil team silver medal with experienced pair Ryan Choi Chun-yin and Cheung Ka-long and fellow youngster Leung Chin-yu, and often took on the role of closing the match ahead of his senior teammates. Ho’s exploits have earned him a huge amount of media as well as social attention, but the 17-year-old said he was unfazed. “I wouldn’t say there was too much pressure. I don’t really like reading about me on social media, so I always just swipe away immediately,” the left-handed fencer said. “Since I wasn’t paying much attention to what was said about me, I did not feel too much of the influence either. “It was my first Asian Games, and I think the biggest takeaway was realising that I wouldn’t be too nervous if I was asked to close out a bout. I was asked to take on the same role in the recent World Cup in Japan, and there wasn’t much weight on my shoulders, thanks to the experience I got from the Asian Games.” While Ho believed his new role on the team was proof that he was entrusted by the coach and his teammates, the mastermind behind the city’s foil team re-emergence, Greg Koenig, again described it as a “happy problem” he had faced before. “Cheung was there, and Choi has been in that role [to close out bouts] for the past two years, and now I have Harris,” Koenig said. “I think that’s just great for us, and I cannot be happier.” The Frenchman added that Ho, who will compete at the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, could expect to be given a lot of opportunities to gain international experience this season. While there are young athletes coming through, there are also some more experienced ones pondering their next moves. Veteran rower Chiu Hin-chun, who won gold in lightweight men’s single sculls, said he would definitely still be around for the Los Angeles Olympics in two years, but the 32-year-old was not sure about the next Asian Games in Doha. Karateka Grace Lau Mo-sheung, who won the third Asian Games medal of her career after finishing second in the women’s individual kata behind arch-rival Maho Ono of Japan, said she needed time to sort out what she wanted to do next. “I am going to speak to my coach [William Thomas], but I am still confused,” the 35-year-old said. “It’s been a month since the Asian Games, but I have yet to sit down and think about my future. “Japan felt like a closing; do I still have passion? It’s a yes and no. I need time to think about my priorities because I have been focusing a lot on karate for many years. I may also want to focus on my family, too.” Lau added that she might be tempted to compete at the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Riyadh at the end of the year, but sources told the South China Morning Post the multi-sport games, which were rescheduled several times before later being reassigned to Saudi Arabia, could be postponed until March because of the conflict in the region.

title: Officials pledge to quell dog attacks before inaugural Northern Metropolis Marathon
description: Extra precautions have been put in place along the route for the event, which has drawn about 15,000 runners across four categories.
content: A new race blending urban and countryside views across Hong Kong will take place on Sunday, featuring the newly opened Fanling Bypass as the finish line for the full-marathon route. Organised by the New Territories Heung Yee Kuk to mark its 100th anniversary, the inaugural Northern Metropolis Marathon has drawn about 15,000 registered runners across four categories: the full marathon, half marathon, 10km and 1,600m races. Addressing safety concerns after a recent series of dog attacks in the New Territories, organisers told the South China Morning Post on Monday that extra precautions had been put in place along the route. “Various government departments were very concerned about this issue and gave us a lot of input,” Ricky Chan, the race coordinator, said. “About two weeks ago, we issued notices to facilities along the route, such as car parks, reminding [users] to properly restrain their dogs. Patrol teams will also inspect the course days before the race to re-check the area.” The safety measures follow several dog attacks reported in the region in recent months, the latest occurring on Monday, when a 26-year-old logistics worker was bitten on the left shin by a mongrel in Yuen Long. In September, a 27-year-old woman died after being chased and attacked by a pack of dogs in the same district, while a 33-year-old dog trainer was fatally attacked at a facility in Ta Kwu Ling in August. The full marathon will start at the Heung Yee Kuk Building in Shek Mun, Sha Tin, and will then take runners along the Science Park Waterfront Promenade, Tolo Harbour Highway, Lam Tsuen River and through the Lung Shan Tunnel before finishing at the North District Sports Ground via the Fanling Bypass. The half marathon will begin at the Hong Kong Science Park and also conclude at the Fanling Bypass. Addressing potential cross-border routes in the future, New Territories Heung Yee Kuk chairman Kenneth Lau Ip-keung said while the idea of running across the Shenzhen border was feasible at a policy level, hosting full marathons on Hong Kong’s busy roads remained challenging. “I had previously thought about cross-border routes like the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge or running through the Lok Ma Chau Loop,” Lau said. “Cross-border events are not a problem at the national level, but it depends on practical arrangements. “Hong Kong is small and holding a full marathon involves busy roads, which makes it very difficult. We hope the Northern Metropolis Marathon will get better and better in the future.” Chan said runners could collect their race packs between October 28 and 31, with baggage check-in required 30 to 45 minutes before start times. The race will bring about extensive road closures, with traffic diversions expected to be put in place in phases from around at 2am on Sunday. Police advised runners to use public transport, with MTR services starting at 4.20am, and organsiers putting on free event shuttles and special overnight buses. Ng Hing-cheong, Chief Inspector of Police Enforcement and Control Division Traffic New Territories North Region, said the southbound section of the Fanling Bypass and the northbound section of the Lung Shan Tunnel would be closed from 3am. Closing the tunnel would impact the entrances from Fanling Highway northbound, and southbound to Lung Shan Tunnel northbound would be closed, requiring drivers bound for Heung Yuen Wai to detour via the Fanling Bypass northbound and Sha Tau Kok Road. The right-turn lane from Po Wo Road northbound onto Fanling Highway southbound will also be closed, with motorists advised to U-turn at the Jockey Club Road roundabout. For the Fanling Bypass, closed sections include Fung Ling Road northbound and the southbound lanes of the bypass towards Fanling Highway. Vehicles will be prohibited from entering the bypass southbound from Ma Sik Road. Westbound drivers on Ma Sik Road will be diverted via So Kwun Po Road, while eastbound traffic can detour via Fanling Lau Road, Luen Yip Road, and Jockey Club Road. Southbound motorists on Sha Tau Kok Road (Lung Yeuk Tau section) can similarly detour via Luen Yip Road and Jockey Club Road to reach Fanling Highway. Roads will reopen in stages, with the Lung Shan Tunnel northbound expected to reopen at 11am, followed by remaining Fanling roads at around 3pm after the races finish.

title: Factory-gate prices are key barometer for China, but is the latest rebound a true recovery?
description: Analysts are sceptical the latest rebound signals a fundamental improvement in supply-demand dynamics, as seen in the previous two upswings.
content: While the eyes of the world are fixed on the US Federal Reserve’s policy meeting later this week and the trajectory of American inflation, observers of the Chinese economy are closely tracking a different metric: the producer price index (PPI). For the world’s manufacturing powerhouse, factory-gate prices have long served as a key barometer of the country’s economic health, and early signs of a recent rebound have raised questions about whether it is a solid, sustainable recovery or a mere flash in the pan. “PPI is one of the most important indicators for gauging China’s economic cycle,” said Raymond Yeung, chief Greater China economist at ANZ Bank. “Over the past 10 to 20 years, movements in PPI have reflected the health of China’s economy more accurately [than gross domestic product].” A look back at the past decade reveals that China’s two major PPI upswings were driven by tangible improvements in supply and demand fundamentals – first during Beijing’s 2015 “supply-side structural reform” initiative, and later amid a pandemic-driven surge in global reliance on Chinese manufacturing. In late 2015, Beijing launched supply-side reforms to cut excess capacity in industries, such as steel and coal, which propelled a jump in PPI. The index reversed from a 5.9 per cent year-on-year decline in December 2015 to 7.8 per cent growth in February 2017, according to data compiled by financial data provider Wind. The next major PPI upswing came during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns disrupted supply chains across much of the world, while China’s vast and resilient manufacturing base helped meet surging global demand for goods, driving up factory-gate prices. China’s PPI then climbed from a 3.7 per cent year-on-year decline in May 2020 to a peak of 13.5 per cent in October 2021, according to official data compiled by Wind. Over the past few months, the country’s PPI is once again showing fresh signs of recovery, particularly following global energy market volatility and surging semiconductor prices amid an ongoing tech supercycle. In March this year, as the US-Israel war on Iran drove up global energy prices, China’s PPI emerged from more than three years of negative territory and climbed to reach 5 per cent year on year in September, its highest rate since mid-2022. But analysts are sceptical that the latest rebound signals a fundamental improvement in supply-demand dynamics, as seen in the previous two upswings. “The situation this time is different from the past rounds, as it is primarily driven by imported inflation,” said Yeung from ANZ. While upstream industries holding inventory might benefit from the surge in bulk commodity prices, Yeung cautioned that downstream companies are likely to suffer from rising costs. David Zhang, a macroeconomics and policy analyst at Trivium China, said the latest rebound was “very different” from 2016, when supply-side capacity cuts were accompanied by a property and infrastructure investment boom that boosted demand. “Today, domestic property and investment demand remain weak, while overcapacity has yet to be fundamentally addressed. It is difficult to interpret the rebound as a sign of a broad-based improvement in domestic supply-demand dynamics,” he said. “Domestic end-demand [also] remains weak, leaving companies with limited room to pass on costs to consumers.” Meanwhile, Beijing’s campaign to curb “involution”, or cutthroat competition, has emerged as another key policy variable for economists to watch, though any meaningful structural improvement will take time to materialise. “Using policy tools to reduce overcapacity and control cutthroat competition will take a relatively long time to actually reflect in the true PPI cycle,” Yeung said. Zhang said the anti-involution campaign had made some initial progress, mainly in curbing disorderly price competition in the short term. “Addressing the structural supply-demand imbalance – and actually getting excess capacity to exit the market – is much more difficult and will take longer,” he said.

title: China’s tax offices issue disclosure orders as offshore asset grace period ends
description: With the 90-day grace period now expired, officials are attempting to spur voluntary reporting of ownership, documentation.
content: Local tax bureaus across China are continuing to step up oversight following the expiration of the country’s grace period for the reporting of offshore trusts last Thursday, part of an ongoing push to spur voluntary tax disclosures. Municipal tax authorities in Beijing published notices for 21 individuals on the official website last Thursday – the expiry date of the 90-day grace period – ordering them to submit tax documentation linked to offshore trusts. The notices, issued to “tighten tax collection over offshore trusts”, direct taxpayers to carry out a self-review of any offshore trusts they established or hold an interest in and furnish relevant documents to tax authorities within 15 days in compliance with the law. Earlier this month, tax authorities in Qingdao – a coastal hub in China’s eastern Shandong province – issued a comparable yet more pointed notice to a local taxpayer. It said “data matching” had uncovered information relating to overseas financial accounts and told the recipient to verify the nature of those accounts. The tax office directed the taxpayer, surnamed Sun, to submit documentation covering the trusts and affiliated offshore listed companies. “It is not wholly the case that tax authorities are unable to locate these individuals. Authorities may have already reached out to some of the people named in the notices before issuing them,” said Tian Zhiwei, a professor at Shanghai University of Finance and Economics. “Tax bureaus are issuing these public notices for two reasons. They are establishing a complete procedural trail to ensure any subsequent penalties or tax recovery actions are procedurally sound. The other purpose is to issue a warning to others,” Tian noted. I suspect they are facing challenges lining up funds or contesting the applicable tax treatment Ye Yongqing, Anli Partners “The notices are expected to send a signal pushing other high-net-worth individuals holding offshore trusts to carry out voluntary self-review and lift compliance standards across the industry,” he added. China has ramped up efforts to tax offshore assets this year. Figures released by the Ministry of Finance last Friday show proceeds from individual income tax exceeded 1.34 trillion yuan (US$200.93 billion) in the first three quarters, climbing 14.1 per cent from a year earlier. That rate of increase outstripped the 6 per cent expansion for value-added tax – China’s largest tax category – and the 7.1 per cent growth of corporate income tax. Ye Yongqing, a tax lawyer with Beijing-based law firm Anli Partners, said his clients had wrapped up filings and settled payment of their taxes tied to their offshore trusts. “To my understanding, most taxpayers in the first batch served with tax notices have already settled the taxes. As for those who haven’t, I suspect they are facing challenges lining up funds or contesting the applicable tax treatment,” Ye added. Greater attention has been paid to the enforcement of tax rules on China’s wealthy, especially its super-rich. Data from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index shows eight of the world’s 500 wealthiest individuals are among those potentially affected by the offshore trust tax measures, having established trusts in tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands and the Cayman Islands. The group includes Ding Lei, head of Guangzhou-based game developer NetEase, with roughly US$37 billion in offshore holdings, and Huang Zheng, founder of e-commerce powerhouse PDD Holdings, who had US$29 billion of assets outside mainland China as of mid-October. Last month, Haidilao International Holding published a filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange, revealing that co-founders Zhang Yong and his wife Shu Ping offloaded 259 million shares of the company, in a deal worth around HK$2.75 billion (US$350.55 million) at the time. The disclosure said the disposal was undertaken to satisfy their personal funding needs and financial arrangements. Many market participants speculated the proceeds would be used to cover tax obligations arising from their offshore trusts. The finance ministry issued the rules governing taxation of offshore trusts this summer. The provisions stated that founders are subject to tax upon settlement of offshore trusts established between 2023 and 2025. This month, the State Taxation Administration added that the threshold qualifying for an extended statute of limitations for tax recovery applies where unpaid individual income tax totals 100,000 yuan or more. “From the cases our team has handled, the extended tax recovery period is mostly five to eight years – longer than we normally anticipated,” Ye Yongqing noted.

title: China drafts rules to protect trade secrets from ‘foreign entities’
description: Provisions on trade secrets opened for public feedback, designed to protect ‘national sovereignty’ and ‘development interests’ against foreign entities.
content: China has drafted special rules to protect the country’s trade secrets and is seeking public feedback on the proposed strictures, the Ministry of Commerce said on Monday. In the draft document, the ministry said the rules apply “where a foreign entity engages in acts infringing upon Chinese trade secrets in the course of international economic, trade and related activities” and those acts endanger or pose a real threat to “China’s national sovereignty, security and development interests”. Under the draft rules, the ministry could impose one or more measures on foreign entities found to have engaged in prohibited conduct, including restricting or banning their trade in goods, technology and services involving China and curbing new investment in China. The drafted rules come as China has built a leading position in sectors such as electric vehicles, batteries and rare earth processing, in which technological know-how and trade secrets are central to competitiveness. Other potential measures include limiting the entry of entities’ personnel and transport vehicles into China, revoking or restricting work permits and residence rights for entities’ personnel within the country, and imposing fines proportionate to the severity of the offence. Foreign entities were defined as foreign corporations, other organisations or individuals. “Keeping trade secrets has indeed become more important in the context of China’s ‘competition’ with the US and the EU,” said Xu Tianchen, a senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit. “Especially as China has adopted a more open-door policy to international visitors, companies will want to step up their vigilance against potential commercial espionage.” The commerce ministry’s draft rules follow a separate draft plan it issued with the Ministry of Science and Technology earlier this month, proposing export bans that would affect 14 technologies in sectors ranging from artificial intelligence to biotechnology and photovoltaic solar power. Xu added the new proposed rules would set out how governments and businesses should respond. The new rules would also authorise the commerce ministry to investigate whether foreign entities’ conduct represents a threat to China’s sovereignty, security or development interests. Foreign entities under investigation would be required to cooperate and provide relevant information, while they would be allowed to mount a defence. If an entity fails to cooperate or “otherwise obstructs” the probe, however, the rules would permit the ministry to issue a ruling based on the available facts. Companies and individuals could also report alleged infringements by foreign entities to the ministry, according to the draft document. The draft rules are now open for public comment, with feedback due by November 24. Last week, the US State Department announced that it was imposing sweeping sanctions under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act on five Chinese entities suspected of stealing trade secrets from American companies. The Chinese firms included Shanghai Zhisuan Technology, a firm founded by former Google software engineer Ding Linwei, venture capital firm MiraclePlus and three related entities. In response, the commerce ministry said it “firmly opposed” the move, which it said “stigmatised Chinese companies” and seriously undermined their rights and interests. It added that the rapid development of Chinese artificial intelligence companies was driven by years of work in fundamental research and sustained investment in innovation, and had nothing to do with the theft of trade secrets. Some analysts warned China’s new rules could increase trade frictions and deepen distrust with trade partners. “This is in line with a more forceful strengthening of economic statecraft in China,” said Miguel Otero-Iglesias, a senior analyst and China specialist at the Elcano Royal Institute. “The consequence is threefold: more state control, more trade friction and more distrust among economic players.”

title: Why pro-Palestinian comedian Sammy Obeid refuses to stay silent
description: Obeid, who is openly critical of Israel and has gone viral with clips on the Israel-Gaza war, has two Hong Kong shows on October 27.
content: “Two wrongs don’t make a right. If you wrong a wrong, you get a wrong. If you wrong that wrong, it is a wrong-wrong. If you wrong that wrong-wrong, it’s a triple-wrong. How many more wrongs until we get this right? The easiest way to make things right is to give people rights. When you give people rights, they can do right. And rights are very powerful – they undo all wrongs.” This is one of stand-up comedian Sammy Obeid’s most viral clips, where he cleverly dissects the Israel-Palestine situation while keeping the audience laughing. Obeid made headlines in August 2025 when two of his planned Singapore shows were cancelled. The comedian accused Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority of trying to censor his material, which often criticises Israel’s actions in Gaza, though officials said his permit was rejected over a late application. In contrast, he was able to perform his material in Hong Kong freely the following month. Despite the setbacks, clips of his criticism against Israel have gone viral. Obeid claims his Instagram account has jumped from around 300,000 followers to 1.3 million in the past year. On October 23, Obeid shared on his social media account that he was refused entry into Japan – one of the stops on his current tour – due to having the wrong visa. Japan subsequently rejected his request to be allowed to continue to Seoul, the next stop on his tour, instead requiring him to return to the US on the same airline he arrived on. Working together with Hong Kong’s Backstage Comedy, he is set to return to the city to perform two sets in SoHo House on October 27. From calculators to comedy Obeid, who is Lebanese-Palestinian-American, grew up in California and graduated from UC Berkeley with a double major in applied mathematics and business administration. After graduating, he put his analytical skills to use as a maths teacher. “I never actually quit,” he says. “I mean, I got fired from my teaching job in 2011.” He famously turned down a job at Google to pursue comedy full-time. The choice included a lot of sacrifice, starting with living on a daily budget of US$10. “I would eat a lot of chips and salsa,” he says. In 2010, he embarked on a mission to set the world record for the longest streak of consecutive comedy performances. He beat the previous record on day 731, continuing until he reached 1,001 nights. This historic streak led to appearances on Conan and America’s Got Talent and landed him the gig as host for Netflix’s 100 Humans. Being in the spotlight also puts him at the mercy of hecklers. He is candid when asked whether comedians need to develop a thick skin to handle potential harassment during live shows. “You can play through it, but I don’t think you have to be OK with it,” he says. “I wouldn’t say it hurts me, but it doesn’t feel good.” I don’t want any opportunities that are contingent on the fact of whether I’m silent or not on genocide Sammy Obeid During a recent performance in San Francisco, an audience member interrupted Obeid’s set, asking if he had any jokes about Jewish children “being put in modern microwaves … because that is what the Palestinians did”. The exchange, which has amassed more than 1.3 million views on YouTube, sees Obeid challenging the allegation, demanding evidence and debunking the heckler’s claims while stressing that he opposed the killing of anyone. Finally, he turned the confrontation into a punchline, addressing Israel directly: “If you want to come to my shows, send your best. This is not your best.” When asked if tackling such heavy subjects takes an emotional toll, he says it is difficult. “I mean it’s always hard to make light of anything that is dark, it’s hard emotionally. It’s not hard for me technically though. But you know, I’m doing my best.” Obeid is comfortable being known as a pro-Palestinian comic because it aligns with his beliefs. “I would appreciate if one day Palestine is free and I don’t have to do this any more. I just wouldn’t have to constantly be reminding the world that the US is funding a genocide in Palestine.” He says that with the ever-evolving Middle Eastern conflict, he spends a lot of time consuming news – whether for his routine or to provide clear and informed responses to his audience. “Yeah, you have to spend a lot of time listening and consuming news. I have to constantly refresh.” Since the invasion of Gaza, many prominent artists and creators have faced systemic blacklisting, cancelled contracts, and severe professional or legal consequences for public advocacy. In 2023, Hollywood veteran Susan Sarandon was abruptly dropped by her long-time representative, United Talent Agency, after speaking passionately at a pro-Palestinian rally. In September, the rapper Macklemore – a vocal advocate for Palestine – was ousted from Ed Sheeran’s world tour, with Sheeran maintaining an apolitical stance and stating his concerts were not political forums. This perceived corporate neutrality backfired, sparking public accusations of “selling out”. Recently, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher, Faber, were forced to completely withdraw her novels, including Normal People and Intermezzo, from sale across the United Kingdom. Asked if he feared similar restrictions, Obeid replies, “I don’t want any opportunities that are contingent on the fact of whether I’m silent or not on genocide. I wouldn’t consider those opportunities. I would consider them traps.” Obeid remains optimistic about change. “I think you have a massive awakening now and it’s reaching a critical mass where there will be no turning back from that and people will not continue to tolerate it,” he says. “I do believe that the world is moving in the right direction.” “Sammy Obeid: High Key in Hong Kong”, October 27, 7.30pm and 9pm, Soho House, 33 Des Voeux Rd West, Sheung Wan. For more information, visit here.

title: Brazil draws record Chinese investment. Could Lula’s industrial strategy complicate ties?
description: The re-elected leader has championed closer economic ties with Beijing but also wants his nation to move up the value chain.
content: China and Brazil are expected to sustain close economic ties following the re-election of Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as president, though his push to strengthen domestic industry and production could complicate the outlook for Chinese companies operating in Latin America’s largest economy, analysts said. Lula defeated right-wing challenger Flavio Bolsonaro in Sunday’s run-off election, securing a fourth, non-consecutive term. Following his victory, Lula told reporters and allies at a hotel in Sao Paulo that “Brazil refuses to be anyone’s backyard” – a remark widely seen as a pointed message to Washington. Chen Fengying, a researcher at the Beijing-based China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations, said Lula’s plans to diversify Brazil’s international partnerships and maintain strategic autonomy from the United States could create opportunities for Beijing. Chinese investment, she added, could also help Brazil upgrade its economy. “[Lula’s win] is good news,” Chen said. “Political shifts in Brazil are closely intertwined with economic and trade policies. Given Lula’s generally friendly stance towards China, bilateral economic and trade ties between China and Brazil are likely to remain stable at the very least.” Chen said she also expected the two countries to deepen technological cooperation, arguing that China “is the only country that can rival the US in the tech field”. She projected further growth in bilateral trade, saying Brazil’s rich natural resources complemented China’s vast manufacturing capacity. Since Lula’s return to the presidency in 2023, his government has sought to deepen economic ties with China while attracting Chinese investment to support Brazilian industries and improve its technological capabilities. Chinese companies invested more money in Brazil than in any other country last year, committing a record US$6.1 billion spread across 52 projects, according to the Brazil-China Business Council. That followed Lula’s visit to Beijing in May 2025, when he attended a summit with Latin American leaders and returned with 27 billion reais (US$4.7 billion) in investment pledges from companies such as Great Wall Motor and Meituan. Trade between China and Brazil hit US$171 billion in 2025, an increase of 8.2 per cent year on year, according to Brazilian government data. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, with demand for oil, soybeans and other commodities underpinning the relationship. But Brazil’s efforts to attract Chinese capital are joined by another goal: keeping more of the economic benefits at home. For Lula, closer ties with China are seen as an opportunity to build his country’s industrial capabilities, rather than remain dependent on imported technology and finished goods. In an October interview with a Brazilian podcast, Lula said Brazil should develop its own electric batteries rather than “depend on the Chinese”. He also called for Brazil to produce its own chips and mobile phones. In the same interview, Lula said China could bring technology to Brazil’s rare earth industry, while insisting that critical minerals should be processed domestically. He described Chinese investors as “bold” and said Brazil was “taking advantage” of the opportunity. Chim Lee, a senior analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said these ambitions could make Brazil a more complex market for Chinese companies, even as bilateral relations remained strong. “We’re likely to see sustained momentum behind projects backed by intergovernmental cooperation, such as infrastructure investments in ports and railways, as well as energy and resources,” Lee said, describing the election result as a “plus” for China-Brazil relations. However, stronger political ties would not necessarily make it easier for Chinese businesses to operate in Brazil, Lee said, citing the Lula government’s efforts to promote local production and protect domestic employment. “The reality on the ground for Chinese enterprises is a bit more nuanced,” Lee said. “Lula’s government has implemented tariffs on Chinese goods and rolled out rules that effectively push carmakers to localise production.” “Similar policies encouraging domestic processing in the mining sector are already being developed, and we can expect more down the line.”

title: Harry Kane primed to pip Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe to ‘world’s best’ Ballon d’Or glory
description: The 70th edition of the award will be hosted in England for the first time and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years.
content: England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide-open race to be crowned Ballon d’Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world’s best footballer. The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner, Stanley Matthews, and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years. Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double, and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup. “I’d love to be able to achieve something like that. It would be a massive milestone in my career,” the 33-year-old said. But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane mean the outcome is far from certain. “I think my wife and my family would prefer to know … it’s very stressful for everyone,” he added. “I can see why they don’t tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don’t know.” ‘I deserve it’ Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain’s Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d’Or winner one day. However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain’s World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit. Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona teammates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi. That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony. “For me, Mbappe and me, we’re the two best players in the world,” Yamal said last month. “I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I’ve won.” Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France. The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies. His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition’s history on 22. “Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out,” Mbappe said. “Who am I voting for? Myself.” In the match-up between the two La Liga-based Ballon d’Or challengers on Sunday, Mbappe scored twice as Real Madrid beat Spanish leaders Barcelona 2-1 in their “clasico” at Camp Nou on Sunday to get back into the title race. Mbappé struck in each half for Madrid, with a fortunate ricochet in the 41st minute and the winning goal in the 87th after Raphinha had equalised for the Catalan club. The result ended Barcelona’s bid to become the first team to win their opening 10 La Liga matches. They had matched Real Madrid’s nine victories from nine games in 1968-69. Madrid stayed in third place but moved within three points of Barcelona. Atletico Madrid are second, two points behind Barcelona. One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in Fifa’s rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking. The Ballon d’Or goes to the player who accrued the most points. Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player’s overall marketing value. Alexia Putellas is the front runner to win the women’s award for the third time with Aitana Bonmati’s three-year reign to come to an end after an injury-hit year. Putellas, winner in 2021 and 2022, was part of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses. Her former club teammate, Poland’s Ewa Pajor, is the main challenger to Putellas after she netted 11 Champions League goals in Barca’s latest triumph.

title: Apple iPhone Duo price premiums evaporate in China’s scalper market
description: Resellers forced to drop premiums by hundreds of dollars as social media buzz about durability and compatibility issues pares demand.
content: Scalpers in mainland China are slashing prices on Apple’s newly released iPhone Duo after the US tech giant’s first foldable smartphone drew mixed early consumer reviews over durability and software glitches. In Shenzhen’s Huaqiangbei electronics market, a vendor surnamed Shen on Monday cut the premium on a black iPhone Duo with 1 terabyte of memory – one of the most popular models – by 2,800 yuan (US$420), bringing the asking price down to 24,300 yuan from more than 25,000 yuan when the device hit shelves on Friday. Interest rebounded slightly once prices softened, Shen said. “Noticeably more customers have been asking for quotes today after learning mark-ups were coming down,” the vendor said. “Inventory remains tight.” Similar price cuts unfolded on Idle Fish, China’s largest second-hand trading platform. Numerous iPhone Duo listings on Monday showed prices 1,000 to 2,000 yuan lower than opening-weekend offers, with some base models commanding premiums as low as 300 yuan over official retail prices. Idle Fish, also known as Xianyu, is operated by Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post. The rapid drop in scalper premiums follows strong initial demand when pre-orders opened on October 16. The passport-style foldable sold out across Apple’s official channels within minutes, pushing estimated delivery dates into early next year. Momentum slowed over the weekend as early adopters took to social media to complain about fragile hinges and screen fractures. Other users flagged app compatibility issues, with many platforms still updating user interfaces for the wider inner screen. Despite the complaints, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, said initial demand in China – the world’s largest market for foldable phones – and the rest of the world was “in line with expectations”. Lam cautioned, however, that enthusiasm was expected to wane once early users got their devices. “Because of the iPhone Duo’s premium pricing, sales momentum in China will taper off rapidly after the first month or two,” Lam said. “The high price point has already screened out potential buyers, while foldable smartphones remain a niche segment.” A report by research firm IDC last week estimated Apple would ship 10 million iPhone Duos worldwide in its first 12 months, with the company capturing 31 per cent of the global foldable market this year and taking the crown in both shipment volume and revenue by next year. IDC identified production bottlenecks as Apple’s biggest near-term hurdle. “If supply falls short, or delivery times are too long, frustration builds up among customers and the early momentum cools,” Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president for worldwide client devices at IDC, said in the report. “Apple’s short-term challenge may be less about persuading people that the experience is worthwhile and more about getting the device into their hands.”

title: China’s airlines are adding 288 domestic routes. Can the sector’s recovery keep up?
description: More flights to Canada, India and Kazakhstan are also planned as the sector navigates sluggish passenger growth and high fuel costs weigh on major carriers.
content: Chinese airlines plan to add 288 domestic routes for the 2026-27 winter-spring travel season, with tropical Hainan and ski destinations in Xinjiang popular among travellers. International flights to some countries are also set to surge by 40 per cent. Most of the new domestic routes will connect coastal cities with tourist hotspots in central and western China, according to figures from the Civil Aviation Administration of China (CAAC). The new flight season began on Sunday and runs until March 27. The winter-spring schedule coincides with the switch from daylight saving time to standard time in some countries, helping airlines maintain consistent timetables, the CAAC said in a circular published last week. The regulator of the world’s second-largest civil aviation market said operational standards had also been adjusted to account for snow, ice and reduced visibility. The schedule is designed to meet rising demand around major national holidays, including the Lunar New Year in February. Routes from major hubs Shanghai and Beijing to Haikou and Sanya are among the most popular, as travellers head to the warm, sun-drenched cities on the southern island province of Hainan to escape colder weather elsewhere. Others are heading in the opposite direction, drawn to the snow-capped peaks of Altay in the far-western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, with bookings for November and December soaring 60 per cent compared with a year ago, according to the CAAC. Tickets to “snow cities” such as Harbin, Changchun and Jiamusi, as well as Heaven Lake, a crater lake on Mount Paektu along the China-North Korea border, are also in high demand amid a winter sports boom first sparked by the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics. Ski suits, boots and other gear are flying off the shelves there, Xinhua reported. International services are also expected to increase. The CAAC said flights operated by Chinese airlines to Canada, Belgium, India and Kazakhstan would grow by 40 per cent. Flights between China and Vancouver are among those expected to rise substantially, with services now departing from Shenzhen, Chengdu, Xiamen and Qingdao in addition to Shanghai, Beijing and Guangzhou. Flight numbers to the United States, major European nations and Southeast Asia would remain largely stable during the new travel season, according to the regulator, while services between mainland China and Hong Kong, Macau and Taipei would increase. On Monday, flag carrier Air China launched a service between Beijing and Reykjavik, Iceland, which flies three times a week with a stop in Copenhagen, Denmark. The airline plans to operate 36 European routes during the new season, serving 24 destinations across 19 countries with about 480 flights each week. New services to Jordan and Madagascar, along with a new route between Moscow and Haikou, will also be launched, though the CAAC did not specify the operator. Existing services between Moscow and Haikou would be increased, it said. The expansion comes as China’s civil aviation sector continues to face financial pressures, despite recovering traffic. Stubbornly weak domestic demand and uneven growth across industries continue to hinder its return to pre-Covid peaks, while the country’s sprawling, still-expanding high-speed railway network presents formidable competition. About 91,000 domestic passenger flights will operate each week during the new season, according to the CAAC, down from more than 97,000 during the previous season, which ran from March to October. The civil aviation sector handled about 380 million passenger trips in the first half of 2026, up 1 per cent year on year. The “big three” state-owned operators – Air China, China Eastern Airlines and China Southern Airlines – all reported steep losses, made worse by surging fuel prices linked to the US-Israel war on Iran. In 2025, industry-wide revenue, including income generated by airlines and airport operators, grew by 3 per cent year on year to 1.14 trillion yuan (US$171 billion). The industry’s total profit reached 6.5 billion yuan in 2025 after turning a profit a year earlier for the first time since 2020, according to official data.

title: Meet Meghan Markle’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Jnr – why has he apologised to her?
description: As the Duchess of Sussex’s father faces an investigation over alleged child sexual abuse material in the Philippines, her estranged half-brother has made headlines by contacting authorities and issuing a public apology.
content: The Philippine interior minister confirmed Sunday that Thomas Markle Snr, father of the Duchess of Sussex Meghan Markle, is under investigation for alleged child pornography, as it emerged that a damning letter shared with his daughter was penned by his ex-wife. Roslyn Loveless, who was married to Thomas Markle Snr until divorcing him in 1975, wrote and sent the letter to London’s Metropolitan Police, the department confirmed to BBC News on Saturday, putting the year at 2019. Initial accounts said the letter was sent in 2018. The police force later shared it with Markle and Prince Harry, the Met said. Loveless died in 2024. Loveless had two children with Markle, Samantha Markle and Thomas Markle Jnr, Meghan Markle’s older half-siblings, BBC News recounted. Markle Snr and Doria Ragland married in 1979 and had Meghan, their only child, in 1981. They divorced in 1987. It was Thomas Markle Jnr who discovered the stash of disturbing images and videos of girls no more than 10 or 11 years old when cleaning out his father’s residence in Cebu, Philippines, while he was in hospital having his leg amputated earlier this year after a stroke, according to previous reports. He notified an FBI hotline, the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children, and other law enforcement agencies. On Saturday, Philippine interior minister Jonvic Remulla confirmed that the Philippine National Police had seized a laptop belonging to Markle Snr and a “trove of child pornography materials,” People reported. Meghan Markle said she was “deeply distressed” at the allegations and revealed it as the reason for her long-standing estrangement from her father. Markle Snr vehemently denied the allegations. “This is bulls***,” he said to the Daily Mail from a Florida rehab centre, where he’s recovering from the amputation. “It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.” Here’s everything you need to know about Meghan Markle’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jnr. He is estranged from Meghan Markle Thomas Markle Jnr was born on September 17, 1966, in Los Angeles, USA, to parents Thomas Markle Snr and Roslyn Loveless. Thomas Jnr, 60, also has an older sister named Samantha. Despite being half-siblings, Thomas Jnr and Samantha have had a strained relationship with Meghan. In 2018, ahead of her nuptials to Prince Harry, a source close to the now- duchess reportedly told people that “Meghan has no relationship with her half-siblings, nor has she ever had one”. Around that time, Thomas Jnr made headlines after he publicly claimed that his father had not been invited to Meghan and Prince Harry’s wedding. In December 2017, Samantha also criticised Prince Harry after he appeared in an episode of Radio 4’s Today programme in 2017 and claimed that the royals were “the family that I suppose she’s never had”. “She has a large family. She always did. Our dad is amazing and completely self-sacrificing,” Samantha wrote in a post on X. “We made it so that she had two houses. How fun it was!” Thomas Markle Jnr has tried to make amends with his half-sister Despite being estranged from his half-sister for several years and dedicating both his Instagram and YouTube accounts to criticising her, Thomas Jnr is now making an effort to make amends with Meghan in light of the recent allegations against their father. “I’m so, so sorry Meghan. I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years,” the 60-year-old, who reportedly works as a window fitter, told The Sun. “Having seen what I’ve seen, I believe the man I’ve been defending and caring for is a monster. And I’m ashamed that I spent years taking his side when you fell out with him. I know we’re not close but I can still remember holding you when you were a baby and looking after you when you were small. So please accept my apology and know that I wish you and your family all the best for the future.” Thomas Jnr had relocated with his father to the Philippines and had been caring for him for four years when he discovered the stash of child pornography. Is Thomas Markle Jnr married? Thomas Jnr got engaged to Darlene Blount in 2019. While the couple eventually split, he had reportedly planned to extend an invitation to the wedding to both Meghan and Prince Harry at the time. Thomas Jnr has been married twice previously, to Tracy Dooley and Johannes Rawha. He reportedly shares sons Thomas and Tyler with Dooley.

title: Asia’s answer to NCAA basketball takes big step forward with new 18 team season
description: Universities from across the region will compete in two conferences between November and April, with championship week next summer.
content: Asia’s answer to NCAA basketball has taken another big step forwards, with 18 universities weeks away from the start of a two-conference season. The teams involved in the Asian University Basketball League will play between November and April, with a championship week, similar to the sweet 16 or final four, pencilled in for next August. A 12-strong Eastern Conference and six-team Southern Conference will compete in a total of 54 games, with universities from 11 different places across the region taking part. Nine from the east and three from the south will then progress to August’s event, which will run instead of the AUBL Hangzhou tournament that has been held for the past two years. “This is a landmark moment for university basketball in Asia,” Jay Li Jintian, the league’s CEO, said. “For the first time, the continent’s best college teams will be tested home and away, and that changes everything. “This season will connect different cultures and styles of basketball, bring the game to more fans than ever and give student-athletes new opportunities to travel, compete and learn. Those experiences will shape the stars of tomorrow and build a stronger future for Asian basketball.” Universities from China, South Korea, Japan, Mongolia and the Philippines make up the Eastern Conference, and will be divided into groups of three, with each team playing its group opponents twice in a home-and-away format. Reigning AUBL champions Shanghai Jiao Tong will get the new season under way on November 22, when they travel to Seoul to take on Yonsei University. Two days later, the South Korean side, one of the country’s longest-standing collegiate powerhouses, will face off against Tsinghua University at Sangnoksu Kim Yeon-koung Gymnasium in Ansan. From there, the conference’s teams will compete at regular intervals until the end of March. In contrast, the Southern Conference, which includes the Chinese University of Hong Kong and 2025 AUBL champions National Chengchi University from Taiwan, will be limited to five days in Hanoi in April. The tournament, which also includes teams from Australia, Indonesia, Macau and Vietnam and takes place from April 7 to 11, will decide who goes to the championship week. The brainchild of Li, who previously worked for the NBA in the United States and as Yao Ming’s right-hand man in China, the AUBL concluded its Series A funding round, which was led by Blue Pool Capital, the family office of Brooklyn Nets owner Joe Tsai, in early April. The funding, typically used to generate cash for development and expansion, was built on the Alibaba Group co-founder’s seed investment in May last year. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post, and Tsai is chairman of the board. Other new backers included the likes of Marc Lasry, former co-owner of the Milwaukee Bucks, and Bolt Ventures, the family office of Philadelphia 76ers co-owner David Blitzer.

title: Landmark Chinese diplomatic art exhibition in London reinvented in Hong Kong 91 years on
description: The ‘commemorative tribute’ to the Royal Academy’s 1935 show of Chinese art includes a book launch and the reuniting of 15 objects.
content: In 1935, an exhibition of Chinese art held by the Royal Academy at London’s Burlington House marked a landmark in Chinese diplomacy. Nine decades later, the event is being reinvented at Christie’s Asia-Pacific headquarters in Hong Kong. “The Royal Academy International Exhibition of Chinese Art 1935-36: A Commemorative Tribute” runs until November 6 and combines the launch of a six-volume publication about the London exhibition with the reuniting of 15 objects from it. The bilingual English-Chinese publication, published in Hong Kong by Asian art gallery Eskenazi, was spearheaded by Daniel Eskenazi – who runs the gallery with his father, Giuseppe – after a forgotten cache of original exhibition photographs resurfaced in Britain. Some 3,000 glass-plate negatives measuring 8 inches by 10 inches (20cm by 25cm), originally taken by photographer A.C. Cooper to produce postcards for the original exhibition, were rediscovered before the Covid-19 pandemic. Chinese art scholar Regina Krahl was alerted. “[Krahl] came to us three years ago and said, ‘Would you be interested in publishing them?’” Eskenazi says. “I said, ‘Definitely, because the exhibition was totally unique.’” While the 1935 catalogues featured small thumbnail images and grouped disparate mediums, the new publication reproduces the archival photographs at full scale and divides the objects into volumes dedicated to specific materials, such as ceramics, jades and bronzes. The entries have been translated into Chinese alongside the original English, with attributions, dates and current institutional or private provenances updated where modern research has permitted. “What really took the time was finding where the things are today, the afterlife, the stories,” says Sarah Wong, president of the Oriental Ceramic Society and co-author of the volumes. The original London exhibition drew more than 400,000 visitors and featured loans from 21 countries, including more than 700 imperial objects sent by the Chinese government aboard the British Royal Navy cruiser HMS Suffolk. “The Chinese loans were unique because they hadn’t left the Palace Museum before in Beijing,” Wong says. These ranged from ancient bronzes, rare paintings and calligraphic works to ceramics, textiles, jade and other categories. “There were also loans from over 200 collections in 21 countries, and the king and queen were also involved,” Eskenazi says. “I hope that this project will encourage people to work together again.” The London exhibition featured pieces from the Palace Museum in Beijing that were later returned to China. Around a thousand other pieces featured remain in museums around the world, while another thousand are now in private hands. The exhibition was a watershed for how Chinese cultural heritage was presented internationally, says Camellia Ng Ni-na, an assistant professor of history and sociology at Hong Kong Shue Yan University. “Previously, China had participated in world expos under the late Qing dynasty [1644-1911], but it was mostly miscellaneous crafts,” Ng says. “For the 1935 London exhibition, the Palace Museum played a leading role. It was the first time an overseas exhibition used an art historical approach to show Chinese culture, rather than to exoticise or use an anthropological approach.” Ng notes that while the exhibition fostered bilateral diplomacy during the early Chinese Republican era – especially important during the Second Sino-Japanese War and before the outbreak of World War II – it initiated a fierce and important domestic debate about international loans of national treasures. Scholars in Beijing voiced concerns regarding maritime transit safety and insurance terms. Curators such as Fu Zhenlun, the assistant director of the Chinese delegation, also criticised display errors at Burlington House. Reuniting imperial treasures The 15 items on show in Hong Kong include a late Western Zhou dynasty (1046BC-771BC) bronze ritual food vessel (gui) from the 9th to 8th century BC – which was formerly in the Adolphe Stoclet collection and is now in a private collection in the United States – and a pair of cinnabar lacquer elephants dating back to the rule of the Qianlong Emperor (1736-1795) and lent to the 1935 show by Queen Mary. Eskenazi notes that releasing the book and hosting the loans in Hong Kong reflects an eastward shift in the Chinese art market over the past century. “In 1935, this was Asia coming to London,” he says. “Now this is the centre. It’s now West going East.” “The Royal Academy International Exhibition of Chinese Art 1935-36: A Commemorative Tribute”, Christie’s Asia-Pacific headquarters, The Henderson, 2 Murray Road, Central. Until November 6.

title: Meet Travis Knight: Wildwood director and Nike billionaire Phil Knight’s son
description: The CEO of Laika, whose stop-motion fantasy film is tipped for an Oscar, started out as rapper Chilly Tee before leaving the music industry behind.
content: After a murder of crows kidnaps her little brother, a young girl ventures into an enchanted forest filled with talking animals and other magical beings, where a looming war will decide everyone’s fate. This is the fanciful tale told in Wildwood, from the stop-motion animation studio Laika – an ambitious project that took 16 years to make it to the big screen, and already a front runner for next year’s Oscars. “To put that in perspective, 16 years ago, Barack (Obama) was then a fresh-faced president in his very first term. Oh, it was a better time, my friends,” director Travis Knight said at the film’s premiere in Los Angeles. “This movie exists because hundreds and hundreds of people poured years of their lives into trying to tell the most beautiful story that they could using their hands, using their imagination,” Travis explained in an interview with AFP. “That is something that computers can’t do,” added the filmmaker, who is also the CEO of Laika, the US studio behind Coraline. Travis is also the son of Nike billionaire Phil Knight, who co-founded the sportswear giant and served as its chairman and CEO until he stepped down in 2016. Here’s everything you need to know about Laika CEO and billionaire heir, Travis Knight. Travis Knight’s older brother died in an accident Travis was born in September 1973 to parents Phil Knight and Penelope “Penny” Knight (née Parks). In 2004, his older brother, Matthew Hatfield Knight, died tragically in a diving accident. He was 34 years old. In his memoir Shoe Dog, which was published in 2016, Phil wrote at length about his two sons and his regret about not spending enough time with them during their childhood. “I told myself it didn’t matter what I said. Matthew never understood, and Travis always understood – they seemed born with these unvarying default positions. Matthew seemed to harbour some innate resentment toward me, while Travis seemed congenitally devoted,” he wrote. It was Travis who informed his parents of his brother’s passing. Phil and Penny Knight were in the cinema watching Shrek 2 when their younger son called them outside to deliver the news. “Penny fell to the floor. Travis helped her up. He put his arm around his mother and I staggered away, to the end of the hallway, tears streaming,” Knight Sr wrote. “I recall seven strange unbidden words running through my head, over and over, like a fragment of some poem: So this is the way it ends.” Matthew is survived by his wife and children. Aside from his late older brother, Travis may also have a younger sister named Christina, although reports on this are conflicting, with most accounts stating that Phil has two sons. He is a former rapper turned animator Travis grew up in Portland, Oregon and attended Portland State University. He briefly pursued a career in music as a rapper, going by the moniker Chilly Tee and signing a deal with hip-hop producers The Bomb Squad. He released his first and only studio album, Get Off Mine, in 1993, and decided to leave music behind. In 1998, Travis joined Will Vinton Studios as a stop-motion animator. His father was a minority investor in the studio before he acquired it in 2003 and later rebranded it as Laika, LLC. In 2009, Travis, who had also served as the lead animator on the studio’s hit stop-motion film Coraline (2009), was named Laika’s CEO. Following the success of Coraline, Travis went on to direct and produce various films, including The Boxtrolls (2014), Kubo and the Two Strings (2016) and Missing Link (2019), all of which earned Academy Award nominations for best animated feature film. Is Travis Knight married? There is little information available on Travis’ personal life. He is married and lives with his wife, Maryse Knight, in Oregon. It is unknown if they have any children. Additional reporting by AFP

title: The Hong Kong Council for Testing and Certification recognises local students tackling real-world safety at Hong Kong Science Fair 2025-26
description: Special award from HKCTC honours secondary school teams that have proven their inventions work beyond the laboratory.
content: Great inventions demand more than imagination. They require uncompromising safety, rigorous testing and the credibility that comes from repeated verification. Testing and certification (T&C) do far more than ensure that products meet strict standards. They provide inventors with a structured road map to validate ideas, transforming creative ingenuity into credible, market-ready solutions. To introduce T&C concepts to young innovators, The Hong Kong Council for Testing and Certification (HKCTC) returned as the strategic partner for the second consecutive year at the Hong Kong Science Fair (HKSF) 2025-26. Building on last year’s success, HKCTC once again presented the “HKCTC Testing and Certification Special Award”. The Award encourages students to grasp fundamental T&C concepts and apply testing methodologies throughout their research and development, from proposal to final prototype. By recognising projects that combine creative innovation with a clear understanding of practical T&C principles, the Award inspires students to pursue science studies and consider future careers in the T&C industry. Beyond competition-based recognition, HKCTC actively nurtures future talent by developing teaching kits, hosting hands-on workshops and arranging laboratory visits. Putting innovation to the test Eight secondary school finalist teams pitched their innovations to an expert judging panel comprising HKCTC members Dr Cheung Kwai-chung, Dr Jack Cheng, Dr Lesly Lam and Robert Lok. “Creativity and practicality constitute the highlights of this project, and the students demonstrated an exceptionally high capability in conducting experiments and testing procedures,” Cheng said. “The gold award-winning team demonstrated a profound environmental consciousness. In the current market, their concept stands out as both innovative and distinctive,” Lok added. The panel also offered valuable feedback on bridging the gap between classroom ideas and commercial production. Cheung emphasised that more extensive experimentation and structured testing protocols are imperative for these concepts to become viable. Lam appreciated projects that demonstrated exceptional precision, using targeted testing protocols to verify core functionalities and operational performance. He remarked that executing the right and targeted assessments is critical, particularly given the finite time and commercial resources available in real-world scenarios. Gold Award Project: No Pouch? Ouch! School: St Paul’s Convent School Students: Charlotte Yuen Hui-ching, Hannah Wong Lok-yiu, Eunice Li Yuk-ting, Wat Tze-yue Teacher: Charlotte Po Traditional knee pads rely on rigid plastic shells that protect the patella but restrict movement, leading many athletes to forgo them. The team crafted a knee pad using a non-Newtonian fluid made from tapioca starch and water. It remains soft and flexible during normal movement but hardens instantly upon impact to absorb shock, delivering robust protection without the encumbrance of rigid plastic. The panel remarked that the design possesses substantial commercial and practical appeal. Beyond the invention, the project deepened the team’s appreciation for the T&C industry. Overcoming challenges like mould contamination by iteratively testing various preservatives, they realised that comprehensive laboratory evaluation is not merely a binary pass-or-fail exercise, but a crucial mechanism for ensuring consumer product safety. Silver Award Project: Li-Guard School: Po On Commercial Association Wong Siu Ching Secondary School Students: Lai Chun-yin, Shen Chun-lok, Yip Ho-yi, Chan Sze-ki Teacher: Wong Chan-fai To address the rise in power bank explosions, the team developed “Li-Guard”, a solution engineered to pre-empt hazardous battery failures. The team explained that under normal conditions, a battery remains stable. But if overcharged or damaged, it can inflate with gas and risk bursting. “Li-Guard” detects the onset of dangerous inflation, sounds an alarm and severs the current long before an explosion can occur. While conventional safety systems monitor temperature alone, a failing battery releases gas and expands before reaching critically high temperatures. “Li-Guard” integrates pressure sensing to track these minute pressure changes, enabling much earlier intervention.
