The rigorous development process shifted the team’s perception of the T&C industry from a mundane administrative exercise to a vital scientific discipline. After meticulously troubleshooting a microscopic sensor misalignment that caused erroneous alerts, the team discovered that proving a device’s safety requires the precise, investigative mindset of a detective. Bronze Award Project: When Pectin meets Carbon School: Man Kwan Pak Kau College Students: Huang Chun-chieh, Cheung Tsun-yin, Chan Wan-ching Teacher: Ho Wai-yan Aligning with “Hong Kong’s Resource Circulation Blueprint 2035”, this project converts commercial organic waste into a valuable medical commodity. By extracting natural pectin from discarded citrus peels, the team formulated a biodegradable absorbent sponge to treat chronic, highly exudative wounds, addressing both local food waste and the escalating healthcare demands of an ageing population. “We extract pectin from orange peel and turn it into a gel-like material that absorbs liquid from wounds. Adding a moderate amount of activated carbon improves the sponge’s absorption, but too much causes clumping. There is an optimal range, around 20 to 40 per cent. Since the material is natural, it biodegrades in soil instead of becoming long-term waste,” the team proudly presented. Following the conclusion of the competition, the team now understands that every claim must be supported by standardised and repeated testing. “Even though we conducted various tests, our methods were still not rigorous enough. This gave us a new perspective on reliability, reproducibility and proper standards,” the team said. Looking ahead: The next generation of testers Riding on this year’s success, HKCTC will continue as a strategic partner of HKSF 2026–27 and will once again present the “HKCTC Testing and Certification Special Award.” Secondary school teams are encouraged to start planning early and embed T&C thinking into their research projects. Details can be found via the QR codes below, and you are invited to follow HKCTC’s social media platforms.

title: China’s AI race needs data fuel. Can a new state-owned giant deliver?
description: Beijing is supporting the entity with mega state-backed enterprises, including the country’s major telecoms carriers and power grid operators.
content: Beijing is making an ambitious bid to turn China’s vast ocean of data into fuel for artificial intelligence and economic growth with the launch of a centralised national data group, though experts warn its success will depend on tearing down entrenched data-sharing barriers. The venture – established on October 20 as a centrally managed state-owned enterprise headquartered in Xiongan New Area, Hebei province – signals Beijing’s intent to translate its digital trove into competitive advantage. Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, Vice-Premier Ding Xuexiang described the move as a “major strategic decision” aimed at strengthening China’s competitiveness in AI and the digital economy, the South China Morning Post reported last week. By coordinating data resources at the national level, the group was expected to lower the costs of sharing and using data, accelerate its transformation into commercially valuable assets, and support the development of China’s economy, said Zhou Lisha, research director at Tsinghua University’s Institute for Modern State-Owned Enterprises. The move was expected to help drive economic growth by unlocking the value of China’s vast data resources, Zhou said in comments recently published by the university’s Xiuzhong College. The initiative underscores Beijing’s intensifying drive to ramp up the infrastructure underpinning its growing AI industry. Sun Yi, a professor at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the new group could help establish unified data standards and coordinate data collection and procurement, providing high-quality data sets for domestic AI models and embodied AI applications, including robotics. Such efforts could lower the overall cost of training AI models, Sun was quoted as saying in a report by state media People’s Daily on Monday. Beijing is backing the entity with a slew of mega state-backed enterprises, including the country’s major telecoms carriers and power grid operators. That structure could allow it to tap into its backers’ incumbent resources and infrastructure, analysts at Guohai Haitong Securities said in a clients’ note last week. Yu Yun, head of the digitisation department at China Southern Power Grid, one of the data group’s shareholders, said the company would connect its energy-sector data-sharing infrastructure with the group’s national platform to facilitate data circulation and develop applications integrating computing power and electricity resources, according to Monday’s report by People’s Daily. The strategic push comes amid rapid expansion. China’s data industry grew 15.7 per cent year on year to 6.78 trillion yuan (US$1.02 trillion) in 2025, with the number of companies operating in the sector reaching 482,000, statistics compiled by the National Data Administration showed. Yet some experts have flagged potential headwinds, warning that the group must navigate fragmented data standards, unclear ownership rights and the difficulty of coordinating resources held by different companies and government agencies. Yu Fenghui, a senior researcher affiliated with Pangoal Institution, a Beijing-based think tank, said long-standing barriers to data sharing and commercialisation remained, including inadequate safeguards for transactions and inconsistent standards across regional trading platforms. The industry’s main challenge had shifted from a lack of regulations to fragmented rules that hindered data flows across regions and industries, Yu was quoted as saying in a recent report by the Securities Times. Beyond technical and regulatory hurdles, the new data group faces an institutional balancing act. An editorial published by the state-backed People’s Posts and Telecommunications News last week warned that the group’s biggest challenge would be striking a balance between its state-backed role and market-oriented operations. “Excessive administrative intervention could squeeze out innovation by private enterprises, while an excessive pursuit of commercial profits would undermine its original mission,” the editorial said. The group should act as an “enabler rather than a replacement” for existing businesses by focusing on infrastructure, data-sharing standards and major applications, it added.

title: Why Zhou Xun risked it all for that amazing long take in The First Taste of Loneliness
description: The Chinese actress and director Gu You talk about the audacious 20-minute unbroken scene and how loneliness brings one closer to happiness.
content: In The First Taste of Loneliness, one of the highest-profile Chinese art-house film debuts of 2026, three generations of women – played by Zhou Xun, Xi Meijuan and Wang Shengdi – struggle to put their lives back on track after the death of their family’s patriarch. This beautifully crafted family drama from Chinese writer-director Gu You (previously known as Gu Xiaogang) premiered in competition at the Busan International Film Festival in South Korea earlier this month. Zhou stars as Jiang Yue, a successful fashion director who pauses her career following her father’s death to settle his affairs and provide emotional support for both her grieving mother, Luna (Xi), and her teenage daughter, Moon (Wang). After years apart, the tragedy reunites them under one roof. Rather than causing a permanent rift between them, the overwhelming sense of loneliness and uncertainty brings them closer together. “At this stage in my life, I have witnessed the full spectrum of human experience,” Zhou tells the South China Morning Post, just days before winning the Busan festival’s gender-neutral prize for best actor. “I’ve seen classmates pass away or fall ill. I’ve witnessed all sorts of things happen to family members – and director Gu’s script explores precisely these themes. I absolutely loved his debut film [2019’s Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains], and ever since, I’ve really wanted the chance to work with him.” Expanding the ‘Shanshui’ universe The film marks the third instalment in Gu’s “Shanshui” (“Landscape”) series, which draws inspiration from traditional shanshui scroll-like paintings. It follows his previous films, Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains and Dwelling by the West Lake (2023). He recently revealed there will be a fourth instalment that may lean more towards genre cinema. “Every experience of loneliness brings a person one step closer to happiness – one step closer to that ultimate, perfect fulfilment,” he says. “In this movie, the three generations experience different moments of loneliness, which are in fact moments of experiencing and growing into an understanding of ultimate happiness.” The 38-year-old filmmaker from China’s Jiangsu province graduated with a degree in fashion design before moving into documentary filmmaking and studying at the Beijing Film Academy. During that time, he reveals, he suffered his own pangs of isolation while watching a film featuring a famous photograph of the Earth taken from space, titled Pale Blue Dot. “At that moment, I felt a sense of what we often call human nothingness,” he says. “From a grand, cosmic point of view, everyone is an incredibly small existence.” Cosmic symbolism continues in Gu’s work, with his new film featuring numerous references to the moon. “In Chinese culture, especially within Zen culture, the moon is used as a metaphor for ultimate happiness or absolute fulfilment,” he says. “The moon represents ‘wholeness’, ‘the most perfect fortune’ or ‘the most flawless image’ – essentially, the ultimate perfection of things.” He goes on to explain how the moon is always there, always whole, even if it is not entirely visible. It can also be seen mirrored in rivers, seas or even a cup of tea; bodies of water also feature prominently throughout his work. Bringing the metaphor back to his film, he continues: “We can compare a person’s life to the moon, and these women happen to be its different earthly reflections. These three distinct paths allow them to experience three different stages and forms of loneliness in a person’s life: for instance, romantic love, a career – a highly intense career – and finally, family. “These are the fundamental things we all experience throughout our lives. So, the allegory in this movie is that while we are going through these experiences, we hope people won’t forget to look up at the moon.” Painting with long takes Much like his contemporary Bi Gan, Gu’s films feature long takes and sequences that defy traditional filmmaking rules regarding linear time and space. Characters from different eras can be seen sharing the frame simultaneously, evoking how our memories and dreams bleed into one another. Early on in The First Taste of Loneliness, Gu stages an audacious unbroken sequence lasting some 20 minutes, in which the camera glides across the Qiantang River and in through the window of the family’s sixth-floor apartment. After observing Jiang Yue and her mother for some minutes, it exits over the balcony and heads off across the rooftops until it descends, seeking out her daughter, who is preparing to graduate alongside her classmates in the schoolyard. Before cutting to the next scene, the lens spins around to reveal that Jiang Yue is already at the school, ready to collect her child. “It unfolds just like a painting, like an ancient Chinese long scroll,” Gu says, acknowledging the painterly aesthetic that continues to define his landscape cycle. “Anyone from any cultural background naturally hopes to create new cinematic languages. For me personally, I really wanted to explore the relationship between traditional Chinese shanshui painting and cinema.” Racing against the camera Gu says a significant amount of time was spent blocking and staging these sequences, especially in public spaces where a film star of Zhou’s stature would attract immense attention. “I was incredibly excited,” Zhou says. “I absolutely love shooting long takes, but throughout my career, I haven’t had very many opportunities to work in this specific way.” At this moment, Zhou leaps to her feet and proceeds to run around the spacious hotel suite we are talking in. “The camera moves through the apartment, spinning around and around, before heading towards the balcony to capture my photo,” she says. “As it goes back towards the balcony, I have to duck and hide behind the camera’s line of sight to stay out of the frame.” She ducks and weaves to illustrate her point. “The moment it flies out the window on a drone, I immediately run out of the apartment and dash down six flights of stairs – all within maybe 50 seconds. There was no lift or car waiting! I just jumped onto the back of the fastest motorcycle of my life to race over to the school.” Speeding through the streets of Hangzhou, Zhou and her driver kept a close eye on the drone as it made its way towards the schoolyard. If she slowed down, they risked being caught on camera and ruining the elaborate sequence. “I must be faster!” she says excitedly in English. “If I’m slow, the camera can maybe see me. So I must go faster than the camera. Yeah!” The impact of Jiang Yue’s reveal at the end of this audacious, seemingly impossible sequence is bound to leave audiences in genuine disbelief. “When it was inside the apartment, it was actually completely handheld,” Zhou says, reverting to Mandarin. “Then the operator has to transition that smoothly from hand to the drone. Then after the drone flies across, it has to be hooked onto rails at the schoolyard. “In those transitions, it has to be perfectly seamless. No shakes or clicks can happen, and you only have one take to get it right, so it was incredibly challenging.” “So crazy,” Gu chuckles – responding, perhaps, as much to the theatrics of his leading lady as to the incredible technical efforts of his cast and crew. title: Dr Ron Roukema on education, leadership and life at Hong Kong International School
description: The HKIS educator reflects on a career spanning the United States, Shanghai and Paris, his Christian faith and his mission to help students thrive.
content: I WAS BORN in October 1972, in New Jersey, in the United States. My parents were both immigrants – young adults who migrated during World War II, in the early 1940s. My father is Dutch and my mother is Italian, from Sicily. As children, we were always told that if we worked for the state, we’d be well taken care of. MY MUM WAS a nurse and she met my father in New York. She worked in a hospital, and he was a police officer. My father retired when he was in his 40s after he broke his back. We then moved to North Carolina, which we chose because it was the exact halfway point between my two sets of grandparents (in New Jersey and Florida). MY FAMILY IS made up of educators. I’m the youngest of five siblings. I have three older sisters, and my parents adopted the son of my father’s friend, when I was about 12. My eldest sister is a university professor and runs a business that does training with government departments. My middle sister retired in one state, moved to another and continues to teach in public schools. My youngest sister is a psychologist and also runs a business working with the government. My brother’s birth father was also in the police force; they were having problems at home, so he lived with us until he was 20. It was just like having a bigger brother, but also a friend who was a role model in some ways. I know he’s a firefighter now in the mountains, but I haven’t seen him in 15 or 20 years. I LOVE SCHOOLS in general. I grew up in a family where everybody enjoyed going to school. I was in about 20 organisations and clubs in secondary school, playing sports and joining activities to make friends. I was voted “Most Involved” and I was also the lead in the school musical, captain of the wrestling and baseball teams, and field conductor for the marching band. Every now and then, I’d choose classes to be with friends, only to regret it when the classroom turned into more play than study. GROWING UP, WE didn’t really have the funds to pay for university. I got a full scholarship as a teaching fellow, to teach in the state of North Carolina for four years after graduation, in exchange for tuition. During university (at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill), I continued to play baseball and also did cheerleading. I got my master’s at East Carolina University and my doctorate at North Carolina State University. MY WIFE AND I went to the same secondary school, but we didn’t meet until university – which is good, because I grew up a lot between the time that I met her and the time that I graduated. I was a fourth-year student, and she was a first-year student. She’s an accomplished photographer and has taught photography at different levels. We’ve been married for 28 years. MY FIRST JOB was as a fill-in teacher of kindergarten classes at Southern Pines Elementary; that lasted about three months before I realised that was the wrong age group for me. I had kids tell me, “I have to go to the bathroom.” I’d reply, “Well, just go down the hall and go to the bathroom.” But they were like, “No, no, no. We have to walk as a class.” Learning to teach kindergarten was very different. After that, I went back to Pinecrest High School to teach secondary-school history. MY FIRST ADMINISTRATIVE job was the last year that Southern Pines Middle School existed (2000). I was tasked with converting the academic framework into an International Baccalaureate Primary Years Programme and helping my former colleagues transition, either to other schools or to different areas of education. ACTUALLY, I NEVER wanted to go into administration. I love teaching. But Joyce Edwards, my associate principal at the time, wanted me to go along with her because she thought I asked good questions. Joyce gave me two options: be the middle-school principal at the new school we’d just built, or move to Durham, in North Carolina, and get a doctorate and go to work at this new school out there. SO, I MOVED to Durham, in 2000. I helped introduce technology programmes at Eno Valley Elementary School as an administrator, where they told me it would take three to five years to build a technology programme. We built it in seven months. IN 2007, AROUND the time that my wife and I were expecting our first child, I was offered a job at an international school in Beijing. But instead of going there, we headed to Shanghai American School, where I served as the founding principal of the middle school at the Pudong campus. I worked there for several years before taking my first headship, reporting directly to the board, at Marymount International School, in Paris, France. WE WERE HAPPY in Paris. We stayed for four years. It was a great school that aligned with my beliefs and philosophies. When our second daughter was born, we started thinking about moving back to Asia. One of the things that drew me towards Hong Kong International School (HKIS) is my Christian faith and the way the school embraces Christianity. WHAT’S THE PURPOSE of knowledge? I think that’s why religion is important to me, because to understand and to learn – it has to be for a greater purpose, and that greater purpose, in the end, is understanding God’s word and what he hopes for us. In the meantime, it’s also about using your knowledge to serve others and develop a culture that people want to be part of, and to understand that everything we do and everything that happens is for a greater purpose. MY FIRST IMPRESSION of Hong Kong was in 2007 – right here in this very office, purely by chance. HKIS was hosting a meeting for middle-school principals, and this office I’m in was previously a boardroom. I joined HKIS as the upper-primary principal in 2014. About a year later, they asked me to move into a larger role, as the associate head of school, or what they called the provost at the time, because of my background in education and the knowledge that I had built up over 20-plus years of experience, which was what the school was hoping for and needing at the time. So, I supported them in that role. DURING THAT FIRST visit, we brought Eva, our oldest, and went to Hong Kong Disneyland. On a trip to Stanley, I ran into the then-head of school, Richard Mueller. We were having lunch at Pizza Express with my wife’s cousins when Richard and his wife walked by and we started chatting. That brief encounter showed me how close and open people in Hong Kong are across both the expat and local communities. It made me feel that I would be happy here, both on an academic and personal level. I AM HORRIBLE with raising my own children, in the sense of being a parent and an educator at the same school where they go and I work. My oldest graduated two years ago, my youngest is in Year Five and my second daughter is in Year Seven. Whenever I go to an open house or a play to support my kids, I usually get pulled away. It’s hard to just be a dad there, because other parents don’t see me for my kids – they see me for them. STILL, FOR THE most part, my kids have loved having me around. I walk my son to school every day, and he’s very happy to do it. Whenever my oldest saw me in secondary school, she’d run over, give me a hug and make sure her friends got to say hello. I WORK IN Hong Kong, but I live in North Carolina. Every summer and Christmas, we go home and see family and friends that we went to school and university with. We have a nice home there – the kind of place people want to be. No dates, no deadlines, but we know that’s eventually what we’ll go back to. It’s just exciting to be around people who have the same origins that I have. I’M PART OF what we call the “US Gourmet Eating Club”, where we go eat fast food in Hong Kong. It’s just a bunch of people; some are associated with the school, some are not. We get together for new restaurant openings. We’re looking forward to the opening of (American fast-food restaurant) Dairy Queen here in Hong Kong – we joke around and call it “gourmet”. MY JOY OF working in schools started before I had kids, and it will continue after they have grown up. I feel like I’ve made an impact in each role I’ve held. When I was a teacher, it was daily conversations to help people make decisions that were impactful. Most of my conversations today are about helping students develop lifelong skills, so that they can be successful in the future. I’m interested in seeing how communities come together and grow. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. This story was made possible with support from Hong Kong International School

title: UK’s unity threatened by pact between Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland
description: First ministers of the three semi-autonomous regions of the UK align on EU future as London brushes aside threat to union.
content: The leaders of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland signed a pact on Monday that threatens to lead to the break-up of the United Kingdom. The first ministers of the three semi-autonomous regions of the UK told Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his government to prepare for constitutional change and that their future lies with the European Union. “For people watching across these islands – for people watching around the world – there could be no clearer sign that Westminster’s time is coming to an end,” they said in a memorandum of understanding, referring to parliament. The announcement came about 48 hours after US President Donald Trump waded into the waters of the politically contentious issue when he said he would “love to see” a reunified Ireland during a trip to visit his golf course hosting the Irish Open. It is the first time the leaders of all three countries are either from pro-independence parties, or pro-unification in the case of Northern Ireland, which was partitioned and remained part of the United Kingdom when Ireland won independence from Britain over a century ago. Burnham’s spokesman brushed aside the threat and said the prime minister strongly believes in the union and was more focused on lowering the cost of living than dealing with constitutional debates. “The United Kingdom is at its best when people come together around our shared values and problem solving, rather than division,” Tom Wells said. Nicola McEwen, director of the University of Glasgow Centre for Public Policy, said the summit was symbolically important but had no legal significance. “I don’t see the threat to the union being bigger today than it was yesterday,” McEwen said. In the late 1990s, the UK passed legislative acts that decentralised government through the process of devolution, giving each country except England some level of policy independence and self-governance through their own parliaments. But tensions have remained with the UK-wide government in London, which retained control over national issues and those concerning England. Scotland’s John Swinney and Northern Ireland’s Michelle O’Neill called for independence referendums in their countries, while Rhun ap Iorwerth did not provide a timetable for one in Wales. The three leaders appeared in their political capacity, rather than their official one, possibly because O’Neill is in a power-sharing government with the Democratic Unionist party. Northern Ireland’s Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, of the DUP, accused O’Neill, of the Sinn Fein party, of “weaponising” the role of first minister by signing the agreement. “I am first minister in the north of Ireland,” O’Neill replied. “This is about historic change happening all around us.” Scotland tried unsuccessfully to break away in 2014, with voters rejecting a referendum 55 per cent to 45 per cent. But McEwen said support for Scottish independence has grown since Brexit, in which the UK formally left the European Union in January 2020, following a referendum in June 2016. Swinney, leader of the Scottish National Party, said he believed voters would now vote for independence if the UK government approved a referendum. Burnham told parliament last week he would allow such a vote to be held if there was a “clear consensus” in Scotland but later sent Swinney a letter saying a vote was “off limits”. The 1998 Good Friday peace accord that ended three decades of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as “The Troubles”, requires a vote on unification if polls there indicate it would likely pass, a threshold the UK government says has not been met. Ireland would also have to approve the change in a referendum. Burnham has made devolution a major theme since taking office less than two months ago but his focus has been on regional governments across England, a reflection of his years as mayor of Greater Manchester. Swinney tried to turn Burnham’s ideology to his advantage, saying his frequent talk of devolution “leads you to the logic of recognising the right of the people of Scotland, in my case, to decide their own future”. Beyond any threat of departing the union, McEwen said the greatest impact of the three joining forces could be that they agreed to cooperate with each other routinely and that could help to exert more influence on the UK government. “It does keep on the agenda that question about, well, if the United Kingdom is a union based on consent, what is the pathway where it looks like that consent may no longer be there?” McEwen said. “Any UK government has been very reluctant to engage in that discussion.”

title: Hong Kong malls see ‘gradual recovery’ with new stores and events: Hang Lung CEO
description: Leasing situation ‘steadily improving’ with new stores set to ‘open one after another’ in fourth quarter and beyond, Weber Lo says.
content: The outlook for shopping centres in Hong Kong is improving, and the business will thrive if operators use new stores and attractive events to counter locals’ fondness for cross-border shopping trips, according to the CEO of Hang Lung Properties. The company’s malls recorded growth in July, and business would be “even better” in the fourth quarter owing to a full pipeline of new shops preparing to open, said Weber Lo Wai-pak on the sidelines of an event on Monday. “Hong Kong shopping malls need to focus on getting the fundamentals right and offering the public new products and activities,” Lo said. “If there are engaging events, foot traffic will actually stay.” Hang Lung’s malls recorded single-digit sales growth in July, while operating performance remained in line with the broader market as the retail sector continued a “gradual recovery”, Lo said. However, many people left Hong Kong during the recent summer holidays, so the company would still need to “observe the situation” for a few more months, he added. The leasing situation in Hang Lung’s shopping centres in Causeway Bay was “steadily improving”, Lo said. “I expect further improvement in the fourth quarter as new stores open one after another,” he said. “Some shops are currently undergoing renovation, so there is a waiting period involved.” Things would “keep getting better over the next 18 months”, he added. Adriel Chan, chair of Hang Lung Properties, said merchants’ willingness to invest in Hong Kong and open new stores showed confidence in the local market. “If Hong Kong’s shopping malls can be made more attractive, comfortable and convenient, I believe Hong Kong consumers will continue to shop locally,” he said. Hang Lung Properties owns the large-scale shopping complex Fashion Walk, with Hang Lung Centre serving as a key element. The massive, four-level retail space at Hang Lung Centre – spanning 4,274 square metres (46,000 square feet) – was for many years one of H&M’s largest stores in Asia. Following the closure of the store in late February upon the expiration of its lease, the ground-floor retail space has been leased to the local pharmacy chain Lung Fung Group. The first and second floors feature mainland Chinese women’s fashion brand W. Management, and restaurants will be introduced on the remaining floors, according to market sources. On the other side of Hong Kong’s harbour, Hang Lung held an opening ceremony on Monday to celebrate the launch of the Amoy Footbridge, a community infrastructure project supporting the continued development of Kowloon Bay. The bridge was fully funded and built by Hang Lung Properties, the majority owner of the residential complex Amoy Gardens. “Following the opening of the footbridge, Amoy Plaza recorded single-digit percentage growth in foot traffic,” Lo said. “Many food and beverage outlets only appeared after the bridge opened, with the second floor alone gaining over 20 new tenants.” According to Lo, the occupancy rate at Amoy Plaza was currently close to 100 per cent, and rents were expected to rise in the future.

title: Bird murals take flight across winding trails of Hong Kong’s Lantau Island
description: The Flock Project is painting the city’s birds on abandoned village homes, inspiring street-art scavenger hunts that celebrate wildlife.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
It all began with a blank wall in the garden of a home in Mui Wo – the start of what artist Dominic Johnson-Hill calls “a wonderful little schoolboy adventure”.
Craving a splash of Hong Kong nature, Johnson-Hill teamed up with British bird muralist Rob Aspire to paint a red-billed blue magpie in his garden.
What began as a quiet home project in 2024 spilled onto the winding trails of Lantau Island. Known as the Flock Project, the duo’s vibrant, painted plumages have now populated the walls of abandoned nooks across the island, morphing crumbling ruins into a living gallery. The project has even inspired hikers to go on scavenger hunts looking for the bird murals.
“You’re making use of these abandoned buildings ... turning them into something that celebrates local wildlife,” said Johnson-Hill, 54. “It’s given me an incredible purpose: celebrating all of these birds while exploring and learning about Hong Kong’s wildlife.”
Rooted in his 17 years of experience making art in mainland China, Johnson-Hill creates his work in auspicious sets of eight – this is why the magpie mural was just the start.
“I told my wife, ‘I need to do another seven birds to finish the set,’” he explained.
To curate his subjects, he asked local ornithologist Paul Aston to compile a list of the region’s most striking species. According to Johnson-Hill, about 80 bird species are residents of Lantau Island. Hong Kong sits along the East Asian-Australasian Flyway, welcoming more than 580 bird species, many of which are seasonal nomads.
“[Aston] told me these incredible stories about how most of the birds on Lantau just come and go,” Johnson-Hill said. “Some go to Africa, others to Myanmar and Vietnam. I love the fact that these birds are just so free – they don’t see borders. They just move with the weather and the food.”
After finishing the first eight birds, he wanted to create his second series and raised about HK$22,000 through crowdfunding and selling T-shirts. The money allowed him to expand his project to Chi Ma Wan and other far-flung corners of Lantau Island.
Last April, the project went viral when a hiking influencer mapped out a trail connecting the murals. Hikers began flocking to Lantau for a street-art scavenger hunt, with chalk arrows drawn on paths guiding visitors to the hidden art.
“On weekends, sometimes we’d have over 100 people following the route,” Johnson-Hill said. “It was wonderful because I started meeting all these lovely people.”
Set to be finished in October, his third series will mark the final set of birds confined to Lantau Island, and his fourth is slated to branch out to Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and Lamma Island.
In 2023, Johnson-Hill attempted to have a traditional art career in Hong Kong, hosting formal gallery exhibitions, but he felt unfulfilled.
So he moved into public art: “It’s so wonderful to create something and then let it go. There’s no commercial element to it; it’s art in its purest form,” he said.
The Flock Project has been his creative rebirth. “It’s a lot of fun because you have to go out and find these houses,” he said.
But tracking down owners of abandoned homes is often impossible, and the impermanence of street art hit home when his sunbird mural was painted over by the property owner a month later. While online fans fumed, Johnson-Hill embraced the fleeting nature of the craft.
“I told everyone to calm down,” he said. “Some birds just stay for a little while, just like the birds of Lantau, and then they fly away. Nothing stays forever.”
Every series has a show-stopper. For the first series, Johnson-Hill and Aspire trekked about 860 metres up Sunset Peak. To keep crowds from swarming a villager’s remote stone cottage, they painted a majestic bird onto the roof, visible only from a neighbouring hillside.
For their most ambitious project yet, the duo waded into an abandoned mine shaft, clearing a fallen tree with a chainsaw before standing knee-deep in water for eight hours to complete a mural of a waterhen.
“With the reflection in the water, it turned out so whimsical,” Johnson-Hill said, adding that a video of the mural racked up over 250,000 views on Instagram.
“The artist is a perfectionist in the greatest sense – he spends the first hour or two just on the eye.”
A post shared by Wang Tong Art | FLOCK Bird Murals HK (@wangtongart)
For Johnson-Hill, finding your passion isn’t about coasting on what you already know, but leaning into what frightens you most.
Public speaking used to terrify him as a kid, but he discovered his passion for it by challenging himself.
“Passions aren’t just things you naturally enjoy,” the artist noted.
“Sometimes they’re things you’re terrified of, hidden behind childhood anxieties. If you push through that fear, you find incredible skills.”
His unorthodox creative journey began 20 years ago in Beijing, where he opened a shop selling T-shirts featuring everyday Chinese objects. That leap of faith eventually transformed him into the artist he is today.
To him, true creativity relies on embracing the unpredictable.
“When you’re young, try as many things as you possibly can: be a barman, a waitress [or] a gardener. Enjoy the serendipity of life and take opportunities that don’t seem to make sense,” he said.
“If you want to go into the creative world, one of your greatest responsibilities is to go out, explore and enjoy life.”

title: Hong Kong racing a ‘unique cultural icon’, Lee says, as season opener brings in 12,000 visitors
description: Chief Executive John Lee calls sport a ‘key driver’ for city’s mega-event economy, after Ka Ying Rising bags record-extending win at Sha Tin.
content: Racing returned to Hong Kong on Sunday, with world-class performances on and off the track, a crowd packed with travelling supporters, and an occasion the city’s leader called a “unique cultural icon”. Some 12,280 visitors, 74 per cent more than last year, made the trip to Sha Tin Racecourse to watch superstar Aaron Kwok Fu-shing get things under way, before Ka Ying Rising powered to a record-extending 21st straight win. The world’s best sprinter took home the HKSAR Chief Executive’s Cup in front of John Lee Ka-chiu, who led the celebrations for the opening ceremony and said he had noticed “many overseas visitors” at the track. It was strong evidence, the chief executive added, of the sport’s status as a “key driver of the mega-event economy”. “Last season, Sha Tin and Happy Valley racecourses attracted over 400,000 visitors from the mainland and abroad – a figure that doubled compared with the previous season,” Lee wrote in a post on his official Facebook page. “This not only demonstrates the strong appeal that the racecourse experience – combining world-class racing, dining and entertainment – holds for global travellers, but also reflects the tangible results of policies implemented since the current administration actively promoted horse racing tourism in the 2024 policy address.” Lee added that the government would continue to work with various sectors to attract more visitors to the city’s major events. “We aim to invite them to deeply experience Hong Kong’s unique charm as a meeting point of East and West and an international tourism hub, while working together to tell the Hong Kong story well,” he wrote. In total, a crowd of 43,920 turned out for what Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges, the Hong Kong Jockey Club CEO, said “was one of the most impressive opening [meetings] we’ve had”. According to the club, total betting turnover reached nearly HK$1.3 billion, and while that was 7.7 per cent lower than last year, it did not come as a surprise to Engelbrecht-Bresges, who was more concerned with the “absolute record when it comes to tourists”. “It shows that the strategy of racing tourism definitely did work and we are extremely delighted that the chief executive in his post highlighted this,” the club’s CEO said. “I think it [the turnover] is a soft start but not in a way of concern because many trainers, especially with the significant heat, we knew they would start slowly. This is a little blip, but today is about the atmosphere and the sport.” And when it came to the sport, Ka Ying Rising’s victory was the highlight for many, including Erin Ross and her husband Dion, who had travelled from New Zealand for a seven-night stay in the city. “We came on holiday to explore Hong Kong and were excited to find out a few weeks ago that Ka Ying Rising was racing today,” Erin Ross said. “We got a bit scared earlier this week with rumours of a possible injury, so we’re really happy he was able to race.” Dion Ross, who has followed the horse since the lead-up to last year’s Everest and called the margin of victory magnificent, praised the scale of Sha Tin, which he said was “a lot busier than racecourses in New Zealand or Australia”. The day officially got under way shortly after 11am, when Kwok, serving as the club’s Year of the Horse ambassador, delivered his first live performance of its theme song, “Go Go Go”. And following a traditional lion dance, Lee struck the gong in front of jockeys and dignitaries to signal the start of the season. Among those nearby was Shenzhen resident Liu Jianxuan, who was born in a Year of the Horse. Carrying a plush doll horse and waiting eagerly for the opening race, he said he had set off early from home with his girlfriend for the occasion. “I was mainly looking forward to opening day because the atmosphere is always better on the first day,” Liu said. “There are many more people today than usual since everyone hasn’t watched a race for two months. “My Chinese zodiac sign is the Horse, so I have a special passion for horses. Plus, racing is a defining part of Hong Kong culture, so I come over whenever there’s a meeting.” Liu’s girlfriend, Yang Yujie, who was visiting for the first time, said she was drawn primarily by curiosity and the live entertainment on offer. “I really enjoy events with a vibrant live atmosphere. Taking advantage of the weekend, I came here to join this opening event after the two-month break, expecting a grand celebration,” she said. Surprised by the traditional cultural elements in the performances, Yang added that she planned to return for future marquee race days to experience the atmosphere again. Also making her first visit was 41-year-old Ou Bijun, a dedicated fan of Aaron Kwok for 30 years. Leaving Foshan at 6am, she arrived at Sha Tin and was already in place and waiting for things to start hours ahead of time. “Seeing him perform at the racecourse was so exciting. Because of him, I also pay attention to horse racing sometimes, so I’m going to line-up for those plush horse charms later – I’ve always found them cute,” she said. According to Ou, almost 100 members of Kwok’s fan club travelled to watch him perform, and said she planned to learn more about racing before trying her luck. “I haven’t had time to explore the racecourse in detail yet,” she said. “I’ll learn a bit more first before placing a few bets.” Additional reporting by Jay Rooney

title: US denies it tried to influence Malaysia’s political leadership in 2014
description: The response came after PAS leader Hadi said a US envoy once asked the party whom it would propose as prime minister if it took power.
content: The US rejected a claim by Malaysia’s opposition Islamist party that Washington once sought to influence the country’s choice of political leadership, calling the allegation false. “The United States has never sought to decide Malaysia’s political leadership,” US embassy in Malaysia Charge d’Affaires David H. Gamble Jnr said in a statement on social media on Sunday. “Any account to the contrary is false.” Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) president Abdul Hadi Awang said at the Islamist party’s annual congress on Saturday that a US ambassador once asked the party whom it would propose as prime minister if it took power. Hadi said the meeting took place around the time of former president Barack Obama’s visit to Malaysia in 2014, when PAS was part of Pakatan Rakyat, an opposition alliance that was later dissolved. He said the then-US ambassador had requested to meet him and he attended with former PAS secretary general Mustafa Ali. According to Hadi, the ambassador asked: “Who does PAS propose as prime minister?” The cleric said he responded: “Who does America agree with?” and it left the ambassador “stunned”. The remark drew laughter from delegates at PAS’ gathering in Kelantan state, which the party has ruled for decades. Hadi said he later recounted the meeting to former prime minister Mahathir Mohamad, who told him it was a “good response”. Takiyuddin Hassan, currently PAS’ secretary general, was also invited to a separate meeting with the US embassy then, he said at a briefing on Saturday. An embassy representative had asked whether PAS planned to topple the Barisan Nasional government at that time, according to him. “We didn’t say anything as we don’t want any interference from another country,” Takiyuddin said.

title: Calls for Hong Kong anti-stalking law after man acquitted of following teen girl
description: Magistrate said charge of loitering did not address defendant’s actions, and lawmakers urge government to revisit proposal for dedicated legislation shelved in 2014.
content: Lawmakers and a government adviser have called for anti-stalking legislation to close a loophole that makes prosecuting repeated harassment difficult in Hong Kong, following the acquittal of a man who followed a teenage girl to her secondary school classroom. Some experts said the government should revisit a proposal for such legislation raised 26 years ago, after the magistrate who acquitted the defendant of a loitering charge also noted the absence of laws to criminalise stalking under certain circumstances. Unlike many jurisdictions with dedicated legislation to protect victims, Hong Kong can only prosecute suspects under a patchwork of different laws, with even the statutes on doxxing viewed as insufficient to punish cyberstalking. The 57-year-old government statistician was found not guilty on August 25 of following the 16-year-old girl to her school and loitering outside the classroom in July last year. The man also allegedly followed her during her commute to school for two to three years. He told police the girl resembled an old friend and he wanted to know her. Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong said that loitering causing concern was inappropriate for addressing the defendant’s actions, which could not be handled under existing criminal laws. Lam also noted that the Law Reform Commission had suggested introducing legislation targeting stalking in the past. The commission raised the suggestion in 2000, but the Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Bureau put it on hold in 2014 after concluding that there were “no favourable conditions for us to pursue the matter further”. Ronny Tong Ka-wah, a barrister and a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, suggested launching a new public consultation on the legislation. “The government back then shelved the proposal because it said society had not reached a consensus on this law … But presently, I honestly see no reason to object,” he noted. Tong added that although it was possible to pursue civil action against a stalker, the threshold for an injunction application was high. Typically, ordinary people will be unable to afford the lengthy proceedings. Dedicated legislation would better protect the public, he said. Lawmaker Alex Fan Hoi-kit, a barrister by profession, said the government should review the commission’s suggestion again and take into account changes in Hong Kong law over the years. Doxxing that exposed a person’s personal information online became prosecutable under the Personal Data (Privacy) (Amendment) Ordinance enacted in 2021. Fan said the acquittal should prompt authorities to reconsider whether to go a step further regarding criminal liability for stalking. Legal sector lawmaker Nick Chan Hiu-fung raised doubts over whether the privacy laws could address cyberstalking, which took many forms. “Privacy legislation cannot serve as a surrogate for anti-stalking laws,” the lawyer said. Chan said that consultation with different stakeholders took time, but he stressed the proposal should be examined again. However, veteran criminal lawyer Stephen Hung Wan-shun said enacting proposed legislation that had been shelved so long ago would be highly unlikely. Hung, a commission member, said the existing loitering law might be enough to cover offences in various scenarios, as the key to securing a conviction was proving suspects were in a place where they should not have been. But Hung noted that the defendant in the latest case was present at the school during its open day, which made his appearance legitimate in a way. “If one wants to resurrect the commission’s proposal, there must be something significant to have happened,” he said. “It has been shelved for many years; it would be difficult for the government to bring it up for discussion.”

title: Young Malaysians brew goal for traditional tuak drink to become national success
description: Given the drink’s origins in Sarawak, industry players have to balance between adhering to traditional processes and commercial limitations.
content: At Raffly Langi’s family longhouse in Sarawak, on Malaysian Borneo, the tuak rice wine did not come in a branded bottle or a tasting flight. His aunt has brewed the drink for Gawai, the harvest festival celebrated by Dayak communities, an umbrella term for indigenous groups in Sarawak whose longhouses have long been centres of family, rituals and communal life. She made it from steamed glutinous rice and a cake called ragi, prepared with rice flour, yeast and spices to kick-start fermentation. Once ready, the tuak was drawn from a jar and served without flavouring. Years later, 33-year-old Raffly has carried that family recipe to the Klang Valley, the urban region around Kuala Lumpur, where he produces tuak under the brand Tuak Alus and develops modern flavours for drinkers who are unfamiliar with the traditional brew. Tuak traditionally comes in sweeter indu, or female, and drier laki, or male, versions, but artisan brands now also offer flavours derived from pandan, pineapple and roselle. The drink can still be bought in Sarawak for US$5 to US$7.50 in an unlabelled plastic or glass bottle, while at Klang Valley pop-ups, producers sell premium bottles and promote brand collaborations and tasting flights, with prices around US$25 or more each. But as it moves from longhouses into mainstream markets, brewers are confronting a persistent question: how much can tuak be changed before the culture that gives it meaning fades? Keeping tradition alive For Raffly and Kuin John, the 39-year-old founder of Tuak Sun Borneo, their craft is inextricably linked to the women who have taught them the drink’s brewing process. “The basic method of making tuak is something I will always keep because it was taught to me by my mother,” Kuin said. She makes a traditional ragi from rice flour, ginger, jicama root and pepper, and lets the drink ferment for at least three to four months to give it a deeper character. “Most importantly, I still respect the traditional taboos and practices passed down from the older generations, [because] even as I modernise the business, these are the parts I don’t want to lose,” Kuin told This Week in Asia. In Raffly’s case, his aunt is the main inspiration for the drink. “The way I learned it throughout all the years, it’s always from my auntie. She’s the one that was always making the tuak in the house,” Raffly said. But preserving that foundation does not mean reproducing every part of her process. Raffly now uses a commercial rice steamer and dehydrator, after batches of ragi dried in the sun repeatedly failed. The machine, he said, was “the key to making the ragi consistent”. For Raffly, authenticity does not require every ingredient to come from Sarawak. Alus sources glutinous rice in West Malaysia, where supplies are more readily available, but continues buying Sarawak’s nipah palm sugar, or gula apong, for indu. Unpredictable gula apong stocks have spurred Alus to develop its pandan and sour-plum versions, which require less palm sugar than indu. “We try to get all the resources from Sarawak, but it’s not efficient for us to maintain production every month,” Raffly said. His aunt has not insisted that authenticity depends on a particular rice or sugar. “It’s the feeling and the taste of the tuak that make it different,” he said. Raffly’s business partner, Ayden Chong, 31, was emphatic that their business should not be rigid in adhering to traditional tuak-making. “There’s a sacrifice and there is adjustment, that we need to make hard decisions … but it is what it is,” he said. Chong, who hails from Perak, said his first taste of tuak came during a visit to a Sarawak longhouse over a decade ago. Mindful of tuak’s cultural significance, he said Alus had tried to hire Sarawakians to work in the Klang Valley and create a community around the drink, instead of just marketing it as alcohol. “I always tell people we are sharing the culture,” he said. “I’m not trying to sell you things.” With tuak’s rising popularity and commercial potential, some Sarawakian politicians have embraced the drink as a symbol of their state. At the launch of Borneo Tuak Festival 2026 in the state capital of Kuching last July, Snowdan Lawan, Sarawak’s deputy tourism, creative industry and performing arts minister, described the drink as a “living heritage”, where a family recipe could become a source of income, brewers could build brands and young people could see a future in inherited knowledge. At the same festival, Gerald Rentap Jabu, the state’s deputy youth, sports and entrepreneur development minister, said building tuak into a recognised Sarawakian product required an ecosystem with quality rice production, research into tuak production and opportunities for young entrepreneurs to develop new products without compromising authenticity. Licensing gap As more tuak entrepreneurs seek to expand their business, they say that current legislation poses a stumbling block. Malaysia’s excise law distinguishes domestic tradition from commerce, defining “native liquor” as customarily made by natives in Sabah and Sarawak for their own consumption and not for commercial use. Work like fermenting, bottling or adding ingredients to liquor intended for sale is treated as manufacturing, requiring a customs licence tied to specified premises. Retail sales are separately licensed. For small producers such as Alus, this leaves a gap between home brewing and conventional commerce. “Pop-ups are still the way because we can’t afford retail,” Chong said. Establishing an approved brewery would require equipment, specialist employees and – by his estimate – an eight-figure investment even before compliance audits. Alus and other tuak brewers are seeking to partner with established Sarawak distilleries, according to Raffly. The Royal Malaysian Customs Department has not responded to This Week in Asia’s questions about excise application and licensing requirements for small commercial tuak producers. Consistency challenge Micky Vincent, a fermentation researcher who lectures at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak, said the composition of yeast and other microorganisms in ragi would typically affect tuak’s alcohol content, aroma and acidity, making quality results difficult to reproduce. “This batch might be good and you become the best brewer for the year. But next year … you buy the ragi from the same auntie, it could be a bad one, it could be masam [sour],” he said. A bioethanol specialist by training, Micky and his students have collected ragi from across Sarawak and isolated about 20 yeast species, retaining five for their ability to produce alcohol and aroma, and suitability for food use. His method directly applies the selected yeast strains to cooked rice instead of using a traditional ragi cake. His own label “Tuak Bioteknologi Borneo” includes novel flavours like coconut and vanilla. Micky said commercial producers should document their fermentation and hygiene protocols and analyse alcohol, residual sugar and organic acids before bottling. But standardisation should not require having a single recipe, he added. “It’s my protocol; it’s their mother’s recipe or tradition. But what we can fight for is the same product.” SAGO Group, a food innovation platform that organises the Borneo Tuak Festival, convened brewers and other stakeholders in 2024 to draw up a tuak manifesto, proposing reforms covering licensing, food safety, research and market access. In a joint written response on Tuesday, SAGO founders Arif Abdul Rahman, Ehon Chan and Evelyn Teo said they were unaware of any policy change arising directly from the manifesto. Because the issues could involve multiple government and other agencies, SAGO had called for coordinated discussions among stakeholders and different licensing tiers proportionate to the scale of producers and risks. “The most immediate issue remains the absence of a clear and proportionate pathway for small producers to move from home or community-based production into legitimate commercial activity,” they said. Malaysia’s new generation of tuak producers are not content with just making it big at the national level and are aiming for the global market. Chong said the Alus sour-plum variety had proved popular with Japanese and Korean customers at the brand’s events, as they were already familiar with plum wines as part of their drinking cultures. “If you have the skills, the right people, the right place and more equipment, this is actually going global,” said Chong, adding that he and Raffly had not decided on their export plans. Kuin said: “Exporting tuak is one of my hopes and ambitions, where I can introduce Sun Borneo’s tuak and send it overseas, so more people get to know about tuak as part of Sarawak’s heritage and culture.”

title: Filipino-Americans rattled by Trump’s migrant-chasing ‘xenophobia’ games
description: Immigrant advocates say the ‘frightening’ games normalise human suffering and violence, deepening fear among the migrant communities.
content: The recent release of classic arcade games on the White House website, which allow players to deport migrants and build a border wall, has stoked more fear and anger among Filipino-Americans, as observers call out the “xenophobic” tactics in US President Donald Trump’s widening immigration crackdown. Analysts and immigrant advocates described the games, unveiled on Thursday, as “frightening”, trivialising the human toll of the policies and normalising hostility towards migrants, particularly among younger people. “CAN’T STOP WINNING. Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” the White House said after launching the games, including Rio Run. It lets users chase immigrants next to the Rio Grande River running through the Texas-Mexico border, featuring border tsar Tom Homan. Another Tetris-based game instructs players to “build the wall” by stacking blocks and “protect the border from the coming horde”. The company on Friday said it did not grant permission for the White House to reference its visuals or gameplay. The United States has expanded its immigration blitz in recent months, arresting, deporting and holding people in poorly maintained detention centres, including those authorised to stay in the country. In July, a record number of immigrants were deported, while the arrests hit 49,571, legal scholars and researchers at the Deportation Data Project said. ‘Xenophobia and scapegoating’ On Tuesday, green card holder and cancer-stricken Loreto Javar was released on “humanitarian grounds” after languishing more than two months at a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centre, forcing him to miss treatments. The 73-year-old Fife, Washington resident was arrested in the US on an old criminal charge from the Philippines while applying for citizenship. The case also prompted Filipino grass-roots rights organisation Malaya Tacoma and labour alliance Tanggol Migrante Movement to slam Philippine embassy and consulate officials for what they called an “attempt to claim credit for the release after failing to act with adequate urgency or cooperating with Javar’s family”. “We know of Filipinos who are wary of going to the grocery stores, churches or to even drop their kids off at school. Trump continues to promote this culture of fear, submission and surrender from migrants of all nationalities,” said Jom Dolor, deputy secretary general of migrant workers’ rights group Migrante USA. “Xenophobia and scapegoating still persist in how immigrants are made to do essential yet most unseen and unsung labour, and simultaneously blamed for the current economic decline and crisis in the US.” Dolor accused the Philippine consulate of not doing enough to help its citizens abroad despite the huge remittances from the diaspora in the US. Dustin Paul, a Filipino-American content creator, said the culture of fear and anger was palpable in the online and offline communities. “I observe reactions every single day, not only from my followers but also from the families experiencing it. So many of us are angry. A lot of us are sad,” Paul said. “We know ICE has been around for a while, way before the Trump administration, but the amount of individuals being arrested during this administration who have no criminal record is absurd,” he said, adding that the games belittling immigrants’ suffering were “disgraceful and disrespectful”. “The individuals being detained are fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, hard workers and neighbours. Families have been ripped apart and it’s embarrassing for our government to display what they go through as games.” The TikTokker said he had “made it a point” on his platform to argue that ICE raids targeted “anyone who immigrated from another country”, disputing the myth of the “model minority” attached to Asian-Americans. Model minority Leland Tabares, an assistant professor of race, ethnicity, and migration studies at Colorado College, said the ICE raids were “very frightening” to members of the Asian diaspora, creating simultaneous cultures of fear and silence that reinforce the model minority trope. “On the one hand, a lot of people are doing a lot to raise visibility about this, but on the other hand, those in the most vulnerable positions are often the ones who are most worried, and therefore most unwilling to speak out,” Tabares said. According to Paul, the games were intended to “normalise what’s happening in our country when it comes to immigrants” by trying to “cater to younger generations as much as possible”. Tabares said the gaming platform advanced Trump’s “two-front war on America”: a material war against real people, as well as a culture war. “The game becomes a way to domesticate these kinds of violence and makes them very accessible to us … it’s naturalising this cultural climate of disenfranchisement and containment,” he said. It also plays a role in reproducing the model minority concept that has divided other migrant communities and people of colour, he added. Tabares said the strategy marked a gamification of the “American dream” while the retro aesthetics served as a callback to the nostalgia built in “Make America Great Again” (Maga) ideology. They turn “America into a kind of game where if you play your role and do well, you will succeed in life, hiding structural inequalities”, he said. “The games naturalised xenophobia as a playful, leisurely activity, which is frightening.”

title: 72-year-old hiker dies after collapsing on challenging Hong Kong trail
description: Police were alerted on Sunday morning to incident involving 72-year-old man surnamed Kwok at Ap Lei Chau’s Yuk Kwai Shan, known for sea views.
content: An elderly man has died after collapsing while hiking on a scenic yet notoriously challenging hill in southern Hong Kong. Police received a report at 9.13am on Sunday from a passer-by regarding the 72-year-old man surnamed Kwok, who collapsed at Yuk Kwai Shan on Ap Lei Chau. A Government Flying Service helicopter airlifted Kwok, who was unconscious and had sustained scratches to his head and feet, to Pamela Youde Nethersole Eastern Hospital in Chai Wan. He was later pronounced dead, with the exact cause of death awaiting an autopsy. Yuk Kwai Shan, also known as Mount Johnston, is a scenic spot popular for its sea views but is considered a dangerous destination because of its steep terrain, lack of established trails and limited shade. Police have previously cautioned residents against hiking in the area. The location has seen several emergency incidents recently. In April, three hikers required rescue by firefighters after losing their way during a rainstorm. In August last year, three other hikers were taken to hospital in a single day after suffering bee attacks on the hill.

title: How to take care of your dog during Hong Kong’s summer heat and thunderstorms
description: Extreme heat and storms can severely affect dogs, both physically and emotionally. Here are some expert tips on caring for yours.
content: If you think this summer has been brutal, imagine how it feels for our pets, especially dogs. Whether cooped up in air-conditioned flats or kept in outdoor village compounds, dogs face severe physical and psychological strain during extreme weather. This link between environmental stress and pet reactivity comes amid a greater community focus on dog behaviour and safety in urban spaces. Hong Kong has recorded its hottest summer on record. Climate change is not only raising temperatures but also making typhoons in Asia stronger, wetter and more destructive by warming sea surface temperatures and loading the atmosphere with moisture. So what can dog owners do to take better care of their pets, now that the summers are hotter, wetter – and longer? “Dogs manage their body temperature by balancing internal heat from metabolism and exercise with external heat absorbed from their environment,” says veterinary surgeon Jacqueline Tong at Mid Levels Veterinary Centre on Hong Kong Island. “To prevent overheating, they primarily rely on evaporation through panting, such as evaporating moisture from their tongue, and sweating minimally through their paws.” Dogs also cool down by conduction by making direct contact with cool surfaces, often lying on their bellies as blood vessels close to the skin dilate to shed heat, Tong says. When it gets extremely hot, airflow and shade are not enough. Dogs have to rely almost entirely on panting and lying on cool floors. In hot weather, especially when animals are kept mainly outdoors, this can trigger behavioural changes that could be misconstrued as problematic. When heat triggers irritability Heat triggers psychological strain in dogs, leading to a noticeable drop in patience, says Jack Chan, the dog training director at Dogather, a pet training centre in Yuen Long, in Hong Kong’s New Territories. Dogs become easily irritated under thermal stress, which can manifest as sudden restlessness, continuous pacing, whining and even uncharacteristic bursts of anxiety or aggression. “The most immediate sign of heat stress is acute lethargy,” Chan says. “When temperatures soar, dogs instinctively seek out shade, refusing strenuous exercise and opting to rest to regulate their core body temperature.” Their interest in food often plummets at the same time, he adds, as the body redirects energy away from digestion to focus on cooling down. Paws, pavement and heatstroke Tong advises owners to do a quick test, “putting their hand on the pavement for five seconds. If they feel it’s too hot for their hands, it’s too hot for the animal as well”. Some pet products on the market designed to help actually hinder, says Debbie Ngai, founder and service director of the Hong Kong Animal Assisted Therapy Association. “While putting shoes on dogs seems like a good way to protect their paws from the burning hot pavement, it actually disrupts their natural biology,” she says. “Dogs rely heavily on their paws to sweat and release body heat, so trapping them in shoes can severely limit their ability to cool down. In extreme heat, this well-intentioned practice can quickly become dangerous.” To prevent heatstroke, Chan recommends making a cool environment a priority and providing constant access to fresh water. “During the peak summer months, owners must adjust their training routines and completely avoid forcing dogs into high-intensity workouts,” Chan says. “Instead, the focus should strictly be on their immediate safety and physical comfort.” Taking a dog for walks in the early morning or late at night is best, Ngai suggests. Sniffing is a big part of how a dog experiences the world, so dogs kept indoors due to extreme weather could be allowed to sniff for hidden snacks. Foraging mats, designed with fabric folds, pockets or silicone ridges in which to hide dry food or treats for the dog to sniff out, help relieve their pent-up energy and anxiety. Keeping your pet inside during peak temperatures is the only foolproof way to ensure they stay safe Jacqueline Tong, veterinary surgeon Tong warns that, as in humans, heatstroke in animals can also lead to death. Observe early warning signs: “If a dog shows a slowed reaction time, starts panting persistently, or actively seeks out shade, they are signalling that they desperately need to cool down,” Chan says. “When dogs cannot cool themselves, overheating damages cells and triggers systemic inflammation, which can quickly lead to fatal heatstroke,” he says. “The intense heat disrupts the immune system and causes severe clotting disorders, visible as skin bruising or bleeding gums.” Chan stresses: “Before full, life-threatening heatstroke occurs, dogs suffer heat exhaustion, showing fatigue, weakness, vomiting or diarrhoea. Left unchecked, this escalates to multi-organ failure as the heart, lungs, liver and kidneys shut down. Owners must act immediately at the first sign of distress, because without rapid intervention, this internal damage will lead to death.” “The absolute best way to protect dogs from extreme heat,” Tong says, is to “keep them indoors with fans or air conditioning running. If you must take them outside, never leave them unattended, and always perform the five-second pavement-heat test. “When outdoor exposure is completely unavoidable, dogs must have uninterrupted access to deep shade and fresh water at all times. Ultimately, keeping your pet inside during peak temperatures is the only foolproof way to ensure they stay safe.” Storm anxiety and barometric pressure Just because the sun is not beating down on the pavement does not mean a dog is unaffected by Hong Kong’s extreme weather. Beyond rising mercury, atmospheric instability brings its own psychological toll. “Dogs are deeply attuned to nature, and their natural instincts remain sharp even when living in highly urbanised environments,” Ngai says. “Long before humans notice an approaching storm or typhoon, dogs can sense subtle shifts in the atmosphere.” “They detect falling barometric pressure, rising humidity and changes in the way the air smells. For many pets, this sensory shift triggers an immediate stress response, causing them to grow anxious or lose their appetite well before the first drop of rain falls.” These weather shifts take a physical toll, too, particularly on senior dogs. Changes in air pressure can aggravate joint pain and arthritis, Ngai says, making older pets visibly uncomfortable and restless. During these early stages of a storm, a dog’s natural impulse is to seek comfort and safety. They may become clingy, looking to their owners for reassurance, or may simply want to rest quietly in a secure spot. When the actual storm hits, the sudden onslaught of heavy rain and thunder intensifies this anxiety. To help them cope, pet owners can encourage them to mimic natural survival behaviours. In the wild, dogs instinctively retreat to dark, enclosed spaces such as caves to shelter from severe weather. At home, owners can recreate this sense of security by providing an “undercover shelter”. Setting up a covered crate, a cosy den under a desk or a quiet, enclosed corner allows anxious dogs to retreat, feel hidden and safely ride out the storm. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Alexandra Eala crashes out of US Open after Zheng Qinwen downs Keys in epic upset
description: Filipino loses three-set battle to friend Iva Jovic, while Chinese star fights back to stun Madison Keys and reach the fourth round.
content: Iva Jovic ⁠and Alexandra Eala put their friendship aside for three hours at the US Open on Saturday before the 18-year-old American prevailed to reach the fourth round. The home hope’s 7-5, 3-6, 7-5 triumph at Arthur Ashe Stadium was a rare bright spot for the New York crowd, who had earlier watched China’s Zheng Qinwen overcome Madison Keys in stunning fashion. On the brink of losing the third set 6-0, Zheng rallied to complete a remarkable 1-6, 7-6, 7-5 victory. Jovic and Eala already shared the court in New York during Fan Week when they teamed up with their fathers for a light-hearted doubles hit. There was little room for sentiment once the match began on Saturday, however. Jovic edged a tight opening set, but Eala responded ⁠in the second, the 21-year-old raising her level to force a decider. The final set ‌again featured momentum swings, with Jovic trailing 4-2 before fighting back to close out the victory and extend her head-to-head ‌record against Eala to 3-0, with a win on each of the ⁠three surfaces. “That felt ⁠like a marathon. I felt like I lost my sanity five times over to win that ‌match. But it’s really worth it for this feeling,” Jovic said. “I’m usually not one that ‌shows that ‌many emotions. But this one really meant a lot to me. It’s ‌everything to have another match at the US Open.” Jovic’s victory was a welcome ⁠bright spot on a day Taylor Fritz, Keys ⁠and Amanda Anisimova were among the home players eliminated. Of the three, Keys’ departure from the tournament was perhaps the most surprising, given Zheng’s performances over the past year as she continued to recover from elbow surgery. A former world No 4, the Chinese star’s ranking had dropped so far she had to go through qualifying to earn her place in the main draw. It has all made for an emotional spell at Flushing Meadows for the 23-year-old, who felt she “forgot how to compete” during her enforced absence but could now feel her competitive fire burning. “I have a lot of emotions when I’m playing the qualifying matches,” she said. “I was even crying after I won the third match to reach the main draw, and you know, the main draw is just the beginning. “For today, after coming back from 0-5, the first thing in that moment I thought, ‘Please, I don’t want to be beaten 6-0’.” She got her game on the board, and saved a match point at 5-1, and she was off and running. “Then I felt I have a lot of energy. I can just keep pushing, keep fighting,” she said. “At the end when I won the match, it’s like, ‘Wow, that’s incredible.’ “Finally, one time the luck is on my side because all these three, four months I have been suffering a lot.” With few matches under her belt this year, Zheng said it took her some time to get to grips with Keys’ big forehand. And when she held serve for 5-1 in the third she could immediately feel Keys’ conviction wane. “I see there is some, maybe, doubt or, I don’t know, not as clean [hitting] as before,” Zheng said. “She started to make a lot of mistakes in that moment, and I start to feel like, ‘OK, I need to be there. I need to keep fighting, don’t give up, and let’s see what’s going to happen’.” Keys said her struggles were something that had been building. After she earned her big lead in the third, she said: “I got really scared, like I couldn’t swing … I felt like I couldn’t play tennis any more.” For Zheng, it was a reminder never to let go of a match until the final point. “Tennis sometimes feels like roller coaster,” she said. “So this gives me also lesson that in a tennis match you always have to be there. “It doesn’t matter if you are winning or losing. You have a match point or you don’t have a match point, you just need to concentrate every single point as long as you can.”

title: Tesla to exhibit Cybercab robotaxi in China: can it spark buzz amid slow sales?
description: While the company stresses the tour does not signal the vehicle will be sold in China, some observers believe it could still bolster the brand’s position.
content: Tesla is facing weaker sales in China this year, but the American electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer is looking to generate a buzz in its second-largest market by exhibiting its new self-driving vehicle, the Cybercab. The robotaxi – which operates entirely without a steering wheel, pedals or rear-view mirrors – would debut in major Chinese cities, including Beijing and Shanghai, starting mid-September in a showcase of product design and technological sophistication, according to Tesla China. However, the company clarified that the Cybercab exhibition did not indicate the cars would be sold in China, nor that Tesla’s robotaxi business would operate there any time soon. Still, industry observers and automotive dealers noted that the promotional tour could strengthen Tesla’s brand visibility in the world’s largest EV market, bringing potential longer-term benefits. “It will convince thousands of visitors at Tesla showrooms that the company remains a global leader in autonomous driving,” said Steve Shi, a manager at Juchen Auto Trade, a China-based car service firm. “Despite facing stiff competition here, Tesla still has a large fan base in China who want to buy its cars.” The Cybercab entered mass production at Tesla’s Texas Gigafactory in April. The two-seat model relies entirely on a self-driving system to navigate public streets without traditional manual controls. Tesla China’s announcement on Friday followed its Shanghai Gigafactory reporting a 7.9 per cent month-on-month decline in deliveries in August. The assembly plant – Tesla’s largest production hub worldwide – handed 86,166 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles to customers in China and abroad last month, compared with 93,579 total deliveries in July, according to data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA). The CPCA has yet to release a breakdown dividing the Shanghai plant’s August figures into domestic and overseas sales. Between January and July, Tesla delivered 266,204 vehicles to Chinese buyers, down 12.4 per cent from a year ago. Throughout 2025, the Shanghai Gigafactory produced about 851,000 vehicles for both domestic sales and exports, accounting for 52 per cent of Tesla’s global total. China remains Tesla’s second-largest market worldwide, behind only the United States. Last year, the EV maker reported sales of about 625,000 vehicles on the mainland, down nearly 5 per cent from 2024. The US carmaker established itself as an early front runner in China’s premium EV segment after its Shanghai factory began deliveries of the Model 3 to domestic customers in late 2019. By 2025, however, Chinese smartphone vendor and EV start-up Xiaomi had emerged as a formidable challenger in the domestic market, with deliveries of its fully electric SU7 surpassing those of Tesla’s Shanghai-produced Model 3.

title: Cold comfort: Japan’s Hokkaido battles cockroach surge amid global warming
description: Rising temperatures and ‘artificial environments’ enable the insects to thrive in a region once considered too hostile for them, experts say.
content: In all his five decades of living in Hokkaido, Makoto Watanabe cannot recall ever being confronted by a cockroach.
