But he admits being alarmed by reports that the despised insects are taking advantage of global warming to gain a foothold in a part of Japan where winters were previously considered too hostile for large colonies to emerge. “When I was a university student in Tokyo 30 years ago, I used to see them in my accommodation and I absolutely hated them,” Watanabe told This Week in Asia. “Since I moved back here, I have always thought that one of the big advantages of living in a place where it is so cold for much of that year is that there are far fewer insects, but cockroaches in particular,” said Watanabe, an academic who lives in the town of Eniwa. But Hokkaido has changed in those 30 years. According to Japan Meteorological Agency statistics, the average daytime temperature across the nation’s most northerly main island is 23 degrees Celsius (73.4 degrees Fahrenheit), rising to 29 degrees in major cities such as Sapporo, in the summer. That is 1.5 degrees higher than three decades ago. More recently, localised summer temperatures have spiked as high as 35 degrees, a figure that was unthinkable even a decade ago. Winter temperatures have also become milder, with the mean average at minus 3.7 degrees in January 1996, but up to minus 2 degrees in January this year. “The environment in the north of Japan has changed a lot and while it used to be difficult for cockroaches to thrive there, they are now finding ways into the ‘artificial environments’ that have been created by development,” said Dr Koichi Goka, head of the Invasive Species Research Team at Japan’s National Institute for Environmental Studies. According to Goka, the “heat island” effect has multiplied in big cities as modern industrial, business and residential units are fitted with heating units, as well as double glazing and other forms of insulation that make them comfortable environments for people and insects. This means a species previously rare in Hokkaido is now making itself comfortable in its new surroundings. “Cockroaches arrive in Hokkaido through human activity – attached to vehicles or in cardboard containers for food or consumer products – and they are increasingly finding places where they can survive even over the harsh winter months,” Goka said. Cockroaches are typically found in tropical or subtropical regions, but three varieties have apparently evolved to the point that they are able to withstand Hokkaido winters. The black cockroach grows to about 3cm long and has shiny black wings. The “brown-banded” variety is smaller and red-brown in colour. Increasingly common is the Japanese cockroach, which lives outdoors in more southern latitudes but has adapted. And Goka believes it is likely that a tipping point has been reached, with the insects having hit a critical mass and Hokkaido’s temperatures set to continue rising. “They are established in Hokkaido now and it will be very difficult – if not impossible – to eradicate them now,” he said. “They have found their ways into buildings and homes, so they have a foothold.” The owner of a Hokkaido-based pest extermination company told the Fuji News Network broadcaster that requests to deal with cockroach infestations were very rare a decade ago, but he had received 50 such requests since the start of this year. By the end of the year, he said, he expected the number of call-outs to have doubled.

title: Letters | Bid-rigging isn’t new. Hong Kong must revisit old complaints
description: Readers discuss reforms to the system around building renovation projects, and a lesson from Zhu Rongji’s life.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. The fire at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po, which claimed 168 lives, exposed a system in which flat owners – the people who pay for and live with the consequences of building renovation decisions – are practically powerless. One question deserves an answer: why did it take a tragedy to force the authorities to act? Owners across Hong Kong have filed complaints about rigged tenders and suspicious contracts for years, but little happened. Yet within months of the fire, investigations were launched. The obvious inference is that such malpractice is widespread, but extraordinarily difficult to prove. Collusion leaves few fingerprints – bids can be steered through consultant specifications, tender evaluations and proxy-stacked meetings that all look legitimate on paper. If malpractice only surfaces after a catastrophe, enforcement is reactive. That must change. Investigations and prosecutions should be standing practice, not post-tragedy theatre. I therefore urge the government and the Independent Commission Against Corruption to revisit complaints lodged by owners over the past 20 years concerning large-scale renovation projects. The industry’s problems did not begin two years ago; many owners who reported suspected collusion were turned away. Those files deserve a second look. Reform must also be structural. Owners are laypeople facing consultants, contractors and managers who run tenders for a living. Owners typically see only a glossy proposal and a recommendation, while the documents needed to scrutinise a deal are often unobtainable. Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court did what the law allowed – questioning a roughly HK$330 million project, requisitioning a meeting, voting out their management committee – yet still could not escape the contract. The consultation on amending the Building Management Ordinance is welcome. Four reforms deserve priority: stronger approval thresholds for large contracts, with tender documents published to all owners; a cap on proxy harvesting; mandatory declarations of interest, with false declarations criminalised; and a genuine mechanism for exiting contracts signed in questionable circumstances. After Wang Fuk Court, this should be treated not as a routine legislative tidy-up, but as a once-in-a-generation opportunity to return control of buildings to the people who own them. Victor Tan, Wan Chai Zhu Rongji and the long runway Zhu Rongji, who died last month aged 97, was 59 when he became mayor of Shanghai in 1988, the year I was born. It was the first time he had truly run anything. The premiership came a decade later. As a child, I knew him only as the official on television who lost his temper when nobody else did. In 1998 he said he had prepared a hundred coffins: 99 for corrupt officials, one for himself. That willingness to be disliked was earned. Orphaned by nine, Zhu graduated from Tsinghua and spent nearly 20 years in the political wilderness. He was around 50, when his old bureau chief Yuan Baohua brought him into the State Economic Commission. What he did in that interval is the whole lesson. He had “no resentment against Heaven, no quarrel with men”, as Confucius put it. He emerged with his competence sharpened. We often offer “A vessel great, it is the slowest made” as consolation, as though the vessel forms itself while you wait. It does not. Zhu was not waiting; he was working, unwatched. Nor did he forget who opened the door. In 2018, days before his 90th birthday, he travelled to pay respects to Yuan, then 102. None of this is to say there was no pain. Restructuring the state sector cost tens of millions their jobs; my father lost his. But an appreciation of Zhu that omits the cost is a press release. Zhu’s life offers no reassurance that things work out; for two decades there was no evidence his would. It might offer a job description for the interval: be good at the work while nobody is watching, refuse to blame the weather, be willing to be disliked once the work matters, and keep faith with those who kept faith with you. He took real command at 59 and did a lifetime’s work in the 15 years that followed. For anyone counting, that’s a long runway. Luo Chen Jun, Singapore

title: Red tape, high cost: can Hong Kong’s new yacht scheme chart a smoother course?
description: Participants sailing to Guangdong province’s Dongao Island say voyage was eventful although bureaucracy and costs were hurdles.
content: Retired harbour pilot Alex Yu Chi-leung sailed his 50-foot wooden yacht, Bowline, from Causeway Bay in Hong Kong to Dongao Island in Zhuhai under a new cross-border yachting scheme last week, but bureaucratic hurdles and shallow waters tempered the excitement of the leisure trip. It was Yu’s first voyage under the scheme, but it could also be his last unless mainland Chinese authorities improve certain requirements. “If the procedures are simplified – because right now they are too numerous, complicated and ambiguous – then I will come back again,” he said. “If I have to do a massive round of work just to sail for one or two days, I might as well sail in Hong Kong.” He added that he would rather take a commercial ferry to Dongao for a holiday. Still, the 66-year-old veteran mariner gave the voyage a score of 60 out of 100 and viewed it as a worthwhile test run. Yu was among 139 participants aboard 16 yachts from Hong Kong and Macau that sailed to Dongao under the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau individual yacht scheme. Launched in June, the scheme allows eligible Hong Kong and Macau vessels to enter designated Guangdong waters for tourism. The voyage, which took place over the weekend, was the scheme’s largest cross-border flotilla to date. It gave visitors a taste of the island’s seafood, hotel suites and natural scenery. An eventful voyage Early on August 29, the flotilla left the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club in Causeway Bay for Dongao, about 36 nautical miles (53.7km) southwest of the city. The journey took between 6½ and 8½ hours, depending on the yacht’s speed. For participants such as 60-year-old financial executive Noel Chan and his 16-year-old son Nigel, it was family time. Chan sailed his 45-foot cruiser, Rampage, in 15-knot winds, while the pair chatted and shared drinks on deck. “The wind speed was very good, conditions were great,” Nigel Chan said. Mabel Tsim, an IT professional and sailor, described the eight-hour journey as a stress-relieving bonding experience. She compared Dongao Island’s idyllic setting and sea views with those of a Southeast Asian resort in Thailand or Bali, Indonesia. “For us as crew members, we focus on the journey itself,” she said. “The destination is a place for leisure, but more importantly, the process is sailing … For city dwellers, it is very stress-relieving.” But hardware limitations soon became apparent. Immigration procedures at the designated port on Guishan Island took about 20 minutes – visitors entered a building, went upstairs for home return permit and baggage checks, then waited downstairs while officers checked vessel documents. However, there was only one yacht berth, meaning vessels had to circle at sea for about 15 minutes while waiting for the previous yacht to clear. One yacht suffered an incident at the port when its propeller broke off and sank to the seabed. After navigating intermittent rain, the fleet arrived at Dongao, an island heavily reliant on mainland families visiting at weekends. But its temporary pontoons proved inadequate, with one yacht running aground twice in shallow water. In the end, 13 of the 16 yachts stayed on the island for one night, while the rest remained for two. Before setting sail, a yacht typically had to spend thousands of Hong Kong dollars to meet government requirements, including a US$1,500 vessel inspection and 3,000 yuan (US$447) in clearance fees, excluding hotel, food and other expenses. For some participants, the time and expense were still worthwhile. “I think out of 100 marks, I would say 85 to 90, so no such complaint … [the mainland is] really, really helpful for this [scheme] … [they] didn’t give you any hassle,” Noel Chan said. His son Nigel compared the cost of sailing to Zhuhai with a friend’s experience in the United Kingdom. “It’s 100 per cent more affordable, and it’s a much more pleasant experience,” he said. While committed sailors and industry advocates regard the scheme’s early problems as necessary growing pains on the path to a world-class Greater Bay Area maritime economy, more pragmatic yacht owners remain divided over whether sailing north is worth the effort. The yacht economy For those with a team to navigate the administrative hurdles, the value proposition can be striking. Noel Chan said he spent just several thousand yuan on Marriott sea-view suites and other expenses for his group of 12. He said the trip cost a fraction of a comparable stay in Hong Kong, and voiced concern that it could lead to a further outflow of Hong Kong consumer spending to the mainland. “You go to Hong Kong, have a bad dinner, you spend that money already. So I think it’s a big challenge [for the] Hong Kong economy,” he said. “The money moved here again by sea instead of Hong Kong cars going [through the northbound vehicle scheme].” The flotilla was a boon for some hotels. A representative from the island’s five-star Gree Dongao Hotel said that the flotilla booked nearly 70 rooms, filling the 268-room property on August 29. The hotel is part of the state-owned Zhuhai Gree Group, which has invested about 4 billion yuan since 2009 to develop a high-end hotel cluster on Dongao. The cluster also includes a 257-room Marriott and the cliffside Alila resort, which has 103 suites and is already attracting Hong Kong yachting people. Dongfa Seafood Restaurant co-owner Zhou Shunfang, 60, marvelled at the flotilla but said she had not seen an influx of high-spending yacht guests. She suspected touts had intercepted them at the pier before they discovered her long-established restaurant. Charting a smoother course Liao Kai, president of the Zhuhai Yacht Association, said about 50 yachts had obtained temporary nationality certificates, allowing them to use the scheme to travel to the Greater Bay Area. Participants broadly agreed that the cross-border experience would require major upgrades to both its policy framework and physical infrastructure before it could unlock the full economic potential of Greater Bay Area waters. At the policy level, reducing the barriers to entry is crucial. The Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club had called for cross-border costs to be harmonised, vice-commodore Joseph Chu said. He suggested that northbound fees should be cut from thousands of Hong Kong dollars to match the nominal HK$58 charged for southbound vessels. He argued that equalising the fees would turn special expeditions into more frequent trips, similar to Hong Kong residents travelling to Shenzhen for afternoon tea before returning home. Yu echoed the call for less bureaucracy. He urged authorities across the border to drop the allegedly redundant “temporary nationality certificate” and accept surveys carried out by Hong Kong-approved professionals, rather than requiring separate and costly mainland inspections. Workarounds to reduce costs are also emerging. Liao said traditional commercial shipping agencies had charged tens of thousands of dollars for customs clearance, prompting the Zhuhai Yacht Association to set up a dedicated agency to deal with paperwork. The move helped reduce outbound clearance fees to around 3,000 yuan for the flotilla. On the water, relatively simple logistical changes could reduce delays. Noel Chan recommended staggered arrival times for yachts at clearance ports such as Guishan, to prevent bottlenecks that leave vessels circling offshore. Tsim said authorities should find a way to process several boats at once. She also called for less rigid point-to-point travel rules, allowing yachts to visit more than one destination on the same itinerary. Infrastructure remains a major constraint. Both Yu and Noel Chan said robust floating moorings, and more of them, were urgently needed at destinations such as Dongao Island to stop yachts having to “double park” in unsafe conditions. Gao Jun, an associate professor at Sun Yat-sen University’s school of tourism management, said Zhuhai needed to improve tourist spending opportunities and amenities to extend the value chain beyond its 20-year manufacturing base in Pingsha. By taking advantage of new self-navigating repair policies in Jinwan, cross-border access points and related services, Zhuhai aims to capture longer-term value from yacht maintenance and berthing, rather than relying solely on weekend tourism. Liao said four yachts had successfully sailed to Jinwan, undergone major repairs and returned to Hong Kong since the self-navigating vessel repair policy was launched in March. He added that more than 20 other vessels were applying to use the service. Industry leaders urged patience. Chu compared the scheme’s early administrative and infrastructure problems with the chaotic early days of Hong Kong International Airport before it developed into a global aviation hub. Stakeholders are now preparing for the anticipated launch of southbound travel. Liao said he had heard from local authorities that the southbound scheme might open in September.

title: China begins mining iron from tailings, low-grade ore that can meet its demand for decades
description: Scientists have found a way to turn waste into a valuable resource on an industrial scale, reducing China’s dependence on iron ore imports.
content: China has launched a world-first industrial-scale facility to extract iron from previously discarded mine tailings and ultra-low-grade ore, turning waste into a valuable resource that can reduce its dependency on overseas supply. According to the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) last Tuesday, a production line capable of processing 5.56 million tonnes of refractory iron ore and tailings per year has passed official checks and is now running steadily. China is the world’s largest iron ore user, absorbing more than half the global supply. However, relying on imports for more than 80 per cent of its needs – mainly from Australia and Brazil – has long undermined its bargaining power and supply security. On the other hand, China has the fourth-largest iron ore reserves, yet most are low grade, and nearly half are too hard and costly to process with standard methods. So huge amounts remain unused. The new breakthrough aims to make those hard-to-use ores viable. State broadcaster CCTV reported that the technology could fundamentally strengthen China’s ability to secure its own iron resources and reduce its heavy dependence on imports of the strategic commodity. After iron ore is mined, the first step is to separate iron-bearing minerals from waste rock. The usual methods use magnetism or density differences, but they do not work when the ore has very low iron content. Researchers at CAS’ Institute of Process Engineering have come up with a new magnetising roasting technique. In short, this fine-tunes the process so that non-magnetic iron minerals become magnetic – turning old waste into usable material. Zhu Qingshan, head of the research team, told China Science Daily on Thursday that the technology traced back to the very founding of the institute’s predecessor – the Institute of Chemical Metallurgy. The late academician Guo Musun began experiments as early as 1959, but the work was later suspended. In 2004, Zhu took over and restarted the research under Guo’s advice. In the early years, it was even hard to find corporate partners. Today’s mature technology, he said, was the result of a half-century scientific marathon. According to CAS, this is the first time worldwide that low-grade iron tailings have been processed on a large industrial scale. The technology boosts iron content from 11 per cent in the tailings to 65 per cent in the concentrate. Looking ahead, the technology could unlock the use of nearly 30 billion tonnes of refractory iron ore and around 10 billion tonnes of iron-bearing tailings across China. The project that just passed inspection consists of three production lines, each with an annual capacity of 1.85 million tonnes. They went into operation in January in Anshan, Liaoning province – a traditional steelmaking heartland. “The facility now produces 2.2 million tonnes of iron concentrate per year,” a manager from Ansteel, a state-owned steel giant, told CCTV on Wednesday. While no official price details are available, the process uses 35 per cent less energy than comparable methods, which cuts costs. The project has also been included in China’s first official list of green and low-carbon demonstration projects issued by the National Development and Reform Commission. However, this project alone will not end China’s need for imports from Australia and Brazil. In 2025, the country imported over 1.25 billion tonnes of ore – far beyond what this single line can produce. Still, the technology turns waste tailings into a useful reserve and opens a new path forward. According to CAS, the project is a core part of a larger plan by Ansteel Group to reprocess 24 million tonnes of iron tailings per year.

title: Face Off: Should secondary schools have esports teams for students to join?
description: Each week, two readers discuss a hot topic in a parliamentary-style debate that doesn’t necessarily reflect their personal viewpoints.
content:
If you are interested in joining future Face Off debates, fill out this form to submit your application.
Some schools are considering whether competitive gaming should be incorporated into student activities. While some critics argue that esports will lead to excessive screen time, I believe secondary schools should establish esports teams, provided that proper teacher supervision and regulations are in place.
Esports can help students develop a wide range of transferable skills. For example, in the competitive game League of Legends , players must coordinate with their teammates, adapt to rapidly changing situations and perform under pressure. These abilities are not only essential in esports competitions but are also highly valued in academic and professional settings. Contrary to the common misconception that gaming is a waste of time, students can sharpen their skills in a structured environment by joining an esports team.
In a 2024 study of adolescents published in the journal Front Psychiatry, Canadian researchers compared 67 esports players with 109 recreational gamers. For 74.6 per cent of esports players, there were positive effects on their social relationships. Many also reported improvements in their motivation, concentration and mental health. These findings challenge the stereotype that gaming leads to social isolation.
Opponents may argue that secondary schools should not establish esports teams because gaming can lead to addiction, poor academic performance and excessive screen time. In fact, esports directly challenge this mindset. The issue is not whether students play games, as many already do. The real question is whether schools should provide a structured environment that transforms gaming into a platform for personal growth, teamwork and independence.
The same study also found that esports players spent more time online and were more likely to exhibit problematic gaming behaviours. But the study concluded that prevention and supervision are essential. In a Canadian school programme mentioned in the report, students were required to exercise, maintain academic standards and attend workshops about healthy lifestyles in order to be part of the team.
Schools therefore should provide a controlled environment where healthy habits can be reinforced , rather than leaving students to navigate gaming culture on their own.
In recent years, competitive gaming, or esports, has exploded in popularity. This trend has prompted some teachers and students to support the creation of official esports teams in secondary schools. While the idea of playing video games competitively at school might sound appealing to teens, introducing esports into school is ultimately bad for students’ health, academic focus and overall well-being.
First, the introduction of esports goes against a school’s responsibility to promote healthy lifestyle habits. Secondary school students already spend many hours in front of screens, whether for homework or entertainment.
Creating an official school esports team would require students to sit through hours of training sessions after school. Excessive screen time and lack of physical activity can cause health issues, such as poor posture, wrist pain and sleep loss. Unlike traditional sports teams that build heart health and physical agility, esports teams would only tie students to chairs and screens.
Furthermore, esports can be addictive and time-consuming. High-level competitive gaming demands intense focus and practice. Managing schoolwork, test preparation and family time is already a difficult balancing act for most teenagers.
Also, if schools validate video games by forming official teams, it could blur the lines between healthy fun and academic distraction. Students may struggle to prioritise their studies, leading to a drop in their grades. The instant excitement and rewards of gaming can easily overshadow the long-term rewards of studying hard.
Finally, the social environment of online gaming is often harmful to the positive character-building that school activities should encourage. While traditional sports teach sportsmanship, face-to-face communication and emotional strength, too much gaming can lead to social isolation, as digital interactions replace meaningful, real-world relationships. And even in a supervised school environment, gaming culture could encourage toxic behaviour and online bullying.
While esports may offer a well-paying career path for a select few, the benefits are outweighed by the risks to the average secondary school student’s physical health, academic success and mental well-being. Schools should focus their limited resources on promoting physical sports, arts and interactive clubs that encourage students to step away from the digital world, rather than pull them further into it.

title: Signalling fault disrupts Hong Kong high-speed rail service, delaying 15 trains
description: Rail services have since resumed after 45-minute disruption to northbound trips on Sunday morning, Transport Department says.
content: At least 15 high-speed cross-border train services were delayed in Hong Kong after a signalling fault prompted a 45-minute disruption of northbound journeys on Sunday morning. The Transport Department said at around 8.30am that the MTR Corporation had notified authorities that high-speed rail services at the West Kowloon terminus of the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong Express Rail Link would be delayed due to a “signal fault”. At around 9.15am, the department said the MTR Corp had resolved the signal issues, and high-speed rail services were gradually resuming normally. It said passengers could check the official 12306 train service app, the relevant MTR website and announcements at the station for details. According to 12306, at least 15 northbound trains from the West Kowloon terminus were delayed, including those to Futian, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Fuzhou, Zhangjiajie, Xian, Tianjin and Chengdu. A government spokesman said on Sunday night that the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department had asked the rail operator to conduct a comprehensive review of the incident. The operator had to submit an investigation report within a month to explain the cause and propose improvement measures, he said. Some passengers took to Chinese social media platform RedNote to voice their frustration over the disruption. “I don’t know what happened in West Kowloon station from about 7am to 8.30am, but all trains were stuck and weren’t allowed into the station,” a RedNote user wrote. “I waited on the train for about one hour before I could finally get off.” Another user travelling to Shenzhen to shop said his train was scheduled for 9.40am, but was delayed by about 20 minutes. Smart Transportation Alliance executive director and ex-lawmaker Gary Zhang Xinyu, a former MTR Corp engineer, said the delay might have been caused by signalling equipment, such as transmitters and detectors, beside the tracks. “The components of signal facilities are like computers or phones we use ourselves,” he said. “That’s not something you can completely avoid.” He said that the repair time on Sunday morning fell within the normal range and hoped that enhanced daily maintenance would reduce the likelihood of such outcomes. Cross-border train services had suffered signalling faults before. On July 1, 2023, signalling problems at the West Kowloon terminus led to a temporary suspension of services. Four trains between Hong Kong and Shenzhen were cancelled, and more than 10 were delayed. The disruption sparked an outcry from travellers, with some stranded at the terminus or on the train. The MTR Corp offered refunds to affected passengers In a separate incident on May 8, 2023, a signalling equipment malfunction near the West Kowloon terminus reportedly led to 26 trains being cancelled. Service gradually resumed after the MTR Corp repaired the equipment in about 1½ hours that day. Affected passengers were switched to other trains or offered a refund.

title: Junior Chinese customs officer killed in mudslide just 4 days into job deeply moves public
description: Her younger sister shares a touching memory online, recalling Li’s promise to take parents to Beijing during next Spring Festival holiday.
content: The tragic death of a junior Chinese customs officer on the Sino-Nepal border, who had only been in her position for four days before being killed in a catastrophic mudslide, has stirred immense heartbreak online. Twenty-four-year-old Li Leiyang began her role as a plant quarantine officer at the Customs at Gyirong Port in Tibet on August 21, according to a report by news portal 163.com. On August 26, while Li was working at her desk, a glacier collapsed in Nepal, triggering a mudslide and floods that travelled 22km in just seven minutes, devastating the Gyirong Port area. This disaster destroyed 27 structures, including the Customs building where Li was located, along with roads and facilities. The aftermath left only the steel framework of the Customs building, as seen in photographs taken after the event. To date, 31 deaths have been confirmed in China’s Tibet region, primarily in the severely impacted Gyirong Port area, while 1,344 people have lost their lives in Nepal. Additionally, thousands remain unaccounted for on both sides of the border. As search and rescue operations are ongoing, a rescue team leader dispatched from Sichuan province to assist his counterparts in Tibet, informed Beijing Daily on August 29 that their equipment had not detected any signs of life in the affected area. Li is among the 541 people missing on the Chinese side whose bodies have yet to be recovered. On September 1, the Gyirong Port Customs authority held a morning ceremony to honour their lost colleagues. Her death captivated millions of internet users in China after they learned of her long and challenging journey to secure the position, which she enjoyed for only four days. Li hailed from a rural family in Anhui province in eastern China. She earned an associate degree from Anhui University of Applied Technology, a relatively unknown institution in the region. After years of hard work to improve her educational background, she was admitted to Anhui Agricultural University, from which she graduated with a bachelor’s degree. Li then successfully passed the demanding graduate school entrance exam for the prestigious China Agricultural University (CAU) in Beijing, from which she graduated months ago with a master’s degree in resource utilisation and plant protection. To secure a position at Customs, regarded by many as an “iron bowl profession,” Li took the highly competitive public servant enrolment test, scoring first among 2,000 applicants. In a social media post announcing its new staff members, the Gyirong Port Customs authority shared that Li described herself as a “hard-working and courageous person with a stable mood.” Her hobbies included planting flowers, reading, and playing with cats and dogs. “As a new member of the Customs, I will seriously fulfil my duty as a plant quarantine officer. My love for this land will motivate me to work hard in safeguarding the biological safety line at our country’s border,” Li wrote in her introduction. Her younger sister shared on social media that Li had once promised to take their parents on a trip to Beijing during the Spring Festival holiday next year. “We never expected that after working for only four days, we would no longer be able to reach you by phone. Our parents and I are waiting for you at home,” her sister lamented. “It is difficult to secure a government job. Who would have imagined that your first salary would also be your pension?” Li’s story has sparked a significant outpouring of emotional responses from internet users in China. “Her entire life was spent preparing for exams. She only experienced the joy of life for four days. Her life is so tragic!” lamented one internet user. Another echoed: “Fate is too cruel to her. I feel deeply sorry for her. Rest in peace, girl.”

title: Hired, then what? Malaysia’s deaf workers push past entry-level jobs
description: A job offer is only the first step, deaf Malaysians say. True inclusion means equal opportunities and room to rise.
content: Yap Yee Lin has been serving espresso at a Starbucks in Malaysia since 2012, longer than many of his colleagues have worked anywhere. But it was only last year, after 13 years with the company, that he was promoted to shift manager at a branch in Kuala Lumpur’s Bangsar Village II. The wait says less about Yap, who is deaf, than it does about how rare that kind of promotion still is for deaf workers in the Southeast Asian nation – and how much has had to change around him to make it possible. Yap, 36, works at what Starbucks calls a Signing Store: an outlet staffed by deaf baristas working alongside colleagues trained in sign language, where visual alarms replace buzzers and dual screens allow staff who cannot hear to confirm an order without it needing to be called out. The Kuala Lumpur branch was the first of its kind in the world when it opened in 2016 and has since become something of a flagship for corporate inclusion. “The hearing and the deaf, they are also given the opportunity to be independent and an opportunity for promotion,” Yap said. Across Malaysia, structured career progression for people with disabilities remains the exception rather than the rule. And it often depends on their employer taking the initiative. Room to rise The idea for a Signing Store has its roots in a project that Starbucks began rolling out in 2016 to create job opportunities for people with disabilities, according to Rina Siew, head of sustainability and social impact for Berjaya Food, the licensee that operates Starbucks in Malaysia and Brunei. At first, deaf recruits were mainly employed as cleaners, but the company soon found that offering routine work with little room for career growth was unsustainable. Deaf employees wanted to become baristas, Siew said, so the coffee giant worked to make it happen. “That was how the concept of the Signing Store was born,” she said. “We wanted a place where they could build their careers like all of us here at Starbucks.” Achieving this meant redesigning the outlets themselves, training hearing staff in Malaysian Sign Language and integrating deaf employees into the same professional-development and performance-review track as everyone else. “At Starbucks, we have a career progression plan for all partners,” Siew said. A decade later, the results are clear to see in the company’s organisational structure. Starbucks Malaysia now has its first deaf store manager-in-training, based in Penang, alongside deaf shift managers working in branches across Kuala Lumpur, Johor and Sarawak. Globally, the company operates more than 26 Signing Stores, including in the United States, Japan, South Korea and China. Siew said the ultimate goal was to make that level of inclusion the norm rather than the exception, incorporating it into Starbucks everywhere, not just a few designated branches. Standing in the way of the ambition to hire more workers with disabilities is a lingering workplace stigma, however. Some employers still viewed deaf staff as less productive, or asked why they should receive the same pay as hearing colleagues, Siew said, adding that there was also a chronic lack of sign language interpreters. “Interpreters in Malaysia are really scarce,” she told This Week in Asia. Wong Yi Xiang, 34, knows that struggle all too well. He joined Starbucks six months ago, after a job search hamstrung not by his qualifications, but by communication difficulties. “My biggest barrier is communication, especially during interviews, because some employers do not understand deaf people,” he said. “All I want is a fair chance to show my work-related skills.” What Wong really desires from a workplace is simple: hearing colleagues willing to meet him halfway and learn enough sign language to work alongside him as an equal. Opportunities for deaf people are scarce in Malaysia and many employers who do hire them largely treat it as a quota-filling exercise – a truth Yap knows from firsthand experience. “It’s difficult for deaf people to look for a job,” he said. “In most places, you only get one or two [deaf employees].” A place to belong More than 800,000 people were registered as persons with disabilities in Malaysia in 2024, according to the country’s Department of Statistics, representing 2.4 per cent of the population. Employment among that group has inched upwards: 4,209 people with disabilities held civil service jobs in 2024, the latest year for which figures are available, up from 3,901 the year before. Yet the main obstacle remains acceptance and understanding, according to the Malaysian Federation of the Deaf. Its executive director Mohamad Sazali Shaari, who is himself a member of the deaf community, said deaf jobseekers were still routinely asked to prove their competence before being considered for a role in a way hearing candidates rarely were. “Limitations arise when colleagues are not accommodating of deaf employees’ communication needs or when there is poor access to information,” he said. “This can become more difficult in workplaces with high staff turnover, where new colleagues may not understand the support deaf employees need, undermining efforts to build an inclusive workplace.” Government incentives had helped, Sazali said, but this was not the same as a sense of belonging. “We will never feel welcome if our needs aren’t in place and sensitivity towards these needs will help to ease our discomfort in society at large,” he said. Malaysia’s government has said it is pushing for precisely that kind of change in perspective. At a gathering in December to mark the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, the cabinet minister who oversees social welfare, women’s rights and family development said the country should move away from viewing disabled citizens as a group in need of assistance and start treating them as one capable of contributing, creating and leading. “This shift requires a change in mindset: from sympathy to respect, from simply giving to empowerment and from assistance to the recognition of rights,” Women, Family and Community Development Minister Nancy Shukri said. Malaysia is not alone in trying to move disability employment beyond simply getting people into work. Singapore has set a target of 40 per cent employment among resident people with disabilities aged 15 to 64 by 2030, up from the 34.7 per cent recorded in 2024-25. Its Ministry of Manpower said in March that 6,800 employers had received government wage support to hire 10,800 residents with disabilities last year, with a separate scheme helping more than 2,400 disabled jobseekers find work over the previous four years. Even so, officials in the city state have drawn many of the same conclusions Starbucks reached in Malaysia – that getting people through the door is not the same as offering them a place to belong. “Inclusive workplaces cannot be built on incentives alone,” said Shawn Huang, senior parliamentary secretary for manpower, during a parliamentary meeting about the country’s annual budget, adding that Singapore would also focus on training, employer support and career resilience. For Yap, helping manage a Signing Store means more than just a pay cheque; it is a way of being accepted by society. After years of seeing deaf workers elsewhere relegated to one or two token roles per company, a shift manager’s badge feels like a quiet victory. “I really enjoy it [my job],” he said. “There are so many tourists coming here from all over the world. I really thank them for coming to visit our place and it’s a really amazing experience for us.” Wong, earlier in his career, is thinking about what he can pass on rather than what he has been given. “I hope to become a coffee master and learn more about coffee,” he said. “I want to share my knowledge about my work and teach other people.”

title: Elderly riders bear brunt of rising New York City subway attacks
description: A woman, who ended up in hospital after being shoved onto the tracks at a station, said ‘nobody’s doing anything’ about the spike in assaults.
content: Attacks on elderly straphangers are fuelling a spike in felony assaults within the New York City subway system, according to New York Police Department’s transit chief Joseph Gulotta. As the NYPD contends with a 9 per cent jump in felony assaults in the city transit system this year, the department’s transit chief said roughly half of all attacks on the rails are targeting a few select groups. “What is driving them is assaults on police officers, assaults on MTA workers and assaults on the elderly,” Gulotta told a news briefing at the NYPD’s Manhattan headquarters on Friday. “When you put those three together, that’s almost 50 per cent of felony assaults.” “That’s something we’re really geared up on. It’s something we take very seriously.” Police have investigated 435 assaults in transit this year through the end of August, compared with the 397 reported by that time last year. Elderly people were the victims in 17 per cent of the attacks, officials said. Police made up another 21 per cent of the victims. While assaults in the subways are up, random attacks are down by 8 per cent, from 69 last year to 63 this year, police said. Unprovoked felony assaults decreased by 4 per cent, from 71 last year to 68. Those arrested for assaults are mostly repeat offenders, police said. The transit chief revealed the new data on attacks targeting elderly commuters just days after a 65-year-old woman, whose leg was broken in three places after a mentally ill stranger shoved her onto the tracks at a Bronx subway station in an unprovoked attack, blasted city leaders for failing to protect riders. “The situation has got to stop,” an outraged Lydia Zuniga told The New York Daily News from her hospital bed last week. “The city isn’t doing anything regarding crazy people. They’re running the subways, and nobody’s doing anything about it.” Zuniga was waiting for a Manhattan-bound No 5 train at the elevated E. 180th St. station near Morris Park Avenue in West Farms at about 1.45pm (local time) on August 27, when her attacker stormed up to her, she said. Other attacks targeting seniors include a 70-year-old woman who was hurled onto the tracks at the 57th St.-Seventh Avenue station in Midtown on July 18. And on April 11, Anthony Griffin, 44, was shot dead by police for slashing three elderly victims with a machete and calling himself “Lucifer” at Grand Central Station. Gulotta said that roughly two out of every three assaults in transit result in an arrest, and that most New Yorkers report feeling safe riding the subway despite the rise in violence. “[To have] 71 per cent of people feeling safe on the subway is an incredible number for us,” the transit chief said. In Zuniga’s case and in the assault on the 70-year-old woman, their attackers did not last long on the streets. Zaki Smith, 36, was captured just two days after the attack inside the 57th St. station and charged with attempted murder, felony assault and misdemeanour assault, police said. And one day after the attack on Zuniga, Juan Nieves, 29, made his way to a psychiatric clinic seeking help, where he confessed to the attack, according to law enforcement sources. He is charged with attempted murder, assault and reckless endangerment as a hate crime, police said.

title: Opinion | In an era of extreme summers, it’s time to look beyond air conditioning
description: In Hong Kong, air conditioning is ubiquitous but conventional models harm the environment. More responsible solutions are needed.
content: The Labour Department recently upgraded its Heat Stress at Work Warning system, making it easier for higher-tier alerts to be sent out, so that employers and workers, especially those who have to work outdoors, can react quickly during very hot weather. Unfortunately, the most we seem to be able to do is issue warnings and recommend passive mitigation measures such as relaxing the work schedule, resting in the shade and staying hydrated. We are sitting ducks as temperatures peak year after year. This has been a testing summer with multiple record-breaking hot days across the globe. In 2024, Hong Kong’s hottest year on record since 1884 saw 52 very hot days (33 degrees Celsius or higher) and just two extremely hot days (35 degrees or higher); the highest temperature hit that year was 35.7 degrees in September. This year, we have already seen three extremely hot days in August alone and a record high of 36.9 degrees – according to the Observatory in Tsim Sha Tsui; at the Sheung Shui weather station, the mercury hit 39.8 degrees. This is a terrifying rate of increase. How much human action has contributed to the extreme weather we are experiencing is up for debate. Are the heatwaves, super typhoons and storms, torrential rains and floods, and severe droughts around the world the result of irresponsible climate crimes we have committed? While it is easy to point fingers, empirical science demands solid evidence and data analysis. What we do know, for certain, is that the heatwaves in Asia are linked to a strong El Nino pattern developed in the Pacific Ocean when waters became warmer, affecting trade winds. No country in Asia was entirely spared from the extreme weather and all have developed some form of advisory system and national processes to battle the heat. Hong Kong was able to handle the heat a bit better but only because we are spoiled by the convenience of air conditioning. From high-end homes in wealthy neighbourhoods to deteriorating tenement houses in dilapidated districts, condensation units are a familiar sight and strolling in the city’s overly air-conditioned shopping malls has become a sport for common folk during the summer. In contrast, European countries, for instance, were not so lucky. Many had no air conditioning but this was not only because of regulatory restrictions, historic preservation mandates or environmental concerns. The continent historically enjoyed mild and short summers, so buildings tended to adopt passive cooling measures, which used to be able to handle the warmest days; it would be a technical challenge to retrofit many of these structures. Also, given that energy costs in Europe are significantly higher than in North America or Asia, air conditioning is a luxury few can afford. If architecture is the creation of an artificial environment and the objective is to provide a beautiful, functional and comfortable space for users, then we must find tangible answers in design and engineering to combat discomfort – including the sweltering summer heat – but not at the expense of the interests of others. Air conditioning may seem the obvious and most convenient solution but conventional models harm the environment by raising outdoor temperatures and releasing greenhouse gases or hydrofluorocarbons into the atmosphere. If there is an urgent frontier in the design and construction industry, it is to responsibly create buildings and development that offer healthy and comfortable environments even under extreme climate conditions. Architects and engineers need to adopt available design measures such as erecting exterior surfaces with good insulation to reduce heat gain, encouraging cross-circulation and air flow, applying heat-reflective or radiative cooling paints, adopting shading devices, overhangs and canopies, installing photovoltaic panels and building roofs to capture, store and convert solar energy to electricity, as well as integrating greenery and water features into building and urban design to reduce the urban heat island effect. The goal is to implement all of our technical know-how to lower heat gain, lowering our reliance on air conditioning. We must hold on to the belief that not all the building technology to battle climate change has been conceived of and invented. While some economies, such as in the Middle East, continue to pursue taller, bigger buildings and vanity projects, China years ago banned any construction over 500 metres, shifting the architectural focus towards creative solutions and new technologies that enhance constructibility, efficiency, sustainability – and user comfort and need. A great prototype can be found in Yuncheng, a city in China’s northern Shanxi province, where 200 nozzles installed on the rooftops of residential towers spray a water mist to cool the air around the buildings. According to one resident, the mist was “cooling and purified the air” and “the temperature felt about four or five degrees lower”. The fine mist evaporates, never reaching the streets below, and the rainbows it creates were icing on the cake. This low-tech solution, requiring no compressor or refrigerant, is an example of a creative but simple solution. In the age of robotic technology and artificial intelligence, ingenuity can still offer solutions to pressing and immediate climate problems. Although robots and AI cannot really sense thermal discomfort, the recurring heatwaves must prompt efforts to explore if and how the technology can spark out-of-the-box thinking and offer solutions for this real and existential problem facing the world. Improving human life in this way would validate technology’s worth – more than the generation of crowd-pleasing images or kung fu performances that offer spectacle but little further value.

title: Why Chelsea football shirts are making Hong Kong fans nervous about crypto laws
description: Caught between their favourite football club and Hong Kong’s Stablecoins Ordinance, fans want to know if they can wear the tops openly.
content: English Premier League football club Chelsea’s lucrative new front-of-shirt sponsorship deal with a stablecoin issuer has left Hong Kong fans and retailers concerned about whether wearing or selling the top counts as illegal promotion under digital currency laws. Chelsea signed the deal with Circle to feature its USDC stablecoin brand on player jerseys for the 2026-27 season in late August, just three months after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) warned Premier League clubs about partnering with unauthorised crypto and finance businesses. Circle’s UK arm, Circle UK Trading, is an FCA-regulated company providing certain financial services. But USDC is not issued or regulated under the laws of the United Kingdom, nor is it distributed by a licensed stablecoin issuer in Hong Kong. Only two stablecoin issuers are currently licensed in Hong Kong – Anchorpoint Financial Limited and HSBC. Ahead of the enactment of the Stablecoins Ordinance on August 1, 2025, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) warned on its website that “it will be illegal for any person to … actively market the issue of unlicensed [fiat-referenced stablecoins] to the public”. Winnie Choi, a Chelsea fan of 12 years, was among those worried about breaking the law. “After looking up the law, I still do not understand whether it is a problem to wear the jersey,” she said. Choi suggested that the HKMA issue a clear, “down-to-earth” guideline on whether wearing the shirt with the USDC logo constituted promotion. Danny*, a club supporter for more than 20 years, said ordinary football fans would not have the awareness to identify if the shirt promoted an unregulated stablecoin. “If I wear it, who will enforce the law? Will I be arrested by police?” he said. Danny said he would not buy the new jersey until authorities clarified whether it was legal to wear it. Hammer Chung, owner of football apparel shop DirectSoccer in Mong Kok, said he was unsure whether it was legal to sell replica jerseys with the USDC logo. He added that he hoped regulators would clarify the matter. But Chung noted that many of the kits for other football clubs that he sold also bore the logos of illegal gambling websites. “Are we also promoting for them by selling the shirts?” he said. The HKMA said it would not comment on individual cases, but noted the ordinance prohibited the “active marketing” or advertising of unauthorised stablecoin activity in Hong Kong. Whether an act constituted actively marketing to the public was determined on a case-by-case basis, a spokesman said. Factors considered by the HKMA included the languages used in the marketing messages, whether they targeted people living in the city, whether a Hong Kong domain name was used and whether a detailed marketing plan was in place to promote the activity. A specific exemption was provided to publishers and live broadcasters who merely published content created by others, as long as they satisfied the relevant conditions set out in the provision and considered the relevant facts and circumstances, he said. Blockchain expert Louis Li Sze-chung expressed concerns that fans donning the new Chelsea shirt in public could be “problematic”, as it all depended on how the HKMA defined active marketing. “There are so many grey areas,” he said, adding that he dared not wear T-shirts sporting the logos of unlicensed crypto trading platforms after the licensing regime was put in place by the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). Li said USDC was the second-largest stablecoin in the world, and it was ridiculous that it was labelled as “unlicensed” under local legislation. He also said it was difficult to regulate the promotion of cryptocurrencies within a certain jurisdiction in the age of the internet because they were issued globally. “How can you say something legal in other countries is illegal here?” The ordinance provides an exemption for promoting unlicensed stablecoins across various media and digital platforms, including live broadcasts, provided the person did not devise and exercised no control over the content of the advertisement. “A group of players on TV is wearing [shirts with] this logo … it’s impossible that it isn’t an advertisement. We’re looking at them the entire game, right?” Li said. Tanna Chong, head of public policy at VerifyVASP, a digital assets compliance company, called for enhanced consumer protection through disclaimers before every match, similar to warning messages in moneylending advertisements. “They would be clear reminders that the programme contains these materials [about cryptocurrency], and that those companies actually do not have a licence in Hong Kong,” she said. Chong, who helped draft the ordinance during her time in government, said there was no hard and fast rule to define active marketing, noting that it was a concept determined on a case-by-case basis considering various contextual factors. She said neither Circle nor Chelsea had control over the broadcasting of matches in Hong Kong, which involved a deal between NowTV and the Premier League, and had not actively implemented a marketing campaign in the city. Circle was not “by way of business providing services” in the city either, she added. She also reassured fans that there was no problem with wearing the Blues’ shirt with the USDC logo, as wearers were not the service provider. “Unless [the wearer] is a Circle employee walking down the street in a Chelsea jersey. In that case, you need to establish that Circle instructed him to wear it with the intent of targeting a Hong Kong audience,” she said. An HKT spokesman said Now TV strictly complied with all relevant Hong Kong laws and regulations. The South China Morning Post has reached out to Circle and Chelsea FC for comment. The West London club’s latest deal followed a collective agreement by all 20 Premier League clubs to phase out front-of-shirt gambling sponsors. But the Blues are not the first team to partner with the crypto sector. OKX and Kraken, both virtual asset trading platforms unlicensed in Hong Kong, are the sleeve sponsors of Manchester City and Tottenham Hotspur. Chelsea itself also partnered with crypto platform BingX, which is also unlicensed in Hong Kong, for an official training kit front sponsorship. During their visit to the city last month, Chelsea players wore the training kit with the BingX logo during an open training session at Kai Tak Stadium. Players from City and Spurs also wore kits sporting the OKX and Kraken logos during their friendlies in Hong Kong in August this year and July last year, respectively. Similar clauses regulating the promotion of unlicensed virtual asset trading platforms are present in the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance. The SFC said it would not comment on specific cases. It added that it would take into account all marketing and advertising activities in their totality in considering the appropriate course of action. Kraken said that it maintained jurisdiction-specific controls designed to ensure its activities complied with applicable local laws. The trading platform also stressed that its partnership with Tottenham Hotspur was a global brand sponsorship. It did not reflect an offer, solicitation or promotion of Kraken’s virtual asset trading services in jurisdictions where those activities were restricted, it added. The SCMP has reached out to Manchester City, OKX, Tottenham Hotspur and BingX for comment. *Name changed at interviewee’s request.

title: After Evergrande, China’s new rules spark unease amid developers’ debt resolution progress
description: China’s property downturn worsens as regulators accelerate reform of the commercial housing sales system, sending jitters through the sector.
content: With the saga surrounding Evergrande founder Hui Ka‑yan ending in his life sentence and the ongoing financial struggle of mainland developers, analysts said challenges remained for troubled operators getting away from the vicious cycle of a sluggish property market, even though risk resolution had largely been completed for some cases. Despite the difficulty, better-capitalised state-owned enterprises would prove more resilient and should gain market shares amid uncertain earnings outlooks, they added. “Just as we thought China’s property sector was entering a ‘sweet spot’ – fewer incremental policy shocks and a more organic path to a cyclical inflection point – regulators are intervening again,” Michelle Kwok, head of Asia real estate and Hong Kong equity research at HSBC, said in a report on August 31. Now in its fifth year since the Evergrande crisis began, China’s property downturn has spurred regulators to launch a series of stabilisation measures. Chinese authorities issued a joint notice on August 28 to accelerate reform of the commercial housing sales system, with a clear push towards completed-home sales. “While the direction has been signposted before, the timing is a meaningful negative surprise,” Kwok said. “Although the China Securities Regulatory Commission simultaneously rolled out capital market support measures, we still expect a sector-wide knee-jerk sell-off as investors reprice for a longer cash conversion cycle, higher upfront funding needs and uncertainties tied to earnings recovery,” she added. Besides, the cap on total debt service-to-income had risen to 60 per cent from 55 per cent, and the maximum mortgage term was extended to 40 years from 30 years, according to the policies. “Recent regulatory changes place even higher demands on developers’ cash flow and financial management capabilities,” said Lulu Shi, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “For companies that have already defaulted, it will be even more difficult to restart land acquisition and restore sales momentum under these tightened conditions.” The property development sector is capital-intensive and heavily reliant on internal cash generation, which depends primarily on sales and access to funding, Shi added. “For cash-strapped Chinese developers, breaking out of the vicious cycle of a sluggish property market remains extremely challenging,” she noted. Several mainland developers reported interim results in August signalling progress on debt resolution and financing coordination, despite still posting losses and shares of mainland developers such as Country Garden and Sunac traded lower after their result announcements. “This suggests the market remains cautious about property fundamentals,” said Yan Yuejin, vice-president of the E‑house China Research and Development Institute, a Shanghai-based property consultancy. “New policies including completed‑home sales rules have drawn mixed readings. Some see them positive for the industry’s long‑term outlook, while others worry about near‑term funding stress.” For developers to regain real operational momentum, the key lies in accelerating asset and project disposals to boost cash inflows, alongside active engagement of external institutional investors in debt restructuring – strategies that deserve thorough review by the companies, Yan added. Country Garden, one of China’s largest residential real estate developers, released its first half‑year report on August 28 after completing onshore and offshore debt restructuring. The Hong Kong-listed firm posted revenues of 44.1 billion yuan (US$6.6 billion) and a net loss of 15.62 billion yuan for the first six months. While still loss-making, it narrowed losses by roughly 16.3 per cent year on year, according to its earnings statement. Sunac, a mainland residential-focused developer that completed onshore and offshore debt restructuring, reported sales of 16.35 billion yuan over the six-month period, down 18.2 per cent year on year. Its net loss came in at 12.54 billion yuan, slipping 2.1 per cent year on year, its interim results showed on August 28. The developer said it had completed revitalisation of 12 key projects in China, with some 11.2 billion yuan expected in capital injection. Yet it still carried substantial off-balance-sheet obligations including trust loans, project development loans and supplier payables, leaving heavy debt pressure on the company.

title: Hong Kong star touted as ‘next Venus Williams’ set for 4th Asian Games in 2nd sport
description: Tipped to follow in American great’s footsteps, Venise Chan spying padel glory after claiming six ITF titles, Pickleball World Cup silver.
content: Christened the “future Venus Williams of Hong Kong tennis” after reaching the national championships final at 12, Venise Chan Wing-yau is grateful in hindsight that she was spared the social media glare that shines so harshly on today’s emerging stars. Still, a quarter of a century later and Chan is still putting herself out there. Still very quick to get the hang of her chosen sport, too. After switching her focus to padel at the beginning of this year, Chan will represent Hong Kong in what is the world’s fastest-growing racquet sport on its Asian Games debut this month. It will mark a return for Chan to the multi-sport spectacular, 12 years after she competed in the last of her three Games as a tennis player. In the intervening period, Chan carved out a career in pickleball and was part of the city team that reached the World Cup final in America last year. After originally trying padel with a colleague from Carret Private Capital, where she works as a risk and compliance director, Chan started thinking in January that “maybe I could try for the Asian Games”. “Once I started playing, I didn’t stop,” she said. “I’m sure there are other people who want my spot and to play for Hong Kong, but I think I was lucky and the timing was right. I took the opportunity and really wanted to do well this year.” Ranked No 9 in Asia and at 282 in the world, but top of the tree in Hong Kong, Chan was recently with the city squad for a camp in Bali, where she also partnered Spanish world No 72 Alba Perez Momha to the quarter-finals of a competition on Padel’s second-tier Cupra FIP Tour. Currently competing in Paris, Chan grew accustomed to spending long periods away from family and friends as she chased tennis success. “I have open-minded parents who allowed me to do online schooling and go around the world to get [ranking] points,” she said. It was back at home in 2002, however, that the 12-year-old Chan claimed a succession of notable local scalps on her way to the national final at Victoria Park. A contemporary South China Morning Post report hailed a “little slip of a girl” who was “the future Venus Williams of local tennis”. Describing herself today as a “part-time social media influencer”, and with an Instagram following pushing 57,000, Chan said: “I didn’t feel like there was too much spotlight on me; I was in newspapers but there wasn’t any social media. “Also, when you’re younger, you’re less stressed. I just wanted to get out there and try to win; I didn’t have any pressure.” By the time she won the first of her six ITF singles titles on the hard courts of Manila at 16, Chan was finding the expectation she imposed on herself “tougher to handle”. “My mental state was much better from about 12 to 15,” she said. “Afterwards, I began to feel I had to do well.” Maintaining a sharp focus on studying helped alleviate the pressure “because I always want to challenge myself in different areas and not do well in just one thing”. “I never saw a sports psychologist because I was never super stressed,” Chan said. “My parents supported me, and weren’t the types to yell at me if I didn’t do well, so there was no need to overstress. “My motivation comes from inside, so it’s not like I was forced to do anything.” A competitor in all four junior grand slams, Chan played on the unforgiving American collegiate circuit, ranking 15th and 17th in 2010 and 2011, respectively, while majoring in marketing and entrepreneurship at the UW Foster School of Business in Seattle. “I focused on studying and tennis. I didn’t go out a lot and wasn’t hanging out with friends, but I had a goal in mind, so I was fine with it,” Chan said. “Everything you do comes with sacrifices and having that focus set me up for the next phase of my life.” Chan, 37, would have the opportunity to pursue a “student lifestyle” when she obtained her philosophy master’s degree from Cambridge University, directly after a persistent back problem forced her premature tennis retirement in 2013. “My dad had always told me you can’t just have a Plan A, because if you get injured it’s the end,” Chan, who reached a career high of world No 340, said. “I was fine with having to stop playing tennis. I got into business, because I needed to make money. It’s the real world, isn’t it?” Also the founder of Asia Aces Pickleball Academy in Wong Chuk Hang, and given some financial support from her domestic team, The One Padel Academy at Go Park Sports, Chan said that she “doesn’t see myself as having played competitively for the past 10 years”. “Although I was playing pickleball [in competition since 2020] I felt I was using a recreational mindset to play at a competitive level,” she added. Last November, soon after the Pickleball World Cup final, which Hong Kong lost to the USA, Chan told the SCMP that she was “not going to kill myself chasing sporting success”. Ahead of her fourth Asian Games, where alongside partner Debbie Lau Hiu-wai her goal is to “win every match and get a medal for Hong Kong”, Chan said she had tried to retain her equanimous outlook. “I want to win, but it’s not that it’s a must, and I’ll feel really sad if I don’t,” she said. “I try hard but winning or losing is part of life. I like to challenge myself, and this is another challenge.” Planning to weigh up her sporting future after the Games, Chan said that having no squash background had meant the toughest ask in padel was trying to adapt to the enclosed courts and the ball staying in play after it hits the wall. After padel beat pickleball to the Asian Games punch, Chan expects her new sport to win the race for Olympic recognition, too. “Padel is much more organised and has one entity overseeing it internationally, but in pickleball they’re still fighting up there,” she said. The mother of a three-year-old son, Chan added: “It’s a very good thing to show people that even at my age and with a kid, you can still do this. You can still have goals and dreams after having a child.”

title: Viral Jennie clip tests limits of South Korea’s AI deepfake laws
description: Severe legal threats fail to deter a wave of teenage offenders who see digital victims as nothing more than pixels.
content: For a few seconds during Blackpink member Jennie’s headline set at Tokyo’s Summer Sonic festival last month, it looked like something had come undone. She turned away from the crowd, adjusted herself and then, the moment was gone. But online, the clip never disappeared – and more than 10 million views later, it has become the latest test of South Korea’s fight against AI-enabled sexual abuse. Fans were quick to cry deepfake, dissecting the footage frame by frame for signs of possible AI manipulation and calling for it to be taken down. The K-pop star’s agency, OA Entertainment, neither confirmed nor denied the clip’s authenticity, merely saying in a statement on August 18 that it had “recently identified ongoing misconduct targeting the artist [Jennie] across online communities and social media platforms”. It added that it was working with lawyers to pursue civil and criminal action, vowing “no compromise or leniency whatsoever”. The account believed to have first posted the video has now been suspended, but no official police or prosecutorial follow-up has yet been announced. If pursued, the case is set to become a high-profile test of South Korea’s revised deepfake laws. Enacted in 2024, their scope has since been broadened to punish not only those who create or distribute sexually exploitative AI-manipulated material, but also those who possess, save or watch it. Yet legal experts say a viral clip of disputed authenticity also exposes the practical limits of enforcement, from proving who made it to who knowingly spread it around. South Korea’s legal framework is “relatively proactive in establishing strong criminal penalties for this kind of abuse”, according to Bang Suk-ho, a senior legal adviser and head of the AI industry centre at Seoul-based law firm Lin LLC. “But simply strengthening the law does not make crime disappear,” he told This Week in Asia. “If anything, we’re in a phase where technology has led to more crime while making it harder to detect criminals.” Evolving abuse South Korea overhauled its legal arsenal against deepfakes two years ago in the wake of public fury over Telegram-based sex crime rings that distributed doctored images of women and girls, including students and servicewomen, via encrypted chat rooms. The scandal carried echoes of the notorious Nth Room case of 2020, which first exposed how platforms based overseas could be used to produce, sell and blackmail victims with sexually exploitative material. But the newer deepfake cases were different in one crucial aspect: demonstrating how convincing abuse material can now be conjured from an ordinary photo, then rapidly circulated and viewed by large numbers of people, before anyone – victim or investigator – knew who had made it. Under amendments to South Korea’s Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes that came into effect in 2024, creating sexually explicit deepfakes carries penalties ranging up to seven years in prison or a fine of 50 million won (US$36,800). Possessing, purchasing, storing or knowingly viewing such material can carry up to three years in prison or a fine of up to 30 million won. Campaigners got some of the harsher penalties they were calling for, but the new law also raised difficult questions about proving intent – and how to actually enforce it. Tougher sentencing rules had pushed prosecutors to seek “increasingly harsher sentences”, which in turn had influenced court decisions, said An Gab-chul, a lawyer at Gammyung Law Firm in Seoul who specialises in sexual crimes. Yet An said the new measures “often fall short in practice and do not function as effectively as they should”, further arguing that procedures for removing illegal material should be simplified. The Jennie case shows why. Before any prosecution can begin, investigators need to establish whether the footage was indeed fabricated, trace who posted it first and prove whether those who shared it knew it was fake. “The apprehension and punishment of offenders is another major problem, as it’s difficult to identify the operators of platforms based overseas,” An said. “Extraditing them may raise conflicts with foreign laws, and overseas servers are outside the jurisdiction of South Korean law.” That difficulty was borne out in police data presented late last month at a forum hosted by Amnesty International Korea, which showed that authorities had filed 26,697 data requests with foreign messaging services and platform operators but received responses to just 15,466 of them, or 58 per cent. The rest went unanswered. For An, the more immediate concern is often more basic: identifying who is behind an anonymous account before the evidence disappears. “The biggest obstacle in online sexual crimes today is preventing suspects from destroying or tampering with evidence,” he said. “In the case of anonymous accounts, it can take a long time to identify the actual user. Investigators often have to contact operators of overseas servers to determine who is behind an account before the person behind the account shuts it down or destroys evidence.” In viral celebrity cases like Jennie’s, that delay can be especially damaging, as reposts and screenshots multiply and vanish long before investigators can establish where the material originated. Still, South Korean courts have shown they can impose prison sentences for AI-generated sexual abuse material when investigators do identify the person responsible. In June, a man convicted of creating and distributed deepfakes of K-pop girl group Aespa was sentenced to two and a half years in prison, alongside an 80-hour sexual violence treatment programme and a seven-year ban from working with children and adolescents. Moral disconnect Criminal penalties alone cannot solve the issue, according to Bang, who finds the psychological side of these offences more unsettling. Whereas committing a crime in person forces the offender to confront their victim, he argues that screens remove this human element. “In the virtual world, that awareness of wrongdoing … becomes much weaker, especially among younger people,” Bang said. “The younger the users, the wider the gap tends to be between their awareness of wrongdoing and the severity of the punishment. As a result, their awareness of the seriousness of these crimes, and of the harm caused to victims, is becoming weaker.” Last year, deepfake-related offences accounted for 35.2 per cent of all cybersex crimes uncovered by police, or 1,553 cases in total – the single largest category, according to statistics presented at the Amnesty forum. Of the 3,557 people apprehended in 2025, almost half – 1,761 – were teenagers and over 90 per cent of deepfake suspects were in their teens or twenties. One case last month involved a teenager being referred to prosecutors after allegedly creating sexually explicit deepfakes using photographs of about 20 girls his age and sharing them on social media. “So this is not something that can be solved simply by strengthening the law, like an endless game of cat and mouse,” Bang said. “We’ve already seen that from experience.” This is not something that can be solved simply by strengthening the law, like an endless game of cat and mouse Bang Suk-ho, AI legal expert Won Eun-ji has seen it too. As executive director of Team Flame, the investigative group that helped expose the Nth Room digital sex-crimes and blackmail scandal in 2020, she has watched high-profile cases like Jennie’s capture the kind of public attention that ordinary victims rarely receive. “The government, media and society as a whole are not paying enough attention to this issue,” she said, noting that even today, many investigations only began after victims forced the issue. “The police and authorities need to further specialise and strengthen their capabilities in tracking and investigating such cases.” Her final point was one she wanted readers to reflect on: that viral moments like the Jennie clip showed the public had a role to play too. “Most of us may not be perpetrators or victims, but that does not mean we are unrelated to the issue,” Won said. “Whenever we come across deepfake sexual abuse material, it is important to report it to the platform, and remember that when someone opens up about being victimised, it is important to support them. We shouldn’t just be bystanders.” Amnesty International Korea framed the challenge in still broader terms, saying the real task ahead was for society to ask “why this violence continues to occur and how we can change the environment in which violence occurs and spreads”. “Digital sexual violence should be understood as a form of gender-based violence,” the organisation said in a statement. “We need to address the structural causes that allow such violence to persist, as well as creating change in the digital environment that provides it a platform.”

title: Hong Kong’s hottest new openings, from Italian eatery Il Presidente to Fujian cuisine hotspot Quan
description: Discover Hong Kong’s freshest F&B openings: divine Italian at Il Presidente, Parisian-inspired Bistrot’s Suzette, tempting Japanese treats at Truffle Donut and contemporary Chinese fare at Quan.
content: Il Presidente Italian la dolce vita finds an exciting home on Duddell Street, at the Marcello Scognamiglio- and Félix de Arriaga Balanzat-led Il Presidente. Building on the runaway success of Trattoria Felino, the co-founders highlight regional favourites such as agnolotti all’ossobuco and costoletta alla Valdostana (breaded veal chop stuffed with Fontina and smoked ham). Dix Design has draped the 70-seater restaurant in sumptuous sunset tones, set against white-clothed tables, high-pile carpets and rich rosewood walls to bring the retro look to life. Behind the bar, Simone Ciambrone shakes up cocktails that capture stand-out moments in 20th century Italian history.
