Shop M2, M/F, Baskerville House, 13 Duddell Street, Central Bistrot’s Suzette Beloved French bolt-hole Jean May might have taken its final bow earlier this year, but F&B darling Tiffany Lo’s “modern bistronomy” philosophy lives on in her culinary curation of the new Bistrot’s Suzette. From chicken-liver parfait with red-onion compote and beef bourguignon to crowd-pleasing steak frites and the signature crêpe soufflé à la Suzette, Lo’s fingerprints are felt on the menu of rustic dishes as the consultant chef shapes a Parisian-inspired dining experience around seasonal produce, familiar flavours and nostalgia that feels like a warm embrace. Shop G02, Cullinan Sky Mall, Kai Tak Truffle Donut One of Japan’s most popular nama doughnut brands makes its Hong Kong debut. Truffle Donut, from Tottori prefecture, relies on Camellia-flour dough enriched with pumpkin for its signature pastry’s characteristic texture, the technique achieving a soft, delicate interior padded out with sugary and savoury fillings, and a crisp outer shell. Choose between 10 flavour options, including three local exclusives – mango pomelo, durian and pistachio – or sample them all to sate your sweet tooth. Shop OT G03A, G/F, Ocean Terminal, Harbour City, Tsim Sha Tsui Quan Lai Sun Dining’s latest gastronomic offering puts the sophistication of contemporary Fujian cuisine and next-generation talent front and centre. Executive chef Justin Yang – the youthful runner-up of China’s hit cooking competition The Divine Dish and winner of the Michelin Guide Chengdu’s Young Chef Award in 2024, recognising his work at the city’s one-star Hokkien Cuisine – leans on his Quanzhou heritage and progressive palate to put forth a concept rooted in balance and artistry, seen in such creations as the chilled mantis shrimp with sea urchin and Fuzhou drunken pork ribs. 5/F, CCB Tower, 3 Connaught Road Central, Central

title: Argentina threatens to sanction oil projects around Falkland Islands
description: On Saturday, oilfield services firms including Schlumberger and Halliburton said they do not and will not work on projects near the islands.
content: Argentina has announced that it will investigate and sanction oil companies working near the Falkland Islands without authorisation, after President Javier Milei said the “winds of change” favour his country’s claim to the archipelago. Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war in 1982 over the South Atlantic islands, a British overseas territory that Argentines call Las Malvinas. Argentina’s presidency said in a statement on Friday that it had ordered the opening of proceedings to “investigate and penalise” 45 entities “linked to the exploration and exploitation of hydrocarbons” around the Falklands. The statement did not name the entities involved. According to Argentine media, they include British, US, Canadian, Israeli, Danish and Dutch companies. On Saturday afternoon, oilfield services companies Schlumberger, Halliburton and Baker Hughes issued statements saying they do not and will not work on hydrocarbon projects near the islands. Later, Milei shared a news item on social media reporting the statements, along with an acronym that translates to “everything is going according to plan”. The Falklands are located about 600km (372 miles) east of Argentina’s southernmost tip and administered by Britain. The Falklands war in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentine government after 74 days of conflict that killed 649 Argentines and 255 British troops. In a speech on Thursday, Milei renewed claims to the Falkland Islands and announced tougher sanctions on companies linked to oil projects nearby. “There are winds of change in the world that are favourable to our claim,” Milei said. Milei’s speech followed comments from US President Donald Trump on Monday that the United States was reviewing its position on the Falkland Islands. According to media reports, Washington has threatened to oppose Britain’s sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago if it does not increase its Nato defence spending. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting responded by asserting Britain’s “unshakeable” commitment to the Falklands. “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” he said in a social media post on Friday.

title: A Hong Kong ice cream truck in Vancouver? Watt A Truck brings the city’s flavours to Canada
description: Experience Hong Kong nostalgia in Vancouver with Watt A Truck, a solar-powered ice cream truck offering Asian dessert flavours.
content: In Vancouver, people hear the music first – “The Blue Danube” by Johann Strauss II – then see a red, white and blue patterned truck pulling up shortly after. As impossible as it may seem, that can mean only one thing for people from Hong Kong – a Mister Softee truck is in town. Or is it? Although it is not the same beloved ice cream dispenser – renamed Mobile Softee in 2010 – found in Hong Kong, Watt A Truck looks remarkably similar and offers nostalgic soft-serve ice cream. “We wanted the truck to look like the Hong Kong truck; otherwise, there’s no point,” says co-founder Wayne Poon Wing-tai, 35, who immigrated to Canada from Hong Kong in 2009. Poon says he and his business partners had considered launching a truck for some time. It took about a year to bring the idea to life and secure the necessary licences. Watt A Truck made its debut in early May at the Vancouver Hong Kong Fair, an annual weekend event celebrating Hong Kong culture. The truck sells a classic waffle cone with soft-serve ice cream for C$5 (US$3.60), as well as C$10 sundaes in flavours including mango sago, matcha red bean, pistachio, crunchy Horlicks and caramel popcorn. The menu also features C$9 ice cream floats in flavours such as Hong Kong-style milk tea and yuen yeung. ‘Who doesn’t like ice cream?’ This summer, Watt A Truck has appeared at parks, street festivals, corporate events and even weddings across Vancouver. Its regular locations include David Lam Park near Granville Island, Lipont Place in Richmond, and Metrotown Station in Burnaby. “Yesterday we went to a seniors’ home [for Chinese elders] and the residents were so happy to see the ice cream truck,” Poon says. “Ice cream is too cold for them to eat, so we prepared Hong Kong-style desserts, like black sesame pudding, red bean soup with mandarin peel and tofu fa.” Poon is well-versed in Chinese desserts. He and his wife, Aurelia Au, 35, also own Snackshot, a shop serving Hong Kong-style desserts, from red bean soup and steamed milk egg custard to sesame rice balls in ginger soup and durian coconut sago. The couple opened the dessert bar in Vancouver’s Marpole neighbourhood in 2017, and have since expanded to Richmond and Kingsway. Watt A Truck is their first food truck, and they have quickly seen the advantages of being mobile. Recently, they were invited to serve ice cream desserts to the cast and crew of HBO’s The Last of Us, currently filming its third season in Vancouver. “At first we were surprised they wanted us to come,” Poon says, “but when it comes down to it, we’re serving ice cream. And who doesn’t like ice cream?” Offering Asian and Hong Kong-style dessert flavours in the form of ice cream is one way the couple hopes to expand their customer base beyond what Snackshot can capture. Running on solar power Watt A Truck also stands out because it runs entirely on solar power – hence the name, a reference to its electric operation. Outfitting a typical food truck costs tens of thousands of Canadian dollars, Poon says, while making one fully green costs considerably more. But he believes the investment was worthwhile. “One of our partners is a bit of a geek, and he was responsible for making the food truck electric,” Poon explains. “We had to install a lot of batteries to power the dessert equipment and soft-serve machine, which made the vehicle heavier, so we had to consider where to distribute the batteries in the truck.” The result is a vehicle that ran for seven hours straight at a community event during the Fifa World Cup in July, serving hundreds of people. Because Watt A Truck is environmentally friendly, municipalities such as Richmond and Burnaby – both home to large Chinese communities – have shown strong interest in hosting it in public spaces. Later this month, Watt A Truck will be at Vancouver International Airport, where it will serve desserts to about 400 operations staff, including maintenance workers and baggage handlers. A validation for the founders The success of Snackshot and Watt A Truck has been validating for Poon and Au. The idea for the former came about during their student days at Kwantlen College (now known as Kwantlen Polytechnic University), when they developed a business plan for their graduation assignment. Their instructor, who was not from Hong Kong, was sceptical. “He couldn’t understand the appeal of our desserts to everyone ranging from teenagers to middle-aged people,” Poon recalls. “He thought our target market was too broad and said, ‘You guys are going to fail.’” The couple persevered, and their efforts paid off. Even the dean of the programme visited their shop and was pleased to see how well it was doing. “Watt A Truck is still new, but we’re having fun,” Poon says.

title: Editorial | As Hong Kong feels the heat, it needs a robust climate resilience strategy
description: Beyond alerts for extreme weather, the city needs a system that protects workers, older people, lower-income households and other vulnerable groups.
content: The record temperature of 36.9 degrees Celsius logged by the Hong Kong Observatory last month is the strongest evidence yet that extreme heat is not just a distant or occasional inconvenience. The rising temperature underlines a growing challenge that many authorities around the world are still grappling with. The city must respond not merely with improved mechanisms for alerts when the mercury soars but with a complete climate-resilience strategy that protects workers, older people, low-income households and communities least able to escape the heat. The city is not alone in feeling the heat in this regard. Some countries in Europe have endured their hottest summer months on record, while the average global sea-surface temperature again reached an unprecedented high. The combination of a warming climate and powerful natural weather patterns is raising the likelihood of heatwaves and extreme rainfall. Hong Kong cannot insulate itself from the global trend. Its dense urban form, ageing population and poorly ventilated homes mean many households, especially those in substandard partitioned flats, are vulnerable. A sizeable outdoor workforce, including construction workers and street cleaners, is also at the mercy of the mercury in the high summer months. The Labour Department’s rapid move to revamp the Heat Stress at Work Warning system is therefore a necessary and welcome step. Higher warnings can now be escalated more readily when the Hong Kong Observatory issues its extremely hot weather special alert or temperatures generally reach 35 degrees Celsius or above. That followed concerns that red or black alerts had never been issued since the three-tier mechanism was put in place in May 2023. Even when the temperature soared to 36.9 degrees Celsius on August 9, the highest since records began in 1884, only the lowest amber warning was issued. The episode may have given the impression that officials who design warning systems from air-conditioned offices do not fully feel the heat faced by those working outside. It also understandably left workers hot under the collar. A work safety warning system that appears disconnected from reality does little to show the government’s commitment to occupational health and safety. Officials say the revised mechanism with a lower threshold will make the issuing of higher alerts easier. It is estimated that the red warning could be issued four to seven days a year as a result, while the black alert could be triggered one or two days a year. In question is not just the colour of the alerts or how many more higher warnings can be expected each year, but whether those affected by extreme heat can really take a break from work. As rightly pointed out by some unionists, the current guidelines for outdoor workers with heavy duties to suspend or take regular rests under the three-tier system are not legally binding. Outdoor workers are usually the ones with the least bargaining power. As some have argued, the revamped system would not mean much if workers and their supervisors still feel compelled to work because of deadline pressure or performance targets. The labour authorities have a role to play in this respect. In addition to more frequent inspections at high-risk outdoor worksites to promote compliance, the implementation of the revised alert system should be closely monitored for necessary refinement. These pragmatic measures could help ensure the mechanism reflects reality and protects workers. The protection from heat stress should also expand beyond the working class. Reports of elderly people hanging around air-conditioned shopping malls to avoid hefty home electricity bills and surveys showing that nearly four in five low-income elderly people reportedly suffer from physical or mental distress during extreme heat are reminders that global warming is no longer just an environmental threat but an issue of public health and social and economic inequality. High-level policy intervention is called for. It is good that Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has pledged to improve urban management and unite efforts to tackle extreme weather events and disasters. This requires visionary and comprehensive strategies to enhance the city’s resilience in different aspects as heatwaves continue to take a heavy toll around the world in the foreseeable future.

title: Write to Win: Which emoji best describes your summer? (Round 1)
description: In our writing contest, students are eliminated one at a time based on your votes and YP editors’ picks.
content:
Read the responses to this week’s Write to Win prompt and vote for the answer you like most using this form .
Mercury: The sunglasses emoji 🕶️ perfectly encapsulates summer, evoking images of long, sunny days, heat shimmering off the pavement and the need to shield your eyes while lounging by the pool or at the beach. It represents confidence, a carefree attitude and a sense of coolness – much like putting on sunglasses before stepping into the bright sunlight.
Venus: My chosen emoji is the plane ✈️ because I travel with my family during the summer holidays. These trips not only allow me to learn about different cultures and lifestyles, broadening my horizons, but they also provide valuable time spent with my family, making my summer truly fulfilling.
Earth: The hourglass emoji ⏳ represents my summer best. Unlike previous years, I could truly relax this summer without university entrance exams looming over me. Now, each falling grain in the hourglass gently reminds me to make the most of this fleeting holiday to create a winning head start.
Mars: I choose cycling 🚴 because it represents how I spend my summer with my family. Riding bikes together is my favourite summer hobby. It allows me to enjoy the fresh air and relax while having a great time with my loved ones on a leisurely bike ride. We appreciate the scenery along the way and enjoy chatting about everyday topics. This activity makes my summer special and strengthens the bond between my family and me.
Jupiter: 💧 The water droplet emoji perfectly represents the intensity of Hong Kong summers. The heat and humidity are so overwhelming that they leave you feeling like a shrivelled prune. I’ve even attempted to use my magical powers to change the weather, but to no avail. Therefore, the only solution is simple: stay hydrated.
Saturn: If I had to choose one emoji to represent my summer, it would definitely be the soft-serve ice cream emoji. 🍦 While Hong Kong is gripped by intense heat, I’ve been craving Mobile Softee ice cream more than ever. As soon as I hear the familiar jingle, I run downstairs immediately. This delightful emoji has truly become the symbol of my summer.
Uranus: 🍦 I would choose ice cream. Summer feels like a slow, colourful melt, much like ice cream under a blazing sun. A single bite always gives me a refreshing chill during the hottest days. Not only does it cool me from the inside out, but it also symbolises the arrival of my long-awaited holiday – finally, I have permission to relax.
Neptune: 📷 The summer I envision would definitely include a camera X that captures all the spontaneous moments. Even though I have my university entrance exams next year, I wouldn’t want my summer to be so dull that I spend all my time at home studying. Instead, I filled my summer with memorable experiences and snapshots that I can look back on with fondness.
Sun: If I had to describe my summer using just one emoji, it would probably be 😫 – I know this is an unusual choice, especially since there are many fun activities to enjoy during the summer holiday. However, the weather can be extremely hot and humid, making it hard for me to breathe properly and enjoy activities like going to the beach.
Milky Way: I will use 🤩 as the emoji to describe my summer. I joined a study tour and arrived in Cambridge on July 14, which marked the start of my summer holiday. When I arrived, I was surprised by how old the city was. As a student who loves history and culture, I was amazed by this. Of course, I felt a bit of culture shock. Compared with Hong Kong, the lifestyle in the United Kingdom is much slower, but I tried to adjust to it. This trip was the most wonderful experience for me to learn English, so I will use the star-eyed emoji to represent my summer.

title: UK’s Prince William to represent King Charles at funeral of Norway’s King Harald
description: Prince William also attended the funeral of Pope Francis last year on the king’s behalf. King Harald’s funeral is to be held on September 9.
content: Britain’s Prince William will attend the funeral of Norway’s late King Harald next week in place of his father King Charles, Buckingham Palace said on Saturday. The heir to the throne is set to represent his father at the funeral on September 9, having also attended the funeral of Pope Francis last year on behalf of the king. British monarchs do not attend funerals of other heads of state per protocol, usually sending another member of the royal family to represent them. Charles, 77, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer but maintains a packed schedule of engagements, released a statement mourning the loss of his “dear cousin” King Harald last week. The two men were second cousins once removed, both being descendants of Britain’s King Edward VII. Charles’ sister Princess Anne will attend in a personal capacity as the godmother of the new king, Haakon VIII. Norway has seen an outpouring of grief for the much-loved monarch, who died on August 28 at the age of 89. Harald – who was known for his warmth, humour and informal style – has been hailed as an inclusive “people’s king” who modernised the Norwegian monarchy during his 35-year reign. His funeral will take place on September 9 at Oslo Cathedral, with mourners including his widow Queen Sonja. Additional reporting by dpa

title: German rocket reaches space as Europe enters satellite launch race
description: Isar Aerospace, which launched its rocket from a spaceport in Norway, plans to offer a commercial ⁠satellite launch service.
content: German start-up Isar Aerospace on Saturday launched its first rocket into space from a site in Arctic Norway, bringing Europe closer to offering satellite flights from its own soil. The uncrewed Spectrum rocket was the first commercial flight to reach orbit from continental Europe, ‌where several nations have said they want a share of a growing market for space missions. “We’re in orbit! And just made European history,” Isar said in a post on social media. The event was a breakthrough for the European launch industry, giving the continent better access to space, Norway’s minister of industry and commerce, Cecilie Myrseth, said in a statement. “The fact that we can now launch satellites from Andoeya strengthens Norwegian and ⁠European security in the turbulent times we live in,” Myrseth said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Isar’s launch site in ‌March, underscoring Europe’s efforts to establish greater autonomy as the global order once championed by the United States is shifting under US President Donald Trump. Blasting off from Norway’s Arctic Andoeya Spaceport, ‌the uncrewed Spectrum, designed for small and medium-sized payloads, carried five small satellites as well as an ⁠in-flight technological experiment, according to ⁠Isar. It was Isar’s second launch, coming 18 months after the company’s first rocket plunged into the sea and exploded in a fiery spectacle soon after ‌take-off from the same site. No one was injured at the time. The March 2025 launch was nonetheless deemed a success by the company for generating large ‌amounts of ‌data for its developers, it said at the time. Saturday’s launch was intended as “both the vehicle’s qualification mission and its first flight ‌carrying payload”, the Bavarian company has said. Global players in the satellite launch market include Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which launches from the ⁠United States, and French ArianeGroup, a joint venture between Airbus and Safran that uses a spaceport in South America’s French Guiana. SpaceX, ⁠a company spanning rockets, satellites and AI, listed on the Nasdaq exchange in June in a record initial public offering. Sweden, with its Esrange launch site, and Britain with its SaxaVord Spaceport in the Scottish Shetland Islands, ‌are the nearest rivals to the ‌Norwegian site, all of which aim to give Europe greater autonomy in space flights. Isar said last week it had secured about €200 million (US$232 million) from the European Space Agency to help fund development of new rockets and expand its testing and launch infrastructure. The German company is also developing a second launch site in Canada.

title: In Focus | Family firms power China’s economy – but what happens when the heirs refuse the throne?
description: About 85 per cent of the private sector is family-run, and family matters may become an economic issue as children decline to inherit operations.
content: Many Chinese tend to label the offspring of the country’s nouveau riche private business founders with the pejorative “fuerdai”, literally “second-generation rich”. They are seen as scions, waiting in the wings to inherit their family’s enterprises and the massive wealth their parents oversaw, a life in the lap of luxury guaranteed. In reality, many of these transitions are plagued by a clash between generations, as the younger generation is unwilling – or unable – to keep the family business going, let alone allow it to thrive. The private sector, the backbone of China’s economy and employment, is now facing a growing succession crisis – one which may see businesses wind down or fold, observers warn, as family matters threaten to send broader tremors throughout the country. In regions like China’s eastern Zhejiang province, a major economic centre, questions over inheritance are becoming more pressing. “I cannot – and probably should not – take over from my father,” said Li Fante, whose family’s factory, like many other businesses in Zhejiang’s city of Wenling, has maintained steady profits. However, he said the work was neither exciting nor lucrative enough to lure him in. “We may not do as well as our parents have done, and the business is boring,” Li said. There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother? Li Fante, Wenling, Zhejiang province When Li’s parents were approaching 70 years old, he said he made an agreement with them to wind down the family business, which produces rubber and plastic parts, after more than 30 years in the trade. He said that disagreements in the family had contributed to the decision. “For us, taking over from our fathers means the beginning of endless quarrels and clashes,” he said. “There is no consensus over how to run a business. So why bother? “Business drive and acumen may not automatically pass from one generation to the next.” Li, who is in his early 30s, used the proceeds from the sale of the factory’s land and its assets to invest in stocks and Shanghai property. Although ostensibly a family matter, Li’s decision – and those taking place among wealthy households across the country – could impact the future of China’s private sector, which accounts for 60 per cent of gross domestic product and 80 per cent of urban employment. More than 85 per cent of the country’s private enterprises are family-run, according to data from the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce, and Zhejiang is a major site of succession debates. The province is one of China’s richest, and its private sector contributes 70 per cent of local GDP and employs many of its residents. The average age of founders from Zhejiang’s top 100 biggest private enterprises was 64 years old, according to a 2025 report from the local government. “This means enterprises entering the succession phase are not isolated ones, but a huge swathe of the most vibrant and productive part of China’s private economy,” provincial authorities said. Data from Wenling’s United Front Work Department showed that, in 2025, close to 60 per cent of local private firms with an annual industrial output of 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million) were in need of “urgent succession planning” to ensure continuity in operations as their founders reached 60 years old. Of 114 private firms surveyed throughout Ningbo and neighbouring cities, including Wenling, 90 were still led by their founders, some aged 70 or older, and about 60 firms had neither a designated successor nor any second-generation family members in management. Only 10 companies of the 114 covered in the survey, conducted between 2023 and 2025 by Ningbo University of Finance and Economics (NBUFE), had come under the control of the second generation. A related NBUFE survey also found close to 20 per cent of the second-generation members of the 114 firms explicitly declined to take over, while 45 per cent remain undecided or prefer to pursue a career other than their family’s business. Su Saier, a deputy professor at NBUFE who led the survey, said most private entrepreneurs in Ningbo – and across Zhejiang broadly – showed limited awareness of succession planning and lacked systematic, long-term arrangements. “Founders have limited willingness to ‘relinquish’ control and there is also a lack of resilience and entrepreneurial drive among their children,” she said. The risks of investment reduction, business closures and broader impact on the economy have researchers worried. “The succession and continuity of private enterprises is no longer a family matter, but a question of regional economic vitality and industrial ecology,” Su warned. “This is particularly true in regions known for their private sector that are China’s economic pillars, like Zhejiang, Jiangsu and Guangdong, where numerous private firms are embedded in industrial and supply-chain networks. “If succession is not smooth at one enterprise, it could put employment, upstream and downstream production and even the broader industrial ecosystem on the line,” she said. Tang Dajie, a senior researcher at the China Enterprise Institute, a private think tank in Beijing, likened family-operated factories to capillaries in the massive Chinese economy. “These factories may not be massive conglomerates themselves, but collectively they could be foundational to the Chinese manufacturing ecosystem,” Tang said. “They usually specialise in a single component, or a minor link in the supply and production chain, that larger manufacturers usually outsource. If they shut down as their founders grey, the resilience and cost-effectiveness of Chinese manufacturing may be at stake going forward.” Li, from the family factory in Wenling, agreed. “The ageing of founders at many factories that do not have a successor may mean potential supply disruptions,” he said. His family factory was one of many producers established in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It now sells moulded plastic auto parts to carmakers like Geely and BYD. Handling succession is not just a test for business owners, but also a challenge for local cadres. If businesses in their jurisdictions wither, officials will have to tackle the subsequent impact on sentiment, jobs and fiscal income. In one recent example, listed kitchenware maker Zhejiang Meida sold a controlling stake to an outside bidder for 1.29 billion yuan in July after its 85-year-old founder failed to convince his children to take over the business. Its stock price subsequently fell. Meida is one of the largest listed firms in its home base of Haining, and employs thousands of workers. Local officials have stepped in following the sudden announcement to save local jobs and retain the local production base, according to people there familiar with the matter. The succession issue has also caught the attention of top policymakers in recent years, with some viewing it as an issue that will make or break the future of the private sector of the world’s second-largest economy. A 2023 Communist Party policy statement on promoting the private economy noted the need for “mentoring and guidance” for the younger generation of private entrepreneurs to ensure “orderly handover and succession”. A dedicated law on the private economy, in effect since May 2025, requires qualified private entities to establish and improve their modern corporate governance system as an institutional foundation for sustainability and intergenerational succession. Specific proposals, like recruiting professional managers to help run and modernise family businesses, have been raised. But Li said this would not help much. “By design, the founding family retains ownership, while professional managers brought in from the outside can leverage their knowledge and management skills to grow the company and get paid with salary, bonus and shares,” he said. “This idea sounds good on paper. “The crux of the issue is that for a small family business, nothing is institutionalised,” he added. “Many business decisions still rest on the founder’s experience, risk-taking, personal connections and even intuition and gut feeling. There is no business model. How can one modernise such a business?” But NBUFE’s Su argued that to make more private businesses more sustainable, the test was how to transform them, regardless of who sat at the helm. Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges Zhejiang Daily “The challenge goes beyond whether the second generation is willing to take over or not, but rather whether modern governance transformation can replace the founder’s personal abilities, experience and authority and adapt the company to the competitive environment of the new era. “The key is who can drive the company’s sustainable development.” Some high-profile examples can provide a model for such a transition. On August 17, Li Shufu, founder of auto giant Geely Auto, put his long-time deputy An Conghui in the driving seat of the 345-billion-yuan business empire, passing over his children. “The most feasible approach is to retain the advantages of the ‘family system’ so that shares can be held by the family, but management positions should be opened to the public, as much as possible to talent outside the family,” wrote Zhejiang Daily – a press organ of the provincial government – in a commentary piece following Li Shufu’s retirement. “The goal is a modern enterprise system with clear property rights, well-defined boundaries between family and business executives for a sound corporate governance structure.” Officials in the province are determined to tackle the issue, as time appears to be running out. “The first generation of Zhejiang entrepreneurs who rose to prominence after the reform and opening-up since the 1980s are now seniors. For them – and local officials and governments as well – handing over the business has become a sword hanging overhead, and the window of time is steadily closing,” Zhejiang Daily said. “Succession is becoming the sternest test for Zhejiang businesses, and everyone has a stake in it to address the challenges.”

title: Opinion | Gen Z is turning filial piety into a career path
description: Tough job and housing markets have graduates questioning whether the old bargain of hard work bringing progress and stability still applies.
content: Hong Kong has always had a simple answer to what young people should do with their lives: study hard, get a job, work harder, buy a flat and eventually complain about the next generation. That formula is becoming harder to sell. A whole lexicon has grown up around Generation Z’s uneasy relationship with work. In mainland China, there are “full-time children”, young adults who stay home and receive an allowance from their parents in return for doing household chores and running errands. Elsewhere, there is the “kangaroo tribe”, an updated version of adults remaining financially dependent on their parents. There are Neets, or young people not in education, employment or training. While the labels differ, the underlying phenomenon is harder to ignore. More young adults are struggling to make the traditional transition to independence. Hong Kong offers an especially revealing case. Consider university graduates with a respectable degree and little work experience. They apply for dozens of jobs, perhaps hundreds, only to find that “entry level” increasingly means “entry level for someone who already has experience”. Employers want experienced workers, but young people need jobs to gain that experience. A position for fresh graduates can demand several years of achievements before an applicant has even had a chance to begin. Against this backdrop, becoming a full-time child looks less absurd than it sounds. If a young adult can stay at home, avoid Hong Kong’s punishing housing costs, receive an allowance and help around the house, why rush into a poorly paid job with little security and even less prospect of progression? This is not necessarily clever economic thinking. Living with parents while searching for meaningful work is one thing; turning dependence into a permanent lifestyle is another. Skills stagnate, professional networks wither and financial independence grows distant. The family home is a safety net, not a career plan. Still, it would be too easy to blame young people when the incentives to move forward have fundamentally weakened. Hong Kong’s housing market is central to the story. Many parents accumulated property under conditions their children will struggle to reproduce, turning the family home into a form of intergenerational insurance. Furthermore, Gen Z is entering the workforce just as artificial intelligence (AI) begins to dismantle the traditional career ladder. For decades, young graduates were told to accept junior roles as an investment in their future. Learn the ropes, make mistakes, build relationships and move up. Now some AI models can perform basic research, analysis, coding, writing and administrative work. The broader problem with AI might not simply be that it eliminates jobs but that it eliminates the very roles through which humans learned how to do the high-level work machines cannot replace. That helps explain a stark shift at universities. In the United States, where tech founders once received rock-star treatment on university campuses, tech executives have been met with scepticism or outright boos. The people who once represented the future now look like a threat to it. Students are not necessarily anti-technology as they are among the first generation to live with AI as an everyday tool. What they are questioning is the bargain attached to it. If corporate productivity gains come from requiring fewer junior employees, where exactly are young people supposed to start? This could also explain why some are less enthusiastic about corporate careers than their parents expect. They have watched previous generations work gruelling hours in finance, professional services and multinational companies while struggling with housing costs, stress and the elusive promise of work-life balance. The destination was supposed to be prosperity. For many, it became a mortgage and a WhatsApp group complaining about work. It is tempting to dismiss Gen Z as entitled, but that misses a structural shift in the career bargain. The old bargain was straightforward. Effort produced progress. If the first rung is disappearing, young people will naturally question the ladder. Companies must rethink how they cultivate talent. If every vacancy demands experience and AI reduces junior tasks, organisations need new ways for young employees to acquire judgment, creativity and professional instincts. Otherwise, the full-time child and the Neet will become less a social curiosity and more of a permanent labour-market symptom. Gen Z is not rejecting work; it is rejecting the idea that any work is automatically worth doing. Hong Kong has spent decades teaching its young people how to compete. The harder question now is whether the economy is giving them anything worth competing for.

title: At least 22 dead, several injured, in fire at DR Congo wedding reception
description: Several people - some alive and some dead - were laid by the roadside outside the event in Kinshasa as attendees tried to help the injured.
content: A fire at a wedding party in Democratic Republic of Congo’s capital Kinshasa left at least 22 people dead, the regional mayor said on Saturday. Several others were injured. The fire started on Friday night and continued into early Saturday in a building in Lingwala in northern Kinshasa. The building’s narrow hallways were constricted by people trying to escape the fire. Several people - some alive and some dead - were laid by the roadside as attendees tried to help those who were still alive. The mayor of Lingwala, Norbert Mushinga, told the Congolese Press Agency that the provisional death toll was 22. He said the toll could rise further. The exact cause of the fire was unconfirmed. “It is a tragedy,” Jacquemin Shabani, Congo’s deputy prime minister and interior minister, said. The minister visited the site on Saturday morning. Deadly fires are common in densely populated areas of Kinshasa where urban development is often implemented without provisions such as fire services. Fires are common during the dry season and several have taken place this year, according to local media.

title: Meet Alix Earle’s influencer sister Ashtin – they’re both on Netflix’s Earle Meets World
description: Ashtin has over a million followers on TikTok, was spotted with Kourtney Kardashian, and is rumoured to be dating Travis Barker’s son Landon.
content: Alix Earle is set to star in her own Netflix reality TV show Earle Meets World. The show, premiering on September 4, will feature her whole family, including her father Thomas James “TJ” Earle, mother Alisa, stepmother Ashley, and her fellow influencer sister Ashtin. “We’re a fun, modern family, and people either think we’re insane or they’re like, ‘Wait, this is exactly like my life’ – and honestly, both are true,” Alix told Tudum about her upcoming show. “The goal is not to be someone different on camera. It’s to show more of who I already am and who my family really is. The fun, the messy, the growth, while capturing the way we help each other through it all.” Despite being involved in several controversies, including her very public feud with Call Her Daddy podcast host Alex Cooper, and her lawsuit with athleisure brand Gymshark after the brand dropped her because of a pro-Israel comment she made on her Instagram Story, Alix continues to be the internet’s favourite “It” girl, and her younger sister Ashtin is following in her footsteps. Meet Ashtin Earle, one of Alix Earle’s self-described “nepo sisters”. Her father was involved in a major cheating scandal Ashtin Earle was born in April 2003 to parents Thomas and Alisa Earle, who split in 2013 after Thomas was involved in an affair scandal with Ashley Dupré, as per Yahoo! Entertainment. Dupré is a former escort who famously made headlines in 2008 after it came out that the former governor of New York, Eliot Spitzer, had hired her services. The scandal led to Spitzer’s resignation and divorce from his wife. That same year, Dupré was involved with Thomas, which attracted media attention to the Earle household. Thomas and Dupré went on to tie the knot, and the couple has since welcomed three children: Izabel Earle, Penelope Earle, and Thomas James Earle II. Despite the family drama, the Earle family remain on good terms with each other and Alix and Ashtin often feature their mother, stepmother and step-siblings in videos. She is the most fashionable Earle While her older sister may boast an Instagram account with nearly six million followers, Ashtin is apparently the most fashionable one in the family. The aspiring model and content creator’s account is more fashion-focused than her sister’s, who found online fame through her candid “Get Ready With Me” TikTok videos. With over a million followers on TikTok, Ashtin is slowly but surely reaching the same influencer status as her older sister. “I still have impostor syndrome when people recognise me. It’s so surreal,” she told L’Officiel about her growing social media presence. “But it’s awesome and exciting, and I’ve gotten so many amazing opportunities. I would not be attending [New York] Fashion Week if it weren’t for this.” Ashtin graduated with a bachelor’s in psychology from Tulane University in New Orleans in 2025. Who is Ashtin Earle dating? While Ashtin has yet to confirm her current relationship status, there is speculation that she is dating Travis Barker’s son, Landon Barker, after he attended the red carpet event for Earle Meets World in Los Angeles on September 1. While the rumoured couple did not walk the red carpet together, they have been spotted spending time together in the past months including at the premiere of Travis Barker’s Louder than Fear documentary on August 11. Ashtin was seen accompanying Barker and his family including his stepmom, Kourtney Kardashian, to their seats at the event, notes E! News.

title: Rolex, Audemars Piguet, Tag Heuer and the rise of pastel watches
description: Major brands are adding models in playful tones to their range, with Hublot, Richard Mille, Dior, Gerald Charles and Norqain also following the trend.
content: Watchmaking is awash with pastel colours. Sorbet shades of peach, baby blue, butter yellow, mint and pink have all tinged the hottest new timepieces, splashed across everything from dials and straps to hi-tech ceramic cases. The pale colour palette has been building for a few seasons now. Last year, Rolex brought delectable ice cream-hued tones to its Oyster Perpetual collection in dusty shades of lavender, sandy beige and pistachio green. The latter colour was reserved for the larger 41mm version and quickly found a fan in Oscar-winning actor and major watch nerd Leonardo DiCaprio, who was photographed wearing the pistachio piece for an Esquire cover shoot. This year, pastels have made a significant statement at Tag Heuer, which has given its Formula 1 timepiece collection a full makeover. Launched in 1986, the Formula 1 was the first watch to carry the Tag Heuer name and looked very different from the traditional Swiss watches of the time, with bright, eye-catching colours and a sporty design rooted in the brand’s motor racing heritage. Last year, the line gained the brand’s light-powered Solargraph movement, and for 2026 a new 38mm version arrives in a whole sweet shop of shades including pastel pink, blue, beige, green and lavender-blue. Timepieces have come sugar coated in pastels at Dior too, which has welcomed three new versions of its La D de Dior watch in soft pink, blue and yellow, each with an iridescent mother-of-pearl dial, matching strap and diamonds pavéed across the bezel and crown. Designed in 2003 by the house’s jewellery artistic director Victoire de Castellane, La D de Dior was conceived with the minimalist watch lover in mind, with a beautifully pared-back round case, and these new additions in particular make for gorgeous wrist candy. Even the house’s sportier Chiffre Rouge, known for its flashes of red, has been splashed with a pastel-pink mother-of-pearl dial framed with a rose-gold bezel smothered in diamonds. The Big Bang, Hublot’s flagship model, is another to have been drenched in pastels. Two models mix a painterly palette of mint green, pink and sky blue across their cases, while a trio of 33mm monochrome versions arrive in peach, mint and petrol blue. There’s also the new 42mm Big Bang Titanium Peach Ceramic chronograph, where that uplifting peach shade pops up across the bezel, skeletonised dial, hands and strap. Audemars Piguet has also made a strong case for pastels, dressing its Royal Oak Offshore in some of the season’s sweetest shades. In a smaller 37mm size, the watches come in turquoise, light blue or bright pink. Tennis star Serena Williams wasted little time putting the pink version through its paces at this year’s Wimbledon, stylishly coordinated with a pink racquet grip for her match against Australia’s Maya Joint. Footballers have also developed a taste for these delectable timepieces. Liverpool striker Hugo Ekitike has been spotted wearing Richard Mille’s extraordinarily rare RM 38-02 Tourbillon Bubba Watson, a 50-piece watch created in soft white with colourblock pastel-pink detailing which, originally designed for golfer Bubba Watson, costs a staggering US$3 million on the secondary market. At Gerald Charles, the buzzy independent maison founded by Gérald Genta in 2000, a new Mini Maestro was unveiled at Watches & Wonders 2026 in discreet tones of ice blue and pink, drawing on the GC58 created by Genta in 2006, a one-off watch that is now preserved at the Gerald Charles Museum at the brand’s Geneva atelier. For a more playful take, Norqain’s new Freedom Chrono Enjoy Life “Sprinkles” delivers just the right amount of pastel colour without being overwhelming. The 40mm chronograph comes with either a “Strawberry” or “Blue Raspberry” dial scattered with multicoloured sprinkles made from Super-LumiNova, meaning they glow blue in the dark. Once every seven days, an ice cream covered in sprinkles appears in the date window. It follows last summer’s original “Ice Cream” watch, which divided its dial into blue, pink and pistachio thirds. Pastel watches are proving surprisingly easy to wear, too, pairing just as naturally with crisp white shirting and soft neutrals as they do contrasted against black, navy or brown tailoring. The styling possibilities are endless.

title: New fashion and accessory drops from brands including Louis Vuitton, Hermès and Dior
description: Make room in your Berluti travel bag for Aigle by Setchu outerwear and CDLP underwear, plus Brunello Cucinelli sunglasses and a Carhartt WIP cap.
content: From technical outerwear and versatile travel pieces to whimsical collaborations and nature-inspired accessories, these nine releases offer all you need to move effortlessly between city life, outdoor adventures and everything in between. Aigle by Setchu Japanese designer Satoshi Kuwata, founder of Milan-based label Setchu, and French outdoor brand Aigle have teamed up for a collection that combines Kuwata’s passion for fishing with Aigle’s technical expertise. Named Aigle by Setchu, the range is equally suitable for city slickers and lovers of the great outdoors. Wardrobe staples such as trench coats, safari jackets and a series of easily packable garments including padded pants and a sherpa jacket reflect Aigle’s focus on functionality and performance. For the range, Kuwata created an origami-inspired logo and a signature double stripe motif. Berluti Berluti’s Fly range provides a curated wardrobe for on-the-go types and frequent travellers. Made of supple lambskin, the Fly leather jacket is fully reversible and lightweight – ideal when temperatures start to drop in the autumn. Pack yours in the equally versatile Fly bag, also made of soft lambskin. The smaller Fly 24h is suitable for everyday wear or an overnight trip, while the roomier Fly 72h is a great option for those who are allergic to checking in any luggage. Brunello Cucinelli The Goldcraft Futura sunglasses from Brunello Cucinelli evoke the world of exploration. Befitting the Italian label’s focus on luxurious materials and top-notch craftsmanship, the glasses are made in Japan of solid 18k yellow gold and will set you back almost US$10,000. Their side shields can also be removed to create a completely different frame. Carhartt WIP Hong Kong-based artist Michael Lau adds a touch of whimsy to Carhartt WIP, the workwear-inspired label, with his second collection for the American brand. Named Flowers: Serendipity and launched with an exhibition at Carhartt WIP’s flagship store in Causeway Bay called “Flowers, Flowers Everywhere” – from the nursery rhyme sung to the tune of lullaby “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” – the range features Lau’s flower characters embroidered on Carhartt WIP’s signature Detroit jacket, a jersey crew neck and a baseball cap. A T-shirt printed with the characters’ colourful universe is also part of the fun range. CDLP Swedish label CDLP’s signature underwear is now available in grey mélange, a shade that was previously impossible to achieve in the brand’s signature Tencel Lyocell, a breathable fabric sourced from dissolved wood pulp. Part of the brand’s Essentials collection, the range includes briefs, socks and tank tops. Dior These striking sandals debuted at the Dior fall/winter 2026-27 show, held on a runway built across a pond in Paris’ Tuileries Gardens. Filled with water lilies similar to those famously depicted by impressionist Claude Monet, the pond represents the tension between nature and artifice at the heart of the collection. Made of green satin and decorated with a pink and yellow water lily, the Dior Nymphéas sandals showcase creative director Jonathan Anderson’s ability to find a fresh way to make an impression with a flower motif. Hermès These boots from Hermès are the ideal marriage of functionality and style. Made of black calfskin and suede goatskin, the monochrome footwear features a very practical notched rubber sole. In true Hermès style, they are also equipped with buckle and zip details. Wear with a frilly dress to add an unexpected finishing touch to an otherwise feminine ensemble. Loro Piana Loro Piana’s textile heritage takes pride of place in the Heddle Tote, a new men’s bag made of cotton canvas, cashmere and silk. With a full cashmere lining, the bag is as luxurious inside as it is outside. Named after a weaving tool, the Heddle Tote comes in earthy hues such as sand and brown, and textures like Irish tweed and Shetland. Louis Vuitton Perfect for on-the-go types, the Louis Vuitton Multipass combines elegance and functionality. Slouchy and easy to carry, the versatile bag comes in an array of colours and materials, including Louis Vuitton’s signature monogram canvas. Staying true to its name, the bag – which comes with an adjustable shoulder strap, a braided chain and a short handle – can be worn several different ways. Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Commemoration held for late Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic
description: The ‘Butcher of Bosnia’ will be buried in Belgrade on Monday in a ceremony expected to draw thousands despite international condemnation.
content: A commemoration was held on Saturday in Belgrade for war criminal Ratko Mladic two days ahead of his burial, attended by dozens of former military staff, family members and officials. Mladic died last week after suffering several strokes while serving a life sentence in The Hague for war crimes committed during the 1990s war in Bosnia. His body was returned to Serbia on a government plane on Thursday, with his casket draped in flags and received with military honours. The 84-year-old will be buried at a Belgrade cemetery on Monday, in a ceremony expected to draw thousands of mourners despite international condemnation. On Saturday, around 300 people gathered at the commemoration ceremony for Mladic at a military facility in Belgrade, organised by an association of retired and active Serbian army generals, according to an Agence France-Presse reporter. His son Darko and other family members also attended, as well as Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic, and officials from the Bosnian Serb statelet, Republika Srpska, including President Sinisa Karan. Dozens of other Mladic supporters crowded in front of the Serbian army house, in central Belgrade, but had to stay outside because the venue was full. Some carried flags or wore T-shirts featuring Mladic in uniform with the caption, “Serbian Hero”. During the ceremony, speakers praised Mladic’s role during the 1990s wars in Bosnia and Croatia, describing him as a “towering figure both as a man and a soldier”. Mladic’s wartime atrocities during the collapse of the former Yugoslavia earned him the nickname “Butcher of Bosnia” in international media. The Hague-based United Nations court convicted him of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed in a UN-protected safe zone. Despite the verdicts, he is still hailed as a hero by some Serbs, particularly in Republika Srpska, where his death was marked with vigils and gatherings. “Thank you [Ratko Mladic] for the existence of Republika Srpska,” Zivomir Ninkovic, a retired Bosnian Serb general, told the ceremony. “For if we didn’t have Ratko Mladic, the way he was with all his characteristics, we would not have the Republika Srpska.” Republika Srpska along with a Bosniak-Croat federation makes up Bosnia since its 1992-1995 war.

title: Competitors dig deep at Hungarian gravedigging contest
description: The event at a cemetery in Nyergesujfalu, northern Hungary, showcases the gravedigging trade and aims to shake off death-related taboos.
content: A gravedigging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38 competitors grabbed picks and shovels on Saturday. The Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators organises the contest to showcase the gravedigging trade and its skills, and shake off death-related taboos. The dry summer-baked soil in the public cemetery in Nyergesujfalu, northern Hungary, proved a worthy adversary for the 19 two-man teams. They huffed and puffed and sweated as they raced for the title of quickest-dug and most stylish grave. “Speed is the main thing here, not the beauty,” said Robert Nagy, the victor with his teammate Laszlo Kiss. “When you have to dig a grave for a funeral, you have to be very careful about the exact dimensions and to make sure that it is beautifully carved.” Their winning time was 1 hour 21 minutes, digging to contest specifications. They shared a cash prize of 200,000 Hungarian forints (about US$640).

title: Egypt sentences TV presenter, 11 others to death in drugs case
description: Sarah Khalifa and 11 others were sentenced to ‘death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang’, state news reported.
content: An Egyptian court sentenced a well-known television presenter and 11 others to death for manufacturing and trafficking narcotics in a sprawling drugs case, official media reported on Saturday. The presenter, Sarah Khalifa, 39, is best known for her programme Mission Impossible, which dealt with issues concerning security and crime. The state-linked Al-Ahram newspaper said a Cairo court sentenced “Khalifa and 11 other defendants to death by hanging on charges of forming an organised criminal gang specialising in procuring materials used in manufacturing narcotics, with the intent to traffic them, and possessing and carrying unlicensed firearms and ammunition”. The verdict came after the court consulted the Grand Mufti of Egypt for his religious opinion, a procedure required by Egyptian law in capital cases. The verdict is subject to appeal. Khalifa also owns a plastic surgery clinic and a production company that specialises in organising parties and events. According to the state-run Akhbar Al-Youm newspaper, the defendants were charged with “manufacturing synthetic drugs with the intent to traffic them, by importing the materials used in manufacturing from abroad”. Al-Ahram reported that authorities seized more than 750kg (1,653 pounds) of narcotics and raw materials, and found two flats used as laboratories as well as unlicensed firearms and ammunition. The court also sentenced Khalifa and others to five years in prison over a separate case involving the kidnapping and assault of a young man. Egypt applies the death penalty for premeditated murder, terrorism, some rape offences and drug trafficking. According to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms, 541 death sentences were issued in Egypt in 2025.

title: 2 pilots killed after Greek air force plane crashes at annual air show
description: Officials said the bodies of the pilots were located during a rescue operation, hampered initially by a fire at Tanagra airbase near Athens.
content: A Greek air force plane crashed at an air show north of Athens on Saturday, killing the two pilots, officials said, as thousands of people attended the event. A fire after the crash sent up large plumes of black smoke. There were no injuries among the spectators. The crash of the twin-seat Phantom F4 jet took place during a low-altitude manoeuvre. Air force officials in Greece said the bodies of the two pilots were located during a rescue operation, hampered in the early stages by the fire on the grounds of Tanagra air force base, 60km (40 miles) north of Athens. Eleven water-dropping planes and helicopters helped 85 firefighters in an effort to contain the blaze, which remained at some distance from the viewing area at Athens Flying Week, an annual air show. Organisers cancelled remaining events planned over the weekend, while the fire prompted an evacuation order in an area near the base. Video footage of the crash showed a plume of smoke rising from the point of the impact followed by a larger, second explosion that happened nearby as the plane broke apart. Cyprus’ Defence Minister Vasilis Palmas said he had called his Greek counterpart, Nikos Dendias, to express the condolences of his government. “It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base,” Palmas wrote in an online post.

title: US ambassador calls violent Israeli settlers ‘terrorists’ after weeks of West Bank unrest
description: Mike Huckabee on Saturday met Palestinian American residents who described the impact of the violence on their lives and properties.
content: The United States ambassador to Israel condemned Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank again on Saturday, calling the behaviour an “act of terror” as he visited Palestinian American residents shaken by months of attacks. Mike Huckabee referred to such settlers as “terrorists”, a word that US officials usually reserve for Palestinian militants. “If there are squatters that come in and put up their own flags and take possession of something that does not belong to them, if they burn a car, if they torch a mosque, if they go into someone’s home and vandalise it, paint graffiti on the walls, that’s a criminal act. But it extends beyond a criminal act. It’s an act of terror,” Huckabee said during his visit to the village of Turmus Ayya, which has reported frequent attacks by settlers over the past year. Such attacks have surged since the war in Gaza began with the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023, according to the UN (United Nations) humanitarian office. Huckabee also used the term “terrorists” last month after weeks of unrest in the West Bank town of Qusra, where settlers surrounded several homes including one owned by a Palestinian American. Days later, residents of the West Bank village of Bazariya said settlers burned a mosque and left a message on a wall in graffiti reading “Huckabee regards from the terrorists” in Hebrew. “I’m glad they admitted it,” the ambassador said on Saturday of the incident, adding: “I don’t think that’s what they intended to do but I do think that they represent a very tiny minority.” A week ago, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the actions of a “handful of rioters”, and the foreign ministry called the settlers’ actions “a disgrace”. Netanyahu’s government is the most ultranationalist and religious in Israel’s history. It has presided over a surge of settlement construction in the West Bank. Most of the international community views settlements as illegal. On Saturday’s visit to Turmus Ayya, the ambassador began his remarks by making clear he was addressing US citizens, who make up a small percentage of the roughly 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank. “I’m very aware that a lot of the American people who live in Turmus Ayya and other communities across this region are not enjoying the life they deserve to live, not enjoying it in a peaceful way,” Huckabee said. “It’s a life that is disturbed by people who have created extraordinary challenges that are unfair and illegal.” The US embassy cannot investigate criminal activity, he said, but it can tell its host government “there are needs that need to be addressed, there are issues that cannot go unnoticed, and specific crimes and acts of terror that cannot continue without that country doing the investigation and adjudication that every person has a right to expect”. Huckabee met about 10 Palestinian American residents who described the impact of the violence on their lives and properties, the municipality told Associated Press. Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and east Jerusalem, in the 1967 Middle East war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. The United Nations and much of the international community consider them to be illegally occupied. Since then, the Israeli government has built nearly 150 settlements that are home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble developed suburbs. Israel’s military operates in all parts of the West Bank but rights groups have said the military frequently turns a blind eye to settler violence. The settlers are Israeli citizens and Israel’s defence minister recently announced plans to fully transfer policing among settlers to the Israeli police.

title: US strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after warships targeted, military says
description: The US military said two of its vessels evaded ‘multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks’ before retaliating.
content: US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it hit three Iranian oil tankers on Saturday, including one off the coast of Kharg Island adjoining Iran’s major oil export hub. CENTCOM said the strikes were conducted after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched ballistic missiles at a pair of US Navy ships. “Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” said Admiral Brad Cooper, CENTCOM’s head. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.” Earlier on Saturday, the semi-official Iranian news agency Tasnim reported that four US missiles struck a tanker around Kharg Island’s anchorage with no reported casualties, and the tanker’s crew was being evacuated. No ‌American personnel were hurt as the US responded to “multiple unprovoked” Iranian attacks, CENTCOM said. Two Iranian tankers were “permanently disabled” near Kharg Island, while another was destroyed in the Gulf of Oman, CENTCOM said on X, adding that the crew members were told to abandon ship before the strikes. Hours later, Iran’s military on Saturday vowed “more severe” retaliatory attacks on US naval vessels if Washington kept up its strikes on Iranian ships. “The US terrorist army is warned that if the evil actions, insecurity and harassment of Iranian ships and the naval blockade of Iran continue, the strikes by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran against US military vessels in the region will be more severe than before and there is a possibility of their expansion,” the Khatam al-Anbiya central command said. Vice-President J.D. Vance downplayed concern over the fighting during a Thursday press briefing, telling reporters he “wouldn’t call it a war”. “Right now, there is no active shooting,” he added. Tit-for-tat attacks have resumed over the past week after a month of relative calm. On August 24, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an “Economic D-Day” campaign under Operation Economic Outcast, a major sanctions and financial campaign declared by US President Donald Trump. While the measures were aimed at Tehran’s shipping, digital assets, aviation, technology and gold holdings, a major shortcoming has been the effectiveness of outlined secondary sanctions. Analysts said Iran is unlikely to feel debilitating pain so long as Washington is unwilling to play hardball with Chinese banks and shipping companies. China has been purchasing over 80 per cent of Iran’s oil. So, apparently impatient with the lack of progress against an adversary that has proven notably adept at weathering US financial strictures for four decades, the president ordered renewed attacks against Iran on August 30. Washington said those pre-emptive strikes were justified to prevent Iran from laying new mines on maritime routes that its forces had spent weeks clearing. Trump’s latest attacks follow his short social media ‌post along with an AI-generated video on August 31 claiming that Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens”. The US and Iran imposed competing blockades after Iran effectively shut the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which carried some 20 per cent of the world’s oil supply before the war, and Washington retaliated by blocking Iranian ports. The conflict, started by Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has lasted half a year with no end in sight despite Trump’s repeated claims said the conflict would be “strictly a short-term excursion” and involve a “four to six week” operation. On Friday, he called the war “small potatoes”, adding “It’s not a big thing”. A US attack on Kharg Island would put further pressure on Iran’s oil industry and its broader economy, ‌which is already reeling from the ‌US naval blockade, but would also invite more Iranian retaliation on US and allied targets and could further entrench US forces in the region. Republicans have recently acknowledged that the war is unlikely to end before the US midterm elections in November. The ruling party and the president have seen steady erosion in popular support amid growing strain on household budgets, leaving them in danger of losing control of Congress after November 3. Brent crude futures closed on Friday at their highest level since July 24 at US$96.28 a barrel. “The duration of the war and persistence of US$4 per gallon-plus gas has raised the household impact of the war from US$500 in additional spend to over US$700 in additional spend,” said Henrietta Treyz, economic policy director with the Veda Partners consultancy. “In other words, high gas prices could be tolerated if they were a blip, but now they’re breaking records at less eye-catching rates.” One option the White House may be considering is a US export ban on diesel, petrol and jet fuel, analysts said, which could provide temporary price relief for consumers but quickly rebound and make matters worse. That could see Trump roll out any such move two to four weeks before the election. The immediate impact of export restrictions would be a glut of refined energy products flooding parts of the United States before export restrictions to Mexico, Canada, Japan, South Korea, Europe and other Asian and Latin American countries destabilise markets. “The ban could create economic feedback that could easily slip into geopolitical destabilisation, not to mention higher prices for US consumers and the rest of the globe,” said Treyz. “Just because the war has gone on for six months and Trump hasn’t declared a national emergency and imposed an export ban doesn’t mean it’s not coming.” In a related development, the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels said that air strikes by Yemeni government forces in the western and southwestern part of the country killed at least three people. Iran is the ‌third-largest producer ‌in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90 per cent of its crude via Kharg Island before the ‌war and the US blockade imposed in mid-April.

title: Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying to give live lecture from space
description: Students from city and neighbouring Macau will be able to participate in ‘Tiangong Class’, with details to be released soon.
content: Hong Kong’s first astronaut Lai Ka-ying and her two fellow Shenzhou-23 crew members will deliver a live lecture from space for students and teachers in the city and neighbouring Macau. Hong Kong authorities revealed on Saturday plans for live broadcasts of “Tiangong Class” to take place soon, without specifying the date and time. The activity, jointly organised by the Hong Kong and Macau governments and the China Manned Space Agency, includes an expert lecture, an in-orbit demonstration and a question-and-answer session to showcase the environment in space. Hong Kong’s Education Bureau will arrange for primary and secondary schoolteachers and students to watch the live broadcast on campuses on the day of the event, while a delegation from Macau will visit the city to attend “Tiangong Class”. A live online broadcast will be arranged on the Information Services Department’s website and Facebook page, as well as local television stations. “This will be a valuable aerospace science education activity, allowing students to watch live demonstrations of science experiments conducted in the unique environment of space, with a view to enhancing their knowledge of aerospace science and stimulating their interest in learning,” a spokesperson said. “Students can also learn from the three astronauts of the Shenzhou-23 crew, who are currently carrying out a manned space mission on the Tiangong Space Station, thereby building their aspirations, encouraging them to be daring to explore, further cultivating their patriotism and strengthening national identity.” The space mission featuring Lai launched in May. Lai, 43, was a police superintendent and a mother of three. She is serving as the payload specialist for the mission. One crew member will remain in orbit for one year to study the long-term effects on astronaut health and to improve in-orbit medical support, while the other two, including Lai, will return in November.

title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino makes an appearance at Under-20 Women’s World Cup
description: Swiss head of world football body has mostly kept out of spotlight since his World Cup sell-off plan fell apart amid widespread opposition.
content: Fifa president Gianni Infantino has arrived at the opening of the Under-20 Women’s World Cup as he faces continuing pressure since abandoning his plan to sell off World Cup profits. Infantino was seen in the stands speaking with Polish football federation president Cezary Kulesza as host nation Poland faced Argentina on the opening day of the tournament on Saturday. Infantino had mostly kept out of the spotlight in the weeks since his World Cup sell-off plan fell apart amid opposition from many Fifa member nations and some of his own officials. The European nations – a quarter of the 24-team field – backed down on a boycott threat last week, citing assurances from Fifa that the plan would not be revived. Legal action over the original attempt rumbles on and Europe has a leading role in efforts to oust Infantino ahead of next year’s Fifa election. A court filing by Fifa on Thursday accused Uefa of running a “smear campaign against Fifa and its leadership” as the European football body seeks discovery of evidence related to the Fifa Forward Enterprise plan. Infantino infuriated football leaders worldwide in July, shortly after the World Cup ended, when his plan for a US$20 billion subsidiary controlling Fifa commercial rights including the World Cup was revealed by British daily The Times. The spin-off was to be 20 per cent owned by investors led by a New York fund created by Joshua Kushner, whose initial money was to pay offers of US$20 million to each of Fifa’s 211 member federations. They were given a mid-September deadline to accept. The Fifa president dropped his proposal within four days. Uefa had support from the Asian Football Confederation and North American football body Concacaf, and there was criticism of the plan and of Infantino from senior Fifa officials.

title: How Asian shipyards in Japan, Korea and Philippines keep US warships battle ready
description: Legal flexibility and regional partnerships allow US Seventh Fleet vessels to undergo complex overhauls closer to potential conflict zones.
content: After being stranded in the South China Sea following a power failure in July, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Benfold was towed to Subic Bay in the Philippines for emergency repairs. The facility is among the repair and maintenance hubs the US Navy has been developing in the region, strategically pushing for allies to perform major maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) work on US naval vessels given the decline of its shipbuilding base at home. The repair work on the Benfold in the Philippine port took about 10 days before it resumed operations. While US law mandates that major warships be built domestically, outsourcing MRO to foreign yards offers more flexibility, especially for forward-deployed vessels. Naval vessels homeported outside the United States are not strictly prohibited from receiving foreign MRO services and deployed US-homeported ships may also be serviced by foreign workers under specific conditions. The capacity of regional allies in the western Pacific, including Japan and South Korea, is particularly vital, given their distance from the continental US as well as Washington’s intensifying strategic competition with Beijing. “By establishing the ability to repair and sustain larger numbers of ships closer to potential conflict areas in the Indo-Pacific, the United States could potentially support extended deployments – including during wartime – by reducing the need to recall ships to the US mainland for repairs,” the Washington-based think tank Centre for Strategic and International Studies said in a recent report. South Korea and Japan’s advanced shipbuilding industries rank second and third in the world, respectively, in terms of capacity. The Philippines and Singapore, meanwhile, occupy strategically important positions in the region and have long served as key partners for the US military. Meanwhile, China at No 1 accounts for more than half the world’s shipbuilding capacity, providing a solid industrial base for its rapidly expanding navy. Shipyards in the region The US Navy runs the US Naval Ship Repair Facility and Japan Regional Maintenance Centre (SRF-JRMC) at its bases in the region. It is headquartered at the Yokosuka Naval Base in Kanagawa prefecture, with detachment sites in Sasebo, Nagasaki prefecture, and Singapore’s Changi Naval Base. The organisation employs local workers and occasionally outsources certain tasks to local contractors. In addition to the directly operated SRF-JRMC, the US Navy has been expanding a network of private companies in the region through its Master Ship Repair Agreement (MSRA). The certification qualifies a shipyard to bid on and perform MRO work on military and support vessels. For instance, the US Navy issued solicitation notices last month, inviting bids from MSRA and Agreements for Boat Repair (ABR) holders to carry out minor repair and maintenance of the America-class amphibious assault ship USS Tripoli and San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS New Orleans, both homeported in Sasebo. Japan Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI)’s Yokohama Dockyard & Machinery Works is the largest ship repair yard in Japan, with abundant experience in repairing civilian and naval vessels. It has two dry docks, seven piers and seven jib cranes. The dock can accommodate huge ships of up to 270,000 tonnes, according to the company. The yard serviced the Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Milius in 2019 as part of a pilot trial – the first time the US Navy had outsourced such work to local Japanese firms. Last year, MHI became the first Japanese yard to secure a regular overhaul contract for the USS Miguel Keith, a Puller-class expeditionary mobile base. Sumitomo Heavy Industries Marine & Engineering is another prominent MSRA holder. The company website says it has focused on repair work mainly for the US Navy in Yokosuka in recent years. They provide repair services to ships belonging to the Seventh Fleet, including nuclear-powered aircraft carriers, and “are engaged in repairing” US Army vessels including landing craft. Sasebo Heavy Industries sits next to the Sasebo Naval Base and shares a dry dock with the US Navy and the Japan Maritime Self-Defence Force. Having suspended new shipbuilding in 2022, the company now focuses exclusively on ship maintenance and repair. Japan Marine United Corporation operates five ship-repair yards across the country, at Isogo and Tsurumi in Yokohama, as well as Kure, Maizuru and Innoshima. The Maizuru facility took part in the repair of the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Fitzgerald last December. South Korea Unlike in Japan, the US Navy does not have a direct ship-repair facility in South Korea. Instead, it collaborates with major local shipbuilders, primarily for logistical vessels. Notably, MSRA certifications for South Korean contractors have been mainly awarded in the past few years, reflecting the US Navy’s strategic shift towards MRO outsourcing. In July 2024, Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI) made history as the first South Korean shipyards to obtain MSRA from the US Navy, shortly after the former acquired the Philly Shipyard in Pennsylvania. Hanwha Ocean conducts its repair works at the Geoje shipyard on an island off the southeastern coast near Busan. It completed South Korea’s first MRO project – maintenance of the USNS Wally Schirra dry cargo and ammunition ship – in 2025 and also worked on the USNS Yukon, a replenishment oiler assigned to the US Navy’s 7th Fleet. HHI secured the overhaul project for the Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo and ammunition vessel USNS Alan Shepard in August 2025 after efforts to tap into the US by forming an alliance with the US-based military shipbuilder Huntington Ingalls. The work was carried out at a berth near HD Hyundai Mipo Dockyard in the southeastern city of Ulsan from last September.
