HJ Heavy Industries, a mid-sized shipbuilder, became the third South Korean firm to pass US Navy evaluations to get an MSRA in January this year, after signing a contract in December to carry out a midlife maintenance contract for the 40,000-tonne Lewis and Clark-class dry cargo ship USNS Amelia Earhart at its Yeongdo shipyard in Busan. SK Oceanplant, another major defence contractor that has built more than 30 South Korean naval and coastguard vessels including the latest Ulsan-class Batch-III frigates, officially signed the MSRA in February. The company operates a 430-metre (1,410 foot) ultra-large floating dock in its shipyard in Goseong on the southern coast and conducts maintenance for more than 30 commercial vessels annually. Samsung Heavy Industries, one of South Korea’s “Big Three” shipbuilders alongside Hanwha Ocean and HHI, has reportedly begun the MSRA application process and aims to complete certification this year. Singapore Strategically located at the entrance of the Strait of Malacca, the crossroads connecting the West Pacific and Middle East, Singapore has long been a hub for US naval operations. Along with the SRF-JRMC’s Singapore detachment, the US Navy primarily works with two local MSRA-holding partners. State-owned defence contractor ST Engineering Marine operates facilities such as its Benoi and Gul yards. Its recent MRO contracts came not only from the Pacific Fleet, but also the Military Sealift Command and Naval Supply Systems Command. It was awarded a contract in February for the regular overhaul of Safeguard-class rescue and salvage ship USNS Salvor. Government-linked Sembcorp Marine held an MSRA before its merger with Keppel Offshore & Marine in 2023 to form Seatrium Limited. Its Tuas Yard has a repair dock that is 400 metres (1,310 feet) long and 14 metres deep, one of the deepest in Asia for mega vessels, while the Admiralty Yard is equipped with multiple dry docks and quays, including one that is 13 metres deep. India The US Navy has also expanded cooperation with India against the backdrop of deepening defence ties under the framework of its Indo-Pacific strategy. It has certified Indian shipbuilders Mazagon Dock and Larsen & Toubro with MSRAs in 2023. Mazagon’s facilities are in Mumbai and Larsen & Toubro runs the Kattupalli Shipyard in Chennai. In 2024, the third Indian MSRA was awarded to state-run Cochin Shipyard. Under these agreements, the Indian contractors will primarily support ships under the US Navy’s Military Sealift Command. The Philippines Although the Philippines lacks an advanced domestic shipbuilding industry, its strategic location as a key hub in the South China Sea has led the US Navy to contract US-owned firms to operate maintenance and repair facilities in the country. The Agila Subic Shipyard in Subic Bay, where the USS Benfold arrived four days after losing power and was repaired in July and August, was formerly operated by Hanjin Heavy Industries Philippines (HHIC-Phil) and is now owned by New York-based Cerberus Capital Management. Colorado-based defence contractor Vectrus (now V2X after a merger) provides services at the site, which features a 500-metre long dock and forms part of the growing network of overseas facilities supporting US naval operations in the region.

title: UK government condemns masked anti-immigrant protesters blocking Dover port
description: ‘Having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating’.
content: Dozens of masked anti-immigration protesters blocked roads leading to Britain’s busiest ferry port on Saturday, clogging traffic and disrupting travellers and cargo vehicles heading for France. The government condemned the action, saying it went beyond peaceful protest. The Port of Dover said Saturday morning that all traffic in and out was “stopped due to an ongoing public order incident” and police said they were “engaging with the protesters”. Video posted on social media showed several dozen men in black, their faces covered, standing across a major road near the port. One clip showed demonstrators linking arms across a main road and shouting “stop the boats.” Chris Vinson, a Conservative Party local councillor, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”. “I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating,” he said. The Labour Party government said “the right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused”. “We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today,” it said in a statement. The National Highways agency said the protest blocked all routes to the port and caused a 6.4km (4-mile) traffic jam. Police were later filmed following protesters towards Dover’s railway station. P&O Ferries said just before midday that “access to the Port of Dover has now been restored”. P&O, which runs services between Dover and Calais in France, said passengers who missed their ferry would be offered the next available crossing. Dover, about 110 km (70 miles) southeast of London, dealt with more than nine million passengers and two million freight vehicles in 2025, according to the port’s website. The town has been the site of previous anti-immigrant protests focused on migrants who cross the Channel from France in small boats. Successive UK governments have struggled to stop people – over 40,000 last year – making the dangerous journey across one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. The issue has been depicted as a crisis by politicians including Nigel Farage of hard-right party Reform UK. He branded the asylum seekers “an invasion” in a Friday speech. Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government says stepped-up law enforcement cooperation between Britain and France has helped reduce the number of people making the crossing so far this year by more than 40 per cent compared to 2025. Mike Tapp, a Labour lawmaker who represents Dover in Parliament, criticised “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. “I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40 per cent and we are working hard to fix the mess,” he wrote on Facebook on Saturday. “Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

title: China launches plan for 3D satellite network to monitor sun and cosmic explosions
description: The project will involve partners from at least five other countries as they track the development of space weather.
content: China has started an international project to build a three-dimensional satellite network between Earth and the moon that will track solar activity and study some of the universe’s most powerful explosions. The project plans to send 30 backpack-sized CubeSats into highly elliptical orbits around Earth in the next four years or so, according to the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory, which will lead the project. The laboratory said on Friday the constellation would “fill a global gap in systematic observations of cislunar space”. Participants include Egypt, Indonesia, Senegal, Serbia and Thailand. A separate group of CubeSats will be sent into orbit around the moon to search for lunar resources, but further details have not been disclosed. “Cislunar space extends from low-Earth orbit to about 2 million km [1.2 million miles] from Earth. It is a new frontier for human activity and a key region for future crewed missions to the moon and the construction of lunar bases,” the laboratory said. Scientists have long relied on individual spacecraft to study this enormous region, leaving many areas unexplored. With dozens of satellites observing from different locations at once, scientists can track energetic particles and magnetic disturbances from the sun as they sweep through the region, revealing how space weather develops. The satellites will also hunt for gamma-ray bursts – immensely powerful flashes from violent events in the distant universe. Detecting the same burst from different locations could pinpoint its source in the sky far more precisely. According to the lab, participating countries will jointly design missions, cover their own costs and share scientific data. China will provide them free instruments to detect high-energy particles, measure magnetic fields and spot gamma-ray bursts. The programme will also offer technical training and common engineering standards to help developing countries play a bigger role in deep-space exploration. “We look forward to working with partners around the world to expand the boundaries of human knowledge of deep space and the universe,” Hu Chaobin, the laboratory’s deputy director, told state news agency Xinhua. Work on the first phase has begun, with overall designs for the spacecraft, instruments and ground control systems expected to be finalised soon. The project is part of a broader push to expand China’s international partnerships in deep-space research. At the conference’s opening ceremony on Thursday, the laboratory also announced it was setting up joint research centres with Thailand’s National Astronomical Research Institute and the Astronomical Observatory of Belgrade in Serbia, according to the local newspaper Anhui Daily. The China-Thailand centre will focus on lunar robots, miniature spacecraft and planetary science, while its Serbian counterpart will study the moon and planets, the sun and space environment, asteroids and other small bodies. Both will run joint research projects and exchanges and train young scientists and engineers. The centres would give “new momentum to science and technology cooperation under China’s Belt and Road Initiative,” Anhui Daily reported.

title: How can future doctors blend clinical rigour with AI fluency and empathy?
description: During Global Education Summit, medical leaders say AI won’t replace doctors, but will reward those who ask better questions.
content: Medical experts have stressed that Hong Kong’s next generation of healthcare professionals must combine clinical rigour with emotional resilience, an open-minded approach to artificial intelligence (AI) and the drive to transform the sector. The remarks came during a panel discussion on the first day of the inaugural Global Education Summit, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier. “We always talk about people going north, going to Shenzhen … for medical services. But I would say that it’s a good thing for a future doctor. You’re going to be a doctor not just for 7 million people. You’re going to be a doctor for 80 million people,” Dr Chung Kin-lai, chief executive officer of CUHK Medical Centre, said on Saturday. Chung was referring to the population of the Greater Bay Area, which is estimated to be about 88 million people. The discussion, titled “Powering Hong Kong’s healthcare talent pipeline: from medical education to research and industry impact”, explored how the sector was preparing young doctors and healthcare talent for this changing landscape. The summit, which runs for two days, brought together about 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents from around the world to discuss regional talent development, AI integration and evolving academic pathways. With AI reshaping clinical workflows, medical leaders warned that traditional metrics for evaluating future doctors were changing. Chung noted that soft skills had become increasingly vital. “The old stuff when we ask about the ingredients to be a good doctor … are something like good language, good presentation, and also something like good memory,” Chung said. “But nowadays, memory is not that important. When you ask the internet, when you ask AI, everything comes up. “I think more important is your training of the other side – the soft side, your human touch. “How you communicate with people, especially with empathy.” Dr Kenneth Tsang, regional chief executive officer of IHH Healthcare North Asia and chief executive of Gleneagles Hospital Hong Kong, highlighted a generational divide in technology adoption. “What we found is that doctors in middle age and above are quite resilient when it comes to adopting AI. They actually resisted taking up AI,” he said. “So we are now actually moving into finding the younger generation of doctors who are very open and already, I would say, very knowledgeable about AI to join us and work with us on AI and healthcare.” With AI tools more prevalent, panellists told students that innovation required asking insightful questions, not just memorising answers. Innovation also required asking insightful questions rather than just memorising answers, said Dr Ricky Chiu, chairman and chief executive officer of PHASE Scientific and adjunct associate professor at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, during the session curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm. “My advice is really right now trying to learn how to ask the question that no one asks or ask the right question,” he said. “If I ask AI what the best way to screen for cervical cancer is, AI will give me a textbook answer. There’s nothing useful about that, right? But if I ask AI, how come these tests are available but yet all the women are still not doing that? And you’ve got a company.” Chiu encouraged students to view healthcare opportunities and career paths beyond traditional clinical roles, outlining three primary ways to contribute: treating patients; teaching doctors; and developing healthcare tools. “A doctor saves lives one at a time, and I think it’s a great life’s work. A good diagnosis can really change people’s lives,” he said. For students and parents considering medical studies, the experts also stressed that young people should ask themselves whether they understood it was a lifelong commitment before choosing this path. Chung warned high-achieving students against choosing medicine out of habit or simply because it was a top priority, noting that the extensive training required could often take 12 to 15 years. Tsang emphasised that real-world clinical readiness hinged on humility, while Chiu urged parents to let their children make their own choices, ensuring medicine was a genuine “lifetime dream”. Echoing the transformation seen in medicine, an adjacent panel discussed the qualities that tech and innovation leaders looked for in the next generation of talent. The panel featured industry leaders including Michael Yue, managing director and general manager of Google Hong Kong, Terry Wong, chief executive officer of the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation, and Yiyin Zhao, managing director of Samsung Electronics Hong Kong. Experts discussed some qualities they valued in future talent beyond academic results, including curiosity, adaptability, problem-solving and resilience. They also stressed the importance of students maintaining “the attitude to keep learning” and the ability to build relationships, work with people, and have empathy for others.

title: Taiwan remains Asia’s ‘most dangerous’ issue, former Singaporean diplomat warns
description: Any cross-strait conflict likely to draw in US with devastating impact on Southeast Asia, Kishore Mahbubani tells Penang Peace Dialogue.
content: Asia is still shackled by “mental colonisation” despite accounting for over half the global population, a former UN Security Council president has said, while warning that Taiwan remains the region’s most dangerous flashpoint. “The big mistake that Asians made after the end of colonial rule [is assuming] that the end of physical colonisation would automatically mean the end of mental colonisation,” veteran Singaporean diplomat Kishore Mahbubani told the inaugural Penang Peace Dialogue in Malaysia on Saturday. The lack of confidence to challenge Western-dominated narratives “continued for several decades”, he added. But the tide may be turning. “What is happening now is a major reversal in history where the Western states are effectively losing their self-confidence and the Asian states are gaining confidence,” Mahbubani said. However, despite this “major transition point in world history”, he said the shift of power towards Asia had yet to reach a tipping point “where the Asian states will have the greatest say in the world [in the way] that the Western states [now] do.” Home to China and India, the world’s two most populous nations, Asia accounts for roughly 60 per cent of the global population, or 4.3 billion people. Mahbubani also said improving China-India relations was vital for Asia’s future, with Southeast Asia needing to play a more active role in pushing for better ties between them. “The relationship between China and India became completely frozen after [the deadly 2020 border clash]. But the good news is that things are now beginning to thaw,” he said. Mahbubani, a distinguished fellow at the Asia Research Institute of the National University of Singapore, twice served as the city state’s ambassador to the United Nations, including two stints as Security Council president – in January 2001 and May 2002. He said that for India to achieve its goal of becoming a manufacturing powerhouse and the century’s third great power, it should engage constructively with China, which commands about one-third of global manufacturing capacity. Turning to regional security, Mahbubani described Taiwan as Asia’s “most dangerous issue.” He warned that any conflict across the Taiwan Strait was likely to draw in the United States, sparking a catastrophic confrontation that would devastate Southeast Asia. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons for defence. Mahbubani urged Taiwan not to declare independence, warning that this would “start a war automatically”. Rather, Taipei should seek creative diplomatic arrangements that preserve the island’s autonomy and way of life under reunification with mainland China in principle, he suggested. “Taiwan should understand where the red lines are and make sure it does not cross the red lines and lead to a war,” he cautioned. The Penang Peace Dialogue is a new annual international forum designed to foster peace and cooperation in an emerging multipolar world. The first edition this weekend brings together roughly 200 academics, policymakers and business leaders from Asia and beyond.

title: Mastering the game: 2 Chinese senior statesmen steal show at World Masters Athletics meet
description: Lyu Mingpu, 92, and Ding Ming, 10 years younger, prove athletic ambition can last a lifetime as they win three gold medals in South Korea.
content: Age may be just a number, but for two of China’s most senior track and field athletes, the numbers they have produced on the global stage have been nothing short of astonishing. At the World Masters Athletics Championships, 92-year-old Lyu Mingpu captured four medals across six events, including two golds, and immediately set a new goal to keep running until he is 100. Similarly, 82-year-old Ding Ming shaved a massive 0.52 seconds off the Asian M80 80-metre hurdles record to win a world title. But beyond their historic podium finishes, the two veterans embody a unique approach to sport, balancing a fierce competitive fire with the pragmatic self-awareness to know their physical limits, proving that athletic ambition can last a lifetime if pursued with caution and purpose. After 13 days of competition, the championships wrapped up in Daegu, South Korea, on Thursday. The 105-member mainland Chinese delegation concluded the meet with an impressive haul of 10 gold, 23 silver and 19 bronze medals. The team’s oldest competitor in the delegation, Jinan native Lyu won gold in the men’s M90 long jump and the M85 4x100m relay. He also secured silver in the M90 triple jump, bronze in the M90 200m, and placed fourth in the 100m and sixth in the 400m. September 3, the World Masters Athletic Championship came to an end in Daegu, South Korea. Lu Mingpu, a 92-year-old from Jinan, Shandong Province, China, won the world championship in the M90 group (90 years and older) long jump event. He signed up for a total of six athletics… pic.twitter.com/qLfCHdrwUT — Walter (@WalterL87309879) September 5, 2026 Lyu had initially entered five individual events, but the relay was an impromptu decision upon arriving in Daegu. “The 85-year-old age group lacked one runner to form a team, so he filled in, and they ended up winning gold,” his son, Lyu Yi, told local media. Despite expressing disappointment with his final placement in the 200m, Lyu was thrilled with his time after edging his opponent by a mere 0.05 seconds. “I am very happy with the result because it broke the national record,” Lyu said. “If I had not chased hard, I would not have broken it.” Rain hampered his long jump performance, restricting him to a 2.05 metre clearance compared with the 2.22 metres he achieves during training. However, the result was still enough to secure the top spot in his age category. His transition to competitive track began at age 71 when he won a bronze medal at a national meet. “Sometimes my body aches, and I think about skipping training, but I grit my teeth and go. After warming up, the pain disappears,” Lyu said. Lyu spent a year preparing for the championships, visiting the Shandong University track at least four times a week for two to three hours per session to practise jogging, stretching, starts and landings. When asked about his health secret, he simply credited consistent exercise. In China’s M90 category, Lyu essentially competes against the clock. “In this age group domestically, I am the only one left on the track,” he admitted. He already holds multiple national records and broke three more at the China Masters in May. He now aims to intensify his training to claim the 400m record. Inspired by other athletes over 100, Lyu refuses to stop. “I cannot give up halfway; I will try to run until I am 100,” he said. “I did not have good conditions when I was young. Now that I do, I just want to keep running.” Earlier in the tournament, on the fourth day of competition, 82-year-old Ding from Anshan, Liaoning province, claimed the men’s M80 80m hurdles title. His 15.99-second finish comfortably surpassed the previous Asian record of 16.51 seconds. For Ding, athletics is a lifelong habit that has evolved into a dedicated post-retirement lifestyle. During his record-breaking race, his focus remained strictly on execution. China’s 82-year-old Ding Ming from Anshan, #Liaoning Province, won the M80 80-meter hurdles final at the 2026 World Masters Athletics Championships, finishing in 15.99 seconds to take gold, and shattering the Asian record for his age group. pic.twitter.com/LrPp0abHFt — iLiaoning (@iLiaoning) August 28, 2026 “From the starting line to the finish, I only thought about one thing: maintaining my form and pushing through to the end,” Ding told local media. After crossing the finish line, he shook hands with every competitor. Ding views the world championships primarily as a gathering for retired athletes and elite amateurs, where communication outweighs winning. “We might not speak the same language, but we shake hands and hug,” he said. “If you win, I won’t be jealous; if I lose, you won’t look down on me. That is sports.” A lifelong sports enthusiast rather than a former professional, Ding began systematic training after retiring. He made his world debut in Lyon in 2015, claimed four golds at the 2019 Asian Masters, and took bronze at the 2024 World Championships in Gothenburg. His Daegu victory came just three months after he set a national age-group record of 16.73 seconds at the China Masters. “Sport is meant to maintain health and reduce the burden on our families, not to create new worries,” he explained. Ding has set no upper age limit for his competitive career, planning to continue as long as he can safely train and navigate outdoors without symptoms like dizziness. “As long as my physical and mental state allows me to go out and return safely, I will keep moving,” he said, adding that he hopes to continue organising and inspiring more seniors to take up the sport. Sanctioned by World Athletics, the biennial World Masters Athletics Championships is widely considered the “Senior Olympics”. Open to global enthusiasts aged 35 and above competing in five-year age brackets, the Daegu edition drew more than 7,000 athletes from 106 countries.

title: Chinese-German team builds ultra-sensitive ‘floating compass’ to hunt dark matter
description: The device detects vanishingly weak magnetic signals, such as those produced by the human brain, and can operate at room temperature.
content: Chinese researchers have developed a table-top magnetic sensor that operates at room temperature and can spot magnetic signals a billion times fainter than the Earth’s own field. The Levitated Magnet Magnetometer (LeMaMa) functions like a compass with a needle that floats in mid-air with virtually no friction. By tracking the needle’s tiny deflections, the team can measure magnetic fields down to the femtotesla level – an advance that could widen the hunt for elusive dark matter particles or monitor brain signals. “The combination of room-temperature operation, tiny components and high sensitivity makes LeMaMa promising for fundamental physics experiments,” Ji Wei, assistant professor at Peking University’s school of physics and corresponding author of the study, told Guangming Daily on August 17. Magnetic fields are everywhere, ranging in strength from about 1.5 tesla for a hospital magnetic resonance imaging machine to the vanishingly weak femtotesla, or a quadrillionth of a tesla, generated by human brain activity. Measuring the tiniest magnetic fields has long been a challenge. Now, scientists from China’s Peking University and Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany have built the world’s first room-temperature ultraprecise magnetometer based on a levitated magnet. Their work was published in the journal Science on August 6. Until now, femtotesla-level measurements have mainly relied on two approaches. One is the superconducting quantum interference device (Squid) magnetometer, which offers excellent sensitivity but must operate at cryogenic temperatures near absolute zero, requiring bulky and expensive liquid-helium cooling. The other is the spin-exchange relaxation free (Serf) atomic magnetometer, which also reaches femtotesla sensitivity but needs heated atomic vapour and only works in a near-zero magnetic field inside heavy shielding – meaning the sample must be brought into the shielded room, limiting close-range, high-resolution detection. LeMaMa works at room temperature, needs no magnetic shielding and is miniaturised. It requires no liquid helium, no heating and no bulky shielded room. The entire device fits inside a vacuum chamber about the size of a lunchbox. This opens up a new path for taking ultrasensitive magnetic detection out of the lab and into the real world. LeMaMa is a bit like a compass. For a compass to be truly sensitive, its needle needs to turn with no resistance – ideally, floating in the air. At the heart of LeMaMa is a tiny sensing magnet just 0.4 mm (less than 0.02 inch) thick. The team suspended another magnet above this “needle” to provide an upwards force that counteracts gravity. But a single magnet alone cannot hold it steady. “It’s like balancing an egg on a smooth table – it might stay for an instant, but the slightest disturbance knocks it over,” Guangming Daily quoted Ji as saying. “To solve that, we place specially designed diamagnetic materials underneath, which push against the magnet instead of attracting it – like an invisible hand supporting it from below.” With these two forces working together, the tiny sensing magnet floats stably in mid-air, becoming a compass without a pivot or suspension thread. When an external magnetic field is applied, the sensor swings slightly. By measuring that deflection, the team can infer the strength and variation of the outside field. To reach extreme sensitivity, they also had to cut down environmental noise. The sensing magnet is housed in a vacuum chamber, and the whole set-up sits on a vibration-isolation stage. In lab tests, LeMaMa showed extreme sensitivity to ultra-weak magnetic signals, despite operating in a strong background field. This means the device can pick up tiny magnetic fluctuations at the femtotesla level – even against background noise from the Earth’s natural magnetic field that is billions of times stronger. The sensor could also help search for new particles such as dark matter. “The team has already applied LeMaMa to detect axion dark matter, improving sensitivity over previous best results by multiple orders of magnitude in a specific mass range,” Guangming Daily quoted Ji as saying. According to a report on the Peking University website, because LeMaMa’s core sensor is just a few hundred micrometres wide, the device is both highly sensitive and small. This makes it well suited for high-resolution magnetic imaging and close-range magnetic field detection. In biomedicine, it could measure neural magnetic signals for brain research and neurological diagnostics. In geophysical exploration, its small size makes it ideal for high-precision magnetic mapping and mineral resource surveying.

title: How bizarre 1969 spy thriller The Chairman pitted Gregory Peck against Mao over ping-pong
description: The Cold War thriller starring Gregory Peck features a surreal encounter with Chairman Mao and a prescient warning about climate change.
content: As the idealistic 1960s bled into the cynical 70s, Hollywood thrillers became increasingly paranoid. But before post-Watergate efforts such as The Parallax View and The Conversation (both 1974) came The Chairman, a globe-trotting 1969 oddity starring Gregory Peck. Instead of the enemy within, the film rattled with anxieties about communist China’s scientific capabilities. It was hardly the sexiest of subjects for a spy thriller – which was reflected in its poor box office showing – but it provided a fascinating insight into real-life East-West relations. Originally developed for Frank Sinatra by writer Jay Richard Kennedy, it was ultimately scripted by Ben Maddow and directed by J. Lee Thompson. The latter had worked with Peck on the rather more gung-ho World War II film The Guns of Navarone (1961). The plot concerns a new enzyme, developed by Professor Soong Li (Chinese-American actor Keye Luke), that enables crops to grow in any climate. American scientist Dr John Hathaway (Peck), his former colleague, is tasked with following Soong to China to bring back the formula. However, Hathaway’s military handlers, led by Lieutenant General Shelby (Arthur Hill), have implanted a recording device in his skull with a secret explosive element that will detonate if he fails. As Shelby puts it: “Think any sane man would walk into China with a loaded bomb screwed into his head?” A fraught Asian shoot At times, the filmmakers were just as bold. Denied access to shoot in mainland China, they decamped to Hong Kong, where they encountered even more problems. As author John Ross put it on his Formosa Files podcast earlier this year, “Hong Kong was dealing with agitation from communist supporters, and the filmmakers were met with demonstrations and threats. Director J. Lee Thompson said that the crew members feared for their safety: ‘In the end, I had to secretly photograph the Hong Kong scenes from cabs or private cars.’” The less said about the climax – which sees Snowdonia, in North Wales, standing in for rural Chinese countryside – the better. Meanwhile, the studio-bound Hong Kong scenes are reminiscent of a Bond movie – which is to say, sexist, racist and far-fetched. Hathaway goes to a busy casino-brothel to meet a contact and is offered “any form of entertainment you wish” by local beauty Ting Ling (Burmese-English actress Zienia Merton). When he refuses, she romances him, then knocks him out. “The pleasures of our city can make you forget,” warns the night manager. While Hong Kong is portrayed as a den of iniquity, the real-life city was not much safer. After a bomb scare, production was moved to Taiwan, where the locals were so incensed that they burned an effigy of Peck. The reason for their ire? A scene in which Hathaway meets Chairman Mao Zedong, founder of the People’s Republic of China, played by Japanese-American actor Conrad Yama. Having landed in mainland China – actually, Taiwan – and seen the requisite number of peasants, paddy fields and propaganda, Hathaway is ushered to a secret palace – Taipei’s spectacular Zhinan Temple – to meet the great leader himself. A surreal encounter with Mao In a sequence so bizarre it might have been taken from an Austin Powers movie, Mao is shown as a smiley old man with a fake wart. He is also incredibly good at table tennis. To begin with, Mao is charming, if needy. “Do you like China?” he asks Hathaway. “Please help us, as first impressions are very accurate.” He then moves into a lecture about the Cultural Revolution, acknowledging the millions of lives lost but arguing this was necessary because the Chinese people “have lived so long like animals, and now they must leap in one generation from the 10th century to the 21st”. Veering a little close to a Bond villain, he warns Hathaway: “That is why we will win, and you people will be thrown onto the pile of human dung we Chinese keep for the fields!” Finally, he offers Hathaway a job helping produce the enzyme on an industrial scale, then finishes with a surprisingly prescient lecture on climate change, telling him “The world is exploding” and that in 25 years, there will be 6 billion people to feed. It is a remarkable scene, especially because the rest of the film is so rote. Not only is it impossible to imagine an Asian film of the era featuring, say, a basketball game with former US president Richard Nixon or billiards with former British prime minister Harold Wilson, but the sequence also seemed to tap into the zeitgeist in ways the filmmakers could not have anticipated. In the years that followed, table tennis would play a pivotal role in the thawing of East-West relations, as part of Mao’s so-called ping-pong diplomacy. Yet even Maddow could not throw much light on the matter – and he wrote it. “It was just a melodrama, which they tried to make concurrent with the politics at the time,” he was quoted as saying in the 1991 book Backstory 2: Interviews with Screenwriters of the 1940s and 1950s. “I didn’t know anything about Mao, to tell the truth. Nobody else did, really, either.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Chinese man, Nepali woman found alive 10 days after flood
description: The man, named only as Luhaitao, was pulled out of a tunnel, while Chandrika Shrestha, 64, was rescued from her buried home.
content: Rescuers pulled out a 64-year-old Nepali woman alive on Saturday from her home, buried under thick mud and debris when the region was struck by massive flooding 10 days ago, killing over 1,300 people and leaving at least 5,500 missing. Emergency personnel said earlier they had rescued a Chinese man, named only as Luhaitao, found alive inside a 225-metre tunnel of the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district. Footage ‌shared by the Nepali army showed him being given ⁠emergency medical attention inside a helicopter, which took him ⁠to an army hospital. He appeared exhausted and disoriented, with dried mud and dust on ‌his skin ‌and clothing. A uniformed doctor with a stethoscope was seen checking his vitals. Members of Nepal’s Armed Police Force cheered later on Saturday as a mud-caked woman, Chandrika Shrestha, was pulled from her buried home in Nuwakot district. “A police team found her as they were clearing the area. She has been airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment,” said police deputy superintendent Iqbal Hawari. A video released by Nepal’s Armed Police Force showed only a part of her house visible, with the lower floors completely submerged by thick sludge. On Friday, ‌rescuers pulled two people from another tunnel at the Upper Trishuli ‌3A Hydropower Station, on the same river. Emergency response teams have been working relentlessly to find survivors since a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through the China-Nepal border following a glacier and rock collapse on August 26. Rescuers ⁠have ⁠said they believe the collapse trapped at least 900 ‌people in ‌tunnels related to six hydropower projects. So far, 1,344 bodies have been recovered in Nepal, according to the national disaster agency, with about 5,000 people missing. Chinese state media said 31 people had been killed and 531 were missing, taking the overall death toll to 1,375, with over 5,500 missing. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Canada and China thaw continues as militaries hold first talks in 8 years amid US pressure
description: The resumption of talks between the two armed forces comes as Ottawa reaches out to Beijing following a series of spats with Donald Trump.
content: China and Canada’s armed forces held their first round of talks in eight years on Friday in the face of growing tensions with the United States. The Chinese defence ministry said there had been a candid and in-depth exchange of views on international and regional issues of common concern. “[Both sides] expressed willingness to strengthen practical exchanges and cooperation between the two militaries, and enhanced mutual understanding and trust,” the ministry added. It was the first meeting through a channel known as the Defence Coordination Dialogue since April 2018 and the fifth since it was launched in 2013. However, during that time, the then Canadian defence minister Bill Blair met his Chinese counterpart Dong Jun on the sidelines of the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore in 2024. China and Canada have been working to reset relations after years of tension by resuming high-level exchanges, expanding direct flights and working to ease trade tensions in areas such as agriculture and electric vehicles. In July, Li Yao, the defence attache at the Chinese embassy in Canada, said the “continued improvement” of relations between the two countries had “created favourable conditions for closer communication and exchanges between the two militaries”. The Chinese statement did not say who led the talks on its side, but General Yang Zhibin, head of the PLA’s Eastern Theatre Command, was in Canada this week for the Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence Conference in Victoria, British Columbia. He met the head of US Pacific Command Samuel Paparo on Monday, ending a two-year break in command-level contact between the two sides. On Wednesday, Paparo called Canada a “close ally” and dismissed a question about a US military attack on Canada as “absolutely and utterly preposterous”. Donald Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st state of the US and he signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” after trade talks between the two neighbours collapsed last month. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had walked away from the talks because of “unreasonable demands” from the US and announced a series of retaliatory tariffs. Carney has also called for Canada and other “middle powers” to play a more active role on the international stage. The country has increased its military presence on the opposite side of the Pacific, taking part in the annual US-Philippine Balikatan exercises for the first time this year. Troops from Japan, Australia, New Zealand and France also took part in the drills. Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty previously said the country’s navy would take part in other exercises in the Indo-Pacific this year, including port calls in Japan. He added there was no contradiction between deeper defence ties with allies and closer trade relations with Beijing.

title: Safety or hostility? Dog owners split over Hong Kong’s crackdown on leash rules
description: ‘The inspections and enforcement are good for protecting the safety of people and pets. They should be continued as we don’t want to see any more tragedies,’ one dog owner says.
content: Hong Kong authorities’ intensified enforcement against dog owners who fail to control their pets has drawn mixed reactions, with supporters welcoming improved safety and critics warning it is stoking panic and hostility. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department carried out inspections and enforcement operations across the city on Saturday following a spate of dog attacks in recent weeks. Among those walking their pets at the West Kowloon Cultural District despite the heat were civil servant Mark Mak, 35, his wife and their two daughters. Mak, who owns a six-year-old dog named Mori, said he always leashed his pet in public to prevent it from wandering or coming into contact with other dogs and disapproved of owners who did not. “The inspections and enforcement are good for protecting the safety of people and pets. They should be continued as we don’t want to see any more tragedies,” he said. Finance sector employee Kim Chan, also in his thirties, walked his nine-year-old black labradoodle, Charcoal, at the cultural district. Chan said that although his dog was well-behaved and non-aggressive, he always used a leash to protect it and avoid affecting others. “The measures can improve protection and remind dog owners of their responsibilities as some people, including children, may be afraid of dogs,” he said. But an owner of a 10-year-old mongrel, who gave only her surname, Cheung, said the stepped-up inspections had created panic in communities. She cited growing hostility from others, including taxi drivers refusing to give her and her dog a ride. “Such measures only spread panic and make people think that having a dog is a problem,” Cheung, in her thirties, said. Staff patrolled the cultural district with signs reminding people to leash their pets, a measure also observed at tech hub Cyberport in Pok Fu Lam, where some dog owners walked with their pets. Retiree Betty Ngai, 63, and her husband were enjoying an outing with their four-year-old poodle at Cyberport. Ngai said she kept her dog on a leash for most of the time outside despite its small size, and supported the government’s reinforced actions in response to recent attacks as a reminder to owners to keep pets under proper control. Authorities stepped up enforcement against dog owners who fail to keep their pets under control during special operations over this weekend and on August 30. The department said officers would step up inspections at public places where dogs congregated, and take immediate enforcement action without warning if keepers were found not to have properly controlled their dogs in accordance with legal requirements. The department earlier said it conducted operations in Yuen Long, West Kowloon, Cyberport and Kai Tak on August 30, and would prosecute three dog owners for failing to keep large dogs on a leash in public areas. Under the Rabies Ordinance, it is an offence to leave a dog unleashed in public areas or at any place from which it may wander into a public space. Offenders can be fined HK$10,000 (US$1,275) upon conviction. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, any dog weighing 20kg or more must be secured in public with a leash of up to two metres. Anyone who fails to comply faces a maximum penalty of three months in prison and a HK$25,000 fine. Last month, a 33-year-old pet training facility owner was mauled by a mixed-breed fighting dog registered as a mongrel. She was found dead nearby after the attack. A 60kg mixed-breed dog killed a miniature poodle and a bichon frise in separate attacks near Yoho Mall in Yuen Long last month.

title: Singapore investigates racism related to China-Nepal disaster, Air India investment
description: Minister K Shanmugam has asked police to look at an ‘online mob’ after various comments, including missing Singaporeans being ‘not our own’.
content: Police are investigating “shameful” racist and xenophobic online comments about the China-Nepal disaster and Singapore Airlines’ (SIA) investment in Air India, Senior Minister K Shanmugam said on Saturday. Mr Shanmugam told reporters that the Ministry of Digital Development and Information will also ask social media platforms to remove comments that breach guidelines. “The media tells me that they had to remove several comments because they were so nasty. I don’t know if all the comments are all made by Singaporeans. But, I will say this – the comments are shameful, nasty, totally unacceptable,” added Mr Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister and coordinating minister for national security. “I have asked police to look into these comments.” Under CNA’s social media moderation policy, users who post hate speech, racist or offensive comments are blocked from commenting on CNA’s social media pages. In cases where such comments are widespread and persistent, CNA may totally turn off comments on its posts, as it did for several news posts related to the China-Nepal disaster. MP Alex Yam (People’s Action Party) also called out such comments earlier this week, describing them as “not just racist” but “downright heartless”. Nine Singaporeans remain missing after devastating floods caused massive destruction in Nepal on August 26. Mr Shanmugam gave several examples of racist remarks made online about the missing Singaporeans, including “no, they are not our own” and “all ABNNs look the same”. He noted that “ABNN” is a derogatory term for Indians. More than a thousand people died in the disaster and Singaporeans remain unaccounted for, he said, yet such remarks continued to circulate online. Mr Shanmugam added that most Singaporeans do not share these views, pointing to more than S$3 million (US$2.4 million) raised by the Singapore Red Cross for relief efforts in Nepal. “Singaporeans are generous, across all races. And it is important that we don’t allow a minority to poison the entire well.” Racist backlash over Air India investment Meanwhile, news that Air India is seeking fresh equity from shareholders, including SIA, has sparked a new wave of “anti-Indian, racist ranting” online, such as “references to snakes, curry, prata, black magic”, Mr Shanmugam said. An “online mob” has also attacked various parties, including the CEO and senior management of Temasek, over their ethnicity. Temasek is the majority shareholder of Singapore Airlines. “It has been said that because the CEO is of Indian ethnicity, he would favour Air India. In the eyes of these people, the CEO’s sin is that he is of Indian ethnicity, even though he is as Singaporean as any of us, he was born here, studied here. That is nasty and libellous,” Mr Shanmugam said. “But for this online mob, however, all of that, the facts don’t matter. What matters is their racism and their own prejudices. If we allow this, in future, everyone can be attacked for their decisions based on their ethnicities. I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things, slowly it becomes normalised, then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it Singapore’s Senior Minister K Shanmugam “These people should be unmasked and dealt with rather than be allowed to hide behind online anonymity.” Singapore is not exempt from “latent racism”, Mr Shanmugam said, adding that authorities have taken a “tough line” to protect the country’s multiracial, multi-religious fabric and preserve social harmony. “I’ve decided to call out these people because you see what is happening in other countries. First, a minority says these nasty things; slowly it becomes normalised; then it becomes mainstream, and political and community leaders will say it,” he added. “Public discourse is then debased. Social harmony is affected. Violence against people of a different skin colour and different religion becomes acceptable.” Racist comments, particularly against Indians in Singapore, have grown more frequent of late, with some originating and “fanned from overseas”, Mr Shanmugam said. “We are a very small multiracial, multi-ethnic country. If we are divided along racial or religious lines, we will lose the unity that has made Singapore strong. There will be feelings of ill will, suspicion, and we will all suffer,” he added. “We should not tolerate this. This is not who we are as Singaporeans.” Temasek’s role in SIA’s decisions A Reuters report last month cited sources as saying that Air India is seeking a further US$1.5 billion in support from owners Tata Sons and SIA, just months after it posted a record annual loss. An SIA spokesperson said last week that the board would “carefully consider any requests for additional capital from Air India, taking into consideration the group’s other capital requirements and Air India’s business strategy”. Workers’ Party MP Kenneth Tiong said in a Facebook post on August 26 that he would not support nor expect any future use of Temasek’s funds to “prop up Air India via Singapore Airlines”. Whether it is SIA or Temasek that “writes the cheque”, there will be a “significant impact” on Temasek, he wrote. “No one, least of all Singaporeans, owes Air India a living … if Singapore Airlines wants to continue its bet on Air India, it should do so on its own two feet, and not on Temasek’s.” Mr Shanmugam said it is SIA’s responsibility to assess its investments in Air India against the resources it has for its “long-term growth and profitability”. “Any decision to invest in Air India lies with SIA, and Temasek as a shareholder in SIA, along with other shareholders, will expect SIA to make its investment decisions responsibly.” Temasek is accountable to the government for its overall portfolio and long-term performance, Mr Shanmugam said, but not for individual investment decisions of its portfolio companies. “Temasek and its subsidiaries decide how to invest across a wide portfolio with investments of varied risks and varied time horizons. Once governments or politicians start directing individual investment decisions, commercial discipline will be compromised,” he added. “Decisions will become politicised – shaped by political considerations, rather than commercial judgment. In the end, Singaporeans will bear the cost.” The government’s general principle is not to intervene in individual investment decisions or pressure companies on how to invest, Mr Shanmugam added. Its role is to ensure professional management in Temasek, and then provide Temasek and its portfolio companies with the “political cover and the confidence which will allow them to make properly considered commercial decisions, free from untoward pressures”. Temasek and many of its portfolio companies, including SIA, Sembcorp, Singtel and CapitaLand, have made substantial investments in India over the years, Mr Shanmugam said. “Temasek’s website says that 43 per cent, nearly half, of its country exposure is to the Americas and China, and seven per cent is in India. But its website also says that India has in fact been its best-performing market over the last decade,” he said. “Mr Tiong is entitled to his views. He is entitled, like any other Singaporean, to ask questions about SIA and Temasek. “But neither his views, nor that of any minister, or any other MP, should substitute for the commercial judgment of SIA’s management and board of directors – boards which have knowledgeable and independent members, and management which has professionals whose primary responsibility is to consider and make these decisions.” Asked by a reporter to respond to Mr Tiong’s statement that no one “owes Air India a living”, Mr Shanmugam said: “I think he ought to do his homework and look at SIA’s letter and the facts that I put out today, and ask if he is being responsible.” This article was first published by CNA: Police investigating ‘shameful’ racist online comments about Nepal-Tibet disaster, Air India: SM Shanmugam - CNA

title: Asia-Pacific media outlets forge new partnerships ahead of Shenzhen Apec summit
description: SCMP and Nanfang Media Group have signed an MOU to deepen media cooperation, as the southern tech hub prepares to welcome regional leaders.
content: Media outlets across the Asia-Pacific region have gathered in Shenzhen to deepen collaboration on content, talent and technology ahead of the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern Chinese city. Hundreds of media representatives witnessed the launch of several partnerships at the Asia-Pacific Media Forum, which opened in Shenzhen on Saturday after two days of sub-forums in other Guangdong cities as part of a series of events marking the 2026 Apec “China Year”. Themed “building a path to shared prosperity for the Asia-Pacific community: media consensus and action”, the forum announced the establishment of the Asia-Pacific Media Partnership Organising Committee. Its 16 founding organisations include China’s People’s Daily and Xinhua News Agency, Russia’s Tass news agency and Vietnam News Agency. Li Shulei, head of the publicity department of the Communist Party’s Central Committee, said on Saturday that the partnership “provides support for in-depth exchanges and enhanced cooperation” and would “enhance the voice and influence of Asia-Pacific media”. The partnership committee would promote a programme focused on high-level dialogue, coordinated communication, technological innovation and practical cooperation, according to an official announcement. Meanwhile, Huang Kunming, the Communist Party chief of Guangdong province, said the province’s strong technological and economic base could support media organisations to make greater use of AI through technology and software collaborations. During the event, the South China Morning Post also signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Nanfang Media Group, based in Guangzhou, Guangdong’s provincial capital. The two news organisations in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area (GBA) are set to work together on news and content, events and AI innovation. Huang Can, editor-in-chief of Nanfang Media Group, said he expected both sides to “work together to tell the stories of Guangdong and Hong Kong, the GBA and China” to local, regional and global audiences. “The SCMP is honoured and pleased to forge this meaningful partnership,” said Tammy Tam, Publisher of the SCMP, adding that it would help to “explore greater potential for more collaboration in various joint projects, including comprehensive coverage of the GBA and China, in a fact-based and convincing way to the region and the world”. The forum also announced another media cooperation initiative, “Gather in Shenzhen, Create a Better Asia-Pacific”, featuring three main projects covering technology sharing, content co-creation and talent co-development. Meanwhile, the Shenzhen Consensus of the Asia-Pacific Media Forum was also launched on Saturday, reflecting broad agreement on advancing open cooperation, driving digital, intelligent and green development, and strengthening media collaborations. The media forum, a major gathering of Asia-Pacific outlets, comes ahead of the Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting in November. Shenzhen will host this year’s summit, the third Chinese city to do so after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. As part of the series, Hong Kong will host the Apec finance ministers’ meeting for the first time in October.

title: Hong Kong mega bridge’s popularity takes toll on helicopter, ferry services: lawmaker
description: Mark Chong says Sky Shuttle’s suspension and drop in ferry services linked to bridge’s growing use, with vehicle flow reaching 5.2 million in 2025.
content: The number of vehicles using a mega bridge linking Hong Kong with Zhuhai and Macau hit a record high last year, the South China Morning Post has learned, with a lawmaker saying the boom has taken a heavy toll on ferry services and a long-running helicopter service. Transport Department figures obtained by the SCMP showed that vehicle flow via the popular Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge reached a record high of 5.21 million last year, up more than 19 per cent from 4.36 million in 2024. The 2025 figures were the highest in the past five years, following border closures due to the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021. The bridge was opened to traffic in 2018. Average daily vehicle flow via the bridge in June this year reached 15,408, already surpassing the overall average for 2025. The bridge’s peak in popularity coincided with helicopter service operator Sky Shuttle’s announcement that it would axe its scheduled flights between Hong Kong and Macau, which had operated since 1990. Sky Shuttle said the service suspension took into account the coming relocation of Macau Heliport to the new heliport at Macau International Airport Terminal 2. It added that its Macau-Shenzhen route was excluded from this suspension and would operate as a scheduled flight service. Starting this month, the company said its helicopter services would switch to a charter-only model, operating five days a week. The Sky Shuttle network, which links Macau’s Outer Harbour Ferry Terminal with Hong Kong’s Hong Kong–Macau Ferry Terminal, used to offer 54 flights every day since 2008 with fares set at HK$4,580 (US$584) per trip. The service was initially founded in 1988 as a joint venture that was majority-owned by Sociedade de Turismo e Diversoes de Macau, headed by the late Macau casino tycoon Stanley Ho Hung-sun. Turbojet – owned and operated by a joint venture between the Ho family’s Shun Tak Holdings and China Travel International Investment Hong Kong – and its competitor Cotai Water Jet, owned by casino operator Sands China, have consolidated their ferry schedules between Macau and Hong Kong since September 1. Under the new arrangement, some frequencies were cut and while others became unscheduled services. Lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung said he believed the bridge’s advantages – reflected by its boom – had greatly affected the Sky Shuttle business. It also took a toll on Hong Kong-Macau ferry services, which recorded a 6.5 per cent year-on-year drop to 7.74 million passengers in 2025. “The bridge’s greater popularity showed that more commuters were attracted by its advantages over other transport means such as the Sky Shuttle and the Hong Kong-Macau ferry services,” he said. Chong pointed out that Sky Shuttle’s helicopter services were more expensive and prone to weather disruptions, while ferry services were restricted by their schedules. “If you commute via the bridge, you can still arrange a luxury service such as pickup or ride services by a limousine,” he said. Macau government data show 1,112 tourists arrived in Macau via the Outer Harbour heliport in the first seven months of 2026, up 1.7 per cent from a year earlier but down 84.4 per cent from 7,121 in the same period in 2019, before the pandemic. Macau received 24.49 million visitors over the first seven months of 2026. Annual helicopter arrivals peaked in 2013 at 43,218, during the casino city’s gaming boom, according to the Macau government.

title: China’s billion-dollar pet funeral industry stays largely unregulated without public oversight
description: A 'high-end custom' service is priced at around US$1,500, which includes transport via limousine and ceremony led by four uniformed pallbearers.
content: In May, at a pet funeral home in Dalian, northeastern Liaoning province, a grieving couple wept as they tenderly combed the fur of their deceased pet cat, a Silver British Shorthair, bidding farewell to their beloved “fur kid.” The feline, cherished by the couple for eight years, succumbed to heart disease. “Pidan (the cat’s nickname), you will no longer feel pain in that world. Please visit us in our dreams to share your news. I hope we will be a family again in the next life,” said the wife. “Pidan, don’t forget Mum and Dad. Remember to stand your ground when bullied in that world,” the husband implored his cat. After about 10 minutes, the husband gently carried the cat’s body to a van awaiting its transport for cremation. Such sorrowful scenes are a daily occurrence in the pet funeral service industry. The sector has experienced remarkable growth over the past decade, spurred by pet owners’ desires to engage professionals for posthumous arrangements for their pets. According to a national enterprises database, Tian Yan Cha, there are 43,600 pet funeral-related companies across China. In 2022 alone, 27,100 new companies were registered, marking a fivefold increase from the previous year. The market value of this industry reached 10 billion yuan (US$1.5 billion) in 2022, according to a report by consulting firm iiMedia Research. This boom is driven by the rapidly growing pet population in the country. Last year, urban authorities across China recorded around 53 million pet dogs and 73 million pet cats. Pet funeral homes offer comprehensive services, including euthanasia, body preparation, memorial ceremonies, cremation, bone ashes retention, tomb burial, and souvenir creation. Prices vary widely, ranging from 1,000 yuan (US$150) to tens of thousands of yuan (thousands of US dollars), as reported by state broadcaster CCTV. A “high-end tailor-made” funeral service, featuring four staff members in uniform carrying the pet’s coffin and using a limousine for transport, costs 9,880 yuan. Some funeral homes also offer religious ceremonies for pets, charging 1,800 yuan. Among the most expensive funeral options is pressing bone ashes into a “life crystal,” which costs 18,000 yuan (US$2,700). “Holding a memorial ritual may seem straightforward, but it fulfils pet owners’ emotional needs. This formal goodbye allows grieving owners to bid farewell to their pets. People are willing to pay for this emotional value,” explained a pet funeral homeowner in Shenyang, also in Liaoning. A ceremony typically includes floral displays, farewell blankets, memorial walls, paw-print keepsake boxes, and bottles containing a tuft of the pet’s hair. Pet owners often read farewell letters, or sometimes funeral organisers read the letters on behalf of the owners. Zhang Yingjun, a 30-year-old woman who opened a pet funeral store in Dalian in 2022, shared her experience of witnessing many heartbreaking farewells: she did not become numb; rather, she felt deep empathy for her clients. “At first, I cried with them. Then I realised that the more important task was to manage the funeral arrangements effectively and provide a high-quality service for them,” Zhang told CCTV. Despite this rapid growth, the industry remains unregulated, with a significant issue being the absence of a principal supervisory authority. Fu Jian, a lawyer from Henan Zejin Law Firm, told the SCMP that pet funeral businesses must first obtain permission from both the livestock administration authority and the environmental protection authority before opening. However, no specific government department is designated to oversee the entire industry’s development, Fu noted. “The civil affairs authority is responsible for human funerals, the agricultural and livestock authority focuses on the harmless disposal of animals, and the environmental protection authority only monitors gas emissions. Due to this fragmented oversight, many pet funeral homes can operate with malpractice or violations without facing investigation or consequences,” Fu explained. He added that many clauses in pet funeral contracts lack specific details regarding service content or quality due to the absence of industry standards. “When stores fail to honour their agreements or provide subpar services, customers often find it difficult to assert their rights,” the lawyer stated. In 2024, an internet user in Shenzhen expressed his frustration on social media after paying 700 yuan (US$100) for a pet store to cremate his cat separately. However, after reviewing a video the store provided of the bathing process, he discovered it was not his cat. Following multiple discussions, the store eventually admitted to having cremated his cat alongside other pets. “I paid for the service, but now I don’t know what happened to my cat,” the man lamented, adding he received no compensation from the store.

title: Who are Alex Eala’s parents? Meet the supportive family behind the Filipino tennis star
description: Her dad Mike is a corporate executive, while mum Rizza is a former national swimmer and comes from a family of athletes.
content: Twenty-one-year-old Alex Eala is currently riding a career high. This summer has seen Eala beat Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon and also win her first WTA title. She’s at a career-best 18th in the world, and she breezed into the second round of the US Open with a 6-1, 6-2 victory over Mary Stoiana – closing it out with a confident smile. Her victory saw the court – filled with Eala’s fans, many bearing the Philippine flag, erupt into cheers. It was hardly surprising, given the ardent, ever-growing fan base that now surrounds the charismatic tennis star. Hailing from the Philippines, Eala has become the nation’s pride as its biggest sporting sensation since professional boxer Manny Pacquiao. The Filipino has achieved stardom thanks to her ability to dominate on the court and is reportedly on track to become one of the highest-paid female athletes, per Forbes. Instrumental in Alex Eala’s success so far are her supportive parents, Mike and Rizza – here’s everything you need to know about them. Her father Mike Eala is a prominent corporate executive Eala comes from a prominent Filipino family. Dad Michael “Mike” Eala is the brother of sports executive Noli Eala, who formerly served as the 11th chairperson of the Philippine Sports Commission and was a commissioner of the Philippine Basketball Association (PBA). There is little information available about Mike, who is reported to be a corporate executive in the Philippines. He made headlines in August when he took to the court at the Arthur Ashe Stadium during the 2026 US Open Fan Week for an impromptu doubles rally with other father-daughter duos. The proud father has also expressed his support for his daughter calling her a “fast learner” in an interview with the Manila Standard. “She never gets dispirited with every loss; in fact, it makes her stronger and fiercer.” Her mother Rizza Maniego-Eala is a former competitive swimmer Being a competitive athlete is in Eala’s blood – her mother Rosemarie “Rizza” Maniego-Eala represented the Philippines at the 1985 SEA Games in Bangkok, where she took home a bronze medal in the 100-metre backstroke category. Rizza went on to serve as the chief financial officer for one of her home country’s largest telecommunication companies, Globe Telecom, until she retired in 2024. Rizza comes from a family of athletes. Her father, Roberto Maniego, introduced Eala to tennis, and was her first coach. Mike and Rizza also have a son, Michael “Miko” who, like his younger sister, also plays tennis. Is Alex Eala dating anyone? Eala was apparently dating Hong Kong tennis player Coleman Wong, although the pair have reportedly broken up. The two met while training at the Rafa Nadal Academy in Mallorca, Spain, according to The Standard. When asked about their relationship, Wong told The Standard in a recent interview that it was “in the past” and that he found the questions regarding his love life “very troubling”.

title: War on Earth could spill over to the moon, Chinese space scientists warn
description: Study models how geopolitical tension could extend into orbit with rival spacecraft dogfighting, evading each other or blocking strategic routes.
content: In a rare study, Chinese aerospace researchers have explored how a war could one day spill into the vast space between the Earth and the moon, with rival spacecraft chasing and evading each other, trying to slip past defences and even blocking strategic routes. Spacecraft could hide in the complex gravitational environment around the moon, where their trajectories are difficult to predict, before emerging and moving towards targets closer to Earth when needed, according to a team from the Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xian. The craft could also be stationed near “choke points” – regions where important or fuel-efficient routes converge – ready to intercept rivals and potentially force them to break through or take less efficient routes, the researchers wrote in the Chinese-language Journal of Command and Control in July. Such capabilities could have an impact without an actual confrontation, they argued. “Without directly using force, [a country could] compel an adversary to change its route, delay a mission, give up a launch window or incur higher costs,” said Dang Zhaohui, the report’s lead author and an associate professor at Northwestern Polytechnical University’s school of astronautics. “What is at stake in cislunar orbital competition is not any single spacecraft, orbit or route, but the ability to access, control and use space – and to deter adversaries – that they provide.” Cislunar space is the vast region where the gravity of both the Earth and the moon shapes how spacecraft move. Compared with satellites orbiting relatively close to Earth, vehicles there can follow far more complex paths under the pull of both bodies. As modern warfare increasingly depends on space-based capabilities, a conflict on Earth could extend into this region as countries seek to protect their own assets while denying an adversary the freedom to operate there. Research into how such confrontations might play out is still in its infancy, according to the Chinese team. Previous studies have examined only a limited range of locations and scenarios, leaving more complex forms of conflict largely unexplored. The authors sought to fill some of those gaps by grouping possible cislunar conflicts into six types, including pursuit and evasion, attack and defence, blockade and counter-blockade, and deception and identification. The scenarios range from encounters between individual spacecraft to contests over entire regions. In one, decoys, fake manoeuvres or misleading information could deceive an opponent, causing it to waste fuel, reveal its intentions or miss a chance to act. But reality would be far messier, the researchers cautioned. The models often assume spacecraft can be reliably tracked and each side knows what the other wants – assumptions unlikely to hold in such a vast, difficult-to-monitor environment. Future research will therefore need to examine how decisions are made when information is missing or delayed. In a real confrontation, the researchers said, the contest may ultimately be as much about misleading an adversary and seeing through its deception as manoeuvring spacecraft through space.

title: 14 fall ill after dining at Eaton HK hotel restaurant
description: Preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked, Centre for Health Protection says.
content: Hong Kong health authorities have detected seven additional suspected food poisoning cases linked to a hotel restaurant in Yau Ma Tei, raising the total number of affected diners to 14. The Centre for Health Protection said on Saturday it had identified three additional food poisoning clusters involving The Astor restaurant at Eaton HK, after initially announcing two clusters on September 3. “The centre’s preliminary investigations revealed that all five clusters are epidemiologically linked,” it said, adding that 14 people had been affected. It said that officers from the centre and the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department jointly conducted an on-site investigation and required management to implement control measures. “All affected people had patronised the buffet there before the operation,” it said. The latest clusters involve one man and five women who consumed buffet meals at the restaurant between August 29 and 31. Between 16 and 40 hours later, all six developed symptoms including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fever. The centre also said the number of cases in the initial two clusters had risen from seven to eight. None of those affected required hospitalisation, it added. It urged anyone who ate at the restaurant between August 29 and September 2 and later developed gastrointestinal symptoms to seek medical attention immediately. During the joint investigation, authorities examined food-handling processes and hygiene at the premises, and collected food samples for testing. Personnel from the Centre for Food Safety instructed the restaurant to immediately suspend serving the “incriminated food items”, though it did not specify which products were involved. The Astor has temporarily suspended operations to carry out a thorough cleaning and disinfection of the premises. A notice on the restaurant’s online booking platform showed “no availability that meets your search criteria” for reservations on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
description: Russia is now using more jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder for Ukraine to intercept than propeller-powered models.
content: Commuters stranded; ⁠children rushed underground in the middle of the school day; festivals cancelled; walks punctuated by booming air defences. Near-constant drone attacks are the stark new reality in Kyiv, and daily life is likely to get harder. Kyiv has survived many traumas since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Despite the initial shock of war and the advent of attack drones and ballistic missiles, residents adapted and managed to impose a semblance of normality. But as a fifth full winter of war approaches, that is becoming harder to maintain. Over the summer, Moscow began sending swarms of high-speed, jet-propelled drones that are ‌more destructive and harder to shoot down than older propeller-powered models. For the last 10 days, air attacks have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, puncturing Ukrainians’ sense that their country’s own long-range drone campaign against Russia was swinging the war back in their favour. Vitaliia Poliakova and her partner were driving near a bridge on the eastern bank of the Dnipro on Thursday when a jet-powered drone struck the road near their car, injuring both. “We were driving, talking about our own things. Then there was a sudden hit,” the 35-year-old said, speaking in the back of an ambulance. Poliakova had cuts to her right hand and her partner had a bloodied face and right leg. Brutal winter coming Foremost in the minds of many of Kyiv’s three million residents is the approach of winter. Russian attacks have caused regular power and water outages since early in ⁠the war, but their intensity in the last 10 days points to greater disruption. “The last year has been really difficult for us,” said Bohdan, 29, as he surveyed his damaged block of flats, struck in a Russian attack ‌this week. “After this (attack), as you can see, it will probably be even harder, so we’re moving away.” With frontline fighting causing hundreds of casualties a week but yielding little in terms of territorial gains, Russia and Ukraine have engaged in an escalating air war in recent months, hammering each other’s energy and logistics facilities. The UN has verified more than 16,000 civilian ‌deaths so far in the conflict, the vast majority of them in Ukraine. Both Moscow and Kyiv say they do not target civilians, but in Kyiv and the surrounding region, dozens of ⁠civilians have been killed since August 27. Daily life is harder On Monday, repeated air raid alerts halted metro services linking the two sides of the Dnipro River that divides the city. At Osokorky station near the opposite bank to the centre, nurse and psychologist Yulianna Oliynyk and her two sons waited on a packed platform for ‌the alarm to be lifted. “I’m already thinking maybe we should just take sleeping bags and sleep in the metro at the station near the school,” she said. “Last year it was difficult at school and now I honestly don’t even know what to do. I just don’t know.” Roads into central Kyiv ‌are clogged, ‌bus stops are crammed and people are walking long distances to get to and from work. Grocery shopping is becoming more difficult. Large supermarkets close when air raid sirens sound, meaning customers must leave the building mid-shop. Some dairy items ‌are running low as supply chains are disrupted and warehouses are hit. Natalia Petrivska, executive director at the Ukrainian Food Retail Alliance, appeared on television this week to reassure people that they did not need to panic buy. Russia fired more than 2,800 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in August, air force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said, after increasing their use fivefold in July compared with June. Interception rates were at around 60 per cent, he added, compared with more ⁠than 90 per cent for slower, conventional drones. Russia says such attacks have a military purpose; Ukraine says they are designed to break civilian morale and persuade the government to give up territory at a time when Washington appears to be making a new push for peace. Yet polling by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology in August showed attitudes towards Russia hardening. The number of respondents who opposed ceding the unoccupied ‌part of the Donbas region – one of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s ‌key demands – rose to 69 per cent from 62 per cent in April. On the first day of the new academic year this week, pupils at one Kyiv school had just finished their first class when air raid sirens sounded and they hurried to underground shelters to continue their studies. “It’s stressful for them, but the children are becoming better able to adapt,” said headmaster Roman Feshchuk. Around 400 children were enrolled this year at the school, which was damaged in an earlier Russian attack in May, although fewer first-graders had signed up, Feshchuk said. Oleksandra, a young girl wearing a traditional Ukrainian dress and carrying flowers to celebrate the new academic year, said she particularly enjoyed arts and crafts. Asked what she dreamed of, she replied: “That the war will end.”

title: 5 years after sweeping ban, China’s tutoring industry still bleeding parents dry
description: Five years ago, China imposed a sweeping ban on for-profit academic tutoring. But the sector has quietly made a comeback amid intense parental demand.
content: Yin Yue, a mother with a 15-year-old daughter, feels like after-school academic tutoring is everywhere again in Guangzhou, the city where she lives in southern China. Five years ago, China launched a sweeping crackdown that drove much of the industry out of sight. But prep centres had quietly begun popping up again in popular commercial areas across the city, said Yin, a pharmaceutical sales manager in her 40s. In Guangzhou’s shopping malls, these centres are now among the busiest tenants, pulling in crowds of parents and schoolchildren on weekends and weekday evenings, according to Yin. During the summer and winter holidays, they sometimes get so busy that nearby shops and restaurants see an uptick in business. That would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago.
