In 2021, Beijing launched its “double reduction” campaign to outlaw for-profit tutoring in core school subjects such as maths and English, aiming to stamp out an academic rat race that was leading parents to spend eye-watering sums on extra classes for their children. Thousands of providers closed or were forced to restructure during the intense national enforcement campaign that followed, as the authorities introduced tough punishments for tutors found operating without a licence. Yet the crackdown did not dampen the intense competition in the country’s education system – or the demand for extra tutoring that it feeds. And that has allowed the industry to gradually make a comeback, aided by a pause in intensive, high-profile national clampdown campaigns. Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before Yin Yue, mother based in Guangdong province Recent surveys and interviews with parents in major Chinese cities suggest that families across the country continue to spend heavily on after-school academic tutoring, even at a time when China’s uncertain job market and property downturn are dampening overall household consumption growth. Yin’s daughter starts high school next month. To help her get a head-start on next semester’s curriculum, Yin spent more than 11,500 yuan (US$1,700) to send her on an intensive 12-day course covering maths, physics, chemistry and English. In total, Yin said her family had spent close to 70,000 yuan on tutoring over the past year. She felt the extra classes were vital to help her daughter keep up with her peers – after all, they all had private tutors too. “The stronger the students, the more their parents spend,” Yin said. “Everyone is still locked in the same relentless race, spending just as much as before.” A survey of more than 2,100 parents in Zhongshan, another city in southern China, conducted by the Southern Metropolis Daily and released in late August, also found that after-school classes were still the norm. Nearly 70 per cent of the parents surveyed said their children were currently attending subject-based after-school tutoring, while about another 20 per cent said they planned to arrange extra classes for them. Only 8.75 per cent said they had no plans for after-school tutoring. More than 60 per cent of respondents said they spent at least 1,000 yuan per month on after-school tutoring, with 6.45 per cent spending over 5,000 yuan. This represents a big chunk of a typical household budget, given that Zhongshan’s per capita disposable income was about 35,000 yuan in the first half of 2026, according to official data. The top three reasons parents gave for paying for tutoring were that their children were struggling to keep up with school coursework, the intense competition for admission to high schools and universities, and the fact that other students were also taking extra classes, according to the survey. Among affluent Chinese families, the spending on tutoring can be far larger. “In my son’s class, parents spend an average of 10,000 yuan a month on tutoring,” said Guan Jing, a parent based in Beijing. Louis Tan, who runs a manufacturing business in Shenzhen, said he had budgeted 300,000 to 500,000 yuan for academic tutoring over the next three years, as his daughter prepared to take China’s national university entrance exams. He had also set aside another 500,000 yuan for art classes, because his daughter hoped to attend China’s prestigious Central Academy of Fine Arts, Tan added. “When I was young, a kid from a poor background could stand out on natural talent alone,” said Tan, who grew up in a poor rural community in southwestern China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region. “Today, they have to compete against peers getting tonnes of extra coaching.” If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and your child doesn’t, she falls behind Zhang Liang, father based in Hubei province Families in smaller cities are also feeling the pressure. In Jingshan, a county-level city in central China’s Hubei province, truck driver Zhang Liang said he had spent more than 10,000 yuan a semester on tutoring for his 9-year-old daughter, plus 2,800 yuan for 14 days of summer classes. The costs are a burden for the family, which earns about 15,000 yuan a month, but Zhang feels the classes are important for his daughter’s future. “If everyone else is taking after-school tutoring classes and yours doesn’t, she falls behind,” Zhang said. He worries that his kidney stones could one day stop him from driving long-haul trucks, leaving the family unable to afford the tutoring fees. Education appears to be one of the few non-negotiable spending categories for Chinese households at a time of heightened economic uncertainty. China’s per capita consumption rose 3.7 per cent in the first half of the year, while spending on education, culture and recreation increased 4.9 per cent, according to official data. Between 2020 and 2025, education, culture and recreation spending in China grew 71.7 per cent, National Bureau of Statistics data showed. Xiong Bingqi, director of the 21st Century Education Research Institute, said the core problem was the intense competition for places at China’s top schools, which extended from senior high school through to university. The fight for school places helps explain the resilience of demand for private tutoring, according to Xiong.

title: Hong Kong to boost STEAM degrees as city targets two-way global education highway
description: Inaugural Global Education Summit, co-organised by the SCMP and HSBC Premier, brings together 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents.
content: The Hong Kong government will expand science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM) education and allocate more land for higher education to transform the traditional study-abroad trend from a “one-way street into a two-way global highway”, the education chief has said. Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin delivered the remarks on Saturday at the inaugural Global Education Summit, co-organised by the South China Morning Post and HSBC Premier. “We have set a clear goal. By the 2026-27 academic year, 35 per cent of all undergraduate students at our government-funded universities will be enrolled in STEAM disciplines,” Choi said. Saturday’s event brought together more than 5,000 policymakers, educators and parents from around the world to discuss regional talent development, artificial intelligence (AI) integration and evolving academic pathways. Attendees at the two-day summit include principals and admissions officers from more than 40 leading secondary schools and universities, including the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford in the UK. Elaborating on the targets, Choi noted that the drive to expand relevant degree programmes was matched by a broader effort to build the infrastructure needed to connect education, research and industry. “To support this, in the 2025-28 triennium, our universities are launching 27 undergraduate programmes related to STEAM, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, creative industries, sustainable development and data science,” Choi told the summit at the Grand Hyatt Hong Kong hotel in Wan Chai. “These are not theoretical courses,” she said, detailing plans for the flagship Northern Metropolis University Town (NMUT). “We drastically increased the reserved land for the campus area of the NMUT from the initial 60 hectares to approximately 300 hectares. When integrated with surrounding technology paths, industry zones, and vibrant communities, the broad and macro area of the NMUT spans more than 1,000 hectares.” She said the project would follow a “one town, five elements” model integrating education, technology, talent, industry and urban development. Choi noted that Hong Kong had welcomed 30,400 non-local students from more than 100 countries and regions in the 2025-26 academic year, a 30 per cent increase over two years. SCMP publisher Tammy Tam said Hong Kong’s role as a regional hub gave it distinctive strengths in attracting international talent and strengthening its long-term competitiveness. “Hong Kong is uniquely positioned with our open society, international outlook, and deep global connections, most of all with the special governing formula of ‘one country, two systems’, to serve as that elite gateway to the world,” she said. “Hong Kong’s future relies on talent. Nurturing, re-skilling, and attracting bright minds is fundamental to our city’s continued vitality.” Regina Yeung, head of Rewards, Partnerships & Premier, Retail Banking and Wealth, HSBC Hong Kong, said the city had developed into a major global education hub. Citing an HSBC survey, she said: “More than half of non-Hong Kong respondents choose Hong Kong as a global education hub, including 37 per cent choosing Hong Kong as their study destination, while 41 per cent leverage Hong Kong as a support hub for education planning.” A panel, curated by SCMP Learn, the newspaper’s education arm, featured leaders from Hong Kong’s leading universities and explored how local institutions could help shape the future of education. The discussion brought together Professor Jay Siegel, vice-president and pro-vice-chancellor for teaching and learning at the University of Hong Kong (HKU), Professor Irwin King, pro-vice-chancellor for education at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) provost Professor Yike Guo. The panellists discussed how higher education must adapt to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce. “In the next phase of this AI era, universities must integrate more skills and the right attitude into their curriculum,” said King, advising parents not to focus solely on traditional academic performance. He added that CUHK had recorded a 75 per cent increase in non-local student intake last year, attracting applicants from more than 100 countries. “We’re looking for great students who are passionate about what they do. And sometimes the passion is not inside your GPA, but in the extracurricular things that you do and the things that you’re involved with,” he said. Siegel, speaking about early childhood development, warned against exposing young children to AI tools too soon. He said excessive reliance on technology at an early age could impede cognitive development and affect long-term mental health. “If we think that AI is going to turn three- to eight-year-olds into geniuses, then we’ve lost the lesson of child development,” he said. “They create confusion and induce a suppression that shows up in later poor mental health. So we need to use the right tool at the right time.” Guo said changing skill demands were already reshaping enrolment patterns in technical disciplines. “A lot of technical skills will vanish, but adaptability, passion and openness will remain essential.” The afternoon programme turned to the future of talent. Joe Ngai, chairman of McKinsey & Company Greater China, delivered a keynote speech on recruitment in a “post-GPA world”, exploring how AI was personalising education while shifting workforce priorities towards emotional intelligence and adaptability. Ngai noted that generative and agentic AI were driving demand for new talent profiles, such as “M-shaped” AI supervisors and “T-shaped” specialists, operating alongside human-agent collaborations. M-shaped supervisors are broad generalists, while T-shaped specialists have deep knowledge in a single specific subject. A panel on innovation and technology featured leaders, including from Google Hong Kong, who outlined how to nurture “future-ready” talent for a workforce relying less on static technical knowledge and more on curiosity, empathy and a growth mindset. Panellists urged the next generation to become self-driven change agents capable of asking deep questions. The sessions also brought together school leaders across local and international sectors, including Ying Wa College principal Dion Chen, HKUGA College principal Corina Chen, Harrow International School head Rosie McColl and Victoria Shanghai Academy chief principal Shirla Sum. On Sunday, panels will feature admissions directors from leading universities, including the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge and New York University. They will be joined by education specialists offering guidance on pathways to highly selective institutions.

title: ‘Adults playing against children’: China’s Zhang Ziyu is a towering presence on World Cup debut
description: The 19-year-old centre holds her own against WNBA stars with team-high 13 points, shares ‘iconic moment’ with Paige Bueckers after the match.
content: China’s teenage centre Zhang Ziyu sparked a social media frenzy after making her Fiba Women’s Basketball World Cup debut against the United States in Berlin on Friday. Viral images and clips of the 2.2-metre (7-foot-3) 19-year-old towering over WNBA superstars dominated online commentary, drawing praise from US stars while exposing deep tactical divisions among Chinese fans. In her 18 minutes off the bench, Zhang presented an unprecedented physical presence, recording a team-high 13 points, six rebounds and two blocks while making nine of 10 free throws, but the Americans still secured a 94-61 victory in their Group D opener at the Max-Schmeling-Halle arena. Standing more than 25 centimetres (10 inches) taller than the tallest American player, Aliyah Boston, photos of Zhang alongside WNBA stars Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers quickly went viral worldwide, with fans joking that the match-up resembled “adults playing against children”. Among the game’s most celebrated post-match moments was a lighthearted interaction between Zhang and Dallas Wings guard Bueckers. Smiling widely, the 1.83-metre Bueckers walked up to Zhang and used her hand to gauge the 40cm height gap between them. Zhang responded warmly by leaning down slightly, though she still towered over Bueckers by more than half a head. Fiba’s official social media accounts later reposted the photograph, calling it an “iconic moment”. The physical disparity forced Team USA to adjust their usual attacking strategy, relying on high-pressure perimeter defence and fast-break transition play to counter Zhang’s size. “This was a different type of basketball game than I’ve probably ever played in my entire life,” US guard Clark said after recording 14 points and 11 assists. “I’ve never played against a woman of that size. She obviously presented some challenges for us, but you’ve got to give our post players a lot of credit.” US head coach Kara Lawson acknowledged the teenager’s raw potential, noting that her physical advantage was nearly unguardable near the rim. “She’s a wonderful player, and you see how young she is,” Lawson said. “She’s still growing and learning how to play and how to leverage her advantage … If she continues to develop, there’s definitely a place for her.” While international social media marvelled at her stature, Chinese sports platforms erupted into an intense debate regarding her fit in the modern game and her long-term development. Critical commentators pointed to her limited mobility, stamina and vertical leap, arguing that modern basketball favoured speed and perimeter shooting over traditional static centres. “Basketball has updated through three eras, but we are still looking for Yao Ming,” one widely shared comment on Douyin read. Another popular comment summarised the clash of styles as “classical basketball versus modern basketball”, warning that forcing teammates to cover her defensive mobility gaps would exhaust the squad against elite opposition. However, many fans and analysts urged patience, defending the teenager against premature scrutiny in her first major international tournament. “She is only 19. Taking lessons against top WNBA players is completely normal,” a Weibo user wrote, adding that rushing her to overseas leagues such as the WNBA without adequate physical preparation could risk career-threatening injuries, given her heavy frame. China head coach Gong Luming offered a balanced assessment of her World Cup debut, describing her performance as a “passing grade” under intense physical pressure. “For her first time taking part in a tournament of this scale against the world’s strongest team with fierce physical contact, this was a passing grade,” Gong said, noting that China’s overall team mindset and defensive firmness were suboptimal. “We hope she carefully reflects on this experience and finds ways to keep improving.” China will look to regroup before facing their second Group D opponent, the Czech Republic, on Sunday.

title: Macroscope | Trump’s Treasury threat will only accelerate the dollar’s decline
description: While loose talk over bond market interventions may not trigger an immediate sell-off, it will convince foreign creditors to keep trimming their Treasury exposure.
content: US President Donald Trump’s thinly veiled threat to hold a gun to the heads of countries that refuse to maintain or expand their holdings of US Treasury bonds would be absurd coming from anyone other than the highly erratic US president. Nevertheless, it must be taken seriously by markets. Questioned about Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s recent efforts to support the US government bond markets through official buy-backs, Trump said that this tactic represents just one possible type of market intervention. “We have many types of intervention. That’s one. The ultimate intervention is our military. And, uh, if we have to use that, we will,” he said. Making these kinds of threats could set off a wave of selling US Treasuries among the ranks of US creditors around the world. In turn, this would destabilise global bond markets, as well as the markets for equities and other financial assets. The US dollar is still the world’s primary reserve currency, albeit to an increasingly lesser extent as other potential candidates – the euro, yen and yuan – become more widely used. Most likely it will be a combination of all three currencies that reshapes the global landscape, seeing that Trump’s problem-riddled administration has exposed the folly of relying too heavily upon any single country or currency. Trump’s behaviour is highway robbery on a grand scale. Even if the highwayman in question is possibly becoming less of a terrifying figure amid speculation of his willingness to step down in favour of US Vice-President J.D. Vance as difficult midterm elections loom for the Republicans. Even if Trump does step aside, though, his administration’s policies – and not just the economic and financial ones – will live on in his absence. The US government bond market is the biggest in the world. At least for now, it serves as the biggest pool of global financial liquidity underpinning international financial transactions. No one wants it drained by a sudden mass sell-off, but it might already be too late to stem that tide. Japan is the biggest foreign holder of US government bonds, with more than US$1.1 trillion worth as of June. The United Kingdom is second with almost US$940 billion, followed by China (US$633 billion), Belgium (US$482 billion) and Canada (US$459 billion). How might these countries react to the rapidly diminishing value of the world’s leading transaction and reserve currency? As the single biggest holder of US sovereign debt, would Japan join or even lead the charge for such securities? Japan does have a long-standing relationship with the US built on their military alliance. Times change, though, and Trump has been pushing Tokyo hard to both pay the US more for its security umbrella and take up more of the burden for its own defence, all the while imposing tariffs on Japanese goods and other barriers to trade. Meanwhile, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s stimulus plan and other domestic spending priorities are adding up quickly. Liquidating some US bond holdings could be one way of closing the fiscal gap. Japan’s domestic bond market is big and liquid enough to absorb reflows of funds from the United States into it, as well as to absorb inflows from countries exiting the US market. The same goes for China, where new inflows of fugitive international funds from out of the US could easily be absorbed. China has long resisted fully opening up its capital markets to international flows, but again, the world is changing. Having the US dollar serve as the world’s principal reserve currency confers strong international leverage upon the US; Beijing is aware of that. The yuan having a share of that exorbitant privilege – along with others, such as the euro and the yen – could well prove to be useful. The European Union has long striven to achieve a common currency on the continent. Towards that end, it is trying to more closely integrate economic and financial policies. In Canada’s case, there is certainly no love lost between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump. All of this adds up to the growing feasibility of an alliance among key powers outside the US to cautiously accelerate their sales of US government bonds and – for some – secure their share of the privilege that comes with international reserve currency status. Trump might have shot himself in the foot, also hitting the US dollar in the process. The message to investors at large is to continue diversifying out of US dollar assets in general – always with an eye to developments in the US – and into the key currencies mentioned above. That is the way of the future, and it should lead to a better balanced world financial order over time.

title: Why former East Germany became the stronghold of far-right AfD
description: Eastern Germany commissioner says economic disruption and anti-immigrant sentiment are driving voters towards the AfD.
content: More than three decades after Germany’s 1990 reunification, lasting east-west divisions may be thrown into stark relief at Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win big and even hopes to take power at the state level, which would be a first for a far-right party in German post-war history. As much of the east has become an AfD stronghold, the government’s commissioner for eastern Germany, lawmaker Elisabeth Kaiser, herself from Thuringia state in the east, spoke about the historic and cultural factors shaping the region’s distinct politics. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, spelling the end of the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR), many state-owned enterprises were closed, sparking large-scale unemployment and population flight, especially by young women. “That was a difficult experience for many East Germans, one that has persisted across generations, becoming part of a collective East German memory,” Kaiser said. “It involved this sense of devaluation, this experience of loss and the realisation that everything can change overnight.” Decades on, wages and savings remain lower on average, most big business is still based in the west, and eastern Germans – one fifth of the population – are under-represented in politics. Billions spent on infrastructure and to stimulate the economy had borne some fruit – Kaiser said the region was now home to many of the “industries of the future”. She also praised many eastern regions as ideal for young families, with lower living costs and rents, natural beauty, good childcare and excellent universities. Nevertheless, she said there remained “big disparities in wealth” and, among many, a feeling of being “disadvantaged and not seen”. The AfD’s hostility to migration resonates in much of the east, even though it has fewer foreign-born residents than the west. While western Germany’s post-war economic recovery was fuelled by “guest workers”, the east invited contract workers from socialist “brother states” such as Vietnam and Mozambique. They “were very much physically separated from East Germans” and on time-limited contracts, Kaiser said, meaning that the former East Germany “was not an immigrant society”. While state propaganda praised the GDR as internationalist, she said there was also “racism, xenophobia and right-wing extremism which unfortunately erupted in the 1990s” – an era known as the “baseball bat years” for its attacks on foreigners. More recently, she said, resentment had spread especially about Syrian and Afghan asylum seekers and the notion of “all the extra things they were getting for free”. Kaiser also addressed warnings that the former East Germany was being romanticised, a nostalgic trend known as Ostalgie. “In times of crisis people remember positive things from their past,” she said, adding that populists were using “emotionally charged elements from the GDR era”. One icon is the Simson-brand scooter, often ridden by the AfD’s lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. “Back then it was a symbol of freedom because it enabled you to move around,” Kaiser said. While older voters may remember feeling more secure in the GDR, Kaiser said it was often forgotten that “that was because everything was so controlled and surveilled”. She also pointed out that many in the east took pride in the peaceful revolution of 1989 and saw it as proof that collectively they were “capable of toppling a system”. The AfD advocates closer ties to Russia despite its invasion of Ukraine and “hybrid attacks” Berlin has blamed on Moscow. Kaiser said the socialisation of many former East Germans had fostered a “strong anti-Americanism” and a lingering scepticism of the transatlantic alliance which had not eased during the current US administration. Many in the east are keen on renewed diplomacy with Russia – a path which Kaiser says the Kremlin showed no willingness to follow. The Soviets’ tight grip over Eastern Europe had left behind “an element of fear of the Russians”, Kaiser said, “a feeling that you shouldn’t provoke them”. Some in the west have suggested the richer part of Germany should stop “subsidising” the east. Kaiser says she finds such ideas “disastrous” and that they “annoy me as an East German”. She said cutting transfer funds would “only strengthen the victim role that the AfD always likes to adopt”. Amid current geopolitical ruptures and economic stagnation, Kaiser said many in the east were especially fearful of change, given their turbulent history. She pointed out that in parts of the west, the AfD and their far-left competitors were also on the rise, and said Germany as a whole should view the east as a political “seismograph”.

title: Police probe death of Tesla driver after collision on Hong Kong road
description: Crash along Island Eastern Corridor temporarily closes some Central-bound lanes near North Point Ferry Pier.
content: Police are investigating the death of a 54-year-old driver of a Tesla whose vehicle collided with two other cars along Hong Kong’s Island Eastern Corridor. The police force said it received a report at 10.37am on Saturday that the man was driving west along the corridor when he was suspected to have lost control of the Tesla and collided with two other vehicles near the North Point Ferry Concourse Promenade. Police added that the Tesla driver sustained “no superficial injury”, but was rushed unconscious to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai. He was certified dead at 12.08pm. The driver of one of the other vehicles was a 44-year-old man. The force did not specify whether he sustained any injuries in the accident. Dashcam video of the incident circulating online shows a black Tesla drifting across lanes before colliding with a white seven-seater and another white vehicle, which appears to drive away without stopping. Images of the incident showed the airbags had deployed in the Tesla while the right side of the white seven-seater was dented. The Transport Department said that due to the accident, some Central-bound lanes of the Island East Corridor near North Point Ferry Pier were closed to traffic at one stage.

title: Rich Dad, Poor Dad author’s vast debts spark awe – and some bitterness – in China
description: Robert Kiyosaki’s claim to be US$1.2 billion in debt has sparked heated debate in China, where property investors have suffered steep losses.
content: The revelation that Rich Dad, Poor Dad author Robert Kiyosaki has amassed a staggering debt pile has sparked heated discussion in China, where property investors have suffered painful losses in recent years amid a deep market downturn. The 79-year-old Japanese-American author, who inspired generations of investors to take on leverage to scale up their investments, claimed in a series of podcast interviews over the summer that he owed US$1.2 billion. His ex-wife and long-term business partner Kim Kiyosaki clarified in an interview with Vanity Fair in late August that the figure covered borrowings related to investments in roughly 1,500 flats, which were shared with his partners rather than personal liabilities. In China, where Kiyosaki’s 1997 bestseller Rich Dad, Poor Dad was also a huge hit, the news has sparked an outpouring of comments on social media – especially from property investors who said they regretted following his advice. Many users said they had bought flats after reading Rich Dad, Poor Dad, only to fall victim to China’s property downturn, which has led to steep falls in housing prices and left huge numbers of investors in negative equity over the past five years. Others recalled reading the book when they were younger and credited it for encouraging them to invest in stocks and funds, in posts on the Chinese social media platform RedNote. There was also some cynicism over the sheer scale of Kiyosaki’s liabilities, with some users noting that ordinary people would never be able to secure US$1.2 billion worth of loans – especially if most of the borrowing was linked to property investment. While Kiyosaki’s vast debt pile has sparked schadenfreude, and some scepticism – with Vanity Fair estimating his personal debt likely amounted to roughly US$30 million to US$60 million – the eye-watering liabilities are part of a deliberate strategy. The author claims to generate an annual income of about US$3 million from his investments. “There does appear to be a stark contrast when a personal finance educator carries massive debt. However, this is precisely the real-world application of the logic in his book,” said Yan Yuejin, vice-president of the E‑house China Research and Development Institute, a Shanghai-based property consultancy. “At the heart of the book, it indicates the distinction between assets and liabilities, and the argument for borrowing money to acquire cash‑flow‑generating assets.” Kiyosaki’s debt was essentially project-level liabilities from property investments, Yan explained. This is a common strategy among large‑scale US property investors, who refinance against asset appreciation to roll over and expand their investments, while insulating themselves from personal risks through limited liability companies. The author set out this principle in Rich Dad, Poor Dad, which spent six years on The New York Times bestseller list after its release in 1997. The book also gained huge popularity in China, where many readers regard it as their introduction to personal finance. The book is framed around two father figures. The “Poor Dad” refers to Kiyosaki’s biological father, a well-educated teacher with a stable public sector job, but who struggles financially. The “Rich Dad”, portrayed as his childhood friend’s father, is a less-educated, but savvy entrepreneur who built wealth through investments. But speculative property investment has become a riskier game in recent years. Higher interest rates in the US had driven a notable rise in financing costs, while rent growth had cooled, Yan noted. Kiyosaki’s strategy would be harder to replicate today. According to Yan, his portfolio consists of rent‑generating properties with relatively steady cash flow. Plus, he entered the market early in the 1970s, giving him a very low cost basis for his assets. The risks tied to this debt hinge on asset-side valuations and cash flow coverage. For now, the model can remain viable as long as there are no extreme market shocks, according to Yan. Kiyosaki himself has acknowledged that his operating model – high-leverage, large-scale and long-term investing – is barely replicable for most people. He has repeatedly warned readers, “Don’t follow my example.” “This represents him taking his own investment philosophy to its extreme. Average readers need to recognise the huge gap between underlying principles and real‑world execution,” Yan said.

title: Philippine Vice-President Duterte-Carpio posts bail over alleged Marcos death threat
description: The legal battle threatens Duterte-Carpio’s 2028 presidential bid as a Senate impeachment trial reaches the 10th week.
content: Philippine Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio posted bail at a Manila courthouse on Saturday, a day after an arrest warrant was issued over her alleged death threat against the country’s president. Duterte-Carpio was charged last month with “grave threats” stemming from a late-night news briefing in which she claimed to have hired a hitman to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, his wife and a congressman cousin should she be cut down first. She later said the comments had been misconstrued. The alleged assassination threat also forms a crucial element of her ongoing Senate impeachment trial, where a guilty verdict would see her removed from office and permanently banned from politics. “The vice-president voluntarily appeared before the court that issued the warrant, so there was no need for her to be arrested,” her lawyer Lawrence Lim said after Duterte-Carpio emerged from the regional courthouse holding a court order confirming she had posted a cash bond. Before entering, Duterte-Carpio had told reporters she feared for her life. “I don’t want to [post bail] if no one is watching,” she said, claiming to be the victim of police harassment. “Will they throw me into the [jail] and then one night I die in my sleep?” she said. Under the Philippine legal code, a criminal conviction on the “grave threats” charge would carry a jail term of up to six months. The vice-president’s legal team issued a statement on Friday saying she had “no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies”. Justice department officials have rejected her lawyers’ argument that she cannot be prosecuted for offences that are also tied to her impeachment. Duterte was impeached in May by the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, on charges that also included corruption. A guilty verdict in the Senate – where her trial recently concluded its ninth week – would spell an end to a planned run for president in 2028. Duterte first announced her candidacy in February.

title: 3 arrested for allegedly acting with seditious intent outside MTR station
description: Police spokesman says their acts were also suspected of smearing the force with the intention of inciting hatred against government and law enforcement agencies.
content: Hong Kong national security police have arrested three people on suspicion of acting with seditious intent over a gathering outside Prince Edward MTR station to mark a 2019 protest flashpoint there. A police force spokesman said on Saturday that two men and a woman were arrested on Thursday, noting that some people were allegedly shouting seditious slogans and holding white flowers outside the station on August 31. “The people concerned were suspected of spreading false information and attacking the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government with lies,” the spokesman said. He added that their acts were also suspected of smearing the police force with the intention of inciting hatred against the government and its law enforcement agencies. Prince Edward MTR station became a flashpoint during the anti-government protests seven years ago, when a controversial police operation on August 31, 2019, resulted in riot officers pursuing protesters into train carriages and beating people with batons and using pepper spray. Gatherings outside the busy MTR station subsequently became a near-monthly occurrence. At least 14 people were arrested in the Prince Edward neighbourhood during a 2020 gathering. The force spokesman slammed those peddling lies about events in the station in 2019. “It is a lie manipulated by people with ulterior motives to spread lies, attack the Hong Kong government and smear the police force, attempting to achieve their political objectives by endangering public peace,” the spokesman said. The two men and a woman were arrested under the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance for “doing an act with seditious intention”. The maximum punishment for the charge is seven years’ imprisonment. Police also seized exhibits from the homes of the three suspects, without disclosing what they were. Two suspects remained in custody as of Saturday afternoon, while the third was bailed out from Hung Hom police station at 3pm.

title: K-drama casting news about Jung Hae-in, Kim Mu-yeol, Shin Se-kyung, Kim Nam-gil and more
description: Jung Hae-in and Shin Se-kyung will star in romantic drama Love Virus, while Lee Jung-eun and Kim Mu-yeol will lead action series The Shooter.
content: Netflix has confirmed the casts for two major new series, while top actors circle fresh romantic and courtroom dramas. Here is our latest round-up of Korean drama casting news. The Shooter Netflix has announced the cast for The Shooter, the latest action series from A Shop for Killers director Lee Kwon. The show will be led by Parasite actress Lee Jung-eun and Kim Mu-yeol, who is basking in the global popularity of the Netflix hit Teach You a Lesson. Lee will play Jeong Suk-ja, an elderly woman who picks up a gun decades after she last held one for the sake of her grandson, whom she raised while working alone in a restaurant. Suk-ja takes on the dangerous Chunghwa Group gang following an attack on him. Kim will appear as Seo Yeon-woo, a man who helps Suk-ja exact revenge against the Chunghwa Group. Lee and Kim previously worked together on Juvenile Justice. Also confirmed to appear in the series are Heo Joon-ho (Bloodhounds), Choi Sung-eun (The Sound of Magic), Bae Na-ra (The Wonderfools), Seo Hyun-woo (Sold Out on You) and Moon Jong-won (Uncle Samsik). Love Virus Jung Hae-in (Something in the Rain) and Shin Se-kyung (Captivating the King) have been announced as the leads of the forthcoming TVING drama Love Virus. Jung will portray Ha Do-woon, the successful son of a wealthy family whose brains and athletic prowess complement his good looks. Shin will play dentist Kang Chae-rin, who has always drawn attention for her beauty and never wanted for anything. The romantic drama explores a sensitive crossroads for the couple: after nine years together, and having never been with anyone else, Do-woon and Chae-rin agree to take a break and date other people to test their love before getting married. This will be Jung’s third romantic drama on the trot, following his 2024 hit Love Next Door and the amnesia romcom Our Sticky Love, which debuted on Netflix last month. Shin was last on screens in the big-budget action spy thriller Humint, which was released during the Lunar New Year holidays earlier this year. The Shady Lawyer Kim Nam-gil (The Fiery Priest) and Lee Joo-bin (The Divorce Insurance) have been approached to lead the legal drama The Shady Lawyer. Set in the high-stakes world of civil litigation – a legal area that churns through 12,000 cases a day – the series will focus on hustling lawyers who enter a game of money and deception. Kim is considering playing Jang Do-young, a lawyer who views civil litigation as a gambling table and tackles cases with reckless abandon. Meanwhile, Lee is looking at the role of Cha Ha-kyung, who is more interested in winning cases than earning money. Together, the two navigate fierce legal battles. In addition to a special appearance in the drama Mad Concrete Dreams this year, Kim also led the Netflix series Trigger last year. He will next be seen in the SBS drama Nightmare alongside Lee Yoo-mi. Lee Joo-bin last appeared alongside Ma Dong-seok (aka Don Lee) in the occult action series Twelve and the rural romcom Spring Fever with Ahn Bo-hyun. The Shady Lawyer is scheduled to be released on ENA early next year. No Crushing Allowed Our Beloved Summer and Melo Movie creator Lee Na-eun is returning to Netflix for her next series No Crushing Allowed, which will star Moon Sang-min (Wedding Impossible), Shin Shi-a (Resident Playbook), Lee Min-jae (Weak Hero Class 2) and Choi Hee-jin (Heavenly Ever After). This teen romantic comedy will focus on rival girls’ and boys’ schools that are separated by a physical wall and a rule that bans any interschool dating; anyone caught breaking it will be expelled. Moon will play model student Chi-won, the student council president at the boys’ school, while Shin is set to portray So-ran, his counterpart at the girls’ school, who is adored by everyone. Chi-won and So-ran are bitter rivals, yet complicated emotions begin to erupt between them. No Crushing Allowed will be helmed by Lee Soo-hyun, who recently directed the show Filing for Love.

title: Malaysia’s PAS eyes new pecking order as it rekindles ties with Umno
description: Analysts say their renewed courtship gives Umno greater leverage over Anwar while allowing both sides to test cooperation limits.
content: Malaysia’s biggest Islamist opposition party has used its annual convention to reopen the door to former rival Umno, while signalling that any reunion will come with a new pecking order as the party sets its sights on leading the federal government. The recalibration comes after a partnership involving Umno and the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS) jointly toppled Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s coalition in Negeri Sembilan last month, weeks after Umno crushed Pakatan Harapan (PH) in Johor. With the parties now backing calls for an early general election – not due until February 2028 at the latest – analysts say their renewed courtship gives Umno greater leverage over Anwar while allowing both sides to test cooperation without yet settling the harder questions of seats and leadership. Anwar’s PH has suffered bruising losses in three state elections since last November, most significantly ceding control of Negeri Sembilan after nearly eight years in power. The common thread in the two state contests on the peninsula was a hard tilt towards Malay dominance in the political structure. Nearly 4,000 delegates and observers attended the opening of PAS’ 72nd muktamar in Kota Bharu on Friday, which was held alongside celebrations marking the party’s 75th anniversary. PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang arrived in a buggy before inspecting a guard of honour formed by the party’s maroon-uniformed volunteer corps, then laid out seven priorities for the next national election. “PAS is prepared to cooperate with any party on matters that benefit the country without compromising its policies and principles,” Hadi said in his policy address. Hadi also ordered PAS to defend every parliamentary and state seat it won at the last general election while targeting further gains in Pahang, Perak and Selangor. “Every state and parliamentary seat that we won in GE15 must be defended,” he said. Old partners, new pecking order Umno secretary general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki led a delegation from the Malay nationalist party, its first appearance at a PAS muktamar since 2019, when the two were partners in the now-defunct Muafakat Nasional pact. “This is not MN,” Asyraf said, referring to Muafakat Nasional, while backing efforts to bring Malaysia’s two biggest Malay-Muslim parties closer together. PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man said any cooperation with Umno-led Barisan Nasional (BN) would be scrutinised and guided by the party’s powerful Majlis Syura Ulama, including the choice of election candidates. PAS holds 43 parliamentary seats – making it the biggest single party in parliament, and governs Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis. It is a founding component party of the opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition. The gathering also came after PAS formally severed political cooperation with Bersatu, another PN component, in June and excluded it from this week’s convention. Hadi on Friday said PAS already had a candidate for prime minister but refused to reveal a name before the election. “The time has not arrived yet. We do not know yet who has more seats, or who has fewer,” he told reporters. During Friday’s convention, Terengganu delegate Wan Mat Sulaiman offered a prime ministerial candidate from the state, pointing to the PAS administration led by Menteri Besar Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, who also chairs PN. “We are not just playing identity politics, but we are also able to prove PAS has the ability to govern well and show the best performance,” Wan Mat said. Syaza Farhana Mohamad Shukri, a political-science associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia, said PAS appeared increasingly convinced that “it is perhaps their time to lead”. “Numerically PAS is bigger than Umno, but it has always been assumed that with more experience Umno would take the lead,” she told This Week in Asia, although she cautioned Umno could still “get its way”. Ahmad Mohsein Azman, a senior analyst at BowerGroupAsia, said there remained “considerable hesitancy” inside Umno and BN about working with PAS. “Seat negotiations will be the first main hurdle should this dynamic formalise ahead of the next general election,” he said. A pact without vows Analysts say an informal arrangement may suit both parties better than another formal alliance. In Negeri Sembilan, BN won 18 seats and PN seven after coordinating to minimise clashes, giving them a combined two-thirds majority. “An informal understanding may actually suit both PAS and Umno better than rebuilding Muafakat Nasional,” said Amir Fareed Rahim, strategic director at risk consultancy KRA Group. “It allows them to avoid splitting the Malay vote while postponing the most difficult questions: who leads, whose brand dominates and where Bersatu and Wawasan fit.” The next rehearsal is already under way in Melaka, where the state government’s term expires in December and an election must be held by February. Hadi confirmed on Friday that PN and BN had started negotiations. BN remains part of Anwar’s federal government and is separately discussing Melaka election arrangements with PH, leaving the coalition negotiating with rival blocs at the same time. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on Thursday called for the next general election to be held early, saying it would be “better” to seek a fresh mandate, and Tuan Ibrahim backed the proposal within hours. Anwar said on Friday he would consider the call, but stressed that the federal government remained stable. PAS leaders are also expected at next week’s Umno general assembly after receiving a formal invitation. Amir said the next test would be whether symbolism gave way to machinery, including a joint seat-negotiation committee or coordinated planning to avoid three-cornered contests. “If Umno begins dealing directly with PAS rather than treating it solely as a PN component,” he said, “that would signal that the relationship is becoming a strategic realignment rather than ceremonial courtship.”

title: New reality for China’s entertainment sector as AI drama goes prime time
description: Fully AI-generated, 30-episode Journey to the West series debuts, as shifting production economics transform the industry.
content: From low-quality “slop” such as soap operas starring humanlike cats and dating shows featuring anthropomorphic fruit, to increasingly slick productions realistic enough to pass for live action, artificial intelligence-generated video dramas have become almost inescapable on Chinese social media feeds. This week, the format graduated to prime time. A fully AI-generated adaptation of the classic Chinese novel Journey to the West debuted on Hunan Satellite Television, a major state-owned broadcaster known for its hit entertainment programming and its streaming platform Mango TV. The 30-episode series, with each instalment running about 40 minutes, went from commission to broadcast in just three months. Production is still ongoing – the director told local media that later episodes would be continuously refined based on audience feedback. The premiere delivered a sharp jolt to China’s long-depressed media and entertainment sector. Shares in Mango Excellent Media, the listed unit of the Hunan broadcaster, hit their 20 per cent daily trading limit twice this week before paring gains. The surge added more than 13 billion yuan (US$1.9 billion) to its market value, signalling a strong return of investor enthusiasm. “This sends a clear signal of policy support,” said Guo Guo, a Beijing-based producer at a leading film and television company. “AI drama is going mainstream.” The technology has hit the accelerator across the content industry. Guo, who began working on AI-generated content (AIGC) projects this year, said a 10-person team could turn out a 100-minute vertical drama in a week, while a more sophisticated long-form production could move at the rate of one 45-minute episode a week. Viewers can be surprisingly immune to the glitches Liu Zhanhao, producer According to the China Netcasting Services Association, 367,000 microdramas were released across Chinese platforms in the first half of this year. More than 74 per cent were AI-generated – an average of more than 1,500 new AI dramas a day. Production teams are rapidly adapting to the new landscape. On a fully AI-generated project, many fixtures of a conventional set – art departments, set crews, cinematographers, lighting technicians and actors – were no longer required, bringing costs down “exponentially”, said Liu Zhanhao, a producer who also moved into AI content this year. In their place is a new kind of worker known in the industry as a “card puller”: part prompt engineer, part visual editor. They feed reference images and prompts into a model, then repeatedly adjust the inputs until it produces a usable shot. Liu’s latest project, a 120-minute science-fiction mystery billed as a premium AI drama, is scheduled to appear on Mango TV this autumn. “The large model developers are the newest claimants on the profits of the film and television industry,” Liu said. His team iterated with the technology quickly, shifting from ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 to Seedance 2.5 in July once it was available, and spent most of the budget on generation. Video generators are still far from perfect. Maintaining consistency of characters and settings, interpreting complex texts and overcoming limits on clip length remained bottlenecks, Liu said. Guo had the same view, saying the models still struggled in scenes with especially high “emotional density”. Platforms are nevertheless urging producers to make more. Streaming services including Mango TV, iQiyi, Tencent Video, and Douyin and ByteDance’s dedicated short-drama platform Hongguo are offering cash subsidies and algorithmic traffic boosts for AIGC productions. Volume has arrived faster than quality. “Viewers can be surprisingly immune to the glitches,” Liu said. “They’re watching what we call ‘brain-off’ gratification dramas. They want the twists, the melodrama, the exaggeration. They’re chasing a feeling.” Ivy Yang, founder of Wavelet Strategy, a consultancy, believed short drama was the format most likely to devolve into cookie-cutter AI slop. “Even before AI, the production logic was to cater to templates that algorithms rewarded – the domineering CEO, the revenge arc, humiliation followed by a comeback, time travel – at the lowest possible cost, highest speed and strongest possible dopamine hit,” Yang said. She added that AI has pushed the cost of replicating those formulas towards zero. “The immediate effect [of consuming this kind of content] is a systematic rise in tolerance for low-quality content,” she said. Yang also worried most about younger viewers, who were still developing their narrative and aesthetic judgment. What was being eroded was “patience – for ambiguity, for set-up, for anything that asked the viewer to do some of the thinking”, she said. Producer Liu said he expected inferior productions to be eliminated quickly as competition intensified, much as China’s once-ubiquitous copycat mobile phones eventually disappeared. China’s cyberspace watchdog this week said it scrubbed millions of pieces of AI content – fake news, explicit and violent material, impersonation and safety violations involving minors – in a sweeping campaign against abuse of generative technology. “The film and television industry is anxious about AI,” said Bryce Gu, who still produces live-action series. Distributors now asked for AI involvement in almost every project, he said, including some for which the technology was plainly ill-suited. “The industry has always been protected by formidable barriers to entry, and AI has largely lowered them,” Gu said. “It can help a talented person get noticed much faster. But it cannot supply the talent.”

title: Middle East war drives 35% rise in Hongkongers’ overseas help requests
description: ‘The rise mainly came from the military conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. Of the rest, half involved lost identity documents,’ immigration chief says.
content: Hongkongers’ requests for help from overseas jumped 35 per cent in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, the city’s immigration chief has revealed, attributing the rise to the war in the Middle East. Director of Immigration Benson Kwok Joon-fung said on Saturday that his department had received around 3,160 requests for assistance from Hong Kong residents overseas between January and August this year. “The rise mainly came from the military conflict in the Middle East earlier this year. Of the rest, half involved lost identity documents,” Kwok said. The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. The conflict upended global air traffic as Middle Eastern flight hubs were deemed unsafe, disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and triggered a global fuel crisis. Tensions at the strategic strait escalated again recently, prompting Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways to further cancel flights to Dubai and Riyadh up to and including November 30. The immigration chief urged residents to keep a close eye on their passports and other personal identity documents when travelling overseas, as a lost document could hinder a person from leaving some countries. “It also takes time to reissue the passport. Even though Chinese consulates and the Immigration Department will endeavour to help residents, it still takes some time,” Kwok said. He also shed light on the revamped Huanggang Port border checkpoint, the city’s second round-the-clock crossing after the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge control point. He assured people that immigration systems had worked well during large-scale drills at the crossing over the past weeks. The revamped Huanggang control point will be the first to use a “joint inspection” clearance model, where passengers need only present one identity document to cross the border, departing from traditional clearance methods that require travellers to clear two separate counters. While the immigration chief said the opening date for the revamped crossing had yet to be decided, he added that city authorities and their Shenzhen counterparts had continued to make minor adjustments to various systems at the site. Kwok said he expected the number of passengers using the revamped crossing to exceed 100,000 per day when it opened. The department has also been testing a new “seamless” e-channel clearance lane at the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge crossing since June, with an estimated 50,000 regular travellers allowed to join. Kwok revealed that 13,000 passengers had registered for the trial, with the two “seamless” lanes used around 80,000 times so far.

title: US envoys put forward ‘number of ideas’ on Ukraine to Putin, Kremlin says
description: Ahead of their first trip to Kyiv, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin as Washington tries to revive negotiations to end the conflict.
content: US envoys proposed a “number of ideas” on how to end the Ukraine war in “frank” talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin late on Saturday, Moscow said, ahead of their first trip to Kyiv. US President Donald Trump’s business partner Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met Putin for more than three hours, the Kremlin said, as Washington tries to revive negotiations to end Europe’s worst conflict since Word War II. Their visit to Moscow comes after the war – which has killed hundreds of thousands and forced millions to flee their homes – escalated this summer. It also follows a visit last month to Moscow by John Ratcliffe, the director of the CIA. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks “extremely frank”, saying the Americans “put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement”, but did not elaborate. The Russian side told the Americans that Moscow was “confident” it could achieve its military goals of seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine, Ushakov added. It was Kushner and Witkoff’s eighth visit to Moscow during the war – but it will be their first in the Ukrainian capital, hit by deadly Russian strikes throughout the war. Both Russia and Ukraine have vowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days to allow for the negotiations to take place. In televised comments before the talks, Putin said Russia would ensure the safety of the envoys in Kyiv – a city Moscow has pounded with deadly strikes throughout the war. “We will do everything that depends on us to ensure the safety of the negotiation process and mediators such as yourselves,” Putin told Witkoff and Kushner. A day earlier, Kyiv said Russia had struck the headquarters of its SBU security services in the city’s historic centre with a drone. Russia’s TASS news agency reported the Americans had flown out of Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was expecting the envoys on Sunday and it was unclear how they would get to Kyiv. Ukrainian airspace has been closed since Moscow launched the war in February 2022 and visiting leaders have been arriving by train. Earlier on Saturday, Putin had thanked Trump for persisting in his efforts to end the war – launched by Russia in 2022 – despite it being “not simple”. Of the envoys’ trip to Kyiv, he said: “No matter what happens next, contacts of this kind are undoubtedly always beneficial.” Trump said on Friday his envoys were bringing a “proposal” to end fighting. “We have an idea for peace,” he said, without elaborating. Moscow occupied large swathes of eastern and southern Ukraine. Putin has insisted Moscow is intent on seizing the rest of eastern Ukraine. Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow after a summer of escalation that saw a drastic rise in civilian deaths on both sides. Kyiv said on Saturday that Russian strikes had killed 10 people across the country – including a child and his family members in the Kharkiv region and two people outside Kyiv. Both Moscow and Kyiv have said they would halt strikes on each other's cities to allow for negotiations. “The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky – who had offered a truce during the US visits – later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow. “From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” Zelensky said. On Saturday, Putin said he had “noted that the Ukrainian side significantly reduced” its strikes on Russia and Moscow. US efforts have so far not led to a breakthrough in the war – which has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions. As peace efforts stalled, in part because of Washington’s war with Iran, Moscow and Kyiv stepped up their long-range attacks. As the US envoys were in the Kremlin, Ukraine said Russian attacks had killed three members of the same family in the city of Chuguiv in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. “As a result of this shelling, almost the entire family was killed: a 19-year-old girl, an 11-year-old boy, and a 45-year-old man,” regional leader Oleg Synegubov said. Earlier on Saturday, Russia struck Kyiv’s suburbs and in the Dnipro region, where local officials said five people had been killed. Zelensky accused Moscow of trying to disrupt the visit of the US envoys with overnight attacks on Kyiv’s two airports – as well as on the civilian targets.

title: Visitors urge Hong Kong to ease restrictions as Sai Kung trail registration begins
description: Hundreds visit Po Pin Chau trail on the first day of a real-name booking system, with some calling for less rigid rules and greater flexibility.
content: Hundreds of Hong Kong residents and visitors braved the heat on Saturday morning to visit a popular Sai Kung trail overlooking hexagonal rock columns, as a trial reservation system requiring real-name registration came into force, prompting some calls for easing restrictions. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department announced the arrangement last month, capping visitor numbers at 2,000 per designated day between 9am and 5pm for the Po Pin Chau section of the High Island Geo Trail. The countryside reservation system is the city’s first. It was implemented in response to overtourism concerns, largely driven by mainland Chinese visitors. While about 1,800 registrations were made for the full day, only 900 actually showed up via prior bookings or by registering on-site, the department said. “We’ve also made use of drones to monitor the trail in real time and we’d be able to communicate with staff at the entrance swiftly. It’s a management model we’ve used for past golden weeks that we found effective,” said department director Mickey Lai Kin-ming. He conceded that the one- to two-minute verification process on site could be sped up to under a minute. Among the first visitors to Po Pin Chau under the registration system was Doreen Sun, a tourist from Beijing visiting the trail for the first time. The education professional, in her thirties, said she had planned her four-day trip to Hong Kong specifically to hike and had visited Po Pin Chau with a friend after seeing recommendations on the mainland social media platform RedNote. “There is a need for such a registration system,” she said. “The presence of many staff for verification here also guarantees safety.” The department previously said the system was put in place to protect the narrow trail from excessive wear and tear, prevent overcrowding and improve the visitor experience, adding that the quota would be further reviewed. No fees will be charged for bookings or penalties for failing to turn up – for now. The roughly 1km-long (1,094-yard) trail is within the Unesco Global Geopark at Sai Kung East Country Park and passes giant hexagonal volcanic rock columns dramatically jutting out from the sea, providing a viewing platform overlooking them. Hongkonger Moon Kok booked the 11am slot to take her mother, with whom she lives, and her aunt, who was visiting from Guangzhou, to Po Pin Chau for the first time. “The booking system itself was not difficult, but it would be better if we could amend the booking before our visits, such as adding an extra person,” said the researcher, who is in her twenties. She added that some family members had been unable to join them as a result. Kok said the number of visitors on the trail was comfortable at its current level, but warned that any more would feel excessive and could create safety concerns, given the narrow and steep steps. Her mother also suggested that authorities should indicate the difficulty of the hike so prospective visitors could assess whether it was suitable for them. The reservation system applies to Saturdays and Sundays from September 5 to 20, the three-day weekend over the Mid-Autumn Festival starting on September 25, and October 1 to 7 – the mainland’s National Day “golden week” holiday. Lawmaker Steven Ho Chun-yin said the coming golden week holiday would be an “examination” for the system, urging the department to prepare by making arrangements, including coordinating with public transport operators. Sai Kung district councillor Christine Fong Kwok-shan, also a lawmaker, said the 25km/h (15.5mph) speed limit on the narrow roads leading up to the trail might require more publicity as she observed many vehicles driving at high speeds. Greenpeace campaigner Ha Shun-kuen said that despite visitor numbers not reaching the government cap, he observed crowd jostling along the narrow trail. “Today was only a normal weekend. I’m worried that the situation will be worse when it’s the October golden week. We know that the 2,000 ceiling was based on past data, but we focus more on the capacity of the ecosystem,” Ha said. He also said that opening a viewing platform in 2024 worsened vegetation loss on Po Pin Chau, and the site’s popularity as a tourist spot directly exacerbated the problem on its ridge. “To really make ecotourism a success, we cannot rely only on controlling crowds. We also need measures that actively restore the environment so it is protected, enabling the long-term development of ecotourism,” Ha said. He added that the government had the right to close off certain sections of the trail seasonally to allow the ecosystem to recover, highlighting that some plant cover was entirely gone and that some tree roots had been exposed. During previous golden week holiday periods, popular beaches were littered with rubbish, with reports of visitors at environmentally sensitive areas trampling on coral reefs while snorkelling and catching marine creatures. The reports sparked controversy, prompting authorities to cordon off certain areas and experts to call for a comprehensive, top-down ecotourism policy led by a single designated authority to safeguard the environment.

title: China expands currency swap with Egypt as trade ties reach new heights
description: New factory and energy projects in Suez zone back gradual shift away from US dollar in bilateral investment.
content: Egypt’s expanded currency swap with China may help bring the yuan into wider use in trade and investment, but experts say any reduced reliance on the US dollar will not happen in a hurry. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Egyptian counterpart Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi this week backed greater use of their currencies, while linking closer financial ties to plans for new factories, energy projects and digital infrastructure. A joint statement released on Wednesday during Xi’s state visit to Cairo also envisions building Egypt up as a regional industrial and logistics hub, leveraging Chinese technology transfers and investment to anchor Cairo’s role within the expanded Brics emerging economies bloc as a gateway for regional and global markets. However, analysts said whether genuine domestic capacity would increase depended on Egypt’s negotiation of the terms. Cairo already has a 30 billion yuan (US$4.47 billion) swap arrangement with Beijing and has borrowed through a panda bond issued in China’s domestic market. Whether Egyptian and Chinese companies use the yuan regularly will be the main test of the currency push. The People’s Bank of China and the Central Bank of Egypt renewed the swap in June, extending it for three years and increasing its value from 18 billion yuan, also known as the renminbi. In their statement, Xi and el-Sisi “welcomed the renewal of the local currency swap agreement and the expansion of its scale”, and encouraged Chinese and Egyptian financial institutions to support industrial and development investment, infrastructure and green and digital projects. John Calabrese, a non-resident senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, said “the reference to yuan use is probably significant”. It signalled “an effort to deepen financial ties, reduce reliance on the dollar and advance the international use of the renminbi, mirroring what China is doing with other partners”, he said. Egypt has faced recurring foreign currency shortages in recent years, although dollar availability has improved. Settling some trade in yuan could reduce the demand for dollars, but it will not resolve the country’s broader foreign currency needs, according to observers. Lauren Johnston, a China-Africa specialist and senior research fellow at the AustChina Institute, described the expansion as a gradual step and more “a continuation than a revolution”, saying the swap was small compared with China’s arrangements with parties such as Indonesia or the European Central Bank. “The key question is whether it is actually drawn down and used,” she said. Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, also said the yuan’s internationalisation would not happen in a single breakthrough. “There is no determining moment but each step counts,” Sun said. “By creating more currency-swap partnerships, the renminbi is gradually extending its reach. It still faces significant headwinds, which makes the incremental approach even more important.” The yuan push extends beyond Egypt, with African governments using or considering currency swaps, yuan-denominated borrowing and conversions of dollar debt into renminbi, including in Kenya, Ethiopia, Mozambique and Zambia. Chinese customs data shows that Egypt imported nearly US$20 billion of goods from China in 2025 but exported only about US$819 million back. Under the swap, each central bank can provide the other with its currency up to an agreed limit. Egyptian banks and companies could therefore obtain yuan for transactions with China without first buying US dollars. Egypt raised 3.5 billion yuan in 2023 through Africa’s first sovereign sustainable panda bond, according to the African Development Bank. The currency push also has an existing industrial base. By mid-2026, the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone had attracted more than 200 companies and more than US$4.7 billion in investment. El-Sisi announced this week that the zone would enter a third expansion phase, with new factories and projects able to create more opportunities to use yuan and Egyptian pounds for investment, equipment and supplier payments. The leaders also outlined the hub ambition for “industry, logistics, clean energy and the digital economy connecting Asia, Africa and Europe”. Proposed areas include electric vehicles, shipbuilding, renewable energy, desalination, agriculture, data centres, semiconductors, cybersecurity, aerospace and key mineral supply chains. “Egypt is one of the potential winners from the reorganisation of global supply chains,” Johnston said. “It is close to Europe and the Middle East and also offers access to African markets. “This could become one of China’s more advanced industrial clusters in Africa, supported by Egypt’s proximity to major markets, its Brics membership and its links to sub-Saharan Africa.” The joint statement encouraged local production, training and technology exchanges. “Egypt has the potential to develop its own production capability through the deal, but it depends on how the government captures the opportunity and negotiates arrangements that cultivate local capacity rather than simply turning the country into a conduit for Chinese exports,” Sun said. Johnston said that developing production hubs via foreign direct investment was “one way for China to address its trade-balance challenge”, referring to China’s huge global trade surplus and pushback from several trading partners. “Instead of concentrating the gains and losses through exports, overseas production spreads them across more countries,” she said.

title: Learning to make small talk has a big impact on Hong Kong teens
description: Small Talks Circles, founded in 2010, hosts events for students to practise their conversational English with local leaders.
content:
Every week, Talking Points gives you a worksheet to practise your reading comprehension with exercises about the story we’ve written.
Nathaniel Sung remembers feeling nervous as he tried speaking in English to Hong Kong’s Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin.
Coming from a school where he was mostly taught in Chinese, Sung was worried about his English skills.
“We’re surrounded by Cantonese. English could be an auxiliary language,” said the 18-year-old, who graduated from SKH St Simon’s Lui Ming Choi Secondary School this year.
Helping students like Sung develop conversational skills was the purpose of this event hosted by Small Talks Circles, an NGO broadening students’ horizons beyond academics.
“The knowledge [from] ... the books is very rigid. But through STC [Small Talks Circles], you have the opportunity to ask questions to people who you only see on TV,” Sung said.
The group’s 78-year-old founder, Philip Leung, encouraged Sung and other participants to speak more and not be afraid of making mistakes.
“I see students transform from being anxious and nervous to being a public speaker,” Leung said.
Since 2010, Small Talks Circles has hosted about 10 events every year for students to practise English in conversational settings. They often invite professional leaders from different backgrounds to speak with programme participants.
Leung believes these skills are key to holistic development.
“You need to have a basket of things, a balance of profile, to make you a complete person, an outstanding individual,” he said.
When Leung worked in the United States in the 1980s, he met university students from Asia and was disappointed by the lack of balance in their approach to life. They struggled to make conversation and focused solely on doing well in classes and finding good jobs.
“This is not a balanced education. This is only one snippet of education. Education goes far beyond that,” Leung said. “You need [social skills] ... when you step out of the campus into a real-world situation. You need to know how to deal with people.”
Decades later, this prompted Leung to start Small Talks Circles as a space for students to get a taste of the real world.
Leung said some hesitated at first when speaking English – some even mixed in Chinese – but would slowly become more confident. He was pleased when they became brave enough to grab a mic at an event.
“They’re doing well now. Even though it’s not perfect, it’s not going to be perfect anyway,” he said.
Anson Ho, Sung’s classmate, said Small Talks Circles empowered him with skills to run events and lead others. The 17-year-old recalled guiding younger pupils during an overnight camp.
“[Leung] taught all the skills that I needed to operate in this event, and you just have 100 per cent, full control,” he recalled.
The student noted the importance of taking the initiative to learn about communication.
“You have to be the active one. You have to be brave to try and maybe fail sometimes so that you can grow from that,” he said.
Another participant, Jack Ching, who graduated from Harbour School, foresees that these soft skills will come in handy when he begins his career.
“Without good communication, it is hard to transmit ideas,” the 18-year-old said. “This is a very important skill that I learned from STC: to network with people that are community leaders.”

title: Overhead display left dangling at airport’s Terminal 2, investigation under way
description: Airport Authority says a maintenance team promptly attended to the malfunctioning screen and cordoned off the area.
content: An overhead electronic display was left dangling in the air at Hong Kong airport’s newly reopened Terminal 2, prompting authorities to pledge a detailed investigation. A spokesman said the incident occurred at about 8.30am on Saturday, when a suspended screen “experienced a technical fault”, triggering its fall-arrest safety system. “The Airport Authority takes the incident very seriously and will conduct a detailed investigation into the cause, with a view to further enhancing the stability of the system,” the spokesman said. Terminal 2’s departure facilities reopened on May 27 as part of the airport’s HK$141.5 billion (US$18.1 billion) three-runway system upgrade. Passengers using the terminal can check in, clear immigration and undergo security screening there before returning to Terminal 1 for departure. A maintenance team promptly attended to the malfunctioning screen and cordoned off the area, the authority said. Photos and videos of the incident circulated widely on social media, with users expressing outrage over a safety hazard emerging just months after the terminal’s reopening. Footage posted on Threads shows the circular screens swaying, secured to the ceiling by two cables. “Terminal 2’s design is great. Having spent a few hundred million Hong Kong dollars, the whole thing was about to collapse within a few months of opening,” one user said.

title: Japan, US to advance cooperation on US$550 billion trade deal
description: Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa affirms no higher US tariffs on Japanese goods and supply chains for critical minerals to be reinforced.
content: Japan and the United States have confirmed they will advance cooperation on investing in strategic sectors and honour the other terms of a trade deal they reached last year, even though President Donald Trump’s tariff policies have changed significantly over time. “We reaffirmed that last year’s agreement remains unchanged,” Japan’s Trade and Industry Minister Ryosei Akazawa told reporters in Washington on Friday, after meeting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer separately. Akazawa said the US would not impose any higher tariff rates on goods from Japan than those agreed to bilaterally in July last year. He also said he agreed with the US officials that the two countries would reinforce supply chains for critical minerals. During his meeting with Greer on Friday, Akazawa said they shared the view that China’s “arbitrary export controls” posed a risk of causing “significant damage to the supply chains of both Japan and the United States”. Japan has stuck to the trade deal’s terms, even after the US Supreme Court invalidated Trump’s sweeping country-specific tariffs in February. Under the agreement, Japan has committed US$550 billion to US-based projects in strategic industries, such as oil and gas, critical minerals and nuclear power, through investments, loans and loan guarantees to be issued by the end of Trump’s second term. In return for the investment commitment, the Trump administration set tariffs on Japanese cars and other products at 15 per cent, lower than initially threatened, and later promised to give the country “no-stacking” treatment. Under the special treatment, imports from Japan with pre-existing tariffs of 15 per cent or higher are exempt from further levies. In mid-February, Japan and the US announced the first three projects, worth about US$36 billion, which include a gas-fired generating facility in Ohio, the largest of its kind in US history, to power artificial intelligence data centres.
