When Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi visited Washington in March to meet Trump, the countries unveiled three more projects worth a total of US$73 billion as the second batch under the trade agreement. One of them is the construction of small modular reactors by GE Vernova and Hitachi in Tennessee and Alabama, estimated to cost up to US$40 billion, while the other two involve building natural gas generation facilities in Pennsylvania and Texas. At the time, Japan and the US said they were working on additional “promising projects” associated with small modular reactors and large-scale nuclear reactors, as well as crude oil infrastructure aimed at increasing exports to Japan. On Friday, Akazawa said he and Lutnick discussed the progress of the six investment projects a day earlier. Akazawa declined to offer any information on projects that are in the pipeline, including when a third batch may be announced. But he added, “I would just like to point out that discussions regarding AI and semiconductor manufacturing are becoming an increasingly significant factor in the consideration of the US$550 billion investment from Japan to the United States.”

title: Hong Kong’s leader outlines 3 key new growth drivers ahead of first 5-year plan
description: John Lee highlights gold clearing system, attracting global enterprises to innovation hub and developing university town as key initiatives.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has identified financial services, innovation and technology, and education as three key new growth drivers ahead of the unveiling of the city’s inaugural five-year development blueprint and annual policy address, calling on individuals and industries to show vision and plan for the future. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Saturday that Hong Kong’s first five-year plan would outline broad strategies, set clear development directions and align with the nation’s 15th five-year plan, while the policy address would focus on specific measures. He said the two documents were closely linked and mutually reinforcing. Lee urged Hongkongers and all sectors to adopt a long-term vision and plan for the future, expressing confidence in his ability to energise the market and create “new gains” for the city. “We will remain pragmatic, continue to unleash market vitality, and constantly cultivate new growth drivers for Hong Kong,” he said of the city’s five-year plan. Lee highlighted initiatives that he said had injected new momentum and created fresh opportunities: ensuring the effective operation of the central gold clearing system; developing a commodities trading ecosystem; attracting leading global enterprises to the Hetao innovation hub, the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park in the Lok Ma Chau Loop; and developing a university town in the Northern Metropolis. Benjamin Hung Pi-cheng, chairman of the Financial Services Development Council, a government think tank, said the establishment of the Hong Kong Gold Exchange in January last year was a strategic and visionary move. “There are only a handful of markets in the world that provide gold trading, refinery and storage services, and Hong Kong aims to be among these three-in-one markets,” he said. “The development is also timely amid intensifying geopolitics, as capital is flowing from the west to the east.” Hung said gold was the starting point for the development of the commodities ecosystem, which would later be extended to other precious metals. “This will ultimately enhance the city to have pricing power and more say in the precious metals market,” he added. This is seen as Hong Kong’s attempt to challenge London’s dominance in global bullion price-setting. Hong Kong is also competing head-on with Singapore on gold storage services. Vincent Ma, CEO of the Hetao technology park, said the innovation hub had attracted more than 100 technology companies, providing a solid foundation for further development. He said the completion of the innovation park’s main building, originally scheduled for a later date, had been brought forward to the end of this year, with its initial occupancy rate expected to reach 75 per cent. Tim Lui Tim-leung, chairman of the government’s University Grants Committee, said the university town in the Northern Metropolis would cover more than 1,000 hectares (2,471 acres), including 300 hectares of campus space. “The university town will be developed with five elements: education; technology; talents; industries; and urban development,” he said. “We will transform Hong Kong’s academic research into the power of commercialisation.” The university town will be located near the Hetao innovation park, facilitating the cross-border flow of enterprises wishing to expand into the mainland, and vice versa. At least 19 tertiary institutions have expressed interest in establishing a presence in the Northern Metropolis. China’s 15th five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, requires Hong Kong to contribute to the nation’s development. It also supports the city’s efforts to become a high-end talent hub and to consolidate and enhance its status as an international financial, shipping and trading centre. Lee said the government had received a strong response to an earlier public consultation on the city’s five-year plan, describing the feedback as “valuable and diversified” and as “providing an important reference and insights”. During the two-month consultation, which ended in late August, the government held more than 100 sessions to gather views, with Lee personally conducting about 30 of them. It received more than 16,000 public submissions. About 80 per cent came from individuals and focused on livelihood issues, while the rest were submitted by organisations, including political parties, think tanks, academic groups and business chambers. Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the annual policy address are due to be announced on September 16.

title: Typhoon Saudel: days of flooding trigger fatal landslide in central China
description: At least one person is dead and 11 are missing after the disaster struck a town in Suichuan county early on Saturday.
content: At least one person was killed and 11 are missing after they were buried by a landslide in central China as the region continued to battle severe flooding caused by Typhoon Saudel. The landslide hit Gaoping, a town in a mountainous area of Jiangxi province, at around 4am on Saturday, according to state broadcaster CCTV. It said rescue teams were rushing to the disaster site. The accident followed days of torrential rain brought by the outer bands of Typhoon Saudel and a cold front. Floodwaters have inundated Suichuan county, where the landslide struck, trapping residents, triggering road collapses and severely disrupting essential public services. The local water supplier issued an emergency notice warning that raw water quality had reached unsafe levels as a result of the floods and advised residents to let their tap water settle in containers before use. Local fire and rescue departments have been working around the clock to evacuate stranded residents. On Friday, firefighters using rubber dinghies navigated severely flooded and impassable roads in Shuangqiao township to rescue a pregnant woman. She arrived safely at a local maternity hospital and successfully delivered a baby girl shortly after noon, according to the local authorities. In Yaqian town, responders also had to evacuate an elderly resident whose house had been cut off by the floods after they suffered a heart attack. Meanwhile, workers battled heavy rain to repair optical cable connections for more than 300 households who had been cut off from the telecoms network. The local traffic management bureau set up temporary traffic controls on key roads in Jinshi town following a series of road collapses. The typhoon caused severe disruption to air services along the country’s east coast after it first made landfall further north in Zhejiang province last week. Flights from major hubs, including Ningbo, Wenzhou, Taizhou and Zhoushan, were all affected – along with routes to and from Hong Kong, Taiwan and Okinawa – but services have now returned to normal. China’s Ministry of Natural Resources has upgraded its geological disaster defence response for Jiangxi from Level IV to Level III, citing the suspected mudslide. It added that a working group had been sent to the site to oversee and guide the rescue operations. The ministry also ordered an advance team of provincial natural resources experts to provide immediate technical support for the search and rescue efforts. Local authorities were urged to step up patrols, monitoring, and early warning systems to prevent similar secondary disasters. The China Geological Survey and the ministry’s technical guidance centre have also been told to provide additional analysis. Neighbouring Fujian province was also severely battered by Typhoon Saudel, prompting China’s National Development and Reform Commission to allocate an additional 100 million yuan (US$15 million) to support recovery efforts on Friday. Several parts of the province saw record daily levels of rainfall on Thursday and Friday, including Putian city where 416.5mm (16.4 inches) – a local record for September – fell in the space of 24 hours. Some surrounding villages recorded more than 500mm over the same period. The deluge caused extensive flooding and several people are missing. Floodwaters in Huating town in the city’s Chengxiang district rose to heights of up to 3 metres (10 feet), submerging homes. The 1,000-year-old Taiping bridge in Fengting town was swept away by raging floodwaters on Thursday, though no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, near the scenic Fujian Tulou heritage complex in Nanjing county, floodwaters of up to 5 metres uprooted a 600-year-old banyan tree that was a well-known local landmark. Fujian’s tea production sector also suffered a staggering blow, particularly in Fuding city – one of the country’s primary tea producers. In some areas, tea shops and storage facilities were submerged under up to 2 metres of water. Tonnes of high-value tea inventories have been ruined and local officials said the direct economic losses caused could reach 330 million yuan. The Jiangxi landslide was the latest deadly accident caused by extreme weather in recent months, and once again highlights the vulnerability of China’s mountainous regions to environmental change. The nation is still reeling from a catastrophic debris flow on its border with Nepal, triggered by a glacier collapse on August 26. The resulting flash floods and landslides devastated border infrastructure, wiped out entire settlements and killed hundreds of people. According to the latest figures, 31 people have been confirmed dead while 531 are missing in Tibet’s Gyirong county, where search and rescue operations are continuing around the clock. Across the border in Nepal, the death toll has reached 1,342 while another 4,898 people are missing. Earlier this summer, southwestern China was also hit by fatal landslides, including a massive slope failure in Chongqing’s Pengshui county on July 17 that claimed 42 lives and buried residential buildings along the Wu River.

title: ‘Mini-dictatorship’: students slam far-right turn at Argentina-run residence in Paris
description: Residents allege surveillance and far-right meetings as they claim Argentina House at Cite Universitaire has become ‘a space of fear’.
content: Weeks before President Javier Milei visits France, scrutiny has grown around an Argentina-run university residence in Paris supposed to promote peaceful coexistence but which activists say instead restricts lodger freedoms and hosts European far-right figures. Paris city officials have demanded the foreign ministry investigate Argentina House, one of dozens of homes run by foreign nations or French institutions on an international campus in the French capital. The Cite Universitaire campus, or Cite U, was set up after World War I as lodgings for youth to form lasting connections with their peers across the globe. But campus sources and former house residents, most speaking anonymously for fear of reprisal, say that the one run by Argentina had gone awry since a Milei appointee, fervent Catholic lawyer Santiago Muzio, became its director in 2024. “The house used to be a space for community, culture, and art. Today it’s a space of fear, control, surveillance, cameras,” said an Argentine who lived there during the last academic year. Residents said their access to common areas such as the lounge or the outdoor barbecue – an epicentre for socialising in Argentine culture – had been restricted. They claimed constant fear drove them to speak in whispers inside the house, with its director frowning on topics such as LGBTQ rights and the forcibly disappeared during Argentina’s 1976–83 military rule. “It’s a mini-dictatorship,” said another student, who lived there during the same period. As France’s far-right eyes its best chance yet to win power in presidential elections next year, various reports have emerged of far-right figures holding meetings in its rooms. Two think tanks linked to the far-right in Poland and Hungary in November were in Argentina House to present a plan to dismantle much of the European Union, according to left-wing media outlet Basta!. In May, it hosted a meeting against euthanasia in Europe. Neither the residence nor Argentina’s ministry of human capital with authority over the site responded to repeated requests for comment. Blandine Sorbe, of the foundation that manages the Cite Universitaire, said she was working to have the issue of the house’s management “raised” at a diplomatic level before Milei’s visit to Paris in late September. The Paris city hall had requested French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot’s team to conduct an investigation in a letter dated July 30. Asked about the matter on Tuesday, Barrot responded: “We are currently in talks with the Argentine authorities and their representatives in Paris.” Cite U hosts around 12,000 students, academics and artists of some 150 nationalities. Argentina House has, since it opened in 1928, welcomed generations of learners from Argentina and other countries, including Argentine-French novelist Julio Cortazar. These days, students pay between €620 and €1,210 a month (US$720 to US$1,400) to sleep in one of its 70 to 80 beds. Life at the house, like all others across campus, is supposed to be ruled by Cite U’s “charter of values”, which includes respect for human rights and privacy, and prohibits discrimination based on gender or sexual orientation. But, says house director representative Laurent Schneider, Muzio has refused to sign it. He said he could not, “in good conscience”, sign a document that recognised gender equality and non-discrimination based on sexual orientation, according to Schneider. A source familiar with the residence said the director had posters defending LGBTQ rights taken down. But the breaking point, campus sources said, was when under Muzio, the residence in February removed a plaque “in homage to the 30,000 disappeared and victims of state terrorism (1974-1983)”, saying it was for construction work. Milei’s government says the figure is much lower. Students responded by holding a commemoration in Germany House, and campus authorities put up a similar plaque across the street. Argentine House then did not allow 13 students viewed as being against the plaque’s removal to remain in dorms during the summer holidays, said one of them, an academic researcher called Salvador Calanni. He said it felt like “political persecution”. Sorbe said around 10 of those students were rehoused for July and August. When it came to applying for the new academic year, Calanni said he was among 42 people Argentina House rejected in what he called an opaque admission process. Cite U encourages houses to take in foreign students to boost mixing, but the director of another house said he could no longer recommend Argentina’s halls. “Imagine sending someone there and them stumbling into a far-right meeting,” he said.

title: Reflections | From prison and poverty to Chinese emperor: the rags-to-riches tale of Liu Bingyi
description: Spared execution as a baby, imperial family member Liu Bingyi grew up a palace outcast, but this served him well after taking power in 74BC.
content: In Belgium, Clement Vandenkerckhove, a 26-year-old former car salesman, has recently been formally recognised as the son of Prince Laurent, the younger brother of the country’s king, Philippe. Vandenkerckhove was born out of wedlock when his mother, the Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, and Prince Laurent had a relationship in the 1990s. A DNA test confirmed the paternity, and a private ceremony earlier this year made Vandenkerckhove a prince of Belgium and gave him rights to his father’s private inheritance. But he will receive no royal allowance, perform no official duties and have no place in the line of succession. The idea of a man living an ordinary life before suddenly discovering – or reclaiming – his place among royalty is not new. More than 2,000 years ago in China, an even more remarkable version of this story unfolded. Its protagonist did not merely reclaim a title: he rose from imprisonment and obscurity to become emperor. Few rulers in Chinese history had a more extraordinary path to the throne than Liu Bingyi, known in history as Emperor Xuan of the Western Han dynasty. Born into the imperial family, he was only a few months old when the witchcraft crisis erupted in 91BC. His grandfather, Crown Prince Liu Ju, was accused of plotting against his own father, the increasingly paranoid Emperor Wu, who believed he was the victim of a conspiracy involving sorcery. The accusation resulted in the execution of Liu Ju and many other members of the family. As a baby, Liu Bingyi escaped execution but was imprisoned. His survival owed much to Bing Ji, a prison official who at his own expense arranged for women prisoners to nurse and care for him, thus preserving the life of a prince of the blood. Liu Bingyi was released during an empire-wide amnesty and was raised for a time by his grandmother’s relatives before being reinstated as a member of the imperial clan. But his adolescence was far removed from the grandeur of court life. The disgrace attached to his family left him marginalised within the palace. This neglect left him in modest circumstances, but it also gave him the freedom to travel in and around the capital, mingle with ordinary people and learn first-hand the injustices and economic difficulties they faced. His unexpected elevation came in 74BC, when his uncle, Emperor Zhao, died without an heir. The powerful regent Huo Guang installed the Prince of Changyi as emperor, but deposed him after only 27 days for supposedly improper conduct. Bing Ji, by then a senior official, recommended the 18-year-old Liu Bingyi for the throne. Huo Guang agreed, believing the obscure young prince would be easy to control. Initially, the new emperor had little real power. Huo Guang and his family dominated the government and military, and Huo’s wife arranged the murder of Empress Xu – Liu Bingyi’s beloved wife whom he had married in poverty – to install her daughter, Huo Chengjun, as empress. The young emperor endured his grief and humiliation while patiently building his own power base. After Huo Guang’s death in 68BC, Liu Bingyi gradually reclaimed imperial authority and moved decisively when the Huo clan eventually plotted against him, killing many of its members and demoting Huo Chengjun, who killed herself some years later. As the sole ruler, Liu Bingyi channelled his experience of ordinary life into practical government. He strengthened the administration, punished corrupt officials, reduced taxes and eased the burdens on the population. His 25-year reign was celebrated as a period of stability and prosperity, something Bing Ji could scarcely have foreseen when he first encountered the helpless infant in his prison.

title: Taiwan’s opposition parties split over mayoral race, threatening 2028 election alliance
description: Dispute between TPP and KMT over tech hub candidates could have ‘butterfly effect’ and spill into other battlegrounds, analysts say.
content: A rupture between Taiwan’s two opposition parties over a mayoral race threatens to spill into November’s elections and erode the fragile trust underpinning their potential 2028 alliance. The main opposition Kuomintang (KMT) and smaller Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) have both registered candidates for mayor of Zhubei, the biggest city in Hsinchu county, after weeks of negotiations failed to produce a joint contender. The KMT has nominated Hsinchu county councillor Wu Hsu-chih, while the TPP’s Chiu Chen-yuan, a former deputy mayor of Hsinchu city, registered on Thursday and vowed to stay in the race. The confrontation has exposed sharply different interpretations of an earlier understanding over electoral cooperation, prompting warnings that the dispute could hurt the opposition in Zhubei, the Hsinchu county magistrate race and other battlegrounds. More importantly, analysts said it could damage the mutual trust the KMT and TPP would need to jointly challenge the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in the 2028 election for the island’s highest office. “An election is like a battlefield. A seemingly insignificant split can produce a ‘butterfly effect’,” said Chang Yuan-hsiang, a political science professor at Soochow University in Taipei. He warned that the dispute could become “the first domino” to fall in the November local elections and eventually undermine cooperation between the opposition parties in 2028. To set fire to an entire forest for the sake of one tree – frankly, even today I still cannot understand why this has happened Huang Kuo-chang, TPP chairman Zhubei is no ordinary local battleground. Chang described the affluent technology hub as the “diamond in the crown” of Hsinchu county. Home to more than 220,000 people – nearly 40 per cent of the county’s population – Zhubei has benefited from the Hsinchu Science Park and its concentration of semiconductor, technology, biomedical and artificial intelligence (AI) industries. Its younger population and large number of technology workers have also made it fertile ground for voters outside the traditional KMT-DPP divide. In the 2024 election for the island’s top leadership position, then TPP chairman Ko Wen-je won more than 38 per cent of the vote in Zhubei. In the simultaneous legislative party-list ballot, the TPP secured 32.6 per cent there, narrowly ahead of the KMT’s 31.9 per cent. Those numbers are central to the TPP’s anger. TPP chairman Huang Kuo-chang said the parties had a long-standing understanding that his party would not contest the Hsinchu county magistrate race and would support KMT candidate Hsu Hsin-ying, while the TPP would field the candidate for Zhubei mayor. Huang acknowledged there was no agreement “in black and white” but said the arrangement had been repeatedly confirmed. He accused the KMT of failing to honour its commitment after the party’s chairwoman, Cheng Li-wun, told him last week that she was unable to resolve the Zhubei dispute. “To set fire to an entire forest for the sake of one tree – frankly, even today I still cannot understand why this has happened,” Huang said. The KMT sees the matter differently. It held a primary in June that Wu won and has argued that cooperation should mean selecting the strongest candidate, potentially through opinion polling, rather than automatically conceding the race. Local KMT figures also believe Wu can win Zhubei and question why the party should surrender a winnable constituency. Hsu’s office has denied breaking any promise, saying she remained committed to the parties “jointly fielding a candidate”, but stopping short of acknowledging an agreement to yield Zhubei to the TPP. Ko, the TPP’s founder and former Taipei mayor, said Cheng should personally resolve the dispute with Huang, warning that failure to do so could affect cooperation in areas including Yilan and New Taipei. KMT legislator Lee Yen-hsiu has similarly warned of a “butterfly effect”, saying protest votes from angry supporters could become “the last straw” for blue-white cooperation, referring to the KMT and TPP’s respective colours. For the KMT, however, the bigger danger may lie beyond Zhubei. Analysts said the KMT risked winning small but losing big, as TPP supporters – particularly Zhubei’s large pool of independent voters – could not be expected simply to switch to the KMT if Chiu withdrew, with some potentially backing the DPP in the closely fought Hsinchu county magistrate race. “Winning on the small battlefield of Zhubei but losing on the large battlefield [across Taiwan] would not be worth it,” said Lin Yu-fang, a former legislator and senior official at the National Policy Foundation, a KMT-affiliated think tank. Lin added that the KMT could “win the battle but lose the war”. He suggested that KMT chairwoman Cheng should persuade Wu to withdraw. “The KMT relies on TPP cooperation in the legislature and would need its support in numerous local races – and potentially in 2028,” Lin said. Analysts said the 2028 contest was ultimately the more important consideration. “With Ko unable to run because of the corruption case against him and Huang currently uncompetitive in opinion polls, the TPP would face difficulties mounting a competitive bid,” Chang said. But without its own candidate at the top of the ticket to boost its party-list vote, the TPP would also need concessions to preserve its political influence, he added. Chang noted that the TPP had proposed three principles for future cooperation: a formal agreement between the parties, a comprehensive primary process and a coalition government. Such an arrangement could preserve the TPP’s role even if its candidate did not head a joint opposition ticket. But it would require considerably more trust than is evident in Zhubei. “If the KMT continues to adopt a ‘big brother’ mentality and refuses to make concessions, causing blue-white cooperation to collapse once again, [William] Lai Ching-te will be the one who ultimately benefits,” Chang said, referring to the island’s leader.

title: Asian Angle | After Nepal-Tibet floods, recovery depends on grass-roots solidarity
description: Rebuilding devastated border villages means backing local support networks long after foreign aid money disappears.
content: Hearts across the globe are aching for communities along the Nepal-Tibet border. Late last month, a catastrophic flash flood ripped apart whole villages and swept away dozens of vital bridges and roads. It has claimed the lives of more than 1,000 people, with authorities racing to find thousands more who are unaccounted for and free hundreds of workers trapped in a hydropower tunnel. In the wake of the flood, the world has rallied to support ongoing rescue and humanitarian efforts. But as with any disaster, shifting from rescue to recovery will be far from straightforward. Soniya, co-author of this article and a Nepali national, experienced this firsthand while providing humanitarian assistance to communities rocked by the deadly 2015 Nepal earthquake. Our research shows local communities are critical to ensuring disaster-hit regions can recover and rebuild. In the wake of disaster It is difficult to comprehend the scale and severity of the Nepal-Tibet floods. Families around the world are grieving, with many still wondering whether their loved ones are even alive. Aside from the tragic human cost, the floods have destroyed whole networks of critical infrastructure. In the worst-affected districts, roads, bridges, power lines and river gauges have collapsed, cutting off the very channels needed to get medical aid and supplies to stranded residents. The demand for these local infrastructure services is at an all-time high, as displaced families seek shelter, the injured search for hospitals and people wait hours and days for their deceased relatives to be identified. Our research team studies how communities, government agencies, not-for-profit organisations and businesses work together in the wake of disasters. Our research shows local communities consistently carry the weight of disaster recovery. People whose homes remain standing, whose phones still work or who live outside the danger zone often become the first source of support for those who have lost everything. From the ground up Several remarkable stories of rescue and resilience are emerging out of Nepal. There is the school teacher who saved the lives of hundreds of students, after receiving several phone calls warning of an imminent flood. There are also people from upstream villages who alerted downstream communities of the coming deluge. These stories illustrate the crucial role communities play in disaster warning and response. Formal agencies alone may not have the resources to forewarn communities with the same speed as a local teacher. Instead, they can work alongside informal networks, such as the guthi of Nepal. Guthi are a kind of social support system that looks after the religious sites, rituals and general welfare of a specific community. Local social networks can also be repurposed for disasters as phone trees, where one person alerts several others, complementing formal warning systems. These networks range from women’s microfinance and cooperative groups to community forest user-groups, which collectively manage local woodlands. These groups often know who is living alone, which households have older people in them and which trekking lodges fill up during peak periods. This knowledge is indispensable and, if sought before disaster strikes, could save lives. When infrastructure fails to meet urgent needs, communities improvise and self-organise. In partnership with emergency responders, locals carry patients across damaged roads, relay messages when communication networks fail and turn schools, monasteries and homes into shelters. Community networks may need to evolve during and after disasters. This could involve establishing new communication channels or using existing networks for different purposes. In Nepal, for instance, local transport networks have already pivoted to deliver water, food and clothes to flood-ravaged regions. Meanwhile, restaurants are distributing hot meals to households that community groups have identified as being particularly vulnerable. When attention fades Community-led responses are perhaps most valuable in the recovery phase. In the aftermath of disaster, streams of international aid and funding can dry up. Media coverage often wanes or diverts to the next fire or flood. During this period, disaster-hit communities do their best to return to daily life. They may need substantial support to do so, particularly in the form of consultation to help rebuild their future, including their homes, businesses and social networks. Nepal’s parma system may support recovery in an informal way. Parma is a type of reciprocal labour exchange in which households lend a day’s work to a neighbour and then receive one back. If outside help has not arrived and reconstruction grants are months away, parma can be used to clear debris, salvage intact belongings or housing materials and set up temporary shelters. Agencies can build on this existing system by providing tools and supplies, while communities contribute skills, labour and local knowledge. Along the Nepal-Tibet border, the long road to recovery has only just begun. In the midst of profound grief and loss, local communities are already mobilising to provide support to their most vulnerable neighbours. Governments and international organisations would do well to follow their lead. Soniya Rijal is a Postdoctoral Research Associate in organising around extreme events, University of Sydney. Nader Naderpajouh is an Associate Professor and Head of School of Project Management at the same university. This article was first published by The Conversation

title: Bangladesh measles outbreak nears 1,000 child deaths as hospital wards overflow
description: An epidemic is sweeping the country, with at least 986 children dead since March and cases topping 180,000 following vaccine campaign delays.
content: Bangladesh’s deadliest measles outbreak in decades is nearing the grim milestone of 1,000 child deaths, as a devastating epidemic sweeps through the country and crowded hospital wards fill with struggling babies. Cries of sick children and the hiss of oxygen machines fill the air at Dhaka’s Shishu Hospital, where Rima Akter keeps a vigil beside her nine-month-old son. “Just an hour ago, a child died, and they wheeled him out in front of us,” 30-year-old Akter said on Thursday. “We saw two children die today.” Akter’s son Sabit Haque is one of scores filling the children’s hospital’s measles wards. At least 986 children have died since March, while suspected and confirmed cases have surged past 180,000, according to the latest health ministry figures. Measles is highly contagious, spreading through coughs and sneezes, and has no specific treatment once caught. Complications can include brain swelling and severe breathing problems. Although anyone can catch the disease, young children are particularly vulnerable. The South Asian nation of 170 million has rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but case numbers continue to climb. More than 1,000 suspected cases are reported daily. “I’ve been running to and from multiple hospitals since July to get my son the proper treatment,” said Sanjana Islam Modina, 19, cradling her six-month-old son Ayan, who has an oxygen tube fixed to his nose. Small dark spots covered Ayan’s head, fading from the angry red rash left by measles. He was first admitted to hospital with pneumonia in July, then contracted measles before finally securing a bed at the capital’s specialised children’s hospital in mid-August. Ayan spent 15 days in intensive care, before improving enough to return to the dedicated measles ward. The hospital currently has 101 children admitted with suspected or confirmed measles. “His lungs were already very weak from the pneumonia, then with measles his breathing was affected more,” Modina said, while trying to soothe her wailing baby. “He’s been on oxygen constantly for the last five days.” Most cases recorded in Bangladesh during the current outbreak have been among children aged between six months and five years. Doctors say many of the children arriving at hospital are already critically ill, with malnutrition further weakening their ability to fight the virus. Ayan has also been diagnosed as malnourished. “The doctors gave my son a special milk specifically designed for malnourished children,” said Modina, wiping sweat from his tiny forehead. The outbreak has exposed gaps in Bangladesh’s efforts to protect its youngest. SM Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for health, called the outbreak “devastating”. Bangladesh had previously made major advances in vaccination against infectious diseases, but a measles drive planned for 2024 was delayed by the uprising that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. Workers’ strikes and political instability delayed a 2025 campaign. The country has since rolled out a mass vaccination drive to combat the outbreak, but the number of cases continues to climb. “There was a gap of a significant number of children missing the doses,” Hyder said. “Healthcare workers … are vaccinating these children to close the gap.” Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and former director of the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research, said Bangladesh should consider a broader vaccination campaign to contain the outbreak. Rahman said public awareness was also crucial, stressing preventive measures including isolating infected children, handwashing and the use of masks by carers. Worried mother Akter needs no reminder of how quickly the sickness can spread. “We are aware of how contagious this disease is; our son was first admitted for bronchitis,” she said. “After being released, we had to come back for measles.”

title: Letters | Could Indonesia be sued for the haze in Malaysia? Yes and no
description: Readers discuss a recourse for victims of transboundary air pollution, tourist spending, tourism videos past and present, and Hongkong Post’s options.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to “Malaysia’s air quality turns hazardous as Indonesian wildfires burn” (August 31). Four areas in Malaysia’s Bornean state of Sarawak recorded hazardous air quality, with Air Pollutant Index readings above 300. Serian, closest to the frontier with Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, recorded a reading of 476. That’s nearing the threshold of 500 for declaring an emergency. Are there remedies for victims of the man-made transboundary haze? Little is known of a transboundary air pollution case brought before the International Court of Justice. Ecuador sued Colombia in March 2008 for alleged aerial spraying of toxic herbicides at locations near, at and across the countries’ border. Ecuador contended that the spraying had caused serious damage to people, crops, animals and the natural environment on the Ecuadorian side and posed a grave risk of further damage over time. The spraying was allegedly carried out as part of Colombia’s plan to eradicate illegal cocaine crops. Under international law, a state is considered to have violated the law if the actions or omissions causing the harm are attributable to the state or constitute a violation of the international obligations of that state. In that case, it was contended that Columbia’s failure in carrying out due diligence regarding the spraying parameters constituted a breach of the no-harm principle. Under the principle, a state is responsible for carrying out due diligence in regulating and controlling activities within its jurisdiction, including private conduct, to refrain from causing significant harm to the territory of other states. The principle has been recognised by the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, which came into force in 2003. If the aerial spraying case is a precedent, then Indonesia can be sued for its failure in regulation and enforcement regarding the conduct of palm oil and pulpwood plantations – conduct which has caused significant transboundary damage to neighbouring countries. Unfortunately, it might not happen. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations has its own way – the Asean way, which emphasises informal and non-legalistic procedures, to cite political scientist Timo Kivimäki. Transboundary haze victims in Southeast Asia have been without remedies for years now. Mohamad Hafiz Hassan, lecturer, Faculty of Law, Multimedia University, Malaysia More tourists isn’t necessarily better Hong Kong welcomed nearly 50 million visitors last year. That is an impressive-sounding figure, though still below pre-pandemic levels. Meanwhile, spending per overnight tourist fell from HK$6,614 in 2018 to HK$5,503 (US$702) last year. Comparing our numbers to those of other tourist destinations around the region gives some reason for optimism. Japan – a paradise for many Hongkongers – only had 42.7 million international arrivals last year, while South Korea was far behind with 18.7 million. However, the number of visitors does not necessarily equate to an economic boost. Shrinking tourist spending is hurting local businesses. However, for many Hongkongers, the rising number of tourists causes discomfort, as they compete for seats on public transport, for example. The Tourism Board is bending over backwards to attract more tourists, but its staff should be doing more to attract more people from not just the mainland but all over the world. That way, our reputation as an international city will shine. This is a material world, and tourism is about making money. Hongkongers are unlikely to appreciate an influx of tourists who spend very little money here. Randy Lee, Ma On Shan No clichés please Though one would assume it’s not for Hongkongers, the Tourism Board’s latest effort to attract tourists – short videos under the theme “Only in Hong Kong” – is a pastiche of clichés. In fact, some of the imagery looks similar to the award-winning video produced more than three decades ago for the tourist association by Louis Ng and Film Factory. Like the song says – “You say it best when you say nothing at all” – perhaps it might be best for the Tourism Board to take a nap until the city has something truly new to show the world? Hans Ebert, Wan Chai Can Hongkong Post explore options elsewhere? I refer to your editorial, “Hongkong Post must look beyond belt-tightening” (August 25). In the 1970s, the McKinsey Report recommended that the government hive off services including the post office, but this didn’t come to pass. If the post office had been hived off, the story would be different today. See how well Link Reit has done, for example. Unfortunately, given the current dominance of courier giants such as SF Express, even if Hongkong Post was to be privatised, the new company would face stiff competition. Might there be opportunities elsewhere in the Greater Bay Area, or through the Belt and Road Initiative? To tap them, the postmaster would have to venture out of their comfort zone. Lo Wai-kong, Yuen Long

title: Southeast Asia’s extreme heat exposes holes in safety net for outdoor workers
description: Many Southeast Asian cities lack adequate heat risk assessments, and have weak regulations protecting outdoor workers, a report says.
content: When the day heats up, small business owner Chung Kee Wa, 68, changes how he tends his oil palm plantation in Yong Peng, in Malaysia’s southern Johor state. Oil palms younger than three years offer little shade, so he tends them in the early mornings and evenings, spraying pesticide, applying fertiliser or weeding. “We try our best to avoid going to the plantation around noon,” Chung said. He carries extra drinking water and, as a smallholder, decides when to slow down or change his hours. But not everyone shares that luxury. Many construction, agriculture and platform workers across Southeast Asia lack that flexibility because employers or output determine their schedules. Southeast Asia is getting hotter, with the annual mean temperature rising by 0.14 degrees Celsius (0.25 degrees Fahrenheit) to 0.2 degrees per decade since the 1960s, according to an Asian Development Bank report in June. Many Southeast Asian cities lacked adequate heat risk assessments, and regulations protecting outdoor workers from extreme heat were either weak or unenforced, the report said. A September 2024 research brief by the International Labour Organization estimated that heat stress could erase 3.7 per cent of working hours in Southeast Asia by 2030 – equivalent to 13 million full-time jobs. Countries like Singapore are taking note. Its Ministry of Manpower (MOM) said on August 28 that an average of six work-related heat disorder cases were reported annually from 2023 to 2025, with no fatalities. It enhanced its Heat Stress Management Framework in September 2024, requiring measures focused on “drink, rest and shade”, alongside heat acclimatisation, wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT) monitoring and emergency response plans. Those doing heavy physical work must rest for at least 10 minutes per hour when the WBGT registers 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit). This rises to 15 minutes at 33 degrees. WBGT combines temperature, humidity, wind and radiant heat, measuring environmental heat stress more comprehensively than air temperature alone. From December 1, employers must also provide heat-stress training, cool drinking water near work areas, suitable clothing and emergency cooling provisions such as cold water, ice packs or water sprays. MOM will recommend that shaded rest areas be ventilated and insulated or cooled. The ministry told This Week in Asia it found 56 companies with heat management lapses in the first half of 2026. These included failures to monitor WBGT, implement acclimatisation programmes or establish emergency response procedures. The companies were warned and some were fined. Worker, not environment But environmental readings are only part of assessing the strain on outdoor workers, according to Jason Lee, director of the Heat Resilience and Performance Centre at the National University of Singapore’s Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine. Individual risk also depends on clothing, physical condition and the intensity and duration of the task. “We are worried about a hot worker, not just a hot environment,” he said. In Bangkok, delivery rider Koy Phanida has reorganised her work day around the heat. “During very hot weather, I work from about 7am until 1pm, take a break until 5pm, then work again until 8pm or 9pm,” the 38-year-old said. “On days that are not hot, I work all day from 7am to 5pm.” She rests and recharges at home because the platform provides no facilities, stretching her working day to 13 or 14 hours. “I have experienced headaches. I stop to find a cool place, take medicine, rest for a while and monitor my symptoms,” she said. She neither sought medical care nor reported the headaches, saying she would not receive any compensation for doing so. Koy’s unrecorded headaches illustrate Lee’s concern that reported heat illness may understate its burden. “Heat can aggravate cardiovascular or respiratory conditions, without being recorded as the trigger,” Lee said. “Compounding this, workers who seek treatment at nearby neighbourhood clinics may not be captured in official workplace or hospital data, creating additional gaps in heat-illness surveillance.” Malaysia’s Department of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH) recorded only eight occupational heat stress-related cases between 2017 and 2025, director general Hazlina Yon told local media last month. “Under-reporting on heat stress is definitely a concern,” said Wong Yan Ke, regional campaign officer for climate and forestry at the Asia-Pacific regional office of Building and Wood Workers’ International, a global union federation. Local and migrant workers might avoid reporting symptoms for fear of being labelled “malingerers” or “disruptive”, potentially affecting future work, he said. Employers might also under-report to protect their safety records. Drinking water is often seen as the best solution to the heat but it is just one aspect. “Resting, is the most powerful, followed by aerobic conditioning, heat acclimatisation, cooling, and then finally hydration,” Lee said. “The power of water breaks lies in the breaks.” Lower heat strain could improve productivity, morale and worker retention while reducing accidents, Lee added. Understanding risks Since Singapore’s 2023 national heat advisory, several industries have sought researchers’ help to understand and address rising heat risks. Malaysia uses DOSH guidelines rather than a stand-alone heat regime. Employers who fail to manage heat risks in the country could face fines of up to 500,000 ringgit (US$124,000), two years’ imprisonment or both under the Occupational Safety and Health Act’s general-duty provision. Smaller firms, however, might need incentives or support to adopt such measures, Wong said. He pointed to South Korea as a potential model. South Korean employers must provide at least 20 minutes’ rest every two hours when the apparent temperature reaches 33 degrees, while public-construction guidance allows contract extensions and says delay damages should not be imposed for heat-related overruns. “Currently, DOSH’s guidelines are generally all right, but they are non-binding. There needs to be more teeth,” Wong said. He called for the guidelines to be updated because they predated climate change becoming a central workplace concern and conditions had changed significantly. Thailand sets statutory WBGT ceilings of 34 degrees for light work, 32 degrees for moderate work and 30 degrees for heavy labour. Its standard does not mention self-employed workers, according to WIEGO and HomeNet Thailand. A study of 300 informal, seasonal sugar cane harvesters in Nakhon Sawan – conducted from January to March 2023, and published in February 2025 – found they averaged 10.1 working hours daily without formal breaks. Researchers assessed their exposure against the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists’ recommended threshold limit value of 26.6 degrees effective WBGT for heavy work. Exposure exceeded that threshold during 90.9 per cent of working time in the hotter study month of March 2023. Ultimately, heat protection in Southeast Asia may depend less on specified temperatures than on who controls the pace when thresholds are reached. For Koy, the heat changes her working hours, but not her financial commitment. “Various reasons, including the financial rewards, make us want to earn more, so we work more,” she said.

title: After 66 years, Kau Kee’s first shop offers fish balls ‘every Hongkonger has eaten’
description: Second-generation owner Anita Lee has modernised the family business so customers can now directly buy the products once supplied only to industry.
content: Anita Lee Yan-kwan grew up around a traditional business that supplied fish balls to Hong Kong’s street food stalls and eateries. But for decades, Kau Kee Food Factory’s signature product was known only among industry operators until Lee, a second-generation owner, opened the company’s first retail store late last year. Kau Kee has operated as a silent giant in the food industry for 66 years, supplying its fish balls to nearly 1,000 eateries and snack stalls across the city. But it finally opened its first bricks-and-mortar shop in Mong Kok last December. “Before opening the retail shop, if you were to ask people about Kau Kee on the street, they would probably not know about it,” Lee said. “Yet it’s likely almost every Hongkonger has eaten our fish balls.” The 30-year-old politics graduate and former civil servant made a career pivot during the Covid-19 pandemic and took charge of the family business even as mask mandates and social distancing rules crippled the street food scene. It left Kau Kee, which was relying solely on manufacturing and wholesaling at the time, in a precarious position as orders from food stalls dropped drastically. “Our business took a really big hit and was severely affected. Since everyone was wearing masks, they stopped eating fish balls on the street. With the economy being so poor, people were spending less money overall,” Lee said. She launched the company’s first online store to sell the products directly to consumers in 2023. Lee recalled how anxious she was about running a factory business at the outset – to say nothing of meeting her parents’ expectations. “Our entire background and expertise was in factory manufacturing. I needed to figure out how to scale production and perfect standard operating procedures,” she said. “Running a retail store requires a completely different skill set. It involves managing people, inventory and, most dauntingly, marketing and promotion – areas where a traditional brand has the least experience. “It’s been a massive challenge because we are starting from scratch.” To compete, Lee leaned into the brand’s greatest strength by cutting out third-party mark-ups and reselling fees and offering its products at a nostalgic “throwback price” of HK$10 (US$1.28) for 10 pieces – roughly half the current market average. “Since we are a factory selling directly to our own shop, we have eliminated the middleman,” Lee explained. “Removing that extra layer means we can give back to the customer. We want people to know that a lower price doesn’t mean inferior ingredients. It simply means better value because we are reaching the consumer directly.” Unlike mass-produced supermarket versions designed for immediate consumption at home, Kau Kee’s recipe was specifically engineered for the street food environment, she said. “Our fish balls contain more fish meat so they stay chewy and don’t become soggy or bloated, even after soaking in curry sauce for half an hour or longer at a busy food stall.” Lee also revealed the secret ingredient to their shop’s signature “king of fish balls” – tuna. “Adding tuna is special because it has a high fat content, giving the fish balls a rich, fragrant oiliness you can really taste,” she said. Lee’s modernisation of the brand also includes “Instagrammable” touches, such as a 3D-printed oversized fish ball model, which has helped attract a new generation of customers and tourists, who now make up about 30 per cent of her customer base. For Lee, the venture is about ensuring the pulse of the 66-year-old business continues to beat while planning her next storefront. “I hope the first store is just a starting point,” she said. “I hope the many years of history will continue.” Driven by a sense of cultural pride, Lee has experienced a mounting sense of frustration at seeing local icons overshadowed by an influx of foreign snack chains. “Nowadays, there are more types of snacks from Korea and Taiwan. But for Hong Kong-style snacks like fish balls and siumai, it feels like only a few old shops are left and they are slowly declining,” she said. “This is a vital part of Hong Kong’s history that has accompanied so many of us. There is no reason for shops from elsewhere to thrive here while we don’t”.

title: How China’s new railway artery bolsters Hong Kong’s ties to the capital, central heartland
description: Completing a vital transport corridor, the high-speed route aims to accelerate economic integration between southern business hubs and northern megacities.
content: A new high-speed railway section connecting Beijing to Xiongan and central Chinese provinces is poised to begin operations this month, filling a missing link in the 2,370km (1,472-mile) train journey from the nation’s capital to Hong Kong. By enabling more direct connectivity and train services to and from Hong Kong for northern and central regions, China aims to inject fresh development impetus into the Greater Bay Area – an integrated economic hub linking several southern cities – and inland regions. The Beijing-to-Hong Kong high-speed line is a combination of individual sections that have gradually become operational over the years, including a link that opened in 2018 and connects Hong Kong and Guangzhou via Shenzhen. The latest section, which will complete the railway, is from Beijing to the Xiongan New Area – a state-level megacity in Hebei province, as well as a signature project of President Xi Jinping, aimed at relieving urban pressure on the capital. From there, the railway will continue to the central province of Henan and extend into Hong Kong. China Railway Group said that once the different sections of the network were fully interconnected – expected in 2027 – direct, express services will be substantially boosted for Hongkongers travelling to the national capital and into the mainland’s central heartland. Currently, there are only two daily bullet train services between Beijing and the Hong Kong West Kowloon terminus, with travel times varying between eight and 10 hours each way. With the full railway operational, agrarian regions and tourist hotspots in Hebei, Shandong, Anhui and Jiangxi provinces will also have express rail connections to the Greater Bay Area. “When the full railway [between Beijing and Hong Kong] is up and running, central regions can expect more tourism and investment, while Hong Kong can be further [integrated] into the national rail network for synergised development,” said Li Jianjie, a researcher with the Institute of Public Policy at the South China University of Technology in Guangzhou. “For Hong Kong, although it already welcomed mainland China’s bullet trains back in 2018, most train services are within Guangdong province,” Li added. “With the full rail line between the city and Beijing taking shape, [Hong Kong will have a] dedicated direct link to the capital city. It marks an elevation of its status in China’s national transport.” The Beijing-Hong Kong express rail link, which runs parallel to the existing link between Beijing and Guangzhou, will also alleviate congestion and meet the demand from rising ridership between central mainland regions and Guangdong, China’s largest provincial economy.

title: The culinary science behind baked stuffed crab shell at Hong Kong’s T’ang Court
description: Executive chef Wong Chi Fai turns local blue and Alaskan king crab into a crisp-topped, creamy shellfish classic, stripping away the mess of whole crab.
content: T’ang Court has spent more than a decade holding three Michelin stars at The Langham, Hong Kong, with a menu that puts refined Cantonese cooking and tradition ahead of spectacle. Executive chef Wong Chi Fai has been at the restaurant for over 25 years, overseeing dishes that draw on classic Cantonese cooking while meeting the demands of a hotel’s fine-dining room. The baked stuffed crab shell is one of those long-standing dishes. The inspiration was not to reinvent crab, but to simply remove the inconvenience that can come with eating it. As Wong puts it, “almost everyone loves the delicate sweetness of fresh crab”, but extracting the meat from a whole crab “can be a messy, tedious affair that interrupts the flow of a meal”. The dish began with a straightforward question: “How can we elevate this experience so our guests can enjoy the pure, unadulterated luxury of fresh crab with complete ease?” Rather than serve the crab whole, the kitchen picks the meat, folds it through a cream sauce, returns it to the shell and bakes it. Diners still get the visual of the crab shell, but none of the mess with claws, legs or shell. “Every night after service, our culinary team hand-picks the sweet, succulent meat from both fresh local blue crabs and Alaskan king crabs,” says Wong. Local blue crab contributes delicate sweetness, while Alaskan king crab brings a richer, robust texture. Wild seafood also shifts day by day. The two variations of crab vary in moisture content and sweetness depending on season, weather and ocean conditions, requiring the chefs to adjust seasoning and cooking time in response. Wong says maintaining a consistent result “requires decades of culinary intuition”. Hand-picking is one of the dish’s most time-consuming stages. The meat has to be removed cleanly without breaking it down too much. “A single fragment of shell ruins the guest’s experience,” Wong says, which is why every portion is inspected by hand. It is a small detail that underpins the whole point of the dish. The next morning, the kitchen makes the sauce fresh. Finely diced onions are sautéed first, a step Wong says helps control their moisture, before the crabmeat is combined with a “rich, velvety cream sauce”. The filling is spooned back into the shell, dusted with “a whisper-thin layer of breadcrumbs”, then baked to order. “We did not want to mask the crab or over-process it,” Wong says. “Our goal was to showcase its pristine sweetness at its absolute peak.” The onion and cream act as a base for the crab’s natural umami and oceanic character, rather than competing with it. The technique is also more finicky than the finished dish lets on. In high heat, fresh seafood can release water, while a cream-based filling can split or become loose. Wong describes this as “the culinary science hidden beneath its traditional surface” – specifically, thermodynamics and emulsion control. Too much heat can dry out the crab, while too little leaves the filling insufficiently set. “Through years of testing, we cracked the precise threshold of temperatures needed at every step,” Wong explains, “from the initial wok-searing of the onions to control moisture, to the exact baking temperature that sets the interior filling into a cohesive, velvety matrix without splitting the cream or drying out the crab meat.” It is, he adds, “pure chemistry disguised as Cantonese comfort.” Anatomy of a Dish Name: Baked stuffed crab shell with crabmeat, onion and cream sauce Restaurant: T’ang Court at The Langham, Hong Kong Price: HK$360 Main ingredients: Local blue crab, Alaskan king crab, finely diced onion, cream sauce and breadcrumbs Flavours: Wong describes it as “a study in contrasts – crisp on the outside, silky and rich within”. Every spoonful is meant to deliver sweet crabmeat with gentle onion and cream richness, still warm from the oven, under a thin, crispy breadcrumb lid – a toastiness that doesn’t overwhelm the seafood. Presentation: The finished product is sent out in the restaurant’s bespoke golden crab dish, with a napkin wrapped around the shell’s edges to make the hot shell easier to hold and helping it reach the table at the right temperature.

title: Your Voice: Child abuse, pressures of productivity and funky dressing
description: This week, students write about the city’s child protection laws, romanticising productivity and the joys of adding colour to your outfits.
content:
Have something to say? Send us a letter using this form.
Natalie Wong Lok-yi, St Margaret’s Co-educational English Secondary and Primary School
Did you know that some of Hong Kong’s current child protection laws related to sexual offences originate from British common law as early as 1956 – a time long before the internet, smartphones or social media existed?
I became deeply aware of the urgent need for action after reviewing the government’s proposed legislative updates. Although the public consultation period recently ended, our focus on child protection must persist. The government’s proposed overhaul addresses critical issues, particularly with new measures aimed at criminalising grooming, tackling the abuse of power in positions of trust and standardising the age of consent at 16.
While our system addresses many issues, it fails to adequately support child survivors of long-term, repeated sexual abuse. Consider the challenge of recalling the exact order of items you purchased during a grocery run on a random weekend years ago. You may remember buying groceries, but expecting to list each item perfectly from memory is nearly impossible, if not completely unfeasible.
Yet, the current legal framework places children who have experienced repeated abuse over many years under a demanding standard. If a victim makes even minor mistakes in their memory concerning specific timelines or locations amid their traumas, their entire testimony can be deemed inadequate.
In reality, traumatised children who experience ongoing abuse often cannot recall the exact details of every incident, including when and where it occurred. Thankfully, the Hong Kong Bar Association recently supported the establishment of a specific offence for continuous child sexual abuse, reversing its position from 2001. The association highlighted the importance of legal safeguards, such as requiring explicit consent from the Secretary for Justice, while endorsing the policy in principle to ensure fair trial procedures in prosecutions.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung has also indicated that the government will actively consider establishing this offence while keeping in close contact with the legal sector.
For far too long, our laws have been expecting young victims to carry the impossible burden of flawless memory alongside their trauma. The law should be on the side of children, not against them. With the rare opportunity we have to fix this historical blind spot as legislative discussions move forward, the public and our lawmakers should keep pushing until our statutes provide complete, uncompromising protection for every child.
Social media often romanticises productivity in a toxic way. Waking up at 5am, having a bowl of granola for breakfast and colour-coding your notes is not the only way to define a day well spent.
Moreover, social media often equates a lack of ambition with laziness. In a landscape filled with company founders and Ivy League students, not aspiring to reach that level can appear idle.
At school, the practice of comparing résumés and LinkedIn profiles creates pressure that drives an obsession with performance. As a result, ambition may stem not from personal goals, but from a subconscious need to prove one’s worth to others.
Students often forget that social media is just a highlight reel – not the complete picture. Over time, we internalise ambition and productivity as indicators of success. It becomes easier to cling to this illusion of purpose than to confront the guilt that comes from not measuring up.
In my opinion, productivity is not predetermined, and ambition should not be viewed as a badge of honour.
Taking time to relax and watch your favourite show can be just as productive as writing an essay.
Moreover, a person with ambitious goals is not inherently better than someone who is satisfied with their current situation.
Funky socks are bright, eye-catching pieces of your outfit that often go unnoticed. They are bold fashion statements that are not overly jarring.
Some people are not fully convinced about the funky socks trend, criticising their appearance as childish and unprofessional. However, what’s wrong with enjoying your funky socks, especially while you’re working?
Unless your client is particularly fussy, a little contrast in an otherwise professional environment is not a big deal.
Wearing funky socks can help you feel more relaxed and improve your mood, as they add a touch of humour throughout the day.
Funky socks aren’t necessarily better than plain white socks; they feel the same and offer the same warmth and protection. However, the unique designs can spark conversations.
When you are wearing a plain suit or uniform that doesn’t say much about you, why not showcase your personality with funky socks? Look for socks featuring your favourite superhero or your favourite food.
Funky socks are versatile and can complement any outfit, whether you’re wearing shorts, trousers or a skirt. As long as the dress code allows it, you should have no trouble choosing your own unique socks.

title: Bolivian military barracks explosion leaves 2 dead, 14 missing and dozens injured
description: Officials say the blast originated from the defence ministry’s fireworks stockpile at a facility in the western city of Viacha.
content: At least two people were killed and dozens injured on Friday after an explosion at a military barracks in the ‌Bolivian municipality of Viacha, about 30km (20 miles) from La Paz, Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said. His ministry said in a statement that 14 people were missing. The blast occurred at around 2.30pm in an area used to ⁠store pyrotechnic material, authorities said. While the cause has yet to ‌be established, officials said the blast originated from the defence ministry’s fireworks stockpile. Earlier, the Viacha health director, ‌Rita Nebraska, had told local television that between 10 and ⁠15 ⁠people were believed to have died in the incident, while 62 people were ‌injured. Fourteen of the wounded were transferred to hospitals in La Paz, including a girl ‌with ‌third-degree burns, she said. Police said more than 50 people ‌were injured and dozens of homes damaged, largely by windows shattered in the blast. Video footage shared on social media showed a column of thick black smoke billowing from the barracks, which is in the city centre. Ambulances, medical teams and ⁠police were deployed to the military complex to assess the ⁠damage and evacuate the wounded to health centres. Nebraska said firefighters had warned that a heat source remained ‌at the ‌site, raising the risk of another explosion, and urged residents to stay at least 150 metres away. An investigation has been launched into the cause of the explosion.

title: ‘Can’t live without fighting’: Myanmar youth find solace in bareknuckle lethwei
description: Amid five years of devastating conflict, young fighters embrace the traditional bloodsport as both self-defence and refuge.
content: In a country consumed by conflict, a sport defined by brutality dominates: Myanmar’s lethwei martial art, where headbutts are encouraged and knockout blows are the aim of the game. “I can’t live without fighting,” said 19-year-old Su Luck, who enters the ring under the paradoxical pseudonym “Peace Prize”. “I have never once considered giving up this passion,” she said. Lethwei is traditional Burmese boxing, distinct from Thai kickboxing because head blows are permitted and fighters compete bareknuckle, fists protected only with wraps of thin gauze. It is known as the “Art of Nine Limbs” because each contender’s two fists, elbows, knees, feet and head are considered viable weapons to take down opponents. In a country where many have been dragged into the five-year-old civil war, the popularity of a tooth-and-nail national sport is obvious to some. “It’s not only a sport, it’s our art of self-defence,” veteran fighter and coach Saw Kyaw Thein Tuu said. “Guns are of no use if they run out of bullets on the battlefield,” the 73-year-old added. “This art will help them defend and fight enemies anytime.” But others find the ring not a training ground for hostility but a space for the Zen of self-improvement. “Even when I take hits to the face, I accept it as my own weakness, as a sign that I still have more to learn,” said Su Luck, who dreams of becoming a teacher. She is a rising star in the sport, which is dominated by men. “I never think I’ve become perfect,” Su Luck added. On parade grounds across Myanmar, legions of youngsters march in formation either for the military or the array of armed groups who have battled it out since the 2021 coup ousted democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi’s government. But at the start of the monsoon season in Hpa-an – capital of Kayin state, Myanmar’s lethwei heartland – more than 100 teenagers and young adults rose for dawn to march in devotion to the sport. Under limestone karsts that dagger the brightening sky, they lap a racetrack to raise their pulses before shifting to a sports hall filled with battered punch bags. Inside, coaches from the Kayin State Traditional Lethwei Organisation hector them to jab harder and kick higher in sparring sessions, leaving them sopping with sweat. For many, their hero is the Burmese-American fighter Joshua Van, the reigning champion in the flyweight division of the internationally renowned Ultimate Fighting Championship. But his title in the mixed martial arts competition was won without lethwei’s signature moves, which were banned for being too dangerous. Fighter Moe Hein is refining those methods during a two-week training camp at Hpa-an, though he does not relish it when they inflict pain. “In some matches when the other person gets battered, bruised or cut because of me, I don’t feel happy inside,” the 22-year-old said. “But since it’s a sport, I’ll try to hit him and he’ll try to hit me too. That’s just how it is.” Myanmar’s civil war, Asia’s deadliest active conflict, has killed more than 100,000 people on all sides, according to ACLED, an organisation monitoring media reports of violence. Coach Saw Kyaw Thein Tuu said he had witnessed lethwei deaths too, as it pushes the boundaries of sport. “I have been to 200 matches in my life and there were six people killed. We had to deal with the police,” he said. “Our Myanmar traditional lethwei should not be considered a sport,” he mused. “It should be thought of as another type of game.” In Kayin state, more than 260,000 people are living displaced, according to United Nations data. Armed factions vie for control of the border state’s lucrative trade routes to Thailand and internet scam centres, which have thrived in the chaos of wartime. Along the six-hour drive from the commercial capital Yangon to Hpa-an are more than a dozen checkpoints manned by the military, militias or armed non-uniformed men. Despite its brutality, Su Luck said lethwei offered another way. “Compared to fighting outside, it’s more honourable to fight in the ring,” she said. “On the stage, when two fighters challenge each other and compete, it has more dignity and respect.”

title: Inside Hong Kong’s red-hot Pokemon card market, where Pikachus sell like stocks
description: Hong Kong has evolved into a global centre for the booming Pokemon card trading market, with rare collectibles traded via tokenised funds.
content: Not so long ago, Pokemon cards were little more than schoolyard treasures in Hong Kong. But the trading cards are now evolving into a sophisticated new asset class, driven by millennial nostalgia and the forces of global capital. In today’s red-hot market – where rare Pikachus sell for vast sums and crime is a real problem – a complex trading ecosystem is emerging, complete with professional grading, tokenised funds and institutional-grade storage facilities. Pokemon card valuations have skyrocketed around the world in recent years, with influencer Logan Paul making headlines in 2021 by spending over US$5 million to acquire a Pikachu Illustrator card. It has since been resold for nearly US$16.5 million. But trading in Asia has come to revolve around Hong Kong, the world’s biggest cross-border wealth management hub, where investors benefit from ultra-low capital gains and sales taxes, according to analysts. Collectors, speculators and even institutions in Hong Kong are increasingly investing in this risky new asset class, as appetite for alternative investments grows in the city’s financial sector. “The demand is coming from a real and growing collector base, not just short-term speculation,” said Albert Cheng, business director for Hong Kong, Taiwan and North Asia at Azimut Group. “We’re also seeing a generational shift where younger investors are putting money into assets they actually relate to and enjoy, like Pokemon cards.” “On top of that, grading services, online marketplaces and tokenisation are making the market more accessible and liquid,” he added. “Of course, some individual cards may be overpriced, but I think the collectible asset class itself has long-term staying power.” Globally, the market for trading card games – including Pokemon cards – could reach US$23.5 billion (HK$183.3 billion) by 2030, growing at a 6.5 per cent compound annual growth rate, according to a report by the Hong Kong Trade Development Council. And the Asia-Pacific region stands out as the market with the deepest demand and most active secondary market, according to market intelligence firm Strategic Market Research. For investors, Hong Kong’s financial system offers the regulatory framework and liquidity needed to treat cards not as toys, but as tradeable certificates of value. But does the boom mark the arrival of a new, durable asset class, or is it merely a bubble? The market’s emergence was initially driven by sentiment-driven collectors such as Pokemon TMFT, an influencer who has attracted a following on Instagram by posting about his efforts to amass the world’s greatest Pokemon card collection. For Pokemon TMFT, whose real name is unknown, the cards’ attraction lies in their emotional resonance. As a child, his mother bought him packs of Pokemon cards as a reward after he had done his chores. During his mother’s battle with leukaemia, he carried a rare card depicting a mother carrying a baby. “Looking at that card gave me strength,” he said. But the rare card trade is increasingly being taken over by professional investors, who are purely interested in speculating on the cards as assets. New market initiatives are turbocharging this trend, with the emergence of tokenised funds that fractionalise ownership and improve liquidity for high-value assets. In March 2026, MemeStrategy – a Hong Kong-listed digital asset investment company – launched what it called the world’s first tokenised Pokemon card fund in partnership with the private market operator Evident. By packaging rare cards – such as the “Van Gogh Pikachu” edition – into on-chain tokens, such funds make it easier for investors to buy into the market. But the trade’s growing financialisation also carried “substantial hidden risks”, said Paxson Fung, founder of the financial services firm CityLinkers Group, in an interview with Hong Kong Commercial Daily. Unlike equities or real estate, these collectibles generate no cash flow. Their value is tied entirely to market sentiment, cultural relevance and consensus on rarity – making them highly vulnerable to liquidity shocks and shifts in public taste, according to Fung. The market is also far from homogenous. While the value of high-end collectible cards jumped 29 per cent last year, lower-grade, mass-market modern cards declined in value by more than 40 per cent, according to data from the Card Ladder Pokemon Index and alternative assets reports by Geiger Research and Altar. The rising number of cards in circulation also risks diluting scarcity and putting further downward pressure on non-premium items, critics warn. In 2025 alone, 26.6 million cards were graded by Professional Sports Authenticator and other authentication services. However, market observers are still upbeat about the Pokemon card market’s long-term prospects. “Pokemon cards are a proven model,” said Lu Fangzhou, an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong’s business school. “They have proven their value for a much longer time [than some other alternative assets, such as NFTs].” For Lu, Pokemon cards are unlikely to be a bubble. Since the sports trading card market dates back to the 19th century, he expects new-generation blue-chip IP trading cards to sustain their relevance for another 20 years or more, though it remains to be seen how high prices could rise. With government backing and a strong cultural base, Hong Kong had the potential to be a hub for trading card investing, though that would ultimately depend on trading volume as a function of demand, Lu added.

title: India and Japan swap young workers for expertise to meet each other’s needs
description: From stealth warship tech to a 500,000-strong talent exchange, Tokyo and New Delhi are pairing Japanese precision with Indian scale.
content: India’s largest-ever business delegation, 200 executives strong, touched down in Japan late last month in search of money, machinery and manufacturing know-how. At its head was Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, whose four-day tour from August 24 to 27 not only laid the groundwork for next year’s 75th anniversary of diplomatic ties but also worked to solidify an economic partnership now expanding into shipbuilding and defence. “We believe in the principle of continuous improvement and we are looking at Japan being our partner in this journey as we progress from a US$4 trillion economy today to a US$30 trillion economy by 2047,” Goyal told a joint gathering on August 24 that included representatives of Keidanren, a Japanese business federation representing more than 1,500 companies. The talks spanned a range of sectors, from semiconductors to artificial intelligence, according to the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry. Goyal later told reporters that Japanese firms had already invested about 14 per cent of a 10-trillion-yen (US$63.9 billion) pledge announced last August.
