At the current pace, he said the 10-year foreign direct investment goal would be reached within three to four years. The delegation’s India tour built on a flurry of recent high-level exchanges. Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi visited India from August 19 to 20, hot on the heels of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s trip in July. India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh, has been conducting its own parallel courtship, with Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath pitching Japanese companies on a proposed 500-acre “Japan City” near the new Noida International Airport, serving the capital region. “What makes the partnership especially interesting is the complementarity,” said Arijit Chatterjee, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. What makes the partnership especially interesting is the complementarity Arijit Chatterjee, business management professor “Japan has technology, capital and an ageing workforce, while India … has scale, labour and a huge market, so the objective is increasingly to combine Japanese know-how with Indian people and production capacity rather than simply attract Japanese FDI.” For a “young, populous state” like Uttar Pradesh looking to build its industrial capacity, Japan was “particularly attractive”, Chatterjee said, “because it brings not just capital but decades of expertise in precision manufacturing, automobiles, robotics, skills and industrial supply chains”. This “complementarity” is visible in India’s Haryana state, which has been working with Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture since June to train and place up to 50,000 young workers and technical professionals over five years in critical industries such as semiconductors and vehicle production – a direct response to the acute labour shortages afflicting many of Fukuoka’s major companies as Japan’s workforce rapidly ages. “Japan can provide training, work experience and exposure to advanced manufacturing practices, while India provides talent,” Chatterjee said. “I see youth mobility as an important complement to Japanese investment and technology transfer: India gains skills, jobs and human-capital development, while Japan gains access to a young, trained workforce it increasingly needs.” Goyal offered another vivid example: the Indian subsidiary of Suzuki Motor Corporation, which first invested in the country in 1989, is now worth more than its Japanese parent company – surpassing it in market valuation as far back as 2015. US$10 billion surge Historical precedents showed the Japan-India relationship was already primed to strengthen, but analysts told This Week in Asia that rising US tariffs and the push to diversify supply chains away from China had accelerated the shift. Last year, the two countries set an aspirational target of exchanging more than 500,000 personnel, in both directions, by the end of the decade. Capital has followed a similar trajectory. “We were sub-US$2 million in assets under management, I think until 2020. Now fast forward to 2026, and we’re close to US$300 million,” said Rajeev Ranka, a partner at Incubate Fund Asia, a Japanese venture capital firm focused on Indian start-ups. He estimates that Japanese firms have completed roughly US$10 billion in Indian mergers and acquisitions over the past five years. “There is a lot of interest and action which is supported by on-the-ground travel and people visiting [India] from Japan,” he said. Dattesh Parulekar, an assistant professor of international relations at Goa University who specialises in India’s foreign policy and diplomacy, said the bilateral relationship was undergoing a “seminal transformation” – moving from what he characterised as a “donor-recipient fiscal equation” to a partnership built on joint innovation, including on defence systems. Partners in arms Earlier this summer, Japan and India agreed to jointly develop stealth technology for Indian warships, fitting them with the Japanese-developed Unified Complex Radio Antenna (Unicorn) system, which reduces a vessel’s radar profile by combining cluttered antenna arrays into a single, compact structure. Talks have also turned to naval shipbuilding and design – an area where India has long lagged behind China, Japan and South Korea, which together controlled more than 90 per cent of the global shipbuilding industry in 2024. Japan had been exploring the possibility of a joint shipbuilding venture with India for a long time, said Vivek Mishra, deputy director of strategic studies at the Observer Research Foundation think tank in New Delhi. “Japan would be a perfect partner [for India],” he said. Uttar Pradesh recognised as much, according to Parulekar, who said part of the state’s appeal to Japanese industry was its “surging ambition to spearhead defence manufacturing” through six dedicated industrial corridors, anchored around Lucknow, Kanpur, Aligarh, Agra, Jhansi and Chitrakoot. “I think cooperation is likely to increase on both the civilian and military sides, with shipbuilding becoming an important part of the broader industrial relationship,” said Chatterjee, noting that India was seeking Japanese investment and design expertise in equal measure. A robust domestic shipbuilding industry was the surest foundation for naval expansion, he added – especially relevant as India races to build a 200-ship navy within the next decade.

title: Being Chinese | A Singaporean in Guangzhou wonders: why do I feel so at home here?
description: Guangzhou set me at ease in a way other cities didn’t. I began to understand what it means to be descended from early Chinese migrants.
content: On a recent trip to China, I was on a rumbling subway train when I was struck by a strange sense of homecoming. It was as if I had been transported back to my childhood, and suddenly I was completely at home among all the strangers in the subway carriage – even though it was my very first time in Guangzhou. The funny thing is that nothing special happened on that ride. I just had a moment to observe my surroundings and realise how much my husband and I – both Chinese Singaporeans – resembled the everyday people around us. We were all roughly the same height and had the same colouring. Many of the other passengers had large almond-shaped eyes with double eyelids and low nose bridges with rounded tips, rather like mine. Although I had visited China many times and taken the subway in cities including Beijing, Shanghai and Chongqing, I had never felt this way before. While I would not invite a second look in most parts of China, I often felt like an “other”. If I am being honest, my nagging feeling in those other cities might have been that in contrast to the often taller, fairer and well-groomed Chinese women, my tropical tan, short stature and make-up-free face were more likely to conjure an image of a homely hobbit, standing among ethereal elves. Fundamentally, however, the feeling of otherness extends beyond mere looks. It is in the subtle things, like having to strain the ear to understand the different melodies of spoken Chinese across the country and tasting somewhat recognisable, yet strange, Chinese flavours – such as heavily seasoned pancakes and grilled meats with cumin. Here in southern China, every other man in the street looked like he could be a long-lost uncle or distant relative. If I was a hobbit, so were people around me. In Guangzhou, capital of Guangdong province, I realised I had felt othered because I had been visiting the wrong cities all along. Here in southern China, every other man in the street looked like he could be a long-lost uncle or distant relative. If I was a hobbit, so were people around me. Besides, the cuisine was often familiar and comforting: soups, lightly cooked seafood, rice-based dishes, except in a wider variety and at lower price points than in Singapore. But the most delightful surprise was the brand of Chinese spoken in Guangzhou. The Mandarin was easy to understand – sometimes the accent sounded like that of our Chinese Malaysian brethren across the Causeway, at other times, it was exactly how Chinese Singaporeans would speak. The icing on the cake was the casual use of Cantonese; twice, I even heard conversations in Teochew. Growing up in 1980s Singapore, I learned English and Chinese at school, but at home, my mother tongue was Malay-laced Teochew, as taught by my paternal grandparents. I also picked up Cantonese by osmosis, while devouring undubbed TVB dramas, broadcast from Johor, Malaysia, with my grandmother. Although my Cantonese is not as fluent as my Teochew, I usually have little trouble understanding it. As I grew older, the highly successful Speak Mandarin Campaign in Singapore meant that there were fewer opportunities to converse in dialects outside the family. But I loved speaking dialects and trying my luck wherever possible, whether it was ordering Teochew rice porridge at hawker centres or chatting with random elderly women. Alas, over the past decade, these encounters have dwindled dramatically. On the few trips I have taken to Hong Kong, I have tried speaking Cantonese, but the somewhat baleful impatience of shopkeepers and service staff mostly leaves me shy and stuttering. So imagine my delight on my first morning in Guangzhou, when an elderly lady approached me in the hotel lift lobby and asked in Cantonese which floor the restaurant was on. I not only directed her to the correct floor, but we also discussed the quality of the breakfast buffet. Only after she thanked me warmly and said goodbye did I realise that I had just conversed entirely in Cantonese without stammering. After that encounter, I became braver and spoke Cantonese whenever I could for the rest of the trip. At times, shopkeepers would smile at me in surprise. As I recounted later to a friend, Guangzhou somehow feels more receptive to poor Cantonese than Hong Kong. It rewards those who try to speak the local dialect, even if they don’t sound perfect. Sadly, I did not have a chance to travel to the Chaoshan region, also in Guangdong province, and try my Teochew on hapless native speakers there. But since returning from Guangzhou, the idea of visiting my ancestral city, Shantou (Swatow), has arisen more than once. While there is probably no hope of tracking down any ancestral village there since the elders in my family died without providing any information, there remains a deep curiosity. Even though the last three generations of my family were born in Singapore, the trip has helped me understand what it means to be descended from immigrants. It is the experience of feeling a strong, mysterious sense of belonging in a place you have never visited before. It is at once unexpected and enlightening, as if parts of yourself, previously unknown, are now revealed.

title: Chinese food delivery platform sparks buzz after rider flies to Singapore for curry puff run
description: Founder of Hong Lim Curry Puff notes that this unique order showcases city state’s rich flavours to an international audience.
content: A Chinese man dressed in a food delivery uniform has sparked widespread curiosity online after he was seen in Singapore buying curry puffs for a customer in China to fulfil a “cross-border food order.” On August 31, Chloe, a Chinese woman living in Singapore, shared a video depicting the man in a Meituan uniform waiting at Hong Lim Curry Puff, a snack shop located in PLQ Mall, about a 17-minute drive from Changi Airport. Meituan is among China’s largest food delivery platforms. Chloe informed the SCMP that she approached the man when she noticed he appeared to be having difficulty communicating with the shop staff. To her surprise, he was wearing a Meituan uniform and explained he was fulfilling a “cross-border order.” The man revealed that a Chinese business owner who had enjoyed the shop’s curry puffs during a previous visit to Singapore was eager to have them again and placed an order through Meituan. He mentioned that the customer paid 2,400 yuan (US$360) for his flight ticket and spent S$13.5 (US$11) on curry puffs. However, he chose not to provide additional details about the customer or any tips received. The SCMP reached out to Meituan but had not received a response by the time of publication. The video has sparked both fascination and doubt online. One netizen commented: “Spending big on a food craving sounds crazy, but it’s totally worth it. I would do the same once I become rich.” Another questioned whether the encounter was staged as part of a marketing stunt. Chloe clarified that she did not receive any sponsorship or was hired to film the video, describing it as a genuine coincidence. Shop founder Victoria Loh told local media that the cross-border order recognised her efforts and provided an opportunity to share Singapore’s flavours with a broader audience overseas. Some users expressed doubts about the man’s identity and raised concerns regarding visa regulations, noting that it was unusual for him to remain in full delivery uniform while abroad. China and Singapore implemented mutual visa-free travel arrangements in February 2024. One Singaporean internet user remarked: “Meituan, come soon,” expressing frustration regarding the pricing and service quality of local delivery apps. Chloe also joined the calls for Meituan to expand into Singapore, joking that she would be delighted to serve as the platform’s spokesperson. According to local reports, sightings of people carrying Meituan delivery bags in Singapore have often involved local delivery riders who bought the bags from Taobao. Meituan’s international food delivery brand, Keeta, currently operates only in Hong Kong, Brazil, and the Middle East, as per an industry insider. According to Singapore-based venture firm Momentum Works, Keeta has registered two entities in Singapore: Keeta and Keeta Technologies. However, both appear to exist solely as registered entities without any clear operational activities.

title: How some grey-market crypto ATMs in Hong Kong can turn users into fraud victims
description: Tucked away in laundromats and arcades, machines offer easy access to crypto, but coming regulations will protect consumers, experts say.
content: Inside a tiny self-service laundromat in Quarry Bay in the east of Hong Kong Island, next to a wall of washing machines, stands a waist-high cryptocurrency terminal with signs reading “Elon Musk recommends Dogecoin” and “Buy bitcoin in one minute”. In order to obtain Dogecoin through the ATM, customers feed Hong Kong dollar notes into a slot and scan a QR code. The equivalent amount in cryptocurrency is then credited into their digital wallet. Such machines have proliferated across the city in recent years as interest in cryptocurrencies has risen. Many are installed at 24-hour unstaffed shops such as laundromats and claw-machine arcades. As of 2024, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) found about 200 virtual asset retailers in the city, which included such ATMs. According to Coin ATM Radar, a global geographical tracker, there are currently 236 crypto ATMs in Hong Kong – concentrated in Mong Kok, Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai and Quarry Bay – offering a dozen different types of cryptocurrencies. However, these ATMs operate in a legal grey area, with the city still in the process of setting up a regulatory regime for over-the-counter cryptocurrency trading. Potential tools in financial scams Some lawmakers and industry insiders warned people of the potential investment risks associated with scams, weak consumer protection and money laundering that ATMs posed. Legislator Johnny Ng Kit-chong said scams involving ATM cryptocurrency transfers were growing increasingly common across the world and often took two forms. The first was through fraudulent machines that accepted cash but did not dispense any crypto, or vice versa. The second was through human actors, such as when fraudsters posed as officials or wooed targets romantically to get them to transfer cash or crypto through a fake ATM controlled by the scammers. “Because blockchain-backed transactions are irreversible and ATMs lack robust verification, recovering these funds is nearly impossible,” Ng said. Two operators, Coinhero and Coinunit, claim to be running Asia’s largest crypto network. A check on their websites found that Coinhero lists its transaction fees online and offers customer support via WhatsApp, email and an actual flagship store in Causeway Bay, while Coinunit’s only channel is a web contact form. Another operator is Canada-based Localcoin. Its CEO, Tristan Fong, said the company had 30 ATMs in Hong Kong and operated consumer protection controls remotely. “We have best-in-class, real-time on-and-off-chain transaction monitoring tools that can be deployed anywhere on earth,” he said. Fong acknowledged the risks of money laundering and scams but noted that other financial services also faced such risks. His company monitored transactions and issued scam warnings to combat illicit activity. Fong welcomed the city’s planned regulation and dialogue with lawmakers on rules for the sector. “Clear rules in Hong Kong would protect consumers, raise standards across the industry, and benefit operators with the ability to implement strong and sophisticated controls,” he said. “We look forward to reviewing the framework when it is published. We will comply fully with any new requirements.” The South China Morning Post has reached out to Coinhero for comment. Regulatory proposal in the works In response to queries from the SCMP, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau said it was finalising legislative proposals with the SFC to regulate virtual asset dealers, including crypto ATM operators, virtual asset custodians and advisory and management service providers. “We are now finalising the legislative proposals, with a target of introducing the relevant bill into the Legislative Council later this year,” it said. The bureau stressed that operators should also “comply with other applicable laws and regulations in Hong Kong”. Andrew Fei, a partner at law firm King & Wood, said that even without a dedicated virtual asset dealer licensing regime, ATM operators remained bound by the city’s existing statutes, including criminal laws. But a specific licence would impose more robust consumer protection, know-your-customer standards, financial resources, risk management and other requirements to help ensure that crypto ATMs were operated in a safe and compliant manner, he added. Fei said shop owners who allowed crypto ATMs on their premises appeared to have straightforward commercial motives, such as drawing foot traffic, and their legal exposure hinged on what they “reasonably suspected” or knew about the operators’ legitimacy. “For criminal liability to attach to shop owners that merely allow the ATMs to be placed in their premises, they would need to have at least some knowledge or suspicion that the ATM operator is doing something illegal,” Fei said. “If they don’t know or suspect anything, then I don’t think the shop owner would be criminally liable.” He suggested that regulators establish an orderly timeline to allow existing market participants to prepare for and obtain the new virtual asset dealing licence before the regime formally comes into effect, to avoid disruption of existing client-facing activities, especially those carried out by financial institutions. Singapore bans crypto ATMs. Other jurisdictions such as Australia allow such services, despite the government’s warning in 2025 that such machines are “one of the highest risk money laundering channels”. Future demand and legitimacy of crypto operators Syed Musheer Ahmed, the founder of Advisory FinStep Asia, a fintech, crypto, and virtual asset advisory firm, said customers of cryptocurrency ATMs in Hong Kong could be small-amount crypto investors, or visitors from jurisdictions where crypto trading was forbidden. “The broader crypto exchange activities globally have come down in the past six months,” Ahmed said, noting that the retail interest for local investors could have gone down. As of Friday, one bitcoin traded at about US$80,630. An SCMP reporter who observed the Quarry Bay laundromat for three hours on a weekday afternoon found that not a single person used the ATM. Fong of LocalCoin said demand for cash-to-crypto transactions had cooled in Hong Kong, with both transaction volumes and average sizes declining. But he argued ATMs were still useful for consumers seeking quick access to digital assets. “We’ve also seen ever-growing numbers of fake crypto exchange websites,” he said. “Concerns about these websites also drive first-time crypto buyers to our machines, because their physical presence in a trusted retail location creates a high level of comfort.” Leon Liu, a researcher at the blockchain network Tron, said the location of the ATMs was not incidental, as laundromats and claw machine arcades were typically unstaffed and opened round the clock – a business model that minimised the cost of running ATMs. But Jack Poon, professor of practice in fintech and entrepreneurial finance at Polytechnic University, warned that unstaffed machines could be platforms for money laundering, as users had no way of knowing whether the cryptocurrency they received came from a legitimate source or illegal activity. He also pointed to the collapse of cryptocurrency platform JPEX, which allegedly committed the city’s biggest financial fraud involving HK$1.6 billion (US$204.1 million) and more than 2,700 victims in 2023, as a cautionary precedent for what happened when an operator had no accountable presence in the city. “A lot of people put money in there without protection. When the operator pulled the plug, a lot of people suffered,” he said. “It was very difficult for Hong Kong law enforcement or regulators to help investors recover their money because the entity was not even in Hong Kong.” According to police, 969 cryptocurrency-related cases were recorded in the first six months of this year, with losses totalling HK$2.68 billion. Those losses amounted to 77.9 per cent of the figure in all of 2025. The number of cases declined by 11.1 per cent to 2,234 in 2025 from a year earlier, while the figure in 2024 was 2,513, a 26.4 per cent drop from 3,415 in 2023. Losses in 2025 totalled HK$3.44 billion, down by 1.7 per cent from 2024. Police did not record the breakdown of cases related only to crypto ATMs.

title: Why Hong Kong fencing ace Ryan Choi can take Djokovic inspiration amid technique tweak
description: Ex-world champion aiming to emerge from injury ready for Asian Games medal quest, music career providing perspective.
content: He is by every measure England’s greatest bowler, but even James Anderson was reduced to mediocrity after an abortive attempt to remodel his action. The owner of 704 Test wickets, Anderson spent most of his country’s 2004-05 tour of South Africa out of form and out of favour, and dejectedly bowling at single stumps on practice strips as he tried to relocate the pace and swing that had characterised his progressive initial years in international cricket. Ironically, it was a stress fracture of the back, precisely the issue his new action was supposed to prevent, that persuaded Anderson to return to the tried-and-tested method that would allow him to become one of the finest bowlers cricket has seen. For Anderson’s idiosyncratic dip of the head at the point of delivery, read Ryan Choi Chun-yin’s “leap, crouch and charge forward”, the tenet of the explosive and “crazy” technique that underpinned the Hongkonger’s ascent to the top of the fencing world last year. The 2025 Asian and world champion, Choi has latterly been bedevilled by a left hamstring complaint that has required him to trade his combative style for an unfamiliar pragmatic approach. At the recent Kerry World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, Choi competed with a “five-to-10-per-cent tear in my muscle”. “If I’m warmed up I can do most stuff, but I cannot have a super big lunge,” Choi told the South China Morning Post. “My main tool is to attack but, sometimes, when I do that, I worry a bit. That affects me against some of my opponents. “But I’ve been working out other ways [to compete]. Even with my injured leg, I’ve been trying to improve my defence, or to attack without lunges.” While Anderson said he felt like he was “trying to impersonate someone else” during his tinkering years, Choi has been “training with a doubtful heart” since June’s Asian Championships. Already nursing the hamstring problem in India, Choi relinquished his individual crown following a quarter-final defeat by eventual champion Kyosuke Matsuyama of Japan. “Every day I have to worry about my leg: will the injury come back or will it get more serious?” Choi said. “One or two years ago, I might have given up, or thought in a very negative way, but I understand now that for every good result you have to go through this process. “When you bounce back from the bottom part of your mentality, you achieve something unexpected.” It is entirely possible that this period of reflection and recalibration could leave Choi with a richer toolbox and broader understanding of himself on the piste. After winning the Masters in 1997 by a runaway 12 strokes for the first of his 15 major titles, Tiger Woods went away and rebuilt his swing. Subsequently, Woods related that he had quietly watched back the entire tournament hoping to identify one area for improvement. “I didn’t see one flaw; I saw about 10,” he said. The challenge Woods successfully navigated was that of bedding in the changes amid a relentless cycle of competition. Choi has been confronted with a similar task. With the dust barely settled following July’s world championships, which were staged hot on the heels of their Asian equivalents, the Asian Games fencing programme in Japan will begin on September 22. “The best way to heal is to rest but there’s always been another competition, so I’ve not been able to properly deal with the injury,” Choi said. “That’s been the most challenging thing for me.” Although he rose to No 1 in the global foil standings after becoming the city’s first fencing world champion last year, Choi currently resides at No 7. His individual world title defence ran aground in the last-16, before a gut-wrenching end to the men’s team foil final, when Hong Kong were beaten 45-44 by Italy after the city team had held a 40-36 lead when Choi stepped up to contest the anchor leg with Guillaume Bianchi. Greg Koenig, the Hong Kong head coach, duly granted his athletes two weeks holiday, telling them: “do not think or speak about fencing”. Opting to coach youngsters in Taiwan and Hawaii, along with teenage teammate Harris Ho Shing-him, Choi, 28, could not help “reflecting on my fencing”. The second-highest-ranked Asian foilist, Choi said: “There had been a lot of pressure, and a lot of upset, because I didn’t do as well as I wanted in the Asian or world championships. “This time helped to distract me, and to find the positive energy to get back in shape.” Aiming to improve on the individual and team bronzes he claimed in 2023, Choi would shake hands right now on going to the Asian Games with less than five per cent of his muscle still torn, although he is hopeful of reducing the damage to “zero per cent”. Also a team silver medallist in 2018, Choi will have a scan at the end of next week, after which Koenig plans to “push him a bit more”. “It’ll be intense training, and with his experience, [the short preparation] can be enough for the Asian Games,” Koenig said. Back in 2018, a chronic elbow injury forced Novak Djokovic to rip up the serve responsible for the majority of the 12 grand slams he had already won and start again. After some teething problems, more surgery, and six months when he experienced “mental hurdles when I had to compete”, Djokovic emerged to win that year’s Wimbledon and US Open, before adding another 10 majors over the following five years. When he encounters his own mental hurdles, Choi thinks of “how much I sacrificed over all these years”. “If one day is hard, it’s nothing,” he said. “No matter how challenging things become, I know I have the ability to overcome them.” While he is not alone among illustrious sportspeople in massaging his technique, Choi is also following in the footsteps of celebrated athletes such as Shaquille O’Neal, Oscar De La Hoya and Armand Duplantis in launching a music career. In March, he released his debut solo single, “My Most Hated Male Singer”. Along with singer Phil Lam, he voiced “Break Through the Sky”, the theme tune for HOY TV’s Asian Games coverage. Choi said that branching into music had invited more scrutiny on his private life and on “how I look”. “People are harsh,” he said. “I feel like I’m naked to the public, that they can judge me from head to toe. I used to care a lot about what people thought of me. This has made me start paying more attention to myself and to the people who love me, not to those who don’t like me, so it’s good for me.”

title: Golden years: in Southeast Asia, growing old is big business
description: From Singapore to Thailand, private operators and luxury resorts are cashing in, as more retirees seek care on their own terms.
content: Helen Fung’s home felt empty. After her husband died last October, she found herself rattling around a house in Singapore with only a domestic helper she could not get along with for company. She turned down her children’s invitations to move to England, put off by London’s grey winters, and instead checked herself into an assisted living facility. On a recent Monday afternoon in St Bernadette Lifestyle Village at Trevose Crescent, tucked away in the leafy residential estate of Bukit Timah, Fung celebrated her 92nd birthday. Carers wheeled and walked eight fellow residents to the dining table before breaking into song. Goaded into a speech, Fung kept it brief: “I’m very happy to be here.” The home, a refurbished two-storey bungalow, is one of a growing number of assisted living facilities springing up as Singapore’s population ages. The city state officially became a “super-aged” society this year, with more than one-fifth of its population over 65. These facilities offer a much-needed middle ground for older people who can no longer live independently but do not require the round-the-clock medical care of a nursing home. Staff help residents with daily tasks such as dispensing medication and writing letters, while some facilities include memory care units for those experiencing cognitive decline. Assisted living is a nascent but fast-growing segment of Singapore’s multibillion-dollar silver economy. The government has provided more than 1,100 such flats since 2021, and private real estate operators are also increasingly entering the market. For residents like Fung, what matters most is feeling part of a community, keeping their independence and being treated with dignity. Despite her early-stage osteoporosis, she moves around the home without a walking frame, sometimes forgoing afternoon sessions of mahjong to journal in her room instead. “I’m fitting in little by little – I’ve learned to get to know more of the residents and our different timetables,” she said. “I told my family I’ll probably stay here until the time comes.” For fellow resident Soo Soo Cheng, 90, her single room is a world away from the six-bedded ward she shared at her previous nursing home. “It was like a dormitory and nothing private like this. I was getting really uncomfortable,” she said. Now she spends her days in a bright orange armchair by the window, walking frame within reach, while carers take care of tasks like printing copies of bills and helping her to bed when her spine acts up. “I’m thankful for a place like this, where I can do things on my own and yet never have a dull moment,” she said. “Time seems to fly.” A middle ground Southeast Asia is ageing rapidly and its social welfare systems are increasingly grappling with a thorny question: what happens to the people who can no longer manage entirely on their own, but do not need a hospital bed? Assisted living – offering medical and social care scalable to residents’ needs – has emerged as an answer. It was designed for people whose needs fell somewhere between the intensive clinical care of a nursing home and what a domestic helper, who cannot reasonably be expected to manage a medical emergency, could provide, said Janice Chia, founder of Ageing Asia, a Singapore-based social enterprise focused on the business of growing old. In Singapore, more people are ageing alone – an estimated 83,000 by 2030, according to the Ministry of Health – while shrinking family sizes are increasing the caregiving burden shouldered by adult children. “Assisted living provides independence and privacy without the seeming unpopular burden of managing foreign domestic helpers,” said Kelvin Tan, who heads the applied ageing studies programme at the Singapore University of Social Sciences. Options in the city state range from government-run flats to private luxury apartments, with monthly bills ranging anywhere from three to five figures, depending on location, room size and level of care required. In 2021, Singapore introduced community care flats aiming to support independent ageing in a social environment. Five such projects have launched so far. The Housing Development Board announced in July that from its sixth project, launching in October, the eligibility age for assisted-living public housing estates would be lowered from 65 to 55, alongside lower fees aimed at improving affordability. Estimated fees for a 15-year lease – currently S$40,000 to S$49,000 (US$31,400 to US$38,500) for a basic package – will drop to between S$26,000 and S$28,000 from next year, according to Vanguard Healthcare, which operates the developments. “The cost is a big advantage for average Singaporeans looking for an accessible offer,” Tan said. Private operators are also scaling up their operations. St Bernadette Lifestyle Village, which runs eight facilities island-wide, offers a mid-tier option priced from S$3,000 to S$6,000 a month. Care homes were “less a business venture than a necessity”, said founder Belinda Wee, who has observed elderly residents growing unsettled in nursing homes due to a lack of socialising. About 80 residents lived in St Bernadette’s homes last year, up from 19 in 2023. Well-heeled pensioners gained a luxury option last month with the opening of Perennial Living, a S$260 million, 195,000 sq ft development in northeastern Singapore featuring a hydrotherapy pool, a traditional Chinese medicine clinic and a karaoke lounge. A basic package for a 330 sq ft studio flat starts at S$8,000 a month, while a 565 sq ft two-bedder costs more than S$13,000. The hefty price tag has raised concerns about the affordability of retirement, though experts note the project is aimed squarely at the upper end of the market. Chia said its prices should be viewed in the category of premium hospitality and care, rather than general assisted living. Sign-ups have been gradual and interest has been “positive”, according to Perennial Holding’s chief executive Pua Seck Guan, who projected a 30 per cent occupancy rate after a year and 80 per cent after two. More new entrants were expected to join the assisted living sector, Chia said, as Singapore’s shift from live-in caregiving to mainstream services gave firms the confidence to invest. But she urged regulators to pace approvals carefully given the dearth of healthcare workers. Singapore needed to recruit about 6,000 nurses, healthcare professionals and support staff every year to meet demand, the Health Ministry said in 2024. It previously estimated that a healthcare workforce of 82,000 would be needed by 2030. “This figure is the one worth dwelling on, because it shows care capability cannot simply be commissioned. Sites can be approved considerably faster than carers can be trained, deployed and retained,” Chia said. Ageing in luxury With its circular driveway and plush lobby, Perennial Living looks more like an upscale hotel than a home for the elderly. The development aimed to set a “new benchmark for senior living in Singapore”, Pua said – reflecting a surge in luxury senior living facilities across Asia as operators recognise their target demographic wants more than just care and medical services. More than US$500 billion is expected to pour into the silver economy across six Southeast Asian markets – Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam and the Philippines – by 2030, according to Ageing Asia. Retirees today were wealthier, healthier and more assertive than any generation before them, the social enterprise said in a report released last month, making the business of ageing the Asia-Pacific’s “largest commercial opportunity”. “Baby boomers, the biggest savers of all generations, have spent their lives making choices and are expected to hold onto that autonomy into their older age,” it said. At Homerly International Senior Living in Thailand, residents walk long, tree-lined avenues within a large, serene gated community, accompanied by nurses, with their pets padding along behind them. The resort, which provides assisted living and nursing care, is one of hundreds of retirement communities popping up across a country with abundant land and a growing healthcare workforce. A month’s stay – including round-the-clock medical care, physiotherapy, pool villas shaded by trees and two staff members in attendance – starts at US$2,200, with the top-end pool villas commanding a price tag of around US$4,500. “Here you’re not a patient, you are a resident. We treat people with dignity,” general manager Rene Pisters said. “You have somebody with you all the time if you need it and the feeling that if something happens to you, there is a nurse sitting here.” Malaysia is seeing a similar boom in luxury homes for the elderly, driven by changing expectations of ageing, according to N. Raaj Selvarajan, group chairman of regional healthcare infrastructure investor Hemrish Group and founder of its flagship senior living brand Sukha Golden. Residents increasingly wanted privacy, wellness and access to care without the institutional feel traditionally associated with elderly care, he said. Demand for its luxury Sukha Senior Resort has surged since it opened in March last year – all rooms are fully occupied, with interested residents placed on a waiting list. Capitalising on the boom, Selvarajan said plans to expand regionally were under way, with projects in Indonesia and Vietnam in the pipeline. “The opportunity is not simply that Asia is ageing; it is that people want to age differently,” he said. Crossing borders For Singaporeans who feel priced out of their own super-aged society, homes for the elderly have become an unlikely engine of Malaysia and Thailand’s recent tourism boom, as families shop for similar care standards at a fraction of the cost. The Straits Resorts Medini, a retirement home in Johor just a 15-minute drive from the border, has built its business around Singaporean demand. “Consistent and encouraging” is how founder Elvira Tan describes cross-border interest in the facility, which offers rooms from S$4,300 a month, bundling in personalised care and grooming services, arts activities and social programmes. Industry insiders expect the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone and Rapid Transit System Link, set to open in January, to further boost demand. “You can obtain the most expensive level of care in Malaysia for about one-third the price of the same level of care in Singapore,” said Kashif Ansari, group CEO of real estate market intelligence group Juwai IQI. Cultural familiarity and the absence of a language barrier eased the transition for would-be residents considering homes across the causeway, he added. “Families with a senior who needs potentially years or even more than a decade of care, naturally want the highest quality service and the lowest cost they can possibly obtain,” he said. “Malaysia has a real competitive advantage in this sector and operators hope to make the most of it.” Money goes further in Thailand too. Facilities in Bangkok and Chiang Mai are attracting a growing number of Asian retirees, including from Singapore and Hong Kong, looking for care comparable to what they can get at home at a fraction of the cost. Thailand hopes the care and wellness industry will become a defining part of its economy in the years ahead, as more people grow old and spend money on a curated retirement. Care standards were high, Homerly’s Pisters said, adding that his company helped elderly residents with bureaucratic hurdles such as visas and bank accounts. “The demand is huge, and it will only get bigger,” he said.

title: Angkor Wat marathon: 6,500 runners race through Cambodia’s ancient Khmer empire
description: This year’s Angkor Empire Marathon saw participants race through misty forests and villages, and past ancient temples and rice fields, as dawn broke over Cambodia’s spectacular Angkor Archaeological Park.
content: Under the cloak of darkness, runners gather in their hundreds at the entrance to the Angkor Wat temple complex, in Cambodia’s Siem Reap. They wait in groups, stretching muscles to pumping house music while a little way off, apsara dancers and traditional Khmer musicians help lift the early-morning energy. Volunteers, many of whom have been at the site since 2am, hand out bottles of water to a crowd of runners and spectators that started arriving at 3.30am, ahead of the staggered starts of the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon. From a small stage framed by the stone carvings of mythical Nagas at the main-road end of the causeway that crosses the moat to Angkor Wat, two emcees shout out motivational phrases in Khmer and English. As the clock ticks down to 4.30am and the start of the first of four races – the full, 42km (26 miles) marathon – pacers make their way to the starting line, competitive racers cramming in behind, waiting for the klaxon to sound. With minutes to go, dignitaries deliver speeches from a stage, wishing competitors luck, thanking sponsors and praising the event’s success over the years. “Angkor Wat always has such a special vibe, so it will be exciting to run among all of the ancient temples,” says Christine Hellington, 32, an Australian who recently moved from Cambodia to Vietnam and is competing in her first marathon. “I’m hoping the atmosphere will help push me through, so I can actually finish it.” National Olympic Committee of Cambodia (NOCC) president Thong Khon, Chinese ambassador Wang Wenbin and NOCC secretary general Vath Chamroeun together light a torch with a blazing flame to officially open the event, then the klaxon sounds and the runners set off towards Siem Reap city, roared on by spectators young and old, who are lining the road. For many competitors, such as Hellington (who did manage to complete the 42km, in five hours and 34 minutes), this marathon’s appeal isn’t just about finishing. Unlike conventional city races, in which competitors run in the shadow of skyscrapers and urban landmarks, here, runners spend much of the course among the temples, settlements and reservoirs that once formed the heart of the Khmer Empire (802-1431). According to Thong Khon, the 11th Angkor Empire Marathon (which took place on August 2) saw a 25 per cent increase in the number of competitors compared with last year. Of the 6,500 total, 1,050 were international runners hailing from 51 countries, with the bulk having come from China, Japan and Britain. Over the two days before the races, entrants were required to visit the Royal Angkor Resort, on the outskirts of Siem Reap, to collect their race gear: their race number – mine was 7008; a T-shirt; a drawstring bag; and a lanyard. Here, the competitive spirit was already being stirred, with pre-race activities ranging from football target practice to mini runs, as well as games and freebies dished out by sponsors. Volunteers and officials were in attendance to offer advice and encouragement. At 4.30am on the day itself, 1,000 people set off on the full marathon. At 5.30am, another 1,000 took on the half-marathon, and the 10km (six miles) attracted 3,000 runners, who set off at 5.40am. The final 1,500 took part in a 3km (1.9 miles) fun run, and set off at 5.50am. Each route started and ended on the road at the entrance to the Angkor Wat complex. The 42km route led deep into the Unesco-crowned Angkor Archaeological Park, passing Ta Prohm – the temple featured in the 2001 film Lara Croft: Tomb Raider – and sacred Srah Srang, a vast reservoir known as the “Royal Bath”. The runners pushed through the ancient capital of Angkor Thom, home to the multifaced Bayon temple, and past some of the park’s lesser-known places of worship, including East Mebon, Pre Rup, Banteay Kdei, Prasat Top and Ta Keo, all of which took on an unearthly aspect in the mist. With a section through Siem Reap city and another through a traditional village, Preah Dak, where the smell of num banh chok – the Khmer breakfast dish of rice noodles – wafted through the air, it’s easy to see how the race made it onto Forbes Travel Guide’s “12 Marathons Worth Travelling For in 2026” list, rubbing shoulders with China’s Great Wall Marathon and the Boston Marathon, in the United States. Clutching his finisher’s medal, Vann Chan Thada seems energised after having completed his second Angkor Empire Marathon, in four hours and 55 minutes. “The marathon was really challenging with the [searing heat], but it was really exciting with the views on the route that we ran,” says the 25-year-old Cambodian. “Running through the ancient temples gave me a different vibe compared with running in the city. We ran in the early morning under the tree-lined shade, and the sunrise with the temples made us feel like we were running through the golden era of ancient Angkor.” The 10km race is timed to begin as the sun starts to peek from behind Angkor Wat. In addition to serious athletes, families and groups of friends are taking part, chatting, laughing, stopping to snap selfies and cheer each other on along the way. The 10km is the perfect option, in other words, for beginners such as me. The seasoned racers storm ahead at the sound of the klaxon, leaving us more casual runners space to take in our surroundings and shoot photos before setting off. Rays of sunlight pierce a high canopy dripping with cooling condensation along the road from Angkor Wat to Angkor Thom’s South Gate. Mist hovers above waterways and the silhouettes of temples suddenly emerge from the treetops, creating a whimsical atmosphere that feels as though it’s been lifted from a fairy tale. Dawn is also when nature springs to life, the treetops alive with birdsong and the faint morning call of gibbons. Unperturbed by the pounding feet of thousands of runners, mischievous macaques join spectators on the sidelines, snatching discarded water bottles from the road with which to rehydrate. Crossing the finish line to energising cheers in one hour and 34 minutes leaves me just enough time to compose myself before English expat Jim Thompson, 46 and dripping in sweat, does the same. “I’ve run before in very uninspiring places, but the key difference is that this race has the temples of Angkor Wat as a sublime backdrop to your achievement of running,” says Thompson, who is no stranger to the experience, having competed in the Angkor Wat International Half Marathon in 2013 and 2014. The longer-established half marathon is a separate NOCC event that takes place around the temples in December each year. “The setting in ancient Angkor Wat is the No 1 highlight; the way that the temples slowly emerge from the darkness into the dawn, and all the while this beautiful mist appears in the sunlight, raining back down onto the runners. All of the other participants were a definite highlight, too, spurring you on to the finish.” The Angkor Empire Marathon was launched in 2014 as an international event designed to promote Siem Reap and the Angkor Archaeological Park as a destination for sports tourism while contributing to charitable and community initiatives. This year’s marathon came at a challenging time for Cambodia’s tourism sector, which is struggling to rebuild international visitor numbers after the Covid-19 pandemic. Figures from the Ministry of Tourism reveal the nation welcomed 1.75 million international arrivals in the first half of 2026, marking a 47.9 per cent year-on-year decline, the dramatic drop attributed to the closure of land borders with Thailand due to the ongoing conflict between the two nations; the Middle East war and its impact on airfares; and the negative publicity regarding online scam centres operating in Cambodia. Angkor Enterprise recorded a 31.69 per cent drop in ticket sales for the Angkor Archaeological Park during the same period, highlighting the importance of finding new ways to draw visitors to Siem Reap. The return of thousands of runners to Angkor Wat offered a welcome boost, a renewed energy having been injected into the city during the race weekend. Restaurants and bars were bustling and shopkeepers engaged in lively bartering to sell their wares. Tuk-tuk driver Mr Chai secured a steady flow of customers throughout the marathon weekend, he says: “Business has been very quiet lately, so it has been good to be busy and see so many people at the temples again.” Furthermore, proceeds from the Angkor Empire Marathon and Angkor Wat International Half Marathon directly benefit children’s hospitals, landmine victims and disability support organisations, and the Cambodian Red Cross, among other humanitarian initiatives. Athletic pursuits in the days of the Khmer Empire – as depicted in bas-relief on the walls of Angkor Wat – served a dual purpose, being a form of military preparation for soldiers as well as a major element of social entertainment. Likewise, today’s Angkor Wat runs are bifunctional: helping to revitalise the local tourism industry while raising funds for charitable causes. The entry fee for the full marathon for international competitors this year was US$75. It was US$65 for the half marathon, US$50 for the 10km and US$25 for the fun run, with tickets available at checkpointspot.asia. The 31st Angkor Wat International Half Marathon will take place on December 6; to register, click here. The date for the 12th Angkor Empire Marathon has not yet been set, although a different event – the Marathon Trail Angkor, which is a series of off-road runs – is scheduled for January 23, 2027; to register, click here The writer was hosted by Angkor Village Hotel, in Siem Reap

title: Tetris says it didn’t give White House permission for ‘Build the Wall’ game
description: The company says it takes copyright infringement ‘very seriously’ and is currently reviewing the matter.
content: Tetris said on Friday that it did not give permission for the White House to use the game’s iconic imagery for a controversial online arcade that the Trump administration released on Thursday. “The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of Build the Wall and did not authorise or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game,” Tetris said in a statement. “We are currently reviewing the matter,” the statement continued. A block-stacking game called Build the Wall included instructions to “protect the border from the coming horde.” The arcade-style games and promotional content used by the Trump administration contain images that resemble games created by Tetris and other major game developers including Sega, Microsoft-owned Xbox and the Flappy Bird Foundation. “At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them,” Tetris said in a social media post. “P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously,” the post continued. Promotional content posted by the White House on social media also included images that resemble trademarks and designs from Microsoft-owned Xbox. Microsoft did not respond to requests for comment, and the Sega Corporation could not immediately be reached. The White House released several games on Thursday, with a placeholder that teased another one “coming soon”. The web-only games, which were published on the official White House website under a new page called “arcade”, sparked condemnation for racist themes and prompted questions about potential copyright violations. In one clip, the letters from the Sega logo transform into Maga, a term that stands for Make America Great Again, which US President Donald Trump turned into his campaign slogan during his first presidential run for the 2016 election. A game called Flappy Bill features a bald eagle carrying a document in its claws that tries to avoid smashing into columns of various heights, against a background that resembles Washington. “This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the president’s many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said in a statement on Thursday. Rights groups criticised the White House. “Makes me sick. They’ve been playing games with people’s lives for years, now they’ve made a video game of what they’re doing,” said Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas. “There’s no attention paid to the quality of life for human beings, both those in their game or those in real life. We who live in the borderlands are US citizens and yet are treated with suspicion and violence,” she added. The game designers “have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others”. Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken several actions since returning to power aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings. His White House meanwhile has long used social media stunts to ram home its points and troll liberal opponents, and has sparked a backlash from several artists by using their music without permission. The White House is trying to convince voters that Trump’s second presidential term has been successful ahead of the midterm election in November. The balance of power in Congress will also be at stake when Americans go to the polls in just over two months.

title: Editorial | E-filing failures should be a wake-up call for public services
description: The blunder reflects negatively on Hong Kong’s ‘smart city’ ambition and pursuit of seamless online public services.
content: Imagine being fined for failing to file your online tax return on time even though you are absolutely sure you have done so, only to find out later that it wasn’t your own fault. For nearly 5,200 Hong Kong taxpayers, this scenario became reality after tens of thousands of people left their eTAX returns incomplete due to unclear wording and interface design. There were even two prosecutions before steps were taken to rectify the blunder. Commissioner of Inland Revenue Benjamin Chan Sze-wai rightly apologised for the inconvenience caused to the affected, saying the tax department had an “unshirkable responsibility” to fix the problem. He assured the public that no taxpayers would be penalised over the incident, adding that penalty remissions would be granted, payments refunded and the two prosecutions withdrawn. “The system is under the Inland Revenue Department and is not ideal … We will continue to improve the system and hope that such misunderstandings will not happen again,” he said. The confusion should not have happened in the first place. Worse, an investigation initiated by the city’s Ombudsman revealed that similar problems were spotted as early as 2022, but were not resolved until tens of thousands were caught last year. It was found that ambiguous instructions on the eTAX submission and signature interface misled users into thinking that authenticating themselves via iAM Smart completed their filing, when in fact they had to return to the eTAX platform and wait for confirmation. Between May 2 last year and January 31 this year, 489,425 taxpayers tried to submit electronic returns using a digital signature on iAM Smart for the 2024-25 tax year; of these, 33,019 ended up with incomplete submissions. The tax department conceded that the failed submissions were due to various factors, such as user actions or network anomalies. About 80 per cent of the 33,000 affected taxpayers had reused “iAM Smart” to sign and submit their tax returns successfully before penalty notices or notices of estimated assessment were issued, including some 14,000 who did so within the same day of the first attempt. The department later adopted steps to address the issues, including pop-ups, confirmation messages, enhanced wording and autosave. That does not exonerate the department of inadequacies in providing a reliable online public service for everyone. As noted by the maladministration watchdog, the national 15th five-year plan has dedicated a chapter to the advancement of digital China, proposing strategic planning to elevate the level of digital intelligence development and digital government infrastructure. The incumbent Hong Kong administration is also committed to promoting digital government and smart city operations. The tax filing blunder is more than a system hiccup. It reflects negatively on Hong Kong’s “smart city” ambition and the pursuit of seamless online public services. The online tax filing system in question was widely used. Even though the majority managed to do so without any issues, the systemic issue had implications that ripple far beyond inconvenience for some users. The blunder inevitably erodes trust, creates legal liability and exposes coordination gaps across digital government systems. The episode serves as a wake-up call for government agencies and public bodies running online public services. Currently, residents can access more than 1,300 online services by the government, public and private bodies via iAM Smart, a one-stop personalised digital service platform announced in the 2017 policy address. Whether it’s business registration, social welfare, healthcare or education, each agency should proactively audit its digital workflows for ambiguous wording, unclear completion signals and inconsistencies across platforms so as to avoid similar hiccups. Hong Kong has long promoted itself as a modern city with full digitalisation of government services. Yet the tax filing episode shows how easily that undertaking unravels when different arms of the administration do not speak the same digital language. Users cannot be faulted for assuming that using the official authentication step via iAM Smart equalled accomplishing the task. The problem highlights a classic coordination failure that has no place in an efficient and effective administration.

title: ‘I enjoy the hunt’: why Hong Kong shoppers are turning to second-hand luxury fashion
description: Hong Kong’s younger shoppers are embracing preloved designer items for their affordability, sustainability and investment value.
content: Bending over trays of jade pendants, gemstone brooches and old watches, Dianne Gupta takes her time as she sifts through a heap of tangled necklaces and rings. “I enjoy the hunt. It’s like finding hidden treasure when I see something I like,” she says, drifting from stall to stall along Apliu Street, well known for second-hand and vintage stalls, in Hong Kong’s Sham Shui Po neighbourhood. Several years ago, Gupta – who has been buying preloved items since she was a child – found a pair of Miu Miu flats for HK$35 (US$4.50) at a charity shop in Central, on Hong Kong Island. She is chasing that same high today. She is not alone – shoppers around the world are increasingly turning to different kinds of outlets and spaces to look for luxury fashion. This is also the case in Hong Kong, where Japanese resale brand Ragtag recently opened a store in Causeway Bay, joining a growing roster of second-hand luxury players in the city. Ragtag, which sells authenticated pre-owned designer pieces and streetwear labels, follows in the footsteps of fellow Japanese retailers such as Brand Off and 2nd Street, which already have a strong presence in Hong Kong. A 2026 study by luxury fashion intelligence platform Designer Signals found that the Asia-Pacific second-hand luxury goods market is estimated at roughly US$10.1 billion this year. It also found that it is expected to reach US$18.9 billion by 2034, with Hong Kong one of the region’s key luxury hubs. A growing demand for sustainability So what sparked the trend? “Some people had a very negative perception of [thrifting] – that [it] was dirty,” says Gupta, for whom thrifting began as a financially responsible way to refresh her wardrobe. “I think the more traditional thinkers would be worried about getting bad juju from the item’s previous owner.” The city’s attitude towards second-hand shopping, however, has changed. “Resale is moving into mainstream retail locations and, in some cases, more premium environments,” says Barrie Chan, senior director and head of retail at real estate adviser Savills. “That changes consumer perception. That makes second-hand fashion feel less like a fringe activity and more like a legitimate lifestyle retail category that can sit alongside conventional fashion brands.” Local consumers, especially among the younger crowds, are more environmentally conscious and, as demand grows for sustainability and premium products at more accessible prices, re-commerce is fast becoming a mainstream habit. Rather than engaging in pure ‘consumption’, today’s Hong Kong clients place a much higher emphasis on an item’s ‘value retention’ Elsa Shen, head of Hana Vintage Every year, 92 million tonnes of textile waste are produced globally. A 2025 report by Hong Kong-based environmental NGO Redress found that the city discards more than 400 tonnes of textile waste daily. “I think that really did kind of turn me off from fashion for quite a bit,” says Gupta, who recalls attending a university class that opened her eyes to the negative impact the fashion industry had on the environment. The trend is further fuelled by social media, where creators often share videos of themselves thrifting at local charity shops and posting “haul” clips showcasing Y2K clothing items and vintage luxury finds. What drives second-hand shopping? Elsa Shen, the head of Hana Vintage, a Shanghai-based luxury resale boutique that opened a Hong Kong branch in 2024, identifies the rising cost of living in the city as a primary driver among her customers for shopping second-hand. “The changing economic environment has prompted consumers to become more rational,” Shen says. “Rather than engaging in pure ‘consumption’, today’s Hong Kong clients place a much higher emphasis on an item’s ‘value retention’ and its ‘liquidity’ within the secondary market.” Shen also notes that her customer base in Hong Kong, while largely dominated by women aged 25 to 55, has seen two shifts in the past few years. “First, our customer base is noticeably trending younger,” Shen says, noting that Gen Z customers in their early 20s are starting to buy vintage bags because “they want to avoid clashing styles with others” and also because they resonate with the concept of environmental circularity. Secondly, the shop’s proportion of male customers has increased. “They are mostly looking for gender-neutral styles or large-capacity travel bags,” she says. According to Shen, the most popular luxury items among Hongkongers are timeless pieces such as the Hermes Birkin 30 and 35 and the So Kelly. Chanel’s Classic Flap series and Louis Vuitton’s classic monogram pieces are also in high demand and consistently sell out. At Hana Vintage, each bag is priced according to an exacting formula: brand, style, condition, accessory completeness and real-time market trends; with classic styles commanding higher prices and collectors’ items carrying what Shen calls a “scarcity premium”. “When boutique retail prices rise, second-hand prices typically follow,” Shen says. At her boutique, discounts can range from 30 per cent to 90 per cent below retail, depending on the bag and market conditions. In practice, bags in good condition typically sell at 60 per cent to 70 per cent of their original price. Even so, given where luxury pricing sits today, second-hand luxury buyers still have to dig deep into their pockets. “[Our] customers highly value the coexistence of practicality and investment potential,” Shen says. “They prefer versatile, classic investment pieces that work just as well for daily commutes as they do for evening dinners, and which maintain high liquidity in the resale market.” The downsides of second-hand shopping However, just as second-hand shopping has become more accessible and the presence of online resale marketplaces has grown in Hong Kong, so too has the prevalence of counterfeit goods as well as concerns about the quality of preloved designer items. In May, the Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department seized an estimated HK$16 million worth of counterfeit products, including watches, bags and clothing. “Trust is fundamental, particularly because the quality of counterfeit products continues to improve and some pieces can be difficult even for professionals to assess,” says Daisuke Hirano, head of Japanese subsidiary Tin Pan Alley, which manages resale chains including Ragtag. “Experienced buyers conduct the initial authentication, while high-value luxury bags and accessories are also checked using AI-enabled authentication services such as Entrupy before being offered to customers.” In 2023, Carousell, a popular resale platform in Hong Kong, launched “Certified Luxury”, a programme that ensures that preloved luxury goods go through authentication checks by trusted experts to assess their quality and legitimacy. Another downside to the trend is that, despite an emphasis on eco-conscious shopping, the increased accessibility of second-hand goods is leading to overconsumption – a constant concern for Aurianne Ricquier, circular fashion programme director at Redress. Ricquier notes that the same online trends that have raised awareness about the importance of sustainability and normalised shopping second-hand are now encouraging overconsumption. “Social media is important to shift mindsets around second-hand because all of us spend so much time on it,” she says. “However, there’s a direct clash with most of the social media content, which is pushing us to buy more stuff all the time.” It is a concern that has been eating away at Gupta. While her thrift-spot videos perform well, she knows she may be encouraging more consumption. Her response has been to share more upcycling and making-of content, and to be more selective about what she promotes. Ragtag’s Hirano puts it bluntly: “Resale is not automatically sustainable simply because an item is pre-owned. Its value lies in extending the useful life of products, maintaining their quality and creating trusted circulation.” The Japanese brand is hoping to place greater emphasis on local buy-back services in Hong Kong and develop a high-quality source of pre-owned luxury inventory. Going forward, for resale to become more sustainable, Savills’ Chan points to creating a stronger buy-back system. “A resale business becomes more sustainable when consumers are not just buying second-hand items, but also selling products back into the system,” Chan says. “Strong buy-back activity would suggest that circular fashion is becoming a habit rather than an occasional purchase.” In Hong Kong, this is already happening on a community level. Organisations such as Redress and community groups like Old But Gold, Top Swop and Swop Society hold clothing-swapping events throughout the year to encourage locals to prolong the lifespan of garments.

title: Top 10: A habit you promise to quit in the new school year
description: From doomscrolling to revenge bedtime procrastination, students share the bad patterns they hope to break to get ready for the coming academic term.
content:
Our next question: What is your funniest memory from the summer holiday? To take part, drop us a line via this form by 12pm on Tuesday, September 8 .
Aahana Mukhi, 16, Island School: Scrolling on social media while eating breakfast. At 6.30am, my algorithm is my companion. This is the ideal environment to get sucked into an endless waterfall of memes and mini-vlogs. Not only does this habit increase my screen time while shortening my attention span, but it also leaves me feeling sluggish. This term, I want to replace my screen with a physical book. With a packed school calendar, time to read books is scarce. Dedicating these 30 minutes to fuelling my imagination will wake my brain up instead of draining it.
Bobo Lau, 16, HKFYG Lee Shau Kee College: It’s 2am – you’re scrolling on your phone after a hectic day at school. This is a phenomenon known as “revenge bedtime procrastination”, and it is a habit I want to break. Day after day, I have gone to school exhausted, repeatedly promising myself to go to bed earlier that night. But it is so tempting to reclaim the time you lost to studying. However, staying up late for “me-time” not only leads to higher risks of hypertension, stroke and coronary heart disease, but it also affects your mental health, making you more susceptible to stress and depression. It is time I break this loop.
Valerie Chiu, 16, St Mary’s Canossian College: Staying up late. Oftentimes, I start working too late in the evening while scrolling through social media. This has led to having to rush to finish tasks even later into the night. I recognise that this creates a vicious cycle of daytime exhaustion that has detrimental effects on both my health and work efficiency. Overcoming this habit is not merely a matter of better scheduling. I believe it requires a shift in mindset to truly respect how precious time is.
Alden Hou, 15, South Island School: You’re at home, doomscrolling on your social media of choice or on a game with your friends, when you realise you have an assignment or a test to study for. I relate. At its core, procrastination is not about being lazy or disorganised; it’s often used to cope with stress, the fear of failure or feeling overwhelmed. Instead of tackling homework or revising for the test, we seek short-term relief by doing something we find enjoyable or less demanding (such as writing this article). But the relief is temporary, and the task doesn’t disappear. Instead, it looms larger, with the pressure building as the deadline nears.
Valerie Shek, 16, The Independent Schools Foundation Academy: Procrastinating. Way too often I find myself putting off assignments until the very, very last possible moment, leaving me stressed, overwhelmed and rushing to finish work. This term, I want to break the toxic cycle and start working on tasks as soon as they are assigned, breaking them down into small and manageable steps. I also plan on setting personal deadlines that are earlier than actual due dates, so I can thoroughly check my work before submitting.
Huang Ziyan, 17, Harrow International School Hong Kong: Saying “I have to study” to turn down school events, concerts or spontaneous activities with friends. While this year is set to be the most academically intense yet, stepping into my senior year has made me realise the true value of the small moments that have shaped my experience and who I am at school. In the new term, I promise to say yes to all the last-minute dinners, formals and play openings – to live, to laugh and enjoy every minute in this final chapter of my secondary school life!
Connie Liu, 15, St Rose of Lima’s College: Last year, I constantly doom‑scrolled on Instagram, sent reels and memes to my friends, or simply lay in bed doing nothing. After every bout of procrastination, I would tell myself the same thing: this behaviour was understandable, since my heavy school workload exerted tremendous pressure on me. As a result, I got trapped in a vicious cycle of putting off schoolwork and making excuses. Deep down, I was aware of how it harmed my academic performance as I pulled all‑nighters to meet deadlines. I was also left worn‑out and had far less time to pursue my interests.
Allegra Khomara, 17, King George V School: In my last year of secondary school, I promise to stop telling myself “just one more episode” or “just one more chapter”. When I get caught up in a great show or a new book, I use that phrase to delay studying or sleep. But one episode turns into five, and 10 minutes turns into two hours. That temporary contentment turns into dread the moment I look over at the unfinished homework on my desk. This year, my goal is to balance relaxation and studies.
Janice Adele Cheung, 12, Yew Chung International School of Hong Kong: My summer often has late nights filled with endless scrolling, gaming or hanging out with friends. Being carefree in the moment but carrying a bad sleep routine into the school year can be damaging. Sleep is the foundation of focus, memory and emotional balance. Academic success depends on a clear and rested mind. The consequences also extend to social life. Friendships and teamwork thrive on energy and positivity, but exhaustion drains both. Students who are tired may find themselves disconnected from peers or unable to contribute fully in group activities. Breaking this habit requires discipline.
Cherish Chiu Cheuk-wing, 16, Leung Shek Chee College: There is a Chinese phrase: “A day’s plan starts with the morning.” The new school year is a great time for me to change and wipe away all my bad habits. In junior forms, I never revised after class since I believed having fun was essential. However, the countdown to university entrance exams has begun. Regularly revising every day is key to retaining knowledge, and I won’t have to cram for exams at the last second. Starting each day with focused study will build steady progress and reduce anxiety.

title: In Focus | Talk is growing of a Tesla-SpaceX merger. Will geopolitics throw a spanner in the works?
description: Security concerns in Beijing and Washington could create ‘bottleneck’ if Elon Musk attempts to combine the two flagship companies.
content: One by one, Tesla Model Y Ls roll out of the company’s end-of-line inspection bays, gleaming in black, white and gold. They are a mix of left-hand and right-hand drive – one of many signs the electric vehicles (EVs) produced here are destined for ports around the world. The company touts a total assembly time of less than 40 seconds at its sprawling Gigafactory in Lingang, a coastal area on the far southeastern edge of Shanghai. From there, Tesla says, a finished car can reach the port and be loaded onto a ship within an hour. In July, one roll-on/roll-off vessel carried 7,738 Teslas out of Shanghai, marking an all-time record for a single shipment of finished vehicles from a Chinese port. The factory delivered 93,579 vehicles that month. As of July, more than half of the cars made there were exported overseas this year. But because of its location, this highly efficient manufacturing powerhouse could present a vulnerability in Washington for Tesla CEO Elon Musk, whose sprawling empire spans EVs, autonomous driving, rockets, satellite internet, humanoid robots, artificial intelligence and brain-computer interfaces. While his EV business relies heavily on China’s supply chain to fulfil global demand, Musk’s commercial aerospace company SpaceX has become a core national security contractor for the Pentagon. That poses a dilemma for the CEO, as he looks to navigate the geopolitical waters between the world’s two biggest economies. Musk must perform a balancing act between the competing interests, which would require a complicated, ring-fenced strategy for his China operations to satisfy regulators in both Washington and Beijing, according to industry observers. “Musk is not yet choosing between the United States and China. He is trying to establish a balance between several tracks of [his] offerings,” said Marina Yue Zhang, associate professor at the Australia-China Relations Institute at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS). “But the danger to maintain this balance lies in an uncertain geopolitical landscape.” The challenge could intensify if Musk were to bring his businesses closer together. Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another Seth Goldstein, Morningstar Currently, Wall Street is abuzz about a possible merger between SpaceX, whose close ties to the US government and Pentagon heighten national-security sensitivities, and Tesla, due to an ever deeper technology overlap between the two firms, from AI to robotics. While Musk has not commented on a merger, the usually outspoken tech mogul has also not publicly denied the speculation. “Tesla and SpaceX are increasingly going to be suppliers to one another,” said Seth Goldstein, senior equity analyst at Morningstar. Tesla supplies solar panels, batteries and potentially cargo casings for SpaceX’s Starship launch vehicle, while SpaceX provides its Grok AI model and Starlink satellite internet for Tesla’s cars and potentially its humanoid robot Optimus, according to Goldstein. The merger would make “operational sense” as it would allow Musk to transfer engineering talent between Tesla and SpaceX projects more smoothly without triggering corporate compliance concerns, Goldstein said. Tesla’s China footprint could complicate such a move, with a merger raising concerns on both sides of the Pacific: Washington’s wariness towards a core partner maintaining a major manufacturing base in China, as well as Beijing’s misgivings about allowing a US defence contractor to operate within its borders. The concerns sparked speculation that Musk may be forced to decouple from China. A Wall Street Journal report in late July, citing unidentified sources, said Tesla had been instructed to separate its China business to pave the way for a potential merger with SpaceX. However, Musk was quick to dismiss it as “absurdly fake news”. “This has never even come up in a discussion ever,” Musk said on his social media platform X, formerly Twitter. Tesla and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the subject. Can Tesla do without China? At stake is Tesla’s sprawling Shanghai manufacturing ecosystem, which accounted for over half of the company’s total global EV deliveries in 2025. Lingang does not just host the Gigafactory, China’s first wholly foreign-owned car plant. It also has the still-expanding Megafactory, Tesla’s energy-storage manufacturing plant, as well as a dense network of Chinese suppliers capable of meeting the company’s standards on cost, quality and scale. Nearby are plants operated by – among others – automotive supplier Joyson Electronics, which provides Tesla with steering wheels and airbags; battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Limited (CATL) and Faway Dongyang, a producer of car bumpers. Inside Tesla’s own factory, crates bearing the names of Chinese suppliers such as Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Suzhou Current Power Technology, Lingyun Industrial and Suzhou Dongshan Precision Manufacturing can be seen along the production line. Many are based within the manufacturing belt that stretches across the country’s east coast, through Shanghai and the provinces of Jiangsu and Zhejiang. Tesla says more than 95 per cent of the parts used at its Shanghai factory are locally sourced.
