It works with more than 400 Chinese suppliers, more than 60 of which have gone on to enter Tesla’s global supply chain. China is critical to Tesla in three interconnected ways: scale, cost efficiency and speed of innovation, said Zhang of UTS. “Shanghai is not simply an inexpensive assembly base. It sits inside an unusually dense network of battery, electronics, casting, motor, tooling and automation suppliers,” she said. “That proximity allows Tesla to alter designs, resolve manufacturing problems and scale production much faster than it could through a dispersed supply chain.” Divesting China “would impair Tesla’s production volume, cost structure and manufacturing-learning loop”, Zhang added. Musk himself was once a frequent visitor to Shanghai. Over a roughly 18-month span between 2018 and 2020, he met Li Qiang – then Shanghai’s Communist Party chief, and now China’s premier – four times, according to a city government account. Musk returned to Shanghai in 2023. His later public visits to China in 2024 and 2026 were centred largely on Beijing. Most recently, he joined US President Donald Trump’s entourage for a state visit to China’s capital in May. Over those years, Musk’s role changed within China and globally. With the establishment of the Shanghai facility, he became one of the country’s most important foreign manufacturing investors. And in the years since his purchase of Twitter, he has accrued immense influence over public discourse and geopolitics, especially in the world’s two largest economies. The more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised Marina Yue Zhang, University of Technology Sydney Between Washington and Beijing Musk’s geopolitical calculus now must include the stringent obligations for SpaceX that come with being a US military contractor. Among the multibillion-dollar agreements the company has made are a US$4.16 billion deal for satellites designed to track airborne missiles, and a US$2.29 billion contract to build a space-based network for satellite communications, both signed with the Space Force of the US Department of Defence in May. Contracts from the US government accounted for around 20 per cent of SpaceX’s total revenues in 2025, the company said in its prospectus. The relationship between SpaceX and the US government is perceived as symbiotic, with each side reliant on the other. Musk said his company had become a “vital element” of the country’s national defence in June. But Zhang said Washington would expect significant compartmentalisation in Musk’s China business. “[The US] may tolerate civilian Tesla manufacturing in China under the same ultimate holding company, but only if that activity is demonstrably isolated from classified programmes, military-relevant AI, controlled technical data and sensitive defence supply chains”. Questions will also be raised from the Beijing side, although China values Tesla as a flagship foreign investment, she said, adding that China could require a ring-fenced Chinese subsidiary or restrictions on data, algorithm and technical access to maintain leverage over the EV maker’s local operations. How Musk plans to navigate between Washington and Beijing will be “the real bottleneck” in a potential merger, according to Zhang. “The commercial case is relatively easy to articulate. The harder question is whether those synergies can be realised without creating unacceptable channels between an American defence contractor and Tesla’s Chinese operations.” She said the CEO would need to “construct an exceptionally clear institutional firewall”, but added this could create a paradox: “the more effective the firewall, the fewer merger synergies can safely be realised.” Tesla lays the first bricks Tesla could be taking early steps to build such a firewall within its production network. A former engineer who worked on battery development for the company said the firm had, years ago, launched an internal effort aimed at building a supply chain that was less dependent on China. It was, in practice, “almost an impossible task,” the engineer said, speaking on condition of anonymity, because Chinese companies were present at almost every layer of the industry. Tesla did ask some suppliers to build production capacity outside China in this effort, the former engineer said. CATL was among the companies that were approached, but the battery maker shelved its direct investment plan in the US in 2022 as geopolitical tension mounted. Japan’s Panasonic and South Korea’s LG Energy Solution, however, have deepened their ties with Tesla in the US market. Still, the former engineer cautioned against reading every effort to diversify production through a geopolitical lens. Hardware companies routinely build parallel supply chains, the engineer said, often for more pragmatic reasons: cost, efficiency and resilience. “A patchwork of regulations and economic incentives has increasingly pushed companies such as Tesla to build a more ‘China-free’ supply chain, or scrutinise suppliers much more closely, sometimes several tiers down,” said Leah Yu, a partner at Jincheng Tongda & Neal Law Firm. Sources of pressure included import restrictions linked to forced labour, national security rules covering connected vehicles, tariffs and tax incentives favouring US-made batteries and components, Yu said. SpaceX faced a harder technology firewall, she added, as export controls were layered on top of supplier-security requirements associated with its aerospace and national security work. These controls could restrict not only sourcing, but also which suppliers and personnel were allowed access to the necessary technology. Goldstein of Morningstar said that ring-fencing Tesla’s Chinese EV and battery operations could address the demands of both governments. However, to allow a merger to proceed, regulatory authorities in both the US and China might still demand that Tesla sells off its Chinese operations or move to a non-controlling stake. While a China divestment could hurt Tesla’s cost efficiency, the EV maker traditionally competes on its autonomous driving technology as a differentiator rather than price, Goldstein said. Gearing up for the ‘biggest product ever’ However, even compared with EVs, China could prove more indispensable for the production of Optimus, which Musk has called “the biggest product ever”. “So far, the largest reliance on China is likely the rare earth metals used to produce magnets for motors that are required for every joint in a humanoid robot,” Goldstein said. “Tesla will likely try to source rare earth metals from suppliers outside China, but this may be difficult as China controls the vast majority of supply today.” Musk addressed the rare earth issue in April, admitting that Beijing’s restrictions on exports of the critical minerals affected the production of Optimus. “We’re working through that with China,” Musk told investors in an earnings call. A continued grip on rare earth elements – and the crucial magnets made with them – could hurt Musk’s ambitions for the humanoid robot, which he projected to be a US$10 trillion sales generator. Beyond rare earth magnets, Optimus remains heavily reliant on China’s supply chain, even with its primary manufacturing rooted in the US. “There is an overlap in key‑component supply chains between Optimus and Tesla EVs, and Tesla leverages existing Chinese partners to co-develop and produce joint modules, dexterous hands and other key parts,” said Ethan Qi, associate director at Counterpoint Research. Tier-one suppliers including Tuopu Group, Zhejiang Sanhua, Xusheng Group and Glory Mica are veterans in Tesla’s EV value chain with years of proven partnerships, according to Qi. “They fully back Optimus V3’s mass production plan,” he said. Amid geopolitical uncertainties, these Chinese partners would willingly relocate or expand their capacity beyond China to mitigate the impacts of tariffs, as they anticipate strong sales prospects from Optimus, Qi added. These delicate and complex adjustments could move fast. Ark Investment Management’s chief futurist Brett Winton said he expected a SpaceX and Tesla combination to be announced before the end of 2026. Tesla’s China operations could pose a “smallish wrinkle” in a potential merger with SpaceX, a major US defence contractor, but it was not necessarily “a stumbling block”, Winton said in a video podcast posted on X on August 11. “The fact that Tesla owns its own factory there is really an anomaly … and an underestimated testament to Elon Musk’s ability to navigate political choppiness in different ways,” Winton said. Rather than addressing the questions raised by the podcast directly, Musk responded on X with an endorsement that has become commonplace for the CEO. “China is awesome. I strongly encourage people to visit.”

title: Opinion | What Sputnik couldn’t do to American science, Beijing has
description: The US’ new tech strategy shows Washington is adopting the core lesson of China’s rise: tech leadership is a national security imperative.
content: The US government owns 9.9 per cent of Intel, converted out of US Chips Act grants, alongside a golden share in US Steel, US$400 million in the rare earth mining firm MP Materials and stakes in roughly 30 firms worth US$26.7 billion. In 2025, Nvidia and AMD gave up 15 per cent of their China chip sale revenues in exchange for export licences. The country that spent four decades advising its allies against picking winners now runs a portfolio. The United States has not fully turned to state capitalism, but it has accepted something it resisted for 80 years. Technological leadership is a security objective in its own right, pursued with the instruments of security policy rather than an economic advantage that pays security dividends. The National Security Science and Technology Strategy, unveiled on August 18 and the first such document bearing this name since Bill Clinton’s in 1995, is where that proposition appears in writing. Most of it reads as such documents often do. Then comes a sentence that gives away the game: the US should avoid contests where capable adversaries can readily counter its moves and should not spend on replicating what a rival has already built better. Countries do not redraw the board while they are winning. Washington has adopted the tactics of a fighter with reach who declines to trade blows in the clinch: keep it long, concede the inside, win where your arms are. That is rational enough, and also what fighters do once they have felt their opponent’s power. The rest of the document follows from that concession. Foreign investment, firms and personnel touching American research face tighter scrutiny, though a presidential memorandum had already turned the Committee on Foreign Investment in the US against Chinese money in strategic sectors in February 2025. Research security has gone from a compliance chore to a branch of statecraft. Three domains are ring-fenced for battlefield advantage – undersea, space, artificial intelligence and autonomy – above an enabling technologies list running through hypersonics, directed energy, semiconductors and nuclear energy. The strategy document reaches furthest into American life through alignment. Agencies are steered towards milestone contracts with competing vendors, told to place federal money where it complements private capital rather than crowding it out, and to expedite clearances so expertise moves between laboratory, firm and department at commercial speed. The universities enter the same architecture through vetting. The scale registers only against what it replaces. Franklin D. Roosevelt asked Vannevar Bush, director of the Office of Scientific Research and Development, in 1944 how wartime science might serve the peace. Bush’s answer, delivered to Truman the following year, was that Washington should pay for basic research and then decline to direct it, since nobody could say in advance which inquiry would bear fruit. Harry Truman vetoed the first attempt to create the National Science Foundation (NSF) and it was not until 1950 that the foundation was established, but the principle held: the state funded, the scientists chose. When Sputnik was launched in 1957, the US answered with money, students and two new agencies: Nasa and the directed military research shop that became the Defence Advanced Research Projects Agency. Both came into being alongside the NSF rather than take its place, and scientists still chose. The Soviet Union frightened the US for 30 years without changing how it organised science. China has managed it in about 10. A reversal in the US position is unlikely. The technology strategy document exists because the Chips and Science Act requires the government’s science office to produce one after every National Security Strategy. Export controls began under US President Donald Trump’s first term and have continued to grow since. Particular mechanisms will be litigated, and some will be abandoned. The premise beneath them has survived two changes of party, and no serious candidate in either proposes restoring what came before. The strategy commits the US to attracting top-tier global talent in critical national security fields. Even so, a new Department of Homeland Security rule that takes effect from September 15 caps student visas at four years in a country where doctoral and postdoctoral programmes usually take longer to complete. The strategy did not write that rule, which is the point: it promises talent that another arm of the same government is turning away. The regime also taxes what it defends. Vetting deters the collaborations it exists to make safe, and money directed at named technologies is money withheld from the unnamed. This was Bush’s point as the transistor was not on anybody’s list of priorities. The grant machinery has been reshaped to match this new paradigm. By April, the NSF had made 613 awards this financial year, a fifth of its 2021-24 pace, with the National Institutes of Health at about 10,000 awards against a normal 18,000. Building a fabrication plant takes about 18 months. A condensed-matter physics programme takes the better part of a decade, and the process begins with a high school graduate choosing between Michigan and Munich. Washington has learned the lesson Beijing taught it: technological leadership is a security objective, not an economic advantage that pays security dividends. However, the advantage the US is defending was built by attracting the people who made the discoveries and giving them room to work. A state can buy Intel, subsidise a fab and fence off a supply chain. It cannot command the next transistor into existence. That is decided by the people still willing to come to Ann Arbor and Berkeley, and whether the US looks like the place to do it.

title: Who is Shiyazh Pete, the first Navajo Nation player to sign an NFL contract?
description: Pete, who was recently released by the Dallas Cowboys to the disappointment of many fans, went viral for his locker room speech this month.
content: Shiyazh Pete, an offensive lineman and NFL hopeful who turned heads earlier this week after a video of him giving an empowering locker room speech to his teammates went viral, has been released by the Dallas Cowboys. The disappointing news was announced on August 31 by Pete’s agent, Brett Tessler, via X. “The Dallas Cowboys are releasing my client Shiyazh Pete (OL, Kentucky). Had a memorable pre-season and should get the opportunity to continue developing somewhere this season,” Tessler wrote. The news is not only a setback for Pete but also for his fans who support him as the first member of the Navajo Nation to sign an NFL contract. Here’s everything you need to know about the 23-year-old. Shiyazh Pete is from the Navajo and Salish tribes Pete was born in May 2003 in Ronan, Montana to parents Natani and Geraldine Pete. Pete’s father Natani is a captain in the US Army and is from the Salish and Navajo tribe, while his mother is Navajo. According to the UK Athletics website, Pete speaks basic Navajo as well as some American Sign Language. Standing an impressive 205cm tall, Pete has played sports since he was young and learned martial arts early on, notes the Navajo Times. He also wrestled, ran track and cross country and even played basketball. It wasn’t until he was in the seventh grade that Pete played his first American football game and fell in love with the sport. Pete said in an interview with the Navajo Times that football had made him “more of a good person.” “I feel like I can talk honestly with people a lot more than I used to, and it’s a good way to know people, and the brotherhood that you expand and create in football is very worthwhile and something that I cherish,” he said. He excelled in both sports and academics Pete was attending Red Valley-Cove High School in Arizona, but later transferred to Shiprock High after teachers noticed his potential in both athletics and academics and recommended to his parents that he transfer. At Shiprock, Pete attained a 3.8 GPA while taking college-level courses and won two leadership awards from the school’s American football programme. He is the first Navajo to sign with the NFL Pete continued to pursue the sport in college and played a season for the University of Kentucky in 2025 after four seasons at New Mexico State University. It was during his time at Kentucky that Pete caught the eye of Cowboys offensive line coach Conor Riley, who scouted him. After going unselected in the 2026 NFL draft, Pete signed a three-year deal with the Dallas Cowboys as an undrafted free agent. Pete became the first Navajo player to sign with the NFL. While Pete may not have made it onto the Cowboys’ roster, he may still sign with another NFL team or continue as a free agent.

title: Perfumes from Tom Ford, Aesop, Byredo and Penhaligon’s that inspire wanderlust
description: These heady, atmospheric eaux de parfum evoke destinations around the globe, from Taormina in Sicily to Mumbai, Cairo and Marrakech.
content: Let these uplifting, emotion-stirring fragrances from Tom Ford, Aesop, Byredo and Penhaligon’s take you on an olfactory journey to trending destinations around the globe. Perhaps their scent will even inspire a physical journey to explore one of these places for real. Tom Ford Taormina Orange Tom Ford Beauty’s Private Blend Taormina Orange Eau de Parfum (US$305/50ml) has a sharp citrus scent that captures the spirit and essence of the charming resort town perched on the cliffs of Sicily. Byredo Mumbai Noise Luxury fragrance brand Byredo’s Mumbai Noise Eau de Parfum (US$235/50ml) is a dark, woody and spicy scent that celebrates the vibrant contrasts of the city. It contains notes of davana, coffee, tonka beans and sandalwood. Penhaligon’s Cairo British perfume house Penhaligon’s is loved for its theatrical scents and fancifully decorated glass bottles. This Cairo Eau de Parfum (US$300/100ml) showcases profiles of Damask rose and saffron with warm vanilla. Aesop Marrakech Intense Be whisked away to the Red City with a single spritz of Aesop’s Moroccan-inspired scent. Marrakech Intense Eau de Parfum (US$158/50ml) features a blend of woody, spicy and floral notes.

title: Mistrial declared in Lindsay Clancy child killings case
description: Jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether the former nurse was criminally responsible for the deaths of her three kids.
content: A judge declared a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial on Friday after jurors said they could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for killing her three young children. The mistrial, on the seventh day of deliberations, leaves the case unresolved and allows prosecutors to take the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse to trial again. Neither Clancy, her family nor the jury showed any emotion as the judge announced the mistrial. The deliberations took a dramatic turn late in the week when Judge William Sullivan said he was going to declare a mistrial on Friday before suddenly changing course and giving her defence lawyer a chance to appeal to the top court in Massachusetts. The emergency appeal was quickly denied. The trial has generated intense interest for more than a month, deeply dividing the public and drawing attention to issues around maternal mental health after childbirth. Clancy’s lawyer said she was suffering from a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her children, the youngest just eight months old, then tried to take her own life. Prosecutors, who said Clancy knew what she was doing, now must decide whether to put Clancy on trial again, drop the charges or try to negotiate a plea deal with her lawyer. Prosecutors said Clancy acted deliberately when she strangled five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan Clancy with exercise bands on January 24, 2023. They said she contrived to get her husband out of the house by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, never disputed that she killed the children but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she had postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth. Over 21 days of testimony, jurors heard how Clancy’s mental health had collapsed after Callan’s birth. Deeply anxious about a planned return to work, unable to sleep and experiencing what she described as a disturbing brain fog, Clancy sought care from experts in post-pregnancy mood disorders, who prescribed multiple psychiatric medications. Clancy’s family members testified that she expressed concern about her mental health decline. Her former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, described her as a “very nurturing, very loving mother” who was “begging for help”. In early January, she checked herself in to a psychiatric hospital for more intensive treatment, but her stay was short. She killed the children 19 days after she was discharged, leaving their bodies in the basement of the family’s home in coastal Duxbury, Massachusetts. Clancy jumped from a second-story window immediately after and remains paralysed from the waist down. Prosecutors conceded that Clancy had severe mental illness, but insisted she was able to understand and control her actions. They emphasised that although she claimed to have heard a male voice commanding her to kill the children, she never disclosed hearing voices to her mental health providers before the killings. In its latter stages, the trial became a battle of medical experts. Kirk Heilbrun, a forensic psychologist hired by prosecutors to evaluate Clancy, testified that he did not believe her story about having heard voices. And he said he did not believe she had acute psychosis when she killed the children, but rather took their lives so they would not “suffer” after she killed herself. Phillip Resnick, a forensic psychiatrist who testified for the defence, said that Clancy was “clearly psychotic” and was not in control of her actions. “It was almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings,” said Resnick, who spent hours interviewing Clancy after the killings. He said she was also likely to have been experiencing bipolar disorder. At the start of the trial, Clancy’s ex-husband Patrick Clancy described the horror of returning home to find his children. Prosecutors played a seven-minute emergency call in which he could be heard finding the bodies. In interviews, he has said he has forgiven her and believes her actions were the result of mental illness. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller
description: The US was the only vote against the resolution for a shift to the Equal Earth cartographic projection over the traditional Mercator map.
content: The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe. Aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the US voted against it and six other states abstained. The new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”, the resolution said. It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569. Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps “guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions”. “They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation.” The US, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are “the reason this institution is losing its credibility”. “Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice,” US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote. The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate – in part due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map. It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America. A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger. “Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe,” said one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, in 2025. France – which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map – announced on Friday that it would abandon the Mercator projection. In that map, “the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or Southeast Asia”, while “Greenland appears almost as big as Africa”, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said. “Changing maps obviously doesn’t change the world,” he said. “But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth.” The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

title: Trump threatens to cut trade with some countries if Fed doesn’t lower rates
description: The message suggests the US president is running out of patience with the central bank just months after Warsh took over from Powell.
content: President Donald Trump intensified pressure on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates, threatening to cut off trade with certain economies with which the US has a deficit if the central bank does not act. Trump issued his demands on Friday in a lengthy social media post after a stronger-than-expected August jobs report, which could bolster the case for Fed officials to raise rates at their next policy meeting starting September 15. In his post, the president exhorted his hand-picked Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he called “great”, and board members to “get smart” and “BE PATRIOTS for a change”. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” Trump posted. “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!” Trump said the US Supreme Court, which struck down his previous tariff regime, had acknowledged his authority to do that. But if he moves forward with trade embargoes, it would almost certainly trigger a legal challenge. It was unclear how such an action would help lower US borrowing costs. The message shows that Trump is running out of patience with the Fed just months after Warsh took over from Jerome Powell, whom the president routinely attacked over the bank’s policy decisions. Trump had pulled back on his pressure campaign against the Fed after Warsh became chair, but the post amounts to a resumption of it. The president’s approval ratings have plummeted ahead of November’s midterm elections, as polls show Americans have panned his handling of the cost of living and the war in Iran. US jobs growth unexpectedly surged in August, with non-farm payrolls adding 162,000 positions, and the unemployment rate held steady. Investors boosted bets on a rate hike at the Fed’s upcoming meeting in response, sending stocks and short-dated bonds lower. Trump, who regularly touts a booming stock market as vindication for his policies, bristled at the slide in a subsequent post. “We just got GREAT Numbers on Jobs, the Market should go UP, because our Credit and Economy are better but, as always, for the past 25 years, the Stock Market goes DOWN, because we’re living under False Reality that if things are good, you’ve got to ‘KILL IT’ because of a ‘fear’ of Inflation,” Trump said. The president went even further than his top White House economic adviser, Kevin Hassett, who earlier on Friday said that the jobs numbers strengthened the case to keep interest rates the same. “We respect the Fed’s independence, but I think the argument for holding steady would be pretty strong,” Hassett said on CNBC.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? is a haunting Vietnam war drama
description: The Vietnam war drama, in competition at the Venice Film Festival, explores trauma, redemption through a US Marine’s true-life journey.
content: 4/5 stars “We were taught to treat Asians like they were less than human,” says Allen Nelson in Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People?, a true-life drama about a former US Marine faced with a reckoning. Screening in competition at this year’s Venice International Film Festival, this often powerful work is based on Nelson’s memoir of the same name. Somewhat surprisingly, Shinya Tsukamoto, the cult Japanese director behind Tetsuo: The Iron Man (1989) and Bullet Ballet (1998), adapted it in what is only his second English-language production. As the end credits tell us, this New Yorker was buried in Japan; in that country alone, he gave more than 1,200 talks about his horrifying experiences in the Vietnam war. How he reaches the point of being able to share his trauma is the film’s true focus. It starts with a young Nelson (Mark Merphy) sleeping rough in an abandoned building after returning from Southeast Asia. A chance encounter leads an old school friend to implore him to speak to the children she teaches about his time overseas. Barely able to utter a word, he is left floored when a girl asks the very question that forms the film’s title. Elegantly weaving elements of Nelson’s life before, during and after Vietnam, the film asks not if he killed, but why. This question certainly occupies his therapist, Dr Daniels (Geoffrey Rush), whose sessions with the older Nelson (Rodney Hicks) provide the backbone of the story. Ravaged by PTSD, Hicks’ Nelson is a mess of a man, plagued by night terrors – to the point where he almost strangles his wife, Linda (Tatyana Ali), in front of his young stepson, Sean. The flashbacks to Nelson’s time in the Marines are harrowing, with Tsukamoto showing his penchant for extreme violence – sometimes a little too gleefully – as Nelson’s platoon rips through villages. “Don’t think. Follow orders. Kill,” he is told, but he has no idea why. “We fight for freedom … black people not free in America,” screams one Viet Cong soldier, and there is a genuine sense here that Nelson and his fellow grunts were simply programmed to kill, then discarded on the scrap heap. Powered by a terrific, haunting performance from Hicks, best known as a playwright and theatre actor in the US, the film is a striking but never sentimental psychological portrait from Tsukamoto. Far from his comfort zone, and all the better for it, the director pays tribute to Nelson – a man who learned to address his demons in a way few ever do. Alongside Spike Lee’s 2020 film Da 5 Bloods, Mr. Nelson, Did You Kill People? is a crunching reminder of the senseless horrors of the Vietnam conflict. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: 5 EU nations plan to send rejected migrants to non-EU ‘return hubs’, target 2027
description: Rights groups have criticised the plan, arguing that European nations cannot guarantee the rights of migrants would be respected.
content: Denmark and four other European Union countries agreed on Friday on a model for “return hubs” in non-EU nations and hope to begin sending migrants to the facilities as early as 2027, an official said. The announcement, made after a one-day meeting in Copenhagen, is the latest development in an effort by EU states to send people whose asylum requests have been rejected to third countries outside the bloc. “We are moving forward towards what is actually a fundamental transformation of the common European migration and asylum system,” said Morten Bodskov, Denmark’s minister of immigration and integration. He briefed reporters alongside counterparts from Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece. The five countries have been negotiating with governments mainly in Africa over potential sites, pioneering the initiative for the whole of the EU. Human rights groups have criticised plans to deport migrants to centres or prisons in third countries, arguing that European nations cannot guarantee their rights will be respected there. Bodskov rejected the idea that “return hubs” were a euphemism for detention and deportation centres and said the International Organization for Migration and the UN Refugee Agency would monitor the centres. “We are not talking about camps, we are talking about opportunities, for a new chance for irregular migrants who cannot return to their own country today and who have no legal grounds to be in our countries,” Bodskov said. The UNHCR said that it “has not been approached with details of such a proposal”, and therefore “cannot comment on the specific arrangements being discussed or on what any potential role for UNHCR might entail”. Although the ministers did not specify which third countries were being considered, Bodskov said they expect to reach their first deal by early 2027. He acknowledged that the concept of “return hubs” was mocked only a few years ago and deemed incompatible with EU and international law. EU laws, however, have changed due to public and political pressure for tougher measures against irregular migration. European lawmakers voted in June to allow member states to set up centres outside the EU on their own or in small coalitions, and send rejected asylum seekers there instead of to their home countries. “This is something new and it’s groundbreaking,” said Bart van den Brink, the Netherlands’ minister of asylum and migration. In early August, a spokeswoman for the Rwandan government said it “was natural” for her government to negotiate with European countries and others to potentially host asylum seekers who were not allowed to live elsewhere. Speaking to Royal FM Kigali, Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo cited an emergency transit mechanism established in Gashora in 2018 for people evacuated from Libya, who could stay there until they were resettled in third countries. Makolo said one of the ideas discussed was to offer a “safe place” where people who have nowhere else to go could get medical care, training and rest while their asylum applications were processed, until they could go back home if safe or get resettled to yet another country. “We want to be part of a solution to a big global problem,” Makolo said. It remained unclear what countries in negotiations with EU nations would gain in return for taking Europe’s rejected migrants. Migrant rights groups have criticised European efforts to set up migrant centres abroad where it may be difficult to monitor and enforce human rights. In an emailed statement, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O’Flaherty, said that “vague assurances of compliance with human rights law are not enough”. “States need to commit to the guardrails necessary to prevent setting up human rights black holes,” he said. The European ministers in Copenhagen emphasised that the new hubs would abide by European and international law. Van den Brink, the Dutch immigration minister, said technical talks and missions to potential partner countries would be used “to gain more insight into the human rights situation and the living conditions of the refugees”. “Because we want to do this in a European way, in line with our values and international law and human rights at its core.” Brussels-based rights group PICUM condemned the meeting in Copenhagen. “EU leaders may call these centres an ‘innovative solution’, but outsourcing migration control is an old tactic to simply move people out of sight and evade human rights obligations,” group director Michele LeVoy said.

title: Why the EU is giving Arctic shipping the cold shoulder as China and Russia push ahead
description: Its opposition to the commercialisation of Arctic transit comes amid rising anxiety over Beijing and Moscow’s closer polar collaboration.
content: As Beijing and Moscow double down on the Arctic shipping route, Europe is hitting the brakes. Despite being the main destination for goods along the route and accounting for most of the world’s shipping giants, Europe opposes the commercialisation of Arctic transits, wary of fragile polar ecosystems and navigational risks amid rising anxiety over Russia and China’s closer polar collaboration. “In Europe, cooperation between China and Russia on container shipping is often viewed as another example of deepened collaboration between the two countries in the Arctic since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022,” according to Patrik Andersson, an analyst at the Swedish National China Centre at the Swedish Institute of International Affairs. Andersson said the collaboration fitted into a broader partnership, which in recent years had expanded to include joint military drills in Arctic-adjacent areas, coastguard cooperation in the Arctic Ocean and joint projects in the mining and energy sectors. Europe’s concerns are reflected in an updated EU Arctic policy that is expected to be issued later this year. In recommendations for the policy released late last year, the European Parliament warned that expansion of Sino-Russian ties in energy, infrastructure and polar shipping “risks consolidating a geopolitical axis of resource exploitation and restricted access”. The recommendations proposed condemning Russia’s restrictions on freedom of navigation on the Northern Sea Route, which runs along Russia’s Arctic coast from near the Barents Sea to the Bering Strait. The position underscores a long-standing rift between Brussels and Moscow over the route’s legal status. Moscow has long claimed special jurisdiction over the Northern Sea Route – a major segment of the Northeast Passage – invoking Article 234 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos), also known as “the Ice Clause”, to enforce strict “non-discriminatory” environmental and navigational regulations “over ice-covered areas” in its exclusive economic zone. However, the European Union has pushed back, arguing that shrinking sea ice owing to climate change undermines Russia’s legal basis to invoke the Ice Clause for control. The EU further contends that Moscow’s transit restrictions and bans on foreign military vessels are discriminatory and clearly violate Unclos. In its recommendations, the European Parliament called for applying international law to counter efforts that either legitimise contested shipping corridors or project geopolitical influence under the guise of scientific or economic cooperation. Europe is concerned that commercialising the route could cement Russia’s control and development of the Arctic. Echoing these concerns, Karen van Loon, a research fellow in the security and defence programme at the Clingendael Institute, a Dutch think tank, noted that payment for use of the route directly fed into Russian state interests. “A service that routinely pays for Russian permits, icebreaker assistance, pilotage or other infrastructure supports a transport corridor operated by the Russian state,” van Loon said. “It also helps Moscow present the Northern Sea Route as a successful international project despite its isolation from Europe.” She added that receiving a vessel did not imply legal recognition of Russia’s authority over the route, allowing European countries to accept port calls while still challenging Moscow’s claims under international law. Alongside the tensions between the EU and Russia, major European shipping giants, especially top container carriers, have reaffirmed their commitment to steer clear of Arctic transit. They are driven mainly by environmental concerns, doubt over commercial viability and severe navigational hazards. “For many Western shipping companies, the geopolitical and reputational risks so far outweigh the commercial incentives,” Andersson said. Asked if, like its Chinese counterparts, Maersk would consider the Arctic route as other maritime chokepoints are squeezed, Vincent Clerc, CEO of the Danish shipping giant, told Bloomberg TV last month that he did not view the passage as a meaningful substitute. Beyond environmental concerns and extreme weather unpredictability, the route “relies on sanctioned Russia to provide icebreakers and escorts throughout those waters”, Clerc said, describing the route as unlikely to play a significant role in global shipping in the coming years. The head of MSC, the world’s largest container shipping company, had a similar view. “Our position at MSC is clear. We do not and will not use the Northern Sea Route,” Soren Toft, CEO of the Geneva-headquartered company, said in January. “Safe navigation cannot be assured. “The risks for crews remain too high. And increased traffic would put additional pressure on fragile ecosystems and local communities.” In 2019, four of the world’s five largest shipping companies – MSC, Maersk, CMA CGM and Hapag-Lloyd – signed a voluntary commitment launched by Ocean Conservancy, a Washington-based marine environmental NGO, pledging not to send ships through the Arctic. China’s Cosco Group did not sign the pledge. With the Arctic warming four times faster than the rest of the world, its ecosystems were already under intense stress, Ocean Conservancy said, noting that unpredictable or even perilous conditions made each trip hazardous. “Shipping companies comprising more than 60 per cent of global container capacity have decided that Arctic shipping is not worth the risk,” it said. “We strongly agree.” European analysts have questioned the route’s overall commercial viability, despite the time savings and the ability to bypass geopolitical conflict zones. Andersson said the savings in time and fuel were offset by high insurance premiums, the need for specialised ice-class vessels and elevated operational costs in harsh Arctic conditions. The economic impact of Europe staying away from the route was negligible, he said. Meanwhile, the risks are real. According to global insurer Allianz Commercial, Arctic shipping presents a markedly higher risk profile than conventional trade routes. Operational risks dominated Arctic waters, with machinery damage and failure accounting for nearly half of all reported casualties. Last month, a Russian tanker suffered serious damage to its hull while navigating through Arctic sea ice, resulting in an insurance payout of 53 million roubles (US$609,000), according to Russian insurer AlfaStrakhovanie. The Russian insurer said icebreaker assistance did not eliminate the physical risks associated with Arctic navigation. The Arctic’s remoteness and lack of infrastructure, such as port state control, tug availability and repair facilities, also made these risks particularly acute, said Captain Anastasios Leonburg, senior marine risk consultant at Allianz Commercial. For shipping in polar waters, the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) international code provides the regulatory baseline by requiring vessels to obtain a polar ship certificate based on ice conditions. But Leonburg said the framework, in force since 2017, was inadequate on its own. Major marine insurers were applying improved due diligence requirements for Arctic transits, mandating pre-voyage surveys and specific warranties regarding vessel suitability, crew competence and operational planning, he said. “We expect these requirements to become more widespread and more rigorous across the industry as traffic volumes increase,” Leonburg said. Enforcing stricter compliance could help Europe regain some leverage, van Loon said, adding that Europe’s strongest influence lay not in competing with Russia for control of the route but in the ports and commercial services needed for ships using it to reach European markets. European authorities could use sanctions screening, insurance and financial rules, as well as environmental and safety standards, to determine the conditions under which vessels using the Northern Sea Route entered European ports, she said. European countries are already putting this strategy into practice. Last December, Denmark, joined by France, Germany and the Solomon Islands, submitted a proposal to the IMO requiring ships operating in the Arctic to switch to cleaner fuels to reduce black carbon emissions. The move illustrates how Europe is using stricter environmental compliance to assert its influence over polar shipping. However, Jian Junbo, director of the Centre for China-Europe Relations at Fudan University in Shanghai, said Europe should not view the Northern Sea Route solely through a geopolitical lens. He argued that European environmental and safety standards could improve governance along the route and should not be used to obstruct its development. “A shipping route is an international public good that should be accessible to all countries,” Jian said.

title: US job market rebounds with 162,000 new jobs, far surpassing expectations
description: The latest labour data may increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise its key short-term interest rate at its next meeting.
content: The US job market rebounded in August as employers added a surprising 162,000 jobs. The unemployment rate stayed at a low 4.1 per cent. The jobs report, issued by the Labour Department on Friday, could be good news for President Donald Trump two months before midterm elections in which the health of the economy is weighing on voters’ minds. Hiring far exceeded the 65,000 forecasters had expected, according to a poll by FactSet. Labour Department revisions also looked good, adding 55,000 to June and July payrolls. Employers created 21,000 jobs in July; the Labour Department had originally reported that they would cut 23,000. Restaurants and bars added 59,000 jobs last month, construction companies 22,000 and manufacturers 16,000. And the US labour force – the number of people working or looking for work – jumped by 683,000 last month after falling in June and July. Yet many households are struggling with the high cost of living, and wage gains are not helping much. Average hourly wages rose 3.1 per cent last month from a year earlier, the weakest year-over-year increase since May 2021. Friday’s report may increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise its key short-term interest rate when it next meets on September 15-16. Solid hiring sends a signal that current borrowing costs are not necessarily high enough to restrain the economy and cool inflation. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said last week that inflation, at 3.7 per cent according to the Fed’s preferred measure, remained too far above the central bank’s 2 per cent target, and added that without further progress, they would have “work to do”. With hiring seemingly healthy, the Fed’s focus will shift to a critical inflation report that is being released next week. On Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller said he was leaning towards keeping the Fed’s rate unchanged, but would support a hike if inflation comes in high. Contributing to inflation is the struggle that US employers have had dealing with a shortage of workers – the result of Trump’s immigration crackdown and the retirement of baby boomers. Some are responding by using technology for tasks that human beings used to do. Employers have been reluctant to let go of the staff they have, so most Americans enjoy unusual job security and unemployment is low. “It’s a very strange labour market,’’ David Kelly, chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, wrote in a commentary on Monday. The No 1 puzzler: hiring is weak, but lay-offs are rare. Employers have not been eager to take on new workers. The Labour Department reported Tuesday that gross hiring – before subtracting people who lost or left their jobs – fell 5 per cent to fewer than 5.1 million new jobs. The United States does not need as many jobs as it did until recently to keep the national unemployment rate from rising. Trump’s immigration crackdown and baby boomer retirements mean fewer people are available for work. More than 1.3 million people have dropped out of the US labour force over the past year. As a result, the “break-even’’ rate of monthly hiring, 155,000 in 2023-2024, has dropped, perhaps to nearly zero, according to a Federal Reserve study. Instead of looking to hire from a diminished pool of available workers, “businesses are increasingly focused on boosting efficiency through technology and AI and increasingly seek to do more with their existing workforce”, EY-Parthenon economists Gregory Daco and Lydia Boussour wrote in a commentary this week. Even if they are not hiring aggressively, companies are reluctant to let go of the staff they have. They retain memories of the unexpected labour shortages that followed the end of COVID-19 lockdowns. So unemployment remains low. For the past year, the number of people applying each week for unemployment benefits – a proxy for lay-offs – has stayed in a historically low range of around 200,000 to 230,000. The result is what economists call a “no-hire, no-fire” labour market in which those who have work enjoy job security, but times are tough for young workers trying to land entry-level jobs or unemployed people seeking to get back to work.

title: 2 floors of Rumsey Street car park to close for 6 weeks for Interpol meeting use
description: Hong Kong police plan to take over the seventh and eighth floors of the Rumsey Street car park in Sheung Wan for six weeks from November.
content: A public multi-storey car park in Hong Kong’s central business district will be partially closed for about six weeks from November as the city prepares to host a meeting of Interpol’s top governing body for the first time. Hong Kong police plan to take over the seventh and eighth floors of the Rumsey Street car park in Sheung Wan to set up a traffic coordination command centre. “The centre is planned to accommodate 240 electric cars to be used by participants of Interpol’s general assembly travelling to and from the airport, hotels and meeting venues,” the police force said in a paper to be tabled for discussion at a meeting of Central and Western District Council next Thursday. “The seventh and eighth floors of the car park will be used as a traffic coordination command centre from November 1, 2026. After the general assembly concludes, it will reopen to the public on December 12.” The car park was chosen because it was on Hong Kong Island and close to hotels and the meeting venue, “which is conducive to the coordination and dispatch of vehicles” for the conference, police said. The 94th Interpol general assembly will be held from November 30 to December 3 at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai. While Hong Kong is making its debut as host, it marks China’s third time, with Beijing having hosted in 1995 and 2017. The general assembly is Interpol’s highest governing body, with member countries gathering to discuss international policing issues and foster collaboration. Interpol has 196 member countries. Hong Kong participates as part of China’s Interpol national delegation, operating locally as a sub-bureau under Beijing’s National Central Bureau. City officials have said that hosting the event in Hong Kong serves to demonstrate the professional image of the city, while Hong Kong police are committed to enhancing collaboration within the global law enforcement community. Police said they would monitor traffic conditions and take measures to ensure smooth traffic flow around the car park while the two floors were closed. The Rumsey Street facility is one of 10 government-run multi-storey car parks. It has nearly 1,000 parking spaces for cars, vans, and motorcycles. The top floors of the building are occupied by government offices while the lower levels are used as a public car park.

title: IVF clinic’s embryo specimen mix-up linked to ‘intentional unlawful conduct’
description: Watchdog says it has ordered Heal Fertility to comply with law and code of practice to prevent recurrence of similar incidents.
content: A mix-up of embryo biopsy specimens may have been caused by “intentional unlawful conduct” at a private fertility clinic, which breached the code of practice for reproductive technology by lacking sufficient protective measures, a Hong Kong regulator has found. The Council on Human Reproductive Technology said on Friday that, following an investigation into the incident, it had ordered service provider Heal Fertility to comply with the Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance and the code to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents. “The council confirmed that no embryos were mixed up or wrongly implanted into the human body in the incident,” it said. The council also put the clinic’s licence under review. It concluded that “intentional unlawful conduct by an individual” was the main cause of the embryo biopsy specimen mix-up at Heal Fertility’s clinic in Central. The council said it would continue to provide professional support to police in an ongoing criminal investigation into the case. The incident came to light earlier this year when a genetic testing laboratory at the Chinese University of Hong Kong found that embryo biopsy specimens sent by Heal Fertility did not belong to the intended patients. Only one of seven specimens from the first woman was hers, while neither of two specimens attributed to the second woman was correct. The clinic, which opened in 2023 as part of the New Frontier Group co-founded by former financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung, was notified of the mismatches on May 26 and June 4. The council subsequently suspended most operations at the clinic. Council chairman Professor Raymond Liang Hin-suen said the Department of Health had filed a police report. A Malaysian employee responsible for extracting the specimens was interviewed by police in late July but left Hong Kong the following day and resigned. She is now wanted in connection with a fraud investigation handled by the organised crime and triad bureau. Heal Fertility apologised to affected clients and submitted an internal investigation report to health authorities on July 29. The council also noted that Heal Fertility, after identifying the mix-up, did not report the incident to the department within the required time frame. It reminded the clinic that all licensed day procedure centres must strictly comply with licence conditions set by the Council, the Department of Health and relevant codes. While Heal Fertility has since implemented improvement measures regarding the handling and storage arrangements of embryos and embryo biopsy specimens, the council’s assessment of the clinic’s response remained guarded. “There is still room for further enhancement in Heal Fertility’s overall performance and operational arrangements,” it said. The council said it had drawn up improvement requirements, would issue a formal letter on Friday and reinspect the premises before making a licensing decision. Until then, Heal Fertility may only provide three services related to the storage of gametes or embryos. Separately, the council has resolved to review the code of practice, targeting completion next year. Key areas include strengthening the incident reporting mechanism and optimising security and handling procedures for biological samples.

title: Play-off win by Hong Kong Bulls no guarantee of Chinese Basketball Association league spot
description: To win promotion, a team in second tier must finish in top two of NBL, beat a CBA team in a play-off and then be screened by China officials.
content: Hong Kong Bulls will earn the right to compete in the top tier of the Chinese basketball league if they finish in the top two of the National Basketball League this season and beat one of the two lowly Chinese Basketball Association league teams in a two-leg play-off. However, a play-off series win would not guarantee straight passage to the top tier for any teams, but only the right to be screened – using several guidelines – by Chinese basketball officials. Teams will then face an anxious wait of 60 days before learning their fate on the CBA website. While the set of documents released by the sport’s governing body in China was billed as “seeking advice” from the clubs, sources told the South China Morning Post that it would be the final decision and would be implemented next April to bring back the promotion and relegation system – for the first time since 2005 – between the two leagues. The soon-to-be-announced promotion and relegation system differs from previous versions reported by Chinese media. Still, senior Bulls executives believe “all is good”, given the three-time defending champions had shown their ambition over the past few seasons. “We proved last year [during the pre-season CBA Cup] that NBL teams were capable of challenging CBA teams,” Bulls general manager Leo Sun Xinwei said. “[The plans were not] the same as what were circulated before, and there will be no expansion to 21 teams for the next season, but it is understandable. “If four NBL teams manage to crack into the top tier all at once, it might bring a negative effect to the CBA, so the current plans could be slower, allowing capable teams to go up, and ensuring a smoother transition. “There isn’t any impact for us as we don’t aim to finish second, third or fourth. We always want to win the league, the play-off tie and prepare ourselves for the new chapter.” The admission checklists for the two Chinese leagues were expected to be similar, with teams awaiting promotion needing to comply with “more than 50 requirements”, including salary cap compliance checks, team training facilities and match arenas. “I’d say the arena could be our biggest issue regarding the CBA assessment,” Sun said. “Even the NBL has such an assessment, and that’s why we couldn’t play at Southorn Stadium, as it didn’t meet the league’s requirements.” The next NBL season, which runs from late November to early April, could feature as many as 21 home matches – including the play-offs – for the Bulls, but the team reckon “we could probably host six to 10” at Kai Tak Arena. That number would only grow in the top-tier league. In the past three seasons, CBA teams have had to play 21, 23 and 26 regular-season games at home. Finding a permanent arena for their home matches, whether in the NBL or the CBA, has long been the priority of the Bulls officials, but plans to renovate Southorn Stadium “will take more time”, said a spokesman for the Hong Kong Playground Association, which owns the multi-purpose arena in Wan Chai. “This remains an active project,” Stefan Ma said. “Due to its complexity and the need to integrate various suggestions, the process will take time. “We will continue working on it to enhance our facilities for the users and public.” The Bulls have also stepped up and purchased their own NBA-calibre floor to be used at Kai Tak when they play there, drastically reducing the floor changeover time at the arena from “approximately three days to just four hours”. “We intend to always host our home matches in Hong Kong; we do not want to do it across the border if it’s manageable,” Sun said.

title: Chinese team extracts uranium from seawater at 8 times the US target rate
description: Researchers developed a material that they say opens up a ‘novel approach’ to recover the nuclear fuel from the world’s oceans.
content: Chinese researchers have found a way to extract uranium from seawater at several times the target rate set by the US Department of Energy, putting China at the forefront of a global quest to tap into a vast source of nuclear fuel. The team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Qingdao did this using a material they developed called PhosCage – a sponge-like molecular structure filled with phosphate groups that act as chemical traps. In a statement, the researchers said they had recovered up to 50.4mg of uranium for every gram of the adsorbent from natural seawater samples – more than eight times the US target of 6mg per gram. They then turned PhosCage into millimetre-sized beads that are easier to deploy and retrieve in the open ocean. The beads captured 22.55mg per gram and continued to work through seven cycles of reuse. “This work opens up a novel approach to extracting uranium from seawater and lays the groundwork for adsorbents that can capture more uranium and eventually be used on a large scale,” the team from the CAS’ Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology said in the statement. The technology could be particularly important for China, which has sizeable uranium reserves but uses far more than it produces as it expands the use of nuclear power. In 2024, domestic mines produced just 1,600 tonnes of uranium – a fraction of the roughly 13,000 tonnes required by its nuclear reactors, according to the World Nuclear Association. That has left China heavily reliant on imports. The world has about 7.9 million tonnes of known uranium resources on land. But the oceans hold an estimated 4.5 billion tonnes, much of it accumulated over time as uranium was washed from rocks by rain and carried by rivers into the sea. The Mediterranean alone contains an estimated 12 million tonnes of uranium – enough to meet the world’s current nuclear fuel needs for about 180 years. But getting at it is extremely difficult. A tonne of seawater contains only about 3.3mg of uranium, so the element must be sifted from vast quantities of water. And uranium is not alone. Seawater is a soup of dissolved elements, some far more abundant than the prize itself. Vanadium is especially troublesome because it can stick to the same chemical traps, making the two difficult to separate. For years, scientists at US Department of Energy national labs in Tennessee and Washington have tried to crack the problem. Oak Ridge National Laboratory developed special fibres that grab uranium, while Pacific Northwest National Laboratory tested them in flowing natural seawater from Washington’s Sequim Bay. By 2016, the best US adsorbents were collecting around 6mg per gram after extended exposure to seawater. But the method remained far more expensive than land mining, and the DOE largely pulled back after its programme wrapped up in 2018. The Qingdao team’s work overcame some of the major extraction hurdles, according to two papers published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials and Separation and Purification Technology. For instance, in tests with several metals present, the bead-like material showed a clear preference for uranium, including over vanadium – one of the hardest elements to separate from it. However, the experiments have limitations. The researchers collected seawater off the coast of Qingdao and ran 25 litres (6.6 gallons) of it through a laboratory flow system, instead of leaving the adsorbents in the open ocean, where waves, currents and marine life would make the job much harder. Meanwhile, neither study put a price on the uranium it recovered. The researchers said further work would focus on scaling up the materials and bringing down the overall cost of extracting uranium from seawater.

title: Thailand suspends building of 49 data centres as resource strain concerns grow
description: The move comes as governments the world over are tightening oversight of data centres even as tech investments in such facilities surge.
content: Thailand’s embrace of data centres hit a speed bump after the government suspended construction of 49 server farms as public concerns about the power-hungry facilities’ impact on communities intensify. The projects were halted to give officials time to develop new industry regulations, expected to be announced in a month, Danucha Pichayanan, secretary general of the National Economic and Social Development Council, said at a press briefing on Friday. Danucha spoke after the first meeting of the country’s data centre supervision commission, led by Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas. “Today’s decision doesn’t mean Thailand is closing the door to data-centre investment because the industry is critical to the country’s competitiveness,” Ekniti said. “We simply want clear and consistent standards in place to ensure the industry can grow sustainably.” Thailand would establish uniform oversight of data centres in operation as well as those being developed, Danucha said. Governments the world over are tightening oversight of data centres as the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence has led to a surge in such facilities. Global data centre spending is set to reach US$31.6 trillion through 2050 to meet the world’s growing appetite for AI, an investment boom with no precedent in history, according to PricewaterhouseCoopers. At the same time, the tech industry, led by US giants such as Microsoft and Amazon.com, is trying to blunt a backlash against data centres that threatens to slow the buildout. At least 75 projects, worth about US$130 billion combined, were blocked or delayed by local opposition during the first three months of this year, according to research group Data Centre Watch. Protesters cite concerns about environmental impact, resource consumption and more broadly how AI could upend employment and society. In the US, the data centre backlash is becoming a force in the November midterm elections. Thailand is experiencing a proliferation of data centres as tech investment soars. The Southeast Asian nation has emerged as a regional destination for AI and cloud infrastructure as global technology companies including Alphabet’s Google, Amazon and Microsoft build out data centre capacity. In May, the government approved TikTok System (Thailand)’s data infrastructure expansion, including data-hosting services, servers and storage facilities. The government approved 88 projects with a total investment of 886 billion baht (US$27 billion) related to artificial intelligence and data centres in the first six months of the year, according to Board of Investment data. Tech investment in the first half has already surpassed the 623 billion baht recorded for all of 2025. Data centres’ drain on power and water is now causing the government to rethink its approach to the industry. It is weighing higher electricity rates for large data-centre operators and stepping up scrutiny of projects in densely populated areas after concerns emerged over facilities being developed in central Bangkok. Bangkok authorities temporarily halted approvals for three other projects after complaints over a data centre being built next to a hospital exposed a regulatory gap that allowed such facilities to seek permits as warehouses, Governor Chadchart Sittipunt told reporters before the meeting on Friday. There should be some environmental impact reviews of data centres, he said. Nationwide, 35 data centres are now in operation, while 117 proposed facilities are awaiting investment approvals, according to Danucha.

title: Robot guide dog debuts in China amid severe lack of furry counterparts
description: With wheels and four legs, aid for visually impaired people represents push to expand AI and robotics into more applications.
content: A Chinese defence industry research facility has unveiled what it calls the world’s first wheeled and legged robot guide dog for visually impaired people, in an example of the sector’s push into a growing range of civilian applications. Hangzhou-based Zhiyuan Research Institute, affiliated with China North Industries Group, the country’s largest defence contractor, launched the robot, dubbed Xiaoyuan, on Friday at the China Care and Rehabilitation Expo in Beijing. Equipped with wheels for smooth movement on flat ground and four legs for climbing stairs, the robot was designed to help visually impaired people navigate independently, according to the institute. The wheeled design allowed the robot to move quietly, an important feature for those who rely on their hearing to perceive their surroundings, the institute said. Meanwhile, it could also identify overhead obstacles such as low-hanging branches, which could be difficult to detect with traditional mobility aids such as canes. The robot offered centimetre-level outdoor positioning accuracy, with an error margin of less than 30 centimetres, while its obstacle-avoidance success rate was at least 99 per cent indoors and 96 per cent outdoors, according to the institute. Xiaoyuan is connected to services including disability federation systems, an accessibility map and a remote assistance portal for volunteers, allowing users to seek help remotely when needed. China has more than 17 million people with visual impairments, according to a report by state-run Xinhua News in May, citing the China Association of Persons with Visual Disabilities (CAPVD). By comparison, the country has only around 400 guide dogs in service, according to CAPVD, which added that a guide dog costs around 200,000 yuan (US$29,776) and takes about a year to train. The institute said it had reached strategic cooperation agreements with disability groups in the eastern province of Zhejiang, its capital Hangzhou and Inner Mongolia, and had begun pilot deployments and trials at locations including Hangzhou’s metro system and shopping centres. Other developers are also working on expanding the application of robotics and AI in China. For example, Beijing-based AI Robotics and Hangzhou-based RoboCT have developed exoskeleton robots used at hospitals and rehabilitation centres to help patients regain mobility.

title: Why are fuel and petrochemical prices outpacing crude – and how long will it last?
description: Global refined-product exports were down 25 per cent year on year in August, with losses concentrated in Russia and the Persian Gulf, analysts say.
content: This summer, David Chen, a Chinese national living in Japan, got an unexpected lesson in global industrial supply chains – delivered through a bag of potato chips. When popular Japanese snack brand Calbee replaced its signature colourful packaging with monochrome designs, Chen initially assumed it was a marketing gimmick. “Then news reports explained the switch stemmed from a naphtha supply crunch. I even looked up the word,” Chen said. Naphtha, a flammable liquid processed from crude oil, might not be a household name, yet it serves as a foundational input in polyester fibres, packaging and industrial solvents. The squeeze has prompted Japanese media to coin a new term: “naphtha bankruptcies”, reflecting mounting anxiety among some companies over securing vital oil-derived inputs. A June survey by corporate research firm Tokyo Shoko Research underscored the widespread impact, finding that about 80 per cent of more than 7,000 responding firms had difficulty procuring oil-derived products. However, behind Japan’s localised squeeze lies a wider strain on global supply. According to late-August estimates by Goldman Sachs analysts led by Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby, global refinery outages – which take refining capacity offline or force facilities to reduce output – stood 60 per cent above seasonal norms. Market and industry analysts attributed the tight conditions to two main pressures: mounting geopolitical conflict and fuel export controls from China, which has the world’s largest oil-refining capacity. “At first, the industry blamed supply-side tensions on falling crude oil supplies driven by the US-Iran conflict. But June marked a turning point,” wrote Ni Ji, an analyst at Shanghai-based Orient Securities, in a mid-August report. Combined with supply shortfalls, oil-derived product prices are extremely likely to stay elevated Yan Lili, Xinhu Futures While the temporary reopening of the Strait of Hormuz in June eased crude supply constraints, prices for petroleum products stayed much firmer, Ni added. “That was when the industry realised global refinery outages were the real driver,” he wrote. Yan Lili, an analyst at Zhejiang-based Xinhu Futures, said the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine had severely affected global fuel production. “Disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz have forced some Asian refineries heavily dependent on Middle East crude to shut down or scale back output. In parallel, Ukrainian drone strikes have targeted Russian refineries, pushing Russian refinery runs to their lowest level since 2024,” Yan said. At the same time, Beijing imposed temporary curbs on fuel exports in March after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The restrictions, intended to safeguard domestic supplies, were lifted in July, but Yan cautioned their effects were still being felt. “Even though the curbs have been removed, we expect fuel export volumes to remain constrained within the year,” Yan noted. According to the August research note by Goldman Sachs, total global exports of refined products fell 25 per cent year on year in late July and August, with the Persian Gulf and Russia accounting for 75 per cent of the decline. Market analysts said there was no immediate fix for the supply squeeze, while Goldman Sachs analysts projected global refinery processing levels would return to seasonal norms in the second half of next year. As outages have dragged on, prices for major oil-derived products, including jet fuel, have significantly outpaced crude since March. Data from the International Air Transport Association showed the global average jet fuel price last week stood at US$156.85 per barrel, marking a 74.2 per cent year-on-year rise. Brent crude futures, by comparison, had climbed about 30 per cent year on year as of August 28. The Goldman Sachs analysts estimated that average diesel and jet fuel profit margins were still triple last year’s levels, while dated Brent was up “only” 34 per cent year on year. “China will soon enter its peak fuel consumption season, and Northern-Hemisphere winter will further boost diesel demand. Combined with supply shortfalls, oil-derived product prices are extremely likely to stay elevated,” warned Yan of Xinhu Futures. Still, industry analysts said the unusually high profit margins were not enough to spur large-scale global investment in new refineries. “Led by Europe, developed economies have long been unwilling to expand refinery throughput amid high costs and carbon-reduction constraints, not to mention the rapid advance of electric vehicles,” explained Ni of Orient Securities. Against this backdrop, some ambitious Chinese companies that expanded overseas in earlier years could be well placed to benefit. “Refining assets stand poised for a market re‑rating,” wrote Chen Kangdi, an analyst at Shanghai-based Guolian Minsheng Securities, in a mid-August research note. The first phase of the Brunei refining-petrochemical complex, in which Zhejiang-based private firm Hengyi Industries holds a 70 per cent stake, has 8 million tonnes per annum of crude distillation capacity. A second phase is getting under way this year. “Constrained by China’s fuel export quota regime, the Brunei facility can sell fuels directly to global markets. This creates considerable asset scarcity and the complex stands to keep benefiting from higher prices,” Chen added. PetroChina, which has interests in several overseas refineries, posted first‑half net profit of 103.9 billion yuan (US$15.48 billion), up 22 per cent year on year. Chokwai Lee, a director of equity research at US-based Morningstar Equity Research, said in a late-August report that these robust earnings reflected PetroChina’s “strengthened upstream integration” as well as solid trading returns in its marketing segment.

title: Hong Kong Marathon expects to welcome record number of runners after increasing quota
description: Organisers also announce the new 5km harbourfront run and expanded youth run, both set to be staged 24 hours before the main races.
content: The 2027 Standard Chartered Hong Kong Marathon will welcome a record 78,000 runners after significantly increasing its half-marathon quota in a quest to “further promote long-distance running, elevate race standards and increase the scale of the event”. A new 5km harbourfront run and expanded youth run, both set to be staged 24 hours before the main races happen on Sunday January 17, will swell overall competitor numbers to 84,000. Explaining the decision to raise their half-marathon numbers from 25,000 to 29,000, the Hong Kong, China Association of Athletics Affiliates (HKAAA) said they had “recognised the strong demand” for the 13.1-mile (21.1km) event and its “role as a crucial stepping stone to the marathon”. First staged in 1997, the SCHKM will next year celebrate its 30th birthday. Kwan Kee, chairman of HKAAA, said his governing body had “always been committed to developing the SCHKM into one of the highest-standard long-distance running events in the region”. “Completing a half marathon is a vital milestone for runners who are progressing towards the marathon, so our historic decision to increase the half-marathon quota will broaden the pathway for more experienced runners and mark a new chapter in the SCHKM’s development,” Kee added. Beginning on Nathan Road in Tsim Sha Tsui and finishing in Victoria Park, the men’s and women’s full marathons boast a combined prize pot of US$314,800. Melaku Belachuw of Ethiopia won last year’s men’s race, nine years after he first claimed the Hong Kong title. Women’s honours went to Bahrain’s Shitaye Eshete. Stretching from Kai Tak Sports Park to Shing Kai Road Garden, the inaugural harbourfront run has space for 3,000 competitors. The youth run, aimed at 10-to-15-year-olds, is increasing its quota from 2,500 to 3,000 participants.
