Haze is a recurring seasonal problem in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and peat fires in Indonesia can travel across national borders and affect neighbouring Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore. Sarawak has been the worst-hit Malaysian state by the haze, with several areas having hazardous air levels in the past few days. The haze this year has been particularly severe, with elevated fire activity in several provinces in Indonesia, including Kalimantan, and prolonged dry conditions contributing to worsening pollution across parts of Borneo. Satellite data from Indonesia’s Forestry Ministry on Friday detected 717 hotspots nationwide likely caused by forest fires since August 1. The data showed 103 active hotspots in the past 24 hours alone. Indonesian authorities have deployed firefighting resources and attempted to induce rain. Indonesian police announced on Friday that they had arrested 112 people suspected of starting the recent forest and peatland fires in 10 provinces on Sumatra and Borneo islands. The suspects were local farmers accused of deliberately burning land to clear areas at lower cost. Indonesia has also suspended the business licenses of five companies over alleged forest and land fires within their concessions in the Kalimantan province. Pipit Subiyanto, a senior police official at Indonesia’s National Police criminal investigation agency, said authorities were investigating 167 cases involving the deliberate burning of some 4,700 hectares (11,700 acres) of land across nine provinces.

title: India’s push to secure place in global chip supply has ‘secret weapon’: its people
description: Building up its pool of design talent can gain it a spot higher up in the value chain by turning ‘Make in India’ to ‘Engineer in India’.
content: India is betting big on domestic manufacturing of semiconductors – the microscopic brains that power everything electronic from cars to AI processing – in an ambitious bid to slash imports and boost its local industry. But observers say the country should set its sights even higher upstream on the value chain by mobilising its “secret weapon” – a talent pool that could realise its dream to turn “Make in India” into “Engineer in India”. New Delhi earlier this week launched the second phase of its mission with a budget of US$13 billion to build an industrial ecosystem spanning chip design to manufacturing. Building on the first phase, which focused heavily on foundational industrial set-up, the second expands support across the entire supply chain, including developing a large manpower pool. The move on Monday comes as other countries in the region, such as Japan and Singapore, outline multibillion-dollar development plans for their semiconductor industries following chip shortages during the Covid-19 pandemic that exposed dependency on a handful of East Asian manufacturers. Delhi has already approved 12 semiconductor manufacturing projects across six states. Three – Micron, Keynes Semicon and CG Semi – have started commercial production this year. They primarily handle assembly, testing and packaging rather than advanced wafer fabrication. An industrial partnership between India’s Tata Electronics and Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation plant in the western Indian state of Dholera is targeting to roll out its first batch of chips in December. Tata also signed a US$11 billion memorandum of understanding with Dutch technology giant ASML on May 16 to make advanced chips for industries ranging from car manufacturing to AI. In for the long-term Analysts say that building a semiconductor industry ecosystem requires strong implementation and planning over the long term because it needs a complex value chain divided into design, fabrication, as well as assembly and testing. “Establishing a complete semiconductor ecosystem is a marathon, not a sprint,” said Anndy Lian, a Singapore-based adviser to governments on information technology systems. He suggested that India build not only fabrication units for complex microchips and integrated circuits but also downstream systems to handle back-end processing after they are made. “These are less capital-intensive and faster to operationalise than fabs, allowing the country to build a skilled workforce and supplier network while major fabs remain under construction.” Hard infrastructure is also vital because highly sensitive semiconductor manufacturing needs pure water, uninterrupted power and specialised chemicals. “A single voltage fluctuation can ruin a wafer batch. India must create plug-and-play industrial parks where utilities are guaranteed to international standards, not just promised,” Lian said. Though India has lagged behind in semiconductor manufacturing such as the US, China and Taiwan, it has a strategic advantage because it has been a hub for semiconductor research and design. It has the world’s largest pool of chip design engineers – but lacks fab-floor operators – responsible for day-to-day manufacturing of silicon wafers – and process engineers who transform raw silicon into working microchips. Bolstering its large talent pool would be a crucial “secret weapon” for India in gaining a competitive edge, Lian said, urging public-private partnerships with universities offering specialised semiconductor curricula. “The goal should be to move from Make in India to Engineer in India.” According to a report by government think tank NITI Aayong in May, India imports 90 to 95 per cent of its semiconductors. This dependence could become a major economic and strategic vulnerability as domestic demand is projected to exceed US$200 billion by 2035. India’s Information Technology Minister Aswini Vaishnaw told reporters earlier this month that the country had set a target of developing 100,000 engineers for the semiconductor industry. The global semiconductor industry is projected to face a shortage of about 1 million workers by 2032. India has already achieved its target of developing 85,000 semiconductor engineers in four years, against a target timeline of 10 years, according to the minister. Semiconductor design programmes are now offered in 355 universities across India, including institutions in smaller towns and cities. Chip consciousness In addition, the federal government runs programmes subsidising up to 50 per cent of project costs for semiconductor manufacturing, supplemented by support from state governments. Indian policymakers were conscious about the criticality of semiconductors in technology systems, said Sunil Sinha, an economics professor at the Institute for Development and Communication in Chandigarh. “That is why there is a serious effort to increase semiconductor production in India. Still, the issue is not just production of chips but what generation chips you are producing. Is it something on which AI can ride upon?” he asked. Raj Kapoor, founder and CEO of India Blockchain Alliance said that the second phase of India’s semiconductor mission showed there was growing recognition that the challenge would be to not just build fabrication facilities but an entire ecosystem to support them. While the Tata-ASML agreement showed India’s intent for advanced chipmaking, the true test would be translating that into access for the country’s longer-term semiconductor ambitions, he said. India’s strategy is notably different from the technological race pursued by the global semiconductor leaders to produce cutting-edge chips. Delhi appeared more focused on manufacturing chips where “demand remains substantial and barriers to entry are lower”, Kapoor said. Still, Sinha said, even the most basic chips would have a significant economic impact because that meant local industries would not need to import them.

title: Chinese armed trainer jets drive away Philippine aircraft over Scarborough Shoal
description: At least three JL-10s carrying PL-5 missiles were involved in incident at disputed atoll in what could be a more cost-effective tactic.
content: China sent armed trainer jets to drive away Philippine light aircraft over the disputed Scarborough Shoal on Wednesday, in a potentially more cost-effective tactic for its increasingly frequent air confrontations over the South China Sea. At least three JL-10 trainers carrying PL-5 air-to-air missiles were involved in the incident over the shoal, according to a video clip posted to social media by the People’s Liberation Army Southern Theatre Command. The footage showed the Chinese jet’s electronic systems locking onto three Philippine aircraft, identifying their models as a BN-2A Islander utility aircraft, a C-208 single-engine turboprop and a PA-31T twin-engine turboprop. A green crosshair was also shown tracking one of the aircraft. “Philippine aircraft, you have intruded into the territorial airspace of China’s Huangyan Dao. Leave immediately, leave immediately. Otherwise, we will take measures,” a Chinese pilot was heard saying in both Chinese and English over the radio. Scarborough Shoal – a coral atoll which is known as Huangyan Dao in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines – has been a major flashpoint between the two countries in recent years. China has controlled the area since 2012 and released baselines for the territorial sea around it in 2024. The Philippines – which challenges the Chinese claim with occasional ship and aircraft activities in the area – filed its own territorial sea baselines for the shoal with the United Nations in July. “Such patrols are aimed at further enhancing control of relevant sea areas and airspace and serve as an effective countermeasure to cope with all sorts of rights violations and provocative acts,” the PLA Southern Theatre Command said in a statement. The PLA’s multirole heavyweight J-16 fighter jet and an H-6 strategic bomber were also seen in the video, but it was the first time JL-10 trainers armed with air-to-air missiles have been shown taking the lead role in such an operation. It came after the Philippines sent the same three light aircraft to patrol over Scarborough Shoal on August 21. The light aircraft fly at relatively low speeds, with the slowest capable of only about 260km/h (162mph) – well below the minimum controllable speed of modern high-speed fighter jets. According to a commentary on state broadcaster CCTV, this creates an asymmetric challenge for Chinese fighters tasked with tracking, escorting and warning these targets whose flight characteristics are vastly different. The JL-10, meanwhile, has good low-speed manoeuvrability. The twin-jet lead-in trainer has a minimum controllable speed of around 210-260km/h and can carry a range of missiles and guided bombs to launch an attack if needed. It is also significantly cheaper to buy and operate than the J-16 fighters. The trainer is estimated to cost about US$10-15 million per aircraft on the international market, compared with nearly US$100 million estimated for a J-16. The PL-5, a short-range infrared homing missile, first entered service in the 1980s. Although it is no longer among the most advanced air-to-air missiles in the PLA Air Force’s inventory, pairing the relatively inexpensive missile with the JL-10 provides a cost-effective option for dealing with slow-moving aircraft. Wednesday’s operation was apparently also a PLA training exercise, with a trainee pilot heard in the video telling his instructor that it was good to see the South China Sea for himself. Previously, the PLA had mainly deployed much more expensive combat aircraft for such missions. In October last year, the Philippine Coast Guard claimed a Chinese J-16 had engaged in “aggressive interference” with a Philippine reconnaissance aircraft carrying journalists. Last month, the PLA Southern Theatre Command deployed H-6K bombers with advanced heavyweight supersonic YJ-12 anti-ship missiles for a joint exercise around Scarborough Shoal.

title: Bargain sale, collapsed deal reflect Hong Kong’s struggling retail property market
description: While North Point shop deal falls through, former home of Insomnia bar in Lan Kwai Fong sells for 60 per cent less than its 2015 value.
content: A foreclosure sale in Hong Kong’s Lan Kwai Fong area and a cancelled shop transaction in North Point reflect the impact of weak consumer spending on Hong Kong’s retail property market, which will remain under pressure through the end of the year, according to analysts. The Lan Kwai Fong property, home of well-known bar Insomnia until it closed in 2024, recently changed hands for 60 per cent less than its value in a 2015 sale. Meanwhile, the deal for the large street shop on King’s Road in North Point abruptly fell through after two months. The retail property market would continue to struggle through the end of the year because banks were unwilling to lend, while the future outlook depended on whether they were prepared to loosen the credit taps, said Edwin Lee, founder and CEO of Bridgeway Prime Shop Fund Management. “There are still many foreclosed properties on the market, but the biggest issue is that banks are taking a very cautious stance on commercial real estate mortgages,” he said. “For large-scale transactions exceeding HK$50 million [US$6.4 million] – or even over HK$100 million – buyers are often required to pay all cash. Since very few buyers have the financial capacity to do so, owners are forced to offload properties at steep discounts.” The former home of Insomnia, Shop A on the lower ground floor of Ho Lee Commercial Building at 38, 42, and 44 D’Aguilar Street, recently sold for HK$58.68 million, reflecting a price of about HK$18,178 per square foot, according to market sources. Market records showed that the original owner bought the shop for HK$168 million via a corporate acquisition in 2015, at the peak of the retail property market. In early 2024, the owner listed the shop for sale with an asking price as high as HK$250 million. Over the subsequent years, the property suffered a paper loss of more than HK$109 million, representing a decline of over 60 per cent. Insomnia’s shutdown came amid a slump for nightlife establishments as Hongkongers increasingly opted to travel to Shenzhen for leisure and consumption. The property ultimately fell into the hands of receivers and was put up for multiple auctions. However, Lan Kwai Fong remained a valuable location – a unique cultural and entertainment landmark that had been emulated by cities across mainland China, said Stanley Poon, managing director at Centaline Commercial. “Even with the retail property market currently in a slump, the location’s strong appeal ensures that a monthly rent of just over HK$200,000 remains competitive,” he said. “Based on the latest transaction price, the projected yield exceeds 4 per cent, suggesting the buyer has secured a bargain at a ‘rock-bottom’ price.” Meanwhile, Shop B on the ground floor of the Chu Kee Building at 433-437 King’s Road in North Point registered a transaction at HK$48.8 million in June, according to Land Registry records. However, the sale of the property, which has about 2,000 sq ft of gross floor area, was cancelled on Wednesday. Land Registry records showed that the property is owned by Tin Yick Hong Realty, a long-established local commercial property investor, which bought it for HK$75 million in September 2013. Lee said that the large ground-floor shop involved in the cancelled transaction was currently leased to Korean eatery Seoul Noodle Shop at a monthly rent of HK$150,000.

title: Asian Games: triathlete Brown ready for assault on glory, questions remain over Elg’s fitness
description: Hong Kong head coach Andrew Wright also states that Oscar Coggins could claim gold in Japan and book his Olympic spot.
content: After a protracted period of being stalked by injury and illness, Bailee Brown is “100 per cent” fit for an assault on Asian Games glory this month, but teammate Robin Elg is training alone as he grits his teeth through a stubborn shin complaint to race in Japan. A mixed relay bronze medallist in 2018 and 2023, Brown required four surgeries on a badly broken finger following a trail running fall in December 2024. Months earlier, she suffered from an E coli infection and norovirus, while more recently Brown was laid low by a bone stress problem. “She’s showing no signs of having any issues and is back on a full run programme,” Andrew Wright, the Hong Kong head coach, said. “As these guys get older, they’re able to [mentally] cope better with setbacks. Everyone at a high level is dealing with something, you just don’t always hear about it.” The situation for Elg is far more complicated. Following the National Games last November, when he was part of Hong Kong’s silver medal mixed-relay team, Elg was diagnosed with a stress problem in a fibula. “We’ve not been able to shift it, no matter what tactic we’ve tried, or which intervention we’ve used,” Wright said. “This thing is just persistently there.” While his teammates had a 4½-week altitude camp in mainland province Yunnan, before transferring to their current Thailand base, Elg has stayed in Hong Kong to use an AlterG Anti-Gravity treadmill, which allows him to run at a lower percentage of his body weight and minimise impact on the offending bone. Wright said Elg was “running big sessions that will translate nicely onto the road”, but acknowledged that the combination of being isolated from teammates, and having no answer for his leg pain, had been “extremely difficult” for the athlete. “It’s very up and down in terms of mental health when you’re going through injury and not with your team, but he has a very good support network around him,” said Wright, adding that if Elg was ever “feeling so overwhelmed that he couldn’t handle it” he would immediately join the city squad overseas. “We haven’t really thought too much beyond the Asian Games, because I don’t think it’s necessarily useful when there are so many unknowns,” Wright said. Wright has finally been granted his wish for a concerted unbroken training block with Cade and Tallulah Wright, the twins who will join Brown in the Hong Kong women’s team in Japan, and who are no relation to the coach. Tallulah Wright finished her international relations degree this summer, while Cade has one more year of her mathematics degree remaining. “It’s been massive to have them with us, and we’re at a stage where none of the athletes have been this fit,” Andrew Wright said. “They’ve never operated on such a professional level, and I’m really glad to see it. It’s not that common in Hong Kong to get people to this stage.” Andrew Wright said long-time stand-out Brown was profiting from the sisters beginning to compete on her level. “You don’t want to be far better than anyone else and not have that positive pressure, because you don’t get the best out of yourself in those conditions,” he said. “It’s a big problem in Hong Kong where there’s nobody coming up and putting pressure on these guys, then they’re subconsciously too comfortable in their position as the best in the team.” After the Games mixed-relay on September 21, Cade Wright will dash from Nagoya to Spain to compete in the under-23 World Championships four days later. “It doesn’t help Olympic qualification, but there are some races where if an athlete really wants to do them, there’s value in it,” Andrew Wright said. Looking forward to Los Angeles in two years, Wright said it was a “one hundred per cent realistic” prospect that Oscar Coggins, his leading male, could claim Asian Games gold and book his Olympic spot. Coggins finished 33rd in the Tokyo Games in 2021. “He’s been flawless the entire year, and he’s operating like a world-class athlete,” Wright said. “It’s amazing to see and to be around every day, and very inspiring. It’s going to be the hardest Asian Games by a long way, but I’ve never seen him this fast across all three disciplines. We’re aiming for the top spot, for sure.” Two high-profile city triathletes not in the Asian Games team, Jason Ng Tai-long and Hilda Choi Yan-yin, are training in Hong Kong with a view to qualifying for November’s Asia Triathlon Sprint Championships in Jordan.

title: Who is ‘Boston’ singer Stella Lefty’s billionaire father, Eric Lefkofsky?
description: Lefty has been making headlines for the wrong reasons lately – but what do you know about her Groupon co-founder dad, worth an estimated US$5.5 billion?
content: Stella Lefty is one of the biggest overnight sensations of 2026. Her breakout country-pop hit “Boston” peaked at number 2 on Billboard’s Hot 100 chart, and her debut album Long Way Home is currently No 4 on the Top Country Albums chart. Unfortunately, the 24-year-old singer-songwriter’s burgeoning success has done little to keep controversy at bay. First, listeners noticed a resemblance between “Boston” and singer Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season”, but Lefty claimed in an interview with Vanity Fair that she “wasn’t thinking about Noah Kahan” when she wrote the song. She ultimately credited Kahan as a co-writer on the track. An even bigger discourse around her success involved her perceived status as a so-called nepo baby or an industry plant. Lefty, whose real name is Stella Lefkofsky, is the daughter of Groupon co-founder Eric Lefkofsky, whose net worth is estimated to be US$5.5 billion, per Forbes. Here’s everything to know about Eric Lefkofsky. What’s Eric Lefkofsky’s background? Eric Lefkofsky was born on September 2, 1969, to a structural engineer father and a teacher mother, according to Grubstakers. He hails from Southfield, Michigan, and attended the University of Michigan, where he earned a bachelor’s degree before completing his Juris Doctor at its law school, according to How They Did It. The 57-year-old is married to philanthropist Elizabeth Lefkofsky and has three children, including two sons and daughter Stella, per Vanity Fair. He has several companies View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tempus (@tempus.ai) Lefkofsky’s entrepreneurial career began at university, when he launched a carpet-selling business after splitting from a girlfriend, writes Forbes. His biggest breakthrough came with the e-commerce company Groupon, which he co-founded with Andrew Mason and Brad Keywell in 2008. The Glencoe, Illinois-based businessman is also the founder and CEO of Tempus, an AI-powered precision medicine start-up, which, in 2024, became his fourth company to go public. He founded the venture after his wife, Elizabeth, was diagnosed with breast cancer and his daughter’s friend, Olivia, passed away from cancer. Lefkofsky also founded the companies MediaBank, Echo Global Logistics and InnerWorkings and co-founded Lightbank and Pathos AI. “In my adult life, I’ve started five companies. I’ve basically had five good ideas in 20 years,” he said, per Forbes. In 2006, Eric and Liz Lefkofsky established the charitable Lefkofsky Family Foundation, and they are heavily involved in philanthropy. Lefkofsky has also written the book Accelerated Disruption: Understanding the True Speed of Innovation (2007). He introduced Stella Lefty to country music Speaking to music magazine The Line of Best Fit, Lefty recalled growing up listening to country music because her father would play it in the car. She referred to him as “the biggest Swiftie”, her “favourite person on the planet” and her “musical everything”, who once listened to Brad Paisley and Tim McGraw in the car with her after her first break-up.

title: Malaysian prince ‘more than happy’ to pay US$1.6 billion levy linked to Singapore land deal
description: Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim, who is reportedly looking to sell a 16.6-hectare site in Singapore, says he is willing to absorb levies in both countries.
content: The son of Malaysia’s king has dismissed a report that a potential tax bill of more than S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) is complicating his plans to sell 16.6 hectares (41 acres) of land in Singapore, saying he was “more than happy” to absorb levies on both sides of the causeway. “As a regular taxpayer, this is normal. No complication and more than happy to contribute to both countries. Should make it double,” Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim posted on social media on Thursday, hours after the Bloomberg report emerged. The crown prince of Johor, Malaysia’s closest state to Singapore, even cheekily added the hashtag #gameisrigged, which he often uses when criticising football-related issues. According to the report, Ismail is looking to sell a 16.6-hectare site in Singapore’s Tyersall Park area, where the Johor royal family has owned land for more than a century. The plot, which reportedly included a parcel the prince obtained through a land swap with the Singapore government last year, would be worth between S$3.8 billion and S$4.7 billion if rezoned, Nicholas Mak, chief research officer at local property portal Mogul.sg, told Bloomberg. Singapore’s Urban Redevelopment Authority said Ismail had applied to develop the land for residential use in March. It proposed rezoning the land to allow for the development of mansions known as good class bungalows and low-rise housing. Under Singapore law, rezoning a property would incur a levy known as a land betterment charge. Mak estimated this could range from S$2.5 billion to S$2.7 billion while another analyst, Tay Kah Poh, first vice-president of the Valuation and General Practice Division of the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers, said it could be as high as S$3 billion. The tax, payable to the Singapore Land Authority, would have to be settled by the land’s owner at the time its development is approved. Bloomberg reported that the prince was asking the buyer to foot the bill, resulting in some Singaporean and Malaysian property developers balking at the additional cost. As a result, Ismail’s representatives were looking for buyers from the US and elsewhere, its sources said. Ismail is the eldest son of Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, Malaysia’s current king and one of the country’s richest men. The Johor royal family has a net worth of around US$5.7 billion, according to a Bloomberg estimate. A sports enthusiast, Ismail owns Johor Darul Ta’zim football club and was president of the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM) from 2017 to 2018. Last November, when the FAM was embroiled in a scandal involving seven heritage players, the prince said he would absorb the cost of bringing their case to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

title: Louis Koo’s production firm disputes HK$149m lawsuit, says claim ‘incomplete’
description: One Cool Film Production accuses Sino Hero Ventures of breaching confidentiality principles and omitting that it was dissolved for three years.
content: Hong Kong film actor and director Louis Koo Tin-lok’s production company has rejected allegations that it owes HK$149 million (US$19 million) in outstanding debts to an offshore firm, saying the claim is incomplete and violates confidentiality principles. In a statement published on social media on Friday, One Cool Film Production said the civil lawsuit lodged by Sino Hero Ventures on Wednesday had concealed crucial details about a HK$70 million loan extended to Koo’s film production business in September 2019. “The case presented by the plaintiff is incomplete. In particular, the plaintiff did not reveal the fact that [it] had been removed from the company registry and dissolved for nearly three years, during which we could not contact its authorised personnel,” the statement said. The defendant in the High Court case also alleged that the plaintiff, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, had unlawfully disclosed details of their agreement that were protected by legal privilege. “The company reserves all rights to pursue the matter. We will handle this matter with lawyers in a solemn manner,” the statement added. Koo, one of Hong Kong’s most recognisable home-grown film stars, has appeared in more than 110 local productions after rising to fame as a television actor in the late 1990s. The 55-year-old won best actor trophies in both the Hong Kong Film Awards and Asian Film Awards in 2018 for his performance in the action thriller Paradox. He was also recognised abroad last year, winning the Extraordinary Star Asia Award at the New York Asian Film Festival. He played a leading role in the 2024 blockbuster martial arts film, Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In, which has rekindled public interest in the Kowloon Walled City. According to the latest lawsuit, Koo and his company failed to repay the HK$70 million loan and interest by a 2022 deadline. The writ claimed the total outstanding amount had snowballed to HK$149.4 million as of August 27. The artist was separately sued by a business partner two years ago for allegedly defaulting on the repayment of an HK$8.3 million loan related to a fashion joint venture.

title: Who was Gloria Steinem’s late husband, David Bale – the father of Christian Bale?
description: The celebrated feminist has died at age 92 – we look back at her life and legacy, including her marriage to environmental and animal welfare advocate David Bale.
content: Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author and activist who became the most visible symbol of the US women’s movement and remained a fierce and eloquent advocate for equality for six decades, has died. She was 92. Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, was a hugely recognisable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centres, at rallies and marches. “You can’t do it on the phone or on the web,” she told Associated Press in a 2015 interview. “You have to be there with all five senses. It should be obvious that people can’t empathise with each other unless we’re in the same room.” Steinem, who had been in declining health, died Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to a post on her social media page. She had recently completed a memoir, to be released this fall. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard,” the post said. “Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.” Though Steinem had recently become more frail physically, her wit and humour remained totally intact. Her friend and fellow activist, Abigail Disney, said she’d visited Steinem’s Manhattan home a bit over a week ago, as those close to her gathered by her side. “She was just as funny and just as sharp as I have ever known her,” Disney said. And, she said, generous. “Everything Gloria did was rooted in kindness,” Disney said. “It flowed through her political activism.” Like Steinem, her late husband David Bale – who is the father of actor Christian Bale – was also an activist who dedicated his life to environmentalism and animal welfare. Here’s everything you need to know about Gloria Steinem’s late husband, David Bale. David Bale was born in South Africa David Charles Howard Bale was born in South Africa to English parents, according to the British Heritage website. His father, Phillip Bale, was a Royal Air Force pilot. Bale’s childhood was spent across England, Egypt and the Channel Islands. As an adult, he worked as a commercial pilot “in the hope[s] of establishing air rescue and food supply flights in Africa,” according to The New York Times. Following his years as a pilot, Bale established himself as an entrepreneur and imported skateboards and jeans from Asia into the United Kingdom before moving to America in 1990, as per ABC News. He was married thrice Bale, a passionate activist, worked for various causes throughout his lifetime. He served as a board member of World Education Inc., an NGO dedicated to providing adult education programmes for third-world countries. He was also on the board of the animal rights group, Ark Trust, and worked with the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund International. Bale and Steinem met in 1999 at a fundraiser for Voters of Choice, as per The New York Times. The couple wed in 2000. Their marriage sparked debate at the time as people questioned Steinem’s decision to wed Bale despite her being famously outspoken about her negative outlook towards matrimony and its impact on women. “Though I’ve worked many years to make marriage more equal, I never expected to take advantage of it myself,” the late activist said in a statement released by Voters for Choice that year. “I hope this proves what feminists have always said – that feminism is about the ability to choose what’s right at each time of our lives.” Prior to Steinem, Bale was a two-time divorcee. He wed his first wife, Sandra Kreunen, in South Africa and welcomed daughter Erin Kreunen with her. After they split in 1964, he went on to tie the knot with Jenny James, a British circus performer. Bale welcomed three more children with James; Louise Bale, Sharon Bale, and Christian Bale. The couple divorced in 1991. What did David Bale die of? Only three years into their marriage, Bale died of brain cancer in December 2003. Christian Bale has previously spoken fondly about his father. “There was a great complexity to my father,” the Dark Knight actor told GQ in a 2012 interview. “He was a devoted family man. But, in the same breath, he simply was not suited to an anchored life. He should have been somebody who had a backpack, an old map, a bit of change in his pocket and that was it – roaming the world.” With additional reporting from AP

title: China pushes to speed up key infrastructure builds amid investment declines
description: The NDRC urges faster work on major projects and the six networks initiative to reverse falling investment.
content: China’s top economic planner has held meetings over two consecutive days on accelerating major construction projects, signalling urgency over bolstering fixed-asset investment as economic momentum slows. The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) met with representatives from several ministries on Thursday to review the progress of the 109 major projects proposed under the country’s latest five-year plan. Officials called for accelerating the implementation of ongoing projects and promoted the early commencement of new projects, according to a statement released on Friday. The NDRC also held a meeting on Wednesday on strengthening financing mechanisms for China’s six networks, an infrastructure programme under the five-year plan to upgrade the country’s water, electricity, computing, telecommunications, logistics and underground pipe systems by 2030. Authorities at the meeting called for strengthening of information-sharing with financial institutions, encouraging the participation of private capital and better leveraging the role of government investments, according to a separate statement. The two meetings followed a slew of similar sessions held by the NDRC last month, including a rare national meeting convened last Friday to promote investments in areas such as technological innovation, industrial upgrading and urban renewal, with officials pledging faster disbursement of fiscal funds for major construction projects. Beijing’s priority was now set on boosting investment, said Song Yu, chief China economist at UBS Securities. Overall fixed-asset investment, covering major areas such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction, fell 6.7 per cent in the January-July period. This was despite 2026 being the first year of China’s new five-year plan cycle, which typically sees stronger investment as authorities begin work on planned projects laid out in the new development blueprint. As of August 28, only about 67 per cent of China’s annual quota of special local government bonds had been issued, while 800 billion yuan (US$119.2 billion) of policy financing tools remain unused, according to Song’s estimates in a report on Monday. “The focus is on spending the money [that’s] available now on projects,” Song said. “There could be a round of additional support later in the year, with adjustments to annual bond issuance and other plans.” The decline in investments has dragged on China’s economic growth, which slowed to 4.3 per cent in the second quarter, the softest quarterly expansion since late 2022. China has set a target of expanding its economy by between 4.5 and 5 per cent for the year, but growth has become increasingly uneven, constrained by soft domestic consumption and investment but buoyed by strong exports and the technology sector. The NDRC also held meetings last month to speed up the issuance of the new policy-based financial instruments, increase support for private investment projects, and coordinate support policies for the six networks initiative. On Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang chaired a State Council executive meeting, urging acceleration of construction of the urban underground pipe network, part of the country’s urban renewal push, to eliminate safety hazards at their source and improve urban functions.

title: Can Hong Kong outshine Singapore as central banks rethink gold custody amid global risks?
description: City in race to lure bullion custody as geopolitical risks intensify scrutiny of gold storage, Goldman Sachs report says.
content: As the Netherlands moved gold out of the US and Canada over geopolitical concerns, attention is turning to whether Hong Kong can capitalise on central banks rethinking where they keep their bullion. The city faces competition from Singapore, which is expected to launch central bank gold-vaulting services in October as part of efforts to cement its status as a gold trading hub in Asia. Where central banks chose to store gold came down to three factors, said Iggy Ioppe, a Wall Street veteran with more than two decades of experience across proprietary trading and private capital markets. “Legal certainty, political neutrality and the ability to get the metal out and use it in a crisis without needing anyone’s permission,” he said. “Hong Kong has no capital controls today and free convertibility is foundational policy. [The question] is what a reserve manager believes about them under stress, 10 to 20 years out.” A real gold hub isn’t a vault, it’s a financing rail … That’s what makes London sticky, gold there doesn’t sit, it works Iggy Ioppe, Theo Where central banks stored gold appeared increasingly a growing priority for reserve managers, according to a Goldman Sachs report on August 14. The Bank of England was the top custody location among reserve managers, ahead of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, the report said. But holding gold at these hubs exposed investors to political risk, including freezing or restricted access. Switzerland and France were the most common alternatives for those seeking to diversify beyond the world’s two main gold settlement networks, the report added. Hong Kong should ensure that stored gold “remains beyond the reach of political direction in a genuine crisis, its legal framework offers the neutrality a reserve manager assumes in Switzerland, and its market is deep enough to sell size into without moving the price”, said Ioppe, who is also chief investment officer of Theo, a New York-based tokenisation platform financing the global gold trade. “None of that is unique to Hong Kong, it’s what any new venue must prove.” Ioppe said a “real gold hub isn’t a vault, it’s a financing rail: the ability to lease, collateralise and mobilise the metal around the clock, not just keep it safe. That’s what makes London sticky, gold there doesn’t sit, it works.” Hong Kong is positioning itself as a regional gold trading hub, with plans to expand vault storage capacity to 2,000 tonnes within three years. As part of this initiative, the city recently launched a trial gold clearing and settlement system involving 11 Chinese and international banks. Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing has made its fourth attempt since the 1980s to relaunch its US dollar gold futures contract. The Financial Services and Treasury Bureau said it was “actively promoting Hong Kong’s gold storage, clearing, and risk management services” among Belt and Road economies. InvestHK, the government's investment promotion arm, said Hong Kong holds a strong competitive edge over Singapore in luring central banks seeking to safeguard bullion. The city’s gold trading volume reached 1,700 tonnes in 2025, according to the agency. It was also a crucial conduit for gold flowing into mainland China, which absorbed around one-third of the city’s gold exports for retail, jewellery, central bank reserves and investment, “a role set to be further strengthened by mutual market access in the future”, it added. “This speaks volumes about the paramount importance of stability in the custody of large-volume bullion,” said Benjamin Wong, head of transport, logistics and industrials at InvestHK. Backed by the central government’s support, “Hong Kong has world-class financial infrastructure and a well-established common law system”.

title: How natural disasters are putting China’s neighbourhood diplomacy to the test
description: Sudden Himalayan mudslides and Southeast Asian flooding potentially trigger diplomatic friction and highlight need to boost warning systems.
content: Cross-border disasters along China’s frontiers are putting Beijing’s neighbourhood diplomacy to the test as climate shocks grow and expose strategic vulnerabilities. The stakes were highlighted last week after a sudden glacial collapse in the Himalayas unleashed a torrent of mud and flooding that ravaged nearby villages and the Gyirong Port between China and Nepal, leaving more than 1,250 dead in Nepal and 21 dead in the Tibet autonomous region. Thousands also remain missing. Beyond the Himalayas, a wave of extreme weather also battered China’s southern frontiers, with torrential rain triggering severe flash flooding and landslides on China’s borders with Vietnam and Laos last week. The record floodwater level submerged economic zones and forced the closure of a crucial checkpoint between China and Laos, as well as several key highways and an airport in the developing Southeast Asian country, over the weekend. Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow and director of the Centre for South Asia Studies at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said dealing with climate-driven disasters would be a “new subject” for China’s foreign policy. Amid the bitter power rivalry with the US, China has in recent years shifted its focus to ties with neighbouring countries, which it sees as crucial to national security and a buffer against pressure from the West. At a high-profile central working conference on neighbourhood diplomacy last year, Chinese President Xi Jinping said neighbourhood was the “foundation of security and development” and that maintaining stable ties with immediate neighbours would be a top priority in China’s overall diplomatic strategy. Liu said environmental crises that spilled across borders could threaten this strategic foundation. “Instability across our borders will inevitably affect China, posing a new challenge for China’s peripheral diplomacy,” he said. Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub, said climate disasters were becoming increasingly transboundary in nature – a reality to which China’s foreign policy must adapt. “Environmental shocks no longer stop at national borders, making cross-border climate management an inescapable reality for China’s neighbourhood diplomacy,” Li said. As China and Nepal slowly advance their own rescue operations, the August 26 disaster is potentially a diplomatic flashpoint. Shortly after the deadly floods, sentiment on social media suggested China should bear responsibility. Without evidence, some accused China of not issuing an early warning while others blamed the event on Chinese-built infrastructure in the region. In a social media post, the Chinese embassy in Nepal deemed the theories “fake news”. Chinese researchers have said the disaster was triggered by a sudden collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. On Wednesday, Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told local TV that Nepal was demanding climate compensation from China, the US and India as “a matter of justice”. He said that as the world’s biggest emitters of greenhouse gases, those countries had made “extremely large” contributions to climate change and left smaller nations to pay the price. The statement drew a prompt response from Beijing, with China’s foreign ministry saying climate change should be considered a global challenge requiring the collective efforts of all countries. “We will strengthen cooperation with Nepal and the rest of the world to jointly prevent and mitigate the negative impact of climate change,” ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said. Khanal later shifted his position, telling the Chinese ambassador in a meeting on Thursday that the country would not seek compensation from any specific country, including China, but through international frameworks, such as the UN climate convention and the Paris Agreement, according to a statement from China’s embassy in Kathmandu. Citing Nepalese government sources, Reuters reported that Kathmandu planned to rebuild an early-warning system with seismic sensors, cameras and a satellite link at a border settlement on the same river corridor along the border with China where the glacier collapsed a week ago. Li, in Washington, said the deluge had underscored the need to scale up early-warning systems between China and its immediate neighbours, which he said would be “one of the most effective tools” available to reduce environmental and ecological crises. China shares land borders with 14 countries, making it vulnerable when disasters cross borders. However, managing transboundary natural disasters usually involves issues such as state sovereignty and political trust, according to Liu. Even as satellite technology and remote sensing allow China to monitor cross-border hazards, they may be seen as a security threat by neighbouring countries. “When cross-border disasters strike, affected nations naturally demand answers on causation and liability,” Liu said. “Yet much of the origin lies beyond China’s jurisdiction, meaning that China can restore degraded ecosystems within its own borders, but it is simply beyond reach when environmental shocks originate in sovereign neighbouring territory.” Liu added that the existing regional framework related to cross-border disaster prevention remained largely a non-binding declaration or memorandum of understanding, which lacked explicit rules on mandatory compliance, liability or cost-sharing in joint relief efforts.

title: Opinion | Despite rivalry, China-India coexistence is not a pipe dream
description: India has no interest in endless confrontation, and Beijing has every reason to prefer a predictable India to another unresolved front.
content: When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping met at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, the encounter was short and carefully choreographed while the message was warm. Modi had earlier said that stable and predictable ties between the two nations matter for a multipolar Asia and world. The larger moment will come on September 12 and 13, when Xi is expected to visit New Delhi for the first time in seven years. He is likely to lead a delegation of some 400 officials to the Brics summit. How should we read this? No honest account of the emerging thaw in Sino-Indian relations can leave out the leader who is not at the table. US President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs on Indian goods imposed last year have pushed Delhi and Beijing closer than any charm offensive could have, even though the tariff rates were reduced this year. When China’s envoy offers to stand firm with India against outside pressure, the strategic logic writes itself. That said, a friendship powered by a shared irritation can cool once the irritation fades. India hedges by instinct, and one day it could gravitate back towards the West. That is not a reason for gloom. Rather, it is a reason to build something durable now, while there is an opening and the will to act on both sides. For much of the past five years, Beijing was content to let the freeze along the Line of Actual Control set the tone. However, a China facing sustained pressure from the United States and an uncertain global economy has every reason not to keep a second front open with a rising neighbour of more than 1.4 billion people. Xi has made the shift explicit, telling Modi the two should be partners rather than rivals. In Beijing’s view, the dragon and the elephant should dance together, not trample each other. Two armies that came to blows in 2020 are unlikely to rebuild trust through hotlines and meeting points overnight, but the direction of travel is encouraging. Days before the Bishkek summit, the two sides announced an eight-point consensus on the boundary question: two new military hotlines in the eastern and middle sectors, two additional meeting points for senior commanders, an expert group to pursue an “early and substantial harvest” of boundary delimitation, the reopening of three border trading posts and more pilgrims for the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra. Alongside these run the quiet enablers of a normal relationship, from restored direct flights to easier visas. This is how trust is rebuilt, one working mechanism at a time, and the willingness to institutionalise restraint is itself a sign that stability now serves both countries. The economy is where India has the most to gain, and where hope is most justified. China’s rare earths and processed critical minerals gave it a chokehold that Delhi felt keenly when export curbs threatened Indian factories. Yet the same thaw that eased the border tensions also loosened those flows, a sign Beijing understands that overused leverage is lost leverage. Bilateral trade is worth more than US$100 billion a year, though the balance still tilts heavily towards China. Chinese investment builds factories and transfers technology on Indian soil, meeting Indian scale and demand. As one commentary in this newspaper put it, the time to capitalise on warming ties is now. For the relationship to be truly mutual, though, Beijing must pay attention to Delhi’s needs. What does India need? First, dependable access to the minerals and inputs China can otherwise throttle, so that supply security replaces uncertainty. Second, real market access for goods where India is strong, from pharmaceuticals to software to farm produce, so the trade relationship stops being a one-way street. Third, investment that creates Indian jobs rather than deepening dependence. Beyond the realm of commerce, India needs verifiable calm on the frontier and steadier Chinese conduct in the neighbourhood. None of these asks is unreasonable. Each is simply the price of the stability Beijing says it prizes, and meeting them would make the improvement in ties stronger for both sides. This brings us to the biggest question of all: can two Asian powers build a relationship founded on coexistence rather than permanent suspicion? There is good reason to think the answer is yes. India has no interest in endless confrontation with a more economically advanced neighbour, and Beijing has every reason to prefer a predictable India to another unresolved front. Coexistence does not erase the border or the wider rivalry. It simply means choosing management over rupture. For now, both sides are choosing exactly that. Beijing appears ready to invest in a durable relationship with India. Delhi, growing surer of its own economic footing, looks ready to meet it halfway. That is more than most expected a year ago, and it could well outlast any joint statement.

title: South Korea weighs ‘contributions’ to Hormuz as US pressure mounts
description: If carried out, the deployment would mark South Korea’s first dispatch of troops overseas at the request of the US in 22 years.
content: South Korea is moving towards the possible deployment of naval assets to the Strait of Hormuz under mounting pressure from Washington, potentially making it one of the first US allies to contribute militarily to the strategically vital waterway, observers have said. The government has reportedly drawn up plans to deploy military assets, including a naval logistics support ship and P-8A maritime patrol aircraft, to the strait. If carried out, the deployment would mark South Korea’s first dispatch of troops overseas at the United States’ request in 22 years, since the Zaytun Division was sent to Iraq in 2004. The Chosun newspaper, citing an official at the presidential office Cheongwadae, reported on Friday that Seoul was considering the deployment, which would require approval from the National Assembly. “We are reviewing various measures related to preparedness on the Korean peninsula and we can manoeuvre within the scope that does not significantly undermine our readiness posture,” the official told journalists. “We have repeatedly discussed ways to make substantial contributions to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, and in fact, such contributions would include military involvement.” Cheongwadae said last month it was closely discussing “practical and military contribution measures” with Washington, while taking into account South Korea’s military readiness on the Korean peninsula and domestic legal procedures. It was the first time the government had publicly referred to the possibility of a military contribution. Asked whether consultations were also under way with the United Kingdom, France and other countries, the official said: “We are reviewing various aspects and are in the stage of consulting necessary countries during the review process.” Under South Korean law, the government must secure National Assembly approval before dispatching a newly formed military contingent overseas. Any proposal must specify the deployment’s purpose, force size, area of operations and duration. The official said it was “somewhat ambiguous” whether the current situation in the Strait of Hormuz could be considered a cessation of hostilities, adding that South Korean authorities were conducting a comprehensive review of the circumstances and any mission would be limited to non-combat activities. Yonhap news agency quoted the same Cheongwadae official as saying the government was “reviewing possible ways” to help ease tensions in the strait, but that “nothing has been decided” and consultations with the National Assembly had not yet begun. Cheongwadae reiterated in a notice to the media on Friday that “references to combat participation, non-combat operations and search activities were merely general descriptions of various options, and nothing has been decided regarding any substantive form of contribution”. The statement came hours after the government denied reports that it had already decided to deploy military assets to the strait. The Chosun newspaper nevertheless reported that the government had informed Washington of its intention to dispatch a new naval logistics support ship, P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and other assets. Other reports said the contingent could also include explosive ordnance disposal personnel. The apparently conflicting statements have fuelled questions over how far Seoul’s planning for a potential military contribution has actually progressed. A senior military official told SBS on Thursday that discussions with relevant countries over potential ports of call and operational bases were under way. A P-8 deployment would require access to an airport in a nearby country for take-offs, landings, refuelling and maintenance, while a logistical support ship would require ports for docking and resupply. Observers say the military appears to be reviewing options – including on missions, potential ports of call and operational bases – ahead of a political decision. Risks and pressure A deployment could face significant political opposition at home, particularly if it is perceived as drawing South Korea into conflict with Iran. Boo Seung-chan, a lawmaker from the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, said any dispatch could trigger a political backlash because it would put South Korean troops in danger. “The government appears to be in agony under unprecedented pressure from Washington, but who would want to send our young soldiers to a war which was not started by us?” he told This Week in Asia. “Ultimately, it will depend on public opinion whether the National Assembly will give a green light to it or not.” The Trump administration has repeatedly singled out South Korea over its reluctance to help the US in its war against Iran. “We got very little help from other countries,” US President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News that aired on Sunday, complaining that Washington had spent billions of dollars helping other countries without receiving sufficient support in return. “We helped them, but when it came to helping us, I didn’t put on a heavy sell, but I just said, ‘Would you like to participate?’ and they all said, ‘No, thank you’,” Trump said. “And I said, ‘OK, thank you very much. I appreciate it.’ But I think you have to remember this stuff. I really do.” Trump also pointed to the US military presence in South Korea. “We have thousands and thousands – like, in South Korea, as an example, we have 40,000 soldiers over there,” he said, recalling that he had asked Seoul to “give us a little hand with Iran”. South Korea hosts about 28,500 US troops. Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies, highlighted the enormous pressure South Korea was under from Washington to contribute to the war effort against Iran. Doo said US officials had focused heavily on South Korea’s possible contribution to ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz during the twice-yearly Korea Integrated Defence Dialogue held in May. “Now South Korea is supposed to return to the table with an answer” at the next round of talks later this year, Doo said. Seoul was also under pressure to make progress on its promised US$350 billion investment in the US, the construction of South Korea’s first nuclear-powered submarines with Washington’s consent and the restoration of wartime operational control of South Korean forces from the US military, he said. President Lee Jae Myung is expected to visit the US later this month to attend the United Nations General Assembly. “Talks over all these key issues appear stalled and the Hormuz deployment would serve as the only possible way out of this quagmire,” Doo said. Shin Beom-chul, a senior research fellow at the Sejong Institute, said the government’s apparent shift towards considering a Hormuz deployment could be linked to US moves to resume dialogue with North Korea. “At a time when the US could engage North Korea and potentially bypass South Korea, the government may be seeking to repair and strengthen its relationship with Washington through the deployment,” he said. Kim Yeol-soo, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for Military Affairs, predicted that South Korea and the US could reach an agreement on a deployment within weeks, with about 150 South Korean servicemen potentially being sent. “To avoid getting caught in the crossfire, South Korea should send a clear signal to Tehran that its mission is not to antagonise Iran but to secure freedom of navigation and peace,” Kim said. However, Professor Yang Moo-jin at the University of North Korean Studies was adamant that South Korea should not deploy forces while the legality of the Iran war remained in dispute. “Using the lives of young people – the very people who represent our future hope – as a tool of diplomatic negotiation runs counter to the spirit of national sovereignty that places young people at the centre of our society,” Yang said. “With tensions already running high, expanding the scope of South Korean military activities could increase the risk of becoming directly entangled in an armed conflict.”

title: Can Avengers: Doomsday and the Russo brothers save the Marvel Cinematic Universe?
description: Marvel superhero films have recently struggled at the box office, but the Russo brothers’ return could help turn the tide.
content: Before they were the most-trusted hands behind Marvel’s largest epics, American filmmakers Joe and Anthony Russo presided over a slightly less potent assemblage of talent: the Bluth family of Arrested Development. Beginning with Arrested Development (14 episodes directed) and Community (34 episodes), the Russo brothers established an especially keen sense for the rhythms and intersections of ensemble casts. “For whatever reason, Joe and I have always really been drawn to ensemble storytelling,” Anthony says. “Maybe it speaks to the fact that we work as a team.” “We grew up in a very large Italian family full of colourful personalities,” Joe says, citing their Ohio upbringing. “It was complex family dynamics. We all grew up on the same street; people lived in different houses. We spent dinners together on Sundays. “We were always interacting with a large amount of personality and interpersonal dynamics. I think that’s how we see the world and see stories.” That inclination has served the Russos well in the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), particularly in the sprawling superhero films Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Avengers: Endgame (2019). But even for the Russos, Avengers: Doomsday is a unique juggling act. It brings together the Avengers, the Wakandans, the New Avengers (from the Earth-616 alternative universe), the Fantastic Four (from Earth-828) and the original X-Men. “The MCU is this massive experiment in how vast, how much scope can an ensemble really have?” Anthony says. “If we have a taste and talent for ensemble storytelling, we’re certainly pushing ourselves further than we ever have before.” The Russo brothers have been knee-deep in work on Doomsday and its 2027 follow-up, Avengers: Secret Wars. They are finishing work on Doomsday – scoring, editing – while, in their words, “soft prepping” production on Secret Wars. “When you’re doing one of these movies it’s the hardest thing you’ve ever done,” Joe says. “When you’re doing two of them, it’s almost inconceivable. But it’s the second time around we’re doing two back to back.” When the Russo brothers were last at the helm in the MCU, Endgame marked the apex of Marvel as a cultural force. Conceived as the culmination of a decade of movies, Endgame became the second highest-grossing film of all time, with US$2.8 billion in ticket sales. Walt Disney will bring it back to US cinemas as Avengers Endgame: Encore this month. Since Endgame, the MCU has undergone plenty of expansion and experimentation. But phases four, five and six of the MCU have also been notably rockier than the first three phases. Kevin Feige, president of Marvel Studios, has acknowledged that oversaturation played a role in the downturn. For the first time, Marvel was not immune to the ups and downs that affect the rest of the movie world. The Marvels in 2023 tapped out with just US$206 million in ticket sales. Captain America: Brave New World in 2025 landed the worst CinemaScore – a B minus – for a Marvel film. Doomsday aims to reinvigorate the MCU. It features not just the return of the Avengers and the Russos, but also Robert Downey Jnr. The former Iron Man star plays the villain Doctor Doom. Downey has said he would not have come back if the Russos had not, too. So there is a get-the-band-back-together quality to Doomsday, expected to be among the highest-grossing yet. Do the Russos feel that the film will, after some MCU stumbles, restore order in the Marvel universe? “It’s a great question. It’s part of the unique challenge,” Anthony says. “The thing that Joe and I have always appreciated about our collaboration with Marvel is: our job isn’t to answer for the entirety of the MCU. We intersect it in a very specific way. It’s that intersection which is where we can make sense of things.” Of course, Spider-Man: Brand New Day (US$2.3 billion worldwide) has already nearly matched Endgame in box-office might. Anthony, “buzzing” from the movie, calls the film’s reception “a wonderful challenge”. It took something extra to bring the Russos back to Marvel. They were coaxed back, Anthony says, by a “foundational narrative concept” suggested by co-writer Stephen McFeely. “We never want to coast on the capital that already exists,” Anthony says. “We want the greatest value of the film to reside in the new thing it’s bringing to the table.” Orienting the film around Doctor Doom, however, was not the initial plan. Originally conceived as Avengers: The Kang Dynasty, the fifth Avengers film went through considerable retooling after Jonathan Majors (who played Kang the Conqueror) was dropped from the franchise after being convicted of assaulting his ex-girlfriend. The Russos eventually stepped in. But the revamped production meant going into shooting with an unfinished script. “We always view the script as a living organism,” Joe says. “We’re improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors. We like to see what the actors bring to the characters, and sometimes you don’t get the actors until a few days or few weeks before you shoot them. And a lot of the time, that’s when the magic happens.”

title: Fake customer service drives 56% jump in phone scam losses to HK$900 million
description: “Every one hour, a resident falls for a scam after answering a fraudulent call,” police superintendent says, as force reveals latest figures.
content: Impersonating customer service staff is the “most rampant tactic” used by phone scammers, Hong Kong police have said, revealing the number of such fraud cases rose by 45 per cent to 4,830 in the first half of 2026 compared with a year ago. Despite the increase, deception cases overall fell slightly between January and June, dropping by 0.7 per cent compared with the same period last year, Superintendent Kwok Ching-yee of the commercial crime bureau said on Friday. Losses also fell by 0.8 per cent to HK$3.51 billion (US$447.6 million), she noted. “Among phone scams, impersonating customer service was the most rampant tactic, accounting for nearly half of the cases. In other words, in the first half of this year, one resident fell victim to a phishing scam every four hours,” Kwok said. “Every one hour, a resident falls for a scam after answering a fraudulent call. On average, victims of each phone scam lost at least around HK$270,000.” Although the numbers of most online scam cases registered a year-on-year decline, phishing scams rose by 61 per cent to 1,113 cases, and phone scams rose by 45 per cent to 4,830. Losses from phone scams alone reached HK$900 million in the first half of the year, a 56 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2025. Police also carried out a cross-departmental operation on a phone scam syndicate, raiding two hotels in Yuen Long and Tsuen Wan over the past two weeks in connection with 203 cases involving HK$320 million. They arrested 269 suspects, comprising 188 men and 81 women. Kwok said the syndicate primarily impersonated customer service staff from courier companies such as the delivery platform SF Express and electronic payment platforms like Alipay. “They sent fake SMS messages to residents or even called the victims, falsely claiming issues such as delivery failures, account anomalies, urgent payments required or the urgent need to cancel allegedly activated paid services or insurance policies,” she said. She explained that scammers would urge their victims to click on links that would lead them to fake websites mimicking the actual companies, organisations or banks. “The scammers then instructed the victim to enter their personal information, such as account numbers and passwords,” Kwok added. Separately, police smashed a local crime syndicate that used artificial intelligence to help carry out money laundering, arresting 15 suspects. The syndicate used Hong Kong identity card photos created with AI to open online accounts with banks and stored value facility operators, using them to launder crime proceeds. The acting chief inspector of the cyber security and technology crime bureau, Ng Kam-chung, said 210 suspicious applications were made and 42 accounts were opened between November last year and this July. “Among these, 14 were used for money laundering, laundering a total of about HK$1.13 million in crime proceeds,” he said. Ng said the suspects included two ringleaders, with one responsible for making the forged identity cards and the other recruiting accomplices. “The syndicate obtained HKID data from lost or stolen identity cards,” he explained. “The mastermind then used photo editing software and AI tools to remove the original headshots from the identity cards and replaced them with their accomplice’s photos to generate fake identity cards. “They then uploaded the fake ID to pass digital identity verification, thereby opening accounts and laundering money. To evade detection by the institutions, the syndicate would sometimes further edit the fake ID cards to create different appearances, such as changing their hairstyle or glasses.” Meanwhile, the city’s de facto central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority said major retail banks had recently discovered about 400 cases involving contactless mobile payments bound with payment cards. It urged users to exercise extra caution and avoid clicking on any suspicious links.

title: Suspect deemed unfit to stand trial for alleged role in deadly hold-up 35 years ago
description: Jury rules Wen Wenye, 61, cannot be held criminally liable for murder and attempted robbery in 1991 due to cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer.
content: A mainland Chinese man has been deemed unfit to stand trial for his alleged involvement in a deadly shooting during a botched robbery in Hong Kong 35 years ago, after he was diagnosed with a cognitive impairment caused by lung cancer. A High Court jury of four men and three women ruled on Friday that Shenzhen resident Wen Wenye, 61, could not be held criminally liable for murder and attempted robbery because he was unable to understand the legal proceedings and give instructions to his lawyers. A “special hearing” will still be held before the jury to decide whether Wen indeed took part in the crimes at Shun Fat Company, a second-hand goods shop on Pei Ho Street in Sham Shui Po, on June 9, 1991. The defendant will not be convicted in any event, but the court can impose appropriate measures if the jury decides that he committed all the acts alleged in the original indictment. Wen has been remanded in custody since his arrest at the Shenzhen Bay control point on November 11, 2023. During his incarceration, he was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer, with mutated cells spreading to his brain. He underwent surgery to remove damaged brain tissue on July 24, 2024, but has used a wheelchair since. Two government psychiatrists found that Wen could barely concentrate or recollect past events, to the extent that he appeared to have forgotten why he had gone to the mainland after 1991 and returned to Hong Kong more than three decades later. In court, the defendant appeared drowsy and inattentive, with his head leaning backward and his mouth slightly open. He almost slid off his wheelchair on multiple occasions, prompting prison officers to help him up and reattach his hearing aid. In his opening speech, on-fiat prosecutor Mark Wei Ho-tong said one robber fatally shot store employee Cheng Kai-lam with a pistol, while his accomplices attempted to break open a jewellery display case. But the three robbers fled without stealing anything after the shop’s owner triggered a security alarm and called police, the court heard. Police later identified a getaway car abandoned near the scene and seized a bloodstained shirt, which forensic analysis in January 2024 found contained Wen’s DNA. Officers also found that the defendant’s right palm print matched one of the samples lifted from the shop’s display case. Wei said that while there was no direct evidence pointing to the robbers’ identities, the jury could be sure that Wen was one of them based on the overall circumstantial evidence. The hearing before Mr Justice William Tam Yiu-ho is expected to last 11 days.

title: Mandhana becomes top women’s run-scorer as India put Hong Kong to sword in Asia Cup
description: Smriti Mandhana takes career total to almost 11,000 runs with blistering century in Dubai as India cruise into semi-finals.
content: India’s Smriti Mandhana became the leading ⁠run-scorer in women’s ⁠international cricket after smashing ⁠a century in her side’s Women’s Asia Cup thrashing of Hong Kong on Thursday. The India vice-captain surpassed former skipper Mithali Raj’s tally of 10,868 international runs during a ‌blistering 124 off 64 balls, including 14 fours and seven sixes. Mandhana now has 10,880 runs across formats. The left-hander also posted her 18th international century, moving past former Australia captain Meg Lanning and South Africa’s Laura Wolvaardt, who both have 17 hundreds, ⁠to become the leading century-maker in women’s international cricket. India scored 193 for five in their 20 overs in Dubai and then bowled out Hong Kong for just 56, winning by 137 runs. “I didn’t know ‌all of this happened,” Mandhana said. “But I love batting and am happy to contribute. There are days when ‌you hit balls from the stumps. There are days when ⁠you edge one. ⁠It’s extremely unpredictable.” Mandhana’s knock powered India to their impressive total after they were put in ‌to bat, with opener Shafali Verma’s 28 the next-highest score in the innings. The 30-year-old said ‌Hong Kong’s ‌disciplined bowling made life difficult early on. “They were disciplined in the ‌power play, bowled really well and the energy they showed was something ⁠we’ll learn from,” added Mandhana, who also dedicated her achievement to her ⁠family. Mandhana, who made her India debut in 2013, became the first Indian woman to score international centuries in all three ‌formats when she ‌registered her maiden Twenty20 international hundred last year. India advanced to the semi-finals of the Asia Cup after restricting Hong Kong to a modest total, with Deepti Sharma claiming three wickets. Opener Natasha Miles top-scored for the city side with 15, while all-rounder Marina Lamplough (14) and wicketkeeper Yasmin Daswani (11) were the only other batters to get into double figures.

title: China’s AI ‘little giant’ Yunxi Technology files for Hong Kong IPO: sources
description: The confidential filing could see the hi-tech provider listed in Hong Kong by year-end.
content: Yunxi Technology, officially one of China’s “little giants”, has submitted a confidential initial public offering application to Hong Kong’s stock exchange, according to people familiar with the matter. The Guangzhou-based start-up was valued at 10 billion yuan (US$1.27 billion) in its latest private funding round and was working with Bocom International on the deal, aiming to raise “several hundred million [US] dollars”, said the people, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue. While the listing is targeted to take place by the end of this year, the timing and size remain subject to change, the people said. High-profile backers include Chinese billionaire Jack Ma’s Yunfeng Capital and investment firm HSG. Yunxi did not immediately respond to South China Morning Post’s request for comment. Founded in 2016, Yunxi provides end-to-end digital growth products and tools to help major clients across the consumer goods, retail, real estate and automotive sectors integrate artificial intelligence into their operations. The company is one of China’s nationally recognised “little giants”, a label awarded by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology to specialised, innovative small- and medium-sized enterprises that focus on niche markets, master core technologies and hold high market shares. By November 2025, China had nurtured over 17,600 such firms, with plans to expand that total to 22,000 by 2030, according to a recent ministry notice. According to a source familiar with the transaction, Yunxi had applied to list under Chapter 18C of the Hong Kong stock exchange rules – a specialised framework designed for high-growth firms in advanced technology sectors. Official data from the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing showed that by the end of March, 14 companies had gone public under this specific chapter, raising a combined HK$28.4 billion (US$3.62 billion), with additional applications under review.

title: Apple poised to unveil most expensive iPhone yet, fuelled by memory price surge
description: TrendForce says 20 per cent increase is “moderate”, with memory costs for 256-gigabyte iPhone 18 Pro model up nearly 400 per cent in a year.
content: Apple’s next flagship smartphone, the iPhone 18 Pro, could cost as much as US$1,319 for the base configuration as skyrocketing memory costs push smartphone prices to record highs, according to a recent report. Prices for the new iPhone line-up were projected to rise by 10 to 20 per cent, driven by soaring memory costs, market research firm TrendForce said in a report released on Thursday. Compared with the baselines of US$1,099 for the iPhone 17 Pro and US$1,199 for its Pro Max variant, consumers would be facing a substantial price increase. However, TrendForce said the increase represented a “moderate pricing approach” by Apple, given that memory costs for the 256-gigabyte iPhone 18 Pro model were estimated to be nearly 400 per cent higher than at this time last year. Apple would absorb part of the soaring component prices to maintain market share, amid a weak global macroeconomic environment and more cautious consumer spending, TrendForce said. Apple is set to hold a product launch in California on Wednesday morning, where TrendForce expects the company to announce the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and its first foldable phone, with the standard iPhone 18 and other models to follow in the first quarter of next year. The foldable iPhone, which is expected to feature a dual-camera set-up and a conventional capacitive fingerprint sensor, could start from US$2,099 to US$2,299, according to TrendForce estimates, with the top of the line version potentially costing more than US$3,000. The initial production of the foldable model is currently limited to only a few hundred units a day to meet Apple’s high quality standards, according to a report by Nikkei Asia on Friday that cited anonymous sources. Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The projected price increase for iPhones comes as the smartphone industry struggles with a severe memory supply crunch, triggered by surging demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure. Supplies of conventional memory for consumer electronics have been squeezed as a result. The memory crunch is expected to drag global smartphone shipments down 16.7 per cent this year, which would mark their steepest annual contraction on record, according to the latest data from IDC, a market research firm. Major smartphone players have been passing higher costs on to consumers. This week, Chinese brands including Huawei Technologies, Xiaomi and Honor announced price increases for existing models, with some mark-ups reaching 1,000 yuan (US$149). Globally, over 40 per cent of smartphone models have had their prices increased this year, marking a first for the industry, Counterpoint Research said in a report released on Thursday.
