New launches were 25 per cent more expensive year on year, while retail prices for existing smartphone models had, on average, surged 15 per cent this year, with the prices of some models nearly doubling, the Counterpoint report said. “Memory has become a key driver of smartphone [manufacturing] costs, resetting pricing across the industry and leaving [brands] with limited room to absorb higher costs,” Counterpoint research director Tarun Pathak said. “Consumers are responding by delaying upgrades, pushing purchases around big sales events or turning to the pre-owned market.”

title: Philippine court orders Sara Duterte to be arrested for threatening President Marcos, his wife
description: The alleged ‌threats are also among the allegations included in the impeachment ⁠complaint against the Philippine ‌vice-president.
content: A court in the Philippines has issued a warrant of arrest against Vice-President Sara Duterte-Carpio over death threats she made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr. The warrant involves three counts of grave threats, according to a court order that also set bail at 120,000 pesos (US$1,900) for each count. The charges were first filed last month, based on a National Bureau of Investigation criminal complaint in February 2025. Duterte’s lawyer, Paul Lawrence Lim, on Friday confirmed the Quezon City regional trial court “has issued a warrant of arrest against the vice-president”. His client “has no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies”, he added. In November 2024, the vice-president claimed after a late night news briefing that she had hired an assassin and instructed him, if she were ever murdered, to kill Marcos, his wife, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and his cousin, then house speaker Martin Romualdez. Duterte-Carpio has since denied making those threats. The alleged ‌threats are also among the allegations included in the impeachment ⁠complaint against Duterte, who is being tried before the Senate ⁠sitting as an impeachment court. A conviction could remove her from office and derail her presidential bid ‌in 2028. Duterte-Carpio also faces accusations of misappropriating over US$10 million in “confidential funds” from her time as vice-president and education secretary, a position she held between 2022 and 2024. Observers say the latest move marks a “significant development for the rule of law”. Duterte-Carpio’s arrest was the “first time in Philippine politics that a sitting vice-president was issued a judicial arrest warrant”, said Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of the polling firm Momentum Research. “It is significant precisely because of how rarely the coercive power of the law reaches people at the very top of Philippine politics,” he added. The timing was “inevitably politically charged”, he said. “But political rivalry cannot, by itself, invalidate legal process. Otherwise, every powerful politician could escape accountability simply by declaring themselves persecuted. Her best protection against both executive overreach and trial by publicity is to participate fully in the court process and avail herself of due process under the law.” Both sides benefited from this due process, said Darwin Angeles, a lecturer at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s College of Law. “The process favours both the state, which will be given the opportunity of presenting the merits of its case, but also the vice-president, who will be afforded due process, which includes the right to a fair, impartial, and speedy trial.” Jean Encinas-Franco, a political-science professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman, called the arrest warrant a matter of “the law finally catching up”, but acknowledged that the move would be seen by Duterte supporters as political persecution amid the ongoing impeachment trial. The vice-president has not shown up to a single session since the impeachment court convened in May. If impeached, she will be barred from seeking public office. Duterte-Carpio declared in February that she planned to run for president in the 2028 elections. Political impact “The supporters of Sara will raise hell and will still invoke political persecution. At least law enforcement officials have already decided that there’s enough of a case to issue a warrant of arrest,” Encinas-Franco said. “But that’s not the end in itself for the accused. It means that she will have a day in court to face her accusers.” In terms of optics, the arrest warrant would be seen as “very political” and a result of the ongoing fallout from Duterte-Carpio’s partnership with Marcos, once known as the “UniTeam”, she said. “People will say that they’re doing this because Sara is running [for president]. But these two things can be true at the same time.” As grave threats are a bailable offence, Duterte-Carpio’s lawyers intended to “post bail ASAP”, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told ABS-CBN News. Angeles said the warrant of arrest would not affect the impeachment trial. “As a matter of law, the criminal case and the impeachment trial involve different legal liabilities: criminal responsibility vs fitness to remain in office. Both the Senate impeachment court and the regional trial court possess jurisdiction to hear and decide the cases before them,” he said. For the Senate, this comes under the constitution while the regional court will try it under the penal code. Technically, both can happen simultaneously, according to Nathaniel Candelaria, an assistant professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman. Meanwhile, observers agree that the arrest will lead to a hardening of each political faction’s supporter base especially heading into the 2028 polls. “Her supporters will definitely see this as a politically motivated arrest. Her critics will see this as part of the rule of law. Regardless of how one sees this, this may affect her chances in 2028, especially those who are undecided,” Candelaria said. Arguelles said the warrant gave the Duterte camp a powerful narrative of persecution to cement support. “Rodrigo Duterte in The Hague, Sara Duterte impeached and now facing arrest – the family can present these not as separate accountability processes but as one sustained campaign to eliminate the Dutertes from national politics,” he said. However, overarching national sentiment may complicate this, as 80 per cent of Filipinos say they find her threats against Marcos and his family unacceptable, according to a Momentum Research poll in July. “The political danger for the Marcos camp is overreach: a process perceived as selective or politically directed could also turn this into political capital and give the Duterte base another reason to close ranks,” Arguelles said. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Hong Kong’s City University disciplines students over orientation camp misconduct
description: Camp organisers admit serious mismanagement, dissolve executive committee after video of half-naked man carrying woman at party sparked concern.
content: Hong Kong’s City University has disciplined students over an orientation event with a disco theme in which a half-naked man was seen carrying a woman wearing only a bra and shorts, two days after the institution said it had “zero tolerance” for improper conduct. The institution said on Friday that all students involved in the orientation camp incident on August 27 had admitted their mistakes, formally apologised to the university and accepted disciplinary action. “The university’s student discipline panel has completed its investigation into the incident and imposed disciplinary penalties on the organisers and the students involved,” it said. “In accordance with established procedures, further details will not be disclosed to protect student privacy.” It added that the event organiser, the Management Sciences Society under the CityU student union, had acknowledged serious mismanagement, immediately dissolved its executive committee and apologised to the community. The university took disciplinary action two days after expressing “grave concern” over the “serious mismanagement and inappropriate behaviour by certain individuals” at the event. The orientation camp sparked public discussion after a video showing the conduct at a disco-themed party went viral online. The clip has since been removed from Instagram, where it was first posted, but continues to circulate on other social media platforms. CityU said it fully understood the concerns raised by parents and the wider community, and hoped society would allow the students involved space to make amends, learn from the experience and grow as they took responsibility for their actions. “The university hopes that through this incident, the students involved will recognise that breaching university rules and causing disruption to the public and participants carries responsibility and serious disciplinary consequences,” it said. It added that its Student Development Services would provide additional workshops on student activity management for organisers of similar events. It has also set up a dedicated hotline to offer mental health support and other help to students in need. Public concern over university orientation activities has increased in recent years amid allegations of sexual harassment at some events. In 2023, a second-year undergraduate at the University of Hong Kong was arrested and charged with groping a first-year student at an orientation event but was later acquitted by a court. There were also reports of students playing kissing games during a Lingnan University orientation event, while allegations of rape and voyeurism emerged at an event held by the Education University of Hong Kong in the same year.

title: 2 US sailors sent back to Abraham Lincoln warship after drunken Pattaya fight
description: Police said the ‘trivial’ incident happened near the Thai resort city’s nightlife hotspot Walking Street.
content: Two sailors from the US aircraft carrier making a port call to Thailand were sent back to the ship after a drunken altercation, Thai police said on Friday. Police were alerted to a “small scuffle” involving the sailors in the early hours of Thursday near Pattaya’s nightlife hotspot Walking Street, city police chief Colonel Anek Srathongyoo said. “The sailors were drunk and they were fighting, making loud noise,” he said. He described the incident as “trivial” and said local residents had only called police to prevent it from escalating. The unidentified sailors were not charged as “they did not violate any Thai law”, Anek said. The US Navy sent the pair back to the ship, he added. The USS Abraham Lincoln’s arrival has drawn global media interest after reports of deteriorating living conditions on board after more than 280 days at sea. It has also put the spotlight on Pattaya, a resort popular with foreign tourists with a reputation for its nightlife, including sex tourism. Authorities launched a crackdown on sex workers ahead of the ship’s visit, although they denied it was linked to the sailors’ arrival. The police chief said there had been no other notable incidents since the Lincoln docked, and one Pattaya masseuse said it had been calmer than previous military port calls. Nattakamol Chartmontri, who has worked in Pattaya for several years, said many of the sailors appeared “young, well-behaved and rule-abiding”. Pattaya businesses had been hoping for a windfall from the visit, which comes during low season, but Nattakamol, 48, said it had so far stayed quiet. “People on social media are so hyped about [the sailors], but actually, they have not made a significant difference to Pattaya businesses,” she said. US Democratic lawmakers called last month for an investigation into conditions on the Lincoln following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises. US President Donald Trump dismissed the concerns, which have fuelled criticism of his dragging war on Iran, although the Lincoln was replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.

title: China arrests 52 Singaporeans in Guangxi pyramid scheme crackdown
description: The detentions come amid a broader push by Beijing to curb illicit financial schemes and cross-border fraud networks.
content: Fifty-two Singaporeans have been arrested and detained in China’s Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region following a law enforcement operation targeting suspected pyramid scheme activities and related offences, according to Singaporean authorities. Singapore’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Singapore Police Force revealed the arrests in a joint statement on Friday, noting that Chinese authorities were still investigating the cases. Sim Ann, Singapore’s second minister for foreign affairs, said consular officers from the country’s embassy in Beijing and its consulate in Guangzhou had visited all 52 detainees to check on their well-being, help with administrative matters and relay messages between the detainees and their families. Sim, who is also the second minister for home affairs, has met relatives of most of the detainees to offer support during what she called an “understandably difficult time”. While officials did not give details of the operations involved, multilevel marketing scams have repeatedly been targeted in police crackdowns in Guangxi. These include the long-running “1040 Sunshine” scheme, which dupes people into paying 69,800 yuan (US$10,390) on the false promise of a 10.4 million yuan return. Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on police crackdowns targeting the scam as early as 2014. The ministry stressed that Singapore “does not intervene in foreign judicial systems, just as we expect foreign governments to respect our laws and legal process”. The ministry said it would continue to press for due process under Chinese law and urged citizens to remain vigilant against schemes requiring upfront payments or recruitment fees. The detentions come amid a broader push by Beijing to curb illicit financial schemes and cross‑border fraud networks. Organising or leading pyramid schemes is a criminal offence in China. Between 2021 and 2025, market regulation authorities across the country investigated and handled 212,800 illegal cases involving pyramid schemes and direct sales, according to China’s State Administration for Market Regulation. During the five-year period, law enforcement officials shut down more than 8,400 venues used for pyramid schemes, the top market regulator said. The enforcement actions in Guangxi coincide with heightened scrutiny and law enforcement operations involving foreign nationals across China. Early last month, Beijing announced it had taken action against more than 100 Philippine nationals for allegedly working or living in the country illegally. That move followed an operation in mid-May, when Philippine authorities raided a steel plant and arrested 70 Chinese citizens accused of illegal employment. The Chinese embassy in Manila criticised the raid’s legality at the time, asserting that subsequent investigations had proved the workers held valid documents. All affected Chinese nationals have since been released. In late June, China’s foreign ministry said that two Japanese nationals had been detained for alleged legal violations. On the same day, Tokyo said it had been told by China that the people were suspected of smuggling items banned from export.

title: John Lee urges banks to finance city’s tech growth, expand offshore yuan business
description: City leader calls for closer partnership between government and banking sector in four areas as Hong Kong seeks strategic growth.
content: Hong Kong’s leader has urged the banking sector to support financing the city’s creation of a new economic engine in innovation and technology (I&T) while expanding offshore yuan business, a key area for aligning with national strategies. Speaking at a Hong Kong Association of Banks event on Friday, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu called for closer partnership between the government and banking sector in four areas. They are: expanding offshore renminbi business; encouraging I&T through finance; developing commodity trading; and strengthening financial security and market integrity. “Strategic growth hinges on technological self-reliance and high-quality development. That very much includes the Northern Metropolis,” Lee told the annual Distinguished Speaker Luncheon. The Northern Metropolis would integrate university town areas with I&T and industry, providing an environment for living, working and travelling, he noted. “It will become a breakthrough point for our city’s rapid development,” he said. Lee also pointed to the Northern Metropolis Financial Advisory Task Force, which comprises 23 banks and was set up to support the development through financing. Authorities are pouring billions of Hong Kong dollars into the megaproject near the border with mainland China, aimed at creating a new engine for I&T. Beyond issuing bonds to finance new infrastructure, authorities are also encouraging developers and companies to co-develop projects within the Northern Metropolis. Lee also said Hong Kong, as the world’s largest offshore renminbi business hub, was uniquely positioned to spearhead the yuan’s internationalisation. This included enriching the yuan liquidity pool, expanding offshore renminbi investment and risk management products, and reinforcing financial market infrastructure. “The national 15th five-year plan charts the country’s course for high-level opening up and the internationalisation of the renminbi stands as a strategic priority,” he said. Lee added that the government looked forward to working more closely with banks to innovate yuan-denominated products, enable cross-boundary trade settlement and broaden the global use of the renminbi. The city would also expand mutual market access schemes with the mainland, including Stock Connect, Bond Connect, Wealth Management Connect and Swap Connect. Hong Kong was also pursuing developments in commodity trading, with the gold market as an entry point, launching a trial operation of the city’s central clearing and settlement system for gold in July, Lee noted. He called for strengthening financial security and market integrity as technologies rapidly evolved. “A thriving international financial centre must be anchored in a safe, trusted and secure environment,” he said. Lee said the city’s first five-year plan, to be unveiled on September 16, would help capitalise on the national blueprint. “The plan will leverage Hong Kong’s unparalleled roles as a ‘superconnector’ and ‘super value-adder’, linking mainland capital and enterprises with global markets while bringing in international capital, technology and talent,” he said. “It helps that, under ‘one country, two systems’, our institutional strengths – our common law system, free flow of capital, simple and low-tax regime and seamless connectivity with global standards – remain rock solid.” Sun Yu, chairman of the Hong Kong Association of Banks, said in his speech that the organisation and the banking industry continued to seize new opportunities by deepening engagement with emerging markets while backing the real economy, particularly through efforts to support the accelerated development of the Northern Metropolis and foster transformation of small and medium-sized enterprises. The association has submitted the Hong Kong Banking 2030 Report to the government, offering recommendations to advance the industry and help the city in consolidating and strengthening its position as an international financial centre. Details of the report will be available next week. Kevin Tsui Ka-kin, co-founder and director of economic research at the policy think tank Pagoda Institute, said Lee could be appealing to banks to be more generous with loans to the innovation and technology sector. “But the banks have their own calculations. It is not easy to convince them,” he said. Tsui noted that local banks had accumulated bad debt in recent years, primarily driven by special loan schemes introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic to assist SMEs, alongside the downturn in property development. “The chief executive might see this and ask them not to suddenly cut off the credit flow,” Tsui said. He added that local banks were traditionally conservative when lending to the tech sector due to higher risk. “There are so many projects, so they diversify their investments. Even one hit out of 100 isn’t guaranteed,” he said. Unlike the US innovation sector, which benefited from a vast ecosystem of venture capital and private funds operating at a much larger investment scale, Hong Kong’s tech start-ups relied heavily on government funding rather than bank financing, he said. “Banks tend to take low risks and stick to traditional mortgages,” Tsui said.

title: Philippines’ Duterte-Quiboloy ties on show at world’s largest arena launch
description: Though in custody on sex charges, Apollo Quiboloy still drew 80,000 followers and Duterte backing for his 75,000-seat Kingdome launch.
content: The presence of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s youngest son at the opening of detained televangelist Apollo Quiboloy’s 75,000-seat Kingdome stadium this week offered a striking display of how ties between the Duterte family and the Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KJC) have endured despite the criminal cases surrounding its founder. Observers say the lavish inauguration, attended by an estimated 80,000 people alongside Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, proved the organisation’s ability to maintain its political and institutional influence, even with its founder behind bars. The event on Tuesday also featured an official city council tribute to Quiboloy and his church. Quiboloy, who denies all allegations against him, remains in custody in the Philippines on charges of human trafficking and sexual abuse. Authorities are also reviewing a formal US request for his extradition. Touted by local officials as a new architectural landmark, the Kingdome is now the world’s largest indoor arena, surpassing the 55,000-capacity Philippine Arena owned by another megachurch, the Iglesia ni Cristo (Church of Christ), in Bulacan province north of Manila. The venue, where construction began in 2012, sits on the sprawling 30-hectare (2.15 million sq ft) KJC compound in Davao City. The site was the location of a 16-day police operation before the self-appointed “Son of God” pastor surrendered in September 2024. His legal counsel later called the surrender an “ultimate sacrifice” to avoid further “lawless violence” in the compound. Quiboloy and eight associates were indicted by a US federal grand jury in 2021. He is wanted by the Federal Bureau of Investigation on charges of sex trafficking by force, fraud, coercion, sex trafficking of children, conspiracy and bulk cash smuggling. He is also accused of running a labour-trafficking scheme that forced church members on fraudulent visas to solicit donations for a non-existent charity. Former church members have given evidence of alleged sexual abuse and exploitation at Philippine Senate hearings. Quiboloy is currently being held at Pasig City Jail facing non-bailable charges of qualified human trafficking, child abuse and sexual abuse. As of Thursday, the Philippine Justice Department was evaluating the US extradition request and had not set a deadline for filing an extradition petition in court. Arjan Aguirre, an assistant professor of political science at Ateneo de Manila University, told This Week in Asia that the KJC’s enduring clout showed how the megachurch’s influence had morphed beyond its pastor’s physical presence. It had become a “multifaceted organisation with the capacity to exert influence across political, economic, educational and media institutions”, Aguirre said, adding that Quiboloy’s status “is embedded in the organisation’s resources, institutions and relationships, which can continue to operate and mobilise support even when he is behind bars”. Quiboloy founded the KJC in 1985 in Davao City. While the church claims over 7 million members, authorities dispute that figure. A network of entities remains tied to Quiboloy and the church, most prominently Sonshine Media Network International (SMNI). Other assets include the Jose Maria College Foundation, construction firm ACQ Solomonic Builders and foundations such as the Sonshine Philippines Movement and Children’s Joy Foundation, which Senate witnesses alleged were involved in moneymaking schemes. “What this tells us is that Quiboloy’s power has become institutionalised: KJC is no longer simply an extension of one religious leader, but a network of institutions capable of sustaining his influence and political connections even in his absence,” Aguirre said. Sebastian Duterte’s attendance at the opening of the Kingdome highlighted the decades-long alliance between his family and the evangelist. Quiboloy has long been a close friend of Sebastian’s father, who previously called the pastor his “spiritual adviser”. Months before the police raid, Quiboloy appointed former president Duterte as an administrator of KJC assets, pointing to what lawmakers called “intertwined interests”. In February, a Makati court issued an asset-preservation order covering 12 bank accounts, 37 properties and 25 vehicles registered under Quiboloy’s name and that of the church’s executive pastor. Before winning the presidency in 2016, Rodrigo Duterte acknowledged receiving lavish gifts from Quiboloy, including real estate and flights on his private jet. “The Dutertes’ and Quiboloy’s spheres of influence are closely entwined, particularly in Davao City,” Aguirre said. “Their relationship is best understood as a mutually reinforcing political and organisational alliance: the Dutertes provide access to political power and government resources, while Quiboloy provides a network of followers that can be mobilised for political support.” Undiminished influence Gino Trinidad, a political-science instructor at Ateneo de Manila University who studies state-church relations, said that “SMNI played a considerable role in legitimising the Duterte administration through its content and reportage”. The alliance was tested after the end of Duterte’s presidency and the subsequent falling-out between the Marcos and Duterte families. Government investigations into SMNI soon followed, leading to the network’s suspension shortly before Quiboloy’s arrest. Yet the crackdown has done little to erode the KJC founder’s standing among followers. “Quiboloy’s arrest and eventual imprisonment did not diminish his legitimacy to the believers of his church. It might have actually added to his influence,” Trinidad said. “Members firmly believe his arrest was an injustice, and now that he is in prison, they have to show their utmost support and reverence to him.”

title: Hong Kong’s 106 billionaires, Treasury yields hit recent highs: the numbers moving markets
description: China’s expanding outbound capital and US bonds’ surging yields are in spotlight this week.
content: China has been expanding its outbound-investment channels, with a new quota granted and greater overseas allocation by the nation’s pension fund. However, the financial world beyond the mainland is seeing volatility as US bond yields hit 20-month highs. Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week. US$6.84 billion in new quotas for mutual funds China’s foreign-exchange regulator approved US$6.84 billion in new, qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) quotas for mutual funds, insurers and banks’ wealth-management units by the end of August, according to data from the State Administration of Foreign Exchange, expanding their capacity to invest in overseas assets. Eighteen money managers, including China Asset Management and GF Fund Management, received US$100 million each, while more than 20 Chinese banks’ wealth-management units received quotas for the first time. Hong Kong has 106 billionaires, second only to New York Hong Kong remained the world’s second-largest billionaire hub with 106 billionaires, trailing only New York, which had 164, according to wealth data provider Altrata. Beijing and Shenzhen also ranked among the world’s 15 cities with the most billionaires, helped by wealth creation from the AI boom. US 10-year Treasury yield hits 20-month high The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 4.78 per cent on Tuesday, its highest level in 20 months, as investors sold government debt amid concerns over the country’s fiscal outlook. The move came as US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told G20 finance ministers that Washington was a leader in tackling sovereign debt problems in emerging markets, even as rising borrowing costs in the US highlighted the challenges facing the country. Benchmark yields in Japan and the UK have also climbed to multi-decade highs. China’s national pension offshore assets hit record US$86 billion China’s National Social Security Fund more than doubled its offshore investments in three years to a record 580.02 billion yuan (US$86 billion) at the end of 2025, as it sought higher returns through greater exposure to overseas markets. Offshore assets accounted for 15.23 per cent of the fund’s total assets, the highest proportion on record, according to its annual report released on Tuesday.

title: Another Chinese EV maker joins grid in Europe, with Xiaomi to launch sales next year
description: Xiaomi Auto says it has signed agreements with eight car dealer groups to build a sales and service network in Germany.
content: Chinese tech firm Xiaomi will start selling electric cars in Europe next year, it announced at a consumer electronics trade show in Berlin on Thursday, adding to the growing list of Chinese carmakers expanding into the European market despite EU tariffs on China-made electric vehicles (EVs) and growing wariness across the bloc. Xiaomi Auto, the group’s EV arm, said it would enter several European markets including Germany, where it had signed agreements with eight car dealer groups to build a sales and service network ahead of the launch. The immediate obstacle would be Brussels’ countervailing duties on Chinese EVs. Since Xiaomi did not participate in an EU anti-subsidy investigation launched in 2023 – it only launched its first EV in China in March 2024 – it is likely to be hit with the highest duty of 35.3 per cent on the cars it exports to the EU, on top of the standard 10 per cent import duty. Xiaomi declined to comment on whether it was in discussions with the European Commission on a price undertaking offer that would spare it the levy. At the launch event at IFA Berlin, Xiaomi executives struck a positive tone on its expansion to Europe. “Xiaomi Auto is committed to long-term investment in Europe,” said Yu Liguo, vice-president of Xiaomi Auto and head of its international business. Alongside its research and development centre in Munich, he said partnerships with local dealers would be key to its European expansion. But momentum at home has slowed. Xiaomi’s July deliveries rose 2.7 per cent year on year to 31,267 but fell 10 per cent from June, according to the China Passenger Car Association, while Xiaomi said August deliveries stayed “above 30,000”, against 36,396 a year earlier. Its EV and AI segment posted a 2.6 billion yuan (US$387 million) operating loss in the second quarter of the year, its second consecutive quarterly loss. Germany, where Xiaomi chose to make its announcement, is also a demanding market, with Chinese rivals BYD, Xpeng, Leapmotor and Nio already present. BYD, Xpeng and Leapmotor are expanding their European production footprint: BYD in Hungary, Leapmotor at partner Stellantis’ factory in Spain, and Xpeng through contract assembly with Magna in Austria. Yu said local partnerships were “at the heart” of Xiaomi’s long-term commitment to Europe. The firm said it planned to add more European dealers to the eight in Germany ahead of the launch.

title: Could Roman concrete have clues on how Pyramid of Giza was built – and saved?
description: Insights into how the ancient concrete grows denser could help create a low-carbon modern version and explain how the Great Pyramid endured.
content: The enduring mystery of how the ancient Egyptians built the Great Pyramid of Giza – with its 2.3 million multi-tonne stone blocks – has puzzled researchers for centuries. Mainstream archaeology holds that the pyramids were constructed from natural limestone or granite blocks precisely cut and hauled into place. An alternative scientific theory suggests the blocks might have been cast from an early form of concrete, but that idea has long faced a critical question: how could such an artificial material survive for more than 4,500 years, while some modern buildings could suffer wear and damage in merely a few decades? Now, a new study on nearly 2,000-year-old Roman concrete may provide a materials-science clue that breathes new life into the concrete hypothesis. Published in the peer-reviewed academic journal Science Advances in July, the research reveals that ancient Roman concrete not only resists decay but actually grows stronger over centuries through a self-healing process. A team led by Zhu Xiaohong of Beijing University of Technology, with collaborators from the University of California, Berkeley, the University of Michigan, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, analysed concrete taken from a communal latrine at Hadrian’s Villa in Tivoli, Italy. Using high-resolution imaging, they discovered the material’s remarkable durability stems from the gradual formation of calcite crystals that fill pores and microcracks. The healing process was driven in part by carbonation, in which calcium-rich compounds in concrete react with moisture and atmospheric carbon dioxide to form calcium carbonate. Carbonation is often considered a durability problem in modern reinforced concrete because it lowers the material’s pH, potentially allowing embedded steel to corrode. But the researchers found that the same chemical process can contribute to mineral growth and densification in ancient unreinforced concrete. “For unreinforced concrete, carbonation may be a good thing,” Zhu said. This insight could extend far beyond Rome. Zhu draws a speculative connection to the Pyramid of Giza, pointing out that ancient Egypt and Rome shared a deeper technological lineage than often assumed, including the use of lime or volcanic-ash-based binders. If Egyptian builders used a calcium-rich, concrete-like mixture, the same sort of long-term mineral growth seen in Roman concrete might have transformed initially workable material into the dense, rock-hard blocks we see today. “The builders of the pyramids may not have deliberately poured the hard stone blocks we see today, but may instead have discovered through experience a mixture that could ‘grow’ over time,” Zhu said. He suggests that some calcium-rich building materials could have continued to evolve after construction through carbonation, mineral deposition and pore filling, producing increasingly dense structures over long periods. Under this hypothesis, dense calcite crystals could form around older mineral phases and inside pores and fractures, potentially reinforcing the material while reducing pathways for water to penetrate. Such mineral growth could continue for centuries, allowing parts of the material to become progressively denser, slowing further deterioration. He compared the proposed mechanism with natural calcite formation, in which calcium dissolved in water can move through pores and fractures before precipitating again as crystalline material. “In other words, time is not only an eroder; it can also be a sculptor,” Zhu said. But Zhu stressed that he had not directly studied the Pyramid of Giza and his proposal did not establish that the pyramid blocks were made from concrete or artificial stone. “This is only a reasonable hypothesis from the perspective of materials science,” he said. Zhu’s judgment stemmed from research in the field of cement and cooperation with field authority Ian Richardson, of the University of Leeds. “In fact, all ordinary Portland cement, as well as natural lime-clay or volcanic ash rich in calcium sources, undergo carbonation,” he said. Portland cement is the most common type of cement used around the world. “It has only been around for 200 years, yet you can see it almost anywhere on Earth. It is the second-most-used material by humans after water,” Zhu said. “I and Professor Richardson have also studied the patented cement from 1824, where modern Portland cement was patented in Leeds in Britain. “We analysed its production technology and composition, and the related research has been incorporated into textbooks on cement chemistry by Professor Richardson.” The ancient Rome sample contained volcanic rock fragments, lime and volcanic ash materials commonly used in Roman concrete, but the researchers found that mineral growth within the material played an important role in maintaining its long-term integrity. Over time, the continual growth of calcite creates a self-healing effect, closing cracks and mitigating further damage caused by environmental stresses or mechanical loads Zhu Xiaohong, Beijing University of Technology In particular, dense layers of calcite formed around older mineral phases and within pores and fractures, reinforcing the material while reducing pathways for water to penetrate. Rather than occurring only during construction, this mineralisation could continue over long periods, filling voids and small cracks and making parts of the concrete progressively denser. “Over time, the continual growth of calcite creates a self-healing effect, closing cracks and mitigating further damage caused by environmental stresses or mechanical loads,” the study’s authors wrote. Zhu said the process occurred in a wide range of calcium-rich cementitious materials. But whether carbonation was beneficial depended strongly on how the concrete was used. In ancient unreinforced concrete, carbonation could instead contribute to densification and long-term durability. The Roman example could eventually inform the design of modern concrete by shifting attention away from initial strength towards long-term behaviour. For the future cement design, “experiments on a thousand-year timescale are impossible, but with a three-dimensional validation system combining accelerated testing, numerical modelling and geological analogues, we can make credible predictions”, Zhu said. The approach could allow researchers to engineer controlled mineralisation so that concrete responded to its environment by gradually filling pores and microcracks rather than simply deteriorating. “For ordinary buildings, ecological design that is ‘sufficient and continuously sufficient’ is far more valuable than engineering that pursues extremely high strength without durability,” Zhu said. He said he was continuing to examine historic construction materials, including samples from Hagia Sophia in Istanbul. “Cement and concrete have always been rather remarkable and great materials, but people may overlook them because they are so common,” Zhu said. “Although it is not exactly a hot research topic, I feel that our research is quite meaningful.”

title: Hong Kong proposes grade 2 heritage status for Kennedy Town selfie spot sea wall
description: Heritage assessment panel proposes listing New Praya’s century-old sea wall as historic structure amid plans to build new pedestrian walkway.
content: A sea wall at a popular selfie spot on Kennedy Town’s waterfront could soon gain grade two status after Hong Kong authorities proposed listing it as a historic structure, although experts say creative storytelling will be key to bringing the site’s heritage to life. According to a document from the Antiquities and Monuments Office, the Historic Buildings Assessment Panel recommended that the New Praya sea wall be given grade two status following an assessment. Subject to members’ endorsement, the office would upload the proposed grading to the Antiquities Advisory Board’s website for a one-month public consultation, the document said. Hong Kong classifies historic buildings into three grades. Grade two is for structures of special merit, for which efforts should be made to achieve selective preservation. According to authorities, the New Praya sea wall may be more than 100 years old and is believed to be one of the oldest along the northern shore of Hong Kong Island. In its proposal to build an offshore pedestrian walkway along New Praya, the government earlier said the sea wall’s potential heritage value would continue to be taken into account. Ivan Ho Man-yiu, chairman of the Harbourfront Commission, said the proposed grading was unlikely to affect plans for the new walkway, as the sea wall’s heritage value had already been considered in the design. “The boardwalk we are currently proposing is at a distance from the sea wall, and the alignment has been thoroughly evaluated to ensure that it will not affect the sea wall in terms of construction,” he said. Ho noted that the sea wall was not currently visible to people standing along the waterfront. He proposed setting aside areas on the new pedestrian walkway where tourists and residents could stop to view it. He also called for better education and promotion of the historic structure, including interactive ways for visitors to learn about the site’s past rather than relying solely on photographs and text. “I hope we can make better use of technology and integrate it into our harbourfront to give the public a whole new experience,” he said. “Besides serving as a pedestrian walkway that connects the waterfront, this boardwalk can also let people view the sea wall and learn about its history.” Professor Kwong Chi-man, chair of the history department at Baptist University, said the New Praya section was likely to be the only historical sea wall remaining on western Hong Kong Island. Kwong compared recent and historical aerial photos, which showed the sea wall was likely to have been constructed in the early 1900s. He added that the sea wall, which had prevented Japanese forces in World War II from landing in that part of the city, should still be relatively intact. “The sea wall has also witnessed prosperous industrial and urban development on western Hong Kong Island, as the area features residential development, slaughterhouses, warehouses and the Hongkong Rope Manufacturing Company,” he said. He said the area’s industrial elements were almost wiped out in the 1970s. New Praya, which stretches 200 metres (219 yards), has become a hotspot for mainland Chinese tourists in recent years, with many visiting to take selfies against the harbourfront backdrop. But the lack of a pedestrian walkway along the waterfront has led visitors to gather on the road, creating safety risks. Authorities have proposed building a pedestrian walkway linking Cadogan Street Promenade and Belcher Bay Promenade at both ends. The walkway is expected to be 200 metres long and 10 metres wide, requiring the reclamation of 0.25 hectares. Reclamation is expected to begin in mid-2028 and be completed in mid-2031. Additional reporting by Edith Lin

title: Chinese basketball players aiming to take team to new heights at Fiba Women’s World Cup
description: Campaign starts against the US, but Dallas Wings player Li Yueru will miss the tournament after her passport was lost in the post.
content: Opponents will be looking up to China during the Fiba Women’s World Cup, starting with the United States. The Americans and everyone else will have to navigate around and over some of the tallest women on the planet: China’s 19-year-old Zhang Ziyu stands 7-foot-3 (2.2 metres). The US team are already familiar with 6-foot-10 Han Xu from her Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA) games with the New York Liberty. If not for a passport mishap, Zhang and Han would be joined by another centre – 6-foot-7 Li Yueru, who plays with the WNBA’s Dallas Wings. Li posted on social media Wednesday that her passport was lost in the post and she will not be able to compete. China opens their campaign against the four-time defending champions in Berlin on Friday. Zhang wasn’t playing when the US beat China 83-61 in the 2022 World Cup final in Sydney for a fourth consecutive gold medal. She made her senior debut at the Women’s Asia Cup last year and helped China capture bronze, averaging 14.8 points and 5.5 rebounds in the tournament. Han praised her performance at that tournament and said she was ready to step onto the world stage. “World Cup is a good moment for her, for the whole world to know her,” Han said. “I am so excited to play with her again.” Both of Zhang’s parents played basketball and it was her mother who encouraged her to take up the sport. As one of the oldest players in the Chinese team at 26, Han takes on the responsibility of looking out for her younger teammates. She points out that Zhang is still “very young” and just starting her career. “She’s a little girl, you know, like the heart is soft,” she said. If Zhang plays on Friday – she missed China’s pre-tournament warm-up against France on Tuesday and did not practise during the brief time-slots open to media Wednesday and Thursday – her height alone will ensure she stands out against the tournament favourites. “She’s good,” Han said on Wednesday. “She just needs some rest ... she has (a) big body and tall girl, and she needs some time to rest a little bit.” On Thursday she said Zhang had practised “a little bit” earlier before the media was allowed in. US guard Sonia Citron, also making her World Cup debut, says they will be prepared either way. “I think just try to make it difficult for her, you know, to guard her as a team,” Citron said. “Just don’t leave anybody on an island, but yeah, I think we’ll prep everything and then be ready.” Few expect China to go further than they did in 2022, with France and Australia expected to be most likely challengers for the US. But Zhang’s introduction gives the Chinese an extra weapon they did not have four years ago. “At the last World Cup, we played our best, but before we played, we never thought we would do so well, but we gave 100 per cent,” Han said. “I’ll try to do the same or better and try to focus every single game. Especially me, I just try to focus because there’s so much noise around me.”

title: Snow in Malaysia? Viral highway fun dampened by soapy truth
description: Police said the white-topped Shah Alam Expressway that mesmerised motorists was caused by a rain-activated soap spill from a lorry.
content: A “wintry wonderland” on a highway in tropical Malaysia left motorists awestruck – until a police revelation melted away the viral moment and turned it into a road safety warning. Social media videos showed thick white foam carpeting several lanes of the Shah Alam Expressway as vehicles drove through the “snowy” route. The spectacle was extremely unusual in Malaysia, where there is no traditional winter season and temperatures remain relatively uniform throughout the year. However, that did not stop Malaysians from proposing their own theories, such as one social media user who likened it to a scene from “a Korean movie, but there’s a Saga”, referring to the Proton Saga, one of Malaysia’s best-known locally made cars. Others suspected the road smelled of popular fabric-softener brands like Downy or Softlan, with a commenter asking: “Who’s washing clothes by the highway?” As the online sleuthing continued over the white-topped road, Shah Alam district police chief Assistant Commissioner Sarudin Samah attributed the incident to soap residue, believed to have spilled from a lorry on August 24, near the Kota Kemuning interchange. Sarudin said firefighters had spread sawdust over the foam but the leftover detergent came back to life when a deluge hit the area on Thursday. “Heavy rain caused the remaining soap residue to produce foam along about 500 metres of the highway,” he said in a statement late on Thursday. Police said the foam, covering a stretch on the Klang to Kuala Lumpur side of the expressway, was spotted in the afternoon. Hours later, the Malaysian Highway Authority issued an alert about the liquid spill near the Kota Kemuning interchange and blocked the left lane, leading to slow-moving traffic. “Please slow down and follow the instructions of personnel at the location,” it said. Sarudin said the highway concessionaire also carried out a second clean-up at the site. While some motorists warned others about the slippery surface, many were reluctant to let Malaysia’s brief taste of “winter” disappear without enjoying it. “Malaysia already has snow,” one commenter said. Another asked whether the foam had been cleared because, if not, they wanted to drive through and “play in the snow”.

title: White House video games depict migrant captures, building border wall
description: Five online games promote President Donald Trump’s agenda, drawing sharp criticism from rights groups.
content: US President Donald Trump’s White House on Thursday unveiled a website featuring classic arcade games - but with a “Maga” twist, in which players can deport migrants and build a border wall. Rights groups swiftly criticised the release of the online games, which comes as the Trump administration steps up its mass arrest and deportation programme for undocumented migrants. One game called Rio Run - an updated version of the game Snake - features a digital version of US border tsar Tom Homan chasing migrants with different skin colours next to the Rio Grande river on the Mexican border. Another game based on the block-stacking game Tetris is called Build the Wall. “Protect the border from the coming horde,” the instructions say. A third involves collecting nets to put in so-called “Trump accounts” - investment accounts containing a US$1,000 deposit for children born in 2025 through 2028. The White House account on X posted a video with the “Make America Great Again” logo Maga, based on the logo of video game maker Sega. “CAN’T STOP WINNING. Build the wall. Deport. Fill a Trump Account,” it says. “This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the President’s many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American,” the White House said in a statement. “This is an effort to further contrast between a culture of fun and winning and the dark socialist vision Democrats have for America.” Rights groups criticised the White House for the gaming website. “Makes me sick. They’ve been playing games with people’s lives for years, now they’ve made a video game of what they’re doing,” Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas, said. The game designers “have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others”. Adriana Jasso, programme coordinator for AMIGOS San Diego Community, who works at the border, said the arcade-style games showed a fundamental “lack of seriousness” from the administration. “The cruelty, the extremity of the administration... is no longer surprising,” she said. The White House seems intent on dehumanising and ridiculing migrants, even as people die in detention centres, she said. “This presents the issue as if it were a game, when in fact it is not.” Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken several actions since returning to power aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings. His White House meanwhile has long used social media stunts to ram home its points and troll liberal opponents, and has sparked a backlash from several artists by using their music without permission.

title: Body of war criminal Mladic returns to Serbia with military honours
description: Huge funeral expected for the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, who died last week in a UN detention facility aged 84.
content: Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic’s body arrived in Serbia on Thursday, where it was received with military honours. The casket, draped in the Serbian flag, was carried from the plane by six soldiers after arriving from The Hague, accompanied by Mladic’s son Darko and Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic. The body was then driven from the airport under police escort, reportedly to a Belgrade military hospital. Mladic died last week while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war. Pro-government media broadcast images of dozens of people, mostly young men, gathered on footbridges over the motorway, displaying banners honouring Mladic and lighting flares as the convoy passed. The same outlets reported details of the funeral, including a public service at a church scheduled for Monday, but no details have been officially confirmed. Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said earlier Thursday that the state would provide “every kind of logistical and transport support” and he expected tens of thousands to gather for the funeral. The court ordered a full inquiry into the circumstances surrounding Mladic’s death, which had to be completed before his family could take possession of the body. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Monday criticised plans to bury Mladic with state honours. “Regarding Ratko Mladic, the glorification of war criminals is contrary to fundamental European values and has no place in the European Union or in countries that aspire to become members,” Kos said in Slovenia. Mladic, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was convicted of atrocities committed during Bosnia’s war, which killed around 100,000 people and forced 2.2 million from their homes. His role in the killings earned him the nickname the “Butcher of Bosnia”, particularly for his role in the Srebrenica massacre, Europe’s worst atrocity since World War II. Mladic was the military face of a brutal leadership alongside former Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic and ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic. After receiving the body, the military hospital said it would carry out a postmortem examination “at the request of Mladic’s family and the justice minister”. Dr Ivan Lekovic, deputy head of the hospital, said: “All findings, including the postmortem results and those of all analyses and examinations, will be provided to the family and the relevant institutions as soon as possible”. Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic said last week that Mladic “will receive all the military and state honours to which he is entitled”. Vucic said only that the funeral would be “dignified and in accordance with the family’s wishes”.

title: Deleveraging clouds China’s AI trade as rising US Treasury yields, inflation fears persist
description: The outstanding balance of stocks bought with borrowed money dropped to US$390.1 billion on Thursday after a brief rebound in August.
content: Chinese leveraged traders continue to unwind their bets on stocks, as unease over rising global bond yields and a lingering oil shock add uncertainty to the artificial intelligence trade. The outstanding balance of stocks bought with borrowed money dropped to 2.62 trillion yuan (US$390.1 billion) on Thursday after a brief rebound in August, according to data from China Securities Finance. That was 13 per cent below an all-time high of 3.01 trillion yuan set on June 25. Meanwhile, short positions on stocks rose to 29.2 billion yuan, near a two-year high. The subdued risk appetite aligned with global caution about risk assets after long-duration US Treasury yields rose to multi-year highs and Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh signalled an interest-rate increase unless inflation moderated. Stocks were also capped by Beijing’s reluctance to introduce a broad stimulus package even after key economic data fell short of estimates in July. The pattern indicates that deleveraging, which began during the July sell-off in tech stocks, has yet to run its course and that a strong rebound may still be elusive given that margin trading is a barometer of risk sentiment. The Star Market 50 index, the chip-heavy gauge at the centre of China’s AI trade, is approaching a previous low triggered by the biggest-ever monthly decline in July. The index tumbled 26 per cent that month, tracking a global tumult of tech stocks on jitters over whether massive AI investments would translate into monetisation. Even after the unwinding of leveraged positions, margin traders still have heavy exposure to tech stocks. Zhongji Innolight, a maker of optical transceivers used by US hyperscalers, had 31.5 billion yuan of leveraged positions on Thursday, the second most on the mainland’s three stock exchanges, while its rival Eoptolink Technology was in fifth place with 19.2 billion yuan, according to data from East Money Information. AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies had 17.5 billion yuan in margin trading balances, ranking eighth place, while ChangXin Memory Technologies, China’s biggest maker of DRAM chips, logged 11.1 billion yuan, putting it among the top 15, the data showed. Meanwhile, household appliance manufacturers were the most-shorted stocks. Air-conditioner maker Gree Electric Appliances and appliance giant Midea Group topped the list with bearish positions of 739 million yuan and 612 million yuan, respectively. Deleveraging would be less of a hindrance for Chinese stocks, while major headwinds were expected to come from rising US Treasury yields and possible redemption of domestic mutual funds that concentrated on tech companies, said Meng Lei, a strategist at UBS Group.

title: How chef Jason Liu reconnects with his Chinese roots at his new Beijing restaurant
description: Long before the Michelin stars, Jason Liu forged his path blending Chinese flavours and Western flair. He continues his journey at Ling Yun.
content: In China’s fine-dining circle, Jason Liu He-sen cuts an unusual figure. Shy and soft-spoken with modelesque looks, the quietly ambitious chef commands attention both behind the pass and on the runway. Liu blurs the line between food and fashion, and his growing influence extends well beyond the kitchen. He walked the runway at Hermès’ spring/summer 2024 menswear show in Shanghai and soon after became the first chef to partner with Nike for its “Yes, Chef!” campaign, during which he wore the sportswear giant’s C1TY trainers. Now 33, Liu has emerged as one of China’s most prominent figures in French-Chinese gastronomy. He recently opened a new restaurant, Ling Yun, near Beijing’s Forbidden City. Its name is inspired by the Chinese idiom ling yun zhuang zhi, which describes towering ambitions that reach the clouds. Ling Yun comes almost a year after the closure of his original Beijing restaurant, Ling Long, which opened in 2019 and earned a Michelin star – and Liu a Michelin Young Chef Award – in 2022. A deep-rooted passion for tastes of China Liu, who is from Taiwan, initially dreamed of becoming an artist, but his ambitions gradually changed as his sisters began praising his home-cooked meals. He began to see the kitchen as a canvas on which he could express himself while building a stable future for his family. “I grew up in a military dependents’ village in Taipei,” Liu says, referring to the enclaves built in Taiwan during the 1940s and 50s to house Republic of China Armed Forces servicemen and their families. “The village brought together people from across China. It grounded me in the flavours of traditional Chinese cooking.” Liu took his first step into the kitchen at a Western restaurant when he was 14. Two years later, he enrolled at Taiwan’s Kai Ping Culinary School while working at the Grand Hyatt Taipei, and eventually gained experience at Taipei restaurants Paris 1930 and Bellini. His big break came in 2017 when, at just 23, he was appointed head chef of Bistro 3 in Beijing. “Armed with a foundation in Western techniques, I saw it as an opportunity to challenge myself,” he says. But Liu’s passion for Chinese flavours never left him, and he steered the Western cuisine at Bistro 3 towards a fusion style by incorporating local flavours and ingredients. In 2018, he forged an even deeper connection with his Chinese culinary roots by embarking on a year-long pilgrimage across mainland China, tracing the Eight Great Traditions of Chinese cuisine through Guangdong, Sichuan, Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Fujian, Hunan, Anhui and Shandong provinces. The insights he gained from the expedition culminated in the opening of the original Ling Long in Beijing and, in 2023, the Shanghai outpost, which continues to wow diners at its location within Waldorf Astoria Shanghai on the Bund. Ling Long Shanghai’s multi-course menu spotlights xian (or umami) dishes made with Chinese ingredients and French techniques. In 2024, it was awarded a Michelin star and debuted at No 36 on Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list. In 2026, it came in at No 9. “Ling Long, which means exquisite, delicate and transparent … symbolises my wish to present traditional cuisine with exquisite clarity,” Liu says. One of Liu’s signature dishes, Shandong Wagyu, features Shandong beef cooked three ways (deep-fried, pan-seared and roasted), marinated in and served with home-made Fujian oyster sauce for added umami. “Shanghai has always been a competitive market,” Liu says. “Opening there was a test.” Modern Chinese cuisine with one foot in tradition But Liu is not resting on his laurels with his latest opening. “Ling Yun reflects another side of how I see traditional Chinese cuisine,” he says. “While the new space will continue to serve modern Chinese cuisine, it will carry a stronger imprint of traditional Chinese philosophy, style and aesthetics.” The debut menu offers a glimpse of this evolution. Liu’s garlic-dressed toro is inspired by suan ni bai rou – a Sichuan dish of thinly sliced pork belly in a pungent garlic sauce – but swaps pork for silkier tuna belly flesh. The dish, which arrives in a pool of spice-laced soy sauce, is based on a recipe Liu picked up while visiting Chengdu. Smoked sugar cane chicken is another dish that draws inspiration from classical Chinese preparation. What first appears to be a roasted piece of chicken has a layer of concentrated meat broth jelly tucked between the crisp, smoky skin and succulent meat. The jelly melts into the chicken as it warms up, amplifying the meat’s savoury richness. Despite Ling Yun’s focus on Chinese cuisine, Liu insists his ambitions extend beyond it. A glance around the cavernous, chapel-like space – with its starched linens and all the trappings of a haute-cuisine restaurant – reveals the scale of his aspirations.

title: 2 trapped workers rescued alive from Nepal tunnel 9 days after floods
description: The two are among hundreds of hydropower workers missing since a wall of mud and debris swept through the country last month.
content: Two hydropower workers were pulled from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal on Friday, a rare ray of hope on the 10th day of rescue efforts after catastrophic Himalayan flooding. Rescuers cheered as one man was pulled from a muddy opening, video released by the energy ministry showed. He was helped to his feet by rescuers, and later carried on the backs of the emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter. A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers carried him away on an orange stretcher. “As long as there is breath, there is hope!” Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha said in a statement. “Rescue operations are continuing in all the affected tunnels. Let everyone’s efforts and prayers continue. We have not lost hope.” Rescuers called it a “miracle” after the August 26 glacial and mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, which has killed at least 1,280 people and left more than 5,500 missing. “I am so happy, my heart is lighter,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of rescued worker Kabir Maharjan, said. The men, both Nepali, were named as Sanjay Shah, 30, a mechanical foreman, as well as Maharjan, 45, a mechanical supervisor, by Home Minister Sudan Gurung. The prime minister’s office said that Shah was in a “stable condition” and that Maharjan was in intensive care. Lakshmi Naini, who said Maharjan is her brother-in-law, waited outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where he was rushed to by helicopter. “It’s a miracle! I am very happy,” she said. “I heard he is alive through social media and I could not believe it.” “I have no words to express how I feel,” said another relative, Shyam Maharjan, 45. The two were among hundreds of hydropower workers who had been missing since a wall of mud and debris swept through the region on August 26 after a vast glacial and rock collapse on a mountain on the China-Nepal border. Searches were continuing at the Trishuli 3A tunnel where the two men were rescued, as well as multiple other sites, with at least 12 hydropower projects smashed by the floods. The government had initially said it believed more than 100 workers could be alive inside multiple tunnels. Nepali rescuers, aided by experts from India, China and South Korea, have continued searching for survivors feared trapped inside hydropower tunnels, but teams had repeatedly hit walls of hard-packed debris. Until Friday, none of the tunnel workers had been confirmed alive. Australian rescue expert Arnold Dix, who has been supporting the operation remotely, said that the rescue efforts were “back in miracle country” after a “week of 24/7 heartache”. Earlier on Friday, Dix said teams at the Trishuli 3A hydropower project believed they had heard a faint response from inside the tunnel. “They believe they received a faint response from inside saying, ‘hunchha’, yes or OK,” Dix, president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association, said, adding that he was en route to Nepal to join the rescue effort. He said rescuers had called into the tunnel: “Don’t worry, we are rescuing you.” Dix was a main adviser during the Himalayan rescue effort that successfully freed all 41 Indian workers trapped inside a collapsed under-construction road tunnel in 2023. Dix said teams had dug through debris blocking the tunnel for 50 to 60 metres (164-196 feet) and had been hoping for a breakthrough at any moment. Less than an hour later, rescuers pulled the two men to safety.

title: Trade chief Greer ‘optimistic’ the US and China can stabilise ties
description: He expects announcements on Board of Trade and American agricultural sales when Chinese leader visits Washington later this month.
content: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said both Washington and Beijing were seeking stability in their relationship and that he remained optimistic about ties ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected visit to the United States later this month. “I am optimistic. The Chinese very much want to have a stable relationship. That’s the word they use: stability. We’re in favour of that as well,” Greer said in an interview with Fox News on Thursday. He also said announcements on operationalising the US-China Board of Trade and incentivising US agricultural sales to China would be the likely outcome of the summit between Xi and US President Donald Trump in Washington, which confirms reports by the South China Morning Post. “We expect we’ll also have some deliverables on the Board of Trade that we’ve talked about,” he said. “We’re getting together with our Chinese counterparts,” he added. The creation of the Board of Trade was announced in May following Trump’s visit to Beijing, alongside a new Board of Investment, as mechanisms for managing business ties between the world’s two largest economies. Under the trade mechanism, both sides are identifying non-sensitive sectors and products eligible for a tariff-reduced trade capped at US$30 billion for each side. The SCMP reported last month that the Board of Trade was likely to be operationalised during Xi’s visit, even as discussions on the investment forum remained stalled. Greer explained how the arrangement could work, with both sides identifying products that could be shielded from future trade measures, particularly goods where American production is limited and there is little concern about imports from China. “It’s looking at different products,” Greer said, adding that the US could pick areas where it may “want to leave it alone” if it imposes trade measures in the future. He cited “toys and games” and “fireworks” as examples of non-sensitive products, saying the goal was to find areas where the US could “trade with China in a balanced way that doesn’t threaten our economy”. In July, the Chinese embassy in Washington said agriculture and aviation were among the sectors selected for tariff-reduced trade, adding that the two sides had “set a guiding objective of expanding two-way agricultural trade” and agreed “in principle” to include agricultural products in a framework for reciprocal tariff reductions. The SCMP also reported last week that the bilateral trade truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, was likely to be extended. “We are not looking for a giant comprehensive trade agreement with China,” Greer said. “We’re looking to manage this relationship.” On Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing that the two countries should maintain the steady momentum in economic and trade ties.

title: Hong Kong’s young skateboarders set to shine at the Asian Games in Japan
description: Katniss Wong and Kamus Wong are pursuing Olympic dreams and are inspired by idols like Sky Brown.
content:
In a skateboard team where the oldest member is merely 16, Katniss Wong Yi-huen and Kamus Wong Yeuk-ching stand out as the youngest competitors in the city’s Asian Games delegation, which consists of 580 athletes participating in 38 different sports.
And while Kamus Wong is already 12 years old, her teammate could end up celebrating her 12th birthday at the Games’ opening ceremony at Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya on September 19.
“I started skateboarding about two years ago after I came across it while watching those reels on Instagram, and then a friend of mine introduced me to the sport,” Katniss Wong said.
“Participating in the Asian Games feels like a huge matter for me. I am quite nervous but excited at the same time; I’ll keep working hard.
“Of course, I’d like to win a gold medal in some tournaments going forward, but for now, it’s just about doing the best I can, and performing the tricks and techniques I’ve learned.”
A pupil at the ESF South Island School, Katniss Wong finished seventh in the Asian Championship final in April and also took part in the World Skateboarding Tour World Cup in Rome in June.
The youngster wants to follow in the footsteps of skateboarding idols, Olympic medallists Sky Brown and Arisa Trew, and also compete at the Olympics, with her first opportunity coming in Los Angeles in two years.
“I wish to train and compete in different places to learn as much and try as hard as I can, and compete in more tournaments worldwide,” the 11-year-old said.
“I think the happiest thing about skateboarding was when you mastered some new tricks; it could be difficult when you couldn’t do something, and you would be unhappy. But it’s about keeping trying and keeping going, and you’ll get better eventually, just like me!”
A post shared by katniss 🙈 (@katniss__hh__)
Kamus Wong, meanwhile, who finished a place below her teammate in the regional championship, is not the first skateboarder in her family.
“We used to ski as a family, but the global pandemic locked down everything,” Dio Wong, her father, said. “So my wife and I started skateboarding, and before we knew it, our daughter also started.
“She started around six years ago, but has been practising more seriously over the past two years.”
A student at Baptist University Affiliated School Wong Kam Fai Secondary and Primary School, Kamus Wong said skiing and skateboarding “felt alike”, and the most difficult part of her practice was to “link all my moves together”.
Her father added his daughter’s school has been “very supportive” and she had been granted some extra off days to practise and compete at the Games.
“She will practise at some state-level facility in Nanjing before the Asian Games, and will only start her new school year afterwards,” he said.
Apart from the two youngest delegation members, Yuna Wan Hiu-yin, Li Pak-lam and Gu Jiahuan, who are between 13 and 16 years old, will make their Asian Games debuts, and coach Cheung Hang-tat said the newest generation of athletes could be the future of the sport in the city.
“Our athletes are really young; some of them – Wan, Li and Gu – will head to Paraguay for the WSG Park Skateboarding World Championship immediately after the Games,” he said. “I believe we’re developing in a positive direction.
“A golden age for skateboarding would be 14 to 20 years old. We have a lot of moves coming off the stairs, the bowl or the half-pipe, so athletes are prone to falling and we need to have a strong physique. Also, when we’re younger, our centre of gravity is lower, making it easier for us to absorb the force.”
A post shared by ⋆🥞˚࿔𝐊𝐚𝐦𝐮𝐬⋆˚꩜｡🍥 (@ssk_kamus_ssk)
For the first time, Hong Kong is also sending teams to the Games in modern pentathlon, wrestling, rhythmic gymnastics and padel.
Pentathletes Shum Chun-hei and Liu Hei-yu said they grew up swimming and started devoting time thinking the sport was “new and interesting”.
Shum, 16, said modern pentathlon had “taught me a lot” since he started about two years ago.
“It’s quite fun and enjoyable as it contains some different sports,” he said. “Most importantly, it taught me to look at different things with a calm and open mind.
“For example, even if you didn’t perform well in one event, you still have a chance to catch up, so you won’t be so negative.”
Diocesan Girls’ School pupil Liu said practising for the five events – fencing, an obstacle discipline, swimming and the combined laser-run – was a “great test” for her both physically and mentally.
As for wrestler Isaac Wong Ching-shing, he believed his sport, which featured at the first modern Olympics in 1896 and the second Asian Games in 1954, was “definitely the toughest one” of all.
“I was really interested in combat sports to start with, and then I decided to take one sport seriously; it’s been four years since I’ve been doing this,” said the 18-year-old, who will compete in the men’s freestyle 57kg category on the penultimate day of the Nagoya Games.
“I think wrestling is the toughest sport of all. It’s really challenging because it’s a six-minute sprint compared to other sports.”
A participant at the recent under-20 World Championships in Slovakia and the under-23 Asian Championships in Vietnam, Wong said wrestling was still developing in Hong Kong.
“It’s our first Games, and we might not be that strong compared to other countries, but we’re growing,” he said. “I’m more focused on my performance, knowing that if I can do that, I can get good results.”

title: China’s Xi eyes Apec trilateral; no outrunning deadly Nepal floods: SCMP’s 7 highlights
description: From an Air China jet grounded in New York to a Hong Kong school’s legal settlement, here are top stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Xi, Trump and Putin may hold trilateral meeting at next Apec forum, Kremlin says A senior Russian aide suggested on Tuesday that Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin could hold a trilateral meeting at the next Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. 2. China demands rights guarantee as US firm secures 100-year Venezuelan oil deal China has demanded protection of its interests in Venezuela after a US-backed energy company was granted 100-year concessions covering oilfields previously operated by Chinese and Russian firms. 3. China-Nepal floods: first research shows no one could have outrun debris flow Not even the world’s fastest sprinters could have outrun the devastating floodwaters that struck a border crossing between China and Nepal last week, according to one of the first peer-reviewed assessments of the disaster. 4.
