China teen with zero programming skills earns US$2,600 in 3 days selling AI study app A 13-year-old girl in China has earned 18,000 yuan (US$2,600) in just three days from an artificial intelligence (AI) product she developed to assist parents in supervising their children’s study habits.

title: Milei escalates Argentina’s Falklands dispute with UK as Trump hints at US policy shift
description: Argentine president moves to block offshore oil project and bolster naval presence following US leader’s comments on UK alliance.
content: Argentine President Javier Milei escalated his country’s dispute with Britain over the Falkland Islands on Thursday, vowing new measures to halt an oil project near the British-controlled archipelago and praising US President Donald Trump for saying Washington could reconsider its neutral stance on the islands’ sovereignty. Milei cast Trump’s comments as proof that his close relationship with the US president – criticised by political opponents as overly deferential – was paying dividends. “The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said in a nationally televised speech. The Argentine leader then announced sweeping actions aimed at stopping the development of the deep-sea Sea Lion oil project, about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands, where British company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum plan to begin drilling in the coming months and start pumping oil in 2028. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own. He threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in the offshore drilling and announced new funding for a naval base in Argentina’s southernmost province of Tierra del Fuego to bolster the country’s military presence near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas. “Argentina will not stand idly by,” Milei said. “Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security.” Milei’s effort to refocus attention on the Falklands is a striking turn for a leader who has faced criticism at home for warming ties with Britain and professing admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the British prime minister detested in Argentina for leading the campaign to retake the archipelago during the 1982 Falklands War. The two-month conflict, which killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders, remains a sore point in Argentina over four decades later. The sovereignty claim is enshrined in Argentina’s constitution and frequently invoked as an expression of national identity, from banknotes to World Cup soccer chants. It is also one of the few causes that cuts across the country’s stark political divides, giving Milei, who is up for re-election next year, a welcome political opening as his approval ratings slip and the economy sputters. “We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy,” Milei said. “But there are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them.” “He wants to use the legitimate sovereignty claim over the Malvinas Islands to regain ground ahead of the election year and serve US interests in its dispute with Britain,” said Nicolas del Cano, a leftist opposition lawmaker. Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former coloniser, Spain, and that Britain has illegally occupied them since 1833. Britain rejects that claim, citing the islanders’ desire to remain a British overseas territory. For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing claims while recognising Britain’s de facto administration of the islands. Any departure from that position would be a major diplomatic affront and inflame already high transatlantic tensions. On Monday, Trump stirred concern in Britain when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the decades-old dispute. “I always review every position,” he replied. “That’s just one of many.” Then, in an interview aired Thursday with British broadcaster GB News, Trump dodged directly answering a question about whether the US would “come to the aid” of Britain in another conflict over the Falklands. Instead, he repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran. “Your country was not there to help me,” Trump said, recalling Britain’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer, telling him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign. “It was pretty sad, the whole thing.” The Trump administration has floated the Falklands as leverage before: an internal Pentagon email leaked in April first raised the prospect of Washington reconsidering its position on the islands as one possible way to punish Nato allies that declined to join the US war on Iran. Downing Street has long insisted that Britain would not yield sovereignty over the Falklands. “Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders’ right to self-determination is paramount,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s spokesman, Tom Wells, said earlier this week, pointing to a 2013 referendum in which the roughly 4,000 people living in the Falkland Islands voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a British overseas territory. Under pressure from Argentina’s populist opposition, which accuses him of neglecting Argentina’s sovereignty claim, Milei has grown more vocal on the Falklands as plans for large-scale oil production around the islands raise the economic stakes of the dispute. In his speech, Milei warned that the Sea Lion project could usher in a broader Falklands oil boom, enriching the islands with resources Argentina claims as its own and further entrenching Britain’s presence. There was no immediate response early Friday from Downing Street. “If we allow it, we will be creating an incentive for the British government to deepen the occupation of the islands and the exploitation of our resources,” Milei said. Milei vowed to fast-track sanctions against companies involved in oil projects around the islands and extend penalties to suppliers, shareholders and directors. His proposed legislation could also bar companies tied to such projects from operating or signing contracts in Argentina. Despite slashing public spending elsewhere as part of his austerity drive, Milei also pledged more money to build a naval base in Tierra del Fuego and upgrade Argentina’s telecommunications capabilities there to strengthen the country’s presence in the South Atlantic. “A poor country without armed forces can hardly make effective progress on its sovereignty claims,” he said.

title: Cathay Pacific extends Dubai and Riyadh flight suspension through November
description: Hong Kong flag carrier says extension due to situation in Mideast, with services to both cities cancelled up to and including November 30.
content: Hong Kong flag carrier Cathay Pacific Airways has extended the suspension of passenger flights to Dubai and Riyadh until the end of November, keeping its Middle Eastern routes grounded for a total of nine months. The airline attributed the extension to “the latest developments in the Middle East”, confirming that services to both cities were now cancelled up to and including November 30. “Affected travellers will be offered the flexibility to rebook, reroute or refund their tickets,” it said. Cathay added that it would continue to review the timing for resuming freighter services to Dubai and Riyadh, while closely monitoring the evolving situation in the Middle East. The announcement comes amid a fresh exchange of strikes between the United States and Iran this week, threatening to reignite a conflict that began in February and had slipped into a diplomatic stalemate. Tensions have mounted further as the US steps up pressure through a naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Cathay first cancelled flights to Dubai and Riyadh on February 28. On July 2, it announced plans to progressively resume passenger and freighter services to the Middle East from September 1, putting tickets back on sale. But on July 17, the airline postponed the planned resumption until late October, again citing developments in the region. It also dropped its previous plan to resume freighter services to Riyadh from August 1, without providing a new timeline. Meanwhile, Emirates continues to operate flights from Hong Kong to Dubai, while Qatar Airways maintains its route to Doha, after both carriers gradually resumed services in March.

title: Debunking the ‘Tina’ doctrine: Nomura warns AI-driven rally masks US vulnerabilities
description: Bank flags US risk premium as AI surge falters, undermining ‘Tina’ or ‘there is no alternative’ to dollar assets.
content: The artificial intelligence boom has signalled growing risks in the US economy and capital markets, with a setback in the technology rally potentially triggering a sharp correction in US assets and weakening the dollar, according to a Nomura report. “The AI boom has masked a rising US risk premium,” Nomura analysts led by Rob Subbaraman said in a report on Thursday, warning that the concentration of global savings in US dollar assets had left investors increasingly exposed to a reversal in the AI-driven US equity rally. The ratio of US net international investment position (NIIP) liabilities to the combined assets of all net creditor nations has risen to 80 per cent, according to the Japanese investment bank. US NIIP liabilities reached US$21.9 trillion in 2025, equivalent to 71 per cent of gross domestic product, while the country’s portfolio liabilities have quadrupled to US$37.4 trillion in March 2026 from US$9.2 trillion before the global financial crisis, the bank’s data showed. “We attempt to debunk the assumed robustness of ‘Tina’,” the bank said, referring to the belief that “there is no alternative” to US assets. The growing exposure meant a sharp decline in US equities could have broader implications for global capital flows, particularly if foreign investors began to reduce their holdings of US assets, according to Nomura. Despite the strong profit growth of US equities supported by the AI boom, the bank flagged high valuations, uncertain adoption, competition from cheaper Chinese large language models (LLMs) and constraints on computing power, memory and electricity. A setback in AI could expose vulnerabilities masked by the equity rally and trigger a broader risk-off move, according to the bank. Foreign investors’ large exposure to US portfolio assets, together with leverage and circular financing linked to the AI investment boom, could amplify the impact, it added. Nomura estimated that US portfolio assets would need to fall by more than 30 per cent – comparable to a global financial crisis-scale repatriation – to fully offset the decline in US portfolio liabilities.

title: China stands to gain from US visa restrictions targeting African countries
description: The White House has slashed the number of places issuing visas on the continent at a time when Beijing is looking to open its doors.
content: The latest US visa restrictions on citizens of African countries are facing increasing criticism that they are not only punitive but also likely to backfire by driving those nations closer to China. Since August 1, visa services have been suspended in 25 African cities, forcing applicants to travel to other approved locations, sometimes in another country. Travellers from 30 African nations must also post a US$20,000 bond, which is refundable if they depart on time. Separately, 26 countries face full or partial US visa bans, and many African nations were included in a broader immigration ban targeting 75 countries that was recently struck down by a federal court in New York. Overall, Africa was the continent hardest hit by Donald Trump’s travel bans and visa restrictions. The State Department justified the latest policy by saying it was intended to strengthen “national security by promoting more uniform screening, vetting and adjudication standards”. But critics, including members of Congress, have warned that these policies may be hurting the country’s global standing and creating openings for China, which has long been keen to bolster its image as a reliable partner for Africa. The continent holds 30 per cent of the world’s critical minerals, with China leading the way in securing mining rights and supply chains. “The Trump administration is clearly thinking about US global influence in a different way than in the past” and is retreating from the idea of a “big global presence”, said Julia Gelatt, the associate director of the US immigration policy programme at the Migration Policy Institute, based in Washington. “Stephen Miller, who is the White House adviser on immigration, has talked about stopping immigration from ‘Third World countries’, and it seems like some of that has really led to a focus on African countries,” she said. Last year, the White House banned travel from 12 countries, including seven African ones, and partly restricted three other African nations before pausing immigrant visas for 75 countries worldwide, more than a third of them African, in January. The most recent measures have now halved the number of US embassies and consulates able to issue visas in Africa. Part of the justification for stopping immigrants from the poorer countries is that they are often refugees who then become dependent on government sustenance. But administration officials have not provided proof that refugees are more likely to receive public benefits, according to the Migration Policy Institute. “Some African populations are coming as refugees and other Africans are coming as very high-skilled workers, and those folks are not relying on government support,” Gelatt said. “Certainly, there have been accusations of racial bias.” The policies pursued by the Trump administration against African countries, such as immigration restrictions and tariffs, may just be helping write China’s script in Africa, according to an August 6 report by the US Congressional Research Service. The report said that while the US was imposing tariffs, China had cut duties on all African exports and was now pushing its currency, the yuan, as an alternative to the US dollar. It added that Beijing was also criticising Washington for bullying other countries while presenting itself as a reliable alternative. Henley & Partners, a UK-based firm specialising in global residence and citizenship planning, drew a contrast between the two countries in its latest Global Mobility Report. The report concluded that “the current path of nationalism the US is following may result in isolation on both economic and political fronts” at a time when China’s openness could help it “to cultivate deeper international trust and cooperation”. China appears set to further this advantage by expanding the number of countries eligible for visa-free travel. Although critics have pointed out that so far this has only been extended to two African countries, Mauritius and the Seychelles, others have said African travellers would still find it easier to enter China than the US. “My first business trips were to Italy, then later the US before China,” said Odi Otti, who runs Caltec Nigeria Limited, a firm that imports tools and machinery. “In my experience, getting a visa to China has been the easiest, all done in four or five days.” With the current restrictions, Otti said he had no immediate plans to seek a US visa. “Not with those bonds and all the hostile behaviour,” he said.

title: Letters | Queen Mary Hospital lift defects raise larger questions for Hong Kong
description: Readers discuss oversight of critical public infrastructure, a better development model for the Northern Metropolis, and a project in Hung Shui Kiu.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. I refer to “Hong Kong suspends contractors over Queen Mary Hospital lift defects” (August 15). With only a small fraction of 28 lifts in a new clinical block at Queen Mary Hospital operating at an acceptable level and the roll-out of clinical services delayed, public attention has understandably focused on rectification works and contractor accountability. However, viewing this solely as a hospital project’s failure risks missing a larger, more troubling picture. This incident did not arise in a vacuum. Hong Kong has already been warned about lift management, contractor oversight and asset reliability in the public sector. In 2023, the Audit Commission’s review of lift and escalator maintenance in public rental housing estates found more than 32,900 lift failures between 2020 and the end of April 2023. The review also identified lifts that were out of service for extended periods, repeated failures within short intervals and weaknesses in monitoring contractor performance. Some lift suspensions lasted up to 89 days. Major public projects are meant to go through numerous checks before opening to the public. Equipment is tested, defects are identified, repairs are carried out and systems are reviewed before final acceptance. That raises the question: how did such significant problems at Queen Mary Hospital emerge after so many checks and approvals had supposedly been completed? Hong Kong should take this opportunity to conduct a wider review of how critical infrastructure projects are planned, monitored and approved across government departments and public bodies. Such a review should target the larger issue – how can performance be uplifted to increase long-term reliability? The public expects hospitals, public housing estates, transport facilities and other essential infrastructure to work when they are needed. The question is no longer whether one project experienced lift failures. The question is whether Hong Kong’s broader system of oversight is sufficiently robust to ensure that critical public infrastructure is truly ready before it enters service. Stephanie Y.K. Hasancebi, Sham Tseng Let’s not be beholden to real estate developers again Development of the Northern Metropolis, a key component of Hong Kong’s five-year plan, is advancing steadily. I suspect the model of development is very much the same as what made today’s Hong Kong. Perhaps we need a rethink – a better model of development, one which does not leave us beholden to real estate developers and those who boost government coffers. The five-year plan will be the most consequential development plan in Hong Kong’s history. It will give us a chance to create a better society in terms of city planning, resource allocation, ecological preservation and social welfare for the grass-roots community. Aesthetics, greenery and climate mitigation are key to creating a world-class city. Our country parks give us an advantage. Future planning should make sure we retain our natural heritage alongside urban development. It would appear our focus in the five-year plan is only on the economy, and not so much on other software components. I urge the government to provide a clear road map that would incorporate other important considerations as well. T.C. Ng, North Point Northern Metropolis development the way to go In my letter, “Increasing cross-harbour toll will not ease tunnel congestion” (August 4, 2010), I noted that one way to effectively address this problem would be to create business centres in the New Territories. To my glee, a consortium comprising mainland Chinese firms and a local developer has now been granted a massive project in Hung Shui Kiu. This is not only a gigantic project, but it lays the groundwork for confidence – a sentiment reinforced by Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho’s remark that these enterprises have cast a tangible “vote of confidence” in the Northern Metropolis. There is a wise saying, “Well begun is half done.” I hope this applies to the Northern Metropolis development, which can and will further uplift Hong Kong’s growth. The reason is simple: unity. The consortium’s concerted effort is no more than the opening chapter; unity across every sector of Hong Kong – be it implicit or explicit – is the very engine that will enforce collective accountability and help the city develop. Ho Kam-tong, Yuen Long

title: US Open: Alexandra Eala marches on, as China’s Zheng Qinwen regains ‘competitive fire’
description: Filipino star cruises into round 3 at Flushing Meadows, as Zheng survives three-set battle and Felix Auger-Aliassime wilts in New York heat.
content: Alexandra Eala of the Philippines brushed ⁠aside Ukrainian Oleksandra Oliynykova ⁠6-1, 6-4 on Friday to reach the third ⁠round of the US Open, keeping alive the buzz for her fervent following in New York. The 21-year-old left hander lost to Oliynykova in Strasbourg earlier this year but had the right formula this time around; Eala needing little more than ‌an hour to book a third-round meeting with No 14 seed Iva Jovic of the USA. “My patience and the consistency of my focus [were] the key to winning the match today,” Eala said. Fresh from claiming her first career title in Washington last month, Eala won the opening four games across a dominant first set, striking ‌11 winners to none from her opponent. The two players traded breaks in a far more competitive second set, where Eala broke from the baseline in ‌the seventh game before slamming her foot on the gas and wrapping up the win with an ⁠unreturnable serve. The first player from the Philippines to win ‌a WTA Tour-level match, Eala was urged on by her compatriots in Louis Armstrong Stadium, where signs in Tagalog urged her to “fight ‌on”. “I think ‌we all represent something [and] I’m proud of what I represent,” Eala said. The fleet-footed, wide-smiling Eala has ‌catapulted herself into fans’ hearts as quickly as she has surged up the rankings, having ended 2025 ⁠world No 50 and arrived at Flushing Meadows 18th in the global standings. Eala, who last year exited the US Open in the second ⁠round, reached the fourth round at Wimbledon this summer for her deepest run at a major, and she said that experience was fuelling her New ‌York campaign. “I do feel like a ‌more well-rounded player and more mature,” Eala said. “I guess with time comes maturity and more intelligence. “I think I just have more knowledge ... in terms of tennis and competing at the very high level. [I know] what I’m capable of and believe in myself.” Zheng Qinwen, meanwhile, celebrated demonstratively after outlasting Yulia Putintseva 6-4, 2-6, 6-1 in her second-round match; the 2024 Olympic gold medallist relishing the return of her game – and her competitive fire. The Chinese former world No 4 endured an injury-plagued 2025 that included a longer than anticipated recovery from elbow surgery. She missed the Australian Open in January and has struggled to regain her form, and the mindset of a champion. “Before the surgery, for me winning was like drinking water,” Zheng said. “Everything came naturally, everything was fluent. “After my surgery, I had some tough matches against the best players in the world [and] I was close but I didn’t get them. “I totally lost the dynamic of how to compete. “I really felt for the first time in this tournament I found myself, I found my fire back during the competition.” Zheng plummeted so far in the rankings that she had to go through qualifying to seal her US Open berth. She grudgingly acknowledged that grinding through the qualifiers might have helped her regain her competitive edge, but that didn’t alleviate the sting of tumbling outside the top 100. “It took a while for me to accept my ranking dropped to 125 and that ‘OK, I need to actually play qualifiers’,” she said. Now she’s in the thick of the main draw and will face 2025 Australian Open champion Madison Keys for a place in the last 16. Zheng is looking forward to the test, and likely a chance to step back onto one of the main show courts after toiling through two rounds out of the spotlight. “I used to always play on the big court,” she said. “I need to fight to get everything back.” Two-time champion Naomi Osaka overcame Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 to set up a third-round date with Elise Mertens, a 6-2, 7-6 winner over Maria Timofeeva. In the men’s draw, No 3 seed Felix Auger-Aliassime wilted in baking temperatures in Louis Armstrong Stadium as he was ousted in four sets by unseeded Karen Khachanov. Beaten 6-7, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2, Canadian Auger-Aliassime said: “After a set and a half, I just couldn’t feel well and was dizzy and seeing spots and couldn’t recover. I thought maybe it would pass, but it didn’t.” Russian Khachanov will next play Benjamin Bonzi after the Frenchman beat Peru’s Ignacio Buse 6-2, 7-6, 6-0.

title: US probes deadly strike on Iran wedding that experts link to US munition
description: Vice-President J.D. Vance says Washington is investigating reported attack ‘because obviously we care’.
content: US Vice-President J.D. Vance said that the United States ⁠was investigating a deadly strike on an Iranian wedding earlier this week that an analysis published by Reuters showed likely resulted from a direct hit by a US munition. An explosion that ripped through a wedding celebration in southern Iran on Tuesday likely resulted from a direct hit by a US munition and not a ricochet off another target, according to an analysis on Thursday by weapons experts who reviewed images and video verified by Reuters. The United States has not accepted responsibility for the incident. ‌US President Donald Trump’s administration is facing growing domestic public pressure to end a war that is weighing on his approval ratings ahead of crucial November midterm elections. Iranian state television on Thursday said that a 22-year-old woman had died in hospital following the strike that hit a home during a wedding, taking the total reported death toll to five. Iranian officials said that nearly 70 were wounded. Funeral-goers assembled in the late afternoon on Thursday outside the village of Kuhestak in Sirik County, along a stretch of the Strait of Hormuz coast that was hit by heavy US air strikes late on Tuesday to mourn their loved ones. Vance told reporters on Thursday that the United States was looking into the incident. “We’re investigating it because obviously we care. We ⁠want to know,” he said. “If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran, when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better ‌from them,” Vance added. The US military said it was aware of the Iranian reports but it “never targets civilians”. A US official speaking on condition of anonymity said the government was looking at various scenarios related to the casualties at the wedding, including whether they were caused by a US strike, some sort ‌of ricochet of an Iranian air defence missile, or an errant interceptor itself. Reuters shared video and images of the incident with four military weapons experts who said the ⁠damage was consistent with a direct hit, as ⁠opposed to secondary damage from a munition ricocheting off a different target. Three of the experts said the munition was likely a US weapon, rather than an errant Iranian air defence missile. One of the experts said the weapon may have simply ‌missed its objective. The incident came some six months after a missile destroyed a primary school in an incident that Iranian officials said killed more than 175 children and teachers. Reuters previously reported that an initial, internal US military investigation showed US forces were likely responsible for ‌that strike. ‌The Pentagon has not publicly released the findings of its probe. At the funeral on Thursday for four victims from the wedding, Iran’s Mehr news agency video showed a pickup truck carrying ‌a flag-draped coffin beneath a canopy of palm fronds. A reporter in front of the truck said: “This is the body of Martyr Amir-Mohammad Karimi, a 4-year-old child who was martyred in an attack on ⁠the country’s south by the criminal American regime”. In other footage of the funeral, mourners threw petals into the air as doleful music played from a loudspeaker. A casket was carried past a row ⁠of soldiers standing at attention with rifles. “If it was a military location, it wouldn’t be so painful. This was a wedding ceremony, but they turned people’s joy into mourning,” the semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted a local man as saying. Washington launched the air strikes on Tuesday, hitting what it said were military targets along the coast in retaliation for Iranian attacks on ‌shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran reported 18 dead in the last US assault. It responded on Wednesday to the US strikes with attacks on US bases in Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, and carried out further attacks early on Thursday, saying it was targeting another US base, in Kuwait. Kuwait’s military said its air defences had intercepted missiles and drones. But following that, the war’s biggest flare-up since July appeared to subside, with no more major attacks from either side reported on Thursday.

title: Malaysia arrests 6 over drugs supplied to pilot caught with Ecstasy pills in Jakarta
description: Police said the suspects were taken into custody during a special operation conducted last month.
content: Six Malaysian men have been detained in connection with a drug smuggling case involving a 39-year-old Malaysia Airlines pilot detained at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport in Indonesia. The six were arrested following information obtained during questioning of the pilot by a team of Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) officers sent to Jakarta from August 11 to 15. Bukit Aman NCID director Commissioner Hussein Omar Khan said the six had allegedly acted as suppliers and couriers who provided drugs to the co-pilot. “All six, aged between 23 and 50, were arrested in a special operation conducted by the NCID from August 20 to 28,” Hussein said on Friday. “Investigations and intelligence gathering found that they played roles as upline and downline members of the drug distribution syndicate involving the co-pilot,” he said. “Further investigations are being conducted, and all six have been detained under the Dangerous Drugs (Special Preventive Measures) Act 1985.” Under the Act, police have the power to detain suspects for up to 60 days to facilitate investigations before further detention orders are issued. Hussein said the NCID would also share information obtained with the Indonesian national police. The pilot was detained at the international arrival terminal of Soekarno-Hatta International Airport after arriving from Kuala Lumpur on Malaysia Airlines flight MH727 on July 28. He was detained at about 11.30pm local time after Indonesian customs officers found his luggage suspicious during an X-ray scan and directed him to an examination room after he collected his baggage. A subsequent inspection uncovered 14 packages containing 70,114 Ecstasy pills weighing about 25kg (55lbs) in his luggage, as well as 4 grams of methamphetamine in his carry-on belongings. The drugs were estimated to be worth 45 million ringgit (US$11 million). According to Indonesian police, the co-pilot had allegedly been promised 50,000 ringgit to transport the drugs to Jakarta, where they were to be collected by another individual from a hotel. This story was first published by The Star

title: France digs in on Pacific islands claim as Vanuatu turns to UN’s top court
description: Vanuatu says it will seek UN General Assembly opinion if Paris does not accept the ICJ’s jurisdiction on the disputed outcrops.
content: France is facing pressure to consent to the International Court of Justice taking up a decades-old territorial feud with Vanuatu, after Paris firmly reasserted its sovereignty over two strategically vital Pacific islands. Vanuatu filed an application with the UN’s top court earlier this week seeking recognition of its claim over the uninhabited Matthew and Hunter islands. However, the case cannot proceed without French consent, prompting Vanuatu to warn it would seek a UN General Assembly opinion if Paris blocks its ICJ bid. The ICJ, also known as the World Court, will not immediately accept the case. Under the court’s rules, the case can only proceed if France agrees international judges have jurisdiction over its disputes with other states. “No action will be taken ⁠in the proceedings unless and until France consents to the Court’s jurisdiction in the ‌case,” the ICJ said in a press statement on Tuesday. France on Wednesday insisted on its sovereignty over the uninhabited islands of Matthew and Hunter, which are some 300km (190 miles) east of the French territory of New ‌Caledonia and southeast of Vanuatu. Eleonore Caroit, a junior minister at the French foreign ministry, said Paris had taken note of the move by Vanuatu over the islands and would give its response in due course. While the tiny islands cover less than 1 sq km of land, their ownership guarantees an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) of 350,000 sq km. Control over these territorial waters dictates fishing rights and the exploitation of rich seabed resources. Modern France still has overseas territories across the globe, from the Caribbean to the Indian Ocean and Pacific, legacies of the colonial era that are now vital strategic footholds for Paris. Vanuatu, which won independence from joint British and French rule in 1980, also claims sovereignty over the uninhabited outcrops. “France’s position is clear and firm,” Caroit said at a conference of Pacific islands hosted by Palau on Wednesday. “It is a position of dialogue and openness, but above all, it is a reaffirmation of France’s sovereignty over these islands,” said Caroit. The sides must “discuss, negotiate, and try to find solutions without relinquishing sovereignty – that was never on the table”, she added. Paris acknowledges the request by Vanuatu to open the case and will respond regarding “jurisdiction” and “the merits of the case”, she said. If Paris refuses to accept the court’s jurisdiction, Vanuatu plans to request an advisory opinion through a majority vote in the UN General Assembly, Vanuatu Environment Minister Ralph Regenvanu said at the forum. In 2025 France and Vanuatu agreed to new ⁠rounds of bilateral negotiations about the islands and the demarcation of the maritime boundaries between ⁠the territories after two earlier rounds of talks in 2018 and 2019. Earlier this year, Vanuatu said the new talks had reached ‌an impasse and it ‌would take its case to an international court. Vanuatu Prime Minister Jotham Napat had accused France of colonialism over the dispute, threatening to use “all diplomatic and international legal means” if discussions broke down. The ICJ, the United Nations’ highest court, deals with disputes between states and violations of international treaties. It often rules on disputes between countries about land and maritime boundaries. Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Boost for EVs: Chinese carmaker Chery to begin testing solid-state batteries next year
description: Chairman says it plans to invest US$1.49 billion in the new battery technology over the next two years.
content: Chery Automobile, China’s largest car exporter by deliveries, will begin testing its solid-state batteries next year, aiming to spearhead commercialisation of a technology likely to further spur the electrification of the global automotive industry. Yin Tongyue, the chairman of the state-owned carmaker, which is based in central China’s Anhui province, said on Thursday that it would invest 10 billion yuan (US$1.49 billion) in the new battery technology over the next two years, with 1,200 engineers to be deployed in the hunt for innovative breakthroughs. “Multiple [battery] technology plans are being laid out,” he told the World Power Battery Conference in Yibin, Sichuan province, the National Business Daily reported. “We will not install them in our vehicles unless they prove to be absolutely safe.” He said the solid-state batteries to be tested next year would have an energy density of 400 watt-hours per kilogram, double that of the batteries used in existing electric vehicles (EVs). Solid-state batteries, which use a solid electrolyte to conduct ions between electrodes, are widely seen as a superior alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries, which rely on liquid or ­gel-based materials. Analysts said the technology promised higher energy density, improved safety and longer driving range. Even if the new tech gets mature, battery makers have to bring down the costs to make it affordable to consumers Eric Han, Suolei But no solid-state batteries have been installed in mass-produced EVs. And just a handful of cars – such as some premium models from Shanghai-based Nio – use semi-solid-state batteries, where liquid is added to solid electrolytes to improve performance. Compared with liquid-based batteries, solid-state variants are less prone to overheating or catching fire in the event of overcharging or collisions. Yin did not reveal when Chery cars equipped with solid-state batteries could hit the market. In June, Robin Zeng Yuqun, chairman of Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL), the world’s largest EV battery producer, told a forum that mass production of solid-state batteries would not happen until 2030. On a scale of one to nine, the technology had only reached level four to date, he said. Eric Han, a senior ­manager at Shanghai consultancy Suolei, said Yin and Zeng’s contrasting views might “attract more attention from the public as more drivers in China are now opting for electric cars”. “Even if the new tech gets mature, battery makers have to bring down the costs to make it affordable to consumers,” he said.

title: US wants foreign warships for its navy. Japan is hoping to be picked
description: Should Washington commission Mogami-class frigates, it will become Japan’s largest deal since relaxing the rules on weapon exports in April.
content: Japan’s Mogami-class warship is turning out to be a hot item among global navies. Australia is buying 11, New Zealand is considering putting in an order – and now, even the United States is showing interest. According to a US Naval Institute report published on Tuesday, government and naval planners are looking at three possibilities: Japan’s Mogami-class frigates, South Korea’s Chungnam guided-missile frigate and Turkey’s Istanbul-class warship. This is the first time since World War II that a major foreign design will be built for the US Navy. Until recently, US law prohibited foreign-built warships from entering service with the navy, but the White House last month instructed the Pentagon to consider obtaining foreign designs by invoking a national security interest waiver. Washington was contemplating having two of the vessels constructed in foreign shipyards before construction would be transferred back to yards in the US “as part of the Trump administration’s push to rapidly expand the fleet”, the report said. If Washington decides on the Mogami-class fleet, this will be a significant development in Japanese sale of advanced military systems to the US, according to Masayuki Masuda, a senior official at the Ministry of Defence’s National Institute of Defence Studies. “It is a well-known fact that the US is having serious problems with its domestic shipbuilding sector and is not able to keep up with demand, so this would make a lot of sense,” he said. “Mogami ships are very advanced and have a smaller crew complement than other comparable vessels, which will be attractive to the US Navy. This would also deepen interoperability between the Maritime Self-Defence Force and the US Navy, as well as with Australia and, potentially, New Zealand.” The Royal Australian Navy has signed a US$7 billion deal with Japan to provide 11 enhanced Mogami-class warships. The first three will be built in Japan and delivered by 2030 and the rest constructed in Australian shipyards. At 142 metres (465 feet) in length and weighing 6,200 tonnes fully loaded, the enhanced Mogami class has a stealthy hull form and is powered by a combined diesel and gas propulsion system, giving it maximum speeds over 30 knots. It is armed with 32 vertical launch cells for missiles, including the Tomahawk. The vessel is also capable of operating at extended ranges – a critical consideration for Pacific operations – as well as a highly integrated combat information centre, extensive automation and the ability to deploy helicopters and unmanned systems. New Zealand is also reportedly interested in replacing its two Anzac-class frigates with the Japanese design, although no deal has been signed. “The US is already familiar with Japanese technology and standards in its warships and knows that Japanese shipyards will be able to meet their requirements,” Masuda said, adding that Washington might ultimately decide to share the project among all three nations. Natural partners William Yang, a Taiwan-based security analyst for the International Crisis Group, said Washington’s shift to commissioning foreign-built warships reflected the Trump government’s attitude towards its allies. “This administration has clearly set out a vision for the next phase of its alliance with partners that places a lot more emphasis on those allies to shoulder more responsibility for defence,” he said. Equally, the US is placing greater emphasis on shipbuilding for defence development, although that is constrained by blockages in domestic output – and that makes Asian nations with a long history in the shipbuilding sector natural partners, according to Yang. And the pressure to launch more hulls is becoming more acute. “The US has fallen behind China in the number of warships it has available and if the US wants to play catch-up, then it needs to commission more ships from its allies,” he said. Should Washington commission Mogami-class frigates, it will become Japan’s largest deal since relaxing the rules on exporting lethal weapons in April and could add new impetus to its defence sector. “In the last year or so, we have seen Japan strengthening its defence equipment sector and deepening its defence cooperation with allies across the Indo-Pacific region,” Yang said, pointing to agreements with Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia to supply weapons systems. “And while the data does not point to Japan providing domestically developed fighter jets to other countries, for example, I do see this as Japan identifying naval vessels as a strength and putting strategic priority on this area.” Japan’s traditional areas of strength – such as cars and electronics – had already moved to other countries or were in the process of being poached by rivals, so Tokyo was looking to build up another domestic industry, Yang said. Tokyo has announced plans to invest heavily to develop new shipyards and upgrade facilities that have fallen into disrepair – with an eye on the anticipated demand for servicing of US warships in the region, according to Nikkei. The paper reported in January last year that an estimated 1 trillion yen (US$6.9 billion) in public and private investment would be required – in part for the construction of a new “national dockyard”.

title: Why snakes have no limbs
description: Ancient snakes had four limbs, but after millions of years, their bodies have become long and streamlined.
content:
Most humans would struggle to navigate the world without arms and legs. But long ago, ancient snakes slowly lost their limbs through evolution.
But why would losing limbs be good? Imagine trying to squeeze through a narrow tunnel with four limbs that might get in the way. For an animal that travels through tight spaces, a long, streamlined body can make movement easier.
Today, snakes’ long, flexible bodies help them in many environments. They push through soil, move across land, swim through water and wind their way among branches.
Snakes belong to the Squamata order of reptiles, alongside lizards. The squamate lineage dates back at least 240 million years.
Snakes’ ancestors had four limbs, but these disappeared after millions of years of change.
Fossil evidence shows that ancient snakes lost their front limbs first, while some kept their back limbs and parts of the pelvis. This two-legged body form was useful for millions of years before most snakes eventually lost their external hind limbs as well.
The snake Najash lived about 95 million years ago. Its fossils include a partial skeleton with small back limbs and a pelvis.
Discoveries like this show that the change from a four-limbed ancestor to today’s long, limbless snake was a slow process (see graphic).
Natural selection favours traits that help organisms survive in their environments. If smaller limbs allowed some early snakes to move more quickly, they may have been more likely to survive and produce children. Over many generations, traits with reduced limbs became more common.
As their limbs became smaller, snakes transformed in another way: their bodies grew longer and grew many more vertebrae. Muscles now bend the snake’s flexible backbone and shift the belly’s skin and scales. This allows snakes to travel well without legs.
This is an example of how evolution does not always make organisms “better” in every way. Instead, it favours traits that suit a certain environment and way of life.
Most modern snakes have no outside limbs. But pythons and boas have tiny, claw-like structures called “pelvic spurs” near the cloaca at the base of the snake’s tail. These pelvic spurs are remnants of their ancestors’ hind limbs and offer a glimpse into snakes’ four-legged past.
In fact, male pythons and boas use their pelvic spurs while courting females, so these leftover “legs” still have an important job.

title: Evolution slithers along: how ancient snakes lost their limbs
description: Over millions of years, natural selection helped these reptiles adapt to burrowing through tight spaces with a long, streamlined body.
content:
As humans, most of us would struggle to navigate the world without arms and legs. But long ago, ancient snakes gradually lost their limbs through evolution.
But why would losing limbs be beneficial? Imagine trying to squeeze through a narrow tunnel with four limbs projecting from your body. Instead of helping, those limbs might get in the way. For an animal that burrows or travels through tight spaces, a long, streamlined body can make movement easier.
Today, snakes’ long, flexible bodies help them push through soil, move across land, swim through water and wind their way among branches.
Snakes belong to the Squamata order of reptiles, alongside lizards. The squamate lineage dates back at least 240 million years. Snakes’ ancestors had four limbs, but millions of years of gradual change produced the limbless bodies of modern snakes.
Some of the oldest fossils proposed to be early snakes date to about 167 million years ago, during the Middle Jurassic period. These early fossils consist mainly of fragments of jaws and other skull bones, which reveal little about what the animals’ bodies or limbs looked like.
Nonetheless, early snakes are thought to have already begun their transition to having four reduced limbs.
Younger snake fossils provide a clearer picture.
For instance, fossils of the snake Najash , which lived about 95 million years ago, include a partial skeleton with small hind limbs and a pelvis.
Discoveries like this one show that the transition from a four-limbed ancestor to today’s long, limbless snake body was a gradual process (see graphic).
Fossil evidence indicates that ancient snakes lost their forelimbs first, while some retained hind limbs and parts of the pelvis. This two-legged transitional body form remained successful for millions of years before most snakes eventually lost their external hind limbs as well.
Natural selection favours inherited traits that help organisms survive and reproduce in their environments.
If smaller limbs allowed some early snakes to move more efficiently, those individuals may have been more likely to survive and produce offspring. Over many generations, traits associated with reduced limbs became increasingly common.
As their limbs became smaller, snakes underwent another major transformation: their bodies grew longer and developed many more vertebrae. Coordinated waves of muscle movement now bend the snake’s flexible backbone and shift the belly’s skin and scales, allowing snakes to travel efficiently without legs.
This is a clear example of how evolution does not always make organisms “better” in every way. Instead, it favours traits that suit a particular environment and way of life.
Most modern snakes have no external limbs. However, pythons and boas possess tiny, claw-like structures called “pelvic spurs” near the cloaca at the base of the snake’s tail. These pelvic spurs are remnants of their ancestors’ hind limbs and offer a fascinating glimpse into snakes’ four-legged past.
In fact, male pythons and boas use their pelvic spurs while courting females, so these leftover “legs” still have an important job.
Young Post has partnered with Hong Kong Science Museum and Hong Kong Space Museum to encourage your pursuit of science. Every month, the museums answer questions about the world around us, the cosmos and beyond.

title: Opinion | 3 easy wins to modernise Hong Kong’s education system
description: Reform must address AI-disrupted assessment, expand global learning in the curriculum, and offer alternative pathways beyond the DSE.
content: Much has been said about Hong Kong’s vitality as a higher education hub. Yet, a radical rethink of our primary and secondary school system is equally necessary. The need for a blueprint has never been clearer. Our world is increasingly defined by the powerful forces of automation enabled by artificial intelligence (AI), geopolitical tensions and flux, as well as conflicting values and perspectives. Workplaces and communities alike demand talent in possession of relational intelligence, technological literacy and pragmatism, and functional dexterity. Here are a few reasonable conjectures. Those who can communicate with empathy and contextual awareness are more likely to secure increasingly scarce entry-level jobs. Those who embrace the reasonings of technology while remaining aware of its pitfalls will see their productivity enhanced. Those who can straddle multiple disciplines are less exposed to the risks posed by a well-trained AI agent. The billion-dollar question is whether Hong Kong is equipping its youth with these desired characteristics. Or is a mixture of inertia and risk aversion holding us back from genuinely upskilling our workforce? To positively disrupt the status quo, three low-hanging fruit should be pursued. Firstly, the purpose and format of school assessments must change. While rote memorisation and recall-centric quizzes may have rightfully ceased to be the primary mode of assessment, AI also poses challenges for in-school submissions. A third way is needed. Much greater emphasis must be placed on verbal communication and the in-depth dialogical cross-examination of ideas. We should introduce shorter but smartly designed examinations that test higher-order evaluative and comparative skills, coupled with a mandatory in-person viva voce – an oral examination of their answers – with suitable workload support offered for examiners. Having taught debating at Eton College and philosophy at Oxford University and the University of Hong Kong, I have experienced the virtues of oratorical advocacy as a pedagogical tool: one that prompts flexibility in thought, precision in diction and an appreciation of emotions and intuitions – skills that matter greatly as text-based outputs are increasingly replicable through generative AI. Be it a corporate or research setting, the success of many presentations hinges not on what was said, but how it was said. The Hong Kong government has pledged reforms to attract more senior secondary students to science and mathematics subjects. While technological literacy should be lauded, we should be careful not to cultivate another brick in the wall, but to nurture architects who can imagine, build, use and dismantle walls with maturity and dexterity. Studying the ethics, governance and socioeconomic effects of technology is as important as making sense of machine learning. Secondly, it is high time senior secondary students were given the opportunity to organically explore and learn about the world beyond Hong Kong, through less curated and more authentic first-hand experiences. The scope of exploration should extend beyond the mainland and encompass Southeast Asia (we are within a five-hour flight of most of its capitals), Northeast Asia (with which we enjoy long-standing cultural ties), and Central and South Asia. For all the talk of our city being a “superconnector” and a bilingual metropolis, our education system is surprisingly limited in linguistic and cultural training offerings. Six “Other Languages” – French, German, Japanese, Korean, Spanish and Urdu – are offered in the Diploma of Secondary Education (DSE), with Hindi joining the ranks in 2028. Arabic (spoken by 422 million) and Bahasa Indonesia/Malay (around 300 million) are not available. Hong Kong should position itself as a hub for those aspiring to understand Asia from up close. This behoves recruiting and training the right calibre of teachers and instructors to spearhead the drive for greater linguistic and cultural internationalisation in the local curriculum. Whether it be in understanding China or neighbouring countries, students would benefit immensely from immersion, which pierces their bubbles of insulation. Deeper dialogues, goal-oriented collaborations and competitions, and more frequent interactions are sorely needed – and can be accomplished with the aid of digital technology. Intention is also key – students should be given ample background information to understand the purpose of field trips. That a school’s secondary students spent seven out of 12 hours of their trip to Guangzhou on a coach bus in 2023 spoke volumes to the dearth of understanding of the mainland – and its travel conveniences – among some of our academic administrators. Schools and teachers should also be given the green light to host constructively critical – as opposed to unilaterally affirmative – discussions concerning China’s developmental successes and bottlenecks, as well as its wider standing in the world. Finally, Hong Kong must strive to internationalise not just its higher education sector, but also its secondary school curriculum. The internationalisation of DSE, the city’s university entrance examinations, has been floated by lawmakers. If this drive is to succeed, Hong Kong’s government must take a more proactive stance in communicating the strengths, values and uniqueness of the DSE – as a regionally competitive and internationally significant education offering. On the flipside, the government should also consider introducing alternative curricula – such as the International Baccalaureate or A-levels – into public schools. Such options should not only be available to those who can afford to attend international schools. Non-international school students deserve the same degree of optionality and flexibility. The three proposed reforms cannot resolve all the issues in Hong Kong’s education. Yet they could perhaps provide a start.

title: Chinese teachers publicly shamed on stage for students’ low test scores, sparking outrage
description: Photos of the incident quickly went viral, drawing over 100 million views on social media and sparking nationwide fury.
content: An impoverished county in southwestern China issued an apology for arranging its primary and junior secondary school teachers on stage to pose for photos alongside prominent characters depicting humiliation due to their students’ low test scores. The images, which went viral on social media, sparked widespread public condemnation. They were captured at an internal meeting organised by the Leibo County Education Bureau in Sichuan province in late August, as reported by Zhengzai News. During an award and punishment session, over 20 primary school teachers were instructed to stand on stage for a group photo, with a large screen behind them displaying the median scores from their students’ most recent exam, which were below 30 out of a total of 100. Two large Chinese characters, chi ru, meaning “humiliation” in English, were prominently displayed in the centre of the screen, directly behind the teachers. Later, another group of 20 junior secondary school teachers, whose students’ average scores fell below 15 out of 100, also took the stage for group photos, similarly featuring the humiliating characters on the big screen. These photos rapidly circulated online, and the incident of public humiliation directed at the teachers garnered over 100 million views on a leading social media platform alone. “This is ridiculous! Do they ever respect teachers?” questioned one internet user. Another outraged user commented: “I am disheartened to read this news report. Are the education bureau’s leaders treating teachers as their slaves? I believe these leaders should resign immediately.” Leibo is a remote and impoverished county in Sichuan province, predominantly inhabited by the Yi ethnic minority. Many residents include left-behind children, whose parents work in larger cities for better opportunities. A junior secondary school teacher in Shanghai, who wishes to remain anonymous, expressed empathy for the teachers, acknowledging the challenges of teaching and enabling students to achieve high scores in such a disadvantaged area. “Their parents are absent from home, so there’s no one to supervise their studies. When students do not apply themselves, teachers have no authority to discipline them. Consequently, students often lack seriousness in their studies, which understandably results in extremely low scores,” said the Shanghai teacher. Domestic media criticised the local authorities for their actions. “Rather than identifying the specific factors contributing to students’ poor performance, the authorities merely shamed the teachers. This constitutes a crude and heavy-handed management approach that fails to motivate educators. Furthermore, it complicates the retention of current teachers,” stated news portal guancha.cn in a commentary on August 27. In light of public backlash, the Leibo county government issued an apology on August 28. “What we did at the meeting was a wrongful act of disrespect towards teachers. It has caused psychological harm to those involved,” the statement read. “We feel deeply guilty about this and are reflecting on our mistake,” the authorities added, noting that an investigation into the incident is ongoing. Despite the State Council of China’s clear stipulation in 2020 through its New Era Education Assessment Reform Plan that schools and authorities should not solely prioritise students’ scores, this trend remains largely uncorrected. Schools whose students excel in significant examinations, such as the secondary school entrance exam and the national university entrance exam, continue to be favoured within society, with their headmasters gaining more opportunities for promotion within the education system.

title: Wilczek’s Multiverse | Cats and mind-full mechanics: what happens when quantum physics meets the brain
description: Legendary experiments in ‘cat-turning’ from the 1850s can teach us about will, control and goal-seeking behaviour.
content: Cats are wonderful gymnasts. Their ability to land on their feet – even when dropped upside-down – caught the attention of two of the nineteenth century’s greatest mathematical physicists, Sir George Gabriel Stokes and James Clerk Maxwell. The remarkable feats of cats inspired these theorists to perform, in the 1850s, legendary experiments in “cat-turning”, as Maxwell later described: “There is a tradition in Trinity that when I was here I discovered a method of throwing a cat so as not to light on its feet, and that I used to throw cats out of windows,” he wrote. “I had to explain that the proper object of research was to find how quick the cat would turn round, and that the proper method was to let the cat drop on a table or bed from about two inches, and that even then the cat lights on her feet.” These pioneering experiments in cat-turning were limited by the available technology. High-speed photography revolutionised the subject. Etienne-Jules Marey developed a chronophotographic camera that could record 12 frames per second, and in 1894 he published a classic, delightful series of stop-action photographs that reveal the sequence of actions through which cats reorient themselves on the fly (literally) and stick the landing. In 1969 a now-classic dynamical model appeared. Even today the subject is not exhausted: a 2026 study began replacing idealised hinges and cylinders with measured properties of a real cat’s spine. Similarly, human divers and gymnasts learn how to guide themselves, catlike, through routines that reorient their bodies in motion. For the cat much of this control may be reflexive; in a human athlete it can be planned, rehearsed and revised. These abilities seem, on the face of it, to violate the spirit of Newtonian mechanics, which says that accelerated motion occurs through the action of physical forces, not willpower. That tension, I think, is one reason that cat-turning fascinated Stokes and Maxwell. A second, more technical reason has to do with the relationship between angular momentum and angular motion. Starting with zero angular momentum and with no external torque, the cat nevertheless changes its orientation. This would be impossible for a rigid body, but by executing a closed loop in its space of possible shapes the cat manages to rotate. A big part of the reason why classical Newtonian mechanics was difficult to discover, and a big part of why it is such a towering intellectual achievement, is that it required a kind of cognitive dissonance. Specifically, it required – and still requires – people to reconcile two very different, quasi-contradictory descriptions of motion, both successful and convincing within their domains of application. There is the “common sense” understanding of movement, in which the concepts of will and purpose are central. This is the way we live our everyday lives: when we reach out to pick something up, we don’t compute forces and accelerations, we just decide to do it. Then there is classical mechanics proper – austere, rigorously mathematical, and deterministic – from which those concepts are excluded. Before the mechanical world-view took hold, self-directed motion was often treated as evidence of an animating principle – a soul – absent from inert matter. Today, science has understood that matter, embodying a system of known, (relatively) simple, mathematically formulated laws, can support the sort of complex emergent behaviour we find in molecular biochemistry, neurobiology and synthetic intelligence. With that understanding, we can bring mind back into mechanics without sacrificing its integrity. The abilities of cats, divers and gymnasts don’t really evade the laws of physics, of course – if they did, we’d promptly change the laws. The fruitful way to engage this problem is not to deny the role of mind in mechanics, but rather to welcome it in. The cat does not invent a new force; it chooses a path in shape space and uses its muscles to redistribute its mass. Ordinary mechanics translates that path into rotation. Thus, to do justice to cat-turning we must enrich mechanics’ vocabulary and its stock of concepts. We can call this expanded subject – which brings ideas about will, control and goal-seeking behaviour into mechanics – “mind-full mechanics”. Its technical ingredients flourish under names such as biomechanics, control theory and robotics. Mind-full mechanics names the conceptual innovation they share in common. In mind-full mechanics, we let ourselves assume that our cat, diver or gymnast can change its shape by acts of “will”. “Will” is the product of minds that have plans aimed at achieving goals, monitor progress, and respond to cues from the external world. Purpose is not a new force; it is a new way of organising forces. Ordinary mechanics – basically, physics according to Sir Isaac Newton – governs how willed shape changes get translated into motion through space. Will is not a force. It is a policy for choosing and coordinating forces. To describe the purposive motion, we need both forces and minds. This hybrid approach defines mind-full mechanics. It is how biologists, athletes and trainers generally think about the mechanical issues they deal with. Allowing for mind and will spices up mechanics considerably. It invites new kinds of questions and permits new kinds of answers. What degrees of freedom can mind-full acts of will call into play? What kinds of observations can guide good choices? How can feedback help to provide stability? What is the role of practice and learning? How did cats’ abilities evolve, and how can athletes move more efficiently or more beautifully? Engineers who design machines for transport, manufacturing, or many other purposes practice mind-full mechanics. Consider, for example, what goes into designing a self-driving car. Sensors provide perception, computers implement a control policy, and actuators translate the policy into forces. The sensors and computers form a narrowly focused mind, while the actuators are like muscles that it activates. Modern “mechanical” engineers learn not only physical mechanics but also control theory, operations research and optimisation. These playful and practical aspects of mind-full mechanics should not obscure its profundity. It is a big step to connect mind and matter. Here we do just that, concretely and successfully. With feet planted on the ground, then, let us contemplate the clouds. Mind-full mechanics shines a bright light into the murky philosophical question of free will versus determinism. The fundamental equations of present-day physics suggest that the complete physical state of a closed system fixes its future. But that is rarely the question we are interested in. We usually have only approximate knowledge of a few aspects of the state of a system, and our interest is focused on limited aspects of its behaviour. For instance, it would be hopelessly difficult, not to mention silly, to try to do psychiatry by evolving the patient’s fundamental wave function. (“How are your gluons arranged today?”) Usually, we have approximate knowledge of a few aspects of our system, and we want to predict a few aspects of how it is likely to behave. Given only that partial information, many underlying states remain possible, leading to a range of possible macroscopic outcomes that we often describe probabilistically. Determinism names a property of a dynamical theory: given a complete state of a closed system at one time, the theory prescribes its later state. But an agent never possesses that complete description and, more importantly, does not pose that question. Its question is not simply “What will happen?” but “What will happen if I do this rather than that?” It has partial information, several available actions, and a goal. It faces a problem of control. Those alternatives do not contradict determinism. If I perform action A, one consequence follows; if I perform action B, another follows. Deliberation is the physical process through which one of those conditions is made actual. Memories, reasoning and imagined consequences are among the causes that shape the choice. Choice is not outside the causal chain; it is one of its links. In philosophical language, determinism is an ontological claim, not an epistemic gift. That is, it says something about the ultimate nature of reality, not about our knowledge of reality. Determinism does not imply predictability across all contexts, and it does not erase the inside perspective of an embedded, finitely informed agent. From outside, an idealised complete description will contain one trajectory. From inside, the agent encounters information, counterfactuals, goals and handles. For people-oriented questions, physical determinism is rarely a useful language. We can’t know a person’s complete “state of mind” in the sense of physics. And we wouldn’t be able to use that information even if we had it – the calculations required are much too hard. In practice, if we want to predict how someone will behave, we try to understand their state of mind using concepts like knowledge, motivation and mood and to figure out how their personality will translate that state into action. For the questions at hand, ontological determinism is largely academic. This applies to our self-awareness, too. Free will is not an illusion, but a useful and legitimate way to understand ourselves. It is very plausible, I think, that free will is how intelligent minds process, and experience, determinism. In short, free will is what determinism looks like from the inside. The quantum state of a closed system evolves deterministically, just as in classical physics. There is a new wrinkle: no embedded observer can measure everything about the complete quantum state, even in principle, without changing it. Quantum theory only widens the classical gap between formal description and experienced reality; it does not create it. Another famous physics cat – Schroedinger’s – dramatises the gap between a complete formal description and an uncertain experienced outcome. The falling cat dramatises a different gap: between a trajectory described from outside and a future navigated from within. Of the two cats, the falling one may teach us more about free will.

title: How China’s AI race is shrinking job market, forcing workers into low-paid, manual roles
description: White-collar, corporate jobs could be in the firing line as artificial intelligence proves quicker at tasks requiring data-heavy tech skills.
content: For four years, Beijing-based Clare Zhang worked as a research analyst at a corporate advisory firm, helping companies assess technologies and competitors for projects they planned to list – until late last year, when she was told that artificial intelligence had reduced the number of analysts the company needed and could afford. Her job involved combing through company filings and public records to produce market and competitor studies that sometimes ran to 500 pages. But AI could increasingly collect and organise the information, analyse data and generate charts in a fraction of the time. Zhang said the company’s human resources department explicitly cited AI when dismissing her, explaining that it could no longer justify employing so many analysts. Two of her former colleagues were laid off shortly afterwards. The pressure soon spread beyond individual jobs. Zhang recently learned that her former boss was also struggling with a declining number of clients, as they increasingly brought research in-house with AI, though her team had warned clients that AI could invent sources and produce convincing but unreliable findings. “They would rather trust AI because our reports were considered too expensive,” Zhang said. In May, a Chinese court ruled it was illegal for a company to terminate an employee on the grounds that an artificial intelligence replacement would be cheaper, after a 35-year-old worker, who oversaw AI-generated responses at a Hangzhou fintech firm, was fired over refusing a demotion and pay cut. The company told him his role could be replaced by AI. While Zhang’s case predates the court’s ruling, she is among a growing number of junior white-collar workers facing pressure from AI, particularly in repetitive roles involving the collection and processing of public information, such as basic research, content production, accounting and administrative work. Over the past three years, AI has evolved from chatbots capable of generating basic text and images into increasingly sophisticated systems that can write code, analyse data, conduct research and handle customer-service tasks, forcing many to seek positions less vulnerable to replacement. After losing her job, she submitted 40 to 50 applications in her first month and explored legal work, only to find opportunities in both fields drying up. Still looking for another research position, Zhang said she was preparing for the possibility of becoming a domestic organiser, childcare worker or supermarket packer. “If nothing else works, I’ll have to do physical labour,” she said. “Those jobs are harder for AI to replace.” AI’s disruption of employment did not begin this year. The International Labour Organization already warned last year that a quarter of jobs worldwide were potentially exposed to generative AI, although transformation rather than outright replacement was the more likely outcome. In China, 33.2 per cent of 40.01 million job postings published between January and April involved tasks considered highly exposed to AI, according to a report released by ShanghaiTech University in July. Basic operations, accounting, visual content production and telephone sales were among the most vulnerable fields. The researchers analysed more than 700 million postings across five recruitment platforms between 2022 and 2026. They found that the greatest pressure fell on entry-level and mid-tier positions requiring one to three years of experience and paying between 5,000 yuan and 8,000 yuan (US$743 and US$1,189) a month, while jobs in manufacturing, healthcare, in-person care and equipment maintenance remained relatively resilient. At the same time, AI is creating new demand. A separate PwC study released in July found that AI application roles increased by nearly 90,000 last year, or 50.8 per cent, while development positions rose by about 30,500, or 15.5 per cent. [AI] has mainly stripped out the people in the middle – those who used to turn a client’s idea into a finished product Juno Zhu, Beijing “Occupations most affected by AI are absorbing new skills at a faster pace,” PwC said. “This presents both challenges and opportunities.” For Beijing-based illustrator Juno Zhu, AI has not ended his career so much as forced him to keep changing course, from hand-drawn picture books to AI-assisted comics and short-form dramas. He studied animation and spent nearly nine years building a career in visual storytelling, only to watch AI tools improve every few months and steadily reduce the number of people needed to complete a project. “People say AI creates new jobs, but I don’t think it has created many,” Zhu said. “It has mainly stripped out the people in the middle – those who used to turn a client’s idea into a finished product.” Work that once took a team of 10 can now be handled by two or three people, he said, while an entire short drama that previously required at least three months can sometimes be produced in one. Zhu has since learned to use the same tools disrupting his profession, but worries they are erasing the value of his nine years of experience. One prospective employer told him a recent graduate earning 5,000 to 6,000 yuan a month could now produce work of a similar standard with AI. Meanwhile, changing industries offered little comfort. Zhu said employers increasingly wanted people who could contribute immediately, leaving little room for a 33-year-old newcomer to learn on the job. “They don’t support you going in and learning any more,” he said. “You have to be ready to work from the moment you arrive.”

title: UK scientists invent the first balloon that can fully break down in 9 months
description: Researchers at Imperial College London hope to make the ‘Bioloon’ available for people to buy in two years.
content:
Balloons are used around the world for parties, but they can harm nature. They do not break down and can hurt ocean life and birds. Because of this, researchers in the United Kingdom are making balloons more eco-friendly.
Scientists at Imperial College London have made the first fully biodegradable balloon called the “Bioloon”. They hope to make it available for people to buy in about two years.
Juliana Cumming is a PhD student at the university and co-creator of the Bioloon. She spent three years creating her balloon formula.
In a laboratory, the 29-year-old showed a flask with a yellow liquid. When it hardens, it turns into a soft, stretchy material that feels like a regular balloon. But it falls apart in nine months, unlike regular balloons.

title: In Focus | Faster and cheaper: why Hongkongers are heading north for medical care
description: Lower costs and fast service across the border draw patients to Guangdong, leaving Hong Kong’s private doctors squeezed.
content: Soon after becoming a mother, Hong Kong resident Sarah Tam enjoyed eight hours of sleep a night and yoga sessions at a post-partum care centre in neighbouring Shenzhen, where carers looked after her newborn around the clock. Tam, a 30-year-old social worker who gave birth in mid-July, spent a month at the facility in mainland China, recovering from delivery with total peace of mind. She said she felt completely at ease leaving her baby in their care, which allowed “mothers to truly focus on resting”. In Hong Kong, new mothers commonly hire a specialised post-partum carer, known locally as a pui yuet, to assist with baby care and recovery at home. However, round-the-clock confinement care in the city can cost upwards of HK$70,000 (US$8,927). The steep price tag prompted Tam and her husband to cross the border to a post-partum care centre in Shenzhen. For just HK$40,000, Tam stayed in a hotel-style room equipped with a queen-sized bed, en suite bathroom, sofa, steriliser, bottle warmer and fridge. The package also covered six meals a day, daily essentials such as nappies and baby clothes, 24-hour newborn care and maternal wellness treatments including massages and facials. During her stay, Tam breastfed her baby for around 30 to 60 minutes a day, leaving bottle-feeding and daily care to centre staff the rest of the time. On days when her husband or other visitors were around, she kept the baby with her for five to six hours. “It’s great value for money,” she said. “The stay averaged around HK$1,500 to HK$1,600 per night … inclusive of three meals, three snacks, baby care, various services and activities.” Tam is part of a growing wave of Hong Kong residents travelling across the border for medical and healthcare services, from routine check-ups and dental work to specialised inpatient procedures. Many of these services match or surpass local quality standards, at a fraction of the cost. Capitalising on the influx of non-local patients, Guangzhou – the capital of Guangdong province and a core city in the bay area – is also positioning itself as a regional hub for medical tourism. Experts noted the northbound wave could ease pressure on Hong Kong’s public healthcare system and raise mainland medical standards, while forcing local private providers to rethink their business models to stay competitive Relieving the burden but hurting the private market?
