Medical and healthcare services are a strategic priority for integration under the Greater Bay Area development plan, a national blueprint linking Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in Guangdong province. According to mainland health authorities, Hong Kong residents made 700,000 visits to Shenzhen medical facilities in 2023. Across Guangdong, 30,575 patients from Hong Kong and Macau received inpatient hospital care that year, a 125.6 per cent increase compared with 2018. “When the mainland offers much lower costs and significantly improved medical standards, it is only natural that people cross the border for care,” said Dr Ko Wing-man, Hong Kong’s former secretary for food and health and honorary president of the Greater Bay Area Medical Professional Development Association. Cheaper cancer therapies across the border are among the most sought-after treatments among Hongkongers. Data from Guangzhou United Family Hospital shows that pembrolizumab – an immunotherapy drug used to treat various cancers – costs 17,918 yuan (HK$20,894) on the mainland, whereas the market price for the same drug in Hong Kong is nearly double, at 30,360 yuan. The breast cancer combination therapy pertuzumab and trastuzumab costs 10,321 yuan at the Guangzhou facility, whereas the same treatment in Hong Kong costs more than five times as much, at 55,872 yuan. Ko said that the flow of patients to the mainland could ease pressure on Hong Kong’s public hospitals, much like public-private partnerships or the Voluntary Health Insurance Scheme, which redirects patients towards private healthcare options. Hong Kong authorities have introduced several measures to facilitate the northbound trend, such as enabling residents to share electronic health records with select bay area medical facilities and expanding the healthcare voucher scheme for elderly residents to 21 regional institutions. Despite these measures, Ko stressed that the government was not pushing the city’s patients across the border. “It has never been a case of the government asking people to go north for medical services, or the city’s healthcare sector sending patients away to the mainland,” he said. However, Ko acknowledged that some patients who previously used private healthcare services in Hong Kong might also be drawn to the mainland. A 2024 survey of 203 private practitioners conducted by the Association of Private Medical Specialists of Hong Kong revealed that 71 per cent reported a decline in patient numbers over the previous year. Nearly 40 per cent of the respondents of the survey – which had not been released to the public previously – said they believed the decline could be due to patients turning to services in the bay area. Competitive pricing and greater transparency Shadow Lu, a 33-year-old financial planner, visited a dentist in Shenzhen for the first time in 2023 for a root canal procedure, which cost her around 13,000 yuan. She said a similar treatment would have set her back by HK$20,000 to HK$30,000 in Hong Kong. Pleased with the outcome, she returned for follow-up dental work in February this year. “On my first visit, I was drawn purely by the price. For my second visit, I returned to the same dentist as I found his skills were very good,” Lu said. Lu also noted greater transparency on the mainland, where consumer review platforms offered extensive patient feedback and detailed profiles of individual practitioners. Using a customer review app popular on the mainland, she could check comments from those who had used the service before choosing a dentist. “Service in Hong Kong is expensive, and there isn’t much reference for me to check whether a dentist is capable or not,” she said. Cross-border maternal care is also expanding. Onyuma Maternity Centre in Shenzhen’s Longgang district – a 40-minute drive from the Heung Yuen Wai border checkpoint – is one of the few post-partum confinement centres on the mainland run by Hongkongers. Operations director Eva Cheng Pui-yin said the business opened in 2023 after conducting thorough market research. “Our company invested in mainland China early on. In recent years, we expanded into the ‘big health’ sector in light of the Greater Bay Area’s prospects, with maternal care being a key focus,” she said. To her surprise, the number of clients from Hong Kong grew from an initial trickle in the early years to a consistent six to seven bookings every month. Foreign nationals working in Shenzhen or Hong Kong also used their service, she added. Cheng attributed the shift to evolving consumption patterns, convenient transport and the exceptional value for money that Hong Kong mothers could enjoy on the mainland. Standard packages at Onyuma Maternity Centre cost roughly 40,000 yuan and include dedicated cross-border hospital pickup, alongside help with newborn travel permit applications. The most luxurious package costs 120,000 yuan, and includes a 900 sq ft two-bedroom suite designed for visiting families, as well as an unlimited supply of baby products, among other perks. Amid the trend towards post-partum confinement across the border, Cheng reminded mothers to exercise caution when selecting services. “Some businesses engage in aggressive price wars, some of them fold abruptly and leave mothers in distress, while others add hidden fees after check-in,” she warned. “Price is important, but institutional stability, quality and reputation matter just as much.” Regional medical ambitions Guangzhou United Family Hospital has witnessed a significant increase in both Hongkongers and foreigners seeking its services. The private facility is operated by the New Frontier Group, which was co-founded by Hong Kong’s former financial secretary Antony Leung Kam-chung. Executive general manager Zhang Xuming said the hospital projected a 75 per cent year-on-year increase in Hong Kong outpatient visits this year, while surgical operations for Hong Kong patients were expected to surge by 230 per cent. Common procedures included cardiac stenting, joint replacements and gallbladder surgeries, he said. “An operation could be arranged for patients the day after an examination, if no major problems are identified,” Zhang said. Apart from quick arrangements, surgeries at the facility were around 30 to 50 per cent cheaper than similar procedures offered at Hong Kong’s private hospitals, he said. While mainland patients accounted for 70 to 80 per cent of admissions, Zhang expected the proportion of non-local patients – especially those who are not from Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan – to increase. “[Medical tourism] could help raise Guangzhou’s profile internationally,” he said. Guangzhou authorities are working to position the city as a major medical tourism hub, leveraging its top-tier hospitals, expert medical staff and international links via Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport, one of China’s busiest aviation hubs. The airport handled more than 10 million international and cross-border passengers as of July 3 this year, a year-on-year increase of around 20 per cent. In April, the Guangzhou International Medical Tourism Service Centre was set up by the government to provide one-stop support to non-locals amid the growing demand for healthcare services. Guangzhou vice-mayor Lai Zhihong said at an August conference in Hong Kong that the centre had partnered with 17 local hospitals to assist non-mainlanders with healthcare access, insurance payment processing, accommodation and transport. Last year, Guangzhou provided outpatient services to 168,000 non-local patients and inpatient care to around 15,000 foreign visitors. Calls for caution Tim Pang Hung-cheong, a patients’ rights advocate with the Society for Community Organisation, warned that while the mainland offered cheaper medical options, Hong Kong patients faced potential hurdles regarding quality consistency and dispute resolution. “In the event of a medical dispute, most patients would be unsure of how to seek redress – whether to approach the hospital directly or navigate an unfamiliar complaint system,” Pang said. He also cautioned that diagnostic imaging conducted on the mainland might not always align with Hong Kong protocols, potentially complicating follow-up care back home. “Is the imaging done according to the technical specifications used by Hong Kong? Are the reports written according to Hong Kong standards?” he said. Pang emphasised that in the long term it would be crucial to achieve a win-win situation in which patients enjoyed benefits from both sides of the border – value for money on the mainland and quality service in Hong Kong. The market has already shown signs of integration amid the trend of northbound medical tourism, with some insurers in Hong Kong now covering healthcare services provided on the mainland. “Medical costs are lower across the border, yet insurance premiums remain broadly the same,” Pang said. “The market will naturally adjust based on the comparative advantages of both systems.” As cross-border competition grows, former health chief Ko urged Hong Kong’s private healthcare providers to sharpen their competitive edge. “How can we make use of our standards that are on par with international practice, or our medical culture, to facilitate more people coming?” he said. “These are the areas we need to think about.”

title: ‘Point of grievance’: Philippines urged to rethink school safety approach
description: A new bill aims to establish a comprehensive safety framework, but experts say measures must target mitigating violence much earlier.
content: As pressure mounts in the Philippines for authorities to act on strengthening school security after two fatal shootings in eight weeks, safety experts say any measure must look at mitigating violence much earlier, even before a child brings a weapon to the campus gate. A bill pushed by lawmaker Bam Aquino will require schools to establish a comprehensive safety framework, including localised safety plans with guidelines on prevention, emergency response and recovery. The bill also includes establishing common standards for safety infrastructure, such as the use of surveillance cameras, mandatory screening and visitor management. Aquino, who chairs the Senate Committee on Basic Education, urged immediate approval of the bill as he invoked the names of students who died in the recent school attacks, warning that no more names must be added to the list. “We cannot accept that this will be part of a normal school life. We cannot wait for the next incident to happen before we act,” Aquino said on August 26. The Philippines was rocked by two separate student shootings this year: first at a public high school in Tacloban City in central Philippines in June where three pupils died, and then at the Ateneo de Zamboanga Junior High School in Zamboanga City in the south that claimed two lives, including that of the perpetrator. The bill consolidates existing proposed measures that seek to address the rise in school violence, including anti-bullying protections, mobile phone use regulations in school, digital and social media literacy, and the expansion of mental health and child protection services. Also included are proposals to improve school-based counselling, establish safety and risk-prevention systems, and adopt a whole-of-community approach. Other officials, such as Education Secretary Sonny Angara and Philippine National Police Chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez, have expressed their support for the bill. ‘Point of grievance’ The measure comes as public pressure mounts on lawmakers to act on the shooting incidents, as authorities continue to probe possible causes, including bullying and allegations of radicalisation through social media. An overwhelming 93.2 per cent of Filipinos viewed school violence as a problem, while 75.8 per cent urged tighter security measures, according to a survey by independent polling firm Momentum Research conducted in August. Meanwhile, 77.2 per cent also saw bullying as a key reason behind the rise in school-related violence, the same poll found. Authorities are also looking into potential links between social media and online gaming platforms such as Roblox as pathways for radicalisation, including alleged references to nihilistic violent extremism communities. Analysts meanwhile have tied the rise in school shootings across the region to a possible emergence of memetic violence, marked by premeditation, attention to aesthetics, and a drive for notoriety through mass violence. Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow of Verve Research, said the trend appeared to be spreading across Southeast Asia, but attributed it to more of a “confluence” than a copycat problem. Just two weeks before the Zamboanga shooting, a student in Nonthaburi, Thailand, opened fire at his public high school, killing nine and injuring 23 others before taking his own life. Across the region, Thailand’s cabinet declared school safety a national priority while Malaysia has faced calls to draw up a National School Safety Master Plan following a series of violent attacks. Munira stressed that policymakers should look beyond schools, citing the attack carried out by a 14-year-old at the Siam Paragon shopping centre in Bangkok in 2023 that killed three people. “The reason they’re attacking the school is one, because it’s the most accessible place. Two, the school is apparently their point of grievance. So what happens if they cannot access the school? Is that going to discourage them from attacking the school?” Munira said. “We need to think not just about securitising the school [...] we need to work out what’s provoking these kids to this extent.” Munira cautioned against relying on measures such as metal detectors at campus gates as that would create a heightened sense of tension in the school environment and institutions might lack the resources to implement them. Hyper-vigilant initiatives also led to security fatigue, which could cause lapses, she noted. “I feel like it’s a wasted resource to spend on this … we shouldn’t be guarding the school at the expectation that a child is going to bring a weapon. We need to be able to identify signs that kids might act out in a very unhealthy way,” Munira said. The analyst cited Singapore as an example of how countries could look into preventive measures and an assessment of cumulative behaviours. In May, the city state’s authorities managed to foil a mass stabbing attempt a month before it was to be carried out, after someone raised the alarm about the suspect’s behaviour. Child safety advocates share similar views, adding that prevention “should not begin only when someone reaches the school gate carrying a weapon”. “By that point, several opportunities for earlier intervention may already have been missed,” said Ysrael Diloy, a child protection specialist at the non-profit Stairway Foundation’s Safeguarding, Training and Consultancy Unit. “An effective school safety system should be able to receive concerns early, assess them appropriately and connect the child or situation to the right intervention before the risk escalates. This requires coordination among schools, families, mental-health professionals, local authorities and, where there is a credible threat, law enforcement.” Diloy said child safeguarding included investing in early detection and intervention, but warned against automatically labelling every child showing concerning behaviour as a potential offender. “The child may also be a child at risk who needs protection, psychosocial support, family intervention or specialised services. The objective should be to address the underlying risks and needs early enough to prevent escalation,” Diloy said. He lamented that identifying children at risk and implementing appropriate interventions remained a challenge for many schools in the Philippines. Beyond physical safety Advocates have also stressed the importance of protecting both the physical and psychological safety of children in safety frameworks. “The proposed Comprehensive School Safety Act is important because it can move us from reacting to individual tragedies towards a coordinated system for prevention, response, and recovery,” Joanna Herrera, a clinical psychologist and executive director of the non-profit organisation Circle of Hope, told This Week in Asia. “But the law will protect children only if schools have realistic local plans, trained personnel, clear accountability, and adequate resources to implement them.” Schools must therefore coordinate with families, village officials and local governments, as well as law enforcement, health services and social welfare authorities, she added. Herrera stressed that safety also depended on whether bullying was addressed, if children felt they belonged, and if they trusted an adult enough to disclose a threat or crisis. She called for a layered system of prevention to be woven into daily school life, as early and coordinated intervention when distress and safety risks emerged was crucial. This included training students, families, teachers and staff in culturally adapted mental health literacy – such as shared and non-stigmatising language for stress, mental health, and help-seeking – and educating school personnel in mental health first aid, crisis response and prevention. Creating regulating, relationship-centred school environments through predictable routines and calm adult responses could also help children learn to make wise choices, she added.

title: A house divided: Asia still split on Infantino’s future, HKFA won’t say where loyalties lie
description: Hong Kong football bosses still refusing to say whether they support under-fire Fifa chief, who is rumoured to be planning Asean Cup visit.
content: While the famously taciturn Football Association of Hong Kong, China is refusing to pick a side, elsewhere in Asia battle lines are being drawn between those that support Fifa president Gianni Infantino and those who want him kicked out of the game. With little more than two months to go before the deadline to nominate a challenger in next year’s election, a look at who stands where shows a region deeply divided, with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) aligning with its counterparts in Europe and North America, but in direct opposition to some of its member nations. Having stayed tight-lipped since Infantino’s plan to sell off the World Cup to private investors was exposed, the HKFA this week told the South China Morning Post that they had “noted the recent discussions regarding Fifa Forward Enterprise [FFE]” and had “no available information to be released at this stage”. That followed weeks of association chairman Eric Fok Kai-shan avoiding every possible public event where he might have been asked to voice an opinion. Later this month, the city will stage the Challenge Division of the inaugural Fifa Asean Cup; playing group fixtures against Laos and Brunei for the right to reach a final where the winners will bank US$300,000. The whole 10-day tournament could be worth around US$500,000 to the HKFA, while it is rumoured that Infantino could pay a visit during the competition. Indonesia, which is hosting the cup’s Premier Division, has also predictably aligned itself with the Swiss lawyer, who last year chose the country’s capital, Jakarta, as Fifa’s “operational hub” for Southeast and East Asia. “We are thinking [about] what we can do to bring everyone really on board with Fifa to develop the game in every corner of the world, to invest in every corner of the world,” Infantino said when announcing the alternative Asean Cup, which will begin on September 24, less than one month after the final of the five-week Asean Hyundai Cup, which celebrated its 30th birthday this year. Last week Davor Suker, the former Real Madrid, Arsenal and Croatia striker, who is friends with Fok, told the SCMP that Infantino was “doing a great job”. A Fifa ambassador, Suker is also an ex-president of the Croatian Football Federation; a relatively small operation that is grateful for any additional financial support, its national team’s ability to consistently punch above its weight notwithstanding. And it is the largesse of football’s global governing body on Infantino’s watch that means he has plenty of associations in his corner. Around six weeks before his FFE proposal was made public, Infantino told Fifa’s member associations that their roughly US$2 million annual handouts would be boosted by 20 per cent. He reminded them, too, that before he took office in 2016, they were receiving US$250,000 per year. Little wonder that the likes of Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Lebanon and Yemen have their flags planted firmly in the Infantino camp. According to several sources, those countries were among a number present when Infantino was holding private talks with the more impoverished Asian nations to promise them US$8 million each before the next Fifa presidential election in March. The president of the Lebanese Football Association, Hashem Haidar, was joined by Qatari counterpart Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani as a co-signatory on a statement “expressing our full support” for Infantino, and “reaffirming our confidence in his leadership and continued commitment to the development of football worldwide”. Unsurprisingly, football chiefs from Saudi Arabia, the 2034 World Cup hosts, added their backing for Fifa’s embattled leader, saying in a statement they supported his efforts to “restore unity across ⁠the football family and continue growing the game for the benefit of all”. The United Arab Emirates Football Association has “reaffirmed its confidence” in Infantino, while the Philippine Football Federation said it “stands behind” Infantino, citing the “expanding commercial and financial assistance” to member associations that resulted in a “more inclusive World Cup”, which serves as a “reminder that when developing nations get real investment, the game becomes more competitive for everyone”. Infantino reportedly also has approval from India and Kuwait. In contrast, Jordan, Iran and Bahrain are not fans, while Japan, South Korea and China have opted to keep their own counsel. The AFC, along with Concacaf and Uefa, rounded on Infantino, calling his plan a “fundamental breach of trust”, adding that his actions were not those of “a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him”. Still, the 56-year-old does not necessarily need the confidence of continental confederations to survive. With all 211 member nations getting a say next March, he is busy circling the globe in a quest to secure the 106 votes he would require in a two-way battle for office. Anyone wanting to oppose him has until November 18 to submit their candidacy. In 2019 and 2023, Infantino was voted in by acclamation, having beaten Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa of Bahrain, Jordan’s Prince Ali Al Hussein and the Frenchman Jerome Champagne in the race to replace Sepp Blatter 10 years ago. Today, Prince Ali and Sheikh Salman are among Infantino’s most vehement critics. Prince Ali recently accused him of “blackmail”, saying that Infantino told him during the World Cup that his endorsement would “go a long way to helping our FA out”. “We did not endorse him before and certainly will not now,” Prince Ali said. In his position as president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman was the organisation’s signatory on the letter calling for Infantino to be unseated. Sources suggest that Asian nations would unite behind a popular candidate against Infantino. There is a fear of being marginalised should a European less obliging than the present office holder be elected. The divisive Prince Ali would not have universal support, with Qatari Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain president, seen as a more unifying figure. He is unlikely to stand, however. Concacaf boss Victor Montagliani is the most likely to stand, but whether the Canadian would be popular enough in Asia is far from certain.

title: Pipes, power and petaflops: what’s behind China’s massive ‘6 networks’ investment
description: With US$1 trillion earmarked for this year alone, a look at where and why Beijing is investing, where progress stands and what comes next.
content: China’s biggest economic buzzword this year could be the “six networks”, as Beijing aims to use infrastructure investment to inject fresh momentum into an economy facing persistent headwinds such as weak domestic demand and a prolonged property downturn. The scale is substantial, with investment expected to exceed 7 trillion yuan (US$1 trillion) this year alone, according to the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC). During the five years through 2030, combined investment in just three of the six networks – water, power grids and underground utility pipelines – is projected to exceed 16 trillion yuan. The South China Morning Post breaks down what the six networks are, why they matter, how much progress China has made and what comes next. What are the six networks? The programme covers the national water network, power grid, computing network, next-generation communications network, urban underground pipeline network and logistics network. While some of these involve traditional infrastructure, others are closely tied to China’s push into artificial intelligence and other hi-tech industries. For example, the computing network links data centres and other computing resources across the country; the upgrade to a “new type power grid” aims to absorb more renewable energy and meet rising electricity demand; and the next-generation communications network covers technologies including 5G, 6G and satellite communications. Why do they matter? Beijing sees the networks as tools to stabilise investment and boost employment. Investment in the water network alone is expected to create more than 3 million new jobs in the coming years, while funding for the power-grid improvements is projected to unlock more than 10 trillion yuan in total supply-chain investment. The networks also underpin China’s ambitions in the global AI race. Expanding data centres require reliable electricity, while computing hubs need high-speed communications links. Upgrading the power grid is also critical as China adds large amounts of solar and wind capacity. “Over the longer term, China’s ‘six networks’ should be understood primarily as an effort to upgrade and replace existing infrastructure, rather than simply build more of it,” said Xing Zhaopeng, a senior China strategist at ANZ Research. This would help stabilise investment without adding excessive new capacity, he added. China’s overall fixed-asset investment, covering major areas such as infrastructure, manufacturing and property construction, fell by 6.7 per cent year on year in the January-July period. What progress has been made? Among major milestones, China’s intelligent computing capacity reached 1.882 million petaflops, 2.5 times the level a year earlier, according to a July report published on the NDRC’s website. The term petaflops means one quadrillion (one-thousand trillion) of a specific kind of computing operation, called a floating-point operation, per second. The country is also deploying an upgraded version of 5G, known as 5G-Advanced, with enhanced capabilities such as higher speeds, while key 6G technologies have entered testing, the report said. In logistics, the Pinglu Canal is on track to open to navigation later this month, supporting surging trade with Southeast Asia. The 134km (83-mile) canal links Nanning, capital of the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, to the Gulf of Tonkin, also known as the Beibu Gulf, between China and Vietnam. What can be expected next? Experts said this year’s 800 billion yuan in policy-based financial instruments would be channelled primarily into the six networks. With climate risks and natural disasters becoming more pronounced, urban underground infrastructure could receive greater attention in the near term, while computing and transport were likely to remain longer-term priorities, Xing said. In late August, the Ministry of Transport and NDRC released a logistics construction plan aimed at lowering transport costs and improving efficiency by 2030. The plan focuses on expanding rail freight, upgrading major highways and ports, improving inland waterways and boosting cargo-handling capacity at key airports.

title: Have you been to the Great Wall of China?
description: Why the answer to the question of whether you have been to the Great Wall of China is trickier than it might seem.
content: Every visitor to China eventually has the same conversation. Someone asks if you have been to the Great Wall. You say, “Yes”, and they ask which bit. You realise, often for the first time, that the question is more pointed than it sounds. There is, in the end, one Great Wall: a 2,000-year building project begun by competing kingdoms before China was unified, linked and extended by the first emperor after unification, Qin Shi Huang, and rebuilt in the Ming period, from 1368 onwards, into the version everyone now pictures. What survives is another matter. A national survey completed in 2012 counted 10,051 wall sections, 1,764 trenches and ramparts, 29,510 watchtowers, and 2,211 forts and passes, with a total length of 21,196.18km (13,170.7 miles). Two-and-a-half-thousand years of collapse, farming, desertification and warfare did to the wall what time does to everything eventually: broke it into many parts. Badaling: the one everyone means Badaling is one of the famous sections closest to Beijing, the first to open to the public, in 1957, and the one most visitors picture when they think of the Great Wall. It is also the most heavily developed section, and the most crowded. Both its north and south stretches have cable cars, and the north side has added a toboggan slideway, with little one-person sledges sent back down the slope at a speed Ming-dynasty officials presumably did not intend. It is here that you can see the most-photographed stretch of the Great Wall, though your legs may be less amused than your eyes. A stone marker partway up declares, “If you do not reach the Great Wall, you are not a hero”, a line attributed to Mao Zedong, a challenge few visitors can resist. It is worth doing once in the way it is worth seeing Stonehenge or Uluru once: partly for the pleasure of saying you have and partly because the climb, like the slogan, flatters the stubbornness in us all. After that, you understand why anyone with any sense goes elsewhere. Mutianyu: the harder climb Mutianyu is what Badaling would be with better manners: fully restored, with fewer crowds. It has its own cable car, though I did not take it. I climbed instead, the whole way, to a summit where the view was exactly as advertised: mist sitting in the valleys, the wall running off in both directions further than seemed reasonable. I was 20 years younger than I am now, which explains the attempt. My legs ached for a full fortnight afterwards. I had not, of course, climbed anything more dangerous than a well-maintained tourist site with a gift shop at the bottom, but it did not feel that way at the time. Jiankou and Gubeikou: the sections that were never fixed And then there are the parts of the Great Wall that were never restored at all, and they don’t want you to forget it. Jiankou, west of Mutianyu, is the section every serious hiker gets talked into and every sensible person gets talked out of. It is steep enough that parts of it are effectively a scrambling route, with crumbling brick, no railings and a reputation for sending overconfident visitors to hospital each year. I have stood at the bottom of it and made a series of choices I do not regret. Gubeikou is its quieter cousin. Around 120km (75 miles) northeast of central Beijing, it makes an easy enough side trip for anyone with a car and a half-day to spare, but feels far removed from the crowds and polish of Badaling or Mutianyu. Unrestored and properly rugged, it was a key pass between the steppe and Beijing, and a site of repeated fighting across the centuries. This is the Great Wall as it still looks in the imagination, before anyone tells you how much of it has been rebuilt. Simatai: the only one open after dark Simatai solves a problem you did not know you had: the Great Wall closes at sunset everywhere except here. It is the section most promoted for night visits, with the stretch between towers five and six lit from within and the lights of Gubei Water Town glowing below. Gubei Water Town itself is a reconstructed northern water town built in the 2010s, criticised by purists for lacking the patina of the real thing and entirely unbothered by the criticism. You stay the night, soak in a hot spring and go up by cable car as the lanterns come on. Not everything has to be authentic to be worth doing. From Wangjing Tower, the city lights of Beijing can sometimes be seen on the horizon at night, a reminder of just how far the capital has grown towards a wall built to keep its predecessors out. Shanhaiguan: where the wall meets water At the eastern end, the wall simply walks into the sea. This section, Shanhaiguan, the “First Pass Under Heaven”, guarded the coastal route into China. A few kilometres south of the former Shanhaiguan town but part of the same defensive complex, a stone causeway built in the Ming period runs into the Bohai Sea, at Laolongtou. This is the only point along the wall where you can stand on stonework with waves breaking against your ankles. The original structure was destroyed in 1900, during the Boxer rebellion, and rebuilt in the 1980s, meaning much of what you see is newer than it looks. Watching the sea do what it has always done to that stretch of granite, this stops mattering rather quickly. The other four Beyond these six sections that I have walked, four others round out the familiar 10. Juyongguan, the closest of the great passes to Beijing, sits in a horseshoe-shaped valley and was considered a major line of defence before the capital. Huanghuacheng, north of Beijing, is the section where the wall disappears into a reservoir. Huangyaguan, near Tianjin, hosts a marathon along its watchtowers each May. Jiayuguan, far to the west, marks the point where the Ming wall reaches the Gobi Desert. None were built with views in mind. They were built to stop people and did the job well. What the great wall actually is Put the 10 together and what you get is, in the end, quite simple, even if nothing about getting there (either conceptually or physically) was: one wall, one continuous ambition, left to fall apart in its own particular way at every point along its length. It is climbable at Badaling and Mutianyu, crumbling at Jiankou and Gubeikou, and confusing everywhere else, because the famous fragments and the forgotten ones are, technically, telling the same 2,000-year story from wildly different points in its disrepair. The wall is simply too long, too old and too broken to be summed up by any single visit, which is why, “Have you done the Great Wall?” never has a sensible answer.

title: Help! Where do I fit in after my divorced parents remarry?
description: Each week, we respond to a question from our readers and give advice and resources they can turn to.
content:
Do you have a personal question you’ve been too afraid to ask? Whether it is about school, family or your social life, you can share it with us through this form . Don’t worry, you’ll remain anonymous.
How should I handle it when my divorced parents remarry? Both of my parents have new families now, and it feels like they have moved on. But I’m just stuck in the middle, and I have no idea where I am supposed to fit.
Seeing your parents split up and find new families can be stressful and confusing, especially if it feels like you’re stuck in the middle. When dealing with complex family relationships, it is natural to feel sadness, anger, uncertainty and even a sense of betrayal .
Take time to feel and reflect on your emotions. This could mean writing about it in a journal, talking to a friend, taking walks to be alone with your thoughts, listening to music or making art. Spending this time with your emotions can reduce your distress and help you think more clearly about what to do next.
While your parents’ relationships have changed, their new marriages do not erase their roles as your parents. You still share your past experiences – and the chance to build more memories in the future. If you feel comfortable, talk to your parents about how you are feeling. It can be helpful to hear their reassurance that you are still part of their family.
Beyond hearing their words, quality time together is also key. You can continue to enjoy family time with them even if it looks different from before. What do you enjoy doing with your parents? Make plans with them to continue these activities regularly. Even if you don’t do these with both parents and can’t see them as much as you used to, you can create a schedule of having one-on-one time with each parent every week or every other week.
While it is important to maintain your individual relationships with your parents, you can also be open to spending time with their new partners and families. You do not have to pretend that everything is perfect, but being polite and trying to talk to them can help ease any tension. This creates an environment where everyone can get to know each other over time.
If you feel anxious, talk to your parent and look for ways to make these meetings more comfortable for you. You can do an activity that you all enjoy or keep the initial meetings shorter until you feel more at ease around them.
Experiencing divorce can affect children’s self-esteem, but the truth is that your family structure does not define your worth. Focus on your goals, your studies, your hobbies and the kind of person you hope to become – that is where your worth lies.
It can feel isolating to be “stuck in the middle”. But other people have experienced something similar even if the exact details are different, and family counsellors are trained to handle situations like this. Support is there, whether you confide in someone you trust, a school counsellor or a mental health professional.
You can also consider the services below.
Mental Health Support Hotline, a 24-hour hotline and support on WhatsApp: 18111
Open Up, a 24-hour online text emotional support platform: openup.hk
This question was answered by clinical psychologists from Shall We Talk, a mental health initiative under the Department of Health launched with the Advisory Committee on Mental Health.

title: Another Chinese national dies in US immigration custody, raising profiling fears
description: Wei Lianyong, 51, reportedly died in Northern Mariana Islands on August 23, after he was found unresponsive at a local detention facility.
content: The Chinese-American community expressed anger and concern on Thursday over the death of a Chinese national in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody on US territory. Wei Lianyong, 51, reportedly died in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) on August 23, although the scandal-plagued agency did not disclose the death until this week. “Asian-Americans, Chinese-Americans, should be very concerned about this and very energised to stop what is essentially an attack on the existence of the community,” said Gabriel Chin, professor at the University of California, Davis School of Law. “We should not accept the idea that Chinese immigration is a bad thing because it’s Chinese because that’s inevitably going to affect the position of US citizens of Chinese ancestry.” Wei was arrested on August 21 by the Northern Mariana Islands Department of Public Safety on criminal charges following an alleged assault on a family of five at their home, according to ICE. The next day, he was taken into ICE custody in advance of deportation proceedings in Saipan, the archipelago’s capital. On the morning of August 23, ICE said he was found “unresponsive” in his prison cell and taken to a local accident and emergency hospital where “life-sustaining interventions were initiated” before he “passed away” at 7.30am. The cause of death remains under investigation, it added. Wei reportedly fifth Chinese national to die in custody of ICE or US Border Patrol Wei is at least the fifth Chinese national who has died in the custody of ICE or the US Border Patrol since March 2025, according to Associated Press tracking. Chinese-American advocates said ICE has been recruiting so rapidly under US President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration and deportation policy that standards are not always great. “You see it in terms of the ICE agents who are field agents who have no idea what they’re doing and are constantly doing things like accidentally shooting somebody who’s completely innocent,” said Justin Sadowsky, legal director with the Chinese-American Legal Defence Alliance, an advocacy group. A related outcome is the rise of deaths in custody due to heat, lack of food, insufficient medical care or mental stress tied to incarceration. “It’s not surprising that eventually this would happen to a Chinese person in the Northern Mariana Islands. It was just a matter of time,” Sadowsky said. Analysts added that the Trump administration’s immigration policies are part of a broader pattern seen in recent years that has scapegoated immigrants and Asian-Americans for Covid-19, eroding US competitiveness and the more cutthroat economy. “What we are seeing in Saipan is the tragic, inevitable result of an aggressive use of government power,” said Chris Kwok, a New York-based Asian-American Community Organiser. “You cannot separate this lack of transparency and basic duty of care from the broader, hostile climate being engineered right now. “When an administration is simultaneously trying to dismantle birthright citizenship and ramping up opaque ICE detentions, it sends a terrifying message to Asian-American and immigrant communities: your existence is viewed as illegitimate, and your rights are expendable,” he added. “We will deport you to random third countries. We don’t care if you die in our custody.” ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said it notified the Chinese consulate and his next of kin “or other designated contact”. It was not immediately clear what part of China Wei came from. The Chinese Consulate General in Los Angeles confirmed it was notified of Wei’s death. “We have expressed serious concerns to the relevant US authorities over this incident and required a timely and thorough investigation into the cause of Mr Wei’s death, notification of the findings, measures to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents, and assistance to the family of the deceased in handling the aftermath,” the consulate said in a statement. Beijing has also repeatedly raised concerns with Washington about detainee treatment, medical intake delays and overall conditions inside federal detention centres. DHS, which described Wei as a “criminal illegal alien from China”, said he was charged with assault with a dangerous weapon, disturbing the peace, assault and battery, and aggravated assault and battery. It did not say whether charges were dropped after his death, why the death was not revealed for nine days and whether a medical exam was performed as required. “ICE is committed to ensuring that all those in custody reside in safe, secure and humane environments,” the agency said. “All people in ICE custody receive medical, dental and mental health intake screenings within 12 hours of arriving at each detention facility.” CNMI is a US territory in the North Pacific Ocean located roughly three-quarters of the way from Hawaii to the Philippines. The 14-island archipelago currently has a population of around 42,000, of which around 3,300 are of Chinese descent. US government ignores international protests over deaths in ICE detention: analysts Analysts said the Trump administration has largely brushed aside protests from foreign governments over deaths and treatment of their citizens in ICE detention, although Beijing has a louder voice than most others. “Given the upcoming summit meeting and President Trump’s responsiveness to individual appeals and contacts with international leaders, if this gets brought up at the summit, Trump is likely to respond,” said Chin. Often, added Sadowsky, any such people-to-people issue at summits becomes part of a broader negotiation involving tariffs and related issues. “My guess is the United States government isn’t going to publicly admit wrongdoing or apologise. That just doesn’t seem to be what the United States government is doing with ICE these days,” he said. “Maybe this could be used to attract concessions from China, but I don’t expect it to resolve the issue.” The Chinese community is hardly the only community facing such treatment, but the number of people facing discrimination and ill-treatment is on the rise, Sadowsky said. “There’s definitely been an increase in stops, including stops of US citizens, and ICE harassing Chinese people, because they’re casting wide nets and using racial profiling.” “I don’t expect anything other than it’s going to get worse,” he added. Unlike most of the rest of the US, the local government controlled the territory’s labour and immigration policy between 1978 and 2009, creating a loophole that attracted large numbers of Chinese. Under these carve-outs, clothes made on Saipan could be legally labelled as “Made in the USA” and shipped to the mainland United States duty-free and quota-free, while avoiding US federal minimum wage standards or many immigration restrictions. That led dozens of Chinese-owned textile factories to employ tens of thousands of mainland Chinese contract workers, mostly young women, resulting, by the late 1990s, in foreign contract workers vastly outnumbering the local population.

title: Editorial | Hong Kong’s fight against aggressive sales tactics is far from over
description: The latest cases are reminders that high-pressure selling has not disappeared and underline the need for stronger consumer safeguards.
content: The pursuit of beauty often comes at a price, though not everyone can or should be expected to fork out a fortune for it, especially when aggressive sales tactics are involved. Recent incidents where routine visits to beauty parlours and department store counters turned into financial ordeals that left customers out of pocket do nothing for the city’s image and confidence in the sector. The tale of an 88-year-old woman having her credit card kept by a salesperson at a department store and swiped multiple times within hours for skincare products, a device and treatment sessions worth HK$100,000 is the latest example of strong-arm sales practices, a problem regrettably still found in beauty and other services. The incident was reported by the South China Morning Post days after a woman said she had been pressured into transactions of more than HK$60,000 at a local outlet of beauty chain Opatra London last month. More complaints followed and prompted the arrests of three people so far. The Customs and Excise Department said it had received 38 calls for help linked to the chain, with reported losses ranging from HK$1,800 to more than HK$200,000, totalling more than HK$3 million (US$382,629). The controversy surrounding Opatra started with a viral online video in which a woman cried outside an outlet in New Town Plaza shopping centre and claimed she had been cheated. The authorities took enforcement action as more complainants came forward about alleged malpractice across the beauty industry, while the United Kingdom-based company issued a statement saying the operation in Hong Kong was independently owned and run by a local distributor. Isolated as they seem, the incidents reflect a long-standing culture of high-pressure selling among some traders that erodes consumer confidence and undermines legitimate businesses in the industry. The playbook is similar. It typically involves prolonged sales pitches that wear down resistance, retention of customers’ credit cards for repeated transactions, unwanted physical contact and time-limited offers. Victims tend to be impressionable customers who are vulnerable to emotional manipulation and lack awareness of their rights. Legally, such malpractice already falls under the tightened Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and undue influence that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice. Despite a maximum jail term of five years and a fine of HK$500,000, the pressure to meet sales quotas and profits, as well as keen competition among traders, tempts some to step out of line. Over the past six years, the authorities logged about 5,000 complaints relating to the prepayment mode of consumption against beauty and fitness services. There is no evidence to suggest this is a widespread problem. But the repeated cases of vulnerable people victimised by strong-arm sales tactics in some sectors underline the need for stronger law enforcement and safeguards. In the case of gym membership deals, some customers ended up paying large sums of money or borrowing from agents referred by aggressive salespeople. There were cases in which the victims were taken to moneylenders, where they were given loans for gym plans tailor-made for their credit limits. A statutory cooling-off period has been proposed for customers to pull out of gym and beauty centre deals. The seven-day cooling-off period, along with a 14-day refund window for prepaid contracts above a certain monetary threshold, gives consumers a practical exit route from high-value deals signed under pressure. A proposed two-year cap on contract duration and a ban on contracts that only start more than three months after signing are also useful tools to curb the long, front-loaded payment plans that amplify losses when things go wrong. Overdue as they are, the legislative amendments are among many more steps needed to better protect consumers. There are concerns that one-off product purchases are still not covered. The latest cases are reminders that aggressive sales tactics have not disappeared. There needs to be timely legal reform and strong enforcement action so that confidence in businesses and legitimate sales practices will not be dented by individual bad sheep.

title: How Hong Kong’s Category III adult films made sex and gore mainstream in the 1990s
description: The adults-only, Category III rating was introduced in 1988, making stars of actresses including Shu Qi and Amy Yip.
content: While Western exploitation films of the 1960s and 70s – gory, sex-crazed shockers such as Herschell Gordon Lewis’ Blood Feast (1963) and Russ Meyer’s Faster, Pussycat! Kill! Kill! (1965) – were largely confined to low-rent drive-in cinemas, Hong Kong took a decidedly different approach. The introduction of the Category III rating in 1988 gave rise to an adults-only genre that did not just lurk in the underground – it conquered the mainstream. Although local martial arts films had been marketed on their violent content since the late 60s, exploitation films proper did not make an appearance in Hong Kong until the early 90s, following the introduction of the new classification. Category III marked the first time the city had an adults-only rating for films. Previously, movies were open to all ages. The new rating led to an explosion of films featuring soft-core sex, gore and extreme violence. Movies such as Sex and Zen (1991), Dr Lamb and Naked Killer (both 1992) and the notorious The Untold Story (1993) dared to go where no Hong Kong film had gone before – and, for a few years, audiences loved them for it. Most of these films look shoddy today, and a few, such as the misogynistic Dr Lamb, which features necrophilia, are as repulsive now as they were back in the 90s. In retrospect, the Category III phenomenon is more notable for its unique social characteristics than for its cinematic qualities. Unlike American exploitation films, which were largely confined to the era’s rebellious youth and dirty old men, Hong Kong’s Category III films were an extension of the booming mainstream industry rather than a separate underground genre. Some, such as Sex and Zen, even became box-office hits. Crossover stars and genre-bending Established Hong Kong stars such as Simon Yam Tat-wah and Rachel Lee Lai-chun (originally known as Loletta Lee) were happy to appear in Category III films. Some actresses who made their names in the genre, including Veronica Yip Yuk-hing and Shu Qi, went on to become serious actresses – a career progression that had proved nearly impossible for performers with similar experiences overseas. A defining quality of Category III films was their mixing of genres. Since the 80s, Hong Kong films had routinely crossed genres – most notably with popular kung fu comedies – to appeal to all audience tastes in a single movie. In the 90s, producers took this a stage further, mixing and matching genres with abandon. Sex and Zen was a period costume drama that combined lowbrow comedy – its hero receives a horse-penis transplant – with plentiful sex scenes, while its sequel added a supernatural element. Naked Killer was a thriller about an assassin, combining gunplay, action and soft-core sex. The killer, played by Chingmy Yau Suk-ching, targets male sexual abusers, by shooting or mutilating their genitals. In the film’s most notorious scene, a dismembered penis is mistaken for a hot dog. Crime and police stories also featured heavily in the mix. “Some of the earliest Category III films were based on famous criminal cases, like 1989’s Sentenced to Hang, which is generally considered to be the first Category III movie,” says Grady Hendrix, co-author of These Fists Break Bricks (2021). In 1991, free-to-air television broadcaster ATV aired Hong Kong Classified Cases, a documentary series about notable real-life criminal cases. The series later became fodder for films such as Dr Lamb and My Better Half (1993), which were often spiced with controversy. “Suburb Murder [1992], which was based on the Braemar Hill murders [in 1985], got a Category III classification but was pulled from release after protests from the families of the victims,” Hendrix says. “The producers later blamed what seemed to be a fictitious notice from the film classification board for pulling it from theatres.” The accidental birth of a genre Category III may now be regarded as a genre, but it began as a simple certificate of classification. The adults-only category was introduced under the Film Censorship Ordinance of 1988, following pressure from the public and the film industry. Before the ordinance, there were no age restrictions on cinema-goers, so all films had to be edited for family audiences. The Television and Entertainment Licensing Authority (TELA) could also ban films if they contained scenes of sex or violence deemed inappropriate for Hong Kong viewers. It was the banning of two high-profile Western films – Alan Parker’s voodoo thriller Angel Heart (1987) and Martin Scorsese’s epic The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), which featured nudity and sexual content – that raised the public’s ire. Hong Kong was now a modern city, so why couldn’t its residents watch the same films as audiences elsewhere? Following what the SCMP described as a “survey of public tastes and tolerance” conducted by TELA, the Category III rating was introduced. “It is intended that films which are currently banned because they go beyond the standard of not suitable for children will in the future be allowed to be shown unless they are grossly [indecent] or too violent for public taste,” a government official told the SCMP in 1988. The effect on Hong Kong’s film scene was not quite what the authorities had intended. Distributors and filmmakers had previously shied away from adult content because the criteria for acceptance or rejection by TELA were vague. The new Category III classification, while not precisely defined, provided a workable framework: hardcore pornography remained off the table, but breasts and buttocks were fine, fleeting female full-frontal nudity was tolerated, as was extreme violence. Initially, Hong Kong cinemas were flooded with Japanese soft-porn films and Western exploitation imports. Seeing an opportunity to make quick money, local filmmakers swiftly ramped up production of their own salacious movies. Category III soon became an identifiable brand. Even though Category III could be sleazy, it was never thought of as pornography Grady Hendrix, co-author of These Fists Break Bricks By 1991, a whopping 81 per cent of the 370 films submitted for classification, including imported titles, had been rated Category III. The Hong Kong public, eager to see what it had been missing, embraced them. Category III films became the latest trend, reflecting the city’s modernisation and international status. Watching a Category III film carried no social stigma. “Audiences knew the distinction between Category III and hardcore porn, which was sometimes referred to as ‘Category IV’,” Hendrix says. “Even though Category III could be sleazy, it was never thought of as pornography.” Sex symbols and a changing tide Local actresses did not mind appearing in the films either, or so they claimed. Amy Yip Chi-mei, dubbed the “champion of breasts” by the tabloid press, was the first actress to capitalise on the Category III boom. She became Hong Kong’s first bona fide sex symbol after bursting into the limelight with Erotic Ghost Story (1990) and Sex and Zen. Yip was soon eclipsed by Veronica Yip, a sharp-witted actress who made her name in a trio of Category III films released in 1991: Take Me, Hidden Desire and Pretty Woman. Although she had few qualms about nudity, Veronica Yip soon used her Category III stardom to jump-start her career as an all-round entertainer. By the mid-90s, public fascination with Category III films had faded, mirroring the broader Hong Kong film industry’s box-office decline. The genre had lost its novelty, and with 1997 approaching, audiences increasingly dismissed it as frivolous and somewhat tawdry. “At their height, Category III movies probably made up 25 per cent of the movies produced in Hong Kong,” Hendrix says. “But as the overall industry slumped, so did Category III. “In the late 1990s and early 2000s, a lot of Category III titles were only released on VCD, and with the rise of the internet, the idea of watching softcore movies in movie theatres felt about as retro as lighting your house by candlelight.” Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Hong Kong poised to top New York, London in finance-hub ranking: GFCI creator
description: ‘It’s going to happen,’ creator of Global Financial Centres Index says, as long as city maintains openness and predictability.
content: An Asian city will eventually overtake London and New York as the world’s leading financial centre, with Hong Kong well placed to compete for the top spot given its legal predictability and low tax burden, according to the creator of a closely watched ranking of financial hubs. “It’s going to happen because it’s so tight,” said Michael Mainelli, chairman of London-based think tank Z/Yen Group, in an interview with the South China Morning Post on Tuesday, referring to the narrowing gap between Hong Kong and the traditional leaders. In the March edition of the Global Financial Centres Index (GFCI) – compiled twice a year by Z/Yen and Shenzhen’s China Development Institute – Hong Kong placed third, trailing London by a single point and New York by two. The next edition is set for release later this month. Mainelli attributed the tightening race to a broader structural shift towards Asia, which now accounts for roughly 40 per cent of global finance. “At some point, there will be an event,” he said, meaning a change at the top of the rankings. Recent macroeconomic volatility, including geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, had weighed on the ratings of some major hubs, but Hong Kong’s underlying framework was unusually resilient, Mainelli said. Central to that, he said, was Hong Kong’s common law system, which let international firms sign and enforce contracts on terms they already understood. Mainelli noted that while many jurisdictions lacked regulatory predictability, Hong Kong sought to retain confidence in the rule of law through its judicial independence. He contrasted Hong Kong’s environment with regulatory friction in the United States. As an example he cited differing opinions from courts on whether Kalshi’s sports-related contracts were gambling subject to state laws or financial derivatives regulated federally – a conflict likely headed to the Supreme Court. Fiscal discipline offered another durable edge for Hong Kong, Mainelli said. State expenditure as a share of gross domestic product – a better indicator of stability than individual tax breaks – was roughly 15 per cent in Hong Kong, compared with around 19 per cent in Singapore and more than 40 per cent across Europe, he said. Following rival tax-incentive announcements from Singapore and Hong Kong, Mainelli cautioned that frequent policy shifts could erode business confidence. “The more a centre flips its tax regime around to suit circumstances, the less confident I am your tax regime is stable,” he said, “Predictability is what international participants are after.” The March GFCI survey revealed that predictability was the primary regulatory demand among businesses, outranking response speed, flexibility and overall quality. Cost was identified as the least significant consideration. Mainelli dismissed concerns that fast-growing mainland Chinese hubs like Shanghai and Shenzhen – ranked sixth and ninth, respectively – would eclipse Hong Kong. Instead, he argued that their growth reinforced Hong Kong’s role as an open, common-law gateway to mainland capital. The city’s investments in gold-trading infrastructure, including a central clearing and settlement system that began trial operations in July and a plan to expand vault capacity near the airport to more than 2,000 tonnes, would “benefit Hong Kong enormously”, Mainelli said. Looking ahead, he said that the city’s main long-term challenge involved balancing mainland integration with global accessibility. “The biggest real threat to Hong Kong … is probably the government losing sight of how much openness matters to business,” he said, adding that the one country, two systems framework remained highly effective as long as commercial openness was preserved. Hong Kong’s eventual rise to the top of the ranking hinged on it continuing to “treat everybody fairly”, he added.

title: Trump takes mail-in ballot fight to US Supreme Court
description: This is the second time the administration has turned ‌to the top court, after the curbs ordered by the president were blocked by a US judge.
content: President Donald Trump’s administration asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to let it enforce a new US Postal Service rule tightening the use of mail-in ballots, moving swiftly after a judge temporarily blocked the regulation ahead of November’s midterm elections. In an emergency request, the Justice Department asked the Supreme Court to lift Boston-based US District ‌Judge Indira Talwani’s order temporarily preventing the USPS from enforcing the new rule, which it adopted following an executive order by the Republican president to restrict mail-in ballots. The USPS regulation would impose new voter-specific data and ballot envelope standards, and potentially refuse the delivery of ballots that do not comply, which critics say could disrupt thousands of legitimate votes as the November 3 vote approaches. Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the election. Critics say restricting mail-in ballots would stand to disproportionately ⁠benefit Republicans given that Democratic voters traditionally have been more likely to use mail-in ballots. It is the second time that the administration has turned ‌to the Supreme Court as it defends Trump’s directive against legal challenges by states and voting rights groups. On August 24 the court lifted an earlier injunction imposed by Talwani in June blocking Trump’s order. That decision, powered ‌by the court’s 6-3 conservative majority, faulted a coalition of mostly Democratic-governed states for suing too soon, but left the door ⁠open to another challenge. The ⁠court’s three liberal justices dissented. Under the new USPS rule, states must provide lists of mail ballot recipients to the postal service ‌and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique bar codes. The postal service could then refuse to send out ballots that do not comply with the new standards or ‌are associated ‌with voters who do not appear on the lists. Trump, who signed his executive order targeting mail-in ballots in March, has for years ‌cast doubt on their security, although evidence of voter fraud is rare. Trump has made false claims of widespread fraud in US elections including ⁠his 2020 loss to former Democratic President Joe Biden. The administration in its written filing on Thursday urged the Supreme Court to allow it to ⁠implement an “important federal policy to protect the mails from being used to commit voter fraud”. A coalition of mostly Democratic-governed states and Washington DC, as well as a number of voting rights groups, challenged the new USPS rule. Talwani issued a temporary order on ‌August 27 blocking the rule for 14 ‌days, finding that it is likely to have violated the US Constitution, under which the states administer elections, and would be impossible for the states to comply with given the rapidly approaching midterms. The Justice Department asked the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals to put the judge’s order on hold, but did not wait for a decision before turning to the Supreme Court. Talwani also held a hearing on Thursday to consider whether to issue a longer-term injunction.

title: US urged to consider military strikes to stop China achieving AGI first
description: Former White House staffer calls for espionage and cyber options as Washington prepares for a potential Chinese breakthrough.
content: The United States should start preparing for scenarios where extreme measures must be taken to stop China from achieving artificial general intelligence (AGI), according to a former White House official, including state-backed espionage and military strikes on Chinese data centres. Jacob Stokes, deputy director of the Indo-Pacific Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security (CNAS), said at an online event on Thursday that various US agencies, including the Department of Defense and the National Security Agency, should begin assessing what intelligence they need to justify taking such actions. “Trying to think through the particulars of that will be especially important, in part because it will help policymakers … start to work backwards based on the unique nature of the technology, in the same way that in a past era, policymakers would learn about nuclear weapons and … work backwards from the science to the policy implications,” he said. In a new CNAS report published last week, the former Obama administration national security staffer called for the US government to consider the feasibility of diplomatic, espionage, cyber and kinetic measures to prevent China from achieving AGI first. AGI is a hypothetical AI system that can achieve human levels of performance across a wide variety of tasks. The report, titled “Superpowers and AGI”, explores how the imminent arrival of AGI might affect US-China geopolitical competition. The US currently enjoys a months-long lead over China in frontier AI models, according to Epoch AI. However, China could make a “surprise technological breakthrough” that means it is close to achieving or achieves AGI first, Stokes wrote, citing China’s advances in areas such as robotics and other forms of “embodied AI”. If this were the case, the US government should consider extreme actions such as military strikes on the data centres that train and run the Chinese AGI system, Stokes wrote, including preventive strikes before China develops AGI. As AI technology grows in importance economically and militarily, the data centres that form the backbone of the AI industry have emerged as military targets. In March, Iran bombed Amazon data centres in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain as part of its conflict with the US. According to Stokes, US government agencies would have to work out what facilities to attack and with which weapons, while considering the risk that the strikes lead to a general war between the two countries. William Hartung, an arms analyst at the Project on Government Oversight, a Washington non-profit organisation, also warned that any strikes on Chinese data centres would “risk starting a shooting war between two nuclear armed powers that could have tragic consequences for all concerned”. “Striking Chinese data centres based on how they might or might not be used in the future would be the height of recklessness,” he said. Another option would be to reverse engineer or “steal” China’s AGI technology, Stokes wrote, which would be justified “legally and normatively” because of China’s own alleged history of stealing US intellectual property. However, he noted that the US government and intelligence apparatus have “not been organised for espionage to gather technological secrets for decades”. The stark assessment comes as US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are set to have talks in Washington later this month on AI governance as the technology continues to improve, posing growing risks to national and global security. The “best case scenario” for the talks is that the two sides find the talks “constructive”, Stokes said on Thursday, rather than any expectations of any breakthroughs on key governance issues.

title: Meet Grigor Dimitrov, the Bulgarian tennis player dating 3 Body Problem star Eiza Gonzalez
description: Once dubbed “Baby Federer”, the former Wimbledon boys’ singles champ has dated Maria Sharapova and Nicole Scherzinger, and was even linked to Serena Williams.
content: Bulgarian tennis star Grigor Dimitrov was eliminated in the first round at the 2026 US Open in New York following a defeat to Australia’s Alexei Popyrin. While Tuesday’s match may have been disappointing for Dimitrov, the 35-year-old is one of Bulgaria’s top tennis players, and once reached a career high of No 3 in the ATP singles rankings. His impressive professional tennis career aside, Dimitrov’s dating history is equally remarkable. From former tennis player Maria Sharapova to The Pussycat Dolls’ Nicole Scherzinger, Dimitrov has dated some of the biggest names in both the sporting and the entertainment world. He is currently in a relationship with Mexican actress and 3 Body Problem star Eiza Gonzalez. Here’s everything you need to know about the Bulgarian tennis player and Eiza Gonzalez’s boyfriend. He was born into a family of athletes Dimitrov was born in 1991 to Dimitar Dimitrov and Maria Dimitrova. Dimitrov’s father is a tennis coach and his mother is a physical education teacher who formerly played volleyball. It was Dimitrov’s father who first introduced the tennis player to the sport and coached him throughout his formative years. Dimitar quickly realised that not only did his son love tennis, but he also had a real talent for the game. In a 2014 interview with the Financial Times, the father-son duo recalled Dimitrov spending day after day practising on the court in their hometown of Haskovo, Bulgaria. “He [Dimitar] was a very strict man and throughout the summer we would be out there on the court at the hottest times of the day but I loved it. I was enjoying it so much and I think that’s what made us work so well together. We were pulling each other up and striving for greatness,” Dimitrov told the Financial Times. A stellar tennis career As his talent grew, Dimitrov left Bulgaria and joined an academy in Barcelona when he was only 13 years old. He soon rose through the ranks and won the boys’ singles title at Wimbledon in 2008, when he was 17. His skills on the court earned him the moniker “Baby Federer” after Roger Federer, whose former coach Peter Lundgren remarked that Dimitrov’s abilities were better than the Swiss legend’s at the same age. Dimitrov went on to defeat the likes of Novak Djokovic and Andy Murray in matches and was ranked world No 3 in 2017. He remains the most successful tennis player from Bulgaria. His dating history Dimitrov and Eiza Gonzalez confirmed their relationship via Instagram in 2025, and have since made a few high-profile appearances together. Before Gonzalez, Dimitrov was known to be in a relationship with supermodel and actress Mădălina Ghenea. Dimitrov dated Nicole Scherzinger from 2015 to 2019 and Maria Sharapova from 2012 to 2015. He was also briefly rumoured to be dating Serena Williams in 2012.

title: Ecuador’s ex-president and Chinese ambassador seek to avoid jail over belt and road dam
description: Sentenced over US$76 million in bribes, Lenin Moreno and former ambassador Cai Runguo want Ecuador’s top court to spare them prison.
content: Former Ecuadorian president Lenin Moreno and a former Chinese ambassador to Quito asked the country’s highest court on Thursday to spare them the five-year sentences handed down last week over a US$76 million bribery scheme. Moreno was convicted of bribery by a three-judge panel of the National Court of Justice over contracts for Ecuador’s largest hydroelectric project secured by a Chinese state contractor. The judges found unanimously that he had used his position as vice-president, held from 2007 to 2013 before he won the presidency in 2017, to help secure financing for the Coca Codo Sinclair plant, built by Sinohydro, a unit of Chinese state group PowerChina. But the former president has not been detained and remains in Ecuador, and if the conviction is upheld, he would serve his term at home rather than in prison, because he is paraplegic. The judges will take up his request on September 7 and, if it is granted, his prison term would be suspended and replaced with conditions such as periodic reporting. “I have not received a single cent from Sinohydro, so please do not come and tell me that I am an accused man,” Moreno told reporters after the ruling was read out. He has said the case was motivated by a desire for revenge by Rafael Correa, the president who made him his running mate and then turned on him after Moreno moved rightward and let investigators pursue his allies. Correa was convicted in absentia in 2020 and lives in Belgium. The plant at the centre of the case is the costliest ever built in Ecuador, in the Amazon basin 100 km (62 miles) east of Quito. Sinohydro signed a US$1.9 billion contract in 2009 and China’s Export-Import Bank lent about US$1.68 billion the next year, on condition that a Chinese company do the work. The deal predated Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road Initiative by four years, but was later rebranded as part of the investment strategy and set the template for what the programme would look like in South America. Coca Codo Sinclair has since become a case study in the risks of that model, never running at its full 1,500 megawatt capacity because of defects present from the outset, with a congressional report counting 17,499 cracks by 2022. Ecuador still depends on the dam for about a quarter of its electricity, and its weak output added to the blackouts of up to 14 hours a day during the 2024 drought. From ambassador to Sinohydro representative Cai Runguo was China’s ambassador in Quito from 2007 to 2011 and was honoured by Correa shortly after Sinohydro won the contract. Within months of leaving the embassy, he joined the company he had dealt with as a diplomat, becoming its legal representative in 2013. Prosecutors said Cai met Moreno while both were in office, pushed the financing through and later helped arrange the payments. He received five years, as did former Sinohydro representatives Yang Huiju and Song Dongsheng, along with Conto Patino, a friend of Moreno’s. Cai has not appeared publicly in Ecuador since around 2016. Twenty of the 21 defendants were convicted, among them Moreno’s wife, daughter, two brothers and a sister-in-law, all of whom were sentenced as accomplices. Those who had held public office, Moreno among them, were barred from public service for life, and reparations totalled more than US$163 million. The payments ran from 2009 to 2018 and came to about 4 per cent of the contract, prosecutors said, most of it passing through a firm linked to Patino and accounts in Panama, disguised as consultancy fees. The case grew out of a 2019 leak about an offshore firm registered in Belize by Moreno’s brother and tied by investigators to the payments. The evidence against Moreno rested largely on a recording of a March 2010 interview, authenticated through forensic voice analysis, in which the judges found he admitted lobbying the Correa government for someone connected to Sinohydro. Moreno argued that the contract was signed and executed under Correa, and that responsibility lay with Jorge Glas, who succeeded him as vice-president and ran the energy portfolio, now serving a corruption sentence of his own. A narrow point in time Article 630 of Ecuador’s criminal code allows judges to suspend a prison term of up to five years, but an anti-corruption reform in February 2021 added bribery to the offences excluded from that benefit. Moreno’s lawyers argued that the earlier text, which barred suspension only for sexual and domestic violence offences, should govern because the bribery began in 2009, 12 years before the reform. Cai’s lawyers made the same argument, telling the court he rejected the conviction and would appeal but was asking for suspension now because it was the only stage at which the law allowed it. “Considering that the benefit whose application is sought was in force on the date of the events, I ask you to set a day and time for the hearing,” Moreno’s filing said. Thirteen of the convicted made the same request and 12 will be heard, after the court threw out one as late. The judges delivered their verdict orally and have yet to issue the written judgment, which starts the clock on appeals. And the sentences fell on individuals rather than on Sinohydro, whose international arm was folded into PowerChina International in 2016. The company has not commented on the verdict and the Chinese embassy in Quito did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Prosecutors said at least 10 requests for banking and corporate evidence sent to China since 2019 went unanswered.

title: Opinion | China’s robot revolution may not arrive in the way you expect
description: Electric vehicles generally travel abroad as finished, branded products. Chinese robotics could spread differently.
content: China’s robots have become skilled at commanding a stage. At last month’s World Robot Conference in Beijing, humanoids sorted parcels, packed phones and performed household chores. Unitree Robotics, whose machines can run, dance and perform martial arts, made an equally dramatic entrance on the Shanghai stock market, closing its first day of trading at more than five times its offer price.
