The spectacle is real, and so is the engineering achievement behind it. However, this can obscure a more useful way to think about China’s robotics boom. Two different bets are taking shape. One asks how much capability can be packed into an increasingly versatile body. The other asks how much useful intelligence can travel across different bodies. Unitree is a leading example of the first approach. Its strength in locomotion and motion control has helped push Chinese humanoids forward at remarkable speed, yet founder Wang Xingxing has also been candid about the software challenge ahead. He said last month that a breakthrough allowing robots to handle unfamiliar environments and tasks could come in two or three years in an optimistic case, or it could take as long as a decade. That uncertainty does not make humanoids a bad bet. Rather, it shows how difficult the physical world is. Language models can learn from an immense digital record. Robots must deal with gravity, glare, clutter, deformable objects, unexpected obstacles and mistakes that can damage equipment. A demonstration might last minutes; an industrial customer expects a system to work shift after shift. There is also a question of priorities. A household robot that folds laundry or sweeps the floor makes for a charming demonstration. Given that global youth unemployment stood at 12.4 per cent last year, automating household chores might not be the productivity revolution many economies most urgently need. If a young person is out of work and at home, outsourcing the dishes to a humanoid hardly feels like the breakthrough the economy is waiting for. Stanford computer scientist Fei-Fei Li has framed the deeper challenge as spatial intelligence. Artificial intelligence must do more than recognise the world; it must understand three-dimensional space well enough to reason and act within it. Her work is also a reminder that a robot need not look human. Intelligence can inhabit many forms. That helps explain a very different Chinese approach. Mech-Mind Robotics, now in the process of listing in Hong Kong, does not primarily build robot bodies. Its core products provide what it calls the robot’s “eye, brain and hand”: 3D cameras, perception and planning software and end effectors, or tools that sit at the end of a robotic arm. The commercial ambition is to make these capabilities standard enough to work across different machines and industries rather than redesign the system for every customer. The firm’s prospectus says more than 29,000 units of its products have been deployed globally and that it has worked with more than 100 Fortune Global 500 companies. Revenue rose from 180.8 million yuan (US$26.9 million) in 2023 to 388.8 million yuan in 2025, when overseas business contributed more than half of sales. The company remains loss-making, so these numbers are not necessarily proof of future success. The figures are not a customer retention rate, but they do suggest that a high share of sales comes from repeat business. Two of the industry’s biggest challenges are getting robots to adapt what they learn to new situations and obtaining enough real-world data to train them. Factory deployment therefore matters twice: it generates revenue but also exposes systems to the awkward exceptions from which better robotics can learn. For global manufacturers, this suggests that the robot revolution might not arrive as a wholesale replacement of existing machinery with humanoids. It could arrive incrementally as better vision, planning and manipulation are added to machines already on factory floors. That also changes how Chinese robotics can reach world markets. Electric vehicles generally travel abroad as finished, branded products. Robotics could spread differently: Chinese cameras, perception software and end effectors could be integrated into industrial systems whose robot bodies are made elsewhere. Investors might need a different scorecard too. Beyond impressive demonstrations, they should ask if the technology can be standardised. How much custom engineering does each deployment require? Do customers buy again? Can lessons from one factory transfer to another? Can the business travel across industries and borders? The humanoid and industrial intelligence paths could eventually converge. As software improves and costs fall, humanoids should become more useful. Industrial systems are already becoming more adaptive. China’s robot race is not simply about building machines that look human. It is about turning intelligence into something repeatable, transferable and economically useful. The robot that eventually wins might still look human. The more important question is whether it keeps earning its place after the audience has gone home.

title: Holdout juror preventing verdict in Lindsay Clancy’s US child murder trial, lawyer says
description: A note from the foreman suggests that one juror ‘refuses to listen’ to the judge about what constitutes reasonable doubt.
content: A single juror in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial is preventing the jury from reaching a unanimous verdict, her lawyer said in court on Thursday, after deliberations stretched into a sixth day over whether to convict the Massachusetts woman of killing her three young children. Defence lawyer Kevin ‌Reddington made that statement shortly after the jury sent Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, a note that prompted him to reinstruct jurors on what would constitute “reasonable doubt”. After the jury was sent back to continue deliberating, Reddington moved to have a holdout juror removed, saying a note from the jury’s foreman indicated “there’s one juror who refuses to listen to the law that you’ve given him or her on reasonable doubt”. “If we come back here in half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, it’s a shame,” Reddington ⁠told the judge, who declined to remove the juror. The jury sent Sullivan a note a day earlier that said: “After much deliberation, we are still unable ‌to come to a unanimous decision.” They sent a similar note on Tuesday. But on both days, the judge instructed them to continue deliberating. If the jury does not reach a verdict and Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to ‌decide whether to retry the case, which has included more than 80 witnesses and more than 300 exhibits. Asked during a lunch break ⁠about his thoughts on the ⁠state of the deliberations, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside the courthouse that “we’ll hang on and find out”. On the question of whether prosecutors in his office would retry the case if ‌it ended in a mistrial, Cruz said only: “I’ll talk when this is all over.” Clancy, 36, faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder. If found not guilty by ‌reason of ‌lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. She has admitted to strangling her three ‌children to death on January 24, 2023, with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with ⁠a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life that left her paralysed. During the six-week trial, defence lawyer ⁠Kevin Reddington sought to convince jurors that Clancy was in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed Cora, five; Dawson, three; and eight-month-old Callan. Testimony from family members, including Clancy’s now ex-husband, Patrick, showed how she had struggled with her mental health in the months after ‌the birth of her third child, repeatedly ‌seeking treatment from healthcare providers who prescribed her a myriad of drugs. Prosecutors do not dispute that Clancy, a former labour and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, had been dealing with mental health issues. But they argued she was able to appreciate the wrongfulness of killing her children and intentionally chose to do so anyway, opting to kill them because she had decided to kill herself and was convinced they would suffer without her. If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Scientists studying cockroach milk and nose-blowing win Ig Nobel prizes
description: The event was moved to Europe after 35 years in the US, with organisers fearing it has become ‘unsafe’ for their guests to visit the country.
content: Ten research teams were honoured on Thursday at a satirical science awards ceremony that was hosted outside the US for the first time due to travel concerns. Researchers who studied milk from cockroaches and analysed soil health using underwear received Ig Nobel prizes celebrating unusual and imaginative contributions to science. The awards organised by a digital magazine called the Annals of Improbable Research shifted to Europe after 35 years in the US over concerns about attendees being able to get visas. At a convention centre in Zurich, Switzerland, research teams received a custom trophy resembling a cross between a mushroom and a human foot. Among them were Matilda Brindle and Stuart West from the University of Oxford and the Florida Institute of Technology’s Catherine F. Talbot, who reconstructed the evolutionary history of kissing, and the late Dr Tokuji Unno who investigated the science of blowing one’s nose. Another research team buried 1,000 pairs of underwear in more than 25 countries to study how critters in the soil helped them decompose. As per tradition, audience members fashioned paper planes and hurled them towards the stage to kick off the show. For future ceremonies, organisers plan to alternate between Zurich and other European countries. The 2027 ceremony will be held in the Belgian city of Antwerp. Previous iterations took place at Harvard University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Boston University, but there are no immediate plans to return to the US. “During the past year, it has become unsafe for our guests to visit the country,” Marc Abrahams, master of ceremonies and editor of the magazine, said in an email in March. The Nobel Prizes, which have no relation to their cheekily named counterpart, will be announced at the start of October.

title: ICE officer charged with lying to investigators in shooting of Venezuelan man
description: Christian Castro shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year.
content: Federal prosecutors have charged a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer with lying to investigators about the events leading up to the shooting of a Venezuelan man during the Minneapolis immigration crackdown earlier this year, according to a person familiar with the matter. The person was not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on condition of anonymity. The person said Christian Castro, the officer who authorities say shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in the leg in January, has been charged with making false statements to federal investigators. The federal charges, which remain under seal, follow Castro’s release from jail last week after Texas’ governor refused to immediately sign an extradition warrant to hand him over to Minnesota authorities, who have charged him separately with assault and false reporting of a crime related to the same shooting. Federal authorities had initially accused Sosa-Celis and another man of beating an officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel during the confrontation. But federal prosecutors dropped charges against the men after video evidence showed the officers may have lied about the encounter, and officials opened an investigation. Earlier this week, a federal prosecutor working on the case told lawyers for Sosa-Celis and other victims that Justice Department officials blocked the prosecutor’s push to bring a more serious civil rights charge against the officer for the shooting, ProPublica reported. But the person familiar with the investigation disputed the prosecutor’s characterisation, saying the civil rights probe is continuing and there has been no final decision on whether to bring additional charges. The prosecutor, Matthew Evans, was fired on Thursday and is now under investigation for alleged obstruction of a grand jury probe, the person said. An automatic email response from Evans’ Justice Department account said he was on leave. Other attempts to reach him were not immediately successful. Castro was initially arrested in May in the Minnesota case, and he was held in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico, while Minnesota officials sought his extradition. But Texas Governor Greg Abbott refused to immediately sign off, citing continuing investigations of fraud in government social service programmes in Minnesota, which Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there. Minnesota officials had sought to stop the sheriff in Cameron County, Texas, from releasing Castro, out of fear that he would flee to Mexico. According to a lawsuit filed by Minnesota, Castro had a conversation with a woman, while he was incarcerated, where he spoke about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico after his release. But Castro was released a week ago after a federal judge refused to order Texas to extradite him. The Department of Homeland Security previously called Minnesota’s prosecution of Castro “unlawful and nothing more than a political stunt”, saying only federal authorities have jurisdiction in the case. Castro was suspended from ICE without pay in February while federal authorities conducted the investigation. “The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct,” ICE’s acting director at the time, Todd Lyons, said then. “Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated. ICE remains fully committed to transparency, accountability, and the fair enforcement of our nation’s immigration laws.” Minnesota officials alleged that Castro, 52, fired through the front door of a home and shot Sosa-Celis in the thigh. Castro and another officer had chased a different man, Alfredo Alejandro Aljorna, to the Minneapolis apartment duplex where he and Sosa-Celis lived. Minnesota prosecutors said the officer then falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel. Lawyers for Sosa-Celis and Aljorna, who Minnesota officials have said were legally in the US, did not immediately respond to emails on Thursday.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Wild Horse Nine movie review – Martin McDonagh returns with jet-black comedy
description: Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell, delivers razor-sharp satire and award-worthy performances.
content: 4/5 stars With Wild Horse Nine, the fifth film of his much-heralded career, Martin McDonagh returns to the joys of his first. The director’s 2008 debut, In Bruges, was a sublimely written tale of two hitmen arguing in the picture-postcard town of the title. Similarly, his latest introduces us to two CIA operatives bickering as they head to the remote Chilean territory of Easter Island in 1973. That is not to say Wild Horse Nine – screening in competition at the Venice International Film Festival – feels like a rehash of In Bruges; far from it. Here, McDonagh presents a jet-black comedy set at a time when the CIA was moving all the pieces on the geopolitical chessboard. A married father of two, Lee (Sam Rockwell) is under instructions from his heroin-addicted boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) to keep an eye on Chris (John Malkovich), a veteran of that fateful day in Dallas a decade earlier when John F. Kennedy was assassinated. Now the ailing Chris is threatening to write an explosive memoir, much to MJ’s chagrin. Already, he has lost all sense of propriety, openly discussing on an aeroplane how many people he has killed and blatantly telling two shocked students he meets in Santiago airport that he and Lee have come “to destabilise your democracy”. More chillingly, he later tells them that a military coup to overthrow the country’s president, Salvador Allende, will see hundreds tortured. Their reason for heading to Easter Island, where they join the tourists to see “the heads” – the mysterious, carved statues that adorn the coastline – will become clear. But as hinted by The Rolling Stones’ “Out of Time” on the soundtrack, this is a story where the spectre of death looms large, just as suspicion and terror cling to these characters. “Don’t trust Lee,” reads a note that Chris carries with him. The power of Wild Horse Nine lies in the Rockwell-Malkovich double act. Rockwell, who won an Oscar for his work on McDonagh’s 2017 film Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, is brilliant, but the real pathos comes from a world-weary Malkovich, who must surely be a major contender this coming awards season. Buscemi, meanwhile, is gloriously entertaining, and Parker Posey is in acerbic form as Lee’s spouse Marge, left to deal with the fallout of her husband’s line of work. Scripting with not a shred of concern for political correctness, McDonagh has crafted a bleak but darkly funny character study, one that plays out on the world stage. Riotously entertaining, Wild Horse Nine will make you laugh, feel guilty and then laugh some more. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Mercury-bound spacecraft on home stretch of nearly decade-long voyage: ‘brilliant moment’
description: The BepiColombo successfully separated from the mother ship and will head for the planet’s orbit.
content: Two Mercury-bound spacecraft left their mother ship behind on Thursday and headed down the home stretch of their nearly decade-long voyage to the solar system’s smallest and closest-to-the-sun planet. The linked European and Japanese spacecraft separated as planned from their cruiser, but controllers had to wait two anxious hours to receive confirmation via radio signals. The crucial operation was broadcast from the European Space Agency’s control centre in Germany, more than 200 million km (124 million miles) away. “It’s a brilliant moment,” said lead project scientist Geraint Jones. If all goes well, the conjoined spacecraft known as BepiColombo will enter orbit around Mercury in November and split from each other in December to map and study the entire planet from different altitudes. As of Thursday, the spacecraft still had 3.3 million km (2 million miles) to go before reaching its destination. Launched in 2018, the BepiColombo mission is named for the Italian mathematician who took part in Nasa’s Mariner 10 mission to Mercury in the 1970s. Only one other spacecraft, Nasa’s Messenger, has explored the puzzling, scorching planet that is just a little bigger than our moon. “How tiny Mercury is, and still it holds some of the biggest mysteries of our solar system,” mission manager Santa Martinez said earlier this week. Added Jones: “There’s a huge amount still left to be learned.” BepiColombo already has travelled more than 10 billion km (6 billion miles) on its roundabout route, according to Martinez. It needed nine planetary fly-bys to reduce its energy enough to be caught in Mercury’s orbit. The last fly-by, in January 2025, yielded stunning photos of Mercury’s impact craters and volcanic plains. Beginning next spring, a slew of science instruments on the European and Japanese spacecraft will study the magnetic field that envelops Mercury, the planet’s dense interior, and the geologic processes at the surface, including the hollows, or depressions, that scientists believe are being eaten away by minerals vaporising from rocks. It is a strange world of contrasts. On a planet where the temperature can top 427 degrees Celsius (800 degrees Fahrenheit), the poles are frigid with deep, permanently shadowed craters packed with ice. Given Mercury’s proximity to the sun, engineers had to design the spacecraft to withstand “extremely punishing” conditions, said the European Space Agency’s Ignacio Tanco, a mission operations chief. “It’s essentially equivalent to operating with a very hot pizza oven running right on your back,” he said. Science observations should begin next spring, with the European Space Agency covering most of the mission’s €1.7 billion (US$2 billion) cost.

title: Just 4 of 28 lifts at Queen Mary Hospital block set for service once repairs done
description: Architectural Services Department says remaining lifts had suffered frequent operational instability and requires urgent follow‑up.
content: Only four of the 28 lifts at Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block will operate normally following minor repairs, while work must be carried out on the rest until the end of the year, according to Hong Kong’s architectural authorities. The Architectural Services Department said on Thursday only four lifts serving non‑clinical facilities at the HK$13.5 billion (US$1.72 billion) block were in acceptable condition and would undergo minor repairs later. The remaining lifts had suffered frequent operational instability and required urgent follow‑up, it added. The department expected work to be completed in the fourth quarter of this year. The block, part of the Pok Fu Lam hospital’s first‑phase redevelopment, was mostly completed last year and began opening in phases last November. Clinical services have yet to move in, as repeated lift faults – including sudden drops that trapped staff – have kept most of the elevators out of service. Authorities said last month that the defects emerged during final testing, with installation and performance failing to meet contract standards. The government ordered contractors to complete repairs promptly and reserved the right to pursue liability for the delays. It had also suspended the main contractor and lift subcontractor from tendering for public works, saying the firms would need to bear the full cost of remedial works. The main contractor for the first phase of the redevelopment was a Paul Y-Able joint venture. The lift subcontractor, Anlev Elex Elevator, is a subsidiary of ATAL Engineering Group, founded by Otto Poon Lok-to, the husband of former justice secretary Teresa Cheng Yeuk-wah. All 28 lifts had received permits from the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department by July last year after it reviewed the subcontractor’s testing reports and conducted on-site inspections. The situation has raised questions over how the lifts passed the tests while being unreliable. Former lawmaker Michael Tien Puk‑sun said that from his understanding, the repair work was originally expected to be completed by next month, but the latest statement from authorities suggested that the deadline could slip to December. He warned that the delays had already had a major impact on the Hospital Authority and patients, and urged the department to fix the problems by October.

title: Hong Kong Nepalese man searches for cousin missing in flood: ‘I cannot sleep’
description: Y.B. Gurung said he last spoke with his cousin shortly before massive glacial collapse and was asking Chinese embassy for help.
content: A Hong Kong Nepalese man is searching for his cousin who is missing after the catastrophic flood struck the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet. Y.B. Gurung, a 64-year-old retiree, told the South China Morning Post that he last spoke with his tour guide cousin Raju Gurung, 40, at 8am on August 26, shortly before a massive glacial collapse triggered the flash flood that washed away villages and left at least 1,225 people dead. “I cannot sleep every night. I am praying every day that he was rescued,” Gurung said on Thursday. At the time of the disaster, his cousin was leading a 42-member team on a pilgrimage into Tibet. The family has tried desperately to locate him by reaching out to the Chinese embassy, but to no avail. As of Wednesday, China had confirmed 21 deaths and 541 missing people. In Nepal, the death toll rose to 1,252 as of 10am Thursday, with about 4,875 people still missing. Yau Tsim Mong district councillor Aruna Gurung said about 60 Nepalese residents in Hong Kong hailed from the Trishuli River region, which had been devastated. She confirmed two members of the local Nepalese community had died in the disaster. “The Nepalese community here is seeking help to verify information and asking for materials and donations to be delivered to those in need in the region,” she said. “We are deeply worried about the situation.” The Non-Resident Nepalese Association Hong Kong said it had raised HK$126,311 (US$16,100) in relief funds as of Wednesday. The organisation also said it estimated Hong Kong’s Nepalese community would come together and eventually contribute about HK$1 million. Satya Gahatraj, the women’s coordinator for the association, said the group had cancelled its five-day celebrations marking the Hindu women’s festival of Teej. The event was originally scheduled to start on September 13. The association will join two other local Nepalese NGOs and the office of district councillor Gurung to hold an event next Monday to mourn the victims, with support from the Nepalese consulate. The Hong Kong Red Cross will also offer support services at the event. The association encouraged Hongkongers seeking to donate to do so through the consulate, which would pass the funds directly to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund. No 2 city official Eric Chan Kwok-ki signed a book of condolence at the Nepalese consulate on Thursday. “In this difficult time, Hong Kong stands with the government and people of Nepal,” he wrote on social media. “We sincerely wish the injured a speedy recovery, and hope the affected people can rebuild their homes and return to normal life as soon as possible.”

title: China-Singapore security team claims breakthrough in hacking Starlink terminals
description: Darknavy gains full administrative control over SpaceX’s user terminal allowing research into the system’s security programmes.
content: A team of cybersecurity experts has announced they successfully compromised the latest Starlink user terminals, crossing the security boundaries of the world’s largest satellite constellation. In a post on its social media account on Tuesday, Darknavy, an independent cybersecurity research institute headquartered in Singapore and Shanghai, said it had used sophisticated hardware attacks to gain full administrative control over the terminals, allowing it to run any custom code on the devices. This gives researchers unprecedented freedom, according to the pot, by reopening a long-missing entry point for in-depth security studies of the Starlink satellite system. Starlink, SpaceX’s low-Earth-orbit satellite internet service, works by connecting user terminals to satellites in near-Earth orbit, which then relay data through ground gateways to the wider internet. As newer satellites are gradually equipped with laser links, some satellites can also communicate directly with one another via laser, reducing reliance on ground stations while improving transmission speeds and expanding global coverage. In battlefield conditions like those in Ukraine, where no local ground gateways exist, Starlink terminals can still gain access to the internet by routing signals through satellites that connect to gateways in neighbouring countries. The terminal acts as both an antenna and a router, making it a critical node for direct communication with the satellites. Until now, research into the satellite system’s security had largely stalled because the terminals could not be hacked. At the Black Hat USA conference in 2022, Lennert Wouters of KU Leuven showed an attack on the first-generation Starlink antenna using voltage fault injection – an advanced hardware attack method. SpaceX later added targeted defences into its models, and for years, multiple top international research teams failed to breach the updated terminals. Last March, Darknavy bought a Starlink Standard Actuated terminal in Singapore, disassembled its antenna, and began analysing its firmware. At the time, the company noted in a blog post that “developers and hackers contend not only in the digital realm but also against the constraints of cosmic physics”. Now, by taking control of the terminal, researchers might be able to legally explore the interaction between Starlink satellites and ground equipment – simulating, injecting, intercepting, and analysing communication protocols to uncover vulnerabilities across the entire satellite network. Darknavy’s case shows that even under the latest and strongest protections, systems can still have weaknesses. The firm said on Tuesday that further details of the research could not be disclosed at this stage and the official website would serve as the main source of information. The South China Morning Post has contacted SpaceX for comment about the findings.

title: Outcry over ‘weapons of love’ forces Hong Kong charity to scrap student contest
description: Po Leung Kuk calls off student eco-bag design competition intended to promote family harmony and counter domestic abuse.
content: A leading Hong Kong charity has called off a student eco-bag design contest meant to counter domestic violence following public backlash over its directive for pupils to draw inspiration from objects commonly linked to household abuse. Po Leung Kuk confirmed on Thursday that it had scrapped the competition, which was organised by its family crisis support service and funded by the Social Welfare Department. The charity said the event “might have caused misunderstanding and concern”, although its original intent was to encourage transforming conflicts into non-violent expressions of love. The charity thanked the public for their feedback, reaffirmed its commitment to opposing domestic violence and promised to continue promoting family harmony through more appropriate campaigns. According to the now-cancelled contest’s promotional material, primary school pupils were invited to turn household items often associated with domestic violence in Hong Kong – including kitchen knives, belts, insecticide, wine bottles, clothes hangers and umbrellas – into cartoon mascots as “weapons of love”. The contest was originally scheduled to run from August 15 to October 15 this year, with winning designs to be printed on reusable bags and distributed to schools. Promotional slogans included “Rather than using a sharp knife [to attack], slice fruit instead and share the sweetness” and “Rather than spraying insecticide, extinguish sharp tongues with praise”. The campaign poster went viral on social media, sparking heated debate. Critics accused the contest of beautifying domestic violence, disregarding victims’ trauma and normalising violent imagery for children. Some internet users said turning instruments of abuse into mascots would be akin to rubbing salt into the wounds of domestic violence victims.

title: Extra funds push Taiwan’s defence spending past NT$1 trillion for the first time
description: The island’s cabinet approves supplementary budget, with heavy investment in missiles, drones and classified programmes.
content: Taiwan’s cabinet approved a supplementary defence budget of NT$145.7 billion (US$4.6 billion) on Thursday, pushing the island’s total defence-related spending for this year above NT$1 trillion for the first time. The additional funding is expected to raise this year’s overall defence spending from 3.32 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) to about 3.83 per cent, the highest level in decades. The supplementary budget, which still requires legislative approval, is aimed at plugging gaps left after opposition lawmakers cut NT$470 billion in May from an eight-year NT$1.25 trillion special defence package proposed by the government. Of the additional funds, NT$133.4 billion would go towards military investment, including missiles, unmanned systems and two classified programmes, according to the cabinet’s approved budget. Seven projects, including the locally developed Chiang Kung, or Strong Bow, mid-tier anti-tactical ballistic missile system, would receive NT$13 billion, while another NT$55.9 billion would fund three uncrewed-system programmes, including coastal surveillance drones. Two classified programmes would account for NT$64.5 billion. Another NT$7.3 billion would be used to replenish urgently needed ammunition, while NT$900 million would fund a tactical network programme designed to integrate intelligence across different operational domains. The package also includes NT$2.5 billion to expand military recruitment and NT$1.6 billion to broaden combat-unit allowances and eligibility. Taiwanese Premier Cho Jung-tai said the supplementary funding was necessary because defence procurement could not be allowed to stall after lawmakers reduced the government’s original special defence package. “Defence cannot afford a gap,” Cho said. He said the government hoped the additional funding would allow the military to acquire more than 600 coastal surveillance drones, more than 40,000 coastal attack drones and an initial batch of more than 100 small suicide unmanned surface vessels by next year. Cho stressed that the uncrewed systems were intended to equip specialised units across the island and strengthen Taiwan’s asymmetric warfare capabilities. The government also hopes orders of those systems will expand local production capacity and establish a “red-free” supply chain that excludes mainland Chinese components. The supplementary funding would bring Taiwan’s total defence-related expenditure this year from NT$949.5 billion to about NT$1.1 trillion. The increase comes just two weeks after the cabinet approved a record NT$1.12 trillion defence budget for next year, equivalent to 3.01 per cent of projected gross domestic product (GDP). Although the 2027 budget figure is only about NT$27.4 billion, or 2.5 per cent, higher than this year’s total after taking into account the supplementary funding, the composition of the two defence spending packages differs. This year’s supplementary spending is concentrated on urgent procurement, particularly missiles, ammunition and large numbers of relatively inexpensive unmanned systems, according to cabinet officials. Next year’s budget, by contrast, represents a broader expansion of regular defence spending. Military investment alone is expected to rise by NT$97.5 billion to NT$259.1 billion, covering weapons procurement and programmes including US-made High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, F-16V fighters and anti-submarine helicopter maintenance. Strong Bow will also shift to the regular budget next year, with the defence ministry planning about NT$36 billion for the programme through 2032. Taiwanese leader William Lai Ching-te has pledged to increase overall defence spending to 5 per cent of GDP by 2030 amid mounting military pressure from Beijing and calls from Washington for the island to spend more on its own defence. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: India grapples with ‘endemic’ menace of age fraud in sports, experts want stiffer sanctions
description: Country’s chaotic birth registration system has allowed older children to compete against younger ones, potentially earning great rewards.
content: No fewer than 500 wrestlers were disqualified from India’s under-17 championships for age fraud in June, highlighting a scourge experts believe ⁠is baked into the country’s sporting culture and ⁠needs to be combated in the same way as doping. The exclusions at ⁠the Gonda meet were the latest in a string of age-fraud cases and came less than a year after some 20 teams were expelled from India’s top schools football tournament, the Subroto Cup, for fielding over-aged players. “It is endemic,” leading sports lawyer Aahna Mehrotra, who has written a paper on the subject, said. “Age fraud runs across most disciplines that have age-group competition, and it is at its worst at the sub-junior and junior levels, where the rewards are highest and the ‌scrutiny is lowest.” India’s chaotic system of birth registration and the absence of a single digital database for athletes have long left the door open for unscrupulous parents and coaches to exploit. For those who have a couple of years shaved off their actual age, the potential rewards can be great. The unfair advantage of extra years of growth can lead to scholarships, sponsorships and fame. In the case of the national sport, it could also give aspiring cricketers a head start in the pursuit of a life-changing Indian Premier League contract worth millions of rupees. PSM Chandran, president of the Indian Federation of Sports Medicine, said it should be punished in the same way as another modern scourge of sport. “Age fraud is very much there, ⁠and the system is inadequate to stop it,” he said. “The federations have not done enough. The cricket board has taken a lead in recent times but we need more from other federations. “We have ‌such strict punishment for doping. Why can’t we have something similar for the age frauds?” Given that context, it is no surprise that when Vaibhav Sooryavanshi exploded onto the cricket scene in his early teens, doubts about his age immediately swirled around the internet. If anything, though, the prodigiously talented Sooryavanshi could be ‌considered something of a poster boy for attempts to rid Indian sport of age fraud. The Board of Control for Cricket in India said Sooryavanshi, who made his ⁠international debut for India at the age of ⁠15 earlier this year, had been subject to bone density tests since the age of eight. The tests are mandatory for players in BCCI-approved tournaments. No silver bullet In 2012, the BCCI was the first sports body in India to adopt the TW3 method, ‌which assesses skeletal maturity through an X-ray of the left hand and wrist. India’s football and tennis federations have since adopted the method. Chandran, a sports medicine expert with decades of experience, does not see it as a silver bullet, though. “Certain bone tests are ‌done in ‌clinics that have no commitment to sports,” he said. “I’m aware of incidents where an athlete submitted the bone test of someone else, and it has happened more than once.” Mehrotra, the founder of AM ‌Sports Law & Management Co, said the TW3 method had “raised the floor”, but was not without its limitations. The test is useful up to about the age of 16, she said, and can also ⁠unfairly flag a naturally early-maturing, big-boned teenager as overage. India’s Sports Ministry has drafted a code against age fraud in sports that Mehrotra says is a step in the right direction. “One cannot eliminate the ⁠menace 100 per cent overnight, so the realistic goal is to make it far harder to commit and far more costly to attempt,” she said. “There has been a lot of conversation around criminalising doping in India. An evaluation of a similar consequence for people who aid minor athletes commit this fraud may be helpful.” Criminal deterrent The proposed Sports Ministry code shifts ‌the emphasis from catching people out later in life ‌to locking identity early in a central, digitally locked database. It also recommends combining documentary checks with TW3, MRI, dental and physical examinations, and introduces criminal deterrence while offering an amnesty window for athletes to correct records without punishment. Mehrotra said the legal deterrence in the code had to be routinely enforced “because a criminal consequence that is announced but never enforced is worth nothing”. At the same time, she argued, authorities needed to remember that young athletes are often victims, and not the architects, of age fraud. “Protect the accused as seriously as you pursue the guilty, which means robust appeals and, because these are minors, strict data protection,” she said.

title: Over 1,700 Indonesians get food poisoning after eating state-issued free meals
description: As of Tuesday, 50,000 individuals ‌contracted food poisoning, according to a lawmaker who criticises the ‘failure of the system’.
content: Another 777 students and teachers contracted food poisoning in Indonesia’s Central Java after consuming government-issued free meals, a school principal said on Thursday, bringing the total number of people made ‌ill by the scheme to more than 1,700 in just a week. In separate incidents in three other locations this week, 950 Indonesians had fallen ill as a result of food poisoning linked to the programme, a member of a parliamentary commission overseeing health said. President Prabowo Subianto launched the multibillion-dollar free meal programme last year to improve nutrition for tens of millions of children, but the costly scheme has been dogged by allegations of corruption, leadership changes and a ⁠spate of mass food poisoning outbreaks. In a senior high school in Lasem, Central Java, 752 students and 25 teachers have been ‌suffering from diarrhoea and vomiting after consuming free meals on Wednesday, said the school’s principal, Juhartutik. The students in Lasem were given grilled chicken. Before it was distributed, a food taster found that some ‌of it was “slimy”, Juhartutik said. “The slimy ones had already been set aside … The kitchen operator said the ⁠food was cooked at ⁠3am and it was eaten at noon,” she said, adding that most of the victims were sent home. Joko Paryanto, a local doctor who treated ‌the victims, said 15 students and teachers had been hospitalised. Sudaryono, head of the National ‌Nutrition ‌Agency, which oversees the US$12.94 billion programme, told a parliamentary hearing that the food poisoning cases would be handled “seriously”. On Tuesday, 664 students fell ill in Sidoarjo, East Java, said Herawati Yuwantina, a local official. In two other ‌cases on ‌Wednesday, 49 people in the East Java city of Nganjuk and 237 in the West Sumatra region of Agam contracted ‌food poisoning, said Charles Honoris, a lawmaker and member of the sole political party outside the governing coalition, citing local health ⁠department data. Charles wrote on social media that they were not isolated incidents. “This is a failure of the system,” he said. The National Nutrition ⁠Agency, which oversees the $12.94 billion programme, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the food poisoning cases. It suspended the kitchen linked to the Sidoarjo case on Wednesday. As of September 1, 50,000 individuals ‌had been affected by food poisoning ‌cases, Charles said, citing health department data. Improper food storage and late delivery of cooked meals are often to blame for the food poisoning. In July, a survey by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed only one-third of people were satisfied with the scheme, with poisoning cases cited as a major reason.

title: MTR Corp sues Opatra operator over HK$347,000 unpaid rent and fees at Sha Tin mall
description: Court document shows rail operator, as landlord of Citylink Plaza in Sha Tin, suing Sayles Retail for the outstanding payments.
content: Hong Kong’s railway operator has sued the local distributor behind embattled beauty brand Opatra London for allegedly failing to pay more than HK$347,000 (US$44,248) in rent and other fees at one of its shopping malls. A court document reviewed by the South China Morning Post on Thursday showed the MTR Corporation, as the landlord of Citylink Plaza in Sha Tin, suing Sayles Retail, the local operator for the UK-based beauty chain, for the outstanding payments. Opatra London has faced intense scrutiny and law enforcement action over the past month following online customer complaints about aggressive sales tactics, leading to the arrest of three individuals – including a saleswoman – by the Customs and Excise Department. Customs officers alleged after the latest arrest on Wednesday that the saleswoman used aggressive sales tactics to pressure a customer into making purchases at a now-closed Opatra London branch in New Town Plaza in Sha Tin. Another Opatra London outlet was located in neighbouring Citylink Plaza. The SCMP previously reported that at least one top executive of Sayles Retail resigned in late August, after customs officers arrested two of the firm’s managers over alleged coercive and misleading sales practices. The legal writ revealed that Sayles Retail failed to pay monthly rent, management, air-conditioning, promotion, and other fees starting in July, totalling HK$347,426. The MTRC Corporation also demanded Sayles Retail pay interest at 3 per cent per annum over the outstanding payment, as well as all legal costs and incurred expenses. The filing also revealed that Sayles Retail ceased operating its Citylink Plaza store on August 16 without the landlord’s consent. The rail operator is demanding the company vacate and return the premises in addition to settling all outstanding fees and accrued interest. All four Opatra outlets in the city, including the flagship store in Causeway Bay, have been closed since the controversy flared up last month.

title: Beijing bets on a US$1 trillion sports boom to revive consumption, job market
description: China is looking to leverage fitness and events to stimulate local economies, as new five-year blueprint aims to nearly double the economic output of the athletic sector.
content: China plans to expand the scale of its sports industry to at least 7 trillion yuan (about US$1 trillion) over the next five years, turning to sporting events, outdoor activities and fitness spending to boost consumption and support local economies. The fresh target was detailed by officials at a press conference on Thursday as part of Beijing’s 15th five-year plan for the sports sector, and the goal represents a big jump from the 3.84 trillion yuan recorded in 2024, according to the most recent data. China’s General Administration of Sport said the country would cultivate home-grown event brands, improve the spectator experience, and use competitions to stimulate spending across dining, accommodation, transport, tourism, retail and entertainment. Policymakers were also betting that the expansion would create jobs and support a broader commercial ecosystem centred on sporting events. The plan comes as Beijing seeks to stimulate consumption and employment, aiming to offset a prolonged property downturn and persistently weak household spending that continue to weigh on local government revenue, the job market and national economic growth. Unlike one-off purchases of subsidised consumer goods, participation in sports can generate recurring spending on training, equipment, travel and entertainment. Meanwhile, relatively inexpensive local competitions can draw spectators into restaurants, hotels, shops and tourist attractions. The Jiangsu Football City League has offered an early example of the model that policymakers hope to replicate. Last year, in its inaugural season, the provincial league staged 85 matches and attracted more than 2.43 million spectators, while relatively low ticket prices and rivalries between the province’s 13 cities helped turn matches into wider tourism and shopping occasions. In the first nine months of last year, 213 sporting events monitored by Jiangsu authorities attracted 5.73 million visits and generated 3.54 billion yuan in consumer spending. Similar gains have been recorded elsewhere. Shanghai’s 182 domestic and international sporting events generated an estimated 13.5 billion yuan in direct economic impact in 2025, with the Formula One Chinese Grand Prix alone accounting for 2.47 billion yuan. Those results have encouraged policymakers to step up support for the industry. The sports administration said it would foster online broadcasting, digital training, virtual sports and intelligent venue operations, while using digital technology to create new forms of sports consumption. To increase the availability of events, Beijing plans to improve the quality of competitions and spectator participation while increasing ticket supply to address strong demand for popular events. Technology and manufacturing form another pillar of the strategy. The sports administration said it would support research into high-performance competition equipment and smart wearables, while accelerating the replacement of imported equipment and encouraging the commercialisation of domestic sports technologies. Beyond consumption and employment, improving public health is another important element of the strategy. Amid a rapidly ageing population and a growing chronic disease burden, Beijing is increasingly treating physical activity as part of its national health agenda. By 2030, China aims to increase per capita sports venue space to about 4 square metres (43 square feet) from 3 square metres currently, while also raising the proportion of people who exercise regularly to about 40 per cent from roughly 38.5 per cent. The country also intends to build or renovate more than 5,000 small sports parks, fitness centres, multifunctional courts and public skating facilities.

title: Moonshot AI – creator of Kimi K3 model – has filed for Hong Kong IPO: sources
description: The leading Chinese AI start-up has confidentially filed for a Hong Kong listing and aims to go public early next year, sources say.
content: Chinese artificial intelligence start-up Moonshot AI – developer of the leading Kimi K3 model – has confidentially filed for an initial public offering in Hong Kong, according to two people with knowledge of the matter, as the firm seeks to tap public markets to fund its rapid expansion. The Beijing-based company was targeting a Hong Kong listing as early as the first quarter of 2027, the sources told the South China Morning Post, asking not to be identified as the information was private. The timeline remained subject to regulatory approvals and market conditions, they added. Moonshot said it “doesn’t comment on market rumours or speculation” in a response to a query sent by the SCMP on Thursday. The company was also looking to undertake a final financing round ahead of the IPO, which could value it at around US$50 billion, the people said. The IPO and financing plan indicate the company is looking to accelerate fundraising as China’s AI labs step up competition with leading developers in the United States. Moonshot made headlines in July with the release of its Kimi K3 model: the world’s largest open-weight AI model with more than 2.8 trillion parameters, which refers to the sophistication of AI systems with larger sizes usually indicating stronger capabilities. The release of K3 sent shock waves across the US AI industry, as the model approaches the performance of leading proprietary systems in Silicon Valley while maintaining the price edge offered by Chinese open-source models. At the unveiling of K3, Moonshot said the system delivered “open-frontier intelligence”, citing independent benchmarks to claim the new model outperformed leading products from Anthropic and OpenAI in some capabilities, while acknowledging that its “overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models.” The model currently ranks as the top Chinese model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, along with Z.ai’s GLM-5.3. It is also far cheaper than leading US models: its price per million output token is 50 per cent lower than OpenAI’s 5.6 Sol and 70 per cent lower than Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5. Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR) – a key metric that projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – has been growing rapidly since earlier this year. The company’s ARR is expected to reach US$1 billion by the end of the year, doubling from an estimated US$400 million to US$500 million as of mid-2026, according to a research note published by Nomura Securities in July. The rapid growth was driven in part by growing adoption of the company’s developer platform, Nomura said in the report. Moonshot is also exploring a revenue share deal with overseas cloud service providers including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, under which the platforms could share up to 30 per cent of revenue from services hosting its Kimi K3 model, according to a Reuters report last month. Moonshot is not the only Chinese AI firm looking to go public. Rivals including Hangzhou-based DeepSeek and Shanghai-based StepFun are also reportedly preparing for IPOs. DeepSeek is planning to list on Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market while also raising funds via a pre-IPO round, the SCMP reported last month. Additional reporting by Coco Feng

title: Defendant knew sexual acts with sister as teen ‘seriously wrong’, court told
description: Prosecution argues man, now 24, knew alleged sexual acts with sibling on five occasions were inappropriate.
content: A man who engaged in sexual acts with his younger sister when he was just a teenager knew his behaviour was “seriously wrong”, prosecutors have told Hong Kong’s High Court. Senior Public Prosecutor Karen Ng Ka-yuet said on Thursday that the older sibling, believed to have been aged between 11 and 14 at the time of the alleged offences, was fully aware that the acts involving his sister, three years younger, were inappropriate. The five alleged incidents took place on unspecified dates only weeks apart, sometime between 2013 and 2016, at the family’s home in Sha Tau Kok. The sister, now 20, filed a police report in 2021. The defendant, now 24, has denied four counts of incest and three counts of indecent conduct towards a child under the age of 16. Ng said the indecent acts were charged separately from the incest counts because they concerned different sexual conduct. The prosecution’s evidence draws on statements from the defendant, in which he admitted to these acts. The sister is not set to testify in court. Ng told the court that the defendant had initiated the first sexual act and made subsequent requests over a period of about two months. While the prosecution’s opening remarks described most of the alleged acts as sexual intercourse, rather than rape, Ng explained that it was only necessary to prove the defendant had intercourse with the person, whom he knew to be his sister, for the offence of incest. The jury heard the defendant had admitted to police that he engaged in such acts with his sister, telling officers: “At that time, I was very young, but I admit that I did do it. I now regret it a lot as well.” Ng claimed the language used by the defendant towards his younger sister during the alleged incidents showed he had “a clear degree of maturity beyond a child of similar age”. “The repeated sexual acts between brother and sister, as admitted to by the defendant, could not be excused as being childish, playfulness, naughtiness or simply innocent,” she said. The senior prosecutor asked the jury to look at the circumstances behind each alleged act, arguing that it would become clear to them that “the defendant – even when he was just between 11 and 14 years old – knew what he was doing to his younger sister was seriously wrong”. The trial continues on Friday.

title: China prepares next phase of national SME fund to boost tech start-ups and IPOs
description: A new phase of the state-backed fund is set to target early-stage hard-tech firms that are IPO-ready.
content: China will soon launch the second phase of a National SME Development Fund with a focus on IPO incubation and channelling private capital into backing innovative, early-stage entities and projects with long-term prospects in hard tech. The fund’s second phase was confirmed as the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), together with nine other ministries and agencies, released China’s 15th five-year plan for promoting the development of small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The second phase would enhance support for inclusive financing and initial public offering readiness, MIIT officials said at a State Council Information Office press conference in August. The national fund would provide a “guiding and catalytic role”, the officials said, expressing confidence that it would continue to attract and pool more venture and private capital for investment in tech-focused SMEs. The fund’s first phase was established in September 2015 and as of March this year had spawned 46 sub-funds with a total capital pool exceeding 120 billion yuan (US$17.6 billion) invested in more than 2,000 enterprises, as well as 92 IPOs, according to data from China Galaxy Securities. With an overall return of around 15 per cent, the fund had also completed exits from over 200 funded projects reached specific milestones. “SMEs, especially early-stage and technology-based ones, are still held back by light assets, high risk and long research and development cycles, making it difficult for them to obtain traditional credit support, when most investors chase mature projects,” said Wu Jing, a China Galaxy Securities analyst, in a note published on Monday. “Featuring risk sharing and long-term investment, the national SME fund can step in to help,” Wu said. Other measures from the just-released five-year plan for SMEs include support for direct and equity financing. China’s various regional equity trading platforms would develop specialised boards for the SMEs accredited by MIIT as “specialised, refined, distinctive and innovative” companies, also known as little giants or SRDIs, for their niche in advanced manufacturing and cutting-edge tech. The country’s bond market would also set up a tech board to help qualified SMEs issue bonds for financing. SMEs, mostly private ones, make up the bulk of the Chinese economy and contribute to a large share of government fiscal income and urban jobs. Yet many continue to grapple with headwinds, ranging from insufficient funding, tepid domestic demand and depressed business sentiment, despite Beijing’s strong tech push and the boom in artificial intelligence and other tech sectors. Private sector investment slumped 9.4 per cent year on year in the first seven months, according to data from the National Bureau of Statistics.

title: Opinion | What a Trump official’s dig at Harvard means for Hong Kong
description: As higher education in the West gets caught up in political theatre, Hong Kong can capitalise on the international education market shift.
content: A cabinet secretary fretting about his daughter’s university choice might once have been considered a private family matter. In Donald Trump’s America, it has become official content. US transport secretary Sean Duffy recently appeared with his family in a road trip series carried on the department’s YouTube page. In one episode, his daughter, Paloma, said if she were admitted to Harvard University, she would probably urge her parents to let her attend. Duffy, however, warned the university had become adept at taking “good young girls” and corrupting their minds. Parents worry about their children’s futures. They are also free to hold firm views about Harvard, faith, politics and the value of an elite education. But this was a serving cabinet member who turned a domestic matter into content for a government-linked video series. It shows how much American politics has changed. The boundaries between public office, personal branding, family life and political messaging have blurred. A university becomes a symbol of everything one side fears about the other. Harvard is not merely a symbol. It is a major research university whose name still carries immense global weight. Paloma is hardly alone in seeing it as an opportunity difficult to refuse. Having grown up in a conservative family and attended a conservative school, she said studying in a more liberal environment might offer balance. That ought not to be controversial. University is meant to broaden minds, exposing students to new ideas, people and ways of thinking. Yet the Duffy exchange was never really about educational philosophy. It reflected the broader Trump administration battle with Harvard and other elite institutions, portrayed as politically uniform, hostile to religion and disconnected from ordinary America. Its disputes with universities have involved funding, admissions, campus policies and ideological bias. In this atmosphere, a young person’s college decision becomes another front in a political conflict. For overseas students, it reinforces an impression that American higher education has become more uncertain, politicised and difficult to access. For Chinese families, the calculation has become more complex. An American degree, especially from an Ivy League university, still carries considerable prestige. But that must now be weighed against high costs, shifting visa rules, weaker post-graduation prospects and a political climate that can appear hostile. Reports of the Trump administration considering a US$100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training, the post-graduation employment programme for international students, have added to the uncertainty. Critics warn it would deter international graduates and weaken innovation – and could face legal challenges after a similar H-1B fee was struck down. Nor is the reassessment confined to the United States. Australia is no longer an automatic choice as high fees and living costs are being weighed against fewer certain career benefits. The United Kingdom has become a less straightforward destination as restrictions on most students from bringing dependants contribute to a fall in demand. With Canada, higher financial requirements and tighter controls have made the study-to-work pathway less predictable. The result is a broader shift in the international education market. Parents still want quality, but they are also looking for affordability, safety, proximity, employability and, for many, a connection to Asia. Hong Kong faces strong competition from cities such as Singapore, Tokyo and Kuala Lumpur, but has a major advantage: five universities in the global top 100. Our appeal is not only academic. Students study in a major financial and professional centre, close to the Chinese mainland and in Asia. They gain access to our networks, commercial culture and role as a bridge between China and the world. Enrolment of non-local students in undergraduate and postgraduate programmes has grown. These students contribute to the broader economy. They rent homes, eat out, use public transport, visit cultural venues and support local shops and services. A cohort drawn from mainland China, Southeast Asia, Belt and Road Initiative economies and elsewhere gives local students a wider regional network before their careers even begin. The long-term gains are even greater. Some graduates will remain, adding to our pool of researchers, professionals, entrepreneurs and innovators. Others will leave, taking their personal and professional ties to the city with them. In time, they may become clients, collaborators, investors, founders and informal ambassadors. Hong Kong’s decision to expand the capacity for non-local students is not simply an education policy. It is an investment in talent, international connection and economic confidence. The Duffy conversation may seem like an odd starting point for Hong Kong. But it captures a significant change. In the West, higher education is increasingly caught up in political theatre and policy disruption. Across Asia, students and parents are making more practical calculations about cost, access and career outcomes. Hong Kong’s advantage is it can offer ambitious students and their families respected universities, international horizons, closeness to home and a direct stake in Asia’s future.

title: Orangutan in Indonesia dies after exposure to haze fires, abnormalities in lungs
description: The 20-year-old male orangutan was unable to stand and was struggling to breathe when a joint team of rescuers found him.
content: An adult male orangutan found struggling to breathe in a palm oil plantation on Indonesia’s Borneo died hours after being rescued, authorities said on Thursday. The orangutan, named Sampurna and believed to be around 20 years old, was found by residents on Sunday morning in Ketapang district, West Kalimantan, an area affected by wildfires. He was unable to stand and was struggling to breathe when a joint team from the West Kalimantan Natural Resources Conservation Agency and the Indonesian Foundation for the Rehabilitation of Forest and Wildlife (YIARI) arrived, the Forestry Ministry said. Video footage showed veterinarians giving Sampurna oxygen and intravenous fluids before taking him to a YIARI rehabilitation centre. His condition deteriorated, however, and he died later that day, the ministry said in a statement. “We deeply regret that Sampurna could not be saved,” said West Kalimantan natural conservation chief Murlan Dameria Pane in the statement. A postmortem examination found abnormalities in his lungs, heart and kidneys, suspected to be linked to prolonged smoke exposure and acute hypoxia, or a lack of oxygen, the ministry said. Sampurna had been monitored by YIARI’s Orangutan Protection Unit on August 16 and was still moving actively at the time. About two weeks later, he was found collapsed in a plantation near areas affected by fires. His death highlights the threat that forest fires pose to orangutans, which depend on increasingly fragmented forests across Borneo. Fires can destroy food sources and habitats, forcing the critically endangered animals into plantations and other areas where they are exposed to smoke and potential conflict with people. Sampurna’s rescue was one of several involving orangutans in West Kalimantan during the current fire season. Indonesia has been experiencing a severe dry season, with forest and land fires affecting parts of the country. According to the Forestry Ministry, fires burned around 202,004 hectares nationwide between January and July this year.

title: Mexican foreign minister to meet Wang Yi in China as US demands trade ties rollback
description: Two-day trip expected to ‘promote steady growth’ of ties, Beijing says, with Roberto Velasco also set to open new Chongqing consulate.
content: Mexican Foreign Affairs Secretary Roberto Velasco arrives in China on Sunday for his first official visit as his country navigates increasing US pressure to roll back Chinese trade ties. The two-day visit will take place at the invitation of Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in Beijing on Thursday. He said China expected the visit to be an opportunity to deepen mutual political trust and cooperation, and “promote the steady growth” of ties to better benefit both nations. The Mexican foreign ministry earlier confirmed the visit in an overnight social media post, noting that Velasco would meet Wang in Beijing and also inaugurate Mexico’s new consulate in Chongqing. “This visit will allow for strengthening political dialogue and the cooperation agenda between both countries,” the post read. Velasco, who took office in April, faces a delicate diplomatic balance. Mexico’s largest trading partner, the United States, is pressuring the Latin American nation to mirror its trade barriers against Chinese steel and aluminium as it reviews the 2020 US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). The push – first reported by Bloomberg in July – is widely believed to be aimed at restricting Beijing’s economic footprint in North America. Chinese companies, including major electric vehicle manufacturers such as BYD, have rapidly expanded their industrial footprint in Mexico as part of a nearshoring trend. However, Washington has repeatedly vowed to curb China’s presence in its neighbouring country, warning that the firms might be using Mexico as a transshipment hub to bypass US tariffs. Another Bloomberg report last month said that Mexico was considering new anti-dumping measures on select Chinese and other foreign goods, alongside higher import tariffs on others. Such a move would deepen Mexico’s alignment with the US as it seeks to protect and renew the USMCA trade pact, which underpins its preferential access to the US market. Trade tensions with China flared after Mexico approved sweeping tariffs of up to 50 per cent on more than 1,400 products from non-FTA countries, a measure that took effect on January 1. The move was widely seen as an attempt to appease Washington ahead of the high-stakes USMCA review talks that began in July.

title: Chinese military’s AI attack chain lags foreign models: researchers
description: PLA focuses largely on support functions while offensive combat uses are exploratory, says paper that drew heavily on US military analysis.
content: China’s military AI models trail their foreign equivalents in performance, concentrating on support functions rather than combat, according to a study by Chinese researchers. The findings appeared in a paper by researchers affiliated with the Armed Police Force Shandong Corps and the Engineering University of People’s Armed Police, published in the journal Defence Industry Conversion in China in July. “The military’s AI applications are mainly used in auxiliary fields such as intelligent question-answering and content generation,” the authors wrote. “They still lag considerably behind foreign large language models in performance, while offensive applications in actual combat remain at an exploratory stage, with relatively limited theoretical and empirical research.” The paper comes as AI moves from an emerging military technology to a core component of the strategic competition between the United States and China, with both militaries exploring the use of artificial intelligence to sharpen command and control. The US is pushing to make AI a foundational part of its armed forces, with the Pentagon calling for an “AI-first” warfighting force and faster deployment of AI across combat, intelligence and decision-making. China, meanwhile, is pursuing its own military AI agenda, seeking to integrate emerging technologies into the People’s Liberation Army and build a more interconnected force in which multiple platforms and weapons systems can work together as a “system of systems”. In August, state broadcaster CCTV reported that the Chinese air force was using an AI-enabled system to draw up battle plans for operations involving more than 100 units, using what the PLA called an “intelligent-strike planning system”. The system was designed to help commanders and pilots by prioritising targets, coordinating attack waves and assigning specific tasks to units, CCTV reported, adding that it had been used “multiple” times. The journal paper drew heavily on an American military analysis published in Military Review, a professional journal of the US Army, in early 2025. Written by officers from the Virginia Army National Guard, the article examined the integration of AI with cyber and information operations, drawing on previous US military operations and state-led exercises as case studies. The Chinese authors found that the US military’s use of AI in these operations showed three capabilities that could shape future offensive warfare. These were the abilities to expand AI military applications from information processing to direct attacks; to achieve physical facility damage and cognitive effects in cyberattacks; and to integrate AI into military command and decision-making. They called for China to build an “autonomous and controllable AI attack chain” capable of identifying and striking battlefield targets; of generating code to attack adversary networks and command chains; and of conducting strikes in the cognitive domain. The authors also said China’s military had yet to develop a sufficiently large pool of personnel trained systematically in AI and big data, highlighting a potential gap between the country’s rapid civilian AI advances and their adoption on the battlefield. In 2017, the State Council, China’s cabinet, released a development plan setting out a path to make China the world’s leading AI power by 2030. That same year, systematic efforts to develop disciplines in big data and AI began across the PLA, the authors wrote. Nearly a decade on, the effort has yet to produce a professional cadre of any scale, the paper said. And specialists recruited directly from industry lack a military background and are constrained in operational settings. To close the gap, the authors proposed sending serving personnel to civilian universities for specialist training and drawing civilian experts into military exercises and routine combat-readiness duty.

title: Celebrated US feminist activist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
description: The life of the Ms Magazine co-founder was the subject of a feature film, The Glorias: a Life on the Road, based on her 2015 memoir.
content: Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author and activist who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the US women’s movement and a fierce advocate for feminist causes throughout her life, has died. She was 92. With her trademark streaked hair parted down the middle and large aviator glasses, Steinem, a co-founder of Ms Magazine, was a hugely recognisable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centres, at rallies and marches. She died on Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation’s social media pages. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard,” the posts said. “Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humour.” Steinem enjoyed writing and spending time in the community in recent years, the posts said. She also hosted talking circles for hundreds of people in her home. “You can’t do it on the phone or on the web,” she told The Associated Press in a 2015 interview. “You have to be there with all five senses. It should be obvious that people can’t empathise with each other unless we’re in the same room.” She began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret. She credits a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favour of abortion rights, with changing her career path. “That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me,” Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told the AP in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v Wade. “Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy.” Though she soon became a known activist, those who watched Steinem denounce discrimination for so many years likely never suspected that she had to overcome a deep fear of public speaking. She would have simply stuck to writing, she said, if only editors at the time had been willing to let her write about the women’s movement. But they weren’t interested, she told the AP in 2015. “So I ended up going out and speaking, which was my nightmare,” she said. “I mean, I was terrified. But I’m grateful, even though I still get scared even now.” Time hardly slowed Steinem down; well into her 80s she was travelling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence. “Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half,” she once said. “It shouldn’t need a name, and one day it won’t.” As the years went on, Steinem’s visibility endured. At 83, she sat in the front row of her first fashion show, guest of designer Prabal Gurung. A few days after her 85th birthday, she was leading a women’s “talking circle” at an off-Broadway play celebrating her life, where one by one, women in the audience – many fighting tears – rose to thank her and tell their own stories of discrimination. In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film, The Glorias: a Life on the Road, based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore. And at 91, she collaborated on a picture book with Liberian peace activist and Nobel laureate Leymah Gbowee aimed at inspiring young people to change the world. Rise, Girl, Rise: Our Sister-Friend Journey. Together for All was published in February.

title: CNBC to close Hong Kong operations, scrap international shows in major overhaul
description: CNBC spokesman says programming from Hong Kong ended on Wednesday and ‘small number of employees’ had been affected by the closure.
content: US business television network CNBC is closing its Hong Kong office and pulling the plug on several flagship international daily shows as part of a major operational overhaul across Asia and Europe. The decision was communicated to staff on Wednesday in an internal memo from the company’s executive management. According to the memo seen by the South China Morning Post, the broadcaster’s management said it made “a number of very difficult decisions” after evaluating its international programming, commercial viability, and resource deployment over several months. “As our production needs in Asia evolve, we have made the difficult choice to close our Hong Kong bureau,” the memo read, adding that London, Singapore, Beijing and Abu Dhabi would remain as key production hubs providing studio, editorial and technical capabilities. A number of roles across several international teams and locations would be eliminated, with affected employees being notified personally, it read. A CNBC spokesman confirmed to the SCMP on Thursday that programming produced from the Hong Kong office had concluded the day before. He said “a small number of employees” had been affected by the closure of its local operations, but declined to comment on individual employees’ circumstances or the support being offered to them. The decision was part of broader changes to CNBC’s international programming and production needs and was not driven by changes in the local operating climate, he added. The spokesman said CNBC would continue to provide editorial coverage of Hong Kong, China and the wider Asia-Pacific region through its teams in Singapore and reporters based in Beijing. The broadcaster’s move saw the immediate cancellation of the business-day programmes Inside India, The China Connection, and Europe Early Edition. Feature series including CNBC Meets and Built for Billions will also wrap up once current broadcast runs conclude. The restructuring follows Comcast’s spin-off of its cable networks – including CNBC and MSNBC – into Versant Media Group at the start of this year, which triggered earlier newsroom lay-offs. Despite shuttering its physical presence in Hong Kong, CNBC said it would maintain its commitment to international audiences.

title: Leave it to the experts, district councillor told after chaotic deer rescue
