description: Footage from district councillor shows him and two others freeing animal by forcefully pulling its rear legs – causing the barking deer to struggle.
content: A wildlife expert and social media users have expressed concerns about the forceful approach used by a district councillor and two other men to free a trapped barking deer, warning they should have sought help from professionals. Tai Po district councillor Chan Siu-keen posted footage of the incident on social media on Wednesday, with the clip showing him and two other men freeing the animal, also known as a muntjac, from a railing by forcefully pulling its rear legs – causing the barking deer to struggle. But some social media users said that barking deer could be easily frightened and potentially die of a heart attack from shock. Chan said he discovered the trapped animal, crying out helplessly, as he passed by Hung Lam Drive in Tai Po Kau. “It was injured and unable to move, and its body was bleeding. Everyone immediately joined forces to carefully lift it out and release it back into the forest,” he said. The clip also shows that, after the trio pulls the barking deer out of the fence, they lift it over the railing and drop it on the other side, causing it to briefly roll down a slope. It then quickly disappears into the forest. Chan defended the trio’s approach, arguing the animal was trapped and bleeding. “I cannot leave it injured and bleeding like this,” he said. “Returned to the wild – may all living beings be protected and may life thrive endlessly.” But Gary Ades, head of fauna conservation at Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden, said the rescue method was not recommended. He said Chan and his team should have sought help from experts from organisations such as the Hong Kong Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals and the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department. Ades warned that the trio could be in breach of the Wild Animals Protection Ordinance by rescuing the barking deer themselves. “The deer was clearly injured from the video, and although the three men helping may have thought the wounds were superficial, without a professional full assessment of the injuries this could not be certain,” he said. “There are also legalities related to disturbing or handling protected wild animals, and this is another reason to call for professional help rather than handling the animal yourself – you may be breaching the wild animal protection ordinance.” While the three men had shown “commendable concern” and managed to free the barking deer, Ades emphasised that there were existing procedures for handling trapped wild animals. “The existing procedures ensure that the wild animal or deer receives some expert assessment and whether it should be released or sent for veterinary medical care and, on full recovery, released back to the wild,” he said.

title: 5 of the best things to do in Hong Kong this weekend, September 4-6
description: Caviar ice cream, a poster exhibition, a super fashion showcase, a showing of a Wong Kar-wai classic and more await you this weekend.
content: Starting September with a bang, the city is serving up everything from major fashion showcases and underground art exhibitions to caviar on gelato. If runway shows and designer labels are not quite your scene, or dessert is not your thing, there is also a three-day health and wellness festival happening at the same time. Here are five things to do this weekend. 1. Messina x Nomad Caviar Ice cream purveyor Messina has teamed up with Hong Kong-based Nomad Caviar for a limited-edition collaboration for the ultimate guilty pleasure for this week only. Each scoop of two custom gelato flavours – a sour cream and roasted potato gelato as well as an olive oil gelato – is crowned with premium Ossetra caviar. The collaboration runs until Monday, September 7, at Messina in Central, on Hong Kong Island, priced at HK$128 (US$16.30) for a single scoop, HK$143 for a double, and HK$153 for a triple, with additional caviar topping available at HK$50 for 8 grams. Click here for details. Messina, 37 Pottinger Street, Central 2. The Mihn Machine The Mihn Machine, from September 4 to 11, brings together more than 100 posters created by Belgrade-based designer Stevie Whisper as art director for Hong Kong’s underground club Mihn. Whisper has been designing posters for the space since September 2025, and this is the first time his works will be presented as large-format pigment prints while marking one year of his creative direction for the venue. The posters will be on display on the ground floor of Villa Serene in Central. Having been involved with more than 700 music and cultural events since 2006, Whisper’s style has helped define a generation of Belgrade’s underground scene through his art, which has also been exhibited in Shanghai, Beijing, New York and Melbourne. The graphics range from puzzles and direct illustrations to imaginative abstractions, drawing from Serbian origins and also the visual identities of club culture. Villa Serene, 3 Staunton Street, Central 3. Centrestage The 11th edition of Centrestage, Hong Kong’s annual flagship fashion event, is running from now until September 5. This year’s showcase brings together some 270 brands from 24 countries and regions, with more than 30 fashion shows marking a record high for the event. The exhibition is free to both industry buyers and the public with more than 40 events across its four-day run. A major highlight is the debut of the Hype pavilion, which is dedicated to streetwear labels founded or led by Hong Kong celebrities and influencers. Brands taking part include Claro by Rosita Kwok, Ogis by Vincent Wong, Pick and Match by Kelvin Kwan and Kit Wan Studios by Kit Wan. A fashion show is scheduled for Friday. International brands take up the rest of the exhibition, including designs from South Korea, the Faroe Islands, Austria, Slovakia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam and Colombia. For more information, click here. Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre, 1 Expo Drive, Wan Chai 4. Longevity and Wellbeing Fest Throughout the weekend, Airside and Manulife will be hosting a wellness festival, featuring over 60 activities led by more than 30 instructors and guest speakers covering fitness, mental well-being and lifestyle. The three-day event at the Airside shopping centre is organised into four main sections: movement activities such as yoga, breathwork and CrossFit exercises, panel discussions on holistic living, a wellness market that includes workshops and pop-ups as well as interactive mental health game booths. The sessions are designed to encourage movement as a foundation for long-term health, with instructors and medical experts guiding participants through practices that balance physical exertion with mental relaxation. The event runs from September 4 to 6, with limited quotas subject to availability. For more information on tickets and scheduling, click here. Airside, 2 Concorde Road, Kai Tak 5. Days of Being Wild Wong Kar-wai’s big-budget period drama, which failed at the box office in 1990 but etched the director’s name into Hong Kong cinema’s hall of fame, sees him unveil his unbridled art-house sensibility as an aspiring cinematic auteur despite the commercial constraints of filming with an all-star cast. Conceived as a two-part film before it bombed – thus the cryptic epilogue that turns out to have prefigured Tony Leung Chiu-wai’s part in 2000’s In the Mood for Love – Wong’s second feature turned Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing into the most remembered playboy in Hong Kong film history via his unhappy affairs with women, as well as a fruitless search for his birth mother. Don’t miss this round of screenings of the film’s 4K restored version – or its 35mm film print in the following week. Read more about the film here. Days of Being Wild opens in cinemas on Friday.

title: Hong Kong regulator reclassifies certain funds with exposure to private markets
description: The industry has increasingly focused on the risks of what was previously a booming private credit industry.
content: Hong Kong’s market regulator has reclassified some of the city’s authorised funds with exposure to private market assets above a certain amount as complex products, raising the threshold for selling these products to retail investors. Funds with exposures to direct or indirect private market assets amounting to 50 per cent or more of their net asset value would be recategorised. The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) said that it observed some funds gaining indirect exposure to private market assets through layered structures and complex instruments, which might lack transparency. This structure made it difficult for retail investors to fully understand the underlying risks, the SFC said in a circular released on Thursday. Due to low liquidity, valuation challenges and higher credit risks, funds with exposure to private credit and private equity would need to enhance their transparency regarding underlying investments and associated risks, according to the SFC. Funds classified as complex products are subject to the SFC’s selling requirements, which include ensuring product suitability, the regulator added. “The enhanced guidance strengthens Hong Kong’s regulatory framework for retail funds with private market exposure by increasing transparency and introducing appropriate investor safeguards,” said Elisa Ng, executive director of investment products at the SFC. Market attention has increasingly focused on private credit market risks over the past year. Last December, HSBC Asset Management suspended the sale of a retail fund involving private credit following questions from the market about potential hidden risks. The regulatory decision means funds exposed to private market assets must clearly disclose three key factors in their offering documents: the extent and means of exposure, the nature and characteristics of underlying assets and the key risks, along with their potential impact on the fund and investors. The SFC urged fund managers to review their existing funds, update offering documents as soon as practicable and maintain proper communication with distributors. For new funds, applications may face closer scrutiny and may not be processed under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

title: India targets weapons self-reliance with fully local assault rifle
description: India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine.
content: India is touting its locally manufactured AK-203 Sher assault rifle – an advanced version of Russia’s powerful Kalashnikov – as an important milestone for the “Make in India” initiative to reduce reliance on foreign-made weapon systems. The Sher, or Tiger, will replace the older, heavily criticised Indian National Small Arms System (INSAS) service rifles used by the Indian Army. Complaints about the INSAS emerged just a year after it was adopted by the army. Indian soldiers fighting the high-altitude Kargil war in 1999 against Pakistan-backed forces in Ladakh, then a part of Kashmir, said the firearm tended to jam or its magazine would crack in the freezing temperatures. After the Sher was successfully test-fired on August 23 at an ordnance factory in the northern town of Amethi, experts celebrated having cracked the Kalashnikov code without having to import any parts. This is a significant victory as most of India’s military weapon systems – from Su-30MKI fighter jets to several warships and submarines – come from Russia. India has been slowly trying to reduce its reliance on Russian-made weapons, as Moscow prioritises its own needs for its ongoing war with Ukraine, by buying equipment from France, Israel and the United States as well as boosting domestic manufacturing. “End-to-end manufacturing of the [AK-203] rifle creates much more than a weapon system. It reflects a building of capabilities in metallurgy, precision engineering, quality control and world-class testing,” said Rakesh Kapoor, former Indian Army deputy chief of staff. “The AK-203 Sher is not merely a rifle. It is a manifestation that India can take world-class technology, absorb it, master it and eventually manufacture the entire product itself.” Indo-Russian Rifles, a company established in 2019 under an agreement with Russia to make the AK-203, is preparing to submit the rifle to the Indian Army for trials this month, according to local media. The rifle is considered important in the country’s fight against insurgency as separatist militants in India’s Kashmir region during the height of unrest in the 1990s relied on Kalashnikovs, which earned a reputation for reliability. At about 3.6kg to 3.8kg (8lbs to 8.4lbs), the AK-203 is about 600 grams (20oz) lighter than the INSAS, has double the range at 800 metres (2,600 feet) and boasts heavier calibre cartridges that can kill rather than only injure targets. “Russia brought the design, [and] India has progressively developed the manufacturing ecosystem around it. With 100 per cent Indian components and input materials, the project demonstrates technology absorption and indigenous manufacturing capabilities,” Kapoor said. “This also meets the larger strategic intent of creating resilient supply chains.” In many ways, an assault rifle is more important for the soldier than heavy weapon systems such as tanks and missiles. “For a soldier, a rifle is not merely a piece of equipment; it is an extension of the soldier himself. Given Indian terrain and operating conditions, the weapon has to be reliable in all conditions in which the soldier operates,” Kapoor said. India has one of the most diverse terrains in the world, spanning towering snow-capped mountains, vast fertile plains, dry deserts, high plateaus and long tropical coastlines. “Therefore, robustness of military equipment is an imperative,” he said. ‘Significant achievement’ Early feedback – including from troops in the Siachen Glacier, considered the world’s toughest and highest battlefield – had been positive, said Sanjay Iyer, a former brigadier with the Indian Army. But he urged that equal importance be paid to quality standards – otherwise “India will have re-created the Kargil problem with a better rifle”. Part of the reason soldiers encountered problems with INSAS rifles during the Kargil war was because of problems with ordnance-factory ammunition and gun oils, he said. An entirely locally made weapon marked “a significant industrial achievement” with now more than a hundred medium and small enterprises sitting across the supply chain, Iyer said. Indigenous content moved up from 25 per cent in July 2024 to 50 per cent by 2025, before achieving complete local manufacturing. Over 601,000 rifles would be delivered by December 2030, ahead of a contractual promise of October 2032, the Press Trust of India reported last July, citing a senior official. While fully domestic manufacturing was an important milestone, “it is certainly not a design achievement”, Iyer said. “The intellectual property remains Kalashnikov’s. India cannot redesign the weapon at will, and export freedom rests with the joint venture.” The AK-203, at least 25 per cent cheaper than imported versions, could be used to arm the police and “be available for exports from 2030”, Iyer said. Indian small arm exports have climbed nearly 10-fold from 7.79 billion rupees (US$82.5 million) in the 2018 financial year to 72.16 billion rupees in the 2025 financial year. “So the market is real,” he added.

title: Norway seizes Russian ship over US$4.2 billion claim by Ukrainian energy firm
description: Naftogaz was awarded the sum after Russia seized its assets when it invaded Crimea in 2014, while Moscow calls the seizure ‘piracy’.
content: Norway had seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a US$4.22 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow’s seizure of its assets when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, officials said late on Wednesday. The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard, according to Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz. The Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesperson as saying the Norwegian ‌action was “piracy”. ⁠Russia ⁠lodged ⁠a formal protest with Norway’s ambassador in Moscow on ‌Thursday after Norwegian authorities seized the Russian vessel. The ‌Russian foreign ministry ⁠said Moscow had demanded ⁠the vessel’s release and would work to ‌secure its ‌return. The Svalbard governor’s office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held on Svalbard, adding: “The governor will take care of the crew and passengers on board the vessel in collaboration with Trust Arktikugol”. It was not immediately clear how many passengers and crew were on the ship. Arktikugol is the Russian company that manages Moscow’s assets on the archipelago. Svalbard, a Norwegian territory since 1925, lies midway between the North Pole and the European mainland and is governed under a 1920 treaty that also allows citizens of signatory states, including Russia, to settle there without a visa. The ship arrived ⁠on Tuesday in Barentsburg, a Russian-operated coal mining settlement on Spitsbergen, the largest island in the archipelago, with a party of Russian scientists, according to a journalist who was accompanying ‌them. Andrei Gorbunov, editor-in-chief of Komsomolskaya Pravda (KP) radio, said the vessel had docked without incident and the expedition members had headed ashore. News did not emerge until Wednesday evening that the ship had been seized. “This seizure has had no impact on the expedition participants or the ship’s ‌crew. No one has been arrested. We are all going about our business as usual,” Gorbunov wrote on KP’s website. “For the time being, the Professor ⁠Molchanov is simply forbidden from leaving the port ⁠of Barentsburg. It is completely unclear how long this ban will last.” Naftogaz has previously won court orders to seize two Trust Arktikugol properties in Svalbard, including a rental guest house, ‌but Russia has raised legal challenges. Naftogaz has been pursuing Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea. A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz US$4.22 billion plus interest ‌and legal ‌costs. “Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award,” said Naftogaz acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko. Norway said the matter was a legal one between Naftogaz ‌and Russia and did not involve the Oslo government. “As a party to the case, Russia can demand that the district court reassess the case,” the Justice Ministry said. Covington said it ⁠had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a vessel used for commercial cruises, for months. Anticipating its arrival, Naftogaz’s lawyers applied to a court for the vessel to be arrested and ⁠compulsorily sold. The application was approved on Monday by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court, which required the governor of Svalbard to enforce its order, supervise the ship and ensure that it is not moved. Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement across several jurisdictions, including the US, France, Britain and Finland, where Russian assets have ‌been frozen. Russia is appealing, saying no notice was ‌given. “We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid,” the Ukrainian company said. Barentsburg is one of two Russian settlements on Svalbard, along with Pyramiden. Together they have 392 residents out of a total population of 2,914, according to Statistics Norway. The Svalbard Treaty restricts military use of the archipelago, but the islands are not a demilitarised zone. Russia has frequently accused Norway of militarising the islands, which Oslo denies.

title: Are Z.ai and MiniMax heading down opposite financial paths months after Hong Kong IPOs?
description: Post-earnings results suggest an emerging divide as differing revenue growth and model capabilities may shape their market standing, analysts say.
content: When two of China’s leading AI pioneers went public in Hong Kong in January, they pitched investors on a shared promise: capturing the explosive demand for artificial intelligence at home and abroad. Their first-half earnings, however, suggest that narrative could be splintering into two different trajectories. While Beijing-based Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, is winning over market analysts on the back of surging revenue and top-tier model performance, its Shanghai rival MiniMax is facing mounting scepticism over lagging technical benchmarks and questions about its growth projections. Z.ai on Monday reported a nearly 400 per cent year-on-year surge in first-half revenue to 953.9 million yuan (US$142 million). By contrast, MiniMax’s revenue grew 283 per cent to US$116.6 million, according to its financial report released last week. The commercial gap appeared even wider when measured by annual recurring revenue (ARR), a metric used by software companies to project 12-month revenue based on current monthly subscriptions. Z.ai co-founder and chief scientist Tang Jie said during an earnings call that the company’s ARR had reached US$1.6 billion based on August’s results. MiniMax founder and CEO Yan Junjie, meanwhile, said its ARR had reached US$800 million in August – half that of Z.ai. However, Yan later acknowledged in a private post-earnings call that MiniMax had calculated the figure by taking revenue from a single week in August and multiplying it by 52, according to a person familiar with the matter. Using that same method, Z.ai’s ARR would reach US$2 billion, Tang noted. Tilly Zhang, a technology and industrial policy analyst at Gavekal Dragonomics, described MiniMax’s maths as “creative”, suggesting the company might have highlighted a traffic peak following the July 31 launch of its flagship H3 video model. Doubts about MiniMax’s outlook have also been reinforced by model performance. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, MiniMax’s latest flagship M3 model scored 45, trailing both Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 and Chinese start-up Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, which both scored 60. HSBC analysts including Ritchie Sun last week more than halved their price target for MiniMax from HK$760 (US$96.92) to HK$330, noting the company had to “invest more to stay competitive”. Also last week, JP Morgan analysts including Olivia Xu said MiniMax remained in “catch-up mode” when judged solely on model capabilities. Market sentiment, meanwhile, has warmed towards Z.ai. On Wednesday, CMB International analysts including He Saiyi raised their price target for Z.ai by 32 per cent to HK$1,985, citing an effective balance between model consistency, raw intelligence and task cost. On Tuesday, Macquarie analysts including Ellie Jiang highlighted Z.ai’s advanced capabilities and frontier positioning, although they slashed their target price by 21.5 per cent to HK$1,693, pointing to broader market volatility. HSBC analysts also cited competition as a significant risk to Z.ai, cutting its target price from HK1,500 to HK$1,375. In post-earnings trading, Z.ai shares fell 1.3 per cent in their first session since the results, closing at HK$1,099 on Thursday – 8 per cent below their pre-announcement close. MiniMax, meanwhile, rose 3.8 per cent in its first post-results session and ended Thursday at HK$354.60, gaining 17 per cent over the same period. Despite the broader divergence between the two companies, they continue to burn through substantial amounts of cash to fund model development and compute capacity. Z.ai’s research and development spending in the first half rose 33.6 per cent to 2.13 billion yuan. Its gross profit margin narrowed to 26.4 per cent from 50 per cent a year earlier, while its adjusted net loss widened 12.1 per cent to 1.96 billion yuan. MiniMax’s research and development expenses more than doubled to US$296.9 million as the firm sought to build an “independent and controllable” computing cluster partly using Chinese chips. While its gross margin improved to 17.9 per cent from 12.1 per cent, its adjusted net loss jumped 111.2 per cent to US$293 million. Beyond their rivalry, both firms face broader structural challenges. Revenue growth was constrained by “a very real compute shortage”, forcing both companies into aggressive data centre capital expenditure plans, Gavekal’s Zhang said. Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Robert Lea and Jasmine Lyu also warned recently that neither Z.ai nor MiniMax currently possessed the competitive edge or resources to compete head-to-head with Chinese tech giants like Tencent Holdings, ByteDance and Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post. Still, Alex Liu, internet and media analyst at Bank of America Global Research, noted that both firms showed “meaningful commercial scale” and differentiated themselves through “faster execution, deeper focus and stronger product iteration”.

title: 21 men, including private tutors, arrested for possessing child porn, unlawful filming
description: Hong Kong police uncover chat group with sexual images of children and upskirt photos, including some allegedly taken by tutors during class.
content: Hong Kong police have arrested 21 men on suspicion of possessing child pornography and upskirt images, including private tutors accused of surreptitiously filming their students during classes. Superintendent Wong Yick-lung of the Kowloon East regional headquarters said on Thursday that officers had uncovered a social media chat group containing child pornography, as well as upskirt images taken on public transport and in shopping centres. “The arrestees included private tutors who allegedly discreetly took intimate photos of their female students during class and then discussed them with other members online,” he said. The 21 men, aged between 19 and 47, included students, technicians, cleaners and construction workers, among other occupations. They were arrested on Monday and Tuesday and released on bail. Chief Inspector So Chi-bing of the Kowloon East regional crime unit said that among the arrested men, eight were apprehended on suspicion of possessing child pornography, while 13 were accused of unlawful filming and publishing intimate images without consent. Officers also uncovered 7,200 child pornography images and more than 120 surreptitiously filmed videos on some of the electronic devices seized during the arrests. In total, officers confiscated 24 smartphones, three tablets, 11 computers and 53 external storage drives during the operation. The chief inspector said police would continue to investigate the sources of the photos and footage, as well as whether the arrested men had been involved in other sexual offences. So warned that people who joined online groups to look at child pornography or other intimate photos taken without consent were “effectively accomplices” and risked facing criminal charges as well. “[Those] inciting and abetting others to take upskirt photos or upload photos taken without consent could be committing an aiding and abetting offence, which carries the same criminal liability as those who have taken the photos,” he added. The chief inspector also urged parents hiring private home tutors to use police background checks to ensure the applicants did not have a history of sexual offences. First launched in late 2011, the Sexual Conviction Record Check scheme allows organisations to check prospective employees, contract staff and outsourced service providers for convictions related to a specified list of sexual offences. The scope of offences covered includes voyeurism, rape, indecent assault, indecency with children under 16 and child pornography. The scheme was expanded in 2025 to cover volunteer teachers and sports coaches. Each check is valid for 36 months, during which time the employer can review the employee’s record an unlimited number of times. In June this year, authorities proposed overhauling Hong Kong’s sex crime laws to enhance protections for children and mentally incapacitated people. Under the government’s plan, sexual assault against minors under 16 and people with mental impairment will carry a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment, up from the current two years. A new range of offences has also been proposed, including making it an offence to cause children or people with mental disabilities to witness sexual acts, watch sexual imagery or send sexual images. Public consultation on the sexual offence reform concluded in August, with Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung saying more than 90 per cent of suggestions from residents supported the proposed amendments.

title: Historic Hong Kong pawn shop gets new lease on life as vibrant community space
description: One Bite Social and Lion Rock Heritage Foundation transform Chun On Pawn Shop into pop-up community and exhibition space.
content: Inside a pre-war building in the heart of Hong Kong’s busy Wan Chai, coffee, curios and Cantopop are now the fresh attractions breathing new energy into a historic pawn shop that closed its doors two years ago. As the nostalgic tunes of late Cantopop legend Leslie Cheung Kwok-wing spin on vinyl and fill the air, curious passers-by step inside to see the shop – located in the venerable tong lau or tenement building – that has been granted a new lease on life. Built in 1924, the four-storey structure became home to Chun On Pawn Shop for more than eight decades ago. After ceasing operations in 2024, the shop reopened in mid-August as a pop-up community and exhibition space. The venue now features old pawnbroking artefacts, historical photographs and workshops and community activities. At 11am on Thursday, roughly a dozen residents dropped by to explore the building, whose ground floor was traditionally covered by a large screen to protect the transactions and privacy of clients. Paula Chan, a retiree who has lived in Wan Chai for 50 years, said she was drawn by the nostalgic charm of the pawn shop while on her way to purchase groceries at the nearby wet market. “I was curious about what a pawn shop looks like and how it operates, as I rarely get to see the layout behind the counter,” Chan said, adding she found the calligraphy particularly interesting. The tenement building is one of the few pre-war buildings in Wan Chai that has retained its original structure. Terrazzo finishes can still be found on the walls. Run by One Bite Social, a non-profit that promotes the rethinking of urban spaces, the project is funded by the Lion Rock Heritage Foundation. The pawn shop switched names and ownership several times throughout the 20th century. In 1963, it was bought by the family of property developer Lo Shiu-tong, who later founded the real estate firm Yu Tai Hing. Under the current set-up, the ground and first floors offer seating for the public. While the higher floors, which operated as a storage space, are now closed, photographs display their original layout and architectural details such as the pitched roof. Amy Li Choi-ying, 24, a social worker who has lived her whole life in Wan Chai, spent 45 minutes relaxing in the space with a cup of coffee. “There are many historic buildings with unique Hong Kong characteristics that have yet to be discovered,” Li said, noting overseas countries such as Japan or the United Kingdom allocated significant resources to conserving century-old monuments. “Rather than dismantling old buildings, can the government and non-profits innovate ways to turn them into social spaces?” she said. In 2024, the pre-war tenement in Wan Chai was classified as a grade three building under the city’s three-tier system for historical buildings, meaning it has some merit but did not qualify to be considered a possible monument. Only those with grade one accreditation are considered buildings with outstanding merit that warrant every effort to preserve them. For another visitor, a 70-year-old retiree surnamed Chan, the exhibition brought back memories of the city’s post-war era, when pawnbrokers were a vital financial lifeline for struggling families. “Pawn shops, especially during that era, offered hope to residents,” Chan said. “Even HK$10 back then was a huge help, as a Chinese fried dough stick cost only 50 cents,” she said with a chuckle. Retiree Irene Lui, a 70-year-old Wong Tai Sin resident who visited the exhibition, added that seeing the authentic pawn receipts was the highlight of her visit. The pop-up community hub will remain open until December 19, mirroring the traditional four-month redemption window pawnbrokers gave clients to reclaim their items.

title: China’s rare earth cerium drug can kill gout pains once and for all: scientists
description: Nanoparticle ‘sweeper’ drug eases joint inflammation and cartilage damage from the painful form of inflammatory arthritis in rat trials.
content: One of the world’s most abundant rare earth elements could offer a comprehensive, long-lasting treatment for gout, a Chinese team has found. The extremely painful form of inflammatory arthritis has plagued humanity for millennia. “No other pain is more severe than this, not iron screws, nor cords, nor the wound of a dagger, nor burning fire” – that is how the ancient Greek physician Aretaeus described the disease in the second century AD. More than 55 million people worldwide had gout in 2020, according to US health data, with the number expected to rise by 70 per cent by 2050. The disease begins with raised uric acid levels in the blood, or hyperuricemia. Consistently high uric acid causes the formation of joint crystals that trigger severe, sudden pain attacks. If left untreated, this monosodium urate (MSU) crystal build-up can lead to joint deformities, kidney damage and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Researchers with the school of pharmaceutical sciences at Shanghai Jiao Tong University are now holding out hope, with a medication based on rare earth oxide nanoparticles that could target the cause of gout and relieve its severe pain. Animal studies showed that the drug not only lowers uric acid levels but also reduces the formation of gout crystals, alleviates inflammation, and inhibits osteoclast or bone breakdown activity, thereby addressing all painful symptoms of gouty arthritis (GA), the team said. This is a feat no existing treatment has ever achieved. The study was published online this week in the peer-reviewed journal Biomaterials, ahead of the February 2027 print issue. “It is believed that this work establishes a comprehensive multi-stage intervention strategy for GA treatment and provides insights for managing other inflammatory diseases,” corresponding author Wang Yin, an associate researcher at the university, wrote in the paper. Wang and his team developed a multifunctional “sweeper” drug, with a core structure made up of hollow nanoscale oxides of cerium – the most common rare earth element. The world’s largest rare earth mine, the Bayan Obo deposit in northern China, is a light rare earth deposit mainly composed of fluorocarbonate cerium minerals. The newly created drug consists of spherical nanoparticles, with a core or inner layer and an outer layer, and an overall diameter of around 100 nanometres. Different drug components can be added to each layer, with the nano size allowing for slow release within the body. For the core layer, the Shanghai team used uricase – an enzyme that breaks down uric acid – protected inside hollow cerium oxide nanoparticles. This protective shell allows the uricase to safely clear uric acid without being destroyed by proteases – or specialised enzymes that break down proteins. The outer layer is made of modified chondroitin sulphate, a compound designed to capture excess nitric oxide. By neutralising nitric oxide, this outer shield helps to reduce painful inflammation, the animal tests showed. Additionally, it can inhibit MSU crystal growth and provide joint lubrication. After synthesising the nanoparticles, the team confirmed their efficacy in lab cultures before testing them on rats. They established a rat model of acute gout based on the pathological onset of the disease in humans, and directly injected the drug into the joint cavity. The anti-inflammatory effect was superior to single use of uricase, chondroitin sulphate, or its modifier compound o-phenylenediamine, and comparable to direct hormone injection for emergency pain relief in gout, the team wrote. Moreover, the drug can remain in the joint cavity for up to five days, achieving a long-lasting local effect that hormone therapy cannot accomplish. Compared with a control group of untreated rats, the drug reduced crystal build-up in the kidneys but it did not completely clear it. However, joint inflammation and cartilage damage were almost fully healed, with tissue in the treated rats back to near-normal levels. This indicates that the drug can reduce inflammation and crystal formation during acute gout flares, thereby protecting bones. But the trials also indicate limitations. Because the drug is injected directly into the joint with minimal absorption into the bloodstream, it cannot effectively treat high uric acid levels throughout the body. In terms of safety, researchers reported that the nanomedicine was non-toxic to cells, safe for the blood, and caused no liver or kidney issues in the animal trials. The drug’s “unique advantages are unmatched by single-target agents” and provides a “rational basis for designing next-generation crystallisation inhibitors”, Wang wrote. “Beyond GA, this multi-target, cascading sweeper presents a versatile therapeutic strategy for other crystalline diseases … or inflammatory disorders,” he concluded.

title: Disposable fashion trend among Chinese tourists sparks waste and health concerns
description: One shop sells around 15,000 items per month, with bestselling products ranging from US$1.5 to US$7.5, comparable to a budget meal.
content: The trend of wearing disposable clothing while travelling gained popularity among Chinese internet users this summer, drawing criticism for its environmental impact. The term “disposable clothing” recently had gone viral on social media, with its hashtag accumulating 6.8 million views and 135,000 discussions on one platform. People shared their experiences of wearing disposable clothing on their trips, highlighting it as an economical choice. One individual noted that she bought five sets of clothes for her seven-day journey, spending no more than 200 yuan (US$30) in total. As the term implies, she had no intention of keeping the clothes after her travels. Most disposable garments are designed for social media appeal, including vibrant long skirts, cloaks, and outdoor jackets that are deemed unsuitable for everyday wear. A women’s apparel shop owner shared with the Chinese media outlet City Express that his store offers various clothing styles tailored to different occasions. For instance, he stocks photogenic skirts for seaside adventures in May, traditional hanfu attire for the Dragon Boat Festival, and exotic skirts for travellers heading to Xinjiang. The shop owner revealed that he sells around 15,000 items monthly, primarily to customers aged 18 to 30. His best-selling items range from 10 to 50 yuan (US$1.5 to US$7.5), comparable to the price of a budget meal. He noted that while most customers do not return, his shop consistently attracts new clientele. Some individuals dispose of the clothes upon returning from their trips, while others sell them on second-hand e-commerce platforms. Although some embrace the trend as a cost-effective option, disposable clothing has faced backlash for contributing to waste and potential health issues. “Disposable clothing is inexpensive, but it still undergoes all the stages of production, transportation, and sale. The more we discard, the more waste we generate,” commented one individual. According to the United Nations Environmental Programme, 92 million tonnes of textile waste are produced globally, with production rates doubling while the lifespan of textiles has decreased by 36 per cent from 2000 to 2015. Furthermore, only eight per cent of textile fibres were sourced from recycled materials in 2023, and clothing and textiles account for 11 per cent of plastic waste. These inexpensive disposable garments are often made of plastic, exacerbating the waste problem. Additionally, disposable clothing made from low-quality materials poses health risks. Cai Shangwei, professor and director of the Cultural Industry Research Centre at Sichuan University, informed Vista that disposable clothing sold on second-hand platforms may also have hygiene concerns. “It’s all about photogenicity. Disposable clothing exists solely for photos. Why can’t people simply enjoy the scenery on their journeys?” criticised one online observer. “The world is a vast photo studio,” commented another.

title: As hordes head to Shenzhen, Hong Kong bars, restaurants sign up for more floor space
description: More food and beverage outlets ‘incorporating unique experiential elements into the dining journey’, says CBRE’s Lawrence Wan.
content: Hong Kong’s food and beverage (F&B) operators, both new and existing players, signed leases for 155,000 sq ft of new floor space in the second quarter of this year, a record high for the sector and more than double the amount registered in the first quarter, according to property consultancy CBRE. In the first half of the year, they snapped up 230,000 sq ft of new space, CBRE data showed. However, analysts said the city’s selective and narrow-based retailing recovery was forcing brands and retailers to be more creative and adopt novel tactics to keep attracting consumers, with that trend particularly evident in the F&B sector. “Our frontline observations suggest that an increasing number of F&B operators are enhancing their offerings by incorporating unique experiential elements into the dining journey,” said Lawrence Wan, executive director and head of retail leasing at CBRE Hong Kong. “Examples include restaurants featuring live music performances, Korean restaurants employing native Korean-speaking staff to create a more authentic atmosphere, Japanese eateries engaging diners through traditional drinking games with chefs, and venues showcasing carefully curated vintage furniture sourced from Europe.” The trend reflected a shift in consumer preferences, he said, with food viewed as just part of the total dining experience. Another property consultancy, JLL, said restaurants that had employed innovative offerings included Le Petit Chef and The Magic Table at Grand Hyatt Hong Kong, where immersive technology was used to turn the dining table into part of the entertainment experience. It said Dans le Noir? at Le Meridien Hong Kong offered meals served in complete darkness, encouraging diners to rely on taste, smell and touch rather than sight. Meanwhile, concepts such as Jing and 7 Paintings combined multi-course menus with immersive visual presentations, art, history and interactive elements, creating a narrative-led dining experience that went beyond the food itself. Others, such as the Magistracy Dining Room, located in a restored heritage building, and The Grand Buffet, Hong Kong’s only revolving restaurant, used their unique settings as a key element of the dining experience, JLL said. Competition has intensified, not only within Hong Kong but also from Shenzhen’s rapidly evolving dining and entertainment scene Michelle Chiu, JLL Sofa Bar Livehouse, a live music salon operator from Chengdu, the capital of southwestern China’s Sichuan province, secured about 3,100 sq ft of street-front retail space at The Centrium in Central last month for its inaugural Hong Kong venue, CBRE said, with the new location expected to open by the end of this month. “Sofa Bar represents a new emerging model of a lifestyle-driven, lounge-centric concept,” said Daniel Yip, director for retail leasing at CBRE Hong Kong. “Rather than relying on high-turnover seating or rigid dining layouts, these spaces blur the line between a boutique showroom, a social hub, and a classic lounge.” The use of unique concepts to lure diners was increasing amid a challenging retail environment, analysts said. Savills, another property consultancy, citing separate market estimates, said Hong Kong residents’ total outbound spending was estimated to have reached HK$50 billion (US$6.37 billion) last year, representing about 9 per cent of the city’s total consumption. Additionally, about 8 million sq ft of new retail space was expected to be completed between last year and 2029, it said, which was likely to weigh on retail rents. “Competition has intensified, not only within Hong Kong but also from Shenzhen’s rapidly evolving dining and entertainment scene,” said Michelle Chiu, director of retail at JLL. “As a result, many operators, particularly in the premium segment, are investing in experiential dining concepts such as projection-mapped shows, immersive storytelling and sensory-led experiences to attract customers and create destination appeal.” However, while Hongkongers were eager to try new concepts, Chiu said experiential dining did not guarantee long-term success. “Diners may come for the novelty, but they return for consistently good food, service and value,” she said.

title: US looks to warship designs from Japan, South Korea and Turkey, reports say
description: It comes after Trump signed a memorandum calling for foreign shipbuilding capacity and investment as US industry struggles to meet demand.
content: Washington is considering using Japanese, South Korean or Turkish frigate designs to expand the country’s naval fleet as the American shipbuilding industry struggles to meet demand, according to US media reports. The move comes after President Donald Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum on August 13 calling for the use of foreign shipbuilding capacity and investment. However, the plan is likely to face strong opposition in Congress. Potential contenders for the US Navy’s new guided-missile frigate include Japan’s Mogami-class, South Korea’s Chungnam-class and Turkey’s Istanbul-class, USNI News reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter. “The president has directed the navy to aggressively increase domestic shipbuilding capacity, including leveraging the proven shipbuilding skills and industrial expertise of our allies,” US Navy spokesman Ron Flanders was quoted as saying. According to the report, the cooperation could follow the “Finland model”. That would see foreign shipbuilders constructing the first two hulls and investing in US facilities, workforce, technologies and supply chains before production is transferred to American shipyards. If it goes ahead, it would be the first time the US has bought a major surface combatant from a foreign partner since World War II. US law requires major navy and coastguard vessels to be built in domestic shipyards, unless the president grants a national security waiver. The navy can still acquire foreign-built auxiliary or sealift ships. In the August White House memorandum, Trump invoked the waiver, determining that it was “in the national security interest” to allow foreign suppliers to participate under the “Finland model”. The model was first used in the coastguard’s medium icebreaker programme, under which Finnish shipyards built initial hulls based on Canadian designs and then transitioned construction to a US shipyard. The memorandum said a lack of capacity and competition in domestic shipbuilding had resulted in large backlogs for navy orders. It also said an “atrophied shipbuilding industrial base, coupled with diminished adjacent supplier bases, has expanded delays and increased costs”. The Trump administration has been pushing to expand overseas shipbuilding, with several senior officials openly discussing the possibility of outsourcing warship construction abroad. The Pentagon included US$1.85 billion in its 2027 budget for a feasibility study examining the potential outsourcing of warship design and construction to South Korea and Japan. The Istanbul-class guided-missile frigate is also being considered after a meeting between Trump and Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan during the Nato summit in Ankara in July, according to USNI News. But lawmakers representing states with major shipbuilding industries are seeking to curb the White House’s efforts to buy foreign-built warships. The 5,500-tonne Mogami-class frigate by Japan’s Mitsubishi Heavy Industries has a stealth hull with a high degree of automation. Australia has ordered 11 of this class for A$20 billion (US$14.3 billion) – the first three to be built in Japan and the remaining eight in Australia. The 4,300-tonne Chungnam-class is South Korea’s latest frigate built by Hyundai Heavy Industries, SK Oceanplant and Hanwha Ocean. In the past few years, many US Navy officials have visited these shipyards. Hanwha Ocean bought the Philly Shipyard in Philadelphia in December 2024 and pledged a US$5 billion investment to upgrade and revive the facility. The US Navy has previously looked to foreign design and investment, most recently in the Constellation-class frigate programme. The frigate was originally based on an Italian design, with Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri investing in a US shipyard to build the vessels domestically. But it was cancelled following extensive design modifications, labour shortages, major cost overruns and delays. Work will continue on only two hulls already under construction, but the first ship will not be delivered until 2029. It was due for delivery this year.

title: ‘Nepal is not closed’: tour operators battle flood fallout, urge visitors to return
description: As the death toll mounts, travel bosses and guides work round the clock to reassure anxious tourists and salvage the peak autumn season.
content: Rajendra Lama’s phone has barely stopped buzzing. In between coordinating rescue operations for flood survivors with the Nepal Mountaineering Association and running his travel company, he spends his days communicating with anxious tour groups, trying to persuade them not to cancel their trips. “We have a crisis in one part of the country, but we’re open elsewhere and are not affected by the floods,” said Lama, a tourism entrepreneur with over 20 years of experience. “I’m just trying to communicate that to my clients.” Catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border on August 26 grabbed global headlines, as tsunami-like waves – a mix of water, sediment and boulders – raced down from the Himalayas, submerging villages more than 100km (62 miles) downstream across northern and central Nepal. Over 1,200 people have died, with more than 4,000 still missing – among them some 600 tourists, many of whom were pilgrims bound for Mount Kailash, a site in the Tibet autonomous region revered by Hindus and Buddhists. Terrifying social media footage has alarmed visitors planning trips during Nepal’s peak September-October travel season, when post-monsoon skies offer unobstructed mountain views. But tourism operators stress that most of the country, including the popular Everest and Annapurna regions, remains safe and unaffected. Bharat Jung Pandey, president of the Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents, said the crisis had caused disruption, but mass cancellations had not yet occurred. By contrast, during last September’s youth uprising, tourist arrivals plunged to roughly 79,000 – down from the typical monthly average of 90,000. Tourism is a crucial pillar of Nepal’s economy, contributing 6.6 per cent to gross domestic product and supporting more than 1 million jobs in 2023, according to the World Travel and Tourism Council. Yet the sector has endured multiple shocks, from Covid-19 disruptions to the Iran war. North America and European arrivals fell by nearly 25 per cent and 19 per cent, respectively, at the start of the spring travel season in March, though an influx of Asian visitors offset much of those losses, limiting the overall decline to just 1 per cent. Juliana Shrestha, co-founder and head of business development at Duluwa Outdoors, said recent flooding had affected bookings, prompting her company to divert itineraries. “Most places are still operational,” she said. “We haven’t had any cancellations but definitely there are safety concerns from people flying in soon. As tourism entrepreneurs, our first response is always to communicate the real scenario, and we’re doing that now.” Tourism associations and high-level government officials have stepped up outreach. Last Thursday, a day after the disaster, the Trekking Agencies’ Association of Nepal published safety statuses for major trails, recommending detours around affected areas. Two days later, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal urged visitors to “support the country’s key economic pillar”. On Tuesday, Tourism Minister Khadak Raj Paudel appealed directly to travellers, saying that “Nepal is not closed” and remained ready to welcome guests. Even so, some experts argue the response from the Nepal Tourism Board, the country’s national tourism organisation, was delayed. “For a country that has faced multiple crises, we were late in communicating that Nepal is largely safe,” said Nisha Onta, founder and executive director of the Kathmandu-based Governance Lab think tank. “We have to communicate promptly in a factual manner, without being too rosy, while also saying Nepal is open and safe to visit.” In response, industry experts and entrepreneurs have worked with the Nepal Tourism Board to build upon the Nepalnow.travel platform, overhauled earlier this year, to provide updated safety information and show the nation is actively responding to the crisis and remains open for business. “When people spend so much money to come here, the minimum they expect is a safe and secure trip,” Onta said. “So we have to assure them how we would respond in case there’s a natural disaster, our rescue plan and preparedness.” As Nepal prepares to revise legislation governing its tourism and mountaineering sectors, analysts say lawmakers must integrate climate-driven policies to address disaster response and overtourism – safeguarding the environment, local mountain communities and visitors alike. Shrestha said he was hopeful that Nepal’s reputation as a “loved and valued destination” would help with a swift recovery, noting that annual arrivals had exceeded 1 million since 2023 following past setbacks, from earthquakes to the pandemic. But analysts warn that increasingly frequent natural disasters pose an existential threat over the long term, calling the recent catastrophe a wake-up call to improve climate governance. “This is an existential crisis,” Onta said. “What if we don’t have the roads, security and safety? What will we show to people who come to see our mountains if we don’t protect them? It’s very critical for our industry to deeply reflect and come up with action plans.”

title: Russia’s equestrian federation latest to be allowed back into international sporting fold
description: Move follows International Olympic Committee’s decision to ⁠lift suspension of Russian Olympic Committee, with several sports following.
content: Russia’s equestrian federation has said the sport’s ⁠global governing body (FEI) ⁠would lift its ban on ⁠Russian athletes and officials from October 5 and allow international events to be held in the country again. Russian and Belarusian athletes have been barred from representing their countries under their national flags ‌at FEI events since March 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, though some have competed as neutral athletes. The FEI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside normal business hours in Switzerland. The move follows the International Olympic Committee’s decision in July to provisionally ⁠lift its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC). The Russian equestrian federation said on Wednesday the ‌FEI Council had approved the move after what it described as extensive negotiations between the national body and international officials. Russia ‌will also be permitted to host FEI-sanctioned competitions from October 5, ⁠subject to compliance ⁠with FEI regulations, it added. The IOC banned the ROC in 2023 after the national body ‌took over sports groups in occupied areas of Ukraine following Moscow’s invasion of the country. The International Basketball ‌Federation lifted ‌restrictions on individual Russian and Belarusian players, coaches and officials on ‌Tuesday, while leaving any decision on the return of national teams and clubs ⁠to international competition to its central board in December. The International Ski and Snowboard ⁠Federation said on Wednesday that Russian and Belarusian athletes would be eligible to compete during the 2026-27 season if they signed a ‌neutrality declaration and met ‌anti-doping requirements. Participation will remain limited to individual events, with no national flags, anthems or uniforms permitted. Other international federations, including aquatics, motorsport, modern pentathlon, wrestling and gymnastics, have also eased restrictions on Russian and Belarusian athletes.

title: Meet Colombian singer Maluma’s girlfriend, Susana Gómez, who’s expecting their 2nd child
description: The Medellin-born architect, interior designer and jewellery company founder was the likely inspiration behind the reggaeton star’s hit single, ‘Junio’.
content: Colombian superstar Maluma recently collaborated with Hot Wheels to create a custom car for its Challenge Accepted campaign. The partnership is personally significant for the “Felices Los 4” singer, who told People that the model car brand has been “part of [his] whole life” and ignited his love for cars. His contribution to the 2026 Global Legends Collection is a Toyota Land Cruiser, reflecting his family-man instincts. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Hot Wheels (@hotwheelsofficial) “It’s a car that is made to put your whole family in it. My priority right now is my family and getting to the right places in a very safe way,” the 32-year-old, who is expecting his second child, a son, with girlfriend Susana Gómez, explained to People. The rapper further shared that his firstborn, daughter Paris, is “so in love with Hot Wheels”, and the soon-to-be father of two is hoping his son will be too. “I can’t wait for my baby boy to be here with us and do the same activities that I like doing with Paris,” he said. So, who is Susana Gómez, who may have inspired Maluma’s song “Junio”? She’s a Colombian creative Susana Gómez was born on November 11, 1992 and hails from Medellín, Colombia, which is also where Maluma was born. According to People, the 33-year-old is an architect and interior designer in her home country. In 2023, she and her sister, Juliana Gómez, founded a jewellery company called Sileo Timeless. The siblings are described as the creators and designers of the brand, per its website, and its pieces are made by artisans in Colombia using gold, diamonds and other precious stones, per People. How did she meet Maluma? According to HOLA, Gómez had been in Maluma’s orbit long before they started dating. Not only did they have mutual friends, but she is also close to his mother, Marlli Arias, sister, Manuela Londoño, and aunt, Yudi Arias. “So many years looking for love elsewhere and I didn’t realise it was next to me,” the rapper declared during a concert, right before announcing that Gómez was expecting their first child through the music video for “Procura”. They welcomed daughter Paris Londoño Gómez in March 2024. Are Maluma and Susana Gómez engaged? The couple was first linked in 2020, and the rapper supposedly hard-launched their relationship on Instagram in December 2021 with a blurry photo of him kissing a woman in front of a Christmas tree. While the post has now been deleted, the lucky lady was assumed to be Gómez. In 2023, during Maluma’s 29th birthday celebrations, he playfully pretended to pop the question, but according to reports, the couple is not yet engaged. Gómez has been married and divorced before, per HOLA.

title: About 4 in 5 young, affluent investors in mainland China turn to offshore assets: study
description: Affluent investors are using exposure to the assets for returns and to manage risk.
content: Young Chinese investors are increasingly turning to offshore assets for wealth preservation and diversification, with more than four-fifths of those surveyed reporting some exposure outside mainland China, a recent study by the CFA Institute showed. About 81 per cent of young Chinese investors surveyed had offshore investments, with such assets accounting for an average 43 per cent of their portfolios, according to the report. The study, conducted in December by the CFA Institute – which trains financial professionals – surveyed 300 young, affluent investors in mainland China between the ages of 18 and 44. The findings suggest offshore diversification has moved beyond a niche preference among wealthy Chinese investors, despite the country’s monetary policies, according to the report. “Despite capital controls, exposure to offshore assets is already mainstream among young, affluent investors, driven primarily by the need for asset preservation and international diversification,” researchers said in the report. Investors with international experience – studying, working or engaging in business outside mainland China – had the highest level of offshore exposure, with 93 per cent holding offshore assets and allocating an average 45 per cent of their portfolios to such investments. Investors in tier-one cities allocated an average 45 per cent of their portfolios offshore, compared with 40 per cent among those in other cities, the report showed. Wealth preservation was the most common reason for investing offshore, cited by 55 per cent of respondents, followed by portfolio diversification at 54 per cent and global economic and industry trends at 50 per cent, according to the institute. Other motivations included access to types of investments unavailable domestically, cited by 44 per cent, and hedging against domestic market or currency risks, cited by 41 per cent. The findings indicated that offshore investing was being used not only to seek returns, but also as a form of risk management. The trend means wealth managers and advisers would need to develop cross-border capabilities that integrate investors’ onshore and offshore assets into a coherent portfolio, taking into account risk, liquidity and currency considerations, said the CFA Institute.

title: For India, Bangladesh’s talk of joining ‘Islamic Nato’ raises red flags
description: Joining the Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani security alliance offers Dhaka leverage, but could also threaten its non-aligned stance.
content: Bangladesh’s potential entry into a defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan could give Dhaka fresh leverage in its dealings with India, but observers warn the move risks fracturing its long-standing strategic neutrality and alarming a hawkish New Delhi. Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament on August 27 that Bangladesh was considering joining the Mecca pact, a security framework signed last month. Earlier reports citing unnamed sources said the invitation originated from Riyadh. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humayun Kabir also told reporters: “If there is a security arrangement among Islamic nations in the Middle East, it is not unusual for us to consider participating. It is being viewed positively.” Under the agreement signed on August 7 in Mecca, an armed attack against any signatory is treated as an attack against all members – earning the arrangement the informal moniker “Islamic Nato.” Shafi Md. Mostofa, an associate professor at the University of Dhaka, said that joining the pact would compel India to be “much more cautious and respectful while dealing with [Dhaka].” Bilateral relations have frayed in recent months amid the continued exile of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina in India, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s delayed visit to Delhi and ongoing border and migration disputes. But Shafi cautioned that formal membership would severely test Bangladesh’s traditional diplomatic balancing act. “A formal collective-defence commitment would be qualitatively different from Bangladesh’s existing issue-based defence partnerships,” he said, referring to current defence ties centred on practical cooperation such as technology transfers and training rather than formal alliances. He added that Delhi would be deeply concerned given the prominent role played by its arch-rival Pakistan. “Joining would inevitably reduce some of the ambiguity that has traditionally allowed Bangladesh to maintain productive relations simultaneously with competing powers,” Shafi said, particularly amid the current Middle East instability involving Israel, Iran and the United States, alongside the ongoing wars in Gaza and Lebanon. Elizabeth Roche, an associate professor of practice at the O.P. Jindal Global University’s Jindal School of International Affairs, said joining a Middle Eastern security bloc could give Bangladesh significant “leverage”. “[Dhaka] can be seen as part of a perceived group of influential nations,” Roche said, adding that Bangladesh’s large Middle East diaspora is a critical economic factor. Around 5 million Bangladeshi citizens live and work in the six Arab monarchies that make up the Gulf Cooperation Council, including 2.64 million in Saudi Arabia alone. Roche added that an anxious India had been closely watching Bangladesh’s post-August 2024 rapprochement with Pakistan. Since Hasina’s ousting, Dhaka has revived high-level diplomatic engagements, eased trade restrictions and resumed direct maritime links with Islamabad for the first time since 1971. Sohini Bose, an associate fellow at Observer Research Foundation think tank, said joining the bloc aligned with the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s (BNP) historic tendency to emphasise Islamic solidarity. “In the current context, it will allow the country to break free of its traditional geopolitical associations with India, China or the US and forge an alternate identity,” Bose said. But she questioned whether Bangladesh – still recovering from severe domestic economic strain, high inflation and slumps in exports and investment – could realistically honour mutual defence obligations. “A practical revisit of its domestic capabilities and development aspirations is necessary before any commitments are made,” Bose said, warning that closer military ties could draw Pakistan nearer to India’s eastern border and the Bay of Bengal – a region Delhi views as its “primary area of interest”. Syed Munir Khasru, chairman of the international think tank IPAG Asia-Pacific, said that regional volatility and oil trade disruptions near the Strait of Hormuz highlighted Bangladesh’s need for stronger security arrangements. “As the world’s third-largest Muslim-majority country by population, Bangladesh joining such an arrangement would give the grouping greater geopolitical and strategic weight,” Khasru said. While Saudi Arabia is central to Bangladesh’s remittance economy, Turkey has become a key defence provider, supplying military hardware and training. He added that as the UN’s second-largest troop contributor, Bangladesh would bring institutional expertise to the pact rather than acting merely as a recipient of aid. Still, Khasru said that Dhaka must balance strategic opportunity against exposure to foreign rivalries. “The objective should be to gain additional strategic options without creating new vulnerabilities or turning Bangladesh into a party to rivalries that do not directly serve its national interest,” he said.

title: South Korean police seek tycoon behind K-pop supergroup BTS to be indicted
description: Bang Si-hyuk is being investigated for alleged investor fraud over the initial public offering of the agency Hybe.
content: South Korean police are pushing for an indictment of music tycoon Bang Si-hyuk, the chairman of the agency behind K-pop supergroup BTS, over alleged investor fraud. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency referred Bang to the Seoul Southern District Prosecutors’ Office on Thursday, asking him to be indicted on a charge of violating the Capital Markets Act, according to the police agency and the prosecutor’s office. Police have been investigating Bang, the billionaire founder and chairman of Hybe, over allegations that he misled investors in 2019 by indicating that Hybe had no immediate plans to go public, prompting them to sell their shares to a private equity fund shortly before the company proceeded with an initial public offering. Police earlier said that the fund might have paid Bang around 200 billion won (US$147 million) in a side deal that promised him 30 per cent of post-IPO stock sale profits. South Korean media reported that police referred four other people, including Hybe executives and private equity fund officials, to prosecutors on Thursday as well, asking for their indictment. Hybe officials have said Bang denies any wrongdoing. “We have consistently responded to the allegations with objective evidence and facts,” Bang’s legal team said in a statement on Thursday. “We expect the allegations to be fully and transparently resolved through the legal process.” Police earlier sought Bang’s arrest twice in April and May. But prosecutors rejected those requests, saying police failed to provide sufficient grounds for his arrest and failed to comply with prosecutors’ demand for further investigation of Bang. Observers say prosecutors could again ask for further police investigation, rather than indicting Bang immediately. News of Bang’s legal troubles flared after BTS returned and launched a much-awaited world tour earlier this year after a nearly four-year musical hiatus due to the band members’ mandatory military service in South Korea.

title: Disgraced lawmaker William Wong to face 4 charges, including dangerous driving
description: Wong, who allegedly drove while drunk and crashed his car into two parked vehicles at the CUHK campus in July, will appear in court next Wednesday.
content: Former Hong Kong lawmaker William Wong Kam-fai, who allegedly drove and crashed his vehicle while in an intoxicated state two months ago, will appear in court next week to face four criminal charges, including dangerous driving. Police on Thursday confirmed that Wong was set to appear in Sha Tin Court next Wednesday morning to face four charges: driving under the influence of alcohol, dangerous driving, failing to stop after an accident and failing to report an accident. The 66-year-old politician was arrested in July after crashing his car into two parked vehicles at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) campus. Wong allegedly drove away from the scene and later parked elsewhere, outside a staff residence. A security guard reported the incident to police. The disgraced lawmaker was released on bail and reported to police in late July. Following his arrest, Wong apologised for “causing inconvenience” to the Legislative Council and becoming the first lawmaker of the current term to resign. He was also suspended from duty at the university, where he was an associate dean of its engineering faculty. Wong is also a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), the country’s top political advisory body. In Hong Kong, dangerous driving is punishable by up to three years’ imprisonment.

title: Dutch advisory council urges EU to seek China deal – but brace for backlash
description: To correct growing economic imbalances, policymakers advise taking stronger defensive measures, despite risk of rising domestic costs.
content: The Netherlands and the EU should press for a trade deal with China to address imbalances, but must be ready to consider measures that could invite retaliation – and bear the associated costs – according to members of a council that advises the Dutch government. The recommendation marks a significant shift in mindset for one of the European Union’s most committed free-trade nations as the next round of China-EU trade talks in October approaches. Both sides traded fire again this week, with EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic urging Beijing on Wednesday to deliver concrete results by October or face “harsher measures”, and China’s Ministry of Commerce hitting back on Thursday by urging Brussels to stop “threatening market closure at every turn”. “It would be quite important to get an agreement with China that will be beneficial for both,” Ab Klink, a member of the Netherlands Scientific Council for Government Policy and a former health minister, told the South China Morning Post on Monday. “On the other hand, if it’s impossible to reach an agreement, then you have to think as the European Union about the next options.” Klink chaired the project group behind a report that the council presented to the Dutch government on Thursday. Focusing on “rebalancing trade” and “boosting innovation”, the report urged the Netherlands to reduce its economic dependencies in an era of increasing geopoliticisation. The Netherlands is no stranger to such actions. The report’s introduction highlights Washington’s successful pressure on The Hague to restrict tech giant ASML from exporting advanced chipmaking machines to China in 2019, then expanding that ban in 2023. Additionally, the ongoing saga surrounding Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and its Chinese owner, Wingtech, has unleashed chaos across the European automotive supply chain. The report acknowledged that acting would carry its own costs. Government support would be needed, trading partners might retaliate, and prices could rise – drawbacks that the scientific council said had discouraged the EU and member states from employing such robust responses. But the report urged policymakers to weigh these costs against the potential damage of geoeconomic coercion, trade shocks and long-term economic costs, and to “seriously consider” all policy options, even if they prove painful. The Netherlands was not trying to strike first against China, and an agreement would be greatly preferable to a trade conflict, Klink said. However, he noted that the Netherlands and Europe must develop a similar policy capacity to China for a worst-case scenario. This “strategic symmetry” – where Europe would pursue the same policy towards China that China pursues towards Europe – is one of three potential approaches presented by the council to address the trade imbalance with China. International coordination could be another option, as the report said it was preferred by economists and proposed by the IMF, where countries with excessive surpluses or deficits work cooperatively on macroeconomic adjustments. French President Emmanuel Macron has been advocating for similar coordination between Europe, China and the United States, but so far with little visible success. The report also rated it unlikely, noting that it would go against China’s national strategy while no international body could enforce the changes. Stronger trade defence measures are the third path presented by the report, as it deemed the EU’s current instruments – designed for product-by-product review – inadequate for what the report called economy-wide market distortions. We are cognisant of the legitimate concerns that China has here, and what we hope is that China sees the same thing in the situation with Europe Haroon Sheikh, Netherlands Scientific Council for Government Policy “The goal for us is still open, free trade. It’s not about closing our markets, but about making sure there is this level playing field,” said Haroon Sheikh, a research fellow with the council and member of the report’s project group. “We are cognisant of the legitimate concerns that China has here, and what we hope is that China sees the same thing in the situation with Europe,” he said, noting that China should understand the EU’s legitimate concerns about China’s “artificial advantage” that could lead to the deindustrialisation or the destruction of European industries. As an independent advisory body, the scientific council provides only analysis and does not make decisions. The more challenging part, some analysts said, would be implementation. “It’s easy to agree on the idea that action is needed – the sooner the better, the more the better – but the Netherlands trying to use its choke point … that is the difficult one,” said Frans-Paul van der Putten, founder of Dutch consulting firm ChinaGeopolitics. The fact that China was catching up in the semiconductor sector, where the Netherlands has held a commanding lead, was another source of concern, according to van der Putten. Media reports that China had begun manufacturing home-grown immersion deep-ultraviolet lithography machines sent ASML stocks falling in July. While analysts said China’s progress remained modest, further restrictions were seen as likely to accelerate Beijing’s domestic push to build its own semiconductor industry.

title: 75.8% of flat owners at block unscathed by Tai Po fire agree to sell to authorities
description: Housing Bureau says 188 households at Wang Chi House have signed sale and purchase agreements as part of buy-back scheme.
content: More than 75 per cent of homeowners at the only block spared the worst of last November’s deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court have agreed to sell their flats to the Hong Kong government, with authorities to press ahead with acquisition procedures. The Housing Bureau said on Thursday that 75.8 per cent of the flats at the estate’s Wang Chi House, or 188 households, had signed sales and purchase agreements as of Wednesday. “[The] government confirmed that it will continue to take forward the acquisition work of Wang Chi House and sign assignments with its owners progressively to complete the relevant procedures on title acquisition,” a spokesman said. In the aftermath of the fire, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 others, authorities announced a plan to buy back flats in the eight-block subsidised housing estate in Tai Po. Under the scheme, the government is acquiring flats at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the owners have paid their land premiums. Participants can use the cash compensation to buy a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to purchase new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement. Buy-back offers were initially sent to the owners of flats in the other seven blocks, before the scheme was extended to Wang Chi House. Authorities previously said they reserved the right to cancel the acquisition plan if fewer than 75 per cent of the owners at Wang Chi House agreed to sell their homes by October 15. The bureau said that 99.3 per cent of owners of flats across all eight blocks, or 1,971 households, had confirmed their intention to sell via acceptance letters before the scheme wrapped up on Monday. It added that 1,595 owners had already signed sales and purchase agreements with the government as of Wednesday. Authorities said they would swiftly follow up on acquiring the remaining estate properties.
