The South China Morning Post earlier spoke to six residents determined not to sell, several of whom maintained that no financial package could compensate for the loss of their long-time homes and communal ties.

title: Louis Koo, his production house sued for HK$149 million over failed loan repayment
description: Sino Hero Ventures accuses Hong Kong film star and his company, One Cool Film Production, of failing to repay HK$70 million borrowed in 2019.
content: Hong Kong film actor and director Louis Koo Tin-lok and his production company have been sued for more than HK$149 million (US$19 million) for allegedly failing to repay a loan from an offshore firm seven years ago. The latest lawsuit compounded the legal troubles of the 55-year-old artist, who was sued by a business partner two years ago for allegedly defaulting on the repayment of a HK$8.3 million loan related to a fashion joint venture. Sino Hero Ventures, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, a reputed tax haven, initiated civil proceedings in the High Court on Wednesday accusing Koo and One Cool Film Production of failing to repay a HK$70 million loan the plaintiff extended on September 6, 2019. Koo played a leading role in the 2024 blockbuster martial arts film, Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In, which has rekindled public interest in the Kowloon Walled City. According to the writ, seen by the South China Morning Post on Thursday, the interest under the terms of the loan accrued at a monthly rate of 1 per cent, or 12 per cent per annum, and rose to 1.5 per cent per month, or 18 per cent per annually, in the event of a default in repayment. The due date of repayment had been extended twice until the end of 2022, but the defendants had only repaid HK$13.9 million since January that year, the writ said. The plaintiff assessed the total outstanding amount as HK$149.4 million as of August 27, adding that default interest would continue to accumulate until full payment or the court’s final determination of the case. Koo, one of Hong Kong’s most recognisable home-grown film icons, has appeared in more than 110 local productions after rising to fame as a television star in the late 1990s. He won best actor trophies in both the Hong Kong Film Awards and Asian Film Awards in 2018 for his performance in the action thriller Paradox. He was also recognised abroad last year, winning the Extraordinary Star Asia Award at the New York Asian Film Festival.

title: Macroscope | Asia is not on the edge of a new 1997-style financial crisis
description: While risks to Asia’s financial stability exist, they have nothing to do with the policy and structural weaknesses behind the 1997 crisis.
content: Doom-mongering pervades financial markets, especially these days when there are mounting concerns about a rise in interest rates and an artificial intelligence-fuelled bubble in stock markets. The alarmism invariably stems from attempts by commentators and analysts to connect the dots, many of which are unlikeable or misperceived. Nowhere is this more apparent than in Asia. Nearly 30 years after the Thai baht lost its peg to the US dollar, causing widespread contagion across the region that morphed into a full-blown systemic crisis, comparisons are being drawn between today’s vulnerabilities and the ones that brought about the 1997 Asian financial crisis. In a report on August 31 titled “Nope, it’s not 1997”, HSBC said that while the differences between the current threats facing the region and those in the run-up to the crisis “outweigh the similarities”, there are some parallels. The bank pointed to the sharp rise in US Treasury yields, the collapse in the Japanese yen and excessive optimism in the technology sector. While all three of these risks pose a threat to financial stability, they have nothing to do with the policy-related and structural weaknesses that were at the root of the 1997 crisis. Not only are there no parallels, the main victims of the crash – Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and South Korea – have rid themselves of the financial and regulatory deficiencies that amplified the shock soon after the crisis erupted. Rigid currency pegs were jettisoned, monetary policy was tightened sharply, concerted action was taken to stem capital outflows and reforms to address severe weaknesses in the corporate and financial sectors were implemented. Malaysia even imposed capital controls for a short period. According to the International Monetary Fund, which provided financial support for the most vulnerable countries in exchange for the enactment of tough reforms, “strategies adopted proved successful in restoring financial market confidence and stability, and in achieving a resumption of economic growth, in most cases by late 1998.” Current account balances improved dramatically, especially in Thailand, while domestic capital markets became more liquid and transparent, allowing countries to borrow in their own currencies. Banking systems have been well-capitalised for many years, underpinned by effective macroprudential regulations. While there are some 1997-type vulnerabilities in a few countries – particularly Indonesia, which suffers from poor governance – these are idiosyncratic as opposed to systemic. The financial and economic threats facing Asia today are global ones. Bond markets are in turmoil everywhere. The combination of a renewed spike in energy prices amid the resumption of hostilities between the United States and Iran, the surge in debt issuance by leading tech firms and concerns about rising fiscal deficits is driving up yields on long-dated bonds. Japan is at the centre of the sell-off. On September 1, its 10-year government bond yield hit 3 per cent for the first time since 1996. The Bank of Japan (BOJ) is under intense pressure to raise interest rates more aggressively to help prop up the yen even though domestic demand is weak. Expectations for borrowing costs have shifted sharply, with markets currently pricing in a one percentage point rise in interest rates to 2 per cent by next July. As JPMorgan noted in a report on September 1, “an acceleration in BOJ rate hikes could trigger a major correction in Japanese equities, which in turn could lead to an unwinding of [short positions in the yen].” A sharp sell-off in Japanese stocks, on top of the pressure on the country’s bonds, could deliver a shock to global markets. However, many Asian central banks have been ahead of the curve. As the US Federal Reserve dithers over whether to raise interest rates this month even though the US is close to full employment and inflation remains stuck above target, Indonesia, South Korea and the Philippines have already tightened their monetary policy. India is likely to be the next major economy in the region to lift interest rates. Although inflationary pressures stemming from the energy supply shock and the AI boom have forced the hand of Asian policymakers, central banks’ hard-earned inflation-fighting credibility has helped underpin Asia’s resilience to successive shocks. In fact, one might ask whether the lessons of the 1997 crisis were learned too well. The lingering fear of destabilising capital outflows, which amplified the impact of the crisis, helped dissuade some Asian countries from liberalising their financial markets more aggressively to attract more foreign investment. A good example is South Korea. In June, index provider MSCI said it would continue to classify the country’s equity market as an emerging market, partly because of regulators’ reluctance to make the won fully tradeable abroad. In India, meanwhile, the share of domestic government bonds owned by foreigners stands at just 4.1 per cent, slightly lower than in China, according to JPMorgan data. The fact that the ghost of the crisis still haunts parts of Asia is reassuring. While the region is still vulnerable to global shocks, a 1997-type meltdown is not on the cards.

title: Remembering Lau Siu-ming, pioneering Hong Kong dancer and revered actor
description: From wartime refugee to classically trained dancer to on-screen villain, Ming Sir’s artistry and mentorship have shaped generations of actors.
content: Lau Siu-ming, the veteran Hong Kong actor who played some of the most unforgettable villains in Chinese-language film history, has died at the age of 94. His story – from war refugee to classically trained dancer, and from stage to silver screen – is all the more remarkable because his career was built not on youthful leading-man looks but on artistry, physical precision and a mentoring spirit that shaped generations of actors who followed. Lau’s artistic journey is one of reinvention, shaped by a childhood that might have broken a lesser spirit. Born in Hong Kong in 1931, Lau was 10 when Japanese forces invaded and occupied the colony, and spent his teenage years as a refugee on the mainland. He eventually made his way back to the city, where a performance by a Chinese arts troupe at the newly opened Hong Kong City Hall in 1962 left him spellbound. A journey to Europe and back Determined to study dance in France, he took a job working in the cargo hold of an ocean liner to pay his way to Europe. His talent and perseverance earned him a scholarship to the Ecole Superieure de Danse de Cannes Rosella Hightower in France in the early 1960s. Hightower, the legendary American dancer and school founder, recognised his unique story and encouraged him to incorporate his Chinese heritage into his ballet work. His graduation duet with Hightower, Rebirth of the Phoenix, was staged at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees in Paris, to widespread acclaim and caught the attention of French dancer, choreographer and opera director Maurice Bejart. Lau went on to become the first Chinese choreographer to work for a French dance company. Lau later performed and choreographed for the Brussels Ballet du XXe Siecle, becoming the first Hong Kong dancer to star on an international stage. Upon returning to Hong Kong in 1967, Lau devoted himself to dance education and choreography. He created the city’s first ballet, Sea Love, founded several dance and arts groups and was a founding member and vice-president of the Hong Kong Dance Federation. Yet, Lau remained characteristically modest about his achievements. “There’s not much to crow about,” he told the South China Morning Post in 2006. “I once did well enough to the point of being invited to study under the best in the field – but I haven’t repaid their efforts with impressive results. That’s why I never want to talk about it.” In the 1970s, he served as dance director for TVB’s flagship variety show Enjoy Yourself Tonight. The role eventually opened the door to acting, with a guest appearance in the TVB anthology series Star Collection in 1975. At 48, Lau made his feature film debut in Tsui Hark’s The Butterfly Murders (1979), portraying the enigmatic scholar Fang Hongye. It marked the beginning of a second career that would make him a household name. An extraordinary filmography Over the following decades, he built an extraordinary filmography that included the TVB dramas The Shell Game II (1981), The Legend of the Condor Heroes (1983), Police Cadet ’84 (1984) and The Breaking Point (1991), showcasing his range in roles as both hero and villain. For many viewers, Lau is inseparable from his portrayal of the tree demon, also known as Lao Lao, in Tsui Hark’s A Chinese Ghost Story trilogy (1987-1991). The androgynous, terrifying villain – whose long tongue ensnared victims – remains one of the most iconic figures in Hong Kong fantasy cinema, and a childhood nightmare for generations. He also delivered a masterful performance as the hypocritical leader Yue Buqun in Swordsman (1990), bringing nuance and complexity to the classic wuxia character. In the two Casino Tycoon films (both 1992), he portrayed the scheming gambler Nie Aotian – inspired by the real-life gambling figure Yip Hon – with such intensity that, on one occasion, he found himself in a surreal situation. At a press conference for the 2017 TVB drama Bet Hur, Lau recalled that, while filming overseas earlier, he was allegedly kidnapped by local gangsters who were convinced by his on-screen portrayal of a triad boss. They took him to meet their leader, who demanded that Lau kneel and serve him tea. Once the misunderstanding was cleared up, however, the gangsters praised his acting and treated him as an honoured guest. Beyond these signature roles, Lau’s filmography included the comedy Front Page (1990) and the action film China Strike Force (2000). His final on-screen appearance was in the ViuTV drama The Gutter in 2020. “However small a character – even if it’s just a small cameo that only lasts for a few seconds – if I’ve spent time sculpting my performance, I’d already regard it as something for my best-of collection,” he said in the SCMP interview. Revered by other actors Known affectionately as “Ming Sir”, Lau’s influence extended far beyond his own performances. A revered figure in the industry, he served as a mentor to countless stars. Actors such as Lau Ching-wan and Francis Ng Chun-yu held him in such high esteem that they regularly visited him with their families, seeking his wisdom on both life and craft. Actress Charmaine Sheh Sze-man once named Lau as one of the two most important mentors of her career. She recalled a car journey during which Lau used water as a metaphor to explain the highest state of acting – to be fluid and natural, adapting to each scene like water taking the shape of its container. The philosophy, she said, has stayed with her ever since. Actress Monica Chan Fat-yung, who worked with him on the 1992 drama The Key Man and later on Bet Hur, shared her grief on social media, recalling how Lau – who suggested her character call him “Dou Dou”, a playful take on “old dad” – “taught me so much … an actor of exceptional skill and a kind senior who cared deeply for younger artists”. In recognition of his lifetime of work, Lau received a Hong Kong Dance Award in 2002, followed by an honorary fellowship from the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts in 2007. In 2013, he received TVB’s “Thousands of Stars” lifetime achievement award for his acting. That same year, the Hong Kong government awarded him the Medal of Honour for his contributions to the performing arts. Lau also served on the Art Form Panel (Dance and Multi-Arts) under the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, advising on the cultivation of young artistic talent. In 2019, he received a Life Achievement Award from the Hong Kong Arts Development Council. Lau’s later years were marked by profound personal loss and declining health. After his wife, Cheung Wai-ling, died from cancer in 2012, he spoke of feeling as though he had lost his most loyal audience member. In his final years, he suffered from seven ailments and relied on a wheelchair for mobility. Lau turned down most work invitations, telling reporters that he needed to rest.

title: Exclusive | ByteDance to expand massive AI data centre cluster in Inner Mongolia, source says
description: As Chinese tech giants ramp up artificial intelligence spending, TikTok’s parent company is set to expand data centres in Ulanqab.
content: TikTok parent ByteDance is seeking to expand its computing capacity by building out more data centres in north China’s Inner Mongolia autonomous region in the next two years, according to a person familiar with the matter, another example of a Chinese tech giant stepping up its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company had been in preliminary talks with local data centre vendors to add between five and six gigawatts’ worth of compute in the city of Ulanqab, the person said, who asked not to be identified due to the private nature of the information. Typically, the cost of upfront investment for a one-gigawatt AI data centre was around 160 billion yuan (US$23.8 billion), according to a research note published by Soochow Securities last month, meaning that ByteDance’s new facility – at between five and six gigawatts – could cost roughly 800 billion to 960 billion yuan. The planned massive AI data centre cluster would be located in Ulanqab’s Jining district, an area that has attracted computing facility investments from other major Chinese technology companies including Huawei Technologies, short video and AI developer Kuaishou, e-commerce giant Alibaba Group Holding, as well as Apple, the source said, adding that ByteDance was aiming for delivery by early 2028. ByteDance did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Thursday. The data centre push comes as the company reportedly secured a US$29.6 billion loan from a group of banks, the second-largest dollar-denominated loan in Asia this year, according to a Bloomberg report on Thursday. The financing underscores ByteDance’s push to expand its AI capabilities as Chinese tech companies ramp up spending on AI infrastructure. According to recent earnings results, Alibaba and Tencent Holdings have both increased spending on AI-related infrastructure and computing resources as they race to build out their AI capabilities. Alibaba’s capital expenditures increased 75 per cent while Tencent’s jumped 176 per cent in their latest quarter, according to their most recent quarterly results. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. ByteDance already had operations in Ulanqab, according to local government and media reports. Volcano Engine, ByteDance’s cloud computing unit, signed a deal last month with the Ulanqab municipal government to set up a computing facility in the city, according to a report by the Ulanqab Daily in late August. AI data centres in the city had been providing computing support for companies including ByteDance, Huawei and Alibaba, in areas spanning training AI models and autonomous driving simulations, according to a statement from Ulanqab officials. ByteDance has been developing its own AI models and applications, including its Doubao chatbot, while investing in the computing infrastructure needed to train and run those systems. The growing concentration of AI infrastructure in Ulanqab has attracted other major Chinese technology companies. Chinese AI start-up DeepSeek was developing a major data centre in Ulanqab with about one gigawatt of computing capacity. RedNote, the Shanghai-based lifestyle social media platform, was also planning a 600-megawatt AI data centre with around a 15-billion-yuan (US$2.2 billion) budget, excluding semiconductor costs, the SCMP reported in July. Ulanqab’s emergence as an important data centre hub in northern China was helped by its access to relatively inexpensive, renewable energy and cooler temperatures that could reduce cooling costs for power-intensive computing facilities. However, the rapid expansion of data centres in Ulanqab also raises questions over water use in a region where the local government says water resources are relatively scarce. Data centres can consume significant amounts of water for cooling, particularly as AI systems require increasingly powerful computing equipment which generates more heat. The city has called for tighter control of water consumption and use of water-saving technologies on new cloud computing projects, reflecting the constraints facing the city as it expands its computing infrastructure.

title: Tech race flashpoint: Huang, Musk push back on AI guard rails amid heated US-China rivalry
description: US tech leaders warn strict rules could blunt innovation and prevent the harnessing of economic gains from rapidly advancing AI.
content: US tech titans including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Tesla’s Elon Musk are pressing global powers to curb artificial intelligence regulations, warning that strict guard rails risk suffocating innovation as the US and China compete in an intensifying technological arms race. Speaking at a G20 meeting alongside US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on Wednesday, Huang urged policymakers to pursue AI regulations targeting “actual and pragmatic harm” rather than “hypothetical theoretical harm”. He argued that excessive regulation and fear could prevent countries from capturing the economic benefits of rapidly advancing AI. “The worst outcome is that you don’t take advantage of it, that you are left behind,” the billionaire chip executive said. The high-profile call comes as Washington moves to ease regulatory hurdles for home-grown developers, drawing sharp rebukes from Beijing, and as US executives ramp up lobbying against potential bans on open-weight AI models, framing open technology as vital to maintaining global technological leadership. Musk delivered a similar message at a G20 session on Tuesday, saying countries should create an environment “relatively free of regulation” in which new technologies were “default legal as opposed to default illegal”. The Tesla chief singled out the European Union as a jurisdiction where high levels of regulation had inhibited technological progress. We’re very strong advocates that open source shouldn’t be something that people try to restrict or lock down Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Platforms Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg also cautioned against restricting access to open-source AI, arguing that widely distributing the technology could itself contribute to safety by preventing powerful systems from becoming concentrated among a handful of companies or governments. “We’re very strong advocates that open source shouldn’t be something that people try to restrict or lock down,” Zuckerberg said at the G20 meeting on Tuesday. “I think it’s a very important part of creating a good future for everyone.” The warnings highlighted the US-China race to develop increasingly capable AI systems and the infrastructure needed to power them, with developers on both sides pushing models towards new levels of performance and autonomy. Anthropic on Wednesday released Claude Fable 5.1, which it described as its most advanced model for coding and complex knowledge work, alongside a restricted-access version called Mythos 5.1. Fable 5.1 scored 66 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, topping the global chart, six points ahead of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, two of China’s leading open-weight models. OpenAI teased its coming Astra model on Wednesday, saying it might reach a “critical level of cybersecurity capability” that could allow it to discover and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities across well-protected systems without human assistance. The tech executives’ remarks also added to a wider debate over how far governments should go in regulating increasingly powerful AI systems. Huang and other US technology leaders have previously pushed back against potential government restrictions on open-weight models, an arena currently dominated by Chinese labs. Meta expanded its open-weight line-up last month with Muse Glimmer, a lightweight model capable of running locally on personal devices, alongside its flagship Llama series. Nvidia broadened its open-weight ecosystem by launching Nemotron 3.5 Lightning the same month. Washington’s moves to ease AI regulations, alongside aggressive lobbying by US tech companies, have drawn criticism from Chinese state media. A commentary published by Yuyuan Tantian, a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, on Sunday accused Washington of weakening AI regulatory standards to “maintain technological hegemony”. It pointed to US President Donald Trump’s June executive order shortening the voluntary pre-release review period for advanced AI models to 30 days from 90. At a G20 meeting, China’s science and technology minister Yin Hejun said there was an urgent need for countries to work together to address the opportunities and risks posed by AI, according to a statement published by the Ministry of Science and Technology on Wednesday.

title: US military’s cyber unit plan threatens South Korea’s diplomatic balancing act
description: A proposed dispatch of specialist troops signals Washington’s focus is expanding beyond the Korean peninsula, experts say.
content: The potential deployment of an American army specialist unit capable of integrated operations across domains, including cyberspace, to South Korea could further reorient the US military’s role on the peninsula from deterring North Korea towards containing China, analysts say. Recent reports that the Pentagon is considering moving elements of the Second Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF), currently deployed in Germany, to South Korea have drawn attention to potential changes in the structure of the 28,500-strong US Forces Korea (USFK). The deployment has not been officially confirmed, with the specific size and composition of the dispatch yet to be revealed. South Korea’s defence ministry declined to comment on the reports. This Week in Asia has also contacted the US Department of Defence. The reports came after General Xavier Brunson, commander of the USFK and the Combined Forces Command, said last year he was considering introducing an MDTF to enhance situational awareness and intelligence capabilities. Hundreds of troops are set to be deployed from the Second MDTF’s Multi-Domain Effects Battalion, which handles cyber, information and space operations, according to reports by The Wall Street Journal, Yonhap news agency and The Chosun Ilbo newspaper. The MDTF is the US Army’s latest rapid-deployment formation, designed to conduct operations across land, maritime, air, cyber and space domains. It was developed in part to counter the anti-access/area-denial capabilities of countries such as China and Russia, which seek to restrict US military access and freedom of operation in their regions. The military established its first MDTF in 2019 and now operates three such units – two of which are already in the Indo-Pacific region. Washington reportedly aims to complete the deployment of the battalion to the Korean peninsula within this year. The potential move is part of a broader restructuring of American forces, which also includes the reassignment of Texas-based armoured units to a newly established Western Hemisphere Command. Broader regional implications Yu Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, said an MDTF deployment to South Korea would have “broader strategic implications in terms of deterring China”. “If elements of the task force were stationed in South Korea, they could potentially be linked to broader operations across the Indo-Pacific, including areas such as the Yellow Sea and the East China Sea,” he said. “This could indicate that the Korean peninsula is increasingly being viewed not only as a forward position for deterring North Korea, but also as a potential hub for multi-domain operations aimed at monitoring and deterring broader regional threats, including those posed by China.” The potential deployment also signals a broader transformation in the character of USFK, Yu said, from being centred primarily on “large-scale forward-deployed ground forces” towards one built around advanced capabilities combining “long-range precision fires with intelligence, space, cyber and electronic warfare capabilities”. “For South Korea, therefore, the most important issue is not simply whether an MDTF is deployed, but which capabilities are deployed, what missions they are assigned, against which potential adversaries those missions are directed, and how the forces would be employed in a contingency outside the Korean peninsula,” he said. The move comes as Seoul and Washington remain divided over the concept of USFK’s “strategic flexibility”. Washington has pushed to expand USFK’s role to include the wider Indo-Pacific region. Seoul, however, has maintained that its primary focus should remain on the Korean peninsula. In May, USFK’s Brunson drew backlash from both Seoul and Beijing for calling South Korea a “dagger in the heart of Asia” aimed at China. “Seoul would need to ensure that the core missions of USFK – deterring North Korea and defending the Korean peninsula – are not weakened,” Yu said. If MDTF capabilities were to be employed in a regional contingency, such as a crisis in the Taiwan Strait, South Korea and the US would need to establish clear arrangements regarding “prior consultation, command and control, operational employment and the division of responsibilities between the two militaries”, he said. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. While many nations, including the US, do not officially acknowledge Taiwan as an independent state, they oppose any use of force to alter the existing status quo. Caught in middle Seoul is fighting an uphill battle to balance its security alliance with Washington against its economic and diplomatic ties with Beijing. During a meeting with South Korea’s National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac last month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged Seoul not to play favourites and Washington to abandon what he described as its “hostile” policy towards Pyongyang to ease tensions on the Korean peninsula. China hoped South Korea would “achieve genuine strategic autonomy, refrain from bloc confrontation and taking sides, and develop relations with major powers including China and the United States in parallel and without contradiction”, Wang was quoted as saying by Xinhua news agency Doo Jin-ho, a research fellow at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, said China would “feel uncomfortable” about the potential deployment if it saw it as being aimed at deterring Beijing. “South Korea could be again caught up in the blowback as a result of the entanglement with its ally, the United States,” he said. From a military perspective, the deployment could give South Korea opportunities to learn from the US in areas such as cyberspace and space warfare, Doo said. But strategically and politically, it could “push Seoul deeper into a dilemma” by contributing to tensions in the region. “South Korea should engage in active discussions with the US side to make sure that the move will be focused on deterring the North instead of China,” he added. Kim Yeol-soo, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for Military Affairs, however, dismissed concerns about a potential Chinese response. “China would have little reason to react sensitively to the deployment of an MDTF battalion numbering a few hundred personnel”, he said, adding that the primary mission of the battalion would be surveillance of North Korean missiles and cyber warfare rather than direct military operations beyond the Korean peninsula. “This will help enhance South Korea’s military preparedness and deter North Korea. South Korea should put the priority on deterring North Korea as long as the battalion stays on its soil,” he said.

title: US$1.6 billion levy complicates sale of Singapore land by Malaysian king’s son
description: Tunku Ismail Ibrahim is seeking to sell 16.6 hectares of land, with his representatives courting buyers from the US and elsewhere.
content: A Malaysian royal’s plan to sell a tract of land in the heart of Singapore faces a complication: a tax bill that may exceed US$1 billion. A levy known as a land betterment charge has emerged as a sticking point in negotiations between some prospective buyers and the current owner, the eldest son of Malaysia’s billionaire king, according to people familiar with the matter. The owner wants any buyer to foot the bill, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. The tax, imposed when the government gives planning permission or other approvals that increase the value of land, may run north of S$2 billion (US$1.6 billion), according to estimates by three local property analysts. It is a potential stumbling block for what may be one of Singapore’s biggest-ever real estate deals. Tunku Ismail Ibrahim, son of Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, is seeking to sell 16.6 hectares (41 acres) of land, including a plot he obtained in a 2025 land swap with the city state’s government that would enable any properties being built on his land to be further away from the Botanic Gardens, a Unesco World Heritage site. In March, Singapore’s Urban Redevelopment Authority said Ismail had applied to develop the land for residential use, and the agency was proposing rezoning it to allow for development of mansions known as good class bungalows and low-rise housing. A representative for Ismail, the crown prince and regent of Malaysia’s southernmost state of Johor, declined to comment. The Singapore Land Authority, which administers the tax, said it does not comment on market speculation concerning landowners’ intentions or potential private transactions. The tax would be payable by the land’s owner at the time its development is approved, although owners can nominate one or more other parties to pay. The timing of any government approval for development is unclear. Some Singaporean and Malaysian property developers have chafed at the additional cost, as well as uncertainty over the exact size of the bill given the deal’s complexity, people familiar with the matter said. Ismail’s representatives have cast the net wider, seeking buyers from the US and elsewhere, the people said. The levy is designed to ensure that economic benefits from allowing land to be developed are returned to the community. The Singapore Land Authority said that the amount payable “will be determined following the grant of permission to develop the land, in accordance with the provisions of the LBC Act”, referring to legislation that came into force in 2022. The charge could range from S$2.5 billion to S$2.7 billion, according to an estimate by Nicholas Mak, chief research officer of Mogul.sg, a local property portal. The levy may be almost S$3 billion, said Tay Kah Poh, first vice-president of the Valuation and General Practice Division of the Singapore Institute of Surveyors and Valuers. He cautioned that the figure may be lower, citing a lack of information about the value of the land before rezoning. Another property valuer, who asked not to be identified discussing a sensitive subject, estimated the tax may be more than S$2 billion. The land itself may be worth S$3.8 billion to S$4.7 billion if rezoned, according to Mak. The analyst who asked not to be identified estimated it may be worth at least S$3 billion. The Johor royal family has owned land in an area known as Tyersall Park for more than a century. Their estate inspired the setting of the 2013 book Crazy Rich Asians, which was later adapted into a hit film. The tax law allows for exemptions and relief in some cases. The rezoning proposal was also subject to public comment. A government notice indicated there was a hearing in July for objections and representations submitted in response to the proposed rezoning. An Urban Redevelopment Authority spokesperson said hearings are only offered to those who submit comments within the requisite notice period.

title: Hong Kong weightlifter’s journey; history of five-kernel mooncakes: 7 Lifestyle highlights
description: From a layered sanctuary flat in Singapore to the risks of hepatitis B, here are seven stories from SCMP’s recent reporting.
content: We have selected seven Lifestyle stories from the past seven days that resonated with our readers. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. ‘Who cares if you’re bulky?’ Hong Kong-born weightlifter on power and femininity Fresh off the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, Hong Kong-born Tammy Wong is still buzzing – and not just from the adrenaline. The 30-year-old weightlifter, who represented England in the women’s 48kg category, finished with a combined total of 160kg (352lbs), just 7kg shy of a podium finish, and five off her own personal best. 2. Yayoi Kusama, Japanese artist famous for pumpkins and polka dots, dies aged 97 Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese avant-garde artist whose obsessive polka dots, towering pumpkin sculptures and mesmerising Infinity Mirror Rooms captivated audiences worldwide, has died at the age of 97. 3. 1 in 20 Hongkongers has hepatitis B, many unaware. What are the risks? David, who is in his forties and works in finance in Hong Kong, does not remember a life without hepatitis B, a viral infection of the liver. “I have been a … carrier for as long as I can remember,” he says. “I found out early on as a child since I was born with it – my mother is a carrier, too.” 4. This Singapore flat is a layered sanctuary that gradually reveals itself When the front door of this flat in Singapore’s Pinnacle@Duxton swings open, nothing of the interior is visible: an L-shaped foyer blocks the line of sight, while a low platform compresses the space before it opens out into an expansive living area. 5. Hunger replaced joy: Hong Kong woman’s 20-year eating disorder after dad’s death For more than two decades of Janet Leung’s life, hunger replaced her joy. After losing her father, endless food maths filled her head, drowning out other thoughts. Her anxiety around eating kept others at a distance. 6. How Josie Ho rejected her billionaire heiress destiny for indie filmmaking Josie Ho Chiu-yee has spent her career dismantling assumptions and forging her own identity through unbridled creativity. When it came to pursuing a music career, the daughter of the late Macau casino magnate Stanley Ho Hung-sun rejected the easy path of Cantopop ballads and blockbuster fluff, instead favouring 1980s-inspired punk rock and genre movies. 7. What are five-kernel mooncakes? A history of the protein-packed treat When you think of mooncakes, the ones that come to mind tend to be the classic sweet lotus paste versions with salted egg yolk, or maybe a more modern interpretation like one with a salty-sweet baked custard filling.

title: China rejects G20 trade-imbalance claims, says no need to devalue yuan
description: Beijing ‘deeply regrets’ a consensus was not reached after opposing some of the language used, and China urges deficit countries to cut spending.
content: China has fired back at critics of its trade imbalances at a Group of 20 gathering, with the central bank firmly denying that Beijing deliberately pursues trade surpluses, while also vowing that it would not weaponise the yuan to boost exports. In the face of concerns over export reliance, People’s Bank of China governor Pan Gongsheng said the country remained committed to expanding domestic demand, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Wednesday. “Addressing global imbalances requires all countries to promote their own structural reforms,” Pan was quoted as saying during the two-day G20 meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors, which ended on Tuesday. Pan’s remarks came amid renewed scrutiny over China’s trade surplus, which hit a record US$1.2 trillion last year. Speaking publicly after the G20 meeting, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called China’s current account surplus “unsustainable” and cited opposition from Beijing as the reason the group failed to issue a unanimous statement. The US Treasury instead issued a statement, late on Tuesday, that was “agreed by all G20 members present except China”. It pointed to four specific paragraphs that China had objected to, including one on taking steps to “eliminate non-market policies and practices that exacerbate imbalances”. “In particular, countries with excessive and persistent external surpluses should remove distortions that constrain domestic consumption and that result in an overreliance on exports for growth,” that paragraph added. A spokeswoman for China’s commerce ministry, Huang Ling, refuted Bessent’s remarks on Thursday. “The use of multilateral forums such as the G20 to hype up so-called ‘economic imbalances’ and ‘overcapacity’ is essentially promoting protectionism and seeking pretexts to exert pressure and restrictions on China,” Huang said. At the G20 meeting, which took place in the US state of North Carolina, Pan added that deficit countries should cut fiscal deficits and raise saving rates, while surplus countries should promote consumption and investment growth. “China has neither the need nor the intention to gain a competitive advantage in trade through currency devaluation,” Pan said. China also opposed a section urging the International Monetary Fund to strengthen its surveillance of structural drivers of global imbalances, as well as wording that addressed debt challenges and improving debt sustainability. It also objected to a paragraph expressing concerns over disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a critical Middle East chokepoint for global oil shipments. The Chinese foreign ministry had said on Wednesday that China “deeply regrets” that a unanimous statement was not possible at the G20 meeting, adding that members should coordinate on global economic issues in an objective, fair and balanced manner. In his speech at the meeting, Pan attributed the deepening global imbalances to rising trade protectionism, the broad application of national security issues, and unpredictable policy. With foreign trade enterprises increasingly using exchange rate hedging tools and the proportion of yuan trade settlement rising, trade with China is no longer as sensitive to exchange rate fluctuations, Pan said. Goldman Sachs analysts said they expected Beijing to continue to favour gradual yuan appreciation against the US dollar to balance China’s objectives of growth in hi-tech sectors; self-reliance in key inputs and technology; and further yuan internationalisation. Expecting incremental broad US dollar deflation in the coming years and relatively lower inflation in China, the bank’s analysts wrote in a research note on Wednesday that the yuan could appreciate gradually on a sustained basis “without major impact on Chinese manufacturers’ relative competitiveness or loss of global manufacturing share”.

title: Xi Jinping’s call for Mideast to build own security framework is a message to US: expert
description: Beijing gives weight to Cairo’s water security but China’s president does not criticise Ethiopia or its Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.
content: Chinese President Xi Jinping has urged Middle Eastern nations to build a self-led security model, nudging them to cut reliance on Washington following further US-Iran military clashes. But, on his first visit to Egypt in a decade, he did not position Beijing as an alternative security guarantor. He made the proposal during talks with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi at Cairo’s Ittihadiya Palace on Wednesday. Beijing and Cairo also aligned on Gaza, Red Sea security and Sudan, while China gave greater weight than it had previously to Egypt’s concerns over an Ethiopian megadam on the Nile. Analysts said the meeting reflected Egypt’s efforts to strengthen relations with China while maintaining its ties with the United States. The meeting came days after the US launched fresh strikes against Iranian Revolutionary Guard targets following attacks on oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. The fighting raised fears of further disruption to oil shipments and pushed crude prices higher. “The people of the Middle East should be masters of their own affairs,” Xi said, according to state news agency Xinhua. He called for opposition to outside interference and said countries in the region should determine their own future, proposing what he described as “a common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable” approach to security in the Middle East. “The fundamental way to achieve lasting peace and stability in the Middle East is through development,” Xi said, referring to Beijing’s view that economic growth, trade and regional cooperation could help address the underlying causes of conflict. Without naming any countries, Xi also said major powers outside the region should “abandon double standards”, and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of regional countries. El-Sisi praised China’s “objective and impartial position” and said Cairo would work with Beijing to ease tensions and explore a regional security framework. John Calabrese, a non-resident senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, said Xi’s emphasis on “common security” carried a message about Washington’s role in the region. “This can be read as an implicit, if thinly veiled, reminder of the limits of the US role as the region’s security guarantor, an affirmation of emerging localised arrangements such as the Mecca Defence Pact, and an alignment with Iran’s long-standing call for external security powers to reduce their presence in the region,” he said. Calabrese said, however, that Xi was not offering China as a new external guarantor. “Despite Xi’s calls for expanded bilateral military and security cooperation, Beijing appears to be advocating a more regionally owned security architecture rather than assuming the role of the region’s new external guarantor.” Xi and el-Sisi said they supported the creation of a sovereign, independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, based on the borders of June 4, 1967, and opposed any plan to relocate Palestinians “for any reason or under any name”. They called for consolidation of the Gaza ceasefire, unrestricted access for humanitarian aid and the return of the Palestinian Authority to Gaza as soon as possible, according to a joint statement released after the meeting. On the Red Sea, China and Egypt said responsibility for governance and security rested mainly with states bordering the waterway. They called on those countries to strengthen regional cooperation, protect freedom of navigation and keep international trade moving. On Sudan, where a civil war has pitted the Sudanese Armed Forces against the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces since 2023, China and Egypt called for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity to be respected, its state institutions preserved and interference in its internal affairs avoided. They also backed a ceasefire and a Sudanese-led inclusive political process. The joint statement also gave greater recognition to Egypt’s concerns over Nile water security. China said it understood the importance of the Nile as Egypt’s “main lifeline” and that it recognised Cairo’s “legitimate rights to safeguard its water security, food security and development interests”. China and Egypt called on all Nile Basin countries to follow international law, including the principle of avoiding harm to other states. The joint statement did not directly criticise the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dam is a massive hydroelectric project built by Ethiopia on the Blue Nile, designed to expand its electricity grid. Egypt relies on the Nile for over 90 per cent of its fresh water and views the dam as an existential threat, fearing Ethiopia’s control over the river’s flow could cause severe water shortages, damage agricultural land, and compromise its own energy generation at the Aswan High Dam during dry periods. Ethiopia says the dam is essential for electricity generation and will not harm Egypt or Sudan. “By explicitly recognising the Nile as Egypt’s ‘lifeline’ and affirming its ‘legitimate rights’ to safeguard water and food security, Xi is giving greater rhetorical weight to Cairo’s concerns,” Calabrese said. “With the [dam] now operational, Egypt’s water-security situation has become more acute. But Xi stopped short of criticising Ethiopia or questioning the [dam].” David Shinn, a China-Africa specialist and former US ambassador to Ethiopia, said China came close to agreeing with Egypt on Nile water usage and accepted that Red Sea security was mainly the responsibility of littoral countries. “These statements will raise questions in landlocked Ethiopia, the source of most Nile water reaching Egypt,” Shinn said. “China is clearly reaching out to strengthen ties with Egypt, and Cairo is responding enthusiastically in an effort to diversify its global relationships.” Egypt’s regional influence and control of the Suez Canal made it important to China, which had invested in port and storage projects there to support Mediterranean trade, he added. The talks produced more than 20 cooperation documents covering the Belt and Road Initiative, artificial intelligence, trade, industrial and supply chains and the digital economy. Despite the expanding relationship with Beijing, analysts said Cairo was unlikely to turn away from Washington. “Egypt will still want to maintain good relations with the United States, which provides US$1.3 billion in military aid annually, far more than anything China provides,” Shinn said. Zhiqun Zhu, a professor of political science and international relations and director of the China Institute at Bucknell University, said Egypt had taken a balanced and pragmatic approach to maintaining good relations with great powers. “It has strong military, security and economic ties with the United States. Egypt is unlikely to take sides in the growing US-China rivalry,” he said.

title: Chinese chipmaker Enflame 4,073 times oversubscribed in Shanghai IPO amid Nvidia race
description: The last of China’s ‘four little dragons’ to go public has drawn millions of retail investors, despite odds of securing an allocation at less than 0.03 per cent.
content: Enflame Technology, one of China’s leading AI chipmakers, has sparked a retail frenzy for its 6.12 billion yuan (US$910.9 million) initial public offering in Shanghai’s tech-heavy Star Market, underscoring growing investor appetite for home-grown alternatives to Nvidia. The Tencent Holdings-backed chipmaker saw the retail portion of its IPO oversubscribed by 4,073 times, with about 7 million online investors alone submitting orders for 42.1 billion shares, according to its filing to the exchange on Wednesday. The high demand amounted to an allocation rate for individual investors of just 0.025 per cent. That made it one of the lowest in mainland China this year alongside robotics maker Unitree Robotics, whose rate was just 0.018 per cent, or about one successful lot for every 5,500 applications. The strong market response highlights Enflame’s role as a crucial player in Beijing’s accelerating push for semiconductor self-sufficiency. The Shanghai-based company – often dubbed one of China’s “four little dragons” in the AI chip sector alongside Moore Threads, Biren Technology and MetaX – is the last of the four firms to go public. The odds of securing Enflame shares are lower than MetaX’s 0.033 per cent and Moore Threads’ 0.036 per cent. Retail investors, meanwhile, are flooding the market, betting that Enflame will match the first-day pops of 693 per cent and 425 per cent achieved when its two rivals debuted in December. Priced at 142.18 yuan (US$21.16) per share, Enflame expects to raise 6.12 billion yuan to fund the research, development and production of its fifth- and sixth-generation AI chips. Kevin Chen, a 35-year-old A-share investor in Shanghai, bid for 6,500 of the chipmaker’s shares on Wednesday. “I applied based on my strong confidence across China’s hard tech sector, just as I did with ChangXin Memory Technologies and Unitree Robotics this year,” Chen said, though he acknowledged having low expectations of actually securing an allocation. Enflame said it would announce the results on Friday. Beyond the retail scramble, Enflame also attracted a strong line-up of strategic investors. Tencent led the pack, securing a 4.06 per cent stake through a subsidiary with a 36-month lock-up. Other prominent investors included memory chipmaker GigaDevice, smartphone and electric vehicle maker Xiaomi, chip packaging and testing company Tongfu Microelectronics, and telecommunications giant ZTE.

title: Iran targets US bases in Kuwait despite warnings from Trump
description: Iran launches missiles and drones at Gulf neighour following US strikes that killed at least 19.
content: Iran attacked US military bases in Kuwait on Thursday, despite US President Donald Trump threatening further strikes in a fresh flare-up six months into the war. Trump said his military was prepared to attack Iran “any time we want” after extensive US bombardment of sites across the country left at least 19 Iranians dead. Tehran retaliated by hitting US military targets across the Middle East, including in Kuwait, Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Iraq’s autonomous Kurdistan region. The clashes deepen the ongoing impasse in the war, as Iran maintains a stranglehold on the Strait of Hormuz oil export route and the US presses its counter-blockade of Iranian ports. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned the United States that Iran had adopted a “new strategy” in the war that “will shatter your foundations”. Kuwait’s army said Thursday it was intercepting a missile and drone attack from Iran, with Iranian state TV confirming that Tehran was targeting US bases in the Gulf state “in response to America’s crimes against the Iranian people”. In a statement, Kuwait’s foreign ministry called the strikes “a direct threat to its (Kuwait’s) security and stability, and the safety of its citizens and residents on its territory, and a grave breach of the rules of international law”. The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks, saying it was trying to stop Tehran placing sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said Sunday’s strikes resulted in “casualties” and responded by targeting US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Projectiles also struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company. Aside from military action, Washington has vowed to choke Iran’s economy, threatening to slap sanctions on its trade partners. Energy Secretary Chris Wright pledged on Wednesday that a US plan for expanded sanctions targeting the Islamic republic’s economic partners would deliver “absolutely maximum pressure”. Trump also mused on Wednesday renaming the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic shipping lane that Tehran has effectively shut for six months, as “Trump Strait” - although he implied later that he wasn’t serious. It's got a nice ring to it pic.twitter.com/Fmzc9iUu8u — The White House (@WhiteHouse) September 2, 2026 “Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???” the US president wrote on Truth Social. Iran’s pummelling of US military targets across the region came after a US attack that hit a wedding in the country’s south, prompting fury from Tehran. The Iranian Red Crescent said shrapnel from the missile attack in the coastal town of Kuhestak killed four people, including a child, and wounded more than 50. The US military did not address the attack directly. US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards. Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States “Satan”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan,” he posted on X. ⁠Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news ⁠agency reported on Thursday ⁠the deaths of six more military personnel from US strikes this week, bringing the military death toll to at least 13. Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities. Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks “truly distressing” “I hope they all return to the negotiating table because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people,” he said. “The Americans are on the other side of the world and nothing happens to them.” A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Kuhestak following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background. “It is a very saddening incident,” Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV. “Thank God the casualties were not higher.” The war erupted on February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed. Israel’s defence minister said meanwhile that his country was prepared to respond “with great force” if attacked by Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September. “For now, they are striking throughout the region except us,” Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli media outlets. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Operators of over 60% of subdivided flats apply for 3-year window to meet rules
description: Hong Kong housing chief Winnie Ho says applications as of Monday involved more than 70,000 subdivided units from about 20,000 complete flats.
content: Operators of more than 60 per cent of subdivided flats in Hong Kong have applied for a three-year grace period to give themselves more time to comply with a regulatory regime rolled out six months ago, the housing minister has said. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin said on Thursday the applications received as of Monday covered than 70,000 subdivided homes from about 20,000 complete flats. This was more than double the 34,000 applications received by August 10. Monday marked the deadline for the initial six-month “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance, which took effect in March. Landlords who applied during this period were eligible for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in recognition fees per subdivided flat until February 2029. A second six-month registration round, offering smaller fee discounts, is under way and will conclude the overall one-year application period. “The early bird initiative has brought about a very significant rise in registration applications,” Ho wrote on social media. “Hong Kong has roughly 110,000 subdivided units. In other words, the registration applications have covered over 60 per cent of the city’s subdivided units.” She added that the registration application numbers also reached about 90 per cent of the estimated 80,000 subdivided flats expected to continue operating under the new regime. Under the ordinance, only subdivided flats that comply with the minimum requirements and are certified as “basic housing units” can be leased legally on the market from next March, with the exception of those registered for the grace period. The grace period runs from March next year to February 2030, and aims to give landlords time to refurbish and certify properties. Landlords have to bear the renovation and certification costs, and pay the government HK$3,000 per subdivided flat to have the properties recognised as basic housing units. Ho urged more operators on Thursday to sign up for the grace period. The registration window for the grace period ends on February 28 next year, but applicants can still receive the HK$3,000 waiver in recognition fees per subdivided home until February 2028 and enjoy a half-price discount in the subsequent year. Ho also said operators of 120 subdivided flats had applied for certification as of Wednesday. According to the government’s website on Thursday, the city already has 41 basic housing units. Hayson Chan Hin-hay, chairman of the Hong Kong Basic Housing Units Operators Association, said some landlords had yet to register for the grace period due to property ownership issues. He added that others did not plan to register as they had either withdrawn from the market or planned to operate illegally. But Chan said it was too early to tell whether landlords who had registered for the grace period would definitely renovate their properties and operate as basic housing units. “Many landlords have yet to decide. It costs them nothing to register for the grace period,” he said. Kenny Tse Chi-kin, vice-president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, said the current number of registered subdivided homes was an encouraging step. The surveyor said he expected the remaining operators to sign up for the three-year grace period to avoid falling afoul of the law. Tse added that the next step after the grace period registration would be for owners to get their properties certified by professionals to ensure compliance with the new standards. Vincent Cheng Wing-shun, a member of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, said he hoped the government could proceed with the certification applications in an orderly fashion so that the market could familiarise itself with the new regime as soon as possible and speed up the refurbishment process. He also raised concerns about whether remaining operators felt incentivised to register for the grace period, as the early bird offer would only become less appealing. The legislator suggested the government continue to encourage landlords to register for the grace period through different channels, such as organising talks at districts with relatively low registration rates. Cheng added that the government could consult records to help proactively reach out to landlords using written or electronic notices. Scott Leung Man-kwong, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, echoed the need to entice the remaining operators to sign up for the grace period. He also said the grace period registration process could help the government better understand the situation regarding subdivided flats and pave the way for future enforcement work. Under the law, a basic housing unit must measure at least eight square metres (86 sq ft), have a ceiling height of 2.3 metres (7.5 feet), a window and a waterproof toilet, among other safety, hygiene and fire safety requirements. The Housing Bureau earlier estimated that about 70 per cent of the city’s 110,000 subdivided flats required only minor rectifications, while the rest needed major renovations.

title: Luxury homes in Singapore’s largest money laundering case hit the auction block
description: A total of 25 properties, including a 4-bedroom penthouse, are expected to fetch millions in the auction.
content: Another 14 luxury condominium units and a grade A office at Suntec Tower One forfeited in connection with Singapore’s largest money laundering case will be put up for sale at auctions this month. The properties, located in prime areas such as River Valley and Orchard, will be auctioned by real estate firms Edmund Tie & Company (ETC) and Knight Frank. As of Thursday morning, a total of 25 properties have been listed for auction. ETC will auction units at South Beach Residences, 8 Saint Thomas and Paterson Suites at UIC Building on September 23. Five units at South Beach Residences at Beach Road will be put up at guide prices of between S$4.45 million (US$3.5 million) and S$25.32 million. They include three 2-bedroom units, one 3-bedroom unit, and a 6,727 sq ft (624 square metres) 4-bedroom penthouse on the 42nd floor. A 3-bedroom unit and a 4-bedroom unit at 8 Saint Thomas, a freehold development in River Valley, will also go under the hammer at guide prices of S$4.4 million and S$5.72 million, respectively. At Paterson Suites, a freehold property near Orchard MRT, a 3-bedroom unit will be put up at a guide price of S$5.18 million. Knight Frank will hold the auction for the Suntec Tower One office, as well as units at Sloane Residences and Gramercy Park, on September 17 at its office at Ocean Financial Centre. The 3,498 sq ft office at Suntec has a guide price of S$11.5 million. The agency described the space as a premium grade A office space that is fitted and ready for occupation. Two 3-bedroom units at Sloane Residences, a freehold property at Balmoral Road, have guide prices of between S$3.6 million and S$3.7 million. Meanwhile, one 2-bedroom and study, one 3-bedroom and two 4-bedroom units at Gramercy Park at Grange Road will be put up at guide prices of between S$3.8 million and S$7.6 million. Apart from Knight Frank and ETC, SRI has also been appointed to conduct auctions of 10 luxury condominium units at Martin Modern and Wallich Residence so far, with guide prices ranging from S$2.238 million to S$6.78 million. Some selected properties will also be offered for sale through an expression of interest process run by List International Realty, outside the auction process. They are among more than 80 real estate properties and 1,000 luxury items forfeited in Singapore’s S$3 billion money laundering case. Auditing firm Deloitte said last Saturday that the assets will go to auction from September 7 and be sold in phases between September 2026 and mid-2027. Deloitte, appointed by the Singapore Police Force in July 2025 to manage and realise the non-cash assets forfeited in the case, said the composition and number of items in each phase are still being finalised and may change as authentication and preparatory work continues. The money laundering case emerged after island-wide raids in August 2023 uncovered millions of dollars earned from an illicit gambling ring based in Southeast Asia. The 10 offenders, all originally from China, have since been convicted and deported after serving their sentences. This story was first published by CNA

title: US universities limit internships for international students after a federal advisory
description: New guidance restricts non-degree-required training, impacting F-1 visa holders’ internship and off-campus work options.
content:
International students in the United States are encountering fresh challenges regarding internships and off-campus employment due to recent decisions by several prominent universities to suspend or limit specific types of Curricular Practical Training (CPT).
CPT is a type of work authorisation that permits international students to engage in internships and practical training that aligns with their academic programmes.
The changes follow two directives in August from the Student and Exchange Visitor Programme (SEVP), a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which take a stricter view of when CPT can be authorised.
Universities including the University of Pennsylvania, New York University (NYU), the University of Southern California, the University of Washington, the University of Rochester and the University of California, Berkeley have paused pending applications or limited CPT to internships that are mandatory parts of a degree programme.
On August 12, the SEVP issued a message reminding school officials of their responsibility when approving CPT.
The guidance said CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and directly related to a student’s major. It also stressed that the training should generally be necessary to complete the degree and required for all students in that programme.
The SEVP also warned the school officials that approving CPT carried personal responsibility. By signing off on a student’s work authorisation paperwork, officials certify that the position meets federal requirements. Improper approvals could have consequences for both the university and the individual official, including possible loss of the school’s SEVP certification.
The agency also warned schools against using CPT to provide employment opportunities rather than as part of an academic programme.
On August 24, the SEVP issued another message reinforcing that CPT is allowed only as an integral part of an established curriculum.
UC Berkeley was among the first major universities to respond.
In an August 13 letter to students, the university’s international office said the new federal criteria were “narrow in nature” and raised questions about existing CPT practices.
The university then suspended applications for “course credit CPT” that were considered integral to a programme but were not formal degree requirements. The university said it would continue processing CPT that was required for the degree.
UC Berkeley’s current CPT guidance continues to reflect the suspension. The university now considers “integral” practical training to mean either a degree requirement for all students in the programme or a necessary component of a master’s thesis or doctoral dissertation.
The University of Pennsylvania announced a universitywide pause on August 29, putting new and pending CPT requests on hold while it reviewed its academic programmes and procedures in response to the federal guidance.
The university stressed that CPT had not been eliminated and that pending applications had not been denied.
It also highlighted a key change in how academic credit was treated, telling students: “Under the guidance, receiving academic credit is not enough by itself.”
NYU updated its guidance on August 31, saying the federal guidance established a stricter interpretation of CPT rules.
Under the university’s reading, CPT may be authorised only when it is an explicit, mandatory degree requirement of a programme.
NYU said CPT authorisations already approved for the autumn term would remain valid, but pending requests had been frozen.
USC has taken a similar position. It said CPT based on an elective course did not meet the federal requirements. As of August 24, the university said CPT would generally be limited to practical training required for graduation.
The University of Washington has also paused new CPT requests that are not required work experience for all students in a degree programme.
At the University of Rochester, optional internships, clinical experience and other practical training, including those tied to elective internship courses, are no longer considered eligible under the university’s interpretation of the guidance.
Other campuses within the University of California system, including UCLA and UC Davis, have also issued guidance.
The changes apply to international students from all countries on F-1 visas.
However, the restrictions could have a major impact on Chinese students, who make up one of the largest international student groups in the US and often rely on internships during undergraduate and master’s degree programmes.
For students who already have internship offers for the autumn semester, the key question is whether the CPT has already been authorised.
At universities that have issued guidance, CPT already authorised on official paperwork generally remains valid.
Students should also remember that they cannot begin off-campus work until they have received the required CPT authorisation.
On the Chinese social media platform RedNote, a user identifying as a Columbia University PhD graduate said the policy was “truly driving international students into a corner”.
“Doesn’t this completely cut off any path for international students to intern in the US?” the user wrote.
A user who said they were a UC Berkeley journalism student noted that a “short-term policy reversal” appeared unlikely. The person cited an email from the university’s international office stating that the suspension of CPT approvals had been “extended indefinitely”.
Another RedNote user, who listed the University of Southern California as his school, posted a scathing reflection, saying that he had “really believed it” when people had promised him the STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and mathematics – were stable and technical skills were in demand in the US.
“I was completely misled. When policies shift like this, all of it falls apart in an instant,” he wrote.
Frustration over US President Donald Trump’s second term has been a dominant theme of discussions on the Chinese platform.
One user, whose post showed an Illinois IP address, said: “This is only one year and eight months into Trump’s term; the ‘good days’ are still ahead of us.”
A Los Angeles-based user replied: “It’s only been a year and a half? It feels like half a lifetime has passed.”

title: Amid global risks, younger investors favour tangible bars as paper gold loses shine
description: Gen Z buyers are driving demand for bullion, spurred by geopolitical tensions, inflation and the appeal of owning gold outright.
content: Sussi Ye began buying gold bars in small batches at the start of the year, slowly building a hoard now worth about 200,000 yuan (US$29,700). Despite the metal’s price swings since then, she has not sold a single gram. “I prefer investing in physical gold instead of gold-linked financial products,” said the 32-year-old resident of Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province. “I like that it’s tangible, you can hold it, and that gives you a sense of security. If I get married someday, I can still have these gold bars crafted into wedding jewellery.” Ye’s instinct reflects a broader shift in global gold markets. Demand for physical gold among Gen Z was rising, as geopolitical tensions and market uncertainties fuelled interest in owning gold outright rather than through paper-based products, according to the London-based dealer IBV Gold London. “Younger investors have experienced a lot of uncertainty – inflation, geopolitical tensions, volatile markets and concerns about the strength of currencies and the wider economy,” said Yuvana Singh, manager at IBV Gold London. “Because of that, they are thinking more seriously about diversification at a relatively young age and turning to gold.” IBV Gold London, which serves clients ranging from family offices to institutional investors, said nearly a third of its inquiries over the past year came from buyers aged between 18 and 28. Gold was no longer seen purely as an investment for older or wealthy investors, Singh said. “It is becoming much more mainstream among younger people,” she said, adding that she was seeing more first-time buyers who had never owned gold before. [Gen Z investors are] looking for something tangible … rather than simply having exposure to its price Yuvana Singh, IBV Gold London Ownership of gold jewellery among consumers aged 18 to 24 had surged to 62 per cent from 37 per cent five years ago, according to a World Gold Council survey of more than 3,000 Chinese consumers last year. Demand for gold bars and coins reached 474 tonnes in the first quarter, up 42 per cent year on year and the second-highest quarterly total on record, led by Asian buyers, according to the council. Gen Z investors “are looking for something tangible … rather than simply having exposure to its price”, Singh said. Investors often worried that “if you later decide that you actually want physical gold, the process of converting that investment into bars or coins isn’t necessarily straightforward”, she added. Depending on the paper gold product, “there can be redemption requirements, fees, minimum amounts, or simply no option for the individual investor to take delivery of the underlying gold”, Singh said. Paper gold refers to financial products such as exchange-traded funds, futures and options that mirror gold’s price movements but do not grant investors physical possession of the metal. IBV Gold London operates a single vault in the UK capital’s Mayfair district, serving clients worldwide in storing their bullion and coins. About 20 per cent of its customer base comes from Asia, including mainland China, Hong Kong and Singapore. BullionVault, the world’s largest online physical precious metals service for private investors, said its first-time users aged 16 to 27 hit a record in 2025 and matched that full-year total in just the first half of 2026. It serves more than 130,000 customers globally. Spot gold was trading at about US$4,425 an ounce as of Thursday, about 21 per cent below January’s record intraday high of US$5,602. Deutsche Bank expected gold to reach US$4,700 per ounce by the end of the year, while Morgan Stanley predicted prices would rise to US$5,000 by 2027.

title: Hong Kong considers DNA testing amid concerns over ‘fighting dog’ classification
description: Authorities studying use of genetic testing to identify breeds, but physical characteristics remain key to classification.
content: Hong Kong authorities are considering genetic testing as a supplementary tool for identifying breeds, an official has said after enforcement action against suspected fighting dogs sparked public concern. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) also said on Thursday that owners could keep existing fighting dogs, provided they complied with statutory requirements, and urged owners not to abandon their pets. Dr Michelle Yeung Lee, the department’s principal veterinary officer, said the AFCD relied on dogs’ physical characteristics to determine whether they belonged to a fighting type. “It is the method adopted internationally, and our risk assessment focuses on dogs’ physical characteristics. If they have certain features, they are likely to cause more significant harm,” she said. Lee also noted that, despite advances in technology, genetic tests currently available were not sufficiently accurate, as the reference databases used by service providers could differ. On Wednesday evening, the AFCD said it would examine the latest applications of genetic testing methods, with a view to considering their use as supplementary identification tools in the future. It added that most dogs had genetic traits from a range of breeds, and that canines carrying genes associated with fighting dogs might not develop all the relevant physical traits. This justified its reliance on physical observation rather than genetic testing, the department said. Under the Dangerous Dogs Regulation, four types of dog – pit bull terrier, dogo Argentino, Japanese Tosa and fila Brasileiro – are classified as fighting dogs. It is illegal to import them or their crossbreeds into Hong Kong, or to breed them locally. The AFCD stepped up inspections and enforcement actions in response to the death of a woman after she was mauled at a pet training centre and the killing of two smaller dogs in canine attacks only days apart in mid-August. The department has since seized at least three canines deemed to have physical traits associated with fighting dogs. Yeung said the department had received more complaints from residents about suspected fighting dogs after the attacks. But the seizures have also prompted public concern, with advocacy groups calling for greater clarity over the department’s classification mechanism and warning that the enforcement action could lead to dogs being abandoned. Yeung said on Thursday that owners could still keep their dogs, even if they fell within the fighting-dog types, as long as they met statutory requirements. These include neutering the dogs, securely muzzling them and keeping them on a leash no longer than 1.5 metres (4.92 feet) in public places. The animals must also wear special collars. She added that owners concerned about their pets being classified as fighting dogs could take them to the department’s animal management centres for assessment. “For existing fighting dogs, if sufficient measures were adopted, they could still be kept. Residents should not abandon their dogs out of [regulatory] concerns,” she said. The first of two attacks in August to come under the public spotlight was the fatal mauling of smaller dogs in Yuen Long by an unleashed 60kg (132lbs) canine believed to have mastiff ancestry. The second occurred days later. The victim, a 33-year-old woman, was found dead near her pet training centre in Ta Kwu Ling after being attacked by a 30kg dog with traits associated with pit bull ancestry. In both cases, the dogs’ licences listed their type as “mongrel”, prompting questions over the effectiveness of Hong Kong’s dog-classification system.
