Addressing those concerns, Yeung said the department would seek to provide more detailed descriptions of dogs’ types during future licensing exercises. Following the incidents, authorities pledged to review the definition of fighting dogs and related regulations to strengthen public safety.

title: Retired Cardinal Joseph Zen, 4 others lose appeal over failure to register protest fund
description: Defendants were convicted in 2022 for failing to register legal defence fund that supported people involved in Hong Kong’s 2019 protests.
content: Retired Catholic leader Joseph Zen Ze-kiun and four other activists have lost an appeal against their convictions for failing to register their legal defence fund for those involved in the 2019 anti-government protests in Hong Kong. The Court of Appeal on Thursday upheld a magistrate’s findings that the now-defunct 612 Humanitarian Relief Fund fell within the definition of a society under the Societies Ordinance and its members were required to register the group with police or ask for an exemption. The court found the registration scheme was constitutional and that it did not impose an unacceptably harsh burden on the exercise of the right to freedom of association. The three presiding judges also ruled that the fund was not a validly constituted trust but instead a vehicle for supporting the 2019 protest movement, with the appellants sharing mutual rights and obligations to achieve that end. Zen, 94, was the fund’s trustee alongside singer Denise Ho Wan-see, former Lingnan University academic Hui Po-keung and ex-opposition lawmakers Margaret Ng Ngoi-yee and Cyd Ho Sau-lan. They were each fined HK$4,000 (US$510) after a trial in 2022. The sixth defendant, fund secretary Sze Ching-wee, did not file an appeal against his conviction and HK$2,500 fine. Ng said the five appellants intended to take their case to the Court of Final Appeal. “The definition of a society under the ordinance is very, very wide, which can potentially affect many people. So we feel this matter does not only affect the 612 Fund but also the entire civil society of Hong Kong,” she said. The court ruled that the ordinance was not so overly wide that it defined a society as a club, company or business partnership or any “association of persons” that shared similar characteristics. Despite rejecting the original trial magistrate’s view that the definition of a society should be as wide as possible to safeguard national security, the court said the law should still be sufficiently broad to achieve that objective. Chief Judge of the High Court Jeremy Poon Shiu-chor and Court of Appeal justices Aarif Barma and Derek Pang Wai-cheong found that the law was clear and definite enough for anyone to understand when a registration would be required. The judges also ruled that a voluntary notification scheme, as proposed by some of the appellants, would be far less effective in achieving the legitimate objective of safeguarding national security, public safety and public order. The defendants are also part of an ongoing investigation by police’s national security department into the group’s alleged collusion with foreign forces to impose sanctions on Hong Kong. No charges have been laid yet in that case, but the travel documents of those involved have been confiscated. The Societies Ordinance stipulates a local organisation must register with the societies officer, who is the police commissioner, or ask for an exemption within one month of its establishment. Otherwise, organisers could be fined HK$10,000 upon a first conviction. Prosecutors said the fund accepted nearly 100,000 donations collectively worth HK$270 million between June 2019 and October 2021, with some of the money used to subsidise anti-government protest organisers, international lobbyists and foreign organisations hostile to Beijing. Those receiving subsidies from the fund included the now-dissolved Civil Human Rights Front, the Taiwan-based Judicial Reform Foundation and the New Hong Kong Cultural Club, a pro-independence group founded by Hongkongers in Canada. The fund’s dealings with overseas bodies were revealed after police invoked the national security law’s implementation rules to compel the five trustees to hand over information, including the personal details of donors and recipients. The case also sparked internal inquiries by the city’s two legal professional bodies after national security police complained about “suspected misconduct by solicitors and barristers” in their provision of legal services. The Hong Kong Bar Association cleared 38 barristers of wrongly accepting payments from the fund but sent letters of advice to four members over “technical” breaches for failing to keep some required documentation. The Law Society of Hong Kong sent “warning or closing letters” to some members on the basis that they had “compromised or impaired their integrity and the reputation of the profession”, but the body did not reveal the number of lawyers involved. The government has proposed regulating crowdfunding by requiring anyone planning to collect public donations to apply to authorities for approval to proceed, but pressure groups have expressed concerns that the move would threaten their survival.

title: 3 women charged with fighting in Hong Kong mall granted bail, banned from venue
description: Trio make first appearance in court after confrontation over their children’s quarrel in shopping centre play area devolved into brawl.
content: A Hong Kong court has granted bail to three women after they were charged with fighting in the children’s play area of a shopping centre and barred them from returning to the venue. Leung Lai-ha, 68, her 34-year-old daughter Ng Ka-wun and Xu Yang, 34, made their first appearance at Kwun Tong Court on Thursday to face charges after their altercation on August 26 at the atrium of APM shopping centre in Kwun Tong. Their confrontation was captured in a video posted on social media, and the three defendants face a joint count of fighting in a public place. The video appears to show the adults engaged in a physical fight, with Xu slapping Leung and the elderly woman hitting back at Xu and her five-year-old daughter. Ng then enters the fray, scuffling with Xu as the fight devolves into a brawl. The video, which drew widespread attention online, did not show how the argument arose but captured Xu’s daughter allegedly being knocked to the ground. Court documents seen by the South China Morning Post on Thursday revealed more details of the defendants’ identities. Xu, who is from mainland China, holds a two-way entry permit and makes frequent trips to Hong Kong. She said she was unemployed. Ng is an insurance agent, while her mother Leung is a retiree. Both are Hong Kong residents. Apart from the charge of fighting in a public place, Leung also faces a separate count of common assault for allegedly hitting the five-year-old girl. At the hearing, Leung and Ng’s lawyer asked the court for time to submit a letter of negotiation to the Department of Justice. Xu requested permission to leave Hong Kong as her family lived across the border. But Acting Principal Magistrate Li Chi-ho rejected her request after considering Xu’s risk of absconding. Before granting bail to all three defendants, he imposed conditions including barring them from leaving Hong Kong and prohibiting them from returning to the shopping centre. Li also increased the cash bail from HK$1,000 (US$128) to HK$5,000 for all three defendants. The next hearing will take place on November 5.

title: Beijing ramps up coastguard patrols and scientific surveys near Taiwan
description: There has been weeks of increased activity to the east of the island following maritime boundary talks between Japan and the Philippines.
content: Beijing said it conducted a routine patrol in waters east of Taiwan on Thursday, the latest in weeks of ramped-up activity by coastguard and other vessels that has alarmed the island. China Coast Guard spokesman Jiang Lue said a formation led by the Putuoshan vessel carried out a “law enforcement” patrol “in accordance with the law”. He said the formation had strengthened control over the waters since last month, safeguarding the rights and interests of Chinese citizens. “The China Coast Guard will continue to strengthen law enforcement patrols in waters under Chinese jurisdiction, resolutely safeguarding national territorial sovereignty and maritime rights,” Jiang said. The patrol followed weeks of increased mainland Chinese coastguard operations and scientific activities in waters east of Taiwan, after Japan and the Philippines opened maritime delimitation talks on the area that Beijing has called illegal and a violation of its rights. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is legally committed to supplying it with weapons. Also on Thursday, mainland Chinese media reported that the Ministry of Natural Resources conducted a marine geophysical survey in waters east of Taiwan that ran from August 10 to 31. The ministry’s Second Institute of Oceanography carried out the survey to “gain a comprehensive understanding of the basic geology and sea floor structure characteristics of waters under China’s jurisdiction”, the report said, adding that it would provide a “scientific basis for China to carry out comprehensive governance of its jurisdictional waters” in the area. The ministry in June dispatched oceanographic research vessel Xiangyanghong 22 also to waters east of Taiwan, saying it was aimed at studying local ecological conditions as part of marine conservation efforts. But it was viewed as an effort by Beijing to exercise control in the waters following maritime boundary talks between Manila and Tokyo in May. Japan and the Philippines do not share maritime borders but their extended continental-shelf claims overlap in waters east of Taiwan, where Beijing maintains its own exclusive economic zone and continental-shelf rights. China’s foreign ministry has called the boundary talks “illegal and void”. Taiwan’s Coast Guard Administration last week said Beijing had deployed a record number of coastguard, scientific research and other ships near Taiwan’s waters last month, warning of an increasingly severe situation. Beijing’s increased activity has also drawn concern from the US and European governments, which said the actions threatened regional stability and the freedom of navigation and safety of international shipping. Washington also called the actions “destabilising”. Beijing rejected the criticism, saying the patrols were lawful and necessary to safeguard its maritime rights and regional order.

title: Feng shui and art guide a 1,400 sq ft Hong Kong apartment’s redesign
description: To optimise energy flow, interior designer Quinn Wong reworked the Ho Man Tin flat using clever design and indigo blue threads.
content: What do you do when your feng shui master declares that your front door sits in the wrong place – but moving it is impossible because of strict building rules? Such was the dilemma facing Suki Tai, the young director of her family’s textile business. Her new 1,400 sq ft (130 square metre) flat in Ho Man Tin, Kowloon, was her first solo home, and when she bought it she had not anticipated that good fortune would hinge on a door. For help, she turned to her friend, interior designer Quinn Wong of Studio Quinn, for a little design alchemy. “The feng shui element was very strong and perhaps the biggest challenge of this project,” recalls Wong, who grew up between Australia and Hong Kong and set up her eponymous design studio in 2024. “We had multiple conversations about how best to incorporate it into the interior since there were so many boxes to tick and balance, including building regulations, the apartment layout and design aesthetics,” she says, “and all of this incredibly detailed planning meant the project took a year to complete.” To remedy the entrance issue, Wong created a partition wall facing the front door, carving out a small transitional hallway. She then framed the threshold between this foyer and the main living and dining area in a bold indigo-blue surround – larger than the front door and with a slightly raised step. “By becoming the ‘main’ entrance, the frame sidestepped the compromised feng shui posed by the front door and also introduces the dining space in a very dramatic way,” Wong says. “The colour won the feng shui master’s approval, as he felt the apartment was lacking the water element, and it fit with Suki’s taste, too.” The indigo shade became a visual thread throughout the home. It reappears as shelving in Tai’s study, on a custom-made sofa and sideboard, and along dado-height panelling in the main bedroom. The panelling offers both style and flexibility – which Wong needed so she could follow the feng shui master’s recommendation to change the bedroom layout every year. “Due to the positioning of the doorway and windows, there are only two walls the bed can be positioned against. The blue panels act as a sort of extended headboard, providing cohesion whatever the configuration,” Wong says. “Additionally, all the furniture is loose [the bedroom also features a reading area] and the bed is deliberately light and easy to move.” The colour also came to the rescue elsewhere, drawing attention away from what Wong describes as a “perfectly nice but rather nondescript timber flooring” inherited from the developer. “The flooring is the biggest aspect of the apartment but, as it was brand new, it would have been wasteful to pull it all up, and I advised Suki to spend her budget elsewhere,” she says. Similarly, Wong united the kitchen and bathrooms, installed by the developer, with the rest of the flat by incorporating similar materials – wood and marble – to maintain a sense of flow. Originally laid out as a three-bedroom, three-bathroom flat, the apartment lacked generous living space. Wong repurposed the third bathroom as a corridor that separates private and public zones. To stop it from feeling enclosed, she introduced open shelving to let in light from the dining room and added an aquarium as a feature, again complying with feng shui recommendations. Not quite as expected, a sculptural rock rather than fish sits within it. “I didn’t want the upkeep of fish but needed more water in the apartment,” Tai says. “Quinn came up with some imaginative and inspired details – my plants are also all water-based – that helped me to incorporate items stipulated by the feng shui master without the decor looking too rooted in the ancient practice.” Having turned the second bedroom into a study, with a daybed for guests, Tai decided to transform the third into a dressing room. Wong used a combination of materials and art deco details – inspired by the flat’s balcony balustrades – to ensure the latter did not feel boxy or monotonous. Tai’s impressive contemporary art collection further influenced the interior palette. Though she initially envisaged a minimalist aesthetic, she quickly warmed to Wong’s suggestion of drawing colours from her artworks into lighting, wallpaper and soft furnishings. The result balances sophistication and playfulness, much like Tai herself. “I initially wanted a neutral and minimal interior, but by the end of the project, I was asking Quinn to add more colour and pattern because I loved it so much,” she admits with a laugh. title: Businessman acquitted in murder of Malta journalist that brought down government
description: Jury acquits Yorgen Fenech, accused by prosecutors of masterminding 2017 car-bomb killing of Daphne Caruana Galizia.
content: A Maltese court on Wednesday acquitted tycoon Yorgen Fenech of orchestrating the car-bomb killing of investigative reporter Daphne Caruana Galizia, sparking outrage from her family and media freedom advocates. The wealthy businessman had stood accused of masterminding the 2017 assassination of 53-year-old Caruana Galizia, which sparked unprecedented protests and brought down a government. Caruana Galizia’s family said in a statement that Fenech’s acquittal was “denying her the justice she deserves”. Her son Matthew Caruana Galizia said jurors had made a “terrible decision... that our country may never recover from”. The European Centre for Press and Media Freedom said the verdict sent “a disturbing message to those who attack and kill journalists”. Dubbed a “one-woman WikiLeaks”, Caruana Galizia had exposed corruption at the highest level in the country, shining a spotlight on murky links between Malta’s business and political elites. Her slaying shocked the world and put Malta, the European Union’s smallest member state, in the spotlight over its apparent rule-of-law failings. The killing also led to a political crisis, and the resignation of then-premier Joseph Muscat in January 2020 after widespread anger and mass protests over his perceived efforts to protect friends and allies from the investigation. A two-year public inquiry published in July 2021 concluded that the state should “shoulder responsibility” for the murder due to the “atmosphere of impunity” the government had created. Fenech, a tycoon whose business interests spanned the energy and tourism sectors, was arrested on his yacht in 2019 as he tried to sail out of Malta after a middleman in the murder was offered a pardon to identify those involved. Prosecutors had accused Fenech of ordering the journalist to be killed because she was on the brink of publishing a compromising article about his uncle. Five people have been convicted so far in relation to the murder for supplying the explosives and carrying out the killing. In June 2025, Robert Agius and Jamie Vella were convicted of supplying the bomb that killed Caruana Galizia and sentenced to life in prison. The three men who carried out the murder - brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio together with Vince Muscat - are serving prison sentences after being found guilty of their role. A 437-page report written by a panel of three judges in 2021 found that the state had shirked its duty to protect Caruana Galizia and subjected her to personal attacks and verbal abuse from politicians. The atmosphere created a “favourable climate” for her assassination, and there was “convincing evidence” that her killers knew they would be protected by “persons in the highest state positions”. “Accountability is now overdue for all those who enabled, facilitated, or protected her murderers,” the family said in their statement on Tuesday. “Nine years after Daphne’s brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed.” Media watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) said it was “beyond outraged”. “The verdict means that almost nine years since the assassination of Daphne Caruana Galizia, the Maltese authorities have failed to identify and convict the mastermind. “Full justice must be served and Maltese authorities must implement the long overdue measures protecting journalists and media freedom,” it added. The Maltese government issued a statement saying it “took note” of the verdict and was “committed to ensuring that justice is served”.

title: Meet the other OFWs offering humorous takes on ‘crazy’ life in Philippines’ Makati
description: Young workers, drawn by the financial district’s expatriate-style amenities, satirise the high costs while navigating its hustle culture.
content: Young professionals in Makati City are humorously redefining OFW as “overworked” or “on-site” Filipino workers, parodying the high costs and urban convenience of Metro Manila’s premier financial district. In the Philippines, OFW generally refers to overseas Filipino workers who move abroad in search of better opportunities and pay. But recently, the initialism has been given a new meaning by some Makati residents who post social media reels chronicling their expatriate-style lifestyle, complete with the city’s skyscrapers, manicured parks and coffee shops. The videos also satirise aspects of OFW life, with tongue-in-cheek lines about homesickness and working hard to provide for the family. “The idea came from my own experience,” said Nick Tumbagahan, who has documented a day in his life as an “OFW” – leaving his Makati condominium, walking to his morning coffee spot, heading to the office, then unwinding after work at the gym. The native of Bacolod City in the central Philippines was a seafarer overseas before moving to Makati for work. “Like many people in Makati, I left home in search of better opportunities. One day, I jokingly referred to myself as an ‘OFW in Makati’ and it resonated,” Tumbagahan said. The trend offers a snapshot of everyday life for city workers and urban dwellers, from local parks and popular running routes to affordable lunch places in the business district. One of Tumbagahan’s videos showcased a go-to lunch spot at a shopping centre’s basement selling budget meals for 95 pesos (US$1.52), garnering thousands of views. The ‘overseas’ costs The idea of being an “OFW in Makati” has resonated with residents in part because of the stark contrast between living and working in one of the country’s most expensive urban centres. “It’s funny because it’s true,” said Justine Poblete-Delos Reyes, who has lived on the outskirts of Makati’s central business district for two years. “Makati feels like a different world and the cost of living is crazy.” She moved to the city after her husband, a lawyer, found a job nearby. They welcomed a baby last year, making the question of settling down in Makati over the long term more pressing. “We’d like to own our own property, but I don’t think it’s feasible here because it’s so expensive,” she said. “But we are content where we are now. There’s a community here and it’s family-friendly.” Makati City accounted for 5.5 per cent of the national economy in 2025, generating a gross domestic product of 1.27 trillion pesos, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority. Land scarcity has driven up property values and rents in hubs such as Makati, with prime land values averaging 1 million pesos per square metre, according to Joey Roi Bondoc, director and head of research at Colliers Philippines. A one-bedroom condominium unit could cost 248,000 pesos per square metre, Bondoc said. “The concentration of premium residential developments, malls, schools and healthcare facilities also contributes to higher living expenses in these locations,” he added. The city had also become a popular choice for expatriates, Bondoc said, as well as “high-level executives, entrepreneurs, young professionals and investors seeking premium locations” close to workplaces and schools. Wealth gap Lurking beneath all Makati’s conveniences is a wide income disparity, according to Michael Ricafort, chief economist at Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation. “The wealthiest families also reside near those CBDs, thereby explaining the large inequality compared with fringe areas,” he said. Makati’s property market is evolving as the Philippines has become one of the world’s least affordable places to buy a home, compared to local incomes, with 55 per cent of respondents saying they struggled to afford housing in Gallup’s 2025 World Poll. Condominium prices in Metro Manila reached 19.8 times the median annual household income in 2024, a study last year by the Urban Land Institute found, far exceeding its affordability threshold of five times annual income. House prices in towns were even less affordable, at 33.4 times the median annual income, said the institute, which has its regional headquarters in Hong Kong. While many of Makati’s daytime workforce commute from outside the city, those who choose convenience over hours spent in traffic are often forced to rent. Eric Gonzales, a data privacy consultant, shares a one-bedroom unit with his partner, who works as a social media manager, paying 26,000 pesos per month in the upscale Salcedo Village neighbourhood, which he said was “quite cheap for this area”. “Our rent could eat up half of one’s salary, even more if you factor in the electric bill, Wi-fi and association dues. It’s definitely a challenge financially speaking, but it does help having someone with you for that,” Gonzales said. Gonzales, who used to spend 400 pesos on motorcycle-hailing fees to commute to Makati, said living near his workplace was much easier. “I’m assuming a lot of these people who can afford to live here probably work in corporate jobs that can afford to pay them enough to live here in the first place … so there’s that convenience factor of probably already being closer to work,” he said. He said food, groceries and eating out were also “much more expensive”, but “that’s the price you pay for that extra convenience and being at the centre of it all”. Why they stay Ricafort said the city still had room for improvement, suggesting that better public transport infrastructure could help narrow the property price gap and improve access to areas outside the central business district. “Traffic congestion and longer travel times amid a lack of fast mass transport systems tend to put a premium on those CBDs,” he said. For many Makati residents, however, the city’s work-life balance and lifestyle options still make living there worth the cost. “I live an active lifestyle and there are a lot of options for people who are also in their fitness journey. There are also a lot of good restaurants and the theatre scene is very much alive here,” said Joe Ramos, a lawyer and fitness instructor in the city. “I work hard and people who work hard deserve to enjoy the fruits of their labour.” Ramos said he chose Makati in spite of its hustle culture because everything he enjoyed was in the city, adding that could not afford to lose hours every day to heavy traffic. “Work is hard, so finding some levity around your work situation can help manage the stress. It doesn’t have to be taken too seriously, and sometimes you can even find helpful tips on things to do or cheap finds,” he said. While Tumbagahan said Makati could be hectic, “it’s also where I’ve built my career, friendships, routines and opportunities”, he added. “I joke about it a lot through the OFW in Makati content, but that’s also because I’ve genuinely enjoyed calling it home.”

title: On the Menu | I’m in my ‘just fine’ dining era, and no-fuss neighbourhood restaurants are all I need
description: In the era of best this and top that, ‘just fine’ works just as well, in my opinion. Great restaurants don’t need awards or influencer kudos.
content: I don’t know who needs to hear this, but sometimes it is OK to be ordinary. I am talking about restaurants that make great food and create a comfortable environment for its diners, but have neither the ambition nor the so-called skill to gain a spot on the multiple award lists around the world, or to – God forbid – land itself in a well-meaning reel of the influencer du jour. Or maybe put it this way: I am bored with everything being touted as the next viral moment, the must-try, the “run, don’t walk” destination that you simply must visit before you perish. Inevitably, places become inundated with portable-light-toting vloggers who tend to hype up the food so much it often feels like the restaurant is set up to fail. It is also strange when this kind of hyperbole falls upon neighbourhood staples that have served regulars for decades. I am in two minds about this: on the one hand, it is fantastic when a humble family-run restaurant gets more attention. On the other, more often than not they were doing just fine on their own, supported by a community of local diners, who suddenly find it much harder to get a seat at the table. ‘Oh my gawd you guys’, expecting every meal to be life changing is extremely exhausting for everyone involved Charmaine Mok I am not saying smaller venues should not be held in the same regard as a high-end restaurant, recognised in guides and immortalised in dramatic slow-mo cinematography; surely, every accolade helps prolong its lifespan in an increasingly challenging climate. But there is a distinct frustration when this hype machine descends upon a humble neighbourhood staple. While any independent joint deserves financial survival, the disconnect between internet hyperbole and real life leaves expectant diners deflated. “How did this place get one Michelin star?” they declare incredulously, unaware of the possibility that the restaurant never even asked for it in the first place. Anyway, I would hazard that most of these places would just be as happy chugging along catering to a steady stream of regulars who would ask about their day, not an obnoxious creator letting the hot food go cold as they adjust their gimbals. I am not sure when we all expected every meal to be transcendent. As long as the food is cooked as expected, the drinks are cold and the staff are happy, a great meal should be more about the people and the conversation around the table than anything else. Because, “oh my gawd you guys”, expecting every meal to be life changing is extremely exhausting for everyone involved. Is there a culinary equivalent of lying flat?

title: Creative industry mourns Hong Kong advertising ‘queen’ Kitty Lun
description: Tributes pour in for advertising veteran and Meta creative leader, who was behind some of the city’s best-known public service campaigns.
content: The global advertising industry is mourning the death of Meta Greater China creative shop chief Kitty Lun Kit-ying, who drowned in a swimming pool at a residential complex in Hong Kong earlier this week. A source close to the investigation confirmed on Thursday that Lun was identified as the 70-year-old woman who died after drowning in the pool of Ville De Cascade in Fo Tan on Monday. She was seen swimming at about 5.20pm that day and was later pulled unconscious from the pool. Resuscitation was attempted before she was rushed to Prince of Wales Hospital, where she was pronounced dead, the source said. Crowned the “Queen of Public Service Advertising in Hong Kong”, Lun masterminded several campaigns over the course of her career that became familiar to Hong Kong households. Her most recent role was head of Meta Creative Shop for Greater China. “Kitty championed the creative and advertising community throughout her career, and she was a visionary leader who shaped our creative direction and nurtured our people over the years,” a Meta representative said on Thursday. “She will be remembered for her exceptional talent, kindness and generosity, and for the profound impact she had on all who had the privilege of working with her.” Born and raised in Hong Kong, Lun studied communication at the city’s Baptist University before moving to Syracuse University in New York to pursue a master’s degree in advertising. Her best-known work included a television advertising series for the Independent Commission Against Corruption. The series, known as “Our Advantage Is ICAC”, featured absurd scenarios in which a voice-over described images of a deer as a horse, a black screen as “white” and vice versa, and a cup of contaminated water as clean, illustrating the dangers of corruption. Another of Lun’s well-known campaigns was “Life has no Take 2”, created for the government’s youth crime prevention initiative. In a ceremony speech for Baptist University’s communication school in June, Lun urged graduates to move beyond “accuracy” and towards “truth” by engaging with daily life and connecting with people in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). “I use AI every day. It’s amazing at ‘what’. It analyses data, it gathers information, it generates, it iterates, it translates and it optimises,” she said. “But it cannot come with me to Mong Kok, and talk to young juvenile delinquents and the young drug addicts, and listen to their lives, their helplessness and what desperation they were having.” LIA Chinese Creativity, a global awards show created by the London International Awards that celebrates top Chinese-language advertising, also paid tribute to Lun on Thursday. “We are deeply saddened by the passing of Kitty Lun, one of Hong Kong’s most respected advertising and creative leaders,” it said. “Throughout her remarkable career, Kitty created countless memorable works and inspired generations of advertising professionals with her creativity, passion and dedication to the industry.” Fellow advertising industry leader Chris Kyme also spoke highly of his long-time colleague, saying: “Kitty Lun was probably unrivalled as a Hong Kong-bred creative leader, female or not, who just kept powering her way across the industry.”

title: Unstable Tibetan Plateau risks cascading disasters as glacier losses mount in Nepal, China
description: Experts find downstream erosion is critical to scale of destruction as death toll continues to rise from China-Nepal landslide and floods.
content: Glaciers on the Tibetan Plateau are likely to become more unstable, which may lead to more collapses and collateral disasters, a senior climate official warns as the death toll from last week’s catastrophic landslide and flood on the China-Nepal border continues to rise. “Over the past 60 years, the glacier area on the Tibetan Plateau has shrunk by around 24 per cent, with around 7,000 small glaciers disappearing completely,” Gao Rong, deputy director of China’s National Climate Centre, said on Wednesday. “Looking ahead, the structural stability of glaciers across the Tibetan Plateau will decline further. Glacial disasters are likely to become more frequent and could amplify in destruction and reach through cascading effects.” As of Wednesday, China had reported 21 people dead and 541 missing following a glacier collapsed at Langtang Lirung on the Nepalese side of the border on August 26. In Nepal, the death toll rose to 1,252 as of 10am Thursday, with about 4,875 people still missing. Beijing has stepped up cross-border support to its neighbour. Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on Wednesday that China’s second batch of emergency supplies arrived in Kathmandu on Tuesday afternoon, accompanied by five DNA identification experts. A third shipment and a second expert team were being prepared. After working for seven days, Beijing on Wednesday cleared the road to Gyirong Port, which was hit hardest on the Chinese side by the mudslide. Heavy machinery has reached the checkpoint area to aid a deeper search. The mudslide created by the glacier collapse travelled 22km (13.7 miles) along the valley and reached the Gyirong Port border crossing in just seven minutes, according to an initial assessment last week. Scientists stress that hazard evaluations can no longer rely solely on measuring initial collapses. A study released on Tuesday, led by the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, alongside the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Wuhan University and other institutions, found that downstream erosion was critical to the scale of destruction. Analysing satellite and field data from Gyirong county, researchers found that collapsing ice and rock swept down the 22km valley, scouring the riverbed, dragging bank debris with it, and mixing with water, turning a high-elevation collapse into a devastating mudslide. Therefore, the Chinese research suggested, disaster risk assessment in the high-mountain cryosphere – or frozen areas – must look beyond the initial failure volume of material breaking away from the mountain, and include the valley bulking potential – the capacity to increase the size of a landslide as it travels downhill – and downstream exposure. “What truly determines risk is not just how much collapsed on the mountain, but how much can be entrained in the gully, and what critical infrastructure and populations downstream are exposed to the hazard chain,” it said. An article published in Nature on Wednesday highlighted the urgent need to upgrade future monitoring and forecasting systems. The disaster proved difficult to predict because it was triggered by the sudden failure of a high-altitude glacier-rock system rather than typical signals, such as extreme rainfall or rising glacial lakes, according to the article. Manoochehr Shirzaei, a geophysicist at Virginia Tech in Blacksburg, told Nature that conventional monitoring tools fell short in predicting such disasters, and stressed the need to have better integrated detection systems. The article said: “What is still largely missing is a regional satellite-based system that routinely searches for accelerating glacier and rock-slope deformation and then connects that information directly to downstream flood and avalanche modelling.”

title: Hong Kong Education Bureau urges schools to prioritise student needs in regulations
description: Schools face scrutiny after incidents involving strict uniform and grooming inspections that affect students.
content:
Hong Kong’s education officials have urged a school to take into account the needs of students while implementing regulations. This reminder follows an incident where many students had to stand in a lengthy queue outside the school in the rain to have their uniforms and hairstyles inspected on the first day of the new academic year.
Similarly, the Education Bureau addressed another school where students who were found not adhering to hair grooming standards were required to stay on campus until they were able to reach their parents.
Dozens of online posts showed a long queue of students standing outside the campus of Kowloon Tong School (Secondary Section) on Tuesday, with some claiming they were waiting for teachers to inspect their uniforms and hair.
Teresa Hon Pui-yee, the school principal, sent a letter to parents later that day defending the inspections, although she noted the school had since reviewed the process.
“In order to establish discipline, cultivate students’ sense of responsibility, and prepare for the student photo shoot on Thursday, class teachers reminded all parents and students [last] Saturday that the school would conduct a uniform inspection on Tuesday,” she said.
However, she explained that because a relatively large number of students arrived at a later time on Tuesday, they were required to queue outside the campus to wait. She pledged that students would not be marked as late if they tapped their cards when school started.
Hon maintained that students should arrive at school early to ensure sufficient time to hand in assignments and prepare learning materials, which she said would help their education and physical and mental well-being.
A bureau spokeswoman said it contacted the school to follow up on the situation.
“The Education Bureau reminded the school to consider students’ actual needs when enforcing school rules and to make appropriate school-based arrangements,” she said.
“The Education Bureau will maintain contact with the school concerned and provide suitable advice and support.”
In a separate incident involving Kowloon’s Tang King Po School, posts on a social media platform claimed that it not only enforced strict grooming rules, but also required students who did not meet the standards to remain on campus while they contacted their parents to inform them of the situation.
Some posts claimed that about 300 students were sent to the school hall and had to call their parents before they were allowed to leave.
According to some posts, the school required that hair not cover eyebrows or ears, nor touch the collar at the back.
The boys’ school has been approached for comment.
The bureau spokeswoman said it contacted the school and also reminded it to consider students’ actual needs.
“Under all circumstances, school staff should maintain discipline while respecting students’ self-esteem, right to education, individual differences and health,” she said.
Schools should draft rules that foster student self-discipline, but formulate them through communication with stakeholders to ensure understanding and consensus, she added.

title: Venezuela’s Maduro seeks dismissal of US charges, citing immunity
description: Nicolas Maduro’s lawyer says head-of-state immunity bars US prosecution over drug trafficking charges.
content: Ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro urged a US judge on Wednesday to dismiss criminal drug trafficking charges against him, arguing he should be immune from prosecution as the head of a sovereign country. The charges, filed in Manhattan federal court, formed the basis for the US military’s raid on Caracas and capture of Maduro on January 3. The Venezuelan leader, who has been held ‌in a Brooklyn federal jail since his seizure, has pleaded not guilty and is scheduled to go on trial on June 1, 2027, if his effort to dismiss the case is unsuccessful. The principle that sitting heads of state are immune from prosecution abroad is a long-standing tenet of international law seen as fundamental to diplomacy. Maduro’s push to persuade Manhattan-based US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to dismiss the case will test US courts’ general reluctance to apply international law in criminal cases. Maduro’s lawyer, Barry Pollack, made the assertion of immunity in a motion to dismiss Maduro’s indictment. Hellerstein had given Pollack a deadline of Wednesday to file the motion. Pollack ⁠said Hellerstein lacked jurisdiction both because sovereign heads of state enjoyed complete immunity and because the acts that Maduro is accused of would have been part of his official duties. “This ‌unprecedented prosecution violates the absolute immunity from criminal jurisdiction to which heads of state and foreign officials acting in their official capacities have been entitled for hundreds of years,” Pollack wrote. Pequeño regalo de amor y esperanza Envío estas fotos como un pequeño regalo a todos mis nietos y nietas, a los niños y niñas, y a toda la gente noble que nos ama. pic.twitter.com/Z6u3130arn — Nicolás Maduro (@NicolasMaduro) August 30, 2026 Pollack wrote that Maduro was falsely accused and “vehemently denies” the allegations. A spokesperson for the ‌Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Legal experts have told Reuters ⁠that Maduro faces an uphill battle. Washington ⁠has not recognised Maduro as Venezuela’s president since 2019, and courts tend to defer to the US president and his cabinet in disputes over who is recognised as a foreign country’s leader. US criminal cases involving heads ‌of foreign states are extremely rare, but precedent offers little encouragement for Maduro. In 1990, a federal judge in Miami rejected former Panamanian military leader Manuel Noriega’s attempt to assert head-of-state immunity in part because he never officially held the ‌title of ‌president. The United States stopped recognising Maduro in 2019, when he was inaugurated after a 2018 election the US said was rigged. The US also called his 2024 re-election ‌fraudulent. Maduro says both votes were fair and has long accused Washington of seeking his ouster to gain control of the South American country’s oil wealth. Pollack wrote that Washington’s assessment ⁠that Maduro lacked legitimacy was not relevant. “Unlike in Noriega, the Executive Branch does not dispute that Mr. Maduro was Venezuela’s head of state, but instead merely claims that, after ⁠2019, he did not occupy that position legitimately,” Pollack wrote. Since Maduro’s capture, his vice-president and socialist ally Delcy Rodriguez has run Venezuela and increased cooperation with the Trump administration. Last month, the two countries reached an unprecedented deal that would see the US take over around ‌one-fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves. Pollack wrote that ‌it was “incongruous” for the United States to recognise Rodriguez, who was appointed by Maduro, and not Maduro. He pointed to statements by Rodriguez and officials in her government in January and February indicating that they still considered Maduro Venezuela’s legitimate head of state. Rodriguez’s government has since gone silent on the matter. Some murals of Maduro in Caracas have been painted over in recent months. Prosecutors have until October 2 to respond to Maduro’s motion to dismiss the indictment, and Hellerstein will hold a hearing on the dismissal effort on November 17.

title: Review | Venice 2026: Ink movie review – Danny Boyle charts the gritty birth of The Sun newspaper
description: Ink tells the story of Rupert Murdoch’s takeover of UK newspaper The Sun and its transformation into the popular tabloid aimed at the working class.
content: 3.5/5 stars Set in a seedy 1960s world of smoky pubs and grimy snooker halls, where deals are done on napkins, Danny Boyle’s Ink is a stark reminder of how British media changed forever with the creation of The Sun. Opening this year’s Venice International Film Festival, this latest venture from Slumdog Millionaire director Boyle comes adapted by James Graham from his own play. Not that you would know it; there is nothing theatrical about Boyle’s staging here. Initially taking centre stage in Boyle’s film is prickly entrepreneur Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce, playing him with good grace), who buys the ailing paper from the Mirror Group back when it had no real identity. In comes editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell), a former hack at the highly successful Daily Mirror, who – under Murdoch’s instructions – creates a newspaper designed to appeal to ordinary, working-class men and women. Typically, characters are introduced with on-screen titles carrying their names – a trick Boyle previously pulled off in his landmark Irvine Welsh adaptation Trainspotting (1996), which shares a similar energy to Ink. Among the most significant is Jules Davies (Claire Foy), a fictionalised amalgam of various women who worked on Fleet Street, where all British newspapers were once based. Here, she battles ingrained sexism as she suggests to Lamb what women might want to read. Assembling his team like George Clooney putting together a gang of criminals in Ocean’s Eleven, Lamb brainstorms his vision for The Sun, a populist paper that prioritises sport, television coverage and scantily clad women on Page 3. Even the design of the paper shakes things up, with italics used to emphasise ‘The Sun’ on the masthead. No, argues Lamb, the sloped typeface is not slouching; “It’s [like] Gene Kelly in Singin’ in the Rain.” Despite a fractious relationship with Murdoch (who argues “We want our readers to feel alive”), Lamb anchors the film, as desperate to give the British establishment a kick up the backside as he is to boost sales. O’Connell plays him vividly, fresh off his controversial role as Sir Jimmy in Boyle’s 28 Years Later. Arguably, amid the nostalgic shots of rattling printing presses, the film does not dive deep enough into what The Sun contributed to the dumbing down of popular culture. It also features bizarre dreamlike sequences that fall flat, meaning it is never quite the super soaraway movie Boyle intended. However, he is a skilled enough director to keep viewers engaged to the very end of this tabloid shaggy-dog tale. Want more articles like this? Follow SCMP Film on Facebook

title: Letters | China-Nepal floods: engineering fixes are only a band-aid
description: Readers discuss the best long-term defence against Himalayan disasters, the Iran war, and the Ukraine war.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. Every monsoon season, the Himalayan regions of Tibet and Nepal face the threat of recurring, destructive debris flows. These mud-and-rock avalanches are not purely random natural disasters. They stem from inherently fragile mountain geology, extreme terrain and increasingly unstable climatic conditions – risks steadily aggravated by human-induced environmental degradation and global warming. The fundamental geological vulnerability comes from long-term tectonic movement. As the Indian plate continuously pushes northward into the Eurasian plate, the Himalayan bedrock remains permanently fractured and loose. The 2015 Nepal earthquake significantly worsened this fragility. Post-event satellite mapping recorded over 24,000 landslides across central and western Nepal. Importantly, most fractured hillsides did not collapse immediately. Seismic weakness lingers for years, turning routine monsoon rain into repeated debris-flow triggers. Steep valley topography amplifies the danger. Climate change has now become the most concerning accelerating factor. Intense monsoon downpours saturate already fractured slopes, while rising temperatures speed up Himalayan glacier retreat. This creates hundreds of unstable glacial lakes held together by weak natural embankments. Events such as the 2021 Sindhupalchowk flood and the 2025 Gyirong debris flow demonstrate how climate change is turning rare disasters into recurring threats. Engineering measures certainly help reduce harm. Controlled glacial lake drainage, slope stabilisation works, early-warning systems and careful land-use planning can shield communities from immediate danger. Yet infrastructure can only mitigate damage; it cannot fix the root environmental and climatic drivers. The clearest lesson from years of repeated Himalayan disasters is simple: sustained environmental protection is the most effective long-term defence. Healthy mountain ecosystems stabilise slopes naturally through vegetation cover, root structures and soil retention. Deforestation, unregulated hill construction and ecological disturbance weaken this natural protection, leaving slopes far more vulnerable to collapse during heavy rain. Meanwhile, human-caused global warming continues to destabilise glaciers, expanding high-risk glacial lakes year by year. Protecting alpine forests, restoring mountain vegetation, limiting disruptive highland development and slowing global warming can gradually reduce slope fragility and cut disaster frequency. Engineering protects communities when hazards strike. But preserving nature prevents these disasters from happening in the first place. P.L. Yuen, past president of the Hong Kong Institution of Engineers Does Trump remember how the Pearl Harbour attack started? I refer to “Trump declares ‘mission accomplished’ in Iran as conflict drags on” (August 27). US President Donald Trump’s delusional “mission accomplished” claim will have little or no credibility internationally and at home in America. On the contrary, for most observers, it is hard to see how his threatening, bullying strategy of economic asphyxiation could succeed in defeating Iran. History has some harsh lessons on the use of such aggressive economic strategies by nations to get what they want. In 1941, an allied embargo against Japan led by the United States to force Tokyo to abandon its imperial ambitions in Southeast Asia helped to trigger the attack on Pearl Harbour and the beginning of the Pacific War. Trump and his supporters would be wise to be careful what they wish for in pursuing the strategy. In any case, it may be too late for this desperate strategy to succeed. Terry Hewton, South Australia China’s urging or not, Putin is unlikely to end war I refer to “Zelensky urges China to use its diplomatic weight to end Russia’s war with Ukraine” (August 26). In 1967, the Israeli politician Abba Eban said, “Men and nations behave wisely when they have exhausted all other resources.” Obviously the latter may take years or even decades. Recall the Bosnian war (1992–1995), Iran-Iraq war (1980–1988), Vietnam war (1954–1975) and even the Thirty Years’ war (1618–1648) in Central Europe. I can’t imagine Russian President Vladimir Putin eating his leek with a wry smile and signing a treaty now, when he has rejected peace talks. There may be a remote possibility of Volodymyr Zelensky sewing his case up if the Kremlin has a new leader. In the meantime, the Ukrainian president’s appeals to China count for nothing. Mergen Mongush, Moscow

title: Mainland Chinese investors buy Hong Kong tech stocks in AI pivot, sell financials
description: Net buying surges for third straight month as AI pivot benefits MiniMax, Alibaba and Tencent, while investors eschew traditional industries.
content: Chinese mainland investors rotated into Hong Kong stocks tied to artificial intelligence and pulled out of companies in traditional industries in August, taking advantage of a market dip to boost bets on the world’s most cutting-edge technology. AI model developer MiniMax Group logged net buying of HK$10.1 billion (US$1.29 billion) last month, the most among the Hong Kong-listed companies available for China’s onshore investors through southbound trading within the cross-border Stock Connect scheme, according to financial data provider Wind. Alibaba Group Holding and Tencent Holdings, the Chinese hyperscalers that have ramped up AI adoption, ranked second and third, attracting buying of HK$7.86 billion and HK$6.72 billion, respectively. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor, China Construction Bank, China Life Insurance and Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) were among those that bore the brunt of selling, the data showed. The shift underscored the appeal of Chinese technology stocks trading in Hong Kong after the latest results from chipmaker Nvidia indicated that demand for AI infrastructure remained robust in spite of rising funding costs. The Hang Seng Tech Index dropped 4.3 per cent last month, offering a dip-buying opportunity to mainland traders, who currently account for about 30 per cent of stock transactions in the city. Yangtze Optical Fibre and Cable Joint Stock, MiniMax’s rival Z.ai, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp and Xiaomi were also among mainland investors’ most favoured stocks, luring inflows ranging from HK$1.6 billion to HK$3.2 billion, according to the Wind data. Meanwhile, Hua Hong led the list of most-sold stocks, as China’s onshore traders let go of HK$3 billion worth of shares last month. Meituan, the biggest on-demand delivery firm in China, came second with net selling of HK$2 billion amid stiff competition in the food delivery segment. China Construction Bank, China Life and ICBC saw outflows ranging from HK$579 million to HK$1.03 billion, the data showed. Pop Mart International, the maker of the popular Labubu toys and other collectibles, suffered net selling of HK$600 million, as its latest results showed slowing sales. Sector-wise, information technology attracted the most net buying at HK$21.8 billion, while financial firms were the least favoured, with an outflow of HK$15.4 billion. Mainland investors poured a total of HK$10.4 billion into Hong Kong stocks in August for a third consecutive month of net buying. However, buying momentum moderated from the previous month’s inflow of HK$62.9 billion. Hong Kong stocks could trade sideways in a narrow range in the near future, as the market contended with China’s deployment of fiscal spending, a scheduled summit between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump and a decision on interest rates from the US Federal Reserve expected later this month, according to CGS International.

title: Low jet flyover of packed Cape Town stadium sparks South Africa safety probe
description: South Africa’s aviation regulator is reviewing flight data after daring Airlink manoeuvre before Springboks match.
content: A low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger jets before a rugby match at Cape Town’s DHL Stadium is being reviewed by South African aviation authorities after it drew safety concerns, officials said on Wednesday. The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it had obtained flight data recordings and requested additional information from regional carrier Airlink as part of its assessment. A full report with recommendations would be issued once the review was complete. “It is therefore critical that we interrogate this past weekend’s events … to determine if there were any safety concerns which warrant a review,” the agency said in a statement. Airlink has withdrawn plans for another flyover at the coming rugby match in Soweto, according to the SACAA, which is responsible for regulating aviation safety and security. The flyover ahead of the Springboks-All Blacks rugby match on August 29 drew huge cheers from an estimated crowd of about 56,000, but also sparked a debate over the safety risks after video footage by spectators inside and around the stadium spread online. Deandra Peters, 25, a pilot and aviation enthusiast attending her first live rugby match, said the crowd in the stadium was electrified by the spectacle in a way that was difficult to capture on video. Planning. Precision. Performance. ✈️✈️ Spectacular scenes of Airlink’s double Embraer flyover at the DHL Stadium. Airlink is Proud Official Sponsor of Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry, presented by Castle Double Malt 🏉#Airlink #FlyAirlink #FlyTheLink #Skybucks #RugbysGreatestRivalry pic.twitter.com/3tPNepftLS — Airlink (@Fly_Airlink) August 29, 2026 “You can watch the planes fly over, but you can’t recreate what it felt like to be inside a stadium full of Springbok supporters absolutely losing their minds,” she told Associated Press. “The atmosphere was electric – the noise, the pride, the emotion. It was a very uniquely South African moment.” Airlink on Wednesday said the manoeuvre had been carefully planned and rehearsed and that safety was “the first consideration at every stage of the process”. It said each aircraft had three senior captains aboard, with more than 75,000 combined flight hours across the crews. Earlier this week, Airlink had provided the data from the planes’ black boxes to the civil aviation authority for review. The SACAA said it would examine flight data to determine whether any safety concerns warranted a review. The airline acknowledged the enthusiasm generated by the spectacle while also recognising what it described as the “valid questions and concerns” that followed. “We never intended to become the news or upstage Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry,” Airlink CEO de Villiers Engelbrecht said in a statement. look how low this flyover looked. two airlink passenger jets just flew over dhl stadium in cape town ahead of the springboks vs. all blacks match. pic.twitter.com/5r5nB1j9ti — Michael Rusch (@weeddude) August 29, 2026 The regulator said the airline had made applications for three flyovers. The most recent one in Cape Town was the second, while the first flyover took place in Johannesburg on August 22. Both were approved in line with the requirements for special air events. Airlink has withdrawn its application for a flyover scheduled for September 1, over Johannesburg’s FNB Stadium. The airline said forecast weather conditions were unfavourable for a safe formation flyby. SACAA confirmed that the application had been withdrawn. South African rugby has a long tradition of stadium fly-bys at major matches, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept over Ellis Park before the Springboks faced the All Blacks. Last Saturday’s fly-by was unusually low and dramatic, drawing international attention, with some aviation experts later questioning whether the aircraft had left too little margin for error. Global flight tracking service Flightradar24 said its analysis showed the lead aircraft was at one point about 12.5 to 14 metres (41-46 feet) above the stadium’s highest structure. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

title: China’s Xi seeks trade routes in Egypt, Central Asia to bypass tariffs and Western rules
description: Presidential tour highlights strategy of shifting manufacturing abroad, shielding domestic exporters from growing global barriers.
content: President Xi Jinping’s journey from Central Asia to Egypt highlights Beijing’s efforts to strengthen alternative trade, energy and manufacturing networks across Eurasia and Africa, analysts said, as wars and tariffs expose a reliance on vulnerable supply routes and overseas markets. Xi arrived in Egypt on Tuesday for his first visit in 10 years after attending a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where state leaders including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to deepen economic and financial ties. According to a joint statement issued by China and Egypt on Thursday, the two sides will explore cooperation in renewable energy, data centres, semiconductors and space applications, as well as critical-mineral supply chains, agriculture and car manufacturing. The two countries also welcomed the renewal and potential expansion of their bilateral currency-swap agreement and called for greater use of the yuan and Egyptian pound in trade and investment settlements. Ahead of Xi’s visit to the North African country, both he and his Egyptian counterpart, President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi, signed op-eds that were published in each other’s leading newspapers, outlining their vision for closer bilateral ties, including expanded Chinese investment in the strategic bridge between Africa and the Middle East. Xi’s journey comes amid a continued US-China tariff war and mounting geopolitical instability, as wars disrupt shipping routes, drive up energy prices, and – together with extreme weather – deepen threats to global food security. The trip reflects a coherent strategy to diversify trade routes and expand access to resources and markets through Central Asia’s overland links and Egypt’s manufacturing base and Suez Canal gateway, according to Su Yue, principal economist for China at the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU). “Alternative trade routes and overseas production give Chinese companies more options and reduce dependence on direct exports from China,” she said. In Xi’s article, which ran on Tuesday in major Egyptian publications, he called for China and Egypt to capitalise on the latter’s strategic position linking the Arab world with Africa and use it to deepen Chinese engagement across both regions, according to a Xinhua readout. On the same day, Sisi’s op-ed ran in People’s Daily, a Communist Party mouthpiece, and said that Cairo aimed to attract more Chinese companies and industries, including manufacturers of electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, renewable energy, electronics, desalination equipment, components and shipbuilding. The two countries should also deepen technology transfers in telecommunications, artificial intelligence and space science, Sisi said, identifying those sectors as priorities for the next stage of bilateral economic and technological cooperation. The Egypt visit followed Xi’s appearance in Bishkek, where he promoted deeper trade, energy and connectivity ties between China and other SCO economies. Xi pledged continued cooperation with member states on solar and wind projects, the development of an AI application centre, and 100 joint science and technology projects over the next three years. China will also support upgrades to the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route – widely known as the Middle Corridor – and establish a centre in Tianjin to promote cooperation among ports and border crossings across SCO member countries, according to a Xinhua readout on Tuesday. A declaration signed by China and the SCO’s other nine members called for reforms to global financial institutions, aiming to give developing countries greater representation and influence at the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. Furthermore, the declaration called for greater use of the bloc’s transit potential, more resilient energy supply chains, and deeper cooperation on agriculture and food security. The offer is transactional: financing and investment without the conditions Western lenders attach Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Ankura Consulting The EIU’s Su said Central Asia’s energy and mineral resources, along with Egypt’s access to African and Middle Eastern markets, formed part of a broader Chinese strategy to localise production and reduce exposure to geopolitical disruptions. But growing trade through third countries could draw greater scrutiny from the United States and European Union over sanctions evasion and transshipment, she warned. There was also a political logic to Beijing’s approach, according to Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China-based managing director at Ankura Consulting. That thinking, he said, entails finding partners to support the institutions and initiatives that China has built to compete with the Western-led order, including Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative and, more recently, its global governance, security, civilisation and development initiatives. “The offer is transactional: financing and investment without the conditions Western lenders attach,” Montufar-Helu said. “At a moment when the US has pulled back from multilateral institutions and is actively disrupting global trade rules, it’s not surprising that the offer resonates across the Global South.” The two relationships are already underpinned by rapidly expanding commerce. China-Egypt goods trade rose 19.7 per cent to US$20.8 billion in 2025, according to Chinese customs data. The surge was said to be largely driven by Chinese exports of machinery and manufactured goods, alongside investment in Egyptian infrastructure and industrial estates. Similarly, China-Kyrgyzstan trade increased 19.8 per cent to US$27.2 billion, dominated by Chinese consumer and industrial exports, while minerals, energy and transport infrastructure remained central to their broader economic relationship. Additional reporting by Mandy Zuo

title: Singapore to host Brazil, Japan, Paraguay in star-studded football festival
description: The Mizuho Blue Challenge will take place at the city’s National Stadium during the Fifa international window in November.
content: Singapore will host a series of blockbuster football fixtures during the Fifa international window in November, including a World Cup rematch between Brazil and Japan, organisers announced on Thursday. The Mizuho Blue Challenge will also involve the hosts and Paraguay, with four matches taking place in the space of five days at the city’s National Stadium at The Kallang. Singapore will take on Paraguay in the opening fixture on November 13, with Japan and Brazil facing off a day later in a rematch of their last 32 clash in Houston, which the South Americans won 2-1. A double-header on November 17, with Singapore taking on the five-time World Cup winners and Japan battling Paraguay, promises to be the highlight of the week at the 55,000-seat venue. In a statement, organisers The Kallang Group and Dentsu Sports International said the event was being backed by the Mizuho Financial Group and would also be part of the Singapore-Japan 60th Anniversary celebrations to commemorate 60 years of diplomatic relations between the two countries. “The Mizuho Blue Challenge – The Kallang Football Series Singapore represents a significant milestone in The Kallang Group’s growth as we evolve from operating venues to creating world-class event properties that Singapore can proudly call its own,” Daryl Yeo, the group’s COO and CEO, said. “As we expand our portfolio of signature events, this inaugural tournament reflects our commitment to bringing premier sporting action to Singapore and creating more opportunities for fans and communities to come together.” Brazil’s players will be making a second trip to Asia inside a matter of weeks, with a game against India on October 3 in Kolkata already pencilled in for the international window that runs from September 21 to October 6.

title: China rivalry ‘no excuse’: US Democrats allege corruption in Trump’s mining deals
description: Lawmakers say strategic competition over critical minerals doesn’t justify abandoning safeguards that prevent funds from being misused.
content: US Democratic lawmakers on Wednesday accused the Donald Trump administration of using the critical minerals contest with China as an excuse for corruption – alleging billions of dollars in deals were enriching the president’s family and friends. “Competition with China is no excuse for abandoning safeguards that prevent taxpayer funds from being misused for private enrichment,” said Linda Sanchez, the Democratic lawmaker from California, at a Ways and Means Committee hearing titled “Strategic Partnerships to Secure Critical Resources and Supply Chains”. “We also cannot say that because China is a strategic competitor, every mining deal is automatically a good deal.” The Trump administration has poured billions of dollars into domestic and overseas mining projects, acquired stakes in US mining companies and established bilateral and international partnerships in a bid to break China’s chokehold on critical mineral supply chains. Beijing holds a near monopoly in the processing of major minerals such as graphite, gallium, tungsten, germanium and rare earth elements – metals that are critical to military systems, semiconductor manufacturing and robotics. While US industry leaders and mining experts have welcomed the investments on national security grounds, many have raised concerns about a lack of transparency and favouritism in awarding mining contracts. Sanchez cited multiple mineral agreements, including the Commerce Department’s US$1.6 billion investment in USA Rare Earth, one of the companies at the forefront of America’s bid to challenge China’s global dominance in rare earth production. She alleged a potential conflict of interest in the deal, as Cantor Fitzgerald – owned by the sons of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – acted as the lead placement agent for the private share offering tied to the government’s investment. Lutnick denied the allegations on Wednesday, brushing off the issue as “minor stuff anyway”. “I had no idea that Cantor was involved with the company at all. Never came up to me. I then passed it to my team,” Lutnick told CNBC. “My kids bought my companies, so I am no longer involved in my old companies at all.” During the congressional hearing, another Democratic lawmaker from California, Judy Chu, said while there was “broad agreement” that America needed to strengthen critical mineral supply chains, recent agreements had raised credible questions about conflict of interest. “But if the federal government is going to spend billions of taxpayer dollars doing it, the public deserves to know where that money is going and who is benefiting,” she said. The lawmakers also cited a June New York Times report that said Trump’s and Lutnick’s families had financial ties to 14 companies working with the federal government on mineral deals. Public Citizen, a non-profit, released a report on Wednesday alleging that companies with little mining experience or expertise were being awarded federal contracts, citing the administration’s infusion of more than US$2 billion into the sector last month. “The massive amounts of taxpayer funds involved in these deals require public disclosure of terms, ownership, financing and government guarantees to avoid corrupt practices,” said Melinda St Louis, director of Public Citizen’s Global Trade Watch, who testified at the hearing. Last month, Trump held a round table with several mining company executives, announcing deals worth over US$2 billion and more than US$180 million in investments for mining workforce development. “We are putting our miners back to work, and we are reclaiming America’s rightful place as the minerals superpower of the world,” Trump said. “We are making mining great again.” China has increasingly leveraged its dominance in critical mineral supply chains, imposing export controls on raw materials and related technologies as retaliation against US tariffs, sanctions and restrictions on advanced chip exports. Its export controls on seven rare earths in April, imposed in retaliation for US tariffs, triggered temporary factory closures around the world. A temporary US-China truce reached in Busan, South Korea, in October last year prevented further escalation but highlighted the deep vulnerabilities in supply chains. Last week, the South China Morning Post reported that the Busan agreement is likely to be renewed during the expected meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump later this month. However, the administration is racing to move away from China-linked supply chains. Washington has signed bilateral and multilateral agreements – including the Forge Initiative, a partnership of more than 50 countries, and the State Department-led Pax Silica coalition of 24 nations – aimed at building supply chains for critical minerals and strategic technologies outside China. Despite a whole-of-government approach, the US continues to face near-term supply chain challenges. In July, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington was still not receiving sufficient critical mineral exports from China. “We are getting a flow of critical minerals from China. It’s not as much as we would want. It’s not at the pace we would want, but we are getting them,” Greer said during his testimony before the Senate Finance Committee. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also raised the rare earths issue during his July video call with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng, saying that he expected Beijing to “fully meet” its commitments on rare earths. However, China said it followed a “responsible and non-discriminatory approach” on its rare earth export controls and the measures were not “targeted at any specific country”. “Given the dual-use nature of rare earth-related items, China has adopted relevant measures pursuant to its export control regulations,” embassy spokesman Liu Chang said in July. “We need to wake the hell up,” said Mike Kelly, the Republican Congressman from Pennsylvania, during the hearing. “This is not a political issue. This is a policy issue. This is about the safety and the security of the United States of America.”

title: In Iranian town, a wedding shattered by deadly strike during US air attack
description: As US forces targeted Iran’s coastal infrastructure, explosions tore through a home where guests had gathered to celebrate.
content: A US missile hit a home in southern Iran where dozens were gathered to celebrate the wedding of a fisherman’s daughter, according to a rights group and Iranian media. Iranian state media said four people – two women and two children – were killed and more than 60 were wounded. The rights group said one of the children, a teenager, was killed by another strike on a nearby communications tower. Heavy explosions shook the coastal town of Kuhestak on the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, and security footage carried by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency showed fireballs lighting up the night sky. It came amid the latest round of American bombardment in southern Iran that the US military said was targeting air defences, radar systems and maritime assets. Kuhestak is one of a string of small towns that dot the barren coastline along the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that has become a central front in the six-month war. Kuhestak is located about 30km (18 miles) from the town of Minab, where dozens of children were killed in a US missile strike that hit a primary school on February 28, the opening day of the war launched by the US and Israel. US Central Command spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the US military was looking into the reports of the strike on a wedding. He would not say if the military had launched a formal investigation. Little information has come out of the remote area. A missile smashed into the wedding party At least one missile hit the home of Ali Mallahi, a fisherman who at the time was celebrating the wedding of his daughter, state media said. “The missile completely destroyed the ceiling of the house,” Mallahi said in an interview with state TV as he pointed to the hole. He said a neighbouring house that shares the same yard was hit by another missile. Like most of the town’s population, Mallahi belongs to Iran’s Baloch ethnic minority. There was no immediate video footage of the moment of impact. But videos aired by Iranian media showed a crater, and walls and the roof of the building heavily damaged, with a smashed car nearby and debris – including wedding guests’ shoes – scattered around. Four people were killed, dozens wounded The state news agency IRNA and state TV said two women and two children, aged 4 and 16, were killed, and at least 68 were wounded. Just after the strike, Ahmad Nafisi, the province’s deputy governor, had told Iranian state television that five people were killed. There was no explanation for the change. At the hospital in Minab where wounded people were taken, Iranian media showed at least two girls and a woman in bandages. One of the children looked like she was still in shock. A man at the hospital with bandages on his head and arm said he was heading to the wedding when he heard jets overhead. The explosion hit as he arrived. “Blocks were falling and hitting people’s heads. And many small children and women that were there were terribly injured. So many,” he said in a video posted by the Iranian Red Crescent, which did not identify him. Nearby port was also targeted Also hit in the round of strikes was a communications tower at Kuhestak’s port, about 100 metres from Mallahi’s house, according to state media. At least two missiles hit the communications tower and another hit a pier at the port, Moein Arjomand, director of the Balochistan Human Rights Documentation Network, told Associated Press, citing witnesses who spoke to his group. The group, which maintains contacts with Baloch communities in Iran, said the 16-year-old was killed by shrapnel as he rode his motorcycle near the communications tower, rather than at the wedding as reported by Iranian media. Iran’s health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 wounded in Tuesday night’s US strikes across Iran. Separately, state media reported that four members of the Revolutionary Guard and 10 Basij volunteer fighters were among those killed in the strikes. Iran’s parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out over the wedding attack, while Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman branded it a “war crime”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan,” Ghalibaf wrote on X, referring to the United States and Israel. “Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan.” United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres was “deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran,” and called for ⁠an immediate cessation of military action, his spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The Secretary General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including ‌the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution,” Dujarric said. The deaths would be in addition to the 3,636 people documented as killed in Iran as of April 7, including 1,701 civilians, according to the Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA), an independent Iranian rights group. The US has reported 18 ‌military personnel killed and more than 750 wounded since the conflict began.
