Expert says fragments point to US weapon A weapons expert told Associated Press that images of fragments of ordnance that Iranian media said was used in the strike on Mallahi’s home, indicated that it was an “American air-delivered guided weapon”. N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services, initially identified the weapon as a SLAM-ER cruise missile, an air-launched missile that can be retargeted in-flight by a human operator. But after examining further imagery, he said it was more likely to be a JSOW, a type of guided bomb, though he did not rule out a SLAM-ER and said multiple weapons may have hit the site. US Central Command declined to comment on the analyst’s findings. Additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Reuters

title: Hong Kong’s first high-end expo with yachts and supercars to launch in November
description: SCMP learns inaugural Festival of Connoisseurs to receive some of HK$100 million set aside for MICE sector under 2026-27 budget.
content: Hong Kong will roll out its first cross-industry exhibition for high-end products ranging from haute jewellery to supercars, yachts and private jets in November, as part of efforts to attract big spenders and cement the city as a global conference and event capital. The South China Morning Post learned on Wednesday that the inaugural Festival of Connoisseurs will receive some of the HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) set aside in Hong Kong’s 2026-27 budget to attract large-scale international exhibitions to the city. Event organiser Informa Markets will use AsiaWorld-Expo, located near Hong Kong International Airport, as its primary venue for the event running from November 4 to 6. Other elements of the exhibition will be held in various locations across Hong Kong in an unprecedented “city-as-your-showroom” format. A source said the exhibition was the first of many such projects to involve the meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) sector. “The government is in discussions over other projects, which will elevate Hong Kong’s offerings and experiences on MICE events and, of course, will in turn boost high-end tourism,” the insider said. “The festival will be spread across several days, cater to different appetites of high-net-worth individuals and maximise interactions with them in iconic venues.” In its latest budget, the government allocated funds to help cement the city’s position as a global MICE hub. Informa, one of the world’s largest commercial trade exhibition organisers, is set to reveal more details about its event on Thursday afternoon. The inaugural festival will feature supercars, yachts, haute jewellery and luxury timepieces, premium travel, arts pieces, upmarket properties, private planes, fine dining and rare spirits, as well as top-end wellness services. Informa and the Tourism Board are teaming up to turn the Festival of Connoisseurs into a flagship event to be held annually until 2028, with plans to progressively expand the exhibition’s scale and global reach. Next year’s event is set to be held in the summer. The festival is expected to bring Hong Kong high-profile global events such as the Monaco Yacht Show, the Palm Beach International Boat Show, the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show, Jewellery Arabia and the Top Marques Monaco supercar show. The Tourism Board earlier said major international conventions had helped boost business travel in July, contributing to the 3 per cent year-on-year increase in visitor arrival levels to about 4.5 million that month. Government figures also showed that the city greeted 2.51 million MICE visitors in 2025, a 7 per cent increase from the previous year. Among that figure, nearly 57 per cent stayed overnight and generated HK$10.7 billion in total spending.

title: Hong Kong clampdown after dog attacks sparks rush for canine DNA tests
description: Government response to string of violent dog brawls may lead to pet abandonments, animal welfare groups say.
content:
A spate of dog attacks in Hong Kong has triggered a rush of canine DNA testing. It comes as the government clamps down on dog breeds classified as “fighting dogs”.
The city’s Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department stepped up sudden inspections and seizures of suspected fighting dogs after a recent string of violent incidents. These include one last month where the 33-year-old owner of a pet training facility was mauled by a mixed-breed dog registered as a mongrel. She was found dead nearby shortly after the attack.
There has been mounting public backlash to the impoundings. One advocacy group has urged authorities to introduce a one-year grace period for owners to voluntarily declare pets with fighting-breed traits.
The recent attacks exposed major loopholes in the city’s self-declaration microchip registration system.
The animal registered as a mongrel was later found to carry genetic traits of the pit bull terrier – one of four fighting breeds strictly banned from import and unauthorised breeding in Hong Kong.
As panic spread among dog owners, commercial testing centres saw a surge in clients seeking genetic proof to prevent their pets from being impounded.
Clement Lai Yat-lung, founder of pet testing firm Hero DNA, said inquiries had surged more than fivefold over the past week, jumping from about 10 to between 50 and 60. He noted that many dog owners, particularly those with mongrels, were anxious about government enforcement and hoped a DNA test result would prevent authorities from seizing their pets.
He said one client who adopted two mongrels was recently harassed on the street, and “an elderly woman even hit one of the dogs with an umbrella”.
Mark Mak Chi-ho, founder of the Non-Profit Making Veterinary Services Society, said that while the crackdown boosted demand for DNA tests, it could prompt anxious owners to abandon their pets out of fear of breaking the law.
“What I am particularly concerned about is free-ranging dogs ... Most of them are mongrels, which have mixed appearances from many different breeds. If the animal’s head is bigger, or it is stronger, people may call it a fighting or dangerous dog,” he said.
Mak called for greater clarity on regulations and reassurance to dog owners that if their pets were registered and sterilised, they would not be breaking the law, regardless of their canine’s breed profile.
Shelters have recorded an uptick in surrender inquiries. Kent Luk Ka-chit, founder of Paws Guardian Rescue Shelter, said daily calls about abandonment had risen to two or three a day, compared with one or two a week previously. He cited a case in which a dog owner brought his licensed pet to the department for vaccination and was told the animal was suspected of being a fighting dog.
The pet was subsequently detained, and the owner later abandoned the dog, he said.
“If their dogs are classified as fighting dogs, owners face heavy responsibilities going forward,” Luk explained.
Luk criticised the government’s approach, calling for public education rather than heavy-handed seizures.
“Authorities could introduce a grace period so that owners who are uncertain about their pets’ breeds can bring them in for inspection,” he added.
Lau Chun-hoi, coordinator of the NGO Animal Welfare Advocacy Alliance, said during a radio programme that enforcement actions had increased the pressure on dog owners, prompting some to abandon their pets. He said his group had recorded a 50 per cent month-on-month increase in dog abandonment cases, adding that he had personally handled 16 cases.
The importing, breeding, selling and keeping of fighting dogs without a licence is prohibited in Hong Kong.
Anyone in possession of a fighting dog commits an offence if the owner fails to produce a veterinary certificate proving that the animal has been neutered. Those convicted face a maximum penalty of a HK$50,000 fine and six months in jail.
The law also requires that dogs weighing more than 20kg be secured in public with a leash up to two metres long. Offenders face a maximum penalty of three months in jail and a HK$25,000 fine.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu has promised to review laws governing dangerous dogs.

title: 5 beauty highlights from Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Laura Mercier and more
description: 111Skin launched an at-home treatment for your complexion, while Wicked star Michelle Yeoh sported a blonde bob at Schiaparelli’s Paris haute couture show.
content: Recent happenings and product releases in the world of beauty include a four-week at-home treatment for your complexion; sophisticated, semi-matte finish lip liners; and a certain A-list actor’s fabulous blonde bob. 111Skin Think of 111Skin’s Exosome Face Lift 4-Week At-Home Treatment as a boot camp for your complexion. It contains a two-step product pairing that is formulated to target signs of ageing, such as tightening sagging skin and reducing the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles. Key ingredients include 111Skin’s proprietary NAC Y2 complex and a Milk Thistle extract, which helps clear out senescent “zombie” cells that accumulate and cause dull-looking skin. Chanel Beauty Les Extraits de Chanel is an exclusive line comprising 11 of the maison’s signature scents – including the iconic No 5, 1957 and Coromandel – in highly concentrated formulations, with each fragrance housed in a distinct hand-sealed bottle and designed to be applied drop by drop onto your skin. Fans of the brand might also take a fancy to the Les Extraits de Chanel purse spray edition – particularly useful when travelling and for quick touch-ups. Laura Mercier One too many late nights? No one has to know – just use Laura Mercier’s new Secret Brightening Under Eye Setting Powder that is specially formulated to smooth the area and lock your concealer into place. The product is infused with light-reflecting pearls and colour-correcting pigments to give you that perfect, airbrushed finish under your eyes. Louis Vuitton Legendary make-up artist Dame Pat McGrath, who was named the creative director of La Beauté Louis Vuitton in 2025, is elevating the house’s make-up collections with her creative vision and signature aesthetic. The French label’s latest release is the LV Crayon, an elegant lip liner, which features a smooth, creamy formula and glides on flawlessly. It is available in 10 hues and can be accompanied by a suite of accessories sold separately. Michelle Yeoh’s new bob Michelle Yeoh can absolutely rock a chin-grazing cut. The 64-year-old actress debuted a platinum blonde bob with exposed darker roots at the Schiaparelli haute couture show in Paris this July. Guests did a double take when they saw the Wicked star climb the venue staircase, sporting a short wispy crop with sunglasses and an off-the-shoulder dress with feathered trim.

title: Late Hong Kong dance pioneer Lau Siu-ming remembered for outstanding achievements
description: Culture minister among those paying tribute to late performer, known as Ming Sir, for his artistic contributions to sector.
content: Representatives of Hong Kong’s arts and culture scene have praised the outstanding achievements and contributions of the late Hong Kong actor and dancer Lau Siu-ming, who died on Wednesday at the age of 94. Lau, affectionately known as Ming Sir, died at about 6pm on Wednesday, according to media reports citing voice actor Ding Yue. Although the cause of death was not specified, Lau had reportedly been critically ill in recent years. “Ming Sir devoted his life to dance and the performing arts. His talent and dedication will always be remembered. We deeply mourn his passing and pay the highest tribute to his outstanding artistic achievements,” Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui said in a statement issued early on Thursday. Born in 1931, Lau was among the first Hong Kong dancers to pursue formal training in Europe. He was known for incorporating his experiences and Chinese heritage into his work. He was later invited to perform with the Brussels Ballet du XXe Siecle. Rebirth of the Phoenix was among his best-known works and was performed in France during the 1960s, according to the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts. “He studied and worked with some of the greatest artists of the times while on scholarship at l’Ecole Superieure de Danse de Cannes Rosella Hightower,” the academy said on its website. After returning to Hong Kong in 1967, Lau moved into television and film, appearing in numerous popular productions that were widely loved by audiences. “His nuanced acting and versatile image left a precious artistic legacy in Hong Kong’s film and television culture,” minister Law said. “His professionalism and passion made significant contributions to the sustainable development of Hong Kong’s cultural sector.” In addition to founding dance and arts groups, Lau served on the Leisure and Cultural Services Department’s Art Form Panel (Dance and Multi-arts), advising on the nurturing of new artistic talent and the expansion of audiences. Lau was awarded an honorary fellowship by the academy in 2007 in recognition of his contributions to the performing arts sector. He also received the Hong Kong Arts Development Council’s Life Achievement Award in 2019. Lawmaker Kenneth Fok Kai-kong said Lau’s death was a great loss to Hong Kong’s arts sector. “I remember visiting him in hospital this past January. He was already very weak, yet he still held my hand tightly, eagerly wishing to pass on his many hopes and expectations for the industry,” Fok wrote in a social media post. “That sincerity and passion remain vividly etched in my mind to this day.”

title: From gym workouts to shopping, Thailand’s friend-for-hire does it all for a fee
description: A new kind of gig economy booms in an increasingly solo society, offering companionship for photoshoots, travel and fitness.
content: “Friend-for-hire” services have started taking off in Thailand as the country’s social landscape changes with an ageing population and a rise in the number of unmarried people. The service is a new type of gig work in which people are paid to act as companions, for instance accompanying someone on a trip to take photos or even joining them in indoor rock climbing. Although no official figures are available, industry players say demand for professional companions has increased in recent years due to the rise in people living alone, changing lifestyles and the influence of social media. According to global market research company Euromonitor International, 29.5 per cent of Thai households were single-person households in 2025, exceeding the global average of 21.9 per cent. And that growing segment has created rising demand for products and services designed for independent living, such as single-seat restaurant tables and solo travel. For many clients, however, the motivation for hiring a companion is convenience rather than loneliness. Ainthuon Rattanawaraporn, a university student and content creator from Bangkok, said she initially used the service out of curiosity but soon found it solved a problem – friends were sometimes too busy to come with her on trips but she was not yet comfortable travelling alone. “I also wanted someone to take pictures for me,” she said. Unlike asking friends for favours, hiring a companion allowed her to freely request specific photo angles and compositions because photography was part of the service. “I don’t want to bother my friends by asking them to take hundreds of photos during a trip,” she said. “With a hired companion, I can tell them exactly what kind of pictures I want.” The growing demand has created new income opportunities for people like Thanaporn Charoenchuea, a 20-year-old university student who started her “Snap Like a Bestie” service. Within about two months, she had served more than 50 clients. She said her customers are not simply looking for someone to take photographs. “They want someone who can make them feel comfortable while capturing natural-looking photos,” she said. Apart from taking photos, Thanaporn spends much of her time chatting with clients, helping shy or introverted people relax before posing for pictures. “The biggest challenge is making sure every client enjoys both the experience and the final photos,” she said. “I love photography and meeting new people, so I find the job both enjoyable and rewarding.” On busy days, she accepts up to three appointments, each lasting between one and three hours. She only accepts bookings in public places after screening clients through their social media accounts. For another companion service provider, Penkawin Wangniwetkul, known as Ice, the business has evolved well beyond photography. After leaving her full-time job as a television co-producer, Ice spent several years working as a presenter, master of ceremonies and online marketing host before entering the companionship business about three months ago. The opportunity came unexpectedly after relatives suggested she accompany two elderly women on shopping trips and outings. “I realised there was genuine demand for someone who could simply accompany people,” she said, adding that she later began posting about the experience on social media, leading to more referrals. Today, clients hire her for activities including running, gym workouts, aerobics, shopping, spa visits, cafe hopping and even indoor rock climbing. A typical booking lasts two to three hours and she charges 1,000 baht (US$30) per hour. Ice has served more than 10 clients and intentionally limits bookings because she continues to work as an MC and presenter. She also screens every client before accepting an assignment. Her clients have included public figures, including an actress she accompanied to a veterinary clinic. She has also received requests to attend wedding receptions as a companion, although she was too busy to accept. Despite growing demand, Ice is selective. She turns down requests that could compromise her safety or make her feel uncomfortable, including accompanying male clients to late-night entertainment venues. The service has also expanded to trips outside the city. Company employee Sasiprapa Nookong is among those who hired a companion during a trip to Chiang Mai. Sasiprapa said that while travelling with a friend, they decided to spend one day pursuing different interests. Her friend planned to go hiking, while she preferred visiting cafes around the city, so she contacted a university student offering the service after seeing reviews on social media. “I believe this service meets the needs of people who occasionally want company, not long-term companionship,” she said, echoing others in stressing that safety should always come first when hiring strangers. Sociologist Narupon Duangwises of the Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn Anthropology Centre wrote in a report that interacting with hired companions may provide emotional comfort for people who find it difficult to make friends in everyday life. But he noted that one feature distinguishing friends for hire from traditional friendship is the ability to choose a companion based on physical appearance, unlike friendships that develop naturally. He therefore suggested that service providers establish clear rules and boundaries to protect themselves and prevent situations such as sexual harassment or other forms of violence.

title: Japan goes on student suicide watch as school term starts
description: Government data shows student suicide spikes in September, when children return to school after a long summer break.
content: Sayoko is watching her 13-year-old son more closely than he probably realises as he settles into his first year of junior high school in Yokohama. He is keeping up with his classes and is fortunate to be popular because of his sporting prowess. But Sayoko, who did not want to give her full name, remembers having a hard time at the same age, so she is alert to any sign that her son might be unhappy. “I was not good at sport and did not have a large circle of friends and, of course, there were always the ‘cool girls’ of the class who could be unkind,” she said. “It was not too bad for me and I came through it in the end, but no parent wants their son or daughter to be so desperate that the only choice they have is to kill themselves.” A tragedy close to home has made that fear even more palpable. The teenage son of one of her husband’s colleagues ended his own life about four years ago. Since then, Sayoko has gone out of her way to avoid the man. “I don’t know what I would say to him,” she said. “Perhaps I am wrong not to try to be normal around him, but I fear anything I say will be the wrong thing.” After a record number of children took their own lives in Japan last year, parents and teachers have once again been urged to look out for warning signs as the school year starts. This period has become associated with a heightened risk of student suicide. The Children and Families Agency has designated August 20 to September 9 as a time for “intensive efforts” to identify those at risk and strengthen suicide prevention measures. As part of the campaign, the government agency has released a video called “The video to watch when you don’t want the summer holidays to end”, telling young viewers that they do not have to struggle alone and can seek free, anonymous support by phone or online chat. Difficult time “For a lot of young people, this is one of the most difficult times of the year,” said Fujiko Yamada, founder of the Child Maltreatment Centre in Kanagawa prefecture. “They have just had a really long summer vacation when they have not had to study, they have been able to be lazy and play with their friends and go on holiday with their families, and all of a sudden they have to go back to school,” she said. “For lots of them, school is a place of rules, where they have to study and they are under pressure to get good grades. They have to get up early and many of them go to cram school in the evenings. Even wearing a school uniform again can be stressful.” On top of school pressures, teenagers might also have issues in their personal lives such as disagreements with parents or friends, or family financial worries, Yamada said. “I speak with children who are not going to school but know they should be. These are those who just can’t bring themselves to go for whatever reason,” she said. “Too often, I see an attitude of ‘all or nothing’ in them, and that means that if they can’t go to school, they do not know what they should do, and killing themselves looks like the only choice they have.” A total of 538 students killed themselves last year – a record high since the government started tracking figures in 1980. The previous record of 529 was set in 2024, according to the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, significantly higher than the 289 deaths recorded in 1980. The number of male students who died by suicide decreased by 20 from the previous year while the number of female students increased by 36. Suicides were up 24 per cent among junior high school girls. September had the highest incidents of student suicides last year, at 59. The ministry’s annual report identified “school problems” – specifically a fear of academic failure, arguments with other students, worries about their future careers and bullying – as the largest cause for a pupil taking his or her own life. Other reasons include health concerns and problems at home. Japan’s overall suicide rate has actually been steadily declining. A total of 19,097 deaths were recorded in 2025, down 1,223 from the previous year – marking the first time the total had dropped below the 20,000 mark since records began in 1978. Signs of stress Research suggests that child suicide rates in other countries follow a similar pattern, spiking in late August and early September as young people go back to school, as well as at the start of the academic year in the spring. A US study published in the April 2024 edition of the Journal of Human Resources showed that, as in Japan, academic stress, economic instability and ongoing post-pandemic disruptions were contributing factors, along with heavy social media use, cyberbullying, screen addiction and deteriorating mental health. “We need parents, in particular, to notice changes in their children, to look for signs of a young person who is struggling,” said Vickie Skorji, senior adviser to the Tokyo-based TELL Lifeline. “In many cases, these are young people who have had mental health issues before but have had time off over the summer and are now going back to school,” she said. “That has a tendency to exacerbate problems and children who were already struggling can be pushed over the edge.” Japan ranked first out of 43 nations for children’s physical health in a Unicef study released last year, but only 32nd on that same list for mental well-being. Anxiety and depression are the most common signs of mental health conditions among children, according to Skorji. “We are telling parents to look out for changes in their children’s behaviour, withdrawing from friends and family and not being interested in the things that they once enjoyed,” she said. “Sleep is another important indicator. Changes in sleep patterns are often signs, along with not eating and general irritability.” This year, TELL is running the Step Up Challenge, a nationwide campaign to raise awareness of the issues facing young people and provide them with hope and support. “Every parent needs to know what that could look like in their children and when the signs are there, getting support is vital. They cannot afford to think it’s just a young person acting like a young person,” Skorji said. “Parents need to talk to their kids and yes, sometimes that can be hard, but not talking to them can be fatal.” If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page.

title: Opinion | How Hongkong Post can ensure it’s not boxed out of the future
description: Regardless of which direction is chosen for the postal service, any reductions in staffing must be done with sensitivity and transparency.
content: The great debate about what to do with Hongkong Post has begun. There will be many twists and turns before we know the final outcome, but one thing is clear: it is vital to keep the staff on board at every step. We ultimately want to have an organisation of committed professionals running a world-class outfit. Early indications are that there could be problems. We are here because of a sharp deterioration in the post office’s financial position starting in 2017-18. A loss of more than HK$100 million (US$12.8 million) that year was followed by losses of over HK$200 million in 2018-19 and more than HK$300 million in 2019-20. Total losses in the past eight years amount to HK$2.9 billion, and the Legislative Council recently approved a HK$4.6 billion capital injection to cover the expense of maintaining the postal service’s operations for the next three years while a review considers options for the long term. This is a far cry from the heady days of 1995, when the post office was turned into a trading fund. That means it enjoyed more flexibility in business matters but had more responsibility for its overall financial situation. The sudden swerve to substantial losses does not mean the original decision on trading fund status was wrong, but it is a reflection of the enormous changes in the operating environment in recent years. Mail volumes everywhere have collapsed as people switch to email and other forms of electronic communication. Why bother with a long letter from home to a child studying overseas when you can make a free call on your mobile phone and see each other in the process? The situation is still changing. In the past, the post office could count on substantial revenue from philatelic sales to offset shortfalls in other areas. In the era of screens and electronic games, though, do children still collect stamps with the same fervour of previous eras? Will this funding stream also fade in time? Options being floated for the future include wholesale privatisation, corporatisation or reversion to normal government department status. Notwithstanding the success of private courier firms in operating profitable businesses conveying small parcels and important documentation, I am not sure writing the government completely out of the script on postal services would ever be politically acceptable. For one, there is a need to maintain relationships with other postal jurisdictions, and that is a matter for the government. This leaves us with corporatisation or standard government department mode. Whichever way we go, a measure of taxpayer support will be required, either to reflect the public service aspect of the corporation’s work or standard expenditure estimates for a government department. Regardless, all practicable means of running the services in the most commercially sensible way must be considered. That means cutting spending, boosting revenue or most likely a combination of the two. Given that 65 per cent of Hongkong Post’s spending is on staff costs, any meaningful reduction will require cuts in staffing. That will mean closing some existing post offices, starting with ones not frequently used. This will not be popular, but it must be done. It is not the rental savings that will be critical but the cost of staffing a full-service outpost. In essence, a postal operation comprises four elements: selling stamps to pay for future service, conveying posted envelopes safely to a sorting office, carefully sorting the mail, and delivering the sorted mail safely to addressees. Steps two to four need to be executed by vetted, reliable staff. Anybody can sell stamps, so in future most stamps should be sold via self-service vending machines or convenience store outlets. Only a few should be sold at fully staffed post offices, and these offices should be reduced to a bare minimum. Another way to improve post office finances is to charge appropriately for services. Charging HK$2.40 for local letter delivery is far below the actual cost. Moving quickly and steadily to HK$5 with annual reviews thereafter would be a reasonable approach without causing serious social damage. A programme along these lines would gradually restore the post office to financial health and reduce the burden on taxpayers of maintaining a reasonable service. However, the staff implications would require careful handling. Any reduction in overall numbers should be achieved by natural wastage, possibly supplemented by a voluntary redundancy scheme. A recent episode sets an unfortunate example. Some officers had apparently been recruited on the understanding they would become permanent civil servants upon successful completion of their probation period. Now, they will be offered a limited-term contract with no guarantee of permanent status later. The small cost savings of this manoeuvre are not worth the loss of trust. It might be legal, but it does not seem honourable. Is this what a good employer would do?

title: US export curbs have reshaped China’s tech scene around ‘chokepoints’: report
description: China’s tech start-ups now focus far more on key ‘chokepoint’ technologies, especially in the chip supply chain, Morgan Stanley report finds.
content: Chinese technology companies seeking public listings are increasingly concentrated in areas where Beijing is trying to break its reliance on foreign technology, as years of US export controls reshape the country’s pipeline of stock market hopefuls. About 20 per cent of companies that have launched initial public offerings on Shanghai’s Star Market so far this year are engaged in tackling key technological “chokepoints” facing China, compared with just 8.1 per cent in 2022, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis of 229 IPOs between 2022 and mid-July 2026. About 60 per cent of firms in 2026 contributed to China’s push for supply chain self-sufficiency, up from 41 per cent four years ago, said the report published on Friday. China’s critical tech bottlenecks have also narrowed since 2022, from a broad mix of strategic goods to a focus on the semiconductor supply chain, according to the investment bank. Driven by expanding foreign trade curbs, the pressure points have moved upstream to raw materials, complex machinery, specialised parts and core manufacturing tools. Of the 21 companies Morgan Stanley identified as addressing chokepoints this year, 19 are in the semiconductor supply chain. There is a particular focus on chokepoints in electronics, with 15 of the firms coming from that sector. “As the chokepoints expanded in the past three to four years, more domestic companies became dedicated in those areas and by 2026 some of them had grown to a stage ready to tap into the capital market to further scale up,” the bank’s analysts wrote. Washington has imposed sweeping controls on China’s semiconductor sector since 2022, restricting the country’s access to advanced computing chips and the equipment needed to manufacture cutting-edge semiconductors. A major escalation in December 2024 restricted various chipmaking equipment and categories of semiconductor-development software. The administration of US President Joe Biden further curbed access to high-bandwidth memory used for artificial intelligence and blacklisted Chinese organisations including semiconductor factories, equipment manufacturers, and investment firms linked to China’s military ambitions. While US President Donald Trump has since eased some restrictions on advanced AI processors, including allowing Nvidia’s H200 chips to be sold to China under certain conditions, the broader pressure on the supply chain remains. Soaring R&D costs The report also found that China’s technological push was becoming increasingly expensive – and risky. Companies in the 2026 IPO cohort spent twice as much on research and development on average compared with their 2022 counterparts, while R&D spending per employee also doubled, according to Morgan Stanley. Annual pre-IPO capital expenditure for companies in 2026 stood at 716 million yuan (US$107 million), more than four times the 174 million yuan average recorded for the 2022 cohort. Morgan Stanley analysts said the heavier spending reflected a “genuine need” for capital, as companies working deeper in strategic supply chains required significant investment not only in research but also to scale their technologies into commercial production. For example, the blockbuster IPO of chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies in July showed how capital raised through public markets could help expand its dynamic random-access memory production capacity. The expansion could benefit Chinese chipmaking-equipment suppliers seeking to replace US vendors across more stages of production, although there was still a lack of domestic alternatives in deep-ultraviolet lithography equipment, the analysts said. However, the new generation of listings comes with greater risks for investors. Only 46 per cent of the 2026 companies were profitable at scale, down from 72 per cent in 2022. Their median return on equity (ROE) – a key measure of net profit generated per dollar of shareholder investment – was 10 percentage points lower than the 2022 batch, with average ROE down by more than 17 percentage points. The numbers suggest many firms are less commercially proven despite their technological progress, according to the report. “We think eventually it is commercial validation that will drive post-IPO performance and investor interest in new IPOs,” the analysts said.

title: Chinese entrepreneur launches itch-scratching services, earning US$15,000 a month
description: Zhang aims to expand to 100 outlets nationwide; aspires to elevate novelty service into a recognised profession throughout the country.
content: A man in southern China has launched an itch-scratching chain brand, generating monthly earnings of 100,000 yuan (US$15,000) from his two outlets. This surprising venture is spearheaded by 32-year-old Zhang Xiaoqiao, who opened his first itch-scratching store in Shenzhen’s Baoan District in early May, followed by a second location in the city’s Futian District a month later, as reported by the Xiaoxiang Morning Herald. At these two venues, branded as Suma, staff wear specially designed pointed nails to gently scratch customers’ bodies while they lie face down on beds, similar to a massage setting. Charging 300 yuan (US$40) per hour, the service aims to alleviate stress and enhance sleep quality. Occasionally, staff will scratch specific itchy areas to help customers relax and even elicit laughter. “In first-tier cities, people generally experience high levels of stress. As a result, this service is in great demand,” Zhang shared with the media. Since there are no precedents for this type of service in China, Zhang had to independently research and develop effective scratching techniques from the ground up. According to Zhang, his two stores collectively generate a gross income of 100,000 yuan monthly and have already reached the break-even point while also starting to turn a profit. “We serve both male and female customers, with males comprising about 70 per cent,” Zhang noted. “Some customers have said our service is more relaxing than a massage, leading to a strong base of returning clients.” Zhang, a native of Hubei province in central China, is no stranger to exploring new ventures. Following his graduation from a lesser-known university, he tried seven different jobs in a single year. Before turning 30, he had founded two companies in the cross-border e-commerce sector, though both struggled to succeed. Two years ago, he was involved in the we-media industry but failed to make a significant impact. Last year, while browsing short videos on social media, he came across a clip featuring a woman scratching her husband’s itches. He noticed many viewers commenting that they would pay for someone to do the same for them. He recalled a comforting childhood memory of his father often scratching his back, which helped him fall into a peaceful sleep, inspiring him to open an itch-scratching store. Now, Zhang frequently faces the question: “Is itch-scratching a legitimate job?” He plans to open 100 outlets nationwide and, more importantly, hopes to establish itch-scratching as a widely recognised profession. The story has sparked considerable attention and humorous discussions across Chinese social media. “Are you considering taking on an apprentice? I want to learn from you and open a store in Shanghai,” quipped one user. Another person commented: “I’m intrigued by the service. Itch-scratching sounds like a great way to feel comfortable and completely relaxed.” However, some sceptics question the viability of the business, with one person wondering: “Are there really that many people willing to pay 300 yuan for a scratch?”

title: China launches largest-ever academic misconduct crackdown after ‘Student Geng’ scrutiny
description: NSFC names more than 40 researchers at 31 institutions in its biggest disclosure to date, following blogger’s allegations in April.
content: Four Chinese academics who lost posts at leading universities after a high-profile blogger flagged their research for misconduct have come under official investigation by China’s leading funder of basic research. The National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) published details on August 26 of 31 new misconduct cases at universities and hospitals across China, involving more than 40 researchers – its largest such public disclosure to date. Among them were four prominent professors publicly named in April by a blogger and PhD dropout known as Student Geng. All four had been recognised by the National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars – an honour that frequently serves as a stepping stone to admission into China’s top science and engineering academies. Three had served as deans or associate deans of their respective schools. Geng’s revelations on social media triggered the NSFC’s largest-ever investigation into academic misconduct. Naming the four academics in its August notice, the foundation revoked their funding and titles, ordered them to return more than 10 million yuan (US$1.49 million) in previously awarded grants, and barred them from reapplying for funding for three to seven years. Within China’s research community, the move is widely seen as a death sentence for an academic career. The NSFC announcement came nearly two months after President Xi Jinping called for a crackdown on academic misconduct. Addressing a joint meeting of the National Science and Technology Awards, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Chinese Academy of Engineering and China Association for Science and Technology, Xi called for “stricter standards” and “more concrete measures” to tackle misconduct and “foster a clean and upright research ecosystem”. China has continued to increase investment in scientific research. Under the 15th five-year plan, Beijing has set a target for society-wide research and development spending to grow by at least 7 per cent annually from 2026 to 2030. But the rapid expansion of research funding has also heightened concerns about academic misconduct and oversight of research spending. The NSFC is China’s main funder of basic research. In 2025, it approved 58,777 projects, with total funding of 38.7 billion yuan. This year, it approved 69,563 projects – a more than 18 per cent increase. Since 2022, the foundation has periodically published notices detailing its handling of research misconduct and funding-related violations. In recent years, Student Geng has emerged as China’s most prominent online whistle-blower on academic misconduct. Ahead of the NSFC’s latest notice, leading international journals had retracted papers co-authored by the four disgraced professors. Many of Student Geng’s other allegations, however, have yet to draw a public response from academics, universities or the foundation.

title: US teens say they don’t use critical thinking when depending on AI
description: The study, published by Common Sense Media, finds that almost three-quarters of American teens have not been taught how to use AI safely.
content:
Print head: Critical thinking gets lost when teens use AI
A survey has found that teens are not using their critical thinking as they depend more on artificial intelligence (AI).
The study was published by a US media advice group called Common Sense Media. The survey involved more than 1,000 US students aged 13 to 17. It found that students were giving up on “critical thinking” as more classrooms use chatbots.
About 40 per cent of those using AI said these tools did not help them learn. They believe that depending on chatbots means that they come up with fewer ideas on their own.
Around six in 10 of the teens who use AI say they use it to get answers for schoolwork. A quarter of them don’t change the answers.
When schools block AI platforms, 59 per cent of pupils turned to personal devices to access chatbots.
But almost three-quarters of those surveyed said they have not been instructed or advised by teachers about how to use AI safely.

title: In Focus | Her nude became a sticker: Hong Kong women say image abuse thrives despite law
description: Advocates say city’s voyeurism laws need more teeth and call for tougher action on non-consensual image leaks and illicit group chats.
content: Five years after a nude photo was taken without her consent, a woman opened Instagram to find the image had been turned into a sticker and sent back to her in a chat. Terrified that the sticker could already be circulating widely, the victim reached out to Emilia Wong Yue-kiu, a women’s rights activist and adult content creator who advocates for bodily autonomy. But Wong was pessimistic that reporting the case would help, noting it was just one of countless similar messages for help she had received in recent years. “Senders of the sticker may not even know where they got it from, and have no idea who the girl is, but they sent it around nonetheless. What offence did they commit then?” she said. Advocates say Hong Kong’s voyeurism laws have been insufficient to tackle the circulation of intimate images obtained without consent and the surreptitious online chat rooms where members post such images. They are urging city authorities to establish faster takedown mechanisms to better protect victims. Legal framework and enforcement gaps Hong Kong’s laws against voyeurism – encompassing four main offences – were enacted nearly five years ago in October 2021, to plug a legal loophole in tackling acts such as upskirting and revenge porn. These four offences are voyeurism, unlawful recording or observation of intimate parts, publication of images originating from the two aforementioned acts, as well as the publication or threatened publication of intimate images without consent. Official data obtained by the South China Morning Post shows that among the four voyeurism-related offences, the number of prosecutions in relation to arrests per year for publishing or threatening to publish intimate images without consent has been the lowest. Between October 2021 and March this year, authorities recorded 545 cases, made 258 arrests, launched 46 prosecutions and secured 33 convictions. That means only 17.8 per cent of arrests for this offence led to prosecutions over that period. Cheryl Yip Cheuk-yi, advocacy officer at the Association Concerning Sexual Violence Against Women, said her organisation’s experience with victims and its work to take down intimate images have shown that the need to prove an intention to cause distress, humiliation or alarm to the photographed individual under the law was a high threshold to reach. For cases involving online groups where people share or leak intimate images taken without consent, she said proving that someone who did not take the image – and may not know the person depicted – intended to cause distress could be difficult. “Perhaps they were thinking that this is a leaked image, and I’m merely sharing it with other people. The requirement to prove their motive may not be something that could be handled here,” Yip said. She added that subtle browbeating could also be challenged in courts, citing an example of someone saying “see you on a forum”, which a victim might interpret as a threat to post intimate photos but which could be dismissed as not constituting a threat. The advocacy officer also described the legality of resharing intimate images obtained without consent that a person did not take as a “grey area”, saying the law offered little clarity on such actions. Data from the organisation’s sexual violence victim support service showed that 63.3 per cent of image-based cases – 178 out of 281 – between 2019 and 2023 involved repeated incidents rather than one-off occurrences. Yip suggested city authorities reference the United Kingdom, which created a specific offence for sharing such images without consent, even if there was no malicious intent involved. “No matter what a person’s intention may be, publishing or threatening to publish intimate images without their consent would create the same level of harm,” Yip said. Legal interpretations and limits But barrister Michelle Wong Lap-yan, who has advised victims of sexual violence, said it did not matter whether the person knew the victim or whether the person had taken the image in voyeurism-related cases. “One of the guilty mental elements regarding the unconsented publication of intimate photos taken without the victim's consent is that the person is reckless as to whether the image originated from the commission of the unconsented taking of intimate photos,” Wong said. For example, if a photo showed clear signs of being taken without consent – such as an upskirt image inside an MTR train – a person ignoring those circumstances could be found reckless in court, she said. The barrister added that publishing intimate images that were taken with consent, but without authorisation for publication, was also a crime. But in the case of a non-consensual nude photo turned into a sticker and circulated, Wong admitted that it could be difficult for prosecutors to prove whether one could deduce that the photo was taken without consent, as well as the circumstances around how the sticker was sent and circulated. Advancing technology poses new threats Both Yip and activist Wong highlighted advancing technology as another threat – both in surreptitious filming equipment and in the increasingly elusive nature of online chat groups where such images are circulated. The latter, especially, has made collecting evidence for a case and taking down non-consensual images more difficult than before, according to both advocates. Wong said filming equipment has become much more sophisticated and accessible in the five years since the law took effect, making filming equipment ever harder to detect, but much easier to obtain. For instance, hidden cameras could be fitted on shoes or inside bags, while some appear as accessories placed near phone cameras that would refract the lens so as to film in 360 degrees. Wong said many of these tools were sold on e-commerce platforms for less than HK$100 (US$12.75). Other tools included software that keeps phone screens blank to view, despite a filming function being switched on. “With these, one can simply take a bag and place it underneath a girl’s skirt for upskirting,” Wong said. “You don’t even need to point a phone at the person to take photos.” While online chat rooms for sharing explicit sexual content were not new to Hong Kong, Yip and Wong said these groups have increasingly hidden their activities behind layers of evasive mechanisms to avoid detection and potential criminal liability. Activist Wong, who uncovered an upskirting group with tens of thousands of local members in 2018, said the scale of such groups had greatly shrunk since the voyeurism laws came into place, with group administrators making access to illicit photos more secretive. Unlike the large, publicly accessible groups with boisterous discussions and doxxing she had uncovered eight years ago, these groups now have only a few thousand members, compared with tens of thousands in the past, she said. Some required referrals from trusted members before admitting newcomers and used cryptocurrency for payments, Wong added. Chat room organisers have also adopted self-destructing messaging methods, which have become widely popular in recent years. “They would now put out really descriptive prompts about a video they would post, then say they would upload it for five minutes before the content was deleted. If members could catch that window, they could see it,” Wong explained. Wong added that bans on online discussion within the groups were effectively another way to evade criminal liability, as there would be no trace of individual members commenting on shared images or requesting payment details for access. Yip said some groups were no longer run by individual administrators but by bots or other built-in systems, making it more difficult for her organisation to request the removal of images or prove they had been posted. Directly posting intimate images on forums or publicly accessible online messaging groups has in fact become rare, according to Ip. “Now, they would post a link, which would be connected to a bot once clicked. Users would have to type some keywords to access the non-consensual image. This is a grey area, as they could say they had never posted the picture,” the officer explained. Faster takedowns are urged Yip called on Hong Kong authorities to establish faster mechanisms for removing non-consensual content to strengthen protections for victims, some of whom may be reluctant to enter lengthy judicial processes that can take years. The officer said that, for most victims reporting cases to non-governmental organisations or the police, the most pressing concern was stopping the circulation of their images. Expedited civil-law channels for removing non-consensual intimate images online exist in some overseas jurisdictions. Singapore launched its Online Safety Commission in June. The commission can issue removal directions and restrict perpetrators’ accounts, with legal authority over online platforms, administrators, internet access providers and app distribution services. Various Canadian provinces also provide for civil claims and urgent court orders to remove images. Activist Wong said Hong Kong could draw on these overseas mechanisms, but cautioned that authorities would need to address how any system would operate on foreign platforms and within jurisdictional limits, given that online activity easily crosses legal borders. Yip noted that, to her knowledge, Hong Kong authorities had not invoked a court disposal order available under the law to require a person to take steps to remove the intimate image concerned at any stage of legal proceedings. “As an NGO, we have no legal authority to demand these platforms take any action. If these orders are issued with legal power, these platforms have to follow up,” Yip said. Barrister Wong said online platforms were not subject to a specific statutory duty to pre-screen user content. Their civil liability for non-consensual intimate images would arise only if they were notified of the content and failed to remove it promptly. “But whether it is effective against foreign platforms is questionable. Primary criminal responsibility rests with the individual uploader under the Crimes Ordinance,” Wong said, noting that city courts had warned of the need to balance freedom of expression against platform liability. But activist Wong said Hong Kong society could not simply rely on the law to address the invasive threat posed by upskirting and image leaks, and that a broader cultural shift in attitudes towards women was needed. “This is intrinsically bullying, which cannot be reversed by law. We need women’s social status to rise, better sex education and less taboo on discussing sex,” she said.

title: Indian Premier League club bosses, Hong Kong cricket aim ‘to go global’ with Sixes
description: India giant JSW Sports, co-owners of Delhi Capitals, become tournament’s commercial partner, with event chiefs planning worldwide circuit.
content: The co-owners of an Indian Premier League (IPL) powerhouse have joined forces with Hong Kong cricket chiefs in a bid to convert the city’s unique Sixes tournament into a global phenomenon. Boasting an ownership portfolio that includes Pretoria Capitals, Bengaluru FC and Pro Kabbadi League team Haryana Steelers, alongside the IPL’s Delhi Capitals, JSW Sports on Wednesday signed a deal to serve as the commercial partner of the Hong Kong Sixes. After being mothballed for seven years, the Sixes made a triumphant return in 2024, then over three days last year drew more than 10,000 fans to its Tin Kwong Road Recreation Ground home. While both parties sounded their intention to take this year’s edition “to new heights”, the overarching goal is to create a worldwide Sixes circuit that features up to six stops. “Our vision is to build this into a much bigger format, and to go global with it,” Cricket Hong Kong, China [CHKC] board member Anurag Bhatnagar said. “To do that, we need strategic partners, people who have the bandwidth, and the expertise and finance, to help us.” Bhatnagar said the plan was to add one overseas Sixes tournament next year, then continue to grow at the same pace going forwards. The proposed 2027 event would probably be staged in Asia, potentially in the Middle East, before the Sixes branches out to Africa and Europe. Bhatnagar said mainland China was another likely host. “The idea is to scale it up with one additional venue every year for the next five years, and at the end of it we should have a global series, comprising five to six events, hosted in different regions of the world,” Bhatnagar said. “We’ve spoken to other boards and received absolute enthusiasm. I think we can quite easily lock in the next three venues whenever we’re ready.” JSW Sports also looks after the commercial rights of a number of leading Indian athletes, including international all-rounder Axar Patel, and in 2018 it established the Inspire Institute of Sport, India’s first privately-funded high-performance Olympic training centre. Divyanshu Singh, the JSW Sports CEO, said his company was “at a juncture where we feel it’s a good time to transition from franchise ownership to IP [intellectual property] ownership and IP partnerships”. “[The Sixes] is a very exciting property, which has been growing,” Singh said. “Also, cricket in international formats attracts fandom that is unparalleled compared to franchise cricket. “This year, we want to create much more fandom and commercial growth.” With the major T20 franchise leagues around the world numbering double figures, and international cricket operating on a 12-month treadmill, Sixes has its work cut out to find a gap in a saturated market. Bhatnagar said that not being “a vanilla franchise cricket event” gave the shorter format a leg-up. “The majority of those leagues are not sustainable, commercially or otherwise,” he added. “Sixes is a fast-paced, short-duration event, and I think it’s perfectly positioned for Gen Z and Gen Alpha, with the shortening attention spans. “It’s countries playing each other. You have India against Pakistan, and Australia vs England, all the great rivalries, happening in one day. That doesn’t happen anywhere else and it sets us apart from the franchise leagues.” This year’s Sixes will be staged from October 30 to November 1 and broadcast on Sony Sports Network. After weak India teams flopped in the past two editions, Singh said work was under way to “ensure we have a great Indian squad”. “We understand the value of stardom, but also I think we’ll ensure there is strong cricket … and great fans,” he added. JSW Sports have signed up for an initial one-year with terms already in place for a further two years. Burji Shroff, the chairman of CHKC, said the two sides were eyeing a long-term relationship. “We look for partners with integrity and good reputations, and JSW has those qualities,” Shroff said. “It’s easy for us to take the Sixes to another level alongside them. Going global is one of the big attractions, and we want to get higher-calibre players here to thrill the fans.” Separately, after Indian officials led grumbles over accommodation and facilities for the forthcoming Japanese Asian Games, CHKC’s stance is that they are “comfortable” with the hotel booked for them by the Sports Federation and Olympic Committee of Hong Kong, China, and the set-up at host venue Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin. Also on Wednesday, the Hong Kong men’s team slumped to a 32-run defeat by Bahrain at the ACC Premier Cup in Kuala Lumpur. Having beaten Saudi Arabia on Monday, the city side will play their remaining group matches against hosts Malaysia and Nepal on Saturday and Tuesday, respectively. The top two advance to the semi-finals, while the tournament winners qualify for next year’s Asia Cup. Hong Kong’s women face India in their second Asia Cup game on Thursday, six days after they suffered a six-run defeat by Thailand in their opening fixture.

title: SHKP clinches rare MTR station-top megaproject in Hong Kong’s Tuen Mun
description: Developer has now won two projects in the area, which combined are expected to deliver nearly 6,800 flats.
content: Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHKP) subsidiary Bright Grand Enterprises on Thursday won the tender for MTR Corporation’s Tuen Mun A16 Station Phase Two Property Development. SHKP had already clinched phase one of the development last November. The second phase’s residential portion spans 249,979 square metres and is expected to yield around 5,510 homes, while its commercial component comprises 31,100 square metres and will house a large-scale shopping mall at the podium level. Combined, the two phases are expected to deliver a total of 6,790 flats in Tuen Mun Area 16. SHKP said it would primarily construct small to medium-sized units. “Projects built on top of stations in well-developed communities are increasingly rare, so we have great confidence in its development,” said Victor Lui, deputy managing director at SHKP. Tender submissions closed on Wednesday, with market sources saying other top Hong Kong developers including CK Asset and Henderson Land Development were among the bidders. A consortium of Sino Land, Kerry Properties, China Overseas Land & Investment and Great Eagle also submitted a bid, they added. MTR Corp said a total of four bids were received. David Tang, managing director of property and international business at MTR Corp, said Tuen Mun was a mature community, with the project situated atop a railway station and offering comprehensive amenities. Vincent KC Cheung, managing director at Vincorn Consulting and Appraisal, earlier estimated the project’s accommodation value at HK$4,000 (US$510) per square foot. “With a total gross floor area of nearly 3 million square feet – including the commercial component – the project is valued at close to HK$12 billion,” Cheung said. Alvin Lam, director at Midland Surveyors, noted that MTR Corp had not launched such a large-scale single tender project in a long time. “The scale of this development exceeds that of the topside projects at Tai Wai, Tsuen Wan West, and Nam Cheong stations from over a decade ago, comprising residential components alongside a large shopping mall and transport facilities,” he said. Lam added the residential portion would likely consist of small to medium-sized flats catering to the mass market. According to tender documents, the phase two development is located beside the Tuen Mun River and the Area 16 Station of the MTR Tuen Mun South Extension, which is under construction. The project has a maximum total gross floor area of 281,079 square metres (3.02 million square feet). Bidders were required to propose an upfront payment, with the winner to pay in four instalments under a fixed profit-sharing ratio of 15 per cent. The project attracted 28 expressions of interest when the submission period closed in July. Consolidated market valuations ranged from HK$7.5 billion to HK$12.1 billion, translating to about HK$2,500 to HK$4,000 per square foot of floor area, with total investment costs projected to exceed HK$20 billion.

title: Exclusive | New Zealand ‘must never be seen as a proxy’, former PM Helen Clark warns
description: Calling the US Pacific strategy a ‘game of bluff’, Clark urges Wellington to defend its independent foreign policy tradition.
content: Helen Clark spent nine years running New Zealand and eight more running the United Nations’ development arm. Now, the former prime minister has a warning for the country she once led: do not let the scramble for Pacific security deals crowd out its much-vaunted independent foreign policy tradition. Speaking to This Week in Asia in Singapore on Tuesday, Clark argued that Wellington’s recent flurry of defence diplomacy – including a defence cooperation pact with Papua New Guinea, a joint security declaration with the Cook Islands and talk of joining a fledgling Australia-Fiji alliance – risked the Pacific’s future as “a zone of peace”. For decades, New Zealand’s foreign policy has rested on two pillars: independence from superpower blocs and a Pacific kept free of nuclear weapons. Both are now being tested. Australia’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines under the Aukus pact with the United States and Britain is perhaps the clearest example of how. “The Australians being in the market for nuclear submarines isn’t helpful – not that it’s clear they’ll ever get them, but what they’ll get is an American base for nuclear submarines,” said Clark, 76, who was in Singapore to deliver the keynote address at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ International Conference on Cohesive Societies Interlude event. “I think there are a lot of people who would think, as I do, that we should be focusing on keeping the Pacific as a zone of peace.” New Zealand’s current government, a coalition of the National Party, ACT and New Zealand First, has reportedly been weighing joining Aukus’ so-called Pillar 2, which focuses on sharing advanced military technologies other than nuclear submarines. But Clark questioned the very premise underpinning the pact: that the US could indefinitely guarantee Pacific security while also juggling commitments elsewhere. She invoked Australian strategist Hugh White, who has long argued that China’s rise makes US primacy in East Asia and the Western Pacific increasingly unsustainable, and that Washington may need to share power rather than assume it can remain dominant. Clark pointed to the recent war on Iran as a case study in US overreach, arguing that Washington did not spend enough on its military to maintain Western Pacific dominance, and noted it had been preoccupied this year with the Iran conflict. “Apply that to the Asia-Pacific context. It’s not real, is it? So this is all a game of bluff. The key thing is to find what the geopolitical balance in the Pacific is going forward,” she said, adding that traditional US allies and partners wanted to see its continued involvement but had begun to lower their expectations. Proxy principles Clark said Wellington needed to guard against perceptions that it was becoming an instrument of great power rivalry. “New Zealand must never be seen as a proxy,” she said. “There have been some unfortunate moves by the current government, but I don’t see that as a long-term trajectory for New Zealand.” One of the defining moments of Clark’s tenure as the country’s 37th prime minister, from 1999 to 2008, was her refusal to send combat troops to the Iraq war in 2003, since the US-led invasion lacked a UN mandate. Wellington instead deployed non-combat military engineers and medical personnel to assist with post-war reconstruction. More recently, she has criticised Washington’s unilateral tariffs, saying they “cannot be consistent with World Trade Organization rules”, while arguing that countries retain the agency to trade without the US through smaller groupings. Clark acknowledged public concern that the current administration was aligning more closely with Washington and abandoning New Zealand’s independent foreign policy, but said the balance would shift with a change of government. “Generally, New Zealanders have been quite proud of their independent foreign policy and New Zealand taking stands based on principle and law, and not just putting up their hand because a great power asked it to,” she said. She has also criticised Wellington’s decision to join a small group of nations that formally rejected the World Health Organization’s new pandemic rules earlier this year, reportedly warning that it risked turning New Zealand into an “irrelevant” and “quirky actor with little to contribute” on the world stage. Foreign Minister Winston Peters recently provoked a diplomatic complaint from Beijing after telling China-born Green Party MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to “go back to your own country” during a parliamentary debate on July 29. Clark called Peters’ comments “damaging” to New Zealand-China relations. Engaging Beijing On China itself, Clark said its position on the world stage had shifted since her time in office, pointing to President Xi Jinping’s recent keynote address on global artificial intelligence governance. “Power abhors a vacuum,” she said, adding that China’s continued success provided opportunities for all. “We need to continually work on how we maintain good engagement and dialogue, notwithstanding that we may have concerns about issues within and around China.” That same instinct for de-escalation shapes her views of Taiwan, saying that no country should give Beijing a reason to act – a formula that rules out “unilateral declarations of independence” as much as it does acts of coercion. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US and its allies, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but do oppose any attempt to take the self-governed island by force. “What we should all be doing is employing every good office we have diplomatically to ensure that this doesn’t happen,” Clark said. “You have to calm it down. These kinds of ambivalent arrangements can go for a very long time if everyone keeps their heads.” It is a philosophy that naturally extends to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ consensus-driven decision-making approach, often criticised for its glacial pace but defended by Clark as a feature, not a flaw. “Asean is very aware that it represents a very wide range of countries with different histories, different orientations, but the key thing is that it stays together and it works for common positions, which may take a long time to get to, but that is part of the process,” she said.

title: Nancy Kwan’s enduring legacy, six decades after the release of The World of Suzie Wong – interview
description: The Hong Kong-born actor left her home city to forge a path for Asian performers in Hollywood, navigating the accompanying xenophobia and sexism of the 1960s. PostMag talks to the Flower Drum Song star about life, loss and leading the way.
content: To many, Nancy Kwan Ka-shen is the actress who rose to international stardom for her role in the 1960 film The World of Suzie Wong, based on the book of the same name, about a sex worker in Wan Chai who meets a wealthy American (played by William Holden). Kwan’s story, however, is far richer than any single role. From breaking barriers for Asian actors in Hollywood and standing her ground in an industry that was rigid and often prejudiced, to founding her own ballet studio, producing films and television advertisements across Southeast Asia, and starring in more than 50 films spanning decades, she has lived a life of relentless creativity, resilience and grace. Now 87, Kwan’s path to celebrity was as serendipitous as it was extraordinary. In August 1959, she stumbled upon a casting call for The World of Suzie Wong. “I thought it was dreadful because all I did was giggle,” she tells me over a FaceTime call from her home in Los Angeles, in the United States. “I was really quite silly. I was surprised I got a job at all. But they seemed to like it, so I ended up in Hollywood doing more screen tests. Eventually, I got the role.” Initially, France Nuyen had been cast, but when the French-American actress withdrew, Kwan’s ballet-trained poise and expressive presence made her the perfect replacement. The film catapulted her to global fame, subtly transforming Hollywood’s perception of Asian women at a time when “yellowface” – casting non-Asian actors in make-up to portray Asian characters – was still widespread. Even decades later, her magnetism remains palpable. Behind her, a poster of Suzie Wong seems almost to lean towards the camera, a reminder that the character and the woman who portrayed her remain inseparable in the public memory. Yet Kwan’s memoir, last year’s The World of Nancy Kwan, reveals a keen awareness of her own agency, her understanding that her story is as much about heritage and personal resilience as it is about fame. Born in 1939 to Kwan Wing-hong, a prominent, Cambridge-educated Chinese architect, and Marquita Scott, a British model and aspiring actress who would leave the family before the start of World War II but later reconnect with her daughter in the US, Nancy grew up in a family whose legacy was intertwined with Hong Kong’s development and global affairs. Her great-grandfather, Kwan Yuen-cheung, was the city’s first Western-trained dentist; her great-grandmother, Lai Amui, survived the mainland’s Taiping rebellion (1850-64) to become one of the first Western-trained nurses in Hong Kong. Her great-uncle Kwan King-leung studied alongside Dr Sun Yat-sen and later served as physician to the Empress Dowager of the Qing dynasty (1644-1911). “I don’t know if great-uncle Kwan King-leung’s friendship with Dr Sun Yat-sen endured, but I think it is extraordinary that the man who is considered the father of modern China spent his formative years in the Kwan household,” Kwan writes in her memoir. Kwan also recalls how, although she has only hazy memories of it, her father (who later remarried) had to hide her and her brother in wicker baskets to travel to Macau by boat and then onwards to mainland China to flee the war after Japan’s attack on Hong Kong in 1941 – an event remembered locally as “Black Christmas”. Later, Kwan learned that her father had served covertly with the British Army Aid Group, assisting soldiers stranded behind enemy lines in their escape from Japanese forces. Some media have even described him as a “Chinese James Bond”. The family returned to Hong Kong in 1945, resuming their lives amid the city’s post-war recovery. Hollywood was never Kwan’s first passion. Ballet had captivated her from childhood, and she trained in Britain, attending the prestigious Royal Ballet School, in London. “I’ve always continued with ballet,” she says. “Then I branched out – jazz and other kinds of dance. Nowadays, I take tai chi.” That disciplined movement would define her screen presence, most memorably in Flower Drum Song (1961). “Hermes Pan, the choreographer, told us, ‘Don’t dance like this; this is jazz.’ We did jazz because that’s what the piece called for. It was all about keeping ballet at bay,” she recalls, a glimmer of mischief in her eyes. At the time of filming, Kwan had no idea how historic the movie would become. “I just thought, ‘Oh, Flower Drum Song, all great.’ But it was the first time a major Hollywood studio made a film with a mostly Asian cast – that was a real achievement. I didn’t know the business that well back then,” she admits. “It wasn’t until my friend [the late Chinese-American actor] Benson Fong told me, ‘Nancy, this is the first time they’re making a film with an all-Asian cast,’ that I thought, ‘Wow, OK, this is bigger than I realised.’ It was very exciting.” Decades later, that trail-blazing spirit echoed in the meteoric success of Crazy Rich Asians, the 2018 film adapted from Kevin Kwan’s 2013 novel, starring a predominantly Asian cast and capturing the global imagination. The connection is more than thematic: Kevin is Nancy’s cousin. “Nancy really paved the way for me to pursue my own creativity,” Kevin, 53, tells me over the phone. “The first time I saw her in Flower Drum Song, I could hardly believe my eyes – just this glamorous creature in my own family. It was always inspiring.” He fondly remembers the rare glimpses of authentic Hong Kong and the nuanced female characters Nancy brought to the screen. He recalls her performance in the late-1980s miniseries Noble House, adapted from the James Clavell novel, that was shot in Hong Kong, which also starred Pierce Brosnan and Deborah Raffin, as it offered him an immersive look at his heritage. “It was remarkable to see her playing a sassy, empowered secretary, and years later, seeing her in Dragon: The Bruce Lee Story [1993] as Lee’s boss was another milestone,” he says. “She was there at every significant stage, paving the way for younger talent, for stories like my own.” Kevin attributes her success to her perseverance. “She never gave up, no matter the hardships or controversies. She was the first woman to return to Hong Kong and run her own film studio, and she got through everything with determination. Even now, in her 80s, she carries herself with the energy and poise of someone decades younger – not just physically, but in spirit,” he says. Nancy navigated Hollywood’s entrenched racial attitudes, which often reduced Asian actors to exoticised caricatures. She admired Anna May Wong – considered to be the first Chinese-American film star in Hollywood, in the 20s – and her ability to get through the barriers she faced. “I didn’t know much about her until I came to Hollywood and found out she was really the first Asian actress from Los Angeles,” Nancy recalls. “I think I met her niece – she comes to a lot of my screenings and book signings – a very lovely girl. I read up on Anna May Wong and even did a documentary about her, doing the voice-over, so I learned a lot about the struggles she faced, especially when they didn’t use Asian actors – they used Caucasians dressed up as Asians, like Luise Rainer in The Good Earth [1937]. She was trying to work during that era, and it was very difficult. When we did Flower Drum Song, the producer told me [Wong] was going to have a role, and I was so excited to work with her. Sadly, she passed away just a few weeks before filming.” Private life and career are intertwined in Kwan’s reflections. Decades spent in Los Angeles, a brief return to Hong Kong to manage her father’s company and the routines of long-term partnership and care illustrate a life shaped by both focus and balance. “I came back when my father was ill and, sadly, he passed away,” she recalls. “After that, I was offered the chance to run a company in Hong Kong. I thought, ‘Why not?’ But I quickly realised it wasn’t for me. Being a CEO meant more lunches and meetings than actual work – I wanted to be on the ground, doing things myself. By then, my son was ready to start high school, so that’s why I moved back to Los Angeles.” Her memoir is filled with vivid, intimate stories of Hollywood encounters. She recounts her then-boyfriend Maximilian Schell, in a fit of jealous rage, hurling his “Best Actor” Oscar at her, and the time she turned down the lead opposite Elvis Presley in Blue Hawaii (1961). “I was asked to meet someone at Paramount Studios about a film,” she recalls. “I didn’t know it was Elvis. I walk onto this empty stage, and then suddenly, he appears with a few of his friends. He sat me down and sang the ‘Hawaiian Wedding Song’ – I was floored. He was such an entertainer. Of course, I applauded and made a fool of myself.” Despite the allure, Kwan politely declined. “I told them I’d already signed for Flower Drum Song. Both roles were historic in their own way, but I felt committed to this one,” she says. She fondly remembers meeting Ursula Andress, who casually mentioned she was about to star in a “B” movie called “007” with Sean Connery, and her own friendship with Bruce Lee, whom she first met in Hong Kong and grew close to while filming The Wrecking Crew (1968), for which he served as martial-arts adviser. “He was going to teach Sharon [Tate] and me some kung fu for a fight scene. That’s how I got to know Bruce quite well. We would hang out at the house, and he often told me about his plans to return to Hong Kong and make martial-arts films,” she remembers. That now-famous fight scene between Tate and Kwan is immortalised in Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film, Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, in which Margot Robbie, playing Tate, is shown watching that exact scene in a cinema. In her memoir, Kwan also reflects on Tate’s kind nature and tragic death, revealing the personal impact it had on her. The memoir confronts other heartbreaks. Kwan opens up about the loss of her son and “best friend”, Bernie Pock, whom she shared with her first husband, Peter Pock.
