Regulatory and institutional gaps also risked the effectiveness of advancing partnerships and business relations, as both regions had limited familiarity and knowledge of each other’s markets, they said. “The main constraint is geography,” said Barbora Valockova, a research fellow at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy’s Centre on Asia and Globalisation. “Central Asia is landlocked and far from Southeast Asia, and overland routes involve multiple borders, transport modes and regulatory systems.” Lin noted that both regions were in the “early stages” of cooperation, and said the challenge of turning agreements into commercially viable projects remained. “Governments can open doors and establish frameworks, but private companies will only support initiatives if there is sufficient market demand, scale and profitability,” she said. “Differences in regulatory systems, market conditions and business practices can also slow implementation.” Central Asia also lacked a centralised and institutionally integrated bloc, such as an Asean equivalent, to ensure the effectiveness of an inter-regional mechanism, Hoo said. Economic ties between both regions had been experiencing “emerging momentum”, said Insebayeva, who urged greater support and working mechanisms in the form of business forums, investment facilitation and educational exchanges. Singapore’s role While Singapore is well positioned to bridge both regions due to its connectivity and business-friendly environment, analysts say direct links between all economies are needed for commercial viability. The city state was a “natural choice” due to its institutional credibility and technical expertise, and could provide a trusted platform for firms unfamiliar with Southeast Asia, Insebayeva said. She noted that Kazakhstan had long drawn inspiration from Singapore in areas such as public administration and financial services, a practice that built trust. Singapore’s existing partnerships with countries in the region could be a model for multi-regional cooperation, Insebayeva said, citing a bilateral services and investment agreement with Astana which came into effect in March last year. “Singapore should be seen as a facilitator rather than the sole gateway,” said Joanne Lin, senior fellow and Asean Studies Centre coordinator at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. “It can connect businesses, capital and expertise across the two regions, but success will ultimately depend on commercially viable opportunities and stronger transport and business links.” Singapore’s coming Asean chairmanship was an optimal time to take its existing strong bilateral ties to a multi-regional level, Valockova said, but added that deeper multi-regional ties would require participation from other major Southeast Asian economies such as Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia. “The realistic goal is an open and flexible network of partnerships that strengthens economic resilience and connectivity,” she said.

title: China dealt blow as US-backed firm takes over Venezuelan oilfields
description: Venezuela was the biggest recipient of China’s lending to Latin America, and Beijing is unlikely to recover debts, one analyst says.
content: A US-backed company’s takeover of Venezuelan oilfields, some of which were previously managed by Chinese firms, has dealt a blow to Beijing’s oil-backed loans and yuan trade networks, analysts say. Through North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a private company, the White House said the US had secured access to oilfields with 65 billion barrels of proven reserves in Venezuela – around one-fifth of the Latin American country’s total supply – including sites previously operated by Chinese firms. “Oil development in Venezuela is effectively dominated by the United States,” said Cui Shoujun, a professor at Renmin University of China’s School of International Studies. “[China’s] likelihood of recovering its debts has decreased,” he added. Venezuela was the largest recipient of Chinese state-backed lending in Latin America, having borrowed more than US$100 billion since 2000, according to US research lab AidData. Most of these were structured as oil-backed loans, requiring shipments of crude to Chinese state buyers, with proceeds going into a Beijing-controlled account to service the debt. While official data is patchy, and Beijing has largely frozen new lending in recent years, Venezuela’s outstanding debt to China is estimated at over US$10 billion. The recovery of those payments now looks increasingly unlikely with the latest US-Venezuela oil deal, details of which were announced by the White House on Monday night, Washington time. Venezuela is likely to be a cautionary tale about the risks involved in occupying ‘real estate’ that the Trump administration has set its sights on Erica Downs, Centre on Global Energy Policy The interim Venezuelan administration – formed after the US military ousted former president Nicolas Maduro in early January – granted NABEP 100-year concessions across 17 oilfields, several of which were run by Chinese and Russian firms. The agreement gave the Pentagon a 35 per cent equity stake in NABEP’s parent company, while the US State Department gained the right to buy 20 per cent of produced crude at cost, along with a right of first refusal over all remaining production. The deal was a “direct hit” to China’s non-dollar trade networks, said Dylan Loh, an associate professor at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University. “Replacing discounted Venezuelan crude forces Beijing onto open markets, while shifting oil sales back into US dollars stalls petroyuan momentum in Latin America,” Loh said. Petroyuan refers to the settlement of oil transactions in the Chinese currency and independent Chinese refiners – known colloquially as teapots – have previously used non-dollar clearing channels to purchase US-sanctioned Venezuelan crude. Deprived of one major source of heavy crude, teapots now face margin compression, Loh said. Erica Downs, senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Centre on Global Energy Policy, similarly noted that the US takeover in Venezuela, as well as the war in Iran, have “generally been bad news for the teapots, which previously counted on discounted crudes from both countries along with Russia to boost their bottom lines”. Among Chinese state-owned companies, China National Petroleum Corporation has the most at stake given its joint venture with Venezuelan energy giant PDVSA, which produces oil for debt-servicing, Downs added. China’s foreign ministry responded to the takeover on Tuesday, saying the country’s rights and interests in Venezuela must be protected. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven reserves of oil, estimated at 303 billion barrels – or around 17 per cent of global reserves, according to the US Energy Information Administration. About half of Venezuela’s total crude exports of 1.1 million barrels per day were sent to the United States in August, according to S&P Global, with the remaining bound for destinations such as India and the Caribbean. Meanwhile, China, previously the top buyer of Venezuelan crude, has taken no shipments in the past few months. Loh noted that in addition to the United States securing additional crude supplies, the takeover “had the added effect of pushing Chinese and Russian influence out of the western hemisphere.” Washington has framed the move as “reasserting the Monroe Doctrine”, a foreign policy position named after former president James Monroe that sought to establish US power across the Americas. China is now likely to be more wary of investments in Latin America, said Cui of Renmin University. Downs expected Chinese companies in energy, mining and infrastructure in particular to be more cautious in making deals in the region, especially in the short term. “Venezuela is likely to be a cautionary tale about the risks involved in occupying ‘real estate’ that the Trump administration has set its sights on,” Downs said.

title: Chevron to expand Venezuela oil operations with US$7 billion plan
description: The US energy giant aims to double production, even as analysts warn that the nation’s decrepit infrastructure would take years to fix.
content: Oil giant Chevron confirmed that it would expand operations in Venezuela after US President Donald Trump announced an ambitious deal to develop the nation’s oil reserves and give the Pentagon a stake in the profits. Chevron, the only US oil company with a major presence in Venezuela, said on Wednesday that it had been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, where it has active operations. The company plans to invest more than US$7 billion over the next five years, with the goal of more than doubling its current production to about 600,000 barrels a day. “Chevron’s history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country’s deep resource potential,” CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement. Venezuela holds the world’s largest proven reserves, totalling more than 303 billion barrels of crude oil, according to Opec’s 2025 Annual Statistical Bulletin. Saudi Arabia is a distant second with 267 billion barrels. Yet because Venezuela’s energy infrastructure is severely degraded and the nation is operating under international sanctions, its daily production is just over 1 million barrels, compared with the 10 million to 11 million barrels that Saudi Arabia produces each day. The US produces almost 14 million barrels per day. Chevron, the second-largest US oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. “President Trump’s mission in Venezuela is straightforward. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity and prosperity to the people of Venezuela,” Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Wednesday in Caracas, Venezuela. “I believe the deals that are signed today – tens of billions of dollars of investment, ultimately many thousands of jobs – are critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity and prosperity for everyone in Venezuela.” The White House confirmed on Monday that it was partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners, NABEP, as part of Trump’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry. Yet the agreement has been met with scepticism from energy experts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s oil industry, which is in disarray after years of neglect. There are also questions about whether Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodriguez, has the authority to give NABEP 100-year rights over 17 oilfields with reserves of 65 billion barrels – and whether future Venezuelan or American administrations would overturn the agreement. Venezuela’s constitution states that arrangements like the one that the US announced this week must be approved by the National Assembly, which has not happened, said Ian Vasquez, vice-president for international studies at the Cato Institute. “The deal lacks legitimacy since it was agreed to with a dictatorship that has clung to power for decades through violence and by committing what was probably the largest electoral fraud in Latin American history in 2024,” Vasquez said. “The agreement was also reached under overwhelming pressure, military and otherwise, from the United States. As such, any future Venezuelan democracy will question the deal, thus undermining confidence in the current arrangement.” Wright pushed back against criticism on Wednesday during a joint press conference with Rodriguez. “This is a deal that’s a massive win and benefit for the people of the United States of America and a massive win for the people of Venezuela,” he said. “Because what it’s going to do is take resources that are underground, not helping anyone, and invest capital and money and technology and bring them to the surface to better the lives of Venezuelans, better supply energy to Americans.” Trump has eyed Venezuela’s oil since the January capture of then President Nicolas Maduro and has pressed to get US businesses back into the country. “We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in,” he said that same month. He suggested again on Monday that other US oil majors were preparing for a return, though other than Chevron, there is no evidence of that. ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods said in January that Venezuela was “ uninvestable”. An Exxon spokesman said this week that “nothing has changed”. The history of US oil majors in Venezuela explains the hesitation. Venezuela nationalised its oil industry in 1976 and created the state-owned company Petroleos de Venezuela S.A. A second nationalisation occurred in 2007, when President Hugo Chavez pushed foreign oil companies into state-controlled joint ventures and seized the assets of companies that refused. Chevron agreed to a joint venture. Others, including Exxon and ConocoPhillips, refused, and Venezuela took their assets. Trump has said that the agreement with Venezuela would “substantially lower” petrol prices in the US. However, analysts have repeatedly warned that Venezuela’s dilapidated oil infrastructure will require years of restoration work and tens of billions of dollars to resuscitate. “It could take two to four years to get new greenfield facilities online in the Orinoco region,” Amy Jaffe, director of the Global Energy, Climate, and Sustainability Lab at New York University, said in an email. “Other places where there is no pipeline and other kinds of support infrastructure could take longer.” Meanwhile, the national average price for a gallon of regular petrol jumped overnight to US$4.12, according to the motor club AAA. That is 93 cents more than it cost at this point last year.

title: China urges global AI cooperation, not rivalry, ahead of Xi-Trump summit
description: With the high-stakes meeting just weeks away and tech tensions escalating, Beijing uses a G20 ministerial forum to advocate collaboration on the emerging technology.
content: China’s science and technology minister Yin Hejun has called for global cooperation to manage the opportunities and risks posed by artificial intelligence, as Beijing and Washington face renewed trade and tech tensions ahead of a planned meeting between their leaders later this month. Speaking at the G20 Innovation Ministerial Meeting held in the United States, Yin said the development of AI and other emerging technologies had entered an “unprecedentedly active” period, with opportunities and challenges coexisting, according to a statement published on the website of China’s Ministry of Science and Technology on Wednesday. “There is an urgent need for countries to work together to address them,” Yin was quoted as saying in the statement. The G20 gathering was held from Monday through Tuesday. Yin’s remarks come as AI and other advanced technologies have become increasingly entangled in the broader rivalry between the world’s two largest economies, with Washington weighing further restrictions that could hamper China’s technological ambitions. The US has already rolled out a series of measures affecting Chinese tech products, including restrictions on foreign-made advanced drones, robots and connected power inverters. In response, Beijing has tightened export controls on dual-use drone technology. But the recent flare-up, wrote a group of Citi Research analysts led by Yu Xiangrong in a research note last month, was “unlikely to materially disrupt China’s AI exports”. The analysts explained that direct US-China trade in the sector was “already suppressed at the aggregate level, limiting the potential first-order impact of further restrictions”. Meanwhile, Washington is currently mulling potential restrictions on Chinese data centre equipment and open-weight models. At the G20 ministerial meeting, Yin said Beijing would continue to prioritise technological innovation and expand high-level opening-up in science and technology. On AI, Beijing officially promotes what it calls a “people-centred” and “upwards and beneficial” approach, while aiming to promote global AI capacity-building and help bridge the digital divide for developing nations. The ministerial gathering also highlighted the divergent approaches of China and the US on AI governance, with Washington pushing a largely hands-off approach that limits new regulation of the technology. Yin’s counterpart, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and co-host of the two-day meeting, cautioned against restrictive new rules and called on countries to adopt the “Carolina Principles” by taking a hands-off approach to AI regulation, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The two-day gathering offered Washington and Beijing a crucial window to engage directly on AI policy, just weeks before President Xi Jinping’s planned September 24 visit to the US, where he is expected to discuss a wide range of trade and economic issues with his American counterpart Donald Trump. Yin’s appeal for international cooperation echoed Xi’s message at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July, where the Chinese president stressed the importance of greater openness and cooperation in AI, as well as international coordination on its development, governance rules and technical standards. During the ministerial gathering, Yin also held talks with science and technology ministers and representatives from the United Kingdom, Argentina and other nations to explore bilateral and multilateral cooperation, according to China’s science ministry.

title: China’s Inner Mongolia pitches affordable homes, fast train to lure Beijing commuters
description: The region is highlighting commuter transit times and booming AI economy to entice the capital’s residents.
content: Inner Mongolia autonomous region’s government is launching a campaign to lure homebuyers from Beijing, pitching the area’s cheaper housing and high-speed rail links amid an artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre boom that is driving up demand for talent and investment. The region’s housing authority, together with officials from Hohhot, Chifeng, Ulanqab, and Duolun county, concluded a three-day property showcase titled “I Have a Home in the Grasslands” in Beijing on Monday, according to the region’s official newspaper. The event presented nearly 20 development projects spanning primary residences, wellness communities, and holiday flats. Authorities pitched a “dual-city” lifestyle, stressing the high-speed rail that connects Ulanqab to central Beijing in as little as 1.5 hours. Price was another key selling point – average prices for commercial housing across Inner Mongolia were about 5,800 yuan (US$863) per square metre, while Hohhot homes cost roughly one-sixth as much as those in Beijing, the report said. The push comes as parts of Inner Mongolia are undergoing an economic shift. As the global artificial intelligence boom fuels a scramble for more computing power and electricity, Ulanqab has emerged as a major data-centre hub, with its cool climate and ample renewable energy making it an attractive location for the industry. Under a three-year plan running through 2028, Ulanqab would focus on green computing for training and running large AI models, while encouraging investment in liquid cooling, computing hardware and AI software and talent. At the same time, the region’s housing market, like much of China’s, remains under pressure. Sales value and floor area of commercial properties, including residential homes, in Inner Mongolia fell 6.2 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively, in the first half of this year, according to regional government data. The region has introduced a series of measures to shore up demand, including allowing buyers from Beijing and other regions to receive the same benefits as local buyers, and promoting a policy that would allow buyers to receive a “certificate on handover” – property ownership documents when they take possession of their homes. The measures echo a broader push by Beijing to rebuild confidence in China’s housing market. Last week, the central government unveiled reforms aimed at shifting home sales away from the long-standing presales model, while tightening safeguards for buyers who purchase homes before construction was finished.

title: In Bishkek, US envoys shadow the SCO summit in challenge on Beijing and Moscow’s turf
description: Central Asian countries in focus as Washington pursues outreach serving to blunt Chinese influence in strategically valuable region.
content: As China and Russia rallied dozens of countries in Bishkek to shape a multipolar world order, Washington’s envoys were splitting the spotlight by meeting several Central Asian presidents in the Kyrgyz capital this week. The manoeuvring showed that the US was likely to continue its outreach to the region and seek to blunt Beijing’s influence, but it would be “unrealistic” for Washington to force Central Asian countries to choose sides, according to a leading Chinese analyst. US Senator Steve Daines and Sergio Gor, America’s special envoy for South and Central Asia, met Kyrgyzstan’s Sadyr Japarov, Tajikistan’s Emomali Rahmon and Uzbekistan’s Shavkat Mirziyoyev separately in Bishkek on Monday. The US diplomatic duo’s exchanges with the three leaders took place as Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin were in town for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s annual summit. The summit brought together the three Central Asian presidents alongside other notable leaders, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Xi met with Japarov and Mirziyoyev on Monday, while Putin held talks with his Uzbek, Kyrgyz and Tajik counterparts on Monday and Tuesday. Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kazakhstan are among the SCO’s founding members. The SCO has drawn greater global attention, as some view it as a vehicle in which China and Russia can pool their influence to compete with the US in international politics, or as an alternative diplomatic space outside Washington-led institutions. As former Soviet republics, the five Central Asian states – including Turkmenistan – have long been regarded as Moscow’s backyard. Beijing’s footprint there has also expanded in recent years with deeper and broader economic ties. Washington has placed higher emphasis on the region through the “C5+1” framework, referring to the Central Asian countries and the US. In February, Gor told a forum in Bishkek that Central Asia was an area that the administration of US President Donald Trump had “prioritised”. Once the main stage of the “Great Game” between the British and Russian empires more than a century ago, Central Asia’s geopolitical importance has regained prominence under the Sino-US strategic competition, particularly as artificial intelligence and semiconductors have emerged as points of contention. Washington has sought to build a critical minerals supply chain beyond China, while Central Asia has vast potential in tungsten, uranium, antimony, molybdenum and rare earths as well as proximity to the Trans-Caspian corridor connecting Europe. Given the Central Asia countries’ relative wealth of rare earths and critical minerals, the Trump administration has attached great importance to cooperating with them, according to Wu Xinbo, who heads Fudan University’s Institute of International Studies in Shanghai. “I think the US will continue to maintain its economic and diplomatic engagement in Central Asia,” Wu said. Washington’s push could effectively amount to vying with China and Russia for influence in the region and countering Beijing’s efforts to develop economic and trade relations with the neighbours, he added. According to official statements from the Kyrgyz, Tajik and Uzbek governments, their leaders’ talks with Daines and Gor all stressed the importance of the C5+1 platform. The discussions involving the two senior US government officials with Mirziyoyev and Rahmon each covered energy and critical minerals, while the meeting with the Uzbek president also touched on AI. In a social media post on Tuesday, Daines said he had visited Kazakhstan, adding that he “always appreciates seeing the positive impacts of trade and investment between our two nations”. Gor wrote separately on Tuesday that he had had a “very insightful” conversation with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, saying: “Commercial diplomacy between our two countries is at record levels and growing.” Still, Central Asian states have appeared to pursue a balanced foreign policy approach between China, the US and Russia, establishing C5+ formats with other international players such as the European Union and Japan. As the fierce contest between China and the US continues on AI, Kazakhstan is now the only country to have joined both the Beijing-backed World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation and the Washington-led supply-chain initiative Pax Silica. Uzbekistan recently sought to follow suit. But Washington has reportedly warned Pax Silica members that they could be excluded from the coalition if they also sign up for Beijing’s competing mechanism. According to Wu, the warning made it clear that Washington wanted to force some countries to choose between China and the US. “But personally, I think that the odds [of reaching that point] are not high,” he said. “Central Asia’s economic and geopolitical ties with China far exceed those with the US. “In the long run, I think it is an unrealistic goal for the US to try to counter China and Russia in this region.” Daines’ Central Asia trip came days after his latest visit to China, during which the close Trump ally toured several Chinese technology companies in the countdown to of Xi’s planned summit with Trump in Washington. Wu described the Montana Republican’s trips as more of a personal itinerary. He noted that Daines was not running in the US midterm elections in November. His Senate term is set to expire in January next year. “I don’t think his visit to China this time is mainly about playing the role of a messenger,” Wu added.

title: Jockey Club delays mainland China races as turnover hits record HK$331.7b
description: Club’s operating surplus could suffer for next few years over investment in basketball betting and new races at mainland facility.
content: The Hong Kong Jockey Club has revealed it will delay introducing regular racing at its Conghua Racecourse in mainland China as it reported record financial results despite a “challenging and fast-changing environment”. The club on Wednesday reported wagering and lottery turnover rose by 3.6 per cent over the previous financial year to a record HK$331.7 billion (US$42.30 billion), despite “a very difficult environment, including the ever-expanding threat of illegal gambling”. The club also said it contributed HK$39.3 billion to the community, while football betting turnover rose by 3.6 per cent to a record HK$179 billion and racing turnover rose by the same proportion to HK$143 billion. Racecourse attendance also benefited from a tourism surge, with visitor numbers more than doubling to 401,259 during the 2025-26 season, up by 105 per cent year on year. But the club, the city’s sole licensed gambling operator, warned it expected its operating surplus to fall “over the next few years” due to heavy investment in basketball betting and its Conghua training facility in Guangzhou, Guangdong province. It had initially planned to open the venue next month, but had decided to delay that after receiving the latest “risk assessment from the relevant mainland departments”. “Following discussions between both parties, it was agreed that we will continue to work closely together to devise appropriate mitigation measures,” the club said. “As such, the originally scheduled October event will be postponed to a later date.” It is understood the delay may be about a few months while both sides continue to review and work out more details for the launch later. The club will not be allowed to offer betting on the races at the facility, due to the mainland’s laws on gambling. The club also highlighted the impact of the government’s pause on granting a licence for regulated basketball betting – a service it had already “invested substantially in” ahead of a launch that was originally planned for this month. A source previously told the South China Morning Post it had already invested HK$400 million for preparatory work, including a dedicated basketball betting system, and that a further HK$600 million was planned to be committed. The club said it had “invested substantially in its technology, including in the customer digital experience and in a new sports wagering platform – initially to be launched together with basketball betting”, which has now pivoted towards football betting. With a heavy investment in the Conghua Racecourse, “it will take time for revenue to be fully realised and, as a result, the club’s operating surplus is set to drop further over the next few years”, the club said. There had been bad news for the club earlier in the day, when it was announced that Romantic Warrior, who has won more prize money than any horse in racing history, had been forced to retire through injury. Despite the setbacks, chairman Martin Liao Cheung-kong was quick to praise his organisation’s racing and commitment to the community. A collaboration with China Travel Group and its coordination with the Hong Kong Tourism Board’s mega-events strategy was highlighted as a key part of the tourism success, while initiatives such as Racing with Golf, Racing with Rugby and Racing with Football helped to showcase the city. “This year, perhaps more than any other, highlighted the strength of the club’s racing and its enduring commitment to its purpose: the betterment of our society,” Liao said. “The unprecedented success of our horses cemented Hong Kong’s position as one of the global leaders in horse racing, while also attracting record numbers of tourists to our racecourses. “Meanwhile, our licensed and regulated football betting service also achieved gratifying results. Above all, despite a very difficult environment, including the ever-expanding threat of illegal gambling, the club maintained its strong support for the community and for the charities that depend upon us.” The club’s status as a global leader on the track was also cemented by champion gallopers Ka Ying Rising and Romantic Warrior, who shared the Horse of the Year crown last season in an unprecedented tie. Chief executive Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges praised the club’s “outstanding results both on and off the track”, despite a “challenging and fast-changing environment”. “Thanks to the success and agile implementation of our long-term strategies we achieved outstanding results both on and off the track,” he said.

title: Opinion | China-Egypt joint drills a show of Beijing’s military reach
description: As recent air drills in Egypt indicate, after decades of building economic interests abroad, China is developing the ability to put military power behind them.
content: China is beginning to match its economic presence abroad with the military reach required to operate across it. The clearest evidence came from Egypt. Chinese J-16 fighters flew there recently, supported by YU-20 tankers that refuelled them in the air. The Chinese jets are taking part in Egypt’s “Eagles of Civilisation” alongside Egyptian Rafales and MiG-29s. This is the first time China has sent the jets to Africa, providing experience in moving a combat force across continents and operating with a major Arab military. Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt commemorates 70 years of diplomatic relations. Over those decades, ties have evolved from diplomacy and trade into infrastructure, technology and now military cooperation. Chinese economic interests are deeply embedded around the Suez Canal. Chinese companies have established manufacturing and logistics operations, using Egypt as a production and distribution base linking their supply chains to European, African and Middle Eastern markets. That footprint is still growing. Egyptian firms signed 17 export contracts worth US$168 million with Chinese buyers last month. Beijing’s investment in Egypt in the first half of 2026 is estimated at up to US$2 billion, with much of the funds going into the expansion of existing projects. Beijing has also extended zero-tariff treatment to Egyptian goods, removing duties that had reached 30 per cent. Yet the commercial relationship remains asymmetric: Egypt’s trade deficit with China exceeded US$18 billion last year. The stakes rise when China’s economic footprint needs to be secured. Ports, factories, logistics networks and supply chains are exposed when instability disrupts access to them. The further Chinese interests extend, the more useful a military presence capable of reaching those regions becomes. The drill provided a glimpse of that capability. For years, China’s expanding global presence had been primarily commercial. Then, the Belt and Road Initiative built infrastructure, opened markets and established Chinese companies in strategic locations. The next stage is military reach to protect that economic presence, and Egypt shows what that transition can look like. A similar pattern is emerging in technology. Huawei Technologies has bid to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centres for the Egyptian government using Ascend chips, while Washington is trying to pull together a competing proposal involving Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Microsoft. Egypt’s AI strategy aims to raise the gross domestic product contribution of its information and communications technology sector to 7.7 per cent by 2030, making access to American and Chinese technology suppliers part of a wider effort to build a domestic technology industry. This also gives Cairo bargaining power over which companies gain a position in this strategic sector. The Chinese presence is therefore extending across the sectors that matter to Beijing’s long-term position in Egypt: manufacturing, logistics, technology and defence. Cairo, however, is not building its relationship with China at the expense of other partnerships. Egypt remains a major recipient of US military assistance and operates a mixed fleet of American, French and Russian aircraft. It has expanded relations with China, maintained ties with Russia, cultivated European and Gulf partners, and joined the Brics grouping. Defence procurement reflects the same approach. Egypt has reportedly shown interest in China’s J-10C as it diversifies its fighter fleet. The exercises give Egyptian forces exposure to Chinese systems while Cairo continues to operate Western aircraft and maintain its defence relationships. That gives both sides something they want. China gains access and operational experience in the Middle East and Africa. Egypt gains another military supplier and major power with an interest in maintaining close ties. The same calculation extends into security policy. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi declined to attend White House talks in February last year after US President Donald Trump pressed his proposal to relocate Palestinians from Gaza. Egypt has also kept a distance from US military operations against the Houthis, despite the economic damage to the Suez Canal. The canal’s revenues fell by 61 per cent in 2024 as attacks on Red Sea shipping diverted vessels away. Cairo had a direct interest in restoring navigation and protecting the canal, yet its response was shaped by its assessment of what those interests required. This is where China’s growing presence becomes useful to Egypt. Chinese foreign direct investment can sit alongside American defence assistance. Chinese technology can compete with American tech. Chinese aircraft can train with Egyptian aircraft while Cairo keeps using Western systems. For Washington, the calculation is more uncomfortable. Cairo only needs credible alternatives to make American boldness more costly, and each additional supplier, investor or military partner gives Egypt more room to resist pressure from any one of them. The implications extend globally. Washington and Beijing frame their rivalry around competing strategic camps. Cairo shows middle powers can keep both sides invested without giving either one exclusive influence, using the resulting competition to extract investment, technology, military capabilities and diplomatic leverage. For China, the larger significance is the narrowing distance between its economic presence and its ability to project military power. Beijing, after decades of building economic interests abroad, is now developing the logistics, access and operational experience required to put military power behind those interests. Egypt is where that transition is becoming visible as China’s economic interests and military capabilities are beginning to connect. Cairo has an incentive to allow this because a more capable China gives Egypt another powerful relationship. The next geopolitical challenge will be how far China can extend this model, and how much military reach its global economic footprint can support and its rivals stand.

title: Indonesian wildfire haze forces 1.4 million students to move to online learning
description: Toxic air pollution levels have forced 12,800 schools across six provinces in Sumatra and Borneo to close.
content: About 1.4 million students in six Indonesian provinces ⁠had shifted to online ⁠learning due to poor air quality ⁠triggered by forest and land fires, an official said on Wednesday. As of September 2, around 1.43 million students from 12,874 schools in six of the provinces hit hardest by forest and land fires had been studying remotely, Gogot Suharwoto, an education ministry official, told the media. Indonesia has intensified efforts to contain haze caused by wildfire in the six provinces, which include Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra on the island of Sumatra, as well as West Kalimantan, Central Kalimantan, and South Kalimantan on Borneo. Of the ⁠1.43 million students, 1.1 million were in West Kalimantan, Gogot said, the province that has ‌recorded the most extensive wildfires so far this year. The remote learning period would last from Monday until Friday and ‌would be continuously evaluated every three days, Gogot said. The decision to conduct ⁠online learning would ⁠be based on the air pollution standard index in each region, he said. Remote learning would be ‌imposed when the index exceeded 200 in a particular location, Gogot added. A majority of regions in Kalimantan ‌recorded air ‌pollution readings in excess of 200 on Wednesday, with some even exceeding 1,000, Forestry ‌Ministry data showed. Southeast Pontianak region in West Kalimantan province was the worst hit, ⁠with a reading of 1,023. Indonesia’s air quality classification system considers readings above 300 as “hazardous”. “School principals ⁠are authorised to take immediate action in urgent situations. They do not have to wait until conditions worsen or spend too long consulting with other ‌authorities,” Gogot said. Forestry ministry ‌data showed that about 200,000 hectares of land were burned by wildfires in the first seven months of the year, nearly doubling in July alone. Wildfires burned around 73,310 hectares of land in six priority provinces, according to forestry ministry data.

title: China’s US$10.8b trade short cut: new Pinglu Canal prepares to supercharge Asean shipments
description: Delivery of first command vessel looks to signal imminent opening of megaproject connecting inland factories directly to Southeast Asian markets such as Vietnam.
content: Aptly dubbed the Pinglu 001, the first command and management vessel for the Pinglu Canal was delivered on Monday and will soon enter service as China prepares to open the strategic waterway designed to support surging trade with Southeast Asia. The delivery marks one of the final steps before the 72.7 billion yuan (US$10.8 billion) megaproject is expected to officially open later this month after years in the making. The canal is a signature project for the world’s second-largest economy as it seeks to accelerate freight flow and slash transit costs with its largest trading partner, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). A fleet of command vessels will patrol the 134km (83-mile) canal to oversee navigation and handle emergency responses. The waterway links Nanning, capital of the Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region, to the Gulf of Tonkin, also known as the Beibu Gulf, between China and Vietnam. The command ships are capable of operating in both coastal and inland waters and can carry up to 50 operational personnel. Their smart navigation systems will undergo testing at shore-based facilities in Qinzhou, Guangxi, where the canal empties into the sea, according to the state-run People’s Daily. The canal’s debut is expected to align with the 23rd China-Asean Expo, scheduled for September 17 to 21 in Nanning. Despite its relatively short length, the waterway is expected to have an outsized impact as Beijing attempts to redraw regional development patterns and further diversify trade relations. Designed to accommodate 5,000-tonne vessels, Pinglu is China’s first river-to-sea canal, and it looks to cut the transit route between inland Guangxi and the ocean by 560km (348 miles). By connecting an extensive network of rivers and tributaries to the sea, landlocked regions in China’s south and southwest – including the provinces of Yunnan, Guizhou and Sichuan – will gain faster access to Asean and global shipping lanes. This offers a critical logistics artery for moving goods such as textiles, timber, plastics, electronics and steel, particularly as Vietnam remains a popular destination for Chinese manufacturers shifting production. China-Asean trade soared 24.7 per cent to US$744.4 billion in the first seven months of the year, according to Chinese customs data. Bilateral trade with Vietnam surged 33.7 per cent to US$215.1 billion over the same period. Trialling a fleet of command ships prior to the canal’s opening is an indication that authorities expect the waterway to instantly carry a lot of shipping Qu Ke, CCB International Robust trade with Southeast Asia helped China weather a renewed trade war with the United States in 2025. Beijing now seeks to accelerate diversification for exporters while injecting fresh economic impetus into inland regions close to Asean, with the Pinglu Canal serving as a critical piece of infrastructure to form a link. There are expectations that the waterway could see immediate and heavy use. “Trialling a fleet of command ships prior to the canal’s opening is an indication that authorities expect the waterway to instantly carry a lot of shipping following its opening, especially for goods to and from Vietnam,” said Qu Ke, a transport analyst at CCB International in Hong Kong. The cost of water transport is lower than moving goods by land or rail, he said, adding that the canal’s 5,000-tonne capacity and efficiency could be further enhanced via intermodal logistics and the adoption of new technology. “Goods and sub-assemblies from factories across China’s western and southwestern interior can first be delivered to Nanning – a major city with sound transport connections – before they are loaded into vessels and shipped down the Pinglu to reach Vietnam to cut costs and time,” Qu said. Pinglu’s first shipping route, however, will be to the island province of Hainan, according to state media reports. Hainan, now China’s largest free-trade area by size, is located just across the Gulf of Tonkin. Both Guangxi and Hainan are positioning themselves at the forefront of China’s economic integration with Asean.

title: How Japan aims to convert ageing warships into leverage to counter China
description: Tokyo plans to send retired destroyers to Manila and Jakarta, but it may not demand alignment against China as part of deal.
content: Japan’s plans to transfer ageing warships to the Philippines and Indonesia could turn older military hardware into geopolitical leverage, deepening regional security ties while helping Tokyo counterbalance Beijing’s growing influence, observers say. Such transfers, they said, fit into Tokyo’s broader security assistance toolkit to strengthen partners’ capabilities and forge longer-term defence relationships through equipment, training, maintenance and interoperability – expanding Japan’s regional influence without demanding alignment against Beijing. The broader effort is aimed at cultivating what Tokyo calls a “desirable security environment” by taking a more active role in shaping the region’s security architecture. Providing retiring warships is an important element of that push. The Philippines expects to receive five Abukuma-class destroyer escorts within two to three years, while Tokyo and Jakarta are discussing the transfer of Asagiri-class destroyers, the first of which was retired in March after 38 years of service. An analysis published on August 25 by Japan’s National Institute for Defence Studies (NIDS), the defence ministry’s main research institute, suggests Tokyo could eventually broaden the pool of equipment for such transfers. NIDS researcher Akinori Ishihara pointed to Japan’s transfer of ageing but still operational warships to Russia during World War I after newer vessels reduced their relative importance in Japan’s future fleet. Ishihara argued that the key consideration was not whether equipment was new or old, or active or retired, but whether Japan could transfer it and still maintain the defence capabilities it needed. That could open the door to retiring equipment early to make it available for transfer, the NIDS analysis suggests. As Japan introduces more advanced, automated and uncrewed systems, some older platforms could become less critical to the Japan Self-Defence Forces structure before reaching the end of their planned service lives, expanding the pool of equipment available for transfer to regional partners. Hirohito Ogi, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Geoeconomics in Tokyo, said such an approach made sense for vessels with relatively limited air-defence capabilities designed mainly for peacetime and grey-zone operations. As China’s precision-strike capabilities became increasingly sophisticated, such ships were unlikely to survive high-intensity combat, he said, arguing that Japan should retire them as early as possible and renew its capabilities. Retiring equipment, however, is only one part of Tokyo’s expanding security aid toolkit. A key mechanism is the Official Security Assistance framework, a grant-based military aid programme Japan launched in 2023 to provide equipment and infrastructure to partner countries. Tokyo has increased its budget from 2 billion yen (US$12.5 million) in the 2023 financial year to a record 18.1 billion yen this financial year and plans to continue expanding the number of countries covered by the programme. Tokyo has used the programme to supply equipment ranging from patrol boats and coastal radars, to surveillance systems and drones, with maritime security being a major focus. Both the Philippines and Indonesia are recipients, reflecting Japan’s efforts to strengthen partners along strategically important waterways. Sebastian Maslow, an associate professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Social Science, said Japan had increasingly embraced arms transfers as a foreign policy tool since overhauling its export restrictions in 2014, a process that culminated in a further major easing of the rules earlier this year. He said Japan’s main strategic objective was to strengthen defence cooperation with Indo-Pacific partners to deter China’s growing influence. Japan’s evolving strategy was “designed to counterbalance China’s rise by preserving the status quo in the region” with arms transfers, helping Tokyo arrive at the centre of emerging bilateral and minilateral defence networks, according to Maslow. The Philippines provides a concrete example of that strategic logic. Maslow pointed to increasingly active mainland Chinese naval operations southeast of Taiwan, particularly around the Bashi Channel and Philippine Sea, with vessels subsequently deploying deeper into the Pacific and around Japan’s islands. Ogi said that strengthening the Philippine Navy’s ability to monitor and track those movements would “directly contribute to Japan’s security” and could also help deter a Taiwan contingency. The warships would add to a growing range of Japanese maritime security equipment provided or offered to Manila, including coastguard vessels and TC-90 aircraft, while the two sides have also explored the potential transfer of Japan’s ageing Type 88 surface-to-ship missiles. The value of second-hand platforms could also extend beyond the hardware itself. Tokyo is discussing training, maintenance and sustainment with Manila, potentially keeping Japan involved throughout much of the equipment’s remaining service life. Indonesia presents a different case as Jakarta seeks to preserve its strategic autonomy, even as defence cooperation with Tokyo expands. Misato Matsuoka, an associate professor at Teikyo University, said Indonesia’s value to Japan did not depend on Jakarta siding with Tokyo against Beijing. She described Tokyo’s approach as “influence without demanding alignment”. Cooperation with Jakarta could show that Japan’s expanding security role did not necessarily amount to bloc-building, she said, a particularly significant point given Indonesia’s influence within Asean and the region’s broader preference for strategic autonomy. Building on this perspective, an analysis for Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies by Chaula Rininta Anindya and Adhi Priamarizki described Jakarta’s ties with Japan as one of “strategic convenience” rather than alignment, while cautioning that Beijing might still view closer defence cooperation as an attempt to constrain China. Maslow said Indonesia’s position as both a Japanese security partner and a close partner of China would test “how China will respond to new defence cooperation in the region”. For Matsuoka, Japan’s longer-term influence could lie less in locking Indonesia into Japanese hardware than in making itself more relevant within the country’s security institutions through training, maintenance and other cooperation. Japan’s influence, she said, could be greatest when it did not require Indonesia to become “Japan-aligned”. According to Maslow, that reflects a broader transformation in Japan’s regional role. He said Tokyo was expanding its traditional economic role into the security sphere, moving “from building production networks to establishing defence networks”.

title: Teen spectator in VIP seat hauled out of arena after hurling basketball at China players
description: NBA star Yang Hansen scores buzzer-beating shot to beat Lebanon in World Cup Asian qualifier and keep team on track for global showpiece.
content: Yang Hansen scored a dramatic late winner to give China an 89-87 victory over Lebanon in their Fiba Basketball World Cup Asian Qualifiers clash on Monday, in a game almost overshadowed by a fan throwing a ball that hit the home star. The 21-year-old Yang sealed the win at the Xishi Basketball Centre in Zhuji, Zhejiang province, with a buzzer-beating bank shot, improving China’s record to 5-3 in the second stage of qualifying and keeping them third in their group. China had squandered a six-point lead with 40 seconds remaining after a series of defensive lapses and a foul on a three-point attempt allowed Lebanon to tie the game at 87-87 with 4.1 seconds left. The dramatic finish followed a bizarre disturbance in the fourth quarter. After Yang was fouled and fell to the floor, a teenager in a front-row VIP seat picked up the loose ball and hurled it back onto the court. The ball struck China captain Zhao Jiwei before bouncing towards Yang while he was still on the floor. Security personnel promptly tackled the spectator, who was later identified as the 16-year-old son of a local sponsor, physically hauling him out of the arena. 昨天男篮世预赛现场极端观众用球砸杨瀚森 pic.twitter.com/v1otRcLG7J — 半糖主义ʰᵃˡ (@BTzhuyiY) September 1, 2026 Prominent basketball commentator Su Qun said the teen threw the ball because he was angry over a series of uncalled physical fouls committed by Lebanon’s naturalised centre, the American-born DJ Funderburk, but missed his intended target. “His intended target was either the referee or the Lebanese player, but his aim was terrible,” Su said, noting China only narrowly avoided a team technical foul or venue penalty. “Cheering or criticising referees is understandable, but throwing objects on the court is illegal,” Su added. “Because a minor is involved, I hope the public refrains from doxxing him and allows him to learn from this mistake.” Local media reported that police issued a stern reprimand to the 16-year-old spectator following his ejection, adding that he was currently awaiting further administrative action at home while the investigation continued. The incident ignited fierce debate across Chinese social media. While a minority of netizens attributed the act to an overly emotional youth defending a national team star, an overwhelming majority condemned the behaviour, with many raising concerns over spectator sportsmanship and questioning whether the teenager’s privileged access as a sponsor’s child contributed to the outburst. “Sitting in the front row, they are either rich or influential,” one widely shared comment on Weibo read. “Perks of being a sponsor’s child acting so wilfully.” Other commenters urged the public and event organisers to address spectator etiquette and venue governance. “The first lesson in sports education is learning the rules,” one widely shared online comment read. “Fans should focus on Yang’s heroic buzzer-beater rather than the chaos in the stands, while ensuring the minor takes responsibility without facing online harassment.” Yang delivered a dominant performance off the bench, recording 19 points, nine rebounds, three assists and one block while shooting 8-of-9 from the field in 26 minutes of play. “We specifically practised this tactic in training; we just applied it on the court,” Yang said after the game. “If it went in, we won; if not, we would have played overtime. I just brought what I worked on during the Summer League onto the court.” Teammate Wang Junjie praised the centre during postgame interviews. “We had this play set up and found Hansen clearly, and he lived up to expectations,” Wang said. “Hansen – NBA! Super high level!” Chinese basketball team officials confirmed on Monday that Yang will miss China’s next qualifier window in late November against Saudi Arabia and Lebanon as he returns to the United States to prepare for his second NBA season with the Portland Trail Blazers. Despite his coming absence, the performance solidified Yang’s standing as the new focal point of China’s national team. Taking to social media after the match, Yang wrote: “Grounded through thousands of strikes and blows, standing firm against winds from all directions. “Thank you to the coaches, teammates and every fan who cheered for us. We won this hard-fought victory together. I am with you all, go Team China!”

title: Education Bureau steps in after students wait in rain for uniform and hair checks
description: Authorities remind two schools to think about students’ needs after complaints about long lines outside campuses while inspections carried out.
content: Hong Kong education authorities have reminded a school to consider the needs of students when enforcing rules after many were forced to wait in a long line outside the campus in the rain to have their uniforms and hair checked on the first day of the new academic year. The Education Bureau also made a similar call to another school, where students deemed to have failed with hair grooming rules were told to remain on campus until they could contact their parents. Dozens of online posts showed a long queue of students standing outside the campus of Kowloon Tong School (Secondary Section) on Tuesday, with some claiming they were waiting for teachers to inspect their uniforms and hair. Teresa Hon Pui-yee, the school principal, sent a letter to parents later that day defending the inspections, although she noted the school had since reviewed the process. “In order to establish discipline, cultivate students’ sense of responsibility, and prepare for the student photo shoot on Thursday, class teachers reminded all parents and students [last] Saturday that the school would conduct a uniform inspection on Tuesday,” she said. However, she explained that because a relatively large number of students arrived at a later time on Tuesday, they were required to queue outside the campus to wait. She pledged that students would not be marked as late if they tapped their cards when school started. Hon maintained that students should arrive at school early to ensure sufficient time to hand in assignments and prepare learning materials, which she said would help their education and physical and mental well-being. A bureau spokeswoman said it contacted the school to follow up on the situation. “The Education Bureau reminded the school to consider students’ actual needs when enforcing school rules and to make appropriate school-based arrangements,” she said. “The Education Bureau will maintain contact with the school concerned and provide suitable advice and support.” In a separate incident involving Kowloon’s Tang King Po School, posts on a social media platform claimed that it not only enforced strict grooming rules, but also required students who did not meet the standards to remain on campus while they contacted their parents to inform them of the situation. Some posts claimed that about 300 students were sent to the school hall and had to call their parents before they were allowed to leave. According to some posts, the school required that hair not cover eyebrows or ears, nor touch the collar at the back. The boys’ school has been approached for comment. The bureau spokeswoman said it contacted the school and also reminded it to consider students’ actual needs. “Under all circumstances, school staff should maintain discipline while respecting students’ self-esteem, right to education, individual differences and health,” she said. Schools should draft rules that foster student self-discipline, but formulate them through communication with stakeholders to ensure understanding and consensus, she added.

title: Man arrested as Hong Kong customs seizes HK$42 million worth of ‘space oil’
description: Customs and Excise Department officers uncover workshop with etomidate materials and production equipment capable of making 160,000 cartridges.
content: Hong Kong customs has arrested a man and seized HK$42 million (US$5.3 million) worth of the illegal narcotic “space oil” from a workshop fitted with a semi-automated production line capable of churning out as many as 160,000 cartridges in a short span. Senior Investigator Chan Kit-lun of the Customs and Excise Department’s drug investigation bureau said on Wednesday officers intercepted a suspicious man the previous day and escorted him to a property in Kam Tin, Yuen Long. Inside, they found more than 3,000 suspected cartridges containing etomidate, or space oil, about 13.4kg (29.5lbs) of liquid etomidate, 3kg of etomidate powder and a range of drug-manufacturing and packaging equipment. Investigators found that the syndicate had installed a semi-automated production line featuring a high-precision liquid-filling machine. Chan said the seized raw materials, if fully processed using the production line, could have yielded up to 160,000 etomidate cartridges in a short time, posing a serious risk if released onto the market. Etomidate is an anaesthetic that authorities reclassified from a Part I poison to a dangerous drug in February last year. The suspect will be charged with one count of manufacturing a dangerous drug and one count of trafficking in a dangerous drug. He is expected to appear at Tuen Mun Court on Thursday. Under Hong Kong law, drug trafficking carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment and a HK$5 million fine.

title: Saleswoman arrested over aggressive sales tactics, third suspect linked to Opatra
description: Source says saleswoman suspected of pressuring customer at now-closed Sha Tin New Town Plaza outlet formerly run by Sayles Retail.
content: Hong Kong customs officers have arrested a woman on suspicion of using aggressive tactics to sell skincare products at a local beauty chain formerly operating under the Opatra London brand, bringing the number of arrests in the case to three. The Customs and Excise Department said on Wednesday that the beauty consultant, 22, allegedly pressured a customer into making purchases at the now-closed Sha Tin New Town Plaza outlet, which was formerly operated by Sayles Retail. The local woman reportedly used excuses such as “the facial treatment is not yet finished” to keep the customer in the shop before persuading her to buy products, the South China Morning Post has learned. “When selling beauty products, the saleswoman exerted undue influence and engaged in improper business practices that led the consumer to make a purchase decision she otherwise would not have made,” said Leung Ka-ho, senior investigator of customs’ trade descriptions investigation bureau. He said the department had received 38 calls for help linked to the chain. The reported losses amounted to more than HK$3 million (US$382,629), with individual cases ranging from HK$1,800 to more than HK$200,000. Customs officers last month arrested two staff members – a 42-year-old Hong Kong man and a 25‑year‑old woman, both managers linked to the brand – over similar tactics. They were later released on bail. Opatra’s headquarters in the United Kingdom has repeatedly distanced itself from the controversy and said the Hong Kong outlets were independently operated under a distribution agreement. The company also announced that it had suspended ties with Sayles Retail and pledged full cooperation with authorities. Investigators are trying to locate three directors of the local company but have not confirmed whether they are in Hong Kong. The company is reportedly facing lawsuits over unpaid rent totalling HK$795,000. All four Opatra outlets in the city, including the flagship store in Causeway Bay, were closed with the brand name covered.

title: Has India’s Modi found new mediator clout after talks with Putin, Iran?
description: Analysts say while India could act as a potential bridge in engaging parties locked in conflict, ensuring a resolution works will be harder.
content: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Iranian leader Masoud Pezeshkian at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit have put the spotlight on New Delhi’s ability to mediate major conflicts. Positioned between Russia and the West, and with working ties across rival camps in the Middle East, India is seen by some analysts as a potential bridge in conflicts where few countries can still speak to all sides, though they note access does not necessarily translate into leverage. On Monday at the summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Modi urged Putin to end the conflict in Ukraine, saying that every day spent at war set humanity back. “As you know, India supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to extend its support to every such endeavour,” Modi said. In a separate development, Pezeshkian requested Modi to use India’s wide-ranging contacts to help steer other parties away from conflict, according to a statement from Iran. “We believe that the solution to the issues we face lies in dialogue and cooperation, and that all available capacities must be mobilised to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict,” he said. The two meetings highlighted the role Modi could play in easing conflicts where India had consistently avoided taking sides while urging peace, analysts said. “Modi’s call to Putin to move from endless war to an end to the war, and Iran’s request that he use India’s contacts to pull others back from conflict, show Delhi testing a new role,” said Srinivaasan Balakrishnan, director of strategic engagements and partnerships at the Indic Researchers Forum think tank. “India has the rare ability to talk to Moscow, Tehran and the West all at once. That access is real. Turning it into settlements is harder. Mediation works only when the parties want an exit and trust the messenger. India has the first part. It still has to prove the second.” Top leaders at the SCO – a Eurasian grouping that includes China, Russia, India, Pakistan and Iran – signed a joint statement after the two-day summit condemning military strikes on Tehran and backing a declaration endorsed by all 10 member states, including India. The statement stopped short of naming Israel and the United States. India had disassociated itself from an SCO statement in June last year that condemned Israeli military attacks on Iran. Three months later, Modi signed the Tianjin declaration that described the US strikes against Iran as a violation of the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter. The latest declaration comes ahead of a Brics summit in Delhi on September 12 to 13. “The Bishkek declaration registered concern over West Asia, backed diplomacy over force, and left little doubt that conflict would follow the leaders to Delhi,” Balakrishnan said. The resolution of conflict was expected to emerge as “a prominent theme rather than a side conversation” at the Brics summit, with both Putin and Pezeshkian due to attend, along with Chinese President Xi Jinping, UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres and other prominent leaders, he added. “The implications could be significant if India uses its chairmanship well. A host that can still speak to Moscow, Tehran and the West is better placed than most to keep the discussion from collapsing into bloc rhetoric,” Balakrishnan said. This could have an impact internationally, as Brics would be framed as an instrument of peace, stability and economic support for a strained world, he added. “Whether the theme matters will depend on whether India can talk to everyone without becoming anyone’s instrument.” Harsh Ramaswamy, an independent political commentator, said Modi’s meetings with Putin and Pezeshkian at the SCO showed that both respected his political stature as a leader elected to three consecutive terms as India’s prime minister. However, resolving either conflict will be an uphill task for Modi. Putin would come under pressure from other political leaders in Russia if he suddenly tried to end the war, Ramaswamy said, adding that Modi was likely to find it equally difficult to persuade US President Donald Trump to end the Iran conflict despite his friendship with the American leader. “He [Modi] may be very friendly with everybody and people respect him, but that does not give you the privilege to change a country’s politics,” he said. Kingshuk Nag, an independent political commentator and author, said Modi would like to play a role in such key international issues and try to project India’s image as well, but the extent of his success remained to be seen. While India has the ability to engage both Washington and Moscow, and has strong ties with Israel and Iran, it may be too early to call Modi a “new mediator in global disputes”, according to Uday Chandra, a political-science professor at India’s Ashoka University. “Now these relationships may be acquiring greater or at least new diplomatic value,” he said. “Iran’s request that Modi use India’s ‘extensive contacts’ is, therefore, significant.” While little had changed in India’s diplomacy, “changes in geopolitics place a new value in India’s multilateralism [approach]”, Chandra said. “The SCO and the coming Brics summit will certainly make India’s multilateralism more visible in world politics.”

title: Ireland must prepare for Northern Ireland reunification vote, foreign minister says
description: Helen McEntee urges preparation for an eventual border poll as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham insists reunification is ‘off the table’.
content: Ireland needs to be prepared for a vote on whether to reunify with the UK’s Northern Ireland region, Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee has said. “I do believe that there will be a border poll at some stage,” McEntee told reporters in Wicklow, Ireland, ahead of a European Union foreign ministers meeting on Wednesday. “It is for the people of Northern Ireland to decide this and it is only where there’s a view that there may be a majority that we should move forward on this.” Her comments came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any conversation about uniting the Republic with Northern Ireland was “off the table”, comparing it to Britain’s divisive Brexit referendum. Burnham made the comments during a recent visit to Northern Ireland, signalling he would stick with the position of past prime ministers. The issue of a border poll, as the vote on unification is known, is contentious in both the UK and Ireland, which act as co-guarantors of the 1990s peace accord that largely ended sectarian violence between British unionists and Irish nationalists in Northern Ireland. A vote can only be called by the UK’s Secretary of State for Northern Ireland when it “appears likely” that a majority of people in the region would support reunification, as stipulated in the landmark Good Friday Agreement. Support for Irish unification is growing in Northern Ireland, especially among younger voters, but recent polling suggests there is still no clear majority in favour. Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who leads McEntee’s Fine Gael’s coalition partner Fianna Fail, recently said talks of unity made him “go bananas,” claiming appetite was not strong enough yet for a poll. “We are strong supporters of the Good Friday Agreement,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told reporters in Wicklow, where he was attending the meeting as a guest. He declined to comment on McEntee’s remarks.

title: Frontier AI at a cost: what Anthropic’s Fable 5.1 means for the US-China model race
description: The US firm’s new models claim top position on leading benchmarks, though steep operating costs against Chinese rivals highlight a growing divide.
content: Anthropic’s powerful new Claude Fable 5.1 model has widened its lead in performance benchmarks over Chinese rivals, even as budget-friendly open-weight models from China continue to gain commercial traction globally. The American company said on Wednesday that Fable 5.1, along with a restricted-access version called Mythos 5.1, was the world’s most advanced model for software coding and complex knowledge work. The standard version scored 66 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, taking the top spot globally and pulling six points clear of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3, both leading Chinese models. Fable 5.1 also claimed first place on San Francisco-based Vals AI’s index for handling complex, real-world tasks across sectors such as finance, coding and law. Anthropic’s earlier Opus 5 and Fable 5 models trailed closely in second and third place. The benchmark results prompted industry insiders to weigh in on whether leading labs in the United States were pulling further ahead of Chinese competitors. Yuchen Jin, a technical staff member at US artificial intelligence platform Databricks, called Fable 5.1’s capability leap “insane”, while some observers noted its performance shattered claims that Chinese open-weight developers had already closed the gap with the frontier. However, a stark price gap points to a sharp divide between the two countries’ approaches. Despite Anthropic slashing cache read prices by 75 per cent, reducing overall user expenses by up to 45 per cent, Fable 5.1 still costs US$3.69 per task on the Intelligence Index, compared with just US$0.84 for Kimi K3 and US$0.68 for GLM-5.3. Cached reads refer to the process in which an AI model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored. “That’s where I think the market starts to split naturally,” wrote Tory Green, co-founder of AI infrastructure firm io.net, on social media on Wednesday. “Cheap open models eat more of the routine agent work, while Fable gets called when the task is hard enough to justify the premium.” Chinese AI developers, meanwhile, continue to scale up performance. Tech giant Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, released Qwen3.8-Max-0902 on Wednesday. The upgraded model topped Arena AI’s benchmark for front-end web development tasks, beating Opus 5 and Kimi K3. Meanwhile, Z.ai founder Tang Jie told investors this week that its coming GLM-6.0 model aimed to achieve recursive self-improvement – a capability that would allow it to autonomously train its own successor. Vals AI CEO Rayan Krishnan said on social media on Wednesday that Fable 5.1 had already shown strong signs of this capability in early testing. As the US-China AI race accelerates, safety and oversight concerns are also intensifying. Anthropic rival OpenAI teased its coming Astra model on Wednesday, stating that it featured “a critical level of cybersecurity capability” that would enable the system to discover and exploit unknown vulnerabilities across well-protected systems without human intervention. While OpenAI promised strict guardrails and restricted access, safety researchers expressed alarm after The Information reported on Tuesday that Astra used a “recurrent depth” architecture – a design that boosts performance but obscures how a model reaches its conclusions. Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at Redwood Research, warned the technique impaired oversight, saying it “may be the single worst development for AI security [and] safety to date.”

title: Iran wins SCO backing against US strikes. Will it be enough?
description: Despite strong rhetoric out of Bishkek, support from groupings like the SCO and Brics may be more symbolic than substantial, analysts say.
content: As the US resumes strikes on Iran to force an end to the six-month-old war, Tehran is turning to multilateral groupings like the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) and Brics for political and diplomatic cover. At the SCO summit in Bishkek on Tuesday, world leaders made veiled references to the instability in the Middle East without naming the United States directly, in apparent tacit backing for Iran. The Bishkek Declaration closing the summit, meanwhile, explicitly condemned the military strikes on Iranian territory as violations of international law. While that could be read as a win for Tehran, observers say the support may prove to be more symbolic than substantial. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s trip to the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan this week was only his second visit abroad since the joint US and Israeli strikes began in late February. He held bilateral talks on the summit sidelines with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of Pakistan, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The diplomatic push came as the US resumed military strikes on Iran after a weeks-long pause in hostilities. American forces struck fresh Iranian targets on Tuesday, pointing to Iranian military threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and US assets in the region. In Bishkek, Chinese President Xi Jinping was among the top SCO leaders who indirectly criticised the US. The “shadow of war continues to haunt the world”, Xi said in his address on Tuesday, warning the assembled leadership that they “must prevent external forces from … undermining regional stability”. In a separate meeting with the Eurasian bloc’s dialogue partners, the Chinese leader said the vast majority of the world did not condone conflict and confrontation, urging “major countries” to take the lead in honouring the rule of law. As Iran’s main economic lifeline and largest trading partner, China is under mounting US pressure to sever those ties – including threats of secondary sanctions on Chinese banks. Iranian state news agency IRNA reported that Pezeshkian and Xi held a brief meeting on the sidelines of the SCO summit, without providing further details. When asked to comment on the report, China’s foreign ministry said only that Xi had “friendly exchanges” with various leaders at the event. The war on Iran is expected to be on the agenda when Xi travels to Washington later this month for a summit with US counterpart Donald Trump. Sun Degang, director of the Centre for Middle Eastern Studies at Fudan University, said sanctions would have no impact on China’s support for Iran and might backfire on the US. “China’s trade, economic and energy cooperation with Iran is resilient and will not end because of US sanctions,” he said. “If the US insists on intensifying sanctions, it will drive more countries to oppose it, and it also runs counter to the free-trade principles that the US itself champions … Sanctioning Iran hurts not just Iran and its trading partners but the US itself.” The SCO summit concluded with member states issuing a joint declaration condemning the military strikes on Iran, reaffirming their support for Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and calling for de-escalation by political and diplomatic means. Apart from Iran, which joined in 2023, the 10-member SCO includes China, Russia, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, India, Pakistan and Belarus. Li Lifan, director of the SCO centre at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, said Iran would have hoped to obtain security assurances from the SCO, as it was “an important geopolitical pivot state and hopes to gain support from friends across the world”. Iran, he said, would also expect to gain greater international recognition, particularly from the Global South, at the Brics summit in India this month. The Brics grouping of major emerging economies is often viewed as a counterweight to Western dominance. Iran joined the expanded bloc in 2024, alongside original members China, India, Russia, Brazil and South Africa. Sun at Fudan University said mechanisms such as the SCO and Brics were particularly “important assets” for Tehran to “achieve a diplomatic breakthrough” against the backdrop of renewed attacks and growing US pressure. “Eurasian countries, represented by China, Russia, India, Pakistan and other Central Asian states, form Iran’s reliable strategic rear,” he said. “This time, the SCO’s emphasis on multipolarity and its opposition to unilateral sanctions and military pressure brought Iran important political, diplomatic and economic support.” Tuesday’s SCO declaration also condemned attacks or threats of attacks on peaceful nuclear facilities, saying such actions posed a threat to international peace and stability. Member states also agreed that a country bore full responsibility for its own nuclear security. Iran’s nuclear ambitions have been at the centre of its dispute with the US, with US forces previously striking Iranian nuclear facilities. Sun pointed out that India, in particular, had frequent interactions with Iran despite its warm ties with Israel, reflecting New Delhi’s “determination not to join a united front behind US sanctions on Iran”. He called this stance an “important gain” for Tehran, but cautioned that neither Brics nor the SCO was a military alliance, and that support for Iran varied across member states.
