Ian Hall, professor of international relations at Griffith University, said: “Iran gained a lot from the [SCO] summit, at least diplomatically.” Hall pointed to the bloc’s condemnation of the ongoing strikes on Iran as violations of international law, its call to end military action and economic sanctions, and its backing of Iran’s right to a civil nuclear industry. “These are significant and unequivocal statements, even if they likely do not signal that SCO members will lend more material support to Iran than they have already lent.” He was also sceptical that multilateral frameworks like the SCO and Brics could play any peacemaking role. “They’re not designed for that purpose. But what they can do is amplify their members’ unhappiness about important developments.”

title: Hello, sailor: Thailand’s Pattaya rolls out welcome mat for USS Abraham Lincoln crew
description: Over 5,000 sailors and Marines have arrived in the Thai resort city for their first shore leave in 286 days.
content: At Risa’s Massage, Fai cancelled her holiday to be at work this week; suitmaker Tito has laid on a made-in-24-hours special for US Navy visitors and hawker Pui is aiming to sell 15 watches in the five days the USS Abraham Lincoln will be in Pattaya. On Wednesday, the Thai resort city began to welcome over 5,000 sailors and Marines, finally on shore leave after being at sea for a record 286 days. It is a timely visit for the US crew – and an economic tonic for a city facing a sharp drop in tourism, partly caused by the war being fought by those aboard the aircraft carrier. Outside the Hard Rock Hotel, which is hosting some of the US servicemembers, Pui Kanda was among the cluster of taxi drivers, hawkers and other hopefuls waiting for them to hit the city. “It’s been very quiet in Pattaya. We have had few visitors this low season so I’m hoping to make some money from these American sailors,” she said, showing her wooden display box of timepieces. “I’m hoping to sell all 15 of my watches. I like to sell to the Americans; they don’t really bargain and they have lots of money.” Next to her, a Thai taxi driver, who gave his name as Sam, showed a laminated card with an array of entertainment possibilities – bars and massage parlours, cabaret shows, shooting ranges and tiger petting zoos. “I will take them anywhere they want to go,” he said with a grin. “We are here to make sure they have a good time.” On Wednesday morning, the hulking Nimitz-class carrier was guided by tugboats to shore at Laem Chabang deep sea port around an hour outside Pattaya. It is joined in Chonburi province – home to Pattaya – by support vessels and a large crew for rest and recuperation before they set sail on Sunday. Well-deserved rest The carrier has been at the centre of a row over the treatment of uniformed personnel fighting President Donald Trump’s war on Iran. Its record nine and a half months at sea has given rise to allegations of poor living conditions, mental health strains and supply shortages. “Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, said in a statement. “What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations.” But in the well choreographed world of shore visits, few sailors wanted to talk about their experiences – certainly not within earshot of their superiors. Instead it was eyes forward on their first evening out for months. “I’m going to go slow and steady,” said one young sailor in a crumpled blue US navy shirt, who did not give a name, as he took out a wad of cash from an ATM. “But then again this is my first time in Pattaya, so who knows?” Extra police have been deployed by Thai authorities to make sure the visit passes uneventfully. Meanwhile, the sailors have been advised by their commanding officers to avoid seedier parts of the city as well as steer clear of cannabis, openly on sale. Keeping them out of trouble is the US Navy’s Shore Liaison Group. “We’re like shepherds,” one member told This Week in Asia. “Just here to keep everything smooth.” Thailand is America’s oldest treaty ally in Asia – a link stretching back to the 1833 Treaty of Amity and Commerce. Pattaya owes its transformation from a fishing village into a nightlife hub to the presence of US troops during the Vietnam war. The U-Tapao airbase an hour outside the city was used in sorties over Vietnam. At the end of the war, businesses, bars and the associated sex work moved to Pattaya as some US personnel stayed on – or returned on regular trips. The visit was a “clear demonstration of our enduring commitment to our allies and partners in Thailand, and we are all very excited to make Thailand the first port visit on our historic deployment”, said Captain Dan Keeler, the carrier’s commanding officer. “We’re very very happy to be here … it’s a well deserved break for all of the crew and we really look forward to our time here to get a little rest and relaxation.” Pattaya is just as eager for the low-season boost – after a year in which hotel occupancy rates slumped to around 25 per cent Tito, who goes by one name, has been selling suits on Pattaya’s beachfront for over 30 years. He has drafted in more staff for the expected rush for fitted suits selling from 7,000 to 10,000 baht (US$210 to US$300). “We know how to work fast for these visits – we have a very short time to cut and fit the suits,” he said. “But the US Navy is good business for us every time they come here.” As the first arrivals entered the Hard Rock Hotel – throwing bemused smiles or cheekily posing for the media – the buzz began to build around the beach. Waving to customers along a hyper-competitive row of massage shops, Fai, who had deferred her holiday because “everyone says we will make big money”, was getting anxious. “When are they coming?” asked the 28-year-old, who gave only one name.

title: Hong Kong to mark National Day with 23-minute fireworks show featuring sunflowers
description: HK$18 million show on October 1 will feature 31,888 pyrotechnic shells exploding over Victoria Harbour celebrating nation’s achievements.
content: Hong Kong will stage a 23-minute fireworks display over Victoria Harbour on National Day on October 1 under the theme “Eternal Radiance”. The HK$18 million (US$2.3 million) extravaganza, exclusively sponsored by insurance provider Sun Life Hong Kong, will mark the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China. Coordinated by the Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau, the show will launch 31,888 pyrotechnic shells from nine firing points on three barges and six floating pontoons at 8pm. “The display not only celebrates our nation’s achievements but also reflects our heartfelt wishes for Hong Kong’s continued prosperity and success,” Sun Life Hong Kong chief executive Clement Lam Ka-yin said. “Through our support for this iconic annual event, we hope to bring people together, share the joy of the occasion and showcase Hong Kong’s vibrancy and unique appeal as a world-class international city.” Fireworks designer Wilson Mao Wai-shing, head of Pyromagic Multi-Media Productions, said the display – titled “Eternal Radiance: Fireworks in Bloom, Illuminating our Country” – would unfold in eight scenes. The company, which also designed last year’s National Day fireworks, said there would be no drone show for the second year running. Among the expected highlights will be the second scene, set to Shirley Bassey’s “You Are the Sunshine of My Life”, featuring layered gold and red rings resembling sunflowers to symbolise hope, warmth and optimism. In the finale, red and gold fireworks will burst like a rising sun over the harbour in a tribute to the spirit of Chinese culture. The show will be capped by a 20-second salvo of a range of fireworks exploding simultaneously in a dense barrage of sound and a burst of spectacle, Mao said. Temporary audio systems will be installed around the Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui and Golden Bauhinia Square in Wan Chai. Prime vantage points for the public holiday spectacle include Tsim Sha Tsui, Wan Chai, the Mid-Levels and Central, while RTHK Radio 4 will broadcast the synchronised background music live during the display.

title: ICAC sets integrity standards for government computers to fight misuse
description: Independent Commission Against Corruption unveils standards after revealing procedures for government computer systems had loopholes.
content: Hong Kong’s Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) has unveiled standards for the use of government computer systems after uncovering loopholes, including requiring bureaus and departments to ensure compliance when requesting digital project funds. Danny Woo Ying-ming, commissioner of the ICAC, said on Wednesday that an investigation had found that some procedures for government computer systems had loopholes that raised the risk of corruption. “Once systems are abused, data is tampered with and proper procedures bypassed, not only will it incur corruption risks, but it can also damage the government’s integrity,” he said at a ceremony introducing the standards. Woo said that as of July, all government bureaus and departments were mandated by the Digital Policy Office to assess whether their computer systems complied with the standards when requesting funds under the Capital Works Reserve Fund for administrative computer systems. The integrity assurance standards cover 12 steps for internal work processes and focus on users, system administration and monitoring. Requiring government organisations to assess their compliance with the standards was intended to prevent corruption-related risks, the ICAC said. Such risks include unauthorised data access, ineffective due diligence, circumvention of rules and over-reliance on manual steps, such as checking and sampling, that could be prone to manipulation for corruption. Lillian Cheong Man-lei, the city’s acting technology minister, said during the ceremony that authorities had sought to strike a balance between safety and development when implementing digital measures. Describing the ICAC’s standards as a tool to bolster integrity and data safety, she said government organisations would be able to pre-empt corruption by integrating anti-graft elements early on in their work processes. “Incorporating integrity measures into our computer systems will make our use of innovation safer, more steadfast and win residents’ trust,” Cheong said. She added that adopting these measures would bolster civil servants’ awareness of conflicts of interest and the need for integrity. The standards called for government organisations to clearly define all access rights and grant staff access to various data and systems in accordance with their operational needs. They also advocated the use of more secure access methods, such as two-factor authentication. To prevent data tampering, the anti-corruption agency urged government organisations to adopt watermarks, encryption measures and blockchain technologies. The agency also pointed out that reliance on paper declarations stating there were no conflicts of interest risked omission, loss, falsification or backdating. The ICAC added that manual processes such as checking and sampling could also be susceptible to manipulation. The agency called for the introduction of mandatory electronic conflict-of-interest declarations and automatic repetitive data processing.

title: How a Hong Kong maker of authentic shrimp roe noodles is leading a comeback
description: Wing Lok Noodle Factory’s second-generation boss shares how the 50-year-old company is thriving by innovating a dying traditional craft.
content: Ha zi mein, or dried shrimp roe noodles, are a Cantonese household staple. Traditionally made from broth-infused dough that is steamed and then immediately baked dry to eliminate moisture, the noodles release the broth when boiled, turning the hot water into a rich, nutritious soup. As mass-produced versions dominate supermarket shelves, the artisanal craft of making ha zi mein – which is listed as part of Hong Kong’s intangible cultural heritage – is becoming increasingly rare. But Wing Lok Noodle Factory, a humble operation in Hong Kong’s Kowloon Bay neighbourhood that celebrates its 50th anniversary in 2026, has been leading a ha zi mein renaissance by producing noodles with fun new flavours such as black truffle, curry seafood, pepper pork and Sichuan spicy beef. The company’s second-generation owner, Angus Chan Hon-kit, says traditional ha zi mein making goes back a long time – “maybe 100 years” – but was nearly lost. “As technology advanced, manufacturers began prioritising convenience and lower costs,” the 38-year-old says. “However, my father always made ha zi mein the traditional way.” Wing Lok Noodle Factory produces completely dehydrated noodles that do not need chemical preservatives, which makes them healthier than mass-produced instant noodles. From humble beginnings to established noodle supplier Chan’s late father, Chan Keung, began learning the ha zi mein trade at 14 years old. In 1976, when he was in his early twenties, he opened a small stall in Hong Kong’s Wong Tai Sin district to supply dried noodles to street vendors who sold cart noodles or chow mein. By 1980, the success of his business enabled him to move Wing Lok Noodle Factory into a proper unit in Kowloon Bay. Angus Chan says his father’s noodles became very popular among local wholesalers in the following decades, but the noodle factory remained relatively unknown to the general public. “My dad would make separate batches [of ha zi mein] in the authentic, traditional way for customers who appreciated it and could afford it,” he says. “There will always be real gourmets with high standards for food and flavour.” Fast forward to 2015, and the ageing Chan senior faced the same problem as many small heritage businesses: he struggled to find someone to take over. His son was the natural first choice, but had been working for more than six years in aviation logistics, in a job that paid well and did not demand the same dedication as noodle making. “I didn’t want the burden of being tied down by a business,” Angus Chan says. “Then, one day, my dad said to me, ‘I’m exhausted. I want to retire. A friend of mine may buy the factory for HK$200,000.’ I thought, ‘What? HK$200,000 for 40 years of your life’s work?’ “It felt like such a waste. So I decided to come back and give it a shot. If I succeed, great. If not, I could always go back to working at the airport.” Upon taking over the factory, the younger Chan realised it was even more difficult than he anticipated. There was no formal structure; his father handled everything himself, from taking orders to accounting and issuing invoices. “I assumed the company was well-developed with proper systems in place, but I had to restructure the entire organisation, hire more staff and start building our own brand – for 40 years, we never had a brand of our own.” Turning a little-known legacy into a popular brand The turning point came when Angus Chan read an article in a local Chinese-language magazine that ranked the top five store-bought ha zi mein in Hong Kong. Four of the five were produced by Wing Lok for other companies to sell under their brand names. He found himself wondering why Wing Lok did not just build its own brand. “That way, we would be free from price pressures imposed by retailers asking us to compromise on ingredient quality. With our own brand, I can use premium ingredients so everyone gets to have better food.” He eventually shifted from mostly working in the office to learning how to make noodles himself, which enabled him to better understand how the business worked and earn the respect of the sifus, or veteran workers. In 2018, he suggested making speciality coriander-flavour noodles to appeal to younger consumers, which caused friction. “My dad really protested against it. We had a big argument,” he says. “He was like, ‘Are you mad? How on earth can you make coriander ha zi mein?’” “I said, ‘Why don’t we just try and test the market?’ It was a big hit and quickly sold out. People were queuing to snap them up. That’s when my dad realised the potential of innovation. He turned around and even started researching how to intensify the coriander flavour himself.” In the eight years since launching the coriander noodles, Angus Chan has developed more than 10 speciality flavours and recently released single-serving packs with topping kits. Each variation took between three and six months of research and development, but he says the hard work was worth it to ensure the components, texture and flavour profile were up to par. Most recently, he spent nine months developing a soon-to-be-released new cup noodle variety. Finding more fans in Hong Kong and abroad Angus Chan is thankful to the sifus who were willing to adapt to the new business model, and was happy when his father told him he was proud of the new Wing Lok brand before his untimely death in 2023. Now in his 11th year of running the company, Angus Chan has transformed his late father’s legacy into a well-known retail brand in its own right, with stockists in markets including Japan, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada and Australia. The brand also continues to support much of Hong Kong’s noodle wholesale market. In the years to come, he hopes to encourage locals to turn away from cheaper mass-produced ha zi mein variations in favour of better-tasting traditional ones. “Authentic ha zi mein is really delicious with a rich broth,” he says. In the meantime, he hopes to take the Wing Lok brand further and find more fans around the world. “Over the past few years, we’ve attended various international trade shows. The Japanese were amazed that boiling water alone turns the dried noodles into a rich broth. And while some Westerners may find traditional ha zi mein too fishy, they found our flavoured variations fascinating. “And for the Hongkongers who have emigrated overseas, they often come back and buy them by the boxful [or place online orders] because they treat it as comfort food and a taste of home.”

title: EU trade enforcers descend on Beijing demanding China fix ‘untenable’ imbalances
description: Brussels officials hold talks in the Chinese capital as they seek a commitment to reduce surging exports to the bloc.
content: A delegation from the European Commission has been locked in talks with Chinese officials in Beijing, as the sides look to find a diplomatic off-ramp from a looming trade war before an October deadline set by Brussels. The EU team was spearheaded by Denis Redonnet, the bloc’s top trade enforcement officer, who was recently made point person on China trade policy – a recognition that in EU circles, talk of partnership has largely been usurped by rivalry and competition. Later this month, the European Union’s top trade official, Ditte Juul Jorgensen, will follow Redonnet to the Chinese capital, she confirmed on Wednesday, as Brussels assesses whether Beijing is willing to make the sort of concessions that could see them avoid sliding into a damaging tit-for-tat exchange in the autumn. “We see an engaged China in these talks, but of course the challenges are very, very significant,” Jorgensen told a hearing at the European Parliament on Wednesday. The commission wants Beijing to commit to reducing its surging exports to the bloc, which have expanded at breakneck speed in recent months. In July alone, China extended its trade surplus over all but three EU members compared with a year earlier. “What we see in relation to China is … increasing concentration dependencies, including in strategic sectors – that is a risk to the EU,” Jorgensen said. “We see that as a result of a number of Chinese domestic policies, but of course also of China’s competitiveness in a number of these sectors, we have an increasing trade deficit,” she added, describing it as an “untenable situation”. Brussels suspects that the exports are turbo-boosted by undeclared subsidies, an undervalued currency, and rampant industrial overcapacity caused by weak domestic demand, years of investment-led growth and state support that has kept production expanding even as consumption has lagged. It fears that these factors propel products to European shores at prices that are undercutting local producers and that could, if left unchecked, deindustrialise swathes of the European economy. “We are working with very concrete proposals. Let’s see how our Chinese counterparts would react to them … But if simply there will be no action, then of course it will be much more difficult for us just to talk about these issues,” EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic told Politico on Monday. But in the Belgian capital, expectations are well managed as to what can be achieved before October, when it must decide what to do. The face-to-face meetings followed a stream of online contacts through August, but these sessions produced no breakthroughs. While Beijing has made conciliatory noises around reducing its gaping trade surplus with the EU, it is thought to prefer to do this by buying more European goods. Such a dynamic would resemble, in part, what US President Donald Trump agreed with China during his first term – the “phase one” trade deal that analysts say did little to address structural problems in the relationship. “These ongoing talks are not just talks – they have to give a proof of concept by October. We have been very clear that these global imbalances that exist cannot continue and there has to be a rebalancing,” Jorgensen said. The Beijing meetings are expected to inform how tough European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen talks on China during her State of the Union speech on September 16, which will in turn help set the agenda for a meeting between Sefcovic and Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao, planned for the second week of October. In the past, von der Leyen has used her annual address to announce investigations into subsidies in China’s electric vehicle sector, a ban on products made using forced labour, and a rival to Beijing’s core infrastructure drive, the Belt and Road Initiative. There is speculation that if negotiations do not make progress, she could announce new instruments or investigations. Jorgensen confirmed on Wednesday that the bloc was developing a “diversification instrument”, which could compel companies in critical sectors to increase their number of suppliers, but added that it was still “early days” in the tool’s development. “That is a consideration relevant for climate, relevant for the energy transition, relevant for our economic security, and the need to rebalance. To be clear, it is that degree of concentration, that degree of dependence on any one supplier – whoever that supplier is – that is in and of itself a risk,” Jorgensen said. During a speech last week von der Leyen warned that “being a partner [with China] does not mean accepting permanent imbalances”, noting that while Chinese imports into the EU had risen 45 per cent in five years, “our exports to China are falling”. “We have seen that this dependence can be used as leverage against us. We must therefore ensure that fair conditions are respected. Dialogue with China remains necessary, but it must produce results. And when dialogue is not enough, we must be ready to make full use of our instruments,” von der Leyen said at the annual conference of France’s main employers’ federation, MEDEF. Her State of the Union remarks later this month will help set the tone for a debate between the bloc’s national leaders in Brussels in mid-October, when they are expected to bless defensive measures against Chinese goods. Already, influential member states have been laying the groundwork for this scenario. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has flip-flopped dramatically on China policy since coming to office, appears to have come closer to Brussels’ thinking in recent weeks. Asked last week whether he backed car industry calls for EU tariffs on Chinese plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, Merz said he had instructed his cabinet to come up with proposals. “I have asked the Federal Cabinet to now quickly gather and document all proposals that we could consider in terms of appropriate responses. We note that German industry has also apparently changed its opinion regarding these global imbalances. We will not only address this issue, but we will make decisions,” Merz said after a cabinet retreat. At the same press conference, Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that “when we see that others are not playing by the rules, we cannot be naive”. “The issue now is protecting the steel industry, the automotive industry, the chemical industry and the pharmaceutical industry, both in Germany and in Europe,” Klingbeil said. “We had a very serious debate about where we need to improve in order to reposition ourselves economically, but also about how we face competition, especially the increasingly unfair competition we are experiencing. Therefore, we agreed – the chancellor confirmed this – that we will discuss appropriate measures in the cabinet soon.” Also last week, an advisory board to the Dutch government urged The Hague to back tougher measures on China, or see industry hollowed out. “Doing nothing in this situation therefore also comes at a high price. Our dependencies will increase and we will be hit hard economically. A strong response also comes at a price,” read the report from Wetenschappelijke Raad voor het Regeringsbeleid, an independent advisory council. “The longer we wait, the greater the pain will be in the future.”

title: Meet Robert De Niro’s 7 children – from actors to a broker and an aspiring model
description: Starring in Netflix’s thriller The Whisper Man, the 83-year-old has built a blended family spanning four relationships and an age gap of over 50 years.
content: Two of Robert De Niro’s seven children, Drena and Julian, are following in their famous father’s footsteps, and the Godfather star is fully aware of the pressure that comes with their famous surname and “nepo baby” status. “It’s a commitment,” the 83-year-old, who is starring in Netflix’s latest thriller The Whisper Man, told People in a recent interview. “And you have to show, especially if you’re a kid in a situation like mine, no matter what [the kids] say, how they behave, what they do, they’re saying, ‘Show me’,” he said. “And if you don’t look like you’re really sincere about it and busting your ass and working hard, it’ll have a negative impact.” “If you really can, over time, cumulatively impress people that you really are sincere about it and will go the distance, then it’ll work the other way 10 times,” the two-time Oscar winner continued. Here’s everything you need to know about De Niro’s seven children – and the five decades between them. Drena De Niro Born on September 3, 1971, Drena is the oldest of De Niro’s children. She was adopted by the actor at five after her mother, Diahnne Abbott, married him in 1976. She then took on his surname. De Niro and Abbott divorced in 1988. She began her career as a model before dabbling in DJing and fashion consulting. At 25, she made her acting debut in the 1996 film Grace of My Heart. She has since appeared in Joy, Hands of Stone and A Star is Born, the last of which also starred her late son Leandro De Niro Rodriguez. Drena, who is about to turn 55, made the Goodfellas actor a grandfather when she and her then-boyfriend, artist Carlos Rodriguez, welcomed their son in 2003. In July 2023, Drena announced that Leandro had died at the age of 19 but did not reveal his cause of death. Raphael Eugene De Niro De Niro and Abbott welcomed their son, Raphael Eugene De Niro, on November 9, 1976. Rather than following his parents into acting, the 49-year-old built a career in luxury real estate, helping stars such as Renée Zellweger and Kelly Ripa find their dream homes in Manhattan. After founding the De Niro Team at Douglas Elliman in 2004 – amassing over US$600 million in early sales – he transitioned his eight-person group to Brown Harris Stevens this January, per Business Wire. Raphael shares three children with ex-wife Claudine De Matos and is currently married to fashion stylist Hannah Carnes. Airyn De Niro After his divorce from Abbott, De Niro began dating Miami Vice star and model Toukie Smith in 1988. The couple welcomed twins Airyn De Niro and Julian Henry De Niro, via IVF surrogate, on October 20, 1995, before separating the following year. Born Aaron Kendrick, Airyn publicly came out as transgender in 2025. Having stayed out of the spotlight for years, the 30-year-old recently opened up about pursuing a modelling career inspired by her mother. “Honestly, if I could be on the cover of Vogue with her or recreating one of her pictures, that would be a dream come true,” Airyn told Them magazine. Julian Henry De Niro Airyn’s twin brother, Julian Henry De Niro, chose a path in acting, making his screen debut in 2016’s In Dubious Battle alongside James Franco and Selena Gomez. He went on to portray a young Barack Obama in Showtime’s 2022 anthology series The First Lady, before stepping onto the Broadway stage in 2023’s revival of The Sign in Sidney Brustein’s Window opposite Oscar Isaac and Rachel Brosnahan. Elliot De Niro In 1997, the Meet the Parents actor married American socialite Grace Hightower, and a year later they welcomed a son together, Elliot De Niro, on March 18, 1998. De Niro shared Elliot’s autism diagnosis in 2016 while advocating for the inclusion of the controversial documentary Vaxxed at the Tribeca Film Festival, of which he is a co-founder. “Grace and I have a child with autism, and we believe it is critical that all of the issues surrounding the causes of autism be openly discussed and examined,” he said at the time, speaking about his son’s diagnosis for the first time. Elliot, now 28, is known for his skills as a tennis player and has competed in the Special Olympics, the world’s largest sports organisation for children and adults with intellectual disabilities. In 2018, he was featured in ESPN’s Special Olympics: 50 Game Changers series. Helen Grace De Niro De Niro and Hightower initially split in 1999 and fought for Elliot’s custody in court. However, their divorce was never finalised, and in 2004, the couple renewed their wedding vows, per People. On December 23, 2011, they welcomed their second child, Helen Grace De Niro, via surrogacy. Helen is now 14. De Niro and Hightower separated for good in November 2018 after two decades of marriage. Gia Virginia Chen-De Niro View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Spill Room (@thespillroom) On April 3, 2023, the actor welcomed his daughter, Gia Virginia Chen-De Niro, with his partner, Tiffany Chen, 45. He then shared more details a week later on CBS Mornings, revealing his daughter’s full name and a photo of the newborn in a striped pink sleepsuit.

title: Walmart’s Sam’s Club accelerates expansion in China as membership passes 10.7 million
description: Company to open 13 new stores this year, bringing total to 76, as value prices and exclusive goods prove to be a winning formula.
content: US membership-only retailer Sam’s Club has sped up its expansion in China this year, with the launch of its sixth Beijing location on Monday drawing long queues of eager shoppers. The Walmart-owned warehouse retailer has found a winning formula in China, with its value pricing and exclusive goods attracting middle-class consumers even as some foreign brands shut down stores or pull out of the country. Sam’s Club said last month that it had 10.7 million paid members in China as of June. Its total annual membership revenue could hit 3 billion yuan (US$450 million) this year, with its basic and premium memberships priced at 260 yuan and 680 yuan a year, respectively. “The appeal of Sam’s Club is the breadth and quality of goods offered along with wholesale pricing,” said Cathy Chao, senior director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “Many goods are unique and cannot be found through alternate channels, and consumers hold a general impression of consistently high-quality goods at a reasonable price, which can justify the membership pricing.” In addition, the membership model encouraged frequent visits by consumers seeking to maximise the value of the annual fee, Chao added. The company said that it planned to open 13 new Sam’s Club stores nationwide this year, including in several lower-tier cities, bringing the total to 76. The warehouse retailer has strengthened localisation by launching more China-specific products. Its top seller varies by city: sweetcorn in Beijing, local brand Bright Dairy milk in Shanghai and sweet bananas in Guangzhou, according to the company’s list in August. In Walmart’s earnings report for the quarter that ended on July 31, China was a stand-out market, with sales increasing nearly 21 per cent to US$7 billion on the back of Sam’s Club’s momentum. Beijing authorities summoned Sam’s Club in June over frequent food-safety problems, and the company said it had initiated internal reviews and corrective actions. A quick leadership reshuffle followed, with former Alibaba vice-president Liu Peng appointed as president of Sam’s Club China.

title: We don’t need no education, we just need board control: Hong Kong skate tweens Games bound
description: There are also teams in modern pentathlon, wrestling, rhythmic gymnastics and padel competing for the first time at the event in Japan.
content: While their classmates are adjusting to the new school year, five young Hongkongers will be putting some of their non-academic skills to the test in Japan. And in a skateboard team where the oldest member is just 16, Katniss Wong Yi-huen and Kamus Wong Yeuk-ching are the two youngest competitors in the city’s Asian Games squad of 580 athletes across 38 sports. And while Kamus Wong is already 12 years old, her teammate could end up celebrating her 12th birthday at the Games’ opening ceremony at Paloma Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya on September 19. “I started skateboarding about two years ago after I came across it while watching those reels on Instagram, and then a friend of mine introduced me to the sport,” Katniss Wong said. “Participating in the Asian Games feels like a huge matter for me. I am quite nervous but excited at the same time; I’ll keep working hard. “Of course, I’d like to win a gold medal in some tournaments going forward, but for now, it’s just about doing the best I can, and performing the tricks and techniques I’ve learned.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by katniss 🙈 (@katniss__hh__) A pupil at the ESF South Island School, Katniss Wong finished seventh in the Asian Championship final in April and also took part in the World Skateboarding Tour World Cup in Rome in June. The youngster wants to follow in the footsteps of skateboarding idols, Olympic medallists Sky Brown and Arisa Trew, and also compete at an Olympics, with her first opportunity coming in Los Angeles in two years. “I wish to train and compete in different places to learn as much and try as hard as I can, and compete in more tournaments worldwide,” the 11-year-old said. “I think the happiest thing about skateboarding was when you mastered some new tricks; it could be difficult when you couldn’t do something, and you would be unhappy. But it’s about keeping trying and keeping going, and you’ll get better eventually, just like me!” Kamus Wong, meanwhile, who finished a place below her teammate in the regional championship, is not the first skateboarder in her family. “We used to ski as a family, but the global pandemic locked down everything,” Dio Wong, her father, said. “So my wife and I started skateboarding, and before we knew it, our daughter also started. “She started around six years ago, but has been practising more seriously over the past two years.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by ⋆🥞˚࿔𝐊𝐚𝐦𝐮𝐬⋆˚꩜｡🍥 (@ssk_kamus_ssk) A student at Hong Kong Baptist University Affiliated School Wong Kam Fai Secondary and Primary School, Kamus Wong said skiing and skateboarding “felt alike”, and the most difficult part of her practice was to “link all my moves together”. Her father added his daughter’s school has been “very supportive” and she had been granted some extra off days to practise and compete at the Games. “She will practise at some state-level facility in Nanjing before the Asian Games, and will only start her new school year afterwards,” he said. Apart from the two youngest delegation members, Yuna Wan Hiu-yin, Li Pak-lam and Gu Jiahuan, who are between 13 and 16 years old, will make their Asian Games debuts, and coach Cheung Hang-tat said the newest generation of athletes could be the future of the sport in the city. “Our athletes are really young; some of them – Wan, Li and Gu – will head to Paraguay for the WSG Park Skateboarding World Championship immediately after the Games,” he said. “I believe we’re developing in a positive direction. “A golden age for skateboarding would be 14 to 20 years old. We have a lot of moves coming off the stairs, the bowl or the half-pipe, so athletes are prone to falling and we need to have a strong physique. Also, when we’re younger, our centre of gravity is lower, making it easier for us to absorb the force.” For the first time, Hong Kong is also sending teams to the Games in modern pentathlon, wrestling, rhythmic gymnastics and padel. Pentathletes Shum Chun-hei and Liu Hei-yu said they grew up swimming and started devoting time thinking the sport was “new and interesting”. Shum, 16, said modern pentathlon had “taught me a lot” since he started about two years ago. “It’s quite fun and enjoyable as it contains some different sports,” he said. “Most importantly, it taught me to look at different things with a calm and open mind. “For example, even if you didn’t perform well in one event, you still have a chance to catch up, so you won’t be so negative.” Diocesan Girls’ School pupil Liu said practising for the five events – fencing, an obstacle discipline, swimming and the combined laser-run – was a “great test” for her both physically and mentally. As for wrestler Isaac Wong Ching-shing, he believed his sport, which featured at the first modern Olympics in 1896 and the second Asian Games in 1954, was “definitely the toughest one” of all. “I was really interested in combat sports to start with, and then I decided to take one sport seriously; it’s been four years since I’ve been doing this,” said the 18-year-old, who will compete in the men’s freestyle 57kg category on the penultimate day of the Nagoya Games. “I think wrestling is the toughest sport of all. It’s really challenging because it’s a six-minute sprint compared to other sports.” A participant at the recent under-20 World Championships in Slovakia and the under-23 Asian Championships in Vietnam, Wong said wrestling was still developing in Hong Kong. “It’s our first Games, and we might not be that strong compared to other countries, but we’re growing,” he said. “I’m more focused on my performance, knowing that if I can do that, I can get good results.”

title: Chinese couple’s surgery fundraising highlights how sudden fame ignites support, backlash
description: Public praise for similar content creators often hinges on specific virtues, restricting how disability is portrayed.
content: A woman in China, suffering from severe scoliosis, has gone viral after accusations that she is “making money by doing nothing” surfaced. This scrutiny followed the revelation that her boyfriend, Yan Ruize, worked gruelling food-delivery shifts to fund her much-needed surgery. He Ling, 23, hails from southwest China’s Sichuan province and was diagnosed with congenital scoliosis – a sideways curvature of the spine – at five years old. Now, at just 1.35 metres tall and weighing 31.5kg, she requires surgery estimated to cost around 300,000 yuan (US$45,000). After completing secondary school, He worked in a mobile phone parts factory, where she met Yan in 2021. Subsequently, she trained as a manicurist and began running a stall at a night market. When the factory where Yan was employed shut down, the couple initially depended on He’s income. In 2024, Yan became a food delivery rider, often working up to 14 hours a day to gather funds for her operation. Recently, a social media creator filmed their story, which went viral, garnering over 18 million views and significant public support. As reported by Fengmian News, online fundraising efforts approached 100,000 yuan, bringing He closer to her surgery goals. However, the surge in online attention also attracted criticism. Some netizens questioned how someone struggling to afford medical expenses could still indulge in manicures, while others accused He of “selling misery” and “doing nothing for money.” In response, she removed her manicure and clarified that she was not solely reliant on contributions from her boyfriend or donations, emphasising that she also worked long hours and engaged in regular live-streaming. Across China, individuals with disabilities or illnesses are increasingly sharing their personal experiences and turning them into public narratives. For instance, Huang Ying, 31, from northwest China’s Ningxia Hui autonomous region, lost her sight after a childhood fever. She became the first visually impaired student in China to enter a prestigious university through the competitive gaokao exams. On Douyin, she shares her studies, travels, and daily life with over one million followers. In Guangdong, southern China, 27-year-old Yang Tiejun has transformed the involuntary shaking of his left arm – caused by three brain haemorrhages that left him partially paralysed – into material for humorous videos, attracting nearly 900,000 followers. Yet, the praise showered upon such creators often hinges on common virtues like being “hard-working, strong, or optimistic,” reinforcing narrow expectations regarding how disabilities should be portrayed. Lei Jing, a sociology-of-emotions researcher at Hunan Institute of Science and Technology, argues that even well-intentioned encouragement can inadvertently bolster identity and class divisions, perpetuating social exclusion. In a 2024 paper published in Disability Research, communication scholars Duan Yongjie and Zhang Yuanyuan described this phenomenon as a form of “secondary stigmatisation.” Duan and Zhang caution that algorithm-driven platforms can amplify repetitive narratives, creating “echo chambers” that confine creators to simplistic identity labels, while online hostility and suspicion exacerbate stigmas and diminish their confidence. The platform economy, in which visibility often translates into income, leaves many creators grappling with relentless pressure to chase traffic and monetise their content. Daidaimeng, an influencer with cerebral palsy and 60,000 followers, shared in a video that after four years of live-streaming and advertising, she had earned only 86,900 yuan (US$13,000). She partly attributed this to not appearing “disabled enough” to retain attention, stating that more sensational videos – such as attempts to run – were often necessary to prevent viewers from scrolling past her content. Her experience exemplifies the paradox of social media, where platforms may amplify disabled voices while rewarding only portrayals that conform to public expectations. Guo Zhiling, a researcher focused on Deaf culture, notes that some Deaf creators feel compelled to attempt speaking or singing on camera, driven by the curiosity of hearing audiences regarding their voices. Guo pointed out that this pressure can skew representation, favouring polished and elite portrayals of Deaf experiences while obscuring less visible realities in the quest for clicks. Fabricated stories have also contributed to public scepticism, placing genuine disabled creators under greater pressure to validate their lived experiences. In May, a blind influencer from Beijing, known as “Hug the Blind Rabbit,” claimed she was struck by an electric bicycle on tactile paving. The video garnered over 100 million views and widespread support from public figures before police later revealed the incident had been staged. The influencer was subsequently detained, and her account banned, with many netizens accusing her of “exploiting sympathy.” These controversies provoke broader questions regarding how patients and individuals with disabilities should be perceived online. One user with the handle @rainism825 remarked that they should not be reduced to merely inspirational stories but rather allowed to express emotions such as anger, sadness, and despair. The user further added that when visually impaired individuals confront danger, the focus ought to be on inadequate accessibility and limited public awareness, rather than questioning their decision to go out in the first place. Furthermore, in a 2025 paper published in New Media & Society, Lu Pengyun and Guo Zhiling emphasised the need for social media platforms to embed equality into algorithmic designs and governance while reducing barriers to diverse and non-mainstream content.

title: India defies Iran war oil shock to keep 8% growth on track
description: With tax cuts and a factory boom offsetting oil volatility, analysts expect momentum to hold – if El Nino doesn’t wreck the harvest.
content: India’s stronger-than-expected first quarter growth has bolstered analysts’ confidence that it can sustain its momentum through the rest of the financial year and remain the world’s fastest-growing major economy – even as it remains exposed to high oil prices caused by the US-Iran war. The Indian economy grew 7.8 per cent in the April-June quarter, comfortably beating the Reserve Bank of India’s forecast of 7 per cent growth, despite the disruption that the Middle East conflict has caused to global energy markets and financial sentiment worldwide. “While energy will undoubtedly be a headwind for the economy, I suspect that it will sustain the momentum … and surprise analysts on the upside,” said Jamus Lim, an associate professor of economics at ESSEC Business School Asia-Pacific, who predicted annual growth “clocking in closer” to 8 per cent. Global oil prices had risen far less than some analysts predicted at the start of the war, he said, when projections as high as US$200 per barrel were being bandied about. Benchmark Brent crude rose 1.3 per cent to US$95.91 a barrel in Asian morning trading on Wednesday, after the US launched a barrage of renewed air strikes on Iran that briefly pushed prices to a five-week high. India, which imports most of its oil and gas, is seen as especially exposed to such price spikes, though the government has so far shielded households from the worst of the impact through limited, staggered price rises. Lim said prices were unlikely to climb much further in the coming months as the cooling and travel demand generated by the northern hemisphere’s summer travel season wound down. “Of course, this doesn’t mean all sectors [in India] will flourish. I am particularly concerned about the rural economy, which is already starting to feel the effects of a strong El Nino year and seeing incomes being hit,” he said. Farm output and allied sectors grew a modest 3.6 per cent year on year in the first quarter, held back by a dry start to the June-September monsoon and mounting concerns that El Nino weather patterns will affect rainfall later in the season. The upside surprise was driven largely by tax cuts on goods, services and incomes earlier this year that lifted consumer spending, with personal consumption rising 7.1 per cent, up from 6.8 per cent a year earlier. Private investment nearly doubled its pace, surging to close to 12 per cent from just 5.8 per cent previously. “Given the challenge with the monsoon and rain deficit, going forward, growth will depend on how manufacturing and services will compensate,” said Dilip Chenoy, chairman of Bharat Web3 Association and former secretary general at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry. High factory utilisation rates had encouraged more companies to expand capacity, he said – a trend aided by the government’s production-linked incentive programme to boost domestic manufacturing, which has benefited industries from carmaking to mobile-phone production. “I am confident that in the next two or three quarters, growth will be around the same range,” Chenoy said, adding that government missions to build up semiconductor manufacturing and the AI industry could further help India withstand both the fallout from the Iran war and Washington’s higher import tariffs. Borrowed growth? India has spent months trying to conclude a long-pending trade deal with the United States, its largest export market. Exports have held up well this financial year, aided by new trade agreements with Britain and the European Union. “Indian industry has diversified exports and that is reflected in the numbers,” Chenoy said. That resilience comes despite concerns over inflation from higher international oil prices and policymakers’ struggle to shore up the rupee, which has weakened alongside other Asian currencies amid the US-Iran conflict. Households are becoming more indebted to maintain their consumption growth Sunil Sinha, economics professor Sunil Sinha, an economics professor at the Institute for Development and Communication in Chandigarh, said the rupee’s slide had prompted foreign institutional investors to sell Indian shares along with other emerging market assets, but added that the weaker currency had also made exports cheaper. “That may be one of the reasons apart from diversification for the export growth,” he said. Should the Iran war persist into next year, Sinha warned that India would likely experience greater fuel-driven inflation as companies lose the ability to absorb higher input costs rather than passing them on to consumers. Higher consumer spending, partly fuelled by a rise in personal borrowing, had been a key driver of India’s recent growth, he added. “Households are becoming more indebted to maintain their consumption growth. But this kind of consumption growth may not sustain,” Sinha said. ANZ Bank said in a report on Monday that signs of improving urban consumption were emerging in segments such as vehicles, though this had yet to translate into broad-based spending. “We expect growth to remain robust towards year-end and into 2027, supported by resilient consumers and recovering investment,” said Alexandra Hermann Prasad, lead India economist at Oxford Economics. “But rising inflation and still elevated uncertainty will weigh on spending.”

title: China’s No 2 foundry Hua Hong invests US$2b in new fab to meet surging AI-driven demand
description: Project is via a joint venture with state-backed investment entities under China’s National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund.
content: Major Chinese foundry Hua Hong Grace Semiconductor is pouring US$2 billion into a massive capacity expansion in the Chinese chip production hub of Wuxi, racing to meet skyrocketing domestic demand for AI infrastructure and bypass US tech curbs. The fresh capital would fund the construction of a new 12-inch speciality line, its third facility in the eastern Chinese city, the country’s second-largest contract chipmaker said in a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange on Tuesday. Once fully operational, the expansion will add 55,000 wafers to its monthly production capacity, representing a roughly 30 per cent increase to its total capacity in Wuxi. The project will be carried out through a joint venture with state-backed investment entities, including the Hua Xin Fund, a vehicle for China’s National Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund, also known as the “Big Fund”. Hua Hong and its Shanghai subsidiary are providing US$1 billion and US$1.1 billion respectively, holding a controlling 51 per cent stake, while the state entities will provide the remaining capital. The state capital injection will bring total funding for the project to US$4.2 billion, according to the filing. The latest move underscores the urgency among China’s major chipmakers to expand capacity to meet the demand for AI chips driven by the country’s massive infrastructure buildout and chip self-sufficiency drive. Hua Hong’s existing fabrication plants in Shanghai and Jiangsu are operating at full utilisation rates, hitting 103 per cent in the second quarter, according to the company’s earnings report released in August. Construction on the new Wuxi facility, dubbed Fab 9B, began in March. It will focus on speciality technology chips which are commonly used in power management systems, microcontrollers and data centres. In a May earnings call, Hua Hong chairman and president Bai Peng said the company “did not see any impact” from US export controls on equipment procurement for the new project. The expansion follows existing developments in Wuxi, where Hua Hong operates Fab 7 – a 12-inch plant running at 95,000 wafers per month – and Fab 9A, a second plant under construction with a planned monthly capacity of 83,000 wafers. China’s largest chipmakers - from foundries like Hua Hong and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp to integrated device manufacturers like Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation and ChangXin Memory Technologies - are investing aggressively to expand their production capacity this year, despite being largely cut off from the most advanced chipmaking equipment due to strict US export controls. Surging AI demand has already brought a windfall to Hua Hong. In the second quarter, its net profit jumped 385.9 per cent year on year to US$38.6 million, while revenue reached a record US$717.5 million, up 26.8 per cent from a year earlier.

title: Advocacy group urges Hong Kong to let residents tap pension savings for homes
description: Federation of Public Housing Estates says recent cuts to MPF administration fees make now an ideal time to relax withdrawal restrictions.
content: A Hong Kong advocacy group has urged the government to let residents use a portion of their mandatory pension savings for home purchases, one of several proposals submitted ahead of the policy address later this month. The Federation of Public Housing Estates noted on Wednesday that recent cuts to administration fees for the Mandatory Provident Fund (MPF) – the city’s compulsory retirement scheme – would generate higher savings for its 4.8 million members, making this an ideal time to relax withdrawal restrictions. “Offering flexibility in using the Mandatory Provident Fund will be especially helpful to young families under 40 who wish to buy homes,” chairman Man Yu-ming said. Vice-chairman Scott Leung Man-kwong, who is also a lawmaker, suggested allowing withdrawal of partial pension savings for buying homes to strike a balance between flat ownership and retirement protection. “The sum may not cover the down payment, but it can help offset expenses,” he said. “We believe that the proposed measure could help homebuyers, especially those with more pension savings.” Leung noted that Singapore allowed residents to withdraw a proportion of their pension to buy homes under certain conditions, while requiring them to refund their accounts if they sell their properties. He suggested Hong Kong adopt a similar rule to curb speculation. In 2024, the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority rolled out a centralised electronic platform to replace the separate systems used by the MPF’s 12 trustees. The authority said earlier in March that the electronic platform would cut administration fees for 378 investment funds by more than 21 per cent from April 1. By the end of 2024, 125,000 MPF accounts held HK$1 million (US$127,543) or more, with 10 per cent belonging to workers under 40. Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po previously said in February that the government had reviewed similar proposals but chose not to proceed due to market volatility and retirement security concerns. The federation submitted its proposal to the government in late August, ahead of the September 16 policy address, which will be delivered alongside the city’s first five-year plan aligning with national development. It also urged the government to relaunch the Tenants Purchase Scheme – which allows public housing residents to buy their flats at a discount – noting that no new estates have been added to the original 39 since 2005. Currently, such tenants can still buy their homes, while the Housing Authority also sells vacant flats under the scheme to eligible buyers. As of the end of 2025, about 30,000 of those designated homes remained unsold. The federation suggested that the government could offer existing tenants the option to move to other public rental estates to speed up sales of the remaining flats. It added that the measure could serve as a reference for the scheme’s possible relaunch. In March, the Housing Authority announced it would conduct a study this year to gather public feedback on potentially restarting the scheme while safeguarding public housing resources.

title: Denmark sends conscripts to Greenland, signalling aim to boost Arctic ‌defences
description: Trump has repeatedly demanded to acquire Denmark’s semi-autonomous territory while Russia has warned against Nato’s Arctic expansion.
content: For the first time in recent history, Danish ⁠conscripts have been deployed to ⁠Greenland, as Denmark moves to ⁠bolster its presence in the Arctic after US demands to acquire the territory. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish island, citing national security concerns and accusing Copenhagen of neglecting Arctic defence. Denmark and ‌Greenland have firmly rejected the idea. The conscripts are part of the first cohort under Denmark’s new extended conscription programme, aimed at producing soldiers able to operate in one of the kingdom’s most strategically important and challenging regions. “It shows presence that we’re here and not just thinking of our own skin. And also thinking of the ⁠people in Greenland,” 19-year-old conscript David said. Copenhagen has pledged billions of dollars to strengthen Arctic ‌defences after Denmark’s defence minister acknowledged years of underinvestment in the region. “Of course, we are a part of a bigger picture of the strategic ‌communication about Greenland, but our role here is just to continue the training ⁠of the conscripts, ⁠the soldiers, and get more experience with the training in the Arctic terrain and climate,” company commander Captain Laura ‌Jepsen said. The conscripts are taking part in Arctic Endurance, a Danish military exercise that trains soldiers for combat and survival in ‌extreme ‌cold-weather conditions. The drill forms part of Arctic Sentry, a Nato mission launched this year ‌to strengthen the alliance’s Arctic presence and ease tensions within Nato after Trump’s remarks about Greenland. Russia, ⁠which maintains the Arctic’s largest military footprint, has criticised Nato’s growing activity in the region, describing ⁠it as a direct security threat that increases the risk of confrontation. China has increased its activity in the mineral-rich region, mostly in partnership with Moscow. Training north of ‌the Arctic Circle, the ‌conscripts moved through a landscape of bare rock and open expanses with no trees in sight. “I think it sends a message that Denmark is reinforcing itself for the future,” Anton, 22, one of the conscripts, said.

title: BYD, Leapmotor buck EV market slowdown as pressure piles up on small rivals
description: China’s leading EV makers saw sales surge in August, with BYD up 17.8 per cent from last year and Leapmotor up 80.7 per cent.
content: Top performers BYD and Leapmotor clawed their way up higher in terms of sales last month, even as China’s electric vehicle (EV) market was shrinking amid weaker consumer demand. However, smaller players were expected to face falling sales and mounting losses for the rest of the year as competition got fiercer, according to analysts. BYD, the world’s largest EV builder, saw its sales in August surge to the highest in nine months, climbing 17.8 per cent from a year ago to 440,293 units, it said in a statement on Tuesday. The rosy performance added to evidence that the Shenzhen-based carmaker – spurred on by its new model launches and buoyant exports – was returning to solid footing despite a bumpy start in 2026. Leapmotor, known for its relatively inexpensive smart EVs, extended its record-setting run to a fifth month, delivering 103,129 vehicles to customers around the world and logging an 80.7 per cent year-on-year increase, according to a statement by the EV manufacturer. Leapmotor’s overseas presence is bolstered by a partnership and joint venture with European carmaker Stellantis. “A widening gap between the winners and the bottom players would force some underachievers to exit the market in the coming one or two years,” said Phate Zhang, founder of Shanghai-based industry data provider CnEVPost. “The leading EV assemblers, with production scale and research strength, are set to increase their global market share because of their advantages in pricing and innovation.” Chinese carmakers sold a total of 614,000 EVs, including pure electric and plug-in hybrid cars, to domestic buyers in the first 23 days of August, down 12 per cent from the same period in 2025, preliminary data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) showed. On Friday, BYD reported a 30 per cent year-on-year jump in its second-quarter earnings, which hit 8.2 billion yuan (US$1.22 billion), beating a consensus estimate of 8 billion yuan from a Bloom­berg analyst survey. Between April and June, BYD achieved overseas sales of 471,091 vehicles, up 82.5 per cent year-on-year, aided by a global energy crisis prompting more consumers to opt for battery-powered cars. Over the past few months, the EV behemoth also unveiled a clutch of new models under its premium and mass-market brands, such as Denza and Sealion. The new cars helped drive a sales spree, attracting consumers with new tech-powered features such as high-performance batteries fit for superfast charging. Among the nearly 30 Chinese ­carmakers that solely produce EVs, only BYD and Leapmotor were profitable in the first half of the year. Their ­counterparts struggled to break even, battered by high research and development costs and price competition that ate into their profit margins. From January to July, Chinese carmakers delivered a total of 5.67 million EVs to domestic customers, down 12.5 per cent from the previous year, according to the CPCA. Global consultancy AlixPartners predicted at the end of June that further price reductions offered by mainland carmakers to retain their market share in the second half of 2026 could exacerbate their worsening business outlook.

title: China cracks down on AI ‘slop’, clearing out clutter from WeChat, RedNote, Douyin
description: Clampdown sweeps across 2,400 websites and apps as cyberspace watchdog escalates fight against generative tech abuse.
content: China is cracking down on artificial intelligence-generated “slop” – low-grade, mass-produced synthetic content cluttering social media and news feeds – as part of a sweeping campaign against the abuse of the generative technology, the country’s top internet watchdog said on Wednesday. In a statement posted to its website, the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) said it had scrubbed more than 5.61 million pieces of harmful or illegal content and removed some 49,000 accounts during its latest enforcement drive. The clampdown swept up 2,400 websites and apps, targeting some of China’s biggest digital spaces, including TikTok’s sister app Douyin and rival Kuaishou, as well as RedNote and Tencent Holdings’ WeChat. Authorities focused on reining in AI-driven fake news, explicit and violent material, impersonation and safety violations involving minors. The response underscores Beijing’s growing concerns over the accessibility of generative AI. As tools become cheaper and more sophisticated, creators can produce convincing deepfakes and clickbait in seconds, challenging existing moderation systems. The CAC said creators on Douyin, Kuaishou and WeChat used AI to turn literary classics such as Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Journey to the West into sensationalised, low-grade “digital swill” to attract traffic. Other accounts used AI-generated “digital humans” and fabricated news stories to run deceptive marketing campaigns targeting elderly users, the regulator said. Chinese internet platform operators were strengthening their internal guard rails, according to CAC. Developers behind leading chatbots, including ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen, had tightened training data reviews, enforced stricter output bans and embedded clearer identification for synthetic content. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The CAC pledged to continue monitoring risks associated with AI-generated and synthetic content and take measures to prevent the “abuse and malicious use” of AI, while vowing to support the technology’s development.

title: US universities curb international student internships following federal warning
description: The restrictions could have a major impact on Chinese students, who often pursue off-campus work experience while studying in the US.
content: International students in the United States are facing new hurdles when it comes to internships and off-campus work after several major universities paused or restricted certain forms of Curricular Practical Training (CPT). CPT is a form of work authorisation that allows foreign students to take part in internships and other practical training related to their studies. The changes follow two directives in August from the Student and Exchange Visitor Programme (SEVP), a division of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which take a stricter view of when CPT can be authorised. Universities including the University of Pennsylvania, New York University, the University of Southern California, the University of Washington, the University of Rochester and the University of California, Berkeley have paused pending applications or limited CPT to internships that are mandatory parts of a degree programme. What changed? CPT itself has not been banned. On August 12, the SEVP issued a message reminding school officials of their responsibility when approving CPT. The guidance said CPT must be an integral part of an established curriculum and directly related to a student’s major. It also stressed that the training should generally be necessary to complete the degree and required for all students in that programme. The SEVP also warned the school officials that approving CPT carried personal responsibility. By signing off on a student’s work authorisation paperwork, officials certify that the position meets federal requirements. Improper approvals could have consequences for both the university and the individual official, including possible loss of the school’s SEVP certification. The agency also warned schools against using CPT to provide employment opportunities rather than as part of an academic programme. On August 24, the SEVP issued another message reinforcing that CPT was allowed only as an integral part of an established curriculum. It again warned that violations could put a university’s certification at risk. Universities begin tightening CPT rules UC Berkeley was among the first major universities to respond. In an August 13 letter to students, the university’s international office said the new federal criteria were “narrow in nature” and raised questions about existing CPT practices. The university then suspended applications for “course credit CPT” that were considered integral to a programme but were not formal degree requirements. The university said it would continue processing CPT that was required for the degree. The university described the move as a precaution, saying it was acting to minimise risk to its international office advisers and the university. It said it was temporarily suspending course credit CPT applications until further notice. UC Berkeley’s current CPT guidance continues to reflect the suspension. The university now considers “integral” practical training to mean either a degree requirement for all students in the programme or a necessary component of a master’s thesis or doctoral dissertation. The university later warned students that the suspension could continue for the foreseeable future. The University of Pennsylvania announced a universitywide pause on August 29, putting new and pending CPT requests on hold while it reviewed its academic programmes and procedures in response to the federal guidance. The university stressed that CPT had not been eliminated and that pending applications had not been denied. It also highlighted a key change in how academic credit was treated, telling students: “Under the guidance, receiving academic credit is not enough by itself.” NYU updated its guidance on August 31, saying the federal guidance established a stricter interpretation of CPT rules. Under the university’s reading, CPT may be authorised only when it is an explicit, mandatory degree requirement of a programme. NYU said CPT authorisations already approved for the autumn term would remain valid, but pending requests had been frozen. USC has taken a similar position. It said CPT based on an elective course did not meet the federal requirements. As of August 24, the university said CPT would generally be limited to practical training required for graduation. The University of Washington has also paused new CPT requests that are not required work experience for all students in a degree programme. At the University of Rochester, optional internships, clinical experience and other practical training, including those tied to elective internship courses, are no longer considered eligible under the university’s interpretation of the guidance. Other campuses within the University of California system, including UCLA and UC Davis, have also issued guidance. What Chinese students need to know The changes apply to international students from all countries on F-1 visas, not just Chinese students. However, the restrictions could have a major impact on Chinese students, who make up one of the largest international student groups in the US and often rely on internships during undergraduate and master’s degree programmes. For students who already have internship offers for the autumn semester, the key question is whether the CPT has already been authorised. At universities that have issued guidance, CPT already authorised on official paperwork generally remains valid. Students should also remember that they cannot begin off-campus work until they have received the required CPT authorisation. On the Chinese social media platform RedNote, a user identifying as a Columbia University PhD graduate said the policy was “truly driving international students into a corner”. “Doesn’t this completely cut off any path for international students to intern in the US?” the user wrote. A user who said they were a UC Berkeley journalism student noted that a “short-term policy reversal” appeared unlikely. The person cited an email from the university’s international office stating that the suspension of CPT approvals had been “extended indefinitely”. Another RedNote user, who listed the University of Southern California as his school, posted a scathing reflection, saying that he had “really believed it” when people had promised him the STEM fields – science, technology, engineering and mathematics – were stable and technical skills were in demand in the US. “I was completely misled. When policies shift like this, all of it falls apart in an instant,” he wrote. Frustration over US President Donald Trump’s second term has been a dominant theme of discussions on the Chinese platform. One user, whose post showed an Illinois IP address, said: “This is only one year and eight months into Trump’s term; the ‘good days’ are still ahead of us.” A Los Angeles-based user replied: “It’s only been a year and a half? It feels like half a lifetime has passed.” Additional reporting by Cao Jiaxuan

title: China cuts thousands of Japan flights as strained ties send travellers elsewhere
description: Mainland carriers scrap more than 30 per cent of flights to Japan as travellers turn to South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia.
content: Thousands of scheduled flights from mainland China to Japan were scrapped during a record-breaking summer travel season for domestic carriers, as travellers pivoted to other Asian destinations amid strained diplomatic ties. A total of 2,312 flights were cancelled in July and August, accounting for 30.7 per cent of scheduled flights, according to aviation data provider Flight Master DAST. July saw 1,195 cancellations, or 31.4 per cent of scheduled flights. Chinese airlines shifted capacity towards other Asian markets where demand remained stronger. Japan dropped out of the top three international destinations for mainland departures during the July-August period, ranking behind South Korea, Thailand and Malaysia, according to Flight Master. Li Hanming, an independent aviation analyst, said 780 China-Japan flights were cancelled in September, based on announcements that no tickets were available. He said the cancellations covered between 150 and 200 routes. The pullback contrasted sharply with a record-breaking summer for China’s aviation sector, as airlines carried more passengers while keeping fares low to stimulate demand. Mainland airlines transported 153.64 million passenger trips between July 1 and Monday, a historic high and up 4.4 per cent from a year earlier, Flight Master estimated. International passenger traffic rose 3.1 per cent during the period. The July-August period typically brings a surge in travel by students and families as schools and universities close for summer. The average passenger load factor, measuring the share of available seats filled, climbed to 87.4 per cent during the period, up 1.7 percentage points from a year earlier, according to Flight Master. August set a new high at 88.8 per cent. The decline in travel comes as relations between Beijing and Tokyo have continued to deteriorate since November, when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made controversial remarks on Taiwan. Among the measures instituted in response to the dispute were travel warnings against trips to Japan from Beijing. Demand has fallen consistently, leading the mainland’s airlines to slash flights on their routes. Tokyo’s decision to raise foreign-visitor visa fees from July 1 has also made visits less appealing for visitors from the mainland, with the cost of a single-entry visa increasing from 3,000 yen (US$18.54) to 15,000 yen, and fees for multiple-entry visas jumping from 6,000 yen to 30,000 yen. Tourist arrivals from the mainland plunged 56.1 per cent year on year in July, extending a downward trend that began in December 2025, according to data released by the Japan National Tourism Organisation. For the first seven months of the year, mainland visitors plummeted 56.3 per cent year on year. Flight capacity from the mainland to Japan recovered to just 46.4 per cent of the level seen during the same period in 2019, Flight Master data showed. By comparison, flights to South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam, Russia and Indonesia, among others, had already surpassed their 2019 levels.

title: Former care home warden guilty of raping intellectually disabled female resident
description: Chung Pui-kei, former assistant warden at Tai Po home run by Hong Chi Association, convicted of raping resident five times in 2024.
content: A former assistant warden at a care home run by Hong Kong’s largest NGO for people with intellectual disabilities has been convicted of raping a female resident five times two years ago. Wednesday’s High Court verdict against Chung Pui-kei moves a high-profile case towards its resolution after it sparked intense public anger and government warnings, leading the Hong Chi Association to appoint an independent review committee headed by a former Law Society president to overhaul facility oversight. The jury of five men and two women found Chung guilty of five counts of raping the mentally incapacitated resident who lived at a Tai Po home operated by the association. The jury rejected the 38-year-old defendant’s contention that the 23-year-old victim might have fabricated the allegations out of grievance or jealousy after her romantic feelings for him went unrequited. The trial heard that the woman, whose intellectual functioning was equivalent to that of a nine-year-old, considered Chung a “very friendly” warden who often chatted with her, played video games with her, and occasionally gave her marshmallows. Prosecutors accused the defendant of abusing the woman’s trust and raping her three times in a male staff room and twice in her room between July 13 and August 9, 2024. The woman said she had sometimes refused or expressed discomfort, but had not dared to speak out for fear of being scolded by the accused. Police recovered condoms and other items associated with sexual intercourse from Chung’s locker. They also seized a bedsheet from the woman’s room that contained the defendant’s semen and the complainant’s DNA. Giving evidence, Chung denied ever having sex with the woman and said their interactions had been limited to casual conversation. Seeking to explain his presence in the women’s ward on August 9, 2024, Chung said he had gone there to inspect the area after receiving a report of a suspected fire. He said he decided to stay and spent an hour with the woman because she was having difficulty sleeping that night. Asked to explain the semen on the bedsheet, the former assistant warden insisted that he had not ejaculated, while suggesting the bodily fluid could instead have been his sweat. A hospital psychiatrist confirmed that the woman had been diagnosed with bipolar affective disorder but said she had not displayed psychotic symptoms during two assessments in August and November 2024. Senior Public Prosecutor Human Lam Hiu-man rejected the defendant’s account as far-fetched and illogical. She stressed that the woman had been mentally stable and that her allegations could not have resulted from hallucinations. While Chung claimed the woman had romantic feelings for him, Lam said the defendant could not have expected a mentally incapacitated person to consent to sexual conduct. Defence counsel Lawrence Hui Cheuk-lun sought to discredit the woman’s account by highlighting discrepancies in her version of events. The lawyer referred to surveillance-camera footage that appeared to show the woman entering Chung’s room voluntarily. He also questioned why she had not suffered physical or psychological trauma. Mr Justice Douglas Yau Tak-hong will pass sentence on October 14, pending a victim impact report and psychiatric and psychological assessments of the accused. Chung has remained in custody since being charged on August 17, 2024. The defendant was also originally charged with committing a grossly indecent act on a male resident at the home on August 3, 2024.
