However, prosecutors later dropped the charge, citing insufficient evidence. The case is the second in which an association employee was found guilty of raping an intellectually disabled resident in the NGO’s care. The association and the Social Welfare Department revealed Chung’s case in separate statements published more than two months after the start of criminal proceedings. The labour chief defended the delay, saying authorities had to consider the feelings of victims and their families. The association also said in a reply at the time that it had no intention to conceal the crime. The department also issued a written warning to the care home after an investigation found that it had failed to put effective measures in place to protect residents from abuse.

title: Opinion | How the SCO chips away at US power without an alliance system
description: The SCO’s significance is practical: it gives those who do not want their future defined in Washington a forum to coordinate and hedge.
content: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) was born 25 years ago as a modest mechanism for managing borders between China, Russia and four Central Asian states. At its anniversary summit in Bishkek this week, it looks more consequential – and harder for the United States to dismiss. The timing is important. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine remains unresolved, while the war between Iran and the US has turned the Persian Gulf into another theatre of strategic competition, with energy markets again exposed to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. The SCO now brings together China, Russia, India, Iran, Pakistan, most of the Central Asian republics and Belarus, alongside partners including Turkey and multiple Gulf states. Its 10 full members represent more than 3.4 billion people and roughly a quarter of global GDP. However, its growing importance is not simply a matter of size. President Xi Jinping has called for the SCO to assume a larger role in technology and security and to help create a “universally secure environment”. He has presented it as a model of cooperation without formal alliances, confrontation or targeting third parties, urging members to focus on development, security, people’s well-being and dialogue. Calling the SCO an anti-American alliance is a mistake. Its members have different interests. India and China remain strategic competitors; India and Pakistan have long-standing tensions; and Central Asian governments want room to manoeuvre between Moscow, Beijing, Ankara, Brussels and Washington. Turkey remains a North Atlantic Treaty Organization (Nato) member while pursuing a larger Eurasian role. The SCO has neither Nato’s military command nor the European Union’s supranational institutions. Its significance is more practical: it gives states that do not want their foreign policy defined in Washington a forum to coordinate, negotiate and hedge. Rather than creating a coherent rival bloc, the SCO is helping normalise a world in which Washington is no longer the indispensable venue for every major geopolitical discussion. Xi’s language reflects that ambition. By stressing cooperation without alliance or confrontation, Beijing is offering the SCO as an alternative model of international organisation. Whether that model is as inclusive as advertised is debatable, but its appeal is growing. The organisation’s agenda has expanded beyond its original security mission. Trade, energy, transport, technology and finance now sit alongside counterterrorism and regional security. Technology could prove especially important. Xi wants the SCO to play a larger role in technology and security, reflecting a broader shift in the sources of geopolitical power. Digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence, data and technology standards increasingly shape national security as much as conventional military capabilities. SCO members have discussed greater use of national currencies, financial cooperation and new development mechanisms, including an SCO development bank. None threatens the US dollar’s central position today, but Western sanctions and restrictions on access to financial infrastructure are encouraging some countries to develop alternative channels for trade and payments. The wars are reinforcing that trend. Russia has become more dependent on Asian markets, while its energy ties with China remain substantial. Beijing was still buying about 2 million barrels a day of Russian crude in 2025. The war in Ukraine has underscored the value of continental energy supplies and transport routes that reduce China’s exposure to maritime chokepoints. Beijing does not need the SCO to become a military alliance. The organisation gives China a platform for expanding economic connectivity and political influence without obliging it to provide security guarantees to every member. Washington should take the SCO seriously. A strategy built too heavily around tariffs, technology restrictions and pressure on third countries to choose sides can encourage exactly the hedging that makes institutions such as the SCO more valuable. Economic pressure has its uses, but sustained pressure also gives other countries reasons to seek alternative suppliers, markets, technologies and payment systems. The US has legitimate interests in Ukraine, the Middle East, freedom of navigation, technology security and the dollar-based financial system, but Washington needs to distinguish between adversaries and institutions. The SCO’s 25th anniversary shows that Eurasian states are building cooperation mechanisms that can survive disagreements among members. While Washington cannot stop that evolution, it can decide how to respond. That means working with Central Asian states where interests overlap; maintaining strong channels with India and Turkey; competing with China without treating every Chinese initiative as hostile; protecting technological advantages without accelerating parallel systems; and keeping diplomatic contacts open with governments whose cooperation could become important on energy, terrorism, proliferation and conflict. The SCO is unlikely to become the Eurasian equivalent of Nato. Its importance is that it is becoming part of the infrastructure of a more fragmented international system where power is distributed more widely and middle powers have more choices. The question for Washington is whether it is prepared for a world in which it is no longer the country around which everyone else must organise.

title: Indonesia investigates reports of 8 citizens fighting in Russia’s war against Ukraine
description: Jakarta says it has to determine if the eight people were recruited through job offers but then duped into joining Russia’s military.
content: Indonesia on Wednesday said the government was ascertaining reports that eight of its citizens who applied for civilian jobs allegedly ended up fighting in Russia’s war against Ukraine. Coordinating Minister for Legal, Human Rights, Immigration and Corrections Yusril Ihza Mahendra said authorities were checking the identities and hiring processes involved, which offered attractive perks such as high pay, non-combat duties and fast-tracking Russian citizenship. “We are taking the information from Ukraine seriously. But we cannot draw conclusions before all the facts have been verified,” Yusril said on Wednesday. According to state news agency Antara, he said the government must determine whether they had actually been fighting alongside Russian forces. Yusril’s response came after Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service last week said it had accessed documents allegedly linking the eight Indonesians to Russia’s military. The agency added that recruiters lured foreigners with job offers and later sent them to the battlefield. Yusril said the eight people could have been duped into joining the Russian military and were possibly unaware of the consequences of deliberately representing a foreign army without presidential permission. “If our citizens were recruited through job offers but then directed into military service and sent to a conflict zone, we must determine whether they are victims,” Antara quoted him as saying. Russia’s ambassador on Tuesday said Moscow was ready to help Jakarta in connection with the case upon request. Sergei Tolchenov also said his country’s embassy in Indonesia did not conduct any recruitment for the Russian armed forces, Tempo news magazine reported. Under Indonesian law, an individual’s citizenship can be revoked in certain cases, including joining a foreign military without presidential authorisation. Yusril said action would be taken against the eight people if the “facts prove that the requirements for loss of citizenship have been met”. Russia has in the past conducted a purported enlistment drive in Asia in a bid to bolster its defences following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, a Ukrainian military intelligence report said at least three Filipinos had been killed on the Russian front lines in recent years. In January, a former member of a paramilitary arm of Indonesia’s national police lost his citizenship after joining a Russian mercenary group fighting in Ukraine. Muhammad Rio said in a social media video that he earned a monthly salary of 210,000 roubles (US$2,434), along with a signing bonus of 2 million roubles. More than 18,000 foreigners from 128 countries and territories have fought or are currently fighting for Russia in Ukraine, CNN quoted a Ukrainian brigadier general as saying last year.

title: 7 ways to reduce dark circles under the eyes without using make-up or needles. Think coffee
description: There are many reasons for dark circles under your eyes, and each has its own remedy, say experts, who share 7 non-invasive treatments.
content: Dark circles are one of the most prolific skin concerns across all ages, and reasons range from alcohol to hormones to lack of sleep and genetics. “Dark circles are slightly misleading because they are not really one condition,” says Dr David Jack, an aesthetic doctor based in London’s Harley Street. “What we perceive as darkness underneath the eyes can come from increased melanin in the skin, visible blood vessels through very thin eyelid skin, changes in the underlying anatomy that create shadow, or a mixture of all three.” The colour can offer some indication of the cause. Jack says brownish circles are more suggestive of pigmentation, while blue, purple or reddish tones can indicate a greater vascular component. If you find that darkness noticeably changes according to the direction of the light, then facial structure and shadow may be the cause. So before investing in another concealer, here is what you can do to make dark circles under the eye less noticeable without make-up – or a syringe. 1. Choose your eye cream according to the cause While they may look the same, not all dark circles respond to the same skincare. “For pigmentation, I tend to look for ingredients that regulate melanin production and improve overall skin quality,” Jack says. “Vitamin C, niacinamide (vitamin B3), azelaic acid and carefully formulated retinoids can all be useful, although the eye area is particularly prone to irritation, so stronger is certainly not always better.” As the skin is so thin under the eyes, it is crucial to look after the skin barrier alongside using active ingredients. “Hydration is key to help with the skin texture when someone has dark circles,” says Nadia Aminian, senior aesthetician at the Taktouk Clinic in London. “The more dehydrated the skin, the worse everything looks, so I always look for ceramides and hyaluronic acid in an eye cream … alongside an active ingredient to treat the dark circles.” Retinoids may be particularly useful for thin-looking skin – or for people who are older – Jack says, as over time they can improve collagen production and skin quality, potentially making the under-eye area appear less translucent. 2. Don’t expect hyaluronic acid to fill hollows Hyaluronic acid has become synonymous with “plumping” skincare, but is it more than surface level? “Hyaluronic acid is another ingredient that can make the skin look smoother and more hydrated, but topical hyaluronic acid obviously cannot replace volume in a tear trough,” Jack says. As we age, changes around the eye socket and midface can deepen the tear trough, creating a shadow beneath the eye. “This distinction is important as eye creams can improve the skin, but they cannot significantly alter the anatomy underneath it,” he says. “If the darkness is predominantly caused by hollowing or shadow, endlessly changing eye cream is unlikely to solve the problem.” So if you have worked your way through several supposedly brightening eye creams without much difference, the product may not necessarily be the problem – it may be targeting the wrong cause. 3. Use caffeine for a temporary morning fix Your morning coffee can do more than make you seem more awake. “Caffeine constricts the blood vessels under the eyes, increasing the circulation around the eyes,” Aminian says, explaining that caffeine also helps with puffiness and oedema, which is why eye creams and gels that include caffeine are recommended for use in the morning. But don’t expect permanent results. “Personally I believe this is a temporary fix,” Aminian says. 4. Reach for something cold “Cold causes vasoconstriction and can reduce swelling, so a cold compress or chilled eye mask can be quite effective on mornings when the eyes look particularly puffy,” says Jack. Aminian says cold compresses, eye masks and facial massage “can make the eyes look brighter, fresher and de-puff them instantly”. But remember that more vigorous is not necessarily more effective when it comes to massage. “I would be cautious about vigorous massage because eyelid skin is extraordinarily thin and repeated rubbing can cause irritation and potentially worsen post-inflammatory pigmentation,” Jack says. 5. Stop rubbing your eyes This could be one of the most overlooked causes of worsening dark circles, according to the experts. Jack says that rubbing the eyes is “probably the big one”. “People with hay fever, eczema or sensitive eyes often do it unconsciously, and chronic friction and inflammation can contribute to pigmentation,” he says. Being too aggressive when cleansing or applying skincare can also exacerbate dark circles. Rather than rubbing skincare vigorously into the area, handle the delicate skin gently – and if itchy eyes are causing you to rub them repeatedly, address the underlying cause rather than trying to treat the resulting darkness. 6. Treat sunglasses as skincare SPF may not immediately spring to mind when you are trying to brighten dark circles, but leaving the eye area exposed could be making pigmentation more noticeable. “UV exposure stimulates melanogenesis, so somebody with a pigmentary component to their dark circles may notice them becoming darker following sun exposure,” Jack says. Small changes to your skincare and daily habits may make a visible difference UV rays can also contribute to collagen breakdown and skin ageing over time, potentially making some of the vascular and structural causes of dark circles more apparent. The problem is that the eye contour often gets easily missed when applying sunscreen, to avoid getting any in the eye. Jack’s solution is straightforward and does not require another chemical product: sunglasses. “Sunglasses are particularly useful because they provide physical UV protection and reduce squinting,” he says. “I would therefore consider daily broad-spectrum SPF and sunglasses part of the ‘treatment’ rather than simply general skincare advice.” 7. Work out whether sleep is actually the problem Getting more sleep is probably the first piece of advice anyone with dark circles hears – but more early nights will not always erase them, as dark circles are “actually genetic or anatomical” in most cases, according to Jack. Other lifestyle factors, however, can temporarily emphasise them, too. As we know, dehydration can make the skin look less plump – alcohol and salty food also encourage fluid retention, making morning puffiness more obvious. “In someone with a pronounced tear trough, this can actually exaggerate the adjacent shadow,” Jack says. So good sleep and hydration may improve how the area looks, but persistent circles are not necessarily evidence that you need more rest or water. If pigmentation, dehydration or puffiness are the reasons, small changes to your skincare and daily habits may make a visible difference. But if your dark circles are predominantly genetic or caused by the structure of your face, even the most diligent routine is unlikely to make them disappear completely. As Jack says, “this is why diagnosing the cause is much more useful than simply buying something labelled for dark circles.”

title: Air China Boeing 747 grounded in New York following gate refuelling incident
description: Beijing-bound Boeing 747-8 inspected after fuel truck reportedly tears lines from wing ports at JFK.
content: A Boeing 747-8 operated by Air China reportedly suffered a fuel leak at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport early on Monday, forcing the cancellation of the flight. No injuries were reported in or around the aircraft, which was expected to operate flight CA982 from New York to Beijing that day. The leak is said to have occurred between 1am and 2am while the plane was parked at the gate, according to posts on Chinese social media. It was being refuelled when the fuel truck moved away with two hoses still connected to the plane, damaging the fuel ports and spilling fuel onto the tarmac, according to a post on Shanghai Observer, a social media outlet of the Jiefang Daily, and a video circulating on other social media platforms. The South China Morning Post has not independently verified the video. Photos shared online appeared to show airport personnel inspecting the aircraft’s fuel ports and refuelling equipment, as well as cleaning up what appeared to be fuel on the ground. Several passengers who said they were booked on the flight posted a cancellation notice they said had come from Air China. It attributed the cancellation to “fuel guarantee”, apparently referring to arrangements to refuel the aircraft. The notice did not mention a fuel leak, aircraft damage or a refuelling truck. The notice circulating on social media has not been independently verified. Air China confirmed on social media on Wednesday afternoon that flight CA982 had been unable to depart as scheduled after the “unusual movement” of a fuel truck damaged parts of the aircraft during ground refuelling. Flight-tracking platform Umetrip showed the flight – which was scheduled to depart JFK at 2.05am on August 31 and arrive in Beijing at 6.40am the following day – as cancelled. One passenger who said they were booked on the flight wrote on social media that they had arrived at JFK at 9pm and had begun boarding around 1am. “We were halfway through boarding when we were told to get off the plane for reasons that were unclear,” the passenger wrote. They said that Air China had given passengers little information and left them waiting until morning, when they were finally told the flight had been cancelled. Passengers were then asked to collect their baggage. The airline said in the brief statement that it had initiated its emergency contingency plan for international flights to assist affected passengers. The Aviation Safety Network, an online database of aviation accidents and incidents, has listed the incident while noting that the only information available came from news, social media or unofficial sources. “During the refuelling process, the unexpected movement of the refuelling truck caused damage to the fuel port and a fuel leak, which led to the cancellation of the flight,” the website said. The website’s description of the incident was posted hours before Air China’s statement. The aircraft, registered as B-2486, is a Boeing 747-8 that entered service with Air China in 2014, according to the website. The four-engine widebody aircraft has the capacity to seat 365 passengers. The Boeing 747-8 uses a pressure-refuelling system, with refuelling points beneath the wings to connect with hoses from ground equipment. If a refuelling vehicle moves while hoses remain connected to the aircraft, the resulting tension can damage the refuelling connections and cause a fuel spill. Additional reporting by Carol Yang

title: 4 top watch moments in August, from Drake’s Daytona to Sam Altman’s bespoke Vanguart
description: Watch Ho & Co founder Jackie Ho channels personal yum cha memories in a Selten collaboration, while Ryan Reynolds steps out with an F.P. Journe Automatique Lune.
content: August may traditionally mark a midsummer lull, but high horology showed no signs of slowing down. Celebrities are getting into watches more than ever, from Sam Altman’s custom order of Vanguart pieces to Drake’s one-of-one “iced-out” Daytona. Meanwhile, high-horology heavyweights Wei Koh and Guillaume Tetu launched Legare with a piece inspired by a dual-escapement pocket watch, as brands like Selten collaborate with Watch Ho & Co to release a stunning dim-sum-centric piece for their third anniversary. Here are our favourite timepiece moments from August. Sam Altman’s Vanguart commission In an era where celebrity wristchecks are routine, and tech titans like Mark Zuckerberg are serious about high horology, OpenAI founder Sam Altman is taking his own turn. To show he’s been bitten by the watch bug, Altman commissioned seven custom pieces from Swiss independent brand Vanguart. The Vanguart x OpenAI collection is limited to the seven pieces and is based on the brand’s titanium Orb model, which starts at US$180,000, according to The Wall Street Journal, or CHF150,000 per watch, according to industry media. The model is known for its distinctive curved case, which features a function indicator (between manual and automatic) at 12 o’clock. It also features a cambered “winding mass”, which rotates to wind the watch in automatic mode. Altman’s pieces are modified to sport the OpenAI logo at 12 o’clock, and the winding mass is inscribed with a quote from Altman – “Compute is Destiny”. The caseback also features a line of code in Python, suggested by Vanguart CEO Axel Leuenberger. As Vanguart president Mehmet Koruturk explains, “This means that artificial intelligence must be used for peaceful purposes. This commission will remain unique in our history.” Celebrity wrist games View this post on Instagram A post shared by champagnepapi (@champagnepapi) Canadian hip-hop star Drake made headlines when he posted on August 15 that Rolex had sent him the One of One Piece Unique Ice Gradient Daytona with the words “Freeze The World” engraved on the caseback. The piece itself appears to feature entirely gem-set parts – from dial to indices, bezel and bracelet – all in a careful gradient going from blue to white. “Crafted to celebrate the record-breaking milestones of 2026. Please do not get your local jeweller to recreate,” Drake captioned his Instagram post. Meanwhile, actor Ryan Reynolds is getting stuck into the hobby in a completely different way. The Deadpool star has recently been spotted in increasingly stunning pieces, ranging from the F.P. Journe Automatique Lune “Nacre” in pink gold to creations by more obscure makers like Lederer and Haldimann. Most notably, Reynolds shared on Instagram in August that he would begin horology classes, “for no reason other than curiosity and a love of this strange mash-up of art and engineering”, per Robb Report. August was a muted affair in terms of red carpets, but that didn’t stop attendees of the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA) Awards, which honours players and teams across English professional football, from showing their best timepieces. In particular, Arsenal midfielder Declan Rice, who was named in the PFA Premier League Team of the Year, sported the white, skeletonised Richard Mille RM 55-01 alongside his subtle monochromatic tuxedo. New releases, near and far Some of the best watch releases this month come very close to home. Hong Kong watch club Watch Ho & Co celebrates its third anniversary by teaming up with Selten once more to present the deeply personal and nostalgic Yum Cha. Designed to evoke the woven pattern of a bamboo dim sum steamer basket, the watch reflects the communal spirit of a traditional dim sum meal. These gatherings are a core memory for founder Jackie Ho, who spent many mornings at dim sum spots with his grandmother. Emerging local label Nectere introduced The Eclipse – a reimagining of its original Order From Chaos design featuring a signature asymmetrical case inspired by the moon’s dark silhouette and golden halo. Atelier Wen, meanwhile, unveiled a two-tone collaboration piece with Massena Lab, giving us the Inflection Shuo, which pairs the model’s full tantalum construction with a dial featuring meticulous hand-tremblage. Urwerk also demonstrated masterful finishing with the UR-1001 Amadeus. Housed in an elaborately baroque-engraved titanium case, the pocket watch displays time via wandering hours and retrograde minutes, alongside a day-date complication using the same format. The reverse face features an “oil change” indicator to track service intervals, along with 100- and 1,000-year tracking scales. Horologer Ming, on the other hand, released the 57.05 Comet, a worldtimer that solves a simple, fundamental problem with tracking time across the globe. A patent-pending additional outer bezel can be shifted to adjust the time for cities that observe daylight saving time, leaving countries that don’t observe it static. Established brands were generally quiet, but Longines and Omega focused on subtle refinements this August. Longines updated its Master Collection most notably by introducing its first-ever Chrono Monopusher, simplifying the pusher layout on the crown side. Omega also updated its Speedmaster 38mm collection – long a vital, smaller size for its most recognisable complication – across seven different colour variations designed to align more closely with the traditional Speedmaster Moonwatch. Wei Koh and Guillaume Tetu launch Legare What happens when you take a pocket watch with two escapements, flip the movement and reframe it as a wristwatch? That was the starting point when Revolution Watch founder Wei Koh and Hautlence co-founder Guillaume Tetu teamed up to launch Legare. The brand’s debut timepiece, the Chapter 1 AGP Inverted, is limited to 25 pieces each in untreated German silver and black rhodium. The Chapter 1 AGP Inverted takes inspiration from a symmetrical, dual-oscillator 1933 pocket watch – a piece that also inspired the Philippe Dufour Duality in 1996. According to Legare’s site, the watch was a graduation project by Albert-Gustave Piguet (no relation to Audemars Piguet), who would go on to develop the Lemania Calibre 2310, one of high horology’s most famous chronograph calibres. Legare inverted the movement for the 1933 piece so both escapements are visible on the dial side, joined by a differential that averages out rate errors for greater accuracy.

title: South China Sea island build-up heightens Vietnam’s security concerns
description: Hanoi voices strong objections after reports emerge about Chinese construction works in the Paracels archipelago.
content: Vietnam faces heightened security in the South China Sea amid reports of construction works in the Paracels archipelago – which Beijing calls Xisha Islands – with analysts saying that the latest developments could alter the strategic balance in the contested waters. Hanoi voiced its strong objection after reports citing satellite imagery said new Chinese infrastructure had appeared on Yagong Island, called Ba Ba Island by Vietnam. “Vietnam ⁠resolutely opposes this, has made serious representations and affirmed its position on the matter, and demands an immediate end to such activities and that they not be repeated,” Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Pham Thu Hang said on Friday. “Vietnam reiterates that all ⁠foreign activities in the Paracel Islands, including at Ba Ba Island and at Hai Sam Reef, conducted without Vietnam’s permission are ⁠completely illegal and null and void,” she added, using Vietnam’s name for Antelope Reef. The Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative (AMTI) reported on August 14 that China had completed land reclamation at Antelope Reef. First signs of major infrastructure have emerged at the new artificial island, including a “likely airstrip”. Beijing has not commented on the current reports, but has consistently framed its activities in the region as one of sovereign rights. Chong De Xian, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said that given existing Chinese infrastructure across the South China Sea, additional installations could strengthen Beijing’s surveillance and operational abilities. “For Vietnam, this potentially means a tighter operating environment, where any presence or activity around the Paracels could be detected earlier, tracked more closely, and challenged more quickly,” Chong said. China controls seven fortified outposts in the Spratly Islands, covering roughly 1,300 hectares (3,200 acres) of reclaimed land equipped with major military airbases, deepwater ports and missile systems, according to AMTI. Beijing has occupied the Paracel Islands since 1974, when it seized them from the former South Vietnam navy. Vietnam, which claims the entire archipelago as its ‌own, ⁠has moved in recent years to expand its own network of bases in the Spratlys, which lie further south. Noraini Zulkifli, senior lecturer at the National Defence University of Malaysia’s Department of International Relations, Security and Law, said the situation “carries genuine potential for escalation” as Vietnam could interpret the new installations as a “direct threat to its sovereignty and national security”. This could alter the strategic balance in the northern South China Sea, she added. “If left unmanaged, the militarisation of contested islands risks increasing the frequency of maritime incidents, heightening the chance of miscalculation,” Noraini said, adding that Hanoi’s “open opposition” signalled a willingness to internationalise the dispute. It also suggests that Vietnam is keen to reinforce its legal claims under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) and invite external players such as Asean, the United States and Japan to play a stabilising role, according to Noraini. Under Unclos, Vietnam claims include a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea, a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, and a continental shelf totalling roughly 1 million sq km (390,000 square miles). An integrated intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network “could put persistent pressure on Vietnamese fishing vessels”, said Van T. Pham, founder and director of The South China Sea Chronicle Initiative, a Vietnam-based independent research organisation that analyses maritime activities in the disputed waters. Indirect response Ray Powell, director of Stanford University’s SeaLight Foundation, said China’s Paracel buildout might be, in part, an indirect response to Vietnam’s ambitious construction programme in the Spratly Islands. “While Beijing has not directly interfered with those, it is strengthening its position in the Paracels,” he said. “It may see this asymmetric response as a way to impose costs on Hanoi without creating a direct confrontation and perhaps driving it closer to Manila’s more adversarial position.” Unlike the Philippines, which takes a confrontational approach – including maritime pushbacks and frequent drills with allies – Vietnam has traditionally held a quieter stance towards Beijing on the South China Sea. However, Hanoi has over the years expanded artificial land in the disputed Spratly Islands to about 1,100 hectares, building military and maritime infrastructure across 27 sites on at least 18 reefs, according to AMTI. Vietnam’s latest objection should be seen as part of a pattern, Chong said. While Hanoi usually tries to avoid unnecessary escalation, it periodically objects on record when Chinese activities cross areas it claims. In March, Vietnam formally protested China’s land reclamation and dredging activities at Antelope Reef. “In this case, the reported construction was already public, and keeping silent would have risked looking like acquiescence, especially on a sovereignty issue as sensitive as the Paracels,” he said. “Vietnam’s open opposition serves to preserve Hanoi’s sovereignty position, signals that it does not accept Chinese activity there, and reassures domestic audiences that the issue is not being ignored.” Before Hanoi issued its formal response, there was evidence of growing public frustration in Vietnam, with the issue generating over 2 million social media posts, Van said. “The response of Vietnamese authorities appears to be lagging behind public awareness, particularly among younger people,” he said. “Vietnam may face growing pressure in balancing the management of its bilateral relationship with China and the need to manage domestic politics in a way that maintains its legitimacy at home.”

title: Malaysian under fire for competing at transgender beauty pageant in Thailand
description: The Department of Islamic Development Malaysia said it would summon the contestant in the Miss Equality World event for questioning.
content: The Malaysian Islamic Development Department (Jakim) will summon a Malaysian participant in the Miss Equality World 2026 pageant in Thailand for questioning, following the circulation of social media posts. In a statement on Tuesday, Jakim director general Dr Sirajuddin Suhaimee said Jakim would work with state Islamic religious authorities and relevant agencies to take action against the individual in accordance with existing laws and regulations. He said the participant’s involvement in the transgender beauty pageant was regrettable and had caused public concern. Sirajuddin said the act went against religious values and human nature, as well as contravened Malaysian laws. “Jakim and the state Islamic religious authorities will not compromise with any efforts to normalise such behaviour,” he said. A video circulating on social media showed an individual, believed to be a man, wearing women’s clothing and speaking at the competition in Bangkok last Sunday, prompting criticism online. Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Hasan said the contestant’s action, which tarnished the country’s image, was also incompatible with Islamic teachings and Malaysia’s cultural norms. “Religious authorities will work with the relevant agencies to examine possible action under existing laws,” he said on Tuesday, state news agency Bernama reported. Malaysia’s sharia laws, which apply only to Muslims, ban cross-dressing and other expressions of gender nonconformity. In Kuala Lumpur, sharia law allows for fines of up to 1,000 ringgit (US$247) or a year in prison for Muslim men who wear women’s clothing in public and are deemed to be posing as women. This story was first published by The Star

title: Former Malaysian minister arrested  in state haj fund corruption probe
description: Malaysia’s anti-corruption agency says the ex-minister is being investigated for his links to a hotel lease agreement in Saudi Arabia.
content: A former Malaysian minister has been remanded for five days as part of an anti-corruption inquiry into the management of the country’s state haj fund. The suspect, who is in his sixties, was detained at about 4.30pm on Tuesday after he went to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) headquarters in Putrajaya to have his statement recorded. MACC confirmed the arrest in a statement on social media but did not release the former minister’s identity. “The arrest was made around 4.30pm and it is linked to a hotel lease agreement in Saudi Arabia,” it said. The ex-minister arrived at the Putrajaya Magistrate’s Court for remand proceedings at 10.25am on Wednesday. He is being investigated in connection to the Royal Commission of Inquiry report on Lembaga Tabung Haji. The report, which was made public on July 29, outlined various weaknesses in the state haj fund management and operations between 2014 and 2020. The former minister is the latest figure to be caught up in the investigation by the anti-corruption agency following the release of the report. Last week, an ex-finance ministry official, who was the fund’s former chairman, was held for seven days at the MACC headquarters. He is expected to be released on Wednesday. The CEO of the fund was also detained in connection with the same investigation, along with seven others who were suspected to be involved in corruption. In the report, the royal commission outlined questionable accounting practices, weak oversight and large investment subsidies which showed the fund would have recorded a net loss of 1.4 billion ringgit (US$350,000) rather than the 3.4 billion ringgit profit it showed in that period. The finding was submitted to the king in August 2022 but remained unreleased until it was declassified just three days before the Negeri Sembilan state election. Last Saturday, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said investigations on issues raised in the report would continue, assuring people that the country should not suffer further losses. “If no action is taken, the country will suffer losses, but when action is taken, I get criticised. I don’t understand,” he told reporters in Penang. “I said 12 billion ringgit was lost. How was it lost? When was it lost? Investigate who was responsible for the loss.” The commission launched the inquiry in 2021 to examine the management and operations of the state-run haj pilgrim funds board from 2014 to 2022 after independent reviews flagged governance concerns. Tabung Haji was established in 1963 to help Muslims save and invest for their haj pilgrimage to Mecca. It is one of the country’s largest Islamic financial institutions, playing a central role in organising Malaysia’s annual haj pilgrimage. Over 63 per cent of the Malaysian population – 21.8 million of the current 34.4 million – are Muslims.

title: Chinese carmakers eye full hybrid market; BYD posts US$1.2 billion profit: 7 EV reads
description: From Tesla recalling 3 million cars in China to carmakers being told to focus on quality, here are seven EV stories you may have missed.
content: We have put together stories from our coverage on electric and new energy vehicles from the past two weeks to help you stay informed. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. After gaining EV sway, Chinese carmakers eye full hybrid market Chinese carmakers, already at the vanguard of electric vehicle (EV) technology and production, are looking to make a dent in international marques’ full-hybrid vehicle stronghold as they continue to disrupt the global car industry’s pecking order. 2. Chinese authorities tell carmakers to focus on quality, not tech offerings China’s shrinking car market has received another reality check as regulators step in to police the hi-tech offerings that carmakers use to drive sales. 3. BYD posts US$1.2 billion profit in second quarter on surging global demand China’s electric vehicle (EV) giant BYD saw its earnings jump 30 per cent in the three months from April to June, ending a five-quarter losing streak as buoyant overseas sales and premium models enhanced its net margin and profitability. 4. Writing the rulebook? China to steer world’s first solid-state battery standards A Chinese-proposed international standard for automotive solid-state batteries has been approved as a new work item by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) – marking the first of its kind for the advanced power systems and the nation’s latest effort to shape rules in emerging industries. 5. Tesla forced to recall record 3 million cars in China over door-handle issue Tesla has issued the largest-ever product recall in mainland China’s electric vehicle (EV) market, as Elon Musk’s firm pledges to fix a door-handle issue affecting nearly 3 million cars. 6. China’s new traffic safety law set to clarify liability for fully automated cars Beijing could soon hold carmakers legally responsible for traffic violations when autonomous driving systems are in use, marking an important step towards clearing regulatory hurdles to wider commercialisation. 7. Parts shortage piles pressure on Chinese carmakers racing to boost intelligence Chinese smart vehicle makers have been hit by another setback as a global components shortage collides with surging prices of raw materials, driven by the artificial intelligence boom.

title: 9 children, 5 others injured after 2 buses collide at Hong Kong primary school
description: Thirteen people sent to hospital, including driver of one of the buses, after accident at Good Hope Primary School cum Kindergarten in Ngau Chi Wan.
content: Fourteen people, including nine children, have been injured in a collision involving two school buses at a Hong Kong girls’ primary school. The Fire Services Department said on Wednesday that it dispatched 10 ambulances to handle the accident at 1.26pm at Good Hope Primary School cum Kindergarten, located at No 381 Jat’s Incline in Ngau Chi Wan. Eight of the 14 injured people were sent to United Christian Hospital in Kwun Tong for treatment, while another five were admitted to Kwong Wah Hospital in Yau Ma Tei. One person was classified as a red case under the department’s casualty triage system, meaning that immediate on-site treatment was required. A second was classified as yellow, meaning the victim sustained serious and potentially life-threatening injuries, but the person’s condition was not expected to deteriorate significantly over the coming few hours. The others were classified as green cases, denoting minor injuries. Nine children, one of the bus drivers, a bus escort and three other school staff were among the injured, according to police. The injured driver sustained injuries to his foot, including bleeding.

title: As oil tops US$97, US-Iran war escalation has markets bracing for supply risks
description: Fresh military strikes in the Middle East have sent energy prices surging, leaving traders to grapple with renewed volatility.
content: An overnight escalation in hostilities between the United States and Iran pushed global oil benchmark Brent futures above US$97 a barrel at one point on Wednesday, marking their highest intraday level since early June – though analysts said prices are unlikely to match the peak seen earlier this year. The latest surge followed fresh US air strikes on Iranian targets on Tuesday, prompting retaliatory strikes by Tehran. Iran launched missiles and drones at sites across the region and targeted US-linked assets in Jordan, according to an Associated Press report on Wednesday. CNN also reported on Tuesday that Iranian state broadcaster IRIB had cited multiple explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy-shipping chokepoints. After the US Central Command announced the attacks on social media on Tuesday, Brent crude climbed more than 5 per cent to about US$95 a barrel, and continued to trade in volatile fashion around that level during Wednesday’s Asian session. “Traders are bracing for further supply disruptions. In the near term, we see no practical path towards a resolution between the US and Iran, so hostilities are set to persist. That will keep global crude prices well-supported,” said Yan Lili, an analyst at Zhejiang-based Xinhu Futures. Beyond the geopolitical risk premium, Zhao Xuyi, an analyst at Shanghai-based Guotai Junan Futures, said shipping represented “an even more critical factor underpinning oil prices”. Reuters reported on Tuesday that two supertankers loaded with Saudi crude were struck by unknown projectiles in near-simultaneous incidents as they sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz late Monday. Both tankers were carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi crude. “The strikes will lend additional support to high crude prices by eroding shipowners’ willingness to send vessels through this corridor. Should the Red Sea crisis drag on, Middle East crude exports could retreat to subdued levels,” Zhao said. US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would face renewed US strikes at “a much harder and higher level” if it retaliated, shortly after American forces announced the attacks. Despite the risks, analysts said they did not expect crude prices to revisit March’s intraday peak of over US$119 a barrel, citing mounting domestic political pressures on Trump. Meanwhile, the yield on the 10-year Treasury note – which measures the annual compensation investors demand for lending to the US government over a decade-long horizon – climbed to over 4.8 per cent on Wednesday, hitting its highest level since January 2025. That suggests ordinary consumers in the US could face higher borrowing costs in the coming weeks and months. “High oil prices are expected to once again stoke US inflation. With the US midterm elections looming, I do not expect these growing hostilities to persist for a prolonged period. Investors should be cautious about the Taco trade,” said Zhao of Guotai Junan Futures. Taco is a Wall Street acronym that stands for “Trump always chickens out”, referring to the view that the US president tends to back away from aggressive threats when the market comes under pressure. The intensifying US-Iran conflict has also raised market expectations for a possible quarter-percentage-point increase in the federal funds rate target range at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting scheduled for September 16. The Federal Reserve kept its target range at 3.50 per cent to 3.75 per cent at its July gathering. According to the CME FedWatch Tool – which derives odds from federal-funds futures pricing – the implied probability of such an increase stood at 70.2 per cent as of Wednesday afternoon, up from 65.43 per cent on Monday. Data from the US Bureau of Economic Analysis showed that the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index – the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge – rose 3.7 per cent year on year in July. The headline gauge has now run above the central bank’s 2 per cent inflation target for 65 consecutive months.

title: China’s AMEC unveils 6 chip-making machines in a day, boosting self-reliance ambitions
description: A rapid R&D drive is powering the firm’s transition beyond its core business.
content: Chinese chip equipment giant Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment (AMEC) has unveiled six new machines – at different stages of commercialisation – in a single day as the company accelerates research and development to feed soaring local demand driven by Beijing’s self-reliance push. The new line-up, announced at an industry conference in Wuxi on Tuesday, spans several steps in chip production, including etching tools that carve microscopic patterns into wafers, deposition systems that build ultra-thin layers of material and the complex equipment used to make silicon-carbide power chips. Unveiling six tools simultaneously marks a notable shift for AMEC as it accelerates its transformation from an etching specialist to an all-around semiconductor equipment firm. Four of the six new products are deposition tools. The global etching and deposition markets are dominated by US and Japanese giants like Lam Research, Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron. During an investor briefing last month, AMEC said it had cut its product development cycle from three to five years down to two years or less. The company poured 2.04 billion yuan (US$303.5 million) into research and development in the first half of the year – a 36.9 per cent year-on-year surge representing 30.5 per cent of its total revenue. It currently has more than 20 new machines under development across six equipment categories. Tuesday’s announcement was AMEC’s second large batch of product releases in six months, following the unveiling of four new machines at Semicon China in March. AMEC has developed 54 types of semiconductor equipment, including 26 etching machines and 24 thin-film deposition tools, as well as chemical mechanical polishing and metrology equipment. Its products now cover more than 30 per cent of front-end semiconductor equipment categories. Over the next five years, company chairman Gerald Yin Zhiyao said in an earnings forecast last month, AMEC aims to expand its coverage to more than 60 per cent of the high-end integrated-circuit equipment market through internal development and acquisitions. It is also expanding manufacturing capacity. AMEC currently has about 600,000 square metres of factory space and plans to increase that to 900,000 square metres over the next five years, with new facilities under development in Shanghai’s Lingang area, Guangzhou and Chengdu. The expansion comes as Chinese equipment makers collectively gain ground amid Beijing’s push for semiconductor self-sufficiency and increased spending by domestic chipmakers. Other domestic equipment makers have also stepped up product announcements. Piotech unveiled at least seven new machines at Semicon China this year, while Naura Technology Group introduced at least five new tools in the first half of the year. Bernstein Research estimated that Chinese suppliers accounted for about 31 per cent of China’s dry-etch equipment market and 27 per cent of deposition equipment in 2025. AMEC and Naura Technology are already the two dominant, domestic dry-etch suppliers, while AMEC has been expanding rapidly into deposition products. The shift is part of a broader effort by Chinese toolmakers to move beyond breakthroughs in individual machines and build more comprehensive product portfolios. In a report last month, Goldman Sachs said China’s semiconductor equipment industry was expanding from etching and deposition into more advanced models, such as high-aspect-ratio etchers and atomic-layer deposition systems, as well as new categories including inspection and metrology equipment. The investment bank expected Chinese suppliers to account for 38 per cent of wafer-fabrication equipment revenue in China by 2028, up from 31 per cent in 2026.

title: Philippine fast-food giant Jollibee picks Hong Kong over New York for spin-off’s listing
description: Company’s plan to list international arm in Hong Kong underscores city’s IPO diversification drive.
content: The parent company of Philippine fast-food giant Jollibee plans to spin off and list its international operations in Hong Kong instead of New York in a strong endorsement of the city’s initial public offering (IPO) diversification efforts. Jollibee Foods Corp (JFC) said in January that it intended to list its overseas arm, Jollibee Foods Corporation International (JFCI), in the United States. The company has now selected Hong Kong as its listing destination. “Hong Kong offers the market depth and investor relevance to support JFCI’s long-term ambitions and is best positioned to recognise the value of its distinctive business profile and growth potential,” the company said on Tuesday. JFC added that bourse operator Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) also provided access to a broad base of global and regional investors, making it well suited to support a business aiming to expand beyond Asia, including continued growth in North America. The company said these characteristics provide a strong platform for JFCI as it seeks to build a leading global food and beverage business with roots in the Philippines. More than 150 Southeast Asian companies are currently listed in Hong Kong, raising more than US$4.3 billion in total, making the city the preferred overseas IPO hub for the region, HKEX CEO Bonnie Chan Yiting said in April. She added in August that about 10 foreign companies had already applied to list in Hong Kong. JFCI operates fast-food chains across Asia, including Hong Kong’s Michelin-rated restaurant chain Tim Ho Wan, known for its signature baked barbecue pork buns. It delivered strong double-digit growth in 2025, with segment revenues reaching 126.8 billion pesos (US$2 billion) – a 27 per cent year-on-year increase – driven by strong momentum in Vietnam, the company’s largest overseas market by store count, according to its annual report. Founded in 1975, JFC has aggressively expanded abroad to boost its global brand recognition. Its latest move was the full acquisition in February of All Day Fresh, a Korea-headquartered hotpot and all-you-can-eat restaurant brand. By the end of 2025, JFC’s global footprint had expanded to 10,341 stores across 33 countries, including China, the US and South Korea, according to its annual report. More than 6,850 stores were located overseas.

title: Chinese research team may have cracked secret to crossbreeding Asian and African rice
description: Scientists identified three genes that make it hard to combine the two varieties – and also highlighted a possible solution.
content: Chinese scientists have identified a genetic barrier that makes it hard to crossbreed African and Asian rice varieties – a discovery that could lay the foundations for creating high-yielding hybrids. While both Asian and African cultivated rice varieties have distinct strengths, crossing them often produces offspring with sterile pollen and low yields. A research team has now identified three genes that act as a barrier to reproduction – and also a possible way round the problem. “This discovery provides an important theoretical foundation and valuable genetic resources for breaking the reproductive barrier between rice species and breeding new, ultra-high-yielding hybrid rice varieties,” the official China Science Daily reported last Friday. Such Asian-African crosses “could potentially increase yields by more than 10 per cent compared with existing Asian hybrid rice varieties”, one of the authors of the study told the newspaper. The research, conducted by a team led by Wan Jianmin at Nanjing Agricultural University’s State Key Laboratory for Crop Genetics and Germplasm Enhancement and Utilisation, was published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on 28 August. African and Asian rice are the only two species out of the 24 in the Oryza genus that have been domesticated to produce food for humans. Asian rice offers high yields and excellent eating quality, making it a global staple. Meanwhile, African rice is generally lower-yielding but has other valuable traits, including the ability to tolerate high temperatures, drought and poor soils, alongside a natural resistance to various pests and diseases. Scientists hope crossing the two will result in new varieties that combine high productivity with greater resilience. Following years of research, the Chinese study identified a genetic barrier to crossbreeding these species that lies within one rice chromosome. When the two species are crossed, a genomic region known as RHS3 aborts around half the first-generation pollen grains created, while the others develop normally. They identified three genes behind this process, which they named mao, dun and jia – or spear, shield and armour. African cultivated rice has the complete spear-shield-armour system, but Asian cultivated rice has only the armour gene. In hybrid offspring, the team found, pollen grains received different gene combinations. Roughly half inherited the complete three-gene system and developed normally, while the other half inherited only the armour, aborted and died. He Xiaodong, a doctoral student at the university and co-first author of the paper, said that a protein encoded by the spear – known formally as ORF10 – damaged the mitochondria supplying energy to rice cells, killing the pollen. However, protein from the shield (ORF16) binds to the spear, neutralising its toxicity, while the armour gene (ORF4) works alongside the shield to send the neutralised spear to a cellular “recycling centre”. Crucially, the research team identified one genetic resource, known as a germplasm, that is broadly compatible with both varieties and which effectively stops the spear’s activities. When crossed with both Asian and African rice, this is enough to largely overcome the drop in fertility. However, the team acknowledged that their research only provided a theoretical foundation for creating new hybrids, adding that further work was needed to create suitable agricultural materials and address issues such as grain quality and pest resistance. China already has some of the highest rice yields in the world – roughly 7.2 tonnes per hectare (6,400lbs per acre) – but is investing heavily in research aimed at boosting crop production as part of its efforts to improve food security. Recent developments include a study in the journal Vita about a new hybrid rice variety that can be cloned with almost 99 per cent efficiency, allowing farmers to replant harvested seeds without losing the crop’s high yield and other desirable traits. Meanwhile, a hybrid wheat variety known as Jingmai 189 reportedly achieved nearly double the national average yield in a trial in the Taklamakan Desert.

title: Southeast Asia’s scam gangs regroup after Cambodia’s purge
description: Dislodged from Cambodian compounds, cyberscam cartels have been setting up shop in Laos, Myanmar and even Malaysia.
content: Cambodia says it has flushed out a scam industry estimated to have stolen tens of billions of US dollars last year alone, but a string of arrests in recent days suggests the gangs behind it may have simply changed address. Scam centres proliferated across Cambodia during the pandemic, when hundreds of thousands of jobless young people were pulled into defunct casino complexes to target victims worldwide with bogus romance, cryptocurrency and investment frauds. Chinese criminal networks found an easy foothold in a country with a reputation for entrenched corruption, but that foothold brought intense pressure from Beijing, and later Washington, to dismantle the shadowy trade. The sector operated largely in the open despite government denials of complicity or profit. It also triggered a human trafficking crisis, with tens – perhaps hundreds – of thousands forced to work in scam compounds. In July, the United Nation’s Office on Drugs and Crime estimated that scam-related losses across the Asia-Pacific reached between US$88 billion and US$114 billion in 2025 alone, a sum that it said “even at the low end, outstrips the GDP of several countries in the region”. For comparison, Cambodia’s gross domestic product in 2025 was around US$50 billion, while Myanmar’s stood at roughly US$82 billion, according to World Bank estimates. Displaced, not destroyed Cambodia’s Information Ministry said in February that more than 250 scam sites had been closed down as its crackdown gathered pace, with 48,000 foreign nationals deported. By the end of last month, large-scale scam activities had “been brought fully under control”, according to Chhay Sinarith, the minister overseeing the anti-scam drive. “There are currently no online scam compounds remaining in the country,” he said on Friday after a meeting with diplomats the day before. Yet advocates are sceptical, telling This Week in Asia that many scam bosses had simply relocated to harder-to-detect condominiums and hotels within Cambodia, or fled to the lawless border areas of Myanmar, special economic zones of Laos or further south into Malaysia. “We have received reports indicating that approximately 10,000 to 20,000 foreigners may have been transferred from Cambodia to Myanmar following the crackdown,” said Jay Kritiya, a coordinator at the Civil Society Network for Human Trafficking Victim Assistance (CSNHTV). The NGO, which works to rescue trafficking victims, estimates that more than 13,700 people from countries as diverse as India and Ethiopia remain trapped in Myanmar’s scam compounds. “Victims who were rescued reported that they were transferred and resold from Cambodia to Myanmar,” Jay said. Further evidence of scam gang migration has also surfaced. On Saturday, Thai highway police in the southern province of Chumphon stopped a suspicious van carrying five Chinese nationals bound for Malaysia. Two had passports without valid entry stamps, while the other three carried no travel documents at all. According to the police, the men admitted “they had crossed from Cambodia into Thailand via illegal natural border crossings, intending to travel onwards to Malaysia”. Investigators said they were now tracing the group’s links to call centres “and related online fraud networks”. Meanwhile, frontier areas of Myanmar controlled by ethnic armed groups and government-allied militias continue to shelter scam operations that traffic people into forced labour. Last week, Thai police in Kamphaeng Phet province, near the Myanmar border, rescued a Chinese woman who had apparently been kidnapped in Bangkok and was being trafficked across the frontier when the car she was travelling in was stopped for inspection. “The driver rolled down the window … we observed four men: two in the front and two in the back,” Police Major Chakkaphet Khrueacha of Mueang Kamphaeng Phet Police Station told reporters. “In the middle of the back seat, a woman was covered with a blanket while the men tried to shield her from view.” The woman screamed for help, but the driver reportedly drove off in an attempt to evade the police. “When they reached the intersection, the occupants pushed the woman out of the vehicle and sped off,” Chakkaphet said. Later reports suggested the woman had opened the door herself to escape. NGOs working to rescue victims from Myanmar’s scam compounds say the crackdowns have been largely cosmetic, merely pushing operations into new areas that stretch along the long border with Thailand. CSNHTV said last month that it had located at least eight scam compounds in territory controlled by the Karen National Army, whose warlord leader Saw Chit Thu is under US sanctions for running scam centres. The group has lobbied authorities to investigate evidence provided by rescued scam compound victims to build criminal cases against the bigger criminal entities behind the industry. “We need to move from case-by-case rescue to network-level intervention,” Jay said. “That means identifying the locations and people trapped inside the compounds, securing their rescue, identifying and prosecuting the perpetrators, freezing and seizing criminal assets, dismantling the networks and their support structures and preventing the same operators from simply relocating or recruiting new victims.” In a report published on August 6, CSNHTV said it had recorded more than 13,670 people trapped in cyber scam compounds controlled by various armed factions along the Myanmar-Thai border including Chinese, Indian, Ethiopian and Filipino victims. Laos has also emerged as a burgeoning scam hub, with security experts at the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and elsewhere saying that criminal networks increasingly embed themselves in the country’s slew of lightly policed special economic zones, many of which are run by Chinese investors. The impoverished, landlocked country has arrested some 6,200 people linked to cybercrime this year alone, according to the Laotian Times newspaper, many of them Chinese and Thai nationals. One of the larger raids came in early August, when police detained more than 260 people at the Thatluang Special Economic Zone, a gleaming new expanse of high-rise condominiums and Chinese-run businesses built on the outskirts of Vientiane.

title: China widens access to overseas stocks, handing out nearly US$7b in QDII quotas
description: Expansion aims to ease tight supply of cross-border investment products following crackdown on non-compliant offshore investments.
content: Beijing’s recent granting of new outbound investment allocations will help ease tight supply of cross-border investment products, including those invested in US securities, as Chinese investors look globally for diversification, according to analysts. The foreign-exchange regulator granted US$6.84 billion of qualified domestic institutional investor (QDII) quotas to mutual-fund firms, insurers and banks’ wealth-management units in the latest round of approvals by the end of August, according to data released by the State Administration of Foreign Exchange. Eighteen money managers, including China Asset Management and GF Fund Management, received allocations of US$100 million each, while more than 20 banks’ wealth-management arms were granted quotas for the first time. Observers said the move shows that policymakers, after tightening scrutiny over non-compliant offshore assets, are making an effort to open up legitimate investment venues amid increasing demand for diversification. “The expansion will help to ease tight supply of cross-border investment products and meet real and legal household demand for overseas asset allocations,” said Wu Jing, an analyst at China Galaxy Securities. “The release of quotas will add to product supply and rein in unreasonable premiums.” The expansion fulfils the foreign-exchange regulator’s pledge in July to increase allocations of overseas investments to meet rising demand from Chinese investors, who are struggling with a prolonged decline in home prices and falling returns from fixed-income assets. Demand for overseas financial products offered through official channels increased after Beijing cracked down on illegal offshore stock accounts opened by Chinese investors. In addition to the Stock Connect programme that allows mainland residents to invest in Hong Kong stocks, QDII is the most popular channel for accessing foreign assets. It allows financial institutions to offer domestic investors fund products, mostly targeting overseas stocks, after getting foreign-currency quotas from the government. Mainland mutual-fund firms have 337 QDII funds under their management, with the investments ranging from US and Hong Kong stocks to bonds and commodities, according to financial data provider Wind. The best performer this year is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) investing in South Korea’s semiconductor stocks, logging a 76 per cent gain. The worst-performing funds are those targeting Hong Kong-listed tech stocks, with an average loss of nearly 30 per cent. With new quotas in hand, some fund-management firms are loosening restrictions on subscriptions and launching new products. China Universal Asset Management increased the daily cap for its QDII fund tied to global medical stocks to 80,000 yuan (US$11,900) from 2,000 yuan starting on Wednesday. Fullgoal Fund Management kicked off the sale of a new ETF tracking the Hang Seng Tech Index on Tuesday. An increase in product supply may curb speculative trading of QDII funds on the secondary market. Such funds have frequently traded at substantial premiums to net asset values this year, triggering trading suspensions as warnings of investment risks. By the end of August, China had approved a total of US$183 billion in QDII quotas for 196 financial institutions since the start of the programme in 2006, according to the official data.

title: Tencent’s Hy4 model gains in open-source AI rankings after ecosystem-driven training
description: On the DeepSWE benchmark, the Hy4 preview scored 64.3, surpassing Alibaba’s Qwen-3.8 Max at 56.6 and DeepSeek-V4 Pro at 62.7.
content: Tencent Holdings’ use of its vast product ecosystem to train its new Hy4 preview model gives it an edge in developing AI agents and brings its flagship model suite back into the top tier of open-source offerings, according to analysts. The Chinese tech giant’s “differentiated product-plus-model strategy”, where preview models were first deployed across Tencent’s suite of products, enabled it to collect user data before feeding the information back into subsequent rounds of training, Goldman Sachs analysts said in a research note on Monday. “We view this closed-loop approach as particularly relevant for productivity and coding workloads, where real-world task trajectories, user interactions and evaluation signals drive model differentiation in the agentic AI era,” said the analysts led by Goldman’s head of Asia internet research Ronald Keung. They added that the Hy4 preview brought Tencent’s Hunyuan series back to the forefront of open-source models, with notable gains in coding capabilities over Hy3. Released on Friday, Hy4 preview ranked eighth globally on Tuesday on Code Arena’s WebDev leaderboard – a real-time competition evaluating large language models on real-world coding tasks – just behind Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and outperforming Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen 3.8-Flash-Next in ninth place. By comparison, Tencent’s previous generation, Hy3, ranked 34th on the same benchmark on Tuesday. On the DeepSWE benchmark, which tests software engineering capabilities, the Hy4 preview scored 64.3, surpassing Alibaba’s Qwen-3.8 Max at 56.6 and DeepSeek-V4 Pro at 62.7. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. Hy4 represented “another big step up” for Tencent as it closed the gap with leading domestic AI developers, HSBC analysts Charlene Liu and Ritchie Sun wrote in a research note on Monday. The bank attributed the model’s progress to high-quality training data sets co-created with internal domain experts across software engineering, gaming, finance and security. Hy4 was co-designed to power Tencent’s WorkBuddy – a workplace agent built to execute complex tasks rather than simply answer queries. The model preview showed early signs of a recursive self-improvement loop, where an AI system uses its own generated outputs to continually refine and train itself without human intervention, according to the analysts. However, HSBC cautioned that the model took longer than expected to reason through complex tasks and tended to over-verify its own work, though post-training and user feedback could resolve these issues over time. The Hy4 preview marks a significant leap in scale, featuring 770 billion parameters – a 2.6-fold increase over Hy3’s 295 billion parameters – and a context window that quadruples to 1 million tokens, up from 256,000. Despite its expanded size, analysts from both banks noted the attractive cost efficiency of the model. On Monday, Tencent said it had successfully compressed the full 1.5-terabyte Hy4 preview into a lightweight 214-gigabyte version. The compression drastically lowered hardware requirements for on-device deployment while retaining performance on standard tasks, the company said. Tencent last month reported a nearly threefold surge in second-quarter capital expenditure to 52.8 billion yuan (US$7.8 billion) – a 176 per cent year-on-year increase – driven by aggressive investments in AI infrastructure and core model development. The heavy AI push helped drive better-than-expected top-line results. Second-quarter revenue rose 11 per cent year on year to 204.8 billion yuan, beating average analyst estimates of 202.8 billion yuan compiled by Bloomberg. The Shenzhen-based giant, which operates the world’s largest video game business by revenue and China’s dominant social network WeChat, said in its earnings release that the full commercial iteration of the Hy4 series would launch later this year.

title: Exclusive: The Boar brings authentic British pub experience to Hong Kong’s Central
description: British pubs, once common across the city, have dwindled in the past decade, but there’s a new opening hoping to revive the tradition.
content: If a good pint is what you’re after, Matt Richardson may have a solution. As one of the brains behind The Boar, a new British public house (where the shortened form and better-known term, “pub”, comes from) and restaurant in Central, he has been working to bring an authentic watering-hole experience to Hong Kong – even travelling to Ireland to perfect the Guinness pour in time for the establishment’s September 1 opening. “I’m going to Dublin in two weeks, just to study it,” Richardson tells me about his late-August plans to visit the Guinness Storehouse. We’re sitting inside his office on Elgin Street, just one step from his latest venture. “Between me going right to the source and us [ensuring] that we’ve got the best beer lines, coolers and cleanliness … that’s the best we can do, that’s what makes a great Guinness. Every little bit counts, because the liquid in the barrel is not even the main element.” Originally from Milton Keynes, northwest of London, Richardson has kept himself busy in the nine years he’s been in Hong Kong. He is the founder and managing director of Big Top Hospitality, the group behind Australian restobar Bourke’s, American-style saloon Honky Tonks Tavern, Mediterranean seaside terrace Terracotta Lamma, fresh pasta bar Twist in Sheung Wan, and bagel joint and delicatessen Mendel’s. With five restaurants already in his portfolio, the British restaurateur is finally opening something that connects him to his roots, but with a name that pays homage to his time in both Hong Kong and Britain. “Boars are the largest land mammals in Hong Kong, but you can also find them all around the UK,” explains Richardson. “Here, they’re kind of loved, aren’t they? You walk up The Peak, and people are super excited to see a little family of boars walking around. I quite enjoy it.” Behind the pass, he has brought on two British chefs with fine-dining pedigrees: executive chef Graham Long, who has worked in Michelin-rated kitchens across London and launched culinary concepts for luxury hotels in Hong Kong. Day-to-day kitchen operations are run by head chef Jake Bennett, who cut his teeth at several Simon Rogan restaurants, including three-Michelin-star L’Enclume in Britain’s Lake District. Most recently, he was at The Baker and The Bottleman, in Wan Chai. “I jumped on board as soon as I found out [Richardson was opening a pub],” says Long. He recalls how the pair began brainstorming the making of The Boar over a few pints. “I’ve always felt that pubs were missing in Hong Kong to a degree. You’d think there would be more, given Hong Kong’s history and the expat community that’s here.” Despite its name, however, the pub and dining room will not be serving wild boar. In Hong Kong, it’s illegal to kill or capture the animal. In Britain, they were hunted to extinction several hundred years ago, before being reintroduced into the ecosystem in recent decades by farms. “I’ve cooked it professionally before. It’s not that common any more, but we used to get it from our game dealer. I actually prefer normal pork, to be honest, but it’s nice,” Long admits. So, if boar is not on the menu, what is? Classic pub grub, of course, including Welsh rarebit, sticky toffee pudding and pork cheek and lobster pie, as well as courses that speak to British sensibilities, such as Eton mess and coronation chicken salad. With both chefs coming from haute-cuisine backgrounds, the dishes reflect their technical discipline. “We want to make the best version of everything. Yes, we’re going to do fish and chips, but we want to make sure it’s the best fish and chips we can possibly do,” Long explains. As for their Scotch eggs, these will be made with British sausage meat, black pudding and Japanese eggs, then fried to order. “You know, nothing beats a Scotch egg. Hopefully, nothing will beat our Scotch egg,” says Long. The Boar will offer two menus, with “downstairs” serving casual bites such as prawn cocktail toast, the signature BLT sandwich, Guinness and treacle bread with salted English butter, broccoli and Stichelton tart, and more, while “upstairs” hosts a more formal dining format, with celeriac and mushroom Wellington, roasted turbot chop, baked Chilean sea bass and chargrilled rib-eye steak to look forward to. (Sunday roasts are in the works, too.) “It’s where we get to have a little bit more fun, be a bit more chef-y, have a few more luxury ingredients and a more sit-down experience,” says Long. One of the highlights of the upstairs menu is the roasted duck, dry-aged for two weeks in-house – no short cuts, all processed by the Boar team – and served with buttered turnips, carrots, a sauce of port and citrus, and toller’s pie, a play on the timeless shepherd’s pie in reference to the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a medium-sized gun-dog breed traditionally trained by hunters to find, flush out and retrieve shot game. Moving into Flaming Frango’s old space on Elgin Street, the two-storey location, with an expansive ground floor and quirky structural nooks, has just the right bones to make it feel like a British pub – but Richardson has a fresher take in mind. “We want it to feel more like a modern pub, because we feel it would be unjust to try and transport something you’d find from the laneways in London [to Hong Kong] – that would be too theatrical,” says Richardson. Instead, he explains he was inspired by his favourite pub, The Pelican, a Michelin Bib Gourmand spot in London’s Notting Hill neighbourhood. “It’s a totally different experience from what people might know of the pub world, but the aesthetics, the feel, is that,” he says. “So, downstairs, think brighter colours and nice wood textures, but lots of nods to the things you might recognise from a pub back home, like the way we do the edgings on the tables and footrests and textures. And then when you move upstairs, this will have a different feel – more green, a bit more opulent.” For Long and Richardson, The Boar is more than just another restaurant opening. “I spent most of my adult life in London and, generally, when I wasn’t working in a kitchen, I was in a pub,” recalls Long, whose time in the city included a stint at two-Michelin-star Pied à Terre, then helmed by Shane Osborn. “Wherever you grow up, everyone has their local pub,” Long says. “[A pub is] shaped by the community that it’s in.” Richardson agrees: “When I’m back home [in Britain, the go-to pub is] just wherever my friends are.” Creating that sense of community here in Hong Kong – where both restaurateur and chef have settled, and for not an insignificant amount of time – is top of their minds when it comes to shaping the destination. “We let the food, the drinks and the genuine hospitality speak for themselves,” says Richardson, adding that every visit to The Boar “feels like coming home”.

title: CityU investigates after clip shows man carrying woman in bra, shorts at disco night
description: Student society behind event apologises for incident and acknowledges that some participants behaved inappropriately.
content: Hong Kong’s City University (CityU) has launched an investigation after a video surfaced showing a half-naked man carrying a woman wearing only a bra and shorts during a student-led orientation event. The university issued a statement on Wednesday stressing “zero tolerance” of improper conduct after the clip appeared online showing the behaviour during a disco-themed party. The clip has since been removed from Instagram, where it was first posted, but continues to circulate elsewhere on social media. The event’s organiser – the management sciences society under the CityU Students’ Union – apologised for the incident and acknowledged that some participants had behaved inappropriately.
