The society said the incident had taken place on the evening of August 27, the first day of its three-day orientation programme. “Our members urged and reminded participants to avoid misconduct during the activity, but we failed to prevent the acts in a timely manner,” it said in a statement posted on social media. “We bear full responsibility for failing to manage and monitor the event scene well.” The society said it would cooperate with the investigation by the Students’ Union and the university, adding that it was willing to accept disciplinary arrangements made according to established procedures. At a special meeting on Wednesday, the Students’ Union Council passed a no-confidence motion that dissolved the society’s executive committee. The university expressed “grave concern” over the “serious mismanagement and inappropriate behaviour by certain individuals” at the event. “We are also deeply concerned about the unnecessary disturbance experienced by participating students. A student discipline panel has been established without delay,” it said. CityU added that the university maintained a “zero-tolerance” policy towards any improper conduct and would take disciplinary action according to the seriousness of the incident. “The purpose of orientation activities is to help new students understand university life and prepare for their academic studies and growth,” it said. “Any conduct that deviates from this purpose, undermines student dignity or damages campus culture will not be tolerated.” The university cited its policy requiring all organisations hosting orientation activities to undergo anti-sexual harassment training and comply with institutional guidelines. According to the Students’ Union website, the management sciences society serves undergraduates studying business decision analytics and global operations management. Public concern over university orientation activities has risen in recent years following media reports of suspected sexual harassment during such events. In 2023, a second-year student at the University of Hong Kong was arrested and charged with groping a first-year student at an orientation event, but was later acquitted by a court. There were also reports that some students played kissing games during a Lingnan University orientation event, while allegations of rape and voyeurism arose at an event held by the Education University of Hong Kong in the same year.

title: Hidden Japanese omakase, ‘excellent’ Cantonese: a Hong Kong bartender’s restaurant picks
description: Carna by Dario Cecchini head bartender Jason Yu shares where he enjoys steak, pasta, ‘incredibly personal’ omakase and no-fuss Cantonese food.
content: Jason Yu is the head bartender at Carna by Dario Cecchini at the Mondrian Hong Kong hotel and creator of the drinks behind its cocktail pairing dinners. He spoke to Andrew Sun. When it comes to food, I value balance, intention and craft. I like dishes where the seasoning, aroma, texture and finish all work together. It does not have to be complicated or fine dining. I am often most drawn to home-made or handcrafted dishes with top ingredients because they usually carry a sense of care and a personal story. A lot of that came from my grandmother’s cooking. She had a special soy sauce blend for her steamed fish. She also cooked with dried mandarin peel or made tea with it, blending peels of different ages to create layers of aroma and depth. She even created sweet, sour, aromatic plum wine infused with family memories. Those experiences shaped how I create cocktails today, especially my interest in balance, infusions and handcrafted elements that carry emotion. On days off, honestly, I usually prefer to cook at home. But if I go out for dinner, I like L’Atlantis (Golden Beach, 18.5 miles, Castle Peak Road, Tuen Mun. Tel: 2618 9866). I enjoy the casual and peaceful atmosphere and simple steaks or pasta. It feels removed from the city, which is perfect for a day off. The staff are also incredibly hospitable. I would take new visitors to Hong Kong to Chi Shing Restaurant (1/F, 71 Chatham Road South, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 6230 9498), a humble and sincere Cantonese restaurant that consistently serves excellent food. The chef, Chi Gor, was formerly with Forum Restaurant on Hong Kong Island. Chi Shing has a strong Cantonese foundation, but the atmosphere remains relaxed and down-to-earth. For me, this represents a true Hong Kong dining experience – proper food, warm hospitality and no unnecessary fuss. For a splurge meal, I would choose Open Meal (Shop 118, 1/F, Lee Bo Shopping Centre, 3 Tsing Ho Square, Tuen Mun. Tel: 6087 9075). It is a hidden Japanese restaurant inside an old commercial building. There are only a few seats, so the experience feels incredibly personal. It is reservation-only and does tailor-made omakase menus. The chef also remembers my preferences but always recommends new dishes based on what he knows I enjoy, so every visit is a new experience. I usually take one holiday a year, travelling around Europe for food. I absolutely loved my last trip to Seville, Spain. I visited a place called Espacio Eslava (Calle Eslava, 3, Casco Antiguo, Seville. Tel: +34 954 90 65 68) three times during the trip. It has the best octopus ever and the house wine, Bodega Bideona Laderas Tempranillo, was superb. The price was very reasonable. Our new cocktail pairing dinner initiative at Carna by Dario Cecchini (39/F, Mondrian, 8A Hart Avenue, Tsim Sha Tsui. Tel: 3550 0339) aims to make dining more playful, approachable and creative. The next dinner is scheduled for September 17. My process starts with the kitchen, studying the flavour, texture and structure of each dish. I then create a cocktail that helps the dish shine. It gives me new dimensions to work with: acidity, bitterness, sweetness, aroma, texture and temperature. The drinks can elevate flavours, refresh the palate or add another layer to the experience without overpowering the food.

title: US journalist jailed for 2 years for working as a Chinese agent
description: Thomas Weir Pauken II worked for state media in Beijing and admitted to working at the direction of people tied to China’s intelligence services.
content: An American journalist who lived in Beijing, worked for Chinese state media and pleaded guilty to acting as an agent for Beijing was sentenced on Tuesday to two years in federal prison. Thomas Weir Pauken II, 51, was also sentenced to three years of supervised release and barred from overseas travel during that period, according to the US Justice Department. He also used the alias Tom McGregor. His father, Thomas Pauken, chaired the Texas Republican Party in the 1990s and later ran for governor. Pauken has been in custody since his arrest in February, and he admitted in June to acting as an agent of China in the US without notifying the attorney general, as required under federal law. In a social media post on Tuesday, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said that from at least 2019 until February 2026 Pauken “operated at the direction and control of people he knew worked for the PRC’s Ministry of State Security (MSS)”. The bureau added that he recruited potential intelligence assets, issued taskings, sent reports to MSS contacts, received at least US$100,000, and made several trips from China to the US to meet people who could provide information to him, and ultimately to Chinese intelligence. Assistant attorney general for national security John A. Eisenberg in a statement said Pauken had “betrayed his country for money” and “exploited his US citizenship and corresponding ability to travel to the US without restriction”. Pauken’s lawyer has said he believed his work could promote peaceful US-China relations and advance religious freedom in China. Pauken moved to China in 2010 and worked for state-run organisations including national broadcaster CCTV and Xinhua. According to court papers, his principal handler, identified only as “Cathy”, was introduced to him in 2017 by a man who allegedly worked as a speech-writer for President Xi Jinping during the Donald Trump administration’s trade disputes with China. The filings say Cathy subjected him to a lie-detector test and told him his reports were being passed on to senior Chinese leaders. The Justice Department said Pauken sold reports to a group from Wuhan seeking information on technology and the Justice Department, and was asked to find an expert who could help them with cyber espionage. The FBI arrested Pauken at a Washington hotel after he encouraged an unnamed official in President Trump’s administration to contact a woman in China whom he believed to be an intelligence officer. “This case illustrates the lengths to which the Chinese Communist Party will go to undermine our democratic institutions,” said assistant director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in a statement. He added that the sentencing “provides a clear warning: anyone operating as an agent of a foreign government against the US will be found by the FBI and held accountable”.

title: Flood-hit Nepal urges tourists to return: ‘our mountain trails are waiting for you’
description: The plea comes as the calamity threatens to deter international visitors even from parts of Nepal largely untouched by the disaster.
content: Nepal urged international travellers not to abandon the Himalayas, declaring the country open for tourism as it continues to assess the human and economic toll from catastrophic floods that killed more than a thousand people. “Our mountain trails, trekking routes are still waiting for you,” Tourism Minister Khadak Raj Paudel said in a video message on social media, using the hashtag #NepalCalling. “Your coming to Nepal this time does not mean only a holiday. It’s a big support to the country fighting this catastrophic tragedy of flash flood.” The plea comes as harrowing images of destroyed villages, roads and bridges – and reports of deaths following last week’s floods – threaten to deter tourists even from parts of Nepal largely untouched by the disaster. One of Asia’s poorest economies, Nepal faces a daunting reconstruction effort as higher fuel costs from the Iran war, weaker tourism and slowing growth weigh on the economy. The disaster has compounded the challenges facing the nation’s 36-year-old Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who rose to power this year on a wave of Gen Z disaffection. The disaster was triggered last week by a glacial collapse that sent ice, mud, rocks and water surging through a valley in Nepal, wiping out entire settlements in its path. Videos showed people running for their lives as walls of water and debris swallowed buildings, tore down bridges and power lines, and washed away trees, boulders and vehicles. So far, about 590 foreigners from 39 countries remain missing, according to figures from Nepal’s foreign ministry. The total death toll in Nepal has climbed to at least 1,114 as of Wednesday morning, with rescue operations continuing. Nearly 4,000 people are still unaccounted for. Specialist teams from Nepal, India, China and South Korea are meanwhile trying to reach workers missing from flood-hit hydropower projects, pushing into tunnels and digging from above in an effort to find alternative access points. Teams have made it hundreds of metres into some tunnels before encountering passages completely blocked by debris. Nearly 950 workers at hydropower projects remain unaccounted for, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal (IPPAN), though it’s unclear how many were underground when the floods struck. India’s Ministry of External Affairs said its tunnel rescue team overcame several challenges such as restricted access space and marshy tunnel floors to move deeper, and would continue its efforts to try and rescue any individuals that may still be trapped inside. Nepal’s Home Minister Sudan Gurung said on Tuesday that authorities had “not lost hope” of finding survivors. The disaster has damaged infrastructure, including at least 12 hydropower projects in Nepal’s Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts, according to IPPAN. “The scale and extent of the damage caused by this disaster are becoming increasingly clear as access has improved and more details are now available,” Nepal’s foreign ministry said in a separate statement. “Given the magnitude of the destruction, Nepal anticipates requiring substantial international support during the rehabilitation and reconstruction phase. “This has been an exceptionally painful and difficult time for Nepal.” At least 11,993 people have been rescued so far in Nepal, with emergency crews relying on helicopters and other aircraft to reach communities cut off after floods and landslides destroyed roads and bridges. On Wednesday morning, India said a fifth aircraft departed for Nepal with an 11-member rescue team, specialised equipment and 5.5 tonnes of essential medicines.

title: Malaysian heritage site caught in row over non-local staff
description: A viral video shot at the Sultan Abdul Samad Building has sparked a backlash, despite management insisting the worker was not a tour guide.
content: Images of a migrant worker apparently guiding visitors around one of Kuala Lumpur’s best-known heritage sites have triggered a backlash in Malaysia, with critics asking why locals were not hired instead. The row erupted after photos and video circulated online showed visitors being shown around the Sultan Abdul Samad Building, a colonial-era landmark that has overlooked the capital’s Independence Square since the 19th century. Sharp-eyed viewers noticed that among the staff in KL City Gallery uniforms was a man in a sash reading “May I help?” who social media users claimed was non-local. The clip quickly ricocheted across social media, with commenters demanding to know why an employee helping to explain Malaysia’s national story of independence and sovereignty to visitors was not a local hire. KL City Gallery apologised on Monday, confirming that the man was a foreign national but insisting that he had never been appointed as a tour guide. “The staff member concerned is not a tour guide and has never been appointed by the company to carry out the duties of a tour guide,” it said in a statement. “The wearing of the sash created confusion regarding the role and identity of the appointed tour guides.” Every guide currently working at the site was a Malaysian citizen, it said, adding that steps were being taken to prevent a similar mix-up from happening again. The explanation did little to quell the criticism online, as social media users demanded to know what roles migrant workers actually performed and why they were stationed at the gallery. “Hire university students, part-time local staff,” one user wrote, while another suggested recruiting Malaysian retirees instead. Several people who said they had previously visited the gallery claimed to have encountered non-Malaysian staff members, though others identifying themselves as guides or recent visitors disputed suggestions that foreign nationals had been conducting tours. “Then who are they?” one user asked, with others urging the gallery to explain what jobs the workers had been hired to do. This Week in Asia could not independently verify the nationality of the workers pictured. The controversy appears to have stemmed from a video posted on Sunday by Kumaar Family, a Malaysian-American family vlog with more than 800,000 YouTube subscribers. Several social media users said they recognised the footage from the channel. Kumaar Family has previously worked with Tourism Malaysia on travel content aimed at both domestic and international audiences. This Week in Asia has contacted KL City Gallery for further comment on the number and nationality of workers it employs and the roles they perform. National identity Completed in 1897, the Sultan Abdul Samad Building once housed the seat of the British colonial administration in Kuala Lumpur and overlooks Dataran Merdeka (Independence Square), where the British flag was lowered ahead of Malaya’s independence in 1957. Part of the complex reopened to the public in February as a centre for exhibitions, culture and tourism after an 11 month-restoration under Warisan KL, a government-backed programme to rejuvenate some of the capital’s most important historic buildings. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who launched the wider heritage programme last year, has previously described the building as a symbol of Malaysia’s journey from colonial rule to independence and national sovereignty. The episode comes as Malaysia continues to grapple with its dependence on migrant labour even as the government seeks to prioritise jobs for citizens. Speaking in parliament in July, Anwar said employment opportunities should be prioritised for Malaysian citizens, while acknowledging that some industries needed migrant workers. “We do need foreign workers, that’s a statement,” he said, adding that recruitment syndicates had for decades allowed people to “amass wealth”. Malaysia permits migrant workers in several sectors, including the service sector, subject to government quotas and other conditions. Awkward timing The gallery row coincided with an announcement from Dhaka on Sunday that Malaysia would recruit around 200,000 Bangladeshi workers over the next six months, beginning in phases from the end of September. Malaysia had restricted the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in 2024 amid reports of debt bondage, forced labour and workers arriving in the country to find the jobs they had been promised did not exist. Mir Shahe Alam, Bangladesh’s state minister for local government, rural development and cooperatives, told reporters on Sunday that roughly 800,000 registered Bangladeshi nationals already worked in Malaysia, and that Dhaka had asked Kuala Lumpur to regularise those without documentation. Malaysia’s government has said it wants to reduce the share of migrant workers in the national workforce to about 10 per cent by 2030, down from the current 13 per cent.

title: Should the Philippines ban Roblox?
description: Online gaming platform is sparking concern about safety and radicalisation over its alleged links to school shootings.
content:
Roblox has become a hot topic in Southeast Asia as officials scrutinise whether young users are being exposed to harmful subcultures on the gaming platform. But analysts warn that it might just be a convenient scapegoat for wider failures in how children are protected on and offline.
Most recently, Roblox has been linked to the August 18 school shooting in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga, where a student brought two firearms to a private school, live-streamed the attack and killed one schoolmate before taking his own life.
Authorities were quick to identify the cause.
The suspect was a “Roblox fanatic”, Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso said.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla characterised the attack as a “case of desensitisation to violence” linked to the games children play online and called for a total Roblox ban.
Remulla also said that authorities had a “great degree of confidence” that Roblox had influenced the shooter’s actions, even as they had yet to conduct a forensic examination of his devices.
“Roblox in itself is not a dangerous game. It is the chat group ... That is where the coaxing happens, where the radicalisation takes place,” Remulla said.
Roblox, which reported 123 million average daily active users globally in the second quarter of this year, is not a single game but an online platform. It is built around user-created virtual worlds and includes chat features that safety advocates say can make it easier for children to meet strangers or be drawn into harmful communities.
Online games have been scrutinised as a potential pathway for radicalisation since a school shooting in the Philippine city of Tacloban that killed three students in June. One of the suspects was found to have been an avid player of the German video game GoreBox.
Philippine officials met Roblox executives in Singapore last month to discuss measures to protect Filipino children from online harm. After the meeting, Department of Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda said Roblox had agreed to strengthen child safety protections for users in the Philippines.
While concerns about Roblox are valid, not every new platform is a threat, according to Munira Mustaffa, executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow at Verve Research: “We risk repeating the same mistake we did with TikTok back in the early 2020s,” she said.
“It’s the same conversation all over again. Tomorrow will be a new platform but the same debate. It will never end unless we understand what exactly is the problem and what we are countering.”
If you have suicidal thoughts or know someone who is experiencing them, help is available. In Hong Kong, you can dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. You can also call +852 2896 0000 for The Samaritans or +852 2382 0000 for Suicide Prevention Services. In the US, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For a list of other nations’ helplines, see this page .

title: Higher typhoon warning possible based on Saudel’s course after rare resurgence
description: T1 signal will remain in force in Hong Kong, but tropical cyclone could change course after rare resurgence, bringing uncertainty.
content: Hong Kong’s weather forecaster could issue a higher typhoon signal closer to the weekend after Tropical Cyclone Saudel experienced a rare resurgence, with the potential to change course over the South China Sea and edge towards the Pearl River Delta. The Observatory said the No 1 typhoon signal would remain in force for the rest of Wednesday and into Thursday morning, as Saudel was expected to linger over the northeastern South China Sea and remain about 300km (167 miles) or more from the city. “Under the combined effect of Saudel and the northeast monsoon, local winds are occasionally strong offshore and on high ground. The No 1 signal is expected to remain in force for the rest of [Wednesday] and into [Thursday] morning,” the forecaster said. Saudel is a name provided by the Federated States of Micronesia and refers to the guards of a legendary ruler of Pohnpei, one of the country’s islands. Hong Kong is expected to remain mainly cloudy on Wednesday, with a few squally showers and maximum temperatures of about 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit). But the Observatory warned that Saudel would gradually turn westwards on Thursday and skirt the coast of eastern Guangdong, bringing uncertainty in the days that followed. “It will edge closer to the vicinity of the Pearl River Delta again on Friday. There will be rather large uncertainties over its intensity by then,” the forecaster said. “The Observatory will closely monitor Saudel’s movement and assess the need to issue the strong wind signal No 3 as it edges closer to the Pearl River Delta.” Kok Mang-hin, a senior scientific officer at the Observatory, said it remained uncertain whether Saudel would track closer to land or stay out at sea. “If it skirts closer to land, Saudel will weaken more quickly. However, if it stays mostly over the sea off the coast of eastern Guangdong, it will weaken more slowly,” he told a radio programme. Saudel made landfall in the eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang on Friday morning. It later strengthened again, prompting the Observatory to issue the No 1 typhoon signal on Monday evening. Kok said the storm had earlier weakened into an area of low pressure, but intensified into a tropical depression on Monday. “As the remnants [of Saudel] moved back over the ocean from land, they were able to reabsorb energy from the sea, supported by a relatively ample supply of moisture. This allowed associated convection currents to regenerate,” he said. “Therefore, it re-intensified into a tropical depression again over the southeastern coastal waters of Hainan Island.” Kok added that it was rare for the remnants of a tropical cyclone to re-intensify, citing the case of Tropical Storm Son-Tinh in 2018. Observatory records showed that Son-Tinh strengthened into a tropical storm before degenerating into an area of low pressure over northern Vietnam in July that year. The low-pressure area associated with the storm’s remnants then made a sharp turn eastwards and intensified into a tropical depression over Beibu Wan in China. Son-Tinh first prompted the Observatory to issue a No 1 typhoon signal and then upgrade it to a No 3 signal. All warning signals were cancelled before Son-Tinh intensified and led to another No 1 signal.

title: Netanyahu accuses security officials of intentionally not waking him on October 7
description: Israeli prime minister repeats assertions about 2023 security fiasco as he faces pivotal elections.
content: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused security officials on Tuesday of intentionally failing to wake him on the morning of Hamas’ October 7 attacks, a day after his wife claimed an opposition figure knew of the onslaught in advance. Netanyahu is heading into close-fought elections later this year, and has come in for sustained criticism in the national debate over who is responsible for the failures that led to the October 7, 2023 security fiasco. The prime minister has alleged in the past that security officials refrained from waking him that morning, insisting that the attack would have been contained if he had stepped in earlier, but only in recent days has he begun to claim that the move was intentional. “Why didn’t they wake me? Because they knew that I, as prime minister of Israel, would immediately have ordered to put the entire army on alert, to wake up all the towns (on the Gaza border) … It’s so obvious that all of this could have been done. This has been hidden from the public,” the premier said during a live interview on Instagram. Netanyahu’s assertions echo those he made in another podcast interview published Monday, in which he blamed the military’s top brass and Ronen Bar, head of the Shin Bet security service at the time, for refusing to wake him to avoid the “miscalculation” of a military escalation with Hamas. “They didn’t believe Hamas would attack,” he added. “They knew exactly what I would do.” His remarks on Tuesday came after his wife Sara, in a separate television interview broadcast the night before, claimed that opposition figure Yair Golan was aware of the plan for the Hamas attack before it happened. The comments drew outrage from the opposition and a lawsuit threat from Golan, a former deputy military chief of staff who heads Israel’s centre-left Democrats party. On the morning of October 7, upon hearing about the Hamas attack, Golan rushed to southern Israel to rescue at least six people at the site of the Nova music festival, where at least 370 people were killed. Sara Netanyahu claimed that Golan was “already dressed and ready” at dawn that day, “while others knew nothing, including the prime minister”. Her interview was broadcast on Israel’s Channel 14, which is close to the government. In a post on X, Golan threatened to sue the first lady for 2.5 million shekels (around US$830,000) unless she issued “an apology within 24 hours and compensation to be donated to survivors of the Nova” festival. “Sara Netanyahu spread a false conspiracy in an attempt to rewrite October 7, turning those who went out to save lives into traitors and those who abandoned Israel’s security into victims,” he said, in a jab at the prime minister. Golan’s party strongly condemned her “vile and deceitful” remarks. “Spreading conspiracies against Major General Yair Golan, and smearing his heroism on October 7, is crossing a red line that borders on insanity,” it wrote on X. Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who has emerged as the front runner to challenge Netanyahu in the coming October election, slammed the “mad conspiracy of betrayal” spread by the premier’s wife. Sara Netanyahu’s accusations reflect recurrent conspiracy theories among a part of the Israeli political class. According to a poll conducted for Channel 13 in August, 40 per cent of Israelis, and 63 per cent of voters for the current right-wing coalition, believe that internal treason led to the October 7 attack – the deadliest day in Israel’s history. Hamas’ attack on Israel resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Militants also took 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead, into Gaza. Israel responded with a massive offensive in Gaza that has killed at least 73,462 people, according to the Palestinian territory’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

title: China’s pension fund doubles offshore investments to new high in quest for higher returns
description: Hong Kong market to benefit as lower growth and interest rates make it harder for fund to ‘rely solely on domestic assets’, analyst says.
content: China’s national pension reserve more than doubled its offshore investments over the past three years to a record 580 billion yuan (US$86 billion), as the state fund increasingly sought higher returns by diversifying its portfolio beyond domestic assets. Offshore investment assets held by the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) reached 580.02 billion yuan at the end of 2025, accounting for a record 15.23 per cent of its total assets, according to an annual report released by the National Council for Social Security Fund on Tuesday. Offshore assets accounted for 9.8 per cent of the fund’s assets in 2022 at 282 billion yuan, rising to 346 billion yuan in 2023 and 438 billion yuan in 2024. The growth in offshore allocations comes as Beijing seeks to broaden investment channels for mainland institutional capital, with Hong Kong emerging as one potential beneficiary. Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People’s Bank of China, said in July that China would continue to increase the share of foreign-exchange reserves allocated to assets in Hong Kong. Financial regulators have also taken steps recently to facilitate investments by mainland insurers in Hong Kong-listed exchange-traded funds. Lower interest rates on the mainland meant the fund had to seek higher yields elsewhere while ensuring geographical and asset-class diversification, which aligned directly with national policy, according to Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators. “Hong Kong serves as an ideal platform for capital going global,” Tang said. “Through the Stock Connect scheme, funds can directly invest in select overseas products and foreign companies listed in the city.” Tang added that beyond equities, Hong Kong offered access to a broad array of international investment tools, derivatives and fund products, enabling mainland institutions to buy virtually any global asset class. “Lower nominal growth and interest rates in China have made it harder for the fund to rely solely on domestic assets for returns,” said Gary Ng, senior economist at Natixis. “The increase likely reflects strategic overseas diversification, amplified by strong global market performance.” Hong Kong equities could have contributed significantly to the increase amid the market rebound in 2024 and 2025, Ng said, citing attractive valuations and access to technology companies not readily available in mainland-listed, yuan-denominated shares, known as A shares. Hong Kong’s IPO market has surged, raising HK$209.9 billion (US$26.8 billion) in the first half of 2026 – a 92 per cent jump from a year earlier – driven largely by mainland listings, KPMG data showed. The bond market has drawn similarly strong demand, with government green and infrastructure bond sales in May attracting about HK$239 billion in orders, 8.6 times the amount on offer. Tommy Ong, managing director of T.O. & Associates Consultancy, said he expected the underlying shift away from domestic assets to continue, noting that “Hong Kong stands to benefit most directly”. Hong Kong’s advantages included its deep pool of US dollar-denominated bonds – especially sustainability-focused issuances aligned with Beijing’s strategic goals – and an equity market that offered greater stability than regional peers like South Korea and Japan, Ong said. Familiarity with dual listings, where Hong Kong-listed shares typically traded at a discount to their mainland counterparts, was another advantage, while investing in Western jurisdictions carried heightened regulatory and asset-freeze risks, he added. The NSSF “actively seized offshore market investment opportunities” in 2025 and optimised its existing holdings, according to the annual report. The fund would closely monitor changes in the macroeconomic environment and capital markets and adopt a strategy of “promoting stability through proactive action”, increasing stock allocations when markets experienced sharp corrections, the report added. The fund also plans to adjust the structure of its equity investments, increasing allocations to industrial and strategic investments, according to the report, which added that it would continue to take a long-term view of China’s capital markets, strengthen its role as a source of patient capital, and invest more in technology and innovation. It generated 390.7 billion yuan in investment income last year, a 13.2 per cent return, while its total assets reached 3.8 trillion yuan. Domestic equities also rallied strongly last year. The Shanghai Composite Index gained 18.4 per cent in 2025, while the Shenzhen Component Index advanced about 30 per cent and the ChiNext Index surged around 50 per cent.

title: China’s 2026 moon laser communication speed is slower than Nasa’s in 2013
description: Data rates during two-way laser link between Earth and the moon were well behind US experiment over a decade ago.
content: China has pulled off two-way laser communication between Earth and the moon, making it only the second nation after the United States to do so. But the data rates it achieved were well behind those recorded by Nasa more than a decade ago, and that has left space experts scratching their heads. Using telescopes in Yunnan province and an experimental satellite that is now orbiting the moon after a launch mishap in 2024, the team recorded a downlink speed of 100 megabits per second and an uplink speed of 1.25Mbps, according to the Chinese Academy of Sciences, which led the project. By contrast, Nasa’s 2013 lunar laser communications demonstration achieved download speeds of 622Mbps and upload speeds of 20Mbps – roughly six times faster for downloads and 16 times faster for uploads. Jonathan McDowell, a London-based space historian and former Harvard astronomer, said the Chinese and US experiments were comparable. “It sounds like China has not yet reached the data rates the US can achieve,” he said, adding that he did not know what accounted for the gap. Yang Lei, a deep-space laser communications expert and head of the research team, noted the speed advantage of laser compared to other methods in an interview with state news agency Xinhua last week. “An 8K high-definition image of the lunar surface would take about four to five minutes to transmit using a conventional 5Mbps microwave link,” he said. “With a 100Mbps laser link, it would take only about 12 seconds.” The technology is taking on new importance as China and the US prepare to send astronauts to the moon and establish a long-term presence near the lunar south pole, with Nasa targeting its first crewed landing in more than half a century in 2028. On Thursday, Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman said China had delayed its latest Chang’e-7 moon mission, but “at Nasa, we are not slowing down”. “We are not counting them out. They are a very capable rival in the space race and we are not taking the foot off the gas,” he told US cable news network NewsNation. Conventional communications – from everyday 5G networks to China’s Queqiao-2 satellite relaying signals between Earth and spacecraft on the moon’s far side – rely largely on radio waves, which spread like ripples and weaken dramatically over vast distances. Lasers operate at much higher frequencies and can be focused into far narrower beams, concentrating energy and carrying more data faster with smaller, lighter equipment. But that narrow beam also makes long-distance laser communication extremely difficult. “Earth-moon communication is like threading a needle from thousands of kilometres away,” Yang said. At a distance of about 400,000km (248,550 miles), even tiny movements of the satellite or disturbances in Earth’s atmosphere can throw the beam off course, with a minute angular error resulting in a miss of several kilometres near the moon. Yang said the team developed a tracking system that corrected for the satellite’s orbit, atmospheric distortion and the time it took light to travel between Earth and the moon, keeping the ground and space terminals locked onto each other while in motion. The returning signal poses another challenge. After travelling 400,000km, it can be so faint that ground telescopes receive only a few photons at a time, amid interference from moonlight, starlight and city lights – like trying to hear a needle drop on a busy street. The team used ultra-sensitive single-photon detectors and algorithms to extract the signal from the background noise, while new processing and coding technologies helped boost transmission speeds. “We have now opened an ‘information highway’ between Earth and the moon,” Yang said, adding that the technology would provide high-speed data links for China’s crewed lunar missions, planned research base and deep-space exploration.

title: Beaming Alexandra Eala thanks raucous fans after cruising to US Open first round win
description: Philippine tennis star beats America’s Mary Stoiana in straight sets, while fans packed out stands just to watch her practice hours earlier.
content: Alexandra Eala cruised to a straight sets win in the first round of the US Open, then thanked her legions of fans who turned the tournament into a home away from home for the Philippine star. Eala dispatched American Mary Stoiana 6-1, 6-2 in Louis Armstrong Stadium, cheered on by supporters who had packed out the practice court just to watch her train in the hours before her opening match. In a brief on-court interview, the charismatic 21-year-old said the fans made it “such a pleasure to do my job”. Her fans arrived at Flushing Meadows bearing Filipino flags, and wearing hats telling her to fight on “Laban Alex”. They cheered her sizzling groundstrokes, documented her volleys and serves in photos and video, and in some cases FaceTimed with friends or family. And this was only at the practice courts. "Thank you everybody for being part of my journey and making it such a pleasure to do my job." ❤️🇵🇭 Alexandra Eala thanks tennis fans worldwide for their support after her first round win 🥹 pic.twitter.com/8lSUzfI42z — espnW (@espnW) September 2, 2026 It was about four hours before Eala was scheduled to play and every seat at the practice court was filled. Many of Eala’s fans didn’t have tickets for the evening session on Monday in New York. But they’d come to see their idol hit some tennis balls. It was hardly surprising, given the enormous, ardent, ever-growing fan base that now surrounds her. This summer has seen Eala beat Iga Swiatek at Wimbledon and win her first tour singles title, at Washington. She’s at a career-best 18th in the world, and many think she’ll continue her ascent. One of the fans watching on a rainy afternoon was Andrea Belen, at 21 the same age as Eala. Belen, a pre-med student at New York University, said she hadn’t been a big tennis fan until Eala came along — someone who looked just like her. Belen’s family’s is originally from Laguna in the Philippines, but moved to Cleveland and her father also became a tennis fan out of pure admiration for Eala. “It’s his new obsession,” Belen said. “It’s become the family hobby.” She and her friend, Sarah Frederick, had arrived at the practice court long before Eala was to appear, correctly guessing that the seats would fill quickly. Belen explained that in the Philippines, basketball and boxing reign supreme, and the sports heroes are men. “It’s just really nice to see a woman out there,” Belen said. “Also, she speaks in our native language, Tagalog.” Ellene Santos had come to the tournament from Orlando, Florida. Like Belen and Frederick, she did not have tickets for the evening match. But Santos, 67, was thrilled to get her Eala fix, just the same. “I’m happy now,” she smiled. With practice over, four retired nurses, all friends, headed for the exit. They were wearing bright blue hats emblazoned with the phrase, “Laban Alex”. “I love how Alex shows she is so proud to be from the Philippines,” said Joy Rodriguez, 65, explaining her ardent fandom. Her friend, Maria Espiritu, 67, said this was the first tennis tournament she’d ever attended. Nearby, Frances Arespacochaga, 77, was taking photos with fellow attendees. Arespacochaga lives in Manila, and was in the United States visiting her sister in Massachusetts. Together they drove down to see Eala at the U.S. Open — bearing flags. “She’s very intelligent, very articulate,” Arespacochaga said of Eala. “In her interviews you can see her values.” Belen, who FaceTimed with her father during the practice session so he could see Eala, spoke of a special Filipino pride in the achievements of countrymen. Like gymnast Carlos Yulo, who won two gold medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024. “Everyone went crazy,” she said. “We’re not that big of a country so those golds meant so much.” She added: “We’re very loud when it comes to supporting our people.” Should Eala stick around a while at the U.S. Open, it’s bound to get a lot louder.

title: Ukraine’s president warns airlines to avoid ‘drone-infested’ Russian airspace
description: Zelensky threatens to respond to Moscow’s escalating aerial barrages by crowding its skies with drones.
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Tuesday that his country’s drones would make Russia’s airspace “completely unsafe” for the duration of the war, drawing accusations of “state terrorism” from Russian leader Vladimir Putin. Both sides have intensified long-range attacks in recent months and diplomatic efforts led by the United States remain stalled more than four years into Russia’s full-scale invasion. “Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelensky said in his nightly address. “Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said. Air traffic at Russian airports has been repeatedly disrupted by the approach of Ukrainian drones, the number of which has increased in recent months. “Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelensky said. “The sky over Russia is currently for drones … as long as the war continues.” Putin responded by branding Zelensky’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”. “They are asking us to resume negotiations … but you don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said in a televised news conference. The hardening stances came after fresh Russian missile and drone strikes killed at least 12 people in Kyiv and the surrounding region. “We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said. Russia has stepped up its use of ballistic missiles that Kyiv is struggling to intercept due to a lack of ammunition for its air defence systems. But Ukraine has responded by striking Russian infrastructure, ports and even e-commerce warehouses. Putin also acknowledged in his address that Ukrainian strikes had damaged infrastructure inside Russia. “The adversary began delivering strikes on our civilian facilities, including on refineries. Did it cause damage? It did,” Putin said. “And why? Among other reasons, and above all, because they were not protected.” But he said Moscow was gaining momentum on the battlefield. “Russian forces, despite everything, are increasing the tempo of their offensive in the zone of the special military operation,” he said, using Moscow’s term for the war. Zelensky said in his nightly address that Ukraine would clear its drones from Russian skies when its partners requested it, “for the sake of diplomacy, for the sake of negotiations … for specific periods of time and in specific destinations”. But US-mediated efforts to end the conflict have largely stalled since the outbreak of war in the Middle East in February. Even so, Putin struck a warmer tone towards US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, key figures in President Donald Trump’s mediation efforts. “Both Mr Kushner and Mr Witkoff are always welcome guests here, and we are glad to work with them,” he said, describing them as “sincere”. Witkoff and Kushner have held several rounds of talks with Russia as part of Washington’s mediation push, with the last visit to Moscow in January. Highlighting the growing operational risks, aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300km (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were near-certain through 2026, including near Moscow and St Petersburg. “There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short ⁠term deep inside Russian territory,” the alert said. “It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict.” Osprey said Russian military air defences included conventional surface-to-air missile systems capable at all altitudes. Last year, Europe’s ‌top rights court found Russia responsible ‌for the downing of a Malaysian Airlines jet in 2014 at cruising altitude over eastern Ukraine where there was fighting. Putin told Azerbaijan’s leader last year that two Russian missiles had detonated beside an Azerbaijan Airlines plane in 2024 after Ukrainian drones entered Russian airspace, in an incident that led to the deaths of 38 people. Additional reporting by Reuters

title: Letters | Hong Kong’s cleaner transport push must not neglect tyre pollution
description: Readers discuss the need to monitor tyre pollution in the city, a Chinese film about the Iraq war, and the US midterms.
content: Feel strongly about these letters, or any other aspects of the news? Share your views by emailing us your Letter to the Editor at letters@scmp.com or filling in this Google form. Submissions should not exceed 400 words. After a summer downpour, run-off from Hong Kong’s busiest roads may carry more than leaves and litter. It can wash accumulated tyre- and road-surface particles, metals and chemical additives into drains and receiving waters. This overlooked issue deserves attention as vehicle electrification and more frequent short-duration heavy rain converge. As of the end of May 2026, Hong Kong has about 178,000 electric vehicles, representing 19.4 per cent of all vehicles, while more than seven in 10 newly registered private cars are electric. On July 20, the Hong Kong Observatory reported that heavy rain events lasting one to three hours increased significantly between 2000 and 2024. Electric vehicles remain essential to cleaner transport. They eliminate tailpipe emissions, support decarbonisation and, through regenerative braking, can reduce brake wear. But every vehicle, whatever its power source, still uses tyres and roads. The interaction releases particles that may become airborne or remain in road dust until intense rain mobilises them. We do not yet know the scale or composition of this pollution in Hong Kong’s stormwater, where it accumulates, or what environmental or public health risks it may pose. Overseas studies identify potential concerns but cannot reproduce the city’s combination of dense traffic, subtropical weather, vehicle types, road materials and drainage conditions. That uncertainty is a reason to investigate, not ignore, the issue. The government should establish a 12-month monitoring pilot in contrasting locations: a tunnel approach, a bus or goods-vehicle corridor, and an arterial road in a densely populated district. Researchers should collect road dust and stormwater before, during and after major storms, analysing particle quantity, size and composition alongside traffic, road conditions, preceding dry periods and rainfall intensity. The work should unite transport, highways, drainage, environmental and public health authorities with universities and industry. Findings could inform road-material procurement, street cleaning, drainage maintenance and future tyre standards. Hong Kong could also build on existing rain gardens, bioswales and silt traps by testing their effectiveness in capturing tyre- and road-wear particles, while assessing clogging, contaminated sediment, maintenance and worker safety. This is not an argument against electric vehicles, nor a claim that they alone cause the problem. It is an argument for completing the transition they represent. Cleaner transport policy must address not only what leaves the exhaust pipe, but also what is released where tyres meet roads – and where it goes when the rain begins. Ling N. Jin, associate professor, and Zhen Leng, professor, Hong Kong Polytechnic University Chinese film offers a fresh view on war I refer to the report, “Hit film about Iraq war gets Beijing message to wider world” (August 19). For a long time, Chinese cinema has attached great importance to grand narratives, particularly those centred on nationalism, patriotism and loyalty. Once Upon a Time in the Middle East may represent an interesting turn. The film is said to draw on the experiences of Chinese restaurateurs who lived through the Iraq war. Significantly, there is little emphasis on intervention by the Chinese state. Instead, Chinese individuals confront extreme circumstances while continuing to protect vulnerable local people. Their actions arise from human compassion rather than nationality. This may be where the film’s soft power really lies. It recalls untold stories of Chinese people interacting with Middle Eastern societies while experiencing the consequences of war themselves. More importantly, it offers a Chinese perspective from which the world can reflect on the Iraq war not merely as geopolitics, but through its impact on ordinary people. They, after all, are innocent. Jiannan Sun, Beijing US voters must make the right choice in the midterms As midterm elections in the United States approach, let’s hope the voters there consider the rest of the world and we get on the path to responsible leadership of the world, which has been lacking for the last 10 years. I understand the impulse to put the country first. However, the world needs to be united or it could cease to exist. It’s time for the minority to support the majority. Duncan Hancock, Lamma Island

title: As Bessent addresses G20 peers, analysts warn benchmark bond yields near ‘concern zone’
description: With US 10-year Treasury yield at a 20-month high, alarm bells expected to ring if it crosses 5 per cent tipping point.
content: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told G20 finance ministers and central bankers this week that the United States was a leader in addressing sovereign debt issues in emerging markets and low-income countries, but analysts said he was also grappling with serious debt issues closer to home. With the US 10-year Treasury yield rising to a 20-month high of 4.78 per cent, Tuesday’s discussion in Asheville, North Carolina, landed amid a global sell-off of rich countries’ sovereign debt that has also sent benchmark bond yields in Japan and the United Kingdom to levels unseen in decades. Analysts warned that the rise in yields was approaching worrying territory for the global economy as higher borrowing costs worked their way through to governments, companies and households and reduced the amount investors were willing to pay for stocks. “We’re heading into the concern zone, which is the other side of 5 per cent for the 10-year Treasury … where alarm bells would begin to ring,” said Padhraic Garvey, regional head of research for the Americas at ING. Current levels were not a mispricing, Garvey said, but it would be a tipping point if the US 10-year yield rose past 5 per cent and the euro zone 10-year yield reached between 3.5 per cent and 4 per cent. The main driver behind the Treasury yield increase was not higher inflation expectations but higher real yields, he said, adding that was worrying for American companies because they could not increase prices to offset the impact. As investors woke up to that risk, the underlying implication for various risk assets, including stocks, could be significant, he said. They would eventually realise that they had to discount future earnings at a structurally higher real yield, while rising yields would also have direct impacts on products such as mortgage rates. By design, Bessent – or any US treasury secretary – ends up being in a difficult position Anis Bensaidani, BNP Paribas Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for the Asia-Pacific region at French investment bank Natixis, said rising yields would also be an issue for companies seeking to raise money – especially artificial intelligence hyperscalers who were issuing debt. “Everybody needs cash,” she said. “Cash is expensive now … when the US Treasury yield goes above 5 … you need to be an amazing company to pay below the Treasury.” BNP Paribas economist Anis Bensaidani said the higher yields would also translate into higher debt-related costs for governments, such as interest, which would eat into their ability to foster public investment in areas ranging from social welfare and energy to defence and AI. It was “a cocktail of negative things for the global economy”, he said. Garvey said rising yields would also make it more difficult for Washington to correct its debt dynamics as fiscal policies could not fix interest rates, which was partially the reason Bessent would not want the yield to get out of hand. But analysts said Bessent was also in a difficult position as he tried to manage US Treasury yields. The Bank of Japan needed to increase its rates to support the yen against the US dollar, they said, adding the US also needed to cut its fiscal deficit – a challenging proposition. “By design, Bessent – or any US treasury secretary – ends up being in a difficult position,” Bensaidani said, adding that while the holder of the office had to manage higher interest rates and a higher interest burden, which were related to fundamentals, fiscal consolidation was not popular and “politically costly”.

title: Hong Kong woman’s 20-year eating disorder after dad’s death and how she recovered
description: Janet Leung lost more than two decades to severe food restriction. Now, at 46, she reflects on finding peace, therapy and the joys in recovery.
content: For more than two decades of Janet Leung’s life, hunger replaced her joy. After losing her father, endless food maths filled her head, drowning out other thoughts. Her anxiety around eating kept others at a distance. Miserable as she was, Leung could not give up this distraction; it offered an escape from the sideways glances and judgment that she endured in her youth. Hidden inside the grown-up was a 16-year-old girl, stuck in an environment that demanded perfection. Patching a ‘broken window’ One Hong Kong night, when she was 14, Leung woke to a world without her father. Her mother had roused her after an urgent call from the hospital. Leung did not want to get up – she had become accustomed to late-night trips to her father’s bedside in case it was time to say goodbye – but this time, she arrived to news that he had already gone. A blank feeling overcame Leung, and she wondered why her family friends were crying more than she was. Before he died, her father had told the family to live their lives as they normally would. Leung and her sisters departed for a Canadian boarding school in the months following. His death was like a “broken window in her home”. She had lost her father, her protector and her connection to food in a single blow, and would carry her grief deep inside as she grew into adulthood. Food as a love language Long before Leung’s father was diagnosed with diabetes and pancreatic cancer, she had sensed that he needed her support. A weariness clung to him, as ever-present as the factory smell in his hair. He cherished family meals and made batches of barbecue pork buns to share. Food became a love language between father and daughter – by eating what he served, Leung could show him how much she cared. During her childhood, her eating habits were not a priority. She saw beauty in her figure, and had little time for anything but her studies. Her school in Hong Kong was “the kind of school that either you are in the top 10, or you’re invisible”, Leung says. “For me, being invisible is a form of death.” She was told she was overweight and taken to the doctor for weight loss. Her food intake and body size were constantly critiqued. Leung had little motivation to change. Her father had not been a lean man, and she saw him as her protector from the rest of the world’s judgment. His passing stripped Leung of that security. At boarding school, diet culture was inescapable as students struggled under the pressure of being watched. Slowly, Leung developed restrictive eating rules, her thoughts straying towards food more as she ate less. Her weight started to drop in the summer after her first year at school. She fell under a dangerous illusion: by focusing on her body, she could chase perfection while attempting to regain the safety her father once provided. The more she thought about food, the less she thought about him. Focus on body image starts early In Hong Kong, body image concerns can start as early as six years old in children of Chinese descent, according to a 2014 study by Cambridge University Press. The study found that only 25 per cent of children between six and 12 were satisfied with their body size, with about half of the students reporting they wanted to be thinner. As in Leung’s case, multiple factors usually combine to cause an eating disorder, according to Vanessa Yim See-heng, a psychology professor at the University of Hong Kong. They can stem from external factors such as family environment and life stressors, as well as core personality traits like perfectionism. Globally, eating disorders account for an estimated 3.4 million lost years of healthy life each year, according to the Global Burden of Disease study. Leung would go on to lose 20. The physical toll About six months into her restrictive eating, Leung knew something was off. Anxious thoughts, constant mathematics and food analysis consumed her. Panic made her pull out her eyebrows and eyelashes. She could never get warm, her energy plummeted and her mind spun with irrational thoughts about food. Her mother tried to reason with her, which Leung put down to jealousy. The boarding school nurse made her eat meals in front of her, but Leung, unwilling to give up control, felt only irritation. This continued even as she studied at university in Canada, spent time in Hong Kong and took graduate classes in New York. Wherever she was, the days ticked by monotonously, elongated by constant hunger. She spent most evenings alone. In her 20s, Leung developed irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and anaemia. Dull abdominal pain replaced her hunger, and she lost the ability to sleep as aches kept her up all night. At 26, her mother convinced her to move back to Hong Kong to focus on her health. Leung, who still did not connect her ailments to restrictive eating, worked in journalism, finance and investor relations. At 36 and miserable at her investor relations job, she went online and chose a therapist at random. It was a perfect match – Leung found herself experiencing simple moments of joy just a few therapy sessions in. A close bond like the one Leung and her therapist developed is critical for effective treatment, especially for individuals navigating long-term restrictive eating disorders like Leung’s, says Daisy Wu, the centre-in-charge at the Hong Kong Eating Disorders Association. “You need to step into their shoes and show … empathy, to not just push them to gain weight,” Wu says. Even so, disordered eating still ruled her life. Soon after she started therapy, she suffered a bad break-up and was physically ill. One day, as she ran on the treadmill, a voice in her head asked her: “How long will you let people treat you like this?” She realised she was not thinking about her ex-boyfriend, but herself. Unpacking the grief Leung went back to therapy with fresh determination. For three hours a week, she and her therapist examined each belief that Leung held. They unearthed a fountain of guilt. Leung realised she had always regretted not visiting her dad more often in the months before his death. She was haunted by the image of him alone, sick and afraid in a hospital bed. More realisations came, but she started to see herself as she was back then – a child coping in the best way she knew how. Slowly, she started eating more. The fear of gaining weight still tormented her, but her mood began to lift, and aches she had always assumed were unrelated to her eating habits started to subside. In her mid-thirties, Leung completed a master’s degree in creative writing and poured her story onto the page. She spent three straight days writing about her dad to memorialise him, barely sleeping and stopping only to go to work. Talk therapy helped her unpack her suppressed grief, but two years ago, at 44, she realised she was still struggling with behavioural compulsions, like over-exercising. She called the Hong Kong Eating Disorders Association helpline to dive deeper into recovery. A team including a psychologist and a psychiatrist helped her confront her eating disorder head-on, easing her anxiety and expanding her life. The recovery process continues. Now 46, Leung chooses not to act on her panicked thoughts, instead going to sleep and re-evaluating in the morning. She eats at restaurants with friends and has regular meals. In the past, Leung says her mind felt dominated by a relentless thrum like electronic dance music. Now that there is space to breathe, she fills it with simple pleasures – going out with friends, painting her nails, diving into her passion for true crime stories. Each one feels like heaven. “It’s like, people who experience war would find a biscuit very delicious because they don’t have food,” Leung says. “I can appreciate the little things, the little peace that I have now, because it was absolute hell before.” The moments of thrum still come and go, but the bassline soon fades, leaving behind a lilting acoustic melody. If you need eating disorder support for yourself or someone you care about, help is available. In Hong Kong, contact the Hong Kong Eating Disorders Association (HEDA) hotline at 2850 4448 or email heda@heda-hk.org. You can also dial 18111 for the government-run Mental Health Support Hotline. Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: Hong Kong primary schools face record cuts amid declining student enrolment
description: Primary One classes drop by 126 as experts warn of continued challenges ahead.
content:
Hong Kong’s public schools are set to cut a record 126 Primary One classes for the 2026-27 academic year due to a declining student population. A sector leader has cautioned that even tougher times lie ahead.
As reported in the latest Primary School Profiles, the total number of Primary One classes in public schools has fallen from 1,558 in 2025-26 to 1,432 in 2026-27, marking a decrease of 8 per cent.
The guide covers more than 500 local primary institutions and is compiled by the Committee on Home-School Co-operation to help parents select schools for their children.
The contraction hit Kwai Tsing the hardest, where nearly half the district’s 31 primary schools – 14 campuses – were forced to trim their Primary One intake. Tuen Mun and Eastern districts followed, each losing 13 classes.
The latest profiles of more than 500 primary institutions serve as reference materials for parents selecting schools for their children.
The sharp drop in enrolment tracks a collapse in local births dating back to 2020, when Covid-19 pandemic curbs and the aftermath of the 2019 social unrest saw births plunge by nearly 20 per cent year on year to 43,000.
Jessie Cheung Chok-fong, a primary school principal and consultant to the Subsidised Primary Schools Council, warned that the sector faced prolonged hardship.
“The worst is yet to come, and all schools know very well, as the city’s birth rate in recent years has been on a declining trend and the winter for the primary school sector is apparently not yet over,” she said.

title: Joshua Wong admits instigating sanctions against Beijing, Hong Kong governments
description: Jailed activist could face longer term after admitting he urged foreign firms to avoid investing in mainland China, providing tech to city police.
content: Jailed Hong Kong opposition activist Joshua Wong Chi-fung has admitted instigating international sanctions against central and local authorities six years ago, such as urging foreign businesses to avoid investment in mainland China and petitioning an Israeli forensic tech firm to terminate its services to the city’s police force. The High Court heard on Wednesday that Wong, 29, had conspired with fugitive ex-lawmaker Nathan Law Kwun-chung, 33, and others to garner international support for their resistance campaign aimed at forcing Beijing to repeal the national security law and grant Hongkongers greater political freedom. Wong pleaded guilty to a count of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces before Mr Justice William Tam Yiu-ho, a former top prosecutor who oversaw cases involving anti-government protesters in the aftermath of the 2019 social unrest. The activist is set to face additional years behind bars, having already been sentenced to four years and eight months’ imprisonment for conspiring to subvert state power through his participation in an unofficial legislative primary election in July 2020. Defence lawyers suggested Wong be sentenced to 4½ years in jail in the latest case, citing the less serious nature of the offence and the delay in prosecution. But Tam expressed reservations, noting the defendant appeared to have lied about renouncing his previous calls for foreign sanctions in his failed bid to run in the 2020 Legislative Council election. The court adjourned sentencing until an unspecified date. A prosecution summary said Wong and Law, who were the secretary general and founding chairman of the now-defunct political group Demosisto, respectively, plotted to seek foreign intervention in Hong Kong affairs as early as 2016 in pursuit of the city’s self-determination. Wong visited the United States in November 2016 to drum up support for the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, which would allow the country’s president to punish Hong Kong and mainland officials for suppressing basic freedoms in the city. In September 2019, amid the city’s political turmoil, the activist travelled to Washington again to urge the country’s lawmakers to pass the bill. It was signed into law two months later. Between July 2019 and May 2020, Wong, Law and Demosisto also urged the US, Switzerland, Germany, France and Italy, among other nations, to stop exporting weapons and crowd control equipment to the Hong Kong Police Force. In a Facebook post dated May 20, 2020, Wong claimed that he had contributed to the passage of two US laws restricting the export of tear gas and non-lethal munitions to the city’s police. In the weeks leading up to the imposition of the national security law on June 30 that year, Wong, Law and their associates urged the US, Britain and European countries to incorporate human rights terms regarding Hong Kong in their trade deals with Beijing. They also called on foreign governments to terminate any special status previously accorded to Hong Kong as a separate customs territory. Demosisto disbanded just before the national security law took effect, and Law left Hong Kong shortly thereafter. “Since political organisations are the primary targets of the [national security] law, resistance must now go underground, with some, like Nathan Law, fleeing the city to keep speaking out in the international arena,” Wong said in an August 2020 article in The Guardian he co-wrote with fellow activist Glacier Kwong Chung-ching. In an article published in the Financial Times on September 29, 2020, Wong urged local and overseas companies to “consider diversifying their markets to avoid overdependence on China”, noting that they “still have the leverage to call for more human rights and freedom protections” in Hong Kong. Meanwhile, the activist helped Law to publicise an online petition in July 2020 calling on Israel-based forensic company Cellebrite to stop providing phone-hacking technology to Hong Kong police and related security agencies. The company acceded to the demand three months later, stating in a press release that it would stop selling its products to Hong Kong and the mainland. In a “presentencing work report” published on November 22, 2020, Wong revealed that he had also written to electronics giants Sony and Apple to warn them against business ties with Beijing. Prosecutors said the activist’s role in the conspiracy only ended when he was remanded in custody on November 23 that year for his involvement in an unlawful assembly in 2019. The activist, who has been detained since then, was initially expected to complete his sentence on January 7 next year, but was charged in the present case on June 6 last year. In mitigation, defence counsel Derek Chan Ching-lung SC said prosecutors’ delay in charging his client with collusion meant the pending sentence would be almost entirely consecutive to his previous jail term for subversion, making the overall sentence “crushing”. Chan said Wong had “matured substantially” during his six years in custody and urged the court to impose the most lenient sentence possible to allow the activist to “have an end in sight and some hope and a future to look forward to”. “He has had a lengthy opportunity to reflect upon his actions, to reflect upon the path he took, the consequences of his actions and the views he held,” the lawyer said. “He still holds the positive attitude that one day he will be released from prison, where he can still have a positive life and take care of his ageing parents.” Collusion with foreign forces carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment under the national security law, with a minimum jail term of 10 years applicable for serious offences.

title: US judge rules alleged Charlie Kirk killer to stand trial, could face death penalty
description: Defendant Tyler Robinson pleads not guilty to aggravated murder charge in shooting at Utah college campus last year.
content: The murder case against the Utah man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk last year is headed for trial, and the defendant could face the death penalty if he is convicted. Utah District Judge Tony Graf on Tuesday sided with prosecutors who said they had “overwhelming” evidence that suspect Tyler Robinson shot Kirk once in the neck as the ally of US President Donald Trump spoke to a crowd of thousands last September in Orem, Utah. One of Robinson’s lawyers entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf following Graf’s decision. Robinson’s lawyers tried to block a trial or at least take the death penalty off the table, arguing that prosecutors failed to show Kirk’s shooting placed others around him at risk of death. That is an aggravating factor under the law that makes Robinson eligible for capital punishment. Kirk’s family called the ruling “an important step in our family’s pursuit of justice”. Prosecutors said Robinson shot Kirk from a rooftop more than 122 metres (400 feet) away, knowing he could have missed, potentially killing other people. Graf had the option to send the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which carries a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison. The judge said his decision to approve the aggravated murder charge was based on “the documented position of several individuals in and around the canopy area” where Kirk was speaking, among other factors. “Tyler James Robinson shot and killed Charlie Kirk because he disagreed with him, and he did it by firing a high-powered rifle into a crowd of over 3,000 people, which created a great risk of death that anyone would know about,” Ryan McBride, a prosecutor with the Utah County Attorney’s Office, told the court. The hearing Tuesday in state court came after prosecutors in July spent five days presenting what they said was “overwhelming” evidence that Tyler Robinson killed the conservative activist while he was speaking at an open-air event on a college campus. The 23-year-old defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting at Utah Valley University last September. Robinson’s lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death. A “mountain of evidence” shows that Robinson was the killer, including DNA, messages with his romantic partner and posts Robinson made on the communications platform Discord, McBride said. One of Robinson’s lawyers, Staci Visser, argued that the state was trying to “shoehorn” the case into Utah’s aggravated murder statute. Prior case law requires prosecutors to show that there was a high probability – not merely a possibility – that other people could have been killed, she said. Robinson also faces potential sentencing enhancements if prosecutors can show he targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. Prosecutors have argued that an engraved bullet found in the suspected murder weapon shows that Kirk was targeted for how the defendant perceived his politics. The inscription “Hey Facist! CATCH!” is an “overt political reference,” they argued in court documents. A handwritten note that prosecutors allege Robinson left for his romantic partner read in part: “I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it”. They also allege Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out”. Robinson’s lawyers have argued that prosecutors do not have strong enough evidence to prove a political motivation. Robinson’s reported romantic partner, Lance Twiggs, told investigators in a recorded interview that Robinson said the day after Kirk was killed that “he wishes he hadn’t done it”. Later that same day – and only about an hour before turning himself in – Robinson posted “it was me at UVU yesterday” in an online chat room, according to investigators.

title: Fernandez move caps Premier League spending spree as clubs spend US$4.7bn on players
description: Enzo Fernandez makes switch from Chelsea to Manchester City for US$125 million, as club spends US$600 million on midfield makeover.
content: English football flexed its unrivalled spending power by embarking on an unprecedented US$4.7 billion outlay on players in the summer transfer window — and Manchester City saved the biggest signing of the lot right to the very end. Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez became one of the most expensive players in the game’s history by completing a marquee move to City from Premier League rivals Chelsea for £125 million (US$169 million) in the final hours of the window that closed across Europe on Tuesday. City’s spending alone on new players this summer — its first in the post-Pep Guardiola era — soared past US$600 million, a record splurge by a club in a single transfer window. With the expenditure of Chelsea and Tottenham also more than US$400 million, England’s top-flight clubs showed they’re in a league of their own when it comes to financial might. That’s mainly down to the competition’s huge domestic and international broadcasting deals, which dwarf those of its less-watched European rivals, but also because of a recent tweak to the Premier League’s financial rules that now allows clubs with the biggest revenues and turnover — like City and others who regularly benefit from Champions League largesse — to have greater spending power in the transfer market. Deadline day passed with the combined spending of top-flight clubs in Spain, Italy, Germany and France — Europe’s other so-called “Big Five” leagues — coming to US$3.8 billion, according to figures on soccer industry website Transfermarkt. The previous highest spend by English teams in one window was £3.14 billion in 2025. Fernandez, who hasn’t started a game since being sent off against Spain in the World Cup final in July, became the latest big-money signing as part of City’s US$440-million midfield rebuild under Guardiola’s successor, Enzo Maresca, that also includes the arrivals of England’s Elliot Anderson (US$155 million) and Morocco’s Ayyoub Bouaddi (US$117 million). Also joining City on deadline day was Senegal winger Iliman Ndiaye from Everton for an initial US$81 million. Abu Dhabi-controlled City recouped almost US$400 million in sales this window — among the departures were Spain’s World Cup-winning captain Rodri and midfield stalwart Bernardo Silva — and the club let Jack Grealish leave on another season-long loan to Everton on Tuesday. The fee for Fernandez is a joint British record, the same as Liverpool paid last year for Alexander Isak. “He is a complete midfielder: technically gifted, hardworking, tenacious and a goalscorer,” City director of football Hugo Viana said of Fernandez, who joined Chelsea for a then-British record £106.7 million in early 2023. Tottenham’s summer recruitment has been almost as remarkable as City’s, and the London club was active right up to the deadline on Tuesday, signing two players from Chelsea. Ukraine winger Mykhailo Mudryk joined on a season-long loan, a month after he was cleared to play again following a doping case, and defender Tosin Adarabioyo moved on a permanent deal. Chelsea responded to its sale of Fernandez by attempting to sign Senegal midfielder Lamine Camara from Monaco, but Sky Sports reported that the French club backed out of the deal. Liverpool signed 18-year-old goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans from Belgian team Genk in a deal that reportedly could be worth up to £30 million. Brughmans has gone back to Genk on loan for the rest of the season. Newcastle signed Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille for a reported £51 million and sent Nick Woltemade on loan to Juventus, with the German striker having spent just one season in the Premier League after a £69 million move.

title: China approves string of ‘telepathy’ devices amid push to leapfrog Elon Musk
description: Chinese regulators have approved a group of brain-technology products this year, as local start-ups push to surpass Musk’s Neuralink.
