content: China’s health regulators have granted approvals for a string of brain-technology products this year, as domestic start-ups push to transform the treatment of conditions ranging from paraplegia to Alzheimer’s and depression. The approvals come as Beijing bids to lead the world in brain-computer interfaces – devices that allow patients to control digital devices using thought alone – offering generous policy support to help Chinese firms compete with overseas players such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink. The sector in China has become increasingly competitive in recent years, with local governments across the country offering financing support and private investment surging as investors eye a spiralling need for novel health tech solutions in an era of rapid population ageing. Among the brain tech products to win Chinese market approval recently is a system developed by a domestic firm named Tiankai Suishi (Tianjin) Intelligent Technology, which helps doctors assess whether a patient’s cognitive functions have been impaired. The device is a cap studded with electrodes that fits over a patient’s scalp and can be used to read the electrical signals given off by the brain, according to an article posted to the company’s official WeChat feed. It was approved by China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) on August 19, official records show. Tiankai Suishi also sells BCI devices that aid early diagnosis of cognitive dysfunction linked to conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and schizophrenia. It is currently seeking regulatory approval for a product to assist with diagnosing depression. The company, founded in 2023, has registered capital of 10.67 million yuan (US$1.59 million), according to the corporate database Qichacha. It is led by Gu Bin, who completed a doctoral degree at Tianjin University’s medical school, according to Chinese media reports. Another recent approval went to a micro-electrode driver developed by StairMed Technology – a start-up backed by Chinese tech giants Tencent Holdings and Alibaba Group Holding – which is used to help implant BCI devices during brain surgery. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. The approval, granted by the NMPA in June, marks a boost for StairMed’s push to develop a working BCI implant. The company was still trying out its implant, with 18 patients having received it so far, domestic media reported in July. These trials had shown promise, with the implant allowing one paraplegic patient to communicate with customers on the Chinese e-commerce platform JD.com by using their thoughts to operate a digital device, said Zhao Zhengtuo, the company’s co-founder, during an event last month. Shanghai-based start-up Neuracle Medical Technology, meanwhile, in March won China’s first regulatory approval for an implantable BCI device designed to help people with spinal cord injuries regain hand movement. Another start-up, Hangzhou-based BrainCo, is developing BCI products to aid depression screening in partnership with a hospital affiliated to Beijing’s Capital Medical University, according to the company. Local governments are ramping up support for the sector. Eastern China’s Zhejiang province has unveiled plans to encourage related firms to go public, while the southern tech hub of Shenzhen has pledged to help firms expand overseas and complete mergers and acquisitions. China’s ageing population has fuelled a rise in neurological disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease, with cases climbing from about 329 million in 1990 to about 468 million by 2021, according to a study published in the journal Med last year. China’s BCI market is projected to reach 6.14 billion yuan by 2028, according to Xinhua.

title: SOTY 25/26: Linguist (Cantonese) winner went from struggling learner to language advocate
description: Jaden Zhao Ziyu wants students with Mandarin backgrounds like her to feel empowered to learn and appreciate the ‘warmth’ of Cantonese.
content:
For Jaden Zhao Ziyu, Cantonese is not just a school subject. The language is a live score of the jokes, songs and everyday rhythms that have become a part of her identity.
It’s particularly noteworthy because Jaden is a cross-border student; she lives in mainland China and attends school in Hong Kong.
The Form Five student at TWGHs Kap Yan Directors’ College grew up in a multilingual environment, which taught her to recognise the differences between Cantonese and Mandarin as well as appreciate the diverse cultural values each tongue carries.
“Through Cantonese immersion, [the language] has become more than grammar and a tool for communication to me; it is home and a compass for everything I do,” the 16-year-old said.
Jaden said her passion for the language grew because of encouragement from the people around her.
“Their support made me curious,” she said. “The more I learned, the more I became interested in the cultural aspects – films, songs, jokes and daily life. Cantonese stopped being just a school subject; it became part of my identity and gave me a sense of belonging.”
Jaden was candid about the technical linguistic hurdles and psychological barriers she faced. “Putonghua has four tones whereas Cantonese has nine, and using the wrong tone for the same word can completely change its meaning. Consequently, learning Cantonese demanded considerable time and patience,” she said.
Equally difficult was the internal voice that told her she would never master the language. “Changing this defeatist attitude was a significant challenge,” she said.
Her strategy was built on staying steady and being patient with herself. “I adjusted my own perspective by accepting that mistakes are an inherent part of the learning process. I practised consistently and acknowledged small achievements,” Jaden explained.
She measured her success in tiny, human moments: “Every time I noticed myself getting a little better at speaking or understanding, I felt motivated. When I could say a sentence more naturally than before, or when I understood a joke without needing a translation, it reminded me why I started learning,” she said.
To challenge herself, Jaden joined student language competitions, such as the 22nd Biliteracy and Trilingualism Composition and Speech Competition in Hong Kong, where she placed third.
“To prepare for competitions, I used all three languages in daily life,” she said, adding that she spoke with friends, listened to the news, wrote short essays and recorded her voice to find weak spots.
“The competition showed me that my love for languages is a real strength. It gave me confidence and motivated me to dive deeper in the future.”
Jaden said she wanted to use her story to show others they could learn Cantonese too.
She mapped out a mission: to pass on the “warmth of Cantonese” – the small, human textures that make the language. Her goal is to make Cantonese a living language among students with a Putonghua background.
“I have helped organise impromptu speech sessions, trained juniors in communication and debate, and created spaces where mistakes are part of learning,” she said. “I tailor methods – stories and songs for younger learners; conversation practice for adults; and patient repetition for those who struggle with tones.”
Jaden said she was driven by the desire to build supportive learning environments for others that she never got to experience herself.
Jaden said she felt the best way to learn a language was through its culture, to “discover what makes it interesting”.
“My plan was hands-on: visiting community centres, working with minority groups and sharing my story as proof that Cantonese is learnable.”
Memorable moments included seeing quieter students find their voice, peers laugh together at a shared joke in Cantonese and a ripple of confidence that made the language feel communal.
Now, as she evolves from learner to advocate, the young student plans to host more talks and structured mentoring to build a community where all pupils can support one another.
“I want future Cantonese advocates to believe that anyone can learn this language, regardless of their background,” she said. “Above all, I hope the warmth of Cantonese continues to spread.”
Jaden’s commitment to language promotion and cultural preservation was recognised at the 2025/26 Student of the Year Awards, where she won the Linguist (Cantonese) category. The awards were organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club.

title: 3 eye-catching home decor items from Ginger & Jagger, Panconesi and Marc Newson x Taschen
description: From a cactus-legged console to a bookstand for your most treasured coffee-table tome, these statement pieces are instant talking points.
content: Whether you’re searching for sculptural furniture or gem-encrusted decor, the following interior design pieces are sure to bring a little personality to your home, or at the very least serve as conversation pieces. Ginger & Jagger Made of marble and brass, this console from Portuguese furniture maker Ginger & Jagger stands out for its cactus leaf “legs”. It is part of the brand’s nature-inspired Earth to Earth collection. Place it against a white wall to add a sculptural element to a minimalist environment. Marc Newson x Taschen Marc Newson – himself the subject of many coffee table books highlighting his work as one of the most important industrial designers living today – has now teamed up with German luxury publisher Taschen for this very special object. The publisher is known for lavishly illustrated books that are often as visually stunning as the photos printed in them. This tripod bookstand, designed in partnership with Newson and made of acrylic glass, aluminium and steel, is the perfect way to display one of the company’s prized and extravagant Collector’s Editions. Panconesi Italian jeweller Panconesi makes its debut in the world of interior design with Conversation Piece, a collection of jewellery-inspired design objects. Recalling a totem pole, the Ascolto Candelabra is made with a stack of gemstones ranging from aventurine to obsidian. Cylindrical metal vases are embellished with gem-set stems, while in the striking Ascolto Clock, gemstones such as carnelian and malachite are used as hour markers. Additional contributions by Sumnima Kandangwa

title: Singapore jails Indian man who hid US$154,000 diamond in mouth during heist
description: Serasiya Milan Ramnikbhai and his accomplice were caught at the airport following the Chinatown robbery.
content: A thief was sentenced to 26 months and two weeks’ jail on Tuesday for his role in a Singapore Chinatown diamond heist. He had hidden a custom-made fake gem in his mouth, switched it for the real diamond and concealed the genuine stone the same way. Serasiya Milan Ramnikbhai, a 30-year-old from India, pleaded guilty to a charge of theft with common intention. His accomplice, 41-year-old Mangroliya Manojkumar Kurjibha, was handed the same jail term in July. The pair had commissioned a counterfeit diamond in Surat, India, matching the targeted diamond’s specifications and serial number. Serasiya’s lawyer, Amarick Gill, said that Mangroliya formed the plan, sourced the counterfeit diamond, identified the trader Dianoche Diamonds Jewelry, and booked the flights and accommodation. He also instructed Serasiya to conceal the counterfeit diamond in his mouth and swap it in exchange for money. The duo entered Singapore on June 19 this year intending to steal the 4.95-carat diamond, valued at US$154,000, from the store in Chinatown. They asked to view the gemstone at about 3pm, with Mangroliya distracting the sales manager by asking to see several items. Serasiya then spat out the fake diamond and switched it with the real gem, concealing the stone in his mouth. His actions were captured on closed-circuit television footage. Mangroliya then told the sales manager that he would consider the purchase before leaving with Serasiya. The pair returned to their hotel and booked a flight to India departing that evening, but the sales manager examined the fake gem and found it to be counterfeit. The men were arrested at Changi Airport while trying to clear immigration. The genuine diamond was later recovered from Serasiya’s haversack. The prosecutor sought the same jail term meted out to Mangroliya based on the principle of parity. She said there was no material difference in their culpability to warrant an adjustment to the sentence for Serasiya. Gill also sought a jail term similar to what Mangroliya received. He said that his client is married and has a six-month-old son. Serasiya is the family’s sole breadwinner and owns a small shop selling textiles and garments. The lawyer said that the plan was hatched by Mangroliya, who worked in the gem industry, while Serasiya knew nothing of the gem trade. For theft, he could have been jailed for up to seven years and fined. This story was first published by CNA

title: Chinese internet giants set to reap artificial intelligence profits in 2 to 3 years: UBS
description: Despite short term macro headwinds, vast user bases and costs are positioning Chinese firms for gains.
content: Internet platforms with vast data and large user bases will capture a larger share of artificial intelligence profits in two to three years, even though macro headwinds have temporarily fuelled investor caution over aggressive AI spending by Chinese tech giants, UBS analysts said. Investors have been cautious over a weak macro environment in the second half of the year, and greater AI spending for hardware and infrastructure would drag down short-term profits, but the industry’s power balance was set to flip soon, according to Kenneth Fong, head of China internet research at UBS. “This is all about the cycle. Now the capacity constraint is on the upstream... so [they] capture a big chunk of the whole profit pool,” Fong said in an interview on Tuesday on the sidelines of a UBS event in Shenzhen. “But two to three years down the road after the capacity constraint eases, the pricing power will shift to the downstream, where they have the distribution capability, data and users,” Fong noted. “The internet company will start to work again.” To strengthen their AI war chest, Chinese tech giants have been ramping up their capital expenditures in the past quarter, at the expense of their free cash flows. Tencent Holdings nearly tripled its second-quarter capex to 52.8 billion yuan (US$7.85 billion), while it posted a negative free cash flow of 13.8 billion yuan for the first time. Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the South China Morning Post, saw its free cash outflow in the June quarter more than double to 44.7 billion yuan year on year, on the back of a 67.7 billion yuan quarterly outlay. Still, the total spending of Chinese technology firms was eclipsed by their US counterparts, accounting for only one-seventh of that of American giants, as the former faced restricted access to advanced foreign chips and operated at smaller scales, according to Fong. Major Chinese technology firms were both defensive and offensive with their AI spending, as they feared missing out on AI advancements while seeing strong returns in cloud and existing business integrations, Fong said, adding that they are using one year to one-and-a-half years’ annual cash flows for their investments. “Even if AI fails to materialise, they basically give up one year of profit, but at least they can make sure they are still in the game,” Fong said. However, compared with US AI firms, Chinese AI labs and tech giants have stood out with a clear advantage in cost efficiency, according to Xiong Wei, China internet analyst at UBS Securities. The training costs for China’s models are estimated to be less than 10 per cent of those of global leaders, while the average API price of major China models was less than 20 per cent of their comparable global peers, Xiong said at the UBS briefing. “On this basis, domestic model developers are not operating at a loss,” Xiong said. “Rather than burning cash for adoption, Chinese developers are maintaining healthy gross margins while utilising technological innovation to enhance profitability, which continuously optimises their training and inference efficiency even as model usage grows rapidly.”

title: Japan’s deadliest delicacy is getting more dangerous
description: Rising sea temperatures are pushing pufferfish species together, spawning hybrids that even specialist chefs cannot safely prepare.
content: Japan’s most dangerous delicacy is getting harder to prepare safely as warming seas push different pufferfish species into the same waters, where they are inbreeding to produce hybrids whose lethal toxins are not yet fully understood. Fugu – the collective Japanese name for several species of edible pufferfish – is prized as much for the danger surrounding its preparation as for its subtle flavour. Many species contain tetrodotoxin, a powerful neurotoxin with no known antidote that can cause paralysis, respiratory failure and death. Since 1958, anyone wishing to prepare pufferfish for public consumption has had to obtain a licence first, a process that takes at least two years and defeats roughly two-thirds of those who attempt it. Chefs learn to strip out the fish’s liver, ovaries, eyes and skin – tissues where the poison concentrates – with the precision of a brain surgeon and the nerve of a bomb-disposal technician. But that hard-won expertise is now being undermined by climate-induced interbreeding, as experts say Japan’s coastal waters are heating up at roughly twice the global average rate. Spotted pufferfish, once largely confined to the Sea of Japan or East Sea, have spent the past decade steadily pushing northward in search of cooler currents. Some slipped through the Tsugaru Strait – the channel separating Honshu from far northern Hokkaido – where they have met and mated with the region’s native pufferfish species. The resulting hybrids now make up as much as 40 per cent of local catches, according to a recent study of fish caught off Fukushima and Ibaraki prefectures. “We started seeing these spotted fugu on the Pacific coast in 2012 as temperatures in the Sea of Japan became too high for them,” said Professor Hiroshi Takahashi of the National Fisheries University in Shimonoseki, Yamaguchi prefecture. Temperatures in the waters there were “among the fastest rising anywhere in the world”, he told This Week in Asia, adding that the changes in pufferfish had been happening just as fast. Some spotted pufferfish had ventured down the east coast as far south as Tokyo Bay, Takahashi said, only to be driven north again as those waters also warmed. Tiger pufferfish had likewise moved north from their usual range to interbreed with common pufferfish in and around Tokyo Bay, he added. The trouble is not that hybrids are more toxic than their ancestors, it is that nobody yet knows how interbreeding has affected the distribution of toxins. Each species of pufferfish stores tetrodotoxin in a different combination of organs and Japan’s health ministry has not yet been able to establish which parts of the new hybrids are safe to eat and which are not. Until it does, the government has banned the sale or consumption of hybrid fugu – but this ban is almost impossible to enforce. “They are very hard to identify,” said Takahashi, whose team has developed a DNA test capable of distinguishing hybrid fish and hopes to make the technology commercially available to fishermen who currently have no reliable way of screening their catch. Fatal attraction None of this is likely to diminish fugu’s deadly mystique. The dish has been eaten in Japan for centuries, enjoyed despite – or because of – the risks involved. Every year, new tales emerge of amateur anglers preparing the fish to eat against the advice of anxious relatives and not surviving the attempt. Diners speak of a faint numbness in the lips as evidence of a narrow escape and the emperor of Japan is barred from eating fugu altogether, lest even a licensed chef makes a mistake. Urban legend holds that chefs who do poison a customer are honour-bound to end their own life, with their own knife, in atonement – though this is a myth. For their part, Japanese restaurateurs are, perhaps unsurprisingly, keen to play down the risks. A spokeswoman for Miyawaki Fugu Club, an upscale restaurant in Tokyo’s Ginza district, said its chef works exclusively with farmed tiger pufferfish from a long-established supplier, which she insisted were “completely safe”. James Reimer, a professor of marine biology at the University of the Ryukyus, said the fugu phenomenon fit a wider pattern of marine life relocating in response to global warming. “What happens to marine ecosystems is one of the hot-button issues of the day, particularly in Japan, because the waters here are warming at twice the global average rate,” he said. During fieldwork off the Izu peninsula, south of Tokyo, three years ago, local fishermen told him that they had lost virtually their entire kelp crop and that the abalone once abundant in those waters had vanished. In their place, they said they were seeing far more sea turtles, as well as large schools of brightly coloured fusiliers – the prefectural fish of Okinawa, some 1,400km (870 miles) to the south. “Last year, our summer in Okinawa was 30 days longer than average, and we had 120 days when the water temperature was around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit),” Reimer said. He warns that the picture is not simply one of fish and other marine life swimming steadily north in search of more comfortable temperatures, however. Global warming is also destabilising weather patterns, making them less predictable. Waters off Kyushu, the southernmost of Japan’s main islands, that might otherwise suit certain species are increasingly prone to temperature swings that could make them unsuitable after all. Even so, the broader direction is unmistakable. Kyushu’s waters have seen a marked rise in shark sightings in recent years, including large tiger sharks – one more sign of the changes occurring beneath the surface of Japan’s seas.

title: Opinion | China’s multipolar world order must prove it can be peaceful
description: To translate its well-articulated vision into practice, Beijing must flesh out concrete mechanics, starting with institutional design.
content: China has spent years articulating its preferred principles for the world order. In June, it went a step further, bringing many of them together in a white paper on global governance and setting out how its Global Governance Initiative should translate principles into practice. Two ambitions sat side by side: an “equal and orderly multipolar world” and a “universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalisation”. The timing is telling. World leaders will gather in New York this month for the 81st United Nations General Assembly under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation”. The difficult word in China’s formulation is no longer “multipolar”; it is “orderly”. Multipolarity itself is becoming easier to imagine. Middle powers increasingly hedge rather than choose sides, seeking more room to bargain among multiple centres of power. Such diffusion of power, however, is far from the natural company of order. The post-Cold War era was once sustained by an expectation that deeper economic integration would narrow political differences. Francis Fukuyama gave the idea perhaps its most famous expression. Today, if anything has ended, it is not history but the very confidence that history has a single political destination. The problem of the emerging order is therefore not convergence, but sustained coexistence. China is central to this question. Its vision for a multipolar world rests ultimately on the consequential proposition that countries fundamentally different can nevertheless stay economically connected and coexist peacefully. Beijing has good reason to want this to succeed. A more diffused distribution of power could enlarge China’s strategic room for manoeuvre, giving other states more space to engage with Beijing without entering its orbit. But the erosion of hierarchy and the erosion of order are not the same thing: China may benefit from the first while becoming increasingly vulnerable to the second. This relates to the political economy of Chinese power. Major disorder hurts both China and the US. Insecurity, however, changes what types of power are more valued. When governments worry more about war, coercion and physical security, alliances, intelligence networks and security guarantees become more valuable. These are areas of exceptional American strength. Much of China’s influence travels through a rather different portfolio: manufacturing, trade, infrastructure, ports, commodity flows, investment and supply chains. These assets work best when sea lanes are safe, markets remain open and political risk is contained. A dangerous world places a premium on protection. A stable world places a premium on connectivity. Ukraine has shown how prolonged conflict can harden security alignments. The turmoil around the Strait of Hormuz illustrates the commercial side of the same problem even more directly. China has repeatedly called for the restoration of safe and free passage through the strait, describing it as an interest shared by the international community, including – notably – itself. For China, insecurity in a major energy and shipping artery places a geopolitical tax on the networks through which its power travels. It consequently has a material interest in preventing insecurity from becoming the organising principle of a more multipolar world. The Beijing-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement in 2023 offers a preliminary indication of what a different approach could look like. But one diplomatic breakthrough does not constitute a durable order. Restored Saudi-Iranian relations did not produce an architecture capable of containing a wider war. A communique signed in Beijing is one thing. Building institutions that survive the next crisis is another. China itself appears increasingly conscious of this gap. Foreign Minister Wang Yi has argued that repeated turmoil should prompt regional states to explore a new regional security architecture. The harder question is what such an architecture would actually do. Beijing already possesses an extensive vocabulary for its preferred international order. What remains less developed is the connective tissue between them: freedom of navigation could come into tension with sovereign discretion; non-interference may limit serious efforts at mediation; strategic autonomy may strengthen smaller states’ bargaining power while making trade and investment less predictable. Saying that all these principles matter does not by itself explain how an orderly system should respond when they collide. That is the missing middle between world view and practice – and the starting point for institutional design. China could treat global connectivity itself more explicitly as a public good, keeping commercial shipping, energy flows and civilian supply chains functioning when politics deteriorates. This need not require China to reproduce the network of bases, alliances and security guarantees associated with American primacy. The more interesting question is whether Beijing could help devise institutions that perform some of the stabilising functions of hierarchy without reproducing hierarchy itself. China has long asked the world to see it as peace-loving. In a more fragmented age, that will no longer be sufficient. It must also show that it is peace-benefiting: that the sources of Chinese prosperity and influence give Beijing a material stake in international stability. Increasingly, it will also have to become peacemaking – capable not simply of helping governments reach agreements, but of helping create the mechanisms through which agreements can withstand the next shock. The post-Cold War era imagined that convergence would make peaceful coexistence easier. China now has the opportunity – and the interest – to demonstrate something harder: that a world which does not converge might still remain safe and orderly. If it can do so, the strongest argument for multipolarity will certainly not be that it weakens American power. It will be that international order can endure without depending on any single power’s dominance.

title: Chinese workers use parasols and sunscreen indoors to combat ‘office ageing’
description: To relieve anxiety, some workers turn empty milk-tea cups into makeshift humidifiers or keep unusual desk ‘pets’ like rocks and mango pits.
content: A growing number of Chinese workers are sharing tips on social media to combat “office ageing.” Suggestions range from applying sunscreen and using full-face masks to setting up parasols at their desks. Recently, a RedNote user with the handle @lelehangmu from Jiangsu province in eastern China shared that just one month into his job, his complexion had noticeably darkened, and his eyes frequently felt strained. The post quickly resonated with others. Another user reported that she appeared significantly fairer after taking time off, while a third expressed frustration over persistent second-hand smoke in shared office spaces. In response, some workers have started erecting parasols at their desks, donning sun hats or face coverings, and generously applying sunscreen to their faces and arms. Lighting designer Yoki informed a mainland media outlet that offices often favour cool-toned lighting to keep workers alert, with the hope that this will enhance productivity. However, lighting is just one aspect of a larger problem concerning the office environment. Dry air, dust-laden ventilation systems, and elevated carbon dioxide levels can exacerbate the physical discomfort and mental fatigue associated with long hours in the workplace. In the 1980s, the World Health Organization introduced the term “sick building syndrome” to describe a range of symptoms linked to time spent in certain buildings, even when no specific illness could be diagnosed. These symptoms include headaches, nasal congestion, dry skin, throat irritation, fatigue, and poor concentration, often worsening with prolonged exposure and subsiding once individuals leave the premises. The syndrome emerged alongside changes in modern architecture and energy conservation initiatives. To reduce heating and cooling costs, many buildings became increasingly airtight, inadvertently limiting the flow of fresh air indoors. In a 2008 study, Indian social medicine scholar Sumedha Joshi connected sick building syndrome to decreased productivity and higher absentee rates, recommending improved ventilation, regular breaks, and strategies to alleviate workplace stress. On social media, concern about the office environment has expanded from health to appearance. A TikTok trend highlights the contrast between photos taken at the beginning of the workday and those snapped several hours later: polished make-up and bright eyes in the morning give way to greasy hair, dull skin, and facial puffiness by evening. Chinese internet users have also attributed prolonged sitting to forward-leaning necks and rounded shoulders, while others humorously note that habitual frowning while working has etched “thinking lines” into their faces. One netizen posed the question: “I age in the office every day. The company pays for my labour, but who will cover my beauty and health?” In China, some workers are creating their own forms of workplace self-care, turning empty milk-tea cups into makeshift humidifiers or keeping unconventional desk “pets,” such as rocks and mango pits, which they caress or pat to relieve anxiety. Beneath these coping strategies lies a deeper concern regarding working conditions and excessively long hours. As of May, the average working hours per week in China reportedly hovered around 48.2 hours, exceeding the statutory 44-hour limit. As one online observer aptly noted: “A good office is not a perk but a basic right. People should shape the workplace, not be reduced to cogs in cubicles.”

title: Beyond coal: China’s installed solar power capacity crosses historic threshold
description: Beijing says the transition marks a turning point but integrating the 31.5 per cent share still requires a multi-trillion-yuan push to forge a modern grid.
content: Solar power has overtaken coal as China’s largest source of installed power generation capacity for the first time, marking a landmark shift in the world’s largest energy market, according to government data. By the end of July, China’s installed photovoltaic capacity had reached 1,286 gigawatts, accounting for 31.5 per cent of the total, the National Energy Administration (NEA) reported on Tuesday. The agency called the milestone a “signature achievement” in China’s green and low-carbon energy transition. “For over a century, since the birth of China’s electric power industry, the historical pattern of coal power serving as the largest power source has been broken,” the NEA posted on its official WeChat account. The infrastructure milestone comes on the heels of earlier official data showing that coal’s share of generated electricity dropped below 50 per cent for the first time during the first half of 2026. By comparison, solar generation accounted for 13 per cent of total electricity consumption by the end of July. In the first seven months of the year, the country generated 802.4 billion kilowatt-hours of solar power, a 15.5 per cent year-on-year surge. China now produces about 80 per cent of the world’s solar modules and has built what the NEA called the world’s “most complete and most competitive” photovoltaic industrial chain. As large volumes of solar and wind capacity come online, China is also accelerating upgrades to its power grid, aiming to build what it describes as a “new-type power system” capable of integrating the growing share of renewable energy. Investment in China’s new-type power grid was expected to exceed 5 trillion yuan (US$743.8 billion) during the 15th five-year plan period covering 2026 to 2030, the NEA said at a press conference in June. The power system is one of “six networks” that Beijing has pledged to strengthen in high-level meetings in recent months. The broader initiative covers other critical infrastructure, including computing networks, telecommunications and underground utility pipelines. In a note on Monday, Larry Hu, Macquarie Group’s chief China economist, said Beijing had stepped up fiscal support to sustain growth for the rest of the year, following weaker-than-expected economic data for July and the second quarter. “Infrastructure investment, particularly in the ‘six networks’, will be the focus,” he added. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence has also turned reliable energy systems into a critical arena of international competition. Large-scale AI deployment demands vast computing power, while surging computing load is driving sharp increases in electricity consumption. In Changshu, an affluent city in eastern China’s Jiangsu province, electricity consumed by data centres and other computing infrastructure surpassed residential air conditioning demand this summer, according to state broadcaster CCTV. Citing local utility data, the report noted last week that the computing industry contributed nearly half of the city’s incremental power demand, becoming the main driver of summer electricity demand growth.

title: Robots show off their skills at World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing
description: A few humanoids have beaten human records in sprinting, but they have trouble with braking.
content:
The five-day World Humanoid Robot Games took place in Beijing last month. The event included contests based on human sports. It also had challenges to see how robots could perform in places like factories, restaurants and offices.
Two robots ran faster than Usain Bolt’s 9.58-second world record in the 100-metre sprint. That was better than 2025, when the winning robot’s time was more than 20 seconds. But the robots struggled to stop and slammed into a mat placed after ‌the finish line.
Another humanoid ran 400 metres in 39.7 seconds. This is faster than South Africa’s Wayde van Niekerk, who has the world record of 43.03 seconds.
Robots also competed in charging electric vehicles, working in restaurants and handling emergencies.
Hua Rong is the chief marketing officer at robotics firm Zeroth. She said the real test would be after the demonstrations: “The competition will be whether, after the product is sold, it can really solve users’ problems.”

title: Tanker, transporter, controller: China’s Y-20 family expands its Pacific reach
description: Answer to strategic airlift shortage is becoming a family of support aircraft able to sustain combat missions deep into western Pacific.
content: When six Chinese heavy transport planes entered European airspace in April 2022, it was not just their cargo that drew international attention. Bound for Serbia, the Y-20 aircraft had flown thousands of kilometres from China carrying components of the Chinese-made FK-3 surface-to-air missile system. A second wave of six aircraft followed, bringing the operation to 12 sorties in what was then China’s biggest overseas airlift involving the strategic cargo plane. Coming just weeks after Russia invaded Ukraine, the delivery raised concerns among European capitals about Belgrade’s growing military ties with Beijing. But the operation also revealed something significant about Chinese capabilities: the People’s Liberation Army could now use its own heavy transport aircraft to move military equipment from East Asia deep into Europe. At the centre of that capability was the Y-20 Kunpeng, China’s first domestically developed heavy military transport. Four years on, the aircraft is evolving into something considerably more versatile. China has introduced an improved version powered by domestically produced engines, confirmed that the airframe can switch between transport and aerial-refuelling roles, and is using it as the basis for a new airborne early-warning aircraft. What began as China’s answer to a shortage of strategic airlift is becoming a family of support aircraft that could help the PLA move forces further from home and sustain and coordinate combat aircraft deeper into the western Pacific. China’s home-grown heavy airlifter China formally launched its large transport aircraft programme in 2007, with the Xian Aircraft Corporation leading development. The first Y-20 flew in January 2013 and entered PLA Air Force service in July 2016, giving Beijing an indigenous heavy airlifter after years of mostly relying on imported Russian Il-76 aircraft. The platform’s development was driven in part by Beijing’s difficulty in acquiring additional Russian Il-76 transports and Il-78 tankers, according to Andreas Rupprecht, a specialist in Chinese military aviation and author of several books on the subject. Designed to fill that strategic void, the Y-20 can carry a maximum payload of roughly 66 tonnes, with an estimated range of about 3,700km (2,300 miles) at that load. But the Serbia mission highlighted how refuelling stops along the route could extend the airlifter’s reach far beyond its range on a single flight. One of the programme’s most important changes has come under the wings, however. The original Y-20A uses Russian D-30KP-II turbofan engines. The newer Y-20B instead uses four domestically produced WS-20 high-bypass turbofans. The WS-20 offers greater thrust and better fuel efficiency than the D-30, although reliable public figures quantifying the resulting gains in range or payload are not available. More broadly, replacing Russian engines gives China greater control over the production and future development of an aircraft increasingly central to its long-range aviation capabilities. Rupprecht estimates that around 90 Y-20A-family transports and tankers were operational by August 2025, while close to two dozen Y-20Bs were in service or awaiting delivery. From transport to tanker The Y-20 has also helped China address another constraint on its ability to project air power: aerial refuelling. China has developed a dedicated tanker derivative, the YY-20A, which allows combat and other aircraft to fly further and remain airborne longer – an increasingly important capability as PLA operations extend deeper into the western Pacific and across the South China Sea. Its growing utility was on show during joint exercises with Egypt in August, when a YY-20A was photographed refuelling an Egyptian Air Force Rafale – a rare example of a Chinese tanker supporting a foreign-made combat aircraft. But rather than relying solely on dedicated tankers, China is now adding greater flexibility to the Y-20 fleet itself. State broadcaster CCTV confirmed earlier this month that the Y-20B could switch between transport and aerial-refuelling missions by installing additional fuel tanks and removable refuelling equipment. Rupprecht argues that the evidence points towards the Y-20B becoming a common multi-role tanker-transport platform rather than China maintaining entirely separate production lines for B-model transports and tankers. Such an arrangement could allow commanders to shift aircraft between two critical tasks – moving troops and equipment or refuelling combat aircraft – as operational requirements changed. It would also allow the PLA Air Force to generate additional tanker capacity from its transport fleet when required, rather than relying entirely on dedicated tanker aircraft. That flexibility could be particularly valuable during sustained operations further into the western Pacific or over the South China Sea. However, no operational Y-20B has yet been publicly observed fitted with the complete tanker configuration. Rupprecht assesses that the necessary fuel-transfer systems and wiring may already be incorporated into production aircraft even when the external refuelling equipment is absent. Seeing further from shore Yet the platform’s evolution extends beyond transport and aerial refuelling. The Y-20B is also providing the basis for the KJ-3000 airborne early-warning and control aircraft, which has been undergoing flight testing since late 2024. As PLA combat aircraft expand their operational reach, the KJ-3000 is intended to solve another problem: greater range matters little without the ability to detect threats, track targets and coordinate operations across an expanding battlespace. The KJ-3000’s large dorsal radar is designed to provide airborne surveillance and command-and-control capabilities that could complement or eventually replace China’s ageing KJ-2000 fleet, which is based on the Russian Il-76. Its development highlights a broader consequence of the Y-20 programme: China now has a domestically produced large-aircraft platform that can be adapted for specialised roles, further reducing its reliance on imported airframes. That capability is becoming more important as Beijing asks the PLA to operate further from home. A Taiwan conflict could require sustained high-intensity operations while potentially confronting US and allied forces across the western Pacific, while the South China Sea presents another vast operating area. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries, including the United States – Taiwan’s main international backer, do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take Taiwan by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

title: HKU partners with tech giants to offer AI labs at expanded Shanghai campus
description: University’s campus in Zhangjiang Science City, Shanghai, welcomed more than 300 students for new term, with plans to expand intake.
content: The University of Hong Kong (HKU) is partnering with tech giants to offer on-site artificial intelligence (AI) laboratories at its expanded Shanghai campus, which welcomed more than 300 students for the new term earlier this week. The campus in Zhangjiang Science City is also expected to expand its intake next year, when the university’s medicine and engineering programmes launch there. Its computing and data science school opened a base in Shanghai in mid-January. The university signed memorandums of understanding with 17 Hong Kong and mainland Chinese companies, including Unitree Robotics, BrainCo and AgiBot, on Sunday to open joint labs specialising in AI and fintech at the campus. The labs are housed in one of the two new buildings inaugurated at the university’s Shanghai campus the same day. Two other blocks housing teaching and research facilities opened in mid-January, while three other buildings will open later. The entire campus spans more than 30,000 square metres. Speaking at the opening ceremony for the new buildings, university president Xiang Zhang said the Shanghai campus would draw on the mainland city’s strengths in innovation and industry to advance partnerships involving AI and frontier technologies. “As the university that has achieved the best global integration in China, and currently holds the highest QS ranking in the country, we must have the confidence to lead educational reform,” he said, referring to the annual Quacquarelli Symonds league tables. “Our funding is only half that of Tsinghua University, yet our research output and overall academic ranking are comparable to or even higher than Tsinghua’s, so we have the efficiency.” Professor Ma Yi, director of HKU’s computing and data science school, said the Shanghai campus would put computing and AI as its core and explore robotics, engineering and healthcare. He said Hong Kong and Shanghai were highly complementary, with the former having a more internationalised student body. “Shanghai is very rich, especially in technology and computing. Its industry is very complete, covering the Yangtze River Delta and even the whole country,” he said. Ma said students would benefit from the collaboration with companies on campus. “They have on-site space, so our students can do internships and participate in frontier technology without leaving our campus,” he said. The school offers programmes spanning the two campuses, with master’s students spending a semester in Shanghai and undergraduates completing 2½ years in Hong Kong before moving to the other campus for the final leg of their studies and internships. The Shanghai campus has welcomed more than 1,000 students since its launch, including over 300 who started the new term on Monday. Zhangjiang Science City is one of Shanghai’s core artificial intelligence clusters, hosting more than 600 AI enterprises and over 30,000 staff. The various fields represented at the science city include foundation models, computing power, data services and embodied intelligence. Marcus Law, a second-year computer science student from Hong Kong, said he chose the programme to experience Zhangjiang’s research environment and access the mainland’s technology ecosystem. He said that he was primarily interested in bioinformatics and hoped to observe how companies operated, as well as their systems and research directions, during his semester in Shanghai. He said the mainland offered a more vibrant environment for development. “Everything is digitised and convenient – the facilities, transport and food are all very accessible – and the investment in AI is greater than in Hong Kong,” he said. Asked whether he would stay in Shanghai or return to Hong Kong after graduation, Law said he was keeping an eye on developments in the Northern Metropolis and the Greater Bay Area. Tunige Tuerxunbieke, a Kazakh computer science master’s student who grew up in Xinjiang, enrolled at HKU after graduating from Tsinghua University in the same field. She had also applied to universities in the United States but ultimately chose HKU due to uncertainties about the admission of mainland students to AI programmes in the country this year and HKU’s willingness to accept Tsinghua graduates, she said. She said visits to Hong Kong’s Cyberport and the Science Park had left her impressed with the city’s support for student innovation. “Hong Kong universities provide a lot of help for student innovation and place great emphasis on an innovative atmosphere,” she said. “This programme also gives us a lot of freedom. We can intern both on the mainland and in Hong Kong.” She added that she hoped to work in Hong Kong and eventually launch her own start-up there, while continuing to specialise in AI agents. In addition to the campus at Zhangjiang Science City, HKU operates from three other locations in Shanghai. They include the Bund SOHO Base, led by the business school. It became operational in December 2025 and delivers programmes that include executive master of business administration and doctor of business administration degrees for working professionals. The campus at Zhangjiang Science City launched alongside the Bund 22 alumni hub on February 28 this year, while the third location is the Caohejing Base, which opened on March 1 and houses research institutes focused on healthy ageing and urban science.

title: Enflame’s US$900m IPO tests appetite for China’s ‘little dragon’ AI chipmakers
description: Fuelled by Beijing’s tech self-reliance push, the company is set to test investor confidence in specialised hardware.
content: As Enflame Technology gears up for a 6.12 billion yuan (US$910.3 million) initial public offering on Shanghai’s Star Market, the Chinese artificial intelligence chipmaker must convince investors that its specialised chip strategy can withstand fierce competition from Huawei Technologies and other domestic rivals, while reducing its heavy revenue dependence on major backer Tencent Holdings. Online and offline subscriptions open on Wednesday, after the Shanghai-based start-up announced on Monday that it would issue 43.04 million shares at 142.18 yuan (US$21.15) apiece. The debut will cap a historic public fundraising wave by China’s “four little dragons” of AI chips – Enflame, Moore Threads, Biren Technology and MetaX Integrated Circuits – as domestic players race to scale production amid export curbs by the United States on advanced Nvidia hardware. Moore Threads led the parade with an 8 billion yuan Star Market debut in December, followed by MetaX and Biren, which raised 4.2 billion yuan late last year and HK$7 billion (US$897 million) earlier this year, respectively. However, while the sector is benefiting from Beijing’s push for technological self-sufficiency and a nationwide buildout of AI infrastructure, Enflame faces some distinct strategic hurdles. Chief among them is its product road map. Unlike Nvidia and its three domestic peers – which focus on general-purpose graphics processing units (GPUs) capable of handling a wide range of workflows – Enflame has staked its future on domain-specific architecture (DSA). As an advanced evolution of application-specific integrated circuits, DSA is designed to maximise computing efficiency for targeted tasks such as AI inference. “DSA will capture significant market share in standardised enterprise and internet inference tasks,” said Guo Tao, a Beijing-based angel investor focused on AI. But Guo cautioned that its more limited flexibility could create bottlenecks during rapid AI model iterations, giving an edge to GPUs compatible with Nvidia’s software ecosystem across mixed-workload markets. Guo added that the domestic AI chip industry was likely to face a market shakeout over the next two years, increasingly consolidating “around vendors capable of stable, large-scale commercial delivery and optimised customer structures”. That concentration could prove to be Enflame’s second major vulnerability: Tencent is not only its largest shareholder with a 20 per cent stake, but also its primary revenue anchor. According to the company’s prospectus, sales to the social media and gaming giant accounted for 33 per cent of Enflame’s revenue in 2023 and 38 per cent in 2024, before surging to 84 per cent in 2025. “Relying on a single major client is a standard survival path early on,” Guo said. “However, growth becomes constrained by the client’s strategic shifts, while also weakening momentum in the broader commercial market.” Enflame addressed this concentration risk in its prospectus, stating that Tencent’s demand for AI accelerator cards currently “far exceeded” the chipmaker’s supply capacity and that it planned to gradually expand into broader enterprise markets. Beyond commercial adoption, execution could depend heavily on navigating supply chain constraints. While bottlenecks in China’s computing sector had shown signs of easing in recent months, securing foundry capacity and component supplies remained critical, said Jimmy Yu, head of China technology research at UBS Securities. “It’s not just the foundries – high-bandwidth memory, capacitors and printed circuit boards can all become bottlenecks,” Yu said during a media briefing last week. Wednesday’s subscription opening could offer an immediate gauge of retail and institutional appetite for Enflame’s specialised hardware strategy as the domestic semiconductor landscape enters a mature, execution-driven phase.

title: North Korea’s next ruler? Kim Jong-un’s daughter, Seoul’s spies say
description: She has the leather coat and state media backing, but analysts say Kim Ju-ae’s youth and gender will complicate her rise.
content: North Korea has never named her, confirmed her age or acknowledged her as Kim Jong-un’s heir. Yet South Korea’s spy agency says the evidence is now unmistakable: his daughter Kim Ju-ae has “effectively” become the successor-in-waiting. The assessment, delivered in a closed-door briefing to the National Assembly’s intelligence committee, was shared with journalists by Youn Kun-young of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea on Monday. “The NIS sees Kim Ju-ae as having effectively entered the stage of being designated as successor,” he said, referring to South Korea’s National Intelligence Service. Youn added that the agency believed Ju-ae’s increasingly frequent appearances in state media formed part of a deliberate effort to imprint “her image as a leader on the North Korean people’s minds”. The assessment adds weight to Seoul’s view that Kim Jong-un is preparing his daughter to extend the Kim dynasty’s hereditary rule into a fourth generation. Kim Ju-ae made her public debut in November 2022, when North Korean state media released photographs of her accompanying her father to the test launch of a Hwasong-17 intercontinental ballistic missile. She has since appeared at a growing number of military, political and diplomatic events, fuelling speculation that she is being prepared as heir apparent. Her public profile has broadened beyond military events. She joined her father on a trip to Beijing in September, her first known appearance abroad, and in January this year made her first public visit to the Kumsusan Palace of the Sun, the mausoleum housing the remains of her grandfather and great-grandfather, Kim Jong-il and Kim Il-sung. That appearance was widely seen as symbolically significant given the regime’s dynastic succession. State media has also been keen to promote a more martial image, photographing her inspecting and firing a new type of sniper rifle before senior military officials in February, test-firing a pistol and operating a new main battle tank alongside her father in March and attending a performance in July marking the 73rd anniversary of the Korean war armistice. Most recently, she joined her parents at Pyongyang’s Liberation Tower, which honours former Soviet troops, and at the Daesongsan Revolutionary Martyrs Cemetery for the 81st anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese rule. ‘Princess training’ Though many details about Ju-ae remain shrouded in secrecy, analysts broadly agree she is being groomed as a potential successor – but add that she is still young for a formal declaration. Believed to be 13, Ju-ae would need another five years to reach adulthood and become eligible to join the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea, seen as a prerequisite for any formal path towards leadership. “She is still receiving princess training for possible succession. There is no sign that the party has made any decision to make her successor, even internally,” said Oh Gyeong-seob of the Korea Institute for National Unification. Oh and others argue that the real marker to watch for is bureaucratic, not photographic: an appointment to a senior party or military post, such as a seat on the Central Military Commission or the Party Central Committee. Ri Il-gyu, a former North Korean diplomat who defected after serving as a political counsellor at the embassy in Cuba, described a shift in terminology in the Chosun Daily last month. Ju-ae was first called “beloved offspring”, he wrote, then “respected offspring”, before being elevated to “the great one who guides the way”. Internal party lecture materials now describe her as “the new star of Joseon” and “General of the New Star”, he added. “Her central role in public appearances carries clear political meaning,” Ri wrote. “Kim Jong-un’s early efforts to imprint his young daughter on the public reflect long-term calculations for succession.” State protocol reinforces the message in subtler ways too: Ju-ae is invariably positioned beside or near the centre of the action alongside her father, dressed at times in a leather coat that echoes his own – visual shorthand tying her to the “sacred” Paektu bloodline from which the Kim family claims its legitimacy. A three-rung ladder Succession in North Korea is a three-rung ladder, according to Professor Yang Moo-jin of the University of North Korean Studies: education, internal designation and finally, an official announcement. By his reckoning, Ju-ae has barely stepped onto the first rung. “She has no party post and there is no sign that Ju-ae is at the centre of a personality cult,” he said. Ju-ae featured in no discussion at the Workers’ Party’s ninth congress in February, he said, and was conspicuously absent when a senior Chinese delegation led by No 4 official Wang Huning met Kim Jong-un in Pyongyang in July. The real test of her status would come at the next party congress, Yang said. “We have to wait and see until the 10th party congress due in 2031, when she will be 18, to see what kind of official title she dons.” Even reaching adulthood clears only the first hurdle. North Korea’s deeply patriarchal political culture could complicate any attempt to install a daughter rather than a son as supreme leader. North Korea has never had a female leader and defectors describe a society where Confucian-inflected male chauvinism endures beneath the state’s official socialist ideology. Oh said Kim Jong-un could help clear the way for his daughter by removing potential rivals within the ruling elite. “Her father would pave the way for her succession through purges and executions as he himself did after seizing power following his father Kim Jong-il’s death in 2011,” Oh said. “But at the end of the day, it would depend on her own ability to overcome those challenges in the future by removing uncooperative political elites.” Summit signals The succession assessment was not the only headline to emerge from Monday’s briefing. The NIS also reportedly told lawmakers that it had obtained blueprints for North Korean missiles and was analysing them. It further said that a summit between Kim Jong-un and US President Donald Trump “could be possible at any time”, according to Youn – though it stressed there was no confirmed evidence of direct contact between the two governments, only “signs” pointing towards dialogue. It would be their fourth meeting. Trump and Kim met three times in 2018 and 2019, but talks collapsed after their ill-fated Hanoi summit failed to produce a deal on denuclearisation. Speculation over a repeat encounter has been building for weeks, driven largely from the American side. Pyongyang has offered no direct response to Trump’s overtures and continues to denounce what it calls Washington’s hostile policy towards the North. As Oh put it: “These differences are very hard to be narrowed down.”

title: China’s tech push fuels fastest profit growth in 4 years amid signs of economic divide
description: AI demand and local chip substitution spark boom for tech firms, leaving traditional industries far behind.
content: Artificial intelligence demand and technological domestic substitution drove profit growth for Chinese listed companies to its fastest pace in four years in the first half of 2026, underscoring the nation’s “K-shaped” economic structure as it transitions away from credit-fuelled expansion. Profit for firms on the chip-heavy Star Market under the Shanghai Stock Exchange surged more than fourfold from a year earlier in the six months to June, while those on the similarly structured ChiNext board in Shenzhen rose 33 per cent, according to a report by the China Association for Public Companies. That outpaced the 19.5 per cent increase for all 5,557 mainland China-listed companies, marking the fastest growth since 2022. The interim earnings season wrapped up on Tuesday. The disparity reflects Beijing’s push for technological self-reliance after policymakers set the goal of prioritising the tech industry in the AI race against the US. China’s big tech platforms are accelerating AI adoption by using home-made chips to support computing power, while memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and other AI hardware companies have boosted capacity after tapping capital markets. “Technology and high-end manufacturing are becoming the new engines of economic growth in China,” said Zhang Qiyao, analyst at Industrial Securities. About one-fifth of listed companies unveiled buy-back plans worth more than 200 billion yuan (US$29.8 billion) by the end of August, the report said. China Reform Holdings and China Chengtong Holdings Group – members of a so-called national team of state buyers – spent more than 60 billion yuan increasing stakes to support stock prices. AI computing power, price increases in memory products and the push for domestic substitutes for hardware drove an acceleration of earnings growth Li Haoyang, China Merchants Securities CXMT, the most valuable company on the Star Market with a capitalisation of 3.8 trillion yuan, posted a profit of 77.6 billion yuan in the first half, swinging from a 2.33 billion yuan loss a year earlier. Net income for Cambricon Technologies, dubbed China’s challenger to Nvidia, more than doubled, while Zhongji Innolight, which supplies optical transceivers to US hyperscalers, recorded a 241 per cent profit jump. CXMT started trading on the Shanghai bourse in July, while Zhongji Innolight completed a dual listing with a Hong Kong debut that month. The resilience in earnings has been reflected in stock performances. The Star Market 50 index has risen 23 per cent this year even after a tech sell-off in July, beating the CSI 300 Index of predominantly old-economy firms that has barely budged. The divergence will probably strengthen throughout the year. While China’s economic data trailed economists’ estimates across the board in July, investors expect Beijing to bolster growth by ramping up support for the tech sector rather than rolling out a broad stimulus package. Revenue for Star Market companies rose 39 per cent year on year in the first half, while ChiNext companies grew 22 per cent, outpacing the average 7.6 per cent growth for all listed firms, the association said. “AI computing power, price increases in memory products and the push for domestic substitutes for hardware drove an acceleration of earnings growth,” said Li Haoyang, analyst at China Merchants Securities.

title: Accepting failure key to success for perfectionist Pedrey Ng as Asian Games debut looms
description: A perfect IB score and desire to aim high form one side of Pedrey Ng’s character, but not settling for second best almost ruined everything.
content: She scored a flawless 45 in her IB exam, but it was accepting she did not have “to be perfect at everything” that cured Pedrey Ng Wing-lam of the temper tantrums threatening to undermine a promising table tennis career. Poised for her Asian Games debut this month, the 22-year-old is five years into a quantitative finance degree from Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, having opted against studying overseas to maximise her sporting potential. “I believed in myself … it’s my dream to play in the Olympics and win a medal for Hong Kong,” Ng said. “That’s something not everybody has an opportunity to do, and if I want to be an athlete, it has to be while I’m young.” As a child, Ng juggled table tennis with rugby, swimming, athletics, cross country, tennis and ice skating, but a place in a select squad at 10 narrowed her focus, and one year later she was elevated to Hong Kong’s youth table tennis team. Ng had actually come to the sport because of her older brother, Pedro, who was a keen player and is partially responsible for Ng’s English name. “My childhood best friend was called Audrey and I wanted the same name but my mum didn’t allow it,” Ng said. “I combined Audrey with my brother’s name and got Pedrey.” While Ng’s parents did not want a daughter named Audrey, they backed her devotion to the sport – on condition she completed her International Baccalaureate (IB). “The Hong Kong coach asked if I wanted to switch to being a full-time athlete in secondary four, but I liked studying and didn’t want to give up so young,” she said. A pupil at St Paul’s Co-educational College, she finished her schooling in some style, albeit Ng was initially awarded an IB score of 44 after her theory of knowledge and extended essay were both graded one mark beneath A. “I appealed and they both became As,” she said. “But I wasn’t in the newspaper, and couldn’t take a photo of the 45, so that was unfortunate.” Ng’s achievement was all the more impressive because she was already combining academics with regular travel for table tennis. “I’m determined and I aim high. I was really competitive when I was young and I didn’t want to lose at anything,” Ng said. A loathing for coming second extended to playing board games with her family, and Ng’s inability to control her emotions grew into a “really serious problem”. “I wanted to be perfect, and I couldn’t accept it when I missed a stupid point,” she said. “Losing one game would mean losing the whole match.” Playing for Hong Kong under-15s in an Asian Junior and Cadet Championship, Ng “lost my temper and made us lose”. “The coach was really mad, and she scolded me,” Ng said. “That’s when I started to realise this was a major problem of mine and I had to face it. I’d thought I was doing well, so why would I need to change anything?” Ng spoke to coaches and sports psychologists at Hong Kong Sports Institute. She uses self-talk and writes in a diary to allow her to “know more about myself, and understand why I would think how I had at certain points in matches”. “It’s a big change for me,” she said. “Sometimes you’re just really mad that you lost a point, and you forget everything and lose your temper. “But I don’t really get frustrated with myself now. Before a match, I get ready to accept whatever happens, and I have a plan in my head for how I’ll respond if I’m playing badly. If you’ve mentally prepared, nothing will come as a surprise.” With her degree extended over eight years, Ng now considers herself a full-time athlete. “I began training much more after going full-time, so I expected my results to get better but that didn’t happen,” Ng said. “We went to lots of overseas competitions with very strong opponents, and I lost much more than I did as a junior. “I learned to accept that I’m not a perfect person. There’s no need to be perfect in every single aspect of life, and realising that made me happier and much more optimistic. “I enjoyed time with friends more, but I also began to enjoy playing table tennis instead of only enjoying the feeling of winning, which led to better results.” One of those better results came in May in a 3-2 defeat to naturalised German Han Ying in the World Team Table Tennis Championships. The 43-year-old is ranked No 17 in the world and was a team silver medallist at the 2016 Olympics. “She is really strong, and I didn’t expect it to be so close,” Ng said. “It was the first time I enjoyed a whole match. I was smiling and playing my ‘A’ game the entire time.” Ng cited playing in front of “home support” in Chengdu for her first major tournament, the 2024 ITTF Mixed Team World Cup, where Hong Kong claimed bronze, as another high, along with the pair of bronzes she won from last year’s World University Games. A reserve for the 2024 Olympics, Ng soaked in the “intimidating atmosphere” in Paris, and wondered whether she could perform “under such high pressure”. “That pushed me to train harder,” she said. “A lot of players can play really well technically, but using your ability in a competition requires a lot of mental strength and mental training.” The singles world No 80, Ng and partner Doo Hoi-kem are third in the doubles global standings after their runners-up finish at last month’s World Table Tennis Europe Smash. Training with Doo’s coach, Zhang Rui, since 2023, Ng says the pair have been the biggest influences on her professional growth. “They’ve changed my perspective as a person, and showed me you just have to accept failures,” Ng said. Along with an eye on her post-sport life, Ng chose to study quantitative finance because it suits her aptitude for “calculations, logical thinking and solving puzzles”, all qualities that aid her table tennis. “Competing on your own, you have to study your opponent, and they all pose different challenges,” she said. “You’re constantly solving puzzles, so it’s very interesting for me.” Now set for the Asian Games, Ng, who was a reserve in Hangzhou three years ago, is aiming to just enjoy the moment and not think about the results. “This is such a blessing,” she said. “I went last time as a sparring partner, now I’m competing as one of Hong Kong’s major players. This is a great improvement for me.”

title: Xi, Trump and Putin may hold trilateral meeting at next Apec forum, Kremlin says
description: Senior Russian aide confirms possibility of all three leaders meeting in Shenzhen in November ‘was discussed’ at this week’s SCO summit.
content: A senior Russian aide suggested on Tuesday that Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin could hold a trilateral meeting at the next Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Leaders of the 21-member grouping are scheduled to meet in Shenzhen, the Chinese economic powerhouse in southern China, on November 18 and 19, setting up the possibility of Xi and Trump meeting four times this year. Asked on Russian state television about ⁠the possibility of such a meeting, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said: “This issue was discussed, yes.” Ushakov spoke from Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, at the two-day summit of the China-led Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) attended by Xi and Putin that ended on Tuesday. Putin confirmed in May his intention to attend the Apec meeting but Trump has not yet done so. Trump’s presence may depend in part on whether Xi agrees to attend the December 14-15 Group of 20 meeting at the US president’s Doral golf course resort in Florida. “And ⁠if ⁠it turns out, as has been said, ‌then the three of them will be able to ‌have ‌a meeting,” Ushakov said. The Chinese embassy in Washington said “We have nothing to offer at this time,” and White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said: “We have no announcements regarding President Trump’s attendance at Apec at this time.” Even as Trump has been complimentary of Xi, however, tensions continue to fester in the bilateral relationship. Bessent criticises China at G20 Finance Ministers meeting On Tuesday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called out China for refusing to agree to a joint communique at the G20 Finance Ministers meeting this week in North Carolina. “It is clear that the country with the world’s largest and unsustainable current account surplus, the People’s Republic of China, was the dissenter,” he added. “I think that the fact that 19 countries did want to address this shows the sheer enormity of the problem.” Ushakov said Putin plans to attend the Apec summit and to hold talks with both Xi and Trump, either bilaterally or in a joint format. But US analysts said any such three-way meeting could undercut long-standing US alliances. “It wouldn’t surprise me because clearly Trump is seeing this Shenzhen trip as a chance to see all of his most authoritarian friends,” said Zack Cooper, senior fellow with the conservative American Enterprise Institute. “It would send just an incredibly problematic message to American allies and partners, right? Trump continues to berate many of our closest allies from Canada to Europe to [South] Korea.” While this could help Beijing and Moscow in their long-term bid to weaken Western ties, it could also undercut Western unity, Cooper added. “It will just further accelerate the drive from a lot of US allies to decrease their reliance on the United States,” said Cooper, a former National Security Council and Department of Defence official. “And it may embolden Russia and China to test those alliances even more. So I think it’s a very problematic possibility.” A major factor as Trump weighs whether to attend the Apec conclave could be whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un agrees to meet him. Late last month, Trump told reporters he expected to meet with Kim this year, adding that North Korea has 57 nuclear weapons. Trump declined to say whether his goal in any such meeting was North Korea’s denuclearisation, even as he used the opportunity to undercut former US presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama. “I don’t want to talk about that, but I do have a good relationship with Kim Jong-un as you know, you’ve seen,” Trump said. “He didn’t like Biden. He didn’t like Obama. He didn’t like anybody. But he likes me.” Jeremy Chan, senior analyst with the Eurasia Group consultancy, said Trump’s recent displeasure with South Korea – seen in his decision to cut short the US-South Korean Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises in mid-August – may be in part driving his outreach to Pyongyang. Trump has reportedly been unhappy with Seoul’s slow movement on fulfilling a pledge to invest US$350 billion in the US and on reducing its trade surplus, an issue the US president focuses intently on. “There’s any number of things that could have just got stuck in his craw,” said Chan. “Trump in some ways is more mercurial than Kim is.” Xi may play influential role in leaders sitting down together Analysts added that Xi could play broker leading up to any meeting before the end of the year between himself, Trump and Putin, either at Apec or at the G20. “Xi will also offer to broker a tripartite meeting,” the Scowcroft Group consultancy said in a report. “Trump has previously said he would include Putin. Xi will suggest that he will try to deliver the Russian leader.” Kevin Nealer, a partner at Scowcroft and one of the report’s authors, added that the decision to invite Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov to this week’s G20 also sent a jarring signal. “Four years into the Russian invasion of Ukraine, allowing a sanctioned Russian Finance Minister to attend a US-hosted G20 meeting is antithetical to US interests,” he said. “Ratifying Russian aggression … and getting nothing in return is simply bizarre.” Additional reporting by Nayan Seth

title: Lofter saga rumbles on as Mong Kok project renamed, owners push for quick sales
description: Distressed 139-unit project has been rebranded as One Edward, as owners seek to move on after death of Lofter founder Carol Chow Pui-yin.
content: A residential project previously managed by troubled Hong Kong developer Lofter Group is returning to the market under a new name, as its owners push to quickly sell the flats by courting mainland Chinese and longer-term investors with competitive prices. The 139-unit project at 1 Ki Lung Street in Mong Kok, formerly known as Upper Prince, has been renamed One Edward after its ownership group took over the development from Lofter. The relaunch could serve as a test case for the future of projects associated with Lofter, after company founder Carol Chow Pui-yin was found dead in May, with the developer facing mounting financial and legal pressure. “The owners are keen to accelerate sales, of course,” said Kenny Kong, project director and spokesman for One Edward Development Limited. One Edward Development on Tuesday appointed Centaline Property Agency as the project’s exclusive sales agent and said its first sales arrangements could be announced within 48 hours. One Edward published its sales brochure under its new name on Friday, making it the first residential project previously managed by Lofter to return to the market since Chow’s death. The development received its occupation permit on June 25 and the units will be sold as completed flats. “We moved the handover to November as potential mainland Chinese buyers may need more time to arrange funds,” Kong said. Lofter acted as the project manager and was never the main owner of the development, according to Kong, with the underlying ownership group remaining unchanged before and after the restructuring. After the board removed Lofter from its development and project management roles in February, the company retained only a 1.5 per cent stake, he said. Founded in 2012, Lofter grew to become a well-known Hong Kong developer by pursuing an asset-light strategy focused on acquiring and redeveloping ageing properties in the city’s urban districts. But its expansion faltered during the pandemic, as interest rates rose and the property market experienced a downturn. In May, Lofter and an affiliate were sued for HK$130 million (US$16.6 million), while another Lofter-linked asset – One Bedford Place in Tai Kok Tsui – was taken over by Bank of East Asia and later acquired by Singapore-listed Wee Hur Holdings. The flats at One Edward range from 19 square metres to 45 square metres (205 to 487 sq ft). Kong said their prices would be set with reference to recently launched projects and that buyers could expect “a pleasant surprise”. The sales push comes as Hong Kong’s housing recovery becomes more selective, with quick-turn investors retreating and demand concentrating in competitively priced projects in established urban areas. “Buyers may expect the price to be a bit lower,” said Raymond Cheng, a veteran property analyst and research director of Mingze Capital International. “They may also ask whether the project’s previous financial difficulties have affected its overall quality.” Rising rents could nevertheless strengthen the appeal of smaller flats to longer-term investors, with Centaline estimating One Edward could generate rental yields of about 4 per cent. Cheng said a 4 per cent rental yield would be relatively high for Hong Kong’s residential market, suggesting the developer might need to price the flats conservatively to achieve that return.

title: Trump puts pressure on squeezed US oil refiners to ease pump prices
description: Industry executives were also asked how the US can process more Venezuelan crude.
