content: President Donald Trump pressed US oil refiners to boost domestic production of petrol and diesel during a closed-door meeting on Tuesday, as he contends with high prices and mounting cost-of-living concerns before November’s midterm elections. Trump made clear he wanted lower prices at the pump for Americans and asked executives how to increase refining capacity, according to a White House official who provided details on condition of anonymity. The official said industry representatives were aligned with that goal and that the discussion touched on regulatory changes, faster permitting and additional investments. The face-to-face pressure highlighted the political peril for a president who campaigned on reining in energy costs only to see them spiral amid the US war on Iran. US fuel prices are at the highest seasonal level ever with petrol now fetching more than US$4 a gallon and diesel nearly US$6 a gallon on average nationwide, according to the American Automobile Association. In return, Trump got an earful about federal biofuel-blending requirements, as some refining executives used the hour-long meeting to argue that quotas forcing them to mix alternative fuels into petrol are raising pump prices, according to people familiar with the conversation who asked not to be named because it was private. Roughly a dozen executives from fuel refining and distribution companies joined Trump in the White House Cabinet Room for the discussion, followed by a quick visit to the Oval Office, some of the people said. They reflected a who’s who of industry, with leaders of smaller independent fuel makers such as Delek US Holdings Inc. alongside representatives from large refiners, including PBF Energy Inc., Marathon Petroleum Corp., and Valero Energy Corp. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who heads Trump’s National Energy Dominance Council, were in the session alongside other officials. The gathering was dominated by talk about the Renewable Fuel Standard, the federal law that compels refiners to blend corn-based ethanol, soy-based biodiesel and other alternative fuels into petrol and diesel, people said. Industry representatives took aim at the administration’s decision to set record-high biofuel-blending quotas, with some casting the targets as unattainable and describing them as driving up petrol costs, some of the people said. Tensions on the issue were heightened after Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency on Monday granted a host of small refineries exemptions from some of those mandates. At the same time, in a blow to the owners of large refineries, the administration also said it would seek to ensure other, non-exempted facilities are on the hook to blend those waived volumes in their stead. Renewable fuel quotas are a particularly thorny subject for Trump, dividing the agriculture and oil industries, two key constituencies. Administration officials on Tuesday acknowledged the political dynamic in suggesting their hands were tied on the issue, some of the people said. Trump convened the meeting as the Iran war continues to disrupt the flow of crude and refined petroleum products, feeding higher costs for petrol and diesel. It is a pressing concern for Trump, who has struggled to allay voters’ pocketbook concerns ahead of elections to determine which party controls Congress for the next two years. While petrol prices have fallen from this year’s peak of more than US$4.50 a gallon in May, they remain about US$1 higher than at the February 28 start of the war – much less the US$2.79 low Trump notched in January. Trump says prices will eventually ease and that Americans understand his stated aim of preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. He told reporters on Monday he could not say with certainty prices would drop before the election. The president is also seeking to unlock more crude flows from Venezuela, tapping a guaranteed share of at-cost production from North American Blue Energy Partners, a privately held company that has been granted 100-year concessions on 17 oilfields. Any increased Venezuelan output would be likely to flow to US Gulf coast refineries that are optimised to process the nation’s particularly heavy crude, though significant increases in production are unlikely in the short term. Refiners in Tuesday’s meeting were asked how the US can process more Venezuelan crude – and how the administration can make that easier, people familiar with the conversation said. While some refiners are already importing volumes from Venezuela – particularly Valero and Chevron Corp. – taking on more will not make geographical sense for some facilities across the US, industry representatives said. Participants also praised Trump for a Jones Act waiver that has allowed foreign ships to transport oil and other commodities around the US. Trump initially issued a broad waiver to ensure adequate fuel supplies and lower costs amid the war, but pared its reach in August.

title: Editorial | China’s anti-corruption campaign is here to stay
description: Hong Kong has a role to play as a new national law seeks to expand the anti-corruption legal framework beyond the country’s borders.
content: China’s anti-corruption campaign has proved to be a sustainable drive rather than a transient clean-up exercise. More than 13 years after President Xi Jinping launched the crackdown with a pledge to hunt both “tigers and flies”, it has become a pillar of Communist Party governance. Its continuing escalation in the run-up to key leadership changes anticipated next year carries a strong and clear message: corruption is not merely individual misconduct within the government structure but a systemic threat to the authority and well-being of the nation. That message matters profoundly to China’s future development. A country of immense scale, with an economy undergoing a difficult structural adjustment and bearing increasingly consequential global responsibilities, cannot afford public power to be compromised by private privilege. Not only does corruption destroy the level playing field for all and weaken confidence in institutions and leadership, it also entrenches local interests and encourages the pursuit of short-term personal benefits over the long-term public good. The scale of the problem has been put into perspective in a recent series of reports by the South China Morning Post. There were no fewer than 65 investigations involving senior officials in 2025, compared with 19 in 2013, when Xi took over as president. Nearly 1 million party officials were disciplined last year. The figures for 2026 suggest that the momentum has continued rather than slowed down. Provincial governments have accounted for a large share of senior targets, while officials in resource-rich provinces have been particularly exposed. Retirement, once seen by some as a protection against further scrutiny, has ceased to provide immunity. This is an important shift. It signals that anti-corruption enforcement is becoming a permanent discipline rather than a campaign that fades away over time. It also dispels an old assumption that distance from Beijing gives local cadres greater latitude. The traditional saying, “the mountains are high and the emperor is far away”, is increasingly incompatible with probes targeting senior officials across the country and scrutinising complex financial arrangements. There is no sign of the crackdown easing in the run-up to the expected leadership change in the coming year. Xi’s anti-corruption policy is being further institutionalised with a new law to expand legal powers beyond borders. The proposed Anti-Cross-Border Corruption Law, submitted for its first reading by the National People’s Congress Standing Committee last month, is expected to provide a clearer legal framework for pursuing cross-border corruption, recovering assets, collecting overseas evidence and addressing the flight of suspects and illicit gains. Its detailed provisions are yet to be published but the direction is unmistakable: China is seeking to adapt its anti-corruption regime to the reality that public-sector corruption increasingly has extraterritorial dimensions. Historically, there has been a link to Hong Kong in this respect, the city being a free and open gateway to China for the world and therefore a convenient exit for illegitimate gains. As it drives cross-border anti-corruption efforts, the new law will have an impact on the city and beyond. As a special administrative region of China and a global financial centre, Hong Kong has added responsibility to step up cooperation. When handled with care and through the proper avenues under the “one country, two systems” model, the new law will become an opportunity for Hong Kong to strengthen its financial regulation safeguards and proactively align with the state anti-corruption policy, which is in the interest of the country and the city. Collaboration on this front is also in line with Hong Kong’s zero-tolerance approach to corruption. The Independent Commission Against Corruption and other regulators have long been ready to step up with robust enforcement action when needed. The anti-corruption campaign may well unfold with sustained, if not stronger, magnitude and effort. A corruption-free China is pivotal to the nation’s rising stature as a global power characterised by stability and prosperity, without which it cannot strive for better growth and development for the country and the world.

title: 14 new Hollywood movies to watch in autumn 2026, from Digger to Avengers: Doomsday
description: Street Fighter, The Social Reckoning and the new Hunger Games film also make our list of the most tantalising upcoming Hollywood movies.
content: Autumn is one of the most bountiful seasons on the moviegoing calendar, as a growing crop of potential awards contenders emerges alongside a mouthwatering array of holiday entertainment and bona fide blockbusters. This year is no exception, with many of Hollywood’s biggest stars unveiling their latest works, and some of the most formidable franchises in recent memory returning to the big screen. Here are 14 of the most tantalising prospects to arrive between now and Christmas (opening dates are for Hong Kong). 1. Heart of the Beast Brad Pitt reunites with Fury director David Ayer to tell the story of a retired US special forces officer who crash-lands in the Alaskan wilderness with his dog, also a seasoned combat veteran. The film promises to be as much a celebration of the military’s highly skilled four-legged operatives as a brawny survival thriller about war heroes battling the elements and their own inner demons. (Opens on September 24.) 2. Digger Tom Cruise is already being hotly tipped as a best actor contender for his larger-than-life performance anchoring Alejandro G. Inarritu’s political black comedy. Cruise plays a billionaire oil tycoon who finds himself at the centre of a global catastrophe for which he is largely responsible, while also becoming humanity’s only hope of survival. Giving off strong Dr. Strangelove vibes, the film is an acerbic satire that promises to delight and infuriate in equal measure. (Opens on October 1.) 3. Other Mommy Academy Award winner Jessica Chastain takes on double duty in the latest horror offering from hit factory Blumhouse-Atomic Monster, produced by James Wan. Adapted from Josh Malerman’s novel Incidents Around the House and directed by Rob Savage (Host), the film sees Chastain play a mother battling to protect her young daughter from a supernatural entity known as “Other Mommy” that looks just like her. Jay Duplass and Severance star Dichen Lachman also feature. (Opens on October 8.) 4. The Social Reckoning Aaron Sorkin won an Oscar for penning The Social Network, which charted the meteoric rise of Facebook. He wrote and now directs this sequel in which Succession star Jeremy Strong plays Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg during the 2021 leak that exposed the company’s awareness of the harmful impact of its platform and lack of action to counter it. Best actress winner Mikey Madison (Anora) co-stars as corporate whistle-blower Frances Haugen. (Opens on October 8.) 5. Street Fighter Past attempts to bring Capcom’s beloved fighting video game to the big screen have wavered from bad (the 1994 version starring Jean-Claude Van Damme) to abysmal (2009’s The Legend of Chun-Li), but this latest iteration appears to be embracing the property’s campier elements. Noah Centineo (next to be seen as Rambo) stars alongside Andrew Koji, Callina Liang and Jason Momoa, as well as WWE veterans Roman Reigns and Cody Rhodes. (Opens on October 16.) 6. Klara and the Sun Taika Waititi (Jojo Rabbit) helms this adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian science fiction novel about a solar-powered “Artificial Friend” named Klara (Jenna Ortega), who is chosen by an ailing teenager (Mia Tharia) to live with her family in the countryside. Waititi appears to have injected a good deal of his trademark quirky humour into Ishiguro’s story, which sees a well-intentioned AI strive to make human lives better. What could possibly go wrong? (Opens on October 22.) 7. Clayface The DC Universe takes a dark turn as its latest entry skews hard into the realm of visceral body horror. Directed by James Watkins (Speak No Evil) from a screenplay by Mike Flanagan (Doctor Sleep), the film stars Tom Rhys Harries as a rising film star whose face is disfigured by gangsters. After turning to a shady backstreet scientist (Naomi Ackie) for help, he emerges as the shape-shifting anti-hero Clayface, a notorious adversary of Batman. (Opens on October 22.) 8. Ebenezer Johnny Depp stars in his first major Hollywood role in eight years, playing the iconic curmudgeon Ebenezer Scrooge in a new adaptation of Charles Dickens’ perennial festive favourite, A Christmas Carol. The film promises to delve deeper into the character’s backstory and boasts an ensemble that includes Andrea Riseborough, Daisy Ridley and Ian McKellen as Jacob Marley. Fans will be hoping that Depp’s triumphant return proves to be more festive cheer than overstuffed turkey. (Opens on November 12.) 9. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping While a prequel series to the Jennifer Lawrence-led franchise seemed unnecessary, 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes emerged as a surprising reinvigoration of the dystopian death match saga. This second instalment focuses on Katniss’s future mentor Haymitch Abernathy – here a 16-year-old tribute from District 12 played by Joseph Zada – as he is selected to compete in the Second Quarter Quell. Ralph Fiennes, Kieran Culkin and Elle Fanning also star. (Opens on November 19.) 10. Focker-in-Law The latest instalment in the family-focused comedy franchise that pits Robert De Niro’s retired CIA agent Jack against his unassuming son-in-law Greg (Ben Stiller) now adds Ariana Grande to the mix. Olivia (Grande) is an FBI hostage negotiator engaged to Greg’s mollycoddled son (Skyler Gisondo). Hilarity ensues when the family convenes for the holidays. After quickly winning over the typically suspicious Jack, Olivia becomes determined to free her betrothed from his overbearing parents. (Opens on November 26.) 11. Hexed Disney Animation’s latest feature-length fantasy follows Billie, a typically awkward and unpopular teenage heroine. After she is expelled from high school, she discovers that she is descended from witches and is transported – together with her mother – into the magical realm of Hexe. Hailee Steinfeld headlines the voice cast, which also includes Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster, Walton Goggins and Stephen Fry. Fawn Veerasunthorn, the Thai-born director of Wish (2023), takes the helm alongside Jason Hand. (Opens on November 28.) 12. The Cat in the Hat Loosely based on the beloved children’s book written and illustrated by Dr Seuss, this animated feature casts Bill Hader as the voice of the eponymous feline, tasked with entertaining a pair of human children. While that pretty much covers the original narrative, the film gives The Cat a complicated backstory involving the “Institute for the Institution of Imagination and Inspiration, LLC”, but one suspects audiences will be attracted by brand recognition alone. (Opens on December 3.) 13. Avengers: Doomsday Marvel Studios is hoping to restore faith in its flagging superhero franchise, going so far as to bring back Cap, Thor and other original Avengers who had been put out to pasture, while casting Robert Downey Jnr as new nemesis Doctor Doom. As if that was not enough, 2019’s box-office-busting finale Avengers: Endgame is being re-released on September 24 in an extended “Encore” edition to prime audiences for this all-new multiverse-fuelled adventure. (Opens on December 16.) 14. Dune: Part Three The third and final chapter in Denis Villeneuve’s epic adaptation of Frank Herbert’s hugely influential science fiction opus takes place around 20 years after the events of its predecessors. Based primarily on Dune Messiah, the film sees Paul (Timothee Chalamet) ruling as a ruthless emperor whose reign comes under threat from a scheming new enemy, played by Robert Pattinson. Zendaya returns as Paul’s former lover Chani, mother of his two children, as do Florence Pugh, Rebecca Ferguson, Javier Bardem and Anya Taylor-Joy. (Opens on December 17.)
