title: US Congress seeks to identify foreign countries behind scam calls
description: Inquiry comes as US government reports tying much of the financial damage from scams to Chinese criminal networks based in Southeast Asia.
content: US lawmakers are trying to identify which foreign countries are the biggest sources of unlawful robocalls targeting Americans, as Congress steps up efforts to combat a surge in phone scams. The inquiry follows a string of US government reports tying much of the financial damage from scams to Chinese criminal networks based in Southeast Asia. The House Energy and Commerce Committee’s Communications and Technology Subcommittee passed the bipartisan “Foreign Robocall Elimination Act” on Tuesday, which would direct the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to establish an inter-agency task force focused on unlawful robocalls originating overseas. “Everyone with a phone has received a robocall or scam call,” said Representative Tom Kean Jnr, a Republican from New Jersey. “Robocalls originating from overseas pose an especially nefarious threat. Congress has taken strides to identify and to trace back illegal robocalls.” Under the House bill, the task force would study the volume of unlawful robocalls originating inside and outside the US and determine which foreign countries serve as the main departure points for the most calls entering the country. It would also assess the financial losses and identity theft associated with foreign-originating robocalls, examine how countries could work together to authenticate international calls, and consider incentives for foreign governments to cooperate with US law enforcement. Tracing fraudulent robocalls remains nearly impossible as scammers routinely spoof caller ID data and route automated traffic through an untraceable web of global telecom networks. The legislation would allow the FCC to require that some voice service providers post a bond before certifying themselves in the agency’s Robocall Mitigation Database. It would also provide legal immunity for an industry consortium conducting traceback investigations, shielding it from lawsuits over sharing or publishing the information it gathers on suspected unlawful robocalls. A companion bill has already passed the US Senate. China is not mentioned, but … The legislation does not mention China or any Southeast Asian country by name. However, major scam compounds are concentrated in Southeast Asia, including Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos, with US officials and international investigators linking many operations to Chinese transnational criminal groups. The compounds often rely on trafficked workers who are lured by fake job offers and then forced, under threats of violence, to carry out online scams. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission said in a March report that the US government estimated Americans lost at least US$10 billion to Southeast Asia-based scams in 2024, with higher losses projected in 2025. The commission said Chinese criminal organisations were the major force behind industrial-scale scam centres in the region. The House Select Committee on China released a May 2026 investigation, similarly saying China-linked scam centres concentrated particularly in Cambodia and Myanmar are part of a broader criminal ecosystem involving fraud, human trafficking and money laundering, also estimating the fraud losses by Americans at around US$10 billion annually. Fraudsters are increasingly using artificial intelligence to generate convincing voices, messages and online personas, enabling them to pose as relatives, employers or government officials. The technology has been used in romance scams, fake job offers, investment fraud and sextortion. A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington previously told the South China Morning Post that China and the United States have been cooperating to combat transnational scam crime, describing it as a “common responsibility” and saying the efforts had produced positive results without providing significant detail. The spokesperson said the two countries had engaged in practical cooperation in areas including combating telecommunications fraud and online gambling, repatriating and pursuing fugitives, and that the efforts had produced “many tangible results”. Separately, on Tuesday, the committee’s Commerce, Manufacturing and Trade Subcommittee advanced H.R. 5967, the Strategic Task Force on Scam Prevention Act. The bipartisan bill would direct the US Federal Trade Commission, working with the US Department of Justice, to convene an inter-agency task force to develop a national strategy for combating scams.

title: Mainland China stepping up preparations for Taiwan blockade, report says
description: Defence ministry says PLA exercises are increasingly focused on plans to cut off the island and control air and sea routes.
content: Taiwan’s defence ministry has warned that the People’s Liberation Army is stepping up its preparations for a blockade of the island, adding that it is sharpening its plans to break such a cordon in response. The assessment was made in the ministry’s “2026 China Military Power Report”, which was submitted to the legislature this week along with its five-year force development plan and next year’s proposed defence budget. The report said recent PLA exercises were increasingly focused on the “joint blockade and control” of the island’s external air and sea routes. “Combined with annual PLA training, the exercises have increasingly focused on maritime and air blockades or quarantines, joint firepower strikes, seizure of comprehensive battlefield superiority and joint amphibious landing operations,” it said. The aim was to strengthen the PLA’s ability to target Taiwan, as well as carry out anti-access and area-denial operations to counter potential foreign intervention, the report continued. Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has never ruled out the use of force to reunite it with the mainland. Most countries, including the island’s main international partner the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force and is legally bound to supply it with weapons to defend itself. The report also said targeted exercises had simulated blockades or quarantines, military-law enforcement operations and long-range live-fire strikes. Meanwhile, the PLA continued to send warplanes and drones across the median line – a nominal boundary dividing the two sides of the Taiwan Strait – and warships had approached waters near the island’s contiguous zone, which extends 24 nautical miles (44km) beyond its coast. To counter such threats, Taiwan’s military said it would strengthen its C5ISR (command, control, communications, computers, cyber, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance) networks and use AI-assisted systems as part of its decision-making process. The island has also begun testing how it would counter a PLA blockade in practice. During this year’s Han Kuang exercises, the island’s largest annual war games, countering a maritime quarantine and blockade played a central role for the first time. In one scenario, Taiwan’s western ports and shipping routes were assumed to have been blockaded, forcing foreign assistance and critical supplies to enter through a “strategic lifeline” off the east coast. In an exercise designed to test the coastguard’s integration into naval command-and-control structures, a Yung Feng-class minesweeper was used to clear a shipping route. Navy and coastguard ships then formed a protective screen around a landing platform dock playing the role of a merchant vessel carrying vital supplies. The exercise also tested the island’s ability to sustain its forces during a blockade by using ground forces to secure ports on the east coast of the island, while civilian trucks and heavy port equipment were mobilised to unload and transport supplies inland. Other exercises simulated the relocation of defence production after an attack and the use of civilian factories to produce kamikaze attack drones. However, the ministry said the PLA’s ability to launch a full-scale amphibious assault was “still insufficient”. It said this would require simultaneous landings at multiple locations while maintaining air and sea superiority, as well as delivering reinforcements and supplies. Chieh Chung, a research fellow at the Association of Strategic Foresight, a Taipei-based think tank, said this year’s defence ministry report devoted considerably more attention than last year’s to the PLA’s focus on joint amphibious landings. While agreeing with the assessment of the mainland’s ability to carry out such operations, Chieh said the report showed that Beijing was accelerating preparations for a potential military campaign against Taiwan. He also said the Han Kuang exercises had provided a “rather comprehensive” test of a range of multi-domain denial measures to counter the blockade, adding that this approach was “moving in the right direction”.

title: Meet Tim McGraw and Faith Hill’s daughter, Maggie McGraw – who just got engaged
description: Unlike her 2 sisters, who work in entertainment, Maggie has a master’s from Stanford and is an intelligence analyst for Major League Baseball.
content: Tim McGraw and Faith Hill’s middle daughter, Maggie McGraw, just got engaged. According to an Instagram post shared on August 30 by the McGraws’ eldest daughter, Gracie, Maggie’s boyfriend James Rubin proposed “in the greatest, most Maggie way possible, filled with flowers and family”. The carousel of images includes a snap of Maggie sipping bubbly while showing off her engagement ring. Gracie wrote in her post that she and her youngest sister, Audrey, helped Rubin set up the proposal. Gracie added to her brother-in-law-to-be, “Thank you @jamesrubin170 for making my sister the happiest lady in all the land.” Here’s everything to know about Tim McGraw and Faith Hill’s daughter, Maggie McGraw. She has a master’s from Stanford Maggie McGraw was born in August 1998 and is the second of McGraw and Hill’s three daughters. Unlike her sisters – Gracie is an actress and Audrey, a singer – Maggie did not pursue a career in entertainment. She attended Stanford University as an undergraduate, then completed a master’s degree in sustainability and science, graduating in 2021. “We are so incredibly proud of our Maggie May!” her father wrote at the time of her master’s graduation. “I have such admiration for her work ethic, her fierce love of her family, and especially her passion to make the world a better place … Go get ’em my sweet girl! Proud Pop!” She works for Major League Baseball Maggie began her career by briefly working as a legislative correspondent for the US House of Representatives in 2022. She went on to spend a year as a legislative aide working on foreign affairs, defence and veterans’ issues for the US Senate. Since March this year, Maggie has worked as an intelligence analyst for Major League Baseball. Who is her fiancé? While she may have grown up the child of country music legends, Maggie has chosen to remain largely out of the limelight. There is little information available on her fiancé, but in a recent birthday post dedicated to Maggie, Gracie mentioned that Maggie was living with “the love of [her] life”, and their three cats and one dog, in New York. “It’s the most wonderful sight to behold,” Gracie gushed. Rubin first appeared on Maggie’s Instagram in 2024, when she shared a snap of the two of them in black tie. “A moment for the dress (and the date),” she captioned the post.

title: Opinion | Nepal-China floods highlight a growing front of the climate change crisis
description: Rising sea levels, extreme weather and drought all remain concerns, but destabilised ice and snow at high altitudes is increasingly a threat.
content: On August 26, a section of glacier collapsed at an altitude of more than 5,000 metres on the Nepalese side of the Himalayas. The falling ice and rock accelerated down a steep valley at about 50 metres per second, scouring debris and transforming into a high-speed mudslide that slammed into Gyirong Port on the Chinese side just seven minutes later. The force of the flow largely buried and obliterated the border facilities. Hundreds of people, many of them travellers, remain missing on the Chinese side. Across the border in Nepal, entire villages were swept away, leaving hundreds dead and thousands unaccounted for. For decades, the defining image of climate vulnerability has been the low-lying island nation, where rising seas threaten to erase entire communities from the map. That threat is real, urgent and unfinished business. However, the catastrophic mudslide that tore through the China-Nepal border forces us to look beyond the waterline and consider a more complex, multidimensional map of climate risk. The iconic risk remains sea-level rise. It is slow, inexorable and already under way. Coastal megacities from Shanghai to Mumbai to New York are investing heavily in sea walls and surge barriers. Small island states are exploring relocation treaties and purchasing land abroad as a form of climate insurance. The very predictability of this threat has allowed societies to develop institutional responses. The second most immediately felt climate risk is extreme rainfall and the catastrophic flooding it brings. For several years, traditionally drier places such as Beijing and large swathes of inland China have suffered disastrous floods that overwhelmed infrastructure, affecting millions and exposing the limits of urban drainage systems never designed for the intensity of rain now falling from a warmer atmosphere. The third risk is drought. This summer, a severe and persistent drought, coupled with record-breaking heatwaves, created a crisis across much of Europe. The prolonged lack of rainfall pushed major waterways, including the Rhine, Danube and Loire, to historically low levels, disrupting river transport and forcing cargo vessels to reduce their loads. France alone faces an estimated €10-15 billion (US$11.6-17.4 billion) in heat-related losses and a projected 35 per cent drop in maize yields. Across Europe, low river levels and wildfires have exposed unexploded ordnance from World War II that had long been submerged or buried – another stark reminder of how climate change is already profoundly affecting our lives. The Gyirong disaster has brought a fourth threat into terrifying focus. Scientists call these events “cryo-hydrological hazards” – disasters born from destabilised ice, snow and meltwater in rapidly warming high mountain regions. The high-altitude China-Nepal border region, which has long been valued by travellers for its dramatic ice-covered peaks, is warming significantly faster than the global average. Since 1981, the number of snow-cover days in southern Tibet has fallen by an average of 12.36 days per decade. Between 1985 and 2020, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau lost roughly 18 per cent of its glacier area. The cascade was a classic cryo-hydrological disaster chain: a high-altitude glacier fracture triggered an ice-rock avalanche that rapidly evolved into a high-speed debris flow. Travelling roughly 22 kilometres in minutes, the mudslide slammed into Gyirong Port and largely levelled the border facilities. The extreme speed left virtually no window for early warning. This is not a one-off. In 2022, a glacier collapse on Italy’s Marmolada peak killed 11 climbers. In 2025, a rockslide and ice collapse in the Swiss village of Blatten claimed a life even after the area was evacuated. The Alps, like the Himalayas, are becoming increasingly unstable as permafrost thaws and glaciers retreat. Europe is among the fastest-warming continents. Mountain communities now face a threat that is sudden, catastrophic and often virtually unpredictable. The Gyirong disaster shows that a warming planet also thaws permafrost and forces ice to retreat, removing the structural “glue” that once held together steep mountain slopes. A warm spell, heavy rain or minor tremor can now produce far more destructive outcomes than a generation ago. For mountain communities across the Hindu Kush Himalayas, the Alps, the Southern Alps of New Zealand, and Alaska, this is a daily reality. The question is whether we can expand our imagination of climate vulnerability to include the valleys below the falling mountains. Yet even as these cascading hazards multiply and claim lives without regard for nationality or ideology, the world remains consumed by interstate enmity. In the face of a planetary crisis that respects no borders, why do we still pour so much energy into rivalry rather than shared resilience? The world has spent decades preparing for the ocean to rise. It is time we also prepare for the mountains to fall and recognise that the real enemy is the one that threatens us all.

title: Congress advances new bill to give US edge in open-source AI race with China
description: Legislation to promote adoption of US open-source models while publicising the risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts.
content: The US Congress on Tuesday advanced a new bill that seeks to establish American global leadership in open-source artificial intelligence, an area where China currently dominates, by promoting adoption of US open-source models and publicising risks associated with using their Chinese counterparts. The legislation was one of several proposals marked up in the US House of Representatives targeting China amid escalating tech competition between the two countries. Congressional committees “mark up” a proposed bill by reviewing it line by line, debating its merits and voting on changes or amendments before deciding whether to send it for a full House or Senate vote. Introduced last week, the Open-Source AI Leadership Act, H.R. 10152, would direct the US Department of Commerce to identify barriers to adopting US open-weight models and compile data on their adoption relative to Chinese ones. Open-weight, or open-source, models are AI models that are released freely over the internet, allowing users with the necessary hardware to download and customise them for their own use. While leading US AI models including OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are mostly closed-source, meaning that they can only be accessed through official channels, most leading Chinese models are released as open-weight models. “This legislation targets a serious problem,” said Gabe Evans, a Republican from Colorado who sponsored the bill. “Unfortunately, the companies that are leading in the open-source and open-weight models are Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot, and these are deeply intertwined with the Chinese Communist Party.” Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post. During the bill’s mark-up session on Tuesday, Evans told the subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade that US companies are increasingly falling behind their Chinese counterparts in the global market for open-weight models. According to data compiled by AI newsletter Interconnects, Chinese open-weight models saw more than 328 million downloads globally last month, more than double those of their US counterparts, following a raft of new powerful releases including Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s updated V4 Pro. US companies admit experimenting with Chinese open-weight models An increasing number of US companies have disclosed that they are experimenting with Chinese open-weight models, which are generally cheaper to use than leading US models, including Airbnb, Perplexity and Facebook owner Meta Platforms. A key component of the new bill would establish a single point of contact at the Commerce Department responsible for promoting the use of US open-weight models among US companies, government agencies, states and qualified foreign partners. The department should also publicise, no later than 18 months after the bill is enacted, various risks associated with using Chinese models, including censorship, supply chain vulnerabilities and misuse risks. While the idea of boosting US competitiveness in open-source AI enjoyed bipartisan support in Tuesday’s mark-up session, some Democrats expressed concern that the bill, in its current form, gives the administration “open-ended” authority to block or promote certain transactions. Lori Trahan, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said that her concerns about the current wording were fixable. The “single biggest threat to a dynamic American open source ecosystem” today is the uncertainty surrounding the Trump administration’s regulatory approach towards the AI industry, she added, which she accused of being “ad hoc, opaque and blunt”. The bill advanced to the full committee by a voice vote, where it will be marked up again before heading to the House floor for a final vote if approved. However, it is unclear whether the bill will be approved as a stand-alone bill, particularly with the House going into recess next month ahead of the midterms. The congressional effort follows the release of a high-profile public letter in July, signed by almost every US tech giant, including Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta, calling for US leadership in open-weight AI models. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang said in a social media post at the time that the world “needs both frontier closed models and frontier open models”. The letter was released amid ongoing speculation that the Trump administration might introduce restrictions on open-weight AI models to mitigate their national security risks and combat China’s growing influence, a move widely opposed by US industry players. A provision in the new House bill states that it does not authorise the Commerce Secretary to “ban, restrict, or otherwise make unavailable an open artificial intelligence model in interstate or foreign commerce”. Subcommittee Chairman Gus Bilirakis held a mark-up of 12 bills on Tuesday seeking to “strengthen American competitiveness and enhance consumer protections”, including several addressing competition with China. Those included the Memory Chip Competitiveness Assessment Act and the American Quantum Competitive Act. The bills “direct the Commerce Department to get serious about where our supply chains are vulnerable and how we outcompete China in the technologies that matter most”, Bilirakis said.

title: UK’s Burnham pledges to restore hope as he makes House of Commons debut as PM
description: His vow to ‘unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility’ was a marked contrast to his predecessor Starmer’s downbeat pronouncements.
content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham faced lawmakers in the House of Commons on Tuesday for the first time since becoming UK leader six weeks ago, with wars in Europe and the Middle East weighing on his promise to kick-start the economy, ease the cost of living and oversee a radical redistribution of power from London to Britain’s regions. On the day parliament returned from its summer break, Burnham said he would “unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility in every postcode in Britain”. “We can make this next decade better than the last,” he said. “We can lift the prospects of all our people and places. We can put more power into every postcode. We can let Britain believe again. We can bring back hope.” It was a marked contrast to the downbeat pronouncements of Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, who tended to accentuate the scale of the challenges Britain faced. After a string of missteps and local election defeats, Starmer was pushed out as leader by his own Labour Party just two years after winning a landslide 2024 election victory. Starmer quit his seat in parliament on Tuesday after 11 years, saying he wanted to “focus on other issues: international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world”. A special election will be held within weeks to replace him. Since taking office as the new Labour prime minister on July 20, Burnham has travelled around the country promising to deliver renewed national optimism. He has announced a series of modest money-saving measures aimed at giving “breathing space” to people and businesses, including a tax cut on domestic energy bills and a lowering of levies on pubs and nightclubs. Burnham, a former lawmaker who was elected to parliament in June after almost a decade away as mayor of Greater Manchester, expanded on the diagnosis of Britain’s ills he set out during his campaign. He said the country had taken “a series of wrong turns” since the 1980s. “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country deindustrialised,” he said, adding that the UK’s 2016 vote to leave the European Union had added “a decade of low growth”. He said that greater public control over water, energy and transport could drive economic growth and ease households’ financial burden, though it was unclear to what extent he planned to reverse decades of privatisation of key pillars of the economy. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham’s economic diagnosis was “completely wrong”. “He thinks that if government spends more money, we will all get richer,” she said. “He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.” Opponents also have questions about No 10 North, a second prime minister’s office in Manchester. Burnham says it will help drive plans to give local leaders more powers and spread economic growth around the country. Critics call it an expensive gimmick. Burnham said No 10 North will oversee “the biggest redistribution of power this country has seen” by helping regions of Britain establish powerful local authorities to give people more “ownership and control” over their communities and lives. Opinion polls suggest Labour has seen a “Burnham bounce” in popularity, but the new leader faces a stack of domestic and foreign problems. In his first foreign trip as leader, Burnham visited Kyiv last month to underscore Britain’s support for Ukraine and share technology for making long-range missiles. In response, Russia accused Britain of taking part in the war on Kyiv’s side. Burnham said that UK support for Ukraine “will not change, whatever the threats we face”. Like other European countries, the UK is under pressure to spend more on the military in response to threats from Russia and weakened US support for Europe. Burnham’s government will have to provide details in the coming weeks on how it plans to fund an increase in defence spending to meet Nato’s target of 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product by 2035. Burnham also faces a contentious decision on whether to give the green light to more oil and gas production in the North Sea, a move supported by US President Donald Trump that faces opposition from advocates of clean energy. Burnham did not address that directly, but said Britain would “meet the climate challenge”. He said he would attend the international Cop31 climate conference in Turkey in November.

title: UN report confirms Syria was building nuclear reactor during Assad rule
description: Syria’s Deir el-Zour site bombed by Israel in 2007 was an undeclared nuclear reactor under construction.
content: Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor in Deir el-Zour under the leadership of ousted former president Bashar al-Assad, according to a UN report seen Tuesday by Associated Press. Inspectors with the UN nuclear watchdog visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work that confirmed the existence of a long-suspected nuclear site, according to the confidential report circulated to member states. Based on this visit, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported that it is “able to establish that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities as required under the NPT Safeguards Agreement”. This information included a nuclear reactor under construction in Deir el-Zour, a fuel fabrication plant and another site used for fuel storage during the rule of Assad. Under Assad, Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear programme that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province. Following Assad’s ouster, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites. The site in Deir el-Zour only became public knowledge after Israel launched air strikes in 2007 that destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it. Israel is believed to have its own undeclared atomic weapons programme that makes it the only country in the Middle East with nuclear bombs. Israel neither confirms nor denies having atomic weapons. The IAEA took samples at the site in 2024 and reported last year that they contained uranium particles. The new Syrian authorities have also expressed an interest in developing a civilian nuclear energy programme and said any nuclear material found in the country would remain in Syria’s custody under international safeguards. The IAEA reported Tuesday that its inspectors visited the Deir el-Zour site on August 29 “to monitor progress on the excavation work”. “Based on observations made at the location, the Agency confirms that the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor.” In its confidential report, the IAEA said three locations were “functionally related” to the Deir el-Zour site. One was related to “conversion and/or fuel fabrication activities”, another was for “temporary storage of construction material”, and another was for the “temporary storage of construction materials being transferred to/from” the site, as well as for “planned reprocessing activities”. During the visit to Syria, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi and a team of senior inspectors also visited a previously undeclared site in the country. Syria notified the agency of the site’s existence in a July 17 letter and invited the IAEA “to cooperate with the Syrian authorities in the inspection and verification of the site and of any nuclear material to be potentially found”. The IAEA said in its report that this new site contained “natural uranium metal in the form of fuel rods with cladding.” The agency verified the material and confirmed “the presence of around 73 tonnes of natural uranium metal”. The agency reported that “all of this nuclear material is currently subject to Agency containment and surveillance measures”.

title: US military carries out new strikes on Iranian targets as hostilities flare
description: Iran targets American interests in Gulf states after US forces attack Iranian air defence sites, radar systems and maritime assets.
content: The US military launched new air strikes on Iran on Tuesday, marking the latest escalation in a six-month war that has seen President Donald Trump alternate between threats, economic sanctions and force. US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on social media that the attacks were in response to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) recent attempted attacks on commercial ships in the strategic Strait of ‌Hormuz and against American service ‌members deployed ‌to the ‌region. “The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines,” Trump said on his Truth Social platform. “If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level.” CENTCOM said it attacked Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, minelaying capabilities and communications sites. Oil prices rose as tensions escalated. Brent crude oil climbed above US$96 a barrel, its highest level in about two and a half months, coming ahead of the November US midterm election, where affordability has been a central theme. Iranian media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, Bandar Abbas, Konarak and Chabahar. Near Sirik, a strike on a wedding killed five people and wounded 50, according to the Iranian Red Crescent. Tehran launched retaliatory strikes against US interests across Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq. Jordan’s military reported intercepting 10 ballistic missiles while three landed in remote areas, as Kuwait and Bahrain also responded to incoming fire. In recent weeks, as US military pounding showed few signs of forcing Iran into submission, the Trump administration turned to economic pressure, which saw oil shipments through the strait return to around half their pre-war levels as attacks abated. In late August, Washington doubled down with an aggressive campaign of sanctions and financial isolation, a so-called “Economic D-Day” under the US Treasury Department’s Operation Economic Outcast. But Tehran has displayed surprising resilience after enduring decades of US and global sanctions, and the US announcements gave few specifics on what was new. Evidently concluding that financial pressure was not having the desired effect – in part, analysts say, because Washington has appeared unwilling to impose secondary sanctions on China, which bought some 80 per cent of Iran’s oil in 2025 – the US attacked Iran’s Larak ‌Island on Sunday, marking the first known strikes in several weeks. This prompted Iran to respond with missiles at two US airbases in Jordan. Tuesday’s US strikes came a day after two oil supertankers were hit in quick succession as they tried to exit the strait, according to maritime security consultant Marisks. Analysts said US pressure on China to end its financial support for Iran, a nation it has maintained diplomatic relations with for 55 years, has clear limits. Beijing’s grip on the global supply of strategic rare earth minerals means that Washington is reluctant to push too hard. And Trump wants a successful summit in Washington with Chinese President Xi Jinping later this month. Trump has become increasingly frustrated with his inability to prevail over Tehran in a war he started after criticising his predecessors for becoming entrenched in “forever wars”. But that has not stopped him from declaring victory. “We’ve already won in many ways, but we haven’t won enough,” he said at one point in recent months. “We won everything. We have all the cards,” he said at another. With enough US pressure, Beijing might be willing to make some modest concessions, said Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund of the United States, citing Chinese contacts. “The Chinese aren’t going to abandon Iran, but could there be a reduced amount of oil imported for a while? That could be a possibility,” she said. “But it’s not something China is going to want to announce.” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a 60-day June Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) aimed at halting the conflict. “I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the MOU, the Islamic Republic of ⁠Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), which includes Russia and China. But Iranian officials have shown little outward sign of bowing to pressure. “If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will ‌be able to export oil,” Iranian parliament speaker ‌Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was quoted as saying by Iranian media. Washington is “addicted to making excessive demands”, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran, “and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”. Analysts added that Iran used the just-concluded SCO summit, where Pezeshkian spoke, to reach out internationally. “The summit was important for Iran, especially given close ties with Beijing, as it followed the US ‘Economic D-Day’ threats,” said Farwa Aamer, South Asia initiatives director with the Asia Society Policy Institute. “Iran is looking to mobilise support from fellow members and would likely make the same ask when the Brics summit convenes in a few weeks,” she added, referring to a key grouping of emerging market economies. “The anti-West signalling, while avoided by some, will find its way into these summits.”

title: Carney fires back at Trump as US-Canada trade fight escalates: ‘stop trying to be tough’
description: Canadian prime minister urges Washington to end online taunts as bitter trade war shakes relations between the historically friendly neighbours.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the Trump administration on Tuesday to “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough”, as he pushed back against a fresh wave of attacks from Washington. Carney said US-Canada trade talks could resume if Washington became serious about negotiations, but he also accused the US of pursuing terms that he said could leave Canadian industries “gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out”. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” Carney said. “It’s not constructive, but that’s their democracy.” His comments came after a new barrage from Washington since trade talks collapsed August 21, including Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” and social media posts taunting Canada. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also said Canada could not go “tit-for-tat” with a US economy 13 times larger, while US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth mocked female Canadian cadets online. Hegseth on Monday posted an image from a cadet training centre in British Columbia showing two young women in uniform, adding “this is real” alongside a Canadian flag. Carney called the post “beneath their office”. The Pentagon stood by it on Tuesday, with deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss saying: “The X post speaks for itself”. Carney said the US approach in the talks would have left Canadian industries effectively as subsidiaries of American companies or imposed terms under which they would be “gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out”. “We’re not going to – of course, we’re not going to accept those terms,” Carney said. Carney said Washington sought an “uncompetitive” deal for key industries, including autos, while pushing changes affecting French-language and cultural protections. He said any of those issues was enough to block an agreement. Carney said Washington also sought limits on Canada’s future trade deals. “Canada is a sovereign state,” he said. “We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals.” Carney was also buoyed by Monday’s Liberal sweep of three special elections, including a decisive win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Quebec, where the Conservatives fell to third place. The victories brought the Liberals to 173 seats in the 343-seat House of Commons and reinforced Carney’s position as he confronts Trump over trade and Canadian sovereignty. Nelson Wiseman, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto, said Trump’s annexation threats carry particular weight in Quebec. “Quebecers have the most to lose in an apocalyptic scenario where the US absorbs Canada and the status of the French language disappears,” he said. US-Canada trade talks collapsed after the two sides failed to reach a deal, and Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly US$20 billion in Canadian goods. Canada responded with plans for tariffs on US products. Trump has repeatedly talked about making Canada the 51st state.

title: Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
description: Berlin says it will shut down a Russian consulate and take other actions, citing ‘hybrid attacks’ by Moscow.
content: The German government on Tuesday blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures. The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on August 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilising European nations. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are “known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine”. He said the device pointed to “a high degree of technical expertise” and painstaking planning, but carrying out the plan appears to have been left to “low-level” agents. Dobrindt told reporters that intelligence points to “people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities”, though he didn’t specify which ones. “Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport.” Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that “with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship”. He said the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective September 18. The Russian House cultural centre in Berlin also will be closed, though that may take some time. Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to European Union sanctions lists “in the context of hybrid attacks”, step up entry controls for people from Russia and increase “pressure on the shadow fleet”, a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions, Wadephul said. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of “shadow fleet” ships. The Russian ambassador was summoned to the Foreign Ministry in Berlin. Wadephul later told ARD television that “Germany can at any time show a stronger reaction, (but) that is not necessary at this point”. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said there would be a “fitting response” to the planned closures, Russian state news agency Tass reported. She rejected claims of Russian involvement in the attempted drone attack, calling them a “far-fetched and contrived pretext” for Berlin to escalate tensions and arguing that “as usual, no convincing or serious evidence has been presented whatsoever”. Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. It is also home to Nato’s Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to Nato battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions. In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics centre at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organised by Russian intelligence. Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials since the invasion of Ukraine. That includes organising plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defence technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. In May, Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to the AP findings and said Moscow is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. He demanded that AP “name one proven fact”. The EU has slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, targeting roughly 3,000 people and entities. EU foreign ministers will meet in Ireland Wednesday. European allies rallied around Germany after Tuesday’s announcement. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that he had spoken with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and “Nato stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig”. In mid-August, the German Cabinet approved plans to give the country’s intelligence services broader powers for actions such as disabling sabotage and hacking attempts. The planned reform, which had been in the works for months, still requires parliamentary approval. Hours before Tuesday’s German statement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who has frequently warned that Russia is carrying out a campaign of sabotage against Nato countries, said Poland has been targeted by new acts of sabotage including arson within the past “dozens of hours”. He spoke the day after a fire broke out at WB Electronics, which the Polish government has described as Europe’s biggest drone manufacturer. Prosecutors said Monday they launched an investigation based on suspicions of the “participation of foreign intelligence activities against the Republic of Poland”, without elaborating on what country might be responsible. They said the fire in Skarżysko-Kamienna destroyed warehouse facilities and caused damage estimated at least 15 million zlotys (US$4 million).

title: Bank of America VP Erin Piacenti killed in Times Square stabbing
description: The suspect, Pamela Cisneros, was killed on Monday as police responded.
content: A ⁠Bank of America ⁠vice-president, Erin Piacenti, was ⁠killed in a stabbing at Times Square on Monday. Piacenti, 32, was a vice-president in BofA’s business selection and conflicts unit, according to her LinkedIn profile. “We are shocked ‌and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones,” the US banking giant said in an emailed statement on Tuesday. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Monday ‌in a press briefing that a woman carrying multiple knives stabbed two people in Times Square before police ‌used a taser and fired their weapons. BofA’s Manhattan office is ⁠located a ⁠stone’s throw from Times Square at One Bryant Park. The bank also has other locations ‌across New York, the heartbeat of the American financial system. Piacenti sustained stab wounds in ‌the incident ‌and was later pronounced dead, the NYPD said. NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch ‌added that the attacks appeared random and unprovoked. “The investigation remains ongoing ⁠by the NYPD Force Investigation Division,” the NYPD said in a statement, ⁠adding that the suspect, Pamela Cisneros, a 49-year-old woman, was killed on Monday as officers responded. The incident comes after the fatal ‌shooting of a ‌senior Blackstone executive last summer when a gunman, carrying an assault rifle, walked into the lobby of a midtown Manhattan office building and opened fire.

title: Power failure halts trams running between Hong Kong’s Wan Chai and Admiralty
description: Disruption comes after westbound line between North Point terminus and Tin Lok Lane halted for several hours on Monday.
content: Tram services between Wan Chai and Admiralty in Hong Kong were suspended on Tuesday night because of a power failure, the second such incident in two days. The Transport Department issued a special traffic bulletin at 9.37pm, saying that Hong Kong Tramways had notified it that eastbound and westbound services between Admiralty MTR station and Tonnochy Road had been suspended because of an electricity fault. The department said at 11.58pm that normal services had resumed. The disruption was the second in consecutive days. On Monday night, westbound services between North Point terminus and Tin Lok Lane were suspended at about 6pm following a power failure. Services resumed at 11.30pm. A Hong Kong Tramways spokeswoman said an initial investigation by its engineering team had found that the two incidents involved different parts of its power supply system and were unrelated. “The incident on Monday night was caused by a sudden fault in the overhead power line system, while the incident on Tuesday night resulted from a fault in the underground power supply cable system,” she said. “Hong Kong Tramways apologises for the inconvenience caused to passengers... Our engineering team is conducting a thorough investigation in a bid to prevent similar incidents from recurring.”

title: In Focus | China, global trading partners watch closely as Trump takes on Canada
description: Ottawa’s resistance tests the limits of US pressure as countries weigh diversification, leverage and the reliability of Washington deals.
content: The latest trade war between the United States and Canada marks a turning point with key lessons for China and other major US trading partners as well as risks, say analysts and former trade officials, as US President Donald Trump continues to put his blunt stamp on global institutions. The breakdown in ties between Washington and Ottawa, one of the largest trade relationships in the world, opens one more front in the president’s disruptive path that could fuel a backlash and further distrust to Beijing’s benefit. “Should Canada succeed in weathering the storm of US retaliation while standing up for its national interests, others may follow a similar ‘get tough’ approach,” said Wendy Cutler, senior vice-president with the Asia Society Policy Institute. “There is no doubt that a growing number of partners are relating to Canada’s growing frustration with Washington, overall, and the heavy-handedness it brings to the negotiating table.” “Beijing must be enjoying watching the volley of words and actions between Washington and Ottawa,” added Cutler, a former senior negotiator at the Office of the US Trade Representative. “It would not be surprising if Beijing steps up its efforts to woo Ottawa into its court.” Talks collapsed late last month after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney broke off negotiations, accusing the US of acting in bad faith with “unfair and uneconomic” late-stage changes. The US countered that Ottawa was abandoning prior commitments, as Trump weighed in, calling Canadian negotiators “clowns” and “nasty people”. Never one to back down from a fight, the mercurial president then set his sights on Ontario Premier Doug Ford, calling him “Flunky Ford” after Ford said that Trump could “kiss my a**”. Trump followed this up with an executive order to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, known as such for almost 400 years, as “Lake America”. Ford countered that Trump’s name game resembled a skit from the television comedy show Saturday Night Live. “I have a lot of real estate on my a**, so he has a lot of room to kiss,” he said. “I just do. I’m a big dude. What can I say?” Amid the mudslinging are huge stakes involving a US$900 billion annual trade relationship, the world’s second-largest after the US and Mexico, and huge risks for Canada, whose economy is 8 per cent of its southern neighbour’s size. Trump has a long history of issuing oversized threats to show dominance and gain leverage. Wall Street traders hope he will back down, a pattern dubbed “taco”, short for “Trump always chickens out”. As it stands, however, Washington has imposed 50 per cent tariffs effective August 22 on some US$20 billion of Canadian imports; raised concerns over Canadian imports of Chinese EVs; demanded veto power over Canada’s independent trade policy; and tried to undermine Canada’s French labelling and media content requirements, a huge red line for the bilingual nation. Ottawa has countered with a pledge to match the punitive US measures “dollar for dollar” effective September 8. Trump further threatened to raise tariffs to 50 per cent effective January 1 on the hugely consequential steel and auto trades. And he has declined to automatically renew the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement, leading to a July 1, 2027, review deadline. One lesson voiced by Carney and increasingly internalised by the 200 nations that trade with the US is the lack of certainty in any agreement negotiated with Washington. “There’s no such thing as a deal any more when it comes to the US, at least with the current administration,” said Abishur Prakash, geopolitical strategist at The Geopolitical Business, a Toronto-based advisory firm. “This is a Wild West-type scenario.” The European Union and United Kingdom crafted deals with the US, Japan pledged US$500 billion and South Korea pledged US$350 billion, only to see the US administration come back for more, examples not lost on Carney, he said. “That’s proven to him that it’s never-ending, that every six months the trade demands return,” Prakash said. “He’s trying to say, ‘hey, you want a deal, let’s make a deal. But if you don’t want to make a deal, this is the consequence’.” Or, in Carney’s words, Washington’s signature is increasingly “written in pencil”. What had distinguished Carney, previewed in his World Economic Forum speech last January, was the need for middle powers led by Canada to push back, he said, even as other world leaders had rushed to Washington to appease the transactional president. By some indications, China led the way by forcing Washington to blink after Liberation Day, using its grip on strategic rare earth minerals. But Canada is far smaller and more interdependent. That said, Canada is the single-largest export market for almost all major rust belt and battleground states, including Michigan, Pennsylvania and North Carolina, coming into the midterm elections, according to the Ottawa-based Macdonald-Laurier Institute. “While some might be predisposed to think that China holds more aces in hand than Canada, that’s not necessarily true because Canada still holds the energy and fertiliser [cards],” said Nicole Bivens Collinson, managing principal with law firm Sandler, Travis and Rosenberg, formerly with the USTR and the Commerce Department. “We have to be careful we’re not overplaying our hand.” But Carney is walking a delicate line. While he has a few “nuclear” options, such as cutting off Canadian electricity that some 20 US states draw on, he wants to avoid alienating Americans, most of whom have soured on Trump. And while Carney’s domestic popularity has soared – over 70 per cent of respondents supported his decision to end trade negotiations with the US leader, according to an Abacus Data survey – that will almost certainly decline if the crisis drags on and Canadian employment and economic growth sink. “It will last and increase if Canada turns out to be right,” Prakash said. “However, if Washington doesn’t fold … the US has so many cards to play. And if Trump were to play just two of them, we would all be bleeding to bits in Canada.” Another lesson reinforced by this crisis is that global trade negotiations increasingly move at a blistering pace. And while China has used its rare earths leverage effectively, the US, Japan and others are racing to blunt this massive vulnerability by rapidly expanding mining and processing. “If I were China, I would probably know that I have a limited amount of time,” Bivens Collinson said. “If the United States is willing to do that to their trading partners to the north of the border, they’re going to be willing to do that to China.” “I would be taking this as a lesson to be heeded, and to recognise that I’ve got a shelf life on these cards that I’m holding.” While the immediate US-Canada mud fight dominates headlines, the crisis also has more fundamental implications as long-standing US-led structures are increasingly unwound and economies race to bolster bilateral ties that exclude Washington as the US hub frays and its many spokes start to break away. Canada’s 10-year diversification target aims to expand non-US exports by US$300 billion, an effort being replicated worldwide. “You have to adapt to survive and sometimes when you’re forced to adapt, diversification is the only way,” said Ashley Kalyn, international trade specialist with Peacock Tariff Consulting. “This is a case study for China and other countries right now because it shows both the possibilities and the limits of responding to US pressure.” “China will be watching Canada very closely,” she added. “Canada demonstrates that this isn’t only about China or the other state’s practices. Washington right now is fundamentally changing how things are.” Analysts questioned whether, given how economically and politically counterproductive the Canada trade war was, Trump offered terms knowing they would be rejected and had other geopolitical reasons for challenging Canadian sovereignty. Instability could serve his repeated call for Canada to become the “51st state”, which has amplified pro-independence movements in Western Canada. Others see this test of wills as a precursor to the dissolution of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) covering 520 million people and a combined GDP of over US$33 trillion, which was negotiated during Trump’s first term. His decision to delay imposing 50 per cent car tariffs until after the election, unpopular in both countries, has fuelled this theory. “US-Canada relations are more fraught than the market is pricing in,” said Henrietta Treyz, economic policy director with consultancy Veda Partners. “US businesses have been able to stave off the ‘nuclear option’ of triggering a withdrawal from the USMCA within six months, but they haven’t been able to do more than that, despite months of opportunity and years of forewarning.” Increasingly erratic US policy has seen China’s soft power grow almost by default as Washington has launched wars, undercut allies, embraced unilateralism, taken on the United Nations and Nato and alienated many US voters. But Trump’s willingness to threaten other countries’ sovereignty – whether through one-sided trade deals, language politics or force – could also concern Beijing, analysts said, given sensitivities over Xinjiang, Hong Kong and Tibet. “Chinese are playing a fabulous game of staying quiet and observing, just watching, keeping its doors open, quite confident if this trade fight snowballs,” Prakash said, adding that anti-Washington anger is palpable in Canadian pubs and coffee shops. “If the USMCA is scrapped, it may also push Mexico to say no, then you have both sides of the US open to China. “The biggest question mark is what is going to be achieved by a trade fight with Canada?”

title: Key investor Kushner blames football power struggle for World Cup plan collapse
description: Venture capitalist says his company would not have ⁠become involved in Fifa boss Infantino’s proposal had it known how it would play out.
content: Investor Joshua Kushner has blamed power struggles within global football for the outrage over Fifa’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup, admitting his firm “would not have gotten involved” if it had anticipated the backlash. The first comments by venture capitalist Kushner – the brother of Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump – since the plan collapsed came on Monday, as European governing body Uefa prepares a criminal case against Fifa president Gianni Infantino. “While we stand behind the motivations of FFE [Fifa Forward Enterprise], we failed to appreciate the political dynamics of global football, and the lengths some would go to,” Kushner said in a statement. “Had we known what this would devolve into, we would not have gotten involved,” added Kushner, whose firm Thrive Capital worked on the deal in private for months, and would have spearheaded the investment process. FFE was a plan to bring private investment into Fifa events, including the World Cup, by selling stakes in a new US$20 billion commercial subsidiary. Fifa said the proposal would have raised US$4.2 billion to benefit poorer football-playing nations, and that member associations could have voted to reject it. Infantino withdrew the proposal in late July in the face of a fierce backlash from Uefa and other stakeholders in the game. Critics said the plan had been hatched in secret to profit its investors, with Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin dubbing the proposal a “shady, opaque back room deal”. Uefa has called for Infantino’s removal, and accused the Fifa president of “criminal mismanagement”. According to legal documents seen by AFP, Uefa is gathering evidence for a potential criminal complaint in Switzerland, where both Uefa and Fifa are based. US media has reported Kushner is being targeted for subpoenas, with Uefa asking a New York judge for permission to demand Kushner and his firm hand over documents and sit for depositions related to the saga. Kushner and Thrive are not expected to be defendants in the Uefa case and have not been accused of wrongdoing. “Money in football has historically been concentrated amongst a small group of countries,” said Kushner’s statement. “The idea behind FFE was to direct more capital and equity equally amongst all 211 member countries, providing significantly more investment to underdeveloped nations to nurture local talent, support grass roots football, enhance the fan experience and ultimately grow the global game everywhere. “It was an idea that every member association would vote on, not an obligation or determination.” He added: “Thrive has a long track record of being a partner to all constituents.” Kushner is also a key investor in the ongoing, record US$12.5 billion purchase of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most successful teams in NBA history.

title: China-Nepal floods: first research shows that no one could have outrun debris flow
description: First Chinese study of the disaster shows debris reached speeds of 19 metres per second when it struck a border crossing in Tibet.
content: Not even the world’s fastest sprinters could have outrun the devastating floodwaters that struck a border crossing between China and Nepal last week, according to one of the first peer-reviewed assessments of the disaster. Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) calculated that the surface velocity of the debris flow was 19 metres per second (62 feet per second) when it struck the checkpoint at Gyirong Port in Tibet. This is almost twice Usain Bolt’s average speed when he set the 100 metres world record of 9.58 seconds in 2009, and 50 per cent higher than his top speed. In a paper posted online on Tuesday by the Chinese-language journal Yangtze River, the team used digital models and frame-by-frame analysis to reconstruct the event, which was triggered by the collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. “This disaster involved a continuous transition from ice avalanche to debris flow, then to mudslide and finally to flood,” wrote the team from CAS Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. “The time from the occurrence of the ice avalanche to its impact on the Gyirong Port was extremely short, and the effective response time was limited, which put forward higher requirements for rapid identification, information transmission and emergency decision-making.” The collapse of the glacier in Langtang Lirung on the Nepalese side of the Himalayan border created an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow that quickly reached Gyirong Port, almost 22km (14 miles) away, and then continued to cascade downstream. The floods killed at least 16 people in China, while another 546 are still missing. In Nepal the death toll has risen to 1,058 with 4,606 people still missing. The researchers calculated that the floods still had a surface velocity of around 11.7 metres per second by the time they reached a bridge on Nepal’s Trishuli River 52km away from the border crossing. This meant that it took between 46 and 75 minutes for the flow to reach the bridge, “providing a potential time window for downstream disaster response”. But the team said this was not the same as an actual warning time because factors such as monitoring, communications and the ability to respond all came into play. The Nepalese authorities have criticised the Chinese government for failing to provide timely warnings once the flow had crossed the border. The floods and other similar events have shown how difficult it is to detect and monitor high-altitude ice avalanches. The Chinese researchers concluded that a feasible response to such incidents could include tracking the potential route of the resulting ice flows and ensuring warnings are issued as soon as possible. This could be done by moving monitoring points further upstream and by using multiple sources such as remote sensing, water level monitoring and seismic data. The team also said such avalanches could create temporary dams in narrow valleys – and although these created further risks, they could also buy more time for evacuations and emergency response efforts. Some media reports have said that Chinese researchers had warned of a flood risk in this region a year ago, pointing to research published online in July last year just days after a bridge at the border crossing was destroyed when the natural dam holding back a glacial lake collapsed. Scientists from the Chengdu University of Technology looked at how glacial lakes were rising as a result of climate change and said there was a risk of further incidents upstream from the bridge. Although the research called for better early warning systems for upstream floods, it did not examine the potential for a glacier collapse. The CAS researchers said that while climate change would have an effect on the stability of glaciers and other ice formations, it was not the only factor. The team also said further research was needed on ways to improve disaster detection and early warnings. They also warned there was some uncertainty about their research because it had relied on limited data and estimates rather than direct measurements and field verification. In a second study published on Tuesday in the CAS-run journal Science Bulletin, another team described the catastrophe as a sudden failure driven by long-term glacier dynamics rather than an immediate trigger such as heavy rainfall. The researchers from institutes in mainland China and Hong Kong also found that seismic precursor signals hours before the collapse coincided with smaller-scale snow and ice activity witnessed on-site.

title: ‘Worst yet to come’ as Hong Kong schools cut record 126 Primary One classes
description: Contraction hits Kwai Tsing hardest, where nearly half the district’s 31 primary schools forced to trim Primary One intake.
content: Hong Kong public schools have slashed a record 126 Primary One classes for the 2026-27 academic year amid a shrinking student population, prompting a sector leader to warn that the “worst is yet to come”. According to the latest Primary School Profiles, the total number of Primary One classes across public schools dropped from 1,558 in 2025-26 to 1,432 in 2026-27, representing a net decrease of 8 per cent. The guide covers more than 500 local primary institutions and is compiled by the Committee on Home-School Co-operation to help parents select schools for their children. The contraction hit Kwai Tsing the hardest, where nearly half the district’s 31 primary schools – 14 campuses – were forced to trim their Primary One intake. Tuen Mun and Eastern districts followed, each losing 13 classes. The latest profiles of more than 500 primary institutions serve as reference materials for parents selecting schools for their children. The sharp drop in enrolment tracks a collapse in local births dating back to 2020, when Covid-19 pandemic curbs and the aftermath of the 2019 social unrest saw births plunge by nearly 20 per cent year on year to 43,000. Jessie Cheung Chok-fong, a primary school principal and consultant to the Subsidised Primary Schools Council, warned that the sector faced prolonged hardship. “The worst is yet to come, and all schools know very well, as the city’s birth rate in recent years has been on a declining trend and the winter for the primary school sector is apparently not yet over,” she said. In March, the Education Bureau announced that a record 15 primary schools would not be allowed to operate subsidised Primary One classes this school year. Among them, four opted to close within three years, eight chose to merge with other campuses, two pivoted to private Primary One classes and one was exempted from submitting a survival plan. Across the city, 100 public primary schools reduced their intake by one Primary One class, 21 lost two and Tsz Wan Shan Catholic Primary School in Wong Tai Sin cut three. Eighteen schools expanded their intake: 17 added one class, while the newly established Erudite Government Primary School in Sai Kung added two to operate three classes this year. The city’s low birth rate has continued to decline between 2021 and 2025. Official data released last month revealed that Hong Kong recorded fewer than 30,000 births from mid-2025 to mid-2026, a 15.6 per cent year-on-year decline. It was the first time since official records began in 1962 that the city recorded fewer than 30,000 births in its midyear population update, breaking the previous midyear low of 32,600 in 2023. The bureau earlier estimated that the population of six-year-olds eligible for Primary One will fall to 40,600 in 2027 and plummet further to 31,500 by 2029. Parents applying for public Primary One places in the coming discretionary stage must submit their choices by September 25, with results released on November 23. Principal Cheung said schools would try their best to promote themselves during the discretionary stage in the Primary One admission system. “What schools can do now is to do everything they can to let parents know their features and strengths,” she said. “I think school-sponsoring bodies and schools with one or two Primary One classes will have to carefully study the possibility of merging with other schools. “Merging with other institutions allows students to go to the same school after their original school closes down,” she said, adding that at least some pupils would feel “they are still together instead of going to different schools”. Cheung added that the city’s drive to attract talent in recent years had not benefited primary schools much, as incoming professionals were not likely to send their children to the city when they were only six to seven years old.

title: What’s next after China court freezes US$318m in Nexperia assets amid Wingtech battle?
description: Bitter custody fight sparked by Dutch intervention has affected European supply lines, and assets look to remain frozen for years.
content: A Chinese court’s order to freeze 2.14 billion yuan (US$318 million) in Nexperia-affiliated assets has cemented the operational independence of its Chinese manufacturing engine from its European headquarters, leaving its local facilities increasingly isolated amid a prolonged custody battle. The Dongguan Intermediate People’s Court in the southern province of Guangdong, where Nexperia’s biggest assembly and test plant is located, has frozen the equity interests in four subsidiaries owned by the Dutch firm, Wingtech said in a Monday filing to the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Meanwhile, equity interests in another Chinese entity owned by Itec BV, a chip tool maker spun off from Nexperia in 2021, have also been frozen. The ruling, affecting 2.14 billion yuan worth of combined assets across the cities of Dongguan, Shanghai and Wuxi, is due to last for three years, until August 2029. The move is designed to “protect Chinese subsidiaries’ assets from being transferred or pledged as collateral”, while their daily operations would not be affected, said Luo Zhiyu, a partner at the DeHeng Law Offices in Beijing who specialises in cross-border transactions and overseas listings. The order marks a major development in the saga that saw Wingtech file a lawsuit against Nexperia and three of its executives in May under China’s anti-foreign sanctions law, demanding the restoration of full control over Nexperia and 8 billion yuan (US$1.17 billion) in compensation. The case has not yet gone to trial. The asset freeze may be revoked after the case proceeds to a court ruling, Luo said. It typically takes three months for the intermediate court to issue a ruling after a hearing is scheduled, though appeals could push the timeline to months or years, he added. Lawyers Yuan Yao and Ge Jingyi at Shanghai-based Joint-Win Partners estimated that the process could take several months if the most optimistic scenario plays out and the two sides reach a settlement. However, if the case were to proceed through normal litigation, it could take one to three years, “or even longer”, they said. Nexperia said in a statement on Monday that the court measures related “solely to entities in China that have been operating outside” its governance structures since October, adding that it was “reviewing the court order and its available legal options”. Itec did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. The saga began last September when the Dutch government intervened to restrict Wingtech’s control over the chipmaker – a decision that was later suspended. But in early October, a Dutch court ousted Wingtech founder Zhang Xuezheng as Nexperia CEO. The power struggle has led to a virtual break-up of Nexperia’s China team – responsible for about 70 per cent of its global output – and its operations outside the country. For example, the plant in Dongguan used to source wafers – a key material – from Nexperia’s German and British factories, but that supply has been cut off since October. Last month, Nexperia’s China subsidiary announced plans to shift its entire product line to a domestic 12-inch wafer supplier, in pursuit of what it called “independent operations”. Shanghai-listed Wingtech, the Chinese owner that has sold most of its other electronics businesses to focus on semiconductors, has suffered steep financial losses. It reported a net loss of 189 million yuan in the first quarter, swinging from a net profit of 261 million yuan in the same period a year prior. That followed an 8.7 billion yuan net loss for all of 2025. The company has also faced a delisting risk warning since May, after its auditor reported scope limitations, citing an inability to verify Nexperia’s overseas financial records. Wingtech said it could be forced to delist if such limitations were not resolved this year. Wingtech has also mounted a legal challenge in the Netherlands, where the local court in February upheld CEO Zhang’s suspension and ordered an investigation that was expected to last up to six months. No updates have since emerged. Wingtech reiterated on Monday that it would “continue to exhaust all legal measures to regain full control of Nexperia”.

title: China’s Li pledges to address US firms’ ‘reasonable concerns’ at Beijing meeting
description: Chinese premier urges US companies to invest more in China, while calling on Washington to take similar steps to strengthen trade ties.
content: Chinese Premier Li Qiang has urged US companies to deepen their presence in China, pledging to address their concerns while calling on Washington to reciprocate, as Beijing gears up for President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to the United States later this month. The remarks came as Li met a delegation from the US-China Business Council – led by its chair, Visa CEO Ryan McInerney – at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on Tuesday. Li said China would address the “reasonable concerns” of US companies and ensure a fair and competitive market, while urging Washington to “take concrete steps” to address issues raised by Beijing and implement the outcomes of recent bilateral trade talks between the two sides. “China may be the only market in the world that combines the two qualities of being large and new,” Li said, pointing to the country’s fast-growing smart and green consumption sectors. Li added that frictions were normal given the scale of bilateral trade between China and the US, and that solutions could be found to any issues through mutual respect and consultation. The US-China Business Council represents more than 270 US companies operating in China, including Visa, Medtronic, 3M and Pfizer. McInerney and other delegation members said the meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump in May had provided stable expectations for bilateral economic cooperation, and that US businesses would continue to expand investment in China and remain “long-term partners” in its development, according to Xinhua. On Monday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent took aim at China’s global trade surplus in his opening address at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, raising concerns over “excessive imbalances”. Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s foreign ministry, said on the same day that Beijing had never deliberately pursued a surplus and opposed unilateral tariffs. In US dollar terms, China’s total bilateral trade with the US rose by 2.3 per cent in the first seven months of the year, while the country’s total foreign trade jumped 21.8 per cent, according to Chinese customs data.

title: Apple’s new CEO Ternus takes over from Tim Cook after 15 years
description: The transition to a new CEO comes at a pivotal time for Apple as it navigates artificial intelligence challenges in the industry.
content: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus takes the helm of the iconic tech giant on Tuesday, ending Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure during which the company’s value skyrocketed to US$4.6 trillion thanks to the iPhone’s enormous popularity. The transition to a new CEO comes at a pivotal time for Apple. Artificial intelligence has unleashed the greatest upheaval within the industry since Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in 2007. Apple has got off to a rough start in AI after stumbling in its efforts to deliver new features built on the technology, as promised nearly two years ago. Earlier this year, it unveiled new artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasising a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the iPhone maker tries to catch up with rivals. Ternus faces challenges that will force him to step outside his comfort zone in hardware engineering. Beyond finding ways to keep Apple competitive in the artificial intelligence race, he will need to navigate supply chain questions and relationships with figures such as US President Donald Trump, who offered public praise for his predecessor on Tuesday. Serving as Apple CEO will also require soft skills, including developing relationships with important figures. Cook cultivated ties with Trump as he navigated the company through business challenges, including Trump’s trade and tariff war targeting countries in Asia, where Apple has extensive manufacturing supply chains. Although he is handing over the CEO reins at Apple, Cook is widely expected to help the company maintain a good relationship with Trump after he shifts to his new role as executive chairman. Ternus worked on some of Apple’s signature products under Cook, including the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro. He will headline next week’s launch of the latest iPhone at Apple’s Cupertino, California, headquarters.

title: Suspected cyberattack puts data of 33,054 customers using group-buying app at risk
description: Privacy watchdog receives report of data breach from TVB-owned Neigbuy, while police learn of six cases of scammers posing as staff.
content: The private data of about 33,000 customers of TVB-owned group-buying platform Neigbuy has been compromised in a suspected cyberattack, with police saying they have received six reports of scammers posing as staff.
