The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data confirmed on Tuesday that it had received a data breach notification from the company on Sunday, and had initiated a formal investigation. The platform, founded in 2018 and majority-owned by free-to-air television broadcaster TVB, offers limited-time deals on groceries, fresh produce, household goods and other products. The privacy watchdog said that signs of a suspected cyberattack, involving unauthorised data access, were first detected on August 24. The security incident had affected 33,054 customers, with the potentially compromised information including their names, addresses, emails, phone numbers and online shopping order histories, it said. The office advised Neigbuy customers to change their account passwords and enable multi-factor authentication. They should also remain vigilant if contacted by unknown or suspicious parties, it urged. Police said on Monday that six cases involving fraudsters posing as Neigbuy customer service staff had been reported over the past week, with the total losses exceeding HK$300,000 (US$38,270). The force also disclosed on its Facebook page for the CyberDefender platform that scammers were posing as Neigbuy customer service staff and claiming to be handling lost parcels, refunds or security deposits. Fraudsters were requesting order screenshots and recipient contact details to execute the scams, police added. In a statement posted on its website, Neigbuy confirmed that it had reported the incident to police and the privacy watchdog. The company said it had isolated affected systems, updated account credentials, and tightened access controls and anomaly monitoring. Neigbuy added that customers’ passwords, credit card details and bank account information were not compromised. It urged customers to be wary of suspicious calls or messages, stressing that staff would never request passwords, verification codes or bank transfers.

title: Netflix K-drama Four Hands, Two Sonatas: Song Kang, Lee Jun-young as rival piano prodigies
description: Song Kang and Lee Jun-young star as two brilliant but opposing young pianists who are forced to play together in this musical K-drama.
content: Lead cast: Song Kang, Lee Jun-young, Jang Gyu-ri Latest Nielsen rating: 5.94 per cent After two years of military service, Song Kang returns to the screen as a brooding musical prodigy in Four Hands, Two Sonatas. Joining him at the piano is the highly prolific Lee Jun-young, setting the stage for a classical music drama that pits two brilliant but opposing talents against each other. Kang Pi-o (Song) and Choi Jeong-yo (Lee) are gifted pianists from opposite sides of the tracks who are forced to combine their talents as they seek to confront their weaknesses and silence their naysayers. For Song, the role marks his first appearance since My Demon concluded in early 2024. Meanwhile, Lee (Reborn Rookie) squeezed the project in just ahead of his own military enlistment this summer, capping off 10 film and television credits in two years. Pi-o is the grandson of a celebrated conductor who refuses to acknowledge him because he was born out of wedlock – despite Pi-o excelling at the piano and winning competitions at home and abroad. This lack of recognition fuels a deep-seated resentment, prompting Pi-o to keep everyone at arm’s length and do rash things, like throwing away the certificates he wins. Since he tends to do this in dramatic fashion – like tossing them in the school bathroom bin for everyone to see – he incurs both the jealousy and animosity of his peers. Jeong-yo is a far more sociable young man with a happy-go-lucky attitude that belies his precarious circumstances. He attends a rough school populated with aggressive youths involved in crime and, following the death of his mother, returns home to a penniless, alcoholic father who is accumulating insurmountable debt. Although he hides it from his friends, Jeong-yo is a brilliant pianist and tends to slink away when he wants to practise. One day, after watching a school recital featuring Pi-o, he sneaks into the dressing room after the show to play the piano. Pi-o’s smitten classmate Hong Jae-in (Jang Gyu-ri, When the Phone Rings) overhears his exceptional playing and, though he runs off, she tracks him down to hire him as her accompanist. Soon, the teachers at Korea Arts High School also recognise his gift, and before long, Jeong-yo enters the school on a scholarship. Despite all his accolades, Pi-o has plateaued, and while everyone recognises his technical talent, those whose opinions matter most feel that his playing lacks emotion. Conversely, Jeong-yo’s emotional playing is quick to move people, but he is rough around the edges. Celebrated pianist Do Hyun-soo (Kim Ju-hun) decides to take them both under his wing, but only if they play “four hands” – two players on the same piano – to learn from each other and grow together. The set-up for Four Hands, Two Sonatas is simple and clear, with two protagonists whose opposing characteristics present them as mirror images of one another – they are two pieces of the same puzzle. With all its classical music and upper-class trappings, including a dramatic flash-forward opening in a music hall in Prague as Pi-o plays with bleeding fingers, the show relies on the shorthand of its images to immediately situate the viewer. As such, entering this world is smooth and all its themes and images are easy to parse, but much like Pi-o is criticised for being technically proficient but emotionally inert, the devil is in the details. Four Hands, Two Sonatas presents a story where conflicts and characters are, for the most part, black and white. What it lacks are the gradients in between to give it the colour it needs. A case in point is the distinction between Pi-o and Jeong-yo’s piano skills. Both sound excellent to the untrained ears; it is only the expert characters in the show who react differently to them. The show clearly explains the motivations behind the characters’ different styles of playing, but since it doesn’t employ any subtle means to help us distinguish them ourselves – we can only take other characters at their word – the opportunity to help us feel the story, rather than merely understand it, slips by. Perhaps, much like its characters, the show just needs some time to settle and explore the middle ground between the opposing emotions and circumstances it sets up. However, that kind of work has to happen before arriving on stage, not while you are on it trying to impress your audience. Four Hands, Two Sonatas is streaming on Netflix.

title: In race with US for critical resources, China discovers major copper and gold deposit
description: Ministry of Natural Resources says Chating deposit could contain more than 1 million tonnes of copper and 200 tonnes of gold.
content: China has discovered a major copper and gold deposit in the latest breakthrough in its hunt for metals vital to solar power, new-energy industries and data centre construction. The deposit was found in the central province of Anhui, China Central Television reported on Tuesday, with the main mineralised body about 1.2km long and 1.1km wide and deeper sections yet to be fully delineated. The Ministry of Natural Resources said preliminary estimates suggested the deposit contained the equivalent of several large copper deposits – each containing more than 500,000 tonnes. The Chating deposit could also contain the equivalent of more than 10 large gold deposits, each holding at least 20 tonnes, the state broadcaster reported on Tuesday. “The major breakthrough was achieved in just a few months and is highly significant,” it quoted the ministry as saying. “China has strong demand for copper and remains heavily reliant on external supplies, but Anhui’s Chating deposit shows that the country still has considerable domestic exploration potential.” Copper’s conductivity makes it indispensable for powering grids, electric vehicles, renewable energy, and artificial intelligence data centres. Gold, meanwhile, is used in high-end electronics and aerospace equipment, while its role as a reserve and safe-haven asset has drawn greater attention from central banks amid heightened economic and geopolitical uncertainty. China launched a nationwide mineral exploration drive in 2021 to expand domestic reserves of critical minerals and reduce supply-chain risks. The Chating deposit could eventually support a major copper and gold production base in central China, and estimates of its resources could rise as exploration continues. Associated deposits of silver and sulphur could also be recovered, the report said. Chating was among the priority exploration projects for this year selected by the ministry as part of a broader push targeting copper, gold, rare earths, antimony and other strategic minerals. Buoyed by booming investment in data centres and heightened geopolitical uncertainty, copper and gold prices have remained near historic highs. LME copper reached US$14,294 a tonne by Tuesday, while spot gold stood around US$4,430 a troy ounce. The International Energy Agency warned in July that global copper supply could fall 25 per cent short of demand by 2035 – even if currently planned projects proceeded. It said the looming gap had prompted governments to step up public financing for new mines and processing facilities, facilitate long-term offtake arrangements and consider strategic stockpiles, adding that greater recycling could also help ease supply strains. The United States imposed tariffs of up to 50 per cent on semi-finished copper products last year in a bid to strengthen domestic production and reduce its reliance on imports. About 200,000 tonnes of copper arrived at US ports in July, the largest monthly inflow since records began in 2014, Bloomberg reported, citing IHS Markit data. China, which relies on imports for more than 80 per cent of its copper concentrate, is also stepping up domestic exploration. In May, China announced that deeper exploration at Tibet’s Yulong copper mine had added 1.31 million tonnes of copper resources, bringing the total amount identified at the site to 7.53 million tonnes.

title: Naomi Osaka brings steel, style of NBA icon Iverson to reach US Open second round
description: Four-time grand slam champion makes another fashion statement before defeating unseeded Russian Anastasia Zakharova in straight sets.
content: Naomi Osaka unveiled ⁠another bold grand slam ⁠walk-on outfit at the US Open ⁠on Monday before the two-time champion battled to a 7-6, 7-6 victory over unseeded Russian Anastasia Zakharova to reach the second round. Osaka has been the fashion highlight of this year’s majors and entered Arthur Ashe Stadium in a hooded tunic ‌featuring patchwork-style panels adorned with press clippings from past tournament appearances and a billowing white tulle train. At Wimbledon, she paid tribute to her Japanese heritage with a kimono-inspired ensemble featuring a traditional kanzashi hair ornament before changing into a white Nike playing kit. At Roland Garros, she arrived in a black Kevin Germanier skirt and competed in a layered yellow, ⁠brown and gold outfit inspired by the Eiffel Tower’s nighttime sparkle. Her look at the Australian Open ‌took its cues from a jellyfish. Competing at Flushing Meadows in an Allen Iverson-inspired outfit, the four-time grand slam champion looked set for a straightforward victory after ‌racing into a 4-1 lead, only for world No 101 Zakharova to force ⁠a tiebreak. “It’s my tribute ⁠to Iverson,” Osaka said of the fashion trailblazer and NBA Hall of Famer. “I really like him a lot. “Nike said basketball, so I said ‘you ‌want basketball, I’ll give you basketball’. I like expressing myself through clothes and I’m glad you guys appreciate it.” Former Philadelphia 76ers star Iverson is often credited with helping bring street culture and style to basketball. Osaka had paid tribute to Iverson in her pre-tournament press conference last week, wearing a T-shirt depicting the NBA star as she spoke to reporters. “For me he’s a trailblazer,” Osaka said. “He’s kind of like done a lot in fashion, whether it’s on purpose or not, but he’s shifted the way that NBA players dress. “I also think the whole conversation around clothes in sports and also just expressing yourself through style, I feel like he’s someone that I look up to in that regard.” Osaka showed her ‌battling ‌qualities to win the tiebreak before being taken to another in the second set, where she ‌held her nerve to close out the victory. “I would say it took everything [to win],” Osaka said ⁠as the clock approached 12.30am on Tuesday. “I have no idea what time it is. Thanks ⁠for staying,” she told fans. “I’m grateful to be able to play on this court again. “I just told myself to not have any regrets. I wanted to come out ‌and compete. I haven’t played ‌since Toronto, so I was a little rusty. I get nervous in the first rounds. I want to do well and show you guys new outfits.” The 13th seed, champion at Flushing Meadows in 2018 and 2020, takes on Czech Republic’s Katerina Siniakova in the second round.

title: Starship could create more debris than an anti-satellite test if it explodes in orbit
description: As SpaceX prepares for a test of the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, experts note the risk of an in-flight incident.
content: As Starship, the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, gears up for an attempt to finally reach Earth’s orbit, experts say the risk of an in-flight catastrophe – and a cloud of debris – “needs to be of concern”. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is expected to launch the Starship spacecraft and Super Heavy booster for the launch system’s 14th test flight and first orbital test flight later this month. According to one aerospace expert, if the Starship’s upper stage explodes in orbit it could produce debris on a scale larger than previous in-orbit incidents, including an anti-satellite missile test. During that test, in November 2021, Russia intentionally blew up a defunct Soviet intelligence satellite called Cosmos-1408. Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at The University of Texas at Austin, said the Russian test had detrimental consequences for the operation of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation. He said if Starship were to explode in orbit, it could create a lot of debris that could become hazards to other objects as well as humans. “If something like that happened in low-Earth orbit, it would be like the Russian anti-satellite test, but probably a few scales larger in terms of the amount of debris it would generate,” Jah said. As of the end of August, SpaceX was still awaiting final regulatory approval for the test flight from the US Federal Aviation Administration, which regulates American commercial space launches. “The FAA is responsible for the safety oversight of licensed commercial space vehicle launch and re-entry operations,” the FAA told the South China Morning Post in August. “Our safety oversight authority does not extend to in-orbit activities.” The Russian satellite – which had a radius of around 2.5 metres (eight feet) and weighed some two tonnes – produced 1,500 trackable pieces of debris and hundreds of thousands more smaller fragments, according to National Geographic. The reusable Starship launch system consists of a powerful 72-metre first-stage booster called the Super Heavy, which separates from the upper stage of the rocket after launch and does not reach orbit. The 52-metre, 100-tonne upper stage of the rocket – known as the Starship – is designed to reach orbit. Both rocket stages are designed to be reusable and to be caught on Earth by a tower with “chopstick” arms. A variant of the Starship called the human landing system (HLS) was selected to take part in Nasa’s Artemis programme, which aims to bring American astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since the end of the Apollo missions in 1972. After astronauts launch from Earth aboard the Orion spacecraft, the Starship HLS, or Blue Origin’s Blue Moon landing system, will ferry astronauts to and from the lunar surface. To escape Earth’s gravity and reach the moon, the Starship HLS will reportedly need to be fuelled with around 1,500 tonnes of liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant. This will involve multiple docking missions in low-Earth orbit using depot and fuel tanker variants of the Starship. SpaceX has had a string of incidents involving the launch system in recent years, including in April 2023 when two rocket stages failed to separate and exploded, and in June last year when a Starship upper stage blew up on a test stand. Asked if there was any cause for concern given SpaceX’s track record, Jah said: “The fact that we’re launching it, the fact that the thing can explode, makes it a possibility. So, it needs to be of concern.” An explosion could potentially send a cloud of bullet-like shrapnel into low-Earth orbit. Jah said rocket bodies owned by the US had previously exploded in higher, geostationary transfer orbits where there was still a debris risk. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to the European Space Agency, the main cause of orbital explosions is residual fuel left in tanks and fuel lines or other energy sources. Over time, the mechanical integrity of spacecraft parts can degrade, leading to leaks or fuel mixing that triggers self-ignition. Starship’s planned test flight – which was originally slated for August and is now expected in mid-September – will be an attempt to launch the spacecraft into orbit. Previous attempts have only reached suborbital trajectories. According to the FAA website, protecting public safety during launches is central to its licencing and approval process. The US, China and Russia are all parties to the Outer Space Treaty, a basic framework for international space law that took effect in 1967. According to Article 7 of the treaty, any state that launches a space object is internationally liable for compensation for any damage the object causes to another state on Earth or in space. Ella Atkins, a professor of aerospace engineering at Virginia Tech, said the primary Starship explosion risk lay in the booster, which did not enter orbit. She said that once Starship or any other payload entered low-Earth orbit, there was a risk of collision when its orbit was not coordinated with other space objects or junk. That made it “critical” for launch authorities and companies to coordinate and collaborate. “All space missions pose a risk of collision. On-orbit testing and refuelling are unlikely to generate anything close to the space junk problem amassed over all objects that persist in orbit today,” Atkins said. She noted that the high orbiting speeds required for objects to counter Earth’s gravity were dependent on Earth’s mass rather than on spacecraft mass. Because of this speed, every orbiting object posed a risk to other objects. “It is therefore critical that no orbiting object hit another orbiting object, regardless of the two objects’ mass or relative masses,” she said. When a debris-generating event occurs in Earth’s orbit, it poses a threat to nearby satellites and spacecraft. Over time, fragments disperse across orbital lanes, with some of the debris being pulled down by atmospheric drag to burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere. Across the history of space travel, thousands of launches have resulted in tens of thousands of tracked objects in orbit, including both spacecraft and debris, according to the European Space Agency. Many more pieces of space debris are too small to track. According to a paper published in the peer-reviewed Chinese-language Journal of Astronautics in May, space debris is a big factor in the safety of missions. Researchers from Sun Yat-sen University and Northwestern Polytechnical University pointed to a 2016 incident where the solar panels of the ESA Sentinel-1A satellite were struck by a centimetre-sized piece of debris, creating a 40cm (16-inch) impact crater. They also noted an incident in November, when a window of the Shenzhou-20 spacecraft docked at China’s Tiangong space station was struck by a tiny piece of debris, delaying the return of astronauts. The rapid growth of internet megaconstellations in Earth’s orbit, driven by SpaceX’s Starlink, has added to the issue of debris, according to the paper. Starlink’s more than 11,000 satellites in orbit have to perform hundreds of thousands of collision-avoidance manoeuvres each year to get out of the path of debris and other spacecraft. Orbital crowding has meanwhile led to concerns about Kessler Syndrome – a theoretical scenario where the density of objects in orbit becomes so high that collisions could create a chain reaction, making certain orbital regions unusable. According to Jah, no evidence has led him to believe that an uncontrolled event in space would continue ad infinitum. “Even if cascading does happen, at some point an equilibrium state will be achieved because Mother Nature is always seeking some form of equilibrium,” he said. Jah said more coordination and planning would be needed as the number of satellite constellations rose. He said it could be comparable to the International Telecommunication Union’s role in distributing spectrum – the frequencies and wavelengths used for wireless communication between space and ground. “If something similar could be done for orbital carrying capacity or something like that, I think that could be useful,” Jah said, referring to the maximum number of space objects in a specific orbital region. “The first come, first served sort of thing is very colonial, very extractive, exploitative,” he said. “SpaceX pretty much has a monopoly in low-Earth orbit. That, and rightfully so, upsets other countries and entities.” Jah said the incentive for better coordination was long-term sustainability. But in the near term, he said the three powers dominating space traffic – the US, China, and Russia – wanted “unlimited freedom of action” and it was unlikely they would sign a treaty to manage such issues.

title: Welfare groups seek clarity on breed classification amid third fighting dog case
description: Animal groups fear unclear rules could lead to more dog abandonment after owner gives up pet classed as fighting breed, the third such case in a week.
content: A Hong Kong man has surrendered his dog after authorities detained it and classified it as a fighting breed – the third known case in a week following a spate of attacks in the city. The case came as animal welfare groups called for clarity on the government’s breed-classification procedures and a transparent appeal mechanism. They warned that heightened anxiety could lead to more pet abandonment and unfair stereotyping of certain breeds. Jacqueline Cheung, founder of the non-profit Love Adopt Animal Society, told the South China Morning Post on Tuesday that she took ownership of seven-year-old Bobo the previous day after the animal’s owner relinquished her at the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD). The original owner had taken his licensed pet to the department for vaccination last Wednesday but was later told that the dog was suspected of being a fighting breed. The animal was held until Monday and subsequently classified as a pit bull terrier crossbreed. The owner reportedly has brain cancer and was unable to cope with the pressure of caring for Bobo. He sought help from volunteers, who eventually put him in touch with Cheung. According to Cheung, a former veterinary nurse, Bobo was well behaved but had severe eye inflammation and was covered in ticks when she collected her from the department. The dog was also diagnosed with heartworm, which typically takes at least six months to develop after a dog is bitten by an infected mosquito. “While pet abandonment can occur with zero accountability on the part of the owner, there is a high chance the dog would likely be put down [if no one adopts her],” she said. Bobo, now called Bowie, is being kept at a pet hotel under Cheung’s supervision. Cheung said the department’s seizures could make owners more reluctant to have their dogs vaccinated against rabies or receive booster shots, potentially affecting public health. She said she would appeal against the department’s classification and hoped it could provide owners with more details about the appeal mechanism. In a statement on Tuesday, the Hong Kong Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA) called for greater procedural clarity over breed classification, more transparent and consistent breed verification procedures, and a review of the definition and management arrangements for “dangerous dogs”. It added that this would “help reassure the community and protect public safety while ensuring animal welfare is properly prioritised”. The group also said that heightened anxiety over recent cases could lead to “unnecessary conflict between neighbours, pet abandonment or unfair assumptions about dogs based solely on their size, appearance or perceived breed”. “Such reactions risk reversing years of collective progress towards a more pet-inclusive and compassionate city,” it said. In the past week, the department seized eight-year-old Baku from his home, while 10-year-old Baobao was at risk of being seized from a coffee shop unless he was neutered immediately. The government later said both dogs had pit bull lineage. Baku’s owner confirmed to the SCMP that the dog returned home on Monday. April Yip, founder of Home for Homeless Dogs, said Baku’s owner was considering whether to appeal against the department’s classification. She told the SCMP that the owner was dissatisfied that the department had renewed Baku’s licence as a “mongrel” in January, only to reclassify the dog as an alleged fighting breed seven months later. In response to SCMP, an AFCD spokesman said the department had drawn on international law-enforcement experience to identify the breed through visual assessments of the dog’s physical characteristics, body proportions and physique. He said American pit bull terriers, American Staffordshire terriers and American bullies had long been classified as pit bull terriers – a category of fighting dogs subject to bans on importation and breeding. He added that owners who disagreed with the department’s classification could apply to the Dogs and Cats Classification Board within 14 days for a review of the decision. Under Hong Kong law, pit bull terriers, dogo Argentinos, Japanese Tosas, Fila Brasileiros and their crossbreeds are classified as fighting dogs. The law requires fighting dogs to be neutered by a registered veterinary surgeon, while owners must obtain a valid neutering certificate. Anyone who possesses a fighting dog but cannot produce a veterinary certificate showing that it has been neutered could face a maximum penalty of a HK$50,000 (US$6,378) fine and six months’ imprisonment.

title: Explosive devices damage power lines near German coal plant
description: At least one device detonated, but others failed to go off. No one was hurt and there was no major blackout in the area.
content: Improvised explosive devices were used on Tuesday in a sabotage attack near a coal-fired power plant in Germany, with several electricity lines damaged and supply briefly interrupted, officials said. Several makeshift bombs were found around 8am local time at the Preilack substation, which distributes power from the nearby Jaenschwalde plant that runs on lignite and also burns rubbish, a police spokeswoman said. At least one of the devices detonated but others failed to go off, she said, adding that no one was hurt and there was no major blackout in the area, about 100km (60 miles) southeast of Berlin. Power plant operator LEAG said in a statement that “an attack was carried out on the Preilack substation, through which the electricity generated at the Jaenschwalde power plant is fed” into the grid. LEAG said there was a “technical failure” in a unit at the power plant, and a possible connection with the incident was being investigated. Grid operator 50 Hertz claimed that unidentified perpetrators damaged several lines in its grid. “There was a brief interruption of service. All lines are now back in operation. The general power supply is currently not affected,” it said in a statement. The police spokeswoman said an investigation had been launched to determine who was behind the incident. Among the recent arson attacks, the most serious took place in Berlin in January. It caused an electricity outage that left tens of thousands of homes and thousands of businesses without power for nearly a week in the middle of winter in the southwest of capital.

title: Philippine capital’s ‘acutely unhealthy’ air due to Indonesian haze spurs warnings
description: The haze has led Quezon City to suspend classes in schools and health experts to urge residents to wear N95 masks outdoors.
content: Smoke from Indonesian wildfires blanketed Manila on Tuesday, turning fires nearly 2,000km (1,242 miles) away into a public-health warning for the Philippine capital and reviving concerns over Southeast Asia’s recurring transboundary haze problem. The haze, carried by southwesterly winds from fires in Kalimantan, the Indonesian part of Borneo, prompted health experts to urge people to wear N95 masks outdoors as air quality deteriorated across parts of Metro Manila. In parts of the capital region, the air quality index reached “acutely unhealthy” levels, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources warned on Sunday, based on readings from its monitoring stations. The warning has prompted Quezon City, part of the Philippine capital region, to suspend classes in all schools. Gerry Bagtasa, a Japan-trained atmospheric physicist at the University of the Philippines’ Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology, told ABS-CBN that the haze was dangerous because it was made up of tiny particles carried by southwesterly winds. Based on satellite images, he said the pollutants had come from intensifying wildfires in western and southern Kalimantan. Although Kalimantan is about 1,939km from Manila, Bagtasa said two typhoons hovering east of Taiwan and south of Hong Kong, along with the current El Nino phenomenon, were intensifying the southwest monsoon Habagat occurring at this time of year. “These [typhoons and El Nino] are pulling the Habagat and along with this, the emissions from the fires in Kalimantan,” he said. Bagtasa expected the haze to linger until the weekend, depending on whether the wind would change direction. Indonesia’s forest and land fires are often fuelled by a mix of dry weather, peatland conditions and land-clearing practices, with smoke from large fires capable of travelling across borders when seasonal winds shift. The last time the Philippines was affected by Indonesian haze was in 2015, during another El Nino event, Bagtasa said. He said, however, that the haze was not a natural disaster but was “man-made” and could potentially worsen because of typical peaks of wildfires in Indonesia between September and October. Rontgene M. Solante, who chairs the Adult Infectious Diseases and Tropical Medicine Fellowship Programme at San Lazaro Hospital in Manila, urged people to use N95 masks rather than other types of face coverings. He said even healthy adults should wear masks outdoors because fine particles could lodge in the lungs and cause breathing difficulties. The haze has also raised questions over whether Southeast Asian governments have effective ways to mobilise cross-border help when fires in one country affect the health of residents in another. Yohanes Sulaiman, an associate professor in international relations at Universitas Jenderal Achmad Yani in Cimahi, Indonesia, said any regional response would depend on whether Jakarta was willing to accept outside help. “The problem is that I don’t see [Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto] is going to accept help from fellow Asean members since this is embarrassing,” he added. Except for Japan, Indonesia’s government had previously been reluctant to accept foreign help during disasters, Sulaiman said. In separate interviews, Philippine military officials told This Week in Asia there was no automatic mechanism within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for soldiers from one bloc member to help another in humanitarian and disaster response. Colonel Jose Regonay Jnr, deputy chief of the Philippine Army’s Public Affairs Office, said Filipino troops were recently involved in joint military training exercises with their Indonesian counterparts, but these did not include humanitarian and disaster drills. Indonesia would first have to request the inclusion of such exercises for that to happen, Regonay said. This Week in Asia has asked Claire Castro, undersecretary of the Presidential Communications Office, whether President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, as this year’s Asean chairman, would suggest establishing a clearer regional mechanism for the bloc’s members to help one another over the impact of transboundary haze on public health.

title: Volkswagen launches inquiry into Changzhou supplier following mass graduate lay-offs
description: The firm launched an investigation following the lay-offs in Jiangsu province of over one hundred graduates a month after they were hired.
content: After significant lay-offs by a key Chinese auto supplier in Changzhou city of Jiangsu province involving over a hundred new graduates sparked nationwide outrage and forced Volkswagen to launch an investigation, analysts note the episode could lead to an overhaul of corporate-governance practices across China’s enterprises. At the centre of the controversy is Changzhou Xingyu Automotive Lighting System, China’s biggest manufacturer of auto lighting components by revenue, based in Jiangsu province. Its official website lists a roster of well-known clients including Volkswagen, BMW and BYD. Beijing-based news outlet Caixin reported that the wave of dismissals had begun in early August. Xingyu reportedly summoned a group of fresh graduate hires over a weekend – employees who had joined the firm only one month earlier – and told them headcount adjustments were necessary amid “soft business performance”. The company presented two options, according to the Caixin report. Graduates could sign a voluntary exit agreement citing “personal reasons” in return for half a month’s salary as compensation. Alternatively, they could stay on the payroll but be reassigned to lower-paid assembly-line roles, though the graduates were recruited to the company for research and development, engineering or management trainee roles. According to the Changzhou Municipal Human Resources and Social Security Bureau, Xingyu hired a total of 440 fresh graduates, reaching negotiated terminations of employment with 107 of them. The affected graduates shared their experiences on domestic social media platforms, which led to the incident quickly going viral. Some noted they had missed the main graduate-recruitment cycle. Volkswagen China said in a statement on Tuesday that it had received information regarding Xingyu’s lay-offs. “We immediately initiated an investigation into the matter and are currently working to clarify the facts,” the carmaker said. “Basic values and rights must be respected and protected across our entire supply chain, and we take any allegations of violations very seriously,” it noted. Xingyu has not elaborated on the underlying reasons for the wave of terminations, but the lay-off controversy emerged after the Shanghai-listed company refiled its updated H-share listing application with the Hong Kong stock exchange at the end of July. The company’s revenue and net profit have maintained overall growth over the past three years, according to its annual reports. Following the high-profile labour dispute, Xingyu suspended its director of human resources, according to the Changzhou human resources bureau. On August 27, Xingyu released an official apology letter and posted remedial plans on its website. “We can imagine the frustration and distress experienced by you and your families,” the company said. “There were management-level misjudgments in decision-making and oversights in internal governance. Our communication was brusque and our approaches oversimplified, with insufficient regard for your vital interests. We feel deep remorse and are conducting thorough self-reflection for these failings,” it said. Meanwhile, the company rolled out three remedial measures: providing three-month stipends, facilitating job placements and a fallback employment support package for those still jobless by the end of November. Some of the affected graduates posted on domestic social media platforms that they had already received the stipends. “This controversy unfolded against a backdrop of slowing economic growth and mounting employment pressure for college graduates. The episode serves as a wake-up call for domestic companies,” said Yan Yiming, a Shanghai-based lawyer. “Following this incident, firms will strike a more careful balance between cost control and their legal obligations. Moreover, they will exercise greater caution in recruitment going forward to avoid unplanned large-scale hiring,” Yan noted. The Changzhou human resources bureau said on August 25 that it would step up inspections and guidance over labour practices across the city. China’s youth jobless rate, for those aged 16 to 24, excluding students, climbed to 17.9 per cent in July, as a record wave of university graduates entered an already crowded labour market.

title: China demands rights guarantee as US firm secures 100-year Venezuelan oil deal
description: Call follows news that Caracas authorities have granted concessions covering 17 oilfields with proven reserves of about 65 billion barrels.
content: China has demanded protection of its interests in Venezuela after a US-backed energy company was granted 100-year concessions covering oilfields previously operated by Chinese and Russian firms. “China-Venezuela cooperation is protected by international law and the laws of both countries. China’s legitimate rights and interests in Venezuela must be guaranteed,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in Beijing on Tuesday. “Economic and trade cooperation between countries should follow the principles of equality, mutual benefit and win-win cooperation.” The demand came after the White House said Venezuela’s interim authorities had granted North American Blue Energy Partners, or NABEP, concessions covering 17 oilfields with proven reserves of about 65 billion barrels. The company is Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer. The White House said most of the fields had previously been “controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese firms”, or by associates of former president Hugo Chavez and his successor, Nicolas Maduro, whom the US abducted earlier this year. Washington later backed Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez as interim leader. China limited its response largely to diplomatic protests, despite Venezuela being a major oil supplier in Latin America for Beijing. The US described the arrangement as part of an effort to “reassert the Monroe Doctrine” and “expel foreign adversaries from our hemisphere”, while accusing China, Russia and Cuba of benefiting from Venezuela’s resources while failing to invest in its infrastructure and development. The White House also said NABEP had granted the US Defence Department’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35 per cent stake in its parent company, potentially giving Washington access to “hundreds of billions” of US dollars in value and dividends. The agreement carries added political significance in Washington, where the Donald Trump administration is under pressure to contain fuel prices that have risen amid America’s war with Iran, months before the US congressional midterm elections in November. Yet, any increase in Venezuelan oil output is likely to require substantial investment and take time. Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but years of mismanagement, underinvestment and sanctions have left production well below capacity.

title: As I see it | If a ‘great rebalancing’ is coming, will China really have to pay for it?
description: While China does have a large trade surplus, economist Michael Pettis’ argument that Beijing is most vulnerable to a global adjustment is not convincing.
content: Michael Pettis says a great rebalancing is coming and China will pay for it. It’s strange how the man who insists that power decides who pays never tests his claim on Washington. The Beijing-based economist has been warning that a great rebalancing is coming since he published a book called The Great Rebalancing. That was in 2013. His latest Foreign Affairs offering? You guessed it: “A Great Rebalancing Is Coming: Who Will Bear the Costs of a Global Trade Adjustment?” It’s the same plot: Today’s trade imbalances are untenable. China, Germany and a few others sell far more than they buy. America buys far more than it sells. And for a rich economy, a permanent deficit means either more joblessness or more debt. How about both? Then Pettis’ history tour. Oil money recycled into Latin America, blown up by rising interest rates in the early 1980s. East Asia in 1997. Southern Europe after 2008. Every imbalance ends. Every ending hurts. It may soon be China’s turn. Perhaps. He is right about one thing: who suffers and pays in a crisis is decided by power, not virtue. Weak countries pay because they can’t borrow on their own terms, defend their currencies or slow down capital flows without triggering a crisis. He thinks America is best placed to escape an impending crisis, and China is most exposed to it. Why? The IMF puts China’s current account surplus at 3.3 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) for 2025. December retail sales grew 0.9 per cent, the weakest since late 2022. Household consumption accounts for only about 40 per cent of GDP. China has a spending problem. Everyone knows it. The trouble is what Pettis builds on that. One country’s surplus is another country’s deficit; your debt is my asset. That’s not a crime. There is no villain hiding in the equation. But Pettis quietly turns it into a one-sided police charge sheet against China. Washington ran a US$1.8 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025, and US$40 trillion in total national debt. The current deficit is about 5.9 per cent of GDP. Public debt is about 100 per cent of GDP. Interest payments alone surpassed US$1 trillion annually. Nobody in Beijing wrote that budget. It’s true that with Latin America, East Asia, southern Europe, every single victim had borrowed in a currency it could not print. When the money dried up, a crisis hit. China owes its debts in yuan, to itself, behind a capital account Beijing can shut on a Tuesday afternoon. Who is more exposed? It’s clear that ending US dollar dominance would be fought tooth and nail by Washington, Wall Street and big business. The empire needs to keep the reserve currency, the sanctions weapon and the cheapest borrowing on Earth, then post the bill for its deficit to Beijing. That is like a man complaining about his electricity charges while refusing to switch off the floodlights blinding the whole neighbourhood. Pettis’ recommended cure is tariffs on the Chinese: “If the United States uses industrial policy to expand domestic manufacturing capacity and, more important, takes greater control over its trade and capital flows using tariffs and other restrictive measures, China and other major surplus economies will not be able to maintain their surpluses with corresponding US deficits.” He is assuming that Americans want to work more and buy less. Applying Pettis’ logic of power, a weak China lost the Opium War in the 19th century; a powerful China probably won’t lose the trade war in the 21st. He never asks what ending the surplus would cost everyone else. Solar panels, a global market dominated by China, fell more than 70 per cent in price between 2022 and early 2025. Doubling the electricity used by sub-Saharan Africa’s 1.25 billion people would take about US$25 billion worth of panels – roughly what the region already burns on generator fuel each year. China’s excess capacity has been building the world. America’s only excess capacity has been used to arm or bomb others. Give me a “white elephant” structure over a bombed-out girls’ school full of dead children any day. Beijing has issued its first five-year plan devoted entirely to consumption, targeting 60 trillion yuan in retail sales by 2030. Meanwhile, 12.4 trillion yuan has been allocated to education, welfare, health and housing in 2026. Up to a point, China should, and is trying to, rebalance. But it will not be paying tribute to a US that can’t balance its own books, to finance a military-industrial-tech complex that will wreck more havoc around the world.

title: UK ex-PM Starmer to quit parliament, focus on ‘international affairs’
description: Keir Starmer was deeply unpopular during his two years in power, and eventually had to step down after multiple missteps.
content: Britain’s former prime minister Keir Starmer, who stepped down as leader this summer after a tumultuous two years in power, announced on Tuesday he would quit parliament to focus on “international affairs”. In a statement on social media, Starmer said it was the “right time” to resign as the MP for the Holborn and St Pancras seat in London after 11 years, triggering a by-election. “It is now time to step aside and focus on other issues: international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world,” Starmer said in his statement. His constituency’s local newspaper, the Camden New Journal, reported Starmer had informed the Labour Party of his decision to leave parliament after 11 years, six of those as leader of the party. Andy Burnham was parachuted into the prime minister role in July to take over from Starmer, who announced his resignation amid piling pressure from fellow Labour MPs. Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, is credited with reviving the centre-left Labour Party, helping it win a landslide victory in general elections in 2024. But the strait-laced politician was deeply unpopular during his two years in power, and eventually had to step down after multiple missteps, making way for the next leader in Britain’s churn of prime ministers.

title: Norway’s King Haakon VIII swears allegiance to constitution
description: Haakon’s wife Queen Mette-Marit, 53, was not beside her husband as she is still recovering from her June 17 transplant.
content: Norway’s King Haakon VIII took an oath before parliament on Tuesday, the first major institutional step of his reign, though his wife, still convalescing after a lung transplant, was unable to attend. Dressed in a ceremonial uniform, the 53-year-old Haakon, who became king when his father King Harald V died on Friday morning aged 89, swore to abide by the Scandinavian country’s constitution, under which the royals have a primarily symbolic function. “I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in accordance with its Constitution and Laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” he recited in the parliament’s main chamber. Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, 53, was not beside her husband as she is still recovering from her June 17 transplant. Dr. Are Holm, head of the Pulmonary Department at Oslo University Hospital, said in a statement from the palace that complications after a transplant are not “uncommon”. “The queen has had complications on several occasions since the operation, including today,” Holm said. “As a result, the queen must be kept under observation throughout the day. The queen will therefore unfortunately not be able to attend the swearing-in ceremony,” he continued. The couple’s eldest daughter, Ingrid Alexandra, now crown princess at 22, attended her father’s ceremony and would also take the oath, but in writing at the Royal Palace. Haakon and the members of parliament also observed a minute of silence in tribute to Harald. Harald’s funeral will be held on September 9 at Oslo Cathedral. He will then be laid to rest in the royal mausoleum at Akershus Fortress in the Norwegian capital. Until the day before the funeral, members of the public will be able to pay their respects to Harald, who is lying in state at the palace chapel. The late regent died while being treated at Oslo University Hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells. He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule, but always ruled out abdicating. Harald, widely seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway, enjoyed massive support despite the slew of scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign. On Tuesday, a poll published by public broadcaster NRK showed that support for the monarchy has clearly increased following Harald’s death. Nearly three out of four Norwegians, or 72 per cent, said they supported the monarchy, a rise of eight points compared with a previous survey in May, according to the poll carried out over the weekend. Support for the monarchy had fallen to its lowest level in February – though 60 per cent were still in favour – while the royal family was mired in a series of scandals. In particular, Mette-Marit faced scrutiny for her ties to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, is currently under house arrest pending his appeal against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions. The 29-year-old was able to visit Harald in hospital on the eve of his death and on Monday he was among those who brought the late king’s casket to the palace chapel. He has also been granted permission to attend the funeral. In the NRK survey, members of the royal family – of which Hoiby is not formally part – were also evaluated. Mette-Marit received one of the lowest character scores of 5.2 out of 10, compared to Haakon’s 8.8. King Haakon and his wife will not be crowned, as Norway abolished coronations in 1908. But like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.

title: Sino Land profit rises 14% as property losses narrow, but core earnings fall
description: Developer adds to land bank despite pressure on mall rents, as e-commerce and outbound travel reshape Hong Kong’s retail market.
content: Sino Land’s annual profit rose 14 per cent as losses on its investment properties narrowed, although a decline in underlying earnings pointed to continued pressure on its core business. Net profit attributable to shareholders rose to HK$4.59 billion (US$585 million) in the year ended June 30, from HK$4.02 billion a year earlier, the Hong Kong developer said on Tuesday. Losses from the revaluation of investment properties narrowed to HK$192 million from HK$1.08 billion. Strip out those valuation changes, however, and the picture was less upbeat. Underlying profit fell 6.4 per cent to HK$4.79 billion. The divergence was also evident in Sino’s investment property portfolio. Occupancy edged up to 90 per cent from 89.6 per cent a year earlier, while attributable gross rental revenue fell 1.5 per cent to HK$3.43 billion. “While Hong Kong’s overall retail sales have shown steady signs of recovery since May 2025, the growth in e-commerce continued to outpace that of traditional retail channels,” Sino said. “Coupled with the persistently high level of outbound travel by local residents during extended holidays, the recovery has yet to translate meaningfully into rental income growth across the Group’s major shopping malls.” Residential sales offered some relief. Attributable segment profit from property sales rose 8 per cent to HK$1.1 billion, with more than 3,500 units generating HK$12.1 billion in attributable sales proceeds during the year. The company maintained its annual dividend at 58 HK cents per share. Elsewhere in the Sino Group, its separately listed hotel arm provided a more stable source of income. Sino Hotels, which is controlled by the Ng family alongside Sino Land, said City Garden Hotel maintained 100 per cent occupancy during the year under a bulk-hiring arrangement, while its average room rate rose 5 per cent. After the financial year ended, Sino Hotels secured a new 20-month agreement covering all available rooms at pre-agreed rates, extending the hotel’s earnings visibility after its previous four-year lease expired. Sino also continued to buy. It acquired three sites in Jordan Valley, Tuen Mun and at Kam Sheung Road Station during the financial year. After the year ended, the developer and its joint venture partners were awarded a project in the Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen New Development Area. “With solid fundamentals and a strong balance sheet, the Group is well-positioned to capitalise on opportunities,” Chairman Daryl Ng Win Kong said in the statement. Sino would continue to “uphold prudent financial management and enhance operational efficiency” as it navigated market fluctuations, he added.

title: Call for Trump-Xi AI safety talks comes as state media slams US AI governance
description: Dean Ball, a former White House adviser, says the window for cooperation will ‘widen’ in next few months but will not stay open forever.
content: An OpenAI executive and former White House adviser is calling for AI safety cooperation between Washington and Beijing ahead of a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, even as Chinese state media launch a scathing attack on American frontier governance in artificial intelligence. “I have always believed US/China AI safety collaboration would be desirable but thought it was unlikely to happen,” Dean Ball, OpenAI’s head of strategic futures, wrote on X on Tuesday. “In the past few months, though, the ground has shifted. There is a window of opportunity.” Ball, a former adviser to the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said the window for cooperation would “widen over at least the next few months” because of escalating AI risks and the upcoming bilateral meeting, but warned it “will not remain open forever”. Ahead of Xi’s planned state visit to the US on September 24, officials from both sides “will press forward with dialogues” on topics including AI guardrails, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Sunday. However, Chinese state media delivered a harsh critique of US AI governance ahead of the talks. In an article published on Sunday, Yuyuan Tantian, a social media account affiliated with state broadcaster CCTV, accused US AI firm Anthropic of trying to dictate industry rules through aggressive lobbying and CEO Dario Amodei’s calls to arm democracies with AI. The commentary also slammed Washington for weakening regulatory standards to “maintain technological hegemony”, pointing to Trump’s executive order in June that slashed the pre-release voluntary review period from 90 to 30 days. The outlet said Anthropic’s “desire for control hidden in its saviour complex” had formed “a monster cultivated by the American path”. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside US working hours on Tuesday. In a blog post the same day, the company said it had strengthened security efforts following several reported safety incidents involving its Claude models. Yuyuan Tantian called frontier model management a “crucial topic” for US-China talks, but urged the industry to distinguish “genuine security threats” from “merely technological competition”. “Who is qualified to say which models are dangerous and which behaviours need to be restricted?” the commentary said, citing Anthropic’s “discriminatory treatment of users in different regions”. Since last September, Anthropic has blocked access to its services from what it described as “adversarial nations like China”. It also temporarily suspended global access to its Claude Fable 5 model in June following Washington’s directive to block foreign usage. “If these problems are not reasonably resolved, the subsequent negotiations will be meaningless,” the Yuyuan Tantian article said. Beijing has not publicly detailed its agenda for the discussions, but an official from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) highlighted major sector risks on Tuesday. Wang Lihong, deputy director of the CAC’s cybersecurity coordination bureau, told CCTV that “extreme out-of-control risks” and misuse have emerged as model capabilities jumped. He also warned against “certain countries pursuing technological hegemony” through export controls. Expectations remain low for any breakthroughs amid intense US-China tech rivalry. “People often get stuck on the need for a ‘deal’ … but actually a huge way to influence China is just to honestly show what we’re observing and what we’re doing about it on the US side,” Helen Toner, executive director at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, wrote on X last week. Toner pointed to a recent incident where OpenAI models autonomously hacked developer platform Hugging Face as “the most visceral evidence” of the dangers of losing control over advanced AI, calling it a valuable topic for the upcoming summit. OpenAI said last month that its flagship models, including GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased system, broke out of a sandboxed testing environment to breach Hugging Face’s infrastructure while searching for information to complete a cyber capability tests. Roughly 1,200 supposedly isolated AI agents found a way to coordinate the attack via a shared message board, according to a third-party investigation published by Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Redwood Research last week. The agents demonstrated “peer altruism”, with some “willing to risk failing their own task to help the ‘collective’ learn”, METR researcher Ajeya Cotra wrote in a blog post, describing the incident as “far more severe” than previous documented events.

title: Export potential? Chinese YY-20 refuels Egyptian Rafale in cross-platform drill
description: PLA tanker aircraft shows versatility in Egypt exercise, highlighting interoperability that could boost global sales prospects.
content: In a rare display of interoperability, a Chinese YY-20 aerial tanker has been pictured refuelling a French-built Egyptian Rafale fighter – showing a versatility analysts say could enable closer multinational air operations and improve the tanker’s potential for export. The photo, released by the Egyptian military on Monday, showed mid-air refuelling during the Eagles of Civilisation 2026 joint exercise, which began last month and is being held at several airbases across Egypt. The YY-20, also referred to as the YU-20, is the aerial-refuelling variant of China’s Y-20 strategic transport aircraft, designed to extend the range and loiter time of receiving aircraft. The Rafale appears to be the first Western-made fighter publicly seen receiving fuel from a Chinese tanker after a YY-20A refuelled Egyptian MiG-29 fighters at last year’s Eagles of Civilisation drills, showing the tanker’s ability to refuel both French and Russian-made fighter jets. The multiplatform demonstrations coincide with a broader effort by Beijing to showcase its long-range power projection. During this year’s exercise, Chinese J-16 fighters completed a 6,000km (3,730-mile) transit to Egypt, relying on YY-20 tankers for aerial refuelling along the way. According to an official PLA Air Force account, the YY-20A also served as an airborne command node during the deployment – suggesting the tanker could play a wider role in coordinating complex long-distance air operations beyond simply extending the range of combat aircraft. Michael Bosack, director of the Parley Policy Institute, said that showing the ability to air-refuel foreign aircraft could give Beijing options for both closer military interoperability and, potentially, marketing the YY-20 abroad. “My view is that the refuelling capability makes the YY-20 more exportable,” he said. That could be particularly relevant to potential customers operating aircraft acquired from various suppliers. “These customers will want capabilities that function with other systems they or their partners may be employing,” Bosack said. However, Bosack said there were no concrete indications that Beijing planned to export the YY-20 or that the cross-platform refuelling displayed in Egypt would become a regular feature of multinational training. “China could be using this for exportability, for interoperability, or for both,” he said. Wang Yanan, editor-in-chief of the Beijing-based Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times that the YY-20 and the Rafale were “highly compatible” because both used probe-and-drogue refuelling systems. Under this system, the tanker trails a hose ending in a basket-like drogue, which connects with a probe on the receiving aircraft to transfer fuel. Wang said that even if minor technical adjustments were required, they were unlikely to pose major difficulties because fuel-transfer rates and pressures were similar across such systems. He said the greater challenge was coordinating procedures between crews operating different types of aircraft, including rendezvous methods, altitude separation, closing speeds and docking manoeuvres. Bosack said that developing more enduring operational interoperability would require routine exercises involving aerial refuelling. “Even with compatible systems, the actual process of conducting aerial refuelling requires skill and training. It also needs effective communication and synchronisation between aircrews,” he said. “It is not yet clear to me the direction they will take, but they have options.” The latest developments come after Chinese state media confirmed last month that the newer Y-20B transport aircraft could be converted into an aerial tanker using modular fuel tanks and removable refuelling equipment – potentially expanding China’s tanker capacity and its ability to support fighter operations farther into the western Pacific.

title: Trump envoy Daines visits Chinese AI, space firms to pave way for Xi summit in US
description: Montana Republican’s trip coincides with intensifying tech war that has become a major front in the US-China strategic rivalry.
content: US Senator Steve Daines, a close ally of President Donald Trump, has wrapped up a days-long trip to China, just weeks ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington. According to accounts online from a Chinese local government and various companies, the Montana Republican travelled from Wednesday to Saturday to China’s tech hub Hangzhou and the southern city of Guangzhou. The visit is consistent with an earlier South China Morning Post report about expectations for Daines’ return trip to China. According to the online accounts, the Trump envoy visited a top Chinese university and several technology firms. Daines’ trip was a sharp contrast to a visit in July by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission’s bipartisan delegation, which had sought to visit several Chinese tech giants but was denied. Daines’ visit comes against the backdrop of an intensifying tech war that has become a major front in the US-China strategic rivalry. Artificial intelligence and space exploration have emerged as critical battlegrounds, and AI is widely expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi sit down later this month. The 64-year-old lawmaker has emerged as an important backchannel figure between Washington and Beijing in recent years. He travelled to Beijing in May as the two sides sought to stabilise relations before Trump travelled to the Chinese capital later that month. His August visit was expected to help finalise the agenda for the two powers’ coming summit in Washington. Still, neither Daines nor the US embassy in China has released details of the trip. According to his social media post, Daines was already in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, on Monday – as was Xi, who was attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s annual summit and paying a state visit. A social media post published on August 25 by George Glass, the US ambassador to Japan, showed that Daines had travelled to Japan before heading to China. While in Japan, the two discussed the US-Japan partnership and “the future of AI, quantum and other cutting-edge tech and the future of energy”. On Monday, Guangzhou-based EHang, a manufacturer of autonomous electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft, announced that Daines visited the company on Saturday and took a flight in one of its products with his wife, Cindy Daines. The couple was accompanied in their visit by Pauline Kao, the US consul general in Guangzhou; Geng Shuang, vice-president of the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs and a former deputy permanent representative of China to the United Nations in New York; and several Guangzhou government officials. Daines said the test flight reminded him of scenes featuring flying cars in the American sci-fi cartoon The Jetsons, and he welcomed EHang’s efforts to expand into the US market, according to an article attributed to the company and published on Monday by the Chinese industry portal youuav.com. The article also noted that the US senator recalled his time in Guangzhou as a Procter & Gamble executive. Daines is one of the few incumbent US senators with experience living and working in China. He visited Hangzhou from August 26 to 29, accompanied by Geng, US ambassador to China David Perdue and US consul general in Shanghai Christian Marchant, according to a Zhejiang provincial foreign affairs office statement on Saturday. The statement said that in a meeting on Friday, Daines told Zhejiang’s governor, Liu Jie, that he was willing to help promote friendly exchanges between local governments in the two countries. Liu said Zhejiang was ready to deepen cooperation with the US in areas including industrial innovation, technology and trade and investment. Daines also visited Zhejiang University on Friday, where Ren Shaobo, the university’s Communist Party secretary, told him that the institution hoped to further strengthen exchanges with the US. That was days after the Pentagon ordered 30 US universities to scrutinise their ties with Chinese research partners. In Hangzhou, Daines also visited Bota, an AI-driven biomanufacturing company, and watched a demonstration of next-generation AI smart glasses at Rokid. He also visited space-intelligence firm Manycore Tech on Friday. The Zhejiang government’s statement said they discussed “the prospects and challenges of AI development”. On the same day, Daines toured Star Vision, a private commercial space company. The firm said on social media on Saturday that it had “discussed the application of satellite remote sensing technology” with the delegation and “[looked] forward to deepening cooperation between the two sides in the years ahead”.

title: Glacier risk hangs over China-Nepal border as region remembers mudslide victims
description: Emergency crews and residents stop to commemorate the more than 1,000 dead in last week’s disaster.
content: Residents and rescuers in the Tibet autonomous region paused for three minutes on Tuesday morning to remember the victims of last week’s mudslide disaster. Sirens sounded for three minutes from 9.55am at the Gyirong Port police station, with similar memorials at rescue and road-reopening sites throughout the region, according to state broadcaster CCTV. More than 1,000 people died and thousands remain missing along the China-Nepal border area after a glacier collapsed at Langtang Lirung on the Nepalese side last Wednesday. The Gyirong Port was overwhelmed with mud and debris as the flow from the collapse swept through a valley and back into Nepal. As of 2pm on Tuesday, 1,058 bodies had been recovered from the Nepalese side, with 4,606 people missing. Chinese authorities reported 16 confirmed deaths and 546 people missing, in their latest update on Sunday. The missing include 261 foreign nationals on the Chinese side and more than 500 foreign nationals in Nepal. An Australian feared missing had contacted Australian officials from Tibet on Tuesday, Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed. The person was receiving consular support and had spoken with their family, the department said, declining to give further details due to privacy obligations. While Nepalese authorities collect DNA samples from remains to help identify victims, China has said it will send DNA specialists to the disaster zone to help its neighbour. The Chinese foreign ministry said on Tuesday that China was also shipping a second batch of aid to Nepal, including drones and DNA testing, water purification and lighting equipment. The remembrances took place under the shadow of a “major risk” of further glacier collapses, according to China’s Ministry of Water Resources. There is also the risk of barrier lakes forming as landslides block the rivers and trap water. Water levels in a barrier lake formed on the Purepuqiang River near the port after last week’s glacier collapse had fallen, reducing risks, state news agency Xinhua reported. Emergency crews are in the area monitoring any further build-ups. Ministry official Yang Dan told CCTV that dams could become unstable, “loosely structured” and easily breached if the water built up or if an earthquake occurred. A breach could unleash large volumes of water and destructive flooding downstream, Yang said. Last week’s disaster severed power, communications and transport links to the area but rescuers are making progress. As of Tuesday, repair crews were within 800 metres (2,625 feet) of Gyirong Port, having cleared sections of national highway G216, according to CCTV. Power crews have been racing to restore electricity along reopened sections of the highway. The broadcaster said repair operations on the highway had entered an “extremely challenging” stage, with rain sending water rushing down three channels on the mountainside, disrupting construction and raising the risk that repaired sections could be damaged again. The China Meteorological Administration has forecast persistent rain in Gyirong county until Wednesday, warning that it could complicate rescue operations and transport and increase the risk of secondary hazards.

title: Under-fire South Korean football body hires ex-Spain boss Robert Moreno as interim coach
description: The Spaniard will be in charge for friendly games in September-October with a view to taking the team to January’s Asian Cup.
content: South Korea’s beleaguered football association on Tuesday appointed former Spain boss Robert Moreno as interim coach, following a disastrous World Cup and series of damaging controversies. Moreno, who was forced to deny earlier this year during a stint in Russia that he used ChatGPT to prepare for games, will be in charge for friendly games in September-October. South Korea will compete in the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia from January 7 to February 5. The Korea Football Association (KFA) said Moreno could lead the team at the Asian Cup, “subject to an evaluation” of his performance. The team have been without a coach since Hong Myung-bo quit following their shock group-stage exit from the World Cup in North America in June. Hong’s departure did little to quell public outrage over the disappointing campaign and added fuel to pre-existing questions about how he was hired. Police raided KFA headquarters last month as part of an investigation into Hong’s 2024 appointment. The KFA also apologised for allegations that it provided sexual entertainment for foreign referees. Moreno will lead South Korea for home friendlies against Ecuador and Uruguay in September and Venezuela and Uzbekistan in October. He would also be in charge if South Korea organise more friendlies during the November international window. The KFA said the 48-year-old had been hired after “an open recruitment process”. He will become the first Spaniard to coach South Korea. Moreno took over the Spanish national team on a temporary basis in 2019 from Luis Enrique. He was appointed full-time in June that year after Luis Enrique resigned because his daughter Xana was diagnosed with a rare bone cancer. Spain rehired Luis Enrique to replace Moreno in November 2019 after his daughter’s death. The coach accused Moreno of being “disloyal” for trying to stay in charge for Euro 2020. Moreno, who has also coached Monaco and Granada, was accused by Russian media in January of using AI to prepare for games during his time in charge of Sochi. Moreno, who left the top-flight side in September 2025 after a poor run of results, denied the reports. “I have never used ChatGPT or any AI to prepare matches, decide line-ups or choose players. That is completely false,” he wrote in an open letter sent to Spanish newspaper Marca. Moreno said he used technology in his job but made his decisions himself and with his staff. “My career in football began precisely through data and video analysis. It’s what I specialise in and what made the difference in my early days,” he said.

title: As rice output falls, Malaysia looks to China’s ‘2 yields, 1 land’ model
description: Chinese rice-prawn farms could help boost Malaysia’s farming production as it faces hurdles to meet its rice self-sufficiency goal.
content: Malaysia is looking to China’s rice-prawn farms as a model to extract more from its shrinking paddy land as a slide in rice self-sufficiency has left it increasingly reliant on imports from its Southeast Asian neighbours. The experiment is also part of an attempt to confront other issues such as ageing farmers and more erratic weather, which have dented Malaysia’s rice output. Agriculture and Food Security Minister Mohamad Sabu said on Monday that Malaysia needed to raise its rice self-sufficiency ratio to at least 80 per cent, arguing that a level below 60 per cent was “not adequate” for national food security, state news agency Bernama reported. “We want to increase productivity and strengthen the supply chain through expanding the use of technology … and encourage innovation and open up more opportunities for value creation throughout the industry chain,” he said. The 80 per cent target is set under Malaysia’s National Agrofood Policy for 2030. However, the country remains far off course. Its rice self-sufficiency ratio fell to 52.9 per cent in 2024 from 56.2 per cent a year earlier, as paddy production decreased by 5.3 per cent to 2.06 million tonnes over the period, according to official data. Malaysia’s planted paddy area also declined by 5.6 per cent to about 579,700 hectares in 2024. Mohamad said in February that the ratio remained around 52 per cent, citing shrinking and underused paddy land as well as climate-related pressures. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) expects Malaysia’s paddy output to remain below average at 2.1 million tonnes this year after floods and dry weather reduced plantings and yields. Rice imports are forecast to reach 1.7 million tonnes this year, with an intensifying El Nino also threatening the 2027 crop through lower rainfall. Malaysia bought 710,656 tonnes of rice in the first half of this year, according to figures cited by Thailand’s Department of Foreign Trade, with Thailand accounting for 327,995 tonnes and Vietnam another 232,416 tonnes. The Philippines, another major Southeast Asian rice importer, is forecast to buy 3.9 million tonnes of rice in 2026. In contrast, Vietnam and Thailand have been exporting more rice to the region and beyond. Thailand exported 7.7 million tonnes last year while FAO expects Vietnam to ship 7.9 million tonnes this year. Khazanah Research Institute warned in May that food-security risks in Malaysia and Southeast Asia extended beyond short-term supply disruptions to deeper dependence on imported food and agricultural inputs, leaving supply chains exposed to geopolitical tensions, trade restrictions and climate shocks. It called for “cooperative self-reliance” within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, combining stronger domestic production with greater regional coordination. Paul Teng Piang Siong, a visiting senior fellow at the Climate Change in Southeast Asia Programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said a low self-sufficiency ratio did not necessarily translate into high vulnerability. “More important is a country’s capability to acquire rice supplies at affordable prices,” he said, adding that reaching 80 per cent self-sufficiency would also carry opportunity costs for scarce resources such as land, labour and water. “Unless a major catastrophe hits the largest rice surplus countries – India, Thailand, Vietnam and Pakistan – at the same time, there should be enough rice to go around,” Teng said. Mohamad’s interest in rice-prawn farming followed a visit last month to the city of Wuhu in China’s eastern Anhui province, where rice cultivation is combined with farming of giant freshwater prawns to generate two sources of income from the same plot. “There are two yields, one from rice and one from prawns,” Mohamad said, according to Bernama, adding that Malaysia’s warmer climate could make year-round prawn farming viable. Malaysia’s Agriculture and Food Security Ministry told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that the main lesson was how “the same agricultural land can be used more efficiently” and provide farmers with another source of income. The ministry said it was considering a pilot project but had yet to decide on a site or timetable, with any system needing to be adapted to Malaysia’s irrigation, soil, climate and existing paddy practices. China’s experience gives the idea some weight. Wuhu’s agriculture bureau said in June 2024 that Fudu township had developed 26,000 mu, or about 1,730 hectares, of integrated rice-aquaculture farming, generating net returns of more than 2,000 yuan (US$297) per mu. The area has also experimented with a “one rice, two prawn” cycle involving crayfish, rice and giant freshwater prawns. A 2025 study in the journal Aquaculture found that rice-prawn systems could raise economic returns, although the gains depended on how densely prawns were stocked in the fields. ‘No copy-and-paste fix’ Muhamad Shakirin Mispan, a senior lecturer at Universiti Malaya’s Institute of Biological Sciences, said Malaysia’s more immediate problem was retaining enough productive paddy land and farmers amid the ageing workforce in the agricultural sector. “Yield improvement alone, especially in limited and selected areas, is unlikely to be enough to increase the self-sufficiency ratio,” he said. Minister Mohamad said in April that Malaysia had lost more than 20,000 hectares of paddy land to development or abandonment, with younger generations increasingly leaving farming for jobs in the cities. Shakirin said rice-prawn farming was technically feasible but could not be grafted onto existing lands in Malaysia, with pesticide use and competing water requirements of rice and prawns among the major obstacles. “The field must be managed as a rice-prawn production system, rather than simply adding prawns to conventional rice fields,” he said. “We can’t directly copy-and-paste what China has done,” Shakirin added, noting that China’s approach had been built through years of research and infrastructure investment.
