Rather than as a direct fix for Malaysia’s rice self-sufficiency gap, the Chinese model may help boost Malaysian farmers’ incomes and total output per hectare, and there should be local trials over several planting seasons before wider implementation, according to Shakirin.

title: China tells carmakers, suppliers to avoid price wars abroad to pave way for healthy growth
description: New rules signal push for sustainable expansion as Chinese EV makers pursue long-term gains and influence in global markets.
content: Beijing has ordered Chinese carmakers and component suppliers to refrain from offering steep discounts in overseas markets as they accelerate their global expansion. For the first time, three ministry-level authorities published guidelines governing Chinese carmakers abroad, aimed at improving their global competitiveness, according to a statement by the Ministry of Commerce. “The guidelines aim to promote long-term, healthy development of the Chinese automotive industry in international markets,” it said. “Car companies are urged to strengthen compliance and wield international influence to promote cooperation in the global automotive industry and supply chain.” The guidelines, jointly issued on Tuesday by the commerce ministry, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the State Administration for Market Regulation, did not specify punishments for non-compliance. Initial signs that Chinese carmakers would launch harsh discount wars abroad have prompted regulators to step in Gao Shen, independent analyst Banking on their technological and cost advantages, Chinese electric vehicle (EV) makers and their supply chain vendors – from battery producers to software providers – have been revving up overseas expansion over the past two years, with surging exports and rising local production. A global energy crisis arising from the US-Israel war on Iran early this year boosted deliveries of Chinese-made EVs in more than 200 international markets. Chinese carmakers handed 2.9 million electric cars to customers outside the mainland in the first seven months of 2027, up 120 per cent from a year earlier, according to data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. “Initial signs that Chinese carmakers would launch harsh discount wars abroad have prompted regulators to step in to curb potential vicious price competition,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “It is necessary for the authorities to spell out detailed punishments to avoid ‘involution’ abroad.” Involution, or neijuan in Chinese, refers to intense ­competition that erodes sustainable growth and makes profits elusive. Chinese carmakers, whose vehicles often sell at higher prices abroad, could enjoy a net margin of 20,000 yuan (US$2,975) per car in overseas markets – four times higher than at home, according to Nick Lai, head of auto research for Asia-Pacific at JPMorgan.

title: China’s 3 major airlines bet on international demand for relief from deep losses: analysts
description: Chinese carriers choose low fares, long-term expansion as regional conflicts and weak domestic demand affect revenues.
content: China’s three biggest airlines are expected to absorb steep financial losses from the first half of 2026 – but avoid notable fare increases – in a long game aimed at stimulating air travel, especially on international routes, aviation experts said this week. Air China, China Eastern Airlines and China Southern Airlines all reported widening net losses in the first six months of the year due to fuel price increases driven by the Iran war, according to stock market filings by the carriers. Muted demand for domestic travel was also cited as a contributing factor by analysts. Airfare increases were considered unlikely as the Civil Aviation Administration of China, the country’s civil aviation regulator, indicated last month that the industry would focus on flight safety and passenger demand stimulus through to 2030. China is on track to become the world’s largest travel and tourism market, and the administration’s five-year plan for civil aviation would help build up a “dynamic and high-quality air transport service system to effectively support the expansion of domestic demand and high-level opening up”, per a plan summary released in August. That would mean “lower prices to allow more passengers to take planes”, independent aviation analyst Li Hanming said. China’s plan also emphasised “internationalisation”, with analysts saying that cross-border flights could help the airlines keep balance sheets under control, albeit slowly and only if new aircraft orders were linked to real demand. Chinese airlines’ right to fly over Russian airspace on routes to and from Europe already gives them an advantage over European carriers, which Moscow has barred from its airspace during the Ukraine war. Rapid expansion of China’s visa-free rules for foreign travellers is further boosting business for the airlines. “You can’t put all your hopes on international [travel],” said Mayur Patel, head of Asian operations at British market intelligence firm OAG Aviation. Significant airfare increases were unlikely because they would deter people from flying, Patel added. Airfares on popular domestic routes had fallen as low as 200 yuan (US$29.75) in September as the peak summer travel season ends, according to the China-based Financial News. Net losses attributable to shareholders in the first half reached 2.3 billion yuan (US$342.2 million) for Air China, about 2.2 billion yuan for China Eastern, and 3.7 billion yuan for China Southern. The losses were wider than in the first six months of 2025. China Southern filed a financial report to the exchange on Saturday noting “volatile” interest rates, currency exchange “risks” and the impacts of fuel price fluctuations. The US-Israel war in Iran this year has sent fuel prices surging and chilled traveller interest in flying near the Middle East. Across the world, international air passenger demand fell 0.1 per cent in July this year compared with the same month of 2025, though excluding the Middle East it expanded by 1.5 per cent, the International Air Transport Association said in a statement on Monday. Chinese airlines faced further competition from high-speed rail at home and were not filling their aircraft seat capacity, Patel said.

title: Philippines’ Jollibee eyes Hong Kong over US to list international unit
description: The company is separating its international business, Jollibee Foods Corporation International, ahead of its planned spin-off and listing.
content: Philippine fast food giant Jollibee Foods Corp said on Tuesday it was planning to spin off and list its international operations on the Hong Kong stock exchange, abandoning earlier plans of a ‌US listing. Jollibee Foods said it was progressing in separating its international business, Jollibee Foods Corporation International, ahead of its planned spin-off and listing. The fast food restaurant operator now plans for a Hong Kong listing citing its existing presence in the city and brand recognition ⁠in Asia. The Hong Kong listing could give the company a better price ‌discovery as investors are familiar with its regional growth story and potentially better positioned to understand where the value is going to ‌come from, said Dilin Wu, a strategist at Pepperstone. “HKEX also provides access to ⁠a broad ⁠base of global and regional investors, making it well suited to support a business with ambitions that ‌extend well beyond Asia, including continued growth in North America,” Jollibee said. Hong Kong has become one of ‌the ‌world’s busiest venues for new share sales this year, as improving investor sentiment ‌and robust demand encourage technology and manufacturing companies to raise capital. The first half ⁠of 2026 has seen about US$22.45 billion in new listings in Hong Kong, up nearly ⁠57 per cent from a year earlier and marking the busiest start to a year for the city in five years, according to LSEG data. Jollibee ‌also appointed its ‌current chief financial and risk officer, Richard Chong Woo Shin, as the chief executive officer of JFCI. Shares rose as much as 3.3 per cent, marking their highest level since mid-August, and were in tandem with the benchmark’s 2.3 per cent gain.

title: Swedish chip expert Henry Homayoun Radamson dies in China of ‘sudden illness’, aged 63
description: Sudden death of Guangdong-based researcher, who specialised in the medical use of technology, leaves a ‘profound void’.
content: Award-winning Swedish chip expert Henry Homayoun Radamson has died in Shanghai at the age of 63. Radamson, who moved to China in 2016, was working as the chief scientist at the Guangdong Greater Bay Area Institute of Integrated Circuit and System. The institute said on Tuesday that he died from a “sudden illness” on August 12. In 2023, Radamson was awarded the Chinese Government Friendship Award, which recognises those who have made outstanding contributions to China’s development. He was best known for his research into nanotechnology and its use in medical diagnostics. He also worked on the development of short wave infrared chips. The European Materials Research Society, where he was an executive committee member, said: “His sudden loss leaves a profound void within his scientific community.” The society described him as “a highly respected scientist and a dedicated researcher whose work contributed significantly to the advancement of materials science and semiconductor technologies”. It also said: “He was an intercultural facilitator of research in Europe and China. Throughout his career, he was driven by scientific curiosity, search for innovation and a strong belief in the potential of research to improve people’s lives.” The society added that shortly before his death, he had expressed the hope that his research team “would continue to pursue the development of cutting-edge medical devices and diagnostics, areas to which he remained deeply committed”. After earning his PhD in semiconductor materials from Linkoping University in Sweden in 1996, Radamson spent nearly two decades as a senior researcher at the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm before moving to China in 2016 under the Thousand Talents Plan, designed to attract leading scientists to the country. He worked in the Institute of Microelectronics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences in Beijing, where his research focused on semiconductor materials made from germanium or related compounds. In 2018, when he took up the role of visiting professor at Mid Sweden University, he told the university that he was working on silicon photonics and imaging designed to detect early-stage cancer tumours. Radamson also said his work in Sweden would focus on developing “a prototype chip to detect and indicate heavy metals and other forms of contamination in the water”. In 2019, he was appointed as chief scientist at the Guangdong institute and became a member of the European Academy of Sciences. He was awarded the Swedish Quality Innovation Award in 2019 and the Venture Cup, the country’s largest entrepreneurship competition, in 2011. He told China’s official Science and Technology Daily in 2023 that his research was focused on combining electronics with optical technologies. He said nanotechnology could be used in everything from night vision systems for cars and waterproof clothing, as well as medical imaging and nanorobots used in surgery. “We hope that the device we develop will be as light as a mobile phone and can scan the body directly to detect abnormalities in blood flow and detect tumours at an early stage,” he said in the interview. “Nano chips are faster to calculate and of course more difficult to design and manufacture. We need ultra-clean laboratories to process nano chips. But the continuous advancement of technology is for the public.”

title: Manus resumes solo operations after collapse of US$2 billion Meta deal
description: The AI start-up said its founders would continue to lead the firm as an ‘independent agent lab’, after Beijing torpedoed its acquisition by Meta.
content: The Chinese-founded artificial intelligence start-up Manus announced on Tuesday that it had formally resumed independent operations, more than four months after Beijing blocked its US$2 billion acquisition by Meta Platforms. The company’s founding team would continue to lead Manus as an “independent agent lab”, the firm said in a blog post on its website, as it sought to move on from a months-long saga that has sent ripples through the Chinese and global technology sectors. The announcement came three weeks after Manus notified users that it was erasing some data generated on or after December 29 – the date the company was acquired by Meta – “to comply with regulatory requirements in specific parts of the world”. Manus said on Tuesday that affected users could restore their data through the company’s “restoration portal”. “For some users, this transition required backing up and restoring data, as well as navigating a temporary interruption to access. We know this took you additional time and effort, and we are very grateful for your patience and trust,” it said. The resumption of independent operations marked what the company called the start of its “next chapter”, after the collapse of its Meta deal that could set a precedent for global deal making involving Chinese-founded tech start-ups. Launched in March 2025, Manus is a developer of autonomous AI agents capable of handling complex tasks such as web research and writing reports. Its parent company, Butterfly Effect, was founded in mainland China in 2022, but the firm rebranded as a Singapore-based company last year, laying off China-based staff and removing its digital footprint in China. By relocating to Singapore, the start-up was able to sidestep US technology export and investment controls, allowing it to raise capital from US ventures and access frontier AI models from providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. The move likely also paved the way for the company’s acquisition by Meta for US$2 billion in December, a rare example of US-China cooperation amid a fierce tech rivalry between the two countries. But the transaction raised red flags in Beijing, triggering a months-long investigation. In April, China’s National Development and Reform Commission told the parties involved in the deal to cancel the transaction. Last month, Manus announced it would delete some user data as part of its transition back to independent operations, though it did not disclose how the transaction would be unwound. Chinese tech giant Tencent Holdings was in talks to become Manus’ new largest shareholder, the Financial Times reported in July, with other former early-stage investors – including ZhenFund and HSG – also involved in the talks. Manus vowed on Tuesday to continue advancing its technology. “We will continue to push the boundaries of what general AI agents can do, turning new capabilities into products that help you take on complex tasks and accomplish more in your day-to-day life and work.”

title: Hong Kong-born weightlifting champion Tammy Wong on strength, fear and femininity
description: Three-time British champion Tammy Wong talks about impostor syndrome and her vision of changing the skinny culture among Hong Kong women.
content: Fresh off the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, Hong Kong-born Tammy Wong is still buzzing – and not just from the adrenaline. The 30-year-old weightlifter, who represented England in the women’s 48kg category, finished with a combined total of 160kg (352lbs), just 7kg shy of a podium finish, and five off her own personal best. A three-time champion of British Weight Lifting’s British Championships, Wong played hockey as a child, continuing through university while going to the gym on the side. During the Covid-19 pandemic, she watched women doing CrossFit and weightlifting and thought to herself: “Oh my God – these women are chucking such heavy weights above their heads! I want to do that!” “I got really strong really quickly,” Wong says. “Next thing you know, I was competing at a national level.” She made her international debut at the 2025 European Weightlifting Championships. A sport about both physical and mental strength But her early success did not free her from impostor syndrome. The speed of her rise brought a psychological burden she did not see coming. Starting out relatively late, at age 24, she felt exposed when competing alongside athletes who had begun weightlifting much younger. “Most of the team started as kids. As a kid, you’re fearless,” Wong says. “As an adult, you learn to feel fear.” She adds: “I hated it because I wasn’t ready. I felt like I didn’t earn my place. And you can’t hide, either. You’re on the platform on your own with spotlights on you, everyone watching.” For the next few years, Wong went through the motions, attending competitions she did not truly want to be at, performing to meet others’ expectations rather than for her own satisfaction. It was a draining cycle of validation-seeking and self-sabotage in which every achievement felt unearned. “I felt like I was constantly waiting to be found out,” Wong says. “A lot of lifters actually train but don’t compete because they can’t handle the pressure,” she adds. “You can be really good at training, but not necessarily competing. I was doing it because people said I had loads of potential, but I wasn’t doing it for myself. It took me a long time to actually believe that.” Her personal bests speak for themselves: a 74kg snatch (lifting the barbell from the floor to overhead in one single, explosive movement) and a 91kg clean and jerk (lifting the bar from the floor to the shoulders – the clean – then driving it overhead – the jerk) for a combined total of 165kg. These impressive numbers have propelled her to the national level. I still get funny looks on the Kowloon side – uncles looking you up and down, like ‘why you so jacked?’ Tammy Wong Leaving the corporate world to become a pro athlete In May 2026, just months before the Commonwealth Games, Wong quit her full-time corporate job in business development to be a full-time athlete. Her routine had long been a gruelling one: “Wake up at 6.30am, leave the house at 7.30am, train after work, don’t get home till close to 9pm, dinner, sleep – same thing every day.” She admits she did not realise how burnt out she was until looking back. “Why am I crying on my way home every night?” she recalls asking herself. The experience taught her not to glorify burnout and to prioritise recovery – both physical and mental. “I just got to a point where I’m questioning life choices,” she says. Although Wong was born in Hong Kong, she spent many of her formative years in England, where she attended boarding school from age 10. She has been based in the UK ever since and has visited her birth city only a handful of times over the years, though she did return in August 2026 for a rare extended stay. “I’m turning 30 this year,” Wong says. “I moved everything into storage. I’m sick of doing the same things. I just need to do something fun.” When asked about the chances of a permanent move to Hong Kong, she says it is probable. “Nothing’s stopping me,” she says, adding that her time in Hong Kong is partly about figuring out whether relocating and a full-time career in health and fitness in the city is viable. Over the last few weeks, she has been reconnecting with extended family, getting some paperwork done to renew her Hong Kong ID card and dipping her toes into the local fitness scene. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tammy Wong (@tam_lifts) Coaching sessions at Powerhouse Barbell Club in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood have afforded her a front-row seat to the city’s evolving exercise culture. Her observation is nuanced: while the city has a thriving gym scene, the participation – particularly among local women – still skews heavily towards what she calls “traditionally safe” forms of movement. “Pilates is big right now, which is great, but I feel like a lot of local girls are still very tiny, not really into strength training,” she says. It is a contrast she noticed almost immediately upon arriving. She explains that in the UK, the culture around women and gym-going is more established, with most – if not all – of her peers working out regularly. This differs from Hong Kong, where an old-school mindset lingers. “I still get funny looks on the Kowloon side – uncles looking you up and down, like ‘why you so jacked?’” she laughs. ‘I really want to get more people involved’ Wong, who posts photos of herself competing – always with a red bow in her hair – for her almost 50,000 Instagram followers, fiercely advocates that femininity and strength are not mutually exclusive. She says promoting this message in Asia is particularly important. “I think growing up … you want to be skinny, and you cut so much,” she says, reflecting on the diet culture in parts of Asia. In particular, she is troubled by the resurgence of weight-loss drugs. “For the past 10 years, we tried so hard to go the other way, to gain muscle, but now with Ozempic and the thin look coming back in, I feel like we’re going backwards, and it’s so sad to see,” she says. She already has a vision for what her life in Hong Kong could look like – and it goes far beyond weightlifting. She envisions workshops, community events and a space where women can feel comfortable picking up a barbell for the first time. “I really want to get more people involved and show them what weightlifting is like – because it’s so fun,” she says. “You earn your muscles, you work hard for them. Who cares if you’re bulky?” Like what you read? Follow SCMP Lifestyle on Instagram. You can also sign up for our eNewsletter here.

title: China highlights advanced wartime tech in defence mobilisation law update
description: The first amendment to the law in 16 years is also expected to cover cyberspace, biotechnology and quantum technology, analysts say.
content: China has made the first amendment in 16 years to its national defence mobilisation law to include a fresh focus on new technologies – a move experts said would cover AI and drones. Analysts said the inclusion would make it possible to rapidly convert emerging infrastructure, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and unmanned systems, into defence capabilities. The revised law, passed by the top legislature on Friday, says that “the state promotes the application of advanced technologies in national defence mobilisation and develops national defence mobilisation forces in emerging fields”, according to the text published by official news agency Xinhua. Though the amendment does not specify which “advanced technologies” it covers, Beijing-based military law expert Xie Dan said it referred to cyberspace, AI, unmanned systems including drones, the electromagnetic spectrum, surveying and mapping navigation, biotechnology, as well as maritime, space and quantum technologies. Xie said the amendment, set to take effect on October 1, not only covered technologies but also market entities and specialised talent in these fields. “The Russia-Ukraine conflict further validates the critical role of unmanned, intelligent and cyber technologies in modern warfare, reinforcing the necessity of this legislation,” Xie said. Xie said the benefits of the revision were that it incorporated many civilian hi-tech enterprises and professionals into China’s mobilisation potential. “In peacetime, these capabilities serve economic and social development; in wartime, they can be rapidly reassigned to provide operational support,” he said. For the first time, the revised law formally defines national defence mobilisation, describing it as activities that “guarantee a rapid transition from peacetime to wartime and transform economic and social capabilities into national defence strength”. It says that the law will be enforced if the country’s national sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, security and development interests – a new addition in the revised text – are “under direct threat”. The revised law also includes data and software as part of the military’s reserve capacity, alongside conventional equipment and products. “Modern warfare is data-driven. Intelligence, command and supply are highly dependent on data and software,” Xie said, adding that only by surveying and collecting data during peacetime could China’s military carry out rapid allocation of resources during wartime. Under the new amendment, non-government entities and individuals may serve as supply chain and logistics providers for strategic material reserves. While the previous version of the law only allowed the government to prepare strategic reserves, the revised law encourages enterprises, public institutions and social organisations to increase their preparedness in technology and production capacity. The revised law also encourages non-government organisations and individuals to take on tasks such as storage, transport and distribution. “Modern warfare is highly reliant on the resilience of the supply chain. It’s not enough to rely on only government reserves to cover all wartime consumption. So it is necessary to mobilise existing production capacity, warehousing and logistics capabilities across society,” Xie said. In an article on Monday, Beijing-based defence think tank Dong Fang Hong framed the revision as a systematic adjustment for war preparation. The article noted that the core challenge of modern mobilisation was no longer whether there were resources but whether they could be quickly mobilised. “No matter how big the economic scale and how many social resources there are, if they can’t be quickly identified, precisely organised and legally allocated … then they are just potential resources and not actual defence capabilities,” it said. China has amended a series of laws related to defence and the military in recent years, including laws on national defence education, protection of military installations, military service, the People’s Armed Police, the coastguard and reservists. The latest revision will “help foster a well-developed, interconnected, and efficient national defence legal framework”, according to a Friday article in the People’s Court Daily, a newspaper affiliated with China’s Supreme People’s Court. “Much of the potential of modern warfare lies within society and the market. The legal revision intends to bring dispersed civilian technological capabilities, production capacity and logistics resources into a law-based framework for mobilisation preparedness,” Xie said.

title: Meet tennis No 1 Aryna Sabalenka’s fiancé, Oakberry founder Georgios Frangulis
description: The Belarusian tennis star first got to know the Brazilian entrepreneur – who co-owns Le Mans FC – as an ambassador for his açaí brand in 2024.
content: Belarusian tennis star Aryna Sabalenka is launching her bid for her third consecutive US Open title, and cheering her on from her player’s box will be her new fiancé, Brazilian entrepreneur Georgios Frangulis. The pair got engaged in March, when Frangulis popped the question with a 12-carat sparkler designed by Isabela Grutman, reported People. “It’s 12 carats with, like, two layers of emeralds and a very beautiful cut,” the world No 1 revealed in an Instagram video, with her husband-to-be adding that it was “not easy to find a beautiful, massive stone”. Although the ring fell three carats short of Sabalenka’s dream rock, Frangulis explained that the larger stone would’ve been “too tacky” and “too expensive”. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Aryna Sabalenka (@arynasabalenka) So what do we know about Georgios Frangulis? He’s proud of his Greek heritage Georgios Frangulis was born in São Paulo, Brazil. His father, Eleftherios, grew up in Brazil, but his grandfather, Georgios, hails from Thessaloniki, Greece’s second-largest city. “I feel 100 per cent Greek,” Frangulis told The Greek Herald. Frangulis studied law at Fundação Armando Alvares Penteado, but did not take the bar exam, per Harper’s Bazaar. He moved to Miami, Florida, and later, Venice Beach, California. In 2016, he married Isabella “Beh” Armentano, per Town & Country. It is unclear when they split. That year, he was also diagnosed with thyroid cancer. He’s an entrepreneur and motorsport enthusiast Frangulis founded the popular açaí brand Oakberry in 2016, shortly after undergoing surgery for thyroid cancer. By 2023, he was on the cover of Forbes Brazil. Today, Oakberry has over 1,100 locations across 50 countries, per The Venture podcast. The company’s founder is a fan of motorsports and has competed in over 100 Porsche GT3 Cup Challenge races, per People. He has dreamed of owning a Formula One team since he was a kid, per The Greek Herald. He is a co-owner of the French Ligue 1 football club Le Mans, alongside former F1 drivers Felipe Massa and Kevin Magnussen, and tennis star Novak Djokovic. His relationship with Aryna Sabalenka The four-time grand slam singles champion first crossed paths with Frangulis in Dubai in the autumn of 2023, per Vogue. It was strictly business at first, with the tennis star signing a sponsorship deal with Oakberry. By January 2024, she was an ambassador for the brand, and by April that year, she and Frangulis were publicly linked. Sabalenka’s ex-boyfriend, Belarusian ice hockey player Konstantin Koltsov, had died that March, and Sabalenka revealed to People that Frangulis supported her during that difficult time. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Georgios Frangulis (@georgiosfrangulis) Frangulis is also very supportive of Sabalenka’s career. He told sports website RG that watching her from the box was “one of the most stressful situations [he has] ever experienced” and that he claps as loud as he can. “For me, the most important part comes afterwards – making sure she’s feeling good overall once the match is over,” he said. Sabalenka has said she would like to have the wedding in Greece in September 2027.

title: Meet Tony Romo’s wife, Candice Crawford – sister of Chace Crawford of Gossip Girl fame
description: The ex-Dallas Cowboys quarterback was put on indefinite leave by CBS following an alleged DUI – but who is his wife and the mother to his 3 sons?
content: In July, ex-NFL star Tony Romo was arrested in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on suspicion of driving while intoxicated. The incident was followed by several further alleged offences, prompting CBS Sports to place the NFL analyst on indefinite leave. Romo has worked in the role since retiring from American football in 2017. “Tony accepts full responsibility for his actions and has taken proactive steps to ensure that this isolated civil matter is properly resolved,” a representative for the former Dallas Cowboys quarterback told TMZ, adding that the 46-year-old is in talks with CBS regarding his future with the network. While Romo deals with the fallout, his wife of 15 years, Candice Crawford Romo, has remained largely out of the public eye. The 39-year-old once told DFW Child – a family magazine in the Dallas-Fort Worth area – that she was “really good at digging [her] head in the sand” when it came to handling negative attention surrounding her husband. So who is Candice Crawford Romo? She is Chace Crawford’s sister Candice Crawford was born in December 1986 in Texas to a dermatologist father and teacher mother – both fans of the Dallas Cowboys. Although Tony Romo initially left Candice’s parents starstruck – she hid them in the bathroom when he came to pick her up for a date, per People – the Crawfords are no strangers to the world of celebrity. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Candice Romo (@candiceromo) Candice’s older brother is actor Chace Crawford, known for his portrayals of Nate Archibald in Gossip Girl and Kevin Kohler / The Deep in The Boys. She’s a beauty queen-turned-sports journalist and entrepreneur Candice Crawford Romo is a former Miss Missouri, and competed for the Miss Texas Teen crown in 2003 and 2005, per People. She graduated from the University of Missouri in 2009 with a degree in journalism. At university, she covered the Dallas Cowboys for CBS segment The Blitz. She later worked for CW33 TV in Dallas, hosting programmes like the nightlife show Up All Night and the weekend Dallas Cowboys sports show Special Edition. Her relationship with Tony Romo Candice Crawford met Tony Romo while interning for the Dallas Cowboys, per People. They began dating in 2009, and he proposed in 2010. The couple tied the knot at Arlington Hall in Dallas the following year in the presence of 600 guests, including Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, who attended with special permission in light of a labour dispute prohibiting team owners and players from meeting. Fellow Cowboys alumni Troy Aikman, Dez Bryant and Roger Staubach also celebrated with the newlyweds. The Romos are parents to three sons: Hawkins, 14, Rivers, 12, and Jones, nine. In 2016, Crawford launched the parenting-focused essential oil spray brand Hawk+Sloane with her childhood friend Hollie Siglin. The company was named after the founders’ sons.

title: Chinese mahjong club owner pays US$2,800 over failed first aid, then gets refunded
description: China’s Civil Code shields Good Samaritans from civil liability for accidental harm during rescues.
content: A mahjong parlour owner in central China paid compensation of 19,000 yuan (US$2,800) following a failed first aid attempt on an elderly customer but received a refund after government intervention. On August 17, a man in his 60s, surnamed Luo, visited the mahjong parlour in Hunan province and passed out while resting in a chair. The shop’s owner, Xiao Aihua, sensed something was wrong with Luo and approached to administer first aid. Believing that Luo had suffered from heatstroke, she dragged him a few steps outside to provide him with fresh air. In her panic, Xiao struggled to dial emergency numbers, prompting a neighbour to call an ambulance, which arrived within 10 minutes. A witness reported that Luo was still alive when the ambulance picked him up, but regrettably, he died later. Luo’s family reviewed the venue’s surveillance footage and claimed that Xiao’s first aid procedures were inadequate, arguing that she should be held responsible for Luo’s death. They emphasised that Luo was a regular patron of the mahjong club and believed that Xiao was liable for her customers’ safety. The family demanded compensation of 100,000 yuan from Xiao, threatening to display Luo’s body in front of her shop if she refused to pay. Xiao’s son noted that his mother was deeply distressed by Luo’s family’s claims, resulting in insomnia and dizziness. Concerned for his wife’s health, Xiao’s husband compensated the family with 19,000 yuan. The situation took a turn when Xiao’s family brought the matter to social media, drawing the attention of local authorities. The police conducted an investigation and concluded that Luo had died from a sudden illness, affirming that Xiao had acted out of goodwill in her attempts to assist him. According to China’s Civil Code, there is a “Good Samaritan” provision which protects individuals who voluntarily provide emergency assistance from civil liability if their actions inadvertently cause harm to the person they assist. Under government mediation, Luo’s son agreed to refund the full amount to Xiao. Luo’s son also acknowledged his mistake, stating: “I now understand that she does not need to compensate for things she did not do wrong.” Xiao’s family plans to donate part of the refunded amount to charity, expressing their commitment to continue helping others in the future, unaffected by this incident. “Compensating the deceased’s family could discourage people from helping others in the future,” commented an online observer. “Even though he refunded the money, restoring trust is difficult,” remarked another.

title: Hong Kong tycoon empires and foundations pledge 30m yuan for China-Nepal flood relief
description: Li Ka-shing and business empire, along with Henderson Land Development and Lee Shau Kee Foundation provide help after Nepal-Tibet disaster.
content: Hong Kong tycoon Li Ka-shing and his business empire, along with Henderson Land Development and the Lee Shau Kee Foundation, have pledged 15 million yuan (US$2.2 million) each to support relief efforts for victims of the deadly flash flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border. Nina Wang Charity Management also pledged HK$10 million (US$1.27 million) to support relief efforts. CK Asset Holdings, CK Hutchison Holdings and the Li Ka Shing Foundation, as well as Henderson Land and the Lee Shau Kee Foundation, expressed their condolences to victims of the disaster. The donations were made through the central government's liaison office’s disaster relief account. Last Wednesday, a massive wall of mud and rock collapsed into a river along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, triggering catastrophic flooding. According to Nepalese police, 1,058 bodies had been recovered as of 2pm on Tuesday, with 4,606 people still missing. Chinese authorities have confirmed 16 deaths and 546 people missing, taking the death toll on both sides of the border to 1,074. Over the past week, the city government, local Nepalese community and organisations have moved to provide financial assistance, including allocating HK$50 million (US$6.3 million) from the Disaster Relief Fund, HK$20 million donated by the Jockey Club, and 30 million yuan contributed by the Macau government. A joint institute by Polytechnic University and Sichuan University for disaster management and reconstruction, established with funding from the Jockey Club after the 2008 Sichuan province earthquake, dispatched a team to Tibet to help with the rescue. Led by the institute’s associate research fellow, Li Yao, the team was the first university-based technical force to enter the core disaster zone. Since last Friday, the experts have been conducting drone-based mapping to obtain first-hand data on the material composition and terrain of the avalanche source zone, while investigating mud marks, air-blast traces and slopes along the flow path. “Based on the field data, the team carried out a preliminary assessment of the breaching risk of the landslide-dammed lake in the upper Donglin Zangbo,” it said, referring to a river on site. Their research had provided “a direct scientific basis for the safe deployment of rescue forces, secondary-disaster monitoring and early warning”, it added.

title: UK-Philippines troop deal to boost Nato’s South China Sea reach
description: If finalised, the UK would be the fourth Nato member to reach a deal with the Philippines allowing troops to train on each other’s soil.
content: A proposed troop access deal between the Philippines and Britain marks the latest step in Manila’s drive to draw more European and like-minded powers into its efforts to safeguard the free flow of trade through the South China Sea and neighbouring waterways. The visiting forces agreement would allow troops from both countries to train and operate temporarily on each other’s soil, a move analysts said could deepen the Philippines’ ties with Nato members and reduce its reliance on the US security umbrella. Philippine and British defence officials met in Manila on Thursday last week for the first round of formal negotiations on the pact. “We appreciate the UK’s unqualified support as a like-minded partner in upholding the rules-based international order and preserving freedoms ensured by the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea,” said Salvador Melchon Mison Jnr, defence undersecretary for acquisition and resource management, in a statement after meeting Amy Senior, Indo-Pacific head at Britain’s Ministry of Defence. Talks began last year after London proposed the agreement in a letter from Britain’s then defence secretary, John Healey, to Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro. The agreement would set out terms for British and Philippine troops to take part in joint exercises, training, humanitarian work and disaster response missions in each other’s territory. It would add Britain to a growing list of Manila’s defence partners with troop access arrangements, following the Philippine Senate’s ratification of similar pacts with Canada and New Zealand in August and with France in March. The Philippines also has a reciprocal access agreement with Japan that came into effect in September last year, while its agreement with Australia has been in force since 2012. Tensions between the Philippines and China over their overlapping South China Sea claims have intensified in recent years. Over a single week in July, vessels from both sides clashed multiple times around the Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal. Diversifying defence ties If finalised, Britain would become the fourth Nato member to have a troop access agreement with the Philippines, after the United States, France and Canada. Matteo Piasentini, a geopolitical analyst with the Italian think tank Geopolitica.info and an international relations lecturer at the University of the Philippines Diliman, said the Philippines stood to benefit from military exchanges with Britain, particularly in naval capabilities. Vincent Kyle Parada, a lecturer at the De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde’s School of Diplomacy and Governance, described the proposed agreement’s scope as “mainly administrative”, covering the terms of overseas troop deployment. “Nevertheless, it’s a necessary step to allow the conduct of joint military exercises on Philippine soil. Once finalised, we’re likely to see the UK as a full-fledged participant in the US-Philippine-led Balikatan exercises in the near future,” Parada said. Crucially, the agreement would also amount to a “show of support for the Philippines’ position on the South China Sea”, he added. Speaking at the 2026 Paris Defence and Strategy Forum in March, Defence Secretary Teodoro said the Philippines was seeking broader defence cooperation with Nato, emphasising the need for greater cross-regional coordination “as challenges to global security and stability continuously evolve”. He also discussed security cooperation between Nato and the Philippines with the transatlantic security alliance’s chair Giuseppe Cavo Dragone on the sidelines of the forum. Parada said the involvement of Britain and France as security partners of the Philippines highlighted the Indo-Pacific’s growing importance to both European powers and to Nato. “The two countries have, by far, the largest footprint in the Indo-Pacific, and they showcase perfectly Manila’s emerging status as a focal point for extra-regional engagement, especially as far as defence cooperation is concerned,” he said. “Nato recognises the growing convergence between Euro-Atlantic and Indo-Pacific security, particularly in response to the loose alignment between China, Russia, Iran and North Korea,” Parada added. “There’s an interest there in establishing regional linkages, especially given Nato’s limited Indo-Pacific footprint barring the US.” Piasentini said that Britain and other Nato members would benefit from training in a security theatre outside Europe. “It increases Nato capabilities when the critical mass of countries is trained in a theatre that is not part of Nato,” he said, adding that Nato members wanted to maintain “a cloud of ambiguity” in their relations with China while maintaining a presence in the South China Sea. Julio Amador, CEO of Amador Research Services and a distinguished visiting fellow at Perry World House, said the Philippines would also benefit from cooperating with more countries to enhance its defence needs. According to Parada, closer Nato ties align with Manila’s objective of diversifying its security partners and reducing its over-reliance on the US. Referring to the Philippines’ pursuit of Western partners for deterrence, Parada said: “They generally have stronger militaries and more robust defence industries, but also because they do not have the same inhibitions regarding security-focused cooperation, especially directed against China. Though US-led, Nato is composed of many member countries that share the Philippines’ strategic interests in the Indo-Pacific.” Amador cautioned against a formal alliance between the Philippines and Nato members, however, noting that US President Donald Trump had been pressurising Nato to shoulder more of the burden for European security and to counter Russian aggression in Ukraine. “At this point, Nato will have to focus on its own backyard. But that doesn’t mean that the Nato member states will not diversify their defence partnerships,” Amador said.

title: Subdivided-flat registration rate at 42.5% as ‘early bird’ phase deadline passes
description: Industry observers say ownership complications and low awareness have slowed landlords’ applications under new housing regulations.
content: Property-ownership complications and low public awareness have slowed landlords’ registration of Hong Kong subdivided flats under new housing regulations, industry observers have said, after the government received only 42.5 per cent of the applications expected in the first phase. Monday marked the deadline for the initial six-month “early bird” registration phase under the Basic Housing Unit Ordinance. Landlords who applied during this period were eligible for a waiver of HK$3,000 (US$382) in certification fees per subdivided flat for each of the first three years. The legislation came into force in March to phase out substandard subdivided flats. The government estimates that about 80,000 flats across the city could be accredited, but only about 34,000 units were registered during the first six months. Scott Leung Man-kwong, deputy chairman of the Legislative Council’s housing panel, described the 42.5 per cent application rate as acceptable but said the HK$3,000 discount was not a significant incentive for landlords to apply early. “For inherited properties, sometimes the verification of legal ownership could delay the application,” he told a radio show on Tuesday. “We’ve seen cases where a son inherited a flat from his father that is already subdivided. The tenants continued to pay rent and they did not process the legal transfer of the property. But now, with the application for basic housing units, they will have to do so.” A second six-month registration round, offering smaller fee discounts, is under way and will conclude the overall one-year application period. Landlords have also been given a three-year grace period to renovate and rectify substandard units in line with government requirements. Leung said rents for renovated units could rise, perhaps from about HK$5,000 to HK$7,000, as landlords sought to recoup their costs. But he was confident rents would fall as more public housing and basic housing units became available. Jerry Ho Chi-pang, vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Basic Housing Units Operators Association, said more briefings on basic housing units should be organised in different districts to raise awareness, as some owners might still be unaware of the new regime. “There were some in Tsuen Wan, but that is only one spot. Talks could be held in other areas such as Sham Shui Po, Mong Kok, and Yau Ma Tei. If I’m a Sham Shui Po resident, especially a senior, it’s unlikely I’d trek all the way to Tsuen Wan for a talk,” he said. Fellow lawmaker Vincent Cheng Wing-shun also said sharing sessions involving landlords who had already filed applications could help reassure those who had yet to apply. He said authorities should continue to provide show flats for landlords, offering renovation guidance and budget estimates for converting existing subdivided flats into units that comply with the new government standards.

title: As Chinese chipmakers snap up local gear, self-sufficiency drive faces commercial test
description: Industry leaders caution that the semiconductor equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability.
content: Chinese chipmakers are setting increasingly aggressive targets to source production equipment locally, adding pressure on domestic toolmakers to come up with machines that are reliable in the exacting environment of high-volume wafer production. Several new wafer fabrication plants, or fabs, in the country were setting explicit localisation targets, according to Jie Chen, chairman of Britech Semiconductor Equipment (Shanghai) Corp, who spoke at an industry conference in eastern China’s Wuxi on Monday. “One large customer here in Wuxi is aiming for 80 per cent localisation of equipment at its new fab,” Chen said. Flash memory maker Yangtze Memory Technologies Corp (YMTC) highlights the speed of this transition. Before being targeted under US export restrictions in 2022, American-made tools accounted for about half of YMTC’s equipment, the company said. Now, it is working towards building a fab that relies mostly on domestic machinery. However, industry leaders caution that the equipment sector must now transition from technical viability to commercial reliability, a shift Chen described as moving from a “zero-to-one” phase into a “2.0 era”. “Making one machine is easy, but can five machines be the same as the first? What about 10, 50 or 100?” Chen said, noting that fabs required absolute consistency across multiple chambers and machines. He added that the industry’s “final exam” would come when Chinese toolmakers could win top overseas clients without home-turf advantage. Beijing’s drive to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers extends beyond chipmakers to upstream materials suppliers. Xian ESWIN Material Technology, China’s largest manufacturer of unprocessed 12-inch silicon wafers, told the conference that domestic machinery made up 52 per cent of its production equipment as of June, up from 42 per cent in 2024. The company targets 58 per cent by 2027. These ambitious mandates are delivering windfalls to Chinese toolmakers. Naura Technology Group, China’s largest chip-equipment maker, last week reported first-half revenue growth of about 25 per cent year on year. The company competes against global leaders Applied Materials and Tokyo Electron in the equipment sectors of deposition, etching, thermal processing and cleaning. Etching tool producer Advanced Micro-Fabrication Equipment (AMEC) grew revenue by nearly 35 per cent, while deposition specialist Piotech – a challenger to Applied Materials, Lam Research and ASM International – posted a sales jump of almost 50 per cent during the same period. Domestic substitution is increasingly shifting from simply replacing foreign tools to directly benchmarking against leading overseas suppliers. Liu Erzhuang, chairman and CEO of Productive Technologies Company, said domestic vendors must compete on productivity, not just technical capability. “Technical success is not the final success,” Liu said. “Only when the technology succeeds commercially and in the market can it truly scale.” Productive Technologies said its wet-cleaning platform could process as many as 850 wafers per hour with 16 chambers, matching the throughput of comparable overseas equipment. Domestic suppliers accounted for about 23 per cent of semiconductor equipment sold in China in 2025, a figure projected to hit 39 per cent by 2030, according to market research firm Yole Group. China already accounted for roughly one-third of global equipment demand currently, Yole’s corporate vice-president Gary Huang said. Domestic suppliers are gaining share in a market that is itself continuing to expand rapidly. Goldman Sachs expects China’s wafer-fabrication equipment spending to rise from about US$44.3 billion this year to US$53 billion in 2027 and US$60.7 billion in 2028. That expansion is particularly pronounced in memory. Goldman expects DRAM capacity at ChangXin Memory Technologies to more than double from about 270,000 wafers per month in 2026 to 665,000 by 2030. YMTC, meanwhile, is expected to raise its NAND capacity from about 200,000 wafers per month to around 300,000 after a new Wuhan fab ramps up, according to China Merchants Securities.

title: Hong Kong school starts academic year without replacing head fired for swearing
description: San Wui Commercial Society Secondary School has candidate, but Education Bureau still conducting background checks.
content: A Hong Kong secondary school has begun the new academic year without a principal while authorities vet a replacement for the former head, who was fired for swearing at security guards during a Singapore study trip. Former lawmaker Edmund Wong Chun-sek, who is also a manager of San Wui Commercial Society Secondary School, said on Tuesday that the Education Bureau was currently conducting background checks on the candidate. The school, located in Tuen Mun, was under the temporary leadership of its deputy head for now, he added. “We have completed the recruitment procedures and decided on one candidate, but the Education Bureau is still vetting the appointment,” Wong said. “Of course, the sooner we welcome the new principal, the better.” Wong said the wider process could take time since the bureau had taken three months to vet the previous incumbent. But he stressed that the school would operate as normal, adding that teachers and the institution’s governance team were on the same page. In response to the South China Morning Post’s inquiry, the bureau said on Tuesday that it had reminded the school to strictly follow the relevant procedures in its application and take appropriate administrative measures to ensure that its operations were not disrupted and that students’ wellbeing was safeguarded. The school started recruiting for a new principal earlier this year following the dismissal of Lee Cheuk-hing, who had held the role since 2022, in June after he was filmed swearing at two security guards while leading a study trip to Singapore. The viral footage, which was filmed in late May, shows Lee swearing in Cantonese and shouting words such as “impolite”, “shut up” and “go away” at the two female guards. The two guards appear visibly upset in the clip and point their fingers at Lee during the exchange. In the same video, Lee is noticeably more polite when interacting with a passer-by, who appeared to be ethnically Chinese, prompting accusations of racial discrimination. Lee also faced allegations of sexist behaviour after another video showed him deliberately dropping a HK$1,000 (US$127) banknote and responding “women are this greedy” when a female student reached for the money. After the row came to light, Lee released a tearful video apologising to Hongkongers and “all sectors” in Singapore, urging students not to follow his example, and submitted his resignation on May 28. The school’s management committee said Lee’s behaviour had violated the professional code of conduct for teaching staff, especially guidelines stipulated by the Education Bureau. While Lee had requested his last day to be August 31, the committee instead decided to sack him on June 3. As part of the hunt for his replacement, the school said applicants would need to have “excellent character”. Wong said on Tuesday that the recruitment process was “in a bit of a hurry”, but added that it was understandable that the bureau could need time for checks.

title: China ends dividend tax exemption for expats, applying 20% rate
description: The exemption previously enjoyed by overseas nationals on gains from foreign-funded firms in China was cancelled in an announcement on Tuesday.
content: China’s tax authorities announced on Tuesday that the country would end the tax exemption for dividends earned by expatriates at foreign-funded firms, setting a 20 per cent rate effective immediately. The measures mainly target “interest, dividend and bonus income” for individual income tax purposes, according to a joint statement from the Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration. State news agency Xinhua said the change was needed for the “unification of the tax system”. In 1994, China put in place a tax exemption on dividend and bonus income that foreign individuals earned from foreign‑invested enterprises. At the time, the measure was designed to advance reform and opening‑up and draw foreign investment. A tax‑service hotline representative said that because the guideline was newly issued, immediate confirmation was not available on whether the new rule would cover individuals in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, or foreigners living overseas. “This change upholds fairness in the tax system. Previously, foreign investors received tax‑exempt dividends while Chinese investors paid tax. Such differential treatment runs counter to the principle of tax neutrality,” said Fu Yifu, a special research fellow at Su Merchants Bank in Nanjing, in China’s eastern Jiangsu province. “Foreign investors in China value comprehensive strengths such as its rule‑of‑law environment, market size and industrial support, not merely a handful of tax incentives. Phasing out these remaining differential treatment policies will foster a more efficient, well‑regulated unified market system,” Fu said. The latest measure comes amid a raft of initiatives that Beijing has rolled out in recent months to tighten oversight of cross-border financial flows, aimed at curbing tax avoidance and capital flight. China announced new rules in July, bringing income generated through offshore trusts under its personal income tax regime, closing a loophole that had enabled wealthy Chinese households to shield large sums of income from taxation. With a unified national market taking shape, China is progressively regulating preferential tax policies. “In past practice, some domestic firms rebranded as foreign‑invested enterprises to siphon profits via large dividends and access tax-exempt benefits, causing tax revenue losses. The new rule has fully closed such arbitrage opportunities,” Fu said. In addition, if their tax residence country allowed tax credits, taxes that foreign individuals pay in China could offset their local tax liabilities. Their overall tax burden therefore might not rise materially, Fu added. According to the new guideline, foreign‑funded enterprises would need to withhold and remit tax when paying dividends and bonuses to foreigners, and the foreign firms would file tax returns within 15 days of the month after payment, the statement said. If the enterprise failed to withhold taxes, the foreign individual receiving dividends would be required to pay the tax on or before 30 June of the following year. If tax authorities issued a time-limited payment notice, the foreign individual would be required to comply with that deadline, it added.

title: ‘Carries the region’s hopes’: Xi hails Kyrgyzstan project as China ramps up railway push
description: China’s Kyrgyzstan rail pledge highlights wider drive to knit Asia together and strengthen trade links.
content: As President Xi Jinping hailed a cross-border railway project via Kyrgyzstan during his visit to the Central Asian country, Beijing is accelerating efforts to expand railway links with neighbours – from Mongolia to Vietnam – to boost regional trade and hedge against rising geopolitical risks. Meeting with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Bishkek on Monday, Xi stressed the importance of building a “high-quality China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway”, describing it as “a major transportation artery that carries the region’s hopes for development”, according to state news agency Xinhua. Xi and Japarov pledged in a joint declaration on Monday to ensure the railway’s timely completion while creating favourable conditions to guarantee its traffic volume and operational efficiency. “The railway is more than just a transit line – it is a strategic lever reshaping the regional landscape,” said Li Lifan, an expert on Russia and Central Asia at the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences. “For China, it creates a safer and more efficient supply chain; for landlocked nations like Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, it presents a historical opportunity to transform into land-linked hubs.” The railway is part of China’s expanding cross-border network under the Belt and Road Initiative, as Beijing steps up infrastructure investment to strengthen trade links and regional connectivity across Asia, Africa and Europe. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway appears more valuable in the current environment as geopolitical uncertainty has increased the value of diversification in transport routes Zoey Wang, Fitch Ratings The push has taken on added importance as geopolitical conflicts, including the US-Israeli war on Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war, have disrupted supply chains and traditional shipping routes, increasing the value of safer alternatives for moving goods. “The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway appears more valuable in the current environment as geopolitical uncertainty has increased the value of diversification in transport routes,” said Zoey Wang, director of global infrastructure and project finance at Fitch Ratings. Wang added that resilience had become a key consideration in infrastructure assessment, with neighbouring cross-border rail projects viewed through the same lens. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, spanning more than 500km (310 miles) and due for completion in 2031, will run from Kashgar in China’s far western region of Xinjiang through Kyrgyzstan to Andijan in eastern Uzbekistan. Once completed, it was expected to become the shortest land route linking China with Central Asia, reducing the rail distance from East Asia to southern Europe by 900km and saving seven to eight days in transit time, state media reported. Elsewhere, construction of a second railway crossing between China and Mongolia was more than halfway complete as of Thursday, Chinese state media reported. The 9.91km line, running from Ganqimaodu port in Inner Mongolia to Gashuun Sukhait in Mongolia’s Omnogovi province, will link Mongolia’s largest coal deposit with China and is expected to carry about 30 million tonnes of cargo annually when it opens in 2027. The rail push is also gathering pace in Southeast Asia. Last week, Vietnam’s National Assembly committed more funds to a major line linking its northern border with China. The 391km line will connect the port city of Haiphong to Lao Cai, a mountainous city bordering southwestern China’s Yunnan province, while passing through the Vietnamese capital of Hanoi. In July, during Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul’s visit to China, both sides agreed that enhanced connectivity was a key driver for economic integration and shared growth across the region. They pledged to accelerate construction of the first phase of a 609km railway connecting Thailand with China via Laos, while launching its second phase as soon as possible. The China-Laos railway, which opened in December 2021 and runs from Kunming, Yunnan’s capital, to Vientiane, has already become an important link in the regional network. In the first half of this year, it carried 11.2 million passenger trips and 12.32 million tonnes of freight, including 188,000 cross-border passenger trips, up nearly 26 per cent from a year earlier, according to China State Railway Group. Within China, the high-speed railway network was increasingly becoming a major draw for foreign visitors. Nationwide, Chinese railways carried 12.3 million passenger trips by foreign travellers in the first half, up 33.6 per cent year on year, according to the company.

title: Global investors descend on China’s Shenzhen to ride wave of AI and robotics opportunities
description: Major banks such as HSBC and UBS host thousands of executives in southern tech hub this week to connect foreign capital with domestic firms.
content: Shenzhen, the southern Chinese city home to US-sanctioned telecoms giant Huawei Technologies and drone maker DJI, has seen an influx of investors and business leaders amid rising global interest in Chinese artificial intelligence and robotics. On Tuesday, the tech hub hosted investor conferences led by three international financial institutions – HSBC, UBS and Nomura – with AI, robotics and other emerging technologies featuring prominently on their agendas. More investors could arrive to chase opportunities ahead of November’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting – one of the region’s highest-profile gatherings of political and business leaders. “Robotics, AI and innovative medicines have emerged as new trends in China’s exports,” David Liao, HSBC’s co-chief executive for Asia and the Middle East, said at the bank’s 13th annual China Conference, according to a press release. “In particular, China’s AI infrastructure supply chain is set to create fresh growth opportunities for global businesses and investors.” HSBC’s two-day gathering, which began on Tuesday, attracted more than 1,500 global business leaders, executives and institutional and individual investors, according to the bank. “Asian markets, led by China, will continue to serve as a key hub for global AI exports,” Liao added. Shenzhen is one of China’s leading innovation hubs and home to internet heavyweight Tencent Holdings and electric-vehicle leader BYD. The city’s rising tech firms, including UBTech Robotics, have also been drawing market attention. Swiss bank UBS said that more than 1,000 guests, including clients from Europe, the US and the Middle East, attended its 23rd China A-Share Conference, which kicked off on Tuesday, with a record 125 companies taking part. The strong turnout reflected growing overseas interest in Chinese companies, innovation and opportunities in the A-share market, said Thomas Fang, head of China global markets at UBS, in his opening remarks at the conference. “Technology, particularly artificial intelligence, is a key investment theme in the A-share market this year,” Fang said, adding that China’s AI supply chain was reshaping global competition through cost efficiency driven by targeted research and development, innovation in model architecture and open-source collaboration. UBS is also stepping up its global AI strategy and investment in China, he added. Nomura’s China Investor Forum, running from Monday to Tuesday, drew 500 delegates, including 400 institutional investors, with more than 50 companies taking part, according to its website.

title: Meet John Galliano’s long-time partner Alexis Roche, who’s styled Kendall Jenner
description: The designer’s 2027 show at the Met has been cancelled due to public backlash – meet his loyal partner, who’s styled A-listers such as Charlize Theron.
content: On August 31, New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and John Galliano announced in a joint statement that the exhibition John Galliano: Horizons – which was scheduled to open in May next year and would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala – has been cancelled in light of the 65-year-old designer’s past antisemitic remarks and subsequent conviction in France in 2011. “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it,” Galliano stated, with Met trustee Anna Wintour calling his decision “very courageous and a measure of the man he is”. This exhibition would have made Galliano the third-ever living designer to receive a solo show at the Costume Institute. Now, it has brought renewed attention to his personal life, including his long-time partner, Alexis Roche. So what do we know about Alexis Roche? He’s French Alexis Roche was born in Provence, in southeastern France. He and Galliano share a stone farmhouse in Auvergne, in central France, where Roche’s grandmother was born, per Vogue. Roche studied art and literature before turning his hand to fashion, per his bio on the artist agency Michele Filomeno. He’s a fashion stylist and brand consultant Roche moved first to London, then to Paris in 2003, where he began working as a brand and celebrity consultant for Dior under Galliano. Following the designer’s dismissal from Dior as a result of his antisemitic remarks, Roche left the maison as well, per the Observer. The stylist has since built an impressive CV, working with stars such as Amal Clooney, Uma Thurman, Kate Moss, Charlize Theron and Kendall Jenner. He worked as an artistic image director at Maison Margiela – where Galliano was creative director from 2014 to 2024 – and is a freelance fashion editor. He is credited as a fashion editor and stylist on this year’s campaign announcing a collaboration between Galliano and Zara. His relationship with John Galliano In 2015, Vogue described Roche as Galliano’s partner of 15 years. A decade later, Roche was described by photographer and movement director Pat Boguslawski in an LA Times article as Galliano’s husband. Roche supported Galliano during his struggles with addiction, per Vanity Fair, and even served as his fitting model while the designer was working on Kate Moss’ wedding dress during his recovery. The couple live in an 18th-century house in Gerberoy, in northern France, and also spend time in their Paris flat and Auvergne farmhouse.

title: Pallas-1 sees China’s Galactic Energy join reusable launch push, closing in on SpaceX
description: The orbital mission marks a key milestone for Beijing’s commercial launch sector.
content: Chinese rocket maker Galactic Energy has successfully sent its Pallas-1 medium-to-large reusable rocket into orbit, marking the latest milestone in Beijing’s drive to develop reusable launch capabilities and narrow the gap with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. The two-stage, liquid-propellant rocket lifted off at 10am on Tuesday from a self-built launch pad at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre’s commercial pilot zone in northwestern China’s Gansu province before entering its designated orbit, according to the Beijing-based company. Standing 52 metres tall with a 3.35-metre diameter, Pallas-1 has a lift-off mass of about 283 tonnes and lift-off thrust of 350 tonnes-force. Its first stage is powered by seven in-house developed liquid oxygen-kerosene engines named CQ-50. The rocket is designed to carry up to 7 tonnes into low Earth orbit and withstand up to 25 flights. Galactic Energy did not attempt to recover the booster on Tuesday. The company plans to test re-entry control, grid fins, braking and deceleration systems before attempting a full vertical landing – initially aiming for targeted recovery at sea or on land – to pave the way for high-frequency commercial reuse. The mission aligns with Beijing’s broader push to become a “space power”, an objective enshrined for the first time in the nation’s latest five-year plan. China has logged important advances in reusable rocket technology this year. In July, the state-developed Long March-10B became the country’s first orbital booster to be recovered, using a sea-based net system. LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 later completed an orbital mission before its first stage landed vertically on deployable legs. Neither recovered booster has flown again yet, leaving SpaceX as the global benchmark to beat. The US company routinely reflies its hardware, and last week its B1067 booster completed a record 37th mission, launching 29 Starlink satellites during SpaceX’s 100th Falcon 9 flight of the year. Reusable rockets slash launch costs and boost mission frequency, which is useful for satellite deployment, crewed missions, space-station resupply, and deep-space exploration. Galactic Energy was founded in 2018 by Liu Baiqi and other aerospace engineers. Liu earned a doctorate from Beihang University, where he later taught, before joining the state-owned China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology, one of the country’s leading rocket developers. The company’s portfolio includes two rocket families: the Ceres series of small- and medium-sized solid-fuel launch vehicles, and the larger liquid-propellant Pallas series. Galactic Energy said it had completed 22 successful orbital launches and delivered 89 commercial satellites to orbit. It is also among a group of Chinese commercial rocket makers seeking public listings. The company entered the pre-initial public offering tutoring process in October 2025, while rivals LandSpace and CAS Space are further ahead at the inquiry stage of Shanghai’s Star Market.

title: Opinion | Why US sanctions threats against China aren’t credible
description: Weaponising global payments against Beijing risks triggering a major shock at home – one America’s fragile debt and stock markets cannot afford.
content: The US threat of sanctions on China because of Beijing’s relationship with Iran isn’t credible. The artificial intelligence bubble and its own precarious bond market make the US more vulnerable to a shock than China. Even if the US risks massive self-harm and kicks major Chinese institutions off SWIFT, the global messaging system enabling dollar-based cross-border payments, it will merely accelerate the yuan’s rise. China’s trading partners can easily switch to the perfectly functional yuan payment system, the Cross-border Interbank Payment System (CIPS). The US talking up economic war on Iran reflects the reality that it is running out of ammunition for a hot war. The US has imposed economic and financial sanctions on Iran for decades. Now it aims to impose secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners. As China is Iran’s main trading partner, the US is essentially targeting China. China and the US have traded places since US President Donald Trump initiated the trade and tech war during his first term. At the time, China was grappling with a massive property bubble and a bloated shadow banking system. The government managed to deflate both without triggering a major economic downturn. Today, while China’s growth rate is muted, the economy is resilient and can withstand shocks. By contrast, the US economy has grown a massive artificial intelligence (AI) and stock market bubble. Stock market capitalisation has reached 240 per cent of gross domestic product, higher than in 1987, 2000 and 2007. The fiscal deficit has continued to balloon. As total US public debt tops US$40 trillion, up from US$9 trillion in 2007, bond yields are surging to 2007 levels. The US needs to refinance bonds worth US$9 trillion and issue US$2.1 trillion to cover the deficit. A major shock will trigger a financial collapse, and a financial war with China will bring such a shock. The US’ financial fragility and China’s resilience make it unlikely that the former will initiate an action that can shock its financial system. In a game of chicken, the US will blink first. The US has been sanctioning China in trade and technology through any means it can find. So far, China has been able to absorb the blows without suffering a recession. China is in the crosshairs of US politicians, with or without Iran. Hence, China has no incentive to respond to US pressure on additional sanctions. Kicking Chinese institutions off the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) system has been touted as a nuclear option that would collapse the Chinese economy. If it is implemented, the effect is likely to be the opposite of what is intended. Some 30 per cent of China’s trade was settled in yuan in 2025. If a bank has access to SWIFT, it has the capability to get on CIPS. It is doubtful that anyone will forgo a trading relationship because CIPS is too cumbersome to embrace. A SWIFT ban could also have one unintended consequence: countries that are forced to join CIPS to settle their China trade could begin to use it for trade with countries other than China, thus replacing the role of SWIFT. This would only undermine the dollar’s primacy. Could the US impose sanctions on banks for using CIPS? It is possible, but as most supply chains go through China, that would shut down the global production system. The US financial system won’t survive such a scenario. Given the severity of the potential blowback, the threat of the US barring China from SWIFT isn’t credible. The status quo of the US blocking ships to Iran and Iran controlling the Strait of Hormuz is likely to continue for some time. As I said previously in this space, I believe that peace will be restored after strategic petroleum reserves and the working inventories in the petrochemical industry run out. The pain of high oil prices will eventually bring peace. China is the biggest trading economy in the world. A stable and growing global economy is in its best interests. This is why China’s response to the US sanctions will be to inflict some pain as deterrence, but not enough to derail its economy. While China depends on trade, the US depends on money inflows. It is a natural consequence of the dollar being the world’s reserve currency. A reserve currency is naturally overvalued vis-a-vis the real economy, as the world accumulates wealth in dollars. As long as the dollar remains a reserve currency, the US is unlikely to be competitive in manufacturing. China and the US are the yin and yang of the global economy. If they can coexist, the global economy can function. If they work against each other, the world will experience inflation and liquidity crises.

title: Thailand jails activist over royal motorcade live streaming
description: She had questioned the conduct of police who dispersed farmers protesting along the route of King Maha Vajiralongkorn’s motorcade in Bangkok.
content: A Thai court has sentenced a 25-year-old activist to two years in prison for violating the country’s strict royal insult law, a rights group said, with her lawyer on Tuesday vowing to appeal. A criminal court convicted Tantawan Tuatulanon on Monday over a live streaming she aired near a royal motorcade in March 2022, legal advocacy group Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said in a statement. The court found Tantawan intended to defame Thailand’s highly revered monarchy when she questioned the conduct of police who dispersed farmers protesting along the route of King Maha Vajiralongkorn’s motorcade in the capital, Bangkok. The court said she had insulted the monarchy on multiple occasions, showing her conduct was “not a good-faith exercise of rights”, the group said. Tantawan denied charges of breaching Thailand’s strict lese-majeste law. Her lawyer Khumklao Songsomboon said that she would file an appeal, insisting on her client’s innocence. “This is simply an exercise of freedom of speech questioning the police’s work and right to assembly,” said Khumklao. “We have fought this far and will definitely continue to do so.” Tantawan was granted bail pending her appeal, with a condition barring her from travelling abroad. The court also fined her 600 baht (US$18) for disobeying an official’s order, according to TLHR. Tantawan was previously detained over the same incident, on both occasions going on a hunger strike, the group said. Tantawan and another activist were also arrested in 2024 for allegedly chasing the royal motorcade of the king’s sister, Princess Sirindhorn, and were charged with sedition and computer crimes, with court proceedings still pending, lawyer Khumklao said. Under Section 112 of Thailand’s criminal code, anyone convicted of insulting, defaming or threatening the king or his family can face a prison sentence of up to 15 years per offence. Legal observers and rights campaigners say the legislation is interpreted so broadly that it has become a tool to target dissent.
