Nearly 300 people have been charged under lese-majeste since pro-democracy protests in 2020, according to TLHR. The demonstrations saw tens of thousands of mostly young people take to the streets of the capital, some of whom openly criticised the monarchy.

title: Trump’s US visa pause; elephant’s 100km trek home; rise of SEA-pop: 7 Asia highlights
description: From Filipino migrants in Japan to South Asians rethinking Western education, here are a few highlights from SCMP’s recent Asia reporting.
content: We have selected seven stories from the SCMP’s coverage of Asia over the past week that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing. 1. Why US visa pause could have ‘real consequences’ for Asian applicants Asian workers and families already facing years-long waits for US visas could be pushed deeper into uncertainty by a global pause on immigrant visa appointments, as President Donald Trump’s administration tightens legal immigration through new screening and higher costs, experts warn. 2. Why Filipino migrants are rethinking their futures in Japan When Japan’s embassy in the Philippines extended applications for healthcare jobs on April 15, the pitch was straightforward: 50 positions for nurses and 300 for care workers in Japan, a three- to four-year placement, free Japanese-language lessons in both countries and a daily allowance during training. 3. Trunk road: injured elephant’s 100km trek home drives debate in Malaysia The lonely journey of a bull elephant trying to return to its jungle home has captured the hearts of Malaysians over the past week, putting a spotlight on the plight of wildlife struggling against deforestation and rapidly expanding human activity. 4. Why South Asian students are rethinking Western university education For years, South Asian students – particularly from India – treated an overseas undergraduate degree as the default springboard to an international career. That assumption is now changing. 5. Can Southeast Asian artists replicate K-pop’s global success with SEA-pop? The successes of Filipino acts SB19 and BINI appear to reflect a wider trend in Southeast Asia’s entertainment scene, with more regional acts outperforming Western artists and K-pop bands on streaming charts. 6. Why Malaysia’s push for 15 million Muslim tourists is no sure thing Malaysia sees an opening in the Gulf travel disruption caused by the Iran war, pitching itself as a Muslim-friendly destination for travellers seeking halal food, prayer facilities and family-focused holidays. 7. Can Singapore’s new anti-scam rules help stop online fraud before it occurs? Singapore’s new rules for messaging platforms mark a significant shift in the country’s fight against scams, placing greater responsibility on digital services to help stop fraudsters before they reach potential victims, as the government seeks stronger penalties for non-compliance.

title: Hong Kong primary school students embrace new school year with excitement and caution
description: Education officials promote initiatives for mental well-being as pupils get set to tackle challenges ahead.
content:
On Tuesday, primary school students in Hong Kong headed back to school, feeling a blend of enthusiasm and nervousness about the upcoming year. The education secretary assured that mental health resources will be enhanced in schools.
While visiting the Hong Kong Taoist Association Wun Tsuen School, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin unveiled a new initiative to promote student well-being.
“This initiative encourages students to support and care for one another to prevent campus bullying. Through our collective efforts, we hope to create an environment where students can develop healthily in body, mind, and spirit,” Choi said.
The Education Bureau’s “Forging Relationships, Nurturing Well-being” school campaign, which begins this month, includes a series of talks designed to help parents, teachers and students adapt to the new school year.
Prabhleen Kaur, 11, a Primary 6 student entering her final year of primary school, told the South China Morning Post that she was thrilled to return but felt pressure from coming exams.
“I feel pretty excited because it’s something new and I can’t wait for the future. But I’m also scared because of the challenges along the way,” said Kaur, an Indian student who was born in Hong Kong.
“This year, I know that [Internal Assessment (IA)] exams are really, really important, but I feel like if I focus enough and work hard enough, I can overcome it.
“I’m so scared for the new start, but I’m going to try to make my last year the best year possible.”
Kaur said her goals for the year included improving her academic performance and extracurricular activities, such as singing in the school choir, where she has been a member for six years, and participating in English debate competitions.
Her best friend, Liyana Samreen, 11, also expressed concerns about secondary school placement.
“I also feel a bit nervous because I want to get into a good school,” said the Primary Six student who moved to Hong Kong when she was two.
To manage the academic workload, she suggested forming study groups during recess or lunchtime. “Instead of playing more, we could study more.”
Despite the stress, Samreen was excited to reunite with friends after the summer holidays. She was seen hugging and chatting with Kaur and other classmates while discussing future study plans.
Samreen also arrived with new school supplies, including a backpack, pencil case, water bottle and lunch bag.
“I’m always excited on the first day of school, especially because it’s my last year. And I want to see how other people treat me and if I can find new friends at school,” she said.
Both students said they were looking forward to learning more about artificial intelligence (AI) this term, having already used the technology to build robot cars and create digital animations in previous years.
Jayden Yan Pak-kiu, 7, a Primary 2 student at the same school, said he felt “a bit nervous” and had butterflies in his stomach, which kept him awake until 4am the night before.
“I’m worried that I won’t be able to make more new friends,” Yan said.
He added that his parents prepared a chocolate sandwich for breakfast and told him, “Don’t give up!” at the school gate.
Jayden set a personal goal to “be a more hardworking child” this year, saying the motivation came from within as he anticipated more challenging coursework in Primary 2.
During her campus visit, Choi emphasised the bureau’s commitment to supporting student well-being.
“In the future, we will continue to support our primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong, both in terms of hardware and software, to create a better learning environment for students,” she said.

title: Malaysian police smash cross-border drug ring, seize US$1 million of meth disguised as tea
description: The bust resulted from intelligence sharing between Malaysian and Thai police after a man is caught with suspected drugs in Hua Hin.
content: Malaysian police have crippled a cross-border drug syndicate with the seizure of 86.2kg of methamphetamine worth 4.31 million ringgit (US$1 million) in Penang and Selangor. The bust resulted from intelligence sharing between Malaysian and Thai police after Thai authorities seized 166kg (370lbs) of suspected methamphetamine from a Malaysian man in Hua Hin on August 8. Penang police chief Dennis Lim Kwang Keng said the information led to Ops Zoraptera, resulting in the arrest of four suspects – three Malaysian men and a Thai woman aged between 19 and 25. The Thai woman is the wife of one of the Malaysian suspects, and both were charged in the case. Lim said Malaysian police arrested the four suspects in Selangor on August 13. The following day, police seized a luxury sedan near Hotel Aroma in Butterworth, Penang, and found 83 packets disguised as tea bags containing 86.2kg of methamphetamine concealed in the vehicle. Lim said the syndicate also modified vehicles with hidden compartments to transport the drugs. “Each person involved in transporting a shipment was paid 6,000 ringgit per trip,” he said at a press conference in George Town on Tuesday. Police also seized five vehicles worth 420,700 ringgit, bringing the total value of the Malaysian seizure to 4.73 million ringgit. Lim said the syndicate was believed to have been active since June and the drugs were intended for the local market and possibly overseas. The first three suspects were charged at the Butterworth Magistrate’s Court on Thursday under Section 39B of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 (Act 234), while the fourth was made a prosecution witness. One suspect tested positive for ketamine in a preliminary urine test, while none had previous criminal records. The 86.2kg seizure in Malaysia, combined with the separate 166kg seizure in Thailand, totalled 252.2kg of methamphetamine confiscated through the operations. The case is being investigated under Section 39B of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952, which carries the death penalty or life imprisonment and whipping of not less than 12 strokes upon conviction. Present during the press conference were police officers from the Bukit Aman Narcotics Crime Investigation Department and the Police Narcotics Suppression Bureau of Thailand. This article was first published by The Star

title: Xi Jinping calls on SCO members to team up for bigger global tech-security role
description: The world is at a crossroads and the group should shoulder its responsibility, Chinese president says at Bishkek summit.
content: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation should take on a bigger global role in technology and security, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Tuesday, describing the Eurasian bloc as having vast potential. At the SCO’s summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Xi said the group had shown “strong vitality” since its founding 25 years ago amid the “sobering lessons of the Cold War”. In a veiled reference to Washington’s system of military alliances, Xi said a key lesson from the bloc’s quarter of a century of cooperation was “finding the right way to coexist without alliance, confrontation or targeting any third party”. “Its most significant achievement has been its steady growth into a new type of regional cooperation organisation that now spans the widest territory, encompasses the largest population, and holds the greatest development potential in the world,” Xi said, according to state news agency Xinhua. However, he said, the shadow of the war lingered and the world was at a crossroads, with rivalries between dialogue and confrontation, win-win cooperation and zero-sum competition, and multilateralism versus unilateralism. “Standing at a crossroads concerning the future and destiny of humankind, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation should bravely shoulder its responsibility and proactively guide the course of history,” Xi said. In outlining his suggestions for the bloc, the Chinese leader said countries had to “prioritise security and create a universally secure environment”, and firmly prevent external forces from interfering in the internal affairs of other countries to safeguard regional stability. Xi also called on the group to deepen cooperation in areas ranging from trade and connectivity to artificial intelligence and the digital economy, pledging to set up a “China-SCO Port Economic Cooperation Centre” in Tianjin. In addition, China would implement 100 scientific and technological projects with member nations over the next three years. On the international front, Xi said Beijing was ready to strengthen communication and cooperation with “relevant parties” as well as push for “political solutions” to conflicts, including the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. As the international order frays, the grouping is viewed as a platform for Beijing to advance its ambitions for a multipolar world and cement its position as a leader of the Global South. At a separate meeting with SCO member countries and dialogue partners, also on Tuesday, Xi again pointed to growing “hegemonism” and protectionism, saying the vast majority of countries did not want confrontation but sought an equal place on the world stage. “We must uphold the principle that all countries, regardless of size, strength or wealth, should enjoy equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules,” he said, calling for more representation of developing countries in international affairs. Xi added that a more united and dynamic SCO could advance multipolarity. “Major powers, in particular, should take the lead in abiding by the rules and the rule of the law, and cooperate to address global challenges.” Among the other leaders at the summit are Russian President Vladimir Putin, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. It is the first time the leaders of China, Iran and Russia have appeared together since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Tehran in February. On Monday, Xi met Putin for their second face-to-face meeting this year, pledging to strengthen the role of the SCO and improve cooperation within the organisation. At the summit on Tuesday, Putin described the SCO as becoming an influential centre of the multipolar world and called for state-sponsored provocation to be eliminated. Iran’s Pezeshkian said sustainable security could not be achieved through confrontation but through respect for countries’ sovereignty, calling the attacks on Tehran a blatant violation of international law, Iranian media reported. Also on Tuesday, the Iranian and Russian foreign ministers took part in a group meeting with their counterparts from other member nations, according to Iranian media. These interactions came just two days after the American military resumed attacks on Iran, breaking a weeks-long lull in fighting. Beijing and Moscow are “comprehensive strategic partners” of Tehran and their responses have been subject to international scrutiny. Last week, US President Donald Trump’s administration declared an “Economic D-Day”, threatening sanctions against countries that continue to do business with Iran. The SCO was formally established in 2001 with six countries – China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan – to combat terrorism in Central Asia. It has expanded to 10 full members and increasingly draws global attention as a non-Western multilateral security coordination platform. It is viewed by some as a vehicle for Beijing and Moscow to pool influence and compete with Washington in international politics.

title: Foreign investors expected to eye more China A shares – but pace set to ease: analyst
description: Overseas capital in yuan-traded Chinese stocks faces cooling, as tech sentiment, US yields and yuan strength steer the next phase.
content: Foreign investors are expected to keep adding to their China A-share holdings, though the pace of buying is likely to slow from the surge in the first half of the year, according to a UBS analyst. “We still expect net inflows in the second half, but the pace will be somewhat slower than in the first half,” said Meng Lei, China equity strategist at UBS Securities, at UBS’s annual China A-share strategy conference in Shenzhen on Tuesday. Foreign appetite for A shares – domestic shares of mainland companies denominated and traded in yuan – hit a record in the first half. Overseas holdings reached more than 4.4 trillion yuan (US$654 billion) by the second quarter, the highest level on record, according to Meng. Global fund managers aggressively expanded positions, with holdings under qualified foreign institutional investor scheme surging 87 per cent in value to 272.8 billion yuan by the end of June as buyers piled into companies tied to the artificial intelligence supply chain and green energy, according to financial data provider Wind. The tech narrative and A shares’ unique, self-sufficient industrial chain are very attractive to global investors Meng Lei, UBS Securities However, analysts said several macroeconomic headwinds were tempering foreign capital inflows into onshore bourses. Most of the second-quarter buying was concentrated in technology stocks, tracking swings in global AI sentiment, Meng said. As tech shares pulled back in the third quarter, debate over the sector’s valuations intensified overseas, making international funds more cautious. Rising long-term US Treasury yields – the anchor for global borrowing costs – are also weighing on sentiment, with the 10-year yield standing at around 4.75 per cent at the end of August. “That could make some investors less inclined to allocate to emerging-market equities,” Meng said. “A shares are part of that universe.” Despite these pressures, he said he expected net inflows to persist, pointing to China’s push for technological self-sufficiency as a key structural support. “The tech narrative and A shares’ unique, self-sufficient industrial chain are very attractive to global investors,” he said. The yuan’s ongoing strength is another major draw. Market consensus pointed to further appreciation over the next 12 months, Meng said, which would directly boost the total returns for foreign holders of yuan-denominated assets. Beyond hardware-focused tech stocks, Meng flagged Chinese exporters and high-end manufacturers as prospective targets for overseas capital. “Many of China’s high-end manufacturers have begun going global, and whether in terms of brand recognition or profit contribution, they are already at the global forefront,” Meng said. At the same time, he said a rotation into consumer stocks – a perennial favourite among foreign investors between 2019 and 2021 – was possible but not yet under way. That rotation would likely require “clearer signs of rising household wages and a broader stabilisation across the domestic real estate market”. Beijing unveiled a fresh package of measures in late August to support the property sector, including structural reforms to prioritise completed-home sales over pre-sales. Meng said the property market remained “in a window of observation and verification”.

title: ‘Aloof’ but engaged: what India’s SCO comeback reveals
description: New Delhi’s re-engagement with the China-led bloc serves as a reminder to the US that it has other options, analysts say.
content: Two years ago, Narendra Modi skipped the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s (SCO) summit in Astana entirely, sending his foreign minister instead. That absence was redressed first at last year’s summit in Tianjin and again this week in Kyrgyzstan, where India’s prime minister stood shoulder to shoulder with China’s Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and the leaders of other SCO member states. Analysts say New Delhi’s revived engagement with the 10-member bloc reflects both its hedging against an evermore unpredictable United States and its desire to counterbalance China’s influence at the SCO – even if they expect it to remain a “somewhat aloof member”. Founded in 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, the SCO was originally envisaged as a vehicle for Eurasian security cooperation, expanding over the years to include Pakistan, Iran and Belarus as full members, with a wider circle of Asian and Middle Eastern countries as observers and partners. India joined in 2017, but it has never been an entirely comfortable fit. China is widely seen as the bloc’s dominant force, bankrolling regional trade and infrastructure projects at a scale no other member can match, while the presence of Pakistan, Delhi’s arch-rival, serves as a perpetual irritant. Still, Modi arrived in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek on Sunday to attend the 26th SCO summit, a two-day gathering concluding on Tuesday, where he was expected to address fellow heads of state on regional stability, counterterrorism and economic cooperation. ‘Anti-Western’ aversion Before last year’s summit in Tianjin, there were signs that Delhi was downgrading its engagement with the bloc, said Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia at British think tank Chatham House – citing not only Modi’s 2024 absence but India’s last-minute decision to make the meeting it hosted in 2023 virtual. “This reflects India’s aversion to being part of any organisation that is regarded as overtly anti-Western,” Bajpaee said. That aversion had not simply disappeared, he said, but improved ties with China and strained relations with a US that had imposed steep trade tariffs and pressured India not to buy Russian oil helped motivate Modi’s move. It also came with a price tag, of sorts. “Delhi’s renewed support for the SCO likely came in exchange for Beijing’s support for India’s Brics chairmanship this year,” Bajpaee said, pointing to the next Brics summit, scheduled to be held in Delhi from September 12-13. The two Asian giants, both members of Brics and the SCO, have been gradually normalising ties – opening new military hotlines, resuming direct flights and easing visa restrictions – after the deadly border clashes in 2020 that froze relations for years. Still, “Delhi prefers to project an image as a non-Western rather than an anti-Western power”, Bajpaee said, noting India’s parallel push for deeper ties with the West. The result would likely be India remaining “a somewhat aloof member of the SCO”, he said – engaged, but not fully at home. Yet Delhi’s presence is also what keeps the SCO from becoming dominated by Beijing, according to Ivan Lidarev, a political scientist and research fellow at the National University of Singapore’s Institute of South Asian Studies. An SCO without India might solidify into a Chinese sphere of influence Ivan Lidarev, political scientist “An SCO without India might solidify into a Chinese sphere of influence in Eurasia to India’s detriment and turn the organisation into an anti-US bloc,” he said, adding that this concern was part of why Russia pushed for India’s admission in the first place. For both Beijing and Moscow, the SCO served as a way of keeping Delhi close and limiting how far it drifted towards Washington, Lidarev said, while enabling the slow accumulation of trust. “The SCO has acted as a giant confidence-building measure between Delhi and Beijing,” he said. “It has committed the two to the same vision of multipolarity, with an emphasis on the Global South.” Modi’s appearance in Bishkek serves another, more immediate purpose: paving the way for Xi’s possible attendance at this month’s Brics summit in Delhi. “A no-show by Xi will be a blow to the summit, particularly in light of Modi’s participation in last year’s Tianjin SCO summit and to the thaw in China-India relations,” Lidarev said, adding it could also complicate next year’s Brics summit that China is set to host. There is a message for Washington embedded in all of this, too. India’s push to strengthen the “non-Western side” of its multi-alignment foreign policy strategy amounted to “a careful and increasingly difficult international balancing act”, Lidarev said – one intended to subtly remind the US that India had other options, at a time when trade talks between the two countries appeared to have hit a wall. Diminishing returns? Other observers cast doubt on the continued utility of SCO membership for India, with Shanthie Mariet D’Souza, founder and president of the Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies in Goa, seeing an organisation that offers the country less and less. “China’s growing dominance and the organisation’s consensus-based structure limit New Delhi’s ability to shape its political and security agenda, particularly on issues such as terrorism and regional conflicts,” she said. But she stopped short of calling for India’s withdrawal, noting that the SCO was one of the few forums where India can sit across the negotiating table from China, Russia and the Central Asian states all at once. “Its value is therefore increasingly tactical,” D’Souza said – giving Delhi a venue to raise concerns about terrorism as its presence prevented the bloc becoming an “exclusively China-Russia sphere”. “India may no longer expect major geopolitical outcomes from the SCO, but it cannot afford to abandon it,” she added. Modi’s regional diplomacy did not begin in Bishkek. He spent two days in Uzbekistan first, on a state visit from Saturday to Sunday, meeting President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and formally elevating ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership. The visit yielded increased Indian access to Uzbek uranium and critical minerals, and a bilateral pledge to push two-way trade past US$5 billion by 2030. That stop was no accident of scheduling, according to Balaji Chandramohan, a foreign-policy analyst and research scholar at the University of Madras. He said the SCO allowed India to reaffirm its commitment to Central Asia and the Middle East at a time of considerable global disruption, shoring up both regional connectivity and its own energy security. “India will expand its strategic outreach in the Central Asian region as a part of its extending Look West and Look North Policy,” he said, referring to Delhi’s parallel diplomatic strategies for deepening ties with West and Central Asia as extensions of its own neighbourhood.

title: Review | The Last Song You Left Behind movie review: Japanese teen romance plays a familiar tune
description: Shunsuke Michieda and Meru Nukumi star as classmates who slowly develop feelings for each other over an unusual musical collaboration.
content: 2.5/5 stars Shunsuke Michieda of the Japanese boy band Naniwa Danshi reunites with director Takahiro Miki after the success of 2022’s Even If This Love Disappears from the World Tonight for another adolescent romance that plays an achingly familiar tune. Adapted from Misaki Ichijo’s novel of the same name, The Last Song You Left Behind stars Michieda as Haruto, an orphaned teenager who lives with his grandparents and has a secret passion for writing poetry. When his classmate Ayane (Meru Nukumi) learns of this, she defies convention and approaches him to propose that he write lyrics for her to sing. Ayane reveals she has a severe case of developmental dyslexia, which almost entirely prevents her from reading or writing. Despite this, she is a talented musician who performs regularly at her uncle’s restaurant and yearns to become a pop star. This dream might just come true with Haruto’s help. Miki has built a career creating these soft-focus tales of fumbling first love, from the innovative highs of My Tomorrow, Your Yesterday (2016) to the inherently creepy lows of My Teacher (2017). His latest offering falls squarely between these two extremes, delivering more than enough clichés, conflicts and calamities to fill a greatest hits album. Nukumi took a year of voice and guitar lessons to prepare for her role, and the effort has paid off mightily. Her performances, featuring music produced by Seiji Kameda, provide some of the film’s strongest moments. Less plausible is the severity of her dyslexia, which renders her incapable of reading sheet music or simple words. Yet when Haruto devises a special code of symbols for them to compose with, she picks it up effortlessly. Predictably, the pair slowly develop feelings for each other, but any notion of romance goes unspoken until it is too late. When their song becomes a hit and Ayane is offered a recording contract in Tokyo, the narrative demands that the fledgling lovers and burgeoning hitmakers go their separate ways, without any discussion about pursuing a future – personal or professional – together. The third act reunites the couple a few years later, after Ayane has become an established star, only to throw an unexpected – yet somewhat inevitable – curveball their way to ensure that any hope of a happy future together remains heart-wrenchingly elusive. Ultimately, this tale of a young, talented couple who pool their resources to find success hits as many of the right notes as it misses, without ever finding a fresh hook to call its own. title: How China’s top 2 container ports became the world’s busiest – and beat Singapore
description: The nation’s ports claimed six of the top 10 busiest worldwide, according to a prominent data provider.
content: China’s Yangtze River Delta is now home to the world’s two busiest container ports, a milestone that one industry analyst said reflects the continued resilience of the country’s export sector and the tech-driven efficiency of its maritime hubs. The Ningbo-Zhoushan Port in eastern China’s Zhejiang province overtook the Port of Singapore to become the world’s second-busiest container port in the first half of 2026, according to France-based shipping data provider Alphaliner. During the period, Ningbo-Zhoushan handled 22.9 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) – a standard measure for cargo container volume – compared with Singapore’s 22.74 million TEU. Shanghai, which has held the top spot for years, saw 28.7 million TEU flow through its berths. The two Chinese ports sit less than 100km (62.1 miles) apart. Qu Ke, a transport analyst at CCB International in Hong Kong, said the strength of Chinese ports had been propelled by efficiency gains and the large-scale adoption of smart technologies. “Autonomous trucks, cranes and automatic loading and unloading are becoming a usual sight at Chinese ports, leading to better safety and efficiency,” Qu said. “This is also supported by sound infrastructure, including roads and railways, for seamless, intermodal logistics to continuously feed containers to these ports.” Ningbo-Zhoushan is a joint port jurisdiction formed through a multi-year restructuring that consolidated individual berths scattered across the two cities – an initiative pushed by President Xi Jinping during his tenure as Zhejiang’s party chief between 2002 and 2007. Qu noted that China’s leading ports were also benefiting from the country’s export boom. Official customs data showed that total exports soared 18.5 per cent in the first seven months of the year to reach US$2.52 trillion, with a surplus of US$687.3 billion. For Ningbo specifically, exports rose 8.3 per cent over the same period to 1.27 trillion yuan (US$188.9 billion), helped by resilient orders from the United States – its largest single overseas market – and expanding shipments to Southeast Asia, particularly Indonesia and Vietnam. “The Yangtze River Delta, which includes both Shanghai and Ningbo-Zhoushan, is one of China’s most dominant export hubs, where tech-intensive goods, like electric vehicles, are loaded onto ro-ro ships at Shanghai or Ningbo, not very far away from their factories, and land in Europe or Southeast Asia,” Qu noted. “This is the kind of regional integration, efficiency and synergy underpinning competitiveness.” Factories in the delta region have been running at elevated capacity since the summer to fulfil orders for the coming US festive season, while exporters have also moved to capture demand amid stabilising US-China trade ties. Ningbo-Zhoushan’s busiest routes connect to major American ports including Long Beach near Los Angeles and the Port of New York and New Jersey, while Shanghai Port also ships most of its goods to America, followed by European hubs Rotterdam and Hamburg. Looking ahead, Qu suggested Shenzhen could be the next major Chinese port to overtake Singapore, anchored by the manufacturing and export might of the Pearl River Delta in Guangdong province. Overall, Chinese ports dominated the global container port ranking compiled by Alphaliner, claiming six of the top 10 hubs worldwide. Hong Kong, once the world’s busiest container port in the 1990s, ranked 14th globally in the first half of the year, with container throughput down 3.5 per cent.

title: ‘Unprecedented’ path: eastern and southern China braces for revived Typhoon Saudel
description: Heavy to torrential rain is forecast over the next three days, with authorities warning of floods, landslides and mudslides.
content: Parts of eastern and southern China are bracing for heavy to torrential rain over the next three days, with authorities warning of floods, landslides and mudslides, as Typhoon Saudel re-forms over the South China Sea. Several airports could be affected, including Guangzhou Baiyun, Shenzhen Baoan, Zhuhai Jinwan, Xiamen Gaoqi, Fuzhou Changle, Wenzhou Longwan, Ningbo Lishe and Hong Kong International Airport, according to aviation data platform VariFlight. So far, no large-scale flight cancellations have been announced. Some travellers took to social media to express concern and confusion over whether their flight plans would be affected by the storm’s revival. The unusual development took place early on Tuesday, when a tropical depression formed from the remnants of Saudel strengthened again into a typhoon over the northwestern South China Sea. The storm had previously made landfall in Zhejiang on Friday – marking the third typhoon to strike the eastern province this year – before weakening and being declassified by China’s National Meteorological Centre (NMC) on Sunday. The centre said it would continue to use the storm’s original name, Saudel, and number 2618. As of 1pm on Tuesday, Saudel was about 345km (214 miles) south of the coastal city of Shanwei in southeastern Guangdong province. The storm’s revival followed a rare trajectory, although there were precedents, analysts said. NMC chief forecaster Xu Yinglong told state news agency Xinhua that the change in underlying surface conditions was key to its revival. Moving from land to warm waters reduced friction while providing the system with a fresh source of energy, allowing it to strengthen again, he said. Xin Xin, a weather analyst with China Weather TV, said other examples of revived typhoons were Hagibis in 2014 and Co-May last year. “But Saudel’s path from making landfall in eastern China to re-entering the South China Sea from the south and reviving is unprecedented,” Xin said in a social media post. It came as heavy rain was forecast across parts of eastern and southern China through to Thursday, with some areas expected to see heavy to torrential rain. On Tuesday, heavy rain or torrential downpours were forecast for southeastern Zhejiang, central and eastern Fujian, eastern Guangdong, southern Jiangxi, southern Taiwan, as well as parts of eastern Heilongjiang and northeastern Jilin. Northeastern Fujian could see particularly heavy rainfall. The NMC extended its yellow rainstorm warning on Tuesday, the second-lowest level in China’s four-tier warning system. The centre urged people in affected regions to guard against flash floods, mudslides and landslides. People in mountainous areas and river valleys were advised to stay away from potentially dangerous locations and heed local weather forecasts and warnings. Strong winds were also forecast across much of the South China Sea and nearby waters from Tuesday morning to Wednesday morning. Coastal areas of Hainan, southern Zhejiang and northern Fujian were expected to experience strong winds. Saudel was forecast to move into the northeastern South China Sea later on Tuesday. From Thursday, it was expected to turn around over the northeastern South China Sea and gradually weaken. The Hong Kong Observatory issued a typhoon signal No 1 on Monday as the remnants of Saudel intensified. The No 1 signal is Hong Kong’s lowest tier for a typhoon, meaning that a tropical cyclone is centred within about 800km of the territory and may affect it. The signal will stay in force at least until Wednesday morning.

title: Amid textbook price jump, Hong Kong families call for more government support
description: Low-income students urge return of subsidies as book lists now cost families up to HK$6,000 for the 2026-27 school year.
content:
Wong* and his wife spent about HK$8,000 on new textbooks for their two daughters last month. That’s half of their household income: a permanent injury left the father unemployed, and they rely on his wife, who brings in about HK$16,000 a month.
“My children are a little sensitive about second-hand books,” the former construction worker said. “They feel using old books will make others look down on them.”
He added that second-hand books often contained notes and annotations, and could be unusable if curriculum updates left them outdated. Often, the single-use codes for accessing online learning resources and exercises had already been redeemed.
The couple’s children are entering Form Two and Primary Six at public schools in Kwai Tsing this month.
While the family receives help from a government textbook subsidy scheme for low-income families, they still struggle with other education expenses, such as tutoring that costs about HK$4,000 monthly.
Last year, the Hong Kong government ended a HK$2,500 study grant, forcing an estimated 60 per cent of underprivileged Hong Kong parents to cut back on extracurricular activities and educational support. The scheme, which alleviated financial stress on needy families, has affected nearly 800,000 students.
Prices for a list of school textbooks now range from HK$4,000 to HK$6,000, representing an average increase of 3.6 per cent for the 2026-27 academic year. It is the highest rise since the pandemic in 2020, according to Education Bureau book list data.
Last month, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin said on an RTHK programme that the scrapped student grant was only a temporary measure introduced during the Covid-19 pandemic. She said the textbook subsidy for low-income families was enough.
Cherish Chiu, a Form Five student at Leung Shek Chee College, spent about HK$2,500 on second-hand textbooks for the new term, nearly half of what buying them brand new would have cost her.
The 16-year-old only bought new copies of two workbooks for English and a Chinese mock paper. For her sister, a Form Three student at St Mary’s Canossian College, the book list totalled about HK$5,700.
Cherish explained that all junior form history and Chinese history textbooks had been recently updated, along with the senior form citizenship and social development curriculum.
“Publishers usually amend these textbooks very frequently, forcing schools to update the book list,” she said. “It’s unreasonable because the price is rising too frequently. The HK$2,500 financial support from the government is essential [for Hong Kong parents] … It can lower financial stress.”
Some schools are working to counter the rising textbook prices.
Edith Wong, an English teacher at a subsidised secondary school, shared her institution’s approach.
“We use self-made handouts … and buy just one set of textbooks to cover Form Four through Form Six,” she said.
Wong, who mainly teaches students with special educational needs, added that some teachers use online learning tools and artificial intelligence to create handouts.
“Different schools have different approaches, depending on their focus. We only buy what we will actually use … [to not] waste money,” she said. “[The costs] really are a headache for low-income families, especially if they have two or more kids in secondary school.”
Primary school pupils have also been affected by rising textbook costs. Principal Wong Wai-lap from Lions Clubs International Ho Tak Sum Primary School in Tin Shui Wai pointed to the effects of changed curricula.
“[It] requires purchasing textbooks and workbooks for more subjects. For instance, primary school general studies has been split into humanities and science, increasing the number of books needed,” he said.
“Information and innovation technology and science requirements may call for purchasing single-use experimental materials, which ultimately means students need more money to buy them.”
The principal noted that Education Bureau regulations required a five-year gap before an updated edition could be issued.
This should prevent constant textbook releases, but a loophole to the rule is that minor revisions are allowed. If the changes are minimal, it is not considered a full new edition, Principal Wong explained.
“If publishers could instead provide supplementary sheets of these revisions, parents could simply print and paste them into the pages, allowing them to keep using second-hand books,” the principal said.
*Full name withheld at interviewee’s request

title: Japan relaxes overtime rules under workaholic Takaichi: ‘unacceptable shift’
description: Businesses grappling with labour shortage have called for flexible work hours but critics say the move risks a return to ‘karoshi’ culture.
content: Japan eased overtime regulation starting on Tuesday in a move meant to help spur economic growth but criticised as a relapse into the country’s ingrained workaholic culture. The move comes after the government led by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi – a self-proclaimed workaholic – adopted a growth strategy in July, calling for revisions to the current oversight of work hours. The change in part reflects calls from certain business sectors for more flexible work styles as they grapple with a deepening labour shortage. Roughly 40 per cent of businesses in Japan are operating under specific labour-management agreements that legally allow monthly overtime of up to 100 hours, according to the labour ministry. But those companies were still advised by authorities to cap overtime at 45 hours each month, with that guidance considered on a par with regulation. That was because exceeding that threshold can increase risks for so-called karoshi, or deaths from overwork, a labour ministry official said. Under the new rule that took effect on Tuesday, labour standards inspection offices will no longer pressure businesses into the 45-hour cap. A Japan Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey showed in May that this pressure was “restricting” activity of around 20 per cent of Japan’s small and mid-sized businesses, especially in short-staffed industries such as construction, transport and hospitality. Critics, however, said the move reversed steps taken by Japan to modernise its corporate culture long centred around marathon work hours. Once a bastion for “corporate warriors” fiercely devoted to their jobs, the country has in recent years ratcheted up efforts towards a better work-life balance, especially after the 2015 suicide of an exhausted 24-year-old employee at advertising giant Dentsu. “This is an unacceptable shift away from, and abolition of, the policy that urged companies to shorten work hours,” the National Confederation of Trade Unions in Tokyo, commonly known as Zenroren, said in a statement. The labour ministry stressed that it would keep tabs on companies to ensure they took measures to protect the well-being of employees. It would “continue to provide the necessary guidance if there is a high risk that health problems caused by excessive work may arise”, the ministry said in a statement.

title: City leader Lee hands Hong Kong flag to Asian Games athletes, hails ‘never-say-die spirit’
description: City will send some 580 athletes, competing in 38 sports to Japan this month, with Chief Executive John Lee expecting ‘greater success’ than in Hangzhou.
content: Hong Kong’s leader handed over the city’s flag to the more than 800-strong delegation heading to this month’s Asian Games in Japan on Tuesday, telling them their “never-say-die spirit” was the best reflection of their home. Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu led a ceremony involving some of the 580 athletes scheduled to compete in 38 sports in Nagoya, and said he believed they would have “even greater success” than in Hangzhou three years ago. In 2023, a record squad of 681 competitors returned from the Games in mainland China with a historic 53 medals, winning eight gold, 16 silver and 29 bronze. “The athletes’ perseverance and never-say-die spirit on the field is the best reflection of the Hong Kong spirit,” Lee said, before handing the flag to members of the delegation, which chef de mission Wong Po-kee will head. “It can transcend language and cultural boundaries, show the world our confidence and our soft power, and tell the story of China and the story of Hong Kong. “I believe that our athletes will give their all on the Asian stage and achieve even greater success, bringing more glory to the country and Hong Kong.” Lee, who was joined by Secretary for Culture, Sports and Tourism Rosanna Law Shuk-pui at New Town Plaza in Sha Tin, added that the government would “continue to invest in policies and resources” to support the development of athletes. Hong Kong’s gold medal haul in Hangzhou was the third time, after 2010 and 2018, that the city grabbed eight titles at a single Games. “It will be great if we can surpass those numbers, but we understand the challenges, in terms of a smaller delegation size and the fact that we’re competing in fewer sports,” Wong said. “We’re still discussing our two flagbearers for the opening ceremony. We want them to be selected from sports with great results, while also making a good representation of Hong Kong. We could be looking at those newer sports, or team sports potentially.” The Games will run from September 19 to October 4, with most of the city’s delegation departing three days before the opening ceremony at Paloma Mizuho Stadium. Once again, the Hong Kong Jockey Club has pledged its full support to the city’s squad, with its Athlete Incentive Awards Scheme providing cash prizes for medal-winning athletes and teams. Medallists in individual events will receive HK$1 million (US$127,556), HK$500,000 and HK$250,000, respectively, with teams that win gold, silver or bronze getting double that to split as many ways as is required.

title: Citigroup boosts headcount by 25% on north Asia desk, Invesco names new Asia-Pacific head
description: US financial firms Citigroup and Invesco are continuing to expand in Asia even amid geopolitical uncertainties.
content: US financial institutions Citigroup and Invesco have separately announced that they would continue to expand their presence in Asia, even as the financial industry faces geopolitical uncertainties and Beijing tightens its control on overseas investment. Citi would boost the headcount of its north Asia and Japan corporate banking desk network by 25 per cent following double-digit growth in client activities, it said in a statement on Tuesday. The US lender would also expand its China desk network by adding Brazil and Europe as new hubs, on top of existing centres in Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai, London, New York, San Francisco and South Africa. “The expansion supports the next phase of Chinese companies’ global growth ambitions as they move beyond low-cost manufactured exports and cross-border acquisitions to building hi-tech supply chain ecosystems overseas, focusing on AI infrastructure, electric vehicles, consumer electronics and green energy,” said Toh Jianxun, head of corporate banking at Citi for Japan, Asia North and Australia. US tariffs, the war in the Middle East and the war between Russia and Ukraine had created uncertainties but also led companies to seek diversification of their supply chain and trading partners, adding new opportunities for Citi and other financial firms, according to analysts. Citi, which operates across 90 countries, would add new investments across South America, Europe and parts of Asia to support the overseas expansion activities of Citi’s corporate clients headquartered in Japan, Korea, mainland China and Taiwan. The desks would offer cross-border financing, foreign exchange, payment and other trade services. “Citi is seeing strong client growth across a number of corridors connecting markets in North Asia and Japan with global markets. These investments underline our commitment to clients to invest further to support their growth and expansion,” Toh said. Citi’s client activity linked to Central Asia had also doubled over the past six months, driven by an increase in trade flow and corporate activity between China and the region’s nations, the lender said, adding that there had been a surge in activity in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America. Separately, US fund house Invesco said it would also continue to expand in the region with the announcement of a succession plan for its Asia-Pacific head. Andrew Lo, one of the longest-serving fund managers in the city, would retire in March next year, ending a 32-year-long career with the firm. He would be replaced by Marty Franc, current CEO of Asia (ex-Japan), who would take up the role of senior managing director and head of Asia-Pacific in the first quarter ahead of Lo’s retirement on March 31. The reshuffle comes as the city’s wealth management sector is facing challenges following Beijing’s tightened controls on offshore investment in May, with Hong Kong regulators requiring financial firms in the city to ask mainland investment clients to declare whether their sources of funding came from offshore. After his retirement, Lo would serve as chairman emeritus of Asia-Pacific, continuing to represent Invesco on the boards of its China and India joint ventures and maintaining partnerships in the region, Invesco said in a statement. “Andrew’s legacy is measured not only by the business he helped build, but by the people he developed, the relationships he nurtured and the trust he earned throughout the region and across our firm,” said Andrew Schlossberg, president and CEO of Invesco. Franc also has more than 30 years of asset management experience, including 13 years with Invesco. US-based Invesco, established in 1935, operates in more than 25 countries and manages US$2.5 trillion in assets globally as of June. Hong Kong has been the firm’s regional headquarters for four decades. Invesco’s Asia-Pacific market was its fastest-growing region, according to its financial statement, with assets under management in the region jumping 19 per cent in 2025 to US$321 billion.

title: Carney’s Liberals win 3 special elections in Canada amid trade clash with US
description: By-election wins strengthen Canadian leader domestically as he defends against Trump’s tariffs.
content: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party swept to victory in special elections on Monday, boosting the leader’s parliamentary majority as a trade war with the United States escalates. Carney’s Liberal Party secured three seats, taking the district of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in French-speaking Quebec from the opposition Conservatives, and two other districts in Ontario and British Columbia that were previously held by the Liberals. Carney congratulated the winning candidates in a post on X, saying that voters had “placed their trust” in the government “at this consequential time for Canada”. “Canada is being tested in a changing world, and Canadians are up for it,” he wrote. Relations between former close allies the United States and Canada have soured after trade talks collapsed last month, with Carney saying US negotiators sought restrictions on his country’s trade pacts with other nations. US officials made unacceptable “threats” to the French language and “Quebec culture” too, he added. After Washington slapped Canada with 50 per cent duties, Ottawa announced counter-tariffs of its own. Despite the risks that escalating the trade war poses to Canada, which is heavily dependent on exports to its southern neighbour, Carney can boast of broad support. According to a poll late last month, 76 per cent of the public praised the former banker’s stance towards Washington. Former head of Canada’s central bank, Carney, 61, was not known for his charisma – unlike his flamboyant predecessor Justin Trudeau, from the same Liberal Party – but has nevertheless managed to kindle a patriotic flame among Canadians weary of American attacks. It was trade tension with the United States that propelled him to power – two months after Trump began his second term – as Canadians saw him as a protector of their economy. Replacing Trudeau as leader of his party and the government in March 2025, he won a general election a month later, to everyone’s surprise. The Liberals won the most seats but fell short of a majority. A by-election in April this year changed that, allowing the party to secure the parliamentary majority it needed to push through an economic agenda aimed at reducing dependence on the United States. More special elections are scheduled in the coming months to replace lawmakers who resigned, but polls suggest no threat to Carney’s majority.

title: Former economic crime chief to head discipline team at Hong Kong, Macau office
description: Hua Liebing’s appointment fills vacancy left last year and marks another change in HKMAO’s top ranks.
content: A veteran mainland Chinese economic crime investigator and former police official has been appointed to lead the discipline inspection and supervision group at Beijing’s top office overseeing Hong Kong affairs. Hua Liebing, a former director of the Ministry of Public Security’s economic crime investigation bureau, fills the vacancy at the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office (HKMAO) left by Geng Changyou, who stepped down last year to become secretary of Hebei province’s Commission for Discipline Inspection. The new appointment was revealed on Tuesday when the office updated its organisation chart on its website. It marked another change in the office’s top ranks following the selection of Zhang Dongmei, a former vice-president of the All-China Women’s Federation, as a deputy director in March. Hua’s appointment brings the HKMAO’s senior leadership to seven members. They include Xia Baolong, who has led the office since 2020, and deputy director Zhou Ji, who also serves as the director of Beijing’s liaison office in Hong Kong. The appointment came a day after a meeting of the HKMAO’s leading group for Communist Party building, which was also attended by members of the discipline inspection and supervision group. According to the HKMAO, the meeting stressed the importance of safeguarding national security, which would also help ensure the steady implementation of the “one country, two systems” governing principle. The office pledged to focus on resolving the challenges facing Hong Kong and Macau, support their integration into – and service to – national development, and to promote their long-term prosperity and stability. The office added that it would continue to build a high-performing team on Hong Kong and Macau affairs which would prioritise solid work and performance. Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said the appointment and the meeting reflected the message delivered by President Xi Jinping on the 105th anniversary of the party’s founding in July, in which he stressed discipline and political loyalty. Following the HKMAO’s elevation in 2023 to a unit reporting directly to the party’s central leadership, Beijing had set higher expectations for the office, and the latest moves were primarily aimed at improving the quality of its work, Lau said. “As Hong Kong and Macau affairs are now under the party’s leadership, the requirements for HKMAO personnel in terms of ability, morality, conduct and ideology will be stricter, so as to ensure that the one country, two systems principle is implemented more effectively,” he said. “This is mainly in response to President Xi’s call to exercise full and strict governance over the party. It is not because something has happened in Hong Kong or within the HKMAO.” Born in Jiangsu province in 1967 and a history graduate from Shandong University, 59-year-old Hua has no known previous experience in Hong Kong affairs. Before taking charge of the Public Security Ministry’s economic crime investigation bureau in 2023, he served as deputy head of the Beijing Municipal Public Security Bureau from 2020. Prior to that, he led the bureau’s legal affairs corps. During his tenure in Beijing, he established the country’s first law enforcement and case management centre to centralise and supervise case handling. He also contributed to the development of smart policing in the capital. Hua has also been described as a legal scholar. He has served as deputy director of the Beijing Law Society, an instructor at the People’s Public Security University of China, and a supervisor for master’s students in law at Renmin University of China. In May this year, Hua took part in the long-running operation “Fox Hunt”, which has led to the arrest of more than 880 fugitives who had fled abroad after committing economic crimes, including 38 under Interpol red notices. A red notice is a request sent by Interpol to its member countries worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. The operation also solved 128,000 economic crime cases nationwide, recovering 37.5 billion yuan (US$5.6 billion) in losses.

title: Rain, internet outages hit first day of Hong Kong’s robot convenience stores
description: But visitors praise humanoid robots at new Galbot stores in Hung Hom, Wan Chai and Kai Tak.
content: Heavy rain and internet outages marred the launch of Hong Kong’s first humanoid robot-operated convenience stores on Tuesday, but visitors said they still appreciated the work of the new robots. Embodied-intelligence robotics company Galbot opened two outdoor stores in Hung Hom and Wan Chai and an indoor shop in Kai Tak. The Galbot stores offer a mix of snacks and drinks, along with local offerings such as pineapple-bun and egg-tart-themed merchandise, with prices ranging from HK$14 to HK$139 (US$1.79 to US$17.73). Customers order using a screen and pay by card, WeChat, Alipay or China UnionPay, before the robot retrieves their purchases. Patrons are also welcome to have a casual chat with the robots in Cantonese or English without making a purchase. “Do not miss it – the big star who’s appeared on the Spring Festival Gala is working right here!” one of the robot managers said as it greeted passers-by in Cantonese. At around 11am, several visitors stopped by the store along Hung Hom’s new waterfront to take pictures, although the heavy rain appeared to discourage them from staying too long. Others showed interest but walked away after learning the store did not accept cash or Octopus cards. The night before the launch, the Hong Kong Observatory issued the No 1 typhoon warning signal as Tropical Depression Saudel moved across the northern South China Sea and edged closer to the coast of eastern Guangdong province. Only the indoor outlet in Kai Tak was spared from the rain, but staff said it was still undergoing internet testing as of noon on Tuesday. In a reply to the South China Morning Post, Galbot said network adjustments at some branches had slightly affected the robots’ spatial positioning, requiring some fine-tuning. On-site engineering and operations teams responded immediately to restore normal service, it said. “We will do our best to work through any issues that arise in this early stage of operation and remain firmly committed to accelerating the move of cutting-edge embodied intelligence technology from the laboratory into real urban environments to meet the needs of different markets and bring customers a more diverse, smoother smart retail experience,” it added. Despite the disruptions, several visitors who spoke to the SCMP said they found the novelty of interacting with the humanoid robot compelling. Hung Hom resident Chau On-ta-yueng, 81, said he had heard about the robot convenience stores coming to Hong Kong before and was happy to see them open. “Hung Hom has opened up a lot more places for sport in recent years, and the environment here keeps getting better with government support,” he said. “A store like this, selling snacks and drinks, is a good thing for people who come to walk or exercise in the area.” Chau bought a bottle of oolong tea at the convenience store for HK$15.80, saying the price was “moderate” rather than expensive. He added that conversations with the robot in Cantonese were smooth, but suggested adding more content to make chats more interesting. Vincen Leyden, 60, a tourist from the United Kingdom, came across the store while walking along the Hung Hom waterfront from a nearby hotel. “The service was very good and interesting,” Leyden said. “[The robot] understood me perfectly.”

title: Excitement and anxiety as pupils return to school, aided by new well-being campaign
description: Education chief Christine Choi says well-being initiative encourages students to support and care for one another to prevent campus bullying.
content: Primary school pupils returned to class across Hong Kong on Tuesday with a mix of excitement and anxiety over the year ahead, as the education chief pledged to strengthen mental health support in schools. During a visit to the Hong Kong Taoist Association Wun Tsuen School, Secretary for Education Christine Choi Yuk-lin announced the launch of a new campaign aimed at improving student well-being. “This initiative encourages students to support and care for one another to prevent campus bullying,” Choi said. “Through our collective efforts, we hope to create an environment where students can develop healthily in body, mind, and spirit.” The Education Bureau’s “Forging Relationships, Nurturing Well-being” school campaign, which begins this month, includes a series of talks designed to help parents, teachers and students adapt to the new school year. Prabhleen Kaur, 11, a Primary Six pupil, told the South China Morning Post that she was thrilled to return but felt pressure from coming exams. “I feel pretty excited because it’s something new and I can’t wait for the future. But I’m also scared because of the challenges along the way,” said Prabhleen, an Indian student who was born in Hong Kong. “This year, I know that [Internal Assessment] exams are really, really important, but I feel like if I focus enough and work hard enough, I can overcome it. “I’m so scared for the new start, but I’m going to try to make my last year the best year possible.” Prabhleen said her goals for the year included improving her academic performance and taking part in extracurricular activities, such as singing in the school choir, where she has been a member for six years, and taking part in English debate competitions. Her best friend, Liyana Samreen, 11, also expressed concerns about secondary school placement. “I also feel a bit nervous because I want to get into a good school,” said the Primary Six student who moved to Hong Kong when she was two. To manage the academic workload, she suggested forming study groups during recess or lunchtime, saying: “Instead of playing more, we could study more.” Despite the stress, Liyana was excited to reunite with friends after the summer holidays. She was seen hugging and chatting with Prabhleen and other classmates while discussing future study plans. Liyana also arrived with new school supplies, including a backpack, pencil case, water bottle and lunch bag. “I’m always excited on the first day of school, especially because it’s my last year. And I want to see how other people treat me and if I can find new friends at school,” she said. Both students said they were looking forward to learning more about artificial intelligence (AI) this term, having already used the technology to build model robot cars and create digital animations in previous years. Jayden Yan Pak-kiu, seven, a Primary Two student at the same school, said he felt “a bit nervous” and had butterflies in his stomach, which kept him awake until 4am the night before. “I’m worried that I won’t be able to make more new friends,” Yan said. He added that his parents prepared a chocolate sandwich for breakfast and told him, “Don’t give up!” at the school gate. Jayden set a personal goal to “be a more hardworking child” this year, saying the motivation came from within as he anticipated more challenging coursework in Primary Two. During her campus visit, minister Choi emphasised the bureau’s commitment to supporting student well-being. “In the future, we will continue to support our primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong, both in terms of hardware and software, to create a better learning environment for students,” she said.

title: Japan bear project aims to show coexistence, not culling, can prevent attacks
description: The programme has been credited with prompting both a recovery in bear numbers and fewer encounters with humans in Nagano.
content: As a sensor sounded, scientist Akiko Takii hurried to a bear trap deep in the forests of Nagano in Japan, where rising nationwide attacks have brought fear and resulted in the culling of thousands of the animals. “It’s a small bear, I think, about a year and a half old,” Takii said as she peered at the 15kg (33lbs) Asiatic black bear thrashing in the cage. “It must have just parted from mum.” Its mother was not around, and Takii took blood and fur samples after her co-researcher tranquillised the young female. The animal was too small to be tagged with a GPS tracker, so she was released. The process of trapping, tagging and releasing the animals is part of a pioneering management plan launched in 1995, as authorities realised the bear population was shrinking in the mountainous region in the centre of Japan’s Honshu island. And it is becoming part of a model of coexistence in the region that some experts believe is an alternative to the dominant practice of culling the animals in an effort to prevent attacks. “By not killing too many of them, more bears survive to live out their expected lifespan. In that sense, a healthy bear population is being formed,” Takii said of the process, which is paired with other methods intended to keep bears away from humans and monitor their movement. Another group in the area used specially trained Karelian Bear Dogs to scare bears away, and more than 3,000km (2,000 miles) of fencing was installed near farms, towns and along rivers to prevent encounters. Bears who slip through are tranquillised, tagged and set free far away. The programme has been credited with prompting both a recovery in bear numbers – although the animals are hard to count – and fewer encounters with humans. There is little sympathy across much of Japan for healthy bear populations. Bears have killed six people nationwide since April 1, after a record 13 fatal attacks last financial year, according to the environment ministry. Sightings last year doubled the previous record and bears are increasingly entering the outskirts of towns and cities. The causes are complex and, including variations in the availability of food like acorns, are potentially linked to climate change. Forgotten fruit The emptying out of rural areas due to depopulation and urbanisation is also leaving forests, farmland and buffer zones less managed, according to Shuichi Kitoh, a Tokyo University professor emeritus of environmental ethics. “Due to depopulation, people are no longer involved in nature and the forest like they were before,” Kitoh said. Fruit like persimmons growing on trees that are no longer harvested are an attractive treat for bears, encouraging them to venture farther from their natural habitats and hunting grounds. “It’s not that bears in general are getting [more] ferocious,” Kitoh said. “We have to identify problematic individuals.” The central government’s response has focused largely on culling bears, expanding the process beyond animals in towns to those that wander into buffer zones on the outskirts. Even before the cull guidance was expanded in April, large numbers of bears were being killed – a record 14,000 last financial year, or almost 40 a day. Takii argued Nagano’s coexistence programme offered a different path. While direct comparisons are difficult, some figures appear to show it has helped limit dangerous encounters. Annual sightings have remained broadly stable at around 1,400 in recent years, while some northern prefectures have recorded sharp increases. Last year, Nagano recorded 11 bear-related incidents, including one death, compared with 59 encounters and four deaths in Akita further north and five fatalities in Iwate. Some Nagano residents also feel reassured, including at a school where Takii was teaching children about bears. “Takii understands wild bear behaviour in this area well, and she assures us they are not aggressive,” principal Hiroshi Aruga said. “I am convinced it’s safe to live with them as long as humans don’t offend them.” But for now, that view remains something of a minority. A cap on the number of bears that can be culled annually in Nagano has been doubled to 675, with 227 killed between April and June this year. Takii’s group, the Shinshu Asian Black Bear Research Association, now only does catch-and-release work for scientific study. Its bear dog programme has been halted. Still, Takii’s outreach is continuing, and at the school she allowed children to handle bear pelts and skulls, while teaching the importance of keeping food away from the animals and maintaining a distance. “Bears seem to be some terrifying creatures if we don’t know them well,” said one parent, Mitsuko Sawanishi, after a lesson. “But after the bear class, I think it’s important to keep a good distance from them and live together.”

title: Russia strikes Ukraine capital for sixth straight day, killing at least 12
description: Civilians die in Russian air bombardments as Moscow repels Ukrainian drones.
content: Twelve people were killed and several more injured in Russian air attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region on Tuesday, authorities said, in the sixth consecutive day of ‌strikes on the Ukrainian capital. Attacks both in Ukraine and Russia continue as efforts are ongoing to find a solution to end the deadliest conflict on the European continent since World War II, which started with Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Eight people were killed and another five wounded in Kyiv, three of them children, and fires broke out in different locations around the capital, emergency services said on the Telegram messaging app. In Boryspil outside Kyiv, four people were killed and a further 13 injured in an attack that hit a residential building and other sites, ⁠Governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram. The daily Russian strikes on ‌Kyiv and the surrounding region are disrupting the lives of millions of people. Air raid alerts covered most of Ukraine’s territory in the early hours of Tuesday. Russia has been increasing attacks on Ukraine’s borders, in addition to energy ‌and logistic facilities, and on Tuesday a fresh strike stopped border crossings into Romania – a member of the European Union ⁠and Nato – at Orlivka on ⁠the Danube river. In Russia, a drone attack caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet in the northwest, and Moscow was repelling drones. In Russia’s Samara ‌region, home to a number of major oil refineries some 800km (500 miles) southeast of Moscow, an air attack damaged civilian facilities, the local governor said on Telegram. Russia and Ukraine deny ‌deliberately targeting ‌civilians. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday he held a “detailed and constructive” call with ‌US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that the sides were working to finalise dates for their visit to Ukraine aimed ⁠at advancing peace efforts. The same day, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin that the war needed to end for humanity’s ⁠sake. The Kremlin leader said Moscow was “moving forward along this path”. The conflict has prompted some Nato members, especially those bordering Russia, to bolster their military capabilities, also in the wake of intensifying drone incidents in the border areas. The Nato Baltic air policing mission ‌has briefly activated jet fighters in Latvia, ‌and Finland has restricted air and maritime traffic close to Russia, armed forces of both countries said separately on social media, as drones were flying over Russia’s Leningrad region where Ust-Luga is located. Margus Tsahkna, foreign minister of Estonia, which has also briefly issued air threat alert on Tuesday, in a post on social media thanked Nato for reacting “swiftly and exactly as planned” by putting fighter jets in the air.

title: Asian healthcare deals heat up as investors bet big on brain tech and surgical robotics
description: Family offices and venture investors across Hong Kong and the wider region are reshaping portfolios to capture long-term biotech growth.
content: Private investors in Asia, including family offices operating in Hong Kong, are showing a growing appetite for advanced medical technologies such as brain-computer interfaces and surgical robotics, as healthcare deal activity picks up across the region amid China’s biotechnology boom. “Asia is ageing, so there’s a structural, long-term demand for better surgery and medicine,” said William Chow, deputy group CEO of Raffles Family Office, headquartered in Hong Kong and Singapore. “A lot of the innovation is happening right here in Asia.” The number of healthcare private equity funds involved in Asia-Pacific deals nearly doubled to 129 in the first half of the year, up from 66 a year earlier, Bain & Company data released last week showed. Globally, the healthcare private equity sector logged 184 buyout deals over the same period, while total disclosed deal value fell 18 per cent year on year to US$51 billion. At Raffles Family Office, which manages about US$2 billion in assets, Chow said surgical robotics and brain-computer interfaces were coming up far more often than they did a couple of years ago. Speaking at the MedTech World Asia conference in Hong Kong, Charles Hu, founder and CEO of Hong Kong-based family office Ryoden Medical Holdings, also highlighted neurotechnology and artificial intelligence as crucial areas of investor interest. In a panel discussion on Friday, Hu said AI adoption was moving from drug discovery into clinical use to enhance surgery workflows in hospitals. “That could be anything from placing sensors in our surgical tools, directly having real-time feedback to the surgeon or the doctor about the status of the disease, so that they can pivot or make different decisions,” he said. Buyout deal counts in healthcare private equity across the Asia-Pacific region climbed 24 per cent year on year to 41 deals in the first six months, outpacing the 6 per cent global growth rate over the same period. After the exit-route freeze between 2021 and 2024, Hong Kong’s booming IPO market is once again giving venture investors a way to exit and reinvest Tay Choon Chong, Vertex Ventures China Tapping into this investor interest, SoftBank-backed surgical robotics company Noah Medical has initiated preparations for a Hong Kong public listing, with plans to file its application as early as next year. On the same panel, Irene Hong, founding partner of CEC Capital Group, noted that deal making worldwide had become concentrated in fewer, larger transactions. “Globally, we are looking at record-high volume in terms of dollar amounts, but … [a] record-low number of deals,” Hong said, noting that capital allocation had moved towards emerging technologies like AI, surgical robots and brain-computer interfaces. This active deal making has not, however, translated into easy returns. “Globally, a backlog of unsold assets, compounded by regulatory uncertainty globally, has left fund managers struggling to exit old positions in recent years, even as the IPO [initial public offering] market has picked up in Hong Kong and mainland China”, said Lai Pak-seng, chairman of Asia global wealth solutions at EQT, in a recent interview. The public listings pipeline is nonetheless offering relief for some firms. Tay Choon Chong, managing partner of Vertex Ventures China, said in an interview that five to seven companies in his portfolio – spanning AI, robotics, semiconductors and photonics – were expected to list in Hong Kong this year, up from two last year. “After the exit-route freeze between 2021 and 2024, Hong Kong’s booming IPO market is once again giving venture investors a way to exit and reinvest,” he added. For deals that cannot wait for an IPO, Lai said secondary funds – which involve buying existing stakes in private equity and private credit funds or portfolio companies from investors who need liquidity before a fund’s typical 10-year term ends – had emerged as an alternative exit route. “In Hong Kong, a growing number of private equity firms and family offices are looking into the secondary fund market to add liquidity to their assets,” Lai said. The global secondary market reached US$240 billion in transaction volume in 2025, the largest year on record, according to investment bank Jefferies. Lai said the market was on track to hit another record high in 2026.

title: What are five-kernel mooncakes? A history of the protein-packed Mid-Autumn Festival treat
description: Rich in nuts and seeds, five-kernel mooncakes are making a comeback as a protein-packed alternative to have during the Mid-Autumn Festival.
content: When you think of mooncakes, the ones that come to mind tend to be the classic sweet lotus paste versions with salted egg yolk, or maybe a more modern interpretation like one with a salty-sweet baked custard filling. Historically, however, the first mooncakes were made with a mix of nuts and seeds. The five-kernel (wuren) mooncake – filled with ingredients including walnuts, almonds and sesame seeds – was considered the height of sophistication from the 1950s to the 1970s. With traditional sweet mooncakes increasingly eschewed by the health-conscious, might this protein-packed version make a comeback? Mooncake history Five-kernel mooncakes originated from the Hu cakes introduced during the Han dynasty (206BC-AD220), when Chinese diplomat and explorer Zhang Qian brought back nuts, such as walnuts and sesame seeds, from the western regions, laying the foundation for their use in mooncakes. Later, during the Tang (618-907) and Song (960-1279) dynasties, these small cakes filled with nuts became popular among the common people, gradually becoming associated with the Mid-Autumn Festival. Similar multi-nut-filled cakes appeared in Qing dynasty (1644-1912) publications such as the Chinese classic novel Dream of the Red Chamber and the gastronomical guide Recipes from the Garden of Contentment. Flaky mooncakes containing finely ground pine nuts, walnuts and melon seeds were mentioned, and it can be inferred that they were found in both the imperial court and local regions. The five kernels symbolise completeness and harmony, making it a classic representative of Cantonese mooncakes. The typical kernels would include walnuts, almonds, olive kernels, melon seeds and sesame seeds, which symbolised the virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and trustworthiness – in that order. Long before white lotus seed paste or modern snow-skin flavours took over the market, wuren was the undisputed king of mooncakes across mainland China and Hong Kong. In times of material scarcity, the calorie-dense components of rich nuts, Jinhua ham and cured pork fat were highly precious, luxury food items. Gifting wuren mooncakes was a massive sign of respect. The ‘five-nut fruit mooncake’ In the early 1950s, imported nuts were rare in Hong Kong, so the traditional five-kernel filling was often replaced with the more common peanuts, melon seeds, sesame seeds and candied winter melon. “People in the industry did not dare call the replacement fillings a five-kernel mooncake.
